# Berakhot 5

## Geulah LeTefillah Recap

### Geulah Arichta Review

The Gemara on daf 4b had been engaged with the question of when one davens Shemoneh Esrei at night — whether one first says Shema and then davens, or the reverse — and, more precisely, the ideal of somech geulah letfillah: juxtaposing Shema with Shemoneh Esrei. As a concluding remark on that topic, the Gemara noted that at night we do not always achieve this juxtaposition precisely, because there is a second bracha — Hashkivenu — that intervenes between the conclusion of Shema and the beginning of Shemoneh Esrei. The resolution offered was the concept of geulah arichta: an extended geulah. Once the Rabbis established Hashkivenu as part of the liturgy, even though it is not thematically about geulah, it becomes incorporated into and continuous with the geulah bracha. It is therefore still regarded as a form of juxtaposition. This ongoing tension — between Shema as an independent mitzvah recited in the morning and afternoon, and Shema as something that has been transformed and embedded within the structure of the liturgy — is a thread that will continue to run through the sugya.

### Baruch Hashem Le'olam

Tosfos points out that the distance between Shema and Shemoneh Esrei at Maariv is extended even further in many communities outside Eretz Yisrael, where a third bracha — the lengthy Baruch Hashem Le'olam — was inserted. This bracha was instituted primarily because people davened in the fields outside, and one did not want those who had davened to leave, leaving latecomers to walk home alone in the dark. Accordingly, this additional bracha was added to give everyone a chance to catch up. Notably, Baruch Hashem Le'olam contains eighteen divine names and functions as something of a miniature Shemoneh Esrei in its own right. Tosfos acknowledges that in principle this insertion creates the same problem of failing to juxtapose Shema and Shemoneh Esrei, but argues that once it becomes part of the established liturgy, it too is absorbed into the extended geulah and is therefore acceptable.

## Ashrei & Missing Nun

### Ashrei Three Times Daily

The Gemara, continuing to address liturgical matters, cites Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Avina: whoever says Tehillah LeDavid — which we call Ashrei, a name drawn from the additional pasuk appended before that perek of Tehillim begins, a name which the Gemara itself already uses, suggesting this addition was established at a very early stage — every day, shalosh pe'amim, three times, can be assured of being a ben olam habah. This is why we say Ashrei three times: twice in the morning and once at Mincha. It is worth noting that Rashi associates the three recitations with morning, afternoon, and evening, though in practice we do not say it at Maariv.

The Gemara then asks: mai tama — what is the reason for its special significance? One might suppose it is because of the alef-bet structure of the psalm. The alef-bet as an organizing principle appears to express the idea that the praises are complete and total — from beginning to end, from A to Z, encompassing all possible praise. But if that were the sole reason, one should instead say Ashrei Temimei Darech, the longest perek in Tehillim, which traverses the alef-bet eight times, betamnaya alpin. That alone cannot be the reason.

Alternatively, perhaps it is because Tehillah LeDavid contains the pasuk Poteach et yadecha umasbia lechol chai ratzon — You open Your hand and satisfy the needs of all living creatures. This pasuk articulates the most central and universal expression of divine beneficence: that God provides sustenance for all of creation, not merely for Jews or for human beings. Some have the practice of physically opening their hands when reciting this pasuk as a kind of bodily enactment of the idea. But if that were the sole reason, one should instead say Hallel Hagadol — not Hallel Hamitzri recited on Yamim Tovim, but the Hallel embedded in the Pesukei D'zimra of Shabbos — which likewise contains the expression Nosein lechem l'chol basar, conveying the same idea.

The Gemara therefore concludes: mishum d'is bei tarti — because Tehillah LeDavid has both. It combines the comprehensive quality of the alef-bet structure with the fundamental expression of God's universal beneficence. Together these convey, with the most complete totality, the idea of God's constant and all-encompassing provision for every creature. Presumably, the significance of reciting this three times daily lies in what it does for the one who says it: impressing upon us, day after day, this profound awareness of God's constant sustenance of all creation — and it is this deep, ongoing awareness that is connected to becoming a ben olam habah.

### Missing Nun in Ashrei

Rabbi Yochanan raises a striking question: mipnei mah lo ne'emar nun b'Ashrei — why is the letter nun absent from Tehillah LeDavid? The answer given is that the nun carries with it an ominous association: mipnei sheyesh bo mapalatan shel sonei Yisrael — because it evokes the falling of the enemies of Israel. The phrase sonei Yisrael is a euphemism; the text means Israel itself. The reference is to the pasuk in Amos: Nafla lo tosif kum besulas Yisrael — She has fallen, she will no longer rise, O maiden of Israel. To include a nun verse in a psalm of praise would have risked evoking this dark resonance.

In Eretz Yisrael, the Gemara notes, the difficult pasuk was reread differently: Nafla v'lo tosif linpol, kum b'nos Yisrael — She has fallen, but she shall fall no more; arise, O daughter of Israel. By shifting where the pause falls, the verse is transformed from a sentence of doom into an expression of hope. This is admittedly a striking answer. Among the many alef-bet psalms throughout Tanach, the omission of a single letter in this one psalm is attributed to the fact that it would have evoked this particular pasuk. What precisely this means — and why the association is so powerful — is left open by the Gemara, though other biblical scholars have proposed alternative explanations for the missing nun.

### Somech Hashem L'Noflim

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds a further dimension: afilu hachi chazar bei David u'smachan b'ruach hakodesh — even so, David returned and through divine inspiration anchored the letter nun implicitly in the following verse. For the samech verse that comes immediately after where the nun would have stood reads: Somech Hashem l'chol hanoflim — God supports all those who have fallen. Precisely here, in the verse that follows the missing nun, the word noflim — those who have fallen — appears, but now in a context where God is already providing support. One might even say that the nun is embedded within the samech verse: the idea of nefila is present, but it is immediately preceded by and encompassed within the divine act of support. The absence of the nun is thus not a void but a deliberate theological statement.

### Michael vs Gabriel Speed

Rabbi Elazar Bar Avina — the same authority who introduced the teaching about Ashrei — states: gadol mah shene'emar b'Michael yoser mah shene'emar b'Gavriel — greater is what is said of the angel Michael than what is said of the angel Gabriel. Regarding Michael, the pasuk says Vaya'af elay echad min hasrafim — one of the fiery angels flew to me — a single flight, an immediate arrival. Regarding Gabriel, the pasuk says veha'ish Gavriel asher ra'isi bachazon betchila me'uf bi'af — Gabriel was flying to fly — the doubled language indicating two stages of flight. Michael thus moves more swiftly than Gabriel.

The Gemara then asks: how do we know that the echad — the one — in the first pasuk refers to Michael? Rabbi Yochanan answers: asya echad echad — a gezerah shavah, a linkage between two uses of the word echad. The pasuk in Yeshayahu says echad min hasrafim, and a pasuk in Daniel says vehinei Michael echad hasarim harishonim ba le'ozreni — Michael, one of the foremost officers, came to help me. The word echad connects the two passages and identifies the anonymous one as Michael. The fact that Michael's name does not appear explicitly in Yeshayahu is itself noteworthy: the names Michael and Gabriel appear only in Daniel and in the post-exilic period. Indeed, the Yerushalmi states shmos malachim alu imahem mibavel — the names of the angels came up with them from Babylonia. Before the exile, angels in Tanach appear only generically or by category; the attribution of individual names to angels was something that entered from the Babylonian cultural context at the time of Daniel.

### Ashrei Before Mincha

One might ask why the discussion of Ashrei appears precisely at this point in the Gemara. The preceding sugya had been addressing the juxtaposition of Shema and Shemoneh Esrei — somech geulah letfillah — as it applies to Shacharit and Maariv. But what of Mincha? At Mincha, one does not precede Shemoneh Esrei with geulah, but one does precede it with Ashrei, serving as a kind of buildup and preparation before moving into Shemoneh Esrei. It is worth considering whether the placement of this passage in the Gemara already reflects, or even implies, a liturgical reality in which Ashrei was positioned before the Shemoneh Esrei of Mincha. The precise development and crystallization of the daily liturgy — when Birchos Hashachar was established, when Pesukei D'zimra was formalized, when the various components were fixed in their current sequence — is something the Gemara never sets forth systematically. One finds scattered pieces of the liturgy treated here and there, primarily Shema and Shemoneh Esrei, and one must work to understand when and how the other elements were introduced and consolidated.

### Angels' Flight Speeds

A Tanna teaches: Michael arrives in one movement, Gabriel in two, Eliyahu in four, and the Angel of Death in eight — but during a time of plague, the Angel of Death arrives in one. The speeds are presumably symbolic. Death does not ordinarily come instantaneously — it typically unfolds in stages. The exceptional speed during a plague reflects the swiftness and immediacy of mass mortality. Similarly, the four stages associated with Eliyahu likely allude to the fact that the redemption he heralds — the arrival of Mashiach — will not come suddenly. The world will not simply be normal and then, in an instant, the Mashiach will appear; it is something that unfolds progressively. The distinction between Michael in one and Gabriel in two is somewhat harder to decode thematically, though the gradations in any case paint a picture of a heavenly realm with differentiated levels of speed and immediacy of action.

## Shema Al HaMita

### Bedtime Shema Mitzvah

The Gemara now returns to the topic of Shema. Rabbi Yehoshua Ben Levi states: af al pi shekara adam Krias Shema beveis haknesses — even though a person has already said Shema in shul — mitzva likroso al mitaso — it is a mitzvah to say it again right before going to sleep. This is Krias Shema Al HaMita.

### Rigzu V'al Techeta'u

Rabbi Yosi identifies the source: the pasuk Rigzu v'al techeta'u, imru bilvavchem al mishkavchem vedomu sela — Tremble and do not sin; say in your heart upon your bed, and be still. The word bilvavchem, in your hearts, connects to the phrase al levavecha from the Shema: the words one is to carry on one's heart are the words of Shema — and those words are to be said al mishkavchem, upon your bed. Vedomu sela: then be still, then go to sleep.

The framing of this through rigzu v'al techeta'u — tremble and do not sin — suggests that the bedtime recitation serves as some form of protection or moral orientation against sin, perhaps guarding against improper thoughts at the moment of sleep. But there is another way to understand the underlying logic: the pasuk in Devarim mandates beshochbecha uvkumecha — when you lie down and when you rise. In practice, we say the evening Shema in shul, followed by Shemoneh Esrei, and then one comes home, eats, and only later goes to sleep. The recitation in shul is thus no longer exactly beshochbecha. The bedtime Shema restores that quality, maintaining the sense of the pasuk by saying Shema precisely at the moment of lying down. There is also yet another dimension: vedomu sela may carry overtones of permanent silence — the silence of death. One goes to sleep not knowing with certainty that one will wake, and the bedtime Shema thus takes on an aspect of prayer and bakasha: an acknowledgment that one is, in a sense, surrendering one's soul each night, and a petition to God to restore it in the morning.

### Scholar & Bedtime Shema

Rav Nachman states: im talmid chacham hu ein tzarich — if one is a Torah scholar, he need not recite Shema at bedtime. Rashi explains: sheragil bemishnavo lachazor girsato tamid dayo b'kach — since a talmid chacham is constantly reviewing and thinking about Torah, he is in any case engaged in Torah study right before sleep. This reflects another reading of the pasuk's intent: vedibarta bam beshochbecha uvkumecha need not mean Shema specifically, but may refer to Torah in the broader sense — one should always be speaking and thinking about Torah, including when lying down. The scholar who naturally inhabits that state has already fulfilled the spirit of the obligation.

Abaye, however, qualifies: af talmid chacham mibayei lei l'meimar chad pasuka derachamei — even a talmid chacham should say at least one pasuk of prayer, of rachamei. The example given is: beyadcha afkid ruchi, padita oti Hashem Kel emet — Into Your hand I entrust my spirit; You have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth. This encapsulates the theological heart of Krias Shema Al HaMita: the recognition that when one goes to sleep, the soul is returned to God, and that waking in the morning — the basis for Modeh Ani — is a gift contingent upon divine grace. The bedtime recitation is thus not only about directing one's thoughts or protecting from sin, but also contains a genuine dimension of prayer and petition for the soul's return.

### Rashi-Tosfos Shema Debate

Before proceeding further in the Gemara, it is important to address a significant dispute between Rashi and Tosfos that bears directly on this topic, rooted in the very first Rashi of the masechta. The question is: why do we say Shema at Maariv when it is still well before nightfall, given that the mitzvah of Shema requires tzeis hakochavim? The historical background in Ashkenaz — where midsummer daylight stretched very late, making it socially and practically necessary to daven Maariv earlier — is addressed in a well-known article by Jacob Katz.

Rashi's position is that when we daven early Maariv and recite Shema before the stars appear, we have not yet fulfilled the nighttime mitzvah of Shema. We fulfill it later, through Krias Shema Al HaMita, at which point it is genuinely night. For Rashi, accordingly, the bedtime Shema does double service: it is both the mitzvah of Krias Shema Al HaMita and the fulfillment of the mitzvah of Shema for the night. Rashi holds that one paragraph suffices for this purpose. Many people who daven early Maariv follow this approach today, either saying Shema again when the stars come out or relying on the bedtime recitation.

Tosfos objects strenuously. For Tosfos, the mitzvah of Shema cannot be divorced from its brachos; the mitzvah of Shema must be fulfilled together with the brachos of Shema, as part of the Maariv liturgy. Tosfos therefore argues that davening Maariv before sunset can itself satisfy the nighttime obligation of Shema — there is a halachic position defining that time as sufficiently nocturnal — and therefore the mitzvah is fulfilled at Maariv itself. The bedtime Shema is then exclusively Krias Shema Al HaMita, not a vehicle for fulfilling the mitzvah of Shema as an independent obligation.

The significance of this dispute extends beyond the practical question. It reflects the deeper conceptual issue running throughout these pages: the relationship between Shema as an independent mitzvah and Shema as it exists embedded within the liturgy. For Tosfos, the two are inseparable — one cannot conceive of the brachos of Shema being recited without those brachos serving as the frame for the mitzvah itself. For Rashi, the two can stand independently, and the mitzvah of Shema can be satisfied by a solitary recitation at bedtime, entirely outside the liturgical context. In practice, we tend to follow Rashi's approach.

### Yetzer Tov vs Yetzer Hara

Reish Lakish, cited by Rabbi Levi bar Chama, teaches: l'olam yargiz adam yetzer hatov al yetzer hara — one should always set one's yetzer hatov in battle against the yetzer hara. Rather than waiting for temptation to present itself and then struggling to resist it, one should be in a constant state of proactive engagement, working on one's middos and moral character before the moment of trial arrives.

The pasuk cited is Rigzu v'al techeta'u — tremble and do not sin. If working directly on one's middos achieves victory over the yetzer hara, good. If not, then ya'asok baTorah — one should engage in Torah study. Learning Torah can work indirectly, strengthening one's character rather than attacking the baser inclinations head-on. Again: if that achieves victory, good. If not, yikra Krias Shema — recite Shema. Then: if that too achieves victory, good. If not, yizkor lo yom hamisa — recall the day of death. Ve'domu sela: be silent forever. Keeping in mind the transient nature of this world and the ultimate accountability before God may succeed where direct struggle, Torah, and Shema have not.

The sequence raises a genuine question: it is not immediately obvious why reciting Shema should be more practically effective against the yetzer hara than learning Torah in general. And indeed one might ask whether this passage is concerned specifically with the moment of temptation or with the general ongoing cultivation of character — though the Gemara itself does not resolve this.

### Torah Given at Sinai

The same Reish Lakish, cited by Rav Levi bar Chama, expounds the pasuk: Ve'etnah lecha et luchot ha'even vehatorah vehamitzvah asher katavti lehorotam — And I will give you the tablets of stone, and the Torah, and the commandment that I have written to teach them. Each element of this verse is decoded: Luchot refers to the Aseret HaDibrot, the Ten Commandments. Torah is Mikra — the written Torah. Vehamitzvah is Mishnah — Mishnah focuses on presenting laws straightforwardly, the parameters of one's obligations, which is why it is identified with the word mitzvah. Asher katavti encompasses Nevi'im and Ketuvim — the prophets and the later holy writings. Lehorotam is Gemara — not just the statement of laws but the argumentation, analysis, and discussion that ultimately enables hora'ah, the capacity to rule on new and ambiguous cases. Melamed shekulam nitnu le-Moshe mi-Sinai — this teaches that all of it was given to Moshe at Sinai.

This passage represents one pole of an ongoing debate in Jewish thought about the nature of oral tradition. Some speak as though everything was directly transmitted and we are merely uncovering what was already given. Others hold that the written Torah was revealed at Sinai and the Rabbis were authorized to interpret and derive from it — that much of the oral law was not directly received but was the product of human encounter with the text under principles of interpretation. There are ways to reconcile these positions: one may say that everything was given in potential, since the capacity to derive it was itself divinely granted. This is the spirit of the well-known aggadah in which Moshe, sitting at the back of Rabbi Akiva's beit midrash, does not recognize what Rabbi Akiva is teaching — until someone asks Rabbi Akiva the source of a ruling and he replies: halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai. In some sense everything derived does trace back to Sinai. The present passage is one that emphasizes the most direct form of this claim.

### Shema as Two-Edged Sword

Rabbi Yitzchak teaches: kol hakoreh Krias Shema al mitato ke'ilu ochez cherev shel shtei pifiyot beyado — whoever says Krias Shema at bedtime is as one who holds a two-edged sword in his hand. The source is the pasuk: Romemot El bigronam vecherev pifiyot beyadam — the praise of God is in their throats and a two-edged sword in their hands. The connection to bedtime is established by Mar Zutra, or some say Rav Ashi, who traces it to the earlier verse in that passage: Ya'alzu chasidim bechavod yeranenu al mishkevotam — the righteous will rejoice in glory and sing upon their beds. It is thus the Krias Shema said upon the bed that produces the metaphorical sword.

The sword is wielded against the evil spirits that are active at night — a dimension of the bedtime Shema that goes beyond prayer for divine protection or the moral framing of one's day, and enters the realm of protection from harmful supernatural forces.

### Torah Repels Mazikin

Rabbi Yitzchak further states explicitly: kol hakoreh Krias Shema al mitato, mazikin bedilin heimenu — whoever says Krias Shema at bedtime, the mazikin withdraw from him. The proof-text invokes the word reshef, which the Gemara identifies with mazikin, from the pasuk Mizeh ra'av ulichumei reshef veketev meriri — a verse from the curses in Devarim listing famine and demonic affliction. The sons of reshef will fly away — uf, which the Gemara identifies with Torah, based on the verse Hata'if einecha bo v'einenu — if you avert your eyes from it, it vanishes — where uf appears in the context of Torah study. The mazikin flee before Torah, here understood concretely as the recitation of Shema.

Reish Lakish then broadens the principle considerably: kol haosek baTorah yissurin bdilin heimenu — whoever engages in Torah study, afflictions withdraw from him. The same reshef verse is employed, but now reshef is read not as mazikin but as yissurin — afflictions in general. This is a striking expansion. Protecting oneself from supernatural mazikin through Torah study has a certain internal logic, but claiming that Torah study protects from yissurin in general raises profound questions about tzaddik v'ra lo and rasha v'tov lo. The Gemara is clearly aware of the tension, and the next section addresses it directly.

## Yissurin Shel Ahava

### Torah Protects — Really?

Rabbi Yochanan immediately challenges Reish Lakish's claim that Torah protects from afflictions: ha afilu tinokos shel beis raban yodin osah — even cheder children know this. The pasuk in the Torah states explicitly: if you hearken to God's voice, do what is right, follow the mitzvos, and observe all the statutes — kol hamachalah asher samti beMitzrayim lo asim alecha ki ani Hashem rofecha — all the afflictions I brought upon Egypt I will not bring upon you, for I am God your healer. This divine promise is taught to children. One need not derive it from a complex gezerah shavah involving reshef and uf.

The point of Reish Lakish's interpretation must therefore be something more specific. The implicit question pressing on the Gemara is the one that everyone already knows: it does not always work out this way. Good people suffer. Torah scholars suffer. The promise of protection is not self-evidently borne out by experience.

### Neglecting Torah = Suffe…

The Gemara therefore reads Reish Lakish's teaching not as a general promise that Torah scholars are exempt from affliction, but as a more pointed warning: kol she'efshar lo la'asok baTorah v'eino osek — one who has the capacity to learn Torah and does not avail himself of it — Hakadosh Baruch Hu meivi alav yissurin mechoarin — God will bring upon him particularly harsh and troubling afflictions.

The proof-text is: Ne'elamti dumiyah hechashaiti mitov, uche'eivi ne'echar — I was silent, stilled from good, and my pain was stirred up. Ve'ein tov ela Torah: tov here is Torah, as the verse states ki lekach tov natati lachem, Torati al ta'azovu — I have given you a good gift; do not abandon my Torah. Thus hechashaiti mitov does not merely mean that good things ceased; it means I was silent from Torah, which is the tov. And the consequence is uche'eivi ne'echar — wounding and affliction follow.

This shifts the framework: the world does operate according to a divine moral economy, but within that economy there is a category beyond clear sins of commission — a category of failure to actualize one's potential for Torah. Even that omission carries consequences. The Gemara is operating in a straightforward world of reward and punishment — but is clearly aware that this framework is incomplete.

### God Gave Torah With Joy

Rabbi Levi, or some say Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa, introduces a striking contrast: bo u're'ei she-lo ke-middat HaKadosh Baruch Hu middat basar va-dam — come and see that the ways of God are not like the ways of flesh and blood. When a person sells something to another, the seller is sad and the buyer is happy. This assumes a commercial context in which one sells not as a merchant but out of necessity — selling something dear to put food on the table, parting with something of real personal significance. In such circumstances, the seller grieves while the buyer rejoices.

God's way is different. Natan la-hem Torah le-Yisrael ve-samach — God gave Torah to Israel and was joyous. The proof is in the very pasuk: ki lekach tov natati lachem, Torati al ta'azovu — I have given you this wonderful gift; do not abandon my Torah. The giving is expressed with joy, not with the grief of one who must part with something beloved. The analogy is to a parent who passes on something precious to a child: the giving is a joyous act because the gift expresses love, the depth of the relationship, and the desire to share something of profound significance. God gives Torah to Israel not with reluctance but with delight — and that delight is itself part of the gift.

## Yissurin Shel Ahava (II)

### Yissurin Shel Ahava

Rav, or some say Rav Chisda, sets out a systematic protocol for the person beset by afflictions. Im ra'ah adam sheyissurin ba'im alav — if a person sees that afflictions are befalling him — yefashpesh be-ma'asav — he should examine his deeds. Perhaps there is a sin for which he bears responsibility; he should use the suffering as an occasion for teshuvah, as the pasuk says: nachpasa deracheinu venachkorah — let us search our ways and investigate — venashuva ad Hashem. If, upon examination, a sin is found, he should do teshuvah.

If he examined and found nothing — pishpesh ve-lo matza — then yitleh be-vittel Torah: he should attribute the afflictions to insufficient Torah study. Not all consequences flow from sins of commission; sometimes it is the failure to do what one could and should have been doing, as the pasuk implies: ashrei hagever asher teyassrennu yah, umi-Toratecha telamdennu — praiseworthy is the man whom God afflicts and teaches from Your Torah. The yissurin become a spur to greater Torah engagement.

And if, even then — ve-im talah ve-lo matza — neither sin nor Torah neglect provides an explanation, beyadu'a: one should understand that these are yissurin shel ahava — afflictions of love — as the pasuk states: ki et asher ye'ehav Hashem yochiach — those whom God loves, God will rebuke.

This sequential logic is itself significant. The Gemara does not simply assert that the good are rewarded and the wicked punished and leave it at that. It knows — implicitly, though it will address it more explicitly in a daf or two — that Moshe himself challenged God on the problem of the righteous who suffer. The framework here represents an attempt to work through that problem systematically, preserving the structure of divine justice while acknowledging that sometimes no accounting suffices.

### Accepting Yissurin Lovin…

Rava, citing Rav Sechora citing Rav Huna, teaches: kol she'Hakadosh Baruch Hu chafetz bo, medake'o beyissurin — whomever God desires, He crushes with afflictions, as the pasuk says vaHashem chafetz dake'o hechali — God desired to crush him with illness.

But a condition follows: yachol afilu lo kiblam me'ahava — one might think these afflictions have value even if not accepted with love. The Gemara therefore qualifies: im tasim asham nafsho — if you place your soul as an asham. Just as an asham, a guilt offering, achieves atonement only when brought with conscious intent and awareness — mah asham lada'at — so too yissurin lada'at: the afflictions carry their significance only when accepted intentionally and willingly, with full awareness of what they are.

The reward for accepting them this way: yireh zera ya'arich yamim — he will see offspring and lengthen his days. And further: she'talmudo mitkayem beyado — his Torah will be sustained in his hand, shene'emar vechafetz Hashem beyado yitzlach — the one whom God desires will succeed.

### Soloveitchik on Yissurin

HaRav Soloveitchik offered a reading of this passage that clarifies what yissurin lada'at — acceptance with intention — actually means in practice. The Gemara itself gives an example of yissurin shel ahava: even something as minor as reaching into one's pocket for change and pulling out the wrong coin qualifies. On its face this seems trivializing. But the Rav's insight is that yissurin shel ahava is defined not by the objective nature or severity of the suffering, but by how the person experiencing it interprets and responds to it. If one sees one's difficulties — whatever their scale — as part of one's relationship with God and uses them as an occasion for self-examination, for reflecting on what could be improved, for investigating one's deeds and one's Torah engagement, then even minor disruptions become yissurin shel ahava. They become part of a process of spiritual refinement and relational deepening with the divine. If, however, one simply experiences the hardship as arbitrary misfortune without any interpretive frame of meaning, then the afflictions are not yissurin shel ahava — not because they fail to happen, but because they are not received as such. The designation is thus not an external metaphysical label applied from outside, but a category that is partly constituted by the subjective response of the one who suffers.

## Bikur Cholim Stories

### 1/60 of Suffering

Rav Huna teaches: kol ha-mevaker choleh notel echad mi-shishim be-tza'aro — one who visits the sick takes away one-sixtieth of the patient's suffering. The response to this is an obvious objection: if so, let sixty people visit the sick person, and they will collectively remove all his suffering and restore him. Rav Huna replies: ke-asirit shel peirot — it is like a tenth of the fruit, meaning a tenth of what currently remains. Each visitor takes a sixtieth of whatever suffering is present at that moment, not a sixtieth of the original total. The portions diminish progressively; no finite number of visitors will reduce the suffering to nothing. This sugya appears as well in Bava Metzia daf 30.

### Rav Papa's Illness

Rav Papa was ill. Rav Shimi bar Ashi came to visit him, saw that his condition was becoming difficult — chaza de-takif leih alma — and said to those present: pray for him. The brevity of this account is itself significant: it illustrates bikur cholim in action, showing a visitor who responds to the severity of the patient's condition with urgent intercession.

### Yochanan Heals Chanina

Rabbi Yochanan was ill, and Rabbi Chanina came to visit him. He said to him: chavivin alecha yissurin — are your sufferings beloved to you? Rabbi Yochanan replied: lo hen velo secharan — neither them nor their reward. Immediately Rabbi Chanina said: hav li yadecha — give me your hand. Rabbi Yochanan gave him his hand, and Rabbi Chanina raised him up.

The exchange is remarkable. The question chavivin alecha yissurin is precisely the question the Gemara has been wrestling with — are these yissurin shel ahava, accepted willingly? Rabbi Yochanan's answer is unambiguous: no. He does not want them, and he does not want even the reward that may come from them. And yet Rabbi Chanina heals him — not despite this answer, but without requiring any other. The healing does not depend on Rabbi Yochanan's theological acceptance of his suffering.

### Ein Chavush Matir Atzmo

The pattern recurs: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba was ill. Rabbi Yochanan came to visit him, asked chavivin alecha yissurin, received the same answer — lo hen velo secharan — extended his hand, and healed him. The Gemara immediately raises the question: amai? Why did Rabbi Yochanan need Rabbi Chanina to heal him? Lokim Rabbi Yochanan lenafsheih — let Rabbi Yochanan heal himself, since he clearly has the power to heal others by clasping their hand. The answer: ein chavush matir atzmo mi-beis ha-asurim — a prisoner cannot release himself from prison. The one who is ill is in a kind of captivity from which one cannot, by one's own power, extricate oneself. One requires another person — a visitor — for that.

This principle gives bikur cholim a dimension beyond comfort and prayer. The visitor brings something the patient cannot provide for himself, something structurally inaccessible to the one who is suffering from within the suffering.

### Yochanan Heals Elazar

Rabbi Elazar was ill and was lying in a dark room. Rabbi Yochanan came to visit him. He uncovered his arm — galyeih le-daraeih — and light fell into the room. The beauty of Rabbi Yochanan was legendary; the Gemara elsewhere describes it in extraordinary terms, and here that beauty literally illuminates a darkened room.

Rabbi Yochanan saw that Rabbi Elazar was weeping. He said to him: amai ka bachit — why are you crying? He offered several possibilities. Is it because you did not learn enough Torah? We have learned: echad ha-marbeh ve-echad ha-mameit u-vilvad she-yechaven libo la-shamayim — one who does much and one who does little are equal, so long as one directs one's heart to Heaven. Is it because of insufficient sustenance? Lo kol adam zocheh li-shnei shulchanot — not every person merits two tables, meaning not everyone is granted both Torah greatness and material prosperity. Is it because of children you did not have? Dein girma de-asira'ah bir — Rabbi Yochanan gestured toward a certain bone he carried with him, a relic of a child he had lost, one of ten children who died in his lifetime.

Rabbi Elazar answered: le-hai shufra de-vali be-ara'a ka bachina — I am weeping for this beauty that will one day rot in the ground. Rabbi Yochanan replied: al da vadai ka bachit — for this, you should indeed cry. And they wept together. Then Rabbi Yochanan asked: chavivin alecha yissurin? Rabbi Elazar answered: lo hen velo secharan. Rabbi Yochanan said: hav li yadecha. He gave him his hand, and Rabbi Yochanan raised him up.

The shared weeping is as striking as the healing. Rabbi Yochanan does not dismiss Rabbi Elazar's grief over transient beauty or offer consolation that deflects it. He affirms it: yes, this is worth weeping over. Two great sages, one of them radiating physical beauty that lights up a room, sit together and mourn the inevitable loss of that beauty to the earth. It is only after this moment of shared grief — this genuine human encounter in the darkness — that the healing follows.

# Berakhot 6

## Prayer in Synagogue

### Prayer Heard in Shul

The daf opens in the middle of daf 6 with a series of statements attributed to Abba Binyamin. Having already encountered his teaching about the mazikim, we now pick up with a new Baraita: *tanya abba binyamin omer, ein tfilato shel adam nishmaat ela b'beit haknesset* — a person's prayer is heard primarily in the synagogue. The proof text is *lishmoa el harina v'el hatefilla*, "to listen to the rejoicing and to the prayer," from which the Gemara derives: *b'makom rina sham t'hei tfillah* — in the place of singing, there should be prayer.

The significance of this statement is twofold, and its context is worth appreciating. In the period of the Gemara and the Mishnah, the rabbis were not the institutional leaders of the synagogues. There was a distinct leadership structure for the beit haknesset, separate from the rabbinic enterprise centered in the beit hamidrash, and archaeological evidence supports this as well. This creates a broader question about the relationship between tefillah and Talmud Torah, and between the beit haknesset and the beit hamidrash as competing or complementary loci of religious life. There are in fact other Gemaras that speak of a person's prayer being heard where he learns — not necessarily in the beit haknesset at all. And the statement here is not even specifically about minyan: one might daven at home alone, or in shul alone, or with a minyan at home or in shul. This is a statement about location, not quorum, and it is not self-evident that the synagogue is the superior location.

### Rina & Singing

Given that context, what makes the synagogue the preferred place? The answer the Baraita gives is *rina* — and *rina* is clearly something distinct from *tefillah*. Rashi explains: *beit haknesset shesham omrim hatzibur shirot v'tishbachot b'ne'imat kol arev* — the synagogue is where the community recites songs and praises with a pleasing and sweet voice. The communal singing is not incidental; it is the very quality that elevates prayer in the synagogue over prayer elsewhere. The Maharsha adds a parallel observation: just as Shmoneh Esrei is preceded by *shevach v'tishbacha*, the praises of P'sukei D'zimra, so too the rina of the congregation functions as a proper lead-in and accompaniment to the central act of *bakasha*.

### Shul vs. Beit Midrash

There is also a historical and liturgical context to the prominence of *rina*: the rabbis, particularly after the destruction of the Beit HaMikdash, were consciously trying to recreate something of the Temple experience. The Shirat HaLevi'im — the Levitical singing with instruments — was a defining feature of the Temple service, and the characterization of the beit haknesset as a *mikdash me'at* makes it entirely coherent that communal singing would be understood as one of the central features distinguishing it as a place of prayer.

---

## God's Presence

### God in Congregation

The Gemara continues: *amar Rabin bar Rav Adda amar Rabbi Yitzchak, minayin she'Hakadosh Baruch Hu matzuy b'veit haknesset* — from where do we know that God is found in the beit haknesset? The proof text is *elohim nitzav b'adat el*, "God stands in the congregation of God." Rashi reads *adat el* as referring to the *beit moed*, the place of divine appointment — the synagogue now functioning in the role once occupied by the mishkan. Without a minyan, the beit haknesset itself is already the locus of divine presence, the place God inhabits in the absence of the Beit HaMikdash.

### Ten to One

From this foundation, the Gemara proceeds through a well-known descending series, familiar from the Mishnah in Pirkei Avot. *u'minayin l'asara shemitpallelim she'shechina imahem* — when ten people pray, the Shechina is with them, as proven again from *elohim nitzav b'adat el*, where the divine presence accompanies the congregation. *u'minayin l'shlosha sheyoshvim b'din she'shechina imahem* — when three sit in judgment, God is with them, as it says *b'kerev Elohim yishpot*, "in the midst of God they shall judge." *u'minayin l'shnayim sheyoshvim v'oskim baTorah she'shechina imahem* — when two sit and engage in Torah, God hears and listens, as it says *az nidberu yirei Hashem ish el re'ehu, vayakshev Hashem vayishma, vayikatev sefer zikaron* — then those who feared God spoke one to his fellow, God hearkened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written.

The end of that pasuk, *v'yirei Hashem u'lechoshvei shemo*, prompted an aside from Rav Ashi: *chashav adam la'asot mitzvah v'ne'enas v'lo asah, ma'aleh alav hakatuv k'ilu asah* — if a person intended to perform a mitzvah and was prevented by circumstances beyond his control, Scripture accounts it as if he had done it. The criterion is *ne'enas* — a genuine attempt frustrated by circumstance, not merely an unfulfilled intention among many. This is parenthetical to the main thread, however.

The series then concludes: *u'minayin she'afilu echad sheyoshev v'osek baTorah she'Shechina imo* — even a single individual learning Torah has the divine presence with him, as it says *b'chol hamakom asher azkir et shemi avo elecha u'verachticha* — in any place where I will cause My name to be mentioned, I will come to you and bless you. One might note that this pasuk speaks of God causing His name to be mentioned, not of the human actor doing so; but through the lens of Chazal it is read as referring to Torah study, by which God's name is invoked. It is also worth noting, as one might observe, that the pasuk could very plausibly have been read as referring to tefillah — *mazkir shem Hashem*, the invocation of God's name, is a natural description of prayer. Yet Chazal read it as Torah. This connects to a broader tension running through this entire passage: the eliding and overlapping of tefillah and Talmud Torah as different modes of connecting to God — and the question of whether, at the experiential level, learning Torah is being understood here as a form of tefillah, a direct personal encounter with God rather than a purely intellectual activity.

### Two vs. One Learning

The Gemara then asks: if even one person merits the divine presence, why was it necessary to state the case of two? *ki me'achar d'afilu echad, trei mibaya?* The answer: *trei michtevan milayhu b'sefer zichronot* — when two learn together, their words are written in the book of remembrance, whereas for one learning alone, *chad lo michtevan milayhu b'sefer zichronot* — his words are not so recorded.

What does it mean for words to be "written in the book of remembrance"? If the concern were simply receiving reward for learning, one would receive that whether learning alone or with a partner. The Maharsha offers a compelling answer: when two people learn together, each challenges and corrects the other, and the conclusions they reach are therefore more likely to be accurate and truthful. It is those conclusions — precisely reasoned, tested by dialogue, closer to the truth — that are worth recording. The single learner may produce interesting thoughts, but without the corrective pressure of a study partner, those ideas may not be reliable enough to merit that kind of recording. The merit of the individual is recorded; but the *ideas* themselves are what get written when two learn together. This reflects a broader principle well-established in the Gemara: learning in partnership is the superior form of Torah study.

There is a further dimension here. The progression in this passage moves from tefillah (at ten) to din (at three) to Torah (at two and one). The shift is notable: the list begins with prayer as the paradigmatic religious act and ends with Torah learning. One might observe that when learning is done alone, it can have the quality of a spiritual, personal, almost prayerful activity — an intimate encounter with God. When two learn together, the dynamic becomes more dialogical and intellectual, *az nidberu*, they "spoke" to one another — a different mode of encounter, more public, more corrective, perhaps less purely interior.

### Din as Torah

The Gemara then turns to the case of three: *tlata miba'ei* — if even two merit the divine presence, why state the case of three? The answer: *mahu deteima dina shelama de'alma hu, velo ati Shechina* — one might have thought that the activity of a beit din, sitting in legal judgment, is merely a matter of maintaining social order and worldly peace, not Torah, and therefore the Shechina would not be present. The Gemara therefore teaches: *dina nami havei Torah* — din is also Torah.

This is a striking statement. There is a real temptation — perhaps especially strong in the rabbinic world — to draw a sharp line between the beit midrash, where "real" Torah takes place, and the courtroom, where practical disputes are resolved. One might imagine that the talmidei chachamim are engaged in the genuinely religious work, while the dayyanim adjudicating everyday cases between litigants are performing something more mundane, however socially necessary. The Gemara rejects that dichotomy emphatically. Why is din Torah? In one sense, because to judge correctly requires mastery of halacha — you cannot sit as a dayan without knowing the relevant Torah. But there is a deeper sense as well: Torah is not only the intellectual process of learning; it is that learning *actualized* in the world, shaping society toward justice and toward what God intended. Din is Torah brought into reality. As the Tur opens Choshen Mishpat citing the Midrash: *kol she'oseh din l'amito ke'ilu na'aseh shutaf l'Hakadosh Baruch Hu bema'aseh Bereishit* — anyone who renders true judgment becomes, as it were, a partner with God in the work of creation. A judge spending his days adjudicating disputes may feel far from the beit midrash, but the Gemara insists that he is performing *avodas Hashem* in the fullest sense.

### God Awaits Ten

Finally, the Gemara distinguishes between ten and three: *asara kadim Shechina v'atya* — for ten, God arrives before they do. God is already present, waiting in anticipation. *v'ad d'ati tlata* — for three, God's presence comes only once the activity is underway. The difference is not merely quantitative; it reflects the urgency and eagerness with which the divine presence anticipates communal prayer. *elohim nitzav b'adat el* — God is *standing* there, not hovering above, but present as an active, anticipating participant. This image, of God already at the synagogue waiting for the minyan to arrive, will carry forward into the Gemara's subsequent discussion of what happens when the expected minyan does not materialize.

---

## God's Tefillin

### God's Tefillin Query

The Gemara now transitions: *amar Rabin bar Rav Adda amar Rabbi Yitzchak, minayin she'Hakadosh Baruch Hu meniach tefillin* — from where do we know that God wears tefillin? This transition is not arbitrary. The image of *elohim nitzav b'adat el* — God standing as an equal participant among the congregation — naturally leads to imagining God not merely as a transcendent observer but as a direct participant in religious life, even wearing the same garb as those among whom He stands.

### Swearing by Torah

The proof begins with a pasuk from Yeshayahu: *nishba Hashem biyemino uvizroa uzo* — God swore by His right hand and by His powerful arm. *yimino zu torah* — His right hand is the Torah, as it says *mi'yimino esh dat lamo*, from God's right hand a fiery law for His people. The *zroa uzo*, the powerful arm, must then refer to something in God's left hand. What is God holding when He swears — analogous to a person holding a Torah scroll when taking an oath? The Gemara identifies it as tefillin, on the basis of *hashem oz l'amo yiten* — God gives *oz*, strength, to His people — and *oz* is identified with tefillin through the pasuk *v'ra'u kol amei ha'aretz ki shem Hashem nikra alecha v'yeru mimeka*, all peoples of the earth will see that God's name is called upon you and they will fear you, which a Baraita in the name of Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol applies to the *tefillin she'barosh*.

Tosafot engages with a nuance here: why specifically the head tefillin? One might suppose the *shin* on the bayit and the *dalet* formed by the knot of the straps spell out part of God's name, making those features the source of the pasuk's *ki shem Hashem nikra alecha*. But Tosafot rejects this, pointing out that the straps have the status of *tashmishei kedushah* — accessories that serve the sacred object — rather than themselves being a *davar shebikdushah*. If the *dalet* formed by the straps were considered an actual written letter of God's name, the straps would require the same level of sanctity as the *klafim* themselves; but it is clear that the bayit has greater sanctity than the straps on account of the *shin*, which means the *dalet* does not carry halachic weight as a letter of God's name. What the pasuk means, Tosafot explains, is simply that the *tefillin shel rosh* is visible — worn high on the head, in plain sight — whereas the *tefillin shel yad* is covered by the sleeve and concealed. It is the visibility of the head tefillin that makes it the locus of *v'ra'u kol amei ha'aretz*.

### Mutual Declaration

The Gemara then asks: *hani tefillin d'marei alma mai ketiv behu* — what is written in God's tefillin? Just as we know what is written in our tefillin, what text does God's contain? The answer: *u'mi k'amcha Yisrael goy echad ba'aretz* — who is like Your people Israel, one nation on earth?

The parallel is deliberate and profound. We recite *shema yisrael hashem elokeinu hashem echad* — we declare God's oneness. The word *echad* here may be best understood not merely as the arithmetical claim that there is one God, but as *god alone* — He is our God, and no other. In this reading, the Shema is a declaration of exclusive allegiance: only God is our God. The parallel in God's tefillin is *goy echad ba'aretz* — not that Israel is the only nation on earth, but that Israel is the one uniquely chosen nation, the nation with whom God has an exclusive relationship. Just as we proclaim our singular devotion to God, God's tefillin proclaims His singular devotion to us.

The Gemara makes this mutuality explicit through the pasuk in Devarim: *et Hashem hemarta hayom* — you have elevated and declared God today — *v'Hashem hemircha hayom* — and God has elevated and declared you today. *amar lehem haKadosh baruch hu l'yisrael: atem asituni chativa achat ba'olam, va'ani e'eseh etchem chativa achat ba'olam.* You have made Me the one singular unit in the world — that is the *shema*, *hashem echad* — and I will make you the one singular chosen unit in the world — that is *u'mi k'amcha Yisrael goy echad ba'aretz*.

There is something genuinely beautiful about this image. The tefillin we wear is a *levush*, a garment of identity: *v'ra'u kol amei ha'aretz ki shem Hashem nikra alecha* — they see you and they see God's name upon you. The tefillin identifies us as belonging to God. The Gemara now imagines God wearing a corresponding *levush* — a garment that identifies God, in some sense, as belonging to us. God, in His essence, transcends all particularity and is the God of the entire universe; but in the *levush* He wears, in the relationship He has put on, there is a unique bond with Israel. The power of anthropomorphism here is not to diminish God but to give extraordinary resonance and weight to the religious acts we perform. If God swears by His Torah when He must swear, then our act of swearing by the Torah participates in something that God Himself does. If God wears tefillin, then our daily donning of tefillin is an act that parallels what God does — an act of mutual declaration.

### Four Compartments

The Gemara is not finished, however. *tenach b'chad beita, shear batei mai* — granted, that is in one compartment; but what is in the other compartments? This question has almost the quality of a *reductio ad absurdum* — having entertained the notion of God's tefillin at all, the Gemara now presses the logic through and asks what fills all four compartments. In doing so, it naturalizes the entire premise: very well, God has tefillin with four compartments, so let us determine their contents.

The Gemara identifies four passages from Devarim, each praising Israel's unique relationship with God. *ki mi goy gadol asher lo elohim krovim eilav* — what great nation has God so close to it? *ashrecha yisrael mi kamocha, am nosha b'hashem* — praised are you Israel, who is like you, a nation saved by God? *o hanissa elohim lavo lakachat lo goy mikerev goy* — has God ever done such a thing as to take one nation out of another? *u'letitcha elyon al kol hagoyim* — to place you supreme above all the nations. These are all passages from Devarim that express the theme of Israel's chosen and elevated status among the nations.

The Gemara momentarily objects that these four passages are too many to yield exactly four compartments — but then resolves the difficulty: *ki mi goy gadol* and *u'mi goy gadol* are sufficiently similar to share a compartment; *ashrecha Yisrael* and *u'mi k'amcha Yisrael* are similar enough to share a compartment. That yields four: Israel's greatness, Israel's praise, the Exodus as the defining act of divine election, and Israel's supremacy among nations — each in its own compartment, and all of them written as well on the *tefillin shel yad*, though there in a single undivided space.

---

## Regular Attendance

### Missing a Day

The Gemara returns to the theme of God's presence in the synagogue and what it means for our obligations there. It is worth noting the connective thread: the image of *elohim nitzav b'adat el* — God not merely present but *standing* in the congregation, as an equal participant — is what prompted the discussion of God wearing tefillin, since God is imagined as fully present and personally engaged in the life of the community. That same image now animates the next set of teachings.

*Amar Rabin bar Rav Adda amar Rabbi Yitzchak: kol haragil lavo l'veit haknesset v'lo ba yom echad* — anyone who regularly comes to the synagogue and one day does not come — *haKadosh baruch hu mash'il bo* — God asks after him: where is so-and-so today? He is usually here. The proof text: *mi vachem yirei Hashem shome'a b'kol avdo* — who is it that fears God, listens to the voice of His servant — *asher halach chasheichim v'ein nogah lo* — who has now gone into darkness with no light? If he went for the sake of a mitzvah, then *nogah lo* — the mitzvah is light, and there is no concern. But if he went for something that is merely *reshus* — perhaps a business matter, an early meeting — *ein nogah lo*, it will not be light for him. *yivtach b'shem hashem* — the end of the pasuk counsels: trust in God's name. The conclusion of the Gemara: *mishum d'hava lei livtoach b'shem Hashem v'lo batach* — because he should have trusted in God rather than missing shul for the sake of his livelihood.

This is a striking Gemara. It speaks to an entirely recognizable reality: the regular shul-goer who one morning does not appear. What is notable, though, is the asymmetry. What of the overwhelming majority of the community that never comes to shul in the morning? The Gemara says nothing about them — no divine inquiry, no concern expressed. It is precisely the person who has established a pattern of attendance whose absence registers. His regular presence has created expectations. God, as it were, knows this person, sees what he is committed to, and notices when he breaks that pattern. There is something both demanding and tender about this: God is upset when the regular shul-goer is absent, but that upset is the upset of one who cares, who tracks, who has a relationship with that person. *haKadosh baruch hu medakdek im chasidav k'chut hasa'arah* — God holds those close to Him to the finest standard — and here too, it is not even that this person is more righteous than others in general, but that he has engaged in a practice that creates a particular set of expectations.

### God's Anger at No Minyan

*Amar Rav Yochanan: besha'ah she'HaKadosh Baruch Hu ba b'veit haknesset v'lo matza bah asarah, miyad hu ko'es* — when God comes to the synagogue at the appointed time for a minyan and does not find ten people there, He is immediately angry. The proof text: *madua basi v'ein ish, karasi v'ein oneh* — why did I come and no one was here, I called out and there was no answer.

One might note a slight tension: the earlier teaching said that God arrives *before* the minyan, already waiting. Presumably the intent here is that God arrives at the time when the minyan is expected, and people are still straggling in — six present, seven, waiting for others to arrive — and this failure to be ready provokes divine displeasure. The reaction is thoroughly human in its expression — and, one might add, thoroughly recognizable to anyone who has ever waited for a minyan to form.

The halachic weight of this aggadic teaching is not negligible. One of the Rishonim invokes this Gemara in connection with a famous episode where it was necessary to free a slave named Tevvi in order to complete a minyan. The general prohibition against freeing one's slave was overridden, according to the Ramban, because the gravity of the divine anger when ten are expected and not present was sufficient to justify even transgressing that prohibition. Whatever further questions that raises, it reflects the understanding that this is not merely a rhetorical flourish but a statement with practical halachic implications about the overriding importance of completing a minyan.

---

## Fixed Place (Makom Kavua)

### Fixed Prayer Place

*Amar Rabbi Chelbo amar Rav Huna: kol hakovei'a makom litfillato, Elohei Avraham be'ezro* — anyone who establishes a fixed place for his prayer, the God of Abraham will come to his aid. When he dies, they say over him at his hesped: *ei anav, ei chasid, mitalmidav shel avraham avinu* — where is the humble one, where is the righteous one, from the students of Avraham Avinu. This formulation, *ei anav, ei chasid*, appears to have been a standard liturgical trope of the period, a classic eulogy phrase used for those known for their seriousness in prayer and their commitment to a fixed place.

One point worth noting: *makom kavua* is not simply equivalent to *beit haknesset*. The teaching says *makom litfillato*, a fixed place for his prayer — not *beit haknesset*. For whatever reason a person cannot go to shul — distance, illness, circumstance — the obligation and virtue of *makom kavua* still applies. The two conversations, that of the beit haknesset and that of the makom kavua, are related but distinct.

### Abraham's Model

*Avraham Avinu minalan dekava makom* — from where do we know that Abraham established a fixed place? *dechtiv vayashkem avraham baboker el hamakom asher amad sham* — Abraham arose in the morning and went to the place where he had stood. The word *amad*, stood, means he returned to the same place he had been before. *v'ein amidah ela tefillah* — standing (*amidah*) always connotes prayer, as demonstrated from *vaya'amod Pinchas vayipalel*, Pinchas stood and prayed.

The significance of *makom kavua* goes beyond mere practicality. When a person has a fixed place, his prayer is not something done haphazardly — not done here today, somewhere else tomorrow. There is an identity that accumulates in a place. We are territorial creatures, and we make associations: this place is where I have stood before God, morning after morning, year after year. The place carries the history of those encounters. It is *my* place in relation to God. This is well evidenced by the seriousness with which *makom kavua* is treated in halachic practice — those sitting shivah must move from their usual place, as a sign of disruption; the intensity of feeling when someone occupies one's accustomed seat in shul is not merely territorial pettiness but reflects something real about the relationship between person, place, and prayer.

The symbolism of Abraham as the model is also worth reflecting upon. Abraham represents the very pillar of faith — *elohei avraham be'ezro* — who held his ground through every trial. His going back to the same place is not only a technical precedent for *makom kavua*; it evokes his character as one who, even in his prayer and his arguments with God, did not waver. The one who fixes a place for prayer aspires to be *mitalmidav shel Avraham Avinu* — a student of Abraham not only in the matter of location but in that quality of unwavering, grounded faith that Abraham's return to his place represents.

---

## Synagogue Decorum

### Leaving Shul

*Amar Rav Huna: ha'yotzei mi'beit haknesset al yifsi'a pesi'ah gassah* — one who leaves the synagogue should not take large steps. The concern is not mere decorum but the message one communicates: taking large strides toward the exit signals eagerness to leave, which is unbecoming of someone departing from a place of divine presence.

### Running In

*Amar Abaye: lo amran ela le'meifa* — this applies only to leaving. *aval le'meito, mitzvah le'mirhatz* — but going into shul, it is a mitzvah to run, as the pasuk says *nirdofah lada'at et Hashem* — let us run to know God. The contrast is deliberate: when leaving, one shows reluctance; when arriving, one demonstrates eagerness. Neither is about decorum in the narrow sense — both express the value of what is happening in the synagogue and one's relationship to it.

### Running for Torah

*Amar Rav Zeira: me'reish ki havina chazina lehu le'rabbanan de'rahatei le'pirka be'Shabbata* — early in his life, Rav Zeira would see rabbinic students running to hear the *drasha* on Shabbos, and he would think: *kamechallei rabbanan Shabbata* — they are desecrating the spirit of Shabbos by running. Once he heard the teaching of Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — *le'olam yarutz adam lidvar halacha va'afilu be'Shabbat* — a person should always run to hear a matter of halacha, even on Shabbos, as the pasuk says *acharei Hashem yelechu ke'aryeh yish'ag*, they shall go after God as a lion roars — *ana nami reitna* — he too would run, even on Shabbos.

The apparent tension is real: there is a prohibition against running on Shabbos, and there is a sense of the decorum appropriate to the beit haknesset. Yet running toward *dvar Hashem* — running *for* Torah — is not a violation of what Shabbos or the synagogue is about; it is, in fact, the most authentic expression of what those things are about. The eagerness to receive Torah is more in keeping with the spirit of Shabbos than any formal decorum that would impede it.

### Rewards for Engagement

Since the discussion has turned to running to the *drasha*, the Gemara continues in this vein with a series of statements about where the reward lies in various forms of communal engagement.

*Amar Rav Zeira: agra de'pirka rahata* — the reward of attending the public *drasha* is the running. This is an honest and somewhat arresting observation: most people attending a public lecture do not sufficiently understand or retain what is being taught. Rashi makes this explicit — *ki rubam einam mevinim*, most of them do not really understand what is being said, nor will they later be able to repeat it accurately. What they do earn reward for is the effort of showing up, the act of running to be there. As Rashi formulates it: the one who can repeat a teaching some time later — that is the real mark of understanding.

*Amar Abaye: agra de'kalla dukhka* — the reward of the *kalla*, the large communal teaching before the *regalim*, is the crowding and the pressure. The assumption is again that most attendees are not following the content closely enough to receive reward on that basis. What they receive reward for is being present in that press of people, enduring the difficulty of the experience, choosing to be there. There may also be a connection to the *mazikim*, mentioned earlier in the daf — the protective effect of being part of a large gathering.

*Amar Rava: agra de'shma'ta sevara* — the reward of *shma'ta*, the actual learned halachic discussion, is the *sevara*, the understanding and reasoning one brings to it. This is a different register entirely: *shma'ta* is the domain of talmidei chachamim engaged in serious analysis. There, simply showing up does not constitute the reward. The reward is the intellectual and spiritual effort of arriving at genuine understanding.

*Amar Rav Papa: agra de'vei tamaya shetikusa* — the reward of attending at a house of mourning or a cemetery is silence. At a shiva, the *menachamim* are not to initiate conversation; they are to be present, attentive, and quiet, waiting for the mourner to speak. Speaking about trivial things in a house of mourning misses what is needed. A quiet, attentive presence — simply being there — is the authentic form of comfort, and that is where the reward lies.

*Amar Mar Zutra: igra de'tanisa tzidkasa* — the reward of a fast day is the tzedakah. This can mean that the fast itself is less primary than the way it translates into action — specifically, giving to the poor so they have food to eat, since for those who go without adequate food throughout the week, the fast is a genuine hardship. One might add: fasting also creates an experiential knowledge of hunger that ought to engender greater generosity.

*Amar Rav Sheshes: igra de'hespeda daluyei* — the reward of the eulogy is the wailing, the crying out. In the time of Chazal, the hesped was not primarily a biographical tribute to the deceased but an experience designed to evoke genuine lamentation. The crying out *is* the reward — it is the authentic response, not the eloquence of the words.

*Amar Rav Ashi: igra de'bei hiluli mili* — the reward of attending a wedding feast is the words one says there. Rashi explains: saying words of praise and joy to the *choson* and *kallah*, actively participating in *simchat choson v'kallah* — that is the reward, not merely the act of attending.

---

## Praying Behind Shul

### Behind Shul is Wicked

*Amar Rav Huna: kol hamispallel achorei beit haknesset nikra rasha* — whoever prays behind the synagogue is called wicked, as it says *saviv resha'im yis'hallechun* — the wicked walk around on the outside. The more natural interpretation is that this refers to someone praying outside the building entirely, though interpretations vary.

### Face Direction

*Amar Abaye: lo amran ela d'lo mahadar apei l'bei knishta* — this is said only when one is not turning one's face toward the synagogue. If a person is outside the shul but facing in the same direction as those praying inside — facing toward Jerusalem just as the congregation does — *leit lan bah*, it is not this terrible thing described. The problem is specifically turning one's back to the shul while praying, as though rejecting its direction and its community.

### Elijah's Judgment

The Gemara illustrates with a story: *hahu gavra d'kamtzallei achorei bei knishta v'lo mahadar apei l'bei knishta* — there was a man praying behind the synagogue with his back to it. *chalif eliyahu* — Elijah passed by, or, according to another version of the text, a certain nomad passed by; in either reading, the figure appeared in the guise of a *taya*, an Arab traveler. He said to the man: *kadu bar kayyams k'mei marach* — is this how you stand before your Master? Everyone is inside praying; you stand out here with your back to the shul, your back to God as it were. *shalaf sapsira v'katlei* — he drew his sword and killed him. That is the entirety of the story, delivered without further comment.

### Prayer's High Status

The Gemara then asks: *mai k'rum zalus livnei adam?* — what is meant by the *krum* of the *zalut* of things before people? *amar lei: elu devarim she'omdim berumo shel olam u'vnei adam mezalzelim bahen* — these are things that stand at the very heights of the world, things of the utmost importance, and people treat them lightly. The specific example given is prayer: *kegon tefillah she'olah lemala* — prayer, which ascends on high.

This is a significant statement, particularly in the context of Berakhot. Throughout this daf there is an ongoing tension between tefillah and Talmud Torah. Here, in what may be the most direct acknowledgment of that tension in this passage, the Gemara acknowledges that some people treat prayer as secondary — finish davening quickly, whatever, and move on to more time with learning or with other activities. The Gemara insists: prayer stands at the heights of the world. It *olah lemala*. To treat it lightly — to pray hastily behind the synagogue with one's back turned — is to misunderstand profoundly what prayer is.

The word *krum* is explained through a subsequent teaching. *ki ata rav dimi amar: of echad yesh b'charkei hayam v'krum shemo* — there is a certain bird in the islands called *krum*, *v'keivan shechama zorachat mehapech l'chama gevanin* — when the sun shines upon it, it turns into many colors. When a person is in a state of *zalut*, of being lowly in the eyes of others, his face changes colors like this bird — shifting and exposed under scrutiny.

### Needing Help

*Rav Ami v'Rav Assi de'amri tarveihu: keivan shenitzrach adam labriyot, zalut lifnei adam* — when a person needs the assistance of other people, he becomes lowly in their eyes. And then *ke'ilu nidon bishnei dinim esh u'mayim* — it is as though he is judged by two judgments: fire and water. The proof text: *hirkavta enosh leroshenu banu va'esh uvamayim* — You have placed people over our heads; we have entered fire and water.

The image is one of compounded suffering. It is not enough that a person has come to a place of material need or dependence; on top of that, he must endure the social humiliation of turning to others for help. The diminishment is not only material but existential — the person's face changes colors, he is tried in two courts at once. This is offered as an interpretation of the same phrase *k'rum zalut livnei adam* with which the passage began, now read through the lens of human dependence rather than the specific case of prayer. The daf closes on this image of vulnerability and its double cost.

---

---

# Berakhot 7

## Mincha Prayer

### Rav Huna on Mincha

The daf begins, at the bottom of 6b, with a series of statements transmitted by Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav Huna. The first: *l'olam yehei adam zahir b'tefillat hamincha* — one should always be careful about the Mincha prayer. The proof is that Eliyahu was answered by God specifically at the time of Mincha.

### Elijah & Mincha

The verse adduced is *v'yehi ba'alot hamincha vayigash Eliyahu hanavi* — it was at the time of Mincha that Eliyahu the prophet came forth and said *aneni Hashem aneni*, "answer me God, answer me." The doubled language of "answer me" is explained as two separate requests: first, that fire should descend from heaven to demonstrate the acceptance of his sacrifice, and second — *shelo yomru ma'aseh kshafim hem* — that people should not dismiss the miracle as mere witchcraft. Even after a miracle, people find ways to discount what they have witnessed. In any case, Eliyahu was answered at the Mincha hour, which provides the proof text for the special importance of that prayer.

### Maariv Prayer

Rabbi Yochanan then extends the argument: not only Mincha, but Maariv as well deserves special emphasis. The verse cited is *tikon tefillati ketoret lefanecha mas'at kapai minchat arev* — let my prayer be established like incense before You, the lifting of my hands like the gift of evening. Here *minchah* carries the sense of a gift or offering, not the specific prayer time, and *arev* — evening — grounds the verse in the context of the Maariv prayer.

### Shacharit Prayer

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds Shacharit to the list: *hashem boker tishma koli boker e'erach lach va'atzapeh* — in the morning You will hear my voice, in the morning I will set my prayer before You and look toward You.

One can understand the Gemara's motivation here. Maariv has a somewhat second-class status — there is a debate whether it is *reshut* or *chova* — and people tend to be tired at night and may not bring to it the focus it deserves. Mincha, falling right in the middle of the day amid all its busyness, requires a particular act of will to stop and daven. One understands why the Gemara wants to underscore both. But by the time every tefillah has been given its supporting verse, the reader is left wondering what has actually been accomplished. If everything is equally important, it is not entirely clear that the original point about Mincha has been made.

---

## Simchat Chatan Kallah

### Wedding Feast Obligation

The Gemara continues with another statement of Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav Huna, now moving away from tefillah entirely: *kol hane'eneh misudat chatan v'eino mesamcho* — anyone who benefits from the wedding feast of the *chatan* and does not rejoice him transgresses *b'chamisha kolot*, the five voices. It is notable that the text focuses on the *chatan* alone. The verse cited is *kol sasson v'kol simcha kol chatan v'kol kalla kol omrim hodu Hashem Tzevaot* — the voices of joy, of gladness, of groom, of bride, and of those who praise God. These five voices represent what is meant to be created and sustained at a wedding feast. To attend and eat while merely serving one's own appetite — treating what ought to be a spiritual experience as an occasion for physical gratification — is to transgress all of them. The formulation is reminiscent of what Rav Yisrael Salanter expressed differently: *yenems gashmius is dayn ruchnius* — another person's physical needs are your spiritual needs. Here the inversion is instructive: one is taking something that should be a spiritual experience and reducing it to the merely physical.

### Five Voices Reward

The flip side: if one does rejoice the *chatan* and *kalla*, what is the reward? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says *zocheh l'Torah shenitna b'chamisha kolot* — one merits Torah, which was given in five voices. The verse from the Sinai narrative lists *kolot u'vrakim v'anan kaved al hahar v'kol shofar* and *v'yehi kol hashofar holech v'chazek m'od* — five distinct voices. The Gemara raises an objection: but the verse *v'chol ha'am ro'im et hakolot* implies six voices, not five. The answer is that those additional voices preceded *matan Torah*; at *matan Torah* itself there were only five. The deeper point is that the act of bringing joy to others at their wedding — what amounts to *gemilut chasadim* in its most communal expression — ultimately merits the highest form of speech, which is Torah.

### Todah Sacrifice

Rav Papa offers a different formulation of the reward: *ke'ilu hikriv todah* — it is as though one offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving. The verse is *mevi'im todah beit Hashem*, from the same passage in Yirmiyahu that contains the *kol sasson v'kol simcha*. The connection is significant: when one connects genuinely with another's joy rather than merely experiencing gratitude for one's own blessings, that communal sense is itself an expression of thanksgiving.

### Building Jerusalem

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says: *ke'ilu bana achat michurvot Yerushalayim* — it is as though one built one of the destroyed places of Jerusalem. The verse is *ki ashiv et shevut ha'aretz kevarishonah amar Hashem* — I will restore the land as it was at first. The significance here is transparent, particularly in light of the *nevuah* of Yirmiyahu that underlies one of the *sheva brachot*: the vision that only in messianic times would *kol chatan v'kol sasson v'kol simcha* again be heard in the *rechovot Yerushalayim*. By sustaining and creating that joy, one helps bring about the reality that Yirmiyahu could only envision for the future. This makes the experience of attending a wedding in Jerusalem today particularly charged, given that the *pesukim* in the *sheva brachot* originally expressed a hope that seemed realizable only at the end of days.

---

## Yirat Shamayim

### Yirat Shamayim Power

The Gemara continues with yet another statement of Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav Huna: *kol adam sheyesh bo yirat shamayim devarav nishma'im* — anyone who possesses fear of heaven, his words are heard. The verse is *sof davar hakol nishma et ha-Elokim yera* — the end of the matter, all is heard: fear God. The *pshat* of the verse is simply the concluding injunction to fear God; but the Gemara reads *hakol nishma* — "all is heard" — as conditioned on *et ha-Elokim yera*, meaning: it is when a person genuinely fears God that his words carry the weight of being heard. This is not only a metaphysical promise; experience attests that the humble, genuinely pious person commands a quality of attention that mere charisma does not always produce.

### Tzaddik & Creation

The verse continues: *ki zeh kol ha'adam* — for this is the whole of man. Rabbi Elazar interprets this in the name of the Holy One: *kol ha'olam kulo lo nivra ela bishvil zeh* — the entire world was created only for the sake of this person, the one who fears God. This is the *kol ha'adam* — the whole purpose of humanity. One reading is simply that this is the ideal all should strive toward. Another reading, which the subsequent statements seem to bear out, is that in order for one truly God-fearing person to exist in the world, an entire civilization is required to support and sustain that person — the clothing, the food, the infrastructure of human society all go into enabling this one individual.

### Tzaddik = World

Rabbi Abba bar Kahana offers a distinct formulation: *shakol zeh keneged kol ha'olam kulo* — this God-fearing person is equivalent in worth to the entire world.

### Others Accompany

Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai (and some attribute the statement to Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma) says: *kol ha'olam kulo lo nivra ela letzavot lazeh* — the entire rest of the world was created solely to accompany this person. One cannot live outside society; the *yarei Elokim* needs friends, community, and the full apparatus of human civilization. Everyone else exists to make that possible. These are statements of remarkable hierarchical force — while they celebrate the achievement of *yirat Elokim* as the highest human attainment and the purpose of creation, they assign the rest of humanity an essentially supporting role. It is worth noting that Rambam, in *moreh nevuchim* or perhaps in his *peirush haMishnah*, uses precisely this framework but applies it to the philosopher — arguing that the philosophers who achieve genuine intellectual knowledge of God are the ones for whose sake civilization exists, and everyone else exists to make the philosophers possible.

---

## Greeting Shalom

### Initiate Shalom

Another statement of Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav Huna: *kol she-yodea be-chavero she-hu ragil litein lo shalom yaktim lo shalom* — if one knows that a friend is in the habit of greeting him, one should take the initiative and greet first. Do not wait for the other person to express enthusiasm. The verse: *bakeshu shalom v'radfeihu* — seek peace and pursue it. The point is that creating a sense of connection goes in both directions, and it is important that the greeting not be a one-way street.

### Theft of Shalom

If one greeted another and received no response, *nikra gazlan* — he is called a thief. The verse: *ve-atem bi'artem ha-kerem gezelat he-ani be-vateichem* — you have destroyed the vineyard; the theft from the poor is in your houses. What has been stolen from the poor person is not money but the *shalom aleichem* itself — the acknowledgment of his presence, the sense of being seen and welcomed. That is all he needed, and it was withheld. This is a pointed teaching, and its practical application in daily life — on *shabbos*, on the street, in a community where one encounters strangers — is difficult to miss.

---

## God's Prayer

### God Davens

The Gemara now moves to 7a with a statement of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosi: *minayin she-HaKadosh Baruch Hu mitpallel* — how do we know that God prays? The verse: *va-haviotim el har kodshi ve-simachtim be-veit tefillati* — I will bring them to my holy mountain and make them rejoice in my house of prayer. The Gemara notes that the verse says *tefillati* — my prayer — not *tefillatan*, their prayer. This implies not merely the house where prayer is received, but where prayer is offered.
