The Gemara asks: *mai ki meis atah ve'lo tichyeh* — why both "you will die" and "you will not live"? *meis atah ba'olam ha'zeh, ve'lo tichyeh la'olam ha'ba* — you will die in this world, and you will not live in the World to Come. This is a devastating prophecy to deliver to Chizkiyahu, who was one of the few truly righteous kings in generations.

### Procreation

*Amar lei: mai kulei hai* — Chizkiyahu asked, what is all this about? Yeshayahu's reply: *mishum de'lo asakt be'piryah ve'rivyah* — because you have not engaged in procreation. We know from the narrative that Menashe, Chizkiyahu's son, was a wicked king who was twelve years old when Chizkiyahu died. And since Chizkiyahu received fifteen additional years of life after this encounter, it is clear that Menashe was born during those fifteen years — making him Chizkiyahu's only heir, born after this very episode. The charge was therefore that Chizkiyahu had not fulfilled the mitzvah of *pru u'revu*.

### Wicked Children

Chizkiyahu explains: *mishum de'chazai li be'ruach ha'kodesh de'nafki minai banin de'lo ma'alu* — because I saw through divine spirit that I would have children who are unworthy, who would be sinners. He had deliberately refrained from procreating because he foresaw, through ruach ha'kodesh, that his offspring would be wicked.

## Kishei D'Rachmana

### Don't Worry

Yeshayahu's response is one of the most cited statements in this section of the Gemara: *be'hadai kavshei de'Rachmana lamah lach* — these hidden things of God, why are they your concern?

### Your Obligation

*Mai de'mifkadat ibaya lach le'me'evad* — what you are commanded, that is what you must do. *u'mai de'nicha kamei kudsha brich hu le'eved le'eved* — what God wants, God will do. You do your mitzvot; let God worry about God's calculations. You should have children and not concern yourself with what you foresee through ruach ha'kodesh about their character. The statement also implicitly raises questions about bechirah chofshit — and indeed the entire exchange will continue to probe the tension between divine foreknowledge and human freedom.

### Marry Daughter

Chizkiyahu accepts the argument — at least enough to call Yeshayahu on it. *hashta hav li bartach* — then give me your daughter as a wife. *efshar de'garma zechusach didi ve'didach ve'nafki minai banin de'ma'alu* — perhaps the combined merit of both of us will result in righteous children. Having been told to act on faith rather than foresight, Chizkiyahu puts the challenge back to Yeshayahu: if you believe that, put your money where your mouth is.

### Decree Made

Yeshayahu refuses: *kevar nigzar alecha gezeirah* — the decree has already been issued. As the discussion makes clear, this does not mean Chizkiyahu will necessarily have wicked children — the later Gemara does not bear that out. Rather, Yeshayahu is saying that the edict of death has been sealed: there is no time. The decree has been made and cannot be reversed, and even if Chizkiyahu were to marry now, he would not live long enough to have children.

### Rebuke

Chizkiyahu's response is sharp. He shifts his address — no longer *yeshayahu ha'navi*, but simply *ben amotz* — cutting him down to size, as when the people in the desert referred to Moshe as *ben amram* in frustration. *kalei nevuatcha ve'tzei* — finish your prophecy and get out. *kach mekublani mi'beit avi aba* — this is the tradition I have received from my grandfather's house, from David: *afilu cherev hada munachat al tzavaro shel adam al yimna atzmo min ha'rachamim* — even if a sharp sword is laid at a person's throat, he should not withhold himself from divine compassion, from prayer. Rashi notes that *avi aba* refers to David, who, at the end of Sefer Shmuel, saw the angel with sword drawn and prayed to God — and did not die. The door is never fully closed.

### David's Tradition

Chizkiyahu thus refuses to accept finality. Even the sword at the throat does not foreclose prayer. This is the tradition from David, and Chizkiyahu invokes it against Yeshayahu's own certainty. The Gemara then cites an additional corroboration: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both say *afilu cherev hada munachat al tzavaro shel adam al yimna atzmo min ha'rachamim*, citing the verse *hen yiktleni lo ayachel* — though He slay me, yet will I hope in Him.

## Prayer Sources

### Dreams

Rabbi Chanan adds a further extension: *afilu ba'al ha'chalomot omer lo le'adam: le'machar hu meit, al yimna atzmo min ha'rachamim* — even if a dream-vision comes to a person and declares that he will die tomorrow, he should not withhold himself from divine compassion, from prayer. The reason: *ki be'rov chalomot va'havalim u'devarim harbeh ki et ha'Elohim yera* — for in the abundance of dreams there is much vanity and many words, but you should fear God, who can always change the outcome.

### Turn to Wall

*Va'yisav Chizkiyahu panav el ha'kir va'yitpalel el Hashem* — Chizkiyahu turned his face to the wall and prayed to God. And God granted him fifteen more years of life, vindicating his faith that the edict could be reversed. It is worth noting, as the Gemara implicitly acknowledges, that the issue of the children was not fully resolved — Menashe was indeed born and was indeed wicked. Yeshayahu, who had said *nigzera gezeirah* and refused to give his daughter, was in some sense the more accurate prophet. Had Yeshayahu agreed to the marriage, one wonders whether the combined merit might have changed the outcome for Menashe as well. As *dov* observed in the course of discussion, God's ultimate plan — if Menashe's birth was part of it — came to pass regardless, through the very act of Chizkiyahu's praying for his life. There is a certain irony in that: Chizkiyahu had initially tried to prevent the wicked children by not procreating, then prayed to live and procreated, and the very child he feared was born. *be'hadei kavshei de'rachmana lamah lach.* At the same time, it is also true that Menashe eventually did teshuvah — his story is not simply one of wickedness.

### Walls Heart

*Amar Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: mikirot libo* — from the walls of the chambers of his heart. The phrase *el ha'kir* — to the wall — is read as an expression of the profundity and sincerity of the prayer: *me'ai me'ai ochilah kirot libi* — my inwards yearn; from the very walls of my heart.

### Shunammite

Levi offers a different reading: Chizkiyahu's turning to the wall was a prayer *al iskei ha'kir* — regarding the wall, the chamber. He argued before God: the Shunammite made only one small wall-chamber for Elisha, and yet God brought her son back to life. My grandfather David — *avi aba*, referring to David or Shlomo — covered the entire Heichal with silver and gold. *al achat kama ve'kama* — how much more do I deserve to live.

## Geulah L'Tefillah

### Prayer Cites

The prayer itself continues: *zechor na et asher hithalachti lefanecha be'emet u've'lev shalem va'tov be'einecha asiti* — remember how I have walked before You in truth and with a whole heart, and I have done what is good in Your eyes. This is quoted from Sefer Yeshayahu, which records Chizkiyahu's prayer.

### Semichas

*Amar Yehuda amar Rav: she'samach geulah li'tefillah* — Yehuda says in the name of Rav: what Chizkiyahu is claiming as his merit for the prayer being answered is that he performed *semichas geulah la'tefillah* — he connected the blessing of redemption to the Shemoneh Esrei, saying *ga'al Yisrael* directly before beginning his prayer.

### Merit

This is a significant statement, and it is what the Gemara has been building toward since the beginning of the *semichas geulah la'tefillah* discussion. The Maharsha makes an additional observation: the *semichas geulah la'tefillah* here is not merely the liturgical practice of following *ga'al Yisrael* with *shemoneh esrei* each morning. It was Chizkiyahu's life itself — the story of the destruction of Sancheriv's army, which immediately precedes this narrative, was Chizkiyahu's *geulah*, and it was followed by this moment of prayer. His claim to God is that he responded to the redemption he experienced with tefillah.

This reflection opens a broader meditation. There is a famous tradition that Chizkiyahu could have been the Mashiach had he said *shirah* when the *geulah* of Sancheriv occurred — when he experienced direct divine salvation, he did not respond with song. And yet here, when affliction threatens him, he prays. The two poles of prayer — the *mimamakim* anguish-prayer of someone facing death, and the *shevach* and *hallel* of someone who has just experienced salvation — appear in close proximity in this narrative. The tragedy, if one can call it that, is that it is often only at the moment of *meis atah ve'lo tichyeh* that we turn to God in earnest, while the moments of actual salvation pass without the full response they deserve. And yet the Gemara's teaching is that even the *semichas geulah la'tefillah* of ordinary daily prayer carries enormous merit — merit sufficient, in the case of Chizkiyahu, to have his prayer answered at the moment of his greatest need.

Rabbi Levi offers a second answer to the question of what Chizkiyahu prayed on the basis of: *she'ganaz sefer refuot* — because he hid the Book of Healings.

## Six Reforms

### Intro Six

*Tanu rabbanan: shisha devarim asah Chizkiyahu ha'melech; al gimmel hodu lo, ve'al gimmel lo hodu lo* — our Rabbis taught: Chizkiyahu the king did six things; for three the Sages agreed with him, and for three they did not agree with him. This is an elaboration of a Mishnah in Pesachim.

### Book Healing

*Ganaz sefer refuot, ve'hodu lo* — he hid the Book of Healings, and they agreed with him.

### Copper Snake

*Kitat nahash ha'nechoshet, ve'hodu lo* — he ground up the copper snake that Moshe had made. On one hand, the *nahash ha'nechoshet* was a memory of Moshe's act in the desert; on the other, it had come to be used as a talisman, treated almost as an idol. *ve'hodu lo* — good idea, agreed the Sages; of course it had to go.

### Father Bones

*Girer atzmot aviv al mittah shel chavalim, ve'hodu lo* — he dragged his father's bones on a bed of ropes. His father Achaz was a wicked king. Rather than honoring him at burial in a manner that might lead people to honor or learn from his example, Chizkiyahu used this method of dishonoring his remains. Rashi suggests this served as a form of atonement for the father. The Sages agreed that this consideration trumps *kibbud av va'em*.

### Waters Sealed

*Satam mei Gihon, ve'lo hodu lo* — he sealed the waters of Gihon, and they did not agree with him. This was done when Sancheriv's troops were approaching, so that they would find no water outside Yerushalayim. Yet the Sages did not endorse this action — perhaps because he should have relied on God, or perhaps because of which waters he sealed.

### Temple Doors

*Kitzetz daltot ha'Heichal ve'shigram le'melech Ashur, ve'lo hodu lo* — he cut the doors of the Heichal and sent them to the king of Assyria as a bribe. The Sages were not pleased: do not go bribing the king of Assyria, and certainly do not use the doors of the Heichal as the payment.

### Extra Month

*Iber Nissan be'Nissan, ve'lo hodu lo* — he intercalated an extra Nissan while Nissan had already begun, and they did not agree with him. One can make an extra Adar, but this must be done before Rosh Chodesh Nissan. Once Rosh Chodesh Nissan has arrived, no further intercalation is possible. *zeh nissan ve'ein acher nissan* — this is Nissan and there is no other Nissan; you cannot create a second Nissan. The Gemara explains his error: *ta'ah bi'Shmuel* — he erred based on a teaching of Shmuel. Shmuel teaches that one cannot intercalate the year on the thirtieth of Adar, because the thirtieth of Adar could potentially be declared Rosh Chodesh Nissan. Chizkiyahu reasoned that since it had not yet been formally declared Rosh Chodesh Nissan, intercalation was still permissible. That was his mistake.

## Sefer Refuot

### Don't Pray

The traditional explanation for hiding the *sefer refuot* is that it was a book of medical cures, and — similar to the *nachash nechoshet* — Chizkiyahu was troubled that people were consulting it rather than praying to God when they became ill. When you have a comprehensive book of cures, people use the book; they don't turn to God. This parallels the concern about the copper snake: in both cases, an instrumentality that ought to point toward God becomes a substitute for God.

One might object: are we really not supposed to use good medical advice? Are we supposed to pray instead of treating illness? The Gemara elsewhere draws the drasha from *ve'rapo yerape* — "he shall surely heal" — that *natan reshut le'rofe lerapo't*, the Torah has given the doctor permission to heal. Why does the Torah need to grant such permission? One explanation is that a person might reason: if God made someone ill, let God make them better. No — the Torah teaches that the doctor has not only permission but obligation to practice medicine.

### Rambam

Given this, the Rambam, who was himself a physician, takes strong issue with the explanation that Chizkiyahu hid the *sefer refuot* because it made healing too easy and people stopped praying. In his *peirush haMishnayot*, the Rambam argues forcefully that this reading of the story is incoherent: medical knowledge is itself a gift from God, and God's role as *rofe cholim* is expressed precisely through human beings who develop and apply the art of healing. To suggest that using medical knowledge is somehow a failure of faith is, in the Rambam's view, a distortion.

### Magic Not

The Rambam therefore reinterprets the nature of the *sefer refuot*: it was not a book of genuine medicine at all, but a book of astrological or magical healing methods — fraudulent cures that misled people, more analogous to the *nachash nechoshet* than to a medical textbook. That is what was hidden and why the Sages agreed. It is worth noting, however, that in the context of this narrative — Chizkiyahu's own illness and his prayer to God for healing — the traditional explanation has a certain literary coherence: Chizkiyahu's claim to God is precisely that he directed people toward prayer when they were ill, and now he himself is doing exactly that.

## Merit Others

### Self Merit

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra: kol ha'toleh bi'zchut atzmo, tolin lo bi'zchut acher* — whoever attributes merit to himself — saying "do it for my sake" — in the end, if something is done for him, it is attributed to someone else's merit.

### Others Merit

*Ve'chol ha'toleh bi'zchut acher, tolin lo bi'zchut atzmo* — and whoever attributes merit to others, saying "do it for their sake," in the end it is attributed to him.

### Moses

*Moshe talah bi'zchut acher* — Moshe appealed on behalf of others: *zechor le'Avraham le'Yitzchak u'le'Yisrael avadecha* — remember Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yisrael Your servants; spare the Jewish people for their merit. Yet in the end, the verse attributes the salvation to Moshe: *va'yomer le'hashmidan lulei Moshe bechiro amad ba'peretz* — God would have destroyed them were it not that Moshe His chosen stood in the breach.

### Chizkiyahu

*Chizkiyahu talah bi'zchut atzmo* — Chizkiyahu appealed on the basis of his own merit: *zechor na et asher hithalachti lefanecha* — remember how I have walked before You. Yet when God responded, the salvation was attributed not to Chizkiyahu but to David: *ve'ganoti el ha'ir ha'zot le'hoshi'ah le'ma'ani u'le'ma'an David avdi* — I have protected this city to save it, for My sake and for the sake of David My servant. Not for Chizkiyahu.

### Bitter Peace

*Ve'haynu de'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: de'amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: mai dechtiv: hineh le'shalom mar li mar* — behold, for peace it is very bitter. *afilu be'sha'ah she'shigra lo haKadosh baruch hu shalom, mar hu lo* — even when God sent him peace, it was bitter, because God stated that it was being done for David, not for him.

## Shunammite

### Small Chamber

*Na'aseh na aliyat kir ketanah* — let us make for him a small wall chamber. The Gemara now takes up the story of the Shunammite and her room for Elisha, having already mentioned her in the context of Chizkiyahu's prayer.

### Roof Dispute

Rav and Shmuel dispute the nature of the chamber. One holds that it was an exposed upper story — *aliyah peru'ah haytah* — an attic that had not yet been roofed, and *ve'kiruha* — they roofed it. On this view, *kir* here means a ceiling, not a wall. The other holds it was a large portico — *achsadra gedolah haytah* — and *ve'chilkuha lishnayim* — they divided it in two with a wall, so *kir* means an actual wall. Each view has a difficulty: according to the one who says it was a portico, why does the verse say *kir* — a wall was the modification? Understood — the wall was the construction. But according to the one who says it was an attic, *mai kir*? The answer: *she'kiruha* — they roofed it, meaning the word *kir* reflects the act of enclosing. And the alternative difficulty: according to the view of a second story, that is why the verse calls it *aliyah*. But according to the view of a large room, what does *aliyah* mean? *me'ulah she'be'vatim* — the finest and most excellent of rooms.

### Four Items

*Ve'nasim lo sham mittah ve'shulchan ve'chise u'menorah* — let us place for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp. *amar abaye ve'itayma rabbi yitzchak: ha'rotzeh lihanot, yehaneh ke'elisha* — whoever wishes to benefit from the hospitality of others should follow Elisha's model. When someone provides you with a bed, a table, a chair — that is the appropriate degree of benefit to accept.

### Models

*U'she'eino rotzeh lihanot, al yehaneh ke'Shmuel ha'Ramati* — and one who does not wish to benefit from others' hospitality at all should follow the standard of Shmuel, as it is said: *u'teshuvato ha'Ramatah ki sham beito* — his return was always to Ramatah, for that was his house. Rabbi Yochanan explains: *she'kol makom she'halach sham beito imo* — wherever Shmuel went, his house was with him. He carried his own bed and his own necessities; he did not avail himself of anyone's hospitality. But if one does wish to benefit from hospitality, the model of Elisha — basic necessities, not excess — is the appropriate standard.

## Holiness

### Recognize

*Va'tomer el ishah: hineh na yadati ki ish Elokim kadosh hu* — she said to her husband: behold, I know that he is a holy man of God.

### Women Know

*Amar Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: mikan she'ha'ishah makeret be'orchim yoter min ha'ish* — from here we see that a woman perceives her guests more acutely than a man does. This parallels the story of Manoach and his wife, where the wife understood the nature of the divine messenger more clearly than her husband did.

### Signs Holiness

*Mina yad'ah* — how did she know? Rav and Shmuel disagree. One says: *shelo ra'atah zevuv over al shulchano* — she never saw a fly pass over his table. The other says: *sadin shel pishtan hitzi'ah al mitato, ve'lo ra'atah keri alav* — she put a linen sheet on his bed, and when she laundered it, there was never any nocturnal emission on it — a sign of his wholly pure thoughts. One version of his holiness is metaphysical — an almost numinous quality in which even flies do not approach. The other is quite concrete: his mastery of his own thoughts and impulses.

### Servant Not

*Amar Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: hu kadosh, u'mesharto eino kadosh* — he is holy, but his servant, Geichazi, is not. Geichazi, as the Gemara elsewhere records, accepted bribes and was ultimately stricken with leprosy.

### Pushed Away

*Va'yigash Geichazi le'hadpah* — Geichazi stepped forward to push the woman away when she came to report her son's death. *amar rabbi yosei bar chanina: she'achaz be'hod yafyah* — he grabbed her by the glory of her beauty, which Rashi explains as a reference to her breasts, deriving this from the word *le'hadpah*. The contrast between Elisha's holiness and Geichazi's conduct is thus made vivid.

## Hosting Reward

### Host Scholar

*Amar Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina mishum Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: kol ha'mareach talmid chacham be'toch beito u'me'hanehu mi'nechasav* — anyone who hosts a Torah scholar in his home and allows him to benefit from his property. Note the shift here from the story's protagonist — a *navi* — to the more practically applicable figure of a *talmid chacham*, making the teaching relevant beyond the prophetic era.

### Like Sacrifice

*Ma'aleh alav ha'katuv ke'ilu makriv tamid* — Scripture considers it as though he brought the *tamid* offering, the daily sacrifice. The exact nature of the analogy is not spelled out, but the comparison to the *tamid* — the regular, ongoing sacrifice — suggests that hosting a scholar is not a one-time meritorious act but something with a sustained, daily quality of sanctity.

### Standing

The Gemara then transitions to practical halacha of tefillah: *al ya'amod adam be'makom gavoah ve'yitpalel, ela be'makom namuch* — a person should not stand in a high place and pray, but rather in a low place. Here the aggadic material ends and we move into the halachic teachings of tefillah, which we will take up in the next session.

---

---

# Berakhot 11

## Positioning in Prayer

### High Place Prohibition

We pick up at the bottom of 10b with a series of statements transmitted in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov. The first: *v'amar rav yosef b'rebbi chanina mishum rabbi elazar ben yaakov — al yaamod adam b'makom gavoah v'yitpalel ela b'makom namuch v'yitpalel.* One should not stand on a high place and pray, but rather on a low place. The Scriptural basis is *mimaamakim kraticha Hashem* — "I have called to You from the depths" — which evokes not only the principle of humility but also the experience of Chizkiyahu's prayer. A *tanya nami hachi* reinforces this: one must not stand on a chair, a platform, or any elevated place to pray, because *she'ein gaphut lifnei hamakom* — there is no haughtiness before God. The verse *tfila l'ani ki yaatof*, a prayer of the poor person when he collapses or faints, further underscores the posture of destitution appropriate to prayer.

This principle is implicitly embedded in the language of the Mishnah and Gemara itself. When discussing being called to the Torah, the text uses the language of *oleh l'Torah* — going up — and *aliyah*. When describing leading the davening, it speaks of *yoreid lifnei hateivah* — going down before the bimah. In certain Sefardi shuls, this was given architectural expression through a lowered platform in the center of the floor from which tefillah was conducted, while the Torah was read from an elevated bimah — perhaps because the Torah comes from on high, proclaimed downward to the congregation, while the human being speaks upward from a position of lowliness and awe.

### Torah vs. Prayer Position

The contrast between the elevated bimah for kriat haTorah and the lowered position for tefillah reflects a genuine theological distinction. Torah reading is associated with *aliyah*, with ascent, with God's word being proclaimed from on high. Tefillah, by contrast, is the human voice reaching upward from below. The phrase *she'ein gaphut lifnei hamakom* captures this precisely: drawing close to God in prayer is an extraordinary intimacy, and the very act of prayer demands that we not allow that closeness to inflate our sense of our own importance. The question of why contemporary practice does not enforce the requirement to pray from a low position is a separate discussion, but the Gemara's own position on the matter is unambiguous.

### Humility & Aspiration

The same tradition then continues with a further requirement: *hamitpalel tzarich she'yichavein et raglav* — one who prays must direct his feet, holding them straight, as derived from *v'ragleihem regel yeshara* — the legs of the angels were straight. Here a notable tension presents itself. Having just insisted on the lowliness and humility appropriate to prayer, the Gemara now invokes the angels as a model for how to comport oneself. This is not necessarily a contradiction. Much of our davening is consciously patterned after angelic worship — we recite *kadosh kadosh kadosh* in imitation of the Seraphim, and we aspire to pray as the angels pray. The aspiration toward angelic form and the cultivation of human humility are two simultaneous orientations in tefillah, each true in its own register, and the tension between them is part of what gives prayer its texture.

---

## Eating & Prayer Order

### Eating Before Prayer

The same chain of tradition continues: *lo tochlu al hadam* — "do not eat over the blood" — is interpreted to mean *lo tochlu kodem she-titpalelu al damchem*: do not eat before you pray for your very soul, for your very blood. The prohibition against eating before davening is rooted in this verse. A further statement is then transmitted: *kol ha-ochel ve-shoteh ve-acher kach mitpallel* — whoever eats and drinks and only then prays — *alav ha-katuv omer: ve-oti hishlachta acharei gavecha* — of such a person Scripture says, "You have cast Me behind your back." The Gemara then applies a *al tikri* reading: do not read *gavecha* — your back — but *ge'echa* — your haughtiness. God says: after this person has attended to his own needs and his own haughtiness, only then does he accept the yoke of Heaven?

### Priorities & Divine Acce…

This is a profound statement about the ordering of priorities. Two dimensions are at stake. The first is how one frames the day: does the day begin with tefillah and *ol malchut shamayim*, with the acknowledgment that everything comes from God, or does it begin with attending to one's own body and needs? The second dimension concerns the very nature of the tefillah itself. When a person eats first, satisfies his own needs, and feels fully embodied and self-sufficient, there is a natural swelling of ego that accompanies that experience. Prayer that follows from such a state is qualitatively different — it reflects a posture of *ve-oti hishlachta acharei gavecha*, of having already positioned oneself and one's body as primary. The real point is that one's total dependence on God must be fully acknowledged before one begins to attend to one's own needs. This is *halacha*, with its own parameters regarding what kinds of eating and drinking may be permitted before davening in cases of necessity — but the underlying principle is clear.

---

## Shema Times Ruling

### Three Hour Limit

The Gemara returns to the times of kriat Shema. Rabbi Yehoshua says you may recite Shema until three hours into the day. And the Gemara declares: *amar rav yehuda amar shmuel halacha ke-rabbi yehoshua* — the halacha follows Rabbi Yehoshua. The rationale offered earlier in the masechet was that kings sleep until three hours into the day, and reading Shema within that window still qualifies as the time when people are typically arising.

### Gra vs. Magen Avraham

This ruling generates one of the most practically significant machloket in the laws of Shema. The Gra holds that *sha'ot zmaniyot* — seasonal hours — are calculated from sunrise to sunset, and that the three-hour limit is therefore measured from sunrise. The Magen Avraham holds that seasonal hours are calculated from *alot hashachar* to *tzeit*, a longer span, and that the three hours begin from *alot hashachar*. Although the Magen Avraham's seasonal hours are individually longer, beginning the count 72 minutes earlier means that his *sof zman kriat Shema* typically falls a good half hour or more before that of the Gra. In practice, the assumption is that *sof zman kriat Shema* follows the Gra — the most lenient reading — and this is compounded by the further question raised earlier in the masechet of whether three hours means the beginning of the third hour or the end. We rule leniently that it is the end of three hours from sunrise.

### Night/Day Asymmetry

A conceptual asymmetry warrants attention. For the nighttime Shema, the halacha is that it may be recited throughout the entire night — meaning we interpret *beshochbecha* as referring to the time when people are asleep, not the time when they go to sleep. For the daytime Shema, however, none of the Tannaitic opinions permits recitation throughout the entire day. Even the most lenient view — three hours, because kings sleep until then — treats the relevant period as only the time of arising, not all of waking hours. So the nighttime reading focuses on the period of sleeping, while the daytime reading focuses on the time of waking. The *kesef mishneh* suggests in one place that perhaps *de'oraisa* the Shema could be said all day long, and that the three-hour limit is only rabbinic, intended to maintain some symmetry — but the asymmetry in how the verse is read remains noteworthy.

### Late Shema Reading

*Hakorei mikan ve'eilach lo hifsid* — one who reads Shema after the three-hour mark has not lost entirely; it is as if one has read from the Torah. But Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva adds: *uvilvad shelo yomar Yotzer Or* — provided one does not recite Yotzer Or. Since Yotzer Or is a bracha of Shema, if one is no longer fulfilling the mitzvah of Shema, one cannot recite it.

### Dual Status Brachot

This position is challenged by a *braisa*: *hakorei mikan ve'eilach lo hifsid ke'adam shekorei baTorah umevorech hu shtayim lefaneha ve'achas leachareha* — one who reads after the time still recites the brachot before and after. This is a *tiyuvta* of Rav Chisda's first position. The resolution emerges from the dual status of these brachot: they are simultaneously brachot of kriat Shema *and* brachot of Shacharit. Yotzer Or functions as a bracha of the morning service — about God creating light and darkness — even independent of the mitzvah of Shema. Therefore one can and does recite it even after the time of Shema has passed. This is how we rule. An alternative version of Rav Chisda's statement already reflects this conclusion, and the *tanya nami hachi* confirms it.

### Shema vs. Torah Study

Rav Mani then draws a striking inference: *gadol hakorei Krias Shema be'onasa yoseir meha'oseik baTorah* — one who recites Shema in its proper time is of greater value than one engaged in Torah study. The logical basis is simple: the Gemara itself says that reciting Shema after the time is equivalent to reading Torah. If the lesser state is equivalent to Torah study, then the greater state — reading Shema in its proper time — must exceed it. And this is indeed reflected in halacha: one interrupts Torah study in order to recite Shema. The *mitzvah* of Shema in its time, even when it lacks the intellectual engagement of Torah study, takes precedence.

---

## Shammai vs. Hillel

### Shammai Literal Read

The next Mishnah introduces a new dimension: not just *when* to recite Shema but *how* to physically position oneself during its recitation. Beit Shammai holds: *ba'erev kol adam yatei veyikra uvaboker ya'amod* — in the evening every person must recline and read, and in the morning one must stand. The derivation is from *beshochbecha uvekumecha* — when you lie down and when you rise up — read literally as a prescription for physical posture.

### Hillel Time Emphasis

Beit Hillel disagrees: *kol adam korei k'darko* — every person reads however he happens to be situated. The basis is *u'v'lechtecha vaderech* — and when you go on the way — which demonstrates that Shema may be recited even while walking, i.e., in whatever position or circumstance one finds oneself. When the Torah says *beshochbecha uvekumecha*, Beit Hillel understands this as a reference to time: *b'sha'ah she'bnei adam shochvim u'v'sha'ah she'bnei adam omdim* — the time when people are lying down and the time when people are rising. It specifies *when* to say Shema, not *how* to be positioned.

### Gemara Analysis

The Gemara clarifies both positions. Beit Hillel's reasoning is internally consistent: *beshochbecha uvekumecha* denotes time, and *u'v'lechtecha vaderech* confirms that physical position is irrelevant. But why is Beit Shammai not persuaded by *u'v'lechtecha vaderech*? Beit Shammai responds: if the Torah only meant to indicate *time*, it could have simply said "in the morning and in the evening." The fact that it says *beshochbecha uvekumecha* — when you lie down and when you rise up — implies *shchiva mamash* and *kima mamash* — actual reclining and actual standing. The use of this formulation rather than the simpler alternative is what drives the literal reading.

Furthermore, the observation that the Torah *could* have said "morning and evening" has an additional implication: Beit Shammai apparently treats *beshochbecha uvekumecha* and "morning and evening" as referring to the same time period. The emphasis of *beshochbecha uvekumecha*, then, is not to convey a different time but to convey the required posture. Beit Shammai then also derives from *u'v'lechtecha vaderech* the principle of *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah* — but that belongs to the following discussion.

---

## Osek B'Mitzvah

### Derivation from Uvlechet…

Since Beit Hillel uses *u'v'lechtecha vaderech* to establish that physical position does not matter, Beit Shammai must derive something else from it. The Gemara identifies what: *b'shivtecha b'veitecha — prat l'osek b'mitzvah* — "when you dwell in your house" excludes one who is occupied with a mitzvah. *u'v'lechtecha vaderech — prat l'chatan* — "when you walk on the way" excludes a groom on his wedding night, who is mentally preoccupied with the mitzvah that is about to be performed, and is therefore considered an *osek b'mitzvah* and exempt from reciting Shema.

The Gemara asks: what exactly is the logic of deriving the exemption from *u'v'lechtecha vaderech*? Rav Pappa explains: *ma derech reshut — af kol reshut* — just as going on a journey is an optional, non-obligatory activity, so too the obligation to recite Shema applies when one is engaged in optional activities. If one is occupied with a mitzvah, the Torah's obligation of Shema does not apply. The Gemara then presses: perhaps someone walking on the way is *also* going to perform a mitzvah — why should *derech* imply *reshut*? The answer: if the Torah had simply wanted to say "sitting and walking," it would have written *b'sheves u'v'leches*. The elaboration *b'shivtecha b'veitecha u'v'lechtecha vaderech* — *your* sitting and *your* walking, when you are engaged in your own affairs — is what limits the obligation. When you are doing your own things and the time for a mitzvah arrives, you stop and do the mitzvah. But when what you are doing *is* the mitzvah — when it is God's business rather than your own — you are exempt. This is the source for the broad principle of *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah*.

### Groom Preoccupation

From the derivation, the Gemara draws the practical ruling: *hachones et habetulah patur, v'et ha'almanah chayav* — a man who marries a virgin is exempt from Shema on his wedding night, while one who marries a widow is still obligated. The groom marrying a virgin is anxious — the wedding night carries a degree of preoccupation rooted both in the nature of the mitzvah and, as the beginning of Ketubot notes, in the concern about whether his bride will prove to be a betulah. The groom marrying a widow faces no such preoccupation.

The Gemara asks: *ihai*, if the principle is that being engaged in a mitzvah exempts, why should a groom marrying a widow be different? He is performing a mitzvah as well. The answer: *hai tarid, v'hai lo tarid* — one is mentally preoccupied and the other is not. This distinction then generates a deeper question about the nature of *osek b'mitzvah*.

### Avel's Obligation

If mere preoccupation were sufficient to exempt one from Shema, then perhaps anyone in a state of profound distraction — someone whose ship has just sunk, or who has suffered some major crisis — should also be exempt. The Gemara considers this possibility and rejects it by pointing to the ruling of Rabbi Abba bar Zavda in the name of Rav: an *avel* — a mourner — is obligated in all the mitzvot of the Torah except for tefillin on the first day of mourning, since tefillin are called *pe'er* — glory — and an avel is not in a state of glory, as derived from the verse addressed to Yechezkel, *pe'ercha chavosh alecha*, implying that the rest of the people were directed not to wear their tefillin while mourning. But for all other mitzvot, including the recitation of Shema, an avel is *chayav*. The fact that a mourner is deeply distressed and preoccupied by his loss does not exempt him from Shema. Mere distraction is therefore not the operative factor.

### Mental Engagement

The Gemara resolves the question with a precise formulation: *chatan tarid tirda d'mitzvah — hacha tarid tirda d'reshut*. The groom is preoccupied with a preoccupation that is itself a mitzvah; the avel and the shipwrecked man are preoccupied with matters of *reshut* — personal concerns, not mitzvah activity. What defines *osek b'mitzvah* is not distraction as such, but mental engagement with an imminent or ongoing mitzvah act. The mind of the groom is genuinely caught up in the mitzvah — even if the motivation has a personal dimension — and that mental preoccupation in the context of a mitzvah constitutes *osek*. The avel, despite sitting shiva — which is itself a mitzvah in some sense — is not mentally preoccupied with a specific mitzvah *act* about to be performed, and his distress therefore does not constitute *osek b'mitzvah*.

A line appears in some versions of the text that *u'v'lechtecha vaderech* also exempts *shluchei mitzvah* — those who are on their way to perform a mitzvah — which is conceptually similar to the chatan case, since one need not be in the midst of the mitzvah act itself but be actively on the path toward it. Rashi apparently did not have this line, and it is textually difficult; the core point, however, is now established.

Beit Hillel, for their part, derives *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah* differently. They read *u'v'lechtecha vaderech* at face value — you recite Shema when you are walking on the road, in whatever position. This *pshat* itself implies that physical circumstance is no barrier to the obligation, and from within this reading they simultaneously extract the exemption for one occupied with a mitzvah, without abandoning the plain meaning of the verse.

---

## Shammai/Hillel Stories

### Two Scholars Tale

Having established the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, the Gemara presents a *baraita* that lays out Beit Hillel's position in full: one may stand and recite Shema, sit and recite it, recline and recite it, walk on the road and recite it, or do so while engaged in one's work — all deriving from *u'v'lechtecha vaderech*. A story then follows.

Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah were reclining at a meal. Rabbi Yishmael was reclining and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah was sitting upright. When the time for the evening Shema arrived, Rabbi Elazar reclined and Rabbi Yishmael sat upright. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah said to Rabbi Yishmael: *yishmael achi* — my brother Yishmael — let me offer you a comparison. It is like someone whose friends admire his beautiful beard, and he responds by saying he will go to the barber and cut it off. So too here: as long as I was sitting upright, you were reclining — you were doing the right thing, since you happened to be in the proper position for the nighttime Shema according to Beit Shammai. Now that I reclined in order to be properly positioned, you sat up?

Rabbi Yishmael explained: I was reclining before because I was eating my meal — that was Beit Hillel, who permits any position. When the time for Shema came, I sat up — also Beit Hillel, since I was not deliberately reclining for Shema. You, however, deliberately reclined at the moment of Shema, acting like Beit Shammai. And moreover — *v'lo od* — I was concerned that the students would see you reclining and conclude that one is *required* to recline, thereby establishing the halacha of Beit Shammai for future generations.

The Gemara probes this further: why did Rabbi Yishmael need to sit up? If Beit Hillel permits reclining too, what is wrong with remaining reclined? The answer: had Rabbi Yishmael also been reclining from the start and continued to recline, there would have been no problem. But Rabbi Elazar was sitting upright *until* the moment of Shema and then deliberately reclined — demonstrating through his action that he was being *makpid* like Beit Shammai, that he held reclining at night was required. In that context, Rabbi Yishmael needed to sit up as a counterdemonstration, to prevent students from drawing the wrong halachic conclusion.

### Sukkah Precedent

The Gemara then records a range of opinions about the practical consequence of acting like Beit Shammai. *tani rav yechezkel*: one who acted like Beit Shammai has acted acceptably; one who acted like Beit Hillel has also acted acceptably — perhaps even now, even after halacha always follows Beit Hillel, Beit Hillel's own position does not technically prohibit what Beit Shammai permits.

Rav Yosef, however, says: *asa kedivrei Beis Shammai lo asa velo klum* — one who deliberately acts like Beit Shammai has accomplished nothing and has not fulfilled the mitzvah. The proof comes from a Mishnah in Sukkah: if one sat with his head and most of his body inside the sukkah but left his table inside the house, Beit Shammai invalidates it and Beit Hillel validates it. When the elders of both schools visited Rabbi Yochanan ben Hachoranis and found him in precisely this situation, Beit Shammai told him: if this is how you have always arranged yourself, you have never in your life fulfilled the mitzvah of sukkah.

The point, as Tosafot explains, is significant. The problem of having one's table inside the house is only rabbinic — the concern is that one will be drawn after one's table and will not remain in the sukkah. Biblically, one is already *yotzei*. Yet Beit Shammai was so insistent on their ruling that they declared one who violated even this rabbinic position to have never fulfilled the sukkah mitzvah at all. By analogy, Beit Hillel would similarly declare that one who goes out of his way to act like Beit Shammai in the matter of Shema has not fulfilled the mitzvah. The argument by analogy is acknowledged as not fully conclusive — it shows Beit Shammai's stringency about their own rabbinic rulings, but it does not prove Beit Hillel would respond symmetrically — yet this is the reasoning advanced.

### Tarfon Danger

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak goes further: *asa kedivrei Beis Shammai chayav misa* — one who acts like Beit Shammai is liable to death. This harsh formulation, echoing language used elsewhere in the masechet about reading Shema after midnight, reflects how seriously the rabbis treated violations of their communal rulings. The proof text is the Mishnah we already encountered: Rabbi Tarfon relates that he was on the road and deliberately reclined to read Shema in the manner of Beit Shammai, thereby endangering himself by exposing himself to highway robbers. The Sages said to him: you deserved what happened to you, because you violated the words of Beit Hillel.

This is a striking position. Beit Hillel is typically associated with leniency and accommodation. Here, however, they draw an unusually firm line: someone who deliberately goes out of their way to practice like Beit Shammai — in the matter of physical positioning for Shema — is told he had it coming when he was endangered. Part of what is at stake, it seems, is the nature of the reading itself. Once one insists on reading *beshochbecha uvekumecha* as requiring a literal physical posture, one is committed to a much more literal interpretive approach to the entire verse — an approach that might, for example, lead one to conclude that Shema need only be said when one actually goes to sleep and when one actually rises, and might not apply on nights when one does not sleep. The firmness of Beit Hillel's position here may reflect precisely this concern: the reading of Beit Shammai opens a fundamentally different interpretive framework for the entire obligation of Shema.

---

## Brachot Structure

### Morning/Night Structure

The next Mishnah addresses the liturgical context of Shema. *bashachar mevarech shtayim lefaneha ve'achas leachareha* — in the morning, two brachot before Shema and one after. *uvaerev mevarech shtayim lefaneha ushtayim leachareha* — in the evening, two brachot before and two after. Then the Mishnah adds: *achas arucha ve'achas ktzara* — one long and one short.

### Tosafot Flexibility

There is a debate between Rashi and Tosafot over how to read *achas arucha ve'achas ktzara*. Rashi takes it straightforwardly: of the two brachot after Shema at night, the first — *emet ve'emunah* — is long, and the second — *hashkiveinu* — is short. Tosafot objects: technically speaking, a "short" bracha means a single-line blessing like *shehakol nihyah bidvaro*, while all the brachot surrounding Shema are elaborate paragraphs that open and close with a *baruch atah* formulation — all of them are "long" in the technical sense. What, then, does it mean that one is long and one is short?

Tosafot, in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, reads *achas arucha ve'achas ktzara* as an idiom — it means "whether long or whether short," an expression indicating flexibility. The Mishnah is telling us that in the case of *emet ve'emunah*, there was a degree of textual latitude: *bein yaarich bein yiktzar bah* — whether one wishes to extend it or abbreviate it. This reflects the broader reality that in the period of the Mishnah the precise texts of brachot had not been fully fixed, and there was genuine flexibility in how one formulated them.

### Fixed Structure Rules

The Mishnah then concludes: *makom she'amru leha'arich eino rashai lekatztzar; lekatztzar eino rashai leha'arich* — where the rabbis said to lengthen, one may not abbreviate; where they said to abbreviate, one may not lengthen. *velachtom eino rashai shelo lachtom; shelo lachtom eino rashai lachtom* — where a *chatimah* is required, one may not omit it; where no *chatimah* is prescribed, one may not add one. Short and long here refer to whether a bracha is a full paragraph ending with a *baruch atah* formulation or a single-line blessing without such an ending. When the structure is mandated, one adheres to it; only where the Mishnah explicitly signals flexibility — as with *emet ve'emunah* according to Tosafot — does latitude exist.

---

## Yotzer Or Blessing

### Darkness Language

*Mai mevarech* — what blessing is recited? Rabbi Yaakov says in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: *yotzer or uvorei choshech* — who creates light and creates darkness. The Gemara then raises a question at the top of 11b: why say *borei choshech* — creates darkness — which sounds unpleasant? Why not say *borei nogah* — creates radiance — as a euphemism? The Gemara answers: *kedichtiv ka'amrinan* — we say it as it is written. The verse in Yeshayahu reads *yotzer or uvorei choshech*, and we follow the Scriptural formulation.

### Day/Night Symmetry

The Gemara then presses further: if we follow the verse, the verse also says *oseh shalom uvorei ra* — God makes peace and creates evil. Yet we do not say that in the liturgy; we substitute *uvorei et hakol* — and creates everything — as a euphemism. Why then not similarly use *nogah* as a euphemism for darkness? The asymmetry is pointed: evil is a theologically charged and troubling concept — far more fraught than darkness, which is a simple physical reality. Indeed, part of the theological power of the original verse is precisely to counter the Zoroastrian dualist claim of two deities, one of good and one of evil. Asserting that one God creates both light and darkness, and indeed both peace and evil, is a deliberate theological statement. The hesitation to say *borei ra* in the liturgy is therefore understandable; it is much harder to explain why *borei choshech* should require euphemism.

The Gemara offers a different reason entirely. The answer is not rooted in the aesthetics of the language but in a liturgical goal: *kedei lehasmich midas yom balaila umidas laila bayom* — in order to juxtapose the quality of day with night and the quality of night with day. In the morning bracha, we mention both light *and* darkness; in the evening bracha, we will similarly mention both. The goal is to create a symmetrical awareness of God's creation of the full cycle of day and night, and this purpose overrides any preference for euphemism.

### Rolling Light

But where in the nighttime brachot do we mention the creation of day? The morning bracha mentions darkness — that covers *midas laila bayom*, bringing night into day. *ela midas yom balaila heichi mashkachas lah* — where do we find the day mentioned in the evening? Abaye answers: *goleil or mipnei choshech v'choshech mipnei or* — the evening bracha of *maariv aravim* speaks of God rolling light away before darkness and darkness away before light. This description of the continuous alternation of day and night accomplishes the goal: even in the nighttime bracha, the creation and quality of day is explicitly referenced. Beyond the poetic beauty of this image of God turning over light into darkness and darkness into light, there is again the theological dimension: it is one God who controls both, and that unity of divine governance is explicitly articulated in both the morning and evening prayers.

---

## Ahava Rabba

### Rabba vs. Olam

*U'v'idach mai hi* — what is the second bracha? Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel: *ahava rabba* — great love. Rabbi Elazar similarly instructed his son Rabbi Padas: it is *ahava rabba*. A *tanya nami hachi* confirms: one does not recite *ahavat olam* in the morning but rather *ahava rabba*. The Rabbanan, however, say *ahavat olam*, and support their view with the verse: *ve'ahavat olam ahavtich al kein meshachtich chased* — "I have loved you with an eternal love, therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness." For the evening, the bracha used is *ahavat olam*.

### Integration with Shema

The structure of the second bracha, in both its morning and evening forms, flows naturally into Shema. *ahava rabba* and *ahavat olam* speak of God's love for Israel; that love is expressed above all through the gift of Torah. The Shema then responds: *shema yisrael hashem elokeinu hashem echad — ve'ahavta et hashem elokecha* — hear O Israel and love God in return. *ahava rabba* is therefore more intrinsically a bracha of Shema than *yotzer or* is: it establishes the love relationship between God and Israel, the gift of Torah at the center of that relationship, and leads directly into the declaration of Shema and its command of love.

### Theological Significance

The split — *ahava rabba* in the morning and *ahavat olam* at night — carries theological meaning. In the morning, one feels the abundant blessings of God: the light, the new day, the overwhelming sense of divine largesse. *ahava rabba* — great, abundant love — captures this morning orientation. At night, the mood shifts. The full bracha of *hashkiveinu* speaks of God's protection through the darkness, asking that we be guarded through the night. In that context, what is most comforting is not the abundance of God's love but its *constancy* — that God's love is eternal, *ahavat olam*, and will accompany us through the darkness, through the hard times, through the fear. It is not the overwhelming brightness of the morning's gift that is invoked, but the steady, enduring love that will never abandon us. *ahavat olam ahavtich* — "I have loved you with an eternal love" — is the word of comfort for the night.

---

---

# Berakhot 11b

## Review: Shema Positions

### Humility & Angels

The previous session covered several halachot relating to Shemoneh Esrei, all transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chanina citing Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov: standing in a low place, standing with one's feet together, and not eating before davening. The first two concern how one positions oneself physically, but beyond the mechanics, they speak to a deeper orientation of humility — standing in a low place evokes a sense of distance between oneself and God. At the same time, the requirement to stand with feet together, like the angels, speaks to aspiring toward the angelic. This captures the essential tension in davening: on one hand, we draw close to God; on the other, the vast gap between the human and the Divine is never forgotten.

### Zman Shema

The discussion of the time for Shema concluded that we rule leniently up to three hours into the day. The Hagra takes an even more lenient position, measuring three hours from sunrise rather than from alot hashachar. There remain significant questions about exactly when the zman begins, but the discussion of times was wrapped up and the Gemara moved into the next Mishnah — the debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel concerning how one positions oneself for Shema: lying down at night or standing for the day according to Beit Shammai's more literal reading of the pasuk, versus the Chachamim's approach which is really about the time of day rather than the bodily posture.

### Brachos Around Shema

The session concluded with the times and positions for Shema and moved into the brachos before and after it. In the morning there are shtei brachos before and achat after; at night shtei brachos before and shtei after. The question turns to identifying what those brachos actually are.

### Yotzer Or & Borei

The morning bracha is Yotzer Or Uvorei Choshech. The Gemara notes that this is a pasuk from Yeshayahu — Yotzer Or Uvorei Choshech — but the end of that pasuk in Yeshayahu reads Oseh Shalom Uvorei et HaRa, meaning God creates evil, which raises theological questions and was also intended to reject dualistic notions of divinity. Nevertheless, we euphemize, substituting Uvorei et HaKol. The word Choshech is retained in its literal sense because we want to mention both day and night: God creates both light and darkness, just as at night we say Golel Or Mipnei Choshech Vechoshech Mipnei Or — the first bracha of each tefillah mentions both the present time and its counterpart.

### Ahava Rabbah

The second bracha is Ahava Rabbah in the morning and Ahavat Olam in the evening. The Gemara raised the question of which to say, with debate between the two formulations. The theme of both connects tightly to Shema: God has loved us — Ahava Rabbah, Ahavat Olam — and we are to love God, V'ahavta et Hashem Elokecha. Moreover, the theme of Ahavat Olam and Ahava Rabbah is Torah — that God has given us Torah — and this parallels the central theme of Shema itself: Veshinantam Levannecha Vedibarta Bam, the mitzvah of Talmud Torah.

### Double Duty Brachos

Throughout this discussion, a key question is whether these brachos function primarily as birchos Kriyas Shema or as birchos Shacharis and Maariv. To some degree, a meaningful distinction exists between the two brachos. Yotzer Or is fundamentally a bracha of Shacharis and Maariv — Yotzer HaMeorot, Yotzer Or Uvorei Choshech, Maariv Aravim — whereas Ahava Rabbah and Ahavat Olam are much more directly connected to Shema. Yet they regularly function as a package. As an illustration: someone davening Shacharis after sof zman Kriyas Shema still recites Ahavat Olam and Yotzer Or, because they continue to function as brachos of Shacharis even when they no longer serve as brachos of Kriyas Shema. These brachos truly do double duty — and, as will become apparent, perhaps triple duty.

### Practical Shema Issues

This dual function has direct practical implications. The brachos of Shema are not classic birchos hamitzvah in the manner of, say, taking a lulav — their language is not Asher Kidshanu B'Mitzvosav. They function both as Birchos HaShachar and as birchos Kriyas Shema, and accordingly one does not recite Shema with these brachos outside the context of davening. If someone says Shema before davening, they do so without the brachos.

Yet because there is a special kiyum of saying Shema im brachosecha, interesting halakhic questions arise. If a person fears missing zman Kriyas Shema, they should say Shema without the brachos rather than miss the time entirely. But ideally, Shema is said with the brachos and with tallis and tefillin, since the tallis is reflected in the third parsha of Shema and the tefillin in the first. This leads to practical trade-offs: if the zman is approaching, should one say Shema immediately or quickly put on tallis and tefillin and daven rapidly so as to say Shema with the brachos? If one can make the zman in time, the ideal is to say Shema with the brachos and with tallis and tefillin; if one fears missing the zman, one says Shema first. Some suggest making a tenai — stipulating that the earlier recitation counts only if the later one will not — though this raises its own questions about whether one can conditionally fulfill a mitzvah.

One might also ask: if someone is going to miss the zman, why not simply recite Asher Kidshanu B'Mitzvosav V'Tzivanu Likro Shema as a classic birchat hamitzvah? The answer is that this is not what the Sages instituted. The brachos of Shema were not instituted as classic birchos hamitzvah, a matter to be taken up in fuller discussion later.

---

## Ahava Rabbah & Birkat

### Learning Before Shema

With this context established, the Gemara transitions into a discussion of Birkat HaTorah. Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel states: Hishkim lishnos ad shelo kara Kriyas Shema — if one rises early to learn before having recited Kriyas Shema, tzarich l'varech — one must recite Birkat HaTorah. Mishekara Kriyas Shema — once one has already said Shema, ein tzarich l'varech — one need not recite Birkat HaTorah, shekevar niftar b'Ahava Rabba — because one has already been discharged through Ahava Rabbah.

This reveals that Ahava Rabbah functions not merely as a bracha of Shacharis and not merely as a birchas Kriyas Shema, but also as a Birkat HaTorah. The language of Ahava Rabbah explains why: V'silamdem chukei chayim, v'ten b'libeinu l'havin u-l'haskil lishmoa lilmod u-l'lamed lishmor v'la'asos u-l'kayem es kol divrei Talmud Torasecha b'ahava — it is saturated with the themes of Torah, of teaching and learning. This directly reflects the themes of Shema itself: God loves us by teaching us Torah; we love God by learning Torah and doing mitzvos, as expressed in the first parsha through Veshinantam Levannecha Vedibarta Bam and in the second parsha through the mitzvos. Because the central theme of the first parsha of Shema is Talmud Torah, Ahava Rabbah — which encapsulates this theme — functions as a Birkat HaTorah as well.

### Mikra vs Midrash

Rav Huna draws a distinction: le-Mikra tzarich l'varech — if one is learning pesukim one must make a bracha first (assuming one has not yet said Ahava Rabbah); u-le-Midrash eino tzarich l'varech — but if one is learning the rabbinic derasha of the pesukim, meaning how halacha is derived from them, one does not.

### Mishna & Talmud Disputes

Rabbi Elazar extends the requirement: le-Mikra u-le-Midrash tzarich l'varech — one must make a bracha for both Mikra and Midrash — u-le-Mishna eino tzarich l'varech — but not for learning Mishna. Rabbi Yochanan goes further: af le-Mishna nami tzarich l'varech — even for Mishna one must make a bracha — aval le-Talmud eino tzarich l'varech — but not for learning Gemara, which is analysis of the Mishna. Rava goes furthest of all: af le-Talmud tzarich l'varech — even for Talmud one must make a bracha. Some have the girsa tzarich lachzor l'varech, framing the question as whether after saying Ahava Rabbah one must make a further bracha, but this is not the standard girsa.

### Primary Object Debate

This debate is striking. In virtually any other context in the Gemara, learning Gemara is considered the highest form of kiyum Talmud Torah — the real Talmud Torah. Why, then, is there any question about whether one makes Birkat HaTorah on it?

The answer lies in the nature of Birkat HaTorah itself. There are two ways to understand the bracha. It may function as a birchas hamitzvah — Asher Kidshanu B'Mitzvosav V'Tzivanu La'asok B'Divrei Torah — in which case it applies wherever the mitzvah of Talmud Torah is performed, and Gemara learning would certainly be included. Alternatively, it may function as a birchas hashevach — Asher Bachar Banu V'natan Lanu Torato Torat Emet — a response to the gift of Torah that God has given us. When we experience something magnificent, we respond with a bracha. But what God gave us most directly is Mikra — the written text. The further one moves from Mikra — through Midrash, then Mishna, then Talmud — the further one is from the direct object of divine revelation. The Gemara, using the Mishna as its focal point rather than the pesukim, is furthest removed. In terms not of the mitzvah of Talmud Torah but of the cheftza — the object of Torah to which we respond with shevach — Mikra has the greatest claim.

So the dispute among the Amoraim may hinge on which dimension of Birkat HaTorah is primary: if it is the birchas hamitzvah, the requirement extends to Gemara naturally; if the emphasis is on birchas hashevach for the object of divine revelation, then Gemara stands at the far end of the chain of derivation and its status is less clear.

### Rav Chiya's Practice

The Gemara cites a relevant practice: Rav Chiya bar Ashi reports that many times he stood before Rav, who would be teaching a chapter from the Sifra d'vei Rav — the books of the house of Rav, though it is not certain this phrase carries its specific technical meaning here. First thing in the morning, Rav would wash his hands — netilat yadayim — then make a bracha, and then teach. Since this was done before saying Ahava Rabbah and before Kriyas Shema, Rav had to recite Birkat HaTorah independently. The content of what he then taught was Gemara — Talmud — which demonstrates that one does indeed make Birkat HaTorah before Talmud, not only before Mikra.

### Nusach Birkat Torah

Mah mivarech — what is the text of this bracha? Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says: Asher kideshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu la'asok be-divrei Torah. Different girsaot among the Geonim exist — some have al divrei Torah — but our girsa is la'asok, to involve oneself in Torah learning. This is notable: even in this birchas hamitzvah, the language is not simply "to learn" but la'asok — to labor, to invest oneself with real engagement. This is the classic birchas hamitzvah.

### Ha'arev Na Request

Rabbi Yochanan appends an additional passage: Ha'arev na Hashem Elokeinu et divrei Toratecha be-finu u-ve-fiyot amcha Beit Yisrael — make the words of Your Torah sweet in our mouths and in the mouths of Your people Israel — ve-niyeh anachnu ve-tze'etza'einu ve-tze'etza'ei amcha Beit Yisrael kulanu yode'ei shemecha ve-oskei Toratecha — and may we and our children and our children's children all know Your name and involve ourselves in Your Torah — Baruch Atah Hashem hamelamed Torah le-amo Yisrael.

This is not a birchas hamitzvah; it is a different kind of bracha entirely. It is a request — a bakashah — that God give us the desire and the delight to learn Torah. Strikingly, this mirrors the language of Ahava Rabbah: V'ten be-libeinu l'havin u-l'haskil lilmod u-le-lamed. The chatimah — Baruch Atah Hashem hamelamed Torah le-amo Yisrael — is an extension constituting a further bracha.

### Three Blessing Forms

Rav Hamnuna adds a third formulation: Asher bachar banu mikol ha-amim ve-natan lanu et Torato, Baruch Atah Hashem notein ha-Torah — You have chosen us from all nations and given us Your Torah. Rav Hamnuna declares: zu hi me'ula she-ba-berachot — this is the finest of the blessings. Why? Perhaps because of the theme of chosenness; perhaps also because it is a bracha said independently even outside this context, as we recite it before each aliyah to the Torah. The Gemara concludes: hilkach nemrinhu le-chulhu — therefore, say them all. And indeed we do.

### Synthesis & Integration

Reviewing all three formulations clarifies why Ahava Rabbah functions as a Birkat HaTorah: it contains all three of these elements within it. This threefold structure of Birkat HaTorah also illuminates the earlier debate about which form of Torah study requires the bracha.

The three elements are: first, the birchas hamitzvah — Asher Kidshanu V'Tzivanu — which applies wherever the mitzvah of Talmud Torah is performed, naturally including Gemara. Second, the birchas hashevach — Asher Bachar Banu — a response to the gift of Torah itself, where Mikra as the direct word of God has primary claim. Third, the bakashah of Ha'arev Na — a request for the desire to engage with Torah — which is its own dimension, something rare and moving in that most of our requests in Shemoneh Esrei concern material needs, while here the center of our spiritual aspirations becomes itself the subject of petition: grant us the will to truly invest in Torah.

There is a significant machloket between the Shulchan Aruch and the Vilna Gaon regarding which of these three elements is primary in Birkat HaTorah, and this generates a range of practical questions. Tosafot already raises the question: if one wakes in the middle of the night, must one repeat Birkat HaTorah? If one stops learning during the day and resumes, must one make another bracha? If Birkat HaTorah is a birchas hamitzvah, then — as with leaving a sukkah and returning — each new resumption should require a new bracha. Tosafot, however, holds that even as a birchas hamitzvah, Talmud Torah is fundamentally different: we are always obligated to be learning, and even when we are not, we are perpetually in the process of returning to it. It is a continuous mitzvah, never truly interrupted. Therefore no new bracha is required upon resumption — and there is something beautiful in that framing: at least in principle, we should always be in the process of getting back to Talmud Torah.

If the emphasis falls instead on the shevach dimension, then Birkat HaTorah is like other birchos hashevach which are recited once daily, as with Birchos HaShachar — one does not recite HaNoten LaSechvi Binah each time a rooster crows.

A related question, debated between the Shulchan Aruch and the Magen Avraham, is whether Birkat HaTorah is required when one is thinking Torah without speaking: one performs the mitzvat Talmud Torah by thinking Torah, but there is no verbal object to which the bracha responds. Which element dominates determines the answer.

Returning to the practical bottom line: according to the peshat of this Gemara, and apparently the ruling of many Rishonim, as long as one does not plan to learn before davening, Ahava Rabbah discharges the obligation of Birkat HaTorah — Ahava Rabbah contains all three of those elements. In practice, however, given the centrality of these brachos and the power of articulating what Torah means to us, the custom developed to ensure we recite Birkat HaTorah explicitly by learning a bit before Shema. This raises its own questions: if someone is rushing and says birchos Kriyas Shema to ensure Kriyas Shema bizmanah, does Ahava Rabbah count as Birkat HaTorah? Does it require specific kavana? The Yerushalmi suggests it may count only if one learns extra Torah after Shema — making clear that the bracha was not merely a birchas Kriyas Shema. If no additional Torah is learned, it is framed only as a birchas Kriyas Shema. Several Rishonim therefore require either kavana or post-Shema Torah learning for Ahava Rabbah to discharge the Birkat HaTorah obligation, though the matter remains debated.

---

## Beit HaMikdash Service

### Memuneh's Command

The Gemara now cites a Mishnah from elsewhere — tnan hatam. Those who followed the previous cycle of the Daf will recall that Masechet Tamid concluded with an extended description of the daily service in the Beit HaMikdash and precisely how the morning was organized. At one stage, after the commencement of the korban tamid, the memuneh — the officer appointed over the kohanim — addressed them: Barchu bracha achat — recite one blessing. They did so.

### Aseres Hadibros

They then read the Aseres HaDibros, and then the three parshiyot of Shema: Shema, V'haya Im Shamoa, and Vayomer.

### Emes Veyatziv

They then blessed the people with three blessings: Emes V'yatziv (which concludes with Gaal Yisrael), V'avodah, and Birkas Kohanim. The bracha of V'avodah raises its own question since our current formulation, Hamachazir Shchinaso L'Tzion, was obviously not the one in use. Rashi suggests two possibilities: either She'oscha levadcha b'yirah naavod — the bracha recited before the duchan blessing, invoking that the kohanim's service should be directed entirely to God — or a formulation such as Baruch hamikabel avodas amo Yisrael b'ratzon, a form of retzei, accepting the sacrifice. In any case it was a bracha for the acceptance of the avodah. Their Shemoneh Esrei was therefore compressed: Gaal Yisrael, Retzei, and Birkas Kohanim — not the duchan Birkas Kohanim, which occurred at different times, but nevertheless a component of this abbreviated Shemoneh Esrei.

### One Blessing Debate

Returning to the opening of the Mishnah: mah bracha achat — what was the single blessing before Shema? When Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Yosef arrived at a certain place, the people there asked them this question. They did not know. They went and asked Rav Masnah, who also did not know. They then asked Rav Yehuda, who reported in the name of Shmuel: Ahava Rabbah. Rabbi Zerika, citing Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, says: Yotzer Or.

Both options have their logic. If the Temple service is conceived as a distilled version of Shema and Shemoneh Esrei — and no more — then Ahava Rabbah is the natural choice, being the bracha most directly connected to Shema. If, on the other hand, the goal is a minimal representation of all of davening — Shema plus Shemoneh Esrei — then Yotzer Or adds the component of the morning service, the praise for creation that the other brachos represent. One compelling point is that the kohanim were particularly concerned with not appearing to worship the sun, having been in proximity to the Temple precincts and the rising sun; declaring Yotzer Or Uvorei Choshech affirmed their allegiance to God rather than the heavenly bodies.

There is also the question of whether their davening was primarily a private obligation or had some public dimension — the Mishnah elsewhere indicates that people would daven together with the kohanim — which may also bear on which bracha was appropriate.

### Brachos Not Mkablos

The Gemara then reports: when Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef came, he noted that what Rabbi Zerika said — that it was Yotzer Or — was not stated explicitly but was inferred. De'amar Rabbi Zerika amar Rabbi Ami amar Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: zos omeres brachos ein me'akvos zo es zo — the fact that only one bracha was said proves that the brachos do not hold each other back. If one says only one of the two morning brachos before Shema, one is yotzei that one bracha; saying it does not require having said the other.

### Inference Issues

The inference works only if the single bracha was Yotzer Or. If they said Yotzer Or without Ahava Rabbah, one can demonstrate that Yotzer Or is valid independently. But if one argues they said Ahava Rabbah, the inference fails to prove anything: perhaps the reason they omitted Yotzer Or had nothing to do with whether one holds the other back. Perhaps they simply had not yet reached the proper time for Yotzer Or.

The Gemara pursues this: ei amart bishlama Yotzer Or — if one says the single bracha was Yotzer Or, hainu brachos ein me'akvos — the proof follows, since they said Yotzer Or without saying Ahava Rabbah. Ela ei amart Ahava Rabbah — but if one says they said Ahava Rabbah, how does that prove brachos do not hold each other back? Dilma — perhaps the reason they omitted Yotzer Or was simply because its time had not yet arrived. The Gemara then considers: granted, perhaps when the time of Yotzer Or came they would have said it. Mai brachos ein me'akvos? Then the principle would mean only that the order does not matter — not that one bracha is fully valid without the other.

### Yotzer Or Timing

Implicit in this discussion is that the kohanim said Shema before the time of Yotzer Or — that is, before sunrise. Rashi quotes the Gemara in Yoma that one who said Shema with the kohanim was not yotzei the mitzvah of Shema because they said it too early. Some read this as indicating that the zman Shema — at least according to one view — does not begin until sunrise, so saying it earlier does not fulfill the obligation.

Our standard ruling requires at least misheyakir, and we do not hold that sunrise is required for Shema. However, the Gemara here implies that Yotzer Or may indeed require sunrise. We do not rule this way either — we hold that Yotzer Or may be said from misheyakir — but there remains a serious question about someone davening before amud hashachar (approximately 72 minutes before sunrise, from when Shema is technically permitted): does one say Yotzer Or at that time? Some say yes, some say no. The double nature of the brachos is again relevant here. Ahava Rabbah is closely bound to Shema itself and would presumably be said even if one is davening before sunrise, since it is a birchas Kriyas Shema. But Yotzer Or is simultaneously a bracha of the morning and of creation — and perhaps the sun's appearance is a prerequisite for its recitation, at least according to the reading that Yotzer Or requires sunrise. This could yield a situation where one recites Ahava Rabbah before sunrise without Yotzer Or, with the understanding that they serve different functions even as brachos of the same Shema.

### Shabbat Addition

The Mishnah continues: u'v'Shabbos mosifin bracha achas l'mishmar hayotze — on Shabbat they would add one blessing for the mishmar hayotze, the outgoing watch. Rabbi Chelbo explains: mishmar hayotze omer l'mishmar hanichnas — the outgoing mishmar would address the incoming. What would they say? Mi sheshachan et shemo babayit hazeh, hu yashken beineichem ahava veachva veshalom vereut — May He whose name dwells in this House cause to dwell among you love, brotherhood, peace, and friendship. It is a beautiful blessing — perhaps especially fitting at the transition point when the incoming mishmar is about to face a demanding week of sacrificial service with all the pressures and divisions of labor it entails.

### Ten Commandments Ban

The Gemara reports: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says: af bagvulin bikshu likros kein — they wanted to establish the practice of reading the Aseres HaDibros in the communities outside the Beit HaMikdash as well — ela shekvar bitlum mipnei tarumos haminin — but they had already abolished it because of the complaint of the heretics.

This is instructive. The impulse to say the Aseres HaDibros before Shema makes sense: Shema is itself a distillation of the Torah's central demands — love God, learn Torah, do the mitzvos. The Aseres HaDibros is another such distillation, a declaration of our responsibilities and a kind of re-enactment of Maamad Har Sinai and kabbalas ol malchus shamayim. But the practice was suppressed because of tarumos haminin — the heretical objection. Rashi in the unedited text identifies these minim as talmidei Yeshu — Hebrew Christians. Our standard printed Rashi reads akum, which here must be understood as reflecting censorship, since minim classically denotes Hebrew Christians who kept halacha while believing in Jesus. Their critique would have been to single out the Ten Commandments as the sole genuine revelation, thereby implicitly delegitimizing the rest of Torah. This maps onto the later reality that Christianity, even while rejecting the broader corpus of halacha, continued to embrace the Ten Commandments.

Despite the evident appeal of the practice, subsequent Amoraim who wished to reinstitute it — Rabba bar bar Chana in Sura and Ameimar in Neharde'a — were in each case told by Rav Chisda and Rav Ashi respectively: kvar bitlum mipnei tarumos haminin. The liturgy as established is not to be altered, even when the original reason for the prohibition may not apply in a particular locale.

---

## Ending Determines All

### Wine & Mead Case

The Gemara moves into a discussion of the actual nusach of brachos and what happens when something goes wrong. It begins: pshita — it is obvious — if someone is holding a cup of wine and thinks it is mead, and begins the bracha with the intention of saying Shehakol nihiyeh bidvaro, but then realizes it is wine and ends with Borei Pri HaGafen — yatza. Why is this obvious? Because even had he completed Shehakol, he would have been yotzei — de-nami im amar Shehakol nihiyeh bidvaro yatza, as we learned: al kulam im amar Shehakol nihiyeh bidvaro yatza. The opening intention to say Shehakol was never an error in the first place.

### Switched Intentions

The more interesting case is the reverse: one holds mead and thinks it is wine, begins with the intention to say Borei Pri HaGafen, but then realizes the truth and ends with Shehakol nihiyeh bidvaro. The question is: batar ikkar bracha azlinan — do we follow the beginning of the bracha — or batar chatima azlinan — do we follow the end? The opening intention was for the wrong bracha, but the text concluded correctly.

Tosafot notes that this cannot simply be a question about lack of kavana — we are generally yotzei mitzvos without kavana. Rather, the issue here is that one had an active contrary intention at the opening: one specifically framed the bracha as Borei Pri HaGafen, and the question is whether that framing invalidates the bracha regardless of whether the words were ultimately correct.

### Chatima Rule

A baraita provides the answer through the case of the morning and evening brachos: Shacharis patach beYotzer Or vesiyem beMaariv Aravim — lo yatza. If one opened with Yotzer Or in mind and ended with Maariv Aravim — not yotzei. Patach beMaariv Aravim vesiyem beYotzer Or — yatza. If one opened with the wrong intention but ended correctly — yotzei. The same applies in reverse for Maariv. Klal shel davar: hakol holech achar hachatima — it all goes by how you end.

### Long Brachos Exception

The Gemara resists this conclusion, noting: shani hatam dekaamar Baruch Yotzer Meor — the case of Yotzer Or is different because it is a long bracha, an extended paragraph. When the baraita says patach, it may mean that ברוך אתה ה' יוצר אור was said at the very opening of the paragraph with a wrong mindset, but by the time one reached the chatima — ברוך אתה ה' יוצר המאורות — the mindset was correct. So the bracha may not be a straightforward proof that wrong intent at the beginning is irrelevant; perhaps it only works here because the wrong intent affected only the opening paragraph while the concluding ברוך at the end was said with correct intent.

The Gemara tests this against the positions of Rav and Rabbi Yochanan. According to Rav — kol bracha she'ein bo Hazkaras HaShem einah bracha — a bracha must contain the name of Hashem, which the concluding Baruch Atah Hashem Yotzer HaMeorot provides. This is consistent. But according to Rabbi Yochanan — kol bracha she'ein bo malchus einah bracha — without Melech HaOlam it is not a bracha.
