The only place Melech HaOlam appears is in the opening Baruch Atah Hashem Eloheinu Melech HaOlam, which was said with the wrong mindset. If that opening is discounted, should the whole bracha fail?

### Day & Night Coverage

Rabbah bar Ulla explains why this is not a problem: kedei lehazkir middas yom balaylah u-middas laylah bayom — both brachos, morning and evening, are structured to mention both day and night. Since each bracha intentionally contains elements of both times, even when one begins with the wrong intention — thinking it is Maariv Aravim when saying Yotzer Or — that opening is not entirely without content, because Yotzer Or by design speaks of both light and darkness. It is analogous to the Shehakol case: just as Shehakol is always valid for any food, the opening of one bracha has some relevance even when said in the wrong context, because both brachos encompass both times. Therefore the case remains insufficient to prove the general principle that wrong intent at the opening is always irrelevant.

The Gemara then returns to the klal shel davar, the overarching rule, and notes: klal shel davar le'asuyei mai — what does the general rule include? Lo le'asuyei ha de'amran — not simply to restate the case just discussed. Rather, it includes a new case: bread and dates.

### Bread & Dates Case

The case is as follows: one eats dates and thinks it is bread. One begins with the intention to say Hamotzi Lechem Min Ha'aretz, then realizes and ends with Borei Pri HaEtz. Hainu bahu — this is exactly the same case we have been discussing: one opened with the wrong intention, ended with the right bracha text. The klal tells us it goes by the end. Fine, the principle is confirmed.

But the opposite case is more interesting: one eats dates and thinks it is bread, begins intending to say Hamotzi, and then ends with the bracha for dates — Borei Pri HaEtz. Yatza — this works. Why, if one was thinking Hamotzi at the beginning? De'afilu siyem bidnahama nami yatza — because even if one had completed Hamotzi for dates, one would still be yotzei, since dates also satiate — tamrei nami mizni zanei. Since Hamotzi would have worked even for dates, the original intent was never truly wrong, and the final correct formulation certainly works.

### Rambam's Toch K'dei

Rashi and Tosafot understand the entire discussion as concerning one's mental intent: the text was said correctly, but the wrong bracha was in mind at the outset. Several Rishonim, however, find this difficult — why should mental intent matter if the text was correct? The Ramban offers a different reading. He understands adaata dehachi as referring not to wrong mental intent but to wrong words actually spoken. The scenarios describe situations where one said the wrong bracha aloud and then corrected oneself. The question is whether a toch k'dei dibbur correction — a verbal self-correction made within the brief span defined as toch k'dei dibbur — is effective.

According to the Rambam's reading, the conclusion of the sugya — hakol holech achar hachatuma — means: as long as one says the right words at the end, a toch k'dei dibbur correction of the wrong words said at the beginning is effective. If one said the wrong thing and corrected it within toch k'dei dibbur, the correction stands. If one said the right thing but then miscorrected it — saying the right bracha and then immediately adding a wrong one — the wrong correction does not undo the correct recitation. This is also how we rule in practice regarding toch k'dei dibbur corrections: saying the correct bracha and then incorrectly correcting oneself does not invalidate what was already said correctly, but saying the wrong bracha and then correcting it within toch k'dei dibbur does work.

---

---

# Berakhot 12

## Emet VeYatziv & Emet

### Emet VeYatziv Emet Ve'em…

The daf opens near the bottom of 12a with a teaching of Rava bar Chinana Sabba in the name of Rav: *kol shelo amar emet veYatziv shachrit ve'emet ve'emuna arvit lo yatza yedei chovato* — whoever did not say Emet VeYatziv in the morning and Emet Ve'emuna in the evening has not fulfilled his obligation. The Gemara has been tracing the blessings that surround the Shema — the blessings before it, Yotzer HaMeorot and Ahava Rabba in the morning, Maariv Aravim and Ahavat Olam in the evening, and the distinction between them. Now it turns to the blessings that follow. The point here is not merely that a blessing must be recited after the Shema — that much is known — but that the specific formulation matters. Just as there is a distinction between Ahava Rabba and Ahavat Olam, so too there is a corresponding distinction between the two post-Shema blessings: Emet VeYatziv in the morning and Emet Ve'emuna at night.

The scriptural basis is the verse *lehagid baboker chasdecha ve'emunatecha baleilot* — to declare Your kindness in the morning and Your faithfulness at night. The morning evokes an appreciation of God's manifest beneficence: the light, the world, the tangible gifts of existence — the register of Ahava Rabba. The evening, with its darkness and uncertainty, draws on a deeper register of faith and endurance — the register of Ahavat Olam. Emet Ve'emuna carries that same quality of abiding trust that characterizes the night.

### Rashi: Morning/Evening

Rashi elaborates on this distinction from the angle of content rather than atmosphere. He explains that *birchat Emet VeYatziv kulah al chesed she'asa im avoteinu* — the blessing of Emet VeYatziv is entirely about the chesed God performed for our ancestors: taking us out of Egypt, splitting the sea, bringing them through. By contrast, *birchat Emet Ve'emuna medaberet af al ha'atidot* — the blessing of Emet Ve'emuna speaks also of future hopes, of the anticipation that God will fulfill His promises and redeem us from the dominion of kingdoms. These are not merely parallel formulations; they represent distinct orientations — one looking backward at miraculous history, the other looking forward in faith. Both dimensions, Rashi implies, correspond naturally to their respective times of day: the morning invites gratitude for what has already been given, the night invites trust in what is yet to come.

---

## Bowing & Rising

### Bow Baruch Rise Shem

The Gemara continues with another teaching from the same tradition — Rava bar Chinana Sabba in the name of Rav: *hamitpallel kshehu kore'a kore'a beBaruch, ukshehu zokef zokef beShem* — when one prays and bows, one bows at the word *baruch*, and when one rises, one rises upon pronouncing the divine Name. In practical terms: at *baruch ata*, one bends the knees at *baruch* and is fully bowed at *ata*, and then as one reaches the divine Name, one straightens upright. Shmuel later conveys this same ruling to Chiya bar Rav — addressing him as *bar Oryan*, either son of a lion or a term evoking Torah scholarship — noting it as a *milta maalya*, a beautiful teaching, that his father Rav had said.

### Shmuel's Reasoning

Shmuel explains the rationale: *dechtiv Hashem zokef kefufim* — as the verse states, God straightens those who are bent. It is therefore the utterance of the divine Name that causes the transition from the bowed position to the erect one. God's Name, in its very pronounciation, lifts the one who has humbled himself.

### Contradiction Resolution

The Gemara raises an apparent contradiction: does not another verse indicate that the divine Name inspires humility — *mipnei shemi nichat hu*, because of My name he is humbled? If God's name causes one to become low, how can it also be what causes one to rise? The Gemara resolves this by noting the precise wording: *mipnei shemi* — because of My name, not through the utterance of My name. The awe and fear that God's name inspires generates the humility that drives a person to bow; but when one actually pronounces the Name in prayer, that very act of reaching out to God is what causes one to stand upright.

There is a beautiful dialectic here that runs through the entire discussion of prayer. We stand in a low place but plant our feet together like an angel, simultaneously expressing smallness and aspiring to connection. Similarly here: the bowing expresses the sense of being nothing in the presence of the Divine, and the pronounciation of the Name — the act of reaching out to connect — is precisely what restores the worshipper to an upright stance. The competing themes of awe and connection, humility and aspiration, are not resolved but held in tension.

### Rav Sheshet's Practice

The Gemara moves to 12b and records the practice of Rav Sheshet: *ki kara, kara kachizra* — when he bowed, he bowed like a rod, meaning all at once, dropping immediately to the ground without hesitation, as though a stick had been thrown down. *vechi zakif, zakif kachivya* — and when he rose, he rose like a snake, slowly and gradually, the way a snake rises from the ground beginning from its head. Rashi notes that the swift bowing ensures that the act does not look like a burden one is eager to shed. The emphasis falls on the weight given to the bowing down — the immediate, whole-hearted expression of awe — while the rising is a slower, more effortful process of regaining the strength to stand. The asymmetry itself carries the message: the inclination toward humility is swift and instinctive; the return to uprightness requires gradual effort. Here again the tension is not dissolved but given a particular weighting.

---

## Aseret Yemei Teshuvah

### Year-Round Formula

Following the same chain of tradition — Rabbah bar Chinana Sabba in the name of Rav — the Gemara presents a third ruling, now concerning Shemoneh Esrei rather than the blessings of Shema. Throughout the entire year, in the third blessing of Shemoneh Esrei one says *ha'el haKadosh*, and in the blessing of justice in the middle one says *melech ohev tzedakah uMishpat*. These are the standard formulations of the year-round nusach.

### Ten Days Changes

The exception is the ten days encompassing Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur — the Aseret Yemei Teshuvah. The phrase "ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur" is technically imprecise, since there are only seven days between those dates; the expression refers to the ten days that encompass both. During this period, the formulation shifts: instead of *ha'el haKadosh* one says *haMelech haKadosh*, and instead of *melech ohev tzedakah uMishpat* one says *haMelech haMishpat*. The theme of God's kingship and judgment dominates this season, and both formulas reflect that emphasis — *melech* is foregrounded, and the attribute of justice is stated as identity rather than as a quality God loves.

It should be noted that *haMelech haKadosh* was already the accepted formulation specifically on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur themselves. The question being addressed here is whether that formulation, along with the parallel change to *haMelech haMishpat*, extends throughout the Aseret Yemei Teshuvah — and the answer given by Rabbah bar Chinana in the name of Rav is that it does.

### Rabbi Eliezer Opinion

Rabbi Eliezer takes a more lenient position: even if one said *ha'el haKadosh* during the Aseret Yemei Teshuvah, he has fulfilled his obligation *bedi'avad*. His proof is from the verse *vayigbah Hashem Tzeva'ot bamishpat veha'El HaKadosh nikdash bitzedakah* — the glory of God is elevated in judgment and the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness. When is God's judgment most prominent? These are precisely the Aseret Yemei Teshuvah. And yet the verse continues by saying *ha'el haKadosh*, which shows that even during this period of judgment, *ha'el haKadosh* remains an acceptable formulation. By extension, if *ha'el haKadosh* is acceptable, *melech ohev tzedakah uMishpat* would presumably be acceptable as well.

### Rav Yosef Rabbah Ruling

The Gemara asks: what is the practical upshot? Rav Yosef rules that the year-round nusach — *ha'el haKadosh* and *melech ohev tzedakah uMishpat* — is maintained throughout the Aseret Yemei Teshuvah, and *haMelech haKadosh* is reserved for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur themselves. Rabbah rules that *haMelech haKadosh* and *haMelech haMishpat* are indeed required throughout the Aseret Yemei Teshuvah. The Gemara concludes *ve'hilchata keRabbah* — and the halacha follows Rabbah, which is our accepted ruling.

### Tosafot Later Additions

Tosafot raises a further point. Having established that one must say *haMelech haKadosh* and *haMelech haMishpat* during the Aseret Yemei Teshuvah — and that failure to do so requires one to repeat the Shemoneh Esrei — Tosafot extends this principle to other insertions of the season: *zachrenu*, *mi chamocha*, *u'chtov l'chayim*, *u'veSefer chayim*, and similar additions. The initial position is that since these have become part of the accepted nusach, one who omits them must go back. However, Tosafot then cites a second view — attributed to Rabbeinu Chananel or Rabbeinu Tam — that these additional phrases were introduced later by the Geonim and were never explicitly ruled upon in the Talmud (*d'lo pasik be'Shas befeirush*), and therefore one does not return if one omits them. This is in fact our accepted ruling: one returns for *haMelech haKadosh* and *haMelech haMishpat*, but not for the *zachrenus* and *u'chtavenu* and similar insertions that were added at a later stage.

---

## Prayer for Others

### Sinner for Not Praying

The Gemara presents yet another teaching from Rabbah bar Chinana Sabba in the name of Rav, this time moving beyond questions of nusach and liturgical form to address the orientation and purpose of prayer itself: *kol she'efshar lo levakesh rachamim al chaveiro ve'eino mevakesh nikra chotei* — whoever is able to pray for mercy on behalf of his friend and does not do so is called a sinner. The proof-text is Samuel's declaration: *chalila li me'chato la'Hashem mechadol l'hitpalel be'adchem* — God forbid that I should sin against God by ceasing to pray on your behalf. Not to pray for someone when one could is cast as a sin against God.

This teaching carries a double weight. On one level, it expresses a genuine theology of prayer: if one truly believes that God operates in the world and that prayer can effect change, then to withhold prayer from someone who needs it is a form of abandonment. Statutory prayer performed out of obligation speaks less directly to this living faith than responsive prayer — prayer prompted by an actual situation. The emphasis on *chaveiro* — a friend, another person — adds the dimension of interpersonal responsibility. If one has faith in the power of prayer and a friend is in need, the failure to pray combines a failure of faith with a failure of care, and that combination is called a sin.

### Afflict Self Talmid Chac…

The Gemara goes further: *im talmid chacham hu, tzarich sheyichleh atzmo alav* — if the person in need is a Torah scholar, it is not enough merely to pray; one must make oneself ill over him, investing one's prayer with a depth of personal anguish. The Gemara initially explores whether this is derived from Saul's complaint — *ve'ein choleh mikem alai* — nobody is making themselves ill over me, lamenting that no one was deeply troubled on his behalf. The Gemara questions whether that standard might apply specifically to a king rather than a Torah scholar. The conclusion is instead drawn from the verse *va'ani bechalotam levushi* — and I in their illness wore sackcloth — understood as David afflicting himself in his prayer for others when they became ill. The standard being set is not merely sincere prayer but genuine self-abnegation: prayer that is so deeply felt it registers as a form of personal suffering.

---

## Shame & Forgiveness

### Sin with Shame Forgiven

Shifting from the topic of prayer to a related register of religious and ethical teaching, the Gemara cites Rabbi Chinana bar Abba in the name of Rav: *kol oseh devar aveirah umitbayes bo, mochlin lo al kol avonosaiv* — whoever commits a sin and is embarrassed by it has all his sins forgiven. This is a striking statement. The scriptural support comes from the verse in Yechezkel: *lema'an tizkeri uvoshat velo yihyeh lach od pischon peh mipnei kelimasech bechapperi lach lechol asher asit neum Hashem Elokim* — so that you will remember and be ashamed and have no more occasion to speak because of your humiliation, when I have atoned for you for all that you have done, says God. The link is causal: the shame is the condition of the atonement.

The deeper logic here is not simply that suffering generates atonement, but that genuine shame can produce a transformative experience. If a person truly internalizes the wrongness of what he has done and feels it as humiliation, that emotional reckoning can reshape character and redirect future behavior. *mochlin lo al kol avonosaiv* reflects not a bookkeeping transaction but the possibility of real inner change. The Gemara, however, asks whether this verse applies to the community as a whole — Israel collectively called to account — or also to an individual.

### Shaul Nov Example

The Gemara resolves this question through the case of Shaul. The verse in Shmuel records that Shaul, appealing to the spirit of Shmuel, listed the channels through which he had sought divine guidance: prophets and dreams. Notably, he did not mention the Urim VeTummim. The Gemara observes: *ve'ilu Urim VeTummim lo ka'amar* — and yet he did not say he had tried the Urim VeTummim. The reason, the Gemara infers, is *mishum dekatlei leNov ir hakohanim* — because he had destroyed Nov, the city of the Kohanim, and with it the priestly infrastructure through which one would consult the Urim VeTummim. To mention that avenue would have been to remind everyone of that devastation. His silence, the Gemara reads, reflects shame over what he had done.

This is a relatively oblique expression of shame — not a confession, not an explicit acknowledgment, but merely the omission of a topic he could not comfortably raise. Yet the Gemara treats it as significant. The avoidance itself signals that Shaul recognized the wrongness of his act. From the standpoint of ordinary psychology, one might question whether such silence constitutes genuine shame or merely uncomfortable evasion. Nevertheless, for the Gemara it is enough to establish that Shaul felt the weight of his deed.

### Bas Kol Shaul Chosen

The proof that Shaul was forgiven as a result comes from two sources. The first: Shmuel told Shaul *umachar atah uvanecha immi* — tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. Rabbi Yochanan reads *immi* — with me — as *bimchitzati*, in my portion of the World to Come. This implies that despite his sins, Shaul merited the World to Come, which the Gemara attributes to his shame over Nov Ir Kohanim.

The second source comes from the Rabbis, who cite a different verse. When David asks the Givonim how to atone for Shaul's sins against them, they call for the execution of Shaul's sons and, in that context, the text refers to Shaul as *bechir Hashem* — the chosen of God. The Gemara reads this not as the Givonim's characterization but as the narrator's voice, or more precisely as a divine declaration: a Heavenly voice — *yatzah bas kol ve'amarah* — went forth and declared Shaul to be the chosen of God. The basis for this designation, the Gemara concludes, is precisely that he had been ashamed over the destruction of Nov Ir Kohanim. The degree of shame actually demonstrated was quite minimal — little more than a failure to mention something in a list — and yet the Gemara reads it as sufficient to earn the designation of *bechir Hashem* and full forgiveness of sins.

---

## Parsha Balak Excluded

### Balak Inclusion Attempt

The Gemara now returns to the structure of the Shema and its surrounding liturgy. Rav Yehuda bar Zvida teaches: *bikshu likvoa parshat Balak bekri'at Shema* — the Sages considered including Parashat Balak as part of the recitation of Shema.

### Torach Tzibur Rejection

The consideration was ultimately rejected for a single practical reason: *mishum torach tzibur* — the burden it would impose on the congregation. The parsha is long, and including it would have made the Shema recitation unacceptably burdensome.

### Yetzias Mitzrayim Sources

The Gemara asks what motivated the proposal. The initial suggestion is that Parashat Balak contains the verse *el motzi'am miMitzrayim* — the God who brought them out of Egypt — and could therefore serve the function currently fulfilled by Parashat Tzitzit, which is the vehicle for the separate mitzvah of remembering the Exodus. But this cannot be the full explanation, since the memory of Yetzias Mitzrayim is mentioned in many places throughout the Torah — the prohibition of *ribbis*, the laws of honest weights — and none of those passages were ever proposed for inclusion in Shema.

Rabbi Yose bar Avin therefore identifies the specific verse that made Parashat Balak a serious candidate: *kara shachav ke'ari u'che'lavia mi yekimenu* — he crouched and lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him? Rashi explains that this verse directly echoes the central language of Kri'at Shema — *beshochbecha uvekumecha*, when you lie down and when you rise up. A passage that contains language of lying down and rising up is uniquely suited for inclusion in the context of Shema. The proposal was thus to capture both the theme of Yetzias Mitzrayim and the structural resonance with the act of Kri'at Shema itself through Parashat Balak.

A further question arises: why not select just those two key verses from Balak rather than the whole parsha, thereby avoiding the problem of length? One might say: take *el motzi'am miMitzrayim* and *kara shachav ke'ari* and nothing else.

### Moshe's Divisions Rule

The Gemara dismisses this possibility on the basis of a received tradition: *kol parsha de'paska Moshe Rabbeinu paskhinan, delo paska Moshe Rabbeinu lo paskhinan* — any parsha that Moshe Rabbeinu divided, we may divide; any parsha that Moshe Rabbeinu did not divide, we may not divide. Since Balak is a single undivided unit, we cannot excerpt portions of it for liturgical use. It is all or nothing — and given the length, it is nothing.

This principle is distinct from the related rule that one should not divide a verse when quoting it — a rule reflected in the Gemara's convention of writing *ve'gomer* (implying completion) when citing a pasuk, as opposed to *ve'chulu* (which is used when the citation is not from a verse). *ve'gomer* signals that the verse should be completed; the reader is meant to continue it to its end. That rule governs individual speech and quotation. The rule being invoked here — not dividing a parsha — applies specifically to liturgical incorporation: when establishing something as part of formal tefillah, one cannot take a fragment of a parsha that Moshe did not himself divide.

---

## Parsha Tzitzit Selected

### Tzitzit Five Things

Having established why Balak was excluded, the Gemara turns to the affirmative question: *parshat Tzitzit mipnei ma kavua* — why was Parashat Tzitzit chosen? Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva answers: because it contains not one but five things of significance — and the Gemara will note that a careful reading may actually yield six.

### Three Explicit Elements

The first three are explicit in the text. The mitzvah of Tzitzit itself: *ve'asu lahem tzitzit*. The memory of Yetzias Mitzrayim: *asher hotzeiti etchem*. And the acceptance of the yoke of mitzvot: *ure'item oto uzechartem et kol mitzvot Hashem va'asitem otam* — you shall see them and remember all the commandments of God and do them. This last element ties Parashat Tzitzit directly to the themes of the earlier parshiyot of Shema, which emphasize learning Torah and performing mitzvot. The parsha thus does not merely add a discrete obligation; it deepens and reinforces the overarching theme of the Shema recitation.

### Three Hidden Elements

Beyond the three explicit elements, the Gemara derives three further dimensions from the phrase *velo taturu acharei levavchem ve'acharei eineichem asher atem zonim achareihem* — and you shall not stray after your hearts and after your eyes, that which you go lusting after. These three clauses address three distinct dangers: heretical thought, sexual transgression, and idolatry.

### Heretical Thoughts Warni…

*Acharei levavchem* — straying after your hearts — is identified as *minut*, heresy. The heart in this context carries the sense of intellect and conviction, not merely emotion. The supporting verse is *amar naval be'libo ein Elokim* — the degenerate one says in his heart there is no God — where *be'libo*, in his heart, marks the seat of theological denial. The tzitzit serves as a reminder that keeps the mind anchored to true faith, preventing the intellect from drifting into heretical conclusions.

### Lustful Thoughts Warning

*Acharei eineichem* — straying after your eyes — refers to *hirhur aveira*, sinful thoughts of a sexual nature. The supporting verse is from the story of Shimshon: *vayomer Shimshon el aviv otah kach li ki hi yashra be'einai* — and Shimshon said to his father, take her for me, for she is pleasing in my eyes. The visual register — *be'einai*, in my eyes — identifies sight as the gateway to sexual sin. The tzitzit redirects this visual faculty toward the sacred, guarding against the tendency of the eye to lead astray.

### Idolatry Adultery Metaph…

*Asher atem zonim achareihem* — which might initially sound like it refers to sexual sin — is in fact interpreted as *hirhur avoda zara*, idolatrous thought. The key text is *vayiznu acharei ha'be'alim* — and they went lusting after the Baalim — where the metaphor of fornication (*zenut*) is applied to the worship of false gods. The underlying image is the covenantal relationship between Israel and God as a marriage, so that turning to idolatry constitutes a form of adultery or fornication. This metaphor recurs throughout the prophets. Parashat Tzitzit thus addresses, in its compact final verse, the three great temptations that undermine the foundation of Jewish religious life.

Taken as a whole, the six elements embedded in Parashat Tzitzit are not merely a convenient list of important topics. They echo and amplify the central concerns of the earlier parshiyot: the unity and exclusivity of God (*shema yisrael*), the commandment to love God and fulfill His mitzvot (*ve'ahavta*), and the promise of reward and consequence (*ve'haya im shamoa*). The third paragraph thus rounds out the Shema as a unified declaration of religious commitment, adding the memory of Yetzias Mitzrayim and guarding against the specific temptations most likely to subvert that commitment.

---

## Yetzias Mitzrayim Baleil…

### Mishna Exodus Night

The Gemara now reaches the final Mishnah of the chapter: *mazkirin Yetzias Mitzrayim baleilos* — we mention the Exodus from Egypt at night. This refers not to the Pesach Seder but to the daily mitzvah of remembering the Exodus, ordinarily associated with Parashat Tzitzit in the Shema. The question is whether this obligation applies only by day or also by night. The Mishnah rules that it applies at night as well.

### Rabbi Elazar Difficulty

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya — speaking of himself as *keven shivim shana*, like one who was seventy years old, a reference to the well-known story of his aged appearance — declared that he never merited understanding how to derive a proof-text for mentioning the Exodus at night, until Ben Zoma came and expounded.

### Ben Zoma Derivation

Ben Zoma's derivation rests on the verse *lema'an tizkor et yom tzeischa me'eretz Mitzrayim kol yemei chayecha* — so that you will remember the day of your going out from Egypt all the days of your life. The phrase *yemei chayecha* alone would denote the days; the inclusion of *kol* — all — expands the obligation to encompass the nights as well. The days of your life are the daytime hours; *all* the days of your life includes the full span of each day, meaning the nights alongside the days.

### Mashiach Era Dispute

The Rabbis read the same verse differently. For them, *yemei chayecha* refers to this world, and the addition of *kol* extends the obligation into the time of Mashiach — meaning that even in the messianic era, the Exodus will still be remembered. Ben Zoma responds with a challenge from the prophet Yirmiyahu: *hinei yamim ba'im... velo yomru od chai Hashem asher he'ela et benei Yisrael me'eretz Mitzrayim* — days are coming when it will no longer be said: by the life of God who brought Israel out of Egypt — *ki im chai Hashem asher he'ela et zera beit Yisrael me'eretz tzafona* — but rather: by the life of God who brought the offspring of Israel from the north and from all the lands to which He had driven them. The ultimate redemption will be so encompassing that it will displace the Exodus as the primary oath-reference. If so, why would the Rabbis say we will still mention Yetzias Mitzrayim in the messianic era?

### Primary Secondary Resolu…

The Sages respond: *lo shetei'aker Yetzias Mitzrayim mimekoma* — it does not mean that the memory of Yetzias Mitzrayim will be uprooted — *ela sheteihei shibud malchuyot ikar veYetzias Mitzrayim tafel lo* — but rather that the redemption from the subjugation of all nations will be primary, and Yetzias Mitzrayim secondary to it. The original redemption will retain its standing as the foundational act of divine salvation; it will simply no longer occupy the primary position in the liturgy of praise and oath-taking.

A parallel case is adduced: *lo yikarei shimcha od Yaakov ki im Yisrael yiheyeh shemecha* — your name shall no longer be called Yaakov, for Yisrael shall be your name. Yet God subsequently addressed him as Yaakov. This shows that the earlier name was not abolished; Yisrael became primary and Yaakov secondary. Similarly, Yetzias Mitzrayim remains part of the vocabulary of redemption, but in the messianic age the larger redemption will be primary and Yetzias Mitzrayim subordinate to it.

Further support comes from Yeshayahu: *al tizkeru rishonot, vekadmoniyot al titbonanu* — do not remember the earlier things; do not reflect on the former ones. The Gemara reads *rishonot* as referring to the subjugation by the nations, and *kadmoniyot* as referring to Yetzias Mitzrayim. In the messianic era, says Rav Yosef, this new reality — identified as the war of Gog and Magog — will so overwhelm the prior ones that they will recede into the background.

### Parable Later Afflictions

The Gemara illustrates this with a parable. A man was walking on the road and encountered a wolf, was saved, and told everyone about the wolf. Later he encountered a lion, was saved, and told everyone about the lion — and forgot about the wolf. Later still he encountered a snake, was saved, and told everyone about the snake — and forgot about both. So too with Israel: later sufferings cause earlier ones to recede from consciousness. The greater the subsequent ordeal, the more it overshadows what came before.

This parable presents something of a tension with the resolution offered by the Rabbis. If the point of the parable is that later afflictions cause people to forget earlier ones, it seems to support Ben Zoma's position that Yetzias Mitzrayim will indeed be forgotten in the light of the ultimate redemption, rather than the Rabbinic position that it will be merely secondary. One possible reading is that the parable is precisely the motivation for the mitzvah: because human nature tends to be overwhelmed by the most recent experience, the Torah specifically commands us never to forget the earlier ones. The obligation to remember Yetzias Mitzrayim, even when greater salvations have occurred, is a counterweight to this natural psychological tendency.

---

## Supplanting Names

### Avram to Avraham

The Gemara's discussion of Yaakov and Yisrael as names that did not fully supplant one another leads naturally into a broader treatment of names that did change. A verse from Divrei Hayamim states: *avram hu avraham* — Avram is Avraham. The Gemara explains: originally he was made a father to Aram alone — *av le'Aram*, reflecting the name *avram* — but ultimately he became father to the entire world, *av hamon goyim*, father of a multitude of nations, reflected in the addition of the letter *hei* to form *avraham*.

### Sarai to Sarah

Similarly, *sarai hi sarah* — Sarai is Sarah. Originally Sarai was *sharet le'umata*, mistress of her own nation alone; ultimately she became *sarah*, mistress of all the world.

### Bar Kappara Avram Violat…

Bar Kappara teaches: *kol hakoreh leAvraham Avram over ba'aseh* — whoever calls Avraham by the name Avram transgresses a positive commandment, as the verse states *vehaya shimcha Avraham* — your name shall be Avraham. The new name is not merely descriptive but obligatory; to revert to the old name is to violate a positive mitzvah.

### Rabbi Eliezer Negative

Rabbi Eliezer goes further: it also constitutes a transgression of a negative prohibition, since the verse states *velo yikarei od shimcha Avram* — and your name shall no longer be called Avram. The formulation *velo yikarei* is not merely a statement of fact but a prohibition: do not call him Avram.

### Sarah Different Question

One might ask whether the same rules apply to the name Sarah: should calling her Sarai also constitute a transgression?

### Specific Command Answer

The Gemara answers by noting the precise wording of the divine command regarding Sarah: *sarai ishtecha lo tikra et shema sarai* — Sarai your wife, do not call her name Sarai — this is addressed to Avraham in the second person singular. *lo tikra* — you shall not call her — is a command to Avraham alone, not a universal prohibition for all people. By contrast, the command regarding the name Avraham — *velo yikarei od shimcha Avram* — uses a passive formulation implying a general prohibition against anyone calling him by the old name. Therefore the prohibition applies to the name Avram universally, but the instruction about Sarah was directed only to Avraham himself and does not generate a prohibition for others.

### Jacob Name Change

The Gemara turns to the comparable case of Yaakov. The verse states *lo yikarei shimcha od Yaakov ki im Yisrael yiheyeh shemecha* — your name shall no longer be called Yaakov, for Yisrael shall be your name. By analogy with Avraham, one might expect this too to carry a universal prohibition against using the name Yaakov.

### Scriptural Evidence Reve…

The Gemara rejects this comparison on the basis of a subsequent verse: *vayomer Elokim leYisrael bemarot halayla vayomer Yaakov Yaakov* — and God said to Yisrael in the visions of the night: Yaakov, Yaakov. God Himself reverted to addressing him as Yaakov, which demonstrates that the earlier instruction did not carry the same force as the prohibition regarding Avram.

### Avraham Yaakov Distincti…

The essential distinction is this: by Avraham, the name fully superseded the old one, and reverting to the name Avram constitutes a genuine transgression — both a positive violation according to Bar Kappara and a negative prohibition according to Rabbi Eliezer. By Yaakov, the name Yisrael became primary but the name Yaakov was not abolished; it remains as a secondary name, since God Himself continued to use it.

A practical question that naturally arises is whether one giving a shiur on Parashat Lech Lecha may say "when God spoke to Avram" — using the name that was in effect at the time. The final lines of the Gemara offer some guidance: the Gemara permits a Navi to praise God by recounting *mah dehavei me'ikara*, what happened in the past, including using the name Avram in that context, because the reference is to a historical moment when that was his name. Whether the same latitude extends to other contexts — whether one discussing Avraham's earlier deeds may use the earlier name — remains somewhat ambiguous within the Gemara. The dominant practice of using *avraham* in all contexts would seem to err on the side of stringency, and most authorities treat Bar Kappara's teaching as having at least the force of an *asmachta*, even if not a fully biblical prohibition.

---

---

# Berakhot 12b

## Emet Veyatziv & Emunah

### Intro: Morning/Evening

The preceding discussion on this daf concerned the *brachot* that surround the *Shema* — those recited before and after. We examined *Yotzer HaMeorot* and *Ahava Rabbah* before the *Shema*, noting how *Yotzer HaMeorot* belongs distinctively to the morning (paralleled by *Maariv Aravim* in the evening), while *Ahava Rabbah* and *Ahavat Olam* are tied more to the themes of *Shema* itself and *Talmud Torah*. We even discussed the possibility of reciting *Shema* without *Yotzer HaMeorot* if the proper time has not yet arrived — a ruling that underscores that fundamental distinction. We now turn to the *brachot* recited after the *Shema*: specifically, *Emet Veyatziv* and *Emet Ve'emunah*.

### Emet Veyatziv vs Emunah

Rabbah bar Chinena Sava teaches in the name of Rav: whoever did not say *Emet Veyatziv* in the morning and *Emet Ve'emunah* in the evening has not fulfilled his obligation. The point here is not merely that one must recite a *bracha* at the close of *Shema* — that much is already established — but that the specific formulation matters. Just as there is a distinction between *Maariv Aravim* and *Yotzer HaMeorot*, and a subtler but real distinction between *Ahava Rabbah* and *Ahavat Olam*, so too there is a meaningful difference in the closing *bracha*: *Emet Veyatziv* in the morning and *Emet Ve'emunah* in the evening.

### Psalm Source

The textual basis is drawn from Psalms: *lehagid baboker chasdecha ve'emunatecha baleilot* — "to tell of Your kindness in the morning and Your faithfulness in the nights." The morning is the time of *chesed*, of experiencing God's beneficence and gifts; the evening draws forth a different register — a sense of concern, of darkness, of uncertainty about the night ahead, evoking hope and trust rather than celebration of manifest blessing. This parallels the distinction between *Ahava Rabbah* and *Ahavat Olam* precisely: the morning *bracha* emphasizes experienced love and abundance, the evening *bracha* an enduring love sustained through faith even when God's presence is less immediately felt.

### Rashi: Content Themes

Rashi makes an important observation two lines before the relevant passage. He notes that *Emet Veyatziv* is entirely about the *chesed* God performed for our ancestors — taking them out of Egypt, splitting the sea, and bringing them across. By contrast, *Emet Ve'emunah* speaks also of future hope: we await the fulfillment of God's promise and His faithfulness to redeem us from the power of kings. This is not only a matter of past versus future, of praise versus petition, but reflects the experiential morning-evening difference as well — the same dynamic that distinguishes *Ahava Rabbah* from *Ahavat Olam*.

---

## Bowing & Rising

### Bow at Baruch, Rise at S…

Rabbah bar Chinena Sava teaches another ruling in the name of Rav, this one concerning bodily posture during the *Amidah*: when one bows, one should bow at the word *Baruch*; when one rises, one should rise at *Shem Hashem*. The choreography is precise — bending the knees at *Baruch*, remaining bowed through *Atah*, and straightening as God's name is pronounced.

### Samuel's Reason

Samuel offers the rationale: as it is written, *Hashem zokef kefufim* — God straightens those who are bent. It is therefore the utterance of God's name that causes the worshiper to rise from the bowed position. The name of God is what elevates us.

### Challenge: Name & Humili…

The Gemara raises a challenge from the verse *mipnei shemi nichat* — "because of My name he is humbled." This verse appears to indicate the opposite: that God's name produces a sense of lowliness and humility, not elevation.

### Resolution

The Gemara resolves the tension: the verse says *mipnei shemi* — because of My name, on account of the concept of God's name — not *bishmi*, in the articulation of My name. The contemplation of God's greatness produces humility; but the actual utterance of God's name in prayer is the moment of reaching out and connecting, which is what raises the worshiper upright.

This resolution reflects a dialectic that has run throughout the earlier discussion. Prayer simultaneously requires a profound sense of our own smallness and an act of reaching toward God. We encountered this earlier in the ruling that one should stand in a low place yet with feet together like an angel. Here too: the bowing down expresses our nothingness in the presence of God, while the pronouncing of His name — the act of connection — is precisely what lifts us. Samuel's teaching to Chiya bar Rav, whom he addresses as *bar orayan* — whether "son of a lion" or "son of Torah" — conveys this exact principle: "Let me tell you something beautiful your father said." What follows is the same teaching we have just seen, transmitted in Rav's name.

### Rav Sheshet's Example

The Gemara moves to 12b and describes the practice of Rav Sheshet: when he bowed down, he would bow like a rod — that is, like a staff thrown to the ground, immediately, all at once, without hesitation. And when he rose, he rose like a snake — slowly, gradually, the way a snake rises from the ground, head first. Rashi explains that the bowing should not resemble a *massa*, a burden one is eager to put down; the emphasis must fall on the immediacy of awe before God. The weight is on falling before Him without hesitation, while the rising is a slow, effortful process of regaining one's stature — again capturing that interplay between humility and the dignity of connection.

---

## HaMelech HaKadosh

### Year-Round Phrasing

Rabbah bar Chinena Sava transmits yet another teaching from Rav, now concerning the *nusach* of *Shemoneh Esrei* rather than its physical performance. Throughout the entire year, when one recites the third *bracha* of *Shemoneh Esrei*, one says *Ha'El HaKadosh*; and in the *bracha* concerning justice in the middle of *Shemoneh Esrei*, one says *Melech Ohev Tzedakah u'Mishpat*.

### Ten Days Exception

The exception is the ten days encompassing Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur — the *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah*. It should be noted that technically there are only seven days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, but the expression refers to the ten days as a unit. During this period, one says *HaMelech HaKadosh* instead of *Ha'El HaKadosh*, and *HaMelech HaMishpat* instead of *Melech Ohev Tzedakah u'Mishpat*. The theme of God's *malchut* dominates these days; accordingly, not only does *Melech* remain in the formula (as it always was), but *mishpat* is no longer merely something God loves — it becomes the very expression of His identity. Both *melech* and *mishpat* are intensified.

It is worth noting that *HaMelech HaKadosh* on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur themselves was not really in dispute — the question was whether to extend this formulation across the full *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah*, and whether *HaMelech HaMishpat* follows the same pattern.

### Rabbi Eliezer: Lenient

Rabbi Eliezer takes a more lenient position: even if one said *Ha'El HaKadosh* during the *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah*, one has fulfilled the obligation *bedieved*. His proof is from the verse: *vayigbah Hashem Tzeva'ot bamishpat veha'El haKadosh nikdash bitzedakah* — the glory of God is magnified through judgment, and the holy God is sanctified through righteousness. Rabbi Eliezer reads this verse as referring precisely to the *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah*, when the focus is on God as judge, and yet the verse concludes with *Ha'El HaKadosh*. This suggests that *Ha'El HaKadosh* remains acceptable even during those days, and presumably *Melech Ohev Tzedakah u'Mishpat* as well.

### Rav Yosef vs Rabbah

The Gemara asks what the final ruling is. Rav Yosef holds that one maintains the regular *nusach* — presumably even *lechatchila* one says *Ha'El HaKadosh* and *Melech Ohev Tzedakah u'Mishpat*, and the change to *HaMelech HaKadosh* applies only on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur themselves, not across the intervening days. Rabbah disagrees and rules that one says *HaMelech HaKadosh* and *HaMelech HaMishpat* throughout the *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah*. The Gemara rules: *ve'hilchata keRabbah* — the *halacha* follows Rabbah, as indeed reflects our accepted *psak*.

### Tosafot: Must Repeat

Tosafot notes that if one failed to say *HaMelech HaKadosh* or *HaMelech HaMishpat* during the *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah*, one must repeat the *Shemoneh Esrei*. Tosafot then extends this principle to the additional insertions of *Zachreinu leChayyim*, *Mi Chamocha*, *Ketov leChayyim*, and *uveSefer Chayyim* — all of which were added to the *nusach* by the *Geonim* — and initially suggests that if one omitted these as well, one must return. However, Tosafot ultimately qualifies this: Rabbeinu Tam (or Rabbeinu Chananel, depending on the reading) writes that since these additions were not explicitly ruled upon in the Talmud, one does not return for them. And that is indeed how we rule: one returns for *HaMelech HaKadosh* and *HaMelech HaMishpat*, but not for the *Zachreinu* formulas and similar additions introduced by later authorities.

---

## Praying for Others

### Can Pray = Must Pray

We have now seen three teachings transmitted by Rabbah bar Chinena Sava in the name of Rav: the distinction between *Emet Veyatziv* and *Emet Ve'emunah*; the laws of bowing and rising; and the *nusach* of *HaMelech HaKadosh* and *HaMelech HaMishpat*. A fourth teaching follows: whoever is in a position to pray on behalf of a friend and does not do so is called a sinner.

### Samuel's Proof

The proof is from the words of Samuel to Saul: *Gam anochi chalilah li mecheto la'Hashem mechadol lehitpalel ba'adchem* — "Far be it from me to sin against God by ceasing to pray on your behalf." The implication is that withholding prayer when you could offer it constitutes a sin.

The force of this teaching deserves reflection. People typically engage in *tefillah* as a statutory obligation, which does not necessarily express a deep personal conviction about the way God operates in the world. But when someone responds to a specific situation — when they perceive a friend's need and pray because something is actually at stake — that reflects a real, lived belief in the efficacy of prayer. The *chaveiro* dimension adds an additional layer: it is not only about faith, but about care for another person. If you believe that prayer can help, and your friend needs it, then failing to pray constitutes a kind of abandonment. That gives the entire concept of prayer a dimension beyond obligation — it becomes a means of helping others, something we bear responsibility for.

### Rava: Extra Measure

Rava adds a further requirement: if the person who needs your prayers is a *talmid chacham*, it is not sufficient merely to pray — one must make oneself ill on his behalf. The Gemara asks what the source for this is. The verse cited is Saul's complaint that no one was *choleh* for him — nobody was sick with worry on his account, no one was revealing things to him. The Gemara reads this literally: making yourself sick over the person is the standard required. But perhaps that obligation applies only for a king? The Gemara deflects to a different verse: David's statement, *va'ani bechalotam levushi* — in their illness I wore sackcloth. David afflicted himself when others fell ill, and that becomes the model for how intensely one must pray for a *talmid chacham*.

### Shame Leads to Forgivene…

The teaching shifts now from prayer to moral psychology, though the common thread is the interior life of religious obligation. Rabbah bar Chinena Sava teaches in the name of Rav: anyone who commits a sin and is ashamed by it has all his sins forgiven. This connects to an earlier theme — that internalizing a message through genuine feeling is more transformative than external punishment. When a person feels shame, when they are genuinely embarrassed by what they have done, that experience can catalyze a profound inner transformation. The forgiveness of *kol avonotav* is not merely a consequence of suffering; it reflects the hope that shame will produce real change.

### Shame & Atonement

The textual basis is the verse: *lema'an tizkeri uvoshet velo yihyeh lach od pitchon peh mipnei kelimatecha bechappri lach lechol asher asit ne'um Hashem Elokim* — "in order that you remember and be embarrassed, and no longer have any opening because of your shame, when I atone for you for all that you have done, says the Lord God." The Gemara reads this causally: because you bear the shame, God will atone for you.

### Saul's Example

The Gemara asks whether perhaps this applies only to the entire community, *tzibbur*, in the kind of collective national shame the verse describes — not to an individual. A second proof is therefore brought for the individual case, drawn from the exchange between Samuel and Saul when Samuel's spirit was raised.

Saul says to Samuel: *tzar li me'od uPlishtim nilchamim bi ve'Elokim sar me'alai velo anani od gam beyad hanevi'im gam bachalomot* — I am greatly distressed, the Philistines are fighting me, God has turned away from me and no longer answers me through prophets or through dreams. The Gemara notices something significant: Saul lists the channels through which he sought God's guidance — prophets and dreams — but conspicuously omits the *Urim v'Tummim*. Why? Because he had destroyed Nov, the city of the *kohanim*, and there was no one left to consult the *Urim v'Tummim*. His failure to mention it reflects an acute awareness of his guilt — he was too ashamed to raise the subject. His silence, for the Gemara, is itself an expression of genuine remorse.

The proof that Saul was forgiven: Samuel says to him, *umachar atah uvannecha immi* — tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. Rabbi Yochanan interprets this as *immi bimchitzati* — in my portion in the World to Come. Because Saul bore his shame, even in this minimal and largely passive form of not mentioning what he had done, he merited the World to Come and all his sins were forgiven. The bar for what constitutes meaningful shame, in this teaching, is set strikingly low — and perhaps that is precisely the point.

A second proof is brought from the verse *bechir Hashem* — "the chosen of God" — which appears in the context of the Gibeonites' complaint against Saul. The Gemara argues that it is not the Gibeonites themselves using this honorific but rather a heavenly voice that declared Saul to be God's chosen — and the reason is the same: because he felt shame over the destruction of Nov and withheld mention of it.

---

## Parashat Balak

### Proposal Overview

The Gemara now returns from this extended discussion to the topic of the liturgy surrounding *Kriyas Shema*. Rabbi Abba bar Zutrati cites Rabbi Yehuda bar Zvida: the Sages sought to include *Parshas Balak* as part of *Kriyas Shema*. This is a striking proposal — that a portion of the prophetic narrative concerning Balak and Bilam would become part of the daily recitation of *Shema*.

### Why Balak?

The Gemara first suggests the reason: *Parshas Balak* contains the verse *El motzi'am miMitzrayim* — "God who brought them out of Egypt." The third *parsha* of *Shema* — *Parshas Tzitzis* — is recited largely in order to fulfill the independent *mitzvah* of remembering *Yetzias Mitzrayim*. One might think that *Parshas Balak* could serve this function equally, containing as it does a reference to the exodus. Indeed, the Gemara implies they would have made this substitution had the passage not been too lengthy — *torach tzibbur*, an imposition on the community.

### Objection

The Gemara presses further: many *parshiyot* contain references to the exodus — the prohibition of *ribis*, the laws of honest weights. If the sole criterion were the mention of *Yetzias Mitzrayim*, why should *Parshas Balak* be singled out? The reference to the exodus alone cannot be the full explanation.

### Rabbi Yosi Answer

Rabbi Yosi bar Avin provides the deeper reason: *Parshas Balak* contains the verse *kara shachav ka'ari uchelavia mi yekimenu* — "he crouched, he lay down like a lion, like a whelp — who will rouse him?" Rashi explains that this verse precisely parallels the central theme of *Kriyas Shema* — the lying down (*shechivah*) and rising up (*kimah*) that frame the daily recitation of *Shema*. Thus *Parshas Balak* would not merely supply a reference to *Yetzias Mitzrayim* but would echo the very thematic structure of *Kriyas Shema* itself, making it an organically fitting inclusion.

### Moshe's Divisions Rule

The Gemara then asks: if the critical verse is *kara shachav ka'ari* along with *El motzi'am miMitzrayim*, why not simply recite those two verses and leave it at that? There would be no *torach tzibbur* — just the essential content. The Gemara answers with a principle: *kol parsha d'paska Moshe Rabbeinu paskinan; d'la paska Moshe Rabbeinu la paskinan* — any *parsha* that Moses divided, we may divide; any *parsha* that Moses did not divide, we may not divide. We cannot extract individual verses from *Parshas Balak* for liturgical use; it must be either included in its entirety or not at all.

It is worth distinguishing this principle from the related rule that one does not divide a *pasuk* — that even as an individual, one should not quote only part of a verse. That rule governs individual speech. The principle here is specifically about the creation of official liturgy: we do not construct liturgy by taking selections from within an undivided *parsha*. That is why *Parshas Balak* was ultimately not included — its length made full inclusion impossible, and partial inclusion is prohibited by tradition.

---

## Parashat Tzitzit

### Five Themes

If *Parshas Balak* was not chosen, why was *Parshas Tzitzis* selected for *Kriyas Shema*? Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva explains: because *Parshas Tzitzis* contains not merely one or two significant themes but five essential elements that together make it uniquely suited.

### The Five Elements

The five themes are: the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* itself; *Yetzias Mitzrayim*; *ol mitzvot*, the yoke of the commandments; *da'at minim*, guarding against heretical thoughts; and *hirhur aveira*, the guarding against sinful thoughts — including *hirhur avodah zarah*, thoughts of idolatry. The Gemara notes that some reckon these as six rather than five, leading some to emend the *girsa* accordingly.

### Yoke of Mitzvot

The first three are readily derivable from the text. *Ol mitzvot* is based on the verse *ur'item oto uzchartem et kol mitzvot Hashem* — "you shall see it and remember all the commandments of God." *Tzitzit* itself is stated explicitly: *asu lachem tzitzit*. And *Yetzias Mitzrayim* is stated directly: *asher hotzeiti etchem*. These three are straightforward.

### Heresy Theme

The remaining themes require derivation. *Da'at minim* — heresy — comes from the phrase *acharei levavchem*, "do not stray after your hearts." In the conceptual world of *Chazal*, the heart is not only the seat of emotion but of intellect and thought. Straying after the heart therefore means being led astray by the mind into heretical ideas, into the intellectual rejection of God's existence or sovereignty. The Gemara supports this with the verse: *amar naval belibo ein Elohim* — the degenerate says in his heart there is no God. The *leiv* is the organ of heresy; the *tzitzit* keep the eye and mind anchored to truth.

### Sexual Sin Theme

*Hirhur aveira* — sinful thoughts, specifically of a sexual nature — is derived from *acharei eineichem*, "do not stray after your eyes." The support is from Shimshon, who says of the Philistine woman he desires: *otah kach li ki hi yashra be'einai* — "take her for me, for she is right in my eyes." Desire begins with visual perception; the eyes lead the heart into sin. The *tzitzit*, visible and present, redirect that gaze.

### Idolatry Theme

Finally, *hirhur avodah zarah* — thoughts of idolatry — is derived from *asher atem zonim achareihem*, "you will stray after them." Though the word *zonim* sounds like sexual infidelity, the Gemara explains it refers to spiritual infidelity, citing the verse *vayiznu acharei habalim* — "and they went astray after the *Ba'alim*." The relationship between Israel and God is consistently figured in the Torah as a marriage; worship of false gods is therefore described through the metaphor of adultery. The *tzitzit* guard against this ultimate betrayal.

Beyond the intrinsic importance of each of these themes, they resonate with the broader content of *Kriyas Shema* itself. *Ol mitzvot* echoes the commitment to observe the *mitzvot* expressed in the first two *parshiyot*. The warnings against *minut* and *avodah zarah* echo *Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* — the proclamation of God's unity and the rejection of all that contradicts it. The inclusion of *Parshas Tzitzis* thus reinforces and expands the central themes of *Shema* while simultaneously fulfilling the independent *mitzvah* of remembering *Yetzias Mitzrayim*.

---

## Remember Exodus

### Mishnah Statement

This discussion leads directly into the final *Mishnah* of the chapter. The *Mishnah* states: *mazkirin Yetzias Mitzrayim balaylot* — one mentions the exodus from Egypt at night. The context is *Kriyas Shema*: we know that *Shema* is recited both by day and by night, and that *Parshas Tzitzis* fulfills the separate *mitzvah* of remembering *Yetzias Mitzrayim*. The question the *Mishnah* addresses is whether there is an obligation to remember *Yetzias Mitzrayim* at night as well.

### Rabbi Elazar's Lament

Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah — who was appointed *nasi* and miraculously appeared to age, such that he could say "I am like a seventy-year-old man" — declares that he never merited understanding how to derive the obligation of mentioning *Yetzias Mitzrayim* at night, until Ben Zoma came and explained it.

### Ben Zoma's Proof

Ben Zoma's proof rests on close reading of the verse *lema'an tizkor et yom tzeischa me'eretz Mitzrayim kol yemei chayyecha* — "so that you remember the day of your going out from Egypt all the days of your life." *Yemei chayyecha* would mean simply "the days of your life," i.e., daytime. But the word *kol* — "all" — extends the obligation to the fullness of each day, which includes the night. Thus the obligation to remember *Yetzias Mitzrayim* applies not only by day but by night as well.

### Sages' Counter

The Sages offer a different reading of the same *kol*. For them, *yemei chayyecha* refers to the days of this world, and *kol yemei chayyecha* — "all the days of your life" — means throughout this world, even into the future. The *kol* does not double the daily obligation into day and night; rather, it extends the temporal scope to ensure the obligation is not nullified even in the messianic era.

---

## Remember Exodus (II)

### Messianic Era

The Sages add: *lehavi limos haMashiach* — even in the days of the Messiah, when a greater redemption will have occurred, the memory of *Yetzias Mitzrayim* will not be set aside. The obligation persists across all time.

---

## Ben Zoma's Challenge

### Challenge Posed

The *Baraita* reports that Ben Zoma posed a direct challenge to the Sages on this very point. Would one really continue to mention *Yetzias Mitzrayim* in the messianic era? He cites the prophet's words: *hinei yamim ba'im ne'um Hashem velo ye'amer od Chai Hashem asher he'elah et Benei Yisrael me'eretz Mitzrayim ki im Chai Hashem asher he'elah ve'asher hevi et zera Beit Yisrael me'eretz tzafonah umikol ha'aratzos asher hidachtim sham* — "Days are coming, says God, when they will no longer say 'by the life of God who brought the Children of Israel out of Egypt,' but rather 'by the life of God who brought up and led the descendants of the House of Israel from the northern land and from all the lands where He had driven them.'" The future redemption will eclipse *Yetzias Mitzrayim* as the primary frame of reference; oaths will be sworn by the greater act of redemption. Ben Zoma therefore asks: will *Yetzias Mitzrayim* even be mentioned?

### Sages' Response

The Sages respond: *lo she'te'aker Yetzias Mitzrayim mimkomah* — this does not mean that *Yetzias Mitzrayim* loses its place entirely. Rather, *shibud malchuyot* — the redemption from all the nations — will become the *ikar*, the primary focus, and *Yetzias Mitzrayim* will become *tafel*, secondary, but still present and still remembered.

### Jacob Example

The Sages support this with the parallel of Jacob's name change: *lo yikarei shimcha od Yaakov ki im Yisrael yihyeh shemecha* — "your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name." Yet God Himself later calls him Jacob. This is not a contradiction; it means that the name Yisrael becomes the *ikar* while Yaakov becomes secondary — but both names remain his. So too with *Yetzias Mitzrayim*: it does not disappear; it is simply no longer primary.

### Prophet's Support

Further prophetic support is adduced from the verse: *al tizkeru rishonot veKadmoniyot al titbonanu* — "do not remember the former things and do not contemplate the earlier ones." The Gemara interprets: *rishonot* refers to *shibud malchuyot* — the servitude under the nations; *kadmoniyot* refers to *Yetzias Mitzrayim*. Both will still be remembered, but neither will dominate the consciousness of the redeemed — the new salvation, *hineni oseh chadashah*, will be primary. The school of Rav Yosef identifies this new thing as the war of *Gog u'Magog*.

### Parable of Dangers

A parable is offered: a man was walking and encountered a wolf, from which he was saved. He told everyone about the wolf. Then he encountered a lion and was saved; he told everyone about the lion. Then he encountered a snake and was saved — and he forgot both the wolf and the lion, speaking only of the snake. So too with Israel: *tzaros achronos meshakechos es harishonos* — the later afflictions cause the earlier ones to recede in memory, because the most recent danger seems greatest.

It must be acknowledged that as a parable, this seems to cut somewhat against the Sages' conclusion rather than supporting it — for the man in the story actually *forgot* the earlier dangers, which would seem to support Ben Zoma's view that *Yetzias Mitzrayim* will no longer be mentioned. One reading is that the Gemara's point may be precisely the inverse: because human nature is to focus only on the most recent and most acute experience, the obligation is *davka* to continue remembering the earlier ones. The *mitzvah* exists precisely because the inclination is to forget. The Gemara, however, does not explicitly close this circle, and the tension remains.

---

## Name Changes

### Avram to Avraham

The Gemara now addresses the question of name changes as such, beginning with Avraham. The verse in *Divrei HaYamim* states: *Avram hu Avraham* — Avram is Avraham. The Gemara explains: initially he was made a father — *av* — to Aram alone, to the people of his region, *Aram Naharayim*. In the end he was made a father to the entire world — *av hamon goyim*, the father of many nations. The letter *heh* added to his name captures this expansion of scope.

### Sarai to Sarah

Similarly, *Sarai hi Sarah* — Sarai is Sarah. Initially she was *sarai* to her own nation alone — the possessive form, "my princess." In the end she became *Sarah* without the possessive, a princess to all the world.

### Bar Kappara Positive

Bar Kappara rules: anyone who calls Avraham by the name Avram transgresses a positive commandment, as the verse states: *v'hayah shimcha Avraham* — "your name shall be Avraham." The declaration of the name change carries the force of a *mitzvat asei*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Negative

Rabbi Eliezer goes further: it is not only a positive commandment but a negative prohibition. The basis is *v'lo yikarei od shimcha Avram* — "your name shall no longer be called Avram." This is not merely a statement of fact but an active prohibition.

### Sarah Question

The Gemara asks: if this is so regarding Avraham, should the same not apply to Sarah — that calling her by the old name Sarai would also be forbidden?

### Distinction

The Gemara draws a distinction. In the case of Avraham's name, God's command was given to Avraham in general terms, applicable to all: *v'hayah shimcha Avraham* and *v'lo yikarei od shimcha Avram* — universal declarations. But regarding Sarah's name, the verse reads: *Sarai ishtecha lo tikra et shemah Sarai ki Sarah shemah* — "Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, for Sarah is her name." The address is in the second person singular — *lo tikra*, *you* shall not call her — directed specifically to Avraham, not to the world at large. There is therefore no general prohibition for others to call her Sarai.

### Chronicles Reference

The Gemara anticipates an objection: the verse in *Divrei HaYamim* itself uses the name Avram — *asher bacharta be'Avram* — "who chose Avram." Does this not indicate that calling him Avram is permissible?

The Gemara answers: there the *navi* is recounting the past — he is describing the moment of God's original choice, when the patriarch's name was indeed Avram, and declaring that God chose him then and subsequently gave him the name Avraham. The prophet is narrating what *was*, not referring to the patriarch by his old name as a present designation. The question of precisely when that line is crossed — whether a teacher explaining *Parshas Lech Lecha* may say "when God spoke to Avram" or must say "when God spoke to Avraham" — is left somewhat ambiguous by the Gemara. Most would naturally say Avraham in any case. Whether one would transgress a *lav* or an *asei* by saying Avram in such a context, and whether these are truly biblical prohibitions or function as *asmachta*, remains an open question that the sugya raises without fully resolving.

---

---

# Berakhot 13

## Interruptions & Breaks

### Chapter Overview

The first chapter of *Berakhot* focused primarily on the structural aspects of *Shema*: the times of its recitation, the surrounding *brachot*, and certain postural questions. The second chapter turns its attention to the act of saying *Shema* itself — the internal quality of the recitation, the permissibility of interruptions, and the nature of the intention required.

### Torah Learning & Kavanah

The chapter opens with the following case: one is reading through the Torah — simply learning, practicing the text of *Parshat Vaetchanan*, for example — and the time of *kriyat Shema* arrives. *Im kiven libo yatza* — if he directs his heart, if he reads with the intention of fulfilling the obligation, he is *yotzei*. This seemingly straightforward ruling carries within it a significant implication, which the *Gemara* will immediately interrogate: it appears to demonstrate that *mitzvot tzerichot kavanah* — that the performance of commandments requires intention.

### Bein Prakim vs. Emtza

The *Mishnah* then addresses permitted interruptions. *Biprakim* — at the breaks between sections — one may greet a person of importance out of *kavod*, honor, and may respond to a greeting from anyone. *Uve'emtza* — in the middle of a section — the threshold is higher: one may only initiate a greeting out of *yira*, genuine fear of the person's reaction. Rashi goes as far as to say this means fear for one's life. One may, however, respond even within a section out of a lesser degree of concern.

### R. Meir vs. R. Yehuda

This is the position of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda offers a slightly more lenient framework specifically regarding *responses*. He agrees that in the middle of a section one may only initiate a greeting out of *yira*, but to respond to a greeting, even *uve'emtza*, the threshold is only *kavod*. At the breaks, Rabbi Yehuda holds that one may respond to absolutely anyone — even a person toward whom there is no special concern of *kavod* — since failing to respond to any greeting is itself a form of affront. The underlying principle shared by both opinions is that responding carries a lower threshold than initiating, an implicit *kal vachomer*.

### Section Divisions

The *Mishnah* then enumerates what constitutes *bein haprakim* — the permissible breaks. These are: between the first *bracha* and the second, between the second *bracha* and *Shema*, between *Shema* and *Vehaya im Shamoa*, and between *Vehaya im Shamoa* and *Vayomer*. The units are understood as the full first *bracha*, the full second *bracha*, and then the three *parshiyot* of *Shema* in sequence. These are the halachic units between which interruption is comparatively more permissible.

### Vayomer-Emet Veyatziv

Notably, Rabbi Yehuda adds that between *Vayomer* and *Emet Veyatziv* — the *bracha* that begins immediately following *Shema* — one should not interrupt at all. The phrase *Hashem Elokeichem emet* bridges the two, and Rabbi Yehuda insists that this transition must flow without pause. This is striking: despite Rabbi Yehuda's generally more lenient posture regarding responses, here he draws a sharp line. Interestingly, this raises a question about the common practice of saying *Amen* after *habocheir b'amo Yisrael b'ahava*. The broader concern of *semichat ge'ula l'tefilla* — the imperative to adjoin the *bracha* of redemption directly to the *Shemoneh Esrei* — is even more stringent, as the *Gemara* elsewhere expressed discomfort even with *Hashem sefatai tiftach* as an interruption. The *bracha* before *Shema* does not have the full character of a classic *birchat hamitzvah* — it lacks the *asher kidshanu bemitzvotav* formulation — and that may explain why somewhat greater latitude applies there.

---

## Order of Parshiyot

### R. Yehoshua b. Korcha

With the *Mishnah* now being the first place to enumerate all three *parshiyot* of *Shema* together, the *Gemara* introduces a teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: *Lama kadma parshat Shema leVehaya im Shamoa?* — Why does the first *parsha* precede the second? The answer is: *kedei sheyekabel alav ol malchus shamayim techila v'achar kach mekabel alav ol mitzvot* — so that one first accepts the yoke of heavenly sovereignty and only thereafter accepts the yoke of commandments.

### Ol Malchus First

The structure reflects a theological priority. The first *parsha* — *Shema Yisrael*, *Ve'ahavta* — is centrally about the relationship between the person and God: belief, love, and acceptance of God's sovereignty. The obligations of observance appear only secondarily. The second *parsha*, *Vehaya im Shamoa*, contains the framework of reward and consequence for *mitzvot*, but lacks the foundational declaration of *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad*. The order thus places *ol malchus shamayim* before *ol mitzvot* — love and acceptance of God before the concrete obligations that flow from that relationship.

### Day vs. Night

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha then explains the placement of *Vehaya im Shamoa* before *Vayomer*: *she'Vehaya im Shamoa noheig bein bayom uvein balaila* — *Vehaya im Shamoa* applies both by day and by night, whereas *Vayomer* — the *parsha* of *tzitzit* — applies only by day. Rashi emphasizes that the *mitzvot* of the second *parsha*, including *talmud Torah*, apply at all times, while *tzitzit* is a daytime obligation.

A deeper reading, which Rashi also indicates later, concerns not the *mitzvot* of the *parsha* but the recitation of the *parsha* itself within *Shema*. Recall that the previous *Mishnah* raised the question of whether *Parshat Tzitzit* is said at night at all, since *mazkirin yetziat Mitzrayim* — the remembrance of the Exodus — which is the purpose of that *parsha*, may not apply at night. On this view, *Vayomer* was perhaps understood as a daytime recitation only, meaning the obligation to include it in *Shema* applies only by day. The halachic ruling ultimately follows the position that there is a *mitzvah* to say it at night as well, and indeed to mention *yetziat Mitzrayim* at night. But the *baraita* here may be articulating an earlier, differing opinion.

---

## Kavanah Debate

### Mitzvot & Kavanah

The *Gemara* now directly addresses the opening ruling: *shema mina mitzvot tzerichot kavanah* — apparently the *Mishnah* proves that *mitzvot* require intention. However, the *Gemara* immediately questions this inference: the debate over *mitzvot tzerichot kavanah* is well established, so how can this *Mishnah* simply resolve it?

### Act vs. Fulfillment

The *Gemara* therefore reframes the *Mishnah*'s meaning. When it says *im kiven libo*, it does not mean *kavanah* to be *yotzei* the *mitzvah* — the intent to fulfill the obligation — but rather *kavanah* to read, that is, intention to perform the act itself. There is an important distinction here: even those who hold that *mitzvot* do not require intent to fulfill still agree that one must intend to do the act one is doing. The paradigmatic case used elsewhere is the *shofar*: if a person attempts to clean out the *shofar* by blowing and inadvertently produces the required sound, everyone agrees one is not *yotzei*, because there was no intent to blow at all. The debate concerns whether, once the act is intended, one additionally needs intent to fulfill the *mitzvah*. Here too, then, the *Mishnah* may only be requiring that the person intend to read — not that one must specifically intend to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *Shema*.

### Proofreading Example

But the *Gemara* immediately presses: *veha ka kari* — the person is clearly reading! Unlike the case of the *shofar*, where one could blow without meaning to make a sound, how could someone be reciting words without intending to read? The *Gemara* answers: *bekorei lehagiah* — the case is one who is proofreading. Rashi explains that when one is comparing texts or checking a *Sefer Torah*, one may be mumbling the words as a function of that act of checking, without the recitation rising to the level of a genuine act of reading. The words may even be said aloud, but they serve the purpose of comparison rather than reading as such. In this case, *kavanah* is required to transform the incidental recitation into an act of *keriah*.

*Tosafot*, however, cannot accept this answer. How, Tosafot asks, can one be reciting words without intending to read them? Tosafot therefore understands the *Mishnah*'s *kavanah* requirement differently: it refers to attentiveness to read accurately, not to a formal act-intention. But this reading does not appear to capture what the *Gemara* itself is after. The upshot in any case is that this *Mishnah* cannot serve as a proof for the position of *mitzvot tzerichot kavanah*, since the *kavanah* required may refer only to the intent to perform the act, which is a separate and less contested requirement. The *Yerushalmi*, notably, draws a further inference from this *Mishnah*: that one is *yotzei* the biblical obligation of *Shema* even without the surrounding *brachot*, since the *brachot* are *derabbanan*. Though the full rabbinic package of *kriyat Shema uvirchoteha* carries particular significance — the *brachot* amplify and extend the themes of *Shema* rather than simply framing a *mitzvah* — one nonetheless fulfills the biblical *mitzvah* without them.

---

## Hebrew vs. Translation

### R. (Judah HaNasi) Rule

A *baraita* records the following dispute: *Kriyat Shema kechatvah* — *Shema* must be recited as written, meaning in Hebrew. This is the position of *Rebbi* (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi).

### Chachamim Rule

The *Chachamim* disagree: *bechol lashon* — in any language. Translation is permissible.

### Understanding vs. Act

The *Gemara* probes the reasoning of each position. *Rebbi* derives from the word *vehayu* — "and these words shall be" — that they must remain as they are, i.e., in Hebrew. The *Chachamim* derive from the word *shema* — "hear" — that the requirement is comprehension: in any language by which one can hear and understand. This conceptual disagreement — is *Shema* primarily an act of recitation or primarily a communicative act of understanding? — maps directly onto the subsequent debate about hearing one's own recitation.

### Hearing Requirement

The *Gemara* then notes that *Rebbi*, who derives from *vehayu* that Hebrew is required, must interpret *shema* differently. He therefore uses *shema* to teach *lehashmia le'oznecha mah she'atah motzi mipichah* — one must cause one's ears to hear what one's mouth is saying. The act of *Shema* requires audibility; one cannot recite it below the threshold of one's own hearing.

The *Chachamim*, by contrast, hold that even if one did not hear one's own recitation — *lo hishmia le'ozno yatza* — one is nonetheless *yotzei*. This position coheres with their conceptual emphasis: since *Shema* is primarily about understanding and communicating content rather than performing a formal act of speech, the failure to produce audible sound does not disqualify the recitation, as long as one genuinely engaged with the words.

This fits a broader pattern: *Rebbi*, who insists on Hebrew and on audibility, grounds the *mitzvah* in the act of recitation. The *Chachamim*, who permit any language and do not require audibility, ground it in communication and comprehension. The debate is not merely technical but reflects a deeper disagreement about the nature of the obligation. A further question arises as to whether the standard is that the person themselves must hear, or that the recitation must be objectively audible to someone — a distinction the *Gemara* leaves for subsequent discussion.

The *Gemara* then addresses how each camp handles the other's prooftext. *Vehayu*, which *Rebbi* uses to require Hebrew, the *Chachamim* interpret as requiring that *Shema* be recited in order — *shelo yikra lemafrei'a*, one may not reverse the sequence. And *Shema*, which the *Chachamim* use to permit any language, *Rebbi* interprets as the hearing requirement. The *Gemara* then considers whether the need to cite these prooftexts reveals each side's default assumption about the language of *mitzvot*, but concludes that no clean inference can be drawn: each side needed its prooftext precisely to counteract the inference created by the other's, so neither default can be established from this exchange alone.

---

## Kavanah Scope

### Two Pesukim Rule

The *Gemara* returns to the question of *kavanah* and now sets out to define precisely how much of *Shema* requires it. A *baraita* interprets the *pasuk* of *Shema* closely: *vehayu* teaches that one must not read out of order; *al levavecha* — "on your heart" — that one must have *kavanah*. The question then becomes: is it possible that the entire *parsha* requires *kavanah*? The *baraita* responds: *talmud lomar ha'eileh* — the word "these" limits the requirement. *Ad kan tzricha kavanah, mikan va'eilach ein tzricha kavanah* — only up to this point is *kavanah* required; beyond it, it is not.

The question of exactly where this boundary falls generates a dispute between Rashi and *Tosafot*. Rashi reads *al levavecha* literally as the endpoint — the middle of the third *pasuk*, *Vehayu hadevarim ha'eileh asher anochi metzavcha hayom al levavecha*. *Tosafot* understands *al levavecha* as referring back to the first two *pesukim* — *Shema Yisrael* and *Ve'ahavta* — and that the third *pasuk* itself identifies those two as the things that must be *al levavecha*.
