On this reading, *kavanah* is required only for the first two *pesukim*, because, as *Tosafot* explains, those two *pesukim* speak of *yichud Hashem*, the love of God, and *yirat Hashem* — the foundational matters of faith that constitute *ol malchus shamayim*.

### R. Eliezer

This position — that *kavanah* is required through *bechol me'odecha*, encompassing the first two *pesukim* — is identified as the view of Rabbi Eliezer.

### R. Akiva

Rabbi Akiva disagrees and derives a broader requirement from the phrase *asher anochi metzavcha hayom* — "that I am commanding you today." The present-tense formulation *metzavcha*, Rabbi Akiva argues, refers not only to what has just been said in the first two *pesukim* but to everything God is commanding in this moment, including the remainder of the *parsha*. Therefore: *mikan atah lameid shechol haparsha kullah tzricha kavanah* — one must have *kavanah* for the entire first *parsha*.

### R. Yochanan Rules

Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *halacha keRabbi Akiva* — the ruling follows Rabbi Akiva. *Kavanah* is required for the entirety of the first *parsha*. This ruling is also transmitted in a second version: a *tosefta* states simply that when reciting *Shema* one must direct one's heart, and an *Amora*, Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Yehuda, interprets this to mean that once one has had proper *kavanah* during the first chapter, nothing further is required. Rabbi Yochanan again rules in accordance with this position. Both versions of the ruling converge on the same halachic conclusion: *kavanah* is required for the full first *parsha*.

---

## Keriah & Kavanah

### Mitzvat Types

A further *baraita* refines the analysis by introducing a conceptual distinction not merely about how much *kavanah* is needed, but about the qualitative nature of the obligation in different portions of *Shema*. The framing is striking: the *baraita* frames the obligation as either *mitzvat kavanah* or *mitzvat keriah* — either a *mitzvah* of intention or a *mitzvah* of recitation — as if these are categorically distinct modes of religious obligation.

### R. Zutra Position

Rabbi Zutra holds: *ad kan mitzvat kavanah, mikan va'eilach mitzvat keriah* — the first portion of *Shema*, up to *al levavecha*, constitutes a *mitzvah* of *kavanah*; from that point onward, meaning the remainder of the first *parsha* and the subsequent *parshiyot*, the obligation is one of recitation only.

### R. Yoshiya Reverse

Rabbi Yoshiya reverses the positions: *ad kan mitzvat keriah, mikan va'eilach mitzvat kavanah* — the first portion is a *mitzvah* of recitation, and the second portion is one of *kavanah*. This is initially puzzling, since the phrase *al levavecha* appears in the first part, not the second.

The *Gemara* works through both positions carefully. For Rabbi Zutra's view, the *Gemara* asks: why is the second portion only a *mitzvah* of recitation? The *Gemara* answers: because the second *parsha* contains the phrase *ledaber bam* — to speak of them — which obligates the act of speech. But then the *Gemara* presses: the first *parsha* also says *vedibarta bam* — and you shall speak of them — so it too should require recitation! The *Gemara* responds: *hachi ka'amar* — the correct reading is that the first portion requires *both* recitation and *kavanah*, since it says both *vedibarta bam* and *al levavecha*; the second portion requires only recitation, without *kavanah*.

But then the *Gemara* asks why the second *parsha* — which also says *al levavchem ledaber bam* — should not require both as well. The resolution: *hahu miba'ei lei lekhe'derabbi Yitzchak* — that phrase in the second *parsha* is not teaching the *kavanah* requirement for *Shema* at all. Rather, Rabbi Yitzchak derives from *al levavchem* that *tefillin* must be placed *keneged halev*, opposite the heart. The verse is thus "occupied" with teaching something about *tefillin*, and cannot simultaneously be read as requiring *kavanah* for the recitation of *Shema*.

### First Parsha Both

The conclusion the *Gemara* arrives at — through both opinions — is that the first *parsha* unambiguously requires both *keriah* and *kavanah*. No opinion downgrades the first *parsha*; the real dispute concerns only what follows.

### Second Parsha Nature

For Rabbi Yoshiya's reverse position, the *Gemara* similarly reconstructs: when he says the first portion is *mitzvat keriah*, he means the first *parsha* requires both recitation and *kavanah* — this cannot be read as demoting the first *parsha*. The question is about the second *parsha*. According to Rabbi Yoshiya, *mikan va'eilach mitzvat kavanah* means the second *parsha* requires *kavanah* only, without recitation. This is the genuine disagreement: Rabbi Zutra says the second *parsha* is *keriah belo kavanah* — just read it, no particular *kavanah* required; Rabbi Yoshiya says it is *kavana belo kriya* — just think it, formal recitation is not required.

### Teaching vs. Reciting

This position of Rabbi Yoshiya — that thinking suffices for the second *parsha* — is supported by a striking reinterpretation of the *parsha*'s own language. The *Gemara* notes that the second *parsha* uses the formulation *ledaber bam*, with the additional prefix *le-*, which the *Gemara* now reads as referring to *teaching* Torah rather than *reciting Shema*. *Agmiru benaychu Torah ki heichi deleigresu behu* — teach your children Torah so that they may engage with it, speak of it. On this reading, the obligation embedded in the second *parsha* is not a formal *mitzvah* of recitation at all; it is the *mitzvah* of *talmud Torah* and teaching. The observation that *vedibarta bam* in the first *parsha* uses a simple command form more naturally read as an obligation to perform an act of speech, while *ledaber bam* in the second *parsha* describes a goal or result of teaching, lends some grammatical support to this distinction.

### Comprehension vs. Act

This leads to a broader conceptual clarification about the nature of the *mitzvah* of *Shema* itself. The *Rishonim* raise the question: how does this internal debate about *kavanah* in specific sections relate to the general question of *mitzvot tzerichot kavanah*? If *mitzvot* require *kavanah*, one would seem to need *kavanah* throughout; if they do not, one would seem to need none at all. Some *Rishonim* conclude that the debate about how much of *Shema* requires *kavanah* is really a debate about which portions of *Shema* constitute the biblical *mitzvah* — perhaps only the first two *pesukim*, perhaps the full first *parsha*, perhaps only the first *pasuk* — with the remainder being at most rabbinic.

However, the *Rashba* offers what appears to be the better answer: the *mitzvah* of *Shema* is not simply an act of recitation — that would be *mitzvat keriah*. It is fundamentally *kabbalat ol malchus shamayim* — the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven through the act of recitation. This means the *kavanah* at stake in *Shema* is not the general *kavanah* to fulfill a *mitzvah*, but a specific, content-oriented *kavanah*: one must understand what one is saying and be actively engaging in the affirmation expressed by the words. This is structurally similar to the requirement in *tefilla* that one know what one is praying — not simply that one intends to fulfill an obligation. Accordingly, even according to the view that *mitzvot ein tzerichot kavanah*, one might still require this substantive form of *kavanah* for *Shema*, since without it the *kabbalat ol malchus shamayim* itself is absent.

The *Gemara* frames the different sections precisely in these terms: the first *parsha* — and especially its opening *pesukim* — requires the full merger of recitation and intentional affirmation; the second *parsha*, whose content concerns the framework of *mitzvot* and reward, may require only one or the other. One opinion holds that merely thinking the second *parsha* suffices because accepting the yoke of *mitzvot* can be accomplished by intention alone; the other holds that since the *parsha* obligates speech — or alternatively that the verse there is about *talmud Torah*, which is an act of learning and teaching — formal recitation without *kavanah* is sufficient.

---

## First Pesuk Focus

### R. Meir Opinion

A final *tanna'itic* position now enters: *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad — ad kan tzricha kavanat halev, divrei Rabbi Meir.* According to Rabbi Meir, *kavanah* is required only for the first *pasuk* itself — the affirmation of God's unity and sovereignty. Nothing beyond it — not *Ve'ahavta*, not the rest of the first *parsha* — requires the heightened *kavanah* of *kabbalat ol malchus shamayim*. The core of the obligation is concentrated entirely in that declaration.

### Rava's Ruling

Rava rules: *halacha keRabbi Meir*. The *halacha* follows Rabbi Meir. This stands in apparent tension with the earlier ruling of Rabbi Yochanan that *halacha* follows Rabbi Akiva, requiring *kavanah* for the entire first *parsha*. These are simply two competing *amoraic* rulings, each aligning with a different *tanna'itic* position.

### Long Echad

*Sumchos* teaches: *kol hamarich be'echad, maarichin lo yamav veshanosav* — whoever extends the word *echad* has his days and years extended. The *Gemara* then specifies: *uv'dalet* — the extension is specifically on the *dalet*. Rashi explains that extending the *alef* or *chet* would distort the word, whereas the *dalet*, as the final letter, can be extended without corrupting the pronunciation. Rav Ashi adds a limiting condition: *uvilvad shelo yachtof baches* — one must not race through the *chet* in order to get to the *dalet*, as that would result in an unclear pronunciation of the *chet*.

A narrative follows: Rabbi Yirmiyah was sitting before Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and was observed extending *echad* at very great length. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said to him: once you have *amlichtei* — once you have enthroned God, recognized His kingship above and below and in all four directions — *tu lo tzrichat*, you do not need to continue further.

### Dalet Symbolism

The practice of extending the *dalet* functions as a ritualization of the *kavanah* demanded by the first *pasuk*. Since the entire weight of *kabbalat ol malchus shamayim* is concentrated in this *pasuk*, the deliberate, extended pronunciation of *echad* provides a mechanism for focusing the mind on what is being affirmed: God's singular sovereignty over heaven and earth and all directions. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba's correction makes this explicit — the extension is not an end in itself but a vehicle for achieving the required *kavanah*. Once that *kavanah* has been achieved, the extension should cease. There is additionally a practical dimension noted by some: the concern not to confuse the *dalet* with a *reish*, which would transform *echad* into *acher*, "another" — a catastrophic error in a declaration of monotheism.

---

## Standing Requirement

### Standing Rules

The *Gemara* reports in the name of Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav: *al levavecha be'amida* — the recitation up to *al levavecha* must be said while standing. The *Gemara* initially wonders whether this means only the words *al levavecha* themselves, and immediately clarifies: *ela eima ad al levavecha* — rather, the rule is that one must stand until reaching *al levavecha*.

### R. Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan extends the requirement further: *kol haparsha kulla be'amida* — the entire first *parsha* must be said while standing. The *Gemara* observes that this follows Rabbi Yochanan's own consistent position — *ve'azda Rabbi Yochanan letaimeih* — since he ruled that *kavanah* is required for the entire first *parsha*, the corresponding ritual requirement of standing similarly extends throughout. The two positions track each other: the scope of required *kavanah* and the scope of required standing are aligned.

### Posture Details

*Tosafot* cites the *Yerushalmi* for a significant qualification: *be'amida* here does not mean that one who is sitting must stand up. Rather, it means that one who is walking must stop and stand still. The concern is distraction: walking during *Shema* is insufficiently focused for the *kavanah* demanded, and one must therefore come to a halt. If one was already sitting, one need not rise. This framing connects the standing requirement to the broader concern for *kavanah*: it is not a formal postural *din* but a practical measure to ensure the requisite focus.

---

## R. Yehuda Practice

### First Pesuk Only

A *baraita* records: *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad — zu kriyat shema shel Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi.* This single *pasuk* constituted the *Shema* of *Rebbi*. As the *Gemara* will explain, *Rebbi* was engaged in teaching Torah throughout the day, and by the time his obligations as *Nasi* and as teacher of the community had run their course, he had only the opportunity to recite the first *pasuk* within *zman kriyat Shema*. Implicitly, the *baraita* is making a stronger point than simply noting which part requires *kavanah*: it suggests that at a *bedi'eved* level, at least, the first *pasuk* alone may suffice for the *mitzvah* itself.

### Rav's Question

Rav said to Rabbi Chiya: *lo chazina lei leRebbi demikabel alei malchus shamayim* — I sit in *shiur* all day and I have never seen *Rebbi* perform *kabbalat ol malchus shamayim*. The formulation is telling: Rav does not say he never saw *Rebbi* recite *Shema*, but that he never saw him perform the act of *accepting* God's sovereignty — underscoring that the essence of the obligation is not the verbal recitation but the inner affirmation.

### Eyes Covered

Rabbi Chiya responds: *bar pachti* — and then explains — *be'sha'ah shemavir yadav al panav, mikabel alav ol malchus shamayim* — when *Rebbi* draws his hand over his eyes in the middle of *shiur*, that is when he accepts the yoke of Heaven. He was reciting the first *pasuk* of *Shema* in that moment, marked by the gesture of covering the eyes. He would do this without interrupting the *shiur* as a formal matter, but using that moment of self-collection to fulfill his obligation.

### Making Up Later

This raises the question: *chozer vegomer o eino chozer vegomer?* — does *Rebbi* go back after the time has passed and recite the full *Shema*, or does he rely entirely on what he said during *zman kriyat Shema*? Bar Kafra says: *eino chozer vegomer* — there is no point in going back. Whatever one accomplished during *zman*, one accomplished; after the time passes, one does not return to complete it. Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbi disagrees: *chozer vegomer* — one should return and complete the full *Shema*. Whether this refers to the *mitzvah* of *Shema* itself or to the integrity of the morning *davening* as a whole — the package of *kriyat Shema uvirchoteha* — is itself a question.

### Yetziat Mitzrayim

Bar Kafra draws a telling inference in support of his own position. He observes that *Rebbi*, in the course of his *shiur*, would always find a way to mention *yetziat Mitzrayim* — the Exodus from Egypt. Bar Kafra argues: this makes sense according to his own view that *Rebbi* does not go back to complete *Shema* later. Since the third *parsha* of *Shema* — *Vayomer*, which mentions *yetziat Mitzrayim* — would not be recited within *zman*, *Rebbi* sought to fulfill the separate *mitzvah* of *zecher yetziat Mitzrayim* through some mention of the Exodus during his *shiur*. But according to Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbi, who holds that *Rebbi* does go back and complete the full *Shema* later, why would *Rebbi* bother mentioning it in the *shiur*? He could simply rely on reciting *Vayomer* when he completes *Shema* afterward.

The *Gemara* answers: *kedei lehazkir yetziat Mitzrayim bizmanah* — in order to mention the Exodus *in its proper time*. Rashi explains that *bizmanah* refers here to the *zman* of *kriyat Shema* itself. There is a distinct value — not simply to mention *yetziat Mitzrayim* at some point in the day, but to do so during the period designated for *kriyat Shema*. The placement of this *mitzvah* within the liturgy of *Shema* has transformed it: the ideal fulfillment of *zecher yetziat Mitzrayim* is not merely reciting the Exodus narrative but doing so within the framework of *Shema* and during its designated time. Even if one cannot recite *Vayomer* as part of *Shema* itself, *Rebbi* ensured that the *zecher* would occur during that window, preserving the liturgical structure as best he could.

---

## Sleep During Shema

### Yotzei Asleep

Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat reported in the name of Rav: if a person says *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* and then falls asleep — *yatza*, one is *yotzei*. This ruling, placed in the context of *kriyat Shema al hamita* — the bedtime recitation — reinforces the position that the first *pasuk* may constitute the full extent of the biblical *mitzvah*. The question of how much one must repeat at night, and at what level of obligation the subsequent *parshiyot* stand, is a debate among *poskim*; the *Gemara* here appears to anchor a significant position: at least *bedi'eved*, the first *pasuk* alone suffices.

### Nudging for First

Rav Nachman said to Dar, his servant: *bipsuka kama tzaaran* — for the first *pasuk*, trouble us. That is, if we are dozing off and have not yet said *Shema*, nudge us awake and ensure we are sufficiently alert and focused to say the first *pasuk* with *kavanah*. *Tfei lo tzaaran* — beyond that, do not trouble us. If we wish to fall back asleep after the first *pasuk*, leave us be.

### Rava's Practice

A parallel account concerns Rava. Rav Yosef asked Rav Yosef the son of Rava: what would your father do in this regard? The answer: *bipsuka kama hava kamatzaer nafsheih, tfei lo hava matzaer nafsheih* — for the first *pasuk*, he would exert himself to be focused and present; beyond that, he would not exert himself. Whether this refers to his own self-discipline in staying alert, or to ensuring those around him — children, household — were awake for the first *pasuk*, the message is identical: the first *pasuk* is treated as the irreducible core, and the remainder, while certainly recited when possible, is treated with lesser urgency.

### Lying Down

The *Gemara* then transitions to a related question of posture. Rav Yosef rules: *pirkadan lo yikra kriyat Shema* — one who is lying flat on one's back should not recite *Shema*. The concern here is not distraction or lack of *kavanah* in the ordinary sense, but *kavod* — the recitation of *Shema*, as an act of *kabbalat ol malchus shamayim*, demands a posture of respect and dignity.

### Position Rules

The *Gemara* asks: does this ruling apply only to recitation? Surely lying flat on one's back while sleeping is also problematic, since Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would curse one who slept in that position — *layeit aman degani aparkid* — on grounds of immodesty. The *Gemara* distinguishes: for sleeping, a slight incline is sufficient to remove the concern; but for reciting *Shema*, even a slight incline does not suffice. One must sit up. The two concerns — physical modesty in sleep and dignified posture for *kabbalat ol malchus shamayim* — are related but distinct, and the threshold for the latter is higher.

### R. Yochanan Exception

The *Gemara* notes an apparent exception: Rabbi Yochanan would recline — *metzli* — while reciting *Shema*. The resolution: *shani Rabbi Yochanan deba'al basar hava* — Rabbi Yochanan was a very heavy man, and sitting upright presented a genuine and significant physical burden. Given those circumstances, his reclining while reciting *Shema* was not disrespectful; indeed, given the physical effort that sitting upright would have required of him, reclining was not a posture of casualness but of necessity. Accordingly, the ruling against *pirkadan* does not apply in situations where the physical demands of sitting upright are genuinely beyond a person's ordinary capacity.

---

---

# Berakhot 14

## Shema Interruptions

### Rabbi Meir's Logic

The sugya opens at the bottom of 13b, with the phrase *uvaprakim*, concerning the rules governing interruption during *kriat shema*. The *mishnah* had recorded Rabbi Meir's position that between the sections (*bein haprakim*) one may ask after another's well-being out of honor (*mipnei hakavod*), and one may also respond. The *gemara* immediately presses: when Rabbi Meir says one may respond, under what conditions? If he means one may respond *mipnei hakavod* — out of honor — the statement is redundant. After all, if one may *initiate* a greeting out of honor, it goes without saying (*ein tzarich lomar*) that one may respond, since responding carries a lower social burden than initiating. Why bother stating it?

The *gemara* therefore suggests: perhaps when Rabbi Meir says one may respond, he means one may respond even at a lower threshold — even to an ordinary person, not only in a situation demanding formal deference. This reading is then tested against the *seifa* of the same teaching. In the middle of a section (*be'emtza haperek*), one may ask only out of awe (*mipnei hayirah*), and one may respond. Again the question: respond under what conditions? If the threshold for responding is the same as for asking — *mipnei hayirah* — then again the statement is redundant. It must therefore be that Rabbi Meir means one may respond even *mipnei hakavod*, a lower threshold than *yirah*. But that is precisely the position of Rabbi Yehuda.

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

The *gemara* then notes: *hainu deRabbi Yehuda* — this winds up being identical to Rabbi Yehuda's position. As the *mishnah* records, Rabbi Yehuda says: in the middle of a section, one may ask *mipnei hayirah* and respond *mipnei hakavod*; between sections, one may ask *mipnei hakavod* and respond to everyone (*shalom lechol adam*). The positions are arranged in an ABBA structure, but the substance is the same: Rabbi Yehuda explicitly distinguishes between the threshold required to initiate and the lower threshold required to respond. If Rabbi Meir's mention of responding implies a similar lower threshold, his position collapses into Rabbi Yehuda's.

The *gemara* therefore concludes that Rabbi Meir did not intend a different threshold for responding. He mentioned it not to introduce a new rule but as a rhetorical setup — stating the obvious so that Rabbi Yehuda could then contrast it with his own position, which *does* distinguish between initiating and responding.

### Braita Framework

The *gemara* then introduces a *braita* to make this structure explicit: *chasuri michasra vehachi katani* — the *mishnah* is elliptical, and this is what it should be taken to mean. The *braita* formulates it clearly: between sections, one may ask *mipnei hakavod*, and there is no need to state (*ein tzarich lomar*) that one may respond — it is self-evident. In the middle of a section, one may ask *mipnei hayirah*, and again there is no need to state that one may respond under the same threshold. This is the view of Rabbi Meir: the threshold for responding is identical to the threshold for asking, and stating otherwise would be redundant. Rabbi Yehuda then takes the floor and distinguishes: in the middle of a section, one may ask *mipnei hayirah* but may respond *mipnei hakavod*; between sections, one may ask *mipnei hakavod* and respond to all. The *braita* thus confirms that Rabbi Meir's mention of responding was meant only to set the stage for Rabbi Yehuda's distinction, not to introduce one of his own.

### Tosafot on Kaddish

Before the *gemara* moves on to extend these laws to other contexts, it is worth pausing to examine a crucial application made by *Tosafot* on 13b. *Tosafot* notes that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda — as the *gemara* will state explicitly — meaning that even in the middle of a section, one may respond *mipnei hakavod*. *Tosafot* draws a direct analogy: if one is in the middle of reciting *shema* and the congregation reaches *kaddish* or *kedusha*, certainly responding to honor God's name is equivalent to responding out of honor to a person. There is no greater expression of *mipnei hakavod* than that. Therefore, one interrupts *shema* to respond to *kaddish* and *kedusha*. This rule applies, however, only within *shema*; interrupting *shemoneh esreh* is governed by an entirely different and more stringent standard.

The practical import of this *Tosafot* is considerable. The question of whether to respond to *kaddish* and *kedusha* while one is davening at a different point than the congregation is far more common in practice than the question of greeting a person mid-*shema*. *Tosafot* resolves it by identifying the honor accorded to God's name as the functional equivalent of *mipnei hakavod* toward a person of distinction.

---

## Hallel & Megilla

### Hallel Status

The *gemara* now extends the inquiry beyond *shema*. A *tanna* from the school of Rabbi Chiyya posed a question directly to Rabbi Chiyya: what is the rule for interrupting *Hallel* and *Megilla*? Does the same framework apply as with *shema*? The question formulates a *kal vachomer*: if *kriat shema*, which is biblical (*de'oraita*), may nonetheless be interrupted under the appropriate conditions, then *Hallel* and *Megilla*, which are only rabbinic (*derabbanan*) and therefore of lesser weight, should certainly permit interruption on similar or more lenient grounds. But a counterargument presents itself: *Hallel* and *Megilla* carry the quality of *pirsumei nisa* — publicizing the miracle — which may invest them with a particular gravity that argues against interruption, especially in a public setting.

### Rava's Distinction

Rabbi Chiyya's response is terse: *posek ve'ein bekach klum* — you may interrupt; it is not a concern at all. The phrase *ein bekach klum* suggests not merely that it is permitted but that it carries no particular weight as an issue. It is certainly no more stringent than *shema*, and may even be more lenient.

Rava then provides the precise rule. On days when an individual (*yachid*) completes the full *Hallel* — that is, days on which the complete *Hallel* is recited — the laws mirror those of *shema*: between one chapter and the next (*bein perek leperek*) one may interrupt; in the middle of a chapter (*be'emtza haperek*) one may not. On days when the individual does not complete the full *Hallel* — that is, days on which only *chatzi Hallel* (half *Hallel*) is recited, such as *Rosh Chodesh* — even interrupting in the middle of a chapter is permitted, since *chatzi Hallel* has the status of a *minhag* and carries lesser weight. The assumption throughout is that the interruptions in question are *mipnei hakavod*; it is under that threshold that Rava assigns these different standards.

### Rav Bar Shaba Case

The *gemara* then raises an apparent difficulty. Rav Bar Shaba once came to Ravina on a day when only *chatzi Hallel* was being recited, and Ravina did not interrupt — even in the middle of a chapter — to acknowledge him. But we just established that *chatzi Hallel* permits even mid-chapter interruption, presumably *mipnei hakavod*. Why did Ravina not interrupt?

The *gemara* resolves this with a pointed observation: *shani Rav Bar Shaba delo chashiv alei deRavina* — Rav Bar Shaba was simply not accorded sufficient importance by Ravina. Ravina did not regard him as someone whose presence created an obligation of *mipnei hakavod*; he treated him as an ordinary person (*kol adam*). The case therefore offers an interesting window into how these hierarchies of honor were assessed in practice — but it does not undermine the rule. The upshot stands: full *Hallel* carries the same rules as *shema*, and *chatzi Hallel* is more lenient than either.

### Yachid Definition

The phrase *yamim sheyachid gomer bahen et haHallel* — the days on which an individual completes the *Hallel* — prompts a lengthy discussion in *Tosafot*. The first issue is whether a *bracha* is recited over *chatzi Hallel*, given that it is only a *minhag*. *Tosafot* generally holds that it is. One of the arguments *Tosafot* adduces is that the very fact the *gemara* discusses the rules of interrupting *chatzi Hallel* implies that it is framed by a *bracha* — for in *Tosafot*'s understanding, the laws of interruption are tied to the notion of interrupting an act framed by a *bracha*. Without a *bracha*, there would be nothing to interrupt in a halachically meaningful sense. One might question this assumption — for instance, if a person were uncertain whether he had fulfilled his obligation to read the *Megilla* and was reading it again without a *bracha*, would the laws of interruption not apply? The assumption that interruption rules require a framing *bracha* is not self-evident. But that is *Tosafot*'s position, and it leads him to observe that the *Hallel* of the *seder* night, which is split by the *seudah*, cannot have a *bracha* spanning both halves — an argument against certain opinions that held it did.

Regarding the word *yachid* itself, *Tosafot* notes that strictly speaking it carries no independent significance here — the rules of interruption do not differ between an individual and a *tzibur*. However, others read the phrase as genuinely distinguishing between them. On the days of *chatzi Hallel*, perhaps the *tzibur* has a fuller level of obligation than the *yachid*. There are indeed authorities who hold that the *minhag* of *chatzi Hallel* applies only at the communal level; when an individual recites it in private (*beyachidus*), no *bracha* is recited at all, since the *minhag* was established at the level of the *tzibur* and not at the level of the *yachid*. This reading would give the phrase its full force: it is specifically the individual who on those days does not complete the *Hallel*, whereas the congregation may have a different standing.

In any case, the *gemara* concludes that these obligations — even though *derabbanan* — carry essentially the same status as *shema* for purposes of the interruption rules: no more stringent and no less.

---

## Tasting & Fasting

### Taste Definition

The *gemara* introduces a digression prompted by the phrase *ein bekach klum* used earlier. A *tanna* from the school of Rav Ami posed a question to Rav Ami: if a person is observing a private fast (*taanis*), may he taste food? *Tosafot* understands the discussion to be limited to a private fast; a communal fast may carry different standards. The question turns on how to understand the nature of a *taanis*. When a person accepts a fast upon himself, what precisely has he accepted? One possibility: he has accepted upon himself not to eat or drink (*achilah ushtiyah kabbilah alei*) — and tasting, which does not constitute eating, would be permitted. Another possibility: he has accepted upon himself to derive no pleasure (*hana'ah*) from food — and since tasting does produce pleasure and involves some ingestion, it would be forbidden.

### Revi'it Measure

Rav Ami's answer is direct: *to'em ve'ein bekach klum* — one may taste and it is not a concern at all. A *braita* confirms this: someone who merely tastes does not require a *bracha*, and someone on a fast who tastes does not violate the fast. Tasting is not eating. The *gemara* then asks: up to how much may one taste? Rav Ami and Rav Assi both state: one may taste up to the measure of a *revi'it* — approximately three and a half ounces — and it remains within the category of tasting rather than eating. This is a striking ruling. A *revi'it* is a substantial quantity, and to say that this amount carries neither *bracha* obligation nor a *taanis* violation is a considerable *chiddush*.

### Tosafot Spitting

*Tosafot* immediately qualifies the ruling: *peirush rak shechozer upolet* — the entire permission is contingent upon spitting the food out. Without that, one might ask what distinguishes tasting from eating. After all, food is entering one's mouth, pleasure is being derived, and some degree of ingestion occurs regardless. *Tosafot* answers: what makes *te'imah* categorically different from *achilah* is the intentional act of spitting out, which signals that there was never any intent to ingest. Something does enter the body — sensation requires contact — but the act is fundamentally not one of swallowing or ingesting. It is a sensory assessment, not consumption.

There is a related debate among the *poskim* regarding tasting at the very tip of the tongue — whether that constitutes a distinct category of act from eating, lighter even than the *te'imah* described here. That question may indeed underlie the *gemara*'s discussion of what makes tasting not eating. *Tosafot*'s answer focuses on the spitting out as the decisive criterion.

---

## Greeting Before Prayer

### Altar Metaphor

The *gemara* returns, albeit through another digression, toward the theme of *tefillah*. Rav states: whoever greets another person (*nosein shalom lechavero*) before davening is as though he has made that person into an altar (*bamah*). The statement is grounded in a *pasuk*: *chadlu lachem min ha'adam asher neshamah be'apo ki bameh nechshav hu* — cease from people, for of what value is he? The word *bameh*, meaning "of what value," is read as *bamah*, an altar. By initiating greetings before directing one's wishes and attention to God, a person has effectively offered up his morning efforts to another human being rather than to the Creator. The imagery carries an almost idolatrous subtext: one has erected an altar to a person in the space that belonged to God.

This statement connects naturally to earlier discussions in the *gemara* about eating before davening and about casting God behind one's back (*hashlakas Elohim acharei gavam*). There the concern was doing other things — attending to personal interests — before acknowledging God. Here the concern is more pointed: it is the explicit honor directed toward another person, which carries the specific quality of misplaced reverence.

### Shmuel's Point

Shmuel sharpens the point: *bameh chishavta l'zeh velo l'Eloha* — what are you doing giving significance to this person rather than to God? Shmuel removes any ambiguity. The problem is not incidental — it is the deliberate act of according weight and honor to a human being in a space that ought to be directed toward the Divine.

### Rav Sheshet Q

This raises an obvious difficulty. Rav Sheshet objects: but our *mishnah* explicitly permits asking after someone's well-being (*sho'el beshalom*) between the sections of *shema* — and at that point one has not yet davened! How can the *mishnah* permit this if Rav has just declared it forbidden?

### Incidental vs. Deliberate

Rav Abba resolves the contradiction by drawing a critical distinction: the problem Rav describes is when a person rises early in the morning and goes deliberately to knock on another's door (*mashkim lefischo*) — making a purposeful effort to honor that person before having davened. That is the case of making the person into a *bamah*: a calculated act of deference to a human being that precedes any acknowledgment of God. By contrast, if one simply encounters someone and responds to their presence, it would be insulting not to acknowledge them, and that incidental greeting does not carry the same weight.

It is worth noting that in Roman culture there was an established practice of patronage in which clients would rise early and attend upon their patrons, forming a kind of retinue to show deference. The *gemara*'s critique carries additional punch in that social context: do not make this person your morning priority, do not perform all of that elaborate human homage, before you have at minimum acknowledged God and davened.

---

## Own Interests First

### Personal Matters Ban

Rav Idi bar Avin said in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan: it is forbidden for a person to attend to his personal affairs (*chafatzav*) before davening. This generalizes the principle beyond the specific case of greeting another person. The entire orientation of the morning — attending to one's own interests, conducting one's business, arranging one's affairs — cannot precede the act of prayer.

### Tzedek First

The source is a *pasuk*: *tzedek lefanav yehalech veyasem laderech pe'amav* — righteousness goes before him and places his feet on the path. Rashi explains *tzedek* here as *tefillah* — the prayer which justifies a person before his Creator, which acknowledges God as the source of one's existence and one's day. That acknowledgment must come first. Only after *tzedek lefanav yehalech* — after righteousness has preceded — may one *yesem pe'amav*, set one's feet on the path of the day's affairs. The structure of the day must begin with this acknowledgment, and everything else follows.

This principle applies specifically to the first davening of the day. For *minchah* and *maariv* the concern is of a different character — whether one will forget when the time arrives — not this foundational issue of the proper ordering of one's morning. The morning *tefillah* is uniquely freighted with the demand that a person begin his day by recognizing God before turning to himself.

### God Provides

The same tradition — Rav Idi bar Avin in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan — adds a positive counterpart: whoever davens first and then goes out on his way, *Ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu oseh lo chafatzav* — the Holy One, blessed be He, takes care of his needs. This is the precise inversion of the prohibition: the *mishnah* forbade a person from attending to his *chafatzav* before davening; the *gemara* now promises that if one davens first, God will attend to those *chafatzav* in one's stead. The same *pasuk* is invoked: *tzedek lefanav yehalech veyasem laderech pe'amav* — put righteousness first, and God will set your feet on your path. Here the *gemara* applies this specifically to the context of departing on a journey: if circumstances permit, daven before you leave, and God will ensure things work out.

---

## Aggadic Teachings

### Dreams & Evil

The *gemara* closes this strand with several *aggadic* statements. Rav Yona said in the name of Rav Zeira: whoever sleeps for seven days without a dream is called evil (*nikra ra*). The *pasuk* is: *vesava yalin bal yipaked ra* — one who sleeps sated will not be visited by evil. By reading *sava* not as "sated" but as *sheva*, seven — if you sleep (*yalin*) for seven days (*sheva*) and are not visited (*bal yipaked*) by a dream, then *ra* — you are evil. The underlying belief appears to be that dreams carry some form of spiritual message or communication; if a person goes an entire week without receiving any such message, that absence is itself a negative sign. The statement has been interpreted to mean that if a week passes without the person achieving even a moment of perceiving the temporariness of this world — as on *Shabbat*, which falls within any seven-day period — then the absence of that awareness marks him as *ra*.

### Torah Sleep

Rav Acha the son of Rav Chiyya bar Abba then offers a closer reading of the same *pasuk* from Rabbi Yochanan. The *pasuk* in its plain meaning supports the following teaching: whoever satiates himself (*masbia atzmo*) with words of Torah before going to sleep will not be visited by evil reports (*ein mevasrim oto besoros ra'os*). *Vesava yalin* — if you go to sleep truly sated with Torah, *bal yipaked ra* — evil will not visit you. The connection of these *aggadic* statements to the surrounding *halacha* is not entirely clear from the structure of the passage; they appear to be associated with the same chain of tradition rather than arising organically from the legal discussion.

---

## Shema-Bracha Link

### No Interruption

Returning to the central halachic thread, Rav Avahu said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda. This means the *halacha* is that one may not interrupt between *Eloheichem* — the end of the third paragraph of *shema* — and *emet veyatziv*, the opening of the *bracha* that follows. The intent is to create a seamless statement: *Hashem Eloheichem emet* — the Lord your God is true. These are technically different units of the liturgy, but by not interrupting between them, they are joined into a single declaration.

### Emet Repetition

Rav Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: what is Rabbi Yehuda's reason? Because the *pasuk* reads *Hashem Eloheichem emet* — and we want to embody that *pasuk* in our recitation. This then generates a practical question: when the *chazan* finishes *shema* with *Ani Hashem Eloheichem* and must continue into *emet veyatziv*, does he repeat the word *emet* — so that it closes *shema* and also opens the *bracha* — or does he proceed directly with *veyatziv venachon vekayam*? Rabbi Yochanan's first position, as reported by Rav Abba, is that he does repeat *emet*: the word performs double duty, closing one unit and opening the next, so that *Ani Hashem Eloheichem emet* flows naturally into *emet veyatziv*.

### Emet Emet Problem

Rava disagrees: he should not repeat *emet*. The purpose of the connection is to allow the two units to flow seamlessly into each other; repeating *emet* interrupts that flow by attaching the word more explicitly to what follows rather than allowing it to bridge the two sections. A certain prayer leader who led services before Rava was heard to say *emet emet* twice — once closing *shema* and once opening *emet veyatziv*. Rava's response was sharp: *kol emet emet chasei l'hai* — this person has the *emet emet* sickness. The doubling was treated as an aberration. One wonders whether this sensitivity also reflects the broader concern, present elsewhere in the *gemara*, about doubling words in liturgy — similar to the prohibitions against saying *shema shema* or *modim modim* — concerns that may have been sharpened by the Zoroastrian and dualistic cultural context in which the Babylonian *amoraim* operated, where any apparent doubling could suggest a dual divine authority.

---

## Eretz Yisrael Custom

### Western Skip

Rav Yosef introduces the next topic with characteristic enthusiasm: *kama ma'alya hai shmaita* — how excellent is the following teaching. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, upon returning from *Eretz Yisrael*, reported the practice of *ma'arava* — the west — for the evening *shema* (*arvit*). In *Eretz Yisrael*, the full *parashat tzitzit* was not recited at night. Instead, they would say the opening of the first *pasuk* of the *parasha* — *daber bnei Yisrael ve'amarta aleihem* — and then jump to the end of the final *pasuk*: *Ani Hashem Eloheichem emet*. This created a kind of hybrid *pasuk* combining the beginning of the first verse with the end of the last. The rationale, as Rashi explains, is that the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* does not apply at night; therefore, reading about *tzitzit* in the evening *shema* was felt to be unnecessary, and the passage was abbreviated.

One might also suggest — and this possibility is raised in the discussion — that the practice reflects a different position on whether *zechiras yetziat Mitzrayim* is obligatory at night. If the *mitzvah* of mentioning the Exodus does not apply at night, there is less reason to recite the *parasha* whose primary function in the evening *shema* is to fulfill that *mitzvah*. The hybrid formulation preserved the structural integrity of the liturgy while bypassing the *tzitzit* section.

### Complete or Skip

Abaye responds to Rav Yosef's enthusiasm with a pointed question: *mai ma'alyusa* — what exactly is so wonderful about that? He invokes a ruling of Rav Kahana in the name of Rav: *lo yaschil*, one should not begin the third *parasha* at night; but *ve'im hitchil yigmor*, if one begins it, one must finish it. The objection is clear: the practice of *Eretz Yisrael*, which starts the *parasha* and then cuts it off to jump to the end, violates this principle. Either don't start it at all, or complete it. Rearranging and abbreviating *psukim* is itself problematic — as the principle *kol pasuk de'lo paskei Moshe anan lo paskeinan* establishes: any verse that Moshe did not divide, we do not divide.

### Starting Point

The *gemara* then considers whether *ve'amarta aleihem* constitutes a sufficient beginning to trigger the obligation to finish. Perhaps the opening phrase *daber bnei Yisrael ve'amarta aleihem* does not count as truly starting the *parasha*, and the practitioners in *Eretz Yisrael* therefore felt no obligation to complete it. Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak said in the name of Rav: *daber el bnei Yisrael* alone is not considered starting; but *ve'amarta aleihem* — once one has reached that phrase — is considered starting. Rav Papa then explains the *Eretz Yisrael* position: they held that even *ve'amarta aleihem* is not considered starting until one actually mentions *tzitzit* itself — *ve'asu lahem tzitzit*. Once *tzitzit* has been named, the *parasha* has been entered and must be completed. But before that point, even having said *ve'amarta aleihem*, one may still jump to the end.

### Babylonian Practice

Abaye draws the practical conclusion for Babylonia. Since the practice of *Eretz Yisrael* requires at minimum beginning the *parasha* — they do not allow it to be entirely omitted — we in Bavel will follow them in beginning it, saying *daber bnei Yisrael ve'amarta aleihem*. But since we also hold that once one begins (*ve'im hitchil yigmor*) one must complete the entire *parasha*, we are obligated to say the whole thing. The result is that in Bavel the full third *parasha* of *shema* was recited at night, while in *Eretz Yisrael* an abbreviated version was used. The Babylonian position implicitly endorses *zechiras yetziat Mitzrayim baleilos* — the obligation to mention the Exodus at night — since completing the full *parasha* is predicated on that obligation.

---

## Ani Hashem Connection

### Conditional Emet

Chiyya bar Rav states: if one has said *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* — the closing phrase of *parashat tzitzit* — then *emet* is recited as the transition into *emet veyatziv*. But if one has not said *Ani Hashem Elokeichem*, then *emet* is not said. This ruling reflects the principle established earlier: the word *emet* at the junction of *shema* and the *bracha* that follows is specifically meaningful as an affirmation of *Hashem Eloheichem emet*. If the phrase *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* was not recited — whether because the *parasha* of *tzitzit* was omitted or abbreviated — then there is nothing for *emet* to affirm, and the word loses its function at that junction.

### Yetziat Mitzrayim

The *gemara* immediately raises the obvious difficulty: if one has not recited *parashat tzitzit* and also does not say *emet veyatziv*, how has one fulfilled the obligation of *zechiras yetziat Mitzrayim*? The *bracha* of *emet veyatziv* is the vehicle through which the Exodus is commemorated in the morning liturgy; its evening counterpart, *emet ve'emuna*, serves the same function at night. If neither the *parasha* nor the *bracha* is recited, *yetziat Mitzrayim* has not been mentioned. This is a genuine problem, and it is here that the approach of Rashi becomes clear: Rashi understands the *gemara* throughout to be operating on the assumption that *zechiras yetziat Mitzrayim* is obligatory at night. The abbreviation of *parashat tzitzit* in *Eretz Yisrael* was driven not by rejecting that obligation but by the inapplicability of the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* at night. Mentioning the Exodus remained necessary; the question was how to accomplish it.

### Ga'al Yisrael

The *gemara*'s answer is that even in the case where *emet veyatziv* is not recited in its full form, a *bracha* must still be said — *shema* requires a concluding *bracha*. That *bracha* takes a different formulation: *modim anachnu lefanecha Hashem Elokeinu shehotzeitanu me'eretz Mitzrayim ufaditanu mibeit avadim ve'asita lanu nisim ugevuros al hayam vesharanu lach* — we give thanks before You, Lord our God, for taking us out of Egypt and redeeming us from the house of bondage and performing miracles and mighty acts for us at the sea, and we sang to You. This alternative *bracha* accomplishes *zechiras yetziat Mitzrayim* through its content, and it concludes — as the questioner in the *gemara* correctly anticipates — with *ga'al Yisrael*, the Redeemer of Israel. The *chatimah* of the *bracha* remains unchanged; what changes is the opening portion: instead of *emet veyatziv* or *emet ve'emuna* — both of which are the affirmations connected to *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* — a different *nusach* is used, one whose content centers directly on the Exodus narrative. The *bracha* of *ga'al Yisrael* is the constant; the text leading into it is what varies depending on whether *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* was recited.

### Custom Differences

The discussion as a whole illuminates a period of genuine liturgical flux. The differences between *Eretz Yisrael* and Bavel in the recitation of the third *parasha* of *shema* at night were not merely matters of local custom but reflected substantive halachic disagreements: about the applicability of *tzitzit* at night, about the obligation of *zechiras yetziat Mitzrayim baleilos*, and about the threshold at which beginning a *parasha* obligates one to complete it. In *Eretz Yisrael*, an abbreviated version of *parashat tzitzit* was used, connected directly to *Ani Hashem Elokeichem emet*; some there may also have held that *zechiras yetziat Mitzrayim* at night was less fully obligatory. In Bavel, the *gemara* firmly presupposes the obligation of *yetziat Mitzrayim baleilos* and requires the full *parasha* to be recited. The word *emet* at the junction, the presence or absence of *Ani Hashem Elokeichem*, and the *nusach* of the concluding *bracha* all follow from these underlying positions. The *Bavli* here does not definitively resolve every strand of the *Eretz Yisrael* practice — it leaves open, for instance, the precise extent to which the western communities accepted the nighttime obligation of *zechiras yetziat Mitzrayim* — but the Babylonian position is clear: the third *parasha* is recited in full, *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* is said, *emet* connects it to the *bracha*, and *yetziat Mitzrayim* is commemorated every night.

---

---

# Berakhot 15

## Order of Shema Paragraphs

### Learning, Teaching, Doing

Today's daf begins in the middle of 14b, at the statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: *lama kadma parshat Shema* — why does the first paragraph of *shema* precede the others? Before engaging with this question directly, it is worth noting the context. We had just finished discussing the laws of *bein haprakim* — the permissible interruptions between the sections of *shema* — and the interesting question of how *bein haprakim* applies to responding to elements of the *davening*, such as *kaddish*, during the recitation of *shema*. Now we turn to the question of the order of the three *parshiyot*.

It should also be noted, as was mentioned previously, that *parshat tzitzit* — the third paragraph — was largely omitted at night in *Eretz Yisrael*, either because the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* does not apply at night, or because the *mitzvah* of *zecher yetziat Mitzrayim* may not apply at night. These regional differences are worth keeping in mind as we approach the question of ordering.

A *baraita* is cited: Shimshon ben Yochai teaches that it is fitting for the first paragraph of *shema* to precede *V'haya im Shamoa* because *shema* corresponds to *lilmod* — learning — and *V'haya im Shamoa* corresponds to *lelamed* — teaching. The source for this reading is that *shema* contains the verse *v'dibarta bam*, "and you shall speak of them," while *V'haya im Shamoa* contains *v'shinantam l'vanecha*, "and you shall teach your children" — that is, *V'haya im Shamoa* commands teaching others, not learning oneself. Then *V'haya im Shamoa* precedes the third paragraph, *Vayomer*, because it contains both *lelamed* and *la'asot* — teaching and doing — while *Vayomer* contains only *la'asot*. The structure is thus a progression: learn, then teach, then do.

This is a different organizing principle than *kabbalat ol malchut shamayim* — the acceptance of the yoke of heaven — which was the first reason given. One might compare it to the difference between the *Rambam* and the *Shulchan Aruch* in how they organize their works. The *Rambam* begins with *yesod hayesodot ve'amud hachachamot* — establishing the foundations, the existence of God, and then building outward to *mitzvot* and practical matters. The *Shulchan Aruch* begins immediately with what to do when you wake up in the morning — chronological and user-friendly. The first ordering of *shema* paragraphs (foundation before practical *mitzvot*) parallels the *Rambam*'s approach, while the second (a sequential progression from learning to teaching to doing) has more of the *Shulchan Aruch*'s character.

### Three, Two, One Elements

The *gemara* immediately challenges the *baraita*: does *shema* truly have only *lilmod* and not *lelamed* and *la'asot*? But *shema* contains *v'shinantam* — teaching — and *ukshartem ukhtavtem* — references to *tefillin* and *mezuzah*, which constitute *la'asot*. Similarly, does *V'haya im Shamoa* lack *la'asot*? It too contains *tefillin* and *mezuzah*.

The *gemara* therefore reframes the principle: it is not that each paragraph exclusively embodies one element, but rather that each paragraph contains *more* of one than the next. *Shema* has all three — *lilmod*, *lelamed*, *la'asot*. *V'haya im Shamoa* has two — *lelamed* and *la'asot*. *Vayomer* has only one — *la'asot*. The order reflects a descending richness: three, then two, then one.

### Foundation vs. Chronolog…

The *gemara* then asks: given that we already have the teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha about *kabbalat ol malchut shamayim*, why did we need the separate approach of *lilmod u'lelamed ve'la'asot*? The answer is *chada ve'od ka'amar* — one good reason and yet another. One reason is to first accept the yoke of heaven and then accept the yoke of *mitzvot*. A second, additional reason is the progression of *lilmod u'lelamed ve'la'asot* within the paragraphs themselves. Both reasons apply simultaneously and reinforce each other.

It is worth pausing on the phrase *lama kadma* — "why does it precede?" — which implies that the liturgy was already fixed, and the *amoraim* are reasoning retrospectively about the rationale. This is more like a post-hoc speculation than a legislative act, which is why multiple explanations can coexist.

---

## Rav's Practice & Conflict

### Rav's Daily Practice

The *gemara* now moves from the conceptual ordering of the *shema* paragraphs to a discussion of Rav's actual practice, which bears directly on the theme of *lilmod u'lelamed ve'la'asot*. The report is as follows: *Rav mashi yadei ve'kara krias shema ve'anach tefillin ve'tzali* — Rav washed his hands, recited *shema*, donned *tefillin*, and then prayed *Shemoneh Esrei*.

The hand-washing here is not primarily focused on the question of *ruach ra*; the *gemara*'s concern is the washing that prepares a person for *davening* — a matter of cleanliness in preparation for prayer. This practice leads *Tosafot* into a detailed discussion: if one receives one's *tefillin* (or *tallis*) between *shema* and *Shemoneh Esrei*, can one put them on with a *bracha* at that point, or must the *bracha* be recited afterward? *Tosafot* notes that wearing *tefillin* during *Shemoneh Esrei* takes priority over wearing a *tallis*, though the underlying reasoning is not entirely clear, given that the concern about wearing *tefillin* while reciting *shema* — since one speaks of *tefillin* in the text — is itself a significant consideration. *Tosafot* concludes that Rav's practice demonstrates the importance of having *tefillin* on for *Shemoneh Esrei*, but does not resolve the question of when the *bracha* is made. One cannot interrupt *shema* to make the *bracha*, yet since one is still in the midst of fulfilling the *mitzvah* of *tefillin* even after *Shemoneh Esrei*, a *bracha* beforehand would not constitute a *bracha* after the *mitzvah*'s completion.

### Work Interruption Obliga…

The *gemara* asks: how could Rav have done this — that is, how could he have said *shema* before donning *tefillin*? A *baraita* is cited: one who is digging a niche for a corpse in a burial cave is exempt from *krias shema*, *tefillah*, *tefillin*, and all *mitzvot* mentioned in the Torah — the principle of *osek bemitzvah patur min hamitzvah*, one who is engaged in a *mitzvah* is exempt from another *mitzvah*. However, when the time for *krias shema* arrives, the *baraita* continues: *oleh venoteil yadav u'meni'ach tefillin vekore krias shema umispaleil* — he ascends from the cave, washes his hands, puts on *tefillin*, recites *shema*, and prays.

But this appears internally contradictory: the opening clause said he is exempt from all *mitzvot*, yet the closing clause prescribes a specific order in which he fulfills them. The *gemara* resolves this: the opening clause (*reisha*) refers to a situation where he is the only one working — if he stops, the *mitzvah* ceases entirely. The closing clause (*sayfa*) refers to a situation where two workers are present — he can take a break while the *mitzvah* continues. This resolution itself raises an interesting conceptual point about *osek bemitzvah patur min hamitzvah*: the exemption applies as long as the *mitzvah* is ongoing, even if one personally steps away from it. A slight slowing of efficiency, it seems, does not itself end the *mitzvah*.

In any case, the *baraita*'s closing clause presents the order as: *tefillin* first, then *shema* — the reverse of what Rav is reported to have done. The *gemara* therefore poses the question: *mikol makom kashya le-Rav* — this remains a difficulty for Rav. A resolution is offered: perhaps Rav follows the view of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who teaches that *ol malchut shamayim* precedes *ol mitzvot* — one first establishes the yoke of heaven, and then performs *mitzvot*. Rav's practice of saying *shema* before putting on *tefillin* would thus reflect this priority: the verbal acceptance of *malchut shamayim* comes before the performance of the *mitzvah* of *tefillin*.

### Contradictory Accounts

The *gemara* pushes back on this resolution. First: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's teaching concerns the relative ordering of recitations — saying *shema* before *V'haya im Shamoa*, not the question of whether one should recite before one performs *mitzvot*. The principle *mah kadma kriya lekriya* — one recitation precedes another — does not obviously extend to the relationship between recitation and action. There may be a fundamental distinction: theoretically, the foundation (*ol malchut shamayim*) is prior to practice (*ol mitzvot*); but in actual performance, doing always takes precedence.

Second, and more significantly, a second account of Rav's practice directly contradicts the first. Rav Chiya bar Ashi testifies: *zimnin sagi'in havei kamina kamei de-Rav* — many times I stood before Rav — and the practice he observed was as follows: Rav would rise, wash his hands, make a *bracha* (understood as *birkas hatorah*), teach his students their chapter of *mishna*, then don *tefillin*, and only then recite *krias shema*. So in this account, Rav performed *tefillin* before *shema* — the conventional order. *Rashi* notes that this account also raises the question of teaching Torah before *shema*, since that constitutes a *mitzvah* performed before *kabbalat ol malchut shamayim*. But the sharper difficulty is the reversal of order: one account has *shema* then *tefillin*; the other has *tefillin* then *shema*.

### Late Tefillin Resolution

One attempted resolution: perhaps the times Rav put on *tefillin* before *shema* were times when it was not yet the *zman* for *krias shema*, so he put on *tefillin* first and waited until the proper time to recite *shema*. This is somewhat striking since *tefillin* is normally worn from *mi-she-yakir* onward, which most opinions regard as identical to the earliest time for *shema*, though there are more marginal views that *shema* cannot be said until *netz*.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this resolution: if this explanation is correct, then what was the point of Rav Chiya bar Ashi's testimony? If the order of *tefillin* and *shema* in that account was incidental to a timing issue, there is nothing significant to learn from it regarding the order. The *gemara* therefore proposes that the story was told for an entirely different purpose: *le-apukei mi-man de'amar le-mishnah ein tzarich levareich* — to exclude the view that one need not recite *birkas hatorah* before teaching *mishna*, as opposed to *psukim*. The story was told to inform us that Rav did in fact make *birkas hatorah* when teaching *mishna*; the order of *shema* and *tefillin* was incidental.

Yet the *gemara* remains unsatisfied: *mikol makom kashya le-Rav* — the problem persists. The two accounts of Rav's order with *tefillin* are still in tension. The final resolution is brief: *shlucha hu de-avis* — the messenger erred. According to *Rashi*, this means that the assistant who was supposed to bring Rav his *tefillin* was late. Rav's fundamental practice was to don *tefillin* before *shema*, as the *baraita* and the second testimony indicate. The one occasion on which he said *shema* before *tefillin* was simply because his *tefillin* were not available in time. This then returns us to *Tosafot*'s question: what does one do when one's *tefillin* arrive only after *shema* has begun — can one make a *bracha* on them then, or must one wait?

---

## Tefillin & Shema Require…

### False Testimony Concept

Having established that the norm is to don *tefillin* before *shema*, the *gemara* now articulates the conceptual basis for this requirement. *Ulla* teaches: *kol ha-korei krias shema belo tefillin, k'ilu me'id ed sheker b'atzmo* — one who recites *shema* without wearing *tefillin* is as if he testifies falsely against himself. The *shema* contains references to the obligation of *tefillin*, and by reciting these words while not wearing them, one makes a declaration that is belied by one's own conduct.

*Rashi* reads *b'atzmo* as a euphemism — as if one is offering false testimony about God, since one is declaring God's commandment while behaving as if it does not apply. This reading is somewhat puzzling: the wrong is being done by the person, not attributed to God. A simpler reading might be that by reciting a declaration of obligation one is not fulfilling, one is bearing false witness against one's own obligations — a kind of self-incrimination by hypocrisy.

Notably, the *gemara* does not make this point about *tallis*. This is deliberate: the obligation of *tzitzit* applies only when one is actually wearing a four-cornered garment; there is no freestanding obligation to always wear *tzitzit*. The charge of *k'ilu me'id ed sheker* therefore attaches specifically to *tefillin* and not to *tallis*.

### Incomplete Offering Anal…

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan offers a milder formulation: *k'ilu hikriv olah b'lo mincha v'zevach b'lo nesachim* — it is as if one offered a *olah* without its accompanying *mincha*, or brought a *zevach* without the *nesachim*. The *olah* and *zevach* are still brought; the *mincha* and *nesachim* were required accompaniments in the Temple service. One has not made a mockery of the enterprise, but one has failed to bring the offering in its fullest form. The act of declaring is not false; it is simply incomplete.

This distinction carries practical significance. The question arises among the *poskim*: when one recites *shema* without *tefillin*, is this an independent transgression — the *k'ilu me'id ed sheker* of *Ulla* — or does it merely constitute a lesser *kiyum* of the *shema* itself? This distinction matters in practice. Consider the case where one awakens very late, close to the *sof zman krias shema*: if one can put on *tefillin* and recite *shema* or say the *birchos krias shema* and recite *shema* but not do both within the remaining time, which does one choose? The accepted *pesak* is that one recites the *birchos krias shema* without the *tefillin*. This establishes clearly that the *birchos krias shema* are more central to the rabbinic fulfillment of *shema* than wearing *tefillin*. Nevertheless, the formulation of Rabbi Yochanan makes clear that *tefillin* does constitute an aspect of the fullest *kiyum* of *shema*, not merely an incidental accompaniment.

One might ask whether this concern about *tefillin* during *shema* extends to other contexts — for example, would a teacher who is not wearing *tefillin* be prohibited from teaching the paragraph about *tefillin*? Likely not, and the reason is instructive: when teaching, one speaks theoretically, whereas when reciting *shema*, one is making an immediate, personal declaration of obligation. The *shema* is not a study exercise but a ritual act of self-declaration, and it is at that moment of personal declaration that the embodiment of the *mitzvah* is demanded. Additionally, once the *shema* has been ritualized as part of the *tefillah*, the expectation is that one fully embodies that ritual moment rather than merely enunciating its words.

### Full Divine Kingship

Rabbi Yochanan teaches further: *ha-rotzeh she-yekabel alav ol malchut shamayim sheleimah* — one who wishes to accept the yoke of heaven completely — should do the following in sequence: relieve oneself (*yifneh*), wash one's hands, don *tefillin*, recite *krias shema*, and then pray. *Ve-zo hi malchut shamayim sheleimah* — this is a complete acceptance of divine kingship.

Several points in this formulation are worth examining. First, no mention is made of *tallis*, which is more optional in this context; the *gemara* later addresses *tallis* in connection with *Shemoneh Esrei*. Second, the inclusion of *tefillah* in the rubric of *malchut shamayim* is striking, since one might have assumed *malchut shamayim* was centered entirely on *shema*. The answer appears to be that the *tefillah* is the climax and translation of *malchut shamayim*: having acknowledged God's kingship and one's obligations through *shema*, and having been brought into that relationship, one then turns to God in prayer. This is the meaning of *semichat geulah li-tefillah* — joining the blessing of redemption to the *Amidah* without interruption.

More broadly, the formulation answers the question raised implicitly by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: should one not begin immediately with *malchut shamayim*? The answer here is no. To arrive at a *full* (*sheleimah*) *malchut shamayim*, one must prepare: attending to physical needs so as not to be distracted or behave inappropriately before God, washing one's hands as an act of physical and conceptual self-purification, and donning *tefillin* to enter a particular mindset. These preparatory steps do not delay the *malchut shamayim*; they make it complete. One further observation: *sheleimah* may be understood not merely as a qualitative description of the person's inner experience, but as a statement about the nature of *malchut shamayim* itself. A *malchut shamayim* that remains abstract and theoretical is incomplete; what makes it *shaleimah* is that it translates into how one actually prepares to encounter God — into prayer, into practice, into relationship.

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds: one who performs all these steps — attending to physical needs, washing hands, donning *tefillin*, reciting *shema*, and praying — without interrupting with other matters, Scripture accounts it as though he built an altar and offered a sacrifice upon it: *ke-ilu banah mizbei'ach ve-hikriv alav korban*. The verse cited is *erchatz be-nikayon kapai va-asovevah et mizbechachah Hashem* — I will wash my hands in cleanliness and go around Your altar, God — connecting hand-washing to the encircling of the altar. The earlier formulation was about the fullness of the *korban* — everything brought together including *nesachim* and *mincha*. Here the emphasis is on preparation: not just bringing the *korban*, but building the altar on which it is placed. The effort of preparation is itself given sacred significance.

*Rava* adds a comment: since the verse says *erchatz be-nikayon*, with cleanliness, and not *erchatz be-kapai*, with my hands — it should have been said that this is as if one immersed in a *mikveh*, since the word *nikayon* suggests a complete cleansing rather than hand-washing alone. The *gemara* leaves this remark without a direct reply and the discussion moves on.

---

## Hand-Washing Requirements

### Cleanliness Purpose

Ravina poses a question to Rava: did you see that student of the *rabbanan* who came from the west — from *Eretz Yisrael* — who said that one who has no water with which to wash one's hands may clean them with dirt, pebbles, or wood chips (*afar, tzror, kasmit*)? Rava confirms this, saying *shapir ka'amar* — he spoke well. The textual basis is that the verse says *erchatz be-nikayon*, "I will wash in cleanliness," not *erchatz be-mayim*, "I will wash with water." Thus, *kol midei de-manki* — anything that achieves cleanliness — suffices. This is consistent with the underlying purpose, which here is about cleanliness rather than a formal ritual requiring water specifically.

### Non-Water Alternatives

This point is supported by a statement attributed to Rav Chisda, who would curse someone who would go searching for water at the time of *davening*. If it is time to pray, one should not delay the *tefillah* in pursuit of water; any cleansing agent will do.

### Distance for Water

However, the *gemara* then introduces a qualification: *vahani milei le-kri'at shema* — this leniency of non-water alternatives applies to *shema*. But for *tefillah* — for *Shemoneh Esrei* — one should seek water specifically. And how far must one travel? Forward, in the direction one is already heading: even up to a *parsa* (four *mil*, approximately three miles). But if the water source is behind one, one need not retrace one's steps even a single *mil* (approximately three-fifths of a mile). The *gemara* then adds: for less than a *mil* backwards, one would be required to return.

This creates a textual difficulty, since earlier the same *gemara* cited Rav Chisda's condemnation of postponing *davening* for water — yet now it seems to require doing precisely that for *Shemoneh Esrei*. *Tosafot* addresses this by rejecting the *girsa* of this entire passage, arguing that the discussion about how far to travel for water pertains to hand-washing before bread, not before *davening*. The crucial distinction is that hand-washing before bread connects to the world of *tumah va-taharah* — it is a formal ritual requirement for which a *bracha* is recited, rooted in the stringencies surrounding *terumah* and sacred food. Hand-washing before *shema* and *tefillah*, by contrast, is about cleanliness and preparation — *hachon likrat Elokecha Yisrael* — and does not carry the same formal water requirement.

---

## Hearing Shema Dispute

### Must Hear Shema Obligati…

The *gemara* turns to a new *mishna*. The *mishna* states: *ha-korei et shema v'lo hishmia le-ozno yatza* — if one recited *shema* and did not make it audible to oneself, one has fulfilled the obligation. *Divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — this is the view of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yosi says: *lo yatza* — one has not fulfilled the obligation; one must hear what one says. A second dispute: if one read but was imprecise in articulating the letters (*lo dikdek be-otiotav*), Rabbi Yosi says one is *yotzei*; Rabbi Yehuda says one is not.

These two disputes might seem to cross unexpectedly: one might have expected the position requiring audibility (Rabbi Yosi) to also require careful articulation, and the more lenient position (Rabbi Yehuda) to be lenient on both counts. Yet the *gemara* does not appear troubled by this alignment and we will see how the positions are eventually reconciled. The *mishna* adds further: if one read the *shema* out of order (*l'mafrea*), one has not fulfilled the obligation; and if one made an error and then realized it, one must return to the place of the mistake and continue in order — since simply repeating the omitted verse at the end would mean reciting out of order.

### Rabbi Yose Position

What is the reason of Rabbi Yosi? The *gemara* cites: *dechtiv shema, hashmea le-oznecha mah she-atah motzi mipicha* — "hear, let your ears hear what proceeds from your mouth." The word *shema* in this reading commands the speaker to make the words audible to himself.

Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, holds that *shema* teaches only *be-chol lashon she-atah shomea* — that *shema* may be recited in any language one understands, without any requirement of audibility. And the *gemara* acknowledges that according to Rabbi Yosi, one can derive both teachings from *shema*: it permits other languages and it demands self-audibility.

### Deaf Person Terumah Case

The *gemara* now brings a *mishna* from *Terumot* to illuminate the dispute. The *mishna* states: *cheresh ha-medabber ve-eino shomea lo yitrom* — a person who can speak but cannot hear may not take *terumah* at the outset. The reason, as the *gemara* understands it, is that one is obligated to recite a *bracha* before separating *terumah*, and since this person cannot hear the *bracha* he is reciting, he cannot do so *le-chatchilah*. However, *ve-im taram, terumato terumah* — if he did do it, the *terumah* is valid after the fact.

This case focuses attention on a subtle distinction: the issue is not merely that the recitation must be audible (that others could theoretically hear it), but that the person himself must hear it. This is an unusual demand. One could have formulated the requirement as: one's lips must move and produce audible sound — a standard of articulation. But to say that the speaker must specifically be the one who hears it is a stronger claim. In the context of *shema*, this makes sense: *shema* is fundamentally a declaration directed first and foremost at oneself. *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* is not a prayer addressed to God — unlike *Shemoneh Esrei*, which may appropriately be whispered and which is directed to God — but a personal declaration of faith. If the speaker does not hear what he is declaring, the self-directed nature of the declaration is undermined.

The *gemara* identifies this position with Rabbi Yosi: it is Rabbi Yosi who holds that failure to hear oneself even *be-di'avad* disqualifies. The implication is that the case of *terumah* — where failure to hear results in disqualification *le-chatchilah* but valid *terumah* *be-di'avad* — should align with some other opinion.

### Three Positions Reconcil…

The *gemara* now works through the logical possibilities. Rav Chisda initially identifies the *terumah mishna* as following Rabbi Yosi. But the *gemara* challenges this: Rabbi Yosi says that even *be-di'avad* one is not *yotzei* by *shema* without hearing — so how can the *terumah* case allow it *be-di'avad*? The response is that the *terumah* case is different because the problem there is the failure to hear the *bracha*, which is only rabbinic, and *be-di'avad* the *terumah* is valid because the *bracha* requirement does not *taly milta* — does not determine the validity of the *terumah* itself.

But a further challenge arises: if the *terumah* case is Rabbi Yosi's, then what position corresponds to the *bracha* of *birchat hamazon* — which the *gemara* cites as a case where one may not recite it in one's heart *le-chatchilah*, yet if one did recite it that way, *be-di'avad* one has fulfilled the obligation? That middle position — *le-chatchilah* no, *be-di'avad* yes — does not fit Rabbi Yosi (who disqualifies even *be-di'avad* by *shema*) and also does not seem to fit Rabbi Yehuda if we understand him as fully lenient even *le-chatchilah*.

The *gemara* considers: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda is precisely the middle position — *le-chatchilah* one should hear, *be-di'avad* one need not. And in that case there would also need to be an entirely permissive position — even *le-chatchilah* one need not hear — to account for the *terumah mishna* cited in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bereih de-Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, who says a person who can speak but cannot hear may take *terumah* even *le-chatchilah*.

This gives us three positions: (1) Rabbi Yosi — even *be-di'avad* one is not *yotzei* without hearing; (2) a middle position — *le-chatchilah* one must hear, *be-di'avad* one is *yotzei*; (3) a fully permissive position — even *le-chatchilah* one need not hear.

The question is how to distribute these positions between Rabbi Yehuda and the other authorities. One resolution: the middle position (*le-chatchilah* yes, *be-di'avad* it works) is the position of Rabbi Yehuda *in the name of his teacher* — as we find in a *baraita*: *Rabbi Yehuda omer mishum Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, ha-korei et shema tzarich she-yashmia le-ozno* — one who recites *shema* is required to make it audible to oneself. The word *tzarich* — "is required" — signals a *le-chatchilah* standard without necessarily disqualifying *be-di'avad*. Rabbi Yehuda thus transmits his teacher's position as the middle one.

### Rabbi Meir: Heart Intent…

At this point, *Rabbi Meir* is introduced with a striking position. He cites the verse *asher anochi metzavecha ha-yom al levavecha* — "which I command you today upon your heart." From this Rabbi Meir derives: *achar kavanat ha-lev hen hen ha-devarim* — everything follows the intention of the heart. On this view, not only is audibility unnecessary, but perhaps even the verbal articulation of *shema* is dispensable; pure thought — *hirhur* — may suffice. This opens the question of whether *hirhur ke-dibbur dami* — whether mental contemplation is legally equivalent to speech.

The *gemara* concludes by consolidating the framework: now that Rabbi Meir has been introduced as holding that even *le-chatchilah* one need not hear, we can resolve the apparent tension between the middle position and the fully permissive position. The fully permissive position is Rabbi Meir's — who says *le-chatchilah* it is fine not to hear, and perhaps not even to mouth the words. The middle position (*le-chatchilah* one should hear, *be-di'avad* it is valid) is either Rabbi Yehuda in the name of his teacher, or perhaps Rabbi Yehuda himself if we take his own view to be the middle ground.

In sum, the *gemara* has mapped out three positions with respect to the requirement of hearing *shema*: Rabbi Yosi holds that even *be-di'avad* one is not *yotzei* without hearing; the middle position (associated with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya transmitted through Rabbi Yehuda) holds that *le-chatchilah* one must hear but *be-di'avad* it works; and Rabbi Meir holds that even *le-chatchilah* one need not hear, and perhaps mental intention alone suffices. The open question — which these positions apply to exclusively, and whether *hirhur* alone fulfills the obligation — will continue in tomorrow's discussion.

---

---

# Berakhot 15b

## Hearing requirement

### Mishna debate intro

The *mishna* on 15b opens with a dispute between Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the requirement of *mushma'a l'ozno* — whether one must be able to hear what one is saying when reciting the *Shema*.
