The upshot of all these stories, taken together, is that no proof has yet been brought that the dead directly perceive what happens in the living world. Each narrative admits of an alternative explanation: perhaps the dead learn from recently deceased intermediaries, or from heavenly announcements made by Dumah. This sustained skepticism is itself notable — what one finds surprising is not that the *Gemara* affirms belief in the dead's awareness, but that it so persistently questions it.

---

## Shmuel's Father

### Shmuel's Search

The *Gemara* brings one final story bearing on this question. Shmuel's father had been entrusted with the money of orphans for safekeeping. When the father died, Shmuel was not present, and the father had no opportunity to inform him where the money was held. As a result, people began calling Shmuel *bar achil zuzei deyatmi* — the son of the one who consumes the money of orphans — impugning both Shmuel's reputation and his father's.

Shmuel went to the gravesite. He asked the assembled spirits for *Aba* — his father, whose personal name was indeed Aba. The spirits mocked him: we have many *Abas* buried here. He specified: *Aba bar Aba*. Still they mocked: we have many of those too. He finally identified his father fully: *Aba bar Aba Avuhu deShmuel*.

### Heavenly Yeshiva

He was told that his father had ascended to the *metivta de-rakiya* — the heavenly *yeshiva*. In the meantime, he noticed the spirit of Levi sitting outside the main group in the cemetery. He asked Levi: why are you sitting outside? Why have you not ascended to the heavenly *yeshiva*? Levi explained: all those years during which you did not attend the *yeshiva* of Rabbi Afis — and thereby caused Rabbi Afis anguish through your absence — you will have to wait that same number of years before being admitted to the heavenly *yeshiva*.

Presently, Shmuel's father came down, and Shmuel observed that he was simultaneously crying and laughing. He asked why the crying: *de-la'agya ka'atit* — because soon you will be coming here, you will be dying. And why the laughing: *de-chashivat b'hai alma tuba* — because of the great honor that awaits you in the world of the afterlife.

### Orphan Protection

Shmuel then interceded for Levi — since I am so important, he asked, let Levi be admitted. And they brought Levi in. Then Shmuel turned to the matter at hand: *zuzei deyatmi heicha* — where is the orphans' money? His father told him: go take it from the hold of the millstone. The money on top and on the bottom belongs to us; the money in the middle belongs to the orphans. The reason for this arrangement: if thieves steal, they will steal from the outer layers first — ours — and the orphans' money is protected. If the earth consumes from below, it will consume ours first. The orphans' money is maximally protected in the middle.

This detailed account of where the money is hidden and how it is protected serves to vindicate the father's reputation entirely. As for the proof-value of the story: the father knew that Shmuel would soon be dying. The *Gemara* entertains the objection that perhaps Dumah had announced this — but the father speaks of death as imminent though not immediate, not "tomorrow," suggesting this was not a last-minute announcement. The *Gemara* counters: *dilma shani Shmuel keivan de-chashiv kadmu u-machrezei* — perhaps Shmuel is so important that the announcement of his coming was made far in advance, *panu makom* — make room — so that even his imminent death was proclaimed in heaven long before it happened.

---

## Yochanan's Reversal (II)

### Original Position

Despite all these stories, no definitive proof has been brought that the dead possess direct knowledge of what transpires in the living world. Every narrative has admitted of an alternative explanation. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* now tells us that Rabbi Yochanan — who had apparently maintained that the dead know nothing at all — in the end reversed his position.

### Moshe's Report

The proof that convinced him comes from a verse. *De-amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yochanan*: from where do we know that the dead speak with one another? From the verse: *vayomer Hashem eilav zos ha-aretz asher nishbati le-Avraham le-Yitzchak u-le-Yaakov leimor* — "And God said to him: this is the land I swore to Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, saying." The word *leimor* ordinarily implies "to say [to someone else]." But Moshe is at the very moment of his death. To whom is he supposed to say this?

The *Gemara* answers: God is telling Moshe — go and tell Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. *She-shvu'ah she-nishbati lachem kiyamtiha le-vaneichem* — the oath I swore to you, I have now fulfilled for your children. Moshe, who saw the Land with his own eyes, is to go and report this to the *avot*.

The objection arises: if the dead already know what is happening in the world, why would Moshe need to report this to the patriarchs? *Ei salka da'atach de-la yad'ei, ki amru lehu mai hava* — if they don't know anything, what is accomplished by telling them? The point is that they must have conscious awareness; otherwise the message is meaningless. Rashi notes that Rabbi Yochanan's original position was that the dead have no awareness whatsoever — *einam mevinim klum ela tza'ara de-gufa* — and this verse proves that they are in fact conscious beings capable of receiving and understanding information.

The *Gemara* responds that the reason Moshe is sent is *le-achzukei le-tivuta le-Moshe* — so that the *avot* should be able to express gratitude to Moshe, recognizing his role in bringing about the fulfillment of the promise. This addresses why Moshe specifically must report it, but does not undermine the underlying premise that the *avot* are conscious and communicative.

---

## Speaking of the Dead

### Stone Analogy

The *Gemara* now closes with a series of related statements. Rabbi Yitzchak says: *kol ha-mesaper acharei ha-mes ke-ilu mesaper acharei ha-even* — whoever speaks about the dead, it is as if he is speaking about a stone. This seems to echo Rabbi Yochanan's original position.

### Awareness Question

Two interpretations are offered. Some say: *de-la yad'ei* — the dead are simply not aware of what is being said about them. Others say: *de-yad'ei ve-lo ichpas lehu* — they are aware, but they do not care. They are dead. Either way, on this view, speaking ill of the dead has no consequence for the dead themselves.

### Divine Protection

But then Rav Pappa reports: someone spoke disparagingly of Shmuel after his death. A beam fell from the ceiling and split his skull. Does that not suggest the dead do care? The *Gemara* responds: *shani tzurba m'rabanan* — a *talmid chacham* is different. *De-Kudsha Brich Hu tavei biy'karei* — God Himself defends the honor of Torah scholars. It is not that the dead are aware and react; it is that God actively protects the dignity of *talmidei chachamim*, even after their deaths.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi extends this: *kol ha-mesaper acharei mitatan shel talmidei chachamim nofel b'Gehennom* — whoever speaks disparagingly after the *mita* of *talmidei chachamim* — their deeds or conduct — falls into *Gehennom*. The verse is cited: *ve-hamatim akalkalotam yolichem Hashem es po'alei ha-aven shalom al Yisrael* — those who weigh the deeds of the righteous and render a perverse verdict, God will lead those sinners — even when peace rests upon Israel, even at the moment of their own death — to their reckoning.

### Judging Favorably

The *Gemara* concludes with a ruling from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *im ra'ita talmid chacham she'avar aveira ba-layla al teharher acharav ba-yom* — if you saw a Torah scholar sin at night, do not think ill of him by day. Why? *Shema asa teshuva* — perhaps he repented. And the *Gemara* sharpens this: not "perhaps" — *ela vadai asa teshuva* — one may assume with certainty that he did.

This applies specifically, however, to *devarim she-begufo* — sins between man and God, matters of personal religious conduct. But *aval be-mamono* — in matters involving money, financial dealings with others — *ad de-mahadar l'marei* — one must wait until one actually sees the scholar reform his conduct before extending the benefit of the doubt. This distinction is important: *dan l'chaf zechut* applies classically to an ambiguous action, where we interpret a possible wrong favorably. Here, the case is one where something clearly wrong was observed, and the question is how we regard the person going forward. The *Gemara* rules that in matters between man and God, we assume *teshuva* has been done. But in financial matters, the concern for protecting others' interests means that charitable assumption must await demonstrated change.

---

---

# Berakhot 19

## 24 Places of Niddui

### R. Yehoshua ben Levi

The daf opens approximately five lines down on the wide column of 19a. The preceding context had involved a discussion of how to behave in a cemetery — whether *tzitzis* should drag on the floor and whether the deceased is aware of what transpires — which led into a pair of *aggadic* passages about speaking ill of *talmidei chachamim* after their deaths, including the story of someone who spoke disparagingly of Shmuel and was struck by a falling beam. With that backdrop, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi now makes the following statement: *b'esrim v'arba mekomos beis din menadin al kvod harav* — in twenty-four places, *beis din* will place someone in *niddui*, a form of excommunication, on account of disrespect shown to a *rav*. Moreover, all twenty-four of these cases can be found within the *Mishnah*.

When Rabbi Elazar asks where these twenty-four cases appear, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi responds simply: go figure it out yourself. Rabbi Elazar did precisely that — *nafak dak v'ashkach tlas* — he searched carefully and found three.

### Three Explicit Cases

The three cases Rabbi Elazar uncovered are: (1) one who denigrates *netilas yadayim*, hand-washing — *hamizulzel b'netilas yadayim*; (2) one who speaks disparagingly after the questionable conduct of *talmidei chachamim* — *hamespaper acharei mitasan shel talmidei chachamim*, where *mitasan* here does not carry its literal meaning but rather refers to a kind of divergence or deviation from the proper path; and (3) one who acts with arrogance or entitlement toward God — *hamigis da'ato klapei ma'alah*.

### Akavya ben Mahalalel

The *Gemara* addresses the second case — speaking ill of *talmidei chachamim* — somewhat out of order, since it was the subject most recently discussed. The proof text is a *Mishnah* in *Eduyos* involving Akavya ben Mahalalel. Akavya used to say: *im ein m'shakin lo es hageyores v'lo es hamshuchreres* — a woman who is a convert or a freed slave cannot be made to drink the *sotah* waters, because the verse uses the phrase *B'nei Yisrael*, which he interpreted narrowly to exclude converts and freed slaves. Rashi explains that *B'nei Yisrael* in this context refers not necessarily to the woman herself but potentially to her husband — meaning a woman married to a convert or freed slave would not undergo the *sotah* ritual. The precise scope of the exclusion involves some interpretive complexity.

The *chachamim* disagreed and held that she may drink. They cited a precedent: was there not the story of Karkamis, a freed slave woman in Jerusalem, whom Shemaya and Avtalyon ruled must drink? Akavya responded: *dugma hishkuha* — they only gave her a kind of facsimile, a mock procedure. This response is read two ways. *Tosafos* suggests the procedure was performed with plain water, effectively a placebo, which raises its own questions: why do it at all, and could a placebo even produce the *sotah* effect if she were guilty? Rashi reads it differently: because Shemaya and Avtalyon were themselves converts (*gerim*), they were personally invested in permitting the procedure, and therefore their ruling was partial and should not be relied upon.

Either way, Akavya was making an unflattering claim about Shemaya and Avtalyon — either that they fabricated a procedure, or that they ruled improperly due to personal bias. As a result, *veniduhu* — they placed him in *niddui*. *Umes beniduyo* — he died while still under that *niddui*, never having recanted. Consequently, *vesakal beis din es arono* — *beis din* placed a stone on his coffin, which is understood as a virtual act of stoning, a particularly harsh expression of censure.

One might ask whether it is ever legitimate to criticize a rabbi's conduct. The *Gemara* had previously indicated that even if a sage was seen to act improperly, one should assume he has done *teshuva*. Here, the deeper issue is that Akavya interpreted what happened in a way that reflected badly on Shemaya and Avtalyon — and from the perspective of the *chachamim*, that interpretation was tendentious. The *chachamim* felt they had to defend Shemaya and Avtalyon's honor. The *Gemara* itself does not hesitate to criticize where genuine criticism is warranted, but the concern here is that Akavya was reading the events in a way that served his own legal position while disparaging his predecessors.

Rabbi Yehudah, in response to this account, says: *chas veshalom she'Akavya ben Mahalalel nisnadah* — God forbid that someone of Akavya's stature was actually placed in *niddui*. When the Temple courtyard was sealed shut on Pesach and all of Israel gathered, no one among all of them equaled Akavya ben Mahalalel in wisdom, *taharah*, and *yirat chet*. He could not have said such a thing; it could not have been him. *Ela mi nihu?* — Who then was it? The answer is Elazar ben Chanoch.

### Elazar ben Chanoch

Elazar ben Chanoch *she-pikpek b'netilas yadayim* — he treated hand-washing with contempt, dismissing it as unworthy of observance. For this he was placed in *niddui*. When he died, *shalchu beis din v'henichu even gedolah al arono* — *beis din* sent word and placed a large stone on his coffin. The *Gemara* derives from this that whoever is placed in *cherem* and dies in that state, *beis din* stones his coffin.

This case makes clear that the issue is not merely violating a rabbinic law — everyone violates rabbinic laws from time to time. The problem is *zilzul*, a dismissive attitude, a posture of "why should I bother, it is only rabbinic." That kind of fundamental disrespect for rabbinic authority is what merits *niddui*. Two paradigms now emerge for how one can show disrespect to the *rabbis*: making a disparaging claim about specific rabbis' conduct, and treating a rabbinic enactment as beneath consideration.

### Choni HaMa'agel

The third case — *hamigis da'ato klapei ma'alah*, acting with haughtiness toward God — is illustrated by the famous story of Choni HaMa'agel, the circle-drawer. When Choni prayed for rain and received only a drizzle, he declared that was not what he wanted; when it came in torrents, he declared that was too much; he drew a circle and announced he would not step out until God provided exactly what was needed. The *Gemara* records that Shimon ben Shetach sent him this message: *tzarich atah le-hitnadot* — you deserve to be placed in *cherem*. *Ve-ilmalei Choni atah gozrani alecha nidui* — were you not Choni, I would excommunicate you. But *mah e'eseh she-ata mitchateh lifnei ha-Makom* — what can I do? You behave insolently before God, and He loves you so much that He acts on your wishes nonetheless. *K'ven ha-mitchateh lifnei aviv* — like a child who misbehaves and whose father still indulges him. *Yismach avicha ve-imecha ve-tagel yoledtecha* — your father and mother will rejoice over you.

It is notable that Shimon ben Shetach ends with a verse of praise even while declaring Choni deserving of *cherem*. Rashi understands *mitchateh* as a kind of naughtiness or stepping over the line before God. The dominant quality being illustrated here is less arrogance in the classic sense and more a kind of *entitlement* — acting as though one has a personal claim on God that overrides normal boundaries. The conceptual move then is that this same quality of overstepping toward God serves as an analogical model for overstepping toward rabbinic authority.

### Tudos of Rome

An additional case is introduced: *d'tanya Rav Yosef Tudos Ish Romi hinhig es b'nei Romi le'echol gedayim mekulasim b'leilei Pesachim* — Tudos of Rome established a practice among the Jews of Rome to eat whole roasted goats — roasted entire on a spit — on Seder night. The background to this requires some orientation. The *Mishnah* in the chapter *Makom She'nahagu* records that in places where the custom was to eat roasted meat on Seder night, they ate. There are Sephardic communities that to this day eat roasted lamb on Seder night as a *zecher l'korban Pesach*. The Ashkenazic practice, however, opposes this, since it too closely resembles actually bringing a *korban Pesach*. Tudos went further: not merely eating roasted meat, but roasting a whole goat over a spit in deliberate simulation of the Temple offering.

Shimon ben Shetach sent him the same message he had sent Choni: *ilmalei Tudos atah gozrani alecha nidui* — were you not who you are, I would excommunicate you. *She'atah ma'achil es Yisrael kodashim bachutz* — because you are making Israel eat *kodashim* outside the Temple, in the sense that you are enacting something so close in form to the *korban Pesach* that it blurs the line entirely.

This raises an interesting conceptual question. We began by saying that *niddui* is imposed in twenty-four places *al kvod harav*, on account of disrespect to a rabbi. Yet the cases accumulate in ways that strain that original framing. The case of Choni is about entitlement toward God; the case of Tudos is about a practice that the rabbis found objectionable, though it was not uniformly prohibited — there were communities that maintained such practices. How these become instances of *kvod harav* in any direct sense requires some stretching. Regarding questions about who has authority to impose *niddui*: Shimon ben Shetach was the *Nasi* and *Av Beis Din*, and presumably acted with the backing of other rabbis even if they are not mentioned. There are also certain predefined violations for which *niddui* takes effect automatically — the *Rambam* rules this way regarding a few cases, though the *Ra'avad* disagrees — while other cases require a formal decision by *beis din*.

### Analogies to 24 Cases

The *Gemara* now accounts for how one arrives at twenty-four cases when only three appear explicitly in the *Mishnah*. A *baraisa* is cited mentioning the famous dispute about the oven of *Achnai*, in which Rabbi Eliezer ruled the sectioned oven טהור and the *chachamim* ruled it טמא. The word *Achnai* is explained by Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel: *melamed she-hikifuhu halachos ke'achna* — it teaches that they surrounded the oven with *halachos* like a snake constricting its prey, debating all sides. Rabbi Eliezer refused to concede even when the walls of the *beis medrash* bent inward and a heavenly voice spoke in his defense. Eventually, the rabbis took all the items Rabbi Eliezer had declared *tahor* and burned them before him, and ultimately placed him in *niddui*. This is a genuine case of *kvod harav*: it is one thing to maintain a position in debate; it is another to refuse to submit to the majority ruling even after the fact, which is the classic case of *zaken mamre*.

However, the *Gemara* notes that while the case of the oven dispute itself appears in the *Mishnah*, the episode of the *niddui* does not. So strictly speaking, in terms of what the *Mishnah* explicitly records about *niddui*, there are still only three cases. The resolution is: *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi medamei milsa lemilsa* — Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi draws analogies from case to case, while Rabbi Elazar does not. From the three explicit paradigmatic cases, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi extended the logic — if *niddui* was imposed for *netilas yadayim*, then similar cases must also warrant *niddui* — and so analogically derived twenty-four total cases. It remains somewhat striking to speak of twenty-four definite places in the *Mishnah* when the actual enumeration depends on analogy, but that is the *Gemara*'s resolution.

---

## Burial & Osek b'Mitzvah

### Coffin Near Shema

Returning to the central topic of *Krias Shema*, the *Gemara* cites a *baraisa*: *ein motzi'in es hameis samuch l'Krias Shema* — one does not take out the coffin to begin the burial procession close to the time of *Shema*, because this would create complications regarding *osek b'mitzvah*. Once everyone is occupied with the burial, the principle of *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah* — one who is engaged in one mitzvah is exempt from another — would apply, and people might lose the opportunity to say *Shema* entirely. Better to say *Shema* first, then begin the procession. But *v'im hitchilu ein mafsikin* — if the procession has already begun, one does not interrupt it, because at that point one has become *osek b'mitzvah*.

The *Gemara* challenges this from a report that Rav Yosef's coffin was taken out precisely during the time of *Shema*, without waiting. The response: *adam chashuv shani* — an exceptionally important person is different; one does not delay the funeral proceedings of so distinguished a figure even for this consideration. This raises a genuine question about how one chooses between *mitzvos* when both compete for priority. The *Gemara*'s initial answer is: do the one you may not get another opportunity to do — if you begin with the *meis*, you may lose *Shema*. But when another overriding concern enters, such as the dignity of a great person, that calculus can shift.

### Before/Behind Coffin

The *Gemara* continues with those walking before and behind the coffin — *shel lifnei hamita v'shel acharei hamita*. Rashi's reading is that even those behind the coffin, if they are not as essential as those in front, should slip away to say *Shema*. *Tosafos* offers a simpler reading of the *Mishnah*: the only operative question is whether you are needed for the proceedings. If you are needed, you remain and do not say *Shema*; if you are not needed, you slip away and say *Shema*.

### Eulogizers Saying Shema

A *baraisa* addresses those engaged in delivering the eulogy — *ha'oskin b'hesped*. If the body is lying before them — *bizman she-hameis mutal lifneihem* — they slip away one at a time and recite *Shema*, because not all of them need to be present simultaneously. This raises an interesting question about the scope of *osek b'mitzvah*: can we say that the audience assembled at a *hesped* is also engaged in the mitzvah? The *Mishnah* earlier spoke of those in the row beside the mourners being *osek b'mitzvah*, while those on the outside could slip away individually to recite *Shema*. It would seem that crowd presence is in some way part of the *osek b'mitzvah* status — hence the requirement to leave only one at a time rather than all at once.

If the body is *not* lying before them, *hein yoshvin v'korin* — they sit and recite *Shema* as a group, and the *onen* sits in silence. The presence of the body thus functions as a marker of the degree to which one is genuinely *osek b'mitzvah*: the more immediate the *meis*, the more fully one is engaged in the mitzvah, and the less latitude there is to step away.

### Onen & Tziduk HaDin

While the eulogizers and participants say *Shema* and then stand in prayer, the *onen* — one who has suffered a loss but the burial has not yet taken place — is exempt from prayer and *Shema* and sits in silence. *V'hu omeid u'matzdik alav es hadin* — and he stands and recites *tziduk hadin*, acknowledging the justice of God's judgment. The text of *tziduk hadin* cited here is: *Ribono Shel Olamim, chatasi lefanecha, v'lo nifrati mimeni echad m'elef alfei alafim* — Master of the Universe, I have sinned greatly before You, and I have not received even one one-thousandth of the punishment I deserve. *Yehi ratzon milfanecha Hashem Elokeinu shetigdor pirtzoseinu u'firtzos kol amcha Beis Yisrael b'rachamim* — may it be Your will that You close our breaches and the breaches of all Your people Israel with compassion.

### Abaye's Critique

Abaye objects: *lo miba'ei lei l'einish l'meimar hachi* — a person should not say this. He cites Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish and a parallel teaching in the name of Rabbi Yosi: *l'olam al yiftach adam piv l'Satan* — one should never open one's mouth to the Satan. To declare that one has not received even a fraction of deserved punishment is to invite further punishment. Rav Yosef adds the proof text: when Yeshayahu said *k'meat k'Sedom hayinu* — we were almost like Sodom — the prophet responded by calling them *ktzinei Sedom*, officers of Sodom. You said "almost like Sodom," now I will call you Sodom. The principle: when you open the door to such declarations, worse follows.

### Tziduk HaDin Meaning

Beyond the practical concern about *piv l'Satan*, there is a deeper question about the theological framing embedded in this text. The language of *chatasi lefanecha v'lo nifrati mimeni* frames the death as punishment *directed at the speaker* — I have sinned, and I have not yet received what I deserve. This is a recognizable way that many people think in times of loss: what did I do to deserve this? Yet *tziduk hadin* in its essential meaning — and as expressed in the liturgical text we actually recite, *hatzur tamim po'alo ki chol drachav mishpat* — is not about the mourner's punishment but about vindicating God's justice with respect to the person who died. The declaration is: whatever God has done, to whoever suffers as a result, it is just — even if incomprehensible.

One possible reading of *chatasi lefanecha v'lo nifrati mimeni* that avoids the punishment-toward-me framing is: I recognize how small I am, how vast is the gap between my deeds and what I deserve, and therefore I have no standing to protest that this death is unjust. It is an expression of humility rather than a claim of personal punishment. Still, the *Gemara*'s very discomfort with this text — as Abaye reads it — seems to be precisely that it is framed in terms of the speaker's own reckoning. Rav Soloveitchik's understanding of the *onen* provides an important counterbalance: the *onen* is not merely exempt from *mitzvos* in the technical sense of *osek b'mitzvah*, but is positively entitled to remain in a state of existential questioning — of *what does this mean, what is life about, how is this just?* — before moving into the affirmative world of *mitzvos*. *Tziduk hadin* does not demand that questioning disappear; it holds both the questioning and the affirmation of God's justice simultaneously.

### Return from Burial

After the burial, *kavru es hameis v'chazru* — they buried the dead and turned back. The rule is: if they are able to begin and complete *Shema* — even *perek echad o pasuk echad*, a single section or a single verse — before they must take their places in the *shura*, the comforting line, they do so; if not, they do not begin. The *Gemara* initially reads the *Mishnah* as requiring the entire *Shema* to be completed, then harmonizes: the meaning is that if they can get even one *perek* or one *pasuk* in before the line forms, they should, because that unit constitutes some meaningful fulfillment of the obligation.

This connects to the broader question of how much of *Shema* is biblically required. Whether the biblical minimum is a *perek* or a *pasuk* — a question raised earlier in the tractate — bears on whether it is worthwhile to recite a partial *Shema* when the full text cannot be completed. It might also be argued that even less than the biblical minimum should be recited for the sake of *kabalas ol malchus shamayim*, but the *Gemara* does not pursue that line and focuses on the question of fulfilling the *mitzvah*.

### Shura Lines

The *Gemara* now addresses those standing in the *shura*, the line through which the mourners pass to receive consolation. A *baraisa* states: *shurah ha-ro'ah penimah peturah* — the row that faces inward toward the mourners is *patur*, exempt from *Shema* and prayer, as they are directly engaged in the mitzvah of comforting the mourners. *V'she'einah ro'ah penimah chayeves* — those who are not facing inward are obligated.

### R. Yehudah on Intent

Rabbi Yehudah offers a different and broader criterion: *haba machmas ha'avel patur, machmas atzmo chayav* — whoever came for the sake of the mourner is exempt; whoever came for his own reasons is obligated. This fundamentally reframes the question. Rather than asking about one's physical position relative to the inner or outer row, Rabbi Yehudah asks about intent and purpose. If you are genuinely there for the mourner, you are *osek b'mitzvah* regardless of where you stand. If you are there for your own reasons — to be seen, out of curiosity, or any other personal motive — then even standing in the inner row does not make you *osek b'mitzvah*. This raises a fascinating question: according to Rabbi Yehudah, what of someone in the inner row who is saying *hamakom yenachem* — is he *osek b'mitzvah* if his intent is self-serving? The framing of *osek b'mitzvah* as defined by purpose rather than by action alone is a meaningfully different conception.

---

## Kevod HaBriyes

### Shatnez Removal

The *Gemara* now pivots to what becomes one of the most important halakhic discussions in the daf. Rav Yehudah citing Rav states: *hamotzi kilayim b'vigdo poshtan afilu bashuk* — if someone discovers while walking in the street that his garment contains *shatnez* — a prohibited mixture of wool and linen — he must remove it immediately, even in the middle of the public street, even if doing so causes embarrassment. The reasoning: *ein chochmah v'ein tevunah v'ein eitzah leneged Hashem* — there is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that stands before God. You do not make calculations; if it involves a violation, you act. And this is tied directly to the principle stated on 19a: *kol makom she-yeish chillul Hashem ein cholkin kavod le-rav* — wherever there is a desecration of God's Name, one does not show deference even to a *rav*. The *kavod* that was discussed so extensively in the first section of the daf — the same *kavod* for whose sake people were placed in *niddui* — becomes entirely irrelevant when *chillul Hashem* is at stake.

### Two Paths Case

The *Gemara* then challenges this principle. A *baraisa* states: after burying the dead and turning back, if there are two paths before them — one *tahor* and one *tamei*, one pure and one impure — and another person goes down the *tamei* path, one should follow him even if one is a *kohen*, *mishum kvodo* — out of deference to that person's honor. One does not wish to leave him or to embarrass him by conspicuously taking the other path. But how can this be? Should we not say *ein chochmah v'ein tevunah v'ein eitzah leneged Hashem* — that no calculation of human dignity overrides the prohibition?

### Beis HaPras

The resolution, *targemah Rabbi Abba b'veis ha-pras d'rabbanan*, is that this case does not involve a path that is biblically *tamei*. Rather, it involves a *beis ha-pras* — an area where a grave has been plowed over, scattering small bone fragments throughout the field. As Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel teaches, *menapeiach adam beis ha-pras v'holech* — one may blow the dust before each step to clear away any possible bone fragments and then walk through, implying that the concern about *tumah* in a *beis ha-pras* is rabbinic in nature. The chips of bone may be too small to convey biblical *tumah*; the rabbis were stringent as an added precaution. Since the prohibition is rabbinic rather than biblical, it can be overridden for the sake of *kevod habriyos*. The *Gemara* also notes that a *beis ha-pras* that has been heavily trampled is *tahor*, as the fragments would have been ground down beyond concern.

The emerging principle: *kevod habriyos* — human dignity — overrides rabbinic law, but not biblical law.

### R. Elazar bar Tzadok

Further support: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok testified that they used to leap over the coffins of the dead — *medalgin hayinu al gabei aronos shel meisim* — in order to greet Jewish kings, and not only Jewish kings but even non-Jewish kings, because one who has seen non-Jewish royalty will better appreciate Jewish kingship when it comes. Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok was a *kohen*, and yet he describes leaping over coffins, which would ordinarily convey *tumah*. How could he do this?

### Coffin Exception

The answer comes from Rava: *devar Torah ohel she-yeish bo challal tefach chotzeitz bifnei ha-tumah* — biblically, if there is a handbreadth of open space between the lid of the *aron* and the body inside, that space constitutes a *roof* that stops the *tumah* from passing upward. *V'she-ein bo challal tefach eino chotzeitz* — if there is no handbreadth, the *tumah* passes through without obstruction. *V'rov aronos yesh bahen challal tefach* — most coffins do have this handbreadth. Nevertheless, *v'gazru al she-yesh bahen mishum she-ein bahen* — the rabbis decreed that even coffins with the handbreadth should be treated as if they do not have it, as a precautionary measure. *U-mishum kvod melachim lo gazru bahen* — but because of the honor of kings, the rabbis did not apply this decree in that context. So once again: what appears to be a biblical concern resolves into a rabbinic *gezeira*, which can be waived for *kevod habriyos*.

This requires a note, because the impression one has from standard halakhic discourse is that a *kohen*'s prohibition against contracting *tumah* from the dead is entirely biblical — he walks over a grave and immediately becomes *tamei* according to Torah law. How then can the *Gemara* treat any aspect of coffin-*tumah* as merely rabbinic? *Tosafos* explains: there is a separate rule that a sealed coffin — one sealed on all sides — is treated as an extension of the *meis* itself, and therefore does not create the *tefach* airspace that would stop the *tumah*. The case in the *Gemara* apparently involves a coffin that is not completely sealed; in such a case, the lid creates the requisite airspace and the biblical *tumah* does not pass through. The rabbinic decree extends the prohibition even to such cases — and it is that extension, that rabbinic overlay, that is waived for *kevod melachim*. This explains why in Eretz Yisrael, where coffins are not used, the biblical *tumah* issue is even more acute, since there is nothing at all to create the *tefach* space.

### Kvod Overrides

The *Gemara* then cites the principle in its broadest formulation: *gadol kvod ha-briyos she-docheh lo ta'aseh she-ba-Torah* — great is human dignity, for it overrides a biblical prohibition. This seems to contradict everything the *Gemara* has just established. The question follows immediately: should we not say *ein chochmah v'ein tevunah v'ein eitzah leneged Hashem*?

### Lo Tasur Framework

Rav bar Shava explained before Rav Kahana: *b'lav d'lo tassur* — the principle means not literally every biblical prohibition, but specifically the biblical prohibition encoded in *lo tassur min ha-davar*, the verse prohibiting departure from rabbinic instruction. Every rabbinic law has, standing behind it, this biblical injunction to obey the rabbis. When we say *kevod ha-briyos* overrides a "*lo ta'aseh she-ba-Torah*," we mean it overrides *lo tassur* — that is, we mean rabbinic law, not the full range of biblical prohibitions.

### Rav Kahana's Response

Those hearing this explanation *achiku alei* — laughed at him. Their objection: *lav d'lo tassur d'oraissa hi* — *lo tassur* is itself a biblical prohibition! If you are genuinely violating *lo tassur*, that is a biblical violation. Rav Kahana replied: *gavra raba amar milta, la techiku alei* — when a great person says something, do not laugh at him. The explanation he provides: *kol mili d'rabbanan asmichinhu al lo tassur, u-mishum kvodo sharu rabbanan* — all rabbinic laws are anchored in *lo tassur*, and the rabbis themselves have the authority to waive compliance with their own enactments when *kevod ha-briyos* requires it. Therefore when *kevod ha-briyos* is at stake, one is not actually transgressing *lo tassur*, because the rabbis themselves sanction the deviation.

This requires further unpacking. The violation of *lo tassur* is not simply doing something the rabbis prohibited. Rather, *lo tassur* is violated through an act of rejecting rabbinic authority — acting in defiance of the rabbis because one does not accept their jurisdiction. When one violates a rabbinic law because of *yetzer ha-ra*, or mistake, or *kevod ha-briyos*, one is not rejecting rabbinic authority in that substantive sense, and therefore does not violate *lo tassur*. We call it a biblical-adjacent concern only because *lo tassur* stands somewhere in the background. But the operative rule remains: *kevod ha-briyos* overrides rabbinic law, not biblical law in the direct sense.

### Hashavat Aveidah

The *Gemara* brings one more challenge: *ve-hisalamta mehem* — the verse regarding returning a lost object. The *Gemara* reads this verse both as a command (*do not turn away from it*) and as a permission (*there are times you do turn away*). The cases where one need not return the *aveidah*: if the finder is a *kohen* and the object is in a cemetery; if returning it would cost more in wages than the object is worth; and — most relevant here — *hayah zaken v'eino le-fi kvodo*, if one is an elderly or distinguished person for whom stooping down and carrying the object would be beneath his dignity. In that case, *l'chach ne'emar v'hisalamta mehem* — the verse itself permits non-return.

This appears to be a case where *kevod ha-briyos* — specifically, the dignity of the finder — overrides a biblical *mitzvah*. Should this not serve as a paradigm for a broader principle? The *Gemara* responds: *shani hasam, de-chtiv v'hisalamta mehem* — that case is different, because the Torah itself explicitly wrote the permission. Could we not derive a general rule from it? *Issura mi-mamona lo yalfinan* — we do not derive prohibitions from monetary matters. Returning a *aveidah* is a *mitzvah*, but it is fundamentally a monetary issue. Monetary considerations are evaluated by their own standards: *hamotzi mei-chaveiro alav ha-rayah*, and similar rules. One's dignity outweighs another person's monetary interest. But we do not say one's dignity outweighs a prohibition that is evaluated first and foremost in terms of the *issur* rather than in terms of money.

### Money vs. Prohibition

This distinction between monetary and prohibitive frameworks is significant for the overall structure of *kevod ha-briyos*. At this stage of the *sugya*, the *Gemara* has established that *kevod ha-briyos* overrides rabbinic law — and has worked to bracket or explain away all apparent cases of it overriding biblical law: the *beis ha-pras* case is rabbinic; the coffin case involves a rabbinic *gezeira*; the *lo tassur* framing shows that even the "biblical" formulation ultimately means rabbinic; and the *aveidah* case is limited to monetary matters. The conclusion of this *sugya* — examining precisely when *kevod ha-briyos* does and does not override — will be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Berakhot 20

## Kavod HaBriyot Override

### Previous Summary

We return to the bottom of 19b, where the *sugya* has been examining the principle of *kavod habriyot* — human dignity — and its capacity to override various *halachic* obligations. The *gemara*'s basic position is that *kavod habriyot* does not override a biblical prohibition, such as wearing *kilayim*. An apparent counterexample involving *tumah* was set aside on the grounds that the *tumah* in question was only rabbinic, and a rabbinic concern *kavod habriyot* does override. The *sugya* then concluded with the case of a lost object: one need not return an *aveidah* if bending down to retrieve it would be beneath one's dignity. That, however, was characterized as a monetary matter, subject to different standards than a direct confrontation with a prohibition. Now the *gemara* poses one final question before drawing its conclusions.

### Nazir & Meis Mitzvah

The *gemara* introduces a *braisa*: *tashma* — come and hear. The Torah states that a *nazir* may not become *tamei* even to an immediate family member. The verse singles out his sister (*velaachoso*), even though his mother and father have already been mentioned. The novel teaching concerns a case where someone — even a *nazir* — was on his way to slaughter his *korban pesach* or to perform *bris milah* for his son, and received word that a family member had died. One might have thought he should turn back and become *tamei*. The *braisa* rules: he may not. The *chidush* is not that he cannot become *tamei* — in such a case there are all the more reasons not to — but rather what the extra phrase *velaachoso* comes to permit: becoming *tamei* to a *meis mitzvah*.

A *meis mitzvah* is a corpse that has no one to bury it. Though not stated explicitly in the Torah, the rabbis read into the text the principle that this overriding obligation supersedes all else — even a *kohen gadol*, even a *nazir*, even one on his way to bring a *korban pesach* or perform *bris milah*, must stop to bury a *meis mitzvah*. The additional *braisa* similarly teaches that even a *kohen gadol*, with all his additional reasons to avoid *tumah*, is overridden by the needs of a *meis mitzvah*.

Now the *gemara* pauses to identify the animating principle behind the *meis mitzvah* obligation. What makes *meis mitzvah* different from ordinary cases where a *nazir* is forbidden to become *tamei*? If someone else is available to bury the body, the *nazir* does not become *tamei* even for his own father. The urgency must therefore derive from *kavod habriyot* — human dignity — which makes this situation qualitatively different. This is itself a striking juxtaposition: the preceding *sugya* treated the weight of *kavod harav* and earlier discussions addressed *kavod hameit*, and now we arrive at the force of *kavod habriyot* in this most extreme case.

### Limits of Override

Given that *kavod habriyot* overrides the prohibition against *tumah* in the case of *meis mitzvah*, the *gemara* asks: why not say *ein chochma ve'ein tevunah ve'ein eitza leneged Hashem* — that when God's commandment is at stake, no consideration of human dignity can override it? The answer seems to be that here, in fact, it does override. So why not extend the principle further — why not use *meis mitzvah* as a paradigm showing that *kavod habriyot* overrides all prohibitions? Or alternatively, why not say that all aspects of *kavod habriyot*, not just *meis mitzvah*, override biblical *mitzvot*? That would open an enormous category.

The *gemara* answers: *shev ve'al taaseh shani* — passive non-performance is different. But this requires clarification: who is being passive in the *meis mitzvah* case? The *nazir* is actively becoming *tamei*. What does passivity have to do with it?

### Hutrah or Dehuya

Rashi addresses this directly. He explains that the *gemara*'s answer sidesteps the question by reframing the entire situation: we are not saying that the prohibition of *tumah* is overridden for the sake of human dignity. Rather, the prohibitions against a *kohen* or a *nazir* becoming *tamei* were simply never said to apply in a case of *meis mitzvah*. The *Torah* from the outset never forbade *tumah* in this context — it is, in the classic formulation, *hutra*, permitted, not *dechuya*, pushed aside.

This is the well-known question of *hutra o dechuya*: when I violate *Shabbat* to save a dying person, have I violated *Shabbat* but done so mandatorily, or is there no violation at all in the context of saving a life? Rashi applies this framework here: the *tumah* for *meis mitzvah* was never prohibited; hence one cannot derive from it any broader principle about *kavod habriyot* overriding prohibitions.

But a difficulty remains: even granting Rashi's framing for the *tumah* itself, the *nazir* who buries the *meis mitzvah* will now be unable to bring his *korban pesach* and unable to perform *bris milah* for his son — obligations carrying *kareit* — because *tumah* stands in the way. One cannot say those prohibitions were also never applicable. To this, the *gemara* responds: the failure to perform those *mitzvot* is passive non-performance. He is not actively violating anything; he is simply not fulfilling a positive commandment as a consequence. And *kavod habriyot* does override passive non-performance even of biblical *mitzvot*.

### Synthesis of Override

The *gemara*'s conclusions can now be stated clearly. *Kavod habriyot* overrides, first, rabbinic prohibitions — and this is attested in other places in *Shas*, such as the case of someone in a field on *Shabbat* who, for reasons of dignity, must pick up stones to use for hygiene, thereby actively violating a rabbinic prohibition. Second, *kavod habriyot* overrides certain monetary obligations, such as the requirement to return a lost object, though the precise contours of this category involve only *mitzvah*-related monetary obligations, not, for instance, outright theft. Third, *kavod habriyot* overrides even biblical *mitzvot* when the failure to perform them is passive — *shev ve'al taaseh* — rather than active.

As a concrete example of the third category: suppose that fulfilling the *mitzvah* of *tekiat shofar* would require walking through a public space in a state that profoundly violates one's dignity — say, without clothing — such that remaining in place and missing the *tekia* is the only dignified option. In that case, the passive non-performance of a biblical *mitzvah* would be permissible on grounds of *kavod habriyot*.

### Subjectivity Issue

This synthesis immediately raises a serious difficulty. *Kavod habriyot* is an amorphous standard. How broadly or narrowly do we define dignity? Does dignity mean how others perceive one publicly, or one's own internal sense of self-worth? The category threatens to swallow everything: invoked constantly, it could override almost any obligation. Yet if *poskim* are too cautious to invoke it, the principle fails to serve its purpose. This tension is reflected in the historical observation — made at an Edah conference by Rabbi Ezra Labaton in a *shiur* on the use of *kavod habriyot* in Sephardic *psak* — that Sephardic *psak* tends to deploy *kavod habriyot* more readily within its *gemara*-given parameters than Ashkenazic *psak* does. Whether or not this characterization holds across the board, it illustrates that the principle's application is genuinely contested.

### Kavod HaMeit Question

A further question worth raising here concerns whose dignity is actually at stake in the *meis mitzvah* case. Is the *kavod* we are protecting the dignity of the dead person, or of the living community that must witness an unburied corpse? The *gemara*, particularly as the *Yerushalmi* understands the laws of *onen*, seems to take *kavod hameit* — the dignity of the deceased — as a meaningful concept in its own right. Yet this raises a philosophical difficulty: if *meisim einam yodim me'umah* — the dead have no awareness — in what sense can we speak of honoring *them*?

One response is that *kavod hameit* is really a displaced form of *kavod habriyot* — we honor the dead because of what it means to living society, to how we treat our *meitim* as a collective. But the *gemara* does not seem troubled by the question and treats *kavod hameit* as a self-evident concept. A counterexample makes the point vivid: if one is walking alone through a forest and encounters an unburied body that no living person knows about, there is still an obligation of *meis mitzvah*, even though no community's feelings are affected and no social dignity is at stake. This suggests that *kavod hameit* has an irreducibly independent content — though this only underscores how expansive and difficult to define these categories can be.

### Tosafot Alternative

Tosafot is dissatisfied with Rashi's approach. The argument that *tumah* was never prohibited in this context — the *hutra* framing — can be deployed in almost any case, which makes it a weak analytical tool. Tosafot therefore offers an alternative explanation: the reason *meis mitzvah* cannot serve as a paradigm for *kavod habriyot* overriding all prohibitions is not because of *hutra*, but because the prohibitions of *tumah* involved here — those governing a *nazir* and a *kohen* — are not universal. They apply only to specific categories of people. A non-universal prohibition cannot function as a general paradigm.

### Tzaar Baalei Chayim

One final and genuinely remarkable observation closes this *sugya*. The *gemara* here establishes that *kavod habriyot* is a value extracted implicitly from certain *mitzvot* — never stated as a free-standing commandment — and then given direct operative weight within *halacha*, capable of overriding rabbinic prohibitions and the passive non-performance of biblical ones. There is, as far as can be determined, only one other case in *Shas* where the *gemara* performs this same operation: *tzaar baalei chayim* — the prohibition of causing animal suffering.

The *gemara* in Bava Metzia debates whether *tzaar baalei chayim* is *d'oraissa* or *d'rabanan*. Even if it is *d'oraissa*, there is no explicit *pasuk* commanding care for animal suffering. The source is the implicit value embedded in certain *mitzvot* — most notably the obligation to unload an animal struggling under its burden. The *gemara* extracts that implicit value and gives it direct *halachic* force, to the precise effect that *tzaar baalei chayim* overrides rabbinic prohibitions — the same role *kavod habriyot* plays. These appear to be the only two instances in all of *Shas* where the *gemara* identifies a value implicit within a *mitzvah*, extracts it, and transforms it into an active, independent factor within the *halachic* system with real operative weight.

---

## Miracles & Kiddush Hashem

### Rav Pappa's Question

Four lines into 20a, the *gemara* shifts to what initially appears to be an *aggadic* digression, though its connection to the preceding themes will become clear. Rav Pappa asks Abaye: *mai shna rishonim de'itrachish lehu nisa u'mai shna anan de'lo mitrachish lan nisa* — what is different about the early sages that miracles were performed for them, yet for us miracles are not performed?

### Learning Comparison

Rav Pappa anticipates the most natural answer — that the earlier generations were greater *talmidei chachamim* — and immediately refutes it. In the time of Rav Yehuda, who serves as the representative of the earlier *Amoraim* being compared to, all of their learning was in *Nezikin*. That was essentially the one order they studied seriously and in depth. We, by contrast, learn all six *sedarim* of *Shas* — *shisha sidrei Shas* — and engage in broad and deep analysis across the board. We are demonstrably more learned.

The *gemara* illustrates what Rav Yehuda's limits looked like in practice: when he reached the tractate *Uktzin* — clearly the most obscure and difficult *masechet* of *Taharot* — he encountered the *mishnah* discussing a woman who pickles a vegetable in a pot, or alternatively olives pickled with their leaves, and the question of their status as *tehoros*. He said: *havayot de-Rav ve-Shmuel kachazina hacha* — I see here the kinds of profound questions that Rav and Shmuel would go to town on, but I cannot even begin to navigate them. He was confessing that this *mishnah* exceeded his grasp. Rashi and Tosafot actually disagree about what the *mishnah* itself means: Rashi understands it to concern whether leaves in the process of wilting lose their status as a *shomer* or *yad* for the purposes of transmitting *tumah*, since pickling will cause them to wither. Tosafot argues the question is rather whether the leaves themselves qualify as food, given that pickled leaves might or might not be edible. The very *pshat* of the *mishnah* is disputed — illustrating why Rav Yehuda found it so difficult.

We, says Rav Pappa, have thirteen different approaches to learning *Uktzin* — according to Rashi, thirteen distinct analytical frameworks; alternatively, thirteen different *yeshivot* engaged with it. By any measure, we are greater *talmidei chachamim* than they were. And yet: *ki havei shalif chad mesana, ata mitra* — Rav Yehuda would merely remove one shoe at the outset of a public fast for rain, and it would begin to rain. He barely had to begin the *ta'anit* and the heavens responded. We, *kamesarina nafshin u'mitzavcha katzavchina ve'leika de'mashgach ban* — we afflict ourselves deeply and cry out to God, and no one pays attention. The *gemara* is making a profound and sobering point: greater *Torah* knowledge does not by itself account for closeness to God. The case of *Choni HaMa'agel* comes to mind — he was not known for *halachic* statements, yet he had an extraordinary relationship with divine response. Who is a *chasid* and who is close to God is not always the same question as who is the greatest *talmid chacham*.

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye's response ties this discussion back to the theme of *kavod Hashem* that animates the preceding *sugyot*. He says: *kamai havei kamsrin nafshaihu akdushat Hashem* — the early ones would sacrifice and risk themselves for the sake of defending God's honor, for *kiddush Hashem*. We do not do that. That willingness to give up personal security and dignity for *kiddush Hashem* — not learning breadth — is what distinguished them.

### Rav Adda Example

The example offered is Rav Adda bar Ahava. He saw a certain Samaritan woman wearing a *karbalta* in the marketplace. Assuming she was Jewish, he rose and ripped it off of her. It turned out she was not Jewish, and he was assessed 400 *zuz* — perhaps for the cost of the garment, perhaps also including a payment for the embarrassment, a matter discussed at length in Bava Kamma. He asked her name; she replied *Maton*. He responded: *Maton Maton arba me'ah zuzei shavya* — *Maton* means 200 in Aramaic, so *Maton Maton* cost him 400 *zuz*. This is offered as a paradigm of self-sacrifice for *kiddush Hashem*: he lost money, was shamed, and exposed himself to legal liability — all to protect God's honor against public violation.

### Zealotry Problem

What exactly was the violation Rav Adda was responding to? The most natural contextual reading — given that the preceding *sugya* involved *kilayim* — is that the garment was *sha'atnez*. The principle of *ein eitzah ve'ein tevunah leneged Hashem* — no consideration overrides God's command — would then motivate stripping the garment off even from someone else. Rashi describes the *karbalta* simply as *shem levush chashuv*, an important garment, without specifying *sha'atnez*. The *Mesoret HaShas*, however, cites the *Aruch*, who explains it as a red, seductive garment, thereby framing the concern as *pritzut* — immodesty leading to improper thoughts — which reframes the entire episode in terms of women's dress and male *hirhurim*.

The *Aruch*'s reading is deeply problematic. If the concern is that her garment is provoking illicit thoughts, stripping it off only worsens the situation. Moreover, it frames the episode as a man adjudicating women's dress standards and physically intervening to enforce them — a reading with serious contemporary implications.

Even the *sha'atnez* reading, which is contextually more defensible, carries difficulties. This is being held up as the model of behavior that earned the early sages their miracles. Yet the woman is *beshogeg* — she is not willfully violating. As the earlier discussion in this *sugya* raised: if someone is unknowingly wearing *sha'atnez*, does one even have an obligation to inform them, let alone physically strip their garment? The earlier framework suggested that passive non-performance by a *beshogeg* violator might be grounds for simply letting matters stand. Here Rav Adda goes considerably further — not even informing her and giving her the option to remove it herself, but acting unilaterally. Even setting aside the gender dimension, praising this kind of zealotry presents real difficulties. It resembles an act of *kinah l'Hashem* in the manner of Pinchas — appropriate perhaps in the most extreme and specific circumstances, but a dangerous model to universalize.

It is also important to note the literary and *halachic* context: this is Abaye's response to Rav Pappa's question. It is one sage's answer about why the early generations merited miracles. The *gemara* does not endorse it as a normative ruling, and the voices of *Shas* are multiple. One cannot simply extract this episode and treat it as the *gemara*'s authoritative statement about proper behavior. The connection to the theme of *kavod Hashem* — placing God's honor above one's own financial and social interests — is the central point being made, even if the specific example raises serious independent questions.

---

## Gender Interaction Cases

### Rav Gidel Case

The *gemara* now introduces a series of cases involving the interaction between sages and women, all tied to the *mikveh*. Rav Gidel used to go and sit by the gates of the *tevilah* — the entrance to the *mikveh* — where he would instruct the women: immerse this way, immerse that way. He was evidently offering guidance about proper immersion technique as women entered.

### White Ducks Defense

The rabbis challenged him: *lo ka'mistafi mar mi'yetzer hara?* — are you not afraid of your evil inclination? Speaking to women immediately before they immerse, in such a charged context, surely inflames illicit desire. Rav Gidel replied: *damyan be'appai ki kaki chivri* — they appear to me like white ducks. They simply hold no erotic charge for him whatsoever. This response invites considerable skepticism, and the *gemara* records it without explicit endorsement.

### Rabbi Yochanan Case

Rabbi Yochanan similarly used to sit by the gates of the *mikveh*. He was not speaking to the women; the *gemara* makes clear his purpose was different. His practice was that when the women of Israel came up from the *mikveh* and passed by, they would look at him — *mistaklan bi* — and thereby merit beautiful children like him.

### Conception Belief

This reflects a belief prevalent among the rabbis: that the thoughts and experiences of husband and wife at the moment of conception shape the nature of the children produced. This conviction appears also in the *gemara* in Nedarim, which discusses at length how various improper behaviors or mental preoccupations during marital relations can lead to particular outcomes in children. Rabbi Yochanan, whose exceptional physical beauty was well known, was positioning himself so that the women, having seen him, would be thinking of him — however obliquely — in the context of conception, thus leading their children to be beautiful.

This is somewhat ironic: the *gemara* in Nedarim that discusses this belief also identifies thinking of another person during marital relations as a problem. Rabbi Yochanan seems not to have been troubled by this tension, perhaps because the mental image of him would remain in the background rather than as a focused preoccupation. In any case, the *gemara* does not problematize his practice here on those grounds.

### Ayin Hara Protection

The rabbis questioned Rabbi Yochanan on different grounds: *lo ka'mistafei mar mi'ayina bisha?* — are you not afraid of the *ayin hara*? Sitting publicly as a figure of beauty, drawing the admiring gaze of many women, exposes one to the *ayin hara* — the evil eye, which at its core is about envy. The envy generated by conspicuous beauty or success is what gives the *ayin hara* its power.

Rabbi Yochanan replied: *ana mi-zara de-Yosef ka'asina* — I am from the descendants of Yosef, and the descendants of Yosef are not subject to the *ayin hara*. He cites the verse *ben porat Yosef ben porat alei ayin* — a fruitful child is Yosef, fruitful *alei ayin*. Rabbi Abbahu derives from this: do not read *alei ayin* but *olei ayin* — rising above the *ayin hara*. Rav Yossi berebi Chanina cites a different verse: *ve-yidgu la-rov be-kerev ha'aretz* — they shall multiply like fish within the land. Just as fish in the sea are covered by water and the *ayin hara* has no dominion over them, so too the seed of Yosef is beyond the reach of *ayin hara*.

The *gemara* then offers a second, more ethical derivation: *ayin she-lo ratzah la-zun mi-mah she-eino shelo* — an eye that refused to feed on that which was not his. Yosef refused *eshet Potiphar*, refused to take what was not his — and the *ayin hara*, which operates through envy and covetousness, therefore has no hold over his descendants. One who does not covet is protected from those who covet him.

There is also a striking literary observation worth noting: the verse that establishes Yosef's protection from the *ayin hara* ends with the phrase *banot tzada alei shur* — the women step up to gaze over the wall. The verse itself evokes women gazing upon Yosef, which directly echoes the scene of women looking at Rabbi Yochanan. The *pasuk* being used to explain why Rabbi Yochanan's practice poses no danger is itself a verse about women looking at a beautiful man.

### Contextuality Principle

Beyond the *aggadic* content, these cases carry significant *halachic* weight for the *Rishonim* and *Poskim* on questions of gender interaction. Both Rav Gidel's case — where he speaks with women — and Rabbi Yochanan's case — where he sits to be observed by them — involve interactions that are not intrinsically prohibited but might be problematic depending on whether they lead to *hirhur*, improper thought. What these *gemarot* demonstrate, alongside other cases such as the *gemara* in Ketubot about a sage carrying a bride on his shoulder, is that the permissibility of such interactions is inherently contextual. If the circumstances and the individuals involved are such that no *hirhur* is generated, the activity is not prohibited. This principle becomes important for later *Rishonim* and *Poskim* evaluating a range of situations involving men and women, where the prohibition, if any, is not categorical but depends on what the interaction actually produces in the minds of those involved.

---

## Women & Mitzvot Obligati…

### Time-Bound Principle

The *gemara* transitions to a new *mishnah*: *nashim va'avadim u'ketanim peturin mikriat shema* — women, slaves, and minors are exempt from *kriat shema*. This trio — women, non-free male adults, and children — represents those who stand outside the full category of obligated adult free males. The exemption rests on the general principle of *mitzvot asei shehazman grama*: women are exempt from positive time-bound commandments. Slaves carry the same obligations as women. As for minors, while the *gemara* discusses the age of *chinuch* and the father's obligation to train his son in *kriat shema*, the children themselves bear no immediate personal obligation.

### Tefillin Exemption

The *mishnah* continues: women are also exempt from *tefillin*. The exemption is derived through a *drasha* connecting *tefillin* to *talmud Torah*. The verse *ve'limadetem otam et bneichem* — you shall teach your sons — is read as excluding daughters from the *mitzvah* of *talmud Torah*. The verse immediately following, *ukshartam le'ot al yedechem* — and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand — is linked to the preceding *mitzvah*, so that those exempt from *talmud Torah* are similarly exempt from *tefillin*. An alternative basis is that *tefillin* may be time-bound, since they are not worn at night — though this is itself debated.

### Prayer Obligation

Despite being exempt from *kriat shema* and *tefillin*, women are obligated in *tefilla*. One might have supposed *tefilla* to be time-bound, given that it is recited at fixed times. The *gemara* explains: *derachamei ninhu* — because prayer is *rachamim*. This is a technically significant word. *Rachamim* denotes not merely compassion as an emotional category but the beseeching of God that wells up from within — the non-formalistic core of prayer. This stands in a certain tension with the principle of *tefilla keneged korbanot*, which grounds prayer in the formal structure of the sacrificial service. The *gemara*'s claim is that at its foundation, prayer is this intensely personal experience of turning to God — universal, atemporal, not reducible to a schedule. Upon this foundation, rabbinic and formalistic structures are subsequently imposed; but the core is *rachamim*, and *rachamim* is not time-bound. Women therefore share equally in this obligation.

### Kriat Shema Exemption

The *gemara* asks: is the exemption from *kriat shema* not obvious? It is a positive time-bound commandment, and women are exempt from such commandments. The *gemara* answers that one might have thought otherwise: *kriat shema* involves the declaration of *malchut shamayim* — the Kingdom of Heaven — so central to Jewish faith that perhaps women should be obligated regardless of the time-bound exemption. The *gemara* also suggests one might have argued that since *shema* is said morning and night, it encompasses the entire day and is not truly time-bound in a meaningful sense. The *gemara* rejects both arguments: the standard exemption applies, and women are not obligated in *kriat shema*.

One might observe the interesting structural contrast here. In the discussion of *tefilla*, the *gemara* argues that what appears time-bound is actually not, because the essential human experience of prayer transcends time. In the discussion of *kriat shema*, a parallel argument — that morning and night together encompass the whole day, making it perpetual rather than time-bound — is apparently entertained and then not pursued, the *gemara* simply affirming the standard exemption on the grounds that *malchut shamayim* does not independently override the time-bound classification.

### Mezuza Obligation

Women are obligated in *mezuza*. The *gemara* says this is obvious — so obvious it need not be stated. The potential *hava amina* is that since *tefillin* and *mezuza* are juxtaposed in the Torah, one might derive an exemption for women from *mezuza* parallel to their exemption from *tefillin*, particularly since *tefillin* is linked to *talmud Torah*. The *gemara* rules that this does not follow: *mezuza* is fundamentally about the status of the house, not about the person's obligation in *talmud Torah*, and therefore women are fully obligated.

### Prayer Nature

Returning to the topic of *tefilla* and its underlying nature, the *gemara*'s reasoning deserves fuller examination. The *hava amina* that women might be exempt from *tefilla* runs as follows: since prayer is prescribed for morning, afternoon, and evening — *erev vavoker vetzahorayim* — it resembles a time-bound *mitzvah* and should be exempt for women. The *gemara* rejects this. Even granting that human beings naturally experience a need to pray at different times of day, the fundamental experience of prayer transcends those temporal anchors. The need to turn to God is not morning's need or evening's need; it is the need of a human being as such. Therefore *tefilla* does not fall within *mitzvot asei shehazman grama*, and women are as obligated as men.

The *halachic* consequence of this analysis is significant, and the *gemara* states it without qualification: women are obligated in *tefilla* — by which the *gemara* means *Shemoneh Esrei*, the *Amidah* — at least twice daily, *Shacharit* and *Mincha*, and perhaps *Maariv* as well, though *Maariv* has its own question of *reshut*. Virtually all *Rishonim* and *Poskim* affirm this. Yet for centuries, the practice departed dramatically from this ruling. Women were often illiterate, did not attend *shul*, and did not recite *Shemoneh Esrei* regularly. Private *tehinot* and personal prayers substituted for formal *davening*.

### Historical Practice Gap

The gap between the clear *halachic* ruling and the historical reality has generated significant discussion among *Poskim*. Some looked at the widespread phenomenon of women not reciting *Shemoneh Esrei* and felt compelled to reinterpret the obligation. Rather than holding women accountable for an obligation they were universally not fulfilling, they proposed a distinction between the biblical foundation of prayer — the personal, existential turning to God that requires no fixed formula — and the rabbinic superstructure of fixed texts twice daily at fixed times. Women are obligated in the former; the latter, being rabbinic and time-structured, might be categorized as *mitzvat asei shehazman grama* from which women are exempt. Saying *Modeh Ani* or reciting any personal prayer would then discharge the biblical obligation.

This position is frankly a post-facto accommodation of practice rather than the straightforward reading of the *gemara*. The simple reading — that women are fully obligated in *Shemoneh Esrei* — is what most *Rishonim* say. In contemporary Modern Orthodox communities, this reading has become increasingly prominent, with the recognition that the historical non-practice was a function of social conditions — illiteracy, confinement to the home, exclusion from communal religious life — rather than *halacha*. It is worth noting that in *Chareidi* communities, where one might least expect this, women do in fact recite *Shacharit* and *Mincha* privately, though not in communal settings. It appears that the *Poskim* who grappled with the phenomenon of women not *davening* were addressing conditions that predate the modern period, and that those conditions no longer describe the reality for large segments of the observant community.

### Birkat HaMazon

The *mishnah* also obligates women in *Birkat HaMazon*. This might seem puzzling: even though *Birkat HaMazon* is not formally time-bound, there is a natural rhythm to eating — *b'erev basar le'echol v'lechem baboker lishboa*, evening for meat and morning for bread — suggesting that eating itself follows temporal patterns, which could render *Birkat HaMazon* quasi-time-bound. The *gemara* rules that this does not make it a *mitzvat asei shehazman grama*; women are obligated. The *gemara* will continue to develop the discussion of *Birkat HaMazon* in the next session, and we will address it then.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

A final textual and conceptual debate between Rashi and Tosafot bears noting. Rashi's *girsa* apparently omitted the word *peshita* — "obviously" — before the *gemara*'s ruling on *tefilla*. According to Rashi, the reason is that since *tefilla* in the form we have it is rabbinic, the entire framework of time-bound exemption for women simply does not apply to rabbinic *mitzvot*. The question of *shehazman grama* is a biblical category; for rabbinic obligations, it is irrelevant. Hence the *gemara* does not say *peshita* — of course they are obligated — because that reasoning would not apply; instead it simply states that they are obligated because of *rachamim*.

Tosafot retains the *girsa* of *peshita* and disagrees. Even for rabbinic *mitzvot*, Tosafot holds, we often pattern the obligations after biblical ones, and the principle of *shehazman grama* — with its attendant exemption for women — can apply to rabbinic *mitzvot* as well. The *gemara*'s ruling that *tefilla* is not time-bound therefore remains meaningful and necessary even for its rabbinic form. This debate between Rashi and Tosafot has implications for how one understands the scope of women's exemptions more broadly, and it turns at least in part on which textual reading one accepts.

---

# Berakhot 20b

## Women & Kiddush

### Women obligated Kiddush

The *gemara* opens with a statement of Rav Adda bar Ahava: *nashim chayavot bekiddush hayom d'oraita* — women are obligated in *kiddush* on *Shabbat* biblically. Our form of *kiddush* is recited over a cup of wine and includes the declaration of *mekadesh hashabbat*, but the wine itself is generally understood to be only *miderabbanan*. At its core, however, there is a biblical *mitzvah* of *zachor et yom hashabbat lekadesho* — to declare the sanctity of *Shabbat*. And that biblical obligation, Rav Adda bar Ahava maintains, applies to women as well.

### Time-bound exemption

The immediate challenge is obvious: *kiddush* is a *mitzvat aseh shehazman grama* — a positive time-bound commandment — and the principle is that women are exempt from all such commandments. Abaye attempts to resolve this by saying the obligation is only rabbinic (*miderabbanan*), not biblical. Rava, however, objects on two grounds. First, the statement explicitly says *d'oraita*. Second, and more fundamentally, if we are going to say the rabbis independently obligated women in *kiddush* even though it is time-bound, then we should have obligated them in every time-bound *mitzvah* — which we clearly have not done. There must therefore be something uniquely compelling about *kiddush*. The question is what.

### Zachor v'Shamor link

Rava answers by citing the verse: *zachor ve-shamor* — remember and observe. These two words, appearing in the two versions of the *Aseret Hadiberot*, were spoken simultaneously (*b'dibbur echad ne'emru*), establishing an intrinsic link between *shmirah* (the negative prohibition of *Shabbat*) and *zkhirah* (the positive declaration of *Shabbat*). The principle Rava derives is: *kol she-yeshno bi-shmirah yeshno bi-zkirah* — anyone bound by the obligation to observe *Shabbat*, meaning to refrain from *melacha*, is equally bound in the obligation of *zikira*, meaning *kiddush*. Since women are unquestionably obligated in *shmirat Shabbat*, they are correspondingly obligated in *kiddush*. The practical implication is significant: because men and women share an equal biblical obligation in *kiddush*, a woman can serve as *motzi* for a man. Any objections that have been raised in later authorities are secondary considerations — matters of *zila milta* and the like — but at the level of principle, the equal obligation is accepted.

### Drasha mechanics

One might ask what kind of *drasha* this is. It is not a *kal v'chomer*, nor quite a *gzeira shava* in the technical sense, yet it functions similarly — treating the two usages of the same concept in parallel texts as definitionally linked. The nature of the derivation is that because *zachor* and *shamor* were said simultaneously, their subjects are coextensive: whoever falls within one falls within the other.

A parallel question arises regarding *havdalah*, which many authorities understand to also be biblical, linked to the same *zkhirah* obligation — declaring the boundaries of *Shabbat* both at its beginning and at its end. On this analysis, women would be equally obligated in *havdalah* as in *kiddush*, and could certainly perform it for themselves and potentially serve as *motzi* for a man. There are, however, certain *rishonim* and *poskim* who hold that women's obligation in *havdalah* is only *miderabbanan*, and some go so far as to maintain that a woman cannot even perform *havdalah* for herself — she must hear it from a man. This is a striking position, since it is exceedingly rare in *halacha* for someone to be unable to perform even for themselves a *mitzvah* from which they are partially or fully exempt. The straightforward reading of the relevant *sugyot*, and the position of most *poskim*, is that women are equally obligated in *havdalah* and may at minimum perform it for themselves.

---

## Birkat Hamazon status

### Biblical vs Rabbinic

The *gemara* now turns to *birkat hamazon*. The *mishna* has already stated that women are obligated, and we have noted that *benching* is not time-bound. Yet Ravina poses a sharper question to Rava: *nashim b'Birkat Hamazon d'oraita o d'rabbanan* — is women's obligation in *birkat hamazon* biblical or merely rabbinic? The *nafka mina* — the practical difference — is whether a woman can serve as *motzi* for others. If her obligation is biblical, then *d'oraita* can discharge *d'oraita*. If it is only rabbinic, then she is in the category of *she'eino mechuyav b'davar*, one not fully obligated, and cannot discharge the obligation of those who are biblically bound.

### Tosefta teaching

The *gemara* brings a *tosefta* from *Sukkah* as potential evidence. The *tosefta* states: *ben mevarech l'aviv, ve'eved mevarech l'rabbo, v'ishah mevareches l'baalah* — a son can perform *birkat hamazon* for his father, a slave for his master, a woman for her husband. This would seem to indicate that all three can discharge the obligation of the men, which in turn suggests their own obligation is biblical and equal. However, the *tosefta* immediately adds that even though this is technically true in principle, *tavo me'eirah l'adam she'ishah u'vanav mevarchin lo* — a curse should befall a man whose wife and children must bench on his behalf — since this could only reflect that the man was insufficiently learned or capable. The cultural context is important here: this was a world in which egalitarianism was not a governing value, and in which the general expectation was that men would be more steeped in learning and practice. In such a context, dependence on one's wife for *birkat hamazon* was understood as a social and personal embarrassment.

### Obligation levels

The *gemara* tries to read the *tosefta* as proof that women's obligation is biblical: *bishlama de'oraita, ati de'oraita umapik de'oraita* — it makes sense that a woman could serve as *motzi* her husband only if both share the same biblical obligation. But if her obligation were merely rabbinic, how could *d'rabbanan* discharge *d'oraita*?

The *gemara* immediately deflects this argument. The *tosefta* also lists a minor (*katan*) as someone who can bench for his father. But a minor is not biblically obligated in *birkat hamazon* — so how can he discharge his father's obligation? Clearly the *tosefta* is not making a claim about equal levels of obligation. The *gemara* resolves this: *kegon she'achal shiur derabbanan* — the case is where the father ate only a rabbinic-sized amount, meaning less than the quantity of *saveta*, true satiety, that triggers a biblical obligation. The Torah says *ve'achalta ve-savata u'veirachta* — only when one is truly sated is the obligation biblical. When one eats only a *ke'zayit* or a *ke'beitzah*, the obligation is rabbinic. So the father in this case is a biblical-level person who ate only a rabbinic-sized amount, making his current obligation only rabbinic. And a *d'rabbanan* can discharge a *d'rabbanan*, even if the two parties reach that level of obligation through different routes.

This resolution dissolves the proof from the *tosefta*: the case may be entirely within the realm of rabbinic obligation on both sides, and therefore we cannot infer anything about women's biblical status from it. It also opens a broader discussion in the *rishonim* about levels of obligation: what happens when someone is a "double *derabbanan*" — doubly distanced from biblical obligation — such as a minor performing *megillah* for an adult? The minor's obligation is rabbinic because of his age; the adult's obligation in *megillah* is also rabbinic; but are these the same level of *derabbanan*, or is the minor's a *derabbanan* of a *derabbanan*? These questions ramify in later contexts.
