It is also worth noting that the *tosefta*'s phrasing — *ben mevarech*, *ve'eved mevarech*, *v'ishah mevareches* — may not necessarily imply *motzi* in the fullest sense. One could read *mevarech* as the son or wife leading the *birkat hamazon* aloud while the others repeat after, rather than truly discharging their obligation on their behalf. On this reading, the *tosefta* would not be addressing *yeitziah* at all, and the whole proof collapses from a different direction. In any case, the *gemara* concludes that the question of whether women's obligation in *birkat hamazon* is biblical or rabbinic remains unresolved.

### Rashi's approach

This raises the underlying question: given that *birkat hamazon* is not time-bound, why would women's obligation be less than men's in the first place? The *mishna* states simply that women are obligated — why should that be anything other than fully biblical?

Rashi explains that women may be excluded from the biblical obligation because of the content of *birkat hamazon* itself. The Torah's formulation is *ve'achalta ve-savata u'veirachta et Hashem Elohecha al ha'aretz hatovah asher natan lach* — you shall bless God for the good land that He has given you. The blessing is not merely a response to eating food; it is an expression of gratitude for the Land of Israel. The second *bracha* of *birkat hamazon* — *al ha'aretz ve'al hamazon* — has this as its core. And the Land of Israel, in biblical law, is apportioned through inheritance — a domain from which women are generally excluded as direct heirs. A woman never inherits the land directly as a primary heir; at most she might inherit in the absence of male heirs. Therefore Rashi suggests that the verse's phrase *asher natan lach* — which He gave *you* — does not apply to women in the same way, and their obligation may therefore be only rabbinic.

### Tosafot's view

Tosafot rejects Rashi's approach. If the concern is about who receives the land, then we should also question the obligation of *kohanim*, *levi'im*, *geirim*, and others who do not hold portions of the land. Collectively, the Jewish people received the land, and that collective relationship is what generates the obligation — not one's individual *nachalah*. Rashi's distinction, Tosafot argues, does not hold.

Tosafot instead points to a later *gemara* which states that if one omits the phrases *al brischa shechatamta bivsareinu* and *al torascha shelimaditanu* from *birkat hamazon*, one has not fulfilled the obligation (*lo yatza*). Tosafot takes this *gemara* literally — these phrases are part of the biblical obligation of *birkat hamazon*. Women who do not have *bris milah* in the literal sense, and who are not obligated in *talmud Torah*, are therefore missing essential elements of the biblical text, and on that basis their biblical obligation may not fully apply. Tosafot acknowledges the difficulty: these themes do not appear in the Torah's own formulation of *birkat hamazon*, so it is hard to understand how they can be part of the biblical obligation. But this is Tosafot's attempt to explain why the *gemara* would entertain the possibility of a reduced obligation for women.

### Pshat conclusion

Both Rashi and Tosafot struggle to explain the *gemara*'s *hava amina*. The simple *pshat* of the *mishna* — that women are obligated in *birkat hamazon* — would suggest their obligation is fully biblical, identical to men's. Given that the underlying question is left open by the *gemara*, and given that the *hava amina* behind a lesser obligation is difficult to ground clearly, the straightforward reading remains that women's obligation in *birkat hamazon* is equal to men's.

The question of *zimun* is a separate matter. *Zimun* is a distinct rabbinic institution — the formal introduction to *birkat hamazon* when three or more have eaten together. Whether women participate in *zimun* with men, and under what conditions, involves additional considerations that go beyond the basic question of whether a woman can discharge a man's obligation in *benching* itself. That discussion belongs to a later *perek* and will be addressed in its proper place.

---

## Benching & Divine favor

### Angels' challenge

Before moving on, the *gemara* closes with a *midrash* attributed to Rav Avira — sometimes in the name of Rav Ammi, sometimes in the name of Rav Assi. The *malachei hasharet*, the heavenly angels, address God with a challenge: *kasuv b'torascha asher lo yissa panim v'lo yikach shochad* — it is written in Your Torah that You do not show favor and do not accept bribes. Yet You show special favor to Israel, as it is written *yissa Hashem panav eilecha* — God will lift His countenance to you. How can this be? Tosafot notes that the *pasuk* about God lifting His countenance does not in *pshat* mean favoritism over others — it simply describes a warm and close relationship. Nevertheless, the *midrash* takes up the apparent tension.

### Divine reciprocity

God responds: *v'chi lo essa panim l'Yisrael* — shall I not show them favor? For I wrote in the Torah *ve'achalta ve-savata u'veirachta* — that the obligation to bench is only when one is truly sated. And yet *ve'hem medakdekin al atzman ad ke'zayit ve'ad ke'beitzah* — they are so careful upon themselves that they obligate themselves rabbinically even for as little as an olive-sized or egg-sized amount of food. Because Israel does more than is strictly demanded of them — going beyond the letter of biblical law in their punctiliousness — God in turn acts toward them beyond the strict *shurat hadin*, the line of justice. There is a reciprocity here: Israel's self-imposed stringency in *benching* is met with divine favor that exceeds what strict judgment would require.

---

## Ba'al Keri rules

### Ba'al Keri practice

The *gemara* now shifts abruptly to a different category of person: the *ba'al keri*, a man who has experienced a seminal emission and remains in a state of *tumah* until he immerses in a *mikvah*. The *mishna* states: *ba'al keri meharher belibo ve'eino mevarech lo lefanav ve'lo le'acharav* — a *ba'al keri* thinks the *shema* in his heart, but he does not recite the *brachos* before or after it. Conversely, *ve'al hamazon mevarech le'acharav ve'eino mevarech lefanav* — for *benching*, he recites the blessing after the meal (the biblical obligation), but not the blessing before eating (which is only rabbinic).

The operative principle at work in the *mishna* is that a *ba'al keri* fulfills his biblical obligations but not his rabbinic ones. The *bracha* of *shema* itself — the core *pasuk* — is biblical, so he does it, though only by thinking it. The surrounding *brachos* of *kriat shema* are rabbinic, so he omits them. The *birkat hamazon* after eating is biblical, so he recites it. The *bracha* over bread before eating is rabbinic, so he omits it.

### Rabbi Yehuda disagrees

Rabbi Yehuda dissents: *mevarech lefanav u'le'acharav* — he may recite the blessings both before and after. Rabbi Yehuda is not troubled by the *ba'al keri*'s status when it comes to *brachos*.

### Thought vs. speech

Before the *gemara* addresses the underlying reason for these restrictions, a striking asymmetry in the *mishna* itself demands attention. The *shema* is performed through *hirhur* — silent thought. The *birkat hamazon* afterward, by contrast, appears to be recited aloud. Why the difference?

Some *rishonim* — the *talmidei Rabbeinu Yona* — resolve this by reading the *mishna* uniformly: even when it says the *ba'al keri* "says" *birkat hamazon*, it means he thinks it, just as with *shema*. Both are done only in the mind.

A second approach draws on the particular character of *shema*. Throughout the earlier discussions in *Berakhot*, there is a strong emphasis on *kavana* in *shema* — on the orientation of the heart. Some earlier opinions even framed *shema* primarily as a *mitzvat kavana* rather than a *mitzvat kriya*. On this reading, the threshold for fulfilling *shema* may be lower than for *birkat hamazon* — perhaps one can be *yotzei shema* through thought alone in a way that does not apply to *benching*.

A third approach — raised by a student — inverts the analysis: perhaps the issue is not about the lower threshold for *shema* but about the higher *problem* of articulating it. *Shema* consists of direct words of *Torah* — words that, when spoken aloud, create a more acute tension with the *ba'al keri*'s state. *Birkat hamazon*, by contrast, is a rabbinic formulation, not words of *Torah* in the same direct sense. Therefore the *gemara* may be telling us not that thinking *shema* is sufficient, but that speaking *shema* is specifically more problematic, while speaking *birkat hamazon* — when the biblical obligation demands it — is more permissible. This is an insightful distinction that the *gemara* will partially address in what follows.

---

## Hirhur k'dibbur debate

### Does thinking = speech

Ravina now sharpens the conceptual question latent in the *mishna*: *zot omeret hirhur kedibbur dami* — the fact that the *mishna* instructs the *ba'al keri* to think the *shema* tells us that thinking counts as speech. For if thinking did not count as speech — if *hirhur lav kedibbur dami* — why would the *mishna* instruct him to think *shema* at all? If thinking accomplishes nothing, there would be no point.

### Hirhur k'dibbur

The *gemara* entertains this first position: *hirhur kedibbur dami* — thinking is halachically equivalent to speech. But then an obvious objection arises: if thinking counts as speech, then the *ba'al keri* should simply say *shema* aloud — *yotzi bisftav* — since the result is the same. Why go through the intermediate step of thinking?

The *gemara* answers: *kede'atan beSinai* — it is like the situation at Sinai. What this means requires unpacking. The reason a *ba'al keri* cannot recite *shema* or *tefilla* or *birkat hamazon* aloud is rooted in the experience of *Maamad Har Sinai*. Before receiving the Torah, the men were commanded *al tigshu el isha* — do not approach a woman. The *gemara* understands this not merely as a prohibition against sexual relations, but as relating to the state of seminal emission. Indeed, the *gemara* points out that the three-day requirement was calculated with the women in mind as well: semen might still be present in a woman's body for up to three days after relations. So the concern at *Har Sinai* was not about the act of intimacy per se — intimacy with one's wife is a *mitzvah* — but about the physical state that follows, which is incompatible with the direct, enunciated encounter with the word of God.

This is not a statement that physical life is problematic. The point is more subtle: receiving the Torah, or any reenactment of that encounter — and every learning of Torah can be understood as a microcosmic *Ma'amad Har Sinai* — demands a particular frame of mind. A state of *ba'al keri* represents an immersion in the purely physical that sits in tension with this spiritual encounter. Crucially, the concern at Sinai was about the *spoken* word of God being received. It was not merely that people were thinking Torah — the word was proclaimed aloud and encountered directly. Therefore the restriction on the *ba'al keri* applies specifically to the articulated word: speaking Torah, saying *shema* aloud, is the problem. Thinking it does not carry the same weight.

Tosafot adds a nuance: at *Har Sinai* the people were not themselves speaking — they were listening. Yet the restriction still applied, because the spoken word was present, active, being proclaimed. The word was "out there," not merely internal. This connects to the student's earlier observation: even reading *shema* from a *klaf*, directly encountering the written words of Torah, may present a heightened problem for the *ba'al keri* compared to reciting the rabbinic text of *birkat hamazon*.

The parallel deepens further: the human being reciting *shema* aloud is in some way a microcosmic reenactment of God proclaiming the *Aseret Hadiberot*. Rashi notes that every engagement with Torah can be seen as a reenactment of *Maamad Har Sinai*, grounded in the verse *yom asher amadeta lifnei Hashem Elokecha be-Chorev*. The act of *kriat shema* in particular carries this quality of direct encounter, and that is precisely what the *ba'al keri*'s state renders inappropriate.

So on the first view: thinking *shema* renders one *yotzei*, and the reason not to say it aloud is specifically the *ba'al keri* problem with articulated Torah — but thinking it is both efficacious and unproblematic.

### Hirhur lav k'dibbur

Rav Chisda takes the opposing view: *hirhur lav kedibbur dami* — thinking does not count as speech, and the *ba'al keri* is therefore not *yotzei shema* by thinking it. His reasoning: if thinking were equivalent to speech, then *yotzi bisftav* — the *ba'al keri* should just say it aloud. And if you say he cannot say it because of the *ba'al keri* problem while thinking is equivalent to speech — Rav Chisda does not accept this middle position. He holds that the two cannot be decoupled: if thinking counts, say it; if you cannot say it, thinking does not count. Therefore, according to Rav Chisda, the *ba'al keri* cannot be *yotzei shema* at all until he immerses. He simply cannot fulfill the obligation in his current state.

This leaves the *gemara* with a question: on Rav Chisda's view, why does the *mishna* instruct the *ba'al keri* to think *shema* at all? If he is not *yotzei*, what is the point?

### Participation purpose

Rabbi Elazar provides the answer: *kedei shelo yehei kol ha'olam oskim bo vehu yoshev u'vatel* — so that he should not be in a situation where the entire community is engaged in *shema* and he sits there doing nothing. This is not merely a social concern about appearances. *Shema* is the central act of *kabbalat ol malchut shamayim* — the acceptance of the yoke of heaven, the declaration of faith in God's sovereignty. It is not something one simply sits out when the community is doing it. Even if the *ba'al keri* cannot be *yotzei*, even if his thinking does not count as speech and does not discharge his obligation, there is a distinct value in participating in this act of communal faith. He thinks along, he orients himself toward the same declaration, even though technically he is not fulfilling the *mitzvah*.

This principle has broader application. When one is in the middle of *Psukei d'Zimra* and the congregation reaches *shema*, at the appropriate pause points one should say *shema* along with the congregation — even though one will arrive at *shema* in one's own davening shortly thereafter. The point is not *yeitziah*; it is participation in a communal act of declaring God's sovereignty. One should not be visibly standing aside from that.

The *gemara* then asks a follow-up question: *venigras be-pirkeih* — why must he specifically think *shema*? Why not simply study his regular learning while everyone else says *shema*? The answer provided: *be-davar she-hatzibur oskim bo* — the point is to be doing specifically what the community is doing. It is not merely about avoiding idleness or doing something unrelated; it is about participating in the same shared act.

### Malchut shamayim focus

Having established this principle, the *gemara* asks why it does not apply equally to *tefilla*. The *mishna*'s case of someone who begins *Shmoneh Esrei* and then remembers he is a *ba'al keri* — *lo yafsik ela yekatzer*, he should not interrupt but should abbreviate — implies that if he has not yet begun, he should not begin at all. Why then does he not at least silently participate in *Shmoneh Esrei* the way he thinks *shema*?

The *gemara* answers: *shani tefilla d'leit bah malchut shamayim* — *tefilla* is different, because it does not carry the same dimension of *kabbalat ol malchut shamayim*. The act of *shema* is intrinsically the act of accepting God's sovereignty — *Shema Yisrael*, *ve'ahavta*, the declaration of faith. That is so central a communal and theological act that even a *ba'al keri* who cannot fulfill it must participate in some way. *Tefilla* — *Shmoneh Esrei* — is not that act in the same sense. And here Rashi adds a philological note: the standard formula *Eloheinu Melech ha'olam* does not appear in the *brachos* of *Shmoneh Esrei*, which instead close with *haMelech haKadosh* and similar formulations. More fundamentally, it is not that *Shmoneh Esrei* never invokes God's kingship; it is that *shema* itself *is* the act of *kabbalat ol malchut shamayim* in a way that *tefilla* is not.

The *gemara* then turns back to *birkat hamazon*: the *mishna* says the *ba'al keri* does recite *birkat hamazon* after eating. This is not *malchut shamayim*, so why does he recite it? The answer: *krias shema u'virchas hamazon d'oraita u'tefilla d'rabbanan* — the dividing line is the biblical versus the rabbinic. The *ba'al keri* performs his biblical obligations; he does not perform the rabbinic ones. *Krias shema* is biblical (and additionally has the *malchut shamayim* dimension); *birkat hamazon* afterward is biblical; *tefilla* in its structured form is rabbinic — and so he does not participate in it.

There is an important alternate *girsa* here: on that reading, *shema* gets special treatment because of *malchut shamayim*, *birkat hamazon* because it is biblical, and *tefilla* is set aside because it has neither dimension — it is neither biblically mandated in its specific form nor is it the primary act of *kabbalat ol malchut shamayim*. Even those who hold, like the Rambam, that there is a biblical *mitzvah* of prayer, agree that the specific structure of *Shmoneh Esrei* as we know it is rabbinic. So the demands surrounding *tefilla* are correspondingly less.

It is worth noting here an important historical footnote: concerns similar to those surrounding the *ba'al keri* were applied in certain Ashkenazic communities of the Middle Ages to women who were *niddah*. The idea that a particular physical state renders certain articulations of *shem Hashem* problematic — that one cannot make *brachos*, cannot say *Shmoneh Esrei*, and so on — was extended by some to the *niddah* context, though this was never a uniform ruling but rather specific *minhagim*. The *gemara* here makes clear that the core concern is the articulation of *shem Hashem* in a state that is spiritually incongruent with that encounter, whatever form that state takes.

The *gemara* does not explicitly address why *shema* is done through *hirhur* while *birkat hamazon* is articulated. The *talmidei Rabbeinu Yona* maintain that even *birkat hamazon* is only thought, not said aloud, so there is no asymmetry. The other approach — that *shema*, as direct words of Torah, is more problematic to enunciate, while *birkat hamazon*, as a rabbinic formulation, can be recited when biblically demanded — has much to recommend it, especially in light of the student's observation connecting this to the Sinai parallel.

---

## Biblical sources

### Benching source

The *gemara* now moves to the biblical derivation of *birkat hamazon*. Rav Yehuda asks: *menalan le'Birkat HaMazon le'achareiha min haTorah* — from where do we know that *birkat hamazon* afterward is biblical? The source is the verse *ve'achalta ve-savata u'veirachta et Hashem Elohecha* — you shall eat, be sated, and bless God. The word *ve-savata* — be sated — implies that the biblical obligation applies specifically when one has eaten enough to be truly full. This is what generates the entire distinction between the biblical obligation (requiring *seva*, satiety) and the rabbinic extension to smaller amounts such as a *ke'zayit* or *ke'beitzah*.

### Torah blessing source

Rav Yehuda then asks: *menalan le'Birkat HaTorah lefaneha min haTorah* — from where do we know that *Birkat HaTorah* before Torah study is itself biblical? The source is the verse *ki shem Hashem ekra havu godel l'Eloheinu* — when I call out in the name of God, you shall ascribe greatness to our God. Rashi understands this as Moshe declaring that before he teaches Torah — before *kriat* the name of God — he will make a *Birkat HaTorah* and the people respond *amen* with *havu godel l'Eloheinu*. But more simply, the verse can be read as saying that whenever one is about to "call out" — *ekra* — in God's name, meaning engage with and read the words of Torah, the response and the prerequisite is *havu godel*, to bless and praise God. The *bracha* of *Birkat HaTorah* is therefore not merely a *birkat hamitzvah* in the technical sense, but primarily an act of *shevach* — praise and thanksgiving for God's gift of Torah to Israel. This is the point the Ramban emphasizes: *asher bachar banu mikol ha'amim ve-natan lanu et Torato* — the selection and the gift are what call forth the blessing.

One student notes that *havu godel* may also be the textual basis for *Yehei Shmei Rabba* — a compelling parallel that connects the congregational response to Torah with the central declaration of *Kaddish*.

### Kal v'chomer logic

Rabbi Yochanan then proposes that these two biblical obligations can be derived from one another through a *kal v'chomer*. The reasoning works in both directions.

To derive *Birkat HaTorah* afterward from *birkat hamazon*: *u'ma mazon she'ein ta'un lefanav ta'un le'acharav* — for food, where there is no biblical requirement to bless before, there is nevertheless a biblical requirement to bless after. *Torah she'te'unah lefaneha* — for Torah, where you do make a *bracha* before (and it is more demanding than food in that respect), *eino din she'te'unah le'achareiha* — how much more so should there be a requirement to bless after.

To derive *birkat hamazon* beforehand from *Birkat HaTorah*: *u'ma Torah she'ein te'unah le'achareiha te'unah lefaneha* — for Torah, where there is no biblical requirement to bless after, there is a requirement to bless before. *Mazon she'hu ta'un le'acharav* — for food, where you must bless after (and it is thus more demanding than Torah in that respect), *eino din she'ta'un lefanav* — how much more so should you bless before.

### Challenge to logic

This *kal v'chomer* is problematic on two levels. First, it is circular in a particularly acute way: once you use the *kal v'chomer* to establish one conclusion, you have destroyed the asymmetry that made the *kal v'chomer* possible in the first place. The entire argument depends on one being more demanding than the other in a particular direction; proving symmetry collapses the basis for the inference in the other direction.

Second, and more substantively, the *gemara* challenges both *kal v'chomer* arguments by noting that neither domain is simply "more demanding" than the other — each has its own distinctive quality that may explain the arrangement. *Ma lemazon sheken nehene* — food involves physical benefit, derived here and now. *U'ma la-Torah sheken chayei olam* — Torah leads to *olam haba*, to eternal life. These are qualitatively different, and one cannot simply treat one as a *kal* relative to the other.

These differences may in fact explain the substantive asymmetry of *before* and *after*. For *birkat hamazon*, the blessing comes after because the sense of gratitude and appreciation is most naturally expressed in response to physical benefit already received — *ve-savata u'veirachta*, you ate and were sated, and then you blessed. One could argue the reverse — that hunger and anticipation are themselves occasions for gratitude — but there is a logic to saying that the experience of benefit is what most calls forth the response of blessing. For Torah, by contrast, the benefit is not received during or immediately after the learning in any tangible sense — the reward is *ad mea ve'esrim*, extending to a future that is not experienced at the moment of study. There is therefore no natural logic of responding to benefit already received. Instead, the very act of preparing to encounter Torah — to involve oneself in something of such spiritual magnitude — is itself the moment of heightened awareness, and that is when the *bracha* belongs.

So the *gemara*'s challenge to the *kal v'chomer* is not merely formalistic. The differences between *nehene* and *chayei olam* go to the heart of why the obligations are structured as they are, and that structural difference undermines the attempt to derive one from the other.

### Mishna refutes

The *gemara* closes this discussion by pointing to the *mishna* itself as a *tiyuvta* — a refutation of the position that *birkat hamazon* beforehand is biblical. The *mishna* states: *al hamazon mevarech le'acharav ve'eino mevarech lefanav* — the *ba'al keri* recites *birkat hamazon* after eating but not the *bracha* before. Since the *ba'al keri* performs biblical obligations and omits rabbinic ones, the *mishna*'s ruling demonstrates that only *birkat hamazon* afterward is biblical. The *bracha* over bread before eating — *birkat ha-nehenin* — is only rabbinic. This decisively rules out the possibility that Rabbi Yochanan's *kal v'chomer* succeeded in establishing a biblical *bracha* before food.

The *gemara*'s position at this juncture is thus: *birkat hamazon* afterward is biblical, established by the verse *ve'achalta ve-savata u'veirachta*. *Birkat HaTorah* beforehand is biblical, established by *ki shem Hashem ekra*. The *bracha* over food before eating is rabbinic. And the *bracha* over Torah after — the *bracha* recited at the conclusion of an *aliyah* — is established through Rabbi Yochanan's *kal v'chomer* from *birkat hamazon*, even if that *kal v'chomer* cannot be cleanly run in reverse.

The further question — which parts of *kriat shema* are biblical and which are rabbinic — remains for the *gemara* to address in what follows.

The discussion of *hirhur k'dibbur* that runs through this entire *sugya* has one further application worth noting before concluding. Tosafot addresses the case of someone in the middle of *Shmoneh Esrei* who hears the congregation reaching *Kaddish* and *Yehei Shmei Rabba*. Rashi (elsewhere) rules that the person should be silent and is *yotzei* through *shomea k'oneh* — hearing counts as answering. Tosafot objects: if *shomea k'oneh* means one has effectively spoken, then one has interrupted *Shmoneh Esrei*. Tosafot ultimately accepts Rashi's position, but the resolution lies precisely in the nuanced middle ground explored throughout this *sugya*: *hirhur* — thinking, or even hearing — can be sufficient for *yeitziah* without being treated as literal speech in every halachic context. It is sufficient to be *yotzei* without being considered an interruption of *Shmoneh Esrei*.

This same question surfaces in the debate between the *Gra* and the *Shulchan Aruch* about whether one must recite *Birkat HaTorah* before engaging in Torah study conducted entirely through thought, without any articulation. The *Gra*'s position turns on whether *Birkat HaTorah* is primarily a *birkat hamitzvah* on the *mitzvah* of *talmud Torah* — in which case it would apply even to silent thought, since one is certainly fulfilling the *mitzvah* thereby — or whether it is fundamentally tied to the encounter with the spoken or written word of Torah, the *ki shem Hashem ekra* moment of calling out God's name. On the latter understanding, *Birkat HaTorah* is demanded only when the words are enunciated, just as the *ba'al keri*'s restrictions are triggered specifically by articulation. The same conceptual tension between *hirhur* and *dibbur* that governs the *ba'al keri*'s *shema* runs through the *Birkat HaTorah* debate as well.

---

---

# Berakhot 21

## Shema & Brachot Status

### Ba'al Keri Intro

The discussion on 21a continues in the midst of a broader examination of the *ba'al keri* — one who has experienced a seminal emission — and the question of what he is and is not permitted to recite. A central distinction raised in the *mishnah* concerns the difference between biblical and rabbinic obligations: a *ba'al keri* may recite *shema* and *birkat hamazon*, both of which are biblical in nature, but may not recite the *brachot* that precede *shema* or the *brachot* that precede eating, both of which are rabbinic. This framework — *birkat hatorah* is *de'oraita*, *birkat hamazon* is *de'oraita*, while the *brachot* after *talmud Torah* and before eating are rabbinic — drives the *gemara*'s subsequent analysis.

### Safek Shema/Emes

The *gemara* records a ruling of Rav Yehuda: if a person is uncertain whether he has recited *shema* — perhaps he was distracted and cannot recall whether he said it — he does not go back and repeat it. However, if he is uncertain whether he has recited *emes v'yatziv*, the *brachot* following *shema* that lead into *shmoneh esrei*, he must go back and recite them. The *gemara* immediately provides the rationale: *krias shema* is *derabbanan*, while *emes v'yatziv* is *de'oraita*. The principle at work is that in cases of *safek* regarding a rabbinic obligation, one need not repeat it, but in cases of *safek* regarding a biblical obligation, one must.

### Shema Derabbanan

This ruling is striking, to say the least. *Emes v'yatziv* — a set of *brachot* composed by the rabbis — is classified as biblical, while *shema* — which appears explicitly in the Torah — is classified as rabbinic? Rav Yosef challenges this immediately, and notably his entire challenge consists of just two words from the *pasuk*: *ubeshochavecha uvekumacha* — "when you lie down and when you rise." What more needs to be said? The *pasuk* seems to mandate *shema* directly.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye responds with a bold interpretive move: that *pasuk*, he says, may well be referring to Torah study rather than to the recitation of *shema* specifically. The words *ubeshochavecha uvekumacha* appear in the context of teaching and transmitting Torah — "you shall teach them to your children, speak of them when you sit in your house, when you walk along the way, when you lie down and when you rise." If we did not already have the tradition of reciting *shema*, we might have read those *pesukim* as entirely about *limud hatorah*, about learning and teaching Torah at all times of day. Therefore, Abaye argues, *krias shema* as we know it may indeed be only *derabbanan*, while *emes v'yatziv* carries biblical force by virtue of the commandment to remember *yetzias mitzrayim* each day — *lemaan tizkor yom tzeischa me'eretz mitzrayim kol yemei chayecha*. The third paragraph of *shema*, *parshas tzitzis*, also mentions *mitzrayim*, so either *emes v'yatziv* or that paragraph could independently fulfill the biblical obligation of *zeicher yetzias mitzrayim*.

### Mishnah Test

The *gemara* then tests this position against the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states that a *ba'al keri* thinks *shema* in his heart but makes no *brachot* before or after it, while for food he makes the *bracha* after eating (which is biblical) but not before (which is rabbinic). From this the *gemara* infers that the *brachot* after *shema* are treated as rabbinic in this context — yet if *emes v'yatziv* is truly biblical, the *ba'al keri* should be obligated to recite it. The *gemara* answers: why would you say *emes v'yatziv* here? Because of the mention of *yetzias mitzrayim*. But in this case, *hada'kereh bekrias shema* — the *ba'al keri* has already recited *parshas tzitzis* in his *shema*, which contains *yetzias mitzrayim*. So the biblical obligation has already been fulfilled through *shema* itself.

### Biblical Scope

This leads to an important qualification of Rav Yehuda's original ruling. The obligation to go back and recite *emes v'yatziv* when in doubt applies specifically when one also does not know whether *shema* was recited. If one knows that *shema* was said — which includes *parshas tzitzis* and its mention of *yetzias mitzrayim* — then there is nothing biblical remaining in *emes v'yatziv* that would require repetition.

One might ask whether this biblical obligation can be fulfilled through any mention of *yetzias mitzrayim*, regardless of the specific text. The *gemara* makes no distinction on this point — any formulation that fulfills *zeicher yetzias mitzrayim* satisfies the biblical requirement, whether it is a quote from the Torah itself or rabbinic liturgy. The text of *emes v'yatziv* per se is not what makes it *de'oraita*; it is the content — the remembrance of the Exodus.

The way Tosafot reads the *gemara*, the case in which one must go back and say *emes v'yatziv* is precisely when one also does not know whether *shema* was recited at all. In that situation, no *de'oraita* obligation has been fulfilled, and one must at minimum recite *emes v'yatziv*. Tosafot further suggests that once a person is already obligated to return and say something, there may be reason to go back and say the full package — *shema* together with *emes v'yatziv* — since the *de'oraita* obligation encompasses both the *yetzias mitzrayim* of the third paragraph and *emes v'yatziv* itself.

### Shema Preference

The *gemara* then asks: given that *parshas tzitzis* already carries the biblical content of *yetzias mitzrayim*, why should the *ba'al keri* say *shema* at all? Why not simply have him recite *emes v'yatziv* and fulfill the *de'oraita* that way? The *gemara* answers: *krias shema adifa de'is bah tartei* — *krias shema* is preferable because it contains more. It carries both *yetzias mitzrayim* and *ol malchus shamayim*, the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven. When one must choose, *krias shema* is the richer package. Still, the *gemara* affirms that when one has a *safek* whether *shema* was said, one may begin from *emes v'yatziv*, since once *shema* has been said the entire biblical obligation is covered through it.

---

## Prayer Obligation Rules

### Rabbi Elazar View

The *gemara* now introduces Rabbi Elazar, who articulates what most people would instinctively assume. If a person is uncertain whether he recited *shema*, he goes back and recites it — since *shema* is biblical. But if he is uncertain whether he davened, he does not go back and repeat *shmoneh esrei* — because *tefillah* is rabbinic, and there is no obligation to repeat a rabbinic act when uncertain whether it was performed.

### Prayer Status

This position rests on the assumption that *tefillah* — at least in its fixed, structured form — is *derabbanan*. While there is a well-known dispute between the Rambam and Ramban on this point, even the Ramban concedes that a daily obligation to pray a fixed text three times a day is rabbinic. The Ramban holds that a biblical obligation to pray exists only in a moment of *tzarah*, when a person faces affliction and the natural human impulse is to cry out — in that context, one must direct that cry to God. The Rambam, by contrast, maintains a daily biblical obligation to pray, but even he is explicit that the specific structure — three *tefillos* per day, a defined text — is entirely rabbinic. So in either case, the structured *shmoneh esrei* as a repeated act triggers the rule: *safek derabbanan*, no need to repeat.

### Rav Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan introduces a different sensibility: *u'levai she'yitpallel adam kol hayom kulo* — would that a person could daven the entire day. This reflects the view that prayer at any time, even beyond the fixed obligations, has intrinsic value. For Rabbi Yochanan, not only is there no problem praying more than required, there is something admirable in it. Applied to the case of *safek* — where a person is unsure whether they davened *mincha* — Rabbi Yochanan's position would at minimum encourage davening again, and might even make it obligatory: after all, even if you have already davened, why not daven again?

### Safek Prayer Options

This generates a three-way framework for how to handle *safek tefillah*. The first position, reflected in Rabbi Elazar's ruling, treats *tefillah* strictly as a rabbinic obligation: if you have a doubt, don't repeat it. The second position, Rabbi Yochanan's, welcomes or even requires repetition — since davening at any time has value, there is every reason to daven again when uncertain. The third approach — a middle path widely employed in practice — is to daven again but to frame the repetition conditionally: if I have already davened, let this count as a voluntary *tefillat nedavah*; if I have not yet davened, let this fulfill my obligation.

This conditionality raises its own questions. The efficacy of such stipulations — whether one can declare in advance the dual character of an act — is debated among the *poskim*. The broader issue it touches is the nature of *kavana* and *da'at*: whether and how consciously articulated intention can shape the halachic classification of a ritual act. The question bears some similarity to the principle of *breira*, though that topic involves a distinct set of considerations and goes beyond the scope of the present discussion.

The underlying tension, however, is real and important. Those who disagree with Rabbi Yochanan are not saying there is no value to praying throughout the day. They are saying that the structured, fixed *shmoneh esrei* belongs in its designated time and mode, and that using it outside that structure — approaching it as an obligation when it isn't one — conflates two distinct categories of religious expression. Rabbi Yochanan allows the formal text to serve as personal prayer; the opposing view insists that if you want to pray personally, you should pray personally, not hijack the structured form.

---

## Prayer Interruption Cases

### Wake Mid-Prayer

The *gemara* records another ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: if a person is standing in *tefillah* — in the middle of *shmoneh esrei* — and suddenly recalls that he has already davened *mincha* earlier that day, he must stop immediately, *posek va'afilu b'emtza berachah* — even in the middle of a *bracha*. The *gemara* challenges this from a related case. Rav Nachman reports that when he was studying with Rabba bar Avuha, students asked: if someone accidentally began reciting the weekday *shmoneh esrei* on *Shabbat* — going on autopilot through the middle *brachot* — what should they do? Rabba bar Avuha answered: *gomrim kol ota berachah* — they complete whichever *bracha* they are currently in the middle of, and then transition to the *Shabbat* text. This seems to indicate that one does not interrupt mid-*berachah*, contrary to Shmuel's ruling.

### Private vs Public

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing the two cases. In the *Shabbat* scenario, *hatam gavra bar chiyuva hu* — the person is still obligated to daven *shmoneh esrei*. The rabbis did not impose the full weekday *shmoneh esrei* on *Shabbat*, perhaps because it would be burdensome, or because personal requests are not appropriate for *Shabbat* — but the person remains obligated in *tefillah*. He is simply reciting the wrong text, not an entirely inappropriate act. So the rabbis allow him to finish the current *bracha* and then proceed correctly. But in Shmuel's case, *aval hacha hat'aya hi* — it is simply a mistake. The person has already davened *mincha*. There is no remaining obligation, and continuing the *shmoneh esrei* in this state is entirely out of place. He must stop.

One might ask why the reasoning from Rabbi Yochanan does not apply here: if davening the whole day is valuable, why not let the person finish the *shmoneh esrei* as a voluntary *tefillah*? Both Rashi and Tosafot cite the *Behag* — the early geonic work *Halachot Gedolot* — who distinguishes precisely here. We rule like Rabbi Yochanan in the case of *safek*: if uncertain whether you davened, daven again, because even if you already did, there is value in doing so and the intention was not clearly fixed as obligatory from the outset. But we rule like Shmuel in the case of *vadai*: if you *know* you have already davened and you stand up explicitly to fulfill your obligation, then the act has been defined from the beginning as obligatory structured prayer. Once you realize mid-*shmoneh esrei* that no such obligation exists, you cannot retroactively recast it as voluntary. You are stuck in the genre you entered, and since that genre no longer applies, you must stop.

This is not merely formalism. It touches on something deep about the nature of structured versus personal prayer. The act's meaning is determined not only by its content but by the intention with which it was begun. *Kavana* shapes the act — and once the act is framed as obligatory, one cannot shift it to volitional in the middle. Rabbi Yochanan permits using the formal text as personal prayer, but only when it is approached as personal expression. Blending the two orientations mid-stream is not allowed even by Rabbi Yochanan.

### Home to Shul

Shmuel offers a second ruling: if a person has already davened at home and then arrives at the *beit knesset* to find the congregation in the middle of *shmoneh esrei*, he should not daven again — unless he can add something personal to the prayer. *Im yachol l'chadesh bo davar yachzor v'yitpallel, v'im lav al yachzor v'yitpallel* — if he can add a *chidush davar*, a personal innovation, he may daven again; if not, he should not.

### Chidush Davar

This concept of *chidush davar* is the mechanism by which Shmuel allows the formal text to function as personal prayer. The same authority who said you must stop in the middle of *shmoneh esrei* when you realize you've already davened is now saying: if you can make this prayer genuinely personal — by inserting your own words, adding something that is truly yours — then you may use the formal text again even having already fulfilled your obligation. The *chidush* transforms the act from repetition of an obligation into an expression of personal prayer, which always has value.

The relationship between *chidush davar* and spoken articulation is important. *Hirhurim*, thoughts alone, are insufficient — it must be expressed in some way. But the deeper question of what qualifies as *chidush davar* — whether it must be a new textual addition or whether a wholly different inner orientation suffices — will be the subject of further discussion in the *gemara* later. Rabbi Yochanan holds that approaching the prayer with a personal, non-obligatory mindset is itself sufficient to make it personal. Shmuel insists that something must be done *to* the prayer, something that distinguishes this recitation from the obligatory one. The debate is not about whether personal prayer has value; it is about whether the formal text can ever become personal through mindset alone, or whether it requires an external act of personalization.

One might wonder whether *chidush davar* can take the form of a purely experiential difference — davening the same text in a different setting, with a different *chazzan*, in a different emotional state. This question will be addressed directly later in the *masechet*, where the *gemara* returns to the nature of *chidush davar* and whether inner experience alone can constitute it.

### Two Cases Needed

The *gemara* then explains why both of Shmuel's rulings are necessary and neither can be derived from the other. Had we only heard the first case — that one stops mid-*shmoneh esrei* upon remembering one has already davened — we might have thought that rule applies only when both instances are of the same type: private and private, or communal and communal. If the first *tefillah* was private (*yachid*) and now the person finds himself in a communal (*tzibur*) setting, one might have thought the communal experience is categorically different — *ke'man d'la tzalay dami*, it is as if he never davened in terms of that richer experience — and therefore he may daven again as an obligation, not merely as a voluntary act. Shmuel's second ruling teaches us otherwise: even if you davened privately at home and now you arrive at a *minyan*, you do not repeat the *shmoneh esrei* on account of the different setting. The obligation is the obligation; having fulfilled it privately does not entitle you to repeat it communally.

Conversely, had we only been told the second case — do not daven again when you arrive at *shul* having already davened at home — one might have thought the rule is simply: don't start. Once you have not started, don't begin. But if you are already *in the middle* of *shmoneh esrei* when you realize you've already davened, perhaps you should finish, since stopping mid-stream seems disruptive. Shmuel's first ruling teaches that even in the middle, even mid-*berachah*, you stop. Both rulings are necessary precisely because the logic in each direction is plausible.

The upshot of Shmuel's framework is that in the context of obligatory structured prayer, once the obligation is fulfilled you do not repeat it — not when you find yourself mid-prayer, not when you arrive at *shul*, not in any circumstance — unless you transform the act through *chidush davar* into something other than repetition of an obligation.

---

## Starting Mid-Congregation

### Timing Dilemma

The *gemara* now raises a related scenario: a person arrives at the *beit knesset* and finds the congregation already in the middle of *shmoneh esrei*, but he himself has not yet davened. The question is whether he should begin *shmoneh esrei* now, knowing that the congregation may finish before he does, causing him to miss certain communal responses.

### Modim Standard

Rav Yehuda rules: *im yachol lehatchil uligmor ad shelo yagia shliach tzibur l'Modim, yitpallel* — if he can begin and finish his *shmoneh esrei* before the *shliach tzibur* reaches *Modim*, he should daven; if not, he should not. The cutoff, remarkably, is not *kedushah* but *Modim*. It is forbidden to be in the middle of one's own *shmoneh esrei* when the congregation is saying *Modim*.

### Kedusha Standard

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees and sets a stricter standard: one must be able to finish before the *shliach tzibur* reaches *kedushah*. According to him, the operative concern is the inability to say *kedushah* with the congregation.

### Private Kedusha

The *gemara* identifies the underlying dispute: *mar savar yachid omer kedushah, u'mar savar ein yachid omer kedushah* — one authority holds that an individual may recite *kedushah* within his private *shmoneh esrei*, while the other holds that this is not possible. According to the opinion that *kedushah* can be said privately, one need not worry about missing it with the congregation, since one can say it within one's own *shmoneh esrei*. Therefore the only critical cutoff is *Modim*. According to the opinion that *kedushah* requires communal participation and cannot be said privately, missing *kedushah* with the congregation is itself a serious loss, and one should not begin if that is unavoidable.

### Kedusha Source

Rav Adda bar Ahava provides the source for why *kedushah* cannot be said privately: *v'nikdashti b'toch bnei Yisrael* — "I will be sanctified among the children of Israel." Any *davar shebekedushah* — any act of publicly sanctifying God's name — falls under this verse and requires a minimum of ten. This principle is derived through a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *toch* appears here in *Vayikra*, and the same word appears in the episode of Korach — *hibadlu mitoch ha'edah hazot* — where the congregation numbered ten (excluding the two righteous men, Moshe and Aharon). Just as there *toch* refers to ten, so here *toch* refers to ten. And since *kedushah* is paradigmatically a *davar shebekedushah*, it requires a *minyan* of ten.

It is worth noting that the *gemara* here says *asarah* — ten — without specifying men. The *rishonim* engage with this question. The Rambam writes that a *minyan* consists of *asarah gedolim bnei chorin* and does not explicitly exclude women. The *Shulchan Aruch* does explicitly exclude women, but that formulation is not in the *gemara* itself. Similarly, Rav Moshe, when asked about counting non-observant Jews for a *minyan*, noted that since we derive the requirement from the *meraglim* — designated by the verse as *ha'edah hara'ah hazot*, the wicked congregation — the *halacha* cannot exclude individuals on the basis of their level of observance.

### Kedusha Text/Liturgy

This raises a subtle but important question: if *kedushah* requires a *minyan* because it is a *davar shebekedushah*, what about instances where one reads the words of *kedushah* as biblical text rather than as liturgy? May an individual read *kadosh kadosh kadosh* when reciting the verses of *Yeshayahu*, or *v'nikdashti b'toch bnei Yisrael* when learning *Vayikra*?

The answer lies in the distinction between reciting text *as text* and performing a liturgical act. The *paytanim* and the *halacha* recognize that the same words can function differently depending on their framing. A parallel case is the recitation of *Hashem Hashem Kel rachum v'chanun* in *Selichot*. When said *betzibur* this functions as a *davar shebekedushah*, but if an individual recites *Selichot* alone, the practice is to read those words with the cantillation (*trop*) appropriate to *Vayikra*, treating them as *pesukim* rather than liturgy, and to conclude the verse through its natural ending — even though the liturgical custom cuts off the recitation earlier. This dual framing — the same words, one as text and one as liturgy — illustrates the distinction.

*Krias shema* is in an analogous position. The experience of *krias shema* is fundamentally that of reading biblical text — *krias shema*, the reading of *shema*. The text is Torah, and reciting it participates in the *mitzvah* of Torah reading and declaration of God's sovereignty. *Kedushah*, by contrast, is a dramatic liturgical reenactment — the community collectively scripting and performing the angelic proclamation of God's holiness. It is not recitation of a text; it is enactment of a scene. That categorical difference is what places *kedushah* firmly in the category of *devarim shebekedushah* requiring a *minyan*, while reading the words of *kadosh kadosh kadosh* as part of *psukim* does not carry the same requirement.

A similar consideration applies to *kiddush*. The opening verses of *kiddush* — *vayehi erev vayehi voker yom hashishi*, *vayechulu hashamayim* — are sung in a traditional *niggun*, but that *niggun* is not the biblical *trop*. The question of whether those verses require the same framing distinctions as other liturgical-textual hybrids is a nuanced one, though in practice it is not treated with the same stringency.

### Modim Significance

Returning to the question of why *Modim* is specifically the critical threshold — more so, apparently, than *kedushah* even according to Rav Yehuda — the answer is illuminating. One might have assumed the concern with *Modim* is about the text itself: *modim anachnu lach*, the expression of gratitude, should be said in solidarity with the congregation. But Rashi explains that it is not the text of *Modim* that is the problem; it is the physical act of bowing. If the entire congregation is bowing before God and one individual is standing upright, *nireh ke-kofer be-mi she-chaveirav mishtachavim lo* — he appears as if he denies the God before whom his fellows are prostrating themselves. The problem is the visible, embodied experience of communal submission to God, not the words.

### Tosafot Solutions

This reframing opens the door to a practical solution, which Tosafot attributes to Rabbeinu Tam: when the *chazzan* reaches *Modim* and the congregation bows, one who is still in the middle of his own *shmoneh esrei* should simply bow — without saying anything — in solidarity with the congregation. The bowing itself resolves the visual and experiential problem without constituting an interruption of *shmoneh esrei*.

Similarly, for *kedushah*, Rashi suggests that silent listening can achieve *yetzias* for the individual: *shomea k'oneh* — hearing is like responding. If one silently attends to the congregation's *kedushah* while in the middle of one's own *shmoneh esrei*, one has in effect participated in *kedushah* without speaking, and without creating a formal *hefsek* in one's prayer. Tosafot debates whether this *shomea k'oneh* mechanism, when it achieves the level of considered as if spoken, would itself constitute an interruption in *shmoneh esrei*. The conclusion Tosafot reaches is that since one did not actually speak, it does not constitute an interruption, even if it counts as participation.

The practical outcome, then, is as follows. The *gemara* instructs *lechatchila*: do not begin *shmoneh esrei* if you cannot finish in time. But Tosafot provides solutions for cases where one finds oneself mid-*shmoneh esrei* facing these situations. For *Modim*: bow silently and say nothing. For *kedushah*: listen silently and be *yotzei* through *shomea k'oneh*. These are *bedi'avad* solutions, not license to disregard the *gemara*'s directive, but they address the reality that one cannot always time one's prayer perfectly.

---

## Ba'al Keri Brachot

### Rabbi Yehuda Lenient

The *gemara* returns to the issue of *ba'al keri* with a ruling attributed to Rabbi Yehuda: *mevarech lifnehem v'achareihem* — a *ba'al keri* may recite the *brachot* both before and after *shema*, and presumably also before and after food. Rabbi Yehuda is not troubled by the *ba'al keri* status at all.

### Ba'al Keri Assumption

This immediately raises a question about Rabbi Yehuda's underlying position. The logic of the *mishnah*'s distinctions — where *ba'al keri* is permitted to recite what is biblical but not what is rabbinic — assumes that a *ba'al keri* is restricted from engaging with Torah and God's name at a certain level. If Rabbi Yehuda permits recitation of all *brachot*, he must hold that a *ba'al keri* is not prohibited from *divrei Torah* at all.

### Har Sinai Source

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had provided the source for the prohibition. He derives it from the juxtaposition in *Devarim*: the *pasuk* commands *v'hodatam l'vanecha v'livnei vanecha* — you shall inform your children and your children's children of the Torah — and immediately adjacent is the verse *yom asher amadta lifnei Hashem Elokecha be-Chorev*, the day you stood at Har Sinai. Just as the revelation at *Har Sinai* required those present to refrain from sexual activity — an explicit divine command was issued to maintain that state of separation — so too all engagement with Torah is likened to *Har Sinai*, and therefore a *ba'al keri* should be prohibited. This prohibition extends even to reciting a *bracha*, since any utterance of God's name in a Torah context falls under this framework.

### Smuchim Debate

The *gemara* asks: does Rabbi Yehuda not accept the principle of *smuchin* — the halachic significance of juxtaposition? If so, why does he not draw the same conclusion from the juxtaposition of Torah learning with *Har Sinai*?

### Mishneh Torah Priority

The *gemara* answers by invoking a distinction formulated by Rav Yosef: even authorities who do not generally derive *halacha* from *smuchin* throughout the Torah do give *smuchin* halachic weight when they occur in *Mishneh Torah* — in Sefer Devarim. The reasoning offered in the *rishonim* is that *Devarim* represents Moshe's retelling and reorganization of the Torah. Since Moshe consciously chose how to arrange and juxtapose material in his restatement, the literary decisions carry deliberate and therefore legally significant meaning. Wherever Moshe placed things next to each other in *Devarim*, that adjacency conveys a message.

### Smuchim Examples

The *gemara* demonstrates that Rabbi Yehuda does indeed employ *smuchin* in *Devarim*, through two examples. First, the case of a woman executed for witchcraft: Ben Azzai derives the form of execution — *sekilah*, stoning — from the juxtaposition of the prohibition against a *mechashefah* with the verse about one who lies with an animal, for whom stoning is explicit. Rabbi Yehuda rejects this derivation, preferring instead a logical argument from the categories of *ov* and *yidoni* — forms of necromancy that explicitly carry the penalty of *sekilah* — to establish the execution of *mechashefah* by *sekilah* as well. This shows that Rabbi Yehuda does *not* employ *smuchin* across the Torah generally.

Second, and to establish that Rabbi Yehuda *does* use *smuchin* in *Devarim*: the law that a man may not marry a woman his father had sexual relations with, even outside of marriage. Rav Gidel in the name of Rav establishes this from the juxtaposition in *Devarim* of *lo yikach ish et eshet aviv v'lo yigaleh knaf aviv* with the passage about a man who lies with a woman and the resulting obligations — *smuchin* in *Devarim*. Rabbi Yehuda accepts this derivation and rules accordingly, prohibiting such a union. This confirms that Rabbi Yehuda does apply *smuchin* as a halachic tool when the juxtaposition occurs in *Devarim*.

### Har Sinai Teaching

Given that the *Har Sinai* juxtaposition also appears in *Devarim* — *v'hodatam l'vanecha... yom asher amadta lifnei Hashem Elokecha be-Chorev* — Rabbi Yehuda should, by his own methodology, derive the *ba'al keri* prohibition from it. So why does he permit a *ba'al keri* to say *brachot*?

The *gemara* resolves this: Rabbi Yehuda reads the *smuchin* in *Devarim* here, but does not derive from it the prohibition on *ba'al keri* learning Torah. Instead, he follows what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the juxtaposition teaches: *kol hamelamed et beno Torah, ma'aleh alav hakatuv k'ilu kibelah me'Har Chorev* — whoever teaches his child Torah, Scripture regards it as if he himself received the Torah from *Har Chorev*. The juxtaposition of Torah teaching with the day at *Har Sinai* teaches not that Torah study requires the same physical conditions as *Har Sinai*, but rather that teaching Torah to one's children is itself a participation in *matan Torah* — a reliving of the chain of transmission that began at *Sinai*. It is not a statement about bodily state; it is a statement about the power of transmitting Torah from generation to generation.

Rabbi Yehuda therefore uses the *smuchin* of *Devarim* — as his methodology requires — but derives a different lesson from it than Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi does. And since the juxtaposition speaks to the value of teaching Torah and not to the physical prerequisites for Torah study, it yields no prohibition on the *ba'al keri*. The discussion will continue.

---

---

# Berakhot 24

## Fixed Meal Prep

### Remove Before Meal

The *gemara* opens with a *baraita*: *harotzeh likaneis liseudat keva*, one who wishes to enter a fixed meal — not a casual snack but a serious, formal banquet from which excusing oneself mid-meal would be embarrassing — should first walk ten times four *amot* (approximately six feet each), or alternatively four times ten *amot*, pausing at each interval to attempt to relieve oneself. As Rashi explains, the walking motion can help clear the bowels. This falls under the category of *hilchos derech eretz*: the rabbis are teaching that concern for social dignity is itself a religious value. An authentically religious person takes care to behave with civility toward the social environment in which he operates.

From there the *gemara* turns to a more directly *halachic* ruling. Rav Yitzchak states: *hanichnas liseudat keva choletz tefillin* — one who is about to sit down to a fixed meal must first remove his *tefillin*. The background assumption is striking: a person is wearing *tefillin* throughout the entire day, and the only live questions concern when it is appropriate to remove them.

### Tefillin on Table

Rabbi Chiya disputes not the act of removal but what to do with the *tefillin* afterward. He holds: *manichin al shulchano vechen hadur lo* — one places them on the table, and this is in fact a glory to him. Rashi identifies two distinct concerns underlying this discussion. First, *shema yishtacher betoch seudato veyitganeh bitfillav* — one might become somewhat intoxicated during the meal and behave inappropriately while wearing *tefillin*. (One might have expected the concern to be passing gas, which is a commonly cited issue in *tefillin* contexts, but Rashi identifies inebriation.) Second, Rashi explains the value of *vechen hadur lo*: *mishum demazmino veyachzor veyanichum bish'at beracha* — having the *tefillin* close at hand serves as a reminder and enables one to put them back on at the time of *Birkas Hamazon*. This is directly analogous to the familiar practice of people donning jackets and hats before *benching*.

### Until Blessing

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak specifies the duration of the removal: *ad zman beracha* — until the time of the blessing, meaning *Birkas Hamazon*. The implication is that the *tefillin* are to be put back on for the bentching itself.

---

## Designation vs Use

### Wrap Both Items

The *gemara* now cites a *baraita*: *tzorer adam tefillav im me'otav be'afarkasuto* — a person may wrap his *tefillin* together with his money in his head-scarf (*afarkasuto*), apparently a kind of cloth wrap worn around the head with hanging material that could be used to bundle items. The ruling implies that this does not automatically designate the scarf as a dedicated wrapper for *tefillin*, and it may therefore still be used for other purposes.

### Conflicting Rules

A second *baraita*, however, states the opposite: *lo yatzor adam* — a person may not use the same cloth as a pouch for both money and *tefillin*, even if the two items occupy separate pockets within it. The *gemara* resolves this apparent contradiction: *lo kashya — ha de'azmenei ha d'lo azmenei*. The determining factor is whether the cloth has been designated (*hazmana*) for *tefillin* use. This raises the broader *halachic* question — one that surfaces in various contexts throughout the *gemara* — of when a given object acquires a particular sanctified status: is it use alone that matters, designation alone, or the combination of both? The parallel cases include setting aside a garment for use as burial shrouds or designating a room as a *beis hakisei*.

### Both Required

Rav Chisda articulates a clear position: *hai sudra d'tefillin d'azmanya l'meitzar bei tefillin* — if you designated a cloth scarf to wrap *tefillin*, even so, designation alone is insufficient. You need both designation *and* actual use. If you designated it and never actually wrapped *tefillin* in it, or conversely used it once to wrap *tefillin* without any designation, it remains permissible to wrap money in it as well. Only once both conditions are fulfilled — *tzar bei tefillin*, you actually used it, together with *azmanya*, you designated it — is it *assur l'meitzar bei zuzei*, forbidden to use for money.

### Design Enough

Abaye takes a different position in the classic debate between *Abaye v'Rava* regarding whether *hazmana miltha hi* — whether designation alone carries *halachic* weight. According to Abaye, *hazmana* is indeed *miltha hi*: designation is sufficient and independently effective. If you designated the cloth, then *af al gav d'lo tzar bei* — even without ever having actually wrapped *tefillin* in it — it acquires the status of a *tefillin* wrapper and may not be used for other purposes. Conversely, if you actually used it for *tefillin* but never designated it as such, it does not acquire that status. One might naturally ask: after using something consistently for an extended period, is explicit mental designation still required, or does sustained use itself constitute designation? That remains a broader question, but Abaye's formal position is that designation is the operative act.

---

## Overnight Storage

### Under Pillow

Rav Yosef son of Rav Nechunya posed a question to Rav Yehuda: *mahu she'yanich adam tefillin tachat merashotav* — is it permissible to place *tefillin* under one's pillow at night? The question arises because sleeping with *tefillin* on is problematic due to the concern of passing gas, and simply holding them risks dropping them. Where, then, does one store them? The *gemara* is clear that storing them beneath one's feet in the bed is out of the question — *tachat margalotav*, that is outright disrespect. The question is specifically about *tachat merashotav*, under the head, which is where one stores precious items, and which therefore might be considered a sign of honor.

### Even Wife Present

Rav Yehuda replied in the name of Shmuel: *mutar afillu ishto imo* — it is permissible, even if his wife is with him in the same bed. The plain implication of Shmuel's ruling encompasses even the scenario of husband and wife together in bed, presumably including the possibility of marital relations. This is, at first glance, a striking ruling.

### Wife Forbidden

A *baraita* is then raised as a challenge: one may place *tefillin* under one's head, but *v'im hayta ishto imo, assur* — if his wife is with him, it is forbidden. The *baraita* does offer a qualification: if the spot where the *tefillin* rest is either more than three *tefachim* above the level of the bed (functioning as a kind of separate shelf-space) or lower than three *tefachim* below it (functioning as if buried), then it is permitted. But absent either of those conditions, having *tefillin* under the head while husband and wife are together is forbidden. The *gemara* concludes: *tiyuvta d'Shmuel tiyuvta* — this is a full contradiction of Shmuel's position.

### Protect Tefillin

Remarkably, Rava then states: *af al gav d'tanya tiyuvta d'Shmuel, hilchata kevatei* — although the *baraita* contradicts Shmuel, we rule like him. This is the somewhat startling Talmudic move of *tiyuvta vehilchata* — formally contradicting an authority and yet ruling in accordance with his view. Rava explains: *kol netiruta tfei adif* — anything that better protects the *tefillin* takes precedence. This is directly analogous to the ruling discussed previously that one may hold *tefillin* in a bathroom in order to prevent them from being left unguarded — protection of the *tefillin* overrides other concerns. Here too, keeping the *tefillin* under one's pillow affords them greater protection, and that outweighs the concern about husband and wife being together. The difference from the bathroom case is that there the need was occasional and unavoidable, whereas here it recurs every night; nevertheless, Rava extends the same logic.

### Exact Placement

Having established that *tefillin* may be kept under the pillow even with one's wife present, the *gemara* turns to the specific mechanics of placement. Rabbi Yirmeyah rules: *bein kar lechesset* — between the pillow and the blanket, and *shelo keneged rosho* — not directly beneath where one's head rests, but off to the side. This is more respectful than having one's head pressing directly down on the *tefillin*.

A *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Chiya appears to say something slightly different: *manichin bekova tachat merashotav* — one places the *tefillin* in a hat-like covering beneath one's head, which the *gemara* initially understands to mean that the head rests directly on top of them. Rashi identifies *kova* here as the *tefillin* bag. The *gemara* resolves the apparent tension: *damafki lei lemorsha dechova levar* — one positions the corner or bump of the *tefillin* so that it protrudes to the outside of the bag, away from where the head rests. The bag is under the head, but the head is not resting directly on the *tefillin* themselves. A physical demonstration clarifies this: if the bag is under one's head but the *tefillin* inside are pushed to one corner pointing away, the head rests on the bag without pressing on the actual *tefillin*.

### Alternative Methods

Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi had a different practice altogether: *manach lehu ahashshifa* — he placed his *tefillin* on a stool in the room, and *uforesh sudra ilvaye* — covered them with a cloth. They were not under his head in bed at all; they were nearby on a nightstand, covered.

Bar Kappara's approach is also cited: *tzayar lehu bechilta u'mafik lemorsheihen levar* — he wrapped the *tefillin* in the *kilta*, the canopy material that hung around his bed, with the bump pointing outward. Rashi explains this as meaning that the protrusion of the *tefillin* knot was turned away from the interior of the bed toward the outside — analogous, in a way, to the earlier discussion about whether *tefillin* on a wall should face toward the bathroom or toward the street. Bar Kappara was careful to orient the *tefillin* so that the bump faced outward, away from the bed, as a form of additional respect.

### Mikvah Night Test

Rav Hamnuna son of Rav Yosef then reports a personal testimony: *zimna chada hava yatvina kammai deRava* — "One time I was sitting before Rava, and he said to me: *zil aiti li tfillin* — go bring me my *tefillin*." Rav Hamnuna went to the room, searched, and found the *tefillin bein kar lechesset, shelo kineged rosho* — between the pillow and the blanket, exactly not opposite where his head lay, precisely as had been ruled. He further noted: *v'aydana d'yom tevila hava* — and he recognized or knew that it was the night his wife was returning from the *mikvah*. He understood that Rava was deliberately demonstrating the *halacha* in practice: that even on a night when husband and wife would be together, the *tefillin* could be kept in this manner under the pillow.

One might ask: why was Rava sending his student to retrieve the *tefillin* at that moment? If the point was to demonstrate proper placement, was this a demonstration of where he had stored them the previous night while his wife was with him, or was he taking them out in advance of that evening? Rashi's reading seems to favor the former — that Rava was showing Rav Hamnuna where he had in fact kept the *tefillin* the night before, when his wife had returned from the *mikvah*. There is a measure of ambiguity in the text, but Rashi takes it as a deliberate *halacha lema'aseh*, a practical demonstration of ruling like Shmuel even in the maximally challenging scenario.

In passing, the *gemara* simply assumes without formal statement that the night a wife returns from the *mikvah* is one on which husband and wife are together. The *gemara* never formally declares this an obligatory night; it treats it as a contextual assumption. Rav Moshe Feinstein addresses this point, noting that the husband's obligation of *onah* is fundamentally keyed to his wife's desire, and the assumption that the *mikvah* night is one of shared desire is rooted in circumstance rather than a categorical commandment attached to that night specifically.

---

## Shema Bed Rules

### Two in Bed

A new question is posed — again by Rav Yosef son of Rav Nechunya to Rav Yehuda: *shnayim sheyishenin bemitah achat mahu shezeh yachzir panav veyikra krias shema vezeh yachzir panav veyikra krias shema* — if two people are sleeping in one bed, may one turn his face in one direction and recite *krias shema* while the other turns in the opposite direction? This is not necessarily a husband-and-wife scenario; it could be two brothers or any two people sharing a bed, as was entirely common in earlier centuries. The *gemara* assumes throughout this passage that people sleep unclothed. The analogy to the earlier *tefillin* discussion is evident: we have moved from questions about the bathroom to questions about husband and wife, and now to the broader question of how to define *ervah* in the context of *krias shema* and *davening*. *Shemoneh esrei* is presumably said while standing — but *shema* may be said lying in bed, perhaps just before sunrise, and the question is whether doing so in the presence of another unclothed person is permissible.

### Wife Back-to-Back

Rav Yehuda replied in Shmuel's name: *afilu ishto imo* — even if his wife is with him, back-to-back suffices. Rashi clarifies that Shmuel's ruling was made specifically in the context of *krias shema*, not merely as an analogy from the *tefillin* case. If the ruling holds for a man's own wife — where one might imagine greater concern about sexual arousal — it should hold all the more obviously for a stranger.

### Wife vs Other

This inference is challenged by Rav Yosef: *ishto velo mibaya acher?* — you say it's permitted with his wife, and the case of somebody else goes without saying? That logic, Rav Yosef argues, is precisely backwards.

### Like Own Body

*Aderaba* — to the contrary: *ishto k'gufo, acher lav k'gufo* — a man's wife is like his own body; another person is not. Rashi explains this in psychological terms: husband and wife who have lived together are accustomed to one another's bodies and the encounter does not provoke the same degree of arousal as proximity to a different person. Interestingly, the concern about arousal operates here even in the case of what the *gemara* presumably envisions as two men sharing a bed — the *gemara* is attentive to the possibility that bodily proximity can evoke erotic thoughts regardless of the pairing.

A more formal reading of *ishto k'gufo* is also possible: if a couple is together under a blanket, it is not considered that one person is in the presence of another's *ervah*, since the wife's body is legally assimilated to the husband's own. Under this reading, the concern is not about sexual thoughts at all but about the propriety of being under the same blanket with a distinct person who is unclothed.

This raises the question of why the same logic of habituation does not apply to the *harchakos* governing a married couple during a wife's period of *niddah*. The answer is that the stakes there are categorically different — if proximity leads to transgression, the violation carries *kares*, a grave *halachic* penalty. Here, the context is a matter of two minutes of reciting *shema*, and the level of concern is calibrated accordingly.

### Need Divider

A *baraita* is now raised as a challenge: *hayashen bemitah uvanav uvnei veito betzido harei zeh lo yikra krias shema ela im kein haytah tallis mafsekes beineihem* — if a man is sleeping in a bed with his children and the members of his household, he may not recite *krias shema* unless a garment is arranged as a divider running between the bodies. This *baraita* — which Rashi understands as encompassing one's wife as well, though Tosafot's *girsa* explicitly reads *hayashen bemitah ve'ishto imo* — poses difficulties for both Shmuel and Rav Yosef.

According to Rav Yosef's distinction between wife and others, the ruling that there is no problem with a wife but a problem with *acher* resolves one *baraita* but seems to be contradicted by another. The *gemara* resolves this by arguing that both Shmuel and Rav Yosef can invoke a *tannai* dispute: there are *tannaim* who forbid even with one's wife and others who permit, and each *amora* aligns with a different *tanna*. What emerges from this resolution is a baseline on which all agree: at minimum, husband and wife back-to-back under a blanket may recite *shema*. Shmuel extends this even to unrelated people back-to-back, a position that the *gemara* does not definitively adopt or reject for the *shema* context.

### Buttocks Issue

The *gemara* now raises a pointed question about the back-to-back scenario: *veha ika agavos* — even turned back-to-back, the two people's buttocks are touching. Are buttocks considered *ervah*? This proves to be a pivotal question because it illuminates a broader distinction in *halacha* between two categories of *ervah*.

The first category is objective *ervah* — the genitals — whose uncovered presence or direct contact creates a formal prohibition against reciting *brachot* or *shema*, even when it is one's own body. The second category involves parts of another's body that may provoke sexual thoughts, and this is a much broader and more contextually dependent category that will be developed further in the *gemara*. The question about buttocks belongs to the first category: even setting aside any concern about arousal, is physical contact with another person's buttocks the kind of contact with *ervah* that would render recitation of *shema* improper?

The *gemara* cites a ruling of Rav Huna in support of resolving the question: *agavos ein bahem mishum ervah* — buttocks are not considered *ervah*. The *gemara* attempts to bring further support from the ruling that a woman may sit naked on the ground and separate *challah* and make a *bracha*, since *mipnei sheyecholah lechasos paneiha bakarka* — she can cover her genital area against the ground. But a man may not do this, since in that position his genitals remain exposed. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak demurs: that case could be explained as one where the woman is pressed so flat against the ground that even her buttocks is not exposed, so it does not necessarily prove buttocks are non-*ervah*.

The two-category structure is critical for understanding the subsequent discussion. Objectively, *ervah* is only the genitals. Everything else — the buttocks, the breasts of a woman, pubic hair — does not constitute objective *ervah*. There is a separate and distinct concern about what arouses sexual thoughts, and that category is far broader, but the two must not be conflated.

### Child Age Limits

The *baraita* had specified that small children (*ketanim*) sleeping in the bed present no problem for reciting *shema*. The *gemara* immediately asks *ad kama* — up to what age? Rav Pappa rules: *tinokes bas shalosh shanim veyom echad, vetinok ben tesha shanim veyom echad* — a girl of three years and a day, and a boy of nine years and a day. These ages correspond to the formal *halachic* thresholds at which certain sexual acts are deemed legally significant. This is primarily a formal, technical demarcation rather than a psychological account of when arousal becomes relevant.

### Puberty Ages

A second opinion is offered: *tinokes bas achas esreh shanah veyom echad, vetinok ben shtem esreh shanah veyom echad* — a girl from eleven years and a day, and a boy from twelve years and a day, which is one year before the onset of *halachic* adulthood. The source is the verse from *Yechezkel* describing physical maturity: *ad kedei shedadayim nachonu use'arech tzimayach* — until the breasts have ripened and hair has sprouted. This opinion is concerned with the onset of actual sexual characteristics and the arousal they may produce. Once a child begins showing signs of physical maturity — early secondary sexual characteristics — it is no longer appropriate for them to share the bed with a parent in a state of undress, at least not in the context of reciting *shema*.

Rashi's commentary suggests the concern here extends beyond the specific context of *shema* recitation to a more general question of appropriateness of shared sleeping. The first opinion (three-year-old girl, nine-year-old boy) engages formal *halachic* categories; the second opinion (eleven and twelve) engages the reality of incipient desire. Neither opinion, it should be noted, eliminates the concern entirely — both recognize that beyond a certain point, a parent and child sharing a bed in the nude is problematic.

The *gemara* then returns to the question of how we rule regarding Shmuel's position on the *shema* case, just as Rava ruled like Shmuel for the *tefillin* case. Rav Kahana asks Rav Ashi: given that Rava ruled like Shmuel in the *tefillin* context for the sake of protection, do we likewise rule like Shmuel for the *shema* context?
