Rabbi Yehuda restricts *Musaf* to until seven hours into the day — one hour past noon. Tosafot notes a linguistic distinction: for *Mincha* the *mishnah* says *ad ha'erev*, "until evening," while for *Musaf* it says *kol hayom*, "the whole day." The difference is that *Musaf* may genuinely be recited at any point during the day — even in the morning, before *Mincha* — and therefore the phrasing "all day" is more apt.

---

## Vatikin Ideal

### Sunrise Mitzvah

The *gemara* on the fourth *perek* opens with a tension: a *braisa* states that the *mitzvah* of *tefillah* is specifically at *hanetz hachamah*, sunrise — *mitzvatah im hanetz hachamah* — so that one may juxtapose *geulah* to *tefillah* and begin *davening* at the very start of the day. This seems to imply that the ideal time, or even the required time, for *shacharit* is sunrise, not the entire morning until noon.

### Ideal vs Halacha

The *gemara* resolves this: *ki tanya hahi l'Vatikin* — that *braisa* describes the practice of the *vatikin*, the scrupulously pious. It is an ideal, not a *halakhic* limit. The operative *halakhah* is that *shacharit* is valid until noon.

### Vatikin Timing

Rabbi Yochanan articulates the *vatikin* practice precisely: *vatikin hayu gomrim otah im hanetz hachamah* — the *vatikin* would complete *shema* exactly at the moment of sunrise, so that they could move directly into *shemoneh esrei* at that precise moment. The thrust of the *vatikin* ideal is thus to place *shemoneh esrei* — not *shema* — at sunrise. *Shema* is completed just before sunrise so that *shemoneh esrei* follows immediately at *hanetz*.

---

## Makeup Prayer

### Missed Maariv

Rabbi Yochanan is cited to the effect that if one forgot and failed to *daven Ma'ariv*, one may recite two *shemoneh esrei* the following morning — one for *Shacharit* and one as a makeup for the missed *Ma'ariv*. Similarly, if one missed *Shacharit*, one may recite two *shemoneh esrei* at *Mincha*. The *gemara* is thus introducing the concept of *tashlumin* — makeup prayer — which has no analogue elsewhere in *halakhah*. One does not, for instance, take the *lulav* twice the next day if one missed waving it; yet for *tefillah* such a makeup is apparently available.

### Noon Cutoff

The *gemara* refines the application: up until midday, one who prays receives *s'char tefilla bizmana* — the credit for having prayed in the proper time. After midday, one still receives the credit for *tefillah* itself but loses the additional merit of *tefilla bizmana* — prayer at the right time. This framing initially suggests that *davening* past noon is not a formal "makeup" but simply a late fulfillment, still within the extended period of the morning prayer. The *gemara* will move toward a more structured makeup model.

### Mincha Makeup

The *gemara* raises the case not addressed among those discussed: if one missed *Mincha*, can one recite two *shemoneh esrei* at *Ma'ariv* — one for *Ma'ariv* and one as a makeup for the missed *Mincha*?

### Korban vs Rachamim

This question crystallizes the central theological tension of the entire *perek*. If *tefillah* operates on the model of *korban*, then missing the time is decisive in one direction but not another. Sacrifices offered on the same halakhic day can be made up later in that day — which explains why a missed *Ma'ariv* can be compensated the next morning, since *erev* and *boker* constitute *yom echad*, one halakhic day, as the verse states *vayehi erev vayehi boker yom echad*. But a *korban* from one day cannot be brought the next day: *avar yomo batel korbano*. If *Mincha* belongs to the afternoon and *Ma'ariv* belongs to the following halakhic day, the *korban* model would prohibit any makeup.

The alternative: *kivan detzloota rachamei hi* — since prayer is fundamentally about *rachamim*, about the unrestricted pouring out of the heart to God, one might argue that *kol eima detzabei matzli* — one may pray at any time — and the entire framework of time limits and makeups is secondary to the essential nature of prayer as human communication with the divine.

### Scripture Proof

A *braisa* is cited that appears to deny any makeup for *tefillah*: *me'uvat lo yuchal litkon* — that which is perverted cannot be straightened; *vecheisaron lo yuchal lehimanot* — and that which is lacking cannot be counted. The *braisa* applies the first half of the verse to one who missed *krias shema* of the evening or morning, or who missed *Ma'ariv* or *Shacharit* — these cannot be remedied. The second half is applied to one who was absent when a group gathered for a *mitzvah*; that absence cannot be retrospectively included. This appears to categorically reject the possibility of makeup prayer.

### Willful Neglect

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction: the *braisa*'s prohibition applies specifically to one who *bittlo bemeizid* — who willfully neglected the prayer. Rav Ashi adds that the *braisa*'s own language is precise: it uses the word *bittul*, annulment or negation, rather than *ta'ah*, erring inadvertently — *shema mina*, this itself demonstrates the distinction. One who deliberately skips *tefillah* forfeits any makeup. One who genuinely forgot or erred may make it up in the following *tefillah*.

### Dialectic Resolution

The *halakhah* of makeup prayer thus embodies a genuine synthesis of the two models. Pure *korban* logic would permit no makeup across days and no flexibility whatsoever. Pure *rachamim* logic would impose no time limits at all and render the concept of "making up" meaningless. The actual *halakhah* lives in the tension between them. *Tefillah* carries the formal structure of *korbanot*: fixed times, the possibility of losing the merit of *tefilla bizmana*, and the impossibility of making up a willfully missed prayer. But the *rachamei* foundation of prayer — its nature as the unrestricted cry of the human heart to God — provides the halakhic basis for makeup prayer when a genuine inadvertent error has occurred, even across the boundary between one prayer time and the next. The times matter, but they do not utterly exhaust the meaning of *tefillah*.

---

---

# Berakhot 26b

## Makeup Prayer Structure

### Missed Mincha Setup

The discussion opens at the very top of 26b, building on the previous session's analysis of making up a missed *davening*. The *gemara* had established that makeup prayer is possible even when the original time has passed, grounded in the principle that *tefillot* are not only *keneged korbanot* — patterned after the sacrifices — but are also *rachamei*, a fundamental human outpouring of feeling and petition before God. This dual nature creates an ongoing tension: if prayer were purely *rachamei*, there would be no issue of missed times or fixed texts; one would simply pray whenever the spirit moved. Yet the very existence of fixed times and fixed text at the rabbinic level demonstrates that the *korban* model does impose real constraints, even while the *rachamei* dimension provides a certain latitude — including, notably, the possibility of making up a missed prayer.

The *gemara* now introduces a further complication. A *braita* teaches: if one forgot to pray *Mincha* on *Erev Shabbat*, one prays twice on Friday night — *ta'ah velo hitpalel Mincha b'Erev Shabbat, mitpalel b'leilei Shabbat shtayim*. Similarly, if one forgot *Mincha* on *Shabbat* itself, one prays twice on *Motzaei Shabbat* — and both of those prayers are weekday *davenings*, *shtayim shel chol*, even though the prayer one missed was a *Shabbat Mincha*. The principle, then, is that a missed *davening* is made up at the next available opportunity, even when the character of that opportunity differs from what was missed.

### Obligation Then Makeup

This raises an immediate structural question: in what order does one perform these two prayers, and how does one designate which is the obligatory *davening* and which is the makeup? The *gemara* is explicit: *mavdil barishona v'eino mavdil bashniya* — one recites *havdalah* in the first prayer and not in the second. This formulation dispels any ambiguity left from the previous discussion. The second *davening* is not simply a continuation or an extension of the first time slot; it is a formally designated makeup. The *gemara* insists that the obligatory prayer must come first, and only afterwards the makeup.

The structural consequence is significant: if one recites *havdalah* in the second prayer but not the first — thereby implicitly designating the second as the obligatory *Ma'ariv* and the first as the makeup — the ruling is *shniya alta lo, rishona lo alta lo*. Only the second counts. The first, which was labeled by one's own actions as the makeup, does not fulfill its obligation, because the makeup is only valid when it follows the obligatory prayer.

### Formal vs. Experiential

One might pause here and ask: what is the experiential meaning of davening twice in immediate succession? At the level of inner religious experience, a second *Shmoneh Esrei* offered immediately after the first seems to fulfill very little. It is an honest question. The answer, upon reflection, is that the makeup prayer is not primarily about recreating a meaningful inner experience; it is about discharging an obligation. One owes a *davening*, one missed a *davening*, and one is checking it off the record. The halachic system is concerned with the *chiyuv* having been met.

This tension is precisely what is striking about the structure. The very permission to make up a missed prayer rests on the principle that prayer is *rachamei* — an inner human experience that transcends purely formal categories. Yet the actual mechanism by which one makes up that prayer is thoroughly formalistic: it must be done immediately after, it must be properly designated, and if the designation is incorrect, the makeup does not count at all. The *rachamei* rationale opens the door; the halachic structure governs everything that happens once inside. This interplay between the inner experiential justification and the formal external execution is one of the central dialectics of this entire *masechta*.

This formalistic dominance should not come as a surprise within a halachic system. The formal rules consistently tip the balance. Consider the well-known responsa of *poskim* on whether one achieves better *kavana* davening at home than in *shul*: overwhelmingly, the ruling is to daven in *shul*. The formal fulfillment — communal prayer, *minyan* — is favored over the subjective inner experience, even where the inner experience might, in a given case, be richer. Yet what makes this *masechta* unique is that the tension itself is made visible. Elsewhere, the question rarely surfaces. Here, the dialectic is openly examined.

### Havdalah Contradictions

The *gemara* then confronts a potential objection. One might think that the reason the first *davening* fails when *havdalah* is recited only in the second is because *Ma'ariv* on *Motzaei Shabbat* without *havdalah* is simply invalid — that a *Ma'ariv* missing *havdalah* does not count at all. The *gemara* challenges this assumption with a *braita*: if one forgot to mention *mashiv haruach umorid hagashem* in the second *bracha*, or *uten tal u'matar livracha* in the *bracha* of *birkat hashanim*, one must repeat the *Shmoneh Esrei* — *machzirin oto*. But if one forgot *havdalah* in *Honen Hada'at*, one does not repeat — *ein machzirin oto* — because *havdalah* can still be recited over a cup of wine later. This proves that *Ma'ariv* without *havdalah* in the *Shmoneh Esrei* is nonetheless valid. The *gemara* acknowledges the difficulty: *kashya*.

But as both *Rashi* and *Tosafot* explain, the difficulty is not so severe on reflection. Ordinarily, if one simply davened *Ma'ariv* and forgot *havdalah*, one is *yotzei* — the prayer counts. The issue here is different. Because we are constructing a formal makeup structure, the requirement is that the obligatory prayer be clearly designated as such, and the makeup designated as such. When one placed *havdalah* in the second rather than the first, one labeled them in the wrong order. The first was thereby marked as the makeup, and the makeup cannot precede the obligation. The invalidity of the first prayer does not arise from the absence of *havdalah* per se, but from the misidentification of the two prayers' roles.

This leads to a further observation. The permission to make up a missed prayer is rooted in the *rachamei* principle — in the non-formalistic, inner dimension of *tefillah*. Yet the practical execution is so highly structured that even two consecutive *Shmoneh Esreis*, both technically valid prayers, may fail to fulfill any obligation whatsoever if the formal designation is incorrect. The inner justification gives way entirely to external formal requirements at the moment of execution.

A question arises regarding whether this entire discussion assumes *Ma'ariv* is obligatory, a *chiyuv*. If *Ma'ariv* is a *reshut* — optional — the framework of makeup prayers would look quite different. *Tosafot* indeed notes this: discussions about making up *Ma'ariv* presuppose it is obligatory, a question that will be debated later in the *masechta*. For now, the *gemara* is operating within the framework that *Ma'ariv* is an obligation and must be made up.

### Omitted Insertions

*Tosafot* raises a closely related practical question: what if one did not entirely miss a *Shmoneh Esrei*, but recited it without a critical insertion — for example, on *Rosh Chodesh* without *Ya'aleh V'Yavo*? Must one do a makeup at *Ma'ariv*? *Tosafot* identifies two competing considerations. On one hand, if one was not *yotzei* the *Mincha*, a makeup is required. On the other hand, the makeup at *Ma'ariv* will itself not include *Ya'aleh V'Yavo*, since *Rosh Chodesh* will have ended — so what exactly is being made up?

The resolution turns on a conceptual distinction: is the failure to recite *Ya'aleh V'Yavo* a failure to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *Ya'aleh V'Yavo* within the *Shmoneh Esrei*, or does it constitute a failure to have fulfilled the *Shmoneh Esrei* itself? If the latter, then one simply was not *yotzei* the *Shmoneh Esrei*, and the situation is directly analogous to the *gemara*'s case of davening twice on *Motzaei Shabbat* for a missed *Shabbat Mincha* — the makeup at *Ma'ariv* does not recapitulate the missed content but fulfills the missed *Shmoneh Esrei* obligation. If the former, then repeating the *Shmoneh Esrei* at *Ma'ariv* accomplishes nothing with respect to the omitted *Ya'aleh V'Yavo*, since that cannot be fulfilled after *Rosh Chodesh*.

The ruling that follows — the accepted *pesak* — is that missing *Ya'aleh V'Yavo* in *Mincha* means one was not *yotzei* the *Shmoneh Esrei* itself, and one therefore davens a second *Shmoneh Esrei* at *Ma'ariv* even though it will not contain *Ya'aleh V'Yavo*. The focus is on the uncompleted *Shmoneh Esrei* obligation, not on the specific missing element.

---

## Avot vs. Korbanot (III)

### Source of Prayer

The *gemara* now presents a fundamental *machloket* among *Amoraim* regarding the very foundation of prayer. *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina* says: *tefillot Avot tiknum* — the prayers were established by the patriarchs. *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* says: *tefillot keneged temidim tiknum* — the prayers were established to correspond to the daily communal sacrifices. The *gemara* then notes that there is a *braita* that supports each position.

The question, read carefully, is not a historical one — not simply who established the prayers or when. As the *Yerushalmi* phrases it, the question is *keneged mi* — corresponding to what? In other words, what is the *model* of *tefillah*? The two answers do not address the same dimension. The first answer speaks to an inner human experience of prayer — what were the *Avot* actually doing? The second speaks to a fixed external structure — what do the prayers correspond to in terms of formal religious obligation? This is precisely the *korban* versus *rachamei* tension that has been running throughout the discussion.

### Avot Founders

The *braita* supporting *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina* identifies each patriarch with one of the three daily prayers. *Avraham tikein tefilat Shacharit* — Abraham established the morning prayer, as it says *vayashkem Avraham baboker el hamakom asher amad sham* — Abraham rose early to the place where he had stood, preceding his intercession before God regarding Sodom. *Ve'ein amidah ela tefillah* — standing is interpreted as prayer, supported by *vaya'amod Pinchas vayefalel*.

*Yitzchak tikein tefilat Minchah* — Isaac established the afternoon prayer, as it says *vayetze Yitzchak lasuach basadeh lifnot arev* — Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening. *Ve'ein sichah ela tefillah* — speech or meditation is interpreted as prayer, supported by *tefillah le'ani ki ya'atof velifnei Hashem yishpoch sicho*.

*Yaakov tikein tefilat Arvit* — Jacob established the evening prayer, as it says *vayifga bamakom vayalen sham* — he encountered the place and slept there. *Ve'ein pegi'ah ela tefillah* — to encounter, in this context, means to importune or entreat, supported by the verse *ve'al tifga bi* — do not entreat me on their behalf.

---

## Shacharit Times (III)

### All Prayer Times

The *braita* supporting *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* takes an entirely different approach, grounding each prayer's time limits in the times of the corresponding sacrifices. *Mipnei mah amru tefilat hashachar ad chatzot* — why did the Sages say the morning prayer extends until midday? *Sheharei tamid shel shachar karev ve-holech ad chatzot* — because the morning *tamid* could be offered until midday. *Rabbi Yehudah* disagrees: it is only until four hours into the day — *ad arba sha'ot* — because the morning *tamid* was offered only until the fourth hour.

For *Mincha*: the afternoon prayer extends until nightfall because the afternoon *tamid* — *tamid shel bein ha-arbayim* — could be brought all the way until nightfall. *Rabbi Yehudah* again limits this, holding that the afternoon *tamid* was offered only until *pelag hamincha* — an hour and a quarter before sunset — and thus *Mincha* prayer may only be recited until that point.

For *Ma'ariv*: the evening prayer has no fixed time limit — *ein lah keva* — because the fats and limbs of the sacrifices that had not been consumed by nightfall could continue to be burned throughout the entire night.

For *Musaf*: one may recite *Musaf* all day — *kol hayom* — because the *korban Musaf* could be offered throughout the day. *Rabbi Yehudah* limits this to seven hours into the day — until 1:00 PM — because the *Musaf* sacrifice could not be brought past that point.

---

## Mincha Times

### Mincha Periods

The *braita* continues by specifying the two windows of *Mincha* time. *Mincha gedolah* — the larger, earlier period — begins from six and a half hours into the day, 12:30 PM, and extends through the afternoon. This gives a window of five and a half hours during which *Mincha* may be recited. *Mincha ketanah* — the smaller, later period, considered the more ideal time because it more closely corresponds to when the afternoon *tamid* was actually offered — begins at nine and a half hours into the day, 3:30 PM, and extends until the end of the afternoon.

These two windows reflect the *korban* model directly. The *tamid shel bein ha-arbayim* defined when afternoon prayer was most properly situated, and the gradations of *Mincha gedolah* and *Mincha ketanah* reflect degrees of correspondence to that sacrificial time.

---

## Avot vs. Korbanot (III)

### Three Prayer Stages

Returning to the *Avot* model, attention is drawn to the three verbs the *gemara* uses to describe the prayer of each patriarch. *Avraham* stands — *amidah*. *Yitzchak* speaks — *sichah*. *Yaakov* entreats — *pegi'ah*. These three verbs correspond not merely to three different times of day but to three stages of the prayer experience itself.

The first stage — *amidah*, standing — precedes speech entirely. According to the *Rambam*, the foundational *kavana* required for prayer, even before one attends to the meaning of the words, is the awareness that one stands in the presence of God. This awareness alone — conscious presence before another — constitutes a profound form of connection, even without speech. The second stage — *sichah*, speech — represents the articulation of one's inner state: giving form, narrowing, and expressing what was first experienced as non-verbal presence. Only after that, in the third stage, comes *pegi'ah* — entreaty, *bakasha*, the explicit request. Prayer is often conceived of primarily as petition, but the deepest understanding of the prayer experience encompasses all three stages: non-verbal standing before God, verbal articulation of that connection, and finally the entreaty that emerges from it. This is the structure of *Avraham*, *Yitzchak*, and *Yaakov* as models of prayer.

### Prayer Types Framework

The second observation about the *Avot* model concerns what it means to say that *Avraham* established *Shacharit*, *Yitzchak* established *Mincha*, and *Yaakov* established *Maariv* — if the entire premise of the *Avot* model is that prayer is not about fixed times. The answer is that these are not times of prayer but *types* of prayer. The morning prayer, *Shacharit*, is not defined by the hour at which it occurs but by the quality of experience that morning evokes: the sense of possibility, of vision, of beginning, of going out to engage the world. *Avraham* is the archetype of this mode — *vayikra beshem Hashem*, he pioneered, he brought people to serve God, he fought wars, he was driven by dream and ambition and the desire to transform the world.

*Mincha*, the afternoon prayer, corresponds to the experience of midday and afternoon — not the freshness of morning dreams but the need to sustain, continue, maintain. *Yitzchak* is the model here: he did not pioneer new visions but secured and deepened what *Avraham* had established. He dug the same wells *Avraham* had dug, replicated the same experiences, ensured that *Avraham*'s achievements were not lost. Without *Yitzchak*, *Avraham*'s wells get stopped up. The *Mincha* prayer is the prayer of continuity and sustaining strength through the middle of the day and the middle of a life.

*Maariv*, the night prayer, corresponds to *Yaakov* — a man perpetually beset by danger and uncertainty, running from *Esav*, laboring under *Lavan*, mourning *Yosef*. The night prayer is the prayer of fear, anguish, and helplessness before an unknown future, the prayer of one who does not know what comes next and turns to God for salvation. These are not times but existential postures, and the *Avot* model names them as such.

### Communal vs. Personal

This brings the discussion to a question that might seem to favor the *Avot* model entirely: if prayer in its essence is this inner human experience of morning ambition, afternoon continuity, and nighttime anguish, why overlay it with the fixed external structure of the *korban* model at all? One answer is practical: not everyone is capable of generating that inner experience at will. Fixed times, fixed texts, and regular structure ensure that prayer happens even when the spirit does not spontaneously move. The structure creates the occasion; connection sometimes follows.

But there is a second, deeper answer. The *korban* to which prayer corresponds in the *gemara*'s formulation is the *tamid* — the communal sacrifice. What the formal structure of prayer achieves is not merely regularity but communality. When all Israel davens at the same time, with the same text, whether together in a *minyan* or separately in their homes, prayer ceases to be each person's private conversation with God and becomes a shared act — a community of prayer. The *tefillah* of the *tzibur* is something categorically different from the sum of individual prayers. This communal dimension is precisely what the *Avot* model, in its purely personal and spontaneous form, cannot by itself generate. The *korban* model — the *tamid*, offered on behalf of all Israel at fixed times — provides the structural analog for communal prayer.

The tension between personal inner experience and formal communal structure is not unique to *tefillah*; it is present in every human endeavor that carries the potential for meaning and inspiration. Whether in music, where the discipline of notation and technique opens the door to genuine expression, or in theater, or any other organized form of human creativity — the formal structure is not the enemy of inner experience but its necessary scaffold. One must first master the structure, and then one may forget it. In the domain of *halakha*, however, the formal rules are not ultimately to be forgotten but to be inhabited — which is why the *poskim* consistently favor davening in *shul* over davening at home for better *kavana*, and why the formalistic expression of the makeup prayer dominates even when its inner justification is the *rachamei* dimension of *tefillah*.

---

## Shacharit Times (III)

### Shacharit Cutoff

The *gemara* returns to the halachic debate regarding the time limit for *Shacharit*. *Rabbi Yehudah* holds that *Shacharit* may only be davened until four hours into the day — until 10:00 AM. The *Rabbanan* hold it may be davened until midday — *ad chatzot*. Both ground their positions in the *tamid shel shachar* and when that sacrifice could be offered, though as noted, the *Rabbanan*'s more expansive position also aligns naturally with the broader *Avot* model of prayer as a morning experience that encompasses the whole of the morning.

---

## Avot vs. Korbanot (III)…

### Model Synthesis

Having presented the two *braitot* — one supporting *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina* and one supporting *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* — the *gemara* asks whether the *braita* supporting the *korban* model constitutes a refutation of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*'s position. *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* responds: *le'olam eima lach tefillot Avot tiknum* — the foundational truth remains that the prayers were established by the *Avot*, by the inner human experience of prayer. *Ve'asmechinenhu Rabbanan a'korbanot* — the Rabbis then *affixed* them, anchored them, to the *korbanot*. The *korban* model is a second layer, imposed by the Rabbis atop the foundational *Avot* model.

This synthesis is not merely a diplomatic resolution; it reflects a genuine structure. Prayer originates not from an external demand — here is a text, here is a time, say this — but from an inner human need, the kind of prayer that *Avraham*, *Yitzchak*, and *Yaakov* exemplified. The Rabbis then formalized this inner reality through the mold of the *korbanot*, giving it fixed times, fixed texts, and communal form. The *Avot* model is the foundation; the *korban* model is the architecture built upon it.

### Musaf Evidence

The clearest evidence that the *korban* model exists as a genuine second layer — and is not merely rhetorical — is *Musaf*. *Tfilat Musaf leRabbi Yehoshua ben Levi man tiknah* — according to *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*, who established *Musaf*? There is no *Musaf* among the prayers of *Avraham*, *Yitzchak*, and *Yaakov*. *Musaf* is purely a *korban* prayer, corresponding entirely to the additional sacrifice of *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*. This proves that the *korban* element is real and not merely incidental. *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* therefore must concede that *Musaf* is anchored exclusively in the *korban* structure.

A significant halachic corollary follows: because *Musaf* is entirely a *korban* prayer with no *Avot* foundation, it cannot be made up if missed. The capacity to make up a missed *davening* — as discussed at the outset — rests on the *rachamei* dimension, on the inner human experience that transcends formal time constraints. *Musaf*, having no such dimension, is governed entirely by *avar yomo batel korbano* — once the day has passed, the sacrifice is nullified and there is nothing to make up. *Tosafot* and others draw this distinction explicitly.

The *Rambam*'s formulation of the biblical-rabbinic distinction in the laws of prayer expresses a similar double layer: a biblical obligation of prayer that has no fixed time, no fixed text — one says whatever one wishes — and a rabbinic overlay of fixed times, fixed texts, and all the formal structure. The relationship between *Avot* as foundation and *korbanot* as formal structure is the conceptual parallel.

---

## Shacharit Times (III)…

### Inclusive Cutoffs

The *gemara* now examines a textual ambiguity in *Rabbi Yehudah*'s formulation. When he says *ad arba sha'ot* — until four hours — does he mean *ad ve'ad bichlal* — up to and including the fourth hour, meaning through 10:00 AM — or *ad velo ad bichlal* — up to but not including the fourth hour, meaning only until 9:00 AM when the fourth hour begins?

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this from the parallel formulation regarding *pelag hamincha* for *Mincha*. If *ad* is inclusive, then *ad pelag hamincha* includes the entire *pelag hamincha* period, which would extend to nightfall — making *Rabbi Yehudah*'s position identical to the *Rabbanan* who permit *Mincha* until sunset. That cannot be right. So perhaps *ad* is non-inclusive? But if non-inclusive, then when *Rabbi Yehudah* permits *Musaf* until seven hours — *ad sheva sha'ot* — he would mean only until noon, and there would be no overlap between *Mincha* time (from 12:30 PM) and *Musaf* time. Yet the *braita* presents a case of *shtei tefillot* — two prayers that must be davened simultaneously, choosing between *Mincha* first or *Musaf* first. That case can only exist if there is an overlap. This proves *ad* is inclusive by *Rabbi Yehudah*: *Musaf* extends until 1:00 PM, creating an overlap with *Mincha gedolah* between 12:30 and 1:00.

But then how does one explain *pelag hamincha*? The *gemara* resolves this by reconsidering which *pelag* is meant. The *braita* had determined — based on an explicit ruling — that *Rabbi Yehudah* refers to *pelag Mincha achrona*, the second half of the *Mincha ketanah* period, from 3:30 to 6:00. If one takes that unit — 3:30 to 6:00 — and divides it into two halves, one has *plag rishona* (3:30 to 4:45) and *plag achrona* (4:45 to 6:00). When *Rabbi Yehudah* says *ad pelag hamincha* inclusively, he means through the first half, ending at the beginning of the second half, 4:45 PM — *michei nafik achas esrei sha'ot chasar revi'a* — when eleven hours minus a quarter have passed. This preserves a genuine difference between *Rabbi Yehudah* (until 4:45) and the *Rabbanan* (until sunset), while maintaining the principle that *ad* is inclusive throughout.

The parallel case regarding the order of *Mincha* and *Musaf* when both must be davened in the afternoon also emerges here. The general ruling is that *Mincha* precedes *Musaf* because *Mincha* is *tadir* — more frequent — and the principle is *tadir ve'eino tadir, tadir kodem*. *Rabbi Yehudah* rules the opposite: *Musaf* before *Mincha*, because *Musaf* has a passing time — *zo overet* — and once that window closes, *Musaf* cannot be made up. One should therefore discharge the time-sensitive obligation first. All times cited are in *sha'ot zmaniyot* — proportional hours calculated by dividing the daylight hours into twelve equal parts — and must be adjusted accordingly for any given day.

### Ben Bava Testimony

The *gemara* now anchors the ruling for *Shacharit* in a specific testimony. *Rav Nachman* notes that the *Mishnah* in *Eduyot* already supports this position. *Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava* testified five things — *chamisha devarim* — among them: *ve'al tamid shel shachar she-karav be-arba sha'ot* — that the morning *tamid* was offered in the fourth hour. The word is *be-arba sha'ot*, "in the fourth hour," not *ad arba sha'ot*, "until the fourth hour." This formulation confirms that the fourth hour was included, that it was offered during that hour — meaning the cutoff is inclusive of the fourth hour, through 10:00 AM.

*Eduyot* is referred to as *bechirata* — the select tractate — because it preserves particularly reliable testimony from early authorities, gathered largely at *Yavne* after the *churban*. The general halachic principle is that teachings preserved in *Eduyot* carry special weight and are generally followed.

### Rav Kahana Ruling

*Rav Kahana* issues the ruling: *halakha ke-Rabbi Yehudah* for *Shacharit* — we rule like *Rabbi Yehudah* that the proper time of the morning prayer extends until four hours into the day, until 10:00 AM — *ho'il ve-tnan be-vchirata kevataih*, since we taught in *Eduyot* consistent with his position.

It is worth noting what this ruling actually demonstrates. The testimony in *Eduyot* concerns when the *korban tamid* was in practice offered in the morning. That a sacrifice was always brought before the fourth hour does not automatically prove that davening *Shacharit* after 10:00 AM is invalid — that conclusion follows only if one accepts that *tefillah* is substantively linked to the *korban* structure. The *gemara*'s readiness to derive the prayer time limit from the sacrifice time implicitly affirms the *korban* dimension. This is not in contradiction to the *Avot* model; it reflects the synthesis established above — the *Avot* experience is foundational, but the rabbis connected the formal expression of prayer to the *korbanot*, and it is that formal connection which governs the times.

The practical ruling that emerges: *zman Shacharit* — the proper time of the morning prayer — ends at four hours into the day, 10:00 AM on a day of equal daylight hours. If one misses this window, one may still daven *Shmoneh Esrei* until *chatzot* — midday — but it is considered *tefillah she-lo bi-zmanah*, prayer recited outside its proper time. After midday, the day's *Shacharit* obligation has passed entirely.

---

## Boker Definition

### Manna Melting

Having established the time limit for *Shacharit*, the *gemara* probes its meaning further through an unexpected source: the *manna* narrative. A *Tosefta* or parallel source asks: when the verse says *va-cham ha-shemesh ve-namas* — the sun heated and the manna melted — at what hour did this occur? The answer given is the fourth hour, 10:00 AM. But the verse elsewhere says *ke-chom ha-yom* — like the heat of the day — referring to the hottest part of the day, which is noon. The resolution: *ke-chom ha-yom* refers to when the day is fully hot everywhere; *va-cham ha-shemesh ve-namas* refers to a condition where the sun is hot but the shaded areas are not yet hot. That is the fourth hour — when sun-exposed areas are already warm but the shade remains cool.

### Two Halves

The *gemara* then asks who holds this position — is it *Rabbi Yehudah* or the *Rabbanan*? The Torah commands that the manna be gathered *ba-voker* — in the morning. The manna melted at the beginning of the fourth hour, 9:00 AM. Yet according to *Rabbi Yehudah*, *voker* — morning — extends through the fourth hour, until 10:00 AM. If that is so, the manna would still be melting during *voker* time, which seems problematic — the people collected during *voker* and it melted during *voker* as well. According to the *Rabbanan*, *voker* extends until noon, so the manna melting at 9:00 AM is within *voker* as well.

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty with the observation that the verse writes *ba-voker ba-voker* — "in the morning, in the morning" — doubling the word. This doubling indicates a division: *chalkehu li-shnei bekarim* — divide it into two mornings, a first half and a second half. According to the *Rabbanan*, whose *voker* runs until noon: the first half of *voker* ends at 9:00 AM and the second half runs from 9:00 AM to noon. The manna was gathered during the first half and melted at the transition into the second half — consistent with melting at the start of the fourth hour, 9:00 AM. According to *Rabbi Yehudah*, whose *voker* runs until 10:00 AM: the repetition of *ba-voker* does not split *voker* in two but indicates that the gathering must occur specifically in the earlier part — *le-hakdim lo sha'ah achat* — pressing the collection into the first part of *voker*, before 9:00 AM, after which the manna would melt even while *voker* technically continued.

### Shade/Sun Distinction

*Rav Acha bar Yaakov* offers the principle that identifies the fourth hour specifically as the moment of transition: *eizu hi sha'ah she-ha-shemesh cham ve-ha-tzel tsonen* — which is the hour when the sun is hot but the shade is still cool? That is the fourth hour. This contrasts with *ke-chom ha-yom*, when even the shaded areas are hot — a condition that arrives at noon. The manna, melting specifically at the sun-hot-shade-cool transition, places its melting precisely at 9:00 AM, the beginning of the fourth hour — and this is accepted by all positions as the correct reading of *va-cham ha-shemesh ve-namas*.

### Boker Layers

What is striking about this entire *sugya* is the direction of derivation. The debate between *Rabbi Yehudah* and the *Rabbanan* about how late *Shacharit* may be davened had been grounded in the *korban* model — when was the morning *tamid* offered. But the *gemara* here is probing the meaning of *voker*, and the *manna* narrative has nothing to do with sacrifices. The question of what constitutes *voker* — whether it runs until 10:00 AM or until noon — is a question about the human experience of morning itself, about what part of the day still carries the quality of *boker*, daybreak. The *manna* melting is a natural phenomenon marking the end of early morning; the cooling shade giving way to pervasive heat is the experiential signal that the morning has concluded. In this sense, the *gemara* is entertaining the possibility that the debate between *Rabbi Yehudah* and the *Rabbanan* is not ultimately about the *tamid* but about a more fundamental question: what is *tefillat ha-voker* — what is the morning prayer, and how long does morning last? The *korban* model and the *Avot* model converge on the same time limits through entirely different conceptual routes.

### Manna Prayer Link

One final observation about the *manna* parallel deserves mention. There is a way of reading prayer itself *keneged ha-man* — corresponding to the manna. The daily gathering of manna in the morning — the experience of going out each day to receive one's sustenance from God, never able to store it up in advance — is a paradigm for prayer as daily petition. Just as Israel prayed through the gathering of manna for their daily bread, each morning's *Shacharit* is a turning to God for the sustenance of the coming day. This layer of meaning sits beneath the formal structures of *korban* and *Avot* alike.

---

## Mincha Times (II)

### Mincha Cutoff Debate

*Rav Chisda* turns to *Rabbi Yitzchak* and raises the practical question directly. Having just ruled like *Rabbi Yehudah* for *Shacharit* — because of the testimony preserved in *Eduyot* — what is the ruling for *Mincha*? Does the time for *Mincha* end at *pelag hamincha* (4:45 PM), as *Rabbi Yehudah* holds, or does it extend until nightfall, as the *Rabbanan* hold? *Rabbi Yitzchak* has no answer — *ishtik velo amar lei midi* — he falls silent.

### Shabbat Evidence

*Rav Chisda* then attempts to resolve the question on his own from a practical precedent. *Mi-deRav matzli shel Shabbat b'erev Shabbat mi-be'od yom* — from the fact that *Rav* davened *Maariv* for *Shabbat* while it was still Friday, before sunset. If *Mincha* time ends at 4:45 PM (*pelag hamincha*), then *Maariv* time begins at 4:45 PM, and *Rav*'s early *Shabbat* davening would be consistent with ruling like *Rabbi Yehudah*. *Shema mina halakha ke-Rabbi Yehudah* — this suggests we rule like *Rabbi Yehudah*.

But the *gemara* counters: *mi-deRav Huna ve-Rabbanan lo havu matzli ad orta* — *Rav Huna* and the *Rabbanan* who were present did not daven an early *Shabbat*. From this one infers the opposite — *ein halakha ke-Rabbi Yehudah*.

### No Ruling

The *gemara* concludes with a formal declaration of inconclusive debate: *hashta de-lo itmar hilkhata la kemar vela kemar, de-avad kemar avad u-de-avad kemar avad* — since no clear ruling has been issued like either authority, one who acts like this one has acted properly and one who acts like that one has acted properly. This is an unusual outcome — a genuine *deaved kemar* situation without a definitive *pesak* for *Mincha* times, even while the *Shacharit* cutoff was definitively ruled.

### Mincha/Maariv Link

The *gemara*'s framing of the evidence — using *Rav*'s early *Shabbat* davening and *Rav Huna*'s refusal to do the same — reveals an implicit assumption: the time of *Mincha* and the time of *Maariv* are interdependent. If *Mincha* ends at *pelag hamincha*, *Maariv* may begin at *pelag hamincha*. If *Mincha* extends until sunset, *Maariv* cannot begin until after sunset. This linkage is important in practice, particularly for congregations that daven an early *Shabbat* and wish to daven both *Mincha* and *Maariv* before nightfall.

A real halachic problem arises when a congregation davens *Mincha* after *pelag hamincha* and then immediately davens *Maariv* as well — in the same pre-sunset window. This relies on *Rabbi Yehudah* for the permissibility of *Maariv* beginning at *pelag hamincha*, while relying on the *Rabbanan* for the continuation of *Mincha* beyond *pelag hamincha*. These two positions are not compatible with each other. Strictly speaking, one cannot use *Rabbi Yehudah* to begin *Maariv* while simultaneously using the *Rabbanan* to continue *Mincha*. The *deaved kemar* ruling means one may choose either position, but one may not blend them contradictorily in a single act of davening.

It should also be noted that nowhere does *Rabbi Yehudah* himself explicitly rule that *Maariv* begins at *pelag hamincha*. The connection is inferred by the *gemara*, and the *Rambam* does not directly derive this from the *pelag hamincha* debate but treats early *Maariv* on *Erev Shabbat* as a special case, since *Maariv* is *reshut* — not obligatory in the same sense. Nonetheless, the accepted practical understanding is that *pelag hamincha* functions as a liturgical boundary with implications for both the end of *Mincha* and the potential beginning of *Maariv*.

---

## Davening Etiquette

### Early Shabbat Story

The *gemara* concludes with a narrative involving *Rav*. *Rav ikla l'vei Gneiva* — *Rav* came to the house of *Gneiva*, and there he davened *Maariv* for *Shabbat* while it was still *Erev Shabbat*, before sunset. *Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba* was davening behind *Rav*. When *Rav* finished his *Shmoneh Esrei*, he did not interrupt *Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba*'s davening — he did not take his three steps back in a way that would intrude into *Rabbi Yirmiyah*'s space, nor did he walk in front of him to return to his seat.

### Three Lessons

*Shema mina tlat* — three halachic conclusions are drawn from this incident. First: *mitpalel adam shel Shabbat b'erev Shabbat* — one may daven *Maariv* for *Shabbat* on Friday before sunset, confirming that early *Shabbat* is halachically permitted. Second: *mitpalel talmid achorei rabbo* — a student may daven directly behind his *rebbe*. This is not considered disrespectful; it does not carry the appearance of bowing to one's teacher, and it does not violate any expectation of deference — unlike davening immediately to the side of the teacher, which could raise concerns. Third: *assur la'avor keneged hamitpalelim* — it is prohibited to walk in front of people who are davening. This is derived from *Rav*'s refusal to step in front of *Rabbi Yirmiyah* once that *talmid* had begun his *Shmoneh Esrei*.

### Four Amos Rule

The *gemara* explicitly endorses this prohibition by connecting it to an independent ruling of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: *assur la'avor keneged hamitpalelim* — one may not walk in front of those who are davening. The *gemara* then raises a challenge: did not *Rabbi Ammi* and *Rabbi Assi* walk in front of people who were davening? The resolution: *Rabbi Ammi* and *Rabbi Assi* walked *chutz le-arba amos* — outside the four-*amot* radius. The prohibition applies only within four *amot* of the person davening — one may not enter or cross that space while the person is in the middle of *Shmoneh Esrei*. Beyond four *amot*, passing in front of a davening individual is permitted.

This is a prohibition that is widely violated in practice. Beyond its halachic weight, it is also simply distracting to those in the midst of *davening*, and people ought to be *makpid* — careful — to avoid walking within four *amot* of anyone in the middle of *Shmoneh Esrei*.

---

---

# Berakhot 27b

## Prayer vs. Sacrifice

### Shemoneh Esrei & Avodah

The daf opens at the very bottom of 27a, but before proceeding, an observation from the preceding discussion is worth noting. The question arises whether the fact that *shemoneh esrei* opens with the word *avodah* — in the blessing *retzei* — constitutes an emphasis on *avodah* as such. This is a genuinely excellent point, and it connects to something even more striking that deserves attention: the words that were later added as a preface to *shemoneh esrei*, *hashem sefatai tiftach ufi yagid tehilatecha*, appear in *Tehillim* in a context where the very next *pasuk* reads *ki lo tachpotz olah va'zevach* — that God does not desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, but rather the words of our mouths and the intentions of our hearts. The preface to *shemoneh esrei* thus stands in exact contrast to sacrificial worship: *tefillah* is what God truly desires.

### Tefillah as Substitute

A second observation reinforces this point. The one *beracha* in *shemoneh esrei* that is ostensibly about *avodah* — *retzei hashem elokeinu be'amcha yisrael ubitfilatam* — never explicitly mentions sacrifices at all. It says *ubitfilatam*, "and with their prayer." It speaks of *vahashev ha'avodah*, returning the service, but the language remains abstract.

### Ishei Yisrael

Even the phrase *ve'ishei yisrael* — the most direct allusion to sacrifices within *retzei* — must be one of the most indirect and abstract ways of referring to sacrificial offerings in the entire liturgy. The deliberate absence of explicit sacrificial language from the very *beracha* that is supposed to correspond to *avodah* is striking. One is left to ask: how much are sacrifices really in *shemoneh esrei*, even where one would most expect them to be?

### Tannaim Debate

The broader picture that emerges from this discussion is that there are *tannaim* who view *korbanot* as the ideal and *tefillah* as a substitute or replacement, and there are other *tannaim* who feel strongly that *tefillot* are more desired by God than *korbanot*. These debates intensified in the period following the *churban habayit*, as the rabbinic world grappled with how to understand prayer in relation to a sacrificial system that no longer existed.

### Empty Ritual

However, it is important to note what the *pshat* of *Tanach* itself seems to be saying. The classic prophetic criticism of Israel's sacrificial practice is not that God would prefer verbal prayer in place of sacrifice. Rather, it is that God does not want empty sacrifice — sacrifice without sincerity, sacrifice divorced from ethical conduct. The prophetic ideal, in other words, is not *tefillah* instead of *korbanot*, but rather the vessel of sacrifice filled with genuine devotion and reflected in all aspects of human behavior. That said, this framing is still consistent with the view that verbal articulation can serve as a legitimate substitute — but with the caveat that *davening* itself means nothing if a person's behavior outside the synagogue does not reflect what he was doing inside it.

### Biblical Tefillah

It is equally important to observe that *tefillah* was never absent from Jewish life even when the *beit hamikdash* stood. From *avraham yitzchak ve'ya'akov* through *david hamelech*, who composed *tehillim* — which many scholars understand as essentially the first *siddur*, whether recited alongside the sacrificial service or by those distant from the *beit hamikdash* — the human need and experience of *tefillah* was always present. It is quite possible that *korbanot* and *tefillah* were never seen as simply two alternative modes of the same thing, but rather as qualitatively different, each serving its own distinct function: *korbanot* for *kappara* and certain forms of *avodah*, *tefillah* for personal connection and petition.

### Rambam's Position

The *rambam* in *Moreh Nevuchim* takes the view that *korbanot* were a concession to human nature rather than the ideal form of worship. But even within his legal writings, the *rambam*'s treatment of *tefillah* is also more reserved than one might expect — a matter for another time. One practical note before moving on: since the entire debate about *tefillah keneged korbanot* concerns the standard daily prayers, *musafim* fall outside that discussion entirely, which is precisely why the practice is to include the explicit mention of the *korban* in *mussaf*. Everybody agrees, as the *gemara* established previously, that *musaf* is *keneged korban*, and *musaf* is the one place in the liturgy where we explicitly name the sacrifice.

---

## Davening Behind Rebbe

### Davening Practice

The *gemara* now turns to the very last line of 27a. The *gemara* asks: *rabbi yirmeyah heichi avid hachi* — how did Rabbi Yirmeyah do what he did? The context is that Rabbi Yirmeyah had been *davening* behind Rav.

### L'olam al Yitpalel

The difficulty is immediate: Rav Yehudah teaches in the name of Rav — the very same Rav behind whom Rabbi Yirmeyah *davened* — that *l'olam al yitpalel adam lo keneged rabbo velo achorei rabbo*: a person should never pray beside his *rebbe* (which implies equality) nor behind his *rebbe* (which is problematic either because it appears disrespectful to face the back of one's teacher, or because it can look as though one is bowing down toward him). The irony is sharp: the very *rebbe* behind whom Rabbi Yirmeyah *davened* was the one who taught that one should not do so.

### Rabbi Eliezer

The *gemara* adds a *baraita*: Rabbi Eliezer says that one who *davens* behind his *rebbe*, and several other related behaviors, causes the *shechina* to depart from Israel.

### Five Violations

The *baraita* enumerates the violations: *hamitpalel achorei rabbo*, *vehanotan shalom l'rabbo*, *vehamachzir shalom l'rabbo*, *vecholek al yeshivato shel rabbo*, and *ha'omer davar shelo shama mipi rabbo* — one who *davens* behind his *rebbe*; one who greets his *rebbe* (without the appropriate honorific); one who returns a greeting to his *rebbe* (same concern); one who disagrees with the *halachic* positions of his *rebbe*; and one who says a teaching he did not hear directly from his *rebbe*.

Regarding *noten shalom l'rabbo*: Rashi and *tosafot* explain that the problem is not the greeting itself but the failure to use the honorific — saying *shalom aleichem* as if to a peer rather than as *shalom aleichem rabbi u'mori*. The *maharsha* notes that in another context in the *gemara*, a slave is not permitted to greet his master with *shalom aleichem* at all, given the extreme gulf in status; but Rashi and *tosafot* did not apply that principle here, understanding it as specific to that situation of master and slave. Here the violation is the manner of address, not the greeting itself.

### Shechina Departs

All five of these violations share a common consequence: *gorem lishchina shetistalek miyisrael* — they cause the *shechina* to depart from Israel.

### Talmid Chaver

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction regarding Rabbi Yirmeyah: *shani rabbi yirmeyah bar abba d'talmid chaver hava* — Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba was different because he was a *talmid chaver*, a student-colleague. He revered Rav as his teacher, but he occupied the status of a younger colleague, and therefore it was appropriate — or at least acceptable — for him to *daven* in closer proximity.

### Havdalah Question

### Second-Person Address

The proof that Rabbi Yirmeyah held this *talmid chaver* status comes from the way he addressed Rav. He asked Rav directly: *mi badalta* — "have you separated from *melacha*?" — meaning, having *davened* *maariv* early, did you thereby stop performing *melacha*? And Rav answered: *badilna* — "yes, I have." The proof of colleague status is the second-person form of address. A student speaking to a *rebbe* would have said *mi badil mar* — "has the master separated?" — using the third person out of deference. The fact that Rabbi Yirmeyah used the second person demonstrates that his relationship with Rav was that of a colleague, not merely a subordinate student.

---

## Conflicting Testimon (II)

### Eliezer Ideology

Returning briefly to one of the violations enumerated in the *baraita* — *ha'omer davar shelo shama mipi rabbo*, the prohibition against saying something one did not hear directly from one's *rebbe* — the *maharsha* correctly notes that this seems puzzling. Throughout *shas*, *amoraim* are constantly innovating, developing new ideas, saying things they never heard directly from their teachers. The most pointed answer is that this represents a distinctly *Rabbi Eliezer* position. Rabbi Eliezer the *tanna* famously took pride in the fact that he never said anything he did not hear from his *rebbe*. From what we know of Rabbi Eliezer — from his reputation as a *tanna* connected to the *Shammaite* tradition, and from other stories about him — it is clear that his approach to *torah she'ba'al peh* was one of pure transmission. *Torah she'ba'al peh* for Rabbi Eliezer was not about creativity or innovation but about receiving from your *rebbe* what your *rebbe* received from his *rebbe*, all the way back to *Moshe*. This stands in stark contrast to the approach of Rabbi Akiva — who was himself among Rabbi Eliezer's students — and who embodied the opposite principle, *doresh tagim*, finding new meaning even in the crowns of letters. Rabbi Akiva was, in this very matter, *cholek* on his *rebbe* about the prohibition against being *cholek* on one's *rebbe*, and he said things that he could not possibly have heard directly from his teacher.

---

## Maariv Early & Melacha

### Melacha Separation

Having established that Rabbi Yirmeyah's question to Rav concerned whether *davening* *maariv* early creates a separation from *melacha*, the *gemara* now takes up that question directly: *umi badil* — is it really true that one who *davens* *maariv* early thereby separates from *melacha* and may no longer perform labor?

### Rabbi's Bath Story

The *gemara* raises a challenge from a statement of Rav Avina: *pa'am achat hitpalel rebbi shel shabbos b'erev shabbat* — once, Rebbi *davened* the Shabbos *maariv* when it was still Friday. Afterwards, he went into the bathhouse, taught a chapter of study, and it was still not yet dark. This would seem to prove that *davening* *maariv* early does not create an immediate prohibition against *melacha* — or at least against bathhouse use — since Rebbi did both after *davening*.

### Bathhouse Laws

Rava explains: what Rebbi did in the bathhouse was to go in for steam — *l'hazia*, to perspire — not to immerse in hot water. The rabbinic prohibition on Shabbos is against immersing in water that was heated on Shabbos, and at a secondary level, even in water heated before Shabbos, out of concern that one might come to heat water on Shabbos itself. But Rebbi's visit to the bathhouse predated the enactment of that second layer of the *gezeirah*. So in fact Rebbi was treating it as Shabbos — he just did so at a time when this particular activity was still permitted even on Shabbos.

### Before Gezeirah

Rava's resolution thus shows that the story does not prove one can perform *melacha* after *davening* early. Rebbi was indeed conducting himself as if Shabbos had arrived; it was only the bathhouse prohibition that had not yet reached its later stringency.

### Early Acceptance

The underlying *hava amina* of the *gemara* is now clarified: the question was whether *davening* *maariv* of Shabbos early, while it is still Friday, means one has implicitly accepted Shabbos early — *kabbalat shabbos* — such that one may no longer perform *melacha*. This is similar to what we see on *motzaei shabbos*, where one can *daven maariv* of a weekday early (following the opinion of Rav Yehudah) even while *melacha* is still prohibited. Just as on *motzaei shabbos* the *tefillah* is separated from the practical permission to do *melacha*, perhaps the same logic operates on *erev shabbos*.

### Mistake Case

The *gemara* then brings a case of Abaye, who permitted Rav Dimi bar Livai to perform a certain *melacha* involving baskets — some kind of smoking or preparation process — after he had *davened maariv*. But the *gemara* immediately notes: *ta'uta havai* — this was a mistake. Rav Dimi had *davened* thinking it was already nightfall; the sky was dark from clouds, and he believed Shabbos was over. When the clouds parted and the sun reappeared, it became clear he had *davened* prematurely. The *melacha* permission was predicated on this being an error: he had not intended to *daven* early, he thought it was actually the proper time.

### Community Mistake

The *gemara* then challenges even this: *ve'ta'uta mi hadar* — does a mistake necessarily get undone? Perhaps even a mistaken early *davening* creates a binding *kabbalat shabbos*. And Rav Avidan is cited: *pa'am achat nitkashru shamayim be'avim* — once, the sky was darkened by clouds, the entire community believed it was already dark, they entered the synagogue and *davened* the Saturday night *tefillah* on Shabbos afternoon. Then the clouds dispersed and the sun shone. They came and asked Rebbi — and Rebbi ruled: *ho'il ve'hitpalelu hitpalelu*, since they *davened*, they have *davened*. They were *yotzei*.

### Mistake Counts?

Now the *gemara*'s logic here requires attention. The original question was not whether a mistaken early *davening* counts as *tefillah* — that is what Rebbi ruled upon — but whether it constitutes a *kabbalat shabbos*. The *gemara* seems to assume that if such a *davening* counts as *tefillah*, it also counts as an implicit *kabbalah*. This is a surprising equivalence. One might argue that even if the *davening* is valid, it only establishes *tefillah* if it is genuinely treated as an early *davening*; if a person thought it was already the right time, perhaps the *davening* is valid as *tefillah* but not as a *kabbalat shabbos* — since no *kabbalah* was intended at all. And yet the *gemara* does not reject this assumption in its answer.

---

## Intentional Early Da (II)

### Kabbalat Shabbat

The *gemara* resolves the *tzibbur* case differently from an individual: *shani tzibbur d'lo matrachi'nan lehu* — a community is different; we do not burden them to go back and *daven* again. If the entire *minyan* erred and *davened* early, the *tefillah* stands, and when Shabbos ends they are not required to repeat *maariv*. An individual, by contrast, must have specifically intended to *daven* early for it to count as an intentional early *davening*.

### Rav's Practice

Rav Chiya bar Avin reports: *rav tzalay shel shabbos be'erev shabbos* — Rav *davened* the Shabbos *tefillah* on Friday. This is the paradigm case of deliberate early *davening*.

### Rabbi Yoshiya's Case

And Rabbi Yoshiya would *daven* the *motzaei shabbos tefillah* while it was still Shabbos afternoon.

### Tzibbur vs Yachid

These two cases together — intentional early *maariv* of Shabbos on Friday, and intentional early *maariv* of *motzaei shabbos* on Shabbos — frame the discussion of what exactly such *davening* accomplishes. For the *tzibbur*, a mistake suffices; for an individual, intention is required.

### Rambam's View

The *gemara*'s assumption throughout this passage is that when one *davens* *maariv* of Shabbos early, one has implicitly accepted Shabbos — *kabbalat shabbos* — and the concept of *tosefet shabbos* underlies the entire discussion. This concept appears elsewhere in the *gemara* in connection with *tosefet yom hakippurim*, derived from a *pasuk*, and is then extended to Shabbos. According to many *rishonim*, the extension to Shabbos may be only *derabanan*, but it is present nonetheless.

The *rambam*, interestingly, never mentions *kabbalat shabbos* in this sense. He does speak of *tosefet yom hakippurim* — adding time at the beginning and end of *yom kippur* — but when it comes to early Shabbos *davening*, the *rambam*'s explanation is simply that since *tefilat maariv* is *reshut*, one may *daven* it a little before its proper time. He does not frame this as an implicit *kabbalat shabbos* that transforms the halachic status of the moment. And correspondingly, one will not find in the *rambam* a statement that *davening maariv* early on *erev shabbos* creates a prohibition on *melacha*.

### Kiddush Question

The *gemara* asks the natural next question: if one *davens* Shabbos *maariv* early on Friday, can one then go home and make *kiddush*? *Omer kiddusha al hakos o eino omer kiddusha al hakos?*

### Rambam Kiddush

The *gemara* answers with a ruling from Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *mitpalel adam shel shabbos be'erev shabbos ve'omer kiddusha al hakos* — one may *daven* Shabbos *tefillah* on Friday and make *kiddush* on a cup. And the ruling is: *hilchata kavatei*, this is how we rule.

For the *rambam*, this too does not require the concept of *tosefet shabbos*. When describing the *mitzvah* of *kiddush ve'havdalah*, the *rambam* speaks of designating Shabbos at its beginning and at its end — a little before the beginning, a little after the end. The idea is to mark the holy day, to designate it; and one can make *kiddush* in anticipation of Shabbos that is about to arrive, without the moment of *kiddush* itself creating the onset of Shabbos. Shabbos, for the *rambam*, begins at sunset. The *mitzvah* of *kiddush* can be fulfilled a bit beforehand as a designation and anticipation.

---

## Early Havdalah (III)

### Kiddush on Cup

As noted, Rav Nachman rules that one who *davens* Shabbos on Friday afternoon may make *kiddush* on a cup, and this is the accepted *halacha*.

---

## Intentional Early Da (II)

### Anticipation vs Reality

One might ask: when one says *mekadesh hashabbos* in the *beracha* while it is still *chol*, what exactly is being said? According to the *rambam*'s framework, one is not declaring that Shabbos has arrived; rather, one is saying these words in anticipation, acknowledging that Shabbos is about to come. Similarly, on the *motzaei shabbos* side, saying *havdalah bechonen hada'as* before Shabbos has technically ended is a parallel kind of anticipation — a looking forward or looking beyond — and does not represent a declaration that Shabbos is already over.

---

## Early Havdalah (III)

### Havdalah Timing

The *gemara* turns to the parallel question on *motzaei shabbos*: if one *davens* *maariv* of *motzaei shabbos* while it is still Shabbos afternoon, can one also make *havdalah* on a cup? *Omer havdalah al hakos o eino omer havdalah al hakos?* The *gemara* assumes that if one is *davening motzaei shabbos*, that means one includes *havdalah* in *shemoneh esrei*. But going further and making *havdalah* on a cup — separating the sacred from the ordinary through the formal ritual — when Shabbos has not yet concluded, is a significantly more striking act. It seems to truly declare that Shabbos is already over.

The *gemara* rules: from Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel — *m'toei shel motzaei shabbos ve'omer havdalah al hakos* — one who *davens motzaei shabbos* early may make *havdalah* on a cup. And this is the accepted ruling.

### Tzorech Mitzvah

*Tosafot*, however, adds an important condition. *Tosafot* says: *yesh lomar d'hacha mairi sheyesh lo tzorech mitzvah la'asos b'motzaei shabbos* — this ruling applies specifically where there is a *tzorech mitzvah*, a need related to a *mitzvah*, such as needing to travel to perform a circumcision and lacking wine for *havdalah* if one waits. *Tosafot* adds: *d'vadai tzarich l'hosif min hachol al hakodesh d'oraita* — because one is obligated to add from the weekday onto the holy day (*tosefet shabbos*), making *havdalah* before Shabbos is technically over seems to undercut that obligation. Therefore, *tosafot* requires some form of genuine need — a *tzorech mitzvah* or at least a *shas hadechak* — before one may do this. Critically, *tosafot* makes clear: *u'pshita d'lo matzi l'ma'avad melacha ad chasheicha* — obviously one cannot perform *melacha* until nightfall regardless of having *davened* and made *havdalah* early.

### Summer Schedule

A practical example makes this concrete: in Northern Europe in the summer, Shabbos can end very late. One may *daven maariv*, make *havdalah*, and go to sleep — while still not performing *melacha* until *tzeis hakochavim*. *Tosafot* in fact deals extensively with such situations at the very opening of this *masechet*, since where they lived, the days were long and the demands of the church calendar and civic life meant that nighttime *davening* was often conducted while it was still light outside.

### Tosefet Concern

Beyond the practical issue, *tosafot* expresses a deeper discomfort: there seems to be something more troubling about making *havdalah* — formally declaring the end of Shabbos's holiness — when Shabbos has not yet ended, compared to simply *davening maariv* early. Even if *halachically* permitted in cases of need, the act of *havdalah* carries a weight that makes one hesitate, even when the *din* allows it.

---

## Conflicting Testimon (II)

### Transmission Chain

The *gemara* now presents a striking chain of transmission. Rav Zeira says in the name of Rav Assi, who said it in the name of Rav Elazar, who said it in the name of Rav Chanina, who said it in the name of Rav: *betzad amud zeh hitpalel Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi shel shabbos b'erev shabbos* — right by this pillar, Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosi *davened* the Shabbos *tefillah* on Friday.

### Date Palm

Then *Ula* arrives and corrects the entire account. First: it was not beside a pillar — it was *betzad timra*, beside a date palm.

### Identity Corrections

Second: it was not Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosi — it was Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosi. And third — most significantly — it was not *shel shabbos be'erev shabbos*, *davening* Shabbos *tefillah* on Friday. It was the opposite: *shel motzaei shabbos be'shabbos*, *davening* the *motzaei shabbos tefillah* while it was still Shabbos.

### Mesorah Issues

Of course, it is possible that both stories are true — two different incidents, one involving each practice. But the deeper point here is about the nature of *mesorah* itself. Ula corrects every single detail: the location, the person's identity, and the direction of the early *davening*. If these details, transmitted through a chain of five *amoraim*, could all be incorrect, the transmission is clearly imperfect. This connects directly to what was said earlier about Rabbi Eliezer's ideology of pure, unbroken transmission — the idea that *torah she'ba'al peh* passes perfectly from *rebbe* to student, unchanged. The *gemara* here gently but unmistakably illustrates that even in careful chains of transmission, details can be garbled. In this way, the *gemara* softens what would otherwise be an impossibly rigid standard: one cannot always say only what one heard directly from one's *rebbe*, precisely because the chain is never as clean as the ideal demands.

---

## Early Havdalah (III)

### Daven vs Melacha

One important practical distinction to carry forward from all of the above: *davening maariv* early — whether of Shabbos on Friday or of *motzaei shabbos* on Shabbos — does not by itself end or begin Shabbos in the sense of permitting or prohibiting *melacha*. One may *daven* early and even make *kiddush* or *havdalah* accordingly, but *melacha* is prohibited until Shabbos actually ends at nightfall, and Shabbos does not begin (in the sense of the *melacha* prohibition) until sunset — or, for those who accept *tosefet shabbos*, from the moment one explicitly accepts it upon oneself.

---

## Maariv Obligation

### No Fixed Time

The *gemara* now takes up the *mishna*'s statement: *tefilat ha'erev ein lah keva* — the evening prayer has no fixed time.

### Reshut Status

The *gemara* asks: what does *ein lah keva* mean? If it means one may *daven* the entire night — *kol halaila* — then the *mishna* should simply say so. The additional phrase, *ein lah keva*, implies something more: it signals that the evening prayer has a *reshut* character, that it is in some sense optional rather than obligatory.

### Gamliel vs Yehoshua

Rav Yehudah says in the name of Shmuel: *tefilat arvit* — Rabban Gamliel says it is a *chova*, an obligation; Rabbi Yehoshua says it is a *reshut*.

### Abaye vs Rava

Among the *amoraim*: Abaye rules *halacha kedivrei ha'omer chova*, like the one who says it is an obligation. Rava rules *halacha kedivrei ha'omer reshut*, like the one who says it is optional — though with significant qualification, as discussed below.

### Tosafot Reading

*Tosafot* argues that *tefilat arvit reshut* does not mean absolutely optional — that one simply need not *daven* if one does not feel like it. Rather, *reshut* here means that relative to other *halachic* obligations, *maariv* can be set aside in certain circumstances. It is an obligation, but one with a lower priority that can be overridden by competing obligations. This is how *tosafot* understands *reshut* in this context, and it is sometimes how *tosafot* uses the term elsewhere in the *gemara* as well.

### Rambam's Position

The *rambam* and others read the history differently: *tefilat arvit* began as a genuine *reshut* — a voluntary practice — but was then accepted by the community as an obligation through universal practice. This raises the question of whether the original *reshut* status retains any practical relevance now that the community has accepted it as *chova*, but this is not a question the *gemara* resolves here.

Whatever the precise meaning, it is clear from the *gemara* that *maariv* is treated as an obligation in all of the preceding discussions — every analysis of whether one is *yotzei* if one *daven*s early, whether one must *daven* twice *shacharit* to make up a missed *maariv*, all of these assume a binding obligation.

---

## Student Inquiry

### First Question

The *gemara* now brings a *baraita*: *maaseh be'talmid echad she'ba lifnei Rabbi Yehoshua* — a certain student came before Rabbi Yehoshua and asked: *tefilat arvit reshut o chova* — is the evening prayer *reshut* or *chova*?

### Yehoshua's Answer

Rabbi Yehoshua answered: *reshut* — it is optional.

### Second Question

The student then went and posed the same question to Rabban Gamliel. The act of seeking a second opinion after having already received a ruling is itself not necessarily problematic; one might genuinely wish to hear multiple perspectives on a contested issue.

### Gamliel's Answer

Rabban Gamliel answered: *chova* — it is an obligation.

### Contradiction Exposed

The student then said to Rabban Gamliel: but Rabbi Yehoshua told me it is *reshut*. At that point Rabban Gamliel said: wait — *hamten* — until the *ba'alei terisin*, the shield-bearers, the *talmidim*, enter the *beit hamidrash*. The image is deliberately militaristic: *torah* study as combat, scholars as warriors. Wait until everyone is assembled, and then you will see.

### Public Testimony

When all had entered, the student rose publicly and asked the question again. Rabban Gamliel immediately declared: *chova*. Then he turned to the assembled *chachamim*: *klum yesh adam shecholek badavar zeh* — does anyone disagree? In the very framing of the question, Rabban Gamliel has already expressed his opinion first — before the other voices have a chance to speak — and has made any dissent effectively impossible. Rabbi Yehoshua was cornered: *amar lei Rabban Gamliel — velo mishmacha amru li reshut?* And did I not hear that you said it was *reshut*? The order was then issued: *Yehoshua, amod al raglecha* — stand on your feet, and let people testify against you publicly.

---

## Yehoshua's Shaming

### Standing Punishment

Rabbi Yehoshua stood on his feet. And Rabban Gamliel continued to sit and expound — to lead the *shiur* — while Rabbi Yehoshua was made to stand throughout.

### People Protest

The assembled *talmidim* began to murmur. They told Chutzpit the *torgeman* — the one who served as the voice, the amplifier of the teaching — to stop. They effectively turned off Rabban Gamliel's mic. (The term *amod*, "stop," is the same word used when Rabbi Yehoshua was told to stand — a striking verbal parallel noted by the students themselves.)

### Affliction Complaint

Their complaint: *ad kama nitztar ve'neizil* — how long will Rabban Gamliel go on afflicting us? What kind of culture is this?

### Prior Incidents

They recalled prior incidents. In *Rosh Hashana* the previous year, there had been a famous dispute over the testimony for the new moon. Rabban Gamliel ruled that the testimony was valid and asserted his calendar against Rabbi Yehoshua's calculation. To enforce his authority, Rabban Gamliel required Rabbi Yehoshua to appear before him on what Rabbi Yehoshua believed was his *Yom Kippur* — with his staff and his money — compelling him to violate his own *Yom Kippur* as an act of submission to Rabban Gamliel's authority. The story appears in *Masechet Rosh Hashana*. Similarly, the case involving *bechorot* — which appears in *Masechet Bechorot* — involved another incident where Rabban Gamliel turned on Rabbi Yehoshua: *amod al raglecha*, stand on your feet.

### Other Cases

The references to *Rosh Hashana* and *bechorot* may refer both to the subject matter of those disputes and to the *masechtot* in which the stories appear.

### Removal Decision

The students reached a decision: Rabban Gamliel must be removed. *Ta ve'na'avreih* — let us go and depose him. The question then was: who should replace him?

---

## New Leadership

### Yehoshua Rejected

The proposal to appoint Rabbi Yehoshua was rejected: *ba'al ma'aseh hu* — he is a party to the dispute. To place Rabbi Yehoshua in Rabban Gamliel's position would be too partisan, and Rashi adds that it would inflict too great a pain on Rabban Gamliel himself.

### Akiva Rejected

Rabbi Akiva was proposed — a figure of immense *talmudic* stature — but also rejected. The concern: *dilma anish leh de'leit leh zechut avot* — perhaps Rabban Gamliel, still wielding political power as the *nasi*, would move against Rabbi Akiva, who lacked *yichus*, the family pedigree and genealogical protection that comes with descent from powerful houses. Rashi explains this very practically: Rabban Gamliel, descended from the patriarchal house of *Hillel*, had connections and authority that he could deploy against someone without comparable lineage. Rabbi Akiva's later marriage into wealth was real, but it did not provide the same protection as illustrious ancestry.

### Elazar Chosen

The choice fell on Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah. He was *chacham* — wise. He was *ashir* — wealthy, which matters in terms of practical power and the ability to sustain political obligations, including financial dealings with the house of Caesar. And he was *asiri le'Ezra* — the tenth generation from Ezra, granting him *yichus* that Rabban Gamliel could not easily assail. Ezra is a particularly resonant model: he was both *Ezra ha-sofer*, the *rabbinic* archetype as it were, and a political leader — a dual identity that mirrors the role of the *nasi* itself.

### Qualifications

The qualifications were thus: wisdom sufficient to answer any *Torah* challenge, wealth sufficient to engage the imperial court, and ancestral merit sufficient to protect him from retribution. *De'i makish leh mefarek leh* — if challenged on his Torah knowledge, he could handle it.

### Wife's Advice

Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah went and consulted his wife. She cautioned him: *sofam ma'avirin lach* — eventually they will depose you. Things will settle down, and your tenure will be temporary.

### One Day Worth It

Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah responded with a well-known saying: *lishamesh inish yoma chad bekassa demokre ulemachar lispari* — let a person use a beautiful glass for even one day, even if it breaks the next. The honor of the position, even if fleeting, is worth it. With that, he accepted.

---

## White Hair Miracle

### Youth Problem

Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah was eighteen years old at the time. For someone so young to assume authority over a *beit midrash* of *talmidei chachamim*, he would need to project an appearance of age and gravitas. His wife had already noted this: *leis lach chivvusa* — you don't have white hair.

### Eighteen Rows

A miracle occurred: *isracheish lei nissa ve'hadru lei tamsrei darei chivvusa* — and eighteen rows of white hair appeared on his head.

### Seventy-Year-Old

This is the background for the famous phrase cited from a *mishna* earlier in this *masechet*: *harei ani keven shiv'im shana*, "I am like a man of seventy years" — not *ben shiv'im*, not actually seventy, but *keven shiv'im*, like seventy. He was not actually seventy; he simply looked that old due to the miraculous appearance of the white hair.

### Open Doors

On the day Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah took office, *silkuhu leshomeir hapetach* — they removed the guard who stood at the door of the *beit hamidrash*. The door was thrown open.

### Gamliel's Policy

Under Rabban Gamliel, a strict admissions policy had been in force: *kol talmid she'ein tocho kevaro lo yikaneis leveit hamidrash* — any student whose inside does not match his outside, who is not as sincere as he appears, may not enter the *beit hamidrash*. This was not purely about power — there was also a genuine concern for authenticity, for ensuring that only truly sincere students filled the study hall. But the effect was exclusivity, and the policy was in Rabban Gamliel's hands to define and enforce.

### Benches Added

On the day of the change, many rows of benches were added. A dispute is cited in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: Abba Yosef ben Dosai and the *rabbanan* disagreed — one says 400 rows were added, the other says 700. The numbers may be somewhat exaggerated, but the point is the dramatic expansion of the study hall.

---

## Gamliel's Despair

### Torah Prevented

Rabban Gamliel became troubled. He thought: *dilma chas veshalom maniyati Torah miYisrael* — perhaps, God forbid, my policy held back Torah from Israel. If the *beit hamidrash* could accommodate hundreds more students than had ever been admitted under his watch, then he had been preventing the spread of Torah all along.

### Dream Vision

In a dream, he was shown white casks filled with black ash — vessels that appeared pure and clean on the outside but were filled with worthless refuse on the inside. This vision seemed to validate his original policy: see, the students he had been keeping out were indeed hollow — their exteriors promising but their interiors empty.

### Dream Consolation

The *gemara* immediately corrects this reading: *v'lo hi* — it was not so. The dream was sent *leyituvei da'atei* — to give him comfort, to make him feel better. It was not the truth.
