To engage with *halacha* immediately before *tefillah* is to make a statement that one's life is directed by God's law, that the details of one's conduct are governed by divine concern. That framing — of a life lived under halachic discipline and purpose — is precisely the right disposition from which to approach God in prayer. It is not merely that one's mind is focused; it is that one presents oneself before God as someone engaged in purposeful, God-directed service. One student's formulation captures this well: when the connection between *halacha* study and *tefillah* is made explicit, one's learning becomes integrated into one's sense of divine service rather than remaining a separate intellectual exercise. The *tefillah* is then not an interruption of learning but its natural culmination.

It is worth noting a contemporary parallel: in the *siddur*, after *birkat haTorah*, there is the custom of reciting a passage of Torah. The prayer most commonly associated with preparation for *shmoneh esrei* at *mincha* — where the structure allows for something to be inserted before *shmoneh esrei*, unlike *shacharis* and *ma'ariv* which are fixed around *geulah* and *tefillah* — is *ashrei*. *Ashrei yoshvei veitekha* is perhaps more an embodiment of the spirit of the *mishna*'s *koved rosh* than of *halacha pesuka* strictly speaking, but the practice points to the same underlying concern: one does not simply walk into *shmoneh esrei* cold.

---

## Forbidden States

### Negative States List

The *baraita* continues with an expanded list: *ein omdin lehitpallel lo mitoch atzvut* — one does not stand to *daven* from sadness, *velo mitoch atzlut* — nor from laziness, *velo mitoch sechok* — nor from having just been engaged in excessive laughter, *velo mitoch sicha* — nor from idle conversation, *velo mitoch kalut rosh* — nor from levity, *velo mitoch dvarim betelim* — nor from frivolous talk. Many of these overlap with what came before; together they paint a picture of the mental states that are incompatible with *tefillah*.

### Simcha Shel Mitzvah

The positive counterpart: *ela mitoch simcha shel mitzvah* — one should stand from a joy of *mitzvah*. This is striking, and seemingly in some tension with the emphasis on awe, trembling, and *koved rosh* that has dominated the discussion until now. The *baraita* here introduces a different register: not awe and weight, but joy.

### Rashi's Reading

Rashi elaborates: *simcha shel mitzvah* means *divrei tanchumim shel Torah*, words of consolation and encouragement from Torah. He offers examples: passages adjacent in the *davening* to redemption themes, such as *ratzon yerei'av ya'aseh*, or *lo yitosh Hashem amo*. The point is that one approaches *tefillah* from a state of joy in one's relationship with God, in the awareness of God's care and presence. *Mitzvah* in this context does not refer to performing an act but to this joyful orientation toward divine closeness. This is a markedly different framing from the *halacha pesuka* of the *baraita* — which may speak more specifically to the *rabbinic* class — and a different framing from the *koved rosh* of the *mishna*. These are not so much competing requirements as they are different valid orientations, available to different people or in different circumstances.

### Parting from Friends

A parallel principle is offered: *vechen lo yipater adam mechaveiro lo mitoch sicha velo mitoch sechok velo mitoch kalut rosh velo mitoch dvarim betelim, ela mitoch dvar halacha*. When parting from a friend, one should not conclude the encounter with idle talk, laughter, or levity. The parting should involve a *dvar halacha*. The *Hagra* notes that the text is in tension here: we have just spoken of *simcha shel mitzvah* as the positive frame, and now we return to *dvar halacha*. He therefore marks the textual point and suggests making the two consistent — reading *dvar halacha* here as aligned with *simcha shel mitzvah*. Whether or not one accepts that textual emendation, the underlying tension points to the same two orientations that appeared in the context of prayer: the frame of halachic engagement, and the frame of joyful connection to God.

The *gemara* grounds this in a broader observation: *shechen matzinu binevi'im harishonim shesiyimu divreihem bedivrei shevach vetanchumim* — the early prophets, with one or two notable exceptions such as Yirmiyahu, concluded their prophecies on a positive note regarding Israel's relationship with God. *Simcha shel mitzvah* in this context means ending on a note that expresses the joy of that divine relationship, a kind of *berakhah* of closeness with God.

### Devar Torah Custom

The *gemara* provides a practical illustration: Rav Kahana accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi all the way from Pumna to Beit Tzanisa in Bavel. Upon arriving, Rav Kahana remarked that the palm trees of Beit Tzanisa must be so ancient they date back to *Adam haRishon*. Rav Shimi responded: *adkartan milta d'Rabbi Yose bar Chanina* — you have reminded me of a teaching of Rabbi Yose bar Chanina. Rabbi Yose bar Chanina had expounded the verse *b'eretz asher lo avar bah ish v'lo yashav adam sham* — a land that no person has passed through and no *adam* has dwelt in — by asking: if no one ever passed through, how could anyone have dwelt? The verse must be using *adam* in the sense of *Adam haRishon*, teaching that any land *Adam haRishon* designated for settlement was settled, and any he did not designate was not — which is why Beit Tzanisa retained its ancient palm trees to this day.

Rav Mordechai similarly accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi from Hagronia to Bei Kifi, or some say to Bei Dura. The point in both cases is the custom of accompanying departing guests — a practice with its own halachic context — and of concluding the encounter with words of Torah. The category of *dvar halacha* proves fairly elastic here: what Rav Shimi offers is a piece of rabbinic *aggadah* and textual interpretation, not a practical ruling. This suggests that *dvar halacha* in this context means broadly any substantive Torah teaching. The frame is what matters: that the parting be shaped by Torah rather than by mere small talk. In the world of the *rabbanim*, the natural way to frame a relationship — both in parting and in approaching *tefillah* — is through the medium of Torah. For those outside that world, or in different contexts, *simcha shel mitzvah*, an expression of the joyful relationship with God, serves the same function.

---

## Kavana Requirement

### Heart to Heaven

The *gemara* now focuses directly on *kavanah*. *Hamispallel tzarich sheyachavein libo lashamayim* — one who prays must direct one's heart to Heaven. *Abba Shaul* frames this as a reciprocal relationship: if one prepares and directs one's heart, God's ears will be attentive. This is the core challenge of *tefillah* as the *gemara* understands it, and it is a formidable one. *Tefillah* is not merely the recitation of words; it is communication, the expression of one's inner state. How does one legislate *kavanah*? The tension between fixed prayer and personal prayer — between the communal structure inherited as *tefillot keneged korbanot* and the deeply interior act of turning one's heart to God — has run through the entire discussion of these chapters, and it is this tension that the present *mishna* now addresses head-on.

### Rabbi Akiva's Practice

The *gemara* cites the practice of Rabbi Akiva: *keshehaya mispalel im hatzibur, haya mekatzeir veoleh mipnei torech tzibur* — when he prayed with the congregation, he would shorten his prayer out of consideration for the burden it places on the *tzibur* to wait. But *keshehaya mispalel beino levein atzmo*, when he prayed in private, one might leave him in one corner of the room and return to find him in the other corner — *mipnei kri'os vehishtachavayos*, because of his extensive bowing and swaying, his physical movement in prayer carrying him bodily across the room. Some scholars have suggested that Rabbi Akiva's mystical and kabbalistic orientation may have contributed to a near-rapturous state during private prayer, beyond simple *shokeling*. Whether or not that is the case, the contrast is unmistakable.

### Communal vs. Private

The contrast between Rabbi Akiva's communal and private prayer raises a fundamental question. One explanation is straightforward: there is a *bein adam lachaveiro* dimension to communal prayer — one cannot indulge one's own *kavanah* if doing so burdens the community that is waiting. But the *gemara* may be pointing at something deeper: communal prayer and private prayer exist in different registers. In communal prayer, one participates in a collective act, analogous in its way to the *korban tzibur*, and the communal experience takes precedence over the individual's subjective intensity. In private prayer, by contrast, the full weight of personal *kavanah* can be given free expression.

This surfaces a question that is genuinely unresolved in halachic literature: should one prefer praying with a *minyan* at the cost of some *kavanah*, or praying in private with fuller attention? The *poskim* generally favor communal prayer, emphasizing the external structure of *tefillah betzibur* — in part because *halacha* is better equipped to address and evaluate external forms than internal states, which cannot be quantified or measured. Yet the *gemara*'s presentation of Rabbi Akiva suggests that the private, interior dimension of *tefillah* is equally legitimate and in some respects more demanding. One might also add that the prohibition against audibly vocalizing one's prayer in a way that could distract others in the congregation points to the same tension: when in the *tzibur*, one reins in the more expressive dimensions of prayer for the sake of the communal experience. When praying *beyechidus*, no such restraint is needed.

---

## Tanakh Models

### Windows in Prayer

Rabbi Abba teaches: *le'olam yitpallel adam bevayit sheyesh bo chalonot* — a person should always pray in a house that has windows. The proof is from Daniel, who prayed opposite open windows. There is something to be said for this experientially: the sense of connectedness to the natural world — to sky, light, and the broader creation — can open the person who prays to a sense of divine presence that can be harder to access in an entirely enclosed, artificial setting. The *gemara*'s instruction to pray opposite a window points to this dimension of *kavanah* through the orientation of the body and the eyes toward an opening to the world.

### Three Times Daily

Perhaps one should pray throughout the entire day? The *gemara* answers: it is already made explicit by Daniel — *vezimnin telata*, three times daily. Notably, the proof is drawn from Daniel and not from the sacrificial calendar. The entire framework here is of prayer as a human act of turning toward God, not as a stand-in for *korbanot*. Three fixed times suffice; they divide and mark the day as oriented toward God.

### Toward Jerusalem

Perhaps one may pray in any direction? The *gemara* answers: one prays *neged Yerushalayim*, toward Jerusalem. Whether this is because Jerusalem is the site of the *Shekhinah* or because it connects to the *korbanot* of the *Beit Hamikdash* is left open. But the thrust of the entire *sugya* — which has consistently cited human models of prayer (Daniel, Chana, David) without invoking sacrificial language — suggests that the orientation toward Jerusalem is about the *Shekhinah* and the locus of divine presence rather than about the sacrificial service.

### Silent Prayer

Perhaps one's voice should be audible during prayer? The *gemara* answers from Chana: *vekola lo yishama* — her voice was not heard. The model of silent, inward prayer is thus established from Chana, who will emerge throughout these *sugyot* as the paradigmatic figure for the laws of *tefillah*.

### Personal Requests

The *gemara* asks one final question: perhaps personal petitions should come *before* prayer? The answer comes from Shlomo: the verse places *rinah* — understood as *tefillah* in the sense of *shevach*, praise — before *tefillah* in the sense of *bakashah*, petition. The praise comes first, the petition follows. Fascinatingly, the word *tefillah* in the verse is mapped onto *bakashah*, while *rinah* is mapped onto the *shevach* dimension — an implicit acknowledgment that *tefillah* in common usage means petition, even as the structural priority of praise is maintained.

The *gemara* concludes with a practical clarification: one does not interrupt between *emet veyatziv* and *shmoneh esrei* — *geulah* must flow into *tefillah*. But after *shmoneh esrei*, one may extend as long as one wishes, even as long as the *vidui* of *Yom Kippur*. And Rav Yitzchak bar Ashi adds in the name of Rav: *af yishal adam tzerakhav beshome'a tefillah* — one may also insert personal requests within *shmoneh esrei* itself, in the blessing of *shome'a tefillah*. Thus the balance between fixed structure and personal expression is preserved at multiple levels: brief insertions within the body of *shmoneh esrei* in *shome'a tefillah*, and unlimited personal prayer after the conclusion of *shmoneh esrei* before *oker raglav*. The *gemara* continues with the model of Chana, whose prayers will provide the ground for many further laws of *tefillah*.

---

---

# Berakhot 31b

## Hannah's Prayer

### Kavana from Heart

The Gemara on 31b opens with a statement of Rav Hamnuna: *kama hilchata givarvata ika le-mishma me-hanei karei de-Channah* — how many powerful *halachot* can be inferred from the verses describing Hannah's prayer? The passage builds on the immediately preceding discussion of *kavana* in prayer, including the striking Gemara about Rabbi Akiva and the difference between how he would sway (*shokel*) when praying privately versus in the *tzibbur*. That contrast reflects two concerns simultaneously: sensitivity to others in communal prayer, and the deeper *kavana* that belongs to individual prayer. The verses of Hannah now serve as the primary model for exploring that individual dimension.

The first inference is from the phrase *ve-Channah hi medaberet al libah* — Hannah was speaking from her heart. The Gemara reads this not merely as a description of her sincerity but as a normative requirement: *mikan le-mitpallel tzarich she-yekaven libo* — from here we learn that one who prays must direct his heart. Prayer is not simply the recitation of words; it demands genuine inward engagement with what one is saying.

### Lips Moving Silently

From *rak sefateha na'ot* — only her lips were moving — the Gemara derives *mikan le-mitpallel she-yachtoch bi-sfatav*: one must articulate with the lips, literally "cut" with them. This is a fascinating halachic balance. Normally, *halacha* requires speech to be audible — we encountered a lengthy discussion earlier in Berakhot regarding one who cannot hear his own recitation of *Shema*. Here, the rule is precisely the opposite: lips move, but the voice is not heard. Some *acharonim* raise the question of whether, given that *tefillah* is fundamentally *avodah she-ba-lev* — service of the heart — it might suffice to merely think the words. The general consensus is that it does not suffice, though there is a position (*tzad*) that *tefillah* constitutes a kind of silent speech, distinct from ordinary vocalization.

### No Raised Voice

From *ve-kolah lo yishama* — her voice could not be heard — comes the ruling *she-asur le-hagbi'ah kolo bi-tfilato*: it is forbidden to raise one's voice in prayer. The model of *tefillah* is thus a silent articulation — lips moving without audible sound.

### Drunk Cannot Pray

*Vayachsheveha Eli le-shikorah* — Eli presumed Hannah to be drunk. From this, the Gemara derives *she-shikor asur le-hitpallel*: an intoxicated person may not pray. Even if one might argue that minimal *kavana* could allow for *yetzia*, the fundamental problem is one of standing before God — a drunken person cannot do so appropriately. The identification of drunken prayer with *avodah zarah* is later derived from Hannah's own words: *al titein et amatecha lifnei bat beliyaal*. The Gemara reads *beliyaal* through a *gezerah shavah* with a verse in which people of *beliyaal* led a city to worship false gods. The connection may rest on the disrespect shown to God by appearing before Him in such a state, and perhaps also on the fact that certain forms of idolatrous worship historically involved intoxication and artificially induced religious frenzy.

### Duty to Rebuke

Eli's reproof of Hannah — *Ad matai tistakarin*, how long will you remain drunk? — becomes the source for another ruling. Rabbi Elazar derives: *mikan le-ro'eh be-chavero davar meguneh, tzarich le-hochiho* — if one sees another engaged in behavior that is unseemly, one is obligated to rebuke them. Tosafot makes explicit that the obligation applies even where no formal *issur* has been violated; inappropriate conduct alone is sufficient to warrant a loving correction.

### Judge Favorably

The Gemara then addresses Hannah's response. She says *lo Adoni* — no, my master. The phrase is interpreted in two ways. According to one tradition (attributed to Ulla, and some say Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Hanina), she was saying: *lo adon atta ba-davar hazeh* — you are not the master here, you do not understand what is happening. *Ve-lo Ruach HaKodesh shorah alecha* — the divine spirit was not resting upon you, because you have suspected me of this impropriety.

A second version reads Hannah as saying: *lav ika Shekhinah ve-Ruach HaKodesh gavach* — the divine presence was not with you, *she-dantani le-chaf chovah ve-lo dantani le-chaf zechut* — for you judged me by tipping the balance of guilt, rather than the balance of merit. When one sees another person act in a manner that appears problematic, the obligation is to tip those scales toward merit — *le-chaf zechut* — to assume that the behavior is proper rather than improper.

There is a striking *hagah* worth noting here: how could Eli, a *kohen gadol* equipped with the *urim ve-tumim*, have made such an error? One answer (attributed to the Vilna Gaon) is that the *urim ve-tumim* worked by having the letters of the tribal names rise before the *kohen*, and that the letters *shin, chaf, resh, heh* — which together spell *shikorah* (drunk) — appeared to Eli, when in fact the divine message was *kesherah* (upright), that she was like *Sarah*, barren and praying. This is admittedly a *vort* rather than *pshat*, but it is a beautiful one.

From Hannah's own correction of Eli — *yayin ve-shechar lo shatiti* — Rabbi Elazar derives a further obligation: *mikan le-nechshad be-davar she-ein bo, she-tzarich lehodio* — one who has been wrongly suspected must inform the person who suspected them. One must not allow false impressions to persist unchallenged.

### Appease Wrongly Accused

When Eli recognized his error and said *lechi le-shalom* — go in peace — Rabbi Elazar derives yet another obligation: *mikan le-choshed et chaveiro be-davar she-ein bo, she-tzarich le-fayeso* — one who has wrongly suspected another must appease that person and make peace with them.

### Bless the Wronged

*Ve-lo od* — and not only that — *ela she-tzarich le-varcho*: one must go further and offer a blessing to the person wrongly accused. For Eli did not merely send Hannah away in peace; he blessed her: *ve-Elohei Yisrael yitein et she'elatecha* — may the God of Israel grant your request.

It is worth noting that while this entire passage is introduced as deriving *halachot* of *tefillah*, most of what has been extracted here concerns interpersonal obligations — the duty to rebuke, to judge favorably, to correct false impressions, to seek appeasement, and to bless the wronged. Only one or two of the *halachot* directly concern the laws of prayer itself.

---

## Hannah's Bold Praye (III)

### Tzevaot Divine Name

The passage continues: *va-tidor neder va-tomar — Hashem Tzevaot*. Rabbi Elazar observes that from the day God created the world, no one had ever invoked the divine name *Tzevaot* — the Lord of Hosts — until Hannah did so. *Tzevaot* derives from *tzava*, meaning army or host, evoking the heavenly legions. Hannah chose this name deliberately. As the Gemara explains, she said before God: *Ribbono shel Olam, mikol tzevaei tzevaot she-barata be-olamecha, kashe be-einecha she-titein li bein echad?* — Master of the Universe, with all the hosts of hosts, all the galaxies and universes You have created, is it so difficult for You to give me one son?

---

## Aggressive Prayer

### Poor Man Parable

The Gemara offers a *mashal* to illuminate Hannah's posture: a human king made a feast for his servants, and a poor person stood at the doorway asking for a scrap of bread. When the servants ignored him, he forced his way in to the king himself and said: *Adoni ha-Melech, kol se'udah she-asita, kashe be-einecha liten li prusah achat?* — My master the king, with this entire lavish feast you have prepared, you cannot give me one piece of bread? The parallel to Hannah's prayer is clear: she forced her way, as it were, to the King Himself, bypassing every intermediary, to demand what should have been a simple request. As was noted, the image of forcing one's way into the king's presence echoes the broader theme of aggressive, insistent prayer running through this entire passage.

### Conditional Threat

The Gemara then addresses the phrase *im ra'oh tireh* — if You will see. Rabbi Elazar explains that Hannah was in effect issuing a conditional threat: *im ra'oh* — if You see my affliction, *mutav* — good; but *ve-im lav* — if not — *estater bifnei Elkanah ba'ali* — I will seclude myself with another man in the presence of my husband Elkanah. Once I have done so, he will bring me through the *sotah* process, and I will drink the *mei sotah*. And then — *ve-i atah oseh Toratecha palaster* — You will not be able to make Your Torah into a falsehood. The word *palaster* is of Greek origin; Steinsaltz notes that it derives from the Greek *plastos*, meaning a molder, and is used metaphorically to mean false or counterfeit.

The force of the argument rests on the verse *ve-niktah ve-nizre'ah zara* — she will be cleansed and she will conceive. If a woman suspected of adultery is innocent and drinks the waters, she will bear children.

### Sotah Waters Debate

The Gemara immediately qualifies this: the argument only works according to the opinion that the *sotah* waters cause a barren woman to become fertile — *im hayta akara, nifkedet*. This is the position of Rabbi Yishmael, who derives it from *ve-niktah ve-nizre'ah zara*.

Rabbi Akiva objects: if this were the effect, all barren women would arrange to be secluded before their husbands and go through this process in order to conceive. He argues instead that the verse refers to improvements in the quality of childbearing: a woman who had given birth with pain would now do so with ease, one who had borne girls would now bear boys, one who had borne dark-complexioned children would bear fair-complexioned ones, one who had borne short children would bear tall ones, one who had borne only one at a time would have multiple births. These benefits, while real, are apparently not so attractive as to motivate widespread manipulation of the *sotah* procedure.

According to Rabbi Akiva, then, Hannah could not have been threatening to force God's hand into making a barren woman conceive through this mechanism. How is the double language of *ra'oh tireh* explained? The Gemara answers: *dibrah Torah ki-leshon bnei adam* — the Torah simply speaks in the manner of ordinary human expression. The doubling is not to be over-interpreted.

---

## Hannah's Bold Praye (III)

### Three Women's Mitzvot

The Gemara continues with the three occurrences of the word *amatcha* — your maidservant — in Hannah's prayer. Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina asks why this word appears three times. He explains that Hannah was invoking them as a response to the three *bidkei mita*, or *difkei mita*, that God created for a woman — three obligations whose violation, according to the *Mishnah* in *Bameh Madlikin*, can bring death in childbirth: *niddah*, *challah*, and *hadlakat ha-ner*, the kindling of the Shabbat candle.

These three *mitzvot* correspond in a meaningful way to the domestic sphere of a woman's life: *challah* to the preparation of food, *hadlakat ha-ner* to the light of the home, and *niddah* to the most intimate dimensions of married life. Hannah's point was: *klum avarti al achat mehen* — I have not transgressed any one of these obligations. I have fulfilled all my *mitzvot*. Now give me what I am asking for.

The Gemara then addresses the phrase *ve-natata le-amatcha zera anashim* — You shall give Your maidservant a seed of men. What is meant by *zera anashim*? Several interpretations are offered. Rav understands it as *gavra be-govrin* — a man among men, a person who stands out among others, an outstanding individual, as Rashi explains. Shmuel interprets it as *zera she-mosheach shnei anashim* — seed that will anoint two men — namely Shaul and David, whom her son Samuel would anoint as kings of Israel. Rabbi Yochanan interprets it as *zera she-shakul ke-shnei anashim* — seed that is equivalent in stature to two great people — namely Moses and Aaron, as the verse places Samuel alongside them: *Moshe ve-Aharon be-chohanav u-Shmuel be-korei shemo*.

By contrast, the anonymous *rabanan* offer the interpretation *zera she-muvla bein anashim* — seed that is absorbed among people, that does not stand out. Rav Dimi elaborates: *lo aroch ve-lo gutz* — not too tall and not too short; *ve-lo katan ve-lo ilem* — not too thin and not too fat; *ve-lo tzachor ve-lo gichor* — not too fair-skinned and not too dark; *ve-lo chacham ve-lo tipesh* — not too clever and not too dim-witted. In other words, completely average.

This is striking on multiple levels. It is worth observing that the interpreters who settled on "average" were the anonymous *rabanan* — perhaps, as one might suggest, those who were themselves not so outstanding. But more poignantly, Rashi suggests the motivation was to avoid *ayin hara* — that a child too exceptional in every respect would draw the evil eye. There is also the simpler reading: Hannah was saying she was not asking for anything extraordinary. She did not need a prodigy or a great man. She simply wanted a child, any child. That reading carries its own quiet power.

---

## Samuel & Paskening

### Four Cubits Law

When Hannah returned the following year with the child, she said to Eli: *ani ha-isha ha-nitzevet imcha bazeh* — I am the woman who stood here with you at this place. From this, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives: *mikan she-asur leshev be-toch arba amot shel tefillah* — it is forbidden to sit within four *amot* of a person who is praying. Since Hannah said she was *standing* with Eli, Eli must have been standing as well — which means one cannot sit within the four *amot* of a person in prayer.

Tosafot adds that the word *imcha* is written *malei*, spelled with the letter *heh*: *ayin, mem, chaf, heh*. The *heh* hints that one may sit in the fifth *amah*, but not within the first four. Tosafot also cites the *teshuvot* of the *Geonim* to the effect that the prohibition specifically applies when one is sitting *u-vatel* — sitting idly, doing nothing. If, however, one is engaged in *Kriat Shema* or other *tefillah*, that suffices. This is a meaningful distinction: the concern is not merely that one's sitting will distract the person praying, but that it is inappropriate to be idle in a shared space where prayer is occurring. If you are participating — even in a lesser form of *tefillah* — that resolves the impropriety. The practical implication is relevant to crowded *batei kenesiot*: someone sitting during the *chazzan*'s repetition (*Chazarat HaShatz*) and listening attentively would not violate this prohibition.

### Samuel Paskens

The Gemara proceeds to an astonishing *aggadta*. Rabbi Elazar states: *Shmuel moreh halacha lifnei rabbo hayah* — Samuel had actually ruled on a halachic matter in the presence of his teacher Eli, which as we know is always a grave transgression. Indeed, one Gemara identifies this — ruling in the presence of one's master — as the sin of Nadav and Avihu, for which they were struck dead.

How is this known? The verse states: *vayishchatu et ha-par vayavi'u et ha-na'ar el Eli* — they slaughtered the ox and brought the boy to Eli. What is the connection between those two events? Eli must have been looking for a *kohen* to perform the *shechitah* of the ox brought as a sacrifice. Young Samuel — who was perhaps three or five years old at the time — observed them searching and said: *lamah lachem le-hadurei batar kohen le-mishchat? Shechitah be-zar kesherah* — why do you need to search for a *kohen* to slaughter? A non-*kohen* (*zar*) may perform *shechitah* for a *korban*.

When Samuel was brought before Eli, Eli asked him: *mina lach ha* — from where do you know this? Samuel replied: *mi ketiv ve-shachat ha-kohen?* — Does the verse in *Vayikra* say "and the *kohen* shall slaughter"? It does not. It says *ve-hikrivu ha-kohanim* — the *kohanim* shall bring, referring to the reception of the blood and what follows from that point. The obligation of *kehunah* begins with *kabbalah*, the receiving of the blood. From the point of *shechitah* and before, the act is valid even when performed by a non-*kohen*.

Eli conceded: *meimar shapir kamart* — you have spoken correctly. But he added: *mihu moreh halacha bifnei ravcha* — nevertheless, you have ruled on a matter of *halacha* in the presence of your teacher. *Ve-chol ha-moreh halacha bifnei rabbo chayav mita* — anyone who rules in such a fashion deserves death.

Tosafot raises a natural question: how was Eli already Samuel's *Rebbe* at this moment, since this was the first time Samuel was being brought to him? Tosafot answers that Eli was the *gadol ha-dor*, and since Samuel was coming to study under him, Eli already had the status of his *Rebbe* — and that status carried its obligations from the outset, regardless of how young the student happened to be.

### Not Replaceable

Hannah came before Eli weeping, and Eli said to her: *shivki li d'aktlei* — let me invoke divine punishment upon him, and *u-veina rachamei* — I will pray, and *v-yahiv lach raba minei* — God will give you a greater son in his place.

Hannah replied: *el ha-na'ar ha-zeh hitpalalti* — I prayed for *this* child. Do not speak to me of a replacement. The emphasis on *hazeh* — this one — carries a *derasha*: she was not asking for any child in general, but for this particular child. There is a resonance here with the earlier interpretation of *zera anashim* as meaning simply a child — not a superstar, just a child. And now she says: not even a better child. This one. The one she prayed for. Somehow Samuel survived the episode, though the text does not spell out exactly how he escaped punishment.

This entire narrative foreshadows the story immediately following in the *pesukim*, in which the young Samuel hears God's voice in the sanctuary while Eli does not — a story in which Samuel begins to eclipse his master. It is not difficult to sense that dimension in the background here as well.

---

## Hannah's Bold Praye (III)r…

### Body's Purpose

Returning to the verse *va-Channah hi medaberet al libah*, Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra explains: *al iskei libah* — regarding matters of her heart. And what were those matters? Hannah said to God: *Ribbono shel Olam, kol mah she-barata be-isha lo barata davar echad le-vatalah* — Master of the Universe, everything You created in a woman, You did not create in vain. *Einayim lirot* — eyes to see; *oznayim lishmoa* — ears to hear; *chotem le-hariach* — a nose to smell; *peh le-daber* — a mouth to speak; *yadayim la'asot bahem melachah* — hands to perform labor; *raglayim le-halech bahem* — feet to walk. And *dadim le-hanik bahem* — breasts with which to nurse a child. *Dadim elalu she-natata al libi* — these breasts You have placed on my heart, as the verse says *al libah*. *Lamah?* — Why? *Lo le-hanik bahem?* — Is it not to nurse a child? *Ten li bein ve-anik bahem* — give me a son so that I may nurse from them.

The argument is at once halachic in its structure and deeply human in its content. Hannah is pointing to her own body as evidence of God's unfulfilled purpose. You created me in a way that assumes motherhood; every aspect of a woman's body — including this — was made for a reason. If you gave me the equipment, give me the capacity to use it. It is, as noted, a profoundly poignant image: not merely the pain of barrenness in the abstract, but the specific ache of a body created for something it cannot do.

A digression follows, connected by the name Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra: anyone who observes a fast on Shabbat — which is understood to mean a *ta'anit chalom*, a fast for a disturbing dream, which must be observed immediately even if it falls on Shabbat — *kora'in lo gzar dino shel shiv'im shanah* — even a decree of seventy years' standing will be torn up. Rashi explains that this decree is one that may have been issued from one's youth. The difficulty of fasting on Shabbat, when everyone else is enjoying food and festivity, gives the act its particular power. Nevertheless, *ve-af al pi chein kofin oto le-hista'anet od pa'am achat be-Shabbat* — one must still accept a second fast as a form of consequence for having missed *oneg Shabbat*. The remedy, according to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, is *leisiv tanisa le-tanisa* — to fast for the fast, which somehow restores what was lost.

---

## God's Responsibility

### Aggressive Prayer Models

The Gemara now makes explicit what has been implicit throughout this extended passage: *ve-amar Rabbi Elazar: Channah hiticah devarim klapei ma'alah* — Hannah threw her words toward Heaven. The verb *hiticah* conveys something like plastering or slapping — words hurled upward, almost aggressively. The evidence is the verse *va-titpallel al Hashem* — she prayed *al* God, literally upon God, rather than *el* God, toward God.

Rabbi Elazar adds: Elijah did the same — *ve-ata hasivot et libam achoranis* — and You have turned their hearts backward. Elijah blamed God directly. Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak then asks: how do we know that God went back and conceded to Elijah that He bore some responsibility? The proof is from the verse *ve-asher hare'oti* — and that which I have caused them to do evil. God acknowledges having created circumstances in which human beings are drawn toward sin.

### Three Saving Verses

Rabbi Hama be-Rabbi Hanina states: *ilmale shalosh mikra'ot halalu, nismotetu ragleihem shel sonei Yisrael* — were it not for these three verses, the legs of Israel (a euphemism for Israel itself) would have collapsed. The three verses are:

First, *ve-asher hare'oti* — I have caused them to do evil. God admits to having created in human beings an inclination toward evil — the *yetzer hara*.

Second, *hinei ke-chomer be-yad ha-yotzer, kein atem be-yadi Beit Yisrael* — behold, like clay in the potter's hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel. The word *yotzer* (potter) resonates with *yeitzer* (inclination); God has formed us, and by forming us He has created our inclination as well.

Third, *va-hasiroti et lev ha-even mi-vsarchem ve-natati lachem lev basar* — I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. The implication is that right now, God has not yet done this — and if He has not, it is He who has left us with the heart of stone, the incapacity to fully resist temptation.

Rav Papa adds a fourth verse: *ve-et ruchi etein be-kirbekhem ve-asiti et asher be-chukotai teleikhu* — I will place My spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes. Again, that spirit is something God can give and has not yet given; the absence is, in some sense, His.

The Gemara then returns to Moses. Rabbi Elazar states: *Moshe hitiach devarim klapei ma'alah* — Moses too threw his words toward Heaven. The verse says *vayitpallel Moshe el Hashem* — but the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov reads *aleph* and *ayin* interchangeably, converting *el* to *al*, so that Moshe prayed *upon* God, against God.

### Prosperity & Rebellion

The school of Rabbi Yannai then derives Moses's implicit argument from the place name *Vedi Zahav* at the opening of Devarim. The Gemara reads *Vedi Zahav* as *dai zahav* — too much gold. Moses said to God: *bishvil ha-kesef ve-ha-zahav she-hishpata lahem le-Yisrael, ad she-amru dai* — because of the silver and gold You poured upon Israel, until they said "enough" — *hu garam she-asu et ha-eigel* — that is what caused them to make the calf. The argument is not merely that human beings have a weakness built into their nature, but that the specific circumstances God created — the extraordinary wealth — made sin nearly inevitable.

The school of Rabbi Yannai offers a vivid *mashal*: *ein ari noheim mi-toch kupah shel teven, ela mi-toch kupah shel basar* — a lion does not roar over a trough of straw; it roars after devouring flesh. It is satisfaction and abundance that lead to boldness, and boldness leads to rebellion. When life is lean, one stays on the straight and narrow.

### Spoiled Son Parable

Rabbi Oshaya offers a parallel image: a man had a weak, thin cow with its ribs showing. He fed it *karshinin* — a grain typically reserved for humans — and it began to kick and rebel against him. They said to the cow: what caused you to kick against me? Nothing but the *karshinin* I fed you.

Rabbi Yochanan, in the school of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, offers what is perhaps the most powerful formulation. A man had a son. He bathed him, anointed him with oil, fed him, gave him drink, hung a purse of money around his neck, and then placed him at the entrance to a brothel. *Mai ya'aseh oto bein she-lo yecheta?* — What do you expect the son to do and not sin? You have given him every inducement. You have made him feel entitled, comfortable, and without restraint. This is what God did when He gave Israel all that gold. What were they supposed to do?

Rav Acha son of Rav Huna in the name of Rav Sheshet cites the folk saying: *malei kerisei, zanei bisha* — a full belly breeds bad kinds of sin. The *pesukim* multiply: *ke-mar'itam vayisba'u, sav'u vayaram libam, al ken shechechuni* — they grazed and were sated, their heart grew haughty, and therefore they forgot Me. *Ve-ram levavecha ve-shachachta et Hashem Elokecha* — your heart will grow haughty and you will forget God. *Ve-achal ve-sava ve-dashen u-fanah* — he will eat and be satisfied and be fat and turn away. *Vayishman Yeshurun vayivat* — Israel grew fat and kicked.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan then asks: and how do we know that God went back and conceded to Moses — that He acknowledged His own role in Israel's sin? The verse says: *ve-chesef hirbeiti lahem ve-zahav asu la-Baal* — I gave them much silver and gold, and they used the gold to make the Baal. The verse itself is God speaking, and the emphasis on *I gave* carries the concession: the very wealth I bestowed led them to this sin.

The model of prayer being built throughout this passage is striking in how far it departs from simple supplication. From Hannah to Elijah to Moses, the *aggadata* of this *amud* and a half presents prayer as a form of *ta'anah* — a reasoned argument, even an accusation. It calls to mind the Chassidic tradition of Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, who was known for defending Israel before God through precisely this mode of prayer. What is remarkable is that these models appear here at the opening of the *perek* on *kavana* — as if to say that this kind of engaged, demanding, even confrontational prayer *is* the model for *tefillah*.

---

## Moses Defends Israel

### Go Down Speech

The Gemara now turns directly to the episode of the Golden Calf and Moses's prayer on Israel's behalf. *Vayidaber Hashem el Moshe: lech red* — God spoke to Moses: go down quickly. Rabbi Elazar reads the divine instruction as a demotion: *red mi-gedulatecha* — descend from your greatness. *Klum natati lecha gedulah ela bishvil Yisrael?* — Did I give you this status for any reason other than for the sake of Israel? *Ve-achshav Yisrael chatu, ata lama li?* — Now that Israel has sinned and lost their standing, what do I need you for?

This is a remarkable reversal of the surface reading of the *pesukim*, which seem to position Moses as God's beloved and Israel as expendable. The *midrash* completely inverts this: God's primary concern is Israel; Moses's greatness was always *bishvil Yisrael*, for their sake. When they fall, his status falls with them. God here is not rewarding Moses by offering to replace Israel with him — He is stripping Moses of the basis for his greatness.

### Moses Strengthens

*Miyad tashash kocho shel Moshe* — immediately Moses's strength was sapped. *Ve-lo haya lo koach le-daber* — he had no strength to respond. Having been told he no longer had standing, he felt he had nothing to say. He was not just weakened emotionally; he was rendered halachically mute, as it were — without standing to intercede.

But then God said: *heref mimeni ve-ashmidem* — let go of Me and I will destroy them. The moment Moses heard *heref mimeni* — let go of Me — something shifted. *Amar Moshe: davar zeh talui bi* — Moses realized: this matter depends on me. If God needs me to release Him, then I have the power not to do so. *Miyad amad ve-nitchazek bi-tefillah* — immediately he stood and strengthened himself in prayer.

### King & Counselor

The Gemara illustrates this dynamic with a *mashal*. A king was angry at his son and was striking him severely. The king's closest companion was sitting right there before the king, pained and wishing to intervene, but afraid to say anything — who was he to interfere with the king's discipline of his own son? Then the king said aloud: if not for my friend who is sitting before me, I would have killed you. The companion understood immediately: the king was sending him a message. The king cared what the companion thought. The companion rose and intervened, and he saved the son.

So too here. *Heref mimeni* — let go of Me — was God's message to Moses that Moses could and should intervene. The instruction was not a command to step back but a hidden invitation to step forward.

### Grab Divine Collar

Rabbi Abbahu states: *ilmale mikra katuv i efshar le-omro* — were it not written in a verse, one could not say such a thing. *Melamed she-tafas Moshe le-Hakadosh Baruch Hu ke-adam she-tofes et chaveiro be-vigdo* — it teaches that Moses seized God, as a person might seize his companion by the cloak. *Ve-amar lefanav: Ribbono shel Olam, ein ani manichacha ad she-timchol ve-tislach lahem* — he said before Him: Master of the Universe, I will not let go of You until You forgive and pardon them.

This is one of the most extraordinary images in the Gemara. The power of prayer, in this formulation, is not petition but physical insistence — *grabbing God by the collar*. Prayer does not merely ask; it compels. The image draws its force entirely from the phrase *heref mimeni* — let go of Me — which Moses, in his prayer, refuses to do.

### Three-Legged Chair

When God said *ve-e'eseh otcha le-goy gadol va-atzum* — I will make you into a great and mighty nation — Rabbi Elazar records Moses's response. *Ribbono shel Olam, u-mah kisei shel shalosh raglayim eino yachol la'amod lefanecha bi-sha'at ka'asecha* — Master of the Universe, if a chair with three legs — Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — cannot stand before You in the moment of Your anger, then *kisei shel regel achat, al achat kama ve-chama* — a chair of one leg, built on my merit alone, how much more so will it be unable to stand?

And beyond that: *she-yesh bi boshet panim me-avotai* — I will be shamed before my forefathers. Because they will say: look at this leader God appointed over them — *bikeish gedulah le-atzmo ve-lo bikeish aleihem rachamim* — he grabbed at greatness for himself and did not seek compassion for the people. The point underscores the same theme as before: Moses's greatness is entirely bound up in his role as the defender of Israel. To accept an offer that abandons the people is to abandon the very thing that gave Moses his standing.

---

## Legal Argument Prayer

### Prayer Makes Ill

*Va-yechal Moshe et penei Hashem Elokav* — and Moses importuned God. Rabbi Elazar explains that Moses stood in prayer *ad she-hechelohu* — until he had importuned Him. Rashi reads *hechelohu* as *hiftsir bo*, meaning he overwhelmed God with his prayers. Steinsaltz, however, renders it as "made Him ill" — understanding the root as *choleh*, sickness. This is a striking image in its own right, and one that may be the more vivid reading: Moses prayed until he had, as it were, worn God out.

Shmuel offers a different reading of *vayechal*: *melamed she-masar atzmo le-misah aleihem* — it teaches that Moses surrendered himself to death for them, reading the root as *chalal*, a corpse, in connection with his later plea *mecheini na mi-sifracha* — erase me from Your book.

Rabbi Avram in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak reads *vayechal* as *she-hechilah aleihem midat ha-rachamim* — he caused the attribute of divine compassion to descend upon them.

The anonymous *rabanan* offer yet another interpretation: *chulin hu lecha me'asot ka-davar ha-zeh* — it would be a desecration for You to do such a thing. This reading connects *vayechal* to *chulin* and *chalilah*.

A *beraita* cites Rabbi Elazar the Great: Moses stood in prayer before God *ad she-achazo achilu* — until he was seized with *achilu*. What is *achilu*? Rabbi Elazar explains: *esha de-atzmot* — a burning of the bones, a deep fever. Abaye translates into Aramaic: *eshta de-garmei*. This is not merely a metaphor for exhaustion; the prayer was so intense that it affected Moses physically.

### Release from Vow

Rava offers his own reading of *vayechal*. He connects it to the verse *lo yachel devaro* — a person may not desecrate his word, i.e., may not violate a vow. *Aval acherim mechilin lo* — but others can annul the vow for him. Rava therefore reads *vayechal* as: Moses convened a *Beis Din* and released God from His vow. What was God's vow? When God declares that He will destroy Israel, that constitutes something analogous to a vow; by the mechanism of *hatarat nedarim*, Moses was able to annul it.

### Patriarchs' Oath

Moses then invoked the oath to the patriarchs: *zechor le-Avraham le-Yitzchak u-le-Yisrael avadecha, asher nishbata lahem bach* — remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel Your servants, to whom You swore by Yourself.

Rabbi Elazar explains the significance of *bach* — by You, by Your own name. Moses argued: *Ribbono shel Olam, ilmale nishbata lahem be-shamayim u-va-aretz* — had You sworn to them by heaven and earth, I might have said: just as heaven and earth will eventually be destroyed, so too Your oath can be nullified. *Ve-achshav she-nishbata lahem be-shimcha ha-gadol* — but now that You have sworn in Your own great name, *mah shimcha ha-gadol chai ve-kayam le-olam u-le-olmei olamim* — just as Your great name lives and endures forever, *kach shevuatecha kayama le-olam u-le-olmei olamim* — so too Your oath stands forever and cannot be annulled.

The argument is airtight in halachic terms: an oath sworn in God's own eternal name cannot be undone by any temporal contingency. Moses trapped God, as it were, within His own metaphysical permanence.

### Nations' Slander

Moses then made a pragmatic argument from the verse *vayomru mibilti yacholet Hashem* — they will say God was not able. The word is *yacholet*, in the feminine form. Rabbi Elazar explains that Moses said: *Ribbono shel Olam, achshav yomru umot ha-olam: tashash kocho ke-nekevah* — the nations will say God's power has weakened like a woman's, and *eino yachol le-hatzilam* — He cannot save them.

God responded: *ve-lo kvar ra'u nissim u-gevurot she-asiti lahem al ha-yam?* — Have the nations not already seen the miracles I performed at the sea? Moses countered: *adayin yesh lahem lomar, melech echad yachol la'amod, u-shloshim ve-echad melachim eino yachol la'amod* — they can still say: He could stand up against one king, Pharaoh, but He could not stand up against the thirty-one kings of Canaan. The destruction of Israel before the conquest would look like a failure of the very mission God had begun.

### Divine Concession

Rabbi Yochanan asks: how do we know God went back and conceded to Moses? *She-ne'emar: vayomer Hashem salachti ki-devarecha* — it says: God said, I have forgiven them *according to your words*. The phrase *ki-devarecha* — according to your words — is the concession: Moses's arguments carried the day.

The *Tanna* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael adds: *ki-devarecha atidim umot ha-olam lomar ken* — the nations would indeed have said exactly what Moses predicted had God destroyed Israel.

*Ashrei talmid she-rabbo modeh lo* — praised is the student whose master concedes to him and admits he was right.

The *daf* closes on a remarkable note. God says: *va-ulam chai ani* — yet as I live. And Rava in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak explains: *she-amar lo Hakadosh Baruch Hu le-Moshe: hecheyitani bi-devarecha* — God said to Moses, you have given Me life with your words. *Chai ani* — I have lived. Rashi explains this as meaning that Moses's prayer prevented the nations from claiming that God lacked the power to save — and so Moses, in a sense, restored God's honor in the world. But there is also a deeper dimension: when we pray properly, when we give God the ability to do in the world what God wants to do, we as it were give life to God. The proper prayer of a human being enables divine action in this world.

---

## Praise Before Request

### Praise First Rule

Rav Simai states: *le-olam yesader adam shivcho shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu ve-achar kach yitpallel* — one should always first arrange the praise of God and only afterward pray. The word *yitpallel* here means specifically *bakasha* — petition or request — while in earlier usages the word *tefillah* referred to praise. The distinction maps onto the structure of *Shemoneh Esreh*: the first three *brachot* are praise, and the middle thirteen are *bakashot*.

### Moses Example

The source, as always, is Moses. *Menalan mi-Moshe* — from where do we derive this? From the verse *va-etchanan el Hashem* — and I beseeched God. And how did Moses begin? *Hashem Elokim, atah hachilota leharot et avdecha et godlecha ve-et yadcha ha-chazakah, asher mi Kel ba-shamayim u-va-aretz asher ya'aseh ke-ma'asecha u-che-gevurotecha* — Lord God, You have begun to show Your servant Your greatness and Your mighty hand; who is there in the heavens or on the earth who could do as Your deeds and as Your mighty acts? First, the praise. And only then: *e'evrah na ve-er'eh et ha-aretz ha-tovah* — please let me cross over and see this good land. First the *shevach*, then the *bakasha*. This structure will be developed further as the Gemara continues.

---

---

# Berakhot 32b

## Prayer > Deeds

### Prayer > Good Deeds

We pick up at the very top of 32b. The *gemara* opens with a statement of Rabbi Elazar: *gedolah tefillah yoter mi-ma'asim tovim* — greater is prayer than good deeds. The proof offered is from Moshe Rabbeinu himself. As the *gemara* puts it: *she-ein lekha gadol mi-ma'asim tovim yoter mi-Moshe Rabbeinu* — there is no one greater in their good deeds than Moshe Rabbeinu. Consider what he accomplished: he took *Bnei Yisrael* out of *Mitzrayim* and did everything for them. And yet, *af al pi khen lo ne'eneh ela bi-tefillah* — he was only answered through prayer.

The verse cited is from the opening of *Devarim*, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness: *al tosef daber elai* — "do not speak to me anymore" — and immediately adjacent to it, *aleh rosh ha-pisgah* — "go up to the head of the mountain and I will show you the land." This is an interesting choice of proof-text, because Moshe did not receive what he asked for — he wanted to enter the land of Israel and was denied. What makes this example compelling is precisely that dimension: Moshe was asking something *for himself*, something one might have thought he had earned outright through a lifetime of extraordinary deeds. Yet even this partial concession — being shown the land — was extended to him only in the context of prayer, not on the basis of merit alone.

### Tosafot: Both Required

*Tosafot* enters with an important qualification. On the phrase *gedolah tefillah yoter mi-ma'asim tovim*, *Tosafot* reads *be-lo tefillah* — the statement means that prayer *combined with* good deeds is greater than good deeds *without* prayer. As *Tosafot* explains: *she-harei Moshe Rabbeinu alav ha-shalom af al pi she-hayu biyado ma'asim tovim hutsrakh li-tefillah* — even though Moshe had good deeds in hand, he still required prayer. The point is not that one can lead a life devoid of *ma'asim tovim* and compensate through prayer alone. Such a reading would be a perversion of the values at stake here.

One might ask whether a student in the discussion raised a sharper challenge: could this be a polemic against certain ideas that ritual sincerity alone matters regardless of one's life? In context, that seems a stretch. Still, *Tosafot*'s concern is real: rhetorically, the *gemara* sometimes makes exaggerated statements in order to emphasize the power of something, and one must be careful not to be misled.

A more integrative reading of the relationship between *tefillah* and *ma'asim tovim* was offered in the course of discussion. *Ma'asim tovim* — or for that matter *tzedakah* — could in principle be performed in a purely secular spirit, as an expression of ordinary decency rather than of one's relationship with God. What *tefillah* adds, or what *ta'anit* adds (if understood as supplemental rather than substitutional), is the articulation of those deeds *within* a God-relationship. As one participant put it, an employee can behave in exemplary fashion toward an employer, but without verbalization that relationship remains somehow dormant, unactivated. *Tefillah* is what puts the relationship into words.

### Fasting > Charity

Rabbi Elazar makes a parallel statement: *gedolah ta'anit yoter min ha-tzedakah* — greater is fasting than the giving of charity. The rationale given is *zeh be-gufo ve-zeh be-mamono* — one involves your body, the other involves only your money.

It is worth noting that the comparison *zeh be-gufo ve-zeh be-mamono* appears elsewhere in the *gemara* in a different context — contrasting *tzedakah* with *gemilut chasadim*, where the latter involves giving of oneself and not merely of one's funds. But there the point is about helping another person; one who performs *gemilut chasadim* gives of their own efforts on behalf of someone else. Here, by contrast, the *ta'anit* is a ritual act of self-denial — one's blood and fat are, in a sense, diminished — while the *tzedakah* at least helps another person. This inversion is genuinely challenging when read against the background of the *nevi'im*, who famously said: why do I need your fasts? What I need is for you to clothe the naked and feed the hungry.

One possible way to read this more narrowly: in the context of a *ta'anit tzibbur* — a communal fast day called in response to drought or crisis — the point may be that if you want your *tefillah* to be answered, merely writing a check is not sufficient. Real extension of oneself, real willingness to suffer, is what is required. We recite *tefillah, teshuvah, tzedakah ma'avirin et ro'a ha-gezeirah*, and in that mode the *ta'anit* represents something qualitatively different from *tzedakah*. Read that narrowly, the statement is more defensible. Read broadly, it remains deeply challenging.

It is also worth flagging the *gemara* in 6b, cited by the *Maharsha*, which states *agra de-ta'anita tzidketa* — the reward of a fast day is the *tzedakah* one gives on the fast day. That statement appears to say the exact opposite, and it is striking that Rabbi Elazar's formulation stands in some tension with a number of other rabbinic statements on this point.

### Prayer > Sacrifices

Rabbi Elazar continues: *gedolah tefillah yoter min ha-korbanot* — prayer is greater than sacrifices. This is directly relevant to the broader thematic arc the *gemara* has been building. The proof is from *Yeshayahu*: *lama li rov zivcheihem* — "why do I need all your sacrifices?" — after which it is written: *u-ve-farish'chem kapeichem* — "when you spread your hands in prayer, I do not answer." The *hava amina* embedded in the sequence is that even after God rejected the sacrifices, prayer might still have been accepted. The very next verse's denial of that possibility implies that prayer is on a higher plane than sacrifice — it carried the possibility of being answered even when sacrifice did not.

### Kohen/Murder/Blessing

Having quoted the verse about spreading one's hands, the *gemara* introduces a related ruling. Rabbi Yochanan states: *kol kohen she-harag et ha-nefesh lo yisa kapav* — any *kohen* who has committed murder may not perform *birkat kohanim*, the priestly blessing. The source is *yedeikhem damim male'u* — "your hands are full of blood," the continuation of the very verse just quoted. Hands that have taken a life cannot be the same hands used to bless the nation.

There are difficult questions that arise from tragic cases — a *kohen* whose wagon accidentally ran over someone, for instance — and whether *teshuvah* can restore the eligibility to perform *nesi'at kapayim*. These questions are derived from this very *pasuk*.

What is striking when stepping back is that this single thread of Rabbi Elazar's statements — *tefillah* greater than *ma'asim tovim*, greater than *ta'anit* which is greater than *tzedakah*, greater than *korbanot* — seems, if taken together without *Tosafot*'s qualification, to create a picture where the connection to God through prayer and *ta'anit* outweighs the doing of deeds in the world. Whether that was intended rhetorically or reflects a deeper theological position is a question worth sitting with.

---

## Post-Churban Prayer

### Locked Gates/Tears

The same Rabbi Elazar who just declared prayer greater than *korbanot* now makes a sobering statement about the current state of prayer: *mi-yom she-charav Beit Ha-Mikdash, nin'alu sha'arei tefillah* — from the day the *Beit Ha-Mikdash* was destroyed, the gates of prayer have been locked. The proof-text is from *Eichah*: *gam ki ez'ak va-ashave'a, satam tefillati* — "even when I cry out and call, my prayer has been stopped up." This is set against the backdrop of the *churban*, and it sets up a striking paradox: the very *tefillah* he praised over sacrifices has itself been compromised by the loss of the *Beit Ha-Mikdash*.

But the *gemara* adds an important qualification: *ve-af al pi she-sha'arei tefillah nin'alu, sha'arei dima lo nin'alu* — even though the gates of prayer are locked, the gates of tears have not been locked. The supporting verse — *shema tefillati Hashem, ve-shavati ha'azina, el dimati al techerash* — "hear my prayer, God, hearken to my calling out; to my tears, do not be silent." *Rashi* notes that the phrase "do not be silent" implies something stronger than merely "listen": to be told not to be silent implies that one has already, in some sense, heard. The tears penetrate further than the words.

Why would the *churban* affect prayer and not only sacrifice? As discussed here: the *Beit Ha-Mikdash* was not merely the site of *korbanot*. It was the locus of God's presence among the people, the embodiment of the intimacy of that relationship. Its loss changes the nature of the relationship itself, and that in turn affects the accessibility of *tefillah*, not only of sacrifice. This is one of the more powerful ways to conceptualize what *Tisha B'Av* asks us to mourn — not the loss of animal sacrifice per se, but the loss of a mode of closeness with God that reverberates through every subsequent act of prayer.

On a related note, *Rava* would not declare a fast on an overcast day, relying on the verse from *Eichah*: *sakota be-anan lach me-avor tefillah* — "You have covered yourself with a cloud so that prayer cannot pass through." When there are clouds, that symbolic barrier is already present.

### Iron Wall

Rabbi Elazar adds a second metaphor, even heavier than locked gates: *mi-yom she-charav Beit Ha-Mikdash, nifseka chomat barzel bein Yisrael le-avihem she-ba-shamayim* — from the day the *Beit Ha-Mikdash* was destroyed, a wall of iron has been interposed between Israel and their Father in Heaven. The proof is from *Yechezkel*: *ve-atah kach lecha machavat barzel, ve-natatah otah kir barzel beinecha u-vein ha-ir* — take an iron griddle and place it as an iron wall between you and the city.

A locked gate still implies a gate — something with the potential to be opened. A wall of iron implies a far harsher and more complete separation. These statements together create a post-*churban* theology of spiritual distance, one which stands in obvious tension with the affirmations of the power of prayer that immediately preceded them. The resolution, it seems, lies not in resolving the tension intellectually but in inhabiting it honestly — and, as was noted, in crying.

---

## Extended Prayer

### Long Prayer/Learn Torah

The *gemara* shifts to a series of practical observations about prayer. Rabbi Chanina states: *kol ha-ma'arich bi-tefillato, ein tefillato chozeret reikam* — anyone who extends their prayer will not have their prayer return empty. The proof is from Moshe Rabbeinu: *va-etpallel el Hashem* is followed by *va-yishma Hashem elai gam ba-pa'am ha-hi* — "and God also listened to me that time." The key is in what is left implicit: the full verse reads *va-etpallel el Hashem arba'im yom ve-arba'im lailah* — Moshe prayed for forty days and forty nights. A prayer of that scope and duration was answered.

### Heartache/Solution

Yet Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan offers what sounds like a counterpoint: *kol ha-ma'arich bi-tefillato u-me'ayein bah, sof ba lidei ke'ev lev* — anyone who extends their prayer and then scrutinizes it — or rather, as *Rashi* explains, who waits for it to be answered, constantly looking to see when the response will come — will in the end come to heartache. The verse: *tochelet memushacha machalah lev* — prolonged anticipation makes the heart sick.

What then is the remedy? *Ya'asok ba-Torah* — engage in Torah study. The verse: *ve-etz chayim ta'avah ba'ah* — "the desire brings a tree of life" — and the tree of life is Torah, as it is written *etz chayim hi la-machazikim bah*.

The *gemara* resolves the apparent tension between these two statements: *lo kashya — ha de-ma'arich u-me'ayein bah, ha de-ma'arich ve-lo me'ayein bah* — one who prays at length and then watches anxiously for the response is in a different category from one who prays at length without that anxious scrutiny. The prayer itself is not the problem; the watching is.

Several readings of the *me'ayein bah* present themselves. One possibility is that the expectation itself undermines something — it is like the famous observation that one who runs from honor will find honor chasing him, but only if he is not looking over his shoulder as he runs. Another reading, perhaps more psychologically acute, is that the *gemara* is not saying the prayer won't be answered; it is saying that the expectation of *how* and *when* leads to heartache, because prayers are sometimes answered in ways not anticipated, or only recognized years later. The heartache comes from the gap between what one expected and what one perceives.

There is also a structural point worth noting. Rabbi Yochanan's prescription — learn Torah — may reflect a broader tension between *tefillah* and *talmud Torah* as competing claims on one's time. One who is *ma'arich bi-tefillah* is by definition not in the *beit midrash*. The alternative being offered may not be only about managing one's emotional state, but about a reorientation of priorities: fulfill your obligation in *davening*, bring your requests before God, and then go sit and learn — for that too is a form of connection, and perhaps a more sustainable one than prolonged prayer with its attendant anxious waiting.

### Persist/Retry

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina adds: *im ra'ah adam she-hitpallel ve-lo na'anah, yachzor ve-yitpallel* — if a person prays and is not answered, they should return and pray again. The verse: *kaveh el Hashem, chazak ve-ya'ametz libecha, ve-kaveh el Hashem* — "hope to God; strengthen your heart; and hope to God again." The repetition in the verse is the proof: when the first round of hope does not produce visible results, strengthen yourself and hope again.

Chanah provides the paradigmatic illustration that had been discussed earlier. She had clearly not prayed for the first time when Eli encountered her at the *Mishkan*; she had waited long, never given up, and returned to pray at greater and greater depth. The reaffirmation of faith implicit in repeated prayer is itself something powerful and expressive — not merely a tactical strategy for finally wearing down divine resistance, but a statement about the relationship. One who prays once and expects immediate results treats prayer as a transaction. One who returns, persisting in faith, demonstrates something qualitatively different.

### Four Need Strength

A *baraita* now teaches: *arba'ah tzrichim chizuk* — four things require constant reinforcement. They are: *Torah*, *ma'asim tovim*, *tefillah*, and *derekh eretz* — here understood, as *Rashi* explains, as *parnasah*, one's livelihood and profession.

The sources: for *Torah* and *ma'asim tovim*, the verse *rak chazak ve-ematz me'od, lishmor ve-la'asot ke-khol ha-Torah* — "only be strong and very courageous, to observe and do all this Torah." *Chazak* corresponds to *Torah* study; *ematz* to *ma'asim tovim*. And the doubling of *lishmor ve-la'asot* — observing and doing — captures both the knowing and the acting.

For *tefillah*: *kaveh el Hashem, chazak ve-ya'ametz libecha, ve-kaveh el Hashem* — hope, then strengthen your heart, then hope again.

For *derekh eretz*: *chazak ve-nit-chazek be'ad ameinu* — "be strong and let us strengthen each other for the sake of our people." *Rashi* reads this expansively: *im uman hu, le-umanuso; im socher hu, le-socharato; im ish milchamah hu, le-milchamato* — whatever one's profession, success in it requires ongoing fortification. None of these things — learning, doing good, praying, making a living — come easily or sustain themselves without effort.

---

## Post-Churban Prayer (II)

### God Remembers Israel

The *gemara* cites the verse from *Yeshayahu*: *va-tomer Tzion azavani Hashem, va-Hashem shichekhani* — "Zion said: God has abandoned me; God has forgotten me." Reish Lakish reads the doubled language as the voice of *knesset Yisrael*: a man who takes a second wife may still remember his first — he was at least there, he experienced those years together. But you, God — not only have you abandoned me, you have *forgotten* me. You don't even think about me anymore.

God's response, as rendered by the *gemara*, begins with a staggering enumeration of the cosmos created on Israel's behalf. There are twelve constellations, and for each, thirty armies (*chayyil*); for each army, thirty legions (*ligyon*); for each legion, thirty officers of a certain rank (*rhaton*); for each such officer, thirty colonels (*karton*); for each colonel, thirty lieutenants (*gistra*); and hanging upon each of those, three hundred sixty-five thousand *ribo* — ten-thousands — of stars, corresponding to the days of the solar year. The arithmetic yields numbers approaching billions, and the *gemara* itself notes with some wonder that even this seems an understatement given what we know of the cosmos. And all of this, God says, was created *bishvilekh* — for you. *Ve-at amarat azavtani u-shechachtani* — "and you say I have abandoned and forgotten you?"

The *gemara* then reads the verse: *ha-tishkach ishah ulah?* — God asks: can I forget? The word *ulah* is heard as *olah* — a burnt offering — do you think I will forget the rams you sacrificed before me? Or the *petrei rechem*, the firstborn animals, that you brought in the *midbar*?

*Knesset Yisrael* then responds with a remarkable double move. First: since there is no forgetting before Your throne — *ein shikchah lifnei kisei kvodekha*, a phrase echoed in the *Rosh Ha-Shanah Amidah* — perhaps You will not forget for me the sin of the *egel*, the golden calf, and I will be punished for it still? God responds: *gam eileh tishkachnah* — even these I will forget.

Then the second move: since you are going to forget certain things — *hoil ve-yesh shikchah lifnei kisei kvodekha* — perhaps You will forget for me the good things, like *ma'aseh Sinai*, the covenant at *Har Sinai*? And God responds: *ve-anokhi lo eshkachekh* — I will not forget you.

*Rashi* observes that this is embedded in the very words of the verse: *gam eileh tishkachnah* refers to *eileh* — as in *eileh elokekha Yisrael*, the golden calf; while *ve-anokhi lo eshkachekh* refers to *anokhi* — as in *anokhi Hashem Elokekha*, the opening of the *Aseret Ha-Dibrot* at Sinai. And this is confirmed by Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: *gam eileh tishkachnah* — this is the sin of the *egel*; *ve-anokhi lo eshkachekh* — this is the doing of Sinai.

Placed immediately after the statements about the locked gates and the iron wall, this passage provides something like a theological counterweight. Yes, the *churban* introduced a barrier. Yes, the gates are locked. But God has not forgotten *Bnei Yisrael*. The entire universe was created for their sake. The sins of the *egel* will be forgiven; the covenant of Sinai will never be forgotten. The juxtaposition is not accidental: these are weeks of *shivat de-nechemta*, consolation, and the *gemara* allows these texts to speak to that moment.

One additional layer was noted in the course of discussion: it is a common psychological reality that when a relationship ends — or enters a painful period of distance — one tends to remember its positive dimensions, the ways in which it was nourishing. God's speech here does something similar: in the very moment that *knesset Yisrael* feels abandoned, God reaches back to the constructive, covenantal memories that remain undiminished.

---

## Prayer Integrity

### Hour Before/After

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishnah*, which speaks about *kavvanah* and the practice of *chasidim ha-rishonim*. The *mishnah* states that these early pious ones would wait an hour before prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives this from the verse *ashrei yoshvei veitekha* — "happy are those who dwell in Your house" — and only thereafter *od yehalelucha selah*, they will praise You. First one dwells; then one praises.

The same Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that one must also wait an hour *after* prayer: *ha-mitpallel tzarikh li-shhot sha'ah achat achar tefilato* — *ach tzadikim yodu lishimekha, yeshvu yesharim et panekha* — "the righteous will give thanks to Your name; the upright will dwell before Your face." After the praise, they still sit. One does not rush out. Prayer is not only the verbalized request; it is also the experience of being in the presence of God, the sitting together in that space before and after the words.

A *baraita* states this formally: one must wait an hour before prayer and an hour after, with both practices derived from those same two verses. *Tosafot* notes a practical implication: this is why we recite *Ashrei yoshvei veitekha* — those opening verses — before *Tehillah le-David* at *Minchah*. The *gemara* in Berakhot teaches that one who recites *Tehillah le-David* three times daily is a *ben Olam Ha-Ba*, but the actual *perek* begins with *Tehillah le-David*. The prefatory verses of *Ashrei yoshvei veitekha* were added — particularly at *Minchah*, where there is otherwise only the *Shemoneh Esrei* — as a way of inhabiting this preparatory sitting before one enters *davening*.

As for who the *chasidim ha-rishonim* were: there was certainly a group known as *chasidim* in the period of the Maccabees, pietistic Jews who famously refused to fight on *Shabbat* and who generally refrained from involvement in the broader society. They did not join the *Chashmonaim* because they reasoned that if God wants a *Beit Ha-Mikdash* restored, He will bring it down from heaven. Whether the *mishnah* refers to them as a defined sect or simply to certain pious individuals who prayed with great care and preparation is not entirely clear.

A second *baraita* confirms: *chasidim ha-rishonim hayu shohim sha'ah achat u-mitpallelim sha'ah achat ve-chozrim ve-shohim sha'ah achat* — they waited an hour, prayed an hour, and waited another hour. The *gemara* asks the natural question: if they spent nine hours a day in the framework of prayer, how was their *Torah* preserved and how did their work get done? The answer: *mitoch she-chasidim hem, toratam mishtameret u-melakhatam mitbarechet* — because they were so righteous, their *Torah* was preserved and their work was blessed, requiring far fewer hours to accomplish.

The *Netziv*, Rav Naftali Zvi Yehuda Berlin, notes a significant difference between this *baraita* and the parallel in the *Yerushalmi*, which reads not *toratam mishtameret* — their *Torah* was preserved — but *toratam mitbarechet* — their *Torah* was *blessed*. He argues these two formulations reflect different orientations toward *Torah she-be'al peh*. In *Bavel*, the emphasis falls on process — the *shakla ve-tarya*, the give-and-take, the creative dimensions of legal deliberation. From that perspective, if you do not invest the hours, even correct conclusions cannot be called *toratam mitbarechet*, because the *Torah* itself is the process, not only the outcome. The *Yerushalmi*, by contrast, oriented more toward reaching correct conclusions, can say that even compressed learning produces Torah that is genuinely blessed — just as work that yields results in few hours is work that has been blessed. It is a subtle but telling distinction in the respective characters of the two Talmuds.

### King/Greeting

The *mishnah* rules: *afilu ha-melekh sho'el bi-shlomo lo yeshivenu* — even if a king greets someone during prayer, one does not respond. The reasoning is implicit in the context: when standing before God in prayer, one is in the presence of the King of Kings, and nothing should interrupt that.

Rav Yosef qualifies: *lo shanu ela le-malkhei Yisrael* — this was said only regarding a Jewish king, who will understand. But *le-malkhei akum* — regarding a non-Jewish king, *posek* — one interrupts, because one's life may be at genuine risk.

The *gemara* raises an objection from a *baraita*: if one is *davening* and sees a dangerous man (*anas*) approaching, or a wagon bearing down, *lo yehei mafsik ela me-katzer ve-oleh* — one should not stop, but rather finish up quickly. The *gemara* resolves: *lo kashya — ha de-efshar le-katzer* — if one can shorten and conclude, one does so; if one cannot, one stops. This is not a matter of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* — it is simply about completing one's *davening* where possible.

### Officer Story

A *baraita* tells of a *chasid* who was praying along the road. An officer (*sar*) approached and greeted him; the *chasid* did not respond. The officer waited until he finished. When prayer was complete, the officer confronted him: *reika* — worthless one — does your Torah not say *rak hishamer lekha u-shemor nafshekha* and *ve-nishmartem me'od le-nafshoteikhem* — to guard your life carefully? How could you risk your life by ignoring me? *Im hayisi choteikh et roshekha be-saif, mi hayah tove'a et damkha mi-yadi* — had I cut off your head with a sword, no one could have demanded your blood from me.

The *chasid* asked: permit me to appease you with words. He said: if you had been standing before a human king — *melekh basar va-dam* — and a colleague had come and greeted you, would you have responded? The officer said: no. And if you had responded, what would they have done to you? They would have cut off my head with a sword, said the officer.

The *chasid* then drew the *kal va-homer*: if you, standing before a mortal king — *she-ha-yom kan u-machar be-kever*, here today and in the grave tomorrow — would not have interrupted your attendance upon him to respond to a colleague, then I, who was standing before the King of Kings, *she-hu chai ve-kayam la-adei ad u-le-olmei olamim*, who lives and endures forever — how much more so should I not have interrupted. *Al achat kamah ve-khamah*. The officer was immediately appeased, and the *chasid* went home in peace.

It is worth noting one slight puzzle in the argument: the *chasid* said "if a *friend* came and greeted you." Had one been the officer, one might have taken offense at the word *friend* — "I am not your friend." A more obvious analogy would have been "if an important dignitary came." Perhaps it is an intentional rhetorical choice, deliberately understating the comparison to make the conclusion more powerful. In any event, the point lands.

One also wonders about the *chasid* praying on the road in the first place — *mispalel ba-derekh* exposes one to exactly these kinds of interruptions. Presumably he had no choice in the matter; he was traveling.

### Danger/Interruption

The *mishnah* had stated: *afilu nachash karukh al akeivo lo yafsik* — even if there is a snake coiled around one's ankle, one does not interrupt prayer.

Rav Sheshet qualifies: *lo shanu ela nachash* — this is only for a snake. *Aval akrav, posek* — a scorpion, however, requires that one stop. Perhaps not all snakes are poisonous; but the *gemara*'s further discussion suggests the distinction lies elsewhere. A *baraita* is cited as a challenge: if someone fell into a pit of lions, one cannot testify that he is dead — perhaps the lions were not hungry. But if he fell into a pit filled with snakes and scorpions, one *can* testify that he is dead. This implies that snakes are reliably lethal — so why treat them differently from scorpions?

The *gemara* answers: *shani hatam de-agav itstsama* — it is different there, because the pressure of the fall agitated them and they would certainly attack. A snake that is merely coiled calmly is not necessarily about to bite.

Rav Yitzchak adds: even if one sees an ox (*reish tora*), one stops prayer and moves away. This seems counterintuitive — oxen are not typically thought of as dangerous — but a *baraita* taught by Rabbi Yoshiyah: *merachakin mi-shor tam chamishim amah* — keep fifty cubits (roughly seventy-five feet) away from even an ox that has never gored; and from an ox that has gored (*shor mu'ad*) — *ke-melo einav*, stay out of its entire field of vision. Rav Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Meir adds: even if the ox has its head in its feeding basket, distracted and apparently calm — *salik le-igra, u-shedi darga mitutakh* — go up to the roof and kick away the ladder. This is understood as hyperbole by *Rashi*, but the principle is clear: one does not take chances with oxen.
