Shmuel adds a further specificity: *hani milei be-shor shachor u-ve-yomei Nisan* — this applies especially to a black ox in the spring, *mipnei she-ha-satan merakeid bein karnav* — because the Satan dances between its horns. After the confinement of winter, the animal has energy and is looking for trouble.

*Tosafot* notes that the *Yerushalmi* adds another qualification: if the snake was clearly preparing to strike — *im haya nachash martia lavo kenegdo* — then one stops, because it *is* intending to cause harm. This brings the whole discussion into clearer relief: the question is always whether there is genuine risk. The *mishnah*'s rule is not recklessness; it is a recognition that the default state of a coiled snake is not the same as an imminent attack.

What results from this sequence of qualifications is a significant moderation of the *mishnah*'s dramatic statement. Yes, one maintains one's standing before God and does not interrupt prayer lightly. But if there is genuine danger — a scorpion, an agitated ox, a snake positioned to strike — one takes care of oneself. *Ve-nishmartem me'od le-nafshoteikhem*.

### Chanina/Arod Story

The *gemara* concludes this section with a famous story. In a certain place there was an *arod* — some creature understood to be a hybrid of snake and scorpion, in any case a poisonous reptile — that was injuring people. They came and told Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa. He said: show me its hole. They showed him, and he placed his heel over the opening of the hole. The *arod* came out, bit him — and the *arod* died.

Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa then picked it up, put it on his shoulder, brought it to the *beit midrash*, and said to his students: *re'u vanai, ein arod memit ela ha-chet memit* — see, my sons, it is not the *arod* that kills; it is the sin that kills. At that moment, it was said: *oy lo le-adam she-paga bo arod* — woe to the person that encounters an *arod*; *ve-oy lo la-arod she-paga bo Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa* — and woe to the *arod* that encounters Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa.

*Rashi* cites the *Ba'al Halachot Gedolot*, who in turn cites the *Talmud* of *Eretz Yisrael*: when an *arod* bites a person, whichever of them — man or *arod* — reaches water first causes the death of the other. *Rashi* suggests that a spring miraculously opened beneath Rabbi Chanina's heel. This is an attempt to naturalize the miracle somewhat; though the opening of a spring beneath his heel is itself miraculous, it gives the event a physical mechanism. The *gemara* of course does not frame it this way, and *Rashi*'s citation of the *Bahag* reads as a kind of commentary-level version of what one might call *nissim be-derekh ha-teva* — wonders that follow natural channels.

The placement of this story is worth noticing. It follows directly after the discussion about when one may or may not interrupt prayer in the face of danger. Having carefully qualified the *mishnah* — yes, stop for a scorpion, for an aggressive ox, for an imminent threat — the *gemara* ends with the story of one whose *davening* was so whole, whose piety was so complete, that the creature that bit him died. The juxtaposition carries a message: the *gemara*'s qualifications are correct and reasonable; but for one who has truly achieved *ein chet*, there is a different reality.

---

## Rain/Havdalah

### Rain/Resurrection

The *gemara* now turns to the *mishnah* which discusses where rain and *havdalah* are mentioned in the *Amidah*. The *mishnah* states: *mazkirin gevurot geshamim bi-techiyyat ha-meitim* — the power of rain is mentioned in the *berakhah* of the resurrection of the dead, i.e., the second *berakhah* of the *Shemoneh Esrei*, which begins *mashiv ha-ruach u-morid ha-gashem*. The question the *gemara* asks is *mai ta'ama* — why specifically there?

Rav Yosef answers: *mitoch she-shkulah ki-techiyyat ha-meitim, lefichakh keva'uha bi-techiyyat ha-meitim* — because rain is as weighty as the resurrection of the dead, and therefore they placed it in that *berakhah*.

Why the equivalence? On one level, rain is literally a matter of life and death for agricultural societies. But beyond that, rain and *techiyyat ha-meitim* share a powerful metaphorical relationship. One plants a seed in the earth — it is buried, it decays, it seems to disappear entirely — and then rain comes, and new life emerges from what had been interred. The whole cycle of seed, burial, decay, and rebirth under rain is a living image of resurrection.

And the *berakhah* of *gevurot* — as this second *berakhah* is often called, reflecting God's *gevurah*, His power — is itself structured around many forms of divine life-giving. *Mechalkeil chayim be-chesed, mechayeh meitim be-rachamim rabbim, someich noflim ve-rofei cholim u-matir asurim u-mekayeim emunato li-sheinei afar* — God sustains the living, heals the sick, releases the bound, keeps faith with those who sleep in the dust. *Mashiv ha-ruach u-morid ha-gashem* fits naturally into this catalogue. The *berakhah* is not narrowly about *techiyyat ha-meitim* alone; it is about *gevurot*, the full range of God's power to give and sustain life. Rain belongs there.

The phrase *matzmiach yeshuah* — God who makes salvation sprout — also contributes: *tzemach*, growth from the ground, is yet another image interweaving rain and human origins. As was noted, in *Bereishit* 2, humans themselves were formed from the earth and brought to life. Rain does not merely water crops; it enacts the paradigm by which God brings forth life from what is buried.

### Request for Rain

The *mishnah* continues: *ve-she'elah be-virkat ha-shanim* — one asks for rain in the *berakhah* of the years, i.e., the ninth *berakhah* of the *Shemoneh Esrei*, where one says *veten tal u-matar li-vrakhah*. The *gemara* asks *mai ta'ama* — why there?

Rav Yosef answers: *mitoch she-hi parnasah, keva'uha be-virkat parnasah* — because rain is *parnasah*, sustenance, and therefore it was placed in the *berakhah* that deals with *parnasah*. This distinction between where rain is *mentioned* (second *berakhah*, as part of divine power over life and death) and where it is *requested* (ninth *berakhah*, as a practical matter of livelihood) reflects a careful logic: the theological dimension of rain belongs in *gevurot*, while the pragmatic need for it belongs alongside one's request for a prosperous year.

### Havdalah/Knowledge

The *mishnah* rules that *havdalah* — the declaration distinguishing *Shabbat* from the weekday — is recited within the *berakhah* of *chonein ha-da'at*, the fourth *berakhah* of the *Shemoneh Esrei*, which concerns God's gift of intellect and knowledge. Again, the *gemara* asks *mai ta'ama* — why?

Rav Yosef answers: *mitoch she-hi chokhmah, keva'uha be-virkat chokhmah* — because *havdalah* involves the act of distinguishing, and distinguishing is an act of intellect, and therefore it was placed in the *berakhah* of wisdom and knowledge.

The Rabbis add a complementary rationale: *mitoch she-hu chol, keva'uha be-virkat chol* — because *havdalah* concerns the beginning of the weekday, they placed it in the first *berakhah* unique to weekday *davening*. The first three *berakhot* of the *Shemoneh Esrei* are recited on *Shabbat* as well, but the fourth, *chonein ha-da'at*, is the first specifically weekday *berakhah*. It is the moment one enters the *chol*, and therefore it is where the declaration *mavdil bein kodesh le-chol* belongs.

The *Gra* points out that this dispute about rationale actually explains our current liturgical practice. We begin *havdalah* in *Shemoneh Esrei* with the phrase *atah chonantanu le-adam da'at u-malamed le-enosh binah* — "You have graced the human with knowledge and taught understanding" — which places *havdalah* in the framework of the *berakhah* about *da'at* and *chokhmah*, satisfying the first position. But then we insert *mavdil bein kodesh le-chol* before concluding the *berakhah*. Why specifically there and not at the very opening? Because by the end of the *berakhah*, the *Shemoneh Esrei* has already transitioned to personal requests — *choneinu mei-itkha da'ah binah ve-haskel* — and one does not make personal requests on *Shabbat*. One must therefore declare the separation of *Shabbat* from the weekday — *ha-mavdil bein kodesh le-chol* — before issuing the personal petition *choneinu mei-itkha*. But one does not begin with that declaration; instead one opens with *atah chonantanu*, keeping *havdalah* embedded within the *berakhah* of *da'at*. The *Gra*'s observation is that this ordering satisfies *both* positions simultaneously: the framing is about intellect and *chokhmah*, while the placement of *mavdil bein kodesh le-chol* before the personal petition reflects the view that this *berakhah* is the first *berakhah* of *chol*.

---

---

# Berakhot 33

## Da'at & Intellect

### Gedolah De'ah

The sugya opens in the middle of 33a, roughly six lines before the lines widen, with a teaching of Rabbi Ami. *Amar Rabbi Ami: gedolah de'ah shenitnah bitchilat berakhah shel chol* — great is intellect, for it was placed as the very first of the weekday *berakhot*. The reasoning is that before one can engage meaningfully with *teshuvah*, *selichah*, and all the other petitions that follow, one first needs the capacity to assess and think about one's life. Intellect is therefore the most fundamental thing we ask of God, the prerequisite for everything else.

### De'ah Between Names

Rabbi Ami adds a second observation: *gedolah de'ah shenitnah bein shtei otiyot* — great is intellect because it appears between two of God's names. The verse supporting this is *ki El de'ot Hashem* (I Samuel 2:3): the word *de'ot* is bracketed by divine names, demonstrating how central knowledge is to the divine order.

The passage then makes a striking and seemingly harsh claim: *kol mi she'ein bo de'ah assur lerachem alav* — whoever lacks intellect, it is forbidden to have compassion for them. The proof-text is *ki lo am binot hu, al ken lo yerachamenu osehu* — they are not a people of understanding, therefore their Creator will not have compassion on them. The statement does invite concern about those who are born without certain intellectual capacities, but the context of the verse points in a different direction. The phrase *ki lo am binot hu* does not mean a people that has no intellect; it means a people that is not being thoughtful — that is not using its intellect responsibly. The statement, then, is less about withholding compassion from those unable to think and more about human responsibility: one who brings troubles upon oneself by acting irresponsibly and without reflection has, in a certain sense, received what their choices led to, in the way that a parent sometimes allows a child to learn from mistakes. This reading is reinforced by the parallel statement that follows: *kol adam sheyesh bo de'ah* — whoever has intellect — in which *yesh bo de'ah* must mean uses intellect in one's life, not merely possesses it innately. The *Maharsha*, it should be noted, has his own reading of this passage, understanding the value of compassion itself as rooted in the concept of *de'ah*.

### Da'ah as Beit HaMikdash

Rabbi Elazar then takes up the same structural point — a concept placed between two divine names — and applies it to the *Beit HaMikdash*: *gedolah mikdash shenitnah bein shtei otiyot*, derived from the verse *pa'alta Hashem mikdash Hashem* (Exodus 15:17), where "Sanctuary" appears between two instances of God's name.

Rabbi Elazar then connects the two themes: *kol adam sheyesh bo de'ah ke'ilu nivneh Beit HaMikdash b'yamav* — anyone who has (that is, uses) intellect, it is as if the *Beit HaMikdash* was built in his days. The reasoning follows directly from the structural parallel: just as *de'ah* is bracketed by two divine names and so is the *mikdash*, the person who lives a life of *de'ah* inhabits a kind of sanctified existence analogous to the presence of the Temple. And crucially, *yesh bo de'ah* here too should be read as one who actively employs intellect — not merely anyone who happens to be intelligent by birth.

This is worth pausing over, because it is the same Rabbi Elazar who earlier said that *tefillah* is greater than *korbanot*, and who also said that since the *churban habayit* it is as if the gates of prayer have been sealed. Taken together, these statements form a coherent picture of how one sustains religious meaning without the *Beit HaMikdash*: *tefillah* still matters, and even when the gates of prayer seem sealed, living a life of *de'ah* creates an intimate relationship with God — as though the *mikdash* itself had been rebuilt.

### Vengeance Challenge

Rav Achah Karchinah challenges the logical principle being applied: *ella me'atah gedolah nekamah shenitnah bein shtei otiyot* — if appearing between two divine names makes something praiseworthy, then vengeance too should be declared great, since the verse reads *El nekamot Hashem El nekamot hofia* (Psalms 94:1), with *nekamot* flanked on both sides by God's name.

The response is a direct affirmation: *in, lemilsayehi gedolah hi* — yes, when it is appropriate, that is indeed a great thing. The *Gemara* then cites Ulla's interpretation of why the word *nekamot* appears twice in that verse: one instance represents *nekamah* for good, the other for evil. The positive usage is derived from *hofia mehar Paran* — God's revelation from Mount Paran — which Rashi understands as a reference to the *midrash* whereby the nations' refusal of the Torah resulted in Israel's receiving it, making their loss Israel's benefit, a kind of redemptive *nekamah*.

This connects to a broader theological question: there is a *mitzvah* of *vehalachta bidrachav*, of emulating God's ways. The standard application, as *Chazal* formulate it, is *mah hu rachum af atah rachum, mah hu chanun af atah chanun* — as God is compassionate and gracious, so should you be. But one might ask: why limit the emulation to those particular attributes? The *Rambam* addresses this by arguing that the specific divine names in the verse — *rachum*, *chanun*, and so on — are those whose application has been authorized by the Torah as models for human conduct. The name *El nekamot* then raises a genuine question: is *nekamah* among the attributes we are meant to emulate? The *Gemara*'s answer is that in its proper context it is indeed valuable — but the very difficulty of defining that proper context, and of setting its limits, is what makes these questions about divine attributes and which ones are held up for emulation so consequential.

---

## Insertions Formula

The *Gemara* situates this discussion of *da'at* within the broader topic of where various insertions are made in the *Amidah*. *Mashiv haruach umorid hagashem* is said in the second *berakhah* of *gevurot*; *veten tal umatar livracha* is inserted into *birkat hashanim*; and *havdalah* is inserted into *chonen hada'at*, the first of the weekday petitions, because it marks the transition to the weekday cycle and connects naturally to the theme of *yeshuat da'at*. The *Gemara* treats *chonen hada'at* as the appropriate vessel for *havdalah* precisely because intellect is the gateway to purposeful weekday life.

---

## Chonen HaDa'at Status

### Rabbi Akiva Position

The *Gemara* turns, four lines into the wider section, to a dispute about the precise form of *chonen hada'at*. Rabbi Akiva holds that *havdalah* is recited as an independent, separate *berakhah* on *Motzaei Shabbat* — not inserted into an existing *berakhah* but standing on its own.

### AKG Enactment

Rav Shemen bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* established for Israel the *berakhot*, *tefillot*, *kedushos*, and *havdalot*. This is a general assumption of the *Gemara* — that the *tefillot* as a whole, including the *Shemoneh Esrei*, were composed during the period of the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*, which predates the *churban* and belongs to the early *Bayit Sheni* era. The question then follows: if it was all established then, why is there a debate about whether *havdalah* belongs inside *chonen hada'at* or stands as a separate *berakhah*? Should we not simply look back and determine what the original *takkanah* was?

*Tosafot* raises the obvious difficulty: we have been *davening* since that time — how can there be a debate about something practiced continuously? The most natural answer is that there was genuine variation in practice, and the debate is over which form is correct. This is not without parallel: the dispute between Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam about the order of the *parshiyot* in *tefillin* is a similar case, and the *Bar Kokhba* caves yielded *tefillin* with both orderings, confirming that divergent practices can and do coexist. Even when a basic form was established, the *Gemara* acknowledges — and the *Tosefta* bears out — that there was a period of latitude during which certain *berakhot* could be combined or arranged differently. The *Gemara* then explains concretely how the confusion arose, through the history of *havdalah*'s movement between the *Shemoneh Esrei* and recitation over a cup of wine.

---

## Havdalah History

### Havdalah Transitions

The *Gemara* explains the back-and-forth history of *havdalah*. Initially — *betichilah kvauha bitfilah* — it was fixed within the *Shemoneh Esrei*. Then, as the community became more prosperous — *he'ashiru* — they elevated *havdalah* into a more prominent ritual and established it over a cup of wine, presumably removing it from the *Shemoneh Esrei*. When poverty returned — *he'anu* — they reverted and placed it back in the *Shemoneh Esrei*. This movement back and forth is what caused confusion about the original form and accounts for the debate between Rabbi Akiva and the other *tanna'im* about its precise placement.

### Double Havdalah

Once *havdalah* was reinstated in the *Shemoneh Esrei*, the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* declared: *hamavdil bitfilah tzarich sheyavdil al hakos* — one who recites *havdalah* in the *tefillah* must also recite it over a cup of wine. The *Gemara* cites this in two parallel formulations — first attributed to Rabbi Yochanan via Rav Shemen bar Abba, then again via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in a *baraita* — and then again as a ruling of Rava and Rav Yosef together.

One might ask: if the community had become poor and could not afford wine, how were they now being told to do both? A reasonable resolution is that the ruling means that even if one cannot afford wine, one fulfills the obligation through the *Shemoneh Esrei*, but once resources permit, one should also do *havdalah al hakos*. The *havdalah al hakos* is not merely a redundant ritual — it serves an additional function with its own logic. Just as *kiddush al hakos* frames *Shabbat* in the context of eating, *havdalah al hakos* frames the transition out of *Shabbat* and into weekday eating. This is why the *halakhah* is that even one who has recited *havdalah* in the *Shemoneh Esrei* may not eat on *Motzaei Shabbat* until reciting *havdalah al hakos* — the two performances serve distinct purposes, not redundant ones. Indeed, *havdalah al hakos* has an explicit counterpart in *kiddush al hakos*: just as *kiddush* is said both in the *Shemoneh Esrei* (in *mekadesh HaShabbat*) and over a cup of wine Friday night, so too *havdalah* belongs in both contexts.

### Sufficiency Debate

The *Gemara* then cites Rava's objection from a *baraita* about related cases. The *baraita* states: if one forgot to mention *gevurot geshamim* in *techiyat hameitim*, or forgot to ask for *veten tal umatar* in *birkat hashanim*, one goes back to the proper place. But if one forgot *havdalah* in *chonen hada'at*, one does not go back — *ein machzirin oto* — because one can recite it over a cup of wine. This raises a challenge: the language *mipnei sheyakhol leomra al hakos* — "because one can say it over the cup" — implies that reciting it over the cup is merely an option, available to compensate for missing it in the *Shemoneh Esrei*, not something required as a separate obligation every *Motzaei Shabbat*. The *Gemara* resolves this by rewriting the reading: *lo teima mipnei sheyakhol leomra al hakos, ela eima mipnei she'omra al hakos* — do not say "because one can recite it," but rather "because one will in any case recite it." One who missed *havdalah* in the *Shemoneh Esrei* need not repeat the *Shemoneh Esrei*, because the *havdalah al hakos* that will come later covers it, and both components will be present regardless.

This leads to a sharper question, introduced through a *baraita* taught by Rav Acha Rikha before Rav Chinana: *hamavdil bitfilah meshubach yoter mimi sheyavdil al hakos* — reciting *havdalah* in the *Shemoneh Esrei* is superior to reciting it over the cup of wine. The *baraita* continues: *ve'im hivdil b'zu u'v'zu yanuchu lo berakhot al rosho* — if one recited it in both, blessings should come upon his head. The *Gemara* immediately identifies a contradiction within the *baraita* itself — *hagufa kashya*: if reciting *havdalah* in the *Shemoneh Esrei* alone is superior and sufficient, then adding *havdalah al hakos* afterward would constitute a *berakhah she'einah tzrikhah*, a blessing that is not needed. And the *Gemara* cites Rav (or Reish Lakish, or Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish together) that one who recites an unnecessary *berakhah* transgresses *lo tissa* — taking God's name in vain. While it is generally assumed that this application of *lo tissa* is an *asmakhta* rather than a biblical prohibition, it is worth noting that many *Sephardic poskim* treat *berakhah levatalah* and *berakhah she'einah tzrikhah* with great stringency, holding it to be a genuine biblical violation.

The *Gemara* resolves the internal contradiction by rereading the *baraita*: it should be understood as saying that reciting *havdalah* in one context alone — whichever one — is praiseworthy, and if one managed to do both, it is also fine. This reading, however, effectively presents *havdalah al hakos* as optional when *havdalah* was said in the *Shemoneh Esrei*, which stands in tension with everything the *Gemara* said earlier. The *Gemara* thus reveals that there were in fact two positions: one that viewed the two forms of *havdalah* as presenting a choice (with *Shemoneh Esrei* being the better option), and one that insisted both were obligatory. Over time, the position requiring both prevailed — but the earlier tradition of optionality left traces in these *baraitot*.

### Forgot Both

Rav Chisda asked Rav Sheshet: *ta b'zu u'v'zu mahu* — what is the rule if one forgot *havdalah* in the *Shemoneh Esrei* and also missed it over a cup of wine? The precise scenario requires some thought — what exactly constitutes having "missed" it over the cup? Perhaps one already drank wine, or perhaps the night has passed. In any case, Rav Sheshet ruled: *ta b'zu u'v'zu chozer lerosh* — one must repeat the *Shemoneh Esrei* from the beginning. The *Gemara* does not return to explain the exact parameters of this scenario, but the principle stands.

### Havdalah Like Kiddush

Ravina then asked Rava: *hilkheta mai* — what is the practical ruling? Rava answered: *ki kiddush* — it is like *kiddush*. Just as one recites *mekadesh haShabbat* in the *Shemoneh Esrei* on Friday night and then recites *kiddush* over the cup, so too with *havdalah*: even though one said it in the *Shemoneh Esrei*, one recites it again *al hakos*. The parallel to *kiddush* is a strong one, and if anything strengthens the case for the mandatory double recitation, since *mekadesh HaShabbat* is an explicit, fully formed *berakhah* in its own right — and yet we still require *kiddush al hakos* afterward. How much more so *havdalah*, which in the opinion of the *rabanan* is merely an insertion within *chonen hada'at* and not a standalone *berakhah*, should require the additional ritual over the cup.

---

## Yom Tov After Shabbat

### Blessing Placement

The next section of the *Gemara* concerns *Yom Tov* that falls on *Motzaei Shabbat*, which creates a structural problem: on a regular weekday, *havdalah* is inserted into *chonen hada'at*, the first of the weekday *berakhot*. But on *Yom Tov*, the *Shemoneh Esrei* has only seven *berakhot* — the middle *berakhot* of the weekday are not recited. There is therefore no *chonen hada'at* into which *havdalah* can be inserted. The debate is then between Rabbi Akiva and the *rabanan* about what to do in this case.

The *Gemara* introduces this through a scene: Rav Zeira was riding on a donkey with Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin following behind him. Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin asked: is it true that you said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the *halakhah* follows Rabbi Eliezer when *Yom Tov* falls after *Shabbat* — that is, that *havdalah* is said in *modim*? Rav Zeira confirmed: *in*, yes.

The *Gemara* then asks: if it is stated as *halakhah*, that implies there is a genuine debate — but is there really one here? Perhaps all agree that when there is no *chonen hada'at* available, *havdalah* goes into *modim*? The *Gemara* answers that the *rabanan* do indeed dispute this in the ordinary case during the year, but as for *Yom Tov* after *Shabbat* specifically, perhaps all agree it goes into *modim*. The *Gemara* then raises the position of Rabbi Akiva, who would hold even in this case for a separate *berakhah*. But the response is decisive: the rest of the year we do not follow Rabbi Akiva's position of making *havdalah* a standalone *berakhah* — *de-tamnei sari tikkun taysha sari lo tikkun*, eighteen *berakhot* were enacted, not nineteen. By the same logic, on *Yom Tov* one cannot add an eighth *berakhah* — *sheva tikkun, tamnei lo tikkun*, seven were enacted, not eight. Rabbi Akiva's position is therefore rejected in both contexts.

### Modim Solution

The *Gemara* now seeks to determine the precise weight of the ruling for *Yom Tov* after *Shabbat*. Rav Zeira says to Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin: the formulation he heard was not *halakhah* but *matin* — we incline toward the ruling of Rabbi Eliezer, that *havdalah* is placed in *modim*. This is less than a definitive *pesak* but still an operative guidance.

The *Gemara* then records a range of positions: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi said in the name of *Rabbeinu* — which Rashi identifies as Rav — *halakhah*, that we rule like Rabbi Eliezer. Others say *mattei*, we incline. Rabbi Yochanan said that *modim* is the placement and, going further, that there is no real dispute about it when *Yom Tov* falls after *Shabbat*, since there is simply no other place to put it. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's formulation was the most cautious: *nirin* — it appears correct. Rav Zeira ultimately instructs: take Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's formulation and rely on it — *nekot deRabbi Chiyya bar Abba beyadecha* — precisely because Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba was as careful with his *Rebbe*'s exact language as Rechava of Pumbedita. How careful was Rechava? He cited Rav Yehuda's teaching that the Temple Mount had a double *stoa* — a *stav* within a *stav* — using the term *stav* rather than the standard rabbinic term *istaba*, demonstrating that he preserved the precise word his *Rebbe* used. Here too, one can rely on Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's *nirin* as an accurate transmission of what Rabbi Yochanan actually said.

The upshot is that the practical conclusion — confirmed by Rav Yosef's formulation of *vatodieinu* — is that when *Yom Tov* falls on *Motzaei Shabbat*, *havdalah* is incorporated into the *berakhah* of *mekadesh Yisrael vehazmanim*. The liturgy Rav and Shmuel composed for this purpose — *vatodieinu Hashem Elokeinu et mishpetei tzidkecha* — is described by Rav Yosef as *marganita beVavel*, a pearl established in Bavel: a beautiful piece of liturgy that threads together the distinction between the sanctity of *Shabbat* and the sanctity of *Yom Tov*, using the language *bein kedushat Shabbat likedushat Yom Tov hivdalta*, "You distinguished between the holiness of *Shabbat* and the holiness of *Yom Tov*." The separation is not between the sacred and the mundane, as in the ordinary *havdalah*, but between two degrees of sanctity — and this language captures that with elegance. This is the text we use today.

---

## Al Kan Tzipor

### Silencing Rules

The *Gemara* transitions to a *Mishnah* that lists expressions to be silenced during prayer. Two cases are specified: one who says *al kan tzipor yagi'u rakhamekha* — "Your compassion reaches to the bird's nest" — and one who says *modim modim*, repeating the word *modim* twice. In both cases, the ruling is *meshatikin oto* — the person is silenced. The context appears to be someone leading the prayer or perhaps interjecting during the *davening*, though the exact setting — whether in *Shemoneh Esrei*, in *tachanun*, or during *targum* (the Aramaic translation of the Torah reading, which the *Yerushalmi* names explicitly) — is not entirely clear.

The *Mishnah* also lists *ve'al tov yizakher shemekha* — "and for the good Your name shall be remembered" — as problematic, since it implies praising God only for good things, whereas the principle is that one must bless God for the bad as for the good, a topic the *Gemara* will return to in a later *Mishnah*.

The case of *modim modim* is understood readily: repeating the word creates the appearance of acknowledging two separate divine powers — *mishum de'mechzei ke'shtei reshuyot* — which in a Zoroastrian context was a live concern. Even if unintentional, such formulations cannot be permitted. The *Gemara* presents a case of Rabba waiting until a *shliach tzibbur* finished a passage in which he said *atah chasta al kan tzipor, atah chus verakhem aleinu* — You had compassion on the bird's nest, now have compassion on us. Rabba turned to Abaye and said, see how well this *talmid chakham* knows how to appease his Creator — a remark that Abaye recognized as sarcastic, since Rabba intended to test whether Abaye would catch what was wrong. Abaye responded by citing the *Mishnah*: we silence him.

### Two Concerns

The *Gemara* presents two opinions from *amora'im* in the West — Rabbi Yose bar Avin and Rabbi Yose bar Zvida — about what exactly is wrong with *al kan tzipor yagi'u rakhamekha*.

The first opinion is *mipnei shemattil kinah bema'aseh bereishit* — because it causes jealousy among God's creatures. The expression singles out the birds as recipients of divine compassion, implying that other creatures are not similarly cared for, which gives rise to a kind of hierarchical jealousy within creation. The *Yerushalmi*'s version of this concern frames it slightly differently: the one praying is essentially complaining to God — "You had compassion on the mother bird; why won't You have compassion on me?" — which is a kind of challenge or reproach, finding fault with divine conduct.

The second opinion is *mipnei she'oseh midosav shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu rakhamim ve'einam ela gezeirot* — because the person treats God's attributes as expressions of compassion when they are in fact no more than divine edicts. This is the more philosophically weighty position, and it directly implicates the question of *ta'amei hamitzvot*.

### Ta'amei HaMitzvot

The question of why *al kan tzipor* is problematic opens onto one of the central debates in Jewish thought: should the commandments be understood as expressions of underlying values — as *ta'amei hamitzvot* — or should they be treated as pure *gezeirot*, expressions of divine will whose value lies entirely in the act of obedience?

Rashi's reading of this *Gemara* (which appears similarly in Tractate *Megillah*) supports the latter view: the commandments, including *shiluach haken*, are to be approached purely as matters of obedience. To say that God's compassion reaches to the birds is to suggest that the *mitzvah* is motivated by God's care for animal suffering — and that, according to this position, is a misrepresentation. The commandment is a *gezeirah*, and its entire value is the obedience it demands.

Both the *Rambam* and *Ramban* resist this conclusion, though they approach it differently. The *Rambam* reinterprets *gezeirot* not as commandments without reason but as edicts issued precisely because God cares about His subjects — namely, us. God does not directly care about animal suffering; rather, the commandment is designed to cultivate within us the attribute of compassion, since how we treat animals shapes what kind of people we become. The problem with saying *al kan tzipor yagi'u rakhamekha* is therefore not that we sought a reason for the commandment, but that we found the wrong one — God's compassion is directed at us, not at the bird per se. The *Ramban* takes a different tack: he acknowledges that there is an opinion here which treats it as pure obedience, but he maintains that we do not *pasken* that way, and that the Torah intends its commandments as expressions of genuine values that should inform human life beyond the specific acts commanded.

The two opinions within the *Gemara* can themselves be read as taking positions on this debate from two different angles. The first opinion — that the prayer causes jealousy among God's creatures — may be understood as a critique not of *ta'amei hamitzvot* per se but of applying them too narrowly: by saying God is compassionate specifically toward birds, one has defined the value too restrictively, failing to see that the Torah's concern for compassion extends across all creation, not just one species. The second opinion — that it turns *midot* into expressions of *rakhamim* when they are really *gezeirot* — expresses the opposite concern: any engagement with the underlying value risks undermining the sense of obligation, because once one locates the *reason* for a commandment, one may feel entitled to substitute other means of achieving that value in place of the commandment itself. These two positions thus represent the two risks inherent in the project of *ta'amei hamitzvot*: going too far in defining the value, and going too far in allowing the value to displace the obligation.

---

## Excessive Praise

### Too Many Names

The *Gemara* introduces a case involving Rabbi Chanina. A certain person went down to lead the *Shemoneh Esrei* before Rabbi Chanina and composed an extended litany of divine attributes: *ha'El hagadol hagibor vehanora veha'adir veha'azuz veha'yirei veha'chazak veha'amitz vehavadai vehanichbad* — going on and on well beyond the standard three names. Rabbi Chanina waited until the *shliach tzibbur* had finished and then addressed him: *siyamtinhu lekulei shevakhei demarakh* — have you exhausted all the praises of your Master? *lama li kulei hai* — why all of this?

### Three Names Principle

Rabbi Chanina explains: the three names we use — *ha'El hagadol hagibor* — would themselves be impermissible were it not for the fact that *Moshe Rabbeinu* used them in the Torah (*Devarim* 10:17) and the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* subsequently established them in the liturgy. Once you begin praising God, there is in principle no place to stop — God is infinite, and any finite list of attributes is inadequate. The only license we have to praise God with any words at all is that these specific words were used in the Torah and fixed by the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*. To add further attributes is to step beyond that license without authorization.

### King Parable

The *Gemara* illustrates this with a *mashal*: a king of flesh and blood possessed millions of gold coins, and his subjects praised him for his wealth in silver. This is not a compliment — *vehalo genai hu lo* — it is unbecoming. To praise someone with lesser attributes than they actually possess, even if those attributes are genuinely impressive in ordinary terms, is a form of diminishment when applied to one whose actual stature renders those attributes trivial.

The broader principle is *lekha dumiyah tehillah* — to You, God, silence is praise. Recognizing that no human language can adequately describe the infinite, the most honest posture is restraint. This is consistent with the *Rambam*'s theology of negative theology: any positive attribute applied to God is, strictly speaking, a misrepresentation, because every human concept is finite and therefore categorically inadequate to describe God. In the specific context of prayer, the implication is clear: our license to praise God at all is dependent entirely on the formulations authorized by *Moshe* and fixed by the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*, and the appropriate response to the impulse to say more is to recognize that less — ultimately, silence — is truer.

---

## Free Will

### Heaven's Hands

Rabbi Chanina teaches: *hakol biydei shamayim chutz miyirat shamayim* — everything is in the hands of heaven except the fear of heaven. The verse he brings is Moshe's address in *Devarim* (10:12): *ve'atah Yisrael, mah Hashem Elohekha sho'el me'imakh ki im leyirah* — what does God ask of you but to fear Him? The asking presupposes that it is up to the person to give or withhold — God will not compel it. A person's genetic endowment, the circumstances into which they are born, the full range of natural and historical conditions — all of these may be determined from above. But whether one ultimately chooses to fear God and do what is right: that is the one domain God does not control, and therefore the one domain that is truly ours.

### Treasure Yirah

The *Gemara* then raises an apparent objection: if Moshe says *ki im leyirah*, as if fear of heaven were a modest request, is *yirat shamayim* really a small thing? Rabbi Chanina cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: *ein lo leHakadosh Baruch Hu beveit genazav ela otzar shel yirat shamayim* — God has in His storehouse nothing but the treasury of fear of heaven. *Yirat shamayim* is the rarest and most precious thing there is — all the more so because it is the one thing God does not Himself supply. That it is left entirely to human choice makes it, when genuinely achieved, extraordinarily valuable.

### Moshe Perspective

The *Gemara* resolves the tension between Moshe's casual tone and the rarity of *yirat shamayim* through a *mashal* of Rabbi Chanina: if someone is asked for a large vessel and has one readily available, it feels like nothing to give. If someone is asked for a small vessel and lacks it entirely, even that small request feels enormous. The assessment of difficulty is always relative to the one being asked. For Moshe, who had attained *yirat shamayim* at the highest level, it appeared a simple thing — *in legabei Moshe milta zutraita hi*, for Moshe it was a small matter. But that does not mean it is small for us. The very fact that God treasures it so highly reflects how genuinely rare and difficult it is for human beings to achieve.

---

## Shema Repetition

### Word vs. Verse

The *Gemara* returns to the category of silencing. The *Mishnah* ruled that one who says *modim modim* is silenced. A *baraita* states: *ha-koreh et Shema vekhophlah, harei zeh meguneh* — one who reads *Shema* and doubles it is acting reprehensibly. The *Gemara* notes a distinction: the *Mishnah* calls for active silencing, whereas the *baraita* uses the word *meguneh*, which is less than silencing — the person's behavior is inappropriate, but one does not necessarily remove them or intervene in the same way.

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent tension by distinguishing between two different kinds of repetition: one who repeats each word individually — *Shema Shema Yisrael Yisrael* — and one who repeats an entire *pasuk*. According to Rashi, repeating each individual word is the lesser offense — it is *meguneh* but not grounds for silencing, since it does not create the impression of acknowledging two divine powers; the person simply seems to be repeating themselves. Repeating an entire *pasuk*, however, gives the appearance of directing one *pasuk* to one divinity and the second *pasuk* to another — that is what rises to the level requiring silencing.

*Tosafot* takes the opposite position: it is repeating each individual word that is the more serious problem, while repeating the entire *pasuk* is the lesser issue. This is in some tension with Rashi, and notably has relevance to those who, out of anxiety about having had sufficient *kavanah*, repeat words or passages.

### Kavanah Later

Rav Papa asked Abaye: *ve-dilma me-ikara lo kivan date'yeh ve-hashta kivan date'yeh* — perhaps the reason someone repeats the *pasuk* is that he initially lacked sufficient *kavanah* and is now repeating it with proper intention? This is a recognizable concern: people do in practice repeat words or verses out of concern that they did not have adequate focus the first time.

### Severe Response

Abaye's response is sharp: *havruta klapei shamaya?* — are you pals with heaven? The implication is that claiming one lacked *kavanah* and therefore deserves a do-over is a kind of presumptuous familiarity — as if one can casually admit to God that one was inattentive and expect to simply be given another opportunity. The *Gemara* pushes the point further: *ei lo kivan date'yeh me-ikara, machinan leh bemarzafta de-nafcha ad de-makhvin date'yeh* — if one did not have *kavanah* the first time, we beat him with a blacksmith's hammer until he achieves *kavanah*. The violence of the image is clearly hyperbolic, but the point is serious: the correct response to insufficient *kavanah* is not to normalize the makeup, which in effect rewards the lack of attention and encourages it going forward. By refusing any remedy and insisting that the failure stands, one creates a stronger incentive to have *kavanah* in the first place. The *Gemara*'s approach here is not to deny that people struggle with *kavanah* — it is to say that offering a systematic makeup is precisely the wrong way to address the problem. The *sugya* breaks off at this point, to be continued.

---

---

# Berakhot 34

## Modim & Dualism

### Modim Dualism

Berakhot 34 is the final daf of this *perek* and of the first half of Masechet Berakhot, which has dealt throughout with *Shema* and *Shemoneh Esrei*. Yesterday's discussion concluded with the problem of saying *Modim Modim* — repeating the word *modim* twice — which raises the concern of dualism, as though one were acknowledging two divine powers. A *Tosafot* at the top of 34a is both generally relevant and particularly apt for this time of year.

*Tosafot* raises the question of *amar psuka psuka vekafla* — whether it is worse to repeat each word or each *pasuk* — and then, a few lines below, addresses a related practice: *ve-otam bnei adam she-omrim beis o gimmel pe'amim Shema Yisrael be-Yom HaKippurim*, those people who actually repeat *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* multiple times. This apparently occurred in certain contexts — perhaps when the *Sifrei Torah* are taken out — though the precise occasion is not entirely clear. *Tosafot* rules, following *Rashi*, that *meshaskin otam*, one silences them, since *Rashi* understands the entire problem to be the repetition of the *pasuk* itself. Even according to the reading of *Rabbenu Chananel*, where one would not technically silence them, the practice is still *meguna*, unseemly and to be looked down upon.

*Tosafot* then considers a possible defense: *shema lo chashiv ela kshe-koreh Krias Shema be-onatah*, perhaps the concern applies only in the context of the *mitzvah* of *Krias Shema*, where the focus is *kabalas ol malchus shamayim* — accepting the yoke of heaven — and where the sensitivity to any appearance of dualism is therefore heightened. Outside that specific *mitzvah* context, repeating a *pasuk* might be less problematic. Even so, *Tosafot* concludes: *u-mikol makom tov shelo lomar* — in any case, the safe course is not to repeat.

However, *Tosafot* explicitly defends the practice of saying *Hashem Hu HaElokim* seven times on *Yom Kippur* and *Yom HaArava* — that is, *Hoshana Rabba*. The explanation is *keneged zayin reki'im*, corresponding to the seven heavens, praising God who dwells above all seven. Moreover, *Hashem Hu HaElokim* appears twice in the same *pasuk* in the narrative of Elijah, lending it further scriptural grounding. So *Hashem Hu HaElokim Hashem Hu HaElokim* is a *minhag kasher*, a legitimate practice — while repeating *Shema Yisrael* is not. The distinction *Tosafot* draws is important: the concern about repeating *psukim* is not an absolute prohibition against all repetition, but one that is tied specifically to the dualism concern, and perhaps even more narrowly to the *mitzvah* context of *Krias Shema* itself.

A related question — about repeating individual words within a *pasuk* due to the *niggun* — touches less on dualism concerns and more on whether doing so constitutes a *hefsek* in the *davening* or a corruption of the *pasuk*. That is a separate discussion left for another occasion.

### Yevarchucha Tovim

The first line of the *mishna* on 34a appears in parentheses: *ha-omer yevarchucha tovim harei zeh derech haminus* — one who says "let the good bless You" is following the way of heresy, often associated with certain Hebrew Christian practices. This line is bracketed because it does not appear in our standard text of the *mishna* and is absent from the *Yerushalmi* as well. It does, however, appear in the parallel *mishna* in Masechet Megillah, where the passage about *al kan tzipor yagiu rachamecha* — "Your compassion extends to the bird's nest" — raises related concerns about *ta'amei ha-mitzvos* and the proper framing of divine attributes. That *mishna* in Megillah includes this additional line. The underlying concern with *yevarchucha tovim* may again be a form of dualism — as though only the good praise the good God, implying a separate evil divinity receives the praise of the wicked.

---

## Shliach Tzibur Error

### Error Replacement

After the parenthetical, the *mishna* moves to a new topic: *ha-over lifnei hateiva veta'ah* — someone who leads the *davening* and makes an error. The *mishna* rules *ya'avor acher tachtav*, another person should take his place — even mid-*Shemoneh Esrei*. This could apply in the case where *meshaskin oto*, where we feel it necessary to remove the person; but as *Rashi* and *Tosafot* explain, it may simply be that the *shliach tzibbur* became so confused that he is incapable of continuing, and someone else must take over. *Shemoneh Esrei* mid-*tefillah* and all.

The *mishna* adds: *v'lo yehei sarvan b'ota sha'ah* — when you are asked at that moment of crisis to step in and replace someone, do not stage a show of modesty by saying "No, no, find someone else." The *tzibbur* is embarrassed; it is inappropriate for the *tzibbur* to be waiting without the *Shemoneh Esrei* continuing. If the *gabbai* calls on you, accept.

### Restart Point

*Me'heichan hu matchil?* From where does the replacement begin? *Mi-techilat ha-brachah she-ta'ah* — from the beginning of the *brachah* in which the original *shliach tzibbur* erred or became so confused he could not continue. If he was in the middle of *Atah Chonen*, the replacement begins from *Atah Chonen*; if he faltered in *Shomea Tefillah*, the replacement starts there. One does not go all the way to the beginning of *Shemoneh Esrei*, nor does one resume from the precise word at which the previous leader stopped. The unit is the *brachah*.

This reading — that the case is one of confusion rather than textual error per se — is how *Rashi* and *Tosafot* understand the context, since the *mishna* uses the word *ta'ah*, which normally implies error, not inability to continue. The contextual reading is nonetheless well-founded given what follows.

### Amen Distraction

The *mishna* then addresses a distinct ruling about the *shliach tzibbur*: *ha-over lifnei hateiva lo ya'aneh amen achar ha-kohanim mipnei ha-tiruf* — the *shliach tzibbur* should not answer *amen* after the *kohanim* during *Birchas Kohanim*, because of the concern of *tiruf*, distraction or confusion. It is difficult to imagine how answering *amen* could so thoroughly confuse a person, but the concern is that if he is not *davening* from a *siddur*, answering *amen* shifts his mental focus, and he risks being unable to return smoothly to *Sim Shalom* after *Birchas Kohanim* is complete. If he does have a *siddur* in front of him, the concern presumably does not apply to the same degree — a point the *mishna* will address shortly.

It is worth pausing on the broader assumption embedded here. The *mishna* takes for granted that *Birchas Kohanim* is performed daily — which is the current *minhag Sefardim* and the practice assumed throughout the *Gemara* and all the *mishnayos*. *Tosafot* and the *Rama* must therefore defend the *minhag Ashkenaz* of limiting *Birchas Kohanim* to the *regalim*. Their basic answer — the *Rama*'s in particular — is that *Birchas Kohanim* is associated with *simcha* and the joy of blessing *am Yisrael be-ahava*, and that given the ongoing persecution and economic hardship of Jewish life in Ashkenazic lands, the sense of *simcha* required was absent except on *yom tov*, which itself carries the added association of *simchat ha-regel* and the original context of the priestly blessing in the *Beis HaMikdash*. This reasoning is not in the *Gemara*; the *Gemara* assumes daily *Birchas Kohanim*. What *Tosafot* is doing — and this is characteristic of the *Tosafists* broadly — is not advocating a change of practice, but reconciling an established grassroots reality with the *Gemara*'s expectations.

A parallel can be noted: the *Ashkenazim* similarly do not recite *Shehecheyanu* at a *bris milah*, while *Sefardim* do. The answer given is along similar lines — that the infant's pain makes it inappropriate. These patterns of constriction in expressions of joy likely reflect the lived reality of centuries of *Ashkenazi* life under conditions of oppression more severe than those generally experienced under Islamic rule. That historical asymmetry appears to have had genuine liturgical consequences.

The *mishna* also takes for granted that if other *kohanim* are present, the *shliach tzibbur* who is a *kohen* does not participate in *Birchas Kohanim* — because it would distract him. This despite the fact that other *Gemaros* indicate that a *kohen* who is present and does not *duchen* violates the obligation implied by *koh tevarchu et Benei Yisrael*. Evidently the *mishna* accepts that when both roles cannot be fulfilled simultaneously without distraction, the *shliach tzibbur* is excused from *Birchas Kohanim*. *Tosafot* on the question of whether the *shliach tzibbur* calls out *Kohanim* or prompts each word — *yevarechecha* and so on — explores the extent to which his role in *Birchas Kohanim* is itself a potential source of distraction or interruption, arriving at several positions on the matter.

### Sole Kohen Exception

*V'im ein sham kohen ela hu* — if the *shliach tzibbur* is the only *kohen* present, the *mishna* rules *lo yissa kapav*: he should not *duchen* at all. So great is the concern that he will lose his focus that *Birchas Kohanim* is simply skipped entirely rather than risk the *shliach tzibbur* becoming so confused he cannot continue. *Im havtachato she-hu nosei et kapav ve-chozer li-tefillato* — only if he is personally confident in his ability to complete *Birchas Kohanim* and return seamlessly to his role as *shliach tzibbur* is he permitted to do so. The closing cases thus illuminate what the *mishna*'s concern throughout this passage has been: that someone becomes so confused they cannot continue — which in turn explains *Rashi* and *Tosafot*'s reading of the earlier cases.

---

## Refusal Protocol

### Three Asks

A *baraita* is introduced: *over lifnei hateiva tzarich lesarev* — one who is asked to lead the *davening* must initially refuse. "No, no, don't pick me, ask someone else, I'm not suited for it." *V'im eino mesarev* — if he does not refuse and says, "Great, you want me as *shliach tzibbur*? Wonderful!" — *domeh le-tavshil she-ein bo melach*, he is like a stew with no salt. There is a tastelessness to such eagerness, a lack of refinement and *derech eretz*. One should not be the first to rush toward a position of *kavod*.

However, *v'im mesarev yoter midai* — if he refuses excessively, genuinely and repeatedly declining when the *tzibbur* actually needs him — *domeh le-tavshil she-hiktikhato melach*, he is like a stew that has been ruined by too much salt. At least the tasteless stew is still edible; the over-salted one is not. If the *tzibbur* needs you, that need must ultimately be met.

*Keitzad hu oseh?* So what is the proper procedure? *Pa'am rishonah yesarev* — the first time you are asked, you decline. *Sheniyah mehavhev* — the second time, you begin to stir, to indicate some openness. *Shlishit poshet et raglav ve-tiyored* — the third time you extend your legs and go down to lead. The *Meiri* understands *mehavhev* not as a verbal "maybe" but as a physical gesture of readiness — you signal that you are prepared to go if asked again.

In practical terms, in a *minyan* where people know the procedure, this three-step dance can become formalized and somewhat pro forma — the *gabbai* asks, you decline, he asks again, you gesture openness, he asks a third time, you accept. If the situation is genuinely urgent, however, as the *mishna* above makes clear, that ritual is set aside entirely: you simply go.

### Derech Eretz

This protocol reflects a broader *derech eretz* principle: a person of quality does not present themselves as eager for positions of honor. The initial refusal is not insincere — it is an expression of genuine humility and an acknowledgment that perhaps someone else would be more suitable. But that same *derech eretz* demands that the refusal not be carried to the point of dysfunction. As with many expressions of courtesy, the procedure is understood by all parties involved and serves a real social and spiritual function even when its mechanics are known to everyone — much as expressions of gratitude remain meaningful even when their reciprocation is predictable.

### Three Moderations

A second *baraita* is then cited as a general principle: *shlosha ruban kasha u-miutan yafe* — three things where an abundance is harmful but a small amount is pleasant and appropriate. They are *se'or*, *melach*, and *sarvanut* — sourdough, salt, and refusal. A small amount of sourdough makes good bread; too much ruins it. A little salt enhances flavor; too much makes food inedible. And refusal: a modest initial reluctance is *derech eretz*, an expression of proper character — but too much refusal prevents the *tzibbur*'s needs from being met.

---

## Errors & Returns

### Rav Huna Units

*Amar Rav Huna*: if someone made an error in the first three *brachot* of *Shemoneh Esrei* — for example, failing to say *mashiv ha-ruach u-morid ha-geshem* and already having completed the second *brachah*, making it impossible to insert it — *chozer l'rosh*, one must return to the very beginning of *Shemoneh Esrei*. The first three *brachot* constitute a single indivisible unit. Any error requiring a correction means the entire unit must be redone.

*U-v'emtza'iyot* — for the middle *brachot*, Rav Huna holds that they too form one large unit, from *Atah Chonen* through *Shomea Tefillah*, and any mistake requiring a return means going all the way back to *Atah Chonen*. *U-v'acharonah* — for the final three, *chozer l'Avodah*, one returns to *Retzei*. So Rav Huna's scheme presents three discrete indivisible units; an error in any one sends you back to the beginning of that unit.

### Rav Assi Order

*Rav Assi amar: emtza'iyot ein lahem seder* — there is no fixed order to the middle *brachot*. According to *Rashi*'s reading, this means the middle *brachot* may even be said out of order. If one realizes mid-*tefillah* that one recited *v'tein tal u-matar* when one should have said *v'tein berachah*, and the error is discovered moments later — say, during *Al HaTzaddikim* — one may recite the correct *brachah* of *Barechenu* right there. There is no ordering constraint on the middle *brachot*. This sounds strange, but the underlying principle does have practical application: the *brachot* of *sheva brachot* under the *chuppah*, for instance, are ruled not to be *me'akev* in their order — a very important *halachah* to know should someone accidentally recite them out of sequence. Similarly, if a *ba'al kri'ah* makes the *berachah* after the *aliyah* first, the *halachah* is not invalidated.

### Tosafot Resolution

The *Gemara* then challenges both opinions from our *mishna*, which states *mi-techilat ha-brachah she-ta'ah* — you return to the beginning of the *brachah* in which you erred. *Rashi*'s version of the text includes *tiyuvta de-Rav Assi*, a refutation of Rav Assi, since the *mishna* implies you go back to a specific *brachah* and not that you can make it up wherever you are. Rav Huna's position is defended, albeit with some strain: when the *mishna* says "go back to the beginning of the *brachah*," it means *Atah Chonen*, because Rav Huna considers all the middle *brachot* to be one single *brachah*. This is admittedly a stretch.

*Tosafot* disagrees with *Rashi*'s *girsa* entirely. In *Tosafot*'s reading, the *Gemara* never actually refutes Rav Assi. What Rav Assi means by *ein lahem seder* is not that you may make up a missed *brachah* wherever you happen to be, but rather that you are not locked into a single indivisible unit — you may return specifically to the *brachah* where the error occurred, rather than being forced back to *Atah Chonen*. There *is* an ordering of sorts; it just operates at the level of the individual *brachah*. This is the practice: if you made a mistake in a particular *brachah* requiring a return, you go back to that *brachah*. This is how we rule — and it is *Tosafot*'s reading of Rav Assi, not the two-unit extremes of the *Gemara*'s stated positions according to *Rashi*.

### Yamim Noraim Adds

This discussion of errors and return has direct practical significance for the *Yamim Noraim*. Several *Tosafot* in Masechet Berakhot assume that even the later Geonic additions — *zochrenu l'chayim*, *katvenu l'chayim*, *mi chamocha*, and the like — carry the same obligation of return if forgotten. The *Gemara* itself contains *HaMelech HaKadosh* and *HaMelech HaMishpat*; it was the *Geonim* who added the *zochrenu* insertions. We rule that if those later additions are forgotten, one continues, since they were added after the fact. There is indeed a question why such additions are permitted at all in the first three and last three *brachot*, given what we are about to learn — but *Tosafot*'s approach, characteristically embracing accepted communal practice, treats even these Geonic additions as obligatory in the sense that forgetting them requires return.

At the end of the relevant *Tosafot*, beginning with the word *v'heicha*, Tosafot states: if one erred in the first three *brachot* — for example, one made an incorrect *chatimah*, or failed to say *zochrenu l'chayim* in *Birchas Avot* between *Rosh Hashanah* and *Yom Kippur*, or omitted *mi chamocha* in the second *brachah*, or failed to say *HaMelech HaKadosh* — *chozer l'rishonah*, one returns to the very beginning of *Shemoneh Esrei*. According to *Tosafot*, then, forgetting *zochrenu l'chayim* requires starting over entirely. We do not rule this way in practice. But the structure that emerges from *Tosafot*'s position is clear: for the first three, return to the beginning; for the last three, return to *Retzei*; for the middle, return to the specific *brachah* where the error occurred — and this applies even to the Geonic insertions.

---

## Personal Requests

### No Personal Requests

*Amar Rav Yehuda: le'olam al yishal adam tzorachav lo b'shalosh rishonot v'lo b'shalosh acharonot* — a person should never insert personal requests in the first three or the last three *brachot* of *Shemoneh Esrei*. Personal needs, when inserted, belong only *b'emtza'iyot*, in the middle *brachot*. This is because the middle *brachot* are structurally the *brachot* of *bakashot* — petitions — while the opening and closing *brachot* serve different functions, as the *Gemara* proceeds to explain.

### Master Parable

*Kasavar Rabbi Chanina*: the first three *brachot* are *domeh l'eved she-mesader shevach lifnei rabo* — like a servant setting out praises before his master. One approaches God first with praise. And indeed the first three *brachot* — *Magen Avraham*, *Mechayei Meitim*, *HaMelech HaKadosh* — are not explicitly petitionary, though they carry implicit dimensions of hope and desire. Their primary register is declaration: who God is and what God does.

The middle *brachot* are *domeh l'eved she-mevakesh pras mi-rabo* — like a servant asking for a portion from his master. A *pras* here likely means simply a portion, something to sustain oneself; the image is of genuine supplication. And the final *brachot* are *domeh l'eved she-kibel pras mi-rabo ve-niftar ve-holech lo* — like a servant who has received what he sought and now takes his leave of the master.

This last description is striking. The *Gemara* does not say the servant *thanks* the master — it says he *asks his leave*. And if one examines the final *brachot* of *Shemoneh Esrei*, they do not map easily onto pure *hoda'ah*. *Sim Shalom* is a petition for peace; *Retzei* asks God to accept our prayer and restore His presence to the *Beis HaMikdash*; *Ya'aleh v'Yavo* is embedded in *Retzei* and connected to the *avodah*. *Modim* itself is more genuinely one of thanksgiving, and *ha-tov shimcha u-lecha na'eh l'hodos* is an expression of gratitude. But the *brachah* as a whole resists the characterization of simple thanksgiving.

Perhaps it is more accurate to say the closing *brachot* function as an act of taking leave — *shalom aleichem*, in reverse, a gracious departure — rather than as explicit *hoda'ah*. The *Gemara* itself, interestingly, does not use the word *hoda'ah* at this juncture; it says only that the servant received his *pras* and departs. This may be intentional: the closing section is not so much about thanks as it is about completing the encounter appropriately, acknowledging the presence one has been in, and seeking *shalom* as one withdraws. The fit with *Retzei*, which asks God to accept the *avodah* and restore the *Beis HaMikdash*, remains somewhat difficult to fully account for within this model — not entirely unlike *Shomea Tefillah*, which also asks for acceptance of prayer, raising the question of how the two differ.

There is also a structural observation worth noting: the fact that *Retzei*, which alludes to the *korbanot* and the *Beis HaMikdash*, is placed outside the core middle section is itself suggestive. The entire *Shemoneh Esrei*, as structured, contains no explicit mention of *korbanot*. We open with *Hashem sefatai tiftach* and proceed through praise and petition. Even *Retzei*, which gestures toward *tefillah k'neged korbanot*, is positioned in the concluding section rather than at the center, reinforcing its role as closing frame rather than core petition.

### Communal Needs

*Tosafot* addresses the prohibition on personal requests in the first three and last three *brachot*, citing *Rabbenu Chananel* and *Rabbeinu Hai Gaon*: *davka l'yachid aval tzorchei tzibbur sho'alim* — the restriction applies only to an individual's personal needs; communal needs may be inserted. This is offered as the justification for the *minhag* of saying *zochrenu l'chayim* and similar insertions, as well as for the *krovot* — the liturgical poems inserted into *Shemoneh Esrei* in *Ashkenaz* — during the *regalim*.

*Tosafot* notes that the final *brachot* of *Shemoneh Esrei* are fundamentally about communal rather than personal concerns. Indeed, if one examines the *brachot*, while all are phrased in the plural, some of the middle *brachot* — requests for livelihood, healing, intelligence — can be understood as essentially personal even when phrased communally. By contrast, *Hashiva Shofteinu*, *Tzemach David*, and other *brachot* in the latter part of the middle section are clearly national in orientation: restoring of judges, the Davidic dynasty, the return to the land. The emphasis that the closing *brachot* are more *tzarchei tzibbur* than the middle ones is a genuinely interesting observation.

But this was also the center of a major controversy between *Geonei Bavel* and *Geonei Eretz Yisrael*, and subsequently between *Sefardim* and *Ashkenazim*: whether *piyuttim* and *krovot* could be inserted into fixed sections of *davening*, including the first three and last three *brachot*. In *Bavel*, the answer was essentially no — *tefillah kevuah* is fixed and cannot be expanded with poetic additions. *Sefardim*, influenced heavily by the *minhag* rooted in *Bavel*, largely adopted this position. In *Eretz Yisrael*, where the *piyuttim* were being composed, the culture of liturgical creativity was vibrant and the view was that *Yamim Tovim* demanded something more textured and responsive to the character of the day — something to give the *tefillah* its proper power and flavor. *Ashkenaz* followed *Eretz Yisrael* in this regard. Ruth Langer's work *To Worship God Properly* explores this debate in depth.

*Tosafot*'s citation of *tzarchei tzibbur* as the justification is a one-word defense of an entire *minhag* — characteristic of the *Tosafist* embrace of accepted practice. Even the *zochrenu* insertions, now universally accepted, were at some stage contested in the Geonic period. What became universally accepted eventually, while *krovot* never crossed over into universal acceptance, reflects the complex history of how local liturgical practice solidifies into *minhag* and ultimately into *halachah*.

---

## Prayer Length Signs

### Long vs. Short

A *baraita* presents two contrasting stories, both occurring before *Rabbi Eliezer*. In the first, a student was leading the *davening* and was going on at great length — *ma'arikh yoter midai*. The students complained: "Rabbenu, how lengthy this one is!" *Rabbi Eliezer* responded: does he go longer than *Moshe Rabbeinu*? — *d'ksiv: va-etpallel lifnei Hashem arba'im yom ve-arba'im layla*, "I prayed before God forty days and forty nights" — referring to *Moshe*'s prayer after the *Chet Ha'egel*, pleading for the forgiveness of *Bnei Yisrael*.

In the second story, a different student led and was cutting things very short — *mekatzer yoter midai*. The students again complained. *Rabbi Eliezer* replied: is he shorter than *Moshe Rabbeinu*? — *d'ksiv: Eil na r'fa na lah*, five words, which *Moshe* said in prayer for *Miriam*.

The obvious question is what *ma'arikh* and *mekatzer* mean in these stories. Does the student go long by adding personal compositions and elaborations to the text, the text being fluid in that era? Or does he simply *chazzan* with extensive musical flourish and take a long time? Likely the former: the period of the *Gemara* was one in which the exact wording of *Shemoneh Esrei* was still somewhat fluid, and a *shliach tzibbur* might frame each *brachah* in more or less expansive language. This reading — that the length and brevity refer to the actual textual content — is significant. It means that the use of *Moshe*'s extremes as models is itself a statement: there is no single fixed proper length for *tefillah*. A *shliach tzibbur* leading in a period of relative textual latitude could legitimately go quite long or quite short, provided he maintained a sincere connection. What is also notable is the tension with the later reality: once a printed *siddur* became universal, the sense of latitude effectively disappeared. The printed word fixed what had once been fluid, in ways that are worth reflecting upon.

The *Gemara* then adds: *amar Rabbi Yaakov amar Rav Chisda: kol ha-mevakesh rachamim al chaveiro ein tzarich l'hazkir shemo* — one who prays for a sick friend need not mention their name. The source is *Eil na r'fa na lah* — *Moshe* prayed for *Miriam* without saying her name; God knows whom we mean. This is a practically important ruling: if you do not know a person's Hebrew name, or do not know who the person is beyond "someone who is ill," your *tefillah* is still valid.

### Smooth Flow Sign

*Amar Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani*: the sign that a prayer has been accepted is whether the words flow smoothly from one's lips — a theme we will encounter again in a later story about *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa*. The *psukim* cited in support — *borei niv sefatayim, shalom shalom la-rachok ve-la-karov* — are read as saying: if the *niv sefatayim*, the speech of the lips, is clear and healthy, then *shalom shalom*, peace in abundance. The facility of speech in *tefillah* is taken as a communicative signal of reception, not merely a personal characteristic.

---

## Bowing Positions

### Bow Locations

A *baraita* enumerates the specific *brachot* in which one bows: *ba-Avot techilah v'sof u-v'hoda'ah techilah v'sof* — in *Avot* at the beginning and end, and in *Modim* at the beginning and end. The mechanics: at the word *Baruch* one begins to bend, at *Atah* one is fully bent, and at God's name one rises. These four points — beginning and end of *Avot*, beginning and end of *Modim* — are the prescribed locations of bowing for an ordinary person.

*V'im ba lishuach b'sof kol berachah u'verachah u'v-techilat kol berachah u'verachah* — if someone wishes to bow at the beginning and end of every *brachah*, *melam-din oto she-lo yishcheh*, one instructs him not to do so. Bowing everywhere undermines the distinctive significance of bowing where it is prescribed. Uniformity eliminates meaning.

### Special Status Bowing

*Amar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi mishum Bar Kappara*: for an ordinary person, the rule is as above. A *kohen gadol* bows at the end of every *brachah*. The reasoning is that those in positions of great power and status must go further to demonstrate that even in the highest human roles, one stands before God in humility. The *kohen gadol*'s enhanced bowing requirements reflect the fact that power can corrupt and distort one's sense of proportion; the act of repeatedly bowing throughout *Shemoneh Esrei* instills a corrective sense of human limitation.

The *Gemara* then records a second version attributed to *Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani* in the name of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* in which the *kohen gadol* bows at the beginning of every *brachah*, and the king does something more dramatic still: *keivan she-kara shuv eino zokef* — once the king bows at the outset of *Shemoneh Esrei*, he remains bowed for the entire *tefillah*. The source is *Shlomo HaMelech* at the inauguration of the *Beis HaMikdash*: *vayehi kechalot Shlomo lehitpalel kam milifnei mizbe'ach Hashem mikroa al birkav* — when *Shlomo* completed his prayer, he rose from kneeling. The implication is that he had been on his knees for the entire prayer. Hence the king, whose position is most prone to distorting one's sense of humanity, must bow the entire time.

### Kida vs. Hishtachavah

The *baraita* distinguishes between the forms of prostration mentioned in *Tanach*. *Kida al apayim* — bowing on one's face — is derived from *vatiked Bat Sheva apayim artzah*, Bat Sheva with her face toward the ground. The simple meaning of *al apayim* suggests the face actually touching the ground, though how precisely that is accomplished without also going to one's knees is debated. Some say it means simply bowing one's head forward. *Keri'ah* — bending on the knees — is derived from *mikroa al birkav*, which is explicitly on the knees.

*Hishtachavah* — full prostration — means *pishut yadayim v'raglayim*, extending both hands and legs, lying fully stretched out on the ground, or at minimum fully splayed with the whole body extended rather than merely the face. The two can combine: *vayikdu vayishtachavu* — first the face touches the ground (*kida*), and then full prostration (*hishtachavah*) follows. The phrase *havo navo ani v'imcha v'achicha lehishtachavot lecha artzah* — will we come and prostrate on the ground? — reinforces the image of full prostration spread out on the earth.

### Stone Floor Limit

*Amar Rav Chiyya brei d'Rav Huna: chazina lehu l'Abaye v'Rava de-matzlu atzluyei* — *Abaye* and *Rava* were observed leaning on their side rather than fully prostrating. The context, as *Rabbeinu Nissim* explains with reference to the *Yerushalmi*, relates to the prohibition derived from *v'even maskit lo titenu b'artzechem lehishtachavot aleha* — the prohibition against prostrating on a stone floor outside the *Beis HaMikdash*. Outside the Temple, one may not perform full prostration directly on stone.

This is the actual reason behind the practice — familiar from *Yom Kippur* and *Rosh Hashanah* — of placing a paper or cloth beneath one's knees and face before *nefilat apayim*. It is not, as one might imagine, simply concern for one's suit. The halachic concern is that face and knees should not contact a stone floor. Whether carpeting suffices — as carpeting is attached to the floor and might be considered subsumed within it — is a point of discussion, but many authorities are lenient with carpeting while still supporting the practice of placing something down as an added precaution.

The context in which *Abaye* and *Rava* were leaning rather than fully prostrating appears to be a fast day — *Rav Nisim* understands it as a public *ta'anit* — when the desire for a more dramatic physical expression of prayer was present, but the stone floor made full prostration impermissible, leading to the lateral lean as a compromise. This also opens an interesting broader question: how extensive was *keri'ah* — bending to the knees — during *Shemoneh Esrei* in earlier periods? We associate prostration on the knees with Islamic prayer and assume Jews simply bow at the spine. But perhaps for some people in earlier times, *keri'ah* in *Shemoneh Esrei* was more extensive than what we practice today.

### Modim Bowing

*Tani chada*: a *baraita* says that one who bows at *Modim* is *meshubach*, praiseworthy. *V'tani idach*: another *baraita* says it is *meguneh*, unseemly. *Lo kashya: ha b'techilah ha b'sof* — the two *baraisos* refer to the beginning and end respectively: bowing at one is praiseworthy, bowing at the other is not. Which end is problematic is not explicitly stated, but the *Gemara* applies this to *Rava*'s practice.

*Rava kara b'hoda'ah techilah v'sof* — *Rava* bowed at both the beginning and end of *Modim*. The rabbis questioned him: given that one *baraita* calls such bowing *meguneh*, why does he do it? *Rava* replied: *chazina lei l'Rav Nachman de-kara* — he observed *Rav Nachman* bowing at the beginning and end of *Modim*, and similarly *chazina lei l'Rav Sheshet de-kara hachi* — he observed *Rav Sheshet* doing the same. This is a striking and recurring motif in the *Gemara*: learning *halachah* from direct observation of a teacher's practice.

The *Gemara* responds: but does the *baraita* not say *hakoreia b'hoda'ah harei ze meguneh*? The resolution: *hahu b'hoda'ah she-ba-Hallel* — that *baraita* refers not to *Shemoneh Esrei* but to the *Hodu l'Hashem ki tov* of *Hallel*. *Rashi* identifies this as *Hodu l'Hashem ki tov* specifically. There, bowing is inappropriate — perhaps because *Hallel* is more in the register of joyful praise, and bowing there would strike an incongruous note. At *Modim* in *Shemoneh Esrei*, where the spirit of awe and acknowledgment of God's sovereignty is dominant, bowing is entirely appropriate and, at both points, praiseworthy.

A further version of the *baraita* is cited — *hakoreia b'hoda'ah u-v'hoda'ah shel Hallel harei ze meguneh* — which suggests the prohibition covers both regular *hoda'ah* and *hoda'ah* of *Hallel*. The *Gemara* resolves: *ki tanya hahi b'hoda'ah de-Birkat Hamazon* — that refers to the *hoda'ah* in *Birkat HaMazon*, presumably *nodeh lecha Hashem Elokeinu*. So the full structure that emerges is: bowing in *Modim* of *Shemoneh Esrei*, at beginning and end, is praiseworthy; bowing in *Hoda'ah* of *Hallel* or *Birkat HaMazon* is unseemly.

---

## Error Significance

### Bad Sign Error

The *mishna* states: *ha-mitpalel v'ta'ah siman ra lo* — someone who is *davening* and makes an error, it is a bad sign for that person. *V'im shliach tzibbur hu — siman ra l'sholchav* — if the *shliach tzibbur* makes an error, it is a bad sign not just for himself but for those who sent him — the *tzibbur* he represents.

The *Gemara* asks: on which *brachah* does an error qualify as a bad sign? Is it any error anywhere in *Shemoneh Esrei*, or is there a more specific locus? *Amar Rabbi Chiyya amar Rav Safra mishum chad d'Bei Rebbi*: only an error in *Avot*, the first *brachah*, constitutes a bad sign. Other errors are less significant as omens.

### Representative Principle

The basis for the bad sign in the case of the *shliach tzibbur* is articulated through a legal principle that appears here in an unusual context: *mipnei she-shlucho shel adam k'moto* — because a person's *shaliach* is like the person themselves. In *halachah* literature, *shlucho shel adam k'moto* is a foundational and frequently invoked principle governing agency in *kiddushin*, commercial transactions, and many other domains. But its appearance in the *mishna* is exclusively in the context of the *shliach tzibbur*.

This is arresting. The principle in the *mishna* is not being deployed in a legal-transactional sense. It is making a statement about the nature of communal prayer itself: the *shliach tzibbur* is genuinely the representative of the *tzibbur* before God. He brings the *tzibbur*'s prayers upward. If he makes an error — if his *tefillah* does not flow — it reflects that the gates of prayer are closed, not necessarily to him personally, but to those he represents. One sees a trace of this in the extended *tefillah* that a *chazzan* recites before *Shemoneh Esrei* on *Yamim Noraim*: declaring that he is representing the congregation and does not feel himself worthy. For most of us today, that sense of representation has faded — the *chazzan* is experienced more as a facilitator of communal singing than as an emissary before God. But the *Rishonim*, when they discuss who should serve as *shliach tzibbur*, reflect a profound understanding that this person is genuinely carrying the *tzibbur*'s prayers upward, and that his errors are the *tzibbur*'s bad omen.

### Chanina Prayer Flow

*Amru alav al Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa: she-haya mitpalel al ha-cholim ve-omer zeh chay ve-zeh met* — it was said of *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa* that he would pray for the sick and afterward say: this one will live, and this one will die. When asked how he knew, he replied: *im shegura tefilati befi* — if my prayer flows smoothly from my lips, *yodea ani she-hu mekubal*, I know it was accepted; *v'im lav*, if not, *yodea ani she-hu meturaf*, I know it was rejected — thrown back, unaccepted.

*Rashi* suggests that *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa* may have been composing his own prayers in his own words, not reciting a fixed text, which would mean that the smoothness or faltering of the words was a more immediate reflection of his spiritual connection in that moment. The practical significance: how one's *tefillah* unfolds — whether it flows or stumbles — can be read as a sign of its reception. This is admittedly a difficult idea for many modern sensibilities, which tend toward skepticism about such omens.
