But the *Gemara* presents it with full seriousness: the phenomenon of *tefillah* involves a real connection to God, and the character of that connection can, in certain circumstances, be read in the quality and ease of the prayer itself.

There is an analogy to the *Ba'al Toke'a* on *Rosh Hashanah*: if he has great difficulty producing the *teki'ot*, some take this as a troubling omen. The difference the *Gemara* points to here is that it is not merely a reflection of the individual's skill or state of mind but rather a sign that the *sha'ar ha-tefillah*, the gate of prayer, is or is not open.

### Kavana Requirement

The *Gemara* connects the question of *ta'ah* with the topic of *kavana*. The *baraita* states: *ha-mitpalel tzarich she-yechaven et libo be-kulam* — when one prays, one must have *kavana* for all the *brachot*. *V'im eino yachol lechaven be-kulam*, if one cannot maintain *kavana* throughout, *yechaven et libo be-achat* — it is sufficient to have *kavana* for one of them. That one *brachah* is identified, again by *Rabbi Chiyya* in the name of *Rav Safra*, as *Avot*. This is the *halachic* ruling: if one has *kavana* for *Avot*, one is *yotzei*, even if the rest of *Shemoneh Esrei* was said more automatically.

*Tosafot* connects this to the principle *le'olam ya'amod adam da'ato: im yachol lechaven yitpalel, v'im lav al yitpalel* — that one should assess whether one can have *kavana* and only *daven* if one can. *Tosafot* understands this as referring to *kavana* for *Avot* specifically: if you can have *kavana* for that *brachah*, proceed; if not, the concern is more serious. The *Rambam*, however, takes a different approach. As *Rav Chaim* explains, the *Rambam* distinguishes between two dimensions of *kavana*. The first — *kavana* to know the meaning of the words — is required minimally for *Avot*; without it there, one is not *yotzei*. The second is a different kind of *kavana* entirely: *da lifnei mi atah omed*, awareness throughout that one stands in the presence of God. According to the *Rambam*, this awareness is required for the entire *Shemoneh Esrei*, and its absence at any point is a genuine failing, even if it does not invalidate one's fulfillment of the formal obligation.

---

## World to Come

### Teshuvah Merit

*Amar Rav Chiyya bar Abba amar Rabbi Yochanan: kol ha-neviim kulam lo nitnab'u ela le-massi bito le-talmid chacham* — all the blessings spoken by all the prophets were said only for the benefit of someone who gives his daughter in marriage to a *talmid chacham*, or engages in commerce in partnership with a *talmid chacham* (*oseh prakmatya le-talmid chacham*), or sustains a *talmid chacham* from his property. The entire sweep of prophetic blessing is reserved for those who are connected to — and who support — the *talmidei chachamim*.

*Aval talmidei chachamim atzmam* — the sages themselves receive something categorically different and beyond: *ayin lo ra'ata Elokim zulatcha ya'aseh li-mchakeh lo* — no eye has seen, God, other than You, what You will do for those who wait for You. What awaits those who dedicate themselves entirely to *Torah* is beyond any prophetic imagery, beyond what has ever been seen or described.

### Mashiach Debate

A second statement in the same name: *kol ha-neviim kulam lo nitnab'u ela li-ymot ha-mashiach* — all prophetic blessings relate only to the messianic era. *Aval Olam Haba — ayin lo ra'ata*, the world to come is beyond all prophetic description. This raises the question of what *Olam Haba* means. While the term is commonly understood today through the lens of the *Rambam* as the fate of the soul after death, the earlier and more literal meaning in the *Gemara* is the transformed state of the world that follows the messianic period: the era of *techiyat ha-meitim* and the complete renewal of existence.

*U-pligi de-Shmuel* — this position is in tension with *Shmuel*'s well-known ruling: *ein bein ha-olam hazeh li-ymot ha-mashiach ela shibud malchuyot bilvad* — the only difference between the present world and messianic times is that Israel will no longer be subjugated to foreign powers. No miraculous transformation, no prophetic bounty. *Ki lo yechdal evyon mi-kerev ha-aretz* — the poor will never cease from the land, even in messianic times.

The footnote in the text marks *Shmuel*'s position, because the *Rambam* rules like *Shmuel* and does so with significance. Where the *Gemara* presents *Shmuel*'s view as a single minority opinion, the *Rambam* in his writings cites it as *amru chachamim*, as if it were the rabbinic consensus. This was a deliberate theological and polemical move: the *Rambam* was addressing communities that were dangerously preoccupied with miracles and messianic drama, and he wished to redirect their focus away from supernatural expectation and toward law and reason. By presenting *Shmuel*'s position as consensus, he normalized a demythologized vision of the messianic era.

### Teshuvah Heights

A third statement in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *kol ha-neviim kulam lo nitnab'u ela li-va'alei teshuvah* — all prophetic blessings are reserved for *ba'alei teshuvah*. *Aval tzaddikim gemurim — ayin lo ra'ata*, those who have never sinned receive something beyond prophetic description.

*U-pligi de-Rabbi Abbahu* — this contradicts *Rabbi Abbahu*, who holds: *makom she-ba'alei teshuvah omdim tzaddikim gemurim einam omdim* — the place where *ba'alei teshuvah* stand, the completely righteous cannot stand. The *ba'alei teshuvah* occupy a higher level precisely because they overcame sin and turned back. The *pasuk* is read: *shalom shalom la-rachok ve-la-karov* — peace to the distant one *first*, and then to the near one. The distant one — one who was far from God — is greeted first and with greater emphasis.

*Rabbi Yochanan* responds by interpreting the *pasuk* differently: *rachok* refers to someone who was distant from sin from the beginning — the *tzaddik gamur* who never came close to transgression. *Karov* refers to someone who was close to sin and moved away. So *Rabbi Yochanan* actually reads the *pasuk* as elevating the righteous over the penitent — the reverse of *Rabbi Abbahu*'s reading.

### Hidden Rewards

*Mai ayin lo ra'ata?* — what is the concrete referent of the *pasuk* about what no eye has seen? *Amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: zeh yayin ha-meshummar ba-anavav mi-sheshet yemei bereishit* — wine that has been preserved inside the grapes since the six days of creation, never extracted, never seen. The juice has remained sealed within those original grapes. *Ayin lo ra'ata*, no eye has ever seen it.

*Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani* disagrees: *zeh Eden* — it refers to the Garden of Eden, Eden itself, which no creature has ever seen. *Adam HaRishon* was in *Gan* — the garden — but not in *Eden*. The proof: *venahar yotze me-Eden lehashkot et ha-Gan* — a river came out of Eden to water the garden. *Gan lechud ve-Eden lechud* — the garden and Eden are distinct places. Even *Adam HaRishon* never saw Eden; it remains entirely unseen, the ultimate hidden reward.

---

## Chanina Stories

### Gamliel Son

*Tanu Rabbanan*: a story is told in which the son of *Rabban Gamliel* fell ill. He sent two *talmidei chachamim* to *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa* to pray for his son. When *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa* saw them coming, knowing their purpose, he went up to the upper floor or roof and prayed. When he came down, he told them: go back — you need not speak with me further. *Chaltzata chama*, the fever has left him. They asked: are you a prophet? He replied: *lo navi anochi ve-lo ben navi anochi* — neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet. *Ela kach mekublani*: this is my received tradition — *im shegura tefilati befi, yodea ani she-hu mekubal*; if the words flow smoothly from my lips, I know the prayer was accepted. *V'im lav — yodea ani she-hu meturaf*, and if not, I know it was rejected.

The messengers sat down and carefully noted the exact hour. When they returned to *Rabban Gamliel*, he told them: *HaAvodah* — by God — *lo chasartem v'lo hotartem*, it was not one moment before or after. *Ela kach haya ma'aseh: be-otah sha'ah chalatsato chama* — exactly at that hour the fever broke. And the son asked for water to drink, as happens when a fever lifts.

### Zakkai Son

A further story: *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa* had gone to study *Torah* from *Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai* — which itself establishes the hierarchy of *Torah* scholarship, *Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai* being the greater *talmid chacham*. While there, *Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai*'s son fell ill. *Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai* asked him: *Chanina beni, bakesh alav rachamim ve-yichyeh* — Chanina, my son, pray for my son and he will live. *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa hiniach rosho bein birkav*, he placed his head between his knees and prayed, and the boy lived.

### Servant Officer

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai*: had I pressed my head between my knees all day long, *lo hayu mashgichim alav* — they would not have paid attention to me in heaven. The contrast is arresting: the greatest *talmid chacham* of his generation, yet his prayers would not have been accepted where *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa*'s were — and in only a few minutes at that. His wife pressed him: *vechi Chanina gadol mimcha?* Is he greater than you? He replied: *lav* — no. But *hu domeh ke-eved lifnei ha-Melech, va-ani domeh ke-sar lifnei ha-Melech* — he is like a servant before the king who is always present, always in close proximity; I am like an officer who has audiences only a few times a year.

The intimacy of the servant — constant, familiar, unremarkable in its access — is paradoxically more effective for certain purposes than the formal access of the officer. The *Gemara* here makes a genuine distinction between two human types: the *talmid chacham* who excels in *Torah* and the individual who excels in *tefillah* and proximity to God. They are not the same. *Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai* does not claim that *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa* is his superior in *Torah* — he is quite explicitly his student. But in the mode of *tefillah*, in the intimacy of standing before God, the *Gemara* recognizes a different kind of greatness altogether.

---

## Prayer Setting

### Windows Jerusalem

*Amar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba amar Rabbi Yochanan: al yitpalel adam ela be-vayit she-yesh bo chalonot* — one should pray only in a house with windows. The source is *Daniel*, whose windows in his upper chamber were open toward Jerusalem. *Rashi* explains that windows allow one to look outward toward the heavens, and this supports *kavana* — the awareness of standing before God.

### Chutzpah Behaviors

*Amar Rav Kahana: chatzifa alai man de-matzli be-vikta* — it is like *chutzpah* to me when someone *davens* in a valley, which is presumably a place of traffic and distraction. Prayer requires a setting conducive to *kavana*, and praying where distractions are abundant reflects a certain carelessness about the act itself.

*V'amar Rav Kahana: chatzifa alai man de-mifaresh chatei* — it is also *chutzpah* to one who publicly announces and elaborates on all of his past sins. The *pasuk* is cited: *ashrei nesui pesha kisui chata'ah* — blessed is the one whose transgression is borne and whose sin is covered. The ideal is the covering and moving past of sin, not its public recitation and display. And with these final words of *Rav Kahana*, the first half of Masechet Berakhot concludes.

*Hadran alach.*

---

# Berakhot 35

## Intro & Mishna Categories

### Welcome & Overview

Today's daf is 35, and with it we enter *Kaitzad Mevarkhim* — what can fairly be called the second half of the masechet. The first half was devoted to the fixed daily liturgy: *Shema* and *Shemoneh Esreh*. From this point forward, the masechet turns to *brachot* that arise at various moments throughout the day outside of any fixed liturgy, with the primary focus on blessings before and after eating, followed later by other *brachot* that may occur during the course of daily life.

### Mishna: Blessings

The *mishna* at the top of 35a opens: *kaitzad mevarkhim al ha-perot* — how does one make a blessing over fruit? *Al perot ha-ilan hu omer borei pri ha-etz*: for fruit from the tree, one recites *borei pri ha-etz*. The *mishna* already presupposes that even when fruit is transformed into juice, one would naturally assume the blessing remains *borei pri ha-etz* in its original form. The *mishna* must therefore specify the exception: *chutz min ha-yayin* — for wine one recites *borei pri ha-gefen*. God, after all, did not create wine directly; human processing was involved. Therefore, even in reciting a special *bracha* for this transformed form, we refer to the fruit in its natural state and say *borei pri ha-gefen*.

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic

One notable feature of the *mishna*'s language is its use of the word *ilan* for tree in the body of the rule, while the *bracha* text itself employs *etz*. As one of the participants observed, *ilan* does not appear in the *mikra*, whereas *etz* — as in *etz pri oseh pri le-mino* — is biblical language. This reflects a broader principle: the formulations of *brachot*, particularly their *chatimot*, draw heavily on the language of *psukim*. The same dynamic explains the well-known *machlokret* among *Sefardim* over whether to pronounce *borei pri ha-gafen* or *borei pri ha-gefen* — the form *gefen* appears in *Tanakh* mid-sentence, while *gafen* is the pausal form for end-of-verse; since *gafen* as such never appears as a final word in *Tanakh*, some hold that one must use only the form that actually appears in the text.

### Wine & Bread

Continuing the *mishna*: *ve-al perot ha-aretz hu omer borei pri ha-adama* — for fruit of the ground, one says *borei pri ha-adama* — with the exception of bread. Here too the *mishna* assumes that since bread derives from wheat, one might say *borei pri ha-adama*, as one would for wheat eaten in its natural form. But for bread, one says *ha-motzi lechem min ha-aretz*.

### Hamotzi Prayer

The *bracha* of *ha-motzi* is interesting because it does approach the idea of the finished product — it says *lechem*, bread, not wheat. Yet the emphasis remains on the divine act of bringing forth the wheat from the earth, rather than on the human process of baking. The *bracha* is thus a dual acknowledgment: it names the final human product while directing our attention to God's creative role in producing the grain.

### Categories: Earth & Veg

The *mishna* then states: *ve-ha-yerakot hu omer borei pri ha-adama* — for vegetables one also recites *borei pri ha-adama*, the same *bracha* as for what it earlier called *perot ha-aretz*. This naturally raises the question: what distinguishes *perot ha-aretz* from *yerakot* if both receive the same *bracha*? One way to draw the distinction — and *Rashi* addresses this as well — is that *perot ha-aretz* refers to things that grow above the ground but are not fruits of a tree, while *yerakot* grow in the ground. That said, *Rashi* also includes *kitniyot* (legumes) within the vegetable category, which complicates a simple above-ground versus below-ground division. The precise scope of *perot ha-aretz* versus *yerakot* remains a point of discussion as the *gemara* continues.

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

Rabbi Yehuda dissents on the last category, holding that one should not say *borei pri ha-adama* over vegetables but rather *borei minei deshaim* — creator of types of herbs, or literally grasses. This formulation suggests that the vegetable category extends beyond things that grow below the ground and encompasses a broader range of low-growing plants.

What this *mishna* accomplishes overall is the laying out of the various categories of *brachot*: that *brachot* are differentiated according to what one is eating, that a transformed form of a food in many cases retains the original *bracha*, and that wine and bread are notable exceptions receiving their own distinct *brachot*. What the *mishna* does not yet address is the source of the obligation to make *brachot* in the first place — that is precisely where the *gemara* begins.

---

## Kodesh Hilulim & Neta

### Kodesh Hilulim Source

The *gemara* opens with the foundational question: *mena hanei milei* — what is the source for making *brachot* before eating? *Detanu rabbanan*: the Torah's discussion of *neta revai* — the fourth-year fruit, which must be brought to Jerusalem and eaten there in a manner akin to *maaser sheni* — includes the phrase *kodesh hilulim l'Hashem*, sanctified as a praising to God. This is interpreted to mean: *melamed she-te'unin bracha lifneihem u-le'achareihem* — it teaches that such produce requires a blessing both before and after eating. This is the initial scriptural basis for *brachot* over food.

### Rabbi Akiva Stringency

Beyond this, Rabbi Akiva states: *assur le-adam she-yitom klum kodem she-yevarech* — it is forbidden for a person to taste anything before reciting a blessing. This formulation is striking. Until now the language has been about obligation and praise; here Rabbi Akiva introduces the concept of prohibition, which points toward a qualitatively different concern — that one is not entitled to eat at all without first acknowledging the divine source of the food. One of the participants astutely noted that Rabbi Akiva's emphasis on the prohibition may be rooted in the structure of the *pasuk* itself: three years of *orlah* in which eating is forbidden, followed by the fourth year of *hilulim*, followed by the fifth year in which one may eat. The sequence suggests: forbidden, then praise, then permitted — echoing Rabbi Akiva's insistence that the blessing is a precondition for eating.

### Kodesh Hilulim Query

The *gemara* now questions whether the phrase *kodesh hilulim* is actually being used to teach the obligation to make *brachot*. The word *hilulim* is written in a doubled form and may be carrying multiple halakhic messages simultaneously. The *gemara* therefore asks: is this really the source for *brachot*, or does the verse need to be used for other teachings?

### Hilulim as Chillulim

The *gemara* offers two other things that *hilulim* comes to teach. First, reading the *heh* as a *chet* — the two letters are phonetically related as gutturals and visually similar — gives us *chillulim*, meaning redemption or transfer of sanctity. This teaches that the law of *neta revai* parallels *maaser sheni*: if one does not wish to bring the fourth-year produce to Jerusalem, one may redeem its value onto money and then bring the money to Jerusalem. *Achlei u-vahadar achlei*: transfer the sanctity, then eat — consistent with the following *pasuk* which speaks of eating.

### Shira Over Wine

The second teaching from *hilulim* concerns the scope of *neta revai* altogether. The *gemara* cites the principle: *davar ha-ta'un shira ta'un chillul* — something over which one sings *shira* falls within the category of *neta revai*, while something over which one does not sing is not subject to this law. The question becomes: what is it that one sings over? Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani says in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: *minayin she-ein omrim shira ela al ha-yayin* — how do we know that *shira* is recited only over wine? The source is the parable in *Shoftim* (Judges), where in the famous allegory of the trees choosing a king, the grapevine declares: have I given up my wine *that gladdens the hearts of God and people* that I should have to become king? The *gemara* asks: if wine gladdens people, in what sense does it gladden God? The answer is that it is through the *shira* itself — the Levitical singing performed in the Temple during the wine libation that accompanied each *korban*.

### Wine Gladdens Hearts

This point has significant practical implications. The *Levi'im* sang *shira* not during the slaughter of the sacrifice, not during the sprinkling of the blood, not during the placing of the limbs on the altar — but only at the very end of the *avodah*, when the wine of the libation was being poured. *Ein omrim shira ela al ha-yayin*. This is also the halakhic model for *Kiddush* and *Havdalah* — rituals of verbal praise and sanctification are performed specifically over wine. The *gemara* here already knew of *Kiddush*, *Havdalah*, and *Birkat Hamazon* as wine-based rituals; the expansion to *Sheva Brachot*, *Birkat Erusin*, and *Birkat Brit Milah* over wine, while not sourced in the *gemara*, further reflects this same principle that *shira* and formal praise carry greatest ritual weight when performed over wine.

The upshot of this approach is that *hilulim* is being used to teach that only grapevines fall within the scope of *neta revai*, since only over wine is *shira* recited. If so, the word *hilulim* has already been fully deployed for this teaching and cannot simultaneously be used to derive the obligation of *brachot*.

### Wine Limitation Debate

The *gemara* therefore states: *haniicha le-man de-tani neta revai* — this works out well according to the version of the *mishnah* that uses the term *neta revai*, fourth-year planting, implying the *mitzvah* applies broadly and is not limited to the vine. If that is the case, the word *hilulim* is not needed to limit the category to wine, and it remains available to teach the obligation to make *brachot*. But according to the version that reads *kerem revai* — fourth-year vine — meaning the *mitzvah* is limited to grapevines from the outset, then *hilulim* must be used to explain *why* it is limited to the vine, and cannot simultaneously teach *brachot*. This debate is recorded explicitly: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon *berebbi* disagree — one transmits *kerem revai*, the other *neta revai*.

### Gezeirah Shavah

The *gemara* then proposes a way out for the opinion that holds *kerem revai*: even according to that view, perhaps the limitation of the fourth-year law to the vine is derived not from *hilulim* at all but from a *gezeirah shavah*. A *braita* cites Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the *pasuk* in the context of *orlah* and *neta revai* says *le-hosif lachem tevu'ato* — to increase for you its yield — and elsewhere the Torah speaks of *tevu'at ha-kerem*, the yield of the vine. The word *tevu'ah* appears in both places; this *gezeirah shavah* links the two and can be used to establish that the fourth-year category is vineyard-specific. If the limitation to wine is learned from the *gezeirah shavah*, then *hilulim* is freed up to teach something else — namely, the requirement of a *bracha*.

The *gemara* is quite strict about this principle: once a word has been used to derive one *halacha*, it generally cannot also be used to derive another. As the *gemara* presses further, even granting the *gezeirah shavah*, the word *hilulim* appears in doubled form, but one usage has already been spent on the law of redemption — *chillul*. At most, then, one *bracha* can be derived. And if only one *bracha* is available, the *gemara* reasons it should be the *bracha* after eating, since we already have a precedent for that in *Birkat Hamazon*.

### Beyond Wine

This leaves the *bracha* before eating without a source from *hilulim*. But the *gemara* responds: *ha lo kashya, de-ati be-kal vachomer* — that is not a difficulty, since we derive it by *kal vachomer*. *Keshehu save'a mevarech keshehu ra'ev lo kol sheken* — if one makes a *bracha* when sated, how much more so when hungry? When hungry, the appreciation of God's gift of food is more immediate and powerful; after eating, one has more fully experienced the blessing but perhaps with somewhat less intensity of anticipation. Therefore, a *bracha* before eating follows logically from the *bracha* after. The *gemara* at this stage seriously entertains the possibility that this *kal vachomer* has the force of a biblical derivation.

But even granting all of this, we have only established *brachot* for wine and grapevines. *She'ar minin minayin* — how do we extend the requirement to all other foods?

---

## All Foods Blessing

### Kal Vachomer Logic

The *gemara* attempts to extend the requirement broadly: *di-yalfi mi-kerem* — let us derive from the case of the vine. Just as the vine is something from which one derives benefit and over which a *bracha* is required, so too everything from which one derives benefit should require a *bracha*. But the *gemara* challenges this: perhaps the vine is distinctive because of the law of *olelot* — the unformed clusters that must be left for the poor, a law unique to the vineyard. Maybe the requirement of a *bracha* is connected to that distinctive feature, even if there is no logical reason why it should be. This is the *gemara*'s standard mode of objection when trying to prevent one case from becoming a paradigm: the mere existence of a distinctive characteristic, regardless of its logical relevance, blocks a generalization.

The *gemara* therefore brings in a second case: *kama tochiach* — let grain prove it. We know a *bracha* is required after eating grain because the *pasuk* says *ve-achalta ve-savata u-verachta*, the source for *Birkat Hamazon*. Grain and wine together prove that the principle — deriving benefit obligates a *bracha* — is not about *olelot*. But then grain has its own distinctive feature: *chayevet be-challah*, the obligation to separate *challah* applies to grain and not to wine. Perhaps the *bracha* requirement is tied to *challah*. So the *gemara* invokes the vine to prove it is not about *challah*, and grain to prove it is not about *olelot* — and the reasoning goes in a circle.

### Grain & Seven Species

The *gemara* next attempts to derive the obligation from *shivat ha-minim*, the seven species. The *pasuk* in *Devarim* describing the Land of Israel enumerates the seven species and concludes with the promise *lo techsar kol bah* — you shall lack nothing — followed by the verse *ve-achalta ve-savata u-verachta*. If that verse of *bracha* applies not only to bread but to all seven species, then we have a biblical source for *brachot* after eating all seven species. And then, by the earlier *kal vachomer*, if one blesses after eating, one certainly blesses before. This would give us *brachot* before and after for the full set of seven species.

### Tzad Hashaveh

But the *gemara* again objects: *mah le-shivat ha-minim she-kein chayavin be-bikurim* — the seven species are distinctive because one brings *bikurim* only from them. Therefore the *bracha* obligation might be tied to that unique characteristic. The *gemara* had tried a similar move earlier with grain and wine, using the *tzad hashaveh* — the common denominator — when individual cases failed. When both grain and wine were brought as sources, the *gemara* had observed that both have a *tzad mizbeach*, an aspect of being offered on the altar. Perhaps the *bracha* requirement applies only to foods that have this altar-connection.

### Olives Included

The *gemara* notes that at most one could extend this to olives, since olive oil is also brought on the *mizbeach*. The *gemara* briefly considers deriving this from the word *kerem* in *kerem revai* — one *pasuk* in *Shoftim* speaks of *kerem zayit*, an olive orchard. But Rav Papa rules: *kerem zayit ikri, kerem stam lo ikri* — it may be called an olive *kerem* with a qualifier, but *kerem* unmodified refers only to the vine. So even including olives via the *tzad hashaveh* argument, the challenge stands: the obligation might be limited to things that have an *altar* dimension.

### All Foods Challenge

Having exhausted the *tzad hashaveh* approach, the *gemara* attempts one more avenue: *ela de-yalif lah mi-shivat ha-minim*. If the verse *ve-achalta ve-savata u-verachta* applies to all seven species and gives us a *bracha* after eating all of them, and we apply the *kal vachomer* to get a *bracha* before, perhaps that is broad enough. The *gemara* responds again: *mah le-shivat ha-minim she-kein chayavin be-bikurim* — again, the *bikurim* connection is distinctive. And critically, the *gemara* adds: *ve-od hatenei le-acharav, le-fanav minayin* — all of this still only gives you a *bracha* afterwards; how would you know about a *bracha* before? The *kal vachomer* answers that, as before. But the underlying point is that even for the seven species we cannot escape the objection based on their distinctive status.

There is something conceptually rich about why *bikurim* and *tzad mizbeach* keep appearing as obstacles. Both *bikurim* and the altar offerings involve bringing food to the *Mikdash* with words of praise — the very model that the *hilulim* verse evoked at the outset. The connection between *bracha* and *kodesh* runs throughout: perhaps *brachot* are obligatory specifically for things that enter the sanctified space of the Temple, and not for the ordinary foods of daily life.

### Sevara: Forbidden

At this point the *gemara* sets aside the entire derivational enterprise. *Ela sevara hu* — it is simply a matter of logic. *Assur lo le-adam she-yehene min ha-olam ha-zeh belo bracha* — it is forbidden for a person to derive benefit from this world without a blessing. This echoes and grounds Rabbi Akiva's formulation from the outset, but now with a different emphasis. The earlier approaches centered on *hilulim* — on praising God for His gifts — and could conceivably be satisfied by a *bracha* after eating alone, or at most an obligation before that flows from a *kal vachomer*. Here the emphasis is categorically different: one is simply *not entitled* to eat without first acknowledging that the food comes from God. The *bracha* is not just an expression of gratitude; it is the act of obtaining permission.

The *Tosafot* at the bottom of the *daf* makes this explicit: *asmachta be-alma* — the verse of *hilulim* was only ever a scriptural support for what the *gemara* now understands to be the real foundation. The *gemara* originally considered that the obligation before eating might be fully biblical, whether from *hilulim* directly or through a *kal vachomer*. That possibility is now set aside, and the conclusion is that the *bracha* before eating is rabbinic — grounded in the *sevara* that one may not derive benefit from God's world without acknowledgment — while the *Tosafot* at the top of the *daf* notes the irony: the *gemara* had to work hard to justify why *Shema* starts with "when" rather than "whether," but here no such question arises. Of course one makes *brachot* before eating; it is self-evident that one does not derive benefit without blessing.

---

## Me'ilah Principle

### Forbidden Benefit

*Tanu rabbanan*: it is forbidden for a person to derive benefit from this world without a blessing. The *gemara* now restates the principle in full formal terms, having established it as the operative basis in the preceding analysis.

### Me'ilah Equivalence

*Ve-khol ha-nehene min ha-olam ha-zeh belo bracha ma'al* — whoever derives benefit from this world without a *bracha* has transgressed *me'ilah*, the prohibition of deriving benefit from sanctified property. The force of this is considerable. Everything in the world belongs to God; God's property is, in a sense, sanctified. Just as one who uses property belonging to the Temple without authorization commits *me'ilah* — theft of sanctified objects — so too one who eats without a *bracha* has taken from that which is God's without permission. The *bracha* functions as the mechanism of authorization. This introduces a profound dimension of *kedusha* into the act of eating: just as the earlier *hilulim* framework evoked the *Mikdash* experience of bringing produce with songs of praise, here too the language of *me'ilah* brings the sanctity of the Temple into the domain of the everyday meal.

### Learn from Sage

The *gemara* asks: *mai takantei* — what is the remedy if one derived benefit without a *bracha* and has thereby committed *me'ilah*? The initial suggestion is *yelech etzel chakham* — one should go to a sage. But the *gemara* immediately objects: *mai avid lei* — what can the sage do? *Ha avi issura* — the transgression has already occurred. *Ela amar Rava*: one should go to a sage *me'ikara* — beforehand — *ve-yilamdenu brachot*, so that one learns all the *brachot* properly, *ke-dei she-lo yavo lidei me'ilah*, so as not to come to transgress *me'ilah*. The *Maharsha* adds that this instruction carries particular weight because the laws of *brachot* are genuinely complex — which *bracha* applies to which food, and in what form. Even making the wrong *bracha*, one that does not fulfill the obligation, may leave the person having derived benefit without a valid *bracha*, and thus still subject to the *me'ilah* concern.

### God Owns All

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: whoever derives benefit from this world without a *bracha* is as though he derived benefit from *kodshei shamayim* — sanctified property of Heaven. The *pasuk* says *la-Hashem ha-aretz u-mlo'ah* — the earth and all its fullness belongs to God.

### Before & After

But Rabbi Levi raises an apparent contradiction. That same verse affirms *la-Hashem ha-aretz u-mlo'ah* — it all belongs to God. Yet another *pasuk* says *ha-shamayim shamayim la-Hashem ve-ha-aretz natan li-vnei adam* — the heavens are God's, but the earth He has given to humanity. *Lo kashya*: the contradiction is not difficult. *Kan kodem bracha, kan le-achar bracha* — before the *bracha*, the earth belongs entirely to God; after the *bracha*, having acknowledged that this is God's gift, we have license to use it. The act of blessing transforms our relationship to the food: without it, we are taking what is not ours; with it, we receive what has been given.

### Steal from God

*Amar Rabbi Chanina bar Papa*: whoever derives benefit from this world without a *bracha* is as though he stole from both God and from *Knesset Yisrael*. The *pasuk* says *gozel aviv ve-imo ve-omer ein pasha, chaver hu le-ish mashchit* — one who steals from his father and mother and says it is no sin is a companion to a destructive person. *V-ein aviv ela ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — the father is God (*halo hu avicha kanecha*); *ve-ein imo ela Knesset Yisrael* — the mother is the Jewish people (*shma bni musar avicha ve-al titosh torat imecha*). The phrase *ve-omer ein pasha* — saying it is no sin — is key. *Rashi* explains: one who dismisses the importance of *brachot*, announcing that it is trivial, teaches others to do the same and spreads neglect of the obligation.

### Yeravam Comparison

*Mai chaver hu le-ish mashchit*? *Amar Rabbi Chanina bar Papa*: such a person is a companion to *Yerovam ben Nevat* — *she-hishchit et Yisrael le-avihem she-ba-shamayim*, who corrupted Israel before their Father in Heaven. This comparison may seem extreme, but its logic runs deeper than it first appears. *Yerovam ben Nevat*'s defining sin was preventing the Jewish people from making *aliyah la-regel* — from ascending to the Temple, from bringing their produce, their grain and wine and oil and animals, to the *Mikdash* in acknowledgment and gratitude to God. One who dismisses *brachot* does the same thing at the level of daily life: he severs the sanctity of eating from its connection to divine acknowledgment. He steals not just from God but from *Knesset Yisrael*, because — as *Rashi* elsewhere notes, echoing the *neta revai pasuk* — it is the act of acknowledgment that calls forth continued blessing upon the land. Remove the *brachot*, and you remove the blessing for the entire people.

The two frameworks the *gemara* has now presented — *hilulim* as praise, and *sevara* as the prohibition of unauthorized benefit — both point toward the same profound sanctification of everyday eating. The first evokes the *Mikdash* model: we bring food before God, we sing over it, we acknowledge its source. The second makes an even starker claim: the food was never ours to begin with. Only by blessing do we acquire the right to consume what is, at its foundation, God's property.

---

## Torah & Livelihood

### Ve'asafta Deganecha

*Tanu Rabbanan* raises the verse *ve-asafta deganecha* — you shall gather your grain — from the second paragraph of *Shema*. Given the command in *Sefer Yehoshua* that *lo yamush sefer ha-Torah ha-zeh mi-picha ve-hagita bo yomam va-layla* — the book of Torah shall not depart from your lips, you shall meditate in it day and night — one might conclude that the Torah mandates uninterrupted, exclusive Torah study. *Yakhol devarim ki-chtavam* — perhaps this is literal? The *gemara* answers: *talmud lomar ve-asafta deganecha* — no, you must also gather your grain. *Hanhag ba-hen minhag derech eretz* — alongside Torah one must conduct oneself in the way of normal economic life.

### Rabbi Yishmael Path

This is the position of Rabbi Yishmael: Torah study and *derech eretz* — ordinary work and livelihood — must coexist. The verse *ve-asafta deganecha* appears within *Shema* itself, immediately following the commandments of love and service of God, signaling that gathering grain is not a concession to human weakness but an integrated part of a life properly lived.

### Rabbi Shimon Path

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai disagrees sharply. Is it truly possible, he asks, that a person plows at plowing time, sows at sowing time, harvests at harvest time, threshes at threshing time, and winnows when the wind blows — *Torah mah te-hei aleiha*? When will Torah be learned? If one's days are consumed by agricultural labor across all its seasons, serious Torah study becomes impossible. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai therefore holds that when Israel does God's will, *melachtan na'asit al yedei acherim* — others will do their work for them, as the verse says *ve-amdu zarim ve-ra'u tzonechem*, foreigners will shepherd your flocks. When Israel fails to do God's will, they must do their own work — *ve-asafta deganecha* — and worse, they will serve their enemies.

### Practical Success

The two positions thus represent not merely different philosophies but different visions of what a Torah community looks like in practice.

### Abaye Assessment

*Amar Abaye*: many followed the path of Rabbi Yishmael and it succeeded for them — *alta be-yadam*, they managed both livelihood and Torah. Many followed the path of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and it did not succeed — *lo alta be-yadam*. The failure was likely twofold: they could not sustain themselves materially, and as a consequence their Torah learning was compromised as well.

### Rava Compromise

*Amar Rava le-rabbanan*: please, do not appear before me during Nissan and Tishrei — the months of harvest and planting. He wanted his students to devote those two months to working in the fields so that they could support themselves, and thus have the remaining ten months free to study Torah without distraction. This is a practical compromise, tilting heavily toward learning while acknowledging that some period of sustained work is necessary. It implicitly acknowledges the *Maharsha*'s point: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's path is an ideal appropriate only for a very small number of exceptional individuals. For the many — *harbe asu ke-Rabbi Yishmael ve-alta be-yadam* — Rabbi Yishmael's model is the one that actually works.

The *Rambam*'s treatment in *Pirkei Avot* and *Mishneh Torah* covers similar ground, criticizing those who sit and learn while expecting others to support them, while simultaneously, at the end of *Hilkhot Shemitah ve-Yovel*, holding out the ideal of one wholly devoted to knowing God and freed from material preoccupation — *kodesh kodashim*. These two poles map onto the debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, with the broad community falling under Rabbi Yishmael's model and perhaps a rare few under Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's.

---

## Earlier vs Later Gen

### Early Gen Priority

*Amar Rabbah bar bar Chana amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Yehuda be-rebbi Ilai*: come and see that the later generations are not like the earlier generations. The earlier generations made their Torah *keva* — their primary, defining endeavor — and their work *arai*, secondary and incidental. They did follow Rabbi Yishmael's model: they worked. But Torah was the center of their identity and their time, and work was what they did on the side because they had to.

### Late Gen Priority

*Doros ha-acharonim*, by contrast, made their work *keva* — primary in time, identity, and focus — and their Torah *arai*. They define themselves by their occupation and squeeze Torah in when they can. The consequence: *zu ve-zu lo niskayma be-yadam* — neither succeeded. They neither achieved great material success nor serious Torah learning. The critique is not merely quantitative but structural: when work becomes the center, it reshapes how one approaches everything else, including religious obligation.

### Loophole Examples

A second teaching from the same chain of transmission sharpens this critique concretely. The earlier generations would bring their produce in through the *traksmon* — the main gate of the house — specifically in order to render it obligated in *maaser*. They actively sought to fulfill the *mitzvah*. The later generations bring their produce in through rooftops, courtyards, and side passages — *derech gagot, derech chatzerot, derech chapifot* — in order to exempt it from *maaser*. Since the *maaser* obligation is triggered by the produce entering the house through its main entrance, using back routes is a technical loophole that avoids the obligation. They could still eat the produce in an *achilas arai* manner — feeding it to animals, eating it casually — but could not eat it as a fixed meal (*achilas keva*) without first separating *maaser*.

### Maaser Obligation

*Amar Rabbi Yannai*: the *tevel* does not become obligated in *maaser* until it sees *pnei ha-bayit* — the face of the house, the main entrance — as the *pasuk* says *bi'arti ha-kodesh min ha-bayit*, I have removed the sanctified portion from the house, implying the produce entered through the normal main entrance and thereby became obligated. Rabbi Yochanan adds that even *chatzer* — the courtyard — creates the obligation, since the verse *ve-achlu bi-she'arecha ve-save'u* speaks of eating within one's gates, not merely within one's house. Some hold that this latter position is only rabbinic, but it expands the concept of *pnei ha-bayit* beyond the doorway of the house itself.

### Money & Observance

The critique lands precisely here. The later generations are so focused on their earnings — *melachtan keva* — that this orientation corrupts their observance across the board. They find halakhic workarounds for *maaser* obligations, driven purely by economic calculation. The *keva* of work does not merely crowd out time for Torah; it reconfigures one's entire relationship to *mitzvot*, making one alert to exemptions and loopholes rather than to fulfillment. That which was meant to be *keva* — Torah and its obligations — becomes *arai*, while that which was meant to be *arai* — making a living — becomes the organizing principle of life.

---

---

# Berakhot 36

## Wine's Special Status

### Wine Exception

The *mishnah* establishes a general rule: everything that derives from fruit receives the blessing of *borei pri ha'etz*, with the sole exception of wine, which receives *borei pri hagafen*. Implicit in this rule is a foundational assumption — that even when something undergoes transformation, it retains its original *bracha*. Were wine not exceptional, it would seemingly receive a *borei pri ha'etz* like any other fruit product. The question the *gemara* immediately poses is: why does wine merit its own distinct blessing?

### Transformation Theory

The *gemara* opens by proposing that wine receives a special *bracha* because it has undergone a transformation to a higher state — *ishtani le'iluya* — wine being, in some sense, superior to grapes. But the *gemara* immediately challenges this: olive oil also represents an improvement upon raw olives, yet as *Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Shmuel*, and as *Rav Yitzchak* likewise said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*, the blessing on olive oil is *borei pri ha'etz* — not a distinct blessing of its own. Transformation to a higher state cannot, by itself, be the reason wine receives a unique *bracha*.

The *gemara* answers that the cases are not parallel: the reason no special blessing was formulated for olive oil is a textual impossibility rather than a conceptual one. One could not simply say *borei pri hazayit* — "Who creates the fruit of the olive" — because the word *zayit* denotes the olive itself, not the oil. The fruit of the olive is the olive; God did not directly create olive oil. This reflects a broader principle: the *bracha* we recite must be literally true of what God has directly created, while simultaneously being capable of extension to include the derived product. *Borei pri hagafen* accomplishes this for wine because it refers to the fruit of the vine — technically the grape — but its abstraction allows it to encompass wine as well. A parallel construction for olive oil would require us to say that God created "the fruit of the olive," which is either false (God created the olive, not oil derived from it through human processing) or confusing (the word already names the fruit). One could suggest *borei pri etz hazayit* — "Who creates the fruit of the olive tree" — which is more textually workable, but the *gemara* in the end sets this aside in favor of the deeper answer to follow.

Underlying this discussion is an important conceptual point: *borei pri hagafen* does not say "Who creates wine." Even on wine, we praise God for creating "the fruit of the vine." God created grapes; human beings, in partnership with the natural processes of fermentation, created wine. The blessing acknowledges the natural substrate while extending, through abstraction, to the transformed product. The same move cannot be made gracefully for oil.

### Wine's Dual Function

The *gemara* advances to the substantive reason wine merits its own *bracha*: *Mar Zutra* states that wine satiates — *chamra zayen* — while oil does not. This, in essence, distinguishes wine from oil in terms of importance and functional weight.

But the *gemara* immediately challenges even the claim that oil does not satiate. The *mishnah* in *Nedarim* states that one who vows to abstain from *mazon* — sustaining food — is nonetheless permitted water and salt. This implies that water and salt alone are excluded from the category of *mazon*, while everything else provides sustenance. Does this not include oil? *Rav Huna* resolves the difficulty by noting that the vow in question uses the broader formulation *kol hazan alai* — "anything that provides sustenance to me" — rather than the more restricted term *mazon*. Everything except water and salt provides some degree of sustenance; but not everything shares the identity of *mazon* in the narrower sense. Oil, then, does provide some sustenance — *alma mishcha zayen* — but not to the same degree as wine.

The *gemara* then probes whether wine truly satiates at all. *Rava* would drink wine on *erev Pesach* specifically to whet his appetite so that he could eat *matzah* with greater desire. Wine, on this account, increases appetite rather than suppressing it. The *gemara* resolves this: a large quantity of wine whets the appetite, while a small amount satiates. The question is then pressed further from a verse: *yayin yismach levav enosh* — "wine gladdens the heart of man" — while *lechem levav enosh yisad* — "bread sustains the heart of man." If bread satiates and wine gladdens, how can we say wine satiates?

The *gemara* reframes the position: wine does two things — *sa'id u'mesame'ach* — it satiates and it gladdens. Bread only satiates; it does not gladden. Wine thus combines both functions, and this dual quality is what earns it a unique *bracha*. The combination of biological sustenance and the capacity to elevate one's spirit places wine in a category of its own among foods and drinks.

### Wine Not a Meal

The *gemara* then pushes the reasoning to its logical conclusion: if wine both satiates and gladdens, perhaps one should recite *birkat hamazon* after drinking it, just as after a bread meal. The *gemara* rejects this: *lo kavei inshi sudata alei* — people do not establish a meal around wine. Wine may perform the biological function of filling a person, but it is not the kind of thing around which a meal is organized. One does not sit down to a meal of wine.

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* presses *Rava*: what if someone actually declared that they were making a meal of wine — would *birkat hamazon* then apply? *Rava* responds sharply: such a person's individual perception is nullified — *batla deitei etzel kol adam* — no normal person makes a meal of wine, and therefore one's subjective determination cannot transform it into a *seudah* requiring *birkat hamazon*.

This ruling raises a more general question about when subjective context can affect *halachic* categorization. The *gemara* here is clear that establishing something as a *kovi'at seudah* for purposes of *birkat hamazon* is not the kind of determination that can be left to individual perception. By contrast, questions of *ikar* and *tafel* — which component of a mixed dish is primary and which secondary — do carry a significant subjective dimension, since these categories are by their nature contextual. But whether something constitutes a meal at all is a threshold question about shared norms, not individual preference, and *batla da'ato etzel kol adam* shuts off any argument from individual intention.

---

## Olive Oil Status

### Oil Contradiction

Having concluded the discussion of wine, the *gemara* returns to examine the earlier statement directly: *Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Shmuel*, and *Rav Yitzchak* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*, that the blessing on olive oil is *borei pri ha'etz*. The *gemara* immediately asks: under what circumstances? If one drinks it directly, that causes harm — as the *braita* demonstrates from the laws of *terumah*: one who drinks *terumah* oil pays only the principal, not the added fifth, because drinking oil directly is not the normal mode of deriving benefit. The Torah's obligation of repayment plus a fifth applies only to *ki yochal* — genuine consumption — and pure drinking of oil does not qualify. The oil damages the person; it is not proper consumption. So this cannot be the case for which *borei pri ha'etz* is prescribed.

### Oil in Mixture

Perhaps, then, one eats it through bread — dipping bread into oil. The *gemara* dispatches this quickly: the bread is *ikar* and the oil is *tafel*, and the rule is explicit in the *mishnah*: one makes the *bracha* on the primary item and thereby exempts the secondary. The oil would not receive its own *bracha* at all.

### Ikar and Tafel

The *gemara* therefore identifies the correct case: one drinks the oil by way of *anigron* — a medicinal mixture. *Rabba bar Shmuel* explains that *anigron* is water of beets, a liquid preparation into which oil is mixed. The parallel preparation *asigron* is water from other boiled vegetables. These are drinkable mixtures into which olive oil is combined, and in this context the oil may be consumed in a meaningful way.

But even here the *gemara* objects: normally the *anigron* — the beet liquid — would be *ikar* and the oil would be *tafel*. The principle returns: the *bracha* follows the primary ingredient. The *gemara* therefore narrows the case further: we are speaking of one who has a sore throat — *choshesh bigrono* — and is drinking the *anigron* specifically for the therapeutic benefit of the oil. In this context the oil is the purpose and the primary element. A *braita* confirms the framework: on *Shabbat*, one may not gargle with oil directly, as that is an overt therapeutic act, but one may prepare an *anigron* mixture with a high oil content and swallow it — the act retains the appearance of ordinary eating while providing the curative benefit on the side.

The *gemara* then asks: is this not obvious? If oil in this context is *ikar*, of course one makes *borei pri ha'etz*. The *gemara* answers that there was a reason to think otherwise: since the person's intention is *refuah* — medical benefit — one might have thought no *bracha* is said at all, as it is functioning as medicine rather than food. The *gemara* teaches otherwise: *keivan de'it lei hana'ah minei ba'ei beruchi* — since one derives genuine pleasure and benefit from it, a *bracha* is required.

This leaves open a broader question that the *gemara* does not fully resolve: what is the rule for something that is purely medicinal and provides no food-like pleasure — such as a flavored cough syrup? The *gemara*'s ruling here covers a case where the substance remains fundamentally a food, consumed in a food-like way, even if the motivation is therapeutic. Whether the same applies to preparations that are purely pharmaceutical in character remains an open question.

One further point is implicit in this discussion: if someone were to drink olive oil directly with no therapeutic framework and no *anigron* mixture, purely out of personal preference, would they even make *borei pri ha'etz*? Almost certainly not — *batla da'ato etzel kol adam* would apply. Whether such a person would make *shehakol* or no *bracha* at all is a separate question left open. The key principle established is that *borei pri ha'etz* on olive oil applies in the specific case where oil is the *ikar* in a context where its consumption is recognized as normal.

---

## Wheat Flour Case

### Flour Debate

The *gemara* now moves into a broader discussion of foods consumed in unusual or altered states, extending the principles opened by the *mishnah*. The case is *kimcha de'chitti* — wheat flour eaten plain. A *braita* elsewhere establishes that one who chews raw wheat kernels says *borei pri ha'adamah*. The question is whether this *bracha* is retained when those same kernels have been ground into flour.

*Rav Yehuda* says one still recites *borei pri ha'adamah*. *Rav Nachman* says one recites *shehakol niheyah bidvaro*. *Rava* urges *Rav Nachman* not to dispute *Rav Yehuda*, since both *Shmuel* and *Rabbi Yochanan* — transmitted through *Rav Yehuda* himself — maintain that olive oil receives *borei pri ha'etz* even though it is not in its natural form. If oil retains its original *bracha* despite transformation, so too should flour.

### Flour vs. Oil

The *gemara* rejects the comparison: *hatam leit lei iluya achrina* — for olive oil, there is no higher state to which it can progress. Oil is what it is; there is no further, superior form of consumption that the olive is "supposed to" become. Flour, by contrast, has a higher state available to it: bread. Flour is not in its ideal form. It is an intermediate stage on the way to becoming something else. This intermediate character undermines its status.

One might have framed the issue differently — not that flour has a higher potential state, but simply that flour is not a normal way of eating wheat. People chew kernels; people eat bread; but eating flour directly is not a recognized mode of consumption. The *gemara*'s emphasis on the "higher state" — *iluya achrina* — points to the same underlying reality: flour is not food in its own right. It is not yet at a stage fit for normal consumption.

### Unfit Foods

The *gemara* then asks: does the *gemara* mean to say that anything in an intermediate state that has a higher form to reach receives only *shehakol*? *Rabbi Zeira* in the name of *Rav Mattana* in the name of *Shmuel* rules that a raw gourd — *akra chaya* — and barley flour — *kimcha de'sa'ari* — both receive *shehakol*, precisely because they are unfit for consumption. This is noteworthy: a raw gourd is in its natural state — it has not been processed at all — yet it receives only *shehakol*. Natural form, then, does not protect a food; what matters is whether it is in a state fit for normal consumption.

One might ask: does the ruling about barley flour apply equally to wheat flour? The *gemara* says yes: if anything, the *gemara* should have stated the rule for wheat flour — which is closer to human food — and we would have derived the more obvious case of barley flour from it by *kal ve'chomer*. The reason barley flour was specified is to teach a different lesson: one might have thought that barley flour, which is not genuinely human food and can even cause harm, receives no *bracha* at all. The *gemara* teaches that even here, some *bracha* applies.

### Blessing Floor

This brings the *gemara* to the question of the floor of *brachot*: is there anything one might eat that receives absolutely no *bracha*? The *gemara* raises salt and *zumes* — a type of brine or salt water. A *braita* rules that on salt and brine one says *shehakol niheyah bidvaro*. These are things people eat in negligible quantities and only rarely; yet they receive *shehakol*. How could one have thought barley flour receives less than this?

The *gemara* answers: salt is something people do sometimes put directly in their mouths, even if rarely. But barley flour — *kimcha de'sa'ari* — actually causes intestinal harm, *tehol ve'kashi le'kukiani*. One might have thought that something actively deleterious to health is so far outside the category of food that it warrants no *bracha* at all. The *gemara* teaches: *keivan de'it lei hana'ah minei ba'ei brukhi* — since one derives some pleasure from it, a *bracha* is required.

The upshot of this extended analysis is a set of interlocking principles. First, natural form does not guarantee a food's standard *bracha* — raw gourd in its natural state gets *shehakol*. Second, changed form does not necessarily reduce a *bracha* — olive oil in the appropriate context retains *borei pri ha'etz*. Third, what determines the *bracha* is primarily whether the item is in a normal, fit-for-consumption state and whether consuming it in that way is a recognized mode of benefit. Fourth, the combination of changed form and an intermediate, non-ideal state — as with wheat flour — reduces the *bracha* further, to *shehakol*. Fifth, the floor of the system is *shehakol*: as long as any pleasure is derived, some *bracha* applies.

*Tosafot* adds an important qualification on the wheat flour case. *Tosafot* notes that the *gemara* is likely not discussing flour that has been ground to a complete powder, because in that case there would never be grounds for *borei pri ha'adamah* to apply at all. Rather, *Tosafot* understands that *borei pri ha'adamah* applies only to a coarser, grainier flour that still retains some quality of the original grain. Once something has been so thoroughly processed that it entirely loses its original form — as with, for instance, a product that has been pulverized, fully reformed, and bears no visual or textural relationship to its source — even *borei pri ha'adamah* is no longer appropriate, and the *bracha* falls to *shehakol*. This principle underlies the practical distinction often drawn between regular potato chips, which retain enough of the original form to merit *borei pri ha'adamah*, and products like extruded chips that are reconstituted from flour, which receive *shehakol*.

---

## Planting Intent

### Palm Hearts

The *gemara* now turns to a related but distinct principle: the intent of the one who plants a tree and how that intent shapes the *bracha* on what the tree produces. The case is *kora* — the tender tip of the palm leaf, which *Rashi* describes as the soft new growth of the leaf before it hardens. *Rav Yehuda* rules *borei pri ha'adamah*: it is a kind of fruit, growing from a tree, and merits this *bracha*. *Shmuel* rules *shehakol niheyah bidvaro*: since if left alone it would harden and become inedible — *hava sofo lehakshot* — its status as an edible product is incomplete and therefore it receives only *shehakol*.

### Radish Comparison

*Shmuel* then concedes to *Rav Yehuda* — *shinana, kevatach mistabra* — your position actually makes more sense. After all, a radish also hardens and becomes inedible if left in the ground too long, yet in its edible state it receives *borei pri ha'adamah*. By analogy, the soft tip of the palm leaf should also receive *borei pri ha'adamah* while it is still edible.

But the *gemara* concludes: *velo hi* — this comparison does not hold. The radish is planted with the intent of eating it — *ada'ata de'pugla natei inshi*. The palm tree — *dikla* — is not planted with the intent of eating the leaf tips — *lo ada'ata de'kora natei inshi*. The palm is planted for its dates, its wood, its fiber — not for these incidental edible portions. Because this product falls entirely outside the intent of planting, it receives only *shehakol*. Although *Shmuel* acknowledged the logical strength of *Rav Yehuda*'s argument, the *gemara* rules: *hilchata kevata de'Shmuel* — the law follows *Shmuel*.

### Caper Bush

The *gemara* challenges this principle with the case of the *tzalaf* — the caper bush. The caper bush is planted primarily for its fruit — *ada'ata de'parcha natei inshi* — yet the *mishnah* rules that on *minei nitzpa* — various secondary parts of the bush, including leaf buds and capers attached to the leaves — one recites *borei pri ha'adamah*, while on the *evyonot* — the actual fruit — and the *kaphrisin* — which *Rashi* understands as a kind of shell or casing surrounding the fruit — one recites *borei pri ha'etz*. This creates a hierarchy: the primary fruit of the bush gets *borei pri ha'etz*, while secondary products that are not the main reason for planting get *borei pri ha'adamah*. Why, then, should the palm tips receive only *shehakol* rather than *borei pri ha'adamah*?

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* answers: the caper bush is planted with multiple products in mind. Even if the fruit is primary, the other parts — the leaves, buds, and related components — are also among the things one hopes to harvest when planting. *Ada'ata de'shusha natei inshi* — people plant the caper bush with these secondary products part of their expectation. By contrast, *lo natei inshi ada'ata de'kora* — no one plants a palm tree with the leaf tips in mind. These are entirely outside the intent of planting, and therefore the palm tips fall to *shehakol* rather than *borei pri ha'adamah*.

### Blessing Hierarchy

What emerges from this discussion is a clear three-tiered hierarchy governed by the intent of planting. The primary product for which the tree is planted receives *borei pri ha'etz*. Secondary products that are part of the planting intent — things one hopes to harvest even if they are not the main goal — receive *borei pri ha'adamah*. Products that fall entirely outside any planting intent, which just happen to grow from the tree and which some people may occasionally eat, receive only *shehakol*.

This principle has practical implications that extend beyond the classical cases. The *bracha* appropriate for a given food can, in principle, shift over time as agricultural practice and market demand evolve. If a product that was previously incidental to a tree's cultivation becomes the primary reason for planting — or moves from being an occasional curiosity to a commercially cultivated commodity — its *bracha* may change accordingly. Anything available in a market context was presumably planted *ada'ata de'hachi* — with that product in mind — and would therefore qualify at minimum for *borei pri ha'adamah*, assuming it is in a reasonably natural and processed state. The transition from *shehakol* to *borei pri ha'adamah*, and potentially from *borei pri ha'adamah* to *borei pri ha'etz*, is governed by the accumulated norms of cultivation and consumption.

---

## Modern Applications

### Juice Question

The principles developed throughout this *sugya* bear directly on contemporary practice in ways that remain actively debated. Take apple juice and orange juice. These are clearly transformed from their source fruit — *ishtani* — but they are not in an intermediate state on the way to a better product, and they are not excessively processed. If anything, they represent a highly desirable form of consumption. On the reasoning developed by the *gemara*, one might expect *borei pri ha'etz* to apply. And indeed, there are serious *halachic* opinions that argue exactly this.

However, the prevailing practice is to recite *shehakol*. The historical basis for this practice lies in the reality of the *gemara*'s world: in that era, no one squeezed juice from apples or oranges for direct consumption. Grape juice and olive oil were the only fruits regularly processed into liquid form. Juice from other fruits was considered incidental — a byproduct, almost a sweat of the fruit — not a recognized mode of deriving benefit. It was therefore *ishtani li'greiusa* — a transformation to a worse state — and would have received *shehakol*. Today the situation has changed substantially. Specific varieties of oranges are cultivated expressly for juice production; the juice is the intended product. Many authorities argue that *ada'ata de'hachi natei inshi* — the planting intent has shifted — and that *borei pri ha'etz* is now warranted. Nevertheless, *minhag ha'olam* — the accepted widespread practice — remains *shehakol*, in part because reciting *borei pri ha'etz* on a liquid feels counterintuitive to most people, even though the *gemara* itself does exactly this in the case of olive oil.

### Coffee & Cocoa

Coffee beans and cocoa beans present analogous questions. These are products of trees — the coffee plant and the cacao tree — and they are planted expressly for the derived products: coffee and chocolate. The *ada'ata de'hachi* argument would seem to point toward *borei pri ha'etz* for these as well, and there are those who so rule, particularly for foods with a high concentration of the primary product, such as very dark chocolate. In the case of coffee, there is the additional complication that the beverage is nearly entirely water flavored by the beans, which raises questions of *ikar* and *tafel*.

### Custom Practice

Here too, *minhag ha'olam* is to recite *shehakol*. The tension between a serious *halachic* argument for *borei pri ha'etz* and the prevailing custom of *shehakol* illustrates a recurring dynamic in this area of *halacha*: the principles established in the *gemara* generate expectations that, when applied to modern agricultural and culinary realities, point in one direction, while accepted practice has crystallized around a different norm. The *gemara*'s framework itself provides the tools to argue both ways — the question of *ada'ata de'hachi*, the question of transformation for better or worse, the question of whether a *bracha* appropriate to a liquid differs from one appropriate to solid food — and the debates remain live for those who engage seriously with the underlying reasoning.

---

---

# Berakhot 36b

## Tzlaf & Fruit Definition

### Tzlaf Overview

The sugya opens with a ruling of *Rav Yehuda amar Rav* concerning the *tzlaf*, the caper bush, which produces several distinct products. As established earlier in the discussion, the products for which the bush is primarily cultivated, as well as those which qualify objectively as its fruit, receive the *bracha* of *borei pri ha'etz*. Products that are either secondary in purpose or do not meet the definition of fruit receive *borei pri ha'adama*. This distinction immediately raises a deeper conceptual question: what exactly defines a fruit? Is it purely functional — determined by what the tree is primarily cultivated for — or is there an objective botanical or halachic reality to the category of fruit that transcends the particular use to which it is put?

To explore this, the *Gemara* turns to other areas of *halacha* in which the definition of fruit is equally consequential. What follows is a sustained comparative analysis across multiple halachic domains — *brachos*, *orlah*, *ma'aser*, *kilayim*, and eventually *tumah* and *shemita* — built on the striking assumption that a single unified definition of fruit operates consistently across all of them.

### Orlah & Rabbi Akiva

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: the ruling concerns *tzlaf shel orlah* — a caper bush in its first three years. *Orlah* applies even outside *Eretz Yisrael*, though its status there is rabbinic in nature, making it subject to greater leniency. The ruling is that *b'chutz la'aretz* — outside the Land of Israel — one discards the *avyonos*, which are the fruit of the bush, and may eat the *kafrisin*. The *avyonos* are forbidden because *orlah* applies to the fruit; the *kafrisin* — which *Rashi* identifies as the shell of the fruit and *Steinsaltz* identifies as the floral buds — are permitted.

The *Gemara* immediately presses: does this mean the *avyonos* are a fruit and the *kafrisin* are not? If so, how do we reconcile this with the *braisa* cited earlier in the context of *brachos*, which ruled that one says *borei pri ha'etz* on both the *avyonos* and the *kafrisin*? This is a significant question, and it illustrates one of the *Gemara*'s foundational assumptions: that halachic categories are consistent across domains. In secular legal systems one would never presume that the definition of "fruit" in one area of law necessarily matches the definition in an entirely different area of law. In *halacha*, however, the *Gemara* proceeds from the working assumption that these categories are universal — a methodological premise worth pausing to appreciate.

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by noting that the ruling of *Rav Yehuda amar Rav* follows the position of *Rabbi Akiva*, as stated in a *Mishna* in *ma'asros*. There, *Rabbi Eliezer* holds that the caper bush is subject to *ma'aser* on its *timros*, *avyonos*, and *kafrisin* — all three products are considered fruit for tithing purposes. *Rabbi Akiva*, by contrast, rules *ein misa'er ela avyonos bilvad* — only the *avyonos* are subject to *ma'aser*, because only they qualify as *pira*, as fruit.

### Ma'aser Comparison

The *Gemara* then asks: why not simply state that we rule like *Rabbi Akiva* altogether, in every domain? The answer establishes an important principle. The leniency toward *Rabbi Akiva*'s position is not a blanket adoption of his view across all categories. Rather, it is a product of a specific principle governing *orlah*: *kol ha-meikel b'aretz, halacha k'moso b'chutz la'aretz* — if one takes a lenient position regarding *orlah* in *Eretz Yisrael*, we rule in accordance with that lenient position outside the Land. Since *orlah* outside Israel has the status of *halacha l'Moshe m'Sinai* with an associated tradition of leniency, we are permitted to rely on minority opinions in that domain.

But this does not mean that the underlying conceptual category of fruit is different in different areas of law. The *Gemara* is clear that in *brachos*, *orlah*, and *ma'aser*, the definition of fruit is, in principle, the same. The difference is not definitional but legal: the permissibility of relying on a lenient opinion varies by domain.

### Orlah Leniencies

To explain why we could not simply declare that we rule like *Rabbi Akiva* for all *orlah* purposes outside Israel, the *Gemara* offers a further consideration. One might have assumed that *Rabbi Akiva*'s leniency could only be applied to *ma'aser* of fruit trees, since *ma'aser* of fruit is itself rabbinic even within the Land. Outside the Land it would be doubly rabbinic — a *drabbanan* of a *drabbanan* — and therefore a natural candidate for leniency. But one might have thought that *orlah*, which is *de-Oraisa* in the Land, cannot be treated so leniently even outside Israel. The ruling teaches that nevertheless, for *orlah* outside Israel, we do adopt the lenient position and restrict the prohibition to the fruit itself.

The depth of leniency permitted by *orlah* in *chutz la'aretz* is illustrated by the *Mishna*: *safek orlah* — doubtful *orlah* — is forbidden in *Eretz Yisrael* and permitted in *Suria* (territories conquered by David and the Hasmoneans). Outside of that entirely, the leniency goes further still: one may purchase fruit directly from a vendor's orchard even knowing that some of the trees are *orlah*, as long as one does not witness the vendor picking directly from those trees. The license to create the doubt, not merely to be lenient when the doubt arises on its own, reflects how far the leniency extends.

This raises a further question: given such sweeping leniency for *orlah* in *chutz la'aretz*, why not rely on *Beit Shammai*, who would classify the caper bush as a vegetable and thereby exempt even the *avyonos* from *orlah* restrictions? To this the *Gemara* responds: *Rabbi Akiva bimkom Rabbi Eliezer avdinan kevateih* — we are prepared to rely on *Rabbi Akiva* even though *Rabbi Eliezer* disagrees, because *Rabbi Akiva* represents a recognized minority position. But *Beit Shammai bimkom Beit Hillel eino mishnah* — once *Beit Shammai* has been definitively overruled by *Beit Hillel*, their ruling is no longer even a minority opinion upon which we may rely. This point carries broader significance for the general principle of *da'at yachid bish'at ha-dechak* — reliance on a minority opinion in times of pressing need. Not every position ever articulated constitutes a legitimate minority opinion; a view that has been wholly rejected loses that status.

### Kilayim Dispute

A new halachic category enters the discussion: *kilayim*. While one may plant trees alongside a vineyard, one may not plant grain or vegetables there. The question is how to classify the caper bush. *Beit Shammai* rules that it is *kilayim b'kerem* — it may not be planted in a vineyard, implying that it is not a tree. *Beit Hillel* rules *ein kilayim b'kerem* — it is not subject to that prohibition, treating it as a tree. Yet remarkably, both schools agree — *elu v'elu modim she-chayavin b'orlah* — that the caper bush is subject to *orlah*, which is categorically a law applying to trees. Here, then, is an explicit instance within the *Gemara* itself where the category of "tree" diverges between two areas of *halacha*. What is a tree for *orlah* may not be a tree for *kilayim*.

### Beit Shammai Logic

The *Gemara* recognizes that *Beit Shammai*'s position appears internally contradictory: they call it *kilayim* in a vineyard — implying it is a vegetable — yet agree it is subject to *orlah* — implying it is a tree. The *Gemara* resolves this: *Beit Shammai sepuki mesapka lehu* — they are simply uncertain how to classify the caper bush. Faced with this uncertainty, they apply stringency in both directions: they treat it as a tree for *orlah* purposes, where being stringent means applying the prohibition, and they treat it as a vegetable for *kilayim* purposes, where being stringent means imposing the restriction. The position is coherent as an expression of consistent stringency under conditions of doubt, even if the legal treatment differs across categories. What is striking is that the *Gemara* does not invoke this as a license to treat definitions differently across categories in general. Every prior opportunity to distinguish the categories was declined; the assumption of cross-category consistency holds firm. *Beit Shammai*'s divergent treatment is explained not as a principled distinction between domains but as an application of *chumra* in a case of genuine uncertainty.

### Safek Orlah Rules

The rules of *safek orlah* — doubtful *orlah* — further illuminate the graduated structure of leniency across territories. In *Eretz Yisrael*, doubtful *orlah* is forbidden. In *Suria*, doubt is resolved leniently and the fruit is permitted. In *chutz la'aretz*, the leniency extends even to cases where one has proactively placed oneself into a position of doubt — one may purchase from a vendor's orchard knowing that some trees are *orlah*, provided one does not witness the picking from those specific trees. This graduated framework shapes the entire discussion of which opinions we are prepared to rely upon by domain and by territory.

---

## Kafrisin Status

### Shomer Concept

Even granting that the *kafrisin* are not themselves defined as fruit — whether one accepts *Rashi*'s identification of them as a kind of shell or *Steinsaltz*'s identification as floral buds — the *Gemara* presses a further question. Why should the *kafrisin* not be forbidden under *orlah* for a different reason entirely: not as fruit, but as a *shomer* — a protective covering of the fruit? The *Torah* states *va-araltem et piryo*, and the word *et* is taken to extend the prohibition: *et ha-tafel le-piryo* — not merely the fruit itself but what accompanies it. The *shomer*, the protective covering of the fruit, is included in the *orlah* prohibition even if it does not itself qualify as fruit.

*Rava* formulates the initial criterion: *heicha d'ita bein bi-tlush bein bi-mechubar* — something qualifies as a *shomer* only when it remains attached to the fruit even after the fruit has been detached from the tree. A walnut shell, for example, continues to enclose the fruit after plucking. Here, however, the *kafrisin* — whether shell or bud — is no longer present once the fruit is detached. According to *Rashi*, the shell falls away after plucking; according to *Steinsaltz*, it does not come off with the fruit at all. In either reading, it fails the criterion.

### Shomer Definition

*Abaye* challenges *Rava*'s formulation with a contradiction from the laws of *tumah*. The *pitma* — the hard crown-like protrusion at the base of a pomegranate — is considered a unit with the pomegranate for purposes of combining toward the minimum measure that makes something susceptible to *tumah*. Yet the *netz* — the fine fibrous material inside that crown — does not combine for that measure, indicating it is not considered food. And yet a *braisa* on *orlah* teaches that the *netz* of a pomegranate is *chayav be-orlah*, included in the prohibition as a *shomer* of the fruit. If the *netz* falls away and deteriorates after plucking — making it unavailable in the detached state — and it is still considered a *shomer*, then *Rava*'s criterion that the *shomer* must persist after plucking cannot be correct.

### Pomegranate & Dates

*Rava* revises his position: *ela amar Rava, heicha d'iteih bish'at gmar peira* — a *shomer* is defined as something present when the fruit reaches its state of completion, when it fully ripens. The *kafrisin* is not present at that stage — it has already fallen away before the fruit matures — and therefore it is not a *shomer*.

A second challenge arises from *Rav Nachman* citing *Rabbah bar Avuha*: certain coverings associated with dates under *orlah* — referred to as *mitchali* — are forbidden, and they are described as *hovei vena'asu shomer la-pri*, protectors of the fruit. Yet *Rav Nachman* specifies that these *mitchali* protect the date *be-kuphra* — when the date is still fully unripe. If the *mitchali* is present only in the unripe stage and not when the date has finished ripening, then *Rava*'s revised criterion — presence at the moment of full ripening — would equally exclude them. Yet they are still deemed *shomrim*. The *Gemara* therefore cannot sustain *Rava*'s revised rule as stated.

### Rabbi Yosi Position

The resolution comes through a fundamental dispute about when a fruit is considered a fruit at all.
