## Pesach Matzot

### Pesach Exception

Rav Papa teaches: *hakol modim be-Pesach she-maniach perusa be-toch shleima u-votze'a* — on Pesach, everyone agrees that one places the broken piece inside the whole *matzah* and makes the *bracha* on the combined unit. The context here is almost certainly *pita*-style flatbread rather than the soft *matzot* we use today, which is why placing one piece inside another was a practical option. In our practice, we hold the pieces together and make the blessing over both simultaneously.

### Lechem Oni

*Amar lei mai ta'ama* — what is the reason? *Lechem oni ktiv* — it is written "poor person's bread," and the poor person's bread is characteristically a broken loaf. On Pesach night, the broken *matzah* is not merely an accident of handling; it is itself halachically significant. The *mitzvah* of *matzah* on Pesach night specifically requires what is characterized as the bread of poverty, and a broken piece is that bread by definition.

This creates a genuine tension with the general principle that favors whole loaves. The resolution is the combined holding or stacking: one maintains the *shalem* — the whole *matzah* — for the general preference of wholeness, while incorporating the broken piece to fulfill the specific requirement of *lechem oni*.

### Ashkenazi Custom

The Ashkenazic practice is to hold all three *matzot* — two whole ones and the middle broken one — when making *hamotzi*. The *bracha* of *hamotzi* is directed toward the top whole *matzah*, satisfying the *lechem mishneh* requirement. Then, when reciting *al achilat matzah*, attention turns specifically to the middle broken *matzah*, which is the *lechem oni* and the one through which the *mitzvah* of eating *matzah* is most properly fulfilled. Though one is technically *yotzei* through any of the *matzot*, the broken middle piece is the one that the *mitzvah* specifically demands, and so it receives the focus of the second blessing.

### Multiple Blessings

Tosafot raises the question of whether making two blessings over the same object — *hamotzi* directed at the top whole *matzah*, then *al achilat matzah* — amounts to improperly piling up *mitzvot*. The answer, Tosafot concludes, is that *birchat ha-nehenin* — blessings of pleasure and enjoyment — are not subject to that concern. The principle against multiplying *mitzvot* on a single act applies to commanded obligations, not to blessings tied to personal enjoyment and *hana'ah*. The precedent is clear: we recite *borei pri ha-gafen* over wine at *kiddush* and then say all the blessings of *kiddush* over the same cup, without any concern that this constitutes inappropriate accumulation.

### Rambam Position

The *Rambam* takes a notably different position. He holds clearly that *hamotzi* on Pesach night should be made on the broken piece — the *perusa* — rather than the whole *matzah*. This accords strictly with the requirement of *lechem oni* and makes the broken piece, not the whole one, the primary vehicle of the *bracha*. In practice, the *Sefardic* communities follow the *Rambam*, though there is variation within those communities regarding whether three *matzot* are held to begin with or only two.

---

## Shabbat Lechem

### Double Manna

The Gemara now turns to the Shabbat obligation. Rav Abba teaches: *uvShabbat chayav adam livtzo'a al shtei kikarot* — on Shabbat one is obligated to break bread over two loaves. The reason: *lechem mishneh ktiv* — the verse says double bread, referring to the double portion of *man* that fell on Friday so that the Israelites would not need to gather on Shabbat. Therefore, we maintain two loaves on Shabbat to commemorate that double portion.

The straightforward implication of the Gemara's formulation is that this obligation applies specifically to Shabbat and not to *Yom Tov*. There is a debate among the *rishonim* on this point, partly tied to the question of whether the *man* fell double on *erev Yom Tov* as well. Our widespread practice is to observe *lechem mishneh* on *Yom Tov*, but the Gemara's language here does strongly suggest it is a Shabbat-specific institution. This also clarifies why on Pesach the practice of combining the whole and broken *matzah* is not driven by *lechem mishneh* concerns — the double-loaf requirement does not apply there in the same way — but rather by the competing interests of *shalem* and *lechem oni*.

A significant practical point: the *halacha* requires that two whole loaves be present for *lechem mishneh*, and wholeness is certainly the *lechatchila* standard. However, the absence of a whole loaf does not eliminate *lechem mishneh* entirely. One could technically fulfill the institution with two slices, ensuring that two loaves are represented even if neither is complete. This raises an interesting question left as a *she'ela*: if on Shabbat one possesses a single whole loaf and nothing else, does one make *hamotzi* on the whole loaf and forgo *lechem mishneh*, or does one break it in half to create two pieces and thereby achieve *lechem mishneh* at the cost of wholeness?

### Portion Requirement

Rav Ashi reports: I saw Rav Kahana hold two loaves on Shabbat — *denakit tartei* — and break only one — *u-vatza chada*. One is not obligated to eat from both loaves; having both present satisfies the institution. This is indeed the *halacha* we follow: *lechem mishneh* is a requirement of presence, not consumption.

### Zeira's Piece

Rav Zeira's practice is recorded: *hava batza a-kulei sheruta* — when he took his piece of bread for Shabbat, he would cut a very large chunk, sufficient to last him the entire meal.

### Etiquette Question

Ravina questioned Rav Ashi about this: *v'ha kamitchazi k'ra'avtanusa* — does this not look like gluttony or poor manners, the same quality for which Bar Kappara criticized the student who rushed to bless the poultry? Rav Ashi replied: *keivan de-chol yoma lo ka-avid hachi* — since this is not his normal practice throughout the week, and he does it specifically now, *lo mitchazi ke-ra'avtanusa* — it does not appear to be a failure of manners. He is not acting from habit or lack of self-control; there is a reason for this specific behavior in this specific context. The Gemara does not spell out that reason explicitly, though the connection to the institution of the *man* — which fed the Israelites for an entire day's portion — offers a compelling explanation for why a substantial Shabbat portion carries its own kind of significance.

### Thick Slices

Rav Ami and Rav Assi are reported to have cut very thick slices — *rifta* — sufficient for a person to be sustained for an entire meal. This is presented in the context of Shabbat eating, where the size of the portion connects meaningfully to the theme of the double *man* and the fullness that Shabbat meals are meant to embody.

---

## Eruv Food

### Ami & Assi

The Gemara concludes with a report about Rav Ami and Rav Assi: *ki hava misrami lehu rifta de-eruva* — when they happened to have bread left over from an *eruv* — whether *eruv chatzeirot* or the food set aside for *eruv tavshilin* — *mevarchin aleha Hamotzi Lechem Min Ha'aretz* — they would specifically make *hamotzi* on it and eat it themselves.

### Mitzvah Principle

*Amri* — they said: *ho'il ve-is'avid bah mitzvah chada, na'avid bah mitzvah achriti* — since this food has already been used for one *mitzvah*, let us use it for another. Rather than giving it away or setting it aside, they made a point of eating it themselves and reciting *hamotzi* over it, thereby involving it in the *mitzvah* of Shabbat or *Yom Tov* bread.

### Custom Connection

This principle has become the basis for the *minhag* of specifically eating the food designated for *eruv tavshilin* at the Shabbat or *Yom Tov* meal. Once an object has been sanctified for one *mitzvah* purpose, there is a value in connecting it to another. The Gemara continues with this theme, and this principle resonates with the broader spirit of Shabbat meal practice that the entire sugya has been elaborating — from the structure of blessings and the priority of loaves, through the significance of size and wholeness, to this final note on carrying forward the sanctity of one *mitzvah* into the next.

---

---

# Berakhot 41

## Non-Ground Foods

### Intro: Vinegar & Locusts

The *mishna* on daf 40b closes with the category of foods that do not grow from the ground — having already addressed *adama*, *ha-etz*, *borei peri ha-gafen*, and *ha-motzi*, the *mishna* now turns to what lies outside all those categories. The ruling is: *ve-al davar she-ein gidulo min ha-aretz* — on something that does not grow from the ground — *omer she-hakol nihyah bi-dvaro*. The examples given are vinegar (*chometz*), *novlot* (a kind of spoiled or damaged date, to be examined below), and *govai* (a kosher species of locust). On all of these, one recites *shehakol*.

### R. Yehuda: Min Klala

On this the *mishna* records the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda: *kol she-hu min ha-klala ein mevarchin alav* — anything that is an expression of curse, one does not recite a blessing over it. Locusts, which devastate crops and represent a curse upon the world, fall into this category. Vinegar, at least in antiquity, was typically not the product of deliberate effort but of wine gone bad. These are, in Rabbi Yehuda's view, unworthy of a *bracha*.

This raises two distinct questions. The first is theological. We have already learned elsewhere the principle *ke-shem she-mevarchin al ha-tov kach mevarchin al ha-ra* — just as one blesses over the good, so one blesses over the bad — which would seem to suggest that even unfortunate circumstances call for acknowledgment of God's sovereignty. The second question is more structural: we generally hold that one may not derive benefit without a preceding *bracha*, yet Rabbi Yehuda seems to hold that where the item is an expression of curse, the Torah's *bracha* is not warranted, and therefore deriving benefit from it incurs no obligation. Both tensions are striking and the *gemara* does not fully resolve them here, moving on instead to practical *halacha*.

### Seven Species Priority

The *gemara* next records a dispute regarding the case where *minim harbe* — many different types of food — are set before a person. Rabbi Yehuda rules: *im yesh beineihem mi-min shiva alav hu mevarech* — if one of the *shivat ha-minim* is among them, the *bracha* is made on that item first. The *chachamim* disagree: *mevarech al eizeh mehem she-yirtze* — one may recite the blessing on whichever one wishes. The earlier discussion in the *gemara* (where choice was placed at the bottom of any hierarchy of preference) seemed to favor Rabbi Yehuda's formulation. How this plays out will become clearer below.

### Braita: Shehakol List

A *braita* is now cited that enumerates the categories requiring *shehakol*. These include: meat of domesticated animals, wild animals, birds, and fish (*besar behemot chayot ve-ofot ve-dagim*); dairy products and animal byproducts such as milk, eggs, and cheese (*chalav, beitzim, gevina*); foods that have spoiled — moldy bread (*pat she-i-efsha*), wine that has developed a surface film (*yayin she-hikrim*), or a cooked dish whose form has been ruined (*tavshil she-avar tzurato*); and also salt, brine (*zamit*), and mushrooms and truffles (*kmehin u-fitriyot*). On all of these one recites *shehakol*.

This *braita* stands in evident tension with Rabbi Yehuda's position: it explicitly rules that spoiled and deteriorated foods — bread gone moldy, wine partially turned — do receive a *bracha*, namely *shehakol*. The question of whether the concern is about lack of taste, or whether it is about the theological impropriety of blessing over what has gone bad, remains open.

### Fungi: Root Question

The *gemara* pauses on the case of *kmehin u-fitriyot* — mushrooms and truffles — and asks: *lemeimra d'khmeina u-fitrya la gidulei karka ninhu?* Do we mean to say that fungi do not grow from the ground? They clearly emerge from the ground's surface — perhaps one should recite *borei pri ha-adama*? The *gemara* adduces a *baraita* about vows: one who vows to abstain from *peirot ha-aretz* (fruits of the ground) is forbidden to eat fruit but permitted to eat mushrooms and truffles. However, if he vows to abstain from *kol gidulei karka* — all things that grow from the ground — he is forbidden even from mushrooms and truffles. So they are considered *gidulei karka* in some sense. Why then is *borei pri ha-adama* not recited over them?

### Abaye: No Root Draw

Abaye resolves the difficulty: *mirba ravvu me-ara* — yes, they grow off the ground — *minka la yanki me-ara* — but they do not draw their nutrients from within the ground. Unlike true ground produce, fungi draw on already-decomposed organic matter; they have no root system that processes inorganic nutrients from the soil. They grow from the ground without nursing from it.

The *gemara* then re-reads the *mishna*'s language accordingly: rather than *al davar she-ein gidulo min ha-aretz* (something that does not grow from the ground), the correct reading is *al davar she-ein yonek min ha-aretz* — something that does not draw its nourishment from the ground. The text was imprecise; the principle is about the mechanism of nourishment, not merely the location of growth.

One might raise the question of hydroponics — vegetables grown in water rather than soil, from a species that would ordinarily grow from the ground. In this particular case, the plant is not drawing from the soil at all. The widespread practice is to recite *adama* on such produce, though the question deserves fuller analysis in its own right.

### Novlot Debate

The *gemara* turns to the case of *novlot*, the spoiled dates mentioned in the *mishna*. Two *amoraim* from the school of Rav Zeira and Rabbi Ila dispute the term: one says *bushlei chamra* — dates that have been "cooked" by excessive exposure to the sun while still on the tree; the other says *tamrei d'zika* — dates blown off the tree by the wind.

The *gemara* tests each interpretation against Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that things which are an expression of curse receive no *bracha*. According to the view that these are sun-scorched dates, the description fits: the fruit has been ruined by the elements, a form of natural curse, and it also explains why only *shehakol* (and not *borei pri ha-etz*) is recited — the dates have undergone *ishtani l'reiusa*, a change for the worse. According to the view that they are merely wind-fallen dates, however, it is difficult to call them a curse — they are fully edible, simply fallen early from the tree. The *gemara* proposes *pashra*: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda's *min klala* language refers only to the other items in the *mishna*'s list (the vinegar and the locusts), not to the *novlot*. This resolution is not entirely satisfying.

An alternative formulation reverses the difficulty: according to the view that they are sun-cooked dates, it is perfectly intelligible that the *mishna* would prescribe *shehakol* rather than *borei pri ha-etz* — the dates have been ruined and are *ishtani l'reiusa*. But according to the view that they are merely wind-blown and intact, why would one recite anything less than *borei pri ha-etz*?

The *gemara* concludes: the unqualified term *novlot* in the *mishna* refers to dates that have been sun-scorched (*bushlei chamra*). The distinct phrase *novlot temarah*, found elsewhere, may refer to wind-fallen dates. This leads the *gemara* into the *mishna* of *Demai*.

### Demai Categories

The phrase *novlot temarah* appears in the *mishna* of tractate *Demai*, in a section listing *hakalin she-be-demai* — the lenient categories of *demai*. *Demai* arises when one purchases produce from *amei ha-aretz* who are not meticulous about separating *terumot u-ma'asrot*. While one may assume *teruma* has been separated (since its proportion is negligibly small and *amei ha-aretz* generally would not neglect it), *ma'asrot* remain a concern. The *mishna* in *Demai* lists a set of fruits so commercially insignificant that one may assume even *amei ha-aretz* would not have objected to separating *ma'asrot* from them — and therefore the consumer need not worry about *demai* with respect to these items.

### Fruit Identifications

The *mishna* in *Demai* lists: *hashitin*, *harimin*, *ha-ozradin*, *bnot shuach*, *bnot shikma*, *gofnin*, *nitzpa*, and *novlot temarah*. The *gemara*, with the assistance of Rabbah bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan, identifies each: *shitin* are a variety of unripe or inferior figs (*min te'einim*); *rimin* are jujube berries (fruit of the *ziziphus lotus*); *ozradin* are crabapples; *bnot shuach* are white figs (*te'anei chivarta*); *bnot shikma* are the fruit of the sycamore tree (*duvli*), not normally consumed; *gofnin* are end-of-season grapes of inferior quality (*shilei gofnei*); *nitzpa* is the fruit of the caper bush — our familiar friend from earlier discussions; and *novlot temarah* is the case now under examination.

### Fallen Dates Hekker

The dispute between sun-cooked and wind-blown dates reasserts itself in the context of the *Demai* *mishna*. According to the view that *novlot temarah* means wind-blown dates (*tamrei d'zika*), one can understand why the *mishna* calls them *novlot temarah* with the qualifier — they are intact dates that have merely fallen, so the qualifying word marks their lesser status. According to the view that they are sun-cooked, there is less reason to use different terminology in the two sources. The *gemara* concedes this as a *kashya* but does not press further.

A separate question is posed: if these are indeed wind-blown dates — intact, perfectly edible — why are they listed among lenient *demai* categories? They are, after all, fit for market. The *gemara* answers: *hefker ninhu* — they are presumed abandoned. Dates that fall naturally from the tree are generally assumed by their owners to be of no value to them; people commonly expect others to pick them up, and the owner would in retrospect have acquiesced. This *de facto* abandonment of wind-fallen dates is closely related to the broader *Bava Metzia* discussion of *ye'ush she-lo mi-da'at* — whether unwitting renunciation, before the owner is even aware of a loss, constitutes legally effective *ye'ush*.

However, the *gemara* adds, if the owner explicitly gathered these fallen dates together and processed them as he would normal produce — taking them to a threshing area and collecting them — this changes matters: *she-asaan goren*. Drawing on Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov, the *gemara* rules that *leket*, *shikcha*, and *pe'ah* which a poor person has gathered and processed like a normal crop are rendered *hukbe'u le-ma'aser* — they become obligated in *ma'aser* rabbinically, because through his actions the owner has effectively treated them like his regular agricultural output.

---

## Blessing Priority

### Same Bracha Priority

The *gemara* now returns to the dispute about prioritizing *brachot* when multiple foods are present. Ulla frames the parameters: *machlokes she-be-virchoteihem shavot* — the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim* applies only when the foods share the same *bracha*, such as two fruits both requiring *borei pri ha-etz*. When a single *bracha* must represent the entire group, the question of which food takes pride of place becomes meaningful. Rabbi Yehuda holds *min shiva adif* — a member of the *shivat ha-minim* takes precedence; the *rabbanan* hold *min chaviv adif* — whichever food one personally prefers takes precedence.

### Different Brachot

When the foods carry *different* brachot, Ulla continues, *divrei ha-kol mevarech al ze ve-chozer u-mevarech al ze* — everyone agrees one makes each *bracha* separately, and the order does not matter. This seems straightforward: a carrot and an apple carry different *brachot* (*adama* and *ha-etz* respectively), so one simply recites each in turn, with no priority question.

But one might object: did we not learn several days ago that certain *brachot* take precedence over others — that *borei pri ha-adama* precedes *shehakol*, and that more specific *brachot* take precedence over generic ones? The resolution, following Rashi as explained by Tosafot, is that the earlier discussion concerned the case of *shehakol* competing with a specific *bracha* — there, *shehakol* is so generic that the specific *bracha* clearly prevails. But when two specific *brachot* confront each other — *borei pri ha-etz* and *borei pri ha-adama* — both are specific. Although *borei pri ha-adama* can cover *borei pri ha-etz* retroactively (*be-di'avad*), the two categories nonetheless have independent standing. Each governs its own domain, and when they are truly separate eating occasions, everyone can agree that the order is free.

### Radish & Olive

The *gemara* raises an objection from a *baraita*: *hayu lefanav tzonon ve-zayit* — one had before him a radish and an olive. The radish requires *borei pri ha-adama*; the olive, a member of the *shivat ha-minim*, requires *borei pri ha-etz*. The *baraita* rules: *mevarech al ha-tzonon u-poter et ha-zayit* — one recites the *bracha* on the radish and thereby exempts the olive. This is striking on multiple counts. First, it implies that the *rabbanan* allow — or even recommend — reciting *borei pri ha-adama* and covering *borei pri ha-etz* under it, apparently *le-chatchila*. Second, it passes over the olive entirely despite it being from the *shivat ha-minim*, which seems to contradict Rabbi Yehuda's position.

Adding to the difficulty, the end of that same *baraita* records Rabbi Yehuda's view: *mevarech al ha-zayit she-zayit mi-min shiva* — one makes the *bracha* on the olive, because the olive is from the *shivat ha-minim*. The *gemara* then asks: does Rabbi Yehuda not accept the principle of *ikkar ve-tafel* — that when one food is primary and another accompanies it in a secondary capacity, the *bracha* on the primary exempts the secondary? The *baraita*'s own conclusion states as much: *im machmat tzonon ba ha-zayit* — if the olive is being eaten because of the radish (i.e., to flavor or accompany the radish), *mevarech al ha-tzonon u-poter et ha-zayit* — even Rabbi Yehuda agrees the *bracha* is made on the radish. So Rabbi Yehuda does accept *ikkar ve-tafel*; his disagreement is only about the case where neither is secondary to the other.

### Ikkar v'Tafel

This establishes a clear principle: *kol she-hu ikkar ve-imo tefela mevarech al ha-ikkar u-foter et ha-tefela* — when one food is primary and another accompanies it in a subordinate role, the *bracha* on the primary exempts the secondary. The secondary food is present not as a food in its own right but to serve the primary — to enhance its taste, cleanse the palate, or provide a vehicle for eating it.

### Gemara Rewrite

The *gemara* is now confronted with the full force of the objection. The *baraita* appeared to set up a case where radish and olive are competing on equal terms — neither is *ikkar* and neither is *tafel* — and the *rabbanan* rule that one may recite *borei pri ha-adama* and have it cover *borei pri ha-etz*. That would flatly contradict the earlier conclusion that different *brachot* each have their own independent sphere.

The *gemara* therefore undertakes a radical rewriting of the *baraita*: *ve-chasurei mechsera ve-hachi katani* — the text is incomplete and should be read as follows. The opening case of radish and olive — *mevarech al ha-tzonon u-foter et ha-zayit* — refers specifically to the case where the radish is the *ikkar*, and everyone agrees. The *baraita* then continues: *bameh devarim amurim? ke-she-tzonon ikkar* — this applies when the radish is primary. *Aval im ein ha-tzonon ikkar* — but when it is not primary, then *divrei ha-kol mevarech al ze ve-chozer u-mevarech al ze* — everyone agrees one makes separate *brachot*, each in its own domain, and may choose whichever order one wishes. The disputed case, where Rabbi Yehuda and the *rabbanan* actually disagree, is recast as one involving two foods with the *same* bracha (*borei pri ha-etz*), where the question is which one represents the group.

This is, as the *gemara* itself acknowledges, a substantial rewrite. The *baraita* as written spoke quite explicitly of radish and olive as competing contenders for a single *bracha*. The *gemara* essentially removes that competition from the text and replaces it with a different dispute — one about priority within the *shivat ha-minim* when a single *bracha* must represent the group.

### Rav Ami Debate

The *gemara* now records a direct dispute between Rav Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha. One holds that the *machloket* between Rabbi Yehuda and the *rabbanan* applies only when the *brachot* are equal (*shevichoseihem shavot*) — and when the *brachot* differ, everyone agrees each is recited separately. The other holds that the *machloket* applies *even* when the *brachot* differ (*af be-she-ein birchoteihem shavot nami machloket*) — and the debate extends even to the question of whether *borei pri ha-adama* may *le-chatchila* be used to cover a food requiring *borei pri ha-etz*.

### Pasuk Order Ruling

The *gemara* then asks: according to the view that the dispute extends to different *brachot*, what exactly are they arguing about? If each food will in any case receive its own *bracha*, what difference does the debate make? Rabbi Yirmiyah answers: *le-hakdim* — they are arguing about which one comes first. The basis for this is a principle stated by Rav Yosef (and some say Rabbi Yitzchak): *kol ha-mukdam ba-pasuk ze mukdam le-vracha* — whatever appears earlier in the *pasuk* receives the earlier *bracha*.

### Seven Species List

The *pasuk* in question is: *eretz chita u-se'ora ve-gefen u-te'ena ve-rimon, eretz zayit shemen u-dvash* (Deuteronomy 8:8). This verse lists the seven species in a specific order: wheat, barley, grape, fig, pomegranate — then a second *eretz* — olive oil, and (date) honey. According to Rabbi Yirmiyah's application of this principle, when two species from this list are before a person and each requires a separate *bracha*, the one that appears earlier in the verse is recited first. Rabbi Yehuda holds that this ordering principle governs even when the *brachot* differ; the *rabbanan* may concede the ordering principle absent a *chaviv* factor, but allow personal preference to override it.

Tosafot rules accordingly: *borei pri ha-etz* precedes *borei pri ha-adama* even when the *brachot* differ, following Rabbi Yehuda whose position we adopt as *halacha*. The question of how *chaviv* — personal preference or immediate eating intention — factors into this ordering remains a live one in later *poskim*.

---

## Shiurim Standards

### R. Chanin: Sizes

The *gemara* notes that the use of this *pasuk* as a source for *bracha* priority is challenged by Rabbi Chanin. Rabbi Chanin says: *kol ha-pasuk kulo le-shiurin ne'emar* — the entire verse was stated with respect to halachic *shiurim*, standard measurements, not as a source for the precedence of *brachot*. The seven species serve as the referents for various halachic quantities, each species providing the defining measure for a distinct area of law.

### Wheat: Eat Time

*Ne'emar chita* — wheat is mentioned, and from this we learn the standard of *achilat pras*, the time it takes to eat a half-loaf, which is operative in the laws of *tuma*. As the *mishna* teaches: one who enters a *bayit ha-menuga* (a house afflicted with leprosy) while wearing his clothes — with sandals on his feet and rings on his fingers — becomes *tamei* immediately, but his garments only acquire *tuma* if he remains long enough to eat a *pras*. The time of *achilat pras* is measured with reference to wheat bread (*pas chitin*), not barley bread — Rashi explains that wheat bread is eaten somewhat more readily. Furthermore, the standard assumes one is eating while reclining (*meisev*) and eating the bread with an accompaniment (*u-v'liftan*), as would be normal.

### Barley: Bone Size

*Se'ora* — barley — provides the standard for bone *tuma*. The *mishna* teaches: *etzem keshorah* — a bone the size of a barley grain causes *tuma* by contact and by carrying, though not *tuma* in a tent (*tumas ohel*), which requires a much more substantial portion of the skeletal structure.

### Wine: Reviit

*Gefen* — the grape — provides the standard of *reviit ya'yin le-nazir*: a *nazir* (nazirite) transgresses the prohibition against wine only when he drinks a *reviit* (approximately three and a half ounces). The choice of wine as the referent here is somewhat puzzling, since it is the very substance being measured for the *nazir*'s prohibition. Both Rashi and Tosafot grapple with this. Tosafot suggests that the issue has to do with surface tension — that wine displacement and water displacement yield different results when measuring volume, and the relevant standard must therefore be calibrated to wine. Rashi approaches the matter from the angle of density — wine contains more substance per unit of volume than water — though the precise halachic application of that density difference is not immediately obvious, since *reviit* is a volume measurement. Both explanations strain somewhat, and this remains a point of difficulty.

### Fig: Grogeret

*Te'ena* — the fig — provides the standard called *grogeret*, the size of a dried fig, which is the minimum quantity for which carrying on *Shabbat* constitutes a transgression. *Kegrogeret le-hotza'at Shabbat* — the dried fig size is the standard amount for *Shabbat* carrying.

### Pomegranate: Hole Size

*Rimon* — the pomegranate — provides the standard for holes in vessels and their *tuma* status. A homeowner's vessel, which is not sold commercially, retains its status as a vessel — and thus its susceptibility to *tuma* — even with a hole, as long as the hole is smaller than a pomegranate. The reasoning is practical: a commercial vessel would be removed from sale once any hole appeared; a homeowner's vessel would continue to be used for progressively coarser goods — first liquid, then grain, then fruit — until the hole grew too large even for pomegranates to be stored without falling through. Only at that point does the object cease to function as a vessel and lose its susceptibility to *tuma*. *Kol klei ba'alei batim shiuram ke-rimonim*.

### Kezayis Standard

*Zayit shemen* — the olive — provides what Rav Yosef states is the overwhelmingly dominant halachic standard: *eretz she-rov shiureha ke-zaysim* — a land most of whose measures are the *kezayis*. How much *matzah* must one eat? A *kezayis*. How much of a forbidden substance constitutes a transgression? A *kezayit*. How much food must one consume to be obligated in *birkat ha-mazon*? A *kezayis*. The *gemara* qualifies the claim slightly — not literally *all* measurements, since as we have just seen, some use other standards — but the *kezayis* is correctly described as the central and most prevalent halachic standard of food quantity.

### Date Honey

*U-dvash* — honey, understood here as date honey rather than bee honey — provides the standard for *Yom Kippur*. The amount of food that, if consumed on *Yom Kippur*, constitutes a transgression of the *inuy* (affliction) prohibition is not a *kezayis* but rather *ke-kosevet ha-gasa* — like a large date. The rationale is that on *Yom Kippur* the relevant threshold is not mere eating but genuine abatement of the fast's discomfort, and a *kezayis* alone is insufficient for that purpose; a fuller, more satiating quantity is required.

The *gemara* then addresses the objection: if the *pasuk* is being used as the source for these *shiurim*, what is left for Rabbi Yirmiyah's use of it as a basis for *bracha* priority? The answer is that the *shiurim* themselves are not explicitly written anywhere — they are not derived directly from the text of the *pasuk* as a matter of *derasha*. Rather, they are either *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* (as an alternative reading in the *gemara* suggests with the word *hilchasa*) or derive from rabbinic tradition, and the *pasuk* serves merely as an *asmakhta* — a textual peg for what was already known. The *pasuk*, therefore, remains available to Rabbi Yirmiyah as a source for priority in *brachot*.

---

## Blessing Priority (II)

### Dates & Pomegranates

A practical illustration of the priority principle appears immediately. Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna were sitting together at a meal when dates and pomegranates were brought before them. Rav Hamnuna took the dates and recited the *bracha* on them first. Rav Chisda challenged him: does the master not hold of the principle stated by Rav Yosef — or some say Rabbi Yitzchak — that *kol ha-mukdam ba-pasuk ze mukdam le-vracha*, whatever comes earlier in the *pasuk* gets the earlier *bracha*? The pomegranate (*rimon*) is the fifth species in the first *eretz*, while honey (*devash*) — understood as date honey — is the second species mentioned after the second *eretz*. So the pomegranate, appearing earlier in the verse overall, should take precedence.

Rav Hamnuna replied: *ze sheni la-aretz ve-ze chamishi la-aretz* — this one (the date honey) is second relative to the second *eretz*, while that one (the pomegranate) is fifth relative to the first *eretz*. When the verse restarts with a second *eretz*, the count resets; therefore, date honey as the second item from the second *eretz* precedes the pomegranate as the fifth item from the first *eretz*.

Rav Chisda's response was enthusiastic: *man yahav lan nagdi de-farzla ve-nishme'inach* — would that we had iron legs so that we could always follow you and attend to your teachings! This ruling is the accepted *halacha*: the two *eretz* groupings are counted separately, and proximity to one's respective *eretz* determines priority within and between the groups, with the first *eretz* group taking overall precedence when competing against the second.

Tosafot adds: when a food from the first *eretz* competes with a food from the second *eretz* for priority, the first *eretz* wins.

---

## Foods in Meals

### Mid-Meal Fruit

The *gemara* now introduces one of the most practically significant discussions of the *daf*: what are the *bracha* obligations for foods eaten during and after a meal of bread? The case presented is figs and grapes brought in the middle of the meal (*betoch ha-seudah*). One can easily visualize the setting — a Roman-style reclined meal in which small dishes of fruit are brought between courses, perhaps to cleanse the palate.

### Huna & Nachman

Both Rav Huna and Rav Nachman rule identically: *te'unim bracha lifneihem ve-ein te'unim bracha le-achareihem* — these mid-meal fruits require a *bracha* before eating them but not after. The reasoning operates on two axes. Before: the figs and grapes are not considered a staple part of the meal and are not understood as accompanying the bread in a *tafel* capacity; they therefore require a separate *bracha* before. After: even though they may not be *zan* (sustaining) in the strict sense, *birkat ha-mazon* with its formulation of *ha-zan et ha-kol* (Who nourishes all) covers all food consumed during the meal, and no separate *bracha achrona* is required.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet disagrees and takes a stricter position: *te'unim bracha bein lifneihem bein le-achareihem* — these mid-meal fruits require a *bracha* both before and after. In his view, there is no category of food that receives a *bracha* before but is then covered by *birkat ha-mazon* without its own *bracha achrona* — with one exception to be noted momentarily. The implication is that fruit eaten mid-meal, not being genuinely *zan*, does not fall within *birkat ha-mazon*'s scope.

### Rashi: Flavored Bread

Rav Sheshet's exception is *pas ha-ba'ah be-kisnin* — a form of bread-like food whose exact definition is the subject of major dispute among the *rishonim*, with significant contemporary application to things like pastries, pizza, and *bourekas*. In brief: it is bread in which some element — sweetening, spicing, filling — renders it more of a flavored or dessert item than a true *lechem*. Rashi's view is that *pas ha-ba'ah be-kisnin* is the one case in which a *bracha* is recited before (the *bracha* of *mezonot*) without a corresponding *bracha achrona*, because *birkat ha-mazon* covers it. On Rashi's reading, the broader principle is that *birkat ha-mazon* covers anything eaten in the meal that is in some sense associated with the bread — the bread functions as the organizing center, and what accompanies it, including flavored bread-like foods, is absorbed into its *bracha* sphere at the end.

Tosafot and virtually all other *rishonim* reject this interpretation and do not rule accordingly. The upshot of Rashi's position, were it followed, would be that a substantially wider range of foods eaten during a meal would require separate *brachot* before — any food that is not conceptually linked to the bread.

### R. Chiya: Full Exemption

The *gemara* notes that the view of both Rav Huna and Rav Nachman — requiring a *bracha* before but not after for mid-meal fruit — stands in tension with the position of Rabbi Chiya. Rabbi Chiya states: *pas poter kol minei maachal, ve-yayin poter kol minei mashke* — bread exempts all types of food, and wine exempts all types of drink. Rabbi Chiya holds that any food consumed in the context of a bread meal is covered by *ha-motzi*, requiring no additional *bracha* before or after. Similarly, wine drunk in the context of a meal at which *borei peri ha-gafen* was already recited requires no further *bracha* — a practically important ruling with implications for *kiddush* and for other drinks served alongside wine.

### Rav Papa Halacha

Rav Papa rules definitively on the three categories: *devarim ha-ba'im machmat ha-seudah betoch ha-seudah* — things that come as part of the meal and are eaten during it — *ein te'unim bracha lo lifneihem ve-lo le-achareihem*. They require no *bracha* before or after; *ha-motzi* covered them at the start and *birkat ha-mazon* covers them at the end. This is the ordinary case: meat, vegetables, potatoes — whatever fills the plate of the meal. *Ve-shelo machmat ha-seudah betoch ha-seudah* — things not considered *machmat ha-seudah* but eaten during the meal — *te'unim bracha lifneihem ve-ein te'unim bracha le-achareihem*. They require a *bracha* before but *birkat ha-mazon* covers them after. *Le-achar ha-seudah* — after the meal — *te'unim bracha bein lifneihem u-vein le-achareihem*. Once the meal is concluded, any food eaten requires both a *bracha* before and a *bracha achrona* after.

### Machmas Haseuda

The decisive question is what *machmat ha-seudah* means — and here Rashi and Tosafot part ways fundamentally. Rashi holds that *machmat ha-seudah* means something directly associated with the bread: foods that one eats together with, alongside, or as a vehicle for the bread. On this reading, a dish of oatmeal eaten in the middle of a bread meal — not functioning as a bread-accompaniment — would be *shelo machmat ha-seudah* and would require its own *bracha* before. Rashi's conception is essentially bread-centric: *ha-motzi* covers what is in the bread's orbit; everything else stands outside it.

Tosafot rejects this decisively. According to Tosafot, *machmat ha-seudah* does not require any relationship to bread specifically. Rather, it refers to anything that performs a central function of the *seudah* — the meal itself — which is to say, anything that substantively fills and satiates. What falls *outside* this category is food eaten primarily for its flavor or pleasure rather than to fill: appetizers consumed for their taste before the meal truly begins, or desserts consumed after the main substance of the meal is complete.

### Tosafot vs Rashi

On Tosafot's reading, the defining criterion is functional: does this food do the work of a meal — does it fill? If yes, it is *machmat ha-seudah* and is covered by *ha-motzi* without further *bracha*. If it is present for its taste, its pleasurable qualities, its role as a *hors d'oeuvre* or a dessert, then it is *shelo machmat ha-seudah* and requires its own *bracha* before, though *birkat ha-mazon* still covers it at the end. This is the accepted *halacha*.

### Modern Meal Courses

Applying this framework to contemporary dining involves genuine difficulty. The categories of appetizer, main course, and dessert exist in modern meals as they did in pre-modern ones, but the lines are not always clear. A grapefruit served before the meal functions as an appetizer; is it *machmat ha-seudah* by virtue of being part of the meal's structure, or *shelo machmat ha-seudah* because it is not filling? Many hold that appetizers of this type do require a *bracha* before. Dessert, where the meal's sustaining purpose has been fulfilled and what follows is purely for pleasure, more clearly falls into the *shelo machmat ha-seudah* category — though in practice many do not recite a separate *bracha* on dessert. Some authorities have ruled broadly that in modern Western meals, where the courses are less sharply distinguished than in European or medieval meals, more of the meal's components can be treated as *machmat ha-seudah*.

What the *halacha* does not do is draw the line according to the bread specifically. A filling grain dish — even oatmeal, even rice — is *machmat ha-seudah* on Tosafot's view and requires no separate *bracha*, despite having no connection to bread. And a fruit dessert, however familiar a part of the meal it may feel, requires a *bracha* before because it is not there to fill. The abstract criterion — filling versus flavoring — must be applied to each meal's structure as it actually presents itself, and where the line falls will sometimes depend on the specific meal and occasion.

---

# Berakhot 42

## Wine Exemptions

### Wine Quantity

The daf begins with a review of several key *halachos* concerning *brachos*. The first concerns wine: a *bracha* on wine exempts *she'ar minei mashkim* — other liquids. This is an important *halacha* that many people are unaware of. The *Mishna Berurah* surveys a range of opinions on the matter, from those who require that one drink a very large quantity of wine — almost *koveiah seudah* on the wine — to those who hold that even the smallest amount suffices. His middle position is that one must drink at least a *mlo lugmav*, a majority of the *revi'is*, for *borei pri hagafen* to exempt other *mashkim*. He rejects the view that merely answering *amen* to a *kiddush* could exempt one, though such an opinion does exist.

## Machmat Haseudah

### Rashi vs Tosafot

The next major question is what is covered when one recites *hamotzi* at a meal. Rashi holds that the *bracha rishona* covers things that are fundamentally there to serve as an accompaniment to the bread — *lefapes es hapas*. According to Rashi, something that is a staple of the meal in its own right but not meant to accompany bread, such as oatmeal, would require a separate *bracha rishona*. Tosafot, and the normative ruling, hold instead that the framework is the meal itself: anything that is *machmat haseudah* is covered, while things that are not *machmat haseudah* require a separate *bracha rishona*.

### Definition

What does *machmat haseudah* mean? The general explanation is that it refers to foods that are present primarily for filling rather than purely for taste. Things present solely for taste — such as certain appetizers or desserts — are not *machmat haseudah* and raise questions about whether a separate *bracha* is needed. Although some argue that dessert today is so standard as to be considered *machmat haseudah*, the general consensus follows the more restricted view. A distinct third category is food consumed after the meal has ended: such food requires not only a *bracha rishona* but, according to the Gemara, even a *bracha achrona*, even if *birchas hamazon* has not yet been recited. Tosafot, however, holds that this post-meal phenomenon no longer applies in practice, since dessert today is always considered connected to the meal. One therefore will not encounter a case of eating something during a meal that requires its own *bracha achrona*, though a *bracha rishona* may still be required when the food is not sufficiently connected to the meal.

### Sfek Brachot

One might ask: given all these disputes, why not simply apply the principle of *safek brachos l'hakeil* and be done with it? Indeed, that is the general approach of the *poskim* — but there is a limit. One must first determine what qualifies as a genuine doubt before applying the principle. Moreover, there is a competing consideration running throughout Tosafot, drawn from the Maharim MiRothenburg: one can avoid the dilemma by eating the questionable food after *hamotzi*, thereby covering oneself. This strategy reflects the flip side of *safek brachos l'hakeil*, namely the principle that *assur l'hanos min ha'olam hazeh belo bracha* — it is forbidden to derive benefit from this world without a *bracha*. It is not merely a question of whether one has fulfilled a *mitzvah* of making a *bracha*, but whether one is entitled to derive *hanah* at all without having first recited one. That is why, although the general stance of the *poskim* is *safek brachos l'hakeil*, there is also this parallel strand encouraging one to find a way to cover oneself rather than risk deriving benefit improperly.

## Ben Zoma

### Question Posed

The Gemara now picks up five lines from the bottom of 41b, with the passage *sha'alu es Ben Zoma*. The questioners ask Ben Zoma: *mipnei mah amru devarim habaim machmat haseudah betoch haseudah einam te'unim bracha lo lifnehem velo achareihem* — why did the Sages rule that foods that come as part of the meal require no *bracha* either before or after? He replied: *ho'il upas potartan* — because the bread exempts them. The Gemara then presses: if the bread exempts everything in the meal, then *yayin nami tipater bepas* — let the wine during the meal also be exempt through *hamotzi*. This takes for granted — as the next *Mishna* will make explicit — that one does indeed recite *borei pri hagafen* on wine consumed during a bread meal. This is another *halacha* that many are unaware of: even at a weekday meal with bread, if wine is brought to the table, one must recite *borei pri hagafen*. Wine is not covered by *hamotzi*.

## Wine Exemptions (II)

### Wine Status

The Gemara answers: *shani yayin d'goreim bracha l'atzmo* — wine is different, for it causes a *bracha* unto itself. This sounds somewhat circular, but the point is clarified by the *Rishonim*.

## Ben Zoma (II)

### Wine's Ritual Status

Rashi explains that *borei pri hagafen* is a *bracha* that carries a status beyond ordinary *birchas hanehenin*. We recite it at *kiddush*, at *havdalah* — it functions as a ritual *bracha* and not only as an expression of enjoyment. Therefore, even when wine appears in the middle of a meal, we maintain the elevated status of *borei pri hagafen* as a separate *bracha*.

Tosafot offers a related but somewhat different framing. Both bread and wine, says Tosafot, are singular in that they each have their own dedicated *bracha* not because they represent a class of foods, but because of the intrinsic importance of that particular food itself. Technically, *borei pri hagafen* should have been *borei pri ha'eitz*, and *hamotzi* should have been *borei minei mezonos* — but because of the special status of bread, it receives the elevated *bracha* of *hamotzi*, and because of the special status of wine, it receives the elevated *bracha* of *borei pri hagafen*. Wine and bread are the only two foods for which an entire, distinct *bracha* was instituted for that singular food type alone. Because wine carries that weight and significance, even when it appears in the middle of the meal, we do not allow it to be overshadowed. This holds even when one knew in advance that wine would be served — the planning does not subsume the *bracha*.

## Pas Ha-Ba'ah

### Rav Huna Story

The Gemara now presents the following story. Rav Huna ate thirteen certain types of cakes or wafers — *pas haba b'kisnin* — of which every three cakes equaled a *kav*. These were substantial portions. *V'lo beirech* — and he did not recite *birchas hamazon* afterwards. Rav Nachman challenged him: *adai kafna* — these were eaten out of genuine hunger, or rhetorically: is this not food for hunger? You ate thirteen of these and filled yourself — how could you not bench? The Gemara then gives the *halacha*: *kol she'acherim kove'im alav seudah tzarich l'vareich* — if this is an amount upon which others would normally establish a meal, then even though it falls into the *mezonos* category of *pas haba b'kisnin*, if one is *koveia seudah* upon it, one must recite *birchas hamazon*. The *rav lo beirech* of the story thus refers to the omission of *birchas hamazon*, not to any *bracha* altogether.

### Keviat Seudah Rule

This leads to a broader discussion of *pas haba b'kisnin*: it is normally *borei minei mezonos* and *al hamichya*, but when the quantity consumed constitutes normal *kvias seudah*, or when the food itself is regularly used as a proper meal, it reverts to *hamotzi* and *birchas hamazon*.

### Three Categories

What exactly is *pas haba b'kisnin*? Among the *Rishonim* there are essentially three main positions, each corresponding to a type of food that has the technical ingredients of bread — flour, water, baked in an oven — yet does not function socially or culinarily as bread, and therefore receives *mezonos* status. It may, however, revert to *hamotzi* status under certain conditions.

The first approach, associated with Rashi and broadly the Rambam, is that the dough is sweetened with spices, eggs, or fruit juices, such that it tastes fundamentally different from bread dough. The paradigm case is cake; a croissant would be another example — highly enriched, very sweet, the additives alter the character of the dough itself.

The second approach derives the word *kisnin* from *kis*, a pocket, and understands *pas haba b'kisnin* as a filled dough — some type of pie, *borekas*, *knish*, or similar stuffed baked good. It is dough, but it does not function as bread.

The third approach, associated with Rabbeinu Chananel and others, identifies *pas haba b'kisnin* as a hard, thin, crunchy wafer — crackers, pretzels, breadsticks, and the like. Again, these have the ingredients of bread but do not function as bread in normal social consumption.

The normative practice tends to be lenient and applies *borei minei mezonos* and *al hamichya* to all three categories. However, the question remains: at what point does even a food that falls into one of these categories revert to *hamotzi* and *birchas hamazon*? The answer is: either when the quantity is such that normal people would establish a meal upon it — *kvias seudah* — or when the particular food is used in practice as a meal itself.

### Modern Examples

Several contemporary examples illuminate how these principles apply. The case of *mezonos* rolls is instructive. What makes a roll a so-called *mezonos* roll is the substitution of eggs or fruit juice for water in the dough. But if one has eaten those airline *mezonos* rolls, they taste entirely like a normal roll. For those authorities who hold that *pas haba b'kisnin* requires a genuinely different-tasting dough — not merely a technical substitution — such rolls are highly questionable. Furthermore, they are typically eaten in the same context and function as bread at a meal, which means that *lachen koveim alav seudah*, and the *bracha* would revert to *hamotzi* in any case. *Mezonos* rolls are therefore considered very problematic.

The case of *challah* with raisins is different: the dough itself is not affected by the raisins, which are merely an addition. There may be a question about where to draw the line — at what point does a dough taste sufficiently spiced or enriched to change its character — but the addition of raisins alone does not cross that threshold.

Pizza presents a more complex case. Some argue it is *pas haba b'kisnin* because the dough is covered with and accompanied by other primary ingredients, suggesting that the crust functions more as a base than as bread. But others argue that pizza is simply a meal — not a snack, not a treat — and that most people sit down to pizza as they would to any other meal. If that is the case, then either the social use of pizza takes it out of *pas haba b'kisnin* entirely, or at minimum the quantity is such that *koveim alav seudah* and *hamotzi* applies. Pizza as always requiring *hamotzi* is a defensible position.

Breadsticks raise a parallel question. If they function like pretzels — as a snack — they may well be *mezonos*. But if they are placed in a bread basket and function as bread at the table, a different analysis may apply.

Meat pies and *knishes* complicate things further. If one were to sit down to a meal of shepherd's pie as the central dish, the filling is the meal and the dough is secondary — which might suggest the dough itself is not serving as bread, but the food overall may be functioning as a meal in a way that affects the *bracha*. These lines are difficult to draw.

The general principle is this: *pas haba b'kisnin* foods technically contain the ingredients of bread, but because by convention they function in a non-bread-like way — as snacks, treats, or accompaniments — they are *mezonos* and *al hamichya*. When convention itself changes, or when the quantity reaches *kvias seudah*, the *bracha* reverts to *hamotzi* and *birchas hamazon*.

### Wedding Story

The Gemara now relates the story of Rav Yehuda. Rav Yehuda was arranging his son's marriage into the household of Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva — some type of engagement party or wedding celebration. *Ayitu lekamaeihu pas haba b'kisnin* — they brought before the guests a type of *pas haba b'kisnin*, whatever it was — some cake, wafer, or pie. When Rav Yehuda entered and heard that everyone was reciting *hamotzi*, he asked with some exasperation: *mai tzi tzi dekashmana* — what is all this *hamotzi hamotzi* I am hearing? *Dilma hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz kamvarchitu* — are you actually reciting *hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz*?

They replied: yes! For *detanya Rav Mona amar mishum Rav Yehuda pas haba b'kisnin mevorchin alav hamotzi* — Rav Mona taught in the name of Rav Yehuda that even on *pas haba b'kisnin* one recites *hamotzi*. And moreover, *veamar Shmuel halacha keRav Mona* — Shmuel ruled in accordance with Rav Mona.

Rav Yehuda responded: what Shmuel said was *ein halacha keRav Mona itmar* — that we do not rule like Rav Mona. They had heard his statement correctly but inverted its import — Shmuel said something about Rav Mona, but what he said was that the *halacha* does not follow him.

The guests then pressed Rav Yehuda: but you yourself have said in the name of Shmuel that *lachmaniyos* — some type of sweetened rolls or enriched baked item in the *pas haba b'kisnin* category — may be used for an *eruv* and over them one recites *hamotzi*. Surely you yourself hold they are bread?

Rav Yehuda replied: *shani hasam d'kava sudasa aleihu* — that case is different, because those are used for *kvias seudah*. The point is not merely that a food technically satisfies the definition of *pas haba b'kisnin* while simultaneously being used as a regular meal food. Once such a food is actually used as bread — once people are *koveia seudah* upon it — it is no longer functioning as *pas haba b'kisnin* and reverts to *hamotzi*. Here at the engagement party, by contrast, these were hors d'oeuvres, light fare — *lo kava sudasa aleihu* — nobody was establishing a meal upon them, and so they remain *mezonos*.

### Rav Pappa Visit

The Gemara continues with a parallel story. Rav Pappa visited the house of Rav Huna the son of Rav Noson. *Basar d'gamru sudasaihu* — after they finished their meal, *aysu kameihu midi l'meichal* — they brought before them something to eat, a type of dessert. Rav Pappa took it and ate. The members of the household challenged him: does the master not hold that *gamar assur l'meichal* — once the meal is complete, one may not eat? The *Rishonim* clarify that this does not mean it is forbidden to eat entirely — one may eat, but only after reciting a *bracha*. Once the meal has been designated as complete, any subsequent food is no longer considered part of the meal and requires at least a *bracha rishona*, and possibly even a *bracha achrona* according to the Gemara. The challenge to Rav Pappa thus assumes he ate without reciting a *bracha*.

Rav Pappa replied: *lo salik itmar* — the *halacha* does not say when you finish eating, it says when you perform *salik* — when you have removed the table. In those times, each diner had a personal small table beside him. Even if one declared oneself full and unable to eat another bite, and even if food was subsequently brought out, the meal is not halachically concluded until the table has literally been removed. Until that moment, a new *bracha* is not required.

## End of Meal

### Table Removal

This raises the broader question of when the meal is considered to have ended in a way that requires a new *bracha* for anything subsequently consumed. The episode with Rav Pappa establishes one position: the threshold is *siluk hashulchan* — the physical removal of the personal table.

### Dependent on Host

The Gemara then presents a further story. Rava and Rav Zeira were at the house of the *Reish Galuta*, the political head of Jewry in exile. *U-vatar de-saliku taka* — after their own dishes had been removed and they considered themselves finished, the *Reish Galuta* sent them a special portion from his table. Rava ate it; Rav Zeira did not. Rava asked Rav Zeira: do you not hold that once the table is removed one may not eat — implying Rav Zeira was being stringent? Rav Zeira responded: *anan a-takka de-Reish Galuta samchinan* — we are dependent on the table of the *Reish Galuta*. The meal is not over until he has finished.

### Da'at Ba'al Bayit

This is a significant *halacha* with implications well beyond the specific narrative. The *Rishonim* derive from here a general principle: a guest at someone's home makes a *bracha al da'at ba'al ha-bayit* — on the basis of the host's plans. Since the guest does not know what will be served and when, every *bracha* the guest recites is implicitly calibrated to whatever the host has planned to bring. Tosafot makes this explicit, ruling that when a host brings out fruits one after another, one need not recite a *bracha* on each successive item, because *somchim al shulchan ba'al ha-bayit* — one relies on the table of the host. This is the same principle operative in the *Reish Galuta* story.

The practical limit is that this applies when one is genuinely in the position of being fed by another. When one is one's own host — foraging in one's own kitchen, making individual decisions about what to eat — one cannot invoke *da'at ba'al ha-bayit*. In that case the *bracha* covers only what one had in mind at the time of recitation, not future unspecified decisions. One could in principle recite a *bracha* with an open-ended intent covering a range of foods — but whether a fully generic intent, covering anything one might subsequently decide to take from the kitchen, would suffice is a separate and more complex question.

### Three Immediates

The Gemara then moves to a different formulation of what defines the end of the meal. It cites Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav: *shalosh techofot hen* — there are three actions that must follow immediately upon a prior action. *Tachef lismicha shechita* — immediately after *semicha* one slaughters the animal. *Tachef ligeula tefila* — immediately after *Gaal Yisrael* one begins *tefila*. And *tachef lintilat yadayim bracha* — immediately after *netilat yadayim* one recites the *bracha*. These three are grouped together because the *Yerushalmi* derives all three from *pesukim*.

The *netilat yadayim* in question, in this context, is understood as referring to *mayim acharonim* at the end of the meal — the handwashing that signals the conclusion of the meal, after which *birchas hamazon* must follow immediately. This is the ruling the Gemara adopts as normative: *v'leit hilchata kechol hani shema'teta* — we do not rule like any of the other criteria that were proposed (finishing eating, removing the table, the oil). Instead, the definitive marker of the meal's end is *mayim acharonim*, and *birchas hamazon* must follow immediately upon it.

The Gemara adds that Abaye proposes a fourth *tachef*: *tachef letalmidei chachamim bracha* — a blessing follows immediately in the wake of *talmidei chachamim*, as attested by the verse *vayivarcheni Hashem biglalecha* — God blessed me on your account, what Laban said to Yaakov. Or alternatively from the verse *vayevarech Hashem et beit hamitzri biglal Yosef* — God blessed the Egyptian household on account of Yosef. The cases of Yaakov and Yosef are being invoked as illustrations of the *talmid chacham* whose proximity brings blessing, though it is noted that *tzaddikim* and *talmidei chachamim* are perhaps different categories.

### Mayim Acharonim and Birc…

Tosafot raises a difficulty with the picture the Gemara presents: we have a practice to leave bread on the table before *bensching*, which seems to conflict with an expectation that the table would be removed. Tosafot resolves this by noting that the practice of removing personal trays applied in Talmudic times, whereas today we remove plates but maintain the bread on the table. This distinction also bears on the question of how Tosafot conceptualizes the status of the *afikoman* at the *Seder*: since *halacha* demands that the *afikoman* be eaten, it is as if one is *someich al da'at hahalacha*, and the meal cannot be considered truly concluded until the *afikoman* has been consumed — even if one has otherwise performed *siluk hashulchan*. A halachically mandated eating, by this logic, extends the parameters of the meal.

Regarding *mayim acharonim* itself, Tosafot and the *Shulchan Aruch*, reinforced by the *Mishna Berurah*, indicate that once *mayim acharonim* has been performed, one should proceed directly to *birchas hamazon* — one should not speak and should not eat additional food even with a *bracha*. The *Aruch HaShulchan* dissents, arguing that if one wishes to speak, eat more, or recite another *bracha*, one may do so and then perform *mayim acharonim* again immediately before *bensching*. The *Mishna Berurah* acknowledges this position. In practice, many who do perform *mayim acharonim* follow the *Aruch HaShulchan*.

The further question arises for those who do not practice *mayim acharonim* at all, which is the case in many communities today: what then constitutes the end of the meal? This may revert closer to the earlier Talmudic criteria — clearing the table, or some analogous act — though no definitive answer is offered here. What is clear is that the functional concern remains: once one has signaled through words and action that the meal is over, any subsequent eating is not considered part of the meal and requires a new *bracha*.

## Mishna Coverage

### Before/After Rule

The *Mishna* now sets out a series of rules about which *bracha* covers which. *Beirach al hayayin shelifnei hamazon patar es hayayin she'achar hamazon* — if one recited a *bracha* on the wine served before the meal, that *bracha* exempts the wine served after the meal, even though the meal will have intervened and the post-meal wine constitutes a distinct drinking occasion. Similarly, *beirach al haparperes shelifnei hamazon patar es haparperes she'achar hamazon* — if one recited a *bracha* on the pre-meal snack (presumably a *mezonos* item), that covers the post-meal snack as well, even though wine and these snacks are not covered by *hamotzi* and even though the meal falls between them. The *bracha* before can extend to the corresponding item after, as the two remain loosely connected as part of the same occasion.

### Bread vs Snacks

The *Mishna* then states: *beirach al hapas patar es haparperes* — reciting *hamotzi* on bread exempts the snacks, presumably even those consumed after the meal. This is interesting, since one might have thought that post-meal items are outside the scope of *hamotzi*. Tosafot addresses this by suggesting that the *parperes* referred to in this clause are not truly *mezonos* but rather something closer to bread chips — they are genuinely a form of bread, and therefore even when eaten after the meal they remain within the scope of *hamotzi*. However, *al haparperes lo patar es hapas* — reciting a *bracha* on the snack does not exempt the bread. Even if, as Tosafot holds, both items are technically in the *hamotzi* category, the snack is not of sufficient significance to exempt real bread.

### Beit Shammai

*Beis Shammai omrim af lo ma'aseh kedeirah* — Beit Shammai adds that even cooked foods, such as porridge or stew, are not covered. The Gemara will question precisely how to read this statement of Beit Shammai, as we will see shortly.

## Sitting Together

### Sitting Position

The *Mishna* continues: *hayu yoshvin kol echad mevarech le'atzmo* — when they were sitting, each person recites their own *bracha*. *Heseivu echad mevarech lekulan* — but if they reclined together, establishing themselves as a *kvias seudah*, one person recites for everyone.

This raises a conceptual question. Normally, we do not recite *birchas hanehenin* on behalf of another, since *birchas hanehenin* is about one's personal, subjective experience of benefit — it must be the individual's own acknowledgment and thanks, not a piggybacking onto someone else's *bracha*. We permit one person to be *yotzei* through another's *bracha* only when they are defined as a group, so that the one reciting is expressing the *bracha* of the collective, not merely of themselves. This is the logic of *zimun* at the end of a meal — one person benches on behalf of a group because they constitute a unified entity. The same logic applies at the start: when all have reclined together and established themselves as a group engaged in a shared *kvias seudah*, they are a collective, and one person's *bracha* expresses the *bracha* of all.

What constitutes *heseivu* today, when *haseibah* is no longer our practice? One view is that without *haseibah* there can be no such grouping. Another view holds that *haseibah* is not the operative criterion for us; what matters is *kvias seudah* together. Tosafot, however, maintains that one cannot have *kvias seudah* without bread — that bread remains a necessary ingredient for the collective to function as a group in this sense.

### Wine Categories

The *Mishna* then distinguishes between wine drunk during the meal and wine drunk after. *Ba lahem yayin betoch hamazon kol echad ve'echad mevarech le'atzmo* — when wine comes during the meal, each person recites their own *bracha*, since drinking during the meal is understood as an individual act. Each person drinks because they are thirsty, or not — the drinking during a meal is personal and not a group activity. *Aval le'achar hamazon echad mevarech lekulan* — but after the meal, when everyone brings out wine to share together, the drinking is now a group occasion, and one person may recite on behalf of all. The person given the honor of reciting *borei pri hagafen* on the post-meal wine also recites the *bracha* on the *mugmar* — the incense burned after the meal for fragrance — even though that comes after everything, and possibly even after *birchas hamazon*.

## Wine Customs

### Shabbat/Yom Tov

The Gemara now qualifies the *Mishna*'s rule that wine before exempts wine after. *Amar Rabbah bar bar Channah amar Rabbi Yochanan: lo shanu ela beshabbatot uveyamim tovim* — this applies only on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*. Why? *Ho'il ve'adam kove'a se'udato al hayayin* — because on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, the custom is to sit and drink wine together after the meal. Knowing this in advance, the *bracha* on the pre-meal wine extends to cover the post-meal wine as well.

### Weekday Customs

*Aval bish'ar yemot hashanah mevarech al kol kos vekhos* — at other times of the year, however, one recites a *bracha* on each cup of wine separately. At a weekday meal, there is no established expectation of post-meal drinking, and so each decision to pour another cup represents a new drinking occasion requiring its own *bracha*. This ruling is attributed to Rabbi Yochanan and reflects conditions in *Eretz Yisrael*; it may also reflect a change from the time when the *Mishna* was composed, when the convention of post-meal drinking was more universal.

A parallel teaching is cited from Rabbah bar Mari in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who similarly limits the exempting power of the initial *bracha* to *Shabbos*, *Yom Tov*, and specific occasions of established drinking — such as after visiting a *shvitz* or after bloodletting — where the practice is to sit and drink a substantial quantity of wine. *Ho'il ve'adam kove'a se'udato al hayayin* — because in those contexts one is *koveia* upon wine. Outside those contexts, each cup requires its own *bracha*.

### Changing Intent

The Gemara presents a case that tests the interaction between the default assumption and individual intent. Rabbah bar Mari visited Rava on a weekday. He recited a *bracha* on wine beforehand and then recited another *bracha* on wine after the meal. Rava said to him: *yeyasher* — well done. This confirms the ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that on a weekday the initial *bracha* does not cover the wine after.

Conversely, Rav Yitzchak visited Abaye on *Yom Tov* and recited a separate *bracha* on every cup. Abaye asked: does the master not hold like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that on *Yom Tov* we are generally planning to drink and therefore one *borei pri hagafen* covers all? Rav Yitzchak replied: *nimlach ana* — I changed my mind. I initially planned to take it easy this *Yom Tov* and then decided to join in. Since my initial intent was not to drink extensively, the default assumption did not apply to me and each cup required its own *bracha*. The default assumptions about what is or is not planned on *Shabbos*, *Yom Tov*, or ordinary weekdays are precisely that — defaults. A specific context or specific intent can override them in either direction.

## During vs After

### Question Posed

The Gemara raises a further question. The *Mishna* established that wine during the meal and wine after the meal operate differently in terms of who recites the *bracha*. This raises the question: *ba'u lahem yayin betoch hamazon mah she-yiftar hayayin sheleachar hamazon* — can the *bracha* of *borei pri hagafen* recited on wine during the meal serve to exempt the wine drunk after the meal? The question is not simply about *da'as* — whether one had the later wine in mind — but may involve a categorical difference between the two types of drinking. Wine during the meal is consumed incidentally, to wash down food; wine after the meal is drunk for its own sake, as a drinking occasion. If these are qualitatively distinct categories, then no amount of advance intent may suffice to connect them.

### Amoraic Dispute

The *Amoraim* divide on the question. Rav holds that the wine during exempts the wine after. Rav Kahana holds it does not. Rav Nachman holds it does; Rav Sheshet holds it does not. And Rav Huna, Rav Yehuda, and all the disciples of Rav hold it does not. The students of Rav thus represent the dominant camp: wine during the meal and wine after the meal are fundamentally different types of drinking, and one *bracha* does not carry over to the other. This does seem to reflect a categorical distinction rather than a mere question of intent.

### Mishna Reading

Rav challenges Rav Nachman from the *Mishna*: since the *Mishna* indicates that during the meal each person recites their own *bracha* on wine, while after the meal one person recites for all, it implies that a *bracha* was recited during and yet another is required after. This would prove that wine during does not exempt wine after. Rav Nachman responds that the *Mishna* should be read as presenting two separate scenarios: one in which wine is brought during the meal, and one in which wine is brought only after the meal. The clause stating *echad mevarech lekulan* applies to the second scenario — where no wine was drunk during the meal at all. If wine had been drunk during, the *bracha* on it would, according to Rav Nachman, cover the post-meal wine, and no further *bracha* would be needed.

### Separate Categories

The normative ruling follows those who hold that wine during and wine after are distinct categories. The *bracha* on wine consumed during the meal — which functions as a beverage accompanying food — does not carry over to wine consumed after the meal for its own sake. Partly this may be because bridging from during to after the meal requires that the two drinking occasions also be of the same type; where they are qualitatively different, the *bracha* cannot span them even if intent is present.

## Snack Coverage

### Asymmetry

The *Mishna*'s statement that *hamotzi* covers the *parperes* but not vice versa reflects a structural asymmetry. Bread is the foundation of the meal and is sufficiently significant to extend its *bracha* over lesser items. The *parperes*, even if it technically falls in the *hamotzi* category according to Tosafot, does not carry enough weight to exempt real bread. The two are qualitatively ordered.

### Beit Shammai

The Gemara now turns to the disputed statement of Beit Shammai: *af lo ma'aseh kedeirah* — even cooked foods, such as porridge or stew. The question is whether Beit Shammai is disputing the first clause of the *Mishna* — that *hamotzi* covers the *parperes* — or the second clause — that *parperes* does not cover bread.

On the first reading, Beit Shammai holds that *hamotzi* does not cover the *parperes* and certainly does not cover *ma'aseh kedeirah* — porridge — which one might have thought would be covered as a meal staple. Beit Shammai would hold that *hamotzi* covers only foods that directly accompany the bread as *lefapes es hapas*, not anything simply eaten during the meal. On the second reading, Beit Shammai is arguing against the implied claim that *parperes* might at least cover *ma'aseh kedeirah* even if it cannot cover bread. Beit Shammai holds that *parperes* cannot even cover porridge — the two remain distinct even though both are presumably *mezonos*.

The Gemara concludes with *teiku* — the question is left unresolved. Practically, it does not matter, since we do not rule like Beit Shammai in any case.

## Keviat Seudah

### Sitting Position

Returning to the *Mishna*'s rule of *hayu yoshvin kol echad mevarech le'atzmo / heseivu echad mevarech lekulan*, the Gemara formulates this as: *haseibu in lo haseibu lo* — it is specifically *haseibah* that creates the group; without it, even eating together does not suffice.

### Tosefta

The Gemara then raises a difficulty from a *Tosefta*: ten people were walking along the road and all eating from the same loaf of bread; each must recite their own *bracha*. However, if they sat down to eat — even if each had their own separate bread — one person may recite for all. This seems to contradict the Gemara's ruling that *haseibah* specifically is required, since the *Tosefta* permits group recitation upon mere sitting, not formal reclining.

### Intent to Eat

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the difficulty: the *Tosefta*'s case of sitting together is one where they said *neizail v'neichol lachma biduch f'lan* — let us go and eat there. They planned to eat together. It is not that they merely happened to sit at the same table; they intentionally established a joint meal. This deliberate intent to eat as a group substitutes for *haseibah* and creates the *kvias seudah* necessary for one person to recite on behalf of all.

### Without Bread

Whether this grouping can occur without bread is debated. Tosafot holds that bread is a prerequisite — there is no concept of a *kevius* without *pas*. The *Rambam*, in his overview of *Hilchos Brachos*, uses language suggesting that *kvias seudah* might in principle apply to any food. The *Shulchan Aruch* rules, however, that in practice *zimun* and group recitation apply only with bread.

### Wine Zimun

The Gemara notes one additional case: if three people sit down and drink wine together — with deliberate intent to drink as a group — they may perform a *zimun* on the wine. However, this too is no longer practiced. In most communities, wine is not drunk in a manner of *kevius* — not as a regular, established group activity — and therefore the conditions for a *zimun* on wine are not met in ordinary circumstances.

---

---

# Berakhot 43

## Haseiba & Group Blessings

### Opening Dispute

We begin on daf 43, picking up from the bottom of 42b. The *mishnah* had established that only when people are reclining together to eat bread may one person recite *hamotzi* on behalf of the entire group. The difficulty was a *braita* that appeared to permit this even when the group merely sits, without reclining. The *gemara* resolved the tension by introducing the concept of *kove'ia makom*: if the group explicitly designated a place by saying "let us go eat bread over there," that act of joint designation functions as an equivalent to *haseiba* and allows one person to bless for the group.

### Mishnah-Braita Tension

The underlying question is whether *haseiba* is purely a formal social convention — a matter of choreography defining the character of the meal — or whether it also reflects something about the subjective inner intention of each participant. The *mishnah* requires *haseiba*; the *braita* permits even sitting. This is the tension the *gemara* must resolve.

### Resolution: Designated P…

The *gemara*'s resolution is that when the group designates a shared location for eating, this designation creates the equivalent of *haseiba*. Even without physical reclining, the verbal act of "let us go eat bread in that place" constitutes the group as a group. In one reading, the social construct of *haseiba* itself — independent of any individual's inner state — accomplishes this. In another reading, it is precisely the *kavanah* expressed through that declaration that reframes the gathering: the participants are understood to have intended to constitute themselves as a collective, and this is what allows a single representative to speak for all.

### Group vs Individual

This points to a deeper principle articulated explicitly by the *Ritva*: *birchat ha-nehenin* and *birkat ha-mazon* are fundamentally different from other *berachot* in which one person can discharge another's obligation. Since these blessings concern a highly personal, subjective experience of pleasure and benefit, each individual would ordinarily be required to recite his own *berachah*. The exception arises only when the eating is understood not as a collection of individual experiences but as the shared experience of a unified group.
