In that case, the leader of the group does not speak as a private individual on behalf of other private individuals; he speaks as the representative of the collective. *Haseiba*, or its equivalent, is what accomplishes this reframing — moving the focus from "I am personally experiencing this benefit" to "we, as a group, are having this experience."

---

## Death of Rav & Resolution

### Rav's Death & Mourning

The *gemara* presents a vivid narrative. After *Rav* died, his students followed the funeral bier to bury him. On their way back, they said: "Let us go eat bread at the bank of the river Danak." After they ate, they sat and a question arose among them: does the *mishnah*'s requirement of *haseiba* apply strictly — meaning that since they were sitting on a riverbank and not actually reclining on Roman dining couches, one person cannot bless for the group — or, since they had declared "let us go eat bread in that place," is that equivalent to *haseiba* and sufficient to allow one to bless for all?

They did not know the answer. The *gemara* then records that Rav Adda bar Abba rose and turned his torn garment around to its reverse side — since the students had already rent their garments for their teacher — and rent it again. He declared: "*Rav* has died, and we have not even finished learning from him how to make blessings over food." The act is extraordinary: he rent his garment twice in expression of a grief that was not merely about personal loss, but about the felt inadequacy of what had been transmitted.

### Anonymous Elder's Help

Then a certain elder — *hahu saba* — arrived and presented the contradiction between the *mishnah* and the *braita* to them, and resolved it: once a group declares "let us go eat bread in that place," that designation is like *haseiba*, and one person may bless for all. This is precisely the resolution we have already seen at the beginning of the discussion. The students' question was thereby answered — not by their master, who was gone, but by an anonymous figure.

It bears noting that some authorities understand every instance of the phrase *hahu saba* in the *gemara* as a reference to *Eliyahu HaNavi*, and reading it that way would suggest that Elijah appeared specifically because the students were so grief-stricken, to offer them some comfort by resolving their difficulty.

### Narrative Significance

The narrative arc carries a subtle counter-message. The profound sense of loss — the tearing of garments twice over, the feeling that essential learning had been lost with *Rav* — is real and not minimized. And yet an anonymous figure, or perhaps wisdom arising from within the community itself, is capable of resolving a genuine *halachic* question. One need not have it all transmitted from one's *rebbe*; careful attention to the *mishnah* and the *braita*, and the willingness to think through their tension, can also yield the answer. The loss of a master is irreplaceable, but the tradition is not solely dependent on any single chain of transmission.

---

## Wine & Haseiba Debate

### Rav's View

The *gemara* now continues: *heiseibu echad mevarech* — when they reclined, one person blesses for all. This is the rule we have been discussing. *Rav* says: this applies only to bread (*pas*), which requires *haseiba*. For wine, *haseiba* is not required; one person may recite *borei pri ha-gafen* for the group even without formal reclining. The basis for this appears to be the end of the *mishnah* itself, which speaks of the wine served after the meal — the post-meal drinking — and states that one person blesses for the group, without mentioning *haseiba* at all. The implication is that for wine, the social conventions of group drinking were themselves sufficient to constitute a collective experience, without the need for the structured Roman dining posture.

### Rabbi Yochanan's View

*Rabbi Yochanan* disagrees: even wine requires *haseiba*. Without *haseiba*, one person cannot bless for the group even over wine.

### Two Interpretations

The *gemara* then records a second version of *Rav*'s position, which carries a subtly different nuance. In the first version, *Rav* said that wine does not *require* (*ba'ei*) *haseiba* — meaning it functions without it. In the second version, *Rav* said that *haseiba* does not *help* (*mahani*) for wine — meaning it is never effective for wine, even when present. These are importantly different claims. In the first version, wine can constitute a group experience through social convention alone, and *haseiba* is simply unnecessary. In the second version, the institution of *haseiba* is so intrinsically connected to the bread meal — to the formal Roman dining posture — that it has no conceptual weight when applied to drinking wine independently. Even if people recline while drinking, that does not rise to the level of the socially recognized institution of *haseiba*, which is a feature of the formal meal around bread.

---

## Tosefta: Order of Seudah

### Pre-Meal Customs

The *gemara* raises a challenge from a *Tosefta* describing the full order of *haseiba* — and this *Tosefta* turns out to be a remarkable document that is as much descriptive of ancient Greco-Roman dining customs as it is prescriptive *halacha*.

The *Tosefta* begins: guests enter and sit on benches and chairs — *safsal* and *katedraot*. They would not immediately recline on couches. They waited until everyone had gathered. Then water was brought, and each person washed one hand. This was a customary practice, perhaps because they would be holding the wine cup in that hand. Then wine was brought before the meal began, and each person made *borei pri ha-gafen* for himself individually, because at this pre-meal stage the group had not yet constituted itself as a collective through reclining.

### Meal Begins

Then they went up into the main dining hall. Once there, even though each person had already washed one hand, each one again washed both hands — this time fulfilling the *halachic* requirement of *netilat yadayim* before bread. The one-hand washing before was a social practice; this two-hand washing is the obligatory *halachic* act before eating bread. Interestingly, the *Tosefta* that begins by asking "what is the order of *haseiba*?" proceeds directly to the wine at this point, skipping over the actual moment of reclining and eating bread. Wine is then served during the meal. Although each person had made his own blessing on the pre-meal wine, now, the *Tosefta* says, one person makes *borei pri ha-gafen* for the entire group.

### Post-Meal Wine

This naturally raises the question of how one is making yet another *borei pri ha-gafen* during the meal if the pre-meal *borei pri ha-gafen* was meant to cover wine throughout. *Tosafot* explains, based on *Rashi*, that since the guests moved from one room to another — entering the dining hall — this constitutes a *shinui makom*, a change of location, which necessitates a new *berachah*. This principle has ramifications for many situations in which someone begins eating or drinking in one place and moves to another, and the *Tosafot* opens significant questions about what counts as a disqualifying change of place and what conditions — such as being under the same roof, or having it explicitly in mind — might prevent the need for a new blessing. We will not pursue those questions here, but the underlying reasoning is clear.

### Tosefta-Mishnah Contradi…

What is striking is that the *Tosefta* directly contradicts the *mishnah* on the question of who blesses for wine during the meal. The *mishnah* says that during the meal each person blesses for himself, while one person blesses for the group for the post-meal wine. The *Tosefta* says the opposite: during the meal one person blesses for the group, and before the meal each person blesses individually. The *gemara* does not smooth over this contradiction immediately; it will engage with it in the following discussion.

---

## Resolving Tosefta

### Guests Exception

The *gemara* now addresses how the *Tosefta* can be reconciled with each of the two versions of *Rav*'s position.

According to the version in which *Rav* holds that wine does not *require* *haseiba* — meaning that one person can ordinarily bless for the group over wine without *haseiba* — the pre-meal stage of the *Tosefta* is a difficulty. If wine does not need *haseiba*, why does each person bless for himself before the meal? The *gemara* answers: *shani orchin de-dato'ehu le-me'akar* — guests are different, because their intention is to uproot themselves. They know they are about to move to a different room. This pre-meal gathering is entirely temporary; no one is *kove'ia makom* here for the purpose of drinking. Since there is no genuine fixing of a place to drink, this moment does not constitute a drinking group, and therefore each person blesses individually. In all other contexts, though, group wine drinking would not require *haseiba*.

### Context of Bread Haseiba

According to the second version — in which *Rav* holds that *haseiba* does not help for wine at all and can never constitute a wine-drinking group — the *Tosefta*'s statement that one person blesses for the group during the meal is the difficulty. If *haseiba* never works for wine, how can there be a group *berachah* on wine during the meal?

The *gemara* answers with a principle of contextual inclusion: *dimigo de-mahani lei haseiba le-pas, mahani lei haseiba le-yayin* — since *haseiba* is operative for the bread, it is operative for the wine as well. The *haseiba* of the bread meal defines the entire gathering as a structured collective experience. The wine, served in the midst of a formally constituted bread meal, inherits the character of that meal. It is not the wine that defines the group; it is the bread meal that defines the group. But once you are sitting together as a formal bread-eating collective, the wine consumed within that framework is likewise experienced collectively, and one person may bless for all. By itself, wine cannot trigger the institution of *haseiba*. But when wine appears within the context of an already-established *haseiba* for bread, it partakes of that same character.

---

## Ben Zoma on Wine

### Ben Zoma's Question

The *gemara* now takes up the *mishnah*'s own position — which is the reverse of the *Tosefta*'s — that during the meal each person blesses for himself, while after the meal one person blesses for the group. *Ben Zoma* was asked about this: what is the reason that during the meal each person must make his own *borei pri ha-gafen*, while for the post-meal wine one person may do so for all?

### Choking Explanation

*Ben Zoma* answered: because during the meal *beit ha-bliah einah panui* — the throat is not empty. One explanation of this answer is practical and concerns risk: if a designated person were to recite *borei pri ha-gafen* for the group while the others were still eating, those others would feel compelled to answer *amen* and might do so while food was still in their mouths, with some risk of choking. Therefore the practice is that each person blesses for himself, at a moment of his own readiness, rather than being obligated to respond to another's blessing while still in the midst of eating.

### Group Experience Need

A second explanation runs deeper and connects back to the fundamental principle of group *berachot*: for one person to bless for the group, the group must be in a shared experiential state — all poised to receive the same benefit at the same moment. If one person recites *borei pri ha-gafen* for everyone while some still have food in their mouths and throats, those people are not actually ready to drink. They are not in the same experiential position as the one making the blessing. They cannot drink at this moment. Therefore there is no true shared experience over which a single *berachah* could encompass them all. After the meal, however, when the food has been removed and everyone's throat is clear, the group can genuinely be in the same state of readiness, and one person's *berachah* can represent the collective.

### Shared Experience

This second explanation reveals the full logic of the entire discussion: a *berachah* recited on behalf of a group requires that the group share an experiential state at that moment. *Haseiba* and *kove'ia makom* define the group structurally; but even within a defined group, there must be a genuine shared readiness for the benefit being blessed over. *Tosafot* raises the obvious question: what if no one happens to have food in his mouth at a given moment during the meal? Should the rule not apply? *Tosafot*'s conclusion is that the sages established a general rule that was not applied case by case. For our purposes — and *Tosafot* speaks here in terms of contemporary practice in thirteenth-century *Ashkenaz* — the only meaningful form of group experience that survives is one anchored in the context of bread, and *haseiba* as a formal institution no longer governs the way it once did in the Roman dining world.

---

## Wine & Incense Blessings

### Convention & Hand-Washing

The *mishnah* states that the same person who recites *borei pri ha-gafen* for the post-meal wine also recites the *berachah* on the *mugmar* — the incense that was burned after the meal. The *gemara* asks: why does this particular person receive both honors? The answer the *gemara* gives is that the *mishnah*'s formulation implies that there was already someone more deserving to receive the second honor, yet the person who made the *berachah* on the wine received it anyway. The reason: *ho'il ve-hu natal yadav techilah ba-achronah* — since he was the first to wash his hands for *mayim acharonim*, the post-meal hand washing, he becomes the one designated for what follows. He who performs *mayim acharonim* first is, in a sense, already in the batter's box for the next ritual act.

This seems surprising: the *mishnah* spoke of his reciting the blessing on wine, not of his washing first. The *gemara*'s reasoning assumes a link — that washing first for *mayim acharonim* led to the wine *berachah*, which then carries over to the *mugmar berachah* — even though the *mishnah* itself did not explicitly mention the hand washing.

### Mayim Acharonim Rule

This is supported by a teaching of *Rav Chiyya bar Ashi* in the name of *Rav*: *ha-notel yadav techilah ba-achronah hu mezuman li-verachah* — the one who first performs *mayim acharonim* is designated for the *berachah*. There is a principle, similar in spirit to *ha-matchil be-mitzvah omrim lo gemor* — the one who begins a mitzvah is told to complete it — by which an initiating act in one ritual domain confers a kind of standing or priority in the next.

### Rav Adda Example

The *gemara* illustrates this with a narrative. *Rav* and *Rabbi Chiya* were sitting before *Rabbi* (Yehuda HaNasi) at a meal. *Rabbi* said to *Rav*: "Go wash your hands." *Rav* was alarmed — had he come to the table with unclean hands? Had *Rabbi* noticed something unseemly? *Rabbi Chiya* saw his distress and said to him: "*Bar pachti* — what he means is that he wants to give you the honor of leading *birkat ha-mazon*," and since the one who washes first for *mayim acharonim* is designated for the *berachah*, this is *Rabbi*'s way of conferring that honor upon *Rav*. The parallel to our *mishnah* is clear: washing hands first for *mayim acharonim* carries with it a designation for the leading role in what follows, whether that is *birkat ha-mazon* or the *mugmar berachah*.

---

## Blessing on Smell

### Rabbi Zeira's Question

The *gemara* now turns to a new and significant topic: when exactly does one make a *berachah* on the aroma of incense? *Rabbi Zeira* transmitted in the name of *Rav*: the *berachah* is made from the moment the column of smoke rises up — *mi-she-ta'aleh timraso*.

### Before or After?

*Rabbi Zeira* himself then challenged this: but at that moment one has not yet smelled it. The interlocutor responds with an analogy: when one makes *hamotzi lechem min ha-aretz*, one has not yet eaten the bread — yet we make the *berachah* before eating. The answer is that one's intention is to eat, and the *berachah* is made in anticipation of the benefit. So too here, one's intention is to smell the incense, and the *berachah* is made in anticipation.

The exchange appears obvious on its face, but it carries an implicit and important subtext.

### Nehenin vs Shevach

The deeper question is whether the *berachah* on smell is a *birkat ha-nehenin* — a blessing made before deriving benefit, as is the rule for food and drink, where it is forbidden to derive benefit from this world without first making a *berachah* — or whether it is a *birkat ha-shevach*, a blessing of praise, like the blessing one makes upon seeing a rainbow or blossoming trees, which is made after or during the experience, not in anticipation of it.

The distinction is significant. A *birkat ha-nehenin* functions as a kind of permission structure: before the benefit, one must acknowledge God; only then may one partake. A *birkat ha-shevach* is different in character: one has an aesthetic or spiritual experience, and the *berachah* articulates the praise that experience evokes. The *berachah* on sight — seeing beautiful trees, a rainbow, or extraordinary natural phenomena — is clearly in the latter category. No one holds one's hand over one's eyes until making a *berachah*, then removes it to look. One sees the thing and then praises God.

The question here is where smell falls along this spectrum. Smell is not like eating: it does not fill one's stomach, does not sustain the body in the same way. In some sense it is more like an aesthetic experience than a nutritive one. If that is so, perhaps one should smell first and bless afterward, as with sight. But the position encoded in the *gemara* — and this is the ruling we follow — is that smell is treated as a *birkat ha-nehenin*: the *berachah* is made before smelling, in anticipation of the benefit, on the analogy of *hamotzi* before eating. One piece of evidence in favor of treating it as *nehenin* is the presence of something physical and substantial — the column of smoke, the incense material — that more closely resembles an object of consumption than a purely visual or aesthetic experience.

*Tosafot*, grappling with these questions, reaches the conclusion that if one is uncertain which *berachah* to make on a given aroma, one might fall back on *she-hakol*, treating it as any other case of doubt in *birchat ha-nehenin*. Another view cited by *Tosafot* is that the generic *berachah* in the realm of *besamim* is *borei minei besamim*, and that this serves as the equivalent of *she-hakol* for aromas. That *Tosafot* entertains the possibility of *she-hakol* itself underscores that the category of smell is fully understood as falling within *birchat ha-nehenin*.

### Meorei Ha-Esh Example

By contrast, a well-known parallel case clarifies the distinction between the two types. *Borei meorei ha-esh* — the blessing on fire on *motzei Shabbat* — is a *birkat ha-shevach*, not a *birkat ha-nehenin*. The *mishnah* says one does not make the *berachah* until one benefits from its light — *ein mevarchin ad she-ye'otu le-oro*. This means one looks at the flame first, derives benefit from seeing it, and then makes the *berachah*. The practice of looking at one's fingernails during the *berachah* on fire, as if deriving a specific benefit at that moment, follows from this: the *berachah* comes after or during the experience. One who makes the *berachah* before looking and then looks is following the structure of *birkat ha-nehenin* — which would be a mistake in this case, since *borei meorei ha-esh* is a *birkat ha-shevach*. This parallel helps delineate why the question about smell is so pointed: if smell were categorized as *shevach*, one would smell first and then bless; if *nehenin*, one blesses first and then smells. The ruling is that smell is *nehenin*.

---

## Types of Incense Blessin…

### General Rule

*Rav Chisda* taught in the name of *Rav* — with an alternative attribution to *Zeiri*: all *mugmarot* (types of incense) receive the *berachah* of *borei atzei besamim* — the blessing on aromatic woods — with one exception: musk. Musk, which derives from animal glands or excretions rather than from plant matter, receives instead *borei minei besamim* — a more generic blessing on types of aromatic things, which functions as the *she-hakol* of the *besamim* world.

### Braita Restriction

The *gemara* immediately challenges this with a *braita*: one only makes *borei atzei besamim* on *afarsamon* (balsam) — and specifically on the balsam of the house of *Rebbe* and of the house of Caesar (both of whom apparently held private royal orchards of this extraordinarily valuable plant, which in its time was said to be worth its weight in gold) — and on *hadas* (myrtle) everywhere. Nothing else, according to this *braita*, would receive *borei atzei besamim*. This appears to contradict the broad ruling that all *mugmarot* receive that *berachah*. The *gemara* declares this a *tiyuvta* — a refutation.

### Resolution of Contradict…

*Tosafot* notes that the *Ba'al Halachot Gedolot* did not have the word *tiyuvta* in his text at all, and instead presents a different version of the *gemara* that harmonizes the sources. The reading he proposes is: the *braita* should be understood as saying "myrtle and anything similar to it." That is, the *braita* uses *hadas* as a paradigm example, not as an exclusive list. The principle derived is: *kol she-ikaro la-rei'ach* — anything whose primary purpose in society is its aroma. This excludes items such as quinces and apples (*tapuchim* and *chavushim*), which do have pleasant aromas but whose primary social function is as food. For those, one does not say *borei atzei besamim*. For any aromatic wood or plant whose defining characteristic is its aroma — not its food value or other utility — one does say *borei atzei besamim*, provided also that it has the quality of *etz* (to be further discussed below). This resolution also implies that *borei atzei besamim* can be said even when the material is being burned as incense, not merely when it is present in its natural state.

*Tosafot* further addresses a practical case: a person who enters a house filled with various *besamim* and is uncertain whether what he is smelling comes from an *etz* or from *adamah*. Some authorities say he should make *she-hakol* — since on all things, if one made *she-hakol*, one has discharged one's obligation. The view of *Rabbeinu Moshe* is that he should make *borei minei besamim*, which functions as the generic default in the world of *besamim*. This debate itself further reflects the question of exactly how to classify *birchat ha-nehenin* on smell.

### Balsam Oil

*Rav Chisda* asked *Rav Yitzchak*: what *berachah* does one make on oil of balsam — *mishcha de-afarsamon*? The answer attributed to *Rav Yehuda* is *borei shemen artzeinu* — who creates the oil of our land, *Eretz Yisrael* — reflecting *Rav Yehuda*'s well-known love of the Land of Israel and his tendency to weave references to it wherever possible. The *gemara* gently notes this and asks: for everyone else, who perhaps does not share *Rav Yehuda*'s particular attachment, what would the *berachah* be? *Rabbi Yochanan* is cited: *borei shemen areiv* — who creates pleasant oil. These appear to have been specific formulations for a specific substance of extraordinary value.

### Costus & Oil-Infused

*Rav Adda bar Ahava* rules that *kushta* (costus, a type of spice) receives *borei atzei besamim*. However, *mishcha kevisha* — oil in which aromatic material has been soaked so that the oil absorbs the aroma, with the original substance removed — does not receive a *berachah*, because the aromatic thing itself is no longer *be-ayin*, physically present. This raises a question directly relevant to modern perfumes and essential oils: if the original substance is no longer present and only its absorbed scent remains, does a *berachah* apply at all?

*Rav Kahana* disagrees and holds that even *mishcha kevisha* — oil that has had the aromatic material soaked in it — receives *borei atzei besamim*. But even he would agree that *mishcha techina* — where the aromatic material is ground up and mixed into the oil without being properly steeped — does not qualify, because in that form the aromatic quality has not been effectively released into the oil and the scent is not significant. The scholars of *Nehardea* go further still, ruling that even ground-up material mixed into the oil suffices. The running question throughout is: at what point has the aromatic substance sufficiently manifested itself — either as a physical object *be-ayin* or as a potent aromatic presence — to warrant a *berachah*?

---

## What Counts as Etz?

### Stalks as Etz

Having established the general rule that *borei atzei besamim* applies to aromatic trees and woody plants, the *gemara* turns to the question of what constitutes an *etz* for this purpose. The definition here is broader than the one used for determining whether to say *borei pri ha-etz* over fruit. For fruit, the operative criterion is whether the plant survives from year to year and its main stalk persists; an annual plant producing food receives *borei pri ha-adamah* regardless of how high it grows. Here, for *besamim*, the definition extends to things that grow on stalks.

*Mar Zutra* offers a scriptural proof: in the Book of *Yehoshua*, the verse describing *Rachav* hiding the spies uses the phrase *be-fishtei ha-etz* — in the flax stalks — where the word *etz* is applied to a stalk. This proves that stalks can be called *etz*. Therefore, aromatic plants that grow on stalks may still receive *borei atzei besamim*, even if they would not be considered trees in the conventional sense. It is notable that this broader definition does not carry over into the domain of fruit blessings: barley and wheat, which also grow on stalks, receive *adamah*, not *ha-etz*. The criterion for *etz* in the *besamim* context is evidently more inclusive.

### Daffodil Distinction

A distinction is drawn between the garden daffodil (*narkum de-ganisa*) and the field daffodil (*de-davra*). The garden daffodil receives *borei atzei besamim*; the field daffodil receives *borei ispei besamim* — the blessing on aromatic herbs or grasses. The precise botanical or legal distinction between the two is not entirely clear from the *gemara*. It may be that the cultivated garden variety, by virtue of cultivation, acquires a more substantial or persistent form that rises to the level of *etz*, while the wild field variety does not. Whatever the underlying principle, the *sugya* makes clear that drawing the line between *atzei besamim* and *ispei besamim* requires careful attention to the nature of each specific plant.

### Flowers & Perennials

Similarly, violets (*siglei*), which are straightforward flowers with no woody component, receive *borei ispei besamim*. On the other hand, jasmine (*samlok*) and a species identified as spikenard growing near the sea receive *borei atzei besamim*, presumably because they grow on stems or branches sturdy enough to qualify as *etz* in the sense established above. Taken together, these rulings show that the line between *atzei* and *ispei besamim* tracks something like: does this plant have a sufficiently persistent, woody, or stalk-like structure? A perennial bush or plant with persistent stems may qualify; a flower that blooms annually from the ground does not.

### Fruit Blessings

*Mar Zutra* adds: if one smells an *etrog* or a quince (*chavush*), both of which have a pleasant natural fragrance, the *berachah* is *baruch she-natan rei'ach tov ba-perot* — who has given a pleasant aroma to fruit. The reason is that these are primarily fruits; their defining social function is as food. Despite their lovely smell, they are not *besamim* in the primary sense, and so neither *atzei* nor *ispei besamim* applies. The blessing acknowledges instead the *Creator*'s gift of pleasant fragrance to fruits — a distinct formulation appropriate to this category. The example of *etrog* may also be significant because *etrog* is not typically eaten raw, which might lead one to think it is not primarily a fruit; but it remains fundamentally a fruit, and the blessing reflects that.

---

## Blossoming Trees Blessing

### Trees Blessing Text

The *gemara* now makes a seamless transition from blessings on smell to a related blessing recited in the spring. *Rav Yehuda* taught: one who goes out in the month of *Nissan* and sees trees that are blossoming recites the following: *Baruch she-lo chisar be-olamo klum u-vara bo beriyot tovot ve-ilanot tovim le-hitna'ot bahem benei adam* — Blessed is One who has not withheld anything from His world and who created in it good creatures and good trees for human beings to take pleasure in.

### Scriptural Proof

From where is it known that one makes a *berachah* on smell at all? *Rav Zutra bar Tuvia* in the name of *Rav* derives it from a verse: *kol ha-neshamah tehalel Yah* — all souls will praise God. The *gemara* reads this as pointing to something that the soul benefits from (*neshamah nehenet mimenu*) but the body does not — and that is smell. This derivation is itself noteworthy: rather than grounding the obligation in the general principle that it is forbidden to derive benefit from this world without a *berachah* — which is the standard foundation of *birchat ha-nehenin* — the *gemara* cites a specific verse and specifically distinguishes smell as a benefit to the soul rather than to the body.

### Nature of Smell

This distinction — *ha-neshamah nehenet mimenu ve-ein ha-guf nehena mimenu* — is central to the entire dialectic that has run through this *sugya*. Smell is not like food, which sustains the body; it is not like drink, which quenches thirst and fills the stomach. It is not even quite like sight, which delivers aesthetic experience but leaves no trace on the body whatsoever. Smell occupies a middle position: it is physical enough — there is a substance, a column of smoke, a present object — that it more closely resembles *nehenin* than *shevach*. And yet the *gemara*'s own proof-text underscores that it is not the same bodily *hana'ah* as food. In the end, the ruling is that smell is treated as *birchat ha-nehenin* — the *berachah* comes before one smells. But the *gemara*'s citation of this verse, and its emphasis that the body does not derive the same kind of benefit as from food, preserves the sense that smell is a sui generis category, neither fully reducible to *nehenin* nor fully equivalent to *shevach*.

---

## Oil & Myrtle Customs

### Oil & Myrtle Practice

The *gemara* returns to the customs of the *seudah*. At the end of the meal, oil and myrtle were brought out for the guests, and *berachot* were made on each.

### Shammai-Hillel Debate

*Beit Shammai* holds: one first makes the *berachah* on the oil and then on the myrtle. *Beit Hillel* holds: one first makes the *berachah* on the myrtle and then on the oil. The nature of this debate — which blessing has priority when two distinct items requiring separate blessings are presented simultaneously — has echoes in other *Beit Shammai*–*Beit Hillel* disputes, such as the order of *borei pri ha-gafen* and *mekadesh ha-Shabbat* in *kiddush*. The underlying logic in each case concerns some principle of precedence or importance, though the exact nature of the argument here is not immediately transparent.

### Rabban Gamliel's Ruling

*Rabban Gamliel* intervened to decide the matter: oil is superior to myrtle because oil confers two forms of benefit — one benefits from its aroma (*rei'ach*) and also from anointing one's body with it (*sichato*). Myrtle provides only the benefit of aroma. Since oil provides a more comprehensive benefit, it takes precedence, and the *berachah* on oil comes first — in agreement with *Beit Shammai*.

### Halacha Ruling

*Rabbi Yochanan* rules: the *halacha* follows the one who cast the deciding vote (*ha-machria*). Since *Rabban Gamliel* decided in favor of *Beit Shammai*'s position, the *halacha* follows *Beit Shammai* — an uncommon ruling, given that the general rule is *halacha ke-Veit Hillel*.

### Rav Pappa's Story

*Rav Pappa* visited the home of *Rav Huna the son of Rav Ika*, and when oil and myrtle were brought before them, *Rav Pappa* took the myrtle and blessed on it first — following *Beit Hillel*. His host challenged him: does the master not hold that the *halacha* follows the *machria*, and therefore we should bless on the oil first like *Beit Shammai*? *Rav Pappa* replied: this is what *Rava* said — the *halacha* follows *Beit Hillel*. The *gemara* then comments: this was not actually so. *Rav Pappa* was maneuvering to extricate himself from the embarrassment of having been caught in what appeared to be a halachic error — he had just read the passage teaching that one should cast oneself into a fiery furnace rather than embarrass another person in public, and now he sought a way to avoid his own embarrassment by attributing a position to *Rava*.

### Rava's Explanation

The *gemara* notes that *Rava* had indeed said, in a different context, that the principle *halacha ke-divrei ha-machria* applies only when the *machria* offers a genuine compromise position — a middle path between the two disputants. When a third authority simply sides with one of the two positions without offering any new synthesis, that does not constitute a true *machria*, and the principle does not apply. On the basis of that teaching of *Rava*, one would in fact arrive at the conclusion that the *halacha* follows *Beit Hillel* — not because *Rava* ever said so explicitly about this case, but because *Rava*'s ruling about what qualifies as a *machria* means that *Rabban Gamliel*'s vote does not trigger the principle. *Rav Pappa*, therefore, was not fabricating from whole cloth, but he did slightly misrepresent the position by saying "*Rava* says the *halacha* follows *Beit Hillel*," when *Rava* never said that directly.

---

## Oil & Wine Order

### Oil-Wine Dispute

The *gemara* next records a *baraita* about oil and wine at the end of the meal. *Beit Shammai* holds: one holds the oil in the right hand and the wine in the left hand, makes the *berachah* on the oil first, and then on the wine. *Beit Hillel* holds the reverse: wine in the right hand and oil in the left, and the *berachah* on wine is made first.

### Wiping on Shamash

After the oil is applied to one's hands, the custom was to wipe the excess oil on the head or hair of the *shamash* — the attendant serving at the meal. The idea seems to be that the *shamash* benefits from receiving the remaining aromatic oil. However, if the *shamash* is a *talmid chacham*, one does not wipe the oil on his head; instead, one wipes it on the wall.

### Unseemly for Scholars

The reason: it is unseemly (*genai*) for a *talmid chacham* to go out into the marketplace perfumed. This ruling sets up the following broader discussion of conduct befitting a Torah scholar.

---

## Six Unfitting Things

### Perfumed in Public

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: six things are unbecoming of a *talmid chacham*. The first is going out perfumed into the marketplace. *Rabbi Yochanan* explains: this applies in a place where people are suspected of *mishkav zachar* — homosexual activity — because going about perfumed in such a place would arouse suspicion that one was signaling one's availability. *Rav Sheshet* qualifies: this applies only to having the perfume on one's clothing. If it is on one's body, the sweat will cause it to evaporate, and there is no concern. *Rav Pappa* adds: hair, however, is like clothing in this respect — the oil on one's hair will remain apparent. Others say hair is like the body — it will be absorbed and will not be a problem.

### Alone at Night

The second is going out alone at night — because of *cheshad*, suspicion. People will assume one has a clandestine rendezvous. This applies only if one has no fixed appointment at night. If one has a regular nightly commitment — such as a fixed time to study with a teacher — people know this and there is no suspicion.

### Patched Shoes

The third is going out in shoes that have patches. *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* states this explicitly: it is unbecoming for a *talmid chacham* to go out in patched shoes. The *gemara* then asks: but *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* himself went out in patched shoes! *Mar Zutra the son of Rav Nachman* answers: the problem is specifically *talai al gav talai* — patches upon patches. A single patch on a shoe is unremarkable; but when one has multiple layers of patching, the shoe becomes unseemly. Furthermore, even multiple patches are only a problem on the main body of the shoe (*befanta*); on the heel or sole (*gilda*), it is not a concern. And even on the main body of the shoe, it is only a problem when going out; at home, it matters not at all. Finally, it is only a problem in summer (*yemot ha-chamah*); in the rainy season, wearing worn-out shoes is practical and unremarkable.

### Speaking with Women

The fourth is speaking with a woman in the marketplace. *Rav Chisda* rules: this applies even to one's own wife. The *baraita* confirms: even one's wife, even one's daughter, even one's sister — because not everyone knows who one's relatives are, and people will form suspicious impressions about the identity of the woman one is speaking with.

### Avoiding Am Ha'Aretz

The fifth is reclining in a group of *amei ha-aretz* in the manner of *haseiba*. The reason: one may come to follow their ways. Association with those who are unlearned and who do not conduct themselves with the standards of *Torah* scholarship will, over time, influence one's own conduct and standards.

### Last to Arrive

The sixth is being the last to enter the *beit ha-midrash* — because one will be called *poshea*, negligent. There must always be someone who arrives last; it should not be the *talmid chacham*.

### Large Steps

Some add a seventh: do not take large steps. The *gemara* explains the reasoning: taking large steps removes one five-hundredth of a person's eyesight. The remedy for this is the wine of *kiddush*, which reverses the loss. This is framed as a health concern rather than a matter of propriety — though it is interesting to note that the prohibition on large steps overlaps with the concern about running on *Shabbat*, and the remedy through *kiddush* wine creates a certain symmetry.

### Haughty Bearing

And finally: do not walk with an upright and haughty bearing (*kumah zekufah*). The reason is severe: one who walks even four *amot* with an exaggerated, arrogant posture is considered as if he were pushing away the feet of the *Shekhinah* — for as it is written, *melo chol ha-aretz kevodo* — the entire earth is filled with God's glory. To walk with self-important haughtiness through a world permeated by the divine presence is to assert one's own centrality in a space that belongs to God.

---

---

# Berakhot 45

## Zimun & Mishnah Overview

### Perek 7 Structure

The seventh *perek* of Berakhot, beginning at the top of 45a, turns its focus from the opening *brachot* of a meal to *birkat hamazon* and, in particular, to the institution of *zimun*. It is worth noting why the preceding *perek* concluded with discussions of *birkat hamazon* on fruit and Rabbi Akiva's vegetables: those final passages were likely placed there in order to resolve all distinctions between different categories of foodstuffs — fruit, vegetables, and the like — so that the present *perek* could assume a bread meal throughout and focus exclusively on the act of *birkat hamazon* itself, without being diverted into distinctions among food types.

### Purpose of Zimun

The *zimun* as an institution is not merely the recitation of a few introductory lines before *bentshing*. Its essential purpose is to constitute all those present as a single corporate entity, so that *birkat hamazon* is performed as a group rather than as a collection of individuals. The *mezamen* opens with *rabotai nevarech*, calling on the others to join in blessing, and after the group responds — *baruch she'achalnu mishelo uv'tuvo chayinu* — all are united under a single *birkat hamazon* recited by the *mezamen* on behalf of all.

This is in fact the classical model: not the contemporary practice in which everyone recites *birkat hamazon* individually after a brief shared preamble, but a structure in which the *mezamen* recites the full *birkat hamazon* and the others fulfill their obligation through him. This connects to a broader principle observed earlier in the tractate regarding *brachot hanehenin*: ordinarily one is not permitted to piggyback on another individual's *bracha* through *shomea ke'oneh*. The exception arises when one is acting not as an individual but as part of a group, with a single representative speaking on behalf of all. That is precisely what *zimun* creates.

### Mishnah: Three Eat

The *mishna* opens: *shlosha she'achlu ke'achat chayavin lezamen* — three who ate together are obligated to perform *zimun*. The *mishna* does not immediately elaborate on what constitutes "eating together" or why three is the operative number; instead, it proceeds at once into a series of distinctions concerning the status of the food consumed and the eligibility of different categories of participants.

### Demai Food Status

The *mishna* introduces *demai* — produce purchased from *amei ha'aretz*, the non-rabbinic masses, who were generally presumed to separate *trumot umasrot* but among whom a significant minority did not. Because of this uncertainty, the rabbis required that one who purchased grain from such sources separate *trumot umasrot* again. Nevertheless, *demai* occupied a somewhat intermediate status. Unlike other rabbinically forbidden items, *demai* was permitted under certain circumstances — for example, one could feed guests *demai* when provisions were limited, or a poor person could eat it in times of need. One way to understand this is that the prohibition attaches less to the food itself as a forbidden substance and more to the eater's obligation to separate before consuming. Because the food is not categorically forbidden as a food, one who has eaten *demai* is permitted to participate in *zimun*.

### Food Purity Rules

The *mishna* presents two parallel lists. The first encompasses quasi-permitted foods: one who ate *demai*; *ma'aser rishon* from which *trumah* had already been separated — for once the *Levi* takes his *ma'aser* and separates a tenth of a tenth for the *Kohen*, the remainder is entirely *chullin*; *ma'aser sheni* or *hekdesh* that were redeemed and thus rendered *chullin*; and finally the *shamash* — the attendant or waiter at the meal — who ate at least a *kezayit*. The last case introduces a distinct point: the *shamash* is not a seated guest but the one serving the meal, and the *chiddush* is that despite his role as waiter rather than participant, he is considered to have eaten with the group and may be counted toward *zimun*. All of those in this first list — *mezamnin alav* — may be included.

The second list presents the contrasting cases of genuine prohibition: one who ate *tevel* — produce from which *trumot umasrot* were not separated, a biblical prohibition — *ma'aser rishon* from which *trumah* had not been taken, *ma'aser sheni* and *hekdesh* that were not redeemed and may only be consumed in Jerusalem, a *shamash* who ate less than a *kezayit*, and a non-Jew. All of these — *ein mezamnin alav* — are excluded, whether because of the forbidden status of what they ate, because they are not Jewish, because they are not genuine participants in the meal, or because they did not eat a sufficient quantity.

### Demai Economics

One might observe an interesting economic dimension to the *demai* regulations. If purchasing from *amei ha'aretz* obligated the buyer to separate again, while produce from those known to be careful required no such additional step, this could have functioned as a market incentive favoring the produce of the more observant. Conversely, one could argue the opposite: that produce requiring additional separation would be sold at lower prices, making it more accessible to those who were willing to bear the burden. The relative proportions of *demai* and non-*demai* produce in the market — whether the vast majority was *demai* or only a small fraction — would determine which effect dominated. The question of what percentage of the market was actually *demai* remains somewhat unclear, and these economic implications, while genuinely interesting, are difficult to evaluate without that information.

### Women/Slaves/Children

The *mishna* then turns to *nashim va'avadim u'ktanim* — women, slaves, and minors — stating *ein mezamnin aleihem*, that men may not form a *zimun* with them. The *Gemara* will discuss both whether these groups may perform *zimun* among themselves and what the reasons are for their exclusion from mixed groups, and we will reach that discussion shortly.

Regarding the minimum quantity required for *zimun*, the *mishna* poses the question *ad kama mezamnin* — until how small an amount of food still suffices — and answers *ad kezayit*, even as little as a *kezayit*. The formulation is notably presented as a lower bound rather than an upper one. Rabbi Yehuda dissents, requiring a *kebeitzah* as a more significant measure approaching satiation.

## Three-Person Source

### Gadlu Lashem Proof

The *Gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — from where is derived the requirement that specifically three people eating together must perform *zimun*? Rav Assi answers by citing the verse *gadlu lashem iti uneromemah shemo yachdav* (Psalms 34:4): "Magnify the Lord with me and let us exalt His name together." The structure of the verse maps onto the structure of *zimun*: one calls — *gadlu* — others respond in praise, and then all together do it *yachdav*, as one unified group. The word *yachdav* is central, because *zimun* is not merely a responsive exchange but a transformation of the participants into a single entity, so that the subsequent *birkat hamazon* is an act of the group.

### Ki Shem Hashem

Rabbi Abbahu derives the same institution from a different verse: *ki shem Hashem ekra havu godel lEloheinu* (Devarim 32:3) — "When I call out the name of God, ascribe greatness to our God." Here again the call-and-response structure is explicit: one person calls out God's name and the others respond with praise. While this verse comes from the Torah itself, making it in some respects a more direct source, it lacks the *yachdav* element that makes the Psalms verse especially apt.

### Zimun Institution

One might ask whether citing these *psukim* means that *zimun* is *de'oraita*. The general assumption is that it is not. These verses function more as *asmachta* — pointing toward an institution that the Torah itself validates conceptually — than as a biblical mandate specifically requiring *zimun* during *birkat hamazon*. That said, the possibility that some *rishonim* understood these citations as establishing a biblical obligation cannot be dismissed out of hand and would require further investigation. What the *Gemara* does establish through these verses is the nature and character of *zimun* as a genuine institution: one of calling, responding, and ultimately performing an act of praise in a unified voice.

### Three vs. Two Minimum

This raises the question David posed during the shiur: why does *birkat hamazon* require specifically three participants, while *hamotzei* — the opening *bracha* — does not? Indeed, the two cases differ in more than just the number. By *hamotzei*, the earlier *Gemara* spoke of *haseiva* — reclining together — as the mechanism of group formation, whereas by *zimun* for *birkat hamazon* the requirement is the specific number of three, with no parallel insistence on *haseiva*.

Tosafot addresses this directly. When people come together to begin a meal, they are in the process of joining and intend to remain together; the act of coming together is itself sufficient to constitute them as a group, and two people can be *motzi* one another for *hamotzei*. By contrast, at the conclusion of the meal, the group is in the process of dispersing — *she-mistaleket zeh mi-zeh* — and therefore something more is required to hold them together as a unified entity, namely the formal *zimun* with its minimum of three. One could have argued precisely the opposite — that people who have been sitting together throughout a meal are already more thoroughly constituted as a group than those who have just arrived — but Tosafot's reasoning is that the departing moment demands an active constitutive act rather than relying on existing togetherness.

It should be noted that Rashi, as quoted by Tosafot, appears to require three even for *hamotzei*, while Tosafot himself seems to suggest that two suffice for *hamotzei* without even the formal requirement of *haseiva*, on the grounds that any eating of bread together suffices. The earlier *Gemaras* had established that *haseiva* is needed for *hamotzei*, but Tosafot acknowledges that in the absence of true *haseiva* nowadays, eating bread together may serve as the equivalent joining mechanism. What remains clear is that *birkat hamazon* carries substantially greater weight — it consists of three *brachot*, it is explicitly commanded in the Torah, and therefore the demand for a more formal and constitutive *zimun* with three is understandable even if the first *bracha* does not require it.

## Mixed Diet Zimun

### Kohen Terumah

Tosafot raises a distinct question that emerges from the *mishna*'s discussion of permitted and forbidden foods. The *mishna* excludes one who ate truly forbidden food from *zimun*, but Tosafot notes this is not because of a failure to form a group — it is because a person who ate forbidden food is fundamentally excluded from *zimun* and *birkat hamazon*. Yet this leads naturally to the question: what if two people eat together but one eats food the other cannot eat? The example Tosafot considers is a *Kohen* eating *terumah*: a non-*Kohen* cannot eat *terumah*, so in what sense are these two people sharing a meal?

### Reciprocal Eating

Tosafot cites the *Yerushalmi* for a governing principle: *zimun* is valid so long as at least one party can eat from the other's food. In the case of the *Kohen* eating *terumah*, the *Kohen* can certainly eat the non-*Kohen*'s food, even though the reverse is not true. That asymmetric reciprocity is sufficient to constitute them as a shared eating group for purposes of *zimun*.

### Mutual Vows

The critical limit arises when neither party can derive benefit from the other. If both have taken vows — *nedarim* — prohibiting them from deriving benefit from one another, there is no reciprocity in either direction, and *zimun* between them becomes impossible.

### Modern Examples

This framework generates several practical applications. If one person is stringent regarding *pas akum* — bread baked by non-Jews — and therefore will not eat the other's bread, while the other would readily eat the stringent person's bread, the condition for *zimun* is met, since at least one party can eat from the other's food. Similarly in the case of one person eating *milchigs* and another eating *fleishigs*: the person eating *milchigs* can, after rinsing his mouth, eat *fleishigs* immediately, while the *fleishigs* eater cannot eat *milchigs*. Since the *milchigs* eater can in principle eat from the *fleishigs* eater's food, the condition is satisfied. The practical implication regarding who leads the *zimun* is that preference is generally given to the person eating *milchigs*, precisely because that person is able to eat from all the food present, while the *fleishigs* eater is more constrained. An additional consideration is that some hold *zimun* properly concerns only the shared bread rather than the side dishes, in which case the meat-dairy distinction may be less relevant altogether.

### Medical Barriers

A genuinely open question arises regarding non-*halachic* barriers to shared eating. What if the reason one person cannot eat from another's food is medical rather than *halachic* — celiac disease being an obvious example? The majority view among *poskim* appears to be that it is specifically a *halachic* barrier that creates the relevant exclusion, and a medical one does not. Nevertheless, the question is real, and the case of someone who cannot eat any bread at all — rather than the specific bread of the other participants — is distinct and touches on the separate *halacha* of whether one who did not eat bread may lead or participate in *zimun*. Those questions will be addressed later in the *Gemara*.

## Voice in Blessing

### Amein Voice Level

The *Gemara* records a teaching of Rav Chana bar Abba: from where do we know that one who responds *amein* should not raise his voice louder than the person making the *bracha*? The source is again the verse *gadlu lashem iti uneromemah shemo yachdav* — they are doing it together, *yachdav*, as one unified voice, not with one drowning out the other.

### Metargem Translator

Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi extends this principle to the practice of Torah reading. In the period of the *Gemara*, a *metargem* would translate the Torah reading into Aramaic verse by verse. Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi teaches that the *metargem* may not raise his voice higher than the *korei* — the one reading the Torah text itself. The source is the verse *Moshe yedabeir veha-Elokim ya'anenu b'kol* — Moshe would speak and God would respond to him with a voice.

### Moshe & God Voice

This is a striking *Gemara*, and the *pasuk* itself is genuinely difficult. The verse appears to cast Moshe as the primary reader and God as the responding *metargem* — which is plainly puzzling. The text further specifies *b'kol*, "with a voice," which seems redundant. The *Gemara* reads this as: God responded *b'kolo shel Moshe* — in Moshe's voice, meaning not louder. Tosafot's explanation is as follows: after the first two of the *dibrot*, God spoke only to Moshe and therefore had no need to project His voice for the entire assembled people. Moshe, however, had to speak loudly so that everyone could hear. God, functioning as it were in the role of *metargem*, could in principle have spoken softly — which would have meant the *metargem* was quieter than the *korei*. Therefore, the *pasuk* tells us that God raised His voice to match Moshe's, so that the principle of parity was maintained. The exact reading of the *pasuk* on Tosafot's account remains difficult, but the functional point is clear.

### Reader Lowers Voice

The *Gemara* then presents a *baraita* that introduces the mirror case: if the *metargem* cannot raise his voice to match that of the *korei*, the *korei* should lower his own voice so that the two are equal. This is a remarkable ruling. One might have thought there was no reason to lower the volume of the original Torah reading simply to accommodate the translator; if anything, one might prefer that the *metargem* simply speak more softly. But the *baraita* insists on parity, and in order to achieve it, it is the *korei* who must lower his voice.

### Equal Dignity

The reason appears to be the dignity and status of the *targum* itself. If the translation were consistently quieter than the original reading, it would signal to the congregation that the *targum* is of lesser importance — and yet for most people present, who could not understand the Hebrew, the *targum* was the primary vehicle of comprehension. Undermining its status by reducing its volume would have undermined its function. The principle of *yachdav* — doing it together, as equals — thus extends from the *zimun* context to the *Torah* reading context. Whether the same rationale applies identically across both cases is worth consideration, but the *Gemara* treats the principle as sufficiently analogous to invoke the same verse.

## Two-Person Eating

### Rav vs. R. Yochanan

The *Gemara* now turns to the question of two people who ate together. Three are obligated in *zimun*; but can two optionally perform *zimun* if they wish? Rav and Rabbi Yochanan disagree. One holds *im ratzu lezamen mezamnin* — they may do so if they wish; the other holds that two cannot perform *zimun* even optionally. The *Gemara* attempts a series of proofs to identify which sage held which position.

### Cannot Split Groups

One attempted proof: the *mishna* states *shlosha she'achlu ke'achat chayavim lezamen* — three who ate together are obligated. The implication *shlosha in, shnayim lo* seems to indicate that two may not perform *zimun* at all. But this is rejected: the *mishna* speaks of obligation, and the question is whether two may do so as a *reshut*. A further proof comes from a *baraita* stating that three who ate together may not divide into separate groups. This too might seem to prove that two cannot perform *zimun*, because if two could, why not simply allow the group of three to split? Rashi explains that a member of the group of three might invoke his ability to depart, since two could still form a *zimun*, thereby freeing himself from the obligation. But the *Gemara* responds differently: even four cannot split into two groups of two, and the reason is *she-kiblu lehu be-chova me-ikara* — they undertook the obligation at the outset when they sat down as three, and one does not convert an obligatory performance into an optional one. Rashi cites the well-known principle that *metzuveh ve-oseh* is greater than *eino metzuveh ve-oseh*.

### Servant with Two

A further attempted proof concerns the *shamash* who attends two people at their meal. The *Gemara* teaches that he may eat with them — *harei ze ochel imahem* — even without explicit permission, because it is assumed that they implicitly allow him to eat so that he will become a third for their *zimun*. If, however, he attends three people, he does not eat with them without explicit permission, since they do not need him. The *Gemara* explains that even if two can perform *zimun* only optionally, the diners would still prefer to have a third so that their *zimun* carries the weight of an obligation rather than a mere permission. The sense of performing a *mitzvah* as an obligation rather than as a discretionary act gives it greater significance, and therefore the implicit grant of permission to the *shamash* can be explained even if two is a valid *reshut*.

## Women/Slaves Status

### Separate Groups

A *baraita* teaches: *nashim mezamnot le-atzman ve-avadim mezamnim le-atzman* — women perform *zimun* among themselves and slaves perform *zimun* among themselves. But *nashim va-avadim ve-ktanim im ratzu lezamen ein mezamnin* — if women, slaves, and minors wish to form a mixed group together, they may not do so.

### Rashi: Optional Status

The *Gemara* interjects with a striking formulation: *me'ah nashi ke-trei gavrei damyan* — a hundred women is considered equivalent to two men. Rashi reads this as meaning that even a hundred women occupy the same category as two men: they are not obligated but occupy a *reshut* category. On this reading, the *baraita*'s statement that women *mezamnot le-atzman* establishes that *zimun* among women is valid, but only as a discretionary matter, parallel to the disputed case of two men. This in turn provides the proof the *Gemara* seeks regarding the two-man case: we see that the institution of *zimun* can exist in a *reshut* mode, not only in an obligatory one, and therefore the claim that two may optionally perform *zimun* has a precedent in the practice of women performing *zimun* among themselves.

### Tosafot: Obligatory

Tosafot reads the passage very differently. On Tosafot's account, *me'ah nashi ke-trei gavrei damyan* refers to the ordinary presumption that women do not count for things that require men — *minyan*, *kol davar she-bikdushah*, and the like. The *hava amina* was that the same presumption would apply to *zimun*, meaning women would be excluded. But the answer *shani hatam de-ika de'ot* — there it is different, because there is a multiplicity of minds — comes to reject this presumption for *zimun*. On this reading, the *maskana* of the *Gemara* is not that women are in an optional category but that they may in fact be equally obligated in *zimun*.

Tosafot notes that the *baraita* uses the active term *mezamnot* — they perform *zimun* — not *yecholot lezamen*, they are permitted to do so. He further records that the daughters of Rabbeinu Avraham, father-in-law of Rabbeinu Yehudah, performed *zimun* on the instruction of their father. Nevertheless, Tosafot acknowledges that this was not the widespread practice — *lo nahagu ha'olam ken* — and then pointedly asks: if women are truly obligated, why is this not the practice? This question reflects the major *machloket rishonim* on the matter. Many *rishonim*, including the Hagahot Ashri, held that women are indeed obligated in *zimun*, not merely permitted. The question remains unresolved in Tosafot's discussion.

### Obligation Question

The question of women's obligation in *zimun* is bound up with the prior question of their obligation in *birkat hamazon*. If women are obligated in *birkat hamazon* as a biblical matter — which is the standard assumption — it becomes difficult to understand why they should not equally be obligated in *zimun*, since *zimun* is the mechanism by which *birkat hamazon* is performed in its fullest institutional form. The difficulty is compounded if one follows Tosafot's reading of the *Gemara*, in which the *maskana* establishes that women are genuinely obligated. The question then becomes not whether women have a personal obligation but why that obligation cannot be discharged collectively with men.

### Pritzuta Concern

The *Gemara* resolves this: why can women and slaves not form a mixed group even if each separately has a form of *zimun*? The answer is *mishum pritzuta* — because of concerns about sexual impropriety. In the social context presupposed by the *Gemara*, a mixed gathering of women and slaves at a shared table raised concerns about impropriety in a way that a gathering of men alone, or women alone, did not. This ruling naturally prompts the question of whether the concern for *pritzuta* is contingent on social context and whether it would apply equally in contemporary settings where men and women regularly share meals — a question that has been addressed in recent halachic literature, including discussions that emerged from *Gush* regarding the possibility of mixed-gender *zimun* in contemporary family contexts.

## Two-Person Eating (II)

### Shomea Ke'oneh Only

The *Gemara* returns to the question of two-person *zimun* and now provides what it treats as a decisive proof. Rabbi Yochanan taught, as cited by Rabbah bar bar Chana: *shnayim she-achlu ke-echad echad mehem yotzei be-virchat chaveiro* — two who ate together, one can be *yotzei* through the other's *bracha*. The *Gemara* asks: what does this teach us? We already know the general principle of *shomea ke-oneh* — one who hears a *bracha* is considered as if he recited it himself, and *shama ve-lo ana yatza*, one who heard but did not answer is still *yotzei*. Why then does Rabbi Yochanan need to specify the case of two?

Rabbi Zeira explains: the point is *she-ein birchat ha-zimun beineihem* — that there is no institution of *zimun* between them. Two can be *yotzei* through the mechanism of *shomea ke-oneh* — one recites *birkat hamazon* and the other listens and fulfills his obligation through that — but this is not the institution of *zimun*. They are piggybacking on one another as individuals, not performing the constitutive act of a group. This is significant because it confirms that while two can technically discharge their obligation, it is not the ideal mode. As we have seen and will see again in later *Gemaras*, *shomea ke-oneh* is a *bedi'avad* mechanism for *brachot hanehenin*; the preferred mode is either performing the *bracha* oneself or being part of a genuine *zimun* as a group.

### West's Testimony

The *Gemara* concludes with a brief exchange that assigns positions. Rava bar Rav Chanan reported to Rav Huna that the rabbis who came from *ma'arava* — from the Land of Israel — said *im ratzu lezamen mezamnin*, that two may optionally perform *zimun*. Since these rabbis came from the West, one might assume they were transmitting the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan. But the *Gemara* responds: *lo de-shami'a lehu me-Rav mikamei de-nachit le-Bavel* — no, they heard it from Rav before Rav descended to Babylonia, when Rav was still in the Land of Israel. Thus it is Rav who holds that two may optionally perform *zimun*, and Rabbi Yochanan who holds that they may not. The practical ruling, as we will see when we reach the relevant *Gemara*, follows Rabbi Yochanan: a minimum of three is required for *zimun*, and there is no valid *zimun* with fewer.

# Berakhot 48

## Zimmun Composition

### Minyan Review

The daf opens on 48a with a statement of Rav Yehuda, picking up from the preceding discussion about who may count toward the quorum for *zimmun*. Yesterday's sugya raised pivotal questions about the *minyan* of ten — whether a minor could serve as the tenth, the debates found in Tosafot about whether the same logic might extend to a woman, the device of a minor holding a *Sefer Torah*, and the broader question of whether there are different standards for the person who completes the group of ten versus the group of three. These issues have had profound practical relevance in communities historically struggling to assemble a *minyan*. The Gemara now turns from those questions to the equally daily and practical question of what constitutes a valid *zimmun*.

### Tisha Achlu Dagan

Rav Yehuda, son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat, states in the name of Rav: *tisha achlu dagan ve-echad achal yerak* — if nine people ate grain and one person ate only vegetables, the tenth nevertheless joins to form a *zimmun* of ten, allowing the leader to say *Eloheinu*. The parallel to the previous discussion is instructive: there, the Gemara entertained the idea of a minor counting as the tenth; here the person is certainly an adult, but has not eaten bread. The minimum threshold is that he ate something.

### Majority Threshold

Rav Zeira then reports that he posed a series of questions to Rav Yehuda: *shemona mahu, shiva mahu* — what about eight, what about seven? Rav Yehuda replied that it makes no difference — the same rule applies. Rav Zeira then lamented that he had not thought to ask about six, since he was uncertain whether that would suffice. Rav Yirmiya responds that it was well that he did not ask, since the ruling in the case of nine, eight, and seven rests on the principle that there exists a *ruba* — a majority — who ate bread, and six would equally constitute a majority. Rav Zeira's position, however, is that he requires *ruba de-minchar* — a discernible, obvious majority — and six, being barely a majority, may not meet that standard.

The practical *halacha* follows this latter view: if seven of ten ate bread, one may say *Eloheinu*; if only six ate bread and four did not, one may not.

### Vegetable & Wine Ruling

The Gemara then records the rule: *ve-hacha hilchata* — the practical ruling is that even one who ate a vegetable or drank a cup of wine *mitztareif*, he joins the group. The question of wine is addressed by the principle that drinking is included within the category of eating. The ruling is that such a person may be counted toward the quorum, and even the word *Eloheinu* may be said, since *shitiya bichlal achila* — drinking is subsumed within the act of eating.

### Three-Person Zimmun

The Gemara does not explicitly address the parallel question for the three-person *zimmun* — whether all three must eat bread. This gap is filled by the *rishonim*. Tosafot records two opinions without resolving the matter. The *Shulchan Aruch* brings three positions: one requiring all three to have eaten bread; a second permitting the third to have eaten only *mezonot*; and a third permitting even *shehakol* or vegetables. This is a genuine three-way dispute among the authorities.

### Modern Practice

The *Shulchan Aruch* ideally prescribes that if a third person joins who has not eaten bread, one should proactively encourage him to eat bread — or at least *mezonot* — so as to participate fully in the *zimmun*. In practice, if the third person has eaten only vegetables or some other food, the *zimmun* may nonetheless proceed. The person leading the *zimmun*, however, should certainly be one who has eaten bread.

There is, however, an important qualification shaping modern practice: in the time of the Gemara, the leader of the benching was *motzi* the others — he discharged their obligation entirely. Today, everyone recites *Birkat Hamazon* for themselves; the leader says only the introductory formulas. This shift has led to a degree of practical leniency on these questions, since the stakes of the leader's eating status are considerably lower when he is not discharging anyone else's obligation.

---

## Yannai & Shimon Story

### Yannai's Purge

The Gemara now presents a famous narrative: *Yannai Malka u-malchata kerichu rifta bahadi hadadei* — King Yannai and the queen were eating bread together. The story is set against the backdrop of a well-known historical episode in which Yannai had killed all the rabbis. As a result, *lo hava lei inish levoruchei lehu* — there was no one left who could lead the benching for them. The absence of qualified individuals to lead *Birkat Hamazon* is treated here with the same gravity as the destruction of the rabbinic leadership itself — a striking juxtaposition.

### Shimon Brought In

Yannai said to his wife: *man yahav lan gavra demevarech lan* — who can find us someone to lead the benching? She replied: swear to me that if I bring someone, you will not harm him. He swore. She then produced her brother, Shimon ben Shetach, whom she had concealed from the purge of the sages. They seated him between the king and the queen. The *Yerushalmi* provides additional context: Yannai had been embarrassed in front of Persian visitors who had previously known Shimon ben Shetach as a great sage and inquired about him, making it pragmatically necessary for Yannai to rehabilitate him. The queen, *Shlomtzion Hamalka*, had hidden her brother precisely to make this possible.

### Shimon's Reply

Yannai said to Shimon: *chazi kama yekara avdinan lach* — see how much honor we are giving you. Shimon responded without hesitation: *lav at mokrat li ela oraita hi demokra li* — it is not you who honors me; it is the Torah that confers my honor, as it is written, *salsaleha uteromemeka, techabedeka ki techabkenah* — honor the Torah and it will exalt you; embrace it and it will honor you. Yannai turned to his wife and said: you see — this man does not accept my authority. One can only wonder at Shimon ben Shetach's sense of self-preservation in this exchange, though perhaps his point was precisely that no royal oath could substitute for that relationship.

### Not Eaten Issue

They gave Shimon ben Shetach a cup to lead the benching. He said: *heichi evarech?* — how can I make a blessing? I have not eaten with them. He proposed saying *Baruch she-achal Yannai ve-chaverav* — blessed is the One from whose food Yannai and his companions ate — since he could not truthfully say *nevareich*, which requires the leader to have partaken. Instead, he drank the cup they had given him, effectively joining the meal through drinking. They then refilled the cup, and he led the benching. The Gemara immediately points out, through Rabbi Abba son of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, that *Shimon ben Shetach de-avad legarmei hu de-avad* — what Shimon did, he did as a personal ruling for himself, not as normative *halacha* for others.

### Kezayit Rule

The normative rule, stated by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, is: *le-olam eino motzi et ha-rabbim yedei chovatan ad she-yochal kezayit dagan* — one can never discharge the public from their obligation until one has eaten a *kezayit* of grain. The leader of the benching, who in that era was genuinely *motzi* the others, had to have eaten bread. The reason Shimon ben Shetach's personal arrangement involved drinking rather than eating is that he found himself in an extraordinary circumstance and ruled leniently for himself — and even that ruling is not accepted as binding precedent.

---

## Kezayit vs. Satiation

### Rashi/Tosafot Q

This ruling generates a sharp analytical question raised by both Rashi and Tosafot: the Gemara implies that eating a *kezayit* of bread suffices to enable one to lead the benching and discharge others. But eating only a *kezayit* creates only a *derabbanan* obligation to bench — the *de-oraita* obligation of *Birkat Hamazon* is triggered only by *sevi'ah*, by actual satiation. Yannai, the queen, and the rest of the company had certainly eaten their fill. How, then, could Shimon ben Shetach, had he eaten only a *kezayit*, have discharged a *de-oraita* obligation through a *derabbanan* performance?

### Tosafot Solution

Rashi's answer is that in certain circumstances, a *derabbanan* obligation can indeed discharge a *de-oraita* one — a position Tosafot finds entirely unacceptable. Tosafot offers a striking and counterintuitive alternative: in principle, one can be *motzi* another person in *Birkat Hamazon* even without having eaten at all. The reasoning is drawn from an analogy to other *mitzvot*: if one has already fulfilled an obligation — already heard *shofar*, already read *Megillah* — one can still perform the act again to discharge the obligation of another who has not yet fulfilled it. The mechanism of *motzi* is not dependent on one's own current state of obligation, but on the category of the *mitzvah* itself. The sole reason the Gemara requires the leader to have eaten is so that he can truthfully say *she-achalnu mi-shelo* — that "we ate from His bounty." It is the verbal declaration, not the mechanism of discharge, that requires prior eating.

This is a remarkable position with far-reaching implications. If the only reason the leader must eat is to truthfully say *she-achalnu mi-shelo*, then in a context where that phrase need not be said, one might be *motzi* another even without having eaten at all. Some *Poskim* accept this inference; others find it untenable. The question has practical ramifications: if two people are eating together and one, for whatever reason, cannot bench — would the other be able to bench for him even without himself having eaten? The debate among *Poskim* on this question flows directly from Tosafot's position here.

### Behag View

The *Behag* (*Halachot Gedolot*) offers an entirely different resolution, one that many find more intuitive: when the Gemara says that a *kezayit* is sufficient for one to discharge others, it means that the others have likewise eaten only a *kezayit*. But if others have eaten to satiation and incurred a *de-oraita* obligation, someone who has eaten only a *kezayit* — and bears only a *derabbanan* obligation — cannot discharge them. The *de-oraita* can only be discharged by someone equally obligated at the *de-oraita* level.

The *Behag*'s answer is conceptually comfortable, but it does not fully fit the circumstance of the Yannai story, where it seems clear that the assembled guests had eaten to satiation. Perhaps the Gemara's statement that Shimon acted for himself carries a deeper implication — that even he would not have been prepared to rule this way in ordinary circumstances.

### Modern Leniency

As a practical summary: the *halacha* requires a majority of seven out of ten to have eaten bread for *Eloheinu* to be said; for the group of three, the ideal is that all three have bread, with *mezonot* being a widely accepted fallback, and even vegetables or *shehakol* being permissible after the fact. The person who leads should ideally have eaten to satiation, or at minimum a *kezayit* of bread. In contemporary practice, however, where the *zimmun* consists only of the opening formulas and everyone benches individually, these standards are applied with somewhat less stringency, since the leader is not in fact discharging anyone else's obligation.

---

## Rabban Shimon Rule

### Dipping & Fig

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that if someone came and reclined at the table, even if he dipped only in *tzir* — brine or vinegar — and ate no more than a single *grogeret*, a pressed fig, he *mitztareif* — he joins the group. At first glance, this seems to contradict the ruling requiring a *kezayit* of bread to lead the benching, since a fig is not bread.

### Mitztareif Clarified

The Gemara resolves this cleanly: *mitztareif mitztareif* — the word *mitztareif* means he may join the group for the count of three or ten, but *le-hotzi et ha-rabbim yedei chovatam ad she-yochal kezayit dagan* — to actually lead and discharge others, he must have eaten a *kezayit* of grain. These are two separate questions: what qualifies one to be counted as part of the group, and what qualifies one to lead the benching. The answer to the first is lenient; the answer to the second is not.

### Leaf & Wine

A further ruling is then cited: Rav Chana bar Yehuda in the name of Rava states the *halacha* explicitly — even if one ate only a leaf of vegetable or drank a cup of wine, he may join (*mitztareif*), but to discharge others he must have eaten a *kezayit* of bread. This is the final practical ruling of this section: *achal aleh yerek ve-shatah kos shel yayin mitztareif; le-hotzi eino motzi ad she-yochal kezayit dagan*.

---

## Sources of Benching

### Moshe & Manna

The Gemara now turns from the composition of the *zimmun* to the institution of *Birkat Hamazon* itself, tracing each blessing to its historical founder. Rav Nachman states: *Moshe tikken le-Yisrael birkat ha-zan* — Moshe instituted the blessing of *ha-zan et ha-kol* at the time the *man* fell in the wilderness. This makes sense: the *de-oraita* verse, *ve-achalta ve-savata u-veirachta*, commands blessing for food, but the blessing *al ha-aretz ve-al ha-mazon* could not yet be said — they had not yet entered the land. The blessing for sustenance could be said over the *man*, even miraculous sustenance, because the *man* makes us aware that all food — natural and miraculous alike — ultimately comes from God. This is the conceptual foundation of *ha-zan et ha-kol*.

A note on the Sefardic *nusach*: some versions of the first blessing include the phrase *ka-katuv poseach et yadecha u-mashbia le-chol chai ratzon*, a verse from *Tehillim*. The Rashba notes in a *teshuvah* that this is difficult to reconcile with the view that Moshe instituted this blessing, since that verse had not yet been written in Moshe's time. This textual difficulty remains unresolved.

### Yehoshua & Land

*Yehoshua tikken lahem birchat ha-aretz* — Yehoshua instituted the blessing of *al ha-aretz ve-al ha-mazon* when the people entered the land of Israel. Only upon entering the land could one thank God specifically for the good land.
