One can only imagine what that moment must have meant to Yehoshua — the one thing Moshe could not do, Yehoshua was now able to fulfill. A *mitzvah* that had been latent since Sinai was finally able to be performed in its fullness.

### David/Shlomo

*David u-Shlomo tiknu boneh Yerushalayim* — David and Shlomo together instituted the blessing of *boneh Yerushalayim*. David established the portion mentioning Israel and Jerusalem — *al Yisrael amcha ve-al Yerushalayim irecha* — since he was the one who established Jerusalem as the capital. Shlomo added the reference to *ha-bayit ha-gadol ve-ha-kadosh* — the great and holy house — since it was Shlomo who built the Temple.

### Boneh De'oraita

This raises an immediate question: does *boneh Yerushalayim* not imply a destroyed Jerusalem, as though it were instituted only after the *churban*? The Gemara understands otherwise. Just as *birkat ha-aretz* was a *de-oraita* obligation that could not be performed until there was a land to speak of, so too *boneh Yerushalayim* is a *de-oraita* obligation that could not be expressed until there was a Jerusalem to praise. The verb *boneh* — building — reflects God's ongoing creative involvement in the city and the Temple. Even when Jerusalem stands fully built, God is understood as the one who built it and sustains it, so the blessing is not inherently retrospective or lamenting. It praises God as the builder of Jerusalem in an active, present sense.

### Yavne & Tov

*Ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* was instituted in Yavne, in connection with the victims of Beitar following the Bar Kokhba revolt. Rav Matna states: on the day the slain of Beitar were permitted burial, the sages in Yavne instituted the blessing of *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*. *Ha-tov* — God is good — refers to the fact that the bodies did not decompose; *ha-meitiv* — God does good for others — refers to the granting of burial. In its original form, the blessing was brief: *Baruch Hashem ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*; it was expanded into a full paragraph over time.

### Exile Context

The theological significance of *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* in the context of *Birkat Hamazon* is considerable. Halachically, this blessing is of greater weight than *shehecheyanu* — the latter marks something good for oneself, while the former marks something good for others as well. More broadly, its placement after *boneh Yerushalayim* creates a striking juxtaposition: the benching as a whole thanks God for the good land and for Jerusalem — precisely what the Jewish people in exile do not have. Into this structure of longing and loss, *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* inserts a declaration that even in exile, even when the land is gone and the Temple is destroyed, even when people are being killed, one can still find cause to thank God. The bodies of Beitar's victims were preserved and eventually buried — and from that, a blessing of joy was composed. This is somewhat analogous to *Kaddish*: in the depths of mourning, one proclaims God's greatness. But the orientation here is slightly different — not *tzidduk ha-din*, accepting God's judgment, but rather the active discovery of goodness within a context of exile and loss.

---

## Benching Order

### Four Blessings

The Gemara now presents the formal order of *Birkat Hamazon*: the first blessing is *birkat ha-zan*; the second is *birkat ha-aretz*, i.e., *al ha-aretz ve-al ha-mazon*; the third is *boneh Yerushalayim*; and the fourth is *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*. This is the basic four-part structure of the benching.

### Shabbat Insertion

On Shabbat, one begins and ends the third blessing with *nechama* and mentions *kedushat ha-yom* — the holiness of Shabbat — in the middle: *matchil be-nechama u-mesayem be-nechama ve-omer kedushat ha-yom be-emtza*. Rashi understands this to mean that the standard text of *boneh Yerushalayim* is retained, with the Shabbat insertion placed within it. The blessing opens with the normal *nusach* — which Rashi identifies as beginning with *Rachem* — and concludes with the standard closing of *boneh Yerushalayim*, with the Shabbat material inserted in the middle.

### Tosafot Variant

Tosafot records an alternative tradition according to which the *nusach* of the third blessing is actually changed on Shabbat. The reading *matchil be-nachamenu ve-chotmin be-nechamat Tziyon ircha u-vinyan Yerushalayim* suggests a different opening formula — *nachamenu*, console us — on the grounds that *Rachem*, in its plain sense, is a petition, and one does not offer petitions on Shabbat. Tosafot ultimately rejects this alternative, noting that *nachem* is equally a request and therefore equally problematic by that logic. But the existence of this tradition attests to genuine diversity in the liturgical *nusach* of the third blessing on Shabbat.

### R. Eliezer Flexibility

Rabbi Eliezer takes a broader view: one may insert the Shabbat mention in any of the later three blessings — in *boneh Yerushalayim*, in *birkat ha-aretz*, or in the blessing the sages of Yavne instituted, i.e., *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*. Notably, he does not permit inserting it in the first blessing, *ha-zan*. This parallels the principle in *Shemoneh Esrei* that modifications and insertions are not made in the first three blessings — which form a fixed, foundational unit — but rather in the middle or later blessings. Even where Rabbi Eliezer permits flexibility, he treats the first blessing as inviolate.

Why is Shabbat mentioned specifically in *boneh Yerushalayim* in the standard practice? One possibility is the thematic connection to the *korbanot* — the *musaf* sacrifices — which are associated with both Jerusalem and the special days of the calendar. But the precise connection remains somewhat open, which may itself explain why Rabbi Eliezer was willing to permit the mention in any of the three later blessings.

The related question of *me'akev* — whether omitting these insertions requires one to repeat the benching — follows a nuanced rule: in *Shemoneh Esrei*, most special insertions are *me'akev*, with the notable exception of *Al ha-Nissim* (though *Ya'aleh ve-Yavo* is debated). In benching, the insertion is generally *me'akev* only when the day itself obligates a meal — as on Shabbat and Yom Tov — which gives the Shabbat insertion its special connection to the meal being blessed.

---

## Scriptural Sources

### Ha-Zan Source

The Gemara now proceeds to derive each of the four blessings from Scripture. The *baraita* asks: from where do we know *Birkat Hamazon* from the Torah? The verse is *ve-achalta ve-savata u-veirachta* — you shall eat, be satisfied, and bless. The word *ve-achalta* — eating — corresponds to *birkat ha-zan*. *Et Hashem Elokecha* — God your Lord — corresponds to *birkat ha-zimmun*, the introductory call to bless, since it is in the declaration of God's name that we call others to join in praise, as in *ki shem Hashem ekra havu godel l'Elokeinu*.

It is worth noting the *peshat* emphasis here: the Torah's primary concern, as expressed throughout *Sefer Devarim*, is not simply that one ate and should be grateful for the food, but that one is being brought to a great land — *eretz harim u-vekaot*, a land of hills and valleys — filled with all good things, and should therefore bless God *al ha-aretz ha-tovah*. The thanksgiving for the food is inseparable from the thanksgiving for the land.

### Ha-Aretz Source

*Al ha-aretz* — on the land — gives rise to *birkat ha-aretz*. This is essentially *peshat*: the Torah itself frames the obligation to bless in terms of gratitude for the land, not merely for the food. The *de-oraita* character of *birkat ha-aretz* is therefore well anchored in the plain meaning of the verse.

### Boneh Source

*Ha-tovah* — the good — gives rise to *boneh Yerushalayim*. What makes the land good? Not only its agricultural bounty, but the presence of the *Shekhinah*, the existence of Jerusalem, and the *Beit ha-Mikdash*. The verse *ha-har ha-tov ha-zeh ve-ha-Levanon* is cited — "this good mountain and the Lebanon" — and the Gemara understands "this good mountain" as a reference to Jerusalem. Thus, thanking God for the goodness of the land necessarily encompasses thanking God for Jerusalem as the locus of divine presence. This is what makes *boneh Yerushalayim* a *de-oraita* obligation — not the loss of Jerusalem, but the recognition that it constitutes the fullness of what makes the land "good."

### Tov Source

The phrase *asher natan lach* — which God has given you — gives rise to *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*. The principle is that for everything God gives us, we acknowledge that God acts with goodness toward us and toward others. One opinion in the Gemara had argued that *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* is itself *de-oraita* on the basis of this verse, though this view is largely rejected — the consensus of the *rishonim* is that *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* is *derabbanan*, instituted in Yavne, as established earlier.

This verse, *asher natan lach*, appears in this sugya with considerable versatility: it is used as the source for *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*, for the blessing before eating, and as we shall see, for *Birkat ha-Torah* as well. This breadth reflects a general hermeneutical principle: the act of God's giving — *natan* — implies an obligation of acknowledgment on our part for whatever is given.

The question is sometimes raised whether all this emphasis on the land means that *Birkat Hamazon* might not be *de-oraita* outside of *Eretz Yisrael*. The Gemara, written in Bavel, does not entertain this suggestion. The obligation to bless is treated as universal, and the mention of Jerusalem in the benching is understood as directed toward a future in which Jerusalem will be rebuilt, not as a precondition for the obligation. Just as one acknowledges the land God has given even without living on it, one acknowledges Jerusalem even while in exile.

---

## De'oraita Debate

### Rabbi View

The Gemara now turns to a *Tannaitic* dispute about which elements of *Birkat Hamazon* are *de-oraita* and which are *derabbanan*. The *baraita* first states the majority position from which *birkat ha-zimmun* and the three blessings are derived together. Rabbi (Rebbi) argues that *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* is *derabbanan* — instituted in Yavne — and not *de-oraita*, even according to those who tried to anchor it in *asher natan lach*. This is the view accepted by virtually all *rishonim*. Rabbi further contends that *birkat ha-zimmun* should be derived from a different verse — *gadlu l'Hashem iti u-neromemah shemo yachdav* — rather than from *Et Hashem Elokecha* as in the earlier derivation. This may reflect Rabbi's view that the *zimmun* is not itself *de-oraita* — a position that is overwhelmingly the consensus of the *rishonim*, even if certain sources seem to suggest otherwise.

### Before Eating

The *baraita* then asks: from the verse *ve-achalta ve-savata u-veirachta*, I know only the obligation to bless *after* eating. What is the source for a blessing *before* eating? The *baraita* proposes a *kal va-chomer*: if one blesses when satisfied, how much more so should one bless when hungry, since the hunger makes one more acutely aware of one's dependence on and appreciation for God's bounty. One might ask whether this *kal va-chomer* is truly persuasive — the experience of satiation is itself the occasion that triggers the gratitude expressed in benching, whereas the blessing before eating is a response to anticipated benefit. But the *baraita* takes the *kal va-chomer* seriously.

Whether this argument establishes the blessing *before* eating as *de-oraita* is debated. The conclusion at the opening of the sixth *perek* of this tractate assumed it to be *derabbanan*. Yet the *Tannaim* here seem genuinely invested in establishing its biblical basis. There may be sources that treat the pre-eating blessing as *de-oraita* and not merely an *asmachta*, even if the weight of the *sugya* moves in the other direction.

### R. Yitzchak Source

Rabbi Yitzchak says one need not resort to a *kal va-chomer*. There is a verse that directly supports a pre-eating blessing: *u-veirach et lachmecha ve-et meimecha* — "and He shall bless your bread and your water." Reading the verse not as a divine promise but as a human obligation — *al tikrei u-veirach* God will bless, *ela u-vareich* you should bless — yields a direct *de-oraita* source for blessing before eating. Furthermore, the word *lechem* applies specifically to bread *before* it is eaten; once consumed, it is no longer called *lechem*. Therefore, the blessing over *lechem* must come before the eating.

### R. Nasan Source

Rabbi Nasan goes further afield. He derives the blessing before eating from a verse in the narrative of Shmuel: when young women direct Saul to the city, they mention that *ki hu yevarech ha-zevach acharei chen yochlu ha-kru'im* — Shmuel will bless the sacrifice and only afterward will the invited guests eat. The Gemara understands "bless the sacrifice" as referring to a blessing over the food before eating, not a sacrificial blessing. This derivation shifts the source away from the Five Books entirely, which tends to push it out of the *de-oraita* category — a blessing learned from a narrative in *Nevi'im* is more naturally understood as a *derabbanan* institution with scriptural support, or at most an *asmachta*.

---

## Women Digression

### Reasons Debated

The mention of the women who spoke to Saul at such length prompts the Gemara to ask: *ve-chol kach lamah* — why did they speak so extensively? Three answers are offered. The first is that *nashim davraniyot hen* — women are chatterers by nature. The Gemara does not leave it there. Shmuel offers a second reason: *ke-dei le-histakel be-yofyo shel Shaul* — they wanted to keep looking at Saul, who was famously handsome. As the verse says, *mi-shichmo va-mala gavoah mi-kol ha-am* — from his shoulders and above he was taller than all the people. So strikingly attractive was Saul that they prolonged the conversation simply for the opportunity to gaze at him.

### R. Yochanan View

Rabbi Yochanan offers a completely different explanation that exonerates the women entirely: *lefi she-ein malchut nogaat be-chavertah afilu ke-melo nima* — one reign cannot overlap with another even by a hairsbreadth. Saul's moment had not yet arrived; Shmuel's authority had not yet concluded. Any meeting between them would have constituted the inauguration of Saul's kingship, and that could not happen before the precise moment ordained for it. The women's extended speech served, whether they knew it or not, to delay the encounter until the appointed time.

---

## Birkat Ha-Torah

### Source Question

The Gemara transitions from the sources of *Birkat Hamazon* to a related question: *Birkat ha-Torah minayin* — from where do we derive the obligation of *Birkat ha-Torah*? This question belongs naturally in this discussion for two reasons. First, *Birkat ha-Torah* is understood by many *rishonim* to be genuinely *de-oraita* — unlike the blessing before food, which the Gemara ultimately treats as *derabbanan* — making it the other major *de-oraita* blessing alongside *Birkat Hamazon*. Second, the two obligations are intertwined in an earlier sugya at the beginning of the tractate, where the Gemara proposed a *kal va-chomer* in both directions: just as *Birkat ha-Torah* is said before Torah study, so too one should bless before eating; and just as *Birkat Hamazon* is said after eating, so too one should bless after Torah (at public readings). The convergence of these two sets of obligations explains why the Gemara addresses *Birkat ha-Torah* here in the same breath.

### Rav Shmuel KVC

Rav Shmuel argues for a *kal va-chomer*: *ha-chayei sha'ah mevarech, ha-chayei olam ha-ba lo kol she-ken* — if one blesses for sustenance that nourishes only in this world, how much more so should one bless for Torah, which gives one sustenance for the world to come. From an intellectual standpoint, the argument is compelling. From a purely experiential standpoint it is more complex — the immediate sensory pleasure of food is different in kind from the spiritual benefit of Torah. One might also note that this *kal va-chomer*, modeled on *Birkat Hamazon*, would more naturally suggest a blessing *after* learning — since *Birkat Hamazon* itself comes after eating.

### R. Chiya Analogy

Rabbi Chiyya bar Nachmani, a student of Rabbi Yishmael, offers a different derivation in Rabbi Yishmael's name: *al ha-aretz ha-tovah asher natan lach* — God gave you the good land. And elsewhere it says: *va-etna lach et luchot ha-even ha-Torah ve-ha-mitzvah* — I have also given you the tablets of stone, the Torah, and the commandment. Just as we thank God for the land God has given us, so we must thank God for the Torah God has given us. The parallel is drawn not through a *kal va-chomer* but through the shared language of *natan* — giving. This derivation, like the one from *asher natan lach* for *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*, works through the principle that any divine gift warrants acknowledgment and blessing. Conceptually it suggests a blessing of thanksgiving — one that might come after the fact — though it is used here as a source for the blessing before Torah study as well.

### R. Meir Source

Rabbi Meir derives the source from the verse already cited earlier in this tractate in connection with *zimmun*: *ki shem Hashem ekra havu godel l'Elokeinu* — when I proclaim the name of God, ascribe greatness to our God. The proclamation of Torah — which declares God's revelation — demands that those present respond by ascribing greatness to God. This understanding frames *Birkat ha-Torah* primarily as an act of praise, parallel to the praise-dimension of *zimmun*. There is a subtle but important distinction: *Birkat Hamazon* is primarily gratitude — *nodeh lecha* — while the *ki shem Hashem ekra* model is primarily praise — *havu godel*. Both dimensions are present in *Birkat ha-Torah* as we know it, and the *rishonim* generally understand the blessing to be *de-oraita* in the mode of gratitude and praise rather than as a *birkat ha-mitzvah*.

This is supported by a striking liturgical fact: the blessing recited at a public *keriat ha-Torah* does not include *asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu* — the *birkat ha-mitzvah* formulation. The public reading blessing is purely a blessing of thanks and praise. This aligns with the conceptualization drawn from *ki shem Hashem ekra* and *asher natan lach* rather than from the *mitzvah*-obligation framework.

---

## Bad & Good

### Bad Blessing

The Gemara now shifts to a broader theological principle: *ke-shem she-mevarechin al ha-tovah kach mevarechin al ha-ra* — just as one blesses God for the good, so one blesses God for the bad. Rabbi Nehorai states this principle and asks for its scriptural basis.

### Giving Source

The source is again *asher natan lach Hashem Elokecha* — whatever God has given you. The Gemara reads this expansively: *dayanecha be-chol din she-danecha* — accept God's judgment in whatever way God judges you, *bein midah tovah bein midat puranut* — whether in the mode of goodness or the mode of affliction. Whatever God gives, it is all recognized as coming from God and as part of God's plan.

### Din & Rachamim

This principle finds a beautiful parallel in a teaching of the *Sfat Emet* on *Rosh Hashanah*. He addresses the apparent tension between *Yom ha-Din* — the Day of Judgment — and *middat ha-rachamim* — divine mercy. His insight is that *din* becomes *rachamim* precisely when we present ourselves willingly before God's judgment, when we accept that being in this relationship with a God who cares enough to judge us is itself an expression of love. When one approaches *Yom ha-Din* not with dread but with the recognition that God's attention and care are themselves the expression of a loving relationship, the very act of judgment is transformed into mercy. The parallel to *mevarech al ha-ra* is apparent: seeing even what seems bad as part of God's giving, as *asher natan lach*, is what transforms judgment into relationship, and affliction into something that can itself be blessed.

---

## Required Themes

### R. Eliezer Reqs

The Gemara now turns to the required thematic content of each blessing. Rabbi Eliezer states: *kol she-lo amar eretz chemdah tovah u-rechavah be-birkat ha-aretz* — whoever did not say in *birkat ha-aretz* that the land is "beloved, good, and spacious," *u-malchut Beit David be-boneh Yerushalayim* — and whoever did not mention the kingship of the house of David in *boneh Yerushalayim* — *lo yatza yedei chovato*, has not fulfilled his obligation.

This is a striking ruling. The *de-oraita* source — *al ha-aretz ha-tovah* — requires only the mention of the land and its goodness. Yet Rabbi Eliezer insists that the fullness of that goodness must be expressed: the land is *chemdah tovah u-rechavah*, and its ultimate significance includes not merely the Temple but the Davidic kingdom that sanctified Jerusalem. As Rashi notes, it was through David that Jerusalem became holy — *she-al yado niskadsha Yerushalayim* — so the Davidic monarchy is integral to what *boneh Yerushalayim* is praising. The obligation is not merely to mention Jerusalem, but to recognize the full sacred character of what Jerusalem represents, which includes Davidic sovereignty.

### Brit Required

Nachum ha-Zaken adds: *she-tzarich she-yizkor bah brit* — one must mention the covenant in *birkat ha-aretz*. The connection between covenant and land is explicit in the Torah: leading up to the commandment of *brit milah*, the verse says *ve-nasati lecha u-le-zaracha acharecha et eretz megurecha et kol eretz Kena'an* — I will give to you and to your descendants all the land of Canaan. The possession of the land is grounded in a *brit*, and that covenantal foundation must be acknowledged when thanking God for the land.

### Torah Required

Rabbi Yosi adds: *tzarich she-yizkor bah Torah* — one must also mention Torah in *birkat ha-aretz*. His reasoning, as elaborated by Rashi, reflects the recurring motif of *Sefer Devarim*: the land is possessed and retained through the observance of *Torah u-mitzvot*. As the verse says, *le-ma'an tichyu u-rivitem u-vastem vi-riashtem et ha-aretz* — so that you may live and increase and come and inherit the land. The *mitzvot* are not peripheral to the land; they are the condition of inhabiting it. Acknowledging the land without acknowledging the Torah would be to miss the essential covenantal structure that makes the land meaningful.

### Brit Milah Theme

Plimo adds a further precision: *tzarich she-yakdim brit le-Torah* — the mention of *brit* must precede the mention of Torah, because the *brit* was given in three covenants, whereas — and here Plimo shifts to *brit milah* specifically — the covenant of circumcision was mentioned thirteen times in the *parasha* of *brit milah*. The repetition of *brit* thirteen times in that *parasha* underscores its primacy; it is therefore essential that *brit* — now understood as *brit milah* — be mentioned before Torah. This observation opens the question, which will become explicit shortly, about how women relate to this required mention of *brit milah* in a blessing they also recite.

### Hodaya Frame

Rabbi Abba concludes the list of required themes: *tzarich she-yomar bo hoda'ah techila ve-sof* — one must open and close *birkat ha-aretz* with thanksgiving. This frames the entire blessing as an act of gratitude: *nodeh lecha* at the opening, and *ve-al kulam Hashem Elokeinu anachnu modim lach* at the close. Whatever else the blessing contains — mention of land, covenant, Torah, kingship — it must be held within a structure of thanksgiving from beginning to end.

---

## Improper Forms

### Min Praise

The Gemara establishes a minimum standard: *ve-ha-pocheit lo yifchat me-achat* — if one reduces the content of praise, one must not fall below one positive mention. It is not entirely clear what this "one" refers to — whether to *eretz chemdah tovah u-rechavah* as a unit, or to some other required element. Whatever the referent, the principle is clear: there is a floor below which the content of *birkat ha-aretz* cannot fall.

### Wrong Closing

A serious error in the closing formula (*chatima*) of the blessing is then identified. If in *birkat ha-aretz* one concludes with *manchil aratzot* — He who bequeaths lands (in the plural) — instead of the standard closing referring to *al ha-aretz ve-al ha-mazon*, or if in *boneh Yerushalayim* one concludes with *moshia Yisrael* — He who saves Israel — instead of *boneh Yerushalayim*, this is condemned. The Gemara calls such a person a *bur* — an ignoramus. It is worth noting that the Gemara uses such strong language precisely because people were actually using these formulations — otherwise there would be nothing to censure.

### Exile Variants

These alternative closings can be understood as responses to the difficulty of the *galut* situation. How does one say *al ha-aretz ve-al ha-mazon* while living outside of *Eretz Yisrael*, eating food not grown in the holy land? The formulation *manchil aratzot* — God who distributes lands to all peoples — attempts to universalize the blessing, abstracting away from the specific gift of *Eretz Yisrael* and toward a more general theological claim that all land ultimately comes from God. This is not without grounding: the *Ramban*'s comment at the opening of *Bereishit* about God's ownership of all land and the right to give and take it from nations is a related idea. Similarly, *moshia Yisrael* in place of *boneh Yerushalayim* might reflect a *galut* sensibility that shifts the focus from building Jerusalem — which currently lies in ruins — to the hope of redemption from exile.

The Gemara, however, does not accept either substitution. The specific language of *birkat ha-aretz* and *boneh Yerushalayim* must retain its *Eretz Yisrael* focus and its Jerusalem-centered orientation. Even in exile, the blessing must speak of the specific land and the specific city as they appear in the *pesukim*. To abstract or universalize the closing formula is not a permissible accommodation to exile — it is an erasure of the essential theological content of the blessing.

### R. Elazar Standard

The Gemara concludes this section with a *tanna* of great stringency. A *baraita* is cited: Rabbi Elazar, in the name of Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of *Rabbeinu* (likely Rebbe), states: *kol she-lo amar brit ve-Torah be-birkat ha-aretz u-malchut Beit David be-voneh Yerushalayim lo yatza yedei chovato* — whoever did not mention covenant, Torah, and the kingship of the House of David in their respective blessings has not fulfilled their obligation. This formulation consolidates all the required themes — *brit*, *Torah*, and *malchut Beit David* — and declares that their omission constitutes a failure to discharge one's obligation. Whether this refers to a biblical or rabbinic obligation, and what the practical *halacha* is when someone has benched without these elements, will require further examination. The daf's discussion of these themes continues on the following amud.

---

---

# Berakhot 49

## HaTov VeHaMeitiv

### Debate Setup

The *gemara* on 49a opens with a dispute between Abba Yosi ben Dostai and the Rabbis concerning the blessing of *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*, the fourth blessing of *birkat ha-mazon*. The *gemara* introduces the debate with the words *v'Rabbanan*, appearing approximately twelve lines down on 49a. One authority holds that *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* requires *malchus* — meaning the full formula of *baruch atah Hashem Elokeinu melech ha-olam* — while the other holds it does not.

### Malchus Requirement

It is important to clarify what is meant here by *malchus*: this is not *malchus beit David*, the kingship of the House of David, which we encountered in connection with *boneh Yerushalayim*, but rather *malchus shamayim* — the phrase *melech ha-olam* in the opening of a *bracha*. The question is whether *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* must be introduced with *Elokeinu melech ha-olam* or whether a shorter formula suffices.

The *gemara* explains the logic of each position. The view that *malchus* is required holds that *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* is *d'Rabbanan* — a rabbinic addition — and therefore stands as an independent *bracha*, not organically connected to the earlier blessings of *birkat ha-mazon*. As an independent *bracha*, it requires its own *Elokeinu melech ha-olam*. The view that *malchus* is not required holds that *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* is *d'Oraisa* — that is, it was part of the original structure of *benching* — and is therefore *samuch l'chavertah*, attached to and following from the preceding *brachot*.

### Samuch L'Chavertah

This is the operative literary principle: a *bracha samuch l'chavertah* — one juxtaposed to and continuous with a preceding *bracha* — does not require its own *Elokeinu melech ha-olam*. The *malchus* invoked in the opening *bracha* carries forward through the entire chain. This is familiar from *shemoneh esrei*, where *baruch atah Hashem rofe cholei amo Yisrael*, *baruch atah Hashem go'el Yisrael*, and all subsequent *brachot* carry no *melech ha-olam*, because they all link back to the opening *bracha* in which *malchus* was established. The theme of *malchus* is present by implication; to repeat it would not be *l'vatalah* because it is understood as continuous. The principle, then, is that when a *bracha* was originally established as part of a sequence, the *malchus* of the opening *bracha* is considered to carry through; when a *bracha* stands independently, it requires its own.

### Application to Benching

An instructive parallel is *birkat ha-Torah*. The first *bracha* opens with *Elokeinu melech ha-olam* and closes with *ha-melamed Torah l'amo Yisrael*. The subsequent *bracha*, beginning with a fresh *baruch*, is treated as a new independent *bracha* and therefore opens again with *Elokeinu melech ha-olam asher bachar banu*, closing with *baruch atah Hashem nosein ha-Torah*. It is not treated as *samuch l'chavertah*, and accordingly requires its own *malchus*. The same logic applies throughout *benching*: the three core *brachot* form an original and continuous sequence; *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*, if understood as a later rabbinic appendage, falls outside that sequence and must stand on its own.

---

## Boneh Yerushalayim

### Chatimah Debate

The *gemara* turns to a *baraita*: *mah hu chosem b'vinyan Yerushalayim* — what is the closing formula, the *chatimah*, of the blessing of *boneh Yerushalayim*? The third blessing opens with *racheim Hashem Elokeinu al Yisrael amecha v'al Yerushalayim irecha*. The question is how it should end. Rabbi Yosi the son of Rabbi Yehuda says one ends with *moshia Yisrael* — savior of Israel. This is a striking position, because it was mentioned earlier that one who says *moshia Yisrael* is an ignoramus. Yet here a named *tanna* endorses precisely that formula, which confirms that this *nusach* had genuine traction and could not simply be dismissed.

### Both Themes

The *gemara* challenges: does he mean *moshia Yisrael* to the exclusion of *boneh Yerushalayim*? It answers: *ella eima af moshia Yisrael* — even *moshia Yisrael*. This formulation can be read either as permitting both *moshia Yisrael u-voneh Yerushalayim* together, or as allowing either formula. Rashi reads it as meaning that one may choose either, with both *boneh Yerushalayim* and *moshia Yisrael* being acceptable options. The *gemara*'s own tendency, as we have seen, favors the explicit *boneh Yerushalayim*.

The emphasis on *moshia Yisrael* may reflect a post-*churban* sensibility: from the perspective of *galut*, the restoration of the Jewish people may feel more urgent and immediate than the rebuilding of Jerusalem. A parallel can be drawn to the *bracha* recited after reading *Megilat Esther* — *ha'el ha-moshia* — which is similarly diaspora-oriented in its framing. In *shemoneh esrei* as well, the sequence runs from *mekabetz nidchei Yisrael* to *boneh Yerushalayim* and then to *matzmiach keren yeshuah*, which refers to the house of David — these themes are clearly interconnected.

### One Theme Rule

Rabbah bar Rav Huna once came to the house of the *Reish Galuta*, opened with one theme and closed with two — presumably saying both *moshia Yisrael u-voneh Yerushalayim* in the *chatimah*. Rav Chisda challenged him: is it such a small matter to end with two themes? For we have a *baraita* in which Rabbi says *ein chotmin b'shtayim* — one does not close a *chatimah* with two themes. The underlying principle is *ein osin mitzvos chavilos chavilos* — one does not bundle *mitzvos* together; each deserves its own proper focus.

It is worth noting that the blessing itself opens with multiple themes — *racheim... al Yisrael amecha v'al Yerushalayim irecha* — yet closes with only one. The opening may be expansive, but the *chatimah* must be singular. This creates the problem: if the blessing addresses both the salvation of Israel and the building of Jerusalem, which theme should the closing formula reflect?

### Exceptions

The *gemara* tests the rule. Levi challenged Rabbi with examples that appear to use two themes in a *chatimah*: *al ha-aretz v'al ha-mazon*, *al ha-aretz v'al ha-peirot*, *mekadesh Yisrael v'ha-zmanim*, *mekadesh Yisrael v'roshei chodashim*. Rabbi answered each: *aretz d'mapka mazon* — the land that brings forth the food; *aretz d'mapka peirot* — the land that brings forth the fruit; *Yisrael d'kadshinhu l'zmanim* — Israel who sanctifies the times by establishing the calendar. In each case, what appears as two themes resolves into one: one entity, one act, one attribution to God.

The case of *mekadesh ha-Shabbat v'Yisrael v'ha-zmanim*, which combines *Shabbat*, Israel, and the *moadim*, cannot be similarly resolved. Here the *gemara* says simply *chutz mi-zo* — this is an exception — and explains *hacha chada hi, hatam tarti*: here it is one, there it is two. Rashi explains that the formula means simply that God sanctifies — *hamekadesh* — and that single verb applies alike to *Shabbat*, to Israel, and to the *moadim*. It is one divine act of sanctification applied to multiple objects. By contrast, *moshia Yisrael u-voneh Yerushalayim* posits two distinct divine acts — redemption and construction — and is therefore genuinely *tarti*, two themes.

The objection was raised that *moshia Yisrael* and *boneh Yerushalayim* could similarly be treated as a single theme — the salvation of Israel leads to the building of Jerusalem, just as the land bringing forth food is one concept. But as the *gemara* makes clear, this analogy does not hold: in the other cases, one is ascribing a single action to God, with the second element being an effect or instrument of the first. Here, one is ascribing two distinct actions to God — saving Israel and building Jerusalem — making them genuinely two themes that should not be bundled.

The *gemara* closes this discussion with the principle: *lefi she-ein osin mitzvos chavilos chavilos* — one does not bundle *mitzvos* together.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet offers a practical resolution. The *chatimah* should mirror the opening theme. If one opened with *racheim al amcha Yisrael* — emphasizing the salvation of the people — one closes with *moshia Yisrael*. If one opened with *racheim al Yerushalayim* — emphasizing the city — one closes with *boneh Yerushalayim*. This is a notable position: it allows for the possibility that the entire *bracha*, from opening to closing, focuses not on Jerusalem but solely on the redemption of Israel, without any mention of *binyan Yerushalayim* in the *chatimah*. Given the *gemara*'s insistence that the land's goodness is bound up with the presence of the *Beit Ha-Mikdash*, this is a striking leniency.

### Rav Nachman

Rav Nachman disagrees. Even if one opened with *racheim al Yisrael* — even when the opening theme is the people's salvation — one must still close with *boneh Yerushalayim*. This is our *nusach*. The basis is the verse: *boneh Yerushalayim Hashem nidchei Yisrael yekaneis* — God builds Jerusalem and gathers in the dispersed of Israel.

### Geulah Themes

The *gemara* interprets this verse to mean: *eimatai boneh Yerushalayim Hashem? Bizman she-nidchei Yisrael yekaneis* — when does God build Jerusalem? When He gathers in the dispersed of Israel. On this reading, the building of Jerusalem is the culmination of the ingathering of exiles; one opens with the salvation of Israel and closes with *boneh Yerushalayim* because the latter is the ultimate goal to which the former leads.

Rashi, however, reads the verse differently — that *boneh Yerushalayim* comes first, and *nidchei Yisrael yekaneis* follows from it. On Rashi's reading, the restoration of Jerusalem is not the culmination but the beginning of the process of Israel's salvation. The *chatimah* of *boneh Yerushalayim* is therefore connected to the opening theme of *moshia Yisrael* because the building of Jerusalem is what initiates the *tishu'at Yisrael*. This is not an easy reading of the *gemara*'s plain sense, which suggests the ingathering precedes the building. But Rashi's approach allows the *chatimah* to be seen as *me'ein ha-ptichah* — thematically continuous with the opening — even as the precise sequence of events is understood differently.

The connection between these themes and *birkat ha-mazon*'s agricultural context is suggestive. The imagery of planting runs through the biblical theology of Israel's relationship to its land — *zera Yisrael* — and the verb *matzmiach* appears in *shemoneh esrei* in *matzmiach keren yeshuah* regarding *malchut beit David*, and also in *mechalkel chayim be-chesed mechayyeh meitim matzmiach yeshuah*, where it appears without explicit reference to David. These are themes the *Chachamim* may have been building upon, though the *gemara* does not make the connection explicit.

The double *chatimah* of *Tisha B'Av* — *menachem Tziyon u-voneh Yerushalayim* — raises the question of *ein chotmin b'shtayim* in a different context. The answer, along the lines of what the *gemara* offers here, would be that *menachem Tziyon* is accomplished *through* the *boneh Yerushalayim*, rendering them sufficiently connected to be treated as one theme. More broadly, the *gemara* here treats the requirement that the *chatimah* mirror the *ptichah* with some flexibility — the connection can be one of thematic continuation rather than verbal identity. The stronger general principle tends to be that the *chatimah* should mirror the line immediately preceding it, which is why the insertions of *ya'aleh v'yavo* and *retzei* are placed just before the final line *u-veneh Yerushalayim ir ha-kodesh bimherah ve-yameinu*, so that the *bracha* closes naturally into *boneh Yerushalayim*.

---

## Rav Chisda Incident

### Missing Elements

The *gemara* now relates a significant incident. Rav Zeira said to Rav Chisda: come and teach us some *mishnayot*. Rav Chisda replied: *birchat mezona lo gamrina* — I don't even know *benching*, and you want me to teach you *mishnayot*? Rav Zeira pressed: what do you mean? Rav Chisda explained that he had once eaten at the house of the *Reish Galuta*, had led *birkat ha-mazon*, and Rav Sheshet raised himself against him like a serpent poised to strike — a dramatic expression of fury and censure. The reason: Rav Chisda had omitted *brit*, *Torah*, and *malchus* from the *benching*. Here *malchus* refers not to *melech ha-olam* but to *malchus beit David*, which we established earlier must be mentioned in *boneh Yerushalayim*. Together, *brit*, *Torah*, and *malchus beit David* are required elements of the third blessing, and Rav Chisda had not mentioned any of them.

### Rav Chananel

Rav Chisda explained that he had acted in accordance with the position of Rav Chananel citing Rav: *lo amar brit Torah u-malchut yatza* — if one did not say *brit*, *Torah*, or *malchus*, one has nevertheless fulfilled the obligation.

### Universal Application

The reasoning offered is striking: *brit* does not apply to women, who are not obligated in *brit milah*; *Torah* and *malchus* do not apply to women and slaves, who are not obligated in *talmud Torah* in the classical formulation, and for whom the laws of kingship do not apply in the same way. Since these elements are not universally applicable to all those obligated in *birkat ha-mazon*, they cannot be considered indispensable to the text. The implication is that a required component of a *bracha* must be one that is meaningful and applicable to every person obligated in that *bracha*.

One of the *Rishonim* — understood to be the Rashba — goes further and says that Rav Chisda intentionally adopted a text that was universal, applicable to all, rather than reciting a formula that excluded women and slaves. On this reading, it is not merely that he ruled these elements were not *me'akev*, but that he positively sought a *nusach* that would serve all people equally. This explains why Rav Chisda did not simply say the fuller text as a preferred option even if its omission is not fatal — because he wanted his *benching* to be universally valid in form, not only in effect.

It is worth noting that our standard text says *al brisecha she-chasamta bi-vsareinu*, a formulation that explicitly references *brit milah*. Some manuscripts — including versions noted in the *Gra*'s textual tradition — do not include the words *she-chasamta bi-vsareinu*, reading only *al brisecha*, which would allow women to be included in the general covenant with God without the specific reference to circumcision. The *gemara* itself, while it begins with *brit* in a general sense, quickly connects it to *yud-gimel britot* at the top of the *daf*, referring to *brit milah*, and states explicitly that the requirement does not apply to women — *einam b'nashim* — which strongly implies that the text containing *she-chasamta bi-vsareinu* was at least understood to refer to *brit milah*. Whether the *exact* text included that phrase is a separate question the *gemara* does not resolve.

This discussion connects to the broader debate raised approximately a month earlier in the *masechta* about the level of women's obligation in *birkat ha-mazon* — whether they are obligated *d'Oraisa* or only *d'Rabbanan*. Rashi there points to this very *gemara*, noting that the exclusion of women from *brit milah* and from receiving a portion in the land may bear on the question of their biblical obligation. The *gemara* never spells this out definitively, but the connections are there in the background. The question of *gerim* is also raised — *Tosafot* discusses whether converts, who similarly lack ancestral portions in the land, stand in a different position.

When it comes to the precise legal effect of omitting these elements, it is also worth noting that even when the *gemara* says *lo yatza*, this sometimes functions rhetorically rather than as a definitive ruling of non-fulfillment, and even a literal ruling of *lo yatza* may mean only *d'Rabbanan* and not *d'Oraisa*.

### Challenge

Rav Zeira responded with a pointed challenge: *v'at shavkat kol hanei tannai v'amorai v'pashkat k'Rav* — you abandoned all the *tannaim* and *amoraim* who required these elements, in order to follow the single opinion of Rav? This is precisely what had enraged Rav Sheshet: Rav Chisda had adopted a minority position against a broad consensus of earlier authorities who held that these elements were required and that their omission rendered the *benching* invalid.

---

## Double Malchus

### Malchus Rule

The *gemara* now returns to the question of *malchus* in *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* — here *malchus* in the sense of *melech ha-olam* — consistent with the earlier conclusion that *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* is an independent *bracha* and therefore requires *Elokeinu melech ha-olam*. The *gemara* invokes the principle already stated by Rabbi Yochanan: *kol bracha she-ein bah malchus lo shema bracha* — any *bracha* without *malchus* is not properly a *bracha*. But this principle was already stated once by Rabbi Yochanan. What then is the novel teaching here?

### Double Malchus Theory

Rav Zeira proposes: *lomar she-tzricha shtei malchuyot* — to say that *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* requires two expressions of *malchus*. One for itself — *chada didei* — and one in place of *boneh Yerushalayim* — *chada d'Vanei Yerushalayim* — since *boneh Yerushalayim* closes with *baruch atah Hashem boneh Yerushalayim* or *be-rachamav boneh Yerushalayim*, without *melech ha-olam*. Since that *malchus* was missing in *boneh Yerushalayim*, it is compensated for in *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*, which contains *ha-melech ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv la-kol*. This is reminiscent of Tuesday in the creation narrative receiving two *ki tov* because Monday had none.

### Objection

An objection is raised: if we are compensating for a missing *malchus*, should we not also compensate for *birkat ha-aretz*, which similarly omits *melech ha-olam*? That would require three expressions of *malchus* in *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* — one for itself, one for *boneh Yerushalayim*, and one for *birkat ha-aretz*.

### Response

The *gemara* responds: *birkat ha-aretz* requires no such compensation because *mishum d'havya leh bracha semucha l'chavertah* — it is a *bracha samuch l'chavertah*, attached to the opening *bracha* which carried *malchus*. It was never independently required to have its own *malchus*, so there is nothing to compensate for. Extending the logic: *boneh Yerushalayim* is also *samuch l'chavertah*, and by the same reasoning should require no compensation either. The *gemara* accepts this: *hu ha-din d'afilu Bonei Yerushalayim nami lo ba'ei* — fine, even *boneh Yerushalayim* did not strictly require *malchus*.

### Rav Papa

Rav Papa then reframes the entire matter. The two expressions of *malchus* in *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* are not a compensation for missing *malchus* in earlier *brachot*. Rather, *tzricha shtei malchuyot l'var mididei* — in addition to the *malchus* for itself, there are two more within the *bracha*. The text of *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* already contains *ha-melech ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv la-kol*, and additionally *el avinu malkenu* — so we have *melech* for *boneh Yerushalayim* and *malkeinu* for *birkat ha-aretz*, paying back the missing *malchus* of both earlier *brachot* simultaneously. This is a structurally elegant resolution that ties all four *brachot* together.

---

## Forgotten Insertions

### Shabbat Insertion

Rav Zeira was sitting behind Rav Giddel, who was sitting before Rav Huna. Rav Giddel was relaying teachings from Rav Huna, serving as an intermediary. He taught: if one forgot to mention *Shabbat* in *boneh Yerushalayim*, one recites a separate *bracha*: *baruch atah Hashem Elokeinu melech ha-olam asher natan shabbasos li-mnucha l'amo Yisrael b'ahava l'os u-le-vrit, baruch atah Hashem mekadesh ha-Shabbat*. This *bracha* stands alone with its own *Elokeinu melech ha-olam* because it is not said *samuch* to the rest of the *benching*; it is being inserted after the fact and must therefore stand independently. Note that the *chatimah* — *mekadesh ha-Shabbat* — does not repeat *Elokeinu melech ha-olam*, consistent with the rule that a closing formula need not do so. When Rav Zeira asked who had said this, Rav Giddel replied: Rav. This *bracha* is printed in some *siddurim* and benchers, though unfortunately many benchers omit it.

### Yom Tov Insertion

Rav Giddel continued: if one forgot *Yom Tov*, one recites: *baruch atah Hashem Elokeinu melech ha-olam asher natan yamim tovim l'amo Yisrael le-simcha u-le-zikaron, baruch atah Hashem mekadesh Yisrael ve-ha-zmanim*. Again said in the name of Rav. The *nusach* in our benchers differs slightly: it mentions the specific *Yom Tov* by name, says *le-sason u-le-simcha* rather than *le-simcha u-le-zikaron*, and does not include *zikaron*. These are textual variants between our received *nusach* and the *gemara*'s formulation.

### Rosh Chodesh Insertion

Rav Giddel then taught: if one forgot *Rosh Chodesh*, one says *baruch she-natan rashei chodashim l'amo Yisrael le-zikaron*. Here, unlike *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, the formula has no *simcha* theme — only *zikaron*. Rav Zeira adds that he was uncertain on several points: whether the *bracha* included *simcha*, whether it included a *chatimah* at all — since a short *bracha* does not necessarily require a closing formula, just as *al pri ha-etz* and *borei nefashot* have no *chatimah* — and whether Rav Giddel said this in his own name or in the name of Rav. The *nusach* we have for *Rosh Chodesh* is: *baruch atah Hashem Elokeinu melech ha-olam asher natan rashei chodashim l'amo Yisrael le-zikaron* — no *chatimah*, no *simcha* — which happens to correspond exactly to what was said, without resolution of the uncertainties.

---

## Chozer L'Rosh

### Nachman's Ruling

Giddel bar Minyumi was present before Rav Nachman when Rav Nachman himself forgot — apparently omitting *ya'aleh v'yavo* or *retzei* — and returned to the very beginning of *benching*, *hadar le-reisha*. When asked why, Rav Nachman cited a ruling: *ta'ah chozer le-rosh* — if one erred, one returns to the beginning. This was said in the name of Rav — the same Rav in whose name the special *bracha* was just taught. An apparent contradiction.

### Before HaTov VeHaMeitiv

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction with a qualification attributed to Minyumi bar Chalifa in the name of Rav: *lo shanu ela she-lo patach b'ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* — the ruling to say the special *bracha* applies only if one has not yet begun *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*. *Aval patach b'ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv, chozer le-rosh* — if one has already begun *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*, one must return to the beginning of *benching*.

This is because *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* marks the end of the core *benching*. Once one has crossed into that *bracha*, one has left the essential framework of *birkat ha-mazon*. The insertion of *retzei* or *ya'aleh v'yavo* belongs within *boneh Yerushalayim*; once one has moved definitively beyond it, there is no way to retroactively correct the omission without repeating the whole. The question of what constitutes "beginning" *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv* is significant: according to the *Acharonim*, saying *ha'el avinu* — the first substantive words of that *bracha* — crosses the threshold. If one has said only *baruch atah Hashem Elokeinu melech ha-olam*, one may pivot and end with *asher natan shabbasos li-mnucha* rather than continuing into *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*.

### When to Repeat

The analogy to *shemoneh esrei* is instructive. If one forgets *mashiv ha-ruach u-morid ha-geshem* or recites it incorrectly, one does not return only to that *bracha* but to the very beginning of *shemoneh esrei*. The first three *brachot* function as a unified structure; an error within that unit requires restarting the whole. Similarly in *benching*, the three core *brachot* are a unit; if the required insertion in *boneh Yerushalayim* was omitted and one has already moved past that structure, the entire unit must be repeated. Note that this is an entirely rabbinic requirement — biblically, the precise *nusach* and the obligation to mention special days are rabbinic; the biblical requirement is satisfied by any expression of gratitude for food. The rabbinic structure, however, is what governs most of our practical ritual life.

---

## Rosh Chodesh Rule

### Shmuel's Teaching

The *gemara* cites a ruling of Shmuel, transmitted through a chain of Rav Nachman: if one forgot *Rosh Chodesh* in *tefillah* — in *shemoneh esrei* — one must repeat. But if one forgot it in *birkat ha-mazon*, one does not repeat.

### Reasoning

When Rav Amram was asked by Rav Avin for the reason behind this distinction, he replied that he too had been puzzled and had asked Rav Nachman, who told him that he had not heard the reason from Shmuel himself. They therefore worked it out independently: *tefillah de-chova hi* — prayer is an obligation; one is required to *daven* today regardless. The proper *nusach* for today includes the *Rosh Chodesh* insertion; if one omitted it, one has not fulfilled today's obligatory prayer and must repeat. *Birkat mezona de'i ba'ei achil, i ba'ei lo achil* — *birkat ha-mazon*, by contrast, arises only when one eats; no one was obligated to eat today specifically. Since the meal itself was optional, the *benching* associated with it is not *chova* in the same way, and the omission of *Rosh Chodesh* does not require repetition.

### Distinction

The *gemara* then challenges: by that logic, on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, where one is obligated to have a *seudah*, the *benching* should function like *tefillah* and require repetition if the *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* theme was omitted. The answer is yes — and this is precisely the ruling of Rav: *ta'ah chozer le-rosh*, one returns to the beginning, qualified only by the caveat that one has not yet begun *ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv*. The two positions attributed to Rav are therefore not contradictory: the special *bracha* suffices on days where there is no *chiyuv seudah*; on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, where the meal is obligatory, repeating the *benching* is required when the special insertion was forgotten.

This also explains why *al ha-nissim* on *Purim* and *Chanukah* is not *me'akev*. On *Purim* there is a *mishteh*, but the question of whether it constitutes a fully obligatory *seudah* involving bread is debated, and in any case the obligation is not of the same character. On *Chanukah* there is no *chiyuv seudah* at all. Since neither day obligates a meal in the same way *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* do, the *benching* for those days does not carry the same *chiyuv*, and the omission of *al ha-nissim* does not require repetition.

The question arises about *Shabbat Rosh Chodesh*: one is obligated to eat on *Shabbat*, and if one forgot *Rosh Chodesh* in *benching* on *Shabbat Rosh Chodesh*, must one go back? The *halacha* is that one does not — which is somewhat surprising given that the same reasoning which would not apply to *Rosh Chodesh* alone should perhaps not change simply because it coincides with *Shabbat*. This distinction between *Rosh Chodesh* falling on *Shabbat* and the parallel question in *shemoneh esrei* warrants further analysis — *tzarich iyun*.

---

## Minimum Amount

### Textual Basis

The *gemara* returns to the question of how much one must eat to be obligated in *zimmun* and *birkat ha-mazon*. The underlying debate turns on how to read the verse *v'achalta v'savata u-verachta* — you shall eat and be satisfied and bless. Rabbi Meir reads *v'achalta* as referring to eating and *v'savata* as referring to drinking — not full satiation but an accompaniment to eating that completes the act. On this reading, any significant act of eating triggers the obligation. Rabbi Yehuda reads *v'achalta v'savata* together as describing an eating that itself produces satiation — *achila she-yesh ba savia* — an eating that is inherently filling.

### Meir vs Yehuda

From this, in the context of the *mishnah* here, Rabbi Meir holds that a *kezayit* — an olive's volume — is sufficient for *birkat ha-mazon* and to join a *zimmun*, while Rabbi Yehuda requires a *kebeitzah* — an egg's volume. These measurements stand in an approximately two-to-three ratio, with a *kezayit* at roughly three and a half fluid ounces and a *kebeitzah* at six to ten ounces.

### Parallel Cases

However, the *gemara* notes that in the *mishnah* in *Pesachim* — which discusses when one must return to Jerusalem to burn *basar kodesh* that was inadvertently taken outside the city, and when one may burn it where one stands — the positions appear reversed. Rabbi Meir there says one returns for a *kebeitzah*, and Rabbi Yehuda says one returns for a *kezayit*. This reversal creates an apparent contradiction with the positions in our *mishnah*.

Rabbi Yochanan resolves it simply: *mukhlefet ha-shitah* — the names are transposed; simply switch them. Abaye rejects this approach. He says: *le'olam lo teipoch* — do not reverse them. The positions are internally consistent; the two debates are simply about different things.

### Meir's Reasoning

In the context of *birkat ha-mazon* and *zimmun*, the *amoraim* explain that the dispute turns on the biblical text. Rabbi Meir holds *v'achalta zo achila, v'savata zo shtiya* — the verse addresses eating accompanied by drinking, and an act of eating is measured at a *kezayit*, the standard *shiur* for eating. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the verse requires an eating that produces satiation, which is the measure of a *kebeitzah*.

In the context of the *Pesachim* case — when to return for meat or *chametz* — the dispute is not about biblical texts but about analogy. Rabbi Meir holds *chazarato k'tumato* — returning for the meat is analogous to the *shiur* for *tumah*, and *tumah* from food requires a *kebeitzah*. Therefore one returns for a *kebeitzah*.

### Yehuda's Reasoning

Rabbi Yehuda holds *chazarato k'issuro* — returning is analogous to the *issur* of eating invalid *kodshim*, and the *shiur* for that *issur* is a *kezayit*. Therefore one returns for a *kezayit*. The cases of *chametz* and *kodshim* track together under one or the other model. It may be that each *tanna* took a different case as the paradigm — one anchoring the analysis in *tumah*, the other in *issur* — and then applied it to both.

It should be noted that the framing of this *gemara* is striking: it sounds as though the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda over *kezayit* and *kebeitzah* in *birkat ha-mazon* may be a biblical-level dispute. Other *gemarot* have suggested that the biblical obligation requires actual satiation, with *kezayit* and *kebeitzah* being rabbinic *shiurim*. Here, however, the *gemara* derives these measures directly from *v'achalta v'savata*, suggesting that even a *kezayit* or *kebeitzah* could create a biblical obligation. On Rabbi Meir's reading, the emphasis is on the *act* of eating rather than on being filled — any eating of a *kezayit* is halakhically significant. On Rabbi Yehuda's reading, the requirement is for an eating that has the *potential* to be filling — even if it did not actually satiate in this instance, the volume of a *kebeitzah* is inherently the kind of eating that could.

---

## Zimmun Text

### Three People

The *mishnah* now sets out the text of *zimmun* — the formal invitation to join in *birkat ha-mazon* — according to the number of participants. With three people, the leader says *nevarech she-achalnu mishelo* — let us bless the One from Whose food we have eaten. If the leader himself is one of the three, he says *nevarech*, including himself in the group. If there are three others and he is an additional participant, he may say *barchu* — bless — calling upon the group without needing to include himself.

### Ten People

With ten people, *Elokeinu* is added: *nevarech Elokeinu she-achalnu mishelo*. The addition of God's name reflects the heightened sanctity of a larger assembly. The same distinction between *nevarech* and *barchu* applies when the leader is or is not counted among the ten.

### Hundred People

At a hundred, *Hashem* is added: *nevarech Hashem Elokeinu she-achalnu mishelo*. The divine name is explicitly invoked as the assembly grows.

### Thousand People

At a thousand, one says *nevarech l'Hashem Elokeinu Elokei Yisrael* — God of Israel is added, reflecting the sense that so large a gathering of Israel represents the people as a whole in its collective identity.

### Ten Thousand

At ten thousand, the full formula is: *nevarech l'Hashem Elokeinu Elokei Yisrael Elokei Tzevaot Yoshev Ha-Keruvim al ha-mazon she-achalanu mishelo* — God of Hosts Who dwells upon the cherubim, for the food we ate from His table. The addition of *yoshev ha-keruvim* — a phrase that appears earlier in the *masechta* in the context of the *Kohen Gadol*'s proclamation in the *Beit Ha-Mikdash* — brings the language of the inner sanctum into the *zimmun* of a vast multitude, as if the *Shechinah* is fully present in so great a gathering of Israel. The *mishnah* notes that *echad asara v'echad asara ribo* — the text is the same whether it is ten or ten myriads, which we will see is the subject of dispute.

### Response Formula

Whatever formula the leader uses, the assembled respond in kind, mirroring the exact text but replacing *nevarech* with *baruch*: if the leader says *nevarech Elokeinu*, they answer *baruch Elokeinu*; if he says *nevarech Hashem Elokeinu Elokei Yisrael Elokei Tzevaot Yoshev Ha-Keruvim al ha-mazon she-achalanu mishelo*, they respond with the full parallel text, beginning *baruch Hashem Elokeinu* and so forth through to the end.

---

## Yose vs Akiva

### Yose Position

Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds that the text of *zimmun* varies according to the size of the assembly — *lefi rov ha-kahal hen mivarchin* — deriving this from the verse *bi-mkhelot barchu Elohim mi-mekor Yisrael*: the congregational praise of God scales with the crowd. The expansive formulas of the *mishnah* — adding *Elokeinu*, then *Hashem*, then *Elokei Yisrael*, then *Elokei Tzevaot Yoshev Ha-Keruvim* — all reflect the position of Rabbi Yose HaGlili.

### Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. Just as in *shul* the text does not change based on whether ten or ten thousand are present — one simply says *barchu et Hashem* — so too in *zimmun*, once the threshold is reached, the text remains constant regardless of the numbers. This is a principled rejection of the graduated formula; the sanctity of the assembly does not escalate indefinitely through textual additions.

### Identification

The *gemara* identifies these as the same positions debated earlier in the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* as we have it contains two strands: one set of teachings giving different formulas for different crowd sizes, and one stating that the formula is the same regardless. These are now identified as representing, respectively, the position of Rabbi Yose HaGlili and the position of Rabbi Akiva.

### Ishmael Clarification

Rabbi Ishmael adds a clarification on the *shul* model that Rabbi Akiva invokes: the correct formula in synagogue is not merely *barchu et Hashem* but *barchu et Hashem ha-mivorach* — the full formula we recite today when called to the Torah and at *barchu* in *shacharit* and *maariv*. This is the precise *nusach* of the *beit ha-knesset*, and Rabbi Akiva's analogy to synagogue practice therefore implies that fixed formula as the standard.

---

---

# Berakhot 50

## Nevarech vs. Barchu

### Shmuel's Principle

Today's daf begins at the very bottom of 49b, where the *Gemara* takes up the discussion that followed the *Mishnah*'s treatment of *zimun*. The *Mishnah* had established the different texts for *zimun* — the distinction between *nevarech* and *barchu*, between groups of three, ten, one hundred, and so on — with increasing appellations of God for larger assemblages. That, as we will see, was the position of Rabbi Yose HaGelili, while Rabbi Akiva held that once ten is reached, the text remains constant regardless of size.

The *Gemara* opens with a statement from *Shmuel*: *le'olam al yotzi adam atzmo min ha-klal* — a person should never exclude himself from the community. This is a striking first principle, with implications well beyond the laws of *zimun*. The *Mishnah*, however, seems to present a difficulty: *bishlosha vehu omer barchu* — when three people eat together, the leader says *barchu*, which is addressed to the others and explicitly excludes the speaker. Does this not contradict *Shmuel's* principle?

### Gemara's Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves the tension by reinterpreting the *Mishnah*: *af barchu* — the *Mishnah* means that even *barchu* is acceptable, but it is not the ideal formulation. *Umikol makom nevarech adif* — nevertheless, *nevarech* is better, because it includes the speaker in the blessing.

The *Gemara* then adduces support from a *braita* cited in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava, quoting Rav Yannai: if one has six people, they may divide into two groups of three. This is permitted up until the threshold of ten, at which point division is no longer allowed. Now, the *Gemara* reasons: *iye amart nevarech adif* — if *nevarech* is at least as good as *barchu*, then dividing six into two groups of three makes sense, since neither group loses anything by moving from a potential *barchu* to a *nevarech*. But if *barchu* were actually superior, why would you divide and lose the opportunity to say *barchu*? The fact that division is permitted therefore demonstrates that *nevarech* is at least equivalent. *Shema mina nevarech adif*.

It is worth noting that the word *adif* here does not necessarily mean "better" in an absolute sense. *Tosafot* reads *adif* as meaning "equivalent," while *Rashi* goes further: once you establish equivalence, and you add *Shmuel's* principle that one should not separate oneself from the community, it follows that *nevarech* is genuinely preferable. The *Gemara*'s proof from the permissibility of dividing six into two groups establishes at minimum that *nevarech* is no worse — and *Shmuel's* principle then tips the balance in its favor.

### Braita Support

The *Gemara* then cites a *braita* that states directly: *bein she'amar barchu bein she'amar nevarech, ein tofsin oto al kach* — whether one said *barchu* or *nevarech*, one does not "jump on him" for it, meaning neither formulation is grounds for correction. This language of equivalence seems to somewhat soften the earlier suggestion that *nevarech* is superior, though it certainly confirms that *nevarech* is not inferior.

The *braita* then adds: *vehanidkanim tofsin oto al kach* — the nitpickers do jump on him. The commentary on the side records an interesting philological note: the variant reading *ha-nikranim*, explained via an Arabic cognate as a term for someone who pecks and picks at minor details, like a rooster scratching through a garbage heap. The word, in other words, is simply a colorful term for a nitpicker. According to this reading, the *braita* is actually trivializing any preference between *barchu* and *nevarech* — it is only the nitpickers who make something of it. At the very least, *nevarech* is certainly not inferior, and in light of *Shmuel's* principle, it is the preferred formulation.

It is worth noting in passing that the question of why the *Shulchan Aruch* uses *barchu* in certain contexts, and why the familiar Aramaic formulation *hav lan nivareich* is used in other settings, deserves further investigation — the *Gemara* here does not address those distinctions directly.

---

## Talmidei Chachamim Tests

### Uvetuvo Debate

The *Gemara* continues by citing the *Tosefta*: *umibirkasav shel adam nikkarim talmid chacham hu im lav* — from the way a person recites blessings, one can tell whether he is a *talmid chacham* or not. This was an era before fixed *siddurim*, when the texts of *brachot* were not yet uniformly standardized, and meaningful variation existed. The *Gemara* then offers a series of examples that distinguish learned from unlearned formulations.

The first example: if one says *uvetuvo chayinu* — "and through His goodness we have lived" — that is the formulation of a *talmid chacham*. If one says *umituvo chayinu* — "from some of His goodness we have lived" — that is the formulation of a *bur*, an ignoramus. The difference lies in the preposition: *uvetuvo* expresses that one's entire life flows from God's goodness without qualification, while *umituvo* implies that one has received only a portion of God's beneficence, suggesting an incomplete or insufficiently expansive gratitude.

The *Gemara* raises a challenge from Abbaye to Rav Dimi: the verse states *umibirchasecha yevoreich beis avdecha le'olam* — "and from Your blessing let the house of Your servant be blessed forever." That verse uses the partitive *mi-*, implying not all but some of God's blessing. The *Gemara* responds: *beshe'eila shani* — in the context of a request, the phrasing is different. When petitioning God, one approaches in humility and asks for what one might receive. *Rashi* frames this beautifully: one should ask *k'ani ha'omeid al ha-pesach*, like a poor person standing at the door, who does not raise his head and make grandiose demands.

But even in the context of petition, the *Gemara* cites the verse *harcheiv picha va'amaleihu* — "open your mouth wide and I will fill it" — which suggests one should request maximally. The *Gemara* resolves this by saying that expansive requests are appropriate for Torah: *hahu b'divrei Torah kesiv*. When asking for Torah one may ask without limit, but when requesting material blessing, the proper posture is that of humble supplication. The principle that emerges is that in gratitude one should express the fullness of divine beneficence — *uvetuvo* — while in petition one may be more restrained, though even there the *Gemara* directs us toward ambitious requests in the spiritual domain.

One might observe a tension running through this entire passage: what begins as a guide to precise liturgical formulation quickly becomes a framework for publicly categorizing people as learned or ignorant. It is worth pausing on this. The *Gemara* could have simply stated the correct formulation and moved on. The choice to frame precision as a test of a person's worth raises a genuine question about the purpose of liturgical exactitude — whether it is ultimately about the proper orientation of the heart toward God, or whether it has become a social sorting mechanism. That tension, already present in the *Tosefta* that the *Gemara* is quoting, is something that remains worth sitting with.

### Chayinu vs. Chayim

A second example of the learned-versus-ignorant test: *uvetuvo chayinu* — "we live through His goodness" — is the formulation of a *talmid chacham*, while *uvetuvo chayim* — "there is life through His goodness" — marks a *bur*. The difference, as *Rashi* explains, is that *chayinu* is personal and inclusive — we ourselves live by God's goodness — whereas *chayim* is an abstract theological statement about the existence of life in general. Personal, embodied gratitude is considered more sophisticated than a detached doctrinal claim.

A dissenting position is attributed to one *Nahvilai*, or according to some textual variants, transmitted differently, who held the reverse: *chayim* is actually preferable because it encompasses all creatures, not just Jews or humans. By saying *chayim* rather than *chayinu*, one expresses a more universal divine beneficence. However, the *Gemara* rules: *ve-leit hilchata ke-Nahvilai* — we do not rule like *Nahvilai*. The formulation *chayinu* is the correct one.

### She'achalnu Mishelo

Rabbi Yochanan offers a third test: *nevarech she'achalnu mishelo* — "let us bless the One from whose [food] we have eaten" — is the formulation of a *talmid chacham*. *L'mi she'achalnu mishelo* — "to the One from whom we have eaten" — is the formulation of a *bur*.

The distinction is subtle. *Rashi* explains that the phrase *l'mi she'achalnu* — "to the one from whom we ate" — could be heard as referring to the *ba'al habayit*, the host who provided the meal, rather than to God. The ambiguity arises because *l'mi* suggests singling out a particular individual among others: "that person from whom we ate" — which naturally evokes the host rather than God. By contrast, *she'achalnu mishelo* without the *l'mi* directs the blessing toward God without that ambiguity.

Rav Acha the son of Rava challenges this from Rabbi Yochanan himself, who elsewhere uses the phrase *l'mi she'asah la'avoteinu v'lanu et kol ha-nissim ha'eleh* — "to the One Who performed all these miracles for our ancestors and for us." Does that not use *l'mi* without confusion? The *Gemara* answers: *hatam mochcha milta* — there it is obvious, because *man avid nissi, Kudsha Brich Hu* — who performs miracles? Only God. When the context makes the referent unambiguous, *l'mi* poses no problem. But in the context of eating, where a host is present, the phrase *l'mi she'achalnu* might indeed be misread as gratitude to the person who fed you rather than to God. The contrast between *nevarech she'achalnu mishelo* and *l'mi she'achalnu mishelo* thus turns on whether the blessing's target is clear.

### Al HaMazon Question

A fourth example: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that *baruch she'achalnu mishelo* — "blessed is the One from whose [food] we have eaten" — is the formulation of a *talmid chacham*, while *baruch al ha-mazon she'achalnu mishelo* — "blessed for the food from which we ate" — marks a *bur*. The insertion of *al ha-mazon* limits and focuses the blessing: you are blessing for the food specifically, rather than blessing God in an unlimited sense. When you say simply *baruch she'achalnu mishelo*, your gratitude for the food becomes the vehicle for blessing God comprehensively. When you say *al ha-mazon*, you narrow your blessing to a transaction — God gave food, I thank for the food.

*Tosafot* offers a related reading: *d'mashma d'mevarech l'ba'al habayit hama'achilo* — it sounds as though you are blessing the host who fed you. The reasoning is that of God, *d'ilu Rachmana lav ha-mazon mazkir* — God is not defined by the food; *belo mazon yesh harbe l'varcho*, there is much to bless God for apart from food. When you emphasize *al ha-mazon*, you are implicitly saying the sole reason you are blessing is the food — which fits the *ba'al habayit* perfectly but is a diminished way to approach God.

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua then refines the problem: the issue with *al ha-mazon* arises specifically when there are only three and God's name is not mentioned, so it is ambiguous whether you are addressing God or the host. But when ten are present and one says *nevarech Elokeinu*, the inclusion of *Elokeinu* removes all ambiguity — *mochach milta*, it is obvious who is being addressed. In that case, *al ha-mazon* is acceptable because the context has already clarified the referent. This is actually borne out by our *Mishnah* itself, which includes the phrase *al ha-mazon she'achalnu* only after the full divine address — *Baruch Hashem Elokei Yisrael Elokei Tzvaot yoshev ha-keruvim*.

One voice in the discussion observes that rather than declaring certain formulations grounds for being called a *bur*, the *Gemara* might simply have stated the correct text. The fact that each "incorrect" formulation attracts a dissenting voice — someone arguing that it is in fact legitimate or even superior — does somewhat soften the sting. Still, the framework of *talmid chacham* versus *bur* is a striking way to communicate liturgical preference, and it is worth acknowledging the tension between cultivating precision in blessing and keeping the orientation of prayer focused on God rather than on the speaker's erudition.

It is also of interest that this emphasis on precision in liturgical language appears in a *Tosefta*, which is an *Eretz Yisrael* source. The broader historical pattern tends toward greater fluidity around liturgical text in *Eretz Yisrael* and greater rigidity in *Bavel* — and yet here it is the *Tosefta* itself that insists on precision and categorizes deviations. The comparison also arises naturally: is the threshold of ten for *zimun* analogous to a *davar shebikdusha*? The *Gemara* does not explicitly invoke that concept here, but comparisons to the *minyan* threshold appear nearby in the sugya, and several *Rishonim* do understand the ten for *zimun* along those lines. The implications for who counts toward the ten — a question raised by, among others, Rav Soloveitchik, who reportedly held that the ten for *zimun* is not based on the *devarim shebikdusha* model and that women could in theory count toward it — will deserve further exploration when we reach the relevant sugya in *Megillah*.

---

## Mishnah Contradiction

### Self-Contradiction

The *Gemara* now turns to what it identifies as an internal contradiction within the *Mishnah* itself. The *Mishnah* opens by stating: *echad asarah ve-echad asarah ribbo* — whether ten or ten myriad, it is all the same formulation. Yet the *Mishnah* then proceeds to give distinct texts for one hundred, one thousand, and ten thousand, with different divine appellations for each threshold. The *Gemara* states plainly: *hagufa kashya* — the body of the *Mishnah* is a self-contradiction.

### Rav Yosef's Resolution

Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction: *ha Rabbi Yose HaGelili ha Rabbi Akiva* — the two parts of the *Mishnah* reflect two different positions, those of Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva respectively. The editing of the *Mishnah* has placed two originally distinct and opposing traditions side by side without fully smoothing the tension between them. This is a point worth dwelling on: the *Mishnah* as we have it was not composed from scratch by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi but rather edited from pre-existing oral texts. Those texts were in some cases conflated, and the rough edges were not always resolved. The *Gemara* itself acknowledges this, and it is one of the more candid moments of *meta*-textual awareness in the *sugya*.

### Rabbi Yose HaGelili

Rabbi Yose HaGelili's position is that the text of *zimun* changes with the size of the group: *lefi rov ha-kahal hem mevarchin* — you follow the size of the assembled congregation. His source is the verse *bimkhelot barchu Elohim* — "in gatherings, bless God" — which he reads as indicating that different types of gatherings call for different modes of blessing. The plural *mkhelot* implies that the diversity of assembly sizes is itself significant and calls for varied expression.

### Rabbi Akiva's Position

Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *mah matzinu bevet ha-kneset* — just as in the synagogue there is no distinction between a gathering of ten and a gathering of ten thousand, so too with *zimun*, once you have reached ten, the formulation does not change. Rabbi Akiva thus understands ten as a categorical threshold — once crossed, the *halachic* category is fixed regardless of how many more are added.

What does Rabbi Akiva do with Rabbi Yose HaGelili's proof-text, *bimkhelot barchu Elohim*? He applies it elsewhere: *mibaye lei le-chidetanya* — the verse is needed for the teaching that even fetuses in their mothers' wombs sang the *shirah* at the sea — *shene'emar bimkhelot barchu Elohim Hashem mimkor Yisrael*, "from the source (*mekor*) of Israel," where *mekor* evokes the womb. Rabbi Yose HaGelili can derive the fetus-song from the word *mekor* alone, leaving *mkhelot* for his own teaching about varying assembly sizes. Rabbi Akiva needs *mkhelot* for the fetus, so it is unavailable to support the graduated-text position.

Rava rules: *halacha ke-Rabbi Akiva* — the law follows Rabbi Akiva. *Rabbeinu Chananel*, quoted by *Tosafot*, codifies this accordingly: whether ten, one hundred, or ten myriad, the formulation is the same — *nevarech Eloheinu al ha-mazon she'achalnu mishelo*. He notably includes *al ha-mazon*, though as we discussed, this phrasing is only appropriate when *Eloheinu* has already been invoked. For three, one does not mention *al ha-mazon*.

The question arises whether the threshold of ten for *zimun* is analogous to a *davar shebikdusha*. Interestingly, Rabbi Akiva himself draws the comparison to the *beit knesset*, which is precisely a context of *devarim shebikdusha*. Several *Rishonim* do understand the ten for *zimun* along those lines, which also bears on the question — not resolved here — of whether women count toward that ten.

---
