## Dividing Groups

### Rav Chama's Question

The *Gemara* now relates that Ravina and Rav Chama bar Buzi came to the house of the *Reish Galuta*. Rav Chama began going around trying to assemble exactly one hundred people, so that the *mezamen* could say *nevarech Hashem Elokeinu*. Ravina stopped him: *lo tzrichet* — you need not bother. *Hachi amar Rava, halacha ke-Rabbi Akiva* — Rava has ruled that the law follows Rabbi Akiva, so there is no significance to the difference between ninety-nine and one hundred. The formulation does not change.

### Groups of Three

Rava himself relates: when eating bread at the house of the *Reish Galuta*, where the feasts were very large and very noisy, the practice was to divide into small groups of three and bench privately — *mevarchinan gimmel gimmel*. The *Gemara* asks: why not divide into groups of ten so that one could include *Elokeinu*? Rava explains: *shama Reish Galuta ve-ikpid* — the *Reish Galuta* would be offended if he saw groups of ten forming to leave, as it would signal publicly that people were departing. Groups of three are discreet; a group of ten making its own *zimun* would draw attention. The smaller groupings allowed people to fulfill their obligation without causing offense.

### Hearing Requirement

The *Gemara* then asks: why not simply wait and be included in the *Reish Galuta's* own *zimun*? The answer: *aidi d'avshu kulei alma lo sham'ei* — because the noise was so great that no one could actually hear the *mezamen*. And to be *yotzei zimun*, one must actually hear what the *mezamen* is saying. *Zimun* is not retroactive and cannot be fulfilled through mere presence; active auditory participation is required. This *halacha* has obvious practical implications — at large weddings and gatherings, the question of whether one has genuinely heard the *mezamen* is entirely live.

---

## Zimun Participation

### Benching Ahead

Rabbah Tosfa'ah teaches: if three people ate bread together and one of them went ahead and benched on his own — without waiting for the *zimun* — the other two can still use him for the *zimun*. Since he ate with them and was part of the original group, he counts toward the *zimun* even though he has already benched. However, he himself does not fulfill his obligation of *zimun* through their subsequent *zimun*: *lefi she-ein zimun le-mafrea* — *zimun* does not work retroactively. He ate with them, he can make them a *zimun*, but the *zimun* they make for him comes after he has already benched, and that does not count. He thus falls short of his own obligation.

This case, which will have occurred at any number of meals across the generations when someone inadvertently begins benching before the group has gathered, illustrates a general principle: the *chiyuv* of the individual who was part of the group remains in force, so he can still serve as part of the *zimun* for others — but his own *zimun* obligation cannot be satisfied after the fact.

---

## Two Groups One House

### Seeing Criterion

The *Mishnah* states: if two groups are eating in one house, when some of each group can see the others — *miktzatan ro'im zeh et zeh* — they combine for *zimun*. If they cannot see one another, each group makes its own *zimun* separately. The key criterion is visibility: you need not have eaten together, need not have felt yourself part of the same gathering, need not have shared food. Mere visual access to one another is sufficient to constitute a single group for purposes of *zimun*.

*Tosafot* notes that *bayit* here need not mean a single room — it can include adjacent rooms or spaces where people can see or hear one another. This has practical implications for large gatherings where people spill across multiple rooms, a balcony, or an outdoor area: the question of whether they can see one another becomes the operative *halachic* test.

### Shamash Role

The *Gemara* adds from a *braita*: *im yesh shamash beineihem, shamash mitzarfan* — if there is a waiter moving between the two groups, the *shamash* combines them. The *shamash* serves as a living link between the groups: even if the two groups cannot see one another directly, the presence of a servant moving between them creates a sufficient connection to render them a single group for *zimun*.

---

## Wine and Water

### Rabbi Eliezer's View

The *Mishnah* concludes with what at first glance appears to be a non-sequitur: a dispute about wine and water. Rabbi Eliezer holds: *ein mevarichin al ha-yayin ad she-yiten le-tocho mayim* — one does not recite *borei pri hagafen* over wine until water has been mixed into it. The wine of antiquity was extremely potent and was routinely diluted — the practice was called *mizigah* — and in its undiluted state it was not considered drinkable wine in the normal sense.

### Rabbis' View

The Rabbis disagree: *bein kach u-vein kach, mevarichin alav borei pri hagafen* — whether or not water has been added, one recites *borei pri hagafen*. According to the Rabbis, undiluted wine retains the status of wine for purposes of blessing regardless of the *mizigah*.

The placement of this *halacha* at the end of the chapter on *zimun* is noted as somewhat puzzling. The likely connection is that *zimun* at such meals was often performed over a cup of wine, and so the question of what blessing one recites over that cup is a natural appendage — though the *Mishnah* does not make the connection explicit.

---

## Zimun Participation (II)

### Three From Three Groups

The *Gemara* now returns to the topic of *zimun* with a case that at first appears paradoxical. *Rav Huna* teaches: *shlosha she-ba'u mi-shalosh chavurot einam resha'in lachalek* — three people who came from three different groups may not separate from one another. The scenario is as follows: each person was eating with his own group. Each then left — perhaps running out to the marketplace — while his original group remained. Now these three individuals from three separate groups find themselves together. Because each of them was individually obligated in *zimun* as part of his original group, they can together constitute a new *zimun*. The obligation attaches to the individual who was part of a *zimun*-obligated group, and three such individuals can now combine to fulfill that obligation together.

*Rav Chisda* adds a condition: *ve-hu she-ba'u mi-shalosh chavurot shel shlosha bnei adam* — this applies only when each person came from a group of at least three, meaning a group that was itself obligated in *zimun*. Each individual must have been part of a proper *zimun*-obligated group; only then can the three individuals regroup and make their own *zimun*.

This case raises a genuine conceptual question about *zimun*: the entire institution has been described as something rooted in the shared experience of eating together as a group. Yet here, three people who never ate together — each of whom ate with entirely different people — are combining to make a *zimun*. The *chiyuv* of *zimun* appears to be something that attaches to the individual who participated in a qualifying meal, rather than something that inheres exclusively in the group as such. Whether this represents a principled extension of *zimun* or a more pragmatic accommodation is a genuine question.

### Rava's Limitation

Rava then limits the case significantly: *velo amran ela de-lo akdimu hanhu ve-azminu aleihu beduchtaihu* — this applies only when the group these individuals left behind has not already made a *zimun* for them. If the group they left behind already performed *zimun* and included these absent members — meaning the absent members had already answered to the *zimun* before departing, as described earlier in the *sugya* where a person waits to answer *zimun* and then runs to the marketplace — then *parach zimun mineihu*, the *zimun* has "flown away" from them. They have already been discharged through that first *zimun* and can no longer regroup for another.

*Rashi* explains that "the group included them in the *zimun*" specifically means the absent members actively answered to the *zimun* before leaving, waiting until *ha-zan et ha-kol* was said. In that case they participated in a *zimun* and their obligation is fulfilled; they cannot count toward a second one.

Rava supports this ruling with an analogy to the laws of *tum'ah*: if a bed is split in half — whether stolen, lost, or divided between brothers or partners — it loses its *tum'ah*. *Keivan de-palguha, parach la tum'ah minah* — once divided, the *tum'ah* departs permanently, and if reassembled, the bed only receives new *tum'ah* from that point forward, not retroactively. Similarly, once a person's *zimun* obligation is discharged through the *zimun* of his original group, it is gone — *parach zimun mineihu* — and cannot be reconstituted.

*Tosafot* notes that the analogy to the bed is particularly apt because these beds were assembled from component parts and could be physically disassembled and reassembled. The parallel to an individual being taken out of one *chaburah* and potentially reconstituted with another is structural: just as the reassembled bed does not recover its prior *tum'ah*, the person who has already been part of a *zimun* does not recover a *zimun* obligation by joining a new group.

---

## Wine and Water

### Before Water

The *Gemara* returns to the *Mishnah's* closing topic and cites the relevant *braita* in full. Before water has been added, the *braita* states, one does not recite *borei pri hagafen* over wine — only *borei pri ha'etz*. *Tosafot* notes in passing that this confirms the general principle that fruit juices, at least when they are significant enough not to be *she-hakol*, receive the blessing of *borei pri ha'etz*. Undiluted wine has not yet been transformed into the improved product that justifies the higher blessing of *borei pri hagafen*. Additionally, before water is added, such wine may be used for washing hands — because its legal status at this stage is closer to water than to wine.

### After Water

Once water has been added, the status reverses. Now the mixture is considered wine: *mevarichin alav borei pri hagafen* — one recites *borei pri hagafen*. And, somewhat counterintuitively, once it is wine it can no longer be used for washing hands: *ve-ein notlin heimenu le-yadayim*. Adding water has simultaneously elevated it to wine and removed it from the category of water available for *netilat yadayim*.

### Whose Position

The *Gemara* then asks: *ke-man azla ha de-amar Shmuel?* — whose position aligns with *Shmuel's* ruling that *oseh adam kol tzarchav be-fat*, a person may use bread for any of his needs? This principle addresses the broader question of *bizayon ochlin* — whether using food for purposes other than eating constitutes a disrespect for food. *Shmuel* holds that even bread, which commands the greatest degree of respect, may be used for other purposes. The *Gemara* concludes that *Shmuel's* position aligns with Rabbi Eliezer, who explicitly permitted using undiluted wine for washing hands. The Rabbis, who held that wine is wine regardless of dilution and thus never permitted it for hands, do not necessarily disagree with *Shmuel's* general principle — but that principle clearly emerges from Rabbi Eliezer's position.

*Tosafot* complicates this: the *Gemara* elsewhere rules like *Shmuel* but with a qualification — food may be used for other purposes only when it is not rendered *ma'us* (repulsive or inedible) in the process. If using food for a secondary purpose ruins it as food, *Shmuel* would not permit it. Rabbi Eliezer, by allowing wine to be used for washing hands even though the hands might make it *ma'us*, goes further than *Shmuel*. So the correct reading is not that Rabbi Eliezer simply reflects *Shmuel's* position, but that Rabbi Eliezer actually extends beyond it.

### Kos Shel Bracha

Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Chanina teaches an important qualification: *modin chachamim le-Rabbi Eliezer be-kos shel bracha* — even the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Eliezer when it comes to a *kos shel bracha*, a ritual cup used for *Kiddush*, *Havdalah*, or *Birkat Hamazon*. For a *kos shel bracha*, water must be added before reciting *borei pri hagafen*. *Rav Oshaya* explains: *be'ina mitzvah min ha-muvchar* — when performing a *mitzvah*, we require the best possible fulfillment, and diluted wine is considered superior for that purpose. The Rabbis may hold that the blessing is valid over undiluted wine in ordinary drinking, but for a *mitzvah* cup, the higher standard applies.

This harmonization is also significant for understanding the placement of the *Mishnah's* closing *halacha*. The *Mishnah* has been discussing the *zimun* over wine — and that wine is almost certainly a *kos shel bracha*. On the level of a *kos shel bracha*, there is actually no dispute: all authorities require the water. The apparent debate in the *Mishnah* may thus be more limited in practical scope than it initially appears.

### Medicinal Purpose

The *Gemara* then asks: according to the Rabbis, who hold that undiluted wine is wine regardless, and who do not permit it for washing hands — for what purpose, then, is undiluted wine fit, given that the *Gemara* seems to suggest it is not normally drunk as-is? *Rav Zeira* answers: *chazi le-kuraitei* — it is suitable for a medicinal preparation involving dates, some sort of curative mixture. The *Gemara* is saying that the Rabbis' position, which classifies undiluted wine as wine and assigns it *borei pri hagafen*, is somewhat strained since they admit people do not normally drink it straight. One recites *borei pri hagafen* over it only in the context of medicinal use, which makes Rabbi Eliezer's position — that undiluted wine is not yet properly wine — the more intuitively compelling one.

---

## Respect for Food

### Four Prohibitions

The *Gemara* now cites a *braita*: *arba'ah devarim ne'emru be-fat* — four things were said regarding bread. One may not place raw meat on bread, lest the blood soak in and render the bread unpleasant. One may not pass a full cup directly over bread, lest it spill. One may not throw bread. And one may not use bread as a support for a plate or table — for instance, wedging a piece under an uneven surface to stabilize it. All four reflect the principle of *kavod* for bread, the staple of life, which commands a level of respect not automatically extended to other foods.

### Throwing Food

The prohibition on throwing food raises the question of whether it applies to foods other than bread. The *Gemara* relates that *Amemar*, *Mar Zutra*, and *Rav Ashi* were eating bread together when dates and pomegranates were brought. *Mar Zutra* tossed a piece to *Rav Ashi*. *Rav Ashi* challenged him: *lo savar lei mar le-ha de-tanya, ein zorkin et ha-ochlin* — does he not hold the teaching that one may not throw food? *Mar Zutra* replied: *hahi be-fat tanya* — that teaching refers only to bread. Other foods are not subject to the same stringency.

### Mar Zutra Story

The *Gemara* then challenges *Mar Zutra's* position from a *braita* that states: just as one may not throw bread, so too one may not throw other foods. But another *braita* states: one may not throw bread, but one may throw other foods. Two *braitot* appear to contradict each other.

### Unpalatable Standard

The resolution: *lo kashya — ha bi-midi de-mimas, ha bi-midi de-lo mimas*. The *braita* that prohibits throwing other foods refers to foods that will become *ma'us* — repulsive or inedible — when thrown. The *braita* that permits throwing other foods refers to foods that will not be ruined in the process. A pomegranate in its shell, for example, can be thrown without the seeds being damaged; the food is not rendered unfit. But something that will get dirty or otherwise become disgusting when thrown falls under the prohibition.

The question of throwing bread at the *Shabbat* table — a practice observed in some communities, where pieces of *challah* are thrown to those seated around the table — arises naturally here. The argument for permissibility would be that the bread is not rendered unfit in the process. However, *Tosafot* makes an explicit and significant distinction: *ve-ein zorkin et ha-pas, afilu lo ma'is* — bread may not be thrown even when it does not become repulsive. Bread is categorically different; it may not be thrown regardless of outcome. This would appear to present a genuine problem for the practice of throwing *challah* at the *Shabbat* table.

### Pouring and Throwing

The *Gemara* continues: *mamshichin yayin be-tzinorot lifnei chatan ve-lifnei kallah* — wine may be poured through channels or funnels before a bride and groom. *Rashi* explains this is permitted because the wine can be collected in vessels and is not ruined in the process — the food is not made *ma'us*. Similarly, one may throw roasted seeds and nuts before them in the summer, but not in the rainy season when they would fall into mud. *Tosafot* raises the question of whether nuts in the shell really become *ma'us* even in mud, since the shell protects the contents — and suggests that *nimas* may not require that people refuse to eat the food, but that allowing it to become muddy is itself a lack of respect, regardless of edibility.

The *Gemara* further states: one may not throw pieces of fine bread or cake (*gluska'ot*) even in summer, because that will be ruined. These distinctions collectively build a coherent principle: food may be used for purposes other than eating, and may even be thrown, so long as it is not rendered unfit. The exception is bread, which may never be thrown.

---

## Food in Mouth

### Three Options

*Rav Yehuda* teaches: if one forgot and placed food in one's mouth without having recited a blessing, one should move it to the side of the mouth and recite the blessing. The *Gemara* then cites three *braitot* that appear to disagree. The first says one should swallow the food. The second says one should spit it out. The third agrees with *Rav Yehuda* that one should move it aside.

### Reconciling Braitot

The *Gemara* reconciles the three positions: *lo kashya*. The *braita* that says swallow refers to liquids — one cannot hold liquid to the side of the mouth and recite a blessing without choking. The *braita* that says spit it out refers to solid food that will not become *ma'us* when spat out — something like a hard candy that has not yet been chewed, which can be removed from the mouth, placed aside, the blessing recited, and the food returned to the mouth without any disgust involved. The *braita* that says move it to the side refers to solid food that would become *ma'us* if spat out — one therefore moves it to the side of the mouth, recites the blessing, and continues eating.

### Waste Priority

The *Gemara* presses further: even for the category of food that would not become *ma'us* when spat out — the case assigned to the "spit it out" *braita* — why not simply move it to the side of the mouth? That would be equally valid. The answer emerges from a key principle: when one has liquids in the mouth and the choice is between swallowing without a blessing or spitting out and wasting the liquid, the ruling is to swallow — even *belo bracha*. This is because *bizayon ochlin*, the imperative not to waste food, takes precedence over the obligation not to derive benefit from the world without a blessing. One does not make a blessing after the fact in such a case; the obligation has been superseded by the imperative to avoid waste.

### Mouth Empty Standard

The *Gemara* closes with a teaching transmitted by Rabbi Yitzchak Kaskasa before Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *mishum she-ne'emar yimaleh pi tehilatekha* — because it is written, "My mouth shall be filled with Your praise." The mouth should be empty and available for praise when one recites a blessing. This is the ideal: one's mouth should be clear, unencumbered, and fully directed toward God when giving praise. It is this standard that explains why spitting out is preferred when possible, and why moving the food to the side is considered a workable but secondary solution. The ideal of *yimaleh pi tehilatekha* — the mouth full of praise alone — is the normative aspiration against which the practical accommodations of swallowing and moving-aside must be measured.

---

---

# Berakhot 52

## Kiddush & Wine Order

### Blessing Order

The *gemara* opens with a *baraita* addressing the debates between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* concerning the proper conduct of a meal. The discussion begins at the very bottom of 51b, where the *gemara* takes up the first issue: at *kiddush*, which *berakhah* comes first — *mekadesh ha-shabbat* or *borei peri ha-gafen*?

### Beit Shammai View

*Beit Shammai* says: first you recite the *berakhah* on the day — *mekadesh ha-shabbat* — and only then the *berakhah* on the wine. Two reasons support this position. First, *she-hayom gorem le-yayin she-yavo*: the very reason you are reciting *borei peri ha-gafen* at all is because of the day — because it is *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* that occasions the *kiddush* and thus necessitates the wine. Although we have seen that the general practice was to have wine before a meal even on an ordinary occasion, on *Shabbat* one would certainly be drinking in connection with *kiddush*, and it is the day that creates that necessity. Second, *u-khevar kideish ha-yom ve-adayin yayin lo ba*: in simple chronological terms, *Shabbat* already arrived before any wine was poured, so the day itself preceded the wine.

### Beit Hillel View

*Beit Hillel* reverses the order, saying *borei peri ha-gafen* comes first, and offers two reasons of its own. The first is *she-ha-yayin gorem la-kiddushah she-tei'amer*: while the purpose is indeed to sanctify the day, it is the wine that enables the *kiddush* to be recited at all — the wine is the vehicle through which *kiddush* is expressed — and therefore the wine takes precedence. One might note that *kiddush* can technically be recited over bread or even over *chamar medinah* in the absence of wine, but the argument holds: whatever the *kiddush* is recited over is the instrument that introduces it. The second reason is the principle of *tadir*: *birkat ha-yayin tedirah, birkat ha-yom einah tedirah* — the *berakhah* over wine is a frequent, constant obligation, whereas the *berakhah* of *mekadesh ha-shabbat* occurs only on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*. When one mitzvah is *tadir* and the other is not, the *tadir* takes precedence.

It is worth noting at the outset — and *Tosafot* makes this point explicitly, with the *gemara* itself raising the question later — that by *benching* (*birkat ha-mazon*) we do precisely the reverse: the *benching* is recited and only afterward do we say *borei peri ha-gafen*. There, holding the *kos* while reciting *birkat ha-mazon* and concluding with *borei peri ha-gafen* conveys the sense that the blessing is being said over the wine, even though it comes at the end. Both orderings, in other words, can plausibly frame the experience as one of blessing said over wine — which underscores why neither argument in this debate is wholly decisive on its own.

### Halakhah & Bas Kol

The *baraita* concludes: *ve-halakhah ke-divrei Beit Hillel* — we rule like *Beit Hillel*. The *gemara* immediately asks: *peshita* — is this not self-evident? We always rule like *Beit Hillel*. Why state it?

The answer invokes a well-known tradition: *de-hanpik bas kol* — a heavenly voice (*bas kol*) emerged and declared that the *halakhah* follows *Beit Hillel*. This arose from an underlying procedural dispute: *Beit Hillel* was greater in number, while *Beit Shammai* was reputed to be sharper in analysis. The question was whether *halakhah* follows the majority by sheer numbers or follows the more intellectually rigorous school. Naturally, *Beit Hillel* argued for the majority while *Beit Shammai* argued for superior reasoning. The *bas kol* resolved the matter by declaring that the *halakhah* follows *Beit Hillel*. Elsewhere the tradition attributes *Beit Hillel*'s merit to their humility — they would always present *Beit Shammai*'s position before their own — which perhaps reflects a willingness to genuinely consider the opposing view.

### Why Beit Hillel

But if we always rule like *Beit Hillel*, why must the *baraita* say so here? The *gemara* offers two answers. The first: *kodem bas kol* — this *baraita* may predate the establishment of the general rule. Before the *halakhah* had crystallized that we follow *Beit Hillel* in all cases, each individual dispute still required an explicit ruling. There is, interestingly, something about these debates concerning the conduct of a meal — and as we will see, their deep entanglement with *tumah va-taharah* — that gives them an archaic quality, suggesting they may indeed have been formulated at an early stage of the tradition.

The second answer: *le-achar bas kol* — even granting that the *bas kol* had already been issued, one might follow the view of *Rabbi Yehoshua*, who holds that we do not defer to a *bas kol*. This brings in the famous story from *Bava Metzia* of the *tanuro shel achnai*: *Rabbi Eliezer* declared a particular oven *tahor* while all the other sages ruled it *tamei*. *Rabbi Eliezer* invoked a series of miracles — a river flowing backward, the walls of the *beit ha-midrash* bending — and finally a *bas kol* emerged declaring that the *halakhah* follows *Rabbi Eliezer* in all matters. At that point, *Rabbi Yehoshua* rose and declared *lo ba-shamayim hi* — it is not in heaven; the Torah has been given to us to interpret, and heavenly voices do not override the halakhic process. According to this view, one might take that principle all the way and say we do not follow the *bas kol* even in the *Beit Hillel* ruling, and thus we must explicitly state the ruling here.

### Lo BaShamayim Hi

The principle of *lo ba-shamayim hi* thus represents a far-reaching stance on the autonomy of the rabbinic process. *Rabbi Yehoshua* was not denying the reality of the *bas kol*; he was asserting that the Torah was given to human interpretation, and that even a genuine heavenly communication cannot override the majority. The *gemara* acknowledges that some might extend this position even to the *Beit Hillel* ruling, holding that the question of which school to follow remains genuinely open — though this is emphatically not the *gemara*'s own conclusion.

### Tosafot Resolution

*Tosafot* addresses an apparent tension: if we all agree with *Rabbi Yehoshua* in the *achnai* case, why do we accept the *bas kol* declaring *halakhah* like *Beit Hillel*? *Tosafot* draws a sharp distinction. In the *achnai* case, the majority of sages was already *against* *Rabbi Eliezer*; he was attempting to use a miraculous voice to *override* the majority. Everyone agrees you do not do that. In the *Beit Hillel* case, the *bas kol* was not overriding the majority — *Beit Hillel* already *was* the majority. The *bas kol* was rather settling a procedural dispute that could not otherwise be resolved by the usual tools of majority rule, since each side was claiming that the proper procedure supported its own position. Or, put another way: it was affirming the majority principle itself against *Beit Shammai*'s competing claim that superior reasoning should carry greater weight. The *bas kol* was thus siding with the majority, not supplanting it — and that is a case everyone agrees to accept.

---

## Havdalah Order

### Havdalah Sequence

The *gemara* now turns to an apparent contradiction. A *baraita* teaches: one who enters his home on *Motzaei Shabbat* recites *borei peri ha-gafen*, then *borei me'orei ha-eish*, then *besamim*, and then *havdalah*. This ordering — wine first, then fire, then spices, then the *havdalah* blessing itself — presents an immediate difficulty: if *Beit Hillel* rules that wine comes first, that is consistent. But the order of fire before spices in this *baraita* does not match current practice, where spices precede the *ner*.

The *baraita* continues: if one has only one cup of wine available and wishes to eat a meal — meaning *havdalah* and *birkat ha-mazon* will need to share that single cup — one sets the cup aside until after the meal, then chains together all the blessings following *birkat ha-mazon*: *borei peri ha-gafen*, *ner*, *besamim*, and *havdalah*, all after the *kos* of *birkat ha-mazon*.

### Attribution to Beit

Before addressing the substance, the *gemara* asks: whose position is this *baraita*? Is it *Beit Shammai* or *Beit Hillel*? It cannot simply be assumed to be *Beit Hillel* on the basis that wine comes first, since we have seen that *Beit Hillel* also holds wine first. To identify the attribution, the *gemara* invokes the framework of *Rabbi Yehuda*, who in a *baraita* of his own offers a different account of the *Beit Shammai*–*Beit Hillel* dispute regarding the combination of *havdalah* and *birkat ha-mazon*.

### Proving Shammai

According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* do not actually disagree about *birkat ha-mazon* coming first and *havdalah* coming last; both agree on that framework. Their dispute is only about the order of *ner* and *besamim* within *havdalah*: *Beit Shammai* says *me'or* first, then *besamim*; *Beit Hillel* says *besamim* first, then *me'or* — which is the practice we follow. The *baraita* in question has *me'or* before *besamim*, which according to *Rabbi Yehuda* is the position of *Beit Shammai* alone. Furthermore, the *baraita* places *birkat ha-mazon* before the entire *havdalah* sequence — which is also consistent with *Rabbi Yehuda*'s account, since he holds that both schools agree *birkat ha-mazon* precedes *havdalah*.

This process of identification works through a process of elimination: our *mishnah* (which is *stam*, attributed to *Rabbi Meir*) has a different arrangement and places *birkat ha-mazon* in the middle of the *havdalah* elements. So the *baraita* cannot reflect the *mishnah*'s position. The only framework in which *birkat ha-mazon* unambiguously precedes all of *havdalah* is that of *Rabbi Yehuda*, and within *Rabbi Yehuda*'s framework, only *Beit Shammai* places *me'or* before *besamim*. Therefore the *baraita* is *Beit Shammai* according to *Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Wine Contradiction

Having established that the *baraita* represents *Beit Shammai*, a sharp contradiction emerges. *Beit Shammai* holds that by *kiddush*, the *berakhah* of the day — *mekadesh ha-shabbat* — precedes *borei peri ha-gafen*, because the day is primary. Yet here, by *havdalah*, the very same *Beit Shammai* begins with *borei peri ha-gafen* — wine first. Why the asymmetry? The *gemara* states flatly: *mikal makom kasha* — the difficulty stands.

To clarify the logical structure: once we have demonstrated that the *baraita* reflects *Rabbi Yehuda*'s framework and that within that framework the ordering of *me'or* before *besamim* belongs to *Beit Shammai*, the question is validated. *Beit Shammai* is saying that wine comes first at *havdalah*. But by *kiddush*, *Beit Shammai* insists the day comes first. What principle accounts for this reversal?

### Euley vs. Afukey

The *gemara* answers: *kasavar Beit Shammai, shani euley yoma me-afukey yoma* — *Beit Shammai* holds that entering into the day is fundamentally different from going out from the day. This distinction drives the asymmetry.

### Shabbat Symbolism

*Euley yoma kama de-makdeminan lei adif* — when *Shabbat* is beginning, the sooner we designate and sanctify it the better. We are eager for *Shabbat* to begin. Therefore, we name the day first — *mekadesh ha-shabbat* — before the wine, to express that eagerness and to sanctify the day at the earliest possible moment.

*Afukey yoma kama de-machrinan lei adif* — when *Shabbat* is departing, the later we formally conclude it the better. We do not wish to rush its ending. Therefore, we recite *borei peri ha-gafen* first and only then *ha-mavdil bein kodesh le-chol*, postponing the formal ending of *Shabbat* by even a few moments. It is not merely about the seconds involved in saying *borei peri ha-gafen* — it is about the symbolism. We begin *Shabbat* eagerly and we reluctantly let it go.

This principle has practical halakhic expressions elsewhere. For example, on *Motzaei Shabbat* in *shul*, the *Chanukah* candles are lit before *havdalah* is recited, so that even though candles are already being kindled — which presupposes *Shabbat* has ended — the formal *havdalah* blessing is delayed slightly. By the time one returns home, *havdalah* has already been recited in *shul*, but the sequence in *shul* itself reflects this reluctance to end *Shabbat* too quickly.

The final phrase the *gemara* adds is: *ki heichi di-la lehavei alan ke-masa'i* — so that it should not appear as though *Shabbat* is a burden we are eager to be rid of. Postponing the formal conclusion, even briefly, expresses that *Shabbat* is cherished and not a weight to be lifted.

---

## Meal Before Havdalah

### One Cup Case

Before proceeding, the *gemara* raises a question implicit in the *baraita*'s scenario. The *baraita* described someone who comes home on *Motzaei Shabbat* with only one cup available and proceeds to eat a meal, after which *birkat ha-mazon* and *havdalah* are combined over that single *kos*. But one should immediately ask: is a person permitted to eat before *havdalah*?

In the *mishnah*'s case the difficulty is less acute, since the person may have begun eating during the third *Shabbat* meal before *Shabbat* ended and was simply continuing — there is a rule permitting one who began eating before *Shabbat* concluded to continue eating. But the *baraita*'s case presents someone arriving home on *Motzaei Shabbat*, clearly intending to begin a fresh meal before making *havdalah*. Why would this be permitted?

### Tosafot on Timing

*Tosafot* addresses this directly. He concludes that this *gemara* is indicating that even though one is generally prohibited from eating before *havdalah*, the imperative to recite *birkat ha-mazon* over a *kos* (*al ha-kos*) is weighty enough to override that prohibition. The reasoning is striking: if this person were to make *havdalah* over the wine first and then eat, he would have no cup remaining for *birkat ha-mazon*. To preserve the ability to recite *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos*, it is therefore preferable to eat first — violating the ordinary prohibition against eating before *havdalah* — and to then use the cup for both *birkat ha-mazon* and *havdalah* together.

This is a remarkable inference. In ordinary practice today, the obligation of *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos* is not typically felt to carry such weight. Yet *Tosafot* sees no other way to read this *gemara*: the only explanation for permitting eating before *havdalah* in this case is that *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos* is of sufficient importance to justify it. The *gemara* in *Pesachim* dealing with a nearly identical *sugya* confirms that even if one did eat before *havdalah*, one may still subsequently recite *havdalah* — the very scenario of this *baraita* serving as a proof.

### Kos Requirement

This leads *Tosafot* to a further inquiry about the scope of the *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos* requirement. How many people eating together trigger the obligation? Some hold it only applies with ten, others suggest minimally three (so that a *zimmun* is present). But *Tosafot* observes that if the requirement were only with three, the *baraita*'s entire scenario could be avoided: rather than eating before *havdalah*, one could simply eat alone — no *zimmun*, no *kos* obligation — and make *havdalah* first. The fact that the *baraita* presents eating before *havdalah* as the preferred solution implies that the obligation of *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos* applies even to an individual eating alone. This is quite far-reaching. *Tosafot* himself acknowledges that the prevalent custom (*minhag ha-olam*) is to use a *kos* only with three — or in some communities only with ten — yet the internal logic of the *gemara* seems to push toward an obligation even for one.

### Pagum & Water

*Tosafot* presses further: are there no other solutions that would avoid the need to eat before *havdalah*? Two possibilities suggest themselves.

First, one could make *havdalah*, take a small sip, and then use the remaining wine for *birkat ha-mazon*. The problem is that once someone has drunk from a cup, it is *pagum* — considered impaired — and a *pagum* cup is disqualified for a *kos shel berakhah*. The *baraita*'s failure to propose this solution thus implies that *pagum* is indeed disqualified *le-khatehilah*, and there is no easy workaround.

Second, one could add wine or water to the cup to restore it. Adding wine clearly repairs a *pagum* cup. The question of adding water is more nuanced: *Tosafot* cites the *Yerushalmi* that *Rabbi Yonah* would taste from a cup and then add a small amount of water, thereby rendering it as though it were a fresh cup. Other *Tosafot* are uncertain whether water suffices, partly because this very *gemara* implies there was no simple fix available — otherwise, why permit eating before *havdalah* at all? In contemporary practice, the questions of adding wine and adding water to a *pagum* or insufficiently filled cup remain practically relevant. One who has made *kiddush* from a shared cup and wishes to make *kiddush* again need not pour an entirely fresh cup — adding wine to the partly drunk cup removes its status as *pagum* and reconstitutes it as a valid *kos*. Similarly, when only a small amount of wine remains in a bottle and the cup cannot be filled to the required level, adding water may also be acceptable, as the *halakhah* historically permitted mixing wine with water.

---

## Wine After Meal

### Mishna Scenario

The *gemara* now turns to analyze the *mishnah* itself on a related point. The *mishnah* states: if wine became available after the meal — meaning at the end of the meal, when only one cup is present — *Beit Shammai* says you recite the *berakhah* over it and then recite *birkat ha-mazon*, while *Beit Hillel* says the reverse: *birkat ha-mazon* first, then the *berakhah* over the wine.

### Mishna Meaning

The *gemara* initially reads *Beit Shammai*'s position as: you recite *borei peri ha-gafen*, drink the wine, and *then* say *birkat ha-mazon* — meaning you drink first without using the wine as a *kos* for *birkat ha-mazon*. This would imply that *Beit Shammai* does not require *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos*. But this reading creates a tension with the earlier *baraita* about *havdalah*, where *Beit Shammai* seemed to insist on exactly such a combination.

### Taste & Pagum

The *gemara* therefore rejects the initial reading. *Lo* — that is not what the *mishnah* means. Rather, *Beit Shammai* is saying: recite *borei peri ha-gafen*, set the cup down without drinking, and then use that same cup for *birkat ha-mazon*. Opening *birkat ha-mazon* with *borei peri ha-gafen* would be the reverse of what we do.

But this generates its own problem: *ha-mevarech tzarich li-to'am* — one who recites a *berakhah* must taste from the object immediately. If you recite *borei peri ha-gafen* and then proceed to recite the entirety of *birkat ha-mazon* before drinking, that is too long an interval. The *gemara* responds: *di-ta'amei* — he did taste it. He recited *borei peri ha-gafen* and took a taste. But then: *ta'amo pagmo* — tasting from the cup renders it *pagum*, impaired, and a *pagum* cup cannot serve as a *kos shel berakhah*. The *gemara* therefore says: *di-ta'amei bi-yadei* — he dipped his finger in and licked it. He did not drink directly from the cup; he obtained a taste through his finger, which does not constitute a drink from the cup and does not render it *pagum*.

This precise mechanism — dipping a finger to taste without creating a *pagum* — has a practical parallel. Rabbis who recite *borei peri ha-gafen* before *birkat eirusin* or as part of the *sheva berakhot* ceremony face a similar problem: *borei peri ha-gafen* is ordinarily a *birkat ha-nehenin*, requiring that the one reciting it derive benefit. Unlike *kiddush*, where the blessing is embedded in a ritual context and can be recited on behalf of others without the reciter drinking, a standalone *borei peri ha-gafen* requires personal benefit. The solution sometimes employed is for the officiant to lightly shake the cup so a drop lands on a finger, and to lick that finger after handing the cup to the *chatan* and *kallah* — a technically valid if precarious resolution.

---

## Cup Minimum

### Amount Question

A further technical difficulty: the *mishnah* specifies *im ein sham ela oso ha-kos* — if there is only that one cup. A *kos shel berakhah* requires a minimum measure (*shi'ur*). If only one cup is present and some of the wine is used for tasting, how can the remaining wine still meet the minimum requirement?

### Cup Size

The *gemara* resolves this: the cup held more than one minimum measure but less than two. It was not exactly a single *revi'it* but somewhat more — enough that after dipping a finger and tasting, what remains still meets the minimum.

### Finger Dip

The practical application follows: by dipping only a finger and licking it rather than taking a proper sip, the amount removed from the cup is negligible. The cup retains more than the minimum required measure, it has not been rendered *pagum* through direct drinking, and it can still serve as the *kos shel berakhah* for *birkat ha-mazon*.

---

## Wine After Meal (II)

### Baraita Position

The *gemara* introduces a *baraita* from the school of *Rabbi Hiyya*: *Beit Shammai* says one recites *borei peri ha-gafen* over the wine, drinks it, and then recites *birkat ha-mazon*. This *baraita* appears to say explicitly what the *gemara* had just denied — that *Beit Shammai* permits drinking the wine first and only then proceeding to *birkat ha-mazon*, without using the wine as a *kos shel berakhah*.

### Resolution

The *gemara* concludes: *ela trei tana'ei aliba de-Beit Shammai* — there is a dispute among *tannaim* about what *Beit Shammai*'s position actually is. According to one reading of *Beit Shammai* — the one reflected in the earlier *havdalah* discussion — *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos* is required. According to the *baraita* from *Rabbi Hiyya*'s school, *Beit Shammai* may not require it at all. This leaves the intriguing possibility that in this dispute, *Beit Hillel* is actually the *stricter* position, insisting on *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos*, while one version of *Beit Shammai* does not. The question of whether the obligation of *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos* applies to one person, three, or ten thus remains subject to serious debate among the *Rishonim*.

---

## Cup Minimum (II)

### Fixing Pagum

*Tosafot* addresses the question of repairing a *pagum* cup directly. He writes that the disqualification of a *pagum* cup applies only where an alternative is available. Where no alternative exists — *iy efshar* — one may recite a *berakhah* even over a *pagum* cup. He then adds, citing the *Yerushalmi*, that one may add a small amount of water or wine to the cup to restore it: *Rabbi Yona* would taste from a cup and then add any amount of water or wine, after which he would recite the *berakhah* over it.

Whether water alone suffices is disputed: other passages in *Tosafot* raise the possibility that only wine repairs a *pagum* cup, since the very scenario of the *baraita* — eating before *havdalah* to enable *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos* — implies that simply adding water was not considered a sufficient remedy. If adding water were unambiguously effective, one could make *havdalah*, take a sip, add water, and use the cup for *birkat ha-mazon* — and no one would need to eat before *havdalah* at all. The *baraita*'s silence on this alternative is itself evidence. In current practice, adding wine to a partially drunk or insufficiently filled cup is standard and well-established. A *kos* used for *kiddush* by one person can readily be refilled with additional wine and used by another without concern for *pagum*. The addition reconstitutes the cup as whole, no longer defined by its having been drunk from.

---

## Blessing Asymmetry

### Order Difference

A fundamental question now presents itself. By *kiddush* and *havdalah*, we begin with *borei peri ha-gafen* and then recite the central blessing — *mekadesh ha-shabbat* or *ha-mavdil bein kodesh le-chol*. But by *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos*, the order is inverted: we recite *birkat ha-mazon* in full and only at the very end say *borei peri ha-gafen* and drink. Why the asymmetry?

### Hefsek Theory

*Tosafot* raises this question and begins his answer: *iy mevarech kodem Birkat ha-Mazon* — if we were to recite *borei peri ha-gafen* before *birkat ha-mazon*, then *birkat ha-mazon* would constitute a *hefsek* — an interruption — between the *berakhah* and the drinking. The *gemara* itself could not entertain the possibility of reciting *borei peri ha-gafen* and then waiting until the end of *birkat ha-mazon* to drink; it assumed you would have to drink immediately. Why? Because an extended recitation like *birkat ha-mazon* — three or four *berakhot* — would constitute too long an interruption between the blessing and its fulfillment.

### Psychological End

*Tosafot* offers an additional reason that goes beyond the mechanical question of length.

### Intent Differs

*De-bishlama bi-sh'ar berakhot lo akar da'atei mi-shtiya* — when one recites *kiddush* or *havdalah*, saying those blessings is not a declaration that one is finished. *Kiddush* signals that one is *about to eat*; even *havdalah*, in a sense, signals that one is about to drink. The person's intention to continue with the meal or the wine remains intact. But *birkat ha-mazon ika akiras da'as mi-shtiya* — *birkat ha-mazon* is a declaration of completion. Reciting *birkat ha-mazon* means: I am done eating. If one had first said *borei peri ha-gafen* and then declared through *birkat ha-mazon* that the meal is over, one could no longer coherently drink the wine afterward — the declaration of closure would have intervened and severed the connection. Therefore the wine must come *after* *birkat ha-mazon*, not before, so that drinking remains a valid sequel to the blessing.

### Infinite Loop

*Tosafot* raises one further, characteristically sharp observation. If *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos* applies to every individual eating alone, one might wonder: after drinking the wine at the conclusion of *birkat ha-mazon*, does that drinking of wine require its own subsequent *birkat ha-mazon al ha-kos*, and so on infinitely? *Tosafot* addresses this by invoking *Rabban Gamliel*'s position that a full *birkat ha-mazon* is only required for one of the *shivat ha-minim*, but even aside from that, the chain terminates: the wine drunk after *birkat ha-mazon* is not itself part of a meal requiring *birkat ha-mazon* in turn.

---

## Hand Washing

### Shammai Order

The *gemara* now enters an extended discussion of *tumah va-taharah* as it applies to the conduct of a meal — material that is less directly operative in current practice but that illuminates the underlying logic of several *halakhot* related to washing and the use of vessels. The *mishnah* presents a debate: *Beit Shammai* says you wash your hands first and only then mix and pour the cup of wine; *Beit Hillel* says the reverse.

A *baraita* elaborates: *Beit Shammai omrim: notlin yadayim ve-akhar kakh mozgin et ha-kos* — first wash hands, then pour and mix the wine. *She-im attah omer mozgin et ha-kos techilah* — if you first pour the wine without washing your hands, there is a concern: *gezeirah shema yitme'u mashkin she-achorei ha-kos machmat yadav* — the droplets of wine on the outside of the cup will become *tamei* through the hands.

### Sheni Problem

To understand this, one must appreciate the world that *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* inhabited: a world of *taharah* consciousness even at ordinary meals, where unwashed hands are treated as *sheni le-tumah* — second-degree derivative impurity. In the rabbinic system, when a *sheni* touches a liquid, that liquid becomes a *rishon*. This is a stringency applied specifically to liquids, reflecting the fact that in the biblical *tumah* system, certain bodily fluids — those of a *zav*, a *zavah*, and similar — are an *av ha-tumah* at the highest level. Liquids were therefore treated with heightened stringency, and even rabbinic contact of a *sheni* with liquid elevates that liquid to *rishon*.

The mechanism of *Beit Shammai*'s concern is therefore: unwashed hands (*sheni*) touch the wine droplets on the outside of the cup (*mashkin she-achorei ha-kos*), making those droplets a *rishon*. Those *rishon* droplets then render the cup itself a *sheni*. And *Beit Shammai* holds that one may not use a vessel that has become a *sheni* in the course of a meal.

One might ask: why is liquid the necessary intermediary? Why do the hands not make the cup *tamei* directly? The answer: *yadayim sheiniyot hen, ve-ein sheni oseh shlishi be-chullin* — hands are only a *sheni*, and a *sheni* cannot produce a *shlishi* in non-consecrated food or objects. It can only elevate a liquid to *rishon*, and the *rishon* liquid then makes the vessel a *sheni*. The vessel itself cannot be affected directly by a *sheni*; the liquid is the required conduit.

### Hillel Order

*Beit Hillel* reverses the sequence: *mozgin et ha-kos ve-akhar kakh notlin yadayim* — pour the wine first, then wash hands. *She-im attah omer notlin yadayim techilah* — if you wash first, *gezeirah shema yehyu mashkin she-be-yadayim machmat ha-kos* — the liquid remaining on your freshly washed (but not yet dry) hands will become *tamei* through contact with the cup, *ve-yachzeru ve-yitame'u et ha-yadayim* — and will then render your hands *tamei*.

### Hillel Logic

The key to understanding this reversal is that *Beit Hillel* holds an entirely different premise: it is *permitted* to use a vessel whose exterior has become *tamei* through liquid contact. Since *Beit Hillel* permits using such vessels, the concern that the cup will become a *sheni* does not trouble them — a *sheni* vessel is not a problem. But precisely because such vessels are in use, there is now a real concern that the cup, as a *sheni*, will make the liquid on one's freshly washed hands into a *rishon*, which in turn will render the hands themselves *sheni*. Therefore *Beit Hillel* says: pour the wine first, and only then wash hands — because after washing, you should not handle the potentially-*tamei* cup until the washing is behind you.

### Liquid Conduit

The *gemara* probes the mechanism. One might ask: why does the cup not make the hands *tamei* directly, without liquid as an intermediary? Answer: *ein kli metamei adam* — a vessel, even a *rishon*, cannot render a person *tamei* directly. Only through liquid does the transfer occur. Similarly, why does the cup not make the liquid *inside* it into a *rishon*, so that *Beit Hillel*'s permission to use such vessels becomes irrelevant? Here the *gemara* introduces an important technical principle.

### Outside Tamei

The *gemara* explains: *hacha bi-kli she-nitme'u achorav be-mashkin askinan — tocho tahor ve-gavo tamei* — we are dealing specifically with a vessel whose *exterior* became *tamei* through liquid contact, while the *interior* remains *tahor*. This is a distinct rabbinic rule: if liquid makes the outside of a vessel *tamei*, only the outside is affected. *Nitma tocho, nitma kulo* — if the inside becomes *tamei*, the whole vessel is *tamei* — but when only the outside is reached by the *tamei* liquid, the inside is unaffected.

The *mishnah* articulates this explicitly: *kli she-nitme'u achorav be-mashkin* — a vessel whose outside was made *tamei* through liquid — *achorav teme'in* — only the outside is *tamei* — *tocho ve-ogno ve-ozno ve-yadav tehorin* — its inside, its lip, its ear, its handle, remain *tahor*. If the inside became *tamei*, the entire vessel follows.

This rule is itself a marker of rabbinic origin and intent. Biblically, a vessel can only become a *rishon* — not a *sheni* — and the idea that only half a vessel is *tamei* has no biblical parallel. The rabbis constructed this asymmetry deliberately to signal that these stringencies are rabbinic, lest people treat them as biblical and, for example, burn *terumah* that came into contact with such vessels. By making the rule internally strange — the outside *tamei*, the inside *tahor* — the rabbis communicated that the entire framework is a rabbinic construction and should not be treated with maximal stringency.

For *Beit Hillel*'s practical reasoning: since only the outside of the cup is *tamei*, the wine inside it remains *tahor*. The cup is usable; the food and drink within it are not affected. *Beit Hillel* therefore permits using such vessels. *Beit Shammai*, however, refuses: *assur le-hishtamesh bi-kli she-nitma achorav be-mashkin, gezeirah mishum nitzotzo* — one may not use such a vessel, because there is a concern that liquid will splatter from the outside onto food, rendering the food *tamei*.

### Core Dispute

The *gemara* now states the fundamental disagreement in clear terms. *Beit Shammai savri: assur le-hishtamesh bi-kli she-nitma achorav be-mashkin* — one may not use a vessel whose exterior has been made *tamei* by liquid, on account of concern about splatter (*nitzotzo*). Since *Beit Shammai* therefore ensures the table-vessels are *tahor*, there is no concern that the vessel will make the hands *tamei* — the vessel is clean to begin with. The only concern is that unwashed hands will contaminate the vessel. So: wash hands first, then pour.

*Beit Hillel savri: mutar le-hishtamesh bi-kli she-nitma achorav be-mashkin* — one may use such a vessel, because *nitzotzot lo shechichi* — splatter is uncommon and we do not legislate against it. Since *Beit Hillel* permits using vessels whose exterior is *tamei*, the possibility that the cup is already a *sheni* is a real scenario. Therefore the concern runs the other direction: the cup may make your wet hands *tamei*. So: pour first, then wash.

### Immediately Before

*Beit Hillel* adds a second, independent reason — *davar acher*: *teichef li-netilat yadayim seudah* — hand-washing should lead directly into the meal. The washing of hands has its purpose in relation to the bread, and that washing should immediately precede the *hamotzi*. If one were to wash hands first and only then pour the wine, the wine-pouring would intervene between the washing and the meal, which is undesirable. Therefore: pour the wine, then wash, and proceed directly to the meal.

The *gemara* asks why *Beit Hillel* needs this additional reason when the *tumah* argument already supports their position. The answer: *Beit Hillel* is also addressing *Beit Shammai* on *Beit Shammai*'s own terms. Even if you accept *Beit Shammai*'s premise that such vessels are *assur* — and therefore there is no concern about the cup making the hands *tamei* — *Beit Hillel* says: my ordering is *still* preferable, because the washing should immediately precede the meal. The argument from *tadir la-netilat yadayim seudah* stands independently of the *tumah* dispute.

This final point is not merely theoretical. It bears directly on the *Ashkenazi* custom of washing hands before *kiddush*, then reciting *borei peri ha-gafen*, and only then *hamotzi*. *Tosafot* in *Pesachim* discusses this practice and acknowledges the difficulty from this *gemara*, which seems to favor hand-washing immediately before the bread. He resolves the tension on two grounds: first, the *gemara* here was concerned with the elaborate process of *mezigat ha-kos* — mixing water with wine in precise proportions — which would constitute a genuine *hefsek* between washing and eating; simply reciting *borei peri ha-gafen* after washing is not the same kind of interruption. Second, *kiddush be-makom seudah* — *kiddush* by its very nature introduces and is integrated into the meal; it is not an intervening act but part of the meal's initiation. The *gemara*'s concern does not apply when *kiddush* is the transition directly into eating.

---

## Towel Placement

### Shammai: Table

The *mishnah* continues with a debate about where one places the towel used to dry the hands after washing. *Beit Shammai* says: place the towel on the table. *Beit Hillel* says: place it on the couch (*keset*) — the reclining surface beside you.

A *baraita* elaborates: *Beit Shammai omrim: mekaneach yadav ba-mapa u-manichan al ha-shulchan* — wipe your hands on the towel and set it on the table. *She-im attah omer al ha-keset* — if you keep it on the couch, the concern is *gezeirah shema yitme'u mashkin she-ba-mapa machmat ha-keset* — the liquid on the damp towel will become *tamei* through the *tamei* couch, *ve-yachzeru ve-yitame'u et ha-yadayim* — and then those *rishon* liquids will render the hands *sheni*.

### Couch Risk

The structure of *Beit Shammai*'s concern is thus: the couch (*keset*) may be *tamei*. The wet towel placed on it retains liquid. That liquid becomes a *rishon* through contact with the *tamei* couch. The *rishon* liquid then makes the hands *sheni* when the towel is used again during the meal. Better to place the towel on the table, which *Beit Shammai* presumably regards as *tahor* — or at least less likely to create this chain of transmission.

### Hillel: Couch

*Beit Hillel* says the opposite: place the towel on the couch, not the table. *She-im attah omer al ha-shulchan* — if you place it on the table, there is a different concern: *gezeirah shema yitme'u mashkin she-ba-mapa machmat ha-shulchan* — the liquid on the towel will become *tamei* through the table, *ve-yachzeru ve-yitame'u et ha-ochlin* — and then those *rishon* liquids will render the food *tamei*.

### Table Risk

*Beit Hillel*'s concern thus runs in the opposite direction: the table, with its *sheni* status, makes the liquid on the towel a *rishon*, and that *rishon* liquid then contaminates the food placed on the table. The table poses a greater risk to the food than the couch poses to the hands.

### Liquid Needed

The *gemara* again probes the mechanism. Why isn't the table making the food *tamei* directly? *Hacha be-shulchan sheni askinan, ve-ein sheni oseh shlishi be-chullin* — the table is only a *sheni*, and a *sheni* cannot produce a *shlishi* in non-consecrated food directly; it can only do so through the intermediary of liquid. Similarly, why doesn't the couch make the towel *tamei* directly? *Ein kli metamei kli* — one vessel cannot render another vessel *tamei*. Even a *rishon* vessel cannot make a second vessel *sheni*; it can only do so through liquid. The liquid on the towel is the necessary conduit in both directions.

*Rashi* notes that one might ask: if you are reclining on the couch, won't the couch make *you* *tamei* directly? The answer: you are careful not to place your hands on the couch itself. Your hands do not touch the couch's surface; the concern only arises if the damp towel is placed there and then the liquid mediates the transfer back to your hands.

One might also wonder: what about the various liquids present in food — stews, gravies, broth? *Rashi* addresses this as well, suggesting that such liquids, being embedded within the food rather than existing as independent *mashkin*, do not function as the requisite conduit for *tumah* transfer in this context. Only liquids existing distinctly — pure water, wine, oil, and the like — serve as the conduit.

### Preferring Hands

The *gemara* then articulates the fundamental dispute in structural terms parallel to the *hand-washing* debate. *Beit Shammai savri: assur le-hishtamesh be-shulchan sheni* — *Beit Shammai* holds that one may not use a table that is a *sheni* in the course of a meal, due to concern for *terumah* eaters (*gezeirah mishum ochlei terumah*): *kohanim* who eat *terumah* might inadvertently render it *shlishi* through the table's liquid. Since *Beit Shammai* does not permit using such a table, the table is presumed *tahor*, and the safer place for the wet towel is therefore the table rather than the potentially *tamei* couch.

*Beit Hillel savri: mutar le-hishtamesh be-shulchan sheni* — *Beit Hillel* permits using such a table, because *ochlei terumah zrizin heim* — those who eat *terumah* are careful and will not let the table contaminate their *terumah*.

*Beit Hillel* then adds the *davar acher*: even leaving aside the *tumah* framework, it is preferable that the hands become *tamei* rather than the food. The reasoning: *ein netilat yadayim le-chullin min ha-Torah* — the requirement to wash hands for ordinary eating has no biblical basis; it is entirely rabbinic. The entire concept of hands being a *sheni* while the rest of the body remains *tahor* is a rabbinic construct with no biblical analogue. Therefore, if one must choose between the towel making the hands *tamei* (which is essentially a rabbinic-upon-rabbinic concern) versus the table making the food *tamei* (which, even if only rabbinic in this case, has a biblical basis in the concept of food becoming *tamei*), it is far preferable to risk the hands. *Mutav she-yitme'u yadayim de-leisu ikar me-de-oraisa* — better that the hands become *tamei*, since the entire foundation of their *tumah* is rabbinic, *ve-al yitme'u ochlin de-is lei ikar me-de-oraisa* — rather than the food, whose *tumah* has a biblical root.

The result is that *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* reason from opposite structural premises — whether a *sheni* vessel may be used at a meal — and arrive at opposite practical conclusions about towel placement. *Beit Shammai*, by prohibiting the *sheni* vessel and thus keeping the table clean, makes the table the safe location. *Beit Hillel*, by permitting the *sheni* vessel and worrying instead about the food, makes the couch the safer location — and adds that even if both locations present some risk, it is better for the risk to fall upon the hands, whose *tumah* is the most attenuated in the system, than upon the food.

---

---

# Berakhot 53

## Crumbs vs. Hand-Washing

### Basic Dispute

The Gemara resumes with the *baraita* on *mayim acharonim*: does one first clear the crumbs from the table, or first wash one's hands? The *baraita* presents the positions of both houses: *tanu rabbanan, Beit Shammai omrim mechabdin et habayit ve'achar kach notlin layadayim* — Beit Shammai holds that one first sweeps away the crumbs and then performs *mayim acharonim*, while Beit Hillel reverses the order.

### Beit Shammai View

The reason Beit Hillel prefers *mayim acharonim* first is that if one washes first, the water will spill onto the crumbs and ruin food one might wish to eat later. Beit Shammai does not insist that hand-washing come first; rather, their primary concern is that the crumbs be cleared before any water is introduced. There may also be an argument that *mayim acharonim* should ideally follow immediately upon finishing the meal — particularly given its function of removing filth, odor, and the *melach Sedomit* — but Beit Shammai subordinates that concern to the protection of the food.

### Beit Hillel View

Beit Hillel responds that if the *shamash* is a *talmid chacham*, he will know on his own to remove any pieces of bread larger than a *kezayit* before the washing begins. *U'maniach et hapeirurin she'ein bahen kezayit* — he leaves only the small crumbs that contain less than a *kezayit*. And such crumbs, as Rabbi Yochanan ruled, may even be destroyed directly by hand, since no one intends to eat them. The text uses this to support Rabbi Yochanan's position: *peirurin she'ein bahen kezayit mutar le'abdan beyad*, that fragments below a *kezayit* do not carry the concern of *bizui ochlin*.

### Root: Am Ha'aretz

The Gemara asks: *bemai kamifligi* — what is the root of their debate? The surprising answer is that the dispute turns on whether it is permitted to use an attendant who is an *am ha'aretz*. Beit Hillel holds it is forbidden to employ an *am ha'aretz* as a *shamash*, and therefore one cannot rely on him to sort the crumbs properly; hence, *mayim acharonim* must wait until the crumbs are cleared. Beit Shammai holds it is permitted to use such an attendant — but then one must worry that large pieces will remain on the table when the washing begins, making it necessary to clear the crumbs first.

This outcome is, as the Gemara acknowledges, somewhat ironic. It is Beit Shammai — not Beit Hillel — who displays the more inclusive posture toward the *am ha'aretz*.

### Ruling Beit Shammai

Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Chanina citing Rav Huna establishes: *bechol pirka halacha ke'Beit Hillel* — throughout this entire chapter, the ruling follows Beit Hillel. However, *bar meiha* — except for this case. Here, *hahalacha ke'Beit Shammai*. In the one instance where Beit Shammai's position carries the traditionally Hillel-like sensibility, Beit Shammai prevails.

### Rabbi Oshaya View

Rabbi Oshaya resolves the tension differently: he reverses the attributed positions entirely. According to his version, *Beit Hillel* is the one who permits using an *am ha'aretz* as a *shamash* and therefore requires that the crumbs be cleared first — with the result that the *halacha* again follows Beit Hillel, and the anomaly disappears.

---

## Havdalah Order

### Initial Problem

The Mishnah places the question of *birkat hamazon* and *havdalah* together in a striking way — embedding the *havdalah* components within the structure of *bensching* over a *kos*, as one might do when concluding a *seuda shlishit* that runs into *motzaei Shabbos*. The Gemara's discussion of exactly how these blessings are ordered begins with an episode: Rav Huna bar Yehuda came to the house of Rava and observed that Rava recited *besamim* first — before *ner*. This puzzled him, since the Mishnah seems to indicate that both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that the blessing over light comes before *besamim*.

### Ner Comes First

Rava's response makes clear that on the question of *ner* coming before everything else, there is no dispute: *Beit Shammai ve'Beit Hillel be'maor lo peligi*. A *baraita* confirms this: Beit Shammai's order is *ner, mazon, besamim, havdalah*, and Beit Hillel's is *ner, besamim, mazon, havdalah*. Both houses begin with *ner*.

### Besamim vs Mazon

The actual question is where *birkat hamazon* and *besamim* fall relative to one another. The Gemara is thus asking Rava: why were you performing *besamim* before *ner*, when all agree *ner* comes first?

### Meir vs Yehuda

Rava explains: the *baraita* just quoted, in which there is a three-way debate among the elements, represents the view of Rabbi Meir. But Rabbi Yehuda's position — which the Gemara had already cited on the first *amud* — is that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel never debated the placement of *birkat hamazon* at all. According to Rabbi Yehuda, everyone agrees that *birkat hamazon* comes first, and *havdalah* comes last. What they debated is solely the relative order of *ma'or* and *besamim*. It is in keeping with Rabbi Yehuda's approach that Rava was practicing — doing *besamim* first, in accordance with Beit Hillel — and Rabbi Yochanan rules: *halacha ke'Beit Hillel aliba de'Rabbi Yehuda*. Practically speaking, when combining *birkat hamazon* with *havdalah*, one begins with *birkat hamazon*, concludes with *havdalah*, and within the *havdalah* proper, *besamim* precedes *ma'or*.

The Gemara does not elaborate on the underlying reason for this specific debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel — unlike earlier disputes in the chapter, where the *gemara* probed deeply to find the root of disagreement. One might understand that *ner* carries the more overtly religious message — both as a marker that fire could not be kindled throughout *Shabbos*, and as a memorial to the first creative act of humanity, the making of fire by *Adam HaRishon* after the first *Shabbos*. Beit Shammai may therefore place *ma'or* first because of the primacy of that message. The *besamim*, by contrast, serves to restore the spirit after the departure of the *neshama yeseira*. Beit Hillel may wish to revive the person first, and only then turn to the more formal religious act.

### Shammai/Hillel Order

To summarize the two positions in the *baraita*: *Beit Shammai omrim al hama'or ve'achar kach al habesamim* — first *ma'or* and then *besamim*. *Beit Hillel omrim besamim ve'achar kach hama'or* — *besamim* first, then light.

### Tadir Discussion

One student raised an interesting observation: the distinction between *ma'or* and *besamim* parallels the *tadir* principle. *Ma'or* is performed only once a week, on *motzaei Shabbos*, whereas *besamim* could potentially be encountered more frequently. Beit Hillel, who elsewhere rules that *yayin* comes before *yom* because it is *tadir*, may here be applying the same logic — *besamim*, being the more regularly performed, comes first. This is a compelling parallel for understanding Beit Hillel's position, even if it leaves Beit Shammai's reasoning to be accounted for separately.

---

## Bara vs Borei

### Text Difference

The Mishnah records that Beit Shammai formulates the blessing on fire as *she'bara ma'or ha'eish* — using the past-tense verb *bara* — while Beit Hillel says *borei me'orei ha'eish*, using the present-participial form *borei*.

### Rava Clarifies

Rava observes that on the question of *bara* versus *borei*, there is actually no dispute: *be'bara kuli alma lo peligi de'bara mashma* — everyone agrees that *bara* signifies the past tense. The apparent debate over *bara* and *borei* dissolves once one recognizes that *borei*, too, can carry the sense of past creation. Rav Yosef challenges this by citing multiple biblical phrases — *yotzer or u'vorei choshech*, *yotzer harim u'vorei ruach*, *borei shamayim ve'noteihem* — all of which use *borei* in contexts that clearly encompass God's past and ongoing creative activity. One might add the grammatical observation that some scholars debate whether Biblical Hebrew truly has a present tense, and whether the participial form functions as a verb at all or rather as an attributive adjective — either way, *borei* plainly encompasses past creation. Rav Yosef's challenge therefore lands: there is nothing to dispute between the two houses regarding *bara* and *borei*.

### Singular vs Plural

*Ki peligi be'ma'or u'me'orei* — the real debate concerns the form of the noun. Beit Shammai says *ma'or* (singular), Beit Hillel says *me'orei* (plural). That is where the houses genuinely differ.

### Shammai/Hillel Flames

*De'Beit Shammai savri chada nehora ika be'nura* — Beit Shammai holds that there is fundamentally a single light within a flame. *U'Beit Hillel savri tuva nehora ika be'nura* — Beit Hillel holds that a flame contains many distinct lights, of different colors and intensities. A *baraita* confirms this: Beit Hillel said to Beit Shammai, *harbe me'orot yesh ba'or* — there are many lights within fire, and therefore the plural *me'orei* is appropriate.

### Vilna Gaon

The Vilna Gaon offers a reading in which the two disputes — *bara* versus *borei*, and *ma'or* versus *me'orei* — are not separate but interrelated. He argues that what Beit Shammai describes when it says *bara* and *ma'or* is the *yesod ha'eish*, the ideal or essential form of fire — the Platonic archetype, as it were, which is singular and was created in the past. Beit Hillel, by contrast, describes fire as it actually exists in this world: ongoing (*borei*) and multiple (*me'orei*), because fire in reality consists of many differentiated flames. This interpretation maps neatly onto a broader pattern: Beit Shammai tends toward the idealized, heavenly conception of things, while Beit Hillel is rooted in how things actually appear in the world. It is a notable reading, though not mentioned in the Gemara itself.

---

## Non-Jewish Sources

### Light Lo Shavat

The Gemara now addresses the rules governing what light and *besamim* may be used for the *havdalah* blessing. The starting point is *ein mevarchin* — one may not recite the blessing over light or *besamim* that come from a non-Jew. The case of the *ner* is somewhat understandable: *mishum de'lo shavat* — because the fire did not rest. If the light was kindled on *Shabbos*, it is in some sense the product of a violation of *Shabbos*, and the very meaning of the blessing is that one could not kindle light until now. A fire that was lit in apparent violation undermines that.

### Avodah Zarah Concern

The case of *besamim* is less obvious. Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains: the *baraita* is speaking of fragrances that were used at a feast of non-Jews, and we presume that such a feast was conducted in honor of their gods — *de'mistama mesibat ovdei kochavim l'avodah zarah hi*. Therefore, those *besamim* are associated with *avodah zarah*.

The Gemara then raises a challenge: if the end of the Mishnah specifies *besamim shel avodah zarah* — fragrances connected to idolatrous worship — then the beginning of the Mishnah, which speaks only of *besamim* belonging to a non-Jew in general, must be addressing a different concern, one unrelated to *avodah zarah*. Otherwise, why would the Mishnah need to make the distinction at all?

Rav Chanina of Sura resolves this: the end of the Mishnah is not adding a new case but is explaining the beginning. *Mah ta'am ein mevarchin lo al haner velo al habesamim shel akum* — why may one not use the *ner* or *besamim* of a non-Jew? The answer is *mipnei she'stam mesibat ovdei kochavim l'avodah zarah* — because we assume that these items came from a feast that was dedicated to idol worship. The concern for *avodah zarah* is thus the explanation for the general restriction on non-Jewish *besamim*, while the distinct *lo shavat* concern governs the *ner*.

### Definition Shavat

A *baraita* clarifies the concept of *shavat* and *lo shavat*: *or she'shavat mevarchin alav* — if the light rested, one may bless upon it; *ve'shelo shavat ein mevarchin alav* — if it did not rest, one may not. But what do these terms mean?

If one were to say that *lo shavat* means the light was produced through a *melacha* — a forbidden act — then a light kindled for a midwife or a dangerously ill patient on *Shabbos* should be prohibited, since it was kindled on *Shabbos*. Yet a *baraita* rules explicitly that *or shel chaya ve'shel choleh mevarchin alav* — one may bless on a light that was kindled for such purposes on *Shabbos*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak therefore explains: *shavat machamat aveira* — the relevant concept is not whether the light was kindled on *Shabbos* per se, but whether it was kindled in a manner that constitutes a violation. A light kindled for *pikuach nefesh* was kindled in a fully sanctioned manner and is therefore considered to have "rested." A light kindled without such license, even by a non-Jew who is not commanded, carries the conceptual taint of Shabbos violation.

A further *baraita* reinforces this: a lantern burning continuously throughout the entire day of *Shabbos* may be blessed over at *motzaei Shabbos*. Even though it was burning on *Shabbos*, it was kindled before *Shabbos* and never violated it.

This leads to a parenthetical but practically significant observation. On *Yom Kippur*, the *halacha* requires that the blessing *borei me'orei ha'eish* be recited only over a *ner she'shavat* — a flame that was burning before *Yom Kippur* and remained lit throughout. One might think the opposite: if the purpose of the blessing is to acknowledge that fire cannot be kindled on *Yom Kippur*, the most dramatic demonstration would be to light a new flame the moment *Yom Kippur* ends. Yet the *halacha* requires instead a flame that persisted throughout — a point that has puzzled many, and which does not receive a clear resolution here.

### Nochri Mi'Nochri

The Gemara continues with a *baraita*: *nochri she'hidlik ner le'Yisrael ve'Yisrael she'hidlik mi'nochri mevarchin alav* — whether a non-Jew lit a candle for a Jew, or a Jew lit from a non-Jew, one may bless upon it. *Nochri mi'nochri ein mevarchin alav* — but if a non-Jew lit from another non-Jew, one may not.

The Gemara probes this carefully. Why may one not use a non-Jew's flame taken from another non-Jew? Because *mishum de'lo shavat* — we presume it traces back to a fire that did not rest. But if that is the logic, then a Jew who takes fire from a non-Jew should face the same problem, since the original flame also did not rest. The Gemara offers the reasoning that when a Jew kindles from the non-Jew's flame, what was forbidden continues in the original flame while something new — *atosfes de'heteira* — is added in the Jewish kindling; it is upon that new portion that the blessing is recited.

But then the challenge returns: if fire is continuously self-renewing — if *mah she'akar lo hiniach u'mah she'hiniach lo akar*, what one picks up is not what one puts down — why should *nochri mi'nochri* be prohibited at all? Each moment the flame is new. The Gemara resolves this by invoking the *halacha* that one who carries a flame to *reshut harabbim* on *Shabbos* is *chayav* for the flame itself, even when there is not enough of the underlying material to constitute a prohibited transfer — proof that legally the flame maintains its identity across time. The flame is not a perpetually new entity; it is the same object.

The *maskana* of the Gemara — as Rashi and Tosafos understand it — is that technically, even a flame kindled on *Shabbos* becomes permissible after some time has passed, since new fire has been added to the old. The entire prohibition in the case of *nochri mi'nochri* is a *gezeirah* — a rabbinic safeguard — enacted because of the one specific problematic case: when the non-Jew lit it shortly before *Shabbos* ended, and the very original flame is still burning. To avoid requiring people to make such fine distinctions, the Rabbis prohibited any flame in which the chain of transmission runs entirely through non-Jews, and permitted only when there is Jewish involvement at some point in the chain.

---

## Fire Use Rules

### Fire Outside City

A *baraita* addresses one walking outside a city who sees a flame: *im rov nochrim eino mevarech* — if the majority of the city's residents are non-Jews, one does not recite the blessing; *im rov Yisrael mevarech* — if the majority are Jews, one may. The Gemara immediately notes an internal contradiction: if a majority of non-Jews means one may not bless, then a fifty-fifty split should be sufficient to bless. Yet the second clause implies a majority of Jews is required. The Gemara resolves this by clarifying that even *mechtza al mechtza* — an equal split — is sufficient. The clauses of the *baraita* were phrased as parallel contrasts (*rov nochrim* / *rov Yisrael*) for stylistic symmetry, but the actual ruling is that fifty-fifty suffices.

### Infant Inquiry

A *baraita* presents a further case: one who was walking outside the city and saw a child holding a torch. *Bodek achrav* — one inquires about the child. If found to be Jewish, one recites the blessing; if not Jewish, one does not. The Gemara asks: why does the *baraita* specify a child? Even an adult presents the same question. Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains that the scenario is *besamuch li'shki'at hachama* — immediately after nightfall.
