In that context, an adult found carrying a newly lit torch would almost certainly be a non-Jew, since a Jew would not have had occasion to kindle a new flame so quickly after *Shabbos*. A child, however, might have simply grabbed a flame that was already burning — *im Yisrael hu ikri ve'nakit* — and thus the inquiry is necessary. The reasoning here is somewhat difficult to follow, and the Gemara does not resolve the apparent tension fully.

### Flame Thickness

A *baraita* rules that if one was outside the city and saw a flame, one may bless upon it only *im ava kefi kivshan* — if it is as thick as the opening of a furnace. If the flame is thinner, one may not bless. This introduces the principle that the blessing *borei me'orei ha'eish* is restricted to a flame serving the purpose of providing light.

### Non-Light Purposes

The Gemara explores what it means for a fire to be lit for the purpose of light through a series of apparent contradictions. One *baraita* says one may bless upon the fire of a kiln; another says one may not. The resolution: at the beginning of the kiln's operation, the fire is entirely for the purpose of smelting, not for illumination; but at the end, when material may be added to make the fire bright enough to work by, it serves the additional purpose of providing light, and the blessing may be recited.

The same structure applies to the fire of an oven or stove: at the beginning it is for cooking; at the end, if tended for illumination as well, it qualifies.

The case of the *beit knesset* and *beit midrash* generates a different kind of ambiguity. One *baraita* permits the blessing on such a fire; another prohibits it. The first resolution: if there is an *adam chashuv* present, Rashi holds that the lights are kindled for his honor — *lichvod* — not for illumination, and one may not bless. Tosafos reads the case inversely: ordinarily the lights in a synagogue or study hall are for honor, but the presence of an important person might prompt the addition of extra light for him to see by. Either way, when the lights serve primarily the function of honor, the blessing may not be recited.

An alternative resolution introduces two further variables: whether there is a *chazan* — here meaning a sexton who resides in the building and needs the light — and whether there is moonlight outside. If a *chazan* is present, the light may be understood as serving a practical function of illumination; if moonlight is available, the indoor lights serve only honor. The *poskim* of later generations applied these principles to candles in synagogues in their own time, and there was genuine debate about whether such candles were fundamentally for *kavod* or for light.

---

## Individual vs Communal

### Shammai Individual

The Gemara turns to the case of people seated together in the *beit midrash* on *motzaei Shabbos* when a flame is brought before them. Beit Shammai rules: *kol echad ve'echad mevarech le'atzmo* — each person recites the blessing individually.

### Hillel Communal

Beit Hillel rules: *echad mevarech le'kulam* — one person recites the blessing on behalf of all, *mishum she'ne'emar be'rov am hadrat melekh* — as it is written, "in the multitude of the people is the glory of the King." It is better to perform the blessing collectively.

### Bittal Beit Midrash

The Gemara finds Beit Hillel's reasoning self-evident. Beit Shammai's position requires explanation. The answer: *mishum bittul beit ha'midrash* — if everyone must stop, gather attention, and listen together, more time is wasted from Torah study than if each individual recites the brief blessing on his own schedule without interruption. A supporting *baraita* notes that in the household of Rabban Gamliel they did not say the equivalent of "gesundheit" when someone sneezed in the *beit midrash* — *mipnei bittul beit ha'midrash*.

This passage also touches on the broader question of *rov am* versus individual recitation that arises in other contexts — including *kiddush* and *havdalah* — and the related issue of whether it is *gadol ha'oneh* or *gadol ha'mevarech* that is preferred. Those discussions are not resolved here; the only consideration the Gemara raises in this context is *bittul beit ha'midrash*.

---

## Light/Spices Dead/Bad

### Dead Prohibition

The Mishnah rules: *ein mevarchin lo al ha'ner velo al ha'besamim shel meitim* — one may not recite a blessing over a light or *besamim* that were used for the dead.

### Honor vs Light

The Gemara explains: *ner lichvod hu de'avida* — when a candle is placed in a funeral procession or beside a corpse, it is not there to provide light but to provide honor to the deceased. Since the blessing on fire is contingent on the fire serving the function of illumination, such a flame does not qualify.

For *besamim*, the principle established earlier applies: the blessing on fragrances requires that they be present *lereicha* — for the purpose of providing a pleasant aroma to those present. The *besamim* placed near a corpse are there to mask the odor of death, not to provide a positive fragrance for smelling. That purpose does not satisfy the requirement.

Rav Yehuda citing Rav adds a further distinction: for a *meis* of sufficient importance that candles are carried before the bier both by day and by night, the candles are clearly for *kavod*, and one may not bless upon them. For a *meis* before whom candles are carried only at night — that is, primarily for light — one may bless. The Gemara notes that in any case, the concern of *hana'ah mi'meis* — deriving benefit from the dead — does not extend to such a candle; the connection is too attenuated to trigger that prohibition.

### Bad Smell Masking

Rav Huna extends the principle: *besamim shel beit ha'kisei* — fragrances placed in a bathroom to eliminate unpleasant odors — and *shemen ha'asui le'haavir et ha'zuhama* — oil applied to one's hands to remove filth after a meal — do not qualify for a blessing. In both cases, the fragrance or oil serves not to provide pleasant smell as an end in itself, but to eliminate something unpleasant. The ruling applies regardless of location: if the fundamental purpose of the fragrance is odor elimination rather than the positive experience of *reiach*, no blessing is recited. This principle applies even outside the bathroom — for example, household air fresheners whose function is to mask bad smells.

---

## Spice Blessings

### Perfume Store

The Gemara introduces the case of one who enters a perfume dealer's shop and smells the fragrances. *Afilu yashav sham kol hayom kulo eino mevarech ela paam achas* — even if one sits there the entire day, one recites the blessing only once. But *nichnas ve'yatza nichnas ve'yatza, mevarech al kol paam va'faam* — if one enters and exits repeatedly, one blesses each time. The question of what constitutes a distinct act of smelling for purposes of the blessing is relevant here, and the *poskim* also debate whether an inadvertent smell — one not consciously intended — requires a blessing at all. If *birkat hareiach* is a *birkat hanehenin*, then even unintended benefit would seem to require a blessing; if it is more in the nature of a *birkat hashevach*, the analysis may differ. The prevailing practice treats it more as a *birkat hanehenin*, given that one recites the blessing before smelling.

### Store Purpose

The Gemara raises a challenge: in the perfume shop, the fragrances are arguably not there *lereicha* — not for the purpose of being smelled. If that is so, how can one recite a blessing upon them? This is puzzling, since a perfume store is self-evidently a place of fragrance. The Gemara answers that the fragrances in the store are indeed made for smelling — *heicha de'nirchi inshi ve'nisvei ve'nizbenu minei* — the whole purpose is that people should smell and be attracted to come in and purchase. The good smell in the store is intentional advertising. The *hava amina* is not fully transparent, but the Gemara's conclusion is that the fragrances in a perfume shop do qualify as *lereicha avida*, and the blessing is in order.

A practical question arises from this: when entering a spice shop — such as a commercial spice store — does one recite a blessing? The fragrances there may be incidental to the purpose of purchasing packaged spices rather than intentionally provided for smelling. If one intentionally pauses to smell a pleasing spice, however, one intends to smell and the blessing would seem appropriate. The practical advice: once one begins to enter and the smell begins to reach one, recite the blessing at that moment and then smell deliberately.

### Outdoor Smell

A *baraita* addresses one walking outside a city who smells a pleasant fragrance from an unknown source. *Im rov ovdei kochavim eino mevarech* — if most of the population is non-Jewish, one does not bless. *Im rov Yisrael mevarech* — if most are Jewish, one may bless.

### Rabbi Yosi Concern

Rabbi Yosi disagrees: *afilu rov Yisrael nami eino mevarech* — even a majority of Jews is insufficient. The reason is *mipnei she'benot Yisrael mekatrot lichshafim* — Jewish women sometimes burn incense for purposes of witchcraft. The Gemara pushes back: surely the majority do not practice witchcraft. Rabbi Yosi's concern is more nuanced. There are in fact two minority uses of fragrant burning that disqualify: some burn incense for witchcraft, and some burn incense *legamurei et ha'kelim* — to infuse clothing with scent. This latter purpose is explicitly not *lereicha* in the relevant sense, since the fragrance is not intended to be smelled by people but to be absorbed into fabric. Together, these two minority uses are sufficient, in Rabbi Yosi's view, to make the majority of outdoor fragrances in a Jewish town unreliable for purposes of the blessing — *ve'chol ruba de'lav lereicha avida lo mevorchinan*.

### Regional Practice

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan gives a concrete regional illustration: one who walks in Teveria on *erev Shabbos* or in Tzippori on *motzaei Shabbos* and smells fragrance should not bless, *mipnei she'chazkatah eino asui ela legamurei et ha'kelim* — because in those places it was standard practice to use incense or fragrances for scenting clothing. In Teveria the custom was to do this *erev Shabbos*, and in Tzippori on *motzaei Shabbos*. The fragrance one smells in those places at those times is presumed to be for fabric-scenting, not for the nose.

### Akum Marketplace

A final *baraita* states: if one is walking through a non-Jewish marketplace and deliberately desires to smell the fragrances there — *nitretzeh lehareich, harei zeh chotei* — this person has sinned. Given the *avodah zarah* concerns associated with such a marketplace, the intentional act of smelling — *nitretzeh* — is the critical factor. A related discussion in Masechet *Pesachim* explores the broader question of how intentionality defines a halachic act of smelling, and how to understand situations where one smells inadvertently. Here the Gemara makes clear that *nitretzeh* is what activates the *issur*.

---

## Benefit Threshold

### Benefit Required

The Gemara closes with a principle that applies to the blessing on light: *ve'ein mevarchin al ha'ner ad she'yei'otu* — one does not recite the blessing on *ner* until one actually derives benefit from it. The discussion of this rule, and its practical and conceptual implications, is where the shiur concludes.

---

---

# Berakhot 53b

## Borei Meorei Ha'esh

### Deriving Benefit

The final *amud* of the eighth *perek* opens with a striking *halacha* that most people, in practice, misunderstand. The *mishna* states: *ein mevarchin al ha-ner ad she'ye'otu l'oro* — one does not recite the blessing over the flame until one derives benefit from it. The reason for this sequencing is rooted in the nature of the blessing itself. The *bracha* on the *ner* during *havdalah* is not a *birkat ha-nehenin*, a blessing for pleasure derived — the proof being that one does not recite it at other times during the week. Rather, it is a *birkat ha-shevach*, an acknowledgment and praise, recognizing that fire may now be used, that the creative week begins again, and — according to the *midrash* — that on *Motzaei Shabbos* Adam *Ha-rishon* himself first created fire. Because it is a *birkat ha-shevach*, one performs it *after* the experience, not before. One thus first looks at the flame — at one's fingers, at the light — and only then recites the *bracha*, not the reverse.

### Proximity vs. Use

The *Gemara* immediately opens the question of how literally to understand the requirement of deriving benefit. *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav* says: *lo ye'otu ye'otu mamash* — it does not mean one must actually derive benefit in a literal sense. Rather: *kol she'illu omed bikrov umishtamesh l'oro* — it suffices that the flame is of sufficient quality that were someone standing close to it, they could use it — and moreover, one may recite the *bracha* even from a distance (*brichuk makom*), as long as the flame possesses that quality. *Rav Ashi* similarly rules that even standing far away one may recite the blessing, provided the flame meets that standard. Two distinct principles thus emerge: first, one need not actually use the light; and second, one need not even be positioned close enough to use it.

### Hidden/Unseen Flame

The *Gemara* then challenges this reading from a *mishna*. The *mishna* states: if one had a light hidden in one's chest — perhaps a lamp or lantern — or saw a flame but did not use it, or used it without seeing it, one may not recite the *bracha* until one both sees the flame *and* uses it. The *Gemara* concedes that it is straightforward to imagine using a flame without seeing it — the flame is around a corner, so one receives light without a direct view. But what would it mean to see the flame and yet not use it? The *Gemara* initially suggests this refers to being too far away — but immediately withdraws that reading, since distance, on the view just established, should not disqualify. Instead, the *Gemara* resolves that the case of "seeing without using" refers to a flame that is sputtering out: one still sees a flicker of flame, but it is so weak that no one, not even someone standing immediately beside it, could derive any use from it. This is the only case excluded — not distance, but deficiency in the quality of the flame itself.

### Smoldering Embers

The *Gemara* proceeds with a *baraita*: *gechalim lochashot* — smoldering embers that are still active, whispering — one may recite a *bracha* over them. *Omimot* — embers in the process of extinguishing — one may not, since they are no longer strong enough to constitute a usable flame. The *Gemara* then asks: what precisely constitutes *lochashot*? *Rav Chisda* answers: any ember over which, if one were to insert a wood chip, it would catch and light on its own. If it would require stirring first to cause something else to catch fire, it does not meet the standard. The *Gemara* also notes a textual question about whether the word *omimot* is spelled with an *alef* or an *ayin*, and resolves the orthography from a biblical verse — *arazim lo amamuhu be-gan Elohim* — confirming that the correct spelling is with an *ayin*.

### Flame Quality Test

*Rava*, it should be noted, takes a stricter position: *ya'osu mamash* — one must actually derive benefit. Yet even *Rava*'s formulation is not taken with full literalness; *Rashi* explains that *mamash* means *omed bisamuch*, standing close enough to benefit — not that the act of benefit must be performed. The *Gemara* then asks how strong the flame must be, and records two opinions. *Ulla* says: strong enough to distinguish between an *issar* and a *pundiyon*, two different coins — one might compare this to distinguishing a quarter from a nickel by the flame's light alone. *Chizkiyah* says: strong enough to distinguish between the *meluzma* coin of Tiberias and the *meluzma* coin of Tzippori — essentially, to tell apart similar coins minted in different cities by the quality of the flame. The common denominator is a flame of genuine and usable luminescence.

### Examples: Rav Yehuda

The *Gemara* then offers three historical examples of *amoraim* making the *bracha* on flames at a distance. *Rav Yehuda* would recite the *bracha* on a flame visible in the house of Ada Dayyala, a neighbor, even though *Rav Yehuda* himself was not close enough to personally benefit from it — consistent with his own ruling that distance is not disqualifying. *Rava* recited the *bracha* on a flame in the house of Gurya bar Chama; *Rashi* notes that this neighbor lived close enough that *Rava* could, had he chosen, have used the light — consistent with *Rava*'s stricter position that one must at least be in a position to benefit. And *Abaye* recited the *bracha* on a flame he saw in the house of Bar Avuha. In all these cases, the underlying principle is the same: the flame must be of sufficient quality, and one may bless it even from a distance, at least according to all the positions prior to *Rava*.

---

## No Search for Candle

### Core Principle

The *Gemara* next records a ruling of *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav* that is, practically speaking, equally important and equally unfamiliar to most people: *ein machzirin al ha-or kederach she-machzirin al ha-mitzvah* — one does not go searching for a flame for *havdalah* the way one goes out of one's way to fulfill a *mitzvah*. If one has wine for *kiddush* and does not have it readily available, one buys it, one knocks on a neighbor's door, one finds an alternative. If one lacks a candle for *havdalah*, the ruling is simply to proceed without it. One does not go to the neighbor. One does not make a special effort. If a flame happens to be available, one blesses it; if not, one omits that component of *havdalah* entirely.

### Rav Zeira Practice

*Rav Zeira* relates his personal practice as an illustration: *me-reisha hava mihadarna* — originally, he would search around for a candle for *havdalah*. But once he heard this ruling of *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav*, he adopted it entirely: *ana nami lo mihadarna* — he too stopped searching. *Ella im mikla li mi-meila mevarachina* — only if a flame happened to come his way would he recite the *bracha*. This is a striking posture for *havdalah*, a ceremony that has in later tradition become highly ritualized with dedicated candles, ornate holders, and careful preparation.

### Spices/Components

The natural next question is what applies to *besamim*, the spices. The *Gemara* draws the conclusion *kol she-ken besamim* — all the more so for spices. The reasoning is instructive. The flame at *havdalah* at least marks something significant: the distinction between *kodesh* and *chol*, the first act of creation in the new week. The *besamim*, by contrast, serve only to restore the person — to compensate, as it were, for the loss of the *neshama yeseira*, the additional soul of *Shabbos*. If one need not search even for the more symbolically significant element, certainly one need not search for the more personal one. The *halacha* is therefore clear: if one lacks *besamim* or a candle, one recites *havdalah* without those components and does not go out of the way to procure them.

One might ask whether this ruling connects to the broader category of *birkat ha-shevach* — a category of blessing not triggered by the fulfillment of a commandment but by encountering something noteworthy. Just as one does not go searching for blossoming trees in order to recite *birkat ha-ilanot*, there is a sense in which the candle and spices of *havdalah*, not being the primary *mitzvah* — which began as part of *Shemoneh Esrei* and even when moved to *havdalah al ha-kos* did not inherently include these components — retain a character that does not generate an obligation to seek them out.

---

## Benching Location

### Mishna Dispute

The *Gemara* now shifts entirely to the laws of *birkat ha-mazon*. The *mishna* records the following dispute: if one ate and forgot to recite *birkat ha-mazon* and subsequently left the place where one ate, *Beit Shammai* holds that one must return to that place in order to bench; *Beit Hillel* holds that one does not. This rule applies specifically to bread, because bread establishes the concept of *keviyas makom* — a fixed place where one's meal is set and over which the obligation of *birkat ha-mazon* becomes anchored.

### Gemara Clarification

The *Gemara*, through *Rav Zevid* (and some say *Rav Dimi bar Abba*), clarifies the scope of the dispute. The debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* concerns only the case of *shoche'ach* — one who forgot to bench before leaving. But in a case of *mezid* — one who knowingly left without benching — everyone agrees that one must return to bench. The *Gemara* then asks: is this not obvious? It might have been thought that *Beit Hillel*'s leniency extends even to the *mezid* case, and the *mishna*'s mention of forgetting was merely to highlight the full stringency of *Beit Shammai*. The *Gemara* therefore clarifies: no, the dispute is specifically limited to the case of *shogeg*, and in the case of *mezid* even *Beit Hillel* concedes.

### Tower/Wallet

A *baraita* records the rhetorical exchange between the two schools. *Beit Hillel* challenges *Beit Shammai*: according to your position, imagine someone who ate at the top of a tower, forgot to bench, and has since descended. Do you require him to climb all the way back up? This seems an unreasonable demand. *Beit Shammai* responds pointedly: according to your position, if that same person had forgotten his wallet at the top of the tower, would he not climb back up to retrieve it? If he would ascend for his own financial interest, how much more so — *kol she-ken* — should he ascend *likhvod shamayim*, for the honor of Heaven, to bench in the place where he ate.

### Honor of Heaven

The force of *Beit Shammai*'s argument is that the place where one ate is not merely a convenience but the *halachically* correct location for *birkat ha-mazon*. Returning to that location is an expression of *kavod shamayim* — a level of seriousness about one's obligations to God that should exceed one's seriousness about one's personal financial affairs.

### Two Students

The *Gemara* then recounts two aggadic stories about students, each providing a pointed illustration. One student, in a case of forgetting (*shogeg*), went beyond the letter of the law and returned to the place where he had eaten to bench, conducting himself in accordance with *Beit Shammai*. When he returned, he found *arnaki d'dahava* — a wallet filled with gold coins. The deliberate echo of the tower-and-wallet analogy is unmistakable: he went back for God's honor, and found personal wealth waiting for him. The second student, who had left intentionally (*mezid*) and did not return to bench — a position that even *Beit Hillel* does not sanction — was eaten by a lion. The eating imagery is recursive: he was careless about where he had eaten, and was consumed in return.

It is worth noting that earlier in the *masechta*, the *Gemara* criticized someone for acting in accordance with *Beit Shammai* against the ruling. Here, by contrast, the *Gemara* presents *Beit Shammai*'s stringency as clearly praiseworthy. *Tosafot* makes this explicit: even *Beit Hillel* does not say that going back is wrong — only that it is not required. Going beyond the *halacha* and returning, as *Beit Shammai* demands, is evidently the ideal. The general ruling throughout the *perek* follows *Beit Hillel*, but the aggadah makes clear that *Beit Shammai*'s position represents the aspirational standard.

---

## Benching Location (II)

### Gold Pigeon Story

The *Gemara* continues with a related story. *Rabbah bar bar Chana* was traveling with a caravan when he ate, forgot to bench, and realized that the caravan was about to move on. He calculated that if he told his companions that he had forgotten to bench, they would simply tell him: *berich kol heicha d'mevarchet* — bless wherever you are, God is everywhere, why do you need to go back? He knew that argument would prevail and he would not be permitted to return. So instead he told them he had lost a gold pigeon — *yona d'dahava* — and asked them to wait while he retrieved it. He returned, benched, and when he arrived back at the spot, he indeed found a gold pigeon.

### Dove Symbolism

The *Gemara* then asks why specifically a pigeon. The answer offered is that *keneset Yisrael* is compared to a dove, as the verse states: *kanfei yona nechpa ba-kesef ve-evroteha bi-yerakrak charutz* — the wings of a dove covered with silver, and its pinions with gleaming gold. Just as a dove is saved by its wings — it escapes danger by flight — so too the Jewish people are saved by their *mitzvot*: *af Yisrael einam nitzolim ella be-mitzvot*. *Rabbah bar bar Chana*, by being *machmir* and insisting on benching in the proper place, was saved — and rewarded — through this act of *mitzvah* observance.

One might note that the story raises a separate question: *Rabbah bar bar Chana* told his companions something untrue and also caused them delay and inconvenience for something that was not *halachically* required of him. Without entering into the full discussion of truthfulness and permissible departures from it in the *poskim*, it is fair to observe that the *Gemara* presents the story approvingly, focusing entirely on his *chumra* in the performance of the *mitzvah* rather than on the means he employed.

---

## Time Limit Digestion

### Until When Question

The *Gemara* raises a further practical question regarding *birkat ha-mazon*: *ad eimatai* — until when, after eating, may one still recite *birkat ha-mazon*? The answer the *Gemara* gives is: until the food is digested. But what is the measure of digestion?

### Until No Hunger

*Rabbi Yochanan* says: *kol zman she-eino ra'ev* — as long as one is not yet hungry again. On this view, the window for benching could extend for several hours depending on the size and richness of the meal, since one does not return to hunger immediately after a substantial meal.

### Until Thirsty

*Resh Lakish* takes a different position: *kol zman she-yitzma machmat achilato* — as long as one is still thirsty as a result of having eaten. This is a notably shorter window. The assumption seems to be that once one has drunk enough to quench the thirst generated by eating, the meal has, in a physiological sense, passed. This would in many cases impose a significantly tighter time constraint than *Rabbi Yochanan*'s formulation.

### Four Mil Standard

A challenge is then raised: does not *Rav Ami* in the name of *Resh Lakish* state that the measure of digestion (*shiur ikul*) is the time it takes to walk four *mil* — that is, 72 minutes, on the widely accepted standard of 18 minutes per *mil*? How does this square with *Resh Lakish*'s thirst-based criterion, which could be much less? The *Gemara* resolves: *la kashya* — there is no contradiction. The difference turns on the size of the meal: a large meal (*achila meruba*) and a small meal (*achila mu'etet*) follow different tracks. *Rashi* and *Tosafot* debate which standard applies to which case, but in any event the operative ruling follows *Rabbi Yochanan* — one may bench as long as one is not yet hungry again — with the four-*mil* measure of 72 minutes serving as the general practical benchmark. In practice, the common custom is not to bench more than 72 minutes after the conclusion of eating, though questions remain about whether a sufficiently filling meal might in principle extend that window.

---

## Saying Amen

### Full Blessing Required

The *Gemara* now transitions to a different but related topic: the laws of responding *amen*. The relevant passage concerns saying *amen* after a *Yisrael* whose *bracha* one did not hear in its entirety — in contrast to a *Kuti*, after whom one does not answer *amen* at all, because one cannot be certain to whom he directed his blessing. The *Gemara*'s formulation implies that after a *Yisrael* one may answer *amen* even without having heard the entire blessing. But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this: if one did not hear the complete *bracha*, how could one possibly be *yotzei*? *Chiyya bar Rav* resolves the difficulty: the case concerns one who did not eat together with the group and therefore has no obligation to be *yotzei* through the *bracha* in the first place. The *amen* here is purely a social response — an act of acknowledgment and participation — not a mechanism for fulfilling one's own obligation.

### Amen vs. Yotzei

This distinction is essential and has wide practical ramifications. Saying *amen* and being *yotzei* are two separate functions. When one is attempting to fulfill one's own obligation through another person's recitation — as is common with *kiddush* on Friday night, where family members rely on the *ba'al ha-bayit* — one must hear every single word of the *bracha*. The *Shulchan Aruch* rules accordingly. In practice this is frequently compromised: people begin singing along with the *bracha*, or speak, or fail to attend carefully enough. Missing a substantive word in the *bracha* through which one is being *yotzei* is a genuine *halachic* problem, and one that demands real care, particularly on *Shabbos* night.

---

## Saying Amen (II)

### Rambam View

The *Rambam* takes a position on this question that requires careful attention. He writes: *kol ha-oneh amen harei zeh kemotzi bracha mipiv dami* — whoever says *amen* is considered as though he himself uttered the *bracha*, since the word *amen* encapsulates and ratifies the entire blessing. He further writes that whoever hears a *bracha* from beginning to end, even without saying *amen*, is considered as though he responded *amen*. The structure of the *Rambam*'s formulation implies that the very act of saying *amen* stands in for hearing the entire *bracha* — as though *amen* is a complete substitute.

### Halakhic Practice

The *Kessef Mishneh* — who is the *Beis Yosef* — acknowledges that this is the straightforward reading of the *Rambam*, but rules that the *halacha* cannot be understood this way in light of the *Gemara* just cited. The *Gemara* itself raised the objection: if one did not hear the whole *bracha*, how can one be *yotzei* even by saying *amen*? The answer given was that the case involves one who has no obligation to be *yotzei* in the first place. This implies that saying *amen* alone, without having heard the complete *bracha*, does not discharge the obligation. Despite the *Rambam*'s apparent position, the *halacha* follows the stricter reading.

### Practical Issues

The practical implications are considerable. When one is being *yotzei* through another's recitation, hearing every word is not a matter of etiquette or attentiveness — it is the core *halachic* requirement. This is particularly challenging with *kiddush*, where the *tefach* of people singing along, the noise of the assembled group, or individual inattention can result in missing words. Missing the key language of the *bracha* — the essential formula that constitutes the blessing one is obligated to fulfill — creates a real question as to whether one has been *yotzei* at all. It is something that requires active and conscientious attention.

---

## Respondent vs. Blesser

### Rabbi Yossi View

The *Gemara* records a *tannaitic* dispute on a related question: between the one who recites the blessing and the one who responds *amen*, who is greater? *Rabbi Yossi* holds: *gadol ha-oneh amen yoter min ha-mevarech* — the one who responds *amen* is greater than the one who recites the blessing.

### Soldiers/Warriors

*Rabbi Nehorai* explains *Rabbi Yossi*'s position with an analogy. *Goyarin* — infantrymen — go down into battle first, engaging the enemy in the initial clash. Then the *giborim* — the mighty ones — come down and achieve the actual victory. The one who initiates is not necessarily the one who wins. The person who says *amen*, arriving after the *bracha*, provides the act of affirmation that crowns and completes the whole. The *bracha* without the *amen* is the charge without the conquest. This concept resonates with an insight that the importance of *followers* is often undervalued: a leader with no one following is simply an eccentric. The first follower who signals that the leader is worth following performs an act of social and communal power comparable to the leader's own. When one says *amen*, one declares to all present that this blessing is real, acknowledged, and shared — a communal act of recognition with genuine weight. Indeed, this line — *gadol ha-oneh amen* — is reportedly inscribed in large letters on the walls of the *Altneuschul* in Prague, almost certainly to discourage talking during *davening*.

### Both Equivalent

A *baraita* then offers a resolution: *echad ha-mevarech ve-echad ha-oneh amen ba-mashma* — both the one who blesses and the one who says *amen* are equivalent, *ella she-memaharim la-mevarech yoter min ha-oneh* — except that Heaven rewards the one who recites the blessing more swiftly than the one who responds. This is a *machloket tannaim*, with one view privileging the respondent and another treating them as practically equal while giving a marginal priority to the blesser in terms of heavenly reward.

### Grab Leadership

It is in this context that the practical advice of *Rav* is situated. *Rav* said to his son *Chiyya*: *chatof u'varich* — grab and bless, meaning: seize the opportunity to lead a blessing for a group rather than merely responding. Similarly, *Rav Huna* told his son *Rabbah*: *chatof u'varich*. This advice does not contradict the equal — or slightly superior — status of the *oneh amen*. The question of whether it is better for each individual to recite their own blessing versus have one person lead and others respond is a separate matter, governed by the principle of *berov am hadrat melech* — the glory of God is enhanced when a multitude participates together. The consensus is that having one *mevarech* with the assembled responding *amen* is preferable to breaking up and each reciting independently. But within that structure, *Rav* counsels his son to be the one leading rather than merely responding, in light of the marginal priority the *baraita* accords the *mevarech*.

---

## Children/Context

### School Practice

The *Gemara* records that *Shmuel* asked *Rav* the following question: *mahu la'anot amen achar tinokot shel beit raban* — what is the rule about saying *amen* after children in school who are practicing reciting *brachot*? These children are not reciting *brachot* in a context of obligation or fulfillment; they are practicing. Does the formulation of a *bracha*, absent the context of genuine obligation, warrant a response of *amen*?

### Practice Exclusion

*Rav* answered: *achar ha-kol onim amen chutz mi-tinokot shel beit raban* — one says *amen* after everyone except these children in the school context, *ho'il u-le-lamed asuyin* — since they are reciting solely for the purpose of learning and practice. A *bracha* without genuine context is not a *bracha* in the full sense, and does not generate the response of *amen*.

### Practice vs. Real

However, this exclusion is not absolute. The *Gemara* qualifies: *ve-hani mili bi-d'lo idan maftirayhu* — this applies only when it is not the time of their *maftir*. *Rashi* explains this to mean the time when children were given the *haftarah* to read, as was the historical practice of assigning the reading of the *haftarah* to minors. At that moment, the *bracha* is no longer practice — it is genuine performance in context, and *amen* is appropriate. The *Ra'avad* offers a broader reading: the qualification applies whenever the children are being *poter* themselves, i.e., reciting a *bracha* in genuine fulfillment of their own obligation — such as before eating or before taking a *lulav*. In those cases, even if the reciter is a child, the *bracha* has genuine meaning and warrants the response of *amen*.

---

## Oil/Water Barriers

### Oil Prevention

The *Gemara* now returns to the topic of *mayim acharonim*, picking up from the end of the *mishna*. A debate is recorded regarding whether having oil on one's hands prevents the recitation of *birkat ha-mazon*. *Reb Zilai* rules: *shemen me'akeiv et ha-bracha* — oil on the hands is a barrier to the blessing. One must clean the hands first.

### Zivai: No Block

*Rav Zivai* disagrees: *eino me'akeiv* — oil on the hands does not prevent the blessing. There is no impediment.

### Acha: Aromatic

*Rav Acha* takes an intermediate position: *shemen tov me'akeiv* — specifically aromatic, fragrant oil is the barrier. *Rashi* explains that if it is one's practice to use scented oil and one's hands are coated in it, one must wash before benching. Ordinary oil, however, does not present the same concern.

### Zuhmai: Smell

*Rav Zuhmai* — whose very name, the *Gemara* notes, seems related to the word *zuhama*, meaning stench — offers the broadest formulation: *keshem she-kohen mezuham pasul la-avodah* — just as a *kohen* who is *mezuham*, physically malodorous or blemished in certain ways, is disqualified from the Temple service — *kach yadayim mezuhamot pesulot la-bracha* — so too, foul-smelling hands disqualify one from reciting the blessing. The analogy to the *kohen* frames the recitation of *birkat ha-mazon* as a form of sacred service that demands bodily cleanliness as a precondition.

### Tosefta Source

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* demurs from citing these three authorities. He declares: *ana lo Zilai v'lo Zivai v'lo Zuhmai yadana* — I do not know these figures and cannot rely on their rulings alone. Instead, he grounds his ruling in a *baraita* (or, according to some versions, a tradition in the name of *Rav*): *ve-hiskadishtem vi-hyisem kedoshim* — "you shall sanctify yourselves and you shall be holy."

### Three Sanctifications

The *baraita* proceeds to parse this verse into a sequence of four sacred acts corresponding to the meal. *Ve-hiskadishtem* — "sanctify yourselves" — refers to *mayim rishonim*, the washing of hands before eating. *Vi-hyisem kedoshim* — "and you shall be holy" — refers to *mayim acharonim*, the washing of hands after eating. *Ki kadosh* — "for holy" — refers to the oil, the cleansing that follows. *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* — "I am the Lord your God" — refers to the *bracha*, the blessing of God's name. Three forms of sanctification through water and oil create the conditions of holiness in which God's name is then invoked. The equation of physical cleanliness with *kedusha* — holiness — is thus not merely metaphorical but structurally embedded in the sequence of the blessing.

### Mayim Acharonim

This *drasha* provides yet another source for the institution of *mayim acharonim*. *Tosafot*, notably, rules that in their time *mayim acharonim* was not obligatory, because the practical concerns that generated the original requirement no longer applied. Other *gemarot* ground *mayim acharonim* in the concern about *melach sdomis* — Sodomite salt, which posed a danger to the eyes if transferred from the hands to the face. The present *drasha*, by contrast, frames *mayim acharonim* more in ritual and sanctity terms than in health terms, with the washing representing a preparatory purification before the invocation of God's name.

One might observe that the rationale of *Tosafot* for not requiring *mayim acharonim* in Northern Europe is interesting when viewed against the history of eating utensils. If one no longer handled food directly with one's hands — because of the spread of forks and cutlery — then neither the health concern of *melach sdomis* nor the practical need for post-meal hand-cleansing would apply. The difficulty is that *Tosafot* appears to formulate this leniency in the twelfth century, while cutlery seems to have spread through Northern Europe in the thirteenth century. It is worth noting, meanwhile, that *mayim acharonim* remains widespread among *Sefardic* communities, where, at least historically, food was more commonly handled by hand. In any case, the *drasha* here — connecting hand-washing before and after the meal to the language of *kiddush yadayim*, sanctification of the hands, which appears in *tannaitic* literature as the technical term for priestly hand-washing — suggests a further layer of meaning in which the act of eating and blessing is understood as a form of sacred service, with all the attendant requirements of physical and ritual preparation that such service demands.

---

---

# Berakhot 54

## Intro & Framework

### Perek Structure

The ninth and final *perek* of *Masechet Berakhot* follows the pattern of its predecessor in presenting all of its *mishnayot* at the outset as a single extended *mishnah*. Whereas the earlier chapters addressed *keri'at shema*, *tefillah*, and the laws of *birkat ha-mazon*, this concluding chapter turns entirely to *birchas ha-shevach* — blessings of praise and acknowledgment that one recites in response to particular experiences, places, and phenomena.

### Miracles - Bnei Yisrael

The *mishnah* opens: *ha-ro'eh makom shena'asu bo nissim l'Yisrael* — one who sees a place where miracles were performed for the Jewish people recites *baruch she'asa nissim la-avoteinu ba-makom hazeh*, blessed is God who performed miracles for our forefathers in this place.

### Akum Uprooting

The *mishnah* continues: *makom shena'akar mimenu akum* — a place from which idolatry has been completely uprooted, one recites *baruch she'akar akum me'artzeinu*, blessed is God who uprooted idolatry from our land. It should be noted that the *mishnah*'s own text uses the term *avodah zarah*, referring to the physical idols and images themselves, not the practitioners. The background here is significant: the Torah in *Devarim* commands the eradication of all idolatrous shrines upon entering the land, and this *berakhah* celebrates the actual fulfillment of that mandate. This was composed in the era of pagan Rome, when images and icons were ubiquitous — making a genuinely idol-free locale all the more noteworthy.

---

## Natural Phenomena

### Thunder & Lightning

The *mishnah* then enumerates blessings for a range of frightening natural events: *al hizzikim ve'al ha-zeva'ot ve'al ha-re'amim ve'al ha-ruchot ve'al ha-berakim* — for *hizzikim* and *zeva'ot* (various startling or powerful atmospheric phenomena, to be clarified in the *gemara*), for thunder, for strong winds, and for lightning. For all of these one recites *baruch she-kocho u-gevurato malei olam*, blessed is God whose power and might fills the world. The *halakhah* as we know it does distinguish between the blessing for lightning and that for thunder, though this *mishnah* subsumes them together.

### Shem u-Malchut Debate

This is an appropriate moment to observe something striking about the *mishnah*'s formulation: the text of each *berakhah* is given only as a closing phrase, without the standard opening of *baruch atah Hashem Elokeinu melech ha-olam*. This omission may simply reflect the unwillingness to write God's name unnecessarily, with the full formula assumed.

However, the question cuts deeper. The first *Tosafot* on the *daf* states explicitly — *perush min ha-shamaya* — that all of these *berakhot* require *hazkarat shem u-malchut*, the full *baruch atah Hashem Elokeinu melech ha-olam*. This is indeed how we *pasken*. Yet a number of *Rishonim* hold otherwise, arguing that these *berakhot* were never elevated to the status of formal *berakhot* and were always more in the nature of *tefillot* — expressions of praise — than structured *berakhot*. On this view they never received *shem u-malchut* at all.

The tension arises directly from the *mishnah*'s silence on the matter. Since these *berakhot* are not *samuch l'chaverta* — they are not appended to a preceding blessing in a chain — there would be no independent reason to omit *shem u-malchut* if they were genuine *berakhot*. And yet the *mishnah* never mentions it. The accepted ruling is that they are indeed full *berakhot* recited with *shem u-malchut*, but the *Rishonim* who disagree are drawing on exactly this textual silence.

---

## Yammim & Neharot

### Water & Deserts

For *al ha-yammim ve'al ha-neharot* — exceptional oceans and rivers, presumably ones of remarkable power or scale — and for *al ha-midbarot*, wildernesses and deserts, one recites *baruch oseh ma'aseh bereishit*, blessed is God who performs the work of creation. A practical question arises here as it does throughout: if one encounters these phenomena regularly, does the obligation still apply? The accepted rule is that the *berakhah* applies if thirty days have elapsed since the last sighting.

### Yam HaGadol

*Rabbi Yehuda* rules that one who sees *ha-yam ha-gadol* — the Mediterranean — recites the more specific *baruch she'asa et ha-yam ha-gadol*. This is a dedicated blessing for the Mediterranean in particular. Of course, from our vantage point the Atlantic and Pacific are vastly larger, yet one recites *yam ha-gadol* only for the Mediterranean. The condition *Rabbi Yehuda* attaches is *bizman she-ro'eihu l'frakim* — only when one sees it at intervals, not constantly. If one lives along its shore and sees it daily, the element of wonder and special occasion has dissipated, and the *berakhah* no longer applies.

---

## Good & Bad News

### Rain Blessing

*Al ha-geshamim ve'al ha-besorot tovot* — for rainfall and for good reports — one recites *baruch ha-tov ve-ha-mativ*, blessed is God who is good and does good. Rain is grouped with good news because from the agricultural perspective life depends on it; it is unambiguously welcome tidings.

### Bad Reports

*Al besorot ra'ot*, or in some versions *shemu'ot ra'ot*, on bad reports, one recites *baruch dayan ha-emet*, blessed is the true Judge. How grave must the news be to require *dayan ha-emet*? This is a question that the *gemara* addresses separately.

### Shehecheyanu

*Bana bayit chadash ve-kana kelim chadashim* — one who builds a new house or acquires new objects recites *shehecheyanu*, the blessing of gratitude for reaching a new and significant moment. The question naturally arises for us: *bayit chadash* is straightforward, but what about purchasing a new suit, a new garment, a new appliance? The answer turns on the degree of joy and significance the acquisition represents. In the era of the *mishnah* and *gemara*, acquiring new clothing or objects was genuinely momentous. For us, it depends on context — when it constitutes a meaningful *simhah*, the *berakhah* applies.

### Herzog Anecdote

A well-known story is told about *Rav Herzog*: at the moment Israel declared independence, he rose and recited *shehecheyanu*. Someone standing beside him challenged him — where is the *halakhic* basis for reciting *shehecheyanu* over such an event? *Rav Herzog* replied simply: he was wearing a new tie. The implicit point was that if a necktie justifies *shehecheyanu*, surely the establishment of Jewish sovereignty in the land of Israel does as well. The story carries a genuine edge, though: it underscores how the formal *halakhic* structure of *shehecheyanu* focuses on the acquisition of *kelim* — physical objects and clothing — while events of far greater existential and spiritual magnitude, which generate incomparably deeper *simhah*, find no explicit home in the same framework.

---

## Me'ein Principle

### Bad & Good

The *mishnah* states: *mevarech al ha-ra me'ein al ha-tova ve'al ha-tova me'ein al ha-ra* — one blesses over bad [news] in a manner analogous to the blessing over good, and over good in a manner analogous to the blessing over bad. This is admittedly cryptic and the *gemara* will unpack what the analogous relationship means in concrete terms.

### Tefilat Shav

*Tzo'ek l'shavar harei zo tefilat shav* — if one cries out to God over something that has already occurred, that is a *tefilat shav*, a worthless prayer. God does not alter the past, and praying for a different outcome for an event that has already taken place is theologically incoherent.

### Pregnant Wife Example

The *mishnah* gives the first illustration: *hayeta ishto me'uberet* — if one's wife is already pregnant and he prays, *yehi ratzon she-teled ishti zachar*, may it be God's will that my wife gives birth to a son — *harei zo tefilat shav*. The determination of the child's sex has already occurred; the prayer comes too late.

### Misfortune Example

The second example: *haya ba-derech ve-shama kol tzevahah ba-ir* — one is traveling and hears a commotion in the city, the sound of emergency, and says, *yehi ratzon shelo tehei zo b'tokh beiti*, may it be God's will that this calamity not be in my house — *harei zo tefilat shav*. Whatever has happened has already happened. One may hope in general, but to direct a prayer toward changing an already-determined outcome is futile.

---

## City Prayers

### Entry & Exit Prayers

*Ha-nichnas l'krach mitpallel shtayim* — one who enters a city makes two prayers, *achat b'nichisato ve-achat b'yitziato*, one upon entry and one upon departure. This may seem surprising given the existence of *tefilat ha-derekh*, which addresses the dangers of travel; but entering an unfamiliar city presents its own dangers — unscrupulous people, unknown conditions, the vulnerability of a stranger in an unfamiliar environment. Hence separate prayers are warranted for both arrival and departure.

### Ben Azai View

*Ben Azai* takes a more expansive position: *arba* — four prayers in total, *shtayim b'nichisato u-shtayim b'yitziato*, two at each juncture. His reasoning is that each time one passes through — whether entering or leaving — one should do two things: *noten hoda'ah al she-avar*, give thanks to God for having been protected until this point, and *tzo'ek al he-atid*, call out to God for protection going forward.

### Tzoak Term

It is worth pausing on the *mishnah*'s choice of vocabulary here. The word used is *tzo'ek* — a word that connotes urgent, anguished crying out — rather than the more neutral *mitpallel*. This is somewhat striking. The *mishnah* earlier used *tzo'ek* in the context of a fire engine rushing past, where raw fear and urgency make the term viscerally appropriate. It also appeared in the example of praying for a son while one's wife is pregnant, a situation where the same intensity might seem misplaced. By the time we reach the city prayers, the use of *tzo'ek* may be deliberate — underscoring the real danger that entering an unfamiliar city posed — but it is notable that the term has now become something of a general verb for any earnest supplication, whatever the level of urgency.

### Bad Equals Good

The *mishnah* states: *chayav adam l'varekh al ha-ra k'shem she-mevarekh al ha-tova* — a person is obligated to bless God for bad things just as he blesses God for good things. The theological underpinning is the belief that everything comes from God and ultimately serves a positive purpose. The *mishnah* grounds this in the verse *she-ne'emar ve-ahavta et Hashem Elokekha b'chol levavecha*, and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.

### Two Inclinations

The *drasha* on *b'chol levavecha* reads: *bi-shnei yetzarekha*, with both of your inclinations — *yetzer tov* and *yetzer ha-ra*. Even the *yetzer ha-ra*, one's baser drives and desires, must be channeled toward the service of God. The famous *midrash* makes the point clearly: *imlo yetzer ha-ra lo bana adam bayit ve-lo nasa isha* — were it not for those urges, a person would never build a home or marry and raise a family. The obligation is to find constructive uses for every part of one's inner life.

### Soul & Might

*U'v'chol nafshecha*, with all your soul — *afilu hu notel et nafshecha*, even if He takes your life. This speaks to the obligation of martyrdom, the readiness to give up one's life rather than violate the fundamental obligations. *U'v'chol me'odekha*, with all your *me'od* — with all your wealth, *b'chol mamonekha*.

### Middah Drasha

Then *davar acher* — the *drasha* more directly relevant to the present context. *Me'od* is read not as "muchness" or wealth but as *middah*, measure: *b'chol middah u-middah she-hu moded lekha harei modeh lo* — for every measure that God metes out to you, you thank Him. The pun moves from *moded* to *modeh*: whatever God apportions — whether it appears favorable or not — is to be accepted with gratitude, in the recognition that *middah k'neged middah* in its deepest sense means that every divine dispensation is purposeful. One receives what one receives and responds with blessing.

---

## Temple Mount Conduct

### Eastern Gate

After all this material on *berakhot*, *tefillot*, and *birchas ha-shevach*, the *mishnah* shifts abruptly to rules of conduct at the *beit ha-mikdash* — a transition that may initially seem jarring but proves, as we shall see, to be thematically coherent with the *masekhet* as a whole. *Lo yakel adam et rosho k'neged sha'ar ha-mizrach* — one should not behave frivolously when facing the eastern gate of *har ha-bayit*, because *she-hu mekhuvvan k'neged beit kodshei ha-kodashim* — it is in direct alignment with the Holy of Holies. The entrance gates were oriented so that from the eastern gate one was facing straight through to the innermost sanctum.

### Entry Restrictions

*V'lo yikanes l'har ha-bayit be-maklo* — one may not enter the Temple Mount with one's staff, *be-min'alo* — with one's shoes, *be-fundato* — with a money belt, *uva-avak she'al raglav* — with dust on one's feet. Entry requires a state of deliberate, careful preparation; one does not enter this space casually.

### Shortcut Prohibition

*V'lo ya'asenu kapandarya* — one certainly may not use the Temple Mount as a shortcut to save time getting from one place to another. *Ve-rakika* — and spitting is similarly prohibited. These extensions follow by *kal va-homer* from the other restrictions already enumerated.

---

## Temple Blessing Formula

### Original Formula

*Kol chotmei berakhot she-ba-mikdash* — all the concluding formulas of blessings in the *mikdash* were sealed with *min ha-olam ve-ad ha-olam*: *baruch atah Hashem Elokei Yisrael min ha-olam ve-ad ha-olam*, blessed forever and ever. The *berakhah* then concluded with *baruch chonen ha-da'at*. This was the standard form.

### Sectarian Denial

The trouble began when the *tzedokim* — or, as the manuscripts may read, *minim* — began to undermine this formula. Their claim was *ein olam ela echad* — there is only one world, denying *olam ha-ba* entirely. It is worth noting that this issue is taken with great seriousness in *Sanhedrin*, where one who denies that *techiyat ha-meitim* is rooted in the Torah forfeits his portion in *olam ha-ba*. Whether the sectarians here are *tzedokim* in the historical sense — who, according to the Christian scriptures, explicitly denied the resurrection — or whether *tzedokim* is a scribal censorship of *minim* is a genuine textual question. What is clear is that some sect was actively propagating the view that there is no world beyond this one, and that this threatened to render the concluding formula of *berakhot* theologically ambiguous.

### Sectarian Response

The institutional response was *hitkinu she-yiyu omrim min ha-olam ve-ad ha-olam* — the formula was changed to *min ha-olam ve-ad ha-olam*, from this world to the next, making the affirmation of *olam ha-ba* explicit and unambiguous. The single seal *ad ha-olam* could be read as encompassing only this one world; the new formulation *min ha-olam ve-ad ha-olam* could not be misread in that way.

---

## Name in Greetings

### Greeting Enactment

The *mishnah* records a further *takkanah*: *hitkinu she-yehei adam sho'el bi-shalom chaveiro be-shem* — that people should greet one another using God's name. This stands alongside the change to the *berakhah* formula as one of the institutional responses to the challenges of the period.

### Biblical Proofs

Two scriptural sources are adduced. The first is the scene at the harvest in Rus: *ve-hinei Boaz ba mi-beit lechem va-yomer la-kotzrim Hashem imakhem va-yomru lo yevarkhekha Hashem* — Boaz arrived from Beit Lechem and said to the harvesters, "God be with you," and they replied, "God bless you." Boaz used God's name as a greeting, and it is treated as entirely appropriate. The second proof is from the *malakh*'s salutation: *Hashem imkha gibor ha-hayil*, God is with you, O mighty man of valor. Both passages demonstrate that invoking God's name in a greeting is not only permissible but exemplary.

### Elder Respect

The *mishnah* also cites: *al tivuz ki ziknah imekha* — do not despise [the teaching] because your mother has grown old. The reading applied here is that *ziknei amecha*, the elders of your people, have established this practice; follow their example just as one would follow the example set by Boaz.

### Eis La-Asot

The *mishnah* then invokes: *et la-asot la-Hashem heferu toratekha* — a time to act for God, they have violated Your Torah. *Rav Natan* reads this as: *heferu toratekha*, [we are prepared to] violate the Torah *mishum et la-asot la-Hashem*, for the sake of serving God. *Rashi* underscores this point carefully — and indeed more than once in his commentary — noting that what might appear to be a violation of the rule against unnecessary invocation of God's name is in fact justified here precisely because it serves a greater sacred purpose. The concern being addressed is whether using God's name in a casual daily greeting is inappropriate, and the answer the *mishnah* gives is that when the purpose is to bring holiness into daily life, the *takkanah* is warranted even at the apparent cost of what might look like ordinary usage of the divine name.

### Framing & Kedusha

This is a striking and deliberate way to conclude *Masechet Berakhot*. The discussion of God's name in greetings, of conduct on *har ha-bayit*, and of the *berakhah* formula in the *mikdash* all converge around a single question: how does one bring *kedushah* into daily life in a world without the *mikdash*? It is also worth noting how this ending resonates with the *masekhet*'s opening. *Masechet Berakhot* famously begins by fixing the time for *keri'at shema* according to when the *kohanim* descend for their *tevilah* — a reference to the *mikdash* at the very outset. The *masekhet* thus begins and ends with the *mikdash* as its frame of reference. The entire tractate can be read as an extended meditation on how, in the absence of the *mikdash*, one constructs a life of divine service through *berakhot*, *tefillah*, and *keri'at shema* — and perhaps even through a simple greeting to a friend, conducted in God's name.

---

## Gemara Miracles

### Source Proof

The *gemara* opens its analysis of the first *mishnah* by asking: *mina hani mili* — from where do we know that one makes a *berakhah* at a place where miracles occurred? *Rabbi Yochanan* cites the verse: *va-yomer Yisrael baruch Hashem asher hitzil* — and Israel said, blessed is God who delivered. The model is *Yisrael* himself giving praise; what was sufficient for *Yisrael* establishes the precedent for all generations.

### Public vs Private

This leads immediately to a question: the *mishnah* speaks specifically of *nissim l'Yisrael*, miracles performed for the Jewish people collectively. Does this mean that only *anissa d'rabim* — a public miracle affecting the masses — obligates a *berakhah*, while *anissa d'yachid* — a miracle that happened to an individual — does not? The *gemara* raises this as a genuine issue.

### Lion Miracle

The first story: there was a certain man, *d'hava ka'azil b'Avar Yemina* — who was traveling through *Avar Yemina* — when a lion attacked him and a miracle occurred and he was saved. He came before *Rava*, who told him: *kol eimas d'matyas le-hasam barich* — every time you pass that place, make a *berakhah*: *baruch she'asah li nes ba-makom hazeh*, blessed is God who performed a miracle for me in this place. The *berakhah* is personalized — *li*, for me — and is tied to that specific location.

### Water & Wall

The second story involves *Mar* son of *Ravina*. On one occasion, *hava ka'azil b'Piska d'Aravot*, he was traveling through the valley of *Aravot* and became desperately thirsty. A miracle occurred and a spring of water appeared, from which he drank. On a separate occasion, *zimna chada hava ka'azil b'ristka d'Mechuza*, he was going through the marketplace of *Mechuza* when a wild camel charged at him. A wall collapsed, he entered the opening, and was saved. When he subsequently returned to *Aravot*, he recited *baruch she'asah li nes b'Aravot u'v'gamla* — blessed is God who performed a miracle for me in *Aravot* and with the camel. When he reached the marketplace of *Mechuza*, he recited *baruch she'asah li nes b'gamla u'v'Aravot* — blessed is God who performed a miracle for me with the camel and in *Aravot* — reversing the order.

### Personalization

Several things are notable here. First, *Mar* son of *Ravina* felt at liberty to personalize the formula well beyond the simple *nes ba-makom hazeh* — he named both miracles explicitly and combined them in a single *berakhah*. Second, when he was at each location, he placed that location's miracle first and mentioned the other second — a natural impulse to foreground the miracle relevant to where he was standing. Third, and most importantly for the legal question: these stories demonstrate that even *anissa d'yachid* — a miracle to a single individual — generates an obligation to recite a *berakhah*.

The *gemara* concludes: *anissa d'rabim kuli alma mechayvei l'vrukhei* — for a public miracle affecting *Klal Yisrael*, everyone is obligated to recite the *berakhah*, even if it occurred long ago and one was not personally present. *Anissa d'yachid ihu chayav l'vrukhei* — for a private miracle, the individual who experienced it is obligated, while others are not. This is the distinction: the *mishnah*'s requirement of *nissim l'Yisrael* establishes a category of national miracles that obligate all of Israel in perpetuity, but personal miracles generate a parallel though more limited obligation that falls exclusively on the beneficiary.

---

---

# Berakhot 54b

## Crossings & Wadis

### Baraita Overview

The Gemara resumes near the bottom of 53b and continues onto 54b, where the *mishnah* has been discussing *brachot* made upon witnessing a place where a miracle occurred for the many — and, separately, a miracle that occurred to an individual himself. Now the Gemara transitions to a *baraita*: *tanu rabbanan*, our Rabbis taught.

The *baraita* lists specific locations and objects upon seeing which one must offer praise to God: the fords of the sea (*ma'avarot hayam*), the fords of the Jordan River (*ma'avarot hayarden*), the wadis of Arnon (*ma'avarot nachlei Arnon*), the hailstones of Elgavish at the descent of Beit Choron, the stone that Og King of Bashan sought to hurl at Israel, the stone upon which Moses sat when Joshua fought against Amalek, the pillar of salt that was Lot's wife, and the wall of Jericho that was absorbed in its place. Upon all of these one must give thanks and praise before God.

It is worth noting that the *baraita* does not specify a particular *nusach ha-bracha*, as the *mishnah* had. It also moves fairly quickly from place-centered miracles to objects — the stones, the pillar of salt — indicating that the focus here is somewhat broader than geography alone.

### Red Sea Crossing

The Gemara first asks what the scriptural basis is for each of these. The crossing of the Red Sea is understood from the verse *vayavo'u Bnei Yisrael betoch hayam bayabasha* — the Children of Israel entered into the midst of the sea on dry land. That this location constitutes a place of miracle requires no elaboration.

### Jordan Crossing

Similarly, the crossing of the Jordan River at the time of Joshua is anchored in the verse describing how the *kohanim* bearing the Ark stood fixed in the dry riverbed while all of Israel crossed on dry land: *vaya'amdu hakohanim nosei aron berit Hashem becharava betoch hayarden hachen, vechol Yisrael overim becharava*. The Jordan crossing differed somewhat from the Red Sea in that the water was not split in the same manner — a wall formed at one point while the lower waters drained away — but it was nonetheless a manifest miracle, and the location of the crossing is accordingly a place upon which one recites a *bracha*.

### Wadis of Arnon

The miracle of the wadis of Arnon requires more elaboration, since it is far less familiar. The Gemara derives it from a cryptic verse in *Bamidbar*: *al ken ye'amar besefer milchamot Hashem et vahev besufa ve'et hanechalim Arnon* — "therefore it shall be said in the Book of the Wars of God: Vahev in Suphah and the wadis of Arnon."

The Gemara expounds: *et vahev besufa* is read as *be-sof*, referring to those at the rear of the Israelite camp. At the time when Israel was about to enter Canaan, two *metzora'im* were walking at the back of the camp — as required, since a *metzora* must dwell outside the encampment. The Amorites, aware that Israel would be passing through a narrow mountain passage, had carved out hidden caves in the walls of the surrounding mountains. Their plan was to wait until the Israelites passed below and then attack them from above — a form of guerrilla ambush.

What the Amorites did not account for was the Ark of the Covenant, which traveled in advance of the Israelite camp and would level the terrain before them. As the Ark passed through, the mountains were caused to press toward one another. The protrusions of each mountain entered into the caves of the opposing mountain, crushing all the Amorites who had hidden there. The blood poured out and flowed into the wadi, eventually reaching the place called Vahev. The *metzora'im*, traveling at the back of the procession, witnessed this aftermath — the blood streaming from between the mountains — which the main body of Israel had not seen. They came and reported it to Israel, and Israel gave song.

This is the meaning of the verse: *ve-eshed hanechalim asher nata leshevet Ar ve-nish'an ligvul Moav* — the pouring of the wadis that inclined toward the inhabitants of Ar and leaned toward the border of Moab. The mountains inclined toward one another, and the blood flowed out accordingly. It is upon passing through this wadi that one recites a *bracha*.

It is worth pausing here to observe a broader point. We have now moved, subtly, from miracles that are directly rooted in explicit *pesukim* into territory closer to *midrash* — specifically a *midrash* that interprets cryptic verses. The subsequent entries in the *baraita* will move further still in this direction. The fact that the *baraita* obligates one to recite an actual *bracha* upon encountering these sites suggests that *Chazal* understood these accounts as genuine historical events, not merely rhetorical or homiletical constructs. This question becomes all the more acute when we reach the episode of Og.

## Hailstones Elgavish

### Stones Suspended

The Gemara next asks about the *avnei elgavish* — the hailstones of Elgavish. A *tanna* teaches: these are stones that stood suspended above one person and fell upon another person — two separate events, connected by the same stones.

They stood above one person: this refers to Moses, *ha-ish Moshe anav me'od* — for Moses is called *ish*. When the plague of hail was struck in Egypt, Moses prayed and the hail ceased — but the verse states *va-yachdelu hakolot ve-habarad u-matar lo nitach artzah*, the thunder and hail stopped and the rain did not descend to the ground. The understanding is that the hailstones remained suspended in mid-air after Moses called upon them to cease. They never actually fell. They were thus *al gav ish* — suspended above the person of Moses.

### Beit Choron Context

They then descended upon another person: this is Joshua, of whom the verse says *kach lecha et Yehoshua bin Nun ish asher ruach bo* — Joshua is also called *ish*. And the verse recounts: *va-yehi benosam mipnei Bnei Yisrael hem be-morad Beit Choron va-Hashem hishlich aleihem avanim gedolot* — when the enemies fled before the Children of Israel at the descent of Beit Choron, God hurled great stones upon them. These are the very hailstones that had been suspended since the time of Moses and now came down upon Israel's enemies at Beit Choron. Thus the site of the descent of Beit Choron is a place where one recites a *bracha* — and at least that second location is a definite geographic site.

## Og's Mountain

### Og Plans Attack

The *baraita* next mentions the stone that Og King of Bashan sought to hurl at Israel. The Gemara states plainly: *gemara gemiri lah* — this is a transmitted tradition, not derived from a *pasuk*. What follows is entirely *aggadic*.

Og calculated the size of the Israelite camp: three *parsa'ot*, roughly twelve kilometers across. He reasoned: if I can uproot a mountain the size of the entire encampment and hurl it down upon them, I can destroy them all at once. He went and uprooted such a mountain and carried it above his head, intending to cast it upon Israel.

### Mountain Destroyed

God then sent grasshoppers — or some creature capable of rapid destruction — to gnaw holes through the mountain as Og held it aloft. The mountain cracked and split, and rather than being hurled forward, it collapsed down over Og's own head, settling around his neck. He attempted to pull it off, *hava bei le-mishlafeh*, but could not.

### Og's Teeth

As Og struggled to free himself, his teeth extended outward in each direction — *mashchei shinei le-hai gisa u-le-hai gisa* — and hooked into the holes in the mountain, making it impossible to remove. This is the fulfillment of the verse *shinei rasha'im shibarta* — You have broken the teeth of the wicked. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish teaches: do not read *shibarta* (you broke) but *shirvavta* (you extended). The verse describes not breaking but a grotesque elongation that trapped Og by his own teeth.

### Moses Defeats Og

Moses then came to finish the battle. How was this possible, given Og's stature? The Gemara establishes that Moses was ten *amot* tall — derived from elsewhere in the Gemara, on the grounds that Moses could spread the rooftop tapestries over the *Ohel Moed*, which was itself ten *amot* high, and he could only have done so without a ladder if he were that tall himself. Moses took an axe that was also ten *amot* long, then jumped ten *amot* upward — placing himself thirty *amot* off the ground, roughly forty-five feet in the air — and struck Og at the ankle, *u-machyei be-karsulei*, and killed him.

The story is, of course, fantastical in the extreme — a theater of the absurd, one might say: a mountain cracking over a giant's head, his teeth caught in the rubble, while Moses leaps thirty *amot* to deliver the coup de grâce at the ankle. Yet the *baraita* treats it with full seriousness, requiring a *bracha* upon the site. One might speculate that the practical likelihood of ever encountering this stone is vanishingly small, which perhaps renders the obligation theoretical — but nonetheless the Gemara does not distance itself from the account. The *midrash* about the stone, incidentally, is more modest than the full narrative the Gemara constructs around it; the *baraita* mentions only a stone, while the Gemara elaborates into something considerably more elaborate.

## Stone Moses Sat

### Stone at Amalek War

The *baraita* also includes the stone upon which Moses sat during Joshua's war against Amalek. What is noteworthy here is that the natural expectation might have been to mark the location of the battle itself as the place of the miracle. Instead, the *baraita* focuses on the specific stone where Moses sat — the place where Moses held his hands aloft and thereby determined the outcome of the war. The emphasis is on the object and Moses' role rather than the battlefield itself.

## Lot & Jericho

### Lot's Wife

The *baraita* continues with the pillar of salt that was Lot's wife — derived from the verse *va-tabet ishto me-acharav va-tehi netziv melach*, his wife looked behind her and became a pillar of salt — and the wall of Jericho that was absorbed in its place.

### Punishment vs Salvation

The Gemara raises a sharp challenge. It is understandable that all the others are miracles, *bishlama kulu nisa* — but the fate of Lot's wife was a punishment, *puranuta hi*. Even granting that it occurred through miraculous means, one might have thought it makes no difference whether the miracle involved salvation or punishment. Yet the Gemara's reasoning here is that a *bracha* of thanks is appropriate specifically for a miracle of salvation, not for one of punishment.

### Specific Blessings

The resolution is to modify the text of the *baraita*. For Lot and his wife, one recites two separate *brachot*: upon seeing the pillar of salt that was Lot's wife, one says *Baruch Dayan HaEmet*; upon seeing the place associated with Lot's salvation, one says *Baruch Zocher HaTzadikim*.

This is a striking passage for several reasons. First, if we follow those *rishonim* who hold that these *brachot* require *shem u-malchut*, then we are continually encountering new formulations of blessings — not simply the generic *she-asa nes* formula of the *mishnah*, but novel texts. Second, this is also the first miracle in the entire list that is not a national Jewish experience but rather a family matter of Abraham's relative, and one that occurred long before Sinai. Yet the Gemara creates a specific *bracha* for it. Third, the notion of reciting *Baruch Dayan HaEmet* upon seeing something that evokes divine judgment — even without it being a recent death or a fresh tragedy — is familiar from the practice of reciting it upon visiting a cemetery. Here too, the sight evokes the appropriate response regardless of when the event occurred.

### God Remembers Righteous

Rabbi Yochanan draws out a theological lesson from the *Baruch Zocher HaTzadikim* formulation: even at the moment of God's anger, He remembers the righteous. The verse states, *va-yehi be-shachet Elohim et arei ha-kikar va-yizkor Elohim et Avraham va-yeshalach et Lot mi-toch ha-hafecha* — when God was destroying the cities of the plain, He remembered Abraham and sent Lot out from the upheaval. The deeper point here engages with other *midrashim* that suggest that at moments of wholesale destruction, the destructive force does not discriminate between righteous and wicked — as in the command on the night of *Pesach* that Israel remain indoors, *ve-lo yiten ha-mashchit lavo el bateichem linigof*. Rabbi Yochanan counters: no, God does remember the righteous even in such moments. Lot, who was arguably not himself fully righteous, was saved for the sake of Abraham.

### Jericho Wall

Returning to the wall of Jericho, the Gemara asks: the *baraita* says the wall was *absorbed* in its place — but the verse says it *fell*, *va-tipol ha-choma tachtecha*, the wall fell beneath itself. How are these reconciled?

The Gemara's answer involves geometry. The wall of Jericho was as wide as it was tall — *potya ve-ruma ki hadadi ninhu*, its width and its height were equal. Therefore if the wall had simply tipped over and fallen to the ground, the resulting pile would be as high as the wall was wide — which is the same as its original height. It would not have truly "fallen" in any meaningful sense of being brought low. For the wall to genuinely collapse, it had to be absorbed downward into the ground. Hence the *baraita* correctly describes the miracle as one of absorption.

## Four Thanksgivings

### Four Categories

The Gemara transitions from these historical miracle sites to a more universally applicable *halacha*. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: four categories of people are obligated to give thanks — *arbaah tzrichim lehodot*. All four are rooted in Psalm 107, a *perek* of *Tehillim* devoted entirely to the theme of divine deliverance and gratitude. The Gemara also notes the connection to the *Korban Todah*, the thanksgiving offering described in the Torah, which the Torah does not explicitly associate with particular triggering circumstances. These four categories supply those circumstances.

### Seafarers

The first category is *yordei hayam* — those who descend to the sea in ships. The Gemara quotes the relevant *pesukim* from Psalm 107: they saw the works of God and His wonders in the deep; He spoke and raised a stormy wind that lifted the waves to the heavens and plunged them to the depths; they reeled like drunkards; they cried out to God in their distress; He stilled the storm to a calm; they rejoiced; *yodu la-Hashem chasdo* — they gave thanks to God for His kindness and His wonders to humankind. The theme throughout is crisis, prayer, deliverance, and the obligation to offer public gratitude.

### Desert Travelers

The second category is *holchei midbarot* — those who travel in the wilderness or desert. The *pasuk*: they wandered in the desert in desolate places, found no inhabited city, cried out to God, and were led on a straight path. Again the concluding injunction: *yodu la-Hashem chasdo*.

### Healed from Sickness

The third category is those who were sick and recovered. What is notable here is that the *pesukim* explicitly frame this as a consequence of sin: *evilim mi-derech pish'am u-me-avonoteihem yitanu* — the fools, through their sinful path, are afflicted because of their iniquities. Their appetite fails; they cry out to God; He sends His word and heals them. Unlike the seafarer or the desert traveler, whose danger is circumstantial, the sick person's affliction is portrayed as arising from moral failure. The obligation of thanksgiving nonetheless applies equally.

### Released Prisoners

The fourth category is those who were imprisoned and freed. Here again, sin is implicated — *ki himru imrei el*, because they rebelled against God's word. They dwelt in darkness and the shadow of death; God humbled their hearts through their affliction; they cried out; He brought them out of darkness. *Yodu la-Hashem chasdo*. The recurring structure across all four categories is striking: crisis, divine abandonment or distance, cry to God, deliverance, and mandated gratitude.

## Blessing Formula

### Gomel Blessing

Having established the four categories, the Gemara asks: what precisely does one recite? Rav Yehuda states: *Baruch gomel chasadim tovim* — Blessed is He who bestows good kindnesses. This is the basis of the familiar *birkat ha-gomel*, though our standard *nusach* — *Baruch Atah Hashem ha-gomel le-chayavim tovot she-gemalani kol tov* — is somewhat more elaborate.

### Ten Witnesses

Abaye adds a procedural requirement: one must recite this *bracha* before ten people, *tzarich le-oduyei kammai asara*. The source is the verse from Psalm 107: *ve-yeromemuhu bi-kehal am* — they shall exalt Him in the congregation of the people. A *kahal* constitutes a quorum of ten.

### Two Sages Required

Mar Zutra adds a further requirement: two of those ten must be Torah sages, *rabanan*. His source is the continuation of the verse: *u-ve-moshav zekenim yehaleluhu* — and in the assembly of elders they shall praise Him. *Zekenim* here refers to sages, and since the plural implies at least two, two of the ten must be learned figures.
