# Shabbat 2

## Intro to Shabbat

### Welcome & Seder Moed

Welcome to Masechet Shabbat, the beginning not only of a new *masechet* but of a new *seder*: Seder Moed. Mazel tov to all who completed Masechet Berachot.

### Length & Duration

Masechet Shabbat is a long *masechet* — 156 *dafim* — and we will be studying it for five months. Together with Eruvin, the two will occupy us for eight months. If one includes Pesachim, the first three great *masechtos* of Moed — Shabbat, Eruvin, and Pesachim — will carry us for approximately a year, covering the first half of Seder Moed.

### Structure & Perakim

Masechet Shabbat contains 24 *perakim*. The ordering of *masechtos* within a *seder* generally follows the number of *perakim*, which is why Shabbat, the longest, comes first. (Eruvin has 10 *perakim*, Pesachim likewise 10.) It is worth noting that, in the *Torah* itself, Nissan and Pesach are always first among the *moadim*, so there is a certain rightness to Pesachim appearing early in our sequence as well.

### Primary Topics

One might expect that a *masechet* devoted to Shabbat would be organized primarily around the 39 *melachot*, their *toladot*, and the associated rabbinic prohibitions. In fact, a large portion of the *masechet* — possibly the majority — is devoted to two or three major topics: *hotza'ah* (carrying), *muktze*, and cooking along with the rabbinic restrictions surrounding it. We do not even reach the *melachot* proper until the seventh *perek*.

The order of the first several *perakim* follows a broadly chronological rather than strictly thematic logic. We begin with an introduction to *hotza'ah*, which leads into discussions of what one may and may not do *erev Shabbat*, followed by further elaborations on carrying, then candle-lighting, and related matters — only arriving at the 39 *melachot* partway into the seventh *perek*. There is something significant, perhaps even intentional, in this structure: six *perakim* lead up to the seventh, which addresses Shabbat proper and its *melachot* — echoing the six days of creation leading to the seventh.

### Org: Chronological vs Th…

This contrast between chronological and thematic organization appears elsewhere in the tradition. The *Shulchan Aruch* generally follows a chronological order: *Hilchot Shabbat* begins with *kabbalat Shabbat*, candle-lighting, and the preparations of *erev Shabbat*. The Rambam, by contrast, always organizes thematically. Yet even the Rambam does not open *Hilchot Shabbat* with the 39 *melachot* — he begins with general categories applicable across all *melachot*, focusing particularly on intentionality, and only arrives at the 39 *melachot* at the beginning of his seventh chapter. The parallel is striking: six chapters in the Rambam, just as six *perakim* in the *masechet*, leading to the seventh where Shabbat proper is treated. This appears intentional. Anyone expecting the *masechet* to begin by laying out the *melachot* of Shabbat should be forewarned: we have approximately two months to wait before we get there.

---

## Reshuyot & Hotza'ah

### Mishnah: Two Which Are F…

The first *mishnah* opens: *yetziot haShabbat shtayim she'hein arba bifnim, shtayim she'hein arba bachutz* — the carryings of Shabbat are two which are four on the inside, and two which are four on the outside. This is somewhat cryptic as stated, and its precise meaning will be clarified as the *Gemara* develops. Based on the *Gemara*'s eventual conclusion, the *mishnah* means that there are two biblical and two rabbinic restrictions, both for the person on the inside and for the person on the outside. The *mishnah* then asks *keitzad* — how so? — and introduces its central scenario: *ha'ani omeid bachutz uba'al habayit bifnim*, the homeowner inside his home and the *ani*, the poor person, just outside the door.

### Reshut Hayachid & Harabim

The homeowner stands in a *reshut hayachid*, a private domain, while the *ani* stands in a *reshut harabim*, a public domain. The halachic definitions of these domains, it must be emphasized, are not about ownership but about physical configuration and use.

A *reshut hayachid* for the purposes of Shabbat is an area enclosed by walls — paradigmatically four walls, though three suffice. The criterion is structural enclosure. Even a walled city, in most cases, retains the status of *reshut hayachid* biblically, unless those walls are deemed entirely insignificant.

A *reshut harabim*, by contrast, is not simply everything that is not a *reshut hayachid*. It is a genuine public space — specifically, a major thoroughfare used by large numbers of people for transit, or a major public square serving as a gathering place. The precise threshold — how major the thoroughfare must be, whether it must cut through an entire city, how many people must use it — will be discussed in due course.

One might observe that these two definitions operate on different conceptual axes: *reshut hayachid* is defined by construction (walls), while *reshut harabim* is defined by use (public traffic). This asymmetry has real consequences: a *reshut harabim* that falls out of use is no longer a *reshut harabim* even if topographically unchanged, whereas a *reshut hayachid* is not defined by its patterns of use at all. This asymmetry also helps generate the intermediate category of *karmelit* and raises questions about cases where both criteria are present simultaneously — for instance, a major thoroughfare within a walled city, where it is unclear which definition dominates. Those questions will arise later.

### Karmelit & Makom Patur

Beyond the two biblical domains, there are two rabbinic domains. A *karmelit* is essentially everything in between — an area not enclosed by walls but also not a major thoroughfare. Rabbinically, one must treat it with the stringencies of both a *reshut hayachid* and a *reshut harabim*: one may not carry from a *karmelit* to either biblical domain, nor from either biblical domain to a *karmelit*. And there is a *makom patur* — certain spaces entirely outside the normal zones of use, treated as free zones where these restrictions do not apply. For now, the focus will remain on the primary domains.

### Biblical Carrying Rules

What does the *Torah* prohibit regarding carrying on Shabbat? Biblically, one may not carry from a *reshut hayachid* to a *reshut harabim* or vice versa. Carrying from private to public is called *hotza'ah* — taking out; carrying from public to private is called *hachnasah* — bringing in. As the *mishnah* states and the *Gemara* will explain, both are generically referred to as *hotza'ah*.

A second form of biblical carrying prohibition is *ha'avara* — conveying an object four *amot* (roughly six feet) within a *reshut harabim* itself. Even without crossing domains, picking up an object in the middle of the street, walking four *amot*, and setting it down constitutes a biblical violation.

Critically, both of these prohibitions require two endpoint actions: *akirah* — picking up or removing the object from its resting place — and *hanachah* — setting it down. Without both endpoints, no biblical violation has occurred. One can imagine scenarios where only one endpoint is present: the object was being carried from before Shabbat and was never lifted on Shabbat itself; or someone else did the *akirah* and handed the object to you; or you transferred it to another person who performed the *hanachah*. In all such cases, the full act of carrying has not been completed by any single person.

These requirements — *akirah* and *hanachah* — apply both to *hotza'ah* and *hachnasah* between domains, and to *ha'avara* of four *amot* within a *reshut harabim*.

### Hotza'ah: Non-Creative

A point worth noting before proceeding to the case analysis: *hotza'ah* is categorically different from all other *melachot* of Shabbat. Every other *melacha* involves some form of creation or transformation — some change of state in the physical world. Carrying from one place to another does not, in any obvious sense, create or transform anything. For this reason, the *Rishonim*, including Tosafot, characterize *hotza'ah* as a *melacha geru'ah* — a minor-grade or diminished *melacha*. This does not mean it is any less prohibited; it is equally *chayav mitah* when performed intentionally. But it lacks the natural quality of creative labor.

This characterization raises the question of why it is prohibited at all, beyond the fact that it is derived from the *Mishkan*. Two approaches are offered. One is that there is a subtle element of creativity even in *hotza'ah* — an object's identity and significance are to some degree constituted by its context and location, so transferring it between domains represents a kind of change of state. This is admittedly a stretch. The other approach connects *hotza'ah* to the prohibition against commercial activity on Shabbat. Business activity is only rabbinically prohibited, yet it is the paradigmatic weekday behavior: going to the market, buying, selling, bringing goods home. A central component of that activity is the carrying of goods to and from the marketplace. *Hotza'ah* may thus be understood as standing in for, or being conceptually connected to, the disruption of the Shabbat atmosphere that commercial activity represents.

The non-creative character of *hotza'ah* may also help explain the conceptual model underlying its definitions. The verse in *Yirmiyahu* — *al totziu massa mibateichem b'yom haShabbat* — frames the prohibition as taking from your houses into the public sphere, and the *Gemara* elsewhere derives the *melacha* from the *Mishkan*, where the call to stop bringing contributions (*al yetzei ish*) is understood as occurring on Shabbat. The underlying image is of taking from one's house out into the public thoroughfare — not a symmetric definition for both domains, but an asymmetric one rooted in the concept of one's private space versus the public world outside. This may be precisely why *reshut hayachid* is defined by walls (the conceptual model of a house) while *reshut harabim* is defined by public use.

---

## Ani & Ba'al Habayit

### Setup: Ani & Ba'al

The *mishnah* presents its cases through a vivid scenario. The *ba'al habayit* stands inside — in the *reshut hayachid* — and the *ani* stands just outside the door — in the *reshut harabim*. Between them is the boundary wall. The *ani* wishes to receive food; the question is who performs which part of the transfer, and who thereby bears halachic liability.

### Case 1: Ani Gives

*Pashat ha'ani et yado lifnim venatan letoch yado shel ba'al habayit* — the *ani* extends his hand inside and places something into the hand of the *ba'al habayit*. The *ba'al habayit* simply holds out his hand and does nothing further. Nevertheless, this is a biblical prohibition — the *ani* has performed the *akirah* in the *reshut harabim*, transferred the object across the domain boundary, and completed the *hanachah* by placing it into the *ba'al habayit*'s hand. The *ba'al habayit* played no active role; his hand served merely as a platform — what the *Gemara* will call *ma'aseh itztaba*. The *ani* is *chayav* (liable to bring a *korban* if done *beshogeig*); the *ba'al habayit* is *patur* — and as the *Gemara* will clarify, in this case not merely *patur aval assur* but essentially *patur umuttar*, since he performed no part of the act at all.

### Case 2: Ani Takes

The *ani* extends his hand inside, and this time takes an object from the hand of the *ba'al habayit* — *o natal mitochah vehotzi*. The *ba'al habayit* was holding the object passively; the *ani* performed the *akirah* (removing it from the *ba'al habayit*'s hand), moved it across the boundary, and brought it into the *reshut harabim*, completing the *hanachah* by holding it or placing it down. Again, the *ba'al habayit* acted as a mere platform. The *ani* is *chayav*; the *ba'al habayit* is *patur*.

These are the *shnayim bachutz* — the two ways the *ani*, standing outside, can perform a complete biblical violation on his own.

### Case 3: Ba'al Gives

*Pashat ba'al habayit et yado lachutz venatan letoch yado shel ani* — the *ba'al habayit* reaches his hand outside and places an object into the hand of the *ani*. He has performed the *akirah* inside the *reshut hayachid*, carried the object across the boundary, and effected the *hanachah* by placing it in the *ani*'s hand. The *ba'al habayit* is *chayav*; the *ani*, who did nothing, is *patur*.

### Case 4: Ba'al Takes

The *ba'al habayit* reaches his hand outside and takes something from the *ani*'s hand — *o shenatal mitocho vehi'chnis* — bringing it inside. He performed the full act of *hachnasah*: *akirah* from the *ani*'s hand in the *reshut harabim*, transfer across the boundary, and *hanachah* within the *reshut hayachid*. *Ba'al habayit chayav, ve'ani patur*.

These are the *shnayim bifnim* — the two ways the *ba'al habayit*, reaching out from inside, can complete a full biblical violation on his own.

### Two Become Four

The *mishnah* now addresses the partnership cases — where the two individuals each perform part of the act — and invokes the principle of *shnayim she'asu*: when two people together perform a *melacha*, neither is individually liable biblically. Each has done only half a *melacha*. These cases are nonetheless rabbinically prohibited. It is here that the two become four.

### Partnership: Ani Initi…

*Pashat ha'ani et yado lifnim venatal ba'al habayit mitochah* — the *ani* extends his hand inside holding an object, and the *ba'al habayit* takes it from him. The *ani* performed the *akirah* (in the *reshut harabim*) and the transfer across the boundary; the *ba'al habayit* performed the *hanachah* by taking it into his hand. Both have participated in the act; neither has performed it fully. This is a rabbinic prohibition for both. Following Rashi's principle that we attribute the act primarily to the one who performed the *akirah*, this case is counted primarily as the *ani*'s rabbinic violation, since he initiated the act.

### Partnership: Ba'al Initi…

Conversely, the *ba'al habayit* extends his hand outside, and the *ani* places an object into it — *o shenatan letochah vehi'chnis*. The *ba'al habayit* then brings his hand back inside, completing the transfer and the *hanachah*. Here the *ani* performed the *akirah* (by picking up and placing the object into the *ba'al habayit*'s hand), while the *ba'al habayit* completed the act. Again, both bear rabbinic liability. This case is attributed primarily to the *ba'al habayit* since, although the *ani* performed the *akirah*, the *ba'al habayit* initiated the transfer by reaching out, and it is he who brings it in.

Questions naturally arise here about what precisely constitutes an *akirah* and what constitutes a *hanachah* in these shared scenarios. If an object is resting in someone's outstretched hand, is it already considered *munach* — at rest — so that taking it from there constitutes a new *akirah*? And when someone brings an object toward themselves and simply holds it, at what point is that considered *hanachah*? These questions — what constitutes *akirah* and *hanachah* in edge cases — are not resolved here and will occupy the *Gemara* extensively in the discussions that follow.

One further question is whether these partnership cases are analogous to *chatzi shiur* — the question of whether performing only half a prohibited act carries any liability. They are not identical: *chatzi shiur* involves one person performing a partial act that never reaches completion. Here, the *melacha* is fully accomplished, but through two people. Whether *chatzi shiur* applies to Shabbat at all — and what would constitute a *chatzi shiur* in the context of carrying — is a separate and important question the *Gemara* does address elsewhere.

### Summary: 2 Biblical + 4

The structure of the *mishnah* can now be summarized. The *ani*, standing outside, has two ways to perform a complete biblical violation — taking out or bringing in entirely on his own. These are the *shnayim bachutz*. Similarly, the *ba'al habayit* has two ways to perform a complete biblical violation — the *shnayim bifnim*. Those two become four in each case when one adds the two partnership scenarios in which each is the primary actor (by virtue of performing the *akirah*). Thus: two which are four on the outside, and two which are four on the inside.

A natural question presents itself: why does the *mishnah* begin Masechet Shabbat with this particular scenario — a *ba'al habayit* and an *ani* — rather than with a more systematic exposition of the *melachot*? Tosafot raises precisely this question. He understands why the subsequent *mishnayot*, which address what one may have on one's person before Shabbat begins, belong at the start of the *masechet* — they concern *erev Shabbat* and are chronologically prior. But why open with this case? One answer is that this was a genuinely common scenario, particularly in a world where the poor would come to the door on Shabbat hoping for food. The image of a *ba'al habayit* with his door open and an *ani* standing outside seeking bread was not abstract. Another answer — and perhaps the more resonant one — is that *hotza'ah* is a *melacha geru'ah*, a non-creative act whose halachic details are far from intuitive. So much of the structure of *hotza'ah* — what counts as *reshut hayachid*, what counts as *akirah* and *hanachah*, why partial acts matter — rests on *Torah she'Ba'al Peh*, oral tradition, rather than on any visible logic derived from the nature of the act itself. The *Gemara* elsewhere notes that it is precisely such areas — where the halachic structure is not self-evident — that receive particular emphasis. Beginning the *masechet* here signals to the student that a great deal of what follows will require careful attention to transmitted tradition rather than intuitive reasoning.

The choice of the *ani* and *ba'al habayit* rather than two anonymous individuals may itself carry a message: even when performing an act of *tzedakah* and *chesed*, one does not override the prohibitions of Shabbat. There are other ways to give food to the poor that do not involve a biblical — or even a rabbinic — violation. That point, made through a scenario where someone might naturally assume the good deed justifies the means, is a powerful opening lesson.

---

## Gemara: Av & Toledah

### Why Different Structure?

The *Gemara* opens with a comparative question. It notes that the *mishnah* in Shevu'ot also opens with a formula of "two which are four," as do several other *mishnayot*. But the Shabbat *mishnah* says "two which are four on the inside, and two which are four on the outside" — doubling the formula. The *mishnayot* in Shevu'ot and elsewhere simply say "two which are four," without the inside/outside doubling. *Mai shna hacha d'tani shtayim she'hein arba bifnim v'shtayim she'hein arba bachutz? U'mai shna hatam d'tani shtayim she'hein arba v'tu lo?* — Why the difference?

### Parallels in Other Mishn…

To appreciate the *Gemara*'s question, one must survey the *mishnayot* in Shevu'ot that share this structural formula. The opening *mishnah* of Shevu'ot states that there are two types of prohibited *shevu'ot* which are four. The *Torah* explicitly prohibits oaths oriented toward the future: swearing that one will do harm (*le'hara*) — for instance, that one will not eat tomorrow — or swearing to do good (*le'heitiv*) — that one will eat something tomorrow. If one violates such an oath, one has transgressed a biblical prohibition. Those are the two. They become four through the parallel cases of false oaths about the past — swearing that one did not eat yesterday when one did, or that one did eat when one did not. Thus: two oaths about the future and two about the past — all biblical, all generating liability.

The *mishnah* in Shevu'ot also lists *yedi'ot hatumah* — awareness of *tumah* — as two which are four. One who is *tamei* is biblically prohibited from eating *korbanot* or entering the *Beit HaMikdash*. Those are two cases. If one forgot that one was *tamei* (*ne'elam mimenu*) — as the *Torah* puts it, it was hidden from him — and either ate a *korban* or entered the *Mikdash*, he would bring a *korban* upon realizing his error. Those two cases of forgetting one's *tumah* become four when one considers the parallel cases where one remembered one's *tumah* but forgot the status of the object — that the food was a *korban*, or that the space was the *Beit HaMikdash*. So two primary cases of forgetting one's *tumah* expand to four when one adds the cases of forgetting the sanctity of the object or place.

Then there are *maro'ot nega'im* — the varieties of leprous spots — which are also two which are four. The *Torah* enumerates *se'is*, *sapachat*, and *baheret* as categories of *nega'im*. The *Sages* understand that there are two primary categories, *se'is* and *baheret*, and that *sapachat* designates a derivative — a *toladah* — of each. So *se'is* and its *sapachat*, and *baheret* and its *sapachat*, give us the two which are four. Crucially, *sapachat* is itself mentioned in the *Torah*, though as a secondary term. Finally, the *mishnah* there also lists *yetziot haShabbat* — carryings on Shabbat — as two which are four, referring to our *mishnah*.

### Av vs Av+Toledah

The *Gemara* answers the structural question as follows: *hacha ikar Shabbat hu — tani avos v'tani toldahos*. Here, since this is a *masechet* dedicated entirely to Shabbat, the *mishnah* discusses both the *av* — the primary category — and the *toladah* — the derivative. That is why the formula is doubled: two which are four on the inside and two which are four on the outside, yielding twice as many cases as in Shevu'ot. *Hatam d'lav ikar Shabbat hu — avos tani, toldahos lo tani*. There, in Shevu'ot, Shabbat is not the central subject. Accordingly, only the *avot* are discussed, not the *toldahos*, and so the formula appears only once.

### Av: Hotza'ah, Toledah: H…

The *Gemara* then asks: what is the *av* and what is the *toladah* in the context of *hotza'ah*? The answer: the *av* is *hotza'ah* proper — taking from a *reshut hayachid* to a *reshut harabim*. This is grounded in the *pesukim*: the verse in *Yirmiyahu* — *al totziu massa mibateichem b'yom haShabbat* — and the verse in the context of the *Mishkan* — *al yetzei ish* — which the *Gemara* understands as referring to bringing the contributions from one's home (a *reshut hayachid*) into the camp of the Levites (a *reshut harabim*). The *toladah* is *hachnasah* — bringing from the *reshut harabim* back into the *reshut hayachid*. Thus the *av* is *hotza'ah*, the *toladah* is *hachnasah*, and by treating both, our *mishnah* produces twice as many cases as the Shevu'ot *mishnah*.

### Shevu'ot Puzzle: Two to…

A difficulty now arises. The *Gemara* proposes that the Shevu'ot *mishnah* deals only with the *av* — only *hotza'ah*, taking out. But *hotza'ah* alone yields only two cases (two ways to take something out — the *ani* doing it entirely, or the *ba'al habayit* doing it entirely). How does the Shevu'ot *mishnah* reach four?

One might suggest that the Shevu'ot *mishnah* expands to four by including the rabbinic partnership cases — the *derabbanans* — while still confining itself to the *av* of *hotza'ah* and setting aside *hachnasah* entirely. But this cannot be right. The *Gemara* points to the presence of *maro'ot nega'im* in the same *mishnah*: *dedumya demaros nega'im katani. Ma hasam kulhu l'chiyuva — af hacha nami kulhu l'chiyuva*. The spots of leprosy, where *sapachat* is itself mentioned in the *Torah*, establish that every item in that *mishnah* — all four of the "two which are four" — are biblical transgressions. Therefore, the four cases in the Shevu'ot *mishnah* must all be biblical, not a mixture of biblical and rabbinic. The presence of *tzara'at* in the *mishnah* is the decisive indicator.

### Rav Papa: Chiyuvim & Ptu…

Rav Papa resolves the difficulty: *hacha d'ikar Shabbat hu — tani chiyuvei u'pturei. Hatam d'lav ikar Shabbat hu — chiyuvei tani, pturei lo tani*. Here, in our *masechet*, where Shabbat is the central subject, the *mishnah* discusses both biblical transgressions (*chiyuvim*) and exemptions (*pturim*) — that is, the partnership cases which are exempt from biblical liability but rabbinically prohibited. There, in Shevu'ot, since Shabbat is not the focus, only biblical transgressions are discussed; the rabbinic cases are omitted.

But this pushes the difficulty back: if in Shevu'ot we are restricted to biblical cases of *hotza'ah* alone — the *av* alone — we can account for only two cases, not four. *Chiyuvei mai ninhu? Yetziot! Yetziot tarti havyan* — taking out is only two. So the *Gemara* resolves this by explaining that the four in the Shevu'ot *mishnah* consist of *shtayim d'hotza'ah v'shtayim d'hachnasah* — two cases of taking out (*hotza'ah*) and two cases of bringing in (*hachnasah*). All four are biblical. The two of *hotza'ah* are the *av*; the two of *hachnasah* are the *toladah* — but all four belong to the biblical level.

---

## Hotza'ah Term Analysis

### Shevu'ot: Hotza'ah & Hac…

To summarize the position now established regarding the Shevu'ot *mishnah*: its "two which are four" consists of two ways to perform *hotza'ah* (taking from *reshut hayachid* to *reshut harabim*) and two ways to perform *hachnasah* (taking from *reshut harabim* to *reshut hayachid*). The two of *hotza'ah* constitute the *av*, the primary category; the two of *hachnasah* constitute the *toladah*, the derivative. All four are biblical transgressions. The Shevu'ot *mishnah* includes both *av* and *toladah* — but only at the biblical level, with no rabbinic cases.

### Our Mishnah: Ani & Partn…

Our *mishnah* in Shabbat presents a very different configuration. Its "two which are four" — whether *bifnim* or *bachutz* — does not consist of two ways of *hotza'ah* expanding to four by adding *hachnasah*. Rather, the two are the two ways the *ani* transgresses biblically — once by performing *hotza'ah* entirely on his own, and once by performing *hachnasah* entirely on his own. Those two expand to four by the addition of the two partnership cases in which the *ani* is the primary actor (because he performed the *akirah*). The structure is thus: from two biblical cases to four, where the additional two are rabbinic. An analogous structure applies to the *ba'al habayit* on the inside. This is fundamentally different from Shevu'ot, where all four cases are biblical and the expansion moves from *av* to *toladah* rather than from biblical to rabbinic.

### Hotza'ah Generic Term

This analysis creates a terminological difficulty: the *mishnah* uses the word *yetziot* — "takings out" — to refer to the entire category. But if the *mishnah* in Shevu'ot includes *hachnasah* as part of "two which are four," and if even our *mishnah* includes both *hotza'ah* and *hachnasah* within the *ani*'s two cases, how can all of this be covered by the term *hotza'ah*? Rav Ashi addresses this: *tana hachnasah nami hotza'ah kari lei* — the *Tanna* calls *hachnasah* — bringing in — also by the name *hotza'ah*. The *mishnah* in the seventh *perek* which lists the *avot melacha* formulates the prohibition as *hamotzi mereshut lereshut* — taking from one domain to another — without specifying direction. Transfer from *reshut harabim* to *reshut hayachid* is thus equally covered by the term *hotza'ah*. The word is generic, referring to domain transfer in either direction, even though conceptually the *av* is the outward direction and *hachnasah* is the *toladah*.

### Hotza'ah = Removal

The etymological basis for this usage is as follows: *kol akiras chefetz mimkomo — tana hotza'ah kari lei* — any removal of an object from its place the *Tanna* calls *hotza'ah*. Even when one is bringing something indoors, there is an element of *hotza'ah* — removal — because the object is being taken out of the place where it was resting. The *akirah*, the picking up, is itself a form of *hotza'ah* — a taking out of position — regardless of the subsequent direction of movement.

### Ravina: Implicit in Mish…

Ravina adds that this understanding is actually implicit in our own *mishnah*. The *mishnah* introduces the subject as *yetziot* — carryings out — and then immediately illustrates with a case of the *ani* sticking his hand *inside* and placing something in the *ba'al habayit*'s hand. The first example of *yetziot* is thus a case of *hachnasah*. This demonstrates directly that *hotza'ah* as used in the *mishnah* encompasses *hachnasah* — bringing in — as well.

### Rava: Reshuyot Framework

Rava offers yet another reading of the term. According to Rava, *yetziot HaShabbat* does not refer to the direction of transfer at all — neither bringing out nor bringing in — but rather to the *reshuyot* themselves: *reshuyot katani — reshuyot Shabbat shtayim*, the two domains of Shabbat. *Yetziot HaShabbat shtayim she'hein arba* would then mean: there are two domains of Shabbat which generate four obligations. The exact mapping of this reading onto the breakdown of the *mishnah* remains somewhat difficult, but the fundamental point is clear: the term *hotza'ah* encompasses domain transfer in both directions because it refers primarily to the relationship between the *reshuyot* rather than to the directionality of movement.

### Conclusion: Av-Toledah

To conclude: the *av* of *hotza'ah* is carrying from *reshut hayachid* to *reshut harabim*; the *toladah* is *hachnasah*, carrying from *reshut harabim* to *reshut hayachid*. Both fall under the generic rubric of *hotza'ah*, because the defining feature is the removal of an object from its place — *akiras chefetz mimkomo* — rather than the direction of transfer. The Shevu'ot *mishnah* presents a "two which are four" that moves from *av* to *toladah*, all at the biblical level. Our *mishnah* presents a "two which are four" that moves from biblical to rabbinic, covering both *hotza'ah* and *hachnasah* within the biblical cases themselves. The discussion of *akirah* that underlies all of this — what it means to remove something from its place, and how that interacts with *hanachah* in the various partnership scenarios — will be taken up in the *Gemara*'s continuation.

---

# Shabbat 4

## Previous Principles

### Patur & Domain

The daf begins at the very bottom of 3b with the word *iba'it eima*. Before proceeding, it is worth reviewing several principles that have emerged over the preceding days of learning. First, the word *patur* as it appears in the *Mishna* does not mean fully permitted — it still indicates a rabbinic problem. Second, regarding the location of an object: if an object is resting on your person and you are stationary, the object is considered to be in the same domain that you occupy. A useful way to picture this is that you become like a piece of furniture — the object on you is like an object on a table. Consequently, when you move, it is as though you are lifting the object off that table and removing it from its domain.

### Person as Furniture

This principle has a practical implication: if one finds oneself walking on *Shabbos* outside of an *eiruv* with something on one's person, one should not stop — because stopping is like setting the object down, and then moving again is like picking it up anew. That is the rule when the object rests on one's person and one is stationary.

### Hand in Two Domains

The situation changes, however, when one's body is in one domain and one's hand is extended into another. According to the way *Tosafot* mostly understands the *Gemara*, if one's person is inside, in *reshut hayachid*, while one's hand is extended outside into *reshut harabim* — or vice versa — and the object is held in that extended hand, the object is considered to be in neither domain. It rests in a kind of indeterminate middle zone. The central question the *Gemara* was grappling with is: given that the object is in this suspended state, may one retract one's hand?

The concrete scenario is as follows: one extends one's arm through a window on *Shabbos* without an *eiruv*, and the object in one's hand is now suspended over the airspace of *reshut harabim* — which, as was established, extends only up to *asara tefachim*. The object is neither in *reshut hayachid* (because the hand is outside) nor in *reshut harabim* (because the person is inside). May one pull the hand back in?

### Two Braitot

Two *braitot* were cited earlier, one permitting retraction and one prohibiting it. The *Gemara* offered various interpretations relating to when a *knas* — a rabbinic fine — is imposed and when it is not.

### Kaneis Resolution

The *Gemara* now resolves the tension. Two lines from the bottom of 3b, the *Gemara* states: *iba'it eima le'olam lo knasu* — in truth, no fine was ever imposed to prevent one who extended one's hand *beshogeg*, unintentionally, from pulling it back in. *Velo kashya* — there is no difficulty between the two *braitot*: *kan le'oto chatzer, kan lachatzer acheret* — one case refers to pulling the hand back into one's own yard, the other to dropping the object into a neighbor's yard.

The distinction is this: if one pulls one's hand back into one's own house, one has simply reversed one's action. The net result is as though nothing was done, and we permit that. However, if one's hand is suspended over *reshut harabim* and one then drops the object into a neighbor's yard, one has in effect accomplished something — the object is no longer in one's own domain. Even if the full intention was not realized (perhaps one wanted it in *reshut harabim* itself, not a neighbor's yard), part of the original intention has been satisfied.

This is the substance of the exchange between Rabba and Rav Nachman cited by the *Gemara*: *haita yado mele'ah peirot vehotzi'ah lachutz* — one extended a hand full of fruit outside — *mahu lehachzirah le'oto chatzer?* May one return it to one's own yard? *Amar lei mutar* — it is permitted. *Lachatzer acheret mai?* — what about a different yard? *Ve'amar lei assur* — that is forbidden.

Rabba then asked *u'mai shena* — what is the difference? In either case the object was in this middle zone, neither *reshut harabim* nor *reshut hayachid*, and one is now placing it somewhere. Rav Nachman responded with a somewhat idiomatic expression — *lechi tichol ala kura d'malcha*, weigh out for me a lump of salt — which *Rashi* explains either as a gentle way of saying "sit with it and you'll figure it out," or perhaps a mild expression of amusement at the question. The answer, once one thinks it through: *hatam lo it'avid machshavto, hacha it'avid machshavto* — in the case where one pulls the object back to one's own house, one's intention was not satisfied; we have essentially had one reverse one's action, leaving things as they began. But placing it in another yard means the object has ended up somewhere other than one's original house — part of one's purpose has been achieved.

The conclusion of all this is that while the *Gemara* had entertained the possibility of requiring one to stand with one's arm extended throughout *Shabbos* as a kind of fine — a position that seems extreme and risks the person simply dropping the object into *reshut harabim* and committing a biblical transgression — the resolution is that at least for *shogeg*, one is permitted to pull one's hand back. One may not necessarily drop the object into a neighbor's yard, but one may at least retract. Whether the same leniency applies to *mezid* is less clear; the *Gemara* seriously entertained the possibility that in a case of willful violation we might insist one keep one's arm extended even at the risk of it ultimately leading to a biblical transgression.

That same tension — how much concern do we have that a rabbinic restriction will lead to a biblical transgression — is precisely the issue in the next topic: the bread in the oven.

---

## Bread in Oven

### Remove Before Violation

*Ba'ei Rav Bibi bar Abaye* — Rav Bibi bar Abaye raised the famous question: *hidbik pas b'tanur* — someone stuck dough on the walls of an oven to bake on *Shabbos*. On *Shabbos*, one does not transgress the moment the dough is placed; the transgression requires the food to actually cook. This opens a deeper question about the nature of the transgressive act: is the act completed by the initial placement of the dough on the heat, on condition that it eventually finishes cooking? Or is the transgression constituted by the ongoing process of cooking, such that one is considered to be continuously involved in the act as it proceeds on *Shabbos*?

An instructive parallel is the case of planting a seed, where the *Rashash* notes that the seed must ultimately take root — a process that takes about two weeks according to *halacha*. Yet the act of placing the seed in the ground is the transgression, on condition that it is not a meaningless act, that it eventually takes root. One could ask the same question about cooking: is the transgression the initial placing on the fire, or is it the entire cooking process, of which the placement was merely the beginning?

With that conceptual backdrop, the question is: if one put dough in the oven on *Shabbos* and the natural course of events will result in the bread baking and a transgression being completed — may one remove the dough before it has finished baking in order to prevent the transgression? Ordinarily, removing bread from an oven on *Shabbos* is not a biblical prohibition — it is rabbinically forbidden as a form of skilled labor, *chochmah*, too reminiscent of weekday activity. But here, if one is not permitted to remove it, one will have committed a full violation of *Shabbos*. The question is: *hitiru lo lirdoto kodem sheyavo lidei issur chatas o lo hitiru lo?* Did they allow one to remove the bread before one became obligated in a *chatas*, before reaching the point of having violated *Shabbos* — or not?

### Shogeg vs. Mezid

Rav Acha bar Abaye posed the clarifying question to Ravina: *heichi dami?* — what exactly is the case? If we say the person placed the dough *beshogeg* — unintentionally, having forgotten it was *Shabbos* — and then continued in that state of unawareness, *velo yadei*, still unaware that he had done anything wrong — then who are we permitting to remove the bread? The person himself doesn't know there is a problem. He thinks it is an ordinary day. There is no one asking for permission.

So it must be, says the *Gemara*, *de-adkar ve-iftar* — that the person subsequently remembered it was *Shabbos*. This is a very common real-life situation: one walks into a room without thinking, performs some act, and then suddenly realizes it is *Shabbos*. Here, however, the realization is potentially helpful — if one is permitted to remove the bread at that point, one can actually reverse the problematic situation and prevent the full transgression from being completed.

### Chatas Awareness Rule

But the *Gemara* presses: if the person became aware in the middle — *mi mechayiv?* — even if he does nothing, he would not be obligated in a *chatas*. Why? *Ve-hasnan: kol chayavei chataos einan chayavin ad she-tehei techilasan shegaga ve-sofan shegaga* — all those obligated in a *chatas* are only obligated if they were unaware from the beginning of the act to its conclusion. If one became aware at any point during the commission of the transgression, one does not bring a *chatas*. One is not *chayav misa* because one did not begin the act knowingly, but one is also not *chayav chatas* because one did not complete it in a state of unawareness.

This rule also reveals something important about the nature of the transgression. If becoming aware midway through the process disqualifies one from *chatas* obligation — as though one became aware "during" the transgression — that implies the act of cooking is understood as an ongoing process, not merely the instantaneous moment of placing the dough on the fire. If the transgression were simply the act of placement, then becoming aware afterward would be irrelevant; one was fully unaware at the moment of placement. The fact that awareness in the middle matters strongly suggests that the ongoing cooking is itself considered part of the continuous act, and one is treated as ongoingly performing the *melacha* throughout the baking process.

### No Korban Question

This gives the *Gemara* pause. If becoming aware midway means one would not be *chayav chatas* regardless, why does one need permission to remove the bread? *Tosafot* questions the *Gemara*'s framing: one might think the goal is simply to prevent any violation of *Shabbos*, not merely to avoid the specific obligation of a *korban*. Even if one would not bring a sacrifice, the *melacha* would still constitute a transgression of *Shabbos*, and preventing that would seem a worthy enough reason to permit the removal. For some reason, the *Gemara* does not seem willing to frame it that way — it treats the rationale as being specifically about saving one from a *korban* obligation.

### Mezid Case

*Ella b'meizid* — so perhaps the case is one of willful violation. The person intentionally placed the dough in the oven on *Shabbos*. Now, despite having begun with full awareness and willfulness, a spirit of regret came over him — and the question is whether we allow him, even in this situation, to remove the bread. The *Gemara* notes: *kodem sheyavo lidei issur sekilah miba'ei lei* — the question should really be phrased as whether he can reverse the act before becoming liable to *sekilah* (stoning, the penalty for willful *Shabbos* violation), not before becoming liable in a *chatas*. This confirms that the case is indeed *mezid*.

### Rav Sheshet Challenge

*Maskif leh Rav Sheshet* — Rav Sheshet challenges this framing. He first raises the position *le'olam beshogeg* — that it really is *shogeg* — and asks: *ul'man hitiru? l'acherim* — for whom are we granting permission? Not for the person himself, who has walked away unaware, but for a bystander. Someone else witnessed the situation — passed by, noticed the bread baking, and wants to remove it in order to spare this oblivious fellow from the full transgression and the *korban* obligation. The bystander is contemplating violating a *d'rabbanan* in order to help someone who transgressed *beshogeg*.

*V'chi omrin lo le'adam cheit b'kdei sheyizkeh chavercha?* — Do we tell a person to sin in order to benefit his fellow? This raises profound questions. On one hand, there is clearly a real obligation toward one's fellow: one may not place a stumbling block before another (*lifnei iver, machshol*), one may not be a passive bystander when another is sinning, and there is a genuine *chiyuv* of *tochacha* — of remonstrance, of *l'hafrisho min issur* — separating one's fellow from transgression. These responsibilities are real. Yet it seems that this obligation does not extend to the point of actively transgressing oneself on behalf of another.

The case is actually *shogeg*, which makes the challenge more striking. The person was unintentional, would have been *chayav korban*, and yet even so, Rav Sheshet objects: we would not permit a bystander to violate a *derabbanan* to spare him. The analogy to *chayecha v'chayei chavercha chayecha kodmin* is instructive — one is not halachically required to sacrifice a limb to save another person's life, even though one must take significant steps to help someone in danger. There is a principle of proportionality and primacy of self that runs through *halacha*.

### Allow Removal

*Ella amar Rav Ashi le'olam bemezid* — Rav Ashi returns to the case of *mezid*. *Ve'eima* — and therefore shift the reading of the text: the question was not whether to permit removal before becoming *chayav chatas* (which would not apply to *mezid*), but before becoming *chayav sekilah*. Rav Acha the son of Rava (*Rav Acha brei deRava*) stated that the matter was actually transmitted not as a question but as a ruling: *amar Rav Bibi bar Abaye lo ba'ei* — Rav Bibi bar Abaye did not ask; he declared. *Hidbik pas b'tanur, hetiru lo lirdosah kodem sheyavo lidei issur sekilah* — if one placed the bread in the oven, they did permit one to remove it before becoming liable to *sekilah*. The conclusion is affirmative, and it is in the case of *mezid*.

This conclusion is consistent with a broader theme that recurs throughout Masechet *Shabbos*: the *Gemara* frequently permits one to violate a *derabbanan* prohibition in order to avoid a *de'oraissa* transgression. The concern for human psychology — that if no relief valve is provided, people will simply go ahead and commit the biblical transgression — is a recurring consideration. Whether there is a distinction between cases involving a new act versus reversing a previous act could perhaps be argued, but the conclusion here is the same: even beginning from willful violation, we allow one to violate the *derabbanan* and remove the bread in order to avoid *issur sekilah*.

### Tosafot: Interrupt Act

*Tosafot* raises a sharp question on the entire discussion. If a person willfully placed the bread in the oven, he is hardly the type to suddenly become punctilious about a *derabbanan* prohibition. If we were to tell him he is not allowed to remove the bread, who would listen? He would say: so now, all of a sudden, I'm going to be stringent about a *derabbanan* and thereby become *chayav sekilah*? The practical effect of prohibiting him from removing the bread seems negligible — he would simply remove it anyway.

One could respond that the question is simply whether he receives a demerit for violating the *derabbanan* or not, regardless of whether he would actually comply. But *Tosafot* does not find this satisfying. Instead, *Tosafot* proposes a remarkable *chiddush*: if we were to rule that he is not permitted to remove the bread, then his non-removal would be *ba'ones* — against his will, coerced by halacha. And if the conclusion of the baking process occurred *ba'ones* — because the halacha effectively tied his hands — then he would not be *chayav* for the completion of the act. Crucially, this reasoning again reflects the understanding that the act of baking is an ongoing continuous act: the initial placement was willful, but if the conclusion was *ba'ones* (he wanted to remove it and was prohibited), then the end of the act was effectively forced upon him.

The conclusion that emerges from *Tosafot* is therefore even more powerful: the *Gemara*'s preference is for him to actively violate the *derabbanan* and remove the bread — thereby genuinely interrupting the act — rather than to benefit from the exemption of *ba'ones* at the conclusion. It is better to interrupt the act genuinely and thereby not transgress at all, than to conclude the act under duress and be technically exempt. The commitment to avoiding *chillul Shabbos* is so strong that we prefer one incur a rabbinic violation in order to genuinely prevent the biblical one, even when the alternative would also technically exempt one from liability.

### Tosafot Distinctions

*Tosafot* then turns to address the challenge of Rav Sheshet — *omerin le'adam cheit kdei sheyizkeh chaveircha* — and notes that there appear to be numerous cases in the *Gemara* where not only is one permitted to violate a lesser prohibition in order to prevent another person from committing a greater one, but one may even be obligated to do so. How do we reconcile those cases with Rav Sheshet's position?

*Tosafot* offers several distinctions. The first involves a case where poor people had taken fruit from someone's field, and if the owner did not perform a certain minor *derabbanan* act, the poor people would end up eating *tevel*. In that case, the *Gemara* permits the owner to perform the minor violation. *Tosafot* explains: that case is different because the owner is implicated in the situation. The transgression that is about to occur is connected to the owner's role — the people took the fruit from his field, and he bears some degree of responsibility for what flows from that. He is not a pure third party; he is party to the chain of events. That is why we permit him to violate a *derabbanan* to prevent their sin.

A second distinction relates to the difference between *preventing* someone from sinning before it begins, as opposed to *reversing* a sin already set in motion. There is a meaningful difference between the two. When one can intervene before a transgression has started, the case for permitting a minor violation is much stronger. In the case of the bread in the oven, the initial act has already been set in motion — the transgression has begun. One's moral responsibility to help is considerably reduced when the other person has already dug their own hole, even if through *shogeg*.

A third consideration raised by *Tosafot* concerns the degree to which the person is to blame. If someone is about to transgress through no fault of their own — not willfully, not negligently, but simply by circumstances entirely beyond their control — the case for intervention is stronger. One might imagine a scenario where someone unknowingly purchased food from a store later found to be selling *treifos*, and one would have to violate a *derabbanan* — such as going *chutz l'tchum* — in order to get the information to the person in time. In such a case, the person is entirely blameless and there may be a genuine obligation to intervene.

### Self vs. Others

There is also the distinction the *Gemara* itself draws: the person in whose hands the situation lies — the one who originally placed the bread in the oven — clearly has more latitude to perform a minor violation to save himself from a major sin. That is why the *Gemara* ultimately shifted to talking about the person himself (*me*) rather than a bystander. It is one thing to say *ein omrin le'adam chatei k'dei she'yizkeh chaveircha* — we do not tell *you* to sin for *your fellow's* sake. It is another matter entirely when one is seeking to save oneself.

As for whether the *shogeg* case — where one became aware midway and would therefore not be *chayav korban* — also permits removal, the *Gemara* did not formally return to that question. *Tosafot* indicates that even so, the violation of *Shabbos* itself would remain something one would wish to avoid, and it would follow by analogy that removal would also be permitted in that scenario.

---

## Four-by-Four Requirement

### Poor Man Takes Bread

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Mishna*'s case of the *ani* and the *ba'al habayit*. *Pashat he'ani es yado* — the poor man extends his hand inside the house, takes bread from the hand of the homeowner, and carries it out. In so doing he has performed *akira*, *hotza'ah*, and *hanacha* — the complete act of carrying. The *Gemara* asks: *amai chayav?* — why is he *chayav*? *Ve'ba'inan akira v'hanachah mei'al gabei makom arba al arba v'leika* — we require the removal and placement to involve a space of four by four, and that condition does not appear to be met here. The object was taken from the homeowner's hand, which is not a *makom arba al arba*. Why is the *ani* liable?

### Four-by-Four Meaning

*Rashi* and *Tosafot* offer different explanations of what the *makom arba'ah* requirement means and why it exists.

*Rashi* explains — from about eight lines before the end of the passage — *d'havi chashuv l'meihavi hanachato hanachah v'akira-to akira*: the four-by-four space is what lends *significance* to the act. It is not about the size of the object being carried but about the significance of the act of removal from that place. *Ve'yado lav makom arba hu* — one's hand is not a *makom arba*, and therefore the act lacks the requisite significance.

This connects to a broader difficulty with understanding *hotza'ah* as a *melacha*. *Hotza'ah* is the most conceptually challenging of the *melachot* on *Shabbos*. It is called by the *Rishonim* *melacha geru'ah* — a deficient or weak form of creative labor — because unlike other *melachot*, it does not produce something; it merely moves something. The *Rishonim* therefore focus more heavily on the significance of the activity rather than its result. One way of giving the activity significance is to require that it constitute a meaningful change — not just the movement of an object, but the removal of an object from its space and the placement of it into another space. If something is removed from a significant space, one has changed the nature of that space; one has also changed the status of the object by relocating it. Without a space of four by four, there is no meaningful "space" from which the removal constitutes a genuine change.

*Tosafot* points to a *pasuk*: *al yetze ish mi-mekomo be-yom ha-Shabbat* — do not leave your place on the seventh day. One *drasha* in Eruvin reads this as *al yotzi* — do not take your vessels from their place, connecting it to *hotza'ah*. The phrase *mi-mekomo* — from its place — suggests that the transgression involves removing something from its *makom*, its established space. From this reading, both the concept of place and the requirement of a significant *makom* are anchored in the biblical source for *hotza'ah*.

*Tosafot* quotes *Rabbeinu Tam*: *ein regilut le-hani'ach chefetz pachot me-arba'ah* — it is not normal practice to set an object down in a space smaller than four. He then also cites *Ri*, who distinguishes between *mekomo shel adam* — the personal space of a person, which is *arba amot* — and *mekomo shel chefetz* — the space of an object, for which *Tosafot* ultimately seems to acknowledge that the relevant measure is *arba'ah al arba'ah tefachim*, not *amot*. This is a critical distinction: *arba'ah tefachim* is approximately one foot by one foot — roughly the size of a tray — as opposed to six feet by six feet. The *Gemara* will later entertain the possibility that the person's hand was spread out, or that an apron was involved — clearly indicating the measure is *tefachim*, not *amot*.

### Gemara's Question

The *Gemara* thus presses: *ve-leika* — the four-by-four requirement is not met here. Rava responds: *ha mani Rabbi Akiva hi* — this is the view of Rabbi Akiva. *De-amar lo ba'inan makom arba'ah al arba'ah* — Rabbi Akiva holds that we do not require a *makom arba'ah al arba'ah*. But what exactly is the *girsa* here — is the measurement in *tefachim* or *amot*? From the context, it is *tefachim*, as the subsequent discussion will make clear. The question then is: what is Rabbi Akiva's principle that dispenses with this requirement?

---

## Rabbi Akiva Position

### Kluta Position

Rava identifies the source: *d'tnan*, as we learned in the *Mishna* — *hazorek mereshut hayachid lereshut hayachid ureshut harabim be'emtza* — one who throws an object from a private domain to a private domain with a public domain in between. *Rabbi Akiva mechayev, vechachamim potrim* — Rabbi Akiva declares the person *chayav* and the *chachamim* exempt.

Now, why would Rabbi Akiva say one is *chayav* here? The object never stopped in *reshut harabim* — it flew straight through the air. Yet Rabbi Akiva says: *amrinan kluta k'mi she'huncha damya* — we say that something absorbed in the airspace is considered as though it was placed on the ground. *Verabanan savri lo amrinan kluta k'mi she'huncha damya* — and the Rabbis say we do not apply this principle. Rabbi Akiva's position is thus that once an object passes through the airspace of a domain, it is as though it came to rest there. And if so, it has effectively been placed in that domain — and one is *chayav* not only for bringing it into *reshut harabim* but perhaps even a second time for then taking it from *reshut harabim* into the second *reshut hayachid*.

If Rabbi Akiva can apply this to an object flying through the air — never even touching the ground — then certainly he would apply it to an object held stationary in one's hand: once it is in the airspace of a domain, it is considered fully present there and one is *chayav*.

### Rava's Question

But the *Gemara* raises a challenge: *lemeimra d'pshita leh l'Rava de'bi'kluta k'mi she'huncha damya?* — does Rava simply take it as clear that the debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *chachamim* is about *kluta k'mi she'huncha*? *Uvetoch asara paligi* — and that they are arguing specifically about the case below ten *tefachim*, which is the airspace of *reshut harabim*? *V'ha mibaya ba'i lah Rava* — but Rava himself raised this as an open question! The *Gemara* quotes Rava's earlier inquiry: *lemata me'asara paligi?* — is their argument specifically about the case below ten *tefachim*?

### Two Interpretations

Two entirely different framings of the debate are possible, and Rava himself raised both.

The first interpretation: *Rabbi Akiva savar kluta k'mi she'huncha damya* — Rabbi Akiva holds that something caught in the airspace is like it was placed on the ground, and the Rabbis disagree. On this reading, their dispute is specifically about what happens when the object travels below ten *tefachim* — the airspace of *reshut harabim*. The object passed through the air within that zone, and the question is whether that counts as *hanacha*. *Aval lemala me'asara divrei hakol patur* — above ten *tefachim*, everyone agrees one is *patur*, since that is not the airspace of *reshut harabim*. According to this reading, the debate has nothing to do with the principle of extending beams (*moshe*), and *lo yalpinan zorek mimushit* — we do not derive the law of throwing from the law of handing.

The second interpretation inverts the logic entirely. *Od eima lemala me'asara paligi* — perhaps they are arguing specifically about what happens *above* ten *tefachim*, and the dispute has nothing to do with *kluta k'mi she'huncha* at all. The real issue is whether we learn the law of throwing from the special case of Moshe handing the beams: *d'Rebbi Akiva savar yalpinan zorek mi'Moshe* — Rabbi Akiva holds that throwing from one *reshut hayachid* to another over a *reshut harabim* is analogous to the case of Moshe's Leviyim handing beams from one wagon to another over public ground, which was the prototype for *hotza'ah* in this form. *Verabbanan savri lo yalpinan zorek mi'Moshe* — the Rabbis say we do not derive throwing from that case.

The case of Moshe's beams: the *Gemara* describes a specific scenario from the *midbar* in which Leviyim on wagons carrying the beams of the *Aron* would hand objects from one wagon to the next. Each wagon constituted a *reshut hayachid*, and the transfer occurred over *reshut harabim* in between. That act of handing — *mushit* — over a *reshut harabim* is itself considered a form of *hotza'ah*. The question is whether *zorek* — throwing — is comparable. On the second reading, the debate between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis is not about whether the object rested in the airspace below ten *tefachim*, but about whether throwing is sufficiently analogous to the case of Moshe handing the beams. And if they argue above ten *tefachim* — in the zone that is definitely not *reshut harabim* proper — then according to this reading, *aval lemata me'asara divrei hakol chayav* — below ten *tefachim*, everyone would agree one is *chayav*, because below ten we would say *kluta k'mi she'huncha dami*.

After raising both possibilities, the *Gemara* concludes: *ha lo kashya. Batar d'ibaya hadar ipshita lei* — this is not difficult, because perhaps after Rava raised the question, he ultimately resolved it: *d'savar Rebbi Akiva kluta k'mi she'huncha damya* — Rabbi Akiva's principle is indeed about the airspace below ten *tefachim*, and it is the principle of *kluta k'mi she'huncha*. And if so, the *chiddush* of Rabbi Akiva is radical: not only does one not need the object to be stationary, not only does one not need it to be on a physical surface, but merely passing through the airspace is equivalent to having rested there.

### Akira vs. Hanacha

Even granting all of this, the *Gemara* presses further: *v'dilma hanacha hu d'la bei, akira bei* — perhaps it is only *hanacha* that does not require a four-by-four space according to Rabbi Akiva; perhaps *akira* — the uprooting, the initial removal — still requires that the object be removed from a *makom* of four by four.

Why would *akira* carry a greater requirement than *hanacha*? *Tosafot* points back to the *pasuk* cited earlier — *al yetze ish mi-mekomo* — which, when read as *al yotzi*, emphasizes the act of removal from a *makom*. The very language focuses on removing something *from* its place, giving the *akira* a particular dependence on the concept of *makom*. The act of *hanacha* might not be subject to the same textual emphasis.

Another possible explanation offered relates to the concept of *kluta* itself. *Kluta* derives from a root suggesting absorption or reception — as in *arei miklat*, cities that absorb and shelter. When an object enters a domain's airspace, the domain, so to speak, receives it. That act of entry — of being absorbed — is what *kluta k'mi she'huncha* describes. This dynamic of reception applies to *hanacha*, to placing: the receiving domain takes in the object. But departure — *akira*, leaving a space — is not an act of reception by the destination, and the principle of *kluta* may not apply there in the same way.

In our *Mishna*, it appears from the case itself that even the *akira* did not require four by four, since the *ani* took the bread from the *ba'al habayit*'s hand, which is plainly not four by four. This seems to push back against saying that *akira* requires a four-by-four space. But the *Gemara* cautions that one cannot prove this definitively from the case, since there may be other explanations. As *Rashi* might suggest, one cannot simply assume the *Gemara* has resolved this; perhaps Rabbi Akiva's position covers both *akira* and *hanacha*, but perhaps it extends only to one. The *Gemara* leaves this as an unresolved question.

---

## Tree Branch Case

### Small Protrusion

The *Gemara* now considers a *braita*: *zarak venach agabi ziz kol shehu* — one threw an object and it came to rest on a small protrusion. *Rabbi mechayev, vachachamim potrin* — Rabbi declares the person *chayav*, and the *chachamim* exempt. This appears to be a direct proof that one may be *chayav* even when the object lands on a space smaller than four by four *tefachim* — since *kol shehu* means any size at all.

### Abaye Reframing

The *Gemara* deflects: *hasham kidebayeina lemeimar lekaman kideAbaye* — there, it will be reframed as Abaye reframes it. *De'amar Abaye: hacha be'ilan ha'omed bereshus hayachid venofov noto lereshus harabim* — we are dealing with a tree whose trunk stands in *reshut hayachid* and whose branch extends into *reshut harabim*. *Ve'zarak venach al nofo* — one threw an object from *reshut harabim* and it came to rest on the branch. *Rabbi savar amrinan shadi nofo basar ikaro* — Rabbi holds that we treat the branch as following the trunk. *Verabbanan savri lo amrinan shadi nofo basar ikaro* — the Rabbis hold that we do not say the branch follows the trunk.

### Branch Follows Trunk

*Tosafot* understands this debate in a fairly *peshat* manner: the dispute is about which domain the branch is considered to belong to. If the object lands on the branch and the branch follows the trunk — which is rooted in *reshut hayachid* — then throwing the object onto the branch is considered as though one threw it into *reshut hayachid*, making one *chayav*. If the branch does not follow the trunk, it is considered part of *reshut harabim*, and the object never genuinely arrived in *reshut hayachid*.

But there is a further relevance to the question of four by four: if the branch follows the trunk, then the significance of the trunk — which presumably does have a base of four by four *tefachim* — extends to the branch. The object on the branch is, in effect, considered to be resting on the trunk, which is a *makom arba'ah*. That is why one would be *chayav* according to Rabbi — not because a small protrusion suffices as a *makom* without four by four, but because the trunk provides the four by four and the branch is regarded as an extension of it.

*Rashi*'s reading differs somewhat. According to *Rashi*, the object is actually considered to be in *reshut harabim*, not *reshut hayachid*, but the connection to the trunk gives the branch significance — as though it were a four-by-four space — by virtue of being attached to an object that is itself large and significant. Imagine a table that is four by four *tefachim* with a small extension: placing something on the extension is significant because it is connected to the whole. Both *Rashi* and *Tosafot* agree, however, on the essential point for our purposes: the reason Rabbi says one is *chayav* is because the trunk provides a four-by-four base, not because four by four is unnecessary.

### Cannot Prove Absence

Therefore, says the *Gemara*, one cannot derive from this *braita* that four by four is not required. *Ella* — rather, this case depends entirely on the status of the trunk. It does not demonstrate a general principle that the four-by-four requirement may be dispensed with. The question of whether *hotza'ah* can be *chayav* without any *makom arba'ah* remains unresolved from this source.

---

## Public-to-Public Case

### Window Throw

*Ella ha Rebbi, detanya: zarak mereshus harabim lereshut harabim ureshut hayachid be'emtza* — the following case attributed to Rabbi: one threw an object from a public domain to a public domain with a private domain in between. The object flew through someone's window, crossed through the private house, and landed in the street on the other side.

### Two Transgressions

*Rabbi mechayiv, vachachamim potrin*. Rabbi holds one is *chayav*, the *chachamim* exempt the person. Now, crucially, this case cannot be explained by the principle of Moshe's beams: that principle applies specifically to private-to-private with public in the middle, not public-to-public with private in the middle. So Rabbi's ruling here must reflect a genuine position that does not require the object to come to rest — it flew straight through without stopping — and also does not require a *makom arba'ah*. And *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* adds: *mechayiv haya Rebbi shtayim* — Rabbi would hold one *chayav* for two separate transgressions: *achas mishum hotza'ah ve'achas mishum hachnasah* — one for the *hotza'ah* (carrying out, from *reshut harabim* into *reshut hayachid*) and one for the *hachnasah* (bringing in, from *reshut hayachid* back into *reshut harabim* on the other side). This demonstrates that Rabbi requires neither a *hanacha* on a *makom arba'ah* nor an *akira* from a *makom arba'ah* — the object was in motion the entire time.

### Roofed House Limit

However, *Rava* and *Shmuel* both qualify Rabbi's position: *lo mechayiv Rebbi ella bereshut hayachid mekura* — Rabbi only declares one *chayav* if the private domain through which the object passed was a roofed house. *De'amrinan beisa keman demalya dami* — because we say a house is considered as though it were full. The roof of the house is what makes the airspace of the house count as genuinely "occupied" — when the object passes through that enclosed, roofed space, it is as though it was truly present within the domain. *Aval she'eino mekura lo* — but if the private domain had no roof, Rabbi would not declare one *chayav*. This is the principle of *kluta k'mi she'huncha* at work: a closed, roofed house truly absorbs the object, making the passage through its airspace equivalent to placement; an unroofed space does not.

This limitation is directly relevant to our case. The scenario of the *ani* taking bread from the *ba'al habayit*'s hand does not involve a roofed house through which an object is thrown — it involves taking directly from another's hand in an open setting. Rabbi's position, restricted to *bayit mekurah*, cannot serve as a source for the principle that four by four is unnecessary in the hand-to-hand case.

### Unresolved Hand Case

The *Gemara* thus reaches the end of the *amud* without a resolution to the original question. The case of the *ani* and the *ba'al habayit* — where the object was transferred from hand to hand, with no *makom arba'ah* at either end of the act — remains without a satisfactory answer. The matter is to be continued.

---

---

# Shabbat 7

## Four Reshuyot

### Reshut HaYachid

Before moving forward into new material, it is worth briefly reviewing the four *reshuyot* introduced in the *Tosefta* cited on the preceding *daf*, since the Gemara will occupy itself with their elaboration for another day and a half. The first domain, *reshut hayachid*, was defined as a space of four by four *tefachim* with walls ten *tefachim* high — and this holds even when the walls are technically below the enclosed space, as in the case of a post or a pit. There was a noted debate among the *Rishonim* as to whether three walls or four are required.

### Reshut HaRabim

The second domain, *reshut harabim*, was described as a major public square or thoroughfare, though the *Tosefta* itself does not specify exactly how major. Elsewhere we find an additional criterion of sixteen *amot* — approximately twenty-four feet — in width, and the question of what further factors are required becomes highly consequential. Some authorities maintain that the space must serve 600,000 people daily, or must be a major road running directly between cities; other criteria are brought as well. A related and critical debate between the *Chachamim* and Rabbi Yehuda concerns whether walls can surround a *reshut harabim*, or whether we say *ati rabim umvatli mechitza* — the public comes and negates the walls. If we accept the latter view, as we generally do, then an *eruv* cannot function in a genuine biblical *reshut harabim*. The definition of *reshut harabim* is therefore of enormous practical consequence: if we conclude that most contemporary situations constitute a *karmelit* rather than a *reshut harabim*, it both reduces the relevant prohibition to a rabbinic level and permits the construction of an *eruv*.

### Eiruv & Definition

The stakes, then, are twofold: first, whether a given space creates biblical liability or merely rabbinic; and second, whether an *eruv* is valid. These questions turn directly on how strictly or broadly one defines *reshut harabim*.

### Beit Satayim

One additional point from the prior discussion bears mentioning: even a fully walled enclosure may be treated rabbinically as a restricted domain for carrying if it exceeds a certain size — approximately 5,600 square feet, the measurement known as *beit satayim* — and is not used for habitation. What exactly "habitation" means in this context is itself a broad and somewhat abstract question.

---

## Karmelit Definition

### Karmelit Examples

The Gemara now turns to the third of the four *reshuyot* — the rabbinic domain, the *karmelit*. The *Tosefta* cited a list of examples falling into this category: an ocean, a valley, and the like, as well as a *karmelit* in the narrow sense, which Rashi identifies as a forest. The difficulty the Gemara raises is terminological: since all these cases belong to the class of *karmelit*, why use the word *karmelit* as one item among them? The answer is that *karmelit* has evolved from a proper noun — the name of a specific type of space — into an abstract category name. The Gemara therefore asks what the *Tosefta* adds by listing the term itself.

The response: *ki ata Rav Dimi amar Rabbi Yochanan* — when Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael and transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — *lo nitzrecha ela le'keren zavit hasmucha lereshut harabim*: the novel case being added is a corner niche adjacent to the *reshut harabim*, which one might not have thought to classify as a *karmelit*.

### Keren Zavit

The *keren zavit* is a corner or intruding niche off the main *reshut harabim*. The Gemara notes that sometimes, when the main street becomes overcrowded, people will push into this corner — *de'avda gav dei de'dachki bei rabim ve'ayli legavei* — yet since it is not used in a convenient and direct manner, *keivan delo nicha tashmishtei*, it retains the status of a *karmelit* rather than a *reshut harabim*.

This introduces a theme that will recur throughout the sugya: the distinction between physical proximity to the *reshut harabim* and functional incorporation into it. The Artscroll edition provides a helpful illustration of the configuration: a main thoroughfare with a small niche or side street set off to the side — not a convenient passage, not part of the primary flow of traffic, and therefore not a *reshut harabim*. In fact, anything that fails to qualify as a *reshut harabim* is a *karmelit*, even if it is closely connected to the *reshut harabim*. This is the principle at work.

### Usage Criterion

An important conceptual distinction emerges here between *reshut hayachid* and *reshut harabim*. Ownership is irrelevant to both: a *reshut hayachid* can be owned by the public, and a *reshut harabim* can theoretically be privately owned but fully public in use. What does matter — and this is primary for *reshut harabim* in a way that it is not for *reshut hayachid* — is use. The physical criteria of *reshut hayachid* are structural: four by four *tefachim*, walls ten *tefachim* high. But the defining quality of *reshut harabim* is functional: how it is used, how easily it is traversed, and how directly it serves the public.

And so the question the Gemara continues to press is: for spaces that are adjacent to or partially connected with the *reshut harabim*, what threshold of convenient use must they meet before they are absorbed into the *reshut harabim*? That criterion — *nicha tashmishtei*, convenient or easy use — is going to be the organizing principle of the discussions that follow.

---

## Pillars & Stalls

### Between Pillars

The Gemara brings another ruling of Rabbi Yochanan transmitted by Rav Dimi: *bein ha'amudim nidon ke'karmelit* — the space between the pillars is treated as a *karmelit*. This would seem to be what was meant in the *Tosefta* by the term *istavinah* (also rendered *istava* or *istov*), referring to a colonnaded walkway alongside the stores. Rashi clarifies that the *istova* referred specifically to the booths set up in front of the stores, while the pillars themselves formed a kind of colonnaded corridor through which people did walk.

One can visualize this as something akin to the covered colonnaded street of an ancient city — like the Cardo in Jerusalem — where rows of pillars defined a space alongside the storefronts, through which foot traffic moved but with considerably more obstruction than the open road. People do walk between the pillars, but they must navigate around them; it is not the direct, unimpeded flow of the main thoroughfare.

Why then is this space a *karmelit* and not a *reshut harabim*? The Gemara explains: *af al gav de'darsi bei rabbim* — even though the masses do in fact walk there — *keivan de'lo mistagi lehu behedya*, since they do not travel through it *behedya* — directly, straightforwardly, without obstruction or detour — it is like a *karmelit*. The word *behedya* carries the sense of directly, without circumlocution or circuitous maneuvering.

### Booth Area

Rav Zeira then cites Rav Yehuda: *itztava she'lifnei ha'amudim nidon ke'karmelit* — the booth area in front of the pillars is similarly a *karmelit*. This is notable because Rashi had identified the *istavinah* in the *Tosefta* with precisely these booths. In any case, the Gemara's logical structure is as follows: for one who holds that even the space between the pillars — where people actually walk — is a *karmelit*, it follows *kol shekein* that the booth area, where people merely stand and browse, is certainly a *karmelit*. But for one who holds only that the booth area is a *karmelit*, it might be that the space between the pillars, where movement does occur, would qualify as a *reshut harabim* — *d'nicha tashmishtei*, since it is more conveniently used for passage.

One might ask at this point: what kind of use is being measured? Is it specifically travel, or any type of use? A *reshut harabim* can be either a major road or a major public square, so gathering and standing might also in principle constitute the relevant use. But here, in the context of the colonnaded market, the Gemara's language throughout emphasizes movement and passage — *af al gav de'darsi bei rabbim*, the masses trample through it — suggesting that the primary criterion being assessed is convenience as a means of transit.

### Standing vs. Walking

The Gemara then presents an alternative version (*lishna achrina*) of Rav Zeira's statement, in which the distinction between the booth area and the space between the pillars is made explicit from the outset: the booth area is a *karmelit* because it is a place where people stand; the space between the pillars, in this version, may in fact be a *reshut harabim* because *zimnin de'darsi lah rabbim* — there are times when the masses actually walk through it. The difference between the two versions is subtle but meaningful: the first formulation frames the distinction in terms of degree of ease of use in the abstract, while the second frames it as a categorical distinction between a place of standing versus a place of walking. Whether *reshut harabim* requires specifically a space of travel, or whether any sufficiently convenient and common use qualifies, is a question the Gemara will return to shortly.

---

## Elevated Structures

### Levaina Zekufa

Rava bar Shila cites Rav Chisda: *levaina zekufa birshus harabim* — a brick standing erect in the *reshut harabim* — *ve'zarak ve'tach b'faneha chayav, al gabah patur*. If one throws a sticky object and it adheres to the face of the brick, one is liable; if it lands on top, one is exempt. The Gemara here transitions from definitional questions about domains back to the act of carrying, but the domain analysis remains central. The sticky object in question — the *deveila*, a round of pressed figs or dates — adheres to the side of the brick while it is still within the airspace of the *reshut harabim*, which extends upward to ten *tefachim*. Since it rests, *nach*, within that airspace, one is liable. If it lands on top of the brick, however, we must examine whether the top of the brick is a *reshut harabim* or not.

### Three-Tefach Rule

Abaye and Rava jointly address this: *ve-hu she-gavoha shelosha* — it is only when the brick is higher than three *tefachim* that its top is not part of the *reshut harabim*, *de'lo darsi lei rabbim*, because people do not walk over it when it stands that high. When the brick is less than three *tefachim* high — about nine to ten inches off the ground — people will simply step on it and trample over it, and it is therefore considered part of the *reshut harabim* through its use, not merely through its structural proximity.

This is a striking point. The principle of *lavud* — the rabbinic rule that anything within three *tefachim* of another surface is considered connected to it — might have sufficed to explain why a low brick is part of the ground. Yet Abaye and Rava deliberately do not invoke *lavud* here. They say instead: because people walk on it. This is because, as the Gemara has been establishing, structural connection alone is insufficient for *reshut harabim*; it must also be used as such.
