Were everyone to walk around this low brick, even a structurally connected surface would not be *reshut harabim*.

### Obstruction Debate

The Gemara makes the principle still more explicit: *aval hizmei ve'higi* — thorn bushes or thistles — *af al gav de'la gevihai shelosha*, even if they are lower than three *tefachim*, they are not *reshut harabim*, because people walk around them to avoid the thorns. The structural proximity to the ground is irrelevant; the decisive factor is that the public does not use that space.

This generates a range of opinions. Abaye and Rava hold that only thorn bushes — not soft obstructions — cause people to walk around: thorn bushes people avoid; a brick they step over. Then comes the view that *ve'ki ata Rav amar afilu hizmei ve'higi* — even thorn bushes people will eventually trample through — and therefore they are still *reshut harabim*, but *aval tzoah lo*: excrement is different, because people will walk around it entirely. Rav Ashi goes further still, suggesting that even excrement does not remove a space from *reshut harabim*, either because people do walk through it anyway, or because — as another reading suggests — the relevant criterion is not immediate avoidance but permanence of obstruction, and excrement is not a permanent feature.

What emerges clearly from all these positions is that use, specifically current immediate use, governs domain status. The Gemara may be saying that even temporary circumstances — a pile of dung, a thorn bush — can dislodge a space from *reshut harabim* status, because the masses are not actually using it as such right now. Structural location within the *reshut harabim* is not enough.

A further question arises from the converse direction: what if a space is higher than three *tefachim* but is nonetheless actually used by the *rabim*? Must both conditions be met — structural proximity through *lavud* and actual use — or is use alone sufficient? The Gemara will address this explicitly in the coming *daf*, where it will discuss a platform approximately nine *tefachim* high, about shoulder height, which is conveniently used by the public for placing and retrieving objects. The Gemara will treat that platform as part of *reshut harabim*. This shows that being within three *tefachim* of the ground is not strictly necessary; what is necessary and sufficient is that the space be used by the *rabim* within the ten-*tefach* airspace. Usage is more foundational than structural proximity.

---

## Size & Height Rules

### Four-by-Four Min.

The Gemara now returns to transmissions from Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ein karmelit pechusah me'arba'ah* — a *karmelit* cannot be smaller than four by four *tefachim*. This is a significant ruling that defines the lower boundary of the *karmelit*. Most *karmeliyot* — open fields, valleys, oceans — are vast, and no minimum size question arises. But within the *reshut harabim*, where we find raised bricks, posts, small platforms, and ledges that are neither used by the *rabim* as part of the street nor walled off as a *reshut hayachid*, the question is: what are these small structures? If they are not *reshut harabim* and not *reshut hayachid*, the remaining options are *karmelit* or *makom patur*.

Rabbi Yochanan establishes that a space must be at least four by four *tefachim* — approximately a foot by a foot — to qualify as a *karmelit*. Anything smaller is a *makom patur*, an exempt space. This parallel to *reshut hayachid* is intentional: just as an object must rest on a surface of four by four *tefachim* to be considered to have been placed down in a domain, so too a space must have that minimum area to be classified as a domain at all. The practical application: a fire hydrant or a similarly narrow surface in the street, smaller than four by four *tefachim*, is a *makom patur*.

Rav Sheshet then qualifies: *ve'tofeset ad asarah* — the *karmelit* "grasps" only up to ten *tefachim*.

### Ten-Tefach Limit

What does *ve'tofeset ad asarah* mean? The Gemara raises a first reading: perhaps a *karmelit* requires walls of ten *tefachim*. But this immediately creates a problem, as the presence of ten-*tefach* walls would make the space a *reshut hayachid*, not a *karmelit*. Tosafot therefore offers a better reading — and it is this reading that fits the context — namely, that the *karmelit* may require ten *tefachim* of airspace above it. The question would then be: can a space with a low ceiling, say five *tefachim* high, be a *karmelit*? Perhaps a domain, to function as such, requires not only four by four in area but also a height of ten *tefachim*, just as *reshut hayachid* typically has walls of ten *tefachim* and *reshut harabim* has airspace up to ten *tefachim*.

### Doghouse Example

The Gemara then challenges this possibility. It cites a ruling of Rav Giddel citing Rav Chiya bar Yosef citing Rav: *bayis she'ein besocho asarah ve'kiruyo mashlimo le'asarah* — a house whose interior is only nine *tefachim* high, but whose roof, one *tefach* thick, brings the outer wall to ten *tefachim* total — has the following status. *Al gago mutar letaltel bekulo*: on the roof, one may carry over the entire surface, because the outer walls are ten *tefachim* high, and we imagine them as extending upward, enclosing the rooftop space as a *reshut hayachid*. *Besokho, ein metaltelin bo ela be'arba ammos*: inside, one may carry only within four *amot* — the restriction applicable in a *reshut harabim* and equally in a *karmelit*. The interior, with walls only nine *tefachim* high from the inside, is not a *reshut hayachid*; not a *reshut harabim*; it is therefore a *karmelit*.

This case — which one might call the "doghouse" — demonstrates that a *karmelit* can exist even when the interior height does not reach ten *tefachim*. The *karmelit* here has an airspace of only nine *tefachim*, yet it is treated as a *karmelit*. This refutes the suggestion that a *karmelit* requires ten *tefachim* of interior height.

What then does *ve'tofeset ad asarah* mean? The Gemara resolves: it means that the *karmelit*'s airspace extends upward only until ten *tefachim* — *ve'ad yud hu de'havia karmelis, lema'ala miyud tefachim lo havei karmelis*. Just as *reshut harabim* has airspace only up to ten *tefachim* above the ground, so too the *karmelit*, parallel to *reshut harabim* in this respect. Above ten *tefachim*, the airspace of a *karmelit* becomes a *makom patur*.

This is confirmed by the teaching of Shmuel to Rav Yehuda — *shinena*, "sharp one" — *lo tehei bemilei de'Shabbata lema'la me'asara*: do not concern yourself with Shabbat carrying issues above ten *tefachim*. The Gemara considers two possible meanings of this instruction. Could he have meant that *reshut hayachid* does not extend higher than ten *tefachim*? This is contradicted by the ruling of Rav Chisda — which will be discussed momentarily — that *reshut hayachid* extends to the sky. Could he have meant that *reshut harabim* does not go above ten *tefachim*? That is already stated explicitly in a *Mishna* (*hazorek arba amot bekotel lema'la me'asara tefachim kezorek ba'avir, lemata me'asara tefachim kezorek ba'aretz*) and would not need to be transmitted specially to Rav Yehuda. Therefore, Shmuel must have been referring specifically to the *karmelit* — *ela akarmelit, de'ein karmelit lema'la me'asara* — teaching that the *karmelit*'s airspace similarly does not extend above ten *tefachim*.

### Karmelit Hybrid

The Gemara now summarizes the hybrid nature of the *karmelit*: *ve'akilu ba'rabbanan mikulei reshus hayachid u'mikulei reshus harabbim* — the Rabbis applied leniencies from both *reshut hayachid* and *reshut harabim* in defining the *karmelit*'s parameters.

From the leniencies of *reshut hayachid*: only if the space is four by four *tefachim* is it a *karmelit*; if smaller, it is merely a *makom patur*. From the leniencies of *reshut harabim*: the *karmelit*'s airspace extends only up to ten *tefachim*, not beyond.

Yet in terms of the actual restrictions on carrying, the *karmelit* is treated strictly on both ends: one may not carry from it to a *reshut hayachid*, nor from it to a *reshut harabim*, and within it one may carry only four *amot*. The *karmelit* is thus a hybrid in its definitional parameters, borrowing size and height thresholds from both major domains, while remaining a distinct and fully restricted rabbinic domain in practice.

To summarize the practical contours: a *makom patur* is a surface smaller than four by four *tefachim*, more than three *tefachim* off the ground (since within three it is absorbed into *reshut harabim* by use), and less than ten *tefachim* high (since at ten *tefachim* with sufficient area it could become a *reshut hayachid*). The classic *makom patur* is found in that zone between roughly nine inches and three feet off the ground, with a footprint smaller than a foot by a foot.

---

## Associated Spaces

### Pit Expansion

The Gemara returns *gufa* — to examine on its own terms the ruling of Rav Giddel that was cited earlier in passing. The "doghouse" scenario is revisited. Abaye adds: *ve'im chakak bo arba al arba ve'hishlimu le'asarah mutar letaltel bekulo* — if one dug a pit inside the structure, four by four *tefachim* in area, such that from the floor of the pit to the ceiling is ten *tefachim*, one may now carry throughout the entire interior of the house.

The logic: this pit, four by four *tefachim* with a height of ten *tefachim*, is a *reshut hayachid*. The walls of the house, though not immediately adjacent to the pit, surround it. The remaining floor space of the interior — the areas outside the pit, which themselves still lack ten *tefachim* of interior height — are now permitted for carrying as well. Why? *Havei chorei reshut hayachid* — they become like the "holes of a *reshut hayachid*."

### Holes in Private

The principle of *chorei reshut hayachid* is that the niches and recesses associated with a *reshut hayachid* share its status. In Talmudic construction, stone walls typically had recesses — small niches used for storage. Such a niche, considered in isolation, does not meet the formal criteria of *reshut hayachid*: it is not four by four *tefachim* with walls ten *tefachim* high. Yet because it serves the *reshut hayachid* and is situated within its walls, it is considered an extension of the *reshut hayachid*.

Applied to the doghouse scenario: once the pit creates a genuine *reshut hayachid* within the structure, all the surrounding floor space, though itself lacking the necessary interior height, is treated as associated space — *chorei reshut hayachid* — and acquires the status of *reshut hayachid*. The entire interior thus becomes permitted for carrying.

Tosafot raises an objection from the laws of *sukkah*: we know that in the laws of *sukkah*, the *sechach* must be connected to the walls; a *sukkah* with *sechach* in the middle and walls far off to the side is invalid. Why then does *reshut hayachid* not similarly require the walls to be connected to the central space? Two answers suggest themselves. First, *sukkah* has an additional requirement of *sechach*, and the rule that *sechach* must be connected to the walls is a distinct criterion generated by the interaction of those two elements; the four-by-four pit here has no such roof requirement. Second, and more fundamentally, *reshut hayachid* is not a *house* — it is a *space enclosed by walls*. A *sukkah* is, in essence, an edifice, a dwelling, and as such its walls must actually constitute the walls of that dwelling. *Reshut hayachid* is defined purely as an area surrounded by walls, however distant. The walls enclose the space; they need not be architecturally connected to any particular point within it. This distinction — between a space defined by its enclosure and an edifice defined by its structure — appears to be the underlying conceptual difference.

### Holes in Public

The Gemara now addresses *chorei reshut harabbim* — niches or holes in walls along the *reshut harabim* that face the street and are used by passersby. If *chorei reshut hayachid* share the status of *reshut hayachid*, do *chorei reshut harabbim* share the status of *reshut harabim*?

Abaye says yes: *ke'reshut harabbim dami* — holes in a wall along the *reshut harabim*, if used by the public, have the status of *reshut harabim*. Rava disagrees: *lav ke'reshut harabbim damu* — they do not.

Rava challenges Abaye: if holes in a public domain wall are *reshut harabim*, how does that square with the ruling — also transmitted by Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — that the *keren zavit*, the corner niche alongside the *reshut harabim*, is a *karmelit*? People do sometimes push into that corner. If even that much use suffices to make something *reshut harabim* according to Abaye, then the *keren zavit* should also be *reshut harabim*. What is Abaye's response?

### Convenience Compare

*Hasam lo nicha tashmishtei, hacha nicha tashmishtei* — there, in the case of the corner niche, the use is not convenient; here, in the case of the holes in the wall, the use is convenient. The *keren zavit* requires one to turn off the main path, squeeze into a corner, move against the flow — it is not *nicha tashmishtei*. A niche in a wall at street level, by contrast, into which one can place or retrieve an object without breaking stride — that is *nicha tashmishtei*, convenient use, and Abaye therefore treats it as *reshut harabim*.

This is not a binary yes/no determination but a qualitative continuum. Every case must be assessed individually for the degree of convenience of its use. The contrast between Abaye and Rava is that Rava requires a very high threshold of use to assign *reshut harabim* status — so high that even a convenient wall niche does not meet it — while Abaye draws the line between genuinely inconvenient use (like the *keren zavit*) and genuinely convenient use (like a wall niche). This distinction cuts to the heart of what *reshut harabim* is: not merely a physical territory but a functionally defined space, and the primary question throughout is always how it is used.

---

## Wall Throw Cases

### Sticky Fig Case

The Gemara now returns *gufa* to the *Mishna* cited earlier (*hazorek arba amot bekotel lema'la me'asara tefachim kezorek ba'avir, lemata me'asara tefachim kezorek ba'aretz*) and its accompanying explanation by Rabbi Yochanan. The Gemara had asked: if one throws something at a wall and it hits below ten *tefachim*, it is like placing it on the ground — but *veha lo nach*, it did not come to rest! Rabbi Yochanan resolves this: *be'dveila shemeinah shanu* — the case is one of a fat, sticky *dveila*, a round of pressed figs, that adheres to the side of the wall. The object does in fact come to rest — it sticks to the face of the wall within the ten-*tefach* airspace of the *reshut harabim*, and one is therefore liable.

### Why Not Holes

This raises an obvious question: why construct such an unusual scenario involving sticky figs? Rava poses this to Abaye: if you hold that *chorei reshut harabbim ke'reshut harabbim damu* — that holes in a wall of *reshut harabim* have the status of *reshut harabim* — then there is a far simpler scenario. *Lokmi be'tsror ve'cheifetz ve'danach be'chor* — simply discuss a rock or any ordinary object that was thrown and came to rest in a hole in the wall. No sticky figs required; the object lands in the hole and stays there. Why does Rabbi Yochanan need the peculiar case of the sticky fig?

One answer: *zimnin meshani lei tsror ve'cheifetz miahdar ve'ati* — a rock or hard object thrown at a hole in a wall will typically bounce back. Getting a thrown object to land in a small hole and stay there is actually a less realistic scenario than a sticky fig adhering to the wall face. It is like a carnival game — it looks easy, but in practice the object bounces back. The sticky fig is actually the more natural case.

### Carving Rule

The second and more fundamental answer: *zimnin meshani lei be'kosel de'leis bei chor* — Rabbi Yochanan is speaking about a wall without holes. And the Gemara explains why a wall with holes cannot serve as the clean example we need. The *Mishna*'s first case is: if one throws something *higher* than ten *tefachim* and it hits the wall, it is like throwing in the air — *makom patur*, exempt. This case is structurally parallel to the case below ten *tefachim*. If we imagine a wall with holes, then a hole higher than ten *tefachim* would also need to be considered. But a hole in a wall higher than ten *tefachim*, if it is four by four *tefachim*, is a *reshut hayachid* — not a *makom patur*. One would be liable for landing something there, not exempt.

And even if the hole is smaller than four by four — which might seem to avoid the *reshut hayachid* classification — the debate of Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis applies. The Gemara cites: *zarak lema'la me'asara tefachim ve'halcha ve'nachah be'chor kol shehu banu le'machlokes Rabbi Meir ve'Rabbanan* — if one threw an object higher than ten *tefachim* and it came to rest in even a small hole, the case falls into the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis regarding *chokekin le'hashlim* — carving out to complete the requisite measurement.

The context of this dispute is a doorway with an arch: to be obligated in *mezuzah*, a doorway must be at least ten *tefachim* high with a width of four *tefachim* at that height. A classic arch narrows at the top; the width of four *tefachim* may not be maintained at the full height of ten *tefachim*. Rabbi Meir holds *chokekin le'hashlim* — we imaginarily "carve out" the stone to square off the arch, and if the resulting space would be ten by four, we treat it as if it already is. The *Chachamim* disagree: *ein chokekin le'hashlim* — we do not carve. Applied to a small hole in a wall: Rabbi Meir would say that if the surrounding stone could theoretically be removed to yield a four-by-four space, we treat the hole as a *reshut hayachid*. Therefore, even a small hole higher than ten *tefachim* would, according to Rabbi Meir, be a *reshut hayachid* — and the case of throwing above ten would not be a clean case of *makom patur*.

### No-Hole Assumption

The Gemara therefore concludes: *ela lav shema mina de'kosel de'leis bei chor* — we must conclude that the *Mishna* and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation are dealing with a wall that has no holes at all. This is why the sticky fig is used: a wall without holes means nothing can land in a hole; the only way something can come to rest on the face of the wall is if it is sticky enough to adhere. And this also ensures that throwing above ten *tefachim* results in a clean *makom patur* — there are no holes that could constitute a *reshut hayachid* and complicate the analysis. *Shema mina* — this is indeed the correct inference.

Abaye's position is thus preserved: holes in a *reshut harabim* wall, when conveniently used, do have the status of *reshut harabim*. The Gemara's choice of the sticky fig case was not due to any problem with that principle, but rather to avoid the complications that holes above ten *tefachim* would introduce — complications involving *reshut hayachid* and the dispute of Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis.

---

## Flagpole Height

### Pole Extension

The Gemara returns *gufa* to the ruling of Rav Chisda: *na'atz kaneh be'reshut hayachid ve'zarak ve'nach al gabav* — one thrust a pole into a *reshut hayachid* and threw an object that came to rest on top of the pole — *afilu gavoah me'ah amah chayav, mipnei she'reshut hayachid olah ad larakia* — even if the pole is a hundred *amot* high, one is liable, because *reshut hayachid* extends all the way to the sky. The walls of the *reshut hayachid*, by the principle that they extend upward without limit, encompass the entire column of airspace above them, however high. Something that comes to rest atop a flagpole standing within a *reshut hayachid* — even one surrounded merely by a low fence — has been deposited in *reshut hayachid*.

### Rebbi vs. Rabbanan

The Gemara raises a question: does the ruling of Rav Chisda reflect the view of Rebbi alone, against the *Chachamim*? The problem is that the top of the flagpole is an extremely small surface — far less than four by four *tefachim* — and we have established that resting on a surface of four by four *tefachim* is required for the carrying act to be considered complete. The Gemara cites a *braita*: *zarak ve'nach al gabei ziz kol shehu — Rebbi mechayev ve'Chachamim potrin* — one threw something and it rested on a tiny protrusion: Rebbi holds one is liable; the *Chachamim* hold one is exempt. Presumably, Rebbi does not require the object to rest on a space of four by four *tefachim*, while the *Chachamim* do. Rav Chisda's ruling, which makes one liable for an object resting atop a thin pole, would seem to align with Rebbi.

Abaye's response will open *daf* 7b — and the question of whether four by four *tefachim* is required in *reshut hayachid* will be taken up there.

---

---

# Shabbat 8

## Rav Chisda's 4×4 Rule

### Four-by-Four Requirement

The daf opens with the words *amar Abaye*, picking up directly from the discussion that had unfolded on 7b. The issue at hand was Rav Chisda's statement revisiting the question of whether an object must be placed on a space of four by four *tefachim* in order for that placement to constitute a valid *hanacha*, or whether the object must be taken from such a space in order for the removal to constitute a valid *akira*. After the extended treatment of what constitutes *reshut hayachid*, *reshut harabim*, and so on, Rav Chisda had ruled that if someone threw an object from *reshut harabim* and it landed on top of a flagpole standing in *reshut hayachid*, the person is *chayav* — even though the top of the pole does not measure four by four. This seems to indicate that, at least for *reshut hayachid* and at least for *hanacha*, Rav Chisda does not require a four-by-four surface.

### Tosafot: Extended Walls

One way of understanding Rav Chisda's ruling is the explanation offered by Tosafot, which builds on an idea encountered a few days earlier: when one has a roof over a *reshut hayachid*, we conceptually treat the enclosed space as filled, as though everything within it rests on the ground. Tosafot extends this logic even without a roof. Since we imagine the walls of a *reshut hayachid* as extending upward indefinitely, any object coming to rest within that vertical column is considered to be within the *reshut hayachid* — and therefore does not require a four-by-four surface beneath it.

### Rabbi on Ziz Protrusion

The Gemara seeks to connect Rav Chisda's ruling to a statement by Rabbi (*Rebbe*) that appeared in an earlier discussion. Three lines from the bottom of 7b, the Gemara asks: *lema Rav Chisda d'amar keRebbe?* — perhaps Rav Chisda, who does not require a four-by-four surface (at least in *reshut hayachid*), is ruling in accordance with Rabbi's position. The *baraita* cited reads: *zarak venach al gabi ziz kolshehu* — if someone threw an object and it landed on a tiny protrusion (assumed to be a protrusion within a *reshut hayachid*), Rabbi rules the person is *chayav*, while the *chachamim* rule the person is exempt. The parenthetical implication follows: *alman lo ba'inan makom arba al arba* — you do not require a space of four by four, at least in *reshut hayachid*. This appears to be precisely Rav Chisda's point.

### Abaye's Concession

Abaye responds with a striking concession: *bireshut hayachid d'chulei alma lo peligi d'Rav Chisda* — when it comes to *reshut hayachid*, everyone agrees with Rav Chisda, including the *chachamim* who dispute Rabbi in that *baraita*. This is a significant shift, given that the entire *sugya* of earlier in the week was preoccupied with who could possibly hold that a four-by-four surface is not required. Here Abaye asserts that at least regarding *hanacha* in *reshut hayachid*, no four-by-four is required — and this is universally accepted. The debate in the *baraita*, then, concerns something else entirely, as Abaye goes on to explain.

---

## Tree Branch Query

### Trunk & Branch Setup

Abaye reframes the dispute: *ella hacha be'ilan ha'omed bireshut hayachid venofo noteh lereshut harabim* — the case involves a tree whose trunk stands in *reshut hayachid* but whose branch extends out into *reshut harabim*. The scenario is: someone in *reshut harabim* throws an object and it lands on one of the branches. The object has come to rest on a branch that is physically located in *reshut harabim*, yet the trunk anchoring the entire tree is rooted in *reshut hayachid*.

### Rabbi vs. Rabbanan

The dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbanan in the *baraita* turns on precisely this question: *deRebbe savar amrinan shadin nofo batar ikaro* — Rabbi holds that we throw the branch after the trunk, meaning the branch is legally treated as part of the domain in which the trunk stands. *V'Rabbanan savri lo amrinan shadin nofo batar ikaro* — the Rabbanan hold that we do not apply this principle.

### Object Location Debate

What is at stake is the legal location of an object resting on the overhanging branch. If the branch is considered part of *reshut harabim* — which is where it physically sits — then the object is in *reshut harabim*. If, however, we follow Rabbi and treat the branch as part of *reshut hayachid* by virtue of its connection to the trunk, then the object is in *reshut hayachid*. This is the simplest and most natural reading of Abaye's reformulation, and it is in fact a general question that appears across multiple tractates: when a tree's trunk is in one domain and its branches extend into another, where is an object resting on those branches considered to be? A vivid parallel case — someone fleeing to a *city of refuge* who climbs onto a branch of a tree whose trunk stands within the city — raises exactly the same conceptual problem.

### Liability Consequences

The practical consequences for *hilchot Shabbat* are as follows. If the branch is in *reshut harabim* and the object on it is not resting on a four-by-four surface, the person is exempt — because in *reshut harabim*, a four-by-four surface is required. If, however, we follow Rabbi and treat the branch as part of *reshut hayachid* by virtue of the trunk's location, then the throw constituted carrying from *reshut harabim* into *reshut hayachid*, and no four-by-four is required for *hanacha* in *reshut hayachid* — making the person *chayav*. Alternatively, if the throw covered only two *amot*, not four: if the branch is *reshut harabim*, there is no violation at all; if the branch is considered *reshut hayachid*, the person has carried an object from *reshut harabim* into *reshut hayachid* and is *chayav*. The domain classification of the branch thus determines liability independently of the four-by-four question.

### Cities of Refuge Analogy

This same legal question — whether an object or person on an overhanging branch is considered to be in the domain of the trunk or in the domain of the branch's physical location — is addressed in several other contexts in the Talmud. The *arei miklat* case is particularly vivid: if someone fleeing a *goel hadam* climbs onto a branch that extends outside the city of refuge, while the tree's trunk stands within it, the question of whether that person is protected by the city's sanctuary turns on precisely this point.

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi offers a different reading that, as noted, does not fit well with the language of the Gemara. According to Rashi, the question is not one of domain classification at all. Rather, the branch is not four by four, and the question is whether its connection to the trunk lends it sufficient significance — as though it were four by four. Rashi effectively reduces the dispute to a variation on the four-by-four question itself. However, this reading sits poorly with the Gemara's emphasis on the trunk being in *reshut hayachid* and the branch extending into *reshut harabim*, and with the formulation *shadin nofo batar ikaro*, which speaks of following the branch toward the root — not of borrowing significance from the root. The simple sense of the Gemara is clearly as presented above.

---

## Beehive Domain Rules

### Beehive Parameters

Abaye introduces a new case: *zarak kaveret li-reshut ha-rabim* — you threw a beehive into *reshut harabim*. The beehive is ten *tefachim* high but not six *tefachim* wide. In that case, *chayav*. If it is six *tefachim* wide, *patur*. The beehive is a vessel shaped like a cylinder. The question is whether it constitutes a *reshut hayachid*.

### Geometry & Diameter

A *reshut hayachid* must measure four *tefachim* by four *tefachim* — not in one direction, but as a square area. For a circular object, the relevant question is what diameter is needed to contain a four-by-four square. By basic geometry, the diagonal of a four-by-four square equals four times the square root of two, which is approximately 5.6. Abaye rounds this to six, as Rashi notes. So: if the beehive is less than approximately 5.6 *tefachim* in diameter, the interior does not contain the requisite four-by-four area, and it does not qualify as a *reshut hayachid*. If it reaches or exceeds that diameter, the hollow interior — bounded by walls and standing ten *tefachim* high — constitutes a *reshut hayachid*.

### Rashi: Objects vs. Domai…

Rashi explains the ruling as follows: the Torah obligates one for carrying *objects*, not for carrying *domains*. You carry within a domain; you do not carry a domain itself. If the beehive meets the parameters of a *reshut hayachid* — ten *tefachim* high and four by four in area — it is classified as a domain rather than an object, and one is therefore not *chayav* for throwing it. Once it is smaller than those dimensions, it is simply an object, and carrying it across four *amot* in *reshut harabim* constitutes a full violation.

### Tosafot: Domain Transfer

Tosafot offers a slightly different explanation. The exemption, says Tosafot, is not because the beehive-as-domain is categorically different from an object. Rather, when the beehive lands in *reshut harabim*, it defines its own interior as a *reshut hayachid*. This means the thrower carried from *reshut hayachid* and deposited the object into what, upon landing, became a new *reshut hayachid*. One is not *chayav* for carrying from *reshut hayachid* to *reshut hayachid*. If the beehive is smaller — not meeting the dimensional threshold — then when it lands, its interior does not constitute a *reshut hayachid*, the object has been deposited in *reshut harabim*, and the person is *chayav*.

### Rava's Objection

Rava introduces a further consideration: *afilu eina rechava vav patur* — even if the beehive is not six *tefachim* wide, the person may be exempt. Why? *Ee efshar lekromei shel kaneh shelo yaalu lemala measara* — it is impossible for a beehive made of reeds not to have some small twigs or protrusions that extend above ten *tefachim*. Since *reshut harabim* extends only up to ten *tefachim*, any portion of an object above that height is outside *reshut harabim*. As established earlier in the tractate, if part of an object rests in one domain while another part is in a different domain, the carrier is exempt. Abaye presumably regards those small twigs as insignificant, but Rava maintains that even minor protrusions suffice to take the object outside the parameters of *reshut harabim* entirely.

This principle has a striking implication: virtually any object of significant height, when placed in *reshut harabim*, will have part of itself extending above ten *tefachim* and will thus fall outside *reshut harabim*. One would, on Rava's view, essentially never be *chayav* for carrying a tall object in *reshut harabim*.

### Lavud & Height Math

The Gemara then turns to a variant of the case: *kafa al piha* — the mouth of the beehive is facing downward. In this configuration, the threshold shifts from ten *tefachim* to seven: *shiva umashehu chayav, shiva umechetza patur*.

The reason involves the principle of *lavud*. When an open end of a structure is within three *tefachim* of the ground, we conceptually treat it as though it is already connected to the ground. When the mouth of the beehive faces downward, the open walls are oriented toward the ground, and we can therefore apply *lavud* to extend those walls to meet the ground — treating the object as if it has already come to rest. If the beehive is just over seven *tefachim* tall — say, 7.01 *tefachim* — then when it descends to within three *tefachim* of the ground (that is, when there is 2.99 *tefachim* remaining), *lavud* kicks in and the walls are conceptually extended. The object is treated as having landed, and its total effective height is 7.01 + 2.99 = 10 *tefachim* exactly, still fully within *reshut harabim*. The person is *chayav*.

But if the beehive is 7.5 *tefachim* tall, when it descends to within three *tefachim* of the ground, *lavud* treats it as already landed — yet 0.5 *tefachim* of the object still extends above ten *tefachim*, placing part of the object outside *reshut harabim*. The person is therefore *patur*. Remarkably, even as the beehive continues falling and eventually the full object is below ten *tefachim*, Rashi maintains that since at the moment of the conceptual *hanacha* (via *lavud*) the object was not fully within *reshut harabim*, the person remains *patur*.

It should be noted that *lavud* applies here precisely because the walls — open side facing downward — can be conceptually extended toward the ground. When the flat base faces downward, one cannot extend a floor via *lavud* in the same manner; *lavud* applies to the continuation of walls, not floors. That is why the threshold changes depending on the orientation of the beehive.

### Rav Ashi on Vessel Walls

Rav Ashi disputes this entire analysis: *afilu sheva umachetza chayav*. Even if the beehive is seven and a half *tefachim* tall and the mouth faces down, the person is still *chayav*. His reasoning: *mechitzos letochan asuyos* — the walls of a vessel are made to serve the contents inside, not to function as proper partitions. Just as we do not extend the floor of a base-down beehive via *lavud* because a floor does not function as a wall, so too we do not apply *lavud* to the walls of a beehive even when the mouth faces downward, because those walls exist to contain the vessel's contents, not to serve as the structural *mechitzot* of a domain. Since they are vessel walls and not functional *reshut*-walls, *lavud* does not apply to them, and the object is treated as having landed only when it physically touches the ground — at which point it is fully within ten *tefachim* and the person is *chayav*.

---

## Usage & Domain Status

### Nine Tefachim Pillar

The Gemara introduces a new case from Ulla: a pillar nine *tefachim* high in *reshut harabim*, upon which the masses regularly arrange and rearrange their loads (*verabim mekatfin aleha*). If someone throws an object four *amot* and it lands on top of that pillar, the person is *chayav*. What makes the top of a nine-*tefachim* pillar part of *reshut harabim*?

### Height-Based Usage Tiers

The Gemara articulates a framework of height-based usage tiers. Below three *tefachim*: people walk on it — unless it is something like a thornbush or excrement that people naturally avoid, anything within three *tefachim* of the ground is functionally walked upon and is considered structurally part of the ground and thus part of *reshut harabim*. From three to nine *tefachim*: the space is too high to be walked on but too low for convenient use — this range is a kind of dead zone, neither incorporated into the ground nor used for placing items. At nine *tefachim*: just the right height for people to set down and rearrange loads on their shoulders — a convenient working surface, like a changing table in a public space. Because the masses use it this way, it has the status of *reshut harabim* even though it is not structurally part of the ground. Things in the three-to-nine-*tefachim* range, by contrast, will be either a *karmelit* (if four by four) or a *makom patur* (if less than four by four).

The critical principle here is that usage — not structural connection to the ground — is the primary definitional criterion for *reshut harabim*. Even airspace that is not physically connected to the ground can carry the status of *reshut harabim* if it is genuinely used by the public in the manner characteristic of *reshut harabim*.

### Hole in Ground Query

Abaye asks Rav Yosef: *guma mai?* — what about a hole in the ground? Yesterday's discussion had addressed holes in walls; now the question is whether holes in the ground are similarly considered part of *reshut harabim* if people use them. A hole in the wall can be imagined as a convenient platform for placing objects; a hole in the ground is considerably harder to use conveniently. The question maps directly onto Abaye and Rava's debate from the previous day about holes in walls. There, Abaye held that even less-than-convenient use suffices to make something part of *reshut harabim*, while Rava held that the standard is higher. Abaye's question about holes in the ground reflects his more permissive position; Rava's higher threshold would presumably exclude such holes. Tosafot and Rashi disagree about the parameters of the hole under discussion — Rashi speaks of a hole nine *tefachim* deep (by analogy to the pillar), while Tosafot argues that for holes in the ground, shallower holes are more accessible and therefore more eligible for *reshut harabim* status.

### Basket as Domain

Rav Ada bar Matna challenges Rava with a further case: *haytah kuppa munachat birshus harabim, gevohah asarah u-revachah arba'ah* — a basket in *reshut harabim*, standing ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* wide. Because it is ten *tefachim* high and has a four-by-four interior, one would imagine the walls of the basket extending conceptually to the ground, making the interior a *reshut hayachid*. The ruling: *ein mataltelin lo mitochah lereshut harabim velo mershus harabim letochah* — one may not carry from the basket into *reshut harabim* or from *reshut harabim* into the basket. If it is smaller than those dimensions — less than ten high or less than four by four — it is simply a basket sitting in *reshut harabim*, and one may carry to and from it freely. Parallel reasoning is then applied to a hole: *ve-chein begummah*, and the same applies to a hole in the ground.

### Basket Resolution

The Gemara then asks whether the ruling on holes is a proof for Abaye's position. The suggestion is that if a small hole (less than ten *tefachim* deep and four by four wide) is treated as *reshut harabim*, that supports Abaye's view that holes count as *reshut harabim*. Rava responds that the ruling is not about the smaller hole at all — the comparison to the basket was only about the case that matches *reshut hayachid* dimensions (ten deep and four by four). For holes that don't meet those parameters, the Gemara is simply not asserting *reshut harabim* status; they may well be a *karmelit* or *makom patur* rather than *reshut harabim*. Rava thus deflects the challenge without conceding his position.

### Objects Don't = Domains

Tosafot raises the implicit question here: if a small basket or beehive could be classified as a *karmelit* when it doesn't meet *reshut hayachid* dimensions, then why did we say earlier (in the beehive case) that the person is simply *chayav* because it is an object — and not treat it as a *karmelit*? The answer is a significant principle: objects are not reclassified as *reshuyot* — not as a *karmelit*, not as anything else — unless they meet the full dimensional criteria for a genuine domain. A *karmelit* is itself a rabbinic category, not a biblical *reshut*, and we do not impose even that rabbinic domain-status on an ordinary object simply because it happens to have some enclosed space. Only when an object meets the full dimensions of *reshut hayachid* (ten *tefachim* high and four by four wide) do we treat it as a domain at all.

---

## Eruv in Pit

### Eruv Setup

The next *sugya* introduces a scenario from the laws of *eruv techumin*. One is not permitted to travel more than 2,000 *amot* beyond city limits on *Shabbat*. However, if before *Shabbat* one deposits food at the edge of the permitted boundary, that food establishes one's *Shabbat* starting point there, effectively allowing travel 2,000 *amot* in the opposite direction as well. For this to work, the food must be accessible — in theory, were the person standing at that spot, they could reach and eat it. The case: *hamaniach eruvo bebor* — the person placed the *eruv* food inside a pit.

### Accessibility Problem

A problem arises immediately. If the pit is a *reshut hayachid*, the food is in *reshut hayachid*, while the person is standing in *reshut harabim*. In theory, the person cannot access the food without transgressing. Since the *eruv* requires that the food be accessible and edible at the moment *Shabbat* begins, this inaccessibility would seem to invalidate the *eruv*.

### Pit Depth Criterion

The Gemara explains that the ruling depends on the depth of the pit. If the pit is less than ten *tefachim* deep, it is not a *reshut hayachid* — the *eruv* works. If it is deeper than ten *tefachim*, it is a *reshut hayachid* — the *eruv* does not work. The Gemara then asks: what does it mean to say the food is "above" or "below" ten *tefachim*? If the pit is always ten *tefachim* deep (and thus always a *reshut hayachid*), then whether the food is placed near the top or near the bottom of the pit makes no difference — it is still in *reshut hayachid* either way, and the person cannot access it. *Ma li lemala ma li lemata* — what does it matter if the food is high or low? *Hu bemakom echad veeruvo bemakom acher* — the person is in one domain and the food in another, regardless of food placement. The Gemara therefore concludes that "above" and "below" refer to the depth of the pit itself, not the placement of the food within it.

### Beraita Proof

This reading seems to be confirmed by a *baraita*. If the pit is less than ten *tefachim*, the *eruv* works — implying that the food, though in a pit, is accessible. But this raises a problem for Rava's position: even a pit less than ten *tefachim* would, on Rava's view, be a *karmelit* — and carrying from a *karmelit* to *reshut harabim* is rabbinically forbidden. So how can the *eruv* be valid if the food is in a *karmelit* and the person is in *reshut harabim*?

### Rava's Drabanan Exception

Rava responds by invoking the principle cited by Rabbi: *kol davar she-hu mishum shevut lo gazru alav bein ha-shmashot* — rabbinic prohibitions (*shevut*) were not extended to apply during the period of *bein hashmashot* (the twilight interval between sunset and nightfall). The food must be accessible only during *bein hashmashot*, when *Shabbat* takes effect. If the only obstacle to accessing the food is a rabbinic prohibition (carrying from a *karmelit* to *reshut harabim*), that prohibition does not apply during *bein hashmashot*. Therefore the food is considered legally accessible, and the *eruv* is valid — even if the pit is a *karmelit* rather than *reshut harabim*.

This principle has wide-ranging implications. Applying it broadly, one might think that any rabbinic prohibition could be set aside during *bein hashmashot*. The *poskim* limit the application with two qualifications: first, the act must serve some legitimate *tzorech mitzvah*, not be a casual violation; second, one must not have already accepted *Shabbat* (through candle-lighting or *kabbalat Shabbat*), since that acceptance defines the moment as *Shabbat* regardless of the astronomical time. The principle can nonetheless be practically significant — for instance, for someone stranded outside their home as *Shabbat* begins.

### Rava Reasserts Position

The Gemara makes clear that Rava is not merely offering a deflection. *Ve-lo teima d'chuyei kamidachina lach* — do not think he is just brushing aside the challenge. Rava reaffirms that his position is substantive: the hole is a *karmelit*, not *reshut harabim*, and the *eruv* works not because the pit is *reshut harabim* (as Abaye would have it) but because the rabbinic prohibition on carrying from a *karmelit* is suspended during *bein hashmashot* under Rabbi's ruling. The *baraita* is therefore not a proof for Abaye.

---

## Usage Hierarchy

### Puddle Passage Test

Rava now marshals a *baraita* from the laws of puddles to ground his position systematically. *Haya rekek mayim u'reshut harabim mahalachet bo* — if there is a puddle of water and the public pathway runs through it, *hazorek l'tocha arba amot chayav* — one who throws four *amot* through it is *chayav*. People walk through the puddle, so it retains *reshut harabim* status. The *baraita* repeats this formulation twice — once for a puddle in the summer and once in the rainy season. Each iteration is necessary: in summer, children may splash through puddles for enjoyment, so one might think the puddle counts because it is pleasurable to walk through. Perhaps in winter, when people avoid puddles, it would be different. Conversely, in winter, people walk through puddles because they are already dirty and indifferent, so perhaps in summer, when they would rather stay dry, the puddle would be avoided. *Tzricha* — both cases must be stated, and the upshot of both is the same: people walk through puddles in any season, and the puddle remains part of *reshut harabim*.

### Walking vs. Using

Rava draws a principled distinction from the double formulation. Why does the *baraita* twice emphasize that the *reshut harabim goes through* the puddle? Rava reads this as a deliberate statement: *hiluch al yedei hadachak shmei hiluch* — walking with some degree of difficulty is still called walking and counts as sufficient use to establish *reshut harabim* status. *Tashmish al yedei hadachak lo shmei tashmish* — but use of a non-walking kind, if accomplished only with difficulty, is not considered genuine use for purposes of *reshut harabim*.

### Primary Function Priority

The implication is that the primary function of *reshut harabim* is passage — movement, travel, walking. Those portions of the public domain that serve this primary function retain their *reshut harabim* status even when using them involves some inconvenience (walking through a puddle, stepping over an obstacle). But secondary uses — placing objects, storing goods — must be genuinely convenient to qualify. A pillar at exactly the right height for shoulder-rearranging counts because it is very easy to use. Holes in walls or holes in the ground, where reaching in and retrieving objects requires awkward effort, do not meet the threshold for a secondary use.

### Abaye-Rava Contrast

Abaye does not draw this distinction. For Abaye, any use — whether walking or otherwise — that is carried out, even somewhat inconveniently, suffices to give something *reshut harabim* status. Rava, by contrast, creates a two-tier system: walking uses are treated more leniently (even *hiluch al yedei hadachak* counts), while non-walking uses must be readily convenient. The articulation of this distinction is the conceptual contribution of this *sugya* to the broader discussion of domain definitions.

---

## Bundle in Acts

### Bundle Throwing

Rav Yehuda presents a case: *hai zarza de'kanei* — a bundle of reeds. If one throws the bundle and stands it up in *reshut harabim* (*rama v'zakfeih*), one does not transgress.

### Separate Acts Doctrine

The reason: *lo mechayeiv ad d'akar leih* — one is not liable until one picks the bundle up as a whole. If the bundle is, say, five *amot* tall, one can carry it through *reshut harabim* without becoming liable — by moving one end out of the original four-*amot* zone, allowing it to come to rest, and then moving the other end. Each stage is a separate act. The first act is not *mechayeiv* because part of the bundle remains within the four-*amot* zone. The second act is a new act, and the first act has already been completed and its *melacha* concluded. The acts are distinct and therefore non-cumulative for purposes of *chiyyuv*.

### Carrying Tall Objects

The practical application is immediately evident: a very tall object can, in principle, be moved through *reshut harabim* in increments, each step less than four *amot*, with the whole object coming to rest between steps. Each individual act falls short of the threshold for a *de'oraita* violation, even though the net result is that the object has traveled a great distance.

### Baby Carriage Issue

Tosafot raises a significant practical question: what about a baby carriage? One never picks it up; one merely rolls it. Two separate questions arise. The first, addressed in a *Gemara* in *Ketubot*, is whether lifting is required for *akira*: the answer is no — dragging an object out of its place constitutes *akira* even without lifting. The second question, which Tosafot raises here, is whether continuous rolling (without any moment of rest) is more like the bundle case (separate acts, each under four *amot*) or more like continuous dragging. Because the baby carriage rolls without stopping, Tosafot argues this is a single continuous act — not a series of separate acts. The object started here and ended there, and the movement never broke.

### Dragging vs. Separate Ac…

The contrast with dragging (*kovel*) clarifies the principle. When one drags an object continuously out of its original place — even without lifting — that constitutes *akira*, and the continuous motion through four *amot* in *reshut harabim* makes one *chayav*. The baby carriage, rolled continuously, is similarly one unbroken act. The bundle case is different: each segment of movement ends with the bundle at rest, constituting a genuine break between acts. Tosafot notes, but does not fully resolve, the apparent parallel to the case where someone stops to switch an object from one shoulder to the other — which the Gemara elsewhere rules does not count as a break. The precise line between a meaningful rest and a momentary pause for readjustment remains an open question.

---

## Ledge as Free Zone

### Ledge Setup

The Gemara turns to the *mishnah*'s case of the *iskofah* — a ledge or threshold projecting from a *reshut hayachid* out over *reshut harabim*, which does not measure four *tefachim* by four *tefachim*. A person can stand on this ledge on *Shabbat*.

### Ledge Function

The *mishnah* describes the ledge as a transfer point. A person standing there can take an object from the householder inside the *reshut hayachid* and give an object to the householder; alternatively, he can take an object from a poor person standing in the *reshut harabim* and give an object to the poor person. In other words, the ledge is used as an intermediary between the public and private domains.

### What Is the Ledge?

The Gemara systematically eliminates possible domain classifications. If the ledge were part of *reshut harabim*, then taking something from the householder and placing it on the ledge would constitute transferring from *reshut hayachid* to *reshut harabim* — a biblical violation. If the ledge were part of *reshut hayachid*, then taking something from the poor person in *reshut harabim* and placing it on the ledge would constitute transferring from *reshut harabim* to *reshut hayachid* — also a biblical violation. Could it be a *karmelit*? Even so, carrying between a *karmelit* and the other domains is rabbinically forbidden, and the *mishnah* permits these transfers *lechatchilah* — explicitly and unreservedly. A *karmelit* would still carry a rabbinic prohibition. *Sof sof issura miha ika* — there would still be some prohibition.

### Makom Patur Defined

The Gemara therefore concludes: *ella iskoppa makom p'tur b'alma hu* — the ledge is a *makom patur*, a fourth type of space, a free zone. The term *patur* here does not carry the usual implication of biblical exemption with rabbinic prohibition remaining; rather, *makom patur* is truly free — like free parking. Objects may be placed there from either domain, and taken from there into either domain, without any prohibition whatsoever.

### Makom Patur Criteria

The operative criterion is dimensional: *kegon d'leis bei arba al arba tefachim* — the space must be less than four *tefachim* by four *tefachim*. Any space of four by four *tefachim* has sufficient area to constitute a *reshut*, whether *reshut hayachid* (if ten *tefachim* high or enclosed) or *karmelit* (if in public space but not meeting full *reshut harabim* criteria). A space smaller than four by four *tefachim* is legally insignificant as a domain — just as an object must rest on a four-by-four surface to constitute *hanacha*, so a space must measure at least four by four to register as a *reshut*. Below that threshold, the space is a non-domain, and domain-based restrictions simply do not apply to it.

The one exception: if a space less than four by four is located within *reshut harabim* and is used by the public — like the nine-*tefachim* pillar discussed earlier — it is incorporated into *reshut harabim* by virtue of that use. Otherwise, if not used by the *rabim* and not otherwise enclosed within *reshut hayachid*, a sub-four-by-four space is *makom patur*.

### Dimi on Non-Domain Spaces

The Gemara concludes with a statement transmitted by Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *makom she-ein bo arba al arba tefachim, mutar livnei reshut hayachid u-livnei reshut harabim l'chasef alav* — a space that does not measure four by four *tefachim* may freely be used for placing objects by both the people of *reshut hayachid* and the people of *reshut harabim*. *U-vilvad she-lo yachalifu* — provided, however, that no one uses it as a transit point to pass objects from *reshut harabim* through the *makom patur* into *reshut hayachid* or vice versa. The *makom patur* is a neutral zone, not a corridor. Using it as an intermediate stop for a transfer between the two major domains would effectively accomplish what direct transfer would accomplish, and that remains prohibited.

---

---

# Shabbat 9

## Mekomah Patur

### Ledge Definition

The daf opens at the very bottom of 8b, where the Gemara returns to a point raised in the Tosefta concerning the *makom patur* — an exempt space. The specific case involves a ledge or threshold that is less than four by four *tefachim* in area, a dimension too small to qualify as a significant domain. Because it is less than four by four, this space is a *makom patur*, and it therefore lacks the halachic standing of either a *reshut ha-yachid* or a *reshut ha-rabim*.

### Three Party Exemption

The Tosefta states: *u-vilvad she-lo yitol mi-ba'al ha-bayit ve-noten le-ani, mi-ani ve-noten le-ba'al ha-bayit* — one must not take from the homeowner and give to the poor man, or from the poor man and give to the homeowner, using this ledge as an intermediate stop. That would be problematic because even though each individual step is technically permitted — transferring from a *reshut ha-rabim* to a *makom patur* and from a *makom patur* to a *reshut ha-yachid* — combining them in sequence would easily lead to transferring directly from one domain to the other.

Nevertheless, the Tosefta adds: *ve-im natal ve-natan, shloshtan pturim* — if all three parties did participate in such a transfer, all three are exempt. The Gemara will soon probe this ruling. One might explain the exemption of all three by saying each party performed only half of the forbidden act, as in the famous case in the Mishnah where the homeowner and the poor man each participate equally and are both exempt. But the Tosefta implies something broader than that: even if the person standing on the *makom patur* picked the object up with one hand and placed it in the other — so that the object fully traversed the space — all parties remain exempt because it passed through a *makom patur*. The Gemara seizes on this.

### Rava's Kashya

The Gemara raises the question: *leima tehavi tiyuvta de-Rava* — is this not a refutation of Rava? For Rava stated: *ha-ma'avir chefetz mi-tchilas arba le-sof arba* — one who transfers an object from the beginning of four *amot* to the end of four *amot* in the *reshut ha-rabim*, *af al pi she-he'eviro derech alav chayav* — even though he did so *derech alav*, through or over himself, he is liable. The question is: if passing through the airspace of a *makom patur* in this way still renders one liable, how is that consistent with the Tosefta's ruling that passing through an actual *makom patur* exempts all three parties?

### Rashi on Derech

The term *derech alav* is the crux of the difficulty, and Rashi and Tosafot understand it differently. Rashi reads *alav* literally — "on top of him" — meaning the person lifted the object ten *tefachim* off the ground, above the *reshut ha-rabim*, so that in the middle of its journey it passed through airspace that qualifies as a *makom patur*. Nevertheless, Rava rules, the person is liable. This is structurally similar to the Gemara's earlier discussion of passing an object through a *karmelit* — there, too, the question was whether transiting through an intermediate domain breaks the continuity of the forbidden act — except that here the intermediate zone is a *makom patur*, which might seem an even stronger basis for exemption.

### Tosafot Interpretation

Tosafot, by contrast, reads *derech alav* not as "on top of him" but as "in front of him" — *lefanav*. On this reading, the person did not lift the object ten *tefachim* off the ground at all; rather, the point is that the object passed directly in front of the person while in motion. Tosafot's concern is to resolve the phrase with another Gemara that requires accommodation, and it is that textual pressure which drives this alternative reading. Tosafot himself notes that the term *al gavei* would more naturally mean "in front of," while Rashi's reading of "on top of" would ordinarily require a different phrase. One can evaluate which reading strains the language less, but what is pushing Tosafot is his need to harmonize a different Gemara. In any case, whichever reading one adopts, the Gemara's structural question remains: why is Rava's case any different from the case of the three parties on the *makom patur*?

### Nach vs. Lo Nach

The Gemara's answer is simple and decisive: *hatam lo nach, hacha nach* — there, the object did not come to rest; here, it did. In Rava's case, whether the object passed through the airspace above ten *tefachim* or passed in front of the person, it never stopped. It moved continuously from its starting point to its ending point, and therefore the person is liable despite the intermediate passage through a zone that might otherwise exempt. In the case of the three parties, however, the person standing on the *makom patur* actually set the object down — it came to rest on the ledge — and then picked it up again and transferred it to the next party. That constitutes two distinct acts, each of which, taken alone, is not only exempt but actually permitted: transferring from a *reshut ha-rabim* to a *makom patur*, and from a *makom patur* to a *reshut ha-yachid*. The combined result is rabbinically problematic — because it too easily approximates the full biblical prohibition of transferring from one major domain to another — but both parties engaged in each individual act remain exempt.

Rava's *chiddush*, then, is that when there is no *nach* — no coming to rest — you remain liable even when the object transits a *makom patur*. We previously had to agonize over the analogous question involving a *karmelit*; the case of transit through a *makom patur* is in some ways an even stronger candidate for leniency, and yet Rava rules *chayav*. That is a genuine *chiddush*. The *chiddush* of the Tosefta, by contrast, is not simply that one is *patur* — it is that the combined act, though producing that *patur* verdict, is nonetheless *asur d'rabbanan*. Both points stand.

---

## Iskofah Two Domains

### Iskofah Case

The Gemara moves to the final clause of the Mishnah, which discusses a ledge — an *iskofah* — that serves two domains simultaneously. The case is not a *makom patur* at all, but a ledge that can be classified as either *reshut ha-yachid* or *reshut ha-rabim* depending on circumstances. The specific scenario involves a *chatzer* — a courtyard surrounded by houses — with a ledge positioned at its entrance, opening onto the *reshut ha-rabim*.

### Door Open Status

The Baraita cited by the Gemara states: *iskofah meshameshet shtei reshuyot* — this threshold serves two domains. *Bizman shehapetach patuach, kilfanim* — when the door is open, the threshold is treated as part of the interior, that is, part of the *reshut ha-yachid* of the courtyard or house. Rashi understands the interior to refer to a courtyard; Tosafot extends this to include either a courtyard or a house, though that distinction is not the focus of the analysis here.

### Door Closed Status

*Petach na'ul, kilchutz* — when the door is closed, the threshold is treated as being on the outside, like the *reshut ha-rabim*. Both Rashi and Tosafot, however, are careful to point out that this does not mean the *iskofah* literally becomes a *reshut ha-rabim* in a biblical sense. Biblically, it retains the status of *reshut ha-yachid* — it is, after all, surrounded by three walls. What the Baraita means is only that one is not permitted to carry in that space. Tosafot explicitly states this: when the door is closed, *mid'oraisa* it remains *reshut ha-yachid*, but the rabbinic rule does not permit carrying there.

### Physical Setup

The Gemara's deeper question is: why does the state of the door make any difference at all? To understand this, one must picture the physical setup carefully.

Imagine a courtyard surrounded on three sides by the walls of houses. The fourth side is open to the *reshut ha-rabim*, except that the walls extend slightly inward — or there is a post, a *lechi*, positioned at the entrance — which allows carrying within the courtyard under the rules governing a *mavoi* or *chatzer*. The *iskofah* is the threshold space in the width of the doorway itself, between the interior courtyard and the *reshut ha-rabim*.

The difficulty is this: even when the door is open, the threshold space — the width of the doorway — has only three walls. The two sides of the doorway and the wall behind it give three walls, but there is no beginning of a fourth wall — no *lechi* and no *korah* (beam) — within that doorway space itself. A *lechi* positioned at the outer edge of the courtyard entrance serves the courtyard interior, but what helps the space within the doorway width?

Rav Chama bar Gurya said in the name of Rav: *tocha pesach tzarich lechi acher le-hatiro* — the inside of a doorway requires an additional *lechi* to permit carrying in it. So even if the door is open, the space of the threshold itself lacks the fourth-wall element needed to allow carrying. One might propose that since the doorway width is less than four by four, it has no independent significance — it is *batel* to the *reshut ha-yachid* behind it and piggybacks on that domain's valid *lechi*. But Rav Chama bar Gurya explicitly rejects this: even if the doorway space is less than four by four — even if in isolation it would be a *makom patur* — one still needs an additional *lechi* outside the doorway to permit carrying there.

This then is the standing question: granted that when the door is closed, the space is problematic — only three walls with no fourth-wall element. But even when the door is open, it has the same three walls and no fourth-wall element. What does the open door change?

---

## Korah Beam Analysis

### Rav Yehuda Answer

The Gemara presents two answers to this question. The first is given by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *hacha be-iskofas mavoi askinan* — we are dealing with the threshold of a *mavoi*. Tosafot notes that this implies the earlier discussion was about a house or *chatzer*, but for the purposes of the core halachic question that distinction is not material. The critical detail Rav Yehuda introduces is this: *chetzyo mekureh ve-chetzyo she-eino mekureh, ve-kiroyav kelapei pnim* — half of the threshold space is covered by a partial roof — specifically, a beam — and the covered portion is directed toward the inside.

The physical picture is as follows: the threshold opening is spanned by a beam (*korah*) positioned toward the interior side of the doorway. When the door is open, the space under consideration from the beam outward encompasses the full interior of the courtyard, which is larger than four by four. In that case, the *korah* functions as a valid halachic marker for a fourth wall, and one may carry up to its outer edge. When the door is closed, however, the space directly under the beam — the space between the beam and the closed door — is less than four by four.

### Beam Efficacy Condition

This distinction is what drives the ruling. A *korah* only functions as a halachic device when it relates to a space of at least four by four. If the space it covers or relates to is less than four by four, it is too insignificant for the *korah* to do halachic work. So when the door is open, the *korah* relates to the full interior courtyard — well over four by four — and functions perfectly, extending the *reshut ha-yachid* to its outer edge. When the door is closed, the *korah* is left relating only to the tiny space between itself and the closed door — less than four by four — and therefore cannot function.

### Four-by-Four Rule

It is important to clarify what "four by four" means in this context. The requirement is not that the *korah* itself be four *tefachim* wide — a thin beam can serve perfectly well as a *korah* in a normal courtyard configuration. Rather, the requirement is that the *korah* must relate to a space of at least four by four beneath or beyond it. A *korah* covering or fronting a space less than four by four is halachically inoperative. This is the key to understanding why the open door and the closed door produce such different results: the door changes not the beam itself but the space to which the beam relates.

### Rav Ashi Lavud

Rav Ashi offers a second answer, which is a variation on the same principle but with an added sophistication. *Le-olam be-iskufas bayis askinan* — we may be dealing with the threshold of a house. The case he constructs is as follows: *u-kegon she-kira bi-shtei korot she-ein be-zu arba ve-ein be-zu arba, ve-ein bein zu le-zu sheloshah, ve-ha-delet be-emtza* — the threshold is covered not by a single beam but by two beams, neither of which is four *tefachim* wide, and the gap between them is less than three *tefachim*, with the door positioned in between the two beams.

The principle of *lavud* — the halachic rule that a gap of less than three *tefachim* is treated as if it were closed — allows two adjacent beams separated by less than three *tefachim* to combine and be treated as a single continuous beam. If the two beams together span enough to constitute four *tefachim*, they function together as a valid *korah*, enabling carrying in the space beneath them.

### Door Separates Lavud

But the door disrupts this mechanism. When the door is closed, it physically intervenes between the two beams, severing their ability to combine through *lavud*. Each beam is then evaluated independently, and since neither alone is four *tefachim* wide, neither functions as a valid *korah*. The space in front of the door is left with only three walls and no operative fourth-wall element, and carrying is not permitted.

When the door is open, the two beams are once again able to operate together. Through *lavud* they combine to form a halachically complete *korah*, the space they front is large enough — being the full interior plus the threshold — and carrying is permitted up to the outer edge.

To sharpen the contrast further: had the two beams been a single, solid *korah* genuinely four *tefachim* wide, the door's position between the sub-sections would be irrelevant — it would remain one complete *korah*, and carrying would be permitted even with the door closed. The reason Rav Ashi uses the more complex case of two beams combined by *lavud* is precisely to make the ruling interesting: it is only *because* their unity depends on *lavud* that the door can interrupt their function. The door is not interrupting a solid beam — it is interrupting the halachic fiction by which two separate, insufficient beams are treated as one. Sever that fiction, and both beams lose their efficacy simultaneously. The case of the solid four-*tefachim korah* would have been different, and that contrast illuminates the limits of *lavud* as a halachic tool.

A practical analogy worth noting: if a roof extends over the outer edge of a doorway — even if the space beneath that roof is less than four by four — the roof itself being genuinely four *tefachim* wide would be enough to make it function. The threshold case is intrinsically parallel to that scenario and helps make the abstract rule more concrete.

---

## Distinct Reshut

### Four-by-Ten Rule

The final point of the Mishnah introduces a different case: *iskofah gevoha asara ve-rechava arba'a, harei zu reshuta le-atzma* — if the threshold is ten *tefachim* high and four wide, it constitutes its own domain. This is not merely saying it is a *reshut ha-yachid*; it seems to be saying something more specific — it is a *reshut ha-yachid* that is structurally distinct from the courtyard behind it. The Gemara asks what the force of this ruling is.

### Rabbi Meir Two Domains

The Gemara says this lends support to Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi, who reported a ruling of Rabbi Meir: *kol makom she-ata motzei shenei reshuyot ve-hein reshuta achas* — wherever you find two structurally distinct spaces, each with the halachic status of *reshut ha-yachid*, the question arises whether you may transfer between them freely. The example Rabbi Meir uses is *amud bi-reshut ha-yachid gevoha asara ve-rachav arba'a* — a column or elevated structure standing in the middle of a *reshut ha-yachid*, ten *tefachim* high and four by four in area. Intuitively one might assume that since both the floor and the top of the column are *reshut ha-yachid*, there is no prohibition in placing objects on top of it.

### Filing Cabinet Gezerah

Rabbi Meir rules otherwise: *assur le-katef alav* — it is forbidden to load things onto it. Why? *Gezeira mishum ketef reshut ha-rabim* — a rabbinic decree lest one do the same with a similar elevated structure in the *reshut ha-rabim*. A column ten *tefachim* high and four by four standing in the *reshut ha-rabim* is itself a *reshut ha-yachid* — and transferring from the *reshut ha-rabim* up onto such a column would be a biblical violation. Since placing objects on top of elevated structures does not feel like carrying between domains — it simply feels like placing something on top of a piece of furniture — there is a risk one would do the same thing outdoors without recognizing the prohibition. Therefore, Rabbi Meir prohibits doing it even indoors as a protective decree.

The concern has an intuitive logic: the act of placing something atop a filing cabinet or a high shelf feels categorically different from the act of carrying an object from one room to another. One does not experience it as a domain transfer. That subjective gap between the act and its halachic characterization is precisely the kind of cognitive slip that rabbinic decrees are designed to close.

### Tosafot Limitation

Tosafot raises an obvious limiting question: if this *gezeira* applies to elevated structures inside a *reshut ha-yachid*, does it also apply to carrying from the ground floor of a house to the upper floor? After all, each floor is technically a distinct *reshut ha-yachid*.

Tosafot resolves this by distinguishing between a structure whose status as a separate *reshut ha-yachid* is not visually obvious — like a column or a tall cabinet standing in the middle of an open space — and a structure whose walls are clearly apparent. An upper story, surrounded by visible walls that make its *reshut ha-yachid* status unmistakable, does not trigger the same concern. The worry is specifically for elevated objects whose independent domain status is not intuitively apparent, so that carrying to or from them feels like simply placing an object rather than transferring between domains. By contrast, if one looks through a window between two clearly-walled adjacent houses and passes an object through, there is no concern — the domain boundaries are visually clear. It should be noted that we do not rule like Rabbi Meir in practice, and this position is therefore of theoretical rather than practical import.

---

## Mincha Time Restrictions

### Prohibited Activities

The Gemara now turns to a completely new topic — the Mishnah on 9b — which is the second Mishnah of this chapter. To understand the larger context: this Mishnah is the middle of a three-Mishnah sequence. The first Mishnah addresses the laws of carrying on Shabbat; the third Mishnah will address going out on *Erev Shabbat* with objects in one's pocket, lest one forget them and carry on Shabbat. Bridging these two is the present Mishnah, which establishes a general concern about beginning activities that one might lose track of — potentially forgetting to perform a time-sensitive obligation.

The Mishnah states: *lo yeishev adam lifnei ha-sapar samuch la-mincha* — a person may not sit down before a barber close to *mincha* time *ad she-yispalel* — until he has davened. Similarly: *ve-lo yikanes adam le-merchatz* — one may not enter a bathhouse; *ve-lo le-burski* — nor begin work at a tannery; *ve-lo le-echol* — nor sit down to eat; *ve-lo la-din* — nor convene for a court case. All of these activities risk becoming so absorbing that one will forget to daven.

### No Interruption Rule

The Mishnah then states: *ve-im hitchil, ein mafsikin* — if one has already begun, we do not require him to interrupt. This rule applies because if there will be adequate time after completing the activity, we trust the person to daven afterward. A qualification not stated in this Mishnah but established elsewhere is that if completing the activity will cause one to miss the *tefilla* entirely, one would be required to stop and daven. But assuming time remains, the Mishnah adopts a lenient position: once one has begun, we do not impose the burden of interruption.

The Mishnah adds one exception: *mafsikin li-kri'at shema, ve-ein mafsikin li-tefilla* — we do interrupt for *kri'at shema* but not for *tefilla* (i.e., the *Amida*). This is because *kri'at shema* is a biblical obligation, and the heightened urgency of a biblical commandment overrides the allowance to continue a permitted activity. *Tefilla*, by contrast, is rabbinic in origin, and therefore once one has already begun a permissible activity, we do not impose the interruption.

### Mincha Times

The Gemara asks: *hi samuch le-mincha* — which *mincha* does the Mishnah refer to? The day is divided into two relevant periods. *Mincha gedola* — the "large *mincha*" — begins at the sixth-and-a-half seasonal hour, which on a standard day corresponds to approximately 12:30 PM. This is the earliest time one may daven *mincha*. The rationale for the half-hour offset from noon involves a dispute among Rishonim: Rashi in one place suggests it is simply a practical allowance because people without clocks cannot detect the precise moment of noon; in another place Rashi explains that experientially, the sun does not begin to feel as though it is setting until after the window of 11:30 to 12:30, during which the sun appears directly overhead regardless of where the mathematical midpoint falls.

*Mincha ketana* — the "small *mincha*" — begins at the ninth-and-a-half seasonal hour, approximately 3:30 PM, and this is considered the ideal time for *mincha*. From 3:30 onward there are only two and a half hours of daylight remaining.

The question is which period triggers the Mishnah's restrictions. Logically, one would assume *mincha ketana*: at *mincha gedola*, one still has five and a half hours remaining in the day. How can anyone be concerned about forgetting to daven when there is that much time? The Gemara confirms this initial logic: *eileima le-Mincha Gedola, amai lo? Ha-ika she'os ha-yom tuba* — if it means before *mincha gedola*, why not? You have plenty of time. *Ela samuch le-mincha ketana* — so the Mishnah must mean right before *mincha ketana*, around 3:00 PM.

### Rav Yehoshua Contradicti…

Having established this, the Gemara raises a contradiction with the position of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who said: *keivan she-higi'a zman tefilat ha-mincha, assur la-adam she-yitam klum kodem she-yispalel* — once the time for *mincha* prayer has arrived, it is forbidden for a person to taste anything before davening. The phrasing *assur litom klum* — forbidden to taste anything at all — sounds absolute, suggesting that even if one has already begun eating, one must stop. This stands in tension with the Mishnah's ruling that once one has begun, one does not interrupt.

The Gemara reconciles this by distributing the two positions across the two time periods: the Mishnah's lenient "don't interrupt once you've started" rule applies to *mincha gedola*, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's absolute prohibition applies to *mincha ketana*. This reconciliation, however, pushes the Mishnah's "don't start" rule all the way back to *mincha gedola*. And if one cannot begin at *mincha gedola*, the question returns: why not? There are five and a half hours left.

The Gemara's first answer is that we are not talking about ordinary activities but about specifically extended ones: *u-vetisporet ben Elasha* — the haircut in question is the famously elaborate hairdo perfected by Ben Elasha, where each strand of hair is arranged so that the tip of one hair touches the root of the next — the kind of styling that can consume an entire afternoon. Similarly, *le-kula mirsa de-merchatz* — not merely a bath but the full spa regimen. *Le-burski gedolah* — the full tanning process from beginning to end. *Be-seuda gedolah* — a large meal on the scale of a wedding feast. *Be-techilat din* — a court case from its opening, which may run for days. Only these outsized activities are prohibited beginning at *mincha gedola*. The result is a relatively lenient ruling: ordinary versions of these activities may be begun even at *mincha gedola*, while only especially extended versions trigger the restriction.

---

## Rav Achai Stringent

### Haircut Risk

Rav Achai bar Yaakov offers a far more stringent position. He contends that even ordinary versions of these activities cannot be begun at *mincha gedola*, and he provides a reason for each. Regarding the haircut: *gezeira shema yishaver ha-zog* — we are concerned that the scissors might break mid-haircut. Obtaining replacement scissors or having them sharpened was not trivial — it could require locating a metalworker and waiting an extended time — so what was expected to be a brief visit could turn into hours.

### Bathhouse Risk
