More importantly, when ten people are reading by a single torch, each is individually occupied with his own text, separated in his own space — they do not constitute a mutual-reminder group but rather ten individuals, each independently exposed to the temptation of adjusting the flame.

This raises a contemporary question: does any of this apply to electric light? Nowadays, there is generally no concern about adjusting an electric bulb. However, a dimmer switch introduces a related issue: if the light is set low and one is tempted to raise it to read more comfortably, the analogy to *hataya* may be relevant.

### Wealthy Exception

*Amar Rava: im adam chashuv hu mutar* — Rava rules that a person of high social standing may read by candlelight. The reason: a *chashuv* person would never handle his own lamp; he always has an attendant do it for him. Since he never touches candles or lamps himself, there is no realistic concern that he will come to tip it. This is a striking distinction. On one hand, even if the lamp is placed ten stories high, one may not read by it — *lo plug*. Yet if one belongs to a class of people who never personally handles lamps, the prohibition simply does not apply. The *gemara* is apparently unconcerned about the social stratification implicit in this distinction — in a society where such class differences were simply a reality, applying different rules to different classes of people was unproblematic.

### Yishmael Story

*Metivei: lo yikra l'or haner shema yateh. Amar Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha: ani ekra velo ateh* — Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha declared: I will read; I will not come to tip it. He was either sufficiently vigilant about Shabbat or sufficiently *chashuv* that the concern did not seem to apply to him. *Pa'am achat kara u'vikeish l'hatot* — once, while reading, he was about to tip the candle. He caught himself and declared: *kamah gedolim divrei chachamim she'hayu omrim lo yikra l'or haner* — how great are the words of the Sages who said one may not read by candlelight. The parallel to the Solomonic story about multiplying wives — the very king who declared "they will not lead my heart astray," and whose heart was indeed led astray — is apt. No matter how great one believes oneself to be, one must take seriously what *Chazal* know about human nature.

*Rabbi Natan* reports an even more striking version: *kara vehittah* — he actually did tip it. He did not merely come close; he did it. He then wrote in his notebook: *ani Yishmael ben Elisha karisi vehitisi ner b'Shabbat, uchesheyi­baneh Beit Hamikdash avi chatas shmenah* — I, Yishmael ben Elisha, read and tipped a lamp on Shabbat; when the Temple is rebuilt, I will bring a fat *chatat*, for I was *mechalel shabbat b'shogeg*.

### Torah Engagement

Despite this powerful story, the *gemara* does not overturn the principle permitting a *chashuv* person to read by candlelight. *Amar Rabbi Abba: shani Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha, ho'il u'mashim atzmo al divrei Torah k'hedyot* — Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha was different: when he engaged in Torah, he forgot his own status. He immersed himself so completely that he lost track of who he was, and in that state of total absorption he reached to adjust the lamp just as any ordinary person would. For others who remain conscious of their *chashuv* status even while learning — who never forget themselves entirely in Torah — the concern does not arise, and the permission stands.

---

## Servants Checking

### Vessel Checking

The *gemara* now takes up the case of a *shamash* — a household attendant — checking glasses and dishes to ensure they are clean. One *baraita* permits the *shamash* to perform this inspection by candlelight; another *baraita* prohibits it. These are in apparent contradiction.

### Permanent v. Temp

*Lo kashya: kan b'shamash kavua, kan b'shamash she'eino kavua* — the two *baraitot* address different situations. One concerns a permanent, regular attendant; the other concerns a temporary hire. Rashi and *Tosafot* disagree about which way to read the distinction: according to Rashi, a temporary attendant, having no security in his position, does a careless job and therefore cannot be trusted to inspect properly. A regular attendant, invested in the household, is more careful. *Tosafot* reads it the other way. The essential point is that the *halacha* varies based on the attendant's relationship to the household.

### Oil v. Naphtha

*V'ibait eima, ha v'ha b'shamash kavua, v'lo kashya, ha d'mishcha ha d'nafta* — alternatively, both *baraitot* concern a permanent attendant, and the distinction is between oil and naphtha. Naphtha is a malodorous petroleum substance that no one wants to handle unnecessarily, and therefore a *shamash* using a naphtha lamp would not come to tip it toward himself or the vessels. Oil, by contrast, is something the attendant handles comfortably, and there is a realistic concern he might tip the lamp. Accordingly, checking by an oil lamp is prohibited while checking by a naphtha lamp is permitted.

### Rav Disagreement

*Iba'ya lehu: shamash she'eino kavua v'demishcha mai?* — what about a temporary attendant and an oil lamp? A permanent attendant using oil is prohibited. Is a temporary attendant using oil also prohibited, or does something about his temporary status change the calculus? *Amar Rav: halacha v'ein morin ken* — Rav rules that it is technically permissible (*halacha*), but one should not publicize this ruling (*ein morin ken*), lest it lead people to make errors. *Rav Yirmiya bar Abba* disagrees: *halacha u'morin ken* — one may and should publicize that it is permissible.

### Household Practices

The *gemara* closes with a story that illustrates this dispute in practice. Rav Yirmiya bar Abba — the same one who ruled that one may publicize the leniency — was once a guest at the home of Rav Assi on Shabbat. *Kam shamaya badkei lehu l'or shraga* — Rav Yirmiya's attendant got up and checked the vessels by candlelight. *Amrah leih deviteihu* — Rav Assi's wife said to him: you yourself do not allow our attendant to do this — why is your guest permitting his attendant to do so? *Amar lah: shavkeih, kerabbeih sevira leih* — he told her: leave him alone; he follows the ruling of his teacher. Rav Yirmiya, having ruled that the leniency may be publicized and applied, is acting in accordance with his own *psak*. We in this house are stringent, but he is not to be faulted for following his *rebbe*'s position.

# Shabbat 13

## Candlelight Reading

### Intro & Gezeirot Theme

We begin daf 13 by picking up two lines from the bottom of 12b, at the phrase *v'emet amru*, where the Gemara is wrapping up a series of *gezeirot* — protective rabbinic decrees — concerning Shabbat. The opening theme of this section has been activities prohibited on Shabbat because they might lead to a transgression. The discussion began with carrying on *erev Shabbat* and has moved to various activities one might perform by candlelight, where the concern is that a person will come to tilt the candle to improve the light — a prohibited act on Shabbat. As we will see, the sugya then shifts radically to a different concern: not Shabbat-related at all, but the general principle that doing one thing can lead to something else entirely.

### Chazzan Reading

The Mishnah at the end of 12b states: *v'emet amru ha-chazzan ro'eh heichan tinokot korin aval lo yikra* — even though one may not read by candlelight, they said that the *chazzan* — the community functionary who also often served as teacher of children — may look to see where the children are reading, but may not himself read. This is apparently connected to the ancient practice of reviewing the weekly *parasha* — the *ma'avir sedrah* — prior to or on Shabbat itself, which seems to be a quite venerable custom. The Gemara asks: *mai lav likros* — doesn't the phrase "he may see" actually mean he can read? That would seem to contradict the principle that one may not read by candlelight lest one come to *l'hatot*, to tilt the candle.

### Chazzan Reading Question

The Mishnah's formulation — *ro'eh* without *yikra* — raises the question of what meaningful distinction exists between seeing and reading. The answer given is *lo l'sader rashei parshiyosav* — he may only organize the beginnings of the *parshiyot*. The Rambam explains this to mean that the *chazzan* may find the starting point and read the first two or three words to get the children started, but he cannot conduct a sustained reading on his own. This is confirmed by a further statement attributed to Rabbah bar Shmuel: *aval mesader hu rashei parshiyosav* — he may orient the children at the beginning of the portions, but no more. The Gemara then asks: and he cannot read the entire *parasha*?

### Children Reading Tosefta

At the top of 13a, the Gemara raises a *Tosefta* in challenge: *Rabban Gamliel omer ha-tinokot shel beit rabban hayu mesadrim parshiyoseihen v'korin l'or ha-neir* — Rabban Gamliel says that the young children studying in their master's house — the famous *tinokot shel beit rabban* — would organize their *parshiyot* and actually read by candlelight. The Gemara notes the force of this: *hayu korin l'or ha-neir* — they were reading, not merely identifying, by candlelight. Presumably one would not actively have small children violate a rabbinic decree.

### Eimas Rabban

The Gemara offers two possible resolutions. The first is that *rashei parshiyosav* — "reading" here refers only to reading the beginnings of the portions, consistent with the limitation already established. The second, and more interesting, resolution is *shani tinokot* — children are different. Why? *Ho'il v'eimas rabban aleihem lo asi l'atzloyei* — because the fear of their teacher is upon them, they will not come to tilt the candle. Even on a weekday, no child would dare move the candle without the teacher's permission. The *eimas rabban* functions as an effective deterrent against the prohibited action that the decree was designed to prevent.

### Group Protection Princip…

The *eimas rabban* explanation is one instance of a broader principle at work here: when multiple people are engaged in an activity together as a group, we are less concerned that they will violate the relevant prohibition, because one person will remind the other. This is distinct from a case where multiple individuals happen to be using the same candle independently for their own separate purposes — in that case, each is acting alone and the mutual-reminder dynamic does not apply. But where they are acting in concert, the group dynamic itself provides a measure of protection.

## Zav & Zavah Eating

### Zav Zavah Rule

The Gemara now shifts to a statement entirely unrelated to Shabbat: *ha-zav lo yochal im ha-zava mipnei hergel aveirah* — a *zav* should not eat with a *zava*, because it will lead to *hergel aveirah*, accustoming oneself to transgression. What is this doing in Masechet Shabbat? One explanation is that a whole collection of teachings of the form "do not do A, lest it lead to B" were transmitted together — the prohibition against sitting for a haircut before *Mincha* lest one miss *davening*, various Shabbat-related concerns, and this concern about *zav* and *zava* eating together — and they were all gathered here because the core of the collection dealt with Shabbat. Another explanation is that this statement was part of the famous list of eighteen *gezeirot* enacted in the upper chamber of Chananya ben Guryon, where Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai agreed upon a series of decrees — and our Mishnah is about to describe that list.

### Hergel Aveira Meaning

What does *hergel aveirah* mean in this context? Following Rashi, the picture is as follows. The *tahor* people are eating together, and a *zav* and a *zava*, both being *tamei*, cannot eat with them. They must go off and eat by themselves — and we will see in the Gemara that the assumption is that everyone, not just *kohanim* dealing with *terumah*, was careful about the laws of *tahara*. So the *zav* and the *zava* cannot eat with the *tahor* group, and the concern is that if they eat alone together in private, it will lead to sexual relations — a concern of *erva* and *karet*.

One could ask: why would this require a special *gezeirah*? Would it not already be covered by the general prohibition of *yichud*? Rashi, and similarly the Rambam, apparently assumes we are speaking of husband and wife. A stranger pairing would fall under existing *yichud* concerns, but here the novelty is the case of husband and wife: even though husband and wife are ordinarily permitted to eat together at home even when she is a *niddah*, here the concern is that the private circumstances of being isolated from their normal eating group will create conditions leading to sexual relations. This will open into the Gemara's broader discussion of the *harchakot* between husband and wife during *niddah*.

There is, however, a significantly simpler reading of this passage, advanced by the *Mishnat Eretz Yisrael* commentary of the Safrai family. According to them, there is no need to introduce sexual concerns at all. The *hergel aveirah* is entirely about *tumah*. The reasoning is: of course two strangers who are both *tamei* can eat together — being *tamei* does not obligate you to eat alone. But husband and wife who are both *tamei* eating together is problematic because the next time only one of them will be *tamei*, and being accustomed to eating together, they will continue doing so — causing the *tahor* one's food to become *tamei*. The concern is specifically the husband-and-wife relationship because that intimacy creates habitual patterns that persist even when the *tumah* circumstances change.

### Purity Practice Braita

A *braita* is introduced in which Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: *bo u'rei ad heichan partza tahara b'Yisrael* — come and see how extensively the practice of *tahara* had spread in Israel. He observes that the Mishnah does not need to state that a *tahor* person should not eat with a *tamei* person — that was taken entirely for granted. Even though there is nowadays no technical prohibition against eating one's own food while *tamei*, unless one is a *kohen* dealing with *terumah*, the practice of eating *be-tahara* had become so pervasive that the *tahor* eating with the *tamei* did not even need to be stated; everyone already understood this. The Gemara's observation here is significant from a social-historical perspective: the *chaburot*, the defined eating groups, and the boundaries of who is a *chaver* — a member of such a group — were deeply boundary-defining markers of identity. The only thing that needed to be stated explicitly was the *zav* and *zava* case.

### Zav Parush Case

A parallel case is then introduced: *lo yochal zav parush im zav am ha-aretz* — a *zav* who is normally careful about *tahara* should not eat with a *zav* who is an *am ha-aretz*, one who is not generally careful about *tumah ve-tahara* or about separating *terumot u-ma'asrot*. The concern, again phrased with the language of *hergel*, is *shema yargilennu etzlo* — perhaps he will become accustomed to being in his company.

The Gemara immediately asks: *ve-chi margilo etzlo mai havei* — so what if he becomes accustomed to being with him? What is the concern? The Gemara suggests: *shema ya'achilennu dvarim tme'im* — perhaps the *am ha-aretz* will feed him *tamei* things. But the Gemara objects: *atu zav parush lo dvarim tme'im achal* — the careful *zav* already eats *tamei* things himself, since he is a *zav*! So what difference does eating the *am ha-aretz*'s food make?

### Rava's Hergel Aveira

Abaye and Rava offer different resolutions. Abaye says: *gezeirah shema ya'achilennu dvarim she-einam metukanim* — we are concerned that the *am ha-aretz* will feed him food from which *terumot u-ma'asrot* have not been properly separated. The intimacy created by being thrown together — both excluded from the *tahor* eating group, eating as a private unit — may generate a particular closeness, a sharing of food, and the *am ha-aretz*'s bread may well be *tevel*. The reason the *zav* example is chosen may be precisely because it is a condition that could last many days, creating an extended period of this problematic intimacy rather than just a single occasion.

Rava demurs. *Rov amei ha-aretz measrin hen* — the majority of *amei ha-aretz* do in fact separate their tithes, and our concern about *demai* — produce of uncertain tithe status — is only rabbinic in nature. We would not construct a rabbinic safeguard against another rabbinic concern of this kind. Rava therefore offers a different explanation: *shema yehei ragil etzlo ve-ya'achilennu dvarim teme'im bimei taharato* — we are concerned not about what will happen during the period of *tumah*, but about what will happen afterward. Once the *zav parush* becomes friendly and comfortable with this *am ha-aretz* during the week or more they spend eating together, he may continue to spend time with him even after he becomes *tahor* — and then he will eat food that is genuinely *tamei*.

This debate between Abaye and Rava is instructive for understanding the *zav* and *zava* case as well. Abaye's concern is about what goes wrong immediately, in the present. Rava's concern is about a future consequence of present intimacy. These two frames map onto the two readings of the *zav* and *zava* prohibition: if the concern is what happens right now — they are alone together, the opportunity presents itself — that corresponds to Rashi's reading that the concern is sexual relations, since the *tumah* concern cannot be the issue in the present moment when both are equally *tamei*. If the concern is what might happen later, then the *tumah*-based reading of the Safrai commentary becomes more plausible — they eat together while both are *tamei*, develop the habit, and then continue when only one is *tamei*.

## Husband-Wife Bed Niddah

### Pajamas Question

The Gemara now introduces a new question, which appears to emerge from nowhere but is in fact intimately connected to the preceding discussion: *niddah mahu she-tishon im ba'alah hi bevigdah ve-hu bevigdo* — may a husband and wife sleep in the same bed when she is a *niddah*, provided they are both wearing their garments? By "garments" — *bigdah* — Rashi clarifies that the Gemara means pajamas, since the normal mode of sleeping for husband and wife, as part of the obligation of *onah*, involved *kiruv basar* — physical closeness, sleeping together unclothed. There is indeed a Gemara in Ketubot that states a wife can compel a *get* if her husband insists on sleeping together only while clothed, since *she'erah kesutah ve-onatah lo yigra* encompasses not just the act of sex but the physical intimacy of sleeping together. The question here is therefore whether wearing pajamas constitutes a sufficient *heker* — a meaningful marker — to permit sleeping in the same bed, or whether they require separate beds entirely.

### Cheese & Meat Analogy

Rav Yosef introduces a striking comparison: *ha-of oleh im ha-gevinah al ha-shulchan ve-eino ne'echal* — Beit Shammai holds that poultry and cheese may be placed on the same table together, even though they cannot be eaten together. Beit Shammai is not concerned that having them on the table simultaneously will lead one to eat them together. Beit Hillel, however, says *lo oleh velo ne'echal* — not only may they not be eaten together, they may not even be on the same table. Beit Hillel is concerned that the proximity of cheese and chicken will lead one to eat them together. By analogy, one might argue that husband and wife in the same bed will similarly lead to transgression — even if there is a *heker* of pajamas.

### Da'at Distinction

The Gemara rejects the analogy, however, on a crucial ground: *d'leika de'ot* — in the case of cheese and chicken, there is no *da'at*, no autonomous opinion or will in either the cheese or the chicken. They are inanimate objects sitting in front of you, and since neither can exercise any restraint, the only relevant question is whether you will remember. But where two human beings with *da'at* are involved, there is hope that if one begins to initiate something inappropriate, the other will remember the prohibition and pull back. Two people are present with independent will, and that mutual check is itself a significant safeguard. This, the Gemara indicates, is what makes the husband-and-wife situation different from the inanimate cheese-and-chicken comparison.

The Gemara notes that this logic is confirmed by what the Mishnah states at the end: *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer shenei achsanain ochlin al shulchan echad zeh basar ve-zeh gvinah ve-ein choshashin* — two strangers at an inn may eat at the same table, one eating meat and one eating cheese, without concern. The reason is exactly as stated: since there are two people, one of them should remember if the other reaches toward the forbidden item.

### Strangers Qualifier

However, a qualification is attached to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling. Rav Chanin bar Ami in the name of Shmuel states: *lo shanu ela she-ein makirin zeh et zeh* — this leniency applies only when the two diners are strangers who do not recognize one another. *Aval makirin zeh et zeh asurin* — but if they know each other, it is forbidden. The reasoning is straightforward: a stranger would not have the familiarity to simply reach over and say "Could I have a piece of your cheese?" But friends, being comfortable with one another, might. And once that social barrier is lowered, we become concerned the prohibition will be crossed.

### Know Each Other

This qualification seems to be directly applicable to our case. *Ve-ha hacha nami makirin zeh et zeh ninhu* — a husband and wife certainly know each other well. Why should we not apply the same concern and prohibit them from sleeping in the same bed even with pajamas?

### Two Protective Factors

The Gemara responds decisively. *Hachi hashta? Ha-tam de'ot ika shinui leika* — in the cheese-and-meat case at the inn, yes, there are two people with *da'at*, but there is no *shinui*, no marking, no sign of anything unusual about the situation. Nothing in the arrangement signals that caution is required. *Ha-ka ika de'ot ve-ika shinui* — but in our case of husband and wife in bed, both factors are present: first, there are two people with *da'at*, so one may remind the other, and second, there is a *shinui* — they are wearing pajamas, which is itself a departure from their normal mode of sleeping together, a *heker* that signals "something is different here, be careful."

### Both Factors Present

Thus, according to the Gemara's analysis as presented here, the combination of two protective factors — *de'ot* (the autonomous will of two human beings) and *shinui* (the wearing of pajamas as a sign) — should in principle be sufficient to permit husband and wife to sleep in the same bed during *niddah*. The pajamas function as a constant reminder, and together with the mutual-check dynamic of two people with *da'at*, the conditions would appear to satisfy the criteria by which we ordinarily judge whether A will lead to B. The Gemara has not yet concluded the matter, however, as we will see when the *zav* and *zava* case is reintroduced.

## Zav Zavah Revisited

### Zav Zavah No Sign

The Gemara now brings back the original ruling about *zav* and *zava* eating together, using it as a challenge to the conclusion just reached. If the combination of *de'ot* and *shinui* is sufficient to permit husband and wife in bed during *niddah*, then why are *zav* and *zava* prohibited from eating together? After all, there are also two people with *da'at* in that situation. The implied question is: does the *zav* and *zava* case constitute a difficulty for the reasoning that allowed the husband and wife in bed?

The overall framework being established is this: wherever both factors are present — two people with independent will, and some form of marking or distinction — we are not concerned that A will lead to B. Where only one factor is present, or neither, we are concerned.

### No Shinui in Zav

The Gemara resolves the challenge: *ha-ka nami de-ika shinui leika* — in the case of *zav* and *zava* eating together, there is indeed no *shinui*, no sign or marker present in the situation to serve as a *heker*. They are eating together in what appears to be a completely ordinary arrangement, with nothing to signal that they must exercise caution. Two people with *da'at* alone is insufficient — both *de'ot* and *shinui* are required. Since the *zav* and *zava* case has *de'ot* but lacks *shinui*, the prohibition stands.

This analysis also illuminates what was said earlier about the case in the inn. Extending the logic: if a *heker* were present in the *zav* and *zava* situation — some visible marker indicating the nature of their prohibition — it is conceivable that the concern would be mitigated. The absence of such a marker is what makes the case problematic.

### Biblical Comparison

The Gemara then introduces a *pasuk* from Ezekiel to anchor the prohibition of husband and wife in bed during *niddah*. The verse describes a *tzaddik* who *el ha-harim lo achal* — did not eat toward the mountains (understood by the Gemara as not relying on *zechut avot* but maintaining his own merits), *ve-einav lo nasa el gillulei beit Yisrael* — did not worship idols, *ve-et eshet re'ehu lo timme* — did not defile his fellow's wife through adultery, *ve-el isha niddah lo yikrav* — and did not draw near to a woman in her *niddah*. The Gemara draws a *hekesh*: *mah eshet re'ehu hu bevigdo ve-hi bevigdah assur* — just as being in bed with another man's wife wearing pajamas is prohibited, *af ishto niddah hu bevigdo ve-hi bevigdah assur* — so too, a man may not be in bed with his own wife when she is a *niddah*, even if both are wearing pajamas. This *hekesh* effectively overrides the reasoning that had seemed to permit it.

## Niddah Prohibition Appro…

### Rashi's Yichud

Three major *rishonim* approach the logical basis of this prohibition differently. Rashi understands the connection to *eshet re'ehu* as grounding the prohibition in *issur yichud* — the prohibition of seclusion with a woman who is forbidden to one. By analogy, a man may not be in the same intimate situation with his wife during *niddah*.

### Tosafot Yetzer Hara

Tosafot raises an objection to Rashi: the concept of *issur yichud* obviously does not apply to a husband and wife in their own bedroom — of course they may be secluded together. So Rashi cannot be saying that the prohibition of husband and wife in bed during *niddah* is literally an *issur yichud*. Tosafot instead understands the *hekesh* to be pointing to a different reason: the *yetzer hara* of sexual desire, particularly when the opportunity is so immediate and present, will override a person's normal capacity for restraint. Just as we would clearly be concerned about a man being in bed with another man's wife even with pajamas — because the sexual drive would overpower ordinary inhibition — so too with a man's own wife during *niddah*, the *yetzer hara* is powerful enough that the *de'ot* and *shinui* together are insufficient to guarantee restraint.

### Ramban Intrinsic

The Ramban offers what is arguably the most satisfying explanation, and one that directly addresses the question raised earlier about other forms of physical intimacy falling short of actual sexual relations. The Ramban argues: does anyone truly think that the only reason a man cannot be in bed with another man's wife is the concern that it might lead to sex? Of course not. It is intrinsically prohibited — the physical intimacy itself, even intentional touching short of sex, even the erotic quality of lying together, is on its own terms a violation of the prohibition pertaining to a married woman. Sexual touch, and indeed the general physical and erotic proximity involved, is itself part of the ambit of the prohibition, not merely a step on a slope toward the prohibited act.

The Ramban uses the analogy of *chatzi shiur* — just as one may not eat even a half-*kazayit* of a forbidden food even though that amount does not constitute the full violation, so too sexual intimacy short of intercourse falls within the prohibitory zone of *gilluy arayot*, even if it does not constitute the core act. Applying this to the *niddah* case, the Ramban says the Gemara is not merely concerned that sleeping together in pajamas will *lead* to sex. Even setting aside where it might lead, the physical intimacy of lying together in bed is itself problematic when the woman is a *niddah* — not because of *yetzer hara* overcoming restraint, but because that closeness is intrinsically improper at a time when they are prohibited to one another. This reading also corresponds to the question raised about what is prohibited beyond sex itself — the entire category of *kiruv basar* during *niddah* falls, in the Ramban's view, under a genuine prohibition, not merely a prudential *gezeirah* against eventual transgression.

This debate among the *rishonim* maps onto a broader dispute about the nature of the *harchakot* — the distancing practices between husband and wife during *niddah*. One school of thought holds that all the distancing requirements are *gezeirot*: rabbinic safeguards designed to prevent the couple from arriving at actual intercourse, which is the only act biblically prohibited. On this view, all the *harchakot* are derivative of the concern that A will lead to B will lead to C. The other view, associated with the Ramban, holds that physical intimacy is itself an independent problem during *niddah*, not merely because of where it leads.

### Rav Padda

A statement of Rav Padda now comes into tension with the Ramban's reading. Rav Padda says: *lo asra Torah ela kurva shel gilluy arayot bilvad* — the Torah only prohibited sexual intercourse itself in the *arayot* prohibitions, not other forms of physical intimacy. His proof text is *ish ish el kol she'er besaro lo tikrevu legalot ervah* — the prohibition of *kiruv* is specifically *legalot ervah*, to uncover nakedness, meaning the sexual act itself. The *rishonim* debate whether Rav Padda means to limit only the biblical prohibition or the rabbinic one as well.

Rashi and Tosafot propose various explanations of how Rav Padda's statement limits the rabbinic scope as well. The Ramban, however, offers a reading that he considers the most precise. He argues that *lo asra Torah* sometimes means not prohibited even rabbinically. But his key insight is that Rav Padda's statement applies specifically to the case of *she'er* — one's relatives, including one's wife — as opposed to *eshet re'ehu*, another man's wife. The *pasuk* says *el kol she'er besaro*, which the Ramban reads as referring to the category of relatives. For relatives — one's sister, daughter, mother, and wife — physical intimacy that is not sexual is not prohibited; the prohibition extends only to the sexual act itself. For another man's wife, by contrast, even non-sexual physical intimacy falls within a broader prohibition. This explains why Ulla's behavior with his sister, discussed next, is not contradicted by Rav Padda's statement.

### Ulla's Kiss

The Gemara reports that when *Ulla* would return from the house of study after an extended period away, *havi minashek lela-achvosei* — he would kiss his sisters — *abei chadaiyu*, on their chest, or according to another version, *abei yadaiyu*, on the back of their hands. The point of the report is that Ulla practiced a form of physical affection with his female relatives that would be impermissible with other women — consistent with the Ramban's reading that *she'er*, one's relatives, are treated differently.

### Ulla Contradiction

Yet the Gemara notes that Ulla appears to contradict himself: *upligi didei adidei* — Ulla argued against his own practice — for in another context he stated *afilu shum korva assur*, even any form of physical closeness is prohibited, *mishum lech lech amri nezira sechor sechor le-charma lo tikrav* — as the saying goes, tell the *nazir* "go around, go around, do not even approach the vineyard." One should keep distance from anything that could serve as a temptation.

### Tosafot Resolution

Tosafot resolves the apparent self-contradiction by distinguishing between a general principle and individual application. As a general rule, we do not want people engaging in certain forms of physical contact because we are concerned it will lead to sexual thoughts and activity — hence Ulla's general statement. However, if a person knows with certainty that for him a particular touch carries no sexual resonance whatsoever — as Ulla understood about kissing his own sister — then there is no prohibition applicable to him. The general guideline exists as a safeguard for people who cannot be certain of their own responses, not as a categorical prohibition binding in all cases regardless of individual circumstance. This reading also has implications for the question of non-sexual touch more broadly — for example, the question of handshaking — where some authorities hold that if the touch genuinely carries no erotic significance for the parties involved, there may be no prohibition at all.

## Widow & Eliyahu Story

### Story Setup

The Gemara now brings a *baraita* from the school of Eliyahu — the *Tanna D'Bei Eliyahu* — that appears in *Avot D'Rabbi Natan*. The story: there was once a student who had studied a great deal of Mishnah, had read extensively in *Mikra*, and had spent much time in the presence of Torah sages. Nevertheless, *u-met ba-chatzi yamav* — he died in the middle of his days, at a young age. His wife took his *tefillin* and began making the rounds of the synagogues and study halls. She posed the same question wherever she went: the Torah says *ki hu chayecha ve-orech yamecha* — the Torah is your life and the length of your days. My husband learned much, read much, served the sages — why did he die so young? Nobody could answer her. One time, the narrator — Eliyahu the Prophet, this being *Tanna D'Bei Eliyahu* — visited her, and she recounted the whole story.

### Bleeding Days Strictness

Eliyahu asked her: *bimei niddatach mah hu etzlech* — during the days of your *niddah*, how did your husband behave with you? She answered: *chas ve-shalom afilu be-etzba ketanah lo naga bi* — God forbid, he did not even touch me with his pinky finger. They were extremely strict during the period of active bleeding — stricter, as we will see, than the days that followed.

### White Days Leniency

Eliyahu then asked: *bimei libunech mah hu etzlech* — and during your white days, your *yemei libunah*, how did he behave? She said: *achal immi ve-shassah immi ve-yashan immi be-kiruv basar* — he ate with me, drank with me, and slept with me in full physical closeness, without clothing. *Ve-lo altah da'ato al davar acher* — and it never led to anything further; they were always careful not to have sex. But they were physically intimate together, sleeping *be-kiruv basar*, without the *shinui* of pajamas.

### Eliyahu's Verdict

Eliyahu responded: *baruch ha-Makom she-harago* — blessed is God who killed him. *Shelo nasa panim la-Torah* — he was not able to misrepresent the Torah. *She-harei amrah Torah ve-el isha be-niddat tumatah lo tikrav* — for the Torah says you should not draw near to a woman in her impurity of *niddah*, and physical intimacy, not only intercourse, is included in this prohibition. Eliyahu's verdict is that the husband's death was on account of this behavior during the *yemei libunah*.

### Wide Bed Apron

Rav Dimi, when he came from Eretz Yisrael, offered an alternative reading of the story: *mita chada havai* — it was a wide bed. The understanding was that they were in the same bed but at opposite ends, not actually lying next to each other in *kiruv basar*. They thought the wide bed constituted sufficient separation. Even so, Eliyahu ruled that this was wrong — they should not have been in the same bed at all. This carries direct practical implications: the general ruling is that husband and wife may not share a bed even at opposite ends during *niddah*, even with a pillow or physical barrier between them. The *mita chada* case is the classic basis for the ruling that a wide bed with a divider does not solve the problem.

Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef offered yet another reading: *sinar mafsik beino le-veinah* — there was an apron, a garment from the waist down, separating between them. They thought this approximated *hu bevigdo ve-hi bevigdah* — sufficient clothing to constitute a *shinui* from the waist down even if they were together from the waist up. Yet again, Eliyahu ruled that this was insufficient.

### Taboo vs Halacha

This story has a great deal to teach beyond its immediate ruling. Reading it alongside early writings of *chachmei Ashkenaz* and the *Geonim*, it becomes clear that alongside the halakhic framework of *niddah*, there existed popular practices — not specifically halakhic, but widespread — centered around taboos associated with menstrual bleeding itself. These taboos were not about the woman's halakhic status as a *niddah* but about the menstruation as a kind of ritual impurity in a more visceral, folk-religious sense. We find evidence that women after the bleeding stopped would bathe, wear white, and that the period following the cessation of bleeding was treated with noticeably less strictness than the bleeding period itself — not because of any halakhic distinction, but because the taboo associated with the blood itself had passed.

This appears to be precisely what is going on in the story. The *talmid* — despite all his learning — was not operating from a halakhic framework. He was following the taboo-based common practices of his time: extreme stringency during active bleeding, because the blood itself was the object of the taboo; and then a relaxation to full *kiruv basar* once the bleeding stopped, because in his understanding the danger had passed. He thought he was being pious. He was not. He was replacing *halacha* with custom-based taboo, and the consequences of the two are inverted.

### Chumrot to Kulos

This brings us to what is arguably the central thematic point of the entire passage: the story illustrates the phenomenon of *chumrot* that lead to *kulot* — stringencies that generate leniencies. By being extraordinarily strict during the bleeding days based on taboo rather than *halacha*, the *talmid* created the psychological and practical conditions for extraordinary leniency during the *yemei libunah*. The two are linked. The taboo-based stringency of the active bleeding period and the taboo-based leniency of the white days are two sides of the same non-halakhic coin.

Eliyahu's statement *shelo nasa panim la-Torah shelo ke-halacha* — that the husband misrepresented the Torah, did not follow it as *halacha* — is precisely this indictment. One cannot treat *hilchot niddah* as a system of taboo and superstition. It is *halacha*: an *issur* and a set of safeguards. The entire framing of the earlier Gemara — the comparison to cheese and meat, the analysis of *de'ot* and *shinui*, the careful reasoning about when A leads to B — is the Gemara insisting that *niddah* is to be treated as *halacha*, not as taboo. No kooties, no mystical danger of the bleeding itself. Simply an *issur* of sexual relations during a defined period, with attendant rabbinic safeguards structured rationally around preventing that transgression. And indeed, reading through Masechet Niddah, as we did not long ago, one is struck by how completely absent the taboo framework is from the *Chazal*'s own presentation. They insist on the halakhic character of the material throughout.

Eliyahu's harsh verdict — *baruch ha-Makom she-harago* — must be understood in context. The wife was not merely expressing private grief to her rabbi. She was going from *beit midrash* to *beit midrash*, publicly challenging the Torah's promise of longevity for those who study it, and implicitly threatening the community's confidence in the halakhic framework itself. Eliyahu's response, while undeniably harsh, was addressed to that public challenge. And it is worth noting that *Eliyahu HaNavi* was ultimately, in the tradition, held to have been too harsh — a quality for which he paid his own consequences. That does not, however, diminish the substance of his ruling on *hilchot niddah*, which stands as a clear articulation of the Gemara's insistence that this domain belongs entirely to *halacha* and not to the world of taboo.

# Shabbat 14

## Chananya's Attic & 18 Th…

### New Mishna Context

The daf opens with a new *mishna*, which begins: *v'elu min hahalachot she'amru ba'aliyat Chananya ben Chizkiyah ben Garon she'alu l'vakro* — these are from the *halachot* that were stated in the upper story of Chananya ben Chizkiyah ben Garon, when they came to visit him. The *mishna* records that *nimnu v'rabu Beit Shammai al Beit Hillel* — Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel, and finding themselves with a majority, they seized the opportunity to pass legislation that had long been stalled. The *mishna* signals that everything we have just been learning — the tailor's pin, the scribe's feather, a *zav* and *zavah* not eating together, not sitting down to the barber before *mincha* time — all of these belonged to the *yud-chet davar*, the eighteen things decided in Chananya ben Garon's attic.

### Abaye's Phrasing Question

The *gemara* opens with a linguistic question. *Amar lei Abaye l'Rav Yosef: elu tnan o v'elu tnan?* — Did the *mishna* say *elu* (these following things) or *v'elu* (and these, connecting to what came before)? The difference is significant: *v'elu* would mean that the subjects of the preceding *mishnayot* are themselves among the *halachot* of the eighteen things, while *elu* would introduce a fresh, self-contained list. The *gemara* resolves this from a *braita*: *ein polin l'or haner v'ein korin l'or haner v'elu min hahalachot she'amru ba'aliyat Chananya ben Chizkiyah ben Garon* — the *braita* ends there, with no continuation that could cause ambiguity about direction. *Shma mina v'elu tnan* — we conclude the reading is *v'elu*, connecting backward to earlier material.

It is worth noting that the prohibition against reading by candlelight was clearly an ancient *takanah*. Rabbi Yishmael, who was himself relatively early, recounted that he once nearly tipped a candle while reading *l'or haner* and acknowledged that the sages had been right to forbid it. So certainly the carrying of a quill or pin, reading *l'or haner*, and a *zav* and *zavah* eating together were all from the eighteen things. Whether the prohibition against sitting down before *mincha* reaches back that far is less clear.

### Braita Proof

The *gemara*'s conclusion is that the *mishna* uses *v'elu* — linking the preceding *mishnayot* to the eighteen things. It is not assumed, however, that this encompasses everything in all three prior *mishnayot*. The phrase *min hahalachot* — "from" the *halachot* — indicates a selection, not an exhaustive enumeration. The eighteen things are not fully laid out in a single place; the *gemara* will eventually complete the list.

### Rambam's Listing

The *rambam* takes the more expansive view, attempting to extend the list all the way back to the very first *mishna* — the *ani* and the *baal habayit*, each with two actions that become four inside and four outside, adding up to eight. He then counts approximately five items from the prohibitions before *mincha* time (barber, bathhouse, and related matters), and another five from the things one may not carry on the eve of *Shabbat* and the prohibition of reading *l'or haner*, arriving at eighteen. This comprehensive reading is generally not the accepted position; the standard understanding is that the *mishna* beginning with carrying, and perhaps the *mishna* about sitting before *mincha*, are among the eighteen, but the list in the *mishna* is a partial one.

### Megillat Taanit

The *gemara* pauses for a significant historical digression: *mi katav Megillat Taanit?* — who wrote *Megillat Taanit*? This is an ancient text, unusual in that it was committed to writing even in a predominantly oral culture — perhaps because it consists largely of dates, which are difficult to memorize. It records the days on which fasting and delivering a *hesped* are forbidden, marking minor historical celebrations that were significant at the time even if we no longer observe them. Notably, *Chanukah* in its earliest Rabbinic formulation appears in *Megillat Taanit*, which describes what happened on those days and why one may not fast.

The *gemara* answers: *Chananya ben Chizkiya v'si'ato* — Chananya ben Chizkiya and his colleagues — *she'hayu mechabevim et ha'tsarot* — who held the afflictions dear. On its surface, this suggests a religious orientation centered on fasting and suffering, people who were always looking for an opportunity to fast and therefore needed a calendar of days on which fasting was forbidden. Rashi, however, reads *mechabevim et ha'tsarot* differently: they were *mechabev* the days on which their *tsarah* was imminent and God had saved them. On Rashi's reading, *Megillat Taanit* is a record of those minor miracles and celebratory moments, and its purpose is to mark the days when something good happened — hence the prohibition on fasting.

The tension in these two readings is real. Rashi must somewhat strain against the plain language, which speaks of the *tsar* itself rather than the salvation from it. *Rabban Gamliel* adds: *af anu mechabevim et ha'tsarot* — we too hold the afflictions dear. *Aval ma na'aseh she'im banu lichtov ein anu maspikin* — but if we were to write them all down, we could not manage it; there are simply too many. On the plain reading, this means that suffering under Roman oppression was so constant and pervasive that one could not document all of it. On Rashi's reading, we are saved so frequently — every single day from some threat — that we could not list all the days of divine intervention: *ein anu maspikin la'asot yom tov be'chol yom*.

The *gemara* then adds two further expressions: *davar acher ein shoteh nifga* — a *shoteh* does not feel when he is being struck; *ve'davar acher ein basar hamet margish be'izmel* — dead flesh does not feel the piercing of an awl. Rashi explains these as metaphors for unawareness: *kach kama nissim ba'im lanu v'ein anu makirim ba'hem* — so too, many miracles come to us and we do not even recognize them. But if one reads the passage according to its plain sense — that it is the affliction itself being counted — then the metaphors work equally well in the other direction: after constant suffering, one becomes inured to it, like dead flesh that no longer registers the blade.

At this point the *gemara* raises a factual challenge: is it really true that dead flesh feels nothing? *Ha'amar Rav Yitzchak: kasheh rimah lamet kemachat bivsar hachai* — Rav Yitzchak taught that a maggot's consumption of a corpse is as painful to the deceased's spirit as a needle piercing living flesh, as it is written: *ach besaro alav yichav v'nafsho alav te'eval* — his flesh will ache and his soul will mourn over him. The *gemara* resolves this: *eima ein basar hamet shebachayim margish be'izmel* — what the saying means is that a portion of dead flesh within a living person does not feel the awl. That is the nature of a callus: it is dead skin, with no nerve endings, and piercing it causes no pain.

### Yechezkel Reconciliation

Having discussed who wrote *Megillat Taanit*, the *gemara* records a second major achievement of Chananya ben Chizkiyah. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav: beram zachur oto ish letov, v'Chananya ben Chizkiyah shemo, she'ilmala hu nignaz Sefer Yechezkel* — that person is remembered for good, and his name is Chananya ben Chizkiyah, for were it not for him, the Book of Yechezkel would have had to be hidden away — that is, excluded from the canon, treated essentially as a *sefer chitzoni*. Why? *She'hayu devarav sotrim divrei Torah* — because at the *pshat* level, portions of Yechezkel appear to contradict the Torah. Rashi cites one example: Yechezkel implies that *kohanim* in particular should not eat *neveilah*, which sounds as though non-*kohanim* may — a formulation foreign to the Torah. Beyond that, Yechezkel's description of the *Beit HaMikdash* differs markedly from the Torah's, and various *halachot* embedded in its *psukim* seem to conflict with established law.

*Mah asah?* — what did Chananya do? *He'elu lo gimmel meot garvei shemen* — they brought up 300 jugs of oil, *v'yashav ba'aliyah v'darshan* — and he and presumably a group of *rabbanim* sat in the upper room and worked through every apparent contradiction, finding ways to reconcile Yechezkel with the Torah. Rashi notes that the oil was needed to keep them working late into the night; they essentially locked themselves in for an extended period until all the problems were resolved.

This gives us a portrait of Chananya ben Garon as a figure deeply engaged with the scriptural and textual foundations of Jewish life: he reconciled Yechezkel with the Torah, he authored *Megillat Taanit* together with his colleagues, and his attic served as a kind of gathering place for significant *rabbinic* deliberation. The *rambam* notes, not unreasonably, that it was likely during one of these very meetings — perhaps the one concerning Yechezkel, or the one about *Megillat Taanit* — that the event of our *mishna* took place: finding themselves assembled and with Beit Shammai holding a majority, they took the opportunity to also resolve the eighteen outstanding matters.

---

## Tumah Classifications

### Nine Categories Listed

The *mishna* we now turn to — drawn from *Masechet Zavim* — lists nine categories of things that render a person or object a *sheni l'tumah*, meaning second-degree *tumah*, with the practical consequence of disqualifying *trumah* (*poslot et ha-trumah*): a *sheni l'tumah* that contacts *trumah* renders it a *shlishi*, which is *pasul* and may not be consumed. Most of these nine categories are among the eighteen things decreed in Chananya's attic, as the *gemara* will clarify.

The first two items are: *ha-ochel ochel rishon* — one who eats food that is a *rishon l'tumah* (food that directly touched an *av ha-tumah* such as a *sheretz*) — and *ha-ochel ochel sheni* — one who eats food that is a *sheni l'tumah* (food that touched a vessel that touched an *av ha-tumah*). In both cases the person becomes a *sheni*. This is notable: *de'oraita*, a person can only become a *rishon* by touching an *av ha-tumah* directly; the rabbis extended *tumah* status to a person who merely eats food of a lower degree. The third item is *ha-shoteh mashkin t'meim* — one who drinks *tamei* liquid, either *rishon* or *sheni* (liquid essentially auto-upgrades, as we will see). In all three cases, the person becomes a *sheni*.

The fourth category is *ha-ba rosho v'rubo b'mayim she'uvim* — one who immerses his head and most of his body in drawn water, i.e., water that was collected in a vessel rather than gathered naturally. The fifth is *v'tahor she'naflu al rosho v'rubo shlosha lugin mayim she'uvim* — a *tahor* person upon whom three *lugin* of drawn water fell, i.e., who took a shower. In both cases the person becomes a *sheni*.

The sixth and seventh items are *ha-sefer* and *ha-yadayim*: *sifrei kodesh* — holy scriptures, at minimum a *sefer Torah* — are themselves a *sheni* and convey *tumah* to *trumah*; and *yadayim* — hands — are always treated as a *sheni*, regardless of the rest of the body's status. The eighth item is *ha-tevul yom* — one who has immersed in a *mikvah* that day but before sunset — who is a *sheni* and disqualifies *trumah*. However, the *gemara* will note that *tevul yom* is *de'oraita* (*u'va ha-shemesh v'taher*) and should be removed from the count of the eighteen rabbinic decrees, even though it remains in the *mishna*'s enumeration. The ninth is *ha-ochlin v'ha-keilim she'nitme'u b'mashkin* — foods and vessels that became *tamei* through liquid contact, which we will unpack further below.

The *gemara* notes that a great deal of the eighteen things concerned *tumah v'taharah*, reflecting how central these concerns were to religious life even after the *churban*.

### R. Eliezer vs. R. Yehosh…

The *gemara* asks: *man tana ochel ochel rishon v'ochel ochel sheni mifsil pasli t'muyei lo mtamyei?* — who is the *tanna* who holds that eating a *rishon* or *sheni* renders you *pasul* but not *tamei* in the full sense — meaning you become a *sheni*, not a *rishon*?

*Amar Rabbah Bar Bar Channah amar Rabbi Yehoshua hi* — it is the position of Rabbi Yehoshua. The *gemara* cites a *mishna* from which this is drawn: *Rabbi Eliezer omer — ha-ochel ochel rishon rishon, ve-ochel ochel sheni sheni* — if you eat a *rishon*, you become a *rishon*; if you eat a *sheni*, you become a *sheni*. According to Rabbi Eliezer, you become what you ate. He adds: *ochel shlishi shlishi* — and if you ate food that is a *shlishi* (which can only be *trumah*, since *chullin* does not reach that degree), you become a *shlishi*, relevant only for *kodesh*.

Rabbi Yehoshua, by contrast, holds: *ha-ochel ochel rishon ve-ochel ochel sheni sheni* — whether you ate a *rishon* or a *sheni*, you become a *sheni*. The act of eating *tamei* food produces a single result: *sheni* status. As for eating a *shlishi*: *sheni le-kodesh ve-ein sheni le-trumah, be-chullin she-na'asu al taharat trumah* — you become a *sheni* with respect to *kodesh* but not with respect to *trumah*, and even this applies only when the *shlishi* in question came from *chullin* that was treated with the stringency of *trumah* (*chullin she-na'asu al taharat trumah*).

This last point requires elaboration. There is a practice of eating one's *chullin* in a state of *taharah*. But there is a further level: treating one's *chullin* as if it were *trumah*, being so scrupulous about it that one avoids contact with a *sheni*. The question is whether such *chullin*, once treated with *trumah*-level care, can also become *tamei* like *trumah* — i.e., can it become a *shlishi*? Rabbi Yehoshua concedes that if one has adopted this practice and the food became a *shlishi*, eating it produces *kodesh*-level *tumah*. The reason he concedes specifically in this case, and not for actual *trumah* that became a *shlishi*, is that since the food is ultimately only *chullin*, we are not confident the person guarded it as carefully as he claims, and we suspect its *tumah* may be higher than a *shlishi*. Once we are concerned it may be worse than declared, we treat it more stringently.

The operative holding for our *mishna* — that eating a *rishon* or *sheni* makes you a *sheni* regardless of the degree consumed — reflects the position of Rabbi Yehoshua.

### Eating Foods Reasoning

Having established whose view it is, the *gemara* turns to the rationale. *Ochel ochel rishon ve-ochel ochel sheni: mai ta'ama gazru beh rabbanan?* — why did the rabbis decree that eating a *rishon* or *sheni* renders you *tamei*?

The concern is practical and vivid. A *kohen* may be eating food that is a *rishon* or *sheni* — permissible food, since it is not *trumah* — and at the same table there is a cup of *trumah* wine. Having eaten the *tamei* food, he might absentmindedly wash it down with the *trumah* wine. While the *tamei* food is in his mouth, it is still a *rishon* or *sheni*, and the *trumah* wine entering his mouth at the same moment becomes *tamei*. This is the scenario the decree is designed to prevent. By telling the *kohen* that eating *tamei* food makes him a *sheni*, the rabbis ensure he will not sit down to such a meal while *trumah* is also on the table.

It is worth noting that there is an earlier and distinct *gezeirah* discussed by *Tosafot* — called *pesul geviyah*, the *pesul* of the body — which addresses what happens when a large quantity of *tamei* food has been swallowed and now sits in the stomach alongside ingested *trumah*. That decree operates with a larger *shi'ur* and addresses a somewhat different scenario. The decree we are discussing here is later, more encompassing, and more stringent: even a small amount of *tamei* food eaten renders one a *sheni* and unable to touch *trumah*, owing to the concern about washing it down.

There is also the question of what minimum *shi'ur* of food is required to trigger this status. *Tosafot* assumes the threshold is a *kebeitzah*.

### Drinking Liquids Ruling

The parallel case: *shoteh mashkin t'meim: mai ta'ama gazru behu rabbanan?* — why did the rabbis decree that drinking *tamei* liquid makes you a *sheni*? The scenario is the mirror image: you are drinking *tamei* wine, and your bread happens to be *trumah*. Without the decree, you would reason that you are *tahor*, the bread is *trumah* and *tahor*, all is well — and then you would take a bite of the *trumah* bread while the *tamei* wine is still in your mouth, rendering the *trumah tamei*. By making the consumption of *tamei* liquid produce *sheni* status, the rabbis ensure you will not combine them at the same meal.

The *gemara* then asks: *hainu hach* — is this not the same as the previous decree? Why enumerate them separately? The answer is: *sh'chichi v'ha lo sh'chichi* — the two scenarios are not equally common. It is far more likely that one would eat food and wash it down with a drink than that one would have liquid in the mouth while inserting food. The latter is physically awkward — the liquid tends to go down before one can bring the food in. So the decree about food causing *sheni* status is grounded in a common occurrence; the decree about liquid is extended to the less common case for the sake of symmetry and completeness, even though it would rarely arise in practice.

---

## Drawn Water Immersion

### Cave Water Origin

The next *gezeirah* concerns drawn water. *Haba rosho v'rubo b'mayim she'uvim: mai ta'ama gazru behu rabbanan?* — why did the rabbis decree that immersing oneself in drawn water renders one *tamei*?

*Amar Rav Bibi amar Rav Assi: she-vat'chilah hayu tovlin b'mei me'arah mechunasin* — originally, people who needed to immerse — presumably *kohanim* eating *trumah*, and possibly those obligated to immerse after a *keri* before saying *shema* or davening — would do so in cave water, naturally collected rainwater. Such water, though *halachically* valid, was typically stagnant and malodorous. *Ve-hayu notnin aleihem mayim she'uvim* — and so, naturally, they would rinse themselves with drawn water afterwards, to clean off the unpleasant residue of the *mikvah*.

*Hitchilu ve-asum keva* — but this practice became fixed and routine. People began treating the rinse as an integral part of the purification process. *Gazru aleihem tumah* — the rabbis therefore declared that this drawn-water rinse would render them *tamei*.

### Preventing Misunderstand…

Why exactly did the fixity of the practice necessitate a decree? The *gemara* records a dispute between Abaye and Rava on this point. *Amar Abaye: she-hayu omrim lo elu metaharim ela elu ve-elu metaharim* — Abaye says the problem was that people began saying: it is not the *mikvah* alone that purifies; it is the *mikvah* together with the rinse. This is a theological misunderstanding of what constitutes purification, and the rabbis could not allow it to stand.

Rava challenges this: *mai nafka minei? Ha katavlu behanach* — so what? At least they are going to the *mikvah*. If they think both are necessary, fine — they are still immersing in the *mikvah*. Rava therefore offers a sharper formulation: *she-hayu omrim lo elu metaharim ela elu metaharim* — they were saying not that both purify but that it is specifically the drawn-water rinse that purifies, not the *mikvah* at all. Since clean water produces a more obviously pleasant result, people began attributing the *taharah* to the rinse rather than the *mikvah*. At that point, the concern was that they might stop going to the *mikvah* altogether. Hence the decree: the drawn-water rinse makes you *tamei*, ensuring no one will view it as the operative act of purification.

The scope of this decree in practice raises interesting questions. Rashi reads the decree as applying specifically in the immediate aftermath of the *mikvah* immersion. The practical implication for women immersing in the *mikvah* has been discussed among the *poskim*: some have held that women should wait until they return home to shower, precisely because of this concern. The *Gra*, however, dismissed the stringency, arguing that the only consequence of taking a shower immediately after the *mikvah* is that one becomes a *sheni l'tumah* — and since we are all *tamei meis* in any case, such a concern is irrelevant. There is no prohibition involved; it is simply that drawn water produces a low-level *tumah* that is only consequential in a world where *tumah* is operationally significant.

### General Shower Gezeirah

There is, however, a second and broader *gezeirah* as well. The *mishna*'s next item is *v'tahor she'naflu al rosho v'rubo shlosha lugin mayim she'uvim* — a *tahor* person upon whom three *lugin* of drawn water fell, i.e., who took a shower entirely apart from any connection to a *mikvah* immersion. This person also becomes a *sheni*.

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama gazru behu rabbanan tumah? De-lo ha lo kayma ha* — because if we only declared *tumah* for the drawn-water rinse immediately after the *mikvah*, no one would take the first decree seriously. To make the original decree credible and effective, it had to be generalized: drawn water creates *tumah* whenever it covers the majority of a person's body, regardless of whether a *mikvah* was involved. One can appreciate the practical weight of this: in a world with Roman bathhouse culture and widespread bathing, such a decree had real consequences for those who were *makpid* on eating *chullin be-taharah*. Though one imagines the answer lay in bathing one limb at a time to avoid covering the majority of the body, the broader implications of maintaining bodily purity under this regime are considerable.

---

## Holy Texts Tumah

### Sifrei Kodesh Tumah Reas…

The *mishna* then lists *ha-sefer* — holy scriptures — as conveying *tumah*. This is, at first glance, a striking proposition: the holiest objects in Jewish religious life are declared *tamei*. One might observe that although *tumah* and *kedushah* are in a sense antithetical, both represent a kind of metaphysical status that surrounds an object and generates real-world obligations. In a world where *tumah* was a lived reality, having *sifrei kodesh* generate *tumah* upon contact gave their holiness a tangible, halachic dimension — touching a *sefer Torah* changed one's metaphysical state and prohibited the eating of *trumah*.

The reason the *gemara* gives is concrete and historical: *she-vat'chilah hayu matzni'in et ha-ochlin de-trumah etzel Sefer Torah* — originally, people would store their *trumah* food together with the *sefer Torah*, reasoning that both are holy and belong together. *Ve-amru: hai kodesh ve-hai kodesh* — both are *kodesh*, why not keep them in the same place? The problem was *pesida*: the rats would come for the *trumah* and end up gnawing at the *sifrei Torah*. To remedy this, the rabbis declared *sifrei kodesh* to be *tamei* — meaning that *trumah* stored near them would be rendered *pasul* — thereby eliminating any incentive to store *trumah* alongside holy books.

### Hands Always Sheni

The final item in this cluster of the *mishna*'s nine categories: *ha-yadayim* — hands are always treated as a *sheni l'tumah*. The reason: *mipnei she-hayadayim askaniyot hen* — hands are constantly busy. One never knows where one's hands have been; they scratch, touch, fidget, and handle objects continuously and often unconsciously. Therefore, regardless of the rest of the body's *taharah* status, hands are presumed to be a *sheni* at all times. This is also, it is worth emphasizing, a radical rabbinic innovation in its own right: *de'oraita*, the *tumah* system treats a person as a unit — either entirely *tamei* or entirely *tahor*. The notion that a specific part of the body (the hands) can carry *tumah* independently of the rest is a purely rabbinic construction.

This has practical implications for daily life. Since bread evokes the context of *kohanim* eating *trumah*, and since hands are always a *sheni*, the rabbinic institution of washing hands before eating bread derives from this framework: *kohanim* would always need to wash before eating *trumah*, and the practice was extended as a reminder of that context.

### Direct Handling Conseque…

The *mishna*'s listing of *ha-sefer* as conveying *tumah* refers initially to the *sefer Torah* itself being a *sheni* that disqualifies *trumah* upon direct contact. But the *gemara* adds a related ruling: *af yadayim haba'ot machmat sefer poslot et ha-trumah* — hands that have touched a *sefer* also become a *sheni* and disqualify *trumah*. One might ask: since hands are always a *sheni* anyway, why does this need to be stated? The answer is that if a person had immersed in the *mikvah*, was extremely careful with his hands, kept his eye on them and they touched nothing — those hands would be *tahor*. The decree states that even then, touching a *sefer Torah* renders the hands a *sheni*.

The *gemara* explains this through a teaching attributed to Rav Parnach in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ha-ocheiz sefer Torah arom nikvar arom* — one who holds a *sefer Torah* naked (*arom*) will be buried naked. The *gemara* immediately asks: *arom salka daitach?* — literally buried without shrouds? *Ela amar Rabbi Zeira: arom belo mitzvah* — rather, it means he will be buried bereft of that *mitzvah*: the *mitzvah* he performed while handling the *sefer Torah* directly — whether it was *hagbah*, *gelilah*, an *aliyah*, or study — will not be credited to him. *Belo otah mitzvah*, the *gemara* clarifies: not all his *mitzvot*, but specifically the reward for that act.

The underlying principle is the reverence owed to a *sefer Torah*: it must always be handled through an intermediary. The *yad*, the *tallit* used during *gelilah*, the mantle — all of these exist to prevent direct contact between the hand and the *klaf*. The way the rabbis encoded this reverence in the system of *tumah v'taharah* was by making direct contact with the *klaf* cause the hands to become a *sheni*, giving the obligation practical, halachic teeth. The consequence of violating this — loss of the *mitzvah's* reward — is stated in measured terms; even the *gemara* did not treat it as a catastrophic forfeiture of all *mitzvot*.

An interesting question arises regarding the scope of this decree: does *ha-sefer* refer only to a *sefer Torah*, or to all *sifrei kodesh*? *Tosafot* raises this explicitly, pointing out that in *Masechet Yadayim*, the canonical status of a book is expressed through the idiom of *metamei et ha-yadayim* — whether it renders hands *tamei*. This was precisely the framework for the debate over whether *Shir HaShirim* belongs in the canon, a question Rabbi Akiva answered with characteristic force: the holiness of *Shir HaShirim* is beyond question, *kodesh kodashim*. The same framework governed the canonization of *Yechezkel*. This suggests the *tumah* of *sifrei kodesh* applies broadly to all canonical books, though the *gemara* centers its discussion on the *sefer Torah*.

### Gezeirah Priority Debate

The *gemara* then asks a precise sequencing question: which *gezeirah* came first — the decree that hands touching a *sefer* become *tamei*, or the general decree that all hands are always a *sheni*?

*Eileima hach gazru bereisha* — if the general decree (all hands are always *tamei*) came first, then *hach lamah li?* — why would you need to separately decree that hands touching a *sefer* are *tamei*? That is already encompassed. *Ela hach gazru bereisha* — rather, the first decree was specifically about hands that touch a *sefer*. *Ve-hadar gazru bechulhu yadayim* — and afterward the rabbis extended it: hands at all times are a *sheni*. Once the extension was made, the original targeted decree became somewhat redundant, though there remains a *nafka minah*: if someone immerses, watches his hands carefully and they touch nothing, then immediately touches a *sefer Torah*, those hands are a *sheni* — a status they would not otherwise have had. But for practical purposes, once hands are always treated as a *sheni*, the prior decree is largely absorbed.

---

## Liquid Contamination

### Food Liquid Contamination

The ninth category in the *mishna*: *ha-ochlin v'ha-keilim she-nitme'u b'mashkin* — foods and vessels that became *tamei* through liquid. The *gemara* asks: *be-mashkin de-mai* — through what kind of liquid?

If it means liquid that touched a *sheretz* — an *av ha-tumah* — then the liquid is a *rishon* and the food it touches is a *sheni*, and this requires no special *de-rabbanan*: it is the basic biblical mechanism by which *tumah* propagates. *De-chtiv: ve-chol mashke asher yishateh be-chol keli yitma* — the Torah itself establishes that liquid that enters a vessel becomes *tamei*, and from there the chain of *rishon* and *sheni* is straightforward.

The decree the *gemara* is describing must therefore refer to a different case: *ela be-mashkin ha-ba'im machmat yadayim* — liquid that was touched by hands. Hands are a *sheni*. A *sheni* touching *chullin* liquid should, strictly speaking, accomplish nothing — a *sheni* can only affect *trumah*, not ordinary food or its liquids. Yet the *gezeirah* declares that when a *sheni* (or *rishon*) touches liquid, the liquid is upgraded to a *rishon*. This is the principle identified by *Tosafot*: *kol ha-posel et ha-trumah metamei et ha-mashkin lihyot techilah* — anything that can disqualify *trumah* (i.e., a *sheni* or higher) also renders liquid a *rishon*. The rationale is that liquid becomes *tamei* more easily than food does. Food requires *hechsher* — contact with liquid — before it can receive *tumah* at all; liquid, by contrast, is inherently receptive and is sometimes itself a source of *tumah* (as in the case of a *zav*'s fluids). Given liquid's heightened susceptibility, the rabbis were maximally stringent: any contact with a *sheni* or higher upgrades it to a *rishon*. The chain then continues: the *rishon* liquid touches food, rendering the food a *sheni*.

### Sheni-to-Rishon Upgrade

The principle just described — that a *sheni* touching liquid upgrades it to a *rishon* — is a dramatic rabbinic extension, and the *gemara* attributes it to a decree modeled on the case of liquids that originate from a *zav* (*gezeirah mishum mashkin ha-ba'im machmat sheretz*). The reasoning proceeds in two tiers. First, since the *de'oraita* rule already establishes that certain liquids — specifically the bodily fluids of a *zav*, *zavah*, or *niddah* — are an *av ha-tumah* in their own right (*de-chtiv: ve-chi yarok ha-zav ba-tahor*), and therefore capable of rendering a person or vessel a *rishon*, the rabbis saw fit to extend analogous stringency to other liquids more broadly. The result is a graduated structure: an *av* touching liquid renders it an *av*; a *rishon* or *sheni* touching liquid renders it a *rishon*. Liquid never merely stays at the level it receives from contact — it is always either at its own *de'oraita* peak or upgraded to *rishon* by the *gezeirah*.

This is striking precisely because it is counterintuitive: one would expect *tumah* to diminish as it propagates downward, not to be selectively amplified at the step involving liquid. The amplification reflects the rabbis' view that liquid is a particularly potent vehicle of *tumah* and demands exceptional stringency.

### Vessel Liquid Contact

The ninth category also includes *ha-keilim she-nitme'u b'mashkin* — vessels that became *tamei* through liquid. Vessels, like persons, can only be a *rishon de'oraita*. So if a vessel is becoming *tamei* through contact with liquid, the liquid must be treated, in this context, as an *av ha-tumah* — the only level that can render a vessel *tamei* at all.

The *gemara* again asks: what liquid? *Eileima be-mashkin de-zav* — the fluids of a *zav* or *zavah* or *niddah*? That is *de'oraita*, as established above. *Ella be-mashkin machmat sheretz* — rather, it must be liquid that touched a *sheretz*, and the *gezeirah* is *mishum mashke de-zav*: because some liquids *are* an *av* (those of a *zav*), the rabbis applied analogous treatment to other liquids in certain contexts, such that when liquid that has touched an *av* contacts a vessel, the vessel becomes a *rishon*. The vessel is thereby rendered capable of propagating *tumah* to *trumah*.

---

## Hands Gezeirah Attributi…

### Attribution Question

Having catalogued the content of the eighteen things, the *gemara* raises a question about their attribution: *tamidei Shammai v'Hillel gazru* — were these decrees issued by the students of Shammai and Hillel? Or was it Shammai and Hillel themselves?

### Earlier Tannaitic Gezerot

The *gemara* cites a *braita* that places certain earlier *gezerot* before the era of Shammai and Hillel altogether. *Yosi ben Yoezer ish Tzeredah v'Yosi ben Yochanan ish Yerushalayim* — familiar names from the first *zugot* in *Pirkei Avot* — issued two decrees: that land outside of Israel is *tamei* (since burial practices among non-Jews could not be relied upon, and one might unknowingly walk over a grave), and that glassware (*klei zechochit*) is susceptible to *tumah* even though the Torah's *de'oraita* system of *tumah* for vessels does not include glass. *Shimon ben Shatach* then instituted the *kesuvah* as an outstanding debt rather than money placed in escrow — a reform designed to make divorce economically consequential and thus a genuine deterrent — and also decreed *tumah* on metal vessels.

And then: *Shammai v'Hillel gazru tumah al ha-yadayim* — Shammai and Hillel themselves issued the decree about hands. So the *gemara* has a *braita* that attributes the *gezeirah* about hands specifically to Shammai and Hillel personally, not to their respective schools.

### Shammai-Hillel Role

The *gemara* presses further. One might try to resolve the tension by reading "Shammai and Hillel" in the *braita* as shorthand for their schools and disciples. But Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel establishes a critical point: *shmoneh asar davar gazru u-ve-shmoneh asar nechelku* — the eighteen things were originally matters of ongoing debate, and on this one occasion Beit Shammai's numbers prevailed and the matters were resolved. The eighteen things, in other words, were not uncontested rabbinic legislation; they were *machloket* items on which Beit Shammai's position ultimately won the day. And the significance of this: *v'ilu Hillel v'Shammai lo nechelku ela b'gimel mekomos* — Hillel and Shammai themselves personally disagreed on only three matters, as Rav Huna teaches, and these eighteen were not among the three.

### Hands Paradox

This creates a genuine difficulty. If the *gezeirah* about *yadayim* was made by Shammai and Hillel personally — as the *braita* states — then it predates the eighteen things, which were matters debated by their *schools*. But we are also told that the hands *gezeirah* is among the eighteen things, which are characterized as items that were *in dispute* between the schools before being resolved. How can something Shammai and Hillel personally agreed upon — it was never among their three personal disputes — also be among the eighteen things that were debated between their schools?

This paradox is left unresolved at the end of the *amud*, and the *gemara* will take it up on the following daf.

---

---

# Shabbat 15

## Shammai & Hillel vs. Beis

### Hand Impurity Attribution

The *daf* begins at the bottom of 14b, with the *gemara* addressing a tension in the attribution of the ruling that hands are a *sheni l'tumah* capable of rendering *terumah tamei*. One tradition traces this ruling to the *gezeiros* of *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* as part of the eighteen things. Yet another tradition attributes it to *Shammai* and *Hillel* themselves, not their respective schools. The *gemara* attempts to reconcile these by suggesting that when we say *Shammai* and *Hillel*, we really mean *Shammai* and his *beis midrash*, *Hillel* and his *beis midrash* — meaning they were the same as *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* and all part of the *yud ches davar*.

This reconciliation is immediately challenged. Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: *yud ches davar gazru b'yud ches nechelku* — on eighteen things they issued an edict, and on eighteen things they were divided. The implication in the *Bavli* is that these were the same eighteen: the things that became the *yud ches davar* were originally matters of dispute. The problem, however, is that *Hillel* and *Shammai* are known to have debated in only three areas, and *tumah* of *yadayim* was not among them. Since the *yud ches davar* were things that had been debated, the *takkanah* of *yadayim* cannot be attributed to *Shammai* and *Hillel* as part of that same group.

### Two Stages of Strictness

A second attempt at reconciliation is then offered. Perhaps *Shammai* and *Hillel* and *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* represent two distinct *stages* of the *gezeirah*, not two separate bodies. Under this reading, *Shammai* and *Hillel* ruled that hands that touched *terumah* render it *toleh* — meaning one does not immediately burn it, since after all the *tumah* is only *d'rabbanan*, but one does not eat it either. One waits for the *terumah* to become invalid naturally, and only then burns it. The students, *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel*, then came and extended the ruling: they declared that such *terumah* must actually be burned outright, treating the hands as conferring full *tumah*.

### Ilfa's Challenge

This two-stage reconciliation is rejected on the basis of a ruling by *Ilfa*: *yadayim techilas gezeirasam l'sreifah* — from the very outset, the *takkanah* regarding hands stipulated that *terumah* touched by impure hands must be burned. There was never a preliminary stage in which one merely suspended the *terumah*. The two-stage model therefore cannot apply to *yadayim*.

### Accepted vs. Rejected

The *gemara* therefore concludes with a different resolution entirely. *Shammai* and *Hillel* did indeed attempt to enact the *gezeirah* of *yadayim* — but it was not accepted. One of the foundational principles governing *gezeiros* is that a *gezeirah* does not become binding unless it is accepted by *klal Yisrael*: *ein gozrin gezeirah al hatzibur ela im ken rov hatzibbur yachol la'amod bah* — a decree may not be imposed on the public unless a majority of the public is capable of upholding it, and correspondingly, a decree that fails to achieve acceptance does not take hold. *Shammai* and *Hillel* tried, but the society was not receptive. Then their students came — *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* — and renewed the *gezeirah*, and this time it was accepted. This is a striking resolution: the same ruling, issued by teacher and student alike, succeeded the second time around, apparently because the communal climate had shifted and people had become more receptive.

### Solomon's Takkanah
