The *gemara* then raises yet another tradition that complicates the picture further. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel teaches: *b'sha'ah she'tikein Shlomo eruvin v'netilas yadayim* — when *Shlomo HaMelech* enacted *eruvin* and *netilas yadayim*, a *bas kol* went forth and declared: *beni im hacham libecha yismach libi gam ani* — "My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad." The verse signals divine approval for a human rabbinic initiative. If *Shlomo* himself enacted *netilas yadayim*, how can we attribute it to *Shammai* and *Hillel* or to their schools?

The logic underlying *netilas yadayim* runs as follows: hands are deemed *tamei* as a *sheni l'tumah*, and a *sheni* can render *terumah tamei*. Since eating bread is analogous to the *kohanim* eating *terumah*, the requirement of *netilas yadayim* was extended universally to anyone eating bread. This chain of reasoning is traced back to *Shlomo*. It is noteworthy that two *takkanot* in particular — *eruvin* and *netilas yadayim* — are projected all the way back to *Shlomo HaMelech*.

### Solomon's Kodashim

The *gemara* resolves the tension by distinguishing the scope of *Shlomo*'s original *takkanah*. *Shlomo gazar l'kodashim* — *Shlomo* decreed that hands are *tamei* only in relation to *kodashim*, not *terumah*. If the ruling applied only to *kodashim*, then *netilas yadayim* as we understand it — the washing before eating ordinary bread — would not follow from *Shlomo*'s enactment at all, since the connection to bread eating operates through *terumah*, not *kodashim*. *Shlomo*'s *netilas yadayim* must therefore have been intended specifically for *kohanim* eating *kodashim*, or for individuals who had brought a *korban* and were entitled to eat from it — not the universal practice we observe today.

### Extension to Terumah

It was then *Shammai* and *Hillel* — and ultimately their students — who extended the ruling to *terumah* as well. *Shammai* and *Hillel* attempted this extension but it did not hold. Their *talmidim* then renewed the *gezeirah* and this time it was accepted and became binding. The picture that emerges is a layered legislative history: *Shlomo* enacted the *takkanah* for *kodashim*; *Shammai* and *Hillel* tried to extend it to *terumah* and failed; *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* succeeded in establishing the full extension, culminating in the universal practice of *netilas yadayim* before eating bread.

---

## Eighteen Things

### Three Sets

The *gemara* returns to the earlier statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel — *yud ches gazru v'yud ches nechelku* — and addresses the apparent contradiction with the teaching that *hushvu*, that they reached consensus. The *Bavli* seems to conflate all of these into a single set of eighteen, understanding that the items debated and the items decreed were one and the same group. The *Yerushalmi*, however, presents a considerably more structured picture: three entirely separate sets of eighteen.

### Same Day Debate

According to the *Yerushalmi*, one set of eighteen were things that *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* actively debated, with *Beis Shammai* ultimately prevailing and winning the vote — these are the *yud ches gazru*. A second set were things on which there was always consensus, never a dispute — the *hushvu*. A third set were things that remained as standing *machlokes* and were never resolved — the *nechelku*. The *Bavli*'s reading, by contrast, takes the debate and the decree as the same eighteen, understanding the sequence as: they debated, then *Beis Shammai* won, then the next day *Beis Hillel* conceded and they were *hushvu*. The *Yerushalmi*'s reading is arguably more natural given the order of the words: the *Bavli* has *gazru* before *nechelku*, which would be puzzling if the decree followed from the debate, whereas the *Yerushalmi* treats them as independent categories.

### Rambam's Framework

The *Rambam* engages directly with the *Yerushalmi*'s framework and identifies all three sets. The eighteen things that *Beis Shammai* won by vote — the *yud ches gazru* — are the *tumah v'taharah* rulings discussed in the *gemara* here, the long list of *sheni l'tumah* concerns. These were things *Beis Shammai* was confident they had the votes to win, so they brought them to a vote. The eighteen things that were always consensus — the *hushvu* — the *Rambam* identifies as the *mishnayos* that preceded the current *mishna*, the cases of the *baal habayis* and the *ani*, the carrying before *Shabbos*, the sitting down for a haircut, and so on. And the eighteen things that remained as standing disputes — the *nechelku* — are, according to the *Rambam*, the *mishnayos* that follow in the remainder of the first *perek*. These are the cases *Beis Shammai* chose not to bring to a vote, precisely because they were uncertain of the outcome — they feared that some members of their school might switch sides, and so those debates were left unresolved.

---

## Shammai & Hillel Debates

### Challah Amounts

Rav Huna teaches that *Shammai* and *Hillel* disputed in three areas. The first is the measure of dough that obligates the separation of *challah*. *Shammai* says: from one *kav* of flour. *Hillel* says: from two *kavim*. The *chachamim* say: neither — rather, one and a half *kavim* is the threshold of obligation.

### Measure Conversions

The derivation of these measures requires working through a series of unit conversions. The *Torah* connects *challah* to the concept of *reishis arisoseichem*, which the *gemara* associates with the *omer* of *manna* in the wilderness — the daily portion was an *asiris ha'eifah*, one tenth of an *eifah*. An *eifah* is seventy-two *log*, so a tenth of that is 7.2 *log*. Now, a *kav* is four *log*. However, there was a well-known conversion between the measures used in the *midbar* and the later rabbinic measures: what had been six units in the period of the *Torah* became five units in the later system (*shisha midbariot* equal *chamisha yerushalmiyot*), meaning the later measures were proportionally larger. Multiplying by five-sixths, the 7.2 *log* of the *midbar* becomes six *log* in the later system — which is one and a half *kavim*. This is the position of the *chachamim*. *Hillel* and *Shammai* apply the arithmetic somewhat differently and arrive at two *kavim* and one *kav* respectively.

After a subsequent re-standardization of measures — *mishe'higdilu hamiddot* — the threshold shifted again. Rabbi Yosi rules that five *reva'im* of flour are exempt and five *reva'im* plus any additional amount are obligated. Rashi explains this as a function of Rabbi Yosi's egg-volume calculation being slightly larger than that of the *chachamim*. *Tosafot* offers a different reading: Rabbi Yosi agrees with the base figure of five *kavim* but holds that five *kavim* must remain *after* the *challah* is taken, not that one begins with five *kavim*. Therefore one needs five *kavim* plus a minimal additional amount — a *mashu* — at the outset.

### Mikvah Water Debate

The second debate between *Shammai* and *Hillel* concerns the amount of drawn water (*mayim she'uvim*) that can invalidate a *mikvah*. *Hillel* says: a full *hin* of drawn water invalidates the *mikvah*. A *hin* is twelve *log*, which works out to roughly two two-liter bottles of liquid. *Hillel* adds the notable statement *she-chayav adam lomar bilshon rabbo* — a person is obligated to quote the language of his teacher — the significance of which will be addressed shortly. *Shammai* says: nine *kavim*, which is thirty-six *log*, three times the amount stipulated by *Hillel*, making *Shammai* considerably more lenient on this point. The *chachamim* rule neither like *Shammai* nor like *Hillel*: they waited until two weavers from the Dung Gate in Jerusalem came and testified in the name of *Shemaya v'Avtalyon* that just three *log* of drawn water invalidates the *mikvah* — a fraction of what either *Shammai* or *Hillel* had said — and the *chachamim* upheld that position.

### Weavers' Evidence

The mention of the weavers carries an important lesson: *le'olam lo yimna adam atzmo mibeis hamidrash* — no one should ever exclude himself from the study hall. Weaving was a profession held in low regard, and yet these two weavers possessed a tradition transmitted directly from *Shemaya v'Avtalyon* that proved decisive. The *gemara* connects this to the tractate *Eduyot*, which was taught at the session when the doors of the *beis midrash* were opened to all comers — the policy of inclusion that allowed previously overlooked testimony to be gathered and preserved.

What makes this particularly striking is the *Hillel* dimension. *Hillel* himself was a student of *Shemaya v'Avtalyon*, and his statement *she-chayav adam lomar bilshon rabbo* — I am quoting the exact language of my teacher — is an explicit invocation of that chain of transmission. Hillel is not presenting a personal opinion; he is claiming to directly transmit what he heard from *Shemaya v'Avtalyon*. And yet the *chachamim* backed the weavers' testimony over *Hillel*'s. The text offers no explanation of why. A priori, one would expect the weight to fall on *Hillel*'s side. One can only infer that the *chachamim* found the weavers' tradition more consistent with what they knew — or perhaps that three *log* simply made more internal sense — and that in this particular case they judged that testimony more reliable.

### Gra on Pronunciation

The *Gra* offers an illuminating explanation of why *Hillel* said *mlo hin* rather than simply *hin mayim she'uvim poslin es hamikvah*. The reason *Shemaya v'Avtalyon* used the phrase *mlo hin*, the *Gra* explains, is that they were *geirim*, and as such they struggled with the guttural pronunciation of the letter *hei*. Had they said *hin* with an imprecise guttural, it could have been heard as *ein* — *ein mayim she'uvim poslin es hamikvah*, meaning drawn water does *not* invalidate the *mikvah*, the precise opposite of what they intended. By prefacing the measure with *mlo* — a full *hin* — the meaning could not be misunderstood regardless of how the *hei* was pronounced. *Hillel* himself could have said *hin* clearly and been understood, but he preserved the exact formulation of his teachers — *bilshon rabbo* — including the seemingly redundant *mlo*, because of the obligation to transmit Torah in the precise language in which it was received.

### Blood Stain Timing

The third debate between *Shammai* and *Hillel* concerns the retroactive *tumah* of a woman who discovers a blood stain. *Shammai* says *dayan sha'atan* — we assess it from the current moment, assuming the stain occurred just now. Anything she touched prior to discovery is therefore *tahor*. *Hillel* says *mipkidah lipkidah* — we trace back to the last time she checked herself; if she was last examined three days ago and found clean, everything she touched in the intervening three days may be considered *tamei*. Notably, in two of the three *Shammai*-*Hillel* debates, *Hillel* takes the more stringent position.

### Sages' Compromise

The *chachamim* again introduce a compromise: *me'et le'et mema'et al yad mipkidah lipkidah umipkidah lipkidah mema'et al yad me'et le'et* — twenty-four hours limits the last examination, and the last examination limits twenty-four hours, meaning one applies whichever is the lesser of the two. If she last checked three days ago, she is retroactively *tamei* only for the previous twenty-four hours. If she last checked five hours ago, she is retroactively *tamei* only for those five hours. This is the operative ruling.

### Uncounted Debates

The *gemara* then asks whether there are no other debates between *Shammai* and *Hillel*. It raises the famous dispute over *semicha* on *Yom Tov* — whether one may perform the laying of hands on an animal offering brought as a *nedarim u'nedavos* on *Yom Tov* — where *Hillel* permits and *Shammai* prohibits. Rav Huna's rule, however, limits the count to disputes that were unique to *Shammai* and *Hillel* alone: *heicha d'leika plukta d'revusa* — only where there was no prior standing dispute. The *semicha* debate had been contested across multiple generations of *Zugos* long before *Shammai* and *Hillel*; it was not a debate that originated with them and is therefore not included in the three.

A further case is raised: *habotzer lagat* — one who harvests grapes intended for pressing. *Shammai* says the juice that drips from the grapes during harvest renders them *huchshar*, susceptible to *tumah*, because there are circumstances in which one would want that juice. *Hillel* says they are not *huchshar*. This might appear to be a fourth debate. But the *gemara* notes that *Hillel* was silent in the face of *Shammai*'s arguments — meaning he conceded — and a debate that was conceded does not count as a standing dispute between them.

The very fact that *Shammai* and *Hillel* debated in only three areas should give one pause. We are so conditioned by the ubiquity of *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* disputes that we tend to project the same pattern back onto *Shammai* and *Hillel* themselves. In reality, we have very few halakhic teachings from *Shammai* and *Hillel* individually, and almost no *machlokes* between them — a striking contrast with the hundreds of disputes attributed to their schools.

---

## Early Enactments

### Two Yoseis

Having discussed the attribution of *yadayim*, the *gemara* turns its attention to the earlier *ברייתא* that cited *Yosei ben Yoezer ish Tzreidah* and *Yosei ben Yochanan ish Yerushalayim* — figures known primarily from *Pirkei Avos* as among the earliest of the *Zugos* — as having enacted *tumah al eretz ha'amim*, declaring the land of *chutz la'aretz* *tamei*, and *tumah al klei zechuchis*, declaring glassware susceptible to *tumah*. In the *Torah*, the categories subject to *tumah* include metal, pottery, leather, and wood, but glassware is not explicitly mentioned. From the time glassware began to be manufactured and used, *chazal* eventually ruled that it too could become *tamei* — and this ruling is traced here to the earliest *Zugos*.

### Historical Timeline

The *gemara* challenges this attribution by introducing another tradition: Rav Kahana transmits that when Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosi fell ill, the Sages sent to him requesting that he share a few teachings in his father's name before he died. He responded with a chronological tradition: 180 years before the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash* — approximately 110 BCE — *pashta malchus ha'resha'ah al Yisrael*, the evil empire (Rome) extended its dominion over Israel. Eighty years before the *churban* — approximately 10 BCE — they enacted *tumah al eretz ha'amim v'al klei zechuchis*, the very two enactments attributed to *Yosei ben Yoezer* and *Yosei ben Yochanan*. And forty years before the *churban* — approximately 30 CE — the *Sanhedrin* relocated from *Har HaBayis* and took up residence in the market stalls (*chanuyos*) of Jerusalem.

The *gemara* asks what the halakhic significance of the *Sanhedrin*'s relocation was. Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi says it was to note that *dinei nefashos*, capital cases, could no longer be adjudicated. *Tosafot* is troubled by this: we find that the location requirement — that the *Beis Din* must sit specifically on *Har HaBayis* — applies only to the case of *zaken mamre*, the rebellious elder, where the verse says *el hamakom asher yivchar Hashem Elokecha bo*, and the *gemara* derives *melamed shehamakom gorem* — that the physical location is itself constitutive of the authority invoked against the *zaken mamre*. Elsewhere, *Tosafot* notes, we find no source that the *Beis Din*'s presence on *Har HaBayis* is required for capital cases. *Tosafot* does not resolve the difficulty.

The chronological problem remains: if the enactment of *eretz ha'amim* impurity was 80 years before the *churban*, and if we have a tradition that *Hillel* led his dynasty for 100 years before the *churban* — with *Yosei ben Yoezer* and *Yosei ben Yochanan* several generations earlier still — then the dates plainly do not match. *Yosei ben Yoezer* could not have been active merely 80 years before the *churban*.

---

## Foreign Land Decree

### Ground Suspension

The *gemara* resolves the chronological tension by positing that the *gezeirah* of *eretz ha'amim* unfolded in multiple stages, not all at once. The earliest stage, attributed to *Yosei ben Yoezer* and *Yosei ben Yochanan*, was: *gazru agusha litlos* — if one physically touches the ground of *chutz la'aretz*, one is in a state of suspended *tumah* (*toleh*) with regard to *terumah*, meaning one does not eat the *terumah* but does not burn it either. As for the air of *chutz la'aretz* — traveling through it without touching the ground — *v'lo klum*, there was no decree at all at this stage.

### Air Suspension

The second stage was enacted by the Sages of eighty years before the *churban*. They added the airspace: both the ground and the air of *chutz la'aretz* now render one in a state of *toleh*, suspended *tumah* requiring one to hold the *terumah* but not yet to burn it. So now ground and air both produce suspension, but not burning.

### Six Usha Cases

The third stage, which the *gemara* identifies as *takkanat Usha*, is then introduced. The *mishna* teaches: *al shesh sefeikos sorfin es ha'terumah* — for six categories of doubt, one burns *terumah*. These six are: doubt about *beis hapras* — a field through which a grave was plowed and bone fragments may be scattered; doubt about soil imported from *chutz la'aretz*; doubt about the garments of an *am ha'aretz* — since an *am ha'aretz* is presumed to be careless about *tumah v'taharah*, he may be a *zav* without knowing it, and his clothes may carry *tumah*; doubt about vessels found without known provenance; doubt about human saliva — since it might be the saliva of a *zav* or *zavah*; and doubt about human urine found alongside animal urine.

The last case requires clarification. Rashi reads it as follows: even where it is not certain whether the liquid is human urine or animal urine, the mere possibility that it is human urine is sufficient to require stringency. All the other five cases involve certainty about what the substance is — human saliva, human clothing — but uncertainty about whether the person was *tamei*. Here, by contrast, there is uncertainty about the very identity of the substance, and Rashi says we are nonetheless stringent. *Tosafot* reads it in precisely the opposite direction: when urine appears in isolation one may assume it is animal urine and be lenient, but when human urine appears *alongside* animal urine, the contrast makes it apparent which is which, and one can identify the human urine with certainty — and it is only then that one must be concerned.

The six cases also differ from the *Beis Shammai*-*Beis Hillel* items in that they are not necessarily about *sheni l'tumah*. If the spit or urine truly comes from a *zav*, it would be an *av hatumah*, and one who touches it becomes a *rishon*. The emphasis of *sorfin* here is not about the degree of *tumah* but about the communal commitment to treat even doubtful cases with full stringency — to burn rather than merely suspend.

The *mishna* distinguishes between *vadai magaan* — certain contact, uncertain *tumah* status — in which case one burns, and *safek magaan* — uncertain contact. Rabbi Yosi rules that in a *reshus hayachid* even doubtful contact obligates burning, whereas the *chachamim* say that in a *reshus hayachid* uncertain contact produces only *toleh*, and in a *reshus harabbim* it is *tahor* entirely.

*Ulla* confirms that these six things were all enacted at *Usha* after the *churban*.

### Usha Burning Rule

With this in place, the three-stage history of the *eretz ha'amim* decree becomes clear. Stage one (*Yosei ben Yoezer*): ground produces *toleh*, air produces nothing. Stage two (eighty years before the *churban*): ground produces *toleh*, air also produces *toleh*. Stage three (*Usha*): ground now produces *sreifah* — one burns *terumah* — and air remains at *toleh*, exactly as it was in stage two. The *Usha* innovation was not about the airspace; it was specifically about the ground, and specifically about escalating the consequence from suspension to burning.

---

## Glassware Status

### Glass-Pottery Analogy

The *gemara* turns to the second of the two enactments attributed to the early period: *tumah* of *klei zechuchis*. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Reish Lakish explains the reasoning: *ho'il u'techilas bri'asan min hachol* — since glassware originates from sand, the Sages treated it like pottery (*klei cheres*). Pottery derives from earth; glass derives from sand — and so *rabbanan* applied the same rules of *tumah* to glass as to pottery.

### Lead-Filled Glass

The analogy to pottery immediately raises a problem. If glass is to be treated like pottery, then just as pottery cannot be purified in a *mikvah* — the way to purify pottery is to break it — glass should likewise be incapable of *tahara* through immersion. Yet the *mishna* in the laws of *chatzitza* implies that glass vessels can be immersed in a *mikvah*, since it lists substances like tar and myrrh that constitute an impediment (*chatzitza*) to proper immersion of glassware. Why is immersion possible if glass is like pottery?

### Rabbi Meir's View

The *gemara* limits the permissibility of *mikvah* immersion for glass to a specific and unusual case: a glass vessel that developed a hole and was filled with lead. This is the position of Rabbi Meir, who holds *hakol holech achar hama'amid* — the defining identity of an object follows whatever it is that gives it its structural integrity. A glass vessel with a hole is no longer a functional vessel; its hole renders it incapable of containing anything. What restored it to vessel-status was the lead filling. Therefore its current identity is that of a lead vessel, i.e., a metal vessel. Metal vessels, unlike pottery, can be purified through *mikvah* immersion — and so the lead-filled glass vessel can be immersed.

### Meir vs. Sages

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel records the dispute: Rabbi Meir says the lead-filled glass vessel is *tamei*, the *chachamim* say it is *tahor*. The *gemara*'s understanding is that Rabbi Meir, by applying *hakol holech achar hama'amid*, reclassifies the vessel as a metal vessel — which is susceptible to *tumah* biblically (*de'oraita*). The *chachamim* disagree and declare it *tahor*. *Tosafot* raises the question: even if one does not accept Rabbi Meir's reclassification as a metal vessel, should the vessel not at least be *tamei* as a glass vessel on a *rabbinic* level? The answer implied is that perhaps yes — but Rabbi Meir's unique contribution is the claim that it rises to the level of full biblical *tumah* as a metal vessel.

The practical upshot for the main discussion is that the *mikvah* immersion of glass is permissible only in this special case of a hole filled with lead. For standard glass, the analogy to pottery holds: it can become *tamei*, but it cannot be purified through *mikvah*. The *gemara* will continue with this topic on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Shabbat 16

## Glassware Status

### Sand Similarity

The Gemara on this daf does not begin with the eighteen decrees of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel — we will return to those shortly — but rather with a list of earlier *takanot* that was quoted previously. Two of those *takanot* are under discussion: one establishing that glassware is *mekabel tumah*, susceptible to ritual impurity, and the other declaring the land of non-Jews *tamei*. Both were enacted in the earliest period of rabbinic legislation, attributed to Yose ben Yoezer Ish Tzereda and Yose ben Yochanan Ish Yerushalayim. The Gemara now turns its attention to glassware.

The fundamental question is: why did the Sages decide that glassware would become *tamei*? One cannot simply say that the Rabbis applied *tumah* to all vessels universally, since there are vessel categories that remain *tahor* even rabbinically — stone vessels, for instance. So what was the specific logic for glassware? The Gemara answers that glassware was considered similar to earthenware because it, too, is made from sand. The assumption, therefore, was that glass would carry a status analogous to *kli cheres*, the earthenware vessel.

One immediate difficulty, however, arises from this analogy. A defining feature of *kli cheres* is that it cannot be purified in a *mikveh* — the only path to *taharah* for earthenware is breakage. Yet it is well established that glassware can be immersed in a *mikveh*. The Gemara resolves this by treating the *mikveh*-eligible glass as a special and narrow case: a glass vessel that had developed a hole — and thereby ceased to be a *kli*, since a hole of sufficient size removes an earthenware vessel from the category of *kli cheres* — and was subsequently repaired by filling the hole with lead. In that case, because the lead repair conferred on it the character of a metal vessel, it could be immersed in a *mikveh* according to the position of Rabbi Meir. Normal glassware, however, would remain in the earthenware category and could not be immersed.

### Earthenware Model

With this analogy to *kli cheres* established, the Gemara subjects it to scrutiny. The most prominent and practically significant feature of *kli cheres* is not merely the question of *mikveh* immersion, but the distinctive manner in which it becomes *tamei* and transmits *tumah*. Ordinary vessels — wood, metal, bone — become *tamei* when *tumah* physically contacts any part of them. Earthenware, by contrast, becomes *tamei* only when something is within its airspace; external contact, even with the outer surface or base, does not render it *tamei*. Correspondingly, earthenware transmits *tumah* only from its airspace. If one suspends a *sheretz* — a dead rodent that is a primary source of *tumah* — within the airspace of a pottery vessel without it touching the walls, the vessel becomes *tamei*. Conversely, if one suspends food within that airspace, the food becomes *tamei*.

The Gemara raises the obvious objection: if glass is like *kli cheres*, then touching the outside of a glass vessel should have no halachic consequence. Yet we know from the *Mishnah* in Kelim that this is not the case. That *Mishnah* states that *kli cheres* and *kli nether* — natron, a mineral substance comparable in halachic status to pottery, identified as sodium carbonate — share the same *tumah* rules: *metameim u-mitameim u-metameim me'aviran*, they can receive *tumah* and transmit *tumah* through their airspace. The *Mishnah* then adds: *u-mitamei me'achoreihem ve-ein mitamei migabeihem* — they become *tamei* through their *achorayim* but not through their *gav*.

Rashi's interpretation of these two terms repays careful attention. *Gav* refers to the simple back or exterior surface of the vessel. *Achorayim*, by contrast, refers to what Rashi understands as a secondary receptacle — specifically, the concave underside of the base of a vessel, a surface that faces outward but still has something of the character of a receptacle. Think of a *kiddush* cup: the bowl is the primary receptacle on the inside, but the base, when inverted, reveals a hollow space on what is technically the exterior of the vessel. Rashi holds that this *achorayim* zone can receive and transmit *tumah*, though rabbinically rather than biblically. The biblical rule governs only the primary interior receptacle; the *achorayim* is an extension of that principle at the rabbinic level. The plain *gav* — the simple exterior surface — cannot receive *tumah* at all, though there may be some capacity to transmit *tumah* if contact is made there, a point that the Gemara does not address explicitly. Tosafot has a lengthy discussion engaging with and largely defending Rashi's reading before offering an alternative, though for our purposes Rashi's framework suffices.

The *Mishnah* closes with the statement *ve-shi'areihem metaharan* — the vessel is purified only through breakage. This too is the law of *kli cheres*. The Gemara then points out: the *Mishnah* in Kelim specifies that it is only pottery and natron vessels that share this identical *tumah* profile — *kli cheres ve-kli nether hu de-tumatam shavah* — and nothing else. Glass is not mentioned. If glass truly followed the pottery model, one would expect it to be listed alongside pottery. Its omission implies that glass is governed by a different set of *tumah* rules. This undermines the original rationale for treating glass like *kli cheres*.

### Metal Model

The Gemara pivots. It proposes a new rationale: *keivan de-chi nishtabru yesh lahem takanah* — since when glass breaks it can be repaired, it is therefore treated like metal vessels, *shavinhu k'cheli matachot*. When glass cracks or breaks, it can be mended by applying heat — a process analogous to how a craftsman solders or re-forms a broken metal vessel. In antiquity, glassware was expensive, and artisans had techniques to fuse broken glass back together. This capacity for heat-based repair defines it as metal-like rather than pottery-like.

Tosafot raises a subtle objection: the mere fact that glass can be *repaired* through heat would not by itself have prompted the original rabbinic decision to make it *tamei*. Fundamentally, glass does not begin its existence as a metal object. Tosafot therefore proposes a hybridized account: the Rabbis initially observed that glass was sufficiently similar to pottery — being formed from sand through intense heat — to declare it *tamei*. But having made that decision, they then faced the question of which existing halachic category to assign it to. Given the repairability through heat, they placed it in the metal category, even if the original impetus came from its resemblance to pottery.

One student raised the observation that the manufacturing process of glass is itself analogous to that of metal — both involve applying extreme heat to a raw material and fashioning it into shape — whereas pottery, though also fired at high temperatures, is shaped differently. This may in fact be closer to what the Gemara intends in this shift: not merely repairability but the entire mode of production and material constitution. Glass also possesses the fragility of pottery while sharing the fire-formed character of metal, making it in some respects a genuinely hybrid material.

### Glass vs Metal/Wood

Granting that glass is now being categorized as metal-like, the Gemara proceeds to test this against two specific halachot of metal vessels and discovers anomalies. The first anomaly concerns the requirement for a *beit kibul*, a receptacle. The general rules for susceptibility to *tumah* vary across material categories. Earthenware becomes *tamei* only through its airspace and has no need of a formal receptacle in the ordinary sense. Wood and bone vessels require a *beit kibul* — a spoon of wood becomes *tamei* only because it has a receptacle; a simple wooden board or stick does not. Metal vessels, however, are the most inclusive: even a *pashut* metal vessel — one that is perfectly flat and has no receptacle whatsoever, such as a needle — becomes *tamei*. Metal requires no *beit kibul*.

The *Mishnah* cited by the Gemara states: *klei matachot — pshuteihem u-mekableihem tme'im* — metal vessels, whether simple or receptacle-bearing, are all susceptible to *tumah*. The *Mishnah* continues: *nishbiru taharu* — if they break, they become *tahor*. And then: *chazar ve-asa mehem kelim — chazru le-tumatam yeshanah* — if they were broken and then refashioned into new vessels, they revert to their *old* *tumah*. That is, if a metal vessel was *tamei*, broken (and thereby became *tahor*), and then remade, it does not begin its renewed existence as a fresh vessel susceptible to *tumah* only going forward — it is immediately and retroactively *tamei* again with its original *tumah*. This is a special rabbinic rule applied to metal vessels.

Now contrast the *Mishnah* governing glassware, which groups it with *klei etz*, *klei or*, and *klei etzem* — wood, leather, and bone. That *Mishnah* states: *pshuteihem tehorin* — vessels in these categories that are flat and have no receptacle are *tahor* and cannot receive *tumah*. Only those with a receptacle become *tamei*, and only when any part of them is physically contacted. Furthermore: *nishbiru taharu* — they become *tahor* upon breakage — but *chazar ve-asa mehem kelim, mekablin tumah mikan u-le'aba* — if refashioned, they can receive *tumah* only going forward, not retroactively. The old *tumah* does not return.

The Gemara thus identifies two anomalies in the attempt to categorize glass as metal. First, glass requires a *beit kibul*, whereas metal does not. Second, the old *tumah* does not revert when broken glass is remade, whereas for metal it does. The wood-and-bone category would actually fit glass perfectly — it accounts for both anomalies — but there is no logical basis to place glass in that category. So the Gemara is left attempting to explain why glass, even if metal-like, diverges from the metal template in these two specific respects.

### Anomalies Solution

The Gemara addresses each anomaly in turn. On the question of why the old *tumah* does not return: *tumas klei zechuchis derabanan* — the entire *tumah* of glassware is rabbinic. And *tuma yeshanah derabanan* — the rule that old *tumah* reverts upon remaking is itself rabbinic. Biblically, once *tumah* is gone, it is gone; a remade vessel can contract *tumah* anew but does not restore prior *tumah*. When did the Rabbis invoke the rule that old *tumah* returns? Only when dealing with a vessel whose *tumah* is biblical in nature. When the vessel's *tumah* is itself only rabbinic, the Rabbis did not apply this additional rabbinic stringency — *lo achisu leh rabbanan*. Since glassware is only *derabanan*, its old *tumah* does not revert.

On the second anomaly — why glass requires a *beit kibul* even though metal does not: here the Gemara gives a different kind of answer. *Avdi rabbanan heikera* — the Rabbis deliberately made a distinguishing marker. Specifically: *ki heichi d'lo lishrifu aleih terumah ve-kodshim* — so that one would not come to burn *terumah* and *kodshim* that came in contact with glassware. The logic is elegant. If glass followed all the rules of metal precisely — including becoming *tamei* without a *beit kibul* — then a scholar thoroughly versed in the laws of *tumah va-taharah* would have no way of knowing, from the behavior of glass alone, that its *tumah* status was rabbinic rather than biblical. By ensuring that glass deviates from metal in this one respect, the Rabbis created a built-in signal: anyone who knows the laws will notice that glass requires a *beit kibul* while metal does not, and will thereby be reminded that the *tumah* of glass is rabbinic. Armed with that awareness, one will refrain from treating it with biblical stringency and will not burn *terumah* that comes into contact with it.

This leads to a broader observation. Earlier in the tractate we discussed cases where the Sages were so strict about a rabbinic *tumah* that they required burning *terumah* that contacted it — for example, *beit ha-pras*, or *yadayim* in their status as a *sheini*. In the case of glassware, they went in precisely the opposite direction, engineering the halachah to prevent such burning. The *rishonim* acknowledge that there is no uniform rule governing which rabbinic *tumot* are treated with full biblical stringency and which are not — it varies by case.

### Transparency Theory

Rav Ashi offers a fundamentally different approach at the top of 16b. He maintains: *l'olam l'cheli cheres damu* — glass is and remains analogous to pottery, not to metal. The objection that originally seemed fatal — if it is like pottery, why should touching the outside of a glass vessel render it *tamei*? — is answered by a celebrated principle: *hoil ve-tocho k'varo*, since its inside is like its outside.

The phrase *tocho k'varo* resonates with a famous earlier discussion in the tractate concerning Rabban Gamliel and the standards for admission to the *beit ha-midrash* — whether a student's inner character must match his outward presentation. Here the phrase is given a striking literal application. Glass is, by its physical nature, transparent. There is no visual distinction between inside and outside; what is on the inside can be seen from the outside, and vice versa. Because glass is inherently transparent, the Rabbis did not maintain the usual distinction between the interior and exterior of the vessel. Touching the outside is, in a sense, like touching the inside, since through the glass wall one sees the inside when viewing the outside. The ordinary rule of *kli cheres* — that only the interior airspace matters — is therefore extended to encompass the exterior as well, not because of any categorical shift but because the physical nature of glass collapses the inside-outside distinction.

Under Rav Ashi's account, the other halachic features of glass align naturally with the pottery model. The *mikveh* case is explained by the same special circumstance invoked earlier — a hole filled with lead. The fact that old *tumah* does not revert upon remaking presents no problem, since that is simply not a feature of the pottery category. And the requirement for a *beit kibul* similarly presents no difficulty. On Rav Ashi's reading, the anomalies that required explanation under the metal theory dissolve. The sole departure from standard *kli cheres* rules is the treatment of exterior contact as equivalent to interior contact, and that is fully accounted for by the physical transparency of glass itself.

The upshot is that the Gemara does not definitively resolve whether glass is fundamentally like metal (with two anomalies explained away) or fundamentally like pottery (with one anomaly explained by transparency). Both positions remain on the table.

### Kashering Glass

This sustained Talmudic discussion of glassware's halachic category carries a direct and well-known application to the laws of *kashrus*: the question of whether glassware can be *kashered*. The Gemara does not address *kashering* directly in this context, but some *poskim* have sought to derive guidance from the *tumah* categorization explored here. If glass is like pottery, then just as pottery cannot be *kashered* — because absorbed material cannot be expelled — glass similarly cannot be *kashered*. If glass is like metal, then just as metal can be *kashered*, so can glass.

Many *poskim* push back sharply on this analogical reasoning, arguing that it conflates two entirely distinct frameworks. The *tumah* categorization is a formal halachic taxonomy; the question of *kashering* is a physical one, turning on whether a material absorbs and releases food substances. These are not the same inquiry, and the formal category assigned for purposes of *tumah* does not necessarily answer the empirical question of absorption. From this perspective, glass should be evaluated on its own physical merits — and in fact, common glass does not absorb food substances at all. A student pointed out that glass manufacturers confirm this: ordinary glassware is non-porous and non-absorbent, and specialty industrial glass that does absorb is rare and prohibitively expensive.

Some *poskim* go so far as to hold that glassware does not require *kashering* at all between *milchig* and *fleishig* use, precisely because it absorbs nothing. It was reportedly common in earlier generations for families to maintain a single set of glass dishes used interchangeably, since glass was understood not to absorb taste. In more recent generations, increased wealth and increased stringency have both contributed to a shift in practice, and most contemporary *poskim* are more conservative — particularly with respect to Pesach, where the threshold of stringency is generally higher. The range of opinions among *poskim* today remains real, however, and in pressing circumstances different answers may be given.

The broader methodological point is worth noting: when the Gemara does not address a practical question directly, decisors look for parallel cases in adjacent halachic domains. Sometimes those parallels are genuinely illuminating; sometimes they are merely formal, and applying them uncritically leads to distorted conclusions. The glassware debate is a case study in that tension.

---

## Shimon ben Shatach

### Ketubah Takana

The Gemara now turns to the early *takanot* of Shimon ben Shatach, who predated the era of Shammai and Hillel. Two *takanot* are attributed to him. The first — that women receive a *kesubah* — is mentioned but not analyzed at length here; nonetheless, the essential background is worth laying out.

The broader question of whether *kesubah* is biblical or rabbinic in origin is debated in tractate Kesubos. A potential biblical source is found in the verse dealing with the seduction of a virgin, which states that the seducer must pay *kesef yishkol ke-mohar ha-besulos* — money equivalent to the *mohar ha-besulos*, the bride price for virgins, fixed elsewhere in the Torah at fifty *shekel*, equivalent to 200 *zuz*, the standard amount of a *kesubah*. The difficulty is that the Torah's *mohar* was paid upfront to the father, functioning either as a bride price or, in another reading, as funds held in escrow for the benefit of the wife should the marriage end. The rabbinic *kesubah*, by contrast, is paid at the time of dissolution of the marriage. Whether the Torah's framework is the true source of the rabbinic institution is therefore genuinely uncertain.

What is clear is that the original practice was to pay the *kesubah* sum upfront at the time of marriage, either to the father or held by the bride directly, as a kind of prepaid alimony or substitute for inheritance — since the wife would not inherit from her husband, but these funds would support her after his death. The *Tosefta* records the problem that arose: a husband who wished to divorce his wife could do so callously, without hesitation, because the *kesubah* had already been paid. There was no financial deterrent. The Rabbis found this unacceptable — *shelo yihei kal b'einav le-garshah*, divorce should not be a trivially easy step. Shimon ben Shatach therefore instituted that the *kesubah* would no longer be paid upfront but would remain as an obligation payable only upon dissolution of the marriage. With his assets potentially at stake, a husband would think carefully before divorcing his wife. It is this specific innovation — the deferred payment — that is attributed to Shimon ben Shatach, not the institution of *kesubah* itself.

### Metal Recontamination

The Gemara pivots immediately to Shimon ben Shatach's second *takana*, which is far more directly relevant to the *tumah* discussion: *ve-gazar tuma al klei matachot* — he decreed *tumah* upon metal vessels. At first this seems entirely superfluous: metal vessels are already *tamei* biblically. The Torah itself provides the source in the passage dealing with the vessels seized from Midian, which commands that any vessel of gold, silver, iron, bronze, or other metals that comes in contact with *tumah* must be purified — either through *kashering* in fire or, for *tumah* purposes, through immersion, together with sprinkling of the waters of the *parah adumah*. What, then, did Shimon ben Shatach add?

The Gemara answers: *lo nitzrecha ela le-tuma yeshanah* — his *takana* concerned the rule of *tuma yeshanah*, the restoration of old *tumah* upon remaking. As we established when analyzing the metal vessel *Mishnah*, this rule — that a broken and remade metal vessel regains its prior *tumah* — is itself rabbinic. It was Shimon ben Shatach who instituted it. Why?

### Sheltzion Story

The Gemara provides the historical background through a narrative: *ma'aseh be-Sheltzion ha-malka* — there is a story about Queen Sheltzion, identified with Shlomtzion, a Hasmonean queen. She made a great feast — a wedding banquet — for her son. During the feast, someone died, and as a result all of the vessels under the same roof became *tamei*, since *tumas meis* — the impurity transmitted by a corpse — extends to everything within the same enclosure. All her vessels were now *tamei*.

For those operating in a world where eating *chullin be-tahara* — ordinary food in a state of purity — was the norm, this was a genuine crisis. The standard process for purifying vessels contaminated by *tumas meis* involves sprinkling the waters of the *parah adumah*, and this process spans a week. There was no time. So she broke all the vessels, gave them to the smelter, who melted and remade them, and produced new vessels. Breaking renders a metal vessel *tahor*; once remade, it would be a fresh vessel capable of contracting *tumah* only going forward. The feast could proceed.

The Sages responded: *yachzeru le-tumasam ha-yeshanah* — the vessels revert to their original *tumah*. They enacted the rule of *tuma yeshanah* that very day, effectively closing the workaround that had been exploited.

### Parah Adumah Logic

The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama* — what was the reasoning? *Mishum geder mei chatat nahagu bah* — because of the concern of undermining the institution of the waters of the *parah adumah*. If breaking and remaking a metal vessel were a straightforward path to *taharah* from *tumas meis*, no one would ever bother with the elaborate and arduous process of *parah adumah* purification for vessels. One could always simply melt them down and recast them. The Rabbis feared this would corrode the entire institution.

The Gemara then raises an internal complication: this reasoning works well according to the view that the rule of *tuma yeshanah* applies only to *tumas meis* — since *parah adumah* waters are specifically required for *tumas meis* purification, making the *tuma yeshanah* rule a targeted deterrent. But according to the view that *tuma yeshanah* applies to all categories of *tumah*, not only *tumas meis*, the *parah adumah* rationale cannot be the whole story.

### Abaye & Rava

For this broader application, Abaye and Rava each supply an alternative rationale. Abaye says: *gezeirah shema lo yishvirenu bikhdei taharaso* — the concern is that a person executing this workaround will not break the vessel sufficiently to achieve valid *taharah*. Since remelting and remaking is work, one will naturally want to make the smallest possible break — a hairline fracture rather than genuine breakage — which will not actually remove the vessel's *kli* status and therefore will not actually produce *taharah*. Forbidding the workaround entirely prevents this risk.

Rava says: *gezeirah shema yomru tevilah bas yoma oltah lah* — the concern is what observers will conclude. If they see that a vessel was *tamei* earlier in the day and is now being used in the evening of the same day, they will assume it was immersed in a *mikveh*. And if they believe that, they will draw the erroneous conclusion that immersion in a *mikveh* confers *taharah* effective immediately — the same day — rather than only at nightfall, which is the actual rule.

The Gemara asks what the practical difference (*nafka mina*) is between Abaye and Rava. It answers: *ikka beinaihu ditzraffinhu martzei* — the case where the vessel was broken into many small pieces. According to Rashi, if the concern is that one will not break it sufficiently (Abaye), then shattering it into many small fragments fully addresses that concern, and in such a case one might not apply the *gezeirah*. According to Rava, however, whose concern is what observers will think, even if the vessel is broken into many pieces the observers will still see it used the same day and draw the wrong conclusion — though Rashi also suggests an inverse reading: a vessel broken into many fragments and visibly repaired will display all its solder lines, making it obvious that it was remade, so observers will not mistake it for a vessel that was merely immersed.

Rashi notes with characteristic candor that he cannot identify the source of the debate between the view that *tuma yeshanah* applies only to *tumas meis* and the view that it applies to all *tumot*. Tosafot, for its part, attempts to locate it in the *Tosefta* of Kelim or *Masechet Kelim*, noting a position attributed there to Rabban Gamliel. The Gilyon HaShas records, in the name of Rabbi Akiva Eiger, every place in Shas where Rashi similarly acknowledges that he cannot identify the source of a Talmudic reference — a significant set of admissions that itself reveals something about how the tradition understands the limits of available sources.

---

## Eighteen Decrees

### Return to 18

The Gemara signals a return to the primary subject of the *yud-ches davar* — the eighteen things decreed by Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. The Gemara has been engaged with earlier *takanot* — the glassware decree, the land of non-Jews decree, the *takanot* of Shimon ben Shatach — all of which were relevant background but were not themselves among the eighteen. Now the Gemara reorients and asks: *ve-ha'idach mai hi* — what are the remaining items among the eighteen? We have already counted, from earlier in the discussion, approximately eight or nine: becoming a *sheini* through eating *ochel rishon* or *ochel sheini*, through drinking *mashkin tme'im*, through immersing one's head and greater part in drawn water (*rosho ve-rubo be-mayim shu'uvim*); hands always having the status of a *sheini*; and food and vessels that touch *mashkin* causing the *mashkin* to become a *rishon* and the food and vessels a *sheini*. The Gemara now sets out to identify the remaining items necessary to reach eighteen.

### Drainpipe Vessels

The Gemara cites a *Mishnah*: *ha-maniach keilim tachat ha-tzinor le-kabel bahen mei geshamim* — one who places vessels beneath a drainpipe in order to collect rainwater. This requires some background. The relevant halachic issue here is not *tumah* susceptibility but the laws of *mikveh*: specifically, the category of *mayim she'uvim*, drawn water, which can invalidate a *mikveh* if added before the *mikveh* contains its requisite forty *se'ah* of valid water. The core rule is that water becomes "drawn" — halachically equivalent to water poured from a bucket — if it is collected within a vessel with the owner's intent. Physical drawing is not required; it suffices that one *wanted* the water to be in the vessel, and that intent is itself treated as if one drew it.

The case of the *Mishnah* is: rainwater falls into a vessel placed under a drainpipe. No one physically carried the water; it fell in by itself. If that water then enters a *mikveh*, is it *mayim she'uvim*? The answer depends entirely on whether the owner *wanted* the water to be in the vessel when it fell.

The *Mishnah* specifies that this rule applies equally to large and small vessels. Tosafot explains the significance of mentioning large ones: a vessel so large that it cannot be lifted when full — approximately the size of a *mikveh* itself, forty *se'ah* — is not ordinarily considered a vessel for purposes of *kabbelas tumah*. One might therefore have thought that such a large vessel is not truly a *kli* and thus cannot render the water "drawn." The *Mishnah* teaches otherwise: even this oversized vessel, though it cannot receive *tumah*, is still legally a *kli* sufficient to define water collected within it as drawn. This is a significant point about how the category of *kli* operates in different legal contexts — a vessel can be a *kli* for one purpose without being a *kli* for another.

Similarly, the *Mishnah* includes vessels of stone (*klei avanim*), vessels of unformed earth (*klei adamah* — earthenware not fired in a kiln), and vessels of dried dung (*klei glalim*). All of these lack the capacity to receive *tumah*, yet all are still legally vessels for purposes of the drawn-water rule. The *chiddush* is that *kabel tumah* and *kli* status are not identical; the absence of one does not entail the absence of the other.

### Shammai Position

The *Mishnah* then presents the dispute: *achad ha-maniach ve-achad ha-shochei'ach* — whether the vessels were placed there intentionally or were forgotten there — *posalin et ha-mikveh, divrei Beit Shammai*. Beit Shammai holds that in both cases the rainwater collected is treated as drawn water. Even if one had originally placed a vessel under the drainpipe for some other purpose and then simply forgotten about it — so that when the rain came and filled it there was no active intent at that moment — Beit Shammai considers the water drawn. The prior placement under the drainpipe, even if no longer present in one's mind, is sufficient to define the water as *she'uvim*.

### Hillel Position

Beit Hillel disagrees: *u-Veit Hillel metaharin be-shocheach* — Beit Hillel considers the forgotten vessel's water *tahor* and not drawn. If one did not intend for the water to be collected when it actually fell — if one's mind was elsewhere and one had genuinely forgotten the vessel — then there is no operative intent, and the water cannot be treated as if one had drawn it. Intent at the moment of collection, or at least a sufficiently active and ongoing intent, is required.

The *Mishnah* continues: *amar Rabbi Meir, nimnu ve-rabu Beit Shammai al Beit Hillel* — they took a vote, and Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel. This, says Rabbi Meir, is what happened on the day of the eighteen decrees. This drainpipe case is therefore one of the eighteen things on which Beit Shammai's position prevailed. Rabbi Yosi, however, disputes this: *adayin machloket bimkomah omedet* — the debate remains unresolved; Beit Hillel was not outvoted. According to Rabbi Yosi, this case cannot be counted among the eighteen. The Gemara will address the implications of this disagreement for the count of eighteen below.

### Intent Continuity

The *Mishnah* also records the limits of the dispute with a refinement attributed to *d'vei Rav*: *ha-kol modin she-ke-she-nichah bi-sha'at kishur avim teme'im* — everyone agrees that if one placed the vessels under the drainpipe when the sky was overcast and rain was imminent, the water is *tamei* (i.e., treated as drawn) even if one subsequently forgot about the vessels. At the moment of placement, rain was so clearly impending that the intent to collect was already fully formed. Conversely: *bi-sha'at pizur avim* — if one placed the vessels when the sky was clear and there was no prospect of rain, everyone agrees the water is *tahor*, since whatever general intention may have existed, it was not active at any relevant time.

The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel applies to an intermediate case: one placed the vessels under the drainpipe when it was overcast, then the clouds dispersed (*ve-nitpazru*), and then the clouds gathered again (*ve-chazru ve-nitkashru*) and it rained. The question is whether the continuity of intent was broken by the interval in which the clouds separated. *Mar savar batalah machashavto* — one view holds that the dispersal of the clouds constituted a break in the process, effectively nullifying the original intent; when the rain finally fell, it did not fall within the framework of the owner's active intention, and so the water is not drawn. *U-mar savar lo batalah machashavto* — the opposing view holds that the intent was continuous: the initial placement during overcast conditions established an intent that was not voided by a temporary clearing of the sky, and when the rain eventually fell, it was received within that unbroken framework of intent. This is the core of the Shammai-Hillel debate in the intermediate case, and both sides agree that the operative question is not merely whether intent existed at the moment of placement, but whether the intent remained operative and continuous through to the moment of actual collection.

### Kutim Niddah

Since Rabbi Yosi holds that the drainpipe dispute was never resolved by a vote and therefore cannot be counted among the eighteen, the Gemara needs to identify another item to bring the total to eighteen. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supplies it: *af bnot kutim niddot me-arisatan bo ba-yom gazru* — on that very day they also decreed that the daughters of the *Kutim* — the Samaritans — are to be considered *niddah* from the moment of birth.

The background is as follows. The *Kutim* were halachically considered *geirei emet*, genuine converts, and were therefore treated in many respects as Jews. However, their interpretation of the laws of *niddah* diverged from the rabbinic understanding. The Rabbis held that a woman can attain the status of *niddah* even as a newborn infant — any blood, regardless of the girl's age, can in principle generate *niddah* status. The *Kutim* did not accept this interpretation, and held that *niddah* begins only upon physical maturity. Because of this divergence in practice, there was a concern that *Kutim* women might be regarded as *tahor* when they were in fact halachically *tamei*. The Rabbis therefore enacted a sweeping decree: all daughters of the *Kutim*, from the moment of birth, are treated as *niddot*. This eliminated the ambiguity entirely.

This decree, enacted on the same day as the other eighteen enactments, gives us the number we need to complete the count of eighteen according to Rabbi Yosi's position — substituting for the drainpipe case which Rabbi Yosi excludes. The Gemara signals that the discussion of the eighteen decrees will continue on the following daf, where, among the remaining items, the law of *batzir* — the harvesting of grapes — will be addressed. That case concerns the rule that for food to become susceptible to *tumah*, it must be moistened by one of the seven liquids (*zayin mashkin*), and only if that moisture came *le-ratzon*, with the owner's approval. When grapes are harvested and a small amount of juice is naturally released in the process, Hillel held that this is not *le-ratzon* since the harvester has no interest in that juice; Shammai held that it is. A vote was taken, Shammai prevailed, and this too became one of the eighteen decrees.

---

---

# Shabbat 18

## 18 Things Debates

### Context & Rambam

We begin today on 17b, at the *mishnah* located approximately ten lines from the bottom of the page. At this point in the tractate, we have concluded several *dapim* dealing with the eighteen things debated by *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* — material that had almost nothing to do with *Shabbos* and was concerned primarily with *terumah* and *taharah*. We now return to *Shabbos* proper, and encounter a series of debates between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* that are specifically *Shabbos*-related.

It is worth noting at the outset that the *Rambam*, reading through both the *Yerushalmi* and the *Bavli*, understood that the original eighteen things were matters on which the schools debated and then reached agreement, all gathered into a single list. The *Yerushalmi*, however, speaks of three distinct lists. The *Rambam* follows this approach and identifies the debates we are about to study as a third list of eighteen things — matters that remained points of ongoing disagreement between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*.

## 18 Things Debates (II)

### Soaking & Dyeing

The *mishnah* opens: *Beit Shammai* says one may not soak ink, dyes, or *karshinin* (vetch — a legume used as animal feed) unless they can complete their absorption before the day is out. *Beit Hillel* permits it.

What *Beit Shammai* is establishing, and what we will see repeated across a series of cases, is that one may not initiate a process before *Shabbos* that will continue on *Shabbos* itself — unless that process can be completed while it is still the day before. *Beit Hillel* disagrees and permits beginning such processes even if they continue into *Shabbos*.

One cannot take this position to its extreme, of course — for then one could never place food on a fire before *Shabbos* to cook on *Shabbos*, nor keep candles burning. The lines of distinction will need to be carefully drawn. Already at this stage, it is worth noting that there are two possible explanations for *Beit Shammai*'s position. The first is a standard rabbinic concern: if one begins something before *Shabbos* and it continues into *Shabbos*, this either leads to actually performing *melacha* on *Shabbos*, or at minimum creates an appearance problem — it looks as though one is engaged in *melacha* on *Shabbos*, since the activity is visibly happening for one's benefit throughout the day. The second possible explanation is something the *Gemara* calls *shevisas keilim* — the obligation to allow one's vessels to rest on *Shabbos*, analogous to the requirement that one's animals and servants rest. This could potentially be a biblical concern, not merely a rabbinic one. These two frameworks — rabbinic appearances-based concern versus biblical *shevisas keilim* — will drive the *Gemara*'s analysis throughout this *daf*.

## Beit Shammai Rules

### Ink & Dyes

The *mishnah* continues with parallel cases. *Beit Shammai* says one may not place bundles of flax into an oven unless they have time to be heated through before *Shabbos*. The process involved is a whitening of the flax — part of the preparation of linen — achieved by exposing the bundles to sustained heat. Similarly, *Beit Shammai* says one may not place wool into a vat of dye unless it has time to absorb the dye before *Shabbos*. In each case, *Beit Hillel* permits it.

### Traps

*Beit Shammai* adds: one may not set traps for wild animals, birds, or fish before *Shabbos* unless the animals could have been caught from the day before. *Beit Hillel* permits it. This case is somewhat different from the others, since trapping is inherently uncertain — one never knows whether an animal will be caught. One reading of *Beit Shammai*'s requirement is that there must have been sufficient time, in principle, for the catch to occur before *Shabbos*. *Tosafos*, however, struggles with the plain sense of the text, suggesting perhaps that the scenario envisions a case where capture is virtually certain. This remains somewhat difficult on the straightforward reading of the *mishnah*.

### Non-Jew Sales

*Beit Shammai* states: one may not sell to a non-Jew, load merchandise onto his donkey together with him, or even hoist it onto his back, unless the non-Jew can reach a nearby destination while it is still the day before *Shabbos*. *Beit Hillel* permits it.

This case is qualitatively different from the previous ones. Here, once the sale is completed, the seller is entirely out of the picture — the goods belong to the non-Jew, carried on his own donkey, going to his own destination. Yet *Beit Shammai* requires that he reach his destination before *Shabbos*. The concern here is transparently one of appearances: it looks as though the Jew has dispatched the non-Jew on an errand on his behalf, even if that is not what has occurred. *Rashi* explains *kedei she-yagia l'makom karov* to mean that the destination must be close enough for the non-Jew to reach it while it is still day.

This case illustrates that *Beit Shammai*'s concern extends even to situations involving one's own *melacha* not at all — where the only issue is how things appear. *Beit Hillel*, by contrast, permits it entirely. In a case involving an actual Jew, one assumes the Jew will complete his activity before *Shabbos*; if not, the concern shifts to *lifnei iver*.

### Tanners & Cleaners

*Beit Shammai* continues: one may not give leather to a tanner, nor clothing to a non-Jewish cleaner, unless the work can be completed before *Shabbos*. *Beit Hillel* permits it — and indeed, *Beit Hillel* permits it even if the item is handed over immediately before sunset.

This case is arguably more striking than the non-Jew sale case, because here the non-Jew genuinely will be performing labor on one's behalf on *Shabbos* — laundering one's clothes, or working on one's leather. And yet *Beit Hillel* permits it. The question of why *Beit Hillel* is so permissive here is a significant one with direct *halachic* relevance, and it will require further analysis. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* adds that in his father's household — the *nasi*'s household — they would give white garments to a non-Jewish cleaner three full days before *Shabbos*, so that there would be ample time for the work to be completed by *Shabbos*, in keeping with the stricter *Beit Shammai* practice.

## Agreed Cases

### Oil & Wine Vats

Notwithstanding all their disagreements, both schools agree that one may lower the beam of an oil press and the circular weights of a wine vat before *Shabbos*, even though the pressing will continue throughout *Shabbos*. The process is familiar from archaeological sites throughout Israel: enormous beams or heavy stones are lowered onto crushed olives or grapes, and their weight slowly presses out the oil or juice over many hours. Both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* permit initiating this process before *Shabbos*.

This agreement immediately raises the central questions that will occupy the *Gemara*: what is *Beit Shammai*'s reason for being strict about all the earlier cases, and why does he permit this one? And more broadly, how do we permit the obvious *Shabbos* staples — keeping lights burning and keeping food cooking — given *Beit Shammai*'s concerns?

## Melacha of Lisha

### Rav Yosef Query

Before engaging the broader questions, the *Gemara* first addresses the local issue of the ink. The *Gemara* asks: who is the *tanna* who holds that putting water into the ink mixture constitutes *sheriyasan* — that is, that the very act of adding the water is itself the prohibited action? The underlying assumption of the question is that the activities *Beit Shammai* forbids initiating before *Shabbos* must be ones that, if performed on *Shabbos* itself, would constitute *melacha*. So the *Gemara* is asking: what *melacha* is involved when one adds water to the raw materials for ink?

This is a surprising question, because one might have expected the answer to be *tzvia* — dyeing — since the ink, after all, is a coloring substance. But the *Gemara* understands that one is not really dyeing anything when one makes ink; one is coloring water, not a textile or other material. The *Gemara* instead identifies the operative *melacha* as *lisha* — kneading. The logic is that kneading involves combining small discrete particles with liquid to produce a homogeneous mass. Making ink involves exactly this: combining some material with water to form a unified substance. The parallel to making dough is clear in structure, even if the end product is far more liquid.

*Rav Yosef* answers that the *tanna* must be *Rebbi*, and cites a *baraisa* to make his case.

### Rebbi Dispute

The *baraisa* cited by *Rav Yosef* states: if one person adds flour and another adds water, the one who added the water is *chayav* — liable — for the *melacha* of *lisha*. This is the position of *Rebbi*. *Rebbi Yosei*, however, disagrees: one is not liable until one actually kneads. Merely adding water to flour is insufficient; the kneading itself is the constitutive act.

The *Gemara* understands this debate to be directly relevant to the ink case, since when making ink one adds water but does not knead. If *Rebbi Yosei* requires actual kneading, then no *melacha* occurs by adding water alone, and *Beit Shammai*'s prohibition would lack a *melacha* basis. Therefore, the *tanna* who grounds the prohibition in a *melacha* concern must be *Rebbi*.

### Abaiye Resolution

*Abaye* challenges this reasoning. Perhaps, he suggests, *Rebbi Yosei* only requires kneading in the case of flour, since flour is normally made into dough through kneading — kneading is part of its natural process. But ink, which is not normally kneaded, may be different: perhaps even *Rebbi Yosei* would agree that adding water suffices to constitute *lisha* for a substance whose preparation does not ordinarily involve kneading.

The *Gemara* rejects this suggestion by citing a *baraisa* that explicitly discusses ashes and water: one who adds water to ashes is liable according to *Rebbi*, while *Rebbi Yosei the son of Rebbi Yehuda* requires kneading even there. This *baraisa* appears to demonstrate that even with a non-flour substance — one not normally kneaded — *Rebbi Yosei* still demands actual kneading for liability. The *Gemara* then considers whether *efer* in this *baraisa* might mean dirt (*afar*) rather than ashes, since dirt is something that is normally worked with water into clay or plaster and thus would normally be kneaded, making *Rebbi Yosei*'s requirement of kneading more understandable. But the *Gemara* notes that there are two separate *baraisos* — one says *efer* and one says *afar* — and *Rashi* explains that they derive from different schools (*Rebbi Chiya* and *Rebbi Oshaya* respectively), and so the identical word need not bear identical meaning across independent sources. They may both refer to dirt, with one simply using a less precise term.

The practical dimensions of this debate are considerable. The parameters of the *melacha* of *lisha* remain actively relevant: Does adding water to oatmeal constitute *lisha*? What about substances that one normally stirs but does not truly knead? The concept of *bar gibul* — whether the substance is of the type that is normally kneaded — is central. There is a question among the *rishonim* whether for substances not normally kneaded, liability arises earlier (as *Rebbi* holds) or whether, to the contrary, it is harder to transgress since the act is less defined. *Tosafos* cites other *Gemaras* suggesting that if a substance is not normally kneaded, one does not transgress the *melacha* at all.

One notable contemporary application: *Rav Moshe* was asked whether adding mayonnaise to tuna fish constitutes *lisha*. The argument in favor of permitting it was that the mayonnaise functions as an adhesive rather than a transformative liquid — it causes pieces to stick together without chemically changing them into a unified mass. There is a compelling logic to this distinction. Nevertheless, *Rav Moshe*'s ruling was to be stringent. A reasonable practice is to spread the mayonnaise directly onto the bread rather than mixing it into the tuna, thereby being *machmir* in accordance with *Rav Moshe*'s position while acknowledging the underlying logic of leniency.

## Permitted Activities

### Water & Incense

The *Gemara* cites a *baraisa* listing activities that may be initiated before *Shabbos* and permitted to continue throughout *Shabbos*. One may open an irrigation channel into one's garden immediately before dark on *erev Shabbos*, and the water may continue flowing into the garden throughout the entire day. One may place burning incense beneath clothing before *Shabbos*, and the clothes may continue absorbing the aroma throughout the day — a common practice before the availability of deodorants, whereby garments were perfumed by exposing them to fragrant smoke. Similarly, one may burn sulfur beneath silver vessels so that the blackened designs become visible; one may apply a salve to the eye; and one may apply a medicated bandage to a wound — all before *Shabbos*, with the healing or treatment continuing throughout *Shabbos*.

### Watermill Exception

The *baraisa* contains one notable exception: one may not place wheat into a water mill before *Shabbos* unless the grinding can be completed while it is still day. The obvious question is why this case differs from all the others in the *baraisa*, all of which are permitted.

*Rabbah* answers: *mipnei she-mashmi'a kol* — because the mill makes noise. *Rashi* explains that the noise publicizes the activity and constitutes a degradation of *Shabbos* — it is inappropriate for the day. This connects to a broader concept attested in the *Yerushalmi*, where quiet on *Shabbos* is itself presented as a significant value. The *Yerushalmi* even relates that one of the *tanna'im* heard knocking on a door on *Shabbos* and exclaimed that someone was violating *Shabbos* — so central was the association between *Shabbos* and silence. This approach does not appear to be the general orientation of the *Bavli*, however.

Even within the *Bavli*'s framework, there are two ways of understanding the *mashmi'a kol* concern. One reading is that the noise must be unusually loud — the grinding of a water mill impacts the entire surrounding area and creates a pervasive impression that commerce and labor are being conducted on *Shabbos*. A second, more specific reading is that the particular sound of a mill in operation signals business activity in a way that other ambient sounds do not.

The practical stakes of this question are real. *Tosafos* raises the question of whether we rule *l'halacha* in accordance with the concern of *mashmi'a kol*. If we do, then questions arise about the parameters. Setting a dishwasher on a timer to run on *Shabbos*, for instance — is this a violation of *mashmi'a kol*? *Rav Soloveitchik* apparently held it is not problematic. If the concern is strictly about volume, most dishwashers are not particularly loud. If the concern is about the experiential impression that *melacha* is being performed, that is a broader standard — though even then, the *Shabbos* clock that switches on lights has become normalized, and one does not experience that as the performance of *melacha*. The comparison between a household appliance and a water mill grinding through the night is not trivial; the mill was an industrial operation whose noise permeated an entire community in a way no modern domestic device approaches.

## Shevisas Keilim

### Rav Yosef Proposal

*Rav Yosef* challenges the *mashmi'a kol* explanation. Why invoke a noise-based rationale? Why not say instead that the water mill is forbidden because of *shevisas keilim*? The *Gemara* cites a *baraisa* in support: the verse *u-ve-chol asher amarti aleikhem tishameru* — "and everything I have told you, observe" — appears in a context where the *Torah* has commanded rest for one's animals. The word *u-ve-chol*, "and everything," is understood to broaden that obligation, including a requirement that one's vessels also rest on *Shabbos*.

If *shevisas keilim* is a valid biblical concern, then *Rav Yosef* proposes that this, rather than *mashmi'a kol*, is why the water mill is forbidden. The water mill is a vessel in motion performing labor on *Shabbos* — paradigmatically subject to *shevisas keilim*.

*Abaye* immediately pushes back: if *shevisas keilim* is invoked to explain the water mill prohibition, and if we are operating within the framework of *Beit Hillel* — as we presumably are, since we rule like *Beit Hillel* — then one must explain how *Beit Hillel* permits all the other cases in the *baraisa* and in the *mishnah*, all of which involve vessels of some kind. To say *Beit Hillel* holds of *shevisas keilim* creates an enormous explanatory burden.

*Rav Yosef* attempts to resolve this by defining *shevisas keilim* narrowly: the prohibition applies only when the vessel is physically in motion — when it has moving parts actively performing work. A bowl holding incense, or an oven holding flax, is passive; the vessel is stationary and is not itself performing the *melacha*. The water mill, by contrast, has a wheel in continuous rotation — it is actively working. Under this reading, *Beit Hillel* accepts *shevisas keilim* in its narrow form and that is why the mill is forbidden, while everything else is permitted because those vessels are inert.

The *Gemara* works through this framework case by case. The incense and the sulfur involve no moving vessel — just fire and the material itself. The flax in the oven: the oven is stationary, no vessel moves. The animal traps: *Rashi* explains that the reference is to stationary traps such as a hook (*lechi*) or a net — the fish bites the hook, the hook does not move; the net is spread but does not itself move to capture the fish. Under this very narrow reading, *Beit Hillel*'s *shevisas keilim* can be maintained while explaining virtually every permitted case. The one case that does not fit this framework — the moving wheel of the water mill — is exactly what the *shevisas keilim* prohibition targets.

### Conclusion

The *Gemara* then cites the view of *Rav Oshaya* in the name of *Rav Assi*: who is the *tanna* that holds *shevisas keilim* is *d'oraisa*? It is *Beit Shammai* — not *Beit Hillel*. This resolves the difficulty entirely. *Beit Shammai* holds *shevisas keilim* biblically, and prohibits all the cases in the *mishnah* on that basis — whether the vessel is moving or stationary, since even a passive vessel participating in a *melacha* is subject to the obligation. *Beit Hillel* does not hold of *shevisas keilim* at all. Under this reading, *Beit Hillel* permits all those cases freely, and the water mill is a separate matter entirely — forbidden not because of *shevisas keilim* but because of *mashmi'a kol*.

This is the clean resolution: *Beit Shammai* and *shevisas keilim*; *Beit Hillel* and *mashmi'a kol* as a distinct, limited rabbinic concern for the water mill specifically.

### Appearances View

*Tosafos* notes that before the *Gemara* introduced *shevisas keilim*, there was a different, simpler way of understanding *Beit Shammai*'s position — one that the *Gemara* was implicitly operating with initially. Under that reading, *Beit Shammai*'s concern is purely rabbinic: it looks as though one is performing *melacha* on *Shabbos*, or is involved in *melacha* being performed on *Shabbos*, whether through one's own vessel or through a non-Jew acting on one's behalf. This approach is more internally consistent with the non-Jew cases — the tanner and the cleaner — where there is no vessel of one's own involved at all, and the only issue is one of appearances. The *shevisas keilim* framework, by contrast, struggles to account for those cases without additional machinery.

So *Beit Shammai*'s position admits of two quite different characterizations: either a rabbinic, appearances-based concern of general application, or a biblical *shevisas keilim* obligation. These represent fundamentally different levels of stringency with very different legal implications.

## Cooking & Vessels

### Mafkir Solution

If *Beit Shammai* holds *shevisas keilim* as a biblical prohibition, a pressing question arises: how does *Beit Shammai* permit keeping oil lamps burning through *Shabbos*, or food cooking in a pot from *erev Shabbos*? All of these involve vessels performing work on *Shabbos*. The *Gemara* lists the cases: a barrel (*gigis*) in which beer ferments throughout *Shabbos*; an oil lamp (*ner*) burning throughout *Shabbos*; a pot (*kdeira*) of food cooking through *Shabbos*; a spit (*shaphud*) on which meat roasts. How can *Beit Shammai* permit any of these?

The *Gemara*'s answer is striking: *de-mafkir lehu* — one must declare these vessels *hefker* before *Shabbos*. By relinquishing ownership of one's oven, one's pots, and one's lamps before *Shabbos* begins, one is no longer obligated to ensure their rest — *shevisas keilim* applies only to vessels one owns.
