This is, the *Gemara* concedes, an extraordinary implication: every *erev Shabbos*, under *Beit Shammai*'s view, one would have to formally renounce ownership of one's cooking vessels and lamps. *Tosafos* observes that this creates a similarly interesting question about *shevisas behemto* — the biblical obligation for one's animals to rest — and whether a parallel *mafkir* move could be used to circumvent that obligation, though *Tosafos* rejects that application.

This is a position the *Gemara* has clearly painted itself into, and *Tosafos* points out that the alternative reading — that *Beit Shammai*'s concern is purely rabbinic — avoids all of this difficulty. Under the appearances-based rabbinic reading, one can draw reasonable distinctions between cases that look problematic and cases (like candles and cooking pots) that have been normalized as part of *Shabbos* life.

### Legumes Braita

The *Gemara* asks whose position is represented by the following *baraisa*: a woman may not fill a pot with legumes such as *asasiyos* and *turmasin* and place it in the oven on *erev Shabbos* at nightfall, because these will require the entire duration of *Shabbos* to cook. If she did so, the food is forbidden after *Shabbos* for the amount of time it would take to prepare — since it was the product of *melacha* performed on *Shabbos*, one must wait that duration before benefiting from it. Similarly, a baker may not fill a barrel with water on *erev Shabbos* at nightfall, if the water will be used in a process that continues into *Shabbos*. The question is whether this *baraisa* reflects *Beit Shammai* alone.

### Stirring Fear

The *Gemara* answers: *afilu teima Beit Hillel* — this can even represent *Beit Hillel*. *Beit Hillel*'s reason for forbidding these particular cases is a distinct concern: *gezeira shema yichateh ba-gechalim* — a rabbinic decree lest one come to stir the coals. This is the principle that will dominate the entire third *perek* of *Shabbos*, and we are here receiving an early preview.

The concern is this: if food is placed on a fire before *Shabbos* in a state that is not yet fully cooked, one may become anxious during *Shabbos* about whether it will be ready in time. That anxiety may cause one to forget that it is *Shabbos* and unconsciously stir or adjust the fire to accelerate cooking. This concern applies even according to *Beit Hillel* — it has nothing to do with *shevisas keilim* — and it is the reason the *baraisa* prohibits placing these particular items in the oven so close to *Shabbos*.

This is also why the *mishnah* in the next *perek* will specify conditions under which food may or may not be left on a flame before *Shabbos*, and why the requirement of a *blech* (a covering placed over the flame) exists in practice: the *blech* addresses this stirring concern by creating a physical and psychological reminder that one should not adjust the fire.

The parallel question is symmetrical: given that the stirring concern applies to *Beit Hillel*, how does *Beit Shammai* permit cooking from *erev Shabbos* at all — given that *Beit Shammai* additionally holds *shevisas keilim*? According to the *shevisas keilim* view, *Beit Shammai* must use the *mafkir* solution for the vessels; the stirring concern must then be addressed separately, presumably through whatever mechanism *Beit Hillel* also uses, such as a *blech*.

## Blech Exceptions

### Raw & Cooked

Having established that the primary operative concern for cooking from *erev Shabbos* is the fear of stirring the coals, the *Gemara* now delineates when that concern applies and when it does not. The *Gemara* states: if one has a pot of raw meat — *kdeira chayasa* — one may place it in the oven on *erev Shabbos* even at nightfall without a *blech*. Why? Because raw meat will not be ready to eat that same evening; it will cook only by the following morning. Since one knows the food will not be ready for a very long time, one is not anxious about it, does not think about it, and will not come to stir the fire.

Conversely, if food is already fully cooked — *bashul shapir* — it also does not require a *blech*. There is no concern about stirring when the food is already done.

### Partially Cooked

The only situation that does require a *blech* is food that is partially cooked — *bashul ve-lo bashul*. Food in that intermediate state will finish cooking relatively soon, and one is likely to be anxious about whether it is ready. That anxiety is precisely what the rabbis feared would lead to forgetting it is *Shabbos* and stirring the coals. The *blech* requirement applies specifically, and only, to this intermediate category.

This preview of the third *perek* carries real *halachic* implications. A *cholent* placed on a fire totally raw before *Shabbos* genuinely does not raise the stirring concern — whatever one's practice regarding whether a crockpot requires a *blech* or what modifications a crockpot requires, the raw-food exception is substantively significant.

### Mixed Cooking Times

The *Gemara* extends this analysis to a mixed case: if one has a pot in the intermediate partially-cooked state — which would ordinarily require a *blech* — but then throws in a single raw bone, one need not cover the flame. Since that one piece requires a long time to cook, one's focus shifts to that long-cooking item, and the anxiety about imminent readiness dissipates.

The *Rambam* goes further and holds that throwing in even a raw vegetable — something that would cook quickly — suffices as a *heker*, a distinguishing mark, to eliminate the stirring concern. We do not rule in accordance with the *Rambam* on this point. Nevertheless, the underlying principle is that wherever one element of the pot will require an extended cooking time, the concern of anxious stirring is attenuated even with respect to the other contents.

## Meat Types & Sealing

### Goat Sealed

The *Gemara* now introduces a further series of distinctions based on both the type of meat being cooked and the physical configuration of the oven. If one is cooking goat meat in a sealed oven — where the oven door or opening has been plastered shut — this is permitted. Two independent factors operate here to reduce the likelihood of opening the oven and stirring: first, the seal itself must be broken, which serves as a reminder; and second, goat meat is particularly susceptible to being harmed by exposure to air, so one would naturally be reluctant to open the oven door.

### Ram Unsealed

If, however, one is cooking ram meat in an unsealed oven, neither protective factor is present. Ram meat is not particularly sensitive to air, so there is no disinclination to open the door; and since the oven is unsealed, there is no physical barrier or reminder. This case is therefore forbidden.

### Mixed Cases

The intermediate cases — goat meat in an unsealed oven, or ram meat in a sealed oven — where exactly one of the two protective factors is present, are subject to a dispute between *Rav Ashi* and *Rav Yirmiyah mi-Difti*. *Rav Ashi* holds that as long as one factor is present, the concern is sufficiently addressed and the arrangement is permitted. *Rav Yirmiyah mi-Difti* holds it is forbidden.

A further difficulty is raised against *Rav Ashi*: if even a single protective factor suffices, how does one ever forbid roasting meat before *Shabbos*? The *mishnah* in the next *perek* will state that one may roast meat, onion, and egg before *Shabbos* only if they will be fully cooked while it is still day — implying a concern about stirring even for meat in an oven. According to *Rav Ashi*, one should always have at least some disinclination to open the oven door, so why is any roasting case ever problematic?

### Coals vs. Ovens

The *Gemara* resolves this by distinguishing the type of cooking. The case of the *mishnah* refers to meat roasting slowly on coals on the ground — not inside a closed oven. When cooking on open coals at ground level, the entire situation is exposed: there is no door to deter opening, no seal to break, and the slow-burning coals naturally invite adjustment. This is precisely the kind of setting where the stirring concern is most acute and where even *Rav Ashi* would agree that the prohibition applies. Finally, *Ravina* notes that a raw gourd is analogous to goat meat, since gourd is particularly susceptible to harm from air exposure; one would therefore be highly unlikely to open the oven when a gourd is cooking, and the arrangement is accordingly permitted.

## Summary & Synthesis

### Three Explanations

To summarize the analysis of this *daf*: there are three distinct explanatory frameworks that have emerged for understanding the restrictions on initiating activities before *Shabbos* that continue into *Shabbos*.

The first and simplest is a rabbinic, appearances-based concern: activities that look like *melacha* being done on *Shabbos* — whether through one's own vessels or through a non-Jew — are prohibited by *Beit Shammai* on those grounds. This is a general rabbinic concern with no specific biblical hook, and it accounts naturally for the full range of cases in the *mishnah*, including the non-Jew cases where no vessel of the Jew's is involved at all.

The second is *shevisas keilim* as a biblical obligation. Under this reading, *Beit Shammai* holds that one's vessels must not perform labor on *Shabbos*, parallel to the obligation for one's animals and servants. This generates significant complications: one must declare one's cooking vessels and lamps *hefker* before *Shabbos* to permit their continued operation, a striking and demanding implication.

The third is *mashmi'a kol* — the concern about creating noise that gives the impression of labor being conducted on *Shabbos*. This concern, which *Beit Hillel* accepts, explains the single exception for the water mill in the *baraisa* permitting various preparatory activities.

### Stirring Anxiety

Underlying all of this, and entirely independent of the *Beit Shammai* versus *Beit Hillel* debate, is the concern about stirring the fire — *gezeira shema yichateh ba-gechalim* — which applies according to *Beit Hillel* as well, and which will be the dominant theme of the third *perek*. This concern is not triggered when food is completely raw (no anxiety, long cooking time ahead), nor when food is already fully cooked (no anxiety, nothing left to do). It applies specifically to partially cooked food, where one's anticipation of imminent completion creates the risk of impulsive intervention. Exceptions exist when the physical configuration of the cooking — a sealed oven, susceptible meat, slow coals — makes it unlikely that one would disturb the arrangement. These principles, previewed here on 18b, will receive full and detailed treatment as the tractate continues.

# Shabbat 19

## Selling to Non-Jews

### Beis Shammai's Sale Ban

The daf opens at the bottom of 18b, where a *Tanu Rabbanan* introduces a series of restrictions attributed to Beis Shammai concerning transactions with non-Jews on *erev Shabbos*. This discussion follows naturally from the preceding material about beginning a *melacha* before Shabbos and having it continue — whether on the basis of *shevisas keilim* or some form of rabbinic decree — and the various exceptions that Beis Hillel and even Beis Shammai themselves acknowledged.

The *Baraisa* states: *Beis Shammai omrim v'lo yimkor adam cheftzo l'nochri* — Beis Shammai prohibits selling one's objects to a non-Jew on *erev Shabbos*, and similarly forbids lending to him or giving him a gift, *ella k'dei she-yagi'a l'beiso* — unless there is sufficient time for the non-Jew to reach his home before Shabbos begins.

### Baraisa Definition

The *Mishnah* had used the phrase *l'makom karov* — to a nearby place — which the *Baraisa* now clarifies more precisely: the non-Jew must have enough time to reach his home. Beis Hillel, for its part, requires only that he reach *bayis hasamuch lachoma* — the house at the wall at the edge of the city. This formulation assumes that the non-Jew is traveling to a different city to bring the sold item home, which reflects a social reality in which cities tended to be either predominantly Jewish or predominantly non-Jewish, making it quite natural to assume that a non-Jewish buyer would be departing for a different location.

### Rabbi Akiva Leniency

Rabbi Akiva presents a more lenient position: *k'dei she-yeitzei mi-pesach beiso* — it is sufficient that the non-Jew departs from the seller's doorway. Rabbi Yosi bar Yehuda clarifies that Rabbi Akiva is not introducing a third position but rather explaining what Beis Hillel's position actually was: *lo ba Rabbi Akiva ella l'faresh divrei Beis Hillel* — he came only to articulate Beis Hillel's view. In that reading, Beis Hillel was always as lenient as Rabbi Akiva describes, requiring no more than that the non-Jew leave the house. This coheres with the *Mishnah*'s own formulation, where Beis Hillel simply permits the transaction without specifying distance — a rendering far closer to Rabbi Akiva's version than to the *Tosefta*'s stricter language requiring the non-Jew to reach his home.

### Maris Ayin vs Process

What is the underlying concern driving these restrictions? The situation here is not analogous to *shevisas keilim* in any straightforward sense, since the object has been sold — it now belongs to the non-Jew, and what he does with his own property is no longer the seller's concern. Rather, the concern appears to be one of appearances: a non-Jew departing on *erev Shabbos* carrying an object that formerly belonged to a Jew creates the impression, for any onlooker, that he is handling and transporting it on behalf of the Jew on Shabbos.

This is the thrust of *maris ayin* — not that we distrust any particular individual, but that perceptions are a social reality, and people naturally draw conclusions from appearances without always extending the benefit of the doubt. As one might observe, *maris ayin* assumes precisely that people will form natural inferences and that the experience of Shabbos is shaped in part by those visible realities around us. Beis Shammai is concerned about this; Beis Hillel is considerably more lenient, and it is Beis Hillel's view that we rule by in practice.

### Chametz Sale Case

A parallel *Baraisa* makes the concern more precise. Beis Shammai prohibits selling one's *chametz* to a non-Jew before Pesach unless one knows that he has enough time to finish it before Pesach arrives: *Beis Shammai omrim lo yimkor adam chametzo lenachri ela im kein yodeia bo sheyichleh kodem ha-Pesach*. Beis Hillel, by contrast, permits the sale for as long as a Jew himself may eat the *chametz*: *kol zman she-mutar le-echol mutar limkor*. Rabbi Yehuda further specifies that Babylonian *kutach* — a dip containing breadcrumbs — may not be sold for thirty days before Pesach, since such a spread is consumed gradually over time, consistent with Beis Shammai's position.

This *chametz* case is telling, because it is difficult to sustain a pure *maris ayin* argument here. When a non-Jew eats *chametz* in his own home, there is no obvious visual impression that the Jew is involved — the *chametz* belongs to the non-Jew, sits in the non-Jew's home, and is consumed by the non-Jew. Yet Beis Shammai still objects.

Combining the two cases — the sale of objects and the sale of *chametz* — suggests that Beis Shammai's concern is not primarily one of appearances but of process responsibility. When I sell you something on *erev Shabbos*, I have initiated a process that culminates in you carrying it through Shabbos. When I sell you *chametz* before Pesach, I have initiated a process that culminates in your eating *chametz* — which is mine — on Pesach. Even though you are a non-Jew who bears no personal prohibition, and even though the object now belongs to you, I set this in motion. This reasoning closely parallels the concern about beginning a *melacha* on *erev Shabbos* that continues into Shabbos — whether the dyeing, the ink-making, or the other processes discussed earlier in the *masechta*. There too the underlying concern is not merely one of appearances but of being the initiating party in a process that unfolds across Shabbos.

### Feeding in Courtyard

The *Gemara* at the top of 19a adds a case that illuminates the limits of this process-responsibility principle. *Tanu Rabbanan*: one may place food before a dog in the courtyard on Shabbos itself. If the dog picks it up and carries it out, one is not responsible — *ein nizkakim lo*. Similarly, one may place food before a non-Jew in the courtyard — a *reshus hayachid* — and if he takes it and leaves, one bears no further responsibility.

Tosafos notes that this ruling holds even according to Beis Shammai. Why? Because the critical distinction is the nature of the process one has initiated. When one sells a non-Jew an object on *erev Shabbos* and he does not live nearby, the natural, foreseeable, and intended endpoint of that transaction is the non-Jew carrying the object home — including through Shabbos. The process one began leads directly and obviously into Shabbos. But when one invites a non-Jew into one's courtyard and places food before him, one has begun a process directed entirely toward eating in place, right there. If the non-Jew then takes the food and carries it home, that is a separate, secondary act — not the culmination of what one initiated. Responsibility ends with the first process.

The *Gemara* questions why both cases — the dog and the non-Jew — are needed, since they seem identical. The answer: one might have thought that because you bear an obligation to feed your dog, perhaps leniency applies to your pet uniquely, and the ruling by the non-Jew, where you have no such obligation, would be stricter. The *Gemara* teaches that this makes no difference — in both cases, since the process you initiated was intended to culminate within the courtyard, what happens afterward is not your responsibility.

Taken together, these rulings support a consistent theme running through Beis Shammai's positions throughout this section of the *masechta*: beginning a process that continues into Shabbos — even when the continuation is carried out by a non-Jew acting on his own — implicates the one who began it. The exceptions arise either when the continuation on Shabbos would not itself constitute a biblical violation, or when what happens on Shabbos is genuinely disconnected from what one initiated beforehand.

## Renting Objects

### Rental Prohibition

The *Gemara* continues: *lo yaskir adam keilav lenachri be'erev Shabbos* — one may not rent one's utensils to a non-Jew on *erev Shabbos*. On Wednesday or Thursday, however, this is permissible. This prohibition is presumably attributed to Beis Shammai.

### Sechar Shabbat Issue

Tosafos raises an important analytic point: one cannot explain this prohibition on the basis of *shevisas keilim* as Beis Shammai understands it. Were *shevisas keilim* the operative concern, renting one's utensils on Wednesday or Thursday would be equally prohibited, since the vessels remain one's own property regardless of when the rental begins, and one's vessel performing labor on Shabbos would be just as problematic whether the rental started Friday or Wednesday. Tosafos adds that the same logic would apply to renting an animal — which everyone agrees implicates *shevisas behema* — but that concern applies equally no matter how far in advance the animal is rented.

Tosafos concludes that this is a ruling consistent with Beis Hillel, which does not hold of *shevisas keilim* for utensils — or alternatively that the discussion concerns garments, for which *shevisas keilim* would not be applicable. Given this, Tosafos identifies the operative concern as *sechar Shabbat*: the prohibition against earning income for work done on Shabbos. If one rents a utensil to a non-Jew immediately before Shabbos, the rent received is payment specifically for Shabbos use, making one a beneficiary of Shabbos labor — which is problematic. If the rental begins on Wednesday or Thursday, the payment encompasses work performed across multiple days, and the Shabbos component is absorbed into a broader arrangement that does not constitute *sechar Shabbat*.

Rashi, for his part, explains the prohibition in terms of appearances: renting a utensil on Friday afternoon creates the impression that one is lending it specifically for use on Shabbos. Even so, since it is the non-Jew doing the work for himself and not for the Jewish owner, this is most naturally understood as a Beis Shammai concern — not based on *shevisas keilim*, but rather on the principle of beginning a process that leads into Shabbos. If one rents a hoe to a non-Jew on Friday afternoon and he uses it on Shabbos, one has initiated a process whose natural continuation is Shabbos labor. If the rental began on Wednesday or Thursday, that causal link to Shabbos is sufficiently attenuated that one is no longer understood as having begun the process that culminates in Shabbos work.

## Sending Letters

### Letter Ban

The *Gemara* continues: *ein meshalechin igeret beyad nochri be'erev Shabbat* — one may not send a letter via a non-Jew on *erev Shabbos*. On Wednesday or Thursday it is permissible.

This case is more immediately obvious than the cases of selling or renting, because here the non-Jew is carrying the letter explicitly for the sender. Even if one did not explicitly instruct him to carry it on Shabbos — and even if the non-Jew theoretically had the option to complete delivery before Shabbos — the practical reality is that one is directly commissioning an act of *melacha* on one's own behalf.

The *Gemara* adds: *amru alav al Rabbi Yose HaKohen — v'amrei lah Rabbi Yose HaChassid — shelo nimtza ktav yado beyad nochri me'olam* — it was said of him, referred to as Rabbi Yose HaChassid, that his handwriting was never found in the hands of a non-Jew. He maintained this stringency absolutely, even when giving a letter well before *erev Shabbos*, because there was always the possibility that the non-Jew might still be carrying his letter on Shabbos. The language here is significant: *ktav yado* — his handwriting — highlighting that one's personal script is in some sense an extension of oneself, making one's participation in any *melacha* performed while carrying the letter especially palpable. This gives the letter case a qualitative dimension beyond the selling and renting cases: not only is the non-Jew acting on the sender's behalf, but the sender's own identity is physically present in the process being carried out on Shabbos.

A practical question arises: does this apply to placing mail in a postal box on Friday? The analysis of such cases is typically conducted through the framework of *amira le-goy* — the prohibition against instructing a non-Jew to perform *melacha* on Shabbos — rather than through the specifically Beis Shammai framework of process-initiation that governs much of this section of the *Gemara*. Depositing mail in a postal box on Friday raises questions about whether the carrier is performing work for the individual sender or for the postal service as an institution, and whether the sender has truly "instructed" anyone to do anything. Sending express mail for next-day delivery on Friday would clearly be more problematic. These remain subjects of significant halachic discussion.

## Renting Objects (II)

### Fixed Price Criteria

Returning to the framework of the *Mishnah*'s earlier discussion of giving items to a non-Jewish launderer, the *Gemara* makes explicit two criteria that permit such arrangements: first, the fee must be fixed — *katzatz damim* — rather than calculated hourly; second, the non-Jew must have a theoretical ability to complete the work at some time other than Shabbos. Both conditions must be met.

The rationale for the fixed-price requirement is that if one pays by the hour, then to the extent that the non-Jew works on Shabbos and one compensates him for that specific Shabbos hour, one is effectively paying for — and thereby participating in — Shabbos labor. A fixed fee for the job, by contrast, severs this direct linkage: the non-Jew is doing the work on his own account, for an agreed price, and the question of when he chooses to do it is, in principle, his own.

The requirement that there exist theoretical ability to perform the work outside of Shabbos is equally important, though its application can be subtle. If one drops off a car at a mechanic on Friday and picks it up Saturday night, with no realistic window for the work to have been done other than during Shabbos, that raises concern regardless of the fixed-price arrangement. What counts as adequate theoretical availability is a genuine question — whether the mechanic could, in principle, have rearranged his schedule to complete the work Saturday night after Shabbos matters, even if practically he would not.

These same principles apply, with heightened scrutiny, when the work is performed on one's property. Because construction on a home is visible and public — passersby see workers on the property on Shabbos — there is an additional concern that it appears as though they are doing labor for the Jewish owner. Tosafos addresses this and notes that even Rabbeinu Tam, who maintained in theory that construction work subject to the standard fixed-price criteria could be permitted, did not rely on his own ruling when it came to building his own home. He was more *machmir* in practice. The practical complications are also significant: workers are commonly paid hourly at least at the individual laborer level, even when a contractor charges a fixed fee for the overall project.

The interaction between these two criteria invites close analysis. One might argue, for instance, that a first-class postage stamp constitutes a fixed price for the service of letter delivery. However, the second criterion — that the carrier have realistic ability to deliver other than on Shabbos — is more doubtful, especially if the relevant pickup or delivery cycle falls exclusively within Shabbos. Additionally, the relationship between the sender and the individual carrier is mediated through a large institution, raising the further question of whether the non-Jewish worker performing the actual delivery is doing so for the sender or for the postal service as his employer.

## Sending Letters (II)

### Fixed Price & Timing

The *Baraisa* states explicitly: *ein meshalchin igros beyad nochri erev Shabbos ela im kein katzatz lo damim* — one may not send letters via a non-Jew on *erev Shabbos* unless a fixed price has been set. The *Gemara* then asks how to read the additional requirement — found in the positions of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel — that the non-Jew must have time to reach either his home or the house at the edge of the next city. Is this an independent requirement, or does it apply only when no fixed price has been set?

Rav Sheshes clarifies: when no fixed price has been set — that is, when the non-Jew is effectively being paid by the hour — then the additional time requirement applies, because without a fixed price, the Jew bears a more direct responsibility for the Shabbos labor being performed on his behalf. Beis Shammai requires that the non-Jew have time to reach his home, and Beis Hillel requires that he reach the house at the edge of the next city. With a fixed price, these distance requirements do not apply in the same way, since the non-Jew carries the letter on his own account.

The *Gemara* then addresses a tension with a *Tosefta* that appears to prohibit sending letters even beyond the distance threshold. The resolution is: *ha d'kviei doar b'masa, ha d'la kviei doar b'masa* — one case involves a city with a fixed postal office, and the other does not. In a city with a postal station, the carrier need only deposit the letter at the central office, and recipients will collect their mail from there. In that case, having time to reach the next city suffices. Where there is no such postal office, the carrier must search out the addressee individually, meaning that even arriving in the next city does not end his active labor on the sender's behalf — he continues carrying the letter for the Jew throughout his search. In that case, more time is required.

Notably, even Beis Hillel in this context acknowledges some concern about sending letters on *erev Shabbos*, particularly because here the non-Jew is unambiguously performing a service for the Jew — carrying his correspondence — which makes the Shabbos labor more direct than in the cases of selling objects or feeding a non-Jew in one's courtyard. This places the letter case at the intersection of the Beis Shammai process-initiation concern and the more universally applicable prohibition of *amira le-goy*.

## Boats & Sieges

### Three-Day Boat Rule

A new *Baraisa* introduces the rule concerning sea travel: *ein mafligin bisefina pachos mi-gimmel yamim kodem le-Shabbos* — one may not set out on a boat journey fewer than three days before Shabbos. This is a notably stricter standard than the Wednesday-Thursday threshold that governed the preceding cases of selling, renting, and sending letters.

The reason for the heightened threshold reflects the different nature of the process. A transatlantic or extended sea voyage is not an activity that is "started" in any proximate sense on *erev Shabbos*; it is an ongoing multi-day process, and if one embarks within three days of Shabbos, one's departure is sufficiently close in time that the voyage as a whole is conceptually connected to the Shabbos it will span. One has begun a journey that will be continuing on Shabbos, and because it is fundamentally a much more extended and continuous process than renting a hoe or selling an object, the window of temporal responsibility is correspondingly wider. Some *Rishonim* offer additional explanations: that it takes several days for a traveler to become acclimated to the sea and avoid seasickness that would ruin *oneg Shabbos*; or that embarking too close to Shabbos risks placing oneself in a *makom sakanah* — a situation of physical danger — which would then necessitate *chillul Shabbos*. The three-day threshold corresponds to the principle that more than three days before Shabbos, one is not yet within the conceptual orbit of the coming Shabbos and need not be anticipating its implications.

### Mitzvah & Local Trips

The restriction applies only to discretionary travel: *bameh devarim amurim — l'dvar harashus*, but for a *d'var mitzvah* — a journey undertaken for a religious obligation — one may set out even on *erev Shabbos* itself. The fact that a *d'var mitzvah* overrides this concern demonstrates that the underlying prohibition is rabbinic in nature, since biblical prohibitions are not set aside for the sake of a *mitzvah* in this way, or at minimum that whatever concern animates the rule yields to the weight of religious obligation.

Rabbi, speaking in the *Baraisa*, holds that even in the case of a *d'var mitzvah*, one should stipulate with the captain that he will not navigate the vessel on Shabbos — understanding full well that this is something of a nominal arrangement, since the captain is not actually bound to honor it and the boat will in practice continue sailing. Rabban Gamliel disagrees and holds that no such stipulation is necessary. As for short trips — the *Baraisa* cites the example of sailing from Tzor to Tzidan, a brief journey that would typically occur in connection with the *erev Shabbos* market — these are permitted even on Friday, since they do not constitute the kind of extended process that raises the concern of being bound to a Shabbos-spanning voyage.

The underlying logic of the three-day rule is that it is only when an ongoing process begins within what one might call the Shabbos-adjacent period — the three days immediately preceding Shabbos — that one bears responsibility for what that process entails over Shabbos itself.

### Siege Warfare

The *Gemara* draws a parallel case: *ein tzarin al ayarot shel nochrim pachos mi-gimmel yamim kodem l'Shabbos* — one may not lay siege to a non-Jewish city fewer than three days before Shabbos. The same three-day rule applies, and for a closely related reason: once a siege begins, military exigency will require continuing operations on Shabbos. Rather than creating a situation in which *chillul Shabbos* becomes necessary, one should not initiate the siege within three days of Shabbos.

However — and this is a crucial qualification — *v'im hitchilu ein mafsikin*: once the siege has begun, one does not interrupt it, and it continues even through Shabbos. Shammai himself is cited as deriving this from the verse *ki tatzur el ir yamim rabbim* — "when you besiege a city many days" — *ad ridetah*, until it falls: *afilu b'Shabbat* — even on Shabbos. Military operations once underway implicate *pikuach nefesh* throughout, and so continuation through Shabbos is not merely permitted but required. This parallel illuminates the logic of the boat case: the concern in both instances is not about what happens on Shabbos itself — war and genuine danger override Shabbos entirely — but about deliberately placing oneself in a situation where those overrides will be necessary.

### Garment Practices

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is cited in the *Mishnah*: the house of Rabban Gamliel would give white garments to the launderer three days before Shabbos, while colored garments could be given even on *erev Shabbos* itself, since they require less effort to clean. This stringent practice aligned with the Beis Shammai position, though the house of Rabban Gamliel identified with Beis Hillel — illustrating that personal piety sometimes led individuals to adopt the stricter view even when they did not rule that way for others.

The *Tanya* cites Rabbi Tzadok confirming this as the practice of Rabban Gamliel's household. The *Gemara* derives from this practice the principle that white garments are harder to launder than colored ones — a practical reality that becomes explicit halachic reasoning. The *Gemara* then relates that Abaye, when bringing a colored garment to a launderer who quoted him the same price as for white garments, invoked this very teaching: since the Rabbis had already established that white garments require more effort, the launderer was not entitled to charge the same rate for colored garments.

The *Gemara* appends a practical piece of advice from Abaye: when giving a garment to a launderer, measure it first and measure it again upon return. If it is larger than when given, the launderer stretched and damaged it; if smaller, he shrank it. The competence and honesty of the craftsman matter, and one should protect oneself accordingly.

## Continuing Processes

### Beis Shammai Logic

The *Gemara* now addresses the *Mishnah*'s ruling that both Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel agree that one may place a beam on olives or grapes before Shabbos and allow the press to continue operating through Shabbos — *uve-shavin elu va-elu sheto'anin*. This is noteworthy because Beis Shammai is generally the one prohibiting the initiation of such processes. Why does Beis Shammai agree here?

The *Gemara* poses the question directly: what is the reason Beis Shammai issued a *gezeira* against all the other processes — dyeing, ink-making, and the like — but not against placing the beam on olives and grapes? Tosafos flags that the *Gemara*'s formulation here is significant: it says *gezeira*, not *shevisas keilim*. This confirms that Beis Shammai's concern throughout this section is properly understood as a rabbinic decree against beginning processes on *erev Shabbos* that will continue into Shabbos — not as the more far-reaching principle of *shevisas keilim* — and the *gezeira* is grounded in the concern that either one will come to fiddle with the process on Shabbos itself and commit a *melacha*, or that one will reason from the permissibility of a process begun just before sunset to the permissibility of beginning it on Shabbos directly.

The answer the *Gemara* gives is that the *gezeira* was issued only for processes that, were one to perform them on Shabbos directly, would constitute a biblical *melacha* requiring a *chatat*. Where the act of doing it oneself on Shabbos would not rise to the level of a *melacha de'orayta*, Beis Shammai saw no basis for the decree.

### Olives & Grapes

This leads to the question: why would squeezing olives and grapes not be a *melacha de'orayta*? Squeezing — *sechita* — is a classic biblical prohibition, and olives and grapes are its paradigm cases. The answer lies in the prior crushing. Before the olives or grapes are placed in the press, they have already been crushed — stamped, milled, or otherwise broken down. At that point, the juices will emerge on their own. Placing a beam on them merely accelerates a process that is already underway naturally. The *Gemara* frames the question: who is the *Tanna* who holds that anything that comes about by itself — *de'ati mimmela* — is acceptable?

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina answers: it is Rabbi Yishmael, based on the following *Mishnah*: if one has crushed garlic, unripe grapes (*boser*), or unripe wheat stalks (*malilot*) before Shabbos, Rabbi Yishmael says one may finish the process after dark on Saturday night, while Rabbi Akiva says one may not. The permissibility of consuming the juices that run off naturally after crushing, in Rabbi Yishmael's view, reflects the underlying position that were one to squeeze them oneself at that stage, it would not constitute a biblical violation — because the crushing has already fundamentally completed the productive work, and what remains is merely the natural emergence of liquid.

### Honey Debate

Rabbi Ami, however, suggests the ruling derives instead from Rabbi Elazar, based on a different case: *challot devash she-riskan mibe'od yom* — loaves of honeycomb crushed before Shabbos, from which honey runs off on Shabbos itself. The *Mishnah* there rules that the honey is forbidden; Rabbi Elazar permits it. Rabbi Elazar's leniency implies that even were one to squeeze the honeycomb directly, it would not be a biblical *melacha*, and therefore one need not prohibit benefiting from honey that flows on its own.

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina, however, declines to derive from the honey case. His reasoning: *hatam hu di-me'ikara ochla u-lesof ochla* — honey begins as a food and remains a food even as a liquid; its halachic classification does not change. But in the case of olives and grapes: *me-ikara ochla ve-hashta mashka* — what begins as food ends as a liquid. This transformation is halachically significant. The prohibition of *sechita* is defined in terms of extracting liquid from food. When the endpoint is liquid, the act of squeezing is more clearly a full *melacha*; when the endpoint is still categorized as food — as with honey, which retains the status of a food despite its liquid consistency — the prohibition applies differently. Moreover, squeezing honey from honeycomb is structurally different from squeezing juice from olives: the honey sits interspersed within the wax rather than being absorbed inside a cellular structure, and the act of pressing it out is less clearly analogous to classic *sechita*.

Therefore, Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina maintains that one cannot prove from the honey case that squeezing olives and grapes after crushing would be biblically exempt. A proof must come from a harder case — one where the endpoint is liquid.

### Crushing Threshold

That harder case is provided: Rav Hoshaia arrived from Nahardea with a *Baraisa* in hand. The *Baraisa* states that olives and grapes crushed before Shabbos, whose juices run off on Shabbos, are forbidden — but Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon permit it. Their permissive ruling, allowing one to drink those juices, reflects the position that even were one to squeeze the crushed olives and grapes directly, it would not be a *melacha de'orayta*. This is the explicit proof from the hardest case — olives and grapes, *sechita* in its most classic form — that the crushing threshold matters.

The *Gemara* then notes that Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina had not heard this *Baraisa* and therefore relied on the *Mishnah* with Rabbi Yishmael's ruling about garlic and unripe grapes. Rabbi Elazar, for his part, did not rely on the Rabbi Yishmael source because of a qualification articulated by Rabbi Yochanan: *be'mechusrin dikah kulei alma lo pligi* — where the produce has not yet been crushed, no one argues; squeezing would obviously be a *melacha de'orayta*. The argument only arises, *ki pligi be'mechusrin shechika* — in cases where the produce has been crushed but not yet fully pressed out. And the *Mishnah* with the beam, Rabbi Elazar holds, may not clearly involve produce that has been crushed to a sufficient degree, making it a less reliable proof. He therefore prefers to rest his position on the explicit *Baraisa* about olives and grapes.

The upshot is this: Beis Shammai agrees that one may place the beam on olives and grapes before Shabbos because, once the produce has been sufficiently crushed, even direct squeezing on Shabbos would not constitute a *melacha de'orayta*. The *gezeira* against beginning processes on *erev Shabbos* was limited to activities that would be biblical violations if performed on Shabbos itself. Where Shabbos performance would not be a biblical violation — because the crushing has already done the essential work — Beis Shammai had no basis for the decree, and indeed all authorities agreed it was permitted.

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina ruled in practice like Rabbi Yishmael, permitting one to benefit from juices that ran off naturally after the produce was well crushed before Shabbos.

## Muktzeh Debates

### Rav vs Shmuel

The discussion of the oil press and its byproducts introduces two new halachic categories: *shemen shel badadin* — oil that dripped off during the pressing process on Shabbos itself — and *machatza'os shel badadin* — the mats used in the press. The oil may raise concerns either because of *nolad* — it is a new substance that came into existence on Shabbos — or because permitting one to drink it might lead one to squeeze the olives directly. The mats may be subject to *muktzeh* because they are designated exclusively for a particular professional or commercial function.

Rav prohibits both; Shmuel permits both. Their dispute reflects a fundamental disagreement about the scope of *muktzeh*: Rav holds a broad definition, aligned with Rabbi Yehuda's position, while Shmuel holds a narrow definition, aligned with Rabbi Shimon's position.

### Business-Use Items

Rabbi Nachman extends the same framework to a series of analogous cases: a goat set aside for its milk, a sheep for shearing, a chicken for its eggs, an ox designated for plowing, and dates set aside to be sold at market. These are all items that were not designated for Shabbos or *Yom Tov* use — they were earmarked for commercial or productive purposes. If one finds oneself in need on Shabbos or *Yom Tov* — wanting to eat from the dates, or wanting to *shecht* the animal — may one do so?

Rav prohibits this: if the item was not designated for Shabbos use, it is *muktzeh* and unavailable. Shmuel permits it: the category of *muktzeh* is narrow, and unless an item is fundamentally set aside in a way that makes it off-limits for any ordinary use, it remains available on Shabbos and *Yom Tov* even if it was not actively designated for that purpose.

### Rabbi Yehuda vs Shimon

The *Gemara* identifies this as the classic dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on the scope of *muktzeh*. Broadly stated, Rabbi Yehuda holds of *muktzeh* — items not designated for Shabbos use are set aside and unavailable — while Rabbi Shimon does not hold of *muktzeh*, meaning he recognizes only a very narrow set of cases in which *muktzeh* applies. The practical *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon, which is why Shmuel's more permissive ruling aligns with accepted practice. However, this is not to say that Rabbi Shimon recognizes no *muktzeh* at all; rather, he limits it to exceptional cases where items are truly and fundamentally inaccessible for Shabbos use.

A student who ruled publicly in the town of Chartah of Arguiz in accordance with Rabbi Shimon — permitting items that Rav, following Rabbi Yehuda, would have declared *muktzeh* — was placed into *niddui* by Rav Hamnuna. The *Gemara* expresses surprise: do we not rule like Rabbi Shimon? The answer is that Chartah of Arguiz was Rav's own locale, and one does not issue rulings contrary to the local *posek* within his own jurisdiction, even if in principle one would agree with the position being advanced.

The *Gemara* adds a final illustrative dispute: two students, when permitted to salvage items from a fire on Shabbos, differed in approach — one saved a large quantity in a single large vessel, while the other made four or five trips with smaller baskets. Their debate parallels another dispute among *Amora'im*, between Rabba bar Zavda and Rav Huna, and is brought here in parallel to the ongoing discussion about Rav and Shmuel's differing approaches.

Regarding *nolad* more broadly: the *Gemara* and Tosafos here suggest that most cases involving a change of form would not qualify as *nolad* at all. Tosafos understands *nolad* as applying only to a genuine transformation — such as food becoming juice — not to ordinary changes of state. This has significant practical implications: the question of whether ice or water formed on Shabbos constitutes *nolad* would, on this reading, generally not be a concern. Even in the oil-press case, the *nolad* problem is debated and ultimately resolved through the dispute between Rav and Shmuel. With this, the *Gemara* concludes its extended treatment of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel's debate about processes that begin on *erev Shabbos* and continue through Shabbos.

---

# Shabbat 20

## Fire Prohibitions

### Roasting Restrictions

The *mishna* at the bottom of 19b transitions from a series of debates between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* — concerning processes begun before *Shabbat* that continue into *Shabbat*, whether carried out independently or involving a non-Jew — to a case on which all agree to be strict. Presumably even *Beit Hillel* concurs with this prohibition.

The *mishna* opens: *ein tzolin basar batzal u'veitza ela kedei she-yitzolu mibe'od yom* — one may not roast meat, an onion, or an egg on *erev Shabbat* unless there is sufficient time for the food to complete its roasting while it is still day. The prohibition, then, is against having the roasting continue into *Shabbat* itself.

### Bread & Crust

The *mishna* continues: *ein notnin pat le-tanur im chasheicha* — one may not place bread into an oven as *Shabbat* approaches, *velo charara al gabei gechalim* — nor a wafer or biscuit on top of coals — *ela kedei she-yikremu paneiha mibe'od yom* — unless there is sufficient time for the crust to harden from while it is still day. Once the crust forms, the bread is considered sufficiently cooked that no concern remains.

Rabbi Eliezer qualifies this: *kedei she-yikrem hatachton shela* — it suffices for the bottom crust alone to form. The *gemara* raises the question of which side constitutes "the bottom" in Rabbi Eliezer's view. Rashi understands that the *bavli* envisions bread being baked in the manner of *esh tanur* pita — slapped against the interior wall of the oven. The side pressed against the wall forms its crust last, while the side facing the fire crusts over first. Does Rabbi Eliezer intend the more lenient reading — the face toward the fire — or the more stringent one — the face against the wall?

A *baraita* resolves this: *Rabbi Eliezer omer kedei she-yakrimu paneiha ha-midubakim ba-tanur* — Rabbi Eliezer requires the side adhering to the oven wall to form its crust, meaning the later and more demanding stage. Only then are we not concerned that one might continue fussing with the fire once *Shabbat* has begun.

### Pesach Exception

The *mishna* introduces a notable exception: *meshalshelin et ha-pesach ba-tanur im chasheicha* — one may lower the *Korban Pesach* into the oven as *Shabbat* descends. This rule presupposes the scenario in which *Pesach* falls on *Shabbat*, as on a normal *erev Pesach* one is permitted to cook on *Yom Tov*. The manner of roasting is also a *chiddush* — one might have assumed the *Korban Pesach* was roasted over an open fire, but the *mishna* indicates it was lowered into an oven, with the fire burning inside and the spit holding the animal over it.

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason this is permitted? The answer: *mishum di-vnei chaburah zerizin hein* — because the members of the group are particularly careful. A recurring principle throughout the tractate is that communal groups maintain a heightened level of vigilance; at least one member will be alert enough to prevent any inadvertent *chillul Shabbat*.

A difficulty arises from an earlier teaching that a whole roasting goat — the oven lid being sealed to avoid damaging the meat — creates no concern about stirring the coals even for an individual. The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between the *Korban Pesach*, which is roasted whole and thus less susceptible to exposure, and the earlier case in which the animal had been cut into pieces, greatly increasing the surface area exposed to air. The sealed oven there had a different function, and the cases are accordingly not analogous.

### Fire Vigilance

The *mishna*'s sequence is noteworthy. The laws governing *erev Shabbat* in this *perek* began with the prohibition against reading by firelight — and the underlying concern throughout is unmistakably fire. Unlike most *gezerot* where the worry is that a person will deliberately violate *Shabbat*, the concern here is that one will become preoccupied and *forget* that *Shabbat* has arrived. Fire, in particular, demands constant attention: one fusses with it, adjusts it, and tends to it. It is easy to lose track of time in the process.

This is why even *Beit Hillel*, who generally permit beginning a process before *Shabbat* and allowing it to continue, agree that fire-related activities require extra caution — both that the fire be burning well and that the food be well along in its cooking before *Shabbat* begins.

It is worth noting that the *Mechilta* records a view that the *mishna* of *ein tzolin basar* reflects the position of *Beit Shammai* alone, consistent with their general stringency regarding processes begun before *Shabbat*, and that *Beit Hillel* would disagree. However, that is not how the *gemara* reads it, nor how *Rebbi* understood it. The universally accepted reading is that fire-related concerns are treated with heightened caution by all, arising from a well-established pattern — first visible in the prohibition on reading by candlelight — that with fire, the likelihood of distraction and inadvertent violation is simply too great.

### Fire-Starting Rules

Having addressed roasting and bread, the *mishna* turns to lighting a fire itself. *U-ma'achizin et ha-ur bi-mdurat Beit HaMoked* — one may begin kindling the fire in the *midurat Beit HaMoked*, the chamber within the *Beit HaMikdash* where the *kohanim*, who were required to go barefoot on the cold stone floors, would warm themselves. This fire may be started on *erev Shabbat* even without waiting for it to fully take hold. By contrast, at the top of 20a: *u-va-gevulin kedei she-tochoz ha-ur be-rubah* — outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, the fire must seize most of the wood pile before *Shabbat* arrives.

This reflects the reality of fire-making before modern conveniences. Building and maintaining a fire required sustained effort, and there was genuine concern that a person would continue tending to it and forget the arrival of *Shabbat*. Outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, once the fire has seized most of the wood, it is considered self-sustaining and no fiddling is expected.

Rabbi Yehuda adds: *be-fechamim kol she-hu* — for charcoal, any minimal amount of ignition is sufficient on *erev Shabbat*, since charcoal, once it catches, burns reliably and no further intervention is necessary.

---

## Ma'achal Ben Drusai

### Roasting Standard

The *gemara* asks: *ve-chama* — how well roasted must the meat be? Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rav: *kedei she-yitzolu mibe'od yom ke-ma'achal Ben Drusai* — it must be cooked to the standard of *ma'achal Ben Drusai*. Ben Drusai was reportedly a bandit who, pressed for time, could not afford to cook his meat fully — hence his preference for very rare meat. Rashi identifies him accordingly. There is a debate in the *rishonim* whether *ma'achal Ben Drusai* denotes a third cooked or a half cooked, and it is not entirely clear whether these fractions refer to proportional cooking time or to observable degrees of doneness — what we might call rare versus medium-rare.

This principle is significant well beyond the present context, as it will become central to the discussion of the third *perek*, which addresses the permissibility of leaving food on a fire before *Shabbat*. The *Ashkenazic* ruling is that *ma'achal Ben Drusai* — whether a third or a half cooked — suffices. The *Sephardic* ruling requires the food to be fully cooked. Importantly, however, that dispute pertains to the case of cooking, not to roasting. This *mishna* treats roasting separately from the third *perek*, which deals exclusively with food left cooking on a stove.

Several differences between roasting and cooking are worth noting. Since roasting proceeds more quickly than cooking, all opinions agree that once meat has reached the *ma'achal Ben Drusai* threshold, one need not be concerned. Moreover, the *kula* that applies to raw food left on the stove before *Shabbat* — because raw food will not be ready until the next morning and one naturally forgets about it — does not apply to roasting. Even raw meat being roasted poses a problem, since roasting proceeds rapidly and one remains attentive to it. On the other hand, by the time roasted meat reaches the *ma'achal Ben Drusai* stage, it is so close to completion that no concern about fiddling remains, and no *blech* is required.

### Bishulei Nochrim

A related teaching is cited by analogy: Rav Assi said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, *kol she-hu ke-ma'achal Ben Drusai ein bo mishum bishulei nochrim* — food that has been cooked to the *ma'achal Ben Drusai* standard is not subject to the prohibition of *bishulei nochrim*. The prohibition against food cooked entirely by non-Jews applies to two categories: food that cannot be eaten raw, and food that is *ra'ui la'alot al shulchan melachim* — fit to be served at a royal table. One of the exceptions is where a Jew initiated the cooking. The *gemara* defines the threshold for that Jewish initiation: once the food has reached the *ma'achal Ben Drusai* stage — cooked to a third or half — it is considered to have been adequately begun by a Jew, and if a non-Jew completes the cooking, the food is permitted. The contemporary *Ashkenazic* leniency of a Jew merely lighting the flame is a later development; in the *gemara* itself the standard is *ma'achal Ben Drusai*. The analogy reinforces the principle: if that stage constitutes sufficient "cooking" for *bishulei nochrim*, it likewise constitutes sufficient readiness to permit leaving roasted meat on the fire into *Shabbat*.

### Chananya Cooking

A *baraita* is then cited: *Chananya omer, kol she-hu ke-ma'achal Ben Drusai mutar le-hashehoto al gabei kirah, v'af al pi she-eino grufah u-ktumah* — Chananya holds that any food cooked to the *ma'achal Ben Drusai* standard may be left on a *kirah* (a stove or oven), even without the stove being *grufah u-ktumah* — swept of its coals or covered with ashes.

This is a direct borrowing from the subject matter of the third *perek*. The concept of *shehiyah* — leaving food on the fire over *Shabbat* — and *grufah u-ktumah* — the swept-and-ashed condition that serves as the Talmudic antecedent of the *blech* — are the central concerns of that later chapter. Chananya's ruling bridges the two discussions: for him, whether one is roasting or cooking, *ma'achal Ben Drusai* is the operative threshold, and once reached it eliminates the need for a *blech*. As noted, others disagree regarding cooking: for cooked food left on the stove, some require it to be fully cooked, on pain of needing a *blech*. But for roasting, *ma'achal Ben Drusai* is universally accepted as sufficient.

### Roast vs. Cook

The structural separation of the present *mishna* — which deals with roasting — from the third *perek* — which deals with cooking — is itself significant. Roasting proceeds quickly; the concern that one will fiddle with it dissipates once a certain threshold of doneness is reached. Cooking is a slower and more uncertain process, and accordingly opinions differ as to how far along it must be before one is confident the person will not intervene. Chananya's position is that both roasting and cooking follow the same rule, while others maintain a stricter standard for cooking. The *gemara* makes this connection explicit here, drawing the two discussions together even before the third *perek* formally opens.

---

## Fire-Starting Rules

### Beit HaMoked

Returning to the *mishna*'s ruling that one may begin the fire in the *Beit HaMoked* on *erev Shabbat* even without it seizing most of the wood, the *gemara* asks: *minan milei* — what is the source that one is permitted to be more lenient in the *Beit HaMikdash*?

Rav Huna derives it from the *pasuk*: *lo teva'aru esh be-chol moshvoteichem be-yom ha-Shabbat* — do not kindle a fire in any of your dwelling places on *Shabbat*. The *derasha* is: the prohibition is on kindling fire *be-chol moshvoteichem*, in your dwelling places. But the *Beit HaMikdash* — the *Mishkan*, the sanctuary — is not a dwelling place in this sense; it is the place of the Divine Presence. Therefore, the prohibition does not apply there, and one may kindle fire in the *midurat Beit HaMoked*.

### Pasuk Derivation

The *pasuk* of *lo teva'aru esh* thus provides the conceptual basis for distinguishing between the *Beit HaMikdash* and *gevulin* — the territories outside it. Outside, the prohibition on kindling fire without adequate seizure applies; inside, it does not in the same way.

### Shabbat Fire Issue

Rav Chisda challenges this: *i hachi, afilu be-Shabbat nami* — if the *pasuk* truly exempts the *Beit HaMikdash* from the fire prohibition, one should be permitted to kindle a fire there even on *Shabbat* itself. Yet this cannot be right: while *melachah* is permitted in the *Beit HaMikdash* on *Shabbat*, it is only for the purpose of *korbanot* that are *be-mo'ado* — obligatory in their time. Optional *korbanot* may not be brought, and *melachot* that do not directly serve the *korban* are prohibited even for the *kohanim*. Warming the *kohanim* does not meet this standard. So how can the *pasuk* be invoked?

### Fats & Kohanim

Rav Chisda himself resolves this: *kra ki ata le-mishrei evarim u-fedarim hu de-ata* — the *pasuk* comes to permit the burning of fats and limbs on *Shabbat*. This refers either to the fats of *korbanot* slaughtered on the previous day — a substantial *chiddush* that their burning may continue into *Shabbat* — or to the fats of the *Tamid* and *Musaf* offerings, which need not technically be burned on *Shabbat* but which the *pasuk* permits. *Tosafot* notes some ambiguity about which scenario is intended, going back and forth on the question.

The fire in the *Beit HaMoked* for the warming of the *kohanim*, however, is not covered by this *pasuk*. Its leniency on *erev Shabbat* — that one need not wait for the fire to seize most of the wood — rests on two other foundations. First: *Kohanim zerizim hem* — *kohanim* are conscientious, as *benei chaburah zerizim hem* established earlier. Second: *ein shvut ba-Mikdash* — rabbinic restrictions are generally relaxed within the *Beit HaMikdash* to give the *kohanim* the latitude they need to perform the *avodah*. The upshot is that while we would not permit a *kohen* to kindle fire *le-chatchila* on *Shabbat* itself for their comfort, before *Shabbat* on *erev Shabbat*, we trust the *kohanim* not to tend to it, and therefore we need not require that the fire fully seize the wood.

### Outside Beit Mikdash

For the rest of Israel — *u-va-gevulin* — the standard is more demanding. *Kedei she-tochoz ha-ur be-rubah* — the fire must seize most of the wood pile before *Shabbat* begins.

---

## Fire Seizure Standards

### Rav's Position

The *gemara* asks: *mai rubah* — what does it mean for the fire to seize "most" of the wood? Rav answers: *rov kol echad ve-echad* — most of each individual stick must be aflame.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel offers a more functional and intuitive standard: *kedei she-lo yomru havu etzim ve-naniyach tachteihem* — it is sufficient when one would no longer say, "bring more twigs to lay beneath them." That is, once the fire is self-sustaining to the point that no one would think to add kindling, the threshold is met. Anyone who has built a bonfire will recognize this moment: there is a clear transition from the stage where one anxiously feeds the fire to the stage where it is simply going on its own.

### Menorah Analogy

A *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Chiyya is cited in support of Shmuel: *kedei she-tehei shalhevet olah me-eleha* — until the flame rises on its own. This is drawn from the procedure for lighting the *menorah* in the *Beit HaMikdash*: one would light it until the flame rose independently, without any need for further adjustment. The analogy is not about *Shabbat* concerns per se, but the principle is identical — once the flame sustains itself, the act of lighting is complete. As the *baraita* adds: *ve-lo she-tehei shalhevet olah al yedei davar acher* — it is not sufficient to leave the flame in a state where it still requires external assistance to rise.

### Single Stick Rule

For a single isolated stick — *etz yechidi* — the question of how much must catch fire is debated. Rav says *rov avyo* — most of its thickness. Others say *be-rov heikeifo* — most of its circumference. Rav Pappa rules: *hilchach, beinan rov avyo u-veinan rov heikeifo* — since the matter is unresolved, we require both: most of the thickness and most of the circumference.

### Tannaim Debate

This dispute mirrors a *tannaitic* disagreement. Rabbi Chiyya holds: *kedei she-yishacheit ha-etz mi-mlechet ha-uman* — the stick must be so consumed that it can no longer serve any craftsman's purpose. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds: *kedei she-tochoz ha-eish mi-shnei tzedadin* — the fire must take hold on both sides of the stick. Although, as the *gemara* notes, there is no definitive proof for the latter view, there is a textual allusion (*zeicher la-davar*) from Yechezkel: *et shnei ktzotav achlah ha-eish ve-tocho nachar, ha-yitzlach li-mlacha* — the fire consumed both its edges and its middle was charred; is it fit for any work? Rashi reads this passage as aligning Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's position with the *rov heikeifo* standard (burning on both sides corresponding to most of the circumference), and Rabbi Chiyya's with *rov avyo* (the degree of destruction that removes the wood from useful service). The precise correspondence is not entirely transparent, but that is Rashi's reading.

---

## Ach Digression

### Ach Meaning

The *gemara* briefly departs from its discussion of fire seizure to address a lexical curiosity. The *pasuk* in Yirmiyahu describing Yehoyakim burning the *Megilla* of Eichah reads: *ve-ha-ach lefanav mevo'aret* — the *ach* was burning before him. Yehoyakim, unwilling to accept the prophecy of Yerushalayim's destruction, cast the scroll into the fire. The *gemara* asks: *mai ach* — what is an *ach*?

Rav says: *achvana* — and as Rashi explains, this means *arava*, willow. Shmuel offers a different interpretation: *eitzim she-nidliku be-achvana* — sticks of wood that burned in a bundle together, each lighting the next — *kol ha-eitzim nidlakim zeh mi-zeh katan madlik ha-gadol* — the smaller pieces kindling the larger ones. The image is of a small bonfire where the pieces feed one another.

### Aravas Anecdote

The discussion concludes with an anecdote that confirms the identification of *achvana* with *arava*: *hahu de-amar lehu man ba'ei achvana* — there was someone going around calling out "who wants *achvana*?" — *ve-ishtakach arvasa* — and it turned out he was selling *aravas*, willows. This confirms that *ach* or at least *achvana* refers to the willow.

---

## Fuel Types

### Twigs vs. Bundles

Rav Huna rules: *kanim ein tzrichim rov* — loose twigs do not require the fire to seize most of them; *agdan tzrichim rov* — but if bundled together, most must be aflame. Twigs burn easily and reliably when separate; bundled together, the fire has more difficulty penetrating between them, and therefore a higher threshold is needed. Similarly for date pits: *garinim ein tzrichim rov* — loose date pits do not require a majority to have caught fire, given their surface area and flammability; *netanam be-chutalot tzrichim rov* — but if placed in baskets, where they are packed together and less surface is exposed, most must be alight.

### Chisda Opposition

Rav Chisda challenges this directly: *ipcha mistabra* — the opposite is more logical. Regarding twigs: *mevadran* — when scattered and separate, they do not kindle one another; if one begins to go out there is nothing adjacent to reignite it. *Agdan lo mevadran* — when bundled, they support each other, each relighting the others. So bundled twigs should be the easier case. The same reversal applies to date pits: loose, they are scattered and each risks going out independently; packed in a basket, they sustain one another's combustion. Rav Chisda thus maintains the exact opposite of Rav Huna. The *gemara* presents both positions without resolution, and the implicit appeal to empirical testing goes unexplored.

### Kahana Position

Rav Kahana, according to the text as we have it, takes a split position: *kanim she-agadan tzrichim rov* — bundled sticks require a majority; *lo agadan ein tzrichim rov* — unbundled, they do not. This corresponds to Rav Chisda's view for sticks. For date pits, the ruling is reversed: *garinim tzrichim rov* — pits alone require a majority; *netanam be-chutalot ein tzrichim rov* — in baskets they do not. There are significant textual variants (*girsaot*) in this passage that yield considerably different arrangements of the rulings, and different manuscripts come out all different ways in terms of what the *baraita* is saying.

### Special Fuels

Rav Yosef teaches: *arba medurot ein tzrichim rov* — there are four categories of fire that do not require the fire to seize most of the material. These are: *shel zefet* — tar or pitch, which is highly flammable; *shel gofrit* — sulfur; a third material that according to our text reads *shel gvina* — cheese — which is puzzling, since cheese is not an obvious fuel. The *Gra* emends the reading to *kira*, gourds, though whether gourds make for particularly reliable fuel is also unclear; and *shel revav* — some type of liquid flammable substance, which Rashi identifies as melted wax or oil. These are all materials that, once ignited, burn reliably and need no further tending — the *erev Shabbat* concern about fiddling does not apply.

A *baraita* adds: *af shel kash ve-shel gavava* — even stubble and straw fall into this category. These burn so rapidly and so easily that there is no concern one will need to adjust them — indeed, as was noted, they may burn almost too well.

### Babylonian Wood

Rabbi Yochanan states: *eitzim shel Bavel ein tzrichim rov* — the wood in Bavel does not require a majority to have caught fire before *Shabbat*. This may be because it is particularly oily or especially dry and thus burns readily.

Rav Yosef challenges this: *mai hi* — what wood are you referring to? If you mean *silty* — thin strips of wood — that cannot be easier to handle than a wick. For Ulla will teach at the opening of the next *perek* that when lighting an oil lamp before *Shabbat*, one must ensure that most of the wick extending from the lamp's mouth is actually burning. A wick is specifically designed to draw oil and sustain a flame; if even a wick requires most of its exposed portion to be lit, how could a thin strip of wood be treated more leniently?

Rav Yosef therefore concludes: *shucha de-arza* — the reference is not to ordinary thin wood but to the fibrous, woolly material found between the bark and the trunk of the cedar tree. This substance is highly flammable and, once ignited, burns reliably — which is why it requires no *rov*. The same material, we will see, reappears shortly in the opening of the next *perek*, where it is identified as one of the substances excluded from use as a wick because it burns too readily.

---

## Perek 2 Intro

### Fiddle Concern

The conclusion of the first *perek* and the opening of the second flow together seamlessly. The concern that dominated the first *perek* — that one will fiddle with a fire on *Shabbat* — provides the direct rationale for the *mishna* of *bameh madlikin*, which asks what types of wicks and oils may be used for *Shabbat* candles. If the wick or oil is of poor quality, the flame will sputter and burn unevenly, creating precisely the anxiety that leads a person to adjust it. Even without the specific concern of reading by candlelight, an unreliable flame tempts intervention.

### Candle History

The straightforward reading of the *mishna* suggests that the lighting of candles on *erev Shabbat* was, at its origin, simply a practical necessity: without oil lamps burning from before *Shabbat*, there would be no light for the Friday night meal. During the week, people largely ate before dark; on *Shabbat*, they ate after dark and could not kindle a flame, so they lit before *Shabbat* began. The *mishna* treats this as a practical reality and asks: given that you must light these lamps, what materials may you use?

That said, it becomes evident within the *gemara* and crystallizes in the *rishonim* that candle lighting eventually acquired the status of a *mitzvah*. Some historians argue that even at the time of the *mishna* it was already perceived as ritually significant — not merely as turning on the lights — pointing to references in non-Jewish and pagan sources that take note of the Jewish practice of lighting candles before *Shabbat* as a distinctively religious act. Lighting candles carried connotations of ceremony and sanctity broadly in the ancient world; the practice may have become ritualized even before it was formally classified as a *mitzvah* with a *bracha*. The question of when exactly that crystallization occurred will unfold as the *perek* proceeds.

### Karaite Context

The Karaites interpreted *lo teva'aru esh be-chol moshvoteichem be-yom ha-Shabbat* to forbid any fire from burning on *Shabbat*, even if kindled beforehand. This led them to spend *Shabbat* in cold and darkness. Maintaining fire from *erev Shabbat* — the *cholent* left burning on the fire, the candles kindled before nightfall — became for *Rabbinic* Jews an important institutional counterstatement against Karaite practice.

It is not entirely clear whether the Karaite position was already known in the *Talmudic* period; the first explicit evidence of the dispute comes from the *Geonic* period. It was in that era that the practice developed of reciting *Bameh Madlikin* on *erev Shabbat* as a deliberate affirmation of the permissibility — indeed, the obligatory nature — of burning lights into *Shabbat*. Manuscripts discovered in the *Genizah* contain a remarkable *bracha* that preceded *Bameh Madlikin* in the *Geonic* liturgy, beginning: *Baruch Atah Hashem Elokeinu Melech Ha-olam asher bachar ba-chachamim ve-talmideihem ve-natan lahem Torah me-Har Sinai al yedei Moshe Rabbeinu* — and proceeding to enumerate the chain of tradition from Moshe through Yehoshua, the seventy elders, the prophets, the sages, and their students, culminating in the commandment to observe *Shabbat* and to kindle the *Shabbat* lamp, before going directly into *Bameh Madlikin*. The polemical thrust is unmistakable: the *Rabbinic* tradition from Sinai is the authentic one, and it mandates lighting candles that remain burning on *Shabbat*.

Whatever the earlier history, by the *Geonic* period the *mitzvah* of *hadlakat ner Shabbat* was unambiguously established, complete with a *bracha* — the first description of such a *bracha* appears precisely in this period.

---

## Prohibited Wicks

### Lachesh

The second *perek* opens: *bameh madlikin u-bameh ein madlikin* — with what may one light, and with what may one not light? The *mishna* begins, as it sometimes does, with the prohibited category. The first prohibited wick is *lachesh* (some have the *girsa* *legesh*). The *gemara* identifies this as *shucha de-arza* — the fibrous, woolly material found between the bark and trunk of the cedar tree, the very same substance that was just discussed at the close of the first *perek* as a fuel that burns so readily it requires no *rov*. The *gemara* registers a moment of apparent confusion: surely *shucha de-arza* is just wood; who would think to use a stick as a wick? The resolution is that the reference is not to the stick itself but to the woolly fiber within it — *be-amranitta de-it bah*, the fibrous substance embedded in it. And precisely because this material burns so easily and rapidly, it is disqualified from use as a wick: it will not sustain a steady, even flame.

### Chosen Flax

The next prohibited item is *chosen* (some versions read *chossen*). Rav Yosef initially identifies it as *ne'oret shel pishtan* — the combings of flax, the fibers removed in the combing process. Abaye challenges this, citing a *pasuk*: *ve-haya ha-chason la-ne'oret* — indicating that *chason* and *ne'oret* are distinct things. Abaye therefore redefines *chosen* as *kitna de-dayek ve-lo nafitz* — flax that has been beaten but not yet combed, so that the husks of the flax have not yet been removed. Flax in this state burns unevenly because of the remaining husks, making it unreliable as a wick. To use flax as a wick properly, it would first need to be fully combed.

### Klach Silk

The third prohibited item is *klach*, which is generally assumed to refer to silk. Shmuel remarks: *she'alti le-chol nechutei yama ve-amru li kulcha shemei* — I asked all those who travel by sea, and they told me its name is *kulcha*. This is essentially a straight Aramaic equivalence rather than a substantive explanation. Rav Yitzchak bar Ze'ira calls it *gushkera*, which Steinsaltz identifies with the cocoon of the silkworm, while Rashi reads *hu beit ha-tola'at* — the house of the worm — the same idea. The implication is that *klach* is not fine silk but a byproduct or remnant of the silk-making process, perhaps the discarded casing or dross, which is why one might think to use it as a wick at all. Who would use expensive silk for a wick? It is the discarded material from silk production that raises the question.

Ravin and Abaye were once sitting in the presence of Ravna Nechemya, the brother of the *Resh Galuta* — the lay leader of Babylonian Jewry. They noticed he was wearing *metaksa*, a fine silk garment. Ravin said to Abaye: that must be the *klach* mentioned in our *mishna*. Abaye replied: what we call *shira parnida* is altogether different — that is fine, expensive silk, not the material of the *mishna*. This suggests that the exchange was as much about identifying a substance as about distinguishing grades of material.

### Silk Types

The *gemara* presses on this distinction. A *baraita* states that *ha-shirayim ve-ha-klach ve-ha-sivikin* — various types of silk fabrics, including *sivikin* (which Rashi identifies as a corded silk and ArtScroll translates as "corded silk," made from the softer portions of silk worked into cord) — *chayavin be-tzitzit*, are obligated in *tzitzit*. The *gemara* notes this as a *tiyuvta* — a difficulty — suggesting that *shirayim* and *klach* are indeed listed as separate items. The resolution proposed is: *shira lachud ve-shira parnida lachud* — plain *shira* and *shira parnida* are distinct categories. Under Rashi's reading, *shira parnida* is to be identified with *klach*, while under *Tosafot*'s reading, *shira parnida* is finer than *klach* and thus different from it. The upshot in either case is that *klach* refers to some form of silk — most plausibly a byproduct or lower-grade remnant of the silk-making process — and is disqualified as a wick because it burns too quickly and will not sustain a reliable flame.

### Idan & Desert

The string of the *idan* (*petilat ha-idan*) is identified by the *gemara* as *achvina* — the same word that just appeared in the digression about the *pasuk* in Yirmiyahu, which Rashi there identified as *arava*, willow. A wick must not only burn but must draw oil consistently; the fibrous material from a willow, whatever its burning properties, does not function well as an oil-drawing wick.

*Petilat ha-midbar* — the fiber of the desert — is identified by Rashi as a type of tall grass, perhaps a grass that grows in arid regions and can be braided into a rope-like form. Though it may seem a plausible material, it too fails to draw oil reliably.

### Moss Problem

*Yaroka she-al pnei ha-mayim* — the green growth on the surface of water — refers presumably to moss or algae. The *gemara* asks what exactly this is. The initial suggestion — *uchnisa de-charitzai*, the moss or algae of ponds — is rejected: *ifuhei mapharchi*, it crumbles and is too brittle; no one could seriously attempt to use it as a wick. Rav Pappa therefore identifies it as *uchnisa de-arva* — the moss that accumulates on the hulls of boats.

This identification was confirmed in a well-known anecdote: Ravin and Abaye — the same pair who appeared earlier identifying the *klach* — were traveling through the valley of Tamrurita when they observed what grew on the water there. Ravin said to Abaye: this must be the *yaroka* of the *mishna*. It is notable that the same pair of scholars appears repeatedly in this *perek* attempting to identify the obscure materials listed in the *mishna* against actual specimens encountered in the field.

### Wool & Hair

The *mishna* then states that the list of prohibited wicks was subsequently expanded (*hosifu aleihen*) to include wool (*tzemer*) and animal hair (*sa'ar*). The *tanna* of the *mishna* did not bother including these originally because they were self-evident: wool, when used as a wick, *michzi kavish* — shrivels up and collapses — and will not sustain a flame. Hair *ichruchei michrich* — singes — and cannot draw oil at all. These were so obviously unsuitable that no one would have thought to try them, and therefore the *tanna* required no explicit prohibition.

---

## Prohibited Oils

### Wick-Oil Shift

A *baraita* explicitly demarcates the boundary in the *mishna*: *ad kan psul petilot* — up to this point, the list concerns prohibited wicks; *mi-kan ve-eilach psul shmanim* — from here onward, the list concerns prohibited oils. The transition is marked by the mention of *zefet* (pitch or tar) and *sha'avah* (wax).

### Wax Debate
