The *gemara* observes: *pshita* — it is obvious that pitch and wax cannot be used as oils, apparently because their burning properties, smell, or consistency make them clearly unsuitable as fuel. The *gemara* clarifies, however, that the case of wax (*sha'avah*) required explicit mention: *mahu de-teima li-psila nami lo chazya* — one might have thought that wax cannot even be used as a wick, and the *mishna* therefore tells us *ka mashma lan* — that wax is valid as a wick, just not as a fuel.

This is counterintuitive to the modern reader, since wax candles function precisely through the wax serving as fuel. The distinction in the *Talmudic* world reflects the fact that oil lamps — not wax candles — were the standard technology. Wax as a wick material, without functioning as the liquid fuel drawn up by capillary action, may have been used by applying wax to a fiber wick to help it stay lit — analogous to how modern wax-coated wicks maintain their flame more reliably than bare fiber. Whether one could also use melted wax as a fuel in a lamp-style vessel remains unclear from the *gemara*'s discussion.

### Dross Materials

Rami bar Avin provides lexical clarifications: *atrna psulta de-zifta* — the substance called *atrna* (elsewhere *itran*) is the dross or residue of *zefet*, the material left over after pitch is extracted from the tree. *Sha'avah psulta de-duvsha* — wax is the dross of honey; that is, beeswax is the byproduct of the honeycomb after the honey is extracted, confirming that the *sha'avah* of the *mishna* is indeed beeswax.

### Commercial Use

The *gemara* asks: *le-mai nafka mina* — what is the practical consequence of these identifications? *Le-mikach u-mimkar* — for commercial transactions. If a buyer contracts to purchase *itran* or *sha'avah*, the identification of exactly what those terms denote — dross of pitch, dross of honey — establishes what the seller is obligated to deliver. The *gemara*'s lexical exercise thus has direct application to the law of commerce and trade contracts.

*Tosafot*, in addressing the ruling that wax cannot be used as fuel, notes the practice in Narvona — contemporaneous to *Tosafot* — of using wax candles for *Shabbat*. *Tosafot* records the debate: does the *gemara*'s prohibition on wax as fuel extend to the wax candles of his era? The argument goes back and forth. The ultimate ruling of *Tosafot* — *ela vadai lo shanu ela bi-shemen, ki lo hiniach bi-shemen nami sharei* — suggests that the prohibition was formulated in the context of oil lamps, and that without the oil-lamp framework, the use of wax candles may be permitted. This became the *Ashkenazic* practice; wax and later paraffin candles are taken for granted for *Shabbat* lighting, though the theoretical basis for reconciling this with the *gemara*'s ruling is a matter discussed by the *rishonim*.

---

---

# Shabbat 21

## Wax Candles & Wicks

### Wax as Wick

We begin at the very top of 21a, with the *tanu rabbanan*. Before proceeding, it is worth resolving a question that arose the previous day regarding *sha'ava* — wax. The *Mishnah* listed wax among the substances one may not use for *Shabbos* candle lighting, and *Tosafot* indeed records an opinion that wax candles are prohibited. Ultimately, however, *Tosafot* permits wax candles, and this ruling is codified in the *Shulchan Aruch*.

The reasoning turns on a precise reading of the *Gemara*'s prohibition. The *Gemara* forbids using wax as a fuel — that is, as an oil — in a configuration where a thread wick is meant to draw up liquefied wax from below. In that scenario, wax does not draw up a wick effectively; it must first melt from the heat of the flame, and the mechanics differ fundamentally from oil. A standard wax candle, by contrast, works differently: the wick is surrounded and embedded in wax, such that the wax itself constitutes a very thick wick. *Halakhically*, the entire object is treated as one thick wick, not as a wick drawing fuel from a separated reservoir. It is on this basis that wax candles — and, by the same reasoning, paraffin candles — are permitted.

### Paraffin & Cotton

The same analysis applies to paraffin, which constitutes the majority of candles in common use. The prohibition the *Gemara* targets is the configuration in which wax or another substance sits separated from the wick and is expected to be drawn up into it. Where the material surrounds the wick, the concern does not apply.

---

## Flicker & Draw Issues

### Prohibited Uses

The *tanu rabbanan* continues: *elu devarim she'ein madlikin bahen b'Shabbos* — those things which may not be used to light on *Shabbos* — *aval osin meihen medurah* — may nevertheless be used to make a bonfire. Whether one wants the heat or the light, whether the fire is on the ground, atop an oven, or on some kind of base, all of these configurations are entirely permissible. The restriction — *v'lo asru ela la'asot meihen petilah l'ner bilvad* — applies only to using these materials as wicks in a lamp. The specific concern is the mechanics of oil being drawn up through a wick. Anyone who has tried to use oil *menorot* knows how finicky the process can be, and it is precisely there that the quality of the oil and wick matters.

### Kik & Kikayon

The *Gemara* turns to the question of *shemen kik* — the oil of *kik* — which is among the prohibited oils. *Mai shemen kik?* What is *kik*? Shmuel reports that he asked all the seafarers and they told him: there is a certain bird found in the islands of the sea, called *kik*, and the oil is derived from it. Rav Yitzchak the son of Rav Yehuda offers a different identification: it is *mishcha d'kaza* — oil of *kaza*. Rashi explains that *kaza* refers to cotton, identifying it as oil pressed from the seeds of the cotton plant. The assumption throughout is that these oils do not burn evenly and cause the flame to flicker, which would lead one to adjust the candle on *Shabbos*.

Resh Lakish offers yet another identification: *kikayon d'Yona* — the *kikayon* of Yona. Rashi is careful to note, on the first narrow line of his commentary, that this is not the exact plant under which the prophet Yona sat, but rather a plant of that species. The Steinsaltz edition identifies this as the castor plant. Rabbah bar bar Chana reports having seen such a plant himself — again, Rashi clarifies, of the same species. He describes it: it grows from swamps, it is draped decoratively over the doorways of shops to attract customers, oil is made from its seeds, and the sick people of the west, of *Eretz Yisrael*, rest beneath its branches. The medicinal reference is consistent with what we know of castor oil, and it is notable that the *Gemara* here describes the oil as being made from the seeds without suggesting it is suitable for use as lamp oil, certainly not on *Shabbos*.

### Flicker Reasons

With the identifications complete, Rabbah now provides the underlying rationale for the two categories of prohibited materials. Regarding wicks: *mipnei sheha'or mesachsachet bahen* — the flame will flicker with those wicks. Regarding oils: *mipnei she'einan nimshachin achar hapetila* — they do not draw well after the wick. When oil does not draw up into the wick effectively, the lamp will burn poorly, and one is likely to come and adjust it.

---

## Mixing Oils Debate

### Abaye's Question

The *Gemara* records a question posed by Abaye to his teacher Rabbah. Given that certain oils are prohibited because they do not draw after the wick, what if one adds a small amount of kosher oil — say, olive oil — to the prohibited oil? The reasoning behind the question is that the addition of good oil might cause the mixture to draw after the wick effectively, rendering it acceptable. Do we issue a *gezeira* — a protective decree — forbidding even this mixture, *deilma ati leadlukei binhu*, lest it lead to using the problematic oils by themselves? Or not?

Rabbah responds: *ein madlikin* — you may not use the mixture. His reason: *lefi she'ein madlikin* — because you may not use them. This is, on its face, a tautology, and the *Gemara* itself acknowledges the humor. Rashi understands it as an expression of the principle of *lo plug* — no distinction is drawn. Since the prohibited oils may not be used by themselves, we do not allow the mixture either, lest one lead to the other. An alternative textual reading found in some manuscripts — *lefi she'einan nidlakin* — would instead be a factual claim: even the mixture does not burn as well as one might suppose. The *Gilyon HaShas* of Akiva Eiger notes parallels in the *Gemara* and even in the language of the Torah itself where a statement is essentially self-referential, citing the verse in *Vayikra* regarding blemished priests: *asher yihiyeh bo mum lo yikrav... ki kol ish asher bo mum lo yikrav* — he may not approach because he may not approach.

It is worth noting the broader context: this entire discussion is rabbinic in nature, and we have not yet been introduced in the *Gemara* to any *mitzvah* of lighting *Shabbos* candles per se. The concerns so far have been analogous to the earlier discussions about reading by candlelight and keeping food on the fire — all centering on the worry that one will come to fiddle with the flame.

### Wick Wrapping

The *Gemara* raises a challenge. A *braisa* teaches: if one wrapped a kosher wick around a non-kosher material, *ein madlikin bo* — one may not use it. Yet Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that in his father's house — the house of Rabban Gamliel, the *nasi* — they would wrap a wick around a nut and light it. The purpose of wrapping the wick around the nut is evidently to create a floating wick, of the kind familiar from *Chanukah* practice, where the nut serves as a flotation device keeping the wick suspended in oil.

### Ma'aseh Rav

Rabbah responds that the *tanna kamma*'s ruling presents no difficulty — *maaseh rav*. When a practice is not merely a theoretical ruling but was actually enacted by a great rabbi, that carries greater *halachic* weight. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel testified that this is what they actually did in Rabban Gamliel's household, and that practical precedent overrides the theoretical position of the *tanna kamma*. Accordingly, one should be able to wrap a kosher wick around a non-kosher base, and similarly one ought to be able to mix kosher oil with prohibited oil and use it.

One might object that the *tanna kamma* represents a broader consensus and that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's practice is merely a *da'at yachid*. This is a genuine and more general question about how heavily *maaseh rav* in the *Mishnah* is to be weighed. The comparison to Rabban Gamliel's practice in the previous chapter — where he sent a white garment to a *kohen*, a ruling we do not follow, understood there as a personal *chumra* — is instructive: if the *maaseh rav* represents a *kula*, a leniency, it is arguably more indicative of the normative *halacha* than a personal stringency.

### Floating Wicks

The *Gemara* presses on a residual difficulty: how does one account for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's practice if the *tanna kamma* prohibits wrapping a kosher wick around a non-kosher material? The resolution is that there is in fact no debate here at all. The *tanna kamma* speaks to the case where both materials are being used together as a wick — *l'hadlik*, for actual lighting. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel speaks to the case of *l'hakpos* — using the non-kosher material as a flotation device only, not as a wick. In that configuration, the nut is not functioning as a wick at all and the restriction does not apply. *Bamei devarim amurim* — the prohibition applies only when both are used for the purpose of burning; *aval l'hakpos*, when it is purely for flotation, it is *muttar*.

### Fat & Fish Issue

The *Gemara* introduces a further teaching. Rav Bruna said in the name of Rav: *chelev mehutach* — liquefied fat — and *kirvei dagim shenimochu* — fish innards that have been liquefied — if one adds a small amount of acceptable oil to them, one may use the mixture for lighting. This appears to contradict Rabbah's ruling that mixing kosher oil with prohibited oil is forbidden.

The *Gemara* resolves this by drawing a crucial distinction. Liquefied fat and liquefied fish innards are not inherently problematic — they do in fact draw after the wick. They were only prohibited by rabbinic decree: liquefied fat was forbidden *mishum chelev she'eino mehutach*, lest it be confused with non-liquefied fat, which does not draw properly; liquefied fish innards were similarly forbidden lest they be confused with non-liquefied fish innards. In both cases the prohibition is itself a *gezeira*, a protective fence around materials that are in principle acceptable. Where the underlying material is fundamentally fit and the only reason for prohibition is a *gezeira*, we permit the addition of kosher oil and allow the mixture. Where the oil is intrinsically poor — genuinely incapable of drawing after the wick — adding a small amount of kosher oil cannot remedy that, and the prohibition stands.

The *Gemara* immediately asks: why not extend the *gezeira* further and prohibit even the mixture of liquefied fat with kosher oil, lest it lead to using liquefied fat with no oil added, which itself was prohibited? The answer: *hai gufa gezira*, the liquefied fat prohibition is itself a *gezeira*. *V'anan neiku v'nigzor gezira l'gezira* — we do not pile a *gezeira* upon a *gezeira*. The *Gemara* is aware that this principle is not absolute and that sometimes the *Gemara* does build such layered decrees, but here it declines to do so.

A note in *Tosafot* raises a broader question: is not the entire framework of prohibited wicks and oils already a *gezeira l'gezira*? The underlying concern is that one might adjust the lamp on *Shabbos*, and the prohibition of these materials is a protective fence around that concern. So forbidding even the mixture of good oil with bad is already one level removed from the original concern. One of the *Baalei HaTosafot* — identified as the Rivan — offers a notably different framing: the reason to avoid oils that do not draw after the wick is not, as generally understood, the fear of adjusting the candle (*shema yateh*), but rather the concern that the lamp will go out entirely (*shema yichbeh*), leaving the household without light and thereby undermining *shalom bayis*. This is a significant reframing, because it implicitly treats the lighting of *Shabbos* candles as a genuine *mitzvah* in its own right — one aimed at ensuring light and domestic tranquility in the home — rather than merely a neutral activity hedged about with prohibitions against tampering. Whether this is the plain meaning of the *Gemara* is a separate question, since the concept of candle lighting as a *mitzvah* has not yet been formally introduced at this point in the discussion.

A further practical observation from *Tosafot* is worth noting. One of the *Baalei HaTosafot* records a tradition that if one has even a single kosher candle in the house, the remaining candles in other rooms need not meet the standards of acceptable wicks and oils — since the presence of one reliable light will prevent one from coming to adjust the others. This was apparently a solution to the real practical difficulty of not having sufficient kosher candles available. Whether this logic holds given the stated reason for the restriction is debated: if the concern is that one will fiddle with the problematic candle when reading or eating by it, the existence of a kosher candle in another room seems insufficient protection. Nonetheless, *Tosafot* records a second answer as well: if the concern is adjustment on *Shabbos*, one may use even non-kosher candles for activities that could theoretically be performed in darkness, since there is no inducement to adjust them.

---

## Temple Menorah

### Temple Standards

Rami bar Chama teaches: the wicks and oils that the *Chachamim* said may not be used for *Shabbos* candle lighting are equally prohibited for use in the *Beis HaMikdash* — specifically for the *menorah*. The proof text is *leha'alos ner tamid*, which Rashi understands via the *hif'il* form of the verb: you cause the flame to ascend, but it must then be self-sustaining — *k'dei shetehei shalheves olah me'eleha*. The flame must rise on its own, *v'lo shetehei olah al yedei davar acher* — it must not require external assistance to keep burning. This requirement for self-sufficiency in the *mikdash* parallels the requirement for quality wicks and oils on *Shabbos*.

### Priestly Garments

A *Mishnah* is cited which states that worn-out undergarments and belts of the *kohanim* — *bigdei kehunah* — were torn into strips and used as torches for the *simchas beis hasho'evah*. The *Gemara* notes that since the belts of the *kohanim* contained a mixture of wool and linen (*kilayim*), one might ask whether using such material as wicks — even for the *mikdash* — is consistent with the standard of self-sufficiency established above. The *Gemara* answers: *lo de-butz* — the wicks used for the *menorah* itself were made from the linen garments, not from the belts. Linen is a kosher wick material, and those specific garments were made entirely of linen. The use of the priestly garments for the *simchas beis hasho'evah* torches is in any case in a separate category — *simchas beis hasho'evah shani* — distinct from the *mitzvah* of the *menorah* proper.

---

## Hanukkah Intro

### Rav Huna

The discussion now pivots to *Chanukah*, and it is here that the *Gemara* enters into what is essentially its only sustained treatment of the laws of *Chanukah*. The entry point is the question of whether the same restrictions governing wicks and oils for *Shabbos* apply equally to *Chanukah* candles.

Rav Huna rules: the wicks and oils that are prohibited for *Shabbos* are equally prohibited for *Chanukah* — *bein beshabbos bein bechol* — whether on *Shabbos* itself or on the weekday nights of *Chanukah*.

### Rava's Concern

Rava explains Rav Huna's reasoning. On *Shabbos*, the concern is familiar: using a problematic wick or oil might cause one to adjust the flame, leading to *chilul Shabbos*. But on a weekday of *Chanukah*, why should it matter if one fiddles with the flame? Rava explains: *kasavar kavsa zakuk la* — Rav Huna holds that if the *Chanukah* candle goes out, one is obligated to relight it. The *mitzvah* requires that the candle burn for the full prescribed duration. If one uses unreliable oils and wicks, they may sputter out and one will fail to fulfill the *mitzvah* without realizing it. Therefore, even on weekdays, only reliable materials may be used. On *Shabbos* there is the additional concern that since Rav Huna permits using the *Chanukah* light (*mutar lehishtamesh leorah*), one might come to adjust the flame while reading or eating by it.

### Rav Chisda

Rav Chisda disagrees: *madlikin bahen bechol aval lo beshabbos* — one may use the problematic wicks and oils on weekdays but not on *Shabbos*. His reasoning: *kasavar kavsa ein zakuk la* — if the candle goes out, one bears no further obligation. Accordingly, on weekdays the concern of the candle burning out is not pressing: one has discharged the *mitzvah* at the moment of lighting, provided the candle had a reasonable potential to last the required time. The question of whether a candle had the requisite potential to last is determined at the moment of lighting, not by whether it actually lasts. If one lights a candle with sufficient oil in a sheltered location, the *mitzvah* is fulfilled even if the candle subsequently goes out. On *Shabbos*, however, even Rav Chisda prohibits these materials — because since one is permitted to use the light (*mutar lehishtamesh leorah*), one will read or eat by it and will be tempted to adjust the flame, leading to a *Shabbos* violation.

### Rabbi Zeira

Rabbi Zeira, citing Rav Matna (or, in another version, citing Rav directly), goes furthest: the wicks and oils prohibited for *Shabbos* may nonetheless be used for *Chanukah*, whether on weekdays or on *Shabbos* itself. Rabbi Yirmiyah explains this position: Rabbi Zeira's teacher holds both *kavsa ein zakuk la* — no obligation to relight — and *asur lehishtamesh leorah* — one may not use the *Chanukah* light for personal benefit. The prohibition on using the light removes the concern that one will fiddle with the flame on *Shabbos*, and the absence of any obligation to ensure continued burning removes the concern on weekdays.

The *Gemara* notes that Abaye initially heard this explanation in the name of Rabbi Yirmiyah and rejected it. When the same reasoning was later transmitted to him in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, he accepted it. Abaye then reflected: *ai zakai, gemarti shema'ata me'ikara* — had I merited, I would have learned it the first time. The *Gemara* asks: what practical difference does it make when one learns something? The answer: *nafka mina l'girsa de'yankusa* — material absorbed in youth adheres with far greater permanence. This is not mere sentiment; the *Gemara* treats early learning as qualitatively superior in terms of retention.

It is worth noting that we rule in accordance with this final opinion. On the question of *kavsa ein zakuk la* — if the candle goes out one need not relight it — this is the normative *halacha*. One must ensure at the time of lighting that the candle has the potential to burn for the required duration, but if it subsequently goes out one has discharged the *mitzvah*. Questions can arise in practice — for example, when lighting outdoors in the wind with the protective glass doors open: if at the very moment of lighting the candle had no reasonable prospect of lasting, some authorities question whether the *mitzvah* has been performed even if one immediately closes the doors. In most cases, however, providing sufficient oil and a sheltered location at the time of lighting is sufficient.

### Kavsah Ein Zakuk

The *Gemara* now challenges the ruling of *kavsa ein zakuk la*. A *braisa* states: *mitzvasah mishetishka hachamah ad shetichleh regel min hashuk* — the *mitzvah* of *Chanukah* candles runs from sunset until the foot ceases from the marketplace, meaning until people have stopped milling about in the streets. One might read this as requiring the candle to burn throughout this entire period, implying an obligation to relight if it goes out.

The *Gemara* rejects this reading in two ways. First: the *braisa* is not prescribing the duration of burning, but the window of time within which the *mitzvah* may be performed. Anytime from sunset until the streets empty is a valid time to light. Second: *l'shiurah* — the *braisa* is specifying the required capacity of the oil at the time of lighting. The candle must contain enough oil to burn for that duration; it need not actually do so.

Rabbah bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of *ad shetichleh regel min hashuk*: specifically, until the *Tarmudayim* have left the marketplace. Rashi explains that these were wood vendors — non-Jews who remained open the latest because people would realize only after nightfall that they needed more firewood and would come to purchase it. The choice of non-Jews, Rashi notes, addresses the obvious question of when Jews would be available to see the *Chanukah* lights if they themselves were lighting at that hour.

The question of precisely when the *mitzvah* window opens — at sunset or at *tzeit hakochavim* — is debated among the *Rishonim*, with arguments on both sides. Similarly, the duration until the streets empty: the *Shulchan Aruch* sets this at approximately half an hour, a figure that reflected conditions in his time. There is a well-known story of a rabbi in *Yerushalayim* who maintained his *menorah* burning until midnight because he lived across from a cinema whose last showing ended at that hour. In the *Shulchan Aruch*'s framework, even indoors — following the transition from public to private *pirsumei nisa* due to conditions of *sakanah* — a half-hour duration is generally accepted as sufficient.

### Timing & Duration

The transition from outdoor to indoor lighting reflects a broader historical development. The original *mitzvah* was designed for *pirsumei nisa* aimed at passers-by — the candle placed in the doorframe facing the street. In times of danger, when public display was prohibited by hostile authorities (Rashi references a Zoroastrian prohibition against lighting fires outside designated sacred sites), the practice moved indoors and focused on *pirsumei nisa* within the household. This shift brought with it greater leniency regarding timing, since even late in the evening the family members at home can witness the candles. The contemporary situation, where religious freedom permits public display, has led many to return to placing the *chanukiah* in a window facing outward, which is to be encouraged.

---

## Hanukkah Levels

### One vs. Per Person

The *Gemara* now presents a *tanu rabbanan* delineating graduated levels of *Chanukah* observance. At the basic level: *mitzvat Chanukah ner ish u'beito* — one candle per household. A single person lights a single candle for the entire family; this is the minimum fulfillment. For *hammehadrin* — those who seek to beautify the *mitzvah* — the standard is *ner l'chol echad v'echad*, one candle per individual in the household. The root *hadar*, from which *mehadrin* derives, connotes the beautification of a *mitzvah*, not stringency in the sense of prohibition. It is worth noting the contrast to the contemporary use of *mehadrin* and *mehadrin min hamehadrin* as markers of strict kashrut supervision — the original sense here is entirely about the positive enhancement of *mitzvah* performance.

### Shammai vs. Hillel

For *hammehadrin min hamehadrin* — those who seek the most beautiful fulfillment — there is a dispute. Beis Shammai says: on the first day one lights eight candles, and one decreases each subsequent day: 8, 7, 6, 5, and so on. Beis Hillel says: on the first day one lights one, and one adds a candle each day: 1, 2, 3, up to eight.

There is an important dispute among the *Rishonim* regarding what exactly happens when one reaches the level of *mehadrin min hamehadrin*. *Tosafot* holds that at this level one reverts to a single *chanukiah* for the entire household, because when multiple individuals light different numbers of candles simultaneously, an observer cannot discern the number of nights from the display. Rambam, by contrast, maintains that each individual continues to light individually, with each person's candle count reflecting the number of the night. The practice among *Ashkenazim* follows the Rambam's framework despite the general pattern of ruling like the *Rishonim* of France and Germany — an interesting crossover.

### Dispute Reasons

Ulla reports a dispute between two *Amoraim* of *Eretz Yisrael* — Rabbi Yose bar Abin and Rabbi Yose bar Zvida — regarding the rationale behind the Beis Shammai–Beis Hillel dispute. One opinion: Beis Shammai counts *yamim hanichnasin* — the days still to come — while Beis Hillel counts *yamim hayotzin* — the days that have passed. This is the most straightforward reading. The other opinion: Beis Shammai's descending count parallels the *parei hachag* — the bulls offered in the *musaf* of *Sukkos*, which descended from thirteen on the first day to seven on the seventh — while Beis Hillel relies on the principle of *ma'alin b'kodesh v'ein moridin*, that we ascend in holiness and do not descend.

Rabbah bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan told him of two elders in Sidon who lived at a time when the practice had not yet fully consolidated around Beis Hillel: one followed Beis Shammai and one followed Beis Hillel, each offering his stated rationale — one citing the parallel to the *parei hachag*, the other citing *ma'alin b'kodesh v'ein moridin*.

Several explanations of this dispute deserve mention. The Maharal observes that starting with eight and descending focuses on *potential* — on the eight days yet to come — while starting with one and ascending focuses on *actuality* — on the night one is presently in. This distinction may reflect a broader pattern running through Beis Shammai–Beis Hillel disputes. On a more evocative level, there is an analogy to the optimist and the pessimist: the descending count emphasizes how many days remain — a countdown to the end — while the ascending count reflects an orientation of openness and increasing joy, indifferent to the endpoint. A striking explanation is offered by Rav Shlomo Zevin, who frames the dispute around whether the message of *Chanukah* is about eradicating evil or spreading good. Beis Shammai, whose jurisprudential tendency is often more focused on human failing and the need to restrain it, counts downward in a manner that parallels the diminishing *parei hachag*, which represent the nations of the world declining. Beis Hillel, whose orientation is toward the spreading of positive holiness, counts upward — *ma'alin b'kodesh*. Even the image of the flame, Rav Zevin suggests, is understood differently: fire as a force that destroys the *ra*, or light as a force that spreads the good.

---

## Placement & Shamash

### Where to Place

The *tanu rabbanan* teaches: *ner Chanukah mitzvah lehannichah al petach beito mibachutz* — the *mitzvah* is to place the *Chanukah* candle at the doorway of one's home on the outside. Rashi explains this in terms of the courtyard: people entering and exiting the courtyard should see the candle in the doorframe. If one lives on an upper story (*aliyah*) where the doorway does not face the courtyard, one places it at the window nearest the public domain, so that passersby in the street can see it.

### Time of Danger

*Uvesha'at hasekanah* — in a time of danger — one simply places the candle on one's table indoors and that suffices. Rashi specifies the nature of the danger: a Zoroastrian prohibition requiring that fires be kindled only at their own sacred sites, not in private homes. The transition to indoor lighting — *al shulchano vedayo* — reflects the broader historical shift in how *pirsumei nisa* was understood, from an outward declaration to the public to an inward observance for the family. This is how the *Shulchan Aruch* rules. The question of how far to restore outdoor or visible lighting in contemporary conditions of religious freedom is one where the predominant practice is to place the *chanukiah* in a window.

### Shamash Purpose

Rava rules: *tzarich ner acher lehishtamesh leorah* — one requires an additional candle in order to use the light. This is the basis for the *shamash*. The purpose is twofold. First, since one may not use the *Chanukah* candles themselves for personal benefit (*ein lanu reshus lehishtamesh bahen*), one needs a separate candle whose light is permitted for use. Second — and this is Rashi's emphasis — the additional candle creates the *pirsumei nisa* by demonstrating that one does not need the *Chanukah* lights for illumination. An observer sees the *shamash* and understands that the *Chanukah* candles serve a different purpose entirely.

If there is already a *medura* — a larger fire or torch providing ample light — one does not need a *shamash*, since the abundant light already makes clear that the *Chanukah* candles are not for personal use. However, if one is a *chashuv* person — a prominent individual who would not normally avail himself of the coarser light of a torch and would instead use refined candlelight — then even in the presence of a *medura* one requires a *shamash*, so that observers will perceive the separate candlelight as sufficient for personal use and understand the *Chanukah* candles to be serving another purpose. In contemporary practice, with electric lighting universally available, the concern that prompts the requirement for a *shamash* is in effect answered by the electric lights themselves, which function as the equivalent of the *medura*.

---

## Hanukkah History

### Megillat Taanit

The *Gemara* now asks: *mai Chanukah* — what is *Chanukah*? This launches the *Gemara*'s sole explicit historical account of the holiday. The *tanu rabbanan* begins by citing *Megillat Taanit*: *bekaf-hey beKislev, yomei deChanukah temanya inun, dela lemispad behon udela lehitanot behon* — from the 25th of Kislev are eight days of *Chanukah*, on which one may not eulogize or fast.

*Megillat Taanit* is an early work — one of the earliest pieces of rabbinic writing — that enumerated the days on which fasting and eulogy were prohibited due to historical events. Most of those events have been entirely forgotten; the 25th of Kislev appears on that list without any greater elaboration than the other entries. There is, however, a Babylonian gloss appended to *Megillat Taanit*, and the *Gemara* now incorporates that gloss, which expands upon the bare reference and provides the narrative behind *Chanukah*.

### Greek Defilement

*Keshenichnasu Yevanim leHeichal* — when the Greeks entered the *Heichal*, the inner sanctuary of the *Beis HaMikdash* — *timu kol hashemanim shebaHeichal* — they contaminated all of the oils stored there, the oils that would have been used for the *menorah*. *Ucheshegavrah malchut Beis Chashmonai venitzchum* — when the *Chashmonai* dynasty prevailed and defeated them, they searched and found only a single *pach* of oil.

### Oil Miracle

The cruse of oil bore the seal of the *Kohen Gadol* — *shehayah munach bechotamo shel Kohen Gadol* — indicating that it had not been opened or tampered with and therefore remained *tahor*. It contained sufficient oil to burn for only one day. *Naasah bo nes* — a miracle occurred — *vehidliku mimenu shemonah yamim* — and from it they kindled for eight days.

### Yom Tov Status

The following year, the rabbis established these eight days as *Yom Tov* — *beHallel vehodaah* — with *Hallel* and thanksgiving. Rashi is careful to clarify: this is not *Yom Tov* in the sense of a prohibition on *melachah*. The designation consists of the recitation of *Hallel* and the addition of *Al Hanissim* in prayer and *birkat hamazon*. Notably absent from the *Gemara*'s description of what was established is the lighting of candles itself — an observation that invites reflection.

### Oil Miracle Meaning

Several questions cluster around this account. The most commonly raised is the so-called "*Beis Yosef* question": if there was oil for one day and it lasted eight days, the miracle was only of seven additional days, not eight — and this is the question for which a wide range of answers has been offered. The most intuitive answer, which the Maharal articulates, is that each day only one-eighth of the available oil was consumed, so the miracle manifested on each of the eight days equally.

A different question — why the miracle of the oil was emphasized at all — leads to a historically significant observation. All of the sources contemporaneous with the events of *Chanukah*, and all of the sources originating in *Eretz Yisrael*, focus exclusively on the military victory and the rededication of the *Beis HaMikdash*. The book of Maccabees attributes the eight-day celebration to a parallel with *Sukkos* (whose celebration had been deferred during the fighting). *Al Hanissim* mentions the military victory without any reference to the oil miracle. Josephus, when explaining why Jews light candles on *Chanukah*, suggests only that light symbolizes redemption, with no mention of any miracle involving oil. The miracle of the oil appears solely in this Babylonian gloss on *Megillat Taanit*.

The Maharal addresses this directly. He argues that the miracle of the oil was designed to demonstrate the divine significance of the military victory. One might otherwise attribute the *Chashmonai* triumph to human valor alone, without recognizing God's role. The small miraculous sign — the single cruse burning for eight days — was intended to reveal the divine hand behind the larger events, connecting the military victory to the rededication of the *Beis HaMikdash* and infusing the entire episode with religious meaning. The oil miracle was, in the Maharal's reading, a vehicle for making legible what was truly at stake.

This has implications for how the concept of *mehadrin min hamehadrin* fits into the broader picture of *Chanukah*. One might suggest that the meticulous, layered care invested in *pirsumei nisa* — with its levels of basic, *mehadrin*, and *mehadrin min hamehadrin* — mirrors the extraordinary gesture God made in revealing the divine through this particular miracle. Just as that miracle went beyond what was necessary to make the point, so too the most beautiful fulfillment of *Chanukah* goes beyond the minimum. The fundamental educational question of *Chanukah* — whether the holiday is primarily about the oil miracle or about the historical struggle for religious independence — remains, and the *Gemara*'s account, read together with the Maharal's interpretation, suggests that the miracle of the oil and the victory of the *Chashmonaim* are not competing narratives but interlocking ones: the miraculous cruse gives the war its proper religious meaning, and the war gives the cruse its proper historical context.

---

---

# Shabbat 22

## Megillat Ta'anit Sources

### Megillat Ta'anit

Today's daf is 22a, and we continue our discussion of Chanukah. Before turning to the Gemara proper, it is worth pausing to examine the source most often associated with the Chanukah narrative: *Megillat Ta'anit*. A recent academic volume by Vered Noam has brought serious scholarly attention to this text, which is, in fact, remarkably brief. The entire entry for Kislev reads as follows: *Bi-tlata be-Kislev itnussun timusa min darta, bi-shiva yom tava, va-esrim va-achad yom Har Gerizim, u-va-esrim ve-chamisha pucha Chanukah yomin tamnaya de-lo le-mispade, ba-esrim u-temanya ne-itosei* — and then the text moves on to Tevet. That is it. A few words for each of the four or five days per month on which a *hesped* is prohibited, with no further elaboration whatsoever.

### Textual Variants

Very early on, a gloss on *Megillat Ta'anit* appeared — known in scholarly terminology as a *scholion* (plural: *scholia*) — which provided historical background for each of the holidays listed in the text. This gloss, composed probably at the end of the Tannaitic period and the beginning of the Amoraic period, exists in two significantly different versions: one that appears to derive from Eretz Yisrael and one from Bavel. What we possess today as the standard scholion on *Megillat Ta'anit* is in fact a hybrid of these two early versions, with heavy influence from the Talmud Bavli and extensive grafts from it. Neither of the two original manuscript families contains the story of the oil miracle. The oil miracle, as a historical-textual matter, originates exclusively in the Talmud Bavli, and from there it made its way into the later hybrid recension of the scholion.

### Eight Days Debate

Both early versions of the scholion do attempt to explain why Chanukah is celebrated for eight days, but they do so without any reference to oil. Their reasoning is as follows: when the *Chanukat HaMishkan* was inaugurated it lasted seven days, and similarly the *Chanukat HaMizbeach* in the time of Shlomo lasted seven days — so why eight days here? The scholion explains that they were occupied for eight days rededicating the *mizbeach*, remaking a *menorah*, and attending to the lighting of the *menorah*. One version adds that because all the *kelim* were *tamei*, they had to construct a new *menorah* — the tradition recorded also in the Bavli, that their initial *menorah* was fashioned from their spears covered with lead. But nowhere in either of these early versions is there any mention of the oil being *tamei* or requiring purification. That element belongs entirely to the Bavli.

### Oil Miracle & Presence

The Maharal is troubled by the prominence the Bavli gives to the oil miracle. His fundamental answer is that while the primary miracle of Chanukah was of course the military victory over the Greeks and the rededication of the *Mikdash*, the miracle of the oil served to demonstrate that it was God who was part of that entire process — that it was about God's presence, the *Shechinah*, once again dwelling with *Bnei Yisrael*. This is a point that the *aggadata* we will encounter shortly makes vivid and explicit. Understanding this theological dimension helps clarify why the Bavli places such emphasis on the oil miracle and why it became the defining narrative of the holiday.

### Mehadrin Levels

This framework also informs the discussion of *mehadrin min hamehadrin*. Some want to explain that even if *tahor* oil was not strictly necessary — since *tumah hutra betzibbur* — or even if *tahor* oil could have been obtained by other means, the fact that they went out of their way to perform the lighting *betaharah*, even when it was not strictly required, reflects an act of *hiddur*, of striving for the best possible fulfillment. And mirroring that striving, as the Maharal explains, God went out of His way to demonstrate His involvement and His presence. The miracle of the oil is thus a *nes* that reflects divine reciprocity, and it is in this spirit that the levels of *mehadrin* and *mehadrin min hamehadrin* take on their deeper meaning.

---

## Bava Kamma Parallels

### Overloaded Camel

The Gemara now cites a *Mishnah* from tractate Bava Kamma: *Gitz hayotzei mitachat hapatish veyatza vehizik, chayav* — if a spark flew out from under a hammer and caused damage, the blacksmith is liable. This *Mishnah* is discussing *esh*, fire, one of the four categories of damage caused by one's property. The *Mishnah* continues: if a camel laden with flax was walking through the *reshut harabim* — the public domain — and the overloaded flax extended beyond the permissible width and entered a storekeeper's shop, where it caught fire from the storekeeper's candle, and that fire then spread and ignited a large building, the owner of the camel is liable. Not only is the storekeeper exempt, but the camel owner, by overloading his animal and causing it to exceed the parameters of the *reshut harabim*, essentially added fuel to the flame and is therefore responsible for all resulting damage.

### Storekeeper Liability

However, *hiniach hachanvani nero mibachutz* — if the storekeeper had placed his candle on the outside of his store, in the space that normally belongs to those traversing the *reshut harabim*, then the storekeeper is liable for any damage caused, since it is now effectively his fire.

### Chanukah Exception

*Rabbi Yehuda omer: be-ner Chanukah patur* — Rabbi Yehuda rules that if it was a Chanukah candle, the storekeeper is exempt. The reasoning is that one is entitled to keep Chanukah candles outside, and those traversing the *reshut harabim* during Chanukah must take appropriate care to keep their loads pulled in. There may also be a broader principle at work — that performing a *mitzvah* confers a degree of exemption from certain liability in such cases. These are questions that belong to a full treatment of Bava Kamma.

One notes that Chanukah appears only this once in the *Mishnayot* — three words, *be-ner Chanukah patur*, as a parenthetical statement — and that there is no tractate dedicated to Chanukah the way there is a tractate *Megillah* devoted to Purim. The Ramban suggests this may reflect rabbinic unease with the Chashmonaim — not regarding the *nes Chanukah* itself, but for their subsequent seizure of political authority, which properly belonged to *Beit David*, in violation of the principle that *kehunah* and religious authority must be separated from political rule. Whatever one makes of that explanation, the singular and brief appearance of Chanukah in the Mishnah is certainly worth noting.

### Ten Tefachim Height

Ravina, citing Rava — or according to some readings, in the name of Rava — draws an inference from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling: *zot omeret ner Chanukah mitzvah lehannicha betoch asara* — this teaches that it is a *mitzvah* to place the Chanukah candle within ten *tefachim* of the ground. The reasoning: if there were no upper limit on the permitted height, then the storekeeper should have been told that since he is allowed to keep it in the *reshut harabim*, he ought to place it higher than even a camel with its rider, thereby putting it out of anyone's way entirely. The fact that Rabbi Yehuda grants the exemption without requiring such a height implies that one is *not* required — or indeed permitted — to place it that high.

The Gemara pushes back: perhaps the argument fails because *im matracha lei tuvah ati le-imnu-ei mimitzvah* — if we imposed too great a burden on people, they would simply refrain from performing the *mitzvah* altogether. It is therefore not that one cannot place it higher; rather, we accommodate people by allowing a convenient placement, and once that right has been granted, the responsibility shifts to those in the *reshut harabim* to take due care. This reflects the broader principle in Bava Kamma about how competing rights in the public domain are adjudicated: generally, the person exercising a recognized right is not the negligent party, and the one who fails to account for that right bears the liability. Fire, however, operates somewhat differently, which is why this case requires more careful analysis.

---

## Height Restrictions

### Twenty Amot Limit

The Gemara records that Rav Kahana taught in the name of Rav Natan bar Minyomi, who expounded in the name of Rabbi Tanchum, on daf 22a: *ner shel Chanukah shehinicho lemala me'esrim amah pesula* — a Chanukah candle placed higher than twenty *amah* is invalid. The two standard height thresholds in *halacha* are ten *tefachim* — roughly three feet — and twenty *amah* — roughly thirty feet. The question of whether the candle must be placed within ten *tefachim* was raised above. Here we learn that twenty *amah* is an absolute upper limit.

### Sukkah & Mavoi

The reason offered is *kesukkah u'kemavoi* — as with a *sukkah* and as with a *mavoi*. In both of those domains, something situated higher than twenty *amah* is treated as non-functional because it is not naturally visible from ground level. A *sukkah* whose *sechach* is higher than twenty *amah* is invalid according to one explanation because one will not naturally look up and notice the *sechach*; one senses the walls but not the defining feature above. Similarly, the beam (*korah*) that marks the fourth side of a *mavoi* — the opening that has no wall — must be visible to serve its function as a *heker*, a sign indicating the permissible boundary. If placed above twenty *amah*, it will not be seen and cannot function as such. The same logic applies to *ner Chanukah*: *pirsumei nisa* requires that the candle actually be seen by those passing in the *reshut harabim*, and above twenty *amah* that condition cannot be met.

This ruling raises obvious practical questions for those who live on upper floors. The Gemara noted earlier that one who *dar be'aliyah* places the candle in the window closest to the *reshut harabim*; in Talmudic times, upper floors were generally not more than thirty feet off the ground. Contemporary multi-story dwellings present a genuine *she'elah*, though the possibility of fulfilling the *mitzvah* for the members of one's household — without the requirement of public visibility — remains available, as does the fact that wide streets and greater distances can sometimes allow for meaningful visibility at greater heights.

### Yosef's Pit

The same chain of tradition — Rav Kahana citing Rav Natan bar Minyomi in the name of Rabbi Tanchum — also offers a *derash* on a verse in *Parashat Vayeshev*, the *parasha* always read during Chanukah: *ve-habor reik ein bo mayim* — the pit was empty, there was no water. The Torah already tells us it was empty; surely that implies there was no water. So why add *ein bo mayim*? The Gemara answers: *mayim ein bo, aval nechasim va'akrabim yesh bo* — there was no water, but there were snakes and scorpions. The *Torah Temimah* connects this to the twenty-*amah* principle: perhaps the pit was deeper than twenty *amah*, which is why Reuven, who intended to rescue Yosef, did not perceive the snakes and scorpions within it — they were too far below to be visible. Just as things beyond twenty *amah* upward are invisible to the eye, so too things deeper than twenty *amah* downward cannot be seen. The application to *ner Chanukah* is apparent: visibility is bounded in both directions. The *derash* itself is admittedly somewhat *ikkar chaseir min hasefer* — the twenty *amah* is not mentioned explicitly in the verse — but the principle it illustrates is clear.

---

## Doorway Placement

### Tefach Position

Rabbah rules: *ner Chanukah mitzvah lehannichah be-tefach hasemucha le-fetach* — the proper placement of the Chanukah candle is within a *tefach* of the doorway, on the outside. If placed too far from one's doorway, passersby will not associate it with one's home and will not recognize it as a *ner Chanukah*. The *tefach* in question is approximately three to four inches — the candle must be quite close to the doorpost or door frame, so that its association with one's residence is unambiguous.

### Right vs Left

Which side of the doorway? *Rav Acha bereih de-Rabba amar mi-yamin* — on the right, meaning the right side as one faces inward from outside. *Rav Shmuel mi-Diphti amar mi-smol* — on the left. The *hilchata*, the ruling, is *mi-smol* — on the left — *kedei she-tehei ner Chanukah mi-smol u-mezuzah mi-yamin*: so that the Chanukah candle is on the left and the *mezuzah* is on the right, surrounding the entrant with *mitzvot* on both sides. Presumably the opinion that favored the right held that the right always takes priority and thus both should be on the right; the ruling, however, is that separating them — one on each side — is preferable. This is also the accepted practice.

---

## Counting Money Ban

### Money Counting

Rav Yehuda, citing Rav Assi — though there is a variant reading that attributes this to Rav or to Rav Yirmeyah — states: *assur le-hartzos ma'os keneged ner Chanukah* — it is forbidden to count money in the presence of the Chanukah lights.

### Kedushah Question

When this ruling was reported before Shmuel, he objected: *ve-chi ner kedushah yesh bah?* — does the Chanukah candle possess *kedushah*? If an object is sanctified to the *Beit HaMikdash*, deriving *hana'ah* from it is forbidden. But a Chanukah candle is not such an object — it is used for a *mitzvah*, but it carries no formal *kedushah*. One would not say, for example, that a person cannot fidget with their *tzitzit* because doing so treats a sacred object improperly. Why then should one be prohibited from counting money by the light of *ner Chanukah*?

### Blood Covering

Rav Yosef responds sharply: *hachi dami kedushah yesh bo?* — is *kedushah* really the only basis for such a restriction? Consider the *mitzvah* of *kisuy hadam*: when one slaughters a *chayah* or a bird, the blood must be covered with earth. The verse says *veshafach vechisah* — one spills the blood and covers it. *Bamah sheshafach yechaseh* — the act of covering follows directly from the act of spilling, meaning one uses one's hand or a shovel. But *shelo yechasenu beregel* — one may not kick the dirt over with one's foot, which would be the most natural and effortless gesture. Why? *Shelo yehyu mitzvot buzuyot alav* — so that *mitzvot* should not be degraded in one's eyes. Kicking dirt over something is dismissive; it signals disregard. Therefore the act must be done respectfully. *Hacha nami* — here too, *shelo yehyu mitzvot buzuyot alav*: counting money by the Chanukah candle is not a question of *kedushah*, but of respect. The *mitzvah* must not be treated as a backdrop for mundane activity.

### Reconciling Sources

There is considerable discussion among the *Rishonim* about how to understand this passage and how it relates to the earlier *sugya* on whether one may *hishtamesh le-orah* — derive benefit from the light of *ner Chanukah*. The two discussions appear side by side without the Gemara explicitly connecting them, and the *Rishonim* disagree sharply about how to integrate them.

The *Ba'al HaMaor* takes the following approach. The earlier discussion — whether one may derive benefit from the light — operated according to the view that there is a quasi-*kedushah* to the Chanukah candle, at least in a rabbinic sense: since the *mitzvah* is modeled on the lighting of the *Menorah* in the *Mikdash*, the rabbis treated the candle as if it had borrowed a dimension of the *kedushah* of the *Menorah's* light, and on that basis one should not derive *hana'ah* from it. That was the concern of the earlier passage. The present passage, however, operates on the assumption that there is no such *kedushah* — and therefore generally speaking one may make use of the light. The distinct concern here is that counting money, a particularly mundane and undignified act, constitutes *bizuy mitzvah* — denigration of the *mitzvah* — and is therefore prohibited. According to the *Ba'al HaMaor*, the *halacha* is thus: no formal prohibition on using the light for legitimate purposes, but using it for crass mundane activity like counting money is denigrating and is forbidden.

The Ramban inverts the analysis. He argues that the earlier prohibition on *hishtamesh le-orah* — according to Rashi — was concerned with sustained use of the candle's light for personal purposes, since this would undermine *pirsumei nisa* by making it appear as though the candle was lit for practical illumination. Brief and incidental use, such as glancing at a coin for a moment, should not raise the same concern. It ought to be permitted. Yet the Gemara forbids even this. The Ramban therefore concludes that the answer invoking *bizuy mitzvah* is not merely identifying a denigrating act — after all, counting coins is hardly comparable in its crudeness to kicking dirt over blood — but rather establishing a legal framework: in order to institutionalize the prohibition against denigrating *mitzvah* objects, the rabbis treat the candle *as if* it has *kedushah*, which then generates a blanket prohibition on any use whatsoever. The invocation of *kedushah* is thus not a description of the candle's intrinsic status but a legal mechanism for enforcing *bizuy mitzvah* prevention.

In practical terms: according to the *Ba'al HaMaor*, the prohibition is specifically against degrading, mundane uses, while permissible uses — including fulfillment of other *mitzvot* or even having one's Shabbat meal by its light — remain allowed. According to the Ramban, the prohibition is absolute during the time the candle is burning, precisely because we institutionalize the *bizuy* concern by treating it as *kedushah*-bearing — and therefore any use is forbidden.

---

## Sukkah Decoration Use

### Using Decorations

The Gemara now raises a related question directed to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *noi sukkah mahu lehistapek mimeno kol shiva?* — may one make use of the decorations of the *sukkah* during the seven days of Sukkot? Specifically, if one has hung edible fruits and other foods as *noi sukkah*, may one pluck them down and eat them if one is hungry? The response given was: just as one may not count money by *ner Chanukah*, so too one may not divert *noi sukkah* from its purpose.

### Tanna vs Amora

Rav Yosef objects vigorously: *mari d'Avraham! tali tanya bidla tanya* — God of Abraham! You are making a *Tannaitic* source dependent on a non-*Tannaitic* source. The ruling about *noi sukkah* is derived from a *Baraita* — a *Tannaitic* source. The ruling about not counting money by *ner Chanukah* is an *Amoraic* ruling. One cannot reason from the Chanukah case to establish the *sukkah* case; if anything, the direction of reasoning should be the reverse — we know the Chanukah ruling from the *sukkah* precedent, not the *sukkah* ruling from Chanukah.

### Baraita Prohibition

The *Baraita* reads as follows: *sichachah kehilchasah* — if one laid *sechach* properly — *ve'itra bekarmeyim, uvesadinin, umetzuyarin* — and then beautified it with colored sheets and decorated fabrics — *vetalah bah egozin, afarsekin, shkedim, verimonim, ufarkilei anavim, ve'ataros shel shibolin, yeinos, shemanim* — and hung from the *sechach* nuts, peaches, almonds, pomegranates, clusters of grapes, wreaths of grain, and containers of wine and oil — *assur lehistapek mehen kol shiva* — it is forbidden to make use of any of these throughout the seven days — *ad motzei Yom Tov ha'acharon shel Chag* — until after the conclusion of Shemini Atzeret. Since one may not use them during *bein hashmashos* at the end of Sukkot lest Sukkot still be in effect, one also cannot use them on Shemini Atzeret.

### Stipulation Override

However, *ve'im hisna aleihen* — if one stipulated at the outset that despite designating these items as *noi sukkah* one was not fully devoting them for that purpose and reserves the right to use them at any time — *hakol lefi tena'o* — the stipulation is effective. The details of how such a *tenai* operates need not detain us here; the basic teaching is that the prohibition without a *tenai* is complete, but the restriction can be overridden by a prior declaration.

### Blood Root

Rav Yosef then draws together the threads of this discussion. *Avohon dekulhu dam* — the root, the father of all these rulings, is the case of blood. From the requirement to cover blood properly — and specifically from the prohibition against kicking dirt over it with one's foot — we derive the fundamental principle that *mitzvot* must be treated with dignity. From that root principle flows the teaching about *ner Chanukah* and the teaching about *noi sukkah*. It is worth noting that these three cases are not precisely parallel: kicking dirt over blood is an affirmatively crude act; counting money by a candle is mundane and dismissive; and diverting *noi sukkah* from its *mitzvah* purpose actually removes it from its function entirely — something not true in the other cases. The *Rishonim* are well aware of this complexity.

The *sukkah* case is in fact further distinguished by additional legal features. The *sechach* and *noi sechach* are *muktza* on *Yom Tov*; even an object that falls off the *sukkah* may not be handled. Moreover, a verse — *chag hasukkot ta'aseh lecha* — is interpreted to mean that *shem shamayim*, God's name, descends upon the *sechach*, conferring upon it a dimension of genuine *kedushah*. And according to several *Gemarot*, this *kedushah* extends to the *noi sukkah* as well. The *Rishonim* therefore wrestle with whether the prohibition on *noi sukkah* is about *bizuy mitzvah* or about intrinsic *kedushah* — or some combination of both. The Ramban's answer, as noted earlier, is that the mechanism of *kedushah* is itself the vehicle for institutionalizing *bizuy mitzvah* prevention.

What unites all these cases — *ner Chanukah*, *noi sukkah*, *lulav*, *esrog*, *sechach*, *tzitzit* — is that during the time they are actively fulfilling their *mitzvah* function, they are subject either to *bizuy mitzvah* restrictions or to something approaching *kedushah*. Once the *mitzvah* period ends, however, that status lapses. This is the category of *tashmishei kedushah* — objects used *for* a *mitzvah*, as distinct from objects upon which *shem Hashem* is written, such as *tefillin* and *mezuzah*. A *lulav* after Sukkot, a *ner Chanukah* after it has burned out — these may be used for other purposes or respectfully discarded. The defining characteristic is temporal: the restrictions apply *during* the *mitzvah* period, and there they apply in two dimensions: do not divert the object from its *mitzvah* purpose, and do not use it in a manner that is denigrating. Once the *mitzvah* time has passed, neither constraint applies.

---

## Candle-to-Candle Lighting

### Rav's Prohibition

The Gemara now addresses a related question: *Rav amar ein madlikin mi-ner l'ner* — Rav rules that one may not light one Chanukah candle from another. This has obvious implications for the function of the *shamash*: before, the *shamash* was discussed in the context of making it clear that one is not deriving personal benefit from the Chanukah lights. Here a separate concern arises — if one may not light from one Chanukah candle to the next, one needs another implement to accomplish the lighting.

### Shmuel's Allowance

*Shmuel amar madlikin* — Shmuel rules that one may light from one candle to the next. Once the first candle is lit, it may serve to kindle the others.

### Three Debates

The Gemara presents these positions as part of a cluster of three debates between Rav and Shmuel in which the general rule — that we follow Rav in disputes with Shmuel — is overridden, and the *halacha* follows Shmuel in all three. Abaye testifies: *kol mili d'mar Rabba avid k'Rav, l'bar mihani tlata d'avid k'Shmuel* — in all matters, Rabba, Abaye's teacher, ruled like Rav, except for these three cases where he sided with Shmuel.

The first is the case before us: *madlikin mi-ner l'ner* — one may light from one Chanukah candle to another. The second: *matirin mi-beged l'beged* — one may remove *tzitzit* from one garment and transfer it to another, even while the first garment remains usable. Rav had prohibited this on the grounds that one is removing the *mitzvah* status from the first garment even if the goal is to enable a *mitzvah* on another garment. Shmuel permits it, and Rabba — and by extension the *halacha* — sides with Shmuel. The third: *halacha k'Rabbi Shimon b'gerira* — we rule like Rabbi Shimon regarding dragging furniture on Shabbat.

This third dispute requires context. The *Mishnah* discusses dragging a bed, chair, or bench across a dirt floor on Shabbat. Doing so might inadvertently create a furrow, which would constitute a *melacha* — either the beginning of plowing or an act of construction. Rabbi Shimon holds: *gorer adam mita kisse v'safsal, u'belvad shelo yitkaven la'asot haritz* — one may drag them, provided one does not intend to create a furrow. This is the principle of *aino mitkaven* — an unintended act that may or may not occur does not render the original action prohibited. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, holding that since the furrow might result, the action is forbidden. Rav ruled like Rabbi Yehuda; Shmuel ruled like Rabbi Shimon, and the *halacha* follows Shmuel. The practical importance of this ruling can scarcely be overstated: if *aino mitkaven* were prohibited, the restrictions of Shabbat would be vastly more burdensome — one could not walk through mud, snow, or soft earth, among countless other everyday situations.

---

## Rav's Reasoning

### Bizuy Mitzvah

Why does Rav prohibit lighting one Chanukah candle from another? A rabbinic student sitting before Rav Adda bar Ahava offered the explanation: *ta'ama d'Rav mishum bizuy mitzvah* — the reason of Rav is *bizuy mitzvah*, the lighting being insufficiently respectful toward the *mitzvah*. This might seem puzzling — why would using one Chanukah candle to light another be disrespectful?

### Machish Mitzvah

Rav Adda bar Ahava rejected this explanation sharply, telling the other rabbis present: *lo titzitu lei* — do not pay attention to him. *Ta'ama d'Rav mishum d'ka machish mitzvah* — the reason of Rav is that it looks as though one is *depleting* the *mitzvah*. Literally the candle loses nothing, but as Rashi explains, the visual impression of moving flame from one candle to another creates an appearance as though one is somehow drawing away from the first candle and diminishing it. The concern is the visual impression of depletion, not actual depletion.

### Direct vs Intermediate

The Gemara then identifies the practical difference between these two explanations. *Ika beinaihu d'ka madlik mishraga l'shraga* — the case in which one goes directly from one candle to the other. If the reason for Rav's prohibition is *bizuy mitzvah*, then going directly from one Chanukah candle to the next is actually *permitted* — for there is no disrespect when one *mitzvah* object is used directly to perform another *mitzvah* act. What would be denigrating is using an intermediary — a match or a sliver of wood — because the immediate act of applying the match to a burning Chanukah candle is not itself an act of *mitzvah*; it is a preliminary action, and using a Chanukah candle to fuel a mundane preliminary step is *bizuy mitzvah*. But if one goes directly, the burning candle is immediately and entirely in service of a *mitzvah* act.

If, however, the concern is *machish mitzvah* — the appearance of depleting the *mitzvah* — then even going directly from one candle to the other is forbidden, because the visual impression of drawing light away from one candle and giving it to another is precisely the problem regardless of whether an intermediary is used. In that case, neither direct nor indirect lighting from one Chanukah candle to another is permitted, and one must use a *shamash* instead.

---

## Ma'aser Sheni Analogy

### Coin Counterweight

Rav Avya raises a challenge from the laws of *ma'aser sheni*. In the third and sixth years of the sabbatical cycle, a *ma'aser sheni* — second tithe — would have to be brought to Jerusalem. Since transporting large quantities of produce could be difficult, one could redeem the *ma'aser sheni* onto coins, which then acquired *kedushat ma'aser sheni*, and bring those coins to Jerusalem instead. Now: *ein shoklin kenegdo dinarei zahav* — one may not use such a coin as a counterweight on a balance scale to measure out gold *dinarim*. That would be using an object of genuine *kedushah* for a mundane purpose.

More strikingly, the prohibition extends even to a case in which the weighed gold coins will themselves be used to redeem other *ma'aser sheni*: *ve'afilu lechalel alav ma'aser sheni acher* — even if the purpose of the weighing is to redeem additional *ma'aser sheni*, the use of the *ma'aser sheni* coin as a counterweight is forbidden. This case is closely analogous to the question of lighting *ner Chanukah* through an intermediary: in both situations, the object of concern is being used as an intermediate step toward a valid and even laudable purpose, but the intermediate use itself is problematic.

Rav Avya's argument is as follows: if Rav and Shmuel debate only about going directly from one candle to the next — with both agreeing that using an intermediary is forbidden — then the *ma'aser sheni* case presents no contradiction, since there too using an intermediary toward a *mitzvah* goal is forbidden. But if Shmuel permits even the use of an intermediary — a sliver of wood placed between the two Chanukah candles — then why is the analogous case of the *ma'aser sheni* coin forbidden even when the gold coins will be used for a *mitzvah* purpose?

### Risk of Failure

Rava answers: *gezira shema lo yechawein mishkolosav vechamapki lehu lechullin* — it is a rabbinic decree against the possibility that the weights may not come out correctly. If one places gold coins on the scale and they do not equal the needed amount, one may abandon the whole enterprise and put those coins to entirely non-*mitzvah* use. Because there is a realistic probability that the process will fail and the coins will never actually go toward *ma'aser sheni* redemption, we cannot rely on the stated intention. The intermediary in that case is too unreliable.

In the case of the *shamash* or a sliver of wood used to light the next Chanukah candle, while in theory the match might blow out, the likelihood that the process will succeed is high enough that we do not impose a comparable decree. Rava's answer thus distinguishes the two cases on the basis of the reliability of the intended outcome, and in doing so leaves open the possibility that Shmuel does indeed permit lighting through an intermediary — a question that remains somewhat unresolved.

---

## Temple Menorah

### Testimony & Presence

The Gemara introduces the *Menorah* into the discussion of *ner Chanukah*, at least by way of analogy. A verse states: *michutz laparoches ha'eidus yaaroch* — outside the curtain of the *Edut*, Aaron shall arrange the lamps. The Gemara asks: does God need the light of the *Menorah*? And further: for forty years in the desert, *Bnei Yisrael* walked by God's light — they needed God's light, not the other way around. So why light the *Menorah*? *Ela edut hi l'va'ei olam shehashchina shara b'Yisrael* — it is testimony to all who enter the world that the *Shechinah* dwells within Israel.

This is a striking passage, and it connects directly to the theological dimension of Chanukah developed earlier. The *Chazal* understood the *Menorah's* light as a symbol of God's presence. When the Chashmonaim rededicated the *Mikdash*, the deeper significance of that act was not merely the physical cleaning and restoration, but the removal of the spiritual *tumah* introduced by the Greeks and their idols — and the re-establishment of the *Mikdash* as a place where *Shechinah* could once again dwell. When the *Mishkan* was first dedicated, fire descended from heaven as a sign of divine acceptance. At Chanukah, the sign was different: the miracle of the oil. To understand what the *Menorah's* light represents — testimony to divine presence — is to understand why that particular *nes* was the vehicle for divine confirmation that the rededication had succeeded. It was not simply a wondrous event; it was God demonstrating that He was once again dwelling His presence in the *Mikdash*. This, as the Maharal explains, is the inner meaning of *nes Chanukah*, and the Gemara here, while not spelling out that connection explicitly, provides the theological foundation for it.

### Ner Maaravi

Rav then identifies the specific form this testimony took: *zo ner maaravi* — it is the western lamp. The *ner maaravi* was one branch of the *Menorah* — most commonly understood to be the central lamp, oriented toward the *Kodesh HaKodashim* — and it received the same measure of oil as all the other lamps. Yet two things distinguished it: first, *u-mimena hayah madlik* — they would light the other lamps from it; and second, *u-vah hayah mesayim* — it was the last to be cleaned out and refilled.

The miracle was this: each night, all the lamps were filled with oil and lit. By morning, some or all of the outer lamps would have gone out — particularly on summer nights when there was less darkness to fill. The *ner maaravi*, however, burned on. By a continuous daily miracle, it lasted a full twenty-four hours, still burning when nighttime arrived again. During the day, the other lamps would be cleaned out and refilled; the *ner maaravi* was left burning until the end of the day, at which point it alone was cleaned out, given new oil and a new wick. Then that newly prepared *ner maaravi* was used to light all the other lamps, and the cycle began again. This daily miracle was the testimony — the ongoing demonstration that the *Shechinah* dwelt within Israel.

It should be noted that a certain *Baraita* records that this miracle did not persist for the entire period of the *Mikdash*; there were times when the miracle ceased and the fire of the *mizbeach* had to be used to relight the *Menorah*. But during the period when it obtained, it constituted a daily, visible sign of divine presence.

### Long Wicks

The relevance of the *ner maaravi* to our *halachic* discussion about lighting *ner Chanukah* from one candle to the next is this: the practice in the *Mikdash* was to light the other lamps *from* the *ner maaravi*, which would seem to permit the very act Rav prohibits — using one consecrated lamp to light another. Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty: *targumah b'fitilot ha'aruchot* — they used very long wicks. The wick of the *ner maaravi* was extended all the way to the adjacent lamp and lit directly, without any separation. This resolves the case according to the view that direct lighting is permitted — one need not say there was any violation of the rule.

---

## Menorah Resolution

### Lighting vs Placing

The question raised regarding the *ner maaravi* — that the *Menorah* lamps were lit from each other — remains difficult according to at least one position. The Gemara therefore introduces a broader conceptual debate that reframes the entire question. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua asks: *ee hadlakah oseh mitzvah, madlikin mi-ner l'ner* — if the act of *mitzvah* is fulfilled at the moment of lighting, then lighting from one candle to the next is permitted, because the act is itself a *ma'aseh mitzvah* and cannot be called *bizuy mitzvah* or *machish mitzvah*. *Ee hanacha oseh mitzvah, ein madlikin mi-ner l'ner* — but if the *mitzvah* is fulfilled not through the act of lighting but through the act of placing the candle in its proper position, then the act of lighting is merely preparatory, and using one Chanukah candle to kindle another is an inappropriate use of a *mitzvah* object for a non-*mitzvah* act.

### If Hadlakah

If *hadlakah* — the act of lighting itself — constitutes the fulfillment of the *mitzvah*, then the entire concern about lighting from one candle to the next dissolves. The candle is engaged in a *mitzvah* act at the very moment it is used to kindle its neighbor, and there is no basis for either *bizuy mitzvah* or *machish mitzvah*.

### If Hanachah

If *hanacha* — the placing or positioning of the lit candle — is the operative act of *mitzvah*, then lighting is nothing more than a preparatory step. In that case, using one Chanukah candle to perform a preparatory step toward another candle's eventual placement becomes problematic, for the candle is being used not for a *mitzvah* act but for a preliminary stage, and the concerns of Rav reassert themselves.

---

## Mitzvah Essence

### Held Candle

The Gemara now brings cases to test which of the two positions is correct. Rava rules: *haya tofus ner Chanukah v'omed lo asah v'lo klum* — if one held the Chanukah candle in one's hand while lighting it, and remained standing with it lit in hand, one has not fulfilled the *mitzvah*. At first glance, this seems to support *hanacha*: the candle was lit but never placed down, and therefore the *mitzvah* was not achieved.

### Flashlight Problem

The Gemara immediately rejects that inference. *Hasam haro'eh omer l'tzarcho hu d'nakit lei* — there, the problem is that an observer would say: he is holding it for his own purposes. A person who carries a lit candle around in their hand appears to be using it as a flashlight — moving through a dark space by its light. Such a candle does not broadcast *pirsumei nisa*; its purpose is ambiguous at best. The disqualification therefore has nothing to do with whether *hanacha* is the operative *mitzvah* act; it is because the act of lighting, while held, is not a meaningful act of *mitzvah* lighting at all, since it cannot serve the purpose of *pirsumei nisa* in that configuration.

### Indoor Lighting

The Gemara tries again. Rava rules: *hidlikah bifnim v'hotzia lo asah v'lo klum* — if one lit the candle indoors and then carried it outside to the doorway — recall that the *mitzvah* requires placing the candle at the outer doorway — one has not fulfilled the *mitzvah*. This seems to support *hadlakah*: if *hanacha* were the operative act, then placing the lit candle outside after having lit it inside should be perfectly valid — one performed the lighting (preparatory), and then performed the placing (the *mitzvah*). Yet the ruling is that one has not fulfilled the obligation. *Ee amrat bishlama hadlakah oseh mitzvah, hadlakah bimkomah bainan* — if the *mitzvah* is the act of lighting, this is readily explained: the lighting must occur at the proper location, and lighting indoors does not fulfill that requirement.

### Carrying Problem

But then *ela ee amrat hanacha oseh mitzvah, amai lo asah v'lo klum?* — if *hanacha* is the operative act, why is this invalid? One lit it inside and then placed it outside — the *hanacha* occurred in the right place. The Gemara answers: *hasam nami haro'eh omer l'tzarcho hu d'adlakah* — there too, the problem is the observer. When one walks from indoors to outdoors carrying a lit candle, the passerby sees a person carrying a light and naturally assumes it is being used as a flashlight. The movement itself — the carrying — confuses the purpose and undermines *pirsumei nisa*. Accordingly, the lighting must occur outdoors and the placing must follow immediately and in place, so that neither the act of lighting nor the subsequent positioning of the candle can be mistaken for ordinary domestic use of a light source. We will continue with this debate in the next shiur.

---

---

# Shabbat 23

## Hadlaka vs. Hanacha

### Core Question Setup

We pick up from the very last line of 22b. The question before us is how to understand the *mitzvah* of *ner Chanukah* — a core halakhic and conceptual issue. *Ner Chanukah* is interesting in two respects: first, who are the people obligated, given that the *Gemara* earlier spoke of *ner ish u'veito*, one lamp per household, then every person in the house, then *mehadrin min ha-mehadrin*; and second, what precisely is the obligation — to do what?

### Hadlaka or Hanacha

The *Gemara* frames the question as follows: is it *hadlaka oseh mitzvah* — the act of lighting that constitutes the *mitzvah* — or *hanacha oseh mitzvah* — the act of placing the lamp down? The *Gemara* explores two scenarios where this distinction would make a practical difference. In the first, one lights indoors at a time when the interior is not a valid location, and then carries the lamp outside to the proper spot. The act of lighting was performed incorrectly, but the placement was done correctly. In theory, if *hanacha* is the *mitzvah*, this should suffice. The *Gemara*, however, finds a way to eliminate this difference: carrying the lamp from indoors to outdoors makes it look like a torch rather than a *menorah*, so even from the perspective of *hanacha* it does not work. A parallel scenario in reverse was also considered.

The *Gemara* then continues: *ta shma*, come and hear. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught that if one had a lantern burning continuously from *erev Chanukah* straight through *Shabbat* — a lantern that had been burning for twenty-four or forty-eight hours — and at *motzei Shabbat* wished to use it for *ner Chanukah*, he would need to extinguish it and relight it. The *Gemara* analyzes: if you say *hadlaka oseh mitzvah*, this makes perfect sense — the fact that it has been burning since *erev Shabbat* is insufficient, a fresh act of lighting is required. But if you say *hanacha oseh mitzvah*, why must one extinguish and relight? One should only need to lift it up and set it back down — that act of placement would be the *mitzvah*.

Tosafot raises the obvious question here: if *hanacha* is all that matters, why even extinguish it? Simply lifting and setting it back down should suffice. Tosafot answers that the scenario involves a lamp that was not lit originally for *Chanukah* but rather as a *Shabbat* light. Even granting that *hanacha* is the *mitzvah*, what must be placed is something defined as a *Chanukah* light. Since this was lit for *Shabbat*, it must be relit to acquire that status.
