The *Gemara*'s point remains, however: if *hanacha* is the *mitzvah*, the act of *hadlaka* alone — however defined — should be insufficient, and one would need to perform a distinct act of placement.

### Bracha as Evidence

The *Gemara* then adds a further proof: *midekamivarchinan asher kideshanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu lehadlik ner shel Chanukah* — from the very fact that the *bracha* recited is *lehadlik*, to light, we derive *shma mina hadlaka oseh mitzvah*. This is a strong proof. It is well-attested among the *rishonim* — as in the parallel case of *shofar*, where the *Rambam* derives from the *nusach ha-bracha* of *lishmoa kol shofar* that the *mitzvah* is to hear rather than to blow — that the *nusach ha-bracha* reflects the conceptual definition of the *mitzvah*. This is not always an absolute one-to-one correspondence: when one puts on *tzitzit*, the *bracha* is *lehitatef b'tzitzit*, to wrap oneself, even though the *mitzvah* is not the act of wrapping but the obligation to attach *tzitzit* to a four-cornered garment. Similarly, on *erev Pesach* we recite *al bi'ur chametz* though the act being performed is checking, not burning — though there the *bracha* captures the conceptual purpose rather than the immediate act. Nevertheless, the presumption that the *nusach ha-bracha* mirrors how the *mitzvah* is defined is reasonable and here supports the conclusion: *hadlaka oseh mitzvah*.

### Who Can Light

Now that we have established that *hadlaka oseh mitzvah*, the *Gemara* draws a practical consequence: *hidlika cheresh shoteh v'katan lo asa v'lo klum* — if a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan* lights it, it counts for nothing. Had the *mitzvah* been *hanacha*, one might argue that the identity of the person performing the act of lighting is less significant, since what ultimately matters is the placement. But since the act of lighting is itself the *mitzvah*, it must be performed by someone who is obligated.

There is, however, an immediate exception: *isha vadai madlika* — a woman may certainly light, because she is certainly obligated. The basis for this is Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling: *nashim chayavot b'ner Chanukah she'af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* — women are obligated in the *mitzvah* of *Chanukah* because they too were part of the miracle.

---

## Women & Af Hen Hayu

### Women Obligated

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling — *nashim chayavot b'ner Chanukah she'af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* — establishes that women are fully obligated in *ner Chanukah*. The principle of *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* overcomes the general exemption of women from positive time-bound commandments (*mitzvot aseh she-hazman grama*), since women were themselves included in the miracle and therefore share in the obligation to publicize it.

---

## Hadlaka vs. Hanacha (II)

### Alternative Framework

Before proceeding further, it is worth pausing to consider a more contemporary *lomdus* approach to the *hadlaka*-*hanacha* debate — one that attempts to connect it to the earlier question of whether, if the *ner Chanukah* is extinguished, one is obligated to relight it (*kavta zakuk lah*).

The reframing runs as follows. Rather than treating *hadlaka* and *hanacha* as two distinct acts — lighting versus placing down — one might understand the debate as being about the act versus the duration: is the *mitzvah* the act of lighting, or is the *mitzvah* that the lamp is burning? If the *mitzvah* is the act, then once that act is performed correctly, one has fulfilled the obligation regardless of what happens afterward. If the lamp blows out, that is not one's responsibility — the *ma'aseh mitzvah* was completed. But if the *mitzvah* is the state of burning, then one bears ongoing responsibility to ensure that the lights remain lit throughout the required period — from *shkia* until *ad d'tichleh regel min ha-shuk*.

This alternative framing has a compelling rationale in terms of *pirsumei nisa*. If one lights and the lamp immediately blows out, one may have performed an act, but one has accomplished nothing in terms of publicizing the miracle. It makes conceptual sense that the *mitzvah* would be defined as ensuring that the lights are burning and fulfilling their purpose. This reading aligns neatly with the two disputed positions: *kavta zakuk lah* and *hadlaka oseh mitzvah* seem to form a coherent pair — if one must ensure that the lamp burns, one must relight it when it goes out, and the identity of who performs the lighting is less significant. Conversely, ruling that *hadlaka oseh mitzvah* and *kavta ein zakuk lah* — that if it blows out one need not relight — forms the other coherent pair.

One might also note that from a *hanacha*-as-duration perspective, it would be strange to require any special act of placement: who has ever heard that one must lift the lamp and set it back down? That oddity, already noted above, suggests that *hanacha* as a literal act of placement is not quite the right way to understand the opposing position. Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged that the *Gemara* itself does appear to interpret *hanacha* quite literally — it specifically contemplates the scenario of *mechaba u'magbi'a u'mani'ach u'madlika*, extinguishing, lifting, placing, and relighting, as distinct acts. The parallel to the *kavta* debate is illuminating and worth noting, even if the *Gemara*'s own formulation resists a clean reduction to that single axis.

---

## Women & Af Hen Hayu (II)

### Two Interpretations

Returning to the principle of *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes*: what precisely does this phrase mean? Among the *rishonim* there are two basic interpretations. The first, cited by Rashi, is that women were among the beneficiaries of the miracle — the decrees of *gezeirat Chanukah* threatened all of *Klal Yisrael*, and the *nes* of the war restored freedom of practice and self-governance to everyone, men and women alike. Focusing on the *nes* of the *pach ha-shemen*, that too was a miracle for all of Israel. On this reading, the principle simply means that women were saved along with everyone else.

The second interpretation, also hinted at in Rashi, is that women were among the *vehicles* of the miracle, not merely its recipients. This reading takes on more force when one notes that the *Gemara* invokes *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* in exactly three cases — *Chanukah*, *Purim*, and *arba kosot* of *Pesach*. By *Purim*, the active role of women is obvious: the redemption came through Esther. By *Pesach*, those who take this approach cite the principle that *nashim tzidkaniyot nigalu avoteinu mi-Mitzrayim* — it was through the merit of righteous women that our ancestors were redeemed. Regarding *Chanukah*, Rashi notes the decree of *she-gazru Yevanim al betulot ha-nissuot l'hiba'el la-tofsar techila* — the Greeks decreed that betrothed women would first be violated by the local governor — making women not merely recipients of the miracle but directly imperiled by the persecution that the miracle ended.

### Scope Limitations

This raises an important question that Tosafot addresses: if *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* is a valid principle, why does it not extend more broadly? Women are not obligated in *sukkah* and *lulav* — yet they were certainly present when the miracles of the desert occurred. Moreover, within *Pesach* itself, we use *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* to explain the obligation of *arba kosot*, yet women are already obligated in *matzah* through a biblical derivation — if one is prohibited in *chametz*, one is obligated in *matzah*. Why invoke *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* for *arba kosot* but not rely on it for other Passover obligations? What is the proper scope of the principle?

### Tosafot's Answer

Tosafot's answer is that *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* operates exclusively within the realm of rabbinic *mitzvot*. All three cases where the principle is applied — *Purim*, *Chanukah*, and *arba kosot* — are rabbinic in origin. The reasoning is as follows: when it comes to biblical *mitzvot*, the Torah itself has established a general framework of *mitzvot aseh she-hazman grama* that defines two categories of obligation, one for men and one for women, and we do not invoke *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* to override or modify that biblical structure. But when the rabbis are themselves instituting an obligation from the outset, they take into account the consideration of *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* in defining who is obligated — and *lechatchila* they obligate men and women equally.

### Rav Soloveitchik

A related but distinct explanation, building on Tosafot and perhaps extending it, was offered by Rav Soloveitchik. All three cases where *af hen hayu b'oto ha-nes* applies share not only the feature of being rabbinic, but a second, equally important common denominator: they all possess the quality of *pirsumei nisa* — publicizing the miracle. The *mitzvah* of *hadlaka* on *Chanukah* and the *mitzvah* of *Megillah* on *Purim* are explicitly characterized in the *Gemara* as acts of *pirsumei nisa*. Even *arba kosot*, though less obviously outward-facing, participates in this quality through the broader obligation of *l'har'ot atzmo k'illu hu yatza mi-Mitzrayim* — presenting oneself as though one personally left Egypt — which carries this character of demonstrating and publicizing the freedom that was wrought.

This connection between *pirsumei nisa* and the inclusion of women is not incidental. If the *mitzvah* were simply a matter of commemorating an event to which one was a witness or beneficiary, the logic of inclusion might not be so compelling. But if the essential purpose is to publicize the miracle as broadly as possible, then there is strong reason to include within the obligation everyone who was part of that miracle. *Pirsumei nisa* calls for maximum participation — and therefore the rabbis, in instituting these obligations, specifically defined them to include those who were part of the miraculous event.

On the practical question of whether a woman in a household where the man of the house is lighting can or should light herself: the *Gemara* is entirely clear that *isha vadai madlika*. Whatever hesitancy exists in some *Ashkenazi* practice may be rooted in considerations of *tzniut* or in questions about the nature of the obligation — whether it rests on the household as a corporate unit or on each individual. If one thinks of it as a household obligation, there may be a desire to see the head of the household as the one who performs it. But this is not stated explicitly in the *Gemara*. The *Gemara* also records the rulings of Rav Sheshet and Rav Zeira on related questions: Rav Sheshet holds that a guest (*achsannai*) is obligated in *ner Chanukah*, which implies that the obligation falls on individuals rather than purely on households. Rav Zeira relates that when he was a student lodging away from home, he would contribute a few coins (*mishtatfana b'fritei bahadi ushpiza*) to his host, thereby acquiring a share in the household's *ner Chanukah* lighting. After he married, he no longer needed to do this, since his household was lighting for him back home (*dekamadlikei alai b'go beisai*). These two rulings together suggest a baseline in which the obligation is anchored in the home as a unit, with the individual's obligation fulfilled through membership in or contribution to that unit — a picture that becomes more complex as one moves to the levels of *mehadrin* and *mehadrin min ha-mehadrin*.

---

## Oils & Configuration

### Choice of Oil

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught: *kol ha-shemanim kulan yafein la-ner* — all oils are suitable for the *Chanukah* lamp, *v'shemen zayit min ha-muvchar* — but olive oil is the preferred choice. This ruling is given in the context of *Chanukah*, not *Shabbat*, as is clear from the discussion that follows.

### Why Olive Oil

Abaye relates that originally his master — presumably Rabbah — would seek out sesame oil, explaining *hai mashcha nehora tfei*, that sesame oil burns longer, and longer burning may better serve *pirsumei nisa*. But once his master heard the teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi praising olive oil, he changed his practice and specifically sought olive oil, reasoning *hai tzalil nehora tfei* — that olive oil produces a cleaner and brighter light. The practical question, then, is what better serves *pirsumei nisa*: duration of burning or quality of light? The ruling follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a cleaner, brighter flame is preferred, even if it does not burn as long. Some *rishonim* offer the additional reason that olive oil is preferred because the original miracle of *Chanukah* involved olive oil — but that is not the reasoning given here in the *Gemara*.

### Ink Production

On a related tangent: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi also taught that all oils are suitable for making ink, and olive oil is again the preferred choice. The *Gemara* raises the question of whether olive oil is preferred for the stage of *l'gabel* — mixing the soot with a binding medium to form ink — or for the stage of *le-ashen* — producing the soot itself by burning oil beneath an inverted vessel so that the smoke collects as a black residue. Rav Shmuel bar Zutra's teaching resolves the question by stating that olive oil is superior *bein l'gabel bein le-ashen* — both for mixing and for producing the smoke. Additionally, Rav Shmuel bar Zutra taught that while all smokes are suitable for use as the black pigment in ink, the smoke of olive oil is the most ideal. Rav Huna added that all types of resin or gum serve as a binding agent in ink, but balsam resin (*sraf kataf*) is superior to all others.

---

## Bracha Rules

### Lighting Requires Bracha

Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav states: *ha-madlik ner shel Chanukah tzarich l'vareich* — one who lights *Chanukah* candles is obligated to recite a *bracha*. This had already been assumed in the earlier discussion but is now stated explicitly.

### Seeing Requires Bracha

Rabbi Yirmiyah adds that *ha-ro'eh ner shel Chanukah tzarich l'vareich* — one who merely sees *Chanukah* lights, without having lit them oneself, is also obligated to recite a *bracha*. This applies when one did not recite a *bracha* upon lighting, or when one did not light at all — for example, a guest whose household is lighting for him.

### Three vs. Two Brachot

Rav Yehuda rules: *yom rishon ha-ro'eh m'vareich shtayim v'ha-madlik m'vareich shalosh* — on the first night, one who merely sees the lights recites two *brachot*, and one who lights recites three. *Mikan va-eilach* — from the second night onward — one who lights recites two and one who sees recites one. The question is which *bracha* is subtracted after the first night: *mimaeit zman* — the *bracha* of *zman*, that is, *shehecheyanu v'kiyemanu v'higiyanu la-zman ha-zeh*. *Shehecheyanu* is recited on the first night to mark the arrival of this new appointed time, just as it is recited on the first night of *Yom Tov* but not on subsequent days of the *chag*. Once it has been said, it covers the entire period. If for some reason one failed to say *shehecheyanu* on the first night, it may be said on a later night. But once it has been recited, it is not repeated.

### Shehecheyanu Once Only

The rationale for reciting *shehecheyanu* only once is consistent with how the *bracha* functions throughout the *mo'adim*: it marks the entry into a new period of sanctified time, not each individual day within that period. It is said once on the first night of *Yom Tov* and once at the outset of *Chanukah*, after which the time has already been acknowledged. For one who sees the lights rather than lights them: *shehecheyanu* and *she-asah nissim* are not dependent on performing the act of *hadlaka*. Seeing the lights draws one into the significance of the time and into the sphere of *pirsumei nisa*, and therefore both *brachot* are appropriate even for the one who does not light.

### Daily Miracle

The *Gemara* raises a further question: why is *she-asah nissim la-avoteinu* recited each day, rather than only once? Since it was seemingly one continuous miracle, is not one recitation sufficient? The *Gemara* answers: *neis kol yoma ita* — the miracle occurred anew each day. This answer fits most naturally with the emphasis on *neis pach ha-shemen*, where each of the eight days of burning constituted a distinct and separate miracle. One might alternatively argue that *she-asah nissim* need not assert that a new miracle occurred today versus yesterday — if the act of *hadlakat nerot* is itself *pirsumei nisa*, then each day's lighting calls forth a declaration of the miracle being publicized, regardless of how one counts the miraculous days. The *Bavli*, however, takes the approach that each day's miracle was distinct, and on that basis the daily recitation of *she-asah nissim* is fully justified.

The full set of *brachot* is thus: *asher kidshanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu l'hadlik ner shel Chanukah*, *she-asah nissim la-avoteinu*, and on the first night, *shehecheyanu*. On the first night one who lights recites all three; on subsequent nights, two; one who only sees recites two on the first night and one thereafter.

---

## Rabbinic Authority

### Source of Authority

The *Gemara* then raises a striking question: *v'heichan tzivanu* — where did God command us? This is, after all, a rabbinic *mitzvah*. How can the *bracha* of *asher kidshanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu* — "who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us" — be recited over something the Torah did not explicitly command? The question, it should be noted, could in principle be asked about many rabbinic enactments. But it carries particular force when applied to *Chanukah* and *Megillah*, where the rabbis did not merely add safeguards to existing Torah practice but instituted wholly new ritual observances, including the establishment of what amounts to a new *chag*. This raised a genuine question: from where do they derive the authority to institute such things, and how can a *bracha* that invokes divine command be recited upon them?

### Lo Tasur & She'al

Two answers are offered. Rav Avya says: *mi-lo tasur* — from the verse "you shall not deviate from what they tell you, right or left" (Devarim 17:11), which the Torah directs at the rulings of the rabbinic authorities. Since the Torah itself commands obedience to rabbinic rulings, a rabbinic enactment carries divine backing, and one can therefore say *v'tzivanu*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a second source: *she'al avicha v'yagedcha z'keinecha v'yomru lach* — "ask your father and he will tell you, your elders and they will say to you" (Devarim 32:7), which likewise directs the people to heed the tradition transmitted through the generations of rabbinic leadership.

### Rambam vs. Ramban

There is a significant dispute among the *rishonim* about how to read the *lo tasur* answer. The *Rambam* holds that violating a rabbinic enactment constitutes a biblical transgression — one violates the *d'oraita* prohibition of *lo tasur* whenever one disregards a rabbinic ruling. The *Ramban* disagrees: if every rabbinic enactment automatically carried the force of a biblical prohibition by virtue of *lo tasur*, then the entire distinction between *d'oraita* and *d'rabbanan* would collapse. On the *Ramban*'s view, the *she'al avicha* answer is in fact the more accurate description of the nature of rabbinic authority: the obligation to heed the rabbis is real and binding, and it is backed by the Torah's endorsement of that tradition, but it does not transform every rabbinic ruling into a full-fledged biblical prohibition. These two answers of the *Gemara*, taken literally, may thus map onto this fundamental *rishonic* dispute about the structure of rabbinic authority.

### Rav Amram's Objection

Rav Amram then raises a challenge from a different angle. The *Gemara* had taught that *demai* — produce purchased from an *am ha-aretz* where there is uncertainty whether tithes were properly separated — may be used for an *eiruv*, for *shitufei mevo'ot*, and a *bracha* may be recited upon it. It may also be used for *birkat ha-mazon* and *zimmun*, and the *ma'asrot* may even be separated from it while one is unclothed, and even during *bein ha-shmashot* on *Shabbat*. The challenge is as follows: if any rabbinic obligation requires a *bracha*, then when separating *demai* in a state of undress, how does one recite the *bracha*? The verse *v'haya machanecha kadosh* — "your camp shall be holy" — teaches that one may not recite a *bracha* while unclothed.

### Definite vs. Doubtful

Abaye resolves this with a crucial distinction: *vadai d'divreihein ba'ei bracha, safek d'divreihein lo ba'ei bracha*. A rabbinic obligation that is definite — where the rabbis have unambiguously imposed an obligation — requires a *bracha*. But a rabbinic obligation that is itself rooted in doubt — where the rabbis legislated because of an uncertain circumstance rather than a certain one — does not require a *bracha*. *Demai* falls into the latter category: the rabbis did not say that tithes were definitely not taken; they said there is doubt whether they were taken. The rabbinic obligation is therefore conditional on the doubt, and since the situation is one of *safek*, no *bracha* is recited. Moreover, the *Gemara* notes that the rabbis treated *demai* more leniently than other rabbinic prohibitions — they permitted it to be fed to guests and to the poor — reflecting that the underlying obligation has a weaker character than a straightforward rabbinic prohibition.

### Yom Tov Sheni Analogy

The *Gemara* challenges Abaye's distinction: how does one recite a *bracha* on the *mitzvot* of *Yom Tov Sheni*, which is itself a rabbinic institution rooted in the doubt over calendar calculation — a paradigmatic *safek d'rabbanan*? The *Gemara* answers: *ki heichi d'lo l'zalzulei bei* — so that people should not treat *Yom Tov Sheni* as less significant than *Yom Tov Rishon*. Were no *bracha* to be recited, it would undermine the sanctity of *Yom Tov Sheni* and invite laxity. Therefore the *bracha* is required there as a special measure to preserve the standing of the institution. This is not a general principle applicable to all *safek d'rabbanan* situations, but a specific ruling driven by the need to maintain the *kedusha* of *Yom Tov Sheni* on a par with *Yom Tov Rishon*. Rava offers a further perspective: *rov amei ha-aretz me'asrin hein* — in practice, most *amei ha-aretz* do tithe their produce, such that *demai* is not even a strong *safek* to begin with. The obligation in *demai* is therefore of a particularly attenuated character, providing additional grounds for not requiring a *bracha* in that case.

---

## Two Entrances

### Two Doors Question

Rav Huna asks: *chatzer she-yeish lah shenei pesachim* — a courtyard (or, as Rashi explains, a house within a courtyard) that has two openings — *tzrichah shenei neros* — does it require two sets of lights? The question presupposes that *pirsumei nisa* requires that the lights be visible from the street, and that a house with two doors accessible from different directions raises the concern that one side might appear unlit.

### Different Sides Needed

Rava qualifies: *lo amran ela mi-shtei ruchot* — we require two sets of lights only if the two doors are on different sides of the house. *Aval mei-ruach achat, lo tzarich* — if the two doors are on the same side, one does not need two sets. The reasoning is presented in terms of *chashada* — suspicion.

### Suspicion Concern

The concern is that passersby will suspect the householder of not having lit *Chanukah* candles. Rashi explains the underlying assumption: a house with two doors may appear to observers to house two separate families. If one side has no visible *Chanukah* light, people will assume that the family associated with that entrance has failed to light.

### Local Suspicion

The *Gemara* presses further: whose suspicion are we concerned about? If it is strangers passing through — *chashada d'alma* — then even two doors on the same side should present a problem, since strangers do not know the internal arrangement of the house. If it is the townspeople — *chashada d'vnei masa* — then they know there is only one family in the house, and two doors on different sides should not matter either. The *Gemara* resolves: *l'olam mishum chashada d'vnei masa* — we are concerned about suspicion from the people of one's own town. And the reason two different sides matter even to townspeople is: *v'zimnin d'michalfei b'hai v'lo chalfei b'hai* — sometimes people will pass by one side and not the other. If they see only the unlit entrance, they will conclude — *ki heichi d'b'hai pitcha lo adlik* — that this person did not light at all, without realizing there is a lit entrance on the other side. When both doors are on the same side, a person passing that side will see the candles at one door even if not at the other, and no suspicion arises.

### Why Care About Suspicion?

This prompts a natural objection: *u'mi chashishinan l'chashda* — are we really required to concern ourselves with what other people think of us? The *Gemara* notes that this concern is especially apt in the context of *ner Chanukah*, where *pirsumei nisa* creates a heightened interest in the perception that the entire community is participating in the observance. But the *Gemara* does not rely on this alone.

### Pe'ah Analogy

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that the Torah required *pe'ah* — the corner of the field left for the poor — to be set aside at the very end of the harvest, not at some point in the middle, for four reasons. The *Gemara* enumerates: *mipnei gezel aniyim* — to prevent theft from the poor, since if *pe'ah* could be designated at any point, the landowner might call his poor relative at a moment when no other poor people are present and give it to him exclusively; *mipnei bitul aniyim* — to prevent wasting the time of the poor, who would otherwise have to wait and watch throughout the harvest not knowing when *pe'ah* would be left; *mipnei ha-chashad* — because of suspicion, since if the *pe'ah* was left in the middle of the harvest and is no longer visible by the time the field is fully reaped, passersby will assume the owner never gave *pe'ah* at all and will curse him; and *mishum bal tichleh* — the prohibition against harvesting the corners of one's field entirely. The *Gemara* queries: are not all four reasons ultimately expressions of the same underlying prohibition of *bal tichleh*? Rava answers: no — the concern for *chashad* is distinct from the concern for *mipnei ha-rama'in* — those who might exploit the flexibility to actually avoid giving *pe'ah* by claiming they gave it earlier. The *pe'ah* case thus demonstrates that avoiding suspicion — ensuring that one does not appear to have failed in a *mitzvah* — is a recognized halakhic concern in its own right, and the *Gemara* uses it as precedent for the concern underlying the requirement to light on both sides of a house with two entrances facing different directions.

---

## Oils & Configuration (II)

### Two-Spout Lamp

Rav Yitzchak bar Radifa in the name of Rav Huna rules: *ner she-yeish lo shenei piyot oleh li-shnei b'nei adam* — a lamp that has two mouths — two separate points from which a wick can emerge — counts for two people. Rashi clarifies that this applies when two members of the same household are each fulfilling the *mitzvah* at the level of *mehadrin*, not when two separate households are involved, since the latter would require distinct lamps.

### Combined Flames Problem

Rava introduces a related ruling: *mila ke'arah shemen v'hikifah petilot* — if one fills a plate with oil and places wicks all around the rim, then *kafah aleiha keli* — if one places a vessel over it, covering the central space so that the flames remain separate — *keli oleh l'kamah b'nei adam* — many people can fulfill the *mitzvah* from this single vessel. However, *lo kafah aleiha keli* — if one does not place such a covering — *asa'ah k'min medurah* — the arrangement becomes like a bonfire or torch, as all the individual flames merge into a single large fire in the center. And *afilu l'echad nami eino oleh* — it does not even count for one person. The *mitzvah* of *ner Chanukah* requires a defined lamp or flame, not the appearance of a bonfire, which looks like light needed for practical illumination rather than a *mitzvah* flame. This ruling has implications for the configuration of the *chanukiah*: there are concerns about placing lights in an arc or arrangement where the flames might combine, particularly on the same horizontal plane.

---

## Priorities

### Household vs. Chanukah

Rava rules on a series of priority questions when one lacks the resources to fulfill multiple obligations. First: if one must choose between *ner beito* — light in the home, which Rashi understands as *ner Shabbat* — and *ner Chanukah*, *ner beito adif* — the household light takes priority. The reasoning: *mishum shalom beito* — because having light in the home makes for peace in the home. A dark house leads to discomfort, discord, and difficulty. The *Chanukah* light, being placed outside, does not serve the interior of the home in any case. This ruling implicitly treats *ner beito* as itself a *mitzvah* — not merely a practical convenience — since it is being weighed against a recognized *mitzvah* of *ner Chanukah*. The *bracha* recited on *ner Shabbat*, incidentally, is a *Gaonic* institution not found in the *Gemara* itself, and the precise moment when the lighting of *Shabbat* candles crystallized as a formal *ma'aseh mitzvah* is itself a matter of discussion.

### Household vs. Kiddush

Second: if one must choose between *ner beito* and *kiddush ha-yom* — having wine for *kiddush* of *Shabbat* — again *ner beito adif*, again *mishum shalom beito*. The same principle applies: the light in the home ensures peace and prevents friction, and this concern takes priority even over *kiddush*. The comparison of these two *mitzvot* further underscores the status of *ner beito* as a serious *mitzvah*, since it is not merely said to be more convenient than *kiddush* but is assigned priority on the basis of the distinct value of *shalom bayit*.

### Chanukah vs. Kiddush

Third: if one must choose between *ner Chanukah* and *kiddush ha-yom*, where *shalom bayit* is no longer in play, what takes precedence? Rava posed this question and then himself resolved it: *ner Chanukah adif mishum pirsumei nisa* — the *Chanukah* candle takes precedence because of *pirsumei nisa*. The principle of publicizing the miracle carries sufficient weight to override *kiddush ha-yom*. Tosafot draws a related inference from this: on a *Shabbat* that coincides with *Rosh Chodesh Chanukah*, the *haftarah* read is that of *Chanukah* rather than that of *Rosh Chodesh*, precisely because *pirsumei nisa* takes precedence. This emerges as a broader principle: *pirsumei nisa*, as a defining purpose of the *Chanukah* observance, carries significant weight in resolving conflicts with other obligations.

---

## Mitzvot & Children

### Candles & Sages

Rav Huna teaches: *ha-ragil ba-ner havin lei banim talmidei chachamim* — one who is scrupulous about the *mitzvah* of the lamp will be granted sons who are Torah sages. The verse *ner mitzvah v'Torah or* — "a *mitzvah* is a lamp and Torah is light" — establishes the symbolic connection: the light of the *mitzvah* begets the light of Torah.

### Other Mitzvot

The passage continues with parallel teachings. One who is careful in the *mitzvah* of *mezuzah* will merit a beautiful dwelling — *zocheh l'dirah na'ah*. One who is careful in *tzitzit* will merit fine garments — *zocheh l'tallit na'ah*. And one who is careful in *kiddush ha-yom* of *Shabbat* will merit cellars full of wine — *zocheh u'memalei garvei d'yayin*.

### Historical Examples

The *Gemara* provides historical illustrations. Rav Huna was accustomed to study near the doorway of Rabbi Abin the carpenter (*nagara*). He observed that Rabbi Abin was meticulous in his candle lighting — whether for *Shabbat* or *Chanukah* or both, as Rashi explains. He declared: *trei gavrei rabbei nafki me-hacha* — two great men will emerge from this house. And indeed, from Rabbi Abin's household emerged Rav Idi bar Abin and Rav Chiya bar Abin, both distinguished *amoraim*. Similarly, Rav Chisda was accustomed to study near the entrance of the household of Rav Shizbi — which, since the father had passed away, was now referred to as *d'bei nasha*, the women's household, i.e., his mother's home. He observed that the mother was meticulous in her candle lighting and declared: *gavra raba nafik me-hacha* — a great person will emerge from here. And indeed Rav Shizbi was the one who came forth from her home.

### Proper Timing

The *Gemara* closes the daf with a teaching about timing. Rav Yosef's wife was accustomed to lighting late. Rav Yosef, citing a *baraita*, reminded her: *lo yamish amud he-anan yomam v'amud ha-esh laila* — the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire did not cease, the one completing for the other before its time was up. The *baraita* derives from this verse that the pillar of cloud would not depart before the pillar of fire took over — each was in place before the transition, not a moment late. This teaches, Rashi understands, that one should not light *Shabbat* candles so close to sunset as to be almost too late. Hearing this, Rav Yosef's wife then overreacted and considered lighting very early. An elder (*saba*) then cited a parallel teaching: *uvilvad she-lo yakdim v'she-lo ye-acher* — provided one neither lights too early nor too late. The proper *mitzvah* is performed at its right time — not rushed, not delayed.

---

---

# Shabbat 25

## Prohibited Oils

### Shemen Serefah

Daf 25 begins with the *mishnah* found in the middle of 24b. The *mishnah* opens: *ein madlikin b'shemen sreyfah b'yom tov* — one may not kindle with *shemen sreyfah* on *yom tov*. Having spent considerable time on the theme of Chanukah, we now return to the major subject of which oils and fuels may be used for *Shabbat* lighting. This *mishnah*, however, begins by addressing something one may not use specifically on *yom tov*.

The preceding *mishnah* had already established that one may not use *shemen sreyfah* on *Shabbat*. The *Gemara* there explained that *shemen sreyfah* refers to *terumah tme'ah* — oil of *terumah* that has become *tamei* and which it is a *mitzvah* to burn. This *mishnah* now adds that the same prohibition applies on *yom tov*.

### Rabbi Yishmael/Itran

The *mishnah* then pivots back to *Shabbat* concerns: *Rabbi Yishmael omer ein madlikin b'itran mipnei kvod hashabat* — Rabbi Yishmael says one may not kindle with *itran*, a type of malodorous tar or pitch fuel, because of the honor of *Shabbat*, since the unpleasant smell will drive one from the room. *Vachachamim matirin* — the Sages, however, permit it.

### Permitted Oils

The *mishnah* then enumerates the oils that are permitted: *shemen shumshumin* (sesame seed oil), *shemen egozim* (nut oil), *shemen tnunot* (gourd oil), *shemen dagim* (fish oil — Rashi identifies this as made from fish innards), *shemen pakuot* (which Rashi describes as another variety of gourd), *itran* (the very tar that Rabbi Yishmael prohibits now appears on the permitted list according to the Sages), and *nefat* — naphtha, a petroleum derivative. Steinsaltz notes that this may be the earliest historical source to mention the production of white naphtha, though it merely references it rather than describing its production in any detail.

### Rabbi Tarfon

Rabbi Tarfon takes the most stringent position of all: *ein madlikin ela b'shemen zayit bilvad* — one may kindle only with olive oil, to the exclusion of all other oils.

## Invalid Sacrifices

### Kodshim Comparison

The *Gemara* now turns to *mai ta'ama* — the reason *shemen sreyfah* may not be burned on *yom tov*. As was touched upon previously, there are two possible frameworks. One is that the primary concern is actually a *Shabbat* concern: if one may use this oil on *Shabbat*, the presence of a *mitzvah* to burn it might lead one to tip the lamp to accelerate the burning. The other reading — which sits more naturally with this *mishnah*'s emphasis on *yom tov* — is that the concern is fundamentally a *yom tov* concern.

The *Gemara* states: *l'fi she'ein sorfin kodshim b'yom tov* — because one may not burn invalid *kodshim* on *yom tov*, and since *terumah tme'ah* similarly possesses sanctity and is unfit for use, it falls under the same category. The *Gemara* then turns to establish the source for this rule: *minani milei* — from where do we know that *kodshim* may not be burned on *yom tov*?

### Pesach Notar

The *Gemara* cites the teaching of Chizkiyah, which was also transmitted as a *braisa* in the school of Chizkiyah. The verse by *Pesach* states: *v'lo sosiru mimenu ad boker, v'hanotar mimenu ad boker ba'esh tisrofu* — do not leave any of it until morning, and whatever remains until morning you shall burn in fire. The verse uses the phrase *ad boker* — "until morning" — twice, which is apparently redundant. The *drashah* derives from this repetition: *boker sheni litein lo boker sheni l'sreyfato* — the second mention of "morning" comes to teach that there is a second morning designated for the burning. One does not burn *notar* on *Pesach* morning itself — on the *yom tov* of the 15th — but rather on the morning of the 16th.

This establishes that burning invalid *kodshim* is prohibited on *yom tov* itself. The reasoning is clear: burning is a *melachah*, and burning *kodshim* yields no direct physical benefit of the kind permitted on *yom tov* — it does not qualify as *ach asher ye'aseh l'chol nefesh*, an act performed for human nourishment or physical enjoyment.

A significant conceptual difficulty arises at this point, however. Both Rashi and Tosafot raise the obvious question: if one is permitted to derive benefit from the burning of *terumah tme'ah*, why can one not light with it? After all, when burning ordinary oil for light, one is clearly deriving benefit. Why should the incidental presence of a *mitzvah* to burn this oil remove the permission to use it on *yom tov*?

The *Gemara* itself does not address this directly. Two answers are offered. The simpler one, advanced by both Rashi and Tosafot, is that it is a *gzeirah*: since one may not burn invalid *kodshim* on *yom tov* in cases where no benefit is derived, the rabbis extended this prohibition to *terumah tme'ah* as well, even where benefit is incidentally obtained, in order to keep the entire category closed and prevent confusion. Tosafot offers a more conceptual answer: although benefit from light is indeed obtained when burning *terumah tme'ah*, that benefit is only incidental to the act. The reason one burns *terumah tme'ah* is to fulfill the *mitzvah* of destroying it. The *Torah* permits incidental benefit during the course of destruction, but the act itself is fundamentally one of religious obligation, not personal benefit. Tosafot draws an analogy to the debate about bringing *nedarim unedavot* on *yom tov*: according to the view that this is forbidden, even though one will eat the meat, the act of *shechitah* for a *korban* is primarily an act directed toward God, not an act of meat preparation — and so even where benefit follows, it does not transform the act into one that *yom tov* permits.

### Olas Shabbat

Abaye derives the same prohibition from a different verse: *olas Shabbos beshabbaso* — the *olah* of *Shabbat* in its *Shabbat*, which implies *velo olas chol beShabbos* — and not the weekday *olah* on *Shabbat*. Tosafot explains that an additional *drashah* extends this to *yom tov* as well: an *olas chol* may not be burned on *Shabbat*, and similarly may not be burned on *yom tov*. Crucially, note that what is being prohibited here is not *kodshim tme'im* but rather the burning of legitimate fats and portions of *korbanot* whose burning time has not yet arrived for that particular day. Even though these are valid *kodshim* and their burning is a *mitzvah*, if that burning is not specifically commanded for this *Shabbat* or *yom tov*, it may not be performed. The same logic applies, *a fortiori*, to *kodshim tme'im*.

### Food-Related Actions

Rava derives the prohibition from yet another verse: *hu levado ye'aseh lachem* — the *Torah* permits on *yom tov* only that which is performed for human eating. From *hu* — "it alone" — we learn *velo machshirin*: one may not prepare the instruments of food preparation on *yom tov*, only the act of food preparation itself. Thus one may not sharpen a *shechitah* knife on *yom tov*, as that is one stage removed from the food. And from *levado* we derive *velo milah shelo bizmano* — not even *milah* that falls outside its designated time may be performed on *yom tov*, since it is not food-related and its obligation is not specific to this day.

One might ask: why would I have assumed that *milah shelo bizmano* could be performed on *yom tov*? What grounds would there be for such a view? Rashi explains that one might have constructed a *kal vachomer*: a *kohen* with *tzara'as* may not remove the affected skin to perform the *avodah* in the *Beis HaMikdash*, meaning *tzara'as* overrides *avodah*. Yet *avodah* overrides *Shabbat*. By the transitive property, *tzara'as* is more stringent than *Shabbat*. Meanwhile, *bris milah* overrides *tzara'as* — one cuts away the *tzara'as* on the *orlah* to perform the *milah*. Therefore *bris milah* would seem to override *tzara'as*, which overrides *avodah*, which overrides *Shabbat* — and one might have concluded that *milah shelo bizmano* could likewise override *yom tov*. Hence the verse is needed to teach otherwise.

Tosafot rejects the *kal vachomer* as formally flawed: the reason a *kohen* with *tzara'as* may not perform the *avodah* is not that *tzara'as* defeats the *avodah* in some competitive sense, but rather that such a *kohen* is simply *pasul* to perform the *avodah* — the two are not directly in tension. Tosafot accordingly offers other reasons why one might have supposed *milah shelo bizmano* permissible on *yom tov*, and the verse comes to exclude it.

The overarching principle from all of these derivations is consistent: even acts that are in some sense connected to a *mitzvah*, even acts whose physical execution would normally be permitted on *yom tov* in another context, may not be performed on *yom tov* when the obligation is not intrinsically tied to that day. One cannot burn *notar*, one cannot burn the fats of *korbanot*, one cannot perform *milah shelo bizmano*. And therefore, just as one cannot burn *kodshim* on *yom tov*, one similarly cannot burn *terumah tme'ah* on *yom tov*.

### Shabbaton Override

Rav Ashi offers yet another framework. The Torah designates *yom tov* as *shabbaton* — a day of rest — and this constitutes a positive commandment, an *asei*. Combined with the negative prohibition *lo ta'aseh kol melachah*, *yom tov* carries both a positive and a negative commandment. The principle *ein asei docheh lo ta'aseh v'asei* — a positive commandment does not override a combination of a positive and negative commandment — means that the *asei* of burning invalid *kodshim* cannot override the combined positive and negative structure of *yom tov*. Therefore: *b'Yom Tov hu d'assur* — it is on *yom tov* that it is forbidden.

All of these approaches converge: burning *terumah tme'ah* is analogous to burning *kodshim*, and since one cannot burn *kodshim* on *yom tov*, one cannot burn *terumah tme'ah* on *yom tov* either. As noted, the conceptual bridge — that *terumah tme'ah* is being burned for one's benefit whereas invalid *kodshim* are not — remains unaddressed by the *Gemara* itself and is resolved only through Rashi's *gzeirah* approach or Tosafot's framework of incidental versus primary purpose.

## Terumah Benefit

### Rav's Principle

The *Gemara* now draws an inference from the foregoing: *yom tov hu de-asar* — it is *yom tov* that prohibits this. *Ha be-chol shapir dami* — on an ordinary weekday, however, it is permitted. Specifically, what is permitted on a weekday is to burn *terumah tme'ah* and derive benefit from the resulting light. This raises the question the *Gemara* immediately addresses: how do we know one may derive this benefit at all?

The fact that the *Gemara* needs to establish a source for this tells us something important: the underlying assumption had been that *terumah tme'ah* — as an item possessing *kedushah* that has become unfit — is *asur ba-hana'ah*, forbidden to derive benefit from, in the same way that other invalid sacred items are. The *Gemara* therefore asks: where does the *Torah* permit benefit from *terumah tme'ah*?

Rav teaches: *keshem she-mitzvah lisrof et ha-kodshim she-nitme'u kach mitzvah lisrof et ha-trumah she-nitme'ah* — just as there is a *mitzvah* to burn *kodshim* that became *tamei*, there is a *mitzvah* to burn *terumah* that became *tamei*. This is the first major principle: burning *terumah tme'ah* is not merely a practical measure for disposal — it is an affirmative *mitzvah*. And Rav adds: *be-sha'at bi'urah tehani mimmennah* — at the moment of its destruction, one may derive benefit from it.

### Mishmeret Source

The *Gemara* immediately asks: *hechan amrah Torah* — where exactly does the *Torah* say this? The answer is derived from what Rav Nachman bar Avuha taught in the name of Rav Nachman: the verse states *va-ani hineh natatti lecha et mishmeret trumotai* — "I have given you the guarding of my *terumot*," in the plural. The word *trumotai* implies two *terumot*: one *terumah tehorah* and one *terumah tme'ah*. How does one guard *terumah tehorah*? By ensuring it does not become *tamei*. How does one guard *terumah tme'ah*? By ensuring it is properly disposed of — not left lying around where one might accidentally eat it.

The verse then says *lecha* — "for you." *Shelcha teheh le-hasika tachat tavshilcha* — you may use it to kindle a fire beneath your cooking pot. When you are in the process of guarding the *terumah tme'ah* by destroying it, the *Torah* says *lecha* — it shall be yours — meaning that during the process of its destruction, you may derive incidental benefit from the burning.

Several important principles emerge from this analysis. First, *terumah tme'ah* is *asur ba-hana'ah* — this the *Gemara* assumes without demonstration. Second, there is a *mitzvah* to burn it, established by analogy to *kodshim*. Third, the verse of *mishmeret trumotai* and *lecha* permits incidental benefit during the process of destruction. And as Tosafot explains, because this benefit is only incidental to the primary act of destruction, it cannot be performed on *yom tov*, where one's actions must be directed toward human benefit as their primary purpose.

There is an interesting debate between Rashi and Tosafot regarding the nature of the *mitzvah* to burn *terumah tme'ah*. Rashi gives two reasons: first, it resembles *kodshim* in which there is a *mitzvah* to burn; and second, it must be disposed of to prevent accidental consumption — *mishum takalah*. The second reason sounds entirely rabbinic. The first suggests a closer biblical analogy, perhaps even a biblical obligation. Tosafot raises the question of whether there is in fact a biblical *mitzvah* to burn it specifically. Even if the verse *mishmeret trumotai* implies a biblical obligation to dispose of it, that obligation need not take the form of burning — one could bury it or destroy it by other means. Tosafot leaves open whether a specifically biblical *mitzvah* of burning exists. The *Gemara* itself elsewhere implies that other forms of destruction might also be acceptable — for example, flooding the wine, though that raises its own questions — and this leaves the precise contours of the obligation somewhat indeterminate. What is clear is that however it is destroyed, the *Torah* permits incidental benefit during the process.

### Ma'aser Contrast

An alternative derivation is offered: *ve-iba'it eima mi-Rav Avohu*, from what Rav Avohu taught in the name of Rabbi Yochanan. The verse from the *vidui* recited over *ma'aser sheni* states: *velo bi'arti mimenu be-tamei* — I did not destroy from it in a state of *tumah*. The word *mimenu* — "from it" — is taken to exclude: from *ma'aser sheni* you may not derive benefit when destroying it in a state of *tumah*, but this exclusion implies a contrast: from *terumah*, oil that became *tamei* may be burned and benefit derived during its destruction.

The *Gemara* challenges this inference: perhaps the contrast is not to *terumah* but to *shemen shel kodesh she-nitma* — oil consecrated for *korbanot* that became *tamei*. Perhaps it is oil of *korbanot* that is permitted, not *terumah*. The *Gemara* responds that this would constitute a *kal vachomer*: if *ma'aser*, which is less weighty than *kodshim*, carries the prohibition of deriving benefit during its *tamei* destruction, then *kodshim*, which are weightier, should surely be prohibited as well. Applying the same logic, *terumah*, which sits between *ma'aser* and *kodshim* in relative weight, would also be included in the prohibition. If the verse is coming to permit something, it would logically permit the least weighty option — and between *kodshim* and *terumah*, *terumah* is less weighty.

### Terumah Less Weighty

This generates a genuine debate within the *Gemara*: which is actually weightier, *terumah* or *korbanot*? The *Gemara* first argues that *kodshim* clearly should not be the permitted category — *kodshim chamur*, they are weightier. The mnemonic *Panak Akas* encapsulates six factors by which *kodshim* exceed *terumah* in stringency. *Piggul* — an improper intention during *shechitah* creates an *issur karet* — applies only to *korbanot*, not *terumah*. *Notar* — leaving over the sacrifice past its time creates a *karet* prohibition — likewise applies only to *korbanot*. The *kuf* represents the status of being called a *korban* itself, which carries an inherent gravity. *Me'ila* — the prohibition against deriving improper benefit from consecrated property, which entails a *lav* and requires bringing a *korban* — applies to *kodshim* but not *terumah*. *Karet* for eating them unlawfully. And *assur lo-onen* — a mourner on the day before burial may not eat *korbanot*, a restriction that does not apply to *terumah*. Six distinguishing features make *kodshim* weightier.

The *Gemara* then entertains the counter-argument: *adarabba, trumah lo mematina* — perhaps *terumah* should not be the permitted category either, since *terumah* also has its own stringencies. The mnemonic *Machpaz* encapsulates four of them. *Misah* — a non-*kohen* who eats *terumah* is liable to *misah bidei shamayim*, death at the hands of Heaven. *Chomesh* — one who unlawfully eats *terumah* must return it with an added fifth. *V'ein la pidyon* — *terumah* cannot be redeemed, whereas a blemished *korban* may be redeemed and its sanctity transferred. *Ve-assur le-zarim* — *terumah* is completely forbidden to non-*kohanim*, whereas at least some *korbanot*, such as *shelamim* and *todah*, may be eaten by non-*kohanim*.

The *Gemara* resolves the tension simply: *hanach nefishen* — six outweighs four. *Kodshim* remain more stringent overall. Furthermore, even setting aside the numerical count, the decisive factor is punishment: *kodshim* carry *karet*, while transgressing *terumah* carries *misah bidei shamayim*. Whichever is more severe establishes the greater weight of the category. Rashi explains that *karet* means dying before one's appointed time and childless, whereas *misah bidei shamayim* means dying before one's appointed time but not childless. Tosafot engages extensively with the question, devoting considerable space — visible from page 28 onward — to the distinctions between *karet* and *misah bidei shamayim*. He cites another *Gemara* to argue that *karet* means dying before sixty, while *misah bidei shamayim* does not necessarily specify a time of death but rather that the death is attributed by Heaven to the sin in question. Various interpretations circulate, but the *Gemara*'s conclusion is clear: *karet*, whatever its precise definition, is worse than *misah bidei shamayim*, and therefore *kodshim* remain the more weighty category. *Terumah* is thus less weighty, and it is *terumah* that is the permitted category from the contrast with *ma'aser sheni*.

### Exclusion Logic

At the opening of 25b, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a final derivation. The verse states *reishis degancha tiroshcha veyitzharecha titen lo* — you shall give him the first of your grain, wine, and oil. *Lo velo l'oro* — "to him and not for his light." The *Torah* says that when you give *terumah tehorah* to a *kohen*, the *kohen* should use it for himself, not burn it as firewood for light. If the *Torah* had to exclude burning *terumah tehorah* for light, the inference is: *mikhlal de-vas orah hu* — this implies that *terumah tme'ah* has the quality of being appropriate for burning as light. Tosafot raises the circularity here — the phrase *lo l'oro* was itself read into the verse by the rabbis, and then read back out again as a derivation — but this serves nonetheless as a final *drashah* establishing that benefit may be derived from *terumah tme'ah* during its destruction.

## Candlelighting

### Rava vs Abaye

Returning now to Rabbi Yishmael's prohibition of *itran* due to *kvod Shabbat*, the *Gemara* asks what exactly the concern is. Rava explains: *mitoch she-rei'o ra* — because its smell is so bad, *gezeirah shema yanichenah ve-yetze* — we are concerned that one will leave the room rather than tolerate the smell.

Abaye challenges: *ve-yetze* — so what if one leaves the room? According to Abaye, the entire concern regarding bad wicks and oils is that one might fiddle with the flame. If the smell is so unpleasant that one simply vacates the room, there is no risk of fiddling — one will not extinguish the lamp or interfere with it. So why does it matter if one leaves?

Rava responds: *she-ani omer, hadlakas ner bi-Shabbat hovah* — because I say that candlelighting on *Shabbat* is an obligation, a *hovah*. It is here that the *Gemara* explicitly articulates, for the first time, that there is an obligatory dimension to *Shabbat* candlelighting. If leaving the room means being without light where one needs to be, then the *hovah* is not being fulfilled.

### Chovah vs Mitzvah

Tosafot clarifies the precise *chiddush* of Abaye's statement: the point is not that lighting candles is an obligation — that, Tosafot says, was never in doubt. The *mishnah* later in this tractate teaches that women can face serious consequences for being careless about *hadlakas ha-ner*, and if there are such consequences, the *mitzvah* nature of the act is assumed. What Abaye adds is that the light must be present specifically where one is eating — *bimkom se'udah* — because *de-hovah hu she-yishe bimkom ha-ner mishum oneg*, it is obligatory that one be in the place of the light so as to enhance *oneg Shabbat*. Eating in darkness is not pleasurable, and *oneg Shabbat* requires that one eat by light.

### Rabbi Yehuda Example

The *Gemara* continues with Rav teaching that it is a *mitzvah* to bathe on *Erev Shabbat*. This goes beyond the *reshut* — mere permission — to bathe warmly before *Shabbat*, which was the formulation of Rav Nachman bar Rav Zavda. Rav says it rises to the level of *mitzvah*. What does this *mitzvah* look like?

*De-amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav kach hayah minhago shel Rabi Yehuda bar Elai* — Rav Yehuda taught in the name of Rav: this was the practice of Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai. *Erev Shabbat* they would bring him a vessel filled with hot water, and he would wash his face, his hands, and his feet in preparation for *Shabbat*. He would then wrap himself in linen garments adorned with *tzitzit*, and he appeared like an angel of God.

The image is striking: not merely hygiene, but a deliberate transformation — clean, draped in fine ritual garments, and emanating an aura of holiness. Taking a bath immediately before *Shabbat*, even when one might otherwise feel sufficiently clean, places one in an entirely different mode of consciousness. The act of preparation — being clean, wearing fine clothing, setting the table — is itself an entry into *Shabbat* holiness.

### Tzitzit Digression

This description of Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai's linen garments prompts a brief digression. *Vehayu talmidav mechabim mimeno kanfei kesutan* — his students would hide the corners of their garments from him. Why? Because Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai's practice was to wear linen garments with *tzitzit* that included *techelet* — wool strings — which technically constitutes *kilayim* or *shatnez* (mixing wool and linen). Normally *shatnez* is forbidden, but where a positive commandment such as *tzitzit* is at stake, *aseh docheh lo ta'aseh* — a positive commandment overrides a negative — and the wool *techelet* may be used even in a linen garment.

The students, however, did not follow this practice. When Rabbi Yehuda asked why they were hiding their garments, he said: *lo kach shaniti lachem, sadin b'tzitzit* — have I not taught you that regarding a linen garment and *tzitzit*, *Beit Shammai* exempts and *Beit Hillel* obligates, and we rule like *Beit Hillel*?

The students' response is described as a *gezeirah mishum kesut lailah*: even though we hold in principle like *Beit Hillel*, we refrain from putting the wool strings in, lest one come to do the same with nighttime garments which are not obligated in *tzitzit*, in which case the *shatnez* would serve no *mitzvah* and would be a genuine prohibition. Tosafot explains that on this point we actually rule like *Beit Shammai*, making this one of the instances where *Beit Shammai*'s position is followed over *Beit Hillel*'s. Rashi reads the passage differently, suggesting the students had no *tzitzit* at all on their linen garments — a more striking reading.

### Bracha Debate

Returning to the nature of candlelighting, a critical terminological observation emerges. The *Gemara* used the term *hovah* for candlelighting, while for bathing it used *mitzvah*. This distinction matters. In the context of *mayim acharonim* — washing hands after eating — the *Gemara* in Chullin similarly says *hovah*, and Tosafot there explains that *hovah* can carry a sense of greater obligation than *mitzvah*, but it also suggests a non-ritual, health-based requirement — which is why one does not recite a *bracha* over *mayim acharonim*, whereas one does recite a *bracha* over *mayim rishonim*.

Applying this framework to candlelighting raises a fundamental question: when, and why, did the lighting of *Shabbat* candles become ritualized as a *ma'aseh mitzvah* requiring a *bracha*? The *bracha* itself does not appear in the *Gemara*; it emerges in the Geonic period.

Tosafot records the debate here explicitly. Some authorities argue — based on the word *hovah* — that no *bracha* should be recited over candlelighting, just as none is recited over *mayim acharonim*. *Rabbeinu Tam* forcefully rejects this view: *de-lo dami l'mayim acharonim d'lo havei ela le-hatzala b'alma* — *mayim acharonim* serves only a health purpose, whereas *hadlakas ner hi hovah shel mitzvas oneg Shabbat* — candlelighting is a *hovah* that itself constitutes a *mitzvah* of *oneg Shabbat*, and many obligations do require a *bracha*. Rabbeinu Tam goes further, engaging in a recorded exchange with Rabbeinu Meshullam — found in the responsa of *Sefer Hayashar* — on whether, if lights are already burning from before *Shabbat*, one must extinguish and relight them. Rabbeinu Meshullam holds that there is no ritual act of lighting per se; the entire obligation is simply to have light in one's home on *Shabbat*, and if it is already lit, the obligation is fulfilled. Rabbeinu Tam ultimately concludes that there is indeed an affirmative ritual act of lighting, and one should extinguish and relight — a position not explicit anywhere in the *Gemara* but one that follows naturally once the *bracha* is established and the act becomes understood as a *ma'aseh mitzvah* in its own right.

## Aggada: Peace/Wealth

### Nishiti Tova

Having concluded the legal material for this section, the *Gemara* turns to *aggadeta*, citing the verse from Lamentations: *vattiznach mishalom nafshi nishisi tova* — my soul has been abandoned from peace, I have forgotten goodness. The *Gemara* reads this verse as an allusion to several different forms of physical and domestic well-being.

Rabbi Avahu identifies *vattiznach mishalom nafshi* with *hadlakas ner b'Shabbos*: without candles, one has no peace — one stumbles in the dark, one cannot eat properly, there is no *shalom bayit*. *Nashiti tova* — I forgot goodness — is interpreted by Rabbi Yirmeyah as *beit hamerchatz*, the bathhouse, recalling the extended discussion in earlier pages about the central role of the bathhouse in ancient life. Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to *rechitzat yadayim veraglayim bechamin* — washing one's hands and feet in hot water, connected to the *Erev Shabbat* practice described above. Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha says it refers to *mitah na'ah ve-chelim na'im* — a nice bed and fine vessels in the home, the sense of peace that comes from living amid pleasant surroundings. Rabbi Abba reads it as *mitah mutza'at* — a made bed — and *ishah mekushetet letalmidei chachamim* — an adorned wife for Torah scholars. The juxtaposition of the made bed and the woman described for the benefit of scholars is acknowledged as somewhat difficult, and Rashi's gloss — suggesting the phrase connotes dignity and suitability — is noted as a careful reading of a passage that does not sit entirely smoothly.

### Who is Rich?

The *Gemara* continues with a sequence of teachings on what constitutes wealth. The mnemonic *Mem-Tav-Kuf-Shin* organizes the four opinions. Rabbi Meir says: *kol sheyesh lo nachat ruach be-oshro* — whoever has contentment with his wealth. The *Maharsha* distinguishes this from the famous line in Pirkei Avot, *hasame'ach be-chelko*, noting that the word used here is *oshro* — his wealth — rather than *chelko* — his portion. Rabbi Meir is saying that even a person who genuinely has much can fail to be rich in the meaningful sense if he lacks inner satisfaction, and another with less but a sense of contentment with what he has is truly wealthy.

Rabbi Tarfon offers an emphatically concrete answer: *kol sheyesh lo kuf kramim u-me'ah sadot ve-kuf avadim she-ovdim bahem* — rich is having a hundred vineyards, a hundred fields, and a hundred servants working them. Rabbi Tarfon was himself a man of great wealth, which may explain his frame of reference. The *Maharsha* suggests that even this statement may contain an implicit critique — the more one accumulates, the more one desires, and true satisfaction remains elusive — but this reading requires some inference.

Rabbi Akiva says: *kol sheyesh lo ishah na'ah bema'asim* — whoever has a wife of good deeds. This reflects Rabbi Akiva's own biography, where his wife's selfless devotion made possible his entire life as a Torah scholar. Notably, Rabbi Akiva also taught *marbeh nechasim marbeh de'agah* — one who increases possessions increases worry — which gives his definition of wealth a quality of inversion: real wealth is not measured in possessions at all.

Rabbi Yose says: *kol sheyesh lo beis ha-kiseh samuch le-shulchano* — whoever has his bathroom close to his table. Particularly in an era without indoor plumbing, this was genuinely significant for comfort and dignity. It is known that Rabbi Yose himself suffered from gastrointestinal difficulties, which may give this statement a personal dimension.

## Tzari Oil

### Tzari Concern

The *mishnah* lists *tzari* among the oils one may not kindle with. The *Gemara* explains: Rabbah says, *mitoch she-reicho nodef, gezeirah shema yistapek mimenu* — because the smell of *tzari* — balsam oil — is so wonderfully fragrant, we are concerned that one will be drawn to dip his bread into the oil. By dipping the bread into the vessel of oil, one removes oil from around the wick, causing the flame to be extinguished prematurely — which constitutes *mechabeh*, a prohibited act of *melachah* on *Shabbat*. Thus *tzari* is prohibited not because of unpleasantness, as with *itran*, but for the opposite reason: its fragrance is so enticing that it creates the risk of interference with the flame.

---

---

# Shabbat 26

## Tzari Oil Debate

### Rava's Aroma Concern

The daf opens at the very bottom of 25b, picking up a dispute regarding the position of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who rules that one may not use *tzari* — a balsam-derived aromatic oil — for Shabbat lamp lighting. Rava explains the reason: *mitoch she-reicho nodef*, because the oil has an exceptionally powerful aroma. The concern is a form of *gezeirah shema yistapek mimenu* — we are afraid that someone, overcome by the fragrance, will dip their bread into the oil, thereby either extinguishing the lamp directly or causing it to burn for a shorter duration. That indirect extinguishing is *gram kibbuy*, and it is for this reason that we do not permit the use of *tzari*.

### Abaye's Fire Risk

Abaye, at the top of 26a, challenges Rava's rationale. He asks: why frame the prohibition around the pleasant aroma when there is a far more concrete concern — the fact that it *af*, it floats? Apparently, burning *tzari* causes sparks or flaming particles to float upward and adhere to walls and ceilings, with the real danger of setting the entire building on fire. Rashi notes this as the operative concern. Tosafot raises a sharp objection: if that were the true reason, we should prohibit the use of *tzari* even on weekdays, since the fire hazard is equally present then. Tosafot's own resolution is that on Shabbat, the additional problem is that one would be compelled to extinguish the resulting fire, thereby violating *Shabbos*. Nevertheless, the fire-safety concern itself has broader application.

### Double Concern

The *gemara* reconciles the two positions by invoking the principle of *chada ve-od ka-amar* — one reason and another: the prohibition rests on both grounds simultaneously. First, *mipnei shehu af* — because it floats and can ignite surrounding surfaces, a concern that may apply even during the week. Second, *gezeirah shema yistapek mimenu* — because the aroma is so alluring that one might come to dip bread into it. Both concerns reinforce each other and together underlie the prohibition.

### Story: Balsam Fire

To drive home the extreme flammability of balsam oil, the *gemara* relates a cautionary anecdote. A mother-in-law who despised her daughter-in-law advised the younger woman to anoint herself with *mishcha de-afarsimon*, this fragrant balsam oil. After she did so, the mother-in-law sent her to light a lamp. The young woman went to kindle it, the flame caught hold of her, and she was consumed. The story is clearly not presented for emulation, but it powerfully illustrates just how volatile this oil is — and why the rabbis took precautions surrounding its use.

---

## Tevel & Terumah

### Prohibited Materials

The *gemara* transitions to a *baraita*: *ein madlikin be-tevel tamei be-chol* — one may not use *tevel tamei*, untithed grain that is also ritually impure, even on a weekday. And *ein tzarich lomar b'Shabbat* — certainly not on Shabbat. Similarly, *ein madlikin b'neft b'lavan be-chol* — one may not use white naphtha as lamp fuel even on a weekday, and certainly not on Shabbat. These prohibitions, the *gemara* notes, are clearly not limited to Shabbat concerns alone.

### Tevel vs Terumah

The prohibition on white naphtha is readily explained by the same concern raised earlier: *mipnei shehu af*, it floats and is dangerously flammable. But the prohibition on *tevel tamei* is more puzzling. We learned on the previous daf that *terumah temei'ah* — impure priestly tithe — may be used for lamp fuel, because one may derive benefit from it during the process of its destruction. Since *tevel* is essentially grain that still has *terumah* within it waiting to be separated, why should it be worse than *terumah temei'ah* itself?

### Separation Requirement

The *gemara* answers from a *pasuk*: *va-ani hinei natati lecha et mishmeres terumosai* — "I have given you the guarding of my *terumos*," in the plural. As was discussed previously, the verse speaks of two *terumos* — one *tehorah* and one *temei'ah*. From the *tehorah* we learn that it must be protected and kept separate; from the *temei'ah* we learn it must be burned, and yet one may benefit in the course of that burning. But then comes the central derivation: just as *terumah tehorah* may only be utilized from the moment of its separation — a *kohen* cannot eat *tevel* on the grounds that it contains *terumah* he is entitled to eat, because that entitlement only begins once the *terumah* has actually been lifted off — so too *terumah temei'ah*. The benefit one is permitted during its destruction applies only *mish'as harama v'eilach*, from the moment of separation onward. While the oil still sits within the *tevel* in an undifferentiated state, it is off-limits.

### Benefit in Destruction

This ruling raises a deeper question that Tosafot addresses directly. The argument seems to imply that *tevel* itself is *assur b'hana'ah* — forbidden in benefit — since we needed a special *pasuk* to permit benefit from *terumah temei'ah*, and yet here we learn that even that permission does not extend back to cover *tevel*. But Tosafot clarifies that *tevel* is not *assur b'hana'ah* in the classic sense. One could, for example, use *tevel* as bedding without transgression. What is forbidden is specifically the *hana'ah* that comes through the process of destroying it — one may not burn *tevel* as fuel or feed it to animals in a destructive way. Interestingly, then, *terumah temei'ah* and *tevel* emerge as something like mirror images of one another: *terumah temei'ah* is generally *assur b'hana'ah*, with one narrow exception permitting benefit during destruction; *tevel* is generally permitted in benefit, with one narrow exception forbidding benefit that arises in the course of destroying it.

---

## Shimon ben Elazar

### Tzari Source

The *gemara* returns with a *gufa* — returning to address the body of the ruling of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. He prohibited *tzari* for the reasons already discussed. But Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar also made an independent statement clarifying what *tzari* actually is: *tzari eino ela saraf mei'atzei hakataf* — *tzari* is the sap that exudes from the wood of the balsam tree. This is the same substance mentioned in the *ketoret* passage recited in *davening*. Some understand this identification not merely as botanical information but as the operative reason for the prohibition: sap, as distinct from oil, does not burn smoothly and does not draw well after the wick. Tosafot, however, notes that if this were the *pshat*, there would be no need for the other reasons — the aroma concern and the flammability concern — and it is unclear why the *gemara* would have constructed those explanations at all. In any case, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar establishes that *tzari* is a tree-derived sap, not a conventional oil.

---

## Lighting Oil Positions

### Yishmael Position

The *gemara* now surveys a range of *tannaitic* opinions on which oils may and may not be used for Shabbat lighting, revealing a clear progressive tendency to restrict. Rabbi Yishmael rules: *kol hayotzei min ha-etz ein madlikin bo* — anything derived from a tree, meaning not from fruit but from the wood or other non-fruit parts of the plant, may not be used for lighting. The presumed reason is that such substances do not burn cleanly and do not draw properly after the wick.

### Yishmael b. Broka

Rabbi Yishmael ben Broka goes further still: *ein madlikin ela beyotzei min hapri* — one may only use something that comes from fruit. This excludes not only tree-derived saps but also, for example, fish oil. Sesame oil and olive oil, deriving from fruits of their respective plants, would remain permitted, but animal products and saps would not.

### Tarfon Position

Rabbi Tarfon takes the most restrictive position: *ein madlikin ela beshemen zayit bilvad* — only olive oil, and nothing else. The progression from no restriction to some restriction to fruit-only to olive-oil-only represents a steady escalation, with each opinion narrowing the range of acceptable materials.

### Yochanan Response

Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka rises to respond to this trend. His argument is essentially one of practical leadership: *mah ya'asu anshei Bavel she-ein lahem ela shemen shumshumin* — what are the people of Babylonia to do, who have only sesame oil? *U-mah ya'asu anshei Madai* — what of the people of Media, who have only nut oil? *U-mah ya'asu anshei Alexandria* — what of Alexandria, where only gourd oil is available? *U-mah ya'asu anshei Kapotkia* — and what of Cappadocia, where they have neither this nor that, but only *neft*, naphtha? One may be personally stringent, but a rabbinic leader bears responsibility for *kol Klal Yisrael*, and a ruling that leaves entire communities unable to fulfill *hadlakat nerot Shabbat* is untenable. Rabbi Yochanan therefore concludes: *ein lecha ela mah shemanu chachamim ein madlikin* — the only materials that are forbidden are those enumerated by the early sages in their established list.

This is in fact the *stam* position of the Mishnah itself, which after listing prohibited wicks and oils turns to note that the *chachamim* permit all the oils — sesame, nut, gourd, fish, *paku'ot*, *itran*, and *neft* — precisely the same oils defended by Rabbi Yochanan. The successive generations of *tannaim* attempting to add prohibitions are pushing against an earlier, more permissive consensus, and Rabbi Tarfon's stringency, however personally compelling, cannot be sustained as a communal ruling.

### Shezuri Clarification

Rabbi Shimon Shezuri similarly affirms the permissibility of gourd oil and *neft* — again, materials explicitly permitted in the Mishnah by the *chachamim* — moving in the direction of expansion rather than restriction.

### Sumchos Position

Sumchos states: *kol hayotzei min habasar ein madlikin bo ela beshemen dagim* — anything that derives from animal flesh may not be used for lighting, with the sole exception of fish oil. This effectively permits fish oil while excluding rendered animal fat, which had already been disallowed by the earlier Mishnaic list.

### Oil Consensus

The *gemara* immediately questions whether Sumchos adds anything new: *Sumchus hainu Tanna Kamma* — is this not simply the same as the *tanna kamma*? The prohibition on *chelev*, liquefied fat, was already established by the earlier sages, so what does Sumchos contribute? The *gemara* resolves that the practical difference involves the ruling of Rav Bruna in the name of Rav — namely, the question of whether mixing a permissible oil with a non-permissible animal product renders the mixture acceptable. The two opinions would differ on that point, though the *gemara* notes *v'lo mesaimei* — we cannot determine which opinion goes which way. What emerges overall is a picture of *tannaim* pulling in two directions: some toward expansion of prohibitions, others — culminating in the broad ruling of the *chachamim* — affirming a wide range of permissible oils for communities across the diaspora.

---

## Shimon ben Elazar (II)

### Plant Materials Tumah

The *gemara* returns to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and presents a *baraita* that contains two rulings together: *kol hayotzei min ha-etz ein bo mishum shalosh al shalosh u-masachin bo chutz mi-pishtan* — anything derived from a tree carries no *tumah* of three-by-three, and it may be used as *schach*, with the exception of linen.

The first ruling requires some unpacking. In the laws of garment *tumah*, there are two relevant sizes: three by three *etzba'ot* — finger-widths — which is a very small swath, perhaps three inches by three inches, significant only to someone poor enough to use it as a patch; and three by three *tefachim* — handbreadths — which is a substantially larger piece, perhaps nine inches by nine inches or more, something that even a wealthy person would find a use for and that could function as an actual garment. Here Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says that materials derived from plants — *Rashi* interprets this to include canvas, cotton, and similar plant-derived fibers — do not become *tamei* even at the smaller size of three by three fingers. These are not classic garment materials. The classic materials are wool and linen, *tzemar u-fishtim*, and only those carry the full range of garment *tumah*.

### Plant Materials Schach

The second ruling follows naturally. For *schach* to be valid, two conditions must be met: the material must grow from the ground, and it must not be *mekabel tumah* — susceptible to becoming *tamei*. Plant-derived materials satisfy both criteria. They grow from the ground, and as we have just established, they do not become *tamei* as garments. Therefore they are entirely valid for use as *schach*.

The one explicit exception is linen, *pishtan*. Linen does derive from a plant, but it is itself a paradigmatic garment material — it is the *pishtan* of the Torah's repeated formulation *beged tzemar o beged pishtim*. Because linen functions as a classic cloth, it is considered *mekabel tumah* in the full sense, and therefore it may not be used as *schach*.

---

## Garment Tumah Laws

### Wool & Linen Only

Abaye now notes that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the *tana d'bei Rabbi Yishmael* are expressing the same fundamental position: *amru davar echad* — they said the same thing. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling, just cited, establishes that plant-derived materials are not subject to garment *tumah*. The *tana d'bei Rabbi Yishmael* arrives at the same principle from a different direction.

The *baraita* of the *tana d'bei Rabbi Yishmael* reasons as follows: the Torah speaks of *begadim* — garments — in many contexts without qualification. *Rashi* lists numerous examples: garments that become *tamei* through contact with a dead rodent, through a corpse, through a seminal emission, and of course in the context of *tzitzit*. In all these places the Torah simply says *beged* without specifying material. One might therefore assume that any material used for clothing qualifies. But in one location — the laws of *tzara'at* — the Torah specifies: *beged tzemar o beged pishtim*, a garment of wool or a garment of linen. Rather than reading this as a limitation applicable only to *tzara'at*, the *tana d'bei Rabbi Yishmael* reads it as the Torah's definitive paradigm: whenever the Torah says *beged*, it means something made of wool or linen. *Mah halan tzemar u-fishtim af kol tzemar u-fishtim* — just as there it means wool and linen, so everywhere it means wool and linen.

So according to Abaye, both Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the *tana d'bei Rabbi Yishmael* hold that if a material is not wool or linen, it simply does not qualify as a garment for any *halachic* purpose — regardless of size.

Rava disagrees with Abaye's reading.
