Rabbeinu Tam takes the opposite approach. He treats the *Gemara* in Pesachim as the primary and authoritative source, and *tzeis* does not occur until 72 minutes after sunset. How then does he read this *Gemara* in Shabbat? The three-quarters of a *mil* — approximately 14 minutes — does not mark the end of *bein hashmashot*; rather, it marks its *beginning*, counting backward from the 72-minute endpoint. So *bein hashmashot* occupies the last 14 minutes of that 72-minute window. The first 58 minutes after sunset are, according to Rabbeinu Tam, unambiguously day. One could, in principle, perform *melacha* throughout that period without transgressing *Shabbat*.

### Tam's Geography

It has been widely noted that Rabbeinu Tam lived in France, where at certain latitudes and seasons it remains visibly light for well over an hour after sunset. It would have been phenomenologically impossible for him to accept that 14 or 18 minutes after sunset constitutes nightfall — the sky is still clearly bright. This geographic reality almost certainly influenced his reading of the sources, even if Rabbeinu Tam does not say so explicitly. His position attracted broad support among the *Rishonim* of France and Germany, many of whom lived in similarly high-latitude environments where late darkness was a fact of daily experience. It is telling that the *Ramban*, who lived in Spain, and the *Mechaber*, who lived in *Eretz Yisrael*, also ruled like Rabbeinu Tam — illustrating how a *shita*, once established, can take on a life independent of the geographic considerations that generated it. The *Mechaber* even applies Rabbeinu Tam *l'kula*, treating the period up to 58 minutes after sunset as unambiguous day — a position virtually no one relies upon today.

### Modern Practice

In practice, most communities follow neither the Gra's 14 minutes nor Rabbeinu Tam's 72 minutes. The prevalent practice is approximately 42 to 45 minutes after sunset. This position traces essentially to Rabbeinu Yonah in Berachot, who proposed setting aside the contradictory *Gemarot* and instead going outside to observe when three stars become visible across the sky. When stars appear distributed throughout the heavens, one has certainly met the threshold of three medium-sized stars that the *Gemara* will shortly describe as the marker of night. Based on astronomical reckoning, this corresponds to roughly 42 to 45 minutes after sunset, depending on location and season.

### Latitude Dependence

All of these positions are, in principle, latitude-dependent. Darkness comes at different rates depending on how far one is from the equator and what season it is. The Gra states explicitly that his number is not fixed but varies with location. In Jerusalem, where it grows dark relatively quickly, the practice associated with the Gra's position is approximately 25 minutes after *shkiya* for *motzei Shabbat* — not 14 or 18 minutes. At higher latitudes, even the Gra's figure would extend further. Rabbeinu Tam's 72 minutes is similarly subject to this variation. Rav Moshe Feinstein argues that Rabbeinu Tam's 72 minutes, adjusted for the latitude of America, yields approximately 45 minutes — which would mean that the common American practice of 42 to 45 minutes is effectively a latitude-adjusted Rabbeinu Tam.

### Rav Moshe's View

The difficulty with Rav Moshe's position is the following. If Rabbeinu Tam's 72 minutes were empirically calibrated to France, one could argue that the equivalent in America, given the difference in latitude, is 45 minutes. But Rabbeinu Tam is not making an empirical claim about France — he is presenting a textual argument that the *Gemara* itself, rooted in the realities of *Eretz Yisrael* and Babylonia, requires 72 minutes. There is no way to derive that 72 minutes in those latitudes corresponds to 45 minutes in America. Nevertheless, Rav Moshe maintains this position. His view is that those who follow the 42 to 45 minute practice are in effect following a modified Rabbeinu Tam adjusted for location. The more straightforward understanding of the 42 to 45 minute practice, however, is that it reflects direct astronomical observation of when three stars appear — an approach that does not depend on resolving the contradiction between the *Gemarot* at all.

Practically speaking, there is a strong argument against relying on Rabbeinu Tam *l'kula* under ordinary circumstances. If one routinely performs *melacha* after 45 minutes — effectively rejecting Rabbeinu Tam's *shita* week after week — it is difficult to invoke that same *shita* selectively when a situation of need arises. The coherence of one's *halachic* practice requires some consistency in which positions one takes seriously.

---

## Halachic Rulings

### Rabbi Nechemiah

The *Gemara* now introduces Rabbi Nechemiah's position: *bein hashmashot* lasts for the time it takes a person to walk half a *mil* from sunset — approximately nine minutes.

### Mount Carmel Test

Rabbi Chanina offers a practical illustration: if you want to experience the duration of Rabbi Nechemiah's *shiur*, leave the sun at the top of Mount Carmel, descend to the Mediterranean, immerse in the sea, and return to the top — that interval is the *shiur* of Rabbi Nechemiah. Mount Carmel is located near Haifa, adjacent to the Mediterranean coast, so the geography is plausible. Rashi understands this as a way of expressing the nine-minute half-*mil* — the descent, immersion, and return constituting roughly that amount of time, though the logistics of how exactly going down a mountain, performing a *tevila*, and returning maps onto nine minutes is not entirely straightforward, particularly since *ya'ale* might mean emerging from the *tevila* rather than literally climbing back up the mountain.

### Tosafot Reading

Tosafot offers a fundamentally different reading of the passage. Rather than describing the duration of *bein hashmashot* from sunset, Tosafot understands the scenario as follows: when the sun is still at the top of Mount Carmel — meaning, before sunset — the time it takes to descend, perform a *tevila*, and return gives you an indication of when the sun will have set. In other words, it is telling a *kohen* who wishes to immerse and then eat *terumah* after dark: if you begin your descent when the sun is at the top of the mountain, you will have completed your *tevila* and ascended before sunset, ensuring that your immersion occurs during definite daytime. On this reading, the example is not about the duration of *bein hashmashot* at all but about a practical landmark for knowing when sunset is near — relevant specifically to a *kohen* who needs to time his *tevila* correctly. What remains somewhat unclear is why the *Gemara* specifies the return ascent, since once the *tevila* is complete the *kohen*'s status changes regardless of where he is physically standing.

The extended discussion of *bein hashmashot* now arrives at a crucial ruling. Before examining it, it is worth noting that the most stringent position in this *Gemara* is Rabbi Yehuda's: from sunset until three-quarters of a *mil* is *bein hashmashot*, before which is definite day and after which is definite night. The other positions — Rabbi Nechemiah's half-*mil* and Rabbi Yosi's blink-of-an-eye — are comparatively less stringent in duration. Were it not for the *Gemara* in Pesachim and the subsequent position of Rabbeinu Tam, the natural reading of this *Gemara* would yield *tzeis* at 14 to 18 minutes after sunset as the most stringent available ruling.

### Two-Sided Strictness

Rabbah bar bar Channah said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *halakha k'Rabbi Yehuda l'inyan Shabbat* — we rule like Rabbi Yehuda for matters of *Shabbat*. *V'halakha k'Rabbi Yosi l'inyan terumah* — and we rule like Rabbi Yosi for matters of *terumah*.

### Strictness Explained

The *Gemara* unpacks this ruling. Ruling like Rabbi Yehuda for *Shabbat* is straightforward: it is *l'chumra*, the strict position, meaning *Shabbat* begins at sunset and does not end until *bein hashmashot* is complete. But what does it mean to rule like Rabbi Yosi for *terumah*? The *Gemara* first considers whether it means *kohanim* may immerse during Rabbi Yehuda's *bein hashmashot* period because according to Rabbi Yosi that period is definite day — but this is rejected, since immersion is a *d'Oraita* requirement and one cannot be lenient there.

The correct interpretation: ruling like Rabbi Yosi for *terumah* means that *kohanim* may not eat *terumah* until Rabbi Yosi's *bein hashmashot* — the blink of an eye — has elapsed following Rabbi Yehuda's three-quarters of a *mil*. This is a two-sided strictness. At the beginning of *Shabbat*, we are strict like Rabbi Yehuda and treat sunset as the onset of *bein hashmashot*. At the end of *Shabbat*, we are strict like Rabbi Yosi and do not permit the eating of *terumah* (or, by extension, the performance of *melacha*) until even Rabbi Yosi's instantaneous transition has passed — ensuring that one is in definite night before acting. We are strict at the onset and strict at the conclusion.

This presupposes a clear understanding of when Rabbi Yosi's "blink of an eye" occurs. One might have thought it happens somewhere in the middle of Rabbi Yehuda's *bein hashmashot* window; the *Gemara* establishes that it occurs at the very end — once Rabbi Yehuda's full three-quarters of a *mil* has elapsed, then for that final split second is Rabbi Yosi's *bein hashmashot*, and only after that is it unambiguous night.

### Tosafot Question

Tosafot raises two questions. First: why does the *Gemara* need to switch from *Shabbat* to *terumah*? It could simply have said we are strict at the beginning of *Shabbat* and strict at the end of *Shabbat*. Tosafot answers that the point is to emphasize that this strictness applies not only to the weighty prohibitions of *Shabbat* but even to *terumah*, which — particularly in the present era when *terumah* may be eaten only by *kohanim* in a state of purity — is somewhat less acute as a practical matter. Even so, we maintain the two-sided stringency.

Tosafot's more probing question is: why does any of this need to be stated for a blink of an eye? What practical difference does a split second make? Tosafot suggests that perhaps Rabbi Yosi's instantaneous transition does not occur precisely at the end of Rabbi Yehuda's period but a few minutes later. This would give real content to the ruling — one must wait not just the three-quarters of a *mil* of Rabbi Yehuda but an additional brief interval before eating *terumah* or performing *melacha*.

In any case, the *Gemara*'s ruling as understood here remains tethered to the framework of this *sugya*: *bein hashmashot* is bounded by sunset on one end and roughly 20 minutes on the other, with additional positions derived either from the *Gemara* in Pesachim or from adjustment for geographic latitude.

---

## Stars as Markers

### Star Counting

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: one star visible in the sky — it is still day; two stars — it is *bein hashmashot*; three stars — it is night. This is a striking and practical alternative to the earlier measures. Rather than counting minutes from sunset or watching the sky's color shift, one simply looks upward.

### Baraita Confirmation

A *baraita* confirms the identical rule: one star is day, two stars is *bein hashmashot*, three stars is night. The *baraita* also includes the teaching of Rabbi Yosi bar Avin: one who performs *melacha* during *bein hashmashot* on Friday evening and again during *bein hashmashot* on Saturday night — having thus spanned the ambiguous period on both ends of *Shabbat* — is *chayav chatat*, obligated in a sin-offering. One might think this is impossible to prove, since perhaps both acts of *melacha* fell in whichever half of the ambiguous period was "really" day. Rashi and Tosafot therefore clarify: the ruling applies when one performed *melacha* continuously throughout the entire *bein hashmashot* period on each occasion. In that case, at least some portion of the *melacha* necessarily fell during the actual *Shabbat* — whether night arrived at the beginning or the end of the ambiguous window.

### Chatat Rule

This ruling exposes a deeper conceptual question, which connects to an earlier *Gemara* concerning a *zav*. When we speak of *bein hashmashot* as an uncertain period, are we saying that night truly begins at one specific moment within that window and we simply cannot identify it? Or are we saying something more fundamental: that *bein hashmashot* is by its nature a mixed category — simultaneously quasi-day and quasi-night — not because we lack information but because that is what dusk inherently *is*? The first reading leads naturally to the requirement that *melacha* must span the entire period to guarantee culpability. The second reading would entail a different analysis entirely. Rashi and Tosafot incline toward the first reading, but the second is a genuine alternative.

### Medium Stars

Rabbi Yosi clarifies an essential detail: the three stars are not the large, bright bodies sometimes visible even in daylight, nor are they the faint stars that emerge only well into the night. They are *beinonim* — medium-sized, average stars.

### Rava's Objection

Rava adds a further clarification consistent with the *chatat* discussion above: one is not *chayav* based merely on performing *melacha* at some moment during *bein hashmashot*. The *melacha* must be performed throughout the entire period.

### Astronomy Basis

The common practice of 42 to 45 minutes after sunset is grounded in astronomical observation calibrated to this *Gemara*. When stars are visible across the full extent of the sky, one has certainly reached the threshold of three medium-sized stars visible to the naked eye. Astronomers have calculated that this condition is met approximately 42 to 45 minutes after sunset, depending on latitude and season.

### Conceptual Issue

The *chatat* rule in this context ties directly back to the conceptual question noted above. If *bein hashmashot* is a period of genuine uncertainty — somewhere in these minutes night begins, but we cannot pinpoint it — then one is only unambiguously *chayav* when *melacha* was performed throughout, ensuring it necessarily overlapped with the onset of night. If, however, *bein hashmashot* is an inherently hybrid category, the analysis differs. Both readings have implications for how one understands the structure of this whole *sugya*.

---

## Practical Signs

### Sun/Palm Trees

Rava said to his attendant: since you are not expert in the precise rabbinic calculations of time (*d'lo kaim-lehu b'shiurei d'rabbanan*), here is a practical guide. When the sun is level with the tops of the palm trees — *ad de-shimsha rei-sh diklei* — that is when you should light a candle, because sunset is imminent.

### Animal Signs

On a cloudy day when the sun cannot be seen, different indicators apply. In the city, observe the roosters: they begin settling onto their perches. Rashi explains they take up their roosting positions while it is still day. In the field, observe the ravens: they return to their nests as nightfall approaches.

### Grass Sign

An additional indicator: a type of grass called *adanei* begins to incline toward the west as nightfall draws near.

### Sign Puzzle

This passage raises an interesting difficulty. If *bein hashmashot* is defined by sunset, why are alternative practical signs needed at all? Anyone can look outside and see whether the sun has set. One possible resolution is that these signs are given for situations where the actual sunset is obscured — perhaps by mountains, or by topography that prevents a clear view of the horizon. When one is surrounded by palm trees but cannot see all the way to the horizon, seeing the sun at the treetops is a more reliable indicator than guessing at the moment of actual sunset. It may also be relevant that what counts as "sunset" for *halachic* purposes — observable sunset vs. astronomical sunset at sea level — depends on the observer's elevation and vantage point, adding additional complexity to the simple instruction to "just look at the sunset."

There is a further implication here. The fact that practical signs are given for when to stop *melacha* and light candles — a period *before* *bein hashmashot* properly begins — suggests that the practice of lighting candles was already firmly associated with the transition into *Shabbat*, laying the groundwork for the later institution of lighting candles 18 minutes (or, in Jerusalem, 40 minutes) before *shkiya*.

---

## Six Tekiot

### Six Blasts Intro

A *baraita* teaches: six *tekiot* — shofar blasts — were sounded on *erev Shabbat*. This practice is associated with Jerusalem and the *Beit Hamikdash*, though there was a designated place on the Temple precincts from which the blasts were made, as discussed in the context of tractate Middot.

### First Blast

The first blast served to signal those working in the fields: cease your labor, gather your tools and implements, and begin moving toward the city. Given the distance they needed to travel and the time required to return implements and transition from fieldwork, this blast was sounded well in advance of *Shabbat*.

### Second Blast

The second blast signaled those within the city: merchants should close their shops, manufacturers should cease production, and commerce should conclude. City-dwellers needed less travel time, so this blast came somewhat later.

### Third Blast

The third blast, according to Rabbi Natan, was the signal to light candles. By this point, the community had had sufficient time to wind down its activities, and the act of candle-lighting was the final *melacha* to be performed — beginning to associate it, institutionally, with the arrival of *Shabbat*.

### Tefillin Alternative

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi offers a different understanding of the third blast: it signaled the removal of *tefillin*. Since *Shabbat* itself is an *ot* — a sign — it is inappropriate to wear *tefillin* on *Shabbat*; and since *tefillin* are not worn at night in any case, the third blast marked the point at which *tefillin* were taken off. According to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's reading, when candles were lit is not specified — Rashi suggests it occurred at the fourth blast, though the text does not spell this out.

### Final Three Blasts

After a brief interval — the time it takes to fry a small fish (*k'dei tzliyat dag katan*), or alternatively, enough time to stick bread to the oven wall and let a crust form — a final sequence of *tekiah teruah tekiah* was sounded. This three-part blast constituted the formal announcement that *Shabbat* had arrived and all *melacha* must cease.

### Babylonian Practice

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel raises a question about the Babylonian practice: *ma na'aseh leBavliyim?* The Babylonians sounded *tekiah teruah* and then stopped in the middle of the *teruah* — *veshovtim mitoch meria*. This differs from the *tekiah teruah tekiah* prescribed above, both in the sequence and in the fact that *Shabbat* begins mid-*teruah* rather than after the sequence concludes. The *Gemara* resolves the count: they actually sounded *tekiah*, then again *tekiah teruah*, halting midway through the *teruah*. The *Gemara* responds simply: *minhag avoteihem beyadeihem* — they maintained their ancestral practice. One might note that it is also worth recalling an earlier usage of the phrase *ma na'aseh leBavliyim* — in the context of candle oils — where a similar appeal to the practical realities of communities outside *Eretz Yisrael* was invoked.

---

## Detailed Timeline

### First Tekiah Detail

The *tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* now provides a more detailed narrative account of the six-blast sequence. When the first *tekiah* began — note the language *hitchil litkoa*, "began to sound," suggesting each blast was sustained over some minutes — those working in the fields ceased plowing, hoeing, and all agricultural labor. Notably, those working closer to the city were not permitted to enter until those working further out had also gathered and converged, so that all entered together as a group.

### Suspicion Issue

Rashi explains the reason for this communal re-entry: if some workers returned to the city noticeably earlier than others, the later arrivals might be suspected of having continued working after the blast — violating *Shabbat*. By waiting for the more distant workers and entering together, all are equally beyond suspicion.

### Second Tekiah Detail

When the second *tekiah* began, the shutters (*trisim*) — boards that shopkeepers would remove and place on stands as display tables for their wares — were taken down, the stores were locked, and all manufacturing activity in the city ceased. Yet the kitchens were still active: hot water remained on the stove and pots continued to simmer.

### Third Tekiah Detail

When the third *tekiah* began, those with food on the fire removed it. Those who intended to preserve heat for their *Shabbat* meals performed *hatmana* — wrapping and insulating their pots. Candles were lit. And if bread was still in the oven, one could quickly stick a fresh loaf to the wall and allow a crust to form — the last permissible act before the final announcement.

### Shabbat Arrival

Then came the *tekiah teruah tekiah* — the concluding three-part blast — and *Shabbat* arrived. All *melacha* ceased.

---

## Late Lighting/Shofar

### Late Lighting Leniency

Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina rules: if someone has not yet lit candles by the time the six *tekiot* are completed, he may still light for a brief additional interval.

### Shofar-Blower Travel

The rationale: the Sages allotted time for the *chazan haknesset* — the one who sounded the *shofar* — to take his *shofar* home after the final blast. During that brief window, *Shabbat* has not yet fully "taken hold" in the most practical sense, and candle-lighting may still be performed.

### Objection

The *Gemara* objects: if the permissible window depends on the distance between the *shofar*-blower's position and his home, the boundary of *Shabbat* becomes entirely subjective and flexible — which undermines the whole purpose of the communal announcement system.

### Roof Storage

The *Gemara* resolves this: the *shofar*-blower has a discreet place (*makom tzanua*) on the roof of the building from which he blows, where he stores the *shofar*. He does not carry it home at all — his "travel" is simply ascending or descending a flight of stairs, a fixed and minimal amount of time. The window is therefore defined and consistent.

### Muktzah Problem

This resolution also explains why the *shofar* must be stored immediately nearby rather than carried through the city: *she'ein metaltelin lo et hashofar v'lo et hachatzotzrot* — neither the *shofar* nor the *chatzotzrot* (Temple trumpets) may be carried on *Shabbat*. This is not merely a question of carrying in a domain without an *eruv*, but a matter of *muktzah*: these are instruments designated for a specific sacred function and are therefore set aside and not handled on *Shabbat*. The discussion of *muktzah* will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Shabbat 36

## Intro & Context

### Daf Overview

Daf 36 marks the transition from the second *perek* to the third. The shiur picks up from the bottom of 35b, completing the final discussion of the second *perek* before moving on to the new chapter's opening *mishnah*.

### Shofar Placement

The passage under discussion concerns the *chazan haknesset* — the synagogue sexton — who would sound the *shofar* blasts announcing the arrival of *Shabbat*. After the final blast, the question arose: what does he do with his *shofar*? The Gemara answers that he had a designated hidden place at the top of his roof where he would deposit it immediately, because *Shabbat* was entering at that very moment. Even within a *reshut hayachid*, a *shofar* and *chatzotzrot* (trumpet) are *muktzah* and may not be handled once *Shabbat* begins. This detail sets up the Gemara's subsequent analysis of the precise *muktzah* status of these instruments.

---

## Shofar/Trumpet Muktzah

### Hide Shofar

The Gemara establishes that the *chazan* had to deposit his *shofar* immediately upon the onset of *Shabbat* because *shofar* and *chatzotzrot* carry *muktzah* status. The term *m'taltalin* — normally associated with carrying between domains — here means something more fundamental: the object is *muktzah* and may not be handled at all. Even within a fully enclosed *reshut hayachid*, neither instrument may be moved.

### Braitot Contradiction

The Gemara then surfaces a striking set of contradictions among *braitot*. One *braita* states that neither *shofar* nor *chatzotzrot* may be carried on *Shabbat* — both are *muktzah*. A second *braita* draws a distinction: a *shofar* may be carried, but a *chatzotzrot* may not. Rav Yosef attempts to resolve the apparent contradiction between these two sources by distinguishing between a private *shofar* and a communal one. Abaye challenges this immediately: even a private *shofar*, what renders it permissible? The Gemara answers that a *shofar* is fit for a legitimate use — it can serve as a kind of funnel through which water is given to a child (*tinok*), drawing the liquid from the wide end through the narrow mouthpiece. A *chatzotzrot*, being straight, cannot serve this function as naturally. Yet Abaye presses further: even a communal *shofar* — the very one used to announce *Shabbat* — is fit for that same use when a poor child in the congregation needs it. The *beit knesset* bears responsibility for the poor, and therefore the communal *shofar* too is potentially usable. The distinction between private and public thus collapses. A third *braita* then enters: just as a *shofar* may be carried, so too may *chatzotzrot* — neither is *muktzah* at all. The three *braitot* now represent three distinct positions: both forbidden, one permitted and one forbidden, and both permitted.

### Three Tannaim

The Gemara resolves the contradictions cleanly: each *braita* represents a different *Tanna*. The *braita* permitting only the *shofar* reflects the view of Rabbi Yehuda. The *braita* permitting both reflects Rabbi Shimon. The *braita* forbidding both reflects Rabbi Nechemya. The three positions map onto a spectrum of how broadly or narrowly each *Tanna* defines *muktzah*.

---

## Muktzah Categories

### R. Yehuda View

Rabbi Yehuda occupies the middle position in this spectrum. He holds of *muktzah* in its standard formulation and distinguishes between the *shofar* and the *chatzotzrot* on the basis of their alternative uses. His view is that a *shofar*, because it can be used as a funnel for a child, has a sufficient legitimate use that affects its classification, while a *chatzotzrot* lacks any comparable alternative function. At one extreme, Rabbi Shimon rejects most categories of *muktzah* — he acknowledges only very narrow cases such as *muktzah machmat mi'us* — and therefore has no difficulty with either instrument. At the other extreme, Rabbi Nechemya holds that even a *kli* that might theoretically have a permitted use may only be moved for its fundamental designated purpose. Since a *shofar*'s fundamental purpose is to be blown as a musical instrument — which is itself prohibited on *Shabbat* — Rabbi Nechemya holds that even the *shofar* may not be moved.

### Rashi Shofar

Rashi's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position deserves close attention. Rashi states explicitly that the *chatzotzrot* is a *davar shemelachto l'issur* — an implement whose primary function is a prohibited one — and is therefore forbidden as *muktzah*. The *shofar*, by contrast, Rashi treats as having been recategorized: because it can be used to give water to a child, it is classified not merely as a *kli shemelachto l'issur* used for a permitted purpose, but as a *kli shemelachto l'heter* outright. This is a significant claim. The standard rule is that a *kli shemelachto l'issur* — a hammer, for example — may be moved on *Shabbat* if one needs to use it for a permitted purpose, such as cracking nuts. But the hammer remains classified as a *kli shemelachto l'issur*; it does not thereby become a *kli shemelachto l'heter*. Rashi appears to be saying that the *shofar* is different: its legitimate alternative use is substantial enough to actually reclassify the object. The question naturally arises — why does the same logic not apply to the *chatzotzrot*? Rashi's answer, at least implicitly, is that the *chatzotzrot* has no such legitimate use that could reframe its classification.

### Tosafot Trumpet

Tosafot take a fundamentally different approach. Tosafot accept the general rule that a *kli shemelachto l'issur* may be moved for a *tzorech heter* — a permitted need — without any reclassification of the object itself. On this reading, both *shofar* and *chatzotzrot* are *kli shemelachto l'issur*, and both could in principle be moved for a permitted purpose. Why then does Rabbi Yehuda distinguish between them? Tosafot's answer is found toward the end of their commentary on 35b. The *chatzotzrot* is in a category worse than *kli shemelachto l'issur*: it is something one would never think of using for any other purpose whatsoever. Tosafot invoke the analogy of a bed designated for holding coins — an object that has been so thoroughly set aside from ordinary use that it enters a state of complete exclusion. The *chatzotzrot* is like that: no one would ever consider picking up a trumpet to crack a nut or perform any other incidental task. It has been entirely removed from the realm of alternative usage, placing it in a more stringent category than a standard *kli shemelachto l'issur*.

### Rashi v. Tosafot

The contrast between Rashi and Tosafot thus comes into sharp relief. Rashi resolves the asymmetry by upgrading the *shofar* — reclassifying it as a *kli shemelachto l'heter* on the basis of its alternative use. Tosafot resolve the asymmetry by downgrading the *chatzotzrot* — placing it in a more severe category than *kli shemelachto l'issur* because it has been fully set aside from any alternative use. The two approaches move in opposite directions: Rashi adjusts the *shofar* upward, Tosafot pushes the *chatzotzrot* downward.

It is important to note that this debate between Rashi and Tosafot does not appear to reflect a broader disagreement about the general rule of *kli shemelachto l'issur*. The *gemara* is clear elsewhere that a *kli shemelachto l'issur* may be moved *l'tzorech gufo* — for use of the object itself in a permitted manner. Rashi presumably does not contest this. The key to understanding Rashi's position in this *sugya* is the specific case under discussion: the *chazan* who deposited his *shofar* the moment *Shabbat* entered was not using it for a permitted purpose — he was protecting it. Moving an object to protect it from damage or theft is what is called *mechama l'tzel*, moving from sun to shade, and that is not permitted even for a *kli shemelachto l'issur*. On this reading, Rashi's concern is precisely with that scenario: since the movement here is protective rather than functional, he must find a way to permit the *shofar* through reclassification. The *chatzotzrot*, not being reclassifiable as *l'heter*, remains forbidden even for protective movement. Tosafot, by contrast, appear to understand the case as involving movement for a permitted purpose — and therefore must find a different way to distinguish the *chatzotzrot*, namely by treating it as completely set aside.

### Moving Objects

To summarize the underlying principles: a *kli shemelachto l'issur* may be moved if one needs to use it (for a permitted purpose) or if one needs its place. It may not be moved purely to protect it from damage — that is the prohibition of *mechama l'tzel*. A *kli shemelachto l'heter* may be moved even to protect it. According to Tosafot, Rabbi Shimon categorizes both *shofar* and *chatzotzrot* as *kli shemelachto l'issur* — he does not acknowledge the more severe category into which Tosafot place the *chatzotzrot* — and therefore both may be moved for a *tzorech heter*. They may not be moved *mechama l'tzel*, but for any permitted use they are available. Rabbi Nechemya, at the other extreme, holds that objects may only be moved for their designated purpose, and since the designated purpose of both instruments is prohibited on *Shabbat*, neither may be moved at all. Tosafot add a clarification: even Rabbi Shimon, who permits moving both instruments for a permitted use, would still forbid moving them *mechama l'tzel* — to protect them for their own sake.

---

## Name Changes

### Shofar Names

Having completed the *muktzah* analysis, the Gemara pivots to a terminological observation. The opening *braita* stated that one may not carry "*lo et hashofar v'lo et hachatzotzrot*" — neither the *shofar* nor the *chatzotzrot*. Rashi notes that the order of the listing is puzzling: if the *shofar* is the more usable and presumably less *muktzah* of the two, why mention the prohibition on *shofar* first, since the prohibition on *chatzotzrot* is even more obvious? This apparent inversion provides the occasion for the Gemara to introduce a significant historical fact: the names of these two instruments were reversed in popular usage after the destruction of the *Beit Hamikdash*. What was originally called a *shofar* — the animal horn — began to be called *chatzotzrot*, and what was originally called *chatzotzrot* — the fashioned metal trumpet — began to be called *shofar*. Rav Chisda states this explicitly: among the three things whose names were interchanged after the *churban*, the first pair is *shofar* and *chatzotzrot*.

This phenomenon is not merely antiquarian. The *Sheiltos*, a Gaonic work composed approximately in the seventh century, demonstrates the real-world effect of this shift. When discussing the *mitzvah* of *tekiat shofar*, the *Sheiltos* writes that Jews are obligated to sound the *chatzotzrot* on Rosh Hashanah — using the post-*churban* vernacular in which the word *chatzotzrot* had come to denote what we call the *shofar*.

### Rosh Hashanah

The Gemara asks *l'mai nafka mina* — what practical difference does this name reversal make? The answer: for the *shofar* of Rosh Hashanah. If someone asks what instrument to obtain for the *mitzvah*, one must be careful to use the vernacular correctly. If speaking in the biblical idiom and telling someone to obtain a *chatzotzrot*, he may go and purchase a metal trumpet — and fulfill no *mitzvah* at all. Knowing what the current vernacular means is essential for directing people to the correct instrument.

---

## Other Name Shifts

### Lulav Plants

The Gemara continues with two additional examples from Rav Chisda's list of inverted names. The *aravah* — the willow used for the *lulav* set, the *arvei nachal* — was subsequently called *tziptzafah*, and the *tziptzafah* — a plant that is not valid for the *lulav* — was subsequently called *aravah*. Here too the *nafka mina* is practical: if someone asks which plant to use for his *lulav*, one must communicate in the current vernacular. Telling him to use an *aravah*, if that term now refers to the invalid species, will cause him to perform the *mitzvah* improperly.

### Furniture

The third item in Rav Chisda's list involves furniture. The words *psora* and *psorta* — denoting a large table and a small table respectively — were reversed in common usage. The *nafka mina* here is for *mikach u'mimkar*, commercial transactions. If a buyer orders a *psora* and the seller understands it to mean the opposite size, the transaction is compromised. One must know the current vernacular to conduct business accurately.

### Stomach Parts

Abaye adds a further case to the list. The *hovlila* — one of the cow's stomachs, associated with the grinding of food and characterized by relatively thin walls — and the *beit hakosot* — a later stomach with thick, doubled walls separated by a layer of fat — had their names exchanged. The *nafka mina* here is for *treifot*. Specifically, the Gemara asks: what difference does it make if a needle is found *b'ovi beit hakosot*, in the thickness of the wall of the *beit hakosot*? The ruling is: if the needle has penetrated only one side of the double wall, the animal is *kesherah*, because the fat layer between the walls seals the puncture. Only if the needle has pierced through both walls entirely is the animal *treifah*. In the thinner-walled grinding stomach, by contrast, even a single penetration is a problem. The practical danger of the name reversal is obvious: a *posek* who confuses the two stomachs may declare an animal *treifah* when it is *kesherah*, or vice versa. Precision in terminology is thus a matter of *halachic* consequence.

### Geography

Rav Ashi appends a final case: *Bavel* and *Borsif* — two geographic names that were interchanged. What had been called *Bavel* came to be called *Borsif*, and vice versa. The *nafka mina* is for *gittei nashim*, bills of divorce. The opening *mishnah* of *Gittin* establishes that an agent bringing a *get* from *medinat hayam* — distant lands across the sea — must declare "*bifnai nichtav u'bifnai nechtam*," that the document was written and signed in his presence, because we cannot assume that proper *halachic* procedure was followed in distant locales. However, the Gemara elsewhere clarifies that *Bavel* is exempt from this requirement because its scholars were sufficiently expert in *hilchot gitin*. Knowing which territory is considered *Bavel* and which is not is therefore crucial: an agent arriving from what is now called *Borsif* must know whether that name corresponds to the *Bavel* of the exemption or not.

Rashi offers a second explanation as well: since a *get* must record the names of places, one must use accurate contemporary terminology. Tosafot, however, take strong exception to this second explanation. Tosafot argue that *Bavel* is not a city but a country, and the name of a country (*shem medina*) is not written in a *get* — only the city is recorded. This raises a broader question relevant to *get* practice across the generations: whether the name of a state or province constitutes a *shem medina* that should be omitted, or whether it serves as legitimate identifying information. That question will require attention when the tractates of *Gittin* and *Ketubot* are reached.

With this digression concluded, the Gemara declares *hadran alach bama madlikin* — the second *perek* is complete.

---

## Third Perek Intro

### Perek Context

The transition to the third *perek* follows naturally from the preceding material. The second *perek* dealt with the sequence of *erev Shabbat* preparations — the lighting of candles and the *shofar* blasts heralding *Shabbat*. One of the *braitot* cited there described how, at the third blast, people would remove food from the fire and light the candles — indicating that fire management and candle lighting occurred at approximately the same moment. The third *perek* picks up that thread and addresses the laws governing food left on or returned to the fire as *Shabbat* enters.

### Fire Management

This chapter also connects back to a discussion at the end of the first *perek*, where Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai debated the permissibility of various *erev Shabbat* activities that extend into *Shabbat* itself. While Beit Hillel generally permits work begun before *Shabbat* to continue into *Shabbat*, food on the fire presents a special concern: the anxiety over whether food is cooking properly may lead a person to stir the coals — an act that constitutes a prohibited *melachah*. The third *perek* will develop this concern in detail and ultimately arrive at the *halachic* framework underlying the contemporary practice of using a *blech*.

---

## Kirah & Fire

### Kirah Vessel

The *mishnah* opens: *kira she-hisikuha b'kash u've-givah* — a *kirah* that was heated with straw and stubble. The *kirah* was a large pottery vessel, fixed in place, that functioned as a cooking apparatus. Fire was built inside the vessel, and a cooking pot was placed on the rim, suspended over the heat. The concentrated space directed heat upward efficiently. Rashi confirms this understanding of the vessel's structure.

### Straw Fuel

When the *kirah* is fueled with straw (*kash*) and stubble (*givah*), the fuel burns quickly and leaves no lasting coals. Since the entire concern of this *mishnah* is that a person may come to stir the coals on *Shabbat*, a fire that produces no sustained coals eliminates the concern entirely. Therefore, in such a case, *notnin aleha tavshil* — one may place a cooked dish upon it before *Shabbat* without any additional condition.

### Wood Fuel

When, however, the *kirah* is fueled with *gefes* — which Rashi identifies as a remnant of something like pressed seeds — or with actual wood (*eitzim*), the situation changes. These fuels produce genuine, lasting coals that retain significant heat and continue to burn well into the cooking period. In this case, the concern that a person will stir the coals on *Shabbat* is real.

### Ash Coverage

Faced with lasting coals, the *mishnah* imposes a requirement: *lo yiten ad she-yigrof o ad she-yiten et ha-eifer* — one may not place food on the *kirah* until one either sweeps out the coals entirely or covers them with ashes. Sweeping out leaves only residual heat with no live coals to stir. Covering with ashes — *ketumah* — effectively suppresses the fire and removes the practical temptation to stir. It is worth noting that the *mishnah*'s plain language might suggest that the fire must be entirely eliminated. This would pose an obvious difficulty for the contemporary practice of maintaining a burner covered by a *blech*. The Gemara will address this: the *eifer* covering need not extinguish the fire completely. What it must do is serve as a *heker* — a marker — that modifies the cooking context. This in turn provides the conceptual basis for treating the *blech* as a functional equivalent of the ash covering: it somewhat reduces heat, it serves as a visual reminder, and it is sufficient even though the flame beneath continues to burn.

---

## Shammai v. Hillel

### Shammai Water

The *mishnah* now introduces the first of two debates between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Even once the conditions of sweeping out or covering with ashes have been met, Beit Shammai holds: *chamin aval lo tavshil* — hot water may be left on the *kirah*, but not a *tavshil*, a cooked dish. The scope of Beit Shammai's leniency is limited to water alone.

### Anxiety Concern

The rationale underlying Beit Shammai's distinction is the degree of anxiety that different foods produce. Water is simple: it heats, it boils, and there is no ongoing cooking process to monitor. One is not tempted to intervene, check, or adjust. A *tavshil* — any dish that is actually cooking — involves a prolonged, anxiety-laden process. Is it cooking evenly? Has it burned? Is it too watery? These concerns draw a person's attention and may lead him to stir the coals to raise the heat. It is this anticipatory anxiety that Beit Shammai seeks to preempt.

### Hillel Both

Beit Hillel disagrees: *chamin v'tavshil* — both hot water and cooked dishes may be left on the *kirah* under these conditions. The *halachah* follows Beit Hillel. Beit Hillel's position does not mean that any food in any state of preparation may simply be left on a roaring fire; the prior conditions of sweeping or covering still apply. But once those conditions are met, Beit Hillel imposes no further distinction based on what is being cooked.

---

## Remove & Return

### Shammai Return

The *mishnah* then records a second debate: *Beit Shammai omrim notlin aval lo machzirin* — Beit Shammai says one may remove food from the fire on *Shabbat* but may not return it. Even the hot water that Beit Shammai permitted to remain on the *kirah* before *Shabbat* — once removed, it may not be replaced.

### Hillel Return

Beit Hillel responds: *af machzirin* — one may even return food to the fire. This position, too, follows Beit Hillel, and it becomes the *halachic* foundation for the contemporary practice of removing and replacing a pot of *cholent* on *Shabbat* — subject, as the Gemara will make clear, to a series of carefully defined conditions.

---

## Sheiya v. Chazara

### Question Posed

The Gemara now poses its central question regarding the *mishnah*'s opening clause. When the *mishnah* says that one may not place food on the *kirah* unless it has been swept out or covered — does this refer to *sheiya* (leaving food on the fire from before *Shabbat*) or to *chazara* (returning food to the fire on *Shabbat* after it has been removed)? The question is not merely philological. It determines how stringent the requirement of *grufa u'ketuma* actually is and — critically — whether there exists a category of *sheiya* that is entirely exempt from that requirement.

### Chananya View

The Gemara introduces the opinion of Chananya: *kol she-hu k'ma'achal Ben Drusai mutar le-shahoto al gabei kirah af al pi she-eino garuf ve-katum* — any food that has reached the stage of *ma'achal Ben Drusai* may be left on the *kirah* even if the fire has not been swept out and even if no ashes have been placed. *Ma'achal Ben Drusai* refers to food that has been cooked to approximately a third or half of full doneness — the name derives from a historical figure notorious for eating food in a partially cooked state. The reasoning behind Chananya's leniency is that once food has reached this stage, it is already technically edible. The cook's anxiety diminishes substantially: the food will not be ruined if left alone, and there is far less temptation to intervene. Chananya therefore holds that the concern for stirring does not apply at this stage, and no suppression of the fire is required for *sheiya*.

If Chananya is correct, the *mishnah*'s demand for *grufa u'ketuma* applies only to *chazara* — returning the food to the fire — not to *sheiya*. The Gemara asks whether that is indeed how the *mishnah* should be read.

### Ashkenazi/Sefardi

Tosafot, at the top of 37a, state their position directly: *mishum d'kaima lan k'Chananya* — because we rule like Chananya, the Gemara is compelled to read the *mishnah* in a way consistent with his view, even though the plain sense of the *mishnah* clearly speaks of *sheiya*. Tosafot acknowledge that this reading of the *mishnah* is forced (*dochik*), but maintain it because the *halachah* follows Chananya.

This is the hinge point of the Ashkenazi-Sefardi divide on the *blech*. Ashkenazim rule like Chananya. The practical consequence is that once food is already a third or half cooked before *Shabbat*, one does not require a *blech* merely to leave it on the fire — *sheiya* is permitted without *grufa u'ketuma* at that stage. A *blech* is required only for *chazara* — if one intends to remove the food and return it during *Shabbat*. Sefardim do not rule like Chananya and therefore require *grufa u'ketuma* — implemented as a *blech* — for *sheiya* as well.

### Personal Experience

The practical consequence of the Ashkenazi position is that for food which is well on its way to being cooked before *Shabbat*, the *blech* is strictly speaking not required for *sheiya*. The *Rama* notes that it is preferable to be stringent *l'chatchilah*, but the underlying Ashkenazi *halachah* does not require it. The requirement of a *blech* for Ashkenazim is primarily the *chazara* concern — placing food back on the fire during *Shabbat* — which carries a higher level of scrutiny for independent reasons.

---

## Chazara Stringency

### Stirring Risk

Why does *chazara* generate a stricter standard than *sheiya*, even according to Chananya who is relatively lenient? Two explanations are offered.

The first: the act of handling the pot heightens the risk of stirring. When food has simply been sitting on the fire since before *Shabbat*, one is in a hands-off posture — there is no reason to touch anything. But once a person picks up the pot, moves it, sets it down, and is in the process of placing it back on the fire, he is already actively engaged with the cooking apparatus. In that moment of active handling, it is far easier to think — the flame could be a little higher — and to reach for the coals. The physical engagement creates an elevated likelihood of the prohibited act.

### Cooking Appearance

The second explanation: returning food to a fire is experientially indistinguishable from the act of cooking. The Gemara uses the phrase *mechzi k'mevashel* — it appears like cooking. Regardless of one's subjective intent, the observable act of placing a pot onto a fire on *Shabbat* looks, feels, and functions like an act of cooking, and that appearance itself is something the Rabbis sought to prevent.

### Modern Devices

These two rationales yield different practical outcomes in modern contexts. Consider a hotplate or stovetop with adjustable knobs. If the concern behind the stringency of *chazara* is the risk of stirring — or in modern terms, the risk of adjusting the flame — then even a covered knob that cannot be easily accessed would address that concern, since there is no realistic avenue to inadvertently adjust the heat. If, however, the concern is *mechzi k'mevashel* — the appearance of cooking — then the question shifts: does anyone cook on a particular device? A hot plate, for example, might not evoke the appearance of cooking in the same way a stovetop does. Conversely, consider a crock pot with its knobs fully covered. The adjustment concern is neutralized, but a crock pot is a device people routinely use for cooking, so the *mechzi k'mevashel* concern may well apply. The two rationales thus generate a genuine *nafka minah* in assessing these modern instruments.

---

## Gemara Reading

### Chazara Primary

The Gemara now works through the alternative reading of the *mishnah* — namely, that its opening clause about *grufa u'ketuma* refers primarily to *chazara*. This is the reading that the Gemara pursues in order to be consistent with Chananya.

### Missing Words

To sustain this reading, the Gemara invokes the principle of *chasurai mechasra* — the *mishnah* is missing words and must be supplemented. The *mishnah* as it stands does not make the *sheiya* permission explicit; it must be inserted as an implicit middle section of the text. Specifically, the permission to leave food on the fire without sweeping — Chananya's leniency — is treated as an unstated assumption embedded in the *mishnah* between its first and final sections.

### Three Stages

Under this reading, the *mishnah* unfolds in three stages. First, the *mishnah* establishes the conditions for *chazara*: if the *kirah* was fueled with straw and stubble, one may return food to it; if with wood, one may not return food until the fire has been swept out or covered. Second — the inserted section — the *mishnah* implies a separate rule about *sheiya*: leaving food on is permitted even without sweeping, provided the food has reached the level of Chananya's *ma'achal Ben Drusai*. What may one leave on? That is a debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: water only, or also cooked foods. Third, the *mishnah* closes by clarifying that the permission for *chazara* stated in the first section is itself contested: Beit Shammai holds one may remove but not return; Beit Hillel holds one may even return. On this reading, the middle section — the debate about water versus *tavshil* — concerns *sheiya* without sweeping, while the final debate of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel concerns *chazara*.

### Complexity

This is admittedly a strained reading. The plain sense of the *mishnah* proceeds naturally from conditions for leaving food on (*sheiya*), to what may be left on (the Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel debate about water versus *tavshil*), to whether removed food may be returned (*chazara*). Tosafot acknowledge this openly: the Gemara is pressing the text into an unnatural shape *mishum d'kaima lan k'Chananya* — because the *halachah* has been established in accordance with Chananya, and the *mishnah* must be reconciled with that ruling. The reading is technically possible but requires the interpolation of unstated content, which is why the Gemara frames it under the rubric of *chasurai mechasra*.

---

## Tomorrow's Daf

### Chananya Debate

Tomorrow's *daf* will continue directly from this point, taking up the core debate between Chananya and the Sages. The central question — whether food that has reached *ma'achal Ben Drusai* may be left on an unsuppressed fire before *Shabbat* without any form of *grufa u'ketuma* — will be argued out in full. This is the debate that ultimately drives the Ashkenazi practice of the *blech* and the Sefardi disagreement with it. The Sefardim, who do not rule like Chananya, require *grufa u'ketuma* for *sheiya* as well, making the *blech* a universal requirement regardless of whether one intends to return the food. That discussion, and its *halachic* resolution, awaits.

---

---

# Shabbat 37

## Garuf vKatum: Shehiya vs…

### Mishna Overview

The second chapter of *Masechet Shabbat*, known as *Kira*, addresses the fundamental questions of keeping food on a flame before *Shabbos* and of removing and returning food to that flame. The *Mishna* establishes that in order to leave food on a stove or oven from before *Shabbos*, the oven must be *garuf o katum* — either swept out of its coals or have ashes placed upon them. This requirement, expressed by the *Gemara* as *garuf ve'katum*, functions as a safeguard against the concern that one might come to stir the coals on *Shabbos* in order to intensify the heat. In contemporary practice, the *blech* — a metal sheet placed over the burners — serves as our translation of this concept.

### Chananya's Lenient View

The *Gemara*, however, raises the possibility that the *Mishna*'s requirement of *garuf ve'katum* applies only when one wishes to return food to the flame on *Shabbos* (*chazara*), but not merely to leave food on the flame from before *Shabbos* (*shehiya*). This reading draws support from the position of Chananya, who holds that once food has reached the level of *ma'achal ben drusai* — roughly half-cooked — one may leave it on an untreated flame from before *Shabbos* without sweeping out the coals. As will become clear, this is precisely the ruling adopted by *Ashkenazim*: once food is partially cooked, no *blech* is required merely to leave food on the flame. The *blech* is required only when one wishes to return food to the flame on *Shabbos* itself.

### Gemara's Core Question

The central question of this entire sugya, then, is whether the *Mishna*'s demand for *garuf ve'katum* — and by extension our requirement of a *blech* — applies equally to *shehiya* (leaving food on from before *Shabbos*) or only to *chazara* (returning food to the flame on *Shabbos*). The *Gemara* works through a series of proofs and counter-proofs in order to resolve this question.

### Tocha vs Al Gaba

About ten lines into 37a, the *Gemara* introduces a teaching of Rabbi Chelbo. The text reads: *de'amar Rabbi Chelbo amar Rabbi Chama bar Guria amar Rav: lo shanu ela al gaba aval letocha assur* — "we only taught the leniency with respect to on top of the oven, but inside the oven it is forbidden." The distinction being drawn is between *tocha* — placing food inside the oven, suspended in the hollow — and *al gaba* — placing it on top of or against the outer rim or roof of the oven. 

Rashi explains that *al gaba* may refer either to placing a pot on the outer edge of the oven's rim, or to setting a covering over the opening and resting the pot on top of that covering, making it function much like a stovetop. In either case, the point is that *al gaba* is not the normal mode of cooking; it involves far less direct heat and is far less experiential of an act of cooking than placing something inside the oven proper. The significance of this distinction lies in the concern underlying the *garuf ve'katum* requirement: namely, that one might come to stir the coals. When something is inside the oven in the usual cooking position, both the heat and the psychological experience of cooking are more intense, and therefore the concern about stirring is more acute.

### Applying the Distinction

The *Gemara* now asks how this distinction between *tocha* and *al gaba* bears on our central question. The argument runs as follows: *ee amrat bishlama lehachzir tenan* — if you say the *Mishna* is speaking about returning food to the flame, then Rabbi Chelbo's distinction makes perfect sense. The concern driving *chazara* is not only that one might stir the coals, but also that the act of putting something back on the flame feels experientially like cooking. Placing food inside an open oven is far more reminiscent of cooking than placing it on the outer rim or on a cover. One could therefore understand why, even in a case where the oven has been treated (*garuf ve'katum*), we would still be more permissive about placing food on top than about placing it inside — the latter simply looks more like cooking. In our contemporary terms, putting food into the oven interior is a more cooking-like act than putting it on the stovetop, even if the stovetop is over a live flame.

But if the *Mishna* is speaking about *shehiya* — leaving food on from before *Shabbos* — then the entire concern is whether one will come to stir the coals, not about what the act looks like experientially. In that case, *ma li tocha ma li al gaba* — what difference does it make whether the pot is inside or on top? The concern about stirring is the same either way. Since Rabbi Chelbo does draw this distinction, the *Gemara* initially reasons that his teaching must be addressing *chazara*, the act of returning food, and this in turn would suggest that our *Mishna* too is about *chazara*.

The *Gemara*, however, immediately deflects this inference. *Mee savrat Rabbi Chelbo areisha kaee?* — Who says Rabbi Chelbo is addressing the first clause of the *Mishna* (concerning the conditions for leaving food on)? *Aseifa kaee* — he is addressing the concluding clause, where *Beit Hillel* says *af machzirin*, that one may even return food to the flame. Rabbi Chelbo's distinction between *tocha* and *al gaba* pertains to the end of the *Mishna*, which unambiguously concerns *chazara*. Our question about the beginning of the *Mishna* — whether *garuf ve'katum* is required for *shehiya* — therefore remains open.

### Double Oven Proof

The *Gemara* introduces a new source: *be kirot hamat'imot* — a double oven, two cylindrical hollows side by side within a single unit. The *Tosefta* teaches: *achat gerufa u-ketuma ve-achat she-eina gerufa ve-eina ketuma, mash'hin al gabei gerufa u-ketuma ve-ein mash'hin al she-eina gerufa u-ketuma* — one of the paired ovens is swept and has ashes, the other does not; you may leave food on the treated one but not on the untreated one. 

The *chiddush* here is that even though the two ovens are a single unit and the untreated one is generating heat right beside the treated one, this does not disqualify the treated side. Each compartment is judged independently. Crucially for our question, the language is explicitly *mash'hin* — you may leave food on. This is unambiguously *shehiya*, not *chazara*. And the *Tosefta* says you may not do so on the untreated side. This constitutes a clear proof that *garuf ve'katum* is required even for merely leaving food on from before *Shabbos*, not only for returning it.

---

## Baraita: What Foods Allo…

### Rabbi Meir's Position

Continuing the double-oven *baraita*, the text asks *u'ma hein mash'hin* — what exactly may one leave on the treated oven? Here the *Gemara* presents two versions of the *Beit Shammai*–*Beit Hillel* debate that are considerably stricter than what our *Mishna* records.

According to Rabbi Meir's version: *Beit Shammai omrim ve-lo klum* — *Beit Shammai* says nothing at all may be left on the flame. This is a strikingly severe position: it would mean that on *Shabbos* there could be no hot food whatsoever, a position that begins to resemble the *Karaite* rejection of any Shabbos fire, though there is no evidence the *Tzedukim* took this view. *Beit Hillel*, in Rabbi Meir's version, permits only hot water (*chamin*) to be left on the treated flame, but not cooked food (*tavshil*). And if one removed the pot from the flame, everyone — both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* — agrees it may not be returned. According to this reading, neither school would have hot food on *Shabbos*; at best, *Beit Hillel* would have hot water.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Position

Rabbi Yehuda presents a substantially more lenient and familiar version. In his account, *Beit Shammai* permits hot water but not cooked food; *Beit Hillel* permits both hot water and cooked food. Furthermore, *Beit Shammai* holds that one may remove the pot (*notlin*) but may not return it (*lo machzirin*), while *Beit Hillel* adds that one may even return it (*af machzirin*). This entire structure — the debate about water versus food, the debate about returning — maps exactly onto our *Mishna*, making Rabbi Yehuda the natural candidate for whose opinion our *Mishna* follows.

### Which Opinion?

The *Gemara* now uses this *baraita* to press the question of *shehiya* versus *chazara* further. *Ee amrat bishlama lish'hos tnan* — if our *Mishna* is about leaving food on from before *Shabbos*, then it aligns perfectly with Rabbi Yehuda. The *baraita* in Rabbi Yehuda's version is explicitly about what foods may be left on (*shehiya*) and requires *garuf ve'katum* for doing so. Our *Mishna* would simply be Rabbi Yehuda's position.

But *ela ee amrat lehachzir tnan* — if our *Mishna* is about returning food, and the requirement of *garuf ve'katum* applies only to *chazara* while *shehiya* is entirely unrestricted, then our *Mishna* cannot align with either Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yehuda.

It cannot be Rabbi Meir, because according to Rabbi Meir even *Beit Hillel* only allows hot water on a treated flame. If our *Mishna* is read to mean that *shehiya* needs no *garuf ve'katum* at all, then the *Mishna* implies everyone agrees food may be left freely on an untreated flame — which flatly contradicts Rabbi Meir's *Beit Shammai* (nothing allowed) and *Beit Hillel* (only water, not food, and no returning). The *Gemara* formulates this as: *kashya le-Beit Shammai be-chada u-Beit Hillel be-tarti* — it contradicts *Beit Shammai* in one respect and *Beit Hillel* in two. According to *Beit Shammai* in Rabbi Meir's version, you can leave nothing on any flame, yet our *Mishna* (read as concerning only *chazara*) implies you can freely leave food on an untreated flame. According to *Beit Hillel* in Rabbi Meir's version, you can leave only water on a treated flame and you cannot return food at all — yet our *Mishna* permits both food and returning. In any case, that our *Mishna* does not follow Rabbi Meir is clear regardless of how one reads it.

The problem with saying our *Mishna* is Rabbi Yehuda is more pointed: even Rabbi Yehuda explicitly requires *garuf ve'katum* for *shehiya*. If our *Mishna*'s requirement of *garuf ve'katum* is being read as applying only to *chazara*, that directly contradicts Rabbi Yehuda's position that *garuf ve'katum* is needed even to leave food on.

### Our Mishna's Position

The *Gemara* resolves this by positing that our *Mishna* represents a third, independent position: *tana didan savar lah ke-Rabbi Yehuda be-chada u-falig aleih be-chada* — our *Mishna* agrees with Rabbi Yehuda in one respect but differs in another. It agrees in the general structure of the debate: *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* dispute whether water alone or food as well may be left on, and they dispute whether food may be returned. In this, it follows Rabbi Yehuda precisely. But it differs on the question of when *garuf ve'katum* is required. *D'ilu tana didan savar lish'hos ve-af al pi she-eino garuf ve-katum* — our *Mishna* holds that for *shehiya*, no *garuf ve'katum* is needed; food may be left on an untreated flame. *Ve-Rabbi Yehuda savar be-sh'hiyya nami grufa u-ketuma in, ee lo lo* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that even for *shehiya*, one must have a treated flame.

This is acknowledged to be a strained reading of our *Mishna*. As Tosafot notes, the plain meaning of the *Mishna* seems clearly to require *garuf ve'katum* for *shehiya* as well. The only reason to push the forced reading of the *Mishna* as concerning *chazara* is, as Tosafot explains, because the *halacha* is ultimately ruled in accordance with Chananya — and that is the *Ashkenazi* position.

---

## Somech (Leaning Agai (II)

### Somech Question

The *Gemara* now turns to a distinct but related question: *mahu lismoch bah* — what is the rule about placing a pot not inside the oven or on top of it, but against its outer wall, adjacent to it? The question is whether this mode — *somech*, leaning the pot against the oven — is treated like placing food directly on the flame (and thus subject to the same restrictions) or whether it is inherently more lenient because it is not placed on the heat source itself.

The practical stakes are significant: if *somech* requires no *garuf ve'katum*, then even in cases where one could not otherwise leave food on the flame, one could place it against the outside of the oven and benefit from the radiant heat.

### Somech Allowed

The *Gemara* returns to the double-oven *baraita* as a source for resolving the *somech* question. The two ovens are a single unit, placed side by side, and therefore the pot left in the treated oven is effectively right up against the wall of the untreated oven — yet the *baraita* permits it. The *Gemara* draws from this that even when heat is communicated through an adjoining wall (*af al gav de-ka salik lei havla me-idach* — even though the hot air rises from the other oven), the arrangement is permitted.

The *Gemara* attempts to deflect this proof by noting that *keivan de-madlya shalat beih avira* — in the double-oven case, the pot is suspended with air circulating beneath it and is not directly pressed against the wall, which might render it different from a pot physically leaning against an oven wall. Nonetheless, the *Tosefta* settles the matter directly: *kira she-hesikuha be-gefet u-ve-etzim, somchin lah ve-ein mekaymin ela im ken grufa u-ketuma* — in an oven lit with wood, one may lean food against it (*somchin*), but one may not place food on the flame itself unless it has been treated. This makes explicit that *somech* — placing food against the oven — does not require *garuf ve'katum*, while placing food directly on the flame does.

This ruling has direct practical relevance: even without a *blech*, one may warm food by placing it near the oven, provided there is no independent *bishul* concern and the food is not going to overheat. The area of the *blech* not directly over the burners raises a similar question — whether that region counts as *somech* or whether the *blech*'s heat distribution makes even that area equivalent to being directly over the flame.

---

## Ashes & Reignition

### Tosefta on Ashes

The *Tosefta* continues by addressing two additional scenarios that are treated as equivalent to *garuf ve'katum*: *gechalim she-amemu* — embers that have burned themselves out entirely — and placing thin flax strings (*ne'oret shel pishtan daka*) upon the coals. Either of these is described as *harei hi ke-ktuma* — comparable to having placed ashes. 

This is noteworthy on two levels. First, the case of embers that simply burned out involves no deliberate act on the person's part — the flame extinguished itself, yet this suffices. Second, the case of the flax strings suggests that even a relatively minor act of dampening the flame qualifies, even if it does not fully extinguish it. These two tracks — spontaneous extinction and deliberate-but-minimal intervention — will become important when translating the *garuf ve'katum* concept into the contemporary *blech*, which represents a deliberate action that nonetheless still permits a vigorous flame underneath.

### Reignition Case

With this, Rav Safra's teaching in the name of Rabbi Hiyya becomes critical: *kitma ve-nisla'ava, somchin lah u-mekaymin aleha ve-notlin heimena u-machzirin lah* — if one placed ashes on the coals and the coals then reignited into a full flame, one may nevertheless lean food against it, leave food on it, remove food from it, and return food to it.

This is a striking ruling. One might have thought that reignition would nullify the ashes entirely, as though they had never been placed. Rav Safra teaches that this is not so: the prior placement of ashes retains its legal significance even after the flame reignites. This principle is foundational for understanding the contemporary *blech*, where a fully vigorous flame burns beneath a metal cover. The *blech* is not extinguishing the flame; it is a *heker*, a marker or reminder, and that suffices — just as the ashes, even when the flame reignites through them, retain their status.

The *Gemara* notes that Rav Safra's list includes *somchin lah* — leaning food against the oven. One might infer that this is listed because without the ashes, *somech* would have been forbidden. The *Gemara* immediately deflects this inference: *notlin* (taking food off) is also listed, yet one can obviously remove food from the flame without any *garuf ve'katum*. The reason *notlin* is listed is because the *Tosefta* wanted to convey the idea that once you take it off, you can put it back — *notlin* is listed for the sake of *machzirin*. Similarly, *somchin* may be listed merely as a rhetorical companion to *mekaymin*, not as evidence that *somech* normally requires *garuf ve'katum*.

The *Gemara* pushes back: the analogy of *notlin* to *somchin* is imperfect. Taking off and putting back (*notlin u-machzirin*) are linked because they describe a single process in the same location — you take the pot from the flame and return it to the same flame. *Somchin* and *mekaymin*, by contrast, describe two different places: leaning against the outside wall and placing on the flame itself. There is no inherent reason to mention *somchin* merely for the sake of *mekaymin*. Hence, the inference stands that *somech* without ashes might indeed be problematic — though the *Gemara* ultimately concludes otherwise, as the *Tosefta* clarifies.

---

## Somech (Leaning Agai (II)

### Tosafot's Caveat

Tosafot introduces an important limitation on the permissibility of *somech*. The *Tosefta*'s ruling that *somchin* is permitted — even without *garuf ve'katum* — applies specifically to leaning food against the *wall* of the oven, where the oven's own structure intervenes between the pot and the fire: *deshani hacha de-dofnei kira mafsikin beino u-vein ha-esh* — here the walls of the oven separate the pot from the flame. This is categorically different from placing a pot directly against an exposed, open flame, such as a burner on a stovetop. In that case, with no oven wall mediating between the pot and the fire, *somech* may not be treated so leniently. This caveat from Tosafot is directly relevant to how these principles translate into contemporary kitchen arrangements.

---

## Ashes & Reignition (II)

### Reignition = Fully Cooked

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani, citing Rabbi Yehoshua, addresses the reignition scenario directly: *ktama ve-huv'ara, mash'hin aleha chamim she-huchmu kol tzarchan ve-tavshil she-bishal kol tzarcho* — if one placed ashes on the coals and they reignited, one may leave on the flame water that has been fully heated and food that has been fully cooked.

This is the position that stands in opposition to Chananya, and it is the ruling adopted by the *Shulchan Aruch* (the *Mechaber*, not the *Rema*). The implicit question is: since ashes were placed, why is only *fully* cooked food permitted? If the ashes retained their legal significance after reignition, one might expect the oven to be treated as a fully kosher *katum* oven, on which even less-than-fully-cooked food could remain. The fact that only fully cooked food is permitted suggests that the reignition does diminish the ashes' effect to some degree.

This is the appropriate point to clarify the underlying principle at stake. The question of whether to leave something on an untreated flame is not a *de'oraita* question of *bishul* — the prohibition of cooking on *Shabbos*. Once food is *mevushal kol tzarcho* — fully cooked — the principle of *ein bishul achar bishul* applies: cooking something already cooked is not an act of *bishul* for Torah-law purposes, even if the food continues to improve (*mitztemek ve-yafeh lo*). The question of whether to permit leaving food on a live flame is a *rabbinic* concern — the fear that one will stir the coals to accelerate cooking. This is important because practitioners sometimes focus exclusively on the *shehiya* and *hatmanah* questions and overlook the independent *bishul de'oraita* dimension, which must always be considered separately.

With the rabbinic concern in view, the distinction between *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo* (the food shrinks and improves) and *mitztemek ve-ra lo* (the food shrinks and deteriorates) becomes central. If the food continues to improve as it cooks, there remains a motivation to stir the coals — one benefits from the continued cooking. If the food only deteriorates with continued cooking, the concern evaporates: the only reason to leave it on the flame is to keep it hot, not to cook it further, and so there is no reason one would come to stir.

Thus, the key question being explored is: for the position that opposes Chananya — which requires the food to be fully cooked before leaving it on an untreated flame — is it sufficient that the food is fully cooked, or must one additionally establish that continued cooking makes the food worse (*mitztemek ve-ra lo*)? The *Gemara* notes that Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani does not explicitly distinguish between the two cases, which might suggest he permits *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo* as well.

The *Gemara* deflects this inference: *shani hacha di-katma* — here is different because ashes were placed. Perhaps his leniency is specific to the case where ashes were applied. If so, the *chiddush* of his ruling is not that *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo* is generally permitted on an untreated flame, but rather that the reignition does not render the ashes entirely meaningless. *Mahu de-teima keivan de-huv'ara hadra lah le-milsa ke-me'ikara* — one might have thought that the reignition returns the situation to its original untreated state, as if no ashes had been applied. The ruling teaches us that even after reignition, the ashes retain some significance.

Tosafot here presents two readings. One possibility is that even after reignition the ashes are fully effective, such that even not-fully-cooked food would in principle be permitted, and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani's language is explained on other grounds. The other possibility is that reignition creates an intermediate category: had the ashes never been applied, not even fully cooked food could be left on; had the ashes been applied without reignition, even not-fully-cooked food could be left on; with ashes applied and subsequent reignition, it is a middle case — fully cooked food yes, not-fully-cooked food no.

### Retam Embers

Rabbah bar Bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan restates the same rule: *kitmah ve-huv'arah, mash'hin aleha chamim she-huchmu kol tzarchan ve-tavshil she-bishal kol tzarcho* — after ashes and reignition, only fully cooked food may remain on the flame. He adds, *va-afilu gachalim shel rotam* — even if the embers are those of the *rotam* plant, known for retaining exceptional heat for an extraordinarily long time even after appearing extinguished. One might have thought that since *rotam* embers remain intensely hot, any ashes placed upon them are rendered trivially ineffective by the re-ignition. He teaches that even in this case, the ashes retain their significance. The *Gemara* notes that this is essentially the same teaching as what came immediately before, and distinguishes the two: the first ruling teaches that reignition in general does not nullify the ashes, while the *rotam* addendum teaches that even particularly vigorous reignition through unusually persistent embers does not nullify them.

---

## Lenient View: Shehiya On…

### Rav Sheshet's Teaching

Rav Sheshet, citing Rabbi Yochanan, now presents the lenient opinion in its clearest form: *kura she-sikuha be-gefset u-ve-eitzim, mash'hin aleha chamim shelo huchmu kol tzarchan ve-tavshil shelo bishal kol tzarcho* — if an oven was lit with wood, one may leave on it water that has not yet been fully heated and food that has not yet been fully cooked. And if one removed the pot from the flame — *akar, lo yachazir ad she-yigrof o ad she-yiten eifer* — one may not return it until the oven has been swept out or ashes have been placed.

This is precisely the position of Chananya. The teaching of Rav Sheshet in the name of Rabbi Yochanan makes explicit what had been implied throughout the earlier discussion: *kasavar matnitin lehachzir tnan* — our *Mishna*'s requirement of *garuf ve'katum* pertains only to the act of returning food to the flame. For *shehiya* — leaving food on from before *Shabbos* — no treatment of the flame is required, even if the food is only partially cooked. The *blech* is necessary only when one wishes to return food to the flame on *Shabbos* itself.

### Rava's Defense

Rava observes that Rabbi Yochanan's teaching should not have been necessary, because the same principle is already evident from a *Mishna* at the end of the first chapter (*perek*). That *Mishna* states: *ein notnin et ha-pas be-toch ha-tanur im hasheichah* — one may not place bread in the oven right before *Shabbos* begins, *ela kedei she-yikremu paneha* — unless it has already formed a crust. The implication is that once the bread has formed a crust — not fully baked, but with some initial cooking — it may be left in the oven even over *Shabbos* on an untreated flame. This *Mishna* from the first chapter already demonstrates that *shehiya* on an untreated flame is permitted for partially cooked food. Rava adds that the requirement of *garuf ve'katum* for returning food is equally obvious from our *Mishna*, since *Beit Hillel*'s permission to return food (*af machzirin*) is predicated on the flame having been treated.

### Our Mishna Reread

In light of this, the role of Rav Sheshet's teaching (*diyuka de-matnitin ka mashma lan*) is to provide the correct reading of our *Mishna* in the second chapter. On its face, the *Mishna* there appeared to require *garuf ve'katum* for *shehiya* as well. Rav Sheshet teaches that the *Mishna* should be understood as addressing only *chazara* — the condition of *garuf ve'katum* in its first clause is a condition for returning food, not for leaving it. The *Mishna* from the first chapter meanwhile establishes that *shehiya* is unrestricted. Together, Rav Sheshet, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rava converge: there is no requirement of *garuf ve'katum* if one only wishes to leave food on the flame from before *Shabbos*.

### Ashkenazi Position

Rashi makes this explicit in his commentary.
