He writes: *ve-anan de-mash'hainan kedira agav kira she-eina grufa* — we *Ashkenazim* who leave our pot on an untreated flame from before *Shabbos*, *a-Chananya samchinan* — we rely on Chananya, *ho'il u-tnan stam mishna kevateih* — because the *stam mishna* at the end of the first chapter follows his view, *ve-af al gav de-lo bishal kol tzorko* — even when the food is not fully cooked, *ve-amar Rav Sheshet mishmeih de-Rabbi Yochanan kevateih* — and Rav Sheshet said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan the same ruling, and *de-matnitin de-pirkin mishum chazara hu* — our *Mishna* in this chapter concerns returning, not leaving.

Tosafot states the same position. All of these *Amoraim* are understood to agree that *shehiya* requires no treatment of the flame. The opposing *Amoraim* who hold that the *Mishna*'s demand for *garuf ve'katum* applies to *shehiya* as well are ruled against, and the *Ashkenazi* practice is built on the convergence of the *stam mishna*, Chananya, and Rav Yochanan as cited by Rav Sheshet.

The *Sephardim*, by contrast, rule in accordance with the stricter positions, because the plain meaning (*pshat*) of our *Mishna* clearly requires *garuf ve'katum* for *shehiya*, and all the other opinions are read as a *lo shanu* against Chananya. Accordingly, the *Sephardi* requirement is that food be fully cooked (*mevushal kol tzarcho*) before it may remain on an untreated flame — and even then, as we shall see, an additional condition applies.

The *Rosh*, who began in *Ashkenaz* and moved to *Sepharad*, navigates between the two positions and ultimately leans toward the *Sephardi* ruling, while framing the *Ashkenazi* practice charitably: *hanichu lahem li-vnei Ashkenaz she-mitoch she-machmirim al oneg Shabbat hem somchin a-Chananya* — allow the *Ashkenazim* their practice, for since they are so scrupulous about *oneg Shabbat* and wish to have hot food that has not become overcooked, they rely on Chananya.

---

## Mitztemek v'Yafeh Lo Deb…

### Stringent Position

The *Gemara* now records a version of Rabbi Yochanan's opinion that is considerably stricter. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, citing Rabbi Yochanan, teaches: *kira she-hisikuha be-gefet u-ve-eitzim, mash'hin aleha tavshil she-bishal kol tzorko ve-chamin she-huchmu kol tzorkan* — one may leave on such an oven only food that is fully cooked and water that is fully heated. Furthermore, *va-afilu mitztemek ve-yafe lo* — even though the food continues to improve as it remains on the flame, this is still permitted once the food is fully cooked.

This is the opinion that opposes Chananya: no untreated flame may hold not-fully-cooked food. But on the question of *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo*, Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's version of Rabbi Yochanan is lenient — once fully cooked, the fact that continued cooking improves the food does not create a new restriction.

### The Dispute

This leniency regarding *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo* is immediately challenged. Other Rabbis cite the position of Rav and Shmuel, both of whom hold *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo assur* — once fully cooked food continues to improve with further cooking, it may not be left on an untreated flame. Only *mitztemek ve-ra lo* — food that continues to deteriorate — may be left on. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda responds: he is well aware of what Shmuel says on this matter (*tika mina lach Rav Yochanan ka'amina*) — but he is reporting Rabbi Yochanan's view, which is that once food is fully cooked, it may be left on the flame even if it continues to improve.

### Regional Practice

Rav Ukva mi-Meishan addresses this dispute to Rav Ashi directly, framing it in terms of regional practice: *atun de-mikravitu le-Rav u-Shmuel* — you who are close to where Rav and Shmuel lived and taught, *avidu ke-Rav u-Shmuel* — follow their ruling. In your locale, fully cooked food may only be left on an untreated flame if it is *mitztemek ve-ra lo*. *Anan, ne-ivid ke-Rabbi Yochanan* — we, who are farther away, follow Rabbi Yochanan and permit leaving fully cooked food on the flame even if it is *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo*. Abaye then asks Rav Yosef for a practical ruling on *shehiya*, and Rav Yosef responds that Rav Yehuda himself used to leave food on the flame and eat it. Abaye deflects this: Rav Yehuda's case cannot serve as a precedent for ordinary people, since he had ongoing health concerns (*mesukan*) that would have permitted him to act on *Shabbos* in ways that might otherwise be restricted. Rav Yosef then notes that the practice in *Sura* was to leave food on the flame — presumably even if *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo* — citing Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, a man of great deeds, as a practitioner of this leniency.

### Rav Ashi's Case

Rav Ashi recounts that while in the presence of Rav Huna, *shav lei kasa de-harsena* — they left on the flame some fried or battered fish — *ve-lo yadana* — and he did not know whether to infer from this that Rav Huna held *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo mutar* (since a fully cooked dish was left on), or whether the case fell under *mitztemek ve-ra lo* — because the dish contained flour, and floury preparations generally deteriorate with extended cooking. The uncertainty itself is telling: the presence of flour in the batter introduced ambiguity as to whether this particular food was classified as improving or worsening on the flame.

### Rav Nachman's Ruling

Rav Nachman closes the discussion with a clear ruling: *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo assur, mitztemek ve-ra lo mutar* — if the food continues to improve with further cooking, it is forbidden to leave it on an untreated flame; if it continues to deteriorate, it is permitted. This is the definitive *Sephardi* position: fully cooked food that is *mitztemek ve-ra lo* may remain on an untreated flame; fully cooked food that is *mitztemek ve-yafeh lo* may not.

---

## Practical Applications

### General Principle

The *Gemara* concludes with practical guidance on which foods fall into which category. The general principle: *kol de-is bei mikha, mitztemek ve-ra lo* — anything that contains flour tends to deteriorate as it continues to cook once fully prepared. Such foods are generally classified as *mitztemek ve-ra lo* and may be left on the flame. The one exception noted is *tavshil de-lifta* — a stew made with turnips (or a similar vegetable), whose behavior depends on further conditions.

### Stews with/without Meat

With respect to the turnip stew: *aval leis bei bisra, mistameich ve-ra lo* — if there is no meat in the stew, it deteriorates with continued cooking and is therefore *mitztemek ve-ra lo*, permitting it to be left on the flame. *Ve-ki is bei bisra nami, lo amrin ela de-lo kavya lei le-orchin* — even when the stew contains meat, this leniency applies only when one is not expecting guests. If guests are expected, *kavya lei le-orchin, mistameich ve-ra lo* — the food's shrinkage is considered harmful because there will be less to serve, and thus it is again classified as *mitztemek ve-ra lo* from the standpoint of quantity if not quality.

### Specific Foods

The *Gemara* closes with three specific examples: *lafta, daisa, ve-tamri* — a fig preparation, an oatmeal-type dish, and a date preparation. All three are classified as *mistameich ve-ra lahen* — they deteriorate with continued cooking. These may therefore be left on an untreated flame once fully cooked, according to the *Sephardi* ruling of Rav Nachman.

The *Gemara* here is clearly operating within the framework of the *Sephardi* conclusion: the permissibility of leaving food on an open flame is conditioned on the food being *mevushal kol tzarcho* and *mitztemek ve-ra lo*. As noted throughout, the *Ashkenazi* position relies on Chananya and does not require full cooking for *shehiya*, rendering these distinctions largely academic in *Ashkenazi* practice for the *shehiya* question — though they remain essential for *chazara*, which even *Ashkenazim* agree requires a *blech*.

---

---

# Shabbat 39

## Oven Types

### Tannur Restrictions

Today's *daf* is 39. We pick up in the middle of 38b, wrapping up the previous *daf*. The *mishnah* introduced two new types of ovens: the *tannur*, which is the pyramidal oven used for baking bread, and the *kupach*, which occupies a middle position. The *tannur* is treated with great stringency — even if one uses *kash* and *gvava* (straw and stubble), and even if there are no coals to stir, it remains forbidden. The *gemara*'s discussion centers on just how strict the *tannur* is: whereas with a *kira* one may place something against the outside even over an exposed flame, what is the rule for a *tannur*? *Abaye* ruled that this too is forbidden.

A *baraita* then confirms *Abaye*'s position: *tannur she-sikuhu be-kash u-ve-gvava* — a *tannur* kindled even with straw and stubble — one may not place something alongside it (*ein somchin lo*), and certainly not on top of it (*ein tzarich lomar al gabav*), and certainly not inside it (*ein tzarich lomar le-tocho*). How much more so is this true if one used actual wood and chips (*gefet u-ve-etzim*). The *baraita* thus makes explicit that one may not place something against the outside of a *tannur* even with the most lenient fuel, in accordance with *Abaye*.

At a certain point the precise rationale becomes somewhat unclear. If we are dealing with wood and chips, the concern that one might come to stir the coals is obvious. But by a *tannur* kindled with straw and stubble the same strictness applies, and there the concern is harder to pin down — it may be a matter of *mechzei ke-mevashel* (the appearance of cooking), or it may be a principle of *lo pelug* (no internal distinctions within the category). The *gemara* does not make this fully explicit.

### Kupach Definition

Rav Acha the son of Rava then posed a question to Rav Ashi: *hai kupach heichi dami* — what exactly is the situation with a *kupach*? If it is like a *kira*, it should be permitted even with wood and chips as long as the coals are swept out. If it is like a *tannur*, it should be forbidden even with straw and stubble. Why does it occupy a middle category? Rav Ashi replied: *nafish hevlei mi-kira* — its retained, contained heat is greater than that of a *kira* — *ve-zuta hevlei mi-tannur* — but less than that of a *tannur*. It thus falls into a genuine middle position.

### Kupach vs Kira

The *gemara* then asks what the physical distinction between a *kupach* and a *kira* actually is. Rabbi Yossi the son of Rabbi Chanina explains: *kupach mekom shfisas kdera achas* — a *kupach* has room for only one pot, making it a very tight, heat-retaining space. A *kira*, by contrast — *mekom shfisas shtei kderos* — has room for two pots. Because it is a larger structure, there is greater airflow and the heat is correspondingly less intense.

It should be noted that the distinction between a one-pot and a two-pot space is attested in the *mishnah*, but archaeological and literary evidence suggests the difference runs deeper than mere capacity. The *kira* appears to have had more open or exposed walls allowing greater air circulation, whereas the *kupach* was a tighter vessel with heat rising through holes at the bottom — far more contained. The one-pot/two-pot description may capture one dimension of this reality without exhausting it.

The point is confirmed from a separate *mishnah*: if a *kira* was split lengthwise, it becomes *tehorah* — unusable and thus ritually pure — because it can no longer function as intended. If split widthwise, it becomes *teme'ah*, because one now has two independent *kirot*, each holding a single pot. This demonstrates that a standard *kira* has two separate openings for two separate pots. A *kupach*, by contrast, whether split lengthwise or widthwise, is always *tahor*, since it has only one opening and either split renders it nonfunctional.

### Modern Ovens

This concludes the *mishnah*'s discussion of the distinctions among *kira*, *kupach*, and *tannur*. In terms of practical application today, the broad consensus among *poskim* is that our modern ovens — what modern Hebrew calls a *tannur* — carry the *halacha* of a *kira*. Modern ovens have significant interior space, ventilation, and airflow; they do not resemble the intensely contained, unventilated heat of the ancient *tannur*, which is better approximated by a pizza oven. Accordingly, the various leniencies that apply to a *kira* apply to our ovens as well.

### Blech Practice

We now shift away from *shehiyah ve-chazarah* (leaving food on and returning it to the flame) and turn to the broader issues of cooking on *Shabbat* that will occupy the remainder of the chapter. Before doing so, it is worth drawing together the practical conclusions about the *blech* that emerged in the preceding discussion.

We have been operating throughout with the understanding that the modern *blech* serves as the practical equivalent of *garuf ve-katum* — the swept-out or ash-covered flame of the *gemara*. This understanding is not without complication. Both Rav Moshe Feinstein and Rav Ovadia Yosef, for different reasons, note at the outset that one could argue that no such precaution is required at all for modern stoves. Rav Moshe's reason is technical: the original rabbinic concern was that one might come to stir the existing coals — that is, to rearrange the fuel already burning. Our stoves require no such stirring; the only act that would increase heat is adjusting the knobs, which is effectively adding more fuel. Since the original *gezeirah* was never directed at adding fuel but at stirring ashes, it may not technically apply. Rav Ovadia's reason is more practical: a modern gas or electric flame burns steadily and does not require intervention the way wood fires do, so the underlying concern is simply less present.

Both authorities make this argument not in order to be lenient, but to preempt a symmetrical objection: if the modern stove does not technically require any precaution, then whatever we do may also not technically satisfy the requirement of the *gemara*. The *blech* does not actually begin to extinguish the flame the way ashes do; it merely somewhat reduces the heat. One could therefore argue that it does not replicate what the *gemara* intended by *garuf ve-katum*.

Given this background, there is a further question of what exactly the *blech* must accomplish in order to be valid. The *gemara*'s arrangement served two functions: it covered the heat source, and it provided a *heker* — a visible reminder — that would alert someone who approached to adjust the fire that something was different. On our stoves, the knobs are where one would come to make an adjustment, and the *blech* covers the burners, not the knobs. Some therefore argue that one must place something on the knobs themselves — removing them, taping over them, or otherwise marking them — to create the necessary *heker* at the point of potential adjustment.

The most stringent approach combines both elements: a single piece of metal that covers the burners and extends down over the knobs simultaneously, replicating both functions at once. However, most *poskim* and most common practice hold that covering the heat source alone is sufficient, reasoning that when one approaches the knobs to make an adjustment, one will still notice the *blech* covering the burners and that will serve as adequate *heker*. Rav Aharon Kotler is quoted by Rav Eider as holding that it is sufficient to remove the knobs or mark them with a *siman*, without covering the heat source at all.

This last position raises interesting practical questions. Appliances whose heat source is already enclosed — crockpots, for instance, or the glass-top stoves that are now common — present a particular challenge. If the heat source is already covered by the appliance's design, placing a further covering over it risks creating a problem of *hatmanah* (insulating in a heat-adding medium), particularly if the covering fits snugly on all sides. One resolution is to rely on the position that covering the knobs alone is sufficient. As for the glass-top stove where the burners are already behind glass, one may similarly mark or cover the controls and rely on that as the required *heker*.

Regarding *chazarah* — returning food to the fire on *Shabbat* — the *Ashkenazi* position in principle follows *Chananya* that once food is partially cooked (to one-half or one-third doneness), it may theoretically be left on a fully exposed flame before *Shabbat*. In practice, the *lechatchila* standard follows the more stringent *Sefardi* position: unless the food is at a stage where *mitztamek ve-ra lo* (further cooking would be detrimental), one should cover the flame. For *chazarah* itself, all authorities agree that the flame must be covered. *Lechatchila* one must hold the pot in hand and maintain intent to return it; *bedieved*, the *Mishnah Berurah* holds that one condition alone suffices, and placing it briefly on a counter may in some circumstances be equivalent to holding it. Taking food directly from the refrigerator on *Shabbat* morning and placing it on the fire is not permitted *lechatchila*; at minimum the food must be fully dry or fully cooked, and there must be no appearance of cooking (*lo mechzei ke-mevashel*). Placing such food on a hot plate where no one normally cooks is more permissible; placing it directly on a *blech* remains a concern for *Ashkenazim*, while some *Sefardi poskim* permit even a *blech* in that scenario.

One further creative device deserves mention: the *kedera blech*, sometimes called the *un-blech*, a flat vessel resembling a *blech* but with a thin sealed hollow interior filled with water or oil, designed to sit on the stovetop as a "pot" so that placing food on top of it constitutes *al gabei kli* (on top of a cooking vessel) rather than direct placement on a heat source, which some authorities consider *lo derech bishul*. Whether this device genuinely changes the experiential or legal reality compared to a standard *blech* depends on how one understands the underlying rationale, and the question is live among contemporary *poskim*.

---

## Eggs & Fish

### Egg Cooking Rules

The *gemara* now turns to direct cooking issues. The *mishnah* states: *ain nosnin beitsa b'tzad hameicham bishvil she-titgalgel* — one may not place an egg alongside a hot water pot in order for it to hard-boil and cook. Even though the egg is not placed on the fire itself, its proximity to the heated vessel is sufficient to cook it, and this is forbidden. Similarly, *ve-lo yafki'enah be-sudarim* — one may not crack an egg and fry it on a cloth. The *gemara* understands this second case to be referring to a cloth heated by the sun, not by fire.

This brings into view the fundamental principle distinguishing *bishul chamah* — cooking by the sun — from cooking by fire. Biblically, cooking is defined by use of fire; cooking by sunlight alone does not constitute a biblical violation. However, something that has absorbed heat from the sun presents a rabbinic problem: absorbed heat is visually indistinguishable from absorbed heat derived from fire, since in either case one sees only a warm object without knowing its origin. Therefore, while the rabbis permit frying an egg directly on a sun-heated sidewalk — where the source is obvious — they do not permit frying it on a cloth that has absorbed heat from the sun, since that cloth could just as easily have been heated by a flame.

*Rabbi Yossi* disagrees and permits use of sun-derived absorbed heat as well. His position is the more permissive one, though it does not prevail in normative *halacha*.

One might ask whether the line between fire and sun is a purely formal legal distinction — cooking is definitionally a fire-related act — or whether it reflects the more functional principle that fire is the *normal* method of cooking while sun is not. The practical difference concerns novel heat sources. Rav Moshe Feinstein held that a microwave constitutes *bishul de-oraita* on the grounds that the definition is about normative cooking methods rather than fire per se. Many other *poskim* disagree, holding either that microwave is not yet normative enough, or that fire is simply the formal definitional criterion. A similar question arises with chemical heat packs used by travelers, which generate significant heat through an exothermic reaction without any flame whatsoever.

### Rav Yosef Opinion

The *gemara* asks: *gilgel mai* — if one went ahead and cooked the egg by placing it against the hot pot, what is the status of that act? Is it a rabbinic violation or a biblical one? *Rav Yosef* answers: *gilgel chayav chatas* — one has incurred a *chatas* obligation, meaning it is a biblical transgression.

This is a striking ruling. The *mishnah* does not make this explicit, and the question was genuinely open: one could easily have read the prohibition as purely rabbinic, given that the egg was not placed directly on a flame. The *Ramban*, drawing on the *Yerushalmi*, holds a reasonable position that *bishul de-oraita* requires direct contact with a flame; cooking accomplished through indirect heat — even from a vessel that is boiling hot — is not a biblical act. What *Rav Yosef* does with such *gemara* passages is not entirely clear.

But *Rav Yosef*'s ruling establishes an important principle that most *Rishonim* accept against the *Ramban*: *bishul de-oraita* is possible even when the food is not placed directly over a flame. Both of the cases in the *mishnah* — the egg against the hot pot, and the salted fish rinsed with hot water from a *kli rishon* — share the characteristic that the cooking occurs without direct contact with fire. Yet *Rav Yosef* in both cases rules *chayav chatas*.

### Ein Bishul

The *gemara* supports *Rav Yosef*'s ruling with a proof from an earlier *mishnah* (38a): *kol she-ba be-chamin milifnei ha-Shabbos* — anything that was cooked before *Shabbat* — *shorin oso be-chamin be-Shabbos* — may be re-submerged in hot water on *Shabbat*. This is the principle of *ein bishul achar bishul*: there is no act of cooking after something has already been cooked. Once food is fully cooked, placing it in boiling water on *Shabbat* causes no violation. *Ve-chol shelo ba be-chamin milifnei ha-Shabbat* — but if it was not cooked before *Shabbat* — *madichin oso be-chamin be-Shabbos* — one may only rinse it with hot water, meaning pour hot water over it, but *aval* — one may not submerge it. Submersion in hot water would constitute cooking; pouring hot water merely to rinse or warm it does not.

### Salted Fish

The *mishnah* adds an exception: *chutz min ha-maliach yashan ve-kolyas ha-ispanin* — except for old salted fish and this *kolyas ha-ispanin*, which *Rashi* identifies as a type of fish (*dag she-korei tunina*), understood by some as a mackerel-type or salt-preserved fish. In these cases, *she-hadachatan zo hi gmar melachtan* — rinsing them with hot water constitutes the completion of their preparation (*gmar melachtan*), making them fit to eat. The *mishnah* implies that doing so would be a significant violation.

*Rav Yosef* confirms, in a later *mishnah* (145), that one who pours hot water on such fish is *chayav chatas* — incurs a biblical obligation. Together with the egg case, this establishes that *bishul de-oraita* applies even without direct flame contact, even potentially in a *kli sheni* (secondary vessel), and forms the basis for the category the *gemara* later develops of *kalei ha-bishul* — things that cook easily. The entire discussion about tea and the requirement of three removes (a *kli shlishi*) derives from this principle, since easily cooked substances may achieve *bishul de-oraita* status even in a vessel far removed from the original heat source.

### Gmar Melacha

The language of the *mishnah* — *gmar melachtan* — raises a further question. The phrase echoes *makeh be-patish*, the prohibition against performing the "final blow" that completes an object, even if that final act is not itself a *melacha*. Could it be that the prohibition on rinsing the salted fish is not actually *bishul* at all, but rather *makeh be-patish* — a *gmar melacha* in the sense of completing a food's preparation, even without any cooking? The *gemara* phrase seems to point in that direction.

The *Yerushalmi* indeed adopts this reading explicitly. It states that *makeh be-patish* applies to food preparation, meaning one can incur a biblical obligation by completing the process of making food edible through any act that finalizes it — not only through cooking. This creates a significant difficulty: all the categories of *bishul chamah* and indirect heating that we thought were rabbinic exemptions would seemingly be subject to *makeh be-patish* instead. The *Yerushalmi* cites several examples that do not involve heat at all — chopping, stuffing, and similar acts of food completion.

The *Bavli*, however, effectively ignores this framework. The *poskim* follow the *Bavli* and read both the egg case and the salted fish case as instances of *bishul* rather than *makeh be-patish*, establishing that *bishul de-oraita* is possible even without direct flame contact. Had the *Yerushalmi*'s position been accepted, the restrictions would be significantly more expansive. The *pshat* of the *mishnah* undeniably supports the *Yerushalmi*'s reading — it is difficult to characterize rinsing brine off salted fish as "cooking" in any conventional sense — but the *Bavli* and the *Rishonim* who follow it limit the ruling to cases involving hot water at *yad soledes bo* temperature and frame it as a form of *bishul*.

---

## Sun vs Fire

### Sun Heat Rules

The *gemara* turns now to the next case in the *mishnah*: *ve-lo yafki'enu be-sudarin* — do not fry an egg on a heated cloth. A later *mishnah* is cited for contrast: *notnin tavshil le-toch ha-bor bishvil she-yishtamer* — one may place a cooked dish into a pit to preserve it, or good water into poorer water to cool it, or — and this is the key point — *ve-es ha-tzonan ba-chamah bishvil she-yeichamu* — cold water may be placed in the sun in order to warm it. Direct sunlight is thus permitted for warming or heating.

This raises the question: if the rabbis permit placing water directly in the sun, does even *Rabbi Yossi* agree, or is this only *Rabbi Yossi*'s position? The *gemara* might suggest that direct sunlight is only permissible according to *Rabbi Yossi*.

### Rav Nachman

*Rav Nachman* clarifies: *bachamah dekuli alma lo pligi deshari* — regarding direct sunlight, all authorities agree that it is permitted. *Be-toldos ha-ur* — regarding something derived from fire-generated heat — *dekuli alma lo pligi de-asir* — all agree that it is forbidden. This is the case of the egg placed against the hot water pot: heating via the derivative of fire is universally prohibited, and as *Rav Yosef* ruled, can even constitute a biblical transgression. *Ki pligi* — the dispute between the rabbis and *Rabbi Yossi* — *be-toldos chamah*: regarding something that has absorbed heat derived from the sun. Biblically this is entirely permitted; the rabbinic concern is that absorbed solar heat is indistinguishable from absorbed heat derived from fire. *Mar savar gazrinan toldos chamah atu toldos ha-ur* — the rabbis hold that we decree against using sun-derived absorbed heat lest it be confused with fire-derived absorbed heat. *Ve-Rabbi Yossi lo gazrinan* — *Rabbi Yossi* declines to make such a decree, and permits anything deriving ultimately from the sun, directly or indirectly.

### Hatmanah Concern

The *mishnah* continues: *ve-lo yatminenu ba-chol u-ve-avak derachim* — one may not bury an egg in hot sand or the dust of pathways in order to fry it (*bishvil she-titzaleh*). Here, strikingly, *Rabbi Yossi* does not disagree. The *gemara* asks: *ve-liflog nami Rabbi Yossi beha* — why does *Rabbi Yossi* not also permit this? After all, sand heated by the sun seems like a straightforward case of *toldos chamah*, and *Rabbi Yossi* permits *toldos chamah*.

*Rabbah* answers: *gezeirah shema yatmin be-remetz* — this is a decree lest one come to bury food in ashes. This introduces the separate category of *hatmanah* — the act of surrounding food with material that will retain or add heat in order to keep it warm. The sages prohibited *hatmanah* in heat-adding materials even before *Shabbat*, for a reason parallel to the prohibition against leaving food on an uncovered flame: just as one might come to stir the coals of an open fire, so too if one buries food in hot ashes before *Shabbat*, one might come to stir those ashes on *Shabbat* to raise the heat. Once this prohibition was established for ashes, it was extended to any material that adds heat. Hot sand adds heat, and although one cannot stir sand to raise its temperature, the category is treated uniformly — *lo pelug*.

Even *Rabbi Yossi*, who rejects the decree against *toldos chamah* when it comes to heated cloths and similar surfaces, agrees that the rabbinic category of *hatmanah* — burying in heat-adding substances — applies. Frying an egg on a cloth involves placing the egg *on* a surface; burying it in sand is categorically different. *Rabbi Yossi* accepts that the *gezeirah* of *hatmanah* applies to burial in heat-retaining or heat-adding material, even when the ultimate heat source is the sun.

*Rav Yosef* offers an alternative explanation for why the rabbis prohibited burying the egg in sand: *mipnei she-meiziz afar mi-mekomoh* — because one is moving the dirt. *Rashi* understands this as a concern of *chofer guma* — making a hole, which relates to the *melacha* of *boneh* or *choresh*. *Tosafot* understands it as a *muktzeh* concern — moving dirt that was set aside from use. The practical difference between *Rabbah* and *Rav Yosef* is the case of loose, pre-dug earth (*afar tichuach*): in that case there is no concern about making a hole and arguably no *muktzeh* issue, but there remains the *hatmanah* concern.

### Rabbi Yose

The *gemara* then cites a proof from a *baraita* in the name of Rabban Gamliel: *megalgelin beitzah al gabei gag roteiach* — one may fry an egg on a boiling hot roof. But *ein megalgelin beitzah al gabei sid roteiach* — one may not do so on boiling hot plaster, which has been heated by fire in the lime-burning process. The *gemara* assumes the roof's heat is from the sun (*toldos chamah*), while the plaster's heat is from fire (*toldos ha-ur*).

The *gemara* notes: this works well according to *Rabbah*, who explains *Rabbi Yossi*'s silence by the sand case as a *hatmanah* concern. Burying in sand is *hatmanah*; placing an egg on a flat hot roof is not *hatmanah* at all. So we understand why even *Rabbi Yossi* would allow the roof: there is no *hatmanah* issue there, and he has no objection to *toldos chamah* in general. But according to *Rav Yosef*, whose concern is the moving of dirt, why would the roof be unproblematic? If the roofs of that era sometimes had dirt on them, placing an egg there could involve moving dirt or creating a hole. The *gemara* dismisses this: *stam gagot leit behu afar* — ordinary roofs do not have dirt on them, so the concern does not arise.

---

## Tiberias Waters

### Pipe Setup

The *mishnah* relates: *ma'aseh she-asu anshei Tiveria* — there was an episode involving the people of Tiberias. *Ve-hevi'u silon shel tzonan le-toch amah shel chamim* — they brought a pipe carrying cold water into a channel of hot water. The hot water in that channel derived from *chamei Tiveria*, the famous hot springs of Tiberias.

The hot springs of Tiberias are categorized as *toldos chamah* rather than *toldos ha-ur*. This requires clarification: note that the word here is *ur* — *alef vav shuruk* — meaning fire (cognate with *Ur Kasdim*), not *or* meaning light. *Toldos ha-ur* designates heat derived from flame; *toldot ha-chamah* designates heat derived from any non-flame source, including geothermal heat. Since the Tiberian hot springs are not heated by a flame, they fall into the *chamah* category regardless of their actual geological origin. Biblically, heating water via *toldos chamah* is entirely permitted; rabbinically, the concern about visual indistinguishability from fire-derived heat makes it problematic.

The people of Tiberias ran this pipe presumably before *Shabbat* — *erev Shabbos* — threading it through the hot spring water so that the cold water inside would be warmed by the time *Shabbat* arrived.

### Water Prohibition

The sages responded with considerable strictness: *im be-Shabbat* — if this was done on *Shabbat* — *ke-chamim she-huchmu be-Shabbos* — the water must be treated as if it were heated directly on *Shabbat* on a fire. *Ve-asurin be-rechitzah u-vi-shtiyah* — it is forbidden for bathing and forbidden for drinking, and remains so until *Motzei Shabbos*. *Im be-Yom Tov* — if done on *Yom Tov* — *ke-chamim she-huchmu be-Yom Tov* — it is treated as water heated on *Yom Tov*. Since heating water on *Yom Tov* is permitted for drinking purposes, it is *assur be-rechitzah u-muttar be-shtiyah* — forbidden for bathing but permitted for drinking.

The prohibition on using water for bathing even when heated on *Yom Tov*, despite bathing being a legitimate bodily need, is a matter the *gemara* will address in greater detail. For now, the *mishnah* establishes it as given.

What is particularly striking about this ruling is not merely the prohibition against the act itself, but the strictness applied *bedieved* — retroactively. If they laid the pipe *erev Shabbos*, the act of heating itself occurred before *Shabbat* began. Ordinarily one might expect the penalty to be less severe. Yet the sages applied the same status to this water as to water heated on *Shabbat* itself.

### Heat Addition

*Rav Chisda* draws out the broader principle: *batlah hatmanah be-davar ha-mosif hevel va-afilu mi-boad yom* — the prohibition of *hatmanah* in a substance that adds heat applies even before *Shabbat* begins, even when done while it is still day. This is the key distinction within the laws of *hatmanah*: there are materials that merely *preserve* heat — wrapping food in towels to keep it warm — and materials that *add* heat. Preserving heat is permitted before *Shabbat* and has its own rules on *Shabbat* itself. Adding heat is forbidden in any circumstance, even *erev Shabbos*, because of the concern that one will come to stir the heat-adding material.

The Tiberian pipe, conceptually understood as a form of *hatmanah* — burying the water pipe within the hot spring water that surrounds and adds heat to it — thus violated the prohibition even though it was established before *Shabbat*. *Tosafot* notes that the prohibition of *hatmanah* in heat-adding substances *erev Shabbos* is stated explicitly in later *mishnayot*. The *chiddush* of this passage, in *Tosafot*'s reading, is therefore the *bedieved* ruling: not merely that the act was prohibited, but that one may not benefit from the water afterward, just as one who left food on an open flame in violation may not eat from it on *Shabbat*.

### Ulla & Nachman

*Ulla* then stakes out a surprising position: *halacha ke-anshei Teverya* — the *halacha* follows the people of Tiberias. The very people whom the *mishnah* depicts as having been corrected by the sages, *Ulla* retrospectively vindicates. Whether his reasoning is that the pipe through water does not constitute *hatmanah* in the technical sense, or that the ruling follows *Rabbi Yossi* regarding *toldos chamah*, is not entirely clear. But he holds that the practice was in fact permissible.

*Rav Nachman* responds sharply: *kvar tavrunhu anshei Teveryah le-silonayehu* — the people of Tiberias have already broken their pipe. The practice does not stand, and the *halacha* is not like them. The upshot of the *gemara*'s discussion is that *toldos chamah* is rabbinically prohibited, *hatmanah* in a heat-adding substance is forbidden even *erev Shabbos*, and if either prohibition is violated, one may not benefit from the result even after the fact.

---

## Bathing Rules

### Pre-Heated Water

The *mishnah*'s ruling — that the Tiberian water, treated as water heated on *Shabbat*, is forbidden for bathing — now raises a question of definition. *Mai rechitzah* — what kind of bathing does the *mishnah* mean to prohibit? *Ilima rechitzas kol gufo* — if it means bathing one's whole body — then the implication of the *mishnah* would be that water heated before *Shabbat* is permitted for bathing the whole body. But a *baraita* contradicts this: *chamin she-huchmu me-erev Shabbos*, water heated before *Shabbat*, may only be used the next day for washing one's face, hands, and feet — *le-machar rochetz ba-hen panav yadav ve-raglav* — but not one's whole body — *aval lo kol gufo*. Pre-heated water is already insufficient for full-body bathing.

### Bathhouse Concern

The reason for this restriction is the famous *gezeirat merchatza'ot* — the rabbinic decree arising from the bathhouses. Since Roman bathhouses commonly heated water on *Shabbat* itself and the activity of bathing in hot water was pervasive, the sages feared that permitting full-body bathing even in pre-heated water would make it impossible to distinguish permissible from prohibited cases. The next time one visited the bathhouse, one might unknowingly — or carelessly — use water heated on *Shabbat*, reasoning that what one did at home was also fine. The decree therefore restricts even clearly permissible pre-heated water to partial washing — face, hands, and feet.

Returning to the Tiberian case: when the *mishnah* says that the water is "like water heated on *Shabbat*" and therefore forbidden for bathing, it cannot mean that full-body bathing is forbidden, since that is already forbidden even with pre-heated water. It must therefore mean the prohibition extends even to washing one's face, hands, and feet — the partial washing that would normally be permitted with pre-heated water is also forbidden, because the water is treated as if it were heated on *Shabbat* itself.

### Yom Tov Water

This raises a further complication. The *mishnah* states that if the Tiberian water was heated on *Yom Tov*, it is treated as water heated on *Yom Tov*, and in that case: *assur be-rechitzah u-muttar be-shtiyah* — forbidden for bathing but permitted for drinking. The question is: what type of bathing is forbidden? If "forbidden for bathing" means even washing hands and feet, then the *mishnah* is saying that one cannot heat water on *Yom Tov* even for washing hands and feet.

### Beit Shammai

This leads the *gemara* to ask: *leima tnan stama ke-Veit Shammai* — is the *stam mishnah* here following the position of *Beit Shammai*? For a *mishnah* states: *Beit Shammai* holds *lo yachom adam chamim le-raglav* — one may not heat water for one's feet on *Yom Tov* — *ela im ken reuyim li-shtiyah* — unless one is heating it for the purpose of drinking. According to *Beit Shammai*, heating water on *Yom Tov* is permitted only for drinking, not for any washing purpose. *Beit Hillel* permits it. If our *mishnah* prohibits using *Yom Tov*-heated water even for washing hands and feet, it would apparently align with *Beit Shammai*'s position — which is a concern, since *halacha* does not generally follow *Beit Shammai*.

### Unresolved

This creates a genuine difficulty in reconciling the categories: water heated before *Shabbat* is permitted for hands and face but not for the whole body; water heated on *Yom Tov* is apparently not permitted even for hands and face, which would place the *stam mishnah* in the position of *Beit Shammai*. What category of water is there that is permitted for full-body bathing? And how do we account for the *Yom Tov* prohibition on even partial washing in a way that does not conflict with *Beit Hillel*?

These questions remain unresolved at the end of the *daf* and will be taken up in the next session, which will also address the broader practical question of whether and under what circumstances one may bathe in hot water on *Yom Tov* altogether.

---

---

# Shabbat 40

## Sheiya to Bishul

### Fire vs. Sun Heating

Having completed the discussion of *sheiya* issues, the daf now moves into the heart of *bishul* on Shabbat. The prior daf established a fundamental distinction: using fire to heat something is a potential *de'oraita* violation, whereas heating through the sun — *bishul chama* — is not a biblical concern.

### Toldos Chama/Or

The Bavli refines this distinction through the categories of *toldos chama* and *toldos or*. *Toldos or* — heat derived from fire rather than from fire itself — appears to carry potential biblical status, at least based on the case of placing an egg beside a hot water pot. *Toldos chama*, by contrast, is certainly not a biblical violation, though whether it carries rabbinic force is itself debated: since it can be confused with *toldos ha'or*, it may in practice be treated more stringently than direct solar heating.

### Egg/Kettle Case

The case of the egg placed beside a kettle of boiling water established a further principle: one need not place something directly upon a fire for *bishul de'oraita* to apply. Rav Yosef's reading of the Mishnah makes clear that proximity to an intense heat source is sufficient.

---

## Tverya Water Pipe

### Tverya Incident

The Mishnah records a case involving the people of Tverya who ran a pipe of cold water through the town's famous hot springs — *chamei Tverya* — in order to heat it. The rabbis ruled that this water must be treated as though it had been heated on Shabbat itself, and accordingly one may derive no benefit from it. If the infraction occurred on Shabbat, the water is forbidden for drinking and bathing alike. If the infraction occurred on Yom Tov, the water may be used for drinking but not for bathing the entire body.

The precise nature of the violation is somewhat ambiguous. One reading — which appears to be the Bavli's primary understanding — is that the pipe was set up *erev Shabbat*, creating a concern of *hatmanah*, insulation that is problematic even before Shabbat. An alternative reading, perhaps more naturally suggested by the Yerushalmi, is that the cold water was piped through on Shabbat itself and was actively heated on Shabbat through contact with the springs, constituting *toldos chama* in the most direct sense.

### Rav Ika Query

This leads to a difficulty. If the water was heated *erev Shabbat*, it should in principle be permitted — water heated before Shabbat, after all, may generally be used on Shabbat. Yet we know from elsewhere that even water heated *erev Shabbat* may not be used for bathing the entire body. At the same time, if we are speaking only of hands, face, and feet, that usage is permitted — so why should Yom Tov present any additional problem? The question then is: what is the intermediate category, something permitted when heated *erev Shabbat* but forbidden both on Shabbat and on Yom Tov?

Rav Ika bar Chanina resolves this by specifying that the case involves *lehishtatef pnei kol gufo* — pouring water over the entire body, a full-body shower rather than immersion in a bath — and that the ruling follows a specific Tanna in the following *beraisa*.

---

## Bathing Debate

### Showering Definition

The term *lehishtatef* denotes showering — pouring water over the whole body — as distinct from sitting in a bath. This definition is critical to understanding the three-way tannaitic dispute that follows.

### Three Positions

The *beraisa* records the following positions. Rabbi Meir rules most stringently: *lo yishtatef adam kol gufo bein bechamin bein betzonen* — a person may not pour water over his entire body whether in hot or cold water. The reasoning behind Rabbi Meir's prohibition of cold water is not entirely clear; it may be a concern that beginning with cold water will lead to hot water, or that it will lead to wringing out towels, or to some other prohibited activity. Rabbi Shimon is most lenient: full-body showering is permitted even with hot water, provided that water was heated before Shabbat — immersion in a bath remains forbidden, but showering is allowed. Rabbi Yehuda takes the middle position: *bechamin assur betzonen mutar* — hot water is forbidden, cold water is permitted.

### Resolve Tverya

The Tverya case is now resolved according to Rabbi Shimon. Ordinarily, water heated *erev Shabbat* may be used for a full-body shower per Rabbi Shimon's ruling. Since the rabbis decreed that the water from the Tverya pipe must be treated as though it were heated on Shabbat itself, it loses that leniency — one may neither drink it nor shower with it. Similarly, on Yom Tov, water heated on Yom Tov is permitted for hands and face but not for showering the whole body. Thus the case occupies a precise middle ground: had it genuinely been heated *erev Shabbat*, a shower would have been permitted per Rabbi Shimon; because it is treated as Shabbat-heated water, even the shower is forbidden; and on Yom Tov, even the permitted Yom Tov heating does not extend to the entire body.

---

## Yom Tov Heating

### Yom Tov Problem

This analysis raises a broader and more challenging question: why may one not heat water for bathing on Yom Tov at all? Unlike Shabbat, on Yom Tov fire is permitted for bodily needs. People who smoke, for example, have long claimed — and in some cases legitimately — that smoking qualifies as a *tzorach haguf*, a bodily need permitted on Yom Tov. Why, then, should heating water for a hot bath or shower be categorically forbidden? After all, bathing is surely a bodily need.

The concern that gave rise to the Shabbat restriction is clear enough: the institution of the public bathhouse created a situation in which, if hot bathing from pre-Shabbat water were permitted, bathhouse attendants would inevitably heat the water on Shabbat itself and claim it had been prepared beforehand. That structural concern, however, does not apply on Yom Tov in the same way, since fire is permitted. The Gemara proceeds to address this through a debate between the Rishonim.

### Ramban: Lo Pelug

The Ramban explains the Yom Tov prohibition as a *lo pelug*: since the rabbis prohibited hot bathing on Shabbat even from water heated before Shabbat, they made no distinction and extended the prohibition to Yom Tov as well. This is admittedly a striking *lo pelug*, given how many uses of fire and heat are permitted on Yom Tov. The Ramban's position means the restriction is purely rabbinic with no structural justification on Yom Tov itself — it is simply an undifferentiated blanket decree.

### Tosafot: Taanug

Tosafot, citing the Riva, offers a fundamentally different explanation. In the *tosafot* beginning *u'Beis Hillel matirin*, Tosafot writes *de-rechitza eina ela le-taanug ve-assura kmo mugmar mishum de-ein shava le-chol nefesh* — bathing the entire body in hot water is classified as a pleasure, a *taanug*, that is not universally shared, analogous to burning incense. Since it is *ein shava le-chol nefesh* — not a common bodily need of the general population — it falls outside the category of legitimate Yom Tov use. On Yom Tov one may perform labor for needs that are universal or near-universal; a luxury enjoyed by only a segment of the population does not qualify.

### Modern Practice

This Tosafot carries significant practical implications. If the Ramban is correct that the prohibition is a *lo pelug*, it is a rabbinic restriction with no sensitivity to changed circumstances. But if Tosafot is correct, the prohibition rests on an empirical assessment that hot bathing is not a common need — an assessment that is plainly different in the modern world, where regular bathing and showering are universal practice.

There are indeed *poskim* who rule accordingly, including the *Shemiras Shabbos ke-Hilchatah*, who in at least one extended footnote argues — though his position may evolve across editions — that a hot shower today, given that people shower regularly, should not be prohibited on Yom Tov. One must in any case be careful regarding *sechita* — the prohibition of wringing out — which applies to wet hair and towels; one should allow hair to drip dry or pat it dry rather than wringing it.

The Gemara's assumption that hot bathing on Yom Tov is self-evidently forbidden is thus one that contemporary *poskim* following Tosafot's reasoning may revisit.

A related and unresolved question concerns women who immerse in a *mikvah* on Friday night, typically in heated water. The full-body immersion in hot water would appear to raise the same concerns as bathing. While many *poskim* have noted the tension and offered various justifications — some suggesting that perhaps the water is merely warm rather than hot — the practice has not been discontinued. The implicit acceptance by *poskim* is itself a form of ruling, even if an acknowledged accommodation. Separately, Ashkenazic practice extends even to cold water: the thousand-year-old *minhag* among Ashkenazim is not to immerse the entire body even in cold water on Shabbat. This goes beyond anything in the Gemara, which limited the concern to hot water. Sephardim do not share this *minhag* and in practice will swim in a pool on Shabbat — a topic the daf will address later.

---

## Halacha L'Rav Yehuda

### Vessel vs. Ground

Rav Chisda introduces a distinction to help situate the tannaitic debate. He rules *machlokes b'kli* — the three-way dispute of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yehuda applies specifically when the water was heated in a vessel. *Aval b'karka divrei hakol mutar* — if the hot water is contained in the ground rather than in a portable vessel, all opinions would permit its use, since in-ground heating is less likely to lead to the appearance of, or actual, heating on Shabbat. The intuition is that a vessel of hot water is more easily associated with fire-heated water and therefore creates a greater concern that someone will heat it on Shabbat; ground-based heat seems less susceptible to that confusion.

### Challenge to Distinction

The Gemara challenges Rav Chisda immediately. The Tverya case — the very case that opened this discussion — involved water flowing through a pipe in the ground, clearly an in-ground scenario, and yet the rabbis forbade it. This overturns Rav Chisda's formulation. The Gemara revises his ruling: the debate in fact applies when the water is *b'karka* — in the ground — while water heated in a vessel is forbidden according to all opinions, since a portable vessel of hot water creates far greater concern of actual Shabbat heating.

### Halacha: Hands/Face/Feet

Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda*. The ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda's middle position. This is consequential: it means that on Shabbat, even water heated before Shabbat may not be used for a full-body shower — Rabbi Shimon's leniency is rejected — and certainly not for a bath. Only hands, face, and feet are permitted.

### Explicit vs. Inferred

Rav Yosef then asks Rabba bar bar Chana whether this ruling was received explicitly or inferred from a broader principle. *Mai klala* — what general principle might yield this inference? The candidate is the doctrine recorded in the name of Rav Yannai, citing Rav or Rabbi: *kol makom she-ata motzei shnayim cholekin ve-echad machriya, halacha k'divrei hamachriya* — whenever two opinions disagree and a third takes a compromise position, the *halacha* follows the compromise. Here, Rabbi Meir prohibits even cold water, Rabbi Shimon permits even a hot shower, and Rabbi Yehuda prohibits hot but permits cold — a textbook compromise position. One might therefore have inferred the ruling in Rabbi Yehuda's favor from this general doctrine.

There is a well-known exception to this principle, however: the case of *mikulei matlaniyot* — worn rags used for various household purposes — where Rabbi Eliezer was strict, Rabbi Yehoshua was lenient, and Rabbi Akiva offered a compromise. There the ruling does not follow Rabbi Akiva, for two reasons: first, Rabbi Akiva was himself a student of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua and therefore does not have the independent standing required for the *machriya* doctrine to apply; and second, Rabbi Akiva ultimately reversed his own compromise position and aligned with Rabbi Yehoshua. Tosafot here also notes at some length that not every middle position is a genuine compromise — a *machriya* must be a hybrid that incorporates elements of each extreme, not merely a position that happens to fall between them numerically.

A further question arises: even if the *machriya* doctrine applies in principle, perhaps it applies only when the dispute appears in a Mishnah, not in a *beraita*. The logic would be that Rabbi's editorial framing of a dispute in the Mishnah implicitly signals something about the preferred ruling, while a *beraita* carries no such editorial weight. Since the current dispute appears in a *beraita*, the inference from the *machriya* doctrine might not hold.

Rabba bar bar Chana resolves the inquiry: *ana be-feirush shemi li* — he heard it explicitly. The ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda regardless of these doctrinal questions. The practical upshot is clear: on Shabbat, bathing the whole body in hot water is forbidden even from water heated before Shabbat, and showering the whole body is equally forbidden.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Rav: Limb by Limb

The Gemara now explores the space between the extremes of full-body bathing and hands-face-feet. Rav rules: *le-machar rochetz bahem kol gufo eiver eiver* — one may wash the entire body limb by limb with water heated before Shabbat, washing one limb at a time until the whole body has been washed, as long as the entire body is not bathed simultaneously.

### Shmuel: Limited Areas

Shmuel disagrees sharply: *lo hutru lirkhotz ela panav yadav ve-raglav* — only the face, hands, and feet are permitted. Washing other parts of the body, whether sequentially or otherwise, is forbidden.

### Baraita Challenge

The Gemara challenges Rav's position. A *beraita* states: *chamim she-uchmu me-erev Shabbat, le-machar rochetz bahem panav yadav ve-raglav, aval lo kol gufo* — if water was heated before Shabbat, one may wash one's face, hands, and feet the next day, but not the whole body. Rav responds: *lo kol gufo be-vas achat* — the prohibition of the whole body means all at once; doing it limb by limb is still permitted. He further interprets the permission for *panav yadav ve-raglav* as meaning *ke-ein panav yadav ve-raglav* — individual limbs at a time, not the whole body simultaneously.

### Rava's Teaching

Rava presents Rav's position in a sharper formulation: *amar Rav rochetz bahem kol gufo u-meshayer eiver echad* — one may wash the whole body and merely leave out one limb. This would technically permit showering while leaving one arm outside, for example. The Gemara then marshals the same counter-evidence — that the *beraita* explicitly restricts the permission to face, hands, and feet, and that *eiver eiver* across the whole body is not permitted — and the Gemara declares *tiyuvta*: Rav's position is contradicted.

### Rabba's Practice

Rav Yosef asks Abaye whether Rabba — who had transmitted Rav's teaching in the more lenient formulation — actually practiced according to Rav's ruling. Abaye replies that he does not know. The Gemara asks: why is this even a question? Obviously Rabba would not have followed a position that had been refuted. The Gemara answers: perhaps Rabba had not heard the counter-evidence. Abaye himself testified that Rabba generally followed Rav's rulings in practice: *kol mili de-mar, avid ke-Rav* — all the master's practices accorded with Rav. The exceptions — three cases where Rabba followed Shmuel — were: removing *tzitzit* from one garment to another (*mattilin mi-beged le-beged*), lighting Chanukah candles from one flame to another (*madlikin mi-ner le-ner*), and ruling like Rabbi Shimon on dragging furniture (*halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon be-gireira*).

### Stringency/Leniency Rule

The Gemara responds with a crucial qualification: *ke-chumrei de-Rav avid, ke-kulei de-Rav lo avid* — Rabba followed Rav's stringencies, but not necessarily Rav's leniencies. Since the three cases where Rabba followed Shmuel were precisely cases where Shmuel was lenient, it is possible that Rabba only followed Rav unconditionally when Rav was strict. Here, Rav's position is the lenient one — permitting limb-by-limb washing — and therefore even if Rabba had not heard the counter-evidence, we cannot be certain he would have followed Rav. The question remains open.

The upshot, however, is clear from the Gemara's overall thrust: Rav's position is rejected. One may not wash the entire body limb by limb with hot water on Shabbat, nor may one perform the maneuver of washing the whole body while leaving a single limb out.

---

## Rama's Position

### Rama Allowance

Notwithstanding the Gemara's apparent restriction to hands, face, and feet, the Rama rules that washing other individual limbs is permitted, as long as one does not wash *kol gufo* — the entire body. The Rama's position is that the prohibition targets bathing or showering the whole body; individual limbs beyond the canonical three remain permissible. The distinction between the Rama's ruling and the case rejected by the Gemara is significant: the Gemara's rejected scenario involved washing each limb in sequence with the intent of covering the whole body, or — in Rava's sharper version — literally washing all but one limb. The Rama permits washing isolated individual limbs, stopping short of the totality that the decree was designed to prevent.

---

## Bathhouse Origin

### Sealed Bathhouse

Having established the rules, the Gemara now traces the historical origin of these restrictions. A *beraisa* discusses a bathhouse whose holes had been stopped up *erev Shabbat*. The bathhouses of the period were heated from below through vents; sealing those vents before Shabbat meant the water was not being heated on Shabbat itself. In such a case, *le-motzaei Shabbat rochetz bo miyad* — one may bathe immediately after Shabbat ends, since the water was not heated on Shabbat and thus carries no prohibition.

### Erev Yom Tov Closure

If the holes were stopped up *erev Yom Tov*, then on Yom Tov itself one may enter the bathhouse, perspire from the steam — *nichnas u-meize* — and then go into the outer chamber and pour cold water over oneself. The full bath in hot water is not permitted on Yom Tov, but benefiting from the steam — a *shvitz*, a sauna experience — is permitted, since the hot water generating the steam was covered with planks (*mechupin be-nesarim*), precluding any possibility of actual bathing. When the matter came before the Sages, they ruled even more leniently: even if the hot water is not covered with planks, the steam bath is permitted, as long as the person does not actually bathe in the hot water.

### Bnei Brak Incident

Rav Yehuda records a concrete incident illustrating this ruling: a story involving the bathhouse of Bnei Brak where the holes had been stopped up *erev Yom Tov*. The next day — perhaps the day following the Pesach Seder — Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva entered and *heziu bah*, took a steam bath. Afterward, *yatzu ve-nishtatefu be-veis ha-chitzon*, they went into the outer room and poured cold water over themselves. What made this permissible, the *beraisa* notes, was that the hot water was *mechupin be-nesarim* — covered with planks — so there was no possibility of anyone bathing directly in the hot water.

---

## Progressive Bans

### Initial Permission

The Gemara now provides a remarkable historical account — transmitted in the name of Bar Kapara via Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi via Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi — of how the restrictions on bathing developed in stages, each restriction generating a new loophole that was then closed, until a final reversal was required.

Initially the rule was simple: *be-techila hayu rochtzin be-chamin she-uchmu me-erev Shabbat* — water heated before Shabbat was permitted for full-body bathing on Shabbat. No restriction applied.

### Ban Bathing

*Hitchilu ha-balanim le-hachem be-Shabbat u-me-erev Shabbat huchamu* — the bathhouse attendants began heating the water on Shabbat and claiming it had been heated before Shabbat. This was the structural problem: the public institution of the bathhouse, with professional attendants whose livelihood depended on customers, created an environment where deceptive practice was endemic. The rabbis therefore prohibited hot bathing on Shabbat entirely — *asru et ha-chamin* — even from water genuinely heated before Shabbat. However, they permitted the steam bath — *hitiru et ha-zei'ah* — the *shvitz*, reasoning or assuming that this remained acceptable.

Logically, the distinction is difficult to justify: heating water for a steam bath requires the same fire as heating it for a bath. One possible explanation is that there was a social pressure to leave some avenue open — perhaps reflecting the Roman cultural reality in which bathing had become deeply embedded in daily life, and an absolute prohibition would be unsustainable.

### Ban Steam Bath

The next stage: *adayin hayu rochtzim be-chamin ve-omrim me-zi'in anachnu* — people would actually bathe in hot water and claim they were merely using the steam bath. Since the *shvitz* was permitted, bathers had a ready-made pretext. The rabbis therefore prohibited the steam bath as well — *asru lahem et ha-zei'ah*. In its place, they permitted *chamei Tverya* — the natural hot springs — since that water was not heated by fire at all, being warmed by geological heat or solar energy.

### Ban Hot Springs

In the third stage, *adayin hayu rochtzim be-chamei ha-ur ve-omrim be-chamei Tverya rachatznu* — people would bathe in fire-heated water and claim they had been to the hot springs. This pretense was at least geographically plausible for those in Tverya, though its application elsewhere is puzzling. The rabbis responded by prohibiting *chamei Tverya* as well — *asru lahem chamei Tverya* — and leaving cold water as the only permitted option. Rabbi Meir would have gone further and prohibited even cold water, as recorded earlier in the *beraita*.

### Permit Hot Springs

At this point *ra'u she-ein ha-davar omed lahem* — the Sages recognized that the public simply could not endure such a comprehensive prohibition. The expression *ein rov ha-tzibbur yecholim la'amod bo* is striking: it reflects a pragmatic willingness to reverse a rabbinic decree when it proves unenforceable and causes genuine public hardship. Accordingly, the rabbis reversed themselves and permitted *chamei Tverya*. Hot springs heated by natural means — *chama be-shel chamah* — are permitted. This ruling has significant implications in the Israeli context for the *dud shemesh*, the solar water heater, since water heated by solar energy is in the same category as *chamei Tverya* and is thus permitted for bathing.

The prohibition of the *shvitz*, the steam bath, however, remains in force and was not reversed. Rava notes further that walking through a large-city bathhouse incidentally — *metayel bahen* — without sitting in the steam is permitted, since the steam encountered in passing is incidental. By contrast, the bathhouses of small villages — *kfarim* — are small enough that even walking through them is tantamount to sitting in a sauna, as the steam is dense and concentrated, and this is therefore forbidden.

Rava adds that one who transgresses a rabbinic prohibition is appropriately called *avaryana* — a sinner — as the Gemara demonstrates from the very language of this *beraita*, which calls those who bathed while claiming to be taking a *shvitz* *ovrei aveira* — sinners — even though the underlying violation was purely rabbinic.

---

## Heating Liquids

### Warming Principle

The Gemara transitions to the direct question of *bishul* — cooking — on Shabbat, now addressing the precise thresholds that define forbidden heating of liquids. The operative rule is introduced through a *beraisa*: *mitchamem adam k'neged ha-medurah ve-yotze u-mishtatef be-tzonen* — a person may warm himself before a fire and then go out and pour cold water over himself, benefiting from the combination of body heat and cold water. However — *u-vilvad shelo yishtatef be-tzonen ve-yitchamem k'neged ha-medurah* — one may not first pour cold water over oneself and then stand before the fire, because this constitutes *mafshir mayim she-alav* — warming the water that is on one's body — which is either a *bishul* concern for the water itself or, per Tosafot's reading, is connected to the broader *gezeira* against bathing the whole body in hot water.

### Water Flask

A second *beraisa* addresses the flask of water: *meivi adam kiton shel mayim u-menicho k'neged ha-medurah* — a person may bring a flask of water and place it before the fire. The condition is *lo bishvil she-yechamu, ela bishvil she-tafig tzintan* — not in order for the water to become genuinely hot, which would constitute cooking, but merely to remove the chill. The line between permissible warming and forbidden *bishul* is defined by the concept of *yad soledet bo*, which will be elaborated momentarily.

The *beraisa* also addresses a hot towel, *aluntis*: one may heat a towel and place it on one's stomach on Shabbat. However, one may not bring a vessel of hot water — a *kumkum* — and place it on one's stomach on Shabbat, not only for the practical danger of spilling but because, per Rashi, it may spill and cover the whole body, amounting to bathing in hot water. Tosafot reads the concern differently: the prohibition relates to the risk of the water falling on the towel and leading to *sechita*, or alternatively to the concern that using a hot water bottle constitutes *refuah* — medicinal treatment — which is separately forbidden on Shabbat.

### Rabbi Yehuda: Oil

Rabbi Yehuda extends the discussion from water to oil: *mevia isha pach shel shemen u-menichato k'neged ha-medurah* — a woman may bring a flask of oil and place it before a fire. The condition again is *lo bishvil she-yevashel, ela bishvil she-yafsher* — not that it should cook, but only that it should liquefy, since oil left at room temperature in certain climates becomes semi-solid. The context suggests this may relate to using oil as a lotion applied to the hands, which would need to be in liquid form.

### Rabban Shimon: Oil

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel takes a more restrictive position on oil: *isha sacha yada shemen u-mitchamemet k'neged ha-medurah ve-sacha li-vnah ha-katan* — a woman may put oil on her hand and then hold it before the fire, and she may apply it to her child, without concern that the oil is heating up in the process. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel thus permits oil only when it is already on the body; placing oil directly before a fire, even to liquefy it, is problematic according to his view.

---

## Oil vs. Water

### Oil as Bishul

The Gemara raises the question explicitly: *shemen mahu le-tanna kamma* — what is the status of oil for the first opinion in the *beraita*, who spoke only of water and did not mention oil? Three positions among the Amoraim interpret the range of tannaitic views.

### Lenient: Oil OK

Rabba and Rav Yosef both rule *le-teira* — leniently. According to them, the first *tanna* holds that oil is entirely unproblematic: *shemen af al pi she-yad soledet bo mutar* — oil may be heated even to the point of *yad soledet bo* without constituting *bishul*. The reasoning is *kasavar tanna kamma shemen ein bo mishum bishul* — the first *tanna* holds that the category of *bishul* simply does not apply to oil when it is heated in isolation. Whereas heating water to *yad soledet bo* is meaningful because hot water is actively used — for tea, for cooking — heating oil by itself to that temperature is not a significant or meaningful act and therefore falls outside the definition of *bishul*.

### Strict: Oil Problem

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reads the first *tanna* most strictly: even below *yad soledet bo*, heating oil constitutes *bishul*. On this reading, *kasavar shemen yesh bo mishum bishul ve-hafshara zo hi bishulah* — oil is subject to *bishul*, and merely liquefying it is already considered cooking. The practical implication is that the first *tanna* and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel converge on the same prohibition but differ on the one permitted avenue: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits oil on the body held before the fire (*ke-l'achar yad*), while on Rav Nachman's reading of the first *tanna*, even that would be forbidden.

### Middle: Oil Limits

Rabbi Yehuda takes the middle position: *shemen yesh bo mishum bishul, ve-hafshara lo zo hi bishulah* — oil is subject to *bishul*, but merely liquefying it does not yet constitute *bishul*. Only heating oil to *yad soledet bo* crosses the forbidden threshold.

### Most Strict: Oil

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, as noted, holds that *shemen yesh bo mishum bishul ve-hafshara zo hi bishulah* — even liquefying oil is considered *bishul* — and therefore prohibits placing oil directly before the fire entirely. The only permitted avenue for warming oil is to have it on the body and then stand before the fire.

The Gemara notes that on one reading, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the first *tanna* appear identical, both prohibiting even liquefaction. The Gemara resolves this: *ika beinaihu ke-l'achar yad* — the difference lies in the indirect scenario of oil on the body before the fire. The first *tanna* prohibits even that; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits it.

---

## Yad Soledet Bo

### Yad Soledet Intro

The Gemara now turns to the unifying halachic standard. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel establishes the definitive rule for both liquids: *echad shemen ve-echad mayim, yad soledet bo assur, ein yad soledet bo mutar* — whether oil or water, if heated to *yad soledet bo* it is forbidden; below that temperature it is permitted.

It is important to note what the Gemara is directly addressing here: the question of when heating a liquid itself constitutes *bishul* — the cooking of that liquid. The concept of *yad soledet bo* is subsequently applied by the *poskim* to the related but distinct question of whether a hot liquid is itself capable of cooking other foods placed in it, such as bread placed in hot soup. That broader application — relevant to *bishul achar bishul* and to *keli rishon* and *keli sheni* discussions — is a transfer of the standard developed here, not its primary context in this *sugya*. For solid foods, by contrast, the relevant threshold for *bishul* is functional edibility — whether the food has become *ma'achal ben Drusai* — since the transformation being tracked is a qualitative one. Liquids are different: since their "cooking" consists not in a qualitative change from raw to edible but in reaching a temperature of significance, *yad soledet bo* serves as the operative measure.

### Oil/Water Same

The ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel thus establishes parity between oil and water. Neither the leniency of Rabba and Rav Yosef — that oil is entirely exempt from *bishul* — nor the severity of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak — that oil is subject to *bishul* even below *yad soledet bo* — is accepted. The same standard governs both: *yad soledet bo* triggers the prohibition, and below that threshold both are permitted.

### Infant Scald Test

Rachava defines *yad soledet bo* operationally: *kol she-kreiso shel tinok nichveit* — the temperature at which the stomach of an infant would be scalded. One might ask how this aligns with the more intuitive formulation — whether an adult can keep a hand in the water without recoiling. The *poskim* explain that the tests measure different things in a complementary way: the infant's stomach test applies to the briefest contact, even a momentary touch; the adult hand test asks whether one can sustain immersion for several seconds without being forced to withdraw. These two formulations, taken together, mark the threshold zone. Various *poskim* have attempted to translate *yad soledet bo* into precise Fahrenheit or Celsius values, with typical estimates falling somewhere between roughly 103 and 115 degrees Fahrenheit — but, as Rav Yehuda Herzl Henkin has argued, the Sages themselves defined this threshold experientially rather than numerically, and the proper test remains the hand in the water, not a thermometer reading. The daf will continue exploring these issues in the next session.

---

---

# Shabbat 41

## Kli Rishon/Kli Sheni

### Rebbi & Oil Flask

The *gemara* opens with the account of Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi, who relates: "One time I followed Rebbe into the bathhouse." Presumably it was Shabbos, and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi wished to place a flask of oil into the bath in order to warm it up. Rebbe's response was immediate: take water in a second vessel and place the flask of oil into that second vessel — do not place it directly into the bath itself.

The reasoning is foundational. The bath is considered a *kli rishon* — the vessel in which the water was initially heated — and objects are capable of being cooked in a *kli rishon*. By contrast, placing the flask into a *kli sheni*, a second vessel into which the hot water has been transferred, removes the concern of cooking. Today's *gemara* is, in fact, one of the primary sources for this entire distinction.

A question immediately arises: what was Rebbe doing in the bathhouse in the first place? The *gemara* established earlier that one may not fully immerse in hot water on Shabbos. Rashi notes, and the *gemara* itself will shortly confirm, that the bath must have been *chamei Teverya* — the naturally heated springs of Tiberias, warmed not by fire but by the earth itself.

### Three Inferences

From Rebbe's instruction, the *gemara* derives three *halachic* conclusions: *shema mina shemen yesh bo mishum bishul* — it is possible to violate the prohibition of cooking with respect to oil, resolving the uncertainty discussed in the previous session. Second: *kli sheni eino mevashel* — a second vessel does not cook; this is of decisive importance for later *halacha*. Third: *hafshara zehu bishulo* — mere dissolution, the liquefying of a solid, may itself constitute the act of cooking.

This third inference, however, sits in some tension with the conclusion reached previously, where it was established that cooking a liquid requires it to reach the temperature of *yad soledet bo*. If mere dissolution — even at a lower temperature — were sufficient, that earlier conclusion would be undermined. The *gemara* therefore notes that in practice, even for oil, we require *yad soledet bo*, and the third inference does not represent the final ruling.

### Chamei Teverya

The *gemara* now raises the inference of Ravina: it sounds as though one who cooks in *chamei Teverya* on Shabbos is biblically liable — *hamevashel b'chamei Teverya b'Shabbos chayav*. This would contradict the established principle that heating by a non-fire source is not a biblical violation. Ravina's reasoning is that Rebbe's story must have occurred after the earlier rabbinic prohibition was in place, meaning that Rebbe could only have been in water not heated by fire — i.e., *chamei Teverya* — and yet his concern about placing oil in the bath seemed to rise to the level of biblical prohibition.

The *gemara* rejects this inference, citing Rav Chisda: *hamevashel b'chamei Teverya b'Shabbos patur* — one who cooks in *chamei Teverya* on Shabbos is exempt. The apparent biblical concern in the story must therefore refer only to *makat mardut*, a rabbinic lashing, not a Torah-level violation. What remains is the rabbinic restriction against cooking something in *chamei Teverya* — a form of *toldos chamah* — and it was this concern that prompted Rebbe to insist on using a *kli sheni*.

### Torah in Bathhouse

Before returning to the *halachic* substance, the *gemara* raises a procedural difficulty: how was Rebbe permitted to speak words of *Torah* in the bathhouse at all? The Gemara cites Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that it is forbidden to think about *Torah* in a bathhouse or lavatory.

One might suppose the answer is that Rebbe spoke in a non-Hebrew language, but the *gemara* anticipates this and rejects it. Abaye states clearly: *devarim shel chol mutar l'omram b'lashon hakodesh* — secular matters may be said in Hebrew even in a bathhouse, and sacred content may not be said even in the vernacular. The criterion is the content, not the language.

Yet one might still object: what Rebbe actually said was not an explicit *halachic* ruling — he simply instructed his attendant to use a different vessel. The *gemara* treats even this implicit reference to *kli sheni* as constituting speech of *Torah*. How, then, was it permitted?

The *gemara* answers: *afrushei mei'isura shani* — it is different when one is acting to prevent another from committing a transgression. In such a case, speaking words of *Torah* in the bathhouse is permitted. A parallel case is adduced: a student of Rabbi Meir followed him into the bathhouse on Shabbos and wished to wash the floor; Rabbi Meir told him *ein medichin* — it is forbidden. He then wished to apply oil to the floor, and Rabbi Meir told him *ein sachin* — that too is forbidden, lest it lead to smoothing over holes in the ground. In both cases, Rabbi Meir spoke clear *halachic* prohibitions in the bathhouse, and this was permitted because he was preventing a transgression. The principle is established: *afrushei mei'isura shani*.

### Connected Systems

Returning to the student's original question — if the bath was heated by *chamei Teverya* rather than by fire, why should it be considered a *kli rishon* at all? The springs never cooked anything in the bathtub per se. Rashi addresses this directly: the bath, into which the hot water is drawn continuously from the wellsprings, is considered like a *kli rishon* in which the water was boiled — *af al pi she'he'eviru me'al ha'ur mevashel* — because a *kli rishon*, even once removed from the fire, retains its status.

There is still an apparent difficulty: the bathtub was never itself placed over a fire. But Rashi's understanding seems to be that when hot water flows continuously from its source into a connected vessel, the entire system functions as a single unit. This has significant contemporary implications. When one opens the hot water tap in a home on Shabbos, drawing water directly from a hot water heater, some authorities argue that the water flowing through the pipe remains part of a single connected system and retains the status of *kli rishon*. The cup into which it is poured may itself be considered part of that connected unit rather than a separate *kli sheni*.

This reflects a broader question about where precisely the conceptual break between *kli rishon* and *kli sheni* occurs. One authority cited holds that when water flows directly from a hot water urn through a spigot into a cup, since the water is still in contact with the heat source at the moment of flow, the cup itself might carry *kli rishon* status — in contrast to the classic case of *kli sheni*, where the vessel has already been removed from the fire before the transfer occurs.

### Cooking Definition

This discussion sets up the two central criteria for *bishul* on Shabbos that have emerged across this *daf*: *yad soledet bo* as the required temperature, and the requirement that the act occur in a *kli rishon* rather than a *kli sheni*.
