Rav Ashi offers a more elegant resolution to the entire beehive discussion. The Beraita's formulation — protect the hive *from the sun* and *from the rain* — does not specify summer or winter. It specifies sun and rain. Rav Ashi teaches: *beyomei Nisan u-veyomei Tishrei*, in the spring and fall months, there are days that are sunny and days with rain. In those seasons, the hive is full of honey that the owner could use for himself, so the honey is not *muktzeh* — and the entire difficulty about the two stored winter loaves does not arise.

---

## Rav Huna Citation

### Corpse Principle

Rav Sheshet addresses Rabbi Yitzchak: go tell him, he says to his students, that Rav Huna already anticipated his principle in Babylon. The principle *ein kli nittal ela le-davar ha-nittal* was not a new teaching — Rav Huna had already applied it in a concrete context. Rav Huna's formulation: *osin mechitzah le-met be-Shabbat bishvil chai, ve-ein osin mechitzah le-met bishvil met* — one may erect a partition for the sake of a corpse on Shabbat if it is done for the sake of the living people present, but not directly for the sake of the corpse. The corpse is *muktzeh*, and one cannot move or arrange items directly for the sake of *muktzeh*. Just as Rabbi Yitzchak taught that a vessel cannot be moved for a *muktzeh* object, Rav Huna had already applied the same reasoning to the case of protecting a *met* — and he did so in Babylon before Rabbi Yitzchak's formulation reached him.

---

## Rav Huna Citation (II)

### Corpse Story

The Gemara elaborates on how Rav Huna's principle plays out in practice. Rabbi Shmuel bar Yehuda and Shila Mari both taught the following scenario: if a corpse lies exposed in the sun and must be shielded, two people come and seat themselves beside it. They position themselves near the body, and their presence begins to shade it somewhat. They find that sitting on the hot ground is uncomfortable, so each brings his bed and sits upon it — the bed is being moved for the sake of the living person, not the corpse. Now they find that the sun is bearing down on them from above, so they bring mats and hold them overhead as an awning — since the mat is held by their arms and not by freestanding walls, it does not constitute an *ohel*. Having now established themselves with beds on either side of the body and mats extended over their heads, each person then has reason to leave. Before departing, each one flips his bed upright and slips away. The result is two vertical beds flanking the corpse, with the mat resting on top — a protected enclosure. The elaborate sequence is necessary because one must not create the protective structure directly for the *met*: the beds are moved for the living persons, and the awning is created in a reverse order — covering first, walls after — which is the halachically sanctioned method for forming a temporary *ohel* on Shabbat.

---

## Corpse Movement

### Bed Brigade

The Gemara now turns to the separate question of how a corpse lying in the sun on Shabbat may be moved when no other solution is available. Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, proposes: *hofcho mi-mitah le-mitah* — the corpse may be transferred from one bed to the next in a kind of bed brigade, with people passing it along until it reaches shelter. The degree to which this constitutes *kevod ha-met* is admittedly difficult to appreciate, but it is the method Shmuel permits.

### Infant Loaf

The alternative approach, cited by Rabbi Chanina bar Shmaya in the name of Rav, is: *maniach alav kikar o tinok u-metatlelto* — one places a loaf of bread or an infant on the corpse, and then moves the corpse ostensibly because one is moving the loaf or the infant. This is a permitted technique for the unique case of the *met*, and the Gemara emphasizes its exceptional character. Normally, placing a non-*muktzeh* object atop a *muktzeh* object does not transform the *muktzeh* object into something movable — one is still fundamentally moving the *muktzeh* item, and the presence of a loaf or child on top changes nothing. This technique is permitted only because of the special concern for the dignity of the dead. This is distinct from the principle that a tray bearing both *muktzeh* and permitted items is not itself *muktzeh* — there, the tray is not intrinsically *muktzeh*; its status depends on what it bears. But the corpse is intrinsically *muktzeh*; it does not shed that status because something non-*muktzeh* rests upon it. The Rabbis made an exception for the *met* out of the pressing concern to treat it with dignity.

### Tiltul Debate

The Gemara concludes with a dispute applicable when neither a loaf nor an infant is available to place on the corpse. Where both are present, all opinions agree the technique is valid. The disagreement is about *tiltul min ha-tzad* — indirect movement. The bed-brigade method of Rav Yehuda represents a form of indirect movement: one is not directly carrying the corpse but tipping it from bed to bed, so that the primary action is the movement of the bed and the corpse moves incidentally. One opinion holds *tiltul min ha-tzad shmei tiltul* — indirect movement is still considered movement and is prohibited for *muktzeh*. The other holds *lo shmei tiltul* — indirect movement is not halachically equivalent to direct movement and is therefore permitted.

It is worth noting that even the lenient opinion here does not sanction simply carrying the *met* by means of an intermediary like a bed that one physically holds — that would still constitute direct movement of the *muktzeh* corpse. *Tiltul min ha-tzad* in its precise form means that one performs an action primarily directed at something else, and the *muktzeh* object moves only as a side consequence — as when reaching for an apple one's arm incidentally nudges a wallet aside. The bed-brigade method, understood properly, approximates that structure: one focuses on repositioning the bed itself, and the corpse moves with it as a secondary effect. Whether that approximation is sufficient to escape the prohibition is the crux of the debate, which will be resolved in the following session.

---

---

# Shabbat 44

## Intro: Muktzah Focus

### Kira Overview

Daf 44 picks up at the bottom of 43b. It is worth pausing to note that the chapter of *Kira* is something of a motherlode for the central issues of *Shabbat*. In the course of this *perek* we have covered the *derabbanan* prohibitions of *shehiya* and *chazara*, the key aspects of the *d'oraisa* of *bishul*, all the *derabbanan* ramifications of *bishul*, including *kli sheni*, *yad soledes bo*, *bishul chama*, and *bishul ur*, and now we are in the midst of a *sugya* — extending through the remaining *mishnayot* to the end of the *perek* — devoted to what is perhaps one of the most central and practically consequential discussions in all of *hilchot* Shabbat: *muktzah*.

### Terminology

To be precise about the scope: the *perek* contains treatment of the *d'oraisa* and *derabbanan* dimensions of *bishul*, alongside the laws of *muktzah*. When one considers that *d'oraisa* and *derabbanan* distinctions within *bishul* and the full framework of *muktzah* are all concentrated here in *Kira*, it becomes clear why this *perek* is such a major locus for so much of what is practically relevant to *Shabbat* observance.

---

## Dead Body/TiltulMH

### Dead Body Setup

The *Gemara* at this point returns to the case that prompted the previous discussion: what does one do with a dead body in the courtyard? The discussion arose in connection with the position that one may move an object only for the sake of a non-*muktzah* item — which raised the question of how one may move a *meis* when necessary. The *Gemara* had already established that if one places an infant or a loaf of bread upon the corpse, it is permissible to move it. This is a striking allowance, because the ordinary use of placing something *mutar* alongside something *muktzah* — such as placing a loaf of bread on a tray along with the Shabbat candelabra so that the tray becomes a *basis* for both permitted and prohibited items — presupposes that the *basis* itself is not inherently *muktzah*. Here, however, the *meis* itself is obviously *muktzah*, and yet the fiction of moving it for the sake of the bread is sufficient — and this is universally agreed upon.

### Two Tiltul Types

The debate that follows concerns the case where there is no loaf of bread and no infant. May one then move the *meis* indirectly — *min hatzad* — by shifting it from one bed to another? This is the question of *tiltul min hatzad*. Before proceeding to the *Gemara*'s analysis, it is important to distinguish between two distinct categories.

The first is *tiltul k'alachar yad* — or *tiltul b'guf* — where one moves an item using a body part other than one's hand in the normal fashion: blowing on it, kicking it, moving it with one's elbow. This type of indirect movement is permitted on *Shabbat*, and crucially, it is permitted even if one is doing it for the sake of the *muktzah* object itself — for example, to prevent it from being damaged.

*Tiltul min hatzad* is a distinct category. Here one moves the *muktzah* item with one's hands, but indirectly — either through another object, as in this case where the *meis* is being carried on a bed, or incidentally, as when one reaches for a permitted object and in so doing pushes a *muktzah* item out of the way.

### L'Tzorech Principle

The governing principle for *tiltul min hatzad* is *l'tzorech davar hamuttar*: such indirect movement is permitted only when one is doing it for the sake of a permitted object. If one is reaching for an orange and one's hand incidentally pushes a wallet out of the way, that is permitted — one is moving toward the orange, a permitted item. What is not permitted is to employ *tiltul min hatzad* for the sake of the *muktzah* object itself. One may not, for instance, use an intermediary to relocate one's wallet simply because one wishes to move the wallet.

To summarize the distinction: *tiltul k'alachar yad* with a *shinui* — kicking, blowing, using one's elbow — is permitted even for the sake of the *muktzah* object. *Tiltul min hatzad* — indirect movement with one's hands, whether incidentally or through an intermediary — is permitted only *l'tzorech davar hamuttar*, for the sake of a permitted item, and not for the sake of the *muktzah* object itself.

### Gemara Analysis

This is precisely why the case of the *meis* is debated. Moving the *meis* on the bed constitutes *tiltul min hatzad*, but one is doing so for the sake of the *meis* itself. And it is that combination — *tiltul min hatzad* for the sake of the *muktzah* object — that is at issue.

The *Gemara* frames it as follows. *Ki pligi* — when do they disagree? *D'leis lei kikar o tinok* — when there is no loaf of bread and no infant. One opinion holds *tiltul min hatzad shemei tiltul* — even indirect movement of *muktzah* is considered real movement of *muktzah* and is prohibited. The other holds *lo shemei tiltul* — it does not rise to the level of genuine *tiltul* and is therefore permitted.

The *Gemara* then attempts to cast this as a *Tannaitic* dispute (*leima kitnai*), citing the following: *ein matzzilin et hamet mipnei hadleika* — one may not save a dead body from a fire. But Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish says: *shamati shematzzilin et hamet mipnei hadleika* — I have heard that one may save it from a fire. The *Gemara* initially suggests that they are debating our exact case: perhaps there is no loaf of bread and no infant, and the dispute is over *tiltul min hatzad* for the sake of a *muktzah* object. The *Gemara* then rejects this framing. Perhaps both *Tannaim* agree that *tiltul min hatzad shemei tiltul* — that indirect movement is still considered prohibited movement of *muktzah* — and that the universally agreed allowance of placing bread or an infant on the corpse is assumed. When the *Gemara* says *leima kitnai* and the response is *lo*, it means the proposed *Tannaitic* parallel is rejected.

### Cremation Concern

The *Gemara* instead explains: *dekulei alma tiltul min hatzad shemei tiltul* — everyone agrees that *tiltul min hatzad* for the sake of a *muktzah* object is still considered a prohibited form of *tiltul*. And this is how we rule in practice: one cannot move *muktzah* indirectly or through an intermediary for the sake of the *muktzah* object itself.

Why then does Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish permit saving the *meis* from a fire? *Dechasi alei* — because *mitoch she'adam bahul al meto*, a person is in an acute state of agitation over his deceased relative and will not allow it to burn. *I lo sharit lei* — if you do not give him a permissible route, even one that involves moving *muktzah*, he will simply extinguish the fire, *ati lechabuyei* — which is obviously a more serious violation. This reflects an important principle that recurs in *hilchot Shabbat*: *Chazal* recognized that even a normally observant person, under the pressure of the moment, will simply transgress. It is therefore sometimes necessary to provide a lesser violation as an outlet, so that a more serious one does not occur. A parallel case is the person who finds himself outside the city as *Shabbat* approaches with his wallet, and if given no permissible path, will simply carry it home.

### R. Yehuda Ruling

The *Gemara* then reports: *Amar Rav Yehuda ben Shila amar Rav Assi amar Rabbi Yochanan* — *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish b'meis*: the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish in the case of the dead body. The special allowance applies, even though under normal circumstances one cannot move *muktzah* by *tiltul min hatzad* for the sake of the *muktzah* object.

The *Gemara* then notes briefly, from the *mishnah* preceding the one now under discussion, that even if a vessel was placed beneath a lamp before *Shabbat* to catch the dripping oil, one may not benefit from that oil, since the oil was not *muchan* — not designated for use — and is therefore *muktzah*. A *baraisa* elaborates: the leftover oil in the lamp itself, or oil that dripped into a plate beneath it, is *asur*. Rabbi Shimon disagrees and permits it, consistent with his general position that he does not hold of most categories of *muktzah*: since the oil is now usable, he sees no basis for prohibition, even though it was designated for the lamp when *Shabbat* began.

---

## Muktzah Categories

### Keilim/Muktzah

The discussion of the *meis* and the question of what may be moved for the sake of a *muktzah* object invites a broader clarification of the *muktzah* framework — one that is frequently misunderstood. There are two large categories of things that can be subject to *muktzah* restrictions, and they must be kept distinct: *keilim* on the one hand, and *muktzah* proper on the other.

A *kli* — a vessel or utensil — is in principle an item that is part of one's ordinary sphere of usable objects. Within the category of *keilim*, the *Gemara* draws a fundamental distinction: *kli shemelachto l'heter* versus *kli shemelachto l'issur*. A fork or a pillow is a *kli shemelachto l'heter* — it is ordinarily used for permitted purposes. A hammer is the classic example of a *kli shemelachto l'issur*: it is primarily used for hammering nails, an act prohibited on *Shabbat*.

### Kli L'Issur

What are the practical consequences of a *kli shemelachto l'issur* like a hammer? It may be moved for its own sake — for instance, to crack nuts — and it may be moved if one needs the space it occupies. The one thing one may not do is move it merely to protect it, as when it has been left out in the rain. These restrictions exist because the hammer's primary association is with a prohibited activity; it is not, however, a thing that has been entirely pushed out of one's usable domain. It remains a *kli*.

### Atzmo Category

*Muktzah* proper refers to objects that are categorically set aside — off-limits at the onset of *Shabbat*. The first sub-category is *muktzah machmat atzmo*: objects with no ordinary use that are simply not vessels in any meaningful sense, such as a rock or a stick. If one designates a rock as a paperweight before *Shabbat*, it may acquire a use and thereby shed its *muktzah* status; absent such designation, it remains *muktzah machmat atzmo*. A dead body is another example: it has no practical use in the normal sense, and is therefore *muktzah machmat atzmo*.

### Mius Category

A second sub-category is *muktzah machmat mius* — objects that are *muktzah* because they are disgusting. The oily, malodorous pottery lamp that will be discussed momentarily is the paradigm case: while one will certainly use it again when one needs to light a lamp, it is not the sort of thing one normally handles, and it falls into this category of *mius*.

### Chisron Kis Cat.

A third sub-category is *muktzah machmat chisron kis*: items that are so expensive or fragile that one treats them as entirely off-limits — the valuable vase one would never allow to be casually handled.

### No-Move Rule

The crucial distinction between these categories of real *muktzah* and the category of *kli shemelachto l'issur* is the following: a *kli shemelachto l'issur* like a hammer can be moved for a legitimate purpose, such as using it for cracking nuts or needing its space. Real *muktzah* — a dead body, a burning lamp, a rock — cannot be moved for any purpose whatsoever. The only permissible ways of dealing with real *muktzah* are *tiltul k'alachar yad* (moving with an unusual body part) or *tiltul min hatzad* where it is for the sake of a permitted item.

This distinction is directly relevant to the earlier discussion. The principle of *ein kli nital ela l'tzorech davar hanital* — which we do not rule by — concerns a non-*muktzah* object being moved for the sake of a *muktzah* object, which the rejected opinion forbids. That is a wholly separate question from what may be done with a *muktzah* object itself. A *muktzah* object cannot be moved for any reason; the only exceptions are the indirect methods discussed above, and extraordinary cases like the *meis* where the *Gemara* provides a special dispensation.

One might ask about a *meis* in a contemporary hospital setting, where space must be cleared for another patient. Where a *sakanah* or the needs of a *choleh she'yesh bo sakanah* are present, those override other considerations. But in terms of the *muktzah* laws themselves, real *muktzah* cannot be moved for any purpose in the absence of such overriding factors — though indirect movement and extraordinary circumstances do provide recourse.

The question of frozen food's *muktzah* status is a related one worth noting: there is genuine debate among *poskim* about whether frozen food that cannot be eaten during *Shabbat* is *muktzah*, and the question arises in practical contexts such as whether a frozen *challah* may be taken from the freezer for use as *shtei lechem*. Even if one were to hold it is *muktzah*, however, one could push it aside by *tiltul k'alachar yad* or *tiltul min hatzad* to reach a permitted item.

---

## New/Old Lamps

### Mishnah Text

The *mishnah* states: *metaltelin ner chadash aval lo yashan* — one may move a new lamp, but not an old one. The lamps under discussion are pottery oil lamps, not candles.

### Why Old Bad

Why is an old lamp problematic? Once a pottery oil lamp has been used, it becomes oily, smelly, and generally unpleasant to handle. Under normal circumstances, one would not pick it up without reason; it is kept at a remove until one actually needs to light it again. This renders it *muktzah machmat mius* — *muktzah* on account of its repulsive character. This is the position of the *Tanna Kamma*: even if the old lamp was not burning when *Shabbat* began, it remains off-limits because of its disgusting quality.

### R. Meir View

Rabbi Shimon's position in the *mishnah* is that *kol hanerot metaltelin chutz min haner hadolek baShabbat* — all lamps may be moved, with the sole exception of one that is currently burning. Rabbi Shimon holds essentially no categories of *muktzah*, or at least does not apply them in these cases.

### Issur Category

Why would even Rabbi Shimon prohibit moving a currently burning lamp? One possible explanation has nothing to do with *muktzah* at all: moving a burning lamp might cause it to go out or to burn more quickly, raising concerns of *kibui* or *havarah*. But there is an additional possible ground — a special category of *muktzah* called *muktzah machmat issur*. This category has its primary and essentially exclusive application in the case of a burning lamp. The burning flame is itself performing a *melachah* on *Shabbat*, and therefore the lamp and the wick that support the flame are *muktzah machmat issur* — set aside by reason of the prohibited act they are currently involved in. This conceptual ground for prohibition is relevant beyond the mere concern about extinguishing, because it extends the prohibition to associated objects — such as the oil that drips from the lamp — and its existence as an independent category will have *nafka mina* implications to be explored in the *Gemara*.

---

## Burning Status

### T. Kamma/R. Meir

The *Gemara* now presents a *baraisa*. The *baraisa* reads: *metaltelin ner chadash aval lo yashan* — one may move a new lamp but not an old one: *divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda. So the *Tanna Kamma* of the *mishnah* is now identified as Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *muktzah machmat mius* applies to the old, used lamp.

Rabbi Meir's position is introduced: *kol hanerot metaltelin* — all lamps, new or old, may be moved. Rabbi Meir is not concerned about *muktzah machmat mius*, whether because he categorically rejects that category or because he holds old lamps do not fall within it. The *Gemara* tends to read these disputes as categorical.

### Burning @ Start

However, Rabbi Meir does carve out an exception: *chutz min haner shehidliku bo b'oto Shabbat* — except for a lamp that was lit on that *Shabbat*. The phrase *shehidliku bo b'oto Shabbat* sounds as if it means the lamp was lit during *Shabbat* itself, but everyone understands this to mean a lamp that was burning when *Shabbat* began. Rabbi Meir holds that if a lamp was in a burning state at the onset of *Shabbat* — during *bein hashmashot* — it retains its status as *muktzah* for the entire *Shabbat*, even after it goes out. This is the principle that *muktzah* status is determined at the commencement of *Shabbat* and applies throughout. Rabbi Meir holds *muktzah machmat issur* and its implications for *status at Shabbat's outset*. This is essentially how we rule.

---

## New/Old Lamps (II)

### R. Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon's position, restated in the *baraisa*, is that all lamps may be moved — *chutz min haner hadolek baShabbat* — except one that is currently burning. And if it goes out — *kavsah mutar letaltela* — it immediately becomes permitted. Rabbi Shimon thus rejects the principle that *muktzah* status at the beginning of *Shabbat* defines status for the whole *Shabbat*. While the lamp is burning, he does not permit moving it; once it goes out, he has no objection.

---

## Burning Status (II)

### Goes Out OK

Rabbi Shimon's position thus stands in sharp contrast to Rabbi Meir's. Rabbi Meir says: if it was burning when *Shabbat* began, it remains off-limits all *Shabbat*. Rabbi Shimon says: while it is burning, do not handle it; once it goes out, it is immediately permitted.

The *mishnah* adds an apparently anomalous ruling: *aval kos v'keira v'ashashit lo yazizam mimkoman* — but a cup, a plate, or a lantern, may not be moved at all. This is surprising given Rabbi Shimon's otherwise narrow *muktzah* position. Why would he be more stringent about a cup, a plate, or a lantern than about a lamp?

### R. Elazar View

Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's position is then introduced: *mistapek min haner hakaveh* — once the lamp goes out, one may take the oil from it. This is consistent with his father Rabbi Shimon's view. But he adds: *u'min hashemen hametaftef v'afilu b'shaa shehaner dolek* — one may also take oil that is dripping from the lamp even while it is still burning. Taking oil from within the lamp while it is burning is prohibited — doing so would constitute a form of *kibui*, diminishing the flame. But oil that has dripped into the plate beneath the lamp while the lamp is burning — Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon permits using that oil. He is not concerned about *muktzah* as applied to that oil.

---

## Abaye/R. Elazar

### Agreement

*Amar Abaye*: Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon agrees with his father Rabbi Shimon in one respect and disagrees in another. *Sevira lei k'Rabbi Shimon b'chada* — he holds like his father in one area: *d'leis lei muktzah* — he fundamentally rejects *muktzah*, or at least the relevant categories thereof.

### Disagreement

*U'palig lei b'chada* — he disagrees in one area, going further than his father: *kavsah in lo kavsah lo* — his father holds that one may use the oil only once the lamp has gone out. Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds *af al gav d'lo kavsah* — even if the lamp has not yet gone out, one may use the oil that dripped into the plate beneath it.

### Issur Debate

What is the underlying conceptual dispute? If the only reason one cannot move a burning lamp is the concern that doing so will cause it to go out — *kibui* or *havarah* — and if one rejects *muktzah* entirely in this context, then even the oil that dripped from the lamp while it was burning should be completely permitted. One is not moving the lamp; one has no *muktzah* concern. This is the position of Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon: his sole restriction is the physical act of moving the lamp while it burns, but he holds no *muktzah* concern at all for the burning lamp or its associated oil.

His father Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, appears to hold a category of *muktzah machmat issur*. Things involved in or associated with a prohibited act become *muktzah*. Therefore, while the lamp is burning, not only may one not move it (due to *kibui*), but the oil dripping from it is also *muktzah machmat issur* — it is designated for and associated with the burning lamp. Once the lamp goes out, that *muktzah machmat issur* status dissolves and everything becomes permitted. The practical relevance of the *muktzah machmat issur* category — over and above the *kibui* concern — is precisely this question of the dripping oil.

Rabbi Shimon further rejects the principle that *muktzah* status is fixed at the outset of *Shabbat*: he does not say that because the lamp was burning at *bein hashmashot*, it remains forbidden all *Shabbat*. The other positions, however, do hold this principle — and this is how we rule. If something is *muktzah* when *Shabbat* begins, that status applies for the entire *Shabbat*.

---

## Container Size

### Why Different

The *Gemara* now turns to the anomaly in Rabbi Shimon's position: *mai shna hani* — why are a cup, a plate, and a lantern treated more stringently than a lamp? The lamp, according to Rabbi Shimon, is permitted once it goes out; why not these as well?

Ulla suggests: *seifa atya k'Rabbi Yehuda* — the latter clause about the lantern and the plate reflects Rabbi Yehuda's position, not Rabbi Shimon's. But Mar Zutra challenges this: the *mishnah* uses the word *aval* — "however" — which signals a contrast within the same opinion. It reads as though Rabbi Shimon himself says: lamps are fine once out, but a cup and a plate and a lantern are not. If it were simply a switch to Rabbi Yehuda's position, the contrastive *aval* would be inappropriate.

### Attribution

*Ela amar Mar Zutra* — rather, Mar Zutra says the entire passage belongs to Rabbi Shimon.

### Small/Large

When does Rabbi Shimon allow a lamp that has gone out? *Ner zuta* — in the case of a small lamp. *D'daitei iluvei* — because one's intention rests upon it: one expects it to burn out during *Shabbat* and plans to use the oil afterward. *Aval hani d'nafishi* — but the large containers — the cup, the plate, the lantern — are different because they are large. Under normal circumstances one would never expect such a large container of oil to burn out over the course of a *Shabbat*. One would have had no thought of using it.

The underlying principle is clearer now: Rabbi Shimon does not generally hold that *muktzah* status is fixed by *bein hashmashot*. However, there is an exception: if when *Shabbat* began the object was *muktzah* in a category Rabbi Shimon himself recognizes — namely *muktzah machmat issur*, the burning lamp — and if under normal circumstances one would never have expected the opportunity to use it during *Shabbat* (because it is a very large container of oil that one assumed would burn all night), then even Rabbi Shimon agrees that its status is defined at the onset of *Shabbat* and it remains forbidden even if it goes out.

A *baraisa* is cited to confirm this: *mutar hashemen shebanair veshabekara asur, Rabbi Shimon matir* — leftover oil in the lamp and in the plate is forbidden; Rabbi Shimon permits it. The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by reading the two cases as referring to different-sized plates: in the *baraisa*, the plate is a small one functioning analogously to the lamp — Rabbi Shimon permits it once extinguished. In the *mishnah*'s clause about the cup, plate, and lantern, the plate is a large one akin to the cup — Rabbi Shimon forbids it.

### Status Fixed

To summarize the structure of opinion: according to Rabbi Shimon, a small lamp that goes out during *Shabbat* is immediately permitted, because one had it in mind that it might be used. A large container of oil that one never expected to go out during *Shabbat* is forbidden even if it does, because its *muktzah machmat issur* status was fixed at the onset of *Shabbat* and was the sort of thing that under normal circumstances would have remained inaccessible all *Shabbat*. We rule more strictly than Rabbi Shimon: even in the case of a small lamp, once it is *muktzah* when *Shabbat* begins, that status applies all *Shabbat*.

---

## Metal Candelabra

### Pamot Case

*Amar Rabbi Zeira*: in the case of a *pamot* — a metal candelabrum, as opposed to a pottery *ner* — *shehidliku bo baShabbat*, that was burning when *Shabbat* began, *ledivrei hamatir assur, ledivrei ha'oser mutar* — the one who normally permits would here agree it is forbidden, and the one who normally forbids would here agree it is permitted. This is a striking statement and requires unpacking.

### Two Directions

The one who normally permits is, according to Tosafot, Rabbi Shimon — or according to Rashi, Rabbi Meir, who allows even old lamps (rejecting *muktzah machmat mius*). But here, even that permissive opinion would agree the metal candelabrum is *asur*, because it is currently burning. And the one who normally forbids — who holds *muktzah machmat mius* and says an old lamp is off-limits because it is disgusting — would here agree the metal candelabrum is *mutar*, because a metal candelabrum does not become disgusting with use.

### Category Holders

The *Gemara* is now drawing out an important implication: Rabbi Yehuda, who is normally strict about old lamps because of *muktzah machmat mius*, has never been asked about a burning lamp of the non-disgusting metal variety. One might have supposed he does not hold *muktzah machmat issur* at all, and that the metal candelabrum — even while burning — would be permitted in his view. Conversely, Rabbi Meir, who does not hold *muktzah machmat mius* and permits old lamps, clearly does hold *muktzah machmat issur* (as established from the *baraisa* regarding the lamp burning when *Shabbat* began). The question was whether Rabbi Yehuda holds *muktzah machmat issur* for the metal candelabrum that is not subject to *mius*.

### Braisa Proof

The *Gemara* then cites a *baraisa* that explicitly resolves this: *Rabbi Yehuda omer kol hanairos shel matechet metaltelin* — Rabbi Yehuda says all metal lamps may be moved — because they are not disgusting — *chutz min haner shehidliku bo b'oto Shabbat* — except for one that was burning when *Shabbat* began. This demonstrates explicitly that Rabbi Yehuda does hold *muktzah machmat issur* and forbids the metal candelabrum if it was burning at the onset of *Shabbat*.

### Final Ruling

The *Gemara* therefore revises the original formulation of Rabbi Zeira's statement: *divrei hakol assur* — everyone agrees that a metal candelabrum that was burning when *Shabbat* began is forbidden, because everyone holds *muktzah machmat issur*. And *lo hidliku aleha, divrei hakol mutar* — if it was not burning when *Shabbat* began, everyone agrees it is permitted, because a metal candelabrum does not become *muktzah machmat mius*. The sole remaining exception is Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon, who holds no *muktzah* concern for the burning lamp at all.

By way of a broader principle: if something is not *muktzah* when *Shabbat* begins, it can still become *muktzah* during *Shabbat* if circumstances change — for instance, if a vessel breaks, or if an egg falls into it. But that newly acquired *muktzah* status does not persist beyond the duration of the condition that created it. The status-defining power of *bein hashmashot* operates only in one direction: *muktzah* at the start means *muktzah* all *Shabbat*. But something not *muktzah* at the start can become *muktzah* mid-*Shabbat* only for as long as the triggering condition lasts. This is the principle of *ein muktzah lechatzei Shabbat*: a *muktzah* status that originates mid-*Shabbat* does not persist once the condition that created it is removed.

---

## Bed/Money Basis

### Bed Designation

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: *mita sheyichada lema'os assur letaltela* — a bed that has been designated for holding money may not be moved, even if no money has yet been placed on it and no money is currently on it. The premise is unusual: who uses a bed as a money drawer? But the *Gemara* entertains it. The ruling is that the mere designation is sufficient to render the bed off-limits.

### Tosafot Q

Tosafot raises the obvious challenge: how is this worse than a *kli shemelachto l'issur* like a hammer? A hammer is designated for a prohibited purpose and yet may still be moved for legitimate uses. If we say the bed is designated for money — an *issur* use on *Shabbat* — why can it not similarly be used for other purposes like any *kli shemelachto l'issur*?

### Designation/Use

Tosafot answers by distinguishing: there are objects that, unlike a hammer, would never be used for any other purpose once designated for one role. A trumpet, for instance, is not going to be used to crack nuts; it has a single use. The *Gemara* assumes that a bed designated exclusively for holding money falls into that category — it becomes an object of a single, prohibited use, and thus entirely off-limits.

### R. Nachman Q

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges this with the case of the new lamp: *metaltelin ner chadash aval lo yashan* — a new lamp may be moved. A new lamp was manufactured for lighting, which is its designated purpose and its only purpose. If anything, its designation for a prohibited purpose is more inherent than that of a bed. Yet it is permitted if it has never been used. How then can a designated bed be forbidden before any use?

### Must Use

The *Gemara* resolves this by revising Rav Yehuda's statement: *ela i itmar hachi itmar* — if this was said, here is how it was said. *Hiniach aleha ma'ot assur letaltela* — if one actually placed money upon the bed, thereby employing it in its designated use, then it is forbidden to move it on *Shabbat*, even if the money is not on it now. Once the bed has been put to use as a money holder, it acquires a new identity — analogous to the trumpet, which has only one use — and is permanently off-limits on *Shabbat*. *Lo hiniach aleha ma'ot mutar letaltela* — if one has designated it but has not yet placed money on it, it is still permitted, just as the new lamp is permitted before it has been used.

---

## Status @ Outset

### Desig+Used

The analysis now becomes more nuanced. Three cases are laid out. The first: one designated the bed for money *and* has used it in that capacity. In this case, the bed has been transformed into a money-holder with a singular identity. Even if no money is on it now, and even if no money was on it at *bein hashmashot*, one may not move it on *Shabbat*.

### Desig/NoUse

The second: one designated the bed for money but has never actually placed money on it. This is the case of the new lamp — the designation has not yet been actualized. The bed retains its status as an ordinary bed and may be moved.

### No Desig

The third: one did not designate the bed for money at all. Here it depends entirely on whether money is present. *Yesh aleha ma'ot assur letaltela* — if money is currently on the bed, one may not move it, because it is now a *basis ladavar ha'asur* — a supporter for *muktzah*. *Ein aleha ma'ot mutar letaltela* — if there is no money on it, it is permitted.

### Bein Hashem

The critical qualifier: *v'hu shelo hayu aleha bein hashmashot* — provided that the money was not on the bed when *Shabbat* began. If money was intentionally placed on the bed at *bein hashmashot*, the bed became a *basis* for the *muktzah* money at that moment, and it retains that status for the entire *Shabbat*, even after the money is removed. This is the principle of *bein hashmashot* determining status for the whole *Shabbat*.

One important nuance: for a *basis* to be created, the *muktzah* item must have been intentionally placed on the supporting object. If coins were accidentally dropped on a bed, that does not create a *basis*. If one intentionally placed a wallet on the bed before *bein hashmashot* and then forgot to remove it, the wallet was deliberately placed and the *basis* is established, even though the forgetfulness was unintentional.

The question of whether one may *use* a *muktzah* item without *moving* it — for instance, sleeping on a bed that is a *basis* — is a separate and genuinely debated question among the *Rishonim*.

---

## Drawer/Tumah

### Cabinet Setup

*Ulla* reports a challenge raised by Rabbi Eliezer from a *mishnah* dealing with a *shidda* — a large cabinet — and its *muchni*, a detachable element that is variously understood by Rashi (as a kind of wheel) and Tosafot (as a base or drawer). The *mishnah* is complex and its bulk concerns laws of *tumah* rather than *Shabbat*, which accounts for the extensive Rashi and Tosafot here.

### Detachable

*Bizman shehi nishmet* — if this element (the base or drawer) can be detached, *ein chibur lah* — it is not considered connected to the cabinet for purposes of *tumah*. If one of the items is rendered *tamei*, the *tumah* does not automatically transfer to the other through this connection, because they are treated as separate objects.

### Measure/Seal

*V'ein nimdedes imah* — when detachable, it is not measured together with the cabinet. This is relevant because a wooden vessel that can contain forty *seah* — the volume of a *mikvah* — cannot become *tamei*. If the drawer is detachable, its volume is not counted together with the cabinet's volume when assessing whether the forty-*seah* threshold is reached.

*V'einah metzelet imah b'ohel hamet* — it does not protect the cabinet's contents in a room containing a dead body. The mechanism here, as Tosafot explains, concerns the *tzamid patil*: a tightly sealed vessel protects its contents from *tumah*. If the cabinet is so large as to be beyond the threshold of *tumah*, and has a tight seal, objects inside are protected. However, if the drawer is detachable, its presence does not fully seal the opening where it sits, and the contents of the cabinet may still become *tamei* through that gap.

### Cannot Drag

*V'ein gorerin otah baShabbat* — one may not drag the cabinet on *Shabbat*, *bizman sheyesh aleha ma'ot* — if money is on the drawer or cabinet. Tosafot notes that when a drawer is completely fixed to a cabinet, dragging the cabinet is simply moving the cabinet and the drawer is merely incidental. But when the drawer is detachable, moving the cabinet is understood as moving two separate items — the cabinet and the drawer — and thus if money is on the drawer, one is moving the *muktzah basis* directly.

### If No Money

The *mishnah* implies: *ha ein aleha ma'ot sharya* — if there is no money on it, it is permitted, and the simple reading suggests this is true even if money was on it at *bein hashmashot*.

---

## BH Status Q

### Contradiction

This presents an apparent contradiction. If the *mishnah* about the *shidda* implies that the absence of money *now* renders the object permitted — even if money was present at *bein hashmashot* — then the principle that *bein hashmashot* determines status for the whole *Shabbat* would seem to be contradicted.

### R. Shimon Attr

The *Gemara* resolves this: *ha hi Rabbi Shimon hi* — that *mishnah* about the *shidda* reflects the view of Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold of *muktzah* and does not hold that *bein hashmashot* status defines *Shabbat* status. According to Rabbi Shimon, if the money is not on the object now, it is permitted now.

### Rav/R. Yehuda

*V'Rav k'Rabbi Yehuda sevira lei* — Rav, however, holds like Rabbi Yehuda, and therefore holds that *bein hashmashot* status is determinative.

### Palm Tree

The *Gemara* offers proof: *amar Rav manichin ner gabi dekla baShabbat* — Rav says one may place a lamp on a palm tree on *Shabbat*. The concern would be that having placed the lamp there, one might come to take hold of the tree when retrieving the lamp — and using a *mechubar*, an item still attached to the ground, is prohibited on *Shabbat*. Rav says this concern does not apply, because since the lamp was burning when *Shabbat* began, it is *muktzah* and one will not come to remove it during *Shabbat*.

### Yom Tov

*V'ein manichin ner gabi dekla b'Yom Tov* — but on *Yom Tov*, one may not do so. On *Yom Tov*, a lamp is not *muktzah*. Therefore there is a genuine concern that one might retrieve the lamp from the tree during *Yom Tov* and thereby make use of the tree. The critical distinction is that on *Shabbat* the lamp is *muktzah* for the whole *Shabbat* — it was burning at the onset — and one will therefore not touch it; on *Yom Tov* no such *muktzah* applies and the concern is real.

### Conclusion

*Ei amarta bishlama d'Rav k'Rabbi Yehuda sevira lei* — if Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda, that something *muktzah* at the outset of *Shabbat* remains so all *Shabbat*, then the distinction between *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* is perfectly intelligible. *Ela i amarta k'Rabbi Shimon sevira lei* — but if Rav holds like Rabbi Shimon, who permits the lamp once it goes out, then *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* would be indistinguishable. This proves that Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda, that status is fixed at the beginning of *Shabbat*.

The conclusion is thus firmly established: Rav holds that the status of an object at *bein hashmashot* — the onset of *Shabbat* — determines its *muktzah* status for the entire *Shabbat*. A bed on which money was intentionally placed at *bein hashmashot* is a *basis* for *muktzah* and remains off-limits the entire *Shabbat*, even after the money is removed. This is the ruling we follow, in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, against Rabbi Shimon.

---

---

# Shabbat 46

## Rabbi Shimon & Muktza

### Intro & Rabbi Shimon

The daf begins at the bottom of 45b, continuing the extended discussion that has occupied the Gemara for nearly two pages: which cases of *muktza* does Rabbi Shimon concede are prohibited, and do we rule like him? As we saw previously, Rabbi Shimon agrees that a burning lamp presents a problem — though this may be a case of *huksa l'mitzvaso* (set aside for its commandment) rather than standard *muktza l'shabbos v'yomtov*. He similarly concedes the case of raisins that were pushed aside and are *aino raoy* (unfit), and beyond that he agrees to additional cases: animals on Yom Tov that are normally kept outside the house, newly born chicks, and so on. The Gemara now continues this inquiry.

### Rav Assi Case

Abaye poses a challenge to Rav Yosef. The Gemara reads: *amar lei Abaye l'Rav Yosef* — Abaye said to Rav Yosef: *v'at lo tisbor d'Rabbi Yochanan k'Rabbi Yehuda s'vira lei?* Don't you also agree that Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rabbi Yehuda? The background is that Rabbi Yochanan had been reported as saying "they say the *halacha* is like Rabbi Shimon," while the Gemara yesterday concluded on the basis of other reports that Rabbi Yochanan himself does not hold like Rabbi Shimon but rather like Rabbi Yehuda, and that "they say" refers to others. Abaye now presses Rav Yosef: *v'ha Rav Abba v'Rav Assi ikla l'vei Rabbi Abba d'min Cheifa* — Rav Abba and Rav Assi came to the house of Rabbi Abba from Cheifa, *v'nafal m'norta al glima d'Rav Assi* — and a candelabrum fell onto Rav Assi's coat, *v'lo tiltelah* — and he refused to move it. This was presumably on Shabbat, and the candelabrum, though burning when Shabbat began, had apparently since gone out. Now, in the Mishna, the position that a lamp remains forbidden even after burning out belongs to Rabbi Yehuda (or Rabbi Meir), not to Rabbi Shimon, who permits moving it once extinguished. So why did Rav Assi refuse? *Lav mishum d'Rav Assi talmida d'Rabbi Yochanan hava* — must it not be that Rav Assi is a student of Rabbi Yochanan, *v'Rabbi Yochanan k'Rabbi Yehuda s'vira lei* — and Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rabbi Yehuda? This seems to confirm that Rabbi Yochanan does not rule like Rabbi Shimon.

### Lamp vs. Menorah

The Gemara responds: *k'Rabbi Yehuda s'vira lei d'is lei muktza* — he holds like Rabbi Yehuda that *muktza* applies, and that is why he did not move the *menorah*. But then the Gemara counters: *m'norta ka'amart? m'norta shani* — you're talking about a *menorah*? A *menorah* is different. This is not a reference to a Chanukah *menorah* but rather to a standing candelabrum. As Reish Lakish ruled in Tzidan: *m'norta haniteles b'yado achas mutar l'taltela* — a candelabrum held in one hand may be moved on Shabbat; *b'shtei yado ossur l'taltela* — one requiring two hands may not. Rabbi Yochanan, however, states: *anu ein lanu ela b'ner k'Rabbi Shimon* — the only leniency we have is with a lamp, ruling like Rabbi Shimon; *aval m'norta, bein b'yado achas bein b'shtei yado ossur l'taltela* — but a *menorah*, whether it requires one hand or two, may not be moved. Why this distinction? Rabba and Rav Yosef both offer the same explanation: *ho'il v'adam koveia lo makom* — since a *menorah* is the kind of object to which a person designates a fixed place, it acquires a hands-off quality. One does not ordinarily move one's candelabrum around the house, and even Rabbi Shimon might agree that such an item is restricted. The point stands: the fact that Rav Assi, a student of Rabbi Yochanan, did not move the *menorah* cannot prove that Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rabbi Yehuda in general, since the *menorah* has its own special rationale.

---

## Menorah Components

### Canopy Bed

Abaye, however, presses further: *ve'harei kilat chatanim* — what about a canopy bed? *de'adam kove'a lo makom* — no one regularly moves the canopy of a bed; it too is *kove'a makom*. And yet, Shmuel says in the name of Rabbi Chiya: *kilat chatanim mutar lintota u'mutar leparka be'Shabbat* — you may both spread the canopy and take it down on Shabbat. Ordinarily, erecting a flat overhead structure constitutes an *ohel* (tent) and is forbidden on Shabbat, but a bridal-canopy bed of the type described was fashioned like a teepee — coming to a point at the top — and therefore does not meet the technical definition of an *ohel*, which requires a flat surface of at least a *tefach* in width. So the spreading and collapsing is permitted from the standpoint of *ohel*. But if the canopy is then left in place for months or years without being moved, why may one dismantle it on Shabbat? Should it not be *muktza* on the grounds that it is *kove'a makom*? The objection undermines the proposed rationale for the *menorah*: if *kove'a makom* were itself a sufficient category to prohibit handling, it should apply to the canopy bed as well. Tosafot responds that conceptually such a category does exist — related to *muktza machmat chisaron kis*, precious objects one designates as untouchable — but the *menorah* does not reach the threshold of that category with sufficient force. A floor lamp that one might occasionally need to reposition is not at the same level of "hands-off" as, say, a Ming vase placed permanently on a mantle. So the *kove'a makom* rationale cannot be the reason a *menorah* is treated differently.

### Chulyot & Assembly

Rather, Abaye offers the true explanation: *ella amar Abaye be'shel chulyot askinan* — we are dealing with a *menorah* made of screwable component sections (*chulyot*). Such candelabra could have their arms removed and reattached, allowing one to vary the number of arms depending on how much light was desired. The problem is that screwing arms into a candelabrum on Shabbat would constitute a forbidden act of construction. While the precise halakhic category is debated — whether it is *binyan* (building) in the technical sense, or whether we say *ein binyan b'keilim* (construction does not apply to vessels) and instead apply *makeh b'patish* (the "finishing blow" that completes an object) — either way, assembling such a fixture is prohibited on Shabbat. Therefore, even simply carrying such a *menorah* is forbidden, lest one come to tighten or adjust its parts. As Rashi explains: *shema tipol v'titparek v'yachzirena v'nimtza oseh keli* — one might drop it, it might come apart, and one would reassemble it, thereby constructing a vessel.

### Gezeirah Scope

The Gemara now works through a careful gradation. If a *menorah* genuinely consists of separate *chulyot*, it is forbidden to move, whether large or small, since there is a realistic concern one will come to fix it. But what if the *menorah* is actually a single piece, merely engraved with circular markings (*chidkei*) that make it look as though it is composed of screwable sections — a *marat ayin* problem? Here the Gemara introduces a *gezeirah*: a large such *menorah*, even if not actually made of pieces, is forbidden because it too closely resembles the problematic case. The concern is more pronounced with a large candelabrum, since component-piece *menorahs* are typically large impressive fixtures; a small handheld one is generally constructed compactly and is less likely to involve interchangeable parts. The Gemara therefore concludes: *ki pligi* — where the dispute lies — is by a small *menorah* that has engraved markings but is not actually made of *chulyot*. One opinion (*mar savar gazrinan*) maintains that even this is forbidden, extending the *gezeirah* two degrees from the core concern. The other opinion (*u'mar savar lo gazrinan*) holds that the *gezeirah* does not extend that far. This is a striking Gemara — even a position that in principle accords with Rabbi Shimon's leniency may still prohibit handling a *menorah* for an independent rabbinic reason entirely unrelated to *muktza* in the standard sense.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan's View

### Stam Mishna

The status of Rabbi Yochanan's position remains unresolved. We have now established from multiple angles: Rabbi Yochanan was reported saying "they say the *halacha* is like Rabbi Shimon," which the Gemara interpreted as others say, not his own view; separately, he appeared to hold like Rabbi Yehuda; yet at the bottom of this very page he stated that the only leniency "we" have is *b'ner k'Rabbi Shimon* — by the lamp, ruling like Rabbi Shimon — suggesting at minimum some acceptance of Rabbi Shimon in the lamp case, though perhaps not more broadly. The Gemara now poses a fresh challenge: *umi amar Rabbi Yochanan hachi* — did Rabbi Yochanan really hold like Rabbi Yehuda? *V'ha'amar Rabbi Yochanan halacha kestam mishna* — but Rabbi Yochanan has a general principle that the *halacha* follows a *stam mishna* (an anonymously authored Mishna, presumed to represent the majority view). And consider what the Mishna teaches about the *mukhni shela* — an object that, following Tosafot's reading, refers to a dresser with a detachable base. The Mishna establishes that such a base, being removable, is not considered a single unit with the dresser for purposes of *tuma*: it does not create *chibur* (connection) with it, is not measured together with it to determine whether the dresser is large enough to be exempt from *tuma*, and does not seal the dresser's opening to protect contents from the *tuma* of a corpse in the same room — since the detachable base cannot constitute a proper seal. None of that, incidentally, is our concern; the Mishna belongs to tractate Keilim, and one may be grateful that tractate Keilim has no Talmud Bavli. The relevant portion is the final clause: *ve'ein gorrin ota beshabbat bizman sheyesh aleha maot* — one may not drag the dresser on Shabbat when there is money resting on the base. The implication — which the Gemara draws — is that if there is no money on the base now, one may drag it even if there was money on it at *bein hashmashot* (twilight, i.e., the onset of Shabbat). That is the position of Rabbi Shimon: the status at the onset of Shabbat does not permanently determine an object's status throughout Shabbat. If this *stam mishna* reflects Rabbi Shimon's view, and Rabbi Yochanan rules according to *stam mishnaot*, how can Rabbi Yochanan hold like Rabbi Yehuda?

### Rav Zeira's Answer

Rav Zeira resolves the difficulty: *tehei mishnateinu dehava aleha maot bein hashmashot* — the Mishna should be read as addressing a case where there was money on the base at *bein hashmashot*. The inference that "only when money is actively on it now may one not drag it" is incorrect. The Mishna is describing one scenario: money is currently on the base, so you cannot drag it. A separate and equally valid scenario — not addressed by this Mishna but equally valid — is that money was on it at *bein hashmashot* and is no longer there now. That too would be forbidden. Thus no proof to Rabbi Shimon's position can be derived from this Mishna, and Rabbi Yochanan need not be in conflict with himself. The Gemara then uses a striking phrase: *shelo lishbor devarav shel Rabbi Yochanan* — so as not to "break" the words of Rabbi Yochanan, i.e., lest we create a self-contradiction in his rulings. The phrase *lishbor* — to shatter — is an unusual formulation, and it reflects how much is at stake in harmonizing Rabbi Yochanan's position. The overall picture emerging across these two pages is a sustained push away from Rabbi Shimon: Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rabbi Yehuda, and even Rabbi — who sounded at one point like he accepted Rabbi Shimon's leniency — may in fact hold like Rabbi Yehuda.

---

## Historical Practices

### Rabbi's Ruling

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reports: *pa'am achat halach Rabbi l'Diospora* — Rabbi once traveled to Diospora (which Rashi understands as a place name, though it sounds remarkably like "diaspora"), *v'horah b'menorah k'Rabbi Shimon b'ner* — and he ruled regarding a *menorah* the way Rabbi Shimon rules regarding a lamp, i.e., leniently. The Gemara immediately raises an ambiguity: *ibaya lehu* — a question was left unresolved. Did Rabbi rule that a *menorah* is like Rabbi Shimon's lamp — meaning both are permitted — or did he issue two separate rulings: a *menorah* is forbidden (as we have been saying throughout), and by a lamp we follow Rabbi Shimon's leniency? The Gemara concludes *teiku* — the question stands unresolved. Similarly unresolved is whether Rabbi's ruling concerning the lamp was a narrow ruling limited to the lamp case, or a broader acceptance of Rabbi Shimon's position across the board.

### Criticized Practices

The Gemara records two parallel incidents illustrating the tension. Rav Malkia came to the house of Rav Simlai, *v'tiltal shraga* — and moved an extinguished lamp — *v'ikpad Rav Simlai* — and Rav Simlai was upset, indicating that in his domain this was not done. Similarly, a figure from the Galilee came to the house of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina, moved an extinguished lamp, and Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina was displeased. These incidents show that the position of Rabbi Shimon continued to resurface and find practitioners, but it was consistently met with disapproval by more senior figures. The Gemara's trajectory is unmistakably toward sidelining Rabbi Shimon's broader leniency, even as it cannot fully eliminate it.

### Rabbi Abahu's Practice

A more nuanced case involves Rabbi Abahu: *ki ika le'asrei de'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, havie metalteil shraga* — when he was in the house of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi he would move an extinguished lamp; *aval ki ata le'asrei de'Rabbi Yochanan, lo havie metalteil shraga* — but when he came to the house of Rabbi Yochanan, he would not. The Gemara asks: *ato mima nafshach* — make up your mind. If he holds like Rabbi Yehuda, let him act like Rabbi Yehuda everywhere and not move it; if he holds like Rabbi Shimon, let him move it everywhere. The resolution: *le'olam ke'Rabbi Shimon sevira lei* — he actually held it was permitted, *umishum kevodo de'Rabbi Yochanan, hu dela havie avid* — but out of deference to Rabbi Yochanan, he refrained when in his presence. This is logically coherent: if something is forbidden, one cannot permit oneself to do it even in another's house; but if something is fundamentally permitted, one may choose voluntarily to refrain out of respect. This behavior itself is evidence of Rabbi Abahu's underlying view.

One might ask why Rav Malkia or the Galilean scholar would perform an act in another scholar's home that the host considered forbidden. Perhaps they did not know the host's position in advance, or acted out of habit. In any case, this passage makes clear that the question being debated at this juncture is quite narrow: not whether we accept Rabbi Shimon's global rejection of *muktza*, which nobody is proposing, but merely whether we can follow him in the specific case of the lamp after it has gone out.

This is also the point at which Tosafot and Rashi diverge significantly on what these discussions actually concern. Rashi reads the debate as potentially including even the case where the lamp was burning at *bein hashmashot* — Rabbi Shimon's full position. Tosafot restricts the discussion drastically: he argues that even the most lenient voices in this passage are only addressing a lamp that was not in use when Shabbat began at all, and whose only potential *muktza* problem is *muktza machmat miyus* (set aside by reason of disgust). According to Tosafot, the possibility of ruling like Rabbi Shimon on the case where something was burning at *bein hashmashot* and is now extinguished is not even on the table here — everyone agrees that case remains forbidden. As Tosafot reads it, the upcoming discussion of *muktza machmat miyus* is thus the real subject of the preceding material as well. This matters greatly for practical *halacha*, and reflects a broader methodological point: Rashi provides the baseline reading against which Tosafot argues, but Rashi's reading is not necessarily closer to *p'shat*. It is simply the necessary starting point for the conversation.

---

## Muktza Machmat Miyus

### Oil vs. Naphtha

The Gemara now takes up the category of *muktza machmat miyus* — *muktza* by reason of disgust or repulsiveness — directly. Rav Yehuda rules: *sharga d'mishcha shari l'tiltula* — an oil lamp may be moved (after it is no longer burning); *d'nafta assur l'tiltula* — but a lamp of naphtha, a strongly malodorous pitch-like fuel, may not, because everyone would agree that qualifies as *ma'us* (disgusting). The category of *muktza machmat miyus* is not in dispute; what is in dispute is whether an ordinary oil lamp falls within it. Rava and Rav Yosef both hold: *d'nafta nami shari l'tiltula* — even a naphtha lamp may be moved. Tosafot explains this not as a wholesale rejection of the *miyus* category but as a narrower definition: there is a distinction between something that is malodorous and something that is genuinely disgusting to handle. A naphtha lamp may smell unpleasant, but it is not so disgusting to handle that one would refuse to touch it, and therefore it does not meet the threshold for *muktza machmat miyus*.

### Rav Avya Anecdote

Rav Avya came to the house of Rava with mud-caked legs and sat down on the couch, apparently without wiping his feet. Rava, displeased at his furniture being muddied, sought to call him to account. With characteristic indirection, Rava asked: *mai ta'ama Rava v'Rav Yosef d'amri duvayhu* — why do Rava and Rav Yosef both rule that even a naphtha lamp may be moved? The implication of the question was presumably not lost on anyone in the room, as the theme of *miyus* — disgust and its consequences — was clearly pointed. Rav Avya, whether willfully or obliviously, answered on the merits: *hoil ve-chazei le-khisuyei bei mana* — since even a disgusting lamp can still be used to cover or seal a vessel, it retains a use and is therefore not *muktza*. Rava pressed back: *ella meiata, kol tzerorot shebe-chatzer metaltelin, hoil ve-chazei le-khisuyei bei mana?* — by that logic, all rocks in a courtyard should be movable, since one could always use a rock to plug up a hole in a vessel! And rocks are certainly *muktza*; one cannot eliminate *muktza* simply by imagining some marginal use.

### Vessel Doctrine

Rav Avya's response articulates a fundamental principle: *hai ika torat keli aleiha, hani leika torat keli aleiha* — this lamp has the status of a vessel; rocks do not. A vessel is by definition something created for human use. To strip a vessel of its usable status requires that it become so thoroughly repulsive or restricted that no legitimate use for it on Shabbat can be identified. A rock, by contrast, never entered the category of human utility in the first place; absent a deliberate act of designation (turning it into a paperweight, for instance), it begins and remains *muktza*. A vessel, however, requires far more to cross back out of the category of usable objects.

This principle is then supported by a *baraita*: *hashirim ve-hanezamim ve-hatabaot* — various bracelets, nose rings, and rings. An upcoming chapter of the tractate will establish that certain types of jewelry may not be worn on Shabbat outside of an *eruv*-enclosed space, out of concern that a woman will remove the jewelry to show it to someone, hold it in her hand, and inadvertently carry it in the public domain. Yet, the *baraita* rules: *harei hen ke-khol ha-kelim ha-nitalin be-chatzer* — these items are like all other vessels that may be moved in a courtyard. And Ulla explains: *hoil ve-ika torat keli aleiha* — since they still have the status of a vessel. Even though you may not wear them, you may move them, because the prohibition on wearing them is insufficient to strip them of their vessel-status for purposes of *muktza*. This is contrasted with genuinely precious items — *muktza machmat chisaron kis*, like an extraordinarily valuable object one designates as permanently untouchable — where the vessel-status is overridden by the degree of restriction. But the general principle holds: vessel-status creates a strong presumption against *muktza* that requires a great deal to overcome.

The Gemara concludes with Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's remark: *barich rachmana dela chasfyei Rava le-Rav Avaya* — blessed be God that Rava did not embarrass Rav Avaya. Whether this is gratitude for the preservation of Rav Avaya's dignity, or relief that the exchange produced a sound halakhic answer, or both, is left characteristically open.

---

## Vows & Firstborn

### Vow Case

Abaye presents a challenge to Rava from a *baraita*: *mafirin nedarim be'Shabbat ve-nish'alin l'nedarim shehen l'tzorech Shabbat* — a husband may annul his wife's vows on Shabbat, and one may seek the voiding of vows by a sage on Shabbat, provided there is a Shabbat-related need. The *baraita* thus permits both husband-annulment and sage-voiding on Shabbat. The *muktza* question here is real: if a woman has made a vow forbidding herself from eating a particular food, that food was *assur* to her at *bein hashmashot*, and even if the vow is later annulled during Shabbat, how does it escape *muktza*? Tosafot raises a related and subtle issue: a vow creates a personal prohibition — it is the person, not the object, that is restricted. If only she is forbidden and others are not, can the food be genuinely *muktza*? And even if it can be *muktza* to her, may it not be moved by others? These questions about whether *muktza* attaches to the object or the person, and whether something *muktza* to one person is *muktza* to all, are raised by Tosafot and remain without a clean resolution, though Tosafot suggests that if the vow explicitly forbade the food to all people, or if *migo d'itkatzai bein hashmashot* — since it was restricted at the onset of Shabbat — it might become broadly *muktza*.

### Firstborn Problem

The Gemara's sharper challenge involves the *bechor* (firstborn animal). Rabbi Shimon rules: *kol she'ein mumo nikar me'erev Yom Tov, ein ze min hamuchan* — if a firstborn animal's blemish was not evident before Yom Tov, it is not considered *muchan* (designated and available) for Yom Tov use. The background: a firstborn animal that lacks a blemish must be brought as a *korban* and may not be slaughtered for ordinary consumption. If it has a blemish, however, a *kohen* may slaughter and eat it without the need for redemption. On Yom Tov, slaughtering is generally permitted. So if a blemish appears on the animal on Yom Tov itself — may the *kohen* slaughter it? Rabbi Shimon says: if the blemish was not visible before Yom Tov, it is *muktza* for the entire Yom Tov, even if the blemish is discovered during the day. This appears to be in direct tension with Rabbi Shimon's leniency by the lamp: just as oil left over when the lamp burns out becomes permitted, why does the *bechor* not become permitted once the blemish appears?

The Gemara responds sharply: *hachi hashta* — how can you compare these cases? By the lamp, *adam yoshev umitzappe imatai tichbe nero* — a person sits and anticipates that his lamp will burn out. He knows when Shabbat begins that the lamp will eventually go out and oil will remain; his mental designation of the oil is entirely reasonable. But by the *bechor*, *adam yoshev umitzappe imatai yippol bo mum?* — does a person actually sit and expect a blemish to fall on his animal? Three independent contingencies would all have to materialize: *mi yeimar denafal bei muma* — who says a blemish will occur at all? *Mi yeimar denafal bei mum kavua* — even if a blemish appears, who says it will be a permanent blemish, since only a permanent blemish permits slaughter? And *mi yeimar dimizdakek leh chacham* — who says a sage will be available and willing to render a ruling on the blemish?

Tosafot adds a sharpening observation: Rabbi Yehuda, who generally holds of more *muktza*, actually rules more leniently on the *bechor* than Rabbi Shimon does. This is because Rabbi Yehuda permits a sage to rule on a *bechor*'s blemish on Yom Tov. Since for Rabbi Yehuda the third contingency effectively disappears — the ruling is permitted — the *bechor* is not as thoroughly set aside. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, holds that it is forbidden for a sage to rule on a *bechor* on Yom Tov, making the third contingency a genuine obstacle and rendering the *bechor* fully *muktza*. This observation also reflects a general principle that the Gemara articulated earlier in the tractate: Rabbi Shimon does not hold that *muktza* applies in every case where something was unavailable at the onset of Shabbat, but he does hold that when the object was genuinely set aside under circumstances where a reasonable person would have expected it to remain unavailable, the *muktza* status is maintained.

### Annulment Types

The Gemara now asks why the vow case does not suffer from the same problem as the *bechor*: even if the husband might annul the vow, who says he will? And even if a sage could void the vow, who says one will be found? The response distinguishes the two mechanisms carefully. For husband-annulment, the Gemara — on the basis of the principle stated by Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava — explains: *kol hanoderes al daas baala hi noderes* — when a wife makes a vow, she implicitly makes it subject to her husband's consent. The vow was never fully unconditional; it always carried the understood possibility that the husband might refuse to ratify it. The food was therefore never truly and definitively forbidden in the way the *bechor* was; there was always the standing possibility of the husband's non-acceptance. As a result, the analogy to *adam yoshev umitzappe* — the person who anticipates the lamp burning out — holds here. Just as the oil is quasi-expected to become available, so the vow-forbidden food is quasi-expected to be annulled.

For sage-voiding, a different answer applies: even if one cannot find a trained sage, *sagi lei b'gimmel hedyotot* — three laypeople suffice to void a vow. The availability of three unqualified laypeople is far more assured than the availability of a qualified expert willing to rule on a *bechor*. And here Tosafot's point becomes decisive: for the *bechor*, not only must one find a sage, but one must find a sage who is willing to transgress — since ruling on a *bechor* on Yom Tov is itself forbidden according to Rabbi Shimon. No such obstacle exists with voiding a vow. The difference in the practical availability and halakhic permissibility of the relevant adjudication produces the decisive asymmetry between the two cases.

---

## Unintended Acts

### Challenge to Rabbi Shimon

The final section of the daf circles back to what was presented at the outset as the one thing Rabbi Shimon concedes: a burning lamp. The Gemara asks with fresh urgency — *mi amar Rabbi Shimon kavta mutar l'taltela, kavta in, lo kavta lo* — is it really Rabbi Shimon's position that when the lamp is extinguished it may be moved but when burning it may not? Why exactly? *Dilma bahadi d'nakat lei kavta* — perhaps as you carry it, it will happen to go out. So the concern when moving a burning lamp is that the act of carrying will cause extinguishing. But then the Gemara objects: *ha shamna lei l'Rabbi Shimon davar she'eino mitkavein mutar* — but we know Rabbi Shimon holds that an unintended act is permitted! He is not intending to extinguish the lamp; he merely wants to move it. And the extinguishing is not even inevitable — it is only a possibility. Rabbi Shimon should permit this.

The Gemara cites support from a *baraita*: *gorer adam kissei mitta v'safsal, ubilvad shelo yiskayven la'asos charitz* — one may drag a bench or bed across the ground, provided one does not intend to create a furrow, even though dragging will likely create one. Rabbi Shimon permits this precisely because the furrow-making is unintended. Why then should he not similarly permit moving a burning lamp, with the unintended — and uncertain — possibility of extinguishing?

### Biblical vs. Rabbinical

The Gemara's proposed resolution draws a principled distinction: *kol heicha dechi michaven ika issur d'Oraisa, ki lo michaven gazar Rabbi Shimon mi'd'rabbanan* — wherever the intended act would constitute a Torah-level violation, Rabbi Shimon does not permit the unintended version; he imposes a rabbinic prohibition even when one lacks the intention. *Kol heicha dechi michaven ika issur d'rabbanan, ki lo michaven shari Rabbi Shimon l'chatchila* — but wherever the intended act would be only a rabbinic violation, then Rabbi Shimon permits the unintended act entirely, even *lechatchila*. The bench-dragging falls into the second category: creating a furrow in this manner is not the standard method of making a furrow, and doing it deliberately would itself be only a rabbinic violation — a *shinui* (irregular method). Since the prohibition is rabbinic even when intentional, Rabbi Shimon permits the unintended version. Extinguishing a lamp, however, is a Torah-level prohibition when done deliberately. Therefore Rabbi Shimon applies a rabbinic fence around even the unintended version and prohibits carrying the burning lamp.

This resolution will not survive intact. The Gemara will return tomorrow to challenge this distinction, since Rabbi Shimon is in fact universally understood to permit *aino mitkavein* — unintended acts — even where the intended version would be biblical. The Gemara's answer at this stage is a preliminary position that the next *daf* will address. We will resume there with the question: if Rabbi Shimon truly permits all unintended acts regardless of biblical or rabbinic status, what is his actual reason for prohibiting the moving of a burning lamp?

---

---

# Shabbat 47

## Rabbi Shimon & Muktza

### Lamp & Unintended Acts

The sugya on 47a picks up from the bottom of 46b, where the discussion has centered on the position of Rabbi Shimon and the narrow domains of *muktza* that he accepts. The specific question at hand is this: Rabbi Shimon clearly prohibits moving a burning lamp — that much seems agreed upon — but why? If one moves the lamp and it happens to go out, that extinguishing is unintended. It is a *davar she'eino mitkaven*, and according to Rabbi Shimon, unintentional acts are permitted. So why should moving the burning lamp be problematic?

The Gemara's first proposed answer is that Rabbi Shimon's leniency regarding *eino mitkaven* applies only when the act, were it done intentionally, would constitute a *d'rabbanan* violation. The classic example is dragging a bench across the ground. Even if one intentionally dragged a bench in order to form a furrow, that would only be a rabbinic prohibition, since digging in such a manner is a *shinui* — an unusual mode of performing the prohibited act. By contrast, extinguishing a flame intentionally would in certain circumstances constitute a *d'oraisa* violation of *mechabeh* — for instance, if one's purpose were to produce charcoal. Therefore, the Gemara tentatively suggests, in cases where the intentional act would be *d'oraisa*, Rabbi Shimon holds that even *eino mitkaven* is forbidden rabbinically.

### Rejecting First Answer

Rava challenges this proposed distinction with a pointed *meitivi*. The Mishnah records that clothing merchants may wear the garments they sell in their ordinary manner of transport — even if those garments contain *shatnez* — provided they do not intend to wear them for protection from sun or rain. This ruling is attributed to Rabbi Shimon, as the permissibility turns entirely on the absence of intent. And yet, if one were to intentionally wear *shatnez* for protection, that would plainly be a *d'oraisa* transgression. It follows that Rabbi Shimon permits *eino mitkaven* even in the face of a biblical prohibition. The proposed distinction collapses.

This point has significant practical consequence. A central pillar of Shabbat observance is the principle that an unintended act which will not inevitably occur is permitted — *eino mitkaven* — and this applies even when the potential violation would be *d'oraisa*. The Gemara's challenge from the *shatnez* case confirms this across domains, not merely on Shabbat. One might observe, however, that the *shatnez* example is not as generalizable as it first appears. Rashi explains there that the very definition of "wearing" requires donning a garment with the intent for it to serve as clothing. When the merchants wear the garments to carry them, they are by definition not "wearing" them in the halachically operative sense — they are transporting. If that is correct, then the *shatnez* case is not really an instance of *eino mitkaven* overriding a *d'oraisa* in the usual sense; it is rather a dispute about the definitional scope of the prohibited act. In that reading, the case may not illuminate the broader question of *kavana* and intent across other prohibitions as straightforwardly as the Gemara implies.

In any case, the Gemara now must abandon its first answer entirely. Rabbi Shimon allows *eino mitkaven* even by *d'oraisa* violations, so the concern about extinguishing cannot explain why the burning lamp is off-limits. A new explanation is needed.

It is worth pausing here to note the parallel issue of *huktza l'mitzvato* — the principle that an object designated for a *mitzvah* cannot be diverted from that function. Some had suggested that the burning lamp falls into this category, analogous to the *s'chach* of a *sukkah* which may not be removed. But as Tosafot points out, moving the lamp around the house to illuminate wherever one needs it does not diminish its *mitzvah* function at all — the lamp continues to serve. The only application of *huktza l'mitzvato* relevant to the lamp is benefiting from the oil that has dripped away, which is precisely what the Mishnah prohibits under the formulation *ein nehenin mimenu*. Moving the lamp as such is not the concern of *huktza l'mitzvato*.

### Flame as Muktza

The Gemara now offers Rava's solution: *hanach l'ner shemen u'ftila* — leave aside the lamp, the oil, and the wick. These three components are *muktza* in the eyes of Rabbi Shimon by virtue of a different category altogether: *basis l'davar ha'assur*, a support for a forbidden object. The forbidden object in question is the flame itself. Rashi makes this explicit: *l'davar ha'assur u'leshalheves* — the forbidden thing is the flame, and the vessel is secondary to it while the flame burns within it. It is the flame that is *muktza*, and everything that supports it — the wick, the oil, and the lamp — becomes *muktza* as a consequence of being a *basis* for that flame.

This is a striking category. The flame itself is what is *muktza* in the primary sense, yet the flame cannot be physically moved in isolation. The concept here is that the actively burning flame represents something utterly prohibited on Shabbat, something that Rabbi Shimon acknowledges as *muktza* in a way that transcends the ordinary mechanics of his usually narrow *muktza* position. Everything else functions as a *basis l'davar ha'assur*. This explains why even Rabbi Shimon, who otherwise rejects most forms of *muktza*, concedes that the burning lamp may not be moved.

### Three Components

Tosafot raises a precise analytical question about this ruling. Why must all three elements — the lamp, the oil, and the wick — be considered a *basis*? Could one not say that only the wick, being the most proximate support for the flame, is the *basis*, while the oil and the vessel are more remote?

The answer Tosafot provides is critical. If only the wick were considered a *basis l'davar ha'assur*, then the lamp itself would be a *basis* to two things simultaneously: the wick, which is prohibited, and the oil, which is permitted. And a *basis* that supports both a permitted and a prohibited object is not treated as a *basis l'davar ha'assur* and may be moved. Therefore, the oil must itself be considered a *basis* as well — for if the oil were deemed permitted, it would neutralize the lamp's status as a *basis* to something forbidden. Only by establishing that all three components are in the category of *basis* can we explain why the lamp as a whole may not be moved.
