This generates an important and open question in the laws of *basis*: does a *basis* to a *basis* become a *basis* in its own right? The lamp, oil, and wick are all considered as a single unit serving the flame, so perhaps the rule applies here because they function organically as one integrated system. Whether in a more ordinary case — say, a lamp sitting on a tray sitting on a table — each layer of support would likewise inherit *basis* status is a question that this passage raises but does not fully resolve.

---

## Ash Shovel Case

### Romanus Ruling

The Gemara transitions, with characteristic elegance and without an explicit header, from the discussion of *basis* to a case involving an ash shovel. Rabbi Chanina quotes Rabbi Romanos: Rebbe permitted him to carry a *machta* — an ash shovel or incense burner — together with its ashes. This immediately invites a challenge from Rabbi Zeira, who poses the question to Rav Assi: could Rabbi Yochanan really have endorsed this? For we have a Mishnah which states that a person may lift a child even if the child is holding a stone, or a basket even if it contains a stone — both instances of moving a permitted object together with a *muktza* item. And yet Rabbi Yochanan himself explained in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chana that the basket case only works if the basket is *filled with fruit* — so that the basket is a *basis* to both a permitted thing and a prohibited thing simultaneously.

### Basis Status

This sets up the central principle at stake. When a *basis* serves both a permitted and a prohibited object, it does not take on the identity of a *basis l'davar ha'assur* and may be moved. This is why the fruit-filled basket with a stone can be carried — the basket is supporting the fruit just as much as the stone, and therefore its character is not defined exclusively by the *muktza* content. But, the Gemara continues, if there is no fruit — if the basket is *only* carrying the stone — then it cannot be moved. So why can the ash shovel be moved when it contains ashes, which are genuine *muktza* with no permitted use?

Before proceeding, an important distinction must be kept in mind. *Kli she-melachto l'issur* — a vessel whose primary use is for a prohibited purpose, such as a hammer — is not the same category as true *muktza*. A hammer retains some hypothetical permitted use on Shabbat (cracking nuts, for instance), and therefore does not become a *basis* in the strong sense. The *basis* principle applies only to genuine *muktza* objects, things that are entirely off-limits with no possible permitted use. The ashes in this case are true *muktza* — they have no use — and so the question of *basis* arises acutely.

### Incense Explanation

The Gemara records that upon being confronted with this challenge, the sage was dumbfounded for a moment, quoting the expression from Daniel: he was astonished for a time. Then he offered an answer: *hacha nami de'is bei kartin* — perhaps in this incense burner there were a few small unburned granules of incense mixed in with the ashes. Those granules are not *muktza* — one can smell them directly even on Shabbat, as Rashi explains — and therefore the incense burner is a *basis* to both a permitted object (the granules) and a prohibited object (the ashes), which would allow it to be moved.

Abaye objects: *kartin bei rabbi mi chashivi?* — are tiny granules of incense considered significant in the household of Rebbe? Such items would be entirely beneath notice in so distinguished a setting. The Gemara raises the possibility that even if they are insignificant to Rebbe, they might matter to poorer people, since *vechi teima chazu l'aniyim* — perhaps they are fit for the poor. The Gemara then invokes a *braita* which states that garments of the poor are judged by the standards of the poor, and garments of the rich by the standards of the rich. A small, coarse scrap of fabric is significant to a poor person and may therefore contract *tumah*, while a wealthy person would discard it and it would not. So too, what is trivial in Rebbe's home might be significant elsewhere. But the Gemara rejects this: *li hitye rabbi* — Rebbe permitted this for himself, in his own home. What matters to a poor person is irrelevant to what is significant in Rebbe's household. If the granules are trivial for Rebbe, they cannot transform the incense burner into a *basis l'davar ha'assur v'l'davar hamuttar*.

### Copper Vessel

Rava now intervenes with a counter-proposal. He reports: when I was in the house of Rav Nachman, *havina metalpelinan kanuna agav kitma* — we would move a copper vessel used to hold burning coals for warmth, together with its ashes. Before accepting this at face value, however, Rava first dismisses Abaye's explanation entirely. Two objections: first, excrement is genuinely disgusting, which is what allows the special *agaraf shel rei* exception; ashes are not disgusting and so the analogy fails. Second, the feces in a chamber pot are exposed, whereas the ashes here are enclosed within the covered vessel — and an enclosed vessel loses the urgency that drives the *agaraf shel rei* leniency. Both conditions are absent, so that category cannot save the ruling.

### Ash's Usefulness

The solution Rava offers, as Rashi clarifies, turns on the word *agav* — "together with." The key insight is that, contrary to appearances, it was not the ashes that posed the *muktza* problem. The ashes themselves, Rashi explains, had a legitimate use: *shehayu tzerichim l'afrah lechasos rok o tzoah* — they would use the ashes to cover spittle or excrement on the floor. Ashes spread over something unpleasant served a hygienic function. If a person customarily saved ashes for this purpose, the ashes were not *muktza* at all. In that case, both the vessel and the ashes are permitted. What then is the *chiddush* of the ruling?

### Wood Chips Resolution

The answer, which Rashi makes explicit, is that the vessel also contained unburned wood chips, and those wood chips are true *muktza* — they have no permitted use on Shabbat. The Gemara confirms this explicitly: *v'af al gav d'ika lashivay etzim* — even though there were wood chips in it. So the vessel is permitted, the ashes are permitted, and only the wood chips are *muktza*. The vessel is therefore a *basis* simultaneously to a permitted object (the ashes) and a prohibited object (the wood chips), and since it supports both, it may be moved. The entire discussion has been resolved by recognizing that the problematic element was not what it initially appeared to be.

---

## Wick Problem

### Oil & Wick Issue

The Gemara now raises a new objection from a *braita*: if a lamp contains a remnant of a burned-out wick, it may not be moved — *she'assur l'taltel*. This is a ruling that both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon agree on, according to Rashi. The difficulty is apparent. If the lamp contains both oil and a wick, the oil is a permitted object, and the wick is a *muktza* object. By the principle just established — that a *basis* to both a permitted and a prohibited thing may be moved — the lamp should be permitted. Why can it not be carried?

### Galilee Context

Abaye's answer is striking: *b'galila shanu* — this ruling was taught with respect to the Galilee. Rashi explains that in the Galilee, linen fabric was scarce and therefore even the remnant of a wick was considered a significant and valuable item: *she'ein bgadim shel pishtan metzuyim lahem*. Because of this, the wick remnant was far from negligible — it was a significant object in its own right. But this raises a puzzling reversal: the more significant the wick, one would expect the stronger the case that it constitutes genuine *muktza*, and hence the clearer the problem. Why does the significance of the wick increase the prohibition? If anything, a significant wick should simply make the question sharper.

### Tosafot's Logic

Tosafot offers a far superior explanation. The question of the Gemara, properly understood, is not why the wick is *muktza* — it plainly is — but why the oil does not neutralize the lamp's *basis* status. The lamp contains oil and a wick. The oil is permitted on Shabbat — one can use oil for many purposes. The wick is *muktza*. So the lamp should be a *basis* to a permitted object and a prohibited object, and should therefore be movable. Why not?

Tosafot's answer: *shehaya lahem rov shemen* — in the Galilee, oil was extremely abundant, so plentiful that it was considered cheap and insignificant. *Ul'chach lo batli shivei ptila agav shemen* — because the oil was so plentiful as to be nearly worthless, the remnant of the wick was actually the more significant object in the lamp. The lamp was therefore considered *primarily* a *basis* to the wick, not to the oil. And when the primary content of a *basis* is the *muktza* item, the *basis* is prohibited.

This reading aligns the case perfectly with the earlier ash-and-wood-chips discussion and makes the logic consistent throughout. The principle that emerges is that when determining whether a *basis* is being used for a permitted or prohibited purpose, the relative weight of those objects matters. If the *muktza* item is by far the more significant, the presence of a trivial permitted item does not transform the vessel into a *basis* to both and thereby render it movable.

### Gaon's Comment

Rabbeinu Nissim Gaon, whose commentary appears alongside this passage, provides a poignant historical footnote. He writes: *netarchu b'zeh hashinuy sheshina Abaye harbe min hachachamim v'lo shamati mehem klum v'lo matzati vo l'echad min hageonim perush* — many scholars labored over Abaye's peculiar answer of "in the Galilee," and he had not heard a satisfying explanation from any of them, nor found one in any of the Geonic literature. He eventually discovered an answer through his own diligent searching in Massekhet Nazir — the same answer that Tosafot would later arrive at, concerning the abundance of oil in the Galilee. The observation is a reminder of how hard-won these explanations were, and how much ground scholars had to cover across *Shas* to find the relevant material. Rabbeinu Nissim Gaon predates Tosafot, and whether Tosafot had access to his commentary is not established.

---

## Assembly & Construction

### Self-Assembly Bed

The Gemara shifts to a new topic, though one that echoes an earlier discussion of the *menorah shel chulyot*. Levi bar Shmuel found Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya standing at the entrance to Rav Huna's house, and asked them: *mahu lehachazir mittah shel tarsin be-Shabbat?* May one reassemble on Shabbat a bed of the sort used by traveling metalworkers — a collapsible, self-assembly bed whose pieces fit together in slots or holes? He was told it was permitted.

### Rav vs Shmuel

When they subsequently brought the question before Rav Yehuda, he was alarmed: both Rav and Shmuel had ruled that *hamachzir mittah shel tarsin be-Shabbat chayav chatat* — one who reassembles such a bed on Shabbat has committed a biblical transgression. The gap between the two positions could not be wider: one authority ruled it entirely permitted, while Rav and Shmuel declared it a violation carrying liability for a *chatat* offering.

### Candelabra Cases

The Gemara then brings what appears to be corroborating evidence for the strict view. A *braita* rules that one who reassembles the arms of a *menorah* on Shabbat is *chayav chatat*. What *melacha* is involved? Rashi notes that the principle of *ein binyan b'keilim* — construction does not apply to vessels — means this is not technically *boneh*. Rather, it falls under *makeh b'patish*, the act of completing a vessel or giving it its final usable form.

However, the *braita* then introduces a distinction: if the candelabra has extendable arms — sections that can be inserted to lengthen the reach, like the segments of a paint roller — then one should not reassemble them, but if one does so, one is exempt. And Rabbi Shimon adds a further refinement: a *keren agulah*, a circular type of horn or musical instrument, makes one *chayav*, while a *keren peshutah*, a straight type, leaves one merely exempt.

### Melacha Criteria

Rashi articulates the principles that distinguish these cases with precision. The circular instrument involves *maaseh uman* — it requires skilled craftsmanship — and must be inserted *b'chozek*, with force, in a tight fit. These two qualities — expert assembly and tight fitting — combine to produce a genuine *melacha*. The straight instrument, by contrast, is inserted loosely and is *darkan le-farkam tamid* — characteristically taken apart and reassembled on a regular basis, such that it has no single "finished" state. Because it is constantly adjusted and never permanently assembled, doing so carries no *chiyuv*.

### Loose Fitting Ruling

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel goes further: *im hayah rafeh, muttar* — if the fitting is loose, it is not only that one is exempt after the fact, but it is permitted *ab initio*. The Gemara concludes that Rav and Shmuel, who declared the bed case a *chiyuv chatat*, were speaking of a tightly assembled bed. The opinion that ruled it permitted must have been following Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view: the bed in question was a loose-fitting assembly.

Tosafot adds that it would be unusual for one position to declare something entirely permitted while another pronounces it a *d'oraisa* violation — they must have been addressing different factual situations. The tight case generates *chiyuv chatat*; the loose case is either *patur aval assur* according to the middle view, or fully permitted according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

### Practical Distinctions

These principles carry significant practical relevance. Several factors emerge as defining the boundary of the *melacha*: whether the assembly requires forcing or banging pieces together (*taka*); whether it involves a screw mechanism that tightens into a permanent fit; whether the item is assembled into a single finished state or is routinely adjusted in and out. The more clearly a construction involves tight, expert, permanent assembly, the more serious the concern. At the other end of the spectrum, things that are loosely fitted and habitually adjusted — such as a table leaf, which slides in and out easily and is not designed to remain permanently in one position — present little difficulty.

### Modern Examples

One might ask about common contemporary objects. Regarding toys such as Lego, the concern depends on how they are actually used. Standard Lego pieces that are regularly assembled and disassembled and not left in a fixed configuration present a weaker case; specialized model kits that are tightly fitted and left permanently assembled are more problematic. Mr. Potato Head, which involves loose, easily removable pieces that are constantly rearranged, presents no serious issue.

A clarinet, which comes in several distinct pieces that must be joined together before use, raises a more interesting question. Unlike a table leaf which occupies different states as a matter of course, the clarinet has a clear unassembled and assembled state — like the bed. However, the pieces are not forced together or screwed tightly; they are joined with a cork fitting, greased for smooth insertion, and the fit remains loose enough to adjust. Whether this brings it closer to the loose-fitting case that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits, or whether the functional finality of assembly militates toward at least *patur aval assur*, is a question the sugya raises without fully resolving for every scenario.

### Rava's Position

The Gemara closes this section with a practical application. At Rav Chama's house, there was a *mita galnisa* — a rolling or collapsible assembly bed — which Rava would reassemble on Yom Tov. One of the rabbis challenged him: was he perhaps relying on the principle of *binyan min ha-tzad* — constructing something in a sideways, indirect manner, which would constitute a *shinui* — or at least ensure that only a rabbinic and not a biblical prohibition was involved? But even rabbinic prohibition is still forbidden, the questioner noted.

Rava replied: *ana ke-Rabban Gamliel svira li de-amar im haya rafuy muttar* — I hold like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who ruled that if the fitting is loose it is entirely permitted. Rashi explains that Rava assembled the bed in a deliberately loose fashion. The *chiddush* of this ruling, as noted, is that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's leniency applies even to objects that have a clear finished/unfinished binary state — the key variable is the looseness of fit, not the nature of the assembly process per se.

---

## Spark Catching

### Vessel for Sparks

The final Mishnah of the chapter rules: *notnin kli tachat ha-ner le-kabbel nitzotzot* — one may place a vessel beneath a lamp to catch sparks, thereby preventing them from igniting the floor or furniture. However, *ve-lo yitten le-tocho mayim mipnei she-hu mechabbeh* — one may not put water in the vessel, because that causes extinguishing.

### Why Permitted

The first question the Gemara raises is how placing the vessel under the lamp is permitted at all. Does not the vessel then become a *basis* to the sparks that land in it — and would that not render the vessel prohibited, as it has now become a support for *muktza* matter?

### Sparks Negligible

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua answers: *nitzotzot ein bahem mamash* — sparks, once they die out, leave essentially nothing of substance. They produce a negligible residue that has no halachic weight and does not constitute the kind of *muktza* matter that would render the vessel a prohibited *basis*. The vessel may therefore be placed there and removed freely.

### Water Prohibition

The prohibition on water in the vessel is more complex. At first glance, the concern might appear to align with the position of Rabbi Yossi, who holds that *gram kibbuy assur* — even indirectly causing extinguishing is forbidden — and who does not permit even placing water-filled vessels around a spreading fire on Shabbat to let the fire extinguish itself. But the Gemara objects: Rabbi Yossi's ruling concerns actions taken *on* Shabbat. If the vessel of water were placed before Shabbat, Rabbi Yossi presumably would have no objection. Yet the *braita* states explicitly: *notnin kli tachat ha-ner le-kabbel nitzotzot be-Shabbat* — one may place the vessel on Shabbat itself, *ve-ein tzarich lomar me-erev Shabbat* — and certainly from before Shabbat. But the water is forbidden even *me-erev Shabbat*, certainly and *a fortiori* on Shabbat itself. This prohibition cannot therefore be derived from Rabbi Yossi's position regarding Shabbat actions. The *seder* of the *braita* implies the water is forbidden even before Shabbat begins.

### Proximity Issue

Rav Ashi provides the resolution: *shani hacha mipnei she-mekarev kibuya* — here is different, because placing the water brings the extinguishing close. This is not simply a case of *gram kibbuy* in Rabbi Yossi's sense; even the Rabbis, who generally permit indirect causation of extinguishing in cases of need, would agree this is problematic. According to Rashi, the very act of setting the water in place constitutes a form of *kibbuy*, since the extinguishing is directly enabled at the moment of placement.

### Floating Wicks

Tosafot takes issue with Rashi's formulation and offers its own reading. Tosafot understands the concern to be more specific: the fear is not that the water passively awaits a falling spark, but that the person might actively lift the vessel toward a falling spark, thereby participating directly in the extinguishing at the moment it occurs. It is this possibility of active involvement that renders placing water there forbidden even before Shabbat — lest one come to do it on Shabbat.

A practical question follows naturally from Tosafot's reasoning: what about the common practice of floating wicks in oil that rests atop water? When the oil is consumed, the wick reaches the water and the flame is extinguished. Is that not the same as placing water to cause extinguishing? Tosafot responds: *ain zeh kari kibuya b'yadav keivan she'eino mitkaven lekibbuy klal ella lehagbiya et ha-shemen* — this is not called extinguishing by one's hand, since the person has no intent toward extinguishing at all. The water is placed there to elevate and support the oil, not to extinguish the flame. The extinguishing, when it eventually occurs, is incidental to the entire arrangement. Because the intent and the design of the setup are directed toward keeping the flame burning — by keeping the oil at the right level — and not toward causing it to go out, there is no concern of *kibbuy*. Tosafot therefore concludes that this practice is permitted: *lo shayach lemigezar midi shema yaaseh be-Shabbat u-shari*.

---

## Insulation Intro

### Insulation Materials

The chapter concludes and the next *perek* opens with a new Mishnah: *bameh tommnin u-vameh ein tommnin* — in what materials may one insulate food before Shabbat to retain its heat, and in what may one not? The Mishnah enumerates a series of materials in which insulation is forbidden: *gefet* (grape pressings), *zevel* (dung), *melach* (salt), *sid* (plaster), *chol* (sand) — whether wet or dry — as well as straw, grape skins (*zogin*), cloth padding (*muchin*), and grasses when moist. Dry grasses, however, are permitted for insulation, since they do not generate the same degree of heat.

### Heat Generation Principle

The underlying principle is that the Rabbis prohibited insulating food before Shabbat in any material that actively generates heat — not merely retains heat, but adds to it. This stands in contrast to the previous chapter's topic, which concerned placing food on a flame before Shabbat. Both involve the concern that the food may be cooked or warmed inappropriately on Shabbat, but the *perek* of *hatmana* — insulation — addresses the distinct technique of wrapping food in insulating material.

### Ash Stirring Concern

The reason behind this prohibition is practical and well-grounded in rabbinic reasoning. The most effective heat-adding insulation material, especially in an era of wood-burning stoves and hearths, would be hot ashes. If one insulated one's food pot within hot ashes, the ashes would continue to radiate heat and potentially cook or raise the temperature of the food on Shabbat. The danger is that a person, noticing the temperature dropping, might be tempted to stir the ashes — *chatiya* — in order to increase the heat, which would constitute a prohibited act of kindling on Shabbat. To preempt this, the Rabbis enacted a broad prohibition against insulating in any heat-generating material before Shabbat. This is the theme to which the new *perek* is devoted, and it will be developed further in the coming discussions.

---

---

# Shabbat 48

## Hatmanah Overview

### Hatmanah Defined

The daf begins at the bottom of 47b, immediately following the *mishnah*, where a new *perek* opens. The previous *perek* dealt with leaving food on the fire — *shehiya* — touching along the way on questions of *bishul* and *muktzah*. This *perek* returns to the theme of putting food on the fire before *Shabbat*, but now in a different register: the food is already fully cooked, and the concern is insulating it so that it retains heat. This practice is called *hatmanah* — literally, burying or insulating.

The classic method of insulation was to store cooked food in hot ashes, which would preserve the heat most effectively. That very effectiveness, however, created a rabbinic concern parallel to the concern about *shehiya*: one might come to stir the ashes in order to reignite them and intensify the heat. Accordingly, the Rabbis ruled that one may not perform *hatmanah* — even before *Shabbat* — in any material that adds heat, including hot ashes. This prohibition applies even to materials unrelated to fire, so long as they actively add heat rather than merely retaining it.

### Heat-Adding Materials

The *mishnah* enumerates a range of materials that add heat and are therefore prohibited for *hatmanah*. What all these materials appear to share, at least in significant part, is that they are organic substances whose decomposition releases heat — a process that constitutes the creation of new warmth rather than mere retention of stored warmth. Dung, for instance, releases heat through decomposition. Sand is different: it may retain heat if it was previously heated, but it does not inherently generate heat on its own.

### Gefet vs. Sesame

The *Gemara* opens with a formal question — *ibayah lehu* — about *gefet*. The term was initially understood to refer to the residue of grape pressing, but in fact it denotes the residue from olives: olive twigs or the refuse remaining after olive oil production. *Gefet* is one of the first items the *mishnah* identifies as prohibited for *hatmanah* because it adds heat.

The question the *Gemara* raises is whether the *mishnah*'s prohibition on *gefet shel zeitim* — olive refuse — is limited to olives specifically, with sesame refuse (*shumshumin*) being permitted, or whether the *mishnah* speaks of olives as its primary example while intending to include, *kal va-chomer*, even sesame refuse, which adds some heat though less than olives.

The *Gemara* adduces a proof from a statement of Rav Zeira in the name of one scholar from the academy of Rabbi Yannai. The ruling is as follows: if one has a container (*kupa*) into which a pot has been insulated — say, surrounded by towels or some other heat-retaining but not heat-adding material — and one then places that container on top of a box filled with *gefet shel zeitim*, this is prohibited. The *gefet* underneath functions like a heat-adding base, analogous to a fire below.

This scenario is directly relevant to contemporary practice, as it describes the functional equivalent of placing a wrapped pot on a *blech* — a metal sheet placed over a flame — where the *blech* adds heat and the towel retains it. The combined apparatus, in certain configurations, raises the question of *hatmanah b'mosif hevel*.

The *Gemara* resolves its initial question as follows: the prohibition on sesame refuse applies even to the surrounding configuration, since it does add heat, but only the olive refuse generates enough *hevel* — rising heat — to create a problem when placed underneath. Sesame refuse does not generate sufficient upward heat to constitute *hatmanah* in that configuration, whereas olive refuse does. Thus the two substances are distinguished not by whether they add heat in principle, but by how directionally and forcefully that heat rises.

## Hatmanah vs. Shehiya

### Blech Problem

At this point the discussion calls for a pause to address a fundamental practical question raised by Tosafot. We have learned throughout the previous *perek* about *shehiya*, and we know from the current *perek* that one may not perform *hatmanah* in a material that adds heat. Yet common practice involves placing food on a *blech* before *Shabbat* — a metal sheet over an open flame that clearly adds heat. If wrapping food in towels alongside the heat of a *blech* constitutes *hatmanah b'mosif hevel*, how is this permitted?

This is the foundational question Tosafot raises: what precisely is the line between *hatmanah* and *shehiya*? In Tosafot's time, the typical practice was to insert a pot into hot ashes such that the ashes would surround the lower portion of the pot — a partial immersion that could be considered a form of *hatmanah* even when the ashes had been swept and covered (*garuf ve-katum*). The problem is: if the surrounding material adds heat, why should that not implicate the prohibition of *hatmanah b'mosif hevel*?

### Tosafot's Distinction

Tosafot begins by drawing an inference from the case of *gefet*: since placing a pot-containing box atop olive refuse is prohibited because the refuse raises heat upward, one might conclude that placing coals beneath a pot — even covered with ashes — should likewise be prohibited. As Tosafot states: *sheharei gechalim ma'alim hevel lema'alah* — coals raise heat upward, just like *gefet shel zeitim*. This would seem to call into question not only the *blech* practice but the entire structure of the previous *perek*.

Tosafot raises the difficulty explicitly: *heicha anu matminim al kira shelanu* — how do we perform *hatmanah* on our own stoves and ovens? Placing a pot in an oven that one then turns off involves a heat-adding element. The *Ri* — one of the most important voices in the laws of *hatmanah* — provides the answer that becomes normative.

Tosafot does mention a second answer: that the heat in the case of a cooling oven is dissipating, meaning the oven is losing stored heat rather than generating new heat, whereas the organic materials in the *mishnah* are actively generating new heat through decomposition. Under this distinction, true *hatmanah b'mosif hevel* would require the creation of new heat, not merely the slow release of absorbed heat. However, this answer is not the one Tosafot ultimately focuses on, because if adopted it would force us to explain the entire previous *perek* as dealing exclusively with dissipating heat — an uncomfortable constraint — and would mean that any genuine new-heat scenario during *shehiya* would also be problematic.

The critical answer is that of the *Ri*, which draws the central line between *hatmanah* and *shehiya*:

> *Ve'lo dami l'hatmanah b'davar hamosif hevel, de'lo asru ela k'sh'matminu b'davik saviv hakedera, dumya d'remetz; aval tanur o chafira she'yesh avir bein hadafanos lakedera, ein le'esor yoser mish'ar sha'ah, af al pi shekol hakedera besoch hatanur.*

The prohibition of *hatmanah b'mosif hevel* applies only when the heat-adding material is *davik saviv hakedera* — pressed against and fully surrounding the pot on all sides, analogous to being buried in ashes. If there is an *avir* — an air space — between the pot and the surrounding heat source, it does not constitute *hatmanah* at all, regardless of how much heat is generated.

### Practical Application

This *Ri*'s distinction has far-reaching practical implications. Because a conventional oven has air space between the walls and the pot, placing food in an oven before *Shabbat* is not *hatmanah* — the pot is inside the oven but is not encased in a heat-adding material that presses against it from all sides. Similarly, a *blech* on a stovetop does not constitute *hatmanah* because the pot rests on the *blech* from below but is not surrounded by it.

The more nuanced contemporary question involves covering the pot with a towel while it sits on a *blech*. The towel retains heat; the *blech* adds heat. Does the combination create *hatmanah b'mosif hevel*? The answer depends entirely on whether the towel presses against the pot on all sides. If the towel is draped loosely — forming, as it were, a tent over the pot without compressing against it — there is air space and the arrangement does not constitute *hatmanah*. If, however, the towel is pressed tightly around the pot so as to encase it from all directions, that would be *hatmanah*, and since the *blech* below is adding heat, it would be *hatmanah b'mosif hevel*, which is prohibited.

A similar question arises regarding the *crock pot*: some rule that a crock pot constitutes *hatmanah* because the heating element surrounds the food vessel on all sides, while others permit it on the grounds that the lid is not in contact with the sides and thus the enclosure is incomplete. This Tosafot is the foundational source for that entire discussion, and the *Ri*'s distinction — full contact on all sides versus air space — is the operative principle in contemporary *halacha* for defining *hatmanah*.

## Reish Galuta Stories

### Flask Story

The *Gemara* now introduces two narratives set in the household of the *Reish Galuta*, the political head of the Jewish community in Babylonia. The *Reish Galuta*'s household was notable for wealth and political prominence but not always for *halachic* scrupulousness, and various improper practices are documented in the *Gemara* from that setting.

Rabba and Rabbi Zeira visit the house of the *Reish Galuta*. They observe a servant who places a flask of water (*kuza d'maya*) on the opening of a hot kettle (*kumkuma*). Rabba immediately rebukes the servant. Rabbi Zeira questions the rebuke: how is this different, he asks, from the common practice of placing one pot of water atop another hot pot to warm it — *maya agav maya*?

Rabba responds with a fundamental distinction: *hatam okumi kamokim* — there, you are merely maintaining the heat of something already warm; *hacha ulodi kamolid* — here, you are actively generating new heat in something cold. The servant was placing a flask of cold water directly atop a hot kettle, using the heat of the kettle to heat the flask.

One might initially read this as a concern analogous to *mosif hevel* in the context of *hatmanah*. But the *Rishonim* generally interpret this story as implicating *bishul* rather than *hatmanah*, given the analysis of Tosafot we have just reviewed. With the *Ri*'s distinction in place, this scenario — a pot resting atop another vessel — clearly lacks the full-contact enclosure that defines *hatmanah*.

Tosafot proposes that the straightforward reading of the case is that one flask will reach *yad soledet bo* while the other will not. If the flask placed on top of the hot kettle will ultimately be heated to *yad soledet bo*, that constitutes *bishul*; if it will not reach that threshold, there is no concern. However, Tosafot is not fully satisfied with this reading, because we already know from prior discussions that one may warm food that will not reach *yad soledet bo* — that in itself is not prohibited. So the mere addition of heat, absent *yad soledet bo*, should not be problematic.

Tosafot therefore presses the reading further and suggests the distinction may turn on the temperature of the contents: one flask contained warm water, the other cold. Even more significantly, Tosafot offers a principle that is *normative l'halacha*: one may not place a cold liquid — which is treated for these purposes like uncooked food even if it was previously cooked and cooled — in a position where it has the *potential* to reach *yad soledet bo*, even if one intends to remove it before that threshold is reached. The concern is the placement itself, not only the eventual outcome. This principle, while not derived explicitly from the words of the story, is how Tosafot reads the narrative in light of other *sugyot* and is practically significant.

One practical corollary: if one has a *hot plate* or heating surface that genuinely cannot raise food to *yad soledet bo* under any circumstances, it may be permissible to place food upon it on *Shabbat*, as the *bishul* concern would be absent — though one must still consider any applicable *chazarah* issues.

### Cloth & Squeezing

The *Gemara* then records a second incident from the same visit. The servant spreads a cloth (*satudar*) over the mouth of a barrel used to store water, and places a cup (*natla*) on top of it. The cup would be used to draw water from the barrel, and the cloth was draped beneath it.

A brief digression on the word *natla* is in order. The *Rashba* notes that the term *natla* — the Aramaic word for a cup used to draw water — underlies the expression *netilat yadayim*. The *bracha* uses the term *al netilat yadayim* not merely in the sense of "lifting" the hands, but with specific reference to the act of pouring water over the hands from a cup. The *natla* is the instrument of that pouring.

Rava rebukes the servant for spreading the cloth over the barrel. Rabbi Zeira asks why, pointing out that in another *perek* there is a teaching permitting the spreading of a *parunka* — a cloth — over a barrel containing liquid on *Shabbat*. What is the difference between these two cases?

Rava replies: *hatam lo kapid ilavei, hacha kapid ilavei* — in the case of the *parunka*, the person is not particular about the cloth getting wet; here, the person is particular about it. In the *parunka* case, since the user does not mind the cloth becoming saturated, there is no concern that he will come to squeeze it out. Here, the cloth is one that its owner would not want wet, and were it to become wet — which is quite likely given that it covers a water barrel and a cup is placed upon it — he would squeeze it out in order to dry it.

The concern is *sechitah* — squeezing. Squeezing a cloth can implicate two distinct prohibitions: if done to extract the liquid for use, it resembles *dash* (threshing); if done to clean the cloth, it may implicate a form of laundering. In this case, the servant is not seeking to extract water for use, so the concern is more akin to the cleaning-laundering category. There is some discussion among the *Rishonim* regarding how clear the *d'oraita* concern is in this case, as the primary purpose is simply to dry the cloth, and the cleaning effect is incidental (*eino mitkaven*). Nonetheless, the risk is real enough that the arrangement is prohibited from the outset.

The broader point is that the anxiety around squeezing is pervasive in Shabbat law. The *Ashkenazi* custom to avoid full immersion in water on *Shabbat* similarly derives in significant part from concern about squeezing wet garments.

## Muktzah Materials

### Moving Muktzah

The *Gemara* returns to the topic of *hatmanah* and turns to a related question raised by Rav Ada bar Matna before Abaye. The *mishnah* that the *Gemara* is discussing also prohibits *hatmanah* with *muchin* — small pieces of cloth — when they are moist, while allowing it when they are dry. These cloth pieces are ordinarily designated for sewing purposes; they sit in a sewing kit awaiting use as patches or similar applications, and as such, they are *muktzah* — set aside and lacking a permissible use for *Shabbat*.

The question is: if on *Erev Shabbat* one took these dry *muchin* and used them to perform permitted *hatmanah* around a pot, does that practical use change their status? Can they now be handled on *Shabbat*, their identity having shifted to "insulating material"?

There is a related procedure that the *Gemara* addresses elsewhere — *tiltul min ha-tzad*, incidental movement. Even if the *muchin* remain *muktzah*, one could reach into the insulation to grab the pot, and the cloth would be displaced incidentally rather than directly handled. The question here is more pointed: has the use of the *muchin* for *hatmanah* affirmatively stripped them of their *muktzah* status, making them directly movable?

### Identity Not Changed

Abaye's response is striking in its logic. He says: *ve-chi mipnei she-ein lo kupa shel teven omed u-mafkir kupa shel muchin?* — does the fact that one could not obtain straw for insulation mean that one is prepared to permanently relinquish one's cloth pieces and dedicate them to *hatmanah* every *Erev Shabbat*? Of course not. This was an ad hoc arrangement. Once *Shabbat* is over, the person will go and acquire proper insulating material. The *muchin* will return to the sewing kit. Their fundamental identity has not changed, and therefore they remain *muktzah*.

This principle is genuinely counterintuitive. Ordinarily, one can alter the *muktzah* status of an object by designating it for a *Shabbat*-permissible purpose before *Shabbat* begins — the classic example being a rock designated as a doorstop or paperweight, which ceases to be *muktzah* once assigned that function. The difference here is that the assignment to a new function was purely situational and temporary. The person's intent is clear: as soon as *Shabbat* ends, these pieces of cloth revert to their original role. There is no genuine reclassification of identity.

This raises a further question: what level of designation is required to remove an object from *muktzah* status? A verbal declaration is not strictly necessary; a practical act of designation before *Shabbat* can suffice. However, the more inherently *muktzah* an object is, the clearer and more practical the act of designation must be. And crucially, if the person's own mindset is that the object will return to its former use after *Shabbat*, then even a practical use during *Shabbat* preparation does not constitute a genuine change of identity.

### Baraita Evidence

The *Gemara* attempts to adduce support for Abaye's ruling from a *baraita*: *tomnin b'gizei tzemer* — one may insulate with raw wool shearings; *uvetzipei tzemer* — with partially combed wool; *uvilshonot shel argaman* — with crimson fabric strips; and *uvimuchin* — with small cloth pieces. All these materials are items ordinarily destined for sewing or textile production. The *baraita* then states: *ve-ein metaltelin otan* — one may not move them, as they are *muktzah*.

The *Gemara* observes that this would appear to provide clear support: the *baraita* mentions *muchin* used for *hatmanah* and then says they cannot be moved. But the *Gemara* deflects: *im lo taman bahen ein metaltelin otan* — the *baraita* is stating two independent rules: first, one may use these materials for *hatmanah*; second, under ordinary circumstances they are *muktzah*. It does not necessarily address the case where they were actually used for *hatmanah* — which was the specific question.

The *Gemara* then asks: if this is the reading, what is the *chiddush*? We already know these materials are *muktzah*. The *Gemara* answers: *mahu d'teima chazi le-mizga aleihu* — one might have thought that some of these materials, such as soft cloth pieces, could be used for lying upon and would therefore not be *muktzah*. The *baraita* teaches that no — they are sewing materials, not items with a functional *Shabbat* use, and they remain *muktzah*.

Thus the *baraita* cannot serve as proof for Abaye's specific point, but the overall conclusion of the *Gemara*'s discussion is that even after actual use in *hatmanah*, the *muchin* retain their *muktzah* status, since the use does not genuinely transform their identity.

## Making Vessels

### Pillow Stuffing

The *Gemara* now transitions to a series of topics connected thematically through the common thread of small cloth pieces and the question of what constitutes "making a vessel" (*melekhet keli*) on *Shabbat*. Rav Chisda ruled that one is permitted to replace the stuffing inside pillows on *Shabbat* — if cloth filler has come out, one may push it back in. The implicit reasoning is that this does not constitute a prohibited act of construction.

### Neck Hole Opening

Rav Chanan bar Chisda challenged his father Rav Chisda from a *baraita* that distinguishes between two similar acts: *matir beit ha-tzavar* — undoing the stitching at the neck hole of a garment — is permitted on *Shabbat*, while *poteach* — opening a neck hole for the first time — is not. The case of *matir* involves a garment that was stitched closed temporarily by a launderer or processor; the stitch was made for a transient purpose and was always intended to be removed. Undoing it on *Shabbat* is therefore permitted. But if the garment arrived from the weaver or vendor with the neck opening never having been made — an opening that is needed to complete the garment's function — then making that opening constitutes a completion of the garment, a form of *makeh b'patish*, and is prohibited.

The analogy to suit pockets sewn shut when purchased is apt: cutting open the pocket stitching is the completing act that makes the pocket usable, and this constitutes making a vessel on *Shabbat*.

### Cloth in Cushions

The same *baraita* states: *ve-ein notnin et ha-muchin lo le-toch ha-kar ve-lo le-toch ha-kaset be-Yom Tov, ve-ein tzarich lomar be-Shabbat* — one may not place *muchin* into a cushion (*kar*) or pillow (*kaset*) on *Yom Tov*, and it goes without saying one may not do so on *Shabbat*. This ruling appears to contradict Rav Chisda's permission to replace stuffing.

The *Gemara* resolves the tension with a brief but critical distinction: *ha bachadti ha ba-atiki* — this refers to a new cushion, that to an old one. Inserting stuffing into a new cushion or pillow for the first time constitutes the making of a vessel — the *keli* did not previously exist in functional form. Re-inserting stuffing into an existing pillow from which it has fallen out is not making but restoring, and is permitted. A *baraita* confirms this explicitly: *nashru machzirin otan be-Shabbat, ve-ein tzarich lomar be-Yom Tov* — if the stuffing fell out, one may replace it on *Shabbat*, and certainly on *Yom Tov*.

### Breakage & Repair

This raises a question that is difficult to resolve with clean lines: at what point is something considered broken and its repair considered "making"? The degree to which stuffing has fallen out, the nature of the object, and the regularity with which such disassembly occurs all bear on the analysis.

A number of practical cases illustrate this difficulty. If the temple of eyeglasses falls off, reattaching it with a screw is prohibited — that constitutes a repair requiring a tool and deliberate reconstruction. For some people this happens frequently, which might alter the analysis, since a commonly recurring detachment may indicate that the parts are never truly considered permanently joined. A toothpick or other temporary fill is a different matter, and the permissibility of such improvised solutions depends on whether they genuinely restore function or merely approximate it.

The question of quantity is also raised: does it matter if half the pillow's stuffing fell out versus a small amount? The key variables remain the tightness of fit, the regularity of the occurrence, and whether what is being done constitutes a genuine act of reconstitution. An inflatable mattress or cushion presents an interesting variant: filling it with air for the first time on *Shabbat* might seem like *chadati* — making new — but since such objects are designed precisely to be filled and emptied repeatedly, the act of filling may not constitute the making of a new vessel.

A related question is raised about winding a stopped watch on *Shabbat*: is a non-functioning watch considered not-a-watch, such that restarting it is *makeh b'patish*? Since winding is a regular, recurring maintenance act, most authorities would treat it differently from genuine repair.

A puzzle presents its own set of issues. Assembling a puzzle may implicate *kotev* in the broad sense of creating an image, and if the puzzle is completed and preserved — framed or displayed — the completion could constitute *makeh b'patish*. There are additional concerns prior to reaching that threshold as well.

Rav Yehuda then states in the name of Rav: *ha-poteach beit ha-tzavar be-Shabbat, chayav chatat* — one who opens the neck hole of a new garment on *Shabbat* is liable for a *chatat* offering. This is a *melacha d'oraita*, a violation of *makeh b'patish*.

## Chibbur Debate

### Rava's Distinction

Rav Kahana challenges this ruling by asking: *mah bein zu le-megupat chavit* — how is opening the neck hole of a garment different from the seal of a barrel? The *Gemara* records in the context of barrel seals a ruling that one is permitted on *Shabbat* to open the barrel in order to access its wine. If that is permitted, why is opening the neck hole of a garment prohibited?

Rava answers: *zeh chibbur ve-zeh eino chibbur* — one is considered fully connected, the other is not.

### Rashi Explanation

Rashi explains the distinction as follows. The barrel cover (*megupah*) begins as an independent entity, separate from the barrel itself. Even though it is subsequently affixed to the barrel — *af al pi she-devuka bah* — it is not considered *chibbur* in the full sense, because it was always designed for removal: *she-harei lintol omedes*. It was placed on from the outside for a specific and temporary purpose and was never an integral part of the barrel. The garment, by contrast, was woven as a single unit — *aval ha-beged k'she-nearag kulo chibbur* — and even the closing of the neck opening was part of the initial construction of the garment, not a subsequent addition.

Tosafot offers an alternative and conceptually cleaner reading: the permitted act with the barrel is making a hole in the *cover*, not in the barrel itself. A hole in a cover does not constitute making a vessel; it makes the cover accessible, but the barrel — the actual vessel — is unaffected. Making a hole in the barrel itself would be prohibited. If the cover is not considered an integral part of the barrel as a vessel, then altering the cover is not making or completing a vessel.

### Opening Packages

This distinction has direct bearing on the question of opening packages and containers on *Shabbat*. The central principle emerging from the barrel-and-cover discussion is that making an opening in a separate cover that was not originally part of the main vessel as a single unit is different from making an opening in the vessel itself. If the top of a container — such as the sealed top of a can or the cap of a bottle — began as a separate unit that was subsequently fused or pressed on, there is more room to be lenient, since altering it is not making a hole in the vessel proper.

An additional important factor is disposability. If the container — or its cover — is designed for single use and will be discarded once emptied, it is harder to classify the opening as creating a *keli*, since a disposable container is not truly a vessel in the meaningful sense. Rav Moshe distinguishes further between a package that is discarded immediately upon being opened and one that is kept in use until its contents are exhausted. A glass jar that one washes out and reuses afterward is a stronger candidate for being considered a *keli*, while packaging that is immediately discarded is substantially more lenient.

Tearing packaging apart *derech kilkul* — in a destructive manner, with no interest in preserving the packaging as a functional container — is generally permitted, since the intent is to access the contents, not to fashion a vessel. Tearing open a bag of napkins, for instance, by ripping the plastic into pieces would not constitute making a *keli*.

### Barrel vs. Garment

To summarize the operative distinction: one who makes an opening in a garment that was woven as a single unit, completing for the first time a hole that is integral to the garment's function, has performed *makeh b'patish* and is liable. One who opens or punctures a separate cover that was attached to a vessel — particularly when the cover is not considered part of the vessel itself — has not made a *keli* and may be permitted to do so. The details of each case — whether the cover is truly separate, whether the object is disposable, and how the opening is made — determine the final ruling.

## Temporary Connections

### Three Examples

Rabbi Yirmiyah raises a challenge to Rabbi Zeira from a *baraita* dealing with temporary connections. The *baraita* presents three cases. First, *kovasin* — bundles of laundered garments from multiple owners that were stitched together with a temporary thread during the laundering process, to be separated once the laundry was complete. Second, *shalshelet shel maftechot* — a keychain on which keys were bunched together temporarily, not as a permanent arrangement. Third, a garment that had been sewn together with another garment made of a different fiber combination for transport purposes, creating a temporary instance of *kilayim* — the prohibition against mixing certain fibers — with the understanding that it would be cut apart before being worn.

All three cases involve connections that are avowedly temporary: the thread will be cut, the keychain will be disassembled, and the *kilayim* joining will be undone.

### Tumah Before Undoing

The *halacha* in all three cases is: *chibbur l'tumah ad she-yatchil l'hatir* — they are considered a single connected unit for the purposes of *tumah* until one begins to undo the connection. The practical implication is that if *tumah* touches one garment in a laundered bundle, all the joined garments become *tamei*, because they are treated as a single unit. Normally, one garment cannot convey *tumah* to another separate garment, but if they are treated as one unit, contact with any part of the unit is contact with the whole. This applies even though the connection is purely temporary.

### Hatchet Challenge

This ruling prompts a challenge from a seemingly parallel case. If one takes a stick found nearby and uses it as a makeshift handle for a hatchet head — a clearly temporary and improvised solution — that assembly is considered *chibbur l'tumah*, one unit for *tumah* purposes, but only *bish'at melacha* — during the time the hatchet is actively being used. *Shelo bish'at melacha* — once the work is done and the hatchet set aside — the stick is no longer considered connected to the hatchet head. It is as if the unit immediately reverts to its component parts once it is not in active use.

The challenge is: why does this case differ from the bundled laundry? In the laundry case, the connection is considered to persist even after the work is completed — *shelo bish'at melacha nami chibbur* — until one actively begins to undo the thread. In the hatchet case, once the work is done, the connection dissolves even without any active undoing.

### Intention Matters

Abaye resolves the contradiction by reference to intention and subjective relationship to the object. In the hatchet case, *adam asuy l'zorko l'vein ha-etzim* — a person is prepared to throw the stick into the woodpile the moment he is done working. His mind is already off the stick as a component of the hatchet as soon as he stops using it. It is mentally discarded, even if physically still attached.

In the laundry case, by contrast, *nami nicha lei* — the person actually wants the thread to remain on even after the laundering is complete. Why? Because *d'ei mitnafu, hadar mechaber lehu* — if any of the garments become soiled again, they will be laundered again as a bundle. The person has an ongoing interest in maintaining the connection. Therefore, the thread continues to be treated as a functional *chibbur* until the person actually begins to undo it.

The conceptual distinction, then, is not simply whether the work is currently being performed, but whether the person still has an active interest in maintaining the connection. Where the connection serves an ongoing potential purpose, it remains a *chibbur*. Where it has been mentally abandoned the moment the immediate task is complete, it dissolves without any physical undoing.

## Rabbi Meir Doctrine

### Oven Receptacles

The *Gemara* now asks: who is the *tanna* behind the doctrine that things which are physically connected are treated as a single unit for *tumah* purposes? This general principle — *kol ha-mechubar lo harei hu ka-moho* — underlies the entire preceding discussion. Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: it is Rabbi Meir.

The proof is from a *mishnah*. An oven (*kira*) had attached to it small holders or receptacles for oil (*beit ha-pach*), spices (*beit ha-tavlin*), and a lamp (*beit ha-ner*) — a design somewhat like small cup-holders affixed to the side of the oven. The question is whether these receptacles are considered part of the oven for *tumah* purposes.

Rabbi Meir rules: *mitam'in be-maga ve-ein mitam'in be-avir* — they become *tamei* through contact (i.e., if the *tamei* object physically touched either the oven or one of the receptacles, all become *tamei*), but they do not become *tamei* through *avir* (i.e., if an *impure* object was suspended in the air space of the oven without touching the base, the receptacles do not become *tamei* even though the oven itself does). Rabbi Shimon disagrees entirely, holding that the receptacles are always treated as separate from the oven and are never included in the oven's *tumah*.

### Meir vs. Shimon

The divide between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon tracks the basic question of whether physical connection of originally separate units creates a single halachic entity. Rabbi Meir holds that connection matters; Rabbi Shimon holds that the receptacles, being independently made and merely attached, remain independent.

### Air vs. Contact

The *Gemara* presses Rabbi Meir: if the receptacles are part of the oven, they should be *tamei* whether the *tumah* came through contact or through *avir*. If they are not part of the oven, they should not be *tamei* even through contact. What justifies the split between contact and *avir*?

### Rabbinic Enactment

The *Gemara* resolves the difficulty: *le-olam lav ke-kira damu* — in truth, the receptacles are not biblically part of the oven — *ve-Rabbanan hu de-gazru behu* — it is the Rabbis who decreed that they be treated as part of the oven. And the Rabbis deliberately constructed this unusual split — contact creates *tumah*, *avir* does not — as a *heikher*, a marker, so that people would recognize that the connection is rabbinic, not biblical. The significance of the marker: if *terumah* comes into contact with these receptacles, one should not burn the *terumah* as if it had touched a biblically *tamei* object, since the underlying *chibbur* is only *d'rabbanan*. By making the law function in an anomalous way — different from how it would work for a genuinely single vessel — the Rabbis ensured that practitioners versed in *hilchot tumah va-taharah* would recall the rabbinic status.

This principle is notable: sometimes in the laws of *tumah* and *taharah*, a split ruling is introduced deliberately to preserve the memory that a given rule is only *d'rabbanan*, thereby preventing incorrect stringencies — such as burning *terumah* — that would be inappropriate if the *tumah* is only rabbinic in origin.

Returning to the broader principle: even Rabbi Meir, who holds that connected objects form a single unit for *tumah*, does not hold this biblically. He holds it as a rabbinic decree. It would be difficult to argue that ten sewn garments are one garment *d'oraita* — they plainly are not. The *chibbur* doctrine is rabbinic throughout, and Rabbi Meir is the *tanna* behind it.

Tosafot notes the contrast between the oven-and-receptacles case and the scissors or carpenter's plane cases to follow. The receptacles and the garments are functional independently of one another; they are combined into a single unit by physical connection. The components of scissors or a plane, by contrast, do not function independently at all — they only function when assembled together. Logically, the case for treating the assembled scissors as a single biblical unit is considerably stronger, yet even there the *Gemara* will reach a conclusion that involves rabbinic dimensions.

## Scissors & Plane

### Detachable Parts

A *baraita* introduces the case of *misporet shel perakim* — scissors made of detachable components, the sort that could be routinely taken apart and reassembled. Similarly, the carpenter's plane (*rehatni*) consists of a metal blade fitted into a wooden handle; both components are regularly disassembled for storage and reassembled for use.

The *halacha* stated in the *baraita* is: *chibbur l'tumah ve-ein chibbur le-haza'ah* — when assembled, these items are considered one unit for *tumah* (contact with one component conveys *tumah* to the whole), but they are not considered one unit for *haza'ah* (when sprinkling the waters of the *parah adumah* for purification, one must ensure the water contacts both components separately).

Recall that for pottery vessels, *tumah* can be conveyed through the *avir* — an impure object suspended in the air space of the vessel without touching the base renders the entire vessel *tamei*. For metal or other vessels, *tumah* is typically conveyed through contact. For the scissors or the plane, the principle is that contact with any part of the assembly renders the whole *tamei*, because the assembly is treated as one unit. But when the time comes to purify — by having the ash-water of the *parah adumah* sprinkled upon the object — the two components must each be sprinkled separately. It is insufficient to sprinkle only one.

### Tumah Haza'ah Split

The *Gemara* raises the obvious objection: *mamma nafshach* — make up your mind. If the assembled scissors are one unit, the *haza'ah* should work by touching one component. If they are two separate units, contact with one should not convey *tumah* to the other. Why the split?

### Rava's Resolution

Rava resolves the difficulty with a principled analysis. *Devar Torah, bish'at melacha chibbur, bein l'tumah uvein le-haza'ah* — biblically, when the scissors or plane are in active use, they are one unit, both for *tumah* and for purification. *Ve-shelo bish'at melacha, eino chibbur lo l'tumah ve-lo le-haza'ah* — when not in active use, since the components are disassembled, they are two separate units, neither for *tumah* nor for purification.

That is the biblical picture: one unit during use, two units when disassembled. But the Rabbis departed from this simple scheme in both directions simultaneously. Rabbinically, the assembled scissors are treated as one unit even *shelo bish'at melacha* — even when not in use — for the purpose of *tumah*. And rabbinically, the same scissors are treated as two separate units even *bish'at melacha* — even when in active use — for the purpose of *haza'ah*.

### Final Principle

The result is a consistent asymmetry: *tumah* always treats the assembly as one unit, and *haza'ah* always treats it as two separate units, regardless of whether the scissors are currently in use. The logic, again, is that of rabbinic stringency applied in the direction appropriate to each law. Being strict about *tumah* means it is easier to become *tamei* — so the assembly is always one unit for *tumah*. Being strict about *taharah* means it is harder to become *tahor* — so the assembly always counts as two separate units, requiring that the purification water reach each component independently.

This produces a memorably clean final principle: always one for *tumah*, always two for *haza'ah*. The rabbinic enactment achieves this by extending each rule beyond its biblical scope in the direction of stringency and collapsing the biblical distinction based on *sha'at melacha*.

Tosafot observes that there is a meaningful conceptual difference between this case and the oven-and-receptacles case discussed earlier. The receptacles function independently of the oven; they are separately made objects that happen to be attached. The components of the scissors or plane, by contrast, have no independent function whatsoever — they are only useful together. This makes the case for treating them as a single biblical unit considerably more intuitive, and yet the *Gemara* still frames the full *chibbur* doctrine as rabbinic in its scope. The scissors case cannot serve as a basis for purification without addressing both components, because biblically when the tool is not in use, they are two objects, and the rabbinic stringency only operates to make *tumah* easier to acquire — not to make purification easier to achieve.

With this, the *Gemara*'s extended discussion of *chibbur*, *tumah*, and *haza'ah* — which branched out from the opening themes of *hatmanah* and the making of vessels — concludes. Tomorrow the discussion returns to *hatmanah* and the laws of *Shabbat*.

# Shabbat 49

## Moisture & Heat

### Moist Materials Intro

The daf begins at the top of 49a, several lines into an ongoing discussion of *hatmanah* — the practice of insulating food before Shabbat to retain heat. The Gemara is in the midst of treating certain materials that may be used for *hatmanah* when dry but not when moist, the assumption being that moisture interacting with the material somehow causes additional heat to be released. Among the materials cited are straw, pieces of cloth, and grass.

### Moisture Source Debate

The Gemara raises a pointed question: *lachin machmat atzman o dilma lachin machmat davar acher* — are these materials considered moist because they were originally moist by their own nature, or because they absorbed moisture from an external source? The underlying assumption appears to be that materials that absorbed moisture from elsewhere would not generate as much heat as those inherently moist. The precise science, if any underlies this, is not self-evident.

The Gemara then attempts a resolution. If we say the prohibition applies only to materials moist from an external source, that is easily understood — water was spilled on them, they absorbed it. But if we say they must be inherently moist, the question becomes: how can pieces of cloth possess their own moisture? The Gemara answers: *mimarta deven itmi* — from the wool that comes from the thigh area of the sheep, which is perpetually moist by its nature. Though one might question whether this truly qualifies as *machmat atzman* — after all, the moisture still derives from the sheep's own perspiration — the Gemara appears to accept that since it was always part of the material's original character, it counts as inherent moisture.

### Oshaya's Baraita

The Gemara then cites what Rav Oshaya taught in a *baraita*: *tomnin biksut uvefirot* — one may insulate using old clothes and dried fruit. Rashi explains that "fruit" here refers to small items such as wheat, not the large produce one might first imagine. The *baraita* continues: *aval lo bichsut lacha velo bepeirot lachin* — not with a moist garment and not with moist fruit. Once again the Gemara asks: how can a garment be considered moist from its own nature? And the same answer applies — *mimarta deven itmi* — wool from the thigh area of the sheep. The Gemara does not ultimately resolve the question of whether the prohibition on moist materials applies specifically to those moist by nature or those that absorbed moisture externally, and the matter is left open.

---

## Permitted Insulators

### Mishnah List

The Gemara moves on to the next Mishnah, which continues the discussion of which materials may be used for *hatmanah*. The Mishnah states: *tomnin biksut uvefirot bechanfei yona uvinisoret shel charashim* — one may insulate with garments, with fruit (again understood by Rashi as small items such as beans or wheat), with the feathers of a dove, and with the wood shavings or sawdust of carpenters. The Mishnah adds: *ubinuoret shel pishtan* — and also with the remnants of flax, *afilu daka* — even if fine.

### R. Yehuda Dispute

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees regarding the flax remnants. *Rabbi Yehuda oser bedaka* — Rabbi Yehuda forbids using the fine remnants, *umatir begasa* — while permitting the coarser ones. His apparent position is that fine flax remnants generate heat in a way the coarser ones do not, though precisely how is not entirely clear from the text.

The Gemara poses a subsidiary question: when Rabbi Yehuda made his distinction regarding fine versus coarse material, was he referring to the sawdust of carpenters (*nisoret shel charashim*) or to the flax remnants (*nuoret shel pishtan*)? A *baraita* resolves this: *Rabbi Yehuda oimer neores shel pishtan daka harei hu k'zevel* — Rabbi Yehuda specifically addresses the fine combings of the flax and declares them to be like excrement, meaning they are problematic as they generate heat. The Gemara concludes: *shema mina a'neores shel pishtan kai* — we learn from this that he was referring to the flax remnants. *Shema mina.*

---

## Tefillin & Purity

### Clean Body Requirement

At this point the Gemara pivots, seemingly from left field, into a discussion of *tefillin*. The connection is the phrase *kanfei yonah* — the feathers of a dove — which appeared in the Mishnah and which now provides the link to the figure of Elisha Ba'al Knafayim. Rabbi Yannai states: *tefillin tzrichin guf naki ke-Elisha ba'al knafayim* — wearing *tefillin* requires a clean body, comparable to Elisha the master of wings. What does "clean body" mean in this context?

### Abbayei vs. Rava

Abbayei says: *shelo yafiah bahen* — one must ensure not to pass gas while wearing *tefillin*. Rava adds: *shelo yishan bahen* — one must not fall asleep while wearing them, because sleep creates a *hesech hadaat*, a lapse in awareness that one is wearing *tefillin*. Rashi also raises the possibility that sleep might lead to a seminal emission; Tosafot sets that concern aside as unlikely in practice, though in principle it would be a problem.

There is then a nuanced debate between Rashi and Tosafot regarding the relationship between Abbayei's and Rava's positions — specifically, which of them is being more lenient. According to Rashi, Rava is the lenient one: Rava says we are generally not so concerned that a person will pass gas uncontrollably — people can exercise that control — but we are concerned that one might fall asleep. This reading is admittedly somewhat counterintuitive, since at any given moment one might think the risk of accidentally passing gas is at least as real as the risk of unexpectedly falling asleep.

Tosafot therefore reads the dispute differently. According to Tosafot, Rava certainly shares Abbayei's concern about passing gas; he simply adds to it the further concern about sleep. If one is tired, Rava says, do not put on *tefillin*, lest you nod off. Abbayei's position, by contrast, is that tiredness alone is insufficient reason to forgo wearing *tefillin* — only if one is genuinely worried about passing gas. The practical implication is that according to Tosafot both authorities agree that passing gas while wearing *tefillin* is prohibited; the dispute concerns how proactively one must worry that these situations might arise. Practically, the normative approach involves wearing *tefillin* only during *tefilla*, the period during which one can reasonably maintain full awareness and self-control.

### Elisha Story

The Gemara then asks: *v'amai kari lei Ba'al Knafayim* — why is this figure called "master of wings"? The story is as follows. Once the evil Roman kingdom — *malchut Romi ha-resha'ah* — issued a decree against the Jewish people: *shekol hamaniach tefillin yenakru et mocho* — whoever wears *tefillin* will have his skull pierced. Despite this decree, Elisha would don his *tefillin* and go out into the marketplace — not merely in private, but publicly, as an act of open defiance and presumably as a model for his fellow Jews not to capitulate.

A Roman officer — a *kasdor*, from the Latin *quaestor* — spotted him and gave chase. When the officer caught up to him, Elisha removed the *tefillin* from his head and held them in his closed fist. The officer demanded: *mah zeh beyadecha* — what are you holding in your hand? Elisha replied: *kanfei yonah hen* — these are merely the feathers of a dove. When he opened his hand, they had miraculously transformed into dove feathers. *Lefichach korin oto Elisha Ba'al Knafayim* — and for this reason he is called by that name. While the Gemara does not spell out explicitly how Elisha's conduct relates to the requirement of *guf naki*, the implication is that one who would publicly defy a Roman decree at mortal risk, and who so profoundly identified with the *mitzvah* of *tefillin*, would surely be the paradigm of one who wore them with complete bodily consciousness.

### Dove Symbolism

The Gemara asks: *umai shena kanfei yonah mish'ar ofot* — why specifically a dove's feathers rather than those of another bird? The answer: *mishum didmiya Knesset Yisrael leyonah* — because the congregation of Israel is compared to a dove, as the verse states *kanfei yonah nechpa vakesef*, the wings of a dove covered in silver. Just as the dove's wings protect it, so the *mitzvot* protect Israel: *af Yisrael mitzvot meginot aleihen*.

Rashi explains that dove feathers protect the bird in ways that other birds' feathers do not. Tosafot cites a Midrashic tradition: while other birds when exhausted simply come to rest on a rock, a dove when tired keeps one wing beating while resting on the other, so that even in repose it uses its wings for protection. Whether or not this reflects ornithological fact, the homiletical point stands.

### Tosafot Decline

One of the most historically significant *Tosafot* in this sugya follows. Tosafot addresses a striking social phenomenon: even among Ashkenazi Jewry, whose general level of *frumkeit* was by any measure extraordinarily high, the *mitzvah* of *tefillin* had substantially fallen by the wayside. We have corroborating evidence from other *Rishonim* of that era that *tefillin* and *mezuzah* — things we today consider absolutely basic — had become somewhat neglected.

Tosafot first attempts to address whether the requirement of *guf naki* might explain this lapse. He notes: *sheharei bezeh anu yecholim lehizaher* — you can certainly guard yourself from passing gas. You cannot use that as an excuse to exempt yourself entirely from the *mitzvah*. He then acknowledges what he will not paper over: *ve'ein litmo'ah al mah shemitzvah zo refuya beyadeinu* — one should not be astounded that this *mitzvah* is weak in our hands. He notes that this was already true in earlier generations, citing a *baraita* in the chapter of Rabbi Eliezer regarding circumcision: *kol mitzvah shelo masru atzman yisrael aleha bish'at gezeirat hamalchut kegon tfillin adayin hi refuya beyadeihem* — any *mitzvah* for which Israel did not submit themselves during a period of royal persecution, such as *tefillin*, remains weakly observed in their hands. The fact that in the time of Elisha, most of the Jewish people did not stand up to defend the wearing of *tefillin*, creates some metaphysical precedent that carries forward through the generations.

What is striking about this Tosafot is that it does not, in its typical fashion, reconcile existing practice with the *halacha* and declare it to be acceptable. On the contrary: Tosafot both tempers the criticism — acknowledging that we are not the first or last to fall short here — and simultaneously insists that one must in fact wear *tefillin*. It is a deliberately balanced posture: compassionate toward human frailty, but unwilling to legitimize the lapse.

### Removal Problem

The adjacent Tosafot — *nachmani rosho* — raises what might seem like the opposite question and is equally illuminating. Tosafot cites the principle from Sanhedrin that in a *sha'at hashmad* — when the government is actively attempting to suppress Jewish practice — one should give one's life rather than violate even a minor *mitzvah* or minor custom. Given that, Tosafot is not troubled that Elisha went out wearing *tefillin* publicly in defiance of the Roman edict; that is entirely expected and halachically required. What Tosafot finds puzzling is that he took them off at all — even when being pursued. *Aval hacha eino ose klum ela she'ein lo tfillin berosho sha'a achat* — but here he is doing nothing other than being without his *tefillin* for a moment. You must remove them eventually, and if the officer is already upon you, perhaps this is that moment.

The juxtaposition of these two *Tosafot* is arresting: one Tosafot is troubled that people in the era of the *Rishonim* were lax about *tefillin* during ordinary times; the other is troubled that Elisha removed his *tefillin* even when being chased by a Roman officer. The background to both is the Ashkenazi *Rishonim*'s profound identification with *mesirus nefesh* — indeed, Crusade-era Ashkenaz bore witness to extraordinary self-sacrifice by Jews who chose death over conversion. In that context, Tosafot reads Elisha as a figure whose model of commitment to *tefillin* should have extended even to the moment of being apprehended.

---

## Hides & Muktzeh

### Hides & Wool

The Gemara returns to *hatmanah* with the next Mishnah. One may insulate food using strips of leather or hides — *shlachim* — and these may be handled on Shabbat: *umtaltalin otan*, they are not *muktzeh*. By contrast, shearings of wool — *gizei tzemer* — may be used for insulation but may not be handled on Shabbat, since wool shearings are normally set aside for use in activities prohibited on Shabbat (such as sewing), and thus they carry *muktzeh* status. The practical result is that a pot insulated in wool shearings cannot be retrieved by directly moving the wool. What, then, does one do?

The *Tanna Kamma* says: *notel es hakisui v'hein noflos* — one simply lifts the lid of the pot and the wool falls off incidentally. This is a case of *tiltul min hatzad* — indirect movement — where one is moving the pot cover (which is not *muktzeh*) while the *muktzeh* material moves only as a consequence. Rashi raises a potential objection: should the lid of the pot not acquire the status of a *basis* — a base for *muktzeh* material — and thereby itself become *muktzeh*? Rashi resolves this by distinguishing the case: a *basis* is an object whose purpose is to support the thing resting upon it. Here, the lid exists to cover the pot below, not to support the wool above. The wool is there for the sake of the pot, not the other way around. Therefore the lid's status is unaffected and it may be moved freely.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya disputes the *Tanna Kamma*'s method. He holds that if the pot is stored inside a box filled with wool shearings, one should tip the box over on its side and allow the pot to emerge, rather than reaching in to retrieve it. His concern: once the pot is removed from the box, the wool will collapse to fill the space previously occupied by the pot, and replacing the pot afterward will be impossible. The Sages disagree and say one may simply remove the pot and return it. The nature of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's concern — whether it is a *muktzeh* problem or something else — the Gemara will address.

### Which Hides?

The scene now shifts. Rabbi Yonatan ben Akhnai and Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar were sitting together with Rabbi Chanina bar Chama, and a question arose in the group. When the Mishnah permits insulating with *shlachim* — hides — and states they may be moved on Shabbat, exactly whose hides are being discussed? Are these the hides of a *ba'al habayit*, an ordinary homeowner — in which case the hide functions like a mat or carpet, and it is obvious one would use it? Or is the Mishnah speaking even of hides belonging to a *uman*, a craftsperson — a tanner — who has set them aside for professional processing?

The concern with the tanner's hides is that he would be particular about their condition: he needs to keep them clean, cut them precisely, and deliver them to customers in proper form. Perhaps his hides therefore qualify as *muktzeh*, being designated exclusively for professional use. Or alternatively, even a craftsperson is not so particular that sitting on a hide in his storehouse constitutes misuse — in which case even his hides are not *muktzeh*.

### Yosei's Father

Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar offers his assessment: *mistavra shel ba'al habayit tenan* — it stands to reason that the Mishnah refers only to the hides of a homeowner. A craftsperson's hides, by contrast, are *muktzeh* because of his *hakpadah* — his insistence on maintaining their condition.

Rabbi Chanina bar Chama then contributes a tradition: *kach amar Rabbi Yishmael b'Rebbi Yosei* — this is what Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, reported. *Abba shalkha havah* — his father, Rabbi Yosei, was a tanner.
