The message, as Rashi explains, was: *denigrei dechamra sha'arei* — the stepping of a donkey is barley, meaning: do not go to the trouble and expense of acquiring fancy Libyan donkeys; buy donkeys locally, feed them well, and save yourself the difficulty. This digression highlights, incidentally, that these Libyan donkeys were a significant investment — possibly wilder or less tractable — which contextualizes why they required the more substantial *pagi*.

---

## Sufficient Protection

### Switching Accessories

In the name of Shmuel, Rav Yehuda raises the question of whether the accessories specified for particular animals may be switched — whether animal A may go out with the equipment designated for animal B and vice versa.

### Four Animals Bit

Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosi responds in the name of his father: *arba behemot yotzot be'afsa* — four animals go out with a bit: the horse, the mule, the camel, and the donkey.

### Naaka Limitation

The question is what this statement excludes. It does not seem to limit the equipment used for these four animals — it does not say these animals may *only* use a bit and nothing more. Rather, it limits which animals a bit is *sufficient* for. A *naaka* — a white female camel — cannot go out with merely a bit. *Keivan d'la mintra bei, masui hu* — since the bit does not adequately protect or control it, putting a bit on this animal is considered a *masui*, a burden with no protective function. It is as if one placed a random object on the animal.

### Braita Debate

The deeper question is raised by the *braita*: *ein chaya yotzet be'soger* — an animal may not go out with a *soger*, a collar. *Chananya omer: yotza be'soger u'v'chol davar ha'mishtamer* — Chananya rules that it may go out with a collar and with anything else that protects it.

### Excess = Burden

What is the case under discussion? It is not a large, dangerous animal — a collar would obviously be insufficient for that, and the *Tanna Kamma* would not need to prohibit it on grounds of being a burden. Rashi suggests it is a small animal. But if it is a small animal, a collar is exactly the right control mechanism. The Gemara concludes that the case is a cat. Rashi notes that cats *she'einan ta'avim livroa'ch kol kach* — are not particularly inclined to run away — and therefore a simple string or cord would suffice. Given that, a full collar is *netiruta yeteira* — excessive protection — and the *Tanna Kamma* holds that excessive protection is in the category of *masui*: it has no necessary protective function relative to the animal's actual needs, and is therefore treated as a burden.

### Chananya View

Chananya disagrees: *kol netirot yeteira lo amrinan masui hu* — even excessive protection does not constitute a burden. The item is still *doing something* — it is genuinely protective, albeit more than strictly necessary. The fact that a simpler measure would have sufficed does not convert the more robust measure into something categorically different from protection.

### Cat Case

The Gemara thus understands the dispute between the *Tanna Kamma* and Chananya to hinge precisely on *netiruta yeteira*: the *Tanna Kamma* holds that where something simpler would suffice, the more elaborate protective measure crosses the line into *masui*; Chananya holds that any genuinely protective measure, regardless of whether a lesser one would do, retains its character as *levush* and is not a burden.

---

## Halakha & Example

### Halakha = Chananya

Rav Huna bar Chiya rules in the name of Shmuel: *halacha ke'Chananya* — the *halacha* follows Chananya. Even *netiruta yeteira*, protection that exceeds what is strictly necessary, does not constitute a *masui*.

### Donkey Story

The Gemara closes with a charming narrative. Levi the son of Rav Huna bar Chiya and Rabba bar Rav Huna were traveling together on the road. Levi's donkey moved ahead of Rabba bar Rav Huna's donkey. Rabba bar Rav Huna was clearly the senior figure, and the donkey's moving ahead was perceived as a slight — as if Levi were not according Rabba bar Rav Huna the proper deference. *Chalash daiteih de'Rabba bar Rav Huna* — Rabba bar Rav Huna was hurt.

### Clever Response

Levi perceived this and wished to set things right without making the discomfort more pronounced. His solution was elegant. He turned to Rabba bar Rav Huna and posed a *halachic* question: if one has a rebellious donkey — *chamor she'askav ra'in* — one that does not behave, one that moves ahead on its own as this one just did, *mahu litzet be'pumbiya b'Shabbat* — may such a donkey go out on *Shabbat* with a *pumbiya*, a halter, even though an ordinary donkey might not require one?

### Respect & Halakha

The move accomplished two things at once. It made clear that the donkey's behavior was not intentional on Levi's part — the animal was, as he put it, a rebellious donkey that moved of its own accord. And it placed Levi in the position of *talmid* asking a *shaila* of his *rav*, making the hierarchy visible and respectful.

Rabba bar Rav Huna responded: *hachi amar avuch mishmei de'Shmuel* — this is what your father said in the name of Shmuel — *halacha ke'Chananya*. The ruling follows Chananya, and therefore a rebellious donkey that requires stronger control may indeed go out with a halter on *Shabbat*, since even a more-than-necessary protective measure is not a *masui*. Whether Rabba bar Rav Huna's mood fully lifted the text does not say — but presumably it did.

---

---

# Shabbat 53

## Rings: Tumah vs Shabbat

### Collars & Tumah

The previous amud had concluded a discussion of the *mishna*'s ruling that various *kolarim* — animal collars — may be immersed without being removed from the animal's neck. The *Gemara* had raised two difficulties. First, how can a collar be *tamei*, given that it is used for an animal rather than a person? The *Gemara* offered two responses: either the collar had originally served as a person's necklace and thereby retained its status as a *kli*, or it is considered a human implement insofar as a person uses it to control the animal. Second, why does the collar not constitute a *chatzitza* when it surrounds the animal's neck during immersion? Again, two answers were offered: either the collar was widened and therefore sits loosely, or it is fashioned as a chain with many gaps and therefore does not interpose.

### Student's Ring Question

In the midst of these discussions touching on both *tumah* of *kelim* and the laws of carrying on *Shabbat*, the *Gemara* introduces two illustrative exchanges. A student from the Upper Galilee asked Rabbi Eliezer: *shemati shecholkin bein tabaat l'tabaat* — I have heard that there is a distinction between different types of rings. Rabbi Eliezer replied: perhaps you heard this only with respect to *Shabbat* — *shema lo shamata le'inyan Shabbat* — for as will be established in the next chapter, a ring bearing a seal may not be worn on *Shabbat*, whereas a ring without a seal may be worn. That distinction, however, applies only to *Shabbat*. As for the laws of *tumah*, *d'leinyan tumah davar echad hi* — it is all the same *halacha*.

### Animal vs Human Rings

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this claim. Is it truly the case that all rings are identical for purposes of *tumah*? Surely the *mishna* teaches otherwise: *tabaat adam t'mea* — a ring made for a person is *tamei* as a *kli* — whereas *tabaat behemah v'kelim*, a ring made for an animal or for ornamentation of a vessel, *tehorot* — is *tahor*. There is plainly a distinction in *tumah* as well.

The *Gemara* resolves this: when Rabbi Eliezer said all rings are the same for *tumah*, he was speaking specifically about rings intended for human use, not animal rings or ornamental rings. The discussion therefore narrows to human rings.

### Metal & Wood Rings

But the *Gemara* presses further. Is it truly the case that all human rings are treated identically? A *mishna* teaches: *tabaat shel matechet v'chotama shel almog* — a metal ring with a cedar seal is *tamei*, because the ring is defined by the band that encircles the finger, and a metal *kli* is *tamei*. However, *shel almog v'chotama shel matechet* — a cedar ring with a metal seal is *tahor*, because the ring is then classified as a wooden vessel, and a wooden vessel is not *tamei* unless it has a receptacle, which this does not.

The *Gemara* again retreats: Rabbi Eliezer meant only that all metal finger rings are the same. And this, finally, is where the *Shabbat* distinction re-enters: all metal finger rings are indeed equivalent for *tumah*, but for *Shabbat*, whether the ring bears a seal or not determines whether one may carry it into the public domain.

### Seal on Rings

The upshot of the exchange is that the student had likely encountered the *Shabbat* distinction and misapplied it to *tumah*. The *Gemara* carefully threads through multiple layers — ring for animal versus human, belt-hook ring versus finger ring, metal versus wooden ring — before arriving at the precise scope of Rabbi Eliezer's claim. The ongoing comparison between *tumah* law and *Shabbat* law illustrates that while both depend on the definition of *kli*, the operative categories are not always identical.

---

## Needles: Tumah vs Shabbat

### Needle Question

The student posed a second question to Rabbi Eliezer: *shamati shecholkin bein machat lemachat* — I have heard that there is a distinction between types of needles. Rabbi Eliezer responded as before: perhaps you heard this only regarding *Shabbat* — *shema lo shamata le'inyan Shabbis* — for on *Shabbat*, carrying a standard needle with an eye constitutes a prohibited act of carrying, whereas a needle without an eye, fashioned as a decorative pin worn on a garment, functions as a *tachshit* — an ornament — and one who wears it is not liable. When it comes to *tumah*, however, *da veda achas hi* — both types of needle are treated the same.

### Eye in Needle

The *Gemara* challenges this. Is it really true that all needles are the same for *tumah*? The *mishna* teaches: *machat shenital churah o uktzah* — if a needle has had its eye or its point removed, it is *tehorah*. A non-functional needle is no longer a *kli* and cannot become *tamei*. So needles are not universally equivalent for *tumah* purposes. The *Gemara* refines: Rabbi Eliezer meant only a complete, functional needle. Are all complete needles then the same?

### Rusty Needles

Not necessarily. Another *mishna* teaches: *machat she'alsah chaludah* — a needle that has rusted — *im me'akev es hasefirah tehorah* — if the rust prevents sewing, it is *tehorah*; *ve'im lav tameia* — if not, it is *tamei*. The school of Rabbi Yannai further explained that this applies *vehu sherishumo nikar* — only if the rust leaves a noticeable mark when sewing, rendering the needle unusable. So even a complete needle may be *tahor* if corroded to the point of dysfunction. The *Gemara* refines again: Rabbi Eliezer meant a complete, polished needle.

### Polished Needles

Even this category requires examination.

### Holes & Movement

A *Baraita* teaches: *machat, bein nekuvah bein einah nekuvah, mutar letaltelah beShabbos* — a needle, whether it has a hole or not, may be moved on *Shabbat*. The reason: even a needle with an eye is classified as a *kli shemelachto le'issur*, an implement primarily used for a prohibited act (sewing). Such an implement may be moved *letzorech atzmo uletzorech mekomo* — for its own use or to clear its space.

### Needle Other Uses

Concretely: if one wishes to use the needle to pick one's teeth, that is a permitted use on *Shabbat*. As a *kli shemelachto le'issur*, it may be moved for a *letzorech hetter*, a permitted purpose, and so in either case — with or without an eye — *muktzah* does not apply.

### Hole Matters for Tumah

The *Baraita* then specifies: *velo amrinan nekuvah* — the distinction between a needle with a hole and one without is relevant *ela le'inyan tumah bilvad* — only for the laws of *tumah*. A needle with an eye is a *kli*; one without is not. This seems to directly contradict Rabbi Eliezer's claim that all needles are the same for *tumah*.

The *Gemara* resolves this through Abaye's explanation in the name of Rava: *begalmi* — the case of a needle without an eye being *tahor* refers to an unfinished needle, one still in the process of being fashioned, where the eye has not yet been formed. When Rabbi Eliezer said all needles are equivalent for *tumah*, he meant fully finished needles. Among finished needles, there are two varieties — one with an eye and one without (the pin-type ornament). For *tumah*, both finished types are treated as a *kli* and are *tamei*. For *Shabbat*, however, the ornamental pin may be worn without constituting carrying, while the sewing needle may not.

The broader lesson of both exchanges — rings and needles — is that the definition of *kli* is operative in multiple domains: *tumah*, *muktzah*, and the prohibition of carrying on *Shabbat*. Yet the precise application of that definition differs across these areas, and care must be taken not to import distinctions from one area into another.

---

## Animals & Shabbat Gear

### Mishna: Animals

The *Gemara* now turns to the next *mishna*, which returns to the question of what animals may wear when going out on *Shabbat*. The governing principle is that an animal may bear items that serve to protect or control it, but not things deemed superfluous — those would constitute a *massa*, a burden. The *mishna* states:

A donkey — *chamor* — may go out with a *marda'at*, a saddle cloth, *bizman she'kshura bo* — when it is tied onto the animal. Rams may go out *bilvuvin* — bound, with either their genitals or their hearts covered, as a standard protective measure. Female sheep may go out in three modes: held up to allow the rams access, bound down to prevent it, or with their wool covered to protect it. Goats may go out *tzerurot* — bound — for reasons we will explore, primarily related to protecting their udders or nursing arrangements.

### Disputes on Gear

Rabbi Yose says *oser bekulan* — he forbids all of these cases — *chutz min ha'rechelim ha'kevunot*, with the sole exception of sheep whose wool is covered. Rabbi Yehuda draws a finer distinction: *izim yotzot tzerurot leyavesh aval lo lachalav* — goats may go out with their udders bound if the purpose is to cause them to dry up from lactation, but not if the purpose is to catch the milk and prevent it from going to waste. The significance of these distinctions will be unpacked as the *Gemara* addresses each case.

One might pause to reflect on what this entire chapter means in practice. To modern readers much of this *perek* seems remote — we are unfamiliar with the animals, the equipment, the terminology. Yet for *Rishonim* like *Tosafot*, who kept horses, cattle, and donkeys, these were live questions. And beyond the practical details, there is something striking about what this *perek* implies for the texture of *Shabbat* preparation. The *perek* sits in the middle of a larger sequence dealing with getting ready for *Shabbat*: lighting candles, managing food on the fire, and now — attending to one's animals. Every *Erev Shabbat*, before *Shabbat* began, one would need to go to the stable and remove from one's animals all the extraneous items they could not bear into *Shabbat*. The commandment not to have one's animals work on *Shabbat* extended to this careful preparation — freeing the animals, in a sense, to have their own form of *Shabbat*.

If one's animal went out into *reshut harabim* bearing a prohibited item, the violation would rest on the owner. The imperative to ensure this did not happen meant actively checking and readying one's livestock as part of the *Erev Shabbat* routine.

### Erev Shabbat Prep

The *Gemara* continues. Shmuel states: *ve'hu she'kshura me'erev Shabbat* — the permission for the donkey to go out with the saddle cloth applies only when it was tied onto the animal before *Shabbat* began. Rav Nachman adds that this can be inferred from the *mishna* itself, since the next *mishna* — which presents the mirror image of prohibited cases — states: *ein ha'chamur yotzei be'marda'at bizman she'eina kshura lo* — a donkey may not go out with a saddle cloth when it is not bound to it.

### Tied Before Shabbat

The *Gemara* asks: what does this mean? If it means not tied at all, *peshita* — that is obvious — because it will likely fall off (*dilma nafla lei*) and one will come to carry it (*ve'ati le'atuyei*). Rather, it must mean tied, but not tied before *Shabbat* began. From which we infer — *michlal de'reisha* — that the permission in the first *mishna* means tied from *Erev Shabbat*. *Shema mina* — the inference is confirmed.

### Falling & Carrying

This discussion crystallizes an important structural point about the entire chapter. There are two distinct categories of prohibition regarding what animals (and, as we will see in the next chapter, people) may bear on *Shabbat*. The first is that the item itself does not qualify as a legitimate form of clothing or protection for that species, and therefore wearing it constitutes a form of carrying even while it remains on the body — just as wearing a knapsack is still carrying. The second is that the item would be permissible in principle, but there is concern it will fall off, leading one to inadvertently pick it up and carry it — a rabbinic concern. The first category involves a biblical violation; the second is rabbinic. Both are operative throughout this *perek*.

### Why Before Shabbat

Why does it matter specifically that the saddle cloth be tied before *Shabbat* begins? Several explanations are offered. Rashi suggests that tying it on *Shabbat* itself gives the act the character of placing a burden on the animal, not merely protecting it — and this definitional shift may be significant halachically, even if in other contexts the timing of placing an item does not ordinarily determine its category. *Tosafot* offers a similar reasoning framed in terms of appearance: tying it on *Shabbat* makes it look to onlookers as though one is preparing the animal to transport a load.

### Weekday Appearance

*Tosafot* adds a third explanation attributed to Rav Porat: *de'meichezi ke'ilu mitkaven le'holich behemah le'makom rachok* — it looks as though one intends to lead the animal on a long journey. This concern recurs at several points in the chapter and is best understood not merely as *maris ayin* — the concern about how an act appears to others — but as what might be called *uvda de'chol*, the creation of a distinctly weekday atmosphere on *Shabbat*. Standing in one's barn, saddling up the donkey, tying things onto it on *Shabbat* — that is precisely what one does during the week when preparing for a journey. Even if there is no issue of carrying, even if no *melacha* is involved, this kind of activity jars against the spirit of *Shabbat*. The *Gemara* therefore permits this only when the preparation was completed before *Shabbat* began.

---

## Saddle vs Cloth

### Backyard Question

The *Gemara* now asks a further question: even setting aside the issue of going out into *reshut harabim* — may one place a saddle cloth on a donkey on *Shabbat* within one's own backyard, where there is no carrying concern? Rashi clarifies that this is the precise question being posed. If the concern is purely about going into the street, tying before *Shabbat* addresses that. But what about the act of placing the cloth in the first place, even at home?

### Cloth vs Saddle

Rav Assi bar Natan posed this question to Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Ashi. Rabbi Chiyya answered: *mutar* — it is permitted. Rav Assi pressed: *u'mah bein zu l'uchaf* — what is the difference between the saddle cloth and a saddle? A saddle may not be placed on the donkey even in the backyard. Rabbi Chiyya had no answer and fell silent.

### Saddle Muktzah

Rav Assi then demonstrated the stringency of the saddle's status. If a saddle is already on a donkey, *lo yitlenu be-yado* — one may not simply remove it by hand, because the saddle itself is *muktzah*. To remove it, *molikho umevi'o be-chatzer ve-hi nofel me-eleiha* — one moves the donkey back and forth in the yard until it falls off on its own. The saddle's *muktzah* status makes clear that placing it on the animal is also forbidden. So why is the saddle cloth different?

### Feed Basket OK

Rabbi Zeira intervened on behalf of Rabbi Chiyya: *hana'ch le-shavtei ke-rabbeih sevira lei* — leave him alone, he holds like his teacher Rav. For Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi had himself transmitted in Rav's name: *tolin traska le-vehema be-Shabbos* — one may hang a feed basket on an animal on *Shabbat*. This refers to the kind of bucket that attaches to a horse's head, allowing it to eat without bending down. *Ve-kol she-ken le-marda'as* — and certainly one may put on a saddle cloth, which does something even more necessary for the animal by keeping it warm.

### Pleasure vs Pain

Rabbi Zeira elaborates on the logic: *u-mah hatam de-mishum ta'anug shari* — if putting on the feed basket, which merely makes the animal's eating more pleasant, is already permitted, then *hacha de-mishum tza'ar lo kol she-ken* — when the purpose is to relieve pain or cold, certainly it should be permitted. Reading *Tosafot*'s approach, the underlying question throughout these cases is: how much effort may one exert on *Shabbat* for the sake of one's animal, when the effort involves no *melacha*? The answer seems to be that effort to alleviate pain (*tza'ar*) is clearly sanctioned, and even effort for the animal's pleasure (*ta'anug*) may be permitted — at least according to Rav.

### Feed Basket No

Shmuel, however, disagrees. *Marda'as mutar* — the saddle cloth is permitted; *ve-traska assur* — the feed basket is forbidden. It is an unnecessary exertion. When Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef conveyed Rav's position to Shmuel — that not only the saddle cloth but even the feed basket is permitted — Shmuel replied sharply: *lo yada be-millei de-Shabbata ve-lo kelum* — he knows nothing about the laws of *Shabbat*.

### Agreement on Cloth

When Rabbi Zeira later went up to Eretz Yisrael, he found Rav Binyamin bar Yephet teaching in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *nosnin marda'as al gabei chamor be-Shabbos* — one may place a saddle cloth on a donkey on *Shabbat*. Rabbi Zeira responded with *yasher*, an expression of approbation. The *Gemara* then notes that the same ruling was transmitted by *Arvach* — that is, Shmuel — in Bavel. But since Rav also permits the saddle cloth, why attribute the teaching specifically to Shmuel? The *Gemara* concludes that Shmuel's version of the ruling was distinguished by its ending: *ve'ein tolin traska be-Shabbat* — but one may not hang the feed basket on *Shabbat*. That final clause — permitting the cloth but prohibiting the basket — is what made Shmuel's formulation distinctive and worth attributing to him specifically.

The *Gemara* then notes that all opinions agree: *marda'at mutar* — the saddle cloth is permitted. The remaining question is what distinguishes it from the saddle. The *Gemara* offers one answer: *shani hasam d'efshar d'nafal mimaila* — the saddle is different because it is liable to fall off, and one may come to carry it. Rav Papa offers another answer: the saddle cloth is to warm the animal, and if the animal is cold that constitutes genuine *tza'ar* justifying the effort, whereas removing the saddle is ostensibly to cool the animal — and a donkey, people say, remains cold even in the heat of *Tekufat Tammuz* — so there is less urgency. Rashi clarifies that this second answer pertains specifically to *removing* the saddle, not placing it. Why placing the saddle is prohibited is perhaps better captured by the earlier intuition: a saddle, more than any other item, signals that one is preparing the animal for a journey or loading it with a burden, and that impression alone — whether framed as *muktzah* or as *uvda de'chol* — is sufficient to prohibit it.

---

## Foals & Pain

### Baraita Foals

The *Gemara* cites a *Baraita* listing further cases: *lo yetzei ha-sus biznav shual* — a horse may not go out with a fox tail hung from its head as ornament; not with a red string between its eyes. These are superfluous decorations. The *Baraita* also teaches: *velo syachin b'traskalin shebefihem, l'reshut harabim* — young foals may not go out into the public domain with feed baskets attached to their mouths.

### Backyard OK

The *Gemara* draws an inference: *l'reshut harabim hu delo* — it is specifically into the public domain that they may not go, *ha bechatzer shapir dami* — but in the courtyard it is fine. This supports Rav's position that the feed basket is permitted, at least in the backyard. The *Gemara* then asks: are we speaking of older foals, and the permission is based on *ta'anug* — mere pleasure — thereby proving Rav correct?

### Pain Justifies

The *Gemara* answers: *lo, biktannim* — no, we are speaking of very young foals. *U-mishum tza'ar* — and the reason is pain. A newborn foal has long legs and a relatively small head; bending down to eat requires significant effort and causes real discomfort. Attaching a feed basket to allow the foal to eat without bending is therefore not merely a convenience but a genuine alleviation of suffering. The *Gemara* confirms this reading: *dumya de-kame'a* — it is analogous to the amulet case, which will shortly be shown to involve relieving pain. *Shema mina* — the inference holds. This is consistent with Shmuel's framework: effort for *ta'anug* is forbidden, but effort for *tza'ar* is sanctioned.

---

## Amulets for Animals

### Amulets Forbidden

The *Gemara* returns to the *Baraita*: *velo b'kame'a, af al pi shehu mumcheh* — an animal may not go out with an amulet, even a tested one, and this is stricter than the rule for humans (*zeh chomer b'behemah mibe'adam*). The earlier *mishna*, by contrast, states that a person may not go out with an untested amulet — *she'eino mumcheh* — implying that a tested amulet is permitted for a person.

### Luck & Amulets

The *Gemara* initially reads the *Baraita* as saying an animal cannot use even a tested amulet. But then it refines: *mumcheh le-adam ve-eino mumcheh le-behemah* — the amulet has been tested for humans but not for animals. An amulet tested to help a human will not necessarily help an animal. *Adam de-it lei mazla* — a person has fortune (*mazal*), and the amulet works in conjunction with that. *Behemah de-leit lah mazla* — an animal lacks that fortune, and so *lo mesaye lah* — the amulet does not help it. The rules are therefore structurally parallel: each species may use only an amulet tested for that species. This principle raises interesting broader questions about amulets and about the concept of *mazal*, which the *Gemara* leaves aside here.

The *Gemara* asks: if the rules are parallel, in what sense is the animal's case stricter? The answer: *a-sandal kai* — the stringency refers to shoes, not to amulets. A person may go out wearing shoes; an animal may not, because the shoe is liable to fall off.

### Shoes Stricter

This concludes the discussion of amulets and introduces the general principle that certain items, however purposeful, remain prohibited for animals due to the risk of falling off and prompting carrying — the second category of rabbinic prohibition noted earlier.

---

## Animal Medicine

### No Anointing

The *Gemara* now examines a series of cases related to medical treatment for animals. The *Baraita* teaches: *sachin u-mefarchasin le-adam* — one may anoint and scrape a wound for a person, *ve-ein sachin u-mefarchasin le-behemah* — but one may not do so for an animal. The initial question is whether this prohibition applies even when there is a genuine wound causing pain — which would seem to contradict the principle that *tza'ar* justifies effort. The *Gemara* resolves this: the case is *di-gemar maka* — the wound has already healed, leaving only a scab. Scratching or scraping the scab is thus for *ta'anug* — pleasure — not to relieve genuine suffering. This is therefore consistent with Shmuel's ruling and does not extend the prohibition to cases of actual pain.

### Blood Clots

A further case: *behemah she-achaza dam* — if an animal has a blood clot — *ein ma'amidin otah be-mayim bishvil she-titzztanen* — one does not immerse it in water to help dissolve the clot. But *adam she-achazo dam* — if a person has such a condition — *ma'amidin oto be-mayim bishvil she-yitztanen* — one may immerse him in water for relief. Why is the human case permitted but not the animal's?

### Spices Concern

Ulla explains: *gezeirah mishum shechikat samamanim* — it is a rabbinic decree because of the concern it will lead to grinding spices, i.e., preparing medicinal ingredients. The general rabbinic prohibition against taking medicine on *Shabbat* (*refuah*) exists specifically to prevent the grinding of medicinal spices. The question extends to various non-pharmacological forms of healing — stretches, massage, hydrotherapy — and whether they fall within this rabbinic concern. Here, the *Gemara* concludes that immersing an animal in water for therapeutic purposes is recognizably an act of *refuah* and is therefore prohibited by this decree.

For a person, however, *adam nireh ke-meikar* — a person getting into cool water appears to onlookers simply as cooling off, not as medical treatment. The therapeutic purpose is not apparent, and therefore the decree does not apply. Why not apply the same reasoning to an animal? *Ein meikar le-behemah* — people do not ordinarily immerse their animals in water for cooling; it is not a normal practice. Therefore, when one does it, it is obviously for therapeutic reasons, and the prohibition applies.

### Calling Animal

The *Gemara* then asks: do we in fact apply such decrees to animals? A *Baraita* teaches: *hayeta omedet chutz litchum, koreh la ve-hia ba'ah* — if one's animal is outside one's *tchum*, one may call it and it will come. *Ve-lo gazrinan dilma ati le'atuyei* — and we do not worry that the owner will go outside the *tchum* to retrieve it. This suggests that we do not extend rabbinic precautions to animal-related scenarios.

Ravina resolves the contradiction: the case in the *Baraita* is one where *tchum shelo muvla betoch tchum shelo* — the animal's legitimate space is embedded within the owner's space. The owner may walk to where the animal is. The only prohibition would be physically leading the animal back into the owner's area, since doing so would remove the animal from the space defined by its shepherd's location at the onset of *Shabbat*. Calling the animal and allowing it to come on its own avoids this. The concern in that case is thus minimal and specific, which is why no further decree was added. By contrast, the concern about *shechikat samamanim* is a broader, more general rabbinic category that does apply to animal treatment.

### Disputed Medicine

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds a further layer: *shechikat samamanim gufah tana'i hi* — the question of whether a given act falls within the prohibited category of *refuah* is itself a matter of *tannaic* dispute. A *Baraita* teaches: *behemah she'achlah karshinim* — if an animal has eaten vetch (a grain harmful to it) — *lo yeritzennah bechatzer bishvil she-titrapeh* — one may not jog it in the yard to help it pass the food, for that constitutes *refuah*.

### Jogging Allowed

However, *Rabbi Yoshia* — rendered here as *Rabbi Yoshi* — disagrees and permits it. *Rava* ruled: *halachah ke-Rabbi Yoshia*. Rashi explains that Rabbi Yoshia's leniency rests on the distinction that jogging is not a medicinal act but rather a physical form of care — *refuah* in a non-pharmacological sense — and therefore does not fall within the decree. As noted, this distinction carries significant practical implications for people as well: whether non-medicinal therapeutic activities such as physical exercise or stretching are permitted on *Shabbat* depends precisely on where one draws this line.

---

## Goat Coverings

### Udder Protection

The *Gemara* returns to the final case of the *mishna* and *Baraita*: goats going out with coverings over their udders. The *Baraita* states that they may not go out — *velo izin b'khis shebadadeihem* — with receptacles beneath their udders. Yet another *Baraita* says they may. Rav Yehuda resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, ha de'mehedak ve'ha de'lo mehedak* — there is no difficulty; the difference depends on whether the covering is tight or loose. Rashi's reading is that a loose covering is likely to fall off, leading one to carry it — the familiar second category of prohibition.

### Dry vs Catch

Rav Yosef objects: one cannot simply pick two *tanna'im* at random and declare their views in conflict — the contradiction is between positions of the same *tanna'im*. The *Gemara* cites the *mishna* itself: Rabbi Yose forbids in all cases except sheep covering their wool; Rabbi Yehuda permits goats going out *tzerurot leyavesh* — bound to dry the udders — but not *lachalav* — not to catch the milk. Another resolution: both the permitting and prohibiting *Baraitot* reflect Rabbi Yehuda's position, and the distinction is precisely *leyavesh* versus *lachalav*.

The significance of Rabbi Yehuda's distinction involves at least two considerations. First, tightness: a covering designed to dry the udder would be fastened tightly, reducing the risk of falling off. A covering designed to catch milk would be looser. Second, purpose: a covering that promotes drying serves the animal's welfare — an animal that is no longer nursing but continues to lactate may experience discomfort, and assisting the drying process is a genuine act of care for the animal. By contrast, a covering designed to catch milk serves the owner's economic interest, not the animal's needs, and therefore cannot be classified as protection for the animal. On this reading, it would constitute carrying.

### Antioch Goats

The *Gemara* cites a teaching from Rabbi Yehuda himself: *ma'aseh be-izei beit antukhya she-hayu dadeihen gasim* — there was a story with the goats of Antioch whose udders were very large, and their nipples were so long that they dragged on the ground. Coverings were fashioned for them *kedei she-lo yisretu dadeihem* — so that the udders would not be scraped and wounded. This case is clearly a protective measure for the animal's benefit.

### Three Purposes

The three purposes that emerge from the discussion — drying the udder, catching the milk, and protecting the udder from scraping — map onto distinct halachic categories. Drying: tight, for the animal's benefit, permitted. Catching milk: loose, for the owner's benefit, forbidden. Preventing scraping: clearly protective, analogous to a bandage, and seemingly permitted in all views. The tight-versus-loose distinction thus encodes not merely a practical concern about falling off, but a deeper judgment about whose interests the covering serves and whether it constitutes genuine protection for the animal or an economic device for the owner.

---

---

# Shabbat 54

## Nursing Father

### Story Setup

The daf begins toward the bottom of 53b, with a *baraisa* introduced by *tanu rabbanan*: *ma'aseh b'echad she-meisah ishto v'henichah ben l'yanek v'lo hayah lo sechar yenikah litten* — a certain man whose wife died left behind a child who still needed to nurse, and he lacked the means to hire a wet nurse. *V'na'aseh lo neis v'niftachu lo dadin k'shnei dadei ishah v'heinik et b'no* — a miracle occurred, and he developed breasts like a woman's and nursed his son.

### Rav Yosef's View

Rav Yosef responds to this story with wonder: *bo re'eh kamah gadol adam zeh she-na'aseh lo neis kazeh* — come and see how great this person is, that such an extraordinary miracle occurred to transform the normal workings of nature on his behalf.

### Abaye's Counter

Abaye demurs sharply: *adarabbah, kamah garua adam zeh she-nishtanu lo sidrei bereishit* — on the contrary, how lowly is this person that the order of creation had to be altered for his sake.

### Theology Debate

This exchange opens a genuinely striking theological question. On one level, the debate turns on how one should regard obvious supernatural intervention in the present era. One view celebrates such a miracle as a mark of divine favor; the opposing view holds that in our time, God works within nature rather than by overriding it, and that a miracle of this magnitude — the transformation of a man's body across biological lines — is cause for concern rather than admiration. The issue may also be more personal: that a man's body underwent something akin to a female physiological change, which itself could be the source of Abaye's discomfort. The two framings — one broadly theological, one specific to this individual — need not be mutually exclusive.

### Earning Livelihood

Rav Yehudah draws his own conclusion from the story: *bo re'eh kamah kashin mezonotav shel adam she-nishtanu lo sidrei bereishit* — come and see how difficult it is for a person to earn a livelihood, such that rather than God arranging for this man to find work, the order of creation itself had to change so he could feed his child. The miracle, on this reading, is not a sign of greatness but a testament to the extraordinary difficulty of *parnasah*. Other passages in the *gemara* similarly acknowledge how grueling it can be for people to find sustenance, and this observation fits within a broader Talmudic awareness of the economic hardships faced even in relatively stable periods.

### Rav Nachman's Point

Rav Nachman adds a corroborating observation: *teida de-misrachei shineitav v'lo ivru mezonot* — one can see that miracles of other kinds occur, and yet *mezonot*, adequate sustenance, still does not come. Whatever miraculous things may happen in a person's life, the difficulty of *parnasah* remains. Easier, it seems, for other types of miracles to occur than for God to simply arrange someone's livelihood.

### Scientific Evidence

It is worth noting that modern science offers some context for the physiological dimension of this story. *Scientific American* has reported that males can indeed lactate, possessing all the necessary biological equipment, and that the relevant hormone release can sometimes be triggered by severe undernourishment. The *gemara* itself emphasizes that this man had no money and could not find work — conditions consistent with starvation. At least one ancient literary parallel appears in Tolstoy's *Anna Karenina*, where an Englishman aboard a ship nurses a child. The convergence of the Talmudic account with this scientific possibility does not resolve the theological debate, but it adds an interesting dimension to a story that might otherwise seem purely legendary.

---

## Disabled Woman

### Narrative Setup

A second *baraisa* follows: *ma'aseh b'adam echad shenasah isha gidemet* — a certain man married a woman who was missing an arm. *Velo hikkir bah ad yom motah* — and he did not come to know this about her until the day she died.

### Woman's Modesty

Rav's initial response is admiration for the woman: *bo re'ei kama tzenuah isha zu she-lo hikkir bah ba'alah* — see how modest this woman was, that her own husband never discovered her condition throughout their entire life together.

### Husband's Modesty

Rabbi Chiyya challenges this framing. *Zu drakah bekach* — this is simply her way; women in general incline toward modesty, and a woman with something to conceal has additional reason to be careful. The true *chiddush*, Rabbi Chiyya argues, lies elsewhere: *ella kama tzenua adam zeh she-lo hikkir b'ishto* — how modest is this husband, who never came to see his wife fully. He followed her lead, or perhaps he himself was sufficiently restrained in his own conduct that he simply never sought to see her completely.

### Marital Context

This *gemara* sits in some tension with other passages that discuss marital intimacy. There are *gemarot* elsewhere that suggest the biblical obligation of *onah* entails sleeping together without clothing — not merely the act of intimacy itself. Reconciling those teachings with the apparent praise here for a husband who never looked at his wife carefully enough to notice a missing arm requires careful attention to the range of Talmudic attitudes toward nakedness and modesty within marriage.

### Functional Achievement

One student offered a reading that the *gemara* itself may not foreground but is nonetheless worth considering: perhaps *shelo hikkir bah* carries a broader connotation — not only that he never perceived her physical condition, but that she managed her household so fully and competently with one arm that he never had occasion to notice anything wanting. On this reading, the story's praise is for the woman's remarkable capability as much as for either party's physical modesty. The *gemara*'s framing of *tzenuah* may not easily accommodate this interpretation, but it is a thought-provoking alternative lens.

---

## Animal Garments

### Rams & Levuvin

The *gemara* now returns to the *halachic* discussion of the *mishnah* and what animals may or may not wear on *Shabbat*. The *mishnah* states: *zacharim yotzin belevuvin* — rams may go out with *levuvin*.

### Levuvin Definition

*Mai levuvin?* — what are *levuvin*? Rav Huna says: *totari*, which Rashi explains as tying the rams together in pairs — *shemechabrim otam bekesher shenayim shenayim shello yivrachu* — so that they are paired off and cannot flee. The etymological support: *mah mashma dehai levuvin lishna dekaruvei hu* — where do we see that *levuvin* denotes bringing together? From the verse *libavtini achoti kallah* (Song of Songs), where *levuv* means to draw close. So the rams go out tied one to another.

### Wolf Protection

Ulla offers a different reading. *Levuvin* refers to a leather binding placed *kneged libam* — over the heart of the ram — *kedei shelo yiplu aleihem ze'evim* — so that wolves will not attack them. This is a protective covering at the chest.

### Why Rams Only

The *gemara* immediately asks: *ze'evim adikarim nafli, anekevot lo nafli?* — do wolves attack rams but not ewes? Several explanations are offered in turn. First: *mishum demasgei bereish idra* — the rams walk at the head of the flock and are the first target. But then why don't the wolves simply come around to the back? Next: *mishum deshmeini* — because the rams are fatter and more appealing. But surely there are fat ewes too? Finally, and apparently conclusively: *mishum dezakfi chotmaihu* — because the rams hold their heads high and look around as they walk, which Rashi understands as a kind of provocation to the wolves, who perceive the raised-head posture as a challenge.

### Copulation Control

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a third reading of *levuvin*: *or shekoshrim lahem tachat zachrutam kedei shelo ya'alu al hanekevot* — a binding placed beneath the rams' genitals to prevent them from copulating with the ewes. This interpretation is supported by the parallel structure of the *mishnah*, which goes on to discuss bindings for the female sheep as well, all of which relate to copulation.

### Shchuzot Definition

The *mishnah* states that ewes may go out *shuchuzot*. *Mai shuchuzot?* — what does this mean? *She'ochzim ha'alyah shelahem lemala kedei sheya'alu aleihem zecharim* — one holds the fat tail upward so that the rams can mount them. So here, unlike the case of the rams, the binding is intended to *enable* copulation rather than prevent it. The *gemara* notes the structural parallelism: *reisha kedei shelo ya'alu al hanekevot, seifa kedei sheya'alu aleihem zecharim* — the first clause prevents copulation, the second facilitates it.

### Shchuzot Etymology

*Mai mashma dehai shuchuzot lishna degiluy hu?* — where does *shuchuzot* suggest exposure? The *gemara* cites the verse in Proverbs describing a woman *shit zonah unetzurat lev* — dressed as a prostitute and of a calculating heart. Somehow *shuchuzot* derives from this language of exposure, particularly sexual exposure.

### Kevulot Definition

The *mishnah* also permits ewes to go out *kevulot*. This is the opposite arrangement: *shemechablin alyah shelahem lemata kedei shelo ya'alu aleihem hazcharim* — one binds the fat tail down to prevent the rams from mounting. Sometimes the farmer wants copulation and sometimes not, depending on the season or breeding plans.

### Kevulot Etymology

*Mai mashma dehai kavul lishna dela avid peiri hu?* — where does *kavul* suggest non-productivity? The *gemara* turns to the story of Hiram, who helped Shlomo build the *Beit HaMikdash* and received certain cities in return. He was displeased: *ma hearim haele asher natata li achi?* — what are these cities you gave me, my brother? — and called the land *eretz kavul* (I Kings 9:13). The *gemara* explores what *kavul* means here.

Rav Huna suggests: *shehayu bah bnei adam shemechubalin bakesef uvazahav* — the inhabitants were so encumbered with gold and silver. Rava objects: if people were laden with wealth, why was Hiram displeased? Rav Huna explains: *keivan de'atirei umifankei lo avdei avidta* — since they were so rich and pampered, they refused to work or be conscripted for the king's projects.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a different account: *eretz chumtin hayeta* — it was cracked, muddy land into which one's legs would sink up to the ankle. *Ve'amri inshi ara mechavla* — and people would say it was a land of *kavul*, *delo avda peiri* — that bore no fruit. This idiom of *eretz kavul dело avda peiri* — unfruitful land — is then the connection: binding the ewe's fat tail down renders her, so to speak, unfruitful, preventing the rams from ascending.

### Conceptual Analysis

At this point it is worth pausing over the conceptual difficulty these cases present. The discussion throughout this chapter has generally operated on a distinction between what is protective of the animal — and therefore not a burden — and what serves the owner's interests through the animal's body, which is more like a *masoi*, a load. Yet here, according to the *tanna kamma*, a ram going out with a binding to prevent copulation, or a ewe going out with her tail tied up or down to enable or prevent copulation, is permitted. None of this protects the animal's health or prevents it from running away; it serves entirely the economic or breeding interests of the owner.

One might try to frame this as owner interest without active use of the animal — the owner is not riding it or carrying goods on it, merely arranging its reproductive capacity. But even ornamentation, which is similarly passive, is treated as a *masoi* in other contexts. The more coherent resolution may be that the operative distinction is not function at all, but *norm*: what is regularly and customarily worn by animals of a given type at a given time is not a burden, and what exceeds that norm is. Rabbi Yossi, who disagrees and forbids all of these, at least makes the analysis consistent: if none of it is protective in the immediate physical sense, none of it should be permitted.

### Kvunot Definition

The *mishnah* permits ewes to go out *kvunot* as well. *Mai kvunot? Shemechabnin otam lemila* — one covers the lamb's wool from birth onward to protect it. The *gemara* connects this to the appearance of *se'eis*, one of the *tzara'at* markings described as *ketzemer lavan* — like white wool. Rav Bibi bar Abaye explains: *ketzemer naki ben yomo she-mechabnin oso le-mila* — like the clean wool of a one-day-old lamb that has been kept covered from birth in order to protect and preserve the quality of its fleece.

This too is clearly in the owner's financial interest — protecting the wool's value — rather than the animal's health. Rabbi Yossi's exception permitting *kvunot* while forbidding everything else is perhaps the most difficult element of his position to understand, since protecting wool for commercial purposes seems at least as removed from the animal's welfare as preventing copulation. One possible explanation is that because the covering is there from the moment of birth, it is treated as simply part of the animal's natural state — as close to being clothing as anything can be.

---

## Goat Udders

### Goat Binding

The *mishnah* states: *ha-izim yotzot tzerurot* — goats may go out with their udders bound. Rabbi Yossi disagrees and holds that this is prohibited, except for the *kvunot* case of wool protection.

### Dry vs. Catch

Rabbi Yehudah draws a distinction within the permitted category: binding the udder *le-yavesh* — to dry up the milk — is permitted, while binding it *le-chalav* — to catch the milk — is not. The practical difference between these may be that a binding tight enough to suppress lactation will not slip off, while one designed to catch milk might be loose and could fall, creating a carrying concern. Alternatively, suppressing the milk may be seen as serving the animal — if it is no longer nursing, continued lactation is painful — whereas catching the milk serves only the owner's interest in collecting it.

### Rav's Ruling

Rav rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehudah's distinction: *le-yavesh mutar, lo le-chalav* — binding to dry up the milk is permitted; binding to catch it is not.

### Shmuel's Ruling

Shmuel rules in accordance with Rabbi Yossi: both are forbidden, with the sole exception of the wool protection case.

### Baraita Problem

There is a *baraisa* that reflects Rabbi Yehudah's position directly: *izim yotzot tzerurot le-yavesh aval lo le-chalav* — goats may go out with bound udders to dry up the milk but not to catch it. *Mishum Rabbi Yehudah ben Beseira amru kach halacha* — in principle, this is the law.

### Ben Beseira

However, Rabbi Yehudah ben Beseira adds a crucial practical qualification: *aval mi mafis?* — but who can distinguish? If one person goes out with their goat's udder bound to suppress lactation and another goes out with it bound to catch milk, an observer cannot tell the difference. Since people will not be able to distinguish and will conclude that it is always permitted, we must forbid the entire practice. *Umitoch she-ein mekirin echad ze ve-echad ze assur* — because they cannot be told apart, both are forbidden.

### Final Ruling

*Amar Shmuel, ve-amri lah amar Rav Yehudah amar Shmuel, halacha ke-Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira* — Shmuel rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehudah ben Beseira: the entire practice is forbidden. A competing tradition (*ki asa Ravin amar Rabbi Yehudah halacha ke-tanna kamma*) holds that the *tanna kamma*, who permits all the bindings, is the operative ruling. The *gemara* does not resolve the dispute at length, but the tendency of the discussion seems to favor the stricter position of Rabbi Yehudah ben Beseira, which Shmuel endorses.

---

## Prohibited Items

### Metulteles

The *mishnah* now turns to items that animals may *not* wear on *Shabbat*. *Lo yetzei hagamal bemetulteles* — the camel may not go out with a *metulteles*. Rashi explains the *metulteles* as a kind of cushion or cloth placed beneath the camel's tail to protect it from the chafing of the strap that holds a load in place. Because its entire purpose is functional during the carrying of burdens, it is itself considered a burden when worn.

### Double-Bound OK

A *baraita* clarifies: *lo yetzei hagamal bemetulteles hakeshurah lo biznavo* — it may not go out with the *metulteles* bound only to the tail. *Aval yotzei hu bemetulteles hakeshurah biznavo uvechotarto* — but it may go out with a *metulteles* bound both at the tail and at the hump. Rashi reads the underlying concern here not as the object being a burden in the conceptual sense, but as a concern that it will fall off — and a loose object that falls may then be carried. If it is bound in two places, at the tail and the hump, it will not slip off, and therefore it is permitted.

### Placenta Binding

Rabbah bar Rav Huna adds a related ruling: *yotzei gamal bemetulteles hakeshurah lo beshalyata* — the camel may also go out with the *metulteles* bound to its *shalyata*, its placenta or afterbirth. Apparently animals do not always immediately expel the afterbirth, and because the connection to the afterbirth makes it painful for the camel to try to dislodge the covering, there is no risk that it will fall off and need to be carried. Here too Rashi's logic is that stability — certainty that the object will remain on the animal — is the decisive factor.

### Akud

The *mishnah* also forbids the camel from going out *akud* or *ragul*. Rav Yehudah explains: *akud* means *akeidas yad varegel* — binding a foreleg to a hindleg, one side to the other, *ke-Yitzchak ben Avraham* — as Yitzchak was bound at the *Akeidah*.

### Ragul

*Ragul* means *shelo yachof yado al gabei tzvaro v'yikshor* — one takes a single leg, bends it upward, and ties the ankle toward the top of the thigh, so the animal walks on three legs and cannot run. Presumably this was done to prevent the animal from escaping, but it is considered a burden — perhaps because it is painful, or because it is seen as an extreme and unnecessary measure as compared to a simple tether.

### Textual Fix

The *gemara* raises a challenge from a *baraisa* that seems to define *akud* as binding the two forelegs together and the two hindlegs together separately — a distinct configuration from the hand-and-foot binding Rav Yehudah describes. The *gemara* resolves this by identifying a different *tanna* whose position Rav Yehudah follows: *akud akeidas yad v'regel ke-Yitzchak ben Avraham, ragul shelo ya'akof yado al gabei tzvaro v'yikshor* — one hand bound to one foot, and *ragul* as the single leg bent up. This *tanna* does not include the hands-together-feet-together configuration at all.

### Permitted vs. Forbidden

The *Shulchan Aruch* rules accordingly. The practical upshot is that binding the two forelegs together and the two hindlegs together separately — a more symmetrical and perhaps less painful restraint — is considered a normal and acceptable method of preventing the animal from wandering, and does not constitute a burden. Binding one hand to one foot (*akud*) or bending a single leg up (*ragul*) both exceed this norm, and are therefore forbidden on *Shabbat*.

---

## Commerce & Shatnez

### Mishnah Rules

The *mishnah* continues: *lo yikshor gemalim zeh bezeh veyimshoch* — do not tie camels together in a line and walk them. However, *aval machnis havalim letoch yado veyimshoch* — one may hold multiple separate ropes in hand and lead them that way, as long as they are not tied to one another. And: *uvilvad shelo yichroch* — one must not wind the ropes around one's hand.

### Market Appearance

*Mai ta'ama?* — what is the reason for the prohibition against walking camels in a line? *Mishum d'meichzi k'man d'azil l'chinga* — it looks like one is heading to the market. Walking a line of camels in a row is a quintessentially commercial, weekday activity. This is less a concern about *marris ayin* in the technical sense of others suspecting a violation, and more a direct *Shabbat* concern: the atmosphere and character of *Shabbat* is undermined when one engages in activities that look and feel like commerce. It is not a *Shabbat*-appropriate experience to create in the public space.

### Shatnez Problem

As for the prohibition on wrapping the ropes around one's hand: Rav Ashi explains that the concern is *kilayim de-chavalim* — the ropes may be a mixture of wool and linen, and wrapping and knotting them together could create a *shaatnez* problem.

### Baraita Objection

The *gemara* challenges this: *ha-tokef tekifa achat eino chibur* — a *baraita* teaches that even a single stitch joining wool and linen garments is not sufficient to constitute *shaatnez*. If one stitch doesn't create *shaatnez*, how does wrapping ropes around one's hand do so?

### Resolution

The *gemara* maintains that the concern is indeed *kilayim de-chavalim*, but refines the formulation: *uvilvad shelo yichroch veyikshor* — one must not *wrap and tie* the ropes together. If one twists them together and then knots them, one has created at minimum a category of rabbinic *shaatnez*, even if the biblical prohibition might require something more elaborate such as intertwining the individual strands. The *gemara* treats this level of wrapping-and-knotting as sufficient to require avoidance, without specifying whether it is biblical or rabbinic.

### Camel Walking

The question arises — prompted in the course of the discussion — how one can walk a camel on *Shabbat* at all while holding a rope or lead, without this constituting *carrying*. The answer appears to follow from the earlier analysis: once an item is considered a non-burden for the animal — because it is normal and customary for the animal to wear it — then the owner holding the lead attached to that item is not carrying. An analogy: if someone is wearing a large hat and another person holds the brim to keep it from blowing off, that second person is not *carrying* the hat, because the hat is on someone's body. The collar and lead, being acceptable items for the animal to bear, are extensions of the animal itself rather than independent objects being carried.

### Rope Distance

*Amar Shmuel: uvilvad shelo yetze chevel mi-tachat yado tefach* — one must ensure that the rope does not extend more than a *tefach* beyond one's hand at the far end (away from the camel). Rashi explains that if a length of rope hangs beyond the hand, it will appear as though one is simply holding a piece of rope rather than leading an animal, and may look like carrying.

### Tefach Dispute

The school of Shmuel (*tana de-bei Shmuel*) teaches that the threshold is actually two *tefachim*, not one. Abaye resolves the discrepancy: Shmuel's ruling of one *tefach* is a practical guidance for actual conduct — advising people to be more conservative in practice — while the theoretical limit is indeed two *tefachim*. A second rule applies to the rope between the hand and the camel: *uvilvad sheyagbi'ah min hakarka tefach* — it must be held at least a *tefach* above the ground. If the lead drags along the ground, it no longer looks like one is walking an animal; it looks like one is dragging a rope, which would appear to be carrying.

---

## Species-Specific

### Donkey

*Ein chamor yotzei bemardaat bizman she'einah keshurah lo* — the donkey may not go out with a saddle blanket if it was not tied to it before *Shabbat*. *Velo bezug af al pi shehu pakuk* — and not with a bell, even if the bell has been stopped so that it makes no sound. *Velo besulam shebetzavaro* — and not with a ladder-like device placed along the length of its neck. *Velo biretzuah sheberaglav* — and not with a strap on its legs.

### Bell Reason

*Mishum demichzei keman de'azal lechinga* — the bell is prohibited because even a stopped, silent bell gives the appearance that the donkey is being taken to market. This is the same concern as with the line of camels: it is a visual marker of commercial weekday activity that undermines the character of *Shabbat*. Tosafot notes that one might instead have argued that the bell is simply an ornament that does not protect the animal and is therefore a *masoi*. But Tosafot resolves this by suggesting that the bell is woven into the halter itself, and the halter as a whole is not a burden — the prohibition is therefore specifically because it *looks* like one is going to market, not because the bell itself is a carried object.

### Ladder Purpose

Regarding the ladder-like device on the neck — *sulum shebetzavaro* — Rav Huna explains: *leheicha d'it leh maka delo hadar hayech bah* — if the animal has a wound on its neck, this device prevents it from turning its head and scraping at the wound. Despite this clearly medical purpose, it is still considered a burden. As with several of the items in this *mishnah*, items applied for health purposes that are nonetheless external to the animal's normal state of dress appear to be treated as *masoi*.

### Leg Strap

The strap placed on the donkey's legs, *retzuah sheberaglav*, is used to correct a gait problem — Rashi explains it addresses something akin to knock-knees — so that the animal walks properly and does not worsen its condition. Again, a therapeutic purpose, and again prohibited.

### Chickens

*V'ein hatarnagolim yotzin bechutin* — chickens may not go out with identifying strings. *D'avdi leh simana ki heichi d'lo lichlefu* — these strings are placed on them so that owners can identify whose chickens are whose, preventing them from being confused or switched. And *velo biretzuah sheberagleihem* — nor may they go out with straps on their legs. *D'avdi leh ki heichi d'lo livru mani* — the straps are placed on chicken's legs to limit the range of their kicking and thereby prevent them from breaking things around the house. This is clearly for the protection of the owner's property rather than the animal, and it is not permitted.

### Rams

*V'ein hazcharim yotzin ba'agalah shetachas ha'alyah* — rams may not go out with little wagons beneath their fat tails. *Ki heichi d'lo lachmatan ayata* — so that the fat tail should not scrape along the ground and become injured. This is arguably a protective purpose, but the wagon is nonetheless forbidden — perhaps because it is a distinctly external object, perhaps because it exceeds any ordinary norm for what a ram would wear.

### Sheep

*V'ein harachelim yotzot chanunot* — female sheep may not go out *chanunot*. The *gemara* will explore what this means through several competing explanations.

### Chanunot Options

The first attempt at a definition comes from Rav Acha bar Ulla, sitting before Rav Chisda: *beshaa shegozezin otah, tomnim lah azak beshemen u'manichin lah al padachtah kedei shelo titztanen* — when the sheep is shorn, one takes a cloth soaked in oil and places it on the animal's forehead so that it does not catch a chill. Rav Chisda rejects this: *im ken asita mar ukva* — you have turned the sheep into Mar Ukva. That is, putting an oil compress on the forehead of a sheep is the kind of refined treatment one gives to very distinguished people, not animals.

The second attempt comes from Rav Pappa bar Shmuel: *beshaa shekarat leiled, tomnin lah shnei azakim shel shemen u'manichin lah echad al padekha v'echad al recham kedei shetitchamem* — during labor, one places two oil-soaked cloths, one on the ewe's forehead and one on her womb, to provide warmth. Rav Nachman objects similarly: *amar lei im kein asita yalta* — now you have made the sheep like Yalta (Rav Nachman's wife). The treatment you describe is what one does for a woman in childbirth, not for a ewe.

### Chanun Tree

Rav Huna offers the authoritative explanation: *eitz echad yesh b'charkhei hayam v'chanun shemo* — there is a tree found in the islands called *chanun*, from which *chanunot* takes its name. *Umevi'im kisam u'manichin lah b'chotmah kedei shetit'atesh v'yiplu darnei rasha* — one takes a splinter from this tree and inserts it into the animal's nostrils so that it sneezes, dislodging the lice or parasites living in its head.

### Female Only

The *gemara* asks: *i hachi, zecharim nami* — if this is the purpose, why is it only for the female sheep? *Keivan d'menagchi zecharim bahadadi, mimeila nafli* — because the rams butt their heads against one another, the impact naturally dislodges the parasites. Female sheep, who do not engage in this behavior, require the *chanun* splinter instead. Still, they may not go out with it on *Shabbat*.

### Compassion View

Shimon the *Nazir* offers an alternative identification, naming a different type of wood — *kisam d'ritma*, a splinter from the broom tree — rather than the *chanun* tree. The *gemara* notes the terminological difficulty this creates: according to Rav Huna, the term *chanunot* is readily explained as derived from the *chanun* tree. But according to the other Rabbis who identify a different wood, what does *chanunot* mean? The answer: *d'avidnan lehu milta d'merachminan aleihu* — because one does something out of compassion, from the root *chanun*, to relieve the animal's discomfort whether during shearing or during birth. The name reflects the act of *chanan*, showing mercy, even if the tree involved is not the *chanun* tree.

### Calf

*V'ein ha'eigel yotzei b'gimon* — the calf may not go out with a *gimon*. Rav Huna explains: *bar nira* — it is a small training yoke placed on a young calf to accustom it to bearing a yoke while it is still pliable, since animals that grow up without yokes are difficult or impossible to train later in life.

### Gimon Etymology

*Mai mashma d'hai gimon lishna d'michaf?* — where does the word *gimon* suggest bending down? *D'chtiv halachof k'agmon rosho* (Isaiah 58:5) — will he bow his head like an *agmon*? Here the verse uses *agmon* to mean something that bends, which Ibn Ezra understands as a fishhook; others translate it as bulrush. In any case, *gimon* derives from the idea of bending the neck down under a yoke. The *gimon* is extraneous to the calf in its natural state and is therefore a burden.

### Cow

*V'lo parah b'or hakupar* — the cow may not go out with hedgehog leather on its udder. *D'avdi lah ki heichi d'lo lamtziuha yali* — this leather is placed over the udder to prevent rodents or other small animals from nursing from the cow. Unlike the earlier cases of binding to suppress or catch milk, which at least some opinions permitted, this device is seen as entirely serving the owner's protective interest rather than anything relating to the animal itself, and it is forbidden.

### Strap Between

*V'lo b'retzu'ah shebein karneiha* — and not with a strap between its horns. An earlier *gemara* records a dispute: Rav holds that the strap is forbidden whether it is placed *l'noy* — for ornamentation — or *l'shamer* — to protect the cow. Even a protective purpose does not render it acceptable; for a cow, which requires no elaborate protection, such a strap is excessive. Shmuel, by contrast, holds: *l'noy assur, l'shamer mutar* — ornamentation is a burden, but a strap placed there for the cow's protection is permitted.

---

## Elazar's Cow

### Neighbor's Cow

*Parato shel Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya hayata yotzah biretzuah shebein karneha* — the cow of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah would go out with a strap between its horns, and the Sages were not pleased.

### Attribution

The *gemara* immediately asks: *chada para havi lei?* — did he have only one cow? Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav teaches that Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah would tithe twelve thousand calves from his herd every year. Clearly he was not a one-cow owner.

### Neighbor's Ownership

*Lo shelo hayeta* — the *baraisa* teaches that it was not actually his cow. *Ella she'shchenato hayeta* — it was his neighbor's cow.

### Protest Duty

*Umitoch shelo mikha bah, nikret al shemo* — because he did not protest or prevent his neighbor from doing this, it is called his. He bore responsibility for conduct within his sphere of influence and failed to exercise it, and so the transgression is attributed to him.

### Household

This leads to a sweeping principle taught by Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chaviva — with a parenthetical noting that throughout *Seder Moed*, this group is sometimes cited with Rabbi Yonatan in place of Rabbi Yochanan — *kol mi she'efshar limkhot le'anshey beito v'lo mikha, nitpas al anshey beito*: anyone who could have prevented the people of his household from sinning and did not protest is held accountable for their sins.

### Scope Expansion

The principle extends outward: *be'anshey iro* — if one could have stopped the people of one's city and did not, one is accountable for the city. *V'kol ha'olam kullo* — and if one could have stopped the entire world from sinning, one bears responsibility for the world's transgressions as well.

### Authority

*Amar Pappa: vehani devei reish galuta nitpasu al kulei alma* — Rav Pappa applies this principle directly: the household of the *Reish Galuta*, the Exilarch, wielded sufficient power and authority over the Jewish community that when anyone in the community did wrong, they bore a particular responsibility — and if they failed to intervene, they were held accountable for the sins of the entire world. The teaching ends here, and the *gemara* will continue in this vein in the next daf.

---

---

# Shabbat 55

## Animal Leash Laws

### Leash Requirements

Before turning to the substance of today's daf, which is largely *agadati* in character, it is worth concluding the practical discussion of animal transport from the previous session by examining the relevant passage in *Shemiras Shabbos Kehilchasa*. In section 7, the author states: *v'inyan shevisas beheima hu sheba'al hachayim yidag kach shelo tetzei habeheima l'reshus harabim v'lo l'karmelis b'sha'as shemasa al gabeha* — the obligation of *shevisas behemto* requires the animal's owner to ensure that the animal does not go out into a *reshus harabim* or a *karmelis* while carrying a burden.

In section 8, the *Shemiras Shabbos Kehilchasa* rules: *beheimah she-l'shem shemirasah yesh bitzavar chevel saviv tzavarah, muttar lo l'holichah birshus harabim b'chevel zeh u-vilvad she-ketzehu lo yivlot tefach echad o yoser mitachas yad hamolicho* — an animal that requires a rope or collar for its protection may be led through a *reshus harabim* on that leash, provided that no more than a *tefach* of the leash extends beyond the handler's hand. This is precisely the *psak* of the *Gemara* applied in practical terms: one may walk one's dog or animal on a leash even in a *reshus harabim*, but must ensure the leash does not come within a *tefach* of the ground. The text further specifies: *v'gam yakpid she-chelek hachevel she-bo hu molich es habeheimah lo yikarav k'dei tefach echad samuch la-aretz*.

Additionally, when wrapping the leash around the animal's neck on *Shabbos*, one must be careful not to lean on the animal: *u-cheshe-koreich es hachevel bi-Shabbos saviv tzavar habeheimah yizaher shelo lishaen aleha*. This reflects the assumption, operative throughout this section, that animals are *muktzah*. The question arises whether work animals are likewise *muktzah*, and the answer is yes — the general presumption is that all animals are *muktzah*, and although there is contemporary discussion regarding pets specifically, the *Shemiras Shabbos Kehilchasa* operates with the standard assumption. Beyond the *muktzah* concern, there is a separate prohibition of being *mishtamesh* in *ba'alei chayim* — making use of a living creature — which applies independently.

### Pet Tags & Chips

Section 9 addresses the issue of identification tags on animals, which arose in the previous session in the context of strings tied to chickens. The *Shemiras Shabbos Kehilchasa* rules: *siman heker hatalui al tzavarah shel beheimah, tag, eino shemirah regilah labeheimah, v'assur lehaniach lah latzeit bo birshus harabim* — an identification tag hanging from an animal's neck does not constitute a normal protective covering for the animal, and it is therefore forbidden to permit the animal to go out with it into a *reshus harabim*. This is a direct application of the *Gemara*'s *psak*. Consequently, owners of dogs must take care not to take their dogs out in a place without an *eruv* when an identifying tag is on the animal's collar.

The final clause of this section introduces a distinction: *v'hu siman heker hakavu'a b'ozen habeheimah b'masmer she-alav mispar zihui v'sha'ar pratum eino bichlal zeh, mikeivan shelo nitan le-hasiro* — a mark that is permanently affixed and cannot be removed falls into a different category. This would apply to a microchip implanted in the animal, which by its nature cannot be taken off. In most places, dogs are legally required to carry tags, which means this ruling has direct and immediate practical application.

---

## Leadership & Protest

### Officials' Liability

The *Gemara* yesterday established that Rabbi Eliezer was held liable for his neighbor's cow, because he failed to protest her behavior. The *Gemara* now extends this principle to communal leadership. *Amar Papa: v'hanei d'vei Reish Galusa nispas al kulei alma* — the members of the household of the *Reish Galusa*, who held political authority and were in a position to intervene in the conduct of the entire community, are held responsible for everyone's wrongdoing, since they had the ability to do something about it.

### Elders & Officers

This is supported by a statement of Rabbi Yochanan. The *Gemara* asks: *mai d'chasiv, Hashem b'mishpat yavo im ziknei amo v'sarav* — what is the meaning of the verse that God will come to judgment with the elders of His nation and its officers? If the officers sinned — that is, the political heads who failed to lead the people properly — what did the elders, the sages, do wrong? The *Gemara* answers: *ella eima al zekeinim shelo michu b'sarim* — rather, understand it as God coming in judgment with the elders because they failed to protest against the officers. Sages and religious figures who possess a voice that can be heard, and who are positioned to protest, bear responsibility when they remain silent. They too are held accountable.

### Woman's Plea

The *Gemara* relates that Rav Yehuda was sitting before Shmuel when a certain woman came and cried out before him, complaining of some injustice done to her. Shmuel paid her no attention. Rav Yehuda said to him: does the master not hold by the verse, *otem azno mi-za'akat dal, gam hu yikra v'lo ye'aneh* — one who seals his ear from the outcry of the poor will himself cry out and not be answered? How could you ignore this woman?

Shmuel replied: *Shina'na, reishach b'kriri, reisha d'reishach b'chamimei* — sharp one, if I, your superior, am judged with cold water, then the head above me will be judged with scalding water. In other words, Shmuel does not fully justify his inaction, but points out that the primary responsibility rests with whoever stands above him in the hierarchy. He was not exactly defending what he was doing; he was indicating that someone else bore a far greater share of the responsibility. There may be truth to this — if one is a cog in a system and the system is not functioning properly, there is often a limit to what any individual within it can do. Nevertheless, this did not help the woman, and Shmuel's response has the character of passing the buck, even if it contains a kernel of genuine insight.

### Mar Ukva's Role

The *Gemara* continues: *hava yasiv Mar Ukva* — Mar Ukva was sitting. Mar Ukva is here identified as the one who truly held authority — he was the head of the *beis din*. And it is he who will be judged harshly, for it says: *Beis David koh amar Hashem, dinu lavoker mishpat, v'hatzilu gazul miyad oshek, pen tetzei ka'esh chamasi u-va'arah v'ein mechabeh, mipnei ro'a ma'aleihem* — House of David, so says God, administer justice in the morning, save the one being robbed from the oppressor, lest My anger go forth like fire and burn with none to extinguish it, because of the evil of their deeds. Mar Ukva, the genuine political head who had the capacity to build a functioning system of justice, was not doing so, and thus he is the one who will be judged with scalding fire.

The scenario, as the *Gemara* presents it: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel are present, Mar Ukva is not. Rav Yehuda presses Shmuel on how he can turn a deaf ear to a woman crying out for help. Shmuel does not fully defend his behavior, but deflects the primary accountability upward to Mar Ukva, who as head of the *beis din* had not established the structures necessary for justice to be served. It is striking that the *Gemara* is willing to record such a pointed indictment — evidently the rabbis themselves applied this standard to their own institutional failures. That it did not help the woman in the immediate moment is a sobering reality that the text does not conceal.

### Must Protest

The *Gemara* now presents a related exchange. Rav Zeira said to Rav Simon: *lochechanu mar l'hanei d'vei Reish Galusa* — you, Rav Simon, should rebuke, give *hochecha*, to the members of the household of the *Reish Galusa*, for they are not conducting themselves as they should, whether through their own misconduct or their failure to create a just system. Rav Simon replied: *lo mekablun minai* — they will not listen to me. Rav Zeira responded: *af al gav d'lo mekablun, lochechanu mar* — even if they will not accept your *mussar*, you must nonetheless stand up and protest.

This leads directly into the principle cited by Rav Acha in the name of Rabbi Hanina: *me'olam lo yatzta middah tovah mipi HaKadosh Baruch Hu v'chazar bah l'ra'ah* — never did a good decree go forth from the mouth of the Holy One Blessed Be He and then be retracted for an evil one. This principle is significant for the *Rambam* as well: *Rambam* teaches that a *navi* is proven genuine when his prophecy is fulfilled — but then how do we account for the fact that God sometimes appears to reverse Himself, as in the case of Nineveh, which He threatened to destroy but did not? *Rambam* answers that God may retract a negative prophecy when people do *teshuvah*, but a positive declaration, a promise of good, God does not reverse — with one exception, as the *Gemara* is about to explain.

---

## Yechezkel Vision

### Good Decrees

The one exception to the principle that God never retracts a good decree is what the *Gemara* now elaborates from the vision of Yechezkel. *Chutz midavar zeh* — except for this one matter, as it is written...

### Idolatry & Injustice

The prophecy in question comes from chapters 8 through 10 of Yechezkel. Yechezkel went into exile approximately ten years before the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*, and in this section of his prophecy he describes a series of terrible sins: people worshipping *avodah zarah* within the *Beis HaMikdash* itself, people turning their backs to the Holy of Holies and desecrating it, and beyond the ritual sins, serious injustice as well. He then envisions angels coming to destroy Yerushalayim, but among them one figure — a man dressed in linen — is given the command to place a mark on the foreheads of the righteous, so that when the city is destroyed, the righteous will be protected.

The *pasuk* reads: *vayomer Hashem elav, avor besoch ha'ir besoch Yerushalayim, v'hisvisa tav al mitzchot ha'anashim hane'enachim v'hane'enakim al kol hato'evos hana'asos besochah* — God said to him: pass through the city, through Yerushalayim, and place a mark on the foreheads of all the people who moan and groan over all the abominations being done within it. These are the righteous who bemoan the wrongdoing. Place a mark on their foreheads; they will be saved and protected when the city is destroyed.

### Gabriel's Mark

The *Gemara* now elaborates on this vision. *Amar lei HaKadosh Baruch Hu l'Gavriel* — God said to Gavriel, for the *Gemara* understands the man in linen to be the angel Gavriel, who had the writing implements of a scribe on his person: *lechi v'rishmi al mitzchan shel tzaddikim tav shel dyo* — go and mark on the foreheads of the *tzaddikim* a *tav* in ink, *shelo yishletu bahem malachei chabalah* — so that the *malachei chabalah*, the angels of destruction, will have no power over them. *V'al mitzchan shel resha'im tav shel dam* — and on the foreheads of the *resha'im*, a *tav* of blood, *kedei sheyishletu bahen malachei chabalah* — so that the angels of destruction may proceed to destroy them.
