# Shabbat 57

## Intro & Framework

### Opening & Context

We begin a new *perek* today — *perek* six, *Bameh Isha* — continuing within the sequence of chapters that address preparations for *Shabbat*. To recall the broader context: the tractate opened with concerns about *hotza'ah* and activities before *mincha*, then moved in the second *perek* to lighting candles, the third to placing food on the fire, the fourth to insulating food, and the fifth to what one's animal may carry on *Shabbat* — which is to say, what must be removed from the animal before *Shabbat* begins. That fifth *perek*, though it might initially seem remote from our daily lives given that we no longer keep farm animals, reframed what *Erev Shabbat* means: not merely tending to the home, but going down to the stable, unburdening the animal, ensuring that it too had its *Shabbat*. That is an important dimension of the preparations.

Now we arrive at what one may wear on *Shabbat* — which is both a question of what one dresses in on *Shabbat* itself and of what one puts on Friday afternoon as one enters the day. There is a pleasing structural symmetry here: we have six days of *chol* and a seventh day of *Shabbat*, and correspondingly six *prakim* of preparation before the seventh *perek* turns directly to the *melachot* of *Shabbat*. The sixth *perek* addresses what is considered clothing or jewelry and what is not.

### Rashi's Framework

Before reading the *mishnah*, it is worth examining the first *Rashi* carefully, because he lays out the conceptual framework that underlies the entire *perek*. *Rashi* identifies two distinct concerns — one biblical, one rabbinic — and both appear in the *perek*, though they are not always clearly distinguished in the *mishnah* itself.

The first concern, which *Rashi* characterizes as biblical, is captured in the phrase *de-havi tachshit ve-lo massa* — the item must constitute jewelry or clothing, not a burden. Wearing something on one's body does not automatically render it clothing; a backpack, for instance, is worn on the body but is plainly a burden. The question is whether what a woman wears qualifies as *tachshit* — jewelry or clothing — or whether it is merely something she is carrying on her person. Anything that falls outside the category of clothing or jewelry is, biblically, a burden, and carrying it constitutes a violation.

The second concern is rabbinic. *Rashi* describes it: *ve-ika de-havi tachshit* — there are items that genuinely are jewelry and therefore pose no biblical problem — *ve-gazaru beih rabbanan*, but the rabbis nonetheless prohibited wearing them. Why? *Dilma shalfa u-machavya le-chaverta le-chashivuta* — lest she remove the item to show her friend how beautiful it is. *Ve-dilma ati le-asuyei arba amot* — and then she will walk four *amot* while holding it before replacing it, thereby carrying in the public domain. This same dual structure — a biblical concern and a rabbinic concern — was present in the previous *perek* regarding animals, where loose items might fall off and come to be carried.

### Mishnah Overview

The *mishnah* does not always specify which category of concern is at play, but as the *Gemara* will make clear, this first *mishnah* is primarily addressing the second, rabbinic concern — things that are genuinely jewelry, but that the rabbis worried might be removed and carried.

*Bameh isha yotza u-ve-mah eina yotza* — what may a woman go out with and what may she not go out with? The *mishnah* opens with a series of prohibitions: *lo teitzei isha lo be-chutei tzemer velo be-chutei pishtan* — she may not go out with wool strings or flax strings woven into her hair. *Velo be-retzuah she-be-roshah* — nor with a strap on her head, whether on her forehead or wrapped around her hair. There is then a parenthetical remark: *velo titbol bahem ad she-tirapaim* — she also may not go to the *mikvah* with these strings unless she first loosens them, since the water must be able to reach between the string and the hair. The *Gemara*, as we will see, treats this remark as far more than parenthetical — it is in fact the key to understanding the entire prohibition.

The *mishnah* continues: *ve-lo totfet ve-lo sarbitin* — she may not wear a *totfet* or *sarvitin*, which are types of head ornaments whose precise identity will be clarified in the *Gemara*. *Bi-zman she-einam tefurim* — this prohibition applies when they are not sewn into her hairnet or cap. The *Gemara* will operate on the assumption that a married woman always has her hair covered, and therefore the concern is not about the hair covering itself, which she would never remove in public, but about ornaments attached separately to it. If they are woven into her hairnet, there is no concern; if they are separate, there is.

*Ve-lo be-khvul li-reshut ha-rabim* — she may not go out with a *kvul* into the public domain. The word *reshut ha-rabim* appears explicitly only in connection with the *kvul*, which raises a question: does the prohibition on all the earlier items apply only in the public domain, or more broadly? The *Gemara* will take a stricter position, ruling that all the items listed earlier are prohibited even in the *chatzer*, the courtyard — the semi-private enclosed space shared by several households. The reasoning is that if we permit her to wear these items in the courtyard, she will come to wear them into the street. This is a remarkably expansive decree: even in a space that is technically *reshut ha-yachid*, the rabbis prohibited wearing these items. Yet even under that strict view, the *kvul* forms an exception — it is permitted in the *chatzer* but not in *reshut ha-rabim*, because had the rabbis prohibited absolutely everything outdoors, it would have been an untenable burden on women.

The *mishnah* then lists additional items: *ve-lo be-ir shel zahav* — not with a "golden city," apparently some type of tiara fashioned to resemble a cityscape; *ve-lo be-katla* — not with a *katla*, a type of jewelry we will identify shortly; *ve-lo bi-nezamim* — not with earrings; *ve-lo be-taba'at she-ein aleha khotam* — not with a ring that has no seal. The absence of a seal is relevant: a ring with no seal is purely ornamental and thus rabbinicaly problematic only because she might remove it to show someone. A ring with a seal, however, might not even qualify as jewelry in the first place, since it serves a functional purpose, and could therefore be a biblical violation. *Ve-lo be-machat she-eina nekuva* — not with a needle that has no hole, which functions like a decorative pin.

The *mishnah* concludes: *ve-im yatza eina chayavat chatat* — if she does go out with any of these items, she has not incurred biblical liability, since these are rabbinic prohibitions. Were she, by contrast, wearing a ring with a seal or a needle with a hole — items that do not qualify as jewelry — she would be biblically liable, *chayavat chatat*.

One might wonder how all of this applies today, given that most communities have an *eruv*. But one student's observation is apt and worth noting: if these items are forbidden even in a *chatzer*, which is itself a *reshut ha-yachid*, an *eruv* — which converts the public domain halachically into something resembling a *chatzer* — may not resolve the problem. If the decree reaches into the *chatzer*, it would seem to reach into an *eruv* as well.

---

## Wool/Linen Strings

### Tevila Question

The *Gemara* opens with a striking question, bypassing the conceptual material and jumping directly to the clause about *tevila*: *tvila man d'char shemeih?* — who mentioned immersion? What does the *mikvah* have to do with the laws of *Shabbat*? *Rashi* frames this with his characteristic wit: *mai inyan tvila eitzel hilchot shabbat* — what relevance does immersion have to the laws of *Shabbat*? This is reminiscent of the rhetorical question *mai inyan shmita eitzel har sinai* — what does *shmita* have to do with Sinai? — used to highlight an apparent non sequitur. The *Gemara* raises the question because it has an answer, and the answer reframes the entire first clause of the *mishnah*.

### Nachman's Reasoning

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak amar Rabba bar Avuha* — Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Rabba bar Avuha, offers a reading: *ma taam kamar* — read the *mishnah* as the mention of *tevila* providing the reason for the earlier prohibition. Why may a woman not go out with wool or flax strings woven into her hair? One might think these are so minor that no one would ever remove them to show a friend. What then is the concern?

The *Gemara* explains: *mipnei she-amru chachamim* — because the rabbis have ruled that on a weekday, *lo titbol bahem ad she-terafem* — she may not immerse in the *mikvah* with these strings until she loosens them. *Ve-keivan de-bachol lo titbol bahem ad she-terafem* — and since that is the weekday rule, *be-Shabbat lo teitzei* — she should not wear them on *Shabbat*. Why? *Dilma mishtarmi lah tvila shel mitzvah* — lest an occasion for a required immersion arise on *Shabbat*, most naturally the immersion of a *niddah*.

### Mikvah Removal Fear

A woman is permitted to go to the *mikvah* on *Shabbat*. If she is wearing these strings and must immerse, *ve-sharya lehu* — she will loosen them, remove them from her hair. A brief linguistic aside is in order: the words *assur* and *mutar*, which we conventionally translate as prohibited and permitted, are in fact words about binding. *Assur* means bound, as in *beit asurim*, a prison. *Mutar* means freed, loosened. *Le-hatir* means to undo the knots. This is relevant here: the *Gemara* says she will come to *matir otam*, to loosen the strings — and then, having come out of the *mikvah* with wet hair, she will not bother rewinding the strings into her hair. *Ve-asi le-asvunehu arba amos bi-reshut ha-rabim* — and she will carry them four *amot* in the public domain. That is the concern: not that she will show them to a friend, but that the necessity of removing them for the *mikvah* will lead to carrying them on *Shabbat*.

### Tosafot Minor Items

*Tosafot* presses the obvious question: this logic seems to apply to anything a woman is wearing. If she goes to the *mikvah* on *Shabbat*, she removes all of her clothing — so why are we not afraid she will fail to replace any of them? *Tosafot* answers that major items of clothing a person will certainly replace before leaving the *mikvah*. The concern applies specifically to minor and trivial items, things so insignificant that a woman, emerging from the *mikvah* with wet hair, will not bother to weave them back in and will simply walk home carrying them. It is precisely the triviality of these items that creates the risk.

---

## Porous Strings

### Rav Kahana Query

*Ba'ei minei Rav Kahana mei Rav* — Rav Kahana posed a question to Rav: *shikhi chalalita mai?* — what about braids or strands that are chain-like, with many gaps and openings, through which water flows freely? These are effectively porous. Does the *mikvah* concern apply to them?

### Arig Standard

Rav replied: *ari kamarta?* — are you speaking of something that is woven? *Kol she-hu arig lo gazru* — anything of that woven, porous character was never included in the prohibition. Such items do not present a *mikvah* obstruction concern, and therefore there is no reason to fear she will remove them before immersing. No concern about showing them to a friend, no concern about removing them for the *mikvah* — they are entirely permitted.

*Itmar nami* — this was also stated independently: *amar Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua, kol she-hu arig lo gazru* — anything of this woven, porous character was not subject to the decree.

### Case-by-Case Debate

*Ve-ika de-amri* — there is an alternative version of Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua's statement: *chazina le-achvasi de-lo kapdan alaihu* — I observed my sisters, and they were not *makpid* about these items, meaning they did not trouble themselves to remove them when going to bathe. *Rashi* notes that the reference is not only to *mikvah* immersion but to regular bathing; indeed, *Rashi* argues that one is actually more careful about removing things when washing one's hair in an ordinary bath than when immersing in a *mikvah* for halachic purposes, since for the *mikvah* one need only ensure water can flow through — if the item is porous, one need not remove it. In an ordinary bath, by contrast, one wants clean hair and will naturally remove anything that might impede washing. Rav Huna's sisters did not remove these items even when bathing, demonstrating that water passes through them freely.

### Categorical vs. Individu…

The *Gemara* then asks: *mai ika bein hai lishna u-vein hai lishna?* — what practical difference exists between these two formulations? One version says that all *arig*-type items are categorically excluded from the prohibition; the other focuses on whether a woman is *makpid* — whether she would actually be bothered to remove the item.

The difference emerges in a case where the braids or strings are soiled — dirty. *Le-hai lishna de-amar kol she-hu arig lo gazru* — according to the categorical approach, since this type of item was placed in the "not prohibited" category because water flows through it, it remains in that category regardless of circumstances. Even if the strings are dirty and a woman would naturally want to remove them when washing her hair, that particular circumstance does not change the halachic category. *Le-hai lishna de-amarta mishum kfeida* — but according to the approach that focuses on whether a woman is actually *makpid*, *keivan de-tanifa mikpad kapid alaihu* — since the strings are dirty she will certainly be *makpid* to remove them, even if not for *mikvah* reasons but simply because she does not want her wet hair getting muddied. In that case, on *Shabbat*, she should not wear them, because we can foresee that she will in fact remove them.

So the two approaches differ in their methodology: one makes categorical determinations based on the type of item; the other assesses individual circumstances to determine whether a woman will actually be *makpid* to remove the item, and restricts accordingly.

### Makpid Definition

*Rashi* presents an important clarification about the concept of *makpid*, and in doing so takes issue with his teachers. *Rashi* quotes his *Rabbaim* who argued that if the strings are dirty and a woman does not want them on her when immersing, her unwillingness itself creates a *chatzitzah* problem — that being *makpid* alone, even where water can pass through the item, renders it an obstruction. *Rashi* firmly rejects this. The criterion for *chatzitzah* requires two independent conditions: the item must physically prevent water from reaching the body, and the person must be *makpid* — unwilling to have it there. *Makpid* alone, absent a physical obstruction to water flow, cannot create a *chatzitzah*. If water gets through, the item is not an obstruction regardless of the woman's attitude toward it.

This is actually the operative ruling: we do not follow *Rashi*'s *Rabbaim* on this point. The ruling is that *makpid* without physical obstruction does not constitute *chatzitzah*. This has significant practical application: certain items on the body — bandages, braces, soft casts in some circumstances — through which water cannot pass but which one is not *makpid* about, may fall into a different category, and that determination is indeed discussed in the halachic literature.

---

## Chatzitzim Discussion

### Mikvaot Mishnah

*Tnan hatam* — the *Gemara* now cites the relevant *mishnah* from *Mikvaot*: *ve-eilu chotzetzim be-adam* — the following constitute obstructions for people. The list begins precisely with the same three items as our *mishnah* in *Shabbat*: wool strings, linen strings, and the straps on the head. The parallel is not coincidental. Our *mishnah* in *Shabbat* assumes that a woman does not go to the *mikvah* with these items, and the *Gemara* has now established that this is exactly why they cannot be worn on *Shabbat*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Hair

Rabbi Yehuda in the *mishnah* of *Mikvaot* disagrees: *shel tzemer ve-shel se'ar ein chotzetzin mipnei she-ha-mayim ba'in bahem* — wool and hair strings woven into the hair are not obstructions, because water penetrates between them. He concedes that linen, which lies tight and flat, may obstruct; but he holds that wool and hair allow water to flow through. The *tanna kamma* does not explicitly address hair strings, leaving that question open.

### Rav Huna Clarify

*Amar Rav Huna: ve-chulam be-roshei ha-banot shaninu* — all of this discussion pertains only to hair. This seems straightforward, and the *Gemara* immediately presses: *le-miutei mai?* — what are you coming to exclude?

### Soft on Hard

*Matkif lah Rav Yosef* — Rav Yosef challenges: if you are excluding strings around the neck from the *chatzitzah* concern, consider the following. If wool around the hair — soft around hard — is a *chatzitzah*, how much more obviously would wool around the neck — soft around soft — be a *chatzitzah*, since a soft substance more readily conforms to a soft surface and closes off gaps. Similarly, if linen around the hair — hard around hard — is a *chatzitzah*, how much more obviously would linen around the neck — hard around soft — be a *chatzitzah*. In both cases, whatever is a problem in the hair is certainly a problem around the neck. *Rashi* notes that the logic admittedly requires some unpacking, since one might have thought that something pliable around a pliable surface would actually leave more gaps — but the *Gemara* proceeds on the assumption that the soft-on-soft configuration is more obstructive.

So Rav Yosef concludes: in all cases, the neck version is at least as problematic as the hair version. Rav Huna's statement that "all of this is in the hair" cannot be coming to exclude the neck — the neck would certainly be included.

*Ela amar Rav Yosef* — so what then is the reasoning that Rav Huna must have had? *Lefi she-ein ishah choneket et atzmah* — because a woman does not choke herself. Whatever she wears around her neck she keeps loose. A woman will wind strings tightly into her hair, but a necklace around the neck is kept loose by self-preservation, and therefore water can get through. Thus neck coverings are not a *chatzitzah* — not because the *mishnah* excludes them, but because the physical reality is that they will always be loose.

### Choker vs. Necklace

*Eitiveih Abaye* — Abaye challenges Rav Yosef: but the *mishnah* elsewhere states that young girls may go out on *Shabbat* with strings in their ears — worn to keep the piercing open — but *aval lo be-chabakim she-be-tzavareihen* — they may not wear chokers around their necks. If a woman always keeps things around the neck loose, why would chokers be a problem on *Shabbat*? The *Gemara* is operating on the assumption that the choker prohibition is because she would have to remove it for the *mikvah*. But if the neck is always loose, there should be no *mikvah* concern.

*Amar Ravina* — Ravina resolves this: *hacha be-katla askinan* — we are dealing here with a *katla*. The *katla* was mentioned already in our *mishnah*. *Rashi* understands it as something like a bib or apron that includes a tight choker element at the top. There exist types of neck ornaments — true chokers — that a woman does wear tightly, precisely because a tight band around the neck is considered attractive. *De-ishah choneket et atzmah* — in this case, the woman actually does constrict herself. Therefore, a *katla*-style choker is a genuine *chatzitzah* concern, and one would have to remove it before immersing. Since she would have to remove it before immersing in the *mikvah* on *Shabbat*, she cannot wear it on *Shabbat*. A looser necklace, by contrast, is not a *mikvah* concern and thus is not a *Shabbat* concern.

---

## Totafet & Sarbitin

### Totafet Definition

*Ve-lo ve-totefes* — the *mishnah* also prohibits wearing a *totfet*. *Mai totefes?* — what is a *totfet*? *Amar Rav Yosef: chumsa de-katifta* — a small bundle of spices, which *Rashi* explains was worn to ward off the *ayin hara*.

### Amulet Question

*Amar lei Abaye* — Abaye immediately presses: if this is a spice bundle worn for protection against the evil eye, the problem is not that it is a mere rabbinic issue — it should not be a problem at all. *Tehei ke-kameia mumcheh ve-tishtarei* — let it be treated like a proven amulet, which is permitted to be worn on *Shabbat*. As the *Gemara* will discuss later, amulets that have been demonstrated to be effective — attested by repeated successful use — are considered a form of protective clothing and are not subject to the *Shabbat* restriction. After all, if an amulet is doing its protective work, one has every reason to keep it on and no motivation to remove it. So why should this spice bundle be a problem?

### Amulet Deferred

The discussion of amulets, including the question of whether one may rely on their efficacy and a broader engagement with the rationalist critique — including the *Rambam*'s position — will be addressed when the *Gemara* reaches that topic directly. For now, the implication of Abaye's challenge is that if the *totfet* is a spice bundle for the *ayin hara*, it fits the model of an effective amulet and ought to be entirely permitted.

### Rabbi Yannai

*Ella amar Rav Yehuda mishmeih de-Abaye: apuzaino* — Rav Yehuda, in the name of Abaye, offers a different identification: the *totfet* is an *apuzaino*, apparently some type of head ornament. The precise meaning of the term is unclear — commentators have speculated about its etymology and referent — but the word *totfet* itself, evoking *totafot*, suggests an ornament of that kind.

### Golden Hairnet

*Tanya nami hachi: yotzei isha bi-shvacha muzhevet* — it was similarly taught in a *baraita*: a woman may go out with a golden hairnet. The question naturally arises: if the concern is that she will take off attractive jewelry to show a friend, should not a golden hairnet be the prime candidate? The answer is that a woman would never remove her basic hair covering in public. She would not expose her hair in *reshut ha-rabim*. Therefore, even a magnificent golden hairnet may be worn, because the risk of removal does not exist. *U-ve-totefes u-ve-sarvitin ha-kvuim bah* — and similarly, a *totfet* and *sarvitin* that are affixed to the hairnet may be worn, since the only way to remove them would be to remove the hairnet itself, which she will not do.

### Anatomy Description

*Eizu totefes ve-eizu sarvitin? Amar Rabbi Abbahu: totefes ha-mukefet me-ozen le-ozen* — the *totfet* is something that goes from ear to ear, like a headband across the forehead. *Ve-sarvitin ha-magi'in lah ad le-chayeha* — the *sarvitin* are ornaments that hang down to the jaw. These are the temple ornaments one sees depicted in ancient Near Eastern and Egyptian headdresses: bands across the forehead, pendants hanging down the sides of the face. If woven into the hairnet, they present no problem. If worn separately, a woman might remove them to show a friend, and therefore they are forbidden.

### Poor Women Items

*Amar Rav Huna: aniyot osot otan shel minei tzvu'in* — poor women would make these ornaments from colored, dyed materials rather than precious metals. This is not merely an anthropological note. The point is that the prohibition is not limited to precious or expensive ornaments. Even a beautifully colored piece fashioned from inexpensive materials can be something attractive that a woman might want to display. Within a person's socioeconomic context, even simple ornaments become objects of pride and social display. Therefore, the concern of removal applies regardless of whether the item is made of gold or of dyed fibers.

---

## Kvul Analysis

### Kvul Ambiguity

*Ve-lo be-khvul* — the *mishnah* prohibits going out with a *kvul*. *Amar Rabbi Yannai: be-khvul zeh eini yodea mahu* — Rabbi Yannai frankly admits he does not know what the *kvul* is. Yet he is not entirely without options. He proposes two possibilities: *ee kavla de-avda tenan* — perhaps we are talking about the identifying mark worn by slaves, something like a tag or seal around the neck that identifies whose slave one is; *o dilma kippah shel tzemmer* — or perhaps it is a wool hat, an additional hair covering worn by a woman who already has a *shvacha* hairnet.

The two possibilities are not simply alternate translations — they carry different halachic implications. The question is which one represents the concern of the *mishnah*. If it is the slave's identifying collar, the concern is that the slave will remove it. If it is the wool hat, the question is whether a woman might remove an additional hair covering given that she already has a hairnet underneath — or, more precisely here, given that the hat sits atop the hairnet. One might think that any hair covering is something a woman would not remove in public, but the *Gemara* explores whether a secondary hat, which can in theory be removed without exposing the hair, is something we fear she might take off.

*Amar Rabbi Abbahu: mistabra* — it makes sense to say *kippah shel tzemmer tenan* — that the hat is what the *mishnah* is discussing. And a *baraita* is cited in support: *yotzei ishah bi-kvul* — a woman may go out with a *kvul* — *u-ve-istama le-hatzer* — and with an *istama* into the *chatzer*. So she may wear these items into the courtyard, but not into *reshut ha-rabim*.

### Underneath Hairnet

*Klal amar Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar formulates a general rule.

### Above Below Divide

*Kol she-le-mata min ha-shvacha yotzin bo* — anything worn beneath the hairnet, one may carry, that is, wear, into *reshut ha-rabim*; we are not afraid she will remove it. *Kol she-le-mala min ha-shvacha ein yotzin bo* — anything worn on top of the hairnet, she may not go out with, because we fear she will remove it.

This is counterintuitive at first glance. One might have assumed that whatever is under the hairnet is harder to remove — the hairnet is on top, fixing it in place — while whatever is on top would be easier to take off. But the rule is about motivation, not mechanics. Anything under the hairnet that could theoretically be slipped out without fully removing the hairnet presents a concern in the view of the *tanna kamma* — she could remove it without exposing her hair. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar disagrees: anything under the hairnet is something we are confident she will not remove, since to do so requires manipulating the hairnet in a way she would not do in public. Only if it is above the hairnet — a real cap or hat worn openly on top of her hair covering — are we afraid she might remove it.

The core dispute is therefore about the intermediate case: something beneath the hairnet that could, with effort, be removed without full exposure. The *tanna kamma* in our *mishnah* says that is still a concern and limits it to the *chatzer*; Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says anything under the hairnet is safe.

### Istama Definition

*Mai istama? Amar Rabbi Abbahu: bizyoni. Mai bizyoni? Amar Abaye amar Rav: kalya prukhei* — it is something that catches the sprouting hairs. A woman's hairnet covers the main body of hair, but some strands escape around the edges — in the front, at the back. She would wear a piece of cloth or felt around the perimeter to catch these stray hairs. This item is technically beyond what is strictly required for hair covering, and it is precisely because it is not strictly necessary that we fear she might remove it. Unlike the hairnet itself, which she will never remove, this peripheral cloth she might take off — and therefore she may not wear it into *reshut ha-rabim*.

### Istama Rules

*Tanu rabbanan: gimmel devarim ne'emru be-istama* — three things were said about the *istama*. First, *ein ba mishum kilayim* — it is not subject to the prohibition of *sha'atnez*, the mixture of wool and linen. *Rashi* explains: even if the *istama* is pressed from wool and linen, they are not woven together. Moreover, *Tosafot* adds two further reasons: this material is stiff and does not conform to the shape of the body or provide warmth, and one of the criteria for *sha'atnez* to apply as a halachic "wearing" is that the garment conform and warm. The combination of being merely pressed rather than woven and of being rigid and non-warming means it does not qualify as clothing for *sha'atnez* purposes — and *Tosafot* argues this applies even rabbinically.

*Tosafot* also proposes an alternative explanation: perhaps the *istama* was not primarily clothing at all, but a support structure from which jewelry was hung. If the item exists not as clothing in its own right but as a base for jewelry, it would not be subject to *sha'atnez* since it is not worn *as* clothing.

Second, *ve-eina metamei bi-nega'im* — it does not become impure through *tzara'at* afflictions. Here too the reason is that it is not woven, and being woven is one of the criteria for garments to be susceptible to *nega'im* impurity. Third, *ve-ein yotzin bo le-reshut ha-rabim* — she may not go out with it into *reshut ha-rabim*, since she might remove it, for the same reason discussed above.

### Bride Crowns

*Mishum Rabbi Shimon amru: af ein ba mishum atarot kallot* — in the name of Rabbi Shimon, they added a fourth ruling: this *istama* does not fall under the restriction on bridal crowns. A *baraita* in *Masechet Sotah* records that after the persecutions of Vespasian, in mourning for the destruction of Jerusalem, brides were no longer permitted to wear certain ornate crowns. The statement here is that the *istama* does not qualify as such a crown and is not subject to that restriction. Notably, this ruling lends support to *Tosafot*'s reading that the *istama* served as a support for jewelry, since the fact that this ruling is necessary at all implies that the *istama* was sufficiently jewelry-like that one might have thought it falls under the bridal crown prohibition.

---

## Slave Seals

### Samuel's Distinction

*Ve-Shmuel amar: kavla de-avda tenan* — Shmuel holds that the *mishnah*'s *kvul* refers specifically to the slave's identifying collar, not to the wool hat of a woman. The hat, under Shmuel's reading, is not a problem at all — we are only concerned about the slave's seal.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this by citing Shmuel himself: *ve-amar Shmuel: yotzei eved be-chotam she-be-tzavaro aval lo be-chotam she-bi-khsuto* — Shmuel ruled elsewhere that a slave may go out on *Shabbat* with a seal around his neck but not with a seal on his garment. If Shmuel believes the slave's seal is such a concern that it is what our *mishnah* addresses, how can he simultaneously rule that a slave may wear a seal around his neck?

### Master Requirement

*Lo kashya* — the *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *ha de-avid lei rabei* — when his master affixes the seal, requiring the slave to wear it, we are not afraid the slave will remove it. He is obligated by his master and will not dare take it off. That is the case where wearing around the neck is permitted. *Ha de-avid ihu le-nafshei* — but if the slave himself made the seal of his own accord, without his master's instruction, then we are afraid he might remove it. That is the case that our *mishnah* addresses, and that is the case the slave-seal prohibition concerns.

### Seal Breaking

*Be-mai ukimta le-ha de-Shmuel* — but if the permitted case is when the master requires it, why is even the seal on the garment prohibited in that case? If his master requires him to wear it, he will not remove it from his garment either. *Dilma mifsik ve-mirta* — the concern is that the seal might break off on its own. The seal falls from the garment, and the slave is terrified that his master will think he deliberately removed it. This scenario is strikingly evocative — the fear that a visible marker of identification has been removed, and the consequences of being found without it.

### Folding Concern

*U-miflei u-machei lei a-katfei* — panicked, he takes off his outer garment and folds it over his shoulder so that no one will see he is wearing it without the seal intact. And carrying a folded garment on one's shoulder is carrying, not wearing. *Ki de-Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef amar Rabbi Yochanan: ha-yotzei be-tallis kefula u-menachat a-katfeihu be-Shabbat chayav chatat* — as Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef cited in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: one who goes out on *Shabbat* with a garment folded and placed on his shoulders is liable as one who carries, not as one who wears. A garment must be worn to be exempt; folded on the shoulder, it is simply a carried object. Therefore, even where the master requires the seal and the slave will not willfully remove it, the seal on the garment remains prohibited, because an inadvertent loss of the seal creates a cascade leading to carrying.

The neck, by contrast, does not raise this concern: if the seal around the neck falls off, there is no garment to remove and fold.

### Resh Galuta Rabbis

*Ve-chi ha de-amar lei Shmuel le-Rav Chinana bar Shila: kulu rabbanan de-bei resh galuta* — Shmuel said to Rav Chinana bar Shila that all the rabbis of the household of the *Resh Galuta*, the Exilarch, who wore identifying seals or insignia on their garments — *lo lipku be-sarye ve-lo chatime* — may not go out on *Shabbat* with these sealed garments. The reason is the same: if the seal falls off, the rabbit of the Exilarch's court, frantic about being caught without his mark of office, will remove his outer garment and carry it folded on his shoulder rather than be seen without the seal. *Le-bar minach* — but Rav Chinana bar Shila himself is excepted. *De-lo kefidi alach de-bei resh galuta* — the household of the Exilarch does not hold him to strict account; they will not penalize him if his insignia is missing. Since there is no consequence for him, there is no reason he would panic and remove his garment, and the concern of carrying therefore does not apply to him.

The upshot of this entire discussion: on the garment, the concern is not willful removal but the involuntary loss of the seal and the fear-driven response that follows. On the neck, that chain of events does not apply. And only those who face actual accountability to the Exilarch's household are subject to the restriction; those for whom the household will make an exception are personally exempt.

---

---

# Shabbat 58

## Intro & Context

### Opening Review

The *daf* under discussion is 58a, and we pick up approximately ten lines down with the word *gufa* — the Gemara's own signal that it is now addressing the substance of a previously cited ruling. By way of orientation: the broader *perek* has been cataloguing items that may or may not be worn on *Shabbat*, particularly those that are carried or worn in the public domain. The animating concern in most of these cases is not a biblical prohibition — many of these items are, strictly speaking, legitimate forms of clothing or jewelry — but rather a rabbinic decree rooted in the fear that the wearer might remove the item to show it to someone, or that it might fall off, prompting the wearer to carry it.

### Kvul & Slave Pendants

The most recent discussion had addressed something called a *kvul*, understood by some as a scarf or secondary cap worn beneath a hairnet. The debate there turned on whether a woman would ever remove this underlying garment while outdoors: since she would be reluctant to expose her hair by removing the hairnet, one might argue there is no realistic concern she would take off the *kvul* either. Others, however, understood the *kvul* as a pendant worn by a slave — a form of identification marking him as belonging to a particular master, attached either to his person or to his garment. In that reading, the concern was that if the pendant fell from his garment, he would not want to be seen wearing his clothing without the identifying mark, and would therefore remove his garment and carry it. It is this slave-pendant case — the *chotam* — that now occupies the Gemara's attention.

## Slave Law Excursus

### Ravad on Slave Status

Before entering the Gemara's analysis directly, a brief excursus on the underlying legal landscape is warranted. The slave under discussion is a non-Jewish slave who has undergone *milah* and *tevilah*, thereby becoming obligated in *mitzvot* at the same level as Jewish women. Such a slave is thus himself bound by the laws of *Shabbat* and, in principle, by the rabbinic enactments built upon them.

There is, however, a striking position advanced by the *Ravad* (Rabbi Abraham ben David). When the Torah commands — *lo ta'aseh kol melachah atah uvincha uvitecha avdecha va'amascha* — "do not do any labor, you and your son and your daughter and your slave and your slave-woman," the *Ravad* argues that this *pasuk* is not referring to the halachically integrated slave who has undergone *milah* and *tevilah*. That slave is already independently obligated. Rather, the verse addresses those who are functionally under the master's authority — workers or bondsmen who have not formally entered the halachic category of Jewish-obligated slaves — and the master's obligation is to ensure that they do not perform labor *for him*, even if they may perform labor for themselves.

### Master's Obligation

The verse *lema'an yanuach shorcha va'chamorecha... avdecha va'amascha kamocha* — "so that your ox and donkey shall rest... your slave and slave-woman like yourself" — makes plain that the master bears a distinct obligation with respect to those under his control. Alongside this: *lo ta'aseh kol melachah atah uvincha uvitecha avdecha va'amascha* imposes on the master a prohibition against allowing his slaves to perform *melachah*. Consequently, when a slave who has gone through the halachic process violates *Shabbat*, not only does the slave himself transgress, but the master may be in transgression as well. The master therefore has an independent stake in the *Shabbat* conduct of his slaves.

This framework — that the master's concern for the pendant is legally salient — will prove important momentarily when the Gemara evaluates the conditions under which a slave may or may not go out wearing the *chotam*.

### Categorical Structure Q

One might ask why the *Mishnah* begins with a single declaration of *bameh ha'adam yotze* — "with what does a person go out" — only to subdivide the discussion into the separate categories of men, women, and slaves, each with their own distinct *halachot*. Clothing is highly gendered, and the social norms that determine what counts as an ornament, a burden, or an ordinary garment differ substantially across these categories. Each category will therefore generate different legal consequences; that they were grouped together at the outset reflects the underlying unity of the question, even as the details necessarily diverge. The same social-norm sensitivity that distinguishes men's clothing from women's clothing is precisely what will drive the analysis of the slave's pendant.

## Slave Pendants Analysis

### Samuel's Ruling

The Gemara now addresses the *gufa* — the substance of the ruling. *Amar Shmuel: yotze ha'eved bechotam shebetzavaro aval lo bechotam shebichsuto* — Shmuel rules that a slave may go out on *Shabbat* with the identifying seal worn around his neck, but not with a seal attached to his garment. The rationale is straightforward: if the seal worn around his neck breaks or falls off, the slave has little incentive to do anything about it — he cannot reattach it on *Shabbat*, and leaving it where it fell creates no particular problem for him. But if the seal affixed to his garment falls off, he faces a different dilemma. He does not want to be seen by his master wearing the garment without the identifying mark, and so he might well remove the garment and carry it — an act of *hotza'ah* on *Shabbat*. It is that risk which the rabbinic decree addresses.

A *baraita* is then cited in support: *yotze ha'eved bechotam shebetzavaro aval lo bechotam shebichsuto* — the same formulation as Shmuel's ruling, and therefore *tanya nami hachi*, the *baraita* accords with Shmuel.

### Baraita Contradiction

The Gemara immediately raises a contradiction from a second *baraita*: *lo yetze ha'eved bechotam shebetzavaro velo bechotam shebichsuto* — the slave should not go out with the seal either around his neck or on his garment. This directly contradicts Shmuel, who permitted the seal around the neck.

One resolution offered is that the difference lies in *who made* the pendant. If the master had it made and insists the slave wear it — *de'avid lei rabeih* — then there is no concern the slave will voluntarily remove it, and if it falls off around his neck, he will simply leave it. In that case the neck-worn seal is permissible, as Shmuel rules. But if the slave had it made for himself — *de'avid lei le'nafsheih* — then we are concerned he might voluntarily remove it, and the *baraita* prohibiting it around the neck applies.

### Pendants & Tumah

The *baraita* appends a further ruling: *ve-ze ve-ze ein mekabelin tumah* — neither the neck-worn seal nor the garment-affixed seal becomes *tamei*. This observation prompts analysis. Rashi explains that the pendant is not jewelry, because the slave does not wear it as an ornament or out of any desire to look attractive — he wears it because his master compels him to. It is therefore not susceptible to *tumah* as jewelry would be. Nor, Rashi adds, is it a *kli* — a functional vessel being put to some use; it simply rests on the person without being actively employed.

This is a striking conclusion, however, because it creates an apparent tension. If the pendant is neither jewelry nor vessel, on what basis is the slave *biblically* permitted to wear it at all? If it were merely a burden, he could not. The implicit assumption of the Gemara's entire discussion is that there is no biblical prohibition — the rabbinic decree is the only obstacle in certain configurations. Yet the category that would permit it — clothing or ornament — is also the category that would make it *mekabel tumah*. To say it is neither jewelry nor vessel, and yet is biblically permissible to wear, points toward the conclusion that it functions as a form of clothing. But if so, why is it not *tamei*? The answer may lie in the material: clothing made of metal, as opposed to fabric, does not enter the halachic category of clothing susceptible to *tumah*.

### Status Puzzle

This puzzle — that the pendant appears to occupy no clean halachic category — is genuinely difficult. It is not jewelry, not a functional vessel, not fabric clothing. If it is some form of metal clothing, then the rule that only fabric garments contract *tumah* as clothing would explain its *taharah*, while still allowing it to be worn biblically. But this remains an unresolved tension: if it is clothing, the question is what kind and under what theory; if it is none of the above, the biblical permission to wear it demands explanation.

What the Gemara has established so far, then, is: the slave's identifying pendant is not *mekabel tumah* — it does not become *tamei*. Yet it is biblically permissible to wear. Rabbinically, however, wearing it on the garment is prohibited (lest it fall off and prompt carrying the garment), and wearing it around the neck is subject to further conditions.

The Gemara then reasons: *midekatani zeh vezeh ein mekabelin tumah* — since both forms of the pendant are said not to become *tamei*, and since the pendant is made of a material that *could* in principle be *tamei* (were it fashioned into a proper *kli*), the Gemara infers that we must be speaking of metal pendants. *Shma mina de'matachet* — conclude from this that we are dealing with metal. The inference is clinched by a *Mishnah* establishing that vessels made of stone, dried dung, or unfired earth — *klei avanim, klei glalim, ve'klei adama* — are never *mekabelin tumah*, neither biblically nor rabbinically. If the pendant were made of plaster or clay, it would be trivially obvious that it is not *tamei*, and the *baraita* would be making a pointless observation. The fact that the *baraita* finds it necessary to state that the pendant does not become *tamei* confirms that it is made of metal — a material that, when fashioned into a proper vessel, certainly would be susceptible. Here, however, because it is neither jewelry nor vessel, the metal pendant remains *tahor*.

### Metal vs Plaster

With that established, the Gemara returns to the contradiction between Shmuel and the second *baraita*. Rather than resolving it through the distinction of who made the pendant, the Gemara proposes an alternative: *ve-kan be-shel matechet, kan be-shel tina* — one case involves a metal pendant and the other a plaster pendant. Even when the master had the pendant made and insists the slave wear it, there remains a meaningful difference based on material.

If the pendant is made of plaster, it has essentially no monetary value — it may even shatter upon falling. If it falls off around the slave's neck, he will simply leave it where it lies; there is no incentive whatsoever to pick it up. In this case the seal around the neck is permitted, consistent with Shmuel's ruling. But if the pendant is made of metal, a different concern arises: even though the slave will not voluntarily remove it (the master insists he wear it), if it falls off, the slave faces a dilemma. Leaving a piece of metal — something of monetary value — lying in the public domain is its own problem; the slave may fear his master's displeasure at losing the valuable object, and so he may pick it up and carry it home. That carrying is the forbidden act. Hence the second *baraita*, which prohibits even the neck-worn seal, is speaking of a metal pendant.

### Makpid Criterion

Rav Nachman bar Ami, citing Rabbah bar Avuha, formulates this as a general criterion: *davar ha-makpid alav rabo — ein yotzin bo*. If the master is *makpid* — particular, insistent — about the object's value, and the slave knows he will face consequences for losing it, then the slave cannot go out with it on *Shabbat*, because we anticipate that if it falls, he will carry it home rather than risk his master's anger. Conversely, *davar she'ein makpid alav rabo — yotzin bo*: if the master cares that the slave wear it but is indifferent to its material value, and therefore the slave has no reason to pick it up if it falls, he may go out wearing it. The master's concern — his *makpid*-ness — functions as the operative halachic criterion distinguishing permissible from impermissible configurations.

## Social Norms & Halacha

### Beged Ish/Isha

The broader question underlying much of this discussion is how social norms interact with halachic categorization. This is not a marginal issue: the very categories at stake — *beged ish* and *beged isha*, men's clothing and women's clothing — are defined not by any a priori Platonic essence but by the social realities of a given time and place. The biblical prohibition on cross-dressing (*lo yilbash gever simlat ishah*) does not itself specify which garments belong to which category; that is entirely a function of convention.

A clear example is trousers. When women first began wearing trousers in modern Western society, a period existed during which pants were understood, by virtually everyone, as distinctly men's garments. At that stage, one could plausibly argue that a woman wearing pants was violating the prohibition of *beged ish*. As social norms shifted and trousers were cut specifically for women and worn universally, that argument became increasingly difficult to sustain on the grounds of *beged ish* alone. Today, objections to women wearing trousers are primarily grounded in *tzniut* — a separate and independently operating concern — rather than in the cross-dressing prohibition. The two concerns must not be conflated: *tzniut* and the prohibition of *beged ish* rest on different foundations and are triggered by different conditions.

### Locked Categories?

This raises a significant question that runs through every area of *halacha*: once the *Sages* specifically identified concrete items as falling under a given category — this garment is *beged ish*, this practice violates that rule — do those identifications become permanently fixed even when the underlying social reality has changed? The categories themselves (men's clothing, women's clothing, burden, ornament) are not static; they are defined relationally to social practice. But it is possible to argue that once a rabbinic enactment or identification is articulated in terms of a specific item, it acquires a life of its own and is no longer hostage to shifting conventions.

This question — how much are specific applications "written in stone" as opposed to being revisable when circumstances change — is perennial in *halachic* literature and arises in every domain. In the context of *Shabbat*, what counts as clothing versus a burden, what constitutes a reasonable concern that an item will be taken off and shown to someone, what qualifies as jewelry as opposed to a mere carrying mechanism — all of these determinations are sensitive, to varying degrees, to the facts on the ground. The categories are social constructs, and therefore they track, at least partially, social change.

Alongside this, the question of whether rabbinic concerns are applied categorically or case-by-case also surfaces here. Tosafot's general approach is that once a concern attaches to some members of a category, the decree extends to the whole category, even when the particular circumstances might not generate the specific danger. The Gemara itself is not fully explicit on this point, but the working assumption in many of these cases is that we prohibit the entire category once a systemic concern has been identified.

## Bells & Jewelry

### Slave Bell Rules

The Gemara now turns from the identifying seal to the *zug* — the bell. *Ve-lo bezug shebetzavaro* — a slave may not go out on *Shabbat* with a bell worn around his neck. *Aval yotze hu bezug she-biksuto* — he may, however, go out with a bell woven into his garment. Importantly, *ve-ze ve-ze mekabelin tumah* — both configurations of the bell, whether around the neck or woven into the garment, are *mekabelin tumah*, susceptible to ritual impurity. The bell is jewelry, and jewelry, unlike the identifying pendant, does become *tamei*.

### Loose vs. Woven

The question is why the distinction between around the neck and woven into the garment should matter, given that both are equally jewelry. The Gemara asks: *zug shebetzavaro amai lo?* — why may he not go out with the bell around his neck? The answer: *dilma mipsik va'ate l'atuyei* — we are concerned that the strap may break and he will pick it up and carry it home, since it has value as jewelry.

But if that is the concern, then *zug she-biksuto nami leichosh dilma mipsik va'ate l'atuyei* — the same concern should apply to the bell woven into the garment; it too could come loose and be carried. The Gemara resolves this: *de'micha bei mumcha* — when the bell is on the garment, we are speaking of a case where it is woven in. A bell properly woven into a garment will not simply fall off; the fear of breakage and subsequent carrying does not apply. The bell around the neck, by contrast, hangs on a strap that is vulnerable to snapping.

### Kol She-Arag

This ruling is grounded in the principle articulated by Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: *kol she'arag lo gazru* — anything that has been woven in is not subject to the rabbinic decree. It is worth noting, as both Rashi and Tosafot observe, that this principle appears in a strikingly different application elsewhere in the tractate. In an earlier context, it was invoked in connection with strings woven tightly into a woman's hair — the question being whether tightly interwoven ornaments constitute a *chatzitzah* for immersion, and whether loosely woven ornamental chains in the hair might be permissible to wear on *Shabbat* because they would not be removed for *mikvah*. There, *kol she'arag* addressed whether something is securely attached to the hair. Here, it addresses whether something affixed to a garment presents a concern of falling off and being carried.

This is a point well worth reflection. The same *amora'im*'s statement — *kol she'arag lo gazru* — is being deployed with two distinct meanings in two distinct contexts. Whether both interpretations reflect the original intent of the statement, or whether the Gemara in each case is reading a general principle through the lens of its own context, is a question that David Weiss Halivni has raised regarding the way the Gemara transmits and reapplies earlier *amoraic* formulations.

## Animal Restrictions

### Animal Rules

The *baraita* continues with the case of the *behemah* — the animal. *Ve-lo tetze behemah lo be-chotam shebetzavarah ve-lo be-chotam shebichsutah* — an animal may not go out wearing identifying tags, either around its neck or affixed to any covering it wears. What is remarkable here — and what was flagged in an earlier session as genuinely puzzling — is that by an animal, the identifying tag is treated as a biblical burden (*massa*), not merely a rabbinic problem. Yet by a slave, the identifying pendant is biblically permissible; the restrictions are rabbinic in nature. The inversion is difficult to explain, and no ready discussion of the distinction was found in the *rishonim*.

The animal also may not go out with bells: *ve-lo bezug shebetzavarah ve-lo bezug shebichsutah* — neither around the neck nor woven into a garment placed on the animal.

### Animal Ornaments

The *baraita* states: *ve-ze ve-ze ein mekabelin tumah* — neither the identifying tags nor the bells worn by an animal become *tamei*. The logic in the case of the identifying tags follows from what has already been established: they are not jewelry (the animal has no aesthetic interest in looking adorned), they are not functional vessels in the ordinary sense, and they do not enter the halachic category of *kelim* susceptible to *tumah*. The case of the bells, however, is more complex. The Gemara will need to account for why bells on an animal do not become *tamei*, given that bells on a person are explicitly *mekabelin tumah* as jewelry.

The reference to the animal's *kesut* — its covering — is explained by Rashi as referring to a blanket or headdress placed on the animal for warmth or appearance, a practice attested with camels and horses.

### Bell Tamei Issue

The Gemara immediately challenges the claim that a bell worn by an animal does not become *tamei*. *Ureminhu: zug she-beheimah tme'iah, ve-shel delet tehorah* — a *baraita* teaches that a bell on an animal is *tamei*, while a bell on a door is *tahor*.

The logic of the door's *taharah* is clear: a bell affixed to a door, if nailed down firmly, is considered *mechubar la'karka* — connected to the ground through the structure of the house — and objects attached to the ground cannot contract *tumah*. A bell merely hung on a nail and easily removable would be different; that remains a *kli* and would be *tamei*. But one properly fixed to the door participates in the door's status and is therefore *tahor*.

The *baraita* then adds a critical further ruling: *shel delet va'asao la-behemah — tme'iah*. If the bell had been nailed into the door and was then removed and assigned to an animal, it becomes *tamei*. The reason: it has now been assigned to the category of an animal's bell, and that assignment — *machshavah*, intention — suffices to enter it into the category of things susceptible to *tumah*. Conversely, *shel behemah va'asao la-delet* — if it had been an animal's bell and was subsequently nailed into a door — *af al pi she-chibro la-delet, tamei*: even though it is now affixed to the door, it remains *tamei*. The Gemara provides the governing principle: *she-kol ha-kelim yordim lidei tum'ah be-machshavah ve-ein olim midei tum'atan ela be-shinui ma'aseh* — vessels enter the category susceptible to *tumah* through mere intention or assignment, but they exit that category only through a *shinui ma'aseh*, a genuine physical change to the object itself.

## Sticky Principle

### Door to Animal

The asymmetry embedded in this principle — what might be called the sticky principle — merits emphasis. When the bell was on the door, affixed by nails, it appeared to have undergone a physical change: it was physically integrated into a larger structure. Yet the Gemara does not count this as a *shinui ma'aseh* sufficient to change the bell's status. The reason is that the bell itself was not physically altered; only its location changed, and it was attached to something. The actual object — the bell — remains physically identical to what it was when it was an animal's bell. Nailing it to a door does not change the bell; it merely repositions it. Hence the bell retains its susceptibility to *tumah*.

### Entry & Exit

The underlying principle is sharp: entry into *tumah* status is easy — it requires only *machshavah*, the mental act of assigning an object to a particular use or category. The moment one decides a bell will serve as an animal's bell, it enters that category and becomes susceptible to *tumah*. Exit from that status, by contrast, is difficult — it demands a genuine *shinui ma'aseh*, a physical change to the object itself, not merely a change of location, owner, or intended use. This asymmetry reflects a broader halachic disposition: the status of *kelim* adheres tenaciously once acquired, and superficial changes do not dislodge it.

## Knocker Principle

### With/Without Knocker

Given that a *baraita* says an animal's bell is *tamei*, how is this reconciled with the *baraita* that said an animal's bells do not become *tamei*? The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *ha d'it lei inbal ve-ha d'leit lei inbal* — the one source speaks of a bell that has a knocker (an *inbal*, a clapper inside), and the other speaks of one without a knocker. A bell with a knocker — one that actually sounds as the animal walks — becomes *tamei*. A bell without a knocker does not.

But the Gemara immediately presses: *mama nafshach* — either way, the reasoning seems difficult. If the bell is considered a vessel, then even without the knocker it should be *tamei*, since a vessel is a vessel. If it is not considered a vessel, then why does adding a knocker suddenly transform it into one susceptible to *tumah*?

### Sound Basis

The answer lies in a *derashah* of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan. The verse in the account of the Midianite spoils — *kol davar asher yavo va'esh ta'aviru va'esh ve-taher* — "anything that comes through fire, you shall pass through fire and purify it" — is parsed not for its primary *peshat* meaning (which the *Sages* elsewhere interpret as the source for *kashering* vessels that absorbed *treif* foods), but rather as a basis for the rule that metal objects that produce sound are *tamei*. The *derashah* focuses on the word *davar* — thing or word — and reads it as encompassing even *dibur*, sound. Thus: things that produce sound from metal are to be included in the category of *kelim* susceptible to *tumah*.

The context here is illuminating. The spoils of Midian included musical instruments and bells among the *kelim* brought back from war. Elazar the Kohen instructed the people on how to render these vessels *tahor*. The Gemara reads this as a scriptural basis establishing that sound-producing metal vessels are a recognized category of *kli* with its own rules concerning *tumah* and *taharah*.

### Interpretations

Two distinct understandings of this principle emerge. The simpler reading — and apparently the straightforward reading of the Gemara — is that there is a substantive independent category: metal sound-producers (*mashmi'ei kol*) are *kelim* susceptible to *tumah* by virtue of what they are and what they do, regardless of for whom they are made. On this reading, even a bell hung on an animal enters the category of *kelim* through the knocker, because making sound is itself the defining function that renders it a vessel.

Tosafot resists positing an entirely new category of sound-makers. Instead, Tosafot argues that the real point is functional utility: a person puts a bell on an animal in order to track the animal's location. The bell's sounding serves the owner directly — just as a rod used to guide an animal is considered the owner's *kli* because the person uses it actively, so too a bell whose sound the owner relies upon to locate the animal is the owner's *kli*. Without the knocker, the bell makes no sound, serves no locating function, and is therefore not the owner's vessel. With the knocker, it does serve that function, and it therefore becomes a *kli* susceptible to *tumah*. On this reading, there is no new categorical principle about sound-makers; rather, the knocker is the mechanism by which the person-owner actually uses the object.

### Context Determines

The Gemara now returns to the middle case — the bell worn by a person, not an animal — and notes a complication. The *baraita* stated that bells on a person (*ve-ze ve-ze mekabelin tumah*) are *tamei* in both configurations — around the neck and woven into a garment. But if we have been explaining the animal's case by saying that only a bell with a knocker becomes *tamei*, the same logic should apply to the person's case, and the *baraita* about the person's bells should likewise distinguish between those with and without knockers.

The Gemara resolves this by appeal to a further *baraita*: *ha'oseh zugin la-machteshet, ula-arisah, ula-matpechos sefarim, ula-matpechos tinokot* — bells made for a pounder (where the sound was believed to improve the quality of what was being ground), for a baby's crib, for *Sifrei Torah* wrappings, or for infants' scarves. The *halacha* in each case: *yesh lahem inbal — tme'im; ein lahem inbal — tehorim* — with a knocker, *tamei*; without a knocker, *tahor*. And if the knocker was removed after the bell had one — *nitlu inbeleihen, adayin tumatan aleihem* — they retain their status.

The Gemara then draws a distinction: *hani mili be-tinok de-la-kala avidi lei* — when we require a knocker for the bell to be *tamei*, that is specifically in the case of an infant or a crib, where the *sole purpose* of the bell is to produce sound. Without the knocker, it produces no sound, serves no function, and is therefore not a *kli*. *Aval gadol — tachshit hu lo* — but for an adult, a bell is an ornament even without a knocker, because adults wear bells as jewelry simply for their aesthetic quality. Therefore, for an adult, a bell without a knocker is still *tamei* because it is worn as jewelry; for an infant's crib or the child's scarf, only a functioning bell with a knocker enters the category of *kelim*.

### Watch Analogy

This last distinction — that the same object can function differently depending on context, and that its halachic status as a *kli* tracks its actual function — is illuminating in a broader sense. It calls to mind a *teshuvah* of Rav Moshe Feinstein addressing the question of wearing a watch without an *eiruv* on *Shabbat*. A watch is not obviously jewelry, nor is it obviously clothing; one might argue it is simply a convenient method of carrying a time-measuring device on one's wrist — a burden rather than an ornament. Rav Moshe's answer was that a watch may be worn without an *eiruv* only if one would wear it even if it were not working — because only then is it being worn as an ornament or jewelry rather than as a functional time-piece that happens to be worn on the body. The parallel to the bell-without-a-knocker analysis is clear: when the functional element is absent and the object is still worn, it is worn as jewelry; when the function is the entire point, its removal empties the object of its *kli* status.

## Sticky Principle (II)

### Knocker Removal

Returning to the *baraita*'s statement that removing the knocker does not change the bell's *tumah* status — *nitlu inbeleihen adayin tumatan aleihem* — the Gemara asks: *le-mai chazi?* — to what use can the bell now be put, without its knocker, if it was made for a child or a crib where sound was the whole point? If it serves no function, it should lose its *kli* status. One might also argue that removing the knocker constitutes a *shinui ma'aseh* — a physical change — which, as established, is precisely what is required to exit the category of *tamei* vessels.

Abaye answers: *ho'il ve-hedyot yakhol le-hakhziro* — since any ordinary person can replace the knocker without special skill, the removal is not really a change of the object. It is a trivially reversible act. The knocker is likely removed periodically — when one does not want the bell to sound — and reinserted when desired. Because the object remains what it was, fully restorable by a layman, it retains its status as a *kli* and therefore its susceptibility to *tumah*.

This principle — *hedyot yakhol le-hakhziro* — has broader resonance in the laws of *Shabbat*. It surfaces in discussions about whether reassembling objects on *Shabbat* constitutes forbidden *boneh* or *makeh ba-patish*: if a layman can trivially restore something to its former state, the disassembly may not have genuinely altered the object's status.

## Scissors & Chibbur

### Scissors Rules

Rava challenges Abaye's reasoning by citing the case of the *masporet shel perakim* — scissors assembled from separable components — and the *izel shel rehatni*, the carpenter's plane, which consists of a wooden frame and a metal blade. The rule stated: *chibbur le-tumah, ve-ein chibbur le-haza'ah* — these multi-part tools are considered a single connected unit for the purposes of contracting *tumah* (if one part becomes *tamei*, the other does too), but they are *not* considered a single unit for the purposes of *haza'ah*, the sprinkling of *parah adumah* water (if the water touches one part, the other is not rendered *tahor*).

This seems contradictory. If the two blades of the scissors are one unit, they should be one unit for all purposes — both for contracting *tumah* and for becoming *tahor* through *haza'ah*. If they are separate units, they should be separate for all purposes.

### Raba's Principle

Rava resolves this. Biblically, the rule is as follows: *bish'at melachah* — when the scissors are actively in use (or in the midst of a sewing session even if not at the precise moment of cutting) — they are considered a single unit for all purposes, both for *tumah* and for *haza'ah*. *Shelo bish'at melachah* — when the work session is over, and indeed standard practice was to disassemble the scissors when putting them away — they are considered two separate units for all purposes, both for *tumah* and for *haza'ah*.

### Rabbinic Stringency

The apparent contradiction arises from rabbinic stringency applied asymmetrically. The rabbis decreed that for *tumah*, the scissors should be treated as a single unit even *shelo bish'at melachah* — even when not in use — because people will not make fine distinctions, and inconsistency in *tumah* rules breeds confusion. Conversely, for *haza'ah*, which renders the vessel *tahor*, the rabbis decreed that the scissors be treated as two separate units even *bish'at melachah* — even when in use — in order to be stringent about ensuring full *taharah*. The result: rabbinically, they are always one unit for *tumah* (easy to contract impurity), and always two units for *haza'ah* (harder to achieve purity). This dual stringency recapitulates, in a different register, the sticky principle: entering *tumah* status is easy, exiting it is hard.

## Rava vs. Abaye

### Abaye's Challenge

Rava's challenge to Abaye now comes into focus. If, according to the *halacha* of the scissors, even the position of *shelo bish'at melachah* — when the tool is laid aside and the intention is to take it apart — already renders the components separate vessels, then certainly once the components are physically separated, they are unambiguously two distinct objects. Applying this to the bell: once the knocker is removed from the bell, they are certainly two separate things. The bell without the knocker is no longer the same vessel it was. If that is so, removing the knocker is indeed a genuine *shinui ma'aseh*, and Abaye's answer — that *hedyot yakhol le-hakhziro* prevents the status from changing — appears insufficient. The scissors principle seems to say the opposite: once separated, the status does change.

### Rava's Response

Rava responds with his own answer, displacing Abaye's: *ho'il ve-ra'uy le-hakkisho al gabbei cheres pizi* — since one can still use the bell by banging it against a piece of pottery. A child's favorite instrument, after all, is a pot and a wooden spoon. The bell without its knocker can still be struck against pottery to produce sound. Therefore, Rava argues, the removal of the knocker does not render the bell nonfunctional; it simply changes the mode of use. The bell remains a sound-producing vessel, capable of being used in this alternative fashion. It therefore retains its *kli* status and does not lose its susceptibility to *tumah*. The *hedyot yakhol le-hakhziro* reasoning of Abaye is unnecessary; Rava's reasoning is that the object remains a functional *kli* on its own terms.

### Alternative Use

This alternative-use reasoning is then corroborated by a parallel *memra*. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina both cite the *ho'il ve-ra'uy le-hakkisho al gabbei cheres* reasoning. But Rabbi Yochanan adds a distinct alternative: *ho'il ve-ra'uy lig-mei bo mayim le-tinok* — one can use the bell as a small scoop or ladle to give water to an infant. The bell without its knocker retains its hollow form and can serve as a vessel for liquid.

### Function Change Q

This sets up a question that is explicitly left unresolved at this juncture. Rabbi Yochanan's alternative-use reasoning raises the possibility that a vessel which has become non-functional in its original capacity but can be repurposed for a different function retains its *kli* status. But the question is not trivial: does a change of function preserve the vessel's status, or does the fact that it is no longer being used for its original purpose constitute a *shinui ma'aseh* sufficient to alter that status? Rava's answer — that the bell can still be banged on pottery — preserves the same *type* of use (sound production). Rabbi Yochanan's answer — that it can serve as a water scoop — involves a genuinely different use. Whether these two are halachically equivalent, and whether change of function preserves or disrupts vessel status, remains to be developed in the continuation of the *sugya*.
