---

# Shabbat 62

## Women's Carrying Objects

### Intro & Mishnah Setup

The daf begins with a Mishnah that continues a theme established in prior pages: which objects carried on Shabbat constitute a biblical violation of *hotzaah* and which constitute only a rabbinic concern. The earlier Mishnayot addressed items that men and women may not wear on Shabbat, not because wearing them is itself a biblical transgression, but because of the rabbinic concern that one might remove them in public and come to carry them. The present Mishnah shifts to a different category: items that, even when worn on or about the body, are classified not as clothing or adornment but as carrying outright—and therefore implicate a biblical prohibition.

### Needle with Eye

*Lo teitzei ha'ishah bemachat hanekuvah*: a woman may not go out with a needle that has an eye in it. A needle with a hole is an implement of sewing; wearing it stuck through one's garment is not a form of adornment but simply a convenient method of transport. The needle is carried by being on the body, not worn as clothing.

### Signet Ring

*Velo betaba'at sheyeish aleha chotam*: nor with a ring bearing a seal, a signet ring. As established in earlier discussion, a signet ring was normatively a man's article—used for authenticating documents and transactions—and not the customary ornament of a woman. Accordingly, when a woman wears it, it is classified not as wearing but as carrying around the finger.

### Kulyar & Kovelet

*Velo bekhulyar velo bekoveles*: nor with a *kulyar* nor with a *koveles*. The Gemara will explain that the *kulyar* is some kind of clasp—Rashi identifies it as a *machbenasa*, though precisely what this is and why it would not qualify as clothing is not fully clear, and the Rishonim do not offer extensive discussion on the point. The *koveles*, as the Gemara shortly clarifies, is a small bundle or vial containing aromatic herbs or spices, worn around the neck.

### Aromatic Bottles

*Velo bitzluchit shel pilayton*: nor with a small bottle of *pilayton*. Rashi identifies *pilayton* as *balma*—balsam oil, *mishchat ha'afarsimon*. To clarify: the balsam familiar from northern latitudes is not the balsam of the Talmudic world. The balsam of the Torah is a bush, indigenous to the region, from which an aromatic oil was derived; one of the components of the *ketoret* is commonly identified with it. The *tzluchit shel pilayton*, then, is a small glass flask containing this aromatic oil, worn around the neck so that one would smell pleasant at all times.

### Meir vs. Chachamim

*Ve'im yatze'ah chayevet chatat, divrei Rabbi Meir*: if a woman goes out wearing any of these items she is obligated a *chatat*, a sin-offering—they are classified as carrying despite being on the body. *Vachachamim potrim bekoveles uvitzluchit shel pilayton*: the Sages, however, exempt her with respect to the last two items, the aromatic bundle and the balsam flask. This mirrors the three-way dispute already seen regarding the *ir shel zahav*, the golden tiara, where Rabbi Meir was more inclined to treat items as biblically prohibited carrying, the Sages considered them jewelry subject only to a rabbinic restriction, and Rabbi Eliezer permitted them outright.

One might ask whether wearing aromatic substances raises the separate rabbinic concern of *shchikat samanim*, the prohibition against grinding medicinal spices on Shabbat. That concern, however, applies specifically to medicinal use—not to fragrance applied to the body—and in any case is a rabbinic matter, whereas the Gemara's primary focus here is the biblical question of whether these items constitute *hotzaah*.

## Ulla's Gender Reversal

### Ulla's Reversal

*Amar Ulla: vechilufeihen be'ish*—Ulla declares that the reverse applies to a man. The Mishnah, notably, does not specify what the law is for a man wearing these same items. The implication might simply be that what is customary clothing for men poses no problem. But Ulla goes further: not only is a signet ring not an issue for a man (since it is normatively men's jewelry), but a non-signet ring—the ordinary ornamental ring normatively worn by women—is classified as carrying when worn by a man, and would constitute a biblical violation.

### Clothing Definition

The Gemara pauses to analyze the logical structure of Ulla's claim. *Alma kasavar Ulla*: it emerges that Ulla holds that certain types of clothing are gender-specific—what is clothing for one gender is not clothing for the other. Read carefully, *kol midi dechazi le'ish lo chazi le'isha, midi dechazi le'isha lo chazi le'ish*: there are articles that are genuinely men's clothing and not women's, and vice versa, such that when worn by the opposite gender they do not constitute wearing but carrying.

This is not self-evident. One could argue—and the Gemara raises this possibility—that if the Torah's prohibition of *lo yilbash gever simlat isha* uses the language *yilbash*, "he shall wear," it presupposes that a man putting on a woman's garment is wearing it in the full sense, not carrying it on his body. The very prohibition implies that it counts as *levisha*. Ulla disagrees: when an item associated with one gender is worn by the other, it is not recognized as wearing at all, and therefore functions as carrying for purposes of *hotzaah*.

### Shepherd Sackcloth

*Metiv Rav Yosef*: Rav Yosef raises a challenge. A *Tosefta* teaches that shepherds may go out on Shabbat wearing their distinctive sackcloth garments—rough, coarse coverings—and that this principle extends to anyone who wears such garments, since the *Tosefta* adds that the reason shepherds are mentioned is simply that this is their custom. The implicit question: here is a type of clothing worn only by a specific sub-group, yet it is still classified as wearing and not carrying. Why should the same not apply to a man wearing a woman's garment or vice versa?

### Gender Categories

*Ela amar Rav Yosef kasavar Ulla nashim am bifnei atzman hen*: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by articulating Ulla's underlying principle—women constitute, as it were, their own distinct "nation." Understood in its narrowest, most local sense, this means that clothing is so profoundly gendered that cross-gender wearing is categorically different from one sub-group of men wearing the clothing of another sub-group. A shepherd wearing sackcloth and a nobleman wearing sackcloth are still operating within the same clothing universe; a man wearing a woman's garment, or a woman wearing a man's garment, crosses a categorical boundary. The garment belongs to an entirely foreign domain and is therefore not recognized as *levisha* at all—it is carrying.

This raises a natural question about whether the same logic would apply across national or cultural lines—would a man wearing distinctively foreign men's clothing be considered carrying? The answer is almost certainly no. The principle *am bifnei atzman* seems to be specifically about gender as a category, not about ethnic or cultural distinctions within the same gender. What makes men's and women's clothing categorically different is the gendered nature of clothing itself.

## Women & Tefillin

### Tefillin on Road

The Gemara then turns to a challenge to Ulla's principle from the laws of *tefillin*. *Hamotzi tefillin*: if one finds *tefillin* abandoned in the road on Shabbat and fears they will be stolen or trampled, one may bring them inside by wearing them—donning the *shel yad* and *shel rosh*, carrying them in by wearing, then returning for the next pair. The ruling states *echad ish ve'echad ishah*—this applies equally to a man and to a woman. A woman may wear *tefillin* to bring them inside, and it is not considered carrying on Shabbat.

This is a striking ruling. *Tefillin* are normatively associated with men. If Ulla's principle holds—that wearing the clothing of the other gender does not constitute *levisha* but *hotzaah*—then a woman wearing *tefillin* should be classified as carrying them, not wearing them. Why then does the Gemara permit her to bring them inside by wearing?

### Meir: Not Time-Bound

*Hatam kasavar Rabbi Meir*: the Gemara resolves the difficulty by attributing that earlier ruling to Rabbi Meir's position. *Laila zman tefillin hu veShabbbat zman tefillin hu*: Rabbi Meir holds that *tefillin* may be worn at night and on Shabbat—that there is no time-bound exclusion limiting their wearing. Since *tefillin* according to Rabbi Meir is not a time-bound *mitzvah*, women are obligated in it equally with men. And since women are obligated, *tefillin* are women's clothing as much as men's. There is therefore no cross-gender wearing, and a woman putting on *tefillin* constitutes *levisha*, not *hotzaah*.

### Obligation vs. Reality

This raises a genuinely interesting question about the relationship between halakhic status and social reality. The Gemara has been operating throughout this sugya on the assumption that clothing categories are defined by societal norms—what people in fact wear. Yet here, the classification of *tefillin* as women's clothing is determined entirely by Rabbi Meir's halakhic position that women are obligated, not by the social reality that in Rabbi Meir's time women presumably were not, in general, wearing *tefillin*. Rabbi Meir appears to be saying: regardless of what people actually do, since in principle women are obligated, *tefillin* is women's clothing—and that halakhic reality controls, not the sociological one.

There is a substantial discussion of this question in the corresponding passage in *Eruvin* concerning the wearing of *tefillin* found on the road. The extent to which that Gemara concludes definitively that the ruling reflects Rabbi Meir's specific position regarding women's obligation in *tefillin* requires separate examination. But here in Shabbat the Gemara simply asserts it as the explanatory framework.

This sugya also has implications for broader debates about women wearing *tefillin* and *tallit*. For some, the very identification of these objects with male religious practice makes a woman's wearing of them feel analogous to cross-dressing at a visceral level—an association with Ulla's principle of *am bifnei atzman*. The Gemara itself is not here engaging with the *beged ish* prohibition; it is asking the narrower question of whether the wearing of a gender-associated object by the other gender constitutes *levisha* or *hotzaah* for purposes of Shabbat. But the sugya implicitly raises the connection, and it is worth noting.

## Finger Carrying & Rings

### Finger Carrying Problem

The Gemara now identifies a further difficulty. Even granting Ulla's position—that for a woman a signet ring is not *levisha* but *hotzaah*, since it is men's clothing—the biblical prohibition of *hotzaah* requires not merely moving an object but doing so in the normal manner of conveyance. The normal manner of carrying an object is in the palm of the hand; carrying it on one's finger is *k'le'achar yad*, an abnormal mode of carrying. If the signet ring is not clothing for a woman, it should only be carrying—but carrying in an unusual way—and an unusual manner of carrying is exempt from biblical liability. Why then is the woman *chayevet chatat*?

### Woman Treasurer

*Amar Rabbi Yirmiyah: be'ishah gizbarit askinan*—the Gemara explains that the Mishnah is speaking of a woman who functions as a treasurer or businesswoman. For such a woman, using a signet ring is a regular feature of her professional activity; it is normal for her to have it on her finger as part of her work. Accordingly, while the ring is still not *levisha* for her—because collectively and socially it is men's jewelry—carrying it on her finger is the normal mode of conveyance for a woman in her position. The ring is not her clothing; it is something she regularly carries on her finger for business purposes, and that is a recognized way of carrying it. Hence she is *chayevet chatat*.

The implication is precise: for any other woman who might happen to wear a signet ring, it would not be a normal mode of carrying, and she would not be biblically liable unless she held it in her palm. Only the woman whose regular practice makes finger-carrying the recognized mode of transport incurs biblical liability.

### Spousal Ring Exchange

A further question arises symmetrically: *Rav Yochanan* (cited by Rabbah bar bar Chana) acknowledges that the woman treasurer case explains female liability for wearing a signet ring, but asks—*ish mai ika le'meimar?*—how does the reverse work for a man? If a non-signet ring is women's clothing and therefore constitutes carrying when worn by a man, the same problem recurs: carrying on the finger is not the normal mode of conveyance for men with respect to rings that are not their own. Why would a man be biblically liable?

*Ela amar Rava*: Rava offers a scenario that explains both cases simultaneously. *Pe'amim she'adam noten le'ishto taba'at she'yesh aleha chotam*: sometimes a man removes his signet ring and hands it to his wife, asking her to bring it home and store it—*le'holichah le'kufsa*. The wife then carries it on her finger until she reaches the storage box. This is a recognized real-world practice: when someone hands you a ring to transport, the natural way to avoid losing it is to place it on your finger. Conversely, *pe'amim she'ha'ishah notenet le'ba'alah taba'at she'ein aleha chotam*: sometimes a woman removes her own ring and gives it to her husband to bring to a craftsman for repair—*le'holichah etzel uman le'taken*. The husband then wears his wife's ring on his finger until he reaches the jeweler. Again, the most natural way to transport a ring without losing it is to wear it on the finger.

Rava's solution is elegant: for both men and women, there exist recognized social scenarios in which one carries a ring belonging to the opposite gender on one's finger as a normal mode of conveyance. The ring is not clothing for the person carrying it—it belongs to the other gender's clothing domain—but carrying it on the finger in these contexts is not *k'le'achar yad*; it is the recognized, ordinary way one transports a ring. Therefore the person is liable at the biblical level.

## Rashi vs. Tam

### Rashi's View

Having established Ulla's position that gender-specific items constitute carrying when worn by the opposite gender at the biblical level, the Gemara leaves open a related question: what about the rabbinic dimension? For a woman, a non-signet ring is a rabbinic concern—not because it is carrying, but because there is fear she might remove it to show a friend, thereby coming to carry it four *amot* in *reshut ha'rabim*. Does an analogous rabbinic concern apply to a man wearing a signet ring—which, for a man, is not carrying at all—lest he come to remove it and show it?

Rashi holds that yes, the same type of rabbinic concern operates for men as for women. Items that are attractive or unusual—secondary objects rather than major garments—might prompt the wearer to remove them and display them, regardless of gender. The rabbinic restriction against going out with such items on Shabbat accordingly applies to men as well.

### Tam's View

Rabbeinu Tam disagrees, drawing on other *sugyot*. In his view, the rabbinic decrees about removing and showing garments were specifically formulated with women in mind. The concern that one might impulsively remove a piece of jewelry or an ornament in the public street to show a friend was identified as characteristic of women's behavior in this domain; it was not extended with the same force to men. Accordingly, Rabbeinu Tam argues that all the rabbinic restrictions we have been studying are gender-specific: they apply to women's articles and not to men's. This is not explicit in the Mishnah or the Gemara; it is a reading Rabbeinu Tam derives from other contexts. The question of whether a man wearing a signet ring on Shabbat faces any rabbinic prohibition is thus genuinely disputed between these two positions.

## Kovelet Perfume Debate

### Three-Way Debate

The Gemara now examines the *koveles* and the *tzluchit shel pilayton* more carefully, presenting a full three-way dispute—Rabbi Meir, the Sages, and Rabbi Eliezer—that exactly parallels the tripartite debate over the *ir shel zahav* encountered earlier: *chayav chatat* (biblical carrying), *assur me'derabanan* (rabbinic prohibition), and *mutar le'chatchilah* (entirely permitted).

### Kovelet Definition

*Mai koveles?* What is a *koveles*? *Amar Rav: chumsa d'pilon*—a bundle of aromatic herbs or spices, worn to smell pleasant, analogous to the *tzluchit shel pilayton*, the small flask of balsam oil. *Vechen amar Rav Assi: chumsa d'pilon*. The two items in the Mishnah, *koveles* and *tzluchit shel pilayton*, are thus very similar in function. It should be noted that the precise definition of *koveles* is not entirely clear, and the Rishonim do not resolve it with certainty.

### Three Positions

*Tanu rabbanan*: a *Baraita* teaches: *lo teitzei bekoveles, ve'im yatze'ah chayevet chatat, divrei Rabbi Meir*—a woman may not go out wearing a perfume bundle, and if she did, she is obligated a *chatat*; so says Rabbi Meir. *Vachachamim omrim: lo teitzei*—the Sages say she should not go out, but if she did, she is exempt from biblical liability, since they classify it as *tachshit*, a form of adornment. Why do they nonetheless prohibit it rabbinically? The standard concern: *dilma shalfa umachviya ve'ata le'atuye*—she might take it off, show it to a friend, and come to carry it four *amot*. Someone who encounters a fragrant perfume bottle will naturally want others to smell it: "Look how wonderful this smells!"—and in showing it she might inadvertently carry it.

*Rabbi Eliezer omer: yotze'ah ishah bekoveles le'chatchilah*—Rabbi Eliezer says she may go out wearing it entirely permissibly.

### Woman's Nature

The Gemara probes Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning. *U'vmai kamifligi?* Rabbi Meir considers it a *massa'ui*, a burden—it is not worn as a garment but carried on the body for a functional purpose. The Sages consider it *tachshit*, jewelry, making it rabbinic rather than biblical. Rabbi Eliezer holds that there is not even a rabbinic problem. His reasoning: *man darko le'miremei?*—who is it that typically wears such a perfume bundle? *Ishah she'reichah ra'*—a woman who has an unpleasant body odor. And such a woman, precisely because of her condition, *lo shalfa umachviya*, will not remove it and show it in public, and therefore will not come to carry it. Tosafot clarifies that this is not about creating different laws for different individuals; rather, it is about determining what type of object this is by looking at whose practice it reflects. Since the class of women who wear this sort of item would not remove it in public, the object itself does not implicate the concern that motivates the rabbinic prohibition.

### Eliezer Reconciled

The Gemara then notes an apparent tension in Rabbi Eliezer's position. A *Baraita* elsewhere quotes Rabbi Eliezer as saying one is *poter*—exempt—regarding the *koveles* and the *tzluchit shel pilayton*, language that implies only exemption from biblical liability rather than outright permissibility *le'chatchilah*. The Gemara resolves this: *lo kashya*. When Rabbi Eliezer is in dialogue with Rabbi Meir, who says one is *chayav chatat*, Rabbi Eliezer responds *poter*—"you are not biblically liable." When Rabbi Eliezer is in dialogue with the Sages, who say *poter aval assur* (exempt but rabbinically forbidden), Rabbi Eliezer counters *mutar le'chatchilah*—"it is entirely permitted." His substantive position is consistent throughout; the language he uses shifts depending on which interlocutor he is addressing.

## Keys & Minimum Amounts

### Key Carrying Braita

Having established the three-way dispute about the *koveles*, the Gemara cites a *Baraita* that appears to juxtapose the *koveles* discussion with the question of carrying a key: *lo teitzei ishah bemafteach she'bevyadah*—a woman may not go out carrying her key in her hand. The concern about carrying one's key when there is no *eruv* is of obvious practical significance. If she goes out with it, she is *chayevet chatat*, says Rabbi Meir. Then the *Baraita* adds: *Rabbi Eliezer poter bekoveles uvitzluchit shel pilayton*—Rabbi Eliezer exempts in the case of a *koveles* and a *tzluchit shel pilayton*.

The juxtaposition is jarring: we were discussing keys and suddenly Rabbi Eliezer is talking about perfume bottles. The Gemara resolves this through *chasuri mechasra*—the *Baraita* is incomplete as stated and must be reconstructed. The full text reads: Rabbi Meir says a woman may not go out with a key and, similarly, with a *koveles* or a *tzluchit shel pilayton*—and if she does, she is *chayevet chatat*. Rabbi Eliezer does not dispute Rabbi Meir on the key; he disputes only regarding the perfume bottles, where he says she is exempt (and, as established above, actually holds it is permitted *le'chatchilah*).

### Oil Requirement

*Bameh devarim amurim?*—When does even the more permissive view hold? *Keshe'yehei bah bosem*—only when there is actually aromatic oil inside the flask. Then the flask is serving its function and may be classified as an adornment the woman genuinely wears. *Aval ein bah bosem*—but if there is no oil in it, she is *chayevet chatat*—biblically liable.

This ruling prompts *Rav Adda bar Ahava* to draw a significant inference: *zot omeret: ha'motzi ochlin pachot mike'shiur bikli chayav*—this teaches that one who carries out food in a vessel, even if the food is less than the minimum amount that would independently require biblical liability, is nonetheless *chayav*. The reasoning is as follows: there is a minimum quantity of food below which carrying it out does not constitute a biblical violation. Yet if that sub-minimum food is contained in a vessel, one might have thought the vessel alone generates liability—the vessel is significant in its own right. The case of the empty perfume bottle, however, seems to suggest otherwise: the bottle without its oil is still *chayav*—and if this is because the residual fragrance counts as the "food" in the vessel, then even a sub-minimum quantity carried in a vessel renders one liable.

### Empty Vessel Analogy

The Gemara makes the analogy explicit. *Ein bah bosem, pachot mike'shiur bikli dami*—when there is no oil, it is like carrying a sub-minimum amount of food in a vessel. *Detanya: chayevet*—and the *Baraita* rules her liable. The implication is that the half-grape in a bowl—the paradigmatic case of sub-minimum food in a vessel—does render one biblically liable, since the vessel is secondary to the food and the food, though sub-minimum on its own, is carried along with its vessel as a unit.

This has practical implications in the realm of other Shabbat questions—for instance, the question of pushing a child in a stroller when there is no *eruv*. One principle is *chai nosei et atzmo*—a living being carries itself, and therefore the child may not constitute *hotzaah*. But what of the stroller? The Gemara's logic here suggests that the stroller is entirely secondary to the child being transported and should not independently implicate *hotzaah*. (This is noted as a matter of Talmudic analysis rather than *pesak*.)

### Rav Ashi's Logic

*Rav Ashi* challenges the inference drawn by Rav Adda bar Ahava. He says: in the normal case of sub-minimum food in a vessel—the half-grape in a bowl—one is indeed exempt, because the vessel is secondary to the food. Since the food alone does not constitute a minimum amount, and the vessel exists only as a container for that food, the entire unit does not meet the threshold for biblical liability. *Veshani hacha*: the case of the empty perfume bottle is different, and here is why—*de'leit lei mamasha klal*, there is no physical substance whatsoever. Fragrance is not a tangible object. Unlike a half-grape, which is at least a physical thing (merely insufficient in quantity), the residual scent in an empty bottle has no physical reality at all. One therefore cannot say that the vessel is secondary to the fragrance, as one might say the bowl is secondary to the grape. When there is nothing physical inside, the woman is simply carrying the bottle—a vessel—and the vessel alone is what is being transported. A vessel of significance is a normal object of carrying, and therefore she is *chayevet*. But this does not prove anything about the general rule of sub-minimum food in a vessel; that case remains exempt.

## Agadic: Poverty

### Amos Prooftext

Having been discussing aromatic oils and women's ornaments, the Gemara pivots to an extended *agadata* section anchored in the verse from Amos: *vere'shit shemanim yimshachu*—"they anoint themselves with the choicest of oils." The context in Amos is a prophetic critique of a people who indulge in physical pleasure while ignoring God's word and the prophets' warnings.

### Pilayton Definition

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: zeh pilayton*—this balsam oil we have been discussing is identified as the choicest of all oils. *Metiv Rav Yosef*: Rav Yosef challenges this identification. A *Tosefta* in Sotah records that *Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava* wished to forbid *pilayton* as part of the post-*Churban* restrictions—the series of practices curtailed as a *zecher le'Churban*, a commemoration of the Temple's destruction—but the other Sages did not agree with him. If *pilayton* is the most indulgent and pleasurable of all oils, why did the majority of Sages decline to forbid it? Presumably because it was considered a basic need rather than a luxury. But if it is truly the height of indulgence, as the verse implies, the Sages should have had strong reason to restrict it.

### Joy vs. Indulgence

*Amar leh Abaye: ule'ta'amech*—and according to your logic, Abaye responds, anything mentioned in that verse in Amos should be evidence of forbidden indulgence. But look at the continuation: *hashotim bemizrekei yayin*—"those who drink wine in a *mizrak*." What is a *mizrak*? Rav Ami and Rav Assi debate: one says it refers to a vessel with openings at both ends from which multiple people could drink together; the other says it refers to the practice of tossing cups of wine from one person to another. Either way, a mode of drinking wine that is extravagant and indulgent. Yet when Rabbah bar bar Chana visited the house of the *Reish Galuta* and saw him drinking from a *kniskanin* (the same vessel, according to one opinion), he said nothing—it was not something he felt obliged to protest. So not everything mentioned in the verse is forbidden.

The real criterion, the Gemara explains, is this: *kol midi de'it beih ta'anug ve'it beih simcha, gazru beih rabbanan*—anything that combines both physical indulgence (*ta'anug*) and joyousness (*simcha*) is what the Sages restricted after the *Churban*. *Aval midi de'it beih ta'anug ve'leit beih simcha, lo gazru rabbanan*—but something that involves physical pleasure alone, without the dimension of joy, is not subject to the restriction. It is specifically the combination of indulgence and festive joy that is too much to permit in the shadow of the *Churban*.

This distinction carries practical significance for questions that arise during *sefirat ha'omer* and other periods of mourning observance. There is a widespread practice not to attend certain entertainments during *sefirah*, though this specific restriction does not appear in *Shulchan Aruch*. The Gemara's principle here—that it is the combination of joy and indulgence that is restricted, not pleasure alone—is important for understanding the correct parameters. The issues around *Churban* and *avelut* concern *simcha*, joy, not merely *ta'anug*, physical pleasure.

The passage in Amos continues: *vehashochvim al mitot shen*—"those who lie on beds of ivory"—and *useruchain al arsotam*, "and they stretch out on their couches." *Saruach* is read by the Gemara as related to *sirchon*, stench. *Amar Rabbi Yosi berabbi Chanina*: this means they would urinate in front of their beds while naked—since they were already undressed for sleep, they would relieve themselves without moving, creating a persistent stench by their sleeping place.

*Megadef beh Rabbi Abbahu*: Rabbi Abbahu mocks this interpretation. If the sin being described is merely urinating beside one's bed, how does that connect to the dramatic conclusion of the passage—*lachen ata yiglu be'rosh golim*, "therefore you shall go into exile at the head of the exiles"? That is too weighty a consequence for such an act, and the connection to indulgence described in the verse is weak. *Ela amar Rabbi Abbahu*: rather, the verse describes people eating and drinking together, reclining side by side on their couches, *vedovkin mitoteihen zu bezu*—pushing their beds together—*umachlifin nishoseihen zeh im zeh*—and exchanging wives with one another. The "stench" on the beds, *umasrichin arsotam*, refers to *shichvat zera she'eino shelahen*—seed that is not their own. The stench is thus a euphemism for sexual sin flowing from physical indulgence, and that is what explains the punishment of exile.

### Three Things

*Ve'amri lah bemasnisa tana*—and it was also taught in a *Baraita*: *gimel devarim mevi'in adam lidei aniyut*—three things bring a person to poverty: urinating naked in front of one's bed (*hamashtin mayim bifnei mitato arom*), denigrating hand-washing (*umezalzel benetilas yadayim*), and having one's wife curse him in his presence (*she'ishto mekallelto befanav*).

### Urination Details

*Amar Rava*: the prohibition regarding urinating by one's bed is qualified. *Lo amran ella de'hadar appei le'purya*—this only applies if one faces the bed while urinating, *ve'le'ar'a*—and urinates onto the ground, so that the area around the bed becomes saturated and smells. *Aval le'varai*—if one's back is to the bed, or *aval bemana*—if it is done into a vessel (a chamber pot) which is then removed, *leit lan bah*—there is no concern. The issue is specifically the creation of a lasting stench in the sleeping area.

### Hand-Washing Issue

*Amar Rava*: the concern about denigrating hand-washing applies specifically to one who does not wash at all—*de'lo mashi yadei klal*. *Aval mashi velo mashi*—if one washes incompletely, that is not the problem addressed here. The *Maharsha* notes that this is not necessarily a ruling about whether one has fulfilled the *halakha* of *netilas yadayim*; it is a statement about cleanliness. The concern is the total absence of any washing, not marginal insufficiency.

However, the Gemara qualifies even this: *ve'lav milta hi*, this qualification itself is questioned. *De'amar Rav Chisda: ana mashai melo chafnai maya*—Rav Chisda said he washes his hands with a full double handful of water, completely covering both hands. *Ve'yahavu li me'hashamayim melo chafnai tivuta*—and in return, Heaven gives him full handfuls of goodness. The implication is that washing fully and completely brings abundant blessing; partial washing is not a neutral act that "covers" one. One should wash properly and thoroughly.

### Wife's Jewelry Curse

*Al iskei tachshiteha*: the third cause of poverty—a wife who curses her husband in his presence—is connected to the *tachshit* discussion that immediately preceded this *agadata* section. Rava explains that the wife's cursing is specifically over *tachshit*, jewelry: she wants her husband to purchase jewelry for her and he refuses. *Ve'hanei mili de'is lei velo avid*—and this only constitutes a problem if he actually has the resources to do it but withholds them. The *Maharsha* observes that since the *Baraita* is describing what leads *to* poverty, it implies the person is not yet poor—he has means but refuses to use them for his wife's honor. The *Maharsha* understands the condition to mean that it is a reasonable and not extravagant expenditure given his means, yet he refuses.

A broader reading of these three causes suggests a unifying theme: each one reflects a failure of respect and dignity. Urinating in a manner that creates a stench around one's sleeping place is a failure to respect one's own living environment. Denigrating hand-washing is a failure to respect the act of preparing for food. And withholding jewelry from one's wife—the Gemara in discussions of *kibbud av va'em* and similar contexts identifies providing clothing as a primary expression of *kavod*—is a failure to respect the other. There is also a dimension of miserliness or stinginess running through all three: a reluctance to expend the minimal effort or resources needed to maintain dignity, toward oneself and toward others.

## Daughters of Zion

### Haughty Walking

*Darash Rava brei de'Rav Ilai*: the Gemara now expounds verses from *Yeshayahu* describing the sins and punishments of the *benot Tzion*, the daughters of Zion. The broader context involves the critique of women's indulgence and seductive behavior in Jerusalem—a natural extension of the aromatic oils and jewelry themes throughout this daf. *Ya'an ki gavhu benot Tzion*: the daughters of Zion became haughty. *Shehayu mehalchot bekomah zkufah*—they would walk with a rigidly upright bearing, a posture of arrogance. *Vatelachna netuyot garon*: they walked with an outstretched neck. *Shehayu mehalchot eikev betzad godel*—they would walk very daintily, placing heel directly beside toe, taking small, deliberate steps rather than natural strides. Rashi understands this as a seductive, attention-drawing manner of walking. Rashi notes that the Gemara's description is specifically about married women, making the behavior not merely immodest but adulterous in its intent.

### Eyeshadow & Winking

*Umeshakarot einayim*: and they would glance with their eyes—*dehavi malyan kuchla le'eineihu*, they would fill their eyes with *kuchla*, eyeshadow or eyeliner, *umramzan*, and then wink at men. The combination of painted eyes and suggestive eye contact is understood as deliberate sexual enticement.

### Walking Appearance

*Haloch vetafof*: walking in a floating or teetering manner. *Shehayu mehalchot arukot betzad ketzarot*: tall women would walk beside short women, creating the visual impression that the tall women were floating above the ground, elevated above the crowd.

### Perfume in Shoes

*Uveragleihem te'achasna*: the verse's word *te'achasna* is read in connection with *eres*, the venom of an adder. *Amar Rav Yitzchak debei Rabbi Ami*: this means they would place *mor ve'afarsimon*—myrrh and balsam—*bimnaleihem*, in their shoes. Walking through the markets of Jerusalem, when they would approach the young men of Israel, *bo'atot bakarka umatizot aleihem*, they would kick or stamp against the ground and the fragrance would splatter upward onto the men. *Umachnisos bahen yetzer hara ke'eres be'akhus*: and they would thereby introduce the *yetzer hara* into those men like the venom of a snake. These are again married women, per Rashi's reading—their seductive behavior directed at other men carries the full weight of potential adultery.

### Punishment Reversal

*Mai puraniyoteihem?*—What are their punishments? The Gemara expounds the punishments described in subsequent verses as direct inversions of each transgression. *Ve'haya tachat bosem mak*: in the place where they applied fragrance, the flesh will rot—*nemakim nemakim*, putrefying. *Ve'tachat chagurah nikpah*: instead of the ornate belt, *nikfim nikfim*, wounds—the genital area which was adorned will be afflicted. *Ve'tachat ma'aseh miksheh karchah*: instead of an elaborate hairstyle, *krachim krachim*, bald patches. *Ve'tachat ptigil machagoret sak*: the *Gemara* reads *ptigil* as *petachim*, openings—the places that led to joy and pleasure will instead be covered in sackcloth. *Ki tachat yofi*: in exchange for beauty—and Rava cites a folk saying, *chilufa shufra kifa*: in the place of beauty comes sickness and sores.

### Leprosy & Afflictions

*Ve'sipach Hashem kodkod benot Tzion*: God will strike the heads of the daughters of Zion. *Amar Rabbi Yose berabbi Chanina: melamed sheparcha vahen tzara'at*—this means that *tzara'at* will spread over them. The connection is linguistic: *vesipach* is related to *sapachat*, one of the forms of leprous plague listed in the Torah's *tzara'at* passages.

*VaHashem pitchan ye'areh*: the verse speaks of God "baring" or "spilling out" their *pitchan*, which the Gemara reads as *petachan*, their openings. *Sura amar Rav Yehuda*: in this matter, one opinion holds that *shenishpechu ke'kiton*—they will bleed profusely, like water poured from a pitcher, an affliction of abnormal menstrual bleeding. The other opinion holds that *shenasa'u fetacheihen ke'ya'ar*—their openings will become like a forest, meaning excessive hair will grow there. The Gemara elsewhere assumes that it was customary for women to remove hair from those areas, so this reversal is particularly pointed.

## Jerusalem Men & Cinnamon

### Jerusalem Men

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav: anshei Yerushalayim anshei shachatz hayu*—the men of Jerusalem were arrogant and boastful. Having described the seductive behavior of the women at length, the Gemara notes that the men were no less problematic. *Shehaya adam omer le'chavero*: a man would say to his friend, *bameh sa'adta hayom*—"what did you eat today?" And the conversation would proceed in elaborate sexual innuendo: *be'pat amila o be'pat she'eina amila*—worked dough or unworked dough, alluding to whether the woman involved was a virgin. *Be'yayin gudrani o be'yayin chardali*—white wine or dark wine, referring to the women they had been with. *Be'mita rechavah o be'mita katzarah*—a wide bed or a narrow one. *Ve'chaver tov o ve'chaver ra*—a good companion or a poor one. *Amar Rav Chisda: ve'chulan le'znut*—Rav Chisda states that all of these are allusions to sexual transgression.

### Cinnamon Fragrance

The Gemara concludes on a note of poignant beauty, connecting back to the theme of fragrance that has pervaded the daf. *Amar Rav Chaba amar Rav Yehuda: atzei Yerushalayim shel kinamon hayu*—the trees of Jerusalem were of cinnamon. Cinnamon wood was so plentiful in Jerusalem that it was used as ordinary firewood. *Uv'sha'ah shehayu masikin mehen*: when it was burned, *reichan nodef bechol Eretz Yisrael*—its fragrance would spread throughout all of the Land of Israel, suffusing the entire country with sweetness.

### Post-Churban Loss

*Umishecharva Yerushalayim, nignazu*—when Jerusalem was destroyed, it was hidden away. *Ve'lo nishtayer ela ke'se'orah*—only a tiny amount remains, no more than a barley seed. *Umishtachach be'gizei de'Tzintzmai malkata*—and that remnant can be found in the treasure houses of the queen known as Tzintzmai, whoever she may be.

# Shabbat 63

## Weapons as Ornaments

### Mishnah Overview

The Mishnah on 63a addresses what a man may not carry — or, more precisely, what he may not wear — on Shabbat, such that doing so constitutes the biblical prohibition of carrying in the public domain. The Mishnah states: *lo yetzei ha'ish lo besayif* — a man may not go out with a sword; *v'lo bekeshet* — nor with a bow; *v'lo betris* — nor with a shield; *v'lo be'alah* — nor with an *alah*, which the Gemara will identify as either a type of spear or a mace with a thick head; *v'lo beromach* — nor with a spear. If he does go out wearing any of these items, *chayav chatat* — he is liable to bring a sin-offering, because this is considered carrying, not wearing.

### R. Eliezer's View

*Rabbi Eliezer omer tachshitin hein lo* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that these military items qualify as *tachshitin*, a form of adornment. People do dress in military attire — think of a royal military guard — wearing a sword not because they expect to go into battle that day, but because it is a particular way of presenting oneself. In that sense, it functions as an ornament.

### Sages' Objection

The Sages disagree: *v'chachamim omrim einam ela lignai* — these items are not ornamental but reprehensible. The proof text is the vision of Isaiah: *v'chititu charvotam l'ittim v'chanitoteihem l'mazmerot* — they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning shears — *v'lo yisa goy el goy cherev v'lo yilmedu od milchamah* — one nation will not lift up a sword against another, and they will no longer learn war. War is not an ideal; it is a profoundly negative phenomenon. Therefore, the Sages refuse to recognize weapons as *tachshitin*.

### Tachshitin Concept

What exactly is *tachshitin*? It is not merely a category of things that are aesthetically pleasing. As established throughout these earlier discussions — involving bandages, *kame'ot*, and various other items worn on the body — *tachshitin* describes something that is fundamentally connected to the body, worn on the body rather than merely carried on it. A sword in its scabbard, worn on one's person not out of imminent military necessity but because one appreciates the way it looks, would in an objective description seem to fall into the category of something being worn, not carried.

What makes this sugya remarkable is the Sages' method of excluding weapons from *tachshitin* status. In earlier discussions, the question was framed in terms of societal norms — for instance, Rabbi Meir's view that a gold tiara is not considered "worn" because most people do not wear it. Here, however, the Sages do not invoke a societal norm at all. They invoke a religious and value-based judgment: because war is morally negative and because the prophetic vision is of a world without war, we refuse — regardless of how society treats such items — to recognize them as clothing. The introduction of values as a determinant of what counts as *levisha* is striking and worth dwelling on. It is not that weapons are aesthetically unpleasant; it is that we decline to confer upon them the status of dignified attire.

### Modern Applications

One might ask whether this discussion has any bearing on soldiers carrying weapons on Shabbat in the modern State of Israel. The primary halachic argument in that context is one of *pikuach nefesh*, not *tachshitin*. Rav Goren devoted an entire volume to the laws of Shabbat in the army, and the operative principle throughout is the preservation of life. This distinction is illustrated by a case in which soldiers wished to walk off-base to attend a synagogue on Shabbat: the ruling was that they could leave their weapons on base, because in that specific context the *pikuach nefesh* justification did not apply. The sword-as-*tachshit* argument, therefore, does not appear to be the operative frame in modern military halachah.

---

## War Symbolism Debate

### Weapon Definitions

The Gemara begins by asking: *mai ba'ala* — what exactly is the *alah* mentioned in the Mishnah? The answer given is *kulpa*. The commentary explains: *peirush shevet shemakin bo verosho av* — it is a staff with a thick head, which points toward something like a mace. Steinsaltz identifies it from a Persian source as a club or lance.

The Gemara then returns to the central dispute: *tachshitin hein lo* — Rabbi Eliezer's position that weapons are ornamental. A *baraita* records that the Sages challenged him: *vechi me'achar detachshitin hein lo mipnei mah hein beteilim le'atid lavo lemot haMashiach* — if they are ornaments, why will they be abolished in Messianic times? Why does the prophecy not simply say there will be no war — why does it say the swords themselves will be beaten into plowshares?

Rabbi Eliezer responds: *lefi she'einan tzrichin* — because they will no longer serve a purpose. When there is no war, weapons become pointless. The Gemara immediately pushes back: *vesehavei lenoy be'alma* — but if they look nice, they still look nice, regardless of whether they serve a martial purpose! Abaye responds with the principle *midi dehavei ashraga betihara* — like a candle at midday: something that serves no function in context becomes superfluous and ridiculous. The ornamental quality of weapons is not merely aesthetic; it is rooted in what they symbolize — valor, courage, might. In a world where war is no longer a reality, that symbolism dissolves, and with it the quality that made them ornamental in the first place.

Rivka raises a sharp point: the Mishnah itself already cited the same *pasuk* about beating swords into plowshares. The Gemara, however, is making a fundamentally different kind of argument. The Mishnah's use of the verse is a value argument: the prophetic vision of a world without war tells us that war is a negative symbol and therefore not to be embraced as a positive, ornamental one. The Gemara, by contrast, converts it into a technical question: if weapons are jewelry, why won't you still wear them as jewelry *l'atid lavo*? Rabbi Eliezer's answer — because they will have no function — is also technical. The Mishnah's argument is the stronger one; the Gemara is working on a different register.

The Gemara then notes: *u'pleigi d'Shmuel* — both the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer, who agree there will be no war in the future, disagree with Shmuel. For Shmuel holds: *ein bein ha'olam hazeh limot haMashiach ela shibud galuyot bilvad* — the only difference between this world and Messianic times is the subjugation of exile; politically, Israel will once again be self-governing, but otherwise the world will remain essentially as it is. Even economically: *ki lo yechdal evyon mikerev ha'aretz* — the poor will never cease from the land, even in Messianic times. It is not going to be a miraculous transformation.

This then supports the position of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: *kol hanvi'im lo nitnabu ela limot haMashiach* — all the prophets prophesied only about Messianic times. The great visions of transformation — no war, the wolf lying with the lamb — those are the descriptions of *yemot haMashiach*, not of *olam haba*. As for *olam haba*: *ayin lo ra'ata Elokim zulatcha* — no eye has seen it; we cannot begin to fathom it. The *masye* — the support for Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba — comes from the Mishnah's assumption that there will be no war in Messianic times, consistent with the view that all the great prophetic visions belong to the Messianic era rather than to some even more remote eschatological period.

The Gemara then presents an alternate version, *ika d'amri*: in this reading, Rabbi Eliezer responds to the Sages' challenge by saying *af limot haMashiach einan beteilim* — weapons will not be abolished even in Messianic times. The verse about beating swords into plowshares refers to *olam haba*, not to Messianic times — and on this reading, Rabbi Eliezer sides with Shmuel, who holds that Messianic times will be essentially continuous with the present world. This second version, the Gemara notes, argues on Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, who places the great prophetic transformations within Messianic times itself.

It is worth reflecting on what is at stake in this debate more broadly. The Rambam strongly emphasized Shmuel's position in *Mishneh Torah*, writing *amru chachamim ein bein olam hazeh liyemot haMashiach ela shibud malchuyot bilvad* — as though this were the consensus view rather than one position among several. In *Peirush HaMishnayot* and elsewhere, the Rambam expressed deep frustration with the obsessive focus people placed on the details of Messianic times and *techiyat hameitim* — will a person rise with missing limbs, will he rise in his clothes, and so on. His emphasis was always on the world of *mitzvot* as the project of building a more just society, not on accumulating metaphysical rewards. To that end, he underscored Shmuel's more naturalistic vision. As Dr. David Berger has noted in a striking article, however, there is an irony in this: by insisting that Messianic times need not look miraculous, the Rambam's framework made it easier for messianic claimants to go unchallenged. The argument that "the world looks the same as before" is not available as a refutation if the Rambam himself said it would look the same. This dynamic played out in the case of Shabbetai Zvi and his followers, among Religious Zionists who understand the present era as *reishit tzmihat ge'ulateinu*, and in Chabad's claims regarding the Rebbe. The irony is considerable.

There is a further dimension to the *tachshitin* debate that deserves attention. The well-known idea that *Shabbat* is *me'ein olam haba* — a foretaste of the world to come — is relevant here: if something is so antithetical to the ideal of *olam haba*, can we embrace it as appropriate dress for Shabbat? One might wish to frame the Mishnah's rejection of weapons as *tachshitin* in precisely these terms. However, the Gemara's distinction between *yemot haMashiach* and *olam haba* complicates matters. We describe Shabbat as *me'ein olam haba*, not *me'ein yemot haMashiach* — and even Rabbi Eliezer, who agrees there will be no war in *olam haba*, might concede that point while maintaining that in this world, and possibly even in Messianic times, weapons carry genuine positive symbolic weight. The halachah, on this view, is this-worldly even when it draws on value judgments; and those value judgments must be grounded in this-worldly realities rather than utopian visions of a realm we can barely fathom.

### Biblical Proof

The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama d'Rabbi Eliezer* — what is Rabbi Eliezer's actual textual basis for holding that weapons are *tachshitin*? The answer: *de-chtiv chagur charbecha al yerech gibor hodecha va-hadarkha* — gird your sword on your thigh, O hero — your glory and your beauty. The *pasuk* explicitly says that a warrior wearing his sword thereby acquires glory and beauty. So at least in this world, weapons can be positive symbols. Rav Kahana challenges this proof: *hai b'divrei Torah chtiv* — that verse is speaking about Torah, not about literal weapons. It is a metaphor — keeping the sword of Torah always at one's side, ready to deploy.

### Literal Meaning Principle

Rav Kahana's interlocutor responds: *ein mikra yotzei midei peshuto* — a verse never entirely departs from its plain meaning. Even if the metaphorical reading is valid, the plain meaning retains its force. And crucially, a metaphor has no rhetorical power unless the image it invokes carries genuine weight in the real world. If wearing a sword were not, in fact, a source of glory for a warrior, the metaphor would be empty. One might think of the Artscroll approach to *Shir HaShirim*, where the metaphorical reading is read directly into the text — but as our Gemara implies, the metaphor presupposes the reality it maps onto.

### Learning Methodology

Rav Kahana then shares a striking personal disclosure: *kad havina bar tamnei srei shanin* — when I was eighteen years old, *vehavah gmirna leh lechulei haShas* — I had already learned all of Shas (by which is meant all of *shisha sidrei mishna* and *Torah she-be'al peh* generally). *Beram velo havah yadana de-ein mikra yotzei midei peshuto* — yet I did not yet know that *ein mikra yotzei midei peshuto*, that the plain meaning of a verse retains its standing even alongside a derash.

This is understandable. Someone immersed in the world of *Torah she-be'al peh* — where the halachic reading of a *pasuk* is definitively established — may come to feel that no other reading is legitimate. The *talmud lomar* at the end of this anecdote is pointed: *deligmar inish vehadar lisbor* — one should first learn all the material, and only then begin to analyze it. The Gemara does not criticize Rav Kahana for the sequence of his learning; it holds it up as a principle. Breadth — *beki'ut* — must precede depth — *iyun*. You cannot analyze what you do not yet know exists. And yet even after knowing everything, there are still insights that emerge only later, in the process of reflection. This tension between *beki'ut* and *iyun* is itself a perennial question in Torah education, and there are *yeshivot* today, particularly in Israel, that deliberately structure their curricula along precisely these lines: years devoted to *Tanakh*, then years to *Mishnah* — breadth first, analysis later.

---

## Torah Study Models

### Sharpening Model

Since the *pasuk* about girding the sword has been established as a metaphor for Torah study, the Gemara now develops that metaphor in several directions, each offering a distinct model of *talmud Torah*. Rabbi Yirmiyah said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *shenei talmidei chachamim ha-mechadedim zeh la-zeh be-halakhah* — two Torah scholars who sharpen one another in *halakhah*, debating back and forth, each one sharpening the other the way running one blade against another produces a keener edge — *Hakadosh Baruch Hu matzliach lahem*, God causes them to succeed. The proof text continues from the same *pasuk*: *va-hadarkha tz'lach* — in your glory, succeed. On the reading *al tikrei va-hadarkha ela ve-chadadkha* — do not read "your glory" but "your sharpening" — we get: sharpen one another and you will succeed.

Not only that: *ela she-olim li-gdula* — they rise to greatness. The condition, however, is *al devar emet* — the approach must be truthful. And if success breeds pride, the *pasuk* adds *ve-anvah tzedek* — humility and righteousness are part of the formula. Only then does one *zocheh le-Torah she-nittnah be-yamin* — merit the Torah given in God's right hand.

Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak adds: one merits *dvarim shene'emru b'yemina shel Torah* — the things spoken of on the right side of the Torah. This is explained via the *pasuk*: *orech yamim b'yemina b'smola osher v'chavod* — long life in the right hand; in the left hand, wealth and honor. The apparent paradox — why does the right hand, which is superior, offer only long life while the left adds wealth and honor? — is resolved: *l'mayminim bah*, those who approach Torah in the right way, *orech yamim ika v'chol shekein osher v'chavod* — first they get long life, and of course wealth and honor come with that. *Lam'smilin bah*, those who do it on the "left," *osher v'chavod ika orech yamim lika* — they may get wealth and honor, but not the fullness of long life.

Rashi suggests two readings of *masmilin bah*: either those who learn without sufficient self-sacrifice, or — his alternative — those who learn *shelo lishma*, not for its own sake. This opens onto the well-known distinction in Tosafot between two kinds of *shelo lishma*: the kind that leads to *lishma* — where the motivation is impure but not antithetical to Torah — and the kind that is genuinely destructive, about which the Gemara says *na'asit lo sam mita* and *mutav lo shelo nivra*. The *shelo lishma* that we ordinarily say is acceptable — the normal human mixture of motivations, looking smart, being respected — is the kind that *mitoch shelo lishma ba lishma*, and that is likely what is meant here in the context of *osher v'chavod*.

### Cooperative Model

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, as cited by Rabbi Abba, presents a second model: *shenei talmidei chachamim ha-nochim zeh la-zeh be-halakhah* — two Torah scholars who are *nochim* to one another in *halakhah*. Rashi offers two readings of *nochim*: pleasant with one another, or leading one another. Not the aggressive sharpening of the previous model, but a cooperative, guiding mode of study. The reward here is different: *Hakadosh Baruch Hu makshiv lahen* — God listens to them. The proof is from *az nidberu yirei Hashem* — those who feared God spoke to one another, and then God listened.

*Ein dibur ela nachat* — the word *dibur* here connotes pleasantness or leading. Rashi's preferred reading is "to lead," citing *yadber amim tachteinu* — He will lead nations beneath us. The reading of pleasantness is the more natural one given the context of cooperative study, but the verse's plain sense leans toward leading.

The *pasuk* continues *u'lchoshvei shmo* — and those who consider His name. Rabbi Ami derives from here: *afilu choshev la'asot mitzvah v'ne'enas v'lo asah ma'ala alav hakatuv k'ilu asah* — even one who intended to perform a *mitzvah* but was prevented by circumstances beyond his control is credited as though he had done it. This is a parenthetical derived from the *pasuk* quoted, not the main line of the *talmud Torah* discussion.

Two further *aggadic* statements appear here in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, via the same chain of transmission. First: *gadol hamalveh yoteir min oseh tzedakah* — lending money is greater than giving outright charity, and *umatil bekis yoteir mikulan* — investing in someone's livelihood or business is greater still. Rashi explains that lending and investing better preserve the recipient's dignity while also building self-sufficiency. Second: *im talmid chacham nokeim venoteir nuchshehu benachash hu* — if a Torah sage is vindictive and bears grudges, he is as bad as a snake, *chagreiho al matnecha* — yet still bind him at your loins. The image of binding at the loins is again, deliberately, the image of the sword. A sword can be dangerous and destructive, yet it still serves; similarly, even a difficult Torah sage has much to offer — though one might also note: try to keep the sword in its scabbard. Conversely: *im am ha'aretz hu chasid al tadur bishchunato* — if an ignorant person is pious, do not live in his neighborhood. Rashi explains: unlearned piety can lead to errors in practice, however sincere the motivation.

### Self-Study Model

The Gemara then presents a third model: *shenei talmidei chachamim ha-madgilim zeh la-zeh be-halakhah* — two Torah scholars who are *madgil* one another in *halakhah*. What does *madgil* mean? Rashi understands it as helping one another in the absence of a teacher; Tosafot understands it as actually leading one another into mistakes — not intentionally, but as an inherent risk of learning without proper guidance. The reward here is striking: *Hakadosh Baruch Hu ohavan* — God loves them. Even if mistakes are made, even in the absence of a *rebbe*, the act of coming together to learn is beloved. The proof text: *ve-diglo alay ahavah* — his banner over me is love.

Rava qualifies this: *ve-hu di-yade tzurta di-shma'ta* — it applies only if they at least know the basic shape of the *sugya*, the contours of the discussion. If they are completely at sea, the principle does not apply. And additionally: *ve-hu di-let le-hu rabba be-mata le-migmar mineh* — only if there is in fact no available teacher. If a proper teacher could be found and one chooses instead to muddle through on one's own, no credit is given for the resulting errors.

The contrast between the three models is worth pausing over. The sharpening model produces the most impressive individual achievement — great *talmidei chachamim*, Torah given in God's right hand. The cooperative and listening models produce something qualitatively different: the *Shechinah* is present, God listens, and the withdrawal of that presence — *gormim la-Shechinah she-tistalek mi-Yisrael* — is the consequence of its absence. The self-study model produces simply: God loves you, even with your mistakes. These are three different visions of what Torah study is for, and three different measures of its success.

### Aggadic Digressions

Two *aggadic* statements follow, attributed to Rabbi Chanina bar Idi and Rabbi Assi (or Rabbi Chanina): *kol ha'oseh mitzvah k'ma'amarah ein mevasrim oto b'sorot ra'ot* — one who performs a *mitzvah* properly will not receive bad tidings, derived from *shomer mitzvah lo yeda davar ra*. And — strikingly — *afilu Hakadosh Baruch Hu gozer gzeira hu mevatla* — even a divine decree can be nullified by one who keeps the *mitzvot* faithfully. This is derived from *ba'asher devar melech shilton u-mi yomar lo mah ta'aseh* — who can tell the king what to do? — juxtaposed with *shomer mitzvah lo yeda davar ra*: the one who can push back against the king is the *shomer mitzvah*.

### Bad Dog Story

A statement in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish — attributed variously to Rav Kahana, Rav Assi, or Rabbi Abba — declares: *kol megadel kelev ra betoch beito monei'a chesed mitoch beito* — one who raises a bad dog in one's home withholds *chesed* from one's home, because no one wishes to visit, and the opportunities for *hachnasat orchim* and charity are foreclosed. The proof text: *lamas merei'ehu chesed* — he withholds *chesed* from his neighbor. In Greek, the Gemara notes, a dog is called *lamas*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds: such a person also casts off the yoke of heaven — *ve-yirat Shaddai ya'azov*.

The Gemara then illustrates this with a narrative: a woman entered a house to bake bread, using what was presumably a communal oven. *Navach bah kalba* — the dog barked at her and frightened her terribly. *It'akeir vlada* — she suffered a miscarriage. The owner of the house, hearing the commotion, came and said: do not be afraid, the dog's fangs have been removed and its claws have been trimmed. She replied: *shkol tivusach v'shadi achizrei* — take your kindness and throw it on the thorns. *Kvar nad vlad* — the fetus has already been lost. A powerful illustration that even the bark of a bad dog, with no bite at all, can cause devastating harm.

This narrative, while appearing within the string of *aggadic* statements in the name of Reish Lakish, connects back thematically to the larger discussion. The aggressive, militaristic image of Torah study — *milchamtah shel Torah* — has real costs. The verbal aggression and harsh confrontation that can accompany the sharpening model is not without danger, even if it produces intellectual greatness. The tension between that model and the more cooperative, peaceful vision is not resolved; it is left standing, precisely as the Mishnah left standing the competing visions of whether strength and valor are positive or negative symbols.

### Torah and Action

Rav Huna cites a verse from Kohelet: *samach bachur beyaldutcha veyetivcha libcha bimei bechurotecha veholech bedarchei libcha ubemarei eineicha* — rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart be good to you in the days of your youth, walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes — *ki al kol eleh yeviecha ha'Elokim bamishpat* — for all these things God will bring you to judgment. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between "go enjoy yourself" and "you will be judged" as follows: *ad kan divrei yetzer hara* — up to the word *veda* is the voice of the *yetzer hara*, telling you to enjoy yourself; *mikan ve'eilach divrei yetzer tov* — the reminder of divine judgment is the voice of the *yetzer tov*.

Reish Lakish reads the verse differently: *ad kan divrei Torah mikan ve'eilach lema'asim tovim* — the first part is about rejoicing in Torah study; the second is about translating that Torah into good deeds. Torah is not only about becoming a great *talmid chacham*; it must produce *ma'asim tovim*, a more just and righteous way of living in the world. Here, once again, the image is of joy in learning rather than of swords clashing. And the measure of success is not intellectual dominance but the quality of one's actions. These two competing visions — the aggressive sharpening model and the joyful, action-oriented one — animate the entire sugya, just as the Mishnah opened with the unresolved question of whether symbols of strength belong in our world at all.

---

## Leg Ornaments & Purity

### Biryas Definition

The Gemara now returns to the final portion of the Mishnah: *biryas tehorah* — a *biryas* is *tahor*, ritually pure. The *biryas* is some kind of clasp or ring used to hold up leg coverings — stockings or the lower portion of a garment — and one may go out wearing it on Shabbat. It is *tahor* because it is not itself a garment or ornament; it merely holds up other clothing. And one may wear it on Shabbat because there is no concern that one will remove it and carry it. *Kevalim tme'im* — *kevalim* are ritually impure — and one may not go out with them on Shabbat, and we will presently learn what they are and why they differ from the *biryas*.

Rav Yehuda explains: *biryas zu etzada* — the *biryas* is like a *etzada*, a bracelet, for the leg. Rav Yosef challenges this: the Mishnah says the *biryas* is *tahor*, but a bracelet — *etzada* — is *tamei*, as we know from the narratives of Midian and elsewhere. The Gemara resolves this: *hachi ka'amar biryas tachat etzada omedet* — the *biryas* functions in relation to the leg the way a bracelet does in relation to the arm. It is not literally a bracelet, but rather some ring or band around the leg whose purpose is to hold up the leg covering. That functional, secondary purpose — serving other garments rather than directly adorning the body — is what renders it *tahor* and what distinguishes it from an ornament proper.

### Kevalim Structure

Ravin and Rav Huna were sitting before Rabbi Yirmiyah, who had dozed off. While their teacher slept, the students engaged the question. Ravin proposed: *biryas be'achat, kevalim beshtayim* — the *biryas* involves one band, the *kevalim* involve two, and that is why *kevalim* are *tamei*. Rav Huna corrected him: *elu ve'elu beshtayim* — both the *biryas* and the *kevalim* involve two bands, one on each leg. What distinguishes the *kevalim* is something else entirely: *umatil shalshelet beineihem* — a chain is strung between the two bands, connecting them, *venasu kevalim* — and that is what makes it *kevalim*. The *kevalim*, then, are not merely two leg-bands but a contraption: two rings around the legs connected by a chain running between them.

### Historical Account

This raises an obvious question: why would anyone wear such a thing? The Gemara supplies an account. Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *mishpacha achat hayeta b'Yerushalayim she-hayu pisioteihen gasot* — there was a family in Jerusalem whose members took excessively wide strides, *ve-hayu betuloteihen noshrot* — and as a result their young women would rupture their hymens. In response, *asu lahem kavalayim ve-hetilu sharsheret beineihem shelo yehu pisioteihen gasot* — they fashioned these banded chains to restrict their stride, thereby preventing the rupture.

The *kevalim* thus originated as a functional device for controlling gait — a modesty measure, in fact. What began as a family practice apparently became more widespread. Curiously, the Mishnah's prohibition is directed at men, even though the narrative concerns women. It appears that at some point this form of leg restraint was adopted more broadly by those who wished to walk with a more restricted step.

### Functional Vessel

Since the *kevalim* serve a specific bodily function — adjusting one's stride — the chain that connects the two bands is considered a *kli*, a functional vessel, which renders the whole apparatus *tamei*. The Gemara asks: *u'shalshelet shebo mashavei leih mana* — does the chain truly make it a vessel? On what basis? The Gemara considers the case of an instrument that produces sound as an analogy — *lemashmia kol bichli matchot shehu tamei* — but distinguishes it: a musical instrument is used actively to produce something. Here, the chain simply hangs between the legs. The Gemara affirms nonetheless: *kaavid maaseh* — it does perform an action, namely, restricting the stride. And because it functions purposively in this way, it qualifies as a *kli* and is therefore *tamei*.

Rabbi Yirmiyah, waking up from his doze, heard the students' exchange and said: *yishar kochacha* — well done, that is precisely correct. And that is the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan as well. Because the *kevalim* are a genuine functional vessel rather than merely decorative, they are *tamei*, and because there is no urgency to keep them on — unlike, say, a clasp that prevents one's clothing from falling — there is concern one might remove them in public, and one therefore may not wear them on Shabbat.

---

## Purity of Ornaments

### Tzitz Source

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *minayin l'arig kol shehu shehu tamei* — how do we know that a woven item of any size, however small, is *tamei*? *Mitzitz* — from the *tzitz*, the golden frontplate worn by the High Priest.

### Tzitz Description

Abaye immediately challenges: *vetzitz arig hu* — is the *tzitz* woven? A *baraita* describes it as *kemin tas shel zahav* — a plate of gold, two finger-widths wide, running from ear to ear, with the inscription written on two lines: the divine name on the upper line and *Kodesh La-* below. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose adds: *ani raitiv b'Romi* — I saw the *tzitz* in Rome, where it had been taken after the destruction of the Temple. He reports that *Kodesh LaHashem* was written on a single line, not two — a minority position in tension with the *baraita*, though his testimony is direct and firsthand.

Subsequently, Rav Dimi sent word from Nahardea: *devarim she'amarti lachem taut hem beyadi* — what I previously told you was a mistake. His original claim — that a woven item of any size is *tamei*, derived from the *tzitz* — was erroneous. *Beram kach amru mishum Rabbi Yochanan* — rather, what they said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan is this: *uminayin letachshit kol shehu shehu tamei* — how do we know that an ornament of any size is *tamei*? *Mi'tzitz* — from the *tzitz*. Since the *tzitz* is an ornamental object worn by the High Priest, it establishes that ornaments of any size are susceptible to *tumah*.

### Inclusive Disjunction

The remaining question is the source for the *tumah* of small woven items. *Uminayin le'arig kol shehu shehu tamei* — how do we know even a small woven thing is *tamei*? *Me'o beged* — from the *vav* of *o beged*, "or a garment," which appears in a *pasuk* listing categories of items susceptible to *tumah*. The *vav* — understood as the inclusive "or" — functions to broaden the category, encompassing even items of minimal size.

One might raise a difficulty: throughout many preceding *dappim* we have been discussing minimum sizes for garments — three fingers by three fingers, three handbreadths by three handbreadths. Tosafot addresses this directly: the distinction turns on whether the item was initially made at a larger size or initially fashioned to be small. A remnant of what was once a larger garment retains significance only if it meets the minimum size threshold. But an item initially crafted to function as a garment — however tiny — retains its *beged* status from the moment of its creation, regardless of size. That, according to Tosafot, is what the *o beged* derivation establishes.

The Gemara concludes with a *baraita*: *arig kol shehu tamei* — even a minimal woven item is *tamei*; *vetachshit kol shehu tamei* — even a minimal ornament is *tamei*; *arig vetachshit kol shehu tamei* — and a combination of woven and ornamental, even at minimal size, is *tamei*. This discussion of *tumah ve-taharah* will continue into the next *daf*.

# Shabbat 64

## Tumah: Garments & Sackcl…

### Arig & Tachshit

The daf opens at the very bottom of 63b, where the Gemara has turned from the general topic of what may be worn on Shabbat into an accompanying discussion of *tumah ve-taharah*. The *Tanu Rabbanan* begins: *arig kol shehu tamei* — a woven piece of clothing, even the smallest size, is *tamei*. Normally we speak of a minimum size of three by three fingers, or three by three *tefachim*, depending on whether one is dealing with a remnant of a larger garment. The present case concerns an item made from the outset to be very small — a tiny wrap around a finger, for instance — and for such an item even the smallest size suffices.

The *braita* continues: *ve-tashchit kol shehu tamei* — an ornament, whether made of metal or wood, not a woven cloth, likewise becomes *tamei* at the smallest size. And then: *arig ve-tashchit kol shehu tamei* — a combination of the two, say a brooch with a woven string attachment, is also *tamei* at the smallest size.

### Tosafot: Kol Shehu

This last clause raises a question that Tosafot addresses directly. If each of the two components — the ornament and the weave — is already *tamei* at *kol shehu*, why does the *braita* need to specify the combination? The answer Tosafot gives is that there is a minimum size even to a *kol shehu*; not every infinitesimal thing qualifies. It is therefore possible that each component alone is only half of a *kol shehu*, and only when combined do they together constitute a full *kol shehu*. That combined item is also *tamei*. That is Tosafot's reading of the *braita*.

### Rava's Sources

The Gemara then asks for the biblical sources underlying each of these rulings. Rava answers: *arig kol shehu tamei* is derived from the verse in the context of *sheratzim*, which reads *o beged* — "or a garment." The word *o* is extra, and from it we derive that even the tiniest garment, a *kol shehu*, becomes *tamei*. The ruling that a small ornament is *tamei* derives from *tzitz*, the priestly headplate. And the ruling that a hybrid of ornament and weave is *tamei* derives from the verse in the context of Midian, which states *kol kli ma'aseh* — all articles fashioned for a purpose. The inclusive word *kol* encompasses even a hybrid vessel.

### Midian Challenge

One of the rabbis challenged Rava: that verse is written in the context of Midian, where the booty had been exposed to corpses. This may reflect the strictures of *tumat meit*, a more severe category — perhaps one cannot apply it to the lighter *tumot*. Tosafot raises an additional point: perhaps the verse is not about *tumah* at all, but simply about cataloguing the spoils of war, with no legal implication for the laws of *tumah*.

### Gezeirah Shavah

The Gemara's resolution is a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *kli* appears in the context of *sheretz* and also in the context of Midian. By drawing this verbal equation, whatever we learn about a *kli* in the Midian passage — that even a hybrid vessel is included — applies equally to the laws of *tumat sheretz*. This establishes that hybrid vessels become *tamei* through contact with a dead rodent.

### Sackcloth Distinction

The *braita* concludes with a statement that initially seems strange: *mosif sak al ha-beged* — sackcloth, made from goat's hair, is more strict than a regular garment in that it is *tamei* as a woven item. But a standard *beged* is also *tamei* as a woven item. What additional stringency is being attributed to sackcloth?

### Sackcloth Reinterpreted

The Gemara resolves this by reinterpreting the statement: sackcloth is more strict than a regular garment in that it is *tamei* even though it is not actually woven. It falls within the category of a garment even absent the quality of *arig*. Sackcloth, it emerges, was not produced through a classic weaving of interlaced threads — it was made by a different process, perhaps a twining or twisting — and yet it still carries the *tumah* of a woven garment. The sackcloth is treated as if it were a garment even without being one in the technical sense.

### Twisted Hair Necklace

This raises the natural question: for what practical purpose would one use goat's hair that has not been woven at all? Rabbi Yochanan answers: a poor person would take three strands of goat's hair, twist them together into a sort of braided cord, and hang it around his daughter's neck as an inexpensive necklace. Even such a minimally processed item — twisted but not woven — falls within the category and is *tamei*.

### Baraita: Tuvui V'Arig

A new *braita* now focuses on sackcloth specifically, extending the analysis. The *braita* begins: *ein li ela sak* — I know only sackcloth itself. From where do I learn to include other items?

### Horse Straps Inclusion

The *braita* asks: *minayin l'rabot et ha-kilkali ve-et ha-chavak* — how do I know to include the *kilkali* and *chavak*? Rashi identifies these as straps used on horses — a breast strap and a girth, various types of horse tack made from goat's hair. These are not human garments at all. The *braita* answers from the word *o* in the verse *o sak*: the inclusive *o* extends the category to include these horse straps, which are made of goat's hair even if fashioned for an animal.

### Ropes Exclusion

One might then think to include even *chavalim* and *meshichot* — ropes made of goat's hair. Rashi explains that these ropes were used primarily for measuring, and crucially they had not been twisted at all; they were simply straight lengths of fiber, not processed in any way resembling normal fabric production. Surely even those should be included? The *braita* answers from the word *sak* itself: *ma sak tavui ve-arig af kol tavui ve-arig* — just as sackcloth involves twisting and weaving, so anything covered by this category must involve at least twisting or weaving. Raw, untwisted ropes are excluded. The picture that emerges is: the material requirement is met by goat's hair (and we will see, other animal hairs); the processing requirement demands that the fibers be at minimum twisted together. Straight, unprocessed strands do not qualify.

### Dead Body Extension

The *braita* then moves from *tumat sheretz* to *tumat meit*. By a corpse, the relevant verse reads: *ve-chol kli or ve-chol ma'aseh izim titchata'u* — you shall purify any leather vessel and anything made of goat's hair. The inclusive phrase *kol ma'aseh izim* — anything made of goat's hair — similarly includes the *kilkali* and *chavak*. And the same question arises: might it include even the untwisted ropes?

The *braita* proposes learning the exclusion by analogy from the *sheretz* case: there we established through *o sak* that only twisted or woven items are *tamei*. Apply the same split to *tumat meit*. The Gemara intervenes: can this analogy simply be drawn? *Tumat sheretz* is a lighter category — only a single day's *tumah* — and it is precisely because it is light that it might be more selective about which garments it renders *tamei*. But *tumat meit*, which is far more severe, might encompass a broader range of objects. The argument by analogy can be challenged.

### Logical Critique

The logical critique is sharpened further. One could construct a *kal va-chomer* in either direction: since even the lighter *tumah* of a rodent applies to twisted goat's hair items, certainly the stricter *tumah* of a corpse should apply. The *braita* rejects this reasoning by pointing out its vulnerability: *tumat sheretz* is characterized as more pervasive in certain respects — a rodent transmits *tumah* from the size of a lentil, whereas a corpse requires the size of an olive. Since the Torah treats rodents as *tamei* in cases where an analogous dead body would not be, one cannot assume the laws of garments flow automatically from one category to the other. Logical derivation — whether by analogy or by *kal va-chomer* — cannot bridge this gap.

It is worth pausing here. This pattern is characteristic of *midrashei halacha* — works like Sifra and Sifrei — where the text repeatedly entertains a logical derivation, constructs it in full, and then demolishes it, ultimately returning to a formal hermeneutical proof. One purpose of this process is to clarify the genuine distinctions between categories. Another, perhaps deeper, purpose is to demonstrate the limits of unaided human logic: one cannot simply reason one's way to Torah law. That requires a *pasuk*.

### Beged V'Or Gezeirah

The *braita* therefore concludes: *beged ve-or l'gezeirah shavah* — the phrase *beged ve-or* appears both in the context of *sheretz* and in the context of *meit*. This is not an analogy subject to challenge; it is a *gezeirah shavah*, a formal verbal equation.
