Just as by *sheretz* only twisted or woven goat's hair items are *tamei*, so too by *meit* only twisted or woven items are *tamei*. And conversely, just as by *meit* the verse says *kol ma'aseh izim* — a very inclusive expression — that inclusiveness flows back through the *gezeirah shavah* to *sheretz* as well.

### Bidirectional Gleichung

The *gezeirah shavah* thus operates in both directions simultaneously. From the *meit* passage, the inclusive *kol ma'aseh izim* ensures maximum breadth; from the *sheretz* passage, the limiting word *sak* ensures the requirement of twisting or weaving. One applies to the other in a single ironclad equation.

### Animal Hairs Expansion

But the *braita* now asks a further question: so far we have been speaking of goat's hair. From where do we learn to include items made from the tail of a horse or the tail of a cow? These are hairs rather than wool — biologically quite different from what one would weave into standard fabric. The *braita* answers from the word *o* in *o sak*: the inclusive *o* extends the category beyond goat's hair to other animal hairs as well.

This raises a difficulty. We already used the word *o* to include the horse straps — the *kilkali* and *chavak*. How can the same word now do double duty to include other animal hairs? The Gemara answers: *hanei milei mikami de-leitei gezeirah shavah* — we used *o* to include the horse straps before we had the *gezeirah shavah*. Once we have made the *gezeirah shavah* between *sheretz* and *meit*, the inclusive *kol ma'aseh izim* from the *meit* passage does the work of including the horse straps. The word *sak* from the *sheretz* passage supplies the limiting principle. Since the *o* is no longer needed for its original function, it becomes available to teach the inclusion of other animal hairs.

And then the final step of the argument closes the loop: now that other animal hairs are established as included by *sheretz*, the *gezeirah shavah* carries that ruling across to *meit* as well. One cannot derive it by *kal va-chomer* — the Gemara demonstrates, again, that such reasoning can be challenged from either direction — and so one must rely on the *gezeirah shavah*.

### Mufneh Status

The Gemara then turns to a metatextual point that underlies the entire *gezeirah shavah*. A *gezeirah shavah* built on shared phrases that were not superfluous in their original contexts can, in principle, be challenged by a strong logical argument. Only if the shared phrases are *mufneh* — extra, serving no other function than to enable the *gezeirah shavah* — is the equation ironclad and immune to rational critique. Here the Gemara establishes that the phrase *beged ve-or* is indeed *mufneh* on both sides.

The reasoning proceeds as follows. A *sheretz* is compared by the Torah to *shichvat zera* — seminal emission — based on the juxtaposition of *ish asher yiga be-chol sheretz* immediately after *ish asher tetzei mimenu shichvat zera*. Since the Torah compares them, what causes *tumah* by *shichvat zera* applies to *sheretz*. And the verse by *shichvat zera* already states *ve-chol beged ve-chol or* — any garment or leather becomes *tamei*. Therefore the *beged ve-or* that appears in the *sheretz* passage could have been derived from *shichvat zera* without being stated explicitly. It is superfluous — *mufneh*. By precisely parallel reasoning, the Torah similarly compares *tumat meit* to *shichvat zera*, juxtaposing *ha-noge'ah be-chol tamei nefesh* with *o ish asher tetzei mimenu shichvat zera*. Once again, *beged ve-or* could have been derived for *meit* from *shichvat zera*, and so the explicit statement of *beged ve-or* in the *meit* passage is likewise superfluous.

### Ironcladness of Gezeirah

Since *beged ve-or* is *mufneh* on both sides — both in the *sheretz* passage and in the *meit* passage — the *gezeirah shavah* is fully ironclad. It does not merely carry the suggestion of equivalence between two cases that happen to share similar language; both shared phrases were placed there for the express purpose of enabling the equation. No logical challenge can break it. The entire edifice — which types of goat's hair are *tamei*, why the twisted but unspun ropes are excluded, why other animal hairs are included — rests on this foundation. And the methodological point is as striking as the legal conclusion: human logic, even when it looks quite persuasive, cannot substitute for this kind of formal derivation. The *gezeirah shavah* says what logic cannot securely establish on its own.

---

## Midian Booty & Gaze

### Agil & Kumaz

Having introduced the Midian passage as a source, the Gemara now turns to examine those verses directly — a discussion relevant both to the *tumah* analysis already completed and to the larger theme of women's jewelry that runs through the entire chapter. The verse in question enumerates the jewelry that the *nesi'im* brought as a voluntary offering after the war: *etz'ada ve-tzamid taba'at agil ve-chumaz* — bracelets, bangles, rings, *agil*, and *kumaz*.

Rabbi Elazar identifies the last two items. *Agil*, he says, is *d'fus shel dadim* — a kind of form or ornament worn over the breasts. *Kumaz* is *d'fus shel beis ha-rechem* — an ornament worn directly over the pubic region. Both, in other words, were worn directly against the body in deeply intimate locations — analogous, one might note, to the body piercings and intimate jewelry worn in various cultures, including today.

### Kumaz Etymology

Rav Yosef says: if that is what *kumaz* means, then I now understand the Aramaic translation, which renders *kumaz* as *machoach*. He connects *machoach* to the word *gichuch* — laughter, or more precisely, levity and licentiousness. Rashi glosses this as *leitzanut*. Rabbah then adds that the meaning is embedded in the Hebrew word itself: *kumaz* is an acronym of *kan makom zimah* — here is the place of licentiousness. The ornamentation of the most intimate parts of the body in this manner was understood as serving a context of sexual license.

### Hirhur Atonement

Against this backdrop, the Gemara turns to the narrative surrounding the offering. When the Israelite soldiers first returned from Midian, Moshe grew angry upon seeing that they had kept the Midianite women alive — precisely the women who had seduced Bnei Israel into sin. Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha explains: Moshe said to Israel, *shema chazartem le-kilkulchem* — perhaps you have returned to your corrupt ways, suggesting they had an interest in the surviving women. Some fifty verses later, when the *nesi'im* bring their voluntary offering, they address this implicit accusation directly. They declare: *lo nifkad mimenu ish* — not one of our men was unaccounted for. Moshe responds: then why are you bringing an offering of atonement? They answer: *im midei aveira yatzanu, midei hirhur lo yatzanu* — if we escaped actual transgression, we did not escape lustful thought. They had not acted, but they had harbored *hirhur*, and for that they sought *kapara*.

This is a striking passage. The question of how the Gemara treats *hirhur* — whether the concern is its tendency to lead to *zera le-vatala* or seminal emission, or whether it is problematic in itself — is a broader topic that runs through many *sugyot*. Here it is treated quite plainly: *hirhur* without any accompanying act is grounds for bringing an atonement offering.

### Male Gaze Teaching

Rav Sheshet then asks: why does the Torah list all of the jewelry together — finger rings alongside the intimate body ornaments? To teach us, he answers, that *kol ha-mistakel be-etzba ketana shel isha ke-ilu mistakel be-makom ha-torfa* — anyone who gazes sexually at a woman's little finger, it is as though he gazes at her most private area. The point is not about what body part is visible or covered. The problem is the quality of the gaze itself. A lustful, objectifying look — *zanu eineihem* — is problematic regardless of where it is directed. From a halachic standpoint this is a concern about *hirhur* and the continuous provocation of the *yeitzer hara*; from what we would today call a feminist perspective, it addresses the male gaze and the objectification of women. The Gemara's framing is different from the modern one, but the underlying concern has a recognizable family resemblance. And it is the man's responsibility for how he is looking, not a demand that women cover their fingers.

The jewelry was brought as a *korban* and presumably melted down for use in the *Beis Ha-Mikdash*. One might ask whether there is a concern about using items so associated with licentiousness for sacred purposes, and whether the transformation through melting changes the object's identity. This connects to broader discussions elsewhere about items associated with — though not technically constituting — *avoda zara*, and whether a genuine physical transformation suffices to permit their use. The Gemara here does not address this question directly.

---

## Permissible Items

### Hair Extensions

Having catalogued what is forbidden, the *Mishna* now turns to what a woman may wear. She may go out *be-chutei se'ar* — with hair extensions, whether woven from her own cut hair, from the hair of another woman, or from animal hair. The concern throughout this chapter has been that a woman will remove an item in a public domain to show her friends, thus carrying it without intent. Hair, however, is not a *chatzitza* for *mikvah* immersion, and so we are not concerned that she will remove it to immerse.

### Head Ornaments

She may go out with a *totafet* and with *sarvitin* — types of head ornaments — *bizman she-tefurin be-kavul*, when they are sewn into her head covering, her cap. Since they are woven into the hat, she will not remove them without also removing the hat, which she would not do in public.

### Headscarves & Wigs

She may likewise go out wearing a *kavul* — a type of scarf or hairnet — or a *pea nachrit*, a wig. These, however, are permitted only *la-chatzer*, in the courtyard — not necessarily in the public domain. The full scope of this limitation will be explored in the Gemara shortly.

### Medical Items

The *Mishna* continues: a woman may go out with a cloth in her ear — presumably for an ear ailment — with a cloth in her sandal to protect against calluses, or with a cloth prepared for her *niddah* flow. The last of these raises a question in the early authorities. Rashi explains the purpose as preventing her garments from becoming soiled. Tosafot objects: an item meant to protect a garment and not the body does not have the status of clothing and should not be permitted. Tosafot therefore understands the cloth as protecting the woman's body directly, which gives it the character of a worn item and makes it permissible.

### Mouth Items

The *Mishna* further permits a woman to go out with pepper, salt, or similar items in her mouth, apparently as a remedy for bad breath. The formulation *ve-chol davar she-nittan le-toch piha* — anything placed in her mouth — suggests a broad category.

### Mouth Items Restriction

However, the *Mishna* immediately qualifies this: she may not place these items in her mouth *le-chatchila* on Shabbat itself, and if something fell out, she may not replace it. Tosafot offers two explanations for this restriction. One is that placing a remedy in one's mouth on Shabbat resembles taking medicine, and taking medicine on Shabbat is rabbinically prohibited. Tosafot himself finds this explanation difficult, because if the concern were medicine, one would presumably be permitted to replace a remedy that was already in use before Shabbat began, yet the *Mishna* forbids even that. The second explanation is therefore more convincing to Tosafot: the concern is not medicine but appearance — people who see a woman place something in her mouth and then step outside will suspect she is simply finding a clever method to carry something. This distinction between the two explanations has practical ramifications for how we approach things like mouthwash on Shabbat — whether they fall into a category of medicine or of something else entirely.

### False Tooth

Finally, a woman may go out wearing a false tooth. A golden tooth, however, is subject to a dispute: Rabbi permits it, while the Sages prohibit it — apparently because a golden tooth is something she might be inclined to remove and show her friends in the middle of the street, which would constitute carrying.

---

## Hair Categories Logic

### All Cases Needed

The Gemara asks why all three categories of hair extension must be specified separately — the woman's own cut hair, another woman's hair, and animal hair. Could one not have been inferred from another?

### Age Mismatch Concern

The Gemara constructs a series of arguments to show why each case requires an independent ruling. If only the woman's own hair were mentioned, one might think it is permitted because wearing one's own hair is natural and unsurprising — *d'lo ma'is*, it is not unattractive or incongruous. But another woman's hair might strike people as odd or inappropriate, and she might therefore be embarrassed by it and inclined to remove it in public. Conversely, if only another woman's hair were mentioned as permissible — because at least it is human hair — one might think animal hair, which is from a different species, would generate more embarrassment and a greater likelihood of removal. Each case addresses a distinct concern. The Gemara then specifies a further nuance: a young woman wearing an old woman's white hair, or an old woman wearing a young woman's darker hair, raises its own concerns about color mismatch and the social pressure to remove the incongruous hair.

### Resolution Logic

The Gemara resolves which of these cases is the non-obvious one requiring explicit mention. It is obvious that an old woman wearing a young woman's hair — which looks flattering — might lead her to show it off and remove it. Less obvious is that a young woman wearing an old woman's hair — which is incongruous and unflattering — would also be prohibited. One might think that since it looks so unattractive on her, she would never be motivated to show it off to friends. The *braita* must therefore tell us explicitly: even there, the concern applies, perhaps because the embarrassment of being seen with it creates a different motivation to remove it. The reason the *braita* mentions both: *aidi de-tani zeikeinah be-shel yaldah, tana nami yaldah be-shel zeikeinah* — since it teaches the case of the old woman wearing young hair, it teaches the reverse as well, even though one is more obvious than the other.

---

## Courtyard Debate

### Rav's Rule

The *Mishna* specifies that the *kavul* and *pea nachrit* are permissible *la-chatzer* — in the courtyard. This formulation prompts the Gemara to ask what exactly the courtyard's status is vis-à-vis everything else discussed in the chapter. Rav rules: *kol she-asru chachamim la-tzeis bo le-reshus ha-rabim asur la-tzeis bo la-chatzer* — everything that the Sages forbade in the public domain is likewise forbidden in the courtyard. The concern is that wearing something in the courtyard will lead her to walk out into the street. Rashi specifies that this applies even to a courtyard with an *eruv*.

### Exceptions

The only exceptions are the *kavul* and the *pea nachrit* that the *Mishna* explicitly permits in the courtyard. According to Rav, this means that the general rule — what is forbidden in the public domain is also forbidden in the courtyard — applies to everything discussed in the chapter, and the *Mishna* is specifically carving out these two items as exceptions.

### Anani Opinion

Rabbi Anani bar Sasson, citing Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose, rules differently: *ha-kol ki-kvula* — everything is permitted in the courtyard, just as the *kavul* is. According to this view, the prohibition throughout the chapter was directed at the public domain, and the courtyard was never subject to it. The *Mishna*'s mention of the *kavul* and *pea nachrit* as permissible in the courtyard is not carving out exceptions — it is simply providing examples of the general principle.

### Rav vs. Yishmael

The Gemara points out the difficulty this creates. If, according to Rabbi Anani, the prohibition was never extended to a courtyard, then mentioning the *kavul* and *pea nachrit* as permissible in the courtyard is redundant — of course they are permitted there, as is everything else. The Gemara resolves this by noting that Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose is a *tanna* who explicitly disagrees with the *Mishna*'s framework. He holds that the entire chapter's prohibitions were limited to the public domain, and the courtyard was always permissible.

### Ulla's Rationale

According to Rav, who does distinguish between different items, Ulla explains why specifically the *kavul* and *pea nachrit* are permitted in the courtyard while other items are not: *kedei she-lo titganei al ba'alah* — so that she not appear unattractive to her husband. Even in the courtyard, she must be permitted to wear something presentable, because the alternative poses a risk to the marital relationship.

### Akiva & Shalom Bayit

This is supported by a *braita*: *ve-ha-davah be-niddata* — regarding a woman who is *niddah*, the early sages ruled that she should not apply eye shadow, rouge, or any jewelry, and should not wear colored garments. But Rabbi Akiva came and taught: if you do this, you will make her repulsive to her husband, and the husband will divorce her. Rather, the verse means only that she retains the legal status of *niddah* until she immerses in the *mikvah* — nothing in the verse mandates making her physically unattractive. Rabbi Akiva's sensitivity here — and his known personal history of a deeply romantic attachment to his wife — lends particular weight to his position. The principle established is clear: *shalom bayit* is a halachic value that limits the application of certain stringencies.

---

## Later Authorities

### Tosafot's Ruling

Having established the range of opinions within the Gemara, we now turn to how the later authorities resolved the question in practice — and this is where the discussion becomes particularly striking. Tosafot rules in accordance with Rabbi Anani bar Sasson: *nira de-halacha ke-Rav Anani* — it appears that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Anani, that everything is permitted in the courtyard. The reasoning is twofold: Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose is a *tanna* who explicitly argues, and when there is doubt in a *de-rabbanan* matter, we rule leniently.

### Karmelit Solution

Tosafot then takes an additional step. Rashi had understood that the courtyard discussion referred to a courtyard with an *eruv*. Tosafot disagrees: we are speaking even of a courtyard without an *eruv*. And as for the public domain itself — Tosafot acknowledges that throughout this chapter we have learned that certain items may not be worn in a *reshus ha-rabim*, and one might think that even with an *eruv* the concern applies. But Tosafot notes a further consideration: *ein lanu reshus ha-rabim gamur* — we do not have a genuine *reshus ha-rabim* today. All of the streets in our communities are really only a *karmelit*. Since the rules governing a *karmelit* are rabbinic rather than biblical, and since we rule that everything is permissible in a courtyard without an *eruv*, all of our streets may be treated similarly. Women are therefore permitted to wear rings and all jewelry.

### Rabbeinu Tam

Rabbeinu Tam articulates this position explicitly: a courtyard without an *eruv* functions as the baseline permissible domain, and since all of our streets have the status of a *karmelit* — lacking either the width of eighteen *amot* or the 600,000 travelers that would constitute a true *reshus ha-rabim* — everything that would be permitted in a courtyard without an *eruv* is permitted everywhere. This is the classic Rabbeinu Tam move: an established common practice that appears to flout an entire chapter of Gemara is shown, upon analysis, to be technically defensible.

### Shulchan Aruch

The Shulchan Aruch compiles the full range of opinions. First, anything forbidden in the public domain is also forbidden in a courtyard without an *eruv*. Second, Rashi's stricter position that it is forbidden even in a courtyard with an *eruv*. Third, the view of Tosafot that everything is permitted even in a courtyard without an *eruv*. After setting out the positions, the Shulchan Aruch acknowledges the practical reality.

### Reality vs. Halacha

Women routinely wore rings and all manner of jewelry. Three justifications are offered. The first is pragmatic and somewhat uncomfortable: they are simply not going to listen, and since this is rabbinic, it is better that they transgress unknowingly than knowingly — *mutav yihyu shogegot*. The second is the Tosafot-Rabbeinu Tam position: they are acting in accordance with the lenient opinion, which holds that all of our domains are equivalent to a *karmelit* or a courtyard without an *eruv*, and in such domains everything is permitted.

### Rema: Sociological

The Rema adds a third justification that is qualitatively different from the other two — and it is, in the words of the shiur, one that is remarkable to encounter. The original rabbinic concern was that a woman would remove her jewelry in the street to show her friends, and carrying an item that way would be prohibited. The Rema notes: *de-achshav she-shchichi tachshitin ve-yotzim afilu be-chol* — today, jewelry is so common that women wear it even on weekdays. *Ve-leika le-michash dilma shalfa u-machvya* — there is therefore no longer any reason to fear she will remove it to display it. *Kemo be-yameihem she-lo hayu regilim latzeis bahem rak be-Shabbat* — in earlier times, women only wore jewelry on Shabbat, and the novelty made it something one might show off. But when jewelry is an ordinary part of daily dress, no one removes it in the middle of the street.

This reasoning is of an entirely different character from the *karmelit* solution. The *karmelit* argument leaves the structure of the rabbinic prohibition in place and finds a jurisdictional escape. The Rema's argument says the prohibition itself no longer applies — not because of any technical legal consideration, but because the sociological reality that grounded the original decree no longer exists. Changed social conditions have changed the *halacha*.

The Shulchan Aruch closes by noting that all of this applies to the rabbinic prohibitions. Anything the Gemara treats as a biblical concern — items considered carrying rather than wearing — obviously remains prohibited regardless of sociological shifts or the *karmelit* analysis. But in practice, the entire chapter we have been studying was, as the Rema observes, effectively superseded by changed realities, and the later authorities worked — through a combination of legal reasoning and honest acknowledgment of practice — to bring the two into alignment.

---

---

# Shabbat 65

## Tosafot & Practice

### Courtyard Permission

The daf begins at the very bottom of 64b, continuing the extended discussion of what may and may not be worn on *Shabbat*. Before entering the new Gemara text, it is worth summarizing the crucial ground covered at the close of the previous session, as it bears directly on everything that follows.

The discussion concerns items that women are prohibited from wearing even in a *chatzer*, and *Tosafot* confronts the obvious tension: in practice, women of his era wore precisely these items of jewelry—not only in a *chatzer*, but openly in the public domain. How is this to be reconciled? *Tosafot* offers three answers, all of which are reproduced in the *Shulchan Aruch*.

The first answer is that the Gemara's prohibition applies only to the *reshut ha-rabbim*, whereas wearing such items in a *chatzer* without an *eruv* is permitted. Extending this logic, *Tosafot* adopts the position—significant for the laws of *eruvin* more broadly—that there is no genuine *reshut ha-rabbim* in the present day. That position alone would effectively permit wearing such items in virtually any contemporary context, though the claim that there was a true *reshut ha-rabbim* in Talmudic times but not now is itself difficult to accept at face value.

### Pragmatic Leniency

The second answer is more pragmatic, if less elegant: women are indeed violating the prohibition, but since the transgression is only *d'rabbanan* and they will not heed any objection, it is better to remain silent. The principle of *mutav she-yihyu shogegin* — better that they sin unwittingly than wittingly — underlies this approach.

### Contextual Maris Ayin

The third answer is perhaps the most conceptually striking. *Tosafot* argues that these rabbinic prohibitions were motivated by a specific concern: that a woman would remove her jewelry in the street to show a friend, thereby inadvertently carrying it. That concern, *Tosafot* maintains, is not merely the rationale behind a formal *takana* that remains on the books regardless of circumstances. Rather, the parameters of the prohibition are continuously defined by whether that concern remains a live one in the present social reality. Since women in *Tosafot*'s time no longer engaged in that behavior, the prohibition simply does not apply.

### Takana Permanence

This third approach, while compelling in limited contexts, is potentially dangerous if applied too liberally, since it could be used to dissolve virtually any rabbinic enactment by claiming that realities have changed. The more conservative and generally accepted approach is that once a *beit din* has established a *takana*, another *beit din* cannot uproot it without surpassing the original in wisdom and in numbers — *ad she-yigdal be-chochma u-ve-minyan* — a principle that reflects the system's fundamental resistance to change.

It is important to note that *Tosafot* deploys the contextual argument selectively. He raises it only when confronted with an existing practice that contradicts the Gemara — never proactively, as a grounds for dismantling a *takana* in the abstract. Classic examples include the neglect of *mayim acharonim*, which was instituted as a precaution against *melach sedomit*, a particular harmful salt that is no longer in common use; or the permission to clap and dance on *Shabbat*, where the original concern about inadvertently constructing a musical instrument is no longer realistic. In each case, *Tosafot* uses the contextual argument defensively, to make sense of accepted practice, not offensively, to innovate.

---

## Maris Ayin Doctrine

### Private Maris Ayin

The Gemara now introduces a formal statement: *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav* — Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav — that wherever the *Chachamim* prohibited something on account of *maris ayin*, the concern for appearances, it is forbidden even in the most private of places, *afilu be-chadrei chadarim assur*. The intuitive assumption would be that a prohibition rooted in appearances should only operate where one is visible. Rav rejects that assumption categorically.

### Bell Contradiction

This ruling immediately invites challenge from a *mishnah* discussed earlier in the tractate: an animal may not go out wearing a bell even if the bell is stopped up and making no noise. The rationale given there is *maris ayin* — it looks as though one is leading the animal to market. Yet another *braita* records that if the bell is stopped up, the animal may walk about with it in the *chatzer*. If the concern is only about appearances in the public domain, that is perfectly consistent; if the concern applies even in private, how is use in a *chatzer* permitted? This appears to directly contradict Rav's ruling.

### Tannaim Debate

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by noting that the question is itself a *tannaitic* dispute. At the top of 65a, a *braita* is cited regarding wet laundry: one who has wet garments — say, caught in the rain — may spread them in the sun to dry, but not in a place where the public can see, lest observers assume the laundry was done on *Shabbat*.

### Wet Laundry Case

This is a *maris ayin* concern, and the *braita*'s *Tanna Kamma* permits it in private precisely because there is no one to observe. This supports the view that *maris ayin* does not apply where one cannot be seen.

### Unresolved Status

Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon, however, prohibit spreading the wet laundry even where no one can see, in keeping with Rav's position that *maris ayin* applies even in private. The Gemara thus identifies Rav's ruling with the minority view of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon, while the *Tanna Kamma* and the ruling about the bell in the *chatzer* reflect the majority view that private settings are exempt from *maris ayin*. The Gemara does not issue a definitive ruling. If one examines *Tosafot* at the top of 65a, on the words *amar Rav kol makom she-asru chachamim*, one finds that *Tosafot* cites opinions — *yesh mefarshim* — who rule that the *halacha* does not follow Rav, while also noting that in other contexts *Tosafot* himself rules that *maris ayin* is indeed a problem even *be-chadrei chadarim*. Some of the *Geonim* explicitly rule that it is not a problem in private. *Le-halacha*, the generally assumed *psak* is that *maris ayin* does apply in private.

### D'oraisa vs D'rabbanan

There is, however, a position in the later *poskim* suggesting that even if *maris ayin* applies in private when something looks like a biblical violation, it may not apply when the act merely resembles a rabbinic transgression. The logic is that concerns about appearances generate concentric protective fences, and when one is already at some remove from a *d'oraisa* prohibition, the outer fence need not extend into completely private settings.

### Sensibility Concern

There is a further way to understand the prohibition of *maris ayin be-chadrei chadarim* that goes beyond the purely sociological concern about what observers might conclude. When the *Chachamim* prohibit an action because it *looks* like a transgression, they may not only be guarding against reputational harm or the risk that onlookers will draw incorrect inferences and become more permissive themselves. There may also be a concern about what performing an action that appears to be an *aveirah* does to one's own religious sensibilities — even in complete privacy, and even when no transgression is technically occurring.

To illustrate: placing a piece of non-kosher imitation food in one's mouth, or ordering a soy cheeseburger, may be technically permissible, but one might ask whether it is the right posture for someone who takes the *kedushah* of *kashrut* seriously. If one understands that laws like *kashrut* and *Shabbat* are not merely legislative constructs but carry some degree of intrinsic significance as *aveiros*, then to perform an act that objectively appears forbidden — even to oneself, even in private — may itself be problematic at the level of religious sensibility. This might explain why *maris ayin* applies *be-chadrei chadarim* specifically in cases that resemble a *d'oraisa* violation, where that sense of intrinsic gravity is most pronounced, while being less pressing when only a rabbinic prohibition is implicated.

It should be noted that this distinction between *d'oraisa* and *d'rabbanan* does not emerge from the present Gemara itself. The cases discussed here — the cow walking to market, which resembles a rabbinic violation, and the laundry drying, which resembles a biblical violation — cut across the proposed distinction rather than supporting it. The distinction is a later suggestion offered by certain *poskim*, and the Gemara does not endorse it explicitly.

### Coffee Rich Example

The Coffee Rich episode is instructive here. When non-dairy coffee creamer first became commercially available, its use raised a genuine *maris ayin* concern: pouring a white liquid into coffee at a dairy-free meal looked exactly like adding milk. Early authorities required that the original container be kept on the table to signal to observers that the substance was *parve*. Over time, as communal awareness of such products became widespread, that requirement lost its force. What constitutes *maris ayin* is not fixed in the abstract; it is a function of what a given action actually appears to be within a specific community at a specific time.

The same dynamic applies to women's trousers. In communities and eras where only men wore trousers, doing so would have raised both a *beged ish* concern and a *maris ayin* concern. In parts of the world where women routinely wore trousers, neither concern was applicable. The *poskim* of Eastern Europe simply were not aware of those communities; the perception that drove the prohibition was locally conditioned.

One might note that a change in communal reality need not be driven by initial violation. When Coffee Rich became universally recognized as *parve*, it was not because people disregarded the original ruling and thereby changed the norm — it was because communal knowledge itself expanded. The item in the box on the table communicated the new reality without anyone having to transgress first. Other normative shifts may have been driven in part by initial non-compliance, but that does not provide license to violate deliberately in order to engineer a change. The point is simply that *maris ayin* remains anchored to social reality, and when that reality genuinely shifts, so do the parameters of the prohibition.

---

## Medical Pads

### Ear Pad

The Gemara now turns to a series of rulings regarding items worn directly on the body for medical purposes. A *moch* — a wad of cloth — placed in one's ear to absorb discharge may be worn on *Shabbat*, since it functions as a form of bodily care and is therefore considered akin to wearing rather than carrying. However, *Tani Rami bar Yechezkel*: the wad must be tied to the ear. If it is not secured, there is concern that it will fall out and the wearer will pick it up and carry it without replacing it.

### Heel Pad

Similarly, a wad placed in one's sandal to cushion a heel abrasion may be worn. Again, *Tani Rami bar Yechezkel* adds the condition that it must be tied to the sandal; the same concern applies — that it will fall and be picked up and carried rather than replaced.

### Menstrual Pad

A pad worn by a woman on account of *niddah* — menstrual bleeding — is likewise permitted, subject to earlier qualifications in the Gemara: the pad must be serving the body itself, not merely protecting clothing, for in the latter case it would not be considered a bodily garment and its transport would constitute carrying. Rami bar Chama considered ruling that this pad too must be bound — specifically, tied between the thighs — lest it fall and be picked up.

### Rabbi Yochanan Case

Rabbi Yochanan would go out with a pad in his ear to the *beis medrash*. Rashi clarifies that the referent is not the menstrual pad but an ear pad for his own discharge. His colleagues objected, and the source of their objection appears to be that he had not properly bound the pad to his ear, as Rami bar Yechezkel required.

### Rabbi Yannai Case

Rabbi Yannai went further: he wore such a pad into a *karmelis*. This was even more sharply contested — not just by his immediate colleagues in the *beis medrash* but, the Gemara says, by his entire generation — since one may not carry even into a *karmelis*, and without proper binding, the concern about carrying applied there as well.

### Rava's Leniency

Rava disagrees with the requirement to bind the menstrual pad. His reasoning: *keivan de-mais lo ati le-atuyei* — since the pad becomes repulsive when soiled with menstrual blood, a woman will not pick it up if it falls. The revulsion itself provides the functional assurance that she will not carry it. This distinguishes the menstrual pad from the ear wad and the heel wad, both of which are relatively clean and would present no particular aversion to handling if dropped.

This is an interesting point in light of the Gemara's earlier extended discussion about the *tahor* status of a woman who is a *niddah*. The earlier *Tannaim ha-rishonim* had cultivated a comprehensive system of taboos around menstrual blood — a posture that Rabbi Akiva moved away from. Here the Gemara seems to take it as self-evident that a woman will be sufficiently repelled by the soiled pad to leave it where it falls rather than pick it up.

### Pad with Handle

A question is then raised by Rabbi Yirmiyah to Rabbi Abba: what if the pad has been fashioned with a handle? If the woman can pick it up without directly touching the soiled material, the aversion is removed and perhaps the original concern about carrying is reinstated. Rabbi Abba rules that even so, it remains permitted — *mutar*. Even with a handle, people simply do not handle a soiled pad after it has become contaminated, and we are not concerned she will carry it. This ruling is confirmed independently: *itmar nami*, Rav Nachman bar Oshaya said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a pad made with a handle is nonetheless permitted.

---

## Mouth Remedies

### Pepper & Salt

The Gemara now addresses items held in the mouth for medical or hygenic purposes. It is permitted to go out on *Shabbat* with pepper or salt in one's mouth. *Pilpel l'reach ha-peh* — pepper is used to counteract bad breath, functioning essentially as an ancient breath remedy. Rashi on the *mishnah* explains that this refers to *pilpel aroch*, a long pepper rather than a peppercorn — there is indeed a plant known as long pepper, related to black pepper, and that appears to be the referent. *Galgal melach* — a ball of salt — is used for a *dorshani*, which Rashi identifies as some form of tooth ailment.

This ruling is a significant *chiddush*. Until this point, the Gemara's cases of items worn for bodily purposes all involved things physically attached to or embedded in the body — bandages, pads, wads bound to the ear or sandal. Here the item is simply loose in the mouth, not attached, not a garment, not a bandage in any conventional sense. Yet it is permitted because it is actively performing a therapeutic function for the body while it is there. This is distinct from carrying medicine in a container: a bottle of pills is not doing anything for the body at the moment of transport; it is merely being moved from one place to another for future use. These cases occupy an intermediate category — the substance is present and functional, but not physically integrated with the body in the way a bandage is.

One might ask: could a breath mint be permitted on this basis? Following the logic of the Gemara, a mint serving to counteract bad breath would appear to qualify. As for the question of whether salt used for a toothache runs into the concern of *sh'chikat sammanim* — the rabbinic prohibition against grinding medicinal substances on *Shabbat*, which extends to taking medicine for minor ailments — the relevant distinction is that salt and pepper are ordinary foods, not exclusively medicinal substances. The question of whether they cross into the category of medicine is a genuine one, but their status as natural foodstuffs provides a basis for leniency.

### Spices

The Gemara adds that *zangvila* — ginger — and *dartzuna* — which Rashi identifies as cinnamon — are similarly permitted when placed in the mouth, presumably serving the same function as the pepper in counteracting bad breath.

### Gold Tooth

The Gemara then addresses the false tooth. A silver false tooth is unanimously permitted. A gold tooth is disputed: *Rebbi matir ve-chachamim osrin* — Rebbi permits it, while the *Chachamim* prohibit it. The concern driving the prohibition appears to be that a gold tooth is sufficiently striking or unusual that the wearer might remove it in the street to show someone — and in so doing, carry it.

### Silver vs Gold

Rav Zeira clarifies the scope of the dispute: it is only the gold tooth that is contested. A silver tooth, by contrast, is *mutar* according to all. Rashi offers a further explanation: the concern with the gold tooth is not only that one might display it to a friend, but that one might feel embarrassed to be wearing something so conspicuous and remove it for that reason. A silver tooth is less visually arresting and thus less likely to prompt removal.

### Embarrassment Principle

Abaye then draws together the shared principle uniting Rebbi, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in their various rulings: *kol midi d'miganya bah* — anything that would be embarrassing or unbecoming to remove, one will not in fact remove, and therefore we do not fear that it will be carried. Rebbi's ruling about the gold tooth rests on this: even if a gold tooth is conspicuous, removing it would itself be more embarrassing than wearing it, and therefore the concern that one will take it out in the street is unfounded.

Rabbi Eliezer's application of the same principle: he permitted a woman to go out wearing a bottle of perfume around her neck — *lechatchila*, as a practical matter — on the grounds that women who wear perfume bottles do so because of poor body odor. Removing the bottle would expose that fact, and therefore the embarrassment of removal is sufficient to ensure she will not do so.

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar formulates a general rule: any item situated beneath a hairnet may be worn out — *yotza bah* — because even momentarily removing such an item would expose the hair, which a woman would be unwilling to do, and thus the concern about carrying it in public is removed.

---

## Women's Attire

### Coin Wound

The *mishnah* continues listing items women may wear out on *Shabbat*. A woman may go out with a coin placed against a wound — *sela she-al ha-tzinis*. The Gemara discusses what a *tzinit* is: Rashi explains it as a wound on the underside of the foot, in a location vulnerable to irritation. The coin serves as a protective covering. The Gemara then asks why specifically a coin — could not a hard piece of pottery or a plain piece of metal serve equally well? The Gemara ultimately concludes, based on Abaye's analysis, that a coin possesses all three relevant attributes simultaneously: hardness, the capacity to exude moisture beneficial to the wound, and the image embossed on it. Each attribute alone could be replicated by something simpler, but no single alternative combines all three. Abaye thus concludes that all three properties together are what make the coin uniquely therapeutic for this purpose.

### Ear Strings

Young girls — *banot ktanot* — may go out with strings or even with small twigs, like toothpicks, inserted in their pierced ears. Rashi explains the practice: young girls have their ears pierced but do not yet wear earrings; the strings or twigs serve to keep the holes from closing until the girls are old enough to wear jewelry. The ruling permits this even though what is being worn is neither jewelry nor a medical device in any conventional sense.

### Wearing vs Carrying

This raises the fundamental question: why is this not carrying? The item is not attractive — Rashi explicitly notes that the twig is not jewelry, *lav tachshit l'noy hu*. It is not therapeutic in the way that a bandage or pad is. Yet Rashi explains that it is permitted because *orcha behachi velav masoi hu* — this is simply the norm for how such an item is worn on the body, and therefore it is categorized as wearing rather than carrying.

This formulation is worth pausing over. The defining distinction between wearing and carrying does not reduce to a single criterion — not decoration, not therapy, not attachment. Rather, the principle seems to be: if one always wants the item on one's body and has no intention of transporting it to a different location, it is wearing. Carrying, by contrast, is what one does when the purpose is to get something from one place to another — even if the object happens to be placed on or in the body during transit. A recorder held in the mouth, or a backpack worn on the shoulders, are carrying rather than wearing because the purpose is transportation, not continuous bodily use. Items like the strings in pierced ears, the wad in the ear, the pad between the thighs, the pepper in the mouth — all share the quality of being continuously wanted on the body, not moved toward a destination. The Gemara does not always make this principle explicit, but it seems to be what is organizing these rulings.

### Cultural Dress

The *mishnah* turns to two examples of culturally specific dress: Arab women may go out fully veiled — *re'ulot* — and Median women may go out with a cloak fastened in their manner. These are simply their ordinary garments.

### Universal Norm

The *chiddush* is articulated in the immediately following phrase: *ve-chol adam* — and in fact any person may wear these items. The *Chachamim* speak in terms of the common case, but the principle is general. Once something constitutes normal dress for some identifiable group of people, a member of a different group who wears it is wearing, not carrying — even if in their own community the item is exotic. The category of *levush*, of dress, is not community-specific in the restrictive sense.

### Stone/Nut Fastener

The *mishnah* also addresses a method of fastening a garment: attaching a string to one end and a stone, nut, or coin to the other, then wrapping the string around the stone to close the cloak. This is permitted — but with the caveat *u-vilvad she-lo tifrof l'chatchilah be-Shabbat*: one should not do this fastening for the first time on *Shabbat* itself. The reason, as will become clear, turns on the *muktzah* status of the coin.

A stone can be designated in advance for a non-monetary purpose — as a fastener, as a paperweight — and thereby lose its *muktzah* status. A coin, however, retains its monetary identity regardless of how one attempts to repurpose it, and thus remains *muktzah* even when incorporated into a garment. The *mishnah*'s initial permission — *porefet al ha-even ve-al ha-egoz ve-al ha-matbeia* — covers fastening with a stone or nut; the concluding restriction against doing so *le-chatchilah on Shabbat* applies specifically to the coin.

---

## Mikvah & Rainwater

### Colorful Strings Risk

The Gemara now presents a series of rulings attributed to *Avuha de-Shmuel* — Shmuel's father — regarding his daughters. First: he would not permit his daughters to go out on *Shabbat* with strings in their ears, despite the *mishnah*'s explicit permission for young girls to do so. The Gemara explains that his daughters wore *tzivonin* — colorful strings — and colorful strings are sufficiently attractive that a girl might be tempted to remove them in the street to show to friends.

### Sleeping Separation

Second: he would not permit his daughters to sleep together in the same bed. This was apparently a common arrangement in large families. The Gemara initially considers whether this reflects support for the position of Rav Huna.

### Arousal Concern

Rav Huna had stated that *nashim ha-mesolalot zo be-zo* — women who rub against one another — are *pesulot le-kehuna*, disqualified from marrying a *kohen*. Rashi, apparently seeking to limit the ruling's scope, says this refers to a *kohen gadol*, on the grounds that such contact might compromise the status of *betula*. Rashi also acknowledges, however, that the act carries overtones of improper intimacy. *Tosafot*, drawing on other Gemarot, takes a broader view: this behavior would constitute *zona* in a more expansive sense, disqualifying even for a regular *kohen*.

The Gemara, however, declines to attribute Shmuel's father's ruling to Rav Huna's disqualification. The Gemara rules that Rav Huna's position itself is rejected: we do not regard such contact as constituting *zona*. Shmuel's father's concern was different — *ki heikhi de-lo le-alfan gufa nukhra'ah* — he did not want his daughters to grow accustomed to having another body beside them while sleeping, which might cultivate a premature or misdirected physical need. This is a concern about habit formation and its consequences for young women, not a concern about the formal halachic category of *zona*.

It bears noting that the *d'oraisa* prohibition against homosexual relations applies specifically to male relations, because *bi'ah* halakhically requires penile penetration. The question of how to categorize intimate female contact has no direct *d'oraisa* source. The Gemara raises the issue here in terms of whether it constitutes *zona* for purposes of *kehuna*, and appears to reject that characterization. The *Rambam* attempts to classify it under *ma'aseh Eretz Mitzrayim*, but this is a difficult position given the absence of clear evidence that Egypt specifically practiced this, and the *Rambam*'s categorization is itself debated. This Gemara is thus directly relevant to contemporary discussions, and the trend of the *sugyah* seems to resist categorical prohibition at the formal halachic level, though the behavior is clearly regarded with disapproval.

### Spring Mikvah

Third: Shmuel's father would construct private *mikva'ot* for his daughters in *Nisan* — in the spring — and would lay down mats for them in *Tishrei*, in the autumn. The Gemara first addresses the spring *mikvah*: the Gemara says *mesayeia lei le-Rav* — this supports the position of Rav.

### Rainwater Majority

Rav had stated: *mitra be-ma'arava sahada raba perat* — rain in the land of Israel is evidenced by the Euphrates rising. The implication is that the rivers rise in the rainy season due to an influx of rainwater, and this creates a halachic problem for *tevila* in a river. The problem is as follows: a *mikvah* of rainwater must be stationary — *mei geshamim* that are *zochalin*, flowing, are invalid. A natural river may be used even though its water runs, because the river itself is classified as *mayim chayim*, groundwater. But if a majority of the river's water at a given time is rainwater rather than groundwater, the river is reclassified, as it were, as a rainwater body — and then the flowing water is invalid. One cannot immerse in a river when its majority is rainwater unless the river is standing, which a river by definition is not. Therefore, in the spring — when snowmelt and sustained rainfall cause the rivers to swell dramatically — Shmuel's father was concerned that the majority of the river's water was rainwater, and so he built standalone *mikva'ot* for his daughters rather than permit them to use the river.

### Underground Water

Shmuel, however, disagreed with his father. Shmuel held that *nahara mi-keifei mivrak* — a river rises from its floor. He believed that when the surface level of a river rises due to rain, there is a corresponding rise in underground water feeding the river from below, such that the proportion of true groundwater never actually falls to a minority. On this view, there is no concern about rainwater constituting a majority, and the river remains usable throughout the year.

Yet, the Gemara notes, Shmuel seems to contradict himself: he elsewhere rules that flowing water is only valid for immersion — *ein ha-mayim metaherin be-zochalin* — in the case of the Euphrates during *Tishrei*, the autumn, but not during other seasons. This position aligns with his father's concern during the spring, even though Shmuel's general principle would suggest no concern was warranted. The tension is left in the Gemara without full resolution: all agree that if a river's majority is rainwater it is problematic when flowing; the dispute concerns whether that situation actually arises in practice.

This is an important point for contemporary practice as well. It cannot simply be assumed that any natural body of water constitutes a valid *mikvah*. Beyond the obvious point that some very large lakes are man-made — and thus lack the requisite characteristics of a natural water source — there is the further question of the proportion of rainwater at any given time and season. For rivers and lakes, this requires investigation, and general statistics about seasonal water composition may be consulted, though each situation should be evaluated carefully.

### Mayim Chayim

Rashi introduces an additional dimension by citing his *rabosav*, who raise the possibility that the problem with a river whose majority is rainwater is not only about flowing versus standing water, but about the loss of the category of *mayim chayim* — living water. The Torah specifies that a *zav* must immerse in *mayim chayim*. Rashi's *rabosav* extend this requirement to a *zavah* as well. Given that contemporary halachic practice treats every woman as combining the statuses of *niddah* and *zavah*, this would mean that all women require *mayim chayim* for valid immersion — and that if rainwater becomes the majority in a river, the river no longer qualifies.

Rashi himself rejects this position, and so does *Tosafot*, and *le-halacha* it is definitively rejected. Were it accepted, the entire system of modern *mikva'ot* — which are overwhelmingly constructed using collected rainwater — would be invalidated. One might ask how such a position could have been maintained at all: surely even the *rishonim* who held it needed functional *mikva'ot*. The answer is that in earlier eras, the overwhelming majority of *mikva'ot* were actually wells, drawing on groundwater that unambiguously qualifies as *mayim chayim*. The position was therefore not practically untenable in its historical context, even if it could not survive into the period when rainwater *mikva'ot* became universal.

### Autumn Mats

As for the mats in *Tishrei*: Rashi explains that in the autumn, the river could be used for *tevila* — the rainwater concern was absent — but the riverbed was extremely muddy, and walking through the mud would create a *chatzitzah* problem, an interposition between the body and the water. Shmuel's father would lay down mats so his daughters could enter the water without accumulating mud on their feet. *Tosafot* offers a different explanation: the mats were erected not on the riverbed but as screens providing privacy, without which his daughters would not immerse properly out of embarrassment. These two explanations reflect different understandings of what practical obstacle the mats were designed to solve.

---

## Women's Attire (II)

### Coin Muktzah

Returning now to the question of the coin as a garment fastener: the *mishnah* had permitted fastening a garment with a string wrapped around a stone, nut, or coin, but had added that one should not do so *le-chatchilah* on *Shabbat*. Abaye explains: the later clause of the *mishnah* — *seifa asan le-matbei'ah* — addresses specifically the coin. Wrapping a string around a stone or nut involves no *muktzah* concern, since those items can be designated for use in the garment before *Shabbat*, changing their functional identity. A coin, however, cannot shed its monetary identity by being incorporated into a garment. It remains *muktzah* regardless. Therefore, handling the coin to fasten the garment on *Shabbat* itself is prohibited, and whatever was not fastened before *Shabbat* cannot be fastened on *Shabbat*.

This also resolves the question of the coin placed on the wound: presumably, this coin too would need to have been in place from before *Shabbat*, since moving the coin into position on *Shabbat* would involve handling *muktzah*.

### Nut Trick

Abaye now poses a question: may a woman use a nut — a legitimate garment fastener — as a ruse to carry food for her infant out into the street on *Shabbat*? The scenario is that she cannot carry the food directly, but she wraps the string of her garment around a nut that happens to also be an edible food item. She walks outside wearing the garment thus fastened, then removes the nut and gives it to the child to eat. Is this permitted?

### No Emergency

*Teivai le-man d'amar ma'arimin, teivai le-man d'amar ein ma'arimin* — the question can be posed on either side of the debate about whether one may employ ruses in cases like a burning building on *Shabbat*. In the case of a fire, one may wish to save garments by wearing many layers at once — effectively carrying them without technically carrying — and the question is whether this trick is permitted. The Gemara draws a critical distinction. In the fire case, there is an urgent emergency: if a permissible outlet is not provided, the person will simply carry the garments in outright violation. Permitting the ruse is thus a concession to human urgency. *Aval hacha, ee lo sharis lei lo asi le-afkukei* — here, by the nut, if the ruse is not permitted, the woman will simply not take the food out. There is no emergency that will cause her to violate regardless. Therefore, no concession is necessary, and the ruse need not be permitted.

The Gemara then entertains a counterargument: even for the opinion that prohibits the fire-garment ruse, the present case might be more permissible — because in the fire case, wearing extra garments is sometimes genuinely a mode of transport rather than dress, and thus the action itself carries the taint of carrying even when technically classified as wearing. Using a nut to fasten a garment, by contrast, is simply what people do with garments — it is unambiguously a mode of dress and never a mode of transport. On this view, even setting aside the emergency consideration, the nut ruse is purer in form and might be permitted.

The Gemara does not resolve the question. *Teiku* — it stands unanswered.

---

---

# Shabbat 67

## Healing Incantations

### One-Day Fever

The Gemara opens with *v'amar Abaye* — Abaye states that his mother (his nurse-maid, who raised him as an orphan) taught him the following. The *amud* begins ten lines from the bottom of 66b, at the words *mai teiku*, and the material picks up in the middle of a sequence of remedies and incantations Abaye received from her.

For a one-day fever (*eshta bas yoma*), Abaye's mother instructed: take a white coin (*zuza chivera*), go to where salt is dried out — as salt pans still function today near the Dead Sea — and take an equal weight of salt. Bind it in the hollow of the neck (the small depression where the neck meets the chest) with a string of hair (*nira barka*), and it will heal. If that cannot be done, one should sit at a crossroads (*parashas drachim*) — as Tamar went to *parashas einayim* — and when a large ant (*shumshumana gamla*) is seen carrying something on its back, take it, place it in a copper tube (*guvta d'nechasha*), seal the tube with lead, stamp it with sixty seals (Rashi notes that sixty is an exaggeration), shake it, carry it, and say to the ant: *tunach alai v'tunai alach* — your burden should be on me and my burden should be on you, so that the fever is transferred to the ant.

At this point *Rav Acha the son of Rav Huna* raised a question to *Rav Ashi*: perhaps this same ant was previously used by someone else to absorb his fever. In that case, the exchange would be counterproductive — one would be receiving back the first person's burden rather than shedding one's own. The response is therefore to revise the incantation: rather than a bilateral exchange, say *tunai v'tunach alach* — my burden and your burden are both on you. What is striking here is that they consider it entirely appropriate to raise a logical objection against an incantation and revise its wording accordingly. This implies that they understood there to be some operative mechanism — something being genuinely manipulated — and therefore a question could be posed and a correction made. This is not the posture of people treating these formulas as arbitrary magic.

If neither approach is available, take a new small flask (*kuza chadta*), go to the river, and say: *Nahara Nahara* — river, river, lend me (*oizfen*) a flask of water for a guest who has visited me, the fever being the guest. Fill the flask, spin it seven times around the head, throw it behind the back, and say to the river: take back the water you gave me, for the guest who came to me came in a day and shall leave in a day (*b'yoma asa b'yoma azal*). This is intended to cause the fever to depart.

### Three-Day Fever

*Rav Huna* teaches the remedy for a three-day fever (*eshta silsa* — Rashi notes it may refer to a fever that has returned three times). The treatment requires an elaborate collection of seven items from seven separate sources: seven thorns from seven palm trees, seven splinters from seven beams, seven pegs from seven bridges, seven portions of ash from seven ovens, seven measures of dust from seven door-sockets, seven scrapings of tar from seven boats, and seven seeds of cumin, together with seven hairs from the beard of an old dog (*dikna d'kalba sava*). All of these are bound in the hollow of the neck with a string of hair. One might wonder, practically, about the source of the seven pegs from seven bridges — whether one simply removes them. Perhaps, as one suggestion proposes, the pegs were surplus materials left over after construction, available to those who needed them for healing purposes.

### Intense Fever

*Rabbi Yochanan* teaches the treatment for *eshta tzmirtah*, an intense burning fever — Rashi describes it as one that sets the entire body on fire. Take a knife made entirely of iron, go to where there is a certain type of bush (Steinsaltz identifies it as a mulberry or thorn bush; the word *vardina* suggests something rose-adjacent), and tie a hair-string to it. On the first day, carve into the bush a little (*likhrok bei porta*) and say: *Vayera malach Hashem elav* — "And the angel of God appeared to him" (Shemos 3:2). The relevance is the verse's conclusion: *madua lo yivar hasneh* — why will the bush not be consumed? The invocation draws a parallel: as the bush was not consumed by fire, so too should the fever not consume the afflicted person. The second day, carve a bit more and say the next verse: *Vayomer Moshe asura na v'ereh madua lo yivar hasneh* — "And Moses said, let me turn and see why the bush is not burning." The third day, carve again and say: *Vayar Hashem ki sar lir'ot* — "God saw that he had turned aside to look" — the word *sar*, turned aside, is invoked to suggest that the fever too should turn aside and depart.

*Rav Aha the son of Rava* then proposed to *Rav Ashi* that a fourth verse would serve well: *Vayomer al tikrav halom* — "And He said, do not draw near here" — so that the fever should not draw near to the patient. The response is to restructure the sequence: on the first day, combine the first two verses (since the essential operative phrase is *madua lo yivar hasneh*, and both those verses contribute to it); on the second day say *Vayar Hashem ki sar lir'ot*; and on the third day say *Vayomer al tikrav halom*. Again, a question is posed and the incantation revised — a pattern that recurs throughout this passage.

When actually carving into the bush, one should bow down close to the ground (*leitatei*) and say: O bush, O bush (*hasneh hasneh*), it was not because you were taller than all other trees that the Holy One caused His *shechinta* to dwell upon you, but rather because you were lower than all trees (*mishum d'mikhkat mikol ilanei*) did God choose you. And just as the fire saw Hananya, Mishael, and Azarya in the furnace and fled from before them (*v'arkat min kadmohei*), so should the fire of the fever see Ploni the son of Plonis — the patient — and flee from before him.

The connection between the humility of the *sneh* and the incantation is not entirely transparent. One possibility is that the act of bowing down, making oneself humble, is intended to invoke divine compassion, echoing the theme of God choosing the lowest of the trees.

### Boils

For *simta* — which Rashi identifies as a type of boil — one recites: *baz bazya mas masya kas kasya*. Rashi does not attempt to explain these syllables. The incantation continues: *sharli v'amarli*, and then invokes *ilein malachei d'ishtalchu m'ara d'Sdom* — these are the angels sent from the land of Sodom. Rashi clarifies that they did not literally come from Sodom; it is simply part of the *lachash*. The purpose is healing: *u'l'asya shechinta d'kaivin* — to heal the painful boils.

Further doubled words follow: *bazach bizach bazbazach mas masach kamon kamoch*. The incantation then says: *einaich bich einaich bich* — your appearance is to you, your appearance is to you — meaning, remain contained, do not inflame the skin further. *Ashrichat bach* — stay in your place. Do not spread further. *Zarach k'chlot u'ch'farda d'lo para v'dlo ravya* — your seed should be like something that is contained, like a mule that is neither fruitful nor multiplies. *Kach lo tifrei v'lo tirbei b'gufei d'Ploni bar Plonis* — so should you neither spread nor multiply on the body of the patient.

### Demons & Shades

For *kifa* — which Rashi says may refer to pus-filled boils, or alternatively to a certain type of demonic shade — one says: *cherev shlufa v'chala netusha* — a drawn sword and an extended sling — *lo shmi yochav chulin machovin* — his name is not painful illnesses.

For a shade (*shida*) one says: *havayat d'pakik d'pakuk havayat* — you were bound and blocked up, you were. *Lita tavor u'mshumat* — cursed, broken, and excommunicated (like a *shamta*). *Bar Tit bar Tamya bar Tina* — calling the demon by these names, all variants of plaster or mud. The incantation continues with further phrases that Rashi does not explain.

For the shade of the bathroom (*shida d'veit hachisei*), one says: *akarkafei d'ari v'a'usi d'guryaisa* — on the head of a lion and on the nose of a lioness — *ashkachton l'shida bar shirkai panda b'meshera d'karti* — there can be found the demon whose name is *bar shirkai panda* in the valley of leeks. *Chavtei* — he should be struck, swallowed in the cheek of a donkey, and so banished.

One might ask why an individual addresses demons directly rather than praying to God for relief. This is a profound question, and as the Gemara will make clear within just a few lines, performing incantations of this kind is itself considered forbidden. The observation underscores how remarkable it is that these formulas are transmitted in the Gemara at all.

---

## Rationalism & Magic

### Questioning Incantations

What is perhaps most striking about this entire passage is the recurring pattern in which the Sages treat incantations as subject to rational scrutiny. As noted above, *Rav Acha the son of Rav Huna* asked a pointed logical question about the ant-incantation and proposed a revised formulation. Similarly, *Rav Aha the son of Rava* proposed a better verse for the fever-incantation. In each case, someone raises an objection and the text is actually revised. This suggests the Sages did not view these formulas as arbitrary, inviolable magic but rather as operating through some kind of real — if opaque — mechanism, such that logical questions could be posed and improvements made. They appear to have believed that something was genuinely being manipulated, and therefore the wording mattered.

### Rambam vs. Gra

This naturally raises the broader question of what to make of such material. The *Rambam* is explicit: all of this is nonsense, derived from the mistaken science of the ancient world. Notably, in his commentary on the *Mishnah* and elsewhere, the *Rambam* states that one may recite an incantation over a patient on *Shabbat* — not because it works — but because it is psychologically beneficial, and anything that calms an ill person's mind has value. The *Gra*, by contrast, argues that this entire framing of the *Rambam* is simply wrong, that the *Rambam* was misled by Greek philosophy, and that the incantations in the Gemara are entirely real and operative, as their prevalence in the Gemara itself demonstrates.

The question touches a deep nerve, because underlying it is the problem of authority. For some, it is essential to say the rabbis never erred even in matters of science — because if one concedes error in one domain, how can authority in *halacha* be trusted? The *Rambam* rejects this framing entirely. He argues that one cannot expect the Sages to have transcended the science of their time; that was never the source of their greatness. Their authority derives from their role as transmitters of the tradition and as those authorized to interpret the *Torah* — not from any claim to supernatural scientific foreknowledge. The Sages were limited by the knowledge available in their era, and there is no theological problem in acknowledging that.

### Three Approaches

This yields three distinct positions on how to handle apparent conflicts between Gemara statements and observed reality.

The first holds that we are simply wrong — the ancients got it right, and if the remedies no longer seem to work, that is our failure of knowledge or execution.

The second, associated with the *Rambam*, holds that the Sages were not scientists, that they shared the assumptions of their time, and that being mistaken about empirical matters in no way diminishes their religious authority.

The third — a position often invoked to preserve rabbinic dignity while conceding the empirical point — holds that the facts on the ground have genuinely changed: *nishtana hateva*, the natural order has shifted, and what once worked no longer does. This approach allows one to accept that the incantations no longer function without attributing error to the rabbis.

It is worth noting that the *Geonim* already ruled that one may not rely on the medical recommendations in the Gemara, given that they no longer accord with observed practice. That the *Geonim* themselves made this concession shows that the willingness to set aside Talmudic medical advice is ancient and not a product of modernity.

---

## Clothing on Shabbat

### Bells & Ornaments

With the discussion of incantations concluded, the Gemara turns to close the sixth *perek* with a few remaining points about what may be worn on *Shabbat*. The Gemara mentions that sons of princes (*vnei melachim*) could wear bells and similar ornaments. *Rabbi Yehoshua* identifies the opinion underlying this ruling as that of *Rabbi Shimon*, who holds that all of Israel are sons of kings (*kol Yisrael bnei melakhim hen*) — we are all descended from Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov — and therefore whatever is appropriate to wear for royalty is appropriate for all Jews. *Rava* offers an alternative rationale: the discussion concerns a bell that is actually woven into the garment (*arig bi'ksusa*), and therefore everyone agrees it may be worn, since if it is integral to the garment there is no concern that one will remove it and come to carry it.

### Crutches & Canes

As the *perek* closes, it is worth recalling two pivotal points from the preceding discussion. First, the general rule: all these items that may not be worn on *Shabbat* in the *reshus harabbim* are prohibited out of concern that one will remove them and carry them. *Tosafot* addressed the striking fact that this concern does not seem to govern actual practice — women routinely wear jewelry in public spaces. *Tosafot* offered three answers, all of which were incorporated into the *Shulchan Aruch*: (1) perhaps the ruling follows the opinion that wearing ornaments is permitted even in a *chatzer*, and since we maintain that there is no *reshus harabbim* in the halachic sense today (a position we rely upon for *eruvin*), the concern does not apply; (2) the violation is only rabbinic in nature, people will not listen to a prohibition even if stated, and it is therefore better to remain silent (*mutav yehyu shogegin*); (3) the concern for removing and showing applied only in a social context where such behavior was common, and since that social norm no longer applies, the entire concern lapses.

Second, and of particular practical importance, is the *Tosafot* ruling regarding crutches and canes, which derives from the Gemara's discussion of prosthetic limbs. The Gemara debated whether a wooden leg is considered clothing (and therefore permissible to wear on *Shabbat*) or a burden (and therefore forbidden to carry). *Tosafot* drew a critical distinction: all of that discussion concerned items that are not strictly necessary for ambulation. But anything without which a person cannot walk at all — crutches, a cane, a wheelchair — is considered halachically part of the body rather than a carried object, and may be used even where there is no *eruv*. This ruling is *pasken'd l'halacha* and has significant practical implications for those who cannot walk without such aids.

### Amulets & Amorites

The *perek* closes with the *Mishnah* that bridges these concerns about what may be worn and the broader topic of *darchei emori*. Items worn for medical purposes that are actively functioning on the body do not constitute carrying. But the question arises: what if those items are of a type that seems not merely medical but superstitious? That is the subject of the final *mishnah* and the ensuing Gemara discussion.

---

## Amulets Debate

### Three Amulets

The *Mishnah* states: *yotzin b'veitzat hachargol* — one may go out wearing the egg of a locust or grasshopper (*chargol*, one of the species listed in the *Torah*). *U'v'shen shu'al* — and the tooth of a fox. *U'v'masmer min hatzaluv* — and a nail from a crucifixion. Crucifixion was not unique to any one figure; the Romans executed many people in this manner, and nails from crucifixions were believed to have medicinal properties. All of these may be worn because they serve healing purposes (*mishum refuah*), and an object worn on the body for a healing purpose is not considered carrying. This is the view of *Rabbi Meir*. The *Chachamim*, however, forbid these items even during the week, not because of carrying on *Shabbat*, but because of *darchei emori* — the ways of the Amorites, the prohibited practices of idolatrous peoples.

The Gemara then explains what each item treats. The locust egg (*beitzat hachargol*) is used for an earache (*shichla*). The fox tooth (*shen hasha'al*) is used for sleep disorders — the tooth of a living fox (*d'chaya*) for one who sleeps too much, and the tooth of a dead fox (*d'mita*) for one who cannot fall asleep. The crucifixion nail (*masmer min hatzaluv*) is used for *zirpa* — what Rashi describes as an infected wound, perhaps from metal contact, which one might today associate with tetanus.

### Healing Exemption

*Abaye and Rava* both state a general principle (*de'amri tarvaihu*): *kol davar sheyeish bo mishum refuah ein bo mishum darchei emori* — anything that genuinely has healing benefit is not subject to the prohibition of *darchei emori*. If something actually works medicinally, it cannot be classified as superstitious Amorite practice. The *Rambam* in his *Peirush HaMishnayot* explains the criterion: one determines whether something has *refuah* by observing whether it actually works.

The Gemara then presses the converse: does this mean that something with no healing benefit necessarily falls under *darchei emori*? The question is pressed by a *Baraisa* about a tree that is shedding its fruit prematurely. Two remedies are offered: weighting the branches with stones (*toano be'avanim*) and painting the trunk with a red dye (*sokro besikra*). The Gemara readily explains the rationale for the stones — they weaken the sap flow and thereby prevent the fruit from dropping (*ki heichi delichkush cheilah*). But what good does the painting do? *Mai refuah ka'avid* — what medical benefit does it provide?

The Gemara's answer is striking: *ki heichi delichzeih inish veliv'ei aleih rachamei* — so that people will see the tree is in distress, and will pray for its owner. They see the painted tree, recognize that there is a problem, and pray on behalf of the owner, whose prayers are then answered. This is grounded in the rule derived from the *metzora*, who is required to call out *tamei tamei* — Rashi notes that one might have assumed the announcement should come from others, but the verse specifies that even the *metzora* himself must declare his condition. The reason: *tzarich lehodiya tza'aro lerabbim*, one must publicize one's suffering to the public, *verabbim yevakshu alav rachamim*, so that the community will pray on the afflicted person's behalf.

What is profoundly significant about this Gemara is that the question is asked at all. The inquiry — what good does the painting do? — implies that there must be a rational, explicable mechanism for something to qualify as *refuah* and thereby escape the category of *darchei emori*. It is not enough that people believe it works or that they have seen it appear to work. The Gemara demands an explanation. This is a much narrower definition of *refuah* than one might have expected — and it creates an obvious tension with the lengthy catalogue of incantations reported earlier. If an explanation is required, then virtually everything in that earlier material would seem to fall short.

One response is that *Abaye* and *Rava* may have held the broader empirical standard — anything they believed had been demonstrated to work qualified as *refuah* — while the *stam* of the Gemara, in framing the question the way it does, adopts a narrower, more rationalist standard. Not every *sugya* need be a unified position. Additionally, there is a distinction between *Abaye's* own transmitted traditions from his nurse-maid and the legal framework he articulates jointly with *Rava* — the former being ethnographic and the latter normative.

The painting example also yielded a real-world insight: a kibbutz practice of painting trees turns out to have the genuine benefit of preserving moisture in the trunk — a mechanism the Gemara did not know but which fully vindicates the practice on rational grounds.

### Tree Remedy

*Ravina* then asks: according to whom do we hang dates on a palm tree that is not producing well? *Ki hai tana* — like the *tanna* just cited, meaning the practice is justified because it alerts passersby to pray for the tree's owner. *Tani tana b'perek Amorai kamei d'Rabbi Chiya bar Avin* — a *tanna* taught in the chapters of the *Amoraim* in the presence of *Rabbi Chiya bar Avin*. Rashi explains that this refers to the two chapters of the *Tosefta* on *Shabbat* — chapters 6 and 7 or 7 and 8 depending on the version — which contain the extensive list of what constitutes *darchei emori* and what does not.

---

## Darchei Emori List

### Allowed Incantations

*Rabbi Chiya bar Avin* states: *kulhu yesh bo mishum darchei emori levar mi'hani* — everything in that list falls under the prohibition of *darchei emori* except for these two cases. The first exception: if a bone is lodged in one's throat (*etzem begrono*), one brings another bone from the same species — if a chicken bone, then another chicken or chicken bone — places it on the forehead, and recites: *chad chad nachis bala, bala nachis chad chad* — one by one go down and swallow, swallow and go down one by one. This is not *darchei emori*. The second exception: for a fishbone lodged in the throat (*idra*), one says: *nin'atzta ke-makat, nin'alta ke-tris, shia shia* — you are stuck like a needle, you are locked like a shutter, go down, go down. This too is permitted.

These two incantations are noteworthy precisely because they are incantations — they are not treatments that are obviously explicable in rational terms.
