And yet they are explicitly exempted from *darchei emori*. This seems to support the view that the standard is not rationalistic explicability but rather some form of demonstrated or assumed effectiveness. Whether the *stam* of the Gemara is consistent on this point remains a genuine tension.

Regarding the overall structure of the *darchei emori* list: the *Yere'im* (*Rabbi Eliezer mi-Metz*, a student of *Rabbeinu Tam*) argues that the list of Amorite practices enumerated by the Sages reflects those known at the time of the *Torah* to be the practices of the Canaanite peoples, and that *assur lehosif aleihem* — one may not add to the list. Anything not on the list is therefore permitted. This is a significant limiting principle.

### Forbidden Incantations

The *darchei emori* list continues. *Ha-omer gad gadi u'snuk lo ashkei u'bushkei* — one who says "let my luck increase and not falter, day and night" — *yesh bo mishum darchei emori*. This is a specific incantation for good fortune and falls under the prohibition. This is distinct from a prayer to God expressing the same wish, such as the *yehi ratzon* formulas recited at the *Rosh Hashanah* table with symbolic foods; those are prayers directed to God, not standalone incantations.

*Hu b'shmo v'hi b'shmah* — if a husband and wife in the bedroom refer to each other by the other's name — this too is *darchei emori*. *Donu doni* — an incantation for the strengthening of one's wine barrels — also falls under the prohibition.

### Divine Names

*Rabbi Yehuda* adds a further dimension to two of the above: not only are these practices *darchei emori*, they are actually worse — they invoke the names of real pagan deities. Regarding *gad gadi*: *ein Gad ela lashon avodah zarah* — the word *Gad* is the name of a deity, as the verse states (*Yeshaya* 65:11): *ha-orchim l'Gad shulchan* — those who set a table to the god Gad. Regarding *donu doni*: *ein Dan ela lashon avodah zarah* — *Dan* is also the name of a deity, as the verse states (*Amos* 8:14): *chai elohecha Dan* — by the life of your god *Dan*, associated with the worship at the city of Dan, where one of Jeroboam's two golden calves was erected.

It is striking that two of the names of the *shevatim* — *Gad* and *Dan* — also function as divine names in idolatrous contexts. One possibility is that the tribal names were appropriated by surrounding peoples for their deities, or alternatively that the city of Dan became so associated with idolatrous practice that the god worshipped there simply bore its name. One might similarly note *Tammuz* (*Tamuz*), a month name in the Jewish calendar that is also the name of a deity, as the verse describes: *mevakkot et ha-Tammuz* (Yechezkel 8:14).

### Animal Omens

*Ha-omer la-orev tzrach* — one who says to a raven, "screech," and to a female raven, "screech," and "turn your tail toward me for good" (*v'hachiziri li zenavech l'tova*) — *yesh bo mishum darchei emori*. This was done upon seeing or hearing a raven, which was interpreted as a portent, and the incantation was meant to redirect the omen. *Ha-omer shachtu tarnegol ze she-kara arvit* — one who says to slaughter a rooster because it crowed after dark (when roosters should not crow), *v'tarnegolet she-kar'ah gavrit* — or a hen that crowed like a rooster — *yesh bo mishum darchei emori*. The feeling that one must slaughter such an animal to ward off misfortune is itself the Amorite practice. Many readers will recognize in these passages echoes of folk superstitions that persisted long after the Talmudic period in various Jewish communities — the impulse to neutralize a bad omen by acting against it is ancient and widespread.

### Cooking Superstitions

*Eshteh ve-otir eshteh ve-otir* — reciting "I will drink and leave over, drink and leave over" as an incantation — *yesh bo mishum darchei emori*. The intent to leave something over at the end of a meal can be a fine custom (*v'savanu v'hotarnu*), but articulating it as a ritual formula crosses into Amorite practice.

*Ha-mafka'at beitzim ba-kotel bifnei efrochim* — one who cracks eggs against a wall or places eggshells on a wall in front of chicks to protect them from dying — *yesh bo mishum darchei emori*. *Ha-megis bifnei efrochim* — one who stirs a pot in front of chicks for the same purpose — also forbidden. *Ha-merakkedet v'ha-monah shiv'im ve-echad efrochim bishvil she-lo yamutu* — one who dances while counting seventy-one chicks so that they should not die — *yesh bo mishum darchei emori*. The anxiety about losing one's chicks clearly prompted a variety of such practices.

*Ha-merakkedet le-kutach* — dancing when making *kutach* (a sour-milk based condiment) — *yesh bo mishum darchei emori*. *Ve-ha-meshattaka le-adashim* — insisting on silence while cooking lentils — also forbidden. *Ve-ha-metzavachat le-grisim* — making loud noise while cooking *grisim* (a type of legume) — also forbidden. One might note that elsewhere in the Gemara it is said that the sounds made when grinding spices have a real effect on quality; this list, however, treats the analogous practices as pure superstition.

*Ha-mash-tenet bifnei kederatah bishvil she-titbashel mehera* — a woman who urinates in front of her pot to speed up cooking — *yesh bo mishum darchei emori*.

### Legitimate Methods

In contrast to the forbidden practices, certain methods of speeding up cooking or improving one's lamp are entirely permitted. Placing a twig of *tut* (mulberry) and a piece of glass in a pot will genuinely cause the contents to cook faster — this is not *darchei emori* but a real technique. The *Chachamim*, however, object to the piece of glass not on grounds of *darchei emori* but of *sakana* — physical danger, as glass fragments in food present an obvious hazard.

Placing a clump of salt into an oil lamp (*bul shel melach l'toch haner*) will make it burn more cleanly — this too is a real and permitted method. Placing pottery shards (*charsisa*) beneath a lamp will cause it to burn more slowly. *Rav Zutra* adds: one who covers an oil lamp or leaves a naphtha-burning lamp (*sheraga d'mishcha* or *nafta*) uncovered causes the fuel to burn faster than necessary and thereby transgresses *Bal Tashchit* — the prohibition against wasteful destruction.

### Wedding Toasts

The *Baraisa* then states: saying *chamra v'chayei l'fum rabbanan* — wine and life to the mouth of the rabbis — is *ein bo mishum darchei emori*, not a *darchei emori* problem. It is simply a standard toast.

A story is cited: *Ma'aseh b'Rabbi Akiva she-asah mishteh l'vno* — Rabbi Akiva made a wedding feast for his son, and at every cup of wine brought to the table he said *chamra v'chayei l'fum rabbanan* — wine and life to the mouth of the rabbis. One might ask whether this particular phrase, being a crystallized formula repeated at every cup, could be considered an incantation. The answer is no — it is simply a standard, recognized toast, not a ritual invocation. The version attributed to Rabbi Akiva extended the formula: *chayei v'chamra l'fum rabbanan u'l'fum talmideihem* — wine and life to the rabbis, to the rabbis, and to their students.

An interesting related question arises from the *Tosefta*: whether one may say *asuta* — that is, the equivalent of "gesundheit" — when someone sneezes. Depending on the textual version (*girsa*), some read *yesh bo mishum darchei emori* and others read *ein bo mishum darchei emori*, reflecting genuine dispute about whether so natural an expression crosses any line.

This concludes the sixth *perek*. *Hadran Alach Bameh Isha*.

---

## Seventh Perek Intro

### Six to Seventh

It is worth pausing to appreciate the structure of *Masechet Shabbat* as we move from the sixth *perek* to the seventh. The first six *perakim* have all been, in one way or another, about preparing for *Shabbat*. The tractate opened with the rules of carrying, then moved to lighting candles, putting food on the fire, insulating food, what one may wear — and whether one's animals may wear — as one dresses for *Shabbat*. Two entire *perakim* were devoted to the topic of carrying in its various dimensions — what people and animals may wear and what constitutes forbidden carrying. It is not coincidental that there are six *perakim* before the seventh: six days lead up to the seventh, and these six *perakim* lead up to the *perek* that addresses the *melachos* of *Shabbat* themselves. The *melachos* have been implicit throughout, but now we arrive at the heart of the matter. In a few *dappim* we will reach the famous *Mishnah* that enumerates the thirty-nine *avos melachos*; but first the tractate introduces the framework for liability.

### General Principle

The seventh *perek* opens with a *klal gadol* — a general principle: *kol ha-shoche'ach ikar Shabbat v'asah melachos harbeh b'Shabbatos harbeh* — one who entirely forgot the concept of *Shabbat* and performed many categories of labor on many *Shabbosos* is liable for only one *chatat*, one sin-offering. The reasoning is that only one fundamental error was made: the complete forgetting that *Shabbat* exists at all. No matter how many *Shabbosos* passed and how many types of work were performed, the person made a single mistake, and a single *chatat* is appropriate.

The second case: *ha-yode'a ikar Shabbat* — one who knows that *Shabbat* exists, but made an error about which day is *Shabbat* (perhaps mistaking Friday for *Shabbat* or losing count of the days). This person performed many labors on many *Shabbosos* — *chayav al kol Shabbat v'Shabbat* — and is liable for a separate *chatat* for each *Shabbat* on which the error occurred. The mistake was repeated twenty times if twenty *Shabbosos* passed; twenty sin-offerings are owed. The number of *melachos* performed on each *Shabbat* does not multiply the liability — it is the number of separate *Shabbosos* during which the error was operative.

An important question arises: if the person made one original error (say, miscounting the days by one), then all subsequent *Shabbat* violations flow from that same single error. Why then does the Gemara say one is liable for each *Shabbat* separately? The answer — which will be developed in the ensuing *sugya* — is that the intervening weekdays (*chol*) objectively separate the violations into distinct acts, even if the subjective mistake was one continuous miscalculation.

The third case: *ha-yode'a she-hu Shabbat* — one who knows that it is *Shabbat*, but was unaware that a particular act is forbidden. This is the most common type of error. Such a person is *chayav al kol av melacha u'melacha* — liable for a separate *chatat* for each category of forbidden labor (*av melacha*) about which he was mistaken. If someone never knew that watering plants was forbidden and did so every *Shabbat* for twenty weeks, he owes a single *chatat* — because there was one error, regarding one *av melacha*. But if he also did not know that writing was forbidden, and did that as well, he owes a separate *chatat* for that category. The unit of liability is the number of *avos melachos* misunderstood, not the number of *Shabbosos* on which the violation occurred.

The fourth case: *ha-oseh melachos harbeh me'ein melacha achat* — one who performed many variations of work all falling within a single category. Watering plants, pruning trees, and fertilizing — all are subcategories of encouraging plant growth, a single *av melacha*. Performing all of them yields only one *chatat*, because they all derive from a single root prohibition. This principle — that *toldos* (subcategories) of a single *av melacha* are grouped together for purposes of *chatat* liability — will be at the center of discussion in the pages to come.

---

---

# Shabbat 68

## Klal Gadol - Principle

### New Perek, Shabbat Laws

With daf 68 we arrive at a new *perek* — and, more significantly, a new dimension of *Masechet Shabbat* altogether. The preceding six chapters concerned themselves with preparations on *erev Shabbat*; only now do we enter into the laws of Shabbat proper. The *perek* opens with a *mishna* that begins, *klal gadol amru b'Shabbat* — "a great principle they stated regarding Shabbat" — and this phrase itself will occupy a substantial portion of the *gemara's* attention before it reaches the substantive halachic material.

### Case 1: Forgot Shabbat E…

The *mishna* presents three distinct cases, each defined by the nature of the person's error and each carrying different consequences for the number of *chatat* offerings required.

The first case: *kol hashocheiach ikar Shabbat v'asa melachos harbeh b'Shabbatos harbeh* — someone who forgets the very existence of Shabbat, the fact that there is such a concept in the *Torah*, and over the course of many Shabbatot performs many different *melachos*. When such a person is eventually reminded — perhaps after ten years of unknowing violation — they bring only *achat*, one *chatat* offering. The reasoning is that there was only one fundamental error: forgetting that Shabbat exists at all. Every subsequent violation flows from that single mistake, and therefore a single offering suffices.

### Case 2: Forgot Which Day

The second case: *hayodea ikar Shabbat v'asa melachos harbeh b'Shabbatos harbeh* — someone who knows that Shabbat exists but, as the *gemara* will explain, forgets which day of the week is Shabbat. Perhaps this person's days became confused each week. In such a case, *chayav al kol Shabbat v'Shabbat* — one is liable for every Shabbat separately, because each week constitutes a distinct act of forgetting. The error is not one global mistake but a recurring one, a fresh lapse each week, and therefore the liability is assessed week by week.

One might ask: what if the confusion began with a single initial error — a one-time disorientation from which all subsequent mistakes derived? The *gemara* addresses this and makes clear that, objectively, each week's violation is defined as a separate act, even if causally linked to a first mistake.

### Case 3: Forgot Melacha C…

The third case: *hayodea shehu Shabbat v'asa melachos harbeh b'Shabbatos harbeh* — someone who knows it is Shabbat but did not know, or forgot, that a particular *melacha* or *melachos* were forbidden. Here the liability is *chayav al kol av melacha u'melacha* — one *chatat* for each distinct category of *melacha*. If such a person did not know that watering plants was forbidden, and violated this over ten Shabbatot, they bring one *chatat*. If they additionally did not know that kindling fire was forbidden, they bring a second *chatat*. The principle here is that the liability tracks the category of the error, not the number of Shabbatot on which it was repeated.

### One Category = One Offer…

A final refinement of the *mishna*: *v'oseh melachos harbeh m'ein melacha achas* — if one performs many *melachos* that all belong to the same essential category, they bring only one *chatat*, since the fundamental mistake was one. Watering, planting, pruning, and fertilizing are all *toldos* of the *av melacha* of planting — they all fall under the same heading. Even if performed in many variations on a single Shabbat, a single *chatat* suffices.

### Thirty-Nine Categories

There are several *chidushim* embedded in this *mishna*, and it is worth taking a moment to appreciate them. The *mishna* organizes the *melachos* into categories — *avos* — and the following *mishna* will enumerate thirty-nine of them. The *gemara* will ask: what is the halachic significance of counting thirty-nine? The answer: it informs us that one could theoretically be liable for up to thirty-nine separate *chataos* for a single Shabbat, one for each *av melacha*, if one forgot the prohibition on every individual category.

This is itself a *chiddush*. One might have thought that just as eating from different parts of a *neveilah* constitutes a single prohibition regardless of how many bites one takes, violating Shabbat in multiple distinct ways — planting and cooking and lighting a fire — should be treated as multiple instantiations of the same transgression of Shabbat. The *mishna* teaches otherwise: the different categories of *melacha* are considered independent sins, each requiring its own *chatat*. Within a category, however, all variations are subsumed under a single offering. This dual structure — multiplicity across categories, unity within them — is the first great *chiddush* of the *perek*.

The second *chiddush* is structural: where one's error lies determines the unit of liability. Error about Shabbat's existence generates one *chatat* total. Error about which day is Shabbat generates one per Shabbat. Error about a particular *melacha* generates one per category of *melacha* forgotten. The axis of the mistake is the axis of the obligation.

---

## Klal Gadol - Analysis

### Linguistic Question

With the substance of the *mishna* now established, the *gemara* turns to what might at first appear a marginal linguistic question: *mai ta'ama tana klal gadol* — why does the *mishna* use the phrase *klal gadol*, a "great" principle, rather than simply *klal*? One thinks of the famous formulation in *masechet Avot* — *zeh klal gadol ba-Torah, v'ahavta l'rei'acha kamocha* — where the greatness refers to the sweeping moral scope of the principle. But what warrants the designation here?

The *gemara* considers a first answer: perhaps *gadol* is used because the *mishna* intends to signal that a second, lesser *klal* is coming later. Indeed, the *gemara* in *Shabbat* later introduces another principle — about the minimum quantities required for the prohibition of carrying — and that *klal* is of narrower scope. So the first one is called *klal gadol* to distinguish it.

This framing draws the *gemara* to observe that *masechet Shevi'it* similarly opens its seventh *perek* with *klal gadol amru ba-Shevi'it* — and this parallel is striking: the seventh *perek* of *Shabbat* (the seventh day) and the seventh *perek* of *Shevi'it* (the seventh year) both open with *klal gadol*. This cannot be coincidental.

But the *gemara* notes a difficulty: *masechet Ma'aser* introduces two *klalim* but does not call the first one *gadol*. If *gadol* merely signals that a second *klal* follows, why not by *ma'aser* as well?

### Avot and Toldot

The *gemara* offers a deeper explanation in the name of Rabbi Yossi bar Avin: *Shabbat ve-Shevi'it de-is behu avot ve-is behu toldot* — both Shabbat and *Shevi'it* share the conceptual structure of *avos* (primary categories) and *toldos* (derived subcategories). By Shabbat this is explicit. By *Shevi'it*, the *Torah* only explicitly prohibits four agricultural activities — do not plant, do not prune, do not harvest grain, do not harvest grapes — but these are understood as *avos* from which additional prohibited activities are derived. Since both Shabbat and *Shevi'it* possess this major-category structure, both open with *klal gadol*, a *klal* that belongs to a domain of great scope.

*Ma'aser*, by contrast, has no such *avos* and *toldos* structure, and therefore does not use *klal gadol*.

### Scope Comparison

Yet the *gemara* notes that this explanation, while internally coherent, cannot be the sole basis for the term *gadol* — because as we shall see, Bar Kappara's version of the *mishna* uses *klal gadol* by *ma'aser* as well, and *ma'aser* has no *avos* and *toldos*. Therefore *gadol* must mean something else.

The *gemara* proposes a second explanation: *gadol* refers to relative scope. Shabbat's *issur melacha* is *chamur* — more severe and broader in scope than that of *Shevi'it*. How so? *De-ilu Shabbat ita bein be-talush bein be-mechubar* — by Shabbat, the prohibition applies whether the object of the *melacha* is still attached to the ground or has already been detached. *Ve-ilu Shevi'it be-talush leita be-mechubar ita* — by *Shevi'it*, the *melacha* prohibition applies only to things currently growing from the ground. Thus the scope of Shabbat's *melacha* prohibition is broader, and its punishment is more severe — *chayav mita*, whereas *Shevi'it* carries only a *lav*. Shabbat is therefore *gadol* relative to *Shevi'it*.

### Bar Kappara Version

This comparative logic then cascades down the chain: *Shevi'it* is in turn *gadol* relative to *ma'aser*, because *Shevi'it* applies even to foods fit for animal consumption (*be-maachal beheimah*), and the *pasuk* by *Shevi'it* explicitly includes *"u-livhemtecha ve-la-chayah asher be-artzecha."* Moreover, the *kedushah* of *Shevi'it* applies even to items used as dyes. *Ma'aser*, by contrast, applies only to human food — and biblically, as Rashi notes, only to *dagan, tirosh, ve-yitzhar* (grain, wine, and oil), with the rabbinic extension reaching other fruits and vegetables but still restricted to human food. Thus *Shevi'it* is *gadol* relative to *ma'aser*, and *ma'aser* in Bar Kappara's version is *gadol* relative to *pe'ah*.

### Pe'ah vs Ma'aser Scope

This requires us to examine the scope comparison between *ma'aser* and *pe'ah*. The *mishna* in *Pe'ah* teaches — *klal amru be-pe'ah* (note: no *gadol*) — that *pe'ah* applies to anything that is food, guarded (not *hefker*), grows from the ground, is harvested at one time, and can be stored for preservation. These five criteria determine what requires *pe'ah*.

*Ma'aser*, by Bar Kappara's formulation, shares the first three criteria — food, guarded, growing from the ground — but does not include the latter two: *lekitaso ke-echad* (harvested all at one time) and *machniso le-kiyum* (can be stored). This absence of the latter two criteria means *ma'aser* applies to a broader range of produce. Specifically, figs are excluded from *pe'ah* because they are harvested at different times throughout the year, and vegetables are excluded because they cannot be stored. Both figs and vegetables are nonetheless subject to *ma'aser*. Hence *ma'aser* has broader scope and is called *gadol* relative to *pe'ah*.

### Tosafot Explanation

*Tosafot* raises an interesting question: since both *ma'aser* and *pe'ah* were rabinnically extended to cover all types of produce — fruits and vegetables not covered by biblical law — why did the rabbis apply a narrower scope to *pe'ah* than to *ma'aser*? Why introduce the additional criteria of *lekitaso ke-echad* and *machniso le-kiyum* for *pe'ah* but not for *ma'aser*?

*Tosafot* answers by pointing to the qualitative difference in how the two obligations function. By *ma'aser*, the process is straightforward: you complete the harvest entirely, then set aside a tenth and distribute it. By *pe'ah*, however, the poor are physically present in the field as you harvest — one sees this vividly in the book of Ruth — hovering and waiting for their portion. If the produce is not harvested all at one time, the poor must return repeatedly throughout the season; if the produce cannot be preserved, they may invest significant effort and time only to receive something that quickly spoils. The rabbis therefore determined that it would not serve the poor's interests to obligate *pe'ah* on produce that is harvested piecemeal throughout the year or that rots quickly. The result is a narrower scope for *pe'ah*, driven by practical concern for the very beneficiaries the institution was designed to serve — an approach that is, as one might note, simultaneously paternalistic and realistic.

What the *gemara* accomplishes by raising the linguistic question of *gadol* is to draw a rich set of comparisons across Shabbat, *Shevi'it*, *ma'aser*, and *pe'ah* — mapping a descending hierarchy of scope and severity, while also highlighting the deep structural parallel between Shabbat and *Shevi'it* in their shared system of *avos* and *toldos*.

---

## Tinok Shenishba Status

### Never Knew = Forgot

The *gemara* now turns to the heart of the first clause of the *mishna*: who exactly is the person described as having "forgotten the existence of Shabbat"? Rav and Shmuel, in a joint ruling, identify the *mishna's* case as referring not to someone who once knew of Shabbat and then forgot, but to someone who never knew at all. *Matnitin be-tinok shenishba le-vein ha-nochrim ve-ger shenitgayer le-vein ha-nochrim* — the *mishna* addresses either a Jew who was taken captive as an infant and raised among non-Jews, or a convert who converted in a non-Jewish environment and never had access to knowledge of Shabbat.

### Definitions

The *tinok shenishba* — the infant taken captive — never knew of their Jewish identity, let alone of Shabbat. The *ger shenitgayer bein ha-nochrim* — the convert who converted among non-Jews — presents a somewhat more complex case. A convert knows he or she is becoming Jewish, yet may have done so in circumstances where the full content of Jewish law was not transmitted. One might argue that a convert bears some residual responsibility to seek out that knowledge; nevertheless, the *gemara* treats this case alongside the *tinok shenishba* as the paradigm of "never knowing."

Rav and Shmuel maintain that even such a person, who bears no fault whatsoever, is obligated to bring one *chatat* upon learning of their Jewish identity and of all the violations they unknowingly committed.

### Tosafot Question

*Tosafot* raises a sharp question on the case of the *ger shenitgayer*. By law, a conversion requires a *beit din* of three — *bifnei gimel*. If there was a *beit din*, what do we mean that the person never knew about Shabbat? Is not informing a convert about the *mitzvos* a fundamental part of the conversion process?

*Tosafot* answers: *v'lo hodiu mitzvos Shabbat* — the *beit din* simply did not get around to mentioning Shabbat specifically among the *mitzvos* they conveyed. The *beit din* was present and functional; the oversight was theirs, not the convert's.

### Kabbalat Mitzvot Princip…

This leads *Tosafot* to articulate a significant principle about *geirut*: *bedi'avad*, the failure to inform a convert of the *mitzvos* does not invalidate the conversion. This is distinct from the requirement of *kabbalat mitzvot* — acceptance of the commandments — which must be present. But *kabbalat mitzvot* can function like signing a blank check, as it were: one accepts whatever the *mitzvos* are, even without knowing their precise content. *Na'aseh v'nishma* is the model. The *gemara* here, and a small number of related passages, thus forms a primary basis for the ruling that a conversion performed *bedi'avad* without a full enumeration of the *mitzvos* is nonetheless valid.

---

## Gemara Analysis

### Linguistic Challenge

The *gemara* now subjects the *mishna's* language to scrutiny. If the first case of the *mishna* — *hashocheiach ikar Shabbat* — describes someone who "forgot" the existence of Shabbat, doesn't the very word *shachach* (forgot) presuppose that the person once knew? Forgetting implies prior knowledge. This would seem to contradict Rav and Shmuel, who say the *mishna* addresses someone who never knew at all.

### Case Escalation

The *gemara* initially attempts to resolve this by proposing an escalating reinterpretation of the *mishna*. Perhaps every case in the *mishna* is actually describing the next, more severe level of fault: "forgot the existence of Shabbat" really means "never knew," "forgot which day was Shabbat" really means "knew the existence but forgot it entirely," and so on upward.

### Knew Then Forgot

Following this logic, if one knew the existence of Shabbat and then completely forgot about it — a case more severe than never knowing — then one would be liable not merely once but once per Shabbat, exactly as the *mishna's* second case specifies. The *gemara* thus attempts to show that Rav and Shmuel's position can be reconciled with the *mishna* by reading each clause of the *mishna* as referring to the next level up.

### Reinterpretation

The difficulty with this strategy becomes apparent when the *gemara* tries to apply it consistently. If we are reinterpreting each clause upward, then the third case — forgetting a particular *melacha* — should become: you forgot which day was Shabbat. But there is no further clause beyond the third to describe what happens when you know everything but forget the *melacha*. The chain of re-escalation breaks down. One cannot coherently re-read "forgot a *melacha*" as "forgot which day was Shabbat," since these are categorically different kinds of forgetting — one about Shabbat itself, one about its content. There is no natural way to complete the re-interpretation, and the *gemara* acknowledges the impasse.

### Rejection of Escalation

The *gemara* therefore rejects this entire reinterpretation strategy. *Matnitin ke-shita de-shachach kach* — the *mishna* is taken at face value in its simple reading. One who knew the existence of Shabbat and then forgot about it entirely is treated as a single, unitary error: one *chatat*, full stop. Rav and Shmuel do not claim that "knew and then forgot" becomes like "forgot each week." The *mishna* reads simply on that point.

### Final Position

What Rav and Shmuel are actually saying, now clarified, is a *chiddush* about the *tinok shenishba* case: *afilu tinok she-nishba bein ha-nochrim ve-ger she-nitgayer bein ha-nochrim, ke-hikro be-sof shachach dami ve-chayav* — even someone who never knew Shabbat at all is treated halachically as though they knew and forgot, and is obligated to bring one *chatat*. The *chiddush* is not about escalating liability but about extending liability to the completely blameless. Even total ignorance — not negligence, not carelessness, but complete absence of knowledge — nevertheless generates a single *chatat* offering.

---

## Exempt Position

### Yochanan & Lakish

Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish take the opposing position. Only where there is some degree of fault — where the person knew of Shabbat and subsequently forgot — can liability attach. But a *tinok shenishba* or a *ger shenitgayer* who truly never knew: *patur*, completely exempt, no *chatat* required.

### Korban Logic

This makes immediate intuitive sense. If someone grew up without any knowledge of their Jewish identity — never knew they were Jewish, never had any reason to observe Shabbat, bore no negligence whatsoever — on what basis would one obligate them to bring a sin offering? Clearly they are *onussim*, people acted upon by circumstance, in the fullest sense of the word.

Yet Rav and Shmuel's position is not as counterintuitive as it might appear, once one understands a broader conception of what a *chatat* accomplishes. The *gemara* in *Horayot* illuminates this with a telling parallel: if a *beit din* issues an erroneous ruling and the majority of *Klal Yisrael* follows it and sins in good faith, it is the *beit din* that brings a *korban*. But if fewer than a majority followed the ruling, each individual brings a *chatat* — even though they acted in perfect good faith on the authority of the highest legal body. The individual bears no moral fault; yet the *chatat* is theirs to bring. This suggests that the *chatat* is not solely a mechanism of guilt-processing. It also serves to repair a metaphysical rupture: something in the world was broken by the act, and the offering is the vehicle for restoring it. The person who did the act — however blameless — is the one whose offering effects the repair.

Similarly by *Yom Kippur*, the fundamental *avodah* of *Yom Ha-Kippurim* is described as *ve-chipper al ha-kodesh* — to purify the *Mikdash* itself — because sin, regardless of intent, is understood to impurify the sacred precincts. The *korban* addresses that rupture independent of the sinner's culpability.

This is Rav and Shmuel's conceptual foundation: even one who is entirely blameless performed the act, and the act generates an obligation.

### Horayot Parallel

The *Horayot* parallel clarifies why Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree. One might argue that in the *Horayot* case the individual was part of *Klal Yisrael* and acted as a member of the community responding to its legal authorities — a connection that generates at least some form of communal ownership of the act. A *tinok shenishba*, by contrast, had no connection to that community and no claim on its legal framework whatsoever. For Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, it is the total disconnection of the *tinok shenishba* that places him outside the scope of any *chatat* obligation.

### Rambam Ruling

Remarkably, the Rambam rules like Rav and Shmuel: a *tinok shenishba* who later learns of their Jewish identity brings one *chatat*. The Rambam describes this obligation as *ke-shogeg* — in the category of an inadvertent sinner — by which he appears to mean not that there is some element of negligence, but that the same legal category applies. What matters is not the presence of fault but the fact that one performed the act; the *chatat* obligation tracks the act, not the actor's moral state.

---

## Baraita Details

### Examples

A *baraita* now elaborates the position of the *mishna* in greater detail, providing concrete illustrations of the *tinok shenishba* case. The *baraita* opens identically to the *mishna* — *klal gadol amru ba-Shabbat* — and then specifies: the case of "forgetting the existence of Shabbat" is illustrated by *tinok shenishba le-vein ha-nochrim ve-ger shenitgayer bein ha-nochrim*, someone who spent their life among non-Jews and never knew of Shabbat. Such a person, upon learning of their situation, brings one *chatat* for all the Shabbat violations of their entire life.

### Multiple Categories

The *baraita* then extends this to other categories of prohibition. All the times such a person consumed blood — *achat*. All the violations of *chelev* — one *chatat*. All the acts of *avoda zara* — one *chatat*. The *baraita* is enumerating the thirty-six categories of sin for which a *chatat* is generally brought, and making clear that for each category, regardless of how many times the violation was repeated across a lifetime, the *tinok shenishba* brings one offering per category, not one per incident. The *chiddush* of the *mishna* about categories applies here as well.

### Munbaz Exemption

The *baraita* then introduces a dissenting opinion: *u-Munbaz poter* — Munbaz exempts entirely. A *tinok shenishba* or *ger shenitgayer* who never knew, according to Munbaz, owes nothing. The *baraita* notes that Munbaz articulated this position before Rabbi Akiva, suggesting that the debate between them is the very debate that underlies the disagreement between Rav and Shmuel on one side and Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the other.

---

## Akiva vs Munbaz

### Chotei Linking

Munbaz's argument is built on a verbal *heikesh*, a juxtaposition of terms. He observes that in one place the *Torah* uses the word *chotei* (sinner) to describe a *meizid* (intentional transgressor), and in another context uses the same word for a *shogeg* (inadvertent transgressor). He infers: *mah meizid hayta lo yedi'ah, af shogeg hayta lo yedi'ah* — just as by the *meizid* there is knowledge, so too by the *shogeg* there must be knowledge. A *shogeg* who never had any awareness that the act was prohibited cannot truly be called a *shogeg* and therefore incurs no *chatat* obligation.

### Akiva Response

Rabbi Akiva responds with a *kal va-chomer* that turns Munbaz's argument against itself. *Hareni mosif al devarecha* — let me extend your reasoning further. If you want to compare *shogeg* to *meizid* in terms of knowledge, consider that *meizid* possesses not just prior awareness but knowledge *be-sha'at ma'aseh* — at the very moment of transgression. Following your logic, a *shogeg* would likewise need to know *at the moment of the act* that he is violating. But that would make him a *meizid*. And by Munbaz's logic, even someone who knows while committing the act that it is forbidden could be called a *shogeg* and bring a *chatat*. Munbaz accepts this conclusion — *hen, ve-chol sheken she-osafta* — yes, and that is actually a valid point: there are circumstances where one acts knowing the act is forbidden and yet remains in the category of *shogeg*. This response, however, only deepens the problem; for Rabbi Akiva's interlocutor, a person who knows at the moment of transgression is not a *shogeg* at all but a *meizid*, and Munbaz's response — that one can know and still be *shogeg* — strikes the *tanna kamma* as untenable.

### Baraita Affirmed

The *gemara* then affirms that this *baraita* supports the position of Rav and Shmuel over Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. The *baraita* takes the *tinok shenishba* as the prime example of "forgetting the existence of Shabbat" and assigns that person a *chatat* — the position of Rabbi Akiva and the *tanna kamma*. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, however, align themselves with Munbaz — a *da'at yachid*, a minority opinion, and a relatively obscure one at that, set against the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Akiva. The *gemara* acknowledges the asymmetry: to go against Rabbi Akiva and the *tanna kamma* in favor of Munbaz is a significant choice, but Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish were persuaded that the logic of exempting the entirely unknowing was compelling.

---

## Knowledge Requirement

### Kares Principle

The *gemara* now clarifies the actual *derasha* through which the rabbis understand when a *chatat* is required, and why it differs from what Munbaz derived. The starting point is a general principle: a *chatat* is brought only for sins whose intentional commission is punishable by *kares*. This principle is learned from a juxtaposition in the *Torah* in the context of *avoda zara*.

### Juxtaposition

The *Torah* writes *Torah achas yihiyeh lachem la-oseh bi-shgaga* — one law for those who act in error — and then immediately juxtaposes this to *ve-ha-nefesh asher ta'aseh be-yad ramah... et Hashem hu megadef*, the case of one who acts presumptuously and thereby blaspheming God, a case that carries *kares*. This juxtaposition is between the *shogeg* who brings a *chatat* and the *meizid* who receives *kares*.

### Rabbinic Reading

Munbaz reads this juxtaposition as establishing a knowledge requirement: just as *meizid* implies prior awareness, so must *shogeg*. The *rabanan*, however, read it differently and more precisely. *Hukshu kulam le-avoda zara* — the entire framework of *chatat* is linked to the paradigm of *avoda zara*: *mah le-hallan davar she-chayavim al zedono kares u-veshigagaso chatat* — what characterizes the paradigm is that intentional commission brings *kares*, and inadvertent commission brings a *chatat*. From this the *rabanan* derive the universal rule: a *chatat* is owed only for a category of sin that, when done intentionally, carries *kares*. Shabbat violation is precisely such a sin.

What the juxtaposition teaches, on the rabbinic reading, is not that the *shogeg* must have had prior knowledge — it is that the relevant criterion for *chatat* liability is the severity of the sin, not the cognitive state of the sinner. Any sin carrying *kares* for the intentional violator generates a *chatat* for the inadvertent one, regardless of the degree of the violator's prior awareness.

---

## Modern Application

### Karaites

The preceding discussion concerned itself with the purely halachic question of whether a *tinok shenishba* brings a *chatat* offering — a question most directly relevant in the era of the *Beit Ha-Mikdash*. Yet the conceptual category of *tinok shenishba* has had a long and consequential afterlife in halachic discourse, particularly in the Rambam's thinking and its reception by later *poskim*.

The Rambam's engagement with *tinok shenishba* began in the context of the Karaites. In his earlier writings, the Rambam was sharply hostile to Karaites — suggesting they had no share in the *Olam Ha-Ba*, denying them the status of members of *Klal Yisrael* in meaningful senses. Later in his life, following more positive encounters with certain Karaite communities, the Rambam revised his tone significantly. He argued that one cannot hold Karaites responsible for their rejection of rabbinic tradition, because they were raised within that tradition and educated to believe that the Karaite interpretation was correct and the rabbinic one mistaken. They are therefore in the halachic position of a *tinok shenishba*: their errors are those of people who genuinely did not know otherwise, not of willful rebels.

### Shulchan Aruch

The *Beit Yosef* extended the Rambam's application of *tinok shenishba* further. In a range of practical halachic contexts where a *mechalel Shabbat* would ordinarily be subject to various exclusions and restrictions, the *Beit Yosef* and subsequently the *Shulchan Aruch* held that these sanctions do not apply to Karaites, precisely because their Shabbat violations flow from sincere — if mistaken — religious conviction formed through upbringing and education. They believe they are right and we are wrong; they are not rebels but *tinokei shenishbu*.

### Rav Kook

In the modern period, as large portions of the Jewish people moved away from traditional observance — often through the influence of secular ideologies and a broader societal context that had abandoned religious frameworks — Rav Kook and other later authorities extended the *tinok shenishba* category significantly. Rav Kook argued that the non-observant Jews of the modern era, even those raised in nominally traditional homes, are in a meaningful sense *tinokei shenishbu*, because the overwhelming influence of surrounding society effectively displaced the religious formation that would otherwise have taken hold.

### Inclusivity Tension

This extension of *tinok shenishba* is not without difficulty. It is, as the *gemara* itself illustrates, a category generated in the context of someone who genuinely had no access whatsoever to Jewish identity or knowledge. Extending it to individuals who have access to traditional Judaism but choose — based on upbringing, education, or the ambient culture — not to embrace it introduces a degree of tension. On one hand, the extension is inclusive and compassionate, refraining from categorizing vast numbers of Jews as deliberate rebels against Torah. On the other hand, it carries a patronizing dimension: it effectively says that even a person who has encountered traditional Judaism and consciously rejected it, or who maintains a different form of Jewish identity, is not truly making a free and informed choice — they are simply the product of forces they cannot see past.

The *gemara's* discussion, it should be noted, focuses on the narrow question of *chatat* liability. Interestingly, the Rambam rules like Rav and Shmuel that even a *tinok shenishba* brings a *chatat*, and yet the Rambam is the very authority invoked to extend leniency in other areas. The concept of *tinok shenishba* thus operates on two levels: as a halachic category for *korban* liability, and as a broader conceptual framework — *ke-onuss*, as the Rambam frames it — indicating that the person cannot be held to full moral accountability for conduct that flowed from circumstances entirely beyond their control. It is this second sense, the Rambam's use of *tinok shenishba* as an expression of *ones*, that has proven most consequential for contemporary halachic discourse.

---

---

# Shabbat 69

## Tinok Shenishba

### Munbaz Intro

The daf begins at the *ela Munbaz* passage, six lines down. To situate the discussion: there is a debate between Abaye, Rava, and Shmuel on one side and Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the other regarding a *tinok shenishba* — someone who never knew they were Jewish — who violates *Shabbat*. Rava and Shmuel hold that such a person must still bring one *korban* for all violations. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish hold that no *korban* is brought at all, since there is no fault and no guilt. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's position is, in a sense, the intuitive one — there is simply no culpability. Rava and Shmuel appear to operate from the premise that a *korban* is not exclusively a mechanism of personal guilt but functions to cleanse the very existence of the sin; accordingly, even a faultless actor must bring it. In the end, the *Rambam* rules in accordance with Rava and Shmuel.

This broader debate is paralleled by a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Munbaz regarding the *tinok shenishba*. Rabbi Akiva pressed Munbaz with a *reductio ad absurdum*: Munbaz's position seemed to require that just as the *meizid* — the willful violator — possesses knowledge and awareness, so too the *shogeg* must have had some initial awareness. Rabbi Akiva pushed the argument to its logical extreme and said: if that is your principle, then make it fully like a *meizid* and require awareness even at the moment of committing the sin. And Munbaz simply accepted this, saying: yes, why not?

### Munbaz Position

This acceptance generates the *Gemara*'s question: *v'leMunbaz shegaga b'mai* — according to Munbaz, where exactly is the error? If Munbaz includes within the obligation of a *korban chatat* even someone who is fully aware of the prohibition at the time of the sin, what constitutes the element of *shegaga* — of mistake — that distinguishes this from an outright *meizid*?

The *Gemara* answers: *kegon sheshagag b'korban* — the error lies in the *korban* itself. He knew he was prohibited; he knew the act was punishable by *karet* or *mitah* in a court with witnesses. But he did not know that this was the type of sin that incurs an obligation to bring a *korban*. And that, according to Munbaz, is sufficient error to classify him as a *shogeg* and obligate him to bring the *korban*.

This is admittedly a somewhat circular position. The only reason he is considered a *shogeg* vis-à-vis the *korban* is precisely because Munbaz rules that such a case counts as *shogeg* and thus obligates a *korban*. Perhaps more charitably, it simply means that he lacked awareness that this category of sin comes with a *korban* attached, and that degree of ignorance — limited as it is — is sufficient for the *korban* obligation. It is a notably extreme and expansive position regarding how much awareness one can possess and still be eligible to bring a *korban*.

### Rabbanan Shogeg

The *Gemara* now turns to the mainstream position — the *rabbanan* — and asks: *verabbanan shegaga b'mai*? In an ordinary case where one brings a *korban*, what must the person have been unaware of?

In general, there are two paradigmatic forms of *shegaga*. In the case of, say, eating forbidden fat: either one does not know that *chelev* is prohibited in principle, or one knows the prohibition but is mistaken about the facts — one thought this piece of meat was a steak and did not realize it was *chelev*. There is an error in law and an error in fact; these are the two classic types of *shogeg*. By *Shabbat* there is an analogous structure: one either does not know that this *melacha* is forbidden, or one forgot that today is *Shabbat* — which is analogous to the factual error, like mistaking *chelev* for steak.

But the *Gemara* now probes whether there are additional scenarios of error that still qualify as *shogeg* sufficient to obligate a *korban*. And the *Gemara* is clear that for the *rabbanan*, an error limited to the *korban* alone — *shegagat korban lo shema shegaga* — is not a real error. If one is aware of everything else, aware that the act is prohibited, aware that it is punishable by *karet* or worse, there is ample reason not to commit the act. Being unaware of one minor subsidiary consequence does not render the willful violation anything less than willful.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan's position is striking: *keivan sheshagag b'karet af al pi sheheizid b'lav* — once one has erred regarding the *karet*, even though one was deliberate in violating the *lav*, a *korban* may be brought.

This is a remarkable idea. One can know that what one is doing is biblically prohibited — that it violates a negative commandment — yet if one does not know that it is punishable by *karet*, one may still bring a *korban*. The reasoning, as will emerge, is that a *korban* is only brought for prohibitions punishable by *karet*; there are only thirty-six such sins. If someone knows they are transgressing a *lav* but genuinely believes it is no more severe than an ordinary prohibition — thinking, for example, that eating *chametz* on *Pesach* is no worse than eating *chazir* or *neveilah* — then according to Rabbi Yochanan, such a person brings a *korban*. Not knowing how weighty the sin was, not knowing it was deserving of *karet*, is sufficient. One was intentional in the act, but not with full awareness of its gravity, and that partial ignorance is enough to render the act atone-able and the person eligible for a *korban*.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish says what one would expect from the normative logic of *shogeg*: one must be fully in error. To bring a *korban*, one must think that what one is doing is permitted. One must err both regarding the prohibition itself and regarding the *karet*. If one knows that what one is doing constitutes a violation of a biblical prohibition, one cannot be called a *shogeg* for purposes of the *korban* — regardless of whether one knew about the *karet* or not.

That said, there is a nuance even within Reish Lakish's position. Take *Shabbat*: *Shabbat* carries both a positive commandment — *tishbos*, to rest — and a negative prohibition, *lo ta'aseh melacha*. Someone raised, say, in a non-Jewish household who was taught to think of *Shabbat* as a day of rest — a positive obligation — but never understood it as a punishable prohibition, would know they are supposed to rest but not know they are violating a *lav*. For Reish Lakish, that would still constitute sufficient *shegaga*. Even Reish Lakish does not require one to think the act is completely neutral. What he requires is that one not know it constitutes a violation of a negative prohibition. So long as one lacks awareness of the *lav*, one may still bring a *korban* even according to the stricter view.

The *Gemara* notes, and rules, that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yochanan — a position that is, in its way, quite generous: even someone who knowingly violates a prohibition but is unaware of its gravity is considered enough in error, and enough outside the category of a fully willful sinner, to be entitled to bring a *korban* of atonement.

One might also note that for Reish Lakish, there may be a gap: a person who knows the prohibition but not the *karet* cannot bring a *korban* since Reish Lakish requires full ignorance of the *lav*, yet it is unclear whether such a person would receive *karet* either — since intuitively *karet* picks up where the *korban* ends. The *Gemara* does not explore this question directly.

### Scriptural Source

The *Gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama de'Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish* — what is Reish Lakish's scriptural basis? The verse states: *asher lo te'asena ve'ashem* — "that should not be done, and one has sinned." The *Gemara* derives: *ad she'yishgog b'lav ve'karet she'bah* — only in a case where one erred in the *lo ta'aseh*, where one did not know the act was prohibited, does one bring a *korban*.

How does Rabbi Yochanan handle this verse, which seems to anchor the error specifically in the prohibition itself? He needs it for another purpose — for what is taught in a *baraita*: the phrase *me'am ha'aretz*, "from among the people of the land," in the relevant passage comes to exclude a *mumar* — an apostate who has fundamentally rejected the entire system — from bringing a *korban*. Now, one might wonder: obviously a *mumar* cannot bring a *korban*, since they are acting as a *meizid*. But the *Gemara* constructs a case: the *mumar* today happens to eat what he thinks is a steak, not knowing it is *chelev*. Today's act, considered in isolation, was accidental. Even so, since this person is a *mumar* — prepared to sin willfully — even if they later do *teshuva*, they cannot bring a *korban* for that act. The verse *me'am ha'aretz* categorically excludes the *mumar*.

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, speaking in the name of Rabbi Shimon, derives the same point differently — not from *me'am ha'aretz* but from the phrase *asher lo te'asena ve'ashem* itself, and specifically from a positive formulation: *hashav mi'yediato mevi korban al shigagaso* — one brings a *korban* only if, had they been made aware, they would have refrained. *Lo shav mi'yediato eino mevi korban al shigagaso* — if even with full knowledge they would have gone ahead and done it, no *korban* is brought. In the *mumar* case, even if the act today was technically accidental, since this person was prepared to sin willfully, we cannot say they would have stopped had they known. Therefore, no *korban*.

The two derivations arrive at a very similar conclusion. One approaches it categorically — the person is labeled a *mumar* and excluded as a type. The other focuses on the specific act — asking whether *this* act is the kind for which, had awareness been present, the person would have desisted. There is a *Gemara* elsewhere that attempts to find a case where these two approaches would diverge, but in practice they converge on the same principle: a *korban* is only brought when the person, had they known, would not have sinned.

### Tosafot Challenge

Tosafot raises the obvious question: once we accept the condition of *shav mi'yediato* — that one would have refrained had one known — we must examine how Rabbi Yochanan satisfies this condition in the case where one *does* know the prohibition but not the *karet*.

Rabbi Yochanan must be saying two things simultaneously. First, not knowing the *karet* is enough to prevent one from being categorized as a fully willful sinner — it is a sufficient degree of error to entitle the person to bring a *korban*. Second — and this is what Tosafot highlights — we must also assume that this same person, had they been told the full severity, would indeed have refrained. That is, even though one was willfully transgressing a *lav*, one must have been doing so with the implicit assumption that it was a relatively minor infraction. Had one known it was deserving of *karet*, one would have stopped. The very fact that one was unaware of the severity provides the basis for saying: yes, this person fits the *shav mi'yediato* criterion, because it was the ignorance of the gravity that made the difference.

This is admittedly demanding as an argument. It is worth noting the further tension that arises with Munbaz's position in relation to *shav mi'yediato*: if the only error is regarding the *korban* itself — one knew it was prohibited, knew it was punishable by *karet*, but simply did not know that a *korban* was also involved — it is genuinely difficult to understand how that satisfies the *shav mi'yediato* standard. Can one seriously argue that awareness of the additional consequence of a *korban* would have made the decisive difference? This is a real question, and the *Gemara* does not resolve it explicitly.

The *Gemara* subsequently uses the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish to analyze a *mishnah* concerning the 39 *melachot*. The *mishnah* states that the *avot melachot* are forty minus one. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the number is stated to teach that if one forgot that each category was forbidden — while knowing it was *Shabbat* — one could in principle bring up to 39 *chatat* offerings. Each *melacha* category constitutes a distinct *aveirah*, unlike, say, eating multiple pieces of *chametz* on *Pesach*, which is a single *aveirah* repeated.

The *Gemara* then asks: how can one know it is *Shabbat* if one thinks all 39 *melachot* are permitted? According to Rabbi Yochanan, the answer is clear: one could know that all 39 categories are prohibited at the level of a *lav* without knowing they are punishable by *karet* — so one still "knows it is *Shabbat*" in the relevant sense. But according to Reish Lakish, who requires full ignorance of the *lav*, how can one know it is *Shabbat* at all while believing all these activities are permissible?

The *Gemara* answers: *v'yada lei b'tchumin v'aliba d'Rebbe Akiva* — one can know it is *Shabbat* through the prohibition of *tchumin*, the Shabbat boundaries. Rashi cites a *Gemara* in Sotah where Rabbi Akiva holds that *tchumin* are a biblical prohibition — *lo seitzei ish mimkomo* means one may not leave the city limits, and this is not merely *asmachta* but a genuine biblical *lav*, yet it does not carry *karet*. So one could know it is *Shabbat* because of the *tchumin* prohibition while believing all the *melachot* to be permissible.

Tosafot raises two additional possibilities that the *Gemara* might have offered: first, one could know it is *Shabbat* through the *mitzvas asei* of *tishbos* — the positive commandment to rest — which implies that certain activities are to be avoided, without one knowing that those activities are prohibited with a *lav*. Second — and this is flagged as a strong question by Tosafot Yeshanim — one could know that a *general category* of *melacha* is forbidden while not knowing that the specific act one performed fell into that category. For instance, one could know that planting is forbidden while not knowing that watering plants is also prohibited. Tosafot does not find a fully satisfying answer to why the *Gemara* preferred the *tchumin* explanation over these alternatives.

The *Gemara* following this passage also addresses the concept of *tinok shenishba* in a broader cultural and halachic context. Beyond the narrow question of whether a *korban* is brought, the idea of a *tinok shenishba* — someone who, due to their upbringing, cannot be held accountable for failing to observe the law — becomes a powerful concept of inclusion. The Rambam used it as a basis for a more forgiving approach toward the Karaites. The *Beit Yosef*, author of the *Shulchan Aruch*, followed suit. And in the post-Enlightenment era, with the vast majority of Jews raised in communities that do not consider themselves obligated in *halacha*, the category provides a framework for understanding diminished culpability. One must note, however, that the concept carries an inherent tension: it is, in a sense, patronizing — it achieves inclusion precisely by declaring that a person cannot be held responsible for their own beliefs. Still, as a concept addressing how far awareness and accountability can be expected to reach, *tinok shenishba* remains among the most consequential ideas in *halachic* thought.

---

## Karet vs Korban

### Abaye Shvuat

Abaye now introduces a statement about *shvuat bituy* — the *korban* brought for making a false oath. The *Torah* creates a special *korban oleh v'yored* for one who swears falsely: either about the past (swearing one did or did not do something when the reverse is true) or about the future (swearing one will or will not do something and then violating the oath). This is a *korban* that applies even though *shvuat bituy* is not punishable by *karet* — it is a *lav* without *karet*. Abaye states: *hakol modim b'shvuat bituy she'ein chayavin aleha korban ad sheyishgog b'lav shebah* — everyone agrees that for a false oath one is not obligated in a *korban* unless the error was about the *lav* itself. An error only regarding the *karet* — which in any case does not exist here — is insufficient.

### Karet Gap

The *Gemara* interjects: *peshita* — isn't this obvious? Of course Rabbi Yochanan would agree here. When Rabbi Yochanan says an error regarding the *karet* suffices, he means in cases where there *is* a *karet* to err about. Here, with *shvuat bituy*, there is no *karet* at all, so there is nothing to make an error about except the prohibition itself. What else could the *shegaga* consist of?

### Karet Specific

The *Gemara* responds: no, it is not so obvious. One might have thought — *ho'il v'chiyuv korban chiddush hu* — since the very existence of a *korban* for a false oath is itself a *chiddush*. In the entire *Torah*, we do not find a simple prohibition without *karet* that incurs a *korban chatat* — a *korban* is normally the consequence of *karet*-level sins. Yet here, the *Torah* demands a *korban* even for a *lav* without *karet*. I might have thought that Rabbi Yochanan, precisely because the *Torah* is so demanding in requiring a *korban* in this case, would shift his position and allow even an error regarding the *korban* itself to suffice — effectively adopting Munbaz's position for this exceptional case. *Kama shema lan* that he does not. Rabbi Yochanan remains consistent: outside of Munbaz, no one holds that an error solely about the *korban* constitutes sufficient *shegaga*. Even in this case, Rabbi Yochanan maintains that one must err about the *lav*.

### Shvuat Cases

The *Gemara* now challenges with a *baraita*: *eizo hi shegagat shvuat bituy l'shavar* — what constitutes a *shegaga* in the case of a false oath about the past? The most intuitive answer would be: one forgot — one swore one had not eaten the apple, genuinely believing it to be true, when in fact one had. But the *Gemara* notes that in such a case, where at the moment of the oath one genuinely believes one is swearing truthfully, this is actually closer to *ones* — compelled sin, or at minimum not a false oath in any meaningful sense. The nature of an oath is such that a factual error in one's sincere belief does not constitute a transgression. 

So what does a *shegaga* in *shvuat bituy* look like? The *baraita* provides: *yodea ani sheshvua asura, aval eini yodea im chayav b'korban o lo* — I know that swearing falsely is prohibited, but I did not know one becomes obligated in a *korban* for it. And the *baraita* says one is *chayav*. This seems to vindicate Munbaz — error regarding only the *korban* suffices! The *Gemara* responds: *ha mani Munbaz hee* — this *baraita* follows Munbaz. It does not represent the normative position. According to the *rabbanan* and Rabbi Yochanan, one must genuinely think the act is permitted, or — in cases involving *karet* — not know of the *karet*; and in cases of *shvuat bituy* where there is no *karet*, one must genuinely believe the false oath is permissible.

### Terumah Abaye

Abaye now states a parallel rule regarding *terumah*: *hakol modim b'terumah she'ein chayav aleha chomesh ad sheyishgog b'lav shebah* — everyone agrees that regarding *terumah*, one is not obligated in the *chomesh* until one has erred about the prohibition itself. The background: if a non-*kohen* eats *terumah* accidentally, he must return what he ate and add a *chomesh* — one fifth — which itself becomes *terumah*. The question is what constitutes *shogeg* here.

The easy case of *shogeg* is always a factual error — one did not know this food was *terumah*. The more complex question is the legal-error case. *Terumah* is not punishable by *karet*; it is punishable by *mita b'yedei shamayim* — heavenly death — which sounds more severe but appears to occupy a lower rung in the *halachic* hierarchy than *karet*.

Abaye says everyone agrees — meaning even Rabbi Yochanan — that one must err about the *lav* itself. The *Gemara* asks: is this not obvious? Rabbi Yochanan only allows an error about *karet* to suffice when *karet* is present. Here there is no *karet*, only *mita b'yedei shamayim*, so of course Rabbi Yochanan would require an error in the prohibition. The *Gemara* responds: not so obvious — one might have thought that *mita b'yedei shamayim* stands in the place of *karet* here, and that erring about the *mita* would similarly suffice as *shegaga*. Abaye teaches us that this is not the case.

### Rava Terumah

Rava disagrees with Abaye. Rava says: *mita b'makom karet omedet, v'chomesh b'makom korban ka'i* — *mita b'yedei shamayim* stands in the place of *karet*, and *chomesh* stands in the place of a *korban*. The structure is mutatis mutandis. Just as by the *korban* the *karet* is the key constituent — the *korban* is the mechanism of atonement for a *karet*-level sin, and erring about the *karet* is sufficient *shegaga* — so too here, the *chomesh* is the mechanism of consequence for a sin involving *mita b'yedei shamayim*, and erring about the *mita* is likewise sufficient.

Rava's formulation is revealing. He does not argue that *mita b'yedei shamayim* is so weighty that awareness of it would surely have deterred the person — which would be one way to ground the *shav mi'yediato* argument. Rather, Rava says something more technically precise: *mita* does for *chomesh* exactly what *karet* does for *korban*. The relationship is structural. The *mita* is the constituent element upon which the *chomesh* obligation hinges, just as *karet* is the constituent element upon which the *korban* obligation hinges. The error must occur precisely regarding that constituent element, whatever it happens to be in a given framework. This framing actually illuminates the underlying logic of Rabbi Yochanan's position more clearly: it is not merely about the subjective gravity of the sin in the person's mind, but about the technical relationship between the severity-marker (*karet* or *mita*) and the consequence-mechanism (*korban* or *chomesh*).

The rule of the *Gemara* in practice follows Rabbi Yochanan — and this is in a sense a deeply forgiving ruling, for it means that someone who knew they were violating a prohibition yet simply did not appreciate that it rose to the level of *karet* is treated as sufficiently non-willful to be entitled to bring a *korban*.

---

## Lost in Wilderness

### Lost Setup

The *Gemara* now turns to a very different and more accessible case: what if someone has literally lost track of which day of the week it is? This is not a hypothetical — one could become lost in the wilderness and lose track of the days entirely. What must such a person do regarding *Shabbat*?

### Six vs One

Rav Huna says: *moneh shisha yamim umeshamer yom echad* — one counts six days and then observes the seventh. That is, the first day one becomes aware of the disorientation is treated as the equivalent of Sunday; one counts forward, and the seventh day is kept as *Shabbat*.

Chiyya bar Rav says the opposite: *meshamer yom echad umoneh shisha* — one starts by observing one day immediately (treating the next full day as *Shabbat*), and then counts six days after it. This position is explained by Rashi as analogous to *Adam HaRishon*, who was created in the middle of the week, found himself in the middle without a clear starting point, and yet observed the *Shabbat* that followed his first full day of existence.

The *Gemara* asks: *b'mai kamiflagi* — what is the underlying dispute? One holds *kevriyaso shel olam*: we follow the pattern of creation — six days of work, then *Shabbat*. The other holds *ke-Adam HaRishon*: since one finds oneself in the middle without knowing which day it is, one is like *Adam HaRishon*, and the immediate next day becomes *Shabbat*.

From a religious and experiential standpoint, the six-then-one approach seems more natural — building toward *Shabbat* rather than beginning with it. But the *Gemara* proceeds to a *baraita*: *meshamer yom echad leshisha* — one observes one day for six. This language suggests the six have already passed, implying one counts six and then keeps the seventh — a *tiyuvta* against Chiyya bar Rav. The *Gemara* confirms: *tiyuvta deChiyya Bar Rav tiyuvta*.

### Rava Solution

The more pressing question remains: how can one do *melacha* on any of the six days, given that each of those days is a *safek Shabbat* — a doubt about whether it might be *Shabbat*? Each carries a *safek* of a biblical prohibition.

Rava answers: *bechol yom v'yom oseh lo k'dei parnasato* — every single day one does only the minimum amount of work necessary for survival. And on the one day designated as *Shabbat*, one does no *melacha* at all. The *Gemara* pushes back: *v'hahu yoma leimus* — will one then starve on that day? Rava responds: one does slightly extra work on the day *before* the designated *Shabbat*, so as to have food ready for the following day — analogous to the double portion of *man* collected on *erev Shabbat* in the wilderness.

But then the *Gemara* asks: perhaps today is itself already *Shabbat*, and doing two days' worth of work today is not justified by *pikuach nefesh* — one can survive today on one day's minimum, and tomorrow's needs can be addressed tomorrow with *pikuach nefesh* as justification then. The *Gemara* concedes the point. The revised answer: every day, including the designated *Shabbat*, one does only the minimum work necessary for that day's survival. One never does extra. *Pikuach nefesh* permits only what is required for immediate survival.

What then distinguishes the designated *Shabbat* day from the others? *Bekidusha v'avdalta* — one makes *Kiddush* and *Havdalah*. Even verbally, even without wine or *besamim*, one sets the day apart and demarcates its beginning and end. This preserves the qualitative distinctiveness of *Shabbat* even when the practical content of the day — the minimum work for survival — is the same as any other.

### Partial Knowledge

Rava then addresses the case where one has partial knowledge that allows elimination of certain days. *Im haya makir miktzat hayom sheyatza bo* — if one knows something about the day one departed, one may do as much *melacha* as desired on the day that is thereby eliminated from suspicion.

Rashi explains the case as follows: one knows that one has been traveling for three days. One has forgotten which day of the week one departed, but one knows the number of days elapsed. This means one can identify that whichever day of the week corresponds to the departure day was not *Shabbat* — since one cannot depart on *Shabbat*. That day of the week, recurring each week, is entirely free of the *Shabbat* concern and one may labor freely on it: *oseh melacha kol hayom kulo*.

The *Gemara* asks: is this not obvious? One might have thought that in addition to knowing one did not leave on *Shabbat*, one could also assume one did not leave on a Friday — who goes traveling on *erev Shabbat*? If so, perhaps two days per week could be eliminated. The *Gemara* rejects this: *zimnin d'meshkach shayarta umakrei v'nafik* — sometimes a caravan presents itself and one departs opportunistically, even on a Friday. But one will never knowingly depart on *Shabbat* itself. Therefore only the one day corresponding to one's departure is eliminated with certainty.

### Tosafot Walking

Tosafot raises an additional dimension: what about walking? *Aval l'haleich yachol kol mah sheyirtzeh* — one may walk as much as one wishes each day, including on the designated *Shabbat*, without concern for *tchumin*. Why? Because if one cannot walk, *lo yagia l'olam l'yishuv* — one will never reach civilization. Furthermore, even on the day designated as *Shabbat*, one may continue traveling, since the purpose is to get back to civilization — an ongoing *pikuach nefesh* consideration.

This raises a broader point worth noting. The *Gemara*'s framework imagines that one does just enough each day to survive today. But reality is often more complex: the work done today — carrying food and supplies, for instance — may not be serving an immediate need but rather preventing a future *pikuach nefesh*. Carrying one's canteen today does not save one's life today (one can drink without carrying); it saves one's life several days from now. The answer is that all such activity falls within the broad category of *pikuach nefesh*: if one does not carry and prepare, one will eventually run out of food and die before reaching civilization. This parallels a case where a doctor must travel on *Shabbat* to reach a patient whose life-threatening condition will materialize on Sunday — the *pikuach nefesh* is future-oriented, but the *Shabbat* violation to address it is permitted now. Tosafot alludes to this when addressing the walking question.

---

## Multiple Shabbatot

### One vs Many

The *Gemara* concludes with the question of how many *korbanot* one brings when one violates multiple *Shabbatot*. The principle has already been stated: if one forgot that *Shabbat* exists altogether — *shikhach ikar Shabbat* — one brings only a single *korban* for all violations across all weeks. But if one knew that *Shabbat* exists and forgot which day it was — *yodeia ikar Shabbat* — one brings a separate *korban* for each *Shabbat* that was violated. The question is: from where do we derive this distinction?

### Two Verses

Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuha, says there are two *pesukim*. The first: *veshamru venei Yisrael et haShabbat* — the children of Israel shall observe *the Shabbat*, in the singular. The second: *ve'et Shabbetotai tishmoru* — my *Shabbatot*, in the plural, you shall observe.

The derivation: *veshamru venei Yisrael et haShabbat* — one observance for many *Shabbatot*. This teaches that in certain circumstances all the *Shabbatot* are treated as a single unit, generating only one *korban*. *Ve'et Shabbetotai tishmoru* — each *Shabbat* is treated separately. This teaches that in other circumstances each *Shabbat* is independently significant and requires its own *korban*. As Rashi puts it: *lo masar katuv ela lachachamim* — the *Torah* left the interpretive assignment to the Sages, who applied the singular verse to the case of forgetting the existence of *Shabbat* entirely and the plural verse to the case of forgetting which day it was.

### Rabbi Yitzhak

Rabbi Yitzhak objects — not to the conclusion but to the assignment: *adaraba ipkha mistabra* — on the contrary, the verses should be understood in the opposite way. *Veshamru venei Yisrael et haShabbat* — "the Shabbat" in the singular — should mean: one observance for each individual *Shabbat*, treating each *Shabbat* as a separate unit. Therefore, each separately violated *Shabbat* incurs its own *korban*. And *ve'et Shabbetotai tishmoru* — "my *Shabbatot*" in the plural — should mean: one observance covering many *Shabbatot*, so that forgetting about *Shabbat* entirely is treated as one global lapse, generating only a single *korban*.

The result is identical to Rav Nachman's: forgetting the existence of *Shabbat* yields one *korban*, forgetting which day is *Shabbat* yields one *korban* per *Shabbat* violated. The only difference between Rabbi Yitzhak and Rav Nachman is which verse is assigned to which case. Both readings are equally valid derivations — the *Torah* provides two verses, one evoking singularity and one evoking plurality, and the Sages interpret them to capture both halachic realities. The *Gemara* will continue tomorrow with the question of forgetting about individual *melachot*.

---

---

# Shabbat 70

## Forgetting Shabbat vs Me…

### Rav Safra's Explanation

The *gemara* opens *daf ayin* with a deceptively simple question: *mai shna reisha u'mai shna seifa* — what is the distinction between the first case of the *mishna* and the latter? In the opening case, one who forgot that it was *shabbat* brings a single *korban* regardless of how many *melachot* he performed; in the latter case, one who forgot the individual *melachot* brings a separate *korban* for each category violated. The difference seems self-evident, yet the *gemara* proceeds to articulate it with precision.

Rav Safra states: *kan yedi'at Shabbat hu poresh v'kan yedi'at melacha hu poresh* — in one case it is knowledge of *shabbat* that would have caused him to desist, and in the other it is knowledge of the *melacha*. The logic is straightforward: if the person had been told "it is *shabbat*," he would have stopped everything he was doing, because his single error was forgetting that the day was *shabbat*. All the various *melachot* he performed flow from that one mistake. In the second case, however, had he been reminded that a particular act was a *melacha*, he would have stopped only that act — and each separate *melacha* would have required its own reminder, its own correction, and therefore constitutes its own category of error.

### Rav Nachman's Challenge

Rav Nachman challenges this formulation, raising what initially appears to be a compelling objection: *klum poresh miShabbat ela mishum melachot?* — when one stops because he is told it is *shabbat*, does he not also stop because he now recognizes the act as a *melacha*? The two pieces of knowledge — that it is *shabbat* and that the act is forbidden — operate together in every case. Likewise, *v'klum poresh mi'melacha ela mishum Shabbat?* — when told his act is a *melacha*, he stops because both the identity of the day and the forbidden nature of the act are now clear to him.

His point seems to be that in both scenarios the person ultimately needs both pieces of information to desist, so how can Rav Safra's distinction hold?

Rav Nachman then offers his own formulation. The *korban* is brought *al shgaga* — on account of an error. *Hatam chada shgaga*: when one forgets it is *shabbat*, he has made a single error. *Hacha tuvah shgagot havinan*: when one forgets individual *melachot*, he has made multiple distinct errors — one about cooking, one about planting, and so on.

### Common Ground Between Vi…

On reflection, the two positions are expressing essentially the same point through slightly different language. Both agree that forgetting *shabbat* constitutes one mistake and forgetting individual *melachot* constitutes multiple mistakes. One framing emphasizes what would have caused the person to desist; the other emphasizes the number of distinct errors made. The practical significance of this subtle difference in articulation will become clearer later in the *daf*, where the case of forgetting *both* *shabbat* and the *melachot* simultaneously forces us to confront precisely how we define and count the nature of one's error.

---

## Chiluk Melachot - Source

### Question on Chiluk Melac…

The *gemara* then moves to a foundational question: *chiluk melachot minalan* — from where do we derive the principle that separate *melachot* generate separate *korbanot* altogether? This requires a source, because the assumption otherwise might be that all violations of *shabbat* constitute a single prohibition — much as there is one *lav* of *shabbat* — and therefore one *korban* regardless of how many categories were violated.

### Pesach Analogy

The force of this question is illustrated by analogy. Consider a person who, throughout the day of *Pesach*, forgets entirely that it is *Pesach* and eats bread, then pasta, then cookies. How many *chataot* does he bring? One — because it is a single sin. He violated one prohibition (*lo tochal chametz*) multiple times without any intervening moment of awareness that would divide the acts into separate obligations.

The same logic would seem to apply to *shabbat*: there is one prohibition of *melacha*, and even though we identify thirty-nine categories, perhaps they are all one large category of *chilul Shabbat*. Why should violating *katzir* and then *bishul* in a single state of forgetfulness be any different from eating bread and then pasta on *Pesach* — still just one *korban* for one prohibition? This is precisely the question the *gemara* is pressing: what gives the thirty-nine *melachot* the status of conceptually separate types of *chilul Shabbat*, each generating independent liability?

### Shmuel's Derivation

Shmuel answers: *amar kra*, the *pasuk* states *mechaleleha mos yumas* — those who desecrate it shall surely be put to death.
