The double language of *mos yumas* suggests, in Shmuel's reading, that the *Torah* has expressed a multiplicity of deaths for violations of *shabbat*, implying that a single act of *chilul Shabbat* can carry manifold liability. Since obviously a person cannot die more than once, this doubling cannot be referring to the *mezid* case — and indeed, *Tosafot* adds that the verse *kol ose melacha yumas* already establishes death for willful violation. The principle of *im eino inyan lemezid tenehu inyan leshogeg* therefore redirects this doubling to the inadvertent case, teaching that there can be multiple *korbanos* for a single period of *shabbat* — one for each *melacha* category violated.

The *gemara* clarifies that when speaking of the *shogeg* case, *yumas bemamon* — "death" is understood as monetary cost, that is, the obligation to bring a *korban*. Playful as that phrase sounds, it captures the *gemara*'s point precisely.

### Gemara Questions Shmuel

The *gemara* presses Shmuel: why resort to this derivation from *mechaleleha mos yumas* when there is a much more elegant Tannaitic source? *V'teipokei chiluk melachos meheicha d'nafka lei l'Rabbi Noson* — why not learn it out from where Rabbi Natan derived it?

---

## Rabbi Natan - Fire as Pa…

### Fire as Specific Melacha

The *braisa* records Rabbi Natan's position: *lo tiva'aru eish bechol moshvoseichem beyom haShabbos* — you shall not kindle fire in any of your dwelling places on *shabbat*. This is the one act of *melacha* that the *Torah* singles out by name in the context of *shabbat* prohibition. The question Rabbi Natan asks is: *mah talmud lomar* — what is the point of specifying fire? We already know fire is one of the thirty-nine *melachot*. Why does the *Torah* need to articulate it separately?

### Eileh Hadvarim - 39 Cate…

To understand Rabbi Natan's answer, the *gemara* traces the derivation of the thirty-nine categories themselves. The *Torah* prefaces the *shabbat* laws in *Vayakhel* with the phrase *eileh hadvarim* — these are the things. The *gemara* derives thirty-nine from this formulation: *dvarim*, *hadvarim*, *eileh hadvarim* — the word *dvarim* in its plural form combined with the *heh* of *hadvarim* and the *gematria* of *eileh* (36) yields thirty-nine. It is worth noting that Rav Yoel Bin-Nun proposed an alternative reading: rather than relying on *gematria*, he observed that if one counts the distinct items listed in the accounts of the *Mishkan* in *Vayakhel* and *Pikudei*, one arrives at precisely thirty-nine. In his reading, the *Torah* is indicating that the activities involved in building the *Mishkan* define the categories of *melacha*, and the phrase *eileh hadvarim* — these are the things — makes that explicit.

Either way, the number thirty-nine is established. What is *not* yet established from this derivation is that violating multiple categories generates multiple *korbanos*. Knowing there are thirty-nine forbidden acts does not by itself tell us that they function as thirty-nine independent prohibitions for purposes of *korban* liability.

### Davar Shehaya Baklal

This is where fire enters. The principle invoked here is *davar shehayah baklal v'yatza min haklal lilamed* — a law that was part of a general category and was singled out from that category was not singled out merely to teach something about itself alone, but to teach something about the entire category. Fire was already included among the thirty-nine. The *Torah* chose to single it out and state an explicit prohibition. That singling-out teaches us two things about fire: that it is an *av melacha*, one of the thirty-nine chief categories, and *v'chayavin aleha bifne atzma* — that one bears separate liability for it as a distinct act. And since this is established for fire through the principle of *davar shehayah baklal*, it applies to every one of the thirty-nine: *af kol she'hu av melacha chayavin alav bifne atzmo* — for any *av melacha*, one bears separate liability.

The logic thus proceeds in stages. First, we establish thirty-nine categories from *eileh hadvarim*. Second, we establish that violating even one of them — not necessarily all thirty-nine — already constitutes a violation of *shabbat*, which we learn from the verse *b'charish uv'katzir tishbot*, where the *Torah* specifically names *charish* (plowing) and *katzir* (harvesting). Third, we now ask: if one violates multiple categories, does that generate multiple *korbanos*, or is it still just one? And for that, we invoke the singling-out of fire — each category is conceptually distinct and independently liable.

### Charish and Katzir Objec…

An obvious question arises: if *charish* and *katzir* are also singled out, why couldn't we have derived *chiluk melachot* from them, without needing fire at all?

Rashi offers two answers. First, *charish* and *katzir* are prohibited through a positive commandment — *b'charish uv'katzir tishbot* is a *mitzvas aseh* (you shall rest), not a *lav*. A positive obligation to rest does not generate *korban* liability the same way a *lav* does; one cannot use it as a paradigm for separate *korban* liability. Second, there is a general principle that where the *Torah* singles out two items rather than one — *shnei ketuvim* — we do not derive a general rule from them; they are treated as exceptions. Rashi prefers this second answer, as does *Tosafot*.

*Tosafot* additionally notes a Mechilta that adds a prior stage to the argument: before we can even ask whether multiple categories generate multiple *korbanos*, we must first establish that violating a single category is already a full violation of *shabbat* — perhaps one must violate all thirty-nine to have "desecrated" it in any meaningful sense. It is from *charish* and *katzir* that we learn even one category suffices. Only after that do we proceed to the question of separate liability, which is answered by fire.

### Shmuel and Rabbi Yossi

Given this compelling Tannaitic derivation, why did Shmuel not use it? The *gemara* answers: *Shmuel savar lah k'Rabbi Yossi* — Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yossi. And Rabbi Yossi maintains *havarah l'lav yatzat* — fire was singled out not to teach the rule of separate liability across all thirty-nine, but rather to downgrade fire specifically. According to Rabbi Yossi, fire carries only the status of a simple *lav* — like going beyond the *techum* or having one's animal work on *shabbat* — and is not subject to *karet* or *misas beis din*. This is a striking position. The very singling-out of fire, which Rabbi Natan reads as elevating all thirty-nine to independent liability, Rabbi Yossi reads as removing fire from the full severity of *melacha*. Since Shmuel follows Rabbi Yossi's reading of the fire verse, he cannot use it as a source for *chiluk melachot*, and must resort instead to his derivation from *mechaleleha mos yumas*.

---

## Rabbi Yossi - Achas (II)

### Achas Meihena Juxtaposit…

The *gemara* then asks: if Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yossi, where does Rabbi Yossi himself derive *chiluk melachot*? If fire is unavailable as a source, Rabbi Yossi must have another derivation.

A *braisa* provides the answer. Rabbi Yossi cites the verse in *Vayikra* dealing with the *chatat*: *v'asah me'achas meihena* — and he does [one] from one of them. This verse is not about *shabbat* per se — it speaks of violating one of the commandments and bringing a *chatat* — but it is read through the lens of *shabbat* and its *korban* liability.

### Deriving Overlapping Err…

The *drasha* turns on the juxtaposition of *achas* (one) and *hena* (they, many), along with the additional *mem* prefix in *me'achas* and *meihena*. This juxtaposition teaches that there are circumstances under which one brings a single *korban* and circumstances under which one brings multiple *korbanos*, even for violations occurring within a single *shabbat*.

### One That Is Many, Many T…

The derivation proceeds as follows. *Achas she'hi hena* — one which is many: this is the case of one who forgot it was *shabbat* yet performed many *melachot*. The core mistake was singular — forgetting *shabbat* — but it expressed itself in many acts. Therefore one *korban*. *Hena she'hi achas* — many which are one: this is the case of one who forgot individual *melachot*, performing multiple acts each representing a separate error, yet all on one *shabbat*. Here one brings multiple *chataot*.

From *me'achas* — from one — we learn that even a partial act can constitute a violation. The example is one who intended to write the name *Shimon* and wrote only *shem*: even though he did not complete his original intention, he wrote two letters (the minimum *shiur* for the *melacha* of *ketiva*) and is liable. The *mem* of *me'achas* signals that even doing less than what one intended, so long as the act itself is complete and reaches the minimum measure, is a violation.

From *meihena* — from them — we derive the relationship between *avos* and *toldos*: the main categories (*hena* = the *avos*) generate subsidiary categories (*me'hena* = the *toldos* that derive from them).

Spelling it out fully: *achas she'hi hena* corresponds to the case of *zadon Shabbat v'shiggat melachot* — one knew it was *shabbat* but forgot the individual *melachot*, thus multiple *korbanos*. *Hena she'hi achas* corresponds to *shiggas Shabbat v'zadon melachot* — one forgot it was *shabbat* but knew the acts were *melachot*; since the single error was forgetting *shabbat*, it is one *korban*.

---

## Rabbi Yossi - Achas (II)

### Shmuel's Disagreement

Why, then, did Shmuel not adopt Rabbi Yossi's derivation from *achas meihena*? The *gemara* states simply: *achas she'hi hena v'hena she'hi achas lo mashma lei* — Shmuel is not persuaded that the juxtaposition of *achas* and *hena* teaches this lesson. Combining two words and reading into their conjunction an entire structure of overlapping and distinct liability is not, in Shmuel's view, a compelling *drasha*. He therefore goes to his own source in *mechaleleha mos yumas*, which, although Amoraic and arguably the weakest of the three derivations, is the one he finds compelling.

We are left, then, with three derivations of *chiluk melachot*: fire (Rabbi Natan), *achas meihena* (Rabbi Yossi), and *mechaleleha mos yumas* (Shmuel). *Tosafot* raises the interesting point that Shmuel, as an Amora, appears to be disagreeing with *Tannaim* — though perhaps he had a *mesorah* supporting his position.

---

## Both Forgotten - Korban…

### He'lem Zeh V'zeh

The *gemara* now introduces Rava's question to Rav Nachman: *he'lem zeh v'zeh biyado mahu* — what is the law when someone forgot both? He forgot that it was *shabbat* and he also forgot, for each *melacha* he performed, that those acts were forbidden. He watered his plants thinking it was Wednesday, but even had he known it was *shabbat*, he would have continued — because he had forgotten that watering plants is a *melacha*. He also baked, under the same double forgetting. How many *korbanos* does he bring — one, because he forgot *shabbat*, or two, because he also forgot each individual *melacha* separately?

### Shabbat as Primary Error

Rav Nachman answers: *harei he'lem Shabbat biyado* — the forgetting of *shabbat* is in his possession, and that would have led to all of his actions regardless. Therefore it is one *korban*. The forgetting of *shabbat* is the encompassing mistake that subsumes all else. *V'eino chayav ela achat*.

One might argue the reverse: *adrabba*, say the opposite — *harei he'lem melachot biyado* — the forgetting of individual *melachot* is also in his possession, and those were the independent errors that drove each act. Perhaps those should govern, yielding a separate *korban* for each. The logic is coherent: the *melacha* errors are distinct from one another, and had he even known it was *shabbat*, each *melacha* error would have persisted independently. Rav Nachman, however, holds that *shabbat* is the larger, more encompassing mistake, and when both are present, the *shabbat* forgetting governs.

### Rashi and Tosafot Debate

Rav Ashi reformulates the question in terms of the language from the opening of the *daf*: *im mishum Shabbat kaparish* — if the person would have stopped because of *shabbat* (i.e., being reminded it was *shabbat* would have been sufficient to stop him), then *harei he'lem Shabbat biyado v'eino chayav ela achat* — it is the *shabbat* forgetting that is primary and he brings only one. *V'im mishum melacha kaparish* — if he would have stopped because of the *melacha* — *harei he'lem melachot biyado v'chayav al kol achas v'achas* — it is the *melacha* forgetting that is primary and he is liable for each one.

This formulation raises the question of what "would have stopped him" means when he forgot both. Rashi explains: if someone called out "it is *shabbat*!" and that alone — without any specific mention of the *melacha* — would have caused the person to stop, then it is because hearing "*shabbat*" triggered the realization that the act was forbidden. The reminder of *shabbat* implied the *melacha* prohibition, and therefore *shabbat* was the key piece of information he had forgotten.

*Tosafot* is dissatisfied with this reading. Why should the order of inference from a third party's reminder determine anything? *Tosafot* reframes the criterion as a matter of self-reporting: we ask the person himself which piece of information was more fundamental to his error. If he reports that had he remembered it was *shabbat*, he would have paused, hesitated, and checked whether his actions were permitted — even if he was somewhat ambivalent about the *melacha* question — then *shabbat* was the more foundational forgetting. Conversely, if the *melacha* was the deeper error and *shabbat* was at most an ambivalent uncertainty, then the *melacha* is primary. The criterion is not what an observer would infer, but which error the person identifies as having been the core of his mistake.

### Gemara's Pushback

The *gemara* is not satisfied even with Rav Ashi's reformulation. Ravina responds: *klum parash miShabbos ela mishum melachos?* — the same objection that appeared on *amud alef* resurfaces. When one stops because of *shabbat*, it is because *both* pieces of knowledge — that it is *shabbat* and that the act is a *melacha* — have been engaged. And *klum piresh mi'melachos ela mishum Shabbos?* — when one stops because of the *melacha*, it is again because both factors are now operative. No matter which piece of information triggers awareness, both are necessarily present in the moment of stopping. So if both were forgotten, one cannot locate the "more fundamental" forgetting simply by asking what would have made the person stop.

According to *Tosafot*, what Ravina is really saying is that Rav Ashi has not addressed the true case — where both were genuinely and equally forgotten. Perhaps Rav Ashi handles the case where one forgetting was dominant and the other ambivalent, but where both are real and complete, the question remains open.

### Gemara's Pushback

The *gemara* resolves the impasse — at least at this stage of the discussion.

### Rav Ashi's Criterion

Rav Ashi's criterion (*im mishum Shabbat kaparish / im mishum melacha kaparish*) reflects the same logical structure as the debate at the opening of the *daf*. This is worth pausing on. What seemed earlier like two merely verbal formulations of the same point — "what would have made you stop" versus "what mistake did you make" — may carry genuine practical weight precisely in the case of *he'lem zeh v'zeh*. When you have only forgotten *shabbat*, the two formulations converge: one mistake, one *korban*. When you have only forgotten the *melachot*, they again converge: multiple mistakes, multiple *korbanos*. But when both are forgotten simultaneously, the two framings can point in different directions. "What would have made you stop" requires identifying which piece of information was the decisive trigger. "Where was your mistake" requires counting the errors. These can come apart, and the case of *he'lem zeh v'zeh* is precisely where that divergence becomes visible.

### Ravina's Position

Ravina's ultimate position — *ela lo shena* — is that it makes no difference which information would have caused the person to desist; in all configurations of *he'lem zeh v'zeh*, *shabbat* is the more encompassing category. The forgetting of *shabbat* implies and includes all the individual *melacha* forgettings; the reverse is not true. Therefore, when both are forgotten, we follow the larger category and it is one *korban*.

---

## 39 Melachot - Source (II)

### Rabbi Yochanan's Question

The *gemara* now invokes a *mishna* we have already encountered: *avos melachos arba'im chaser achas* — the primary categories of *melacha* are forty minus one. The *gemara* had asked, *minyana lama li* — why does the *mishna* need to state the number? Surely one can count.

### 39 Korbanot Scenario

Rabbi Yochanan answered: to teach that it is possible to bring thirty-nine *korbanos* in a single state of forgetfulness — *she'im asaan kulam b'he'elam echad chayav al kol achas v'achas* — that one who forgot all thirty-nine categories and violated each one within a single *he'lem* brings a separate *korban* for each. The number thirty-nine is stated to tell us the theoretical maximum: thirty-nine *korbanos* for a single *shabbat*.

---

## 39 Melachot - Source (II)

### Forgetting All vs. Shabb…

This scenario immediately raises a difficulty: if one forgot all thirty-nine *melachot*, one has effectively forgotten everything that *shabbat* prohibits. Doesn't that amount to forgetting *shabbat* itself — in which case, by our earlier analysis, there should be only one *korban*?

### Karetand Lav Framework

The *gemara* resolves this elegantly through Rabbi Yochanan's own position — *kivan d'shagog b'kares af al pi d'mezid b'lav* — that even if one knew the act was prohibited at the level of a *lav*, if he forgot that it was punishable by *karet*, he is considered *shogeg* and liable for a *korban*. Accordingly, one can know it is *shabbat* and know that certain acts are forbidden, yet forget the severity — specifically, that each of these categories is subject to *karet*. In such a case, he brings thirty-nine *korbanos* for the thirty-nine categories he violated while still, in some sense, "knowing" it was *shabbat* (in that he knew the acts were at least prohibitied at the level of a *lav*).

This resolution is specific to Rabbi Yochanan's view. Reish Lakish, who holds that *shogeg* liability requires forgetting even the basic *lav* prohibition — *ad d'yishgog b'lav u'vkares* — faces the difficulty more acutely: if one forgot that all thirty-nine things are forbidden, hasn't he simply forgotten *shabbat*?

### Techumin as Shabbat Know…

For Reish Lakish's position, the *gemara* employs the same resolution offered two days prior: *d'yadah lei b'tchumin v'aliba d'Rabbi Akiva* — one retains knowledge that it is *shabbat* because he knows, at minimum, that it is biblically prohibited to go beyond the *techum* (city limits), which Rabbi Akiva holds is a biblical prohibition. This residual knowledge of *some* *shabbat* prohibition — even if not *melacha* — suffices to establish that he "knew" it was *shabbat*. He then made thirty-nine independent errors about the individual *melachot*, and thus brings thirty-nine *korbanos*. If no such residual *shabbat* knowledge exists and he forgot even *techum*, then his forgetting of all *melachot* collapses into a forgetting of *shabbat* itself, and only one *korban* is brought.

---

## Order of Realization - R…

### Katzar V'Tachan Case

Rava introduces a case of considerable complexity. A person harvested a *k'gogeret*'s worth of grain and ground it — performing two *melachot* — while in a state of *shiggas Shabbat* (having forgotten it was *shabbat*). He then, without any intervening realization that he had sinned, performed the same two acts again — harvesting and grinding — this time in a state of *zadon Shabbat v'shiggas melacha*: he knew it was *shabbat* but had forgotten that these acts were forbidden.

To simplify: he performed two acts under error-type one (forgetting *shabbat*) and then two acts under error-type two (forgetting the *melachot*). Call these "error-one acts" and "error-two acts" respectively.

### Realizing Shabbat First

Now the order in which he realizes his mistakes: first, he becomes aware of his error-one acts — the acts he committed while forgetting it was *shabbat*. At that moment, he becomes obligated in a *korban*, and that obligation encompasses both *ketzira* and *techina* done under error-type one.

### Ktzira Goreret Ktzira

Then he becomes aware of his error-two acts — those committed while knowing it was *shabbat* but forgetting the individual *melachot*. What is his obligation? Rava states: *ktzira goreret ktzira v'techina goreret techina* — harvesting drags harvesting, and grinding drags grinding. Since his first realized obligation already includes an obligation relating to *ketzira*, the subsequent *ketzira* obligation (from the error-two acts) is subsumed within the earlier one; he need not bring an additional *korban* for it. The same applies to *techina*. Thus, having realized mistake-one first, both error-two *korbanos* are absorbed by the first obligation, and he brings only one *korban* total.

### Realizing Melacha First

But reverse the order of realization: first he becomes aware of his error-two acts — those committed while knowing it was *shabbat* but forgetting the *melachot*. This immediately generates two obligations: one *korban* for *ketzira* and one *korban* for *techina*. Then he becomes aware of his error-one acts. The error-one acts, because committed under *shiggas Shabbat*, would normally generate one *korban* (since forgetting *shabbat* is a single error). But in this reversed scenario, since his *ketzira* obligation from the error-two realization already exists, and the error-one *korban* would overlap with it (it too involves *ketzira*), the error-one *korban* is absorbed — *ktzira goreret ktzira*. He need not bring a separate *korban* for the error-one *ketzira*. However, the error-one *korban* also included *techina*, and since a *techina* obligation already exists from the error-two realization, no additional *techina korban* is needed either.

The practical result depends on which realization came first — and the order of recognition determines which obligation "drags" the other into its ambit.

### Abaye on Overlaps

Abaye pushes back on this analysis, particularly regarding the second scenario. He argues: *techina nami goreret techina shem techina achas hi* — the grinding also drags the grinding, by a chain of inclusion. Even if one never actually brings the *korban* generated by the error-one realization (because it was absorbed by the prior error-two obligation), the fact that the error-one *korban* conceptually *included* a *techina* obligation means that when the remaining *techina* obligation from error-two surfaces, it too is subsumed by that chain.

In other words, Abaye holds that inclusion works across links: the error-two *ketzira* obligation absorbed the error-one *korban* (which included *techina*), and therefore the remaining *techina* obligation is also absorbed — even though no actual *korban* was ever brought for the intermediate step. This is a striking claim: an obligation that was itself absorbed, never actualized into a *korban*, nevertheless transmits its power of inclusion to further obligations downstream. The *gemara* will continue this debate on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Shabbat 71

## Two Forgettings Case

### Case Review Setup

The daf opens in the middle of a case that requires some recapitulation. The scenario involves a person who forgot it was *Shabbat* and performed two *melachot* — cutting (*ktzira*) and grinding (*tchina*). While still in that state, he somehow remembered that it was *Shabbat*, but without having realized that he had just sinned, and then immediately entered a second state of forgetting — this time forgetting that these same two *melachot* are prohibited — and performed them again. Viewed in isolation, each of these two states of forgetting would independently generate two *korbanot*. The person then remembered his sins, but sequentially: first he became aware of the first sin (the forgetting of *Shabbat*), and then of the second sin (the forgetting of the *melachot*).

In the first forgetting, the obligation crystallizes upon remembering, generating a *korban* that covers both *ktzira* and *tchina*. When the person then remembers the second sin — which likewise comprises both *ktzira* and *tchina* — the question becomes whether a new and separate *korban* is required.

### Why Two Offerings

The *gemara* concludes that in this case no additional *korban* is necessary, because the *ktzira* of the second sin is already subsumed within the obligation generated by the *ktzira* of the first, and similarly the *tchina* of the second is already subsumed within the first. The second obligation is effectively dragged along by the first.

### One vs Two Forgettings

This raises an important structural question. Ordinarily, we hold that two separate acts of forgetting — with a moment of awareness in between — generate two separate *korbanot* for the same sin. Even if a person forgets, then remembers, and then forgets again and repeats the exact same transgression, the interrupting awareness divides the two episodes into distinct obligations. Why, then, does the case here produce fewer than two *korbanot*, given that there are effectively two different states of forgetfulness at play?

Rashi addresses this directly. He explains that the present case is genuinely ambiguous. On one hand, there was no intervening moment of awareness between the two states of forgetting — the person never realized he had sinned. On the other hand, it is not a single uniform state of forgetting: the person was forgetting different things at different times, first the nature of the day and then the prohibited character of the *melachot*. This ambiguity — neither the clean break of two forgettings divided by awareness, nor the seamless unity of a single forgetting — is precisely what allows for the discussion. The *gemara*'s resolution, at least at this stage, is that once the first obligation is crystallized, it subsumes and drags along the second.

---

## Reverse Order Case

### Reverse Order Setup

The more complicated scenario arises when the person remembers in reverse order. Rather than becoming aware of sins in the sequence in which they were incurred, he first becomes aware of one component — the *ktzira* — of the second forgetting, then of the entire first forgetting (which includes both *ktzira* and *tchina*), and finally of the *tchina* component of the second forgetting. The question is how many *korbanot* this sequence of awarenesses obligates him to bring.

### Rava's Dragging

Rava articulates a principle of *gerera* — dragging. When the person first becomes aware of the *ktzira* of the second forgetting, that awareness generates an obligation in one *korban* for *ktzira*. When he then becomes aware of the entirety of the first forgetting — comprising both *ktzira* and *tchina* — the *ktzira* component of that first forgetting is already represented in the *korban* he is obligated to bring. The overlap, even if partial, is sufficient: *ktzira goreret ktzirah* — the *ktzira* obligation drags along the other *ktzira* obligation, including together with it the *tchina* that accompanies it. In Rava's formulation: *ktzirah goreret ktzirah vetachina she'imah* — the *ktzira* drags the *ktzira* and the *tchina* that accompanies it. However, when the person finally becomes aware of the *tchina* of the second forgetting, that *tchina* stands on its own — *bimkomo omedet* — and requires a separate *korban*, since it was not represented in the first obligation.

The net result according to Rava is that the person brings one *korban* for the initial *ktzira* awareness (which subsumes the combined first forgetting), and one additional *korban* for the final *tchina*. At the end of the day, each category — *ktzira* and *tchina* — receives at least one *korban*.

### Abaye's Position

Abaye extends the principle of *gerera* further. He holds that the *tchina* of the first forgetting itself drags along the *tchina* of the second forgetting — *tachina nami goreret tachina*. Since it is all considered one category of *tchina*, the single *korban* for *ktzira* covers all the various sins committed, even though no *korban* is ever specifically brought for the act of *tchina*. As Abaye puts it: *shum tachina achat hi* — it is all one act of *tchina*. According to Abaye, therefore, only one *korban* need be brought, and it covers everything — a striking conclusion, since nothing in that *korban* specifically represents the *tchina* at all.

---

## Three Olives Proof

### Rava Consistency

Having presented Rava's position, the *gemara* immediately questions whether Rava truly holds the principle of *gerera* in the manner described. The challenge comes from another statement attributed to Rava — *umi it lei leRava gerera?* — does Rava really subscribe to this dragging principle? A different ruling of Rava appears to be in tension with it.

### Three Olives Setup

The *gemara* introduces a new case: a person ate two *zeisim* (olives' worth) of *chelev* (forbidden fat), which carries the penalty of *karet* and requires a *korban chatat* when performed unwittingly. Both olives were eaten in a single state of forgetfulness — *behelem echad* — meaning that even if consumed on different occasions during the week, as long as the person never awoke to the realization of his sin in between, a single *korban* suffices. The minimum measure (*kizayit*) is the threshold for the obligation.

Now, before becoming aware of both sins, the person became aware of only the first olive. He still had no recollection of having eaten the second. In that state — aware of the first, unaware of the second — he went ahead and ate a third olive of *chelev*, this time in the state of forgetfulness associated with his unawareness of the second.

The case therefore has three olives. Olives one and two were eaten in state of forgetting A. Between the first and third eating, there was an intervening awareness of the first olive only. The third olive was eaten in the state of forgetting B (which is the same unawareness that applied to olive two). Then the person eventually becomes aware of both olives two and three.

### Middle Olive Solution

Rava's ruling is both precise and practically ingenious. If one brings the *korban* designated for the first olive, that atones for sins one and two — since both were eaten in a common state of forgetfulness — but not for sin three, which was in a different state. If one brings the *korban* for the third olive, that atones for sins three and two — since both the third and the second share the same state of forgetfulness (B) — but not for sin one. However, if one is astute enough to designate the *korban* for the middle olive — sin two — then all three are atoned for: *niskapru kulam*. Why? Because olive two shares state of forgetfulness A with olive one, so the *korban* for two sweeps in one; and olive two shares state of forgetfulness B with olive three, so the *korban* for two sweeps in three as well. The middle olive sits at the intersection of both states of forgetting, and a *korban* brought for it therefore reaches in both directions.

It is notable that the designation of the *korban* is operative here. The person coming before the *beit din* can be instructed to designate his *korban* for the middle olive, and that single designation achieves complete atonement. There is something striking about this — the obligation is not objectively fixed by the acts themselves; the person retains the power to define which act his *korban* primarily addresses, and the others are subsumed accordingly.

### Abaye Alternative

Abaye, consistent with his broader position, holds that even greater latitude is available: *afilu hevi korban al echad mehen, niskapru kulam* — even if one brings the *korban* for any one of the three, they are all atoned for. The reason lies in the extended chain of *gerera*: if one brings for olive three, that includes olive two; but since olive two is included, a *korban* for olive two would have included olive one; therefore, bringing for olive three ultimately drags in olive one as well through the intermediary of olive two. Conversely, bringing for olive one includes two, and two includes three. The chain of dragging, in Abaye's view, means that any single *korban* reaches all the way through.

As the *gemara* observes, this case is actually a milder form of *gerera* than what appeared in the *Shabbat* scenario, since here all three sins are of the same type — all are *chelev* — whereas in the *Shabbat* case, Abaye allowed a *korban* for *ktzira* to discharge an obligation for *tchina*, which has no representation at all in the *korban* being brought.

### Challenge to Rava

The *gemara* now presses its original challenge to Rava directly. If Rava does not accept the extended form of *gerera* that Abaye employs in the *Shabbat* case — where a *tchina* that has no representation in the first *korban* gets dragged along — then how can Rava in the three-olives case allow a *korban* for olive one to discharge the obligation for olive two? After all, this too involves a partial overlap rather than complete identity: the *korban* for olive one is brought in state A, while olive two also has a connection to state B, which is not at all represented in the *korban* for olive one. From the *gemara*'s perspective, the two cases are roughly analogous — in both, there is some overlap between the *korban* being brought and the sin being discharged, but in both there is also a component of the discharged sin that is not represented in the *korban*. How, then, does Rava permit *gerera* in the three-olives case but not in the *Shabbat* case?

---

## Rava Persuaded

### Rava's Reversal

The *gemara* resolves the tension by reporting that Rava changed his position after debating Abaye on the three-olives case: *batar deshameih me'Abaye savrah* — after he heard Abaye's reasoning, he was persuaded. He therefore conceded that some degree of *gerera* operates in the three-olives scenario. Were he to revisit the *Shabbat* case in light of his revised view, he would presumably accept that the *korban* for the combined first forgetting can include the parallel obligation from the second forgetting.

### One Dragging Rule

The *gemara* then presses further: once Rava has conceded the principle of *gerera*, why does he not go all the way with Abaye and say that the *tchina* of the first forgetting drags along the *tchina* of the second, such that a single *korban* covers everything?

The *gemara*'s answer is a precise limiting rule: *gerera it lei, gerera degerera leit lei* — Rava accepts one dragging, not a dragging of a dragging. The first *korban* can drag in an obligation that has some overlap with it, but it cannot drag in an obligation that is only connected through an intermediate step. The *tchina* of the second forgetting has no representation whatsoever in the original *korban* brought for *ktzira*. It is connected only because the *gerera* of the combined first-forgetting *korban* sweeps in the second forgetting's *ktzira*, and it is only through that swept-in *ktzira* that the *tchina* could theoretically be reached. That is two degrees removed — a dragging of a dragging — and that is too far for Rava.

Rashi sharpens this point slightly. He notes that the reason the *tchina* of the second forgetting cannot be discharged is not merely that it is two steps removed, but more specifically that the combined *korban* only drags in the second obligation because of its *ktzira* component. The *tchina* of that second obligation is being dragged along by virtue of its *ktzira* — it is a passenger on the *ktzira*'s inclusion. That *tchina* does not itself have the power to then extend the drag further to the *tchina* of another separate obligation. The *tchina* of the second forgetting is, in Rashi's formulation, entirely foreign to the original first *korban*, and therefore Rava refuses to extend the *gerera* to cover it.

---

## Rabbi Zeira Question

### Half-Melacha Setup

The *gemara* now introduces a question posed by Rabbi Zeira — something that Abaye and Rava both took as self-evident, but which Rabbi Zeira himself was uncertain about. The new scenario involves a single *melacha* performed in two halves, each half under a different mode of forgetting.

To illustrate with a clearer example: a person forgot it was *Shabbat* and wrote one letter — half of a complete act of writing, since writing a complete word (*shem*, for instance) requires two letters. He then remembered it was *Shabbat* but somehow forgot that writing is prohibited on *Shabbat*, and proceeded to write the second letter, completing the word. Each half of the *melacha* was performed under a different type of forgetting — the first under forgetting of the day, the second under forgetting of the prohibition. At no point did the person realize he had sinned. There was no intervening awareness, merely two different modes of forgetting, each responsible for half of a single prohibited act.

### Combination Question

Rabbi Zeira's question, addressed to Rabbi Assi (or according to an alternative tradition, asked by Rabbi Yirmiyah of Rabbi Zeira), is: *mahu sheyitztarfu?* — do these two halves combine? The stakes are significant. If they combine, the person has completed a full *melacha* and is obligated in a *korban*. If they do not combine — because the two halves were performed in structurally distinct states of forgetting — then neither half independently constitutes a complete prohibited act, and the person may be exempt.

### Separation Answer

The answer given is unambiguous: *chalukin l'chataot v'lo mitztarfin* — since these two modes of forgetting, when a complete act is performed under each, generate separate *korbanot*, they are considered categorically separate states. They do not combine. The reasoning is that the very separateness of the two modes of forgetting — even in the absence of an intervening awareness — is sufficient to treat them as distinct legal states for all purposes. If doing a full *melacha* under each mode would result in two separate *korbanot*, it follows that those modes are considered genuinely separate, and therefore two halves under those separate modes also remain separate and do not merge into a single act.

This stands in direct tension with the assumptions underlying the earlier discussion of Abaye and Rava, which proceeded on the premise that some degree of combination across the two modes of forgetting was possible. Rabbi Zeira's question, and the answer he received, reveal that what Abaye and Rava treated as obvious was actually the subject of genuine halakhic uncertainty.

The *gemara* also takes a moment to acknowledge the distinctly abstract character of this entire sugyah. The cases discussed here are purely academic constructions — no one is bringing *korbanot* in the time of the *amoraim*, and the questions are entirely theoretical. This stands in stark contrast to the first six *perakim* of *Shabbat*, which were deeply embedded in the material world and practical life of the period. The present *sugyah* represents the *gemara* at its most formally speculative, playing with halakhic categories in the absence of any grounding in contemporary practice.

---

## Forbidden Fat Mishnah

### Same vs Different Sins

The *gemara* now examines a *mishnah* in *Kerisos* that bears directly on these questions. The *mishnah* states: if a person ate *chelev* and *chelev* — two separate acts of eating forbidden fat — in a single state of forgetfulness (*behelem echad*), he is liable for only one *korban*. Multiple acts of the same sin within one uninterrupted state of forgetting merge into a single obligation. By contrast, if a person ate *chelev*, blood (*dam*), *notar* (leftover sanctified food), and *pigul* (an offering consumed with improper intent) — all four categories carrying the penalty of *karet* — even in a single state of forgetfulness, he is liable separately for each one: *chayav al kol achas ve'achas*. Different categories of sin, even when committed in a single episode of forgetting, generate separate obligations.

The *mishnah* articulates this as a dual principle. Multiple categories bring stringency, because each carries its own *korban*. But a single category brings its own kind of stringency as well: if one ate half a *kizayit* of *chelev* and then another half a *kizayit* of *chelev* — within the time required to eat half a loaf (*kedei achilat pras*) — the two halves combine to constitute one complete act, and the person is liable. However, if one ate half a *kizayit* of *chelev* and half a *kizayit* of *notar*, those halves do not combine, and the person is exempt.

### Two Halves Debate

The *gemara* asks: when the *mishnah* says that two half-*kizayit* portions of *chelev* combine and the person is liable, is this not obvious? Of course two halves of the same sin combine into a whole act. What *chiddush* is being communicated?

Reish Lakish, in the name of Bar Tutini, answers that the *mishnah* is addressing a subtler case: *kegon she'achalo bishnei tamchuyin* — the two halves were eaten in two different dishes. One half of the *chelev* was in a soup; the other half was in a steak. Although the sin is identical — both are *chelev* — the experiential reality of the eating was different. One might have thought that, just as Rabbi Yehoshua holds that different dishes (*tamchuyin*) divide eating acts and can generate separate *korbanot* when full measures are involved, the same principle would apply in the lenient direction: different dishes would also prevent two halves from combining, exempting the person. The *mishnah* therefore teaches otherwise.

The *gemara* then refines the question of how to understand Rabbi Yehoshua's principle. One might have thought that Rabbi Yehoshua applied the rule that different dishes separate eating acts both *lekula* (leniently) and *lechumra* (stringently). To be stringent: if a full *kizayit* of *chelev* was in the soup and another full *kizayit* in the steak, they are considered separate acts and the person is obligated to bring two *korbanot* rather than one. To be lenient: if only a half *kizayit* was in the soup and a half *kizayit* in the steak, the different dishes would prevent combination and exempt the person. The *gemara* concludes that Rabbi Yehoshua applied his principle only stringently — to multiply *korbanot* — but not leniently. When it comes to two halves, the strict approach is to combine them and obligate the person, and that is what the *mishnah* teaches.

The *gemara* continues by reconsidering the framing. Initially the question was raised on the first clause of the *mishnah* — why must it tell us that two halves of *chelev* combine? But in fact the proper teaching of the Bar Tutini tradition belongs on the final clause — the case of exemption for two different categories. What might seem to be a case of half *chelev* and half blood is actually a case of the same *chelev* eaten in two different dishes. The reason they do not combine is not that they are different substances but that they were in different dishes — and it is that *chiddush* that belongs to Rabbi Yehoshua, who says different dishes separate acts both stringently and leniently. The *gemara* accordingly relocates its question: since the *sof* of the *mishnah* is addressing *chelev* in two different dishes, the *reisha* — the case where two halves do combine — must be referring to the same dish, in which case the combination is indeed not obvious?

### Rabban Gamliel Rule

Rav Huna resolves this. The case where the two halves combine is not simply a case of the same dish with no complicating features. It is a case where the person had a *yedi'ah* — an awareness — in between the two acts of eating. Normally, an intervening awareness divides sin-obligations and prevents combination. The *chiddush* of the *mishnah* is that even with an intervening awareness, the two halves still combine. How so? Because the awareness the person had was only of having eaten half a *kizayit*, not of having committed a complete sin. This is the ruling of Rabban Gamliel: *ein yedi'ah lachatzi shiur* — awareness of having performed only half the prohibited measure does not constitute the kind of legally operative awareness that divides obligations. A *yedi'ah* divides only when one becomes aware of a complete transgression. Awareness of a half-measure leaves the act legally undivided, and the two halves therefore combine notwithstanding the interrupting moment of partial awareness.

---

## Atonement Timing

### Half-Sin Awareness

The distinction just established — that *yedi'ah* of a complete sin divides, while *yedi'ah* of a half-measure does not — sets the stage for the next set of cases. The operative question going forward is not only whether there was an awareness in between, but what the *content* of that awareness was. Only awareness that one has committed a full, complete transgression carries the legal weight to sever one episode of sin from another and generate independent obligations.

---

## Two Olives Separate

### Scenario Setup

The *gemara* now introduces a case that at first appears to be a straightforward application of what has already been discussed, but which in fact opens a new debate. A person ate two full *zeisim* of *chelev* in a single state of forgetfulness (*behelem echad*). This alone would ordinarily generate a single *korban* — two complete acts of the same sin in one episode of forgetting. But the person then became aware of his first act and, separately, became aware of his second act. Rashi notes explicitly that the assumptions of this *sugyah* are in tension with those of the previous one — what was treated as given before is now openly contested.

### Rabbi Yochanan View

Rabbi Yochanan holds: *chayav shtayim* — the person is liable for two separate *korbanot*. Although the two acts of eating were performed in a single state of forgetting, the fact that awareness came in two separate stages is sufficient to divide them into independent obligations. The source Rabbi Yochanan invokes is the verse *al chatato v'hevi* — for his sin he shall bring — which he reads as requiring a separate *korban* for each discrete sin as it becomes known. Every separate act of remembering triggers a separate and independent obligation, regardless of the original unity of the forgetting.

### Reish Lakish View

Reish Lakish disagrees: *eino chayav ela achat* — he is liable for only one *korban*. Since both acts were committed in a single state of forgetfulness, the sins belong to a single undivided episode. When the person becomes aware of the first act and brings a *korban*, that *korban* is brought *me-chatato* — from his sin — which Reish Lakish reads as encompassing the whole category of sin committed in that episode. Even a *korban* brought for only part of a continuous sin-state atones for the whole. Separate awarenesses, in Reish Lakish's view, do not divide what was originally one.

The *gemara* then asks how each *amora* handles the verse that seems to favor his opponent. For Rabbi Yochanan, how does he account for the phrase *me-chatato* — "from his sin" — which suggests that a *korban* for part of a sin suffices for the whole? And for Reish Lakish, how does he account for *al chatato v'hevi*, which seems to require a separate *korban* per sin?

Reish Lakish's answer to the latter is that the verse applies *l'achar kapparah* — after actual atonement has been achieved. If the person became aware of act A and brought his *korban* for A — completing the act of atonement on the *mizbeach* — and only afterward became aware of act B, then B is an independent obligation and requires its own *korban*. But if awareness of B preceded the actual bringing of the *korban*, then B can still be subsumed within the single offering brought for A. What creates the division is not the awareness itself but the completed act of atonement in between.

---

## Atonement Timing (II)

### Complex Scenario

The *gemara* then constructs a deliberately complicated scenario in order to illustrate the point on which Rabbi Yochanan would agree that only one *korban* need be brought. The scenario involves a person who ate one and a half *zeisim* of *chelev*, had an awareness specifically of the one *kizayit* (not of the accompanying half), then ate another half a *kizayit* of *chelev* in a new state of forgetting. When awareness ultimately arrives, the person has an obligation for the one *kizayit*, is unaware of the first half (which was forgotten), and has a new half-*kizayit* from the second eating.

### Why Complicated

The reason the *gemara* requires such a tortured construction is to find a case where even Rabbi Yochanan — who generally holds that separate awarenesses divide obligations — would concede that a single *korban* covers multiple acts. In this scenario, when the person brings a *korban* for the one *kizayit* he is aware of, the accompanying first half is not remembered and is therefore effectively absorbed into that *korban*. The second half, eaten in a separate state of forgetting, might seem like it should combine with the forgotten first half — two halves of the same sin — but it does not, because the forgotten first half has already been subsumed into the *korban* brought for the whole *kizayit*. There is nothing left for the second half to combine with. The second half is therefore simply waived, and the person is exempt from bringing a *korban* for it. This is the scenario where even Rabbi Yochanan would say only one *korban* is brought for multiple sins — not because of dragging in the ordinary sense, but because one component disappears into the main *korban* and the other is left without a counterpart to combine with.

---

## Ravina Ashi Debate

### Three Possibilities

Ravina raises a meta-level question to Rav Ashi. In the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, what exactly is the scenario under discussion? Ravina poses three possibilities. First: perhaps they debate only in a case where awareness arrived before the person had designated (*hafrasha*) a *korban* at all — before any formal setting-aside of the animal. In that case, the debate is whether separate awarenesses alone (*yediot mechalkot*) are sufficient to divide obligations. If Ravina's first framing is correct, then once a *korban* has actually been designated, Reish Lakish would agree with Rabbi Yochanan that the obligations are divided and two *korbanot* are required. Second: perhaps they debate only in a case where the person had already designated the *korban* for the first act before becoming aware of the second. In that case, Rabbi Yochanan holds that the designation itself divides (*hafrashot mechalkot*), while Reish Lakish holds that even a designated *korban* can still incorporate the second sin, since only actual atonement (*kappara*) creates a true division. According to this second framing, if no designation had yet been made, even Rabbi Yochanan might agree that a single *korban* suffices. Third: they argue in both scenarios — both before designation and after.

### Designation Check

The *gemara* argues that it is most reasonable to assume they debate in both cases. The proof comes from the structure of the *gemara*'s earlier answers. When we asked how Reish Lakish accounts for the verse that seems to require a separate *korban* per sin, we answered that Reish Lakish reserves that verse for the case of *achar kapparah* — after actual atonement has been achieved. But if Reish Lakish would agree that two *korbanot* are required once a *korban* has been designated, then why did the *gemara* not frame his agreement in terms of designation rather than completed atonement? The fact that the *gemara* reached all the way to completed atonement as the dividing event — rather than the much earlier and less demanding step of designation — implies that the *gemara* assumed designation alone does not divide according to Reish Lakish. This in turn implies that the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is not limited to the post-designation case, but extends even to the pre-designation case.

Similarly, when we asked how Rabbi Yochanan accounts for the verse that seems to allow a single *korban* for multiple sins, we gave the elaborate answer involving one-and-a-half plus a half. If Rabbi Yochanan would agree that a single *korban* suffices in any case where no designation has yet been made, then there would have been a far simpler answer available: just say that Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Reish Lakish in the pre-designation case. The fact that we did not give that simpler answer implies that the *gemara* assumed Rabbi Yochanan holds two *korbanot* are required even before designation — again suggesting the debate covers both scenarios.

### Rashi Meta-Analysis

Rashi here makes a fascinating observation about the nature of the argument being made. The *gemara* is not citing Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish directly — it is reasoning from the way the *gemara* itself framed their debate to draw inferences about the scope of their positions. In other words, the *gemara* is treating its own earlier formulations as evidence for what was assumed by the Yeshiva about the parameters of the dispute.

Rashi notes explicitly: since the *gemara* had framed the cases in a specific way — using completed atonement as the dividing event for Reish Lakish, and the complex one-and-a-half scenario for Rabbi Yochanan — this framing reflects the assumptions of the *bnei yeshiva* who structured the *gemara*. *Depishita livnei yeshiva she-sidru ha-gemara de-le-achar hafrasha nami patar Reish Lakish* — it was self-evident to those who edited the *gemara* that Reish Lakish exempts even after designation. The editorial choices of the *gemara* itself become hermeneutic evidence about the scope of the underlying dispute.

This is a striking observation. The *gemara* is simultaneously the source of the argument and the object being examined. The *amoraim* Ravina and Rav Ashi are reading the assumptions embedded in the *gemara*'s own discourse back out from the text in order to clarify what was assumed about positions that were never explicitly defined with respect to the question at hand.

### Uncertain Scope

Ultimately, the *gemara* does not accept this line of reasoning as a definitive proof. The *gemara* concludes: *udi'lma sfukei misapka lei* — perhaps the reason those earlier answers were given is precisely because the scope of the debate was unknown, and the answers were formulated in a way that would hold regardless. The complicated case of one-and-a-half and a half, for instance, was given not because we assumed Rabbi Yochanan holds that separate awarenesses alone divide, but because we were uncertain, and that scenario serves as a valid case for Rabbi Yochanan's single-*korban* position under any reading of the debate. Similarly, the reference to completed atonement as the trigger for Reish Lakish's agreement may reflect uncertainty rather than assumption.

The *gemara* closes on this note of acknowledged inconclusiveness: the scope of the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish — whether they argue before designation, after designation, or in both cases — cannot be established with certainty from the structure of the *gemara*'s own earlier answers, because those answers may themselves have been framed in conditions of uncertainty.

---

---

# Shabbat 72

## Chatas vs. Asham

### Overview

Daf 72 opens by completing the discussion of how many *chataos* one must bring under various circumstances — a topic that occupied much of the preceding folio — before transitioning, on the second *amud*, to the far more practically resonant question of what constitutes an intentional versus an unintentional act on *Shabbos*. The two discussions are connected by the underlying question of *kavannah* and awareness, but they occupy very different conceptual territory, and the *sugya* marks the transition clearly.

### Three Asham Cases

To understand where the *Gemara* is heading, it is necessary to first survey the landscape of the *asham*. Unlike the *chatas*, which is a female sheep or goat brought for unintentional violations of a negative prohibition, the *asham* is a male ram and follows a distinct set of rules. The primary cases in which a *asham* is brought are three: *me'ilah* — misappropriating consecrated property; stealing and swearing falsely about it; and the case of *shifcha charufa* — a man who has relations with a woman who is half-slave and half-freed. This third case is notable for a striking feature: the *asham* is brought even if the act was committed *be-meizid*, intentionally. That anomaly will become central to the *Gemara*'s analysis.

These categories appear explicitly in the fifth chapter of *Zevachim*, which is recited as part of the *korbanot* section of the morning liturgy: *asham gezeilos* for theft and false oath, *asham me'ilos* for misappropriation of *hekdesh*, *asham shifcha charufa*, *asham nazir*, *asham metzora*, and *asham talui*. The first five are *asham vadai* — definite guilt offerings — while the *asham talui* stands in its own category.

### Asham Talui & Safek

The *asham talui* is brought when a person suspects he may have sinned but is not certain. The classic case is where two pieces of food were before him — one of forbidden fat (*chelev*) and one of permissible fat (*shuman*) — he ate one but does not know which. Because the forbidden object was concretely present and the doubt is genuine, there is a sufficient basis to bring the *asham talui*. This applies to any case of doubtful violation for which, had the sin been certain, a *chatas* would have been required. The technical term for this is *asham safek* — a guilt offering predicated on an uncertain sin.

### Akiva vs. Tarfon

The *Gemara* in *Kerisos* records a debate about *asham* in the context of *me'ilah*. If a person is uncertain whether he committed *me'ilah*, does he bring an *asham safek* even though the definite violation calls for an *asham vadai* rather than a *chatas*? Rabbi Akiva maintains that one does — the logic of *asham talui* extends to any case of genuine doubt, regardless of what offering the definite sin would have required.

Rabbi Tarfon, however, offers a more economical approach. Since this person, if he eventually discovers he did sin, will in any case be obligated in an *asham vadai*, why should he bring two separate offerings — both of them rams — the one on suspicion and the other on certainty? Instead, Rabbi Tarfon advises: bring one *asham* now, with the stipulation that if it turns out the sin was definite, this will serve as the *asham vadai*, and if the sin never becomes certain, it will serve as the *asham safek*.

### Asham without Knowledge

The *Gemara* draws a striking inference from Rabbi Tarfon's position. For this stipulation to be coherent — for an offering brought before certainty to retroactively qualify as an *asham vadai* — it must be that an *asham vadai* does not require prior *yedia*, prior awareness of the sin, as a precondition. By contrast, the *chatas* is inextricably bound to the moment of awareness: it is precisely the moment of becoming aware (*yedia*) that creates the obligation and defines the act as subject to a sin offering. But by the *asham*, at least according to one view, this is not the case. The sin itself — independent of whether the sinner has yet come to know that he sinned — generates the obligation, and one may bring the offering even before that awareness crystallizes into certainty.

This is the full weight of the phrase with which *Ulla* opens the discussion: *le-man de-amar asham vadai lo ba'i yedia be-techilah* — according to the view that a definite *asham* does not require prior knowledge, we must rethink what role awareness plays in dividing multiple acts of the same sin.

---

## Shifcha Charufa Acts

### Five Acts Question

Having established that *yedia* may not be a constitutive requirement for the *asham*, *Ulla* turns to the case of *shifcha charufa* to draw out the implications. If a man committed five separate acts of intercourse with this half-freed slave woman, and became aware of his sin in between each act, does he bring five separate *ashamim* or only one?

The intuition borrowed from the laws of *chatas* would suggest that awareness divides. By *chatas*, the moment of *yedia* is what creates the obligation, and therefore *yedia* occurring between two acts generates two separate obligations. But if *yedia* is not the constitutive element of an *asham vadai*, then it lacks the power to divide.

### Ulah's Position

*Ulla*'s position is precisely this: since *yedia* is not required for an *asham vadai* — since the sin itself is what obligates, independent of awareness — then awareness occurring between acts has no dividing force. Even across five separate acts with intervening moments of *yedia*, only one *asham* is owed.

### Hamnuna Challenge

Rav Hamnuna challenges this reasoning. Consider the case where a man had relations with a *shifcha charufa*, then designated an animal as his *asham* — *hifrish korban* — and then explicitly said, "Hold off, don't bring it yet; I want to have relations again, and then it will count for both." Surely, Rav Hamnuna argues, the act performed after the designation of the *korban* would generate an independent obligation. If so, doesn't that demonstrate that awareness between acts is equally sufficient to divide them?

### Korban Designation

The response is sharp and clarifying. The two cases are not analogous. When a *korban* has been formally designated — set aside and sanctified — the next act is by definition performed after a concrete, legally significant event has intervened. That creates a genuine division. But mere awareness — *yedia* without *hafrasha* — does not constitute such an event. The principle of *hafrasha* divides; *yedia* alone does not. This is the *chiddush*: even in a case where one is acting intentionally, where one would have expected separate acts to generate separate obligations, the *asham* of *shifcha charufa* resists division unless an actual designation of a *korban* has taken place between acts.

The *Gemara* acknowledges that there is something structurally interesting here. When acts are performed *be-meizid* — willfully — there is already stronger reason to see each act as independent. And yet the *Torah*'s treatment of *shifcha charufa* is a *chiddush* that even multiple intentional acts generate only one *asham*. The division comes only from *hafrasha*, not from awareness.

---

## Rav Dimi Position

### Dimi's Claim

When Rav Dimi arrived from *Eretz Yisrael*, he presented the flip side of *Ulla*'s analysis. *Rashi* notes that they are not in direct dispute; rather, each articulates what follows from a different premise. *Ulla* explored the implications of the view that *asham vadai* does not require *yedia be-techilah*. Rav Dimi articulates the view that it does.

According to the position that *yedia* is indeed a prerequisite for bringing an *asham vadai* — making it structurally analogous to the *chatas* in this respect — then awareness between acts functions precisely as it does by *chatas*: it divides. Therefore, if a man had relations with a *shifcha charufa* five times with *yedia* intervening between each act, he would be obligated in five separate *ashamim*.

### Abaye Analogy

At this point Abaye enters with a comparison that is admittedly not exact but is analytically productive. He notes: by *chatas*, everyone agrees that *yedia* is essential. Yet even there, Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute a related case. The scenario is this: a person ate two *kezaytim* of *chelev* in one state of forgetfulness — one act on Sunday, another on Sunday — and then became aware of the first on Monday and the second on Tuesday. Rabbi Yochanan holds that he brings two *chataos*. Reish Lakish holds he brings one.

What is Reish Lakish's logic? If *yedia* is the dividing element by *chatas*, how can separate acts of *yedia* fail to divide the obligations? This is the crux of Abaye's comparison. He is mapping the case of *yedia* occurring *between* the acts — as in the *shifcha charufa* scenario — onto the case of separate *yedia* occurring *after* the acts — as in the Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute. The analogy is inexact, but *Rashi* and *Tosafot* both try to articulate why it is nonetheless instructive.

The key observation is that *shifcha charufa* is already a *chiddush* in that even multiple intentional acts yield one *asham*. Since the *Torah* has indicated that dividing these acts is harder than usual, if *yedia* between acts is sufficient to divide them here, that should certainly mean that separate *yedia* after acts is sufficient to divide by *chatas*. Put differently: awareness that can break even the harder-to-divide *shifcha charufa* scenario should a fortiori be able to break the more readily divided *chatas* scenario.

### Awareness Comparison

To make the analogy fully visible, it helps to lay out the cases spatially. By *chatas*: if you commit two violations in one state of forgetfulness and then become aware of them in one moment, it is one *korban*. If you commit one, become aware, and then commit another, it is two *korbanot* — that is undisputed. The dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerns a middle case: two violations in one state of forgetfulness, followed by two separate moments of awareness — one on Monday, one on Tuesday. Rabbi Yochanan says two *korbanot*; Reish Lakish says one.

By *asham*: one act followed by *yedia* followed by another act — that is the *shifcha charufa* scenario under discussion. The *Gemara* treats this as analogous to the Rabbi Yochanan–Reish Lakish case, because if *yedia* between acts divides by *asham*, it should correspond to separate moments of *yedia* after the acts dividing by *chatas*.

### Reish Lakish View

After Abaye raises this analogy, *ishtik* — silence. The question lands without an immediate answer. Then the *Gemara* reconstructs what Reish Lakish's position must actually be. If Reish Lakish says one *korban* in the case of two separate post-act moments of *yedia* by *chatas*, then by the same logic, *yedia* between acts by *asham* would also not divide. For Reish Lakish, *yedia* is not in itself a dividing force — even when it is a constitutive requirement for the obligation. The only thing that divides, even according to Reish Lakish, is *hafrasha* — formal designation of a *korban*. This is consistent with what Rav Hamnuna demonstrated, and the *Gemara* invokes him explicitly: *u-che-Rav Hamnuna* — the division by *hafrasha* is the point of agreement; the division by *yedia* is the point of dispute.

---

## Ravin Summary

### All Agree Case

When Ravin arrived from *Eretz Yisrael*, he offered a crisp, three-part summary of where the consensus lies and where the dispute falls. *Hakol modim* — both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish agree — that in the *shifcha charufa* case, if *asham vadai* does not require *yedia be-techilah*, then awareness between acts does not divide, and only one *asham* is owed. This follows *Ulla*'s position: if *yedia* is not constitutive of the obligation, it lacks the power to divide. Even Rabbi Yochanan, who says two *korbanot* by *chatas*, would concede that by *asham vadai* — if *yedia* is not required — a single *asham* suffices.

### Hafrasha Agreement

*Hakol modim* as well that when *hafrasha* — formal designation of the *korban* — occurs between acts, a separate *asham* is required for the subsequent act. This is the case demonstrated by Rav Hamnuna: even Reish Lakish, who does not treat *yedia* as a dividing force, agrees that *hafrasha* divides.

### Knowledge Dispute

The *machloket* between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish plays out specifically in the case where *asham vadai* does require *yedia be-techilah* — according to the view that treats it as structurally parallel to *chatas*. There, the question is whether *yedia* occurring between acts divides them or not. Rabbi Yochanan holds that it does; Reish Lakish holds that it does not. This maps onto their dispute about separate *yedia* after acts in the *chatas* context — and with that summary, the entire discussion of multiple *chataos* and multiple *ashamim* reaches its conclusion.

---

## Intentionality Debate

### Mitasek Definition

The *Gemara* now turns to what will prove to be among the most practically significant distinctions in the laws of *Shabbos*: the line between *shogeg* — unintentional transgression, which obligates a *korban* — and *mit'asek* — a completely incidental act that does not. The word *mit'asek* derives from the root *esek*, involvement or occupation; in its reflexive form, it connotes a person who was occupied with his own affair and the prohibited act simply happened as a byproduct, wholly unintended. The contrast with *shogeg* is precise: a *shogeg* knows what he is doing but is unaware that it is forbidden; a *mit'asek* did not even intend the action that constituted the prohibition.

### Lift vs. Cut

The first case illustrates *mit'asek* clearly: *nitkavein le-hagbi'a et ha-tallush ve-chatach et ha-mechubar* — he intended to lift an object that was detached from the ground (*tallush*), but as he did so, he inadvertently severed something that was still attached (*mechubar*). According to *Tosafot*'s reading of this case, he thought the object was already detached from the tree, reached to pick it up, and in doing so tore it from a delicate twig connecting it to the ground — an act of *kotzer*. Everyone agrees he is exempt. The act he performed — cutting something attached — was not his act at all. He was lifting; the cutting was entirely incidental.

### Cut Mistake

The second case is where the debate ignites. *Le-chtoch et ha-tallush ve-chatach et ha-mechubar* — he intended to cut something detached, took out his knife and cut, but the object he cut turned out to be attached to the ground. He performed exactly the category of act he intended — cutting — but he was mistaken about the status of the object he cut. This is the *machloket* of Rava and Abaye.

### Rava Position

Rava says: *patur* — exempt. His reasoning is *deha lo nitkavein la-chatichah de-issura* — he was not intending to perform a prohibited cut. Now this cannot mean he was unaware of the prohibition, since that would be ordinary *shogeg*. What Rava means is more fundamental: for an act to be "his," it must be the act he envisioned in its essential character. A normal *shogeg* is someone who knows he is performing *kotzer* — severing something from the earth — but believes it is permitted, either because he thinks it is not *Shabbos* or because he thinks this particular act is allowed. That person owns the act. But here, the man did not conceive of himself as cutting something attached to the ground. The act he performed — *kotzer* — was not the act he intended in any meaningful sense, even though physically his knife moved and something was cut. Rava holds that a mistake about the facts of the situation is sufficient to render the act not truly his, placing it in the category of *mit'asek*, and exempting him entirely.

### Abaye Position

Abaye disagrees: *chayav* — obligated. His reasoning is *deha ka michavein la-chatichah be-alma* — he was intending to cut, and he cut. He cannot disclaim the action. The mistake he made was not about what type of act he was performing — he knew he was cutting — but about the factual circumstances of what he was cutting. For Abaye, once a person intentionally performs the physical act that constitutes the *melacha*, a factual mistake about the specific object does not dissolve his ownership of the act. It remains his act; he is a *shogeg* and obligated in a *korban*.

---

## Chomer Shabbat

### Multiple Melachot

Rava proceeds to ground his position in a *braita* that draws a systematic comparison between *Shabbos* and other *mitzvot*. The *braita* states: *chomer Shabbat mish'ar mitzvot ve-chomer sh'ar mitzvot mi-Shabbat* — *Shabbos* is more stringent than other *mitzvot* in certain respects, and other *mitzvot* are more stringent than *Shabbos* in others.

The stringency of *Shabbos*: if a person violated two *melachot* in one state of forgetfulness, he brings two separate *korbanot*, one for each. This is the principle of *chiluk melachot* — the categories of prohibited labor on *Shabbos* are conceptually distinct, and each generates an independent obligation. By other *mitzvot*, violating two categories in one state of forgetfulness yields only one *korban*.

### Categories vs. Acts

The *Gemara* asks: what exactly is being compared? If the point is two different categories — say, *kotzer* and *tochen* on *Shabbos* — versus eating *chelev* and *dam* by other prohibitions, then both cases yield two offerings, and there is no contrast. And if the point is two acts of the same category — *kotzer* twice on *Shabbos* — that is also one *korban*, the same as eating *chelev* twice. The *Gemara* therefore clarifies that the comparison is between two distinct *melachot* on *Shabbos* — which yield two *korbanot* — and the analogous case among other *mitzvot*, where even multiple distinct forms of violation in one forgetfulness yield only one. The clearest example of the latter is *avodah zarah*.

### Avodah Zarah

The principle is cited in the name of Rav Ami: *zivach ve-kitar ve-nisach* — if a person slaughtered a sacrifice to an idol, burned incense to it, and poured a libation to it, all in one state of forgetfulness, he brings only one *korban*. These are three distinct forms of *avodah zarah*, yet they are treated as one violation. The contrast with *Shabbos* is striking. By *Shabbos*, the *Torah* has differentiated the categories of *melacha* to such a degree that each stands independently; by *avodah zarah*, notwithstanding the conceptual distinctions between different modes of worship, a single *korban* covers all.

---

## Other Mitzvot Stringent

### Fat Mistake Case

The *braita* continues with the flip side: *chomer she'ar mitzvot mi-Shabbat* — the respects in which other *mitzvot* are more stringent than *Shabbos*. The *braita* states: *be-sh'ar mitzvot shogeg be-lo mitkaven chayav* — in other *mitzvot*, a person who transgressed without full intention — *shogeg be-lo mitkaven* — is obligated in a sin offering. This is not the case by *Shabbos*, where such a person would be exempt.

The *Gemara* presses immediately: what is this case of *shogeg be-lo mitkaven* by other *mitzvot*? The most natural reading is: *de-savar de-shuman hu ve-achalo* — he thought the fat in front of him was permissible fat (*shuman*) and ate it, but it turned out to be forbidden fat (*chelev*). He was doing the same act he intended — eating — but was mistaken about the factual nature of what he was eating. By other *mitzvot*, he brings a *korban*. By *Shabbos*, the analogous case — intending to cut *tallush* and cutting *mechubar* — yields no obligation. And this, Rava argues, is the proof for his position.

### Avodah Zarah Intent

The *Gemara* pauses to ask: what is the *shogeg be-lo mitkaven* case in the specific context of *avodah zarah*? The question is whether *avodah zarah* has its own internal version of this phenomenon.

### Synagogue Bow

One candidate: *ke-savar beis ha-keneset hu ve-yishtachaveh lo* — he thought he was in a synagogue and bowed toward it, but he was actually in a temple of idol worship and bowed in front of an idol. This would seem to be a case of unintentional worship. But the *Gemara* rejects it as an *asham* case: *harei libo la-shamayim* — his heart was directed toward Heaven. This is not a case of mistaken *avodah zarah* at all; it is an act of prayer directed at God, which happened to take place in front of an idol. The inner direction of worship is what defines the act.

### Statue Bow

A second candidate: *de-chaza andarta ve-sagid lah* — he saw a statue and bowed down before it. But again, the *Gemara* analyzes the act carefully. If he accepted the statue as a god — *kibblah alav ke-eloha* — then his act was *meizid*, fully intentional idolatry. If he did not accept it as a god — *lo kibblah alav ke-eloha* — then bowing before a statue as a sign of respect, without any acceptance of its divinity, is *lav klum* — it is nothing, an act of reverence rather than worship. Neither case is the relevant *shogeg be-lo mitkaven*.

### Ahava Yirah

The *Gemara* therefore identifies the case as: *ella be-ahavah u-ve-yirah* — he worshipped *avodah zarah* out of *ahavah* and *yirah*. According to *Rashi*'s standard explanation, this means he did so for material gain — *ahavas mamon* — or out of fear of harm, but without any genuine belief in the divinity of the idol. He fully intends the outward act of worship; he is not bowing accidentally or directing his heart elsewhere. Yet deep down he does not really believe in the god he is propitiating. He is performing the act knowingly but without genuine religious conviction. This is *shogeg be-lo mitkaven* as it applies to *avodah zarah*.

### Omer Mutar

Rava, however, reads the case differently. He maintains that the operative case is simply *be-omer mutar* — the standard case of *shogeg*, where the person thought the act was permissible. He did not realize that worshipping this deity was forbidden. In Rava's reading, the *braita*'s *shogeg be-lo mitkaven* for other *mitzvot* refers to the plain, classic case of thinking the act was permitted — *omer mutar* — which is the most common form of *shogeg*.

### Analogy Shabbat

The comparison to *Shabbos* then comes into focus. By *avodah zarah*: you knew you were performing an act of worship but thought it was permissible — that is a *korban*. By *Shabbos*: you intended to cut something *tallush* and cut something *mechubar* — according to Rava, that is *patur*. The cases are analogous: both involve knowing the type of act one is performing, while being mistaken about the specific circumstances. Rava argues that the *braita* confirms his position by demonstrating that this class of factual-mistake case is treated differently by *Shabbos* than by other *mitzvot*.

---

## Abaye Counter

### Spit vs. Fat

Abaye responds by denying the analogy that grounds Rava's proof. He reidentifies the *shogeg be-lo mitkaven* case for *she'ar mitzvot* not as thinking one was cutting *tallush* when it was really *mechubar*, but rather as: *de-savar roku u-vala'o* — he thought he was swallowing his own saliva and swallowed it, but it turned out there was forbidden fat in his mouth. He swallowed it unknowingly.

In Abaye's reading, this is the case that is truly analogous to the first, uncontested case of *mit'asek* by *Shabbos* — intending to lift *tallush* and ending up cutting *mechubar*.
