In both cases, the person intended a qualitatively different act from the one that constituted the sin: swallowing spit versus eating forbidden fat; lifting versus cutting. Abaye concedes this case is exempt by *Shabbos* — and it is precisely what the *braita* identifies as the *chomer she'ar mitzvot* case for other *mitzvot*.

### Benefit Principle

Why, then, is the person *chayav* for swallowing the forbidden fat, even though it was utterly unintended? Because of the principle: *sheken neheneh* — because he derived benefit. By *chalavin va-arayot* — forbidden fats and forbidden sexual relations — the experience of benefit creates an inescapable bond between the person and the act. You cannot say "that was not my act" when the substance entered your body and you derived benefit from it. The physical reality of benefit-taking constitutes ownership of the act in a way that cannot be disclaimed.

### No Mitasek

This is why *mit'asek* does not apply to *chalavin va-arayot*. In the domain of *Shabbos*, a person can sometimes say: the act that occurred was not the act I intended, and therefore I do not own it. But where one has eaten or engaged in a forbidden sexual relationship, the reality of benefit-taking forecloses that defense. The act is yours, and at minimum you are a *shogeg* obligated in a *korban*.

### Rava Abaye

To summarize the positions: Rava holds that a mistake about the facts of the object — thinking one is cutting *tallush* when cutting *mechubar* — is equivalent to *mit'asek* by *Shabbos* and exempts entirely. By *chalavin va-arayot* this defense is unavailable due to the principle of benefit-derived ownership, but everywhere else it applies. Abaye holds that once a person intends the category of act — cutting, in this case — and performs it, a factual mistake about the specific object does not dissolve ownership of the act; that remains *shogeg*, obligating a *korban*. The *mit'asek* exemption is reserved for cases where the person intended a qualitatively different act altogether — as in lifting versus cutting — or, where benefit is derived, it does not apply at all.

---

## Martyrdom

### Technical Issue

The final passage of the *shiur* addresses a pointed question that arises from the *Gemara*'s treatment of *ahavah va-yirah* in *avodah zarah* — specifically from Rava's position. If a person who worships an idol out of love of gain or fear, without genuine belief in its divinity, is exempt from the technical *korban* obligation — and by extension, is not truly performing an act of *avodah zarah* — then what is the basis for the principle of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor*? If someone holds a weapon to a person's head and demands that he bow to an idol, and if such a coerced act motivated by fear (*yirah*) is technically not *avodah zarah*, why should one be obligated to give up one's life rather than comply?

### Tosafot Limit

*Tosafot* addresses this question directly. One approach offered by *Tosafot* is to limit Rava's ruling to cases where it is patently obvious to all observers that the worship is not sincere — where the absence of genuine religious conviction is transparent. This would preserve the technical exemption in clear-cut cases while not undermining the principle of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* in ambiguous ones.

### Love of God

A more fundamental resolution, and arguably more satisfying, is that the obligation of martyrdom is not derived from the technical prohibition of *avodah zarah* at all. The source of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* is the positive commandment of *ve-ahavta et Hashem Elokecha be-chol levavcha u-ve-chol nafshecha u-ve-chol me'odecha* — to love God with all one's soul, even at the cost of life. The imperative to die rather than transgress is grounded in the *mitzvah* of love of God and total devotion to Him, not in the technical definition of what constitutes an actionable violation of *avodah zarah*.

The practical implication of this distinction is significant. Even if the act being demanded is not technically *avodah zarah* in the strict halachic sense — for example, being compelled to convert to a monotheistic religion that does not constitute *avodah zarah* — the obligation of martyrdom may still apply. What is at stake is not a precise halachic category of prohibited worship but rather the question of whether performing the demanded act constitutes a repudiation of one's fidelity to God. Where it does, the principle of self-sacrifice derives from love of God and is not contingent on the technical classification of the act as *avodah zarah*.

---

---

# Shabbat 74

## Overview: 39 Melachot

### Daf Context

Today's *daf* is 74, though we begin in the middle of 73b, which we did not finish in the previous session. A few words of introduction are appropriate, because we have been spending considerable time building toward this *mishna*. The *mishna* lists the thirty-nine *melachot*, and the *gemara* had in fact quoted its opening line no fewer than six times before actually arriving at it — building anticipation, as it were — and then once more immediately upon reaching it. The *mishna* on 73a is thus the central location, the canonical listing of the thirty-nine categories of *melacha*.

As we work through the *gemara* examining each category in turn, we should note at the outset something that is, frankly, a little frustrating: the discussion surrounding each *melacha* can be extremely terse. Sometimes this is because a later *perek* will develop that category more fully. Sometimes it is simply terse with very little material anywhere in the *gemara* about the exact parameters. It is genuinely difficult to explain why there is extensive discussion about purely theoretical questions — how many *chata'ot* one brings, or whether one may wear various objects on *Shabbat* — while the thirty-nine *melachot* themselves sometimes receive only a few lines. That said, the rest of the *masechet* does elaborate on many of them, sometimes addressing *de'oraisa* parameters, sometimes *de'rabbanan*, and sometimes leaving the distinction unclear.

### Four Categories

The thirty-nine *melachot* break down into four organizational categories. The process of making bread accounts for eleven *melachot*; making a garment accounts for thirteen; making a *klaf* — a type of parchment with writing upon it — accounts for nine; and the process of building a house accounts for the remaining group. Clothes, food, shelter, and, of course, books: that brings us to thirty-eight, with *hotza'ah* — carrying — standing apart as the thirty-ninth, not falling neatly into any of the preceding categories. The working assumption, which we will see operative throughout today's *gemara*, is that these categories are linked to what was done in the *mishkan*. Even though this is not precisely how the *mishkan*'s activities were categorized at the time, the *mishkan* serves as an organizing principle — a useful framework for thinking about those thirty-nine *melachot*.

### Yereim Position

That said, it is worth recalling the position of the *Yereim*, which holds that according to one approach in the *gemara*, the thirty-nine *melachot* are not based on the *mishkan* at all. Rather, they are grounded in what *Chazal* understood *melacha* to be — the main forms of constructive labor through which people interacted with the world. On this view, the categories are not merely organizational; they are the very reason these activities constitute *melachot*. The *Yereim* further notes: *lama mesarah hakatuv lachachamim* — once it was transmitted to the Sages, it became crystallized. No one can add to it. This is a radically different approach from the one normally taught, but it is the *Yereim*'s reading of one strand within the *gemara*.

### Avot & Toldot

The other essential preliminary concerns the distinction between *avot* and *toldot* — parent categories and their derivatives. A *toldah* is something similar to its *av* either in form or in function. Baking, cooking, and frying, for instance, are all similar in purpose and function — using heat to transform food. Some *toldot* are similar in form but not in function: grinding sawdust resembles grinding wheat into flour in its physical process — taking a whole thing and reducing it to small pieces — but the goal is entirely different. Conversely, some things are similar in function but not in form. As a general rule, one may assume that anything achieving a very similar goal is a *toldah*; things that share physical process but not goal are not always *toldot*.

### Parallel Avot

When something is similar to its parent category both in form and in function, it may not be a *toldah* at all, but rather a parallel *av*. This is the concept that Rashi and the Rambam refer to as *me'ein melacha achat* — "of the same type as one *melacha*" — meaning that an *av* category can encompass a set of parallel activities rather than a single defining act. Planting a seed, planting a tree, and perhaps even grafting are all direct manipulations of the thing one is trying to cause to grow, and so they may constitute parallel *avot*. By contrast, putting down manure, watering, or pruning a tree — where one is working on the surrounding environment to encourage growth rather than directly on the plant itself — would be *toldot*. The closer the resemblance in every dimension, the more likely the activity functions as a parallel *av* rather than as a derivative.

---

## Choresh

### Choresh Definitions

The *gemara* cites a *braita*: *hachoresh vehachofer vehachoretz* — whether one makes a furrow, digs a ditch for the sake of planting, or carves out a narrow channel — *kulan melacha achat hen*, they are all one *melacha*. Notice that the *gemara* does not call these *toldot*; it calls them one *melacha*, because they are all essentially the same thing: working the ground in some way to make it softer and more appropriate for planting. The physical change in the earth — whatever its precise form — serves the function of making the ground more fit for growth.

### Ground Leveling

Rav Sheshet then teaches: if one has a mound of earth — *gavshushit* — and removes it to level the ground, the *din* depends on context. *Bevayit chayav mishum boneh*: if it was done inside the house, where floors were made of dirt, one is liable for *boneh*, building, since leveling the floor is a significant part of the construction process. *Besadeh chayav mishum choresh*: if done out in the field, it constitutes *choresh*, plowing — even though plowing normally involves making a hole while here one is flattening something. The conceptual point is that one is working the ground, doing something to it that makes it more appropriate for planting. Whether that is a *toldah* or a parallel *av* is not entirely clear, but it is certainly within the *choresh* category when performed in the field.

### Filling a Hole

Rava extends the analysis with a parallel case. If one levels the ground by filling a hole — *siluka d'guma* — the same logic applies: *bevayit chayav mishum boneh*, inside the house it constitutes building a floor; *uvasadeh chayav mishum choresh*, in the field it constitutes plowing. Notice that in neither formulation does one's subjective intention determine the category. Rather, it is the objective character of the action — as determined by its location — that defines the *melacha*. This may be operating according to Rabbi Yehuda's view that *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa chayav*, but even so, we must objectively define what the action accomplished, and that determination depends on context.

### Digging for Dirt

Rabbi Abba's teaching presents the classic case of *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa*: *hachofer guma b'Shabbat v'eino tzarich ela l'afrah* — one digs a hole on *Shabbat* but only wants the dirt. Perhaps one needed dirt to cover a mess on a dirt floor, or for some similar purpose. The ruling is *patur*: one is exempt. The *issur* attaches to digging the hole, so why is one exempt? Because this is *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa*. The person performed the exact physical act of digging, and an outside observer would see what looks entirely like a *melacha*. But one's goal was entirely different from the stated purpose of the *melacha* — the purpose as defined by how it was performed in the *mishkan*. Digging a hole is a *melacha* because its goal is either to build something in the house or to make something fit for planting. Here the person is wholly indifferent to the hole; the dirt is the object. Performing the physical act for an entirely different purpose renders one *patur*.

Now, this is normally the subject of the famous dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Shimon holds one is exempt for *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa*; Rabbi Yehuda holds one is liable even so. The *gemara* therefore clarifies: *v'afilu Rabbi Yehuda* — even according to Rabbi Yehuda, *d'amar melacha she'eina tzricha legufa chayav aleha*, who holds that one is liable even when not acting for the *melacha*'s intended purpose — *hani milei metakken*, that is only when one's action is nonetheless constructive. *Hai mekalekel hu*: here, the hole is not making the floor more level, nor making the field more fit for planting. It is, objectively, making a mess. The hole is a *mekalkel*, not a *metakken*. If the hole happened to be dug in a way that would also serve planting purposes, then according to Rabbi Yehuda one would be liable even if that was not the intent. But if it is simply a disruptive hole that serves no constructive function in its location, even Rabbi Yehuda agrees there is no *chiyuv*.

---

## Kotzer

### Harvest Terms

Moving to *kotzer* — harvesting. Having addressed planting and plowing, the *gemara* now turns to cutting growing things. *Kotzer* applies when one picks something that is growing specifically because one wants that thing. Pruning for wood, picking fruit off a tree — any act of detaching a growing thing because one desires it — falls under this category.

The *gemara* teaches: *hakotzer, habotzer, v'hagoder, v'hamasik, ha'oreh* — whether one harvests wheat, harvests grapes, picks dates, picks olives, or picks figs — *kulam melacha achas hen*, they are all one *melacha*. Farmers use a different verb for every type of harvesting, but for our purposes these are all parallel forms of the same act. Crucially, the *gemara* does not call these *toldot* of one another; they are all parallel *avot*.

### Throwing at Dates

Rav Pappa introduces a striking case: *hai man d'shada pissa l'dikla v'atar tamrei* — someone throws a clump of earth or a rock at a palm tree and the dates fall. *Chayav shtayim* — this person has incurred liability for two *melachot*, and if done *beshogeg*, one would bring two *korbanot*. What are the two? *Achat mishum tolesh v'achat mishum mefarek*.

The first, *tolesh*, is the abstraction of *kotzer*: where *kotzer* referred specifically to wheat, the *gemara* here uses *tolesh* — removing something growing from where it grows — as the more general term. One is liable for detaching the dates from the tree. The second, *mefarek*, is understood by Rashi as a *toldah* of *dash*. Just as threshing extracts the kernel from the husk by applying pressure, so too *sechita* — squeezing — extracts juice or content from its container, and *mefarek* operates on the same principle: separating something from within which it is contained.

This model explains, for instance, why the *gemara* elsewhere characterizes milking a cow as *mefarek* — one is removing food from its container. Though Tosafot raises the difficulty that *mefarek* in other contexts is limited to *gidulei karka*, things growing from the ground, not from animals, the conceptual structure remains: *mefarek* is an abstraction of *dash*, the removal of food from that which contains it.

Why are dates specifically a case of *mefarek*? Rashi explains that dates grow in large clusters, much like grapes, so that knocking one loose separates it from the larger mass of which it is a part. Tosafot, however, objects: unlike juice within a grape or milk within an udder, a date in a cluster is not really enclosed within a shell. Tosafot therefore reads the case differently — what one does when striking the date is loosen it from its outer skin, *klipa ha-elyona*, the thin upper peel that covers the date. *U-kshemaka b'tamar mefarek et ha-klipa min ha-temarim*: by striking the date, one separates that outer layer from the date itself. Either way, the result is that throwing at dates generates a double liability: *tolesh* and *mefarek*.

This parallels the earlier observation that pruning can generate a double liability under certain conditions. Here too one act produces two *melachot* from two distinct categories, and since they are separate categories, two *chata'ot* would be required.

### Shinui Objection

Rav Ashi responds: *ein derech telisha b'kach v'ein derech prika b'kach* — throwing a rock at a tree is not the normal manner of *telisha*, nor the normal manner of *prika*. This constitutes a *shinui* — a non-standard method — and therefore one is not liable.

This sets up an important and recurring tension between Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi about the definition and scope of *shinui*. How far outside the norm must a method be before it qualifies as *shinui*? If an action is unusual but equally effective — or even more effective — does it still constitute *shinui*? The classic example is writing with one's non-dominant hand: that is *shinui* because it is both unusual and significantly more difficult, and the difficulty itself is part of what makes it a departure from the standard mode of action. But what of something unusual that presents no additional difficulty and produces the same result? These are the contours of a debate that will recur in later sections of the *gemara*.

---

## Me'amer

### Gathering Definition

The *gemara* continues with *me'amer* — gathering. Having cut the grain, one now gathers it, much as in Yosef's dream. The question of what exactly this *melacha* prohibits is more nuanced than it might initially appear. Does it cover any act of gathering scattered items together? If your children scatter their toys, may you not collect them?

### Salt Gathering

Rava addresses the case: *hai man de-khanif milkha mi-milkhasa* — someone gathers salt from a salt flat, a place where seawater is dried to extract the salt that spreads across a large area, which is then gathered into piles. This is strikingly similar to gathering grain: something has been produced by a drying or separating process, it lies spread out, and one gathers it together. Rava rules: *chayav mishum me'amer* — one is liable for gathering.

### Ground Growth Only

Abaye, however, limits this: *ein imur ela b'gidulei karka* — *me'amer* applies only to things that grow from the ground. This is an important limitation that we sometimes apply and sometimes do not across different *melachot*. We already encountered the question regarding *mefarek* and *dash* — do they apply to milking cows, which does not involve *gidulei karka*? Here, at least for *me'amer*, Abaye explicitly limits the *melacha* to things growing from the ground. Salt, even though its gathering is functionally similar — it is a food substance, it undergoes a processing stage, and then one gathers it — is not *gidulei karka* and therefore does not carry the *issur* of *me'amer*.

### Practical Examples

It follows from Abaye's limitation that gathering toys into a toy box on *Shabbat* is not *me'amer*. What would constitute *me'amer*, then? Twigs that have fallen from trees, scattered across the ground and gathered for firewood — that is a textbook example of *me'amer*, much like the *mekoshish eitzim*.

One useful practical resource here is the illustrated *39 Melachos* set, which presents visual examples with clear distinctions between *de'oraisa* and *de'rabbanan* cases. Among the examples it lists for *me'amer*: piling scattered fruit in an orchard, putting together a bouquet of flowers, and — interestingly — stringing figs, with a note that this applies even at home. The last example is striking, because one might have assumed that *me'amer* applies only where the items lie as they fell, before any prior gathering. One might have expected *ein imur achar imur* — that once something has already been gathered and brought inside, a second act of collecting cannot constitute *me'amer*. Yet the stringing of figs — a process by which figs were pressed tightly together into balls, a distinct stage of processing for sale or storage — raises exactly this question. The details can be found in the relevant *mekorot*, much of it drawn from the *Mishna Berurah*.

---

## Dash & Combing

### Threshing Types

The *gemara* continues with *dash*, threshing. Animals would be driven over a board fitted with cleats, pressing down on the stalks of grain to extract the kernel from the husk. A *tanna* teaches: *ha-dash, ha-menapeitz, v'ha-menafet* — whether one threshes grain, combs flax to remove its seeds, or combs cotton to remove its seeds — *kuleihu melacha achas hen*, they are all one *melacha*.

At first glance this seems straightforward: they all accomplish the same thing, extracting a kernel from surrounding material, just applied to different objects. But there is a meaningful difference. As far as one can tell, the purpose of working the cotton or the flax is to make the cotton and flax themselves usable — not because one wants the seeds. So the goal of the action is inverted relative to threshing: in threshing, one wants the kernels; in combing cotton or flax, one wants the surrounding fibers and the seeds are the byproduct.

### Wool Combing Question

Rashi raises the question directly: why are *menapeitz* and *menafet* not treated as *toldot* of wool combing rather than as parallel *avot* of *dash*? One might say that the object being worked determines the category — that wool, flax, and cotton are materially distinct enough to warrant different classifications. But that still does not explain why the *gemara* does not at minimum call them *toldot* of something. Perhaps the form — separating something from the material surrounding it — places them alongside *dash*; perhaps they are a type of *borer*, separating what one wants from what one does not. Whatever the precise categorization, the *gemara* calls them *melacha achas*, which suggests they function as parallel *avot* rather than as derivatives — even if the reasoning is difficult to unpack entirely.

---

## Separation Melachot

### Three Separation Methods

The *gemara* continues with three *melachot* that are all essentially ways of separating good from bad: *hazoreh*, winnowing — throwing threshed grain into the air so the wind carries off the chaff while the denser kernels fall; *haborer*, selecting by hand to remove dirt and debris; and *meraked*, sifting through a sieve. The *gemara* acknowledges the obvious: *hainu zoreh hainu borer hainu meraked* — winnowing, selecting, and sifting are all conceptually identical.

### Mishkan Principle

Abaye and Rava both respond with a unifying principle: *kol milta dehavya bamishkan, af al gav de-ika dedamya leh, chashiv leh* — anything that was a distinct process in the *mishkan*, even if there exist other activities similar to it, receives its own separate category. Each of these three processes — winnowing, selecting, and sifting — was performed as a distinct operation in the *mishkan*, and that is sufficient to grant each its own *melacha*, regardless of their conceptual overlap. Part of what seems to motivate this ruling is the need to account for thirty-nine distinct *melachot* — though the *gemara* has not yet said so explicitly.

### Kutesh Question

If the principle is that anything done in the *mishkan* receives its own category, then *velichtov nami koteish* — why not also include *kotesh*, the pounding that removes the inner layer of bran from the wheat kernel after threshing but before the fine grinding? The process works as follows: threshing removes the outer husk; pounding removes the inner bran layer still attached to the kernel, yielding whiter flour; then fine grinding produces flour. So why not count *kotesh* as its own *melacha*?

Abaye answers: *sheken ani ochel pitto belo ketisha* — a poor person eats his bread without this step. The bran is not always removed; people who eat coarser bread do not pound the grain at this stage. So *kotesh* was not a universal step in the process.

Rashi adds a further observation: there is actually an ambiguity about which category *kotesh* belongs to. One might classify it under *tochen*, since it involves pounding something and breaking it up. Or one might classify it under *borer*, since its purpose is to remove a part one does not want from the part one does want. Rashi's deeper point is that we are constructing a coherent organizational principle around the process of making bread, and we want to count only steps that are always performed. Since *kotesh* is not always performed, it is not listed — not because it lacks the substance of a *melacha*, but because the list aims to describe a standard, universal process. Since it would in any case be subsumed under *tochen*, there is no harm in omitting it.

### Thirty-Nine Limit

Rava offers a more fundamental answer: *hai mani Rebi hi, d'amar avot melachot arbayim chaser achas* — this *mishna* follows the view of Rebi, who holds there are exactly thirty-nine *melachot*. The number is not merely a convenient count — it is a fixed limit. *V'i chashiv kotesh havu lehu arbayim* — if *kotesh* were counted, there would be forty. Therefore it cannot be included.

The *gemara* then presses: but if we have to reach exactly thirty-nine and cannot exceed it, why do we count three separate *melachot* for what is essentially one process of separation — *zoreh*, *borer*, and *meraked* — while including *kotesh* only once, or not at all? Rashi notes the asymmetry: if *kotesh* is a type of *tochen*, we have two types of *borer* and two types of *tochen*, yet the *gemara* assigned three to separation and one to grinding. Why not swap one of the three separation *melachot* for *kotesh*?

The *gemara* concludes: *ela mechvarta ke'Abaye* — Abaye's answer is the better one. The reason *kotesh* is not counted is not primarily the arithmetic of thirty-nine, but the fact that it was not a universal step in the bread-making process. The arithmetic does play a role — the *gemara* acknowledges that we could have organized things differently and arrived at the same number — but the decisive factor is whether a step was universally performed. This does raise the broader question of whether the thirty-nine are an objective list or an organizational scheme that could have been constructed somewhat differently. The *gemara*'s discussion here suggests, perhaps uncomfortably, that both things are somewhat true.

One further note: Rashi comments that the bread-related *melachot* in the *mishkan* were actually performed not for bread at all but in the processing of plants to extract dye. The "bread" framework is an organizing metaphor, not a description of what literally happened in the *mishkan*. This makes the universality argument somewhat ironic — we are assessing which steps were "always" performed in a process that was never actually about bread — but the organizing principle holds regardless.

---

## Borer Part 1

### Borer Principle

The *gemara* now moves to the *halachot* of *borer* in earnest. A *braita* teaches: if one had before him multiple types of foodstuffs — *borer v'ochel, borer u'maniach*, one may sort and eat, one may sort and set aside. *Velo yavor*: but do not do *borer*. *V'im beirer chayav chatas*: and if one did *borer*, one is liable to bring a sin offering. This is perplexing: it says one may sort and then says do not sort. The *gemara* immediately asks: *mai ka'amar*? What exactly is being said?

What the *braita* is missing is the key criterion: what distinguishes the permitted sorting from the prohibited *borer*? Three different *amoraim* each insert their own criterion.

### Timing Criterion

Ulla says: *borer v'ocheil l'vo bayom* — one may sort if one will eat that day; *u'borer u'maniach l'vo bayom* — one may set aside if it will be eaten that day, which Tosafot explains means setting it aside for someone else who will eat it that day. *U'l'machar lo yivror*: but one may not sort for tomorrow. If one did sort for tomorrow, *chayav chatas* — one is liable.

Rav Chisda challenges this: *v'chi mutar l'afos l'vo bayom? V'chi mutar l'vashel l'vo bayom?* Does one bake for today? Does one cook for today? These are certainly prohibited even if one will eat the product the same day. How does "for today" make any difference?

The implicit logic behind Ulla's criterion — as Tosafot explains — is that selecting food in the context of eating might be classified as part of the eating process, *derech achila*, rather than as food preparation. Baking and cooking, by contrast, are always preparation, never eating. But even granting this framework, selecting for "later today" is plainly not part of the immediate act of eating. The criterion of today versus tomorrow is therefore rejected.

### Quantity Criterion

Rav Chisda proposes instead: *borer v'ocheil pachas m'kishiur, borer u'maniach pachas m'kishiur* — one may sort less than the minimum *shiur*, i.e., less than the volume of a *grogeres* (a dried fig). *V'kishiur lo yivror* — do not sort the minimum amount or more. Rav Yosef challenges with the same question: *v'chi mutar l'afos pachas m'kishiur?* Does one bake less than a *shiur*? The criterion of quantity is likewise rejected. Rashi notes in passing that there is a question of *chatzi shiur* — a biblical prohibition of performing a *melacha* below the minimum — though its application to *melachot* as opposed to prohibited foods is debated.

The underlying idea behind Rav Chisda's criterion — again, as Tosafot explains — was that a small quantity might be considered eating rather than preparation. But this too is rejected: the distinction between preparation and eating is not defined by quantity.

### Method Criterion

Rav Yosef proposes: *borer v'ocheil b'yad, borer u'maniach b'yad* — one may sort using one's hand. *B'kanun u'v'tamchui lo yivror* — one should not use a funnel or a large dish, which facilitates the sorting without being the professional tool; if one did, *patur aval assur* — exempt but prohibited, perhaps because of *shinui* or because it begins to resemble the professional act of *borer*. *U'vinfa u'v'khvara lo yivror* — one certainly should not use a sieve or sifter, the professional vessels for separation. If one uses such a vessel, *chayav chatas* — one is fully liable.

This criterion has considerable logical force: it distinguishes between *derech achila* — the natural manner of eating, which involves using one's hand to pick out what one wants — and the professional activity of *borer*, marked by the use of dedicated tools. The three-tier structure (permitted by hand, exempt but prohibited with a non-standard vessel, fully liable with a professional vessel) also introduces the nuance of *shinui*: using an intermediate vessel is a departure from normal eating but not the full professional mode of *borer*.

Rav Hamnuna objects: *midi kanun v'tamchui tani?* The *braita* never mentioned a funnel or a large dish. Tosafot explains the objection: if there are to be three levels — *mutar*, *patur aval assur*, and *chayav chatas* — based on the specific type of vessel, the *braita* would need to have specified those vessels explicitly. Since it did not, this reading cannot be correct as a *peshat* of the *braita*, even if the underlying legal distinction is sound.

### Immediacy Criterion

Abaye therefore proposes: *borer v'ochel l'alter u'borer u'maniach l'alter* — one may sort if eating immediately; *u'vo bayom lo yivror* — do not sort for later that day; *v'im birer, na'asah k'borer l'otzar* — if one did sort for later, one has done the paradigmatic act of *borer*: selecting into storage, an early stage of preparation. Anything beyond immediate is the biblical *borer*, and one is *chayav chatas*.

Abaye can also claim some support in the *braita* itself: the phrase *borer v'ochel* implies immediate eating, since *ochel* suggests the eating follows directly from the sorting. This is better grounded in the text than the previous criteria, and the *gemara* affirms it: *shapir amar Nachmani* — Rava, hearing the explanation, says that Abaye (whose other name was Nachmani) gave a fine *peshat*.

What exactly constitutes "immediate," *l'alter*? The general accepted definition is the period of last-minute preparation just before a meal — the window during which one prepares things for that same meal, even for the end of the meal. If one's meal is expected to last an hour and one sorts something that will be eaten at the end, that may still qualify as *l'alter* if the sorting occurred within the normal last-minute preparation window. Any *psak halacha* on the precise parameters requires a separate discussion.

---

## Borer Part 2

### Food vs. Chaff

The *gemara* does not settle on Abaye's criterion alone. Rav Huna now introduces the criterion of direction: *borer v'ochel, ochel mitoch psoles* — one may sort food from chaff, removing the food and leaving the waste; *borer u'maniach, ochel mitoch psoles* — or one may set aside food for someone else, still removing the food from the waste. *Psoles mitoch ochel lo yivror* — however, one may not remove the chaff from the food; *v'im birer chayav chatas* — and if one did, one is liable.

The logic here is that removing food from chaff mimics the natural manner of eating — one focuses on the food and takes it — while removing chaff from food is the professional manner of *borer*, the act of the one who selects and prepares produce for storage. The latter is precisely how grain was sorted in its early processing stages: the chaff was removed from the grain, not the grain from the chaff.

Abaye objects: *midi ochel mitoch psoles katani?* The *braita* does not use the language of food from chaff or chaff from food. Abaye therefore stands by his own criterion of immediacy. Nevertheless, the *gemara* does not abandon Rav Huna's distinction — it resurfaces shortly.

### Two Food Types

The *gemara* introduces a further complexity: what if one has two types of food before one — not food and chaff, but two perfectly edible items, one of which one happens not to want? The *gemara* reports a case: *hayu l'fanav shenei minei ochlin — borer v'achal, borer v'hiniach*. One sorted and ate; one sorted and set aside. Rav Ashi says *patur* — exempt; Rabbi Yirmeya mi-Difti says *chayav* — liable.

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya — ha be-kanon ve-tamchuy, ha be-nafa u-kevara*. The case of *patur* involves using a non-standard vessel, while the case of *chayav* involves using a professional sieve or sifter. This resolution reintroduces Rav Yosef's vessel criterion. Notice what has happened: even after the *gemara* affirmed Abaye's answer as the best *peshat* of the *braita*, the other criteria — vessel type and direction (food from chaff versus chaff from food) — have quietly been reinstated through subsequent *sugya* material.

This is the crucial structural question underlying all of *borer*: are these criteria "and's" or "or's"? Must one satisfy all three — immediate, by hand, removing food from chaff — for the act to be *mutar*? Or does satisfying any one of them suffice? The weight of *halachic* tradition is that all three must be satisfied for the act to be *mutar*, and that missing even one renders it a *de'oraisa* violation. This is not stated explicitly in the *gemara* but is where the *halacha* arrives.

### Fruit Basket Story

The *gemara* relates a story involving Rav Bibi. It was his *Shabbat* of attendance — Rashi explains that it was his turn to see to the needs of the rabbis. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi came to visit, and he placed before them a basket of fruit, *shada kammaihu kalkala de-firi*, pouring it out in front of them and letting them select for themselves. The *gemara* notes: *v'lo yadana* — we do not know the reason. Was it *im mishum de-savar ochel mi-toch psolet assur* — because he thought that even removing food from chaff is forbidden, and therefore he did not want to sort for them in advance? Or was it *mishum ayin yafa* — simply a generous gesture, allowing his guests to take what they liked?

Tosafot offers a clarification: perhaps Rav Bibi thought that when the sorting is not *l'alter* — not immediate — even *ochel mitoch psoles* is forbidden. So he did not sort in advance because it would not have been immediate, and the guests sorted for themselves immediately as they ate. Whatever the precise reason, what is significant is what the story quietly demonstrates: all three criteria are still in play. The story follows directly on Abaye's ruling about immediacy, yet it invokes the *ochel mitoch psoles* distinction. Neither criterion has displaced the other.

### Lupine Exception

Chizkiya teaches a case that seems to contradict the established rules: *ha-borer turmusin mi-toch psolet shelahen chayav* — one who removes lupines from their shells is liable. This is striking, because this appears to be *ochel mitoch psoles* — removing food from waste — which we established is the permitted direction. Why is it *chayav*?

The *gemara* explains: *shani turmusin de-shalkei lehu sheva zimni* — lupines are different because they are boiled seven times. Without continued boiling — or without timely removal from their shells — they will rot. The implication is that because of this boiling process, when one attempts to extract the seeds they become soft and mushy. The shells that have not yet been similarly processed are comparatively solid. In some sense, therefore, what appears to be *ochel mitoch psoles* is actually more akin to *psolet mitoch ochel* — one is removing the degraded, mushy component from the still-intact material. *U-ke-psolet mi-toch ochel dami*: it resembles chaff from food. This is admittedly difficult to understand clearly, and the difficulty is compounded by the fact that Chizkiya says the person is *chayav* rather than merely *assur* — a seemingly strong ruling for what might have seemed like an edge case of *ochel mitoch psoles*. Rashi offers several attempts at explanation, none of which resolves the matter entirely.

---

## Tachan

### Chopping Beets

Rav Pappa teaches: *hai man defaris silka chayav mishum tochen* — one who chops up a beet is liable for the *melacha* of *tochen*, grinding. This is a jarring statement. Cutting food into small pieces is *tochen*?

### Cutting vs. Grinding

Tosafot limits the ruling: *davka besilka shayach techina, aval shear ochlin sharei* — only with beets does the concept of grinding apply; for other foods it is permitted. The basis for the distinction is not fully spelled out, but perhaps beets, which are normally not eaten raw, undergo a meaningful transformation when minced very finely — something approaching a real change in substance rather than merely a change in size.

The Rosh, however, reads the text differently. He understands the *gemara* not to be discussing beets at all — he reads *silta* rather than *silka* — and understands the case as one in which a plant has been reduced to something almost dust-like, its leaves removed and the material ground to a fine powder. The Rosh's position is that ordinary cutting of food into pieces is not *tochen*. The question is: at what point does cutting stop being cutting and become grinding? The Rosh holds that real *tochen* requires a genuine physical transformation — reducing a solid to something powder-like — not merely producing smaller pieces of the same substance.

This question has immediate practical implications. Can one make egg salad on *Shabbat*? The analysis involves multiple *melachot*: mincing the ingredients (*tochen*), adding mayonnaise (*losh*, kneading), and so on. The *Tzitz Eliezer* addresses this at length, concluding that it is permitted, relying in part on the argument that mincing food does not constitute *tochen*, and in part on the principle that — by analogy to *borer* — if done *l'alter*, immediately before eating, it falls within the context of eating rather than preparation. One should not *pasken* from these remarks alone, but the framework is instructive.

### Sawdust Example

Rav Menashya teaches: *hai man desalis silti chayav mishum tochen* — one who produces sawdust is liable for *tochen*. This is a clearer case. Sawdust represents a genuine physical transformation: one takes solid wood and reduces it to fine powder. The material is not merely smaller; it has undergone a real change. Notably, this applies even though wood is not food — it is not part of the bread-making process — though it does grow from the ground. This demonstrates that *tochen* is not limited to food but extends to any material that undergoes this kind of transformative reduction.

### Kapid Amishchata

Rav Ashi adds a related but distinct ruling: *ei kapid amishchata chayav mishum mechatech* — if one cuts wood and is particular about the exact size of each piece, one is liable for *mechatech*, the *melacha* of cutting.

This introduces an important distinction between two related categories. *Koreia*, tearing, is a *melacha* that applies to cloth: any productive tearing of cloth, without a requirement of precision. *Mechatech*, cutting, applies to other materials — leather, wood, and similar substances — but carries the additional requirement of *kapid amishchata*: one must be particular about cutting to a specific, intended size. Tearing a cloth napkin at random is *koreia*; cutting a plank to an exact measurement is *mechatech*. The criterion of precision — caring about the exact dimension of the resulting piece — is what transforms ordinary cutting into the *melacha* of *mechatech*. This criterion will recur in later discussions.

---

## Dash & Sechita

### Dash Definition

The *gemara* addresses *dash*, threshing, as the parent *melacha*, and *sechita*, squeezing, as its *toldah*. The *av melacha* of *dash* is the act of threshing grain in the field: an animal walks over a board fitted with cleats, pressing down on stalks to extract the kernel from the husk. The *toldah* is *sechita* — squeezing fruit for its juice — because the act is structurally identical: extracting the desired content from its container. Threshing happens in the field; squeezing happens in the kitchen. The change of venue makes it a *toldah* rather than a parallel *av*.

### Fruit Categories

Not all fruits are equal in this context. *De'oraisa*, the prohibition of *sechita* applies only to olives and grapes. The reason is historical and functional: those were the fruits that were historically processed specifically for their juice — olives for oil, grapes for wine. For all other fruits, squeezing is *miderabanan*, unless it is common practice in a given place to squeeze them for their liquid. In America, for example, it is standard practice to squeeze oranges for juice, and therefore squeezing an orange in America would be *de'oraisa*.

### Lemon Squeezing

The case of lemon is particularly instructive. Unlike oranges, one does not drink lemon juice; one uses it to flavor food. The *halacha* is therefore that one may squeeze a lemon directly onto food on *Shabbat*. The reason is the principle of *mashke haba le'ochel ke'ochel dami* — liquid that goes directly into food takes on the status of food rather than of liquid. Since the juice is being absorbed directly into what one is eating, one is not producing a liquid in any independent sense. However, one may not squeeze a lemon into an empty cup, because there one is creating an independent liquid — *sechita* — even if it is only *miderabanan*. Squeezing onto fish: *mutar*. Squeezing into a cup: *assur*.

---

---

# Shabbat 75

## Cooking: Food & Non-Food

### Kneading & Baking Org.

The daf begins on 74b, five lines from the bottom, with the words *ve-halash ve-ha'ofeh* — kneading and baking. The Gemara opens with a question posed by Pappa: why does our *tanna* ignore the *bishul simmanim* — the cooking of the various plant-based materials from which dyes were extracted — which did in fact occur in the *Mishkan*, and instead record *ofeh*, baking? The answer is *tanna didan siddura de-pas nakat*: our *tanna* is organizing the *melachot* according to the process of bread-making. As previously discussed, this may be merely an organizational principle — the conventional understanding — or it may reflect a distinct conceptual framework for understanding the *melachot*, as the *Yereim* understands it.

### Peg in Oven Example

Rav Aha bar Rav Avira teaches: one who throws a moist peg into an oven is liable for *bishul* — cooking. The Gemara initially asks *pshita* — is this not obvious? Yet the moment we are no longer speaking about food, nothing is self-evident with respect to *bishul*. The Gemara therefore explains the underlying concern: one might have thought the person's intention is *lishuruyei maneh* — to harden the peg, which one does by placing it in the oven and evaporating the moisture. The Gemara's response is *de-mirpa rafi* — first the peg becomes softer — *ve-hadar kamit* — and only afterward does it harden. The precise science may be uncertain, but what matters is the Gemara's conceptual point: *bishul* applies to non-foodstuffs, and the key definition it focuses on is the use of heat to induce softening. By contrast, when it comes to food, the focus is on heat altering taste — whether it renders something edible, whether it improves flavor, and related questions that are themselves subject to debate. When the object is not food, the operative definition shifts to heat-induced softening, mirroring what happens in the normal cooking process.

### Pitch Liquefying

Rava bar Rav Huna adds: one who heats up pitch — liquefying it — is likewise liable for *bishul*. Again the Gemara asks *pshita*, and again there is a genuine concern: *keivan de-hadar ve-ikushi* — since once the pitch cools it will re-harden, one might have thought this does not qualify as cooking. The Gemara rules that it does. The question arises: is the *hava amina* rooted in the problem of *eino mitkayem* — something that does not last? When one heats water it is cooked even though it will cool, and perhaps the same logic applies here: the transformation lasts long enough to serve its function. If one wants liquefied pitch to pour onto a surface, the fact that it will later re-harden is irrelevant — a meaningful transformation has occurred in the interim. In any event, the Gemara treats this as *bishul* without hesitation.

### Cooking Non-Food Items

Two further points emerge from these cases. First, *bishul* is not limited to food. Second, it is not limited to *gidulei karka* — things that grow from the ground. Some other *melachot* are so limited, but one may certainly cook meat and be liable. Pitch, which derives from some petroleum-like substance, is also included. The heat-induced transformation of an object is the core definition of *bishul*, irrespective of what category of object is involved.

---

## Multiple Melachot Exampl…

### Barrel & Oven

With the discussion of *bishul* essentially concluded, the Gemara moves into a series of cases that function almost as puzzles: how many distinct *melachot* can one transgress within a single production process? Rava teaches: one who makes a pottery barrel — *chavita* — is liable for seven *sin offerings*, having transgressed seven distinct *melachot*. One who makes an oven — *tanura* — which is similar pottery but is subsequently glazed and finished, is liable for eight. The Gemara does not enumerate the categories itself; for that one must consult Rashi.

### Rashi's Barrel List

Rashi's enumeration of the seven *melachot* in making a pottery barrel runs approximately seven lines in the standard text. First, grinding up the earth to be used for the pottery — this is *tochen*. One might wonder whether pulverizing clay is truly comparable to the paradigmatic *tochen* of grinding wheat into fine powder, or whether breaking up earth into small pieces is categorically different. Yet Rashi elsewhere rules that mincing beets constitutes *tochen*, so grinding dirt follows. Second, selecting out the stones from the earth — *borer*, selecting. Third, sifting the earth through a sieve — one wants clean, fine material for the plaster or pottery. Fourth, mixing the earth with water to create a moldable clay — this is *losh*, kneading, analogous to adding water to flour to create a homogeneous mass. Fifth, smoothing over the surface — *memareiach*, smoothing, which in the leather context refers to spreading a substance evenly. Sixth, making the fire — *mavir*. Seventh, placing it in the fire — *mevashel*, cooking. One might note a tension: the Gemara's earlier discussion emphasized that *mevashel* requires the object to first become soft, yet fired pottery only hardens. Rashi does not pause to address this. Note also that Rashi does not count digging the hole from which the dirt was extracted, because that constitutes *melacha she'einah tzerichah legufah* — a destructive act whose byproduct alone is desired. Others offer variant lists.

### Makeh BeFatish

The additional eighth *melacha* for the oven is explained by Rashi as follows: after removing the vessel from the kiln, one applies a plaster coating. Now *memareiach* — smoothing — has already been counted. Rashi therefore classifies this final application as *makeh b'fatish* — the last finishing act performed actively and deliberately. A crucial distinction emerges: when an object is merely passively completed by being left in the oven, that passive completion does not constitute *makeh b'fatish*. Only an active, deliberate final act — such as manually applying plaster to the finished oven — qualifies. This raises a general question about *makeh b'fatish b'ochlin*: if *makeh b'fatish* is the generic last act of completion, would finishing a food item also trigger it? The question is noted but not here resolved.

### Boneh & Vessels

There is a noteworthy dispute between Rashi and Tosafot — joined by the *Geonim* — about whether one of the acts in this process should be counted as *boneh*, building. Rashi holds *ein binyan bikeilim* — there is no category of building applied to vessels. Tosafot disagrees, arguing that *ein binyan bikeilim* is not an absolute principle. It means that reassembling a disassembled vessel does not constitute *binyan*, but creating a vessel from raw materials entirely from scratch does constitute *boneh* and the prohibition applies even to vessels. This disagreement has practical *halachic* implications that recur later in the tractate.

### Basket: 11 & 13

Abaye then extends the exercise: one who makes a reed wicker basket — *chalsa* — is liable for eleven *sin offerings*. If one adds a lip around its opening, the total rises to thirteen. The question, as before, is how to enumerate the *melachot* involved.

### Rashi Basket Breakdown

Rashi's analysis of the eleven *melachot* in basket-making proceeds as follows. First, one prunes branches from a tree. Rashi notes that since one also intends to prune the tree — benefiting it — this yields two *melachot* simultaneously: pruning as a form of planting (*zore'a*), and uprooting what is detached from its place of growth — *kotzer*. That is two. Third, gathering the fallen branches into a pile — *me'ameir*, gathering. Fourth, selecting the good ones — *borer*. Fifth, smoothing the sticks to be used — *memachek*. That is five. Sixth, Rashi says one breaks the sticks into two or three pieces — and classifies this as *tochen*. This is admittedly striking, since *tochen* conventionally involves reducing something to tiny particles, and breaking sticks into a few pieces does not obviously fit that description. Rashi's precise reasoning here is not fully elaborated, and this classification does not appear to play a major role in the later *poskim*'s treatment of the parameters of *tochen*. Seventh, cutting the sticks to particular sizes — *mechatech*, cutting to a precise measure. That is seven. Then come three acts associated with weaving on a loom: setting up the frame — *meisach*; weaving — *oreig*; and the third loom-related act as well. That yields ten. Finally, trimming the edges upon completion — *makeh b'fatish*. That is eleven.

The additional two *melachot* that bring the total to thirteen when one adds the lip are *tofer* — sewing — and *kosher* — knotting, since the lip requires some stitching and knotting to attach. The interesting *chidush* in Rashi's list, as noted, is the application of *tochen* to the breaking of sticks — a classification that is difficult to square with the standard parameters of that *melacha*, and one that the *rishonim* do not appear to have leveraged significantly in their practical discussions.

---

## Wool from Live Animal

### Three Offerings

Rabbah bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan: one who spins wool directly off the back of a live sheep on *Shabbat* — a technique in which the animal is brought indoors and the wool is spun directly from it without prior shearing — is liable for three *sin offerings*: one for *gozez* (shearing), one for *menapeitz* (combing, presumably accomplished through the pulling and twisting involved in the process), and one for *toveh* (spinning). Even though all three acts are performed as a single continuous process, each constitutes a distinct *melacha*.

### Rav Kahana: No Derech

Rav Kahana disagrees: *ein derech gezizah b'kach v'ein derech menapeitz b'kach v'ein derech tveiyah b'kach* — this is not the normal way of shearing, not the normal way of combing, and not the normal way of spinning. Accordingly, one is exempt from all three. This reflects the principle that liability attaches only when an act is performed in its normal manner — *derech* — and performing all three in a single unconventional process disqualifies each of them.

### Wise Women's Practice

The Gemara challenges Rav Kahana from a *baraita* cited in the name of Rabbi Nechemia. The verse states *ve-chol ishah chachmat lev beyadeiha tavu* — all wise-hearted women spun with their hands. Rabbi Nechemia explains what made them so remarkable: they drove the goats into the water to wash the wool, then spun the fiber directly off the goats. *Alma tveiyah gabei behemah shemah tveiyah* — we see that spinning directly from a live animal is called spinning.

### Wisdom Exception

The Gemara resolves the challenge: *chochma yesirah shani* — that case involved exceptional wisdom, a special technique that only particularly skilled women could execute. For ordinary people, spinning directly from a live animal is not the normal manner of performing any of these three *melachot*. One might ask whether those exceptional women themselves would be liable — and perhaps for them, since this constitutes their normal *derech*, the liability would apply. Tosafot addresses this: even if one is personally capable of performing the act in this unusual way, *batlah da'ato eitzel kol adam* — one's personal practice is nullified against the standard practice of people generally, and so it is still not considered a normal manner of performance. A further point, raised by a student and worth noting, is that even though we derive the *melachot* from the *Mishkan*, the parameters of what constitutes a normal *derech* are applied as general standards — not simply based on what was done in the *Mishkan* itself.

---

## Feather Processing

### Three-Part Process

The Gemara introduces a *baraita*: one who plucks a feather from a bird, snips it, and strips the feathers from the quill is liable for three *sin offerings*. The question of whether the bird must be alive is an interesting one — *gezizah* involves cutting something off a living creature, and it is debatable whether a dead animal would be included. Rashi clarifies that *kanaf* here refers to the feathers of the wing.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish identifies the three categories. Plucking the feather — *tolesh* — is liable because of *gozez*, shearing. This is not a significant novelty, since shearing refers to cutting something from a living creature for the sake of the detached material. Snipping the tip — *kotem* — is liable because of *mechatech*, cutting to a precise size. *Mechatech* requires that one care about producing a specific size or shape. Rashi explains that one is not merely cutting off the sharp lower tip; rather, one is cutting off the upper tip of the feather, which can be used for down — but only a specific portion of the tip yields usable material. One therefore cuts at a precise location to obtain a precise quantity. Rashi alternatively suggests that since the feather will ultimately serve as a quill, the cut is made at a particular point to produce a usable writing instrument of the right dimensions. Either way, this is *mechatech*. Stripping the feathers from the quill — *memaret* — is liable because of *memachek*, smoothing.

### Memachek Parameters

This last ruling is striking and important. Smoothing in its primary context — leather-making — involves a desire that the smoothed surface be smooth. Here, however, one stripping feathers from a quill has no particular interest in the smoothness of the result; one simply wants to remove the feathers. And yet the Gemara rules it is *memachek*. Unless, that is, one intends to use the quill as a writing instrument, in which case smoothness of the barrel is indeed desired. This ambiguity goes to the heart of *memachek*: must one specifically desire a smooth result, or does the act of smoothing itself suffice regardless of intent? This has significant practical consequences. If one applies a poultice or salve to a wound, spreading it flat across the surface, one does not necessarily want the salve itself to form a smooth layer — one merely wants to apply it. Nevertheless, as we will see, the Gemara rules such spreading constitutes *memachek*. One might ask whether two *melachot* can be violated simultaneously: if shaving, for example, is *gozez* because one cuts from a living body, might it simultaneously be *memachek* because one desires the skin smooth? This is indeed analogous to the present case, where stripping feathers is both an act of removal and an act of smoothing.

### Modern Applications

These questions bear directly on contemporary practice. *Sicha* — applying oil to the skin — is prohibited on *Yom Kippur* but not on *Shabbat*; oil of standard viscosity applied to the skin raises no *Shabbat* concern. The question arises regarding thicker substances: if a cream or ointment thicker than oil is spread smooth across the skin, does that constitute *memachek*? The practical guidance that follows from this is that one should dab such substances on rather than spread them smooth — applying the cream in multiple spots and allowing movement or pressure to distribute it, rather than deliberately smoothing it into an even layer. The same considerations arise with liquid soap — whose viscosity is arguably no greater than oil, and which one does not intend to leave as a thin smooth coating — and with toothpaste, where the question is whether one is genuinely trying to create a smooth spread or merely applying an agent to all surfaces. These remain live questions in *memachek*'s parameters.

---

## Knotting & Unknottin (II)

### Tent Stakes

The Gemara turns to the *melachot* of *kosher* (knotting) and *matir* (unknotting), which will be treated in detail in a later chapter. Here it poses a preliminary question: where did knotting occur in the *Mishkan*? Rava answers: *shekein koshrim biyatdot ohalim* — they would tie down the curtains of the *Mishkan* to the tent stakes. Rashi reads this as referring to *yesodot* — the stakes to which the *yeriyot*, the surrounding curtains of the *Chatzer Ohel Moed*, were fastened.

### Temporary Knot Problem

The Gemara objects: those knots were tied *al m'nat lehatir* — for the purpose of being undone, since the *Mishkan* was periodically disassembled when the camp traveled. This is a significant conceptual point. In other contexts, an object that eventually returns to its prior state — such as liquefied pitch that re-hardens — is not disqualified as non-lasting. Yet the Gemara treats this knot as categorically *al m'nat lehatir*. This suggests that the concept of permanence as it applies to *kesher* (knotting) may be stricter than *eino mitkayem* as applied to other *melachot*. A knot tied even for an indefinitely long period — such as for the entire duration of the encampment, which could last fifty years — might still be considered temporary if there is awareness that it will ultimately be untied. The Gemara elsewhere does note that since the Israelites were entirely dependent on divine instruction, they were prepared to remain in place indefinitely, which would confer permanence. That argument would have worked here as well, yet the Gemara presses to find a different example — suggesting it is interested in locating a case of permanent knotting on its own terms.

### Broken String Knots

Abaye proposes: *shekein orgei yeriyot* — those who wove the *Mishkan* curtains. *Shenifska lahem nima* — if a thread broke during weaving, they would knot it together. This supplies an example of permanent knotting in the *Mishkan* context. Rava then asks: fine, now we have *kosher* — but what about *matir*, unknotting? If two broken threads each had to be knotted, and the two knots wound up directly adjacent to one another in the weave, the fabric would look flawed. One solution would be to undo one of the knots and re-knot differently. But the Gemara rejects this on aesthetic grounds: *hashta lifnei melech basar vadam ein osin kein* — before an earthly king one would not leave such an obvious flaw in fine work; *lifnei melech malchei hamlachim* — before the King of Kings, certainly not. Rashi suggests that in practice they would simply pull the thread out entirely and restart, rather than leave adjacent knots. The Gemara accordingly dismisses this as a source for *matir*.

### Snail Traps

Rava — or according to some, Rav Ilai — proposes the final answer: *shekein tzedei chilazon koshri'in umatirin* — those who set nets to trap the *chilazon* snails, from whose blood the *techelet* dye was produced, would regularly knot and unknot the nets in the course of adjusting them. This supplies both *kosher* and *matir* as genuine *Mishkan*-connected activities. The Gemara is thus willing to trace a *melacha* through a chain of processes — trapping snails, extracting dye, producing the blue thread — several stages removed from the final product. One might also observe that the snails were found by the sea while the *Mishkan* was in the desert, though perhaps this activity occurred before the Israelites departed, near the *Yam Suf*. The deeper point is that the Gemara is prepared to count a *melacha* rooted in an imperfect, problem-contingent part of the process — not only the ideal, flawless execution. There may even be a *mussar* dimension to this: the Torah acknowledges that even sacred work does not always go perfectly, and the responses to those imperfections are themselves part of the process.

### Knot for Permanence

The Gemara then addresses *tofer* — sewing — in this context: *vehatofer shtei tefirot*, making two stitches. The Gemara asks: *vahalo kayma* — two stitches alone will just pull out; they are *eino mitkayem*, not lasting. Rabbah bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan: *vehu she-ksharan* — the ruling applies where one tied a knot at the end of the stitches, preventing them from pulling loose. One might ask whether that terminal knot itself constitutes an act of *kosher*. Perhaps it does; perhaps it depends on whether it is a double, professional knot. In any case, one is liable for *tofer* by virtue of the stitches, which the terminal knot renders permanent. This raises a further question: is the *melacha* of stitching dependent on an act performed after the stitching itself? Until the knot is tied, the stitches are *eino mitkayem*. One might argue that an act performed subsequently to the *melacha* can retroactively render the prior act a completed *melacha* — an interesting principle in its own right.

---

## Tearing for Sewing

### Moth Hole Repair

The Gemara asks where *keria* — tearing — occurred in the *Mishkan*, given the general principle that destruction is only a *melacha* when performed for a constructive purpose. Rabba bar Rav Zeira and Rav Zeira — both of them — answer: *shekein yeriyah shenafal bah darna* — a curtain of the *Mishkan* into which a moth hole had fallen. One would tear away the damaged area around the hole and then resew the gap with a patch in its place. This again illustrates the Gemara's recurring pattern of locating *melachot* in the corrective responses to imperfection within the *Mishkan* process.

---

## Knotting & Unknottin (II)

### Tightening Threads

Rav Zutra bar Tuvia cites Rav: one who stretches and tightens a loose thread of existing stitching on *Shabbat* — *hamoteiach chut shel tefira beShabbat* — is liable for *chatas*. One did not perform the original sewing; one simply found a thread that had become slack and pulled it taut, re-securing the attachment. A practical instance: tightening the knots of one's *tzitzit*, or pulling taut a thread by which a button is loosely attached. In both cases, no new stitches are made, yet the act of tightening constitutes *tofer*. The ruling would presumably apply only where the tightening produces a result that is *kiyama* — lasting — for a meaningful period. If the thread immediately loosens again, it may be *eino mitkayem* and the liability would not apply. But where the act does secure the thread for a significant duration, even without new stitching, it is a form of *tefira*.

One might ask more broadly whether *tefira* is confined to stitching or encompasses other methods of joining two pieces together — gluing, for example. Whether gluing would constitute *tofer* or perhaps *kosher* is a question that the Gemara here leaves open.

At this point the Gemara inserts two additional statements attributed to Rav Zutra bar Tuvia in the name of Rav that are not directly relevant to the discussion of *Shabbat melachot*. One concerns the prohibition against learning even a single matter from a *magush* — which Rav identifies as a blasphemer or idolator rather than a practitioner of witchcraft, as proven by the fact that one is permitted to study witchcraft *lidrosha* (for the sake of understanding and teaching), whereas Rav's blanket prohibition would be inexplicable were the *magush* merely a witch. The second concerns the requirement to calculate *tekufot u'mazalot* — the astronomical seasons and constellations — and the condemnation of one who possesses the knowledge to do so but neglects to do it. Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse *ki hi chochmaschem u'vinaschem le'einei ha'amim* that computing *tekufot u'mazalot* is a positive obligation — the knowledge that even the nations will recognize as genuine wisdom — and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani adds that it leads to the appreciation of divine creation. The *Smag* codifies this as *halacha*, and the *Rambam*, while not specifically emphasizing *tekufot u'mazalot*, does include the study of natural sciences under the *mitzvah* of *ahavat Hashem*, since contemplating the wisdom of creation leads to both love and awe of God.

---

## Chilazon/Snail Trapping

### Trapping & Squeezing

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: one who traps the *chilazon* snail and squeezes its blood — *hatzad chilazon vehapotzo* — is liable for only one *sin offering*, for *tzeida* (trapping). Rabbi Yehuda says: two, because *ptzi'ah bichlal disha* — the squeezing is included in the category of *disha*, threshing, which in this context means extracting something from its natural container. The Rabbis respond: *ein ptzi'ah bichlal disha* — squeezing blood from a snail is not *disha*.

### Disha Limited

Rava explains the Rabbis' position: *kasavri ein disha ela b'gidulei karka* — *disha* applies only to agricultural products, things that grow from the ground. A sea creature such as the *chilazon* is categorically excluded.

### Mefarek Question

This ruling carries significant implications. The Gemara elsewhere categorizes milking as *mefarek* — extracting. Some authorities argue that if *disha* is limited to *gidulei karka*, then milking — which involves a land animal rather than an agricultural product — would be only *d'rabbanan* on a biblical level. Others maintain that milking is an exception or that land animals, which subsist on and are rooted in the earth, might be included within a broader conception of *gidulei karka*. Tosafot raises this possibility but rejects it. A third, counterintuitive position found in some *rishonim* and *poskim* holds that the limitations on the *avot* do not necessarily apply to the *toldot* — so that even if *disha* is restricted to *gidulei karka*, the *tolada* of *mefarek* might not carry the same restriction. This is an admittedly strange position, since one would expect a *tolada* to be at least as limited as its *av*, but it is noted. The practical stakes are high: the question of whether a woman expressing milk on *Shabbat* is a *d'oraita* or *d'rabbanan* concern turns in part on this very issue.

The *Yerushalmi*, as cited by Tosafot, raises an additional question: whether trapping snails constitutes *tzeida* at all. If the *chilazon* is a snail — as is now generally accepted — it does not flee. One goes and scoops them up. Does locating and extracting an immobile creature constitute *tzad*? This is a genuine question in the parameters of trapping that the *Yerushalmi* leaves open.

### Live Squeezing Preferred

Rava raises a further question: why is one not also liable for *netilat neshama* — taking a life — when squeezing the snail? Rabbi Yochanan answers: *shepetza'o meit* — it was already dead when squeezed. Rava counters: even if it was alive, *mit'asek hu eitzel netilat neshama* — the killing is incidental to the purpose of the act. Tosafot notes that *mit'asek* is not the precisely correct term here; what is meant is *davar she'eino mitkavein* — an unintended consequence of an otherwise permitted act. Yet Abaye and Rava have jointly established the principle *modeh Rabbi Shimon b'psik reisha v'lo yamut* — even Rabbi Shimon, who permits unintended acts, concedes liability when the forbidden result is inevitable, as when one cuts off an animal's head and claims not to intend its death. Squeezing a snail until its blood is fully extracted would seem equally inevitable.

### Live Squeezing Preferred

The Gemara resolves the difficulty: *d'kama d'it beih neshama tefei nicha leih* — as long as the snail remains alive, one prefers that it stay alive, *ki heichi d'litzil tziv'eih* — so that the color of the blood will be clearer and of higher quality. It emerges that the blood extracted from a live snail is superior to that taken from a dead one. One therefore actively does not want the snail to die during the process. This converts the situation into a *psik reisha d'lo nicha lei* — an unavoidable consequence that the actor specifically does not desire — and the ruling is that one is exempt in such a case.

### Psik Reisha Parameters

This ruling occasions a notable dispute between Rashi and Tosafot. Rashi holds that the exemption of *psik reisha d'lo nicha lei* applies only when one actively does not want the result. If one is merely indifferent — *lo ichpat lei* — one is still liable. Tosafot vigorously disagrees, marshaling evidence from other *sugyot* to argue that indifference and active non-desire are legally equivalent. The *halacha* follows Tosafot: once one is indifferent to the unintended result, one does not incur biblical liability, regardless of whether one affirmatively does not want it or simply does not care. The three positions — actively desiring the result, being indifferent, and specifically not wanting it — thus collapse into two for practical *halachic* purposes: one either desires the outcome or one does not, and absence of desire (whether through indifference or active preference against) suffices for exemption in a *psik reisha* context.

---

## Slaughtering Analysis

### Rava vs. Shmuel

The Gemara proceeds to *shechita* — slaughtering. The question posed is not about whether *shechita* is a *melacha* (the *Mishnah* plainly lists it), but rather what conceptual category underlies the liability: *shochet mishum mai chayav* — for which *melacha* is one liable when slaughtering? Rava says: *mishum tzovei'a* — for coloring, since the blood colors the skin of the animal's neck at the point of slaughter. Shmuel says: *mishum netilat neshama* — for taking life, which is the natural category for slaughter.

### Staining for Commerce

The Gemara initially appears to press Rava: according to you, there is liability for *tzovei'a* — but no liability for *netilat neshama*? Of course there is liability for taking life as well. Rava clarifies: one incurs a *double chiyuv* — both *netilat neshama* and *tzovei'a*. But Rava feels compelled to explain himself lest future generations mock the *tzovei'a* claim as absurd. *B'mai nicha lei* — why would one actually want the coloring? The answer is *nicha lei d'litnef beit hash'chita dama* — one wants the site of the slaughter to be stained deeply with blood, *ki heichi d'lichazei inshi v'leitu v'lizbnu mineih* — so that passersby will see the fresh blood and know the meat was recently slaughtered, thereby attracting customers. This commercial desirability of the bloodstained neck demonstrates that the coloring is actively desired, making it a direct act of *tzovei'a* with full *kavanah*.

### Rabbeinu Tam

Tosafot raises the question of what constitutes *netilat neshama* when one wounds without killing — as the Gemara implies one is liable for wounding as well. One possibility is that injury is a stage on the path toward death. Rabbeinu Tam advances his famous position: the common denominator of all the cases in which liability arises for *netilat neshama* is the extraction of blood. *Ki hadam hu hanefesh* — the blood represents the soul, and therefore taking blood is a form of taking life. This is why wounding — where blood flows — also falls under *netilat neshama*, while killing without bloodshed, though certainly *netilat neshama* in a plain sense, lacks this additional dimension. On Rabbeinu Tam's reading there are thus effectively two sub-categories: killing an animal outright, and extracting blood through wounding. This framework also bears on the question of why squeezing the *chilazon* does not generate liability for *netilat neshama* — a question Tosafot addresses at some length.

---

## Tanning & Salting

### Salting & Working

The Gemara asks: the *Mishnah* lists both *moleach* (salting) and *me'aved* (working/processing) as separate *melachot*, yet salting is simply part of the process of working leather. Why enumerate them separately?

### Sartat Added

Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish both answer: *afik chad mineihu* — remove one of those two, *ve-ayyel sirtut* — and insert *sirtut*, line-making, which was absent from the list. The process of making leather or other craftwork includes scoring lines as a guide for cutting or writing — *sirtut* — and this had been omitted. Adding it and removing the redundant *moleach* preserves the total at thirty-nine. This exchange reveals something important: the count of thirty-nine is still, at this stage, somewhat fluid. The categories are still crystallizing, and the Rabbis are prepared to reconfigure the list to arrive at the correct total.

### Salting Meat

Since *moleach* has been absorbed into *me'aved*, one might think that salting only generates liability when applied to leather or similar materials undergoing processing. The Gemara immediately applies *me'aved* to food. Rava bar Rav Huna rules: *hai man demalach bisra chayav mishum me'aved* — one who salts meat is liable for *me'aved*. Rava, however, contests this: *ein ibud be'ochlin* — there is no *ibud* (working/processing) when it comes to foods. *Ibud* is a category that applies to materials being transformed — leather, wood, and similar objects. Food is food; applying *me'aved* to foodstuffs is fundamentally excluded. This parallels another exclusion: *tzovei'a* similarly does not apply to foods in many opinions.

### Transformative Salting

Rav Ashi qualifies the position of Rava bar Rav Huna: even that ruling was only intended for a case *deka'ba'i lei le'orcha* — where one is salting for a long journey, making something akin to preserved dried meat or beef jerky. In that case, one genuinely transforms the food — extracting all moisture, hardening it, rendering it something fundamentally different from what it was — analogous to what the processing of leather achieves. That is the kind of transformation that *me'aved* is meant to capture. *Aval leveisa* — but if one is salting for home use a few days hence, *lo matzi inish demashvei michlei etz* — people do not turn their food into wood. Home salting is not sufficiently transformative to qualify. The opposing view holds that no matter how transformative the salting, food is categorically excluded from *ibud*. On that view, heavily preserved salted food still cannot trigger *me'aved*. The two positions thus diverge over whether the exclusion of *ochlin* from *ibud* is functional (depending on the degree of transformation) or categorical.

---

## Scraping, Cutting & Writ…

### Pillar Smoothing

The Gemara turns to *memachek* (smoothing), *mechatech* (cutting to size), and related *melachot*. Rav Ami bar Chanina rules: one who rubs against pillars — the columns of a portico — on *Shabbat* is liable for *misa* for *memachek*. Rashi explains that one is smoothing the floor beneath by dragging one's body along it. Tosafot rejects this reading — presumably because that would more naturally be *boneh* than *memachek* — and instead explains that one is literally rubbing leather against the stone pillars, a direct application of the leather-smoothing process.

### Three Finishing Acts

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites three rulings in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. First: one who whittles the tip of a pole on *Shabbat* — shaping it to a point — is liable for *mechatech*. Although one smooths incidentally in the process, the dominant act is a precise cut to produce a specific shape — namely, a point — and *mechatech* is the governing category, not *memachek*. This illustrates a general principle: when an act can be classified under a more specific category, that category takes precedence over a broader one.

### Salve Smoothing

Second: one who spreads a *ritya* — a medicinal salve or poultice — on a wound on *Shabbat* is liable for *memachek*. This is the critical ruling for a range of practical applications. One might have thought *memachek* requires an intention that the surface itself become smooth — and here one merely wants to apply the salve therapeutically. One does not care whether it lies flat. Nevertheless, the act of spreading it smooth constitutes *memachek*.
