This is the basis for the practical guidance that one should dab such substances on rather than spread them, relying on subsequent movement to distribute the material — whether salve on a wound, cream on skin, or toothpaste on teeth.

### Stone Finishing

Third: one who makes the finishing indentation around the edge of a stone on *Shabbat* is liable for *makeh b'fatish*. This might appear to be *memachek*, since one is smoothing a surface, yet the Gemara classifies it as *makeh b'fatish* — the last finishing act that completes the object. Similarly, one who makes a final decorative incision in a vessel (*hatziyar tziyura b'chli*) or who blows a final adjustment into a glass vessel (*hamnafeiach b'chli zchuchit*) is liable for *makeh b'fatish*. The principle is broad: any last act that brings an object to its finished state is *makeh b'fatish*, which is why the *amora'im* later summarize — *kol midi d'it bei gmar melacha chayav mishum makeh b'fatish* — anything that constitutes the final act of completion is *makeh b'fatish*. The literature on the precise parameters of this principle is extensive.

### Thread Removal

Rabbi Yehuda rules: one who removes a hanging thread from a garment — the kind of loose end left after the garment is otherwise finished — is liable for *makeh b'fatish*, since it is the last act of completion. This applies only *d'kapeid alayhu* — if one actually cares about that thread. If one is indifferent, even though removing it technically finishes the garment, the absence of concern presumably means the garment was never considered incomplete. The converse question — whether removing threads sewn in by manufacturers for packaging purposes, such as the stitching that keeps jacket pockets closed, constitutes *makeh b'fatish* — is probably inapplicable, since the garment was already finished before those threads were added; *makeh b'fatish* is the last stage of the original production process, not the undoing of something added afterward.

### Writing & Erasing

The *baraita* establishes an instructive asymmetry between writing and erasing. If one writes a single very large letter that occupies the space where two letters could have been written, one is exempt — only one letter was written, and the minimum for liability is two letters. However, if one erases a large letter and the resulting blank space is sufficient to accommodate two letters, one is liable. The act of erasing is not measured by how many letters were erased but by how much space is cleared for writing. Rabbi Menachem the son of Rabbi Yosi notes: *zeh chomer b'mochek mib'koteiv* — this is a case where erasing is more stringent than writing.

---

## 39 Melachot & Disputes

### Avot Melachot

The *Mishnah* concludes: *eilu avot melachot* — these are the primary categories of *melacha*. The word *eilu* — these — is precise and exclusive: *le'apukei mid'Rabbi Eliezer* — to exclude the position of Rabbi Eliezer, who rules *d'mechayev al tolada b'makom av* — that if one performs both an *av* and its *tolada*, one incurs liability for each separately. According to Rabbi Eliezer, the number of *chatatot* one can incur is theoretically unlimited, since every *tolada* is distinct from its *av*. The *Mishnah*'s formulation — *these are* the *avot melachot* — excludes this position and establishes that only the thirty-nine primary categories generate distinct liability.

### Rabbi Yehuda Adds 2

The number thirty-nine is stated both at the beginning and at the end of the *Mishnah*. The repetition of the count at the end serves to exclude Rabbi Yehuda, who — as the *baraita* teaches — adds two additional categories: *shoveit*, a method of beating threads into the loom during setup, and *maddek*, a method of beating threads smooth during weaving.

### Refutation

The Rabbis respond to Rabbi Yehuda: *shoveit harei hu bichlal meisach* — *shoveit* is already included within *meisach*, the act of setting up the warp on the loom, since it is part of that preparatory process. *Maddek harei hu bichlal oreig* — *maddek* is already included within *oreig*, weaving, since it is part of the act of weaving itself. These are not independent categories but constituent elements of processes already enumerated. The total therefore remains thirty-nine, and the discussion will continue in the following session.

---

---

# Shabbat 76

## Klal Gadol: Carrying

### Hotza'ah Centrality

The daf begins at the bottom of 75b, at the *mishna*. Having already treated the *klal gadol* concerning the thirty-nine *melachot*, the *gemara* dispatched that material with relative brevity — though the remainder of the *masechet* will return to elaborate on those categories in various ways. We now turn to another *klal gadol*, and what is striking is its subject matter: rather than a principle touching the totality of *shabbos*, we are pulled immediately back into the world of *hotza'ah*, of carrying. Three chapters of the *masechet* have already addressed this topic, beginning at the very opening, and now the entire next chapter will continue there as well. The centrality of *hotza'ah* to the discussions of *shabbos* is worth pausing to recognize — indeed, the very next *masechet*, *Eruvin*, is devoted to it to a significant degree.

### Kashur Le-Hatznia

The *mishna* states: *kol ha-kasher le-hatznia matznin kamohu ve-hotzio be-shabbos chayav* — anything that is fit to be set aside, and which people normally do set aside in that amount, if one carries it out on *shabbos* one is *chayav chatas*. The abstract criterion for *hotza'ah* liability is thus twofold: first, the object must be of a type that is not ordinarily discarded — it is the kind of thing people keep rather than throw away; second, the specific amount carried must itself be a quantity normally preserved and not discarded. Even if an object is valuable in principle, a negligible quantity of it might be tossed out, and that quantity would fall below the *shiur*. The *mishna* then states: *ve-kol she-eino kasher le-hatznia ve-ein matznin kamohu* — anything that fails either criterion — *eino chayav*, one is not liable, *ela ha-matznio* — except for the person who actually set it aside.

### Objective/Subjective

This last clause is quite surprising. Almost universally, a *shiur* is an objective measure, end of story. Occasionally we might speak of a range across classes of people — the garment that a wealthy person discards but a poor person will still use as a patch — but here the *mishna* descends to the individual level: if *you* personally have set something aside as significant, then *you* are *chayav* for it even if no one else would bother with it. The example is illuminating: most people would discard a half-eaten piece of gum, but if you have set it aside for your own later use, it holds subjective significance for you, and you are *chayav*.

What is equally fascinating is the hyper-focus on *hotza'ah* in relation to minimum sizes. Every one of the thirty-nine *melachot* requires its own *shiur*, and some were mentioned in the preceding *mishna* and *gemara* — yet for some reason it is specifically *hotza'ah* around which an enormous body of analysis concerning minimum sizes has crystallized, spanning the remaining *mishnayos* here and the entire next *perek*.

The *gemara* then explains what the language *kasher le-hatznia* — fit to be set aside — comes to exclude. *Rav Pappa* says: *lafukei dam nida* — to exclude menstrual blood. A woman in the midst of her cycle discards the soiled material; no one has any use for it, and it is not the type of thing normally preserved. *Mar Ukva* says: *lafukei atzei ashera* — to exclude wood of an *ashera*, a tree used in idolatrous worship, which is prohibited in benefit and must be destroyed. On *Mar Ukva*'s view, menstrual blood could arguably be set aside — *matznia lei lashunra*, one might preserve it for a cat to consume. The response is *kivan de-chalsha lo matznia lei*: since it causes illness, one would not in fact set it aside. *Rashi* here broadens the point, explaining that feeding human blood to a cat causes the person who fed it to become ill — and *Rashi* does not limit this to menstrual blood specifically but to *dam ha-adam* generally.

*Tosafot* notes that in other *gemaras*, *atzei ashera* is actually treated as something one would set aside, since one has an obligation to burn it — the *mitzvah* of destruction gives one reason to hold onto it. Yet this *gemara* places it squarely in the category of objects with no meaningful use.

### Exclusions Debated

The *gemara* then cites *Rabbi Yose bar Chanina*, who observes that this *mishna* is *d'lo k'Rabbi Shimon* — it does not accord with the view of *Rabbi Shimon* (who is, by default, *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai*). For *Rabbi Shimon*, as we will read in a forthcoming *mishna*, *lo amru kol ha-shi'urin halalu ela le-matzniyeihen* — all the minimum *shi'urim* about to be enumerated in the coming *mishnayos* are not stated for the general population. They apply only to the class of people for whom such amounts are genuinely meaningful, or perhaps only to someone who specifically set the item aside. For everyone else, *Rabbi Shimon* holds that a larger amount would be required for liability. Our *mishna*, by contrast, treats these minimums as universal — anyone who carries them out is *chayav* — while simultaneously holding that an individual who assigns personal significance to a smaller amount is *chayav* for even less.

*Rabbi Elazar* adds a further nuance: the *mishna* also does not accord with *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar*, as taught in a *baraita*. That *baraita* rules that if an object that is not generally fit to be set aside — and whose standard quantity is not normally preserved — is nonetheless set aside by a particular individual, and then someone *else* carries it out, that other person is *chayav* by virtue of the first person's act of designation. *Nitchayev zeh be-machshava shel zeh* — the second person incurs liability through the subjective significance established by the first. This position, while presenting its own difficulties from the standpoint of fairness, has a certain appeal: once an individual has created subjective significance, it radiates outward and governs others as well, rather than remaining a purely personal standard. Our *mishna*, however, does not adopt this position.

---

## Animal Feed Sizes

### Cow/Camel/Sheep

The *mishna* continues: *hamotzi teven ke-melo pi para* — if one carries out straw, the minimum amount is what fits in the mouth of a cow, since straw is what cows eat, and the cow's mouth provides the relevant measure. *Atza ke-melo pi gamal* — a different type of fodder, the straw of legumes (as *Rav Yehuda* explains: *teven she-minei kitniyot*), which cows do not eat but camels do, goes by the camel's mouth. Since the camel is a larger animal with a correspondingly larger mouth, the minimum *shiur* is bigger. *Amir ke-melo pi taleh* — another type of fodder, perhaps grain stalks of a different variety, goes by a sheep's mouth. The principle is that one always looks to the smallest animal that eats the food in question, because that smallest animal's mouthful is the minimal unit of significance.

### Goat/Figs/Dried

*Asavim ke-melo pi gedi* — grass goes by the mouth of a goat. A goat has a smaller mouth than a sheep, and since goats eat grass, and the goat represents the smallest relevant consumer, the measure is accordingly smaller.

*Alei shum va-alei betzalim lachim ke-grogeret* — moist leaves of garlic or onion, which fall into the category of human food, go by the size of a *grogeret*, a pressed fig. The general rule is that all human food is measured by the *grogeret*. Why is the pressed fig and not a *kezayit* the standard? Presumably because a *kezayit*, while sufficient to define an act of eating halachically, does not rise to the level of a quantity that provides even minimal satisfaction, and thus falls short of the significance required for *hotza'ah* liability.

An interesting question arises: what if an item is both human food and animal food, and the relevant animal eats a smaller quantity? Would the animal-food measure lower the *shiur*? The *mishna* appears to hold that once something qualifies as human food, the *grogeret* standard applies. *Yeveshim ke-melo pi gedi* — if those same leaves have dried out and are no longer suitable for human consumption, the *shiur* reverts to a goat's mouthful, since a goat is the smallest animal that would eat them.

The rule, then, is clear in principle: identify the smallest relevant consumer of the item. If a larger animal also eats it, that is irrelevant — one goes by the smallest mouth among those that consume it. A point worth noting: the animals in view are domestic animals, those one actually cares about feeding. Wild animals that are not normally kept would not confer significance in the same way, because what gives the food its objective value is that people are in the business of feeding these creatures.

### Camel Intent Debate

The *gemara* then raises the question of subjective intent in the context of animal feed. *Ki ata Rav Dimi amar*: if one carries out straw in the amount of a cow's mouthful, but one's intention is to feed it to a camel — since camels also eat ordinary straw, even if the primary association of straw is with cows — what is the *halacha*? The camel requires more than a cow's mouthful to constitute a significant feeding; so does the fact that the carrier's subjective purpose is the camel lower the significance of what he is carrying, and thereby exempt him?

*Rabbi Yochanan* initially said: *chayav* — one is liable, because the objective minimum for a cow's-mouth feeding remains intact regardless of one's personal intent. *Reish Lakish* said: *patur* — exempt, because for this person, who is focused on the camel, the amount he is carrying does not yet rise to significance.

The *gemara* notes that at night *Rabbi Yochanan* had said *chayav*, but in the morning — *hadar bei* — he reversed himself, aligning with *Reish Lakish*. *Rav Yosef* approved of the reversal. *Abaye*, however, pushed back: *adrabba*, he argued — the original position made more sense, because *de-chazi le-para*, there is an objective reality that this amount is fit for a cow. How does the carrier's subjective desire to feed a camel undo an objective minimum that exists for the rest of the world?

*Ravin*, upon arriving from *Eretz Yisrael*, then clarified how the debate was actually formulated. When one carries out straw in the amount of a cow's mouthful to feed a camel — *de-kulei alma lo peligi de-chayav*: there is no dispute; everyone agrees one is *chayav*. The objective minimum for a cow's-mouth feeding stands, and the intent to use it for a camel does not diminish it.

### Forced Eating

The actual dispute between *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Reish Lakish*, *Ravin* clarifies, concerns the reverse case: one carries out *atza* — the legume straw normally eaten only by camels — in an amount equal only to a cow's mouthful, intending to feed it to one's cow. The question is whether the carrier's subjective intent to use camel fodder for a cow can raise the *shiur* and render him *chayav* for what is ordinarily a sub-minimum amount of that item.

*Rabbi Yochanan* says *patur* — exempt — and *Reish Lakish* says *chayav*. The crux of *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position is the principle *achila al yedei d'chaka lo shma achila* — a forced or coerced eating does not constitute eating. Even if one forces one's cow to consume this fodder it does not naturally want, that act is not recognized as a genuine feeding. And since the act one proposes to perform with this item is considered halachically meaningless, the subjective intent cannot confer significance on the amount, and one cannot become *chayav* on the basis of that intent.

This is the key distinction: subjective reality can reduce a *shiur* — one who personally sets aside even a small amount of something creates significance for oneself — but only when the act one intends to perform with it would itself be recognized as meaningful. If the intended use is one the *halacha* does not acknowledge — such as force-feeding an animal something it cannot properly digest — then even genuine subjective intent cannot generate *chiyuv*. *Reish Lakish* disagrees: *achila al yedei d'chaka shma achila*, such a feeding is still considered feeding, and therefore the subjective intent is operative.

*Tosafot* notes that the question of *achila al yedei d'chaka* arises in other contexts as well — there is a *sugya* in *Bava Kamma* concerning torts where *achila al yedei d'chaka* is treated as *achila* — and the principle has applications in the laws of *Yom Kippur* and elsewhere.

---

## Non-Combination Rule

### Stricter/Lenient

The *mishna* concludes: *ve-ein mitztarfin ze im ze mipnei she-lo shavu be-shi'ureihem* — the different categories of animal feed cannot combine with one another because their minimum sizes differ. If one has three-quarters of a cow's-mouth measure of straw and supplements it with some *atza* — the legume fodder measured by a camel's mouth — the two quantities cannot be added together to reach the cow's-mouth minimum. The *mishna* thus rules that combination across categories of differing *shi'urim* is not permitted.

*Rav Yosef bar Chanina* then qualifies this principle: *ein mitztarfin la-chamur she-bahem aval mitztarfin la-kal she-bahem* — one cannot combine to the more stringent category, but one can combine to the more lenient. The "more stringent" category here is the one with the smaller minimum — the cow's-mouth measure — because it takes less to reach liability. The "more lenient" is the larger minimum — the camel's mouth — because more is required. So one cannot use camel-fodder to supplement a sub-minimum amount of cow-straw to reach the cow's-mouth *shiur*. But one can use cow-straw to supplement a sub-minimum amount of camel-fodder to reach the camel's-mouth *shiur*, because the stricter material is being deployed toward a more lenient threshold.

What is notable at this point is that the analysis has shifted from the concrete reality of what the camel would actually eat toward a more formal register. The *gemara* is no longer asking whether the camel would consume the combined mixture — it might not eat the cow-straw at all — but is instead applying an abstract rule: the stricter category may be used toward the more lenient. This is worth flagging as a significant structural feature of how *halacha* operates.

### Common Shiur

The *gemara* now challenges this principle with a *mishna* from the laws of *tumah*. The *mishna* there teaches: *ha-beged gimal al gimal* — a cloth garment must be three by three *tefachim* to become susceptible to *tumas moshav* (the impurity conveyed by the seat or lying-place of a *zav*); *ha-sak arba al arba* — sackcloth requires four by four; *ha-or chamesh al chamesh* — leather, five by five; *mapatz shesh al shesh* — a mat, six by six *tefachim*. A *baraita* then teaches that *ha-beged ve-ha-sak ve-ha-sak ve-ha-or ve-ha-or ve-ha-mapatz mitztarfin ze im ze* — cloth and sackcloth, sackcloth and leather, leather and matting can combine across categories. This seems to contradict the rule that different *shi'urim* cannot combine.

*Rabbi Shimon* explains why combination is permitted there: *mipnei she-re'uyim le-tamei moshav* — because they are all fit to convey the impurity of *moshav*. At first glance this sounds circular — we are trying to determine whether the combined amount creates a sufficient *moshav* item, and we are told they combine because they can create a *moshav*. *Rashi* (in *Sukkah*) and *Tosafot* here clarify: the point is that although each material has a different standard minimum, there exists a scenario in which they all share the same minimum — namely, if one deliberately cut out a swath of material specifically designated as a seat. In that case, even a one-by-one-*tefach* piece of any of these materials carries significance. Since in that scenario they all share a common minimum, they can combine across categories even in the ordinary scenario.

*Tosafot* adds a further nuance: combination is permitted only between adjacent categories — cloth with sackcloth, sackcloth with leather — but one cannot leapfrog a category by combining cloth directly with matting. The reasoning for this restriction is admittedly difficult to explain clearly.

The conclusion the *gemara* draws is: *ta'ama de-ra'uy le-tamei moshav* — the reason combination is permitted there is precisely because there exists a common *shiur* across the categories. *Aval eino ra'uy le-tamei moshav* — if there were no such common *shiur*, combination across categories would not be permitted.

### Formal Categories

*Rava* then applies this logic to the animal-feed categories: *hacha nami chazi le-dugma* — here too, there is a scenario in which all the different foods share a common minimum. If one intends to use any of these materials as a sample — a merchant showing a prospective buyer what type of feed is available, for instance — then even the tiniest quantity, *kol she-hu*, is significant. Since all the categories share this common minimum in the sample-use scenario, that formal connection allows combination across categories even in the context of feeding animals.

This is the formal rule operating at full abstraction: it is not that the camel would eat the combined mixture. It is that these categories share a common *shiur* in some recognized scenario, and that formal commonality licenses their combination in other contexts.

Here lies a broader observation worth making explicit. What historically generated these minimum sizes was the concrete reality of animals — cows, camels, sheep, goats — and the amounts their mouths hold. But once those minimums were crystallized into halachic categories, they became formal, abstract measures. We no longer ask in every case whether the camel will eat this combination. We ask whether the formal rules governing these size-categories permit combination. Once a definition or legislation — whether of Torah or rabbinic origin — has crystallized, one applies the rules of the category as it now stands, not necessarily the historical rationale that generated it.

This raises a genuinely interesting question: if societal norms were to shift so that, say, animal husbandry practices changed entirely, would the minimum sizes change accordingly? One could argue that, to the extent these sizes reflect living realities that must remain active, a societal shift would alter the *shiur*. Or one could argue that once crystallized, the category is fixed. The answer is not obvious, and the present discussion of subjective reality complicates it further — since uniquely in *hotza'ah*, subjective personal significance can reduce the *shiur* in a way that has no real parallel among the other *melachot*.

---

## Human Food Standard

### Grogeret Standard

*Hamotzi ochalin ke-grogeret chayav u-mitztarfin ze im ze* — one who carries out food is *chayav* if the amount equals a *grogeret*, a pressed fig, and different types of food combine with one another. The reasoning for combination is explicit: *mipnei she-shavu be-shi'ureihem* — because they share the same minimum. Even if the various foods would never be eaten together — a bit of peanut butter, a bit of something else entirely — they combine formally to the *grogeret* standard, because all human food shares that threshold. This is again the formal category at work.

### Shells/Seeds/Bran

The *mishna* then specifies exclusions: *chutz mi-klipatan ve-ha-garinin ve-uktzeihen* — shells, seeds, and stems or stalks of food do not combine with the food and are not themselves considered food. *Ve-subin u-mursan* — two grades of bran are similarly excluded. These are components not ordinarily eaten and thus fall outside the category of human food.

### Legume Shells

*Rabbi Yehuda* carves out an exception: *chutz mi-klipei adashim she-mitbashlot imahem* — the shells of lentils that are cooked together with the lentils are included, since in that context they are effectively consumed along with the food. The *gemara* asks whether beans (*pulin*) are similarly included. A *baraita* suggests that *Rabbi Yehuda* includes both lentils and beans. The resolution: *ha be-chadti ha be-atiki* — when the beans are fresh, their shells are cooked with them and are thus included; when old, the shells are discarded and excluded. Why are old bean-shells not used? *Rabbi Abbahu* offers the reason: *mipnei she-nir'in ke-zvuvim be-ke'ara* — because they turn dark and look like flies in the dish, making the food unappetizing even if technically edible.

The *gemara* also raises the question of bran: is it true that bran does not combine with food? We have a *mishna* stating that *chameshet reva'im kemach ve-od chayavin be-challa* — the minimum amount of flour for *challa* obligation includes the fine bran and coarse bran along with the flour proper. *Abaye* responds: *she-ken ani ochel pito be-isa belusa* — a poor person may eat bread made with bran-laden dough. Yes — but that is not enough to elevate bran to objective food-status for the purposes of *hotza'ah*. Only the individual who specifically sets bran aside as a food for himself generates subjective significance; the mere existence of a class of poor people who consume it does not establish bran as a universally recognized food. This again raises the pointed question of how broadly or narrowly one defines the population whose habits define the objective standard.

---

## Liquids Shiurim

### Wine/Milk/Other

The *mishna* at the beginning of the next *perek* turns to liquids, where different *shi'urim* apply depending on the liquid's characteristic use. *Yayin ke-dei mzigat ha-kos* — wine: the minimum is the amount needed to mix a cup. The wine of that era was dense and potent; it was customarily mixed with water (either two-to-one or three-to-one) before drinking. The minimum, therefore, is the quantity of this unmixed, dense wine sufficient to produce a full cup of mixed wine — roughly a mouthful. *Chalav ke-dei gmi'a* — milk: the minimum is a swallow. *Devash ke-dei litein al ha-katit* — honey: the minimum is the amount placed on a wound as a medicinal treatment, either human or animal. *Shemen ke-dei lasuch eiver katan* — oil: the minimum is the amount to anoint a small limb, such as a pinky. *Mayim ke-dei lashuf bahem et ha-kilor* — water: the minimum is the amount needed to soften a poultice applied to a wound, *Rashi* specifying an eye-patch.

What is notable is that most of these liquids are measured not by drinking but by non-drinking applications — medicinal, cosmetic. Even when used as a drink, different liquids carry different minimums: wine is measured one way, milk another.

### Revi'it Standard

*U-shear kol ha-mashkin be-revi'it* — all other liquids not specifically enumerated go by a *revi'it*, a quarter of a *log*, approximately three and a half ounces. *Ve-chol ha-shofchin be-revi'it* — even waste-water, dirty or foul water, goes by a *revi'it*. The use-case for foul water, as the *gemara* will explain, exists as well.

*Rabbi Shimon* disputes all the subdivisions: *kulam be-revi'it* — all liquids go by a *revi'it*, making no distinction between wine, milk, honey, oil, or water. Furthermore, *Rabbi Shimon* repeats his broader position: *ve-lo ne'emru kol ha-shi'urin halalu ela le-matzni'eihem* — all these minimums apply only to those for whom such amounts are significant, or to those who specifically set them aside. For others, a larger amount would be needed for liability — the *mishna*'s universal application is rejected.

---

## Dense Wine Amount

### Quarter Revi'it

The *gemara* now establishes the precise minimum for dense wine. A *tanna* teaches: *ke-dei mzigas kos yafeh* — the amount to make a *nice* cup of wine, meaning a full and proper cup. The *gemara* asks: what is a *nice cup*? *Kos shel beracha* — the cup used for *birkat ha-mazon*, which is a *revi'it*. *Rav Nachman* then cites *Rabba bar Abbuha*: the cup of *beracha* requires a *rova revi'it* — a quarter of a *revi'it* — of dense wine, *ke-dei she-yimzagnu ve-ye'amid al revi'it* — so that when diluted with water it reaches a full *revi'it*. If a quarter of a *revi'it* of dense wine, combined with water, yields a full *revi'it*, then the ratio of water to wine is three to one — three-quarters water, one-quarter wine.

*Rava* then observes: *af anan nami tanyana* — we too have taught this. The *mishna* says wine goes by *ke-dei mzigat kos*, and the *tanna* glosses this as *ke-dei mzigas kos yafeh* — a nice cup. The *mishna* further states that all other liquids go by a *revi'it*. Mixed wine — wine already diluted — falls under the general liquid category and goes by a *revi'it*. Therefore, the minimum of dense wine is the quantity needed to produce a *revi'it* of mixed wine, and since *Rava* holds that a proper mixture requires three parts water to one part wine, the minimum of dense wine is one-quarter of a *revi'it*.

### Water in Pitcher

*Abaye* raises two objections. First: a *baraita* in the context of *nida* law describes mixed wine as wine from the *Sharon* valley mixed with two parts water — a two-to-one ratio, not three to one. If the standard ratio is two to one, the minimum of dense wine would be one-third of a *revi'it*, not one-quarter. Second — and more structurally challenging: *mayim be-kad mitztarfin?* The water that will eventually be mixed with this wine is still sitting in the pitcher. If the dense wine, standing alone, cannot be drunk as-is and requires water to be useful, how does one count it as a significant minimum? The significance seems to depend on water that has not yet been combined with it.

### Rava: Intent

*Rava* responds to both challenges. On the ratio question: *yayin ha-Sharoni lachud d'reifi* — the *Sharon* wine used for checking bloodstains is simply a weaker wine, incapable of absorbing as much water. Alternatively, *hasam mishum chazusa* — that *baraita* is concerned with matching a color for *nida* inspection, not with the normal drinking ratio. For drinking purposes, *ba'ei tfei* — one needs more water, and the ratio is three to one.

On the water-in-the-pitcher objection, *Rava* replies: *le-inyan Shabbos midi de-chashiv ba'inan ve-ha nami chashiv* — for purposes of *Shabbos*, the question is what counts as significant, and this too counts as significant. The dense wine, in the quantity of one-quarter of a *revi'it*, is the precise ingredient that will be used to produce the meaningful cup. The fact that the water is still in the pitcher does not diminish the significance of the wine, because the wine is already designated for a recognized, purposive use. Just as a small concentrated packet intended to produce a full beverage is itself a significant item, the quarter-*revi'it* of dense wine is significant because of the cup it is going to become.

*Abaye* must ultimately agree that the water need not be combined — the *mishna* itself is explicit that the minimum is the amount needed to make a cup of wine, not that the water has already been added. What *Abaye* seems to have resisted is the conclusion that one-quarter of a *revi'it* is a significant amount; he inclined toward a two-to-one ratio and therefore a third of a *revi'it*. *Rava* has demonstrated both that the three-to-one ratio is correct and that the significance of the dense wine derives from its intended use, fully realized once it is mixed — and that suffices for *hotza'ah* liability on *Shabbos*.

---

---

# Shabbat 77

## Shiurim: Wine & Blood

### Shiurim Overview

The daf under discussion is 77, and we continue within the perek of *Hamotzi Yayin*, which addresses the various *shiurim* for carrying foods and liquids on Shabbat. By way of orientation: for human foods, the governing measure is always a *gerogeres* (a dried fig's bulk). For liquids, different *shiurim* apply. Wine, when diluted, requires enough to constitute a full *revi'is* — specifically, according to Rav, a quarter of a *revi'is* of undiluted wine, given a three-to-one dilution ratio. This was somewhat contested by Abaye, who appeared to favor a two-to-one ratio, which would have implied a different minimum. With this background in place, we pick up in the middle of 77a.

### Dried Wine: Kezayis

The Gemara introduces a *tana*: *yavesh bikezayis divrei Rebbi Noson* — if wine has dried out completely, Rabbi Noson holds that the relevant measure is a *kezayis*, since the substance is now solid. This is immediately puzzling: solid foods are governed by the measure of a *gerogeres*, not a *kezayis*. Why then does dried wine go by a *kezayis*? Presumably, the answer lies in the fact that it can be re-diluted and restored to wine, so it retains something of its liquid character — yet Rabbi Noson still assigns it a *kezayis*.

Rav Yosef observes that this position of Rabbi Noson is identical to one articulated by Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda: *amru davar echad* — they said the same thing. To establish this identification, the Gemara cites a *braisa* from tractate *Ediyos*, where Rabbi Yehuda reports six matters in which Beit Shammai was lenient and Beit Hillel strict. (Rashi notes parenthetically that there are in fact more than six such matters, but Rabbi Yehuda was testifying to the specific tradition before him in Ediyos, not offering an exhaustive catalogue.) One of these six concerns *dam neveilah* — the blood of a ritually slaughtered animal that was improperly killed. The meat of a *neveilah* is *tamei*; Beit Shammai holds the blood is *tahor*, while Beit Hillel holds it is *tamei* as well — whether because blood is treated equivalently to meat, or on the basis of a particular *pasuk* (as Tosafot discusses).

On the question of quantity, Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda states: *af kishitmu Beit Hillel, lo tim'u ela b'dam sheyesh bo revi'is* — even when Beit Hillel declares it *tamei*, they only do so for blood amounting to a *revi'is*, because that is the quantity which can congeal into a *kezayis*. The reasoning is that blood is *tamei* as a species of meat, and meat of a *neveilah* is *tamei* in a *kezayis*. Therefore, the liquid form is measured by the amount that will yield a *kezayis* of solid — which is a *revi'is*.

The symmetry is striking: Rabbi Noson says that wine which has dried into a *kezayis* solid was originally a *revi'is* of liquid; Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda says that blood which amounts to a *revi'is* of liquid is *tamei* because it can congeal into a *kezayis* of solid. Both affirm a conversion relationship between one *revi'is* of liquid and one *kezayis* of solid. The Gemara therefore identifies them as advancing the same underlying position.

### Density & Conversion

Abaye challenges whether these two authorities can truly be regarded as making the same claim. His objection is grounded in the physical properties of the substances involved.

*Dilma lo hi* — perhaps they cannot be equated. Abaye argues: Rabbi Noson's ruling applies to wine (*d'kalish* — thin, not very viscous). But blood (*d'samich* — thick, more viscous) is a far denser substance. If a *revi'is* of thin wine yields a *kezayis* of dried matter, it does not follow that a *revi'is* of thick blood would yield the same. Less than a *revi'is* of blood — perhaps half, perhaps two-thirds — might already constitute a *kezayis* of congealed solid. So the two rulings cannot simply be read as expressing the same physical conversion ratio.

Conversely, Abaye argues from the other direction: if Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda holds that a *revi'is* of blood is the threshold because it can congeal into a *kezayis*, then applying that logic to wine (which is thinner), a *kezayis* of dried wine would actually represent *more* than a *revi'is* of original liquid. This means one would be *chayav* for carrying out even less than a full *kezayis* of dried wine. In short: neither ruling straightforwardly implies the other, because the *metzi'us* — the physical reality — of different liquids is genuinely different.

This Talmudic exchange points toward a broader conceptual tension. One might ask: at what point does the measure cease to track practical usability and become a formal legal category that operates by its own internal rules? This question surfaced earlier in the tractate as well — by the case of mixed grain types, where the governing question was whether the minimum *shiur* was met, not whether any animal would actually eat the mixture. The same dynamic appears here: once the measure has been assigned, the system operates with its own logic, and the question of whether the substance is genuinely useful in this form becomes secondary.

A related difficulty: if we are speaking of undiluted wine that has dried out, the starting point should have been a *quarter* of a *revi'is*, not a full *revi'is*, since undiluted wine requires only that smaller measure. Why does Rabbi Noson cite a full *revi'is*?

### Rashi: Category Shift

Rashi addresses this directly. He explains: *de-me-ikara havei beih revi'is u-ve-karush revi'is sheleima be'inan de-lav bar meziga* — although the wine may originally have been the denser, undiluted variety requiring only a quarter *revi'is*, once it dries out it is no longer eligible for *mezigah* (the act of diluting wine for drinking). It has departed from the category of concentrated wine-to-be-diluted, and therefore can no longer be governed by the *shiur* of that category. It must now be measured by the standard applicable to ordinary, fully potable wine — and that *shiur* is a full *revi'is*.

This is a notable conceptual move: the drying of the wine does not merely change its physical state; it shifts its legal category. It leaves category A (*yayin chamur*, undiluted wine ready to be mixed) and enters category B (standard wine ready for drinking). Rashi is explicit that the criterion for this shift is the loss of *mezigah* eligibility. What is equally notable is what Rashi does *not* say: he does not ask whether this *kezayis* of dried wine is actually useful or functional. The question is not one of usability but of categorical placement. The substance has been removed from one legal box and placed in another — and within that new box, the *shiur* of a *revi'is* applies. The formalization of the *shiurim* has, in this instance, taken over from the functional reasoning that originally generated them.

---

## Aleph-Ayin & Aramaic

### G'miya Spelling

The Gemara opens the next topic — the *shiur* for milk — with the phrase *chalav kedei g'miya* (milk in the amount of a swallow), and immediately raises a textual question: is the word *g'miya* spelled with an *alef* or an *ayin*? This may seem an unusual digression, but it reflects genuine linguistic uncertainty. For Ashkenazim, for whom *ayin* has lost its guttural quality and sounds identical to *alef*, this question might appear trivial — but in a world where *ayin* was pronounced gutturally, the two letters were meaningfully distinct, and the distinction mattered for scribal and oral traditions alike.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the question by citing the episode in Bereishit where Eliezer asks Rivkah for water: *hagmi'ini na me'at mayim mikadech* — the word for "let me swallow" appears there spelled with an *alef*. This supports the *alef* spelling. (It is worth noting that the word as it appears in the Mishnah may have been spelled with an *ayin*, yet the Gemara uses the biblical spelling to determine the correct form — an interesting deployment of the written Torah to arbitrate oral-tradition orthography.)

### Spelling Questions

The Gemara, now launched on this topic, raises several further spelling disputes. Are the seeds excluded from the *shiur* for carrying food spelled *garinim* with an *alef* or an *ayin*? Rabbah bar Ulla derives the correct spelling from the verse *venigra me'erkecha* — "and it shall be deducted from your valuation" — reasoning that seeds are things that are discarded or deducted, and the root there contains an *ayin*. The derivation is admittedly creative: the word in its biblical context has nothing to do with seeds, but the Gemara is searching for etymological grounding.

Then: is the word *omomos* — describing charcoal that is smoldering or sputtering, neither fully alight nor extinguished — spelled with an *alef* or an *ayin*? Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi cites the verse *arazim lo amamuhu began Elohim* — "the cedars did not overshadow it in the garden of God" — where Rashi explains *amamuhu* means "darkened." Since smoldering charcoal is blackened, this etymological connection supports the *ayin* spelling.

Finally, the word for closing one's eyes — as in the ruling about whether one may close the eyes of a dying person on Shabbat (a question touching on *muktzah* and the prohibition against hastening death) — is it spelled with an *alef* or an *ayin*? Rav Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan cites *ve-otzem einav me-r'ot bera* — "and one who closes his eyes from seeing evil" — where the word clearly appears with an *ayin*.

### Scribal Tradition

The Gemara's method here is revealing. In each case, the orthographic question is resolved by citing a biblical verse — from both Torah and *Nach* — on the assumption that the scribal tradition of the written text is reliable enough to arbitrate spelling disputes in the oral tradition. This reflects a broader confidence in the integrity of scribal transmission: not only the Torah scroll, which was subject to the most rigorous preservation, but even the books of *Nevi'im* and *Ketuvim* were preserved in scrolls that the sages consulted and trusted.

Scholars have noted that the community of scribes in antiquity was in certain respects distinct from the community of sages, with its own traditions, skills, and custodianship of the text — not only the craft of writing but the textual tradition itself. The Gemara's assumption that a biblical verse can settle an orthographic dispute in a Mishnaic term presupposes that both traditions, scribal and rabbinic, were understood to preserve authentic and reliable transmission.

The very fact that these *alef-ayin* questions arise at all is itself significant. One would never confuse an *alef* with a *chet*, because those are quite dissimilar. But *ayin* and *alef* are readily confused when the *ayin* has lost its guttural pronunciation — and the Gemara elsewhere mentions that in Beit She'an, a cosmopolitan city in Eretz Yisrael with significant Greek cultural influence, people were known to pronounce their *ayins* as *alefs*. It seems plausible that in Bavel as well, the guttural *ayin* was beginning to erode — and these textual disputes may be a linguistic symptom of precisely that process.

---

## Shiurim: Liquids

### Milk, Egg, Honey

The Gemara now presents a *baraisa*: one who carries out (*hamotzi*) milk of an animal — the measure is *kedei g'miya*, the amount of a swallow. The measure for a woman's milk (*chalav shel isha*) and for the white of an egg (*loven shel beitza*) is *kedei liten b'mashifa shel kilor* — enough to apply to the smear on an eye patch (*kilor*). The distinction is instructive: animal's milk was commonly drunk, and so it receives the drinking measure. A woman's milk, by contrast, was not typically expressed and stored — it went directly from mother to infant — and so the only context in which it would be carried externally was medicinal, specifically for use on this type of eye patch. The same applies to egg white, which was similarly applied to these patches for therapeutic purposes. Hence both are measured by the therapeutic use rather than a consumption measure.

### Eye Patch (Kilor)

The Gemara then addresses the measure for the *kilor* patch itself: *kedei lishof b'mayim* — enough to apply water to it. This formulation is somewhat puzzling. Rashi explains the measure as the amount used for two eyes — but why not simply describe it as the size required to function as an eye patch? Perhaps, as one might suggest, the patch was used not merely as a covering but as an applicator — held in the fingers and used to apply the liquid directly to the eye. In that reading, the relevant dimension is the patch's capacity to serve as an applicator: large enough to hold water on one portion while leaving another portion free to grip.

Rav Ashi raises a further question: is the minimum size *kedei shipa* — enough to apply the liquid — or *kedei achiza v'shipa* — enough both to grip and to apply, meaning the patch must be large enough to accommodate fingers holding it in addition to the surface area used for application? The Gemara concludes *teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

### Honey for Wounds

For honey, the *tana* teaches: *kedei liten al pi katit* — enough to place on the opening of a wound. Rashi understands *katit* as a type of scraping or abrasion. The measure is not the entire surface area of the surrounding irritation but the wound opening itself. Rav Ashi again poses a question: does *al pi katit* refer to the mouth of the entire wound — the full area of injury, excluding only the surrounding inflamed tissue — or does it refer to the first raised prominence of the wound, excluding even the broader injured area? Once again the Gemara concludes *teiku*.

These unresolved questions are not without practical significance — at least theoretically, the *nafkah mina* concerns the obligation to bring a *korban chatat* for inadvertent violation. One might also observe the broader point being illustrated: these *shiurim*, at least in the present context, do not appear to be received as rigid *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*. Rather, the Gemara is actively working them out through reasoning about typical use — which raises in turn the question, already flagged in the earlier discussion of mixed grains, of the relationship between the conceptual basis for a *shiur* and its subsequent formalization as an autonomous legal category.

---

## Creation & Purpose

### Nothing in Vain

The Gemara now turns in a markedly different direction — one that may seem surprising given the halachic context, but whose connection will become clear. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *kol ma shebara ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu b'olamo, lo bara davar echad l'vatala* — everything that the Holy One Blessed Be He created in His world, He created nothing in vain. Each creature, each natural phenomenon, serves a purpose. The connection to the immediately preceding material is subtle: we have just been discussing honey applied to wounds, and the Gemara is about to explain which creatures were created to provide cures for various injuries.

### Creatures & Cures

The Gemara proceeds: *bara shavlul l'katit* — He created the slug for an abrasion. One applies the slug (or its secretion) to a scraped or abraded wound. *Bara zvuv l'tzira* — He created the fly for a wasp sting; crushed flies were applied to the site of a wasp bite. *Yatush l'nachash* — the mosquito for a snake bite; crushed mosquito was applied to snakebite wounds. *Nachash l'chafafit* — the snake for *chafafit*, which Rashi explains as a type of boil or *shechin*; some preparation from the snake — whether venom or otherwise — served as treatment. *V'samamit l'akrav* — and the *samamit* (understood by Rashi and the primary tradition as a spider, though Steinsaltz identifies it as a gecko) for a scorpion sting.

For the last case, the Gemara elaborates on the preparation: *maiti chada uchma v'chada chivra* — one takes one black specimen and one white specimen of the *samamit*, boils them together, and applies the mixture to the scorpion sting.

The theological claim animating this passage is explicit: every creature serves a purpose. The Maharsha grapples with the obvious challenge: what of creatures that cause pain and harm — what is their purpose? His answer is that creatures capable of causing suffering serve a different but equally intentional divine purpose: they allow a person to atone through *yisurim* (suffering) in this world rather than in the next. The Gemara's focus here, however, is on the positive benefit these creatures provide — the specific medical functions that justify their existence from a human-centered perspective.

One might press the point further: is the argument that everything on earth must benefit human beings? The Gemara seems to be making precisely that claim, at least with respect to these creatures. But as one might note, this is a markedly anthropocentric framing. The psalmist's declaration that *hashamayim mesaprim kevod El* — the heavens declare God's glory — implies a different register of divine purpose, one that extends well beyond human utility. The Gemara here is answering a narrower question in a narrower way: these creatures, which might seem superfluous or merely irritating, actually serve concrete medical functions.

### Five Fears

The Gemara continues with another teaching: *chamisha eimos hen* — there are five instances of fear, all falling under the heading of *eimat chalash al gibbor* — the fear of the weak upon the strong. This phrase functions as a general rubric for what follows, rather than as a sixth example in its own right: in each case, a smaller or apparently weaker creature causes fear in a larger, more powerful one.

The five are: *eimat mafgia al ari* — the fear of the *mafgia* upon the lion. Rashi describes this as a small creature that makes a loud noise and thereby frightens the lion; others identify it as a skunk-like animal whose spray drives off even packs of lions. *Eimat yatush al ha-pil* — the fear of the mosquito upon the elephant, which is greatly distressed by mosquito bites and will go to considerable lengths to avoid them. *Eimat samamit al ha-akrav* — the fear of the spider upon the scorpion; the same creature mentioned above in its curative role is, in its living form, a predator that the scorpion fears, despite being physically smaller. *Ve-eimat senunit al ha-nesher* — the fear of the *senunit* (identified by Steinsaltz as a swallow) upon the *nesher* (which, as Yehuda Feliks and others have established, refers to a vulture rather than an eagle — a point worth noting given the regal biblical imagery associated with the *nesher*). Flocking birds can interfere with birds of prey. *Ve-eimat kilvis al Leviathan* — the fear of the *kilvis*, a small fish, upon the Leviathan, the great sea creature. Rashi explains that this small fish would enter the ear of the great fish, causing it particular distress.

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *mai kra* — what is the scriptural basis for this? The verse *hamavlig shod al oz* — "one who spreads destruction upon the strong" — is cited, with Rashi reading *shod* as *shadud*, the downtrodden or diminished, who can nonetheless project fear onto the powerful.

---

## Animal Observations

### Goats & Sheep

The Gemara transitions to a charming narrative interlude. Rabbi Zeira found Rav Yehuda standing at the entrance of his father-in-law's home in an exceptionally good mood — *d'hava bedicha da'tei* — so good, indeed, that Rabbi Zeira felt this was the moment to ask him about all the wonders of the world: *ei ba'i minei kol chalala d'alma hava amar lei* — had he wished, he could have asked him anything about the open workings of the world, and Rav Yehuda would have answered him.

There is a real question about how to read this passage. One reading is that *bedicha* carries a tone of lightness and even humor: this was not a formal *beit midrash* exchange but a relaxed outdoor conversation, and the questions and answers that follow are playful rather than strictly scientific. Another reading takes the passage more earnestly: the Gemara chose to record these questions and their answers because curiosity about the natural world was considered a legitimate and even valued form of inquiry. This is consistent with the principle that one who can calculate the cycles of the heavens (*tekufot u-mazalot*) and does not do so has failed to appreciate *pe'ulat Hashem* — the work of God — and stands in a kind of negligence. On this reading, a *talmid chacham* of Rav Yehuda's stature was expected to have engaged with these questions precisely because they are part of understanding the divine creation.

Rabbi Zeira's first question: *mai ta'ama izi masgan b'reisha* — why do goats walk in front of sheep? Rav Yehuda answers: *k'veri'ato shel olam* — like the creation of the world, where first there was darkness (*chashocha*) and then light (*nehora*). Since goats tend toward dark coloring and sheep toward white, the order of the animals in the flock mirrors the sequence of creation.

### Sheep vs. Goats

The next question: *mai ta'ama hanei mikhasyan va-hanei migalyan* — why are sheep covered (i.e., their hindquarters concealed by their broad, fatty tails) while goats are exposed? The answer: *hanei de-mikhasyan minaihu mikhasyan* — those from whom we take material to cover ourselves (sheep, whose wool we use for clothing) have their own parts covered; *va-hanei de-lo mikhasyan minaihu, migalyan* — those from whom we do not take material to cover ourselves (goats) remain exposed. This is, as the questioner notes, a notably human-centered explanation — the covering of the animal mirrors our own use of it.

### Tails & Horns

The questions continue: *mai ta'ama gamla zutra kinvaseh* — why does the camel have a short tail? Because it grazes among thornbushes (*kisei*), and a long tail would become entangled in the thorns. *Mai ta'ama tora arich kinvaseh* — why does an ox have a long tail? Because it grazes in swampy areas (*agmi*) and requires a long tail to swat away flies. *Mai ta'ama karna de-kamtza rekika* — why is the antenna (translated variously as "horn") of the locust soft and pliable rather than rigid? Because it lives among blades of grass (*chilfei*), and if the antenna were stiff, it would catch on the grasses and be torn out — which, the Gemara explains, would blind the locust.

### Antennae & Eyes

This leads to Shmuel's statement: one who wishes to blind a locust removes its antennae (*lishlifinu le-karnei*). Whether this means there is some magical connection between antennae and sight, or — more plausibly — that locusts navigate and locate themselves through their antennae, functioning somewhat like a cat's whiskers, so that their removal renders the creature effectively blind by depriving it of its sensory apparatus, the practical observation is the same.

The final question in this series: *mai ta'ama hai timra de-tarnagolta midli le-eila* — why does the chicken's eyelid move upward rather than downward? (Unlike humans, whose upper eyelid descends, a chicken's lower membrane rises.) The answer: *de-dayri adafi* — because chickens roost on beams and ledges high above the ground, and smoke rises. Since smoke and irritants ascend from below, having the lower eyelid move upward provides better protection for the eye against rising smoke. The adaptation is designed, on this account, precisely for the environment the creature inhabits.

---

## Aleph-Ayin & Aramaic (II)

### Aramaic Etymologies

The Gemara now presents an extended series of Aramaic etymologies, tracing common Aramaic words back to Hebrew roots or phrases. The exercise reflects a view that Aramaic, however widely spoken, contains hidden layers of meaning derivable from the holy tongue.

*Dasha* (a door) derives from *derech sham* — the way of the path, the way through which one passes. *Darga* (a step or stair) derives from *derech gag* — the way to the roof. *Matkulisa* (a type of dip or condiment) derives from *matai tichleh da* — when will this be finished? — because dip is used so slowly and sparingly that it seems inexhaustible, lasting far longer than solid foods. *Beita* (a house) derives from *bo ve-isiv* — come and sit — expressing the fundamental hospitality embodied in a home. *Biksa* (a small house) derives from *be-aksa* — a narrow, confined space. *Kufta* (a basket, or perhaps a measuring vessel) derives from *kuf ve-tiv* — turn it over and sit on it — because these baskets were sometimes inverted and used as seats. *Livni* (bricks) derives from *livnei banei* — for your children's children — because a house built of brick will endure for generations.

*Hutza* (a divider between properties, made of weak materials like thorns and thistles) derives from *chatzitza* — a mere partition rather than a proper fence. *Chatzva* (a pail or jug used for drawing water) derives from *shotzev mayim min ha-nahar* — one who hews or draws water from the river. *Kuza* (a small flask or jug) derives from *ke-zeh* — just like this, a little of that — suggesting the casual borrowing or sharing of a small amount. *Shutisa* (a myrtle branch) derives from *shtuta* — foolishness — because the Gemara elsewhere records that great sages would dance with myrtle branches before the bride and groom at weddings, acting in an uncharacteristically loose and joyous manner in the spirit of *mesameach choson ve-kallah*.

*Mashichla* (a large bucket used for bathing) derives from *mashi kuleh* — it washes the entire body. *Mashchalta* (a smaller, finer bucket) derives from *mashi kallah* — it is used by a *kallah*, a bride, or more broadly by people of distinction, since it is the more elegant vessel. *Asita* (the mortar — the vessel that holds spices to be ground) derives from *chasirta* — something lacking or hollow, a cavity. *Buchna* (the pestle — the implement used to strike and grind) derives from *bo ve-akeh-nah* — come and let me strike it.

*Levusha* (a garment) derives from *lo busha* — no shame, for clothing removes nakedness and with it the experience of shame. *Glima* (a cloak, something like a long coat or mantle) derives from *she-na'aseh bo ke-golem* — one becomes shapeless when wearing it, as a heavy outer garment obscures the body's form. *Gulsa* (a finer cape or outer garment) derives from *gali ve-isiv* — reveal and sit — meaning one takes it off before sitting, lest the garment be spoiled. *Puraiya* (a bed) derives from *she-parin ve-ravin aleha* — that one is fruitful and multiplies upon it.

*Bor zinka* (an empty well) derives from *bor ze naki* — this well is empty. *Sudra* (a handkerchief or head-covering, particularly associated with *talmidei chachamim* who wore it as a distinctive mark) derives from *sod Hashem lire'av* — the secret of God is for those who fear Him — suggesting that this garment identified those initiated into the deeper dimensions of Torah. *Apadna* (a large mansion or palace) derives from *apitcha dein* — this is the entrance, the doorway — evoking the place where important matters, business dealings, or charitable requests were transacted.

---

## Growth & Strength

### Three Animals

The Gemara teaches: *shlosha kol zman she-mazkinin mosifin gevurah* — three creatures, the older they grow, the more powerful they become. These are: *dag* (fish), *nachash* (snake), and *chazir* (pig). Fish simply keep growing larger and more powerful without reaching a stage of decline associated with old age. Snakes likewise increase in size and strength — as evidenced by the massive specimens found in places like the Bronx Zoo. And wild boars continue to grow in bulk and ferocity. The underlying observation is that these creatures do not experience senescence in the way other animals do; they grow continuously rather than plateauing and declining.

---

## Shiurim: Liquids (II)

### Oil: Small Limbs

Returning to the *shiurim*: *shemen kedei lasuach eiver katan* — oil sufficient to anoint a small limb. The school of Rabbi Yannai specifies: *shemen kedei lasuach eiver katan shel katan ben yomo* — oil sufficient to anoint the smallest limb of a day-old infant. That is: take the tiniest person possible (a newborn) and the tiniest limb (a pinky, or even a segment of a pinky), and that is the measure. The resulting quantity is extraordinarily small.

The Gemara raises a challenge (*meitivei*): a *braisa* attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states *shemen kedei lasuach eiver katan ve-katan ben yomo* — oil sufficient to anoint a small limb *and* a day-old infant. The conjunction *vav* seems to suggest two separate measures: either a small limb of a full-grown adult, or alternatively a large limb of a day-old infant. If so, the *braisa* does not require both conditions simultaneously, and the resulting measure would be larger than the school of Rabbi Yannai's ruling.

The school of Rabbi Yannai pushes back: *hachi ka'amar* — this is how the *braisa* should be read. The *vav* is not conjunctive but explanatory: *shemen kedei lasuach eiver katan shel katan ben yomo* — a small limb of a day-old infant, with *katan ben yomo* specifying which *katan* is meant. Both conditions are required simultaneously, and the measure is indeed the minute amount they originally proposed.

The Gemara then asks whether this is a debate among *tanna'im*. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, it now appears, holds that the *vav* is genuinely conjunctive and either condition alone suffices — a small limb of an adult, or a large limb of a day-old infant, with these treated as equivalent measures. Rabbi Natan, by contrast, says only *kedei lasuach eiver katan* — a small limb, full stop — which Abaye understands as referring to a small limb of an adult, with no reference to an infant.

The Gemara initially considers whether this represents a true dispute: does Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar hold that both criteria combined (small limb of a day-old infant) is the measure, while Rabbi Natan holds that only one condition at a time need be met? The Gemara rejects this framing: *de-kulei alma eiver katan de-katan ben yomo lo* — everyone agrees that a small limb of a day-old infant is too small a measure and does not constitute the threshold for *chiyuv*. The school of Rabbi Yannai is thus rejected by consensus. The actual debate is between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that a small limb of an adult and a large limb of a day-old infant are equivalent and interchangeable measures, and Rabbi Natan, who accepts only the small limb of an adult and does not allow the infant's limb as an alternative.

The Gemara concludes with a *braisa* in which Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar himself explicitly states *shemen kedei lasuach eiver katan shel katan ben yomo* — establishing the combined measure of small limb plus day-old infant as his definitive position. The *nafkah mina* for all of this, as noted, is the liability to bring a *korban chatat* for carrying oil on Shabbat.

### Water & Sh'chicha

The Gemara turns to water: *mayim kedei lishofet et ha-kilor* — water in the amount needed to apply to the eye patch. This is a strikingly small measure, far less than the amount one would use for drinking. The Gemara now pivots to the conceptual question underlying this and the preceding *shiurim*: how does one determine which use of a substance governs the minimum measure?

---

## Sh'chicha Principle

### Abaye's Rule

Abaye articulates a general principle: *kol milta di-shchicha ve-lo shchicha, azlu rabbanan batar di-shchicha le-kula* — whenever a substance has two possible uses, one common (*shchicha*) and one uncommon, the Rabbis follow the more common use, and they do so even when that results in a leniency (a larger minimum measure, making it harder to be liable). Conversely, *shchicha u-shchicha, azlu rabbanan batar di-shchicha le-chumra* — when both uses are equally common, the Rabbis follow the common use and do so in the direction of stringency, adopting the smaller measure. The underlying logic is that a common use defines what the substance "is" for purposes of the *shiur*, and when two equally common uses compete, the stricter measure governs.

### Wine & Milk

Wine: *shtiyato shchiha, refuato lo shchiha* — drinking wine is common; using it medicinally is not. The medicinal use would correspond to a smaller measure; the drinking measure is larger. The Rabbis follow the more common use — drinking — *le-kula*, as a leniency, resulting in a higher threshold for liability. Milk: *achilato shchiha, refuato lo shchiha* — consuming milk is common; using it medicinally is not. Again, the Rabbis follow the eating measure *le-kula*, treating the larger, more common use as the governing measure.

### Honey: Equal Uses

Honey presents a different situation: *achilato shchiha ve-refuato shchiha* — both eating honey and using it medicinally are common uses. The question of whether a use is "common" in this context should not be understood as a frequency count of individual occasions. Rather, the relevant inquiry is whether someone who possesses honey would be equally likely to be using it for one purpose versus another — whether both purposes are among the primary identified uses of the substance. By that standard, honey is genuinely *shchicha* for both eating and healing. Accordingly, *azlu rabbanan batar refuato le-chumra* — the Rabbis follow the medicinal use *le-chumra*, adopting the smaller measure and thus a lower threshold for liability.

### Water Exception

Water seems to fit the first pattern clearly: *shtiyato shchiha, refuato lo shchiha* — drinking water is overwhelmingly common; using it for a wound patch is not. The Rabbis should therefore follow the drinking measure *le-kula*, which is a much larger amount. Yet the Gemara rules the opposite: the measure for water is the small amount used for the eye patch. Why?

Abaye explains: *be-Galila shanu* — this was taught in the Galilee. In the Galilee, where people were relatively poor, water was the standard liquid used for wound dressings and eye patches, since other liquids like wine, oil, or honey were less accessible. In that regional context, using water medicinally was sufficiently common to elevate it to a primary use. This does not mean that water was used for medicinal purposes more often than for drinking in absolute terms; it means that within the list of primary recognized uses for water in that community, medicinal application appears near the top.

This explanation, however, raises an unsettling implication: does the *shiur* vary by region? If the measure for water as derived in the Galilee reflects Galilean practice, would the measure be different in Judea?

### Rava & Shmuel

Rava offers an alternative that sidesteps the regional specificity: *afilu teima bi-sh'ar mekomot, k'Shmuel* — even in other places, the same result follows, on the basis of a ruling by Shmuel. Shmuel stated: *kol shakyani massu u-metall'lei* — all liquids will heal a wound but will also cause clouding of the vision or some deleterious side effect. *Le-var mimaya* — with the exception of water. *D'massu ve-lo metall'lei* — water heals and does not cause blurring. Because water is uniquely effective for this purpose without side effects, it is preferred for use with the *kilor* eye patch wherever one might be. This makes the medicinal use of water sufficiently prominent — even in places where other liquids are plentiful — to elevate it to a primary recognized use.

### Regional Variation

Yet the question of regional variation does not fully dissolve. The possibility that *shiurim* could differ from place to place sits uncomfortably with the general conception of *shiurim* as fixed and formal legal categories. As the earlier analysis noted, once a *shiur* has been formalized, it tends to operate by its own internal rules, no longer directly beholden to the functional reasoning that originally generated it. The notion that a *shiur* might shift depending on local custom or economic conditions points in precisely the opposite direction — toward flexibility and responsiveness to context. The tension between these two tendencies — the formal fixity of *shiurim* on one hand, and their grounding in lived practice on the other — remains unresolved at the close of this passage, and is to be continued.

---

---

# Shabbat 78

## Liquids: Standards

### Common Uses Principle

The daf begins approximately fifteen lines into 78a, picking up in the middle of the *Mishnah* that catalogs the minimum amounts (*shiurim*) for which one becomes liable for carrying various liquids on *Shabbat*. Before proceeding to the final line of that *Mishnah*, it is worth recalling the elegant principle that *Abaye* articulated in the preceding discussion. He observed that when a substance has both a common use and an uncommon use, we follow the common use to determine the relevant *shiur* — even if that results in a more lenient (smaller) minimum. The rationale is that significance is calibrated by the primary function people actually have for an object. When there are multiple common uses, however, we adopt the strictest (smallest) amount, because even that small a quantity is rendered significant by the fact that it serves a recognized, ordinary purpose.

This principle, while clarifying, still leaves open a subtle question. Water, for instance, is far more commonly used for drinking than for preparing an eye compress. Yet the *Gemara* treats the compress application as a "common use" sufficient to define water's *shiur* for that purpose. The definition of "common use" is thus itself a contextual and perhaps even geographic judgment — the *Gemara* raises elsewhere whether the *shiur* might vary by region — and the broader question of how fixed or malleable these *shiurim* are in the face of changing circumstances remains a live one throughout this section of the *Gemara*.

### Revi'it Standard

With that framework in place, the *Mishnah* concludes: *veshear kol hamashkin berevi'it* — all other liquids go by a *revi'it* (a quarter-log, approximately three and a half ounces). This is the default measure for any liquid not specifically addressed by one of the earlier exceptions.

A *baraita* then expands on this: *dam vechol minei mashkin berevi'it* — blood and all other types of liquid go by a *revi'it*. Tosafot notes that the word *vekol* here should be read as *veshear*, meaning "and all other" liquids beyond those already discussed. The intent is not that every liquid whatsoever requires a *revi'it*, but that blood and the remaining unspecified liquids, having not been granted a smaller *shiur*, default to the standard *revi'it*.

### Blood Exceptions

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar dissents regarding blood. He holds that blood does not require a full *revi'it*; rather, the minimum is *kedei lichol ayin achat* — enough to apply to one eye. His reasoning is that blood was used medicinally for a condition called *barakit*, which Rashi identifies as a type of raised growth or mote on the eye. Since people would apply blood to one eye for this ailment, even so small an amount carries practical significance. (The cosmetic application, which one might assume would involve both eyes, is not the operative use here — and notably, the use need not be one that can be performed on *Shabbat* itself. An object's significance for the purposes of carrying liability is determined by its value and use during the week. Just as one may be liable for carrying a match even though striking it on *Shabbat* is forbidden, blood used medically during the week has its *shiur* defined by that use.)

The *Gemara* then asks which blood is specifically used for *barakit*: it is *dama detarnagola bara*, the blood of a wild rooster. Whether this means the *shiur* for all blood is thereby defined, or only for wild rooster blood specifically, remains somewhat unclear from the *Gemara*'s formulation.

Rabban Gamliel agrees with the measure of one eye's worth but arrives there by a different route. He says blood is applied for *erod*, which Rashi describes as white spots on the eye. The blood used for *erod* is *dama dekharshutin'a* — the blood of a bat. To remember which blood treats which condition, the *Gemara* offers a mnemonic: *gavva le-gavva* — "outside to outside, inside to inside." The wild rooster (*bara*, meaning "outside/wild") corresponds to *barakit*, a protrusion that is, as it were, external. The bat, which Rashi notes inhabits enclosed spaces within a city, corresponds to *erod*, the white spots within the inner part of the eye. Again, whether this *shiur* applies to all blood or only to these specific types is left without a fully explicit resolution.

### Removal vs. Setting Aside

The *baraita* then introduces a critical distinction: *bameh devarim amurim bemotzi* — when do these smaller *shiurim* apply? When one is the *motzi*, the person who simply carries out the liquid. *Aval be-matznia kol shehu chayav* — but in a case where the item was *matznia* (set aside as personally significant), even the smallest amount renders one liable.

Rabbi Shimon responds with the inverse formulation: *bameh devarim amurim be-matznia* — these smaller *shiurim* apply to the case where the item was set aside and given personal significance. *Aval bemotzi eino chayav ela bi-revi'it* — but the ordinary person who merely carries out (without having designated the object as significant) is not liable unless there is a full *revi'it*.

This restates the debate from the *Mishnah* itself. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that the smaller *shiurim* (for honey, milk, blood, and so forth) are the standard measures for ordinary carrying; if the person additionally designated the item as significant, liability descends further to *kol shehu*, any amount. Rabbi Shimon takes the opposite position: the smaller *shiurim* reflect the significance conferred by setting aside; absent such designation, all liquids — even honey, milk, and blood — revert to the default *revi'it*.

### Master-Apprentice Exception

The *Gemara* raises a difficulty with the *Tanna Kamma*'s formulation. The *baraita* reads *be-matznia kol shehu chayav* — "in a case where it was set aside." The *Gemara* notes that Tosafot and Rashi actually read this phrase differently from each other, but following Tosafot's reading: had the *baraita* said *ha-matznia*, it would mean "the one who set it aside" — that is, only the person who personally designated the item would be liable for carrying any amount. That would accord with the *Tanna Kamma*'s baseline view. But the *baraita* says *be-matznia*, meaning "in a case where it was set aside" — implying that anyone who carries it, even someone other than the person who designated it, would be liable for *kol shehu*.

The *Gemara* objects: is that not the rejected view of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who held that once one person confers significance upon an object, it becomes significant for everyone? The *Gemara* cites the example: I set aside my chewing gum because I intend to chew it later. According to the *Tanna Kamma*, that act of setting aside makes me liable for *kol shehu* when I subsequently carry it — but it does not affect someone else who carries it; for them, the standard *shiur* still applies. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar held the more expansive view: once I confer significance, it becomes universally significant.

*Amar Abaye*: the *baraita* is not speaking about the general case at all. It addresses a specific scenario — *betalmid she'amar lo rabbo*, a master who instructed his apprentice. When a master tells his apprentice to clear out a room, and the apprentice does so by carrying items into the public domain, the apprentice is liable for items that carry ordinary significance. For items that lack standard significance but which the master had specifically designated, the apprentice is likewise liable — because his role is entirely subordinate to the master's directives, and the master's designation of significance functionally constitutes significance for the apprentice as well. In all other cases, only the person who actually set aside the object is liable for *kol shehu* when carrying it; no one else's liability is affected by that designation.

The overall framework, then, is as follows. For foods, the standard is *kegrogeret*, the size of a pressed fig. For liquids, the default is a *revi'it*, with specific exceptions for items like honey, milk, and arguably blood, which have recognized uses in smaller quantities. If a person sets something aside as personally significant, the *shiur* drops to *kol shehu* — for that person. And in the unique relationship of master and apprentice, the master's act of setting aside extends that lowered *shiur* to the apprentice as well.

### Dirty Water & Plaster

The *baraita* includes one more point of agreement: *u-modim chachamim le-Rabbi Shimon bemotzi shofchin she-shi'uran bi-revi'it* — the Sages concede to Rabbi Shimon that dirty water (*shfochin*) has a *shiur* of a *revi'it* even in ordinary carrying. This invites a natural question: *shpochin le-mai chazu*? What does one do with dirty water? *Amar Rabbi Yirmiyah*: you use it to mix plaster — *le-gabel bahen et ha-tit*.

But this raises a further difficulty. A separate *baraita* establishes that the *shiur* for plaster (*tit*) is the amount needed to form the opening of a bellows (*pi kur*), the small channel used in smelting. That amount of finished plaster is far smaller than the quantity of plaster one could produce from a *revi'it* of water. If a small quantity of finished plaster has recognized significance, should not the proportionally smaller amount of water sufficient to produce that plaster also be significant — and therefore carry a *shiur* well below a *revi'it*?

The *Gemara* resolves this with *lo kashya*: there is no contradiction, because the two cases involve different states of material. *Ha d'migbal, ha d'lo migbal* — one speaks of plaster already mixed, the other of water not yet combined into plaster. *She'ein adam tore'ach le-gabel tit la'asot pi kur*: a person does not go to the trouble of mixing plaster merely to produce the tiny amount needed for a bellows opening. One would only undertake the labor of mixing if one had a meaningful quantity of plaster to work with. Therefore, the water that has not yet been made into plaster requires a full *revi'it* to be considered significant; it is only the already-prepared plaster, in its finished state, that carries significance in a smaller amount.

---

## Non-Food Shiurim

### Rope vs. Strap

The *Mishnah* now leaves the domain of liquids and foodstuffs and turns to various other items, each assigned its own *shiur* for carrying liability. *Hamotzi chevel* — if one carries out a rope — the measure is *kedei la'asot ozen le-kupa*, enough to fashion a handle for a box. *Gami* — a strap or elastic material — goes by the smaller measure of *kedei la'asot tlai le-nafa u-le-chvarah*, enough to make a hanging loop for a sieve, from which one would hang the sieve in the kitchen.

One might ask why rope is not also measured by the smaller sieve-loop standard, since a rope can obviously serve as a loop as well. The *Gemara* explains: *keivan de-charik be-mana, lo avdi inshi* — because rope chafes against the vessel. People do not use rope to hang a sieve precisely because of its abrasive quality. A box handle, which is used differently and does not require gentle material, is made from rope — and so that larger size is the operative *shiur* for rope, while the softer strap material continues to be measured by the sieve-loop.

A *baraita* adds several related materials. *Hutzin* — wicker — is measured by enough to make a handle (*ozen*) for a wicker basket (*sal ve-khfifa*). *Siv* — a fibrous material that grows between the bark and trunk of a palm tree — according to *acherim*, is measured by enough to place at the mouth of a small pitcher to filter wine.
