One might have thought that since wood could serve such functions, even a minimal quantity would suffice to establish liability. The *Gemara* teaches that this is not so: *kol shehu* — an arbitrarily small amount — is not the standard. The standard use of wood is as firewood, and the *shiur* is determined by that standard use: *ke-dei levashel beitzah kalah*.

---

---

# Shabbat 90

## Matznia & Intent

### Context & Review

The sugya opens by recalling the context established in the preceding discussion. The *mishna* had ruled that if one sets aside even a smaller-than-standard quantity of an item — a practice known as *matznia* — and subsequently carries it out on Shabbat, one is *chayav*. The *gemara* then made the bold extension that even without having formally set the item aside beforehand, the very act of taking it out for an express purpose suffices to confer subjective significance upon it and render one liable. This extension, however, raises the obvious question: if intent alone suffices, what does the *mishna*'s case of *matznia* add? The answer is that the *mishna* addresses the situation where one originally set the item aside but then, at the moment of carrying it out, was not consciously thinking of that purpose — he was carrying it out without any particular intent at all.

### Intent Negation

The *gemara* begins the current amud by asking: why was it not self-evident that the original act of *matznia* would still govern? One might have argued *bitulei batlei machshavto* — that by subsequently carrying the item out without any focused purpose, one has effectively negated one's original intent, and with it the subjective significance one had assigned to the smaller quantity. The *gemara* therefore teaches *kol ha'oseh al da'at rishon hu oseh*: since one is acting in accordance with a broad, general intent, the original intent that gave significance to the lesser quantity remains operative.

### One Kernel Rule

*Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* then states that *Rabbi Meir* — assumed to be the *stam Tanna* of the *mishna* — held that one is *chayav* for carrying out even a single kernel of wheat, provided one is taking it out *lizriah*, for the purpose of planting. The *gemara* asks: is this not obvious? The *mishna* already says *kol shehu* — even the smallest amount — so of course a single kernel suffices. The *gemara* answers that one might have thought *kol shehu* means not literally any amount whatsoever, but rather the smallest of the standard rabbinic measurements — a *kezayis*, a *k'adashah*, or the like — as opposed to the larger *grogeret*. One might not have realized it means something truly beyond the scale of standard *shiurim* entirely. The *gemara* therefore teaches that yes, it means the absolute minimum. But as noted in the prior discussion, the deeper *chiddush* of *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* is the *gemara*'s implicit assumption from the previous session: that even without prior *matznia*, the mere fact of taking the item out for a specific purpose confers the subjective significance. Until now, all the *mishnayot* had addressed only cases of prior *matznia*.

### Kol Shehu Debate

This understanding that subjective intent can redefine the minimum quantity — even below any standard rabbinic measure — opens the floor to a broader inquiry into the limits of subjective redefinition.

## Challenge Minimums

### Symmetry Problem

*Rav Yitzchak brei d'Rav Yehuda* presses the logic: if intent can shrink the minimum below the standard *shiurim*, why cannot intent also expand it? If someone decides that his act of significance is removing the entire contents of his house as one grand unit — *cheishev lehotzi kol beito* — should we not say he is not *chayav* until he has taken out everything, since in his subjective definition that is the singular act of significance? Some *Rishonim*, including *Tosafot*, understand this question as directed not specifically at *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* but at the *mishna* itself: why, if subjective intent governs, does it operate only in the direction of stringency and not leniency?

### Stringency Only

The *gemara* answers that the principle of subjective intent operates only to increase liability, not to diminish it. Intent can make something *chayav* that would otherwise be exempt; it cannot make something exempt that would otherwise be *chayav*.

### Objective Norms

The underlying principle is *batla da'ato etzel kol adam* — when one's personal intent conflicts with the objective norm shared by all people, one's individual intent is negated. Where ordinary people would regard a given item or act as significant, that significance stands regardless of whether a particular individual assigns it weight. The *chiddush* of the *mishna* operates in precisely the opposite direction: when an individual assigns significance to something that other people would not consider significant, his subjective weight elevates it. He cannot, however, use his subjective frame to strip significance from something that the objective world regards as meaningful. This, one notes, also effectively answers the question implicitly: the answer was in some sense obvious, but the question was raising a more fundamental issue — where else in *halacha* do we find minimum quantities defined by subjective intent, even in the stringent direction? The case of *achshavei*, where one's act of eating something normally unfit confers significance upon it, is a related but distinct phenomenon — it concerns the act of giving significance, not the quantitative threshold as such.

## R. Shimon Uniform Rule

### Significance Binding

The *gemara* now notes that our *mishna* does not follow the position of *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar*. The *braita* states: *klal amar Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* formulated a general principle. Anything that is not ordinarily the type of object people set aside, and whose quantity is not ordinarily one that people preserve — *huchshar l'zeh vehitznio* — yet this particular person found it meaningful and set it aside. We know that if he himself takes it out, he is *chayav*. But *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* adds: *uva acher vehootzio* — if someone else then comes and takes out that same object — *nischayav zeh bemachshavto shel zeh* — that other person is liable on account of the first person's intent.

What troubles *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* is the lack of uniformity. If a quantity is *chayav* for one person and not for another, the minimum has become a moving target depending on whose perspective governs. He therefore maintains that once someone has conferred significance upon an object, it carries that significance for everyone. The *gemara* notes that our *mishna* does not follow this view — we do not say that one person's *matznia* creates universal liability for all subsequent actors. For everyone else, it remains the standard minimum. Only the one who set it aside bears the elevated standard for himself.

### Absurd Examples

To illustrate how counterintuitive this principle can become: consider someone who removes chewing gum from one's mouth, wraps it, and sets it aside for later use. For virtually everyone else, this object carries no significance whatsoever — no one would think to set aside chewed gum. Yet if one has done so, according to *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar*, someone else who then carries it out would be *chayav* on the strength of the original owner's intent. The tea bag one intends to reuse serves as a similarly striking example. The *mishna*, by rejecting *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar*, limits subjective significance to the person who created it.

## Intent Changes

### Simple Swap

*Rava* in the name of *Rav Nachman* addresses a new set of cases in which intent changes during the course of carrying. The baseline ruling: if one took out food the size of a *grogeret* intending to eat it — the standard minimum for food — and then, while still in transit and before putting it down, changed one's mind and decided to use it as seeds for planting, one is *chayav*. The reverse — taking it out to plant and then deciding to eat it — is equally *chayav*. The *gemara* asks: *p'shita* — is this not obvious? A *grogeret* is the minimum for eating, and planting requires only a few seeds, so in either direction one had the minimum. The *gemara* answers that one might have thought that the two stages of the carrying act — *akira* (picking up) and *hanachah* (putting down) — must be defined by the same intent. Since subjective intent has been given such weight as to redefine the minimum itself, perhaps an act begun with one definition and concluded with another is not legally a single unified act. The *gemara* rules against this concern: the *grogeret* quantity suffices at either stage regardless of the change in intent, and the act remains one *melacha*.

### Half Size Expansion

*Rava* then poses a genuine question. One took out half a *grogeret* intending to plant it — a minimum for planting. During transit, the item expanded — perhaps it was tightly compressed and unfolded, or perhaps it absorbed moisture — and by the time of *hanachah* it had grown to the size of a full *grogeret*. One then changed one's mind and decided to eat it. *Mahu* — what is the *halacha*?

### Combining Halves

The question is not trivial. At the moment of *akira*, the item did not qualify for the food category — it was only half a *grogeret*. It qualified only for the planting category. By the moment of *hanachah*, it had become a full *grogeret* and one was treating it as food. The question is whether the two halves of the *melacha* can combine: the beginning half defined the act as a planting act, and the concluding half defined it as a food act. Since the subjective intent has been shown to be definitionally significant, perhaps an act whose beginning and end are qualitatively different — each qualifying under a different category — cannot be viewed as one unified *melacha*.

### Original Intent

The *gemara* presents the counterargument: *keivan d'ilu ishtika hava michayev amachshava d'zria* — since, had one simply not changed one's mind and proceeded with the original planting intent, one would have been *chayav*, the subsequent change of intent does not break the continuity of the *melacha*. One cannot escape liability by having added a new intent on top of an already-complete set of conditions for *chiyuv*. Thus one would be *chayav* even here.

### Reverse Scenario

The question is then flipped: one took out a full *grogeret* intending to eat it — satisfying the food minimum at the outset — and during transit it shriveled (or some fell away), reducing the quantity below a *grogeret*. One then changed one's mind and decided to use what remained for planting. *Mahu*? Here the asymmetry is more acute. Had one maintained the original intent of eating, one would have been *patur* at the end, because there was no longer enough for the food category. The only thing that could potentially render one liable is the new intent to use the reduced quantity for planting. But the *akira* was performed treating it as food, and the *hanachah* treats it as seeds. Are these two legally incompatible halves of a *melacha*? The *gemara* leaves open whether *batar hashta azlinan u'mechayev* — we follow the end-state and one is *chayav* — or whether the discontinuity between the two halves is fatal to *chiyuv*.

### Shrink Reexpand

An even more extreme case: one took out a *grogeret* for eating — minimum satisfied. During transit it shriveled below the minimum. Before being put down, it re-expanded to a full *grogeret*. The endpoints both satisfy the minimum; the intermediate period did not. This question is qualitatively different from the preceding ones, because here there is no change of intent at all. The issue is not whether the subjective redefinition of the minimum can bridge two differently-intended halves; it is a question about the nature of the carrying act itself. Does the transporting process itself need to maintain the minimum at every moment? While one might expect the *gemara* to frame this as a question about the centrality of the transporting phase, the *gemara* instead frames it strikingly in terms of *dichui* — the concept of disqualification.

### Permanent Disqualificati…

*Yesh dichui le'inyan Shabbat o ein dichui le'inyan Shabbat*? — Is there a principle of permanent disqualification (*dichui*) applicable to the laws of Shabbat? Normally *dichui* arises in the context of *mitzvot* and *korbanot*: if an animal had a *mum* (blemish) that temporarily rendered it unfit for sacrifice, and the *mum* later healed, some hold it remains permanently rejected. The *gemara* here applies this logic — strikingly — not to qualifying for a *mitzvah* or a *korban*, but to qualifying as the object of a *melacha*. Did the temporary shrinking below the minimum "reject" the object, such that even after re-expansion it can no longer serve as the object of a complete act of *hotza'ah*? By framing it this way, the *gemara* is not emphasizing that the carrying process itself requires an ongoing minimum, but rather that once disqualified at a moment in the middle, perhaps the object is permanently disqualified. All of these questions are left unresolved — *teiku*.

## Throw Food Tamei

### Setup

*Rava* poses a further question to *Rav Nachman*: *Zarak kezayis truma levayis tamei* — one threw a *kezayis* of *terumah* into a house containing a corpse, thereby rendering the house a *ohel* for the purposes of *tum'at meit*.

### Category Separation

The *gemara* immediately asks: *lemai* — for what legal question is this scenario being posed? If the question is about Shabbat liability for carrying from *reshut harabim* into the house — *kegrogeret ba'inan* — food must be the size of a *grogeret*, which is larger than a *kezayis*, so there is no *chiyuv* in any case. If the question is about *tum'ah* — whether the food becomes *tamei* — *k'beitzah ochlin ba'inan*: we require food the size of an egg. At this point, an important dispute between *Rashi* and *Rabbeinu Tam* is directly relevant throughout *Shas*. *Rashi* holds in many places that the *beitzah* standard applies only to the capacity of food to transmit *tum'ah* to the next object in the chain; for food itself to become *tamei*, even a tiny amount suffices. *Rabbeinu Tam* disagrees and holds that even for food to become *tamei* in the first instance, a *beitzah* is required. The *gemara* here states *k'beitzah ochlin ba'inan*, which can be read consistently with either position.

The *gemara* then clarifies: the question is indeed about Shabbat. The scenario is refined: *kegon d'ika pachas mibeitzah ochlin* — in the house there was already less than a *beitzah* of food. Specifically, there was a *beitzah* minus one *kezayis*. The thrown *kezayis* flew in and landed on the existing food, combining with it — *vehai mashlimei lebeitzah* — completing it to a full *beitzah*. This combined quantity now becomes *tamei* in a more significant sense: it can transmit *tum'ah* or, according to *Rabbeinu Tam*, it has now reached the threshold for becoming *tamei* at all. The question is: since the act of throwing the *kezayis* in and having it land has now activated the *tum'ah* category — because the combined food has reached the *beitzah* threshold — does the significance it acquires in the realm of *tum'ah* transfer to confer Shabbat liability, even though a *kezayis* is ordinarily insufficient for *hotza'ah* on Shabbat?

### Why No Transfer

The *gemara* cites a *braita* in which *Abba Shaul* states that one who carries *shtei halechem* or *lechem hapanim* from the *Beis Hamikdash* is liable for Shabbat only at the *grogeret* standard. The *gemara* asks: *v'amai* — why? One might have argued that since the *halacha* of *yotzei* — food taken out beyond the walls of the *Azarah* — applies at a *kezayis*, the Shabbat liability should similarly apply at a *kezayis*. Analogously, why not say that carrying *chametz* or *chazir* should trigger Shabbat liability at the *kezayis*, since that is the quantity of significance in those areas of *halacha*? The *braita* thus implies that the fact that a certain quantity carries significance in another domain of *halacha* does not automatically transfer that significance to the domain of Shabbat carrying. This should answer *Rava*'s question as well.

### Different Moments

The *gemara* responds that the cases are not comparable. *Miyad d'afkeih chutz lechomat ha'azarah ipsil lei b'yotzei* — the *issur* of *yotzei* takes effect at the moment the food crosses the wall of the *Azarah*. The relevant *kezayis* is measured at that moment. By contrast, *ashabbat lo mechayev ad d'mafik lei lereshut harabim* — Shabbat liability does not arise until the carrier brings the food all the way down into the public domain and performs *hanachah*. The two moments of legal focus — the moment of *yotzei* and the moment of Shabbat carrying — are temporally distinct. Because they occur at different times, the *shiur* that applies at one moment cannot be borrowed to satisfy the requirement of the other.

### Same Moment Issue

But the case *Rava* has posed is different: *hacha shabbat v'tum'ah bahadi hadadi ka'asyan* — here, Shabbat and *tum'ah* occur at the same moment. The instant the *kezayis* of *terumah* lands on the existing food and combines with it, two questions become simultaneously relevant: has the combined food crossed the threshold for *tum'ah*? And has an act of Shabbat carrying been completed? Since both questions are asked at the identical moment, perhaps the *shiur* operative for *tum'ah* at that moment can also supply the Shabbat minimum. The question remains open and unresolved. As noted, what the *gemara*'s entire line of inquiry reflects is the broader consequence of having opened the door to subjective redefinition of minimum quantities. Once the *mishna* established that intent can move the minimum, the *gemara* consistently asks: can other frameworks similarly shift what counts as a sufficient quantity for Shabbat liability?

## Bring Back Inside

### Intent Negation

The *mishna* states: *chazar v'hichniso eino chayav ela k'shiuro* — if after having taken the item out one brings it back inside without having used it for its original purpose, one is no longer *chayav* except according to the standard minimum. The subjective significance that had been conferred, for example by intending to plant a single seed, evaporates once one has abandoned that purpose by returning the item without using it. One might have thought that once significance is conferred, it persists — but the *gemara* says it does not.

### Remains Distinct

*Abaye* refines the case: this ruling applies specifically to a scenario *k'gon shezarko l'otzar umikomo nikar* — where one threw the item back into one's warehouse and it remains identifiable in its location, having landed separately from the main pile rather than merging back into it. The item is thus distinct and has not been fully reabsorbed into the general store. One might have thought that since it remains physically separate — *keivan d'mikomo nikar b'milta kamaitah kai* — it retains the significance originally given to it, as if it had never truly been "returned."

### Negation by Warehouse

The *gemara* teaches otherwise: *mid'zarko l'otzar batulei batlei* — the very act of throwing it back into the warehouse constitutes a negation of the original planting intent. Even if the seed remains visually distinct on the warehouse floor rather than having fallen into the main grain pile, the act of return carries legal weight. Since one is no longer planning to plant it, and one has restored it to the domain of stored grain, the subjective significance is extinguished. It reverts to the objective standard minimum — a quantity that a single seed obviously does not meet.

## Unbroken Carrying

### Two Acts Rule

The *mishna* states: *hamotzi ochlim unetanam al ha-iskupa* — one who takes out food and places it on the threshold — *bein she-chazar v'hotzi'an bein she-hotzi'an acher patur* — whether one subsequently takes it from there into the street, or someone else does, both are exempt. The reason is *mipnei she-lo asa melacha b'vat achat* — the *melacha* was not performed as one continuous act. The two stages were separated by an intervening putting-down.

### Karmelit Status

The *gemara* analyzes the nature of the *iskupa*. It cannot be a *reshut harabim*, because then taking the food from the house to the porch would itself be a complete act of *hotza'ah* from *reshut hayachid* to *reshut harabim*, and one would be *chayav* at that point. It cannot be a *reshut hayachid*, because then taking it from the porch to the street would be going from *reshut hayachid* to *reshut harabim*, again producing *chiyuv*. The *gemara* therefore concludes the *iskupa* must be a *karmelit* — an intermediate domain that is neither *reshut hayachid* nor *reshut harabim*. Taking food from a private domain to a *karmelit* and from a *karmelit* to a public domain are each half-acts, neither of which independently constitutes a complete prohibited *melacha*.

## Basket of Fruit

### Whole Basket Rule

The *mishna* further states: *kupa she-mele'ah peirot* — a basket full of fruit — *venetnah al ha-askufa ha-chitzona* — placed on the outer porch, which here functions as a *reshut harabim* — *af al pi she-rov peiroteiha mi-bachutz patur* — even though most of the fruit overhangs into the public domain, one is exempt — *ad she-yotzi et kol ha-kupa* — until the entire basket has been taken out. Even if numerous individual pieces of fruit are wholly within the public domain, since they remain contained within a basket that is not entirely in the public domain, the carrying act is deemed incomplete. This introduces the principle *eged kli shmei eged* — that being bound within a vessel constitutes a form of legal unification — though the precise scope of this principle will be debated.

## Unbroken Carrying (II)

### Rest Principle

The *gemara* explains the *mishna*'s teaching about the *iskupa* more precisely. *Ta'ama denach bekarmelit* — the reason one is exempt is specifically because the food came to rest in the *karmelit*. *Ha lo nach bekarmelit chayav* — had it not rested there, one would be *chayav*. This might have seemed obvious, but it is not, because this ruling is *matisin delo k'Ben Azzai* — our *mishna* does not follow *Ben Azzai*. A *braita* teaches: one who carries from a shop to the main street (*paltya*) by way of the *stav* — the colonnaded walkway in front of the shops, a space that is neither *reshut hayachid* nor *reshut harabim* and functions as a *karmelit* — is *chayav*, because one moved without interruption from one domain to the other. *Ben Azzai* rules *patur*. *Ben Azzai* either holds that traversing an intermediate domain breaks the continuity of the act, or applies the principle of *mehalech ke-omeid* — that walking constitutes a series of discrete micro-resting-points, such that passage through an intervening domain counts as an interruption. Our *mishna*, by ruling that it is only the actual putting-down in the *karmelit* that creates the exemption, implicitly rejects *Ben Azzai*: the mere traversal of a *karmelit* without rest does not break the act.

## Basket of Fruit (II)

### Chizkiyah: Fruits

*Chizkiyah* offers a reading of the *mishna* that sidesteps the concept of *eged kli shmei eged* entirely. He says the ruling — *lo shanu ella b'kupa mele'ah kishuin v'diluin* — applies only to a basket filled with cucumbers and gourds, which are long objects. In such a case, since each individual cucumber extends from inside the house out into the street, no single cucumber has been fully transferred from one domain to the other. The *petur* has nothing to do with the basket as a binding unit; it is simply that each individual fruit object is not yet fully in the public domain. *Aval mele'ah chardal* — but if the basket is filled with mustard seeds, which are tiny, any seed that is over the threshold has been fully carried out, and one would be *chayav*. *Almah kasavar eged kli lav shemei eged* — *Chizkiyah* thus holds that being contained within a vessel does not create a legal unit.

### R. Yochanan: Unit

*Rabbi Yochanan* disagrees. *Afilu mele'ah chardal patur* — even a basket filled entirely with mustard seeds: if the basket is not fully out, one is exempt. *Almah kasavar eged kli shmei eged* — *Rabbi Yochanan* holds that containment within a vessel creates a single legal unit. The individual seeds or fruits are not evaluated independently; what matters is whether the basket — as the containing unit — has been fully transferred.

### Ambiguous Text

*Rabbi Zeira* observes that the *mishna* is read by each *amora* as supporting his own view, but in fact does not definitively prove either position. On one hand, the *mishna*'s concluding phrase — *ad she-yotzi et kol ha-kupa* — emphasizes the basket as the operative unit, suggesting *eged kli shmei eged* in keeping with *Rabbi Yochanan*. On the other hand, the *mishna*'s opening — *af al pi she-rov peiroteiha mi-bachutz* — implies that if all the fruit were outside, even with part of the basket remaining inside, one might be *chayav*, suggesting the individual fruits are what matters, in keeping with *Chizkiyah*. *Chizkiyah* reconciles the *mishna* by reading *kol ha-kupa* as meaning: when it is the type of basket where taking out the "whole basket" is what matters — i.e., long-object baskets — you are *patur* until all the fruit is out. *Rabbi Yochanan* reconciles it by reading *rov peirot* as describing even the scenario where all the fruit are outside, ruling one still *patur* until the basket itself is fully out. The more natural reading of the *mishna*, it must be said, favors *Rabbi Yochanan*: the *mishna* speaks of a basket of fruit, not specifically of long-stemmed vegetables, and its climactic ruling focuses on the basket as the decisive unit.

### Merchant Baskets

A *meitivei* challenges *Chizkiyah* from a *braita* about a *kupas ha-rochlin* — the spice-merchant's basket, which contained multiple compartments each holding different spices or fragrances. *Af al pi she-rov minin bachutz* — even if most of the different varieties are on the outside — *patur ad she-yotzi et kol ha-kupa* — one is exempt until the entire basket is taken out. This appears to present a case where complete, distinct objects of different types are fully in the public domain yet liability is withheld until the basket itself is fully out — which looks like a clear proof for *eged kli shmei eged* and against *Chizkiyah*.

### Long Objects

*Chizkiyah* responds: *hacha b'mai askinan b'urnosi* — this case also involves long objects. *Rashi* explains these as long cinnamon sticks or similar elongated spices, such that most of each individual object's length is on the outside but the trailing end of every item still remains inside. There is no case here of a fully transferred individual item; each object straddles the threshold. Admittedly, this is a strained reading of a *braita* that would naturally suggest independent, distinct bundles of spice — but it is *Chizkiyah*'s only available response.

## Stealing on Shabbat

### Override Principle

*Rav Bibi bar Abaye* challenges from a ruling familiar from *Ketubot* and elsewhere regarding the principle of *kam lei b'drabba minei* — when two transgressions are committed simultaneously, the more severe overrides, and the lesser penalty is not collected. In the paradigmatic case: one who steals a wallet on Shabbat is *chayav* to pay for the theft. The reason is that the two violations — *geneivah* and Shabbat — do not occur simultaneously. *Geneivah* is effected by *kinyan* — acquisition — which takes place when the thief picks up the wallet or draws it into his possession, occurring before the moment Shabbat liability attaches. Shabbat *chiyuv* for *hotza'ah* comes only when the object is brought into *reshut harabim* and put down. Since the temporal gap between the two violations exists, *kam lei b'drabba minei* does not apply, and the thief pays for the theft.

### Dragging Loot

*Haya megarer v'yotze patur she-issur geneivah v'issur Shabbat ba'im k'echad* — but if the thief was dragging a large bag of loot and it crossed the threshold in a continuous drag, the Shabbat violation and the act of *kinyan* for theft occurred simultaneously, and he is *patur* from the monetary payment. This is because *meshichah* — drawing an object into one's domain — serves as the *kinyan* for theft, and if this *meshichah* occurs at the same moment as the *hanachah* completing the *melacha* of Shabbat, both violations arise at once, and the more severe Shabbat violation overrides.

### Vessel Unity

The *gemara* now draws in *eged kli shmei eged*: if we hold that the vessel creates a single legal unit, then when the thief drags the bag, the *kinyan* might be effected as soon as the opening of the bag crosses the threshold — since access to the interior, and thus effective acquisition of everything within, is obtained at that point — even while part of the bag's body still remains in the private domain. But Shabbat liability would not attach until the entire bag — as one unit — has been brought into *reshut harabim*. That would mean *geneivah* precedes Shabbat, and *kam lei b'drabba minei* would not apply, making the thief liable — yet the *mishna* rules him *patur*.

### Mouth Away

The *gemara* resolves this: *d'afkeia derech shulav* — the bag was dragged out with its opening facing away from the thief. If the mouth of the sack faces away, then even with *eged kli shmei eged*, access to the interior is only obtained when the mouth itself crosses the threshold — and by that same moment, the entire bag has crossed. Thus the *kinyan* for theft and the Shabbat *hanachah* occur at the same instant. The ruling of *patur* is coherent.

### Straps & Stitches

The *gemara* probes whether this scenario truly works. *V'ika makom cholna* — what about the stitching at the rear of the bag? One could theoretically unpick the stitching and access the contents from behind even before the mouth crosses the threshold. The *gemara* responds that the bag contains *naskei* — large ingots or bars of silver, objects too large to be extracted through a small tear in the stitching. The only effective access point is the mouth, so the analysis stands.

Further: once we have established the scenario with the mouth facing away and large objects inside, what about the bag's *shnatzim* — straps that encircle the mouth? As the mouth crosses the threshold, the straps, which are still trailing on the private-domain side, have not yet fully crossed. If *eged kli shmei eged* makes the straps part of the vessel-unit, Shabbat liability would not attach until the straps too have crossed — at which point the *kinyan* has long since been effected, restoring the temporal gap between theft and Shabbat. The *gemara* answers: *d'michrach kerichei* — the straps are wrapped tightly around the mouth. When the mouth of the sack crosses the threshold, the coiled straps come with it simultaneously. There is thus a configuration in which the moment of *kinyan* for theft and the moment of Shabbat liability coincide exactly, rendering the thief *patur* — and this remains consistent with *eged kli shmei eged*.

# Shabbat 91

## Spices & Tziruf

### Spice Amounts

The dominant theme of this section of the *masechta* continues to be minimum sizes required to be *chayav* for carrying on *Shabbos*. The *mishna* states: *tavlin kidei letaveil beitza kalla* — spices sufficient to season a light egg, which Rashi identifies as a hen's egg prepared scrambled or fried. That much is the threshold for *chiyuv*. The *gemara* then raises a contradiction from a *braisa*: *tavlin shnayim b'gimmel shemos mimin echad o mishlosha minim assurim umitztarfin zeh im zeh* — spices with two or three different names, whether of one type or of three different types, are forbidden and combine with one another. The plain implication is that different types of spices combine to reach a minimum amount.

### Tosafos: Combining Prohi…

Tosafos has a lengthy discussion on this point. He focuses on the phrase *shnayim b'gimmel shemos*, understanding it to refer not merely to different varieties of the same spice, but potentially to spices with different underlying *issurim*. The key line in Tosafos runs: *d'gimmel minei issur k'gon orlah kilayim kerem v'shel asher v'shel ir nidachas kari gimmel shemos* — that there are times the *gemara* uses the word *shem* to refer to the nature of the *issur* itself. From here Tosafos is drawn into a broader discussion: if one has a small amount of spices from *avoda zara*, a small amount from *orlah*, and a small amount from *kilayim*, and their combined volume equals a *k'zayis*, does he receive *malkus*? He has not consumed a minimum of any single category — yet Tosafos entertains the possibility of a generic *lav* that would combine across different prohibited categories, making one *chayav* even on a mixture of distinct *issurim*. That larger question can be set aside for now. The operative point is that different types of spices combine — both for the purpose of reaching the minimum *shiur*, and for the purpose of *bitul*, where the combined flavor of multiple forbidden spices in a dish prevents any one of them from being considered *batel*.

### Chizkiya: Similar Types

Chizkiya qualifies this principle significantly: *biminin metika shanu hoil v'reuyin l'mateik k'deirah* — the *braisa* was taught only with respect to sweet spices, those that share the function of sweetening the pot. Only when all the spices operate in the same direction, so to speak, do they combine. Spices of different characters — one sweet, one savory, one sharp — do not combine with one another, since they do not work together toward a unified effect on the dish.

### Gemara: Why Similar?

The *gemara* then challenges: if only similar spices combine, how does the *mishna* permit combining different types of spices for the purpose of seasoning an egg? The *gemara* resolves this by saying *hacha nami chazu l'mateik* — in the *mishna*'s case as well, all the spices in question are of the sweet-spice category and function together.

This is a curious *gemara* in two respects. First, Tosafos himself asks why the *braisa* says *reuyin l'mateik* — "suited to sweeten" — rather than simply *mamtikin*, "they sweeten." He then raises a deeper question: if the spices, taken in their combined quantity, do produce a discernible taste, why should it matter whether they are all of the sweetening type? And if they do not produce a discernible taste, why should their being sweet help? Tosafos answers that if they work in different directions — some sweetening, some sharpening, some souring — then even if something is technically tasted, it is a *nosein ta'am lifgam*, a taste that diminishes rather than enhances, and is therefore halakhically disregarded.

Another way to understand the underlying issue is through the question of whether a distinct taste must be identifiable. If multiple spices all contribute to sweetness, then even if one cannot identify the particular sweetness of cinnamon versus honey versus sugar as distinct contributions, the combined sweetness is a recognizable and meaningful flavor. But if they are pulling in different directions, no single recognizable flavor emerges from the combination, and the mixture does not register halakhically as carrying any one of their tastes.

What remains striking is that elsewhere in the *gemara*, when it comes to *tziruf* — combining different items to reach a minimum *shiur* — the rule is entirely formal: as long as all items are measured by the same standard, they combine, even if no animal or person would consume that particular hybrid mixture. The *gemara* never asked, for example, whether a combination of camel food and sheep food would actually be eaten together. Here, by contrast, the *gemara* insists that the spices must actually function together as a unified flavor agent. Why the *gemara* demands functional cooperation in this case but not in others is itself an interesting question that the discussion leaves open.

---

## Dyes & Coloring

### Plant Dyes

The *mishna* lists plant materials used to produce dye: shells of nuts (*klipei egozim*), shells of pomegranates (*klipei rimonim*), *stis*, and *puah* — each sufficient to dye a small piece of cloth used at the opening of a hairnet. The standard is *kidei litzbo'a beged katan*, enough to color that minimal piece of fabric.

### Raw vs. Processed Dyes

The *gemara* raises a contradiction from a *braisa*: *hamotzi samamanim shruyim* — if one takes out dyes that have already been steeped and converted into liquid form — the minimum is only *kidei litzbo'a bahen dugma l'irah*, enough to color a sample swatch placed on the warp of a loom, which is obviously smaller than the amount needed for the hairnet opening. Why does the processed dye require a smaller minimum?

Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha explains: *lefi she'ein adam tore'ach lishros samamanim litzbo'a bahen dugma l'irah* — a person does not go to the trouble of steeping and processing raw plant material just to dye so tiny a sample. Once the dye has already been prepared as a liquid, however, even a very small amount is useful and significant — one would take even a drop of ready liquid to color a swatch. The distinction, articulated earlier in the *masechta* as well, is one of processing stage: the significance of a substance depends on what form it is in at the time it is carried.

---

## Cleansers

### Urine & Natron

The *mishna* turns to cleansing agents. *Mei raglayim* — urine — was used in the laundering process. A *braisa* adds the qualification *ad ben arba'im yom* — until forty days. Tosafos raises several possibilities for what this means: whether it refers to the age of the infant whose urine is in question, whether it means urine that has been aged forty days, or whether the effective period begins or ends at forty days. The *mishna* also includes *neter* — natron, a mineral cleanser. A distinction is drawn between *neter Alexandrit*, Alexandrian natron, and *neter Antipantiron*, which appears to be of a different provenance — Rashi suggests the latter derives from a plant source rather than a mineral one. The standard measure for all these cleansers is the amount needed to remove a stain from the small cloth used at the opening of a hairnet.

### Borit & Shevi'is

The *mishna* also mentions *borit*, commonly translated as soap. Rav Yehuda identifies *borit* as sand, but the *gemara* immediately challenges this: a *braisa* explicitly lists *borit* and sand (*haborit vehakhol*) as two separate items, so clearly *borit* is not sand. The *gemara* then proposes that *borit* is *kavrita* — sulfur (*gafrit*), as Rashi identifies it.

But this too is challenged. A *braisa* states that *borit* was added to the list of items that carry *shevi'is* — sabbatical year — sanctity. The rule is *kol sheyesh lo ikkar yesh lo shevi'is, she'ein lo ikkar ein lo shevi'is*: only something that grows from a root possesses *shevi'is* status; a mineral does not. Since sulfur is mined rather than grown, it cannot have *shevi'is* status, and therefore *borit* cannot be sulfur.

### Borit Variants & Cleaners

The *gemara* then proposes that *borit* is *ahala* — the same substance listed elsewhere, identified by some as aloe, though this identification was discussed and questioned in an earlier *gemara* as well, since different types of plants with that name have quite different properties. When the *gemara* points out that the *braisa* appears to list *borit* and *ahala* as two separate items, the answer is *trei gavni ahala* — there are two varieties of *ahala*, and *borit* refers to one variant while the other name refers to another.

Beyond these, the *mishna* includes *kimuliya*, which Rav Yehuda identifies as *shlof dutz* — a loose, easily-removed type of earth. *Ashlag* is identified by Shmuel, who reports he asked all who traveled by sea and they told him it is called *shunana*, found in the aperture of a pearl and extracted with an iron pick — though precisely what this substance is remains somewhat unclear. All of these cleansers are measured by the same standard: the amount needed to cleanse a small garment.

---

## Sacred Items & Geniz (II)

### Idolatry Items

The *mishna* states that even the smallest amount of items relating to *avoda zara* — appurtenances of idol worship — is significant when carried, as the verse states *velo yidbak beyadcha me'umah min hacherem*: not even the tiniest portion may remain in one's possession; it must be destroyed. Since even the smallest amount carries an obligation to act — namely, to destroy it — even the smallest amount is halakhically significant. This stands in contrast to the general principle, articulated explicitly in an earlier *gemara*, that items subject to *issurei hana'ah*, from which benefit is forbidden and which one desires only to be rid of, were excluded from the category of things that are *matzninin kamohen* — things people wish to preserve. Rabbi Yehuda here takes the position that the obligation to destroy the item is itself sufficient to confer significance on even the smallest amount.

---

## Fragrances & Oils

### Pepper (Pilpeles)

*Pilpeles kol shehu* — the smallest amount of *pilpeles* — is listed in the *mishna*. The *gemara* asks *lemai chazi*, what is it used for, and answers *lereiach hapeh* — to place in the mouth to mask bad breath. Rashi notes in the *mishna* that this is not the same as our pepper, *eino pilpel shelanu*, though the *gemara* must explain what it is used for. The exchange raises an interesting question: if *kol shehu* is truly the smallest discernible amount, could one tiny crumb of a peppercorn have any meaningful effect on bad breath? The answer remains somewhat unclear, though presumably a ground or crumbled amount, however small, was considered sufficient in the context of a time before modern dental hygiene.

### Tar & Fragrances

*Itran kol shehu* — the smallest amount of *itran*, a type of tar or pitch — is used, as Rashi explains, for *tzichosa*, a headache. Commentators identify this with a migraine specifically, noting that the strong odor of tar — whether smelled directly or burned — was used as a remedy. *Minei besamim*, various fragrances, were used to cover bodily odors. The *gemara* adds *hamotzi reiach ra kol shehu* — even a bad smell, in the smallest amount. Rashi suggests bad-smelling substances were used for treatment of the sick, and one explanation is that they were used to drive away *shedim* and *mazikim*.

### Oils, Purple, Metals

*Shemen tov kol shehu* — the smallest amount of fine oil, identified earlier in the *gemara* as myrrh oil. *Argaman kolshehu* — royal purple dye, even the smallest amount; Rashi acknowledges that the reason is not spelled out clearly, *ta'ama lo nishparash*, though he suggests it too may have been used for its fragrance. *U'besolat havered achat* — one fresh rose petal, or according to the *Aruch*, a rose-shaped embroidered ornament used as decoration on a garment.

### Metal Vows

*Minei matechot kolshen* — the smallest amount of various metals. The *gemara* asks *lemai chazi* and cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: *sheken ra'ui la'asot mimenu dorban katan* — even a tiny piece of metal is enough to fashion a small animal prod or a needle.

A *braisa* then discusses the minimum amounts relevant not for *Shabbos* but for vows to the *Beit Hamikdash*. If someone says *harei alai barzel* — I pledge iron — *acherim omrim lo yiphos me'amah al amah*, not less than a *amah* by a *amah* square. Rav Yosef explains this is used for *kaleh oreiv* — a spike-studded panel placed on the roof of the *Beit Hamikdash* to deter ravens attracted by the burning sacrificial meat. The second formulation given in the *gemara* arrives at the same dimension from the opposite direction: the minimum amount pledged is what is needed to construct this device, which is a *amah* by a *amah*.

For copper — *nechoshet* — the minimum implicit in a vow is not less than the value of a silver *ma'ah*. Tosafos raises the obvious question: for gold the minimum is a gold *dinar*, for silver a silver *dinar* — consistent with the smallest unit of each metal's standard coin. Why then for copper does the minimum jump to the value of a silver *ma'ah* rather than a copper *peruta*, which is the smallest copper coin? The likely answer is that a *peruta*'s worth of copper is so negligible an amount that one simply cannot do anything meaningful with it, whereas a *ma'ah*'s worth is at least sufficient to work with.

Rabbi Eliezer specifies: *lo yiphos metzinora ktana shel nechoshet* — no less than a small fork made of copper. Abaye explains its use: *shemechatkin bahen et hapitilot umekanchin et hanerot* — one uses it to adjust the wicks and clean out the lamps of the *menorah*. This tiny delicate implement represents the minimal useful object fashionable from copper, and thus defines the minimum for the vow.

---

## Sacred Items & Geniz (II)

### Torah Waste

The *mishna* lists *makkak sefarim umakkak mitpachot* — the waste matter of sacred books and the cloths used to wrap them — as items for which even the smallest amount is significant, because *shematzninin osan ligenzan*, one sets them aside to place them in *geniza*. Even crumbling fragments, the residue left after the material has deteriorated, must be treated with the requisite care and buried rather than discarded.

### Worms & Pests

Rav Yehuda provides a taxonomy of the creatures or waste associated with these materials. *Makkak* is the name for what eats away at books and parchment. *Takhakh deshira* is what eats silk. *Ila de'invei* is what eats grapes. *Peh dete'einei* is what eats figs. *Haha derimonei* eats pomegranates. Rashi understands these as the creatures themselves. *Kulehu sakanta* — all of them are dangerous to one's health if consumed.

### Peh Worm Story

The *gemara* illustrates the danger with a story. A student was sitting before Rabbi Yochanan eating figs. He said: *Rebbi*, it seems there are thorns in these figs — something sharp and pokey. Rabbi Yochanan replied: *katlei pa ledaden* — the *peh* worm of the figs has killed this person. The student had unwittingly swallowed the worm and taken it to be a thorn. Rabbi Yochanan was alerting him — none too reassuringly — that he was in real danger.

---

## Box of Fragrances

### One Act, Many Items

The final *mishna* of the *perek* introduces a case of *hamotzi kuppat harochlin* — one who carries out a peddler's box of fragrances. Such a box contained multiple small compartments, each holding a different fragrance. Even though there are many different types within the box — *af al pi she'yesh bah minim harbei* — one is only *chayav chattas achas*, a single *sin offering*, because the entire box was taken out in one act. Tosafos acknowledges that this seems obvious: even multiple separate acts of carrying within a single lapse of awareness combine for one *sin offering*, and certainly a single act does. Nevertheless, the *mishna* makes the point explicit, establishing that the multiplicity of compartments and varieties does not transform a single act of carrying into multiple acts.

---

## Seeds & Plants

### Garden Seeds

*Zeronei gina* — vegetable garden seeds — are measured at less than a *grogeris* (pressed fig), since these are not being carried as food. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira says five seeds is the minimum for *chiyuv*. This minimum reflects the practical standard for planting; one does not ordinarily take out a single seed to plant.

### Specific Seeds

For cucumber seeds (*zera kishu'in*), gourd seeds (*zera dilu'in*), and Egyptian bean seeds (*zera pul hamitzri*), the minimum is two. These larger seeds — taken individually in pairs — are of sufficient significance that even two constitutes a meaningful amount for planting purposes.

---

## Locusts

### Kosher Locust

*Chagav chai tahor kol shehu* — a live kosher grasshopper, even the smallest size, renders one *chayav*. If the grasshopper is dead — *meis* — it is treated as food and requires the standard food measure of *k'gerogeris*, the size of a pressed fig.

### Non-Kosher Vine Locust

*Tzippores keramim* — a non-kosher vine grasshopper — is *kol shehu* whether alive or dead. Since it is not kosher and thus not food, the ordinary food measure does not apply. Instead, even the smallest amount is significant because *shematznino lah l'refuah* — one sets it aside for medicinal use, as will be elaborated later in the *gemara*.

### Tanna Kamma vs. Rabbi Ye…

Rabbi Yehuda adds: *af hamotzi chagav chai tamei kol shehu* — even a live non-kosher locust, the smallest amount renders one *chayav*. His reasoning: *shematznino lekatan litzchok bah* — one sets it aside for a child to play with. The Tanna Kamma, by contrast, does not assign significance to a live non-kosher locust. This sets up the question: if a live *kosher* locust is *kol shehu* because children play with it, why is a live *non-kosher* one any different? And conversely, why does the kosher/non-kosher distinction matter for the living creature at all, since one does not eat a live grasshopper? These questions are taken up in the *gemara*.

---

## Seeds & Plants (II)

### Why Minimum Seeds

The *gemara* now addresses the apparent tension between the *mishna*'s minimum of five (or two) seeds for planting and the rule from a *braisa* that taking out manure or fine fertilizing material sufficient for even one head of cabbage — or according to the Sages, one leek — constitutes a *chiyuv*. If even one plant's worth of fertilizer is significant, why are multiple seeds required?

Rav Papa resolves this: *ha d'zari'a ha d'la zari'a* — the two cases describe different stages. The fertilizer case concerns something already planted and growing: once a plant is in the ground, one will indeed go to the trouble of fertilizing a single stalk. Seeds, however, have not yet been planted, and *ein adam tore'ach lehotzi nima achat lezri'ah* — a person does not bother taking out one single seed to plant. The effort of the planting act is only undertaken when one has at least a small meaningful quantity. The same principle applied earlier to dyes: the minimum depends on the stage at which the material finds itself.

A *braisa* is then cited: *hamotzi gar'inim* — one who takes out pits or seeds. If for planting (*im lentiyah*) — two. If for eating (*im lachilah*) — *kemelo pi chazir*, enough to fill the mouth of a pig. Rashi clarifies this refers specifically to a date pit. One might wonder how a single date pit fills a pig's mouth; likely the phrase does not mean literally filling the entire oral cavity, but rather that one is sufficient for the animal to chew on — a single unit constitutes a meaningful portion. Tosafos adds that the phrase envisions selling or giving to a non-Jew for his pig, since there are specific rabbinic concerns about Jews raising pigs that go beyond ordinary restrictions on non-*kosher* items and which arise from other *gemarot*.

If for burning as fuel (*im lehasik*) — *kidei levashel beitzah kalah*, enough to cook a light egg. If for use as counting markers (*im lecheshbon*) — two according to one opinion, five according to *acherim*. Rashi explains the five: up to four items, a person can track mentally without a mnemonic aid, but once the count reaches five, one begins to forget and needs a marking system. The two who say five is the threshold and two is insufficient apparently differ on when external counting aids become necessary.

---

## Hair & Fibers

### Tail Hairs

*Hamotzi shnei nimim miznav hasus umiznav hapara* — one who takes out two hairs from a horse's tail or a cow's tail is *chayav*, because *shematkinah lenishvin* — one puts them aside to use as the trigger element of a snare or trap.

### Pig Hair & Palm Fibers

A single pig bristle (*michsha shel chazir*) suffices, as it is harder and is used in stitching. For the fibrous material wound around the trunk of a palm tree (*tzurei dikla*), two are needed, as they are woven together in basket-making. For the thinner vine-like growth (*turei dikla*), one is sufficient, though Rashi himself acknowledges he does not know what it is used for — *velo yadati lemah chazi*.

---

## Locusts (II)

### Locust for Wisdom

The *gemara* now identifies *tzippores keramim* as *palya be'eri* according to Rav, and Abaye adds that it is found in a very young palm tree that has not yet developed its full growth of fronds and vines. It is used *lechuchmah* — to enhance learning and retention. The procedure described: eat the right half of the creature. Place the left half in a copper tube, seal it with sixty seals — Rashi notes this is not literally sixty but means it is well sealed — and suspend it on one's left arm. The mnemonic for this arrangement: *lev chacham limino velev ksil lismolo* — the heart of the wise is to his right, the heart of the fool to his left — so one eats the right half. One then learns as much as one wishes. Afterward, one must eat the other half to consolidate the learning; failing to do so will cause everything learned to be forgotten, *me'akar talmudo*.

Whether this locust is kosher or not remains somewhat ambiguous in context. Ordinarily one might invoke the principle that *refuah* use permits a non-*kosher* item under certain conditions, but here the purpose is enhancement of learning rather than treatment of illness, which may not satisfy the conditions for that dispensation. It is possible the *gemara* assumes the creature is in fact kosher.

### Rav Kahana Story

The *gemara* then returns to the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the live non-kosher locust. A story is introduced: Rav Kahana was standing before Rav when a *shushiva* — a type of non-kosher locust — was flying near his mouth as he spoke. Rav told him: *shaklei* — move it away from you. Why? *De-lo limru meichal ka achal* — lest onlookers see the creature near his mouth, with it perhaps even entering his mouth, and think he is eating it.

### Alive vs. Dead Debate

But why should it matter if people think he is eating a kosher locust? The *gemara* answers: *ve-ka'avar mishum bal teshaktzu et nafshoteichem* — because eating a live creature, even a kosher one, violates the principle of *bal teshaktzu*, the prohibition against making oneself disgusting. Whether this constitutes a formal technical transgression or is more broadly a violation of the spirit of that *pasuk* is a matter of parameters, but the upshot is clear: one should not eat a live creature. This explains why even a live *kosher* locust cannot be eaten without concern.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Logic

Returning to the dispute: the Tanna Kamma holds that a live non-kosher locust has no significance because parents would not let children play with it. The concern is *dilma achlei* — the child may eat it, and since it is non-kosher, that is a problem. One might ask: if even a live *kosher* locust risks the child eating it alive and transgressing *bal teshaktzu*, why does the Tanna Kamma permit children to play with the kosher one? The *gemara* resolves this: the concern is not that he will eat it alive — *ella dilma mayis ve-achlei* — but that it will die and then he will eat it. If it is a kosher locust and it dies, the child eats it and there is no *kashrus* violation. If it is non-kosher, the parent cannot allow the child to play with it since the death of the creature would lead the child to eat it, a non-*kosher* food.

### Rashi: Direct Feeding

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *ai mayis, katan mispad safid lei* — if it dies, the child will eulogize it, not eat it. Children treat their pets as pets, they do not eat them when they die. Therefore the parent has no concern about non-*kosher* consumption, and a live non-*kosher* locust may be given to a child to play with.

Rashi's comment here has significant implications beyond the immediate case. He writes: *modeh hu de-lo yavinan lei be-yadayim* — even the opinion that a minor eating non-*kosher* food does not obligate the *Beit Din* to intervene (*katan ochel nevelot ein Beit Din metzuvin alav le-hafrisho*) would agree that one may not directly feed the child non-*kosher* food — *de-tanya lo tochlum lo tachilum le-hazhir gedolim al haktanim*. Now, the parent here is not literally feeding the child the locust; he is giving it to the child as a toy. Yet Rashi categorizes the scenario — handing the child a live locust that will likely die and be eaten — as *ma'achil be-yadayim*, tantamount to direct feeding. This raises profound questions about the parameters of the prohibition of *ma'achil be-yadayim*: does placing a child in a situation where non-*kosher* consumption is a foreseeable consequence constitute direct feeding? The *Chasam Sofer* has a celebrated *teshuvah* engaging precisely this question in the context of a parent placing a child in an institution where the child would inevitably be fed non-*kosher* food — whether the act of placement constitutes *ma'achil be-yadayim* given that Rashi extends the concept this far. That *teshuvah* and the broader discussion it generates belongs to a longer conversation, but Rashi's formulation here provides an important foundation for it.

---

## Matznia Principle

### Setting Aside Items

The new *perek* begins with *ha'matznia* — one who formally sets aside an item. *Ha'matznia le'zera u'li'dugma u'li'refuah ve'hotzio be'Shabbos chayav be'chol she'hu* — if one sets aside something for planting, for use as a sample, or for medicinal purposes, and then carries it out on *Shabbos*, one is *chayav* even for the smallest amount. The act of setting aside confers subjective significance on even a negligible quantity.

### Standard Measures

A normal person who did not perform this act of *matznia* — *eino chayav alav ela ki'shiuro* — is *chayav* only upon the standard minimum measures discussed throughout this *perek*. Furthermore, if the person who had set aside the item subsequently changed his mind and brought it back indoors — *chazar ve'hichniso* — he is again *eino chayav ela ki'shiuro*. The return undermines the significance he originally conferred. The seed had its special status because of his intent and that he was carrying it out to use it; bringing it back signals abandonment of that intent, and the subjective significance dissolves with it.

### Gemara: Why Matznia?

The *gemara* raises a sharp question: *lama li le'masni ha'matznia? leisni ha'motzi le'zera u'li'dugma u'li'refuah* — why does the *mishna* need to specify that one *set aside* the item? It should have simply said: one who *takes out* something for planting, for sampling, or for healing is *chayav kol shehu*. The very fact that the *gemara* poses this challenge is itself remarkable. The implicit assumption of the question is that the act of *matznia* — physically setting aside ahead of time — is not what generates significance. Rather, the intent at the moment of carrying out is itself sufficient to elevate even the smallest amount into a significant object. If I take out one seed with the intention to plant it, that intent, expressed in the act of carrying, is what matters — regardless of whether I set it aside beforehand.

This is quite a radical claim. It means that any item carried out with a specific use in mind becomes significant at *kol shehu*, without any prior formal act of designation. And it immediately raises a problem: if intent at the moment of carrying is always sufficient, then why do the *mishna* and *braisa* we just discussed specify different minimum amounts for seeds depending on whether they are for planting, for eating, or for burning? If I take out one seed intending to plant it, should not *kol shehu* apply universally?

### Abaye: Prior Intent

Abaye resolves the first question by reframing the *mishna*'s case. The *mishna* is speaking of a person who *set aside* a single seed — *kegon she-hitznio* — and then *forgot why he had set it aside* — *veshachach lama hitznio* — and took it out simply to bring it somewhere, without any particular use in mind at the moment of carrying. In this case, the intent at the moment of carrying provides no subjective elevation — the person is just moving the seed. One might have thought that since he has no intent now, and has even forgotten his prior intent, the earlier act of setting aside has been fully negated — *bitulei batlei machshavto*. Abaye teaches: *kol ha-oseh al da'at rishonah hu oseh* — what one does is defined by one's original intent. The prior act of setting aside survives the forgetting and continues to define the significance of the object. Therefore, even without a current use-intent, the object remains significant at *kol shehu*.

### Use-Intent Significance

But the *gemara*'s larger implication — that use-intent at the moment of carrying is by itself sufficient to create *kol shehu* significance, even without any prior *matznia* — is still on the table. According to this principle, any time a person takes out even the smallest amount of anything with the specific intent to use it, he has rendered it significant and is *chayav kol shehu*. This eliminates the need for formal prior designation entirely and shifts the operative factor entirely to the moment of carrying.

### Tosafos Challenge

Tosafos presses the obvious difficulty: if intent at the moment of carrying is sufficient to create *kol shehu* significance, then why do we have different minimum amounts for seeds depending on their intended use — two for planting, *melo pi chazir* for animal feed, *beitzah kalah* for firewood? If intent alone determines significance, one seed taken out for planting should be *chayav* regardless of quantity.

Tosafos's resolution is that those measures are not about what is in any individual's mind at the moment of carrying. Rather, they reflect objective use-categories. If the *type* of seed or pit is one that is ordinarily used for planting, the minimum is two. If it is the kind used for animal feed, the minimum is *melo pi chazir*. These standards are defined by what the object is generally used for — its objective category — and not by the subjective intent of the person carrying it. Subjective individual intent generates *kol shehu* significance only in the *matznia* case or when the person carries it out specifically to use it himself. The standard minimum measures, by contrast, represent a formal, category-based threshold that operates independently of any individual's purpose on a given occasion.

---

---

# Shabbat 92

## Egged Kli Shemi Egged

### Basket & Fruit Intro

Today's daf is 92a, and we pick up with a question arising from yesterday's *mishnah*. That *mishnah* established that if one has a basket filled with fruit and carries it out from a *reshus hayachid* — a private domain such as a house — into the street, a *reshus harabbim*, even if most of the basket is on the outside, as long as part of it remains on the inside, the act of carrying is not yet complete. The simple reading of this ruling reflects the idea that the basket renders everything within it a single unit; one does not look at the fruit individually but rather treats the whole as a fruit basket. Even if an entire piece of fruit has crossed into the public domain, it does not matter — it is defined as part of the fruit basket and treated accordingly. This is the position known as *egged kli shemi egged*: being bound within a vessel constitutes a genuine form of binding that creates a single unit. There are, however, other readings of this *mishnah* that downplay the role of the basket — readings that understand the case as involving unusually long fruits of which most of the fruit is outside, minimizing the *chiddush* of the ruling considerably.

### Rava: Gourds & Seeds

The *gemara* continues this debate at the top of 92a, four lines from the top. *V'chein amar Rava* — and Rava said similarly: *lo shanu ela b'kuppah meleiah kishu'in v'dulu'in* — the *mishnah* is speaking only of a basket filled with gourds and cucumbers, meaning fruits so large that even when part of the basket extends outside, no single complete fruit is fully on the outside. *Aval meleiah chardal* — but if the basket is filled with mustard seeds, small enough that whole fruits are certainly outside when part of the basket is, then *chayiv* — one is liable. In that case, Rava holds, one looks at the individual fruits rather than the basket as a whole. *Alma kasavar egged kli lo shemi egged* — this reveals that Rava's view is that being bound in a vessel does not constitute binding, that it does not create a unified unit, and one must therefore assess the individual fruits. This is a demanding reading of the *mishnah*.

### Abaye: All Seeds Exempt

Abaye, by contrast, says: *afilu meleiah chardal* — even if the basket is filled with mustard seeds, *patur* — one is exempt. Even though a thousand mustard seeds are fully outside the threshold, as long as part of the basket itself remains inside, one is exempt. *Alma kasavar egged kli shemi egged* — this reveals that Abaye holds that being bound by a basket is a genuine form of binding, that it creates a single unit, and the basket is assessed as a whole.

### Position Reversal

The *gemara* then introduces a tradition: *kam Abaye b'shitasei d'Rava, kam Rava b'shitasei d'Abaye* — each of them reversed his position, so that Abaye wound up adopting Rava's original stance and Rava wound up adopting Abaye's. They are still in disagreement, but now on the opposite sides of the argument. This is significant for *halacha*, since we almost always rule like Rava against Abaye — and now Rava is the one who holds *egged kli shemi egged*, the straightforward reading of the *mishnah* that the basket creates a single unit.

The *gemara* then states: *v'remi d'Abaye ad'Abaye, v'remi d'Rava ad'Rava* — it will now demonstrate a contradiction in Abaye's own statements and in Rava's own statements.

### Tosafot on Reversal

Tosafot raises an immediate methodological difficulty: since Rava and Abaye each held both sides of this argument at different points in their careers, how does one know that any given statement actually contradicts their final position? It might simply reflect an earlier view since abandoned. Tosafot resolves this by stating directly: *kim lehu l'shas d'hai milsa d'maisi itmar basar d'hadar behu* — the tradition of the *shas* is that the statement which will now be cited was made after they had already reversed themselves, reflecting their later, settled positions. It is worth noting how much of the analysis at this stage rests not on direct textual evidence but on received tradition — the assertion of the reversal itself is not supported by any explicit quotation, and the claim that the next statement dates from after the reversal is likewise simply known. That is the nature of the tradition here.

### Hand vs. Vessel Test

Now the *gemara* proceeds to the apparent contradiction. According to the revised positions — where Rava holds *egged kli shemi egged* and Abaye holds the opposite — what do we make of the following teaching? *D'itmar: hamotzi peiros l'reshus harabbim* — if one carries fruit out into the public domain. *Abaye amar beyad chayiv* — Abaye says, if you did so with your hand, you are liable. *Bikli patur* — but if it was in a vessel, you are exempt. Read simply and without context this seems puzzling: is one liable for carrying an apple in hand yet exempt for carrying it in a basket? The scenario being described, however, is not simple. The case involves an object that is partly inside and partly outside. Carrying "with the hand" means one is standing inside the house while one's hand — holding the fruit — extends into the public domain. The vessel case is our familiar scenario: part of the basket is outside, part remains inside. The question in both cases is identical: does one assess location by what is inside or by what is outside?

In the vessel case: does one go by where the basket is, or by where the fruit is? In the hand case: does one go by where the fruit is, or by where the body is? These are structurally parallel questions, and both hinge on whether one treats the containing unit — the basket, or the person's body together with the hand — as a single entity. Of course, the interesting cases are those where there is meaningful divergence between where the container is and where the contents are; a basket just barely larger than its fruit would not generate much of a question.

Rava, in this cited teaching, takes the opposite position: *beyad patur* — if you extend your hand, you are exempt, *bikli chayiv* — but in a vessel you are liable. According to Rava as quoted here, even though part of the basket is inside, since some of the fruit is outside, one is liable — which is the position that *egged kli lo shemi egged*. This is the reverse of Rava's stated later position. The *gemara* resolves this by saying *ipcha* — reverse the names. Either the citation reflects their earlier views before the reversal, or one simply exchanges the names of Abaye and Rava in this passage. In the end, the *gemara* arrives at two halachic conclusions now attributed to Rava: first, *egged kli shemi egged* — one looks at the basket as a single unit and goes by where the basket as a whole is; and second, that standing inside and extending one's hand outside renders one liable.

This second point raises a problem. The very first *mishnah* of this *masechta* teaches *pashat baal habayit yado lachutz* — if the homeowner extended his hand outside with bread and the poor person took from it, or the reverse, *sheneihem peturin* — both are exempt. Is that not precisely our case — standing inside, hand outside — and yet the *mishnah* says exempt?

### Rashi: Apple vs. Body

The *gemara* resolves this: *hatam lemala migimmel, hacha lemata migimmel* — there, the hand was above three *tefachim*; here, below three. Rashi explains the distinction beautifully. In the case of the first *mishnah*, the reason for the exemption is not that we regard the fruit as still "inside" because the person's body is inside. The fruit, when held in an outstretched hand, is one hundred percent outside. The exemption comes from a different consideration entirely: the fruit has not come to rest — *lo nach*. It has not been deposited. Rashi states this explicitly: *vetaama mishum d'lo nach, velo mishum eged gufeih* — the reason is the absence of *nichah*, of rest, not the connection to the carrier's body. When the hand is below three *tefachim*, the principle of *lavud* applies and anything within three *tefachim* of the ground is treated as resting on the ground, rendering one liable. When the hand is above three, the fruit has not come to rest, and the poor person must take it from the hand before liability can attach.

### Object Unity Resolved

This distinction clarifies why the basket and the apple in the hand belong to entirely different analytical categories. The basket is an *object* — and as a single object, one can coherently say it is partly inside and partly outside, and assess its location accordingly. The fruit and the person, however, are not a single object. The apple is always distinct from the person holding it. When the apple is in an outstretched hand, no one would say the apple is "one unit" with the person such that the apple's location is partly inside because the body is inside. The apple is simply outside. The separate question — whether it has come to rest — is an entirely distinct inquiry. Rashi's formulation makes this precise, and the distinction between the two cases is clean and elegant.

---

## Carrying Methods

### Methods of Carrying

The *mishnah* now turns to a different but closely related topic. *Hamotzi bein b'yimino bein b'smolo* — whether one carries an object in the right hand or the left hand, *b'toch heiko* — held against the chest within one's garment, *o al kteifav* — or on the shoulders, *chayiv* — one is liable in all these cases. *Shekein masa b'nei Kehat* — for this is how the *B'nei Kehat* carried the *mishkan*. The *B'nei Kehat* were responsible for transporting the primary sacred vessels; the *mishkan* was disassembled and they bore the *aron*, the *shulchan*, and the other major vessels on their shoulders and persons.

### Rashi on Methods

Rashi quotes and references a *Yerushalmi* tradition to account for why the *mishnah* enumerates multiple methods — right hand, left hand, chest, and shoulder. The shoulder is explicitly mentioned in the verse *uv'kateif yisau*. As for right hand, left hand, and chest, Rashi notes: *orah ar'a* — that is simply the natural, ordinary way things are carried; no special proof text is required. Rashi further cites, in the name of Rabbeinu Yitzchak bar Yehuda who heard it from Rav Hai, a tradition that it is explicit in the *Yerushalmi*: the verse regarding Elazar ben Aharon ha-Kohen's responsibilities — *u'fkudat Elazar ben Aharon ha-Kohen shemen ha-ma'or u'ktoret ha-samim u'minhat ha-tamid v'shemen ha-mishha* — lists multiple items under his care, and the *gemara* reads this not merely as administrative responsibility but as physical carrying. One flask of oil in his right hand, one in his left; the incense somehow against his chest; the *menahot* on his shoulder. This is how one carries seven distinct items simultaneously — by distributing them across different parts of the body.

### Unusual Methods Listed

The *mishnah* then proceeds to enumerate cases of unusual carrying: *k'l'ahar yado* — by the back of his hand; *u'v'raglo* — on his leg; *b'piv* — in his mouth; *u'v'mafreko* — Rashi understands this as the underarm, while Tosafot argues it means the elbow, and notes that the term in the vernacular of Ashkenaz for the elbow (*elbogen*) corresponds to their reading, whereas the underarm (*axlen*) corresponds to Rashi's. The *mishnah* continues: *b'ozno* — in his ear; *bi's'aro* — in his hair; *u'v'fundato* — in his belt; *u'fih l'mata* — with the opening of the belt facing downward, so that it is a poor container since things would fall out; *bein fundato l'haluko* — between one's belt and one's garment, which is actually a reasonable way to store certain items; *u'vi'sfat haluko* — at the hem of one's garment; *bi'mnalo* — in one's shoe; *bi'sandalo* — in one's sandal.

### Exemption Formula

*Patur* — one is exempt in all these cases — *she-lo hotzi k'derech ha-motzi'in* — because one has not carried in the way that people normally carry. This phrase begins to lay the foundation for the principle of *shinui* — doing something in an unusual manner — and its sister formulation *k'l'ahar yad*, named after the first example given: the back of the hand.

### Shinuy Concept

The term *k'l'ahar yad* is instructive. Literally *l'ahar yado* means the back of his hand. When the *mishnah* uses *k'l'ahar yado* — with the *kaf* of comparison — it is initially describing an actual method of carrying: on the back of one's hand. But this concrete example then becomes the paradigm for an entire conceptual category. Once we understand that carrying on the back of the hand is the prime exemplar of performing something in an unusual way, the phrase *k'l'ahar yad* is generalized to describe that whole category of *shinui*. Tosafot notes that in versions of the text that read *k'l'ahar yado* — with the *kaf* — some understand *b'raglo* (on his leg) as itself an explanation of *k'l'ahar yado*: the leg carrying is the concrete referent and what follows is the broader category.

It is worth noting that one could have read this entire *mishnah* as speaking specifically and exclusively about carrying, since carrying is a *melacha* that is unusually focused on process. Tosafot makes a point that has been discussed at length: unlike *melachot* that produce something — cooking, baking, dyeing — which are broadly defined by their result, carrying produces nothing and is therefore defined entirely by its process. Because carrying focuses on process, every variation in process may be analytically distinct and must be traced back to the *mishkan* individually. That is why the *mishnah* says: this is how *B'nei Kehat* did it. The normal ways are *chayiv* because they reflect the *mishkan* prototype; the unusual ways are exempt because they deviate from it.

### Shinuy Parameters

One might have concluded, then, that *shinui* is a principle unique to carrying. We will see, however, from subsequent *mishnayot*, that *shinui* extends across *melachot* of *Shabbat* more broadly. This generalization raises a series of important practical questions.

First: must *shinui* affect the end result? From the cases in our *mishnah* the answer is clearly no. Whether one carries an object in one's elbow, in one's belt, or in one's hand, the object arrives at its destination equally well. The end result is identical. The same is true of other *melachot*: if one turns on a light switch with one's elbow, the light burns just as brightly. *Shinui* does not require that the end result be compromised.

Second: must *shinui* make the act harder to perform? Or is any unusual method sufficient even if it is just as easy? Flipping a light switch with one's elbow, for example, may not be appreciably harder than doing so with a finger. From a number of cases it appears that something can constitute a *shinui* even when it does not make the act more difficult, simply because it is an unusual way of performing it.

Third: does *shinui* apply outside of *Shabbat*? This is a broader question that touches on *halacha* beyond the laws of *Shabbat*. The *Eglei Tal* — the well-known work on the thirty-nine *melachot* of *Shabbat*, so named because *tal* spelled backwards renders the letters for thirty-nine — addresses this directly. In the context of the laws of writing, there is a discussion of *derech ketivah*, and whether writing with the wrong hand might be invalid. The *Eglei Tal* initially considers the argument that *shinui* is relevant only to *Shabbat* because of the principle of *melechet machshevet* — the requirement that a prohibited labor on *Shabbat* be performed with the full deliberateness of skilled, purposive work. *Melechet machshevet* imposes rigorous standards on how an act must be carried out, and by its very nature, *shinui* undermines the compliance with those standards. One might then conclude that the concept of *shinui* as an exemption is peculiar to *Shabbat* and does not operate in other areas of *halacha*.

The *Eglei Tal* then demonstrates, however, that this cannot be entirely correct. In other areas of *halacha*, performing a prohibited act in an unusual manner also generates exemption: if one eats forbidden food in a *lav derech achilah* — not in the normal manner of eating — one is similarly exempt. So the *shinui* exemption cannot be entirely Shabbat-specific.

### Aglei Tal Framework

His resolution is that there are two distinct types of *shinui*. Some forms of *shinui* are significant enough — so fundamentally different from the normal performance of an act — that they apply across the board, in all areas of *halacha*, because the act is simply not the same act when performed in that manner.
