Rav Hilkiya bar Tuvi then introduces a tripartite structure that clarifies the landscape of the debate. Within three *tefachim* of the ground, *divrei hakol chayav* — everyone agrees one is *chayav*. Above ten *tefachim*, *divrei hakol patur* — everyone agrees one is exempt. The debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *chachamim* occupies the middle range: *mi-gimmel v'ad yud* — from three *tefachim* up to ten.

A *baraita* cited immediately thereafter reinforces this: within three, *divrei hakol chayav*; above ten, it is only a rabbinic prohibition — *mishum shevut* — and if both rooftops belong to the same person, it is even permitted outright. This last point is striking: if one owns both private domains and throws above the ten-*tefach* airspace of the *reshut ha-rabim*, the prohibition is purely rabbinic, and self-ownership of both sides removes even that. The practical force of this ruling may be appreciated by considering the case of two rooftops on opposite sides of a *reshut ha-rabim*: the sole obstacle to throwing between them at roof height is the rabbinic concern about the appearance of carrying between two distinct private domains — a concern dissolved when they belong to a single owner. The concern about crossing the *reshut ha-rabim* itself, above ten *tefachim*, generates no biblical prohibition.

The Gemara addresses an apparent conflict with a ruling of Rav: Rabbah bar Rav Huna reported in the name of Rav that one may not throw from one house to the other across a *reshut ha-rabim*, while Shmuel ruled it is permitted. The Gemara resolves this: the case of Rav's prohibition involves one building taller than the other, creating a significant likelihood that the thrown object will miss and fall into the *reshut ha-rabim*. Were it to fall, one might then go down and retrieve it — carrying in the *reshut ha-rabim*. It is that consequential risk, rather than the throw itself, that Rav prohibits. Rashi notes that the missed throw itself would not even constitute a *melacha b'shogeg*: if an object does not go where one intended, it lacks the character of *melekhet machshevet* — purposive, intentional craft — and is therefore not a *melacha* at all. The concern is the subsequent retrieval.

### Three Logic

The Gemara asks — and this exchange is attributed to either Rav Chisda or Rav Hamnuna — where does this principle of *kol pachas mi-gimmel kelavud dami* — anything within three *tefachim* is considered connected — come from? The answer offered is a functional rationale: *lefi she-ee efshar le-reshut ha-rabim she-tisleket b'melet uv'rehatni* — it is impossible to perfectly level a *reshut ha-rabim* using a plane and roller. Any public thoroughfare will have natural undulations, and therefore the ground effectively extends, in practical terms, for up to three *tefachim* above the theoretical floor. Anything within three is therefore halachically part of the ground.

This explanation, however, immediately runs into difficulties. If the reasoning is purely about the physical character of the *reshut ha-rabim*, it should not apply elsewhere — yet the principle of *lavud* is applied broadly, including to the walls of a *sukkah*. The Gemara cites the *Mishnah* in *Sukkah*: a wall suspended from above is valid if it comes within three *tefachim* of the ground, invalid if it is higher than that — and there, the *reshut ha-rabim* rationale is plainly irrelevant. The Gemara responds that the *sukkah* case operates on a different principle: a gap of more than three *tefachim* at the base of a wall is invalid because *gedayim bokin bah* — goats can pass through, and it is not practically a wall. Less than three, goats cannot pass through, so it functions as a wall.

But the Gemara presses further: *tainach lematah* — that explains the bottom; but what about above? The *lavud* principle is applied also at the top of a wall or between the wall and the *sechach*: if the top of the wall falls within three *tefachim* of the *sechach*, it is treated as if the wall reaches all the way up. That scenario cannot be explained by the *reshut ha-rabim* rationale or by the *gedayim* consideration. The Gemara therefore concedes: *kol pachas mi-shelosha kelavud dami hilcheta gemiri lah* — the principle that anything within three is treated as connected is a received tradition, a *halacha* without a fully generalizable logical basis.

### Lavud Tradition

The Gemara's admission that *lavud* ultimately rests on *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* rather than logic is worth pausing over. The discussion had proposed an elegant functional explanation — the natural unevenness of public thoroughfares — but successive applications of the principle outside the *reshut ha-rabim* context could not be accommodated by that reasoning. The *sukkah* cases, particularly the top-of-wall application, forced the Gemara to acknowledge that *lavud* is a received tradition that transcends any single rationale. It had to be anchored somewhere, and this passage is where the Gemara explicitly does so.

---

## Zorek P.U. to P.U.

### Bayis Kluta

Having analyzed the case of throwing from *reshut ha-yahid* to *reshut ha-yahid* across a *reshut ha-rabim*, the Gemara turns to the reverse: throwing from *reshut ha-rabim* to *reshut ha-rabim* with a *reshut ha-yahid* in between. The *baraita* states: *reshut ha-rabim le-reshut ha-rabim u-reshut ha-yahid ba'emtza* — one threw from one public domain to another with a private domain in between — *Rebbi mechayev ve-chachamim potrin*. Rabbi — Rebbi Yehuda ha-Nasi — holds one is *chayav*; the *chachamim* exempt.

Rava and Shmuel both clarify that Rebbi imposes *chiyuv* only when the intervening *reshut ha-yahid* is *mekura* — roofed, like a house — not when it is an open yard or courtyard. The reason: *bayis k'man d'malya dami* — a roofed enclosure is treated as though it were completely filled. The thrown object, passing through a window, traversing the enclosed space, and exiting through another window, is treated as though it came to rest within the house, because the house, conceptually, is a full, bounded box. When an object enters that box, the principle of *kluta k'mi she'huncha* applies with particular force: the complete enclosure — floor, walls, and roof — creates the most persuasive case for treating the airspace as equivalent to rest. An open courtyard, lacking a roof, does not generate this conceptual filling, and Rebbi would agree with the *chachamim* there.

### Av Toldah

Rav Chana reported in the name of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *mechayev haya Rebbi shtayim* — in this case Rebbi would hold one is *chayav* twice, once for *hotza'ah* — removing the object from the *reshut ha-rabim* into the house — and once for *hachnasah* — bringing it from the house back out to the *reshut ha-rabim*. Rav Chana then raises an objection: to say Rebbi holds *chayav* twice implies *mechayev Rebbi atoldah bimkom av* — that Rebbi holds one brings a separate *korban* for a *toldah* when done together with an *av*. But is that not contrary to Rebbi's own position? The *baraita* teaches that Rebbi derives the number thirty-nine *melachot* from the words *eileh ha-devarim* — and elsewhere the Gemara draws from this that thirty-nine is the maximum number of sin offerings corresponding to the thirty-nine *avot*, implying that doing an *av* and *toldah* together yields only one *korban*, not two. Rebbi explicitly holds that *toldah bimkom av* is only one *chiyuv*.

Rav Yosef then clarifies: the statement that one is *chayav* twice was not said in explanation of Rebbi's ruling about throwing through the house. It was said in explanation of a different *baraita*, dealing with the debate of Rabbi Yehuda and the *Rabbanan*: *reshut ha-yahid le-reshut ha-rabim v'avar arba amot be-reshut ha-rabim* — one threw from a *reshut ha-yahid* into a *reshut ha-rabim* and the object traveled four *amot* within the *reshut ha-rabim*. Rabbi Yehuda holds *chayav* and the *chachamim* exempt. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that this is a debate about *shtayim* — whether one is *chayav* twice. The reason the *chachamim* cannot be understood as exempting entirely is that obviously one has transferred from a private to a public domain — one would be *chayav* at least once. Therefore the debate must be: is one *chayav* an additional time for traversing four *amot* in the *reshut ha-rabim*? Rabbi Yehuda holds yes — twice — and the *chachamim* hold only once.

The attribution of *chayav shtayim* to this debate of Rabbi Yehuda rather than to Rebbi resolves the problem: Rabbi Yehuda is not bound by Rebbi's position against holding *toldah bimkom av* liable independently. Rabbi Yehuda could hold like Rabbi Eliezer that one does bring two *korbanos* for an *av* and *toldah* together.

### Holtz Debate

The Gemara then probes the precise structure of the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Rabbanan*. One possibility: the Rabbis do not fully exempt — rather, they agree one is *chayav* once but dispute only the second *chiyuv*. The object entered the *reshut ha-rabim*, and then — applying *kluta k'mi she'huncha* — one is *chayav* for that entry; then it traveled four *amot*, yielding a potential second *chiyuv*. Rabbi Yehuda imposes both; the Rabbis impose only one. This reading naturally accounts for why the *baraita* specifies four *amot*: the four *amot* represent the second act.

### One vs Two

An alternative reading is proposed: perhaps the Rabbis exempt entirely, and the debate concerns whether *kluta k'mi she'huncha* applies at all. The scenario: one explicitly intended the object to come to rest as soon as it entered the *reshut ha-rabim*, but it flew on and came to rest four *amot* later. Rabbi Yehuda holds *kluta k'mi she'huncha damya* — it is treated as having rested at the moment of entry — and therefore his intention was satisfied; one is *chayav*. The Rabbis hold *lo amrinan kluta k'mi she'huncha* — we do not treat the airspace as rest — and therefore the object never landed where one wanted, the intention was unfulfilled, and one is *patur* entirely. On this reading, there is no second *chiyuv* in the picture at all; it is simply a dispute about whether the action was completed.

The Gemara dismisses this alternative: *lo salka dach-tach* — it cannot hold. Proof comes from the ruling of Rabbi Yehuda on the *melachot*: *Rabbi Yehuda mosif af ha-shovet veha-medakdek* — Rabbi Yehuda added *shovet* and *medakdek* to the list of prohibited labors. The *chachamim* responded that both are *toldot* — derivatives — of existing *avot*. Significantly, the debate is framed as Rabbi Yehuda *adding* these labors. If the question were simply whether Rabbi Yehuda holds thirty-nine or forty-one *avot*, the debate would be stated differently. The word *mosif* — he added — implies he agreed they were *toldot* and was adding them nonetheless, meaning the debate is whether one is *chayav* for a *toldah bimkom av*. And *shema mina* — we derive — that Rabbi Yehuda does hold one is *chayav* for a *toldah bimkom av*, confirming that the debate in the carrying case is indeed about one *chiyuv* versus two.

The Gemara anticipates the objection: perhaps *mosif* means Rabbi Yehuda actually held them to be *avot*, disagreeing with the *chachamim* about their categorization, not about the consequence of a *toldah bimkom av*. The Gemara addresses this: if they were disagreeing about categories, the *chachamim* would not have used the language of *toldot* — they would have simply denied them as *avot*. The exchange makes more sense as a dispute about whether doing a *toldah alongside* its *av* generates an additional *chiyuv*.

Returning now to the question of *chiyuv shtayim*: the Gemara asks, on the assumption that Rabbi Yehuda holds one *chayav* twice, how can that even work here? If one intended the object to land at point A — the moment of entry into *reshut ha-rabim* — one did not intend it to land at point B, four *amot* later. And if one intended point B, one did not intend point A. How can two separate *chiyuvim* attach to a single throw aimed at a single destination? The Gemara resolves: *be'omer kol makom she-tirtze tanu'ach* — the case is where one said explicitly: I do not care where it lands, wherever it stops is fine with me. Since one expressed complete indifference to the landing point, halachically two distinct acts are recognized: the object entered the airspace of *reshut ha-rabim*, and — because of *kluta k'mi she'huncha* — that constitutes act one; it then traveled further and came to rest four *amot* later, constituting act two. Since one had no preference for either location over the other, both are attributed to one's intention, and both generate *chiyuv*.

### Indifference Case

What is conceptually remarkable about this conclusion is the superimposition of two discrete acts onto a single, continuous motion. The object never actually stopped moving between entry into the *reshut ha-rabim* and its final resting point four *amot* away. Yet halakha treats it as though it stopped and then resumed — by virtue of *kluta k'mi she'huncha* at the moment of entry, and then by virtue of the actual stop four *amot* later. One did not initiate two throws; one threw once. And yet, because the *halacha* treats the airspace entry as equivalent to rest, and because one declared indifference to outcome, two acts of *hotza'ah* are recognized, yielding two *chiyuvim* according to Rabbi Yehuda. Rashi observes that if the object had instead missed and fallen into the *reshut ha-rabim* against one's intent, that would not even constitute a *melacha b'shogeg* — the lack of alignment between intent and result in that scenario would be so fundamental as to negate the characterization of the act as *melekhet machshevet* entirely.

---

## Intent Precision

### Intent Subset

The Gemara's final passage, with which the daf concludes, turns explicitly to the question of how precisely one's *kavanah* must match the outcome in order to generate *chiyuv* — specifically in the context of carrying and throwing. The Gemara states: *peshita* — it is obvious — that if one intended to throw something eight *amot* and it only went four, one is *chayav*. The analogy: one who intended to write the name *Shimon* but wrote only as far as *shin-mem* — the word *shem* — is *chayav*, because writing *shem* is included within writing *Shimon*. The intended act subsumes the actual act: four *amot* is contained within the intention to go eight.

### Intent Superset

The harder case — *niskaven lizrok arba v'zarak shmona mai* — is the reverse: one intended to throw four *amot* but the object traveled eight. Two ways of analyzing this are proposed. On one view, *ha-apik lei* — you removed the object from its original four-*amah* domain, and that removal is what constitutes the *melacha* of carrying four *amot* in *reshut ha-rabim*; one is therefore *chayav* regardless of whether it went further. On another view, the landing point matters: *heicha d'ba'ei lo nach* — where one wanted it to land, after four *amot*, it did not land — it traveled further. One's intention was for a specific endpoint, and that endpoint was not realized.

The Gemara then notes the connection to what was just established above. We concluded that one is *chayav* twice in the four-*amot* case only when one explicitly declares indifference to the landing point — *kol makom she-tirtze tanu'ach*. This framing now implies that without such explicit indifference, if one intended a specific result and the object exceeded that intention, one is *patur* — because *heicha d'ba'ei lo nach*, it did not land where one wanted. This is the question the daf leaves open: when the actual outcome is a superset of the intended outcome — not a subset — does *chiyuv* attach? The particularly stringent standard of *kavanah* that governs the *melacha* of carrying, where even carrying an object the wrong direction can exempt, suggests the answer may be no. The resolution of this question is deferred to the following daf.

---

---

# Shabbat 98

## Intent & Carrying

### Eight vs Four

The Gemara opens with a case it labels *pshita* — obvious. If one intended to throw an object eight *amos* through a *reshus harabim* but it traveled only four, one is *chayav*. The reasoning: *harei kasav shem mi-Shimon* — it is analogous to one who intended to write the name Shimon but wrote only the *shin* and *mem*. One is still *chayav* for writing two letters, because the intent to write the complete name subsumed the intent to write its component letters. Intending to throw eight *amos* includes within it the four, so when the object traveled four, that was encompassed in the original intent.

### Four vs Eight

The Gemara immediately reverses course and poses the harder question: *niskaven lizrok arba ve'zarak shmonah* — one intended to throw only four *amos* but the object traveled eight. What is the *halacha*?

The Gemara entertains two possibilities. On one side, *ha-apik lei* — one did ultimately remove the object from its place, and perhaps the very significance of four *amos* lies in the concept that four *amos* constitutes a person's personal space. To transport an object four *amos* is to remove it from its space, and whether it came to rest at 4.1 or 8.0 *amos*, that fundamental act of removal was accomplished. On the other side, *heicha d'ba'ei hanacha* — the act of carrying is defined not only by movement but by where the object comes to rest. If the intended resting place was after four *amos* and the object came to rest after eight, the act performed was not the act intended.

### Shimon Analogy

The Gemara notes that this very question was addressed implicitly in the previous discussion, where Ravina answered Rav Ashi's case — in which an object passed from a house into a *reshus harabim* and continued four *amos* — by saying the person is *chayav* only *b'omer kol makom she'tirtzeh tanuach*, when the thrower explicitly declared indifference to where the object would land. This answer is telling. Why was that qualification necessary? If intending to carry more includes carrying less, or if carrying less *mechayev* one for the additional distance as well, one could have answered more simply: the intent to place the object upon entering the *reshus harabim* included the act of crossing the boundary, and therefore one is *chayav* for both. Or conversely, intending to travel four *amos* subsumes the crossing of the line. The fact that the Gemara required the explicit declaration of indifference demonstrates that none of these simpler answers were available — that intent in carrying must be precise.

### Carrying Requires Precis…

The Gemara therefore reverses even the initial *pshita*: even if one intended eight and the object traveled only four, one would be *exempt*. And it explains why the *Shimon* analogy fails. *Mi dami?* — how can you compare them? *Hasam*, there, writing *Shimon* certainly includes writing the *shin* and *mem*, because one cannot write *Shimon* without first writing those letters. *Hacha*, here, is it true that one cannot throw eight *amos* without having first thrown four? One might say yes — but the critical distinction is that carrying, unlike writing, is defined by its conclusion. The act of carrying four *amos* means picking something up, walking four *amos*, and putting it down. The act of carrying eight *amos* means picking something up, walking eight *amos*, and putting it down at eight. These are not the same act with one nested inside the other; they are distinct acts, each defined by a specific resting place.

This reflects a well-established principle: carrying places a heightened demand on *kavannah*. Across the *lamed-tet melachos*, we find requirements of *meleches machsheves* — intentional, considered action — but by carrying the concern is particularly acute, likely because carrying is a *melacha* defined more by process than by result. One must intend not merely the act of transporting, but the precise destination. If the object travels further than intended, or less far, or comes to rest in a different location, the act performed differs from the act intended, and one is *patur* — unless one explicitly declared indifference to where the object would land, the scenario of *kol makom she'tirtzeh tanuach*, in which case liability obtains regardless of where it ultimately rests.

---

## Reshuyot Combining

### Public-Private-Public

A *Tanna* teaches: if one threw an object from one *reshus harabim* to another *reshus harabim* with a *reshus hayachid* in between — a house, for instance, whose airspace the object passed through — and the object traveled four *amos* in the *reshus harabim*, one is *chayav*; less than four *amos*, one is *patur*.

### Through vs Resting

The Gemara asks: *mai kamashma lan* — what novelty does this teach? Surely if the object traveled four *amos* in a *reshus harabim* one is *chayav*. The Gemara answers with two teachings embedded in the ruling. First, it is *not* teaching that passage through the house triggers liability — that is, we do not rule *kluta k'mi she-huncha*, that the object's passing through the airspace of the house is treated as if it came to rest there. That principle, associated with Rabbi Akiva and others, is here rejected.

### Reshuyos Mitztarfos

The second and remarkable teaching is: *reshuyos mitztarfos* — two separate *reshus harabim* domains combine. If the object traveled two *amos* in the first *reshus harabim*, passed through the house, and traveled two *amos* in the second *reshus harabim*, those two segments combine to constitute the required four *amos*, and one is *chayav*.

This is a striking *chiddush*. Two *amos* in a *reshus harabim* is not merely below the threshold — it is a fully permitted act. One is *mutar l'chatchila* to carry an object fewer than four *amos* in a *reshus harabim*; the prohibition attaches only at four. This is grounded in the concept that four *amos* represents a person's personal space — less than four *amos* and the object has not left its domain. Two such permitted acts, separated by an entirely different domain, somehow combine to constitute a single prohibited act. The *chiddush* is not merely quantitative combination but the joining of two legally independent and individually innocuous movements across a discontinuous path.

One might note an interesting implicit assumption: the Gemara speaks throughout as if a given segment of road can be *reshus harabim* while an adjacent segment, if roofed, is not. The question of whether a partial covering redefines the entire *reshus harabim* is not explicitly addressed here, though we will encounter it shortly. And regarding Rabbi's position — that passing through the house is treated as *hachnasa* and renders one *chayav* for entering — it seems unlikely that Rabbi would simultaneously affirm *reshuyos mitztarfos*, since defining the passage through the house as an independent act of *hachnasa* would be difficult to reconcile with also treating the two segments as halves of a single act of *ha'avara*.

---

## Roofed Public Domain

### Roofed = Exempt

Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda said in the name of Rav Abba bar Avira in the name of Rav Huna in the name of Rav: *hamavir arba amos b'reshus harabim mikora patur* — one who carries four *amos* in a *reshus harabim* that has a roof overhead is exempt.

This applies to any roofed public thoroughfare — an underpass, a vaulted street, a covered arcade. The ruling has contemporary relevance as well. The *Geonim* derived from the concept that *reshus harabim* must resemble conditions in the desert the requirement that 600,000 people traverse a street for it to constitute a biblical *reshus harabim* — a standard that allows most modern communities to permit an *eiruv*. Where 600,000 people do gather, poskim have considered whether the presence of underpasses or overpasses along a major route — sections that are *mekora* — might suffice to remove the entire street from the category of *reshus harabim*. However, the Gemara here implies nothing so sweeping: it treats the roofed segment as losing its *reshus harabim* status locally, not as disqualifying the broader thoroughfare. As will become apparent momentarily, the Gemara assumes that adjacent unroofed sections retain their *reshus harabim* identity even when roofed sections intervene.

### Not Diglei Midbar

Why is one who carries in a roofed *reshus harabim* exempt? *Lefi she-eina doma le-diglei midbar* — because it does not resemble the encampments of the Israelites in the desert, the paradigmatic *reshus harabim* from which we derive the laws of *hotza'ah*. The desert road was open to the sky. A vaulted space is more like a house; once covered, it loses the defining character of a *reshus harabim*.

This raises an important question for *eiruv* construction. The *tzurat hapetach* — the formal gate-like structure of post and lintel that permits carrying — is predicated on the assumption that we are dealing not with a biblical *reshus harabim* but only with a *karmelit*. If a biblical *reshus harabim* exists, a *tzurat hapetach* is insufficient. The partial *mikora* argument — that some coverage somewhere along the route transforms the entire domain — thus has practical stakes, but the Gemara does not endorse it.

---

## Roofed Public Domain (II)

### Wagons Were Covered

The Gemara immediately challenges its own ruling. *Eini?* — is that really true, that the desert camps had no covering? *Ve-ha agalot de-mechusot havu* — but the wagons were covered! Rav in the name of Rabbi Chiyya states: the areas *tachteihen u-veineihen ve-tzideihen* — underneath the wagons, between the wagons, and at their sides — all constituted *reshus harabim*. But this only raises the underlying difficulty: if the wagons bearing the *kerashim* created a covered space, how can one maintain that the desert encampment was the paradigmatic uncovered *reshus harabim*?

---

## Levite Wagon Setup

### Spaces Around Wagon

The Gemara establishes certain physical assumptions about the wagons. Each wagon was five *amos* long and the beams were ten *amos* long, so each beam overhanging two and a half *amos* on each side. The wagons traveled in pairs, and the beams from each pair of wagons would overhang toward each other — potentially meeting in the middle and creating a roof over the space between them. This would mean that the area between the wagons was in fact covered, directly undermining the claim that the desert road was open.

The Gemara answers: *ki kama Rav bedadarta* — Rav's statement refers to the gaps between the beams as they lay on the wagon. The wagon was five *amos* long; each beam was an *amah* and a half wide (as specified in the Torah). Laid across the width of the wagon, one could fit three beams — taking up four and a half *amos* — leaving a half *amah* to be distributed across the two gaps between the three beams. According to Rashi, the beams were stacked in vertical columns with gaps between them, and those gaps constituted the *reshus harabim*. According to Tosafot, the word *bedadarta* refers specifically to the bottom row before subsequent rows were staggered, at which point the gaps would disappear.

### Three Beams & Gaps

The Gemara, however, immediately challenges this. *Orcha de'agala kama havya* — how long was the wagon? Five *amos*. *Pusya de-kersh kama havya* — how wide was a beam? An *amah* and a half. *Kama mosiv* — how many fit? Three — totaling four and a half *amos*. *Pashlei palga de'amsa* — you are left with half an *amah* for the two gaps, meaning each gap is a *tefach* and a half. And a *tefach* and a half is subject to the rule of *lavud* — objects or surfaces within three *tefachim* of each other are treated as connected. The gaps are thus halakhically non-existent, and the beams are treated as one continuous surface. There is no *reshus harabim* between them.

### Four Beams Problem

The Gemara then suggests placing the beams on their depth rather than their width. Each beam was an *amah* deep; placed thus, four could fit on a five-*amah* wagon. Three gaps would divide the remaining one *amah* — six *tefachim* — giving each gap exactly two *tefachim*. But two *tefachim* still falls within *lavud*, so the problem remains. *Sof sof sumcha de-kersh kama havya* — the depth of a beam is one *amah*; *arba* — four fit; *pashla amta* — one *amah* left; *ki shadlei mar beini u'veini* — dividing it among three gaps yields two *tefachim* each — *ke-lavud dami* — still treated as connected.

### Angled Beams Taper

The Gemara now introduces the opinion of *leman de-amar krashim mil-matan ovyan ama u-mil-malah kalin ve-holchin ad ke-etzba* — that the beams were one *amah* deep at the base but tapered toward the top until they were only a finger-width in depth. This is the position we will later see associated with Rabbi Yehuda. If the beams taper as they rise, then the portions of the beams extending beyond the wagon become progressively thinner. By the time they overhang the space between the wagons, the beams are nearly nothing — a point — and the gaps between them have grown correspondingly. What was a two-*tefach* gap at the base becomes open airspace above. The *lavud* problem disappears and meaningful uncovered space — *reshus harabim* — exists between the beams.

### Atzbe'i Columns

For the opinion that the beams maintained uniform depth throughout — *keshem she-mil-matan ovyan ama kach mil-malah ovyan ama* — Rav Kahana offers an alternative: *be-atzbai*. Rashi explains this (with two possible readings) as grouping the beams into combined columns at the two ends of the wagon, rather than distributing them evenly. Instead of four evenly spaced columns with two-*tefach* gaps, two beams are paired at each end, leaving a full *amah* — six *tefachim* — between the central paired groupings. Six *tefachim* exceeds the *lavud* threshold; that central space is halakhically open and qualifies as *reshus harabim*.

The Gemara then asks: *atzbai heichi manchat lehu* — but where exactly are these combined columns placed? *Agava de-agala* — on the floor of the wagon itself.

### Frame Without Floor

This prompts a further question: *agala gufei mikoreh havai* — but the wagon itself is roofed. Even if one has now solved the problem of the gaps between the beams, the entire base of the wagon covers the space beneath it, just as the undercarriage of any vehicle covers the ground below. The Gemara answers: *amar Shmuel bi-teidoth* — Shmuel says the wagons were constructed of pegs or a frame, without a solid floor. The wagon was a structural frame onto which the beams were loaded, but the space between the frame members had no covering. The area beneath the wagon therefore remained open, and the ground-level space under and around the wagon retained its character as *reshus harabim*.

Tosafot raises a broader conceptual objection: given that the majority of the area under the wagon train was in fact covered by the overhanging beams, why focus on the small uncovered gaps as definitive of the *reshus harabim*? The Gemara's implicit answer is that it is the uncovered portion that establishes the domain's identity, not the covered portions created by the cargo in transit. This itself is a significant assumption. One might equally have argued that the structural reality of the space — open sky when the wagons are absent — should define its identity, and the Gemara could have dismissed the entire difficulty on those grounds. It is striking that the Gemara does not take that simpler route, instead engaging seriously with the question of whether the wagon coverings redefine the space beneath them.

---

## Mishkan Beam Design

### R. Yehuda: Tapered

The Gemara now turns from the halakhic implications of the wagon configuration to a description of the *kerashim* themselves. *Tanu Rabbanan*: the beams were one *amah* deep at the base — *mil-matan ovyan ama* — but toward the top they tapered to near-nothing — *mil-malah kalin ve-holchin ad ke-etzba*, until at the top they were only a finger-width. The prooftext: *yihyu tmimim al rosho* — the word *tmimim* is read not as "complete" or "whole" but in the sense of coming to an end, as in *tammu nichratu* and *v'yitmu yemei b'chi evel Moshe* — they conclude, they cease. Thus the beams conclude at the top, coming to a point. This is the position of Rabbi Yehuda.

### R. Nechemya: Uniform

Rabbi Nechemya disagrees: *keshem she-lemattan ovyan ama, kach mil-malah ovyan ama* — the same way they were one *amah* deep at the bottom, so at the top they remained one *amah* deep. The beams were uniform rectangular solids throughout. The prooftext he invokes is *yachdav* — together, meaning one consistent unified form from bottom to top.

Each disputant must address the other's textual support. On the word *tmimim*, Rabbi Nechemya reads it as requiring that each beam be made from a single whole piece of wood — *shlemim ve-lo de-nisra* — complete, not assembled from separate pieces. On the word *yachdav*, Rabbi Yehuda reads it as the simpler instruction that the beams be placed flush and even in a consistent row, not staggered — *d'lo lishlachfinu me-hadadi* — together, aligned.

### Corner Configuration

The Gemara now addresses the corner beams. The Torah specifies six beams for the western wall plus two corner beams — *u-shnei krashim ta'aseh l'miktzo'ot*. The interior of the *Mishkan* was thirty *amos* long by ten *amos* wide. The beams along the length stood side by side, each an *amah* and a half wide. Six beams on the western wall gave nine *amos*; the remaining *amah* on each side was supplied by the corner beams. Each corner beam contributed half an *amah* of interior width to the western face, completing the ten *amos*, while its remaining *amah* of width extended outward, connecting flush with the depth of the lengthwise beams.

This configuration works elegantly according to Rabbi Nechemya, whose beams have uniform depth of one *amah* throughout. *D'ati putya d'hanei u-mamli leh l'sumcha d'hanei* — the width of the corner beam fills in the depth of the lengthwise beam. The corner beam's width on the exterior is one *amah*, the depth of the adjacent lengthwise beam is one *amah*, and they meet perfectly, producing a clean exterior and interior configuration.

### Tapered Corner Problem

According to Rabbi Yehuda, however, whose beams taper toward the top, the corner configuration becomes problematic. The corner beam tapers in one direction while the adjacent lengthwise beam tapers in the perpendicular direction. They will not meet cleanly at the top; one will be coming to a point in one direction while the other tapers in a crossing direction, producing an awkward and irregular junction. *Miman kol nevuchadnetzar behai ayeil u-vehai nafak* — one goes in one direction, the other goes out another, and they do not resolve.

The Gemara answers: *de-shapi lehu ke-turei* — at the corners they would fashion the beams to taper in both directions simultaneously, so that the corner beams rose to a point like a mountain peak, meeting the tapering of both adjacent walls cleanly. While no explicit verse mandates this particular treatment of the corners, the Gemara accepts it as the implied solution.

---

## Pole System

### Central Pole Rings

*Ve-ha-bariach ha-tichon betoch ha-kerashim* — the Torah describes a central pole running through the rings of the beams. The *kerashim* had rings affixed to their exterior faces, and poles were threaded through these rings to bind the beams together into a stable wall, functioning like long bolts running the length of each wall — preventing the individual beams from swaying.

### Three-Way Miracle

*Tana benes haya omed* — a tradition records that the central pole's placement was miraculous. Rashi explains: the verse implies that a single pole ran through rings in all three directions simultaneously — along the southern wall, the northern wall, and the western wall, turning the corners in one continuous passage, which is physically impossible by natural means. Tosafot notes, however, that the *brayta* of *melechet ha-Mishkan* describes three separate poles running along three separate walls, and on that reading the miracle mentioned is a different one. The Gemara does not resolve this dispute but proceeds with the broader description.

---

## Mishkan Curtains

### Inner Curtains

The Torah instructs: *ve-es ha-Mishkan ta'aseh eser yeriot* — you shall make ten curtains for the *Mishkan*. *Orech ha-yeri'ah ha-achat shmoneh ve-esrim ba-amah* — each curtain was twenty-eight *amos* long and four *amos* wide. The ten curtains together formed the inner layer of the *Mishkan*'s covering.

### Width-Wise Coverage

Orienting the curtains lengthwise across the width of the *Mishkan*: each curtain was twenty-eight *amos* long; the interior width of the *Mishkan* was ten *amos*. Subtracting ten for the interior ceiling leaves eighteen *amos*, or nine *amos* falling on each side. The beams were ten *amos* tall and the *adanim* — the silver sockets — added one *amah* at the base.

### R. Yehuda vs R. Nechemya

Here the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya determines the precise coverage. According to Rabbi Yehuda, whose beams taper toward the top, the curtain placed over the top of the wall need not traverse the full one-*amah* depth of the beam; it slopes down naturally from the tapering apex. The curtain therefore descends nine *amos* on each side, covering the full ten-*amah* beam height and leaving only the *adanim* — the sockets at the base — exposed. *Rav Yehudah megalei amah de-adanim* — according to Rabbi Yehuda, the sockets are the only exposed element.

According to Rabbi Nechemya, whose beams maintain uniform depth, the curtain must first traverse the full one-*amah* depth of the beam at the top before it can begin to descend. This consumes one of the nine *amos*, leaving only eight to fall along the side. *Rav Nechemya megalei amah de-krashim* — an entire *amah* of the beam itself is left exposed, in addition to the exposed socket below.

### Length-Wise Coverage

The same calculation applies along the length. The curtains' combined width — ten curtains of four *amos* each — totaled forty *amos*. The interior of the *Mishkan* was thirty *amos* long. After accounting for thirty *amos* of interior ceiling, ten *amos* remained to drape down the rear wall. According to Rabbi Yehuda the tapering beam required no depth adjustment, and the full ten *amos* descended the back wall, reaching the *adanim* and covering even the sockets. According to Rabbi Nechemya the one-*amah* beam depth consumed one *amah* of the drape, leaving nine descending the rear wall and the sockets exposed.

### Goat Hair Curtains

Above the embroidered inner curtains lay a second layer of coarser curtains made of goat's hair: *ve-asita yeriot izim le-ohel*. These differed in two respects: each was thirty *amos* long rather than twenty-eight, and there were eleven rather than ten. Combined width was thus forty-four *amos*; combined length thirty *amos*.

Applying the same width-wise calculation: thirty *amos* oriented across the ten-*amah* interior leaves ten *amos* per side. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the full ten descends each side, *mechase amta de-adanim* — covering even the sockets. According to Rabbi Nechemya, one *amah* is consumed by the beam depth and nine descend, *megalya amta de-adanim* — the sockets remain exposed. This is corroborated by the *brayta*: *v'ha-amah mizeh v'ha-amah mizeh b'odef* — the Torah's explicit mention of the extra *amah* on each side of the goat's hair curtain. According to Rabbi Yehuda, *l'chasot amta de-adanim* — this extra *amah* covers the sockets. According to Rabbi Nechemya, *l'chasot amta de-krashim* — it covers the exposed beam, not the socket.

### Doubled Front Curtain

In the length-wise direction, the eleven goat's hair curtains yielded forty-four *amos* combined. Thirty *amos* covered the interior ceiling; fourteen remained. Of these, two *amos* were designated to be folded over at the front — *v'chifalta et ha-yeri'ah ha-shishit el mul pnei ha-ohel* — doubled down over the entrance, leaving twelve *amos* for the rear.

### Train Behind Mishkan

Of the twelve *amos* remaining to descend the back wall: according to Rabbi Yehuda, all twelve fell down the rear. Ten covered the full height of the beams; two *amos* extended onto the ground behind the *Mishkan*. This is the referent of the verse *chatzi ha-yeri'ah ha-odefet tisrach* — the half of the extra curtain trails beyond. *Tisrach* connotes extension or trailing.

### Mishkan as Bride

According to Rabbi Nechemya, the one-*amah* beam depth consumes one *amah*, eleven descend the rear wall — one covering the socket and ten covering the beam — and only one *amah* trails on the ground. Thus even according to Rabbi Nechemya something trails, though less than according to Rabbi Yehuda. *Tisrach mechavroteha* — it trails beyond its companions, longer than the other curtains, even if only by one *amah* onto the ground.

The Gemara closes with an image from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *l'ma ha-Mishkan domeh* — to what is the *Mishkan* comparable? *L'isha she-mehalechet ba-shuk ve-shuleha mehalchin achareha* — to a woman — a bride — walking through the marketplace with her train trailing behind her. The doubled-over curtain at the entrance served as a veil; the trailing length at the rear was the train. With this image the daf concludes.

---

---

# Shabbat 99

## Beams & Sockets

### Carving Technique

The daf opens with a *baraita* describing the construction of the *mishkan*'s structural elements: *charutzim hayu kerashim vachallulim hayu adanim* — the beams were carved, and the sockets were hollow. What this means practically is that each beam, which was essentially a rectangular solid, had to terminate at its base in two small pegs that would fit into the hollow of the sockets below. To produce those pegs, the craftsmen had to cut away the surrounding material — removing everything that was not the peg — leaving two protruding feet at the bottom of each beam. The sockets, in turn, were square blocks with a hollow cavity, into which those feet would be inserted. That is the entirety of the mechanism described: carved pegs and hollow sockets, fitted together.

### Assembly Method

The visual logic is straightforward. One begins with a full rectangular beam and cuts inward on all sides near the base, producing two narrow pegs. The sockets receive those pegs, and the whole structure locks into place. *Rashi* includes a diagram that clarifies the geometry. The broader halachic significance of this description will become apparent as the *gemara* returns to questions of carrying and domain.

---

## Curtains & Skill

### Hooks as Stars

The *gemara* turns to a entirely different aspect of the *mishkan* — the curtains that formed the roof. The Torah describes two sets of five curtains each, sewn together along their respective lengths and then joined to one another by means of rings (*lula'ot*) and hooks (*krasim*). The *gemara* notes: *venirim krasim belula'ot kekochavim barakia* — the hooks visible through the rings appeared like stars in the sky. From beneath, looking up at this ceiling of curtains, the gold-toned copper fittings would glimmer through, creating the impression of a starlit sky. Whether that visual impression was intentional — whether the *mishkan*'s designers were consciously evoking the heavens — is left open. The curtains themselves were not uniformly blue, so this was not a simple imitation of sky. Yet the image is a striking one: the very structure of the joinery producing an unplanned, or at least unspecified, celestial effect.

### Curtain Materials

A *baraita* then specifies the materials of the two layers of curtains. The lower curtains (*yeri'ot tachtonot*) were woven from *techeiles* (blue), *argaman* (royal purple), *tola'as shani* (scarlet), and *shesh* (linen) — a rich, multicolored fabric. The upper curtains (*elyonot*), by contrast, were *ma'aseh izim*, made entirely from goat hair. On the surface, this suggests the upper curtains were simpler: a single, plain material versus the elaborate combination below.

### Goat Hair Spinning

The *baraita* immediately overturns that assumption: *ugdolah chochmah shene'emrah be'elyonot yoter mimas shene'emrah betachtonot* — the skill required for the upper curtains exceeded that required for the lower ones. The proof is textual. Regarding the lower curtains, the verse says that women of skilled heart (*chachmat lev*) spun with their hands. Regarding the upper curtains, the verse says that women whose hearts *lifted them up* with wisdom spun *et ha'izim* — they spun the goats. The *gemara* cites a *tannaitic* teaching in the name of Rabbi Nechemiah, already encountered a few weeks earlier in the course of study: *shatuf ba'izim vetavui min ha'izim* — the goats were washed in the river while still bearing their hair, and the thread was spun directly from the backs of the goats while they stood there. That is the meaning of "they spun the goats" rather than simply "they spun the goat hair." Spinning directly from a living animal, rather than from sheared and prepared fiber, demanded a level of technical mastery that surpassed even the intricate multicolor weaving of the lower curtains. This passage was cited earlier in the tractate in a halachic context: the *gemara* there raised the possibility that since this technique required extraordinary skill (*chochmah yetirah*), a normal person performing it might not be liable for a *melachah* on *Shabbat*, as it would constitute a *shinuy* — a deviation from standard practice.

---

## Wagons Layout

### Wagon Positioning

With the discussion of curtains concluded, the *gemara* returns to the theme of the *levi'im* and carrying — specifically, the question of *reshut harabbim* and how its dimensions are derived from the *mishkan*. The context is a teaching of Rav in the name of Rabbi Chiya: *agalot tachteihen beneihen vetzideihen reshut harabbim* — underneath the wagons, between the wagons, and at their sides was all *reshut harabbim*. This was noted the previous day in the discussion of whether the overhead beams converted the space into a covered *reshut harabbim*.

### Wagon Length

Abaye states: *bein agalah le'agalah kemlo orech agalah* — the gap between one wagon and the next was equal to the length of one wagon. And the length of a wagon was five *amot*.

### Rashi's Model

*Rashi* explains this as follows. Each wagon was five *amot* long. Two wagons moved side by side, and each was also five *amot* wide — two and a half *amot* for the base of the wagon, and then one and a quarter *amot* on each side for the thickness of the wheels. The full outer width of each wagon, from wheel edge to wheel edge, was therefore five *amot*.

According to *Rashi*, the beams of the *mishkan* were laid across the tops of two side-by-side wagons, overhanging each one. From the outer edge of one wagon to the outer edge of the other was fifteen *amot*: five for each wagon plus five between them, and the beams extended across the entire span with overhangs on the outer edges.

The *gemara* asks about the length: why does the wagon need to be a full five *amot*? The calculation based on the beam widths — whether one and a half *amot* or one *amah* across — yields either four and a half or some similar measure that falls short of five. The *gemara* answers: *ki heichi dela litzdu kerashim* — to prevent the beams from rubbing against one another. A small cushion of space was necessary so that the columns of beams would not wear each other down through friction.

### Base Width

The *gemara* then turns to the width of the wagon's base. Rava states that the sides of each wagon (*tzidei agalah*) were equal to the width of the wagon — two and a half *amot*. So the base of each wagon was two and a half *amot*, with the outer wheel adding one and a quarter *amot* on each side, for a total of five *amot* per wagon.

The *gemara* asks: why does the base need to be two and a half *amot*? Would not one and a half suffice? The answer is: *ki heichi d'lo lidudi krashim* — again, to give the beams sufficient stability so they would not sway. A narrower base would leave too much beam overhanging on each side without adequate support.

One should appreciate just how much overhang is involved here in *Rashi*'s model. The beam extends from beyond the outer wheel on one side, across the full wagon, and out over the wheel on the other side. If the inner support is only two and a half *amot* and the overhang on each side extends considerably further, the structure is not particularly stable — a point *Tosafot* does not let pass.

### Width Derived

The *gemara* now addresses the derivation of the standard width of *reshut harabbim*: *d'kaima lan derech reshut harabbim shesh esrei amah* — we hold that a *reshut harabbim* must be sixteen *amot* wide, and we learn this from the *mishkan*. The *gemara* says that if we learn it from the *mishkan*, the *mishkan* structure itself only yields fifteen: five for each of the two wagons and five between them. How do we arrive at sixteen?

The *gemara* answers: *amta yetirta havai d'hava kai bein Levi* — there was an additional *amah*, the space where the *levi* walked alongside the wagon. If the beams began to slip, a *levi* positioned at the side could catch and adjust them. This guard-walking *levi* occupied an extra *amah* — either a half-*amah* on each side, or a full *amah* on one side — bringing the total to sixteen. That is *Rashi*'s explanation.

### Tosafot's Model

*Tosafot* raises several objections to *Rashi*'s model. First, if two wagons travel side by side and the beams overhang from both, the beams will press against one another in the middle, rubbing away at each other. Second, even accepting the two-and-a-half *amah* base, the overhang on each side is so great relative to the support that the structure is structurally implausible.

*Tosafot* therefore proposes an entirely different understanding. In *Tosafot*'s model, what the *gemara* calls the "two wagons" is in fact one unified structure. Each "wheel" was itself two and a half *amot* thick — not one and a quarter as in *Rashi*. You thus have one large structural unit: two and a half *amot* for the outer wall and wheel on one side, ten *amot* of interior space, and two and a half *amot* for the outer wall and wheel on the other side — a total of fifteen *amot* from outer edge to outer edge. The ten-*amah* interior space is exactly the length of each *mishkan* beam, so no overhang was needed or intended: the beam lay perfectly across the interior of the structure.

This single unified structure had four wheels underneath — two outer wheels and two inner wheels — and interior walls or supports at the points where the inner wheels were located, so that the beam rested on those interior walls rather than spanning freely. The distinction *Tosafot* draws is that what *Rashi* calls "two wagons" and what the *gemara* calls each *agalah* in the context of width refers to half of this single structure — from the outer wall to the first interior support, which was two and a half *amot*, plus the gap to the next half, which was five *amot*. The entire unit read as a unified structure rather than two independent vehicles.

*Tosafot*'s model avoids the problems of opposing overhangs and structural instability. It also allows a single ten-*amah* beam to rest cleanly across the interior without conflict. The *levi* with his extra *amah* still accounts for the sixteenth *amah* on the outside. The *gemara*'s insistence on five *amot* as the measure of a wagon is interpreted by *Tosafot* as referring to each half of the structure, not a separate independent vehicle, with the full structure spanning fifteen.

---

## Mound & Rock

### Dimensions

The *gemara* moves to the next *mishnah*: *chulyat habor vehasela* — the mound of earth (*chulya*) surrounding a well and a rock. The *mishnah* establishes that if either of these is ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* by four *tefachim* in its base dimensions, it constitutes a *reshut hayachid*. One who takes an object from the top of such a mound or rock, or places something upon it while standing in *reshut harabbim*, is liable.

This ruling contains an important conceptual point. A *reshut hayachid* is not limited to the classic model of a cavity surrounded by four walls. Even a solid elevation — a mound of earth or a natural rock — with the requisite dimensions qualifies. The logic is that once you have walls of ten *tefachim* on all sides, those walls are understood to continue upward indefinitely, making the space above them — including the top surface of the mound or rock — part of the *reshut hayachid*. The analogy is to the roof of a building: even if the entire interior were filled with earth, the roof would still be a *reshut hayachid* because the walls define the perimeter and their legal effect extends upward.

The *mishnah* specifies that if the dimensions fall short of ten high or four by four wide, one is exempt. The four-by-four requirement means exactly four in each direction; sixteen square *tefachim* arranged in a shape lacking four in any one direction would not suffice.

### Combination Debate

The *gemara* asks: why does the *mishnah* need to mention the mound around the well (*chulyat habor*) separately from the rock? The mound, as a solid elevated mass with the requisite dimensions, is simply a case of the same *halacha* as the rock — what novel point does it add? The *gemara* answers: *mesaya lei le-Rabbi Yochanan* — it supports the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan, who said that *bor vechuliyasa mitztarfin l'asara* — the well and its surrounding mound combine to reach the measure of ten.

The question is: in which dimension do they combine? Here *Rashi* and *Tosafot* diverge.

*Rashi* understands the combination to be in height. Imagine a well that is only five *tefachim* deep, with a mound of five *tefachim* built up around its opening. For a person standing at the bottom of the well, the total wall surrounding them is ten *tefachim*: five from the depth of the well and five from the height of the mound above ground. The interior of the well thus constitutes a *reshut hayachid*, even though neither element alone reaches ten. The difficulty with *Rashi*'s interpretation is that the *mishnah* speaks of placing objects *on top of* the mound (*al gaban*) and being liable — but on *Rashi*'s model, the top of the mound is only five *tefachim* high and would not itself be a *reshut hayachid*. The liability would attach only to placing something *inside* the well, not on top of the mound.

*Tosafot* therefore reads the combination differently — as combining in width rather than height. On this reading, the mound itself is ten *tefachim* high, so height is not the issue. The problem is that the mound consists of two raised sides flanking the opening of the well, and each side may be only a *tefach* or two wide, with the gap of the well's opening — perhaps two *tefachim* — between them. Taken separately, neither side has the required four *tefachim* in width. But Rabbi Yochanan's principle allows the mound and the well opening together to be treated as a combined unit of four *tefachim*. The basis for this combination is that one could in theory lay a plank across the gap, and since the well and its mound are understood as a single functional apparatus, the gap is treated as bridged even without an actual plank, rendering the entire surface — including the top of the mound — a *reshut hayachid*. On this reading, the liability described in the *mishnah* for placing something *on top* fits perfectly.

*Rashi* and *Tosafot* do not dispute that both types of combination are legally valid. The question is only which scenario Rabbi Yochanan and the *mishnah* are addressing. *Tosafot* argues that since the *mishnah* explicitly discusses placing on top of the mound and being liable, the combination must be one that makes the top of the mound itself a *reshut hayachid*, which only works on the width-combination reading.

---

## Mound & Rock (II)

### Application

The *gemara* then cites a supporting *baraita*: a well in *reshut harabbim* that is ten *tefachim* deep and four wide — one may not draw water from it on *Shabbat*, because doing so transfers from a *reshut hayachid* into a *reshut harabbim* or at minimum into a *karmelis*. The *baraita* confirms that *bor vechuliyasa mitztarfin l'asara*, and the phrasing here — combining to reach ten — aligns textually with *Rashi*'s height-combination reading. *Tosafot* agrees that the *baraita* and Rabbi Yochanan's statement refer to the *Rashi* scenario, but maintains that when Rabbi Yochanan's principle is applied to explain the *mishnah*'s case, the same logic extends to width-combination as well.

---

## Well Usage

### Drawing Prohibition

The *baraita* establishes that one may not draw water from a ten-deep, four-wide well situated in *reshut harabbim* on *Shabbat*, because the act of drawing transfers an object from a *reshut hayachid* into the surrounding space, whether that space is a *reshut harabbim* or a *karmelis*. This is the practical problem that led to the rabbinic practice of constructing enclosures around public wells, or at minimum symbolic corner-post structures, to define the surrounding space as *reshut hayachid* and permit water-drawing.

### Wall Requirement

The *baraita* continues: *ela im kein asu lo mechitzah gevohah asara tefachim* — unless one builds a wall ten *tefachim* high around the well. Only then is water-drawing permitted, because the surrounding area has been converted into a *reshut hayachid* and one is simply moving within that domain.

### Drinking Rule

Even absent a proper wall, the *baraita* allows drinking from the well under one strict condition: *ela im kein hichnis l'tocho rosho ve-rubo* — unless one inserts into the well one's head and the majority of one's body. The concern is that if a person merely leans over the well to draw water — even if the bucket or vessel remains within the airspace of the well — there is a risk that the person will stand upright while still holding the vessel, thereby transferring it from *reshut hayachid* into whatever domain the person is standing in. Only if the majority of the body is actually inside the well can we be confident that the person and the water are effectively together within the *reshut hayachid* and that drinking constitutes movement within that domain rather than a transfer across domain boundaries. This is, practically speaking, a highly precarious requirement, demanding that one suspend the majority of one's body over a pit ten *tefachim* deep in order to drink.

---

## Throwing Clarifications

### Rav Mordechai

The *gemara* records a question posed by Rav Mordechai to Rabbah. There is a post (*amud*) standing in *reshut harabbim* that is ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* wide — in other words, a classic *reshut hayachid* exactly like the rock of the *mishnah*. One throws an object that lands on top of the post. The question: is one liable?

On the surface this appears trivially answered by the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* says one is liable for taking from or placing upon a ten-high, four-wide rock in *reshut harabbim*. But Rav Mordechai raises a consideration: *keivan d'mimakom patur ka-asya* — since the object came from a *makom patur*. In order to land on something that is ten *tefachim* high, the object must have traveled through the airspace above ten *tefachim* in *reshut harabbim*, which is a *makom patur*. Perhaps the trajectory from *reshut harabbim* through a *makom patur* and then down onto *reshut hayachid* interrupts the act, making it a movement from *makom patur* into *reshut hayachid* rather than from *reshut harabbim* into *reshut hayachid* — and thereby exempting the thrower.

### Mishnah Res.

Rabbah, Rav Yosef, and Abaye all respond identically: *matnisin hi* — it is answered by the *mishnah*. The very *mishnah* under discussion describes placing something on a rock of exactly these dimensions in *reshut harabbim* and holds one liable; clearly passage through the higher airspace does not exempt.

Rav Mordechai is unimpressed, accusing all three of repeating each other without engaging the question. He points out that the *mishnah* might not actually address the precise scenario he raised. Perhaps the *mishnah* refers to placing an object directly — without the object ascending above ten *tefachim* first. For instance: a needle thrown into a crack in the rock (*charitza*) near the base, which never rises above ten *tefachim* at all. It enters a fissure that, as part of the floor of a *reshut hayachid*, is itself *reshut hayachid*, without the object ever having passed through the higher airspace. That would resolve the *mishnah* without answering Rav Mordechai's question about an object that does pass through *makom patur*.

The *gemara* notes that even a needle must rise slightly (*ee efshar de-lo midalya purta*), and the crevice scenario is an attempt to minimize that elevation as much as possible. Admittedly, reading the entire *mishnah* as discussing needle-in-crevice is a forced interpretation, and *Tosafot* takes a different view of what Rav Mordechai was really asking.

### Tosafot Theory

*Tosafot* argues that the question is not simply about an object passing through *makom patur* as a way-point in flight. That scenario — an object passing through an intermediate domain in the course of being carried — has already been discussed elsewhere, and transit through a *makom patur* does not exempt. *Tosafot* understands that Rav Mordechai's question is more specific: it concerns the physics of a thrown object that reaches an apex and then falls.

When one throws an object upward, the object travels from *reshut harabbim* upward into *makom patur*, reaches its apex, and then changes direction — gravity takes over and the object falls back down. *Tosafot* suggests that because this change of direction, this cessation of the thrower's energy and transfer to gravitational force, occurs precisely in the *makom patur*, perhaps the act is thereby divided into two separate movements: one from *reshut harabbim* into *makom patur*, and a second from *makom patur* into *reshut hayachid*. If so, the second segment — from *makom patur* into *reshut hayachid* — does not constitute a prohibited carrying act, and one would be exempt.

This is a far more compelling and nuanced question. The needle-in-crevice scenario was an attempt to resolve the *mishnah* under any possible reading, but *Tosafot*'s framing clarifies why the three *amoraim* who simply said "it's a *mishnah*" were failing to engage the real issue: the *mishnah* may address direct placement, whereas Rav Mordechai is asking specifically about the dynamic of a thrown arc that reverses direction in *makom patur*.

---

## Wall Status

### Wall Question

The *gemara* records that Rav Mesha transmitted a question of Rabbi Yochanan. There is a wall in *reshut harabbim* that is ten *tefachim* high but not four *tefachim* wide. Because it lacks the four-*tefach* width, the wall itself is not a *reshut hayachid* in its own right. However, this wall surrounds a *karmelis* — some open, intermediate-domain space — and in doing so converts that enclosed area into a *reshut hayachid*. Now, someone throws an object that lands not inside the enclosed yard but on top of the wall itself — on the wall's upper surface, which is less than four *tefachim* wide. What is the status of that surface?

One might say: the wall lacks four *tefachim* of width and is therefore a *makom patur* — exempt space — neither *reshut harabbim* nor *reshut hayachid*. Or one might say: since the wall has created a *reshut hayachid* in the backyard, it should be considered part of that *reshut hayachid*, as if the entire enclosed space — yard plus wall — is one filled unit (*keman d'malya*), making the wall's upper surface itself *reshut hayachid*.

### Ulla's Logic

Ulla resolves the question by means of a *kal vachomer*: if this wall creates *reshut hayachid* for the backyard it encloses, it certainly — *kol she-kein* — creates *reshut hayachid* for its own thickness. The force of the *kal vachomer* is that it would be incongruous for a structure to extend *reshut hayachid* status to others while being denied that status for itself. The wall is, as it were, more integral to the *reshut hayachid* it creates than the yard it encloses; surely its own surface partakes of that status.

### Precedent

A confirming tradition is then cited: Rav Chisda in the name of Rav, and similarly in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, state that any wall ten *tefachim* high — even if not four wide — that surrounds a *karmelis* and converts it to *reshut hayachid*, renders one who throws an object onto the top of that wall liable. The *kal vachomer* of Ulla is thus formally endorsed as *halacha*: the wall's own thickness shares in the *reshut hayachid* it creates.

---

## Becoming R.H.

### Digging Q.

Rabbi Yochanan poses a striking question. Suppose there is a well that is only nine *tefachim* deep — one *tefach* short of the depth required to constitute a *reshut hayachid*. On *Shabbat*, someone shovels a *chulya* of earth from the bottom of that well, deepening it to ten *tefachim*, and throws the dirt backward out of the well into *reshut harabbim*. Setting aside whatever liability attaches to the digging itself (*boneh* or *choreish*), has this person also committed the *melachah* of carrying? That is: did the person take an object from *reshut hayachid* and deposit it in *reshut harabbim*?

### Simultaneous Acts

The question is: *akirat chefetz ve'asiyas mechitzah bahadi hadadi ka'atu* — the uprooting of the object (the dirt) and the creation of the *mechitza* (the additional *tefach* of depth that makes it a *reshut hayachid*) occurred simultaneously. Perhaps we say that since they occurred together, we treat the well as if it were already a *reshut hayachid* at the moment of uprooting, and the person is liable. Or perhaps we say that since the well was *not* a *reshut hayachid* at the moment the act began, there is no liability: the *akirah* — the uprooting — did not take place from a *reshut hayachid*, and the fact that it became one during the act is insufficient.

### Inverse Q.

Rabbi Yochanan then poses the inverse question. Suppose the well is already ten *tefachim* deep — a proper *reshut hayachid*. One takes a mound of earth from *reshut harabbim* and throws it into the well, and it lands on the bottom, reducing the depth from ten to nine *tefachim*. Has one carried from *reshut harabbim* into *reshut hayachid*? The act began with a valid *reshut hayachid*, but by the time the dirt settled at the bottom, the well no longer qualified. Do we say that the *hanachah* — the placing — and the elimination of the *mechitza* occurred simultaneously, and therefore one is liable because the *reshut hayachid* still existed when the act was completed? Or do we say that since the *mechitza* was removed in the very act of placement, there is no valid *hanachah* in *reshut hayachid* and one is exempt? One might invoke the principle of *kluta k'mi she-huncha damya* — that the moment an airborne object enters a domain it is treated as having been placed there — but that principle's applicability here is itself subject to debate.

### Dates on Wall

To potentially resolve these questions, the *gemara* cites a *mishnah* involving a different case. One throws an object ארבע *amot* in *reshut harabbim* and it strikes a wall: if it hits at a height above ten *tefachim* it is like throwing in the air and one is exempt; if it hits below ten *tefachim* it is like throwing on the ground and one is liable for *hazarak arba amot b'reshut harabbim*. The *gemara* had previously questioned this *mishnah* — the object presumably bounced off the wall rather than coming to rest — and Rabbi Yochanan resolved it by explaining that the *mishnah* speaks of *dveila shemena*, a sticky mass of compressed dates, which adheres to the wall upon impact.

The *gemara* then asks: why is one liable in this case? *Ha kamivtzar me'arba amot* — the mass of dates, once stuck to the wall, reduces the effective traversed distance to slightly less than four *amot* (since the object's resting position is on the wall, not at the full four *amot* of open ground). *Tosafot* rejects *Rashi*'s reading of this objection (that the back of the date rests short of four *amot*), arguing that if that were the case one would be straightforwardly exempt because the four *amot* were simply not completed, comparable to the case of a basket straddling domains. *Tosafot* instead understands the question as follows: a clump of dates protruding from the wall at a height below ten *tefachim* creates a structural protrusion that, if it were a true building element, would interrupt the *reshut harabbim* beneath it. The question is whether that protrusion — created by the act of throwing — has now altered the domain, such that the object did not land in *reshut harabbim* after all.

### Architecture Change

The *gemara* resolves the matter with a crucial distinction. *Hasam lo mevatlei* — in the case of the dates on the wall, the structure is not truly altered. A sticky mass of dates attached to a wall is a temporary accretion; no one considers the fundamental architecture of the space to have changed. The dates will be removed, the wall remains what it is, and the surrounding space remains *reshut harabbim*. Therefore one is liable, and the objection about architectural change does not apply.

*Hacha mevatlei* — in the case of the well, however, the situation is genuinely different. When one throws earth into the well and fills it up, or digs earth out and deepens it, one is truly and permanently altering the physical structure of the space. The *mechitza* is genuinely eliminated or created. The *gemara* therefore declines to derive an answer to Rabbi Yochanan's questions from the dates case: they are structurally dissimilar. Rabbi Yochanan's questions — about both digging and filling a well — remain unresolved.

---

## Plank & Pegs

### Rava Q.

Rava poses a further question. Suppose there are two pegs (*yesedot*) standing in some space, each ten *tefachim* high, but neither is four *tefachim* wide, and they are not enclosing any space that would independently combine their dimensions. By themselves, they have no *reshut hayachid* status — unlike the mound and the well, which are understood as part of a single apparatus. One then throws a plank (*daf*) and it lands across the tops of the two pegs. The plank, now resting atop the two ten-*tefach* supports, spans the gap and creates a surface that constitutes a *reshut hayachid*. What is the *halacha*?

### Simultaneity

The *gemara* asks: is this simply the same question Rabbi Yochanan already posed — whether the simultaneous creation of a *mechitza* and the placement of an object creates liability? *Hainu de'Rabbi Yochanan* — that is precisely what Rabbi Yochanan asked. The well case and this case would seem to be identical in structure, and since we were inclined to say there is no liability when the *akirah* does not begin from an established *reshut hayachid*, the same reasoning would apply here.

### Separation Theory

The *gemara* clarifies that Rava's question is in fact distinct. Rava's scenario involves throwing not just the plank but also an additional object resting on the plank — both thrown together. The plank is the vehicle that creates the *reshut hayachid*; the other object is the one whose carrying we wish to evaluate. Now, it is physically impossible for an object resting on a plank to remain perfectly stationary during flight: *ee efshar de-lo midalya purta* — inevitably, the object rises slightly off the plank at some point during the arc. There is therefore a momentary interval of separation between plank and object. If that separation means the plank lands first — even for an instant — and creates the *reshut hayachid*, and then the object completes its descent and lands within that newly-created *reshut hayachid*, then the act is in fact sequentially ordered: first the *reshut hayachid* came into being, and then the *hanachah* occurred. Under that analysis, one would be liable.

### Unresolved (Teiku)

The *gemara* leaves Rava's question unresolved: *teiku*. However, the framing of the question implies something significant. It appears that if the plank genuinely lands first — if the *reshut hayachid* actually exists, even momentarily, before the second object comes to rest — then liability does attach. One was in control of the entire process; one initiated the throw knowing that the plank would create the *reshut hayachid* and that the object would land within it. The fact that when the act began no *reshut hayachid* yet existed does not automatically exempt, as long as by the time the *hanachah* is completed the *reshut hayachid* is in place. The unresolved question is whether the in-flight separation is sufficient to establish that temporal sequence, or whether the simultaneous nature of the throw collapses the two events into a single undifferentiated act, foreclosing liability.

These questions — of domains coming into existence during the carrying act itself — will continue to be explored in the material ahead.

---

---

# Shabbat 100

## Mayim al Mayim

### Water on Water

The daf opens with a statement of Rava that sets the conceptual framework for much of what follows. *Peshita li*, says Rava — it is obvious to me that *mayim agabi mayim*, water floating on water, is *hainu hanachasan*: that is indeed considered its set location. If one scoops water from the top layer of a pond or well and carries it from a private domain to a public domain, one has performed a proper act of carrying. One has removed the water from the place in which it is *munach* — set, in a fixed location.

This establishes the conceptual axis of the discussion: for carrying on Shabbat to be Biblically prohibited, both the *akira* (removal) and the *hanacha* (placement) must occur at a genuinely fixed, stable location. Something must be taken from a set place and put down in a set way. What follows is a sustained examination of which circumstances qualify as genuinely fixed, and the results are striking.

### Egoz al Mayim

The contrast to water on water is immediate and sharpens the point considerably. *Egoz agabi mayim* — a nut floating on water — is *lav hainu hanachasan*: it is not considered *munach*. If one carries a nut into a *reshut ha-rabim* and sets it down on a pond, or removes a nut from a pond and carries it across a domain boundary or four *amos*, one has performed neither a valid *akira* nor a valid *hanacha*. The nut is not resting on solid ground; it is moving around on the surface of the water and is therefore not in a fixed location.

This is a striking result when placed alongside positions stated elsewhere in the tractate. We have encountered opinions that something passing through the airspace of a *reshut ha-rabim* — *kluta keman shehunacha damya*, "absorbed as if placed" — is considered *munach*; that passing through the interior of a house — *beisa keman demalya dami* — is considered *munach*; that a clump of dates stuck to a wall is considered *munach*. These are all cases of objects in motion or impermanent contact, yet they are treated as having a fixed location. And yet something floating on water is not. Although a date stuck to a wall will eventually fall, at the moment in question it is stable. Something on water, by contrast, is inherently unstable — the water moves, and anything on it partakes of that instability. That basic assumption — that *being on water* disqualifies an object from being considered *munach* — is itself a significant *chidush*, even before the more nuanced sub-cases are examined.

### Egoz Bikli Tzaf

Rava then poses a question about relative location. *Egoz bikli v'kli tzaf agabi mayim mahu*? — what is the law if one places a nut inside a vessel, and that vessel is floating on the water? This is essentially a question about the frame of reference for *munach*.

*Mi amrinan basar egoz azlinan, v'hanyach*? Do we look at the nut relative to itself, and note that its location relative to the dish or the boat is perfectly stable? The nut has not moved relative to the vessel; it is fixed vis-à-vis its immediate container. Or do we say *odilma basar kli azlinan, v'halo nayach*? Do we look at the vessel itself, and since the vessel is not at rest — it too is floating on moving water — the nut is not considered to be in a fixed location either?

This question maps neatly onto broader intuitions about relative location. Anything on earth is fixed relative to some more distant frame of reference. The question is which frame of reference is operative for purposes of *hanacha*. At a certain scale — a vessel the size of a city — one might reasonably argue that the vessel itself defines the environment and the water underneath is irrelevant. But in the case of a nut in a small dish, both can still be manipulated directly, and the question is genuinely open. The *Gemara* leaves it unresolved: *teiku*.

### Shemen al Yayin

The next question picks up on the issue of two distinct liquids — oil floating on wine — and this has a parallel in a debate already recorded in the *Mishnah*. *Machlokes Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri v'Rabbanan*: there is a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the Sages, applied here by the *Gemara*.

The source debate concerns *terumah* and *tum'ah*. If oil is floating on wine and both are *terumah*, and a *t'vul yom* — someone who immersed in a *mikvah* that day and is waiting for nightfall — touches the oil, the question is whether the wine beneath is also rendered *tamei*. A *t'vul yom* has the status of a *sheni*, and touching *terumah* renders it *tamei* as a *shelishi*, a *pasul* that cannot transmit further *tum'ah*. If the oil and wine are a single unit, touching the oil is touching the whole — and the wine is invalidated as well. If they are separate, only the oil is rendered *tamei*, and the wine may still be consumed.

The Rabbis hold *lo pasul ela shemen* — only the oil is invalidated. Oil and wine are distinct; they do not constitute a single liquid unit merely because one floats atop the other. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri disagrees: *shneihem chibbur zeh l'zeh* — they are connected to one another. Since both are liquid, the whole constitutes one unit, and touching any part of it is touching all of it.

Applied to our context: according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, oil on wine is like water on water — it is all one liquid unit, and removing oil from wine counts as removing it from a fixed location, a proper *akira*. According to the Rabbis, the oil on the wine is like the nut on the water — they are separate, the oil is not *munach* in a fixed sense, and one who places or removes it is exempt.

## Bor Reshut HaRabim

### Pit with Mat

Abaye now introduces a series of cases involving a pit in a *reshut ha-rabim*, each of which interrogates how deeply a change within the pit can alter its identity as a *reshut ha-yachid*. The first case: *bor bi-reshut ha-rabim amukah asarah ve-rechevah shmonah* — a pit in the *reshut ha-rabim* that is ten *tefachim* deep and eight *tefachim* wide.
