The ruling of *patur aval assur* applies to a different case, which Rashi describes as the manner in which rabbis wore their shoes: tied in a way that was slightly loose. Such a person might leave the shoes tied and simply kick them on and off without ever undoing the knot — keeping them tied for several days at a stretch, or even longer if they are infrequently worn. While the knot is not truly permanent — eventually one will need to tighten or loosen the straps, particularly in muddy conditions — it is also not undone on a daily basis, and therefore falls into the intermediate category. The ruling of *muttar l'chatchila* applies to the residents of *Mechuza*, who were scrupulous about their appearance and tied their shoes very tightly; such a person must undo the knots each night, and therefore there is no issue whatsoever.

This raises a practical question about *kavvanah* — intention. A knot can only be prohibited at the moment of tying; if one ties a knot intending to undo it that day but then changes one's mind, there is no retroactive violation. The more pressing concern is when a person is semi-aware at the moment of tying that he habitually does not undo the knot for extended periods. For example, one who receives *gelila* on *Shabbos mincha* and ties the *gartel* around the *Sefer Torah* is aware that it will not be untied until Monday — more than a day. This warrants *chumra*. Similarly, one whose *Shabbos* shoes habitually sit tied until the following *Shabbos* would do well to make a practice of untying them *motzei Shabbos*.

### Sandal Scenarios

The parallel resolution for sandals follows a similar structure. The *chayav chatat* ruling applies to *d'toi d'katri ushkhafi* — the sandals of nomadic travelers or merchants, where the shoemaker ties the straps onto the sandal base permanently. The wearers do not detach the straps from the base at all; they merely put the sandal on and off as a unit, with the strap attachment being fixed from the moment of manufacture. This satisfies the *kesher uman* criterion and is truly *kayama*. The *patur aval assur* ruling applies to ordinary people, *b'chumrsa d'katri inhu*, who attach their own straps to the sandal base themselves. While they do reconnect the strap to the base, they do so irregularly — leaving it for a week or a month at a time — and since the attachment is not made by a craftsman, it falls short of biblical liability but remains rabbinically problematic. The *muttar l'chatchila* ruling applies to a sandal shared by two people — not simultaneously, but on a rotating basis. Since two people of different foot sizes must regularly readjust the straps to fit each person, the knot is undone with sufficient frequency that it presents no concern.

### Shared Sandals

The *Gemara* illustrates this last point with a concrete example: *besandal denafki beih bi harei* — a sandal shared by two, worn alternately, requiring regular readjustment of the straps. This is precisely the *muttar* case.

---

## Rav Yehudah's Sandals

### Shared Use Resolution

The *Gemara* proceeds directly to a narrative involving Rav Yehudah, brother of Rav Salla Chasida, who owned a pair of sandals that he and his young child wore on an alternating basis — *zimnin nafik beih ihu, zimnin nafik beih yanukeih* — sometimes he wore them out, sometimes his child did. He came before Abaye to ask what the law was regarding these sandals on *Shabbos*. Abaye's initial response was startling: *chayav chatat* — a full biblical violation. Rav Yehudah was taken aback: he had come not even knowing whether it was rabbinically problematic, and here Abaye was telling him it was a biblical offense. Abaye then asked why he thought it should be permitted. Rav Yehudah explained that since every day, on a regular basis, sometimes he would wear them and sometimes his child would, the straps were constantly being readjusted. Abaye immediately reversed himself: *i hachi, muttar l'chatchila* — if that is the case, it is entirely permitted.

### Abaye's Challenge

Rashi explains why Abaye initially said *chayav chatat*: he had assumed, before hearing the full picture, that the sandal was of the permanently-attached type, perhaps tied with a craftsman's knot, and that there was no regular undoing. Once he understood that the shared use entailed routine readjustment, the ruling shifted completely. The governing principle, restated here clearly according to Rashi: permanent knots are biblical, daily-undone knots are permitted, and those left for a week or more are rabbinically prohibited. The space between a day and a week remains imprecise.

---

## Broken Straps & Vessels

### Yirmiyah/Abbahu

The *Gemara* now shifts to a different category of problem involving sandal straps: what happens when a strap breaks during *Shabbos*. Rav Yirmiyah was walking behind Rabbi Abbahu in a *charmelit* when his sandal strap broke. Tying it back would be at least *asur d'rabbanan*. The problem was that carrying the broken sandal was also rabbinically forbidden in a *charmelit*. Rabbi Abbahu's solution: find a moist reed or similar vegetation — something edible by animals, already available on the ground, and therefore not *muktzeh* — and use it to temporarily bind the sandal. Since it is entirely improvised and everyone understands it will be replaced *motzei Shabbos*, it has no character of permanence whatsoever.

### Abaye/Yosef

A parallel case involved Abaye, who was standing before Rav Yosef when his sandal strap broke — this time in a *chatzer*, a courtyard, so there was no carrying problem. Rav Yosef said: *shevukia* — just leave it. Since it is in a protected courtyard, we can retrieve it after *Shabbos*. Abaye pressed: why is this case different from the Rav Yirmiyah case, where a workaround was found? Rav Yosef's response implied that the sandal had become *muktzeh*. Abaye challenged this: *amana hu* — it is still a vessel, a *kli*, and should not be *muktzeh*. The *Gemara* notes an important distinction: in the Rav Yirmiyah case, the only problem was carrying in a *charmelit*; there was no claim that the sandal had lost its vessel status. Here, by contrast, the instruction to simply leave it implies that Rav Yosef viewed the sandal as having lost its *kli* status and become *muktzeh*.

### Reversing Sandal

Abaye proposed a resolution: *hafichna lah miyamina l'smola* — one can reverse the sandal from right to left. Rashi explains that sandals of this period had two straps: one on the instep (inner) and one on the outer edge. If the outer strap broke, the sandal was considered unusable for its own foot, because people would not bother to repair a broken outer strap — it was too visible and unsightly. Since no one would fix it, it was effectively discarded, making it *muktzeh*. However, Abaye argued that since sandals of the period were made on a relatively flat, non-contoured base — not shaped to a specific foot — one could switch the sandal from right to left. What had been the outer strap would now become the inner strap, and the sandal would remain functional. As long as this salvage was possible, the sandal retained its *kli* status and should not be *muktzeh*.

The *Gemara* notes that the broader question of *shivrei keilim* — the general *muktzeh* status of broken vessels — applies here, though the discussion focuses specifically on the sandal case rather than the general principle.

---

## Inner vs. Outer Strap

### Halakha Position

The *Gemara* now turns to the question of which position we follow. The context is set by a citation of Rabbi Yochanan, who will shortly weigh in. The statement that follows — *mideka matir Rabbi Yochanan aliba d'Rabbi Yehuda, shma mina halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* — introduces a principle: since Rabbi Yochanan goes to the trouble of explaining and defending Rabbi Yehudah's position, we infer that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehudah. This has significant consequences for the *muktzeh* status of a sandal with a broken outer strap.

### Baraita: Sandal Damage

A *baraita* from *Keilim* is cited: *sandal shenipsaku shtei oznav o shtei tartsiyotav* — if a sandal's two ear-flaps or both strap-holders break, or if the entire base is removed, it becomes *tahor*, meaning it has lost its vessel status. If only one of the flaps or strap-connectors breaks, or only a majority of the base remains intact, it remains *tamei* — it is still a vessel. The underlying logic is familiar: *tumah* and vessel-status are coextensive. When a vessel completely loses its functional identity, the *tumah* departs and it becomes *tahor*. When enough integrity remains to still be considered a functional item, *tumah* persists.

### Rabbi Yehudah Position

Into this framework, Rabbi Yehudah introduces a sharper distinction: *nifska pnimis, tamei* — if the inner strap broke, the sandal remains *tamei*, because it is still usable and one would fix the inner strap. *Hachitzona, tahor* — if the outer strap broke, even though only one strap is affected, it is *tahor*, because one would not bother to repair an unsightly broken outer strap. The sandal has effectively been abandoned.

The Rabbis disagree: even a broken outer strap does not disqualify the sandal as a vessel. Only if both straps break simultaneously does it lose its status. One might reverse the sandal from right to left, so even a broken outer strap does not render it nonfunctional.

The halakhic stakes are immediate: if we follow Rabbi Yehudah, a sandal with a broken outer strap is not a *kli* and is therefore *muktzeh* on *Shabbos*. If we follow the Rabbis, it retains *kli* status and may be handled.

Rabbi Yochanan enters the picture with a sweeping statement: *kemachlokes le'inyan tumah, kach machlokes le'inyan Shabbos* — the same dispute about when the sandal loses vessel-status for *tumah* applies identically to *Shabbos*, determining when it becomes *muktzeh*. However — and this is striking — *aval lo le'inyan chalitzah*. When it comes to *chalitzah*, the dispute does not apply in the same way.

The *Gemara* probes this carefully. According to the Rabbis, a sandal with one broken strap (even outer) retains vessel status for *tumah* and *Shabbos*. Why, then, would they say it is disqualified for *chalitzah*? After all, we know from elsewhere that even a left shoe used on the right foot is valid for *chalitzah* — the standards for *chalitzah* are if anything lower, not higher. It would be incoherent for the Rabbis to be more lenient for *tumah* and *Shabbos* than for *chalitzah*.

The *Gemara* then examines the other side: according to Rabbi Yehudah, a sandal with a broken outer strap is not a vessel for *tumah* or *Shabbos*. But could Rabbi Yehudah nonetheless say it qualifies for *chalitzah*, invoking the principle that a left shoe on the right foot works? The *Gemara* rejects this: *heicha delemilsiah lav mana hu* — the principle of using a left shoe on the right foot applies only when the sandal is genuinely a complete shoe for its own purpose. Here, since Rabbi Yehudah holds that a sandal with a broken outer strap is not even a shoe for ordinary use on its proper foot, there is no basis to invoke the left-foot dispensation for *chalitzah*.

The *Gemara*'s resolution is therefore: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about *chalitzah* is not saying the parties converge there while diverging elsewhere. Rather, they dispute *chalitzah* in precisely the same way they dispute *tumah* and *Shabbos*. What his statement teaches is the following principle: the rule that a left shoe on the right foot is valid for *chalitzah* applies only when that shoe is a genuine, complete shoe for its own left foot. A shoe that has lost its vessel status entirely — as Rabbi Yehudah maintains when the outer strap breaks — is disqualified for *chalitzah* as well.

---

## Yochanan/Mishna Tension

### Yochanan Plain Mishna

Rabbi Yochanan's statement that *halacha* follows a *stam mishna* — an unattributed *mishnah* — creates a further difficulty. The inference that Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabbi Yehudah rests on the fact that he elaborated and defended Rabbi Yehudah's position. Since Rabbi Yochanan also holds that we follow the *stam mishna* as a general principle, the *Gemara* asks whether there is a *stam mishna* that contradicts this.

### Problem Stated

There is. The *mishnah* in *Keilim* states: *sandal shenipseka achas me'aznav vetikna, tamei midras* — if one of the sandal's flaps breaks and is repaired, it remains *tamei midras*. The *Gemara* initially reads this as meaning that the sandal retains vessel status whenever only one strap breaks, regardless of whether it is the inner or outer one. If so, this *stam mishna* contradicts Rabbi Yehudah's view that a broken outer strap is sufficient to disqualify the sandal. The *Gemara* tries to read the *mishna* as referring only to the inner strap: *penimis davka* — only the inner strap case yields *tamei*. But then the objection arises: if that is the intent, why does the *mishna* not simply say so? Why draw the distinction at "one strap versus two straps" rather than at "inner versus outer"?

The *mishnah* continues: *nipseka hashniya vetikna, tahor min hamidras aval tamei maga midras* — if the second strap broke (and was repaired), the sandal is *tahor* from *midras* but remains *tamei maga midras*, as something that had contact with a *midras* object. This line requires careful unpacking. When the sandal bore only one broken strap (the inner one, on the Gemara's reading), it remained *tamei midras* — fully an *av hatumah*. Now both straps have broken and been repaired, and the *Gemara* asks: why is it now *tahor midras*? The sandal never ceased being a shoe — each strap was repaired immediately when it broke. Yet its *midras* status was lost.

Rashi offers two readings. In the first, the sandal genuinely stopped being a shoe when both straps were broken simultaneously enough to alter its identity — and since it briefly became a non-shoe (perhaps usable for another purpose, like a backscratcher), it could no longer function as a *midras* vessel. Yet because it was, at that transitional moment, in a sense "touching itself" as it shifted from one vessel-identity to another, it retains *tumah* as *maga midras* — the *tumah* of having had contact with a *midras* object. This is an unusual idea: an object that touched itself. *Tosafos* flags the conceptual difficulty involved. In Rashi's second reading, the sandal never actually stopped being a shoe — each strap was fixed before the next broke — but since by the end of the process both straps have been replaced entirely, it now has the identity of a *new* shoe. The new shoe never received *midras tumah* itself, but it was in contact with the old shoe that bore that *tumah*, and so it is *tamei maga midras*.

This second reading of Rashi introduces the critical concept: replacing all component parts, even sequentially, creates a new identity, even if there was never a moment at which the object ceased to function.

### Four-Strap Resolution

Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef offers a resolution to the contradiction between Rabbi Yochanan's apparent endorsement of Rabbi Yehudah's view and the *stam mishna*: *tehei mishnasenu b'sandal she'yesh lo arba oznayim v'arba tasiyoseihen* — interpret the *stam mishna* as dealing with a sandal that has four flaps and four strap-holders, two on each side. In such a case, breaking "one strap" means breaking one of the outer straps, leaving the second outer strap still intact. Since one outer strap remains, the sandal does not yet lose vessel status even according to Rabbi Yehudah. Breaking "the second strap" means breaking the remaining outer strap — at which point, under Rabbi Yehudah's view, the sandal becomes *tahor*. This reading harmonizes the *stam mishna* with Rabbi Yehudah's position and preserves Rabbi Yochanan's consistency.

The *Gemara* acknowledges that this is a strained resolution — it posits an unusual four-strap sandal that is not the standard case — but accepts it as preferable to allowing Rabbi Yochanan's positions to contradict one another: *shelo lishbor devarav shel Rabbi Yochanan*. It is worth noting the structure of the *Gemara*'s reasoning here. Rabbi Yochanan never explicitly stated he ruled like Rabbi Yehudah; the inference was drawn from the fact that he elaborated Rabbi Yehudah's position. Nor did Rabbi Yochanan ever explicitly invoke the *stam mishna* in this context — the *Gemara* applies his general principle. The resulting tension is therefore built on two layers of inference, yet the *Gemara* treats it as a genuine contradiction requiring resolution.

### Rabin Alternative

When Ravin came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he brought a different tradition: *amar Rav Chanina bar Abba amar Rav, halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* — Rav ruled like Rabbi Yehudah. *Rabbi Yochanan*, however, did not. This resolves everything cleanly: Rabbi Yochanan does not rule like Rabbi Yehudah, and therefore his endorsement of the *stam mishna* — which holds that even a broken outer strap does not disqualify the sandal — is perfectly consistent. The earlier inference that Rabbi Yochanan ruled like Rabbi Yehudah was mistaken, or at least disputed. The *Gemara* responds that there is now a debate among *amoraim* about what Rabbi Yochanan's actual position was: *amorai ninhu ve'aliba d'Rabbi Yehuda* — there are two versions of how Rabbi Yochanan related to Rabbi Yehudah's view.

---

## Ship of Theseus

### Chizkiyah Question

The *Gemara* now presents a question posed by Chizkiyah that has a philosophical dimension reaching far beyond the immediate halakhic context. The *Gemara* had already established in another context that ordinary household vessels lose their *tumah* status only when they develop a hole large enough to allow a pomegranate to pass through — any smaller hole is not enough to render them nonfunctional. Chizkiyah asks: what if a vessel sustained a series of small holes, each no larger than an olive — below the threshold — and each was filled in (with putty or a similar material) before the next appeared, until the cumulative area of all the holes filled over time would, had they all been open simultaneously, equal a pomegranate-sized opening? At no single moment did the vessel have a disqualifying hole. Does it nonetheless lose its *tumah* status?

### New Faces/Identity

Rabbi Yochanan responds by invoking the sandal case: *rebbi, shnisah lanu* — you yourself taught us this. The *mishnah* states that if the first strap of a sandal broke and was repaired, the sandal remains *tamei midras*. If the second strap then broke and was also repaired, the sandal is *tahor midras* but *tamei maga midras*. The question that arises is why: the sandal never stopped being a shoe, so why does it lose its *midras* status? Rabbi Yochanan's answer, attributed here as something Chizkiyah himself had previously taught: *panim chadashos ba'u l'chan* — new faces have come here. Since every critical component has been replaced — even though sequentially — a new identity has been created. Although the object never ceased to exist as a functional vessel, the totality of replacement amounts to a new entity. The same principle answers Chizkiyah's question: if enough of the vessel's material has been removed and replaced that had all of it been gone at once the vessel would have lost its identity, then the sequential replacement constitutes the arrival of *panim chadashos*, a new identity.

### Both Straps New Shoe

The *Gemara* thus articulates a clear rule: a sandal in which both straps have been replaced, even one at a time, is no longer the original sandal. It is halakhically a new shoe. It does not carry the old *midras tumah*, though it is *tamei maga midras* because the new shoe was formed out of, or in contact with, the old one. The parallel for vessels: once enough material has been replaced that the original integrity has been wholly reconstituted with new components, the object has a new identity for purposes of *tumah*.

### Praise & Yeridat Drot

The response to Rabbi Yochanan's elegant resolution is extraordinary. Chizkiyah exclaims: *lais dain bar inash* — this is no ordinary human being, this is an angel. An alternate tradition says: *k'gon dain bar inash* — this is what it means to truly be a human being. From this praise, the *Gemara* transitions to a famous statement attributed to Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rava: *im rishonim bnei malachim, anu bnei anashim; v'im rishonim bnei anashim, anu kachamorim* — if the earlier ones were like angels, we are merely humans; if the earlier ones were human, we are like donkeys. And not like the distinguished donkeys of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa or Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, whose animals refused to eat food that was not theirs — but like ordinary donkeys.

### Yeridat HaDorot

This statement opens onto a much larger theological and intellectual question: the doctrine of *yeridat hadorot*, the decline of the generations. The idea holds that every successive generation stands on a lower spiritual and intellectual *madregah* than its predecessors, moving ever further from *Har Sinai*. There is no question that profound veneration of earlier *gedolim* is appropriate. The question is whether one must subscribe to a particular ideological commitment that later generations are simply nothing compared to earlier ones — and what the consequences of that commitment are.

A useful entry point into this debate is the book by Menachem Kellner, *Maimonides and the Descent of the Generations*, which argues that *yeridat hadorot* — though promoted by certain *Geonim* — was by no means a universally held or ideologically central doctrine. The Rambam, notably, never quotes it and in certain domains, particularly science, explicitly acknowledges that *Chazal* were limited by the knowledge available in their time and that later generations have made advances. This is not a blanket rejection of *Chazal*'s authority, but it is a recognition that the doctrine of generational decline does not have to be foundational.

The deeper question, as Kellner frames it, is: what is the basis of the authority of *Torah She-ba'al Peh*? If one holds that the authority of *Chazal* derives from the fact that they were the most brilliant and holy human beings who ever lived, then any challenge to their perfection becomes destabilizing — contradictions with science must be deflected, later authorities can never genuinely question earlier ones, and the entire enterprise risks becoming more like worship than scholarship. But there is another basis for the authority of *Torah She-ba'al Peh*: the Torah itself empowers *Beit Din*, and authority resides in the institution that is duly constituted and recognized. Just as the authority of a supreme court derives from the legitimacy of the institution rather than from the claim that its members were the greatest jurists who ever lived, so too the authority of the *Gemara* and of *Chazal* can rest on institutional empowerment rather than on the premise of irreversible generational decline. On this view, it is entirely possible to maintain full commitment to *Torah She-ba'al Peh* while engaging honestly with the historical and intellectual record, without requiring the past to be beyond scrutiny.

---

## More Permitted Knots

### Wine/Oil Flasks

The *mishnah* continues with additional examples of permitted knots. *Nodot yayin v'shemen* — leather flasks or pouches containing wine or oil — were typically cinched at the neck with a rope. The *Gemara* asks: is it not self-evident that this is permitted? The novelty, again, is a flask with two handles or ears. One might think that since it is possible to pour from the flask by loosening only one side of the cinching rope, a person might leave the other side tied and never undo the full knot. The *Gemara* teaches that we are not concerned about this; the general practice is to undo both sides, and occasional shortcuts do not transform the knot into a *kesher shel kayama*.

### Meat Pot

*Kdeirah shel basar* — a pot of meat — was sealed with a leather cover tied down. The *Gemara* again asks: obvious, is it not? The novelty involves a pot with a *shlucha* — some kind of spout. One might suppose that since one could pour the contents out through the spout without removing the cover, the tied cover might be left in place. The *Gemara* teaches that we are not concerned: ordinarily the cover is opened regularly, and the occasional possibility of using the spout does not change the character of the knot.

### Animal Pen Rope

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states that one may tie a rope across the entrance of an animal pen. Since animals go in and out of the pen daily, the rope must be untied and retied constantly, and it could never take on a character of permanence. Again the *Gemara* asks: is this not obvious? The novelty is that there are two knots involved — either two separate ropes, one above and one below, or a single rope tied at both ends to the posts. One might think that at least one of the knots would be left in place — if there are two ropes, one might be left; if the rope is tied on both ends, one end might remain knotted. The *Gemara* teaches that we are not concerned: the routine of daily animal management ensures both knots are regularly undone.

### Halakha Rule

The *Gemara* then records: *amar Rav Yosef amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel, halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, meaning that tying such a rope before an animal pen is permitted.

### Abaye/Yosef Debate

Abaye objects to Rav Yosef's formulation: *halacha miklal d'pligi?* — does saying "*halacha* follows him" not imply that there were others who disputed him? Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov was simply adding another example of a permitted knot, with no dispute involved. Rav Yosef replies: *mai nafka lach mina?* — what practical difference does it make? If the *halacha* is as he says, whether or not anyone disputed him is irrelevant. Abaye insists: *gemara gemar, zimereta hi?* — we have a tradition, do you want to reduce it to a mere tune? It matters to understand the full contours of the debate, what the underlying parameters were, and what considerations drove different positions. Even when the *halacha l'maaseh* is settled, understanding the intellectual structure of the disagreement provides insight that simple rule-recitation cannot.

---

---

# Shabbat 113

## Kesher Uman & Weaver's R…

### Bucket & Belt

The daf opens with a new *mishnah* that continues the theme of knots on *Shabbos*. By way of background: we had established that knots which are completely permanent — or, according to the Rambam, a combination of *kesher uman* (a professional knot) and permanence — are biblically forbidden. Knots lacking both of those qualities are permitted, and those occupying an intermediate position are rabbinically forbidden.

The *mishnah* before us introduces a concrete case: *koshin dli bipaskia* — one may tie a bucket to the side of a well using a *paskia*, a belt, rather than a rope. The reason is evident: no one leaves his belt tied to a well. Whatever the objective strength of the knot may be, the subjective and contextual reality is that it will be undone very shortly. This is a significant principle — the nature of the knot is assessed not solely by its physical characteristics but also by the intent and circumstances of the one tying it. However, *aval lo b'chevel* — one may not use a rope, since a rope would normally be left there and would therefore constitute at minimum a rabbinically forbidden knot, and potentially a biblical one depending on its permanence and professional character.

### Rebbe Yehuda's Principle

*Rebbe Yehuda matir* — Rabbi Yehuda rules permissively even with a rope. He then states a general principle: *kol kesher she'eino shel kayama ein chayavin alav* — any knot that is not permanent, one is not liable for. *Tosafot* raises a pointed question: haven't we already established that non-permanent knots are not a problem? And further, Rabbi Yehuda is not merely exempting after the fact — he is permitting the tying *l'chatchila* to begin with. *Tosafot* resolves this by arguing that Rabbi Yehuda's general principle is not actually connected to the preceding line about the bucket at all. It loops back to clarify the very first *mishnah* in this section regarding which knots incur liability — it is a separate and independent statement, not a continuation of the bucket discussion.

### Chevel D'Gardi

The *Gemara* asks: *chevel d'mai* — what type of rope does Rabbi Yehuda permit when tying the bucket to the well? If it is an ordinary rope — *chevel d'alma* — surely that is a *kesher shel kayama*, a permanent knot, and how could Rabbi Yehuda permit it? The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ela chevel d'garde* — it must be referring to a weaver's rope. This is something that closely resembles, or may even be identical in appearance to, a regular rope, but which belongs to a weaver and is used in some professional capacity — perhaps worn as a sash or used in his craft. Come *motzaei Shabbos*, the weaver will need it back; he will not simply leave it attached to the well. The practical temporariness is clear in context even if the object looks indistinguishable from an ordinary rope.

### Mizchilaf/Confusion

With this established, the *Gemara* reframes the entire dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda. The Rabbis hold that we are concerned: *gazrinan chevel d'garde atu chevel d'alma* — we worry that permitting a weaver's rope will lead people to use an ordinary rope, since they look alike. Rabbi Yehuda holds *lo gazrinan* — he is not concerned that people will make this mistake. This is all an inference of the *Gemara*, not explicit in the *mishnah*, but the *Gemara* requires it to explain how Rabbi Yehuda could sanction what he does.

### Slipknot Debate

The *Gemara* now introduces a *baraita* that creates a difficulty: *chevel dli shenifsak* — if the bucket's rope broke and you wish to reconnect the two ends, what do you do? The Rabbis say: *lo yikshrenu ela ovno* — don't tie a proper knot; rather, make a slipknot (*aniva*). Rabbi Yehuda says: you may wrap a belt or sash around it — *korech alav punda o paskia* — provided you do not make a bow. The *Gemara* identifies this as a contradiction: *kashya de'Rebbe Yehuda ad'Rebbe Yehuda, kashya de'Rabbanan ad'Rabbanan*.

The problem, as the *Gemara* unpacks it, is that everyone would presumably agree in principle that a *slipknot* is perfectly fine — it is thoroughly temporary and easy to undo. The assumed structure of the debate was that the Rabbis are concerned about visual confusion (*mizchilaf*) while Rabbi Yehuda is not. Yet here the positions appear reversed: the Rabbis permit the slipknot while Rabbi Yehuda disallows it. Why?

### Rope vs. Slipknot

The *Gemara* resolves the Rabbis' apparent contradiction cleanly: *chevel be'chevel michlaf* — one rope looks like another rope, so the Rabbis rightly worry about confusion in the bucket case. *Aniva be'kshira lo michlafa* — but a slipknot is obviously different from a regular knot; no one will confuse the two. Hence the Rabbis permit a slipknot and their position is consistent.

### Slipknot Permanence

For Rabbi Yehuda, the resolution is more substantive. The *Gemara* says: *hasam lo mishum de'michlafa aniva be'kshira* — Rabbi Yehuda is not concerned that the slipknot will be confused with a permanent knot. That is not his reason for prohibiting it. *Ela aniva gufa kshira hi* — rather, Rabbi Yehuda holds that a slipknot is itself a genuine knot. Even though it can be undone easily, it can remain in place for a very long time. The ease of untying does not determine whether something qualifies as a knot; durability of result does. This is a meaningful principled disagreement about what constitutes a *kesher shel kayama*.

It is worth noting the connection to the earlier *mishnah* where Rabbi Meir held that if a knot can be undone with one hand it is not a problem. One reading of the *Gemara* there was that Rabbi Meir would permit even a well-tied slipknot if it could be undone one-handed — setting up a direct *bar plugta* between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on exactly this question. The practical *halacha* is that a slipknot is not problematic, but the *Gemara*'s analysis makes clear that the issue is not merely one of confusion — it may independently implicate the question of permanence, even for an easily-released knot.

---

## Practical Examples

### Cow & Trough

The *Gemara* cites a ruling in the name of Rav (via Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi): *mevi adam chevel mitoch beiso v'koshro b'parah u'va'eivus* — a person may bring a rope from his own home on *Shabbos* and tie it to his cow on one end and to the feeding trough on the other. The assumption is that since the cow needs to be released, both ends will eventually be untied, and there is no concern of a permanent knot.

### One vs. Both Ends

Rav Acha Aricha (also identified as Rabbi Acha bar Pappa) challenges this from a *baraita*: if the rope on the trough is already tied there, one may tie the other end to the cow, and vice versa — but *u'vilvad shelo yavi chevel mitoch beiso v'yikshor b'parah u'va'eivus* — one may not bring a new rope from home and tie *both* ends fresh. The concern is that when you are done, you might untie only one end, leaving the other as a permanent knot. This directly contradicts Rav's ruling.

Rav Abba resolves the tension: *hasam chevel d'alma* — the *baraita* is discussing an ordinary rope, for which the concern about leaving one end attached is real. *Hacha chevel d'garde* — Rav's ruling refers to a weaver's rope, which, as established in the *mishnah*, will not be left in place because it is needed for the weaver's professional use. The parallel with the bucket case is exact.

### Weavers' Muktzeh

The *Gemara* shifts to a related topic. Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules: *kol k'lei kivoi mutar l'taltalo b'Shabbos* — all of the weavers' vessels (*keilei kivoi*) are permitted to be carried on *Shabbos*. Since we have been discussing the weaver's rope, the *Gemara* now addresses the *muktzah* status of the various implements of weaving more broadly. These are tools used for *melachah* — they are *melachto l'issur* — yet as with any *k'lei she'melachto l'issur*, they may be moved *l'tzorech gufo o l'tzorech mekomo*: for their own use or to free up the space they occupy. The only prohibited reason to move such an item is to protect it from damage — *me'chamah l'tzel*.

The concern the *Gemara* raises goes beyond *melachto l'issur*: perhaps these implements are so valuable or delicate that one is never willing to let anyone touch or handle them — which would make them *muktzah machmas chisron kis*, a far more stringent category that cannot be moved for any purpose. The ruling is that this concern does not apply; the weavers' implements are movable.

### Loom Beams

The *Gemara* records a question posed to Rav Yehuda: *koved elyon v'koved tachton mahu* — what about the upper and lower beams of the loom? These are substantial structural components, not small portable instruments — might they be *muktzah machmas chisron kis*? Rav Yehuda vacillated: *im v'lav v'rafya b'yadei* — he gave no firm answer. The question was subsequently resolved by a tradition from Rav Nachman citing Shmuel: the weavers' implements are indeed permitted to carry, *afilu koved elyon v'koved tachton* — even the upper and lower horizontal beams. However, *aval lo es ha'amudim* — not the vertical posts, which are set into the ground.

### Holes & Posts

Rava asks Rav Nachman: *mai shna amudim delo* — what distinguishes the vertical posts that they cannot be moved? If it is because removing them from the ground creates a hole — *mishum gumot* — that should not be a concern, since the holes are already there and any deepening of them is incidental (*gumot mimeila ka'avin*). The *Gemara* supports this from the *mishnah* about burying turnips and radishes beneath a vine: one may remove them on *Shabbos*, even though doing so disturbs the earth, because the displacement of dirt is merely incidental. Surely the same principle applies here?

The *Gemara* distinguishes: *b'sadeh lo asu l'ashvuyei gumos* — in a field, no one goes to fill in a hole in the ground. *Hacha b'bayis, asu l'ashvuyei gumos* — inside a house, once you have an exposed hole in the floor, you are likely to come and smooth it over. That act of filling and smoothing would constitute a form of *boneh*, at least rabbinically. The prohibition on moving the vertical posts is therefore not a *muktzah* concern at all — it is a concern that removing them will lead to a forbidden act of building.

The parallel question posed by Rabbi Yochanan to Rabbi Yehuda bar Livai receives the same substantive answer: the upper and lower horizontal beams may not be moved, *l'fi she'ein nitlin* — because they are simply not moved. Rashi explains this to mean that since these items are never ordinarily relocated, they attain the status of *muktzah machmas chisron kis* — items so fixed in place by the owner's intention that they are treated as genuinely set aside.

---

## Folding & Hachana

### Folding Clothes

The *Gemara* now transitions to a new *mishnah*: *mekaplin es hakelim* — one may fold garments on *Shabbos*, even four or five times. One may also prepare the beds — spread out the sheets — *milelei Shabbos l'Shabbos*, from Friday night for the sake of *Shabbos* itself, meaning one is going to sleep in that bed on *Shabbos*. But *aval lo mi-Shabbos l'motzaei Shabbos* — one may not make the bed on *Shabbos* for Saturday night. The prohibition here is not connected to any specific *melachah* but to a distinct concern: *hachana*, preparing on one sacred day for the needs of a subsequent day or weekday.

### Yom Kippur Cases

Rabbi Yishmael adds: *mekaplin es hakelim u-matzi'in es hamitot mi-Yom Kippur l'Shabbos* — one may fold garments and prepare beds from *Yom Kippur* for *Shabbos*, in the case where *Yom Kippur* falls on a Friday. Since *Yom Kippur* is of somewhat lesser sanctity relative to *Shabbos*, it can serve *Shabbos* in this way. The *mishnah* also addresses the related case of *chelvei Shabbos*: if *Yom Kippur* falls on a Sunday, the fats of *Shabbos* offerings may be burned on *Yom Kippur* — again, the lesser-sanctified day serves the greater. But the fats of *Yom Kippur* offerings cannot be burned on *Shabbos*, since *Shabbos* does not serve *Yom Kippur*. Rabbi Akiva takes the most restrictive position: neither day's offerings may be processed on the other day — each day stands entirely on its own.

### Hachana Defined

The concern underlying the prohibition on folding garments for after *Shabbos* or making beds for *motzaei Shabbos* is what we call *hachana* — preparation from one day for the next. It is worth noting that some *Rishonim* do not frame the *issur* primarily as *hachana* but rather as *tore'ach b'Shabbos l'tzorech chol* — expending effort on *Shabbos* for weekday purposes. This reframing carries real practical implications. The question of whether one may study on *Shabbos* for an exam on Sunday, for instance, turns partly on which formulation one accepts.

### Intent & Context

A critical qualification is that the prohibition applies only when the action is genuinely done for tomorrow's benefit. Very often something done on *Shabbos* has the incidental effect of making things ready for *motzaei Shabbos*, but that is not the actual motivation. A common example: after *seudah shelishit*, well before *tzeit hakochavim*, clearing the table and removing the crumbs is not *hachana* for *motzaei Shabbos*. The motivation is simply that one does not want a messy room right now. The same logic applies to rinsing a bottle and placing it in recycling — one is not preparing for *motzaei Shabbos*; that is simply how one properly puts things away. The *Mishna Berura* and a growing number of contemporary *poskim* affirm this clearly.

Applying the same principle to folding: when one folds one's garments so that they do not become wrinkled — which is simply the way one treats clothing well — that is not *hachana*; it is attending to the garment for its own sake. The *Aruch HaShulchan* makes this point explicitly, as we will see. Similarly, carrying one's *tallis* home from *shul* after *Shabbos* davening is not *hachana l'machar* — one wants one's *tallis* at home, not left in *shul* where it might be lost or misplaced. The fact that it will then be available for next *Shabbos* does not transform the act into preparation for tomorrow.

---

## Folding & Tikun

### Folding Conditions

The *Gemara* introduces a significant additional restriction on folding that operates independently of the *hachana* concern. The school of Rabbi Yannai taught: *lo shanu ela b'adam echad* — folding is permitted only when done by a single person. With two people folding together — *b'shnei bnei adam lo* — it is forbidden. Furthermore, even with one person: *lo amran ela b'chadashim* — only new garments. Old garments, which are more creased and appear to require greater attention, are forbidden. And even new garments: *lo amran ela b'levanim* — only white ones. Colored garments are also forbidden. And even one person folding new white garments: *lo amran ela she'ein lo lehachalif* — only if one has no other garment available. If one has another garment to change into, the folding is forbidden because then one is plainly not folding for current use but for tomorrow — reverting to the *hachana* problem.

### Nireh Kemetaken

The reason for all these restrictions is stated by Rashi: *keshehem mekapplin otan mafashtin kimteihem venireh kemetakenin* — when garments are folded precisely, one smooths out the wrinkles, and this looks like one is fixing the garment, improving it, making it as good as new. The paradigmatic image is someone pressing their trousers precisely along the crease, smoothing everything perfectly — that is not merely putting a garment away, it is *nireh kemetaken*, it appears like a repair. The conditions enumerated — one person, new, white, no alternative — represent the cumulative threshold below which this appearance of fixing does not arise.

### No Alternative

The final condition — that there be no other garment available — works on two levels. First, if one has a different garment to wear for the rest of *Shabbos*, then one has no need for the folded garment today at all, which means the folding is inherently for tomorrow, raising the *hachana* problem once again. Second, the availability of an alternative also amplifies the appearance of *tikun*, since one is clearly investing care and effort in a garment for future use rather than immediate need.

### Tallit Practice

In practice, one can observe in many *shuls* a range of customs regarding *tallis* folding. Some people fold their *tallis* inside out — reversing the natural crease — precisely on account of this *Gemara*. Others simply roll it up rather than fold it. These practices reflect a concern about *nireh kemetaken*.

### Aruch HaShulchan View

The *Aruch HaShulchan*, however, takes a considerably more lenient position. He argues that this *Gemara* addresses a very specific and exacting type of folding — something akin to pressing a garment's crease with great precision, repeatedly, so that the crease becomes sharply defined. That is *nireh kemetaken*. Ordinary folding along the garment's natural folds, done simply to keep it from wrinkling, is not subject to this concern at all — it is merely how one properly stores a garment. Given this understanding, normal folding of a *tallis* on its natural folds presents no issue.

---

## Kavod Shabbat

### Shabbat Clothes

Rav Huna rules: *im yesh lo lehachalif yachalif* — if one has garments to change into, he should change into them for *Shabbos*. One is obligated to wear special *Shabbos* garments. This flows naturally from the prior discussion of folding: if one has a second set of clothes, one does not even need to fold the current ones — one changes into something designated for *Shabbos*.

### Lowering Hem

But what if one has no special *Shabbos* garments? Rav Huna continues: *yeshalshel bevagdav* — one should lower the hem of one's garment. In the world of the *Gemara*, the hem of working clothes was typically held up for ease of movement. Lowering it to near the ground was a mark of leisure or wealth — one who did not need to run about or labor. Even if one's garment is the same weekday garment, adjusting the hem signals that today is different; it is a day of rest and dignity. Rav Safra objects: *veha mitchazi keramut rucha* — doesn't this look arrogant, like one of the wealthy strutting about? The *Gemara* answers: *keivan dechol yoma lo ka'avid veha'idna hu deka'avid lo mitchazi keramut rucha* — since one does not normally do this and does it only now for *Shabbos*, it does not read as arrogance but as honor for the day.

### Vekibadto Drasha

The *Gemara* now expounds the verse from Yeshayahu: *vechibadto me'asot derachecha* — you shall honor it (*Shabbos*) by refraining from your normal ways. *V'chibadto* — you honor it: *shelo yehei malbushecha shel Shabbos kemalbushecha shel chol* — your *Shabbos* clothing should not be the same as your weekday clothing. The proof from practice: Rabbi Yochanan called his garments *mechabduyotai* — the things that give him honor. Clothing is how one expresses respect, for oneself and for the environment one inhabits. On *Shabbos*, the way one dresses is part of how one honors the day itself.

This raises an interesting tension for those who wear formal attire every weekday — suit and tie daily — since that makes it difficult to have distinctive *Shabbos* garments. One practical resolution is to reserve one's finest suits exclusively for *Shabbos*, or to wear formal items on *Shabbos* — such as French-cuff shirts — that one intentionally avoids on weekdays. The goal is differentiation, not merely formality.

### Gassah Walking

The *Gemara* continues with the verse: *shelo yehei hiluchecha shel Shabbos ke'hiluchecha shel chol* — your walking on *Shabbos* should not be like your walking on the weekday. What does this mean practically? The *Gemara* answers with a ruling from Rav Huna citing Rav: if one is walking on *Shabbos* and encounters a stream, *im yachol l'haniach raglo rishona kodem she'te'aker shniyah* — if one can step across such that the second foot lands on the far bank before the first foot is lifted off the ground, it is permitted. If not, it is forbidden — since jumping or stretching dramatically is not the composed manner of *Shabbos* walking. Rava objects: must one then walk all the way around? That requires more effort. And if one wades through, one risks getting one's garments wet and then wringing them out. The *Gemara* concedes: *keivan d'lo efshar shapir dami* — when there is no practical alternative, it is fine.

### Cheftzei Shamayim

The verse continues: *mimtzo cheftzecha* — from pursuing your desires. *Cheftzecha asurin* — your personal pursuits are forbidden. *Cheftzei Shamayim mutarin* — but pursuits for the sake of Heaven are permitted. This is the source for the well-known ruling that one may make announcements after *davening* for communal and religious purposes — those fall under *cheftzei Shamayim*. Similarly, one may speak about hiring a teacher for one's children — *l'tzorech mitzvah* — even though it involves planning for weekday activity, because it is a divine purpose.

### Speech Rules

The final clause: *v'daber davar — shelo yehei diburcha shel Shabbos k'diburcha shel chol* — your speech on *Shabbos* should not be like your speech on the weekday. Rashi explains this as referring to business talk, market prices, financial accounting — the stuff of weekday conversation. This goes beyond the *mimtzo cheftzecha* prohibition, which concerns actually pursuing one's affairs; here we are told that even idle conversation about such matters — the kind of *shmoozing* one does about business without actively planning anything — is also inappropriate on *Shabbos*. *Tosafot* raises this distinction and cites Rabbeinu Tam, who notes the redundancy if *dover davar* merely repeats what *mimtzo cheftzecha* already covers.

*Tosafot* then cites a remarkable *Yerushalmi* in the name of Rabbeinu Tam: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai had an elderly mother who talked a great deal on *Shabbos*. He said to her, "Mother, it is *Shabbos*," and she fell silent. The implication is that one simply should not be as generally talkative on *Shabbos* as on the weekday — a more sweeping disposition of quiet and restraint. The *Yerushalmi* also notes that even greeting one another on *Shabbos* required some leniency to be permitted, suggesting that there was a genuine sense among some that *Shabbos* was characterized by a quality of stillness. Nevertheless, the mainstream position — reflected in Rashi — focuses on content (business talk, planning, weekday pursuits) rather than on quantity of speech generally.

One final distinction: *dibur assur, hirhur muttar* — speaking is forbidden, but thinking is permitted. One may mentally plan for *motzaei Shabbos* even if one may not vocalize those plans. There is only so much one can reasonably regulate, and controlling one's thoughts entirely is not expected.

---

## Stream & Dirt

### Stream Crossing

The *Gemara* returns to the question of walking on *Shabbos*: *mahu lifso'a pesiah gassah b'Shabbos* — may one take a large step on *Shabbos*? This was asked by Rav of Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yosi. The reply is striking: *ve-chi be-chol mi hutar* — who ever said it was permitted even on a weekday? *She-ani omer: pesiah gassah noteles echad mi-chamesh meos mi-me'or einav shel adam* — a large step removes one five-hundredth of a person's eyesight. The remedy, however, is available: *u-mahadra lei b'kiddusha d'bei shimshi* — it is restored through the *Kiddush* on Friday night. Rashi understands this as referring to drinking the wine of *Kiddush*. The precise meaning of this physiological claim is not entirely clear, and various more metaphorical interpretations have been proposed — among them, that someone rushing through life with great strides does not truly see what surrounds him, and that the slow, deliberate *Kiddush* of Friday night restores that awareness. Whatever the deeper meaning, the practical point is clear: an unnaturally large, rushing step is inappropriate and even harmful, both on *Shabbos* and in general.

The *Gemara* implicitly notes the best practical solution in the stream case: when there is truly no alternative, one takes the large step — *keivan d'lo efshar shapir dami*. The ruling about *pesiah gassah* similarly applies only when the large step is chosen unnecessarily; unavoidable circumstances are treated differently.

### Eating Dirt

A parallel exchange: *mahu le'echol adamah b'Shabbos* — may one eat dirt on *Shabbos*? This was apparently practiced sometimes as a folk remedy. Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yosi responds identically: *ve-chi be-chol mi hutar* — who ever said this was permitted on a weekday? *She-ani omer: af be-chol assur mipnei she-hu malkeh* — even on a weekday it is forbidden, because it is injurious to health. The *Gemara* will continue with the specific hazards of eating dirt.

### Dirt Consequences

Rav Ami declares: *kol ha-ochel me-afra d'Bavel k'ilu ochel mi-bsar avosav* — anyone who eats from the soil of Bavel is as if he ate from the flesh of his ancestors. The Maharsha explains that in Bavel — unlike *Eretz Yisrael* where burial sites were well-known — people were interred throughout the land in the wake of the Babylonian exile, so one is likely consuming decomposed matter of the dead. A more severe formulation is also cited: *ve-yesh omrim k'ilu ochel shkatzim u-remasim* — some say it is as if one ate forbidden crawling creatures and rodents.

The rhetorical basis for this latter claim is traced through Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan. Reish Lakish asks: *lama nikra shema Shinar* — why was Bavel called *Shinar* in the Torah? *She-kol mesei mabul ninaru l'sham* — because all the dead of the Flood were shaken out there, since Bavel sits at a low elevation and everything flowed to it. Rabbi Yochanan similarly: *lama nikra shema Metzula* — why was it called *Metzula*? *She-kol metei mabul nitzlelu l'sham* — all the dead of the Flood floated there.

The *Gemara* objects to the second formulation: those dissolved remains have long since ceased to be *shkatzim v'remasim* in any halachic sense. The answer: *keivan d'malki, gazru beih Rabbanan* — since eating dirt is injurious to health, the Rabbis imposed this rhetoric as a safeguard, framing it as equivalent to having eaten forbidden animals. The language *gazru beih Rabbanan* is striking — it makes this not merely rhetorical hyperbole but almost a formal rabbinic equivalence, intended to deter the practice.

That such rhetoric was necessary suggests that eating dirt was genuinely practiced, which in turn is perhaps evidence of significant poverty in the population the *Gemara* is addressing.

### Clay Case

A concrete case: *hahu gavra d'achal gargashta v'achal tichli* — there was a man who ate gray clay and also ate cress. *V'kadchu tichlaya b'libeih u'meis* — the cress took root in the clay inside his body and caused a fatal fever. Rashi explains: *nikletu ha'tichlim b'adama v'gidlu* — the cress seeds lodged in the clay and literally sprouted, growing within the man and destroying him. This is precisely the kind of case — someone ingesting a seed which germinates internally — that has in fact been documented in modern medicine, lending the *Gemara*'s account an unexpected plausibility.

---

## Ruth Narrative

### Ruth's Preparation

Returning to the theme of *Shabbos* garments, the *Gemara* cites the verse from the Book of Ruth: *v'rachatzat v'sacht v'shamt simlotaich alaich v'yaradt ha'goren* — bathe and anoint yourself and put on your garments and go down to the threshing floor. These are Naomi's instructions to Ruth. Rabbi Elazar comments: *elu begadim shel Shabbos* — these are Shabbos garments. One might ask why the verse needs to say "put on your garments" at all — everyone gets dressed. The answer is that these are not merely any garments but specifically her finest, her special clothes, the equivalent of *Shabbos* dress. *Ten l'chacham v'yichkam od* — give to the wise and they will add wisdom. The *Gemara* now draws a comparison between Ruth and Shmuel as instances of someone who improved upon instructions given to them.

### Ruth's Modesty

Naomi told Ruth to bathe, anoint herself, put on her garments, and then go down to the threshing floor — in that order. But the verse describing what Ruth actually did inverts the sequence: *v'tered ha'goren v'hadar vata'as k'chol asher tzivata chamota* — she went down first, and only then did all that her mother-in-law had commanded. Rashi explains that Ruth realized the wisdom of this reversal: had she prepared herself at home and then walked to the threshing floor in her finest clothes, she would have drawn attention and comment. By going down first and then adorning herself in a private place, she preserved her dignity and avoided the scrutiny of passersby.

### Samuel Case

The parallel case involves Shmuel. Eli instructed him: if the voice calls again, say *daber Hashem ki shomeia avdecha* — speak, Lord, for Your servant is listening. But when God called and Shmuel responded, he said only *daber ki shomeia avdecha* — speak, for I am listening — omitting God's name. Rashi suggests two reasons: either Shmuel was not entirely certain the voice was divine and therefore did not want to invoke God's name without certainty, or he was concerned about pronouncing the name unnecessarily. In either case, Shmuel improved upon his instructions, just as Ruth did.

### Ruth's Knowledge

*V'telech v'tavo v'tilakeit ba'sadei* — she went and came and she gleaned in the field. Rabbi Elazar asks: the verse says both "went" and "came" — why not simply say she went and gleaned? *She-halcha u'vata halcha u'vata* — she went back and forth, back and forth, *ad she-matza b'nei adam ha'mehuganim la'yelech imahem* — until she found a group of properly behaved people to go with. She was careful from the outset about the company she kept.

Then Boaz noticed her. His foreman asked — or Boaz asked his foreman — *l'mi hana'ara hazot* — to whom does this young woman belong? One might wonder: was it Boaz's habit to inquire after young women? Rabbi Elazar explains: *dvar chochma ra'a bah* — it was a matter of wisdom he observed in her. *Shenei shibolim likta, shlosha shibolim eina likta* — when two stalks had fallen, she gathered them; when three fell together, she did not take them, because halachically *leket* (gleanings) applies only to two dropped stalks, not three. Boaz saw someone who knew the *halacha* and scrupulously observed it even when no one was watching.

### Boaz's Choice

The *baraita* adds a parallel observation: *dvar tzniyut ra'a bah* — Boaz also saw a matter of *tzniut* (modesty) in her. *Omedet me'umad* — when she was gathering standing stalks, she stood upright. *Noflot meyoshav* — when she was picking up stalks that had fallen to the ground, she would not bend over; she crouched down instead to avoid immodest posture. It was the combination of halachic precision and refined modesty that captured Boaz's attention.

### Modesty Practice

Boaz then told Ruth: *vatishak Orpa lachamota v'Rut davka bah* — Orpa kissed her mother-in-law and left, but Ruth cleaved to her. Boaz says to Ruth that she should cleave to his young women — *vatidbaki im na'arotai*. The *Gemara* notes the apparent awkwardness of a man using the word "cleave" in addressing a woman. Rabbi Elazar explains: *shari l'idbuki bah* — since Ruth herself was defined by the act of *deveikut* (cleaving) — cleaving to Naomi when Orpa turned back — Boaz's use of that very word was an appropriate echo and expression of admiration.

### Kingdom Hints

Boaz told her: *goshi halom* — draw near. Rabbi Elazar comments: *remez ramaz lah* — he was hinting to her, though not necessarily consciously, that *atida malchut beit David latzet mimech* — the kingdom of the house of David would one day come from her. The word *halom* is the same word that appears in the verse where King David himself said: *mi anochi Hashem Elokim u'mi veiti ki hevi'atani ad halom* — who am I, Lord, that You have brought me to this point? The verbal echo links Ruth's future to David's acknowledgment of his own kingship.

When Boaz said *v'tavalt pitech bachometz* — dip your bread in vinegar — Rabbi Elazar sees a practical message: vinegar is beneficial in the heat. But Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani reads another hint: *atid ben latzet mimech she-ma'asav kashim k'chometz* — a descendant will come from you whose deeds are as harsh as vinegar. That is Menashe.

When Ruth sat *mitzad hakotzrim* — by the side of the harvesters — Rabbi Elazar notes: *v'lo betoch hakotzrim* — not in their midst. Rashi's picture is that Boaz stood at one end and Ruth at the other, with all the harvesters between them. Rabbi Elazar sees in this spatial arrangement a hint that *atida malchut beit David shetehei metchaleket* — the kingdom of David would eventually be divided.

### Wealth Timeline

*Vayitzbat la kali vatochal vatisba* — he handed her parched grain and she ate and was satisfied. Rabbi Elazar expounds on the sequence of verbs in the verse. *Vatochal* — she ate: *bimei David* — this refers to the era of David, a time of basic sustenance and beginning. *Vatisba* — she was satisfied: *bimei Shlomo* — in the era of Shlomo, when there was genuine abundance. *Vattotar* — and there was leftover: *bimei Chizkiyahu* — in the time of Hezekiah, when wealth reached its fullest expression.

An alternative reading is also offered: *vatochal bimei David u'bimei Shlomo* — both David and Shlomo represent the first stage of simply eating, *vatisba bimei Chizkiyahu* — satisfaction came in Hezekiah's time, *vattotar bimei Rebbe* — and the surplus, the peak of wealth, corresponds to the era of Rebbe (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi). This is a remarkable claim: the personal wealth of Rebbe exceeded that of the kingdoms of Shlomo and Chizkiyahu. The *Gemara* supports this: the one who managed Rebbe's stables was said to be wealthier than the Persian king Shabur Malka. Whether this is literal or metaphorical (some suggest it refers to Torah wealth rather than material wealth), the tradition is clear: Rebbe's household represented an extraordinary peak.

### Eschatology

The *baraita* concludes with an eschatological reading of the same verse: *vatochal ba-olam ha-zeh* — she ate, referring to this world; *vatisba l'yemos ha-mashiach* — she was satisfied, referring to the messianic era; *vattotar l'asid lavo* — and there was leftover, referring to the world to come. The progression of eating, satisfaction, and surplus maps onto the three stages of Jewish eschatological history — the present world, the messianic age, and the ultimate future. With that expansive vision, the daf comes to a close.

---

---

# Shabbat 113b

## Kavod Shabbat & Clothes

### Kavod Shabbat Intro

The daf opens in the context of a *mishnah* that dealt with folding clothes on *Shabbat* and various *issurim*, but which gave occasion to introduce the broader theme of *kavod Shabbat*: refraining from extraneous activities, changing one's clothes, and a range of behaviors either performed or avoided in honor of the day. Because *kavod* is so central to this discussion, and because clothing is identified as one of the primary vehicles through which honor is expressed, the *gemara* now turns to a *drasha* on the concept.

### Vesachas Kvodo Drasha

The verse under discussion is *vesachas kvodo yekad yekod kikod esh* — "and beneath his *kavod* burned like the burning of fire" — referring to *Sancheriv*. *Rabbi Yochanan* comments: *vesachas kvodo velo kvodo mamash* — beneath his *kavod*, but not the *kavod* itself. *Rashi* explains that when the army of *Sancheriv* was destroyed, the bodies burned while the clothes were left intact. The explanation for *Rabbi Yochanan*'s reading is consistent with his general outlook: *Rabbi Yochanan l'taimei*, *Rabbi Yochanan* goes according to his own reasoning, for as we learned previously, *Rabbi Yochanan karei l'manei mechabdisai* — *Rabbi Yochanan* calls his clothes "the things that honor me," *mechabdisai*. It is therefore natural that he reads *kvodo* as a reference to clothing, and that the *drasha* emphasizes the clothes being spared while the bodies were consumed.

*Rabbi Elazar* offers a different reading: *tachas kvodo mamash* — *kvodo* refers to the person himself. If the burning is described as beneath the person himself, this must mean the souls were destroyed while the bodies remained intact.

*Rabbi Yishmael bar Nachmani* then adds: *vesachas kvodo kishreifat b'nei Aharon* — like the burning of the sons of Aharon. Just as in that case, *sreifat neshama veguf kayam* — the soul was consumed while the body remained — so too here, *af kan sreifat neshama veguf kayam*.

In any case, these are various *drashot* that tie into the concept of *kavod*, and at least according to *Rabbi Yochanan*, *kavod* refers specifically to one's clothing.

### Biblical Source

*Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *minayin l'shinnui bgadim min HaTorah?* — from where do we derive the idea of changing clothes from the *Torah* itself? After all, we cited earlier the verse from Ruth — *v'rachatzat v'sacht* — put on your *simlotayich*, understood as *bgadei Shabbat*. But where else does the *Torah* indicate that changing into appropriate clothes for different occasions reflects proper honor?

The answer is drawn from the *avoda* in the *Beit HaMikdash*: *upashat et bgadav v'lavash bgadim acherim* — the *kohen* removes his garments and wears other garments to take out the ashes. This establishes a precedent that different functions call for different clothing.

### Derech Eretz

*V'tana d'bei Rabbi Yishmael*: *limadcha Torah derech eretz* — the *Torah* is teaching you proper conduct. *Bgadim shebishal bahen kedera l'rabo al yimzug bahen kos l'rabo* — the clothes in which you cooked the pot for your master you should not use to pour his cup. You wear an apron while cooking, but dress differently when attending or serving at dinner. The point is not that some clothes are inherently better than others, but that clothes must match their purpose. If one wishes to show particular honor for *Shabbat*, one dresses in a manner befitting that occasion.

## Torah Scholars' Dress

### Patched Shoes Disgrace

*Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *gnay hu letalmid chacham sheyeitzei biminalim hametulaim lashuk* — it is a disgrace for a Torah scholar to go out into the marketplace wearing shoes with patches on them. One need not wear expensive shoes, but one should not appear tattered. This is because the Torah scholar represents Torah itself, and his appearance affects how others perceive Torah and those who study it.

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge: *veha Rabbi Chiyya bar Chanina nafik?* — but did *Rabbi Chiyya bar Chanina* go out wearing patched shoes? *Rabbi Abba brei deRav Nachman* answers: *telai al gav telai* — the problem is only when one's patches have patches. As the expression goes, he is so poor his patches have patches. This raises a real difficulty: what is a person supposed to do when he genuinely cannot afford better shoes? The *gemara* will later discuss the community's obligation to provide for Torah scholars, but for now the point stands that even the appearance of destitution — entirely beyond one's control — creates a problematic impression.

This is admittedly a tension that runs much deeper in the tradition. There is an analogous difficulty with the *bigdei kehuna* and the question of *mumim* — how much one accommodates existing social norms about external appearance versus how much one works to reshape those norms. The *gemara* here seems to be accommodating the reality that people judge by externals, even while acknowledging that *ha'adam yireh la'einayim v'Hashem yireh lalivav* — a person looks at what is visible while God looks at the heart. The practical position taken is that, in the interim before broader sensibilities change, the Torah scholar must be mindful of the impressions created by his appearance.

### Stains & Desecration

*Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *kol talmid chacham shenimtza revav al bigdo chayav mita* — any Torah sage who is found with a *revav* — a grease stain, something particularly conspicuous and repellent — on his garment is deserving of death. This is strong language, and it is supported by the verse: *kol mesan'ai ahavu mavet* — all those who hate me love death. The *gemara* reads this as *al tikrei mesan'ai ella mashni'ai* — do not read "those who hate me" but rather "those who cause others to hate me." The Torah scholar who goes about with a disgusting stain on his garment causes people to hate Torah and has, in effect, done something terrible to how Torah and Torah study are perceived.

Here, unlike the case of patched shoes, it may be more within one's control to launder one's clothes — though laundry also costs money, and one should not be cavalier about that reality. Nevertheless, the principle is clear: how one dresses reflects the respect one shows toward the people around oneself, toward the occasion, and toward what one represents. It also directly affects the respect others will accord to those things in turn.

### Revav vs Revvad

*Ravina amar revad itmar* — the word stated was not *revav* but *revvad*. And according to *Rashi*, *revvad* refers to something worse — specifically a semen stain. *V'lo pligi* — and they do not actually dispute one another. *Ha b'glima ha b'levusha* — one refers to the outer garment and the other to the inner garment. *Rashi* explains: for the inner garment, which is less visible, a regular grease stain might be tolerable, but a *revvad* is still unacceptable. The outer garment, by contrast, presents a problem even with an ordinary grease stain.

### Isaiah Nakedness

*Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: what is meant by the verse *ka'asher halach avdi Yeshayahu arom v'yachef* — like my servant Isaiah walked naked and barefoot? *Arom* does not mean literally naked — it means *b'v'gadim bluyim* — with garments in tatters. *V'yachef* barefoot means *b'minalim hamutlaim* — with patched-up shoes. This underscores the point that tattered garments and patched shoes are perceived as tantamount to not being properly clothed at all.

### Chatzitza Stains

A *mishnah* elsewhere teaches: *revav al hamarda* — a grease stain on a saddle is a *chatzitza*, a barrier to valid immersion. This applies when there is still surface grease that has not been fully absorbed, since something is only considered a *chatzitza* when one is *makpid* — when people find it objectionable. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* qualifies: only if the stain is the size of an Italian *issar* or larger does it constitute a problem; smaller than that is not an issue.

Regarding garments: *v'al hab'gadim mitzad echad eino chotzetz* — if a grease stain on a garment appears on one side only, it is not a *chatzitza*. *Me'shnei tzdadim chotzetz* — if it has been absorbed so thoroughly that it is visible on the other side as well, then it is a *chatzitza*. *Rabbi Yehuda* says in the name of *Rabbi Yishmael*: *apilu mitzad echad chotzetz* — even from one side alone it constitutes a *chatzitza*.

*Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish* asked *Rabbi Chanina* about the saddle discussed earlier: *mitzad echad o mi'shnei tzdadim* — does it become a *chatzitza* from one side or only from two sides? *Rabbi Chanina* replied: *zu lo shamati* — I have no explicit tradition on this. But *k'yotze bah shamati* — I have heard a parallel teaching. The *mishnah* records: *Rabbi Yosi omer — hab'nayim mitzad echad* — for *benayim*, one side is already a problem. As for an *am ha'aretz*, only from two sides is it a problem. The *gemara* will explain momentarily that *benayim* here refers to Torah scholars. *V'lo tihye marda chashuva mi'bigdo shel am ha'aretz* — a saddle should not be treated more stringently than the clothes of an ordinary person. Therefore, even the saddle presents a problem only when the stain penetrates both sides — which, it must be said, would require a remarkably heavy stain.

### Scholars & Stains

*Mai Banayim?* — what is the meaning of *benayim* in the *mishnah*? *Amar Rabbi Yochanan: elu Talmidei Chachamim she'oskim bevinyano shel olam kol yimeihem* — these are Torah sages who spend their entire lives engaged in building the world. The *gemara* thus reads *benayim* through the lens of the well-known *drasha: al tikri banayich ella bonayich* — do not read "your children" but "your builders." This designation carries genuine weight: the *gemara* is countering the perception that Torah scholars merely sit and waste time, emphasizing instead that they are the ones constructing the fabric of the world.

With this identification established, the ruling follows naturally: because Torah scholars must be especially careful about their appearance and what it communicates, a stain on even one side of their garment is already a problem. For ordinary people, however, a stain only becomes a *chatzitza* when it penetrates both sides of the garment.

One might ask why the *gemara* needed to invoke *Rabbi Yosi*'s ruling rather than simply citing the *Tanna Kamma*'s position — that for ordinary people a stain is only a problem when it goes through to both sides — and inferring from there about the saddle. The *gemara*'s choice to cite *Rabbi Yosi* specifically remains somewhat puzzling, but the halachic conclusion is the same.

## Talmid Chacham

### Lost Objects Trust

*Ve'amar Rabbi Yochanan: eizehu talmid chacham she-machzirin lo aveidah bitvi'at ha-ayin?* — who is the Torah scholar to whom we return a lost object based merely on visual recognition? It is worth noting that the term *talmid chacham* in this context does not carry its modern connotation of a great *gadol*, but refers more literally to one who is a student of the *chachamim* — still a disciple, but one who devotes his time entirely to Torah study.

Ordinarily, returning a lost object requires the claimant to provide a specific identifying mark — a *siman*. If someone claims to recognize an object by sight without being able to articulate a precise description, that is not normally sufficient, since anyone could make such a claim. Yet the *gemara* entertains the possibility that for a Torah scholar whose integrity can be relied upon absolutely, visual recognition alone may suffice.

### Appearance & Integrity

*Zeh hamakpid al chaluko l'hafcho* — this is someone so attentive to how he presents himself that if he has put on his garment inside out, he will take the trouble to remove it and reverse it so it appears properly. The *gemara* identifies this level of self-awareness and care about one's presentation as a marker of the *talmid chacham* whose word can be trusted regarding lost objects.

This is a striking combination of assumptions. On one hand, the underlying hope — not always realized — is that devotion to Torah leads to greater focus on *middot*, character, and honesty. On the other hand, there is the claim that attention to one's external presentation is somehow connected to that integrity. One might reasonably object that people can be very careful about how they appear without that reflecting anything about their actual character. Indeed, the *gemara* elsewhere offers a more intuitive criterion for this category of trust: someone who has never been *meshaneh b'diburo* — who never misrepresents the truth except in the three cases the *gemara* itself permits for the sake of peace. That seems a more direct measure of the integrity at stake when returning lost objects. The assumption that careful dress correlates with honesty, while interesting, is clearly not airtight.

### Community Support

*Ve'amar Rabbi Yochanan: eizehu talmid chacham she-b'nei iro metzuvim la'asot lo melachto?* — who is the Torah scholar that the people of his town are obligated to perform his work for him, so that he may devote himself entirely to his study? *Ze she-maniach cheftzo v'osek b'cheftzei shamayim* — someone who completely abandons his own pursuits and devotes himself purely to heavenly matters.

The *gemara* qualifies: *v'hani mili le-mipshat b'riftah* — and even this obligation extends only to providing him with bread. It does not entail a fine house or luxury provisions — only basic sustenance. This *gemara* connects to a much larger debate. The *Rambam* famously and vigorously opposed the institutionalization of communal support for Torah scholars who did not work, noting how many of *Chazal* maintained professions. He viewed the social pressure to donate to such support as highly problematic. At the same time, the practice of supporting individuals devoted entirely to Torah has a long history in many communities. The phrase *maniach cheftzo ve'osek becheftzei Shamayim* could be read to mean not merely that one devotes considerable hours to learning, but that one never leaves the *beit midrash* for any other purpose. In any event, the *gemara* is clear that even if such support is warranted, the community's obligation extends to *riftah* — bread — and no more.

### Rabbinic Leadership

*Ve'amar Rabbi Yochanan: eizehu talmid chacham she-memanin oto parnas al ha-tzibbur?* — who is the Torah scholar that the community is prepared to appoint as *parnas* over them? While *parnas* often denotes a lay leader, in this context it almost certainly refers to a rabbinic leader. *Ze she-sholin oto d'var halacha b'chol makom v'omer* — someone who can be asked a halachic question from anywhere and can answer it immediately, *va'afilu b'masechet kallah* — even from *Masechet Kallah*, a relatively small and obscure tractate dealing with *sheva brachot* and matters associated with the wedding.

*Tosafot*, however, attempts to limit this standard on the basis of a later *gemara*, arguing that the requirement is not encyclopedic knowledge of all of *Shas* but expertise in one area — even if that area is as limited as *Masechet Kallah*. That would be a significantly different reading from *Rashi*'s, which understands the standard at face value.

The *gemara* subsequently revisits this question — *kol she'shoalin oto halacha bechol makom ve'omrah, lemai nafka mina? leminuyei parnas al hatzibur* — and qualifies it: *ei bechada masechta, be'asreih* — if he is a master of one tractate, he can be appointed as a local rabbinic authority in his own community. *Ei bechulah tenuyei, bereish metivta* — if he is knowledgeable across the entirety of *Shas*, he can be appointed at the level of *rosh metivta*, a broader regional authority. This graduated standard is what *Tosafot* had in mind when softening the seemingly absolute demand of the original formulation.

At this point, *Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish* returns the discussion to where it began — the question of what type of garment is meant by the ruling that one side of a stain suffices. He says: *elu keilim ha'ulyarin haba'in mimedinat hayam* — these are the bath attendants' robes that come from overseas. *Rashi* explains that these are the special robes one puts on immediately after bathing, which come from overseas and are particularly fine. Since one puts them on having just washed, even a single-sided stain is objectionable.

The *gemara* then asks: *lemeimra dechivari ninhu* — presumably you are saying these are white garments, since stains would show most clearly on white. But *Rabbi Yannai* told his sons: *al tikberuni lo becheilim levanim velo becheilim shechorim* — do not bury me in white clothes or in black clothes. *Levanim* — white — because if he does not merit and goes to *Gehinnom*, he will look like a bridegroom among mourners. *Shechorim* — black — because if he does merit and ascends to a higher place, he will look like a mourner among grooms. *Ela becheilim ha'ulyarin haba'in mimedinat hayam* — rather, bury me in these bath attendants' robes from overseas. The implication is that these robes are not white. *Alma sumkei ninhu* — they must be reddish or some other color. The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, ha biglimei ha belivushei* — the inner garment is presumably white while the outer cloak is a darker color, and the ruling about one-sided stains applies specifically to the outer garments.

## Yom Kippur & Shabbat

### Can YK Serve Shabbat

Having completed the extensive digression about *Shabbat* clothes and Torah scholars, the *gemara* returns to the *mishnah*, which dealt with the relationship between *Yom Kippur* and *Shabbat* — specifically whether one may prepare on *Yom Kippur* for *Shabbat* and vice versa, and whether the fats of sacrifices from one sanctified day may be burned on the other. *Rabbi Ishmael* held that *Yom Kippur* can serve *Shabbat* — that is, preparations or offerings may carry over from *Yom Kippur* to *Shabbat* — while *Rabbi Akiva* disagreed and said neither day can serve the other.

## Yom Kippur & Shabbat (II)

### BeShabbato Limit
