*Tano Rabbanan: Olah Shabbat beShabbato* — the verse regarding the *Shabbat olah* says "in its *Shabbat*," which is read as permitting the fats of *Shabbat* to be offered on *Yom Kippur*, since *Yom Kippur* is the next day and is itself called *Shabbat*. The question is whether this can work in reverse — can the fats of *Yom Kippur* be burned on *Shabbat*? *Talmud lomar beShabbato* — the limiting word *beShabbato* forecloses that direction.

### Kedusha Comparison

The reasoning behind the asymmetry is that even though *Yom Kippur* is called *Shabbat Shabbaton* — doubly sanctified, as a *Shabbat* from *melacha* and a *Shabbat* from eating and physical pleasures — the *kedusha* of the weekly *Shabbat* is nonetheless considered higher, as demonstrated by the severity of its punishment. Violation of *Shabbat* carries the death penalty, whereas violation of *Yom Kippur* carries *kares*. Therefore, when a choice must be made, *Yom Kippur* serves *Shabbat* and not the reverse.

This is the view of *Rabbi Ishmael*. *Rabbi Akiva* disagrees and reads *beShabbato* as limiting each day to serving only itself: *Olah Shabbat beShabbato* — the *Shabbat olah* remains in its own *Shabbat*. What then does the verse come to permit? *Limed al chelvei Shabbat shekravin beYom Tov* — it teaches that fats of *Shabbat* can be offered on an ensuing *Yom Tov*, not on *Yom Kippur*. *Yakhol af beYom HaKippurim? Talmud lomar beShabbato* — one might think even *Yom Kippur*, but the verse limits: only in its own *Shabbat*.

The underlying debate, then, is over which secondary day the verse is permitting. For *Rabbi Ishmael*, the baseline assumption is that *nedarim u'nedavot krevim beYom Tov* — free-will offerings can be brought on *Yom Tov* — and this is already known without a verse. Therefore, when the verse says something can serve *Shabbat*, it must be adding something new: even *Yom Kippur*. For *Rabbi Akiva*, *nedarim u'nedavot ein krevim beYom Tov* — free-will offerings cannot be brought on *Yom Tov* — so the verse is needed precisely to establish that *Yom Tov* may serve *Shabbat* in this way; it does not extend to *Yom Kippur*.

The connection to *Eruv Tavshilin* is worth noting: cooking on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat* is itself a biblical act of preparation, and it is *Rabbi Akiva* who anchors the permissibility of *Yom Tov* serving *Shabbat* in this *pasuk*.

### Tekiah Debate

*Rabbi Zeira* said: when I was in *Bavel*, I used to assume that the following *Baraita* would be agreed upon by everyone: if *Yom Kippur* falls on a Friday, one does not sound the *shofar* — since everyone is already refraining from *melacha*, the usual signal to stop work before *Shabbat* is superfluous. And if *Yom Kippur* falls on a Sunday, one does not make *havdalah* between *Shabbat* and *Yom Kippur* — since they share essentially the same level of *kedusha* and the same prohibition of *melacha*, there is no meaningful distinction requiring formal separation. (One does make *havdalah bein kodesh le-kodesh* between two *Yom Tovim*, but the latter is only *d'rabbanan*, whereas *Yom Kippur* and *Shabbat* share effectively the same standing.)

When *Rabbi Zeira* made *aliyah* to *Eretz Yisrael*, however, he found *Yehuda* the son of *Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi* sitting and teaching otherwise: that ruling applies only according to *Rabbi Akiva*, who holds that *Yom Kippur* cannot serve *Shabbat* in any way. But according to *Rabbi Ishmael*, who permits the fats of *Shabbat* to be offered on *Yom Kippur*, there is a meaningful halachic distinction between the two days — and therefore when *Shabbat* leads into *Yom Kippur*, one should perform a *tekiah* to signal that distinction and alert people that the fats of *Shabbat* may be burned on *Yom Kippur*.

### Shofar Purpose

*Rabbi Zeira* responded: *kohanim zrizim hem* — the *kohanim* are already careful and knowledgeable; they do not require a *shofar* blast to inform them of this nuance. A *tekiah* would only be warranted for something relevant to the broader public.

*Mar Kushisha brei d'Rav Chisda* challenged *Rav Ashi*: do we really say that *kohanim* do not need such signals? The *mishnah* records that three *shofar* blasts were sounded in the *Beit HaMikdash* — three to signal people to stop working and come in from the fields, and three to signal that *Shabbat* itself had arrived and all *melacha* must cease. If these blasts were sounded in the *Beit HaMikdash*, presumably even the *kohanim* needed them.

The *gemara* answers by invoking *Abaye*'s statement in a different context — where the menorah of *Helni HaMalka* in the *Beit HaMikdash* served as a signal for the time of *Shema*, and the *gemara* explained that the *kohanim* themselves said *Shema* before sunrise, so the signal was *l'sha'ar ama d'vi-Yerushalayim* — for all the other residents of *Yerushalayim*. Similarly here: *hacha nami l'sha'ar ama d'vi-Yerushalayim* — the *shofar* blasts in the *Beit HaMikdash* were for the general population, not for the *kohanim* themselves, who were sufficiently expert to know these *halachot* without a public announcement.

## Knivat Yerek

### Trimming Allowance

This discussion of the relationship between *Yom Kippur* and *Shabbat* concludes with a notable practical detail. One thing permitted on *Yom Kippur* that is not permitted on *Shabbat* is *knivat yerek* — trimming vegetables, the removal of leaves from produce. The exact nature of the prohibition on *Shabbat* is not entirely clear; it appears to be *d'rabbanan*, perhaps related to *borer* or a similar category.

On *Yom Kippur*, this trimming is permitted starting from *mincha* time onward — *min hamincha u'lemala* — on account of *agmas nefesh*. *Rashi* interestingly interprets this in the opposite direction from what one might expect: rather than alleviating distress, it is permitted in order to *increase* the sense of *agmas nefesh* — wetting one's appetite as the fast draws near to its end, heightening awareness of the deprivation. The note on the side of the *gemara* offers a different explanation: it is permitted so that one need not spend time after *Yom Kippur* engaged in this preparation, which would needlessly extend the effective experience of the fast.

### YK on Shabbat

When *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*, is the trimming of vegetables still permitted? *Rav Zeira* said in the name of *Rav Huna*, who said in the name of *Rav Yehuda*, who said in the name of *Rav Ami*, who said in the name of *Rav Huna*: *assur b'knivas yereq* — it is forbidden. The *Shabbat* character of the day overrides the leniency permitted on *Yom Kippur*.

*Rav Mana* then cites a *Baraita*: from where do we know that when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat* one may not trim vegetables? *Talmud lomar Shabbaton Shevus* — the verse employs the doubled language of rest. The *drasha* proceeds: *ileima l'melacha v'kasiv lo sa'aseh kol melacha* — if you say this doubled language is only about *melacha*, we already have an explicit verse forbidding *melacha*; therefore the doubled language must be coming to address *knivat yerek*.

*Tosafot* is quick to note that this is evidently an *asmachta* — a rabbinic support adduced from a biblical verse, not a genuine biblical prohibition — since if the prohibition were *d'Oraita*, it would apply on *Yom Kippur* itself for any purpose, which it does not.

*Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* then says in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *Yom Kippur shechal lihyos b'Shabbos muttar b'knivas yereq* — when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*, the trimming of vegetables is in fact *permitted*. The *gemara* challenges this from the *Baraita* just cited, which assumed it was forbidden. The *gemara* responds: *lo l'olam l'melacha* — the doubled language of *Shabbaton Shevus* is not addressing *knivat yerek* at all; it is simply adding an additional positive and negative prohibition regarding *melacha* itself, establishing that refraining from *melacha* on *Shabbat* involves both a *lav* and an *aseh*. *Tanya k'vosei d'Rabbi Yochanan* — a *Baraita* is then cited in support of *Rabbi Yochanan*: when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*, *muttar b'knivas yereq* — one is permitted to trim vegetables.

### Nuts & Seeds

The *Baraita* continues: *maftzin b'egozim umfarchisin b'rimonim min hamincha u'l'ma'ala mipnei agmas nefesh* — one may also crack nuts and remove pomegranate seeds starting from *mincha* time on, by reason of *agmas nefesh*. This applies whether it is a regular *Yom Kippur* or, according to *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position, when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*.

### Rava's Response

The *gemara* reports that in the household of *Rav Yehuda* they would trim cabbage on *Yom Kippur*. In *Rava*'s household they would scrape gourds. However, when *Rava* observed that people — likely his household members or servants — were beginning to do this too early, before *mincha* time, he said to them: *asa igresa mi'ma'arava mishemei d'Rabbi Yochanan d'assur* — a letter has just arrived from *Eretz Yisrael* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* that it is forbidden. He felt they were abusing the permitted leniency, and he responded by invoking an alternative ruling — whether or not he truly held by it — to put a stop to the premature preparation.

*Hadran alach v'eilu k'sharim.* A new *perek* begins tomorrow.

---

---

# Shabbat 114

## Kavod Shabbat & Clothes

### Clothes & Kavod

The daf picks up at the bottom of 113b, continuing a discussion that arose from a *mishnah* dealing with folding clothes and various *issurim*, which provided an occasion to focus on the concept of *kavod Shabbat* — the honor due to the Sabbath — and the role that clothing plays in expressing that honor. Because the discussion has centered on *kavod* and the idea that clothing itself confers honor, the *Gemara* now turns to a *derasha* on a verse that uses the word *kevodo*.

### Sancheriv Derasha

The verse in question is from Isaiah: *v'tachat kevodo yikad yikod kikod esh* — "and beneath his glory shall be kindled a burning like the burning of fire." The subject of the verse is Sancheriv. Three *Tannaim* offer competing interpretations of the phrase *tachat kevodo* — "beneath his glory."

Rabbi Yochanan reads *v'tachat kevodo v'lo kevodo mamash*: beneath the *kavod*, not the *kavod* itself. Rashi explains that this means the bodies of Sancheriv's army burned while the clothes did not. This reading coheres with Rabbi Yochanan's known perspective, cited from the previous discussion: *kari l'manei mechabdosai* — Rabbi Yochanan refers to his clothes as "the things that honor me." It is therefore natural that he would read *kevodo* as a reference to garments, and understand the verse to mean that the bodies burned beneath the clothing while the clothing itself was preserved.

Rabbi Elazar reads *v'tachat kevodo tachat kevodo mamash* — beneath his glory, literally meaning beneath the person himself. This raises an interpretive question: what does it mean to have a burning beneath the person himself, within the person? Rabbi Elazar understands it to mean that the souls were destroyed while the bodies remained.

Rabbi Yishmael bar Nachmani offers a third reading, drawing an analogy to the death of Aharon's sons: *k'sereifat bnei Aharon, mah lehalan sereifat neshama v'guf kayam af kan sereifat neshama v'guf kayam* — just as there the soul was consumed and the body remained intact, so too here the soul was destroyed and the body remained. On his reading, *kevodo* refers to the body, and *tachat* — within or beneath — indicates that only what is internal, the soul, was destroyed.

All three *drashot* connect to the theme of *kavod* and clothing, but it is Rabbi Yochanan's reading that ties most directly to the *kavod Shabbat* discussion: clothing as the bearer of *kavod*.

### Priestly Garments

The *Gemara* now returns explicitly to the question of changing clothes and seeks a biblical basis for the practice. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: from where do we derive *shinuy begadim*, the changing of clothes, from the Torah? The proof comes from the priestly service of removing the ashes in the *Beit HaMikdash*: *u'pashat begadav v'lavash begadim acherim* — the *kohen* removes his garments and puts on other garments to carry out the ashes. The Torah itself thus mandates changing clothes for different functions, providing the biblical model for dressing differently in honor of *Shabbat*.

### Derech Eretz

The *tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* adds a broader lesson: *limidatcha Torah derech eretz* — the Torah is teaching you proper conduct. The illustration given is: *begadim shebishal bahem kederah l'rabo al yimzog bahem kos l'rabo* — the clothes one uses to cook the pot should not be the clothes one uses to serve the cup to one's master. The point is not that some clothes are inherently superior to others, but that clothes should be appropriate to the occasion. One wears an apron while cooking and presents oneself differently when serving or attending dinner. Applied to *Shabbat*: to show *kavod* for the day, one dresses in a manner that is dignified and befitting the occasion.

---

## Torah Scholars

### Patched Shoes

The *Gemara* now shifts from changing clothes for *Shabbat* to a broader concern: how a Torah scholar appears in public regardless of the occasion. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *gnai hu l'talmid chacham sheyeitzei b'minalim hametulaim lashuk* — it is a disgrace for a Torah scholar to go out to the marketplace wearing shoes with patches on them. The concern is not about wearing expensive shoes but about appearing in a way that reflects poorly on the Torah he represents.

### Extreme Poverty

The *Gemara* immediately raises an objection: but Rabbi Chiya bar Chanina went out with patched shoes. The response given is: *betlai al gabi tlai* — the problem is only when patches have patches, when someone is so destitute that his patches themselves require patches. This acknowledges the reality of extreme poverty: one cannot simply be told to buy presentable shoes when the means are unavailable. The *Gemara* will return later to the community's obligation to support Torah scholars, but at this stage it simply notes that when poverty is truly extreme, the standard cannot be applied in the same way.

This raises a deeper tension that runs throughout this section. We live in a world where people form judgments based on external appearances, and how one presents oneself affects how others perceive what one represents. There is an acknowledged problem with this — the value of a person lies within, as the verse says: *haadam yireh laeinayim v'Hashem yireh lalevav* — a person sees the eyes, but God sees the heart. Yet the *Gemara* is operating in the real world, where accommodating social norms has consequences for the public perception of Torah.

### Stains & Grease

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba continues in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol talmid chacham shenimtsa revav al bigdo chayav mita* — any Torah scholar found with a grease stain on his garment is deserving of death. The language is harsh. The proof text cited is *kol mesaneay ahavu mavet* — "all who hate me love death" — read with a *derashah*: *al tikrei mesaneay ela masniey*, do not read "those who hate me" but "those who cause others to hate me." If a Torah scholar dresses in a way that repels people and causes them to form a disgusted impression of Torah, he has committed a serious wrong against the Torah's standing in the world.

### Revad vs Revav

Ravina qualifies the statement: *revad itmar*, not *revav* — it was said with *revad*, not *revav*. According to Rashi, *revad* refers to something even more objectionable than a grease stain. And the two cases are not in conflict: *ha biglimi ha bilvushi* — one refers to the outer garment and the other to the inner garment. A grease stain on the inner garment, which is not visible, would be tolerable; on the outer garment, even that would not be acceptable. The distinction thus reconciles what might otherwise appear to be a contradiction between the two formulations.

### Isaiah Example

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba continues in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, citing the verse about Isaiah: *ka'asher halach avdi Yeshayahu arom veyachef* — "as my servant Isaiah walked naked and barefoot." The *Gemara* explains that *arom* does not mean literally naked, but rather *b'vegadim beluim* — wearing garments in tatters. And *yachef*, barefoot, is interpreted as wearing *minalim hametulaim* — patched-up shoes. The verse thus underscores the point made earlier: that wearing tattered clothing or visibly worn shoes is perceived as essentially equivalent to not wearing clothes at all.

### Saddle Stains

The *Gemara* then cites a *mishnah* from elsewhere: *revav al hamarda* — a grease stain on a saddle — constitutes a *chatzitza*, an interposition, for the purposes of *tevila* to render it *tahor*. The relevance here is that the only thing that constitutes a *chatzitza* is something that one is *makpid* about — that one objects to. The fact that a grease stain on a saddle is a *chatzitza* therefore demonstrates that people are genuinely particular about such stains on their equipment and garments. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies: only if the stain is the size of an *isar italki* or larger does it constitute a problem.

The *mishnah* continues: if a grease stain is on only one side of a garment, *eino chotzetz* — it is not a *chatzitza*; if it has soaked through to both sides, *chotzetz* — it is. Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Yishmael: even one side constitutes a *chatzitza*.

### Saddle Question

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish posed a question to Rabbi Chanina: regarding the saddle — was the *chatzitza* of a stain on a saddle assumed to be on one side only, or must it go through to both sides? A stain heavy enough to soak through an entire saddle would have to be substantial indeed, though perhaps the discussion refers to a saddle blanket rather than the saddle itself.

Rabbi Chanina responds: *zu lo shamati* — I have not heard an explicit tradition on this point. But *k'yotzei ba shamati* — I have heard a similar ruling. From the *mishnah*: Rabbi Yossi says that for *benai'im* — literally "builders" — one side is already a problem, while for an *am ha'aretz* it is only a problem from two sides. This comparison provides an analogical answer: if an *am ha'aretz*'s clothing is only a problem when the stain goes through both sides, then a saddle — which surely should not be treated more stringently than the clothes of a common person — would also require the stain to go through both sides. The question of why the *Gemara* needed to invoke Rabbi Yossi's nuanced ruling rather than simply using the *tanna kamma*'s position for ordinary clothes is noted, but the practical conclusion stands.

---

## Talmid Chacham

### Who is Talmid

Having invoked the category of *benai'im*, the *Gemara* now asks: *mai banayim* — who are these "builders"?

### Builders Derasha

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *elu talmidei chachamim she'oskin bevinyano shel olam kol yemeihem* — these are Torah scholars who are engaged in building the world for all their days. The term *benai'im*, builders, is thus read as a reference to those who build the world through Torah, echoing the well-known formulation *al tikrei banayich ela bonayich*. While from an outside perspective it might appear that those who sit and learn are removed from practical contribution, the *Gemara* asserts the opposite: they are the true builders of civilization.

This reading also explains why the standard for Torah scholars regarding clothing stains is stricter than for ordinary people: they represent something of the highest public significance, and therefore the standards of appearance that apply to them are correspondingly heightened.

### Lost Objects

Rabbi Yochanan now addresses the question of who qualifies as a *talmid chacham* for the purpose of *hashavat aveidah*. The rule is that a *talmid chacham* whose integrity can be trusted may have a lost object returned to him on the basis of *tevi'at ha'ayin* — recognition alone — even without being able to provide a specific identifying *siman*. Ordinarily this would be insufficient, since anyone could claim to recognize something.

### Appearance & Integrity

The *Gemara* defines who merits this level of trust: *ze hamakpid al chaluko lehofcho* — one who is so careful about his personal presentation that if he accidentally puts on his garment inside out, he will take the time to remove it and put it on properly.

This is a striking criterion. The *Gemara* seems to assume a connection between meticulous care about one's personal appearance and the kind of integrity that would make one trustworthy in matters of monetary honesty. The underlying logic seems to be that self-awareness about how one presents oneself to others reflects a broader attentiveness to one's own conduct and its effects on the world.

At the same time, this connection is not without its complications. The care one takes with outward appearance can, in principle, serve as a mask for inner deficiencies of character rather than as a reflection of genuine integrity. A different *Gemara* elsewhere suggests a seemingly more direct criterion for trustworthiness: someone who has never been *meshane b'diburo* — who never misrepresents the truth, except in the three contexts where the rabbis permit a departure from strict accuracy. That standard has a more obvious logical relationship to financial honesty. The criterion of careful dress is noteworthy precisely because it is less obvious, and the *Gemara* treats it as a meaningful indicator of character nonetheless.

### Community Support

Rabbi Yochanan now turns to a different question: who qualifies as a *talmid chacham* such that *benei iro metzuvin la'asot lo melachto* — the people of his town are obligated to perform his work for him, so that he can devote himself entirely to learning? The answer: *zeh she-maniach cheftzo v'osek b'cheftzei shamayim* — one who completely abandons his own pursuits and devotes himself purely to heavenly matters. The *Gemara* qualifies this obligation: *v'hani milei lemitrach b'rifta* — even this communal obligation extends only to providing basic sustenance, bread, not to providing luxuries.

This passage touches on a much larger debate. The *Rambam* argued vigorously against the institutionalization of community-supported Torah study, noting that the great figures of *Chazal* all had occupations and were not supported by the *tzibur*. He objected particularly to social pressure compelling communities to fund such support. A more sympathetic reading might compare the community support of full-time Torah scholars to the way graduate fellowships fund advanced scholarship in fields that are not financially remunerative but that society judges to have lasting value — with the critical caveat that such support requires a rigorous selection process and should not be extended indiscriminately.

The phrase *meniach cheftzo v'osek b'cheftzei shamayim* itself may already encode some selectivity: it may not refer to anyone who spends hours learning, but specifically to one who never leaves the *beit midrash*, who has genuinely and completely abandoned all personal pursuits.

### Three Categories

The *Gemara* now presents a series of related formulations from Rabbi Yochanan, each asking *eizehu talmid chacham* — who is a *talmid chacham* — but for different purposes. First: *kol she'shoalin oto halacha b'chol makom v'omrah* — one who can be asked a *halacha* question from anywhere and can answer it. This is the criterion for appointing someone *parnas al ha-tzibur*, a rabbinic leader of the community. *Tosafot* reads this as referring to mastery within one's area of specialization, even if that area is small — citing *masechet Kallah* as an example, a single *perek* of relatively accessible material focused on the laws of a wedding. Rashi, by contrast, appears to read it more broadly.

The *Gemara* then distinguishes between levels. *Ee b'chada masechta* — if the scholar is a master of one tractate — *b'asrei* — he may be appointed as a local rabbinic authority in his own community. *Ee b'chula tanuye* — if he is knowledgeable across the breadth of *Shas* — *b'reish mesivta* — he may be appointed as a *Rosh Yeshiva*, a more regional or senior authority. These distinctions apply specifically in the context of communal rabbinic appointment.

The section concludes with a return to the *derasha* that opened this discussion. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish offers a different interpretation of *benai'im*: not Torah scholars but rather *keilim ha'ulyarin habaim midinat hayam* — bath attendants' garments that come from overseas, garments of a very particular and fine quality for which people are extremely particular. Even a stain on one side would be objectionable because of their quality. The *Gemara* then notes that since stains would presumably be most visible on white garments, this is the implication. But Rabbi Yannai instructed his sons not to bury him in white garments — lest he not merit and appear like a groom among mourners in *Gehenna* — nor in black garments — lest he merit and appear like a mourner among grooms in heaven. Instead, he requested burial in these bath-attendants' garments from overseas. The *Gemara* concludes that these must be a reddish or other color, and resolves the apparent difficulty by distinguishing between inner garments, which would be white, and outer cloaks, which would be of a darker color.

---

## Yom Kippur & Shabbat

### Olat Shabbat

Having completed the extended digression on the dignity of Torah scholars, the *Gemara* returns to the *mishnah*'s original topic: the relationship between *Shabbat* and *Yom Kippur* in matters of preparation and sacrificial service. The *mishnah* had presented the positions of Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva on whether one can prepare on *Yom Kippur* for *Shabbat* and vice versa. A *baraita* is now cited: *olat Shabbat b'shabbato* — the *olah* of *Shabbat* in its *Shabbat* — is read as teaching that the fats of *Shabbat* that were not burned in time may be burned on *Yom Kippur*, since *Yom Kippur* itself is called *Shabbat*. The verse uses the word *Shabbat* to include another *Shabbat*, and the immediate candidate is *Yom Kippur*, which falls on the very next day.

The *baraita* then asks: might this work in the reverse direction as well — could one bring the fats of *Yom Kippur* on *Shabbat*? The verse answers: *b'shabbato* — only in its own *Shabbat* — limiting the direction.

### Hierarchy Dispute

This is the crux of the debate between Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva. The limiting word *b'shabbato* means we can only choose one direction, and the question is which day serves which. In most people's intuition, *Yom Kippur* — called *Shabbat Shabbaton*, a doubled *Shabbat* — would seem holier. Yet the *Gemara* understands that the *kedushah* of the weekly *Shabbat* is in fact greater, as evidenced by the *onesh*: violation of *Shabbat* carries the death penalty, while violation of *Yom Kippur* carries *karet*. Death is the more severe punishment, indicating the higher sanctity of *Shabbat*. Therefore, when a choice must be made, *Yom Kippur* serves *Shabbat* and not the reverse. This is the position of Rabbi Ishmael.

Rabbi Akiva, however, reads *b'shabbato* as an even more restricting statement: each *Shabbat* can only serve itself. Nothing may be transferred from one to the other. But if so, what does the verse come to teach? Rabbi Akiva says it teaches that the fats of *Shabbat* may be brought on *Yom Tov* — a festival day that follows *Shabbat*. *Yom Tov*, not *Yom Kippur*, is the permissible extension.

### Yom Tov Prep

The *Gemara* unpacks this. According to Rabbi Ishmael, *nedarim u-nedavot kravin b'Yom Tov* — free-will offerings may be brought on *Yom Tov*. If that is already established, then the verse need not be teaching us something about *Yom Tov*, which we already knew. The verse must therefore be extending the permission even to *Yom Kippur*. According to Rabbi Akiva, however, *nedarim u-nedavot ein kravin b'Yom Tov* — free-will offerings may not be brought on *Yom Tov*. It would therefore not be self-evident that the fats of *Shabbat* could be burned on *Yom Tov*, and the verse is needed precisely to teach that *Yom Tov* — not *Yom Kippur* — is the permissible case. This also aligns with the *mishnah*'s theme of *eruv tavshilin* and the general principle of *Yom Tov* preparing for *Shabbat*.

### Yom Kippur Friday

Rabbi Zeira provides a historical account. When he was still in *Bavel*, he assumed that the *baraita* ruling — that when *Yom Kippur* falls on Friday there is no *tekiah* (no series of shofar blasts to mark the cessation of *melacha*), and when it falls on Sunday there is no *havdala* between *Yom Kippur* and *Shabbat* — was universally accepted. The reasoning is straightforward: the *tekiah* on an ordinary *erev Shabbat* signals people to stop working, but if *Yom Kippur* already forbids *melacha*, there is no point. Similarly, *havdala* marks a transition from a higher to a lower *kedushah*, but the difference between *Shabbat* and *Yom Kippur* is marginal — both prohibit *melacha*, with only a difference in the severity of the *onesh* — so no *havdala* is required.

When Rabbi Zeira made *aliyah* to *Eretz Yisrael*, he found Yehuda the son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi teaching that this is only the view of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that *Yom Kippur* cannot serve *Shabbat* at all and thus there is nothing to mark. Rabbi Ishmael, who holds that *Yom Kippur* does in fact serve *Shabbat* in the matter of the sacrificial fats, would require a *tekiah* when *Shabbat* transitions into *Yom Kippur*, to announce to people that the day's *kedushah* is slightly different and that the fats may be offered. Rabbi Zeira responded: *kohanim zrizim heim* — the *kohanim* are diligent and knowledgeable; they do not require a shofar blast to inform them of this *halacha*. A *tekiah* is relevant for matters that affect the general public, not for technical sacrificial laws known to the *kohanim*.

### Shofar Blasts

Mar Kashisha son of Rav Chisda challenges Rabbi Zeira's position, citing the *mishnah* that the shofar blasts on *erev Shabbat* were performed in the *Beit HaMikdash* itself — which would seem to imply that the *kohanim* were among those who needed them. The response, citing Abaye's ruling in a different context, is that the blasts in the *Beit HaMikdash* were intended for the people of Jerusalem generally, not for the *kohanim* themselves. Just as the gold *menorah* of Hilni HaMalka that indicated the time of *Shema* was for the general public while the *kohanim* already recited *Shema* before sunrise, so too the *tekiah* from the *Beit HaMikdash* was for the city's population, not for the *kohanim* who were already well-versed in the relevant *halachot*.

---

## Knivat Yerek

### Tekiah Question

The *Gemara* now raises a further question. Given that *Yom Kippur* has a slightly different *kedushah* from *Shabbat* — specifically, the *halacha* of *knivat yerek*, trimming vegetables, which is permitted on *Yom Kippur* from *mincha* time and onward but not on *Shabbat* — why not blow the shofar at the transition between *Shabbat* and *Yom Kippur* specifically to publicize this? The *tekiah* would serve to inform people: the day is now *Yom Kippur*, and from *mincha* time you will be permitted to trim your vegetables. *Knivat yerek*, it should be noted, is a rabbinic prohibition — some form of *borer* or similar concern, not a biblical *melacha* — and it was permitted specifically on *Yom Kippur* from *mincha* onward. Rashi explains that the permission is granted so that one does not need to rush immediately after the fast to prepare food, which would extend unnecessary discomfort; others understand *agmat nefesh* differently, as whetting the appetite rather than relieving it.

### Tekiah & Permitting

Rav Yosef answers: *lefi she'ein dochin shvut lehatir* — we do not violate a rabbinic prohibition in order to permit another rabbinic act. Blowing the shofar on *Shabbat* or *Yom Kippur* is itself an *issur d'rabbanan*. We would not perform one rabbinic violation in order to announce the permissibility of a different rabbinic act. Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi offers a second reason: *shvut karov hitiru, shvut rachok lo hitiru* — a rabbinic leniency that takes effect immediately at the transition may be announced, but one that only takes effect at the end of the day, at *mincha* time, is too distant to justify making an announcement at the moment of transition.

### Yom Tov Shabbat

The *Gemara* tests these answers against an analogous case. The *mishnah* rules that when *Yom Tov* leads into *Shabbat*, a *tekiah* is sounded — because now many things that were permitted on *Yom Tov* become forbidden on *Shabbat* — but no *havdala* is made, since *Shabbat* is a higher *kedushah* than *Yom Tov*. Conversely, when *Yom Tov* follows *Shabbat*, *havdala* is made between the two — moving from *Shabbat* to a lesser *kedushah* — but no *tekiah* is sounded.

Why is no *tekiah* sounded when *Yom Tov* follows *Shabbat*? One might think a *tekiah* should be blown precisely to tell people: *Shabbat* is over, *Yom Tov* has begun, *shechitah* is now permitted — you can cook, you can slaughter immediately. This is something that takes effect right away, unlike the case of *knivat yerek* at *mincha* time. Yet no *tekiah* is sounded. This demonstrates that we simply do not blow the shofar to announce that something becomes *mutar*. The purpose of a *tekiah* is to signal a stop — to say *assur*. *Havdala* marks a transition, but even when things become permitted, no *tekiah* accompanies that announcement.

This supports Rav Yosef's position: *ela machvarta k'd'Rav Yosef* — the cleaner answer is that of Rav Yosef, who holds that *tekiah* is simply not used as a mechanism for permitting things, regardless of whether the permission is immediate or distant.

### Shabbaton Shevut

The *Gemara* returns to the question of *knivat yerek* specifically when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*. Rav Zeira says in the name of Rav Huna: *Yom HaKippurim shechal lihyot b'Shabbos assur b'knivat yerek* — when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*, trimming vegetables is forbidden. Rav Mana cites a *baraita* that derives this from the verse: *Talmud lomar Shabbaton shevus* — the double language of *Shabbaton shevus* applied to *Yom Kippur* in the Torah. Since the verse cannot merely be repeating the general prohibition of *melacha*, which is already stated explicitly elsewhere, it must be adding the prohibition of *knivat yerek* specifically for when *Yom Kippur* coincides with *Shabbat*. *Tosafot* notes that this is an *asmachta*, since if it were truly a biblical prohibition it would apply to *Yom Kippur* in any case; but the *asmachta* nonetheless supports the rabbinic ruling.

### YK on Shabbat

Rabbi Chiya bar Avin then cites Rabbi Yochanan to the contrary: *Yom HaKippurim shechal lihyot b'Shabbos mutar b'knivat yerek* — when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*, trimming is in fact permitted. The *Gemara* challenges Rabbi Yochanan's view from the very *baraita* just cited, which assumed that *Shabbaton shevus* comes to prohibit *knivat yerek* in precisely this case. Rabbi Yochanan responds by rereading the verse: *Shabbaton shevus* does not come to teach about *knivat yerek* at all. It comes only to tell us that there is both a *lav* and an *aseh* — a negative commandment and a positive commandment — for *melacha* on *Shabbat*. Since the verse *b'lav va'aseh* provides this double reinforcement for the *melacha* prohibition alone, it is not available to extend the prohibition of *knivat yerek* to the case where *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*.

### Mincha Prep

A *baraita* is cited in support of Rabbi Yochanan's position: *tanya k'vasi d'Rabbi Yochanan* — we taught consistent with Rabbi Yochanan — that when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*, *knivat yerek* is permitted, and furthermore, *maftzi'in b'egozim um'farchasin b'rimonim min haminchah ul'ma'alah* — one may crack nuts and remove pomegranate seeds from *mincha* time onward. These preparations for the meal to be eaten after the fast are permitted beginning at *mincha* time, even when the day is *Yom Kippur*. The reason given is *mipnei agmat nefesh* — on account of the distress associated with the fast — so that after *Yom Kippur* one does not need to rush to prepare food and thereby extend the period of discomfort.

The practice was observed in the household of Rabbi Yehuda, where they would trim cabbage on *Yom Kippur*, and in the household of Rabbah, where they would scrape gourd. *D'vei*, "in the house of," in this context typically refers to the household and its members, which would include the women of the house.

### Rabbah's Letter

However, Rabbah observed that people around him were beginning to abuse the allowance — performing these preparations before *mincha* time rather than waiting. When he saw this overextension, he announced: *asa igrasa mimarava mishme'i d'Rabbi Yochanan d'assur* — a letter has arrived from *Eretz Yisrael* in the name of Rabbi Yochanan forbidding it. Whether or not such a letter in fact existed, Rabbah felt it necessary to retract or suppress the leniency because of the way it was being misused, preferring to invoke the authority of Rabbi Yochanan himself to close the door on the abuse.

With this, the *Gemara* concludes: *hadran alach v'eilu k'sharim* — we have completed this *perek*.

---

---

# Shabbat 116

## Kitvei Kodesh & Muktze

### Mishna: Sefer & Tik

The daf begins on 116b with the continuation of a *mishna* that addresses saving *kitvei kodesh* from a fire on *Shabbat*. The *mishna* states: *matzilin tik hasefer im hasefer* — one may save the container or mantle of a *sefer* together with the *sefer* itself, and similarly the bag of *tefillin* together with the *tefillin*. The *mishna* adds: *ve'af al pi she'yesh betokhan ma'ot* — even if there is money inside the container. This permits the incidental movement of *muktzeh* as part of the salvage operation.

The *mishna* then asks: *uleheikhan matzilin otan* — to where may these items be brought? The answer is *lemavoi she'eino mefulash* — to a *mavoi*, a courtyard, that is not open at both ends. *Mefulash* denotes a thoroughfare open on both sides. The implication is that there remains some rabbinic problem with carrying in this *mavoi*, though it is not entirely forbidden. Ben Beteira, however, says *afilu lemefulash* — even to a *mavoi* that is open at both ends, which is a considerably more permissive position and presumably entails a more serious rabbinic concern about carrying.

Two explicit allowances emerge from this *mishna* for *sefarim*: first, one may bring them into a courtyard where carrying is not fully rabbinically sanctioned; second, one may incidentally move *muktzeh* in the process. A third issue — whether and how much one may save before the concern arises of coming to extinguish the fire — is addressed more fully in the subsequent *mishna* dealing with food.

### Mavoi: Mefulash Debate

The *gemara* initially focuses on the *muktzeh* aspect. It then introduces a *baraita* that, unexpectedly, concerns the fourteenth of Nisan falling on *Shabbat* — a digression that will ultimately connect back to the *mishna*'s allowances. Before turning to that, however, the debate in the *mishna* between the majority and Ben Beteira turns on the definition of the *mavoi* into which one may carry. The *gemara* will explore at length what precisely *mefulash* and *eino mefulash* mean, a discussion that will be taken up in full later.

### Ben Beteira Identity

A question arises regarding the identity of Ben Beteira — specifically, why he is referred to by the patronymic alone, without a personal name, and why this figure may be unfamiliar. Ben Beteira is a *tanna* who appears from time to time in rabbinic literature. He features notably in discussions surrounding the question of bringing the *korban Pesach* on *Shabbat* — the famous episode in which *Bnei Beteira* stood in opposition, or at least in tension, with Hillel's ruling, where Hillel invoked a tradition received from Shemaya and Avtalyon. Ben Beteira may also appear in discussions involving Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's ruling to blow the *shofar* in Yavne after the *churban*. In any case, he is a recognized *tanna* whose opinions appear at various points in the Talmud.

---

## Pesach Flaying Debat (II)

### Rabbi Yishmael vs. Sages

The *gemara* unexpectedly introduces a *baraita*: *arba'ah asar she'chal lihyot be-Shabbat* — if the fourteenth of Nisan falls on *Shabbat*. The *korban Pesach* overrides *Shabbat*, but the question is how far that override extends. Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka rules: *mafshitin et hapesach ad hachazeh* — one may flay the *pesach* only up to the chest, working from the legs upward. This allows removal of the *emurim*, the innards designated for the *mizbe'ach*, which may indeed be offered on *Shabbat* as part of bringing the *korban Pesach*. However, one may not flay it completely, since complete flaying would serve the meat — and the meat will not be eaten until *motzaei Shabbat*. The Sages disagree: *mafshitin et kulo* — one may flay the entire *pesach*.

The *gemara* asks: the position of Rabbi Yishmael is intelligible — *dehai avid letzorech gavo'ah*, what you do is for the sake of Heaven, for what is needed on the altar, and since that is permitted on *Shabbat*, so is this. But what is the reasoning of the Sages? Why permit flaying that serves only the meat, which is not needed until after *Shabbat*? Rabbah bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan invokes a verse: *kol pa'al Hashem le-ma'anehu* — all that God has done is for His sake (Proverbs 16:4). The idea, however counterintuitive it may seem to derive a practical *halacha* from this verse in *Ketuvim*, is that all aspects of the *korban Pesach* process, including preparing the meat for consumption, are ultimately in the service of God. One therefore does not draw a fine line between what is strictly needed for the *mizbe'ach* and what is needed for the *hedyot* — it is all part of bringing the *korban Pesach*, whose very purpose is to be eaten. The *gemara* here operates in a mode of *giluy milta* — the verse is not directly *doche Shabbat*, but rather illuminates a general perspective on the latitude one may take.

### Three Explanations

Within the Sages' position, two distinct explanations are offered for permitting complete flaying. Rav Yosef says: *kedei shelo yasriach* — so that the meat does not spoil. Since the entire purpose of the *korban Pesach*, more than any other *korban*, is the *achilah*, the eating, at night, one is permitted to protect that meat even on *Shabbat*. Rava offers a different rationale: *shelo yehei kodshei shamayim mutalim ke-nevelah* — so that sanctified objects of Heaven should not lie about like a carcass, half-flayed and unseemly. For Rava, it is not the practical concern of meat spoiling but rather the inappropriateness, the indignity, of leaving a sacred animal in such a state that justifies complete flaying.

### Meat vs. Kavod Kodashim

The practical difference between Rav Yosef and Rava can be illustrated in two cases. First: *de-manach aphtora de-dahava* — if the carcass is laid on a gold table, treated with great dignity, no one could claim it resembles a *nevelah*. This would resolve Rava's concern but not Rav Yosef's. One might ask, then, why according to Rava it would ever be necessary to flay completely — simply placing it on a gold table would solve the problem. Second: *yoma de-astana* — a day with a strong cold wind, as Rashi explains a north wind, that keeps the meat cool and prevents spoilage. This resolves Rav Yosef's concern but not Rava's.

A parallel is worth noting here. In the chapter of *Perek Rabbi Eliezer de-milah*, the *gemara* discusses performing a *brit milah* on *Shabbat*. The ruling there is that if the *mohel* is still in the process of performing the *milah*, he may continue removing small additional pieces of skin even if they would not render the *milah* invalid — because he is still mid-process. Once he has stopped, he may not return for those pieces. Similarly, here, once the broader activity of preparing the *korban Pesach* is sanctioned on *Shabbat*, even peripheral steps within that process may be included under certain conditions.

The *gemara* then asks: according to Rabbi Yishmael, what does he do with the verse *kol pa'al Hashem le-ma'anehu*? The verse must give him some latitude — he explains it as permitting flaying to the extent necessary for removing the *emurim*: *shelo yotzi imurim kodem she-yafshit ha-or* — one does not remove the innards before partially flaying the hide, because the wool or hair of the animal's skin would contaminate the innards if drawn out without first flaying. Rav Huna the son of Rav Natan explains the technical reason: the fleece or hair would get into the innards and render them unseemly. So Rabbi Yishmael grants latitude to flay insofar as it facilitates removing the *emurim* for the *mizbe'ach*, but no further.

---

## Sefer Torah Precedent

### Basis Distinction

Rav Ashi cites Mar Ukva: *mai hadru lei chavrayya le-Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka* — what did the colleagues say to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka to argue for greater latitude in the *korban Pesach* flaying? The tradition is that they invoked the *mishna* about saving *kitvei kodesh*, reasoning: *im matzilin tik hasefer im hasefer* — if we allow saving the container of a *sefer Torah* together with the *sefer Torah*, should we not permit *nafshit et hapesach meirosho*, flaying the *pesach* from its head completely?

The *gemara* immediately challenges: *mi dami* — how can these be compared? *Hasam tiltul* — there, by the *sefer Torah*, at most we are dealing with moving something, perhaps *muktzeh*, perhaps carrying into an imperfectly sanctioned *mavoi*, but in any case a rabbinic concern about *tiltul*. *Hacha melacha* — here we are discussing *melacha*, actual flaying, which would be a genuine biblical prohibition absent the override of the *korban Pesach*.

Rav Ashi therefore explains: *bitartei pligi* — actually there are two parallel debates by the *korban Pesach*. There is a *muktzeh* dimension — *pligi bitiltul* — and there is the *melacha* dimension — *pligi bimelacha*. The argument from the *mishna* is thus reformulated: *im matzilin tik hasefer im hasefer, lo nitaltel ora agav basar* — if one may carry the *sefer Torah* in its container, should one not be permitted to carry the skin together with the meat? According to Rashi, this addresses the case where the skin is still attached to the meat: the skin is *muktzeh* since it is not usable on *Shabbat*, and the question is whether it may be moved together with the meat. Tosafot disagrees with Rashi's framing, preferring a case where the skin is fully detached, with the argument being that one would use the flayed skin as a kind of carrier or wrapper for the meat — analogous to the *tik* of the *sefer Torah*.

The implication is that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka was arguing not only against complete flaying, but also against using the flayed skin to carry the meat. The colleagues countered from our *mishna*.

The *gemara* rejects this comparison: *hasam na'asa basis ledavar hamutar* — there, the container of the *sefer Torah* serves as a base for something permitted, the *sefer Torah* itself, which is not *muktzeh* at all. *Hacha na'asa basis ledavar ha'asur* — here the skin serves as a base for something forbidden. According to Rashi, the flesh is not edible on *Shabbat* since it is raw. Tosafot goes further: when *Shabbat* began, the animal was still alive, rendering its flesh *muktzeh* from that moment forward. The two cases are therefore fundamentally different.

### External Container

The *gemara* attempts yet another formulation of the argument: *ela hachi ka'amrei lei* — here is what they were actually saying. The *chiddush* of the *mishna* is not simply that one carries the *sefer Torah* in its container together with the money that happened to be inside. Rather, consider this scenario: one had no container around the *sefer Torah*, went to another room where there was a *sefer Torah* container that happened to have money in it, brought that container to the *sefer Torah*, placed the *sefer Torah* inside, and carried it out. In this case, when *Shabbat* began, the container held only money — not a *sefer Torah*. It was therefore a pure *basis ledavar ha'asur*. Yet the *gemara* assumes this too would be permitted, even though the *mishna* does not explicitly state it. And the argument to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka would be: if even this is permitted, should one not be allowed to carry the skin together with the meat, even though the meat is a *davar ha'asur*?

The *gemara* again asks: *ve-hi gufa minalan* — who told you this external-container scenario is actually permitted? If you derive it from the fact that in our *mishna* we did not require the person to shake the money out before saving the *sefer Torah*, that is because *ade-hachi ve-hachi nafla de-leika* — by the time you would do all that, the fire would have consumed everything. But in the external-container case, *ade-hachi ve-hachi lishtaiya* — before you got back with the container, all the money could simply have been tipped out. So the *gemara* at least implies that one should dump the money before bringing the container to the *sefer Torah*. If there is an alternative, one would be expected to use it.

This is why Tosafot insists the comparison must be to a case where the skin is fully flayed off and no longer attached: the argument is precisely that even when there is no other option for carrying the meat — just as there was no other option for saving the *sefer Torah* quickly — one should be permitted to use the skin even though it is a *basis ledavar ha'asur*.

### Rabbinical Labor

After these multiple failed attempts at comparison, the *gemara* arrives at its final resolution: *ella amar bar Abba Ashi le-olam ke-da-amran me-ikara* — really it was as originally said, focusing on the comparison between the *tiltul* allowance by the *sefer Torah* and the flaying of the *pesach*. How does the comparison work despite the objection that *tiltul* and *melacha* are categorically different?

The answer: *kegon de-lo kafid ella a-or* — the case is one where the person has no intention to use the hide, has no interest in the skin whatsoever. Flaying is only a biblical *melacha* when one intends to preserve the skin for use as leather. When one is solely interested in protecting the meat — or maintaining its dignity, in Rava's formulation — the flaying is only a rabbinic prohibition. And the *gemara* then adds: *de-shakil lei bevarzei* — furthermore, the flaying is done in tiny pieces, scraping off small bits of skin rather than removing one continuous piece. This eliminates even the possibility of *psik reisha*, since no usable piece of hide results. Abaye and Rava both rule that Rabbi Shimon concedes the rule of *psik reisha ve-lo yamut* — that even unintended but inevitable results are prohibited — but if no usable result is produced at all, that concern evaporates.

The rough comparison thus emerges: just as certain rabbinic concerns — some *muktzeh* considerations, some issues with carrying in a *mavoi* — are set aside to preserve sacred *sefarim*, so too certain rabbinic concerns around flaying are set aside to preserve the *korban Pesach*. The two cases remain distinguishable in many ways — not all rabbinic prohibitions are equivalent, and the contexts differ. But the general principle that we ease certain *derabbanans* to preserve something sacred is shared between them.

A further question is raised regarding the hide of the *korban Pesach* in general: since by other *korbanot* the *kohanim* receive the hides, what happens to the hide of the *pesach*, which goes entirely home with the owners? The answer is that the owner receives the hide as well, just as the owner receives the meat.

---

## Pesach Flaying Debat (II)

### Shinu'i: Small Pieces

As noted in the final resolution above, the *gemara* establishes that the flaying in the case of the *korban Pesach* must be performed *be-varzei* — by scraping off tiny pieces rather than removing the skin in one continuous motion. This *shinu'i* ensures that no usable piece of hide is produced and therefore eliminates the question of *psik reisha*. Since Abaye and Rava both hold that Rabbi Shimon concedes in a case of *psik reisha ve-lo yamut*, it is essential that the method of flaying produce no usable result. With this modification, the flaying is purely rabbinic in character, enabling the comparison to the *derabbanans* permitted by the *mishna* for saving *kitvei kodesh*.

---

## Mavoi Definitions

### Rav Chisda: Dual Lechaim

Returning to the *mishna*'s debate about where one may carry *kitvei kodesh*, the *gemara* now defines *mefulash* and *eino mefulash* in earnest. The *gemara* asks: *heichi dami mefulash, heichi dami she'eino mefulash* — what exactly do these terms mean? Rav Chisda offers a surprisingly restrictive definition. *Shalosh mechitzot u-shnei lechayayim* — three walls and two *lechaim* (vertical posts at the open end): that is a *mavoi she'eino mefulash*, a closed *mavoi*, one that is entirely in order for carrying. *Shalosh mechitzot ve-lechi echad* — three walls and only one *lechi*: that is a *mavoi mefulash*, an open *mavoi*. This is shocking on its face, since three walls with a single *lechi* is the standard requirement for rabbinic carrying in a *mavoi* according to the normative view of Beit Hillel.

The *gemara* explains that both positions in the *mishna* are *aliba de-Rabbi Eliezer*. Rabbi Eliezer, as taught in the *mishna* in Eruvin, requires *shenei lechayayim* — two posts, one on each side of the opening — in order to permit carrying in a *mavoi*. Beit Hillel requires only one *lechi* or a *korah* (a horizontal beam). So the debate in our *mishna* is understood entirely within Rabbi Eliezer's framework: the majority holds that even for *sifrei kodesh* the *mavoi* must meet Rabbi Eliezer's full standard — three walls and two *lechaim*. There is thus no great innovation, since carrying there is fully permitted. Ben Beteira then says he will be lenient even with only one *lechi*, which Rabbi Eliezer normally would not consider sufficient. The *gemara* is thus pushing the *mishna* to the most restrictive possible reading, anxious to limit the cases in which a rabbinic leniency is being granted on account of *kitvei kodesh*.

### Rava: Two Walls Model

Rava objects to Rav Chisda's interpretation on two grounds. First, the language: *gimmel mechitzot ve-lechi echad mefulash karyat lei* — you call three walls and one *lechi* a *mefulash*, an open-ended *mavoi*? That language suggests a space wide open on both ends, like a thoroughfare. Three walls and a single *lechi* is far from open-ended; calling it *mefulash* is a serious stretch. Second, according to the Sages who require two *lechaim*, carrying into a *mavoi* with two *lechaim* is permitted for anyone — there is nothing special about *sifrei kodesh* that would need to be mentioned. The *mishna* would be stating a trivial point.

Rava therefore proposes a different framework: *shetei mechitzot ve-shnei lechayayim ze mavoi she'eino mefulash* — two *mechitzot* with a *lechi* on each end is the *mavoi she'eino mefulash*. *Shetei mechitzot ve-lechi echad ze mavoi mefulash* — two *mechitzot* with only one *lechi* is the *mefulash*. Now the language *mefulash* is fully appropriate — a space with only two real walls and one post is genuinely open. This framework operates *aliba de-Rabbi Yehuda*, who holds an extremely permissive position. As taught in a *baraita*: if someone has two houses on two sides of a *reshut ha-rabim*, he may place a *lechi* or *korah* on each end — north and south — and carry in the middle, treating the space as enclosed despite it being a full thoroughfare. The Sages respond: *ein me'arvin reshut ha-rabim be-kach* — that does not constitute an *eiruv* for a *reshut ha-rabim* with only two real walls. But Rabbi Yehuda's position is that two walls with a *lechi* on each side are sufficient. Within that framework, Rava explains the debate: the majority requires two *lechaim* (one on each open end), while Ben Beteira permits even with only one *lechi*.

### Rav Ashi: Three Walls

Abaye presses Rava: even granting the language of *mefulash*, according to Rabbi Yehuda who permits carrying with two walls and a *lechi* on each side, if that is sufficient, why does the *mishna* present this as a special allowance for *sifrei kodesh* alone? According to the Sages within Rabbi Yehuda's framework, carrying would be permitted there for anyone. Tosafot anticipates this: Rava presumably holds that Rabbi Yehuda means two walls and two *lechaim* are sufficient only *de-oraita* but not necessarily *de-rabbanan*, so there remains a rabbinic concern that the leniency for *sifrei kodesh* addresses. Nevertheless, the objection stands that the *mishna*'s framing is peculiar.

Rav Ashi offers the final resolution: *shalosh mechitzot u-lechi echad ze mavoi she'eino mefulash* — three *mechitzot* with one *lechi* is the *eino mefulash*. *Shalosh mechitzot belo lechi ze mavoi ha-mefulash* — three walls with no *lechi* at all is the *mefulash*. This operates *afilu le-Rabbi Eliezer* — even within Rabbi Eliezer's framework. Rabbi Eliezer normally requires two *lechaim*. The allowance for *kitvei kodesh* is: *aval le-Sefer Torah be-chad lechi sagi* — for saving a *Sefer Torah*, one *lechi* suffices. And the debate with Ben Beteira is whether even no *lechi* at all — three bare walls with a fully open end — is permitted for saving *kitvei kodesh*.

The resolution is elegant on the linguistic level: *mefulash* naturally describes a space with three walls and nothing at the fourth end — genuinely open. And the debate remains within a three-wall framework throughout, since it is difficult to imagine allowing carrying without three walls absent the radical position of Rabbi Yehuda. Even Ben Beteira requires three walls; he only dispenses with the *lechi* requirement entirely.

What is striking about this entire discussion is how modest the actual allowance for *kitvei kodesh* turns out to be. Carrying the *sefer Torah* with its container that happened to have money: that was *tiltul min hatzad* and *basis ledavar mutar u-ledavar asur*, which under normal circumstances is not really problematic. The innovation with respect to carrying is limited to one fewer *lechi* than normally required, or possibly no *lechi* at all — but always with three walls. The *gemara* resists giving any dramatic license for *kitvei kodesh* and works hard to minimize the rabbinic deviation involved. The deeper point will emerge as the discussion turns to food: the real concern is not how much rabbinic latitude is extended but rather the fear that the person, in his anxiety, will cross a line and extinguish the fire.

---

## Food Salvage Rules

### Mishna: Three Seudos

The *gemara* transitions to the next *mishna*: *matzilin mazon shalosh se'udot* — one may save food for three meals. Human food is saved for a person, animal food for animals. The three-meal rule reflects the *Shabbat* obligation of eating three meals, a topic that will be developed further.

The *mishna* specifies: *naflah deleikah beleilei Shabbat* — if the fire broke out on Friday night, one may save food for three meals. *Beshacharit* — if it broke out in the morning, only two meals, since one meal has already passed. *Bemincha* — if it broke out at *Mincha* time, only one meal, since only one remains before *Shabbat* ends. The assumption is that once *Shabbat* is over one can prepare fresh food. Rabbi Yosi disagrees: *le'olam matzilin mazon shalosh seudos* — regardless of when the fire breaks out, one may always save food for three meals, since three meals is the sanctioned *Shabbat* food quantity in all circumstances.

### Gezerah: Overzealousness

The *gemara* asks a pointed question: since the food is not *muktzeh* and, as Rashi emphasizes in contrast to the *kitvei kodesh* case, the courtyard into which the food is brought is fully kosher for carrying — why limit how much can be saved? *Nitzil tfei* — let one save as much as possible. Rava answers: *mitoch she'adam bahul al mamono* — because a person is so anxious and pressured about his monetary loss, *ai sharis lei asi le-chabbuyei* — if you permit him too broadly, he will become so consumed with salvaging everything that he will come to extinguish the fire. The restriction to three *seudos* is a *gezerah* to prevent this. If you tell him: grab three *seudos* and leave, he will hopefully not lose sight of *Shabbat* in his panic.

This creates an interesting asymmetry: on one side, we extend certain leniencies — permitting carrying into a *mavoi* that lacks the normally required *lechaim* — and on the other side, we impose restrictions — limiting food salvage — all animated by the same concern about the person's behavior during a crisis.

A brief note on contemporary practice: *lehalacha* we are considerably more permissive regarding extinguishing fires on *Shabbat* due to *sakana*, the danger to life, which raises the question of why those concerns were apparently not operative in the *gemara*'s context. One plausible answer is that stone houses with dirt floors, which were the norm in the ancient *Eretz Yisrael* setting and perhaps even more so under Roman occupation where fire brigades existed, simply did not burn in the way that later wooden structures in *Ashkenaz* did.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye raises a parallel: a *baraita* teaches that if a barrel of wine broke on one's roof on *Shabbat*, one may place a single vessel underneath to catch the spilling wine — *mavi kli u-maniach tachteha* — but one may not hold a vessel to catch the drip, nor bring additional vessels to collect what is flowing off the roof. One may perform this one-time act of placing a vessel, but not engage in an ongoing salvage operation. Abaye asks: here there is no fire, nothing being extinguished — what *gezerah* is at work? The *gemara* answers: *gezeira shema yavi kli derech reshut ha-rabim* — we are concerned that in the course of a full salvage operation, the person will bring vessels through a *reshut ha-rabim*, constituting a biblical carrying violation. The parallel underscores a broader rabbinic concern about letting people engage in extended emergency salvage operations, lest they inadvertently commit more serious violations in their haste.

---

## Wine Barrel Salvage

### One vs. Multiple Vessels

The *gemara* now examines the barrel case in its own right. *Nishbera lo chavis be-rosh gago* — a barrel broke on one's roof. *Mevi kli u-maniach tachtav* — one may bring a vessel and place it underneath. But one may not bring another vessel to catch the drip, nor a second vessel to position at the edge of the roof so the wine streams into it as it flows. Placing a vessel beneath the barrel is a single discrete act; anything that looks like an ongoing, organized salvage effort is prohibited.

### Guest Exception

The *baraita* continues: *nizdamnu lo orchim* — if guests unexpectedly arrive, one may now bring additional vessels and collect the wine, since one is ostensibly doing so to serve guests, not to conduct a salvage operation. But: *lo yiklot ve-achar kach yazmin* — one may not first collect and then invite guests. Rather, *yazmin ve-achar kach yiklot* — one must first invite the guests and then collect. Even then, the *baraita* says: *ve-ein maarimin be-kach* — one may not scheme. That is, one may not invite guests as a calculated ruse to justify collecting wine.

### Scheming Debate

Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda disagrees: *maarimin* — one may scheme in this case. The wine is going to waste, and since the underlying concern is merely rabbinic, scheming to prevent monetary loss is acceptable here.

The *gemara* observes that this seems to parallel a broader *tannaitic* debate about *ha'arama* — scheming — in *halacha*, a significant topic that appears across various contexts, from selling *chametz* before *Pesach* to transferring a firstborn animal's ear to a non-Jew. The question of when *halacha* permits, ignores, or prohibits such schemes is a recurring theme.

---

## Pit Animals Analogy

### Mother & Offspring

The *gemara* wonders whether the debate about *ha'arama* in the barrel case mirrors the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding animals that fell into a pit on *Yom Tov*. The *baraita*: *oso ve-et beno she-naflu le-vor be-Yom Tov* — a mother and its offspring fell into a pit on *Yom Tov*. Under normal circumstances, one may not slaughter both on the same day. Rabbi Eliezer says: *ma'aleh et ha-rishon al menat le-shochto* — bring up the first one with the intention of slaughtering it. Then the second one: one may lower food to it where it is, *bishvil she-lo yamut*, so it does not die, but one may not raise it out of the pit, since there is no justification for *shechting* it that day. Rabbi Yehoshua says: bring up the first one declaring intent to slaughter it, then once it is out of the pit, say: actually, I prefer the second one — and scheme to bring the second one up as well. *Ratzah zeh shochet, ratzah zeh shochet* — then one may slaughter either one. Rabbi Yehoshua even goes so far as to permit changing one's mind back to the first animal after the second is already out.

### Alternatives Analysis

The *gemara* cautions against a simple equation of these two debates. Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer's objection to scheming by the animals is specific to that case: *de-efshar be-parnasa* — there is a reasonable alternative, namely lowering food to the animal. Since an alternative exists that prevents any loss to the animal, there is no justification for the scheme. *Aval hacha de-lo efshar* — but in the barrel case, where the wine will simply be destroyed with no alternative, even Rabbi Eliezer might permit scheming. Conversely, Rabbi Yehoshua may permit scheming by the animals not only because of monetary loss but because of *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* — the prohibition against causing suffering to animals, who are sitting at the bottom of a pit. *Aval hacha de-leika tza'ar ba'alei chayim* — in the barrel case, where there is no animal suffering involved, Rabbi Yehoshua might not permit scheming. The two debates thus cannot simply be collapsed into one. Different *tannaim* may take different positions depending on the particular factors at play, and one cannot assume consistency across all cases of *ha'arama*.

---

## Food Salvage Details

### Bread Quality Hierarchy

The *gemara* returns to the salvage of food from a fire and addresses a further *baraita*. *Hitzeipa nikiya* — if one saved fine bread first, *ein matzipin pat hadraah* — one may not subsequently go back to save coarser bran bread. Once you have fine bread for your three meals, who would eat bran bread? There is no purpose in saving it. However: *aval pat hadraah, matzipin nikiya* — if one first saves bran bread, one may then go back and save fine bread as well, since the three meals of bran bread are insufficient, and one may reasonably claim to want better-quality bread for *Shabbat*.

### Holiday Boundaries

The *baraita* continues: *matzilin mi-Yom ha-Kippurim le-Shabbat* — one may save food on *Yom Kippur* for *Shabbat*, in the case where *Yom Kippur* falls on Friday and *Shabbat* immediately follows, since one will have no opportunity to prepare *Shabbat* food and *hachana* from *Yom Kippur* to *Shabbat* is not problematic in this direction. *Aval lo mi-Shabbat le-Yom ha-Kippurim* — but one may not save from *Shabbat* for *Yom Kippur*, since one cannot eat on *Yom Kippur*, and for *motzaei Yom Kippur* there will be time to prepare. *Ve-ein tzarich lomar mi-Shabbat le-Yom Tov* — needless to say, one may not save from *Shabbat* for *Yom Tov*, since *Yom Tov* permits food preparation. *Ve-lo mi-Shabbat le-Shabbat ha-ba'ah* — nor from one *Shabbat* to the following *Shabbat*, since six intervening days allow for preparation. One may, however, save on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat*, since one cannot prepare food on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* may be *mechin le-Shabbat*.

Tosafot raises a question: why would one think it is permitted to save from *Shabbat* to *motzaei Yom Kippur*? After all, *motzaei Yom Kippur* is an ordinary weekday and one does not save from *Shabbat* to a weekday — just as one does not save from *Shabbat* to *motzaei Shabbat*. Tosafot answers: there is a *mitzvah* to eat immediately upon the conclusion of *Yom Kippur*, and one might have thought that this *mitzvah* constitutes sufficient justification. Moreover, given the fast, there is an added concern about delaying the resumption of eating. Alternatively, the case concerns saving food *for Yom Kippur itself* — not for after it — to feed children, who must be fed even on *Yom Kippur*.

### Forgotten Bread

Another *baraita*: *shachach pat be-tanur ve-kiddesh alav ha-yom* — one forgot bread in the oven and *Shabbat* came in. Taking bread out of an oven — *rediyat ha-pat* — is rabbinically prohibited. The *tanna de-bei Rabbi Yishmael* teaches that *rediyat ha-pat* is a *chochma* — a skilled activity — but not a *melacha*, and therefore the prohibition is purely rabbinic. Nevertheless, normally this rabbinic restriction is in force on *Shabbat*.

The question is: does the imperative to have food for *Shabbat* override this rabbinic prohibition? The *baraita* rules: *matzilin mazon shalosh seudos* — yes, one may remove bread from the oven to save three *seudos* worth. This is quite striking, going considerably further than the *mishna*, which never sanctioned the violation of a *derabbanan*. Furthermore: *ve-omer la-acherim, bo'u ve-hatzilu lachem* — one may even announce to others that they may come and save food for themselves. People may thus come and collectively save large quantities of bread, each taking for themselves three meals' worth.

However: *u-keshe-hu rodeh, lo yirdeh be-mardeia* — when removing the bread, do not use the normal baker's shovel that is the standard implement. *Ela be-sakin* — use a knife instead. This *shinu'i* is required. The *gemara* asks: *eini* — is the *shinu'i* really necessary? Since *rediyat ha-pat* is only rabbinic, is it not already permitted in its normal form? The *gemara* answers: *kama de-efshar li-shnuyei meshaninnan* — wherever possible, we prefer to introduce a *shinu'i*. Even when a rabbinic prohibition is being overridden for a legitimate reason, one does not do it in the normal forbidden manner if an alternative mode is available. The *gemara* is thus quite strict in demanding the *shinu'i* even where the underlying activity is already rabbinic. Notably, the very idea that one might not require the *shinu'i* — since the entire prohibition is only rabbinic — is itself a striking position that has no explicit precedent in the *mishna*.

---

## Shabbat Meals

### Friday Preparation

From the salvage discussion the *gemara* transitions naturally to the laws of eating on *Shabbat*. Rav Chisda teaches: *le-olam yashkim adam le-hotza'at Shabbat* — a person should always rise early to spend money on *Shabbat* expenses. The verse states: *ve-haya ba-yom ha-shishi ve-hachinu et asher yavi'u* — on the sixth day they prepared what they would bring. The word *ve-haya* implies immediacy: the very first activity of Friday morning should be preparing for *Shabbat*.

### Lechem Mishneh

Rabbi Abba teaches: *be-Shabbat chayav adam livtzoa al shtei kikarot* — on *Shabbat* one is obligated to break bread over two loaves, the *lechem mishneh*. The source is the *manna*, where the verse records that a double portion fell on Friday. The biblical precedent of *lechem mishneh* thus mandates that one hold two loaves when making *hamotzi* on *Shabbat*.

### Rav Kahana Practice

Rav Ashi reports: *chazina lei le-Rav Kahana de-nakit tartei u-vatza chada* — I observed Rav Kahana hold both loaves when reciting *hamotzi* but break into only one of them. He explained his reasoning from the verse: *liktot ksiv* — the word used is *liktot*, to gather. One is required to hold the two loaves, not necessarily to break into both. This is the common practice of holding both loaves while breaking only one, saving the other for a subsequent meal.

### Rabbi Zeira Custom

Rabbi Zeira had a different custom: *hava vatza akula sheirusa* — he would break bread on every item he was serving at the beginning of the meal, and Rashi explains further that he would cut a portion large enough to last the entire meal. Ravina asked Rav Ashi: *ve-amichzei ke-ravtanusa* — does this not look like gluttony, to have this enormous chunk of bread before him? Rav Ashi replied: *keivan de-chol yoma lo avid, ve-ha'idna hu de-ka avid, lo michzei ke-ravtanusa* — since this is not what one normally does on other days and is done specifically now, it does not look like gluttony. It appears, rather, as something done for *kavod Shabbat*, as part of the lavish and distinguished character of the *Shabbat* meal.

### Eiruv Bread Use

Rav Ammi and Rav Assi had another practice: *ki matlu lehu rifta de-eiruva* — when the bread used for making an *eiruv* was brought to them — whether *eiruv chatzeirot* or, by analogy for our practice, *eiruv tavshilin* — *sharu lei*, they would eat it and begin their meal with it. Their reasoning: *ho'il ve-is'avid bah chada mitzvah, lis'avid bah mitzvah achrina* — since one *mitzvah* has already been performed with this bread, let another *mitzvah* be performed with it as well. They would therefore use the *eiruv* bread specifically for their *Shabbat* meal. Some maintain this practice specifically, using the *eiruv* bread for *shalosh seudos* or some other *oneg Shabbat* purpose, in order to honor the bread that performed one *mitzvah* by giving it another. The discussion of related *mitzvot* of eating on *Shabbat* will continue.

---

---

# Shabbat 117

## Sefer Torah 85 Letters

### 85 Letters Overview

The daf opens by continuing a discussion about a *sefer Torah* that retains eighty-five letters scattered throughout it. Such a *sefer Torah* maintains the status of *kedushat sefer Torah* and would be rescued on *Shabbat*. This principle is derived from the passage of *Vayehi Binsoa Ha'aron*, which functions as a kind of independent mini-*sefer Torah* in its own right, given that it contains exactly eighty-five letters.

### Rabban Shimon View

The *Gemara* now asks: *man tanna de-palig alei de-Rabbi* — who is the *tanna* that disagrees with Rabbi's position regarding the *Vayehi Binsoa* passage as an independent *sefer Torah*? The answer is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. As a *baraita* teaches: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that eventually — in the era of *yemos hamashiach* — this *parsha* will be relocated and written in its proper place. According to this view, it does not belong in *Parshat Naso* but in *Bamidbar*, where the arrangement of the *degalim* and the movements of the camps are described. Why then was it written where it is? *Kedei lehafzik bein puraniyot rishona le-puraniyot sheniya* — in order to separate between the first set of transgressions and punishments and the second set.

### Two Punishments

The second *puraniyot* is clear: immediately after *Vayehi Binsoa Ha'aron*, the Torah states *vayehi ha'am kemit'onenim* — the people began to complain, demanding food and water and eventually meat, as is described at length in this week's *parsha*. But what is the first *puraniyot*? The verse immediately preceding *Vayehi Binsoa Ha'aron* states *vayisu me-har Hashem* — they traveled from the mountain of God.

### Departure Complaint

Rabbi Hama bar Hanina expounds: *she-saru me-acharei Hashem* — that in departing from *Har Sinai*, they had already turned away from God. Even the very act of departure carried within it a sense of abandonment.

### Rashi Tosafot

Rashi, commenting on the phrase *me-acharei Hashem*, explains that within three days of their journey, the *asafsuf* — the mixed multitude — had already begun to crave and desire, and this craving represents the beginning of the process that would culminate in the explicit demand for meat. According to Rashi, it was one continuous process: the desiring began the moment they left *Har Sinai* and reached its culmination when they declared *lama zeh yatzanu mi-Mitzrayim*. The *Vayehi Binsoa* passage serves to introduce a pause into that process.

Tosafot, however, questions Rashi's explanation (referred to as *bakuntres*) and offers a different reading of *puraniyot rishona* in the name of the *Ri*. Rather than referring to the beginning of the craving, Tosafot cites a *midrash*: *vayisu she-nas'u me-Har Sinai derech sheloshet yamim ke-tinok ha-yotzei mi-beit ha-sefer* — they traveled from *Har Sinai* like a child running out of school when the day is done, *she-boreach lo ve-holech lo*, fleeing and going on their way. They ran from *Har Sinai* because they had absorbed so much Torah there and were eager to be free of it. It is this unseemly haste in departing — this flight from the mountain of God — that constitutes the first *puraniyot*. Against that backdrop, *Vayehi Binsoa* introduces a note of order and divine accompaniment: *kuma Hashem ve-yafutzu oyvecha* — even within the movement of the camp, there is a sense of following God rather than fleeing Him.

One might ask: if the text would have read as entirely positive without this interpretive framework — since the passage about Jethro and the invitation *telech imanu* that precedes it is encouraging in tone — is the rabbinic reading perhaps artificially creating a problem in order to offer an artificial solution? Furthermore, since there is a second and arguably a third *puraniyot* that follow in close succession — the *mitonim* and then the *asafsuf asher bekirbo hit'avu ta'avah* — why not place the separator between those? The response to this is that the rabbis were responding to two distinct observations: first, the *nuns* that precede and follow the passage, which bracket it off from its surroundings and demand explanation; and second, a genuine sense that the passage would have fit more naturally in the earlier chapters of *Bamidbar* where the movements of the camps are described. Whether the answers offered are fully satisfying remains open to discussion.

### Proper Location

The *Gemara* asks *heichan mekomah* — where does this passage truly belong? Rav Ashi answers: *bidgalim* — among the description of the camps and their arrangement, a *parsha* earlier in *Bamidbar*, where the basic structure of travel and movement is laid out. That concludes the discussion of a *sefer Torah* retaining eighty-five letters. The question of whether those eighty-five letters must appear in one place or may be scattered remains a matter of debate, left unresolved.

---

## Gilyonim Status

### Margin Question

The *Gemara* now turns to a new question: *ha-gilyonim shel sefer Torah* — what is the status of the margins of a *sefer Torah*? *Matzilim otan mipnei hadleka o ein matzilim otan mipnei hadleka* — do we rescue the blank margins from a fire on *Shabbat*, or do we not?
