# Shabbat 119

## Kavod & Oneg Shabbat

### Previous Kavod Shabbat

We pick up on 119b, six lines down in the wide lines. The previous daf opened a rich discussion centered on *kavod Shabbat* and *oneg Shabbat* — the twin obligations of honoring and enjoying the Shabbat. A central theme was that it is not enough merely to have preparations completed; the *Rishonim* and *Amoraim* emphasize the importance of personal involvement in the act of preparation itself, as one would invest in receiving an important guest. There was also a nuanced discussion about dress during the preparation process — whether one should don fine clothing befitting the day or more workmanlike attire suited to the physical labor of preparing. Even the question of appropriate dress for one's *kavod Shabbat* preparations is treated as a substantive issue rather than a mere aside. This is the broader context within which the following discussion unfolds: the laws of eating and honoring Shabbat.

### Yosef Mokir Shabbat

The famous *aggadata* of *Yosef Mokir Shabbat* — Yosef who honors Shabbat — was treated in detail on the previous daf. The story illustrates not only the reward for honoring Shabbat but the spiritual logic behind personal investment in its observance: when a person throws himself into the preparations with genuine enthusiasm, it reflects an internalized appreciation of Shabbat's sanctity that no mere delegation of tasks can replicate.

## Fire & Shabbat Desecrati…

### Fire & Chillul Shabbat

*Amar Rav Yehuda berei de-Rav Shmuel mishmei de-Rav*: Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Shmuel said in the name of Rav: *ein hadlaka metzuya bemakom she-yesh chillul Shabbat* — fire is only prevalent in a place where Shabbat is desecrated. This statement ties directly into the broader discussion of fire breaking out on Shabbat, which is the formal topic of the *sugya* — namely, what food may be saved when a fire breaks out. Having established great praise for those who honor Shabbat, and having noted that if Israel were to keep two Shabbatot in full observance redemption would come immediately, the *Gemara* now turns to the rhetorical counterpart: the negative consequences of *chillul Shabbat*. The pivot is natural, as the very scenario of a fire on Shabbat invites the question of causation.

### Jeremiah Verse

The source for Rav Yehuda's statement is the verse in Yirmiyahu: *ve-im lo tishme'u elai lekadesh es yom ha-Shabbat ve-lavitasei masa* — if you do not listen to Me to sanctify the Shabbat and to refrain from carrying burdens — *ve-hitzati esh be-sha'areha ve-achla armonot Yerushalayim velo tichbe* — then I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it will consume the towers of Jerusalem, and it will not be extinguished.

### Nachman: Fire Not Put Out

The *Gemara* asks: *mai velo tichbe* — what is the meaning of the phrase "it will not be extinguished"? *Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak*: *be-sha'ah she-ein bnei adam metzuyin le-khabotah* — it will occur at a time when people are not around to put it out, so that it continues to burn. Presumably that time is Shabbat itself, when people are in *shul* and not positioned to fight a fire.

### Midda Kneged Midda

This constitutes a measure of *midda keneged midda* — measure for measure — for not keeping Shabbat. One might ask whether statements of this kind are meant literally as divine retribution, or metaphorically as rhetorical exhortation to greater observance. They are clearly punitive in nature, not descriptive. It is important to note the danger in applying this kind of rhetoric retroactively as a form of *onaat devarim* — causing pain through words — by blaming individuals or communities for tragedies that befall them. The *Gemara*'s intent is plainly to encourage observance, not to provide a framework for finger-pointing at those who suffer. The arrogance of claiming to know precisely how divine providence operates, combined with the cruelty of compounding someone's tragedy with blame, makes such after-the-fact attribution deeply problematic — even if the *Gemara* itself speaks in these terms as a hortatory device.

## Jerusalem's Destruction

### Abbaye: Shabbat Violation

*Amar Abbaye*: *lo charva Yerushalayim ella bishvil she-chillalu bah es ha-Shabbat* — Jerusalem was only destroyed because Shabbat was desecrated within it. The verse cited is: *umishabbotosai he'elimu eineihem* — from My Shabbatot they averted their eyes — *ve-achel betocham* — and I began destruction in their midst. The language of *ve-achel* here connects to the root of *le-hatchil*, beginning, the commencement of devastation.

### Rabbi Abbahu: Shema

*Amar Rabbi Abbahu*: *lo charva Yerushalayim ella bishvil she-bitlu keri'at shema shachrit va-arvit* — Jerusalem was destroyed only because they ceased to recite the *shema* in the morning and in the evenings. The verse cited is: *hoi mashkimei vavoker shechar yirdofu* — woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue intoxicating drink. The continuation of the passage reads: *ve-haya kinnor va-nevel ve-tof ve-chalil ve-yayin mishtehem* — and there was harp, lute, drum, flute, and wine at their feasts — *ve-et po'al Hashem lo yabitu* — but they do not look at the work of God. And then: *lachen gala ami mi-bli da'at* — therefore My people was exiled for lack of knowledge.

Rashi explains this last phrase with reference to the declaration of God's unity — *meyached shemo*, the proclamation of *Hashem Echad*. The broader reading, however, encompasses something more: a failure to perceive God's presence in the world, which is precisely what the *berakhot* surrounding *shema* in *shacharit* are about — *yotzer ha-me'orot*, the creation of light, *ma'aseh bereishit*, the ongoing creation. Instead of cultivating this awareness, the people pursued pleasure.

What is striking about this shift in the *Gemara* is the move to what might seem like a relatively minor infraction — neglecting *keriat shema* — in the context of explaining a national catastrophe. The point may be precisely that before one focuses on gross violations, it is worth identifying the smaller failures that are foundational to the entire religious orientation. A lack of that bedrock awareness of God in the world — the very thing *shema* is designed to cultivate morning and evening — is what ultimately opens the door to the larger spiritual and moral collapse that leads to destruction.

### Rav Hamnuna: Education

*Amar Rav Hamnuna*: *lo charva Yerushalayim ella bishvil she-bitlu bah tinokot shel beit rabban* — Jerusalem was destroyed because the schoolchildren who attended religious instruction were prevented from learning. The verse is: *shefoch al olel bachutz* — pour out wrath upon the suckling in the street. The *Gemara* interprets: *ma ta'am shefoch? Mishum de-olel bachutz* — why is wrath poured out? Because the children are outside rather than in school where they should be.

This too fits the pattern of the preceding statements: perhaps a community is diligent in observance, perhaps it respects authority, but if it does not invest sufficiently in the Jewish education of the next generation, it reveals a fundamental indifference to continuity and to the weight of Torah as the animating force of communal life. That indifference ultimately erodes everything else. It is worth noting that this teaching was eventually translated into practical law: the *Rambam* records in *Hilkhot Talmud Torah* that school children may not be dismissed from learning even for the purpose of building the *Beit HaMikdash* — a legal ruling that reflects how seriously the *Gemara* takes this principle.

### Ulla: Shame

*Amar Ulla*: *lo charva Yerushalayim ela mipnei she-lo haya lahem boshet panim ze mi-ze* — Jerusalem was destroyed because they had no shame before one another for acting improperly. The verse is: *hovishu ki to'evah asu, gam bosh lo yevoshu* — they should have been ashamed, for they committed an abomination, yet they are not ashamed. When a basic sense of shame for misconduct disappears from a society, the practical restraint that shame provides disappears with it. Here again the common denominator with the preceding statements becomes clear: these are not descriptions of some spectacular transgression, but of characterological and attitudinal failures — a way of being in the world that removes the internal and social brakes on sin.

### Rav Yitzchak: Status

*Amar Rav Yitzchak*: *lo charva Yerushalayim ella bishvil she-hushvu katan ve-gadol* — Jerusalem was destroyed because they equated the small with the great, failing to recognize and appropriately honor differences in stature and merit. The verse cited is: *ve-haya kha'am ka-kohen* — the people were like the *kohen* — indicating a total flattening of distinction between laity and religious leadership, a kind of radical equality that left no room even for meritocracy. The continuation — *ve-acharav ha-bok tibok* — signals the inevitable emptying out that follows.

### Rabbi Chanina: Tochacha

*Amar Rav Amram brei de-Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, amar Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, amar Rabbi Chanina*: *lo charva Yerushalayim ella bishvil she-lo hochichu ze et ze* — Jerusalem was destroyed because people did not give *tochacha* — remonstrance — to one another. By failing to rebuke one another's misconduct, people both lose their own sensitivity to what is wrong and implicitly endorse the behavior of others through silence.

The verse cited is: *hayu sareha ke-ayalim lo matze'u mir'eh* — its officers were like harts that found no pasture. The *Gemara* explains: *ma ayal ze rosho shel ze be-tzad zanavo shel ze* — just as harts walk in a line with each head at the tail of the one before it — *af Yisrael she-be-oto dor kavshu pneihem ba-karka, ve-lo hochichu ze et ze* — so too in that generation, everyone buried their faces in the ground and did not look one another in the eye, and thus did not rebuke one another. This failure of moral courage and mutual accountability then led to compounding sin.

### Rav Yehuda: Respect Torah

*Amar Rav Yehuda*: *lo charva Yerushalayim ella bishvil she-bizu bah talmidei chachamim* — Jerusalem was destroyed because they showed contempt for Torah scholars within it. This is closely related to the earlier point about equating the small and the great: when *talmidei chachamim* are not accorded appropriate respect, it reflects a denigration of Torah itself and of its authority over communal life. The verse is: *va-yihyu mal'ivim be-mal'achei ha-Elohim, u-vozim devaro, u-misa'ta'im bi-nvi'av, ad alot chamat Hashem be-amo, ad le-ein marpe* — they mocked God's emissaries, disdained His word, and scorned His prophets, until the anger of God rose against His people, until there was no remedy.

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: *kol ha-mevazeh talmid chacham ein lo refu'ah le-makato* — whoever denigrates a *talmid chacham*, the wound he incurs will have no healing — a direct reading of the phrase *ad le-ein marpe*.

The *Gemara* then draws on an additional verse: *al tigu bi-meshichai u-vi-nvi'ai al tera'u* — do not touch My anointed ones, and do not harm My prophets. *Alu tinokot shel beit rabban* — "My anointed ones" refers to the schoolchildren, who were anointed with oil as part of their initiation into learning, as Rashi notes. *Ve-elu talmidei chachamim* — "My prophets" refers to the Torah sages. Both sets of statements converge: whether one speaks of the youngest children in *cheder* or the most accomplished scholars, the disregard for Torah and its bearers at every level is the thread connecting all of these explanations for Jerusalem's destruction.

## School Children & Torah

### Reish Lakish: Children's…

*Amar Reish Lakish mishum Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah* — Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah, grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: *ein olam miskayem ella bishvil hevel tinokot shel beit rabban* — the world only continues to exist by virtue of the breath of schoolchildren, the pure, innocent words of Torah emerging from their mouths.

### Papa & Abaye Dispute

*Amar lei Rav Papa le-Abaye*: *didi ve-didach mai?* — what about our Torah learning, does it not similarly sustain the world? The response: *eino domeh hevel she-yesh bo cheit le-hevel she-ein bo cheit* — breath that is accompanied by sin is not comparable to breath that is without sin. There is a quality of innocence and purity in the learning of children who have not yet sinned that gives their Torah a distinctive power — not merely intellectual achievement, but something about moral innocence that sustains the world and gives it hope for the future.

### School Priority

*Ve-amar Reish Lakish mishum Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah*: *ein mevatlin tinokot shel beit rabban afilu le-vinyan Beit HaMikdash* — one does not dismiss schoolchildren from their learning even for the sake of building the *Beit HaMikdash*. While much of this discussion has the character of *derasha* and *aggadata*, the *Rambam* codifies this principle as practical *halakha* in *Hilkhot Talmud Torah* — that children remain in school even if the Temple is being built. So seriously does the *Gemara* take the continuity of Torah education.

### City Without School

*Ve-amar Reish Lakish mishum Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah*: *kach mekublani me-avotai* — here is the tradition I received from my forefathers (and some say he attributed it to *Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah*'s own forefathers, presumably *Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi*): *kol ir she-ein bah tinokot shel beit rabban, machrivin otah* — any city that does not have schoolchildren — that has not established a *cheder*, a Jewish school — will be destroyed. *Ravina* adds that the word is not merely *machrivin* — destruction — but *machrimin otah*, invoking *cherem*, a total and more severe form of destruction, conveying an even greater gravity.

## Trustworthiness & Ethics

### Rava: Trustworthy People

*Ve-amar Rava*: *lo charva Yerushalayim ella bishvil she-pasku mimena anshei emunah* — Jerusalem was destroyed because trustworthy people, people of integrity, ceased to dwell within it. This shifts the discussion from the realm of Torah and its study to a more general statement about basic moral character and faithfulness.

### Jeremiah: One Honest Per…

The verse cited is from Yirmiyahu: *shotetu be-chutzot Yerushalayim u-re'u na, u-de'u u-vakshu bi-rchovoteha, im timtze'u ish oseh mishpat, mevakesh emunah, ve-eslach lah* — roam through the streets of Jerusalem and look, seek in its public squares — can you find even one person who acts with justice, who seeks faithfulness? If so, I will forgive it. The implication is that no such person could be found, and therefore it was destroyed. This connects back thematically to earlier material in the *sugya* about *shomer emunim* — keeping faith — and the importance of trustworthiness as a foundational civic and spiritual virtue.

### Ketina: Exception

The *Gemara* challenges: *eini?* — is that really true? *Ve-amar Rav Ketina*: *afilu be-sha'at kishlonah shel Yerushalayim, lo pasku mimena anshei emunah* — even at the time of Jerusalem's stumbling and decline, trustworthy people did not altogether cease. The verse cited is: *ki yitpos ish be-achiv beit aviv, simlah lecha katzin tihyeh lanu* — a man will grab his kinsman from his father's house and say: you have a cloak, be our ruler. The *Gemara* explains the verse's imagery: the "cloak" (*simlah*) refers to *devarim she-bnei adam mitkasim bahem ke-simlah* — matters that people conceal within themselves as a garment conceals the body — meaning, you possess Torah knowledge that you keep hidden. *Yeshnan be-yadecha* — you have this. You should therefore be our leader.

### Rejected Leader Parable

The verse continues: *ve-ha-machshelah hazot tachat yadecha* — and this stumbling is under your hand. The *Gemara* interprets: *devarim she-ein bnei adam omdim aleihem ela im ken nichshalim bahem* — matters so difficult that people cannot truly grasp them without first making mistakes and learning from those errors. The people are saying to this individual: you possess both the concealed knowledge — the fundamentals — and the hard-won understanding that comes only through struggle. Be our leader, our *talmid chacham*.

To this the man responds with an oath: *yisa ba-yom ha-hu le-emor lo eheyeh chovesh* — he will take an oath on that day, saying: I will not be bound. *Ein yisa ela leshon shevuah* — *yisa* here is oath language, as in *lo tisa et shem Hashem Elokecha*. And he explains: *lo eheyeh me-chovshei atzman be-veit ha-midrash* — I am not among those who bind themselves to their seat in the *beit midrash*. You are mistaken about me. *U-ve-veiti ein lechem ve-ein simlah* — in my house there is no bread and no cloak — *she-ein be-yadi lo mikra ve-lo mishnah ve-lo Gemara* — I have neither Scripture nor Mishnah nor Gemara. I am not who you think I am.

The point of the entire *derasha*: this man, when pressured to claim a position of leadership on the basis of Torah scholarship he does not possess, refuses to lie. He openly declares his ignorance. This demonstrates that even in the period of Jerusalem's decline, there existed people of basic honesty.

### Torah vs. Business

The *Gemara* probes: *u-mimai* — but how does this prove trustworthiness? *Dilma shani hasam di-amru lei gmirna, amru lei eima lan* — perhaps he is not refusing to lie out of genuine honesty, but rather out of self-interest: if he claims to be a *talmid chacham*, they will immediately demand that he deliver a *Gemara shiur*, and he cannot. So he is simply avoiding an untenable position.

The *Gemara* responds: *hava lei le-meimar gmar ve-shachach* — if his concern were self-image rather than truth, he could have simply said: "You're right, I was once learned, but I have forgotten." That would have gotten him out of the difficulty without full disclosure. The fact that he admits to never having possessed Torah knowledge at all demonstrates genuine honesty.

The *Gemara* then resolves the apparent contradiction between Rava's statement — that Jerusalem was destroyed because trustworthy people ceased — and the evidence that even in its decline, at least some honest people could be found: *lo kashya, kan be-divrei Torah, kan be-masa u-matan* — there is no difficulty. In matters of Torah, perhaps people retained enough residual respect for Torah that they would not lie about their learning. In business dealings, where the *yetzer ha-ra* is stronger and the temptations greater, they ceased to be trustworthy — and that is what ultimately brought about the destruction.

This is a striking resolution. The *sugya* begins with the centrality of Shabbat observance and the respect for Torah, and ends with the observation that even when other forms of honesty remained, the destruction came from a basic failure of commercial integrity — the loss of faithfulness in everyday economic life. While the earlier causes focused on observance and Torah, the final cause points to fundamental morality and *emunah* in human dealings as the cornerstone without which a community cannot endure.

## Saving Food Rules

### Basket of Bread

The *Gemara* now returns to the practical *sugya* of saving food during a fire on Shabbat, moving from the quantity limitation of three meals to more specific rules. The *Mishnah* states: *matzilim sal malei kikarot af al pi she-yesh bah meah seudot* — one may save a basket full of loaves of bread even if it contains a hundred portions. The basket, as a single object, may be taken out in its entirety — one is not required to remove bread from it in order to limit the quantity. The key is that this is one act of saving a single vessel.

### Single Objects

Similarly: *ve-igul shel dveilah* — a round pressed mass of figs — and *ve-chavis shel yayin* — a barrel of wine — may each be taken out in their entirety as single objects, even if their contents exceed three meals' worth. The principle in each case is that it is a *kli echad*, a single object, which may be carried out as one act regardless of how much food it contains.

### Save for Yourselves

In addition to the single-object exception, the *Mishnah* offers another method for saving more than three meals' worth: *ve-omer la-acherim: bo'u ve-hatzilu lachem* — one may say to others: come and save for yourselves. By relinquishing his ownership and inviting others to take the food, each person who comes may save three meals for himself, and the total amount preserved may far exceed what the homeowner could save on his own.

The *Gemara* follows: *im hayu pikchin, osin imahem cheshbon achar Shabbat* — if they were clever, they would settle accounts with the homeowner after Shabbat. The *Gemara* asks: *cheshbon mai avidtei?* — why is a settlement necessary at all? Once the homeowner declared the food ownerless (*hefker*), ownership passed to those who took it. *Amar Rav Chisda*: this is a matter of *midat chasidut* — a measure of piety. Strictly speaking, those who took the food may keep it; but as an act of righteousness, they would return it.

*Amar Rava*: but how can someone be called a *chasid* here if they intend to be compensated? A true *chasid* would return the food without expectation of payment. The *Gemara* responds: *hacha bi-yerei shamayim askinan* — here we are dealing not with a *chasid* but with a *yerei shamayim*, a God-fearing person with a strict moral code. Such a person operates in a middle register: *ve-lo nicha lei de-lihani me-acherim* — he does not want to profit from another's misfortune, but *u-ve-chinam nami lo nicha lei de-litrach* — he also does not want to expend effort without recompense. He neither appropriates the food as a windfall nor donates his effort for nothing. Therefore, *ve-hachi ka-amar* — this is what the *Mishnah* means: if they were *pikchin*, meaning, if they understood the arrangement clearly enough to know that settling accounts afterward does not constitute *sechar Shabbat* — payment for labor on Shabbat — because technically they were taking for themselves and the food was truly theirs, then they could make such an arrangement after Shabbat without violating any prohibition.

### Where to Save

*Le-heichan matzilin?* — Where may one save food? The *Mishnah* is more stringent about food than it was about sacred books. For *sifrei kodesh*, the *Gemara* earlier allowed saving even to a courtyard with some architectural deficiency. For food, the rule is stricter: *le-chatzer me'urevet* — to a courtyard that is both architecturally complete and has an *eruv*. No allowances are made, because the concern is that permitting too much latitude will lead a person to extinguish the fire actively.

### Ben Beteira Lenient

*Ben Beteira omer*: *af le-she-eina me'urevet* — even to a courtyard without an *eruv*, as long as it is architecturally correct, saving food there is permitted. The tension here is instructive: for *sifrei kodesh*, leniency was extended on account of the sanctity of the texts; for food, the *Tanna Kamma* is stricter than even the standard rule of carrying would require, precisely because of the fear that one will come to extinguish the fire. Ben Beteira disagrees and applies a more lenient standard.

## Saving Clothes & Objects

### Vessels for Shabbat

The *Mishnah* continues: *u-le-sham motzi klei tashmisho* — there one may also bring out vessels and utensils needed for Shabbat use. Rashi understands this to mean objects one will actually use on Shabbat — furniture, household items, and the like — though the precise limits of what qualifies as needed for Shabbat remain subject to discussion.

### Wearing Clothes

By clothing, the *Mishnah* takes a different approach than it does with food. Rather than specifying a fixed quantity, it states: *u-lovesh kol mah she-yuchal lilbosh* — one may wear and take out whatever one is able to wear. *Ve-otef kol mah she-yuchal la-atof* — and one may wrap whatever one is able to wrap. Anything that can be carried out on one's body — piled on, layered, draped — may be taken out, even if far more than one would normally wear.

### Back & Forth

The *Tanna Kamma* permits going back and forth repeatedly: *ve-chozer ve-lovesh u-motzi* — returning, dressing again in additional garments, and going out again. This parallels the loophole by food — where others could be invited to take for themselves — except that here the food equivalent permitted others to act, while for clothing the homeowner himself may make multiple trips, each time loading on as many garments as he can wear.

### Rabbi Yose: 18 Garments

*Rabbi Yose omer shmonah asar keilim* — Rabbi Yose limits this to eighteen standard garments. The *Gemara* enumerates them: a *miktron* (an outer cloak), an *onkli* (a cape), a *punda* (a type of belt), a *kalvuvus shel pishtan* (a linen outer garment), a *chaluk* (a shirt), an *apilyon* (a cape or covering), a *ma'aforet* (a head scarf), two *safarkim* (straps, perhaps for holding up clothing), two *minalim* (shoes), two *anpalyot* (socks), *veis pargad* (boots), a *chagor she-bemotnav* (a belt at the waist), a *kova she-berosho* (a hat), and a *sudar she-be-tzavaro* (a kerchief around the neck) — in sum, eighteen items corresponding to the standard garments typically worn in that era.

### Save with Me vs. For You…

The *Gemara* notes an apparent asymmetry between the two loophole formulations in the *Mishnah*: by food, it says *bo'u ve-hatzilu lachem* — come and save for yourselves — while by clothing it says *bo'u ve-hatzilu imi* — come and save with me. The explanation is that by food, the homeowner is limited to three meals for himself, so in order for more to be saved, the food must actually become the property of others — hence *lachem*, for yourselves. By clothing, however, no such per-person limit applies to the homeowner: he may take out as many garments as he can carry on his body. Therefore, the clothing remains his, and he simply recruits others to assist him — *imi*, together with me.

## Fire Protection Methods

### Fireproof Leather Coveri…

The *Mishnah* now shifts from what may be removed to what may be done in place to prevent further burning. *Rabbi Shimon ben Nanas omer*: *porsin or shel gedi al gabei shidah, teivah u-migdal* — one may spread a goat-leather hide over furniture — a chest, a box, a cabinet — *she-achaz bah ha-or* — when fire has already caught one part of it — *mipnei she-hu mechareich* — because the leather will singe but not burn through. The leather functions as a fireproof cover, protecting the remaining portion of the furniture from the spreading flame. This is an active protective measure, and Rabbi Shimon ben Nanas permits it.

### Vessel Barriers

*Ve-osin mechitza be-chol ha-keilim, bein melai'in bein reikanin, bishvil she-lo ta'avor ha-dleikah* — one may also create a barrier using any kind of vessels, whether filled or empty, to prevent the fire from spreading. The idea is that surrounding the burning item with vessels — even empty ones — can contain or redirect the fire.

### Rabbi Yosi: Water Vessels

*Rabbi Yosi oser bi-khlei cheres chadashim melei'im mayim* — Rabbi Yosi prohibits using new pottery vessels filled with water. His reasoning: *lefi she-einan yekholim lekabel et ha-or ve-hem mipakin u-makhabin et ha-dleikah* — new pottery vessels cannot withstand the heat of the fire; they will crack open, and the water inside will spill out and extinguish the fire. From the *Tanna Kamma*'s silence on this point, the *Gemara* infers that the first opinion permits even this — the indirect extinguishment that results when the vessel bursts and the water douses the flames.

### Water Saturation Method

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: *tallit she-achazah bah ha-or mitzad echad, notnin aleha mayim mitzad acher* — if a garment has caught fire on one side, one may pour water on the other side of the garment. *Im kavta kavta* — if it goes out, it goes out. The mechanism is that the water saturates the unburned portion, and the fire extinguishes itself before reaching the saturated area. This is *geram kibbuy* — indirect extinguishment — rather than active dousing of the fire, and the *Tanna Kamma* of the *Mishnah* permits it.

*Tosafot* raises the question of whether saturating the garment with water involves a concern about *libun* — the prohibited melakhah of bleaching — but that analysis belongs elsewhere.

A *baraita* presents a parallel ruling: *tallit she-achazah bah ha-or mitzad echad — poshtah u-mitkasseh bah, ve-im kavtah kavtah* — if a garment has caught fire on one side, one may remove it, put it on, and if the act of wearing it causes the fire to go out, that is permissible. Similarly: *vekhein Sefer Torah she-achazah bo ha-or — poshto ve-korei bo, ve-im kavtah kavtah* — if a *Sefer Torah* has caught fire, one may open it and read from it, and if the fire goes out as a result, that is permissible.

Both of these cases raise a genuine conceptual difficulty. In what sense are these acts truly *eino mitkaven* — without intention? If one spreads the garment or opens the *Sefer Torah* specifically hoping the fire will be extinguished, this looks less like an unintended consequence and more like a desired outcome achieved through an ostensibly different act. Perhaps the best reading of these cases is that the person genuinely is not intending the extinguishment — he is simply wearing his garment or reading the *Sefer Torah* — and if the fire goes out, it goes out. That reading at least preserves the formal structure of *eino mitkaven*, and the later *Gemara* analysis of the door-and-lamp case suggests that this is indeed how the *Gemara* reads these scenarios.

### Natural Extinguish

The *Gemara* asks why the *baraita* does not simply permit the active use of water, as Rabbi Shimon ben Nanos does. The answer: *keman de-amar ke-Rabbi Shimon ben Nanos* — the *baraita* presumably follows Rabbi Shimon ben Nanos's position. But then the *Gemara* objects: *aima de-amar Rabbi Shimon ben Nanos mishum de-mechareich* — Rabbi Shimon ben Nanos permits only the leather cover because it singes rather than extinguishes. *Geram kibbuy mi amar?* — who ever said Rabbi Shimon ben Nanos permits indirect extinguishment? The *Gemara* answers: yes, he does permit it — as is proven from the fact that the *Tanna Kamma* of the *Mishnah*, by contrast with Rabbi Yosi, permits placing vessels of water that will burst and douse the fire, which is itself a form of *geram kibbuy*. This demonstrates that the first opinion endorses *geram kibbuy* in principle.

## Grama & Fire Out

### Grama Permitted?

*Tanu Rabbanan*: the *Gemara* now addresses the question of *grama* — indirect causation — more broadly, and whether the *Tanna Kamma* truly permits indirect extinguishment through water. The inference from Rabbi Yosi's prohibition: *mikhlal de-Tanna Kamma sharei* — since Rabbi Yosi explicitly forbids the water-filled pottery vessels that will burst and put out the fire, the implication is that the *Tanna Kamma* permits this form of indirect extinguishment. This is a significant ruling, and the *Gemara* proceeds to test its limits through a series of related cases.

It must be emphasized that this is a very important *Gemara* for practical *halakha*. Much of the modern discussion around Shabbat-mode appliances, the devices developed by *Tzomet*, and other indirect methods of activating or deactivating electrical systems draws on the principles being developed here around *grama* and its permissibility.

### Shaking Off Lamp

*Ner she-al gabei tavla* — if there is a lamp on top of a table, one may shake the table and allow the lamp to fall off, *ve-im kavtah kavtah* — and if it goes out, it goes out. This is permitted because the primary act is shaking the table — perhaps for some other purpose, such as clearing or cleaning it — and the extinguishment, if it occurs, is a secondary consequence.

The school of Rabbi Yannai qualifies this: *lo shanu ela be-sho'eiach* — this ruling applies only if the lamp was left on the table by accident, i.e., forgotten there. *Aval be-mani'ach* — but if the lamp was deliberately placed on the table, *na'aseh basis le-davar asur* — the table becomes a *basis* — a supporting base — for a prohibited object, and as such it takes on the status of *muktzeh* itself, making it impermissible to move.

### Door & Lamp

*Ner she-achorei ha-delet* — if there is a lamp burning behind a door, *pote'ach ve-no'el ke-darko, ve-im kavtah kavtah* — one may open and close the door in the normal way, and if the lamp goes out as a result, that is permitted. This case is more straightforwardly *eino mitkaven*: the person genuinely wants to open his door, not to extinguish the lamp. The question is only whether the opening of the door will foreseeably extinguish the flame.

### Rav's Curse

*Lait alei Rav* — Rav cursed at this ruling or at one who would act upon it. The *Gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama lait lei Rav?* — why did Rav curse? One might think it is because Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda that *eino mitkaven* is prohibited, and the *Tanna* who taught the leniency holds like Rabbi Shimon who permits *eino mitkaven*. But surely Rav would not curse everyone who rules like Rabbi Shimon in this domain.

The *Gemara* rejects this explanation: *be-ha afilu Rabbi Shimon modeh* — in this case, even Rabbi Shimon would agree that there is a problem. The reason is the principle of *psik reisha*: *modeh Rabbi Shimon bi-psik reisha ve-lo yamut* — Rabbi Shimon agrees that if an act inevitably produces a prohibited consequence, it is forbidden even if unintended. If the lamp is situated directly behind the door such that opening the door will certainly extinguish it, that is *psik reisha*, and Rabbi Shimon would prohibit it.

### Psik Reisha

The question then becomes one of certainty versus probability. *Psik reisha* requires that the prohibited consequence be definite — if one cuts off a head, it will certainly die. But here, it may not be certain that opening the door will extinguish the lamp; it depends on conditions such as the proximity of the lamp to the door and the force of any draft. This leads some *Acharonim* to develop the category of *karov le-psik reisha* — something approaching but not quite reaching the certainty of *psik reisha*, yet still highly probable. Whether such a near-certainty is treated as *psik reisha* or retains the more lenient status of *eino mitkaven* is itself a significant debate among later authorities.

At minimum, the *Gemara*'s framing here clarifies what was difficult about the earlier cases: the permissibility of wearing the burning garment or opening the *Sefer Torah* rests on the assumption that the extinguishment is genuinely not the person's aim and is not an inevitable consequence of the act. If extinguishment were certain, it would be *psik reisha* and prohibited even for Rabbi Shimon.

### Wind Principle

*Amar Rav Yehuda*: *pote'ach adam delet keneged medura be-Shabbat* — one may open a door opposite a bonfire on Shabbat. The assumption is that a full bonfire will not be extinguished by the draft from an opening door.

*Abaye* questions this: *be-mai askinan?* — what conditions are we discussing? *Eileima be-ruach metzuya* — if we are speaking of ordinary, calm wind, *mai ta'ama de-man de-assar?* — who would ever prohibit opening the door? A normal draft will not affect a bonfire. *Ei be-ruach she-eina metzuya* — if we are speaking of a strong, unusual wind, *mai ta'ama de-man de-sharei?* — why should anyone permit it, if the wind is strong enough that extinguishment becomes likely?

The *Gemara* resolves: *le-olam be-ruach metzuya* — the case is indeed ordinary wind. *Mar savar gazrinan* — one authority holds that we make a *gezeirah*: we prohibit opening the door even in ordinary wind, lest a person grow accustomed to doing so and then fail to be careful when the wind is strong. *U-mar savar lo gazrinan* — and the other authority holds that no such *gezeirah* is necessary; when the wind is strong, a person will naturally be alert to the danger and will refrain.

The broader principle emerging from this discussion is significant: it raises the question of whether *psik reisha* reasoning applies only to cases of absolute certainty, or whether cases of high probability — *karov le-psik reisha* — similarly trigger a prohibition, whether as a matter of substantive law or as a *gezeirah*. The *Acharonim* develop this point extensively from the present *Gemara*. The discussion of *geram kibbuy* — indirect extinguishment — will continue in the following daf.

---

# Shabbat 120

## Gerama & Fire

### Rabbi Yossi Position

The present daf picks up in the middle of 120b, ten lines before the lines widen, at the words *osin mechitza*. Having concluded the previous *mishnah*, the Gemara turns to another *mishnah* that addresses issues central to *hilkhot Shabbat* — in particular, the question of saving property from a fire and the concern that rescue efforts might lead to outright prohibited labor.

The *mishnah* records a dispute regarding placing pottery vessels filled with water around a fire. The fear is that the heat will cause the vessels to burst, releasing the water and thereby extinguishing the fire. Rabbi Yossi prohibits this; the *chakhamim* permit it. The Gemara seizes on this dispute as a window into the broader question of *gerama* — indirect causation — on Shabbat.

### Gerama Definition

*Lemeima*, says the Gemara: *d'rabbanan savri geram kibuie mutar* — the *chakhamim* hold that causing a fire to extinguish itself indirectly is permitted. This formulation is striking, for it sounds like an outright, unconditional permission — some *rishonim* indeed hold that *gerama* is permitted even without any special justification, though at minimum the Gemara implies it is permitted in the context of a fire. *Ve'Rabbi Yossi savar geram kibuie assur* — Rabbi Yossi holds that indirect causation of extinguishment is forbidden.

### Baraita Resolution

Yet *ve'ipcha shemanan lehu* — we have apparently heard that they hold the reverse positions. A *baraita* teaches: *osin mechitza b'kelim reikim u'mle'im she'ein darkan l'hishtaber* — one may make a wall of empty vessels or full ones that will not normally break. This implies that the *tanna* of this *baraita* agrees with Rabbi Yossi that full vessels which would break and extinguish the fire are forbidden, and Rabbi Yossi himself then adds that even the pottery of Kfar Shichin and Kfar Chananya does not normally break — a more lenient position than the *chakhamim*. The positions appear inverted relative to the *mishnah*.

One resolution proposed is to reverse the attributions in the *mishnah* — the *chakhamim* would then be the stringent party and Rabbi Yossi the lenient one, and his statement in the *baraita* about the hard pottery would be understood as arguing against the *chakhamim* on their own terms. The Gemara, however, rejects this: *Rabba bar Tachlifa* says in the name of Rav that the *tanna* who holds *geram kibuie assur* is Rabbi Yossi — this is an established tradition that fixes Rabbi Yossi as the stringent position and cannot be reversed. Instead, the Gemara resolves the *baraita* by reading it as entirely Rabbi Yossi's view — *v'chisorei mechasra v'hachi kattani* — the *baraita* is incomplete and must be read as follows: one may make a wall of empty or full vessels that do not normally break; and vessels from Kfar Shichin and Kfar Chananya likewise do not normally break — because Rabbi Yossi says those vessels do not normally break. The entire *baraita* is Rabbi Yossi's, and the apparent role reversal dissolves.

### God's Name Gerama

The Gemara now presents a genuine internal contradiction: *verami Rabbi Yossi ad Rabbi Yossi* — Rabbi Yossi contradicts himself. A *baraita* teaches that if one has written God's name in ink on one's arm, one may not bathe, anoint, or stand in a foul-smelling place, lest one erase it — for *mechikat Hashem*, erasing God's name, is a *de'oraita* prohibition. Yet if immersion in a *mikveh* for the sake of a *mitzvah* becomes necessary, the *chakhamim* say to wrap a band of reed around the arm and immerse; Rabbi Yossi says simply immerse in the normal manner, provided one does not scrub the arm. Immersing with God's name on one's arm will, naturally, cause the water to wash it away — an act of *gerama* in erasing God's name. Here Rabbi Yossi is not troubled by *gerama*, whereas in the fire case he is.

The Gemara proposes that perhaps the prohibition of *mechikat Hashem* is derived from the verse *lo taasun ken l'Hashem Elokeichem* — "do not do so to Hashem your God" — which forbids only direct action: *assiya hu d'assur, grama shari*. The Gemara then asks: but the same logic applies to Shabbat, where the verse reads *lo ta'aseh kol melacha* — "do not do any labor" — equally excluding indirect causation. This framing makes clear that *gerama* was never a *de'oraita* concern on Shabbat; the entire question is at the *de'rabbanan* level.

### Biblical vs Rabbanic

The Gemara's resolution now becomes a *de'rabbanan* distinction. By the prohibition of erasing God's name, *gerama* is simply permitted — the verse excludes it from the prohibition entirely. By Shabbat, there is likewise no biblical concern, but one might still have expected a *rabbinic* prohibition. The Gemara proceeds to explain why Rabbi Yossi differs on Shabbat specifically.

### Anxiety & Fire

The Gemara's answer is: *mitoch she'adam bahul al mamono* — because a person is agitated over his property. Rabbi Yossi in principle has no conceptual objection to *gerama*; it is permitted even on Shabbat. But in the specific context of a fire, if one is allowed to engage in the elaborate arrangement of water-filled vessels, one's anxiety over the loss of possessions will lead one to go further and directly extinguish the fire. This is the same delicate balance that runs through the entire chapter: if too much is prohibited, people will simply violate Shabbat outright; if too much is permitted, anxious homeowners will overstep in their rescue efforts. *Grama kibuie*, therefore, is permitted in principle, but Rabbi Yossi forbids it by fire due to this special *de'rabbanan* concern — a concern that does not apply in the case of God's name on one's arm.

This prompts a further question: the *chakhamim* who argue on Rabbi Yossi permit the water-filled vessels by fire. But then why do they require covering God's name before *tevilah*? If a person is agitated enough during a fire that we fear *gerama* will lead to direct extinguishment, should we not *a fortiori* be lenient in the case of the *mikveh*, where no such anxiety is present? And if *gerama* is permissible, why does anyone require the covering at all?

At this point the Gemara reconsiders the entire framework. *Ve'dilma*, it asks — does the reed band (*gemi*) even accomplish anything? If it is tight on the arm, it constitutes a *chatzitzah* and invalidates the *tevilah*; if it is loose, the water penetrates anyway and provides no protection for the ink. And one might further think the ink itself is a *chatzitzah* — but a *baraita* resolves this: blood, ink, honey, and milk are *chatzitzah* only when dry; when moist, they are water-permeable and are not a *chatzitzah*. The *gemi*, however, remains problematic.

The Gemara therefore abandons the *gerama* framework for this case entirely, and Rava bar Rav Shila provides the true explanation: *d'kasvari assur la'amod bifnei Hashem arom* — the *chakhamim* hold that it is forbidden to stand naked before God's name. The covering is not about preventing erasure of God's name; it is about not exposing God's name while unclothed. This explains why a loose cover suffices — it need not keep water out, only conceal the name.

The *chakhamim* require one to seek out such a covering, even at some inconvenience, while Rabbi Yossi holds one may simply place one's hand over the arm. The Gemara asks: might one's hand slip? And the response is that the same concern applies symmetrically. The Gemara concludes that the ideal solution — when a loose cover is readily available — is accepted by all. The dispute reduces to whether one must delay the *tevilah* to go searching for a cover when none is at hand.

### Tevilah Ba-Zmanah

This brings us to the question of *tevila bizmana*: is there a *mitzvah* to perform one's immersion precisely at its appointed time, or may one delay? The *chakhamim* hold *tevila bizmana lav mitzvah* — there is no obligation to immerse at the exact time. Therefore, if one must search for something to cover God's name, the *tevilah* may simply wait. Rabbi Yossi holds *tevila bizmana mitzvah* — immersion at its designated time is a *mitzvah* — and therefore one should not be compelled to postpone it in order to search for a cover. Placing one's hand over the arm is sufficient.

A *baraita* is then cited concerning *Yom Kippur*, which categorizes various categories of those who require *tevilah* — *zav*, *zavah*, *metzora*, *bo'el niddah*, *tamei meit* — and specifies whether their immersion falls by day or by night. It concludes that a *ba'al keri* may immerse at any time during the day. Rabbi Yossi says that from *Mincha* onward he need not immerse. This might suggest Rabbi Yossi holds *tevila bizmana lav mitzvah* — why immerse on *Yom Kippur* if one can simply wait until nightfall? The Gemara, however, identifies this Rabbi Yossi as Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda, not the *stam* Rabbi Yossi of our *mishnah*. Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda explicitly holds *tevila bizmana lav mitzvah* — as evidenced by his ruling that a woman in complex cases of uncertain status need only immerse once at the end of the entire uncertain period rather than at every possible time. The *stam* Rabbi Yossi of our *mishnah*, by contrast, holds *tevila bizmana mitzvah*.

The upshot of the entire sugya is that *gerama* is permitted — certainly at the *de'oraita* level, and the language of the Gemara suggests it may be entirely permitted even *de'rabbanan*. The *chakhamim* permit it by fire outright; Rabbi Yossi agrees that *gerama* is in principle permitted but introduces a special *de'rabbanan* concern specific to fires, where agitation over property loss may lead to direct violation. By the *mikveh* scenario, the covering requirement has nothing to do with *gerama* at all, but rests on the separate concern of standing unclothed before God's name. The practical ruling is that *gerama* is at least *assur de'rabbanan* on Shabbat — and this principle underlies many of the leniencies developed by responsa authorities for indirect activation of electrical devices on Shabbat, much of which rests on the *gerama* foundation.

---

## Amirah L'Goy & Katan

### Non-Jew Fire Help

The *mishnah* teaches: *nochri sheba lekhabot* — if a non-Jew comes of his own accord to extinguish a fire, one may not say to him "extinguish it," for that constitutes *amirah l'akum* — enlisting a non-Jew to perform *melacha* on one's behalf. Yet one need not say to him "do not extinguish it" either. *Mipnei she'ein shvitato aleihen* — because his resting is not incumbent upon you. You have no obligation to ensure that a non-Jew refrains from *melacha* on Shabbat. One may not actively engage him, but one need not stop him either.

One might ask: since extinguishing a fire without the purpose of producing charcoal is only a *de'rabbanan* prohibition — it is *melacha she'einah tzrikhah le-gufah* in the view of Rabbi Shimon — why is *amirah l'akum* prohibited even here? *Tosafot* addresses this directly: *ein omrim lo kabbe afilu bidvar de'rabbanan amirah l'nochri shevut* — one may not instruct a non-Jew even for a *de'rabbanan* prohibition. *Amirah l'akum* itself is a *de'rabbanan* prohibition, but it applies regardless of whether the underlying act is biblical or rabbinic.

The Gemara then cites Rabbi Ami: in the case of a fire, the rabbis permitted one to make a general public announcement — to no one in particular — that whoever chooses to come and extinguish the fire will not lose out, and after Shabbat one may pay them for their services. This is not a direct instruction to a specific non-Jew to extinguish the fire; it is a general declaration addressed to whoever happens to hear it, and the non-Jew acts entirely of his own volition. The question of whether one may go further — instructing a non-Jew to engage in *grama kibuie* — is foreclosed by *Tosafot*'s ruling that even *de'rabbanan* acts are off-limits for *amirah l'akum*.

The Gemara attempts to derive support for the permissibility of the general announcement from the *mishnah* itself: if the *mishnah* says "do not tell him to extinguish," this implies that telling him in the general, indirect fashion — "whoever extinguishes will not lose out" — would be permitted. But the Gemara rejects this inference, noting that the *mishnah*'s parallel clause — "do not tell him not to extinguish" — could equally be read to mean that any statement more directive than this silence is forbidden, including the general announcement. *Ella mihacha leka l'mishmana mineh* — one cannot prove either way from the *mishnah*. Nevertheless, *Tosafot* rules that the general announcement is permitted, and this is the practical ruling.

### Yosef ben Simai

A *baraita* recounts: a fire broke out in the courtyard of Yosef ben Simai in Shichin, and the soldiers of the garrison of Tzippori came to extinguish it — apparently from a neighboring village, drawn by the news, perhaps because Yosef ben Simai held a position of authority as an officer of the king. Yosef ben Simai refused to allow them to extinguish the fire, *mipnei kvod Shabbat* — out of concern for the honor of Shabbat. A miracle occurred: rain fell and extinguished the fire. That evening he sent each of the soldiers two *sela'im* and fifty *sela'im* to their commander, rewarding their goodwill even though he had turned them away.

When the rabbis heard of this, they said: he need not have done that. The *mishnah* already teaches that one need not stop a non-Jew from extinguishing a fire on his own initiative. The narrative carries a dual message: it celebrates the extraordinary piety of Yosef ben Simai, while making unmistakably clear that ordinary people should not attempt to replicate it. Miracles are not to be assumed, and the halakha provides an adequate path that does not require turning away help. The concern Yosef ben Simai expressed was perhaps not about a specific halakhic violation — he was not technically violating anything by allowing them to proceed — but about the experiential dimension of Shabbat: having an active firefighting effort underway undermines the spirit of the day, particularly for a public figure whose conduct represented *kevod Shabbat* before the surrounding population.

### Minor Agency

The *mishnah* continues: *aval katan sheba lekhabot ein shomin lo* — but if a minor comes to extinguish the fire, one may not allow him to proceed, *mipnei sheshvitato aleihem* — because his resting is your obligation. Unlike the non-Jew, whose Shabbat rest is not the Jew's responsibility, the minor's Shabbat observance is. The Gemara then asks whether this *mishnah* implies a general principle — that one is obligated to prevent a minor from performing any biblical prohibition (*katan ochel nevelot beit din metzuvin alav lehafrisho*). Rabbi Yochanan answers: no. The *mishnah* is speaking specifically of a case where the minor acts *al daat aviv* — for his father's sake, to benefit his father.

### Acting for Parent

When a minor acts on his own — for example, eating *treifa* food for himself — it is not one's obligation to interfere, at least where the child is below the age of *chinuch* or is not one's own child. *Tosafot* notes that if the minor has reached the age of *chinuch* or is one's own child, the parent does bear an obligation to stop him. But the case of the *mishnah* is different: the minor is extinguishing the fire to benefit his father. In that case he is not acting for himself; he is an extension of the father. Allowing him to proceed is therefore analogous to *amirah l'goy* — it is as if the father had effectively enlisted him, even without explicit instruction.

### Non-Jew vs Minor

This leads the Gemara to ask: if the minor acts *al daat aviv* and thereby becomes an extension of the father, should the same logic not apply to the non-Jew who comes to extinguish the fire for the sake of the Jew? Is he not also acting for the Jew's benefit? The Gemara answers: *nochri l'daatei d'nafshei avid* — the non-Jew acts for his own purposes. Even if his motivation is friendship, anticipated reward, or goodwill toward the Jew, he makes his own autonomous calculation. He is not subservient; he acts because it serves his own interests as he perceives them. The minor, by contrast, acts entirely out of felt obligation to the parent and without the independent judgment of an adult. He therefore functions as a complete extension of the father rather than as an independent agent.

This analysis yields a striking halakhic observation. The *mishnah* appeared to ground the prohibition of allowing one's minor to extinguish the fire in the biblical verse — *atah u'vincha u'vitecha* — which explicitly includes one's children among those who must rest on Shabbat. But the Gemara reframes the entire discussion: the question becomes one of general obligations to prevent minors from performing *issurim*, compounded by the specific concern that when a minor acts for a parent he becomes an extension of that parent, akin to *amirah l'akum*. The affirmative biblical obligation to ensure that one's children rest — implied by the *mishnah*'s language — is effectively subsumed into these generic categories. Some *rishonim* and *poskim* do revisit this independent biblical obligation of *shevisat katanim*, but it is a striking feature of the Gemara's analysis that this dimension nearly disappears from view.

---

## Vessels & Protection

### Covering Candles

The next *mishnah* states: *kofin k'ara al gabei ner beshvil shelo te'echoz bekora* — one may overturn a vessel over a burning candle so that the beam above does not catch fire. This is not an act of extinguishing; it is a protective measure. Similarly, one may cover the excrement of a minor and a scorpion so that one does not step on it and is not bitten.

### Minor Excrement

The *mishnah*'s mention of covering the excrement of a minor prompts discussion. The *mishnah*'s apparent *chiddush* is that one may move a vessel to cover something that might otherwise be *muktzah*. But the Gemara challenges the *chiddush*: *hi atzmah mukhenet le-klavim* — the excrement of a minor is not *muktzah* to begin with, since it has some use. Perhaps the *chiddush* is that it constitutes *nolad* — something new that came into being on Shabbat? A *baraita* teaches that flowing rivers and springs are not treated as *nolad* because their flow is continuous and expected. Similarly, the excrement of a minor is expected and therefore not *nolad*.

The broader context of this discussion arose during a visit of several rabbis — Rav Yehuda, Rav Yirmiya bar Abba, and Rav Chanan bar Rava — to the home of Avin of Neshikaya. The host provided benches for Rav Yehuda and Rav Yirmiya bar Abba but not for Rav Chanan bar Rava, who sat on the floor. Feeling slighted, Rav Chanan bar Rava, overhearing the host teaching his son the version of this teaching about covering the excrement of a minor, declared that the man was teaching his son nonsense — pointing out that there was no *chiddush* since the excrement was not *muktzah*. The host asked how he should teach the passage. The resolution: the teaching should read *al tzo'ah she-l tarnegolim mipnei katan* — covering the droppings of chickens so that the minor does not dirty himself. Bird droppings, unlike the excrement of a minor, are not *ra'uy le-klavim* and would be *muktzah*, and the *chiddush* is therefore that one may cover them to protect the child.

### Bird Droppings

Even so, the Gemara challenges: the bird droppings in the yard could simply be removed as *graf shel re'i* — the rule that permits removing repulsive waste from one's domain. The Gemara responds that *graf shel re'i* allows one to move the waste contained *within* a vessel, not to pick up the waste directly. But another source shows that even repulsive waste may be moved directly — the case of a rat found in Rav Ashi's perfumes, where Rav Ashi instructed that it be taken by its tail and removed. The Gemara concludes that the case of the *mishnah* concerns waste in the garbage area of one's yard — a location where the rules permitting removal of *graf shel re'i* do not apply — and therefore covering it is the only available option.

### Scorpion Trapping

The *mishnah*'s permission to cover a scorpion relates to the laws of trapping on Shabbat. Trapping the scorpion constitutes *melacha she'einah tzrikhah le-gufa* — labor performed not for the sake of the usual objective of that labor (one does not want the scorpion for any productive purpose) — and is therefore only a *de'rabbanan* prohibition in the view of Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Yehuda records that a case involving trapping a scorpion in the town of Arav came before Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who expressed concern that the person might be liable to bring a *chatat* — indicating that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai may have held like Rabbi Yehuda that *melacha she'einah tzrikhah le-gufa* is a full biblical violation.

---

## Killing Dangerous Animals

### Dangerous Animals Kill

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches: *kol ha-mazikin neheragin be-Shabbat* — all dangerous animals that cause injury to people may be killed on Shabbat. *Rashi* specifies that this refers to those that are potentially fatal. Crucially, this permission extends even to proactive killing — if one encounters a poisonous snake or scorpion that is not actively attacking, one may still kill it, since this protects others from danger. This constitutes *melacha she'einah tzrikhah le-gufa*; one is not killing for the usual productive purpose of the labor but purely as a protective measure.

### Five Animals

Rav Yosef challenges this from a *baraita*: *chamisha neheragin be-Shabbat* — there are specifically five animals that may be killed on Shabbat: the fly of Egypt, the wasp of Ninveh, the scorpion of Chadyav, the snake of Eretz Yisrael, and a rabid dog anywhere. These five are either particularly lethal or particularly prone to attacking people. But the *baraita* limits the permission to these five — not all dangerous animals — which contradicts Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's general ruling.

The Gemara asks: whose position is the *baraita*? If it represents Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *melacha she'einah tzrikhah le-gufa chayav* — that such labor is a full biblical violation — then even these five could only be killed if they pose an immediate threat of *pikuach nefesh*. If it represents Rabbi Shimon, who permits *melacha she'einah tzrikhah le-gufa*, then the list of five represents an implicit limitation: only these, not all dangerous animals. Either way, it poses a difficulty for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's sweeping ruling.

Rabbi Yirmiya dismisses the challenge: *dilma meshabeshta hi* — perhaps the *baraita* is a corrupt text. The Gemara does acknowledge that only *baraitot* edited by Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshaya — essentially the *Tosefta* — carry full textual authority; other *baraitot* may contain errors.

### Piety vs Pragmatism

Rav Yosef, however, objects to this dismissal: *ana matniti lah* — that is my *baraita*, a tradition I myself preserve, and it should not be discarded simply because it is inconvenient. Yet he also resolves the difficulty himself: *be'rutzo batreihu de'kulei alma la peligi* — the *baraita* is discussing the case where these animals are actually pursuing and threatening a person. In that case, all authorities agree they may be killed, for it is *pikuach nefesh*. The *baraita* is therefore not about proactive killing at all; it is about reactive self-defense. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling, by contrast, permits proactive killing according to Rabbi Shimon for all genuinely dangerous animals, not only these five.

A *tanna* teaches before Rava bar Rav Huna: *ha'horeg nechashim ve'akravim be'Shabbat ein ruach chasidim nocha heimenu* — one who goes out of his way to kill snakes and scorpions on Shabbat, the spirit of the pious does not rest easily with him. Even if such killing is only a *de'rabbanan* prohibition under Rabbi Shimon, it is unseemly to go about actively hunting these animals. Rava bar Rav Huna responds sharply: *ve'otan chasidim ein ruach chachamim nocha mehem* — those so-called pious people do not find favor with the sages. The sages take a broader view of public welfare, and one should not be excessively stringent at the expense of communal safety.

### Divine Providence

A *baraita* offers a striking theological framing: *nizdamnu lo nechashim ve'akravim* — if snakes and scorpions happen to cross one's path on Shabbat and one kills them, *be'yaduah shenizdamnu lo lehorgan* — it is evident that heaven arranged for them to cross one's path so that one would have the merit of eliminating them. If one did not kill them, *be'yaduah shenizdamnu lehorgo* — they were sent to kill, and a miracle from heaven intervened to spare the person. This framing functions as a theological endorsement of proactive killing: encountering such creatures is itself providential, and acting to eliminate them is meritorious. Ulla (or in some versions, Rabbah bar bar Chana) in the name of Rabbi Yochanan qualifies this: the providential inference — that they were sent to kill — applies only when the animals were actually hissing aggressively at the person, not when they were simply encountered incidentally.

### Incidental vs Proactive

A final story is cited: Rabbah bar bar Chana reports that once a scorpion or snake appeared in the study hall and a certain person stood up and killed it. Rabbi said of him: *paga bo ke-yotzei bo* — "something just like it encountered him." The *baraita* leaves ambiguous whether this was a compliment — the creature was attacking, and he courageously dispatched it — or an insult — he himself behaved like a dangerous creature in going out of his way to kill it.

The Gemara concludes with a practical clarification from the incident involving Rabbi Abba son of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and Rav Zevid, who were sitting on the porch of Rabbi Yanai when a snake appeared from between them. They asked Rabbi Yanai whether one may kill snakes and scorpions on Shabbat. He replied: I even kill wasps — snakes and scorpions, *a fortiori*. The Gemara qualifies this ruling: *dilma le-fi tumo* — perhaps this applies only incidentally. That is, the permission may extend to stepping on or passing over a creature in the course of one's normal movement, but not to going out of one's way specifically to chase it down and kill it. Within the framework of Rabbi Shimon — who treats proactive killing as only a *de'rabbanan* violation of *melacha she'einah tzrikhah le-gufa* — there remains a spectrum of permissibility: some hold it is entirely encouraged, others discourage it, and still others permit it only when done incidentally rather than through deliberate pursuit.

---

---

# Shabbat 123

## Kli Shemelachto L'Issur

### Hammer & Nuts

The daf opens in the midst of a discussion about *kli shemelachto l'issur* — a vessel whose primary function involves a prohibited activity — and the question of whether such an object may be used on Shabbat for a permitted purpose. The Mishnah had already illustrated the principle with concrete examples: using a hammer to crack nuts, or a saw to cut cheese. These examples raise the conceptual question of what exactly is meant by *l'tzorech gufo* — using the object itself for some legitimate purpose.

*L'tzorech gufo* must be understood against the backdrop of two other possible modes of handling such an object. The second is *l'tzorech mekomo* — one does not wish to use the object at all, but simply needs to move it out of the way to clear a space. The third is *mechama l'tzel* — moving the object from sun to shade in order to protect it from damage. These three categories structure the entire analysis of *kli shemelachto l'issur* that unfolds across the daf.

### Mishna vs Rav Yehuda

The Mishnah's ruling appeared quite clear: even vessels designated for prohibited activities may be handled on Shabbat for a permitted purpose. Yet Rav Yehuda sought to read the Mishnah in a far more limited sense, arguing that it addressed only a vessel designated for a *heter* use — which would seem to undermine the Mishnah's entire point.

### Rava's Position

Rava pushed back against this restrictive reading. In his view, the Mishnah's plain intent is that even a vessel whose *melacha* is forbidden may be used on Shabbat for a permitted purpose. This, he argued, is precisely what the examples of the hammer and the saw are meant to illustrate. With Rava's position established, the Gemara turns to an *eitivei* — a challenge from a *braita* — that opens five lines into the daf.

---

## Pestle/Cutting Board

### Beit Shammai/Hillel

The *eitivei* cites a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel concerning the *ali* — the pestle, which in its broad, flat form could serve as an improvised cutting board. Beit Shammai rules: *ein notlin et ha-ali liktzava alav basar* — one may not take the pestle to use it as a surface for cutting meat on Yom Tov. Beit Hillel permits this, reasoning that it serves *simchat Yom Tov*.

### Post-Use Restriction

Crucially, however, both schools agree: *veshavin she-im katzav alav basar she-assur letaltelo* — if one has already cut meat on it, it may not subsequently be moved. This presents a challenge to Rava's position. If the pestle is a *kli shemelachto l'issur*, why should it become forbidden after its permitted use? At worst, it should remain in the category of *kli shemelachto l'issur* — a hammer used for cracking nuts is still moveable after one finishes cracking. Why should the pestle be different?

The Gemara initially considers answering according to Rabbi Nechemia. Rabbi Nechemia represents an extremely restrictive position: any vessel, even one *shemelachto l'heter*, may be used only for its intended purpose — *l'tzorech tashmisho*. A fork may be used to eat, but not to scratch oneself, even though scratching is entirely permitted. Whatever one wishes to use on Shabbat may only be used for its classic, designated function. According to Rabbi Nechemia, then, the pestle's special *heter* to serve as a cutting board — granted only for *simchat Yom Tov* — expires once that use is concluded.

### Rabbi Nechemia

This answer holds that both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel may be operating within the framework of Rabbi Nechemia — a striking conclusion in its own right. The Gemara, however, moves past this resolution upon hearing a report in the name of Rav.

---

## Professional Tools

### Fragrance/Gold Tools

Rabbi Chinana bar Shlamya said in the name of Rav: *ha-kol modim be-sichi zavi u-mezorei* — everyone agrees with respect to these three implements. Rashi offers two readings of what these implements are: instruments used in the production of fragrances, or instruments used in weaving. Whatever their precise identity, they are professional tools of a specialized character, and all authorities agree that they occupy a stricter category than ordinary *kli shemelachto l'issur*.

The reason is *d'keivan d'kapid aleihu* — because the owner is exacting about them. These are tools one guards carefully, keeps designated for their professional function, and would not want anyone handling casually. Consequently, *miyachid lehu makom* — a place is set aside exclusively for them, and they become effectively off-limits. This category is what is generally described as *muktzah machmat chisron kis* — *muktzah* born of concern over financial loss, though the concern need not be specifically monetary. The operative condition is that the owner regards the implement as untouchable for any other purpose. This is what explains why the pestle, as a professional grinding instrument, cannot be moved after its exceptional Yom Tov use: it falls closer to this category of professional tools that one does not wish handled indiscriminately.

This prompts an important conceptual question: does *muktzah machmat chisron kis* apply only vis-à-vis others, or can it apply even for the owner himself? One might imagine a case where the owner is personally comfortable handling the implement but insists that others not touch it. Whether this asymmetry is legally meaningful is indeed a subject of discussion in the *rishonim*, touching on the question of *muktzah l'aniyim* and *muktzah l'ashirim*.

### Tool Gradation

The Gemara then records a *machloket* regarding how broadly this category of untouchable professional tools extends. Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kurnas shel zehavim shanu* — the Mishnah's ruling that a hammer may be used to crack nuts applies not only to an ordinary blacksmith's hammer, which is large and resilient and no one worries about damaging, but even to a goldsmith's hammer — a delicate instrument used to thin out gold. One might have assumed that the precision required of such a tool would render its owner sufficiently exacting about it to prohibit casual use. Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is thus a significant *chiddush*: even that degree of professional delicacy does not push the implement into the forbidden category.

Rav Shemen bar Abba goes further still: *kurnas shel besamim shanu* — the Mishnah's ruling applies even to a hammer used in producing fragrances. Such an implement is doubly precious: it is a professional instrument, and it must remain pristine and free of foreign odors. Even so, one may use it to crack nuts. The Gemara then notes the logical relationship between these two rulings. Whoever holds that the fragrance hammer is permitted *a fortiori* permits the gold hammer, since the fragrance hammer is the more carefully guarded of the two. Conversely, whoever holds that the gold hammer is permitted need not necessarily extend the ruling to the fragrance hammer, since the owner's *kapeidah* regarding the fragrance hammer may be greater.

What emerges is that the category of implements so precious that one refuses to let anyone touch them is an extreme case — far more extreme than one might initially have assumed. The realm of *kli shemelachto l'issur* turns out to be quite broad, reaching even into instruments that seem obviously protected by professional concern.

This is directly connected to a case in the Mishnah that speaks of using a heavy needle to pick a lock, illustrating that instruments are evaluated by their actual function and use-context rather than by reflex categorization.

### Spindles & Pokers

The Gemara adds that spindles and certain pointed weaving tools — *hakush* and *hakarkar* — may also be used on Shabbat, in this case to pierce fruit in a manner resembling a toothpick, connecting back to the principle that instruments with identifiable permitted uses remain in the category of *kli* that may be handled.

---

## Tilul Min Hatzad

### Fig in Straw

The Gemara now introduces a *baraita* that shifts the discussion toward the mechanics of indirect handling of *muktzah*. The case: an unripe fig — *paggah*, which Rashi identifies as specifically a fig — was buried in straw in order to hasten its ripening, much as one today might place fruit in a paper bag. The fig itself is not *muktzah*. But the straw surrounding it may be. Straw designated for animal fodder is not *muktzah*, since feeding one's animals on Shabbat is permitted. Straw designated for use in plaster-making, however, is *muktzah*, since that is a prohibited activity. The *baraita* rules: *muttar letaltela* — the fig may be moved, despite the surrounding *muktzah*.

### Wafer in Coals

A parallel case: a wafer buried in coals to keep it warm. Here the rule turns on exposure. If *im megula miktzatah* — part of the wafer is exposed — *muttar letaltela*: one may remove it, because one grasps the exposed, permitted portion and extracts it. The coals surrounding it collapse incidentally as it is removed, but one is not directly moving the *muktzah*. If, however, the wafer is completely buried, *assur letaltela*: one may not move it, because reaching it would require directly moving the *muktzah* coals out of the way.

### Spearing Method

Rabbi Elazar ben Tadai offers an elegant solution: *tochsim bekush bekarkar* — one may take a spindle or pointer and spear the buried item, whether fig or other object, and extract it. *Vehen minaroat me'alehen* — the surrounding material falls away of its own accord. The point of the spindle naturally displaces the *muktzah* material as it is inserted, but this displacement is incidental to the act of reaching the permitted object. This is the paradigmatic case of *tiltul min hatzad* — indirect movement of *muktzah* — and it is permitted when performed *l'tzorech davar hamuttar*, in the course of accessing a non-*muktzah* item.

The principle can be illustrated in familiar terms: if a permitted object sits behind books on a shelf, pulling out the books will naturally push aside whatever else is there — and this is acceptable, since one is acting on the permitted items and the incidental displacement of other objects is secondary. Alternatively, one could use a body part — an elbow, a breath of air — to move the *muktzah* directly. This mode, *tiltul begufo*, is permitted even more broadly, including in cases where one simply needs the item moved.

### Rav Nachman Ruling

The Gemara records: *amar Rav Nachman halacha k'Rabbi Elazar ben Tadai* — the ruling follows Rabbi Elazar ben Tadai, establishing that *tiltul min hatzad* is indeed permitted in such cases. The operative principle, as the Gemara formulates it, is *tiltul min hatzad lo shemei tiltul* — indirect movement is not legally considered movement.

### Radish Orientation

The Gemara then introduces a complication via a ruling Rav Nachman himself stated elsewhere. A radish buried in the ground: if oriented *mil'mala l'mata* — wider toward the top and narrowing downward — it may be extracted without difficulty, as it simply slides out of the hole and the surrounding earth collapses naturally inward. But if oriented *mil'mata l'mala* — the narrow end upward and the wider portion below — extraction is forbidden, because pulling it upward would require physically displacing the earth around the wider lower portion. In that case, one is not merely permitting the earth to collapse incidentally; one is actively moving it to create space.

This ruling initially appears to contradict Rav Nachman's endorsement of Rabbi Elazar ben Tadai's method. The Gemara resolves the tension by noting that *hadar beih Rav Nachman* — Rav Nachman retracted. The final established principle is that *tiltul min hatzad* is permitted when one is in pursuit of a *davar heter*, with the incidental displacement of *muktzah* material being entirely secondary.

---

## Broken Needle

### Needle Query

The Mishnah states that a standard sewing needle may be used on Shabbat to remove a splinter. Rava the son of Rabba posed a question to Rav Yosef by way of a written inquiry: *machat shenitlah chararah o uktzah* — what is the law regarding a needle that is missing its eye, or missing its point? Is such an object *muktzah*?

Rav Yosef responded from the Mishnah itself: since a needle may be used to remove a splinter, and a splinter does not care whether the needle has an eye or not, the absence of the eye presents no obstacle. The needle without an eye can still perform this function perfectly well. Regarding the missing point, the matter is less obvious — a blunted needle may be less effective. But the missing eye, at minimum, does not compromise the needle's utility for splinter removal.

This ruling carries a significant implication. One might have argued that the determination of whether an object qualifies as a *kli* — and thus falls outside the basic *muktzah* prohibition — should be made at the onset of Shabbat based on whether the object is conventionally classified as a vessel. A broken needle might be thought to have fallen out of the *kli* category entirely, rendering it like discarded refuse — genuine *muktzah*. Rav Yosef's answer is that as long as there is some functional use to which it may be put, it retains its status as a vessel for Shabbat purposes.

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye raises a challenge from the *Mishnah* in *Keilim*: *machat shenital chararah o uktzah — tehorah* — a needle missing its eye or its point is ritually pure. For the laws of *tumah v'taharah*, it has ceased to be a *kli* and, if it had previously contracted impurity, that impurity departs. The implication is that the laws of vessels should be uniform: what is not a vessel for *tumah* should not be a vessel for Shabbat either.

### Tumah vs Shabbat

Abaye himself answers the challenge he has raised — defending Rav Yosef's position. *Tumah ashabbat karmit?* — one may not simply import the definition of vessel from the laws of *tumah* into the laws of Shabbat. For *tumah*, the Torah requires *kli ma'aseh* — a vessel that is, in Rashi's formulation, still in the state as it was made, intact and complete. For Shabbat, the operative criterion is *midi d'chazi* — functionality. As long as the object is usable for something, it retains its vessel status and is not *muktzah*. The two bodies of law employ different definitional frameworks for what constitutes a vessel.

### Rava's Distinction

Rava complicates the picture further. A *tosefta* in *Keilim* directly addresses the Shabbat question and rules: *bein nekuvah bein she'einah nekuvah, muttar l'taltela b'shabbat* — whether the needle has an eye or not, it may be moved on Shabbat. And the requirement of an eye was stated *ela l'inyan tumah bilvad* — exclusively for the laws of *tumah*. This appears to be a direct vindication of Rav Yosef and Abaye.

Abaye, however, interprets this *tosefta* in a manner consistent with Rava's position. *B'golmei askinan* — the *tosefta* speaks of an unfinished needle, one that has not yet had its eye bored. *Zimnin d'mimlich aleihu u'mashvei lehu mana* — the owner may yet decide to complete it and make it into a full vessel. Since it is not broken but merely unfinished, it retains sufficient vessel status for Shabbat purposes even though it lacks the completeness required for *tumah*. Here the gap between the two definitional systems is relatively modest: an unfinished vessel may be functional enough for Shabbat, though not technically complete enough for *tumah*.

### Rava's Distinction

Rava's view, however, is that a genuinely broken needle — one whose eye or point has been removed — is different in kind. *Adam zarkah l'vein gruta'ot* — a person would throw such a needle into his scrap-metal pile. It is not merely incomplete; it has become refuse. In Rava's view, that object has lost its vessel status for Shabbat as well. If it is not a *kli* for *tumah*, it is not a *kli* for *muktzah* purposes either.

### Functional Status

The upshot of this discussion is that all opinions agree the definition of *kli* for *muktzah* is not identical to the definition for *tumah v'taharah*, but they disagree about the degree of divergence. For Rava, the gap is limited: an unfinished vessel may qualify for Shabbat even if not for *tumah*, but a broken vessel falls out of the Shabbat category along with the *tumah* category.
