For Abaye and Rav Yosef, the gap is wider: even a broken needle that has lost its eye retains functional vessel status for Shabbat purposes, so long as it can still be put to some use.

This discussion crystallizes an important conceptual point about *muktzah*. The category of *kli shemelachto l'issur* is fundamentally distinct from classic *muktzah*. Classic *muktzah* — whether *machmat mi'us*, *machmat chisron kis*, or simple objects like sticks and stones that were never part of one's mental universe of usable things — means the object is entirely off-limits, completely hands-off. The category of *keilim* is radically different: these are normal household objects that one uses regularly. At most, they carry certain restrictions on the manner in which they may be moved. It is therefore essential to establish whether an object qualifies as a *kli* — because doing so moves it out of the realm of genuine *muktzah* entirely and into the far more permissive world of *keilim*, where only specific types of movement are restricted.

---

## Infant Care

### Limb Straightening

The Gemara introduces what appears to be a tangential matter: *asuvei yanuka* — the question of whether one may manipulate the limbs of an infant on Shabbat, some form of physical adjustment of its limbs, as Rashi and Tosafot both explain. Rav Nachman forbids this; Rav Sheshet permits it.

### Purgatives

Rav Nachman grounds his position in the Mishnah that follows shortly: *ein osin apiktoizin b'Shabbos* — one may not take a purgative on Shabbat. Rashi notes that this is not strictly a *refu'ah* question in the usual sense — taking a purgative to eat more is not healing an illness — but it nonetheless falls under the rabbinic category of *metakein*, of "fixing" or adjusting the body in a way that resembles prohibited weekday activity. Tosafot, it should be noted, actually locates Rav Nachman's proof in the end of that Mishnah, which explicitly addresses the straightening of an infant's limbs.

### Splinter Analogy

Rav Sheshet responds: *hasam lav orcha hacha orcha* — taking a purgative to eat more is not a normal mode of bodily care; it is unusual behavior. Straightening an infant's limbs, by contrast, is ordinary care — comparable to feeding and hydrating the child. And the proof that normal bodily care is permitted on Shabbat comes from the Mishnah that one may use a needle to remove a splinter. Removing a splinter is not a *refu'ah* in the halakhic sense, nor is it *metakein*. It is simply the normal care of one's body. Rav Sheshet's position is that ordinary physical care of any kind falls outside the prohibition. Rav Nachman's rebuttal is precise: *hasam pakid* — a splinter is a foreign object lodged in the body; removing it is extracting something extrinsic, not fixing the body itself. Straightening limbs, by contrast, involves working directly on the body's own structure, which is why he regards it as forbidden.

---

## Historical Development

### Oleaster Stick

The Gemara turns to a Mishnah concerning *kaneh shel zeitim* — a stick used to turn over olives in a barrel, allowing the owner to assess their readiness for pressing by examining the oil that collects on the rod. The Mishnah rules: *im yesh kesher berosho mekabel tumah* — if the stick has a knot or bulge at its top, it can become *tamei*. *Ve-im lav ein mekabel tumah* — if it has no such feature, it cannot. Yet *bein kach u-vein kach nital b'Shabbos* — in either case it may be moved on Shabbat.

The Gemara asks: why should a smooth stick become *tamei* just because it has a knot? After all, *pshutei klei etz hem* — it is a flat wooden vessel with no receptacle, and *pshutei klei etz ein mekabelin tumah* — flat wooden vessels cannot become *tamei*, since the Torah's paradigmatic vessel is a sack, and just as a sack has a receptacle, wooden vessels must have one as well. The resolution, taught in the name of Rav Nachman, is that the knot functions as a minimal receptacle: *besha'ah shemehapech bezeitim hofcho vro'eh bo* — when one stirs the olives, one draws out the rod and examines the small amount of oil that collects in the hollow formed by the knot, thereby assessing the olives' readiness. This constitutes a *beis kibul*.

This Mishnah proves directly that the definition of *kli* for *tumah* and for Shabbat are not identical. The smooth stick without a knot clearly functions as a useful tool; it simply lacks a technical requirement for *tumah* status. Its Shabbat status is unaffected.

### Rabbi Yosi

Rabbi Yosi states a sweeping principle: *kol hakeilim nitlin* — all vessels may be moved on Shabbat, *chutz min hamassar hagadol vehayated shel machareisha* — except for the great saw and the peg of the plow. These represent the narrow category of professional implements so large and specialized — and so guarded by their owners — that they fall into genuine *muktzah machmat chisron kis* and cannot be moved for any purpose.

### Expanded Vessels

Rav Nachman extends this category: *hai uchla dekatzri ke-yated shel machareisha dami* — the launderer's metal basket, whether used to apply water to garments or to perfume them with incense, is similarly off-limits, as no one would use it for any other purpose. Abaye likewise identifies: *charva de-ushkafi* — the leatherworker's knife; *vesakina de-ashkavta* — the butcher's knife; *de-chatzina de-nargi* — the carpenter's plane. All of these are *ke-yated shel machareisha dami*, treated as the equivalent of the plow peg. They are the sorts of professional tools whose owners would not permit casual use, and they belong to the category of complete *muktzah*.

### Three Vessels

The Gemara then introduces the historical dimension: *barishona hayu omerim sheloshah keilim nitlin beshabbat* — originally, the Sages ruled that only three vessels may be moved on Shabbat. These were: the knife used for cutting pressed figs, a vessel used to skim the froth from a cooking pot, and the small table knife. Every other vessel was forbidden to move — a restriction that strikes one as nearly paralyzing. One naturally wonders how daily life on Shabbat was possible. Yet this was the initial decree.

It should be noted that Tosafot suggests that vessels with receptacles — cups, plates, spoons — were presumably never included in the prohibition. The decree concerned other types of implements. Nonetheless, the scope of the initial restriction was vast.

*Hitiru v'chazru v'hitiru, v'chazru v'hitiru* — then they relaxed the decree, and relaxed it again, and relaxed it further, *ad she'amru kol hakeilim nitlin beshabbat* — until they reached the position with which the Mishnah opens: all vessels may be moved, with the sole exception of the great saw and the plow peg.

This entire progression belongs to what is properly called *gezeirat keilim* — a rabbinic enactment concerning vessels — and it is conceptually distinct from the basic category of *muktzah*. The Gemara now turns to Abaye and Rava's reconstruction of what these stages of liberalization actually were.

---

## Four Stages

### Stage One

Abaye reconstructs the stages of liberalization as follows. The first relaxation permitted *davar shemilachto l'heter* — any vessel whose primary function is a permitted activity — to be moved *l'tzorech gufo*: that is, for the purpose of using the object itself for some permitted function.

### Stage Two

The second relaxation extended permission for *kli shemelachto l'heter* to *l'tzorech mekomo* as well — one may move such a vessel simply because one needs its space, even without intending to use the object itself.

### Stage Three

The third relaxation addressed *davar shemilachto l'issur* — vessels whose primary function is forbidden. These were now permitted to be moved *l'tzorech gufo* — to use the object for a permitted purpose — but not *l'tzorech mekomo*. Moving a hammer to clear a table, on this view, remained forbidden. Additionally, at this stage the permission extended only to moving such an object with one hand; moving it with two hands was still prohibited as too overtly a weekday activity.

### Stage Four

The fourth and final stage was the proclamation of *kol hakeilim nitlin b'Shabbat afilu bishtei yadayim* — all vessels may be moved, even when doing so requires two people. This is the position that now stands as the framework of the Mishnah.

Abaye's reconstruction, however, is stricter than the position we rule by in one important respect: he holds that *kli shemelachto l'issur* cannot be moved *l'tzorech mekomo*, and that *kli shemelachto l'heter* cannot be moved *mechama l'tzel*. Rava will disagree with both distinctions, and the *halacha* follows Rava.

---

## Rava's Stages

### Gufo=Mekomo

Rava challenges Abaye's construction at its foundation. The Gemara records his argument: *ma li l'tzorech gufo ma li l'tzorech mekomo?* — once the Sages declared something permitted, what halakhic distinction can be drawn between using the object for its own sake and simply needing its space? Abaye evidently believed these to be meaningfully different; Rava maintains they are not.

### Rava Stage 1

According to Rava, the first stage of liberalization was the full permission of *davar shemilachto l'heter* — vessels whose primary function is permitted — for all uses: *bein l'tzorech gufo bein l'tzorech mekomo*, whether one is using the object or merely needs its place.

### Rava Stage 2

The second stage extended permission to *mechama l'tzel* for *kli shemelachto l'heter* as well. One may move a vessel whose function is permitted even solely in order to protect it from damage — from sun to shade, for example. This is the ruling we follow.

The third stage then addressed *davar shemilachto l'issur*, permitting movement both *l'tzorech gufo* and *l'tzorech mekomo* — equating these two, as Rava does for *shemelachto l'heter* — but stopping short of *mechama l'tzel*. At this stage, as with Abaye's parallel formulation, individual movement was permitted but movement requiring two people was not.

### Final Ruling

*Ad she'amru kol hakeilim nitlin b'Shabbat afilu bishnei benei adam* — the final ruling reached is that all vessels may be moved even when two people are required. The *halacha* follows Rava throughout. The single remaining restriction on *kli shemelachto l'issur* is *mechama l'tzel* — one may not move it solely to protect it from damage.

An illustrative practical application: pens, pencils, and crayons are *keilim she'melachtam l'issur* — vessels whose primary function is a prohibited one. They are not *muktzah* in the classic sense. They may therefore be moved *l'tzorech gufo* — for instance, to use a pen to manipulate a lock mechanism — and *l'tzorech mekomo*, to clear them from a surface. What one may not do is move them solely to protect them from being damaged. Similarly, even large objects requiring two people to move, such as a computer, fall within the permitted category of *kli shemelachto l'issur* for purposes of *l'tzorech mekomo*, unless they have entered the category of *meyuchad limkomo* — designated to a fixed location in a manner that takes them outside the realm of ordinary *kelim* handling.

---

## Mechama L'Tzel

### Definition

*Mechama l'tzel* literally denotes moving an object from sun to shade — that is, moving it not to use it and not because it is in the way, but solely to preserve it from damage. For *kli shemelachto l'heter*, this is permitted. For *kli shemelachto l'issur*, it is forbidden.

### Conceptual Basis

The conceptual basis for this distinction is important to grasp. When one uses a hammer to crack nuts, one is relating to the hammer as a nutcracker — a tool for the present permitted purpose. When one moves a hammer off a table because it is in the way, one is relating to it as an obstacle or an annoyance, with no particular regard for its nature as a hammer. In neither case is one relating to the object *qua* hammer in its primary forbidden capacity. But when one moves a hammer from the rain because one does not want it to get damaged — when one's motivation is concern for the hammer as a hammer, as one's professional tool — one is at that moment relating to the object in precisely the way one relates to it throughout the week. It is that mode of relating, that self-positioning as the hammer's owner and guardian, that is the problem. The person is not treating Shabbat differently from the rest of the week with respect to this object.

### Hammer Example

The practical implication is pointed: if one's hammer is outside in the rain, the appropriate solution is to find some nuts that need cracking, thereby giving oneself a *l'tzorech gufo* justification for moving the hammer inside. This is not a legal fiction — it is a genuine permitted use. But moving the hammer inside purely to protect it, without any permitted use in view, remains forbidden for *kli shemelachto l'issur*.

This principle also explains the mortar-and-pestle case (*medocha*) that the Gemara revisits at the end of the *amud*. The Mishnah rules that the mortar may be moved if it contains garlic — because then one is in effect moving the garlic and the mortar incidentally — but not if it is empty. Rava resolves the difficulty by identifying the case as one of *mechama l'tzel*: the mortar is being moved purely to protect it or to clear it for safekeeping, and that is the one category forbidden even according to the final, most lenient stage of the rulings on *keilim*.

---

## Nehemiah Era

### Crisis Context

The Gemara provides explicit historical grounding for the entire phenomenon of *gezeirat keilim*. Rabbi Chanina reports: *bimei Nechemia ben Chachalia nishnet mishnah zu* — this Mishnah and the entire restrictive framework it encapsulates was enacted in the days of Nehemiah son of Hachaliah. The verse from the Book of Nehemiah is cited: *bayamim hahema raiti biyehuda dorchim gittot beshabbat* — in those days I saw in Judea that they were treading wine vats on Shabbat, and bringing in bundles of grain. *Chilul Shabbat* was rampant and open.

### Corrective Measure

The rabbinic response was correspondingly extreme: all vessels were declared off-limits. The logic was that vessel-handling is the gateway to productive weekday activity. If people cannot touch their tools, they cannot perform their work. The decree was a sweeping corrective — an overcorrection, by design — intended to erect a sharp barrier between Shabbat behavior and weekday behavior at a moment when that barrier had nearly collapsed entirely.

### Gradual Liberalization

Once the crisis had passed and the decree had achieved its corrective purpose, the process of gradual liberalization began, proceeding through the stages described by Abaye and Rava until reaching the permissive position of *kol hakeilim nitlin b'Shabbat* that stands as normative *halacha*.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer closes the discussion with an observation about the chronological relationship between several restrictive *mishnayot* and *braitot* and the general permission: *kanim u'maklot glustra u'meducha kulam kodem hataras kelim nishnu* — the Mishnah concerning reeds and staffs, the ruling about the *glustra* (a bar or bolt with a rounded protrusion), and the ruling about the mortar and pestle were all formulated during the period before the general permission of vessels was granted. Their stringency, which might otherwise seem puzzling against the backdrop of the lenient ruling, reflects the historical moment of maximum restriction — the period in Nehemiah's era when all vessels were off-limits. The restrictive tone of those passages is thus not a contradiction of the current ruling but a historical artifact of an earlier, emergency enactment.

The essential point to carry forward is the conceptual one. *Kol hakeilim* — all ordinary vessels — occupy a fundamentally different category than classic *muktzah*. Classic *muktzah* is an object that is mentally off-limits, pushed aside, out of one's world of intended Shabbat use. *Keilim* are the normal objects of daily life, and the entire history of the laws governing them is a history of a decree — *gezeirat keilim* — that was imposed in extreme circumstances and then progressively relaxed until the broad permission of the Mishnah was established. Within that broad permission, only one genuine restriction remains on *kli shemelachto l'issur*: it may not be moved *mechama l'tzel*. Everything else is permitted.

---

---

# Shabbat 124

## Kodem Gezeirat Keilim

### Gezeirat Keilim Overview

The daf opens at the bottom of 123b, in the midst of the discussion of *muktzah* as it applies to *keilim* — vessels that are ordinarily used and therefore not *muktzah*. To provide the necessary background: in the time of Nechemiah, owing to rampant *chilul Shabbat*, the Rabbis instituted a sweeping restriction known as *gezeirat keilim*, under which virtually no vessels could be handled on *Shabbat*. Over time there was a gradual pushback, and more and more vessels were permitted. By the period the *Gemara* addresses, the only remaining issues concern either highly specialized professional vessels that are never ordinarily moved, or vessels that fall into the category of *kli shemelachto l'issur* — a vessel whose primary function involves a *melachah* prohibited on *Shabbat* — for which certain restrictions on movement remain.

Against this backdrop, Rabbi Elazar proposes a sweeping historical framework to account for a series of otherwise puzzling *mishnayot*: *amar Rabbi Elazar*, kanim u-maklot, glustra u-maducha — reeds, poles, a door bolt, and a mortar — *kulan kodem l'gezeirat keilim nishnu*, all of these were taught during the ancient period before vessels were permitted. This is his method for dismissing four *mishnayot* that impose extremely restrictive limitations on the handling of these objects. The point is not merely that these *mishnayot* describe an outmoded stringency — it is that we do not rule in accordance with them at all, and the historical framing provides the explanation.

This approach of placing a historical framework on *Torah she-be-al peh* is not without precedent. The *Gemara* itself sometimes distinguishes between *Mishnah rishonah* and *Mishnah achronah*, acknowledging that an earlier teaching was later superseded. Here Rabbi Elazar applies an analogous logic to explain why certain *mishnayot* no longer represent operative *halacha*.

### Kanim - Lechem Hapanim

The first of the four *mishnayot* concerns the reeds used in the *lechem hapanim*. The *Mishnah* states: *lo sidur hakanim v'lo netilatan docheh et hashabbat* — neither the placing nor the removing of the reeds overrides *Shabbat*. This requires some explanation. In the *Beit Hamikdash*, the twelve loaves of *lechem hapanim* were arranged in two columns of six, with thin reeds interposed between each loaf to allow air circulation and prevent spoilage. These reeds functioned essentially as shelves, holding each loaf slightly above the one beneath it. On *Shabbat*, the procedure was to remove the old bread, place the new bread, and only after *Shabbat* reinsert the reeds — the reeds themselves were not arranged or removed on *Shabbat* itself.

The difficulty is evident: these reeds should be entirely permissible to handle. They are a classic *kli shemelachto l'heter* — a vessel whose function is entirely permitted. Why should they be restricted? Rabbi Elazar's answer is that this *Mishnah* originates from the period before *keilim* were permitted in any but the most basic circumstances, a time when even innocuous vessels could not be handled.

One might object: is there not a general rule that rabbinic prohibitions do not apply in the *Beit Hamikdash*? *Tosafot* addresses this directly, citing the principle *ein shevut b'mikdash* yet acknowledging that this rule is not absolute — some rabbinic restrictions did apply even there, and perhaps at this particular moment of crisis, when *chilul Shabbat* was so rampant, the Rabbis extended the restriction even into the *Beit Hamikdash*.

Rashi explains that the reeds were removed together with the bread on *Shabbat*, and then reinserted only after *Shabbat*. The concern reflected in the *Mishnah* thus makes sense specifically in a period when virtually all vessels were forbidden — a state of affairs that no longer applies.

### Maklot - Pesach Sacrifice

The second *mishnah* concerns the poles used for flaying the *Korban Pesach*. The *Mishnah* in *Pesachim* describes how thin, smooth poles were kept in the *Beit Hamikdash* for this purpose: one person would place a pole across his own shoulder and his companion's shoulder, suspend the *Korban Pesach* from it, and flay it. Rabbi Eliezer addresses the situation when *arba'ah asar she-chal lihyot be-Shabbat* — when *Erev Pesach* fell on *Shabbat*. Since the *Korban Pesach* could still be brought on *Shabbat*, the question was what accommodations had to be made. Rabbi Eliezer rules that one should not use the pole; instead, he says, *maniach yado al kteif chaveiro ve-yad chaveiro al kteifo* — one places his arm on the companion's shoulder and vice versa, and flays in that manner.

What is the problem with these poles? One might suggest they are *kli shemelachto l'issur*, but even then, the act of flaying is *l'tzorech gufo* — an entirely legitimate use. Rabbi Elazar's explanation is again that this ruling dates from the period when almost all *keilim* were forbidden — it is a holdover from the era of *gezeirat keilim* in the days of Nechemiah, when restrictions were near-universal.

### Glustra - Door Bolt

The third *mishnah* discusses a door bolt fitted with a rounded knob at its top — a *nagar she-yesh be-rosho glustra*. Rabbi Yehuda rules that one may *shomto min hapetach zeh v'toleh b'chaveiro b'Shabbat* — slip it from one door and attach it to another. Rabbi Dosa goes further and rules that it is simply like any vessel and may be moved freely in the courtyard.

The *Gemara* understands Rabbi Yehoshua's position (evidently the source behind Rabbi Yehuda's ruling) that one cannot move this bolt directly but must drag it, as though it cannot be lifted and carried in the ordinary manner. Rabbi Tarfon, however, permits it fully, stating *harei hu k'chol hakeilim* — it is like all other vessels, which implies that all other vessels are fully permitted. This makes it difficult to argue straightforwardly that this *mishnah* predates the general permission of *keilim*, since Rabbi Tarfon himself seems to presuppose that context. Perhaps the more compelling reading is that Rabbi Yehoshua's tradition was itself a holdover from an earlier period, while Rabbi Tarfon came to correct it — a fascinating instance of one Tanna reflecting an earlier sensibility that his colleague explicitly sought to supersede.

### Meducha - Mortar

The fourth case is the *maducha* — the mortar. The earlier discussion established that one may move a mortar only when it contains a clove of garlic. The question is: even if it is *kli shemelachto l'issur*, one should still be able to move it for its own legitimate purpose. Rabbi Elazar's historical framework provides the explanation — this too is a ruling from the pre-permissive era, and is therefore no longer operative law.

Thus all four *mishnayot* are accounted for under Rabbi Elazar's umbrella explanation: they are relics of a period before *hatarat keilim*, and we do not rule by them.

---

## Rava's Position on Keilim

### Rava - Post-Gezeirah Ves…

Rava rejects Rabbi Elazar's historical framework: *mi-mai*, what compelled you to explain all these *mishnayot* as predating the general permission of *keilim*? *Dilma le-olam achar hatarat kelim nishnu* — perhaps all four were taught after vessels were already permitted, and the restrictions each *Mishnah* reflects are explainable on independent grounds.

### Need Threshold for Reeds

Regarding the reeds of the *lechem hapanim*, Rava explains: *ta'ama mai mishum ivushai* — the reason reeds are used at all is to prevent the bread from going moldy. But *ve-hai purta*, for this brief interval — the new loaves resting without separation for only a portion of the day before the reeds are reinserted after *Shabbat* — the bread simply will not grow mold. There is therefore insufficient need to permit the use of the reeds. Similarly, for the poles used in flaying the *Korban Pesach*: *efshar k'Rabbi Elazar* — it is possible to manage without the poles, as the Tanna himself demonstrates by describing how people use their arms instead. The restriction therefore flows not from the era of blanket prohibition but from the absence of genuine need.

This raises a pointed question. Even granting that the need is not absolute, these reeds appear to be *kli shemelachto l'heter* — a vessel whose function is entirely permitted. Why should a mere deficiency in pressing need restrict the use of something in that category? This consideration has led some *poskim* to conclude that even a *kli shemelachto l'heter* is only permitted when there is some genuine purpose motivating its use — that the general permission of *keilim* after *hatarat keilim* was not a blanket license to handle vessels arbitrarily, but requires at least some threshold of *tzorech*. This is not the way the broad majority practice nor how the general assumption runs — we operate on the premise that a *kli shemelachto l'heter* may be moved freely — but some *poskim* do invoke this *Gemara* as support for imposing at least a minimal threshold of purpose even in that category.

The case of the poles is worth noting in this connection: the poles may actually qualify as *kli shemelachto l'issur* to begin with, which introduces a separate set of considerations, distinct from the reeds.

### Glustra - Domain Analysis

As for the *glustra*, Rava invokes the explanation of the school of Yanai: *k'debei Yanai*, *bechatzer she-eina meureves askinan* — the case involves a courtyard that has not been combined into an *eruv*. The restriction on the bolt is therefore not a *muktzah* problem at all. It is a problem of domain. The bolt sits in the door frame, and the question is whether moving it constitutes carrying from the house into the courtyard.

Rabbi Yehoshua holds *tof hapetach k'dilifnim dami* — the door frame is considered part of the interior of the house. Consequently, moving the bolt from one door directly to another would constitute transferring it from the domain of the house into the courtyard, which is forbidden in a courtyard without an *eruv*. Rabbi Yehoshua's allowance of *shomto* — dragging — reflects an attempt to avoid a direct transfer, though the precise mechanism that makes dragging permissible is not entirely clear.

Rabbi Tarfon, by contrast, holds *tof hapetach k'dilachutz dami* — the door frame is considered part of the courtyard. Since the bolt is already in the courtyard domain, moving it from one door frame to another is simply moving an object within the courtyard, *mana d'chatzer bechatzer kamitaltel*, and is entirely permissible.

This elegantly resolves the problem without invoking *gezeirat keilim* at all — and indeed Rabbi Tarfon's phrase *harei hu k'chol hakeilim* now makes perfect sense as a statement about domain, not as evidence that vessels are already generally permitted.

As for the *meducha*, Rava's answer is simply: *Rabbi Nechemia hi* — that *Mishnah* reflects the position of Rabbi Nechemia, whom the *Gemara* is about to encounter in the next *Mishnah*, and whose approach to *muktzah* and the movement of vessels is considerably more restrictive than the majority view.

So to summarize: we have two approaches to the four restrictive *mishnayot*. Rabbi Elazar situates them historically before *hatarat keilim*. Rava explains each individually — insufficient need for the reeds, alternative method for the poles, a domain concern for the bolt, and Rabbi Nechemia's stringent position for the mortar. A third explanation, applicable in some contexts, is that a vessel can be so specialized or so bound to its professional function that it is genuinely *muktzah* — not merely *kli shemelachto l'issur* but fully set aside. These three categories — the historical period, Rabbi Nechemia's stringency, and genuine *muktzah* — represent the range of explanations available for restrictive rulings in this area.

---

## Kol Hakeilim Mishna

### Mishna Text - Vessel Mov…

The *Gemara* now turns to the next *Mishnah*: *kol hakeilim nitlin l'tzorech v'shelo l'tzorech* — all vessels may be moved both for a purpose and without a purpose. This echoes the formulation of the opening of the *perek*, *kol hakeilim*, and raises the same underlying question: does this apply to *kli shemelachto l'heter*, to *kli shemelachto l'issur*, or to both? Against this permissive majority view, *Rabbi Nechemia omer ein nitlin ela l'tzorech* — Rabbi Nechemia rules that vessels may only be moved for a purpose, and as the *Gemara* will clarify, purpose here means the vessel's designated function.

### Rava - Purpose Definitio…

The *Gemara* asks: *mai l'tzorech u'mai shelo l'tzorech*? What does it mean to move something "for a purpose" versus "without a purpose"? Rava explains: *l'tzorech* means *davar shemelachto l'heter l'tzorech gufo* — moving a *kli shemelachto l'heter* to use it for its own function. *Shelo l'tzorech* means *davar shemelachto l'heter l'tzorech mekomo* — moving it because it is in the way and you need its space. Both of these are subsumed under the permissive rule of the *Mishnah*. What remains forbidden, on the stricter position attributed here to Abaye, is moving even a *kli shemelachto l'heter* to protect it from damage — *mechama l'tzel*. And a *kli shemelachto l'issur* is one degree more constrained: it can be moved *l'tzorech gufo* — to use it for its legitimate permitted function, such as using a hammer to crack nuts — but not merely *l'tzorech mekomo*, not simply to clear it from a table.

### Rabbi Nechemia - Restric…

Rabbi Nechemia goes further: *afilu davar shemelachto l'heter, l'tzorech gufo in, l'tzorech mekomo lo* — even a *kli shemelachto l'heter* may only be moved for its own use and not merely to clear its space. This is the view attributed to Abaye in earlier discussions, and it is one degree more restrictive than the way we rule. We rule like Rava, according to whom a *kli shemelachto l'heter* may be moved for any purpose whatsoever, and a *kli shemelachto l'issur* may be moved *l'tzorech gufo* or *l'tzorech mekomo* — the only forbidden movement being for protection from damage.

### Melachto L'Heter vs. L'I…

The full schema, then, is as follows. According to Rava's ruling — which is the *halacha* — a *kli shemelachto l'heter* may be moved for any reason: to use it, to clear its space, or even to protect it from rain or sun. A *kli shemelachto l'issur* may be moved to use it for a permitted function or to clear its space, but not to bring it in from the sun. Rabbi Nechemia shifts everything one degree more restrictive: a *kli shemelachto l'heter* may be moved only for its own designated use or to clear its space, not for protection; and a *kli shemelachto l'issur* may be moved only for its own designated use. We do not rule like Rabbi Nechemia.

It is worth noting that Rabbi Nechemia's position, as it emerges in other *sugyot* beyond this one, is interpreted even more narrowly by some: that a *kli shemelachto l'heter* may be used only for its classic, primary function — not for some secondary or ad hoc use even if technically permitted. That reading does not emerge explicitly from the language of this particular *sugya*, but it informs how Rabbi Nechemia is understood in other contexts, and the *Gemara* acknowledges that there are different places where his view is discussed and different ways to reconcile them.

---

## Practical Applications

### Clearing Dishes Problem

The *Gemara* now proceeds to a series of practical challenges. Rav Safra, Rav Acha bar Huna, and Rav Huna bar Chinana were sitting and reasoning about what Rabba's position would be, specifically *aliba d'Rabbi Nechemia*: if even a *kli shemelachto l'heter* cannot be moved *l'tzorech mekomo*, then how do we clear the dishes from the table after a meal? The dishes themselves are *kli shemelachto l'heter* — they are ordinary vessels used for entirely permitted purposes — and yet according to Rabbi Nechemia, if one cannot move them simply because one needs their space, the table could never be cleared.

Rav Safra offered the answer: *midi d'hava agraf shel rei* — it is comparable to removing a chamber pot. The Rabbis recognized a special dispensation to move even *muktzah* objects that are disgusting, lest one be demeaned by their continued presence. Similarly, a table full of dirty dishes carries a degree of that logic. Shortly thereafter, Abaye raised this same question directly to Rabba himself, and Rav Safra reported the answer that the colleagues had discussed — attributing it to the group rather than to himself, a gesture of modesty in the presence of the master.

### Chamber Pot Exception

The chamber pot analogy merits brief attention. The rule of *agraf shel rei* represents a specific accommodation for objects whose presence is degrading — the Rabbis could not in good conscience require one to leave such things in place merely because of *muktzah* considerations. Applying that logic to the clearing of dishes extends it to situations of significant discomfort or unseemliness, though the precise scope of the analogy remains a subject of broader discussion.

### Mortar Pestle Cases

Abaye poses a challenge to Rabba from the case of the *meducha*: the *Mishnah* states that a mortar may only be moved when it contains a clove of garlic. If it is a *kli shemelachto l'issur*, there should nonetheless be grounds for moving it *l'tzorech gufo* or *l'tzorech mekomo*. Rabba responds: *hacha be'mai askinan mechama l'tzel* — the case in that *Mishnah* involves moving the mortar to protect it, which is the one category that remains forbidden. That is the only circumstance in which even *l'tzorech gufo* or *l'tzorech mekomo* does not suffice to permit moving a *kli shemelachto l'issur*.

### Pessal - Cutting Board

A parallel challenge is raised from the case of the *pessal* — a broad flat surface used as an improvised cutting board. Both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel permit using it on *Yom Tov* as a cutting board for meat, in the spirit of *simchat Yom Tov*. But the *Mishnah* states that once one has cut meat on it, *asur letaltelo* — it may no longer be moved. Why not? It is *kli shemelachto l'issur*, but *l'tzorech gufo* or *l'tzorech mekomo* should still be permissible. The answer is again: *hacha be'mai askinan mechama l'tzel* — the case is one of protecting it from damage, and that remains forbidden.

### Log of Wood - Yom Tov

A further challenge: the *Mishnah* teaches that on *Yom Tov* one may not support a pot with a log of wood, and one may not support a door with it either. Now, a log of wood on *Yom Tov* is not *muktzah* in the full sense, since one may light fires on *Yom Tov* and use the log for that purpose. It ought therefore to be *kli shemelachto l'heter* — and if so, why may it not be used to support a pot? It is being used *l'tzorech gufo*. The answer the *Gemara* gives is: *keivan d'be'Shabbat davar shemelachto l'issur hu, gezeirah Yom Tov atu Shabbat* — since on *Shabbat* a log of wood is *kli shemelachto l'issur* (one cannot light fires), we apply by rabbinic decree the *Shabbat* status to *Yom Tov* as well. But this raises the deeper question of why even a *kli shemelachto l'issur* status should prevent use *l'tzorech gufo*, and the *Gemara* answers with a crucial distinction.

---

## Vessels vs. Non-Vessels

### Firewood Not a Kli

The *Gemara* introduces a foundational principle: *hani mili heicha d'ika torat kli alav* — all the rules about *kli shemelachto l'heter* and *kli shemelachto l'issur* apply only when the object in question carries the status of a *kli*, a vessel. *Heicha d'leika torat kli alav lo* — where something does not qualify as a *kli*, none of those rules apply and it is simply *muktzah*.

This is the key to understanding the log of wood. Our *perek* is *kol hakeilim* — it concerns vessels. Once an object qualifies as a *kli*, it falls within the domain of usable objects on *Shabbat*; at most its use may be limited to *l'tzorech gufo* and *l'tzorech mekomo* rather than *mechama l'tzel*. But if an object is not a *kli* — if it has no fashioned vessel character — it is fundamentally *muktzah*, not subject to the graduated permissions of *kli shemelachto l'issur* at all.

Firewood is not a *kli*. Its very purpose — being burned — removes it from the category of vessel. It is therefore *muktzah* outright on *Shabbat*, not merely *kli shemelachto l'issur*. If one designated a stick before *Shabbat* to serve as a tool for turning something over a spit, that might give it the character of a *kli shemelachto l'issur*, since it has been assigned a specific instrumental function. But designating wood for use as firewood does not make it a *kli* — firewood as such is not a vessel category. One cannot *meiyached* an object for a function that itself lacks the character of vessel use.

### Equating Shabbat-Yom Tov…

The *Gemara* now interrogates the mechanism by which the *Shabbat* status of firewood is applied to *Yom Tov*. The claim is that since firewood is *muktzah* on *Shabbat*, we apply a *gezeirah Yom Tov atu Shabbat* — a rabbinic extension of *Shabbat*'s strictness to *Yom Tov* — and therefore the firewood cannot be used on *Yom Tov* for purposes other than fire. The *Gemara* challenges this: *u'mi gazrinan* — do we truly equate *Yom Tov* to *Shabbat* in this way?

### Fruit Skylight Example

The challenge comes from the *Mishnah*: *mashilin perot derech aruba b'Yom Tov aval lo b'Shabbat* — one may lower fruit through a skylight on *Yom Tov* but not on *Shabbat*. The practical case is fruit drying on a roof that is about to be ruined — on *Yom Tov* one may lower it through the skylight, which minimizes exertion, but this would not be permitted on *Shabbat*. This demonstrates that we are willing to maintain a distinction between *Yom Tov* and *Shabbat* and do not simply import every *Shabbat* stringency into *Yom Tov*. The *Gemara* responds: *u'mi lo gazrinan* — but we also do equate them in other respects, as the principle *ein bein Yom Tov l'Shabbat ela ochel nefesh bilvad* indicates that for everything unrelated to food preparation, the two days are treated equivalently — even at the rabbinic level.

### Well Animal Debate

Rav Yosef resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, ha Rabbi Eliezer, ha Rabbi Yehoshua* — it is a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, as demonstrated by the teaching about an animal and its offspring that fell into a well on *Yom Tov*. Rabbi Eliezer rules that one may pull up the first animal on condition of slaughtering it and must do so; for the second animal, one may only lower food but may not extricate it, since that effort exceeds what *simchat Yom Tov* demands. Rabbi Yehoshua permits a scheme: one declares intent to slaughter the first animal, pulls it up, then changes one's mind; declares intent to slaughter the second, pulls that one up as well; and then decides which one to slaughter. *Ratza zeh shochet ratza zeh shochet* — whichever one he then prefers, he may slaughter.

This *ha'aramah* — legal artifice — allows both animals to be extricated without directly violating a prohibition, since at each moment of lifting there is an ostensible intention to perform the permitted act of *shechitah*. It is worth noting that *tzaar ba'alei chayim* — preventing animal suffering — may well have been part of what motivated the lenient position, though the *Gemara* frames Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling in terms of permitted *ha'aramah*.

The upshot is that those who are more lenient about *Yom Tov* relative to *Shabbat* follow the approach of Rabbi Yehoshua, while the stricter equation of the two days reflects Rabbi Eliezer's stance. The *Gemara* then notes that this mapping cannot be pressed too far: perhaps Rabbi Eliezer is only strict about the animal case because there is an available alternative — one can lower food to sustain the animal in the well — whereas when no alternative exists he might be more lenient. Conversely, perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua permits the *ha'aramah* only because that particular framing is available; where no permissible framing exists, he might be stricter. So the two positions cannot automatically be exported to every *Yom Tov*/*Shabbat* comparison.

Rav Pappa offers the ultimate resolution: the whole question of whether we equate *Yom Tov* to *Shabbat* may simply reflect the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, which we will return to momentarily.

---

## Beit Shammai vs. Hillel

### Beit Shammai Restrictions

Rav Pappa's resolution invokes an additional *Mishnah*: Beit Shammai says *ein motzi'in et hakatan v'et halulav v'et sefer Torah l'reshut harabbim* — one may not carry a child, a *lulav*, or a *Sefer Torah* into the public domain on *Yom Tov*. This is striking. We might assume there is no issue of carrying on *Yom Tov*, yet Beit Shammai applies restrictions even to objects that seem to involve a *tzorech mitzvah*. The implicit argument of Beit Shammai is that carrying on *Yom Tov* is constrained in ways quite similar to *Shabbat*, at least outside the specific domain of food preparation. Beit Hillel permits this carrying.

### Carrying-Muktzah Link

The *Gemara* now pushes back on Rav Pappa's resolution. Even granting that Beit Shammai is strict about *hotza'ah* — carrying in the *d'oraita* sense — why would that make him strict about *tiltul*, the rabbinic concern of *muktzah*? The reasoning that restricts carrying need not automatically generate a *muktzah* restriction, since the two operate on different levels. At this juncture the *Gemara* introduces one of the most revealing lines of the entire discussion.

### Tiltul-Hotza'ah Connecti…

*V'tiltul gufeih lav mishum hotza'ah hu?* — Is not *tiltul* itself connected to *hotza'ah*? Rashi explains: *hilkhach im mezalzel b'tiltul, mezalzel b'hotza'ah* — if one becomes careless about moving objects, one will come to carry them into a public domain. This single line illuminates the underlying rationale for *muktzah*: at least according to this *Gemara*, the prohibition against moving certain objects on *Shabbat* serves as a fence protecting against inadvertent *hotza'ah*. If one maintains self-discipline about what objects one touches and moves on *Shabbat*, that same mindset will curb one from casually carrying things outside.

Some *Rishonim* understood *muktzah* entirely in these terms — as a fence for carrying. Others explain *muktzah* through the concept of *hekhin*, derived from *v'hekhinu et asher yavi'u* — preparing beforehand. The objects one normally uses are treated as if designated for *Shabbat* use, while objects outside one's routine consciousness are not. Still others, notably the Rambam, ground *muktzah* in the need to make *Shabbat* feel qualitatively different, adding an element of taboo and distinctiveness to the day. And the *Gemara* itself earlier connected *gezeirat keilim* to the social crisis of widespread *chilul Shabbat*, suggesting that restrictions on vessels served a communal psychological function — creating a sense of the inviolate character of *Shabbat*.

What is particularly striking is how thoroughly *muktzah* has come to dominate the popular imagination of *Shabbat* restrictions. Children often attribute every prohibition on *Shabbat* to *muktzah*, which is in a sense an intuitive appreciation — however imprecise — of the way *muktzah* creates a pervasive sense of *Shabbat* as a different order of existence. Half of *Masekhtet Shabbat* concerns carrying and the other major portion concerns *muktzah*, and the *Gemara* here draws a direct line between the two.

---

## Rav's Melachto L'Issur

### Rav - Mar (Hoe) Case

The *Gemara* now affirms that Rav himself holds in accordance with Rava's lenient position on *kli shemelachto l'issur*. The evidence: *De'amar Rav*, Rav said that if one has a *mar* — a hoe or shovel — and wishes to move it *shelo yiganev*, so it should not be stolen, that is *tiltul shelo l'tzorech v'assur* — moving without purpose and forbidden. This represents the one forbidden category: moving a *kli shemelachto l'issur* to protect it from damage or theft. But the very framing of the prohibition confirms the positive: *aval l'tzorech gufo ul'tzorech mekomo mutar* — for its own use or to clear its space, a *kli shemelachto l'issur* may certainly be moved. Rav thus aligns with Rava.

### Shutza Net Story

Additional evidence comes from a narrative: Rav Kahana came to the house of Rav, and Rav instructed his servants *aisu lei shutza l'Kahana* — bring a net (a *kli shemelachto l'issur*) for Kahana to sit on. The *Gemara* reads significance into the phrasing: did Rav not deliberately specify the purpose — *l'tzorech gufo*, for Kahana's seating — to underscore that while use is permitted, moving without need would not be? The implication would be that *l'tzorech mekomo* alone would not be sufficient, contrary to what we have established.

### Net Protection Context

The *Gemara* resolves this in two ways. First: perhaps what Rav actually said was *shiklu shutza mikamei Kahana* — remove this net from before Kahana — which would make it a case of *l'tzorech mekomo*, clearing the space, and Rav was demonstrating that this too is permitted. Second: *iba'is eima, hasam mechama l'tzel hava* — the net was out in the yard and would have been damaged by exposure; Rav deliberately emphasized the purpose of sitting in order to frame the movement as *l'tzorech gufo* and thereby avoid any confusion about the sole category that is forbidden — moving a *kli shemelachto l'issur* merely to protect it from damage. The story thus confirms, rather than undermines, the permissibility of both *l'tzorech gufo* and *l'tzorech mekomo* for *kli shemelachto l'issur*.

---

## Cushion Case

### Rav Mari - Sun Question

Rav Mari bar Rachel had a cushion — a *kli shemelachto l'heter* — lying in the sun. He came before Rava and asked *mahu letiltulei* — may he move it out of the sun? Rava responded immediately: *shari*, it is permitted.

### Rava Permits - Questione…

Rav Mari then began introducing qualifications: he did not really need it, he had another cushion available. Rava brushed this aside: *chazya orchin*, perhaps you will have guests. Rav Mari pressed further — he had more than enough cushions for guests too. At this point the exchange becomes somewhat pointed.

### Gilui Da'at - Strict View

Rava said to him: *galya da'atach k'Rava svira lach* — by your persistent resistance you are demonstrating that you yourself hold the stricter view, that even a *kli shemelachto l'heter* may not be moved *mechama l'tzel*. I hold the permissive position. For anyone else who asks, it is *mutar*; *bedidi asar* — if you want to impose the stringency on yourself, that is your prerogative. This is a classic expression of *gilui da'at* — one's own behavior revealing one's operative conviction — and Rava's response is both pointed and principled: a personal stringency is valid, but it does not become the universal *psak*.

---

## Brooms - Cloth vs. Frond

### Broom Types Distinction

Rabbi Abba citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav: *machbadot shel milta* — cloth rags or cloth brooms used to wipe off surfaces — are *kli shemelachto l'heter* and are *mutar letiltalan b'Shabbat*, permitted to be moved on *Shabbat*. *Aval shel tmara* — brooms made of fronds — since their primary use is sweeping dirt floors, which is forbidden on *Shabbat* because it would level the ground, they are *kli shemelachto l'issur* and may not be moved. *V'Rabbi Eliezer omer af shel tmara* — Rabbi Eliezer says even the frond broom may be moved.

### Frond Broom Prohibition

The *Gemara* asks: in what context does Rav prohibit the frond broom? If the concern is *l'tzorech gufo* or *l'tzorech mekomo*, we have already established that Rav holds like Rava and permits a *kli shemelachto l'issur* in both of those cases. So why would Rav restrict the frond broom?

### Protection - Not Purpose

The answer is that the prohibition must be referring specifically to *mechama l'tzel* — moving the frond broom to protect it from damage. That is the one case in which even a *kli shemelachto l'issur* may not be moved, and that is precisely the scenario Rav addresses. The formulation of the ruling thereby confirms the entire framework: Rav restricts the frond broom only in the context of protection, consistent with his general position that *l'tzorech gufo* and *l'tzorech mekomo* remain permitted.

### Rabbi Eliezer Agreement

As for Rabbi Eliezer's statement that even the frond broom is permitted — the *Gemara* resolves a textual difficulty by proposing a change in reading: rather than having Rabbi Eliezer dispute Rav's restriction, he should be understood as agreeing with it: *v'chen amar Rabbi Eliezer* — and so too Rabbi Eliezer agrees that in the context of *mechama l'tzel* it is forbidden. Both authorities thus align in permitting movement of *kli shemelachto l'issur* for use or space, and in restricting it when the sole motive is protection from damage.

---

## Broken Vessels

### Mishna - Broken Parts

The *Gemara* turns to the next *Mishnah*: *kol hakeilim hanitlin b'Shabbat, shivreihen nitlin imahen* — all vessels that may be moved on *Shabbat*, their broken pieces may also be moved. The qualification: *uvilvad shehen osin me'ein melacha* — as long as the broken pieces can still perform some function. The examples given are a broken kneading trough whose shards can be used to cover a barrel, and broken glass that can be used to cover a small flask. In each case, the piece has some residual utility and therefore retains sufficient character as a *kli* to avoid *muktzah*.

### Rabbi Yehuda - Original…

Rabbi Yehuda imposes a stricter standard: *bilvad shehu osin me'ein melachtam* — the broken pieces must be capable of performing a function similar to their original purpose. A shard of the kneading trough must be large enough to hold porridge, as the original vessel held dough. A piece of broken glass must retain enough curvature to hold oil, as the original bottle held liquids. Rabbi Yehuda requires a functional continuity with the original vessel's character; mere general utility is insufficient.

### Breaking Time Debate

Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel clarifies that the dispute between the *Tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda applies specifically to vessels that broke on *Erev Shabbat*. One opinion holds that what matters is whether the broken piece can do some portion of the original function; the other holds that any function suffices. However, if the vessel broke on *Shabbat* itself — *divrei hakol mutarin* — all agree the broken pieces are permitted, as long as they retain some use. The reasoning: *ho'il u'muchanim agav avihen* — since the vessel was not *muktzah* when *Shabbat* began, its permitted status adheres to the pieces as well.

### Broken Vessels as Firewo…

Rav Zutra raises a challenge from a case involving *Yom Tov*: the ruling that on *Yom Tov* one may use whole vessels as firewood — *masikin b'keilim* — but not broken vessel pieces — *v'ein masikin b'shivrei keilim*. When did these pieces break? If they broke before *Yom Tov*, *eitzim b'alma havu* — they are simply wood, and why should they not be usable as firewood? It must be that they broke on *Yom Tov* itself. Yet the ruling restricts their use — which contradicts the claim that breaking on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* makes things *easier* because the original permitted status adheres.

### Nolad - New Creation

The *Gemara* resolves this by inverting the framework: *ela i itmar, hachi itmar* — the original formulation must be reversed. Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel actually says that the dispute applies when vessels broke on *Shabbat*, and breaking on *Shabbat* makes things *harder*, not easier. The reason: if the vessel changed its character on *Shabbat*, there is a concern of *nolad* — a new entity came into existence on *Shabbat*. One opinion holds that the broken pieces are still considered *muchan*, prepared, since the vessel was permitted at the outset of *Shabbat*, and the pieces retain that status as long as they still perform some portion of the original function. The other opinion holds that if the pieces can only perform a *different* function from the original vessel, they constitute *nolad* — something genuinely new has come into being — and are therefore *muktzah*.

By contrast, if the vessel broke *Erev Shabbat*, *divrei hakol mutarin* — all agree the broken pieces may be used — since the *nolad* concern is absent: the breakage occurred before *Shabbat* began, the pieces had some function when *Shabbat* entered, and there is no newly created entity on *Shabbat* itself. The discussion will continue with further elaboration of these distinctions in the next daf.

---

---

# Shabbat 125

## Burning Vessels

### Three Baraitot

The daf opens in the midst of a sustained discussion of *muktzah* and *Yom Tov*, picking up from the previous amud (124b). The *mishnah* had addressed *kelim* that broke on *Shabbos*, and the *gemara* explored two ways of reading the case: on one view, a vessel that broke on *Shabbos* is advantaged because it began *Shabbos* in a state of *muchan*, ready for use and outside the *muktzah* category. On the other view, breaking on *Shabbos* itself creates a *nolad* problem, and it is better if the vessel broke *erev Shabbos*. With this backdrop in mind, the *gemara* introduces three conflicting *baraitot*.

### R. Yehuda's Nolad

The first *beraita* states: *masikin bekelim ve'ein masikin beshivrei kelim* — on *Yom Tov* one may burn vessels as fuel, but not broken vessels. The second *beraita* states the reverse: *kesheim shemasikin bekelim kach masikin beshivrei kelim* — just as one may burn whole vessels, so too one may burn broken vessels. A third *beraita* states: *ein masikin lo bekelim velo beshivrei kelim* — one may burn neither. (Presumably, the permitted fuel in all views remains ordinary wood.) The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by attributing each position to a different *tanna*. The first *beraita* reflects the view of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that breaking on *Yom Tov* creates a *nolad* problem. Therefore, whole *kelim* may be burned — they are not *muktzah* — but broken vessels, having newly acquired their broken status on *Yom Tov*, are *nolad* and may not be used.

### R. Shimon Lenient

The second *beraita*, which permits burning broken vessels as well, reflects the view of Rabbi Shimon, who does not accept the category of *nolad* at all. In his view, even a *kli* that broke on *Yom Tov* itself may be used.

### R. Nechemia Restrictive

The third *beraita*, which prohibits burning even whole *kelim*, reflects the well-known stringent position of Rabbi Nechemia, who holds that a *kli* may be used only for its intended purpose. Since a vessel's intended purpose is not to serve as firewood, burning it is impermissible. And a broken vessel is doubly precluded — it would both fail the intended-purpose test and, if it broke on *Yom Tov*, raise a *nolad* concern as well.

---

## Leftover Bricks

### Bricks Movable

Rav Nachman rules: *hanei livnei de'ishtayer mibinyana* — bricks left over from a construction project are permitted to be moved (*shari letaltulinhu*). The reasoning is *dechazu lemismach aleihu* — they are fit to lean or sit upon. This is a striking ruling. One would naturally assume that leftover construction bricks are *muktzah*, having been set aside for building purposes. Yet Rav Nachman holds that precisely because the common context of a pile of leftover bricks is one where people would sit on them in passing, no formal act of designation is needed. This ruling anticipates a broader question that will occupy the *gemara* later in the daf: what exactly must be done to transform an object — whether a stone, a brick, or a piece of nature — into something considered *muchan* and not *muktzah*? Rav Nachman's ruling here suggests that context alone, the fact that it is the normal kind of thing people would use, suffices. It is worth noting that this is better than a random stone: a brick is a human artifact, fashioned to be used, even if not currently serving any particular function.

One might raise the question whether moving and arranging these bricks would constitute *boneh*. The *gemara* implicitly sets this aside: since the bricks do not interlock and no *ohel* is being formed, simple stacking would not constitute *boneh*.

### Stacked Becomes Muktzah

However, Rav Nachman qualifies this: *sharginhu vadai aktsinhu* — if one has already stacked the bricks, that act itself constitutes a clear expression of intent to reserve them for future construction. The deliberate stacking demonstrates that the owner has mentally set them aside (*hiktzah*), and they therefore become *muktzah*. The underlying principle is revealing: in the absence of any act of consecration for construction purposes, leftover bricks remain presumptively available and non-*muktzah*. But a positive act of setting-aside reverses that presumption.

---

## Pottery Shards Context

### Shards: Chatzer vs Karme…

The *gemara* continues with closely related cases. Rav Nachman citing Shmuel rules: *cheres ketana* — a small shard of pottery — *mutar letaltela bechatzer*, may be moved in a *chatzer*. The discussion implicitly assumes the shard broke before *Shabbos* to set aside any *nolad* concern. In a courtyard, where people conduct domestic activity and commonly have pottery in use, it is normal to pick up and use a pottery shard — to cover a vessel, for instance — and so such a shard is considered *muchan* and not *muktzah*. However, *aval bekarmelis* — in a *karmelis*, a semi-public domain — it may not be moved, even within four *amos*, because this is framed as a *muktzah* question, not a carrying question. The *karmelis* does not provide the context of active domestic use that gives the shard its presumptive utility.

This leads to a broader question that runs through this entire section of the *gemara*: what makes a *shever kli* — or more broadly, any object of ambiguous status — considered *muchan*? The answer being developed here is context. A shard in a courtyard is the kind of thing one would pick up and use; in a *karmelis*, that is less self-evident.

### R. Nachman: All Contexts

Rav Nachman himself, going beyond his ruling in the name of Shmuel, states: *afilu bekarmelis* — even in a *karmelis*, the shard may be moved. The sole exception, in his own view, is a *reshus harabbim* — a true public thoroughfare — where pottery shards are simply not the sort of objects one normally encounters or uses.

### Rava: Common Use Standard

Rava goes further still: *afilu birshus harabbim* — even in a *reshus harabbim* the shard is permitted, provided one has a use for it at that moment. The *muktzah* question, in Rava's view, should not turn on the specific domain one is currently in. If the object is the kind of thing that is *ra'uy* — fit for use — in *some* common context, that suffices to render it non-*muktzah* universally. One need not demonstrate that it is typically used in the specific location where one encounters it.

### Rava's Shoe Story

The *gemara* illustrates Rava's position through a vivid anecdote. Rava was walking in the *Ritka* — which Rashi identifies as the name of the *reshus harabbim* of *Mechuza*, his city — when his shoes became muddied (*itvassa masaneh*). His attendant picked up a pottery shard from the road and began scraping the mud from Rava's shoe. The rabbinic students who were present began reproving the attendant: one cannot pick up a pottery shard on *Shabbos*! Rava intervened sharply: *lo mistayei dlo gamri* — it is not enough that you yourselves do not know the *halacha*, *ela migmar nami migmri* — you must also proclaim your ignorance to others?

Rava then articulated the principle: *ilu bachatzer havai, mi lo chazi lechasuyei bei mana* — if we were in a courtyard, everyone would agree the shard could be used to cover a vessel; that is effectively our *mishnah*. *Hacha nami chazi ledidi* — here too, in the *reshus harabbim*, I have a use for it. The operative rule Rava establishes is that if an object is *ra'uy* in some common context, it is non-*muktzah* in all contexts. What is required is not that the object be useful specifically where it is found, but that it belongs to the category of things that people actually use — that in at least some, perhaps typical, circumstances it would be considered a usable object rather than garbage.

---

## Discarding Vessels

### Barrel Cover Permitted

Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules: *megufas chavis shenichtesa* — if a barrel has been shattered, *mutar letaltla b'shabbos* — one may move both the cover and the broken pieces of the barrel. A *beraita* supports this: *megufah shenichtesa, hi ushvareha, mutar letaltela b'shabbos* — the cover and the barrel's broken pieces may be moved. As a *shever kli* that retains some functional use, the pieces remain non-*muktzah*.

### Don't Modify Shards

However, the *beraita* immediately qualifies: *v'lo yispus mimena shever lechasuyei bo kli* — one may not break off an additional piece from the barrel in order to use it to cover a vessel. Doing so constitutes an act of fashioning a vessel on *Shabbos*. Rashi extends this further: one may not even smooth the edges of an existing shard, which would be an even graver form of fashioning. Similarly, one may not use a shard to prop up a bed leg (*velismoch bah karei hamita*).

### Pre-Shabbat Disposal

A critical qualification follows: *ve'im zarka b'ashpa — asura* — if one threw the broken barrel into the garbage, it becomes *asur*. This is the key to the *gemara*'s conceptual framework for *shever kli*. A broken vessel, because it retains functional potential, is presumptively non-*muktzah*. But the owner can redefine it as garbage — and once defined as garbage, with no use, it becomes *muktzah*. Context can make something *muktzah* even if its physical properties would otherwise permit use.

### Rav Pappa's Challenge

Rav Pappa challenges this reasoning: if throwing something out makes it *muktzah*, then *zarkeih liglimeh* — if you threw out your coat, does that too become *muktzah*? Rav Pappa resolves this by clarifying the *gemara*'s intent: the operative moment is *mibod yom la'ashpah* — if you threw the item out before *Shabbos*, *erev Shabbos*, when *Shabbos* was set in with the object already defined as garbage, only then is it *asur*.

The resolution distinguishes between two types of objects. A true *kli*, like a garment, does not lose its *kli* status merely by being discarded; its fundamental identity as a functional vessel persists. But a *shever kli*, whose status was already ambiguous — it is functional but was never wholly a vessel in the usual sense — can be definitively classified as garbage through the act of throwing it out before *Shabbos*. Once *Shabbos* enters with the object having been designated as refuse, its status is fixed for the duration of *Shabbos*. Conversely, throwing it out on *Shabbos* itself would not retroactively change its status, since it entered *Shabbos* as a non-*muktzah* item. The broader principle being refined here is that *shever kli* is presumptively better than a random stone or stick because it started as a *kli* and retains that residual character — but that character can be affirmatively negated before *Shabbos* through a clear act of disposal.

---

## Mat Strands & Garment Sc…

### Mat Strands Permitted

Mar bar Hamdura citing Shmuel rules: *kromei d'machatzeles mutar l'taltelan b'Shabbos* — strands that have come loose from a reed mat may be moved on *Shabbos*. The reasoning, which Bar Hamdura explains he received directly, runs as follows: *machatzeles gufah l'mai chazei* — what is a mat itself used for, if not sitting upon and covering things? *L'chasuyei bei afra* — to cover dirt, to prevent dust from rising. Therefore, *hani nami chazu l'chasuyei bei tinofes* — even a single loose strand can be used to cover some filth. This is noteworthy: the strand not only performs some function, it can arguably perform a function *me'ein melachtan* — similar to the original function of the mat itself. Under the more stringent reading of the *mishnah* (associated with Rabbi Yehuda), the standard is that a *shever kli* must be capable of performing something similar to its original function. Even by that standard, the mat strand qualifies.

### Scraps Too Small

Rabbi Zeira citing Rav rules: *shirei pruzmos assur l'taltelan b'Shabbos* — remnants of a *pruzma* (a garment) may not be moved on *Shabbos*. Abaye explains: *b'matlaniyos she'ein bah gimmel al gimmel* — we are discussing scraps of cloth that do not even measure three by three handbreadths. Such a piece, *d'lo chazi lo l'aniyim v'lo l'ashirim* — is not usable by either the poor or the wealthy; it is not large enough even to serve as a patch. When the fragment of a *shever kli* has reached a point where it is too small to perform any reasonable function whatsoever, it exits the category of the usable and becomes *muktzah*.

---

## Broken Ovens

### Oven Debate Setup

The *gemara* now cites a formal *baraita*: *shirei tanur yashan harei hen k'chol hakelim hani-talin b'chatzer* — the broken pieces of an old oven are like all *kelim* that may be moved in a courtyard. This is the position of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *ein nitlin* — they may not be moved. Rabbi Yossi testified in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov in agreement with Rabbi Meir, permitting the broken pieces to be moved.

Before examining the debate, the *gemara* uses the *beraita* to establish the physical context. A *tanur* was a large pottery vessel set into the ground with plaster and used for baking: a fire was placed at the base and pots were set over the top. The *beraita* also mentions the cover of the oven — which is relevant because the cover lacked a handle — a point to be addressed in a later section.

### Abaye's Explanation

Abaye explains the underlying debate: *b'osin me'ein melacha v'ein osin me'ein melachtan kamifligi* — they dispute the case of broken pieces that can perform *some* function but not their original function. A broken shard of oven pottery can perhaps be used to cover a vessel, but it cannot bake bread. Can it nevertheless do something? Of course. Is that enough? That is the debate. Abaye identifies this as the same argument between the *tanna kamma* (understood to be Rabbi Meir) and Rabbi Yehuda in the *mishnah*: Rabbi Meir holds that any function suffices; Rabbi Yehuda holds that the function must be similar to the original function (*me'ein melachtan*). Under Abaye's reading the dispute about the oven pieces is simply an application of the generic *mishnah* debate to a particular case, a very clean and straightforward explanation.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava raises a pointed challenge to Abaye's account: *i hachi, de-miflegi be-shivei tannura, liflegu be-shivei kelim be-alma* — if the debate is simply about objects that can perform some function but not their original one, why argue specifically about broken oven pieces? Argue about broken vessels in general! This challenge has force precisely because there is another, independent dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda involving ovens. Rava reasons that the *tannaim*' choice to argue specifically about ovens must be intentional — it must relate to something particular about ovens, not merely to the generic question of *shever kli*.

---

## Oven in Well

### Oven Setup

Rava therefore proposes that the broken oven pieces under debate are the shards of a very particular kind of oven. He cites a *mishnah* from tractate *Kelim*: *natno al pi ha-bor o al pi ha-dut* — if an oven was placed into a well or into a *dut* (a cistern with a surrounding structure), *ve-natan sham even* — and stones were inserted around it. Rashi explains the configuration: the walls of the well were close to the walls of the oven, and small stones were wedged into the gaps to create a tight fit, preventing heat from escaping around the sides. Since the heat was thus entirely contained within the oven just as it would be if the oven were plastered to the ground, this configuration is treated as equivalent to being plastered to the ground.

The relevance of "attached to the ground" requires brief explanation. Under the laws of *tumah ve-taharah*, objects generally become susceptible to *tumah* only when they are detached from the ground; items connected to the ground are considered part of the earth and are *tahor*. An oven is exceptional: it becomes susceptible to *tumah* specifically when it is attached to the ground. The Talmudic derivation comes from the verse: *tannur ve-khirayim yutatz temeim hem* — an oven and a *kirah* shall be demolished (*yutatz*), they are *tamei*. The word *yutatz* — to demolish, as opposed to *shevirah*, simply to break — implies connection to the ground, since one demolishes something connected to the earth. Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis dispute what this implies.

### R. Yehuda: Connection Re…

Rabbi Yehuda holds: *mechusar netitza tammei* — only that which requires demolition, i.e., something connected to the ground, can become *tamei* as an oven. *She-ein mechusar netitza tahor* — an oven not connected to the ground when first fired is not a true oven and therefore is *tahor*. The *mishnah* in *Kelim* states Rabbi Yehuda's position as follows: *im masik milmata ve-hu nisok milmala* — if one fires from below and the oven heats fully at the top (meaning the heat is well contained by the tight stone-wedged fit), then *tamei*. *Ve-im lav* — if heat escapes around the sides, then *tahor*, because it is not sufficiently equivalent to being plastered to the ground.

### Rabbis: No Connection Re…

The Rabbis hold: *temeim yihyu lachem mikol makom* — the verse's concluding phrase, "they shall be *tamei* to you," is inclusive and requires no condition of ground connection. Once the oven is fired, it becomes *tamei* regardless of whether it is connected to the ground. *Hu ve-hu sak mikol makom* — it makes no difference.

The Rabbis do not ignore the word *yutatz*, however. They interpret it differently: *de-salka da'atach amina keivan de-chavrei be-ara, ke-gufa de-ara dami* — one might have thought that since the oven is connected to the ground, it is like the ground itself and cannot become *tamei*. The word *yutatz* comes to teach *ka mashma lan* that even a ground-connected oven becomes *tamei*. In other words, for the Rabbis *yutatz* does not impose a requirement of connection; it removes a potential exemption.

Conversely, Rabbi Yehuda, who requires connection, must explain the phrase *temeim yihyu lachem*. The answer — attributed to the tradition of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel — leads to the next point.

### First vs Second Firing

Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel clarifies: *machlokes be-heseik rishon* — this entire dispute applies only to the first firing of the oven, when the pottery walls are hardened and the oven acquires its essential identity. It is at that inaugural firing that Rabbi Yehuda requires the oven to be properly connected to the ground. *Aval heseik sheini* — but if the oven was subsequently detached and then refired, everyone agrees that ground connection is not required, *afilu talui be-tzavar gamal* — even if it were suspended from the neck of a camel. Ulla confirms this: even for the Rabbis' position, their ruling that no ground connection is required applies from the first firing; *afilu talui be-tzavar gamal* it would be *tamei*.

---

## Rava Resolves Oven Debate

### Rava's Theory

Rava applies this *tumah ve-taharah* dispute directly to the *Shabbos* question. If the oven was placed in the well without achieving sufficient ground connection as required by Rabbi Yehuda — that is, if heat escaped around the sides — then Rabbi Yehuda holds it was never a proper *kli* in the first place. Since it was not a true oven-*kli*, its broken pieces are certainly not pieces of a *kli*, and therefore they are *muktzah*. The Rabbis, who hold that even an unconnected oven is a valid *kli* susceptible to *tumah*, would naturally permit moving the broken pieces on *Shabbos*.

### Rav Ashi Rejects

Rav Ashi objects sharply: *i hachi, ade-mifligi be-shivrei tanur, lifligi be-tanur gufa* — if that is what they are disputing, they should be arguing about the oven itself, not its broken pieces. If Rabbi Yehuda holds the oven was never a *kli*, that would be the more fundamental question; why frame the debate around the broken pieces? *Hashata tanur gufa le-rabbi Yehuda lo havei mana, ma shevarav mi-ba'ya* — if the oven itself is not a *kli* according to Rabbi Yehuda, there is obviously no question about its pieces. Rav Ashi therefore rejects Rava's explanation entirely.

---

## Tafka Usage Case

### Stovetop Function

Rav Ashi proposes that the debate is exactly what Abaye said it was originally — about broken pieces of a vessel that can perform some function but not their original function — and that there is nothing mysterious about the choice of an oven as the example. *U-ve-osa ma'aseh tafka* — the broken piece of an oven can be used as a *tafka*, which Rashi describes as functioning like a stovetop or grill. Instead of placing fire inside and containing heat within walls (as in an actual oven), one places a fire underneath the broken shard and the shard becomes hot, so that food can be placed on top of it. This is a useful function, but it is structurally different from baking in an oven.

### R. Meir's Argument

Rabbi Meir addresses Rabbi Yehuda with an internal argument: *le-didi* — according to my own position, any function whatsoever suffices and there is no requirement of similarity to the original function. But *ella ledidach* — even granting your position, admit at least that this piece performs something close enough to its original function to satisfy your standard.

### R. Yehuda's Response

Rabbi Yehuda replies: *lo dami* — it is not comparable. *Hasam haseka mibifnim, hacha haseka mibachutz* — in the oven the fire burns on the inside and the walls contain and radiate the heat; here the fire is on the outside. *Hasam be'umad* — in an oven the items being cooked stand upright within; *hacha lav be'umad* — here items lie flat on the surface. The two modes of cooking are fundamentally different and the broken shard's function does not qualify as *me'ein melachtan* — similar enough to its original function.

---

## Covers & Stoppers

### Oven Cover Permitted

The *beraita* that introduced the oven debate also established that the cover of an oven (*kisuyo*) may be moved on *Shabbos she'eino tzarich beis yad* — even if it lacks a handle. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's testimony in the *beraita* covers both the broken oven pieces and the handle-less cover. This ruling is invoked practically: Avida asks, according to whom do we nowadays move the oven covers of *Matza Mechasya* that lack handles? *Ke-Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* — in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. The question of whether a handle-less cover raises *boneh* concerns is connected to the broader issue of whether an object that fits snugly into a structure begins to look less like a movable *kli* and more like a building component. A handle signals that removal is intended and expected; its absence raises that concern, which is part of why the ruling needed to be stated explicitly.

---

## Gourd & Stone

### Tight Fit Required

The *mishnah* introduces a new case: *ha'even shebakiruya* — the stone in the *kiruyah*, a type of hollowed-out gourd used for drawing water. A gourd floats and therefore cannot draw water without ballast. The common solution was to insert a stone to weigh it down. The *mishnah* rules: *im memalin bah ve'einah nofeles, memalin bah* — if when one draws water the stone does not fall out, the gourd may be used and the stone is considered part of the vessel. *Ve'im lav* — if the stone would float out, one may not use the gourd: the stone remains *muktzah*, the gourd may become a *basis* for a *muktzah* object, and the entire assembly is problematic.

This case raises in concrete form the question of what is needed to transform a stone — a piece of nature with no prior history as a *kli* — into a functional vessel component. The *mishnah* will be analyzed further in the *gemara* below.

---

## Window Stopper

### R. Eliezer: Tied Required

The *mishnah* now turns to *pkak hachalon* — a stopper or plug for a window. In the absence of window shades, large pieces of wood or similar material were used to block window openings. The question is whether one may install such a stopper on *Shabbos*. Rabbi Eliezer rules: *bizman shekashur vetalui pokmin bo* — only when the stopper is both tied to the wall and suspended (i.e., not dragging on the ground) may one use it to stop the window. If it is not tied and not suspended, one may not — *ve'im lav ein pokmin bo*. The reasoning is that inserting an unattached, unsuspended piece into a wall opening looks like *boneh* — one is adding a new structural element to the building. But if the stopper is already tied to the wall and hangs suspended, it is recognizably part of the window structure, akin to a shutter, and closing the window with it is not an act of construction.

### Sages: Always Permitted

The Sages disagree: *bein kach uvein kach pokin bo* — regardless of whether the stopper is tied and suspended or not, one may use it. The Sages are less concerned that inserting a temporary stopper into a window constitutes *boneh*, and their position does not require the formalities Rabbi Eliezer demands.

---

## Covers & Stoppers (II)

### Forgotten Stone

The *gemara* now cites a later *mishnah* in the tractate: *even sheal pi hachavit* — a stone placed on the mouth of a barrel as a stopper. The ruling is that one may tip the barrel so that the stone falls off (*mateh al tzidah vehi nofelet*), thereby accessing the barrel's contents. The stone is *muktzah* and the barrel itself is not a *basis*. Rabba citing Rav Ami citing Rabbi Yochanan qualifies: *lo shanu ela beshocheach* — this ruling applies only when the stone was left on the barrel through forgetfulness. *Aval bemaniach* — if the stone was intentionally left there as a stopper, *naaseh basis ledavar haasur* — the barrel becomes a *basis* for a *muktzah* object and the barrel itself becomes *muktzah*. Since the owner knowingly rested a *muktzah* stone on the barrel and left it there through *bein hashmashos*, the barrel is secondary to the stone and acquires *muktzah* status along with it.

### Intentional Cover

Rav Yosef citing Rav Assi citing Rabbi Yochanan presents the inverse ruling, stated in identical terms but with opposite import: *lo shanu ela beshocheach* — the *tuma* that the stone retains *muktzah* status applies only when it was left there by forgetfulness. *Aval bemaniach* — if one intentionally placed the stone there, *naaseh kisui lachavit* — the stone becomes a cover for the barrel, i.e., it becomes a *kli*. By deliberately using the stone in a functional role as a barrel cover, the owner has transformed it from a mere stone into a *kli*, and it is no longer *muktzah*.
