This is the precise inverse of the *shever kli* discussion: there, an object began as a *kli* and broke, and we explored how much it retains its *kli* status. Here, an object begins as a piece of nature and we ask what is needed to elevate it into *kli* status. Rav Assi's position, as transmitted by Rav Yosef, is that intentional functional use alone suffices.

---

## Gourd & Stone (II)

### Action vs Function

The two positions regarding the barrel stone are in direct tension with the *mishnah*'s case of the stone in the gourd. Rabba raises the challenge against his own position (that the stone on the barrel remains *muktzah*): the *mishnah* in the *kiruyah* case says that if the stone does not fall out, one may use the gourd — implying that the tight-fitting stone is automatically rendered a *kli*, even without any deliberate act. Does that not prove that merely using an object functionally suffices to make it a *kli*?

### Rav Ami vs Rav Yosef

The *gemara* responds: *velo hi* — there is no contradiction. *Hasam keivan de-hatka, shavye dofen* — in the case of the gourd, one did something: the stone was fitted tightly, pressed in so it would not fall out, effectively making it a wall of the gourd. That physical integration constitutes an act. Rav Yosef, who holds the opposite position (that functionality alone suffices), is also challenged by the *kiruyah* case: if no action is needed, why does the stone become *muktzah* when it is loose and would float out? The answer for Rav Yosef's position is: *hasam keivan delo hatka, bei bitulei batlei* — there it is not that the absence of an act disqualifies the stone; rather, a stone that will float out is simply not functional, and without functionality there is no basis to treat it as a *kli*.

The *gemara* thus articulates the fundamental dispute: *mar savar ba'inan ma'aseh umar savar lo ba'inan ma'aseh* — one authority holds that physical action is required to transform a stone into a *kli*, while the other holds that demonstrated functionality alone suffices.

---

## Designation of Objects

### Rabbi's Designation

The *gemara* now cites a tradition about Rabbi himself. When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael he reported, in the name of Rabbi Chanina (with an alternative attribution to Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Chanina): *pa'am achat halach Rabbi l'makom echad* — on one occasion Rabbi traveled to a certain place and found *nidbach shel avanim* — a row of stones. It was *erev Shabbos*, and he said to his students: *tse'u v'chishvu k'dei she-neshev aleihem l'machar* — go and think about them, designate them mentally, so that we can use them tomorrow. The report states that Rabbi did not require any physical act (*velo hitchrichan Rabbi l'ma'aseh*) — mere mental designation was sufficient to render the stones non-*muktzah*. This appears to be direct evidence that action is not required.

### R. Yochanan Disputes

However, Rabbi Yochanan disputes this reading: *hitchrichan Rabbi l'ma'aseh* — Rabbi did in fact require that something be done to the stones. The question then becomes: what precisely did Rabbi demand?

### Rav Ami's Version

Rav Ami — who holds that physical action is required — reports that Rabbi Yochanan said Rabbi instructed his students: *tse'u velamdu* — go and arrange them. Rashi clarifies the point: the instruction was not that arranging would suffice to make them non-*muktzah*, but rather the reverse. Because the stones are going to remain *muktzah* (you cannot change their status without real action, and there was no time to do so properly), Rabbi told the students: position them now while it is still permitted to move them, because once *Shabbos* enters you will not be able to. The act of arrangement was not a solution to the *muktzah* problem but an instruction to deal with the stones before *Shabbos*.

### Rav Assi's Version

Rav Assi reports a different version of what Rabbi said: *tse'u v'shifshifu* — go and dust them off, simply brush the dirt off them. This minimal gesture of attention, showing that one has taken an interest in the stones and intends to use them, would be sufficient designation to render them non-*muktzah*. Under this version, no substantial physical action is required — a trivial act of attention suffices.

### Alternative Objects

The *gemara* also notes that the identity of the object in Rabbi's story is itself disputed. Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul says it was *soreh shel koros* — a row of beams, not stones. Rabbi Yochanan ben Shaul says it was *gishra she-safina* — a pole used to test water depth to prevent a boat from grounding. The identification matters: one who says it was the depth-testing pole would certainly agree that the same ruling applies *a fortiori* to a pile of beams; but one who says it was merely a pile of beams might hold differently for the valuable depth-testing pole, which the owner would not want anyone touching, making it *muktzah machamat chisron kis* — set aside due to financial concern. These two versions thus raise distinct concerns: the former is about how one transforms a piece of nature into a *kli*, while the latter is about whether an object's special value causes its owner to mentally restrict its use.

The underlying question of this entire section can be sharpened. The *shever kli* case and the stone-into-*kli* case are mirror images. A *shever kli* started as a *kli* and retains that residual character even in broken form — it is presumptively non-*muktzah* and requires a positive act (throwing it out) to become *muktzah*. An untouched piece of nature has no such presumption; it has never been a *kli* and must acquire that status. Whether acquisition requires physical action, demonstrated functionality, or mere mental designation is precisely what the various authorities dispute.

---

## Vine & Bucket

### Vine Tying Required

The *mishnah* rules: *zemora shekeshurah betapiach, memalin bah beShabbos* — a vine tied to a *tapiach* (some vessel used for drawing water) may be used on *Shabbos* to draw water. If it is not tied, it may not be used: it is merely a random vine and retains *muktzah* status. The tying — a deliberate act connecting the vine to the bucket — is what converts it from a piece of nature into a functional component of a water-drawing vessel.

---

## Palm Pieces as Seats

### Repurposing Palm

The *gemara* introduces a closely related case: *chariyot shel dekel shegigeran le-eitzim* — pieces carved from a palm tree for use as firewood. *Ve-nimalach aleihen lishiva* — and one changes one's mind and decides to use them as seating instead. The situation is analogous to the vine and the stone: an object that had been designated for one use (firewood, a non-*kli* use) and now one wishes to repurpose it as a seat. What does one need to do?

### Designation Debate

The *beraita* states: *tzarich likshor* — one must tie the pieces together (to form a bench-like structure) in order to transform them into seating. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: *ein tzarich likshor* — it is sufficient merely to designate them mentally; no physical act of tying is required. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel may be more lenient here because the palm pieces have already been cut and are thus already under human control, unlike a completely natural stone. Having already been fashioned into something (even if only firewood), perhaps mental designation alone suffices to redirect their use.

---

## Vine & Bucket (II)

### Attached vs Detached

Rav Sheshet resolves the apparent tension between the *mishnah*'s vine case and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient position: even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would concede that the vine tied to the bucket requires actual tying rather than mere designation. *Hacha b'mai askinan — bemichuberet be-aviha* — the case of the vine involves a vine still attached to the ground (*mechuberet*). This is not merely a *muktzah* question; it involves the prohibition of using something attached to the ground (*mechubar lekarka*), out of concern one might come to detach it. A vine attached to the ground is an intrinsically harder case to permit, which is why tying to the bucket is required. One might ask: if the vine is attached to the ground, the concern should be the prohibition of using *mechubar*, not merely *muktzah* — even if it were tied to the bucket, should that not remain prohibited? The *gemara* addresses this: *lemata migimmel* — the vine is within three handbreadths of the ground. Objects attached to the ground but extending more than three handbreadths upward present a greater concern that one might forget they are attached; within three handbreadths, the attachment is obvious and the risk is reduced, making use permissible.

Rav Ashi adds: *afilu teima bitlusha* — even if the vine were detached, we might require actual tying before *Shabbos*. *Gezeira shema yikto* — there is a rabbinic concern that if one were permitted to use a detached vine merely by designating it, one might come to break off a vine from a living plant, which is biblically prohibited. Therefore even for a detached vine, the *gemara* demands the affirmative act of tying it to the bucket before *Shabbos*, rather than mere designation.

The underlying axis of the entire daf thus comes into relief. On one side stands the *shever kli*: it began as a *kli* and, even in fragments, retains more of its non-*muktzah* character, requiring only that one not actively discard it before *Shabbos*. On the other side stand pieces of nature — stones, vines, palm cuttings — which must be brought into the category of *kli* through some act or designation. Whether that act must be physical and substantial (*ma'aseh*), minimal (dusting off), or merely mental (thought alone) is the question around which this entire sugya revolves, with different authorities drawing the line at different points.

---

---

# Shabbat 126

## Perek Intro & Tircha

### Perek Overview

Today's *daf* is 127, and we begin a new *perek*. The previous *perek* dealt with *muktzeh*, but specifically in the context of *kelim* — which, as we learned, is not classic *muktzeh* in the fullest sense. A *kli* is by definition something usable, not something pushed away and set aside, and so while there is a special *gezeirah* limiting the use of *kelim she-melachtan l'issur*, that restriction is in fact quite narrow. This new *perek* continues the *muktzeh* theme while introducing a distinct additional concern: the opening discussion involves clearing out a granary or moving grain in order to make space for guests or for a *shiur*. In this way, the *perek* introduces the important concept of *tircha* on *Shabbat*.

### Tircha Concept

Many people carry a sense that *tircha*, like *uvda d'chol*, is not a fully formalized *halacha* — not a genuine *issur d'rabbanan*, let alone an *issur d'oraita*. Nevertheless, *tircha* is central to the experiential dimension of *Shabbat*. According to some, this experiential dimension is precisely the content of the *mitzvas aseh* of *shabbaton* — that positive obligation to preserve the character and atmosphere of *Shabbat* beyond the formal prohibition of *melacha*. However one frames it, *Chazal* had much to say about avoiding unnecessary effort or exertion on *Shabbat* even when no *melacha* is involved. The practical question is something like: if you have a storage room filled with boxes and someone needs a place to sleep, can you undertake a major clearing operation on *Shabbat* even without any *melacha*? That is one of the central concerns the *perek* addresses.

### Rav Chisda vs Shmuel

Of course, as we clear the space, the question of *muktzeh* re-enters, because the type of grain one must move determines whether it is *muktzeh* at all. The Gemara's discussion opened with a debate between Rav Chisda and Shmuel. The *Mishnah* states that one may move four or five boxes of grain. Rav Chisda reads this precisely: four boxes under certain circumstances where the space is small and one cannot fully empty it, five in larger situations. Shmuel, by contrast, reads "four or five" as idiomatic — a way of saying a great deal — and holds that there is in fact no fixed limit. Both agree, however, that one may not completely empty the space, because once the floor that was covered is fully exposed, one may come to smooth it out — which would constitute a prohibited *melacha*.

### Granary Muktzeh

To reorient ourselves, the Gemara asks: *u'mai aval lo et ha-otzar* — even according to Shmuel, who permits removing large quantities of grain, what does it mean that one may not remove "the granary"? The answer is *she-lo yigmor kulo* — one may not completely empty it, *dilma atei l'ashvuyei gumos* — lest one come to smooth the holes in the ground. On this Shmuel agrees. The point of disagreement is: *aval at'chulei mat'chil* — one may, according to Shmuel, begin emptying a granary on *Shabbat* even if one had never started before *Shabbat*. One can simply not finish it entirely. The Gemara then identifies whose position this reflects: *Rabbi Shimon hee d'leis lei muktzeh* — this is Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold of *muktzeh*.

A clarification is necessary here, because the statement that Rabbi Shimon does not hold of *muktzeh* is genuinely surprising. It cannot mean he rejects *muktzeh* entirely — the *Mishnah* itself states that *tevel* grain is *muktzeh*, and that grain or legumes that are not *ra'ui l'achila* are *muktzeh*. Even Rabbi Shimon holds of certain categories. What the Gemara means when it says *leis lei muktzeh* is that Rabbi Shimon rejects a larger range of *muktzeh* categories than others. He may not hold of *muktzeh machmas mi'us*, or *muktzeh machmas chisaron kis*, or he may define categories more narrowly than Rabbi Yehuda. The categorical statement *leis lei muktzeh* is an abstraction the Gemara uses — but it should not be read as a blanket rejection of the entire principle.

### Min HaMuchan Gap

What exactly is the *muktzeh* concern with granary grain? The grain is stored there precisely to be used eventually — so why would it be *muktzeh* at all? One way to approach this is through the conceptual gap between *muktzeh* in the strict sense — something actively set aside — and *min ha-muchan*, something that has been prepared and is in one's consciousness as a usable item for *Shabbat*. Most things in our ordinary lives fall somewhere between these poles; we assume that items we have not actively pushed away are implicitly *muchan*, on the theory that we would have expected to use them.

Granary grain, however, sits at a genuine border. On the one hand, it is there to be used and has not been *maktzeh*-ed in any active sense. On the other hand, it is the kind of thing one does not expect to use for perhaps a year — the kind of thing so stored away that it may not even implicitly be within the range of what one would anticipate using. A useful analogy: imagine one bought several cases of wine before *Pesach* and stored them in a closet, unopened. On *Shabbat* one needs wine. On one hand, those bottles were never pushed away — why would one not want to use them? On the other hand, they are so thoroughly stored that they may not even be in the implicit mental range of things one would reach for. That, it seems, is the conceptual terrain the Gemara is navigating with respect to granary grain and the debate about whether beginning to use it is permitted on *Shabbat*. Rabbi Shimon, holding of less *muktzeh*, would permit beginning to empty the granary; Rabbi Yehuda and others would not.

---

## Granary Rules

### Granary Paths

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: *ein matchilin be-otzar techila* — one may not begin using the granary from the outset on *Shabbat*. However, *aval ose bo shevil kedei she-yikanes ve-yetzei* — one may make a path through it in order to enter and exit. The Gemara immediately notes the apparent tension: if one cannot begin moving the grain, how is making a path permitted? The resolution is *ose bo shevil be-raglav* — the path is made simply by walking through, *bi-chnisato u-vi-ytziato*, as one enters and exits. One is not picking up the grain and actively moving it with one's hands. That kind of direct handling would be *tiltul b'gufo*; walking through and displacing grain with one's feet is closer to *tiltul min ha-tzad*.

### Tzvuah Tzvurah

A second *baraita* addresses a related case: *tzvuah tzvurah* — a mound or pile of grain. *Bi-zman she-hitchil bah me-erev Shabbat* — if one began using the pile before *Shabbat*, *mutar lehistapek mimena be-Shabbat* — one may continue drawing from it on *Shabbat*. *Ve-im lav* — but if one had not begun before *Shabbat*, *asur lehistapek mimena be-Shabbat*. This is attributed to Rabbi Shimon.

### Rabbi Achai vs Shimon

The Gemara notes a problem: *kelapei laya* — this is backward. Rabbi Shimon is supposed to be the lenient voice regarding *muktzeh*, and yet here his position is the restrictive one? It says *Rabbi Achai matir* — Rabbi Achai is the one who permits. The Gemara resolves this by reversing the attribution: *ela eima* — exchange the names. It is Rabbi Achai who says it is *asur*, and *ve-Rabbi Shimon matir* — Rabbi Shimon permits. This restores the expected alignment: Rabbi Shimon is lenient regarding *muktzeh*.

It should be noted that because the Gemara abstracts Rabbi Shimon's position into the categorical formula *leis lei muktzeh*, it is committed to having Rabbi Shimon take the lenient position consistently. A more nuanced treatment might draw finer distinctions within or across categories of *muktzeh*, but once one adopts the categorical abstraction, Rabbi Shimon must always appear on the lenient side.

### Shiur Amounts

The Gemara asks: *tana, kama shiur tzvuah tzvurah* — what is the minimum quantity of piled grain that triggers the restriction, such that one may not begin using it on *Shabbat*? The answer given is a *letech* — half of a *kor*, which equals fifteen *se'ah*. This is a substantial volume. The implication is that below this threshold, the grain is not considered sufficiently "stored away" to raise the *muktzeh* concern, and even according to the stricter opinions one could move it on *Shabbat*. Notably, the volume of a *letech* corresponds to the combined volume of the five boxes mentioned in the *Mishnah* itself. That equivalence helps anchor the two discussions together.

Subsequently, Rav Nechumi bar Zachai asks Abaye the same question, and Abaye confirms: *shiur tevuah tzeburah, beletech* — the measure of piled grain is a *letech*, citing the same *baraita*.

### Trips vs Load

The Gemara returns to our *Mishnah*'s four or five boxes — all subsequent questions, it emphasizes, are according to Rav Chisda, who holds that the numbers are precise. The question is: *be'arba'ah vechamishah kupot in, tefi lo* — does the limit of four or five mean one must use exactly four or five boxes to carry that amount, i.e., that the number of trips is the binding constraint? The reasoning would be *mi'uta be-hilucha adif* — better to minimize the number of trips, even if each trip involves a greater load. Alternatively, *mi'uta be-mas'oi adif* — perhaps it is better to carry less per trip, even if that means making more trips.

The question has an obvious intuitive resonance: when we move things from room to room, the natural temptation is to maximize how much we carry each time rather than make multiple trips. Presumably on *Shabbat* one would want to limit the sense of labor — but does that mean limiting trips or limiting load?

### Bottle Sizes

The Gemara attempts to resolve this from two *baraitot* that appear contradictory. One *baraita* states: *mefanin afilu arba'ah vechamishah kupot shel kadei shemen veshel kadei yayin* — one may clear four or five boxes of oil and wine containers. A second *baraita* says: *be'asarah uvechamishah asar* — ten or fifteen. The natural reading would suggest a dispute about the limit, and one might say they are debating *mi'uta be-hilucha* versus *mi'uta be-mas'oi*. However, the Gemara rejects this: *dechulei alma mi'uta be-hilucha adif* — all agree that fewer trips is preferable. The difference between ten or fifteen and four or five does not refer to the number of boxes but to the number of bottles within the boxes. *Ha demishtaklei chada chada bekupah* — in one scenario each box holds one large flask, so four or five boxes carry four or five bottles. *Ve-ha demishtaklei tartei tartei* — in another, each box holds two medium-sized bottles, yielding ten bottles in five boxes. *Ve-ha demishtaklei tlata tlata* — in a third, each box holds three smaller bottles, yielding fifteen. And there is a reference to *dikurei de-harfanya* — the pitchers of a certain locale known for their smaller size. The bottom line: the number of trips is fixed at four or five; the number of individual containers varies with their size.

### Guests & Limits

The Gemara raises a further question, again according to Rav Chisda: *hani arba v'chamisha d'ka'amar* — when the *Mishnah* says four or five, is this an absolute limit even when *af al gav de'ika orchin tuva* — even when there are many guests? Or is it rather *hakol lefi ha'orchin* — everything proportional to the number of guests, such that more guests permits more? *Tosafot* notes that if more guests yields a higher limit, one must ask what the baseline is. Since the *Mishnah* gives no such baseline, *Tosafot* concludes that four or five boxes applies even for a single guest. Whether more guests multiplies this is precisely the question.

---

## Space Clearing

### Rabbi Field Story

The Gemara cites the following teaching: *d'amar Rabbah amar Rebbe Chiya* — Rabbah says in the name of Rebbe Chiya: once Rebbe went to a certain place on *Shabbat* and saw that the students were crowded into a small space. He went out to the field and found it filled with *omarim* — bundles of grain. *V'pina Rebbe kol hasadeh kulo* — and Rebbe cleared the entire field of these bundles so the students could sit there.

This is striking on multiple levels. One would expect sheaves of grain standing in a field to carry a stronger *muktzeh* status than grain that has already been brought into a granary — it is in a more primary, unprocessed state. Moreover, the clearing took place outdoors, presumably in a *karmelit*, raising a question of carrying. Rashi addresses this by explaining that Rebbe moved each bundle *pachot pachot me-arba amot* — less than four *amot* at a time, each increment falling within the permitted range in a *karmelit*. One could also ask whether *omarim* in this state are genuinely *ra'ui* for use, given that they have not yet been threshed or winnowed — though if the primary use is animal fodder, they may be considered fit even in this state.

### Individual vs Group

What the Gemara actually introduces this story to resolve is the earlier question: *hakol lefi ha'orchin* — can one move proportionally more for more guests? Since Rebbe (or Rebbe Chiya, per the alternate version attributed to Rav Yosef in the name of Rav Yehoshua) cleared the *entire* field — not a measured four or five boxes — it is evident that *hakol lefi ha'orchin*. Even according to Rav Chisda, a larger group of guests or students creates proportionally greater latitude. *Shma mina* — this can be derived from here.

However, the Gemara notes: *adati iba'i lehu* — there remains a further unresolved question. *Chad gavra mashni l'kulehu o dilma gavra gavra mashni l'nafshei* — can one person clear the entire space on behalf of all the guests, or must each guest clear his own individual portion? The underlying concern is whether the license to exert effort on *Shabbat* is individual and non-transferable.

### Rabbi's Intent

The Gemara attempts to resolve this from the same story: *ta shma v'pina Rebbe* — it says Rebbe cleared it. This implies one person did it for everyone. But the Gemara immediately questions this: *Rebbe b'nafshei pina?* — Do you really think Rebbe, the *Nasi* of all Jewry, personally cleared the field himself, with no one helping?

### Pharaoh Analogy

The Gemara resolves: *ela tziva v'pina* — rather, it means he commanded and it was done. The parallel is to *Paroh*, about whom the verse says *va-ye'esor et richvo* — and he harnessed his chariot — and Rashi explains *sina mekaltelet et ha-shura*, that hatred disrupts the normal order, suggesting that Pharaoh perhaps did this himself in his agitation. But the deeper point is that when a verse says a king "did" something, it means he commanded it and it was carried out. When Bush invaded Iraq, one would not say he personally wielded a rifle. So too here: Rebbe ordered it done, and it was done. The conclusion is therefore *aval kol chad v'chad mafnin etzlo* — but in reality each individual cleared space for himself. The story cannot prove that one person may clear for all.

*Tosafot* adds a brief but pointed comment: *perush kol hasadeh kulah* — the phrasing "the entire field" implies that even if we might have accepted the idea that Rebbe would personally do some of the clearing, no one would imagine that the *Nasi* of Israel personally cleared an entire field. The very scale of the operation implies it must have been done by command.

---

## Hachnasat Orchim

### Greatness of Guests

Since the preceding discussion involved making space for students and guests, the Gemara takes the opportunity to elaborate on *hachnasat orchim*. *Masechet Shabbat* has a habit of digressing into *aggadata* when a suitable opening presents itself, and this is one such moment.

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan: gedola hachnasat orchin k'hashkamat beit hamidrash* — Rabbi Yochanan says: welcoming guests is as important as rising early to invest oneself in *Torah* study. The basis for the comparison is the text of the ruling itself: one may clear space for guests and one may clear space to prevent people from being unable to study — and the two are placed alongside one another as equally weighty concerns. It is notable that the comparison is to *hashkamat beit hamidrash* — one's personal effort in learning — rather than to enabling the learning of others or to some broader communal benefit.

### Guests vs Shechina

Rav Dimi of Nehardea goes further: *yatir me-hashkamat beit hamidrash* — welcoming guests is more important than extraordinary effort in learning. His reading of the same ruling is that guests are listed first, and concern for disrupted study is listed second — and order implies priority.

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav: gedola hachnasat orchin me-hakbalat pnei ha-shchina* — greater is welcoming guests than receiving the Divine Presence. The prooftext is from the story of Abraham's visitors: *va-yomer* — and Abraham said. The word that follows, *Alef-Dalet-Nun-Yud*, is ambiguous: it can be read as an address to the visiting men (*adoni* — "my masters") or as God's name (*Adonai*). The Gemara reads it as *kodesh* — a sacred usage — meaning Abraham was addressing God. The verse *im na matzati chen b'eynecha al na ta'avor me'al avdecha* — if I have found favor in Your eyes, do not pass from over Your servant — is read as Abraham asking God to wait while he attends to his guests.

Rabbi Elazar adds a related teaching: *bo u-re'eh she-lo k'middat ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu middat basar v'dam* — come and see that God's way is not the way of human beings. In human affairs, one of lesser status cannot say to one of greater status: wait until I come to you. Yet Abraham was able to say exactly that to God. This formulation is interesting because it shifts the emphasis somewhat: rather than exalting *hachnasat orchim* per se, it emphasizes God's willingness to set aside, as it were, His own honor — to be *mochal* on His *kavod* — in order that Abraham could fulfill his obligation.

### Peah Mishnah

Rav Yehuda bar Shila, citing Rav Assi citing Rabbi Yochanan, teaches: *shisha devarim adam ochel piroseihem ba-olam hazeh ve-ha-keren kayemet lo le-olam ha-ba* — six things: a person eats their fruits in this world, while the principal reward remains for him in the world to come. These six are: *hachnasat orchim*, *bikur cholim*, *iyun tefillah*, *hashkamat beit hamidrash*, *ha-migadel banav le-talmud Torah*, and *ve-ha-dan chavero le-chaf zechus* — judging one's fellow toward the scale of merit.

The Gemara then raises an objection: *v'ha'anan tnan* — we have the famous *Mishnah* from *Peah*, recited in daily *davening*, that presents a comparable but different list: *kibbud av va-em*, *gemilut chasadim*, *ve-hava'at shalom bein adam le-chavero*, and *talmud Torah ke-neged kulam*. Are these the only such things? The two lists do not match.

### List Reconciliation

The Gemara resolves: *hani nami be-hani shaychi* — the first list is subsumed within the second. Rabbi Yochanan's six items are an elaboration of the *Mishnah* in *Peah*. Specifically: *hachnasat orchim* and *bikur cholim* fall under *gemilut chasadim* — acts of kindness. *Hashkamat beit hamidrash* and *ha-migadel banav le-talmud Torah* clearly fall under *talmud Torah ke-neged kulam*. *Ve-ha-dan chavero le-chaf zechus* falls under *hava'at shalom bein adam le-chavero* — Rashi explains that when one consistently assumes the better of other people, one cultivates a far more generous way of engaging with the world, which in turn encourages reciprocity and creates a much greater measure of peace between people than a world in which everyone assumes the worst.

The harder case is *iyun tefillah*. Rashi makes something of a stretch in placing it under *gemilut chasadim*, suggesting that *tefillah* — which involves acknowledging one's dependence on God and one's gratitude for what one has received — is itself a form of recognizing and acknowledging *chesed*. It is an acknowledgment of having received kindness, and as such fits within the broader framework of *gemilut chasadim*. It is admittedly the less intuitive inclusion, but the logic is discernible.

One might also ask how this fits with the closing line of the *Peah Mishnah*: *talmud Torah ke-neged kulam*. If *talmud Torah* outweighs all else, how can *hachnasat orchim* be compared to *hashkamat beit hamidrash*, let alone said to exceed it? The resolution may lie in the distinction between *hashkamat beit hamidrash* and *talmud Torah* itself: *hashkamat beit hamidrash* refers to the effort and dedication involved in showing up, in making the commitment to learning even when it is difficult — what the Gemara elsewhere calls *schar halicha*. This is not identical to the substance of *talmud Torah ke-neged kulam*, which captures the comprehensive weight of Torah study as such. The comparison of *hachnasat orchim* to *hashkamat beit hamidrash* is therefore a comparison to a specific dimension of the *talmud Torah* complex, not a claim that *hachnasat orchim* outweighs *talmud Torah* in its fullest sense.

### Practical Rewards

The formulation *ochel piroseihem ba-olam hazeh ve-ha-keren kayemet le-olam ha-ba* deserves close attention. The *ve-ha-keren kayemet le-olam ha-ba* — the principal remains in the world to come — is straightforwardly metaphysical: one performs these deeds and is rewarded in the next world. But *ochel piroseihem ba-olam hazeh* — eating their fruits in this world — need not be understood in a narrowly metaphysical sense, as if God arranges some special payment in this life. *Tosafot* raises the question of *schar mitzvah be-hai alma ika o leka* — whether one can genuinely receive reward for *mitzvot* in this world at all — a question with significant consequences, since it was partly the observation that righteous people seem not to be rewarded in this world that led Elisha ben Abuya to apostasy. The Gemara's general approach is *schar mitzvah be-hai alma leika* — do not expect the reward in this world.

But *ochel piroseihem* may simply describe the natural, practical benefits that flow from these actions — the kind of world they create when people live by them. Consider *kibbud av va-em*: the Torah promises *lema'an ya'arichun yamecha* — that your days will be lengthened. This could refer to *olam ha-ba*. But it is also true in a very practical sense that a society in which people care for their elderly parents is one in which people live longer and more dignified lives. This echoes the Rambam's insight in *Moreh Nevuchim*, where he explains the rationale for *gemilut chasadim*: the word *gomel* — which means to bestow — also carries the sense of repayment. The world operates in cycles: today one person has means and another is in need; tomorrow the situation may reverse. A society built on mutual aid and *chesed* is one in which everyone benefits, not because God arranges tit-for-tat rewards but because such a society is simply a better one in which to live. *Hava'at shalom bein adam le-chavero* is self-evident on these terms. And *talmud Torah*, like *iyun tefillah*, shapes one's entire orientation toward the world, infusing everyday life with an awareness of what God wants and how His presence manifests — a benefit that is real and practical even before considering any eschatological reward.

---

## Dan L'Kaf Zechut

### Worker Payment

The Gemara returns to *dan chavero le-chaf zechus* with a series of illustrative stories. *Tanu Rabbanan: ha-dan chaveiro le-chaf zechus, danin oto le-chaf zechus* — one who judges one's fellow favorably will himself be judged favorably. The Gemara is careful not to read this only as a promise of divine reward, though that dimension is present. There is also a realistic, practical dimension: if one habitually assumes the best of others, it becomes very difficult for others to think poorly of him, and it cultivates a generosity of spirit that tends to be reciprocated. The worst human experiences include being suspected of wrongdoing when one is entirely innocent — a suffering the Gemara elsewhere acknowledges by saying one gains great reward for bearing it. That very fact highlights how terrible false suspicion is. A culture in which people assume the best of one another is simply a better world to inhabit.

The first story: a man descended from the upper Galilee and hired himself out to a certain homeowner in the south for three years. On *erev Yom Kippur* (some say *erev ha-regel*), he asked for his wages so he could go home and provide for his wife and children. The employer responded with a succession of *ein li* — I have nothing: no money, no fruit, no land, no animals, no bedding. Each denial seemed plainly false. The worker put his belongings on his back and walked home in despondent silence.

### Employer's Reasoning

After the holiday, the employer came to the worker's home with the full three years' wages — a substantial sum — along with three donkeys laden with food, drink, and delicacies. After they ate and drank together, the employer presented the wages and then asked: *b'mah chashadtani* — what did you suspect me of, each time I said I had nothing?

The worker gave his answers. When you said you had no money: *shema perakmatya b'zol nizdamna lach* — perhaps a great business opportunity presented itself and you invested all available funds. When you said you had no animals: *shema muskarot b'yad acherim* — perhaps they were all rented out. When you said you had no land: *shema arisut b'yad acherim* — perhaps others are sharecroppers on it and you could not convey clean title. When you said you had no fruit: *shema ein m'usarot* — perhaps they had not yet been tithed. When you said you had no bedding: *shema hikdish kol nechasav le-shamayim* — perhaps you had consecrated all your possessions to Heaven.

### Mutual Judgment

The employer responded: *ha'avoda, kach haya* — by the Temple service, that is exactly what happened. *Hadarti kol nechasai bishvil Horkenos b'ni* — I took a vow dedicating all my possessions because of my son Horkenos, who would not study *Torah*, and I did not want him to inherit my property. When I came to my colleagues in the south, *heitiru li kol nedarai* — they annulled my vows, and that is why I am now able to pay you. *U-cheshem she-dantani le-zchus, ha-Makom yadincha le-zchus* — just as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.

The final line raises a question: what does it mean for God to judge one favorably? God knows the truth of one's motivations — He does not need to assume the best. One possibility is that this is simply a blessing by parallel: as you did, so may be done to you. But there is a deeper reading. Very few of our motivations are pure black and white. We act for multiple reasons simultaneously, some more noble and some less. God, in judging us, can choose which aspect of our motivation to emphasize, which framing to adopt. To be judged *le-chaf zechus* by God may mean that God chooses to interpret our actions through the lens of the more positive intentions that informed them, even where less noble impulses were also present. By the same logic, *dan le-chaf zechus* toward another person means choosing to interpret their behavior through its most favorable possible context — recognizing that behind most actions there is a complex web of reasons, and consciously emphasizing the better ones.

### Hasid & Woman

The second story: *ma'aseh be-chasid echad she-padah riva achas bat Yisrael* — a certain pious man redeemed a young Jewish woman from captivity. When they reached an inn during the journey, *u-lemalon hishkivah tachas margelosav* — he had her sleep in the same room, at the foot of his bed. *U-lemachar yarad ve-taval* — the next morning he went to the *mikvah* and then gave a *shiur* to his students. The need to immerse in the morning after being in the same room as the woman carried obvious implications.

### Students' Charity

Before teaching, the *chasid* asked his students: *b'sha'ah she-hishkavti tachas margelosai, b'me chashadtuni* — when I had her sleep at my feet, what did you suspect me of? They answered: *shema yesh bo talmid she-eino baduk le-rebbi* — perhaps there is a student among us whose character you have not yet fully ascertained, and therefore you did not trust her to be outside your room. Even in framing a negative possibility about one of themselves, the students expressed it as a matter of incomplete knowledge rather than established bad character. Then: *b'sha'ah she-yaradti ve-tavalti, b'me chashadtuni* — when I went to the *mikvah*, what did you suspect? *Shema mipnei torach ha-derech ira keri le-rebbi* — perhaps the physical exertion of the journey caused a seminal emission, entirely unrelated to anything involving the woman. The *chasid* confirmed: *ha'avoda, kach haya* — that is exactly what happened. And *keshem she-dantuni le-zchus, ha-Makom yadin eschem le-zchus* — as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.

### R. Yehoshua Story

The third story: *pa'am achat hutzrach davar echad le-talmidei chachamim etzel matronita achas she-kol gedolei Romi metzuyin etzla* — once the Torah scholars needed a certain favor from a Roman matron whose home was frequented by all the great men of Rome, with implications that reflect on her character. They asked: *mi yelech* — who should go? Rabbi Yehoshua volunteered and went with a student. Upon arriving, *chalatz tfillov be-richuk arba amot* — he removed his *tefillin* four *amot* before her threshold, entered, and *na'al ha-delet bifneihem* — locked the door in front of his student. Upon emerging, he went to the *mikvah* and taught.

### Students Interpret

Then, as in the previous story, Rabbi Yehoshua asked his student: *b'sha'ah she-chalatzi tfilli, b'me chashadtuni* — when I took off my *tefillin*, what did you suspect? *Kasavar Rabbi lo yikanesu divrei kedusha be-makom tum'ah* — we assumed you held that matters of holiness should not enter a place of impurity, given that *Chazal* attributed a form of ritual impurity to non-Jews. When he locked the door: *shema davar malchus yesh beino le-veina* — perhaps there was sensitive governmental business to discuss privately. When he immersed: *shema nitza tzinora mipiha al begadav shel Rabbi* — perhaps some of her saliva had landed on his clothing, since *Chazal* attributed to non-Jews an impurity analogous to that of a *zav*. Rabbi Yehoshua confirmed: *ha'avoda, kach haya* — that is exactly how it was. And again: *atem, keshem she-dantuni le-zchus, ha-Makom yadin eschem le-zchus*.

These three stories escalate in the extremity of their circumstances. The point driven home is that one can never know the full context behind another's actions, and one should always strain to find the most favorable explanation possible. Achieving this standard in extreme cases is admittedly difficult, but habituating oneself to it in easier cases is the practice that makes it possible.

One important point deserves mention. The stories prompt a question that was raised in the room: why did these figures — the *chasid*, Rabbi Yehoshua — not act more transparently, so as to forestall suspicion? Michael is correct that *Chazal* elsewhere invoke the principle *ve-heyitem nekiyim me-Hashem u-mi-Yisrael* — one must be above suspicion before both God and Israel. There is a genuine obligation not only to act rightly but to act in ways that minimize the likelihood of false suspicion. One might suggest the figures in these stories were deliberately constructing a teaching situation for their students. But that response is incomplete. The more important lesson may be the asymmetry in how readily we invoke *mara'it ayin* in ritual matters versus in interpersonal ones. The sages were vigilant about appearances in the former domain, and *ve-heyitem nekiyim* functions as the parallel principle in the domain of money and interpersonal ethics. The cases here — involving money, in the first story, and sexual propriety in the others — are precisely the areas of greatest human temptation, and the principle of being above suspicion applies with full force. These questions deserve further investigation.

---

## Muktzeh Conclusions

### Trumah Tahorah

The Gemara returns to the *muktzeh* discussion. *Mafnin trumah tehorah* — one may move pure *terumah* on *Shabbat*. The Gemara asks: is this not obvious? What is the *chidush*? The answer: *tzricha d'mancha b'yad Yisrael* — the novel case is where *terumah* is in the possession of a *Yisrael* rather than a *kohen*. One might have thought: *keivan d'la chazya lei, asur* — since the *Yisrael* cannot eat the *terumah* himself, it is *muktzeh* for him. The Gemara therefore teaches: *keivan d'chazya le-kohen shapir dami* — since it is usable by a *kohen*, it is not *muktzeh*. This connects to a broader principle: an item that is fit for use by some — even if not by the person holding it — is not *muktzeh*.

### Demai Use

The same logic applies to *demai* — produce purchased from an *am ha-aretz* whose *terumot u-ma'asrot* may not have been properly separated, and which therefore must be re-tithed rabbinically before consumption. One might think *demai* is *muktzeh* because the holder may not eat it as is. But the Gemara responds: *keivan d'ei bei mafkar lei le-nichsei ve-havei ani ve-chazya lei* — since one could theoretically annul ownership of all one's possessions, become poor, and then be permitted to eat *demai* as a poor person, it is considered *chazya lei* — fit even for him, at least in principle, and therefore not *muktzeh*. Moreover — and this suffices independently — *de-tnan: ma'achilim et ha-aniyim dmai v'et ha-achsandya dmai* — as the *Mishnah* teaches, one may feed the poor *demai* and likewise army troops. Rashi explains why the poor were given this leniency: the poor must go door to door seeking *tzedakah* and cannot be selective about from whom they accept food, asking only from *chaverim* and not from *amei ha-aretz*. Since they receive from all, they receive *demai* as a matter of course, and the rabbis did not burden them with the obligation to separate tithes from it.

*Tosafot* notes the obvious point: one could simply have said, as with *terumah*, that since *demai* is fit for the poor, it is not *muktzeh* — no need for the theoretical argument about annulling one's possessions. The Gemara goes the extra mile to show that the item is in principle fit even for the holder himself.

### Beit Shammai Hillel

Finally, Rav Huna cites a *baraita*: *Beit Shammai* holds *ein ma'achilim et ha-aniyim dmai v'et ha-achsandya dmai* — one may not feed the poor or army troops *demai*. *Beit Hillel* holds the opposite: *ma'achilim et ha-aniyim dmai v'et ha-achsandya dmai* — one may. The full elaboration of these positions will continue in the subsequent discussion.

---

---

# Shabbat 130

## Bloodletting & Timing

### Frequency & Age Rules

The daf begins on 129b, picking up from where the preceding *perek* left off. Because the end of the previous chapter addressed the status of a woman in childbirth as a case of *sakanas nefashos* — someone for whom *Shabbos* may be violated — the *Gemara* naturally transitions into related health matters, particularly the practice of bloodletting, which was a standard medical intervention of the time. The rabbis recognized, however, that bloodletting also left the patient in a vulnerable state, and so they legislated carefully around it.

*Shmuel* opens with the rule: *porsa de-dama kol tlasin yomin* — the interval between bleedings is thirty days. One does not let blood twice within a single month. *Shmuel* adds further: *u-veina perakim yema'et* — between the chapters of life, one should do even less. *Rashi* explains this as a reference to age: after forty, assuming a lifespan of eighty years, one is in the intermediate chapter and should reduce the frequency. After sixty, the final chapter, one should reduce further still — *Rashi* suggests once every two or three months.

### Prohibited Days & Mars

*Shmuel* also specifies the appropriate days for bloodletting: Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday. *Shabbos* is excluded in any case because of *melacha*. But what of the remaining days? Monday and Thursday are explicitly prohibited: *mi she-yesh lo zechus avos yeza'at dam be-sheni va-chamishi* — only one who has exceptional ancestral merit and wishes to take a risk would let blood on those days. The reason is that both the heavenly court and the earthly court convene on Mondays and Thursdays. The earthly courts would hold sessions in the cities on those days, making them days of judgment. Since bloodletting weakens the body and creates vulnerability, one should not add to that risk on a day of divine scrutiny.

Tuesday presents a separate problem: *mishum de-kaimei lei Ma'adim bi-zuvei* — because *Ma'adim*, Mars, appears in an even hour on that day. The *Gemara* operates within a framework in which seven celestial bodies cycle through the hours of the day in a fixed sequence. *Rashi* spells out the order with the mnemonic *ShTzaM ChaNKaL*: *Shabtai* (Saturn), *Tzedek* (Jupiter), *Ma'adim* (Mars), *Chamah* (the Sun), *Kochav* (Mercury), *Nogah* (Venus), and *Levanah* (the Moon). Beginning from the moment of creation and proceeding through a seven-hour rotation, the mathematics work out such that on Tuesday, Mars always falls on an even-numbered hour. The *Gemara* emphasizes this specifically because Mars governs blood, and an even hour was considered particularly dangerous. It is worth noting that in several European languages — French and Spanish among them — Tuesday's name is etymologically derived from Mars, *Mardi* and *Martes* respectively, which is a remarkable convergence.

Friday poses a further complication: Mars also falls on an even hour on Friday, in the fourth hour. Yet bloodletting on Friday was widespread practice. The logic was pragmatic: people would let blood on Friday, then be hungry enough to eat a substantial meal entering *Shabbos*, which they needed in any case, and those without much money could combine the occasions conveniently. The *Gemara* invokes the principle *shomer pesayim Hashem* — God protects the simple — acknowledging that because the practice was already so entrenched, prohibiting it would be futile. This principle appears again in a responsum of Rav Moshe Feinberg regarding smoking: it is prohibited to begin, but for those already accustomed, *shomer pesayim Hashem*.

The question of how seriously to take astrological considerations is worth pausing over. The belief in astrology was widespread, extending well beyond the *Gemara* into the *Rishonim* — the *Ibn Ezra*, for example, was deeply invested in astrological thinking. The *Rambam*, characteristically, either dismisses these beliefs as simply false or argues that the science has advanced and corrected earlier errors. There is, however, an interesting asymmetry in the tradition: matters that touch on the mechanics of the heavenly spheres and their impact on human events tended to receive more weight than straightforwardly medical or astronomical advice. These texts about bloodletting and dangerous hours occupy a middle register, and even in contemporary *yeshivos*, one does not observe these *Gemaros* being treated with the same normative weight as halachic rulings.

### Dangerous Dates

*Shmuel* goes on to enumerate specific dates that are dangerous for bloodletting. A Wednesday that falls on the 4th of the month (*arba d'hu arba*), a Wednesday on the 14th (*arba d'arba'is*), a Wednesday on the 24th (*arba d'esrim v'arba*), or a Wednesday near month's end when fewer than four days remain — all of these are *sakanta*, dangerous. *Rosh Chodesh* itself and the day after cause weakness (*chulusha*). The third of the month is an outright danger. *Erev Yom Tov* weakens; *Erev Shavuos* actually endangers. The rabbis extended the *Erev Shavuos* prohibition to all *Erev Yom Tov* occasions.

The reason given for the special danger of *Erev Shavuos* is striking: *d'nafik beizika u-shmei tavu'ach* — on that day, a wind goes forth whose name is "slaughter," *because had the Jewish people not accepted the Torah, it would have slaughtered their flesh and blood*. The day carries residual mortal danger, and one should not court it through bloodletting.

### Eating & Bloodletting

*Shmuel* rules that if one eats wheat — or more broadly, eats anything — immediately before bloodletting, the bloodletting only serves to drain what was just consumed. It does not provide the more general health benefit one would otherwise expect. This applies when the purpose is therapeutic (*l'refuah*). However, if the goal is merely to lighten the blood — to relieve a sense of heaviness — then it is effective even after eating.

### Post-Bloodletting Timing

After bloodletting, one may drink immediately. One should eat only after the time it takes to walk a *chatzi mil* — approximately ten minutes — has elapsed. Two questions are then raised and left unresolved in *teiku*. First: is drinking immediately after bloodletting actually beneficial, and does delay make it harmful, or is delay merely neutral? Second: is eating within a half-*mil* beneficial, and is eating before or after that window harmful, or merely neutral? Both questions remain open.

### Barbers & Pricing

*Rav* would announce publicly: *me'a karnei bezuza, me'a reishi bezuza* — a hundred horn-applications (bloodlettings by horn) for a *zuz*, a hundred head-treatments (haircuts) for a *zuz*. *Tosafos* explains that bloodletters and barbers were the same tradesmen, sharing the same sharp instruments. The proclamation was essentially advertising a standard price: a *zuz* per service. As for mustaches — *me'a sepami velo klum* — a hundred mustaches for nothing, meaning the mustache trim was thrown in for free alongside the paid service.

*Rav Yosef* adds a charming postscript: when he was a student in the house of *Rav Huna*, on days when the rabbis were unproductive in their learning, they would say: *haidna yoma de-shapmi hu* — today is a mustache day. He reports that at the time he did not understand the expression, but now he does. Since the barber received nothing for the mustache, a day when one exerts effort and receives nothing — or simply produces nothing of value — became known as a mustache day.

---

## Childbirth & Shabbat

### Umbilical Cord Care

The *Gemara* transitions to matters surrounding childbirth, which connects organically to the preceding chapter's discussion of a woman in labor as a case of *sakanas nefashos*. The *Gemara* states: *vekorshin hatabur* — one may tie the umbilical cord on *Shabbos*. A *baraisa* is then cited: *vekorshin hatabur* — one may tie the umbilical cord.

### Placenta Burial

*Rabbi Yossi* adds: *af chotchin* — one may even cut the umbilical cord. A further practice is mentioned: *vetomnin hashilya kedei sheyeicham havlad* — one buries the placenta so that the infant will be warm, reflecting a medical belief of the time that the placenta provided warmth to the newborn.

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* describes the method of burial as varying by socioeconomic status. Daughters of kings — meaning the very wealthy — would bury the placenta in basins of oil (*b'sefalim shel shemen*). Daughters of the wealthy would bury it in wool sponges or piles of wool. Daughters of the poor would bury it in pieces of cloth (*b'mochin*).

### Cord Cutting Ruling

*Rav Nachman* transmitted in the name of *Rabbah bar Avuha* in the name of *Rav*: the *halacha* follows *Rabbi Yossi* — one may indeed cut the umbilical cord on *Shabbos*, not only tie it.

*Rav Nachman* further transmits: even the *Chachamim* who generally dispute *Rabbi Yossi* would agree that when twins share an umbilical cord, one may cut it to separate them. The reason is *d'manchi ahadadei* — they pull against one another, and if left connected they can endanger each other. Even the more restrictive opinion grants this exception.

### Childbirth Acts Shabbat

*Rav Nachman* transmits a third ruling in the same chain: *kol ha-amur b'parshas tochacha — osim l'chaya b'Shabbos*. Anything described in the passage of remonstration in *Yechezkel*, where God reproaches Israel by describing what proper care at birth looks like — all of those acts may be performed for a woman who has just given birth on *Shabbos*.

### Yechezkel Derivation

The *Gemara* proceeds to derive each practice from the specific language of the *pasuk* in *Yechezkel*: *u-moladosayich b'yom huledet osach* — from the phrase "your birth on the day you were born," the *Gemara* derives *mikan she-meyaldin et havlad b'Shabbos* — that one may assist a woman in childbirth on *Shabbos* (the *hif'il* form indicating another person actively assisting). *Lo kores sarech* — "your navel was not cut" — yields *mikan she-chotchin et hatabur b'Shabbos*, that one may cut the umbilical cord. *U-v'mayim lo ruchatzat l'mish'i* — "you were not bathed in water to smooth you" — yields that one may bathe the newborn. *V'hamlei'ach lo humlachas* — "you were not salted" — yields that one may rub salt on the newborn, which was believed to promote health. *V'hachtel lo huchtalt* — "you were not swaddled" — yields that one may swaddle the newborn on *Shabbos*.

A brief but important remark from *Tosafos* clarifies the nature of this derivation: *lav mikra mafik* — these are not actually being derived as *halachos* from the *pasuk*. Rather, *ella mistama*, since *Yechezkel* mentions these acts in a context of reproach — pointing out that they were neglected — *im ken tzar hu* — if they are not performed, it causes suffering to the newborn. And since *u-v'chulan ein bahem issur d'Oraisa* — none of these acts involves a biblical prohibition (cutting an umbilical cord, for instance, is not a *melacha* in the biblical sense; the most that could arise would be incidental bleeding from certain cutting actions) — the point is simply that where there is no biblical violation and there is real suffering involved, these acts are entirely permitted.

---

## Circumcision Shabbat

### Tools on Shabbat

The *Gemara* now opens the new *perek*, called *Rabbi Eliezer d'Milah*, which is devoted to the *halachos* of *mila* on *Shabbos* as well as *mila* in general. The name disambiguates this chapter from another *perek* whose opening line also features *Rabbi Eliezer* — specifically *Rabbi Eliezer d'ha-oreg*, the chapter dealing with weaving. Since the present chapter lacks a convenient verbal hook in its opening line, it is identified by its subject matter.

The *perek* opens: *Rabbi Eliezer omer: im lo hevi kli me-erev Shabbat, mevi'o be-Shabbat meguleh* — if one did not bring the circumcision implements before *Shabbos*, one may bring them on *Shabbos* itself, and one does so *meguleh*, openly, so that everyone can see that a *mila* knife is being carried. This is permitted because *brit mila* overrides *Shabbos*. Carrying the knife openly removes any suspicion that one is carrying something forbidden.

In a case of danger — where non-Jews have prohibited *brit mila* — one may cover the knife, but *al pi edim*, in the presence of witnesses. Jews, at least, should know what is being carried beneath one's garments, to dispel any suspicion among the Jewish community.

### Multi-Stage Violations

*Rabbi Eliezer* goes further still: *kortim etzim la-asos pechamim la-asos barzel* — one may even cut down trees on *Shabbos* to make charcoal, and use the charcoal to forge the iron for the *mila* knife. In other words, *Rabbi Eliezer* permits violations many stages removed from the *mila* itself, so long as they are necessary for performing the *brit*. If there is no other way, any act required — no matter how indirect — is permitted on *Shabbos* for the sake of *brit mila*.

---

## Akiva Restriction

### Akiva's Principle

*Rabbi Akiva* articulates a sharply contrasting principle: *kol melacha she-efshar la-asotah me-erev Shabbat einah docha et ha-Shabbat* — any *melacha* that could have been done before *Shabbos* does not override *Shabbos*. Only that which could not have been done beforehand — the *mila* proper, which by definition must be performed on the eighth day and therefore cannot be done in advance — is what overrides *Shabbos*. Everything else, in theory, could have been done before *Shabbos* began, and therefore it does not override it.

This principle is not about practical impossibility — it does not matter whether, say, the person carrying the knife was unavoidably delayed. The question is purely theoretical: could it have been done beforehand? If yes, it does not override *Shabbos*. Practically, this means that if the knife was forgotten, one waits until *Motzaei Shabbos* and performs the *brit* on Sunday. There is a strong *mitzvah* to perform *mila* on the eighth day itself — derived from the phrase *u-vayom ha-shemini yimol*, which *Chazal* understand to indicate a special imperative even to the point of overriding *Shabbos* — but once the conditions for that override are not met, one simply performs it as soon as *Shabbos* ends.

---

## Circumcision Shabbat (II)

### Exposure Rationale

The *Gemara* returns to *Rabbi Eliezer*'s ruling about carrying the knife openly and poses the question: what is the reason he requires this? Is it *mishum chavuv mitzvah* — to endear the *mitzvah*, to publicize how important *brit mila* is such that one carries the knife openly on *Shabbos* as a demonstration? Or is it *mishum chashada* — simply to avoid the suspicion that one is carrying something forbidden, with no particular positive statement being made?

The practical consequence is this: if the reason is *chavuv mitzvah*, then carrying it openly is specifically required — *meguleh in, makhuseh lo*. If the reason is only to avoid suspicion, then covering it with witnesses would serve equally well.

*Rabbi Levi* rules: *lo amar Rabbi Eliezer ela l'chavuv mitzvah* — *Rabbi Eliezer* said it specifically to endear the *mitzvah*, not merely to avoid suspicion. A *baraisa* underscores this by formulating the rule as *mevi'o meguleh ve-ein mevi'o makhuseh* — one brings it openly and specifically does not bring it covered. The double formulation — both the affirmative and the negative — implies it must be done this way.

*Rav Ashi* adds that the *Mishnah* itself implies the same conclusion: it states that in a time of danger one covers it. This implies that when there is *no* danger, covering is not permitted. If the sole concern were avoiding suspicion, hiding it with witnesses would presumably always be adequate. The fact that covering is restricted to times of actual danger demonstrates that the exposure serves the affirmative purpose of *chavuv mitzvah*. *Shema mina* — this is a valid proof.

A further *baraisa* records that *Rabbi Yehuda* reported in the name of *Rabbi Eliezer*: in times of danger, the practice was to bring the knife covered with witnesses present. This is essentially a restatement of what the *Mishnah* records. The *Gemara* then asks: when we say "witnesses," does this mean the carrier plus one other person, or two witnesses beyond the carrier? The *Gemara* resolves that it must mean two beyond the carrier — since the carrier cannot formally testify on his own behalf — or alternatively, he and another together would be understood as capable of serving as witnesses in other contexts, satisfying the concern even if not constituting formal *edut*.

---

## Localized Authorities

### Community Variants

The *Gemara* now broadens its lens. It is a striking feature of the *halachic* landscape of the *Chazal* period that different communities followed different local authorities, and what was practiced in one place was not necessarily the standard elsewhere. Three communities are held up as examples.

In the place of *Rabbi Eliezer*, people would actually chop wood on *Shabbos* to make charcoal, to make iron, to forge the *mila* knife — performing the very multi-stage violations *Rabbi Eliezer* permitted. The community genuinely followed his ruling in practice.

### Fowl & Milk Case

In the place of *Rabbi Yose HaGlili*, they would eat *basar of b'chalav* — fowl cooked with milk. *Rabbi Yose HaGlili* held that there was no biblical prohibition on fowl with milk, and moreover that there was not even a rabbinic prohibition — derived from the juxtaposition with *neveila* and the limiting phrase *b'chalev imo*, "in its mother's milk," which explicitly excludes fowl since fowl has no mother's milk. His community acted accordingly.

*Levi* once came to the house of *Yose Rishba* — *Yose* the hunter — and was served the head of a peacock cooked in milk. He did not eat it. When he later came before *Rabbi*, *Rabbi* asked him sharply: *amai lo tshamtemehu* — why did you not put him in *cherem*? He is violating a rabbinic prohibition. *Levi* responded: I recognized that this was the town of *Rabbi Yehuda ben Batera*, the local authority, and I concluded that perhaps *Rabbi Yehuda ben Batera* ruled like *Rabbi Yose HaGlili*. That is indeed the *baraisa*'s teaching: *Rabbi Yose HaGlili omer* — the verse says do not eat *neveila*, and elsewhere it says do not cook a kid in its mother's milk. *Rabbi Yose HaGlili* derives from the juxtaposition that the milk prohibition extends only to animals also subject to *neveila*, while fowl, though subject to *neveila*, is explicitly excluded by *imo* — "its mother's milk" — since fowl has none. He understands this exclusion as total, dispensing with even the rabbinic enactment.

### Reward for Devotion

*Rabbi Yitzchak* then reports that the community that followed *Rabbi Eliezer*'s ruling on *brit mila*, and showed such tremendous devotion to this *mitzvah*, was rewarded: all its members lived to a ripe old age, and moreover, when Rome issued its decree prohibiting *brit mila*, that community was somehow spared from the *gezeirah*. Rather than treating *Rabbi Eliezer*'s position as a dangerous aberration to be censured, *Chazal* pointedly praise the devotion it represented and note its reward — a remarkable statement that might seem counterintuitive given how firmly the majority rules against *Rabbi Eliezer* on this matter.

---

## Joy vs. Displeasure

### Embraced Mitzvot

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* now formulates a broader principle: *kol mitzvah she-kiblu aleihem be-simcha, kegon mila* — any *mitzvah* that the Jewish people originally accepted with joy, such as *mila*, is still performed with joy today. He derives this from the *pasuk* cited at every *brit mila*: *sas anochi al imratecha ke-motze shalal rav* — I rejoice over Your word like one who finds great treasure. *Rashi* identifies "Your word" (singular) as *brit mila*, the singular command Avraham received. *Tosafos* adds that the *perek* in *Tehillim* to which this belongs is *lamnatzeach al ha-sheminit* — the psalm oriented toward the eighth day, directly evoking the eighth-day *mila*. *Tosafos* further cites the *derasha* that *Avraham* made a great feast on the day *Yitzchak* was *higamel* — the word *higamel* being read as *hey-gimel-mem-lamed*, where *hey* and *gimel* equal eight and *mal* means circumcised, encoding the eighth-day *brit mila* in the very word. The point is that joy has accompanied *brit mila* from the outset, and it continues to be marked with a great *seudah*.

### Disputed Mitzvot

By contrast: *kol mitzvah she-kiblu aleihem be-katata* — any *mitzvah* originally received with dispute and displeasure, *kegon arayos* — like the prohibitions of forbidden sexual relations. The *pasuk* records: *Vayishma Moshe et ha-am boche le-mishpechotav* — Moshe heard the people weeping according to their families. The *derasha* is *al iskei mishpechotav* — they were weeping over the newly imposed restrictions within the family, the prohibitions of incest and the related *arayos*. And so those *mitzvos* — *adayin osin osah be-katata* — remain fraught: there is hardly a *kesuvah* written without some attendant dispute about its terms, some measure of contention clinging to the whole domain.

### Martyrdom Mitzvot

*Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* articulates a further principle: any *mitzvah* for which the Jewish people were willing to give their lives during times of governmental persecution — *kegon avodat kochavim u-mila* — like the rejection of idolatry and the practice of *brit mila* (this almost certainly reflects the Chanukah period and similar decrees) — *adayin hi mukhzeket be-yadam*, it remains strong and firm in their hands. By contrast, any *mitzvah* for which Jews did not demonstrate that willingness to die, *kegon tefillin*, is *adayin hi merufeh be-yadam* — weak in their hands. It is somewhat surprising to see *tefillin* named here, given how central it appears among male observant practice. Yet the *Gemara* proceeds to explain in a way that illuminates the weakness.

### Tefillin Weakness

*Rabbi Yannai* states: *tefillin tzrichin guf naki k'Elisha Ba'al Knafayim* — *tefillin* require a clean body like *Elisha Ba'al Knafayim*. *Abaye* explains *guf naki* as *she-lo yafiach bahem* — one may not pass gas while wearing *tefillin*. *Rava* adds: *she-lo yishan bahem* — one may not even sleep in them, out of concern that gas may pass during sleep. The implication is that maintaining this standard throughout the hours of wearing *tefillin* is genuinely demanding, and that historically many did not meet the standard consistently. *Tosafos* attests that even in their own era, *tefillin* was not being worn as diligently as it should have been. Whether because of the *guf naki* requirement or simply through laxity in practice, the observation that *tefillin* is *merufeh* — weakened in Israel's hands — carries historical weight.

### Elisha Story

*Ve-amai karu lei Elisha Ba'al Knafayim* — why is he called the master of the wings? The story: *shepa'am achat gazra malchut ha-risha'ah* — once, the evil government of Rome issued a decree that anyone who places *tefillin* on his head would have his skull pierced. *Elisha* would nonetheless put on *tefillin* and go out into the marketplace, publicly, presumably to bolster the resolve of the Jewish community.

One Roman officer spotted him and gave chase. When the officer caught up, *Elisha* tore the *tefillin* from his own head and held them in his hand. "What is in your hand?" the officer demanded. "The wings of a dove," *Elisha* answered. He opened his hand — and dove's wings were found there.

*Mai shna kanfei yonah* — why a dove specifically, and not any other bird? *Mishum de-damya Knesses Yisrael le-yona* — because the Jewish people are compared to a dove: *kanfei yonah nechpah ba-kesef ve-evroteiha bi-yrakrak charutz* — the wings of a dove covered in silver and its pinions like fine gold. Just as a dove's wings protect it — *Rashi* notes that a dove relies on its wings more than its beak for defense — so too the *mitzvos* protect the Jewish people: *af Yisrael mitzvos meginot aleihem*.

*Tosafos* points out something arresting: even *Elisha* was not technically *moser nefesh* here, since rather than declaring "these are *tefillin*," he denied it and saved himself. One need not go out of one's way to be killed. Still, the fact that *Elisha* wore *tefillin* publicly in defiance of the decree demonstrates a degree of devotion that stands in contrast to the general laxity — and his public witness was precisely the point.

---

## Forgotten Knife Case

### Knife Transport

*Rav Abba bar Rav Adda* reported in the name of *Rabbi Yitzchak*: there was once an incident in which they forgot to bring the *mila* knife from *erev Shabbos*, and brought it on *Shabbos* by way of the rooftops and courtyards — *derech gagot ve-derech chatzerot* — following *Rabbi Eliezer*'s general permission for carrying implements needed for *brit mila*.

### Eliezer Objection

This was, however, done *shelo birtzon Rabbi Eliezer* — not in a manner that pleased *Rabbi Eliezer*. *Rabbi Eliezer* himself would have had them bring it directly through *reshut ha-rabbim*. His position, it emerges, permits the most direct route even if it involves a biblical violation, because the *mila*'s need effectively licenses whatever is necessary. The roundabout path through rooftops and courtyards — technically only rabbinic violations — was more restrictive than *Rabbi Eliezer* would have demanded.

### Quandary Resolved

*Rav Yosef* challenges the formulation of the incident: if it was *shelo birtzon Rabbi Eliezer*, surely it was even more against the will of the *Chachamim*, who would not permit even rabbinic violations for something that could have been done before *Shabbos*. A *baraisa* makes this explicit: the *Chachamim* say that just as you cannot bring the knife through *reshut ha-rabbim*, so too you cannot bring it through rooftops or courtyards or fields. Even these rabbinic violations are not sanctioned when the task was omissible before *Shabbos*. So according to whom was the incident performed?

*Rav Ashi* resolves: *shelo birtzon Rabbi Eliezer u-machlokto* — it was not according to the will of *Rabbi Eliezer* or his disputants. Neither side was satisfied. Rather, *ela birtzon Rabbi Shimon* — it was consistent with the position of *Rabbi Shimon*.

### Shimon's Domain

For *Rabbi Shimon*, rooftops, enclosed fields, and courtyards — assuming they all have sufficient walls — are all a single domain: *kulan reshut achas hen l'keilim she-shavsu b'sochan* — they are all one domain for objects that began *Shabbos* there. If a vessel was in the courtyard or on the rooftop when *Shabbos* began, it may be carried freely among all such spaces without any *eiruv* between them, because *Rabbi Shimon* considers them a single *reshut ha-yachid*. The only need for an *eiruv* is to carry from inside a house into those spaces, or from those spaces back into a house. Something that began in those outdoor spaces can move among all of them freely.

The knife began *Shabbos* in one of those outdoor spaces, and so carrying it from one end of the courtyard complex or rooftops to the other was, according to *Rabbi Shimon*, not even a rabbinic violation. He was the one authority satisfied with what had occurred.

---

## Mavoi Carrying Rules

### Mavoi Without Shituf

This resolution prompts *Rav Zeira* to pose a question to *Rav Assi*: *mavoi shelo nishtatfu bo, mahu le-taltel be-chulo* — if an alleyway did not have a *shituf mavoi* established, and a vessel began *Shabbos* within it, may one carry that vessel throughout the alleyway?

To understand the question: the typical spatial configuration is houses opening into a courtyard, and multiple courtyards opening into a *mavoi*, an alleyway. The *mavoi* has three walls but lacks the fourth. To carry within the *mavoi*, all the courtyards must jointly establish a *shituf mavoi* — a partnership, typically through shared food — which binds them together as a unified domain. The question is: what if this *shituf* was not made? A *chatzer* without an *eiruv* among its houses still permits carrying within the *chatzer* for objects that began there — since it has four walls and serves as a *reshut ha-yachid* — but does the *mavoi* enjoy this same leniency?

Two factors might distinguish the *mavoi* unfavorably: it has only three walls (not four), and it lacks the intimacy of *diyurin* — residents directly opening onto it. People access the *mavoi* only through their courtyards, not directly from their homes, making it a less integrated space.

### Zeira-Assi Discussion

*Rav Assi* was silent and did not answer at the time. Later, *Rav Zeira* found him teaching the following tradition: *Reish Lakish* said in the name of *Rabbi Yehuda Nesia* — the incident in which the *mila* knife was forgotten and brought on *Shabbos* involved precisely a *mavoi* without a *shituf*, and the knife had begun *Shabbos* within that *mavoi*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Account

*Rabbi Oshaya* reported that he had asked *Rabbi Yehuda HaGozer* — the *mohel* — what exactly had occurred, and the *mohel* clarified: it was a *mavoi shelo nishtatfu bo*, a *mavoi* without a *shituf*, and the knife had simply been carried from one end of the *mavoi* to the other (*mehai reisha lehai reisha*). Bystanders who observed someone walking through the alleyway with a knife may have assumed something irregular had occurred, not realizing the knife had simply started there and was being transported within a single, wall-bounded space.

*Rav Zeira* then turned to *Rav Assi*: clearly, from your citation of this incident, you hold that one may carry throughout a *mavoi* that lacked a *shituf* if the object began there. *Rav Assi* confirmed: yes, that is his position. *Rav Zeira* was puzzled — he had asked this question many times and received no answer, and now here was the ruling embedded in a story about *brit mila*. *Rav Assi* replied: *dilma agav shitpach rahit lach gamrach* — perhaps in the rush of moving through your learning you happened across this teaching of *Reish Lakish* about *Rabbi Yehuda Nesia* and the *brit mila* incident, and through that you uncovered the *halacha*. *Rav Assi* acknowledged: yes, that is precisely what happened.

### Paradoxical Carrying

The *Gemara* closes with a ruling transmitted through *Rav Nachman* in the name of *Rabbah bar Avuha* in the name of *Rav*, which clarifies an apparent paradox:

If the courtyards all made their own internal *eiruvin* — joining each courtyard's houses together — then one *cannot* carry throughout the *mavoi* without a *shituf*. If the courtyards did *not* make *eiruvin* — meaning everything is "open" and unresolved — one *may* carry throughout the *mavoi*.

This is left as a striking paradox to contemplate, with the explanation deferred to the following day's *shiur*. The counterintuitive conclusion — that doing the right thing (making *eiruvin* in the courtyards) results in greater restriction in the *mavoi*, while neglecting to do so results in greater permissibility — inverts ordinary expectations and will require a fuller treatment of the underlying principles of *reshuyos* and *eiruvin* to resolve.

---

---

# Shabbat 131

## Machshirei Milah & Mavoi

### Rabbi Eliezer Intro

Today's *daf* is 131. We pick up from the bottom of 130b, in the midst of discussing *Rabbi Eliezer*'s position that *machshirei milah* — preparatory acts for *bris milah* — may be performed on *Shabbos*, overriding the prohibition of *melacha*. The *Gemara* had been examining the case of carrying a knife through courtyards, and made clear that this scenario does not actually hinge on *Rabbi Eliezer*'s ruling at all, since even without an *eruv*, at least according to *Rabbi Shimon*'s position, the courtyards may be considered a single domain by virtue of their surrounding walls — and carrying would therefore be permitted in any event.

### Knife & Courtyards

The *Gemara* then noted that even according to the more restrictive view, the carrying of the knife could be accomplished in a halachically permissible manner through *eruvei chatzeros*, without needing to invoke *Rabbi Eliezer*'s principle at all. This sets the stage for what initially appears to be a tangential discussion but is in fact a necessary clarification of how *eruvei chatzeros* and *shituf* interact in the domain of a *mavoi*.

### Mavoi Shituf

The *Gemara* now introduces a somewhat puzzling statement that, at first glance, seems counterintuitive. Its purpose will become clearer as the discussion unfolds, and it serves as an appetizer for the full treatment of these laws in *Masechet Eruvin* — approximately a month away.

---

## Mavoi Paradox

### Rabbi Zeira's Rule

*Itmar*: *amar Rabbi Zeira amar Rav* — a *mavoi*, an alleyway into which multiple courtyards open, where the courtyards did not perform a *shituf* among themselves, *ein metalatlin bo ela bearba amos* — one may carry within it only within four *amos*. In other words, without the courtyards having joined together to form a unified domain with the *mavoi*, carrying within the *mavoi* itself is effectively prohibited — even for objects that originate within the *mavoi*.

### Abaye & Rabbah

*Amar Abaye*: *Rabbi Zeira* said this teaching but never explained it, until *Rabbah bar Avuha* came and provided the explanation, transmitted through the chain *amar Rav Nachman amar Rabbah bar Avuha amar Rav*.

### Eruv Paradox

The explanation is strikingly paradoxical. *Mavoi shelo nishtatfu bo* — a *mavoi* whose courtyards did not combine into it: *eirvu chatzeros im battim* — if the courtyards each made their own *eruv* together with their respective houses, then *ein metalatlin bo ela bearba amos* — the *mavoi* is off-limits, and one may carry within it only four *amos*. But *lo eirvu chatzeros im battim* — if the courtyards did not even make a local *eruv* with their houses, then *muttar letaltel bekulo* — it is entirely permitted to carry within the *mavoi* for objects that originate there. The more one does in the right direction, the worse the outcome for the *mavoi* — a genuine paradox that demands explanation.

### Chatzrot → Battim

*Rav Chanina Chuza'ah* addresses this to *Rava*: he understands why making an *eruv* in the individual courtyards causes the *mavoi* to become forbidden. The reasoning is *denidku chatzeros vena'asu battim* — the courtyards have been, as it were, uprooted from their status as courtyards and transformed into houses. The entire logic of *eruvei chatzeros* is that multiple houses opening into a single courtyard, though technically within a *reshus hayachid* surrounded by walls, constitute separate domains at the level of ownership and use. The *eruv* — typically performed by joining together in a loaf of bread — creates a legal fiction in which the courtyard is treated as a unified domain owned by a single entity.
