Once each courtyard undergoes this transformation through its *eruv*, it ceases to function as a courtyard and becomes, effectively, a single person's domain — functionally equivalent to a house.

### Rav's Mavoi Rule

This is where *Rav*'s position becomes critical. *De'amar Rav*: *ein mavoi nittar belechi vekorah* — a *mavoi* is not rendered permissible for carrying through a *lechi* (a vertical post) or a *korah* (a horizontal beam) unless the classic configuration is in place: *ad sheyehu battim vachatzeros petuchim letocho* — houses and courtyards must open into it. *Vehacha, battim ika chatzeros leka* — here, once the *eruv* has been made in each courtyard, you have houses but no courtyards. The physical layout hasn't changed, but the legal reality has: each courtyard has been reclassified as a house, and so the *mavoi* no longer has courtyards opening into it — only what are now effectively individual houses. Without the classic configuration, the *mavoi*'s leniencies do not apply.

The inverse case — where no *eruv* was made — is then raised. If the houses never made an *eruv* with their courtyard, they have no access to the courtyard at all, making them legally irrelevant to the *mavoi*. So one might ask: in that scenario, is the configuration not equally deficient? You have courtyards but no accessible houses. The *Gemara* will develop this challenge in the following section.

---

## Bitul Reshut

### Waiving Domain

The *Gemara* responds: even without a prior *eruv*, there is a mechanism — *bitul reshut* — by which all residents could renounce their private domains in favor of one individual. This retroactively creates a unified domain and allows carrying within the courtyard, so the houses are not entirely irrelevant.

### Sof Sof Problem

But the *Gemara* is not satisfied. *Sof sof* — ultimately — if everyone waives their rights to one person, then *bayit ika batim leika*: you effectively have one house, not multiple houses. The classic configuration requires multiple houses opening into a courtyard; *bitul reshut* collapses everything into one, destroying the very configuration that is required.

### Day Division

The *Gemara* attempts a resolution: *deimitzafra ve'ad palga deyoma legabi chad, umipalga deyoma ulefanya legabi chad* — perhaps for the first half of the day one person holds the consolidated rights, and for the second half of the day another person does. In this way, the identity of the individual courtyard is preserved (since no permanent *shituf* transformed it), and access to the *mavoi* is maintained through the rotating *bitul reshut*, while the presence of houses retains legal significance.

The *Gemara* rejects this as well. *Be'idna de'ita lehai leita lehai* — at any given moment when one person holds rights, the other does not. At no point in time does the *mavoi* simultaneously have the classic configuration of a courtyard with multiple house-owners. The paradox remains.

### Rav Ashi Solution

The *Gemara* abandons this entire line of reasoning. *Ella amar Rav Ashi*: *mi garam lachatzeros she'ye'asru batim v'leka* — what is it that would make the courtyards problematic for the *mavoi*? It is the houses — and they are not present in the relevant sense.

*Rav Ashi*'s explanation is considerably more direct. When one wishes to carry an object within the *mavoi* itself — not from the courtyard into the *mavoi*, but within the *mavoi* — the question is whether the courtyards opening into the *mavoi* constitute a separate domain that problematizes the *mavoi*. If the houses have made an *eruv* with their courtyard, then the courtyard has active use flowing in from those houses; it is a domain with significant traffic, distinct from the open *mavoi*. The fact that this separate, active domain is open into the *mavoi* means the *mavoi* is not a self-contained space — it is penetrated by a different domain, and carrying within it becomes problematic.

By contrast, if no *eruv* was made in the courtyard, the houses are entirely cut off from the courtyard. The courtyard has no connection to the houses; it is simply an open yard. In that case, the courtyard is not a meaningfully distinct domain from the *mavoi* — it is essentially an extension of it. The entire space functions as one open area, and carrying within the *mavoi* does not implicate any separate domain. Hence, *muttar letaltel bekulo*.

All of the foregoing, it should be noted, involves purely *rabbinic* prohibitions — the underlying spaces are all, at the biblical level, *reshus hayachid*.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Scope

### Not Universal

With this digression concluded — itself occasioned by the *Gemara*'s discussion of carrying a *milah* knife through a *mavoi* — the *Gemara* returns to the main topic. *Amar Rabbi Chiya bar Abba amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *lo l'chol amar Rabbi Eliezer machshirei mitzvah dochin es haShabbos* — *Rabbi Eliezer* did not make a universal ruling that preparatory acts of any *mitzvah* may override *Shabbos*. The position is more nuanced than a blanket principle.

### Shtei Halechem

The *Gemara* offers the *shtei halechem* — the two loaves brought on *Shavuos* — as a case in point. These loaves must be brought on *Shavuos* itself, and they override *Yom Tov*, or even *Shabbos* if the day falls accordingly. *Rabbi Eliezer* indeed holds that even the *machshirim* — the grinding, baking, and preparation of the loaves — may be performed on *Shabbos*. But critically, *v'lo lamdan Rabbi Eliezer ela migzeirah shavah* — he derived this not from a general abstracted principle, but from a specific *gezeirah shavah*.

The *baraisa* records: *minayin l'machshirin shel shtei halechem she'dochin es haShabbos?* The *Gemara* establishes the *gezeirah shavah* through the word *hava'ah* — "bringing" — which appears both by the *omer* and by the *shtei halechem*. By the *omer*, we know from the verse *becharish uvaktzir tishbos* that since plowing is optional, only optional harvesting is prohibited on *Shabbos* — the harvesting of the *omer*, being a *mitzvah*, may be done even on *Shabbos*. From this we learn that the preparatory act of harvesting overrides *Shabbos* for the *omer*. The *gezeirah shavah* on *hava'ah* then extends this principle to the *shtei halechem*.

The *Gemara* raises the question of whether this *gezeirah shavah* is *mufni* — whether the shared term is truly free of its local function, and thus available to serve as an anchor for the analogy. A *gezeirah shavah* where neither term carries its own contextual load is ironclad and cannot be logically challenged; one where only one side is free can be made, but is open to refutation. *Rabbi Eliezer* himself holds that a *gezeirah shavah mufneh mitzad echad* — free on only one side — may be made but is subject to challenge, *lamedin umeshivin*.

Why would this particular *gezeirah shavah* require both sides to be free? Because it is logically vulnerable. By the *omer*, there is a specific *mitzvah* to perform the act of harvesting — *im matza katzur eino kotzer*, if grain was already harvested, it cannot be used; it must be freshly cut as an act of *mitzvah*. That is why the cutting of the *omer* overrides *Shabbos*. But by the *shtei halechem*, *im matza katzur eino kotzer* does not apply — grain cut weeks earlier is perfectly usable. Thus one could logically challenge any attempt to extend the *omer*'s principle to the *shtei halechem*. The *gezeirah shavah* must therefore be fully *mufni* on both sides to be unchallengeable.

The *Gemara* demonstrates that the *omer* side is indeed free: the verse states *b'yom havichem et omer hatnufah*, "on the day of your bringing the elevation *omer*" — the phrase *b'yom havichem* is understood as superfluous in context and thus opens the verse for the *gezeirah shavah*. And on the side of the *shtei halechem*, the word *tavi'u* is seen as more inclusive than strictly necessary, similarly making that side available. With both sides free, the *gezeirah shavah* is ironclad.

The deeper point is this: *Rabbi Eliezer* needed a specific *gezeirah shavah* to extend the principle from the *omer* to the *shtei halechem*. He did not simply abstract a universal rule from the *omer* and apply it everywhere. This means that wherever he extends the principle of *machshirei mitzvah dochin es haShabbos*, he requires a specific *limud* — and cases he cannot derive separately remain unaffected.

### Extensions

The *Gemara* now attempts to identify what *Rabbi Eliezer* excludes, testing various candidates. *Ve-ha tanya*: a *baraisa* teaches that *lulav ve-chol machshirav dochan es ha-Shabbos divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — *lulav* and all its preparations override *Shabbos* according to *Rabbi Eliezer*. This is striking. Taking a *lulav* involves no *melacha* whatsoever; the act of the *mitzvah* itself does not require violating *Shabbos*. Yet *Rabbi Eliezer* would permit climbing a palm tree and cutting down a *lulav* on *Shabbos* if needed, or cutting an *esrog* — any preparatory act required to fulfill the *mitzvah* that day.

Similarly, *ve-ha tanya*: *sukkah ve-chol machshireha dochan es ha-Shabbos divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — sitting in the *sukkah* requires no violation, yet one may build the *sukkah* on *Shabbos* itself. And *matzah ve-chol machshireha dochan es ha-Shabbos divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — not only on *Yom Tov*, but even on *Shabbos*, may one bake *matzos* to fulfill that night's obligation. And finally, *shofar v'chol machshirav doche es ha-Shabbos divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — one may fashion a *shofar* from an animal's horn, carry it in *reshus harabbim*, and perform any preparatory act required.

The *Gemara* thus finds that *Rabbi Eliezer* extends the principle to a remarkable range of *mitzvos* — including those where the act of the *mitzvah* itself would never require overriding *Shabbos*. The question then becomes: where does he learn each of these, and what does he exclude?

---

## Tzitzit & Mezuzah

### Excluded Items

*Amar Rav Adda bar Ahava*: the cases *Rabbi Eliezer* does exclude are *tzitzis l'taliso u'mezuzah l'pischu* — attaching *tzitzis* to one's garment or affixing a *mezuzah* to one's doorpost on *Shabbos*.

### Consensus

A *baraisa* confirms that all agree — *Rabbi Eliezer* and the *Chachamim* both concur — that *she'im tzitz taliso v'asah mezuzah l'pischu be-Shabbos, shehu chayav*: if one puts *tzitzis* on his garment or affixes a *mezuzah* on *Shabbos*, he is liable.

### No Fixed Time

*Amar Rav Yosef*: the reason is *lefi she-ein kavua lahem zman* — these *mitzvos* have no fixed time. Other *mitzvos*, like *korban Pesach* or the *tamid*, are performed on *Shabbos* because the *Torah* explicitly designates their time — *b'moado*, in their appointed time. Similarly, *lulav* must be taken today and *shofar* must be blown today. But *tzitzis* and *mezuzah* carry no such urgency; one can simply do them tomorrow. Without the weight of a fixed time, there is no basis to override *Shabbos*.

### Abaye Challenges

*Amar lei Abaye*: on the contrary, the opposite should follow. *Michdi ein kavua lahem zman, kol sha'ata v'sha'ata zimneih hu* — precisely because there is no fixed time, every moment is its time of obligation. As *Tosafos* explains: if one does not put *tzitzis* on his garment today, he has failed to perform today's *mitzvah* of *tzitzis*, even if he does it tomorrow. The same is true of *mezuzah*. So why should the lack of a single designated day weaken the demand? The same could be said of *lulav* — if one fails to take it today, he has lost today's *mitzvah*. The frequency of obligation does not seem to strengthen the case; the loss of each day's *mitzvah* is equally real.

### Ownership Condition

*Ella amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* — and some attribute it to *Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua* — the real distinction is *ho'il u'veyado l'hafkiro*: since it is within one's power to renounce ownership of the garment or the house, the obligation is contingent on circumstances of ownership rather than being an absolute personal demand. *Lulav*, *shofar*, *sukkah* — these are unconditional obligations that apply regardless of what one owns or doesn't own; you must fulfill them today, full stop. But *tzitzis* applies only because one happens to own a four-cornered garment, and *mezuzah* applies only because one occupies a particular dwelling. Since the obligation is conditional on the ownership, it does not carry the absolute weight needed to override *Shabbos*.

---

## Lulav Source

### Lulav Question

The *Gemara* now turns to identifying the specific *pesukim* from which *Rabbi Eliezer* derives his position for each *mitzvah*, since we have established that he requires a separate *limud* in each case. *Menalei l'Rabbi Eliezer ha* — where does he learn that *lulav* and its preparations override *Shabbos*?

### Bayom Pasuk

One might suggest learning it from the *shtei halechem* — but *shekein tzorech gavoah*: those loaves are brought as an offering in the *Beis HaMikdash*, a category of sacred service, which cannot simply be extended to the ordinary individual *mitzvah* of *lulav*. Moreover, the more fundamental distinction is that the *shtei halechem* themselves override *Shabbos* — one cannot derive a general principle applicable to *mitzvos* that do not themselves override *Shabbos*. Instead, the *Gemara* cites: *ella amar kra bayom* — the verse states *ulekachtem lachem bayom harishon*, "you shall take for yourselves on the first day." The word *bayom* — on the day — teaches *afilu beShabbos*: even if that day falls on *Shabbos*.

### Bayom Purpose

One might object: perhaps *bayom* simply authorizes taking the *lulav* — why must it speak to the preparations? The answer is that you do not need a *pasuk* to permit taking the *lulav* itself. The concerns about *muktzeh* are only *rabbinic*, and if the *Torah* is speaking to *Shabbos* override at all, it must be addressing the preparatory acts — the cutting of the *lulav*, the trimming of the *esrog*, and so on — which constitute genuine *melachot*.

### Rabbis' Bayom

The *Chachamim* who dispute *Rabbi Eliezer* read the word *bayom* differently. *Hu mibayei lei bayom velo balailah* — the word teaches that the *mitzvah* of *lulav* applies during the day and not at night. There is a risk of deriving from the *shivas yamim* said by *lulav* in the verse that it mirrors the seven days of *sukkah* — and since *sukkah* applies both at night and during the day, perhaps *lulav* should as well. The word *bayom* from *ushmaachtem lifnei Hashem Elokeichem shivas yamim* — "you shall rejoice before God seven days" — at the end of the *lulav* passage, teaches *yamim velo leilos*: only days, not nights.

### Rabbis' Bayom

Where then does *Rabbi Eliezer* derive the day-not-night restriction for *lulav*? *Nafka lei mi'ushmaachtem lifnei Hashem Elokeichem shivas yamim* — he extracts it from that same concluding phrase. And the earlier word *bayom* in *ulekachtem lachem bayom harishon* is thereby freed to teach the override of *Shabbos* for the preparations.

### Arba Minim

One might then ask: since *Rabbi Eliezer* has a *pasuk* for *lulav*, why not simply write the rule by *lulav* and extend it to all other *mitzvos*? The *Gemara* answers: *mishum d'ika l'mifrach* — because the inference can be challenged. *Mah lulav shekein taun arba minim* — *lulav* may be uniquely weightier because it requires four components. The framing here is notable: the *Gemara* uses the language *taun arba minim* — "it requires four *minim*" — suggesting that the fundamental *mitzvah* is centered on the *lulav* and the other *minim* are accompaniments to it, consistent with the blessing *al netilas lulav* rather than *al netilas arba minim*. This distinctive compositional character of the *mitzvah* gives it a weight that cannot simply be extended elsewhere.

---

## Sukkah Source

### Sukkah Question

*Menalei l'Rabbi Eliezer ha* — where does *Rabbi Eliezer* derive that the preparations of *sukkah* override *Shabbos*? Cannot be from *shtei halechem* — *shekein tzorech gavoah*. Cannot be from *lulav* — *shekein taun arba minim*. A separate source is required.

### Shivas Yamim

*Ella gmar mishivas yamim milulav* — a *gezeirah shavah* on the phrase *shivas yamim*. The *Torah* uses *shivas yamim* in connection with both *sukkah* and *lulav* — the seven days of *Sukkos*. *Mah hahlan machshirav dochin es haShabbos, af kan nami machshirav dochin es haShabbos* — just as we derived that the preparations of *lulav* override *Shabbos*, so too the preparations of *sukkah*.

### Night & Day

And why can one not simply write the rule by *sukkah* and derive everything else from there? Because *sukkah* itself has a distinctive feature that gives it greater weight: *shekein noheget baleilot uvayamim* — *sukkah* applies equally at night and during the day, unlike *lulav*, *shofar*, and most other time-bound *mitzvos*, which apply only during the day. This uniqueness means one cannot draw inferences from *sukkah* to those other *mitzvos* — each requires its own derivation.

---

## Matzah Source

### Matzah Question

*Menalei l'Rabbi Eliezer ha* — where does he derive that the preparations of *matzah* override *Shabbos*? Cannot be from *shtei halechem* — *shekein tzorech gavoah*. Cannot be from *lulav* — *shekein taun arba minim*. Cannot be from *sukkah* — *shekein noheget baleilot k'vayamim*, since *sukkah* applies at night as well, while *matzah* is fulfilled only at night (the *seder* night), an inverse distinction.

### Chamisha Asar

*Ella gamar chamishah asar chamishah asar mechag haSukkos* — another *gezeirah shavah* extending the chain. The *Torah* associates both *Sukkos* and *Pesach* with the fifteenth of the month — *chamishah asar*. *Mah lehalan machshirin dochin es haShabbos, af kan machshirin dochin es haShabbos* — just as the preparations of *sukkah* override *Shabbos*, so too the preparations of *matzah*.

### Men & Women

And why cannot one simply write the rule by *matzah* and derive all others? *Shekein noheget benashim k'va'anashim* — *matzah* applies equally to men and women. All the other *mitzvos* under discussion — *lulav*, *shofar*, *sukkah* — are obligatory only upon men at the individual level, while *matzah* carries the distinctive weight of applying universally across gender. That broader scope gives *matzah* a special character from which one cannot automatically derive rules for those other, more restricted *mitzvos*.

---

## Shofar Source

### Shofar Question

*Menalei l'Rabbi Eliezer ha* — where does *Rabbi Eliezer* derive that *shofar* and its preparations override *Shabbos*? The *Gemara* eliminates each prior source in turn: *shtei halechem* — *shekein tzorech gavoah*; *lulav* — *shekein taun arba minim*; *sukkah* — *shekein noheget baleilot k'vayamim*; *matzah* — *shekein noheget benashim k'va'anashim*, while *shofar* biblically obligates only men.

### Yom Teruah

*Ella amar kra*: the *Torah* states *yom teruah yiheyeh lachem* — the day of *teruah* shall be for you. The word *bayom* — on that day — implies that the blowing must happen on that specific day, *afilu beShabbat*, even on *Shabbos*.

### Bayom Purpose

One might ask: why must the word *bayom* be teaching the override for *machshirin*? Why not simply say it is authorizing the blowing of the *shofar* itself? The *Gemara* answers from a *baraisa*: *ha tana d'bei Shmuel* teaches that the verse *kol melechet avodah lo ta'asu* — you shall not perform constructive labor — excludes *tkiyat shofar u'rediyat hapat*: blowing the *shofar* and taking bread out of an oven. These are acts of skill, *chochmah*, not *melacha* in the technical sense. Blowing a *shofar* is not a prohibited labor to begin with; it is only rabbinically restricted on *Shabbos*. Therefore, there would be no need for the *Torah* to explicitly permit blowing the *shofar* on *Shabbos* — it is *rabbanically* restricted. The verse must therefore be speaking to the preparations — the fashioning of the *shofar*, carrying it in the public domain, and any other *melacha* required to enable the blowing.

### Yom Kippur

*Verabbanan* — how do the *Chachamim* read the word *bayom* in this verse? *Hahu mibayei lei bayom velo balailah* — to restrict *shofar* to daytime, not nighttime. And where does *Rabbi Eliezer* learn the daytime restriction for *shofar* if not from here? *Nafka lei mi'beYom HaKippurim ta'aviru shofar, bechol artzechem* — from the verse about the *shofar* of *Yom Kippur*, which also says "the day." The two instances of *shofar* — on *Rosh Hashanah* and *Yom Kippur* — are learned from one another, *vegamrei ahadadi*, to establish the full structure of *teki'os* and the daytime restriction. This frees the word *bayom* in the *Rosh Hashanah* verse to teach the override for *machshirin*.

### Shofar Special

And why cannot one write the rule by *shofar* and derive the other *mitzvos* from it? *Shekein machneset zichronot shel Yisrael la'avihem shebashamayim* — this is a singularly powerful statement. *Tkiyat shofar* is not merely a *mitzvah* like others; it is the vehicle through which the prayers and remembrance of Israel are brought before their Father in Heaven. One might therefore say that the *Torah* made a special allowance for *shofar* on *Shabbos* precisely because of its unique spiritual gravity — it brings Israel's *zichronos* before God — and this cannot be generalized to other *mitzvos*.

This is a striking observation that resonates with a lived reality: of all the *mitzvos* not performed when *Rosh Hashanah* falls on *Shabbos*, the absence of *shofar* is the most keenly felt. *Sukkos* without *lulav* on *Shabbos* is softened somewhat because one still sits in the *sukkah*. But *Rosh Hashanah* without *shofar* is genuinely disorienting.

Similarly, the *shofar* of *Yom Kippur* in the *yovel* — *tiku be'veit din shofar, niftaru avadim levateihem vesadot chozrot leva'aleihem* — was the instrument that activated all the laws of the *yovel*: the liberation of slaves and the return of ancestral fields. That *shofar* too carries extraordinary weight. Both the *Rosh Hashanah* and *Yom Kippur* instances of *shofar* have dimensions of significance that make them sui generis — one cannot apply what is permitted for them to other, less weighty *mitzvos*.

---

## Milah Source

### Milah Question

*Milah ve-chol machshireha dochin et haShabbat divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — finally, the *Gemara* arrives at *milah* itself. *Menalei l'Rabbi Eliezer ha* — where does *Rabbi Eliezer* derive that the preparations of *milah* override *Shabbos*?

### Delay Possible

The *Gemara* raises the challenge: cannot *milah* be learned from all the preceding cases? The reply is *mah le-hanach she-ken im avar zemana batlah* — those other *mitzvos* share the feature that if their time passes, the *mitzvah* is entirely lost. If one did not take *lulav* on a given day of *Sukkos*, one did not perform that day's *mitzvah* — it cannot be made up. If one did not eat *matzah* on the night of *Pesach*, that *mitzvah* is gone. Each of these carries the urgency of an unrepeatable moment.

By contrast, *bris milah* is — as the *Gemara* acknowledges — one *mitzvah*, with one checkmark, that can be performed even after the eighth day. Missing the eighth day is not the same as forfeiting the *mitzvah* entirely; one is handing in the assignment late rather than not handing it in at all. The loss is real — the eighth-day timing carries great significance — but the *mitzvah* itself can still be performed. This structural difference means one cannot straightforwardly infer from the urgency of time-bound *mitzvos* that *milah* enjoys the same license.

### Bayom Pasuk

*Ela hainu ta'ama de-Rabbi Eliezer, de'amar kra: u'vayom ha-shmini yimmol besar orlato* — the word *bayom*, again: "on the day" of the eighth day, he shall be circumcised. *Ve-afilu beShabbat* — even on *Shabbos*.

### Bayom Purpose

Now, at the most basic level, the *pasuk* must first establish that *milah* itself overrides *Shabbos* before one can even speak of the *machshirin*. *Rashi* points out that the underlying rule that *milah* itself overrides *Shabbos* is a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — an oral tradition from Sinai not derived from a *pasuk*. The extra word *bayom* in the written *Torah* therefore serves to teach *Rabbi Eliezer*'s additional layer: that even the *machshirin* — the preparatory acts, the forging of the knife and all that precedes the act — override *Shabbos* as well.

### Thirteen Brits

And why cannot one simply write this by *milah* and derive all other *mitzvos* from it? *Mah le-milah she-ken nichretu aleiha shelosh esreh britos* — *bris milah* is distinguished by the fact that the word *bris* (covenant) is mentioned thirteen times in the passage of *Avraham*'s receiving the *mitzvah*. This gives *milah* a weight and covenantal gravity unparalleled by any other *mitzvah*, such that even if one were willing to override *Shabbos* for it, that reasoning is unique to *milah* and cannot be extended elsewhere.

The overall picture that emerges from this sustained analysis is as follows. *Rabbi Eliezer* applies the principle of *machshirei mitzvah dochin es haShabbos* broadly — extending it even to *mitzvos* like *lulav*, *sukkah*, *matzah*, and *shofar*, whose performance does not itself require overriding *Shabbos*. The only categories he excludes are *tzitzis* and *mezuzah*, either because their obligation is conditional on circumstances of ownership and therefore lacks absolute personal urgency, or — in the view that *Abaye* finds more compelling — because those other *mitzvos* each carry the weight of a specific unrepeatable day, while *tzitzis* and *mezuzah* are contingent obligations. But in every case where *Rabbi Eliezer* does apply the principle, he requires a specific *limud*: a dedicated *pasuk* or an established *gezeirah shavah*. The principle is not, for him, a universal abstraction. We will continue tomorrow with the debate between *Rabbi Eliezer* and the *Chachamim*.

---

---

# Shabbat 132

## Machshirin & Mitzvot

### Machshirin Override

The daf begins five lines from the top, at the double dot (*ad kan*). The Gemara has established Rabbi Eliezer's sweeping position: even *machshirin* — preparatory actions for *mitzvot* — may be performed on Shabbat, and this is true even for *mitzvot* that would not themselves override Shabbat under ordinary circumstances, such as *shofar* or *sukkah*. According to Rabbi Eliezer, if the *mitzvah* itself overrides Shabbat, then its preparatory acts do as well, and if it does not, the preparatory acts still may. This is quite a bold and broad position.

### Rabbis Disagree

The Rabbis dispute Rabbi Eliezer specifically on the question of *machshirei milah* — the preparatory acts for circumcision. The Gemara states: *ad kan lo pligi Rabbanan alei ela bemachshirei milah* — the Rabbis only disagree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding preparatory actions for *milah*.

### Milah Consensus

However, on the core question, there is no dispute: *aval milah gufa divrei hakol docha Shabbat* — the *milah* itself, everyone agrees, overrides Shabbat. This gives rise to the obvious question: *minalan* — from where do we know this?

## Milah Source: Halacha

### Halacha L'Moshe

Ula states that the source is *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — an oral tradition going back to Moses at Sinai. Rabbi Yitzchak concurs. One might think this settles the matter, but the Gemara is not satisfied.

### Kal Vachomer Issue

The Gemara challenges this position by citing a well-known *braita* — found also in the Tosefta and quoted in Yoma — regarding *pikuach nefesh* overriding Shabbat. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah there argues: if *milah*, which involves only one of a person's limbs, overrides Shabbat, then *kal vachomer* — all the more so — saving an entire life should override Shabbat. This *braita* takes for granted that *milah* overrides Shabbat and uses it as the premise for a *kal vachomer*.

The problem this creates is pointed: *v'i salka deitach halacha* — if we say that *milah*'s override of Shabbat is known only through *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, then Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah cannot derive a *kal vachomer* from it. A *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* is, by its nature, an isolated ruling that does not necessarily integrate into the broader logical system of *halacha*. It stands alone. One cannot abstract from it and apply the standard forms of legal inference.

### Bone & Blood Case

The Gemara illustrates this principle with a debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva wished to argue by *kal vachomer* that a *revi'is* of blood from a corpse — which causes *tumah* even under the same roof — should also be a *tumas meis* that obligates a *nazir* to shave and that a *kohen* is prohibited from contracting. His argument ran as follows: an *etzem kese'orah* — a bone the size of a barley grain — causes *tumah* that requires a *nazir* to shave, even though it only conveys *tumah* by contact, not under a roof. A *revi'is* of blood, which is stronger in that it conveys *tumah* even under a shared roof, should certainly obligate a *nazir* to shave. To this, Rabbi Eliezer replied: the rule that an *etzem kese'orah* causes *tumah* is itself a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. And *ein danin kal vachomer me'halacha* — one cannot derive a *kal vachomer* from a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*.

### No Kal Vachomer

It follows that if *milah*'s override of Shabbat rests on *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's *kal vachomer* regarding *pikuach nefesh* would be untenable. The Gemara therefore concludes that the source must lie elsewhere, and it proceeds to explore alternative derivations.

## Gezeirah Shavah Os

### Os Connection

Rabbi Elazar proposes a *gezeirah shavah* based on the word *os* — sign. Shabbat is called *ki os hi beini uveineichem* — "for it is a sign between Me and you." *Milah* is similarly called *v'hayah l'os bris* — "and it shall be a sign of the covenant." Through this verbal analogy, we derive that *milah*, which is an *os*, is performed even on Shabbat, which is an *os*.

### Tefillin Objection

The Gemara objects immediately: *tefillin* is also called an *os* — *v'hayu l'os al yadecha*, "and they shall be a sign upon your hand." If the *gezeirah shavah* from *os* teaches that *milah* overrides Shabbat, should we not conclude that *tefillin* likewise overrides Shabbat? The objection is pointed. There is a certain irony here as well: the very reason we do not wear *tefillin* on Shabbat is that Shabbat itself is already an *os*, making the *tefillin* — also an *os* — superfluous. Yet here we are suggesting that the shared status of *os* teaches the opposite: that the one *os* is performed on the day of the other *os*. The Gemara sets this approach aside and tries another.

The Gemara then shifts to a *gezeirah shavah* from the word *bris* — covenant. *Milah* is called a *bris* repeatedly — *es brisi heifir* — and Shabbat is called a *bris*: *l'dorosam bris olam*. The *gezeirah shavah* would teach that *milah*, which is a *bris*, is performed on Shabbat, which is also a *bris*. But this too raises a difficulty: the only place the Torah explicitly uses the language of *bris* in the context of *milah* is in the verse about an adult male who has willfully refused circumcision — *v'arel zachar asher lo yimol besar orlaso es brisi heifir*. That verse concerns a *gadol*, an adult who has chosen not to circumcise himself. An infant would not be subject to *kares* and would not be implied by this verse. We would therefore know only that an adult's *milah* — which would never override Shabbat since it would never fall on the eighth day — is called a *bris*, and the infant's *milah* remains unaddressed.

The Gemara tries yet again with the word *doros* — generations. Shabbat is described as *l'dorosam bris olam* — "for their generations, an eternal covenant." And the verse about infant *milah* reads *yimol lachem kol zachar l'doroseichem* — "be circumcised, every male, for your generations." Perhaps the shared term *doros* teaches that *milah* is performed on Shabbat. But the Gemara raises the same objection: *tzitzis* is also described with the word *doros*, so should *tzitzis* also override Shabbat?

### Three Terms Test

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves all these difficulties with an elegant answer: *danin os bris v'doros* — we derive the rule by applying all three terms together. Shabbat is described with *os*, *bris*, and *doros* — all three. *Milah* is similarly described with all three terms. No other *mitzvah* shares all three terms with Shabbat: *tefillin* has *os* but not *bris* and *doros*; *tzitzis* has *doros* but not the others in the same configuration. It is this convergence of all three terms that establishes *milah* uniquely as the *mitzvah* performed even on Shabbat.

One cannot help but notice the significance of these three terms — *bris*, *doros*, *os* — in the context of Jewish identity. Shabbat observance and *bris milah* have historically been the twin markers of communal belonging, and it is striking that the Gemara identifies precisely these three shared terms — covenant, generations, sign — as the textual basis for their interrelationship.

## Bayom Derivation

### Bayom Teaching

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different derivation altogether. The verse states *bayom hashmini* — "on the eighth day" — and Rabbi Yochanan reads the word *bayom* as teaching that *milah* is performed on that day, meaning specifically on that day, *afilu b'Shabbos* — even if it falls on Shabbat.

### Korban Challenge

Reish Lakish challenges this. The word *bayom* appears in the context of *mechusrei kapparah* — those who require a *korban* to complete their purification process — where the verse similarly says *bayom hashvi'i* or *bayom hashmini*. Should we conclude from those verses as well that such *korbanot* may be brought on Shabbat?

### Bayom Daytime

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds: in that case, *bayom* teaches something else entirely — *bayom v'lo b'lailah* — that the *korban* is brought by day and not by night. The Gemara asks whether the same answer applies to *milah* — perhaps *bayom* there too teaches only daytime, not Shabbat override. The Gemara responds: by *milah*, the daytime requirement is derived from a different source — *ben shemonas yamim*, where the word *yamim* (days, plural) implies daytime. With the daytime requirement covered by that word, the additional *bayom* is free to teach *afilu b'Shabbos* — even on Shabbat.

But there remains the question about *mechusrei kapparah*. The Gemara explains: by *korbanot* generally, we know that sacrificial service is performed during the day from the verse *b'yom tzavaso* — "on the day He commanded." One might have thought that since the Torah was unusually lenient with *mechusrei kapparah* — allowing them to bring progressively less expensive offerings if they lack funds — perhaps all the standard rules are relaxed for them, and they might even bring their *korban* at night. The verse therefore says *bayom* to confirm that the normal rules apply: daytime only, not nighttime. It is this concern, rather than any Shabbat override, that the word *bayom* addresses in the context of *mechusrei kapparah*.

Rav Avina adds: could we truly have entertained the notion that all rules collapse for *mechusrei kapparah*? Would we have allowed a *zar* — a non-*kohen* — to bring their *korban*? Would we have allowed an *onen* — someone in acute mourning — to bring it? Clearly not. The *bayom* restores the normal framework of rules; once the Torah reasserts that it must be done by day, we understand that all other standard requirements remain intact as well. The conclusion is therefore that *bayom* in the context of *mechusrei kapparah* is not about Shabbat override, while *bayom* in the context of *milah* is free to teach precisely that.

### Shmini Alternative

Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers another approach: the word *shmini* — eighth — is written once in the phrase *uven shemonas yamim* and appears a second time in the Scriptural formulation, and this redundancy teaches that *milah* is performed on the eighth day *afilu b'Shabbos* — even on Shabbat.

The Gemara questions this: the word *shmini* is needed to exclude a seven-day-old infant. But then the Gemara points out that the phrase *ben shemonas yamim* already tells us the minimum age of eight days; the restatement of *shmini* then teaches that the eighth day specifically — and not a later day — is the proper time, excluding a nine or ten-day-old. Between the two, there is no remaining redundancy to teach a Shabbat override.

### Bayom Preferred

The Gemara therefore concludes: *ela mivarta k'Rabbi Yochanan* — the preferable approach is that of Rabbi Yochanan, who derives the Shabbat override from the word *bayom*. A *braita* is cited in explicit support of Rabbi Yochanan's position and against that of Rav Acha bar Yaakov.

## Braita & Kal Vachomer

### Braita Milah

The *braita* states: *shmini yimol afilu b'Shabbos* — on the eighth day one circumcises, even on Shabbat.

### Braita Resolution

The *braita* then addresses the apparent tension with the verse *mechaleleha mot yumos* — those who violate Shabbat are put to death — and resolves it by explaining that this applies to all other *melachot*, except for *milah*. The word *bayom* then confirms that *milah* is performed even on Shabbat.

### Rava's Question

This raises an important methodological observation. The *braita* frames its discussion in terms of competing textual possibilities — perhaps the verse means one thing, perhaps another — and ultimately resolves the question by citing the word *bayom*. But Rava asks: what is the underlying logical tension that the *braita* is articulating? What actual reasoning would have suggested that *milah* overrides Shabbat, and what reasoning would have pushed back against that conclusion? The *braita* as written merely toggles between textual possibilities without explaining the substantive arguments.

This reflects a meaningful distinction between the style of *Midreshei Halacha* — which tend to present competing textual readings without deeper argumentation — and the Gemara's characteristic desire to find the substantive reasons behind each position. Once the *braita* says "you could have read it this way, or perhaps that way," the Gemara wants to know: what are the actual arguments pulling in each direction?

### Kal Vachomer Argument

The Gemara reconstructs the argument as follows. One might have reasoned by *kal vachomer*: *u'ma tzara'at she'docha et ha'avodah, ve'avodah docha et haShabbos* — if the prohibition against cutting off *tzara'at* overrides the *avodah* (a *kohen* afflicted with *tzara'at* on his foreskin, or a person with *tzara'at*, may not cut it off even to enable performance of the Temple service or eating the *Korban Pesach*), and the *avodah* in turn overrides Shabbat (communal sacrificial service is performed on Shabbat), then by the transitive principle, the prohibition of cutting off *tzara'at* is more weighty than Shabbat. Since *milah* overrides the prohibition of *tzara'at* — one circumcises even when *tzara'at* is present on the foreskin — it follows that *milah* overrides *tzara'at*, *tzara'at* outweighs *avodah*, *avodah* outweighs Shabbat, and therefore *milah* is the most weighty of all and overrides Shabbat. A compelling chain of reasoning.

### Tzara'at Rebuttal

The Gemara then reconstructs the pushback: *hadar amar u'mi yeimar d'tzara'at chamura* — but who says that *tzara'at* is actually weightier than Shabbat? *Dilma mishum gavra hu d'lo chazi* — perhaps the reason we do not cut off the *tzara'at* to enable *avodah* has nothing to do with *tzara'at* being more weighty than *avodah* or Shabbat. The real reason is simply that even if one were to cut off the *tzara'at*, the person would remain *tamei* that day. He would need to immerse in a *mikvah*, and only after sunset would he be *tahor* and eligible to perform *avodah*. Cutting off the *tzara'at* would not help him perform today's *avodah* at all. The prohibition against cutting off *tzara'at* is therefore not overriding the *avodah* because it is weightier — it is simply that the two are not in the kind of productive conflict that would trigger any override. There is no immediate *avodah* that the cut would enable. The whole transitive argument therefore collapses: one cannot conclude that *tzara'at* is weightier than Shabbat, and so the *kal vachomer* that *milah* should override Shabbat fails to be airtight. The *braita* therefore concludes that the word *bayom* is what clinches the ruling — and without that verse, the matter would be genuinely uncertain.

This is where Rashi notes that according to the view of *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, the tradition was simply known, and the derivations are being worked out after the fact. As the Gemara makes clear in Yoma in the parallel discussion of *pikuach nefesh*, the Sages produced many derivations for what they already knew intuitively. By the time of the Maccabees, *pikuach nefesh* overriding Shabbat was already a practical reality — the soldiers initially refused to fight on Shabbat, were slaughtered, and then intuited that God must want them to defend themselves. Only later does the Gemara ask *minayin* — from where do we derive it? — and produce a range of textual proofs. The same dynamic applies here: *milah* overriding Shabbat was taken for granted; the derivations are the Sages working backwards to anchor in text what was already known by tradition.

## Milah & Tzara'at

### Milah Overrides Tzara'at

The Gemara now turns to a closely related but distinct question. A *braita* teaches: *milah docha es hatzara'as, bein bizmano bein shelo bizmano* — *milah* overrides *tzara'at* whether or not it is performed on the eighth day, i.e., whether or not it is performed at the prescribed time. By contrast, *milah* overrides *Yom Tov* — and, needless to say, Shabbat — only when it falls on the eighth day, *bizmano bilvad*. But with respect to *tzara'at*, any *milah* at any time overrides the prohibition against cutting off *tzara'at*.

### Besar Derivation

The Gemara asks: *minalan* — from where do we know this? The *braita* derives it from the word *besar* — flesh — in the verse *yimol besar orlaso*. The Torah could simply have written *yimol orlaso* — "circumcise his foreskin" — but it says *yimol besar orlaso* — "circumcise the flesh of his foreskin." This extra word teaches that *milah* is performed even when there is *tzara'at* — a *baheret* — on the site: *af al pi sheyesh sham baheres, yikotz* — even so, one cuts it off.

### Braita Logic

The *braita* then presents its deliberative structure: one might have thought that the prohibition *hishamer benega hatzara'as* — "guard yourself regarding the *nega* of *tzara'at*," understood as a prohibition against cutting off *tzara'at* — applies everywhere, including on the foreskin, so that *milah* would not override it. Alternatively, one might argue that *milah* does override it and the prohibition applies only elsewhere on the body. The *braita* concludes: the extra word *besar* teaches that *milah* is performed even in the presence of *tzara'at*.

### Rava Analyzes

As before, Rava asks what the underlying reasoning is on each side of this debate — the *braita* presents the options without explaining the substantive arguments. The Gemara obliges.

### Kal Vachomer Tzara'at

The initial argument in favor of performing *milah* despite *tzara'at* would rest on a *kal vachomer*: *u'ma Shabbos chamura milah docha oslah, tzara'as lo kol she'ken* — Shabbat is weighty, yet *milah* overrides it; *tzara'at* is surely less weighty than Shabbat, so *milah* should certainly override *tzara'at* as well. If asked whether Shabbat or *tzara'at* is the weightier prohibition, virtually everyone would say Shabbat. It follows that *milah*'s override of the lesser prohibition of *tzara'at* would seem to require no special derivation.

### Tzara'at Counterarg

The pushback: *mi'mai de-Shabbos chamira? dilma tzara'at chamira* — what makes you confident that Shabbat is weightier than *tzara'at*? Perhaps it is *tzara'at* that is weightier. The very same transitive argument applies here: *tzara'at* overrides *avodah* (one does not cut off *tzara'at* to enable performance of *avodah*), *avodah* overrides Shabbat — so perhaps *tzara'at* is weightier than Shabbat, and *milah*, while it overrides Shabbat, does not necessarily override *tzara'at*. Since the argument is genuinely two-sided, we cannot resolve it by *kal vachomer* alone, and the word *besar* is required to establish that *milah* does in fact override *tzara'at*.

## Aseh vs. Lo Taase

### Aseh Principle

The Gemara now presents an alternative approach — the principle of *asei docheh lo ta'aseh*: a positive commandment overrides a negative prohibition. *Milah* is a *mitzvas asei*, and the prohibition against cutting off *tzara'at* is derived from *hishamer* — a *lo ta'aseh*. Accordingly, the positive commandment of *milah* should override the negative prohibition of *tzara'at* as a matter of straightforward principle, without requiring any *kal vachomer* from Shabbat.

### Objection to Aseh

The objection: *asei docheh lo ta'aseh greda* — the principle of a positive commandment overriding a negative one applies only when the negative stands alone. The prohibition of cutting off *tzara'at* is not a standalone *lo ta'aseh*. It is accompanied by a positive obligation as well — *lishmor v'la'asos*, "guard and perform," which is understood as an *asei* component to the laws of *tzara'at*. When the opposing prohibition involves both a positive and a negative obligation, the simple hierarchy of *asei docheh lo ta'aseh* does not apply.

### Braita Resolves

The *braita* therefore concludes: the word *besar* is the necessary textual anchor. Without it, neither the *kal vachomer* from Shabbat nor the principle of *asei docheh lo ta'aseh* would be sufficient to establish that *milah* overrides *tzara'at*. With the word *besar*, the override is explicit.

## Common Denominator

### Besar in Cases

A further difficulty now arises. The word *besar* appears in two specific contexts: by the infant — *uven shemonas yamim yimol besar orlaso* — and by the adult — *asher lo yimol besar orlaso*. The adult gets *kares* for willful non-circumcision, and only an adult is described in those terms. A minor who is older than eight days — a *beinoni* — is neither an eight-day-old infant nor yet an adult subject to *kares*. The word *besar* is not explicitly written in connection with his *milah*. One might therefore argue that only the infant's and the adult's *milah* override *tzara'at* — the infant because of the weight of the eighth-day commandment, and the adult because of the severity of *kares* — but the *beinoni*, lacking either of those special weights, might not override *tzara'at*.

### Abaye's Method

Abaye resolves this with the principle of *tzad hashaveh* — the common denominator. One cannot learn simply from the *gadol* that *milah* overrides *tzara'at*, since the *gadol* has the distinctive weight of *kares*. One cannot learn simply from the *katan* of eight days, since that *milah* has the distinctive weight of being performed at the prescribed time. But what they share in common — the very act of *milah* — is that each overrides *tzara'at*. From this common denominator, *Abaye* concludes: *af kol shehamol docheh es hatzara'at* — every circumcision overrides *tzara'at*, including that of the *beinoni*.

## Tzara'at Not Weightier

### Chain Objection

The Gemara returns to press the transitive argument once more. Rav Safra asks Rava: *mimai de-Shabbos chamira? dilma tzara'at chamira* — what makes you think Shabbat is weightier than *tzara'at*? *Sheken dacha avodah, ve'avodah dacha Shabbos* — *tzara'at* overrides *avodah*, and *avodah* overrides Shabbat, so perhaps *tzara'at* is the weightiest of the three?

### Impurity Reason

The Gemara answers: *hatam lav mishum dechamira tzara'at* — the reason we do not cut off *tzara'at* to enable *avodah* is not because *tzara'at* is weightier. *Ella mishum degavra hu delo chazi* — it is because even after cutting off the *tzara'at*, the person would not be fit to perform *avodah* that same day. He would be *mechusar tevillah* — lacking immersion — and would need to go to the *mikvah* first. Only after sunset following the immersion would he become *tahor* and eligible for *avodah*. Cutting off the *tzara'at* therefore provides no practical benefit for today's *avodah*. The prohibition against cutting *tzara'at* is not demonstrating that it is more weighty than *avodah*; it simply means there is nothing to be gained today.

### Direct Confrontation

The Gemara then raises a sharper version of the challenge: what of *nega'im tehorim* — *tzara'at* lesions that are *tahor* and do not convey *tumah*? In such a case, cutting off the *tzara'at* would not leave the person *tamei*; he would be eligible to perform *avodah* immediately. Yet even there the prohibition against cutting it off applies. Does this not prove that the prohibition of *tzara'at* is indeed weightier than *avodah*?

Rav Ashi addresses this with a fundamental principle: *asei docheh lo ta'aseh* — the rule that a positive commandment overrides a negative prohibition — applies only when the two directly confront each other at the very moment of violation. *Be'idna de'mit'akar lav, kamukim aseh* — at the precise moment the prohibition is being transgressed, the positive commandment must simultaneously be fulfilled.

### No Simultaneous Act

The classic examples are *milah* overriding *tzara'at*, where the act of cutting the *tzara'at* is simultaneously the act of performing the *milah*; and *tzitzis* overriding *kilayim*, where attaching the woolen *tzitzis* to a linen garment involves the *kilayim* prohibition at the very moment the *mitzvas asei* of *tzitzis* is fulfilled. In both cases, violating the prohibition and fulfilling the positive commandment are a single act.

By contrast, when someone cuts off *tzara'at* in order to later perform *avodah*, the two acts are not simultaneous. Cutting off the *tzara'at* is not itself the performance of *avodah*. Therefore, the principle of *asei docheh lo ta'aseh* cannot be invoked to permit cutting off even a *tahor tzara'at* for the sake of *avodah*.

### No Weightier Status

The conclusion follows: the fact that *tzara'at* is not cut off even to enable *avodah* proves nothing about the relative weight of the two prohibitions. It reflects only the absence of direct confrontation, not any hierarchy of severity. *Tzara'at* is therefore not demonstrably weightier than Shabbat, and the transitive argument that would have undermined the *kal vachomer* is itself undermined on both grounds: the *mechusar tevillah* answer (even after cutting, the person cannot perform *avodah* today) and Rav Ashi's answer (the two do not directly confront each other in any case).

## Tannaim Debate

### Rabbi Yoshiya

The Gemara concludes by noting that the underlying dispute between Rava and Rav Safra reflects a *Tannaitic* disagreement, as a *braita* on daf 83b records. Rabbi Yoshiya derives from the word *besar* that *milah* overrides *tzara'at* even when *tzara'at* is present — specifically relying on the textual derivation, since the logical arguments on each side are insufficiently decisive.

### Rabbi Yonatan

Rabbi Yonatan argues that no explicit derivation is necessary for the case of eighth-day *milah*: since eighth-day *milah* overrides Shabbat, which is the weightier prohibition, it certainly overrides *tzara'at* — *Shabbat chamura docha tzara'at lo kol she'ken*. For Rabbi Yonatan, the *kal vachomer* is sufficient for the eighth-day case, and the word *besar* comes to address something else entirely — namely, that *milah* outside the prescribed eighth-day time (*shelo bizmano*) also overrides *tzara'at*, a case that could not be derived from the *kal vachomer* alone. This neatly accounts for the use of the word *besar* even in Rabbi Yonatan's view.

The sugya thus covers substantial ground: the question of where *milah* overriding Shabbat is derived (*halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, various *gezeirot shavot*, and *bayom*), the parallel question of *milah* overriding *tzara'at* (derived from *besar* and extended via *tzad hashaveh* to all cases of *milah*), and the structural question of why the transitive chain of *tzara'at–avodah–Shabbat* does not establish *tzara'at* as weightier than Shabbat, with Rav Ashi's direct-confrontation principle serving as the capstone of the discussion.

---

# Shabbat 133

## Milah & Tzara'at

### Baraita: Tzara'at

The *daf* opens by returning to the *baraita* that derives the laws of *brit milah* from the phrase *basar orlato*, and the *gemara* now extends this analysis to the interaction between *milah* and *tzara'at*. The *baraita* states: even if there is a *baheret* — a *tzara'at* lesion — on the foreskin, one cuts it away together with the foreskin. *Baheret imo* — the lesion is removed along with it. This is the position of Rabbi Yehoshua.

The *gemara* immediately asks: why do you need a *pasuk* for this? The act of removing the *tzara'at* is a *davar she'eino mitkaven* — an unintended consequence. The mohel intends only to perform the *brit milah*; the removal of the *tzara'at* is incidental. And a *davar she'eino mitkaven* is permissible. The *gemara* even gestures at the obvious rejoinder — that this may be a case of *psik reisha* — before proceeding to examine the matter more carefully.

### Abaye vs. Rava

Abaye answers that the *pasuk* is necessary only according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a *davar she'eino mitkaven* is forbidden even when unintended. The *pasuk* comes to override that prohibition and permit the incidental removal of *tzara'at* in the course of *milah*. Rava, however, argues that the *pasuk* is necessary even according to Rabbi Shimon — who generally permits unintended consequences — because *modeh Rabbi Shimon psik reisha velo yamut*: Rabbi Shimon concedes that when a forbidden result is the certain and inevitable consequence of one's action, it cannot be called truly unintended. Since cutting away the foreskin will necessarily remove the *tzara'at* along with it, this is a *psik reisha*, and Rabbi Shimon would ordinarily prohibit it. The *pasuk* therefore comes to permit it specifically in the context of *milah*.

The *gemara* then asks: does Abaye himself not hold that Rabbi Shimon agrees in a case of *psik reisha*? After all, both Abaye and Rava are cited together as stating *modeh Rabbi Shimon psik reisha velo yamut*. The *gemara* resolves this by explaining that Abaye came around to this position only after hearing it from Rava. In an earlier stage of his thinking, Abaye held that even a *psik reisha* would be permissible according to Rabbi Shimon, and therefore the *pasuk* was needed only for Rabbi Yehuda. Once persuaded by Rava's formulation, he accepted that Rabbi Shimon too would require the *pasuk* in a case of *psik reisha*.

### Indirect Removal

The *gemara* then notes that some authorities cite this same dispute — between Abaye and Rava regarding whether the *pasuk* is needed for Rabbi Yehuda alone or also for Rabbi Shimon — in connection with a different *baraita* about *tzara'at*, one not specifically involving *brit milah* but rather the general prohibition against removing a *tzara'at* lesion. The *pasuk* says *hishtamer b'nega hatzara'at lishmor vela'asot* — take great care regarding the *tzara'at* lesion, to observe and to act properly. The *baraita* derives from *la'asot* that one may not actively remove the lesion. However, one may wrap a bandage around one's leg to protect it from friction, or carry a pole on one's shoulder over the site of the lesion, and *im avrah avrah* — if the lesion happens to be worn away as a result, so it is. The prohibition is against active intentional removal; one need not go out of one's way to avoid circumstances that might incidentally cause the lesion to fade.

Here too the *gemara* asks why a *pasuk* is needed, since this is a *davar she'eino mitkaven*. And here too the same dispute plays out: Abaye says the *pasuk* is needed for Rabbi Yehuda, while Rava says it is needed even for Rabbi Shimon, since in a case where the rubbing away is a certain consequence, it would constitute a *psik reisha* and Rabbi Shimon would ordinarily prohibit it.

The *gemara* thus identifies two categories of permissible *tzara'at* removal that require scriptural authorization. The first is active removal during *brit milah*, which is explicitly sanctioned by the *pasuk* derived from *basar orlato*. The second is indirect removal through ordinary activity — wearing garments, carrying objects — where the removal happens incidentally; even here, where the removal may be a necessary consequence, the *pasuk* tells us it is permissible.

### Rav Avin: Intent

The *gemara* then returns to Abaye's earlier position and asks: according to the view that even Rabbi Shimon would have permitted *psik reisha* across the board, what purpose does the word *basar* serve in the derivation? If everything short of active intention were already permitted under Rabbi Shimon's general principle, the specific *pasuk* by *tzara'at* and *milah* would be redundant.

Rav Avin answers: the *pasuk* addresses a case where the person performing the *brit milah* explicitly declares that he intends to cut away the *tzara'at* as well. In such a case one might have thought that since there is now active intent to violate the prohibition of *tzara'at* removal, the act should be forbidden. The *pasuk* teaches that so long as he is performing the *brit milah* and not altering his actions because of the *tzara'at*, it does not matter that he harbors the intent to remove the lesion — the *milah* permits the removal regardless. This is a significant *chiddush*: even explicit intent does not disqualify the act, provided the *milah* itself proceeds normally.

### Minor & Intent

The *gemara* then asks: this explanation works well for an adult performing his own *brit milah*, since one can speak of the adult having such intent. But what about a minor? A minor cannot form the relevant intention. The *gemara* answers by way of Rav Mesharshiya: the case for the minor is that *avi haben* — the father — declares that he intends to remove the *tzara'at* as part of the *milah* being performed on his son. The *chiddush* is the same: even though the father actively intends to remove the *tzara'at*, the *milah* permits this, provided nothing changes about how the procedure is performed.

### Alternative Methods

The *gemara* immediately adds a qualification: even if the *pasuk* permits acting with such intent, one should nonetheless seek to minimize direct conflict where possible. Citing Resh Lakish, the *gemara* invokes the principle that wherever one encounters a positive commandment in conflict with a negative commandment, if it is possible to fulfill both, that is the preferred course; only when it is impossible does the *aseh* override the *lo ta'aseh*. Applied here: if there is another mohel available who does not harbor the explicit intent to remove the *tzara'at*, one should use him instead, so as to avoid the direct confrontation between the *aseh* of *milah* and the prohibition against removing *tzara'at*. It is only when no such alternative is available — *d'leika acher* — that the current mohel, despite his stated intent, may proceed.

It is worth noting that the standard rule of *aseh docheh lo ta'aseh* is not what is operating here in the straightforward sense, since the prohibition against *tzara'at* removal is not merely a *lo ta'aseh* but also a *mitzvat aseh* — making it more weighty than a simple negative commandment. The permission here derives from the specific *pasuk* regarding *brit milah*, not from the general principle. The *gemara*'s invocation of the principle is therefore to press the point that even where a *pasuk* permits the conflict, the preference is always to find a way that avoids it.

One might ask whether, at least in the case of an adult who is not yet circumcised, the solution is simply to wait until the *tzara'at* clears. This is an excellent question, and indeed the *chiddush* of the *pasuk* seems to go beyond mere urgency: even where one could theoretically wait for the lesion to resolve, the *milah* nonetheless licenses the removal. This is not a matter of overriding the *tzara'at* prohibition due to time pressure — it is a more fundamental redefinition of what the act of *milah* permits. That is also precisely why the *gemara* becomes more demanding when the mohel actively intends the removal: if the act itself is what provides the license, that license holds even without urgency, but it should still be conducted in the least confrontational manner possible.

---

## Milah & Yom Tov

### Late Milah

The *gemara* now turns back to the earlier *baraita* and addresses the principle that *yom tov eino docheh* — a *brit milah* that is not performed on its eighth day does not override *Yom Tov*. The contrast with *Shabbat* is worth noting: one might have thought that since *Yom Tov* is less weighty than *Shabbat*, the *aseh* of *milah* could override the *lo ta'aseh* of *Yom Tov* through the standard principle of *aseh docheh lo ta'aseh*. The *chiddush* is therefore more pronounced here — even *Yom Tov* is not overridden by a *milah shelo bizmanah*.

### Chizkiyah Drasha

The *gemara* asks: from where do we know this? Chizkiyah, and the school of Chizkiyah, derive it from the double mention of *ad boker* in the laws of the *korban pesach*. The *pasuk* first states *lo sosiru mimenu ad boker*, do not leave over from the *korban pesach* until the morning of the fifteenth of Nisan, and then says *v'hanosar mimenu ad boker ba'eish tisrofu*, what remains, burn it in fire in the morning. The sages read the second *ad boker* as referring not to the morning of the fifteenth but to the morning of the sixteenth, thereby establishing that the burning of leftover *pesach* meat is performed on the sixteenth rather than the fifteenth. The implication is that burning *nosar* — itself a *mitzvah* — is pushed off from the fifteenth because the fifteenth is *Yom Tov*, even though the *mitzvah* of burning could theoretically be done that day. Since the burning is not specifically a *mitzvah* of the fifteenth — it can wait until the sixteenth — it does not override *Yom Tov*. By the same logic, a *milah shelo bizmanah*, which has no specific urgency of today, does not override *Yom Tov*.

### Pesach Offerings

Abaye derives the same principle from a different *pasuk*: *olas Shabbos b'shabbaso* — the Shabbat *olah* is brought on its Shabbat, and not the *olah* of a weekday on Shabbat, nor the *olah* of *erev Yom Tov* on *Yom Tov*. Although burning leftover fat is a *mitzvah*, since it is not specifically the *mitzvah* of that day, it cannot override *Yom Tov*. The same logic extends to *milah shelo bizmanah*.

Rava derives it from yet another *pasuk*: *hu levado yei'aseh lachem* — it, alone, may be done for you on *Yom Tov*. The word *hu* emphasizes that only what is done for the sake of eating on *Yom Tov* is permitted, and not even *machshirin* — preparatory acts — are included. The derivation *levado v'lo milah shelo bizmanah* excludes a non-eighth-day *milah* from the category of what overrides *Yom Tov*. This is all the more significant because one might have argued the contrary by way of *kal vachomer*: *tzara'at* overrides the Temple service, the Temple service overrides Shabbat, and *milah* overrides *tzara'at* — perhaps *milah* should override Shabbat or *Yom Tov* even when not in its proper time. The specific *pasuk* forecloses that reasoning.

### Yom Tov Nature

Rav Ashi takes a different approach entirely. In his view, no special *pasuk* is needed for *milah shelo bizmanah* vis-à-vis *Yom Tov*, because *Yom Tov* itself carries both a positive and a negative dimension: *shabbaton asei hu* — the requirement that *Yom Tov* be a day of rest is itself a positive commandment, in addition to the *lo ta'aseh* of *lo ta'aseh melachah*. Since *Yom Tov* comprises both an *aseh* and a *lo ta'aseh*, the straightforward rule of *aseh docheh lo ta'aseh* cannot apply — a single *aseh* does not override a *lo ta'aseh v'asei*.

The specific *psukim* that permit *milah bizmanah* to override Shabbat were directed precisely at eighth-day *milah*, as derived from *u'vayom hashemini yimol basar arlato* — "on the eighth day." Those *psukim*, and the special weight they confer, apply only to *milah bizmanah*. Once a *milah* is not performed on the eighth day, it loses that exceptional license and becomes like any other *mitzvah*. Any ordinary *mitzvah* — a single *aseh* — cannot override the *aseh v'lo ta'aseh* of *Yom Tov*, and so *milah shelo bizmanah* does not override it either.

It is worth noting, in connection with this discussion, one important and practically relevant exception to the principle that eighth-day *milah* overrides Shabbat. The *gemara* elsewhere derives this override from the *pasuk* in *Parshat Tazria*: *ishah ki tazria v'yaldah zachar u'vayom hashemini yimol basar arlato*. The *drash* understands *ki tazria* as referring specifically to birth through the natural birth canal — *b'makom shemazra'at*. A birth by cesarean section therefore falls outside this *parasha*, and the *asei* of *milah* in such a case does not override Shabbat. This is a significant and practically important *halacha* that is not always known: a baby born by cesarean section whose eighth day falls on Shabbat does not have his *brit milah* performed on Shabbat. The *halacha* is ruled accordingly.

The *gemara* concludes this section by affirming *halacha k'Rabbi Akiva*, who articulates the general rule that anything that could have been done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat, and that this ruling applies both in the context of *milah* and in the context of *korban pesach*. The *gemara* notes that both rulings must be stated explicitly — one cannot be inferred from the other. If we knew only the ruling by *milah*, we might think that by *korban pesach*, where there is *kares* for failing to bring it, even the preparatory acts should be permitted on Shabbat. And if we knew only the ruling by *korban pesach*, we might think that by *milah*, where the covenant was mentioned thirteen times in the *parasha* of Avraham, even the *machshirin* should override Shabbat. Each ruling is independently necessary.

---

## Milah on Shabbat

### Tzorchei Milah

The *mishna* states: *osin kol tzorchei milah b'Shabbat* — all the needs of *milah* are performed on Shabbat. This encompasses two distinct categories. The first includes acts that are part of the *mitzvah* of *brit milah* itself, which overrides Shabbat. The second includes health-related procedures performed after the *milah* is complete, which are permitted on the basis of *pikuach nefesh*.

### Preparation Issues

The *mishna* enumerates the acts that are permitted: *molin u'porin u'motzatzin* — the cutting of the foreskin, the *priah* (tearing away the thin membrane beneath the foreskin), and *metzitzah* (drawing out the blood from the wound). One may then apply a bandage. Cumin, which appears to have been used to treat the wound, may be applied; if it was not ground before Shabbat, one may chew it with one's teeth and apply it from the mouth. Similarly, if wine and oil were not mixed together before Shabbat, one does not mix them now but rather applies each one separately to the wound. The emphasis in these last cases is that where advance preparation was not done, the procedure should be carried out with a *shinui* — an alteration from the normal manner of performing the act.

### Wrapping & Shinui

The *mishna* further states that one may not fashion a specially cut wrap for the wound *lechatchilah* on Shabbat, but one may take a cloth and wrap it around. If no cloth was prepared at the site of the *brit milah* before Shabbat, one may wrap it around one's finger and carry it there, even from another courtyard. Rashi explains that this wrap serves not merely a medical purpose but also to prevent the skin from moving back over the site of the incision — and so it is more properly understood as part of the *milah* itself rather than purely a health measure.

### Shinui Debate

The requirement to perform these acts with a *shinui* when not prepared in advance raises a broader question. Tosafot note: even though after the *brit milah* the baby has the status of a *choleh she'yesh bo sakanah* — a patient whose life may be at risk — we nonetheless require a *shinui* wherever possible: *kama d'efshar l'shannuyei meshanninan*. This is a striking position, because the standard rule is that for a genuine *choleh she'yesh bo sakanah*, one acts without hesitation and without modification.

What emerges from Tosafot is that the categories of a woman in childbirth and a baby after *brit milah* represent a distinct class: they are treated presumptively as *choleh she'yesh bo sakanah* even without specific indicators that the situation is life-threatening, yet precisely because this is a kind of default classification rather than a case of manifest acute danger, there remains room to require a *shinui* when one can be managed. This is different from the approach taken to an unambiguous medical emergency — a building collapse, a cardiac event — where one acts completely without modification. The two cases we have encountered so far in which a *shinui* is expected, namely childbirth and post-*milah*, form a category of their own, and that distinction is worth bearing in mind.

---

## Continuity of Act

### Kol Tzorchei

At the top of 133b, the *gemara* asks: the *mishna* listed many specific permitted acts, and then said *kol tzorchei milah* — all the needs of *milah*. What does the inclusive phrase add that the list did not already cover?

### Engagement Status

The *gemara* answers by citing a *baraita*: as long as the mohel is actively engaged in the *brit milah* — *kol zman she'hu osek b'milah* — he may return to cut away remaining strands of skin (*tzitzin*), whether those strands are ones that *me'akvin et ha-milah* — that prevent the *milah* from being halachically valid — or those that *ein me'akvin* — that do not prevent validity but leave the *milah* aesthetically incomplete. In other words, even after enough has been done that the *milah* is technically valid and the person is *yotzei*, the mohel may continue cutting, since he is still in the midst of the act.

However, once *peireish* — once the mohel has disengaged, setting down his instrument and stepping back from the procedure — the situation changes. If he then notices that something was left incomplete, he may return only to remove strands that *me'akvin et ha-milah*, that is, strands whose presence renders the *milah* invalid. He may not return to remove strands that are merely cosmetically incomplete. The *chiddush* of *kol tzorchei milah* is thus that continued engagement permits more than the bare minimum required for the *mitzvah* — the mohel may finish the aesthetic work so long as he has not disengaged.

This raises the question: who holds that once one disengages, one cannot return even for *tzitzin she'ein me'akvin*? Perhaps there is a position that even after *peireish* one may return, since the entire act was licensed from the outset.

### Pesach Analogy

Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers: it is Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka. The *baraita* there discusses the case where the fourteenth of Nisan falls on Shabbat. One may flay the *korban pesach* on Shabbat up to the chest — *mafshit et ha-Pesach ad ha-chaze* — in order to reach the *eimurim* (the portions to be burned on the altar), which must be burned that day. This flaying is permitted because it is necessary for the *korban* that must be done on Shabbat itself. Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds that once the *eimurim* have been removed, one may not continue flaying the entire animal, since the remaining flaying serves only to preserve the meat for the evening meal — a purpose that belongs to after Shabbat. The rabbis disagree and permit flaying the whole animal, since that too aids the proper use of the *korban*.

According to Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, once the *eimurim* have been removed, the licensed act is complete, and re-engaging with the remaining flaying is considered a new act rather than a continuation of the same process. The *gemara* finds this parallel to the case of *milah*: once the mohel disengages after completing a technically valid *milah*, returning to remove cosmetically incomplete strands is likewise treated as a new act rather than a continuation.

### Aesthetic Doctrine

The *gemara* immediately challenges this parallel: perhaps by *milah* one should be permitted to return even after *peireish*, because of *Zeh Eli v'anvehu* — the principle of beautifying the performance of *mitzvot*. The *baraita* expounds: *hitna'eh lefanav b'mitzvot* — adorn yourself before God through the *mitzvot*. This means making a beautiful *sukkah*, a beautiful *lulav*, a beautiful *shofar*, beautiful *tzitzit*, a beautiful *Sefer Torah* — with beautiful ink, a fine quill, an expert scribe, wrapped in fine silks. All of this constitutes the *mitzvah* of *Zeh Eli v'anvehu*: to beautify not only the *mitzvah* object itself but all that accompanies it.

Applied to *brit milah*: by going back and finishing the aesthetic work after *peireish*, one is beautifying the *milah* itself. Perhaps, then, the principle of *Zeh Eli v'anvehu* extends the license to re-engage, and one should be permitted to return even after separating. This would distinguish *milah* from the *korban pesach* case, where completing the flaying does not beautify any aspect of the sacrificial act itself and thus cannot be grounded in this principle.

---

## Milah & Yom Tov (II)

### Beautification

The *baraita* on *Zeh Eli v'anvehu* concludes with Abba Shaul's interpretation: *ve'anvehu hevei domeh lo* — glorify Him means become like Him. Abba Shaul reads *ve'anvehu* as *ani va'hu* — I and He — and understands the verse as an obligation of *imitatio dei*. Just as He is compassionate and gracious, so too you should be compassionate and gracious: *mah hu chanun v'rachum af atah heyei chanun v'rachum*.

It is worth pausing here to note that the tradition contains two distinct formulations of this idea of walking in God's ways. One formulation focuses on character traits — *chanun v'rachum*, compassion and graciousness — cultivated internally. The other formulation focuses on actions: just as God clothed the naked and visited the sick, so too should you clothe the naked and visit the sick. These represent two recognizably different approaches to the moral life: one grounded in virtue and the cultivation of character, the other grounded in the performance of specific beneficial acts.

The Rambam was a particularly strong proponent of the character-trait approach. He explains, for instance, the teaching in *Pirkei Avot* that *hakol lefi hamaaseh* — it is all according to the action — as meaning that giving a small amount of *tzedakah* repeatedly is preferable to giving a large amount at once, precisely because frequent giving more effectively cultivates the internal disposition of generosity. This emphasis on character formation, rather than on the magnitude of the act, reflects the Rambam's broader moral philosophy. The Rambam's approach also ties into his theological position: since God cannot truly be described in positive terms, the reason the Torah uses attributes like *chanun* and *rachum* to describe God is not to tell us what God actually is, but to indicate what character traits we should emulate. The *Torah* chose those particular attributes as the model for human striving — rather than, say, God's role in bringing natural calamity — in order to orient human moral development toward *ve'halachta bidrachav*.

The immediate point of the *gemara*, however, is that *Zeh Eli v'anvehu* as applied to *milah* might supply grounds for permitting the mohel to re-engage after *peireish* in order to aesthetically complete the *milah*. The *gemara* takes this suggestion seriously and must look elsewhere for the authority that prevents such re-engagement.

---

## Continuity of Act (II)

### Lechem Panim

Rav Ashi offers an alternative resolution. He identifies the *tanna* who holds that one may not return after *peireish* as the *rabbanan* who dispute Rabbi Yose in a different context.

The *mishna* in the context of *Lechem haPanim* describes the procedure for exchanging the showbread on Shabbat. Four *kohanim* enter: two carrying the two new stacks of bread and two carrying the two *bazichin* (spoons of incense). Four others enter ahead of them: two to remove the existing stacks and two to remove the existing spoons. The ones carrying the new bread stand on the north side, facing south; those removing the old bread stand on the south side, facing north. *Elu moshchin v'elu manichim* — as some draw out, others set down, simultaneously, so that the *shulchan* is never without bread for even a moment. *Tefach shel zeh b'tzad tefach shel zeh* — one person's *tefach* of bread is immediately adjacent to the other's, the old being drawn out as the new is placed in, because the *pasuk* says *lechem panim lefanai tamid* — the showbread must be constantly before Me.

Rabbi Yose holds that even if the old bread is removed first and there is a gap before the new bread is placed, that too is considered *tamid* — continuous — since the bread was there in the morning and will be there again shortly. The *rabbanan* insist that *tamid* means there can be no interruption whatsoever; a single moment without bread on the *shulchan* disqualifies the arrangement from being called continuous.

Rav Ashi draws the analogy: the *rabbanan* here hold that any break in a state or process renders it non-continuous. Applied to *brit milah*: once the mohel has disengaged — *peireish* — there is a break in the continuity of the act. The *rabbanan* would therefore say that returning after this break is not a continuation but a new act, and a new act is not licensed by the original permission to perform *milah* on Shabbat.

This is a striking conceptual move. The *gemara* is comparing the continuity of a static state — the permanent presence of the *Lechem haPanim* — with the continuity of an active process, namely the performance of *milah*. One might object that these are fundamentally different: if we ask whether a static state was uninterrupted, any gap in the state defeats the claim; but if we ask whether an action was continuous, a pause in the middle of the same process by the same actor might be treated differently. The *gemara* nonetheless draws the parallel, and it is from this comparison that the ruling emerges that a mohel who disengages may not return to remove *tzitzin she'ein me'akvin*.

The overall conclusion of this section is therefore twofold: first, so long as the mohel remains actively engaged, he may continue to cut even what is not strictly necessary for the *milah*'s validity — this is the *chiddush* of *kol tzorchei milah*; and second, once he disengages, he may only return to complete what is genuinely indispensable.

---

## Incomplete Milah

### Final Strands
