One might have expected that even a potentially non-viable infant should retain some status as a living being, making any act upon it at least arguably prohibited. Yet the *Gemara* presses the logic to its conclusion: a *nefel* has no *chiyuv* of *bris milah*, and acts performed upon it do not carry the prohibited character of acts performed upon the living. The *Gemara* will continue to explore the implications of this position on the following *daf*.

# Shabbat 137

## Mixed-Up Infants

### Case Setup

The *mishna* on 137a opens with a famous debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua concerning a *mohel* who found himself in an unusual predicament. He had two infants to circumcise: one whose *brit milah* was scheduled for Sunday, and one whose *brit milah* was scheduled for *Shabbat*. He forgot which was which.

### Sunday on Shabbat

In the first scenario, the *mohel* proceeded on *Shabbat* believing he was circumcising the *Shabbat* infant, but in fact circumcised the Sunday infant. Not only did he violate *Shabbat* without proper license for this particular child, but the circumcision itself accomplished nothing halachically — a seventh-day *milah* is of no consequence. The *mishna* rules that he is *chayav* a *korban chatat*: he was *shogeg*, not *meizid*, but he violated *Shabbat* without justification for the child he actually operated on.

### Friday on Shabbat

The second scenario introduces a subtler case. One infant was to be circumcised on Friday and the other on *Shabbat*. The *mohel* failed to perform the Friday circumcision on Friday — the most natural reading of the *mishna* is that he mixed up the infants, circumcised the *Shabbat* infant on Friday, and then on *Shabbat* itself mistakenly circumcised the Friday infant. This is meaningfully different from the first case: although the ninth-day *milah* should not have overridden *Shabbat*, it was at least a valid *mitzvah* of *brit milah*. A seventh-day *milah* is nothing at all; a ninth-day *milah* is still a *mitzvah*, merely one that does not warrant desecrating *Shabbat*.

### Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

In this second scenario, Rabbi Eliezer rules that the *mohel* is still *chayav* a *chatat*, while Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him. It is worth noting the apparent tension in Rabbi Eliezer's overall position: the same Rabbi Eliezer who ruled, just days earlier in our learning, that one may fashion a knife and carry it through *reshut ha-rabbim* to perform a *brit milah* for the infant one has a *mitzvah* to circumcise — that same Rabbi Eliezer rules stringently when the *mohel* mistakes one infant for another.

### Ta'a Bidvar Mitzvah

The *gemara* articulates the principle underlying Rabbi Yehoshua's exemption: *ta'a bidvar mitzvah ve-asa mitzvah patur* — one who erred in the course of performing a *mitzvah* and, through that very error, still accomplished a *mitzvah*, is exempt from a *chatat*. Nobody maintains that such a person did not violate *Shabbat*, and certainly it is not *mutar*; the exemption is purely from the obligation to bring a sin offering. The *gemara* offers a parallel: one who picks up a *lulav* on *Shabbat* and inadvertently carries it into *reshut ha-rabbim* — even there, where there was no license to violate *Shabbat* for the *lulav* at all, the fact that the violation occurred in the context of performing a *mitzvah* and actually succeeded in performing one renders the person *patur* according to Rabbi Yehoshua.

---

## Resolving Dispute

### Rav Huna Version

The *gemara* now confronts a textual tension. *Rav Huna masni chayav* — Rav Huna's version of the *mishna* holds that in the first case (the Sunday infant circumcised on *Shabbat*) everyone agrees the *mohel* is *chayav*. The dispute concerns only the second case (the Friday infant circumcised on *Shabbat*). A *baraita* cited by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar supports this reading explicitly: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua did not disagree when the Sunday infant was circumcised on *Shabbat*, because that constitutes *ta'a bidvar mitzvah velo asa mitzvah* — an error in the performance of a *mitzvah* that did not result in any *mitzvah* being accomplished. On that everyone agrees the *mohel* is *chayav*. Their dispute concerns the Friday infant circumcised on *Shabbat*, where *ta'a bidvar mitzvah ve-asa mitzvah* fully applies.

The *baraita* adds a striking note: both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua derive their respective positions from *avodah kochavim*. One would not have expected this. The explanation is that the *parasha* in *Shelach* dealing with *chatat* — *v'chi tishgu v'lo ta'asu et kol ha-mitzvot ha-eileh* — is understood by *chazal* as referring paradigmatically to *avodah zarah*, and therefore that case serves as the template for determining when a *chatat* is incurred. Rabbi Eliezer reasons: just as by *avodah zarah* the *Torah* says do not do this, and if you do it you are *mechayev*, so too here, no distinction. Rabbi Yehoshua counters: *hasam lo tarid mitzvah* — there, the sin occurred with no connection to performing a *mitzvah*; *hacha tarid mitzvah* — here the person was involved in a *mitzvah* and succeeded in performing one, and that changes the analysis. In practice, of course, what is being derived is not so much from the specifics of *avodah zarah* as from the general proposition of when a *chatat* is incurred — the contrast each *amora* draws is simply whether being engaged in a *mitzvah* context alters that standard.

### Rabbi Meir Version

*Rabbi Yehuda masni patur* — Rabbi Yehuda's version, supported by a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Meir, reverses the consensus case entirely. According to Rabbi Meir, everyone agrees that the Friday infant circumcised on *Shabbat* is *patur*, because a *mitzvah* was in fact accomplished. The debate concerns the Sunday infant circumcised on *Shabbat*. Rabbi Eliezer says *chayav*; Rabbi Yehoshua says *patur*. But here Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning shifts: *hasam lo tarid mitzvah* — and Rabbi Yehoshua responds *hacha tarid mitzvah*, meaning that even though the *mohel* did not ultimately perform any *mitzvah* (the seventh-day circumcision is nothing), he was nonetheless in the thick of performing a *mitzvah*. Being immersed in the activity of *brit milah* is itself enough to exempt according to Rabbi Yehoshua, even without having actually fulfilled a *mitzvah*. The same arguments from *avodah kochavim* apply, with the same structure.

Yet a third *baraita*, attributed to Rabbi Chiya in the name of Rabbi Meir, introduces yet another permutation that seems to reverse the intuitively "better" case: when the Friday infant is circumcised on *Shabbat*, everyone agrees the *mohel* is *chayav* — despite a *mitzvah* having been performed — whereas when the Sunday infant is circumcised on *Shabbat*, that is precisely where Rabbi Yehoshua exempts. This appears paradoxical: how can Rabbi Yehoshua exempt in the case where no *mitzvah* was accomplished but hold liable in the case where a *mitzvah* was?

### License to Override

The school of Rabbi Yannai resolves this apparent reversal with an insight that reframes the entire discussion. The more common scenario when someone circumcises the Friday infant on *Shabbat* is that the infants were mixed up: the *Shabbat* infant was circumcised on Friday, and the Friday infant on *Shabbat*. When *Shabbat* arrives under those circumstances, there is no longer any infant present for whom *Shabbat* may be overridden — the *Shabbat* infant was already circumcised yesterday. *De-lo nitnah Shabbat le-hidachos*: *Shabbat* no longer carries a right to be overridden, because the one infant who could have justified it has already been circumcised. The fact that a *mitzvah* was incidentally accomplished does not save the *mohel* from liability, because he had no license to be violating *Shabbat* at all.

By contrast, in the scenario where the Sunday and *Shabbat* infants were confused and the Sunday infant was circumcised on *Shabbat*, the *Shabbat* infant has not yet been circumcised. *Seifa nitnah Shabbat le-hidachos*: because the *Shabbat* infant is still waiting, there remains a valid license to override *Shabbat*. The *mohel* simply confused which baby was which. This reframes the debate entirely: the critical variable is not only whether a *mitzvah* was accomplished, but whether the *mohel* possessed an active license to override *Shabbat* in the first place.

### Rav Ashi Challenge

Rav Ashi raises a sharp objection to Rav Kahana: even if the *Shabbat* infant has already been circumcised, surely there are other eight-day-old infants somewhere in the world for whom *Shabbat* may be overridden. The *mohel* standing before the Friday infant believed it to be a *Shabbat* infant, and in principle such infants exist — should that general fact not constitute sufficient license?

### Specific License

The *gemara* rejects this. *Le-hai gavra miha lo ishtari* — for this particular *mohel* in this particular situation, there is no license. The license to override *Shabbat* is not abstract and theoretical; it must be grounded in a specific circumstance facing this specific person. The existence of eight-day infants elsewhere in the world, for whom he has no role or assignment, does not grant him personal license to violate *Shabbat* for the infant standing before him.

---

## Timing & Health

### Normal Eighth Day

The next *mishna* opens with a deceptively simple enumeration: an infant may be circumcised on the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, or twelfth day — not earlier, not later under normal circumstances. *K'darko lishmonah*: the ordinary case is the eighth day.

### Bein Hashmashos

When an infant is born during *bein hashmashos* — the twilight period between two days — there is genuine uncertainty about which day he entered the world. If born at *bein hashmashos* between Monday and Tuesday, the *brit milah* is performed on nine days counting from Monday, since perhaps he was born on Tuesday and the eighth day counting from Tuesday coincides with nine days from Monday.

### Holiday Obstacles

The *mishna* catalogs how layered holiday complications can push the *brit milah* further out. If a *bein hashmashos* birth occurs between Friday and *Shabbat*, the *brit* cannot be performed the following Friday (because the infant might be a *Shabbat* infant, making it the seventh day) and cannot be performed on *Shabbat* (because if the infant is a Friday infant, this is the ninth day, and a ninth-day *brit* does not override *Shabbat*). The *brit* therefore falls on Sunday — the tenth day counting from Friday. If the following Sunday is *Yom Tov*, it is pushed to Monday, the eleventh day. If Sunday and Monday together are *Rosh Hashanah* — a configuration our calendar does not permit today, but the *mishna* addresses — neither day is available, and the *brit* is performed on Tuesday, the twelfth day from Friday.

### Sickness Delay

If the infant is ill, the *brit milah* is postponed until he recovers: *katan ha-choleh ein molin oso ad she-yivarei*. This is straightforwardly a matter of preserving the child's life and health.

### Healing as Rebirth

Shmuel rules that if an infant's fever has broken — *chaltzaso chamah* — one does not rush to perform the *brit milah* immediately. Seven days are granted to ensure full recovery. The *gemara* raises the question of whether *me'et le-et* is required: must seven full twenty-four-hour periods elapse, or is it sufficient to count into the seventh calendar day?

A *tanna* from Lod teaches: *yom havraso ke-yom hivaldo* — the day of recovery is treated as the day of birth. Just as from birth the *brit milah* is performed on the eighth day, so too from the day of recovery. The *gemara* then considers whether this analogy works symmetrically in both directions. From birth, *me'et le-et* is not required — a child born at the end of Sunday may have his *brit* first thing the following Sunday morning. But perhaps by illness the standard is stricter, since the concern is genuinely medical rather than halachic: perhaps full seven twenty-four-hour days are necessary to confirm genuine recovery. The *gemara* leaves this as a live question. It should be noted that the *gemara* here addresses only the health concern itself; there are other contexts in halachic literature where the question arises whether the eight-day count from birth is suspended during a period of illness — that question is not resolved here, and the *gemara* speaks only to the recovery period.

---

## Valid Brit Standards

### Corona Visibility

The *mishna* identifies which pieces of residual skin (*tzitzin*) invalidate the *brit milah*: *basar ha-chofeh et rov ha-atarah* — flesh that covers the majority of the *atarah*, the corona. One who has such flesh remaining is still considered an *arel*, and a *kohen* in that state may not eat *terumah*, as the verse states *kol arel lo yochal bo*. The *gemara* notes this applies even to a hemophiliac who cannot undergo circumcision — the status follows regardless of fault.

Rav, in a tradition transmitted through Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba and Rabbi Avin, clarifies the precise meaning of *rov ha-atarah*. The *mishna* does not mean that flesh must cover the majority of the *circumference* of the corona (which is what one might naturally assume). Rather, it means flesh that covers the majority of the *height* of the corona — even in a single location. Accordingly, the entire circumference must be clean: even one small piece of skin anywhere along the circumference that covers the full height of the corona renders the *brit milah* invalid. This is a more demanding standard than a simple reading of *rov ha-atarah* would suggest.

### Obese Infant Case

The *mishna* adds a separate rule: *ve-im haya ba'al basar* — if the infant is very heavy and fleshy, one corrects the appearance *mipnei marit ha-ayin*, out of concern for appearances. This is quite striking. The *brit milah* may have been performed completely and correctly, yet extra flesh around the area could make it appear that circumcision was not done. The context is a society with a prominent public bathhouse culture. There is additionally a historical dimension: during periods of Hellenistic influence, some Jews were not undergoing or were actively reversing their *brit milah*, which would heighten communal sensitivity to appearances in this area.

### Shmuel's Method

Shmuel addresses the practical question of how to assess the obese infant: *ro'in oto* — one inspects him. *Kol zeman she-mitkasheh ve-nir'eh mahul* — whenever he has an erection and appears circumcised at that point, *eino tzarich lamol* — no additional surgery is required, because the flesh stretches and the proper result is visible. *Ve-im lav, tzarich lamul* — if even then he appears uncircumcised, surgery is required. The reasoning is that when the flesh stretches under arousal, the true state of the circumcision becomes apparent. Shmuel's standard: if it *looks* circumcised under those conditions, the infant is fine.

### Rabban Gamliel

A *baraita* records the same rule in the name of Rabban Gamliel, but with a subtle difference in formulation: *kol zeman she-mitkasheh ve-eino nir'eh mahul, tzarich lamul* — whenever he has an erection and appears *uncircumcised*, surgery is required. *Ve-im lav, eino tzarich lamul* — if that is not the case, no surgery is needed.

### Appearance Standards

The *gemara* asks: *mai beinaihu* — what practical difference exists between Shmuel's formulation and Rabban Gamliel's? *Ika beinaihu nir'eh ve-eino nir'eh* — the difference is a middle state where the appearance is ambiguous: not clearly circumcised, not clearly uncircumcised. Shmuel's standard requires that the infant *look circumcised* in order to be exempt from further surgery — anything short of clearly circumcised requires intervention. Rabban Gamliel's standard requires only that the infant not *look uncircumcised* — so in that ambiguous middle zone, Rabban Gamliel requires no further surgery while Shmuel would. Shmuel thus applies the stricter standard.

### Missing Periah

The *mishna* concludes: *mal velo para et ha-milah ke-ilu lo mal* — one who circumcised without performing *periah*, the tearing away of the membrane beneath the foreskin, is as if he did not circumcise at all. The *gemara* understands *periah* to be part of *halachah le-Moshe mi-Sinai* for *brit milah*, and it likewise overrides *Shabbat*. The *gemara* also notes that *periah* made it practically impossible to reverse the circumcision — a consideration not irrelevant to its historical significance.

---

## Brachot & Blessings

### Mohel's Beracha

The *gemara* turns to the *brachot* of *brit milah*. It is notable that these *brachot* do not appear in the *mishnayot* themselves — they are introduced here from a *tosefta* or *baraita*. The *mohel* who performs the circumcision recites: *asher kidishanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu al ha-milah* — the standard formulation of a *birchat ha-mitzvah* over the act itself.

### Father's Beracha

The *avi ha-ben* — the father of the infant — recites: *asher kidishanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu lehachniso bivrito shel Avraham Avinu* — You have commanded us to bring him into the covenant of our patriarch Abraham. The distinction between the *mohel*'s blessing and the father's is carefully calibrated. The *mohel* performed the physical act, so his *beracha* is *al ha-milah*. The father's *mitzvah* is not to personally perform the circumcision but to ensure that his son is brought into the covenant — and his blessing reflects precisely that obligation: *lehachniso*, to bring him in. This framing simultaneously reflects the father's halachic role and elevates the act beyond a surgical procedure into something covenantal. The father is not merely complying with a positive commandment in the way one takes a *lulav*; he is initiating his son into the eternal *brit* of *Avraham Avinu*.

### Assembly's Response

Those standing present respond: *keshem shenichnas la-brit ken yikanes le-Torah u-le-chupah u-le-ma'asim tovim* — just as he entered the covenant, so may he enter into Torah, marriage, and good deeds. This formulation closely parallels the *mishna* in Kiddushin enumerating the father's obligations toward his son: to circumcise him, to marry him off, and to teach him a trade. The three elements of the assembly's response — Torah, *chupah*, and *ma'asim tovim* — map precisely onto those three obligations.

### Ashkenazic Revision

The formulation just described — *keshem shenichnas* — is, however, not the original *girsa* of the *gemara*. The *Bach* establishes, and there is little reason to doubt, that the original text read: *keshem she-hicknasto la-brit ken tachniseyhu le-Torah u-le-chupah u-le-ma'asim tovim* — just as *you* brought him into the covenant, so may you bring him into Torah, marriage, and good deeds. This version is addressed to the father, building directly on his *beracha*: having declared that God commanded him *lehachniso bivrito shel Avraham Avinu*, the assembled guests respond by expressing the hope that he will similarly fulfill his remaining obligations. The blessing is for the father, not for the infant.

The shift to *keshem shenichnas* — refocusing the blessing on the infant rather than the father — was an Ashkenazic emendation rooted in medieval historical circumstance. In Ashkenazic communities of the Middle Ages, the father was very often not present at the ceremony, whether because of persecution, early death, or other hardships. When the father was absent, one could not say *keshem she-hicknasto*, addressed to someone who was not there. The formulation was therefore adjusted to *keshem shenichnas*, which centers on the infant and does not presuppose a living father. Once adopted for cases of a deceased or absent father, it was eventually standardized across all cases, so that today most people are unaware that the original *beracha* was directed at the father entirely. The change in meaning is real and significant: the original assembly's response was a charge and blessing to the father regarding his ongoing obligations; the current version is a prayer for the infant's future.

### Mevarech's Beracha

The *mevarech* — an appointed individual, distinct from the *mohel* and the father, perhaps serving a function analogous to a rabbi or officiant — recites a longer blessing:

*Asher kiddash yedid mi-beten, chok bi-sh'eiro sam, ve-tze'etza'av chatam be-ot berit kodesh. Al ken, bischar zot, El chai chelkenu, tzivah le-hatzil yedidut she'erenu mi-shachat, lema'an brito asher sam bi-sh'erenu. Baruch Atah Hashem, koreit ha-berit.*

"Who sanctified the beloved one from the womb, placed a statute in his flesh, and sealed his descendants with the sign of the holy covenant. Therefore, in the merit of this, the living God who is our portion commanded to save our beloved ones from destruction, for the sake of His covenant that He placed in our flesh. Blessed are You, God, who makes the covenant."

There is a textual question noted by the *Ya'avetz*, Rabbi Yaakov Emden, about whether the correct *girsa* is *tzivah* (He commanded, past tense) or *tzaveh* (command, an imperative addressed to God) — whether we are affirming what God has done or petitioning God to act.

The blessing is notable and striking. Its opening is theologically rich — tracing the covenant in the flesh of the infant back through his future descendants, embedding the *brit* in the very fabric of Jewish continuity. But its ending takes an unexpected turn: the covenant is invoked as protection, as the means by which the beloved ones are saved *mi-shachat*, from destruction. What does this mean? Rashi interprets *mi-shachat* as *mi-gehennom*, from Gehenna — citing the verse *gam at be-dam britech shilachti asirayich mi-bor ein mayim bo* (Zechariah 9:11). On Rashi's reading, the blessing is fully consistent with the covenantal theme: the *brit milah* is what grants Israel its Jewish identity and, through that, ultimate salvation. The notion that *brit milah* protects from *gehennom* is a prominent idea in medieval thought, less so in the *gemara* itself, but that is how Rashi renders the conclusion of the blessing.

One could also read *mi-shachat* more literally — as a reference to infant mortality — and see in this closing phrase a reflection of ancient concern about infant survival, with the *brit milah* understood as a divine sign of protection. Either reading, the blessing closes with *koreit ha-berit*, acknowledging God as the maker of the covenant, which frames the entire ceremony as an act of divine initiation rather than human ritual.

### Geirim Brachot

When the *milah* is performed on a *ger* — a convert — the *mohel* recites the same standard *beracha*: *asher kidishanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu al ha-milah*. The *mevarech* for a *ger* says: *asher kidishanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu lamol et ha-geirim u-lehatif mehem dam berit* — You commanded us to circumcise converts and to draw the blood of the covenant from them. The emphasis on *dam berit*, the blood of the covenant, is significant: converts very frequently require only *hatafat dam berit* rather than full circumcision, and the *beracha* is constructed to cover that case prominently.

The closing of the *mevarech*'s *beracha* for *geirim* invokes the cosmic significance of *dam berit*: *she-ilmalei dam berit lo nitkaymu shamayim va-aretz, she-nemar im lo briti yomam va-lailah chukot shamayim va-aretz lo samti* — were it not for the blood of the covenant, heaven and earth would not endure, as it is written: if not for My covenant by day and by night, I would not have established the laws of heaven and earth (Jeremiah 33:25). The closing is the same: *Baruch Atah Hashem, koreit ha-berit*.

This formulation raises an interesting observation. One might have expected the *beracha* for a *ger* to emphasize what is specifically happening to him — being brought into the *brit shel Avraham Avinu* — parallel to the father's *beracha* for his son. Instead, the significance invoked is generic: the cosmic importance of *dam berit* for the maintenance of the world. While the *beracha* does close with *koreit ha-berit*, acknowledging that a covenant is being made, the specific act of bringing this individual into the covenant of Abraham is not foregrounded. Whether one reads this as a deliberate theological choice or simply a formulation that was standardized for a different reason, it is curious.

### Slaves Brachot

When *milah* is performed on a *Canaanite slave* (*eved*), the formulation is identical in all respects to that used for *geirim*: the same *beracha* over the act, the same *mevarech* blessing invoking *dam berit*, the same closing *pasuk*, and the same *Baruch Atah Hashem koreit ha-berit*. No distinction is drawn between the *ger* and the *eved* in the blessing's text, despite the fact that their entry into the covenant carries different halachic weight. The *eved* has a partial *chiyuv mitzvot* and occupies a unique intermediate status — not a full Jew, not an outsider. Yet the *beracha* says *koreit ha-berit* for him as well, acknowledging that even the circumcision of a slave is a covenantal act. One might have expected some textual distinction to register this difference. The *gemara* records none.

---

## Tollin & Yom Tov

### Eliezer Allows

With the conclusion of the *perek* on *brit milah* — *hadran alach Rabbi Eliezer de-milah* — the *gemara* opens a new *perek*, again associated with a ruling of Rabbi Eliezer. The opening *mishna* shifts entirely to the laws of *Yom Tov*. *Rabbi Eliezer omer: tolin et ha-mashmeret be-Yom Tov* — Rabbi Eliezer permits suspending the *mashmeret*, a sieve or strainer, over a vessel on *Yom Tov*. The practice is to place this filter over a jar and pour wine through it, allowing the wine to pass through while trapping the lees and grape remnants above. Rabbi Eliezer permits setting up this apparatus on *Yom Tov* itself.

### Sages Stringent

The *chakhamim* disagree. *Ein tolin et ha-mashmeret be-Yom Tov* — the Sages prohibit setting it up on *Yom Tov*, even though food preparation is generally permitted on *Yom Tov*. Their reasoning is that this could have been done the day before, and we do not want acts to be performed on *Yom Tov* that could have been completed in advance. However, *aval nosnin li-keli be-Yom Tov* — if the strainer was already suspended prior to *Yom Tov*, one may pour wine through it on *Yom Tov*, since the food-related use itself is permitted. On *Shabbat*, even using a pre-set strainer is prohibited, because it resembles *borer*.

### The Problem

The *gemara* raises a sharp question against Rabbi Eliezer's leniency. If Rabbi Eliezer permits setting up the *mashmeret* on *Yom Tov*, he is apparently sanctioning the construction of an *ohel* — a covered structure — *le-chatchilah* on *Yom Tov*. The large cover placed over the vessel functions halachically as a kind of roof. But we know from another *sugya* that Rabbi Eliezer does not even permit adding a temporary addition to an existing *ohel arai* on *Yom Tov*, let alone creating a new *ohel arai* from scratch.

The source for that position is a *mishna* discussing *pkak ha-chalon* — a stopper for a window or skylight. Rabbi Eliezer permits using it only if it was already tied and suspended before *Shabbat*; otherwise, sealing the window would constitute adding to an enclosure. Rabban Gamliel and the Sages permit it either way. Rabbi Yochanan further clarifies, in a statement attributed to the school of Rabbah bar bar Chanah, that all opinions agree one may not construct a new *ohel arai* on *Yom Tov* — this goes without saying for *Shabbat*. The only dispute is about *adding* to an existing *ohel arai*: Rabbi Eliezer prohibits even an addition on *Yom Tov*; the Sages permit additions even on *Shabbat*. How, then, can Rabbi Eliezer allow the creation of a new *ohel* over the wine vessel on *Yom Tov*?

### Eliezer=Yehuda

The *gemara* resolves this by identifying Rabbi Eliezer's position with that of Rabbi Yehuda. *Rabbi Eliezer savar lei ke-Rabbi Yehuda*. A *baraita* teaches that the distinction between *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* is that on *Yom Tov* one may perform acts directly related to *ochel nefesh*, food preparation. Rabbi Yehuda goes further: *matir af machshirei ochel nefesh* — he permits not only the direct food preparation but even the preparatory acts that facilitate food preparation. Rabbi Eliezer, the *gemara* proposes, holds in accordance with this more lenient position: since constructing the sieve apparatus is preparatory to the food act of straining wine, it is *machshirei ochel nefesh* and thus permitted on *Yom Tov*.

### Milah Parallel

The *gemara* immediately notes the elegant parallel: just as Rabbi Eliezer permitted *machshirei milah* — the preparatory acts enabling *brit milah* — to override *Shabbat*, so too here he permits *machshirei ochel nefesh* to be performed on *Yom Tov*.

The *gemara* presses further, however. Rabbi Yehuda permits *machshirei ochel nefesh* only when those preparatory acts *could not have been performed before Yom Tov*. Things that could have been set up the day before *Yom Tov* are not permitted on *Yom Tov* even according to Rabbi Yehuda. And the sieve, presumably, could have been suspended before *Yom Tov*. So the identification of Rabbi Eliezer with Rabbi Yehuda does not fully resolve the problem.

The *gemara* concludes that Rabbi Eliezer goes one step beyond Rabbi Yehuda. The same pattern obtains by *milah*: Rabbi Eliezer permitted *machshirei milah* even when they could theoretically have been done before *Shabbat*. He takes the same expansive position regarding *machshirei ochel nefesh* on *Yom Tov* — permitting preparatory food-related acts even when they could have been done in advance. The parallel between his rulings on *milah* and his rulings on *Yom Tov* is thus precise and consistent. The remainder of this *mishna*'s discussion will continue in the next *daf*.

---

---

# Shabbat 138

## Sieve on Vessel

### R. Eliezer vs. Chachamim

The daf opens at the very bottom of 137b, two lines from the bottom, picking up a new topic that was introduced after the extensive treatment of *brit milah*. The subject is the act of placing a sieve on top of some type of jar or vessel. Rabbi Eliezer permits doing so on *Yom Tov*, while the *Chachamim* forbid it. The Gemara frames this as a case of *ohel arai* — a temporary tent-like structure — which is striking, since it would never obviously occur to us that stretching something over the top of a jar constitutes an *ohel*. Yet that is precisely the Gemara's framing.

### Ohel Arai & Machshirei

The reason Rabbi Eliezer permits it is that he allows even *machshirei ochel nefesh* on *Yom Tov* — preparatory activities related to food, including things that could have been done *erev Yom Tov*. This framing of the case as *machshirei ochel nefesh* implies that stretching the sieve over the jar could involve a genuine biblical concern of *ohel*, such that Rabbi Eliezer must invoke a specific permissive principle to allow it. The *Chachamim*, however, maintain that it may not be done on *Yom Tov*.

### Tala Mai—Status

The Gemara now poses the question *tala mai* — what is the legal status if one actually did place this sieve stretched over the vessel on *Yom Tov*? Is this a genuine *de'oraita* violation, or something else? This question is characteristic of these later chapters of *Shabbat*, where the Mishnah lists prohibited activities without clarifying whether each prohibition is biblical or rabbinic, leaving it to the *Amoraim* to work out the underlying status.

### Rav Yosef: Chayav

Rav Yosef rules: *tala chayav chatas* — if one stretched the sieve over the vessel, he is liable for a sin-offering. This is a strong position, asserting that the act constitutes a genuine biblical violation.

### Abaye Challenges

Abaye challenges this: *of ohel*? Are we really talking about a true *ohel* here? The force of his objection is that an *ohel* is ordinarily understood as a structure, whereas what we are dealing with is essentially a vessel. Even if one could technically identify a roof-like element in the act of covering a jar — and the analogy to wrapping something tightly in a membrane is useful here — it hardly resembles the kind of independent structure one normally associates with *ohel*. He further presses: does it follow that hanging a jar from a nail would similarly make one liable? Obviously, the mere act of suspending something creates no *ohel*; his point is that something so trivial cannot properly be called a *melacha*.

### Midrabbanan & Uvda

Abaye resolves the question: *midrabbanan hi* — the prohibition is entirely rabbinic. And notably, he does not even characterize it as a rabbinic *ohel*. Instead, he frames it as *uvda d'chol* — a weekday-type activity, the kind of thing one does in the course of ordinary labor on a weekday, which is inappropriate on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* even absent any actual *melacha* category. What constitutes *uvda d'chol* is itself an open question; here it may be associated with the activity of sifting wine, which borders on *borer*, but the concept does not always map neatly onto a specific *melacha*. The upshot of Abaye's position is that when Rabbi Eliezer permits this on *Yom Tov*, there is no great novelty: since it is merely *uvda d'chol* and involves food preparation, it falls within the broad permission to engage in food-related activities on *Yom Tov*.

This leads naturally into a broader contemporary application. The *Shulchan Aruch*, drawing on the *Terumat HaDeshen*, rules that certain uses of specific implements on *Shabbat* are prohibited as *uvda d'chol*. Based on this, some *Acharonim* — including the *Shemirat Shabbat* — extend the principle to forbid the use of labor-saving kitchen gadgets on *Shabbat* as *uvda d'chol*, reasoning that any device reminiscent of large-scale production is inconsistent with the spirit of *Shabbat*. Rav Moshe, however, disagrees, limiting the prohibition to implements associated with large-scale commercial production, and ruling that ordinary small-scale kitchen devices used domestically do not constitute *uvda d'chol*. The parameters of this category thus remain genuinely contested.

---

## Temporary Structures

### Four Prohibited Cases

Abaye gathered together various *Baraitot* and *Mishnayot* — the word *chumrei* here means bundles, not stringencies — and organized them into groupings. He taught the following: *ha-god, ha-mishmeret, kila, v'chisei galen lo yaaseh* — four prohibited structures. The *god* is a leather flask or canteen used for storing wine, which travelers would stretch over poles so that the wind would keep it cool; suspending this large leather pouch creates something resembling an *ohel*. The *mishmeret* is precisely the sieve-over-vessel case of our Mishnah. The *kila* is a canopy over a bed. And *chisei galen* is a type of chair whose leather seat is stretched over an open frame — picture opening the legs of a director's chair and then stretching the leather seat across the top, creating both a functional surface and a kind of roof-like covering. All four of these one should not do on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*.

### Tefach & Liability

If one did perform any of these, the ruling is *patur aval assur* — one is exempt from a sin-offering but it remains forbidden. None of these constitutes a genuine biblical *ohel*; they lack the permanence required and, critically, they are not even made to function as an *ohel* in any meaningful structural sense. These are rabbinic prohibitions only. By contrast, *ohel keva* — a permanent structure — one may not build, and if one did, one would be *chayav chatas*. Two factors distinguish the rabbinic cases from the biblical one: the structures are temporary, and they are not made to serve as genuine *ohalim*.

### Hinged Structures

The Gemara then introduces the category of what is fully permitted: a bed, a *chisei traskal* (a folding chair, like a director's chair, where everything is attached on hinges and one merely opens it), and an *asla* (a similar chair with an opening in the seat used as a toilet). Rashi explains that the bed case involves a bed that was standing vertically against the wall — like a Murphy bed — which one simply lowers down to the horizontal position. When one does so, an *ohel*-like space is created beneath it, yet one has not erected anything; one has only returned something to its natural position. The *traskal* similarly involves a structure that is entirely pre-made on hinges, requiring nothing more than opening. All of these are *mutarin letasam lechatchila* — permitted to be set up at the outset.

The question of an umbrella is directly relevant here. The historical consensus among *poskim* treats umbrellas as prohibited, despite the fact that a fresh analysis might well permit them given these principles, and that tradition carries normative weight.

### Pre-made Principle

The governing principle is important: something already constructed and on hinges, which merely requires opening, is not considered a new act of *ohel* creation. An additional factor that favors all these permitted cases is that none of them are being made *for the purpose of* an *ohel* — a chair, a bed, a table exists to serve the person using it, not to protect the space beneath it. This further distinguishes these cases from genuine *ohel* creation. However, caution is warranted before extending these rulings expansively; a canopy over a baby carriage, for instance, does serve to protect the space beneath it in the manner of an *ohel*, which complicates any straightforward application of the pre-made principle — though it remains true that the structure is pre-assembled and requires only opening. The question of pop-up tents and collapsible cribs follows a similar logic, though the concern of *boneh* may be raised in those cases as well, particularly where legs must be snapped into place.

---

## Wine Sifting

### Wine in Sieve

The Gemara transitions back to a case involving *borer*-type separation before returning to the *ohel* discussion. The Mishnah states that one may not place wine in a sieve on *Shabbat*. The Gemara asks *shimmer mai* — what is the halakhic status if one actually did sieve the wine? Rav Kahana rules: *ha-shimmer chayav chatas* — one who sifted the wine is liable for a sin-offering, making it a biblical violation.

### Challenge: Rav Sheshes

Rav Sheshes challenges this forcefully: how is it possible that the two positions in the dispute are at such extreme opposites? Rabbi Eliezer permits sieving wine *lechatchila* — even at the outset — while the *Chachamim* prohibit it. If the *Chachamim's* prohibition were merely rabbinic, that would be understandable. But to say that Rabbi Eliezer permits something outright while the *Chachamim* consider it a biblical *chiyuv chatas* — can such diametrically opposed rulings really coexist within a single dispute?

### Golden Tiara Case

Rav Yosef replies: why not? There is a precedent. Consider the *ir shel zahav* — the golden tiara or golden city ornament — where we find precisely this pattern. Rabbi Meir rules that a woman who goes out wearing this ornament into the public domain on *Shabbat* is *chayav chatas*. The *Chachamim* rule *patur aval assur* — she is exempt but it remains forbidden. And Rabbi Eliezer rules she may go out wearing it *lechatchila* from the outset. In that dispute, Rabbi Meir's position of *chiyuv chatas* and Rabbi Eliezer's position of *mutar lechatchila* coexist, despite being extreme opposites. The reasoning: Rabbi Meir holds that this type of ornament is not recognized as standard clothing or jewelry that women typically wear, so wearing it constitutes a form of carrying rather than wearing; Rabbi Eliezer holds that it is genuine jewelry and that there is no concern she will remove it to show her friends.

Abaye responds to this parallel with a sharp observation: *mi savrat Rabbi Eliezer ad Rabbi Meir kai*? Who says Rabbi Eliezer in that case is even responding to Rabbi Meir? Perhaps he is responding only to the *Chachamim*, who say *patur aval assur*, and he is telling them it is *mutar lechatchila* — so the opposition is between *assur* and *mutar*, not between *chayav chatas* and *mutar*. Tosafot here admits genuine difficulty. The Tosafot notes that even according to Abaye's reframing, the actual halakhic positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer remain at extreme opposites — one holding *chayav chatas* and the other holding *mutar lechatchila* — even if they are not directly disputing one another. Tosafot openly acknowledges not fully understanding what the Gemara's answer accomplishes.

The Gemara proceeds apparently satisfied that Rabbi Eliezer can hold something is *mutar* even when others hold it warrants a sin-offering. It therefore now asks: *mishum mai matrin bei* — when one warns the person who sieves wine of the category of *melacha* he is about to violate, what *av melacha* is invoked?

### Raba: Borer View

Raba says the relevant *melacha* is *borer*. This might seem to stand to reason. *Borer* is the act of taking food while leaving the waste behind. Here too, the wine passes through the sieve and comes out — that is the food — while the lees and grape remnants remain stuck above — that is the *pesolet*. One is, in effect, extracting the food from the mixture.

### Rabbi Zeira: Meraqed

Rabbi Zeira disagrees and says the *melacha* is *meraked* — sifting. The distinguishing feature of *meraked* is that the *pesolet* is on top and the food comes out below. Here too, the grape sediment remains on top of the sieve while the pure wine falls through beneath — *pesolet mil'ma'ala v'ochel mil'mata*.

### Analysis & Liquids

At first glance this debate seems almost self-answering: the case of wine sieving is obviously more similar to *meraked* than to *borer*, since *meraked* involves a sieve and the same spatial arrangement — refuse on top, food below — whereas *borer* typically involves manually removing food from a pile without a sieve. Rashi makes this explicit: he explains that according to Raba, the act would also qualify as *meraked* — Raba is not denying it resembles *meraked* — but he holds it is additionally classified as *borer* and one could warn the violator on that basis as well. Rabbi Zeira, however, denies that it qualifies as *borer*: for *borer*, the refuse sits at the bottom of the pile and the food is taken out from above by hand, as with legumes. Since the spatial arrangement here is inverted — refuse above, food below — it does not sufficiently resemble *borer* to constitute a proper *hatra'ah* on that basis. Everyone agrees it is *meraked*.

A broader halakhic point worth noting here, though it is not developed in full at this juncture: there is a significant leniency that applies to liquids but not solids in the laws of *borer*. With respect to liquids, if the mixture was drinkable before being sieved, one is permitted to pour it through a sieve on *Shabbat*. This leniency — applied, for instance, to water filters and to orange juice with pulp (permitting its straining for someone who would drink it with pulp anyway) — has no parallel in the laws of *borer* as applied to solid foods. Part of the reason may be that passing liquid through a sieve happens somewhat passively, unlike the active manual sorting characteristic of *borer* with solids. But regardless, the Gemara's conclusion is that one who sieves wine is indeed *chayav* — the act is most clearly analogous to *meraked*, and may also implicate *borer*.

---

## Tallit as Canopy

### Folded Tallit

Rami bar Yechezkel taught: *tallit kfulah lo yaaseh* — one should not spread a folded *tallit* over posts to create a canopy on *Shabbat*. Rashi explains that *kfulah* means a cloth doubled over, such that it not only covers the top but falls over the sides, creating walls as well — making it function even more fully as an *ohel*. The ruling: *patur aval assur* — if one did so, one is exempt from a sin-offering but the act is rabbinically forbidden. It remains a temporary *ohel* and does not carry biblical liability, but it is prohibited.

### Drawstring Allowance

The greater novelty in Rami bar Yechezkel's teaching is what he permits. If the *tallit* has a string or drawstring (*chut o meshichah*) attached to it, it is *mutar limotcho lechatchila* — one may unfurl it at the outset on *Shabbat*. The rationale is analogous to the hinged structures discussed earlier: if a string is already attached and the structure need only be pulled open, one is not creating something new. Even a drawstring mechanism is sufficient to render the act one of opening rather than erecting.

### Tosafos: Tefach Rule

Tosafot introduces an important qualification that distinguishes the drawstring case from the hinged-structure case. With a hinged object like a bed or folding chair, the entire structure is pre-made and one merely opens it — no additional criterion is required. But with a *tallit* and a drawstring, which is not on hinges and involves a more active spreading, Tosafot holds that there must already be a first *tefach* of the *ohel* constructed before one may spread it further. The principle is that one may add to a pre-existing *ohel arai* — this is permitted — but one may not *create* an *ohel arai* from scratch even with a drawstring. If the first *tefach* is already in place, then spreading the remainder merely extends an existing structure rather than originating one. This requirement of a pre-existing first *tefach* applies to the drawstring case specifically; hinged structures do not require even this.

---

## Canopies & Beds

### Rav & Rav Kahana

The Gemara records a playful exchange between Rav Kahana and Rav. Rav Kahana asked: *kilah mahu* — what is the law regarding a canopy over a bed? Rav replied: *af mitah asurah* — why are you asking about the canopy? Even putting up a bed is forbidden. Rav Kahana then asked: so what about the bed? Rav reversed: *af kilah muteret* — why are you asking about the bed? Even a canopy is permitted. Rav Kahana, seeing he was being toyed with, asked plainly about both. Rav then gave the actual ruling: *kilah asurah u'mitah muteret* — the canopy is forbidden, the bed is permitted.

### Carmonite Bed

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing cases. When Rav said "even a bed is forbidden," he was referring to the Carmonian (*karmonai*) bed — a type of bed that is not simply lowered from a vertical to a horizontal position, but requires one to snap the legs into place. This raises serious concerns not merely of *ohel* but of genuine *boneh* — the act of assembling a functional vessel — and also of *makkeh b'patish*, since one might end up banging the legs firmly into their sockets to secure them. When Rav said "even the canopy is permitted," he was referring to the case described by Rami bar Yechezkel — a canopy with a drawstring already attached, and as Tosafot notes, with a first *tefach* already in place, such that one is only extending a pre-existing structure. The straightforward ruling for normal cases is: making a canopy from scratch is forbidden; lowering a bed that was leaning vertically is permitted.

### Rav Huna's Canopies

Rav Yosef reports an empirical observation: *chazina lehu l'kilta d'bei Rav Huna* — I observed the canopies in the household of Rav Huna. They were spread in the evening and thrown down in the morning — *me'orta negidi, umitzfra chavita ramya*. Rashi understands this as evidence that if canopies can be taken down they can presumably also be put up, and that these too were cases involving drawstrings or similar pre-made elements that permitted the act.

### Curtains Permitted

Rav says in the name of Rabbi Chiya: a *vilon* — a curtain serving as a temporary wall — *mutar linototo* — may be hung on *Shabbat*, and *mutar l'parko* — may also be taken down. This introduces the broader question of whether the *melacha* of *ohel* applies to walls as well as roofs. The general assumption is that making a temporary wall, so long as it is not being attached to a permanent structure, does not constitute a prohibited act. A free-standing temporary curtain — a *mechitzah shel tzniusa*, for instance — does not raise an *ohel* concern. The issues that arise with *mechitzot* on *Shabbat* typically involve situations where the partition is being erected to serve a specific halakhic function, which is a separate discussion.

### Wedding Canopies

Shmuel says in the name of Rabbi Chiya: *kilas chasanim* — the wedding canopy used in the bridal suite — *mutar linotosah* — may be erected on *Shabbat*, and *mutar l'parkah* — may be taken down. These wedding canopies, unlike standard bed canopies with flat roofs, came to a point like a teepee. A flat roof that is a *tefach* wide is what creates an *ohel*; a canopy that comes to a point has no such roof and is therefore classified entirely as walls. Since walls are permitted, the wedding canopy may be erected.

### Rav Sheshes: Tefach

Rav Sheshes son of Rav Idi refines this: *lo amran ela she'ein b'gagah tefach* — the permission applies only when the top of the canopy does not reach a *tefach* in width. If the very apex of the canopy is a *tefach* wide, it is forbidden because there is now a genuine roof. But even when the apex is not a *tefach* wide, the permission is further limited: *ela she'pachut mi'shlosha samuch l'gagah* — the top must not reach a *tefach* width within three *tefachim* down from the apex. This is because the principle of *lavud* — that anything within three *tefachim* is considered legally connected — would cause the *tefach* width three *tefachim* below the apex to be treated as if it were the roof itself. One must therefore ensure that no *tefach* of width is found within the top three *tefachim* of the structure.

The Gemara adds a further restriction: *lo amran ela she'ein b'shipua tefach* — even in the slope of the walls, there must not be a *tefach* of width. If there is a *tefach* width in the incline, then *shipuei ohalim ke-ohalim dami* — the inclined walls of tents are treated as the tent roof itself. Rashi acknowledges that taken to its logical conclusion, this rule creates difficulty: if the entire bottom of the canopy is two *tefachim* wide, it seemingly would always be forbidden. Rashi resolves this by suggesting the canopy was purely decorative and not actually placed over the bed. Tosafot offers the alternative that the walls angle outward in a manner that avoids creating a *tefach* of horizontal width at any point, though this reading is difficult. The most straightforward resolution, adopted by Tosafot, is simply that this final line does not belong in the Gemara text at all.

A final condition: *delo necha mipuraya tefach* — the canopy must not hang down a *tefach* below the edge of the mattress. If the canopy extends beyond the edges of the bed and hangs down a *tefach*, then those hanging portions are considered walls and the top portion of the canopy becomes a roof — at which point the structure is forbidden. The entire permission depends on the canopy being understood as consisting entirely of walls converging to a point, with no portion functioning as a roof.

---

## Hats & Clothing

### Felt Hat Permitted

Rav Sheshes son of Rav Idi continues: *hai siana shari* — this *siana*, a felt hat, is permitted on *Shabbat*. Rashi identifies the *siana* as *kova shel levad* — a felt hat. The reasoning is analogous to the bed and the folding chair: the entire structure is pre-made, and placing it on one's head does not involve any act of spreading or construction. One is not making something new.

### Brim Width Debate

The Gemara immediately complicates this: but is it not also taught that a *siana* is forbidden? The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — ha de'ika tefach, ha de'leika tefach* — it depends on whether the brim is a *tefach* wide. A hat with a brim wider than a *tefach* — four inches — presents an *ohel* concern, since the *tefach* threshold is what transforms a covering into a halakhically significant *ohel*. What makes this case somewhat different from the bed or chair is that a hat's brim genuinely functions as an *ohel* — its purpose is to provide shade beneath it — whereas the bed and chair are not made to protect the space underneath them. Still, it remains somewhat anomalous that something entirely pre-made and worn constantly should be treated differently.

### Cloak Tightness

The Gemara presses further: if a wide-brimmed hat is forbidden, then by the same logic, should one not also be forbidden from pulling one's cloak over one's head — creating a *tefach* of covering above? The Gemara resolves this: *lo kashya — ha de'mahedik, ha de'lo mahedik* — the distinction is between holding it tightly and not tightly. Rashi explains that the issue has nothing to do with *ohel* at all. When one holds the cloak loosely over one's head, the concern is that the wind may blow it off and one will rush to retrieve it and end up carrying it in a *reshut harabbim*. When one holds it tightly, that fear does not apply. Under this reading, the *ohel* concern is simply not the operative issue with a cloak held over the head.

### Tosafos: Stiff Brim

Tosafot, citing Rabbeinu Chananel, offers a different reading of *de'mahedik* and *de'lo mahedik*. Tightly (*mahedik*) refers to a brim that is stiff and does not easily bend — *she'eino nichpaf* — which gives the appearance of an *ohel* and is therefore forbidden. Loosely (*lo mahedik*) refers to a flexible brim that bends easily — *she'hu nichpaf* — which does not look like an *ohel* and is therefore permitted. According to this reading, the prohibition is appearance-based: it is not a true *ohel* but *looks* like one, and that is sufficient to forbid it. This position is cited in the *Shulchan Aruch*. In practice, hats are not treated as problematic, which follows Rashi's approach; but the discussion around stiff-brimmed hats based on Rabbeinu Chananel's reading remains a genuine consideration in the sources.

---

## Rami's Letter

### Two Teachings

The Gemara now relates that Rami bar Yechezkel sent a letter to Rav Huna asking him to transmit two particular teachings that Rav Huna had previously taught in the name of Rav — *chad beShabbat v'chad beTorah* — one pertaining to the laws of *Shabbat* and one relating to Torah. The request was not exploratory but confirmatory: Rami bar Yechezkel already knew the substance of these teachings and wished them formally recorded, having sent a written inquiry to elicit a written reply.

### God by Two People

The first teaching relates to the *god* — the leather flask discussed earlier, which when stretched over poles can create a rabbinic concern of *ohel*. The Baraita states: *god bekisna mutar linototo beShabbat* — a *god* held by its straps may be spread on *Shabbat*. Rav qualifies: *lo shanu ela be'bei terei bnei adam* — this was only said when two people are spreading it. *Aval be'adam echad assur* — if one person alone spreads it, it is forbidden. Rashi, citing the *Geonim*, explains the mechanical difference: when one person must spread the leather flask alone, he must tie one end firmly to a post and then stretch it taut to secure the other end, resulting in a tightly-stretched covering that more closely resembles an *ohel*. When two people work together, each holding one end, the flask can be suspended more loosely, and it does not carry the same appearance of *ohel* construction.

### Kila Forbidden

Abaye adds: *u'vekila afilu bei assara bnei adam assur* — and with a *kila* — a true canopy structure, one actually made to function as a roof — even ten people working together cannot permit it, because *i efshar delo mimtacha purta* — it is impossible to spread it without it becoming stretched at least a little. The significance of stretching, as opposed to mere placement, is that a tautly stretched covering has the character of a genuine *ohel*, and no number of people can avoid imparting that quality to a true canopy.

### Oven Leg Cases

The second *Shabbat* teaching involves an oven. *Kira she'nishmeta achat miyarkoteiha* — if a tripod oven has one of its legs slip out of place, *mutar letaltela* — one may still move it on *Shabbat*, since it remains functional and is not *muktzeh*. *Shtayim assur* — if two legs have slipped, it may not be moved, presumably either due to *muktzeh* or due to concern that one will come to fix it.

### Rava: One Leg

Rava takes a more stringent position: *afilu chad nami assur* — even if only a single leg has slipped, the oven may not be moved. His reasoning: *gezeira shema yigsof* — there is a rabbinic decree out of concern that if one picks it up to move it, one will be tempted to push the leg back into place and fix it, which would constitute either *boneh* or *makkeh b'patish*. The *muktzeh* question is not the operative concern for Rava; the concern is the act of repair that might follow from handling it.

---

## Torah Forgetting

### Rav's Prophecy

The Gemara now transitions to an extended *aggadic* teaching connected to the second item Rami bar Yechezkel requested from Rav Huna — a matter relating to Torah. Rav states: *atidah Torah she'tishtakach mi'Yisrael* — there will come a time when Torah will be forgotten from the Jewish people. The verse adduced is from the *tochacha*: *v'hifla Hashem et makotecha* — God will make your smitings wondrous. The word *hafla'ah* is ordinarily associated with wondrous or extraordinary things. Rav reads a second verse — *lachen hineni yosif l'hafli et ha'am hazeh haflei va'fela* — as identifying this *hafla'ah* specifically with Torah, since the verse concludes *v'avdah chochmat chachamav* — the wisdom of its sages will be lost. The wondrous punishment, in other words, is the disappearance of Torah wisdom.

### Kerem B'Yavne

The Gemara cites a *Baraita*: when our rabbis entered the *kerem b'Yavne* — the rabbinic assembly at Yavne after the destruction of the Temple, called a vineyard because the scholars were arranged in rows — they said: *atidah Torah she'tishtakach mi'Yisrael* — Torah will be forgotten from Israel. The verse they cited is from Amos: *hinei yamim ba'im ne'um Hashem Elokim v'hishlachti ra'av ba'aretz, lo ra'av lalechem v'lo tzama lamayim, ki im lishmoa et divrei Hashem* — a hunger will come, not for bread or water, but to hear the word of God. And further: *v'na'u mi'yam ad yam... levakesh et devar Hashem v'lo yimtza'u* — they will wander seeking the word of God and will not find it.

This fear of Torah's loss was not abstract for the scholars at Yavne; it was the lived reality of the post-*Churban* generation. Their urgent effort to gather testimony — the process that produced *Massechet Eduyot* and ultimately led toward the crystallization of the Mishnah — was motivated precisely by this concern. The fear that *Torah she'ba'al peh* would be lost drove the consolidation of traditions, even at the cost of writing down what was traditionally transmitted orally.

The Gemara identifies what *devar Hashem* means in this verse. Three interpretations are offered: *halacha*, knowledge of the messianic end-time, or prophecy. The most striking of these is the first — that what will be lost is *halacha* itself — though the latter two, the end of prophetic guidance and loss of knowledge of redemption, are similarly sobering.

### Woman's Quest

The Gemara explains what the verse's description of wandering means in practice. The image offered: *atidah ishah she'titol kikar shel terumah v'tachzor b'vatei knesiyot u'vatei midrashot* — a woman will take a loaf of *terumah* and wander from synagogue to synagogue and from study hall to study hall, *leda'at im tamei hi v'im tahor hi* — seeking to know whether it is pure or impure. *V'ein mevin* — and no one will be able to tell her. This is the image of wandering to find *devar Hashem* and not finding it.

### Gemara Challenges

The Gemara presses back sharply: *behedya ketiv bei* — but the answer is written explicitly in the Torah! The verse *mikol ha'ochel asher ye'achel* explicitly addresses the transmission of *tumah* to food. How could something so plainly stated in Scripture be forgotten? The implication of the Gemara's challenge is that the scenario being described — total ignorance of whether something is *tamei* or *tahor* — is implausible given that the basic categories are written in the Torah itself.

### Tumah Mechanisms

The Gemara resolves the challenge by redefining what will be forgotten. The woman is not asking whether the loaf is *tamei* or *tahor* in a basic sense — she knows it is *tamei*. What she will not be able to determine is *im rishona hi v'im shniya hi* — whether it is a *rishon le'tumah* or a *sheni le'tumah*. The Gemara immediately challenges again: but this is explicitly taught in a *Mishnah*! The Mishnah in *Avot ha-Tumot* states: *ha-sheretz she'nimtza ba-tanur, ha-pat she'betocho shniya* — if a dead rodent is found in a pottery oven, the bread inside the oven is a *sheni le'tumah*, because the rodent (*av ha-tumah*) renders the oven a *rishon*, and the oven renders the bread a *sheni*. This is standard Mishnaic content; how could it be forgotten?

The Gemara answers with the question that Rav Adda bar Ahava once posed to Rava: why is the bread a *sheni* and not a *rishon*? The reasoning that treats the bread as a *sheni* depends on understanding that *tumah* travels from the rodent to the oven, and from the oven to the bread — two steps. One could mount a logical argument that the rodent, being in the same enclosed space as the bread, should directly render the bread *tamei* as if the entire vessel were filled with *tumah*, making the bread a *rishon*. What will be forgotten is the answer to this question: the understanding that *ochlin mitamin be'avir kli cheres, v'ein kelim mitamin be'avir kli cheres* — food becomes *tamei* through the airspace of a pottery vessel, but other vessels do not. This rule — derived from the verse's specification that food and not vessels becomes *tamei* through the airspace — is what establishes that the rodent does not directly render the bread *tamei*, but does so through the oven as an intermediary. And the proof that the bread is only a *sheni* — not a *rishon* — is that if the rodent directly transmitted *tumah* to the bread, the bread would be a *rishon*; the fact that the verse implies only food (and not other vessels) becomes *tamei* in the airspace shows that the *tumah* travels through the oven, making the bread a *sheni*. It is this level of reasoning — the mechanism by which *tumah* transmits through a *kli cheres* — that will be forgotten. Not the basic facts, but the internal logic that resolves apparent contradictions.

### R. Shimon's View

The Gemara closes this passage with a dissenting *Baraita*: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says: *chas v'shalom she'tishtakach Torah mi'Yisrael* — God forbid that Torah should ever be forgotten from Israel, as the verse states *ki lo tishkach mi'pi zaro* — it will never be forgotten from his descendants. How then does Rabbi Shimon understand the verse about wandering and not finding *devar Hashem*? *Shelo yimtza'u halacha berurah u'mishnah berurah b'makom echad* — what will not be found is a clear *halacha* and a clear ruling in any single place. Torah will not disappear, but clarity will. Every matter will be disputed; nothing will be settled; scholars will disagree on every detail. The *Mishnah Berurah* famously takes its title from precisely this phrase — *mishnah berurah* — clear teaching. This, Rabbi Shimon holds, is what the assembly at *kerem b'Yavne* feared and why they worked so urgently to consolidate testimony: not that Torah itself would vanish, but that the clarity and unity of its transmission would be lost, leaving an endless proliferation of dispute with no resolved and authoritative ruling in any one place.

---

---

# Shabbat 139

## Judicial Corruption

### Rabbi Yose ben Elisha

The daf opens in the middle of an aggadic digression. A *baraita* is cited: *tanya, Rabbi Yose ben Elisha omer, im ra'ita dor she'tzarot rabot ba'ot alav, tze'i u'vdok b'dayanei Yisrael* — if you see a generation upon which many afflictions come, go and examine the judges of Israel. The leaders, the *dayanim*, bear the primary responsibility. Who exactly Rabbi Yose ben Elisha was is difficult to establish; he does not appear in standard biographical sources, and his statement is largely an elaboration and focusing of themes already present in the *pesukim* he cites. What he contributes is the insistence on a single, decisive point of accountability.

### Afflictions from Judges

The principle is stated starkly: *shekol puraniyot she'ba'ah l'olam lo ba'ah ela bishvil dayanei Yisrael* — all afflictions that come into the world come only because of the judges of Israel. The supporting verse is from Micah: *shimu na zot rashei beit yaakov u'ktzinei beit yisrael hamita'avim mishpat v'et kol hayeshara ye'akeshuv* — hear this, O heads of the house of Jacob and leaders of the house of Israel, who despise justice and pervert everything that is straight. The verse continues: *boneh tziyon b'damim v'yerushalayim b'avla* — building Zion in blood and Jerusalem in iniquity.

### Three Sins & Punishments

The *Gemara* identifies three distinct categories of sin and a corresponding set of three afflictions. The verse specifies: *rosheha b'shochad yishpotu* — its leaders judge through bribery; *v'chohaneha b'machir yoru* — its priests teach for pay; and *u'nevi'eha b'kesef yichsomu* — its prophets practice divination for money. The *kohanim* here are understood in their capacity as teachers and legal authorities — the forerunners of the rabbinic role — rather than in their Temple function. The phrase *yoru mishpatecha l'yaakov* underlies this reading. Everyone is for sale, and yet the verse concludes *v'al Hashem yisha'enu* — and they rely on God — expressing a kind of religious self-satisfaction that makes the corruption all the more severe. The *Gemara* notes that they were wicked, *ela she'talu bitchonam b'mi she'amar v'hayah ha'olam* — but they placed their trust in the Creator of the world. Whether this slightly mitigates the condemnation or compounds it by adding hypocrisy to corruption is left ambiguous by the *Gemara's* formulation.

Therefore, *Hakadosh Baruch Hu* brings three afflictions corresponding to the three sins — *gimel puraniyot keneged gimel aveirot she'beyadam* — as Rashi identifies them: the judges, the priests, and the prophets. The three afflictions are drawn from the continuation of Micah: *lachem biglalchem tziyon sadeh techaresh* — because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field; *yerushalayim iyin tihyeh* — Jerusalem will become a wasteland; *v'har habayit l'bamot yaar* — and the Temple Mount will be like a wooded height.

### Jerusalem's Restoration

The *Gemara* continues: *v'ein Hakadosh Baruch Hu mashrei shechinato al Yisrael ad she'yichlu shoftim v'shotrim ra'im mi'Yisrael* — God will not cause His *Shechinah* to dwell upon Israel until evil judges and officers have ceased. The verse from Isaiah is then cited as the promise of restoration: *v'ashiva yadi alayich v'etzrof kabor sigayich* — I will return My hand upon you and purify you as with lye; *v'ashiva shoftayich k'varishona* — and I will restore your judges as at first. The verse concludes with the promise that Jerusalem will again be called *ir hatzedek* — the city of righteousness, *kirya ne'emana* — the faithful city. The entire arc, destruction and restoration alike, passes through the integrity or corruption of those who dispense justice.

---

## Redemption via Justice

### Ulla & Redemption

Directly in the wake of the passage about Jerusalem's restoration, the *Gemara* cites Ulla: *ein Yerushalayim nifdet ela bi-tzedakah* — Jerusalem will be redeemed only through *tzedakah*, or through justice. The supporting verse is Isaiah: *tziyon be-mishpat tipadeh v'shaveha bi-tzedakah* — Zion will be redeemed through justice, and those who return to her through righteousness. There is a textual variant in which the subject is *yisrael* rather than *yerushalayim*, and it is likewise somewhat unclear whether the reference is to the return from exile or to the rebuilding of the *Beit HaMikdash*. But the core point is that redemption comes through the embodiment and enactment of justice.

### Merit vs. Mercy

This principle connects to the broader and well-known tension in rabbinic thought about the nature of the messianic redemption. A *Gemara* elsewhere cites the verse *be'ita achishena* — I will hasten it in its time — and resolves the apparent contradiction by saying: *lo zakhu — be'ita; zakhu — achishena*. If Israel does not merit redemption it will come in its appointed time; if they merit it, it will be hastened. The question is the degree to which redemption comes through divine compassion versus through earned merit.

### Vilna Gaon's Blessing

This question had a practical liturgical consequence. The Vilna Gaon was *makpid* on account of this *Gemara* that in the third *bracha* of *bensching* one should not recite *boneh ve-rachamav Yerushalayim amen* — emphasizing God's compassion as the vehicle of Jerusalem's rebuilding — because *tziyon be-mishpat tipadeh*: Zion is redeemed through justice, not through mercy alone. The correct formulation, on his view, is therefore *boneh Yerushalayim amen*, without the word *ve-rachamav*. The emphasis of Ulla's statement, as the Gaon understood it, is less about the tension between divine justice and divine mercy and more about the necessity of Israel's own enactment of justice as the precondition for redemption.

---

## Chain of Corruption

### Rav Pappa's Pyramid

The *Gemara* now presents an almost one-to-one correspondence between categories of sin and categories of resulting affliction. Rav Pappa says: *i batli yahiri, batli amgushi* — if the arrogant ones would cease, the *amgushi* would cease. Steinsaltz identifies the *amgushi* as Zoroastrian fire-priests in Persia. The verse cited is *v'etzrof kabor sigayich* — I will cleanse you as with lye of your impurities — where the word *sigayich* is read by Rashi as related to arrogance (*yisgeh*, to be lifted up; cf. also *gas*). The end of the verse, *v'asira kol bedilayich*, yields the next correspondence: the *bedilayich*, those who cause separation between Israel and God, are linked to the *amgushi* who headed a rival religion and periodically pressed Jews into service for their sacred fire. A second correspondence follows: *ibatlei dayanei, ibatlei gezirpati* — if the corrupted judges cease, the *gezirpati* (non-Jewish legal officers) will cease — drawn from the verse *hesir Hashem mishpatayich, pina oyvech*: God will remove your corrupt judgment, and your enemies will turn away.

### Broken Staff Metaphor

A further teaching is brought in the name of Rabbi Milai citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, on the verse *shavar Hashem mateh reshaim shevet moshlim* — God will break the staff of the wicked, the staff of rulers. A staff is not here a weapon for striking but a support, something one leans upon. *Mateh reshaim* — the staff of the wicked — *elu hadayanim* — these are the judges. But then: *shenasu makel lechazzaneihem* — they have become a stick of support for their officers. The point is that the corrupt judges bear not only the guilt of their own perverted rulings but also the guilt of enabling all those who work for them. The officers — the *chazzanim* — circulate and exploit the judges' authority: they say, in effect, if you want this summons served, if you want this ruling enforced, you will have to pay for it. The corruption spreads outward from the judges through all the attendant positions of authority that shelter beneath their institutional power.

### Talmidei Chachamim Role

The second half of the verse — *shevet moshlim*, the staff of rulers — is applied as follows: *elu talmidei chachamim shebemishpachot hadayanim* — these are the Torah scholars in the families of the judges. Rashi explains that these judges do not genuinely deserve their positions, but their family members who are learned teach them just enough Torah to maintain an appearance of competence, and defend them when they act improperly. This is a strikingly sharp indictment: it is ultimately the *talmidei chachamim* who are most to blame, because they prop up the unworthy judges, and the unworthy judges in turn prop up all those who perpetuate the corruption around them.

Mar Zutra offers a variant formulation: *elu talmidei chachamim she-melamdim hilchot tzibur le-dayanei bur* — these are Torah scholars who teach communal law to ignoramus judges. The point is not necessarily limited to family members; any learned person who provides just enough knowledge to give an incompetent judge a veneer of authority is complicit in the resulting injustice. There is a notable shift in the analysis here from wickedness to incompetence: the corruption begins with judges who are knowledgeable but venal, and then extends to judges who are simply unqualified but sustained in their positions by those who know better.

This naturally raises questions about nepotism and the practice of obtaining positions through family connections rather than merit, though the *Gemara* does not address that dimension explicitly. What it does say is that the responsibility of those who enable the unqualified — whether as relatives, tutors, or institutional supporters — is at least as grave as that of the incompetent judges themselves.

### Fingers & Tongues

Rabbi Elazar ben Milai in the name of Reish Lakish then turns to the verse in Isaiah: *ki chapeichem nigoalu vadam ve'etzbeoteichem be'avon siftoteichem dibru sheker leshonchem avlah tehgeh* — for your hands are defiled with blood, your fingers with sin, your lips have spoken falsehood, your tongue utters perversion. The *Gemara* maps each element onto a different participant in the corrupt legal system. *Chapeichem nigoalu vadam* — your hands defiled with blood — *elu hadayanim*: the judges, who extend a hand to receive bribes. *Ve'etzbeoteichem be'avon* — your fingers with sin — *elu sofrei hadayanim*: the court scribes, who use their fingers to write out the perverted rulings. *Siftoteichem dibru sheker* — your lips speak falsehood — *elu orchei hadayanim*: the lawyers who advise the litigants, a role the *Gemara* views as inherently suspect, since litigants were expected to present their own cases. *Leshonchem avlah tehgeh* — your tongues utter perversion — *elu ba'alei dinim*: the litigants themselves.

The entire legal system is thus implicated from top to bottom. What is particularly striking about this passage is not merely the extent of the corruption but the precision with which it assigns responsibility. Beginning from the *talmidei chachamim* who enable unworthy judges, continuing through the judges themselves, their officers, their scribes, their lawyers, and finally the litigants — every participant is named and held accountable. The *Gemara* does not treat this as a purely historical or literary exercise on the *pesukim*; it moves between *tannaitic* and *amoraic* voices across generations, suggesting an enduring concern.

---

## Joseph & Aaron

### Joseph as Nazir

The *Gemara* now moves to three apparently unrelated statements, all attributed to Rav Milai in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak from Migdal. The first: *miyom sheparash Yosef me'echav, lo ta'am ta'am yayin* — from the day that Joseph was separated from his brothers, he did not taste wine. The proof-text is the phrase *ulekodkod nezir echav* — literally, to the crown of the head of the one separated from his brothers — which, read through the lens of *nezir*, suggests that Joseph adopted a *nazir*-like abstinence. This is combined with the well-known detail that he had long hair, and the inference is extended to the full *nazir* profile: no wine, no contact with the dead, and distinctive hair. The *Gemara* appears to understand this abstinence as a form of mourning — Joseph, torn from his family, separating himself from worldly pleasures in his grief.

### Brothers' Wine Abstention

Rabbi Yose bar Chanina adds that the brothers likewise did not taste wine during all those years of separation. The proof-text is *vayishtu vayishkeru imo* — they drank and became drunk with him — with the inference being that the emphasis on *imo*, with him, implies that until that moment they had not been drinking at all: *michlal de'ad idna lo* — by implication, until now they had not. A dissenting voice objects that perhaps the verse simply indicates that they did not previously get *drunk*, while they did drink; the response is that *shtiya mi'hava* — drinking they did engage in — but *shichrus de'lo hava* — drunkenness had not occurred until that moment of reunion. One might also wonder, as the *Maharsha* does, whether on Joseph's side it was truly *nazir*-like abstinence or whether *eimas malchus* — awe of the ruler — kept the brothers from drinking. The *Maharsha* also raises a technical difficulty: *vayigalach vayichalef simlosav* — Joseph shaved and changed his garments — which complicates reading him as a literal *nazir*. The *Gemara* may therefore be using the term in a looser, evocative sense rather than asserting formal *nezirut*.

### Aaron & Heart Purity

The third statement of Rav Milai: *bischar de'ra'acha vesamach belibo* — in the merit that God foretold to Moses that Aaron would see him and rejoice in his heart — *zacha l'choshen hamishpat al libo* — Aaron merited that the *choshen mishpat* would rest upon his heart. The *Maharsha* notes that the verse does not merely say Aaron would appear to rejoice — the rejoicing was genuine and internal, free of any hidden jealousy. The reward is therefore fitting: the *choshen mishpat*, which rests on the heart, goes to one whose heart was truly pure. One might note a faint thematic resonance between this and the extended discussion of corrupt judges that preceded it — there, the corruption of the legal system is traced to the total absence of inner integrity; here, it is precisely inner integrity, the heart that genuinely rejoices, that earns the ultimate symbol of judgment placed over the heart. The *Gemara*, however, does not draw this connection explicitly, and the three statements of Rav Milai appear to have been assembled here simply because they share an author rather than because they share a theme.

---

## Responsa & Truth

### Three Questions to Levi

The *Gemara* now transitions back toward the laws of *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* through a narrative about three *sheilot*. The people of Bischar sent three questions to Levi: what is the law regarding a *kilah* (a canopy placed over a bed)? What about planting *kushuta* (hops, a vine-like plant) in a vineyard — is that *kilayim*? And what happens when someone dies on *Yom Tov*? As the messenger was traveling, *nach nafshih d'Levi* — Levi died. Shmuel then turned to Rav Menashia and said: *i chakimas, shalch lehu* — if you are capable, send them a response. This appears to have functioned as a kind of training exercise — here is a real question, let us see how you handle it.

### Canopy Prohibition

Rav Menashia responded: regarding the *kilah*, *chazarna akol tzidi kila velo matzana lah tzad heter* — we have looked at every side of the canopy issue and cannot find any angle of leniency.
