But if there is enough oil to actually cause full leather treatment, *me'abed*, then even incidental transfer is forbidden, because the biblical *melacha* could be triggered regardless of intent.

The *gemara* initially presents Rav Chisda's statement as distinguishing between intent to shine versus intent to treat, but immediately corrects itself: who would ever permit intentionally applying oil to leather even to shine it? The statement is reformulated to hinge on quantity: the question is whether the *shiur* of oil present is sufficient only for *tzach-tzacho* or sufficient for *me'abed*. This makes the ruling far more workable — the permissibility of incidental leather contact depends entirely on how much oil is present on the skin, not on one's stated intention.

---

## Shoe Restrictions

### Tanu Rabbanan: Shoes

A *baraita* teaches: *lo yeitzei katan bemin'al gadol* — a small person should not go out wearing an oversized shoe on *Shabbat*. However, *aval yotzei hu bechaluk gadol* — one may go out wearing oversized clothing.

### Removal Concern

The reason for the shoe restriction is the concern that the poorly fitting shoe will be removed and then carried in a *reshut harabbim*. A garment, even an oversized one, does not generate the same concern.

### Women's Sensitivity

*Velo teitzei isha bemin'al merufat* — a woman should not go out wearing a shoe that is *merufat* — damaged or torn at the top — because women are more likely to be sensitive to wearing items that are damaged or unflattering, and are therefore more likely to remove such a shoe in public and carry it. The concern for men with a clearly oversized shoe is lesser, in keeping with the general principle that men are less bothered by the appearance of what they wear, whereas women are more sensitive to such matters.

### Chalitza Issue

*Velo tachloz bo* — a *merufat* shoe may not be used for *chalitza* because it is not a complete, intact shoe. However, *ve'im chaltza chalitza kesheira* — if such a shoe was in fact used for *chalitza*, the *chalitza* is nonetheless valid *bedi'eved*, since it still qualifies as a shoe in some sense.

### New Shoe Definition

*Ve'ein yotzim bemin'al chadash* — one may not go out wearing a new shoe. The question is what "new" means in this context. Rashi explains that a new shoe has not yet been broken in and does not conform to the exact shape of the foot (*im einena mechuyevet lemidas ragla*). Because of this poor fit, a woman is more likely to remove the shoe in public, triggering the concern of carrying.

### Bar Kappara: Pre-Shabbat

Bar Kappara qualifies: *lo shanu ela shelo yatza bo sha'ah achat mibode yom* — the prohibition of a new shoe applies only if it has never been worn even for a single hour before *Shabbat*. *Aval yatza bo me'erev Shabbat mutar* — if one wore it outside even briefly on *Erev Shabbat*, it is permissible to wear on *Shabbat*, as the minimal prior use suffices to break it in.

---

## Shoe from Last

### Shoe Removal

The *gemara* cites two contradictory *baraitot*. One states that one may remove a shoe from the *imos* (the last — the wooden form on which the shoe is constructed) on *Shabbat*. The other states that one may not. This contradiction needs to be resolved.

### Kelim Debate

The source of the dispute is a *mishnah* in *Kelim*: *minal she'al gabei imos Rabbi Eliezer metaher* — a shoe that is still on the last, Rabbi Eliezer rules it is *tahor*, because it is not yet considered a complete vessel. *Vachachamim metamin* — the Rabbis say it is *tamei*, because they consider the shoe complete once its construction is finished, regardless of whether it has been removed from the last.

This dispute has direct implications for *Shabbat*: according to Rabbi Eliezer, the shoe still on the last has not yet acquired the status of a shoe-vessel, and is therefore *muktzah*. According to the Rabbis, the shoe is complete and is not *muktzah*. The first *baraita* follows the Rabbis' view; the second follows Rabbi Eliezer.

### Raba: Purpose

The *gemara* notes that the ability to remove the shoe from the last depends not only on the shoe's status but on that of the last itself. The last is a tool used for shoemaking — it is a *kli shemlachto l'issur*, a tool whose primary use involves a prohibited labor. Raba rules that a *kli shemlachto l'issur* may be moved *bein l'tzorech gufo bein l'tzorech mekomo* — both for the purpose of its own use and to free up the space it occupies. According to Raba, therefore, the last may be moved to facilitate removal of the shoe — this is *tzorech mekomo*, freeing up space — and the *baraita* permitting removal works out well.

### Abaye: Broader View

Abaye, however, disagrees on the rule for *kli shemlachto l'issur*: *l'tzorech gufo mutar l'tzorech mekomo assur* — it may be moved for its own designated purpose but not merely to clear its space. This creates a problem: if removing the last from the shoe is *tzorech mekomo* — clearing the space inside the shoe so one can use it — then according to Abaye, one cannot move the last at all.

One might initially have thought that pulling the last out of the shoe in order to use the shoe is *tzorech gufo* — one is, in some sense, using the last in the process of extracting the shoe. The *gemara*, however, understands this as *tzorech mekomo* — the last is simply in the way, occupying a space that needs to be cleared. And according to Abaye, that is not a sufficient reason to move a *kli shemlachto l'issur*.

### Loose vs. Tight

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty: *hakha b'mai askinan — be'rafui* — the case concerns a shoe that is loosely (*rafui*) resting on the last, not tightly fitted. When the shoe is loose, one can remove the shoe by handling the shoe itself, without having to grip or directly move the last at all. The last simply stays behind. There is therefore no problem with the last as a *kli shemlachto l'issur*, since it is not being moved; only the shoe is handled.

A *baraita* confirms this: *Rabbi Yehuda omer im haya rafui muttar* — Rabbi Yehuda says if it is loose, it is permissible.

### Rabbi Yehuda Logic

Having established that looseness resolves the problem according to Abaye, the *gemara* asks how this teaching integrates with Raba's view. According to Raba, who permits moving the last for *tzorech mekomo* in any case, why does Rabbi Yehuda specifically require that it be loose? If it is tight, Raba would still permit moving the last. The *gemara* answers: *hee d'Rabbi Yehuda mishum d'Rabbi Eliezer hee* — Rabbi Yehuda's statement is not advancing his own independent position on the last; rather, it is addressing the concern of Rabbi Eliezer regarding the shoe itself.

The *baraita* is explicit: *Rabbi Yehuda omer mishum Rabbi Eliezer im haya rafui muttar* — Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: if it is loose, it is permissible. Rabbi Eliezer holds that the shoe is not yet a vessel so long as it remains on the last. But if the shoe has been loosened from the last — the last is no longer tightly embedded within it, and it has begun to separate — then even Rabbi Eliezer will acknowledge that the shoe has achieved its independent identity as a shoe. The shoe is therefore no longer *muktzah* even according to Rabbi Eliezer, and one may handle it.

Thus the distinction between tight and loose in Rabbi Yehuda's statement is not about the *last* at all — it is about defining at what point, in Rabbi Eliezer's view, the shoe crosses the threshold into *vessel* status.

---

## Carrying Infants

### Taking a Child

The new *perek* returns to *muktzah*. The *mishnah* opens: *notel adam et bno ve'even beyado* — one may pick up one's child even though the child is holding a stone. The stone is *muktzah*, yet because one is fundamentally handling the child, the stone's movement is incidental.

### Raba: Live Infant

The *gemara* now brings a teaching of Raba that connects to this *mishnah*: *hotzi tinok chai ve'kis tali b'tzavaro chayav mishum kis* — one who carries a live infant into a *reshut harabbim* while the infant has a money pouch hanging around its neck is liable for carrying the money pouch. This is not *muktzah* but the domain-crossing prohibition of carrying on *Shabbat*, though the *gemara* treats the two contexts as governed by analogous principles of primary and secondary objects.

### Self-Carrying

The *gemara* asks: why is one not liable also for carrying the infant? Because Raba holds like Rabbi Noson: *chai nosei et atzmo* — a living person carries himself. When one carries a living, mobile person, one is not considered to be doing the prohibited act of carrying that person; their own vitality renders them self-carried. At minimum this requires that they be capable of some form of movement, though how much mobility is necessary is a discussion Tosafot addresses.

### Pouch Independence

But given this, why is the money pouch not considered secondary to the infant and therefore also exempt? The *mishnah* itself teaches: *ha-motzi et ha-chai b'mitah patur af al ha-mitah* — one who carries a live person in a bed is exempt even for the bed, because the bed is *tefeilah lo* — secondary to the person. If the bed is nullified by the live person, why is the money pouch not similarly nullified?

The *gemara* distinguishes: *mitah l'gabe chai mivtali lei* — the bed in relation to a live person is indeed secondary, because the bed is there solely to serve the person, in the manner of something that clothes or supports him. *Kis l'gabe tinok lo mivtali lei* — but a money pouch hanging around a child's neck retains its independent identity. It is not there to serve the child in the way a bed serves its occupant; it remains an independent object that one also has in mind. Therefore one is liable for it separately.

### Dead Infant Case

*Tinok meit ve'kis tali lo b'tzavaro patur* — if the infant is dead and has the money pouch hanging from its neck, one is exempt.

### Work Not Needed

The *gemara* asks why one is not liable for carrying the dead infant. Raba holds like Rabbi Shimon: *kol melacha she'eino tzricha l'gufo patur aleha* — for any labor that is not needed for its own intrinsic purpose, one is exempt. Taking a dead body out of the house is not done because one wants the body in a particular place; it is done because one wants the body out of the current place — precisely the definition of *melacha she'eino tzricha l'gufo*. One is therefore exempt. As for the money pouch, it is either similarly *melacha she'eino tzricha l'gufo*, or — per Rashi — in this case the pouch is more emotionally connected to the dead infant (perhaps one intends to bury the child with it), making it more secondary to the infant than in the live-infant case.

### Mishnah Connection

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishnah*'s case of picking up a child who is holding a stone. The connection is important: the *mishnah* appears to treat the stone as secondary to the child — analogous to the way one might expect the money pouch to be secondary to the infant. This is precisely what prompted Raba's discussion of why, by the live-infant case, the money pouch nonetheless retains independence.

### Child's Yearning

The house of Rabbi Yannai offers an explanation for the *mishnah*'s leniency: *b'tinok sheyesh lo ga'agu'in al aviv* — the case involves a child who has a yearning (*ga'agu'in*) for his father. The stone is not truly nullified or secondary; technically, picking up a child carrying a stone does involve moving *muktzah*. The reason it is permitted is that refusing to pick up a child in such a state of longing and distress would effectively render the child a *choleh* — ill from emotional anguish — and for a *choleh* we permit *issur d'rabonon*. This is a limited justification that depends on the specific emotional circumstances.

### Muktzah Exception

This answer, while internally consistent, is a narrow one — it does not establish a broad principle that objects held by children are always secondary and *batel*. The basket-and-stone case and the *terumah* cases mentioned in the *mishnah* will require their own analysis. The *gemara* will continue to work through these implications in the discussions that follow.

---

---

# Shabbat 142

## Muktzah with Permitted I…

### Intro: Child/Basket Cases

Today's daf is 142, and we pick up on the last line of 141b. The *mishna* there spoke about three related cases: picking up one's son when the child is holding a stone, moving a basket that has a stone inside it, and carrying *terumah teme'ah* together with *terumah tehorah*. The common thread running through all three cases is that *muktzah* is being moved together, as a single unit, with permitted items.

It is worth distinguishing this arrangement from *tiltul min hatzad*. *Tiltul min hatzad* — the indirect motion discussed previously — describes a one-time push, where one moves a *muktzah* item out of the way incidentally in order to reach something else. The cases in our *mishna* are different: the movement is sustained and ongoing, and although one is primarily moving a permitted item, the *muktzah* is along for the ride — a stone in the child's hand, a stone in the basket, and so on. The *mishna* indicates that this is permitted.

As we will see, however, much of today's daf — particularly the first *amud* — proceeds on the assumption that this is fundamentally *not* permitted, and therefore sets about redefining and severely limiting each case in the *mishna*.

### Rava's Secondary Items

Part of what drives the *gemara*'s restrictive reading is Rava's ruling, with which we concluded yesterday: if one carries an infant with a money pouch around its neck into a *reshut harabbim*, one is exempt regarding the infant but *chayav* regarding the money pouch. The pouch is not considered secondary to the infant — unlike clothing, or a chair on which the person sits. Since it is not *tafel* (secondary), one is fully liable for carrying it.

The *gemara* proceeds on the assumption that the same parameters that define liability for carrying also govern the prohibition of moving *muktzah*. If that is correct, then moving a basket with a stone inside, or picking up a child holding a stone, should be treated no differently from carrying the stone directly. This inference will drive a wholesale reinterpretation of the *mishna*.

### Gemara's Challenge

The *gemara* opens with the first case: *notel adam et bno ve-even be-yado* — one may pick up his son while the child holds a stone. But how does this square with Rava's ruling that one would be *chayav* for the money pouch in an analogous carrying case? If the same logic applies here, picking up the child should be treated as directly moving the stone.

### Rabbi Yannai's Exception

The house of Rabbi Yannai answers: *betinok she-yesh lo ga'agu'in al aviv* — we are speaking of an infant who has a particular emotional longing for his father, such that if the father does not pick him up, the child will fall into acute distress. Under those circumstances, the rabbis allowed it — Rashi describes it as approaching a situation of *choleh*, someone whose welfare is at stake — and therefore it is a special dispensation, not a general rule. Needless to say, this is a strained reading of the *mishna*, which states the allowance without any such qualification.

### Stone vs. Coin Question

Proceeding to the top of 142a, the *gemara* asks: *mai irya even afilu dinar nami* — if we are granting a special allowance because the child is in emotional distress, why does it matter whether the child holds a stone or a *dinar*? The allowance should apply equally in either case. Yet Rava himself rules that while a stone is permitted, a *dinar* is *assur*. What is the basis for this distinction, whatever the underlying theory of the *mishna* may be?

The *gemara* answers: *even ee nafal lo ati avuye le-atuyei* — if the child drops the stone, the father will not bother to pick it up. But *dinar ee nafal ati avuye le-atuyei* — if the child drops a coin, the father will come to retrieve it. The concern, then, is that permitting the coin will lead to a direct act of moving *muktzah*. It functions as a kind of *gezeirah* on *muktzah*: we allow the emotional-distress dispensation, but not in a case where there is a realistic risk that the *muktzah* will be directly handled. By extension, anything sufficiently valuable that the father would retrieve it falls into the same prohibition.

### Garment Baraita

The *gemara* then brings a *baraita* in support of Rava's general principle — returning now to the domain of carrying rather than *muktzah*. If someone takes his garments folded on his shoulder, or carries his sandals and rings in his hand rather than wearing them, he is *chayav*. If, however, he is wearing all these items, he is exempt. The *baraita* then addresses a compound case: if someone carries another person outside, and that person is wearing his clothes, with sandals on his feet and rings on his fingers, the carrier is exempt — for the person (*chai nosei et atzmo*, the living being carries himself), and for the clothes (secondary to the person). Rashi notes that the word *tab'otav b'yadav* in the second scenario implies the rings are on the fingers, especially given the parallel with *sandalo b'raglo*, and that the plural form reinforces this reading.

The critical clause follows: *ve-ilu hotzian k'mot she-hen* — but if the person being carried is holding his clothing rather than wearing it, the carrier is *chayav*. This directly supports Rava: something a person holds is not *tafel* (secondary) to that person. Clothing one wears, or a chair one sits in, is genuinely secondary — but an item one merely holds in one's hand remains independent.

The *gemara* then notes that this principle of carrying is being applied to the laws of *muktzah*, which is striking. The laws of *muktzah* have their own distinct parameters — one can perform *tiltul b'gufo*, moving *muktzah* with one's body, as we learned recently, something entirely inapplicable to carrying. Clearly the two domains operate differently. Yet the *gemara* insists on the parallel, and this insistence will drive it to reinterpret every case in the *mishna* as a special circumstance. Let us now turn to those cases.

---

## Basket/Stone/Fruit Case

### Basis (Basis) Principle

The *gemara* turns to the next case: *kalkalah ve-ha-even b'tochah* — a basket with a stone inside. According to the *mishna*, one may move the basket. But the *gemara* raises an immediate difficulty even before the question of directly moving the stone: *ve-havei kalkalah basis l'davar ha-asur* — the basket itself becomes a *basis l'davar ha-asur*, a base for a prohibited item. Since the stone was resting in the basket when *Shabbat* began, the basket acquires *muktzah* status along with the stone, and cannot be moved at all.

### Fruit Requirement

Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *hacha b'kalkalah m'lei'ah peirot askinan* — we are dealing with a basket that contains not only a stone but also fruit. A *basis l'davar ha-asur v'davar ha-mutar* — a base for both a prohibited and a permitted item — does not acquire *basis* status. This is the source of the familiar practice of placing *challah* on a candelabrum tray before *Shabbat*, so that the tray does not become a *basis* solely for the candles. Similarly, a drawer containing both *muktzah* and permitted items does not become a *basis*.

The additional detail that there is fruit in the basket also strengthens the *mishna*'s case in another way: one can now say that one is primarily moving the fruit, just as one is primarily picking up the child — the *muktzah* is merely incidental. The *gemara*, however, having already established its restrictive approach, remains dissatisfied.

### Shake-Out Objection

The *gemara* objects: *v'lishdinhu l'peirei v'lishdyeih l'even v'ninktinhu b'yadeih* — why not simply tip the basket out, allow the fruit and stone to fall together, and then pick up only the fruit? If there is a way to avoid moving the stone, that alternative must be pursued. The *gemara* is entirely consistent in its approach: whenever one has another option, the blanket allowance of the *mishna* does not apply. Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rav answers — as originally stated in connection with the following case in the *mishna* but here applied earlier — that we are dealing with *peirot ha-mitnapnim*, fruit that is easily soiled. Emptying out the basket would ruin the fruit, so that option is not available.

The *gemara* presses further: *v'liernahu niurei* — why not at least shake the basket to dislodge the stone, perhaps turning it at an angle so the stone slides out while the fruit remains?

### Stone as Plug Solution

Rav Chiya bar Ashi said in the name of Rav: *hacha b'kalkala p'chuta askinan* — we are dealing with a basket that has a hole in it, *d'even gufa na'asis dofen l'kalkala* — and the stone itself is serving as a plug for that hole. Shaking the basket to remove the stone would cause all the fruit to pour out through the hole. One cannot be expected to do that. Therefore, there is no viable alternative, and moving the basket together with the stone is permitted.

This is a remarkable reading of the *mishna*. The upshot of the *gemara*'s entire analysis of this case is that the *mishna*'s seemingly general allowance — move the basket with the stone inside — is in fact limited to a very narrow scenario: one where there is genuinely no other way to avoid moving the *muktzah*. The first case of the *mishna*, the child with the stone, is similarly limited to an infant in acute emotional distress. Far from a general rule, each case becomes a barely-recognizable exception.

One might observe that this also has implications for the *basis* question raised by students during the shiur: if the *gemara* demands that one shake out or separate the *muktzah* whenever possible before moving the *heter*, that same logic would seem to require removing the permitted item from the *basis* whenever possible rather than simply moving the whole together. The *gemara* is quite consistent in pressing this conclusion.

---

## Mixed Terumah Case

### Terumah Mixing Rules

The *gemara* now turns to the third case in the *mishna*: *metaltlin terumah teme'ah im hatehorah* — one may carry *terumah teme'ah* together with *terumah tehorah*. The *terumah tehorah* is permitted and not *muktzah*; the *teme'ah* is prohibited and effectively *muktzah*. The *mishna* permits moving them together.

### Rav Chisda's Conditions

Rav Chisda refuses to accept this as a blanket allowance. He rules: *lo shanu ela shetehorah lemata utme'ah lemala* — this applies only when the *tehorah* grain is on the bottom and the *teme'ah* grain is on top, so that there is no practical way to extract the *tehorah* grain by itself. In that case, one has no option but to move everything together.

*Aval tehorah lemala utme'ah lemata* — but if the *tehorah* grain is on top and the *teme'ah* is below, *shakil lei l'tahor v'shavik lei l'tamai* — one should simply remove the *tehorah* grain and leave the *teme'ah* behind. To move the entire mixture in that case is impermissible, because an alternative exists.

### Baraita Challenge

The *gemara* objects from a *baraita*: *metaltlin terumah teme'ah im hatehorah v'im hachullin* — one may carry *teme'ah terumah* together with *tehorah terumah* or with *chullin*. The *baraita* then explicitly addresses both positions: *bein shehatahorah lemala utme'ah lemata, bein sheteme'ah lemala vehatahorah lemata* — whether the *tehorah* is above and the *teme'ah* below, or the *teme'ah* is above and the *tehorah* below. Either way, it is permitted. This appears to directly contradict Rav Chisda.

### Purpose Determines Oblig…

Rav Chisda responds: *matnisin letzorech gufo, braita letzorech mekomo* — the *mishna* addresses the case where one needs the grain itself; the *baraita* addresses the case where one needs the space occupied by the basket.

The distinction is significant. If one's purpose is to access the grain — specifically the *tehorah* grain — and the *tehorah* grain happens to be on top, then one has a viable alternative: simply remove the *tehorah* grain without disturbing the *teme'ah*. In that case, one must do so. But if one's purpose is to clear the location — to move the entire basket out of the way — then removing only the *tehorah* grain would leave one with a basket of *teme'ah* grain still sitting in place. That does not accomplish the goal. Since no viable alternative exists, one may move the whole basket regardless of which grain is on top.

The *gemara* then raises a counter-question against Rav Chisda's own framing: the case of needing the grain could have simply been resolved by saying one always needs to move the basket — in which case there would be no distinction between above and below, since one always needs the whole basket moved. Why did Rav Chisda assume the *mishna* spoke specifically about needing the grain?

### Rava's Reading Context

Rava answers: *matnisin kevasei dika* — the precise language of the *mishna* itself supports Rav Chisda's reading. The indication comes from the end of the *mishna* — which for us is the next *mishna*: one who has money on a pillow may shake the pillow and let the coins fall off in order to use the pillow. Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *lo shanu ela letzorech gufo* — this is only when one needs the pillow itself. *Aval letzorech mekomo* — if one needs to clear the space, then shaking off the coins will not help, since the coins will still be lying on the floor in the same spot. In that case, *metaltelo ve'odan alav* — one may move the pillow with the coins still on it.

Since the *mishna*'s case of the pillow is one where one needs the pillow itself, Rava reasons that the corresponding case of the grain at the beginning of the *mishna* is likewise one where one needs the grain. *Umi-de-seifa letzorech gufo reisha nami letzorech gufo* — since the end of the *mishna* deals with needing the item itself, so too the beginning. This lends retroactive support to Rav Chisda's distinction.

The pattern is by now entirely consistent: the *gemara* permits moving a *heter* together with *muktzah* only when no viable alternative exists. Where one has a way to access the permitted item without touching the *muktzah*, that alternative must be pursued.

---

## Terumah Separation on Sh…

### Rabbi Yehudah's Allowance

After addressing the *muktzah* dimensions of the *mishna*, the *gemara* turns to a different ruling at the end of the same *mishna*: *Rabbi Yehuda omer af ma'alin* — Rabbi Yehudah says one may also perform *ha'ala'ah*, the act of removing a unit of grain from a *dimua* mixture (a mixture of *terumah* and *chullin* that has lost its *bitul*) on *Shabbat*, in order to permit the remainder.

### Why Special Case?

The *gemara* asks: *v'amai, ha ka metaken* — why is this permitted? One is effectively fixing the food, rendering it fit for consumption, which is normally prohibited on *Shabbat* just as separating *terumos u'ma'asros* is forbidden.

The *gemara* first suggests: *Rabbi Yehuda k'Rabbi Eliezer sevira leh* — Rabbi Yehudah holds like Rabbi Eliezer, who maintains *terumah b'eini machata* — that in a *dimua* situation, the unit of *terumah* to be removed is considered as if it were already in a distinct, removed state.

The *gemara* derives this from a *mishna*: if one *se'ah* of *terumah* fell into fewer than a hundred units of *chullin*, rendering the whole mixture *dimua* (prohibited because the *terumah* is not *batel*), and then one unit from that mixture fell into a different container of *chullin*, Rabbi Eliezer says that fallen unit is treated as if it were entirely *terumah* — *vada'i* — and creates a *dimua* in its new location according to its full quantity, not proportionally. The sages, by contrast, say the unit *medama* only according to its proportion: since only 1/90th of it is *terumah*, only that fraction creates a problem in the new mixture. Rabbi Eliezer's position implies that the moment one unit needs to be removed, it is conceptually already removed — and any unit that subsequently departs from the mixture is treated as that designated unit, entirely *terumah*.

The *gemara* then asks whether this reasoning could be applied *le'kula* as well: if the unit is considered already removed, perhaps separating it on *Shabbat* involves no real act of fixing? *Eimar de'shamas leh l'chumra* — we only have evidence that Rabbi Eliezer applies this reasoning stringently, never leniently.

### Mental Designation Method

The *gemara* then proposes a different alignment: *ela hu de'amar k'Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — Rabbi Yehudah holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. A *baraita* records: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, *nosen einav b'tzad zeh v'ochel mitzad acher* — one may mentally designate a unit in one corner of the pile and then eat from the rest. No physical separation is required; mental designation suffices.

The *gemara* connects the two positions: Rabbi Yehudah's allowance to physically separate the unit, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's allowance to merely designate it mentally, share the same underlying logic — if mental designation is sufficient to render the grain permitted, then the *dimua* is not really in need of a full act of *tikkun*. The physical separation is not seen as a formal act of fixing, because the *terumah* in a *batel* *dimua* is already considered conceptually removed. Rabbi Yehudah simply goes one step further and permits the actual physical act as well.

The *gemara* verifies this alignment from a *baraita* on 142b: *Rabbi Yehuda omer ma'alin es hamiduma b'echad u'me'ah* — Rabbi Yehudah permits physical separation. *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar omer nosen einav b'tzad zeh v'ochel mitzad acher* — Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits only mental designation. They are thus in debate. The *gemara* concludes: *Rabbi Yehudah azil k'Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — he follows the same underlying principle but takes it one step further, reasoning that if even the act of mental designation does not constitute fixing, then actual physical separation — which is no more substantial in terms of *tikkun* given that the *terumah* is already *batel* — should equally be permissible on *Shabbat*.

### Fixing vs. Bitul Distinc…

A crucial conceptual distinction underlies this entire discussion. There is a difference between saying that the grain is *fully fixed* and saying that the *terumah* is already *batel*. Under the principle of *kama kama batel*, the *terumah* becomes *batel* sequentially as each unit falls in; one does not need to posit that the designated unit has already been removed. Rather, the *terumah* is genuinely *batel* — though the rabbinic obligation to remove a unit remains. This means that in a second-degree mixture, when a unit from the *dimua* falls into a new container of *chullin*, one need not treat that unit as full *terumah*, because its *terumah* component was already *batel* in the original mixture. The *kama kama batel* principle operates only so long as the proportions remain such that *bitul* applies; once the mixture is detectably *tasted* or a contrary *rov* emerges, one can no longer invoke it.

The point for our discussion is that saying the *terumah* is *batel* does not mean the grain is fully fixed — there is still an obligation to remove a unit. But the prohibition against *tikkun* on *Shabbat* requires an act of real fixing; if the *terumah* is already conceptually *batel*, the act of separation is not a full *tikkun* in the halachic sense, and Rabbi Yehudah permits it.

---

## Barriers to Removal

### Stone on Barrel

The *gemara* now returns to the core *muktzah* theme, turning to the next *mishna*: *ha'even she'al pi hachavis* — a stone sitting atop a barrel. *Mataltah v'hi nofeles* — one tips the barrel and the stone falls off, allowing access to the barrel or its contents.

*Hayta bein hachaviyos* — but if the barrel is positioned among other barrels, so that tipping it would risk knocking them over (Rashi) or there is simply insufficient room, then one cannot tip it in place. In that case, *magbiya u'mataltah v'hi nofeles* — one lifts the barrel, carries it to a suitable location, and then tips it so the stone falls off.

The case of money on a pillow follows: *ma'os she'al hakar, m'na'er hakar vehen noflos* — one shakes the pillow and the coins fall off, allowing use of the pillow. *Hayta alav lishleshes* — if the pillow has a stain or spittle on it, *m'kanchesah b'smartut* — one wipes it with a rag. *Hayta shel or* — if it is made of leather, one may apply water, since leather is not subject to the prohibition of *libbun* in the same way as cloth. Rashi does note, however, that with soft leather there could in principle be a concern of *kibus*, and he addresses the parameters there.

This *mishna* — particularly its instruction to shake the stone off the barrel whenever possible — is presumably what informed the *gemara*'s restrictive analysis on 142a. The *mishna* there seemed to be a blanket allowance; this *mishna* implies that wherever removal is possible it is required, and moving the *heter* together with the *muktzah* is only a last resort.

### Focus on Heter Principle

*Man tana d'kol haycha d'ika issur veheter beheter tarchinan be'issur lo tarchinan* — who is the *tanna* who holds that whenever there is both an *issur* and a *heter*, we focus our effort on the *heter* and not on the *issur*?

The question is abstract in a way that may seem surprising. After all, directly moving the stone would be a straightforward violation of *muktzah*, while moving the barrel (the *heter*) and tipping the stone off involves no direct handling of *muktzah*. One might think the reasoning is self-evident. Yet the *gemara* elevates this into a general principle — whenever one faces a combination of an *issur* and a *heter*, one must focus on the *heter* even if it is more cumbersome — and asks where else we find this principle.

Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel hi* — it is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

### Sorting Majority vs. Min…

*D'tenan, haborer kitnit beyom tov* — if one sorts legumes on *Yom Tov*: Beit Shammai says *borer ochel v'ochel* — one selects the food to eat it immediately, much as one performs *borer* on *Shabbat*. Beit Hillel says *borer kedarko* — one may sort in the normal manner. Normally, the most efficient method is to remove the minority element — typically the *psoiles* (chaff or contaminants) — rather than the food itself. Beit Hillel permits this on *Yom Tov*, and further permits using one's lap (*becheyko*) or a vessel (*vetamchui*) to assist.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then qualifies Beit Hillel's ruling in a *baraita*: *bameh devarim amurim* — when does Beit Hillel permit removing the *psoiles* in the normal manner? *She-ha'ochel merubeh al ha-psoiles* — when the food is more abundant than the refuse, making it easier to remove the minority *psoiles* rather than the majority food. But *aval psoiles merubeh al ha'ochel* — if the refuse is more abundant than the food, *divrei hakol borer ochel* — everyone agrees one must focus on the food. The reason Beit Hillel allows removing the *psoiles* is that it is the more efficient method when it constitutes the minority; if the *psoiles* is the majority, efficiency considerations no longer justify departing from the rule that one focuses on the *heter*.

This is the general principle: we focus on the *heter* unless focusing on the *issur* is significantly easier. The *gemara* then asks: why, then, must one lift and carry the barrel in our case? It would be far easier simply to pick up the stone — which is focusing on the *issur* — and remove it directly. By the logic of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, should we not permit that?

The *gemara* answers: *hacha nami kivan d'ibaei lemishkal lo mishtaklei yayin ad d'shaklei* — in this case too, since one would need to lift the barrel in order to extract all the wine from the bottom, it is not really more laborious to lift the barrel in any case. Focusing on the barrel (the *heter*) is not a significant additional burden, because one would need to lift it to access the contents regardless. Therefore, this is comparable to the case where the *psoiles* is the majority — one must focus on the *heter* and not on the *issur*, since no real imposition is involved in doing so.

It must be acknowledged that the fundamental comparison throughout this passage — between the *borer* question of which category to sort first and the *muktzah* question of whether to handle the stone directly — is puzzling. To pick up the stone is a direct violation of *muktzah*; no one would have imagined this was permitted. To tip the barrel, thereby moving the stone without handling it, is a form of indirect motion entirely distinct from the *borer* analysis. The *gemara* nonetheless draws the comparison and resolves it on the *gemara*'s own terms.

### Money on Pillow Rules

Returning to the case of money on a pillow: Rav Huna said in the name of Rav — *lo shanu ela beshoche'ach* — the allowance to shake the pillow applies only when the money was left there inadvertently. *Aval bemaniach* — if one intentionally placed the money on the pillow before *Shabbat*, *na'asa basis ledavar ha'asur* — the pillow becomes a *basis l'davar ha-asur*, and cannot be touched at all. This ruling applies equally to the earlier case of the barrel and the stone: the barrel is not a *basis* only because the stone was forgotten there, not deliberately placed.

Rabba bar bar Chana, again in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, reiterates: *lo shanu ela l'tzorech gufo* — the instruction to shake off the coins is only when one needs the pillow itself. *Aval l'tzorech mekomo, metaltelo ve'odan alav* — if one needs to clear the space entirely, one may move the pillow with the coins still on it. Chiya bar Rav mi-Difeti teaches similarly in a *baraita*: the allowance to move the pillow with coins on it in the case of needing the space is confirmed.

---

## Placing Permitted on Muk…

### Wallet Trick

*Shachach arnaki b'chatzer* — if one forgot one's wallet in the courtyard, Rabbi Oshaya rules: *meniach aleha kikar o tinok u'metaltela* — one places a loaf of bread or an infant on top of the wallet and then carries it. This case differs materially from everything discussed before. There, one was moving a *heter* with *muktzah* incidentally along for the ride, and the fundamental object of attention was the *heter*. Here, the object being directly handled is the *muktzah* itself, and the purpose of moving it is the *muktzah*. The bread or infant is added precisely to create the appearance of moving a *heter*. Nevertheless, Rabbi Oshaya permits this because of *hefsed mamon* — concern about financial loss.

### Brick Generalization

Rabbi Yitzchak extends this further: *shachach levana b'chatzer, meniach aleha kikar o tinok u'metaltela* — if one forgot a brick in the courtyard, one may equally place a loaf or infant on it and move it. The trick is not limited to items of high monetary value — even an ordinary brick, if one is concerned about its being damaged or lost, qualifies.

### Sack in Reshut Harabbim

Rav Yehuda bar Shila said in the name of Rav Assi: *paam achat shachechu daskia meleah maot b'istatya* — once they left a sack filled with coins in a *reshut harabbim*. They came and asked Rabbi Yochanan, who instructed them: *henichu aleha kikar o tinok* — place a loaf of bread or an infant on it. Now the difficulty is compounded: besides the *muktzah* problem of the coins, there is also the *d'Oraita* prohibition of carrying in a *reshut harabbim*. Rashi explains that the solution involves moving the sack in increments of fewer than four *amot* at a time — *pachot pachot m'arba amot* — thereby avoiding any single act of carrying that would cross the threshold of liability. Together with the bread or infant solution for the *muktzah*, this produces a multi-layered workaround. As we will see in a coming *mishna*, when one is caught outside with money and faces a *Shabbat* violation, the *gemara* is quite willing to sanction approaches that come close to the edge rather than allow an outright violation.

### Rav Ashi's Restriction

Mar Zutra rules: *hilchata k'chol hanei shematata b'shocheach* — the ruling is in accordance with all of the above positions only when the item was forgotten. If one intentionally left it there before *Shabbat*, this dispensation does not apply.

Rav Ashi goes further: *afilu shachach nami lo* — even if one forgot it, none of this is permitted. *V'lo amru kikar o tinok ela l'met bilvad* — the only context in which the earlier authorities ever sanctioned the bread-or-infant trick was in the case of a *meit*, a dead body: out of respect for the dead, when one needs to move the body out of the sun to prevent decomposition, one may place a permitted item on it and carry it. Outside of that specific case, the technique has no application.

### Abaye/Rava on Shekaach

Abaye and Rava, who preceded Rav Ashi, had practiced differently. *Abaye manach kafa akifi* — Abaye would place a ladle on bundles of wheat and carry them. *Rava manach sakina abar yona umataltela* — Rava would place a knife on a slaughtered pigeon and carry it. Both appear to have used the bread-or-infant technique even in cases other than a *meit*.

Rav Yosef, who was their teacher, responded mockingly: *kama charifa shma'atecha d'dardaki* — how sharp, these young ones. He was not objecting to the principle entirely, but to the specific application: *eima d'amri Rabbanan b'shochei'ach, l'chatchila mi amri* — when the Rabbis permitted this trick, it was only *b'shochei'ach*, for something forgotten. Did they say it may be done *l'chatchila*? Here, one had knowingly left the bundles of wheat or the pigeon outside before *Shabbat*, making this a case of *meniach*, not *shachach*.

Abaye replied: *ilav d'adam chashuv ana, kafa kefi lama li* — were it not that I am a person of distinction, I would not have needed to put the ladle on the bundles at all, because the bundles are not even *muktzah* — *d'chazu l'mizga*, one can recline on them, making them a usable item. He only added the ladle to avoid misleading onlookers, given his standing as an *adam chashuv*. Rava said likewise: *ana sakina abar yona lama li, d'chazi l'umtza* — I would not have needed to put the knife on the pigeon at all, because the pigeon can be eaten raw, and therefore is not *muktzah* to begin with. Again, his care with the knife was a measure appropriate to an *adam chashuv*.

The practical *halacha* follows Rav Ashi's restrictive ruling. The voices of Rav Yosef, Abaye, and Rava represent an earlier and more lenient position, permitting the technique at least in cases of *shachach*; but Rav Ashi, as the later authority who gave the *gemara* its final form, rules that the trick is reserved solely for a *meit*.

---

## Pigeon & Intended Use

### Raw Pigeon Edibility

The *gemara* now examines Rava's claim that the pigeon is not *muktzah* because *d'chazi l'umtza* — it can be eaten raw. The *gemara* probes: *ta'ama d'chazi l'umtza* — the reason it is not *muktzah* is that it can be eaten raw. *Ha lo chazi l'umtza lo* — implying that if it could *not* be eaten raw, it would be *muktzah*. But why? It could still be given to a dog — and dog food is not *muktzah*.

### Dog Food & Intended Use

The answer the *gemara* draws from this is that Rava holds like Rabbi Yehudah, who maintains a stricter position on *muktzah* than Rabbi Shimon. The critical point is this: if an item was designated as *ma'achal adam* — intended for human consumption — and on *Shabbat* it becomes fit only for *ma'achal behema* (animal consumption), it is *muktzah*. One still intends to use it eventually for people; the fact that right now it can only be given to animals does not change its intended status. It is therefore classified as *muktzah* because it is not presently fit for the use for which it was designated.

This is precisely why Rava needed to say the pigeon *can* be eaten raw: if the pigeon were entirely inedible by humans in its raw state, its status as *ma'achal adam* would be momentarily suspended, and it would be considered *muktzah*.

### Duck Intestines Precedent

To confirm this, the *gemara* cites Rava's own practice: *tavi li bar avza* — he instructed his attendants on *Yom Tov* to roast a duck for him, *ve-shadi maya li-shunra* — and to throw the intestines to the cat. This seems problematic: the intestines of a duck are in principle edible for humans (in the fashion of sweetbreads), and by assigning them to the cat, Rava appears to be treating *ma'achal adam* as *ma'achal behema*, which should create a *muktzah* problem.

The *gemara* answers: *hasam kivan di-masrach daito alavei mei-etmol* — there, from the outset of *Yom Tov*, it was already clear that the intestines would spoil if saved for later. They had to be disposed of during *Yom Tov*, and since leaving them would cause them to spoil, they were never genuinely designated as *ma'achal adam* to begin with. One knew from the very beginning that the meat would serve the people and the intestines the cat. An item that was never intended as *ma'achal adam* is not *muktzah* when given to animals. Only an item initially set aside as *ma'achal adam* that then becomes edible only for animals falls into the *muktzah* category according to Rabbi Yehudah.

*Hachi nami mistavra, de-Rava ke-Rabbi Yehuda sevira lei* — and indeed this is the logical conclusion: Rava holds like Rabbi Yehudah.

### Nolad & Broken Vessels

The *gemara* adduces further support from a teaching of Rava himself: *isha lo tikanes le-veis ha-eitzim litol me-hen ud* — a woman may not enter the woodshed to take a poker on *Yom Tov*. *Ve-ud she-nishbar asur le-hasiko be-Yom Tov* — and a poker or spit that breaks on *Yom Tov* may not be used as firewood. The basis: *lefi she-masikin be-keilim ve-ein masikin be-shivrei keilim* — while one may use whole vessels as firewood on *Yom Tov*, one may not use broken vessels, because the broken state is *nolad* — a new reality that came into being on *Yom Tov* itself. This demonstrates that Rava holds of *nolad*, which is the position of Rabbi Yehudah.

The *gemara* thus concludes from this: *shma mina de-Rava k'Rabbi Yehuda sevira lei* — one may infer that Rava holds like Rabbi Yehudah. The *gemara* concedes that holding like Rabbi Yehudah on *nolad* does not automatically entail holding like him on the *ma'achal adam / ma'achal behema* distinction — the two issues are logically independent — but the *gemara* groups them together as dimensions of Rabbi Yehudah's more stringent approach to *muktzah*, and reasons that since Rava holds like Rabbi Yehudah on *nolad*, it makes sense that he likewise holds like him on the *ma'achal adam* question. This is why Rava needed to establish that the pigeon was fit for raw human consumption: operating within Rabbi Yehudah's framework, an item intended as *ma'achal adam* that is currently fit only for *ma'achal behema* would be *muktzah*, and Rava had to demonstrate that no such problem arose.

---

---

# Shabbat 144

## Barrel & Squeezing

### Barrel Breaking

The *mishnah* on 144a opens with the case of a barrel that breaks on *Shabbos* and the question of saving wine from it. While this somewhat echoes earlier discussions about saving items from a fire — where there was concern that permitting such activity might lead one to extinguish the flames — the barrel case is harder to understand in terms of any genuine prohibition. The issues raised there involve excessive *tircha* or *uvda d'chol*, though the details need not detain us here.

### Fruit Squeezing

From the barrel, the *mishnah* transitions to the more central concern of squeezing (*sechita*), a topic introduced already at the end of the previous *perek*. The earlier discussion there involved using a sponge to absorb oil — the concern being that one would come to squeeze it out. The *mishnah* then turns to fruit juices: oil and wine that run off from grapes or other fruit, and whether one may benefit from them on *Shabbos*, given the worry that permitting such benefit will lead one to actively squeeze the fruit. On this question, *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *Chachamim* disagree. The *Chachamim* appear to prohibit benefit in all cases, while *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that if the fruit was set aside for food (*le'ochalin*), one may benefit from the juices that run off on their own, since the fruit's designation for eating means there is no concern one will come to squeeze it. A simple example: if one is eating grapefruit on *Shabbos* and some juice runs out, may one drink it? According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, since it was set aside for food, yes.

### Three Categories

The *Gemara* distinguishes between three categories of fruit. First, *zeitim va'anavim* — olives and grapes — where the *Gemara*'s working position is that even *Rabbi Yehuda* concedes to the *Chachamim*: even when set aside for food, one may not benefit from the juice that runs off. Second, *tutim v'rimonim* — pomegranates and strawberries — which are squeezed with some frequency, though not as regularly as grapes and olives; this is the category under active debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *Chachamim*. Third, *she'ar perot* — all other fruits — which are squeezed only rarely, and here even the *Chachamim* agree that the juice presents no problem at all.

### Frequency vs Status

At first glance, the differences among these three categories appear to be simply a question of frequency: everyone squeezes olives and grapes, pomegranates are squeezed occasionally, and other fruits almost never. The two extremes are agreed upon, and the debate concerns the middle case. However, it is important to note that olives and grapes carry an additional dimension that goes beyond mere frequency.

### Oil & Wine Status

What is produced by squeezing olives and grapes? Olive oil and wine — the paradigmatic liquids of the ancient world, and indeed of *halacha* itself. If one were asked to name the most significant liquids, the answer would be water, olive oil, and wine. The point, then, is not only that squeezing olives and grapes is common, but that *halachically* what is produced carries a recognized status: it has a *shem mashkeh*, a formal identity as a liquid. Notably, olive oil and wine are among the seven liquids that render things susceptible to *tumah v'taharah*.

This is why olives and grapes almost certainly constitute the only category where actually squeezing would violate a *d'oraisa* prohibition. If one were to squeeze an orange, even if it were common to do so and not at all done in an unusual manner, the orange juice would essentially be considered a waste product — and therefore one would not have performed the act of truly producing a *mashkeh*. This is also why the case of olives and grapes is agreed upon not merely because of the heightened concern that one will come to squeeze them, but because of the formal status of what they produce. And crucially, if the distinction among the three categories were purely a matter of frequency, those categories might shift over time or by location — but if the *d'oraisa* turns on the status of olive oil and wine as formal liquids, then that category is stable regardless of changing circumstances.

---

## Categories Established

### Yehuda Concedes

The *Gemara* had already demonstrated on the previous day that *Rabbi Yehuda* agrees with the *Chachamim* with respect to olives and grapes. Now it turns to the other extreme. Three lines from the bottom of 144a, the *Gemara* states: *ashkechan Rabbi Yehuda d'modei l'Rabanan b'zeitim va'anavim* — we have established that *Rabbi Yehuda* concedes to the *Chachamim* regarding olives and grapes, since there is a heightened concern that one will come to squeeze them (and doing so would constitute a *d'oraisa* violation). Now the *Gemara* asks: *Rabanan d'modei lei l'Rabbi Yehuda b'she'ar peiros minalan?* — how do we know that the *Chachamim* agree with *Rabbi Yehuda* that the juices running off fruits other than pomegranates and strawberries (i.e., the very-rarely-squeezed category) present no problem at all?

### Baraita Permission

The *Gemara* answers from a *baraita*: *sochtin b'fagin u'v'prishin u'v'ozradin* — one may squeeze prunes, quince, and crabapples. According to *Rashi*, *pagin* are prunes, *prishin* are quince, and *ozradin* are crabapples. Not only is there no concern about benefiting from their juices — one may actually squeeze them *lechatchila* on *Shabbos*, since they fall into the category so uncommon as to carry no *issur d'rabbanan* at all. *Aval lo b'rimonim* — but not pomegranates. The reason pomegranates fall into the middle category, at minimum *assur d'rabbanan*, is then illustrated.

### Pomegranate Status

*Shel beis Menashia ben Menachem hayu sochtin rimonim* — in the household of Menashia ben Menachem, they would press pomegranates for juice. This established practice demonstrates that pomegranate-squeezing is not so unusual or strange, and is therefore subject to at least a *d'rabbanan* prohibition.

### D'Oraisa vs Rabbanan

The *baraita* is thus speaking to the *lechatchila* question — not whether one may benefit from juice that ran off, but whether one may perform the act of squeezing at all. The three levels emerge: *zeitim va'anavim* is *d'oraisa*; *rimonim* and *tutim* is *d'rabbanan*; and things that are genuinely uncommon to squeeze are entirely *mutar*.

### Rational Proof

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge: perhaps the *baraita* permitting the squeezing of prunes and crabapples represents only *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position, who is generally more lenient — so the proof that the *Chachamim* agree would fail. The *Gemara* responds: *u'seha nami Rabbi Yehuda* — fine, even if it is *Rabbi Yehuda*, this *baraita* still tells us something new. Until now, we only knew *Rabbi Yehuda*'s leniency with respect to benefiting from juices that ran off on their own (*yatzu me'atzman*); he was never heard to permit squeezing *lechatchila*. So what can one say? *Keivan d'lav b'nei sechita ninhu* — since these fruits are simply not the kinds of things that people squeeze, even *Rabbi Yehuda* permits doing so *lechatchila*. And if that is so, then the *Chachamim* must agree as well, since the entire debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *Chachamim* was never about the permissibility of the act of squeezing itself, only about the concern of what the act might lead to. Things that no normal person squeezes — there was never any debate about them at all. *Shema mina Rabanan hi* — this is indeed the *Chachamim*'s position too.

This is a striking demonstration: the proof is established not from any explicit text, but purely from a logical argument. One might have supposed that the debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *Chachamim* extended even to the underlying act — that they disagreed about what is *d'oraisa*. But the *Gemara* is convinced otherwise: since these fruits fall into the category of *mutar lechatchila*, this must represent universal agreement.

This raises the important practical question of where to draw the line between the *d'rabbanan* and *mutar* categories. We know the *d'oraisa* category is *zeitim va'anavim* with relative confidence, and perhaps only that — though one might argue that certain strains of fruit grown specifically for juice production (like Valencia oranges) could be treated as *d'oraisa*, since that is their primary purpose. Nevertheless, the prevailing view holds that only olive oil and wine carry *d'oraisa* status. The more interesting line to draw is between *d'rabbanan* and *mutar*, which requires defining how widespread a practice must be before it elevates a fruit into the *d'rabbanan* category. The *Gemara* will address this directly.

---

## Geographic Prevalence

### Rav Nachman Ruling

Returning to the pomegranate case and the household of Menashia Bar Menachem: *Rav Nachman* rules, *halacha k'shvei Menashe Bar Menachem* — the *halacha* follows the practice of the household of Menashia Bar Menachem, meaning pomegranate-squeezing is treated as *assur d'rabbanan*.

### Rava's Challenge

*Rava* immediately challenges: *Menashe Bar Menachem tana hu?* — is Menashia Bar Menachem a *tana*? He was not issuing a *halachic* ruling; he simply made pomegranate juice. How does one rule "like" a pomegranate-juice producer?

### Braita Author

The *Gemara* clarifies: what *Rav Nachman* meant was that the *halacha* follows the author of the *baraita*, who was concerned with the phenomenon of Menashia Bar Menachem's household and ruled that because of it, pomegranate-squeezing is *assur*. It is a pointed and even somewhat playful exchange — particularly fitting for *Purim* — but the meaning was always clear: the *baraita*'s author took note of that practice as evidence of its prevalence.

### One Person Rule

The *Gemara* now presses harder: *u'mishum d'savar k'Menashe Bar Menachem halacha k'moso?* — just because this *tanna* was concerned about the practice of Menashia Bar Menachem, does that mean we must follow suit? *Menashe Bar Menachem havei ruba d'alma?* — is one individual the majority of the world? If a single unusual person makes pomegranate juice, why should that dictate *halacha* for everyone else?

### Thornbush Precedent

The *Gemara* answers by citing a *mishnah*: *hamkayem kotzim bekerem* — one who maintains thornbushes in his vineyard. Does allowing thornbushes to grow there create a *kilayim* problem, given that thornbushes are not normally cultivated for food? *Rabbi Eliezer* says it does — *kadesh*, the vineyard is sanctified as *kilayim*. The *Chachamim* say it does not: only plants that people normally cultivate are relevant, not things that people routinely uproot.

*Rabbi Chanina* explains *Rabbi Eliezer*'s reasoning: *shebechin be'arvaya mekaymin kotzei sadot legmaleihem* — because in Arabia, people cultivate thornbushes in their fields to feed to their camels. Since it is done in some place, even that creates a concern. This demonstrates that a practice common in some subset of society or some geographic region can have *halachic* implications even elsewhere.

### Arabia Example

The *Gemara* objects: *midi irya?* — is that really analogous? *De'arvaya atra* — Arabia is an entire land, a geographic region where the practice is widespread. Because it is genuinely common in that region, it carries implications beyond. That is not comparable to one individual.

### Region Significance

*Hacha batla da'ato etzel kol adam* — here, a single person who makes pomegranate juice should be entirely irrelevant to everyone else. The *Gemara* thus establishes a key limiting principle: only practices that are truly prevalent in a given geographic region can elevate a fruit into the *d'rabbanan* category. One unusual individual is insufficient. The breadth of the geographic region need not be defined with precision, but the practice must be genuinely widespread there.

### Importing Fruit

This in turn opens a broader discussion. What if the practice is common in a different region, not one's own? What if fruit is imported from that region — so that its juice is in fact common locally, not because people press it locally, but because it arrives in pressed form from elsewhere? And what of a further hypothetical: if a fruit is commonly squeezed in Florida but not locally, and the reason it is not common locally is simply that the fruit is not grown there — if one had access to such fruit, one would certainly squeeze it. Does that theoretical prevalence count?

### Most Fruits D'Rabbanan

Based on these considerations — actual local practice, importation, and what one *would* do if one had access to the fruit — the category of *d'rabbanan* turns out to be extremely broad in practice. Almost everything winds up there. It would take something genuinely obscure — a fruit that virtually no one anywhere ever squeezes for juice — to fall into the *mutar* category. Crabapples may be one such example; it is difficult to think of many others. In practice, we assume grapes and olives are *d'oraisa* and virtually everything else is at minimum *d'rabbanan*.

### Lemon Squeezing

There is, however, an interesting *Beit Yosef* that bears on this. The *Beit Yosef* notes that it was very common to squeeze lemons on *Shabbos* — and not lemons onto fish (squeezing into food, which we will address shortly, and which is *mutar*), but simply squeezing lemon juice to make lemonade or add to tea. He struggles to explain how this could be *mutar* given that lemons are commercially pressed at scale. One argument he attempts — that it is not so common to squeeze lemons for plain lemon juice — is difficult to sustain. The strongest argument he can offer is that no one ever drinks lemon juice straight; it is always mixed with something else, so it never functions independently as a *mashkeh*. Regardless, the practical conclusion remains that almost any fruit, unless genuinely rare, falls into the *assur d'rabbanan* category.

---

## Water Squeezing

### Libun & Sechita

A question was raised earlier about the *issur* of squeezing water from fabric — why should that present a problem if squeezing certain fruit juices does not? Squeezing water absorbed into fabric involves two distinct concerns. One is *libun* — the act of cleaning. There is a debate among the *rishonim* about whether *libun* applies only when squeezing out water (since the normal way to launder involves soaking in water and then wringing it out) or even when squeezing out other unwanted liquids, such as wine, since ridding the fabric of an undesirable liquid is itself part of the cleaning process.

### Wine vs Others

The second concern is *sechita* proper — extracting liquid that one actually wants, as when fabric has absorbed wine that spilled from the barrel and one then wrings out the fabric to salvage the wine. In that case, there is a genuine act of producing a *mashkeh*. Some hold that if the fabric absorbed a liquid other than wine or olive oil — one that would not carry *d'oraisa* status even if squeezed directly from its original source — then squeezing it from fabric would only be *d'rabbanan*, not *d'oraisa*. This type of squeezing — liquid extracted from cloth or similar material, understood as a form of *mefarek*, severing a desired product from its containing medium — is compared to the fruit-squeezing cases discussed throughout this *daf*, and some authorities apply parallel limits. Since the *mishnah* itself opened with a case involving wine, the comparison is at least apt in that instance.

### Spill Wiping

There are cases where *libun* presents no concern: for example, *derech lichluch* — wiping up a spill, so that rather than cleaning the fabric, one is in fact getting it dirty. Without reaching the full practical *halacha*, the point is that in such circumstances the act cannot be characterized as *libun* at all, and the concern diminishes accordingly.

---

## Mikvah Invalidation

### Beet Juice Case

The *Gemara* now continues with a case introduced by *Rav Chisda*: *tardin she'sechtan u'nesanan b'mikvah* — one who squeezed beets and placed the beet juice into a *mikvah*. Such beet juice *poslin es ha'mikvah b'shinuy mareh* — it invalidates the *mikvah* by changing its color. The basic rule is that drawn water (*mayim she'uvim*) invalidates a *mikvah* if added before it reaches its full forty *se'ah*, but once the *mikvah* is complete with forty *se'ah*, the problem disappears, and only a quantity of three *log* before completion is problematic. Liquids that are not water, however, invalidate the *mikvah* when they change its color — even when there is already forty *se'ah*, and even in amounts less than three *log*.

### Beet Status

The *Gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: *b'shinuy mareh v'ha lav b'nei sechita ninhu* — why should beet juice invalidate the *mikvah* at all? The color change of the *mikvah* is not itself the problem. If water underwent some chemical reaction and changed color without any foreign substance being introduced, the *mikvah* remains *kasher*. The color change serves only as a measure of the amount of invalid liquid that was introduced. For beet juice to invalidate the *mikvah* by changing its color, it must itself be a halakhically significant liquid — a *mashkeh*. But nobody squeezes beets to make beet juice. This is precisely the point made earlier: it is not merely a question of how common the squeezing is, but whether *halacha* recognizes what is produced as a liquid with formal status.

### Significance Theory

The *Gemara* offers an answer: *keivan d'achshavinehu havu lehu mashkeh* — since one gave this juice significance by choosing to squeeze it, that subjective significance is sufficient to confer upon it the status of a *mashkeh*. And the same applies to *tutim u'rimonim*: *keivan d'achshavinehu*, if one gives it significance by squeezing it, *havu lehu mashkeh*, it thereby acquires *mashkeh* status. *Rashi* notes the striking implication of this position: if subjective significance is what confers *mashkeh* status, then one should be forbidden from squeezing *any* fruit for its juice, since the very act of squeezing constitutes an act of giving significance. On this view, when the *mishnah* permitted squeezing certain fruits, it referred only to squeezing in order to remove excess juice — not to squeezing for the purpose of producing juice. If one squeezes *for the juice*, even unusual fruits would be forbidden, because one's intent has objectively granted the product *mashkeh* status. This is not the *Gemara*'s final position, but it is the position being presented at this stage.

### Rav Papa Answer

*Rav Papa* rejects the underlying premise entirely. Who ever said that something must have a formal *halachic* status as a *mashkeh* in order to invalidate a *mikvah*? *Mishum d'havi davar she'ein osin mimenu mikvah l'chatchilah* — the reason beet juice invalidates the *mikvah* is simply that it is a substance from which one cannot construct a *kosher mikvah* in the first place.

### Mikvah Rule

*Rav Papa*'s principle is: *vechol davar she'ein osin mimenu mikvah l'chatchilah posul es ha'mikvah b'shinuy mareh* — anything that cannot itself serve as a *mikvah* invalidates the *mikvah* when it changes its color. No formal status as a *mashkeh* is required. Even a physically liquid substance, without any *halachic* recognition as a liquid of significance, suffices to invalidate the *mikvah* when it changes its color. The question of whether *Rav Papa* means truly *kol davar* — any substance whatsoever, such as iron rust causing a color change — or whether there must still be some liquid-like character to the substance, remains open. But his point is clear: the formal *halachic* status of *mashkeh* is irrelevant to *mikvah* invalidation.

---

## Mishnat Mikvah

### Wine & Vinegar

A *mishnah* from elsewhere is now cited: *nafal l'tocho yayin o chometz u'mochal v'shinu mar'av pasul* — if wine, vinegar, or *mochal* (the water that runs off olives, distinct from olive oil itself) fell into the *mikvah* and changed its color, the *mikvah* is invalid. The *Gemara* asks: *man tanna d'mochal mashkeh hu?* — operating still with the assumption that only something with *mashkeh* status can invalidate a *mikvah*, who is the *tanna* who holds that *mochal* has *mashkeh* status?

### Mochal Question

The question is sharp: *mochal* is not olive oil; it is merely the watery runoff from olives. Does *halacha* recognize it as a liquid of significance?

### Abaye Position

*Abaye* answers: the *tanna* in question is *Rabbi Yaakov*, as taught in a *baraita*: *Rabbi Yaakov omer mochal harei hu k'mashkeh* — *mochal* is treated as a *mashkeh*. This ruling is not specifically for *mikvah* purposes; it concerns susceptibility to *tumah*. Only something recognized as a *mashkeh* can render other things susceptible to *tumah*, and *Rabbi Yaakov* holds that *mochal* carries this status.

### Initial Juice

But the same *baraita* immediately qualifies: *u'mah tam amru mochal hayotzei betchilah tahor?* — why then did they say that the initial runoff from an olive is *tahor* and does not become *tamei*? The answer is *l'fi she'eino rotzeh b'kiyumo* — because that initial runoff is something nobody retains; it is simply discarded. (The production of olive oil involves a complex process of crushing and pressing, and the first liquids that emerge in a non-processed way are not treated as a desired product.) What everyone throws away is not accorded formal liquid status.

### Shimon Disagrees

*Rabbi Shimon* takes the opposite position: *mochal eino k'mashkeh* — *mochal* does not have *mashkeh* status at all.

### Three Stages

Yet *Rabbi Shimon* himself must account for the fact that the *mochal* that comes out at the final stage of olive pressing — *mochal hayotzei me'ikar beit habad* — is universally agreed to be *tamei*. He explains: *l'fi she'lo efshar she'lo b'tzitzchei shemen* — at that stage, it is impossible that there are not small droplets of olive oil mixed in. So even *Rabbi Shimon* agrees that the late-stage *mochal* is *tamei* — not because it is itself a *mashkeh*, but because of the olive oil present in it.

### Middle Stage

This yields a clear picture of three stages: the initial runoff (universally *tahor*, because it is discarded and given no significance), the final press-house juice (universally *tamei*, either because it is itself a *mashkeh* per *Rabbi Yaakov*, or because of the olive-oil droplets per *Rabbi Shimon*), and a middle stage. This intermediate stage — *mochal* that comes out after the olives have been mounded and are under pressure but have not yet been formally pressed — would not contain olive oil droplets and is not simply discarded. It is this middle case that separates the positions.

### Mochal Debate

The debate between *Rabbi Yaakov* and *Rabbi Shimon*, then, concerns precisely this intermediate stage. *Rabbi Yaakov* holds that *mochal* has *mashkeh* status and therefore this intermediate juice is *tamei*. *Rabbi Shimon* denies *mochal* any *mashkeh* status and holds this intermediate juice is *tahor*, since it lacks olive oil droplets. *Rava* adds that in any case, to invalidate a *mikvah*, formal *mashkeh* status is not required — anything not suitable for a *mikvah* suffices — so the debate between *Rabbi Yaakov* and *Rabbi Shimon* about *mochal* as a *mashkeh* pertains to *tumah*, not necessarily to *mikvah* invalidation.

---

## Squeezing Into Food

### Pot vs Bowl

*Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel* teaches: *socheit adam eshkol shel anavim letoch hakadera aval lo letoch hake'arah* — a person may squeeze a cluster of grapes into a *kadera* (pot), but not into a *kearah* (bowl). This is striking: grapes and olives are the *d'oraisa* category, yet here the *Gemara* permits squeezing them. The reason is fundamental.

### Liquid to Food

When one squeezes a liquid onto food, the liquid effectively becomes food upon contact. Separating food from food — even if the intermediate form is liquid — is not the same as producing a *mashkeh*. It is analogous to cutting a slice from an apple: one is separating food from food, and that is permissible.

### Absorption Cases

The clearest case is when the juice is entirely absorbed by the food — for instance, squeezing a lemon onto fish without skin, where the juice soaks in completely. There it clearly does not exist independently as liquid once it has merged with the fish. Similarly, squeezing onto couscous that fully absorbs the juice creates a new food, not a separate liquid. Even when some juice runs along the side of the fish rather than being fully absorbed, the *halacha* — though it is not entirely explicit in the *Shulchan Aruch* — is that one may do so.

### Intent Cases

A less obvious case is squeezing onto a salad. The juice sits atop the salad rather than being absorbed into it, and retains its physical liquid form. Nevertheless, the ruling in practice is that anything added to give taste to food is considered part of the food, even if it physically remains liquid. Squeezing lemon onto a salad, because its purpose is to enhance the flavor of the food, is treated as producing food rather than a *mashkeh*. Squeezing into tea, by contrast, is adding flavor to a liquid, and therefore produces a liquid — a problem. One cannot squeeze lemon into soup for the same reason.

### Empty Pot

*Rashi*'s reading of the *Gemara* appears to go even further. The contrast in the text is between *kadera* (pot) and *kearah* (bowl) — not between food-containing and empty vessels. *Rashi* seems to suggest that even an empty pot suffices, because squeezing into a pot — by its very context — indicates that one intends to use the juice as an ingredient in food to be cooked. The context alone defines the product as food rather than liquid, even before any actual food is present. This is a more extreme position, and we do not rule in accordance with it. In practice, the ruling is that the juice must go directly into food. If one squeezes a lemon into a small pouring vessel first and then pours it over the fish, that is *assur* — the intermediate step, even if food is the ultimate destination, breaks the connection required for the juice to be classified as food rather than liquid. The *Chazon Ish*'s rejection of the common workaround — squeezing lemon into a spoonful of sugar before adding it to tea — follows this logic: since the intent is ultimately for the tea (a liquid), the intermediate food step does not help.

---

## Milking Rules

### Goat Milking

*Rav Chisda* draws an inference from *Shmuel*'s teaching: *cholev adam ez letoch hakadera velo letoch hake'arah* — by analogy to the grape-squeezing case, one may milk a goat directly over a pot but not into a bowl. Squeezing or milking into a pot indicates that the product is destined for food and thus takes on food status; milking into a bowl produces milk as an independent liquid.

### Tosafot Limit

*Tosafot* limits this ruling to *Yom Tov*: on *Shabbos*, one may not milk at all, even into a pot. This is a significant restriction, and it rests on an important conceptual foundation.

### Edible Source

*Tosafot*'s reasoning is as follows: the entire leniency of squeezing-into-food rests on the fact that when one produces *ochel* (food) from *ochel* (food), nothing qualitatively new has been created. The source is edible food, and the product is edible food — the act lacks significance as a creative act. But when one milks a goat on *Shabbos*, the goat is not *ochel*; it cannot be slaughtered and eaten on *Shabbos*. The goat is inedible in its current state. Therefore, whatever one produces from it — whether it ends up as food or liquid — is qualitatively different from the source, which is inedible. That distinction is sufficient to make the act of milking itself a violation on *Shabbos*, regardless of where the milk goes.

### Unripe Fruit

There is a *nafka mina* to *Tosafot*'s position: the case of squeezing unripe, inedible fruit. According to *Tosafot*, if the fruit being squeezed is itself inedible, then even if the juice goes directly into food, one would be *chayav* — because the permissibility of squeezing-into-food rests on the source being *ochel*, and here it is not. The source's inedibility removes the basis for the leniency entirely.

---

## Mikvah Susceptibility

### Liquid to Food

*Rami Bar Chama* cites the principle: *mashkeh haba le'ochel ochel hu* — liquid that goes into food is food. The question of *haba le'ochel* — whether this means liquid that has actually entered food, or liquid that is intended for food — is a matter of significance that runs through the subsequent cases.

### Zav Milking

*Rami Bar Chama* raises a difficulty against this principle. If a *zav* milks a goat — a *zav* transmits *tumah* not only through touch but through *heset*, moving or shifting an object — then the milk he causes to flow would be *tamei*, since he moves it in the act of milking. This seems straightforward. But the *Gemara* notes the following tension.

### Milk Paradox

If *mashkeh haba le'ochel ochel hu* — if milk destined for food acquires food status — then the milk being milked has *ochel* status, not *mashkeh* status. But then, how did the milk become susceptible to *tumah* in the first place? Food requires contact with a liquid (*mashkeh*) to become susceptible. If the milk is itself food, where is the liquid that rendered it susceptible? The milk can hardly render itself susceptible.

### Initial Drop

The *Gemara* resolves this by invoking *Rabbi Yochanan*'s teaching in a parallel case: *betippa meluchlechet al pi hadad* — there is a drop that sits on the surface of the udder before flowing out. *Hacha nami betippa meluchlechet al pi hadad* — here too, there is a small amount of milk on the nipple of the udder before milking begins. This initial drop is not included in what one intends to eat or use as food; it simply sits there at the opening. Since it is not designated for food consumption, it retains its default status as a *mashkeh*. That drop — as a *mashkeh* — renders the surrounding material susceptible to *tumah*. Everything that subsequently flows out passes through or alongside it, and thereby becomes susceptible. Once susceptible, the milk can become *tamei* through the *zav*'s *heset*.

### Impure Squeezing

*Ravina* raises a further case: *temei met shesachat zeitim va'anavim* — someone who is *tamei* from contact with a corpse (*avi hatumah*) is squeezing olives and grapes. Unlike the *zav*, this person transmits *tumah* only through direct contact, not through *heset*. Let us say he is squeezing out exactly a *kebeitzah* (egg's worth) of fruit.

### Juice Tumah

The fruit, while being handled, has not yet come into contact with a liquid. The person cannot make the fruit *tamei* by handling it — food requires liquid contact to become susceptible. He then squeezes out a small amount of liquid. That liquid now touches the remaining fruit, which could thereby become susceptible and then *tamei*. But the remaining fruit, at that point, is less than a *kebeitzah* — the minimum required to transfer *tumah* onward. Therefore, even though the fruit is now susceptible and *tamei* from the *tamei met*'s touch, it cannot make the liquid flowing out *tamei*, because it is too small. The liquid remains *tahor*. If, however, the fruit is more than a *kebeitzah*, then it would be sufficient to make the flowing liquid *tamei*.

But this analysis depends on the juice being classified as a *mashkeh* in the first place. If *mashkeh haba le'ochel ochel hu* applies here as well, the liquid has food status and cannot render the fruit susceptible — so the whole chain of susceptibility would not begin.

### Bowl Squeezing

*Ravina* answers his own question: *besochet letoch hake'arah* — the case under discussion is one where the person is squeezing into a bowl, not a pot. That is, this is a case of ordinary *sechita* to produce juice as a liquid, not squeezing into food. Therefore the juice retains full *mashkeh* status throughout, the chain of susceptibility functions as described, and the question of *mashkeh haba le'ochel* does not apply.

---

## Bread Gloss

### Grape Gloss
