The daf's analytical arc moves from a broad foundational question — when does access to food constitute prohibited vessel-creation? — through increasingly granular sub-categories. The opening *mishnah* establishes that destructive access to food is permitted when vessel-creation is not the intent. The *Gemara* then examines various configurations: holes in corks, holes in barrel-sides, the difference between tops and sides, and the distinction between making new holes and enlarging existing ones.

### Permitted

The daf permits a substantial range of acts: completely destroying the packaging or barrel to access food; cutting off the top of a barrel (even dramatically with a sword), which is understood as an act of display rather than functional vessel-creation; making a hole in the top of the cork, which does not constitute a standard functional opening; and reinserting a pre-cut pipe that had fallen from an existing hole.

### Prohibited

Prohibited are: making a hole in the side of the barrel in a manner that creates a standard functional pour-spout; smoothing wax over any hole (*memare'ach*); making any new hole, whether or not it rises to the biblical threshold of *boneh* — at minimum it is rabbinically prohibited; and folding a myrtle leaf to create a pipe-spigot, since the act of creating its functionality is itself the problem.

### Analytical Shift

Perhaps the most intellectually striking feature of the daf is the mid-discussion pivot in mode of analysis. The first part of the *sugya* examines the macro question of whether an act transforms a vessel's functional character — turning a storage barrel into a serving vessel. The latter part — particularly Rava's analysis — zooms in entirely on the micro-act of hole-making, classifying holes by directionality (two-directional holes are biblical; one-directional holes are rabbinic by *gezeira*) and ruling on expansion of existing holes through a chain of reasoning about chicken coops and weasels. These two frameworks — vessel-functionality and hole-taxonomy — are not always easy to reconcile, and the *Gemara* does not fully integrate them.

### Modern Cases

The daf's practical implications for contemporary Shabbat observance are considerable and genuinely unresolved at their edges. Disposable packaging — designed to be discarded after a single use — is significantly more lenient than the barrel of the *mishnah*, which was itself a genuine vessel before sealing. Many authorities hold that disposable packaging creates no vessel-creation concern at all. Resealable containers — designed after opening to be closed again and reused — present a far more serious problem, since the opening explicitly confers new functionality. The question of cans (tuna fish, soda) turns in large part on whether the sealed top is more analogous to protective wax (*l'shamer*) or to structural integration (*l'chazek*), and whether the can was a vessel before the top was applied. Given that all of these hole-making concerns may be rabbinic rather than biblical — a position that the *Gemara* by the latter part of the *amud bet* seems to lean toward — there is a basis for leniency in cases of genuine uncertainty. Nevertheless, practice varies considerably, and the *sugya* of 146 makes clear why: the underlying categories are subtle, the analogies to modern materials imperfect, and the two analytical frameworks of the daf not always pointing in the same direction.

---

---

# Shabbat 147

## Marit Ha'ayin

### Forbidden in Private

The daf opens at the very bottom of 146b, transitioning from the laws of food and opening packages to a range of practical *shabbat* applications. The final point of the *mishna* addressed a case where someone's clothes became soaking wet — whether from rain or from walking through water — and upon returning home wishes to remove them. He may lay them out in the sun to dry, but not in a visible location, since passersby will think he did laundry on *shabbat*.

Building on this, the *gemara* cites a ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *kol makom she-asru Chachamim mipnei marit ha'ayin, afilu be-chadrei chadarim asur* — wherever the Sages forbade something on account of appearances, it is forbidden even in one's innermost private chambers. The concern for how an action appears is not dependent on whether anyone is actually watching.

### Tannaitic Dispute

The *gemara* immediately questions this from our *mishna*, which says one may spread out the garments in the sun *but not in front of people* — implying that the prohibition is specifically in public. The *gemara* resolves this by noting that it is in fact a *tannaitic* dispute: a *baraita* records that while the first opinion limits the prohibition to public settings, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon extend the prohibition even to private chambers. The ruling we follow, requiring the prohibition even in private, is thus the more stringent *tannaitic* position.

It is worth noting, however, that this is not without dissent in the *rishonim*. The *Hilchos Gedolos* (*Behag*) rules that the prohibition applies only in public. We rule like the overwhelming majority position — even in private — but there is an interesting contemporary discussion regarding a case where the worst a bystander could think is that one is violating a *rabbinic* prohibition, as opposed to a biblical one. Some *poskim* hold that in such a case the concern for appearances applies only in public.

### Context & Intent

A critical distinction in the laws of *marit ha'ayin* is that the operative question is not whether anyone happens to be watching, but rather: *were* someone to observe this, what would it appear to be? Context can therefore dissolve the concern entirely. If one's raincoats are dripping wet and one hangs them in the bathroom to dry, no one would think laundry was being done on *shabbat* — that simply is not a *marit ha'ayin* problem. The context makes the situation self-explanatory. This is qualitatively different from a leniency based on the mere absence of observers: we do not permit something just because no one happens to be looking, but we do not prohibit it when context makes clear that no violation is being committed or suggested.

### Personal Sensibilities

One might ask why *marit ha'ayin* should be prohibited even in genuinely private circumstances where no human observer is present. One answer is pragmatic: one can never be entirely certain of privacy, and the concern applies as a precautionary matter. But there is a deeper reason as well. The concern for appearances is not solely about what other people will think, nor is it only about preventing others from drawing incorrect conclusions or becoming lenient about *aveiros*. It is also about one's own sensibilities and sense of personal boundaries. Performing an act that has all the outward appearance of being forbidden can itself compromise one's own relationship to the limits of *halacha*, regardless of whether any external observer is present. This is likely among the reasons why the prohibition holds even in private.

---

## Laundering & Garments

### Shaking Tallit

The *gemara* continues at the bottom of the page. Rav Huna rules: *hamenayer talit beShabbat chayav chatat* — one who shakes out his *tallit* on *shabbat* is liable for a *chatat* offering. This is the *melacha* of *kibus*, laundering, and the ruling is unambiguous.

Rashi explains this as *hamenayer talit min ha'afar* — shaking dust out of the garment; that, he says, constitutes its laundering (*libun*). Tosafot disagrees and cites Rabbeinu Chananel's reading that the reference is to dew (*tal*) — shaking the moisture out of the garment. It should be noted that in our printed text of Rabbeinu Chananel the reading actually aligns with Rashi's, referring to dust rather than dew, even if Tosafot cites him otherwise.

### Laundering Without Water

The deeper debate between Rashi and Tosafot concerns whether *libun* — laundering — can occur without the use of water. According to Rashi, vigorous shaking that effectively removes embedded dust or dirt from a garment constitutes *kibus* even without water. According to Tosafot, without water there is no *kibus*, and therefore shaking off dew is the better illustration because the water component is present.

Interestingly, Rashi himself elsewhere seemed to require water as part of *kibus*, and Rabbi Akiva Eiger points to the apparent tension. Here, however, Rashi takes the position that the effective removal of embedded dirt constitutes laundering regardless of whether water is involved.

From the perspective of Tosafot, one might genuinely ask: if a garment is soaking wet and you shake the moisture off, in what sense has it been laundered? The *gemara* elsewhere discusses *sechita* — squeezing — and there are opinions that squeezing water out of a garment constitutes *kibus* even without asking whether the garment is cleaner afterward. This may reflect a view that laundering is defined not only by the result but by participation in the stages of the laundering process: submerging in water, squeezing, drying. Each stage, on this view, is prohibited in its own right even if the garment does not emerge cleaner. Yet if one were to compare the two: taking soaking wet clothes and spreading them out in the sun to dry — as in our *mishna* — seems more clearly an act within the laundering process than simply shaking off surface moisture. The practical ruling follows Rashi overwhelmingly, which carries implications in both directions: *kibus* does not require water, but by the same token, a simple shaking off of surface moisture may not be the classic case.

### Qualifications

The *gemara* then introduces several important qualifications that substantially narrow the scope of the prohibition. First, *velo amru ella bechadti* — this applies only to new garments. Old garments (*atikei*) are not subject to the same concern. The reasoning is that the significance of the cleaning process is diminished when the garment itself is worn and unremarkable; there is no dramatic transformation, and the act does not rise to the level of meaningful *kibus*. This is not simply a matter of intent — even if one did not care much, that does not generally permit a prohibited act — but rather that without the typical laundering process (water, detergent, wringing), the prohibition only applies where one produces a dramatic, meaningful improvement in the garment's appearance. An old, worn garment does not meet that threshold.

Second, *velo amrin ela be-uchmin* — the prohibition applies particularly to black garments. White or red garments (*chivrei ve-sumkei*) are not subject to the same concern, because dust and dirt are far more visible on black, and thus the contrast between soiled and cleaned is far more pronounced. One might add that if the dirt itself were dark, the analysis would presumably shift even for a light-colored garment.

Third, *vehu dekpid alei* — all of this applies only where one is genuinely particular about cleanliness. Here too, the category of *kapid* is doing significant work: if one is not sufficiently *machpid* that the garment be clean to a meaningful degree, the act does not rise to the level of *kibus*. One might suggest that *kapid* means: one would not wear the garment in its dirty state, such that cleaning it constitutes a genuine transformation of use. The question of how these qualifications map onto contemporary fabrics, garment types, and types of soiling is one the *gemara* does not fully resolve.

### Ulla's Challenge

The *gemara* then relates that Ulla came to Pumbedita and observed rabbis shaking out their garments on *shabbat*. He declared: *kama machalin rabanan shabata* — the rabbis are desecrating *shabbat*! Rav Yehuda responded by instructing the students to go shake out their garments right in front of Ulla — demonstrating publicly that the local practice held this to be permitted. The justification: *anan lo kapdinan midi* — we are not particularly *machpid* about it. The implication is that they fell below the threshold of *kapid* that would render the act prohibited.

### Lo Kapdin

Similarly, Abaye was standing before Rav Yosef and asked for his hat. Rav Yosef saw that there was *tal* — either dew or, according to Rabbeinu Chananel, a stain of some kind — on the hat and hesitated to hand it over, apparently concerned that Abaye might shake it off on *shabbat*. Rav Yosef then said: *nefoz shadi* — shake it off, throw it. *Anan lo kapdinan midi* — we are not *machpid* about such things. Again, some middle level of concern that falls short of *kapid* does not trigger the prohibition.

### Surface vs. Deep

As a general principle, it emerges that lightly brushing something off the surface of a garment — where it is merely resting and not embedded — is not *kibus*. The prohibition begins when one is extracting dirt that is embedded within the fabric. The language of the *gemara*, however — *hamenayer*, shaking out — does sound like something more surface-level than deep scrubbing, a point that is not fully resolved.

---

## Carrying vs. Wearing

### Folded Tallit

Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *hayotzei betallis mekupeles munachas al kesefo beShabbos chayav chatat* — one who goes out on *shabbat* with a *tallit* folded up and placed on his shoulder is liable for carrying. It should be noted that *tallit* here does not refer to the ritual four-cornered garment with *tzitzis*, but to a general type of cape or cloak that was worn in that era. The normal manner of wearing this garment was to drape it so that it hung low behind the back. If instead one bundles it all up and has it sitting around one's neck or draped entirely over one shoulder — not flowing down in its normal configuration — that is no longer considered wearing; it is considered carrying. Even though the garment is technically on the body, the configuration determines the *halakhic* category.

### Merchants & Pouches

A *baraita* confirms this: *socharei kesus hayotzin betallisos mekupallos umunachos al kispheihem beShabbos chayavin chatas* — garment merchants who go out with their cloaks folded over and resting on their shoulders on *shabbat* are liable for *chatat*. The *baraita* clarifies that it is not only merchants who are subject to this rule — it is anyone who wears a *tallit* in this configuration. The merchants are singled out because it is their characteristic manner of transporting goods, which illustrates that the folded-over configuration is inherently one of carrying rather than wearing.

Similarly, a storekeeper who goes out with coins bound up in his cloak — essentially a money pouch fashioned from the garment — is liable. Again, the rule extends to anyone who carries objects in this fashion, not only storekeepers. This manner of bearing objects is defined as carrying, not wearing.

### Runners Exception

There is an exception: *rattanim* — messengers or runners — may go out on *shabbat* with their *sudar* (a type of scarf or head covering) folded up and resting on their shoulders. And again, the *baraita* notes this is not limited to runners — anyone may do so — but runners are cited as the characteristic case because this is their normal manner of wearing such a garment.

Why is this different from the merchants' case? The distinction lies in whether the configuration constitutes a normal mode of *wearing* or merely a mode of *transporting* the object on the body. For runners, wearing the *sudar* in this gathered or rolled configuration is a recognized manner of wearing it — analogous to the different ways one might wrap a scarf — and therefore it qualifies as wearing, not carrying. One might have thought that because runners specifically adopt this configuration to keep the garment from falling off during rapid movement, it is a functional choice rather than a genuine wearing position. The *chiddush* is that even so, if this is a recognized way in which people wear such a garment, it is defined as wearing.

### Horkenos Story

Rav Yehuda related that Horkenos the son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Horkenos once went out on *shabbat* with his *sudar* on his shoulder, with a string wound around his finger — apparently to help secure the garment. When the matter came before the Sages, they ruled: even without a string wound around the finger, this is a recognized manner of wearing the *sudar* and requires no additional securing. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak stated in the name of Rav Chisda that this is the accepted *halacha*: one need not wind any string around one's finger, for simply wearing the *sudar* in this folded configuration is sufficient.

### Folding & Creasing

The *gemara* then records that Ulla came to the house of Assi bar Hini, and those present asked: *mahu laasot marzev beShabbat* — what is the law regarding making a *marzev* on *shabbat*? In the context of garments, Rashi understands *marzev* to mean creating permanent creases or folds in a garment — deliberately shaping it in a lasting way. Tosafot, together with the Rambam, understand the question differently: it concerns whether folding a garment in a particular configuration constitutes a manner of *wearing* it or whether it is merely a way of *bundling* it so it does not fall off, which would make it carrying. The discussion, on Tosafot's reading, is entirely continuous with the preceding analysis.

Ulla replied that Rebbi had ruled it is forbidden to make a *marzev* on *shabbat*. The *gemara* then asks: what is a *marzev*? Rav Zera explains: *kisei bavlayita* — the pleated pouches of the Babylonians; i.e., pleated or creased folds in the fabric.

A vivid illustrative exchange follows. Rav Yirmiyah was sitting before Rav Zera and asked: what if I do it *this* way — is it permitted? Forbidden, said Rav Zera. What about *this* way? Also forbidden. The precise configurations are lost to us since the text only records the exchange without the visual demonstration.

Rav Papa then offers a unifying principle: *kol adaata delechnufei, assur; kol deleitnaot, shari* — anything done with the intent to bundle the garment up is forbidden; anything done to make it look attractive is permitted. According to Rashi, *lechnufei* means creating permanent creases in the garment as an end in itself, as opposed to simply arranging it attractively for one's appearance at that moment. According to the Rambam and Tosafot, *lechnufei* means bundling the garment up to keep it off the ground or to prevent it from falling off while moving — which, as argued above, renders it carrying rather than wearing. If the purpose is that the garment looks its best in that configuration on one's body, it is wearing; if the purpose is to bundle or secure it, it is carrying.

The point at which a garment goes from being worn to being carried on one's body is genuinely difficult to define visually. One may still be wearing the garment while bearing it in a non-standard configuration — the question is when that configuration crosses the line. The Rambam's view, for instance, is that lifting a hem to avoid a puddle is not problematic, because one is still wearing the garment. But rolling the entire garment up and changing its fundamental configuration — so that it no longer hangs and drapes in any normal sense — may be carrying. The analogy to a *tallit* worn to *shul* in a place without an *eruv* is instructive: wearing it draped in its normal manner is permissible; wearing it bundled up around the neck is not.

### Rebbi's Folded Tallit

Rav Dimi reported: once Rebbi — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — went out to the field with the two edges of his *tallit* folded and resting on his shoulders. Yehoshua ben Ziruz — identified as the son of the father-in-law of Rabbi Meir — said to Rebbi with diplomatic indirection: would not Rabbi Meir render one liable for a *chatat* in this situation? Rebbi was apparently taken aback — *dikdik Rebbi Meir ad kan?* — Rabbi Meir would be so precise as to require a *chatat* even in this case? Nevertheless, *shilshel Rebbi talliso* — Rebbi lowered his *tallit* and redraped it in its normal configuration, thus conforming to Rabbi Meir's position.

When Ravin later came, he reported an alternate version of the story: it was not Yehoshua ben Ziruz but Yehoshua ben Kupsai, and the challenge was not invoking Rabbi Meir but Rabbi Akiva — *b'zu lo chiyyeiv Rebbi Akiva chattas?* Rebbi's reaction was the same — *dikdik Rebbi Akiva ad kan?* — and he again redraped his *tallit*.

A third version, brought by Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda, holds that the story was not about Rebbi actually wearing his *tallit* this way, but about Rebbi posing the question in the abstract — whether this would be permitted. This version apparently addresses the discomfort of the narrative in the other versions, which could be read as implying that Rebbi had unwittingly violated *shabbat* according to Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Akiva.

---

## Bathing & Towels

### Hot Water Immersion

The *gemara* next addresses bathing on *shabbat*. The *mishna* mentions bathing in cave water or in the hot springs of Tiberias. The *gemara* notes that cave water is compared to the springs of Tiberias — both are hot — which suggests that immersion in hot water is being discussed. The general rabbinic rule is that immersion in hot water heated by fire is forbidden on *shabbat*, lest it lead to going to bathhouses and heating water on *shabbat*. Hot springs that are naturally heated — like Mei Tverya — are permitted. Accordingly, the *gemara* explains that *harochetz* — "one who bathed" — is formulated in the past tense (*bediavad*) to indicate that one was not supposed to have immersed in fire-heated hot water, even if it was heated before *shabbat*.

### Single Person Towel

The *mishna* then addresses drying off: *afilu be-eser aluntiyos, lo yevi'em b'yado* — even if one used ten towels to dry off, a single person may not bring them home. The concern is *sechita*: carrying a wet towel creates a risk that one will come to squeeze it. Even ten towels, each of which absorbs less water individually, do not resolve the concern when a single person is carrying them.

### Multiple People Towel

However: *aval asara benei adam, mistapkim b'aluntis achas* — ten people who dry themselves with a single towel, which becomes thoroughly wet, *mevi'in otan b'yadam* — may bring it home in their hands. The reason: since many people are involved, they will remind one another not to squeeze the towel. This is a general principle in *halakha* — when a group acts together, we are less concerned about inadvertent violations, because the collective serves as a check on individual lapse. This principle parallels the teaching at the end of the first *perek* of the tractate, where placing the *korban pesach* in the oven near *shabbat* is permitted in part because a group is involved and they remind one another.

---

## Oil & Body Care (III)

### Anointing Oil

The *mishna* continues: *sakhnin u'memashmeshin* — one may anoint the body with oil and spread it gently. This is permitted on *shabbat*.

### Vigorous Massage

However, *aval lo misamlin* — vigorous rubbing or massage is forbidden. Such intense physical manipulation is either associated with *refuah* — healing — or constitutes *uvda d'chol*, a weekday-type activity. Even absent oil, a vigorous massage would similarly be problematic.

A *baraita* specifies: one may anoint the stomach (*bnei mei'in*) and massage it gently on *shabbat*, provided one does not do it in the manner one does on a weekday — so as to avoid *uvda d'chol*. The question of which activities fall into the category of *uvda d'chol* is not always transparent; here, what exactly constitutes the weekday manner is ambiguous. If the concern were *refuah*, the framing as *uvda d'chol* would be puzzling; and if it is *uvda d'chol*, the specific mention of the stomach — which has medicinal connotations — is noteworthy.

### Scraping Skin

*Velo misgarerin* — one may not use a scraper on the skin. After anointing with oil, it was common to use a metal scraper to remove the oil from the body. Such scrapers, illustrated vividly in ancient archaeological finds, resembled small spoon-shaped implements in various sizes mounted on a ring. Using them on *shabbat* is forbidden, apparently because of *refuah* or *uvda d'chol*. An exception applies, as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules, if the legs are caked with dried mud or excrement (*tit uvetzoah*) — in that case, *gored kedarko* — one may scrape it off in the normal manner without concern, since this is simply cleaning rather than a therapeutic act on the skin itself.

The *gemara* notes that the mother of Shmuel bar Yehuda had a silver scraper made for him, specifically for use on *shabbat*. Rashi understands this as a specially designated *shabbat* implement. The reasoning may be that a dedicated, ornamental silver scraper is less evocative of the weekday professional procedure, thus reducing the *uvda d'chol* concern — though one may fairly observe that the act itself remains similar regardless of the instrument's material.

---

## Bathing Locations

### Muddy Rivers

*Ein yordin leKardumisa* — one may not descend into the river Kardumisa. The reason: *mishum pika* — because of the mud, one may slip and fall, causing one's garments to become entirely soaked with muddy water. The concern is the resulting need to wring them out or the general dishevelment and damage that would follow.

---

## Medical Treatments

### Broken Bones

*Ve'ein machzirin es hashever* — one may not reset a broken bone on *shabbat*. This falls under the prohibition of *refuah* on *shabbat*. Strikingly, the *mishna* categorizes this as a standard *issur refuah* rather than as a life-threatening emergency requiring the overriding of *shabbat*. In practice today, however, we would immediately classify such a patient as a *choleh kol haguf*, and all the relevant prohibitions of *refuah* would not apply. Our scope of applying *issur refuah* is far narrower than the *mishna*'s categorical treatment would suggest.

### Dislocated Limbs

*Mi shenifreka yado veraglo* — someone with a dislocated arm or leg may not plunge the limb into cold water, which would apparently reduce swelling and pain. However, *aval rochetz hu kedarko* — one may wash normally. And: *ve'im nisrape nisrape* — if one heals in the process, so be it — provided the act itself does not take on the overt character of a therapeutic procedure. Again, practically, we would consider any person with a dislocated limb to fall well within the category of *choleh kol haguf*, and the analysis would proceed accordingly. The *mishna*'s placement of these cases within the category of *issur refuah* remains somewhat difficult to explain within modern *halakhic* practice.

---

## Bathing & Towels (II)

### Shower vs. Immerse

The *gemara* now draws out a distinction from the *mishna*'s phrasing. The *mishna* speaks of bathing in cave water *similar to* the hot springs of Tiberias; the *gemara* notes: just as Mei Tverya is hot, so too here. This implies hot water is involved, yet immersion in fire-heated hot water is rabbinically forbidden on *shabbat*. The *gemara* resolves: *harochetz diavad in, lechatchila lo* — "one who bathed" implies that this was *bediavad*; one should not have immersed in fire-heated hot water to begin with.

From this a further inference follows: *mikal d'lehishtatef kol gufo afilu lechatchila shapir dami* — pouring or showering hot water over one's entire body would be permitted even *lechatchila*. The rabbinic decree (*gezeirat merchata'ot*) was directed at immersing in hot water in a bathhouse context, which would lead to heating water on *shabbat*. It was not directed at showering.

A *baraita* records the dispute explicitly. Rabbi Meir forbids showering (*lehishtatef*) in either hot or cold water. Rabbi Shimon permits it entirely. Rabbi Yehuda holds that hot water is forbidden and cold water is permitted. The practical *halakha* follows the view that showering — as opposed to immersing — is technically not included in the original decree. This is the basis on which contemporary discussions of hot water use in apartment buildings on *shabbat* proceed, with various qualifications depending on the specific setup. The prohibition as applied to showering is a separate question involving concerns about *sechita* (hair), the use of liquid soap, and related issues — but the fundamental *gezeirah* of *merchata'ot* relates to immersion.

The *gemara* then returns to the drying question: *venistapeg afilu be-asara alunti'ot* — one may dry off even with ten towels. The *gemara* explains that both the opening clause and the closing clause of the *mishna* teach a *chiddush*. The opening clause teaches that even with ten towels — where each one holds relatively little water — since it is one individual, there remains a concern he will come to squeeze them, and he may not carry them home. The closing clause teaches that even with one towel shared by ten people — which becomes quite wet — since they are many, they remind one another, and there is no concern they will come to squeeze it.

### Bringing Towels Home

A *baraita* is cited: *mistapeg adam be-aluntit u-menichah be-chalon* — one may dry off with a towel and place it in the window to dry. This is not considered *kibus* (laundering), and people understand the towel became wet from use on *shabbat* rather than from washing. The *baraita* adds that one may not hand the towel to bathhouse attendants (*ulyarin*), because they are suspect to wring it out.

### Rabbi Shimon Lenient

Rabbi Shimon takes a more permissive position: *mistapeg be-aluntit achat u-mevia be-yado le-toch beito* — one may dry off with a single towel and carry it home. This disagrees with the *mishna*'s ruling that one person may not carry towels home. Abaye asked Rav Yosef: how do we rule? Rav Yosef responded by listing the authorities who permit it: Rabbi Shimon, Rebbi, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan. Given such a consensus, the ruling is *muttar*.

The *gemara* then questions how Rabbi Yochanan can rule against a *stam mishna* — Rabbi Yochanan's general principle being that we rule in accordance with an anonymous *mishna*. The resolution: Rabbi Yochanan's version of the *mishna* attributed the stringent ruling to Ben Hachinai by name, not as an anonymous ruling. Having it attributed removes it from the status of *stam mishna*, and the majority view permits bringing the towel home.

### Students Story

Rebbi himself is cited from a *baraita*: when we were learning Torah from Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa — presumably Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai — we would carry oil and towels from courtyard to roof and from roof to an enclosed yard until reaching the wellspring where we bathed on *shabbat*. The *gemara* understands this as evidence that each individual could carry his own towel. Tosafot note that the reasoning may be connected to the fact that students of a rabbi are assumed to follow their master's practice, and therefore Rebbi's personal involvement implies that each individual was permitted to do so. Shmuel's ruling is recorded via Rav Yehuda: one may dry oneself and bring the towel home. Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is recorded by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: the *halacha* is that one may dry oneself and bring the towel home.

---

## Carrying vs. Wearing (II)

### Scarf Below Shoulders

The *gemara* returns to the question of wearing a *sudar* in a way that does not constitute carrying. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *lemata mikispayim* — it must be tied or arranged below the shoulders (specifically, below the shoulder blades). If the garment is not secured below that point, it is not considered properly worn.

Rava applied this practically to the inhabitants of Mechuza. When they were required to bring garments to the troops on *shabbat* — a compulsory service that created an unavoidable carrying concern — Rava told them: *sharvivu behu lemata mikispayim* — drape the garments down below your shoulders. By ensuring the garments hang below the shoulder blades, they are being worn rather than carried, thus minimizing the *chillul shabbat* as much as possible.

---

## Oil & Body Care (III)

### Method Debate

The *gemara* returns to the question of anointing on *shabbat* and the dispute about how to do so in a manner that is not *uvda d'chol*. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina rules: *sach ve-achar kach memashmesh* — first anoint and then rub, because on weekdays the order is reversed — first rub and then anoint. By reversing the order one avoids doing it in the weekday manner. Rabbi Yochanan rules: *sach u'memashmesh be-vas achas* — anoint and rub simultaneously, rather than doing them sequentially as one does during the week.

The nature of the *uvda d'chol* concern here is admittedly unclear. The classic cases of *uvda d'chol* involve either activities associated with *melachos* or activities associated with professional labor. What exactly makes the sequential anointing-and-rubbing process resemble weekday labor is not self-evident. It may be that specifically regarding the stomach (*bnei mei'in*), the concern shades into *refuah*, which would explain the emphasis on doing it differently than on a weekday. But if the concern were *refuah*, one might expect the language of *uvda d'chol* to be replaced by or supplemented with *refuah* language. The category remains somewhat opaque.

---

## Bathing Locations (II)

### Hot Springs Healing

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: it is forbidden to stand on the floor of a *dyumeset* on *shabbat*, because it causes one to sweat (*me'amelet*) and thereby heals. The concern is not the sweating per se but the deliberate use of the *dyumeset*'s properties as a therapeutic process — which constitutes a *maaseh refuah* on *shabbat*. Whether something that can also be done in a non-therapeutic context would be permitted even by a sick person if done without medicinal intent is a legitimate question; context and intent would presumably be relevant.

### Dyumeset Waters

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: the period during which the *dyumeset* is therapeutically beneficial is twenty-one days, and *Atzeret* — *Shavuos* — is included in that count. The *gemara* asks: is *Shavuos* the beginning or the end of the twenty-one day period? A proof is attempted from a statement of Shmuel: all beverages are salubrious from the period of the *Zevach* — i.e., from Pesach — until *Shavuos*. This implies that *Shavuos* is the end-point of the beneficial period. However, the *gemara* deflects the proof: perhaps beverages are more beneficial when the world is cooler, and *Shavuos* marks the end of the cool season. But the *dyumeset* is effective because of its steam and heat, and therefore it may be more beneficial as the world gets hotter — meaning *Shavuos* could be the beginning of its effective period rather than the end. The question is left unresolved.

### Rabbi Elazar Story

Rabbi Chelbo then introduces an *aggadic* observation: the wine of Prugeita and the waters of Dyumeset *kipchu aseret hashvatim mi'Yisrael* — they caused the ten tribes to be cut off from Israel, meaning that these great indulgences led to a life of excess that caused them to abandon Torah and their spiritual heritage.

Immediately illustrating this principle, the *gemara* relates: Rabbi Elazar ben Arach happened to come to Prugeita and was drawn after its exceptional wine. *V'imshich batreihu* — he was pulled in its wake. *I'akar talmudo* — his learning was uprooted. He forgot everything he had learned. When he finally returned, he arose to read from the *Sefer Torah* and wished to read the *pasuk* *Hachodesh hazeh lachem* — "this month is to you," the very first commandment given to *Klal Yisrael*. Instead, he read *Hacheresh haya libam* — "their hearts became stopped up," like a deaf-mute. The words look similar in script, and his processing of the text had so deteriorated that he misread even this foundational verse.

The rabbis prayed for him, and his learning was miraculously restored. Yet the story is a stark illustration of the dangers of indulgence and isolation. It is noteworthy that what he read — *hacheresh haya libam* — is not merely a misreading but an unwitting self-description: his heart had become blocked, unable to receive Torah.

### Torah Community

The *gemara* connects this to the *mishna* in Pirkei Avos where Rabbi Nehorai teaches: *hevei gole le'makom Torah* — exile yourself to a place of Torah. Do not remain where it is comfortable and indulgent; be prepared to give up creature comforts for an environment of Torah learning. And: *ve'al tomar she'hi tavo acharecha* — do not say that Torah will follow you wherever you go, that students will come to you. Why? *She'chaveirecha yekaymuha beyadecha* — your colleagues are what maintain your Torah in your hands. One cannot be self-sufficient; one needs the environment, the peers, the constant engagement of a Torah community to remain sharp. *Ve'al binatcha al tish'en* — do not rely on your own intellect alone. You need your friends, your colleagues, the place of Torah.

A *baraita* then adds that Rabbi Nehorai was not actually named Nehorai — his real name was Rabbi Nechemia, and some say Rabbi Elazar ben Arach himself. This is striking: the person who issued the warning about the necessity of the Torah community may have been the same one who experienced its loss most devastatingly. His name *Nehorai* — from the root meaning light — was given because *sheme'ir einei chachamim bahalacha* — he would illuminate the eyes of the sages in *halacha*. He was the great luminary. And yet when he went to a place where the wine was too good and the Torah sages were absent, even he lost his Torah.

---

## Oil & Body Care (III)…

### Silver Scraper

The *gemara* records that Shmuel bar Yehuda's mother had a silver scraper made for him. Rashi understands this as a *shabbat*-specific implement — a dedicated silver tool for use on *shabbat*. The apparent reasoning is that an ornamental silver scraper is less evocative of the weekday professional procedure and thus may mitigate the *uvda d'chol* concern. As one might fairly note: the act itself is the same regardless of the implement's material. The silver designation signals that this is a *shabbat* implement and thus perhaps shifts the framing from weekday-type activity to something fitting the sanctity of the day — though the concern does not disappear entirely.

---

## Medical Treatments (II)

### Purgatives

*Ve'ein osin apiktvizin beShabbat* — one may not take a purgative on *shabbat*. Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: this prohibition applies specifically to a medicinal substance (*sam*) that one drinks to induce vomiting. However, sticking one's finger in one's throat to induce vomiting is *muttar*. This distinction is initially puzzling — why is the manual method not equally a *maaseh refuah*?

### Waste Concern

The answer is suggested by the next line. Rav Nechemia taught: in fact, even on a weekday it is forbidden to vomit in order to eat more — because it constitutes *hefsed ochlin*, wasteful destruction of food. The fact that the concern is about wasting food — rather than about healing — reveals that inducing vomiting with one's finger is not categorized as *refuah* at all. It is a gluttonous practice, done to enable further eating at a banquet. A liquid purgative, by contrast, is associated with a medical process and thus falls under *issur refuah* on *shabbat*. That the *gemara* frames the concern solely as food waste without reference to the moral dimension of gluttony is itself noteworthy.

### Minor's Limbs

*Ve'ein me'atzvin et hakatan* — one may not *me'atzvim* (arrange or align) the limbs of a minor. Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: however, *lelapufi yanuka beShabbata shapir dami* — a different type of alignment or bundling of a baby's limbs (*lipuf*) is permitted. The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: the *mishna*'s prohibition specifically concerns aligning the spine — *shatzedei bechumrei shidra demichzi kevoneh* — which resembles the act of building, structuring the skeletal frame. Other arrangements or bundling of a minor's limbs that do not rise to that level remain permitted.

### Choleh Leniency

Here again, the *gemara*'s categorical treatment is striking in light of contemporary practice. We would immediately classify any patient requiring bone-setting, limb-resetting, or spinal manipulation as at minimum a *choleh kol haguf* — and in most such cases the patient would likely qualify as *choleh sheyesh bo sakana*. In either case, the *issur refuah* does not apply. Even for a *choleh she'ein bo sakana*, we are *matir* even rabbinic prohibitions based on the circumstances. The practical upshot is that the *mishna*'s categorical prohibitions in this area are far narrower in application than they appear, and the question of how to explain what the *mishna* was addressing — given the narrowness of how we apply *issur refuah* today — remains genuinely difficult.

---

---

# Shabbat 148

## Bathing & Immersion

### Hot Water Rules

Today's daf is 148. Before proceeding to new material, it is worth spending a moment on the *halakhot* that emerged from the previous shiur, particularly around bathing.

The *mishna* there reflects the position of Rabbi Shimon, who permits bathing in hot water — but that ruling applies to *Yom Tov*, not *Shabbat*. On *Shabbat*, based on an earlier *gemara* that addressed the *issur* of bathing in hot water at length, the conclusion recorded in the *Shulchan Aruch*, the Rambam, and virtually all authorities is that bathing the entire body in hot water is prohibited — even by shower — due to concern that people would go to bathhouses and heat water on *Shabbat*. The relevant distinction is therefore as follows: washing individual limbs in preheated hot water is permitted, as is bathing the entire body in cold water; bathing the entire body in hot or warm water is not permitted, regardless of whether it takes the form of a bath or a shower.

A practical question arises about lukewarm water. Since producing lukewarm water requires mixing hot water with cold, and the hot water has been drawn on *Shabbat*, the prohibition appears to derive not merely from the temperature of the water as such, but from the use of the hot water itself. This suggests that even a warm shower remains problematic on *Shabbat* — which is of course what everyone practices. The underlying concern in all of these cases traces back to the *gezeira* regarding bathhouses.

On *Yom Tov* the analysis is different and rests on the concept of *tzorach kol haguf*. Since the majority of people — at least in America — bathe daily with hot water, many *poskim*, including this one, hold that a hot shower on *Yom Tov* is permitted. Even then, one must be careful not to squeeze out one's towel or hair.

### Immersion Customs

What about swimming on *Shabbat*? For *Ashkenazim*, there is a *minhag* going back roughly eight hundred years not to immerse the entire body even in cold water — whether in a bath, a swimming pool, or otherwise — with the sole exception of *mikveh*. The concern is incidental consequences such as squeezing hair or squeezing a towel. *Sefardim*, by contrast, do permit swimming on *Shabbat* provided one does not squeeze anything out. The *Ashkenazi minhag* forecloses the activity entirely due to the concern that one might come to do so. When there are health concerns, the rules differ.

### Removing Dirt

The previous shiur also addressed the question of removing dirt and stains from garments. Although the *gemara* there introduces qualifications — new garments, black garments, and the like — those qualifications must be read alongside an earlier *gemara* that prohibits rubbing a garment vigorously to remove embedded stains, regardless of the garment's type. How are these reconciled?

One approach holds that a genuine stain or something that truly embeds itself in the fabric is prohibited regardless of the garment type, while something trivial like dust presents a problem only with a new black garment where it is conspicuous. A second approach locates the difference in the manner of removal: vigorous rubbing is always prohibited, while a more casual wipe may only be problematic in certain circumstances.

In practice, the operative principle is this: removing something from the *surface* of a garment is generally permitted; rubbing out an embedded stain is problematic. Crusted matter may be scraped off the surface, but once one is working to extract a stain from within the fabric itself, that crosses the line. The use of water, it should be noted, is a separate concern entirely.

The term *makpid* as used in the earlier *gemara* means that the stain is so bad one would not wear the garment without removing it. Those severe restrictions apply more to trivial matters like dust. When one is genuinely working to extract something embedded, the prohibition applies regardless of those qualifications.

---

## Broken Bones

### Bone Restoration

The *mishna* states *ein machzirin et hashever* — one may not restore a broken bone on *Shabbat*. This is a striking ruling, since one might have expected that a broken bone would constitute at minimum a *sakanat eiver* and thus be treated with considerable leniency. Nevertheless, the *mishna* prohibits restoring it.

The *gemara* immediately introduces the view of Shmuel: Rav Chanana bar Taltiya cited Shmuel as ruling *halacha machzirin et hashever* — the *halacha* is that one may restore a broken bone. This is not an opposing *tannaic* source, not a *baraita* or a competing *mishna*, but simply Shmuel's personal ruling against the *mishna*.

### Rabbah's Encounter

The *gemara* then relates that Rabbah bar bar Chana came to Pumbedita but did not attend Rav Yehuda's *shiur*. Rav Yehuda dispatched his attendant — *Rashi* glosses *Ada Dayala* as some type of assistant — with instructions to compel Rabbah bar bar Chana to come. The attendant did so, essentially forcing him to attend. Upon arrival, Rabbah bar bar Chana found Rav Yehuda expounding the *mishna's* ruling: *ein machzirin et hashever*, you may not restore the bone on *Shabbat*. Rabbah bar bar Chana told him: Rav Chanana bar Taltiya said in the name of Shmuel that the *halacha* is *machzirin et hashever* — we do not rule like the *mishna*.

Rav Yehuda's response is telling. He says: Chana of ours — referring to Chana bar Taltiya who was from Pumbedita — and Shmuel of ours. Both the transmitter and the one in whose name it was said were from our own community, *v'lo shmia li* — and I never heard this teaching! *Rashi* reads Rav Yehuda's conclusion — was it not justified that I forced you to come? — as a genuine expression of gratitude. Because of this forced encounter, the entire academy was enlightened by a teaching that had circulated in their own community without reaching them.

### Dislocation Rules

The *gemara* then shifts from broken bones to dislocated limbs. The *mishna* rules that if one's hand or foot has been dislocated, one may not compress it in cold water, though one may wash it in the normal manner — and if it heals, it heals.

The *gemara* records that Rav Avya was sitting before Rav Yosef and made an unusual movement with his arm, asking: if one's hand is positioned like this, what may be done? Rav Yosef ruled it forbidden. He tried another position — also forbidden. In the process, Rav Avya actually injured his own hand. Rav Yosef then asked: what exactly was your question? The *mishna* already rules on this: one who has a dislocated hand or foot may not compress it in cold water but may wash it normally, and if it heals it heals. Why were you asking all these variations?

Rav Avya explained his reasoning: the *mishna* also says *ein machzirin et hashever*, and Shmuel ruled *machzirin et hashever*. If you can restore a broken bone, perhaps the same leniency should apply to a serious dislocation. Rav Yosef's reply was sharp: *kulehu bechada machta machtinhu* — do you think everything is bundled together into a single ruling? *Heicha d'itmar itmar v'heicha d'lo itmar lo itmar.* Where it was said, it was said; where it was not said, it was not said. Shmuel's leniency was limited to broken bones; there is no extension to dislocated limbs. The *halacha* regarding dislocation is construed strictly.

### Theory vs. Practice

This is quite difficult to understand from our vantage point. One can see why a broken bone might be considered more serious than a dislocation, but it is hard to understand either prohibition in light of the way *halacha* is actually ruled today. The accepted *pesak* is that even for a *choleh she'ein bo sakanah* — someone who is ill without danger to life — one may perform acts of healing on *Shabbat*, and may even violate other rabbinic restrictions (with questions about exactly how directly a *Yisrael* may violate a rabbinic prohibition and whether *amirah l'akum* suffices, but substantial leniencies exist). Someone with a broken bone or a dislocated shoulder would almost certainly fall into the category of *choleh kol haguf*, not *michush b'alma* — a mere minor discomfort.

It is therefore quite striking that both the *mishna* and the *gemara* take such strict positions here. The *gemara* does show an initial move toward leniency at least in the most extreme cases, and in practice contemporary *pesak* is quite lenient across this category. How precisely one gets from the *gemara's* strictness to current leniency is a question that would require a careful look at how the *rishonim* and *acharonim* explain and develop this *gemara*.

This concludes *Perek Chavit*, which covered food-related matters — some *de'oraita*, some *de-rabanan* — including concerns around squeezing food, squeezing a towel, bathing, clothing, and, at the end, *refuah*.

---

## Borrowing Loans

### Mishnah Cases

The next *perek* opens with *sho'el adam m'chaveiro* — one may borrow from a friend on *Shabbat* pitchers of wine or oil, provided one does not use the word *halveini* — "lend me." Similarly, a woman may borrow loaves of bread from her neighbor. The *mishna's* explicit identification of women in this context reflects the common halakhic literary practice of writing with men as the default subject; where a woman is the relevant actor in a common scenario, she is explicitly identified. This carries no legal significance: the rules are the same. Sometimes the *mishna* simply illustrates with representative cases — wine and oil as things men might deal with, bread as something associated with women's domestic domain. One should not read legal significance into the choice of examples where the *gemara* itself does not do so.

### Collateral Rules

The *mishna* continues: if the lender does not trust the borrower — he is worried the borrower will forget or fail to repay — he may have the borrower leave a garment (*tallis*) with him, and they settle accounts after *Shabbat*. One might initially ask whether this constitutes a *pikadon* — a formal deposit against a debt, which would be explicitly transactional in character. The key distinction is one of framing and context. Ordinarily, leaving collateral is the hallmark of a formal financial transaction: you owe me one hundred dollars, here is something of value as security. Here, the framing is entirely different: you leave your watch by me, and you pick it up after *Shabbat* — the settling of accounts is deferred and informal.

Crucially, the *gemara* will shortly clarify that the entire rabbinic concern in this area is not that commerce is intrinsically incompatible with *Shabbat* at the rabbinic level, but rather that these activities may lead to writing — a *de'oraita* violation. If that is so, then taking a *mashkon* makes excellent sense: the very existence of the collateral obviates the need for a written record. Even a more explicitly transactional arrangement might be acceptable if the *issur* is only about writing and not about commerce itself.

### She'ilah vs. Halva'ah

There is a significant distinction between *she'eilah* and *halva'ah*, and the *rishonim* understand it differently. *Rashi* holds that *shoel* implies borrowing for a short period with prompt return, whereas *loveh* implies a longer-term arrangement, creating greater concern that the parties will want to document the transaction. *Tosafot* offers what is arguably the more intuitive explanation: *she'eilah* — *shoel* — refers to borrowing a durable object that will be returned as itself. If you borrow my car, you return my car. *Halva'ah* — *loveh* — refers to borrowing something fungible that will be consumed: I lend you one hundred dollars, you spend it, and you return a different one hundred dollars. The paradigm of *halva'ah* is monetary lending, but it applies to anything fungible.

This distinction matters enormously for our *mishna*. When one borrows two eggs from a neighbor, technically this is *halva'ah*: you are not going to return the same two eggs, you will return two equivalent eggs. Yet the *mishna* permits it with the language of *she'eilah*. *Tosafot* explains that although the transaction is technically *halva'ah* in substance, framing it in the language of *she'eilah* — especially when it involves a physical object being taken and an equivalent returned — strongly suggests the domestic, short-term, non-commercial register. Things that are used and given back do not naturally call for documentation. Things that are spent and replaced do. By using the language of *she'eilah*, even if technically imprecise, one places the transaction in a category that does not lead to writing.

### Language Distinctions

The *gemara* poses the question directly: Rabbah bar Rav Chanan asked Abaye — what is the practical difference between saying *hashileini* and *halveini*? The *mishna* restricts the language, but why should the choice of words matter?

Abaye answers plainly: *hashileini lo ati l'michtav* — using the language of *hashileini* does not lead to writing it down; *halveini ati l'michtav* — *halveini* does lead to writing it down. This confirms what had already been suggested: the *Bavli* frames the concern around these business-adjacent activities on *Shabbat* not as an intrinsic problem but as a *gezeira* lest it lead to the *de'oraita* violation of writing. One could have argued that commercial-sounding language is intrinsically problematic because it evokes the world of *mekach umimkar* — commerce and transactions — which is antithetical to the spirit of *Shabbat*. The *Bavli*, characteristically, prefers to anchor the prohibition in concern for a consequential *de'oraita* violation. When one uses language that evokes the domestic sphere of short-term borrowing, it does not lead one to write; when one uses language that evokes formal lending, it does.

### Language Imprecision

The *gemara* is not entirely satisfied with this answer. It presses: *keivan d'bechol zimna d'ba'i l'meimar halveini v'amar lei hashileini* — since in ordinary weekday usage people use these terms imprecisely and are not *makpid* about which one they say, *v'lo kapdi ilei*, so even when someone says *hashileini* it may actually refer to a real loan, and *v'ati l'michtav* — people will end up writing things down even when they use the term *hashileini*. If the terms are used interchangeably in everyday speech, what protection does the preferred terminology actually provide?

### Shabbat Context

The *gemara's* resolution is elegant. On *Shabbat*, since *hashileini* is the only term the rabbis permit — *halveini* is not permitted — *minkara milta v'lo ati l'michtav*: the restriction is self-announcing. The very fact that one must remember to use only the term *hashileini* on *Shabbat* serves as a built-in reminder that one is in a *Shabbat* context governed by *Shabbat* norms. This creates a distinctive register for *Shabbat* borrowing. By establishing that only one term is valid, the rabbis effectively create a signal: every time a person consciously uses *hashileini*, they are reminded that this is *Shabbat*, that records are not to be written, and that the transaction is of the domestic, trust-based variety. The restriction on language thus functions both as a practical safeguard and as a contextual marker.

---

## Uvdin D'Chol

### Shinuy Principle

Rabbah bar Rav Chanan said to Abaye: the rabbis declared that anything relating to *Yom Tov* should be done with a *shinuy* — a variation — as much as possible. This principle applies to activities that, while technically permitted on *Yom Tov*, have the character of *uvdin d'chol* — weekday-type activities. Things that are laborious and mundane in nature, even if permitted, should be performed somewhat differently on *Yom Tov* to distinguish the day. The question is how this principle interacts with competing considerations.

### Water Bucket Case

The case in point involves women filling their water buckets (*chatzvayehu*) from the well. This was a laborious, thoroughly weekday activity. Why do we not require a *shinuy* here?

The *gemara* works through the options. Should those who normally use large buckets use small ones instead? Then they will have to make more trips — *ha ka mafsha behilucha* — increasing *tircha*, exertion. Should those who use small buckets switch to large ones? Then the load becomes heavier — *ha ka mafsha bemasavye*. Perhaps one should drape some type of cloth over part of the bucket as a physical *heker*? The cloth will get wet and one will come to squeeze it — *azil lidei schita*. A non-cloth cover? The rope holding it may break and one will come to tie a knot. Every proposed *shinuy* introduces a new *Shabbat* concern or an unacceptable increase in burden. Therefore — *hilkach lo efshar* — there is genuinely no viable option, and the requirement of *shinuy* does not apply here.

### Competing Values

This discussion brings two values into tension: *uvdin d'chol* on one side and *tircha* on the other. These are not the same concern. *Tircha* refers specifically to physical exertion and effort; *uvdin d'chol* refers to the quality of an activity as weekday-like, pulling one out of the sacred character of the day. The question is: when these values compete, which wins?

### Tosafot's Position

*Tosafot* addresses this question — though in connection with a parallel *sugya* in *Beitzah* rather than directly with our *gemara*. *Tosafot* holds that minimizing *uvdin d'chol* outweighs concerns about *tircha*: if one can make an activity genuinely feel less like a weekday activity by accepting more exertion, one should do so. The more important value is eliminating the weekday character of the activity.

Why then does our *gemara* not require more trips or a heavier bucket — accepting the *tircha* in order to introduce a *shinuy*? *Tosafot* answers: because in this case, going to the well and drawing water, however many trips one makes and whatever size bucket one uses, remains thoroughly *uvdin d'chol* in character. No variation in bucket size or number of trips transforms the experiential quality of the activity. The only value achieved by a forced *shinuy* here would be a *shinuy* for its own sake — not an actual reduction in the weekday character of the activity. That does not justify increasing trips or burden. But where a *shinuy* would genuinely make the activity feel less weekday-like, the reduction of *uvdin d'chol* would justify accepting the additional *tircha*.

### Modern Devices

This tension has direct application to a contemporary debate among *poskim* regarding labor-saving mechanical devices in the kitchen on *Yom Tov*. Assume that concerns of *tochen* (grinding) or *borer* (sorting) do not apply — is there an independent concern of *uvdin d'chol* in using, say, a grater or a peeler?

The *Shmirat Shabbat Kehilchata* holds that such use is forbidden because of *uvdin d'chol*: labor-saving devices, even when no other *melachah* is implicated, introduce a quality of weekday efficiency that is inappropriate for *Yom Tov*. There is a sense in which more primitive methods — involving genuine personal effort — correspond to a simpler, more *Yom Tov*-appropriate mode of being. Rav Moshe, by contrast, drawing on a line in *Shulchan Aruch*, argues that there is no basis for calling labor-saving devices *uvdin d'chol*: since when is saving effort a weekday-like activity? Absent other violations of *borer* or *tochen*, Rav Moshe permits it.

The underlying question — exactly what quality renders an activity *uvdin d'chol* — is genuinely unclear. What is clear from our *gemara* is that the interplay between *uvdin d'chol* and *tircha* is a live halakhic consideration, and that in some situations accepting more *tircha* to reduce *uvdin d'chol* is the correct balance.

---

## Enforcement Strategy

### Musical Instruments

The same Rabbah bar bar Chana said to Abaye: we taught in the *mishna* — *lo mesapkin v'lo metapchin v'lo merakdin b'Yom Tov* — one may not clap, bang rhythmically, or dance on *Yom Tov*. *Rashi* understands this prohibition as targeting a form of mourning behavior, but *Tosafot* disagrees and holds that the prohibition applies even to joyful music-making: even clapping and dancing out of happiness is forbidden on *Yom Tov*. The reason, as the *gemara* in *Beitzah* explains, is the concern that one will proceed to bring out musical instruments, fix them, or make them — a prohibited act.

Rabbah bar bar Chana then observes: *v'kachazeinan d'avdin v'lo amrinan lehu v'lo midi* — we see people doing this and we say nothing. How is that explained?

### Shogeg Principle

The *gemara* responds by citing Rava's related ruling that a person should not sit at the opening of an alley by the *lechi* — the vertical post serving as the halakhic marker — lest an object roll out and he run after it, forgetting the boundary and carrying from *reshut harabim* to *reshut hayachid*. Yet we see that people bring their water vessels and sit at precisely these openings and we say nothing. The answer in both cases is the same: *hanach l'Yisrael — mutav sheyihyu shogegin v'al yihyu mezidin* — leave the Jewish people alone; better that they sin in error than willfully. If rebuke will not be heeded, it is better to remain silent.

### Torah vs. Rabbinic

One might have thought this principle applies only to rabbinic prohibitions: where the violation is only *de-rabanan*, one can concede that unheeded correction accomplishes nothing. But where the violation is *de'oraita*, perhaps one must speak up regardless — both to voice protest and to work harder to ensure compliance. The *gemara* rejects this distinction sharply: *v'lo hi — lo shna b'drabanan v'lo shna b'doraita* — it makes no difference whether the violation is biblical or rabbinic; if the rebuke will not be effective, one remains silent in either case.

### Yom Kippur Example

The *gemara* proves this from *tosefet Yom Kippur*, the biblical obligation to begin *Yom Kippur* early. We observe people eating and drinking until it is literally dark — until the last possible moment, forgoing the addition entirely — and we say nothing. This is a *de'oraita* violation, yet the principle of *mutav sheyihyu shogegin* applies.

### Rishonim Nuances

The *rishonim* qualify this principle significantly. The principle cannot be absolute: if someone is committing a blatant, explicit *de'oraita* violation — theft, for instance — one cannot simply stand by in silence on the grounds that rebuke will be ineffective. The qualifications operate along several axes. First, the more serious and explicit the violation, the less plausibly the person can claim genuine *shogeg* — their status as an inadvertent sinner is weaker to begin with. Second, the more severe the violation, the greater the obligation to attempt correction even against the odds of success. Third, there is the independent dimension of voicing protest: even where one cannot realistically expect compliance, remaining entirely silent may signal acceptance. One must not create the impression that one endorses the conduct.

These considerations also intersect with the *mitzvah* of *tochecha* — the obligation of rebuke — and the question of its limits. The *gemara's* principle is genuinely one of discretion: sometimes silence is the wiser course. There is even a debate among later *poskim* about a *rishon* who concluded a responsum with the phrase *ela hanach lahem l'Yisrael v'chulu* — "and leave Israel alone" — and whether this invokes the *shogeg* principle (meaning what they are doing is wrong, but rebuke is futile) or the entirely different *hanach lahem l'Yisrael* from elsewhere: *im lav nevi'im heim bnei nevi'im heim* — if they are not prophets, they are descendants of prophets — meaning we can trust that they are acting correctly.

---

## Clapping Debate

### Tosefta vs. Bavli

Returning to the prohibition against clapping and dancing: it is worth noting that the *Tosefta's* presentation of this prohibition appears to frame it as an intrinsic problem of *uvdin d'chol*. The specific context in the *Tosefta* involves activities that farmers would do in their fields to scare birds away — making it paradigmatically a weekday labor-type activity. The prohibition, on that reading, is about the intrinsic character of the act, not about what it might lead to. The *Bavli*, as is its characteristic method, reframes the prohibition as a concern about consequences: clapping and dancing may lead one to produce or repair musical instruments — a prohibited *melachah*. The intrinsic *uvdin d'chol* dimension is displaced by a concern about a downstream *de'oraita* violation.

### Tosafot's Rationalization

This *Bavli* reframing has significant practical consequences. *Tosafot* acknowledges that in their day — as today — it was extremely common for people to ignore this prohibition entirely. Rather than applying the *shogeg* principle and saying that people are sinning but one should leave them alone, *Tosafot* goes further and rationalizes the widespread practice. Since the prohibition as framed by the *Bavli* is a *gezeirah* against clapping *because* it may lead to making or fixing musical instruments — and since in *Tosafot's* era (and arguably more so today) people do not trivially make or repair musical instruments in response to festive clapping — *Tosafot* suggests that the *gezeirah* may not apply in such circumstances.

### Consequences Framework

This approach is only available precisely because the *Bavli* has reframed the prohibition as a concern about consequences rather than an intrinsic problem. Had clapping been an intrinsic *issur* — whether as *uvdin d'chol* in the *Tosefta's* sense or for some other inherent reason — there would be no room for *Tosafot's* argument. It is the framing as a *gezeirah* tied to specific consequences that opens the door to arguing that those consequences are no longer realistic. This connects directly to the broader *uvdin d'chol* discussion: the *Bavli* consistently prefers to ground prohibitions in concern for downstream violations rather than in the intrinsic character of an activity, and that preference has real halakhic implications for how the prohibition can be understood and applied.

---

## Ribis & Bread

### Hillel's Ruling

The *gemara* continues. The *mishna* permits a woman to borrow loaves of bread from her neighbor using the appropriate language. The *gemara* asks: does this imply that during the week such borrowing is entirely permitted? If so, this appears to contradict the position of Hillel. The *gemara* cites a teaching: *v'chein hayah Hillel omeir* — Hillel used to say — a woman should not lend a loaf of bread to her friend *ad sheta'asena damim* — unless she first converts it into a monetary value. The concern is *peiros b'peiros* — lending something and receiving back the same category of item, with the risk that the item will have increased in value in the interim. *Shema yokru chitim v'nimtza ba lidei ribis* — perhaps the price of wheat will rise, and when the borrower returns a loaf of bread it will be more valuable than what was borrowed, constituting *ribis*.

### Fixed Prices

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *afilu teima Hillel — ha be'atra de-kayitz damei ha be'atra de-lo kayitz damei.* Even according to Hillel, there are two distinct situations. Where the price is fixed and well-known — *kayitz damei* — the *ribis* concern does not apply. Where the price is indeterminate — *lo kayitz damei* — Hillel's requirement to set a monetary value applies.

### Practical Leniency

*Rashi* explains the mechanism: if the price is fixed and universally known, then even if that price subsequently changes, everyone will know it has changed. The parties can therefore adjust accordingly — one returns the value rather than the object — and the *ribis* concern is avoided. If the price is indeterminate, there is no clear baseline, and the risk that an equivalent quantity represents a greater value is unmanageable without first establishing the monetary equivalent.

In practice this is a real issue for everyday neighborly borrowing. The *halacha* does require sensitivity to the concern even in contemporary circumstances, and it will be discussed at greater length when the relevant material in *Bava Metzia* is reached. Notably, in places where prices are regulated — such as certain staple goods in Israel — the concept of *kayitz damei* may apply with particular force, though even there periodic price adjustments must be accounted for.

---

## Yom Tov Loans

### Rav Yosef

The *gemara* turns to a formal dispute about the legal status of loans made on *Yom Tov*. Suppose one borrowed food on *Yom Tov* and subsequently refuses to repay. Can the lender bring the borrower to *din* — to *Beit Din*? Rav Yosef rules: *lo nitna l'itava* — the loan cannot be adjudicated in court. The entire arrangement is built on trust; it is not a formally enforceable obligation. The reasoning: *de-im amarta nitna l'itava* — if you were to say it is court-enforceable, *ati l'michtav* — the lender would write it down to secure their ability to collect. Converting the arrangement into a real enforceable debt is precisely what creates the pressure to document it. Keeping it on a trust basis means neither party expects written documentation.

### Rava

Rava disagrees: *nitna l'itava* — it is enforceable in court. His reasoning runs in the opposite direction: *de-im amarta lo nitna* — if you say it cannot be enforced — *lo ya'iv leh* — who will give on such a basis? No one will extend the loan if they have no recourse whatsoever. *V'ati limnumey mi-simchas Yom Tov* — and this will result in people being unable to participate in *simchas Yom Tov*. The concern for *simchat Yom Tov* frames this as a *Yom Tov* issue specifically, perhaps even more acutely than a *Shabbat* issue: on *Yom Tov* one is actively cooking and preparing food, and running out of an ingredient mid-preparation is more likely and more consequential. Enabling the *simchas Yom Tov* of the community requires that the lender have some genuine assurance of repayment.

### Mishnah Support

The *gemara* tests these positions against our *mishna*. The *mishna* rules: *eino ma'amino, maniach taliso etzlo* — if the lender does not trust the borrower, he may leave his *tallis* as collateral, *v'oseh imo cheshbon l'achar ha-Shabbos* — and they settle accounts after *Shabbat*.

The *gemara* asks: if the loan cannot be brought to court — as Rav Yosef holds — then we understand why the lender would want to hold the *tallis*: without court enforcement, the collateral is his only security. But if the loan is court-enforceable — as Rava holds — why would anyone bother with collateral? Just give the goods and sue if unpaid.

The *gemara* answers: *lo beina d'eikum bedina v'dayana* — the lender may simply prefer not to deal with the trouble of *Beit Din* and judges. Even if technically enforceable, one might still prefer the simplicity of holding collateral to avoid litigation. This response does not disprove court-enforceability; it merely explains why collateral remains attractive even where enforcement is available.

---

## Shemittah Cases

### Meat Distribution

The *gemara* continues with a new challenge. The case involves a butcher who slaughtered a cow and distributed the meat to customers on *Rosh Hashana* — the first day of the new year. This falls at the transition from the seventh (*shemittah*) year to the eighth. At the end of *shemittah*, outstanding debts are cancelled. The question turns on whether the first day of *Rosh Hashana* was the 30th of Elul (making it a day of the seventh year, the old year) or genuinely the 1st of Tishrei (the first day of the eighth year). *Im hayah chodesh me'ubar* — if it was a full month — the first day of *Rosh Hashana* was the 30th of Elul, the debt falls within the seventh year, and *shemittah* cancels it. *V'im lav* — if not — the debt arose on the genuine first of Tishrei, the eighth year has begun, and *shemittah* does not cancel it.

### Enforcement vs. Voluntary

The *gemara* poses a challenge to Rav Yosef's position. If *Yom Tov* loans are not court-enforceable — *lo nitna l'itava* — why does it matter whether *shemittah* cancels them? *Shemittah* cancels debts that are collectible in court; a debt that can never be brought to court is already unenforceable without *shemittah*. The *gemara* resolves this by identifying a special factor: *shani hasam de'iglai milsa de-chol hu* — in the scenario where *shemittah* cancels the debt, the first day of *Rosh Hashana* turned out to be the 30th of Elul — a weekday, not *Yom Tov*. The loan was therefore a regular weekday transaction, fully enforceable, and properly subject to *shemittah* cancellation. The *Yom Tov* loan rules were never in play.

The final clause of the case — *v'im lav, eino meshamet* — is then pressed into service on behalf of Rava's position. If the first day of *Rosh Hashana* was genuinely the 1st of Tishrei, *shemittah* does not cancel the debt, and the implication is that there is something remaining to collect. This suggests the *Yom Tov* loan *is* enforceable — otherwise *shemittah's* non-application would be meaningless. The *gemara* offers a nuanced response: *dihavi leh v'shakil* — the point is not about court-enforced collection but about voluntary repayment. Even if the lender cannot compel payment, the borrower may willingly come and repay. The distinction between the two clauses of the case is therefore this: when *shemittah* applies, the lender cannot simply accept payment when it is offered. When *shemittah* does not apply, the lender may straightforwardly accept whatever the borrower brings.

### Shemittah Procedure

This leads to an important *mishna* on the *shemittah* procedure. *Ha-machzir chov bishvi'it* — one who returns a debt during *shemittah* — the lender must say: *meshamet ani* — I hereby annul this debt. If the borrower then responds that he wishes to repay regardless, *yekabel mimenu* — the lender may accept. The obligation to annul derives from the verse *ve-zeh devar ha-shemittah*, which requires the lender to formally pronounce words of annulment. Mere silence or passive acceptance is insufficient; the lender must actively declare the annulment, after which voluntary repayment is permitted.

The practical upshot for our case: where a *Yom Tov* loan has been affected by *shemittah*, the lender cannot simply pocket the money when the borrower comes to pay. The lender must first declare annulment. Only if the borrower then insists on paying regardless may the money be accepted. Where *shemittah* has not applied, the lender accepts the money directly as soon as it is offered.

### Collateral Scheme

Rav Avya's approach to securing repayment is also noted. When distributing food on *Yom Tov*, Rav Avya would take collateral — *mashkona* — and the *gemara* here explicitly labels it as *mashkon*, confirming that at least where the concern is about writing rather than business *per se*, openly taking collateral is acceptable.

The *gemara* then describes a scheme attributed to Rabba bar Ulla: after *Yom Tov*, before ever pressing for repayment, he would approach the debtor and ask to borrow some object — say, a car — for an hour. Once he had that object in hand, he would hold onto it until the original debt was paid. This is a somewhat clever workaround: rather than holding collateral at the time of the original *Yom Tov* loan, he would acquire leverage over the debtor afterwards, thereby ensuring repayment without the complications of formal court proceedings.

---

## Erev Pesach

### Fixed-Time Korbanot

The *mishna* introduced the case of *Erev Pesach* falling on *Shabbat* and the arrangement of getting one's sheep while deferring payment. Rav Yochanan derives a broader principle: *makdishin pesachcha be-Shabbat v'chagigatecha be-Yom Tov* — one may sanctify a *korban Pesach* on *Shabbat* and a *chagiga* on *Yom Tov*, even though sanctifying *korbanot* is normally forbidden on both. The principle is *le-tzorech Shabbat* and *le-tzorech Yom Tov*: where there is a genuine need tied to that specific day, the sanctification is permitted. If *Erev Pesach* falls on *Shabbat* and one has not yet sanctified one's *korban Pesach*, one may do so.

### Pesach Example

The *gemara* attempts to derive support for Rav Yochanan's position from the *mishna*: *v'chein Erev Pesach biYerushalayim she-chal lihyot be-Shabbat, maniach talito etzlo v'notel et pishcho v'oseh imo cheshbon le-achar Yom Tov* — you get your sheep first on *Shabbat* and work out payment afterwards. The implicit assumption is that you then sanctify the sheep on *Shabbat* for use as your *korban Pesach* — thus proving that such sanctification is permitted.

### Pre-Sanctification

The *gemara* resists this reading by proposing: *heicha be-mai askinan — bi-mmaneh acherim imo al pishcho* — what we are actually discussing is not acquiring an unsanctified sheep and sanctifying it, but rather buying into a group (*chiburah*) that already has a sanctified *korban Pesach*. One who did not have an animal joins an existing group; the financial settlement deferred to after *Shabbat* represents one's buy-in fee. The sheep was already sanctified; no new act of *hekdesh* occurs on *Shabbat*.

The *gemara* acknowledges that this reading is forced. The *mishna's* plain language strongly suggests one is acquiring a sheep and then sanctifying it — not merely purchasing a share in something pre-sanctified.

### Rav Hoshaia

The *gemara* then cites a *baraita* of Rav Hoshaia that eliminates any ambiguity: *holech adam etzel roeh haragil etzlo v'noten lo taleh le-pischo umakdisho* — one goes to a shepherd, receives a sheep, and *explicitly sanctifies it* for one's *korban Pesach*, then settles accounts after *Shabbat*. The word *umakdisho* — and he sanctifies it — is unambiguous. Here too the *gemara* attempts to retreat: since one regularly buys from this shepherd, the shepherd had already anticipated the buyer's arrival and sanctified it in advance, so the buyer's act of sanctification is rabbinically supplementary at best. This reading is extraordinarily strained. All the cases point in the same direction: one acquires the sheep on *Shabbat* and sanctifies it.
