The *gemara's* attempts to explain them otherwise are not convincing, but they represent the *gemara's* effort to avoid a direct proof for Rav Yochanan from the *mishna* — even as Rav Yochanan's position remains substantively sound.

### General Principle

The *gemara* ultimately resolves the matter through a *stam mishna* that rules: *lo makdishin v'lo maarichin v'lo machrimin v'lo magbihin terumot umaserot — kol elu be-Yom Tov amru, kal vachomer be-Shabbat* — one does not sanctify, evaluate, consecrate, or separate *terumot* and *maaserot* on *Yom Tov*; these prohibitions apply on *Shabbat* as well, *a fortiori*. Rav Yochanan himself holds that *halacha* follows an unattributed *mishna*, and this *mishna* appears to prohibit sanctification on *Yom Tov* and *Shabbat* categorically — in apparent tension with his own ruling.

The resolution is straightforward: *lo kashya — kan be-chovot shekavuah lahen zman, kan be-chovot she'ein kavuah lahen zman.* The *mishna's* prohibition applies to obligations that are not time-bound — sanctifications and dedications that one could perform on any day. Rav Yochanan's permission applies to obligations that are bound to a specific day: the *korban Pesach* must be brought on the 14th of Nisan, the *chagiga* on *Yom Tov* itself. Where the obligation is fixed to today and cannot be fulfilled otherwise, sanctification is permitted on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*. Where there is no such temporal urgency, the prohibition stands. This is the general principle with which the *daf* concludes.

---

---

# Shabbat 152

## Old Age Metaphors

### Intro to Aging

The final pages of *Maseches Shabbos* draw to a close with an extended *aggadeta* — a sustained and richly textured discourse on the infirmities of old age, the nature of the soul after death, and the fate of the righteous and wicked in the world to come. The *gemara* builds much of this discussion on a close reading of *pesukim* from Kohelet, interpreting each image as a precise metaphor for the physical deterioration that accompanies aging.

### Guards of House

The *gemara* opens with the verse *bayom sheyize'u shomrei habayit* — "on the day that the guards of the house will tremble" (Kohelet 12:3). The *gemara* identifies each element of the verse with a part of the aging body. *Shomrei habayit*, the watchmen or guards of the house, are *haksalim veha'atzla'ot* — the ribs and sides, which protect the inner organs as a guard protects a house. *Anshei hachayil*, the strong men who become bent, refer to *shokayim* — the thighs, once powerful, now weakened and stooped.

### Grinders & Eyes

The verse continues: *ubatlu hatochenot* — the grinders cease — which the *gemara* identifies as *shinayim*, the teeth. And *vachoshchu haro'ot ba'arubot* — those who see through the skylights grow dark — refers to *einayim*, the eyes. Each faculty of the body, in turn, fails.

### Caesar Dialogue

The *gemara* then relates that Caesar said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya: *mai ta'ama lo asit levei avidan* — why did you not come to *bei avidan*? *Bei avidan* is a house of disputation — whether between Rabbis and members of various Jewish sects or between philosophers — to which different Sages responded differently, some confident in their capacity to handle intellectual or other challenges, others reluctant to engage. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya had not attended, and Caesar pressed him for an explanation.

### Yehoshua's Decline

Rabbi Yehoshua's response is a cascade of vivid metaphors: *tur talag* — the mountain is snowy, meaning his hair has gone white. *Sachronei glidin* — it is surrounded with frost, which Rashi interprets as his beard and mustache having also whitened. *Kalvei lo navchin* — the dogs are no longer barking, meaning, according to Rashi, that he has lost the clarity and volume of his speech. *Tachneit lo tachnin* — the grinders are not grinding, that is, his teeth no longer function. He pleads old age, couched in precisely the same vivid figurative language the *gemara* has just been unpacking.

### Bei Rav Saying

*Bei Rav* offers another pointed image of old age: *ad d'lo avidna bacheshna* — I search for something I have not lost. Because the elderly become bent over, they appear perpetually to be searching the ground for something they have dropped — though they have lost nothing at all. It may also capture the mental dimension of aging, the sense of reaching for something that is no longer there.

### Youth vs Age

A *baraisa* is cited in the name of Rabbi Yosi bar Kisma: *tava try me-telasa* — two is better than three. This is the riddle of the Sphinx inverted: a person walks on two legs in the prime of life and three — with a cane — in old age. *Vai lah lechada d'azla v'lo atya* — woe to that one which has gone and does not return. The *gemara* asks: what is that one thing? *Yankusa* — youth. Woe to the loss of youth, which, once gone, does not return.

### Roses & Thorns

Rav Dimi elaborates: *yankusa klila d'varda* — youth is a crown of roses. *Savusa klila d'chilfei* — old age is a crown of thorns. The contrast could hardly be starker.

### Meir's Teaching

A teaching transmitted in the name of Rabbi Meir advises: *dok b'kakhei vetishkach b'nigrei* — grind with your teeth and you will find it in your legs. The meaning is that if one eats well and takes care of one's body in youth, the benefit will be felt in old age — in one's legs, one's mobility, one's strength. The verse cited in support is *vnisba lachem v'nihye tovim vera'ah lo rainu* — we will be sated with bread, we will be well, and we will not see evil — implying that even in later years, one who has maintained proper nutrition will be spared suffering.

### Food & Drink

Shmuel says to Rav Yehuda — whom he addresses as *Shinana*, the sharp one — *sharei kayecha v'ayyel lachmech*: open your mouth and let the bread come in. Eat well while you are young. *Arba'in shanin michla ma'aly* — until forty years of age, food is what principally benefits your health. *Mikan v'eilach mishty ma'aly* — from forty onwards, what you drink becomes the more significant factor for your well-being.

## Eunuch Exchange

### Animal Insults

A certain *guza'ah* — a eunuch — who appears according to Rashi to have also been a *Tzadoki*, a sectarian of some kind, said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: *meihacha l'Karchina kama* — how far is it from here to Karchina? Karchina was plainly chosen as a play on *karcha*, meaning bald, and so the question was a veiled insult directed at the Rabbi's baldness.

### Counter Insult

Rabbi Yehoshua responded in kind: *kemeihacha l'Guzina* — the same distance as it is from here to Guzina. *Guzina* echoing *guza*, a eunuch — you call me bald, I call you a eunuch. The *Tzadoki* then said: *barcha karcha b'arba'ah* — a sheared goat costs only four *zuz*, implying that without its hair it is worth almost nothing. Rabbi Yehoshua countered: *ikra shalifa b'tamanya* — a castrated sheep fetches eight *zuz*. The point, as noted from the Sefaria commentary, is that even with the concession of baldness, a castrated animal commands a higher price than a bald one — making the eunuch's situation comparatively worse, not better.

### Barefoot Shame

The eunuch then observed that Rabbi Yehoshua was not wearing shoes. He said: *d'al sus melech* — one who rides on a horse is a king; *d'al chamor ben chorin* — one who rides on a donkey is at least a free man; *dimna'aly b'riglohi bar inish* — one who has shoes is at least human. But *d'lo ha v'lo ha dachafir v'kavir tav mineih* — one who has neither beast nor shoes, who goes about barefoot — it would be better for him to be dug into the earth and buried. This last comment perhaps explains why this exchange appears in the context of a discussion about death and the fate of the body.

### Three Blessings

Rabbi Yehoshua responded: *guza guza, tlat amart li, tlat shamat* — castrated one, you have said three things to me; now hear three things in return. The three things he received were the three insults: the crack about baldness, the comparison of animals, and the remark about the shoes. The three responses: *hadrat panim zakan* — the glory of a man's face is his beard, which the eunuch, being castrated, does not have; *simchat lev isha* — the joy of a man's heart is his wife; *nachalat Hashem banim* — the inheritance from God is children. *Baruch hamakom shemena'acha mikulam* — praised be God who has prevented you from possessing any of these three. When the eunuch challenged Rabbi Yehoshua — *karcha metziyana*, are you really picking a fight? — Rabbi Yehoshua replied: *ikra shalifa tochecha* — is a eunuch going to deliver me rebuke?

## Shimon & Rabbi

### Festival Absence

Rabbi said to Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta: *mipnei mah lo hikbalnu panecha baregel* — why did we not welcome you on the festival, the way my fathers welcomed your fathers? The expectation was that a student would visit his Rebbe on the *regel* to show proper respect to the *Nasi*. Rabbi Shimon's reply, like that of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya before him, is a catalogue of the infirmities of age.

### Obstacle Shift

*Slaim naasu gevohim* — the rocks have become very high. Even the modest inclines and small obstacles of daily life now loom impossibly large. *Krovim naasu rehokim* — things that used to be close now feel very distant; even short distances seem enormous. Rashi adds the interpretation that this may also refer to loss of hearing: people speaking right next to him now seem as if they are speaking from far away. This image resonates with contemporary experience as well. A speaker on disability access once described to a group of rabbis that if they wished to understand why people with physical disabilities did not come to their synagogues, they needed simply to step outside and count the steps — obstacles invisible to those unaffected, but each one a mountain to those who are.

### Cane & Loss

*Mishtayim naasu shalosh* — from two I have become three. He must now walk with a cane. *Umesim shalom babayis batel* — and the one who makes peace in the house has been nullified. Rashi interprets this as a reference to the loss of sexual desire or sexual capacity in old age, though other explanations have been offered relating to digestion or other functions. The plain sense of *mesim shalom babayis* — the one who makes peace in the house — lending itself to other readings as well.

## Kohelet Ch. 12

### Closed Doors

The *gemara* returns to the *pesukim* of Kohelet 12. *Vesigru dlasayim bashuk* — and the doors have been closed in the marketplace. This refers to *nekavav shel adam* — the body's orifices — which no longer function as they once did. The reason given is *bishvil korkevan she-eino tochen* — the stomach no longer grinds as it should, which is a different form of grinding than the failure of the teeth discussed earlier.

### Bird Wake

*Veyakum lekol hatzippur* — and one rises at the sound of a bird. The *gemara* explains: *she-afillu tzippur menaarato mishnato* — even a bird's chirping is enough to rouse the elderly person from sleep. The slightest sound, which a younger person would sleep through entirely, awakens the old.

### Song Failure

*Veyishchu kol bnos hashir* — and all the daughters of song are laid low. Even the sound of male and female singers, which once brought pleasure, now falls upon the elderly person *ke-shucha* — like a burden or something laid low — no longer giving joy.

### Barzillai Truth

The *gemara* now raises the case of Barzillai the Giladi, who said to David: *ben shmonim shana anochi hayom, hayada bein tov lera* — I am eighty years old today; do I any longer know between good and evil? The *gemara* notes: *mikan shedeoseihen shel zekenim mishtanos* — here one sees that the intellect, or more broadly the sensory and experiential faculties, of the elderly change.

The passage continues to elaborate on what Barzillai meant. *Im yit'am avdecha et asher ochal ve'et asher eshteh* — can your servant even taste what he eats or drinks? From this the *gemara* derives: *mikan she'siftoteihem shel zekenim mitrapot* — that the lips of the elderly become cracked, or that their sense of taste diminishes, so that they can no longer properly taste what they eat or drink. *Im eshma od bekol sharim vesharos* — will I still be able to hear the sound of singers? From this: *mikan she'ozneihem shel zekenim mitkavdot* — their ears grow heavy, meaning they lose the acuity of their hearing. Whether the *gemara* understands Barzillai's statement as referring primarily to the intellectual and ethical capacity to distinguish between good and evil, or more to the experiential sense of pleasure and taste, is not entirely clear from the *peshat* of the verse — though the *gemara* leans toward the latter, understanding his complaint as one about failing senses rather than failing moral judgment.

### Maidservant

Rav challenges the reliability of Barzillai's testimony: *Barzilai HaGiladi shakra hava* — Barzillai the Giladi was a liar. As evidence, Rav points to a maidservant in the house of Rebbi who was ninety-two years old and who continued to taste the pots to determine the spices — demonstrating that old age does not necessarily rob everyone of their sense of taste. Of course, this does not mean that Barzillai's experience was not real, only that it was not universal.

### Licentious Fall

Rava offers a different explanation: *Barzilai HaGiladi shatuf be'zimah hava* — Barzillai the Giladi was immersed in licentiousness. *Vekol hashatuf be'zimah, zikna kofetzet alav* — anyone who is given over to uncontrolled sexual behavior finds that old age jumps upon him with particular force. The suggestion seems to be that Barzillai's suffering in old age was more severe than most, which explains why his description sounds so extreme — even harsher than what the *gemara* itself had already described. Rebbi's maidservant represents the norm; Barzillai was a special and self-inflicted case.

## Wisdom vs Folly

### Scholars Wisdom

A *baraisa* — which also appears as a *mishnah* at the end of *Maseches Kinim* — is cited in the name of Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosi. *Talmidei chachamim, kol zman shemazkinin, chochmah nitvosefet bahem* — Torah scholars, the older they become, the wiser they grow. The verse cited in support is *biyeshishim chochmah ve'orech yamim tevunah* — in the elderly is wisdom, and with length of days comes understanding.

### Folk Folly

*Ve'amei ha'aretz*, however — the people of the land, those less versed in learning — *kol zman shemazkinin, tipshus nitvosefet bahem* — as they grow older, they become more foolish. The verse invoked here is *mesir safah lene'emanim* — God removes speech from those who were trustworthy, those who could ordinarily be depended upon for meaningful discourse — *veta'am zekenim yikach* — and the taste of elders He takes away.

### Scripture Split

One might ask: these two *pesukim* seem to be in direct contradiction — one says aging brings wisdom, the other says aging brings foolishness. Rashi resolves the contradiction by splitting the verses along the divide between *talmidei chachamim* and *amei ha'aretz*: one verse describes the trajectory of those devoted to Torah learning, the other describes those who were not.

### Mind Exercise

Beyond the theological framing, there is something genuinely compelling here from a modern perspective. The principle that sustained intellectual engagement across decades preserves mental sharpness in old age finds some support in contemporary research. There is evidence, for instance, that activities like crossword puzzles are associated with delayed onset of dementia and Alzheimer's. More broadly, there is an ongoing debate about whether significant cognitive decline is inevitable in people who do not develop dementia — and some evidence suggests that the more a person has exercised their mind over a lifetime, the more robustly those faculties persist. This maps quite naturally onto what the *gemara* is saying: decades of *talmud Torah* constitute sustained mental exercise of the highest order, and the Sages observed that this produced precisely the effect of preserving and even deepening wisdom in old age.

## Almond & Desire

### Almond Blossom

The *gemara* returns to Kohelet 12, now picking up from *gam migavo'ah yira'u* — even from a height they will fear — which is understood as: *she'afilu gushushit k'tanah domeh lo keharei harim* — even a small mound looks to the elderly person like the tallest of mountains. *Vechatchatin baderech, besha'ah sheholech baderech na'asu lo tohin* — they are fearful when they walk on the road, perceiving every step as a potential danger, afraid they might fall and injure themselves.

*Veyanats hashaked* — the almond tree blossoms. *Zu klivosos* — this is the hip bone, which protrudes from the body in old age.

### Grasshopper Drag

*Veyistabel hachagav* — the grasshopper drags itself along. *Elu agavos* — this refers to the buttocks, which begin to sag.

### Caper Bush

*Vetafer ha'aviyonah* — the caper bush fails. *Zu chemdah* — this is sexual desire, which is lost in old age. The derivation of *chemdah* from *aviyonah* appears to involve taking the *taf* from *vetafer* together with *aviyonah* to yield *ta'avah*, desire — though Rashi clarifies it refers specifically to *chemdat tashmish*, sexual desire.

### Rav's Sigh

Rav Kahana was reciting the *pesukim* before Rav. When he reached *vetafer ha'aviyonah*, Rav gave a great sigh. Rav Kahana understood from this: *shma mina bital lei chemdeh deRav* — I see that Rav has lost his sexual drive. This is a striking moment, not least because Rav was known to have taken temporary wives when he traveled — a practice attested elsewhere in the *gemara* — and so the loss of that drive would have been felt all the more acutely by him.

### God's Command

Rav Kahana then expounds: *mai dechtiv ki hu amar vayehi, zu ishah* — what is meant by the verse "He spoke and it was" — this refers to the woman. *Hu tziva vaya'amod, elu banim* — He commanded and it stood firm — these are children. The point is that God Himself implanted sexual desire in human beings, which leads men to seek marriage and ultimately to produce children. Without that divinely commanded desire, the rational case for investing in marriage and child-rearing would be far weaker — a point that resonates with evolutionary accounts of why male investment in family formation requires such a powerful biological drive.

### Women Baraita

A *baraisa* states: *ishah chemat meleia tzo'ah* — a woman is like a flask filled with excrement. Rashi reads this as a comment about the shared nature of the human body, not specifically targeting women. *Upiha malei dam* — her mouth is filled with blood, a euphemism for menstruation. *Ve'hakol ratzin achareha* — and yet everyone runs after her. The *baraisa* is making the point about the sheer power of sexual desire: that in spite of everything that might rationally diminish attraction, the drive implanted by God is so strong that men pursue women regardless. One might object that the excrement image need not be specific to women — though the menstruation reference immediately following makes it difficult to read it otherwise. What is theologically interesting is the juxtaposition: the *gemara* has just described the loss of sexual drive in old age as something to be mourned, and now frames the drive itself as something divinely commanded and essential to human continuity — without offering a purely religious justification. Rav's sigh over the loss of his desire was a very human moment, and the *gemara* does not shy away from its profundity.

## Eternal House

### Individual Dwellings

The *gemara* now turns to Kohelet 12:5: *ki holech adam el beit olamo* — because a person goes to his eternal house. Rav Yitzchak derives from this that every righteous person receives their own particular dwelling place in *olam ha-ba*. The use of *beit olamo* in the singular — each person's own eternal house — rather than a collective *beit olamim*, suggests individual, differentiated accommodations commensurate with each person's spiritual standing.

### King Parable

The *mashal*: a king and his servants enter a city together. *Keshen nichnasin kulam be-sha'ar echad nichnasin* — when they enter, they all pass through the same gate. Everyone enters *olam ha-ba* through the same portal. But *u-keshen lanin kol echad ve-echad notnin lo mador le-fi kevodo* — when it is time to retire, each person is given lodging according to their honor. So while all enter together, each righteous person occupies their own unique and appropriately calibrated place in *Gan Eden*.

### Youth Darkens

Rav Yitzchak further expounds: *ki ha-yaldut ve-ha-shachrut havel* — because youth and black hair are vanity. *Devarim she-adam oseh be-yalduto mashchirin panav le-et ziknato* — the things a person does in his youth will darken his face in old age. Rashi connects this to the earlier discussion of sexual licentiousness: excessive indulgence in one's youth comes back to haunt a person in old age, bringing shame and consequence.

## Worm & Soul

### Maggot Needle

Rav Yitzchak states: *kashah rimmah la-met ke-machat be-vasar ha-chai* — the maggot eating away at a dead body is as painful to the dead person as a needle piercing living flesh. The dead, it turns out, are not entirely beyond sensation. The verse cited is *ach besaro alav yichav* — even his flesh will pain upon him.

### Soul Mourning

Rav Chisda adds: *nafsho shel adam mitabelet alav kol shivah* — a person's soul mourns for its body for the entire seven days of *shivah*. The soul does not immediately ascend and detach; it remains present, mourning the loss of the body it inhabited. The verses cited are *ve-nafsho alav te'avel* — his soul mourns for him — and *va-ya'as le-aviv evel shiv'at yamim* — establishing that *avel* is a seven-day period.

### Communal Shiva

Rav Yehuda teaches: *met she-ein lo menachamim, holchin asarah benei adam ve-yoshvin bi-mekomo* — if a dead person has no mourners, ten people go and sit in the place where that person used to live. The practice of assembling a *minyan* in the home of someone who dies without family — sometimes observed even today — is rooted in the *gemara*'s understanding that the soul of the deceased is still present and sitting *shiva* as it were, in mourning for its own body. The practice reflects a profound respect: no one should depart this world without others experiencing and marking the loss, and the dead person himself is included in that mourning.

### Dream Gratitude

The *gemara* relates that a certain person died in the neighborhood of Rav Yehuda without any mourners. Every day Rav Yehuda gathered ten people and sat in the place where that person had lived. After seven days, the deceased appeared to Rav Yehuda in a dream and said: *tanuach da'atach shehenachta et da'ati* — may your mind be at ease, for you have set my mind at ease. The gratitude expressed by the deceased in the dream affirms the *gemara*'s underlying conviction: the soul of the departed is present, aware, and genuinely affected by whether it is mourned. Beyond the halakhic dimension, there is something profound here — a statement that no one should leave the world without their absence making some impact, without others pausing to register the loss.

### Hearing Eulogies

Rabbi Abahu states: *kol she'omrin bifnei hameis, yodeiah* — whatever is said in the presence of a dead body, the deceased is aware of it, *ad sheyistom hagolel* — until the coffin is sealed. This has direct implications for the *hesped*, the eulogy. Is a eulogy delivered solely for the comfort of the mourners, or does the deceased also hear it and derive something from it? According to Rabbi Abahu, the deceased hears every word until the moment the coffin is closed. The *gemara*'s treatment of *kavod hameis* — respect for the dead — is thus grounded in a quite literal metaphysical assumption: the soul remains present and aware.

### Awareness Dispute

Rav Chiya and Rabbi Shimon *berabbi* dispute the precise duration of this awareness. One opinion: *ad sheyistom hagolel* — until the coffin is sealed. The other: *ad sheyitachel habasar* — until the flesh is consumed, which could be a considerably longer period. The one who says until the flesh is consumed derives it from *ach besaro alav yichav venafsho alav te'eval* — his flesh pains him, and his soul mourns — implying that the soul remains present and aware as long as the flesh is being consumed by decomposition. The one who says until the coffin is sealed derives it from *veyashov he'afar al ha'aretz keshehayah veharuach tashuv el ha'elohim asher netanah* — once the dust returns to the earth, the spirit returns to God, no longer hovering near the body. The question of whether this occurs the moment the body enters the ground or only when the coffin is sealed is itself a point of subtlety.

## Soul Fates

### Garments Parable

The *gemara* now presents a *baraisa* on the fate of souls, framed by a powerful *mashal*. A human king distributed royal garments to his servants. The wise ones (*pikechim*) folded them carefully, placed them in a box, and preserved them. The foolish ones (*tipshim*) went out and did their work in them, soiling and wearing them out. When the king called for his garments back, the wise ones returned them freshly laundered and gleaming; the foolish ones returned them filthy. The king rejoiced to receive the garments of the wise and was furious at those of the foolish.

For the wise ones he said: *yinatnu kelai le'otzar* — let my garments be placed in the storehouse where they belong — and *vehem yelchu levateihem leshalom* — and they shall go to their homes in peace. For the foolish ones: *kelai yinatnu lechoves* — my garments must first be sent to the launderer — with the clear implication that the soul will require cleansing in *Gehennom* — *vehem yitchabshu beveit ha'asurim* — and they shall be bound in prison.

### Righteous Reward

God says of the bodies of the righteous: *yavo shalom yanuchu al mishkevotam* — they shall come in peace and lie down in their rest. And of their souls: *vehayetah nefesh adoni tzerurah betzror hachayim* — the soul of my master will be bound up in the bundle of life, held under the *Kise HaKavod*, as the *gemara* will elaborate.

### Wicked Punished

Of the bodies of the wicked: *ein shalom amar Hashem lerasha'im* — there is no peace, says God, for the wicked. Precisely what this means for the physical fate of their bodies is not spelled out. Of their souls: *ve'et nefesh oyvecha yekale'enah betoch kaf hakela* — the soul of your enemies shall be slung as from the pocket of a slingshot, shot across the world.

### Eliezer Souls

Rabbi Eliezer elaborates: *nishmatan shel tzadikim genuzot tachat Kise HaKavod* — the souls of the righteous are hidden under God's heavenly chair, as derived from *vehayetah nefesh adoni tzerurah betzror hachayim*. Of the wicked: *zomemot ve'holchot* — they are stretched out and sent across the world. One angel stands at one end of the world and another at the other end, and they slingshot the souls of the wicked back and forth between them — *umekal'in nishmatan zeh lazeh* — as from the pocket of a slingshot.

### Dumah Souls

Rabbah then asks Rav Nachman: what about the *beinoni*, the average person — neither fully righteous nor fully wicked? Rav Nachman demurs: *ei k'ma deshchivna lo amri lacho* — if I were to die, I would not be able to tell you, because he is not himself a *beinoni*, implying he would have access to the answer only from the vantage point of having died as one. Shmuel, however, does offer an answer: *elu ve'elu leDumah nimseru* — both the wicked and the average are handed over to *Dumah*, the angel appointed over souls. But among those given to *Dumah*: *halalu yesh lahem manoach* — some have rest — *halalu ein lahem manoach* — and some do not. The wicked have no rest; the average do, though they are not elevated to the place beneath God's heavenly chair that the righteous occupy. This is a striking *gemara*: the righteous alone attain *olam ha-ba* in the fullest sense; the wicked suffer; the average occupy a neutral, restful but undistinguished state — not punished but not rewarded in any active sense either.

## Dust & Resurrection

### Mari Dust

Rav Mari states: *atidi tzaddiki d'havu afra* — in the end, even the righteous will return to dust, derived from *veyashov he-afar al ha-aretz k'she-hayah* — and the dust shall return to the earth as it was. This appears to be a challenge to the assumption, implicit in the earlier *mashal* of the king, that the bodies of the righteous are preserved intact.

### Grave Diggers

The *gemara* then relates a remarkable story. Grave diggers were digging in the territory of Rav Nachman when Rav Acha bar Yoshiya, who had been buried there, rebuked them from within his grave. They came to Rav Nachman and reported: *nachar ban gavra* — a person rebuked us. Rav Nachman came and asked: who are you? The response: *ana Acha bar Yoshiya* — I am Acha bar Yoshiya. The story rests on the assumption — consistent with what was said of the righteous in the earlier discussion — that not only are the souls of *tzadikim* preserved beneath the *Kise HaKavod*, but their bodies too remain intact in their graves.

### Nachman Challenge

Rav Nachman pressed him: *velav amar Rav Mari atidi tzaddiki d'havu afra* — but did not Rav Mari say that even the righteous will return to dust? How can your body still be present?

### Acha Jealousy

Rav Acha bar Yoshiya replied: *u-mani Mari d'lo yadeina lei* — who is this Rav Mari? I never encountered him, and so I do not *pasken* like him. Rav Nachman then pressed him with the *pasuk* itself: *veyashov he-afar al ha-aretz k'she-hayah* — the dust shall return to the earth as it was. Rav Acha responded: *de-akrayakh Koheles lo akrayakh Mishlei* — whoever taught you Kohelet did not teach you Mishlei. For Mishlei says: *u-rekav atzmos kinah* — and the rotting of bones is jealousy. *Kol mi she-yesh lo kinah b'libo, atzmosav markivim* — anyone who has jealousy in his heart, his bones rot. *Kol she-ein lo kinah b'libo, ein atzmosav markivim* — if one has no jealousy in his heart, his bones do not rot. Because Rav Acha bar Yoshiya harbored no jealousy, his body remained preserved. The verse from Kohelet speaks only of those whose bones are subject to this rotting — not of the *tzadik* who has purged himself entirely of envy.

### Resurrection Only

Rav Nachman then touched him — *gasheshiyei* — and felt actual substance: *chazie d'is bei mashasha* — he saw that there was real physical matter there, that this was not a hallucination or a dream. He said: why not come to my house? Rav Acha replied: *galise da'atakh d'afilu nevi'ei lo kares* — you have revealed that you have not even studied the prophets. For it says: *vi-yedatem ki ani Hashem bifishi es kivroseichem* — you shall know that I am God when I open your graves. Only God — only at the time of *techiyas hameisim* — will the dead be removed from their graves. And the end of the verse: *uvehaalosi eschem mikivroseichem ami* — when I raise you up out of your graves, My people. I can sit up, I can speak, but I cannot leave my grave.

### Second Before

One might ask: how do we reconcile the preservation of the body with the verse *ki afar ata veal afar tashuv* — for dust you are and to dust you shall return? Rav Acha answers: *hahu sha'ah achas kodem techiyas hameisim* — that moment of returning to dust is one second before the resurrection. The body is preserved intact until that final instant, at which point it returns to dust — and then God reconstitutes the dust and resurrects the body. This resolution is elegant: the bodies of the righteous are genuinely preserved, Rav Mari's statement stands, and the apparent contradiction dissolves. Furthermore, one who attended to the earlier discussion will note a significant implication: if the *tzadik's* body does not decompose until a single moment before *techiyas hameisim*, then the earlier opinion — that the deceased remains aware until the flesh is consumed — means that the *tzadik* is aware of everything occurring around his grave until the very moment before resurrection.

## Witch Samuel

### Heretic Question

A *min* posed a challenge to Rabbi Abahu: *amrisu nishmasan shel tzadikim genuzos tachas kisei hakavod* — you say that the souls of the righteous are hidden under God's heavenly chair. *Uva'alas ov heicha askiya l'Shmuel* — so how did the necromancer at Ein Dor raise up the soul of Shmuel? If his soul was beneath the *Kise HaKavod*, far beyond this world, how could she possibly have accessed it? The question is not trivial: it presupposes an internal tension between the doctrine of the soul's elevation and the biblical narrative of Shmuel's apparition.

### Twelve Months

Rabbi Abahu responded: *hasam besoch shneim asar chodesh hava* — that was still within twelve months of Shmuel's death. A *baraisa* teaches: *kol shneim asar chodesh gufo kayam venishmaso ola veyoredes* — for the first twelve months, the body remains preserved and the soul ascends and descends. During that period the soul is still somehow connected to this world, moving between the heavenly realm and the earthly, not yet having fully departed. The necromancer was therefore able to encounter the soul on one of its return visits, when it was accessible in this world.

### After Months

After twelve months: *haguf batel* — the body ceases, it begins to decompose — and *venishmaso ola ve'shuv eina yoredes* — the soul ascends and no longer comes back down. It remains permanently beneath the *Kise HaKavod* and is no longer accessible from below. The witch at Ein Dor could raise Shmuel precisely because she acted within that first year; had she attempted it afterward, she would have found no soul within reach. This brings the *masechta's* final discussion to a fitting close, weaving together the themes of bodily preservation, the soul's postmortem journey, and the limits of what lies within human — or demonic — power to access.

# Shabbat 153

## Death & Eulogies

### Opening & Context

The *daf* opens with a fascinating *aggadata* unit that wraps up a broader disquisition about old age and death — a thread the *Gemara* has been developing in connection with dying generally and on *Shabbat* specifically. We begin at the top of 153a.

### Eulogy as Indicator

*Amar Rav Yehuda brei d'Rav Shmuel bar Shilas mishmei d'Rav* — Rav Yehuda son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas says in the name of Rav: *me'hespeddo shel adam nikkar im ben olam haba hu im lav* — from the eulogy of a person, one can tell whether he merits the world to come or not. This is, admittedly, a somewhat startling claim, since eulogies are notorious for embellishment. Yet the *Gemara* proceeds to work with this principle, and one might observe — as the Ramban does in a related context — that it is forbidden to exaggerate beyond the accepted norm. Even after subtracting conventional inflation, a eulogy still conveys a meaningful picture of who the person was.

The *Gemara* challenges this immediately: *ini*? Is it really true? It cites the fact that Rav himself said to Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, *achim be'hespeda d'hasam kamina* — warm the people up, get them emotionally stirred, at my own funeral. If a person's righteousness naturally produces the appropriate communal response, why would Rav need to give such instructions?

The *Gemara* answers: *lo kashya* — there is no contradiction. *Ha d'mchammu lei v'achim, v'ha d'mchammu lei v'lo achim* — sometimes you try to arouse the crowd and succeed; sometimes you try and do not succeed. The success or failure of the effort is itself the indicator.

### Rashi's Approach

Rashi clarifies that *me'hespeddo shel adam* does not refer primarily to the content of what is said at the eulogy — how lavishly the deceased is praised — but rather to how the *tzibur* responds: how much they cry, wail, and mourn. The depth of the communal emotional reaction is what signals the person's worthiness.

Rashi adds a further nuance, explaining why effort is needed at all, even for a genuinely righteous person. Four lines down in the narrow script, Rashi writes: *l'hespeda v'achim l'olam chimmuma ba'ei* — it truly requires working people up emotionally, *she'ein bnei adam nichmarim kol kach al zaken* — because people do not typically get so torn apart when someone dies after a full old age. If a person dies at 100, even if the loss is profound, the community has been expecting it, and the person lived a complete life. Hence, even for a genuine *tzaddik* who died in old age, the *maggid hesped* must labor to produce the appropriate response — and whether that labor succeeds tells us something real.

### Abaye's Challenge

*Amar lei Abaye l'Rabba* — Abaye said to Rabba: what about a case like yours, master — *d'sane lei kulei Pumbedisa* — where the entire population of Pumbedisa hates you? Rabba was known for rebuking the people of Pumbedisa sharply; the city was cosmopolitan and, Rashi notes, prone to dishonesty and corruption, and Rabba would confront them, earning their resentment. *Man achim hespedeyhu* — who is going to get emotionally stirred at your eulogy? The challenge is pointed: a person can be profoundly righteous and still fail the "eulogy test" because his righteousness made him enemies.

### Rabba's Response

*Amar lei* — Rabba replied: *mistaya at v'Rabba bar Rav Chanan* — it would be enough just you and Rabba bar Rav Chanan. If those two are genuinely torn up at my funeral, that is all that matters. The broader masses who despise him have reasons for that reaction that say nothing about his actual greatness. The *tzibur* that matters is the circle that truly knows a person — and when that circle responds with genuine grief, it is a meaningful signal.

This represents a significant qualification of the principle. The *Gemara* acknowledges that public response in general is not always a reliable gauge. Sometimes a person who is not righteous at all attracts widespread mourning; sometimes the reverse. What matters is the response of those who are the appropriate measure of the person — and that is what tells us about *olam ha-ba*.

### Merit Criteria

*Ba'ei minei Rabbi Eliezer mei'Rav* — Rabbi Eliezer asked of Rav: *eizehu ben olam haba* — who is the person who merits the world to come? Rav replied with a verse from Yeshayahu: *ve'oznecha tishmanah davar mei'acharecha leimor zeh haderech lechu vo, ki sa'aminu vechi sasmilu* — your ears will hear something from behind you saying, "This is the path, walk on it," whether you turn right or left.

Rashi understands this literally: when you die you will hear a heavenly voice or an angel directing you on the path that the righteous have taken, and that itself tells you that you merit *olam ha-ba*. This reading, however admittedly limited in practical guidance, is supplemented by the Maharsha's interpretation. The Maharsha connects the verse to the famous *midrash* on the *pasuk* in the portion of Yisro, where Yisro advises Moshe to *vehodata lahem es haderech asher yelchu vah ve'es hama'aseh asher ya'asun* — and *Chazal* understand *haderech asher yelchu vah* to refer to ethical, interpersonal conduct: burying the dead, caring for the poor, *gemilus chasadim*, and acting *lifnim mishuras hadin*. The Maharsha reads Rav's verse as alluding to that same framework: *haderech zu gemilus chasadim, yelchu zu bikur cholim, bah zu kvurah, ki sa'aminu zeh hadin vechi sasmilu lifnim mishuras hadin*. It is the totality of a person's ethical and interpersonal behavior that is the measure of worthiness for *olam ha-ba*.

### Teachers' Approval

*Rabbi Chanina omer: kol sheda'as rabosav nochin heimenu* — anyone whose teachers derive *nachas* from him, that person merits *olam ha-ba*. It is the teachers specifically, not the parents, whose satisfaction is the indicator. A person who has genuinely grown in learning and character, such that those who trained him are proud of what he became — that is a sign of genuine spiritual achievement.

### Preparation Methods

The *Gemara* now cites *Kohelet*: *vesovevu bashuk hasofdim* — the eulogizers will spread out through the marketplace. *Bnei Galila amri: asei devarim lifnei misascha* — the people of the Galil say: do things so that the eulogizers will speak about them in front of your bed, meaning in front of your coffin as it is carried out. *Bnei Yehuda amri: asei devarim le'achar misascha* — the people of Yehuda say: do things so that the eulogizers will speak of them behind your bed. *Velo pligi, mar ki'asrei umar ki'asrei* — they do not disagree; each follows the custom of his locale, since in the Galil eulogizers walked before the coffin while in Yehuda they walked behind. The underlying message, however, is identical: live in such a way that what the eulogizers say about you is what you would want said. Think about what you want written in your obituary — and then direct your life accordingly toward that end.

### Daily Repentance

*Tnan hasam* — we learned in a *Mishnah* elsewhere: *Rabbi Eliezer omer: shuv yom echad lifnei misascha* — do *teshuvah* one day before you die. His students challenged him: *vechi adam yodea eizehu yom yamut* — does a person know which day he will die? Rabbi Eliezer replied: *vechol sheken!* — all the more so! *Yashuv hayom, shema yamut lemachar* — repent today, for perhaps you will die tomorrow.

### Uncertainty Strategy

The force of this teaching is not merely about ensuring one dies in a state of *teshuvah*, but about using the uncertainty of death's timing as a strategy for living. *Venimtsa kol yamav bitshuva* — the result is that a person's entire life becomes one lived in *teshuvah*. The concern about being prepared at any moment propels continuous ethical and spiritual attentiveness — it is not just preparation for the end but a framework for the present.

### Purity Metaphors

*Ve'af Shlomo amar bechochmato: bechol eis yihyu vegadecha levanim veshemen al roshcha al yechsar* — and Shlomo too said in his wisdom: at all times your clothes should be white and the oil on your head should not be lacking. Rashi understands "white clothes" as referring to the soul — keep your soul clean, do *teshuvah*. The Maharsha reads "clothes" differently from the soul itself: *begadim* are what dress the soul, meaning your *actions* — your actions should at all times be pure, and where they are not, *teshuvah* must follow immediately.

### King's Feast Parable

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai: mashal lemelech sheziman es avadav lise'uda, velo kava lahem zman* — a king invited his servants to a feast but did not specify when it would take place. *Pikchin shebahen kishu es atzman veyashvu al pesach beis hamelech* — the wise ones dressed themselves up and stood at the entrance of the king's palace. *Amru: klum chaser leveise hamelech* — they reasoned that the king's house lacks nothing; the feast can happen at any moment without advance preparation, so they must always be ready. *Tipshim shebahem halchu l'mlachtan* — the foolish ones went off to their work. *Amru: klum yesh seuda v'lo torach* — is there a feast without effort? We will have ample warning.

### Punishment Imagery

*Upitom bikesh hamelech es avadav* — and suddenly the king summoned his servants. *Pikchin shebahem nichnasu l'fanev k'shehen mekushatin* — the wise ones entered before him dressed and ready. *V'atipshim nichnasu l'fanev k'shehen meluchlachin* — the foolish ones came before him dirty. The application is stark: people assume they have time to begin living better, to do *teshuvah*, to start taking their obligations seriously — but tragedy and death can come without warning, *chas v'shalom*, and one cannot wait.

*V'kaas likrat tipshim*. The king was pleased with the prepared ones and angry at the foolish. *Halalu shekishru atzman l'seuda, yeshvu v'yochlu v'yishtu* — those who prepared themselves may sit, eat, and drink. *Halalu shelo kishru atzman l'seuda, yaamdu v'yiru* — those who did not prepare must stand and watch.

### Contrast in Response

The son-in-law of Rabbi Meir adds in Rabbi Meir's name: *af hein nirin k'mashmashin* — even they appear as though they are attending upon the diners, since they stand around them like servants. So the final formulation is sharpened: *elu v'elu yoshvin* — both groups are seated. *Halalu ochlin v'halalu re'evin* — these eat and the others go hungry. *Halalu shotin v'halalu tzemayim* — these drink and the others go thirsty. As the verse in Yeshayahu states: *koh amar Hashem hinei avadai yocheilu v'atem tir'avu, hinei avadai yishtu v'atem titzma'u, hinei avadai yaronu mi'tuv lev v'atem titzaku mikh'eiv lev*.

The sitting at the same table while being unable to eat is, in its way, a more acute exclusion than standing: it makes the person's deprivation absolutely explicit. This connects to the *Gemara*'s teaching elsewhere that *Gehenom* for the *reshaim* may consist of the same experience that is *Gan Eden* for the *tzaddikim* — the same sun that warms and illuminates the righteous destroys the wicked. The famous parable of the feast where all arms are rigid and those in *Gan Eden* feed one another while those in *Gehenom* starve captures the same idea: identical circumstances, utterly different experiences.

### Mitzvot as Prep

*Davar acher: b'chol eit yihyu v'gadecha l'vanim* — the *Gemara* offers an alternative reading of the verse from *Kohelet*. Here, "white clothes" refers to *tzitzit* — the white strings of the *tzitzit*. The Maharsha notes that *b'chol eit*, "at all times," comes to include even circumstances where one lacks *techelet* and the strings are white alone; even in that incomplete form one must wear them. *V'shemen al roshcha al yechsar* — "the oil on your head should not be lacking" refers to *tefillin* of the head. Again the Maharsha notes that *b'chol eit* means even if one lacks the *tefillin* of the arm, one must still ensure one wears the *tefillin* of the head. More broadly, the *Gemara* in *Berakhot* notes that a man surrounded by *mitzvot* — wearing *tzitzit* and *tefillin* — is far more likely to lead a virtuous life overall.

### Aggadic Conclusion

With *Hadran Alach Sho'el*, the *perek* concludes. This was a remarkable unit traversing the territory from death and eulogies through repentance, preparation, and the eternal consequences of how one lives. We now begin the final *perek* of *Maseches Shabbat*: *Mi Shehecheshich Bederech* — what does one do when caught away from home as *Shabbat* begins.

---

## Traveling at Shkiya

### Problem Setup

The final *perek* takes up a practical scenario: a person is traveling and, with his wallet and donkey and all his belongings, finds himself caught on the road as *shkiya* arrives. Something like being stuck in one's car as *Shabbat* is about to begin. What does one do?

### Non-Jew Solution

The *Mishnah* presents the first solution: *noten kiso l'nochri* — give your wallet to the non-Jew traveling with you. If there is no non-Jew, or perhaps no non-Jew one trusts, *u'manicho al hachamor* — place it on the donkey. Once one enters the outer courtyard of the city — a space surrounded by the walls of buildings that constitutes *reshut hayachid* — one may remove from the donkey the *kelim* that are not *muktze*. For the *muktze* items, one unties the ropes — assuming they are a *kesher she'eino shel kayama*, a non-permanent knot permitted to untie on *Shabbat* — and the bags fall down on their own.

### Rationale

*Mai ta'ama sharu lei rabanan l'meitav kiseih l'nochri?* — why did the Rabbis permit giving the wallet to the non-Jew? This is, at minimum, a rabbinic problem of *amira l'akum*, instructing a non-Jew to perform *melacha* on one's behalf. The *Gemara* answers: *kim lehu l'rabanan de'ein adam ma'amid atzmo al mamono* — the Rabbis have established that a person will not stand idly by regarding his money. Even the most observant individual, faced with the prospect of abandoning his wallet, will rationalize keeping it on his person. Therefore, *ei lo sharis lei, asi l'asuyei arba amos b'reshus harabim* — if they do not provide a lesser-prohibited outlet, he will end up carrying it through the public domain in outright violation of a biblical prohibition. The *Gemara* recognizes — as it does in other contexts such as a fire breaking out on *Shabbat* — that sometimes one must find a *muttar* alternative or the person will act in outright transgression regardless.

### Found vs. Owned

*Amar Rabbah: davka kiso* — this dispensation applies only to one's own wallet. *Aval metzia lo* — if one found an object in the street during *Shabbat*, the Rabbis did not permit having a non-Jew carry it. We are not afraid that a person will violate *Shabbat* over someone else's money, since he lacks that visceral attachment.

The *Gemara* pushes back: *pishita, kiso tanya* — of course, the *Mishnah* says "his wallet." One might have thought, however, that the *Mishnah* simply uses the standard case and the same rule would apply even to a found object — *orcha d'milsa kasani*. The *Gemara* establishes: *ka mashma lan* — no, the distinction is substantive. A found object that has not yet been picked up does not trigger the same concern.

### Found Object Status

*V'lo amran ela d'lo asai l'yadei* — that is only when the object has not yet come into his hand. *Aval asai l'yadei, k'kisei dami* — if he has already picked it up, it is treated like his own wallet, and the same concern applies. We are now afraid he will not leave it behind, and so a *muttar* outlet is needed.

*Ika d'amri* — an alternative version presents this as an open question (*baei Rabbah*): if a lost object came into his hand, do we say *keivan d'asai l'yado k'kisei dami* — since it came to his hand it is like his wallet? Or do we say *keivan d'lo tarach bah, lav k'kisei dami* — since he expended no effort, it did not arrive through his labor, and we are not concerned he will violate *Shabbat* for it? The *Gemara* leaves this as *teiku*, unresolved.

### Donkey Solution

*Ein imo nochri* — if there is no non-Jew available, the *Mishnah* permits placing the wallet on the donkey. The *Gemara* confirms: *ta'ama d'ein imo nochri* — the reason is specifically the absence of a non-Jew. *Ha yesh imo nochri, nochri adif* — if there is a non-Jew available, it is preferable to give it to the non-Jew rather than place it on the donkey.

### Legal Distinction

*Mai ta'ama?* — why is the non-Jew preferable? *Chamor atah metzuveh al shevisaso* — regarding your donkey, you are commanded to ensure its rest: *Lo taaseh kol melacha* concludes with *shorcha vachamorcha*, your ox and your donkey. You bear a positive biblical obligation of *shevitat behemto*. *Ee ata metzuveh al shevitato* — regarding a non-Jew, however, you bear no such obligation. He is not under your authority in the relevant sense, and having him carry involves no biblical violation — only a rabbinic one. Hence the non-Jew is the preferred option where available.

### Hierarchy of Options

### Ranking People

The *Gemara* then constructs a full hierarchy. Suppose you have with you a donkey and also a *cheresh* (a deaf-mute), a *shoteh* (one of unsound mind), and a *kattan* (a minor). All three of the latter are not fully *bar daat*, not yet obligated adults. Which is the preferred carrier — the donkey or one of those three?

*Chamor manach lay, cheresh shoteh ve-kattan lo yahiv lay* — it is better to load the donkey than to give it to any of the three. This is not obvious: loading the donkey risks transgressing the biblical obligation of *shevitat behemto*. The *Gemara* explains — and this is a striking passage — *hani adam hani lav adam*: these are people, and the donkey is not.

### Chinuch Concerns

Rather than simply resolving which option involves the lesser immediate technical violation, the *Gemara* takes a broader perspective rooted in *chinuch*. The donkey has no understanding of what is happening. But a *kattan* will eventually become an adult; a *shoteh* or *cheresh* may recover. And beyond those individuals, the broader act of habitually using people — even those currently exempt — to carry on *Shabbat* creates patterns that will influence adult Jewish behavior. The long-term implications outweigh the immediate technical question of whether using the donkey might more directly brush against a biblical prohibition.

### Deaf-Mute Priority

*Cheresh ve-shoteh* — if one must choose between a *cheresh* and a *shoteh*, *le-shoteh yahiv lei* — give it to the *shoteh*. The *Gemara* elsewhere recognizes that a *cheresh* possesses a degree of intelligence; some opinions hold him to be a full *bar daat*. A *shoteh*, while in a state of mental illness, is considered entirely lacking in *da'at*. Hence the *cheresh* is closer to full halachic adulthood, and it would be more problematic to use him.

*Shoteh ve-kattan* — between the *shoteh* and the minor, *le-shoteh yahiv lei* again — give it to the *shoteh*. A minor will become an adult, and the *chinuch* concern looms large.

### Deaf-Mute Status

It is worth pausing to note that the treatment of the *cheresh* in halachic literature raises sensitive and evolving questions. Halachically, *cheresh* refers specifically to the deaf-mute — one who is both deaf and unable to speak. A person who is only deaf but can speak bears no halachic disability. Historically, one might have assumed that few deaf people were also mute; but in fact, prior to hearing aids and modern audiological support, the absence of auditory feedback made normal enunciation essentially impossible for a standard deaf person, meaning most deaf people would indeed have fallen into the *cheresh* category.

Since the establishment of schools for the deaf beginning in the 18th century, and particularly with the development of sign language, there has been significant halachic evolution. The question of whether sign language constitutes speech is debated among *poskim*, and many contemporary authorities hold that a deaf-mute today no longer falls into the traditional halachic category of *cheresh* — a position that represents a major development, though not all *poskim* concur.

### Cheresh vs. Kattan

*Iba'ye l'hu: cheresh ve-kattan* — the *Gemara* raises the harder question: what if one must choose between a *cheresh* and a minor? On one hand, the *kattan* will become an adult, making the *chinuch* concern acute. On the other hand, the *cheresh*, while an adult, has some degree of *da'at* and — depending on the view — may be closer to full halachic standing.

*Aliba d'Rabbi Eliezer lo tiba'ye lach* — according to Rabbi Eliezer, there is no question. A *Tosefta* records that Rabbi Yitzchak says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: *trumas cheresh lo tesei l'chullin mipnei shehu safek* — *terumah* separated by a *cheresh* does not lose its status of *terumah* because his halachic capacity is uncertain. He may be a full *bar daat*, and therefore one would certainly prefer to give it to the *kattan* rather than to someone who might be a full halachic adult violating *Shabbat*.

*Ki tiba'ye lach, aliba d'Rabbanan* — the question arises according to the Rabbis, who hold that the *cheresh* definitively lacks full halachic status. The *Mishnah* teaches: *chamishah lo yitrumu v'im tormu ein trumasam trumah* — five categories may not take *terumah* and if they do it is not effective, including *cheresh, shoteh*, and *kattan*. According to this view, the *cheresh* is definitively not a full *bar daat* and his carrying would not constitute a full *chillul Shabbat*.

So the question becomes: is it better to give it to the *cheresh* — since he is definitively not halachically adult and therefore creates no *chillul Shabbat* concern — but risk that onlookers see an apparent adult Jew carrying on *Shabbat*, leading others to do the same? Or is it better to give it to the *kattan* — since he will become an adult and it is therefore worse for his *chinuch* — but a child is obviously a child and onlookers will not draw the wrong conclusion?

*Ika d'amri l'cheresh yahiv lei, ika d'amri l'kattan yahiv lei* — the *Gemara* records opinions on both sides without resolving the matter. What is most striking across this entire passage is the consistent willingness of the *Gemara* to weigh long-term educational and communal consequences against immediate technical halachic considerations — and in certain cases to allow those broader concerns to override what might seem the technically preferable solution in the immediate case.

### Hidden Solution

*Ein sham lo nochri v'lo chamor v'lo cheresh v'lo shoteh v'lo kattan* — if none of these are available: no non-Jew, no animal, no one exempt from *Shabbat* obligations. *Amar Rabbi Yitzchak: od acheres haysa, v'lo ratzu chachamim l'galosah* — there was another solution, but the Sages did not want to reveal it. Of course the *Gemara* now proceeds to tell us what it is: *molicho pachas pachas m'arba amos* — carry it in increments of less than four *amos* at a time. Each act of carrying is defined by its start (*akira*) and its end (*hanacha*). Walking less than four *amos* between each stop means no single act of carrying meets the *shiur* of a biblical violation. Done sequentially, it obviously covers the full distance home — but each individual segment remains below the threshold.

### Concealment Rationale

*Amay lo ratzu chachamim l'galoto?* — why did the Sages not wish to reveal this solution? *Mishum kevod Elokim haster davar, u'kevod melachim chakor davar* — honoring God sometimes requires concealing a matter; honoring kings requires investigating it. Rashi explains: protecting *kevod shamayim*, preventing people from sinning, sometimes means not spelling out every available leniency. If this solution were public knowledge, people would come to abuse it. The concern is specific: *de-mati le-asuyei arba amos b'reshus harabim* — revealing it might easily lead to actual biblical violation, since it is all too easy to lose count and carry more than four *amos* in one stretch.

### Disclosure Debate

This raises a genuine tension that recurs in *halachic* practice: there are certain leniencies whose existence ought to be known, but whose broad publication may produce the opposite of the intended effect. The concern is not merely about "control" — it is about the educational dynamics of how leniencies function. When a *b'diavad* option becomes too publicly known, it tends to become a *lechatchila*, and the robust baseline obligation loses its force.

At the same time, the problem with non-disclosure in this specific case is obvious: if a person is stranded outside the city with no one to call and no way to find out the ruling, concealing the solution does him no good whatsoever. There is no opportunity to quietly advise him *be'sha'as hadechak*. This makes the case for non-disclosure harder to sustain here, and the tension is real.

### Rabbinic Concerns

There is an important principle underlying the structure of these discussions: *ein domeh gezeiros Chazal zu l'zu* — one cannot straightforwardly extrapolate from one rabbinic enactment or dispensation to another. Each context has its own considerations about how anxious a person will be, what the public visibility of the act is, and what the downstream consequences of permitting it might be. The scenarios of fire on *Shabbat* and financial loss have different profiles, even though both involve the concern that a person under pressure will violate *Shabbat* if no outlet is provided.

### Honor Principle

*Kevod Elokim haster davar, u'kevod melachim chakor davar* — the verse from *Mishlei* sets up the tension elegantly. On one side: the honor of God sometimes requires concealment, the withholding of information that would be spiritually dangerous in unqualified hands. On the other side: the honor of kings — and by extension, the ideal of Torah scholarship — requires investigating and uncovering the truth, bringing hidden matters to light.

The tension between these principles is not merely academic. A *posek* is regularly faced with the question of how much to share. When someone asks a *halachic* question, they are not always asking for a philosophically complete answer — they are often implicitly asking to be helped to *keep halacha*. Spelling out every *b'diavad* pathway in the answer to a practical question can undermine the questioner's sense of the primary obligation. Yet withholding information that the person genuinely needs — especially when they have no other way to access it — crosses a different line.

### Measures Parable

*Tanya: Rabbi Eliezer omer, bo ba-yom gadshu se'ah* — that day they piled up the measure. *Rabbi Yehoshua omer, bo ba-yom machaku se'ah* — that day they smoothed out the measure.

According to Rashi's explanation, this is precisely the debate about whether concealing the *pachos pachos m'arba amos* solution was wise. Rabbi Eliezer holds that it was — like pouring mustard seeds into a basket full of gourds and cucumbers (*le-kuppah mele'ah kishu'in ve-dilu'in, adam noten le-tochah chardal, ve-hi machzeket*): the small additions fill in the gaps and the whole holds together. The concealment creates a protective barrier around the biblical prohibition and the system works.

Rabbi Yehoshua holds the opposite: *domeh le-arivah mele'ah devash, noten le-tochah rimonim ve-egozim, ve-hi mekiah* — it is like a trough full of honey into which you try to force pomegranates and walnuts — it spits them out. If you try to seal off a leniency without actually providing it, people will find the situation untenable and simply violate the prohibition outright. The *chumra* produces its own *kula*: by refusing to provide a legitimate outlet, you drive people to transgress. According to this view, the Sages should have disclosed the *pachos pachos* solution openly.

### Later Implementation

In practice, the *halacha* follows that *pachos pachos m'arba amos* is a valid solution, and the fact that the *Gemara* itself reveals it represents at least a partial embrace of disclosure. The precise balance — teaching the solution where needed while not broadcasting it indiscriminately — captures the middle path between the two positions.

### Rambam's View

The Rambam takes a striking further step. Returning to the unresolved *teiku* about the *metziah* — the found object that came into one's hand — the Rambam rules that while one cannot give it to a non-Jew and cannot place it on a donkey in that case, *pachos pachos m'arba amos* remains available even there. The Rambam's reasoning, as he explains in a *teshuvah*, is that unlike the other solutions — giving to a non-Jew or loading a donkey — which are more visible and public acts, moving an object less than four *amos* at a time is a private, inconspicuous method. Therefore, even for a *metziah*, this lesser-known solution remains accessible. The *Gra* identifies a *Gemara* that may serve as the basis for the Rambam's position, though the Rambam's application extends beyond what the *Gemara* itself explicitly states.

---

## Animal Work Issues

### Work Prohibition

The *Gemara* now returns to the donkey solution and confronts the biblical problem that was set aside earlier. Placing a load on one's donkey on *Shabbat* would seem to transgress the prohibition of *mechamer* — having one's animal perform labor. The verse *lo taaseh kol melacha* concludes with *shorcha vachamorcha*, explicitly including one's animals. The Rambam, it should be noted, emphasizes this not as a *lav* but as the *aseh* of *lema'an yanua'ch shorcha vachamorcha* — a positive obligation to ensure one's animals rest — though the *Gemara* here frames it as a negative prohibition. This distinction will be explored further in subsequent discussion.

### Walking Solution

*De'amar Rav Adda bar Abba: menicha aleha k'she'hi mehalechet* — one waits until the donkey begins walking and then places the load upon it. The halachic significance: *melacha* in the context of carrying is defined by *akira* and *hanacha* — the initial lifting and the final setting down. If the donkey was already in motion when the load was placed upon it, the donkey itself never performed an *akira* — it never lifted the object off the ground. Therefore, no *melacha* was performed by the animal.

### Stopping Problem

The *Gemara* immediately raises the objection: *v'iy efshar d'lo kaima l'hashtin mayim ul'hateil gelalim* — it is impossible that the donkey will not stop at some point to urinate or defecate. When it stops and then starts moving again, that constitutes *akira* and *hanacha*. The donkey will have performed the complete act of carrying.

### Load Management

The solution: *k'she'hi mehalechet menicha aleha* — when the donkey starts walking, place the load on it; *k'she'hi omedet, notleh heimena* — when it stops, remove it. As soon as it starts moving again, replace the load. This requires close, active attention throughout the journey — one must remain constantly aware of the donkey's movements and respond immediately when it stops. The *Gemara* notes this is itself not without purpose: the arrangement makes one acutely conscious of the delicate halachic situation one is navigating.

### Friend as Carrier

*Ee hachi, chaveiro afilu chaveiro* — if this is the approach, the same logic could apply to a friend: have the friend begin walking, then place the load on him while he is already in motion. He never performs an *akira*, and the same technical solution applies.

### Rav Papa's Analysis

### Violation Levels

*Amar Rav Papa* — Rav Papa clarifies the full hierarchy of violation levels. *Kol she'begufo chayav chatas* — anything that, if one carried it oneself, stopping and starting, would constitute a full biblical transgression requiring a *chatas* offering — *b'chaveiro patur aval assur* — when done via one's friend (placing the object on him while he walks), one is exempt from biblical liability but it remains rabbinically forbidden. The technical loophole of the missing *akira* reduces it to a rabbinic level, not to full permissibility.

### Donkey Priority

*Kol she'bechaveiro patur aval assur, b'chamoro mutar l'chatchila* — whatever is only rabbinically forbidden when done via one's friend is entirely *muttar lechatchila* via one's donkey. This seems to apply even beyond the emergency case of the wallet: if the technical *melacha* is absent because there was no *akira* by the donkey, the act is fully permitted from the outset. This explains why the hierarchy places the donkey above giving the load to a Jewish adult, even an unrelated one.

### Running Solution

*Haisa chavilasah munachas al kteifo* — if one has a bundle already on one's shoulder as *Shabbat* begins, *rutz ad she'magia l'veiso* — run straight home without stopping. If one never stops, one never performs a *hanacha* in *reshut harabim*, and the journey is completed without a complete act of carrying.

### Speed Requirement

*Davka rutz* — this is valid specifically when running. *Aval kali kali, lo* — walking slowly, pausing incrementally, is not permitted. *Keivan d'leika hekeira* — since there is nothing visually distinguishing slow walking with a bundle from ordinary carrying, *asi l'mevad akira v'hanacha* — one will almost certainly come to perform a full *akira* and *hanacha* inadvertently. The running itself serves as the *hekeira*, the visible signal that something unusual is happening — and it also keeps one focused on the goal of completing the act without stopping.

### Final Problem

*Sof sof* — the *Gemara* raises the final difficulty: *ki mati l'veiseh, ee efshar d'lo kai purta* — when one arrives home, it is impossible not to stop, even briefly, before crossing into *reshut hayachid*. At that moment one performs a *hanacha*. How does one avoid that final prohibited act?

This question, as Rashi and *Tosafot* note, could equally have been raised about the donkey or the other cases discussed: in all of them, arriving home requires the animal or carrier to stop, which constitutes a *hanacha*. But perhaps in those cases the *Gemara* was not concerned because there was never an *akira* to begin with — without both endpoints, the act of carrying is incomplete. Here, where the *Gemara* may be assuming that the person had been standing still before *Shabbat* began and then started walking — meaning there was a genuine *akira* — the *hanacha* at the end becomes a real concern that must be addressed.

### Shinuy Method

*Dezarak leh k'le'achar yad* — one lets the bundle drop in an unusual manner, *k'le'achar yad*, slipping it off one's back or setting it down abnormally rather than in the standard way. This constitutes a *shinuy* — an alteration from the normal method of performing the act — which reduces the *hanacha* from a full biblical violation to a lesser category.

### Unresolved Timing

The deeper unresolved question underlying this final exchange is when exactly the act of walking began. If *Shabbat* descended while the person was already in motion, there was no *akira* — and without a starting point, the only issue is the *hanacha* at the end, which the *shinuy* addresses. If the person was standing still when *Shabbat* began and then started walking, there is a genuine *akira*, and the full prohibition of carrying applies — making it necessary to address both endpoints. The *Gemara* leaves this tension implicit, and the discussion of the broader prohibition of having one's animal work on *Shabbat* will continue in the following *daf*.

---

---

# Shabbat 154

## Carrying Home Erev Shabb…

### Wallet Outside City

We pick up at the bottom of 153, with the continuing discussion of what a person should do when Shabbat overtakes him outside the city with his wallet. The *gemara* had concluded that one should simply run home without stopping, relying on the principle that continuous motion prevents one from inadvertently setting the object down in a prohibited domain. The *gemara* then asks: what happens when one finally arrives at one's house? The answer is that one sets it down *kil'achar yad* — in an irregular, backhanded manner — upon entering.

### Kil'achar Yad

The reason the *gemara* did not raise this question in the case of placing the object on an animal is that when the animal was already in motion, there was never a proper *akira* — a halakhically significant lifting — to begin with. Consequently, there is less concern about the *hanachah*, the act of setting down.

### Pachos Pachos Me'arba Am…

Tosafot, however, presses further: the same problem should arise in the case of walking *pachos pachos me'arba amos* — fewer than four cubits at a time — through the public domain. At some point the person must transition from *reshut harabim* to *reshut hayachid*, and the question of how to set the object down without a prohibited *hanachah* is equally acute. Tosafot notes that one could stop in a *karmelis* before entering one's house, which would reduce the concern to a rabbinic one. Regardless, Tosafot concludes that the same answer applies: one sets it down *kil'achar yad*.

### Chutz L'techum & Sakana

A further relevant question concerns the *techum* boundary. The *Shulchan Aruch* and the Rama rule on this with an interesting distinction. On one hand, the authorities permitted a range of measures to bring the wallet home — placing it on an animal, and so forth — yet they did not permit placing it on a friend who is in motion, because that would constitute *shnayim she'asu'u*, the paradigm of two people performing an act jointly, recalling the first *mishnah* about the poor man and the householder. So not every rabbinic leniency was granted.

Regarding the *techum* specifically: the Rama rules that if remaining outside the city poses a danger — *sakana* — one may violate *techum* concerns to return to safety. But absent such danger, one must stop at the boundary of one's *techum*, even if that boundary falls well short of the city. If, for example, one's *techum* ends two thousand feet before the city gate and one finds oneself five thousand feet outside the city, one travels two thousand feet and stops. No further movement is permitted unless *sakana* overrides the restriction.

One might ask whether the rabbinic prohibitions apply at all during *bein hashmashot*, the twilight period. There is certainly a position, associated with Rebbi, that rabbinic decrees do not apply during *bein hashmashot*, at least *bemakom mitzvah*, in the context of a mitzvah. That consideration would be relevant here. As for the status of *techum* itself: although Rabbi Akiva holds it to be *d'oraisa*, the accepted ruling is that it is *derabanan*. Yet it is not entirely clear why the authorities drew the line precisely where they did, permitting some rabbinic violations in this case but not others.

### Placing on Minor vs. Ani…

One final point before transitioning to today's *daf* proper concerns the case of placing the object on a minor. There is a debate between the Rambam and Tosafot about whether, in that case, one must also wait for the minor to be in motion before placing the object — analogous to the requirement in the donkey case. This question is closely tied to a fundamental distinction. The donkey case involves a *d'oraisa* concern: causing one's animal to perform labor on Shabbat. But if the child in question is not one's own, there is no *d'oraisa* concern at all, since the obligation of *shvisah* — ensuring rest — applies specifically to members of one's own household. One is commanded regarding one's own children and animals, not another's.

This leads to a conceptually important point. The Rambam apparently holds that the requirement to wait for the animal to be moving before placing the load applies only in the donkey case, precisely because one bears a *d'oraisa* responsibility for one's own animal. By contrast, the minor case — especially if the minor belongs to someone else — involves no such obligation. A question was raised: is one not, in such a case, causing another person to transgress the *shvisah* of their own child? The response is that the obligation of *shvisah* applies specifically when the minor is performing labor for the sake of the person commanded — meaning when the minor's activity is directed toward one's own purposes. When the minor is acting for someone else, that framing does not apply. In any event, the Ramban understands the animal case to be more stringent than the minor case, and that serves as the natural bridge into the *daf*'s opening *gemara*.

---

## Mechamer Achar Behemah

### Full Melachah: Chatas &…

The *gemara* begins with the statement of Rami bar Chama: *hamechamer achar behemah beShabbos beshogeg chayav chatas, meizid chayav sekilah* — one who drives his animal on Shabbat carrying a load is liable to bring a *chatas* if he did so inadvertently, and is liable to *sekilah* — death by stoning — if he did so deliberately. According to this position, *mechamer*, the act of leading one's laden animal, constitutes a full *melachah* in every sense: it is as though the person performed the act himself.

Before proceeding, it is worth noting that the *poskim* — as already developed by the *rishonim* — identify two distinct prohibitions relating to one's animal on Shabbat. The first is the positive commandment of *shvisas behemto*: *lemaan yanuach shorecha vachamorecha* — ensuring that one's ox and donkey rest. This applies even when one is not personally participating in the animal's activity. If one rents one's animal to a non-Jew who works it on Shabbat, one transgresses *shvisas behemto*, even without any direct involvement — but only with respect to one's own animal. This is a *mitzvas aseh*, a positive obligation, rooted in membership in one's household.

The second is the negative prohibition: *lo taaseh kol melacha atah uvincha uvitecha vashorecha vachamorecha* — do not perform any labor, you and your son and your daughter and your ox and your donkey. This verse is understood by one opinion to constitute a genuine prohibition of *chilul Shabbos* at the highest level — not merely ensuring the animal rests, but one actually performing the *melachah* together with the animal. When one directly drives the animal — *atah vechamorecha*, you together with your animal — this may be classified as performing the *melachah* oneself.

The *gemara* presents Rava's reasoning for this first position: *deamar kra lo taaseh kol melacha atah uvehemtecha* — the same verse in which the prohibition of *melacha* carries the penalty of *sekilah* says "you and your animal." *Behemtecha dumya dideich* — your animal is treated like you. Just as one who violates Shabbat through one's own action is liable to a *chatas* for inadvertence and *sekilah* for deliberateness, so too here. Rashi adds that *atah uvehemtecha* specifically connects to the *melachah* of leading — as if one had performed the *melachah* entirely oneself.

An important qualification: if one's animal sets out on its own initiative — say, if one placed food before it and it walked toward the food carrying a load, without one's direct participation in the act of carrying — that would not necessarily constitute *mechamer*, and certainly would not carry the status of *sekilah*. *Mechamer* requires direct, active participation. By way of illustration: if one's cat shreds toilet paper on Shabbat entirely on its own, not only is one not required to stop it, one may even use the shredded paper.

Regarding slaves: the *gemara* assumes that the *mitzvas aseh* of *shvisah* — ensuring rest — applies to minors and slaves. It is specifically with respect to animals that the *gemara* entertains the possibility of a genuine *melachah*, because one is using the animal as one performs the *melachah*, and that may be classified as one doing the *melachah* through it, at the level of *lo taaseh*.

The Ramban notes, however, that there are cases where one would indeed be liable even according to positions that do not accept full *mechamer* liability. If, for instance, one's cow is plowing and one is physically holding the plow and guiding it as the cow pulls, the Ramban says that constitutes performing the *melachah* oneself — because one is directly manipulating the implement of the *melachah* even as the animal provides the motive force.

### Rava's Responses

The *gemara* now records that Rava offers two responses (*shtei teshuvos ladavar*) to the first position — meaning he challenges the claim that *mechamer* is fully equivalent to performing the *melachah* oneself.

His first response: *chada dichsiv, Torah achas yihyeh lachem la'oseh bishgagah, vehanefesh asher taaseh beyad ramah* — there is one law for one who acts in error, and the one who acts presumptuously. This verse concerns *avodah zarah* but is applied to the entire Torah: *huksha kol haTorah kullah l'avodah zarah*. The whole Torah is analogized to *avodah zarah* for purposes of the *chatas* obligation. Just as *avodah zarah* requires a physical act performed by one's own body, so too a *chatas* for any Torah violation requires a physical, bodily act. Since in the case of *mechamer* it is the animal performing the act, not the person, there is no liability for a *chatas*. This is Rava's first answer.

His second response draws from a *mishnah*: *hamechalel es haShabbos bedavar shechayavin al shigagaso chatas ve'al zedonos sekilah* — one who violates Shabbat with something for which the inadvertent act incurs a *chatas* and the deliberate act incurs *sekilah*.
