The *gemara* infers: *michlal de'ika midi delo chayav al shigagaso chatas velo al zedonos sekilah* — there must be a category of Shabbat violation for which one does not bring a *chatas* and does not incur *sekilah*. What is that? The prohibition of *mechamer* — leading one's animal. So one can infer that *mechamer* is a form of *chilul Shabbos* but not of the same category that carries *sekilah*.

The *gemara* pushes back: perhaps the other categories referenced are *techum* according to Rabbi Akiva — who holds *techum* to be *d'oraisa* but not punishable by death — and *havarah* (kindling fire) according to Rabbi Yosi — who holds that the Torah's singling out of the prohibition of kindling indicates it carries lashes but not *sekilah*. If those are the categories intended by the *mishnah*, then *mechamer* might still be subject to *sekilah*. So the inference is inconclusive.

### No Chatas, Yes Sekilah

Rav Zevid teaches the discussion differently. In his version, Rami bar Chama says: *hamechamer achar behemah beShabbos beshogeg eino chayav chatas* — one who leads his animal on Shabbat inadvertently does not bring a *chatas* — *uvemeizid chayav sekilah* — but deliberately he is liable to *sekilah*. This is a striking intermediate position. The absence of a *chatas* for the inadvertent act is conceded — because, as Rava's first argument established, the *chatas* requires a bodily act which is absent here. But the deliberate act, Rami bar Chama argues, still warrants *sekilah*, because there are cases where one incurs *sekilah* without a corresponding *chatas* for inadvertence — as with one who blasphemes (*megadef*), for instance.

### Rava's Logic Challenge

Rava challenges this intermediate position. He cites the *mishnah*: *hamechalel es haShabbos bedavar shechayavin al shigagaso chatas chayavin al zedonos sekilah*. Rava argues that this implies the converse — *ha ein chayavin al shigagaso chatas, ein chayavin al zedonos sekilah*: if there is no *chatas* for the inadvertent act, there is no *sekilah* for the deliberate act. Rami bar Chama's position therefore cannot stand.

At this point the *gemara* itself intervenes with an important logical observation. The *mishnah*'s formulation — "if *chatas*, then *sekilah*" — is a conditional statement, not a biconditional. In elementary logical terms: if P then Q does not entail that if not-P then not-Q. "If P then Q" licenses only the contrapositive: if not-Q then not-P. The *mishnah* tells us that having a *chatas* guarantees *sekilah*. It does not tell us that lacking a *chatas* rules out *sekilah*.

The *gemara* makes this point explicitly: *mi kasni ha ein chayavin?* — did the *mishnah* say "if there is no *chatas* there is no *sekilah*"? No. What it said is: *davar shechayavin al shigagaso chatas chayavin al zedonos sekilah* — if there is a *chatas*, there is definitely *sekilah*. But there may well be something for which there is no *chatas* and yet there is *sekilah*. And what might that be? *Mechamer* — exactly. So the *mishnah* does not exclude *sekilah* for *mechamer*. Rami bar Chama's position, though it arrived at the same result, is not actually refuted by the *mishnah*.

This is thus a technically coherent position: *mechamer* incurs no *chatas* because no bodily act was performed, yet it may still incur *sekilah* because the prohibition is severe enough to warrant capital punishment even without the *chatas*-level requirements.

### Rabbi Yochanan: Exempt

The *gemara* then transmits the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan: *mechamer achar behemto beShabbos patur miklum* — one who leads his animal on Shabbat is completely exempt from punishment. This does not necessarily mean there is no biblical violation, but there is no punishment of any kind.

*Beshogeg lo mechayev chatas* — inadvertently, one does not bring a *chatas*, as established by the *huksha kol haTorah kullah l'avodah zarah* principle: a *chatas* requires a bodily act, and here one performed none.

*Uvemeizid nami lo mechayev misah* — deliberately, one does not incur capital punishment either. The *gemara* invokes the same *mishnah*: *hamechalel es haShabbos bedavar shechayavin al zedonos kares ve'al shegagaso chatas*. Rabbi Yochanan draws the inference that if there is no *chatas*, there is no *sekilah* — and we already noted the logical difficulty with this inference, yet the *gemara* here adopts it in Rabbi Yochanan's name as the operative conclusion.

*Belav nami lo mechayev* — one does not even receive lashes. Why? *D'havei lei lav shenitan le'azharat misas beis din* — the prohibition in question, *lo taaseh kol melacha*, is the very verse that serves as the basis for the capital penalty for deliberate *chilul Shabbos*. There is a general principle that a *lav* given to warn against a capital offense — *lav shenitan le'azharat misas beis din* — cannot simultaneously serve as the basis for lashes. Once the verse is "used" to ground the more severe punishment, it cannot be applied to impose the lesser one on someone not subject to the greater. Therefore, no *malkus* either.

The *gemara* continues on 154b: even according to the view that one does receive lashes for such a *lav*, here one would not. The verse could have read simply *lo taaseh kol melacha uvehemtecha* — do not perform any labor, and your animal. But it says *atah* — you — separately. *Hu nihu demichayev* — it is *you* who are the subject of liability for *melacha*. *Beheimah lo mechayev* — for the animal's actions alone, not only is there no *sekilah*, there is not even *malkus*. The explicit mention of *atah* signals that the animal is categorically distinct from the person for purposes of *melachah* liability.

### Atah vs. Behemtecha

This concluding derivation from the verse encapsulates the *gemara*'s final resolution. Two competing understandings of *atah uvehemtecha* were on the table throughout the discussion: one view read it as equating the animal's labor to the person's own act, grounding full *sekilah* liability; Rabbi Yochanan's view reads it as differentiating them — *atah* and *behemtecha* are listed together precisely because they are not the same, and the liability structure that applies to the person does not apply when it is the animal performing the act.

We *pasken* like Rabbi Yochanan: *mechamer* carries no punishment — no *chatas*, no *sekilah*, no *malkus*. It remains a *lav* in the view of most authorities, though a *lav shenitan le'azharat misas beis din*, and therefore not actionable. The Rambam, as the Ramban understands him, goes further and holds that it is not even a *lav* — only an *asei*, the positive obligation of *shvisas behemto*. That remains a question in the Rambam.

To summarize the two conceptual tracks that run through the *sugya*: there is a *mitzvas asei* — *lemaan yanuach shorecha vachamorecha* — to ensure one's animal rests, which applies even when one is entirely passive, and which applies only to one's own animals. And there is the *lo taaseh*, which applies when one is directly performing the *melachah* together with the animal. The whole discussion of *mechamer* concerns the *lo taaseh* dimension. When one is so directly involved — as the Ramban's example of holding the plow while the cow pulls — the Ramban holds one would be liable. But in the standard case of simply driving the animal, Rabbi Yochanan rules: *patur miklum*.

---

## Unloading at Courtya (II)

### Karni D'Umna & Pillows

Having resolved the theoretical question of *mechamer*, the *gemara* now turns to a practical scenario: one has arrived at the outer courtyard of the city — *higia l'chatzer hachitzonah* — a protected area where the leniencies granted for the journey cease to apply. Now one must unload the animal without handling *muktzah* items. Rav Huna addresses the case where one's animal is carrying glass vessels: *mevi kesasos u'maniach tachteiha, matir hachavalim, vehasakin noflin* — one brings pillows, places them beneath the vessels, unties the ropes, and the sacks fall without the glass breaking.

The *gemara* asks: but we have already established in the *mishnah* that *notlin kelim hanitlin* — one may remove non-*muktzah* items directly. Glass vessels are not *muktzah*. Why the need for pillows? The *gemara* answers: *ki ka'amar Rav Huna bekarni de'umna* — Rav Huna was speaking specifically about the horns of a bloodletter. These are glass instruments used in a medical procedure and, as Rashi explains, they are repulsive and also qualify as *klei umanut* — tools of a craft — and are therefore *muktzah*. They cannot be directly handled.

### Mevatel Kli Me'heichano

The *gemara* immediately raises a further difficulty: *v'ha kamvatel kli meheichano* — is one not invalidating a vessel from its use? By placing the pillow beneath the *muktzah* instrument, the pillow becomes unusable — one cannot move it without causing the glass to fall and break. And the Rabbis did not permit an act that renders a vessel functionally unusable on Shabbat. One might suggest that one can simply lift the pillow and the *muktzah* item along with it, as is often permitted with *basis* situations. But here, moving the pillow causes the glass to fall and shatter. Therefore, the pillow truly is rendered unusable.

---

## Unloading at Courtya (II)

### Small Sacks Solution

The *gemara* resolves this: *bishlifi zutri* — with small sacks. Rashi explains that the vessels are light enough that one can remove the pillow from beneath them by sliding it out gradually — moving the vessel onto another pillow, and then another, until it is close enough to the ground that the final removal causes no breakage. The pillow is thus not truly rendered permanently unusable; it can be retrieved.

### Tevel & Glass Chunks

The *gemara* then raises a *beraisa*: if one's animal was carrying *tevel* — untithed grain, which is *muktzah* — and *ashashiyos*, which the *gemara* will clarify refers to chunks of raw glass rather than finished glass lanterns, one unties the ropes and lets the sacks fall, *af al pi shemishtabrin* — even though they will break. The implication is that one makes no accommodation and allows even breakable items to fall.

### Glass Chunks: Usable Bro…

Why does this not trigger concern for *mevatel kli meheichano*? Because *ashashiyos* here means a large chunk of glass — *kulsya* — which even after breaking remains usable. Rashi suggests that the broken pieces can still serve a purpose; one possibility is that colored glass shards can be used for mosaic work, or the pieces can be remelted. Therefore, it is not a genuine loss. The *gemara* confirms this reading: *dayka nami dekasni dumya detavla* — it can be inferred by close reading, since the *beraisa* juxtaposes these glass chunks with *tevel* — something completely unusable on Shabbat — indicating that the glass chunks too are not fit for Shabbat use (*lo chazi lei*), confirming we are dealing with raw industrial material rather than finished vessels.

The *gemara* asks: then what is the *chiddush* of *af al pi shemishtabrin* — why does the *beraisa* need to specify "even though they break"? One might have thought that even a minor loss — such as the small shards that cannot be salvaged — would give pause. The *beraisa* teaches that we are not concerned with such a minor loss.

---

## Gamliel's Donkey & Tzaa'r

### Honey & Dead Animal

A *beraisa* relates that Rabban Gamliel's donkey was carrying honey. He did not want to unload it until after Shabbat, and by the time Shabbat ended, the donkey had died from the burden. The *gemara* is evidently troubled by this outcome and frames the discussion around the prohibition of *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* — causing suffering to animals.

### Spoiled Honey Use

The *gemara* first asks why the honey could not simply be removed, since honey is not *muktzah*. The answer is *k'shehikdish* — it had spoiled. The peculiar idiom here, *dvash hikdish* ("the honey became sanctified"), actually means the opposite — it soured. Spoiled honey is *muktzah* because it is unfit for normal use. The *gemara* asks: if it spoiled, for what use is it even being preserved? The answer: *likitita d'gamlei* — it is rubbed into the sores of camels as a medicinal salve, a use unsuitable for Shabbat. Hence it is *muktzah*.

### Alternative Solutions Fa…

The *gemara* then considers why other solutions were not employed. Why not untie the ropes and let the sacks fall? Because *mitzru ziki* — the barrels would break, spilling the honey. Why not place pillows beneath? Because *mitanfi* — the pillows would be soiled with honey and thereby rendered unusable, which again constitutes *mevatel kli meheichano*. Unlike the earlier case where the pillows could be retrieved by gradual removal, here they become permanently soiled and unusable. That solution was therefore off the table.

### Tzaa'r Overrides Rabbinic

The *gemara* points out, however, that the concern of *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* — animal suffering — can override rabbinic prohibitions. A classic parallel is the case of an animal that has fallen into a well on Shabbat: one may lower pillows into the well for the animal to rest on, even though this renders the pillows unusable (*mevatel kli meheichano*), because preventing the animal's suffering takes precedence over rabbinic restrictions. If that precedent exists, why did Rabban Gamliel not simply place pillows to reduce the animal's load, notwithstanding the *mevatel kli* concern?

### Gamliel: Tzaa'r Only Rab…

The *gemara* resolves: *kasavar tza'ar ba'alei chayim derabbanan* — Rabban Gamliel holds that the prohibition against causing animal suffering is itself only rabbinic in origin. If that is the case, it is merely a rabbinic concern competing against another rabbinic concern (*mevatel kli meheichano*), and one does not simply override the other.

This is a halakhically decisive point. Whether *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* is *d'oraisa* or *derabanan* has immediate practical consequences: if it is biblical, it overrides rabbinic prohibitions; if it is only rabbinic, it does not. We rule that it is *d'oraisa*, and that ruling has direct application — for example, in the well-known issue of milking dairy cows on Shabbat. Because the cows suffer when not milked, various rabbinic leniencies (having a non-Jew do it, employing an automatic milking device set before Shabbat, and similar arrangements) are permitted, precisely because *tza'ar ba'alei chayim d'oraisa* overrides the relevant rabbinic concerns. Rabban Gamliel, holding it was only rabbinic, let the competing considerations stand — with the tragic result the *gemara* records.

---

## Sides of Animals & Trees

### Rubbing on Donkey Side

Abaye found Rabba, his *rebbe*, rubbing his son against the side of a donkey — *d'kameshafshef lei l'brei agav d'chamra*. Abaye challenged him: is the master using animals on Shabbat? This leads into a broad and practically significant discussion about the prohibition against using animals and trees on Shabbat. The baseline rule is that one may not ride an animal and may not climb a tree on Shabbat, and this has been extended to prohibit using an animal or tree in any manner. The question is what "using" encompasses: does it mean only the top — the riding surface of an animal, the branches and top of a tree — or does it extend to the sides as well?

### Sides Permitted

Rabba responded: *tzedadim heim, ve'tzedadim lo gazru bahem rabbanan* — it is the side of the animal, and the Rabbis did not extend their decree to the sides. The prohibition was against riding and using the animal in the manner of riding; it does not encompass leaning against the flank or using the side of the animal.

### Proof from Undoing Ropes

Where does this principle come from? The *gemara* derives it from our very *mishnah*: *matir hachavalim vehasakim noflim* — one unties the ropes and the sacks fall. The *gemara* asks: is this not referring to a case — *d'chavar gavalki* — where the sacks are combined as saddlebags on both sides of the donkey? When one unties them, one must lean against the donkey to reach both sides simultaneously, thereby using the donkey's flank for support. Since the *mishnah* permits untying the ropes in this configuration, it implicitly permits using the sides of the donkey.

The *gemara* offers an alternative: perhaps the *mishnah* refers to a different configuration — *d'lo havu tzedadim* — one where the bags are not truly saddlebags but are combined by a central loop or peg that one can release without leaning on the donkey at all. Or similarly, *einami b'lachta* — a rope configuration that allows one to free the sacks without any bodily contact with the animal's side. In that case the *mishnah* provides no proof about *tzedadim* at all.

### Sukkah Third Wall

The *gemara* then raises a case from *hilchos sukkah* to press the question. The *mishnah* in *Sukkah* states: if two walls of the *sukkah* are man-made and the third is a tree, the *sukkah* is valid, but one may not use it on *Yom Tov*. (Rashi notes that "going up" into the *sukkah* refers to the standard practice of building the *sukkah* on a roof, so that one ascends to enter it and descends to return to the house.) The question is: what configuration does this envision, and what precisely is the problem?

### Using Top vs. Trunk

One possibility: the tree's trunk serves as a wall, with a shelf inserted into it to support the *schach*. One cannot use the *sukkah* on *Yom Tov* because reaching for items stored atop the *schach* means making use of the *schach*, which is supported by the shelf in the tree's trunk, which means using the side of the tree. If *tzedadim* — the sides — were permitted, there would be no problem.

Another possibility: one has bent the tops of trees over to form the wall, using the treetops and branches rather than the trunk. In that case, the prohibition comes from using the top of the tree, not the side.

The *gemara* tests this by examining the next clause of the *mishnah*: if three walls are man-made and a tree forms the fourth, the *sukkah* is valid and one *may* use it on *Yom Tov*. This creates a difficulty regardless of how one explains the three-wall case. Whether the *schach* rests on the tree's top (bent-over branches) or on a shelf in its trunk, in either case the tree is still involved when three walls are man-made. Why does adding a third man-made wall resolve the prohibition?

The *gemara* answers: *ela hatam beguza deparsachna* — the case involves a pine-type tree whose branches naturally radiate outward along its trunk, forming a wall on their own without any bending or artificial support. The key point, as Rashi explains, is not the species per se but the structural implication: when three man-made walls support the *schach* entirely, the tree's role is purely that of a curtain-wall, bearing no weight. The rule, confirmed by the *mishnah*'s own summary — *zeh haklal*: if one were to remove the tree and the *sukkah* would remain standing, one may use it on *Yom Tov* — is that if the tree bears no structural load, using the *schach* does not constitute using the tree.

This resolves the four-wall case but leaves the question of *tzedadim versus* the top of the tree in the three-wall case unresolved.

### Sides of Sides Debate

The *gemara* considers whether this connects to a *tannaitic* dispute. The *mishnah* forbids using the three-wall *sukkah* on *Yom Tov*; Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir permits it. Perhaps they disagree about whether using the trunk — the *tzedadim* — is forbidden. Abaye says no: *dekuli alma tzedadim asurim* — most likely everyone agrees the trunk itself is forbidden. The dispute, he suggests, concerns *tziddei tzedadim* — things attached to the sides of the tree. If the *schach* rests not directly on the trunk but on a shelf that is inserted into the trunk, then one using the *schach* is making direct use of the shelf and only indirect use of the trunk. One opinion forbids this indirect use; the other permits it.

This distinction is practically decisive. The hammock example illustrates it clearly: if one ties a hammock rope directly to a tree trunk, that is *tzedadim* — using the side of the tree. If one inserts a peg into the trunk and ties the rope around the peg, the direct use is of the peg, and the trunk is engaged only indirectly — that is *tziddei tzedadim*.

### Peg in Tree Case

Rami bar Chama challenges Rava — who denied any meaningful distinction between *tzedadim* and *tziddei tzedadim* — from the following *mishnah*: *na'atz yated be'ilan ve'talah bah kalkalah* — one who drove a peg into a tree and hung a basket from it. The basket contains food intended to serve as an *eiruv* to extend one's *techum*. If the basket hangs above ten *tefachim*, the *eiruv* is invalid; below ten *tefachim*, it is valid. The *gemara* notes: *ta'ama d'na'atz yated be'ilan* — the reason it works is that a peg was driven into the tree. This implies that had the basket been hung directly on the tree without a peg, even below ten *tefachim* it would be invalid — because one would be using the tree to access the food. The *mishnah* specifies the peg because it makes the critical difference: with the peg, one is using *tziddei tzedadim*, which is permitted; without it, one is using the *tzedadim* themselves, which is forbidden.

This challenge shows that a distinction between *tzedadim* and *tziddei tzedadim* is implicit in the *mishnah*, contrary to Rava's position.

### Tree Shaking Solution

Rav Papa offers a different explanation of why the peg matters, one that does not require accepting a distinction between *tzedadim* and *tziddei tzedadim*. Even if one holds that the trunk itself may be used, the *mishnah* may specify the peg for a different reason: *hacha b'kalkalah d'chukah askinan* — the basket has a very narrow opening. If the basket were attached directly to the tree, retrieving the food would require inserting one's hand deeply into the basket, and the jostling — *d'shakil lei ati l'atuyei ilana* — would cause the tree to shake. Shaking the tree is the equivalent of using the treetop, which is unambiguously forbidden. With the peg, the basket hangs freely enough that one can retrieve the food without causing the tree to move.

### Halakha: Trunk vs. Attac…

*V'hilchesa*: the ruling is that *tzedadin asurin* — the trunk of the tree is forbidden — and *tziddei tzedadin mutarin* — things attached to the trunk are permitted. This follows Abaye's distinction rather than Rava's flattening of the categories.

### Ladder & Peg Application

Rav Ashi applies this ruling directly: *hashta d'amrat tzedadin asurin* — now that we have established that using the trunk is forbidden — *hai darga d'madla lo linchei inash a'dikla* — one should not lean a ladder against a palm tree, *d'havei lei tzedadin* — because the ladder rests directly on the trunk and one using the ladder is using the trunk.

How then does one climb such a tree when necessary? *Linchei a'guza l'var midikla* — one places a peg that protrudes from the side of the tree. And when climbing: *v'chi salik lo linach krei a'guza* — one should take care not to rest one's foot on the peg itself, *ella lintach a'kanim* — but rather on the rungs of the ladder. If the ladder rests on the peg and one's foot is on the rungs, one is using *tziddei tzedadim* — the ladder, which is supported by the peg, which is in the trunk — and that is permitted. But resting one's foot directly on the peg means using *tzedadim* — the side of the tree — which is forbidden.

The practical upshot is clear: a hammock hung from a nail or peg in a tree is permitted, since the person is in the hammock which hangs from the peg, not directly on the trunk. One simply must ensure the connection is via an intermediate object — peg, nail, or bracket — and not a rope tied directly to the bark.

---

---

# Shabbat 155

## Bundles & Twigs

### Intro: Pikei & Kiffin

The Mishnah we turn to now belongs to a cluster of rulings concerning a person's farm animals and the question of *tircha* — unnecessary effort on Shabbat — even in contexts where no formal *melacha* is being performed. The Mishnah states: *matirin pikei amir lifnei behemah* — one may open bundles of straw in front of an animal; that is not considered undue effort, since one is simply providing the animal its food. The Mishnah further permits *mefaspasin et hakiffin* — one may spread or scatter the contents, rubbing and loosening the material so it is no longer tightly bundled. The question of precisely what *kiffin* means will be debated in the Gemara. One reading, to be developed below, is that *pikei* are bundles of straw bound in two places — one at the top and one at the bottom — while *kiffin* are bundles bound in three places.

### Why Spread Straw

Why would one spread out the straw rather than simply leave it in a loosened bundle? Rashi explains: *shekhen derekh shemefazrim labehemah ha'asavim, veyafeh la le'ochlan* — it is the normal practice to scatter the grass before the animal, and it is better for the animal to eat it that way. When the hay is compressed, *shekesheim dechukim mitchamemim* — it heats up, *ve'einah merichah reicha kol kach* — the smell does not waft as readily, *vekatzah bahen* — and the animal is less interested in it. So spreading the hay makes it more attractive and appetizing to the animals, and this purpose justifies the additional effort.

### Zirin Prohibition

The Mishnah then states: *aval lo et hazirin* — but one may not undo bundles of *zirin*. According to the first approach to be presented in the Gemara, *zirin* are bundles not of straw but of twigs — the kind that might occasionally serve as animal food when moist, but are not generally regarded as such. The prohibition on undoing these bundles is thus categorically different from the permission to undo straw bundles, and the Gemara will explain the underlying rationale.

### Vetch & Carobs

The Mishnah continues: *ein meraskin lo et hashachat velo et hacharuvin lifnei behemah* — one may not chop up *shachat* (vetch) or *charuvin* (carobs) before an animal, *bein dakah bein gasah* — whether a small animal such as a sheep or goat, or a large animal such as a cow, horse, or camel. Rabbi Yehuda dissents in one respect: *matir becharuvin ledakah* — he permits chopping carobs for a small animal, because carobs are hard and require pre-cutting to be edible for smaller animals.

The overarching theme of this Mishnah is the limit on *tircha* in the service of one's animals. On one hand, there is a duty to feed one's animals — the famous *derasha* on the verses of *Shema* establishes that one must feed one's animals before eating oneself, and *tzaar baalei chayim* is a recognized concern. On the other hand, the Rabbis drew a line against effort that is unnecessary. Farm animals occupy an ambiguous position: one might argue for greater leniency given the owner's responsibility toward them, or for stricter limits given that agricultural labor is quintessentially the domain of weekday work. The Gemara does not resolve this tension explicitly, but whatever threshold applies here is specific to the context of animals and cannot be mechanically applied elsewhere.

---

## Rav Huna's View

### Pikei=Kiffin

Rav Huna offers the following reading of the Mishnah: *hen hen peki'in hen hen kiffin* — the *pikei* and the *kiffin* are the same thing; both refer to bundles of straw. The *pikei* are bound in two places and the *kiffin* in three, but the distinction is incidental. Both may be undone and spread out before the animal. The *zirin*, by contrast, are twigs of cedar — *zirin de'arzei* — which can be used as animal fodder when moist but are not generally so used. According to Rav Huna, the reading of the Mishnah is: one may both undo and spread out straw bundles, whether bound twice or three times, and this same license applies to *kiffin*. What one may not do at all — neither spread nor undo — is the *zirin*, the twigs.

### Non-Food Creation

Why this stark asymmetry? Rav Chisda articulates the rationale behind Rav Huna's position.

### Chisda's Formula

*Kasavar: lemitrach be'ochla tarchinan; leshavei ochla lo mashvinan.* If something is already defined as food, one may exert additional effort to make it more suitable or appealing for the animals. What one may not do is transform non-food into food. The concern with *zirin* is not the physical exertion involved in undoing the bundle — indeed, undoing a bundle is minimal effort — but rather the conceptual act of redefining something. A bundle of twigs is presumed to be firewood. When one unties it and places it before an animal, one is in effect converting it from non-food into food. This is not *melacha* in the formal sense, but it resembles the creation of something, a kind of quasi-*melacha* in the domain of category: one is taking an object understood as firewood and rendering it food purely by context, by the act of placing it before an animal. That act, Rav Huna maintains, is what is forbidden.

---

## R. Yehuda's View

### R. Yehuda's Terms

Rabbi Yehuda reads the Mishnah entirely differently. According to him, *hen hen peki'in hen hen zirin* — the *pikei* permitted at the opening of the Mishnah and the *zirin* forbidden at its close both refer to straw bundles; the difference is merely that *pikei* are bound in two places and *zirin* in three. The *kiffin* in the middle of the Mishnah, which says one may spread them out, are the twigs — *kiffin de'arzei*. Thus Rabbi Yehuda inverts Rav Huna's assignment of the second and third terms.

### Don't Scatter Food

The operative logic according to Rabbi Yehuda is precisely the reverse of Rav Huna's. Rabbi Yehuda has no problem with the conceptual transformation of non-food into food; if the animal will eat something once it is prepared, one may do what is necessary to enable that. What Rabbi Yehuda forbids is additional effort once the item is already edible. Thus the Mishnah, read through Rabbi Yehuda's lens, is saying: one may undo the straw bundles — whether bound twice or three times — but once the bundle is undone and the straw is accessible, the animal can eat it. At that point, spreading and scattering is unnecessary effort, and is therefore forbidden. The animal eats better from scattered straw, as Rashi notes, but that preference does not justify the additional exertion once the food is already consumable.

### Twigs Need Work

By contrast, the twigs — which Rabbi Yehuda identifies as the *kiffin* — may be scattered. Why? Because the animal will not eat them unless they are spread out and loosened. For these items, the extra work is not superfluous; it is what makes them edible in the first place. Since the goal is to make the item food for the animal, one may do whatever is necessary to achieve that goal. The effort is not gratuitous; it is the very mechanism of transformation from inedible to edible.

### Rava's Formula

Rava crystallizes Rabbi Yehuda's position: *kasavar: shavuyei ochla mashvinan; aval mitrach be'ochla — lo tarchinan*. To turn something into food — that is permitted. Once it is already considered food, once the animal can eat it without further preparation — then we do not permit any additional effort. The two positions thus represent diametrically opposed understandings of what is problematic on Shabbat in this domain: for Rav Huna, the problem is creating something, the quasi-*melacha* of converting non-food into food; for Rabbi Yehuda, the problem is purely one of unnecessary exertion once the food is already there.

---

## Testing Positions

### Vetch Test

The Gemara now attempts to determine which position is supported by the sources. It begins with the latter portion of the Mishnah itself. *Ein meraskin et hashachat ve'et hacharuvin lifnei behemah, bein dakah bein gasah* — one may not chop up vetch or carobs before animals, large or small. The Gemara argues: presumably the carobs are analogous to the vetch — *charuvin dumya deshachat*. Just as vetch is soft and readily eaten — *shachat de'orcha*, suitable as is — so too the carobs are soft and suitable. If that is the case, then what the Mishnah is forbidding is additional effort on food that is already edible, which is exactly Rabbi Yehuda's principle. *Alma lo tarchinan be'ochla* — once it is food, we do not permit the extra effort. This appears to challenge Rav Huna.

### Huna Counter

Rav Huna responds: do not read the analogy in that direction. *Shachat dumya decharuvin* — the vetch is like the carobs, not the other way around. Just as standard carobs are hard and not easily consumed without chopping — *charuvin de'akusha* — so too the vetch in this case is hard. And where does one find vetch that is too hard for an animal to eat? *Be'eilei zutrei* — with small foals, young donkeys, for whom even ordinary vetch is difficult to consume. The chopping is thus necessary to make the food edible for those particular animals, and the prohibition, according to Rav Huna, is about creating food from non-food, not about unnecessary effort on existing food.

This point is worth pausing over: whether something is already food or not yet food depends not only on the item itself but on the animal being fed. The same vetch that is edible for a full-grown horse may be effectively non-food for a newborn foal. This nuance surfaces again in the discussion of Rabbi Yehuda's exception for carobs fed to small animals.

### Gourds Test

The Gemara then turns to a separate Mishnah: *mechatchin et hadlu'in lifnei behemah, ve'et haneveila lifnei hakalavim* — one may chop up gourds before animals, and a *neveila* (carcass) before dogs. The Gemara asks: presumably the gourds are analogous to the carcass — *dlu'in dumya deneveila*. A carcass is soft and readily eaten by meat-eating animals; if the gourds are similarly soft and edible without chopping, then the permission to chop them represents a ruling that extra effort on already-edible food is permitted. This would support Rav Huna. *Alma tarchinan be'ochla* — once it is food, we may exert additional effort.

### Huna Counter II

Rabbi Yehuda responds in kind: read the analogy the other way. The carcass is like the gourds — *neveila dumya dedlu'in*. The gourds are hard; so too the carcass is hard. And what kind of carcass is hard? *Devasar pili* — elephant meat, which is difficult to eat without chopping; or *beguryata zutrei* — for small puppies or whelps, for whom even ordinary meat must be specially prepared. Thus the chopping here too is about making something edible, not about improving already-edible food.

### Chanan Test

The Gemara makes another attempt. Rav Chanan from Neharde'a taught: *mefarchin teven ve'aspasta ume'arvin* — one may chop up straw and alfalfa (or fodder) and mix them together. Straw and fodder are among the most obviously and readily edible items for animals; if anything is food in its given form, it is these. Yet the Mishnah permits chopping and mixing them, which seems to indicate that once something is food, one may still do extra effort to improve it. *Alma tarchinan be'ochla* — a seemingly strong proof for Rav Huna's position.

### Preserving Huna

The Gemara declines to accept this as a definitive refutation of Rabbi Yehuda's framework. Perhaps the straw in question is *betivna sarya* — slightly spoiled straw, which the animal would not eat in its current state; the chopping rehabilitates it. And perhaps the fodder is for *aylei zutrei* — young foals who require it to be more finely prepared. Thus even here, the chopping might be classified as making something into food rather than improving already-edible food.

The Gemara does not cleanly resolve the dispute. Both positions find textual support, and each can deflect the challenges directed at it by positing special circumstances. The overall thrust of the sugya, however, seems to favor the principle that the problem is making non-food into food, rather than exerting effort on food already fit for consumption — though the opposing reading is well-supported and cannot be dismissed.

---

## Force-Feeding Rules

### Camel Feeding

The next Mishnah shifts from what is done to the food to how food is delivered to the animal. *Ein ovsin et hagamal* — one may not *oveis* a camel, which means one may not force enormous quantities of food into it — essentially filling its stomach like a trough, as the Gemara will explain. *Velo dorsin* — nor may one use the related technique of *dosin*, pushing food into the animal's throat, though less deeply than *ovsin*. These are two distinct modes of forced feeding, one pushing more deeply than the other. *Aval mal'atin* — but one may *mal'it*, which is to assist the animal in eating, placing food in its mouth without forcing it beyond where the animal could retrieve it.

### Calf Feeding

The Mishnah continues: *ve'ein ma'amirin et ha'agalim* — one similarly may not *ma'amir* the calves; *aval mal'atin* — but one may *mal'it* them. The same distinction between impermissible force-feeding and permissible assistance applies to calves. For chickens, the Mishnah uses the term *mehal'kitin* — one may be *mehal'ket* for chickens, a different verb for what appears to be a related form of assistance. The precise meaning of *mechalkin* will be disputed in the Gemara.

### Water & Bran

The Mishnah then permits: *ve'notnim mayim lemursan* — one may add water to bran, which is how animal feed is typically prepared. This is noteworthy because adding water to grain or flour raises the concern of *lisha* — kneading, a prohibited Shabbat labor. The Mishnah permits adding the water but adds: *aval lo govlin* — one may not knead it. Adding water is permitted; mixing it into a dough-like consistency is not.

### Water for Birds

Finally, the Mishnah distinguishes between categories of animals with respect to water. *Ve'ein notnim mayim lifnei devorim ulifnei yonim shebashovach* — one may not put out water for bees or for doves in the coop. *Aval notnim lifnei avazim velifnei tarnegolim velifnei yonei hardesi'ot* — but one may put out water for ducks, chickens, and Herodian doves (a domesticated species, possibly from the island of Rhodes, associated with Herod's time). The basis of this distinction — whether it concerns ownership, responsibility, or the animals' access to water in the wild — is the subject of the Gemara's discussion below.

---

## Force-Feed Debate

### Ovsin=Fullness

What does *ovsin* mean? Rav Yehuda explains: *ein ovsin la evus betoch me'eha* — one does not make a trough inside its stomach; one does not force-feed the animal to such a degree that its stomach becomes like a trough, packed completely full. The Gemara asks whether such a thing is even possible. The answer is yes — Rav Yirmeyah of Difti testified: *ledidi chazi li hahu taya de'akhla kora ve'atneia kora* — I once saw an Arab nomad who fed his camel an entire *kor* of grain and then loaded a *kor* onto its back. Camels are evidently capable of consuming and carrying extraordinary quantities. The prohibition of *ovsin* addresses precisely this extreme.

### Hamra vs. Malatin

Beyond *ovsin*, there is the more ordinary prohibition of *hamra*, force-feeding, and the permitted *malatin*. Rav Yehuda defines the distinction as follows. *Hamra* — the forbidden force-feeding — pushes food *le-makom she-eino yakhol lehachzir*, to a place from which the animal cannot retrieve it; the animal is compelled to swallow. *Halatah* — the permitted assistance — places food only *le-makom she-yakhol lehachzir*, to a place from which the animal could still expel it if it chose. The animal retains the ability to spit it out; it is participating in the act of eating rather than being subjected to it.

### Chisda: Kli Issue

Rav Chisda disagrees with this framework. In his view, *idei ve-idei le-makom she-eino yakhol lehachzir* — both *hamra* and *halatah* involve feeding to the point of no return, where the animal cannot retrieve the food. The distinction is not anatomical but instrumental: *hamra bi-chli, halatah be-yad* — the forbidden act uses a specialized vessel, the permitted act uses the hand. On Shabbat, taking out specialized farm implements to force-feed one's animals transforms the activity from care-giving into a form of *ovdin de-chol*, weekday agricultural labor. Using one's bare hands, by contrast, retains the character of simple feeding and is therefore permissible. Interestingly, using a vessel actually reduces the physical effort relative to doing it by hand — yet it is the vessel-use that is forbidden. The concern here is not tircha but the character of the act.

### Yosef Challenge

Rav Yosef challenges both positions by citing the Mishnah's rulings about chickens and coop doves. The Mishnah states that one may perform *mechalkin* for chickens — and certainly *mal'atin* — but one may not perform *mal'atin* for coop doves, let alone *mechalkin*. If *mechalkin* means placing food in the hand before the animal and *mal'atin* means simply placing it in front, then by doves one could not even toss food in front of them — which seems extreme. If, on the other hand, *mal'atin* involves placing food in the mouth (and is forbidden for doves), then for chickens both mouth-feeding and force-feeding are permitted, implying that force-feeding per se is not the problem — only using a vessel is.

### Yehuda Defense

Rav Yehuda defends his position: *mechalkin* means placing food in the mouth, *mal'atin* means placing it in front of the animal. Both of these are permitted for chickens, and both involve no force-feeding whatsoever. With respect to doves, the reason even *mal'atin* — the trivial act of placing food in front of them — is forbidden is not because of the nature of the act, but because of the nature of the animal: the doves are not the owner's responsibility, and anything done for an animal not in one's care is impermissible. Force-feeding, by contrast, remains forbidden for all animals regardless.

### Chisda Defense

Rav Chisda maintains his alternative: *mechalkin* for chickens means force-feeding using a vessel, while *mal'atin* means force-feeding by hand. The Mishnah thus permits both for chickens — confirming that force-feeding by hand is allowed — while prohibiting both for coop doves because they are not the owner's animals. The only thing universally forbidden is force-feeding with a vessel.

---

## Ownership Test

### Dog & Pig

The Gemara grounds the distinction between permitted and forbidden animal-feeding in the concept of *mezonotan alecha* — "their sustenance is upon you," meaning you bear responsibility for their feeding. A *baraita* illustrates this with a stark and memorable contrast: *notnin mezonot lifnei kelev, ve'ein notnin mezonot lifnei chazir* — one may place food before a dog but not before a pig. The explanation: *zeh mezonotav alecha ve'zeh ein mezonotav alecha* — for the dog, you bear responsibility (presumably because it is your dog), while for the pig, you do not. A Jewish household does not keep a pig; any pig encountered is unowned from that household's perspective, and one bears no responsibility for it. The practical halacha thus tracks ownership and responsibility rather than the intrinsic character of the act.

### Water Case

Rav Ashi draws the same conclusion from our Mishnah directly. The Mishnah prohibits putting water before bees and coop doves but permits it before ducks, chickens, and Herodian doves. The most natural explanation is: *hani mezonotan alecha ve'hani ein mezonotan alecha* — the former group are not your animals, the latter are. This confirms that even something as trivial as placing water before an animal is forbidden when it is not your responsibility.

### Responsibility Test

The force of Rav Ashi's point is that ownership or responsibility, not the degree of effort, governs this category of rulings. Even the most minimal act — setting out water — is prohibited when directed at animals outside one's care.

### Water Specificity

The Gemara, however, presses back: if the rule is purely about *mezonotan alecha*, why does the Mishnah specify water? One should presumably be forbidden from putting out any food — grain, bread — before such animals. Why does the Mishnah single out water as the forbidden item?

### Necessity Standard

The Gemara resolves this: *shani mayim deshchichi be'agma* — water is different because it is readily available in the swamps and natural surroundings. The prohibition is not simply that the animals are not yours; it is that there is no necessity to what you are doing. When water is plentiful in the environment, placing water before the animals adds nothing — they do not need you to provide it, and therefore doing so constitutes unjustified effort. Food, by contrast, may not be as readily available, and providing it may well be necessary even for animals one does not own. The practical upshot of this reframing is nuanced: the question is not only whether the animal is yours, but whether what you are providing is genuinely necessary given what the animal can access on its own. On rainy days when water is everywhere, even one's own animals would not need water put out; on drought days, the calculus shifts. This provides a practical standard that must be evaluated against actual circumstances.

---

## Dog's Poverty

### Derasha: Dog

Rabbi Yona delivered the following *derasha* at the entrance of the house of the *nasi*. The verse states: *yodeia tzaddik din dalim* — the righteous one knows the judgment of the poor. The *tzaddik* here is the Holy One Blessed be He, and the *dal*, the poor one, is the dog. *Yodeia Hakadosh Baruch Hu b'kelev shemezonotav mu'atin* — God knows that the dog is a poor creature, that food is scarce for it.

### Digestion Law

In consequence of this poverty, God arranged that *shoheh achilato be-meiav gimel yamim* — the food remains in the dog's stomach for three days, allowing it to sustain itself over longer intervals between meals, much as a predator that eats infrequently must extract maximum sustenance from each meal. This has a concrete halachic implication cited from the Mishnah: if a dog swallows flesh from a human corpse and then dies, how long after ingestion does the flesh remain *metamei* — capable of transmitting corpse-impurity — while still inside the dog? *Becheli gimel yamim, me'et le'et* — for a dog, seventy-two hours. For birds and fish, by contrast, the food is consumed almost instantaneously — *kedei shetipol le'or vetisaref* — as quickly as if it had fallen into a fire.

### Proper Conduct

Rav Huna draws a practical moral from the *derasha*: *orach ar'a*, proper conduct, demands that one throw a small piece of meat to a dog when one has it, because the dog is a *dal*, a creature of genuine poverty with little access to food. One should have compassion on it and provide what one can.

### Mari's Rule

Rav Mari qualifies this: *mashach ozneih* — give it a piece about the length of an ear, something small, *ve'chutra batreih* — and then the stick should follow. Like the children's book about the mouse and the cookie: if you show the dog too much kindness without establishing a boundary, it will not leave you alone. One must give a little and then drive it away, so it does not become a persistent nuisance.

### Field vs. City

This advice applies, however, only *be-dabrah* — in the field or open countryside, where animals roam widely and a dog encountered once may not return. *Aval be-mata* — in the city, do not even do this, *de'ati le-misrach* — because the dog will latch onto you. In the city, dogs have smaller territories and less food, and any generosity will result in the dog following one persistently.

### Pappa's Saying

Rav Pappa offers a final aphorism that encapsulates the contrast: *leit de'anyi mi-chalba* — there is none poorer than a dog; *ve-leit de'atir me-chazira* — and there is none richer than a pig. The pig forages and eats virtually anything; it needs nothing from anyone. The dog, dependent on scraps and leftovers, epitomizes poverty among animals.

---

## Hamra vs. Halata

### Hamra Method

The *sugya* concludes with a *baraita* that provides a precise account of the two force-feeding methods. *Hamra* — the forbidden form — proceeds as follows: one makes the animal kneel (*marbitza*), forces open its mouth (*ufokeis et piha*), and feeds it *karshinim* (vetch) together with water simultaneously, all at once.

### Halata Method

*Halata* — the permitted form — is entirely different in character: one feeds the animal while it is standing, gives it vetch separately, and gives it water separately. The feeding is sequential and non-coercive.

### Proof Structure

What does this *baraita* establish? The *hamra* method involves no vessel — it is done entirely by hand, with the animal kneeled and its mouth held open — yet it is forbidden. This directly refutes Rav Chisda's position that the only forbidden element is using a *kli*, a vessel. The *baraita* demonstrates that force-feeding without any vessel can itself be forbidden, and that the distinction between *hamra* and *halata* turns not on the use of a vessel but on the manner and degree of compulsion: simultaneous delivery of food and water into a kneeling animal with a pried-open mouth is categorically different from placing food and water before a standing animal in separate stages. The *baraita* thus provides the strongest support for Rav Yehuda's position that force-feeding per se — irrespective of whether a vessel is used — is what the Mishnah prohibits.

---

---

# Shabbat 156

## Water & Bran

### Mishna Setup

The daf begins at the bottom of 155b, in the context of various rulings related to feeding farm animals. The particular concern that now arises touches on a potential *de'oraita* prohibition: when one adds water to bran, does that constitute *lisha* — the forbidden labor of kneading?

The *mishna* permits pouring water into bran but prohibits kneading it. Abaye reports that he posed the question before his master Rabba: *matnitin mani* — whose position does our *mishna* reflect? Rabba answered that it follows Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda.

### Lisha Debate

The underlying question is why adding water to bran should be permitted at all. When one pours water into flour, is that not itself a form of *lisha*? A *baraisa* frames the dispute explicitly: if one person places flour and another pours water into it, *Ha'acharon chayav* — the latter is liable, according to Rabbi. Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: one is not liable until one actually kneads. Our *mishna*, which permits adding the water, therefore appears to reflect the position of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda.

The *Gemara* pushes back: perhaps the permissive position of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda applies only to flour, which is *bar gibul* — subject to kneading — but not necessarily to bran.

### Bar Gibbul

The *Gemara* introduces the concept of *bar gibul*: bran, unlike flour, does not readily dissolve when water is added. It does not quickly transform into a cohesive dough; one must work it considerably more, and even then it does not reach the consistency of classic dough.

Counterintuitively, the *Gemara* suggests that this very quality — being *lav bar gibul* — might make bran *more* subject to concern, not less. Since bran never achieves a full classical dough, even the earliest stage of mixing is considered significant, a kind of loose mixture being the most one can expect from it. As paradoxical as this sounds, the logic is that when the endpoint is already a degraded form of *lisha*, even the threshold stage is treated as meaningful.

The consequence of accepting this line of reasoning would be troubling: our *mishna* would have no *tanna* to follow. Even Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda would agree that adding water to bran is a problem.

### Baraita Rejects

The *Gemara* rejects this reading outright: *lo salka da'atach*. A *baraisa* states explicitly: *ein notnin mayim l'mursan dibrei Rabbi* — Rabbi holds one may not add water to bran at all. Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda says one may. The *bar gibul* distinction does not alter the fundamental dispute. Our *mishna* does indeed follow Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that adding water alone does not constitute *lisha* — the prohibition applies only to actual kneading.

The broader question of how we rule remains complex. In general practice, one does not add water to substances that will dissolve and form a dough. Where leniency might apply, it is only with a *shinui* — a deviation from the normal manner of preparation.

### Kelli Kneading

The *Gemara* cites a *baraisa*: *ein govlin et hakelli* — one may not knead *kelli*, a type of wheat roasted in the oven that becomes sweet and is used to prepare a mixture called *shasisa* (combined with oil, vinegar, and salt). A dissenting view — *yeish omrim govlin* — permits it.

Rav Chisda identifies the lenient opinion as that of Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda. According to Rabbi, even adding the water creates a problem; according to Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda, since the addition of liquid is permitted, the concern focuses only on the kneading itself. Yet actual kneading is the classic act of *lisha* — how can it be permitted?

### Shinui: Bit by Bit

The *Gemara* immediately qualifies the lenient ruling: *vahani mili huda meshani* — it is only permitted if one does it with a *shinui*. This is a striking feature of certain *melakhot*: while most *de'oraita* prohibitions are guarded by layer upon layer of rabbinic safeguard, here we find a case where even an act that might constitute biblical *lisha* is permitted when performed with a *shinui*.

A parallel case is *tochin*: grinding spices may be permitted on *Shabbat* if both the grinding implement and the surface are each a *shinui* from their normal use — this is actually the ruling in *Shulchan Aruch*, even though *techina* is a *melakha de'oraita*. Bran kneading follows a similar pattern.

Rav Chisda specifies the *shinui*: *al yad al yad* — a little at a time. Even performing the same action in small increments constitutes a sufficient *shinui*, without doing anything qualitatively different. This is itself surprising — one is performing the same *melacha*, merely piecemeal.

The general *psak* as it emerges from the full *Gemara* incorporates multiple criteria together. First, one reverses the order of combining ingredients — if normally water is added to the solid, one adds the solid to the water first. Second, the mixture should ideally be *belila raka*, a loose mixture resembling batter rather than *belila ava*, which is thick dough. The distinction matters because *lisha de'oraita* arguably applies only to a thick dough-like consistency. Third, one employs a *shinui* in the manner of mixing as well, which the *Gemara* will develop further.

### Shatis Method

The *Gemara* notes that all opinions agree that stirring *shatis* — a honey-wheat mixture — on *Shabbat* is permitted. This seems to contradict what was just established about requiring a *shinui*. The *Gemara* resolves the tension: *lo kashya ha be'ava ha berakika* — the cases differ based on whether the mixture is thick or thin. A loose mixture is categorically different from a thick dough.

Yet even for the thin mixture, the *Gemara* immediately adds qualifications: *vahani mili huda meshani* — still only with a *shinui*. Rav Yosef specifies: the normal practice is to add the vinegar first, then the *shatis*; on *Shabbat*, one reverses the order — first the *shatis*, then the vinegar. This is the *shinui* of addition, which addresses how the components are combined.

The question remains whether reversing the order also resolves concerns about the act of stirring itself, or whether a separate *shinui* is needed for that step as well. Rashi's approach is that since the mixture is *belila raka*, it does not constitute *lisha* in the first place, which would explain why no additional *shinui* for stirring is required. Yet this reasoning is in some tension with the requirement to reverse the order of addition — if the loose mixture eliminates the *lisha* concern entirely, why is the order *shinui* needed at all?

The practical *halakha* incorporates all the leniencies together: a loose mixture (*belila raka*), reversal of the order of addition, and a *shinui* in the manner of mixing. The *Gemara* seems to suggest that while any one of these factors might be independently significant, one should seek to combine them all.

---

## Case: Animal Handlers

### Handlers Mixing

The *Gemara* now presents a concrete case. The son of Rav Huna bar Chiyya found the animal attendants of his father's household (*devei nasha* — a term that can refer to the women's household, or, as appears relevant here, to the household after the father's death) actually kneading bran with water and feeding it to the cattle. He kicked them — *batash beih* — insisting they stop, since this appeared to violate the *mishna*'s prohibition on kneading.

It is worth noting what the *mishna* says: *notnim mayim l'mursan aval lo govlin* — one may add water to bran but may not knead it. This attendant was performing actual *gibul*, which is precisely what the *mishna* forbids.

### Maternal Grandfather

Then his father arrived and found him. He said: *hachi amar avuha de'immach* — here is what your mother's father says — meaning the position of his maternal grandfather. He cited a ruling in the name of Rav, transmitted by Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba: *govlin velo masfin* — one may knead, but one may not hand-feed (*maspi*) the food directly into the animal's mouth. Furthermore, *dela lakit bilshoneih machalkitin leh* — if the calf is too young to lap it up with its own tongue, one may assist it in swallowing.

Rashi notes that the prohibition on *masfin* corresponds to the force-feeding issue discussed in an earlier *mishna*. The ruling of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba thus permits the kneading itself, contrary to the son's objection.

### Shinui Required

The *Gemara* immediately intervenes: *vahani mili dameshany* — even this leniency applies only if performed with a *shinui*. This editorial gloss consistently appears throughout the *sugya*, each time the *Gemara* states a permissive ruling, it adds the qualification that a *shinui* is required.

### Cross Stirring

Rav Yeimar bar Shmaya citing Abaye specifies the *shinui* for the kneading motion: *shesi ve'erev* — warp and woof. Rather than the normal elliptical stirring motion, one makes alternating strokes in perpendicular directions — effectively tracing a plus sign rather than circular motions. This is more laborious and less effective, since it does not reach all portions of the mixture evenly.

The *Gemara* itself notes the problem: *lo me'arev shapir* — it does not mix well.

### Vessel Method

This leads to a second alternative: Rav Yehuda rules that one may pour the mixture from one vessel to another — *mena'ar leh l'kli* — achieving mixing through the act of pouring between containers rather than through direct stirring. One may not perform the normal kneading motion, but this alternative method is permitted.

To summarize the full picture that has emerged: there is a debate about whether one may even add water to bran (*Rabbi* vs. *Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda*); where adding the water is permitted, reversing the order of addition constitutes a *shinui* for that step; and the actual mixing may be performed only with a *shinui* — either a little at a time, or with cross-directional strokes, or by pouring between vessels. All of this is ideally combined with the mixture being *belila raka*. What is extraordinary, and acknowledged as such by the *Gemara*, is that these *shinuyim* seem to permit even what might be a *melacha de'oraita*.

---

## Notebooks Section

### Zeiri Notebook

The *Gemara* introduces a new source: *kesav apinkasei di-Zeiri* — it was written in the notebook of Zeiri. Rashi explains *pinkas* as bound writing tablets of the kind used by merchants. The entry records that Zeiri said before his teacher Rabbi Chiya: *ma'u legabbei* — what is the ruling regarding kneading (*gibul*)? Rabbi Chiya responded: *assur* — it is forbidden. This aligns with the *mishna*'s prohibition and with the position of Rabbi.

Zeiri then asked: *ma'u lefarek* — what about *perika*, unloading? Rashi understands this as the transfer of fruit from one animal to another, discussed in an earlier *mishna*. Tosafot, however, interprets *perika* in this context as pouring from vessel to vessel — the same technique Rav Yehuda described as a *shinui* for mixing. On this, Rabbi Chiya ruled: *mutar* — permitted.

### Animal Feeding

Rav Menashya, whose ruling also appears in the context of the *pinkas*, addresses proportional feeding of animals: one may place one standard measure before one animal (*chad kammai chad*), and two before two (*trei kammai trei*). However, three measures before two animals is *assur* — excessive and involving unnecessary labor (*tircha*) on *Shabbat*.

Rav Yosef disagrees and sets no upper limit — *kav va'afilu kabayim* — even a *kav* or two *kabayim* is permitted. Ulla goes further still: *kur va'afilu kurayim* — even a *kur* or two *kurin*. A *kur* is a very large measure, making Ulla's ruling extremely permissive.

### Levi Notebook

The *Gemara* now cites *kesiv apinkasei deLevi* — what was written in the notebook of Levi. Levi recorded that he mentioned before his teacher Rabbi — the *Gemara* glosses: *Rabbeinu Hakadosh*, Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi — that in Bavel people were accustomed to actually knead *shatis* (the bran-and-honey mixture) on *Shabbat*. *Vetzavach Rabbi* — Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi would cry out in protest. *Ve'lais deshmia lei* — and no one would listen to him. *Ve'lais cheilei bidei lemisar* — and he did not have the ability to forbid it by authority, *mide'Yosei bar'Rabbi Yehuda* — because Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda's lenient position provided a basis for the established practice.

This is a notable example of the tension between *psak halacha* and entrenched communal practice. Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi accepted that *lisha* was prohibited and was disturbed by the practice in Bavel. Yet the people there relied on Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda's position, which, once it permitted adding the liquid, opened the door to permitting actual kneading with a *shinui*. The communal practice, backed by a legitimate rabbinic opinion, was beyond his power to overturn.

---

## Astrology Section

### Birth Days

From the notebook of Levi, the *Gemara* transitions — without any apparent thematic connection to the *Shabbat* laws just discussed — to the notebook of his son, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. What follows is a lengthy and remarkable passage on astrological influence.

The notebook records character traits associated with the day of the week on which one is born. Someone born on Sunday (*echad b'Shabbat*) will be a great person — *yehei gavar* — but without one element of the other direction: either entirely righteous or entirely wicked, not mixed. The *Gemara* illustrates with Rav Ashi, who says that he himself was born on Sunday, as was Dimi bar Kakuzta — and while Rav Ashi became the head of a *yeshiva*, the equivalent of a king, Dimi bar Kakuzta became the chief of bandits. The point is full greatness in one direction or the other. The rationale offered is that Sunday was the day on which both light and darkness were created, making it a day of complete extremes.

Someone born on Monday will be angry (*ragzan*), because on that day the waters were separated — a state of conflict and division. Someone born on Tuesday will be wealthy and promiscuous (*atir ve'zanai*), because the vegetation (*deshaim*) was created then — it grows quickly and spreads promiscuously everywhere, symbolizing both wealth and indulgence. Rashi notes that the word for promiscuous growth is used similarly about plants.

Someone born on Wednesday will be wise and luminous — or, according to some, will have a good memory — because the celestial luminaries (*me'orot*) were created on that day. Someone born on Thursday will be a doer of kindness (*gomel chasadim*), because the fish and birds were created then; Rashi explains that fish and birds have their food more readily available to them, symbolizing effortless divine provision, which mirrors the quality of *chesed*.

Someone born on Friday (*ma'alei Shabbata*) will be a *chazran* — one who is always running and pursuing things — just as everyone rushes on *Erev Shabbat*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds: *chazran b'mitzvot* — specifically one who runs after opportunities to perform *mitzvot*, since all the running on *Erev Shabbat* is in preparation for a sacred purpose.

Someone born on *Shabbat* will die on *Shabbat*, because the great day of *Shabbat* was profaned on his account at the moment of his birth. Yet this is immediately qualified: Rava bar Rav Shila adds that such a person will be called the great holy one, *kadisha raba*, by virtue of having been born on *Shabbat* itself.

### Mazal Debate

Rabbi Chanina, upon hearing all of this from the students who reported the notebook of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, responded: go and tell Bar Liva'i — Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — that it is not *mazal yom* — the astrological significance of the day of birth — that determines a person's character. Rather, *mazal sha'ah gorem* — it is the star ruling at the hour of birth that matters.

The framework underlying this position is that the seven celestial bodies rotate through the hours of the day in a fixed sequence. Since neither a day nor a week is divisible evenly by seven, the celestial body presiding at any given hour differs based on the day of the week — a system charted by Steinsaltz in detail.

### Celestial Bodies

According to the *mazal sha'ah* system, someone born under the sun (*chama*) will be luminous and self-sufficient — eating and drinking from his own resources, just as the sun is self-sustaining and provides light to all. But his secrets will be exposed (*razohi galyan*), just as the sun illuminates everything and conceals nothing. If he is a thief, he will not succeed.

Someone born under Venus (*Noga*) will be wealthy and promiscuous (*atir ve'zanai*) — the same traits attributed to Tuesday births in the *mazal yom* system. The reason given is *mishum de'ityalid be'nura* — because a fire was kindled within him, Venus being associated with burning passion. Rashi specifies *yeter tashmish*.

Someone born under Mercury (*chochav*) will be luminous and wise, because Mercury is the *safra de'chama* — the scribe of the sun, always in close proximity to it, absorbing its light and wisdom. In Greek mythology Mercury is the divine messenger, and there may be an echo of that conception here.

Someone born under the moon (*levana*) will suffer much evil, building and destroying, destroying and building — reflecting the moon's constant waxing and waning. He eats and drinks what is not his own, since the moon's light is borrowed from the sun. His secrets will be hidden (*razohi kasyan*), and if he is a thief, he will succeed.

Someone born under Saturn (*Shabtai*) — whose name echoes *Shabbat* and the root of cessation — will have his plans frustrated (*machshavteih betalin*). An alternative view reverses this: whoever plots against him will have their plans frustrated.

Someone born under Jupiter (*Tzedek*) will be righteous (*tzadkan*). Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds: *tzadkan b'mitzvot*, and Rashi specifies here that *mitzvot* refers particularly to *tzedakah*.

### Mars & Blood

Someone born under Mars (*Ma'adim*) will be *ashir dami* — a shedder of blood. This is among the most cited lines in the passage. Rav Ashi immediately qualifies it: *ei umna ei ganva ei tavcha ei mahola* — he may be a bloodletter, a killer, a ritual slaughterer, or a *mohel*. In other words, the astrological inclination toward blood does not determine its expression — that is left to the individual's choices and circumstances.

This observation, if one brackets the astrological framework itself, reflects something recognizable: people are born with different temperaments and inclinations, whether through genetics, upbringing, or socioeconomic circumstance. Much is fixed; what is not fixed — what is always in one's own hands — is *tzadik o rasha*, the moral direction. The *Gemara* elsewhere states that before birth an angel decrees whether one will be rich or poor, strong or weak, but *not* whether one will be righteous or wicked, for that is given over entirely to the individual.

Rava himself states: *ana b'Ma'adim havai* — I was born under Mars, yet I am none of those. Abaye responds: *mar nami anish ve'katil* — but the master also punishes and causes death, in his capacity as a *dayan*. The redirected Mars energy manifests even in judicial authority. One participant noted that Rava once caused the death of Rav Zeira on *Purim*, an incident recorded in Tractate Megillah — another dark echo of *ashir dami* directed through unexpected channels.

### Mazal & Jews

The *Gemara* now addresses whether astrological influence applies to Jews at all. Rabbi Chanina states: *mazal machkim mazal ma'ashir* — the constellation makes one wise, makes one wealthy — *ve'yesh mazal l'Yisrael* — and it applies even to Jews. This is in tension with Rabbi Chanina's own famous dictum that *hakol bidei shamayim chutz me'yirat shamayim* — everything is in the hands of heaven except the fear of heaven. The *Gemara* understands him as saying that astrological influence is real and powerful, though not absolutely determinative.

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *ein mazal l'Yisrael* — the constellations do not govern Jews. He derives this from the verse: *ko amar Hashem el derech hagoyim al tilmadu umi'otot hashamayim al techattu* — do not fear the signs of the heavens, for it is the nations who fear them, not Israel. Rav agrees: *ein mazal l'Yisrael*.

### Abraham Test

Rav Yehuda citing Rav — a passage famously quoted by Rashi in the *Chumash* — derives the principle from the episode of Avram. God took Avram outside (*vayotze oto hachutza*) and showed him the stars. Avram protested: *nistakalti be'itztagninut sheli* — I have looked in my astrology, *ve'eini ro'eh leholid ben* — and I see that I am not destined to have a son. God replied: *tze me'itztagninut shelcha* — step outside your astrology. *She'ein mazal l'Yisrael* — for there is no constellation for Israel.

The *Gemara* then asks: what was Avram's specific astrological concern? *Dekai tzedek be'ma'arava* — his sign, Tzedek (Jupiter), was in the west at the relevant time, which according to Rashi signifies a cooler, less generative position, since the sun rises in the east. God responds: *mahadrina u'mokeimna leh be'mizrach* — I will move the star to the east, to a more generative position.

This is connected to the verse *mi he'ir mi'mizrach tzedek yikra'ehu l'raglo* — who bestirred from the east, Tzedek called to his feet — a *pasuk* from the *haftarah* of the relevant *parasha*, which according to this reading refers not to Avraham himself coming from the east, but to God repositioning the constellation Tzedek in the east for Avraham's sake.

Rashi's comment in the *Chumash*, however, takes a different approach: *Avram eino molid aval Avraham molid* — Avram will not beget, but Avraham will. The change of name itself — the addition of the *hei* — altered the astrological reality. What this implies, importantly, is not that the astrology was simply wrong, but that God intervened to change it. The stars had genuine influence, but God overrode them.

### Shmuel Case

A story involving Shmuel illustrates how *ein mazal l'Yisrael* works in practice. Shmuel and the non-Jewish astrologer Avlat were sitting together, watching men walking toward a lake. Avlat declared that one of the men — identifiable by his astrological sign — would go and not return; a snake would bite him and he would die. Shmuel said: if he is a Jew, he will go and come back.

The man went, returned, and Avlat rose and examined his bundle, finding a snake that had been cut into two halves. He asked the man what he had done. The man explained: each day, the group would pool their bread for a communal meal. That day, one member had no bread to contribute and was visibly embarrassed. The man — so as not to embarrass him — went around collecting as if taking bread from everyone, but made it appear as though bread was also taken from the embarrassed man, and contributed his own bread in that person's stead, *ki heichi d'lo lichsif* — so that he would not be shamed.

Shmuel declared: *mitzvah avadat* — you performed a *mitzvah*. He then went out and expounded: *u'tzedakah tatzil mi'mavet* — *tzedakah* saves from death. And not merely from an unusual or painful death (*misah meshunah*), as another *Gemara* interprets the verse, but *ela mimisah atzmah* — from death itself, from the very death that had been decreed for the person.

This raises a question: if Shmuel believed that Jews are above astrological influence, how did he confidently predict the man would return? It seems he did not know that the man had already performed an act of *tzedakah*; he stated his prediction on general principle. But the story also suggests the mechanism: it was not that the constellation had no hold at all, but that the *tzedakah* had already neutralized it. How Shmuel knew with certainty the outcome is left unexplained.

### Akiva Daughter

Similarly, from Rabbi Akiva: *d'Rabbi Akiva havya lei barta* — Rabbi Akiva had a daughter. The *kalda'ei* — astrologers — told him: *hahu yoma d'aylah l'vei ganana* — on the very day she enters the bridal canopy, a snake will bite her and she will die. Rabbi Akiva's daughter was understandably consumed with anxiety over this prediction.

On her wedding night, she took her hair pin (*machvanta d'tzavta*) and inserted it into a hole in the wall. In the morning, when she withdrew it, she pulled out a snake impaled on the pin — it had been in the wall, waiting, and she had inadvertently driven the pin directly into its eye, killing it.

Her father asked: what did you do? She told him: a poor man had come to the door calling out for food, but everyone was preoccupied with the wedding meal and no one heard him. She rose, took the portion that had been given to her, and gave it to him. Rabbi Akiva declared: *mitzvah avadat* — you performed a *mitzvah* — and went out to expound: *u'tzedakah tatzil mi'mavet* — not from an unusual death, *ela mimisah atzmah* — but from the preordained death itself.

### Rav Nachman

A third case: the mother of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak was told by the *kalda'ei* that her son would be a thief. She therefore never allowed him to walk with his head uncovered. Her reasoning, which she would express to him: *kasei reisheich ki heichi d'teihavei lach eimata d'Shamaya* — cover your head so that the fear of heaven will be upon you. She also urged him always to pray for divine assistance in overcoming his inclinations, though she never told him what the *kalda'ei* had predicted.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak himself never knew why his mother insisted on this. One day he was sitting beneath a palm tree that was not his, studying, and his cloak slipped from his head. *Dali einei chaza l'dikla* — he lifted his eyes, saw the date palm, and his *yetzer hara* overwhelmed him: *salik paskei l'kibura b'shinei* — he climbed up and bit off a cluster of dates with his teeth, taking fruit that was not his own.

The story is instructive beyond its astrological dimension. The *Gemara* here illustrates not only the metaphysical mechanism of *tzedakah* and prayer overriding destiny, but also the practical power of education and habit in reshaping natural inclination — a theme with obvious resonance beyond any astrological framework.

### Rambam Letter

This *Gemara* is deeply striking: throughout the entire passage, not a single opinion unambiguously rejects astrology. Even those who hold *ein mazal l'Yisrael* do not deny the reality of astrological influence on non-Jews, and even for Jews they acknowledge that it has real pull that must be overcome through *mitzvot* or divine intervention. The *Gemara*'s assumption is consistently that the stars genuinely influence human destiny.

The Rambam's letter on astrology addresses this tension directly. He opens with a sweeping condemnation: anyone who examines the science will see that astrology is complete foolishness, refuted by reason through lucid proofs. From the perspective of tradition, he argues that if everything were truly determined by the stars, the entire system of *Torah*, commandments, and *Talmud* would be rendered meaningless.

Confronting the apparent contradiction posed by our *Gemara*, the Rambam does not simply ignore it. He writes: do not regard it as a difficulty that certain sages in the *Talmud* and *Midrashim* appear to maintain that the stars influence human fate. He then offers several possible explanations: perhaps only one or two sages held this view, not the consensus; perhaps they did not mean it literally and there is an underlying *allusion* in their words; or perhaps they addressed it as they did because that was the prevalent belief of their time and place, and they were speaking in those terms to reach their audience without necessarily affirming the underlying premise.

This approach is characteristic of the Rambam's broader method — seen also in his treatment of *Shmuel*'s dictum about messianic times, where he attributes to a single authority what is in fact a minority view and argues that the consensus lies elsewhere. The Rambam concludes that in matters where reason has already established clear proofs, it is not appropriate to abandon those conclusions based on individual statements of the sages — *she'ein raui la'adam la'azov divrei ha'sekhel*.

The question of whether the Rambam himself believed that God directs the world through stellar mechanisms — a more philosophical position distinct from popular astrology — is a more complex matter left unresolved here.

---

## Muktzah Debate

### Gourds Issue

The *Gemara* transitions to a new *mishna*: *mekatzin et hadla'at lifnei habehemah* — one may chop up a gourd in front of animals on *Shabbat*. The concern here shifts away from *lisha* and toward *muktzah*. A gourd, in the normal course of things, is set aside for human consumption — it would typically be cooked. The question is whether its designated status for human use renders it *muktzah* and forbidden from being used for animals.

### Muktzah Principle

The *mishna* addresses this by analogy: one may also chop up an animal carcass (*neveilah*) in front of dogs, even if the animal died on *Shabbat* — meaning that when *Shabbat* began, the carcass was not yet fit for dogs and was presumably intended for human consumption or in a status of set-aside.

The governing principle is: *muktzah le'adam lo havei muktzah livhemah* — something that is *muktzah* for a person is not thereby *muktzah* for animals. The *muktzah* status is person-relative; what is set aside from human use on *Shabbat* is not set aside from animal use.

### Defective Animals

Rabbi Yehuda disputes this: *im lo hayta neveilah me'erev Shabbat asura* — if the carcass was not already a *neveilah* (fit for dogs) from before *Shabbat*, it is forbidden on *Shabbat* — *lefi she'eino min hamuchan* — because it was not designated for this use when *Shabbat* began.
