The *chatzer* is permitted because from the *chatzer's* perspective, the *mavoi* is not fully merged with it — its opening into the *mavoi* is only partial, so the *chatzer* residents are unaffected. The *mavoi*, however, is entirely open into the *chatzer*, and since the *mavoi* residents have not joined in an *eruv* with the *chatzer* residents, the *mavoi* residents are prohibited from carrying. The problem in the *mavoi* is not a deficiency of walls — the walls of the *rachavah* or *chatzer* are adequate from a structural standpoint — but rather the absence of a joint *eruv* joining the two groups. There is thus no contradiction between Rav's rulings: the *rachavah* case assumes a joint *eruv* was made, and the *chatzer* case assumes it was not.

---

## Three-Walled Alley

### Three-Wall Case

The *gemara* now transitions to a new case: the *mavoi ha-asui ke-nadli* — the alleyway shaped like a centipede, that is, a rectangular enclosure with three complete walls and one side entirely open. Having resolved the questions surrounding the *mavoi mefulash* and its variants, the *gemara* turns to this distinct configuration where the issue is not two open ends but rather a single open face on what is otherwise a three-sided enclosure.

### Rav vs Shmuel

The dispute is stated directly. Rav holds that the *mavoi asui ke-nadli* requires nothing on the fourth, open side — the three existing walls are sufficient to permit carrying within. Shmuel holds that a *lechi* or *korah* is required on the open fourth side. The *gemara* will proceed to examine the reasoning underlying this disagreement.

---

---

# Eiruvin 9

## Under the Korah

### Intro: Under Korah

Our daf begins at the bottom of 8b, where the Gemara has been engaged in a complex discussion about *mavoyos* opening into *chatzeros* and various spatial configurations. The Gemara now turns to a more focused question: may one carry underneath the *korah* — the beam that spans the opening of a *mavoy*?

The Gemara had entertained opinions in both directions on this question, and then observed that the answer does not actually depend on the underlying rationale for the *korah*. Some hold that the *korah* functions as a *heker* — a recognizable sign or marker — while others hold that it functions as a *mechitzah*, a halachic partition. Yet regardless of which theory one adopts, the same question remains: does the wall (or the *heker*) operate from the inner face of the beam, or from the outer face? That question can be resolved either way under either theory. So the debate about *heker* versus *mechitzah* does not, by itself, determine whether carrying beneath the beam is permitted.

## Under the Korah (II)

### Rav Chisda: Inside/Outsi…

Rav Chisda states that whatever one's position on the *korah*, there is one point of universal agreement: *bein lechayayim* — opposite the *lechi*, the vertical post that marks the side of the *mavoy* opening — is forbidden (*she'assur*). The prohibition holds regardless of how one understands the function of the *lechi*.

This prompts a natural question: why should the *lechi* be treated differently from the *korah*? After all, the same inside/outside debate that applies to the *korah* could equally apply to the *lechi*. Tosafos explains that the *lechi* is categorically different because, unlike the *korah* — which must be at least a *tefach* wide — a *lechi* may be of infinitesimal thinness. Since the *lechi* is permitted to be arbitrarily narrow, the rabbis ruled that one may not use the space directly opposite it. Were they to permit that space, a person might easily step over an extremely thin post without even noticing, rendering the *lechi* functionally meaningless. Notably, the Gemara itself does not offer this explanation; Tosafos supplies it as a logical rationale for the distinction.

### Rami bar Chama: External…

Rami bar Chama poses a challenge to Rav Chisda. The case: *na'atz shtay yetaydot bishnay kotlay mavoy mibachutz* — someone drove two pegs into the outer face of the two walls of the *mavoy* and rested the beam on them, so that the beam sits flush against the outer face of the walls rather than resting directly on top of them. What is the law in this scenario?

Rav Chisda's answer is ingeniously constructed. He says: *ledvray hamatir assur uledvray ha'ossur muttar* — according to the opinion that normally permits carrying under the beam, this case is forbidden; according to the opinion that normally forbids it, this case is permitted. The logic: the permissive view holds that the beam functions through its outer face. But when the beam is flush against the outer face of the *mavoy* wall, its outer face is now pointing away from the *mavoy* — not connected to it at all. So the permissive view would forbid this configuration. Conversely, the restrictive view relies on the inner face of the beam, and in this case the inner face is flush against the *mavoy* wall — suggesting it should actually be valid. A possible objection is that even the outer face, being within three *tefachim*, could invoke the principle of *lavud* and be considered as though connected. But Rav Chisda apparently holds that physical adjacency alone is insufficient here — the beam must be directly and positionally on top of the *mavoy*.

### Rava: Direct Placement

Rava goes further and argues that even the opinion that normally forbids carrying beneath the beam — the one that relies on the inner face — would also forbid this configuration. His reasoning: *ba'inan korah gabay mavoy veleka* — we require that the beam be directly above the *mavoy*, and here it is not. The beam rests against the side of the walls, not atop them, and that does not satisfy the halachic definition of a *korah*.

### Tzurat HaPetach

Rava draws an analogy to *tzurat hapetach*, the doorframe configuration used as a halachic enclosure. It is well established that in a *tzurat hapetach*, the upper horizontal element must pass directly above the two vertical posts — it cannot be offset to the side. This is precisely why one cannot simply use existing utility poles as a *tzurat hapetach* when the crossbar does not run directly above them. The same principle governs the *korah*: it must sit directly atop the walls of the *mavoy*, not flush against their outer face. Rava offers no further theoretical explanation; he simply identifies this positional requirement as part of the technical definition that *Chazal* assigned to a valid *korah*, much as they assigned it to a *tzurat hapetach*.

### Extended/Suspended Beam

Rav Ada bar Matna raises a challenge to Rava from a *braita*. The *braita* states: *haita koraso meshucha o tluyah* — if the *korah* was *meshucha* (extended) or *tluyah* (suspended). The initial assumption is that *meshucha* means the beam is pulled away from the *mavoy* — protruding outward from the face of the wall, not sitting directly on top — and *tluyah* means the beam is suspended without reaching the side walls on either end. The *braita* then rules: if the gap is less than three [*tefachim*], one need not bring another beam (*ein tzarich lehavi korah acheres*); if it is three or more, another beam is required.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissents and says the threshold is four *tefachim*, not three. This is striking because *lavud* — the principle that objects within three *tefachim* are halachically considered connected — is generally cited as a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, an oral tradition from Sinai. Yet Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel appears to dispute the measurement. The Rambam holds that there can be no disputes regarding a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, and this Gemara is among those that sit in tension with that position.

### Lavud Connection

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction with Rava's ruling by reinterpreting the *braita*. *Idi v'idi mibifnim* — in both cases (*meshucha* and *tluyah*), the beam remains within the interior of the *mavoy*. The distinction between the two is not inside versus outside, but rather: *meshucha mi-ruach achat* — the beam is separated from one wall, not extending all the way to one side; *tluyah mi-shtei ruchot* — it is suspended without reaching either wall on either side.

Why must the *braita* teach both cases? Because one might have thought: from one side, we can apply *lavud* and consider the beam as though it reaches the wall. But perhaps we would not apply *lavud* in two directions simultaneously — that is, we would not extend the beam imaginarily to both sides at once. The *braita* teaches *kamashma lan* that *lavud* can indeed be applied in both directions.

### Rav Ashi: Diagonal Dista…

Rav Ashi offers an alternative reading: *meshucha ve-hi tluyah* — the beam is simultaneously extended away from the edges and elevated above the top of the walls. It is both horizontally displaced and vertically elevated. The scenario is: pegs are driven into the walls at an angle (*akumot*), and the beam rests on them — neither touching the side walls (*she'ein begovahan gimel* — the vertical gap is less than three *tefachim*) nor spanning all the way to the edges (*she'ein be-akmimutan gimel* — the diagonal distance is less than three *tefachim*).

The question Rav Ashi addresses is whether one may apply *lavud* in two directions at once — imaginarily lowering the beam to the level of the wall-top and simultaneously extending it to reach the edge. The concern is analogous to a case in *Sukkah*: can *lavud* attach something to an imaginary extension? The principle is that *lavud* can connect two physical objects within three *tefachim*, but one cannot first imaginarily extend one element and then apply *lavud* to that imaginary extension. However, Rav Ashi explains that this concern is resolved because the diagonal distance — combining both the vertical drop and the horizontal gap — is itself within three *tefachim*. Since the physical edge of the beam is within three *tefachim* of the corner of the wall along the diagonal, *lavud* can be applied directly from one physical point to another, without any intermediate imaginary step.

Tosafos notes the asymmetry with the *Sukkah* case, where *Chazal* permit an imaginarily extended wall to function as a valid wall even without *lavud*. Tosafos explains that the two domains have different operative criteria. In the *mavoy*, one requirement is that the *korah* must be touching — or within three *tefachim* of — the top of the wall. The very fact that the Gemara earlier ruled that a beam flush against the outer face of the *mavoy* is disqualified, even though one might apply *lavud* there, demonstrates that the *mavoy* imposes its own technical standards not fully reducible to those of *Sukkah*.

## Opposite the Lechi

### Lechi Forbidden

Having established that Rav Chisda held the space opposite the *lechi* to be universally forbidden, the Gemara now turns to a *braita* taught by Rav Zakkai before Rabbi Yochanan: *bein halachayayim ve-tachas hakorah nidun ke-karmelis* — the space opposite the posts and beneath the beam is treated as a *karmelis*, not as *reshut hayachid*. In other words, carrying in that space falls outside the halachic benefit of the *mavoy*'s *eruv* designation.

### Rav Yochanan Rejects

Rabbi Yochanan's response is blunt: *puk tani levra* — go teach that outside, meaning, this is not a teaching we accept here. Evidently, Rabbi Yochanan's position is that carrying opposite the *lechi* and beneath the beam is in fact permitted.

### Abaye: Qualified Permit

Abaye says: *mistavra milta d'Rabbi Yochanan tachas hakorah* — the reasoning of Rabbi Yochanan makes sense with respect to beneath the beam. There, one can plausibly permit carrying. *Aval bein lechayayim assur* — but opposite the *lechi*, Abaye maintains, is forbidden, consistent with what Rav Chisda established.

### Rava: Permit (Qualified)

Rava disagrees: *bein lechayayim nami mutar* — opposite the *lechi* is also permitted. Rava is thus the lone authority who consistently permits both spaces.

### Makom Ptur Argument

Rava now explains his basis. He cites a tradition brought by Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a space that is less than four by four *tefachim* is a *makom ptur* — a domain-free zone — and both those in *reshut harabbim* and those in *reshut hayachid* may place objects upon it, provided they do not use it to transfer between the two domains. Rava reasons: even if one considers the space opposite the *lechi* to fall outside the formal *reshut hayachid* of the *mavoy*, since it is a narrow strip less than four *tefachim*, it should have the status of a *makom ptur* — a neutral zone where carrying is permitted from either direction.

### Abaye Refutes Ptur

Abaye refutes this: *hatam b'gavoha gimmel* — a *makom ptur* of that kind applies only when the space is elevated at least three *tefachim* above the floor of the *reshut harabbim*, such as a post or mailbox-like protrusion. A strip of ground-level space cannot be a *makom ptur*. Ground-level space belongs entirely to one of the recognized domains — either *reshut hayachid* or *reshut harabbim* (or *karmelis*). A narrow strip at floor level has no independent neutral status.

### Doorway Needs Lechi

Abaye then marshals a positive proof from a ruling of Rav Chama bar Guria in the name of Rav: *toch hapesach tzarich lechi acher l'hatiro* — if one wants to use the space within a doorframe of a *mavoy*, one needs an additional *lechi* to permit it. This appears to be strong evidence that the space opposite — or rather, inside — the *lechi* framework of the door cannot be used without a separate *lechi*. If the doorframe's own *lechis* were sufficient to permit the adjacent space, no additional *lechi* would be needed.

One might try to distinguish: perhaps the doorframe is four by four *tefachim* wide, giving it the character of an independent domain, and that is why it requires extra treatment. But Rav Chanin bar Rava says in the name of Rav that *af al pi she'ein bo arba'ah al arba'ah* — even if the doorframe interior is less than four by four *tefachim*, a separate *lechi* is still required. This forecloses the distinction.

### Karmelis vs. Public

Rava, undeterred, responds: *hasam d'patuach le-karmelis* — those cases all involve a *mavoy* opening into a *karmelis*, and in that scenario I concede that the space opposite the *lechi* is problematic. But when the *mavoy* opens into a *reshut harabbim*, carrying opposite the *lechi* is still permitted.

The Gemara is startled: what — it is *better* when the *mavoy* opens into a full *reshut harabbim* than when it opens into the less severe *karmelis*? *Yatva b'ara ve-diyura b'shmei shamaya* — is the more grounded domain dwelling in the heaven and the less severe domain dwelling on earth? The categories seem inverted.

### Matza Min Et Mino

The Gemara affirms that yes, counterintuitively, the situation is worse when it opens into a *karmelis*. The principle invoked is *matza min et mino ve-ne'or* — one kind found its like kind and it stirred. The phrase is borrowed from the laws of *kashrus*, where a forbidden substance that had been nullified (*batel*) can be "reawakened" when more of the same forbidden substance is added, combining to produce a perceptible and therefore prohibited taste.

Applied here: the narrow strip of space opposite the *lechi* is in a gray zone — it sits at the cusp of the *mavoy*'s *reshut hayachid*, right at the edge, technically within the walls but not squarely within the *mavoy*'s *hechsher*. If the space outside is a *karmelis*, this ambiguous strip is attracted to the *karmelis* — it finds its like kind and becomes annexed to it, making it prohibited. But if outside is a full *reshut harabbim*, the contrast is stark. That narrow strip, right within the walls and adjacent to a bustling public domain, is not going to be reclassified as part of the *reshut harabbim*. The contrast actually preserves its association with the *mavoy* and keeps it permissible.

### Lechi Conclusion

In summary: the space opposite the *lechi* is treated as a genuine point of controversy. Most of the Talmudic evidence — the various *braisos* and rulings cited throughout this passage — indicates that it is forbidden. Rav Chisda stated at the outset that everyone agrees it is forbidden. Abaye concurs. Rava alone permits it, but must systematically address each piece of contrary evidence by distinguishing cases where the *mavoy* opens into a *karmelis* — in those cases he concedes prohibition — from cases where it opens into a *reshut harabbim*, where he continues to maintain that the space is permitted.

## Consecutive Lechis

### Multiple Lechis

The Gemara now introduces a new dimension to the *lechi* discussion. Rav Huna b'rei deRav Yehoshua cites Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *mavoy sheritzfo belachayayim* — a *mavoy* into which consecutive *lechis* were placed, one after another, all the way along the opening, with gaps between them that are each *pachot pachot me'arba* — individually less than four *tefachim*, but more than three. This scenario, Rabbi Yochanan says, is the subject of the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbanan.

### RSBG: Lavud 4

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that *lavud* applies up to four *tefachim*. Accordingly, all those consecutive *lechis* with gaps of less than four *tefachim* would be treated as connected to one another — effectively merging into a single thick *lechi*.

### Lavud: 3 vs 4

The Rabbanan hold that *lavud* applies only up to three *tefachim*. Since the gaps are between three and four *tefachim* — beyond the *lavud* threshold of the Rabbanan — each post remains an independent *lechi* without being merged with its neighbors.

### Proof Method

Why does this dispute matter? The Gemara reasons that the only way this dispute is meaningful is if we accept that one cannot use the space opposite the *lechi*. According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who applies *lavud* at four *tefachim*, all the posts merge into one long thick *lechi*, and one can only carry up to the inner face of the innermost *lechi* (*mishtamesh ad chuda pnima'i*). According to the Rabbanan, who do not apply *lavud* at that distance, the posts do not merge — only the outermost post counts as the *lechi*, and one may carry up to the inner face of that outer post (*mishtamesh ad chuda pnima'i shel chitzon*). But if carrying opposite a *lechi* were simply permitted, the whole debate would be pointless — one could carry everywhere regardless of whether the posts merge. The debate therefore constitutes proof that *aval bein lechayayim d'chulei alma assur* — opposite the *lechi* is forbidden according to all.

Rava, ever consistent, responds: *hasam nami d'patuach le-karmelis* — that case too involves a *mavoy* opening into a *karmelis*, and in that situation I agree the space is forbidden. The Gemara then reprises the *matza min et mino* argument, arriving at the same conclusion as before.

### Rav Ashi: Independent

Rav Ashi offers a different reading of the consecutive-*lechis* scenario that avoids using it as proof against Rava at all. He reads the case as: *ritzfo belachayayim pachos pachos me'arba bemeshech arba amos* — the consecutive *lechis* extended across a run of four *amos* into the *mavoy*. Why does four *amos* matter? Because four *amos* is the minimum halachic size for an independent *mavoy*. If Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applies *lavud* and merges all those posts into one solid wall, that wall — spanning four *amos* — effectively defines a new *mavoy* within the original *mavoy*. What was a *lechi* is now a wall, and a new interior space of four *amos* is created that has the character of its own *mavoy*, requiring its own *lechi* to be permitted.

### New Mavoi Issue

Thus, according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — *de'amar amrinan lavud, havei leh mavoi, vetzarich lechi acher lehatiro* — applying *lavud* transforms the consecutive posts into a wall, and that wall creates an independent *mavoy*, which in turn requires its own *lechi*. According to the Rabbanan — *lo amrinan lavud, lo tzarich lechi acher* — no *lavud* is applied, no wall is formed, and no new *mavoy* is created; a single *lechi* at the entrance continues to suffice. In this reading, the dispute is entirely about the consequences of *lavud* for *mavoy* formation, and tells us nothing at all about whether one may carry opposite a *lechi*. Rava's position is therefore unaffected.

## Lechi Visibility

### Valid: Inside Visible

When Ravin came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he transmitted a ruling of Rabbi Yochanan: *nira mibachutz ve-shaveh mibifnim* — if a *lechi* is visible on the outside but flush with the wall on the inside, *eino nidon mishum lechi* — it does not count as a *lechi*. This ruling now becomes the pivot for a new discussion. The Gemara introduces the opposing case as the clear baseline: *nira mibifnim ve-shaveh mibachutz* — if it is visible on the inside and flush on the outside, *nidon mishum lechi* — it certainly qualifies. When a person standing inside the *mavoy* can see a protrusion from the wall, the *lechi* is doing its job as a *heker* for those who are carrying within the *mavoy*.

### Disputed: Outside Visible

The disputed case is the reverse configuration: the protrusion is visible to someone standing outside the *mavoy* — it appears as something jutting from the wall — but for those inside the *mavoy*, the surface is flush and the protrusion is invisible. Is that sufficient?

### Rabbi Chiya: Both Valid

A *braita* of Rabbi Chiya's school resolves this directly: *kotel shetzido echad kanus mechaveiro* — a wall in which one side is set back relative to the other. Whether the configuration is *nira mibachutz ve-shaveh mibifnim* — visible outside and flush inside — or *nira mibifnim ve-shaveh mibachutz* — visible inside and flush outside — in both cases *nidon mishum lechi*. Rabbi Chiya explicitly teaches that outside visibility is sufficient.

### Inference Method

The Gemara asks: does the fact that Rabbi Chiya taught this *braita* prove his own ruling? After all, Rabbi Yochanan also must have known this *braita* and yet rejected it — *shemeia lei ve-lo savar lah* — he heard it and did not accept it. Perhaps Rabbi Chiya similarly taught it without personally subscribing to it.

The Gemara rejects this parallel: *bishlamah Rabbi Yochanan lo savar lah, mishum hachi lo tni lah* — it is understandable that Rabbi Yochanan did not hold by this *braita*, because he did not teach it. But Rabbi Chiya, *ee itah delo savar lah, lamah lei le-mitniyah* — if he did not believe it, why would he go around teaching it? The act of teaching constitutes an endorsement. Rabbi Chiya's position is therefore established: a *lechi* visible only from the outside is valid.

### Rabba bar RH: Sufficient

Rabba bar Rav Huna states explicitly: *nira mibachutz ve-shaveh mibifnim nidon mishum lechi* — a *lechi* visible on the outside and flush on the inside is valid. He aligns with Rabbi Chiya's ruling.

### Chatzer Application

Rava now proposes a support for this position from the *mishna* of *chatzer ktana she-nifretza le-gedola* — a small courtyard that opened up into a large one. As discussed in earlier dapim, when the wall between a small *chatzer* and a large one falls, the large courtyard remains permitted (since from its perspective this is merely one opening among many, and it retains the character of a *reshut hayachid*), while the small courtyard is forbidden (since its entire wall is open and it is treated as subsumed within the large one).

Rava asks: if visibility from the outside is sufficient for a *lechi*, then the small *chatzer* should be permitted! The edge of the small *chatzer*'s wall, where it meets the large one, protrudes relative to the large *chatzer*'s wall — visible from the outside (the large courtyard), even if not from the inside (the small courtyard). That should constitute a *lechi* and resolve the small *chatzer*'s problem.

### Rav Zeira: Configuration

Rav Zeira explains why Rava's support fails: *be-nichnasim kotlei ktana le-gedola* — the case of the *mishna* is where the walls of the small *chatzer* extend inward into the large one. In that configuration, there is no protrusion at the edge — the walls run inward and there is simply a break where the wall ends. Nothing juts outward from the plane of the large courtyard's wall. Hence there is no *lechi* at all, whether viewed from inside or outside.

The Gemara then asks: even so, *velima lavud* — the inner edge of the small courtyard's wall may be within three *tefachim* of the outer wall of the large courtyard. Could we not apply *lavud* and treat that gap as if the wall extends flush, thereby creating a notional *lechi* through *lavud*? The Gemara raises a specific measurement scenario to show that this does not always work — *bemuflag mikotel zeh bishnayim u-mikotel zeh be'arba'ah* (Ravina) — the inner wall may be two *tefachim* from one side and four *tefachim* from the other, so that *lavud* cannot be applied on the four-*tefachim* side.

The Gemara then asks: even so, *velima lavud me-ruach achat ve-tishtrei* — at least apply *lavud* on the side where the gap is only two *tefachim*, creating a *lechi* on that one side, and let the small *chatzer* be permitted on that basis.

### Rabbi: Two Planks

The Gemara answers: *Rabbi hee de'amar be-ina shenei pasim* — this is the position of *Rebbi*, who requires two planks — one on each side — and not merely one. While a *mavoy* requires only a single *lechi* at its opening, a *chatzer* according to *Rebbi* requires a plank on both sides of its opening. A single *lechi* via *lavud* on one side alone would therefore be insufficient. This matter, the Gemara signals, will be pursued further.

---

---

# Eiruvin 10

## Courtyard Lechi Case

### Small Courtyard Problem

We begin at the very top of 10a. The *Gemara* had been engaged in a lengthy discussion about whether a *lechi* that is visible from the outside of a *chatzer* or *mavoi*, but flush on the inside, possesses halachic validity. One of the challenges against this position had been the classic case — discussed over the preceding days — of a small *chatzer* that opens into a larger one. In that case, the small *chatzer* is considered fully exposed and carrying within it is therefore prohibited. The question was: why is the small *chatzer* considered fully exposed? Why doesn't the fact that its walls extend beyond the boundary of the smaller space count as *lechis* visible from the outside?

The *Gemara*'s earlier answer was that the walls run flush all the way in, leaving nothing actually extending beyond. The counter-question then arose: since the small *chatzer* was said to be ten *amot* wide and the large *chatzer* eleven *amot* wide, there is a differential of one *amah* — three *tefachim* on each side. Should we not apply *lavud* and treat those extensions as joined? The *Gemara* responded that the division is not even: under the analysis of Rav Zeira and Ravina, there are two *tefachim* on one side and four on the other, so *lavud* can be invoked only on the two-*tefach* side, not the four-*tefach* side. The *Gemara* then noted that even one side should suffice, since ordinarily a single *lechi* is enough for a *chatzer* — and this brings us to where we pick up now.

### Rabbi's Two-Plank Rule

The *Gemara* answers: *Rebbi hi*, this is the position of *Rebbi*. *De-amar beinon shenei passin* — he holds that you need two planks. This rule does not apply to a *mavoi* in the standard sense, but it does apply to a *chatzer*. By way of background: the fundamental distinction between a *mavoi* and a *chatzer* is largely geometric — a space that is longer than it is wide functions as a *mavoi*, while one that is wider than it is long functions as a *chatzer*. A *mavoi* is rectified with a single *lechi*; a *chatzer*, according to *Rebbi*, requires two planks, one on each side of its exposed face. We will examine the details of this distinction in future learning, but for now the operative point is clear: since we are dealing with a *chatzer*, *Rebbi* requires a plank on *each* side, and therefore a *lechi* on only one side is insufficient.

This is supported by a *Baraita*: *chatzer niteret be-pas achat* — a *chatzer* may be rectified with one plank positioned at the point exposed to the *reshut ha-rabbim* — *ve-Rebbi omer bishnei passin* — but *Rebbi* says it requires two planks. We will return to the comparison between *mavoi* and *chatzer* in coming days; for now, this is our answer to the previous difficulty.

The *Gemara* then asks: *hai mai* — what kind of answer is that? *Ei amrit bishlama nira mi-bachutz ve-shaveh mi-bifnim einu nidon mishum lechi* — if we accept the original assumption that something visible from the outside but flush on the inside does *not* have the status of a *lechi*, then the whole structure of the case — one *chatzer* opening into another — makes perfect sense. Moreover, *ve-Rebbi savar lah ke-Rabbi Yose* — we can also say that *Rebbi* holds like *Rabbi Yose*, who maintains that each plank must be at least three *tefachim* wide. On this reading, *ve-de-Rabbi Zeira ve-de-Ravina lessa* — we set aside the special analysis of Rabbi Zeira and Ravina, which posited walls extending inward creating an asymmetric four-and-two division, and instead understand the case straightforwardly.

Now, why does *Rebbi* holding like *Rabbi Yose* matter? The larger *chatzer* is permitted precisely because the opening does not exceed ten *amot* and there is wall projecting inward on each side. If *Rebbi* requires two planks for a *chatzer* to be rectified, and *Rabbi Yose* requires each such plank to be at least three *tefachim* wide, then the large *chatzer* must be exactly one *amah* larger than the small one — three *tefachim* on each side, and three *tefachim* equals one *amah*. This explains precisely why the case was formulated as ten and eleven *amot*.

### Dimensions Challenge

The *Gemara* now raises a sharp objection. *Hai mai* — on the alternative reading, where something visible only from the outside does count as a *lechi*, the case cannot be explained elegantly. Under that approach, we had to invoke Rav Zeira and Ravina's special scenario — walls extending inward — and then explain away *lavud* by positing an uneven two-and-four distribution. But then the precise dimensions of the case become puzzling. Why was it necessary to state that the large *chatzer* was exactly eleven *amot*, one *amah* more than the small one?

*Gedolah be-achas esrei lamah li* — why does it have to be eleven specifically? The *Gemara* offers two possibilities. If the point is to establish the minimum size at which the large *chatzer* becomes halachically sound, then *be-eser ve-shnei tefachim sagi* — ten *amot* and two *tefachim* would suffice, since on the alternative reading *Rebbi* does not hold like *Rabbi Yose* and does not require a full three *tefachim* per plank. The two-*tefach* extension on one side would be enough.

Conversely, if the point of the case is to explain why the small *chatzer* is problematic — that we cannot invoke *lavud* because one side is four *tefachim*, which exceeds the three-*tefach* threshold — then why give an example where the differential is so narrow? *Le-katan ke-hai, le-shmin d'mipok tuvei* — if you wanted to demonstrate that the small *chatzer* is impermissible, give a case where the large *chatzer* is much bigger, twenty *amot* say, so that no one would think to apply *lavud* at all. The very fact that the case was formulated as ten and eleven — a minimal, surgically precise differential — makes no sense unless the reason for the one-*amah* difference is that each plank must be exactly three *tefachim*, consistent with *Rebbi* holding like *Rabbi Yose*.

### Visibility Proof

*Ella lav shema mina* — we must conclude: *nira mi-bachutz ve-shaveh mi-bifnim einu nidon mishum lechi*. If something is visible from the outside but flush on the inside, it does not count as a *lechi*. *Shema mina* — this is a sound proof.

To summarize the arc of the argument: the case of the two *chatzerot* had been presented as a potential challenge to the validity of an outside-visible-only *lechi*. The *Gemara* spent considerable effort over previous sessions trying to construct a special scenario — walls extending inward, uneven *lavud* — that would explain why the small *chatzer* was exposed without conceding the general principle. But now the *Gemara* pulls the rug out: if that elaborate special scenario were true, the case would not have been formulated with the precise dimensions of ten and eleven *amot*. The specificity of those numbers only makes sense on the straightforward reading — that outside-visibility does not count as a *lechi*, and the one-*amah* difference reflects *Rabbi Yose*'s three-*tefachim* requirement, which *Rebbi* accepts. *Shema mina*.

---

## Lechi Mavoi Extension

### Rav Yosef's Doubt

At this point, *Rav Yosef* says: *lo shamia leh hai shemaitah* — I never heard this teaching, referring to the position of *Rav Huna* that had been cited in the preceding discussion, to the effect that a *lechi* visible only from the outside still counts. This statement reflects the well-known historical circumstance: *Rav Yosef* suffered an illness that caused him to forget his learning, and he relied on his students to remind him of what he had previously taught.

### Abaye's Counterargument

*Amar lei Abaye* — *Abaye*, who was *Rav Yosef*'s primary student, responded: *at amart niah lan* — you yourself told us this. *Ve-ha amart niah lan* — and specifically, you told it to us in the context of the following teaching. *De-amar Rami bar Abba amar Rav Huna* — in the name of *Rav Huna*, another ruling: *lechi ha-moshech im dofno shel mavoi*.

### Four-Amah Threshold

The case is as follows. Imagine the thickness of a *mavoi* wall. If a *lechi* extends out from that wall — not into the *mavoi* itself but along the exterior, parallel to the wall — then from within the *mavoi* it appears to be nothing more than a continuation of the wall itself. From the outside of the *mavoi*, however, it is clearly visible as a separate protrusion. This is a textbook example of something *nira mi-bachutz ve-shaveh mi-bifnim* — visible from outside, flush from inside.

What is the *halacha*? *Pachot me-arba amot nidon mishum lechi* — if this extension is less than four *amot* long, it counts as a *lechi*. *U-mishtamesh be-chudo ha-pnimi* — and the usable area of the *mavoi* extends only up to the inner edge of this extension, not beyond it, meaning one may not use the space directly opposite the *lechi* — a matter that had been established in earlier sessions. *Arba amot nidon mishum mavoi* — once the extension reaches four *amot* or more, it is no longer classified as a *lechi*; it becomes, in effect, a wall of a *mavoi* in its own right. *Ve-asur le-ishtamesh bekulan* — and now one may not use the entire *mavoi*, because the *mavoi* is left without any effective *lechi* closing it off. The extension has grown too large to serve as a *lechi* and instead absorbs the identity of a wall, leaving the *mavoi* open.

### Three Inferences

*Shema mina telat* — from this teaching, three *halachot* may be inferred. First, *shema mina bein lechayim asur* — the space directly opposite the *lechi* is prohibited for use; one may only carry up to the inner edge of the *lechi*. This resolves a debate that had occupied the *Gemara* a day or two earlier. Second, *shema mina meshech mavoi be-arba* — the minimum length of a *mavoi* is four *amot*, since it is precisely at four *amot* that this extension stops functioning as a *lechi* and starts functioning as a *mavoi* wall. Third, and most critically for the present discussion, *shema mina nira mi-bachutz ve-shaveh mi-bifnim nidon mishum lechi* — something visible from the outside but flush on the inside counts as a *lechi*, since that is precisely the character of the extension in this case, and it was nonetheless given full *lechi* status.

The first two inferences align with positions that had already been established in earlier *sugyas*. It is the third inference that carries the most weight here.

### Ruling Confirmation

*Ve-hilcheta* — the *halacha* is: *nira mi-bachutz ve-shaveh mi-bifnim nidon mishum lechi*. It does count as a *lechi*.

The *Gemara* immediately registers the tension: *tiuvta ve-hilcheta*? We just demonstrated a contradiction — from the case of the two *chatzerot* — against this very position, and now we rule in accordance with it? *In* — yes, *mishum de-tani Rabbi Chiyya kevataih* — because although the two-*chatzer* case seems to contradict this ruling, there was an explicit *Baraita* taught by *Rabbi Chiyya* that directly supports it, stating that whether a *lechi* is visible on the outside and not the inside, or on the inside and not the outside, it is halachically valid. There is evidence in both directions. The weight of *Rabbi Chiyya*'s explicit teaching tips the scales, and so we rule accordingly.

This is a conceptually striking conclusion. One might have assumed that the entire purpose of a *lechi* — or a *korah* — is to serve as a *heker*, a recognizable marker, for those *inside* the space, reminding them not to carry beyond the boundary. If the marker is only visible from the outside, does it not fail at its fundamental purpose? The *Gemara*'s ruling suggests either that the *lechi* functions more as a formal partition than as a practical reminder, and therefore inside-visibility is not essential; or that *Chazal*, in formalizing the requirement, were satisfied with any form of recognition — even from the outside — as sufficient. The *halacha* stands: outside-visibility is enough. As a practical consequence, those living in the small *chatzer* of the original case would not be able to carry therein under the ruling of the *braita* — but they are not considered to be in a completely open domain, because the extension does constitute a *lechi*.

---

## Wide Opening Solutions

### Ten-Amah Limit

Having completed the discussion of the *korah* and *lechi* — their heights, the spaces below and opposite them, and related questions — the *Gemara* now turns to the second clause of the *Mishna*: if the opening of a *mavoi* is too wide, it must be reduced. *Ve-rachav me-eser yima'et* — if the opening exceeds ten *amot*, you must make it smaller before a *lechi* or *korah* will be effective.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Leniency

*Amar Abaye: tanu rabbanan* — *Abaye* cites a *Baraita*. *Ve-rachav me-eser yima'et* — wider than ten, you reduce. *Rabbi Yehuda omer eino tzarich lema'et* — *Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees and holds that no reduction is required, even for openings wider than ten *amot*. Just as *Rabbi Yehuda* had ruled earlier that the *korah* need not be lowered even when it exceeds twenty *amot* in height, so too here he allows a wider opening without reduction.

*Ve-ad kama* — to what maximum width does *Rabbi Yehuda* permit this? *Savar Rav Acha kamei de-Rav Yosef lemeimar* — Rav Acha proposed before *Rav Yosef* that the limit should be *ad shelosh esreh amah u-shlish* — thirteen and a third *amot* — derived by a *kal va-chomer* from the laws of *pasi biraot*.

### Pasi Biraot Wells

The *pasi biraot* are the special partition-walls constructed around public wells. The scenario is as follows: a well in a public space is four by four *amot* and ten *tefachim* deep, making its interior a *reshut ha-yachid*. Drawing water from it while standing in a *reshut ha-rabbim* would constitute carrying between domains. The rabbinic solution is to erect corner-posts — small L-shaped walls at the four corners — that formally enclose the space around the well. The resulting enclosure looks like four walls with enormous gaps; indeed, there is far more open space than closed space, which ordinarily renders an enclosure invalid. Nevertheless, because the four corners are in place, the entire enclosed area is treated as a *reshut ha-yachid*, allowing people to draw and use the water within it. This is a special *heter*, quite different from the standard rules of *mechitza*. The maximum size of this enclosure, as the *Gemara* will explain, is thirteen and a third *amot* — large enough to accommodate four cows entering and four cows exiting simultaneously, which appears to have been a practical measure of the required access.

The proposed *kal va-chomer*: *pasi biraot*, where we are already extremely lenient in allowing more open space than closed space, nevertheless impose a maximum opening size of thirteen and a third *amot*. A *mavoi*, where we apply the ordinary stricter rules requiring more closed space than open, should certainly not permit openings exceeding thirteen and a third *amot* — for if even the lenient case caps at that figure, the stricter case should not exceed it.

### Analogy Rejection

The *Gemara* rejects this *kal va-chomer*, and does so from two opposing directions. First, one could argue the reverse: *pasi biraot* is so lenient in allowing *parutz merubah al ha-omed* — more open than closed — that we must draw the line somewhere, and so we cap it at thirteen and a third. But a *mavoi*, where we are generally strict and require *omed merubah al ha-parutz*, perhaps enjoys more latitude precisely at the dimension of the opening, since we have already been strict in other respects. Thus the opening of a *mavoi* might be permitted to exceed thirteen and a third *amot*.

Alternatively, the opposite inference could be drawn: precisely because *pasi biraot* is so lenient in one dimension, it can afford to permit thirteen and a third. But a *mavoi*, where no such leniencies exist, might be held to a stricter standard than ten *amot*, and thirteen and a third might actually be too generous. *Klal klal lo* — perhaps for a *mavoi* we allow nothing beyond ten.

In short, the *pasi biraot* is a fundamentally different legal construct, and no inference — in either direction — can be drawn from it to the case of a *mavoi*. The *Gemara* therefore leaves open the question of how far *Rabbi Yehuda* would extend his leniency in the case of the *mavoi*. The *Chachamim*'s position remains clear: ten *amot* is the maximum permissible opening width.

---

## Lengthwise Division

### Post Solution Rejected

The *Gemara* now turns to practical solutions for a *mavoi* whose opening is too wide. Reducing a twenty-*amah* opening to ten is straightforward in principle — but in practice, one may wish to keep the opening as wide as possible. *Tani Levi* — Levi taught: *mavoi she-rachav esrim amah* — if a *mavoi* is twenty *amot* wide — *no'etz kanna be-emtzaito ve-dayo* — simply plant a post in the middle and you are done. The post divides the twenty-*amah* opening into two ten-*amah* openings, each of which can then be fitted with a *korah*, and the problem is solved.

However, the *Gemara* reports that Levi himself — or in another version, *Shmuel* in Levi's name — retracted this: *ein halacha ke-osa mishna*. We do not rule like that *Baraita*. The reason is the principle the *Gemara* will articulate: *atya avira di-hai gisa ve-di-hai gisa u-mevatli* — the air space on this side and that side comes and renders the post inconsequential. A lone post standing in a twenty-*amah* opening, with ten *amot* of open air on each side, cannot be said to divide anything. It simply disappears into the surrounding void.

### Four-Amah Plank

What then is the solution? *Amar Shmuel mishme d'Levi* — Levi's accepted answer: *oseh pas gavoha asarah be-meshech arba amot u-mamido le-orkho shel mavoi* — make a plank ten *tefachim* tall and four *amot* long, and stand it *lengthwise* into the *mavoi*. 

This is the ingenious part. Rather than placing something across the opening, perpendicular to the direction of entry, you insert a plank running *parallel* to the direction of the *mavoi*, extending four *amot* inward from the opening. The result is not a wall across the opening but a dividing partition along the length. Recall that we established earlier that four *amot* is the minimum length of a *mavoi*. An extension of four *amot* therefore does not function as a *lechi* — it is too long — but rather as a *mavoi* wall in its own right. By placing this four-*amah* plank lengthwise, you have in effect created two separate *mavois*, each ten *amot* wide, sitting side by side. Each may then be independently fitted with a *korah*.

### Air Space Negation

Why does this work where the post did not? Because we are no longer trying to make something function *across* the opening, where it would be overwhelmed by the surrounding air space on both sides. Instead, we are creating a partition *along* the length, defining one *mavoi* on each side of the plank. The plank is not a *lechi* subject to being negated by flanking air space; it is a wall. The air space on its sides does not negate it because it is not positioned transversely.

*Tosafot* notes that according to one view, a *tzuras ha-pesach* — a symbolic doorframe — would be needed at the back end, connecting the plank to the rear wall, in order to fully close off each *mavoi* from the other. However, the *Gemara* itself does not state this requirement, and *Tosafot* also entertains the possibility that it is unnecessary — that once the first four *amot* of the *mavoi* are divided by the plank, the two sides are sufficiently defined as separate *mavois*, and the fact that they are joined at the rear is inconsequential.

---

## Gap-and-Plank System

### 15-Amah Example

*De-amar Rav Yehuda* — the *Gemara* presents an alternative solution, one that is more intuitive though technically more involved. *Mavoi she-rachav chamesh esreh amah* — if the *mavoi* is fifteen *amot* wide: *marchik shtei amot ve-oseh pas shalosh amot* — leave a two-*amah* gap and erect a three-*amah* plank. This closes off a five-*amah* section and leaves ten *amot* open — which is within the permissible limit.

The logic: you need to close off five *amot* of the fifteen-*amah* opening. One could simply erect a five-*amah* plank, but *Rav Yehuda* offers a more accessible solution. Within the five-*amah* section you wish to treat as closed, you leave a two-*amah* gap and erect a three-*amah* plank. Looking at that five-*amah* section, the majority — three out of five — is standing wall. The principle of *omed merubah al ha-parutz* — the standing portion is greater than the open portion — is satisfied, and the entire five-*amah* section is considered as if it were fully walled. The remaining ten *amot* constitute the permissible opening.

### Negation Principle

The *Gemara* sharpens the analysis by asking why *Rav Yehuda* did not suggest what might seem like an even more elegant arrangement. Rather than a two-*amah* gap and a three-*amah* plank, why not divide the three *amot* of wall across both sides of the gap? Specifically: a plank of one and a half *amot*, then a two-*amah* gap, then another plank of one and a half *amot*. The result is the same total: three *amot* of wall, two *amot* of gap, covering five *amot* — and the wall on each side is spread more evenly. Why is this not offered as an option?

Here the *Gemara* introduces its second operative principle: *atya avira di-hai gisa ve-avira di-hai gisa u-mevatli* — the air from one side and the air from the other side comes and cancels out what is in the middle. This principle operates at the level of individual segments rather than the totality of the opening. Even if the overall count of wall versus gap satisfies *omed merubah al ha-parutz*, a particular wall segment may be rendered halachically void if there is too much open air on both of its sides relative to its own size.

In the case of a one-and-a-half-*amah* plank flanked by a two-*amah* gap on one side and ten *amot* of open *mavoi* space on the other, the disproportion between the air space and the plank is severe enough to negate the plank entirely. This is not a matter of whether the total wall beats the total gap; it is a micro-analysis of each segment individually. By contrast, when the plank is three *amot* with only a two-*amah* gap on one side and the open *mavoi* on the other, the three-*amah* plank is robust enough that the flanking air space does not render it void.

The distinction between these two principles is essential: *omed merubah al ha-parutz* asks whether, across the entire section one is trying to close, more is walled than open. The air-negation principle asks whether any individual segment of wall is overwhelmed by the open space on both of its sides. Both conditions must be satisfied independently.

### Alternating Walls

The *Gemara* pushes further. Why not use alternating small walls: a one-*amah* plank, a one-*amah* gap, a one-*amah* plank, a one-*amah* gap, a one-*amah* plank — five *amot* covered, with three *amot* of wall and two *amot* of gap? Here the air flanking each individual one-*amah* plank is not larger than the plank itself — one *amah* of gap on each side of a one-*amah* plank — so the negation principle should not apply.

The *Gemara* raises the possibility that from this case we might infer *omed ke-parutz assur* — that when the standing wall is merely equal to the gap (one against one), rather than greater, it is insufficient. But the *Gemara* immediately deflects: *le-olam eima lach mutar* — actually, equal is sufficient. The problem with this arrangement is again the negation principle: even though each local one-*amah* plank has only a one-*amah* gap immediately flanking it, the plank is bordered on its far side by the ten-*amah* open space of the *mavoi*. That extended open air combines with the one-*amah* gap on the near side to overwhelm the one-*amah* plank and negate it. The negation principle is what disqualifies this arrangement, not any failure of *omed merubah al ha-parutz*.

### Spread-Out Walls

The *Gemara* then proposes: *na'avid pas amah u-mechtza, veyarchik amah, veya'aseh pas amah u-mechtza* — make a plank of one and a half *amot*, then a gap of one *amah*, then another plank of one and a half *amot*. This covers five *amot* with three *amot* of wall and two *amot* of gap. Each one-and-a-half-*amah* plank is flanked by a one-*amah* gap on one side and the ten-*amah* open *mavoi* space on the other. But the one-and-a-half-*amah* plank is larger than the one-*amah* gap — so the question is whether it survives the negation principle.

*Innahu hachi nami* — the *Gemara* affirms that this arrangement is indeed valid. One and a half is greater than one; the gap does not overwhelm the plank. *Ve-chulei hai lo atrachu rabbanan* — but *Chazal* did not impose this more burdensome configuration on people. They allowed the simpler solution of a single three-*amah* plank with a two-*amah* gap. The two-plank arrangement is valid if one wishes to use it, but it is not required.

---

## Side-Door Concern

### Abandonment Fear

The *Gemara* now raises a conceptually different concern. Suppose one has erected the three-*amah* plank with a two-*amah* gap, and placed the *korah* over the ten-*amah* main opening. The permissibility of the *mavoi* depends on the *korah* marking the entry point. But what if people begin to use the two-*amah* gap as their habitual exit? If the residents abandon the main door and pass instead through the side gap — which has no *korah* — then the gap becomes the effective entrance of the *mavoi*, and the *korah* over the main opening no longer marks the actual point of entry. The concern is that practical human behavior might undermine the halachic construct.

### Strong Presumption

*Amar Rav Adda bar Matna*: *chazaka ein adam meniach petach gadol ve-nichnas be-petach katan* — there is a strong presumption (*chazaka*) that a person will not abandon a large door in favor of a small one. People naturally use the larger, more convenient opening. There is no realistic concern that the residents will habitually choose the narrow two-*amah* gap over the spacious ten-*amah* main entrance.

### Not a Shortcut

The *Gemara* compares this to a case discussed in an earlier session, involving a *mavoi* whose side wall was breached. There, *Rav Huna* and *Rav Assi* were concerned that people might exit through the breach in the side wall under certain circumstances, thereby compromising the *mavoi*'s status. Why should we not be similarly concerned here?

The *Gemara* distinguishes: *hasam ka-mamit locha, hacha lo ka-mamit locha* — there, the side opening creates a shortcut; here, it does not. When there is a breach in a side wall, exiting through it allows one to bypass the front of the *mavoi* entirely — it is a genuinely more direct route in certain directions, and people may well be drawn to use it habitually. Here, by contrast, the two-*amah* gap is on the same face as the main opening. Exiting through the gap rather than through the main door offers no directional advantage whatsoever — it is simply a smaller version of the same exit. No one would consistently prefer a narrow gap to a wide door when both lead in precisely the same direction. The *chazaka* therefore holds, and the concern is dismissed.

---

## Toilet Seat Debate

### Toilet Seat Setup

The *Gemara* returns, in a different halachic context, to the question of how air space on both sides of a partition affects its halachic status. *Tanan hasam be-Oholot* — a teaching from the tractate dealing with *tum'at meit*: *or ha-atzla* — a leather toilet seat. This was a piece of leather, approximately one *tefach* by one *tefach*, placed over the seat opening of a toilet, with a hole in the center through which waste passed. If this leather seat is suspended above a corpse, or a *ke-zayis* of a corpse, does it function as a barrier that blocks the spread of *tumah* upward, or is the hole too significant to be disregarded?

The principle at work: an object of one *tefach* by one *tefach* can block *tumah* from spreading through it. But if the hole in the center is large enough, the leather around it may not constitute a full *tefach* by *tefach* barrier. The question is: when can the leather surrounding the hole and the hole itself combine — *mitztarfin* — to be considered a full *tefach*, and when does the hole prevent this combination?

### Rav Dimi's Measure

*Ki ata Rav Dimi* — when Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he said: *etzba'im mikan ve-etzba'im mikan ve-etzba revach be-emtza* — two finger-widths on this side, two on that side, and two finger-widths of gap in the middle. Since a *tefach* measures six finger-widths by the pinky-based scale, and two plus two plus two equals six, the entire piece is exactly one *tefach*, divided equally.

### Ravin's Measure

*Ki ata Ravin amar* — when Ravin came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported differently: *etzba u-mechtza mikan ve-etzba u-mechtza mikan ve-etzba revach be-emtza* — one and a half finger-widths on each side and one finger-width in the middle. Since a *tefach* also measures four thumb-widths, and one and a half plus one and a half plus one equals four, this arrangement equals one *tefach* by the thumb-based scale.

### Abaye's Challenge

*Amar lei Abaye le-Rav Dimi* — Abaye challenged *Rav Dimi*: *mi peligi*? Do you and *Ravin* actually disagree? *Rav Dimi* initially responded: *lo* — no. One is measuring by pinky-widths, the other by thumb-widths; both describe a *tefach*, the units simply differ. *Ha be-ravrvata, ha be-zutrata* — one uses the larger unit, the other the smaller.

*Abaye* pressed: *pela'a* — really? You are arguing, *u-va-omed u-va-parutz mi-shetei ruchos palgiton* — and specifically about whether closed space from both sides can be *combined* to exceed the gap. This is not a dispute about units of measurement; it is a dispute about the underlying principle.

### Combining Sides Debate

Abaye's insight is as follows. Both scholars describe a *tefach*-sized piece of leather with a hole of some size in the center. The question is what proportions are necessary for the leather to be considered a halachically effective barrier rather than a perforated non-entity. The critical variable is the relationship between each side of leather and the central gap. Rav Dimi says each side is equal to the gap — two against two. Ravin says each side must be larger than the gap — one and a half against one. Abaye argues that this difference reflects a principled disagreement: can you *combine* the leather on both sides to determine that the combined wall exceeds the hole, or must you look at each side independently?

If combining is permitted, then two plus two equals four, which exceeds the two-finger gap — and the leather is valid even with equal-sized sides. If you must evaluate each side independently, then two equal to two is insufficient — you need each side to individually exceed the gap — and Ravin's arrangement of one and a half against one is necessary.

### Dimi Clarifies

Rav Dimi responds to Abaye's challenge: if I truly held that combining from both sides suffices, I should have given a more striking example — *etzba u-shnei shlishim mikan ve-etzba u-shnei shlishim mikan ve-etzba ushnei shlishim revach be-emtza* — one and two-thirds on each side against a gap that is larger than either side alone, with both sides together exceeding it. That would have been the dramatic statement of the combining principle. Instead I gave an example where each side is equal to the gap — which proves that I am not relying on combining at all.

*Ella ee ika le-meimar de-pliginon, be-parutz ke-omed pligin* — if there is a genuine disagreement between us, it is not about combining versus not combining. Both of us, *Rav Dimi* clarifies, hold that you may not combine the two sides; you must evaluate each side independently. The disagreement is about a different question: must each side individually be *greater than* the gap, or is it sufficient that each side be *equal to* the gap? Ravin holds that each side must be greater — hence one and a half against one. *Rav Dimi* holds that equality suffices — hence two against two.

This maps directly onto the question that arose in the context of *mavoi* partitions earlier in the *daf*: the dispute over *omed ke-parutz* — whether a standing wall that is merely equal in size to the open gap is sufficient, or whether the standing must exceed the opening. The leather toilet-seat case and the *mavoi* partition case thus illuminate the same underlying principle, applied in two very different halachic domains. It is worth noting, as *Tosafot* observes, that the way we define issues of *mechitza* for *eruvin* purposes is not necessarily identical to the way we define whether a barrier is sufficient to contain or block *tumah* — the two legal frameworks overlap but are not coextensive.

---

---

# Eiruvin 11

## Doorframe & Eruv

### Mishna: Tzurat Hapetach

The daf begins at the very bottom of 10b, returning once again to the *mishna*. The *mishna* has already established that a *mavoi* cannot be higher than twenty *amot* or wider than ten *amot*, and now turns to the question of how to remedy those deficiencies. The key principle introduced is: *im yesh lo tzurat hapetach* — if the opening possesses a doorframe, consisting of two posts with a beam across the top, then *af al pi sherachav me'eser ein tzarich lema'et* — even if it is wider than ten *amot*, one need not reduce it. The *tzurat hapetach* defines the entire opening as a doorway by virtue of its frame, regardless of width.

### Modern Eruv Setup

This ruling carries enormous practical significance, for it is precisely this principle upon which contemporary *eruv* construction relies. The standard method of creating an *eruv* in a city involves affixing beams against telephone poles and using the telephone wire as the upper beam, thereby forming *tzurot hapetach* of vast dimensions that encircle an entire urban area. The legitimacy of this practice rests squarely on the assumption that a *tzurat hapetach* remains valid even when wider than ten *amot*.

### Rambam's Limits

It should be noted, however, that the *Rambam* rules that a *tzurat hapetach* does not function for openings wider than ten *amot*. According to his position, the construction of a contemporary *eruv* in the standard manner would simply not be permissible — an extraordinarily stringent consequence. The *Rambam*'s source for this ruling will become clear as the *Gemara* unfolds.

---

## Doorframe Efficacy

### Height Baraita

The *Gemara* on 11a opens by noting what is already established: *ashkachan tzurat hapetach d'mahani berachvah* — we have seen that a *tzurat hapetach* helps when the *mavoi* is too wide. Likewise, from the earlier discussion at the beginning of the *masechet*, we saw that an *amaltara* — the decorative cornice carved into the upper corners of a frame — helps when the *mavoi* is too high, exceeding twenty *amot*, since the ornamentation draws the eye upward and thereby provides the necessary visual recognition. The *Gemara* now asks: *ipcha mai* — what of the reverse cases? Will a *tzurat hapetach* help when the *mavoi* is too high, and will an *amaltara* help when it is too wide?

The logic behind the uncertainty is instructive. The problem of excessive height is arguably one of visibility — the cornice addresses it by making the threshold visually salient. It is not obvious that a *tzurat hapetach* would resolve this, since the *tzurat hapetach* functions by defining the space as a doorway, not by drawing the eye. Conversely, a cornice that addresses a visibility problem may not help when the issue is that the opening is simply too expansive to be conceptualized as a door.

A *baraita* is then cited: *mavoi she'hu gavo'ah me'esrim amah yema'et* — a *mavoi* exceeding twenty *amot* in height must be lowered; *v'im yesh lo tzurat hapetach eino tzarich lema'et* — but if it has a doorframe, it need not be. This is a striking ruling. Perhaps the reasoning is that if the frame itself ascends the sides of the opening, it encourages the viewer to look all the way up. Alternatively, perhaps the entire framework of excessive height is not fundamentally about visibility at all, but rather about defining the space as a doorway — and a *tzurat hapetach* accomplishes exactly that, irrespective of height.

### Reciprocal Question

The *Gemara* then poses the question in the other direction: *amtzur berachvo mai* — does the cornice help when the problem is excessive width? The *baraita* cited lists the cases: a *mavoi* too high must be lowered, a *mavoi* too wide must be narrowed, but if there is a *tzurat hapetach*, no reduction is needed — and similarly if there is an *amaltara*, no reduction is needed.

The *Gemara* asks: *mai lav aseifa* — is this not referring to the final case, meaning the cornice helps when the *mavoi* is too wide? The *Gemara* deflects: *lo, areisha* — not necessarily. Perhaps the *tzurat hapetach* is speaking to the too-wide case, while the *amaltara* is speaking to the too-high case, and the passage tells us nothing about whether a cornice resolves excessive width. The argument for saying it should not is compelling: there is no obvious logic by which a decorative cornice element would address the fundamental problem that an opening is too expansive to count as a doorway.

### Combined Solutions

What the *Gemara* has established with confidence is that a *tzurat hapetach* works not only when the *mavoi* is too wide, but even when it is too high — a conclusion of great practical relevance for the use of *tzurot hapetach* in modern *eruv* construction.

### Tosafot Challenge

*Tosafot* raises an interesting question at this point. Why, *Tosafot* asks, would one need a *tzurat hapetach* to solve the problem of excessive height? After all, a *tzurat hapetach* consists of a post on either side and a beam above. If there are posts on both sides, those posts themselves constitute a *lechi* — a side post — and a *lechi* should be sufficient for a *mavoi*. Why does it matter that the beam is higher than twenty *amot*?

*Tosafot* offers two answers. The first is that perhaps the posts are too thin to qualify as a valid *lechi* according to some opinion that requires a minimum thickness. The second, and more significant answer, is that the *baraita* may be addressing a scenario where a *lechi* alone would not suffice in the first place — such as an outdoor space or a broader configuration where a full *tzurat hapetach* is required and a *lechi* would be inadequate. In such a case, the point is precisely that even a *tzurat hapetach* — which might have been thought insufficient at a height greater than twenty *amot* — remains valid.

---

## Rav's Restriction

### Rav's Correction

The *Gemara* now introduces a major dispute. *Matni lah Rav Yehuda le-Chiyya bar Rav kamei de-Rav* — Rav Yehuda was teaching *Chiyya bar Rav*, the son of Rav, in the presence of Rav himself, and he taught our *mishna* as it stands: *eino tzarich lema'et* — that if there is a *tzurat hapetach*, one need not reduce the opening. Rav intervened and corrected him: *atneiye tzarich lema'et* — teach it to him the other way, that even with a *tzurat hapetach*, one must still reduce the opening. According to Rav, the *mishna*'s ruling that a *tzurat hapetach* exempts one from reduction does not apply when the opening exceeds ten *amot*; the *tzurat hapetach* simply does not function in that case. This, as noted, is the ruling adopted by the *Rambam*.

### Rav Yosef's Inference

Rav Yosef proceeds to draw a further implication from Rav's position: *midivrei Rabbeinu nilmad* — from the words of our master we can derive that *chatzer she-rubba petachim ve-chalonot* — a courtyard the majority of whose perimeter consists of doorways, windows, and openings — presents a condition of *parutz merubba al ha-omed*, where more is breached than stands. Can such a courtyard be enclosed by means of a *tzurat hapetach*? Rav Yosef argues that from Rav's ruling it follows that *einan nitarot be-tzurat hapetach* — even if each individual opening is less than ten *amot*, a *tzurat hapetach* does not resolve the problem of majority exposure.

One should pause here to appreciate the stakes. Contemporary *eruvin* rely not only on the leniency that a *tzurat hapetach* can span more than ten *amot*, but also on the leniency that a *tzurat hapetach* can serve to enclose a space that is overwhelmingly open — where the vast majority of the perimeter consists of nothing but air. According to Rav and Rav Yosef's reading of him, both of these leniencies are denied.

### Logic of Restriction

What is the logical basis for Rav's position? The *Gemara* articulates it: *ho'il ve-yoter me-eser oser be-mavoi* — a gap of more than ten *amot* is inherently problematic in the context of a *mavoi*, and *parutz merubba al ha-omed oser be-chatzer* — majority exposure is inherently problematic in the context of a *chatzer*. Rav's argument by analogy is: just as a *tzurat hapetach* cannot resolve a gap exceeding ten *amot*, so too it cannot resolve the condition of majority exposure. Both are fundamental structural deficiencies that a *tzurat hapetach*, however elegantly formed, cannot overcome.

One can understand this conceptually. The *tzurat hapetach* functions by defining a space as a doorway. One could argue that if an opening is too large, it simply cannot be credibly characterized as a doorway regardless of the frame around it — it is a breach, not a door. By extension, when the majority of the enclosure is breached, even individually valid *tzurot hapetach* may not suffice to transform the overall space into an enclosed domain.

And yet the conceptual distinction between the two problems is also worth noting. The objection to a gap wider than ten *amot* is local: this specific opening is too large to be called a doorway. The objection of *parutz merubba al ha-omed* is global: there is too much unenclosed space overall. Once one installs a *tzurat hapetach* in a particular gap and successfully defines that gap as a doorway, it is no longer treated as a breach but as a passage through a wall — and if every gap receives a valid *tzurat hapetach*, the problem of majority exposure disappears. This is the argument for saying that *parutz merubba al ha-omed* can be resolved by *tzurot hapetach* even if the too-wide problem cannot.

### Gemara Pushback

The *Gemara* pushes back against Rav Yosef's inference. The argument is as follows: the reason a *tzurat hapetach* might not help for a gap exceeding ten *amot* is that we are particularly strict about large gaps. The evidence for this strictness comes from the *patzei birot* — the corner posts surrounding a public well. According to Rabbi Meir, even in the case of the *patzei birot*, where leniency regarding majority exposure is granted by universal consensus, the individual gaps may not exceed ten *amot*. This shows that the ten-*amot* limit is a deeply embedded strictness, cutting across other leniencies.

By contrast, the problem of *parutz merubba al ha-omed* is one where we are comparatively lenient. The *patzei birot* themselves demonstrate this: the entire structure consists of only four corner posts with the majority entirely open, yet everyone agrees it is valid. *Tomar be-farutz merubba al ha-omed* — will you make the same strict argument when the problem is majority exposure? *Ha-oseh be-chatzer, sheken hutra etzlo patzei birot, ledivrei hakol* — this is a recognized area of leniency, so perhaps a *tzurat hapetach* can indeed resolve it.

The *Gemara* then attempts to bring a proof that a *tzurat hapetach* cannot resolve majority exposure from a passage about walls with numerous doorways and windows. The *Gemara* cites a teaching that walls with many openings are acceptable *u'vilvad she-omed merubba al ha-parutz* — provided that the solid portion predominates. This seems to imply that if the majority were openings, even doorways with *tzurot hapetach*, it would not be valid. Rav Kahana deflects this by explaining that the teaching refers to *pichai shimai* — ruined or deformed openings that lack a proper frame. The debate between Rav Rechumi and Rav Yosef as to the precise meaning of *pichai shimai* — whether it means lacking proper side posts or lacking a lintel — converges on the conclusion that such openings do not constitute valid *tzurot hapetach* at all. If one actually installs proper *tzurot hapetach*, the teaching presents no obstacle.

The *Gemara* ultimately notes: *v'af Rav Yochanan savar lah l'ha de-Rav* — even Rabbi Yochanan seems to hold like Rav, that a *tzurat hapetach* does not work for a gap wider than ten *amot*. The narrative that follows will both illustrate and complicate this claim.

---

## Vineyard Case

### Beit Chortan Story

A story is introduced via the chain: *d'amar Ravin bar Rav Adda amar Rav Yitzchak* — Ravin bar Rav Adda says in the name of Rav Yitzchak: there was a certain man from the valley of *Beit Chortan* who drove four posts into the four corners of a field and stretched a vine across the tops of them — *shenatz arba kundisin b'arba pinot hasadeh u-matach zmora aleihem* — thereby creating, in effect, four *tzurot hapetach* enclosing a space that was entirely open. His intention was to use this enclosure to permit planting of *kilayim*, diverse species, within the space immediately adjacent to his vines. This is an astonishing application, for it means using *tzurot hapetach* to enclose a space that is, in its entirety, exposed on all sides — precisely the structure we use today for urban *eruvin*.

### Kilayim vs Shabbat

The case was brought before the Sages, who permitted it for purposes of *kilayim*. Reish Lakish then drew the broader conclusion: *keshem she-hitiru lo l'inyan kilayim kach hitiru lo l'inyan Shabbat* — just as they permitted this for *kilayim*, so too would they permit it for *Shabbat*. Rabbi Yochanan disagreed: *l'kilayim hitiru lo, u'l'inyan Shabbat lo hitiru lo* — for *kilayim* it was permitted, but not for *Shabbat*.

The *Gemara* now asks: what was the critical feature of the case that generated this dispute? Two possible explanations present themselves. First, perhaps the vine was wrapped around the side of the posts rather than stretched directly over the top — *min hatzad* — in which case the issue is not the width of the enclosure but the position of the beam. The *Gemara* immediately rejects this as the basis of Reish Lakish's leniency: Rav Chisda has already ruled that *tzurat hapetach she-asah min hatzad lo asah ve-lo klum* — a *tzurat hapetach* in which the upper element runs along the side rather than directly over the top is entirely worthless, and Reish Lakish could not have endorsed it. Therefore, the vine must have run over the top — *al gaban* — and the dispute must have concerned something else.

The *Gemara* considers whether the gap was less than or more than ten *amot*. If it was less than ten, there is no apparent reason for Rabbi Yochanan to invalidate it for *Shabbat*. The *Gemara* therefore suggests: *ela lav beyoser mi-eser* — the gap must have exceeded ten *amot*, and this is the crux of the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan: does a *tzurat hapetach* remain valid for *Shabbat* when the opening is wider than ten *amot*?

### Reconciling Positions

The *Gemara* then discovers a contradiction internal to each authority's position. A separate *baraita* presents Reish Lakish saying — not in his own name, but in the name of Rabbi Yehuda b'Rabbi Chanina — that a certain type of braiding or stringing (*pe'ah*) works for *kilayim* but not for *Shabbat*. Rabbi Yochanan in this same passage says it works for neither. This contradicts their positions in the *Beit Chortan* case, where Reish Lakish permitted both and Rabbi Yochanan permitted *kilayim* but not *Shabbat*.

The resolution for Reish Lakish is straightforward: *ha deidei ha derabeih* — in the first instance he spoke in his own name; in the second, he transmitted the opinion of his teacher. These need not be consistent. The contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's position is more difficult. The *Gemara* proposes: if we say that in the first case (where Rabbi Yochanan permitted *kilayim* but not *Shabbat*) the vine was *al gaban*, running over the top, then his objection to *Shabbat* would be because the opening exceeded ten *amot*. In the second case (where he permits neither), the vine was *min hatzad*, running along the side — and that disqualifies even *kilayim*.

### Beam Position Key

The *Gemara* then considers whether the debate in the first case could equally be read as concerning the position of the vine rather than the width of the opening: perhaps even in the *Beit Chortan* case the vine ran along the side, and it is *that* which Rabbi Yochanan objected to for *Shabbat*, while Reish Lakish was lenient enough to permit a *min hatzad* arrangement for *Shabbat*. If so, the second case, where the vine was *min hatzad* and larger than ten *amot*, would explain why even Reish Lakish — who in his own name permits *min hatzad* for *Shabbat* — would say it fails for *kilayim* when it exceeds ten *amot*, following the stricter view transmitted from his teacher.

The *Gemara* brings proof for the conclusion that *kilayim* is indeed more lenient than *Shabbat* in this domain: *hatanya, hayu sham kanim ha-dukranin ve-asah lahen pe'ah milmala, afilu b'yoter me-eser mutar* — an explicit *baraita* states that posts with a cord running over the top permit planting of diverse species even when the width exceeds ten *amot*. This demonstrates that for *kilayim*, the ten-*amot* threshold does not apply when the upper element runs directly over the top.

Given this explicit permission for *kilayim* at widths exceeding ten *amot*, the distinction drawn by Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri — who said that up to ten is permitted and beyond ten is forbidden — must be referring to a case where the cord ran *min hatzad*. Only in that degraded configuration does the width become significant even for *kilayim*. The *Gemara* concludes: *ela lav shma mina ela lav min hatzad* — derive from this that when the restriction applies, it is because the cord ran along the side, and even there, up to ten is acceptable and beyond ten is not. *Shma mina* — this is a sound conclusion.

The overall picture that emerges: for *kilayim*, a classic *tzurat hapetach* with the beam running directly overhead is valid regardless of width. When the beam runs *min hatzad*, the width becomes relevant even for *kilayim*: below ten *amot* it may still work; above ten *amot* it does not. For *Shabbat*, the requirement that the beam run directly overhead is absolute. Whether a gap exceeding ten *amot* disqualifies a properly formed *tzurat hapetach* for *Shabbat* remains the great dispute: Rav says it does, the unqualified *mishna* says it does not, and Rabbi Yochanan's position resists the *Gemara*'s attempts to align it definitively with Rav. The *Rambam* rules with Rav; current practice follows the *mishna*'s plain reading, and our *eruvin* depend on both the leniency of width exceeding ten *amot* and the leniency of majority exposure.

---

## Archway & Mezuzah

### Rav Sheshet Story

Returning to the question of what a *tzurat hapetach* must look like, the *Gemara* records Rav Chisda's rulings on the matter. First: *tzurat hapetach she-asah min hatzad lo asah ve-lo klum* — a *tzurat hapetach* in which the upper element runs along the side of the posts rather than directly over their tops is entirely invalid. Second: *tzurat hapetach she-amru tzrichah she-tehei briyah k'dei le-amid bah delet* — the doorframe must be sufficiently sturdy to support a door, should one be leaned against it. Notably, however, even a door made of straw would suffice — what is excluded is only a structure so flimsy it would collapse under any weight.

Reish Lakish adds in the name of Rabbi Yannai an even more demanding requirement: *tzurat hapetach tzrichah heker tzir* — the doorframe must exhibit a recognizable hinge socket. Rav Avya explains that this means something resembling the bracket or loop that would receive a door's hinge — a physical indication that a door could actually be mounted. For Rabbi Yannai, the *tzurat hapetach* must not be merely symbolic but must genuinely resemble a functional doorframe to the point of having this feature.

The *Gemara* then records that Rav Acha the son of Rav Avya found the students of Rav Ashi and asked them: *amar mar midi be-tzurat hapetach* — did the master say anything specific regarding criteria for a valid *tzurat hapetach*? They replied that he had said nothing. From the master's silence, one infers that no special requirements — including *heker tzir* — are imposed beyond the basic structure. We rule accordingly: *heker tzir* is not required, though the requirement of structural soundness (*briyah*) is upheld.

Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet dispute whether the side posts must physically touch the upper beam. Rav Nachman rules they need not (*ein tzrichin liga*); Rav Sheshet rules they must (*tzrichin liga*). Rav Nachman enacted his ruling in the house of the *Reish Galuta*, constructing a *tzurat hapetach* without the posts making contact with the beam above. Upon learning of this, Rav Sheshet instructed his attendant, Rav Gadda, to go and remove the *eruv* — a remarkable act of contravening a colleague's ruling in the house of the *Reish Galuta*. The household caught Rav Gadda in the act and had him imprisoned. Rav Sheshet then went to the door and called out to him by name, and Rav Gadda emerged — an episode recounted with an unmistakable air of the extraordinary.
