This Talmudic incident stands, incidentally, as a striking precedent for the dismantling of an *eruv* one regards as halachically invalid.

### Kippa Baraita

Rav Sheshet later asks Rabbah bar Shmuel whether he knows any relevant *baraitot* bearing on the *tzurat hapetach* discussion. He is told: *tanina kippah* — we have taught the case of an arch. The *baraita* specifies that the minimum dimensions for a valid doorframe — whether for the purpose of *mezuzah* or *tzurat hapetach* — are ten *tefachim* in height and four *tefachim* in width. This is why the posts erected for a *tzurat hapetach* must reach a minimum height of ten *tefachim*; below this they do not constitute a doorway.

### Meir vs Chachamim

The debate centers on a structure that begins as the correct four *tefachim* wide for the first three *tefachim* of height, but then curves inward in an arch, so that by the time it reaches ten *tefachim* in height it is no longer four *tefachim* wide. Rabbi Meir holds the structure valid; the Sages hold it invalid.

Abaye clarifies the parameters of the dispute. All agree that if the arch begins to curve before the structure reaches three *tefachim* off the ground, there is nothing of value — you do not even have the beginnings of a doorframe. All agree likewise that if the total height does not reach ten *tefachim*, the structure is invalid regardless of what happens below. The debate is restricted to the case where the first three *tefachim* are straight and four *tefachim* wide, and the full height reaches ten *tefachim*, but at the ten-*tefach* point the width has narrowed due to the arch.

### Conceptual Framework

The key question is whether one can invoke the principle of *chokekim le-hashlim* — conceptually "carving out" the material to complete a valid form. Rabbi Meir holds that one can: *Rabbi Meir savar chokekim le-hashlim*. Since the arch contains enough material that, in theory, one could carve it into a straight-sided rectangle meeting all the required dimensions, and since the base already has the correct proportions, the structure is treated as if it had already been so completed. The beginning of the correct form exists; the potential for the full form is present; and that potential is sufficient to confer the status of a valid doorway. Rabbi Meir's reasoning parallels the principle *kol ha-omed lizrok k'zaruk dami* — the potential state is treated as realized. The Sages (*Rabbanan savar ein chokekim le-hashlim*) do not accept this: if the actual dimensions at the critical point are insufficient, no conceptual carving saves it.

### Disconnected Posts

This debate has direct bearing on the question of whether the side posts of a *tzurat hapetach* must physically touch the upper beam. According to Rabbi Meir, even where the posts do not technically connect to the top of the structure — since the archway in his scenario is valid despite the actual walls not forming a flush rectangle — the doorframe can still be recognized as valid by virtue of its form and potential. The arch, in which the straight lower section does not physically reach the curved upper section in the rectangular sense, is analogous to a *tzurat hapetach* in which the posts do not literally touch the beam above. Rabbi Meir's ruling thus lends support to Rav Nachman's position that physical contact between posts and beam is not required.

This is precisely what Rabbah bar Shmuel pointed out to Rav Sheshet — and Rav Sheshet, recognizing that this *baraita* constituted evidence against his own ruling, instructed that the *matnita de-kippah* not be disclosed to the household of the *Reish Galuta*, lest it further undermine his position in an already fraught situation.

The conclusion that emerges from practice: the side posts need not physically touch the upper beam. What is required is that the posts be positioned directly beneath the beam — not off to the side — and that the overall structure possess the shape and sufficient stability of a doorframe.

---

## Lechi & Kora

### Shammai vs Hillel

The *Gemara* moves to a new *mishna* addressing the question of *hechsher mavoi* — what is required to render a *mavoi* valid for carrying. Beit Shammai says: *lechi ve-korah* — both a side post and a horizontal beam. Beit Hillel says: *o lechi o korah* — either one suffices. Rabbi Eliezer says two *lechayayim* are required, one on each side. A certain student adds in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, before Rabbi Akiva, that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree at all for a *mavoi* narrower than four *amot* — for such a *mavoi*, either a *lechi* or a *korah* suffices according to all. Their dispute was only for widths between four and ten *amot*. Rabbi Akiva demurs, maintaining that the dispute applied even when the width was less than four *amot*.

### Closed-End Mavoi

One might object that this *mishna* cannot apply to a *mavoi* open at both ends (*mavoi mefulash*), since such a *mavoi* would require at minimum a *tzurat hapetach* at one end — and therefore a *lechi* or *korah* alone would be insufficient regardless of the opinion. Rav Yehuda resolves this directly: the *mishna* is addressing specifically *hechsher mavoi satum* — the case of a closed-end *mavoi*, one that is enclosed on three sides and open at only one end. For such a *mavoi*, the question is what is required at the single open end. That is where the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel applies.

### Wall vs Heker

The *Gemara* then probes the conceptual stakes of the Shammai-Hillel dispute. If Beit Shammai requires both a *lechi* and a *korah*, this would appear to indicate that together they constitute a fourth wall — *arba mechitzot de-oraisa*, that biblically four walls are required. The *Gemara* pushes back: not necessarily. Biblically, perhaps three walls suffice to constitute a *reshut ha-yachid* such that throwing an object from a *reshut ha-rabim* into it violates the prohibition. What Beit Shammai's requirement of both a *lechi* and a *korah* accomplishes is the rabbinical requirement for carrying (*le-taltel*) — and they require this combination because together they define the fourth side as a genuine *mechitza*. Conversely, if Beit Hillel requires only one or the other, this suggests that a single element does not constitute a wall but rather a *heker* — a symbolic marker. Even so, the *Gemara* notes, this need not imply that biblically one needs only three walls; one could push further and say biblically even two walls could define a *reshut ha-yachid*, with the rabbinic requirement for carrying being three.

What matters conceptually is the following: the *Gemara* understands the Beit Shammai-Beit Hillel dispute as precisely the debate that was raised earlier in the *masechet* — does a *lechi* or *korah* function *mishum mechitza*, as a wall, or *mishum heker*, as a mere visual marker? The *Gemara*'s analysis here suggests that requiring both (*lechi ve-korah* together) is consistent with the *mechitza* reading, while requiring only one or the other is consistent with the *heker* reading. Crucially, however, the *Gemara* emphasizes that this conceptual distinction does not settle the question of biblical *reshut* status: the biblical threshold for *reshut ha-yachid* may be lower than what either position demands rabbinically for carrying, and the Shammai-Hillel dispute pertains to the rabbinic level of permission, not to the biblical definition of domain.

---

---

# Eiruvin 12

## Tzurat HaPetach Debate

### Tzurat HaPetach Proof

Before turning to today's primary material, a correction to yesterday's presentation is in order. In discussing whether the side-posts of a *tzurat hapetach* must physically reach the crossbeam, the *Gemara* had adduced a proof from the case of an arch. The proof offered yesterday was attributed to Rebbi Meir's distinctive principle of *gud asik* — imagining the curved portion carved straight — which is in fact a weak basis for a general rule, since that reasoning may be unique to his position. The stronger and more accurate proof is that the *Gemara* establishes that *everyone* agrees: if an arch rises to a height of ten *tefachim* and spans four *amot* in width, the fact that it curves above the posts is legally irrelevant. The top of the arch counts, because the actual physical top of the structure is what matters, even if the upright posts terminate lower down. This is the genuine principle, and its significance extends well beyond the technical dispute about arches: it is one of the foundations permitting the construction of contemporary *eruvin* using a *tzurat hapetach*, which is valid even when most of the fourth side is open and even when the opening exceeds ten *amot* in width — the ruling we follow, in contradistinction to the position of the Rambam.

### Beit Shammai vs Hillel

With that correction in place, the *Gemara* now resumes the discussion of the *Mishnah*'s debate regarding what is required to render a *mavoi* — a dead-end alleyway — permissible for carrying on *Shabbat*. Beit Shammai holds that one requires both a *lechi* (a side-post) and a *kora* (a crossbeam). Beit Hillel holds that either a *lechi* or a *kora* alone suffices. The *Gemara* had been probing whether this dispute reflects a disagreement about function: does the requirement serve as an actual *mechitza* (wall), or merely as a *heker* (a recognizable marker that reminds one of the boundary)?

### Wall vs Heker Theme

These two questions — function and biblical status — constitute the two central themes that will recur throughout this *daf*. The first question is whether the *lechi* or *kora* functions as a genuine wall or merely as a symbolic marker. The second question concerns the relationship between biblical and rabbinic law: does a standard three-walled dead-end *mavoi* already constitute a biblical *reshut hayachid*, with the *lechi* or *kora* required only rabbinically to permit carrying? The straightforward reading is indeed that three walls suffice biblically, and that whatever is required for the fourth side is a rabbinic overlay enabling use of the space. These questions will be examined in depth as the *Gemara* works through multiple opinions.

---

## Rebbi Eliezer Position

### Two Lechayim Question

The *Gemara* now picks up from three lines before the end of 11b. Rebbi Eliezer is quoted: *Rebbi Eliezer omer lechayayim* — Rebbi Eliezer says one requires two *lechayim*. This is a position distinct from all others discussed thus far: not Beit Shammai's requirement of both a *lechi* and a *kora*, and not Beit Hillel's requirement of either one. Rebbi Eliezer says two *lechayim*.

The *Gemara* immediately asks: when Rebbi Eliezer says two *lechayim*, does he mean two *lechayim* together with a *kora* — which would effectively constitute a *tzurat hapetach* and would clearly suggest that he is trying to approximate a genuine wall — or does he mean a novel position of two *lechayim* without any *kora* at all?

### Braita of Uvlin

To resolve this question, the *Gemara* cites a *braita* relating a story about Rebbi Eliezer himself. He once visited Rebbi Yosi ben Perida, his student, in a place called Uvlin. He found his student residing in a *mavoi* that had only one *lechi*, contrary to Rebbi Eliezer's own ruling that two are required. Rebbi Eliezer told him: *beni*, my son, add another *lechi* to make it permissible. The student pushed back: *vechi lesotmo ani tzarich* — do I need to seal it off entirely? Is requiring two *lechayim* not tantamount to demanding that I wall off the entire opening? Rebbi Eliezer replied: *s'tom uvcha* — yes, seal it off; that is what is required.

Now the *braita* continues, and at its end Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is quoted: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not debate the case of a *mavoi* that is less than four *amot* wide — there, everyone agrees no requirement at all applies. Their debate was limited to widths between four and ten *amot*, where Beit Shammai requires a *lechi* and a *kora* together, and Beit Hillel requires either a *lechi* or a *kora*. This position differs from the *Mishnah*, which states that for a *mavoi* less than four *amot*, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that either a *lechi* or a *kora* suffices — not that nothing is needed at all.

### Lechayim Reconciliation

The *Gemara* returns to the question of Rebbi Eliezer. *Tani me'hat* — the *braita* does teach in any case that his student said *vechi lesotmo ani tzarich*, "must I seal it off entirely?" The *Gemara* reasons: if Rebbi Eliezer required two *lechayim* and a *kora*, that would make sense of the student's complaint — because two *lechayim* with a crossbeam spanning between them is a *tzurat hapetach*, and the student would understandably feel that is like constructing a complete wall. But if all Rebbi Eliezer required was two *lechayim* without any *kora*, why would that be called "sealing it off"? It is not such a dramatic requirement.

The *Gemara* answers: *hachi ka'amar* — the student's complaint should be read as: "must I seal it off with *lechayim*?" That is, the student considered the requirement of two *lechayim* an excessive demand, even without a *kora*, and his complaint was rhetorical rather than technical. The upshot is that this exchange does not definitively prove whether Rebbi Eliezer requires two *lechayim* with or without a *kora*. The simpler reading, given that no *kora* is explicitly mentioned in his ruling, is that Rebbi Eliezer means precisely two *lechayim* alone.

---

## Shimon ben Gamliel

### Less Than Four Amot

The *Gemara* now turns to the statement of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel at the close of the *braita* just cited. As noted above, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree regarding a *mavoi* narrower than four *amot* — there, he says, nothing at all is required. This stands in tension with the formulation in the *Mishnah*, where a student quotes Rebbi Yishmael's position that for a *mavoi* under four *amot*, both schools agree that either a *lechi* or a *kora* suffices.

### Rav Ashi Resolution

Rav Ashi resolves this apparent conflict. When Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that less than four *amot* requires *kelum* — nothing — he does not mean literally nothing. He means *eino tzarich lechi vekora keBeit Shammai velo lechayim keRebbi Eliezer* — one does not need the more demanding requirements: not both a *lechi* and a *kora* as Beit Shammai rules, and not two *lechayim* as Rebbi Eliezer rules. All opinions agree that for a *mavoi* under four *amot*, one does not need anything excessive. What *is* needed — *ela o lechi o kora keBeit Hillel* — is still either a *lechi* or a *kora*, in accordance with Beit Hillel. This resolution is admittedly strained, since Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel plainly seems to introduce a third position. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* endeavors to harmonize the sources and treats "nothing" as meaning "nothing beyond what Beit Hillel requires."

### Narrow Mavoi Threshold

Having established the rule for a *mavoi* under four *amot*, the *Gemara* now asks: how narrow can the *mavoi* become before no requirement whatsoever applies — before even a *lechi* or *kora* is unnecessary? Rav Achli, and some say Rav Yechiel, rules: *ad arba'ah tefachim* — until four *tefachim*. Once the opening of the *mavoi* is four *tefachim* or less, everyone agrees that nothing is required at all.

This is not a principle of *lavud* — the rule that a gap of less than three *tefachim* is legally treated as closed. Rather, the reasoning is that an opening of four *tefachim* or less is so narrow that it practically defines itself as a small doorway, and the *mavoi* is considered effectively closed even without any added structure. It is a striking ruling: even though this end of the alleyway is entirely open in a physical sense, if it is narrow enough everyone would agree that no fourth-wall requirement applies whatsoever. One might suggest that since the underlying purpose of the *lechi* or *kora* is to function as a *heker* — a reminder — when the opening is sufficiently narrow, that function is naturally fulfilled by the narrowness itself, and therefore no added marker is needed.

### Psei Chatzer Agreement

Rav Sheshet, quoting Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba quoting Rav, now notes that the Sages agree with Rebbi Eliezer's more demanding position in one specific context: *bepsei chatzer* — by the planks used to enclose a *chatzer* (courtyard), rather than a *mavoi*. The role of the *psei chatzer* has already been introduced: unlike a *mavoi*, a *chatzer* requires something more substantial than a simple *lechi*, and this more demanding requirement is called a *pas* (plank). On this point, Rav Nachman adds: *halacha keRebbi Eliezer bepasei chatzer* — the practical ruling follows Rebbi Eliezer with respect to the *psei chatzer*, meaning two planks are required. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then probes who exactly "agrees" to Rebbi Eliezer here: since the *Gemara* previously recorded the debate between Rebbi and the Sages over whether a *chatzer* requires a plank on both sides or only one, when we say that "everyone agrees" to Rebbi Eliezer's two-plank requirement by a *chatzer*, it is specifically Rebbi's position that aligns with Rebbi Eliezer. The alternative formulation — that we "rule like Rebbi Eliezer" by a *chatzer* — implies that even here there is a debate, just that the *halacha* follows the more demanding position.

---

## Mavoi vs Chatzer

### Different Requirements

The *Gemara* now transitions to a fuller discussion of why a *chatzer* requires more than a *mavoi*. A *braita* establishes that a *chatzer* permits carrying with a *pas* (plank), while Rebbi maintains two *psim* are necessary. This invites a deeper examination of the structural distinction between the two domains.

Why should a *chatzer* demand more? Several possibilities suggest themselves. One is that a *chatzer* is used by all the residents of the houses that open into it, and therefore carries a much higher volume of foot traffic, requiring a more prominent delineation. Another, cited by *Tosafot*, is something of a counterintuitive logic: a *mavoi* opens directly onto a *reshut harabim*, which might seem to call for a stricter requirement for the *mavoi*. But in fact the stark contrast between the *mavoi* and the *reshut harabim* may actually reduce the need for a formal marker there, since the transition is already obvious.

What becomes clear — and this will be reinforced toward the end of the *daf* — is that the distinction between *chatzer* and *mavoi* is not primarily functional but structural. The *halacha* defines these domains not by how they are used or who owns them, but by their physical configuration: a space that is longer than it is wide is treated as a *mavoi* (an alleyway), while a space that is square or wider than it is long is treated as a *chatzer* (a courtyard). The more demanding requirement of the *chatzer* follows directly from this structural characterization.

It is also worth noting at this point the terminological distinction: what is called a *lechi* in the context of a *mavoi* is called a *pas* in the context of a *chatzer*. The difference in name may reflect a difference in required dimensions. As will emerge, a *lechi* may be a mere *mashehu* — any width at all — whereas a *pas* must meet a minimum width threshold. Some positions require the *pas* to be at least three *tefachim* wide; others require at least four.

### Chatzer Pas Dispute

A *braita* spells out the dispute explicitly: *chatzer niteret bepas echad* — a *chatzer* is rendered permissible with one *pas*, while Rebbi says it requires two *psim*. This corresponds to the disagreement we have seen between Rebbi and the Sages about whether the *chatzer* must be enclosed on both sides or only one. The *Gemara* frames this debate in the context of the ruling recorded yesterday — that two *psim* flanking a smaller *chatzer* opening into a larger one explains why the larger one must be an *amah* wider (i.e., three *tefachim* on each side). This makes it clear that certain authorities require both a minimum width for each *pas* and coverage on both sides.

### Pas Dimensions Debate

Rav Asi quotes Rav Yochanan as ruling that a *chatzer* requires two *psim*. Rav Zeira challenges him: did Rav Yochanan not himself teach that the *psim* must each be four *tefachim* wide? If so, how can he require two of them — that would be a very substantial total enclosure, and certainly difficult to reconcile with the *braita* about a *chatzer* of ten and eleven *amot*. Moreover, one cannot say both — four *tefachim* each and two of them — since the arithmetic would not work with the case of a ten- and eleven-*amah* *chatzer*, where each *pas* is only three *tefachim*.

When Rav Zeira later resolved the matter, he explained: *meruach achat bearba'ah, mishtei ruchot mashehu mikan umashehu mikan* — if there is a *pas* on only one side, it must be four *tefachim* wide; if there are *psim* on both sides, even a *mashehu* — a minimal amount — on each side is sufficient. This elegantly reconciles Rav Yochanan's two statements. However, it does not explain the case of the ten- and eleven-*amah chatzerot*, where the *pas* is three *tefachim* on each side. The *Gemara* resolves that as well: that *braita* reflects the opinion of Rebbi, who requires two *psim*, and furthermore holds like Rebbi Yosi, who requires three *tefachim* on each side.

### Ten Eleven Amot

The *braita* taught by Rebbi Ada bar Avimi, before Rebbi Chanina — or some say before Rebbi Chanina bar Pappa — states: the smaller of two connected *chatzerot* is ten *amot* wide, the larger eleven *amot* wide. The reason for this one-*amah* differential is precisely the *psim* on each side: if the larger *chatzer* is one *amah* wider than the smaller, and that *amah* is divided as three *tefachim* on each side, then the opening between them is contained by a *pas* of three *tefachim* on each side. This is consistent with requiring both two *psim* and a minimum width of three *tefachim* each — the position of Rebbi following Rebbi Yosi. It is incompatible with simultaneously requiring four *tefachim* per *pas* and two *psim*, since three *tefachim* twice does not equal four *tefachim*.

### Two Yochanan Statements

To summarize the synthesis: Rav Yochanan's two statements are not contradictory. His ruling that four *tefachim* are required refers to the case of a single *pas* on one side only. His rulings that are compatible with *mashehu* on each side refer to the case where two *psim* are present. The *braita* of Rebbi Ada bar Avimi with its three-*tefach* *psim* reflects a third view: the combined opinion of Rebbi (who requires two *psim*) and Rebbi Yosi (who specifies three *tefachim* as the requisite width).

What emerges clearly from all of this is that by a *chatzer*, the requirement is substantially more demanding than by a *mavoi*. A *mavoi* requires only a *lechi* of any minimal width — a *mashehu*. A *chatzer* requires either one *pas* of four *tefachim*, or two *psim* of any minimal width, or according to Rebbi and Rebbi Yosi, two *psim* of three *tefachim* each.

---

## Shmuel Chatzer Ruling

### One Pas Suffices

Rav Yosef cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: *chatzer niteret bepas echad* — a *chatzer* is rendered permissible with one *pas*. No specification of four *tefachim* or two *psim* is given; the statement is presented simply.

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye immediately challenges Rav Yosef: did Shmuel really say one *pas* suffices? Elsewhere, Shmuel told Rav Chananya bar Shila: *lo ta'avid uvda ella o berov dofen o bishnei pasin* — do not issue a practical ruling unless the *chatzer* has either a majority of its fourth wall closed, or two *psim*. This is a considerably stricter requirement. How can Shmuel simultaneously say one *pas* is enough?

Rav Yosef responds: do I not know about the case in Dura de-Ra'usa, the village of the shepherds? There, a *leshon yam* — a tongue of water from a lake — entered a *chatzer*, and the case came before Rav Yehuda (Shmuel's student), and he ruled one *pas* sufficient. So Shmuel's position of one *pas* is well attested.

### Water Leniency

Abaye, however, is unimpressed by this response: *leshon yam ka'amart*? You are proving from a case involving water? *Kalu she-heikilu chachamim bemayim* — the Sages applied special leniencies in cases involving water. One may not draw general *halachic* conclusions from rulings that pertain to the permission to draw water, since the rabbis deliberately loosened their standards in those cases to enable people to draw water on *Shabbat* — a critical practical need when there was no other water supply.

The principle is illustrated by the case of a *mechitza teluyah* — a suspended partition. Rav Tavla asked Rav: does a suspended partition (one that hangs above the ground without reaching it) permit carrying in a dry, ruined space below? Rav replied: *ein mechitzah teluyah materet ella bemayim* — a suspended partition is only effective for water. The partition is imagined as extending downward into the water, creating a *reshut hayachid* within the water below, enabling one to draw water from that space. This would not work to define a dry space. And the reason is: *kalu she-heikilu chachamim bemayim* — it is a special leniency for water. Therefore, one cannot derive general rules about *chatzer* enclosures from cases involving *leshon yam*.

So the contradiction stands: Shmuel says one *pas* in one place, and two *psim* or the majority of the wall in another. The *Gemara* acknowledges: *mikal makom kashya* — in any case the difficulty remains.

### Pappa Huna Solution

When Rav Pappa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua came from the study hall, they explained: *meruach achat bearba'ah, mishtei ruchot mashehu lekan umashehu lekan* — when Shmuel says one *pas*, he means a *pas* of four *tefachim* on one side; when he says two *psim*, he means a *mashehu* on each side. The two statements refer to two different configurations, both of which Shmuel accepts as valid. This is the same resolution Rav Zeira had offered for Rav Yochanan's statements, and it now applies equally to Shmuel's.

The *Gemara* then turns to Shmuel's third formulation — *rov dofen*, the majority of the wall. Why would Shmuel mention the majority of the wall as a distinct category? Rav Pappa probes: if a *chatzer* has a wall of seven *tefachim*, and one closes off four *tefachim* of it, that four-*tefach* *pas* would constitute the majority of the wall. But then why speak in terms of *rov dofen* at all — why not simply say four *tefachim*? And why should four *tefachim* be the threshold — once you close off more than half of a seven-*tefach* wall, the remaining gap is less than four *tefachim*, and we have established that an opening less than four *tefachim* requires nothing at all. So the entire *rov dofen* language could be shorthand for "enough to reduce the gap to under four *tefachim*."

Two resolutions are offered. First: *kan bachatzer kan bamavoi* — the rule that an opening under four *tefachim* requires nothing may apply to a *mavoi* but not to a *chatzer*, where the higher standards mean that reducing the gap to under four *tefachim* is not on its own sufficient. Second: the rule itself that under four *tefachim* suffices may be disputed — *deRav Achlei gufa tannai hi* — and not universally accepted. Either way, the *Gemara* has shown that by a *chatzer*, the requirements are more stringent than by a *mavoi* at every level.

---

## Leshon Yam Scenario

### Water Into Chatzer

The *Gemara* now presents a *braita* treating a *leshon yam* — a tongue of water from a lake or sea — that enters a *chatzer*. The *braita* rules: *ein memalin heimena beShabbat* — one may not draw water from it on *Shabbat* — *ela im kein yesh lo mechitzah gevohah asarah tefachim* — unless there is a partition of ten *tefachim* height on each side, which would presumably mean the required structure on both sides of the water's entry point, based on the rules we have discussed.

When does this requirement apply? When the opening through which the water enters is more than ten *amot* wide. If the water's opening is less than ten *amot*, no such additional partition is needed to permit drawing water.

The *braita* also appears to assume, incidentally, that carrying within the *chatzer* is never the issue — even when the opening is larger than ten *amot*, one may carry within the *chatzer* without constructing the additional partition. The requirement of the additional wall is tied only to the act of drawing water.

### Carrying vs Water

This asymmetry prompts the *Gemara*'s question: if the *chatzer* has an opening into the lake or sea of more than ten *amot*, the *chatzer* has effectively been breached on one entire side into a space where carrying is forbidden. The rule is that a *chatzer* that is breached along its full width into a forbidden domain is itself forbidden for carrying. So why does the *braita* treat carrying in the *chatzer* as unproblematic and only restrict the drawing of water?

### Giduda Explanation

The *Gemara* answers, near the top of 12b: *hacha bemai askinan de'it leih giduda* — the case here is one where there is a *giduda*, a remnant of a wall. According to Rashi, the scenario is that the *chatzer* had a wall along that side, and the wall partially collapsed or was submerged. The water has now entered the *chatzer* through the breach, but the remnant of the original wall still exists beneath the water's surface — it is simply invisible. Because the wall remains physically present, even if underwater, the *chatzer* retains its enclosed status and carrying within it is permitted.

The permission to carry thus rests on the existence of this submerged wall. However, to draw water from the water itself, the existing structure is not sufficient if the opening exceeds ten *amot*, and an additional visible partition must be constructed.

*Tosafot* offers several explanations for this distinction. One suggestion is that when drawing water one carries it back through the yard toward the house, and at that point, standing near the house, the submerged wall on the far side is not visible, undermining its function as a *heker*. A second and perhaps simpler explanation is that when drawing water — lowering a bucket into the water — there is a realistic concern that the bucket will pass over the submerged wall into the prohibited space beyond; therefore a visible additional partition is required to prevent this. Both explanations preserve the principle that the submerged *giduda* suffices to permit general carrying in the *chatzer* but does not adequately safeguard against the specific risks associated with drawing water when the opening is large.

---

## Lechi Kora Functions

### Lechi Wall Kora Heker

The *Gemara* now directly engages the fundamental question that has been hovering over the entire discussion. Rav Yehuda states: *mavoi shelo nishtatfu bo* — if the residents of a *mavoi* did not join together in the bread (*shituf*), and one erected a *lechi* — *hezorker letocho chayav* — then one who throws an object into it from a *reshut harabim* is liable. This means the *lechi* has created a biblical *reshut hayachid*. But if instead of a *lechi* one erected a *kora* — *hazorek letocho patur* — one is exempt, because the *kora* does not create a biblical *reshut hayachid*.

The implication is: a *lechi* functions as a genuine wall, sufficient to complete a biblical *reshut hayachid*; a *kora* functions only as a *heker* and does not constitute a wall at all.

There is something arresting about this formulation. It implies that the rabbis permit carrying in a *mavoi* that is not a biblical *reshut hayachid* — a *mavoi* with three walls and a *kora* is not a *reshut hayachid* according to this position, yet carrying there is rabbinically permitted. This is a significant departure from the usual assumption that rabbinic permission to carry requires at minimum a space that has already qualified as a *reshut hayachid* on a biblical level.

### Shituf Impact Question

Rav Sheshet challenges this formulation directly: you qualified the ruling with *shelo nishtatfu bo* — that they did not perform a *shituf*. Does that mean that if they *did* perform a *shituf*, then even a *mavoi* with only a *kora* would become a biblical *reshut hayachid*? In other words, does the joint ownership created by the *shituf* — the communal participation in a shared loaf — transform the domain's biblical status? *Vechi kikar zu aseto reshut hayachid vereshut harabim* — does this loaf of bread determine whether a space is a *reshut hayachid* or a *reshut harabim*?

### Shituf Not Defining

Intuitively, there is a kernel of logic to this idea. After all, many people assume that *reshut hayachid* and *reshut harabim* are at least partly defined by private versus public ownership. If so, one might think that the *shituf* — which creates a form of collective private ownership — could contribute to creating a *reshut hayachid*. But the *Gemara* emphatically rejects this. A *braita* is cited: *chatzerot shel rabbim umevoot she-einam mefulashim, bein eirvu uvein lo eirvu, hazorek letocho chayav* — public courtyards and dead-end alleyways, whether an *eruv* was made or not, constitute a *reshut hayachid* and one who throws into them is liable. Biblical domain status is determined entirely by walls, not by ownership or communal arrangements. The *shituf* or *eruv* has no bearing whatsoever on whether a space qualifies as a *reshut hayachid*.

### Mefulash Mavoi Lechi

Since the *shituf* cannot affect biblical status, Rav Yehuda's original formulation must be reread. *Amar Rav Yehuda* — rather than conditioning the ruling on whether a *shituf* was or was not performed, what he actually means is this: *mavoi she-eino raui leshituf* — a *mavoi* for which *shituf* is not even possible. What *mavoi* is impossible to make a *shituf* for? A *mefulash* — one that is open at both ends, passing through from one *reshut harabim* to another. Such a *mavoi* has only two walls (the long sides), not three. Now the ruling makes sense. If one erects a *lechi* — creating a third wall — *hazorek letocho chayav*: biblically, it now has three walls and qualifies as a *reshut hayachid*. If one erects only a *kora*, the third side has no genuine wall; a *kora* is a *heker* only, not a wall. *Hazorek letocho patur* — it remains without three walls and is not a *reshut hayachid*.

*Alma kasavar lechi mishum mechitza, vekora mishum heker* — this establishes clearly that a *lechi* functions as a wall and a *kora* as a *heker*. And this position is shared by Rabbah as well: both agree that *lechi mishum mechitza, kora mishum heker*.

The implications are significant. For a standard *mavoi* with three existing walls, the *lechi* or *kora* for the fourth side is a rabbinic requirement only — the space is already a biblical *reshut hayachid* on the basis of its three walls. But for a *mefulash* *mavoi* that is open at both ends and has only two walls, the *lechi* elevates it to a biblical *reshut hayachid*, while a *kora* does not. The analogy to the laws of *sukkah* is instructive: *shtayim kehilchasam veshlishit afilu tefach* — two complete walls and a third wall of even minimal width constitutes a valid *sukkah*. Analogously, the *lechi* in this context functions as that minimal third wall.

### Rava Position

Rava disagrees. He holds: *echad zeh ve'echad zeh mishum heker* — both the *lechi* and the *kora* function only as a *heker*, as a recognizable marker. On this view, neither structure creates a wall in any meaningful biblical sense. Even a *lechi* does not transform a two-walled *mefulash mavoi* into a biblical *reshut hayachid*.

### Required Walls Type

Rav Yaakov bar Abba challenges Rava from a *braita*: *hazorek lemavoi* — one who throws into a *mavoi*... (and the ruling there implies that the *lechi* makes a decisive difference in terms of biblical liability). This seems to prove that a *lechi* functions as a wall, contradicting Rava's position. Rava responds: *hachi ka'amar* — this is how the *braita* must be read. If the *mavoi* is of the type that requires only a *lechi* — meaning it already has three walls and only needs the *lechi* as a rabbinic fourth-side requirement — then one who throws into it is *chayav*, because it already had three walls and was a *reshut hayachid* before the *lechi* was added. If the *mavoi* requires more than a *lechi* — meaning it has only two walls and needs both a *lechi* and a *tzurat hapetach* to permit carrying — then one who throws into it is *patur*, because without three real walls it is not a *reshut hayachid*. The *lechi* in that scenario does not create a wall; it is only a *heker*. Thus the *braita* does not prove that a *lechi* functions as a wall; it simply reflects the difference in the pre-existing wall count of the *mavoi* being discussed.

---

## Rebbi Yehuda Two Houses

### Two Houses Lechi Kora

The *Gemara* now revisits the famous ruling of Rebbi Yehuda discussed previously. Rebbi Yehuda says: if there are two houses facing each other on two sides of a *reshut harabim*, one may place a *lechi* on each side, or a *kora* on each side, and carry in the street between them. The *reshut harabim* between the two houses is rendered permissible by these minimal structures on each end.

### Rabbis Rejection

The Sages reject this: *ein me'arvin reshut harabim bekach* — one cannot make an *eruv* for a *reshut harabim* with such minimal structures. Clearly the Sages hold that a *lechi* and a *kora* are insufficient to transform a *reshut harabim* into a space where carrying is permitted.

What is the basis of Rebbi Yehuda's position? The *Gemara* explains: *hatam kasavar Rabbi Yehuda shtei mechitzot d'Oraita* — Rebbi Yehuda holds that biblically, only two walls are required to constitute a *reshut hayachid*. If two walls already create a biblical *reshut hayachid*, then the *lechi* or *kora* on each end serves as a rabbinic *heker* sufficient to permit carrying. But his position tells us nothing about whether a *lechi* or *kora* constitutes a wall for purposes of the third wall, since he does not require three walls to begin with.

This is a striking *Gemara*. Rebbi Yehuda's extraordinary leniency — permitting one to carry in an open street between two buildings merely by placing a post or a beam on each end — is not based on any theory that the *lechi* or *kora* builds a third or fourth wall. It is based entirely on his view that two walls alone already create a *reshut hayachid* on a biblical level. The rabbis who reject his position presumably require three walls for a biblical *reshut hayachid* and do not accept that two buildings facing each other provide even two adequate walls for a *reshut harabim*.

---

## Mavoi Chatzer Structure

### Square Becomes Chatzer

Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav: *mavoi she'archo kerachbo* — a *mavoi* whose length equals its width — *eino niter belechi mashehu* — cannot be rendered permissible with a mere *lechi* of minimal width. Once the *mavoi* is as wide as it is long — in other words, square — it takes on the legal status of a *chatzer* and must be treated accordingly, requiring a *pas* of four *tefachim* or two *psim* rather than a simple *lechi*.

### Chiya Confirmation

Rav Chiya bar Ashi, also in the name of Rav, makes the same point from the opposite direction: *mavoi she'archo kerachbo eino niter bekora tefach* — once the length equals the width, even a *kora* of one *tefach* — the standard requirement for a *kora* in a *mavoi* — is no longer sufficient. This confirms from another angle that the transformation from *mavoi* to *chatzer* is triggered by the shape itself, regardless of function.

### Zeira Appreciation

Rav Zeira expresses appreciation for this teaching: *kama nechuvanin shmaita desavi* — how precisely on target is this ruling of the elders. Once the length equals the width — *hava lei chatzer*, it is now a *chatzer* — and *chatzer eina niteret belechi vekora* — a *chatzer* cannot be rendered permissible with a *lechi* or a *kora*. Instead, *ella bepas arba* — one needs a *pas* of at least four *tefachim* (or two *psim* of minimal width).

This reflects an important conceptual theme: domain status is determined by objective physical structure, not by use or ownership. One might have thought that the difference between a *mavoi* and a *chatzer* is how the space is actually used — a *mavoi* is used as an alleyway, a *chatzer* as a courtyard. But the *halacha* determines identity purely on geometric grounds: if a space is longer than it is wide, it is a *mavoi*; if it is not longer than it is wide, it is a *chatzer*. This parallels the earlier principle that *reshut hayachid* status is determined by walls alone, not by ownership or the performance of an *eruv*.

### Zeira Question

Rav Zeira, however, raises a difficulty. Given that a *lechi* does not suffice for a *chatzer* and one needs a *pas* of four *tefachim*, why can a *lechi* not simply count as a *pas mashehu* — a minimal-width *pas*? After all, both a *lechi* and a *pas* are vertical structures placed alongside the opening; why should the mere width of the structure determine whether it satisfies the *chatzer* requirement?

### Nachman Definition

The *Gemara* responds that Rav Zeira has momentarily forgotten the ruling cited earlier by Rav Ami in the name of Rav Yochanan: *pasei chatzer tzrichin she'yehe bin arba* — the *psim* of a *chatzer* must be at least four *tefachim* wide. This is the essential difference between a *lechi* and a *pas*: a *lechi* may be any width whatsoever, a *mashehu*; a *pas* for a *chatzer* must be at least four *tefachim* wide (if only one *pas* is used). A *lechi*, by definition, does not meet this threshold and therefore cannot function as a *pas* for a *chatzer*.

Rav Nachman then states a principle: *naktinan* — we take the following as established. *Eizu mavoi sheniter belechi vekora* — which *mavoi* is rendered permissible with a *lechi* or a *kora*, the less demanding requirement? *Kol she'archo yeter al rachbo* — any space whose length exceeds its width. *Uvatim vechatzerot petuchin letokho* — and furthermore, houses open into yards and yards open into it. So to fully qualify as a *mavoi* entitled to the lenient rules, two conditions must be met: it must be longer than it is wide, and it must have the functional structure of houses feeding into yards that feed into the alleyway.

*Ve'eizu hi chatzer she'eina niteret belechi vekora ela bepas arba* — and which *chatzer* requires the more demanding *pas* of four *tefachim* rather than a *lechi* or *kora*? *Kol she-meruba'at* — anything that is square.

### Shape Irrelevant

The *Gemara* immediately clarifies: does *meruba'at* mean specifically square, to the exclusion of circular or other shapes? *Meruba'at in, agulah lo*? No. *Hachi ka'amar* — this is what the rule means: *ee orchah yeter al rachbah* — if its length exceeds its width, it is a *mavoi* and a *lechi* or *kora* suffices; *ve'ee la, havlei chatzer* — if it is not, it is a *chatzer*. Shape is entirely irrelevant. The space could be circular, triangular, trapezoidal, or any other form. The only criterion is whether the dimension aligned with the flow of entry and exit — what we might call the "length" — exceeds the perpendicular dimension. If it does, it is a *mavoi*; if not, it is a *chatzer*.

### Length Requirement Views

Finally, the *Gemara* asks: how much longer does a space need to be than it is wide to qualify as a *mavoi*? *Vekamah* — how much? Shmuel initially held: *ad pi shenayim berachba* — it must be twice as long as it is wide. By this standard, a street that is ten *amot* wide would need to be at least twenty *amot* long to qualify as a *mavoi*. This is a demanding threshold. Rav, however, citing Rebbi Chiya, rules: *afilu mashehu* — even the smallest excess suffices. As long as the length exceeds the width by any amount at all, even a *mashehu*, the space is classified as a *mavoi* and may be rendered permissible with a *lechi* or a *kora*. The moment it is square or wider than it is long, it becomes a *chatzer* and the more demanding requirements apply.

---

---

# Eiruvin 13

## Rabbi Akiva & R. Ishmael

### R. Akiva's Insistence

We begin on 13a with a review of the preceding passage. A student had reported in the name of Rabbi Ishmael that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not debate the case of less than four *amot*, and Rabbi Akiva flatly insists that Rabbi Ishmael never said such a thing. Yet Rabbi Akiva then declares that we rule like that student's position. The Gemara is puzzled: how could he rule like a student whose claim he just rejected? The answer is that Rabbi Akiva was not issuing a genuine ruling; he was provoking his students in order to sharpen them and see how they would respond.

### Relevance to Chatzer

This raises an obvious question: what practical difference does it make whether Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel debated the case of less than four *amot* by a *mavoi*? After all, we rule like Beit Hillel in any case, who permits a *lechi* or *korah* — so whether Beit Shammai agreed below four *amot* seems entirely moot. The Gemara addresses this by pointing out that such a ruling could carry implications beyond the *mavoi*. If we were to establish that less than four *amot* makes a meaningful halachic difference, that principle might extend to a *chatzer* as well. As discussed previously, a *chatzer* requires a *pas* on either side or a *pas* of four *tefachim*; it is possible that for a *chatzer* of less than four *amot*, a lesser requirement would apply. So there could be genuine halachic ramifications. Nevertheless, the Gemara concludes that Rabbi Akiva insists Rabbi Ishmael never said any such thing, and that his declaration that we rule like the student was made only to challenge and sharpen the other students.

## R. Yehoshua b. Levi

### The Anonymous Student

The Gemara continues, approximately eight lines from the top of 13a, with the statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *kol makom she'ata motzei mishum Rabbi Yishmael amar talmid echad lifnei Rabbi Akiva* — any place you find the formulation that a certain student said in the name of Rabbi Ishmael in the presence of Rabbi Akiva, *eino ela Rabbi Meir* — that student can only be Rabbi Meir. How often this precise formulation appears in the Talmud is uncertain, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's principle is clear: the student who transmitted Rabbi Ishmael's teachings to Rabbi Akiva was necessarily Rabbi Meir.

### R. Meir's Studies

The reason is that Rabbi Meir *shimesh*, studied and attended, both Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva. He was apparently the singular prominent student who served as a crossover between the two great academies. The Gemara proceeds to a *braisa* that will tell us more about this remarkable biographical fact.

## R. Meir the Scribe

### Kankantom Additive

The *braisa* opens with Rabbi Meir's own testimony: *keshe-hayiti etzel Rabbi Yishmael* — when I was learning by Rabbi Ishmael, *hayiti matil kankantom letoch hadeyo* — I would add *kankantom* to my ink. According to Rashi, and as identified by the Steinsaltz commentary, *kankantom* is copper sulfate, and as we will see from the story, its effect is to make ink more permanent and far more resistant to scraping and erasure. Rabbi Meir was a *sofer* — a professional scribe — and he was adding this substance to his ink. Rabbi Ishmael saw him do so and said nothing. *Keshe-bati etzel Rabbi Akiva, asarah alai* — when he came to Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Akiva forbade it to him.

The immediate relevance for the Gemara is simply to confirm that Rabbi Meir studied under both Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva.

### R. Ishmael's Objection

A second version of the story, transmitted by Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Meir himself, presents the account differently. There, Rabbi Meir begins by studying under Rabbi Akiva, who sees him add *kankantom* to the ink and says nothing. When Rabbi Meir then comes to Rabbi Ishmael, Rabbi Ishmael asks: *beni ma melachtecha* — my son, what is your profession? Rabbi Meir answers: *lavlari ani* — I am a scribe. Rabbi Ishmael responds with gravity: *beni hevei zahir bimlachtecha* — my son, be exceedingly careful in your work, *she-melachtecha melachet shamayim hi* — for your work is heavenly work, writing *Sifrei Torah*. The stakes could not be higher: *shema ata mechasser ot achat o meyater ot achat nimtset machriv et kol ha'olam kulo* — if you should lack even one letter or add even one letter, you stand to destroy the entire world.

Both Rashi and Tosafot address which specific letter could be so catastrophic. Rashi suggests that in the verse *ve-Hashem Elokim emes*, if one omitted the *alef* from *emes*, the word would become *meis* — dead — which would be devastating. Or, if *vayidaber Hashem* were written as *vayidabru* with an added *vav*, the result would be deeply heretical. Tosafot raises the example of *Bereishis bara Elokim* becoming *Bereishis bera'u*, potentially implying that God was created. The Maharsha, citing the *Ramban*, adds the kabbalistic dimension: the letters of the Torah collectively form an elaborated divine name, and each letter carries metaphysical weight in the structure of Torah's mystical reality, so that altering even a single letter transforms that whole reality.

It is worth noting that in the era of the *Chazal*, there was greater variance in Torah script than we have today — not in major matters, but in smaller questions such as whether a word was written *malei* or *chaser*. It was the work of the *masores*, the scholars who counted and categorized every single letter, that produced the high degree of standardization we have in our *Sifrei Torah* today. This context only sharpens the force of Rabbi Ishmael's admonition: at a time of less standardization, the temptation toward carelessness was correspondingly greater, and the call for extreme precision all the more urgent.

The Maharitz Chayes, a nineteenth-century scholar, adds a further insight. We know that Rabbi Meir was not only a scribe but was famous for his *drashos* on *psukim* through creative engagement with the letters — the well-known example being his reading of *kasnos or* (garments of leather) with an *alef* as *kasnos or* (garments of light), cited by Rashi. The Maharitz Chayes suggests that Rabbi Meir may have had a practice of noting in the margin of his *Sefer Torah* some symbol or mark corresponding to one of his *drashos* on that *pasuk*. This would explain why Rabbi Ishmael was particularly anxious. Knowing Rabbi Meir's habit of playing creatively with letters, Rabbi Ishmael feared that in a moment of inspiration — say, the idea of writing *kasnos or* with an *alef* — he might inadvertently carry it over into the actual script itself. Hence the urgent warning: be very careful, for your brilliant textual creativity must never bleed into what you actually write in the *Sefer Torah*.

### R. Meir's Response

After Rabbi Ishmael's warning, Rabbi Meir responds: *davar echad yesh li ve-kankantom shemo* — I have this special additive called *kankantom* that I put into the ink. The Gemara then pauses to ask: *mai ka'amar lei u'mai ka'mehadar lei* — what was Rabbi Meir saying, and how was it responsive? Rabbi Ishmael had warned him not to add or drop letters, and Rabbi Meir answered by telling him about an ink additive. What is the connection?

The Gemara explains: *hachi ka'amar lei* — this is what Rabbi Meir was communicating. Not only, he was saying, do I not make mistakes of writing extra letters or fewer letters — *debaki ana*, I am a complete expert in the script and I do not err in that way. But I want you to know how scrupulous I truly am. I am not merely careful about deliberate errors; I am concerned even that *afilu michshla dezevuv nami delma ati veyasiv atage dedalet umachei lei umashvei lei reish* — a fly might land on the script while the ink is still drying, settle on the small protrusion of a *dalet* — the extension to the right of the bar beneath the letter — and obliterate it, transforming the *dalet* into a *reish*. To guard against even that kind of accidental erasure, I add this *kankantom* to my ink to make it impervious to such mishaps. So Rabbi Meir's response was entirely on point: his use of *kankantom* was a further expression of his extraordinary vigilance against any kind of letter alteration, deliberate or accidental.

### Contradictory Versions

This brings us to a genuine textual problem. In the first version, Rabbi Meir says he was by Rabbi Ishmael who said nothing, and then went to Rabbi Akiva who forbade it. In the second version, he was by Rabbi Akiva who said nothing, and then went to Rabbi Ishmael who objected. The Gemara states: *kashya shimush a-shimush, kashya asiya a-asiya* — there is a contradiction regarding the order of study, and there is a contradiction regarding who it was that issued the prohibition.

### Resolution

*Bishlama shimush a-shimush lo kashya* — the contradiction about the order of study is resolvable. The Gemara proposes: *me'ikara ata l'kamei d'Rabbi Akiva* — initially Rabbi Meir came to Rabbi Akiva. *U-mid'lo matzi l'meikav al libei* — but he was not yet able to fully grasp Rabbi Akiva's teaching. This does not mean Rabbi Meir lacked the intellect; rather, he had not yet absorbed sufficient material. *Azal l'kamei d'Rabbi Yishmael, ve-gmar gemara* — so he went to Rabbi Ishmael and there he received the *gemara*, the entire body of transmitted tradition. *Gemara* here means not analytical method but the downloading, as it were, of the entire oral corpus — all the material, everything that needed to be received. *Ve-hadar ata l'kamei d'Rabbi Akiva vesavar svara* — and then he returned to Rabbi Akiva equipped with all the material, and now he was able to learn the analytical acuity, the *svara*, that Rabbi Akiva's teaching demanded.

This reflects an important principle. The Gemara elsewhere famously debates whether it is more valuable to be *Sinai* — one who knows all the material, as if one received the Torah from Mount Sinai — or *oker harim* — one who can uproot mountains, who possesses incisive analytical power. The point here is that the two are not in competition but in sequence: what good is *oker harim* if you do not yet have all the material? How can you analyze and bring all the relevant traditions to bear on a question if you have not yet received them? Rabbi Meir needed to be fully *Sinai* before he could be the preeminent *oker harim* in Rabbi Akiva's academy. Once he had received the entire tradition from Rabbi Ishmael, he could return to Rabbi Akiva and realize his full intellectual potential. So the order of study is reconcilable: Rabbi Akiva first, then Rabbi Ishmael for the *gemara*, then back to Rabbi Akiva for the *svara*.

The contradiction about who issued the prohibition, however, is not resolvable. *Ella asiya a-asiya kashya* — this remains a genuine difficulty. We have two irreconcilable versions, and the Gemara simply acknowledges: *kashya* — it is a problem. With that, the Gemara notes in passing that the entire purpose of quoting this story was to demonstrate that the student who reported Rabbi Ishmael's teaching to Rabbi Akiva must have been Rabbi Meir, since he is the one known student who moved between both academies.

The Gemara then continues with a series of teachings about *kankantom* and the *parshat sotah* that flow from this discussion. A *braisa* is cited in which Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Meir: *lechol matilin kankantom letoch hadeyo chutz miparshes sotah* — for all purposes one may add *kankantom* to the ink, except for the writing of the *parshat sotah*. For the *sotah*, the Torah requires *ve-chasav u-macha* — the priest writes and then erases — and therefore the writing must be of the kind that *can* be erased. *Kankantom* would make erasure impossible, rendering the scroll invalid for the *sotah* ritual.

This raises the question of what Rabbi Ishmael's original objection was. Was he objecting only to using *kankantom* for *parshat sotah*, or was his objection broader, applying to the entire *Sefer Torah*? Tosafot raises this explicitly: *amar Rabbi Yishmael she-haya oser bechol ha-Torah kulah* — Rabbi Ishmael forbade it across the entire Torah. Perhaps, Tosafot suggests, Rabbi Ishmael derived this from the verse *ve-chasav u-macha* through a *gezeira shava* applied universally, reasoning that all halachically valid writing must be of the erasable type — or alternatively, perhaps the prohibition was rabbinic in scope, extending beyond *sotah* as a precautionary measure. Rabbi Meir, by contrast, limited the problem strictly to *parshat sotah*.

Rabbi Yaakov then transmits a further refinement in Rabbi Meir's name: the prohibition applies only to *parshat sotah she-ba-mikdash* — to the actual scroll written for the *sotah* ceremony in the Temple. But if the *parshat sotah* appears within a full *Sefer Torah*, one may use *kankantom* even there. The practical question between the two versions of Rabbi Meir's position is whether one may erase the *parshat sotah* from a *Sefer Torah* to perform the *sotah* ritual. If the *Sefer Torah* contains *kankantom* throughout, it cannot be erased from it, and so you lose the option of using it for *sotah*. Whether that is a concern depends on whether you may even use a *Sefer Torah* for a *sotah* in the first place.

Rabbi Yirmiyah identifies this as the crux of the matter, and the Gemara then examines a parallel *Tannaic* debate: the *tana kama* holds that a scroll written validly for one *sotah* cannot be reused for another woman, while Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya holds it can. The question is whether the same *lishmah* requirement that governs the first case governs the use of a *Sefer Torah*. Rav Papa argues that these are not necessarily parallel: the *tana kama* may restrict use for a different woman because once designated for Rachel, it can no longer be reassigned to Leah — but a *Sefer Torah* written generically, for no woman at all, might nonetheless be usable. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak argues the opposite: Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya's permissive position may apply where the scroll was at least written for *some* woman as a *sotah*, whereas a *Sefer Torah* written with no intent for the *sotah* ritual at all might be unusable for that purpose.

The Gemara further asks whether Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya's position is consistent with the *mishnah* concerning a *get* written for one woman that cannot be used for another (*shim'cha keshmi ve-shem ishtecha keshem ishti* — your name is like mine and your wife's name is like my wife's name). The Gemara distinguishes the cases: by a *get*, the Torah uses the language *ve-kasav lah* — he shall write *for her* — establishing a requirement of *ketiva lishmah*, writing specifically for this woman. By *sotah*, the Torah says *ve-asa lah* — the priest shall *do* for her — placing the *lishmah* requirement on the *doing*, which is the erasure into the water, not the writing itself. The writing is only a preparatory stage; the critical act is the scraping. Accordingly, there may be no requirement that the *ketiva* of the *sotah* scroll be for this particular woman, even if there is some minimal requirement that the writing be oriented toward the *sotah* ritual in general.

## R. Meir's Brilliance

### Meir's Unmatched Brillia…

The Gemara now turns from the story of Rabbi Meir the scribe to a broader portrait of Rabbi Meir's extraordinary intellect. Having shown that Rabbi Meir needed to first study under Rabbi Ishmael before he could fully absorb Rabbi Akiva's teaching, the Gemara moves swiftly to put any resulting questions about Rabbi Meir's capacity thoroughly to rest.

Rabbi Akha bar Chanina states: *gali ve-yadu'a lifnei mi she-amar ve-haya ha'olam she-ein be-doro shel Rabbi Meir kamoso* — it is revealed and known before the One who spoke and the world came into being that there was no one in Rabbi Meir's generation at his intellectual level. This is a striking formulation: it is not a human assessment but a divine one.

### Why Not Rule Like Meir

If Rabbi Meir was unquestionably the greatest mind of his generation, why do we not rule like him as a general principle? It is not that we systematically rule *against* Rabbi Meir, but in standard disputes — Rabbi Meir against Rabbi Yehuda, for instance — we rule like Rabbi Yehuda. It should be noted that the Gemara does say *stam matnisin Rabbi Meir* — that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi used the teachings of Rabbi Meir as the foundation for the anonymous voice of the *Mishnayos*. Yet when Rabbi Meir appears in explicit debate, we often do not rule like him.

The reason the Gemara gives is: *shelo yachlu chaveirav la-amod al sof da'ato* — his colleagues could not reach the bottom of his thinking. He was so profound that nobody could fully comprehend his reasoning. More than that: *shehu omer al tamei tahor u-marei lo panim, al tahor tamei u-marei lo panim* — he could declare something that was *tamei* to be *tahor* and marshal evidence for it, and equally declare something *tahor* to be *tamei* and bring compelling proof. The implication cuts in two directions: not only could others not always follow his argument, they also could not always trust that his argument — however dazzling — was arriving at a sound conclusion. If a person is so brilliant that he can prove anything, then a correct-seeming proof may not be trustworthy, not because he intended to deceive, but because such extraordinary dialectical power can lead even the most sincere reasoner to conclusions that, in the end, most would not accept.

This raises a question about the *sanhedrin* and the requirement that its members be capable of making arguments for purity and impurity — a point the Gemara will develop further shortly.

The tension here is worth sitting with. The Gemara holds up Rabbi Meir as the supreme intellect of his generation while simultaneously explaining why his rulings often do not prevail. And it introduces the unsettling possibility that the same brilliance which makes someone the greatest *posek* in theory can make that person's rulings difficult to rely on in practice. The halachic process requires not only intellectual power but the capacity to carry one's colleagues — to reason in a way they can follow, evaluate, and ultimately endorse.

### The Name Meir

A *tana* teaches: *lo Rabbi Meir shemo, ella Rabbi Nehorai shemo* — his original name was not Rabbi Meir but Rabbi Nehorai. *Ve-lamah nikra shemo Rabbi Meir?* — and why was he called Rabbi Meir? *She-haya me'ir einei chachamim ba-halacha* — because he would illuminate the eyes of the sages in *halacha*.

This is itself a somewhat striking formulation given what was just said about him. If nobody could fully understand his reasoning, in what sense did he illuminate their eyes? The answer seems to be that the encounter with Rabbi Meir's intellect forced his colleagues to elevate their own. They could not keep up with him, but the very effort of trying to engage his arguments sharpened their minds and made them better at *halacha*. It is reminiscent of the *le-chadeid ba-hem et ha-talmidim* — teaching contrary positions in order to sharpen the students — mentioned earlier in this *amud*. The danger that such brilliance might prove false things true does not negate the fact that the encounter with it makes everyone around it more capable.

The Gemara continues: *ve-lo Nehorai shemo* — and the person known as Rav Nehorai was also known by a pseudonym. His actual name was Rabbi Nechemia, or according to another opinion, Rabbi Elazar ben Arach. He too was called Nehorai because *she-man-ir einei chachamim ba-halacha* — he illuminated the eyes of the sages in *halacha*.

There is an important tension the Gemara is navigating. On one hand, it presents Rabbi Meir's intellectual power as potentially dangerous — he could make the false appear true. On the other hand, it immediately affirms that this same power actually improved *halacha* by forcing everyone around him to rise to a higher standard. Intellect is not simply dangerous; it is dangerous *and* indispensable. The question is not whether to have it but how to channel it. This also raises the perennial question of the limits of *halachic* argumentation: if one knows enough sources and possesses enough analytical skill, one can construct a plausible argument for almost any position. What distinguishes a legitimate *halachic* argument from a merely clever one? The answer lies in integrity — not just in whether an argument *can* be made but whether one is genuinely being faithful to what the sources actually require.

### Seeing the Teacher

Rabbi continues this portrait of Rabbi Meir by saying: *hai de-mechadedna mechaberai, de-chazitei le-Rabbi Meir me-achorei* — the reason I am sharper than my contemporaries is that I at least saw Rabbi Meir from behind. *Ve-ilu chazitei mikamei, havei mechadedna tefei* — had I seen him from the front, I would have been even sharper still.

The Gemara cites the verse: *ve-hayu einecha ro'ot et morecha* — your eyes shall see your teacher. This is understood on one level as a practical claim about the completeness of communication: as much as ninety percent of communication is nonverbal, and seeing a teacher's facial expressions, gestures, and physical comportment conveys nuances that words alone cannot. Seeing only a teacher's back captures body movement and posture but misses the face; seeing from the front would yield still more. But there is another dimension here as well. Rabbi Meir was not merely a repository of information or a logical machine; he was a person whose passion and engagement had a galvanic effect on everyone around him. The personal encounter — the *gestures*, the *fire* — inspired students to push themselves further than they otherwise would have. The intellectual sharpening was inseparable from the relational and spiritual dimension of the teacher-student encounter.

One might also read this in light of the famous passage elsewhere about Rabbi Elazar ben Arach, who journeyed to a place of pleasant springs and beautiful surroundings — and forgot all his Torah. Intellect alone, divorced from the living engagement with teachers and colleagues, is ultimately insufficient. What sustains Torah is not brilliance in isolation but the dynamic of living transmission: the face of the teacher, the eyes of the student, the charge that passes between them.

The Gemara cites the verse to support Rabbi's statement — *ve-hayu einecha ro'ot et morecha* — and one cannot help noting the resonance with the famous divine declaration to Moshe in a different context: *panai lo yeira'u ve-ra'ita et achorai* — you cannot see My face, but you may see My back. Here, Rabbi saw the back of Rabbi Meir, and it was sufficient to make him the sharpest of his generation. Had he seen the face, one can only imagine.

### Sumchus & Proofs

The Gemara then introduces Rabbi Meir's student Sumchus: *she-haya omer kol davar ve-davar shel tumah arba'im u-shmonah ta'amei tumah, ve-al kol davar ve-davar shel taharah arba'im u-shmonah ta'amei tahara* — for every matter of *tumah* he could give forty-eight demonstrations of why it was *tamei*, and for every matter of *tahara* forty-eight demonstrations of why it was *tahor*. The Maharsha notes the significance of the number forty-eight: there are said to be fifty gates of wisdom, of which Moshe possessed forty-nine. Presumably no one below Moshe could exceed forty-eight — and Sumchus reached that peak. Crucially, however, Sumchus used his forty-eight proofs to demonstrate what was actually *tamei* and what was actually *tahor* — not to invert them. He absorbed the sharpness of Rabbi Meir but directed it toward truth rather than toward dazzling reversal.

### Anonymous Proofs

A *braisa* then records: *talmid vatik haya be-Yavne she-haya metaher et ha-sheretz be-me'ah va-chamishim ta'amim* — there was a distinguished student in Yavne who could give a hundred and fifty proofs that a *sheretz* — one of the eight ritually impure rodents enumerated in the Torah — was actually *tahor*. This is where the provocative capacity to prove the opposite, which was said of Rabbi Meir, now reasserts itself — but notice that it is attributed to an anonymous figure, not to Rabbi Meir himself, and certainly not to Sumchus. The Gemara seems deliberately to ascribe this inversion-of-truth capacity to an unnamed person rather than to any named sage whose rulings one would want to rely upon.

### Ravina's Failed Proof

Ravina then says: *ani adun ve-ataharenu* — let me try to prove that a *sheretz* should be *tahor*. His argument: *u-mah nachash she-meimit u-marbeh tumah tahor, sheretz she-eino meimit ve-eino marbeh tumah, lo kol sheken* — a snake, which can kill and thereby bring *tumah* into the world, is nonetheless *tahor* — it is not among the eight *shratzim* that the Torah declares *tamei*. If a snake, which causes death and spreads *tumah*, is *tahor*, certainly a *sheretz*, which neither kills nor spreads *tumah*, should be *tahor* — all the more so.

The Gemara dismisses this: *ve-lo hi, ma'aseh kotz be-alma hu* — it is not a valid proof. A snake is like a thorn: it injects venom, it stings. The *tumah* it generates is incidental, a byproduct of its action, not something intrinsic to the snake itself. This fails entirely as a *kal va-chomer*. The argument does not even count as one of a hundred and fifty. The Gemara's willingness to play this game for a moment, only to dismiss Ravina's attempt with a shrug, is itself telling. The entire arc of this section — from the praise of Rabbi Meir's brilliance, to Sumchus using that brilliance for truth, to an anonymous sage proving a *sheretz* is *tahor*, to Ravina's failed attempt — amounts to a sustained corrective: the capacity to prove the opposite is a real and formidable power, but the Gemara is not celebrating it. It holds it up precisely to frame its limits.

## Beit Shammai & Hillel

### The Debate

Rav Abba said in the name of Shmuel: *shalosh shanim nechleku Beit Shammai u-Veit Hillel* — for three years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel debated. *Hallalu omrim halacha k'moseinu ve-hallalu omrim halacha k'moseinu* — each declared that the *halacha* should follow them. The *rishonim* explain that this was not simply each school claiming to be right on the merits; it was a procedural dispute. Beit Hillel was the majority in numbers, while Beit Shammai was the sharper and more brilliant school. The debate was therefore about the ground rules of *halachic* decision-making: does a larger number of voices outweigh greater intellectual acuity, or does brilliance override numbers?

*Yatza bat kol ve-amra* — a heavenly voice declared: *eilu ve-eilu divrei Elokim chayim* — these and these are both words of the living God — *ve-halacha ke-Veit Hillel* — and the *halacha* follows Beit Hillel.

What does *eilu ve-eilu divrei Elokim chayim* mean? The Ritva, drawing on the *Rambam*, offers what is arguably the most principled explanation. The *Rambam* held that the overwhelming majority of *Torah she-be-al peh* was never pre-given as a fixed set of rulings transmitted from Sinai. There is a small body of *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — a handful of direct transmissions — but the rest, the vast majority of the halachic corpus, is the product of human intellect and creativity applied to the interpretation of the written Torah, operating through defined hermeneutical rules such as the *yud-gimmel middos she-ha-Torah nidreshes bahen*. This stands in contrast to another view, based on a certain *aggadita* in the Gemara, that all rulings were given to Moshe at Sinai and disputes arise only from failures of transmission. The *Rambam* rejected this view on both logical and apologetic grounds: it does not accurately describe what the Gemara actually does, which is not recapture a forgotten tradition but reason from texts to new conclusions; and it hands critics — particularly the *Karaim* — the argument that if there are so many disputes, the transmission cannot be trusted.

Under the *Rambam*'s framework, *eilu ve-eilu divrei Elokim chayim* means that the Torah text is genuinely open to multiple legitimate interpretations, and both the position of Beit Shammai and the position of Beit Hillel represent valid readings of what the Torah means. There is no single original meaning that one school got right and the other got wrong. Nevertheless, we must *posken* — practical *halacha* requires a decision. The question then becomes: on what basis do we decide?

### Why Beit Hillel Won

*U-mipnei mah zachu Beit Hillel likboa halacha k'mosan* — why did Beit Hillel merit that the *halacha* was established like them? The Gemara answers: *mipnei she-nochin ve-aluvin hayu* — because they were pleasant and unassuming, *ve-shonim divreihem ve-divrei Veit Shammai* — and they would teach not only their own positions but also the positions of Beit Shammai, *ve-lo od, ella she-makdimin divrei Veit Shammai le-divreihem* — and not only that, they would even mention Beit Shammai's position *before* their own.

The Gemara illustrates this with the *mishnah* in *Sukkah* about one whose head and most of his body were in the *sukkah* but whose table was inside the house. Beit Shammai rules this is invalid; Beit Hillel rules it valid. Beit Hillel invokes a precedent: the elders of both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel once visited Rabbi Yochanan ben HaChoranis and found him sitting in exactly this way — most of his body in the *sukkah*, his table indoors — and they said nothing. Beit Shammai responds that they did indeed say something: they told him, *im kach hayita noheg, lo kiyamta mitzvat sukkah miyamecha* — if you have been conducting yourself this way all along, you have never actually fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *sukkah*. The point for our purposes is that the *mishnah* mentions the elders of Beit Shammai before those of Beit Hillel, which is itself an expression of the principle. And some hold that the very structure of the *mishnah* — always presenting Beit Shammai's position before Beit Hillel's — reflects Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi following the precedent set by Beit Hillel itself, which always taught the other side's view first.

### Lessons on Humility

The Gemara draws a broader moral: *shekol ha-mashpil atzmo, HaKadosh Baruch Hu magbiho* — whoever humbles themselves, the Holy One lifts them up; *ve-chol ha-magbiya atzmo, HaKadosh Baruch Hu mashpilo* — whoever exalts themselves, the Holy One lowers them. *Kol ha-mechazer achar ha-gedolah, gedolah borachat mimenu* — whoever pursues greatness, greatness flees from him; *ve-chol ha-boreach min ha-gedolah, gedolah mechazeret acharav* — whoever flees from greatness, greatness pursues him. *Ve-chol ha-dochek et ha-sha'ah, sha'ah dochakato* — whoever presses the moment, forces things before their time, the moment presses him back; *ve-chol ha-nidcheh mipnei ha-sha'ah, sha'ah omedet lo* — and whoever yields to the moment and does not force things, the moment stands firm for him.

### Engagement vs. Brilliance

The deeper principle here is that Beit Hillel's humility was not merely a character virtue disconnected from their *halachic* standing. Because they did not treat themselves as the sole repository of truth, because they genuinely engaged with Beit Shammai's arguments and taught them — and taught them *first* — they were the school that truly absorbed all the voices. Even if Beit Shammai was sharper, Beit Hillel was the position that fully grappled with the *totality* of the debate. And *that* is what halachic authority requires: not just brilliance, but engagement.

This connects directly to the theme running through the entire *daf*. Rabbi Meir was the most brilliant of his generation, but his brilliance was so self-contained, so far above his colleagues, that it could not be fully relied upon — not because he was wrong, but because nobody could follow the reasoning well enough to endorse it. Beit Shammai was sharper than Beit Hillel, but Beit Hillel's engagement with all views, including Beit Shammai's, made theirs the position that genuinely represented the broader halachic conversation. There is a consistent message here: *halacha* is not a competition in individual brilliance but a collective enterprise, and it is ultimately those who engage all opinions, who are anchored in community and relationship, who earn the right to rule.

There is also a pointed contemporary implication. The tendency to seek out brilliant *rashei yeshiva* in isolation from community life, elevating their rulings simply on the basis of encyclopedic knowledge and analytic acuity, reflects exactly the model that this Gemara critiques. The great *poskim* of earlier generations were not only scholars; they were people embedded in the realities of their communities, who understood the full human texture of the questions they were deciding. Brilliance in a vacuum is exactly what the Gemara is warning against when it explains why we do not always rule like Rabbi Meir — and why we do rule like Beit Hillel.

One final point on the *bat kol*: it might seem paradoxical to resolve an impasse through a heavenly voice, given the general principle that we do not follow a *bat kol* in halachic disputes — as in the famous case of Rabbi Eliezer and the oven. The answer is that there the procedure was clear: *acharei rabbim lehatos* — we follow the majority. The *bat kol* was therefore out of place because there was an established method. Here, the impasse was precisely *about* the procedure itself — whether to go by majority or by superior intellect — and there was no pre-existing rule to resolve it. A procedural deadlock of that kind may be precisely the situation for which a *bat kol* is appropriate.

## Not to Be Created

### The Debate

The Gemara closes with one final dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, this one of a philosophical rather than halachic character. *Shtei shanim va-mechetza nechleku Beit Shammai u-Veit Hillel* — for two and a half years — notably shorter than the three years of the previous dispute — Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel debated.

### The Vote

*Hallalu omrim: noach lo le-adam shelo nivra yoser mi-she-nivra* — one school maintained that it would have been better for a person never to have been created than to have been created. *Ve-hallalu omrim: noach lo le-adam she-nivra yoter mi-shelo nivra* — the other held the opposite, that it is better to have been created. One naturally assumes that the more pessimistic position was Beit Shammai's and the more optimistic one Beit Hillel's, consistent with their general orientations. *Nimnu ve-gamru* — they took a vote and concluded: *noach lo le-adam shelo nivra yoter mi-she-nivra* — it would have been better for a human being not to have been created. This is the more pessimistic conclusion, and it is striking that the vote came out this way — particularly in light of the fact that the previous Gemara ruled like Beit Hillel.

### Examine Your Deeds

The Gemara continues: *achshav she-nivra, yefashpesh be-ma'asav* — now that one has been created, one should investigate one's deeds. *Ve-amri lei: yemashmesh be-ma'asav* — or, in another version, one should feel or examine one's deeds. Is there a difference between these two formulations?
