However, it does not permit *rabbinic* carrying within that space, since one should not benefit from something brought about through a violation of *Shabbat* (*ma'aseh Shabbat*). The *gemara* clarifies that Rav Nachman's restriction was stated specifically in the context of a *mechitza* made through deliberate violation (*meizid*). Where no violation occurred — as in the case of water naturally returning to a well — there is no concern of benefiting from forbidden labor, and the *mechitza* is fully valid for all purposes. Indeed, even if *Shabbat* had begun with the well completely dry and the water appeared only during *Shabbat*, the analysis would be the same: the enclosure is valid and carrying is permitted.

---

## Biblical Status/Rabbim

### Rav Nachman Distinction

With the discussion of *Abaye*'s questions concluded, the *gemara* introduces a statement: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who throws an object into the space of *pasi biraot* is *chayav* — liable for the biblical prohibition of carrying from *reshut ha-rabbim* to *reshut ha-yachid*. This implicitly confirms that the enclosure constitutes a *reshut ha-yachid* at the biblical level.

### Rabbi Eliezer Throws

The *gemara* objects: this seems obvious! If *pasi biraot* did not constitute a biblical *reshut ha-yachid*, how could the rabbis have permitted drawing water there in the first place? The fundamental structure of the laws of *eruv* requires that one first establish a biblical *reshut ha-yachid*; only then may one ask whether rabbinic carrying is also permitted within it. If the enclosure is not biblical, the entire rabbinic dispensation collapses.

The *gemara* therefore reframes the statement: Rabbi Elazar is not teaching about an enclosure around a well but about a person who constructed this same corner-post configuration (*k'ein pasi biraot*) in the middle of a *reshut ha-rabbim* — in an open public thoroughfare — and then threw an object into it. In that case, one might have thought the *reshut ha-rabbim* negates the effectiveness of the *mechitza*, rendering the configuration invalid. Rabbi Elazar teaches that this is not so: even in the middle of a street, this configuration is a *reshut ha-yachid*.

The *gemara* again objects: is this not also obvious? If this configuration were not effective in general as a *mechitza*, it could never work around a well either. The *gemara* therefore arrives at the true *chiddush*.

### Rabbim Non-Negation

The novelty is this: *af al gav d'ka bakei bah rabbim* — even though the general public (*rabbim*) passes through the space. If one constructed the corner-post configuration in Times Square, for instance, with major thoroughfares passing through two of the gaps and another road through the other two, one might think that the presence of a *reshut ha-rabbim* flowing through the gaps negates the wall entirely — that there is no *mechitza* to speak of when the public passes through unimpeded. Rabbi Elazar teaches that *rabbim* do not negate the *mechitza*: the enclosure remains a *reshut ha-yachid* even under these conditions.

This principle connects directly to a dispute that appears in a *mishnah* coming later in *Eruvin*. Rabbi Yehuda rules that if a *reshut ha-rabbim* — a major thoroughfare — passes through the gaps of a *pasi biraot* enclosure, the street must be redirected to the side (*yesakenu le-tzadin*); otherwise the *mechitza* is negated. The *chachamim* disagree and hold that no such redirection is required. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar are cited as stating jointly: *kan hodiucha kochan shel mechitzot* — "here they have shown you the power of walls." That is, the *chachamim*'s position demonstrates how robust a *mechitza* is: even with a *reshut ha-rabbim* passing directly through, the walls are not nullified.

The *gemara* notes that if Rabbi Elazar's ruling were only implicit in his commentary on the *chachamim*'s position in that *mishnah*, one might think he was merely explaining the *chachamim*'s view without personally endorsing it. The present statement establishes that Rabbi Elazar personally rules in accordance with the *chachamim* — that *rabbim* do not negate the *mechitza*.

An important qualification emerges from the *rishonim*: Rabbi Yochanan himself does *not* rule this way. When we reach that *mishnah*, Rabbi Yochanan will maintain that a *reshut ha-rabbim* does negate the *mechitza*. The joint formulation here (*Rabbi Yochanan ve-Rabbi Elazar damrei tavayhu*) refers only to their shared commentary that the *chachamim*'s position reflects great confidence in the power of walls; it does not mean both personally endorse that position as *halakha*. Rabbi Elazar's independent statement makes his personal ruling clear; Rabbi Yochanan's independent ruling is otherwise established.

---

## Head & Body Requirement

### Head & Body Rationale

The *gemara* now examines the requirement, stated in the *mishnah*, that the cow's head and the majority of its body (*rosho ve-rubo*) must be inside the enclosure for the watering to be permissible. To understand this requirement, the *gemara* draws a parallel from a *mishnah* in *Eruvin* (which appears later, on 99b): a person may not stand in *reshut ha-rabbim* and drink from a window opening into a house, nor may he stand inside and drink outside, unless his head and the majority of his body are in the same domain as the liquid he is drinking. The concern is that if only part of one's body is in the appropriate domain, one may inadvertently straighten up and carry the cup back across the *mechitza*. If, however, the head and the majority of the body are positioned where the drinking occurs, the risk of such inadvertent carrying is sufficiently mitigated.

The same logic applies to the cow at the well: the concern is that if only a small part of the cow is inside the enclosure, the cow may step outside and the person holding the vessel will follow, inadvertently carrying from *reshut ha-yachid* to *reshut ha-rabbim*. When the majority of the animal is inside, this risk is deemed sufficiently controlled.

### Question: More Required?

The *gemara* then raises a more refined question: does this requirement of *rosho ve-rubo* apply across all circumstances, or might it vary depending on the degree of control the person exercising?

The *gemara* distinguishes two cases. Where the person is holding the vessel (*nakit mana*) but not holding the cow (*lo nakit lah*), there is no question that *rosho ve-rubo* of the cow is required inside the enclosure: the cow is free to move and the holder of the vessel is subject to the risk of following. But what if one is holding both the vessel and the cow (*nakit mana ve-nakit lah*)? In that case, the person has full physical control over the animal's movements. Perhaps the requirement of *rosho ve-rubo* applies only when the cow is free to move; when the person is in control, even less than *rosho ve-rubo* may suffice.

*Rabba* replied that the *mishnah*'s language resolves this: *u-vilvad she-tehei parah roshah ve-rubah mi-bifnim ve-shotah* — "provided that the cow's head and majority of its body are inside and drinking." The *gemara* then attempts to determine which scenario the *mishnah* is addressing.

### Trough Case Analysis

The *gemara* raises a *braita*: a person may not fill a vessel with water on *Shabbat* and hold it before his animal (*lo yemalei adam mayim ve-yiten be-Shabbat lifnei behemto*). He may, however, fill water and pour it into a trough (*avus*), and the animal will drink on its own. If the prohibition is categorical — one may never hold the vessel without also restraining the cow — then the *mishnah*'s case of *rosho ve-rubo* must be a scenario where the person *is* holding the cow (and the vessel), since holding the vessel alone is categorically forbidden.

However, *Abaye* qualifies the *braita* significantly: the prohibition against holding the vessel before the animal is not a categorical rule, but applies specifically to a case where the *avus* — the trough — is positioned with one end inside the *pasi biraot* enclosure and extends outward into the *reshut ha-rabbim*, yet the trough itself is ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* wide, and thus constitutes a *reshut ha-yachid* in its own right. In such a case, what one might wish to do is carry the vessel over the airspace of the trough — which is *reshut ha-yachid* — directly to where the animal stands outside the enclosure. This the *braita* forbids.

Why? Not because the act itself would be biblically prohibited — but because of a rabbinic concern: the person may notice a crack or defect in the trough (*avus d'mikalkel*), descend into the *reshut ha-rabbim* to fix it, and bring the vessel down with him. After fixing it, he will then carry the vessel back up from the *reshut ha-rabbim* into the airspace of the trough, which is *reshut ha-yachid* — and that constitutes a biblical act of *hotza'ah*.

The *gemara* challenges even this: when the person originally descended, that was not a prohibited act since he did not *intend* to bring the vessel to *reshut ha-rabbim*; it was merely incidental movement. The principle articulated in the name of Rabbi Yochanan is that one who moves objects from corner to corner within a domain and then changes his mind and takes them outside is *patur* — exempt — because the initial *akira* (lifting) was not performed with the intent to remove them to another domain. So here too, the original descent was not an *akira* for *reshut ha-rabbim* purposes. The *gemara* responds: the concern is not for the descent but for what follows — once he is in *reshut ha-rabbim* fixing the trough, he sets the vessel down on the ground, and then when he picks it up again to bring it to the animal, *that* is a full *akira* from *reshut ha-rabbim* with intent to bring it to *reshut ha-yachid*, and that is the act from which the *gezeira* protects.

### Approach 1: Holding

The *gemara* thus presents a first approach: the *braita*'s prohibition of holding the vessel before the animal applies categorically in any normal scenario. Since it is never permitted to hold the vessel without restraining the cow, the *mishnah*'s ruling — that *rosho ve-rubo* is required — necessarily addresses the case where the person *is* holding the cow (and the vessel). In that case, *rosho ve-rubo* of the cow is both required and sufficient, even though the person maintains physical control.

### Approach 2: Not Holding

The second approach (*ika d'amri*) inverts the reading of the first question. According to this version, it may be taken as given that *rosho ve-rubo* suffices when one is holding both the vessel and the cow. The question is whether *rosho ve-rubo* suffices when one is *not* holding the cow — or whether a greater portion of the animal must be inside. The *mishnah* is then cited to show that *rosho ve-rubo* suffices in the case of not holding the cow. And thanks to *Abaye*'s qualification of the *braita*, the prohibition of holding the vessel without restraining the cow is not categorical — it applies only in the special case of the extended trough (*avus*). Outside that scenario, holding the vessel while the cow's head and majority of body are inside is perfectly valid, and *rosho ve-rubo* is sufficient.

The two approaches thus differ in their starting assumptions. The first assumes that holding the vessel without restraining the cow is generally forbidden, and therefore the *mishnah* must be addressing the case where one holds both, in which circumstance *rosho ve-rubo* is required but sufficient. The second assumes that holding the vessel without restraining the cow is generally permitted (the *braita*'s prohibition being limited to the *avus* case), and the *mishnah* addresses that ordinary case, ruling that *rosho ve-rubo* is sufficient even without holding the cow.

---

## Camel Distinction

### Camel Long Neck

The *gemara* then introduces a *braita* about feeding a camel: if the camel's head and majority of body (*rosho ve-rubo*) are inside the *pasi biraot* enclosure, one may engage in *obsin* — stuffing food into its mouth, the manner in which camels are typically fed, as the *gemara* in *Masechet Shabbat* discusses at length. The *gemara* reasons that *obsin* is analogous to holding both the vessel and the cow simultaneously, since one is actively engaged with the animal's mouth. Yet even in this case, *rosho ve-rubo* is required. This seems to refute the first approach's implicit suggestion that perhaps less than *rosho ve-rubo* would suffice when one holds both animal and vessel, since here one holds both and *rosho ve-rubo* is still demanded.

### Other Animals

Rav Acha bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav Sheshes responds: a camel is different (*shani gamal*) because of its long neck. Even when one controls a camel physically, the neck is long enough that the animal can easily extend its head outside the domain. Consequently, *rosho ve-rubo* remains essential for a camel even when the feeder has full control. For an animal with a short neck — a cow, for instance — when the person physically restrains it, the degree of control is qualitatively greater, and it remains possible that less than *rosho ve-rubo* would suffice.

The *gemara* then introduces a second *braita*: for a generic *behema* (animal) with its head and majority of body inside, one may engage in *obsin*. Once again, the *gemara* reads this as equivalent to holding both animal and vessel, yet *rosho ve-rubo* is required. If a generic *behema* also requires *rosho ve-rubo* even when controlled, there is no ground for distinguishing camel from cow.

### Rabbi Eliezer Prohibition

The *gemara* resolves this by arguing that the two *braitot* were not composed together; the word *behema* in the second *braita* also refers to a camel. The *gemara* supports this by citing another *braita*: Rabbi Eliezer prohibits the use of a camel for this purpose altogether, precisely because of its long neck. The neck of a camel introduces a category of risk that cannot be adequately controlled, and therefore Rabbi Eliezer extends his concern to an absolute prohibition in the camel's case. This supports the reading that the halakhic difficulties raised by *rosho ve-rubo* in the *braitot* are specific to the camel's unique anatomy, leaving open the possibility that for other animals — where physical restraint provides full control — the requirements may be less demanding.

---

---

# Eiruvin 21

## Passei Biraot Rules

### Olei Regalim Limit

The Gemara at the very bottom of 21b opens with a statement by Rav Yitzchak bar Adda: *lo hutru passei bira'ot ella le'olei regalim bilvad* — the special leniency of *passei bira'ot* was permitted only for those ascending to Jerusalem for the *regel*, the pilgrimage festival, and not for ordinary individuals. The *passei bira'ot* is a remarkable rabbinic construction that allows the creation of a halachically enclosed space even when the majority of its area remains uncovered — a leniency whose unusual breadth is itself the subject of these restrictions. Notably, the occasion for drawing water under this arrangement was *Shabbat* specifically; *Yom Tov* presented no difficulty in this regard and required no special dispensation.

### Animals Only

A *baraita* then adds a further restriction: *lo hutru passei bira'ot ella legabei behema bilvad* — the arrangement was permitted only for the sake of animals, not for human drinking. The Gemara synthesizes these two statements: *behemet olei regalim*, the animals of those ascending for the *regel*. The cumulative rule is thus doubly limited: the *passei bira'ot* applies only to the animals of *olei regalim*, not to ordinary animals, and not to human beings even among the pilgrims themselves.

### Human Access

If humans are excluded from drawing water through this arrangement, how then do they drink? The Gemara answers: *aval adam mitapes ve'oleh u'mitapes ve'yored* — a person can scale down the wall into the well and scale back up. Notably, the Gemara phrases this with going up mentioned before going down, which is something of an odd reversal. The answer is striking in its austerity: despite the entire elaborate construction of *passei bira'ot*, a human being must climb down the wall of the well to draw his own water.

This leads to a further question. The Gemara invokes an earlier ruling in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: *lo hutru passei bira'ot ella leve'er mayim chayim bilvad* — the *passei bira'ot* was only permitted for a well of live, flowing water, not for collected rainwater. The Gemara presses: if the entire arrangement is for the sake of animals, why should the source of the water matter? An animal has no preference between *mayim chayim* and *mayim mechumasim*. The Gemara answers: *be'inan midi dechazi le'adam* — we require water that is fit for human consumption. Rashi explains that the water itself lends dignity and legal weight to the *mechitza*, and therefore *mayim chashuvim*, water of importance, is required.

### Tosafot Leniencies

At this point Tosafot intervenes to soften the severity of the position considerably. The earlier Gemara had permitted feeding the animal grain within the enclosure, despite grain not being water; Tosafot notes that this is also presumably something *dechazi le'adam*, fit for human use. More significantly, Tosafot poses the obvious question directly: if the *passei bira'ot* is permitted only *letzorech behema*, for the sake of animals, why does it matter whether the water is fit for humans?

Tosafot offers two leniencies in response. The first: *she'im dela letzorech behema ve'nishtayer sham, shari le'adam* — if one drew water for the animal and water remained, that leftover water is permitted for human consumption. The second, and more far-reaching leniency: once the *passei bira'ot* has been constructed and put in place *letzorech behema*, it is thereafter permitted *lechatchila* to draw water even explicitly for a human being. The restriction, according to Tosafot, applies only to the original intent when establishing the arrangement; once legitimately erected for animals, humans may freely draw from it as well. This makes the position far more intelligible and practical.

### Wide Troughs Case

The Gemara then returns to the core ruling: *lo hutru passei bira'ot ella legabei behema bilvad, aval adam mitapes ve'oleh mitapes ve'yored* — a person scales the wall. The Gemara then introduces an exception: *ve'im hayu rechavim, afilu adam nami* — if the walls of the well are too wide to scale, then even a human being may draw water through the *passei bira'ot* arrangement.

Tosafot explains the precise meaning of this exception in light of his two earlier leniencies. In the general case, a person benefits from the arrangement only through leftover water or through drawing *lechatchila* once the setup was made for animals. But where scaling is physically impossible, even those secondary steps are unnecessary: one may *lechatchila* draw water through the *passei bira'ot* directly for a human being, without any prior drawing for the animal's benefit.

---

## Vessel Holding Rules

### Direct Holding Ban

The Gemara now revisits a ruling encountered earlier: *velo yemalei adam mayim ve'yiten lifnei behemato* — a person may not fill a vessel and hold it before his animal so the animal can drink from it directly. The permitted alternative is: *aval memale hu ve'shofech lifnei behema ve'shota me'eleha* — one may pour the water into the trough and the animal drinks from it on its own. The concern, as discussed previously, is that holding the vessel before the animal creates a risk that one might follow the animal out of the *passei bira'ot* enclosure.

The Gemara challenges: if one may not hold a vessel before the animal anyway, what purpose does the *passei bira'ot* serve? The response is that it allows one to fill the trough. But then a sharper question follows: if the vessel cannot be held in front of the animal regardless, why did the earlier ruling limit the arrangement to the case where *rosh ve'rubo*, the majority of the animal, is within the enclosure? Even if the animal were to step outside, since one is not holding the vessel there should be no concern.

### Abaye's Trough Case

It is this challenge that motivates Abaye's clarifying statement: *hacha be'mai askinan* — what is the case we are discussing here? *Be'evus ha'omed be'reshut harabim, gavo'ah asarah ve'rochav arba, ve'rosho nichnas bein hapasim* — a trough standing in the public domain, ten *tefachim* tall and four *tefachim* wide, whose inner end extends into the space between the boards. In this configuration, the trough itself constitutes a *reshut hayachid*, and the concern is that if one is holding the vessel over the trough and sees it is cracked or broken, one might take the vessel into and out of different domains. It is in this case specifically that holding the vessel is permitted, and therefore the requirement of *rosh ve'rubo* — that the majority of the animal be within the enclosure — remains necessary to prevent the person from inadvertently following the animal outside.

The upshot is that the general rule *does* permit holding the vessel before the animal. The prohibition discussed here is confined to this specific configuration of the trough as a *reshut hayachid*, and the *rosh ve'rubo* requirement is the mechanism by which the person is kept within bounds.

---

## Burganin & Geography

### Rav Yirmiyah Bar Abba

The Gemara now turns to a statement by Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba in the name of Rav: *ein burganin be'Bavel u'fassei bira'ot be'chutz la'aretz* — there are no *burganin* in Bavel, and *passei bira'ot* do not apply in *chutz la'aretz*. *Burganin* are small way-stations or huts erected outside a city for watchmen guarding the fields. Halachically, these structures extend the *techum* of the city, provided they are within seventy and two-thirds *amot* of the city boundary — a distance small enough that they are considered attached to the city.

The Gemara explains why *burganin* do not function in Bavel: *deshchichi bidkei* — because flooding is common there, and structures are frequently washed away. Since such huts cannot be relied upon to remain standing, they cannot serve as legitimate extensions of the city boundary. As for *passei bira'ot* in *chutz la'aretz*: *delo shchichi mesivsa* — because there are no *yeshivot* there.

This reasoning reveals something quietly profound. The original justification for *passei bira'ot* was *olei regalim*, the pilgrimage traffic converging on Jerusalem. After the *churban*, the Gemara assumes, the institution would have continued to apply wherever similar conditions of significant travel existed — namely, Bavel, where people streamed to the great academies of Torah learning. In its very assumption, the Gemara has articulated a theological and sociological proposition: the *yeshiva* replaces the *Beit Hamikdash* as the center of Jewish spiritual gravity. The people traveling to Neharde'a and Pumbedisa stand in for the *olei regalim* ascending to Jerusalem. *Chutz la'aretz*, lacking such centers of Torah, has no analogous circumstance and therefore cannot avail itself of the *passei bira'ot*.

### Alternative View

The Gemara then presents an alternative formulation: *ika d'amri*, some say that Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba taught that neither institution applies in either location. In this version, *burganin* do not function in Bavel because of flooding (*deshchichi bidkei*), and they do not function in *chutz la'aretz* because of theft (*deshchichi ganavei*) — thieves will simply take the huts, rendering them unreliable as permanent structures. As for *passei bira'ot*: they do not apply in Bavel because water is abundantly available (*deshchichi maya*), and there is therefore no pressing need for the special institution; and they do not apply in *chutz la'aretz* because the necessary concentration of travelers does not exist there.

### Three Parsaot Story

The Gemara, having just cited Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba, introduces a connected story. Rav Chisda said to Mari, the son of Rav Huna who was the son of Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba: I have heard that on *Shabbat* you traveled from Barnash to the *beit knesset* of Daniel — a distance of three *parsaot*. Now a *parsa* is four *mil*, and the ordinary *techum Shabbat* permits travel of 2,000 *amot* beyond the city limits. Three *parsaot* is twelve times that ordinary distance. How did you manage this? Rav Chisda challenges: surely you relied on *burganin* — but your own grandfather taught in the name of Rav that *burganin* do not function in Bavel.

In response, the grandson went outside and pointed to a series of *masvata* — Rashi understands these as destroyed cities, each one situated within seventy and two-thirds *amot* of the next, so that each ruined settlement served as a connector to the following one. Once one reaches a city, the entire length of that city counts toward one's *techum*, and then another connector can bridge the gap to the next settlement. The arithmetic is staggering: three *parsaot* is 24,000 *amot*, and if each connector spans only seventy and some *shirayim* *amot*, the number of such connectors required is enormous. One must assume that the ruined settlements themselves provided substantial length, with the gaps between them bridged by these small connectors.

Tosafot raises an interesting philological point here. He initially considers whether *masvata* refers to small villages rather than destroyed cities, and notes that in the first chapter of Gittin the word *masvata* appears to refer to large cities. This bears practical significance for the writing of a *get*: since the standard formula designates the location with the word *masa ploni*, one must ask whether that term applies to a town or only to a city. Tosafot ultimately concedes that Rashi's reading — destroyed cities — is correct and that the evidence from this Gemara therefore does not resolve the *get* question. What is clear in any case is that even a destroyed city is halakhically sufficient to extend the *techum* and connect the chain of settlements.

---

## Torah She'be'al Peh

### Boundless Mitzvot

The Gemara now embarks on an extended *aggadic* digression that, as we will see, ultimately circles back to the theme of rabbinic legislation. Rav Chisda relates that Mari bar Mar expounded the verse: *l'chol tichla ra'iti ketz, rechava mitzvatecha me'od* — for all things I have seen an end, but Your commandments are exceedingly wide. David said this and did not explain it. Job said it and did not explain it. Yechezkel said it and did not explain it. And it was not until Zechariah came and explained it.

### Zechariah Scroll

Each figure is cited in turn. David proclaimed *rechava mitzvatecha me'od* without specifying the dimension. Job declared *arucha me'eretz midah, u'rechava mini yam* — greater in length than the earth, and wider than the sea — but gave no precise measure. Yechezkel described a scroll spread out before him, written on both sides — *panim ve'achor* — containing *kinim*, *vahege*, and *vahi*: the sufferings of the righteous in this world, the reward of the righteous in the world to come, and the punishment of the wicked in the world to come. Yet Yechezkel too gave no precise dimensions for the scroll.

It is Zechariah who finally provides the measurement: *ani ro'eh megilla afa, aruka esrim b'amma, ve'rachva eser b'amma* — a flying scroll, twenty *amot* in length and ten in width. These, the Gemara specifies, are divine *amot*, whose precise length is beyond ordinary human reckoning. The Gemara then unpacks the calculation. The scroll is folded, so when unfolded it is twenty by twenty — 400 square divine *amot*. It is written on both sides; if one were to separate and lay those two sides flat side by side, the total would be forty by twenty — 800 square divine *amot*.

By comparison, the verse in Isaiah states *mi madad besh'alo mayim, ve'shamayim ba'zeret tiken* — God measured the heavens with a *zeret*, the span from thumb to little finger, which equals half a divine *amah*. The heavens in both dimensions are thus half a divine *amah* by half a divine *amah* — a quarter of a square divine *amah*. The ratio of 800 to one-quarter is 3,200. Thus, *nimtza kol olam kulo echad mishloshei alafim u'matayim ba'Torah* — the entire world is only one thirty-two-hundredth of the Torah. The scope of *Torah she-be'al peh* — which is what this midrash is understood to concern — dwarfs the entire physical universe.

The Maharsha notes a dimension of this image: the scroll written *panim ve'achor*, front and back, alludes to *pshat, remez, drash*, and *sod* — the layers of meaning that lie folded within the text, some visible on the surface and some requiring the text to be opened and its inner face revealed.

### Two Pots Parable

The Gemara returns to Mari bar Mar's exposition, now on the verse: *ve'hineih shenei dudaim te'enim mu'adim lifnei heichal Hashem* — two baskets of figs set before the sanctuary of God. One basket contained figs that were *tovot me'od*, exceedingly good, like the finest first-ripened figs; the other contained figs that were *ra'ot me'od*, exceedingly bad, utterly inedible. The good figs, the Gemara explicates, represent *tzaddikim gemurim*, the fully righteous; the bad figs represent *resha'im gemurim*, the wholly wicked.

One might conclude that the *resha'im* are a lost cause, that their hope is entirely annulled. But the verse from *Shir Hashirim* — playing on the shared root of *dud* and *duda'im* — intervenes: *haduda'im natnu rei'ach*, the mandrakes gave forth their fragrance. *Elu va'elu atidim sheyitnu rei'ach* — both groups, even the thoroughly wicked, will in the future give forth their goodness. The *resha'im* possess *mitzvot* as well, and ultimately their hidden worth will be revealed in the time to come.

### Rava's Figs

Rava offers a different reading of *haduda'im natnu rei'ach*. Rather than both baskets, the *duda'im* here refers to something else entirely: *elu bachurei Yisrael shelo ta'amu ta'am chet* — these are the young men of Israel who have not yet experienced sin. Like fresh young shoots that have not yet matured, they have not yet acquired the taste of transgression. The Maharsha adds that mandrake plants carry little flavor, which makes the wordplay *lo ta'amu ta'am chet* all the more apt.

Rava continues with the next phrase: *ve'al petacheinu kol megadim* — by our doorways are all manner of delicacies. This refers to *benot Yisrael shemagidot pitcheihen leva'aleihen* — the women of Israel who faithfully report their status as *niddot* to their husbands. An alternate version reads *she'ogdot pitcheihen leva'aleihen* — they bind up their openings, scrupulously observing the laws of *niddah* and refraining from relations during the forbidden period.

### Mandrakes Drasha

*Chadashim gam yeshanim, dodi tzafanti lach* — new things and old things, my beloved I have stored up for you. The Gemara reads this as the voice of the community of Israel speaking before God: *Ribbono shel Olam, harbeh gezeirot gazarti al atzmi yoter mima shegazarta alai* — Master of the Universe, I have imposed upon myself many more prohibitions than You have imposed upon me. The Maharsha connects this specifically to the *chumra* of Rabbi Zeira and other stringencies in the laws of *niddah*, and it resonates broadly with the world of *chumrot* that Jewish communities have layered upon themselves — from *kitniyot* on Pesach to *Yom Tov sheni* — and I have fulfilled all of them. *Chadashim gam yeshanim*: the new ones, the rabbinic additions, alongside the old ones, the biblical commandments.

Rav Chisda then tests a student who was organizing *aggadot* before him, asking: have you heard a good interpretation of *chadashim gam yeshanim*? The student replied: these are the light *mitzvot* and the heavy *mitzvot*. Rav Chisda objected: what does that have to do with old and new? The Torah was not given in two installments, the lighter ones later than the heavier ones. Rather, the correct reading is: *hallalu midivrei Torah ve'hallalu midivrei soferim* — some are from the Torah itself, those are the *yeshanim*, the old; and some are from the sages, those are the *chadashim*, the new. The student's confusion apparently arose from equating the rabbinic, and therefore ostensibly lighter, laws with the *chadashim* — a reasonable but mistaken conflation.

This also illuminates why, in the *drasha* to follow, the *chadashim* — the rabbinic laws — are mentioned first. As Rava will immediately demonstrate, the rabbinic laws demand a heightened vigilance.

Rava expounds the verse from Kohelet: *veyoter mehema beni hizaher asot sefarim harbe* — and more than all this, my son, be careful of the making of many books. *Beni hizaher bedivrei sofrim yoter midivrei Torah* — be more careful about rabbinic law than about biblical law. The explanation offered is that biblical law carries positive and negative commandments, whereas *kol ha'over al divrei sofrim chayav misa* — one who transgresses rabbinic enactments is, as it were, deserving of death. Rashi quotes the verse *u'foretz geder yishchenu nachash* — one who breaks through the fence will be bitten by a snake — framing the rabbinic law precisely as *geder*, a protective fence around the biblical law. To breach it is to expose oneself to the gravest consequence.

One must, however, understand this in context. The Maharsha notes that this cannot be taken in its simple, absolute sense — halachically, rabbinic law is generally treated more leniently than biblical law, and the ordinary rules of *safeik*, doubt, and other principles reflect this. The Maharsha therefore suggests the statement refers specifically to rabbinic laws that protect against biblical violations carrying the death penalty. Even if one accepts a broader reading, it remains rhetorical exaggeration aimed at instilling vigilance, not a strict halachic equation of rabbinic and biblical severity. The statement *chadashim gam yeshanim* now reads with added force: the *chadashim*, the rabbinic enactments, are listed first because it is they that demand this particular vigilance.

Lest one wonder why the *divrei sofrim* were not simply incorporated into the written Torah from the beginning, the verse itself addresses this: *asot sefarim harbe ein ketz* — the making of many books would have been endless. The *Torah she-be'al peh* is genuinely boundless — as the entire calculation from Zechariah's scroll demonstrated, it exceeds the physical universe thirty-two hundredfold — and no written document could have contained it. The written Torah must be finite and manageable; the oral tradition, by its nature, can expand without limit while remaining responsive to the particular needs of each generation and each era.

### Rabbinic Severity

The Gemara concludes this sequence with a comment on the final phrase of the verse: *velahag harbe yegi'at basar* — and much engagement brings weariness of flesh. Rav Papa the son of Rav Acha bar Adda in the name of Rav Acha bar Ulla teaches: *shekol hamal'ig al divrei chachamim nidon betzoa rotachat* — anyone who mocks the words of the sages will be judged in boiling excrement. The word *lahag* is read as *mal'ig*, to mock, and *yegi'at basar* as the excretion of the flesh. But the same phrase carries an alternate reading: if one instead puts in genuine effort — *yegi'ah* — and engages seriously, then *ta'am basar*, it is like the taste of meat, *geshmak*, deeply satisfying. What appears from the outside to be foolishness reveals itself, under proper engagement, to be richly substantive.

The arc of the entire *aggadic* passage is now clear. The *Torah she-be'al peh* is incomprehensibly vast, extending far beyond anything the physical world can contain. It was given this way deliberately, because no written text could hold it. It demands more vigilance, not less, than the written Torah. It encompasses not only the rabbinic *gezeirot* and *takanot* but even the *chumrot* that the Jewish people have taken upon themselves. And to mock or dismiss it brings the gravest consequence, while to engage with it seriously is among the deepest pleasures available to a human being.

---

## Rabbi Akiva Story

### Prison Hand-Washing

The Gemara now presents a narrative that grounds the foregoing abstract discussion in vivid, almost unbearable, human terms. *Ma'aseh be'Rabbi Akiva shehaya chavush be'veit ha'asurin* — it happened that Rabbi Akiva was imprisoned by the Roman government. His attendant was Rabbi Yehoshua Ha-Garsi — Rashi suggests this may be either a place name or a reference to one who ground bran, *grisin*. Each day, Rabbi Yehoshua would bring Rabbi Akiva a measured, fixed quantity of water, the maximum the authorities would permit.

One day the jailer intercepted Rabbi Yehoshua and declared that he was carrying too much water — perhaps, the jailer suggested, intending to use it to soften the ground and dig an escape tunnel. He poured off half and gave Rabbi Yehoshua only half. When Rabbi Yehoshua arrived, Rabbi Akiva said to him: Yehoshua, do you not know that I am old and my life depends on you and what you bring me each day? Rabbi Yehoshua recounted the entire incident. Rabbi Akiva replied: give me the water so that I may wash my hands before eating bread. Rabbi Yehoshua was stunned: there is not enough water here even for you to drink, and you wish to use what little remains for *netilat yadayim*?

Rabbi Akiva's response is striking in its simplicity: *mah e'eseh, shechayavin aleiha mita* — what can I do? One who transgresses this rabbinic enactment is deserving of death. *Mutav amut mitat atzmi ve'lo e'evor al da'at chaverai* — better that I die my own natural death than that I transgress the view of my colleagues and become deserving of a heavenly death. He refused to eat until they brought him sufficient water for *netilat yadayim*.

The word *chaverai*, colleagues, is itself charged with meaning. On one hand, it might seem to reduce the weight of the obligation — these are his own contemporaries who made this rule, not towering earlier generations. And yet it heightens another dimension: the obligation not to betray the integrity of the enterprise one is part of, the commitment to one's colleagues and to the shared *halachic* project they have built together. The two readings amplify rather than cancel each other.

### Sages' Response

When the sages heard of this they said: *mah bizknuto kach* — if he had this inner strength in his old age and in prison, *beyalduto al achat kama vechama* — how much more so in his youth; and *uma beveit ha'asurim kach, shelo beveit ha'asurim al achat kama vechama* — if he was capable of this in prison, how much more in freedom.

Tosafot notes an important qualification: the Gemara elsewhere, in the first chapter of *Eruvin*, states that four things are exempt in the camp, and *netilat yadayim* is among them — and all the more so when there is genuine danger. Rabbi Akiva was thus not halachically required to go to such extremes; *machmir al atzmo haya*, he was being stringent upon himself. This actually reinforces the larger point: the story is not primarily about the technical obligation but about Rabbi Akiva's extraordinary commitment to *divrei chaverav*, the enactments of the sages, even beyond what the law demanded of him.

---

## Shlomo Eruvin

### Bat Kol Rejoicing

The entire foregoing *aggadic* passage — the boundlessness of *Torah she-be'al peh*, the severity of transgressing rabbinic law, the story of Rabbi Akiva's self-sacrifice for *netilat yadayim* — now converges on the theme of the tractate itself. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *beshe'a shetikan Shlomo eiruvin u'netilat yadayim, yatzta bat kol ve'amra* — at the hour when Shlomo enacted *eiruvin* and *netilat yadayim*, a heavenly voice went forth and proclaimed: *beni im chacham libcha yismach libi gam ani* — my son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will rejoice. And further: *chacham beni ve'samach libi va'ashiva chorfi davar* — be wise, my son, and gladden my heart, that I may respond to those who taunt me with a word.

The attribution of *eiruvin* and *netilat yadayim* to Shlomo, accompanied by divine rejoicing expressed through a *bat kol*, grants these institutions a weight that transcends their technical rabbinic classification. Heaven itself celebrated their enactment.

### Field Midrash

Rava expounds the verse: *lecha dodi neitzei hasadeh, nalina bakfarim, nashkima lachramim, nireh im porchah hagefen, pitach hasmadar, henetzu harimonim, sham etein et dodai lach* — Come, my beloved, let us go out to the field, lie in the villages, rise early to the vineyards, see if the vine has flowered, if the unripe grape has opened, if the pomegranates have blossomed; there I will give my love to you.

The community of Israel speaks to God: do not judge me as You judge those who dwell in cities — where stealing, sexual sin, and false oaths abound, driven by commerce and desire. *Neitzei hasadeh* — come to the field, and I will show You Torah scholars who labor in Torah from a place of deprivation, free from all distraction. *Nalina bakfarim* — do not read *bakfarim*, villages, but *bakofrim*, the rebels — come and see those upon whom You have bestowed goodness, and yet they have denied and rejected You. This is a stark contrast between those who study Torah in poverty and those who, having received divine blessing, turn away from God.

This is a striking *drasha* given its source: it comes from Rava, who lived and taught in Mechuza, a prosperous, cosmopolitan city. The historian Yaakov Elman has written extensively on Rava's fraught relationship with the urban culture of Mechuza, its wealthy merchants, and their resistance to rabbinic authority. The strong condemnation of city life that appears here — the cities of the wealthy who deny God despite His largesse — fits precisely into Rava's social context and his ongoing struggle to instill Torah values in an affluent, materially comfortable community.

The *drasha* continues: *nashkima lachramim*, let us rise early to the vineyards — these are the *batei knesiot* and *batei midrashot*. The rows of a vineyard, as elsewhere in rabbinic literature, evoke the rows of the study house, the *kerem b'Yavneh*. *Nireh im porchah hagefen* — let us see if the vine has flowered — these are the *ba'alei mikra*, those who know the written Torah. *Pitach hasmadar*, the unripe grape has opened — these are the *ba'alei Mishna*, whose learning is more developed. *Henetzu harimonim* — the pomegranates, far larger and more developed than the grape, have blossomed — these are the *ba'alei Gemara*, who represent the apex of Torah learning. *Sham etein et dodai lach* — there I will give my love to you; *arecha kevodi u'godli, shevach banai u'vnotai* — I will show You my honor and my greatness, the praise of my sons and daughters and all the *Torah she-be'al peh* they have developed.

### Handles Metaphor

The Gemara then cites: *vayedaber shloshet alfei mashal, vayehi shiro chamisha va'alef* — Shlomo spoke three thousand parables, and his song was a thousand and five. This is interpreted to mean that on every matter of Torah, Shlomo gave three thousand explanatory parables, and on every matter of rabbinic teaching, he offered a thousand and five reasons. The point is the same as before: even the *divrei sofrim*, the words of the sages, are not arbitrary or thin — they carry thousands of deep explanations that are not immediately visible to the surface reader. Rava then expounds the verse from Kohelet: *veyoter shehaya Kohelet chacham, od limad da'at et ha'am, ve'izen ve'chiker, tiken meshalim harbe* — more than being wise himself, Kohelet taught knowledge to the people; he listened, investigated, and arranged many parables. Rashi explains: *d'agmarah b'simanei teamim, kava lah mesoret ve'simanim bein b'teivot hamikra bein b'girsa shel Mishna* — he taught through signs of cantillation, establishing a *mesora* and markers both for the words of Scripture and for the formulation of the Mishnah. In other words, Shlomo established not merely specific enactments but the foundational apparatus of the *masora* — the system of transmission — for *Torah she-be'al peh* itself, just as the written Torah has its own *masorah*.

### Handles Creation

Ulla in the name of Rabbi Eliezer then states: *batchila hayta Torah doma l'kfifa she'ein lah oznayim* — originally the Torah was like a basket or pot without handles — *ad sheba Shlomo ve'asah lah oznayim* — until Shlomo came and made handles for it.

This image is deliberately distinct from the familiar image of a *geder*, a fence. A fence protects against transgression by keeping people away from the prohibited. Handles do something different: they allow you to grasp, to carry, to hold on. Rashi connects this explicitly back to the earlier statement — the *oznayim* refer to the enactments of *eiruvin* and *netilat yadayim*, and also to Shlomo's *gezeira* on *shniyot l'arayot*, the secondary forbidden relationships elaborated in Yevamot. These are not merely prohibitions; they are positive frameworks that enable people to *hold onto* the *mitzvot* and live within them. *Ochzim Yisrael ba'mitzvot sheyitrachaku min ha'aveira* — through them, Israel grasps the commandments and thus distances itself from transgression.

The distinction is worth dwelling on. *Eiruvin* and *netilat yadayim* are not *gezeirot* in the standard prohibitory sense. *Eiruvin* is a constructive act — one builds, one establishes, one makes a *bracha*. *Netilat yadayim* similarly involves a positive ritual with its own *bracha*. These are *mitzvot* in the fuller sense, rabbinic *mitzvot* that give people something to do, something to perform, a handle by which to grasp the larger fabric of *halacha*. The Beit HaG, it is worth noting, includes some of these — *eiruvin*, *mikra megilla*, *chanukah* — within his enumeration of the 613 commandments, reflecting in his own way this sense that these rabbinic enactments have achieved a status that approaches the constitutional.

### Hair Locks

Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva states: *melameid sheyeish lidrosh al kol kotz ve'kotz tilei tilim shel halachot* — on every little thorn, every tiny stroke of a letter in the Torah, one can derive piles upon piles of halachot. This is the capstone of the entire passage on the breadth of *Torah she-be'al peh*: not only is it thirty-two hundred times the size of the physical universe in its totality, but every single letter of the written Torah, every minimal graphical element, contains within it an inexhaustible depth of oral tradition.

---

## Torah Cost

### Raven Metaphor

The Gemara continues with a verse from *Shir Hashirim*: *shachorot ka'orev* — black as a raven. In whom does one find all this Torah? *Bemi shemashkim u'ma'ariv aleihem le'veit hamidrash* — in one who rises early and stays late in the *beit hamidrash*, *shachorot* evoking *shachar*, dawn, and *erev*, dusk. Torah is not acquired casually; it demands the full arc of the day.

### Cruelty to Family

Rava reads the image with even greater harshness: *bemi shemashchir panav aleihem ka'orev* — in one who darkens his face over them like a raven, who denies himself sunlight and all ordinary comfort. And further: *bemi shemeisim atzmo achzori al banav ve'al benei beito ka'orev* — in one who makes himself cruel to his children and members of his household like a raven, completely abandoning their needs in total devotion to Torah study.

This is a striking statement and it is not without tension within the broader rabbinic tradition. The Gemara in Ketubot takes a far more critical view of abandoning one's family for Torah study. Yet here the abandonment is presented in positive terms, almost as a virtue. The *Vilna Gaon* in his commentary on *Mishlei* cites this very passage at length to support the ideal of complete self-abnegation for Torah, including the abandonment of worldly and domestic obligations.

### Ada Bar Matna

The Gemara illustrates this with the story of Rav Ada bar Matna, who went to the house of Rav to study. His wife asked him: what will become of your children, who will provide for them? He replied: *mi shelimu kurmei be'agma* — are there no longer reeds in the swamp? Meaning: let them go find reeds and subsist on whatever the earth provides. It is an extraordinarily unfeeling response, and the Gemara presents it without apparent criticism.

The tension this creates is real and worth acknowledging. The weight of rabbinic literature, including other passages in the Talmud, generally disapproves of this degree of abandonment. That this passage praises it — implicitly, through inclusion and framing — reflects a genuine diversity within the Talmudic tradition on the question of what the pursuit of Torah demands. And as noted above, it is Rava who bears the weight of this position, a man who struggled throughout his career with a community that he felt was insufficiently devoted to Torah and too seduced by the comforts and corruptions of urban wealth. In that context, perhaps, the rhetoric of total sacrifice becomes comprehensible, even if it cannot be universalized.

---

---

# Eiruvin 22

## Review: Rabbim & Mechitza

### Rabbim Negate Mechitza

Before turning to the *mishna* at the bottom of 22b, it is worth reviewing several key principles that emerged in the *gemara* studied on Shabbos, as they are central to *halacha l'maaseh*. The first is the position of Rav Yehuda: *asi rabbim u-mevatteli mechitza* — the *rabbim* passing through a *mechitza* negate it. This principle is critical because it leads to the conclusion that one cannot establish an *eruv* around a street that constitutes a genuine *reshut harabbim*. The *rabbim* would pass through the *tzurat hapesach*, the nominal wall of the *eruv*, thereby negating it as a *mechitza*. For Rav Yehuda himself this was not a difficulty, since he held that two *mechitzot* suffice. But when one combines Rav Yehuda's principle with the position of the *chachamim* — who require three *mechitzot* — the practical result is that an *eruv* cannot encompass a true *reshut harabbim*.

### Island Walls Problem

The second issue is the question raised at the end of the previous *daf*: why cannot an island serve as a *reshut hayachid*? One might simply use the drop of the sea wall as a *mechitza* on all sides, creating a *reshut hayachid* out of the island. The *gemara* never fully resolves this question. One might argue from the principle of *asi rabbim u-mevatteli mechitza* that travel across the island's edges negates the wall — but this negation only operates at points of actual crossing. To take Manhattan as an example: yes, the George Washington Bridge would break through the *mechitza* at that point, but everywhere else along the perimeter, where there is no crossing, why not regard the river wall as a valid *mechitza*?

### Ownership & Natural Walls

Two answers emerge from the *rishonim*. Tosafot suggests that when walls are entirely natural and not manmade, everyone would agree that *asi rabbim u-mevatteli mechitza* applies — and seemingly would extend this to mean that the very presence of *rabbim* within the *mechitzot*, not merely the act of crossing them, suffices to negate the walls entirely. The precise contours of this position remain somewhat unclear. The Ramban, whose answer is more widely cited among the *poskim*, argues that one must be able to perceive oneself as enclosed within the *mechitzot*. When they are so far apart — or so naturally formed — one cannot see oneself as contained. Some *poskim* note the ambiguity: what, precisely, is the threshold? Not every island is ten miles across, and perhaps the Ramban's standard would permit smaller ones.

The third issue from the previous *daf* concerns ownership and the definition of *reshut harabbim*. The *gemara* had noted that Yehoshua surrendered roads to the *rabbim*, yet where those roads were difficult to traverse they remained privately owned. How does ownership bear on the category of *reshut harabbim*? Tosafot holds that private ownership must be combined with the road's impassability; it is the conjunction of the two factors — not ownership alone — that prevents the space from qualifying as a *reshut harabbim* and limits the application of *asi rabbim u-mevatteli mechitza*. The Ramban, however, takes a more sweeping position: something cannot be a *reshut harabbim* at all unless it is literally owned by the public, regardless of the presence or absence of *mechitzot*. According to the Ramban, a privately owned street is categorically exempt from the status of *reshut harabbim*.

To summarize the three critical issues from the previous *daf*: the principle of *asi rabbim u-mevatteli mechitza*; the question of whether island walls can create a *reshut hayachid* across a large space; and the role of ownership in defining *reshut harabbim*.

---

## Pasei Biraot Rules

### Well Types & Pasei

The *mishna* at the bottom of 22b returns to the special leniency of *pasei biraot*. It states: *echad bor harabbim u-ve'er harabbim u-ve'er hayachid osim lahen pasim* — whether the well is a communal cistern of collected rainwater, a communal well of live spring water, or a private well of live spring water, the *pasim* may be erected. The one exception is *bor hayachid* — a privately owned cistern of collected water — for which a genuine *mechitza* of ten *tefachim* surrounding the entire space is required. This is the position of Rabbi Akiva. The concern is twofold: collected water may dry up, and a privately owned well has no community present to remind people that the *pasim* alone do not constitute a full *reshut hayachid*.

### R. Yehuda b. Bava

Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava is considerably more restrictive: *ein osim pasim ela le-ve'er harabbim bilvad* — the *pasim* are permitted only for a communal well of live spring water. Everything else requires a full *mechitza* of ten *tefachim*. This stringent position combines both criteria: public ownership and live water.

### Two Criteria Needed

The *gemara* at the top of 23a records that Rav Yosef said in the name of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: the *halakha* follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava. And Rav Yosef further said in the name of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *lo hutru pasei biraot ela be-ve'er mayim chayim bilvad* — the *pasim* were permitted only for a well of live water.

One might ask: why state both rulings? Is the second not already contained within the ruling that the *halakha* follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava? The *gemara* explains that each statement is independently necessary. Had one stated only that we rule like Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, one might have understood the emphasis to be on his requirement of *rabbim* — public ownership — while perhaps allowing even collected water so long as it is communally owned, reading the word *ve'er* in his formulation as directed against Rabbi Akiva's leniency regarding private ownership rather than as a requirement for live water per se. Conversely, had one stated only the second ruling — that *pasim* require live water — one might have supposed this applies equally whether the well is public or private, since live water does not dry up. Therefore both statements are needed: we follow Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava in requiring both criteria simultaneously, public ownership and live water.

---

## Gardens & Courts

### R. Y.b. Bava Garden

The next *mishna* introduces a new topic, though one thematically continuous with the discussions above. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava states: *hagina veha-karpef she-hen shiv'im amah ve-shirayim al shiv'im amah ve-shirayim* — a garden or open lot that measures seventy and a fraction by seventy and a fraction in area. The "fraction" will be clarified by the *gemara* as two-thirds of an *amah*, yielding approximately 70.67, which is close to the square root of 5,000. That figure represents *beit satayim* — two *se'ah* — derived from the courtyard of the *Mishkan*, which measured 50 by 100 *amot*, totaling 5,000 square *amot*.

It will be recalled that in the opening *mishna* of this chapter, Rabbi Yehuda had held that *pasei biraot* are limited to *beit satayim*, on the grounds that a larger space is not *hukaf l'dira* — not enclosed for the purpose of habitation — and therefore does not achieve the full status of a *reshut hayachid*. The *chachamim* responded that this limitation to *beit satayim* applies only to a *gina* or *karpef*, whereas spaces that are genuinely *hukaf l'dira* — like a courtyard — have no such size restriction. The governing principle, then, is that a space that is not primarily a place of human habitation is limited to *beit satayim*.

Now the *mishna* continues. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava holds that even a garden or lot surrounded by a proper wall of ten *tefachim* — thus fully enclosed — is permissible only if *sheyehei va shomira o beit dira* — there is either a guardhouse or a dwelling within the space — or *shetehei smucha la-ir* — it adjoins the city and is effectively accessible as an extension of it. Even in those cases where the space might arguably qualify as *hukaf l'dira*, he demands something concrete to demonstrate its residential character.

Tosafot addresses what seems to be a natural question: does this restriction apply to a proper courtyard attached to a home? Tosafot answers that it does not; Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava is speaking about spaces that are fundamentally gardens — *lo hukaf l'dira* in their essential character — where a dwelling or guardhouse was added as an afterthought. A space that genuinely began as a residential enclosure is not subject to this limitation. The stringency targets a garden in which a house was later inserted to lend it residential standing, which Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava regards as insufficient. Without some genuine residential feature, even a perfectly enclosed space cannot exceed *beit satayim* — or, more precisely, cannot be used for carrying at all if it is fundamentally *lo hukaf l'dira*.

### Stam R. Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda — here *stam* Rabbi Yehuda means Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai — takes a position slightly less stringent: *afilu ein bah ela bor ve-siach u-me'arah, metaltelin betokhah* — even if the space contains only a cistern, an irrigation ditch, or a cave, one may carry within it. One does not need a full house, but something must be present that gives the space a measure of connection to human use and activity, enough to justify up to *beit satayim*. Without any such feature, according to both Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava and Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai, a fundamentally *lo hukaf l'dira* space is entirely forbidden — not merely limited to *beit satayim* but unusable for carrying altogether.

### R. Akiva Lenient

Rabbi Akiva takes the most lenient position, and it is his ruling that we follow in practice: *afilu ein bah achat mikol elu, metaltelin betokhah* — even without any of those features, one may carry within the space, provided it does not exceed seventy and a fraction by seventy and a fraction. According to Rabbi Akiva, if a *lo hukaf l'dira* space is bounded within *beit satayim*, no additional qualifying element is required.

To clarify how these positions interact: all authorities would agree that a space genuinely *hukaf l'dira* — where habitation preceded and defined the enclosure — carries no size restriction. The debate concerns spaces that are fundamentally *lo hukaf l'dira*. There, Rabbi Akiva permits up to *beit satayim* without conditions; the other two views require some residential feature before granting even that allowance.

### R. Yosi Rectangle

Rabbi Yosi adds a further leniency regarding shape: *afilu orkhah pi shnayim berochbah, metaltelin betokhah* — even if the length is twice the width, one may carry within it. He does not dispute the *beit satayim* limit, but holds that the space need not be a perfect square. This echoes the dimensions of the *Mishkan*'s courtyard, which was precisely 50 by 100 — a two-to-one rectangle. The implicit question, to which the *gemara* will return, is whether Rabbi Akiva requires a perfect square, and if so, what this means for spaces that are naturally rectangular.

### R. Eliezer Notes

Rabbi Ilai then reports three traditions he received from Rabbi Eliezer. First, *vaafilu hu ke-beit kor* — even a space the size of a *beit kor*, which is far larger than *beit satayim*, is permissible; Rabbi Eliezer apparently holds there is no size restriction even for *lo hukaf l'dira* spaces. Second, regarding a courtyard where all residents joined the *eruv* except one who forgot: Rabbi Eliezer holds that the person who forgot may not bring objects from his house into the courtyard, but the others may bring objects into his house — a position not followed in practice, where the ruling is that the courtyard remains permissible but his house is off-limits to everyone. Third, *she-yotzin be-arkavlin be-Pesach* — a certain vegetable may be used for *maror* on Pesach.

Rabbi Ilai adds that he searched among Rabbi Eliezer's students for a colleague who had heard the same traditions and found none, which left him without corroboration — though it is noted that he was certain of his report. The fact that Rabbi Ilai felt compelled to seek confirmation fits with the broader character of Rabbi Eliezer as a *tanna* who was known for transmitting only what he received from his teachers and never innovating.

---

## Ve'od Convention

### Ve'od Question

The *gemara* turns to a literary question: *mai tanna de-katani ve-od* — why does the *mishna* introduce Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's stringency regarding gardens with the word *ve-od*, "and furthermore"? One might say: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava was strict in the previous *mishna* — requiring both live water and public ownership for *pasei biraot* — and here he is strict again, limiting *lo hukaf l'dira* spaces; so we use *ve-od* to link two consecutive stringencies of the same *tanna*.

The *gemara* challenges this: that cannot be the criterion, because we can find two consecutive stringencies attributed to *stam* Rabbi Yehuda in the first *mishna* of the chapter — one regarding *pasei biraot* being limited to *beit satayim*, and another regarding *pasei biraot* in a *reshut harabbim* — yet the *mishna* there does not use *ve-od* between them. So what explains the difference?

### Ve'od Answer

The *gemara* answers: *hasam afsiku rabbanan, hacha lo afsiku rabbanan* — there, the *chachamim* intervened between the two positions of Rabbi Yehuda with a substantial digression, whereas here there was no such intervening digression. In the first *mishna*, between Rabbi Yehuda's two stringencies, the *chachamim* not only responded directly but went on at length — limiting *beit satayim* specifically to *gina* and *karpef*, enumerating what types of spaces may be unlimited, and so on. That constituted a significant departure from the immediate thread. Here, by contrast, the transition was direct.

The *gemara* then raises a further challenge: but we find in *Sukkah* that Rabbi Eliezer's positions are connected with *ve-od* even though the *chachamim* intervened between them. The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing the character of the interruption. In *Sukkah*, the *chachamim*'s intervening statement — that only the first night of *Sukkah* is required — was directly responsive to Rabbi Eliezer's point and did not veer off into independent subject matter. That brief on-point response did not constitute the kind of digression that would sever the connection. In our first *mishna*, the *chachamim*'s response ranged far beyond the immediate issue and introduced a catalogue of independent rulings. That is the interruption that precludes *ve-od*. The rule that emerges: *ve-od* is appropriate when two positions of the same *tanna* are juxtaposed either without interruption at all, or with an interruption that is immediately on-point and confined to the matter at hand. Where the intervening material digresses substantially into independent topics, *ve-od* is not used.

---

## Beit Sasayim Size

### R. Akiva = T.K.?

The *gemara* now turns to the halachic substance of the *mishna*. Rabbi Akiva says that one may carry in a *lo hukaf l'dira* space without any additional requirements, provided it does not exceed seventy and a fraction by seventy and a fraction. The *gemara* asks: *Rabbi Akiva hainu Tanna Kamma* — is Rabbi Akiva simply repeating the position of the first *tanna*? Rashi understands this as a reference to the *Tanna Kamma* at the very beginning of the chapter, who had held that *pasei biraot* need not be limited to *beit satayim* and implicitly placed no additional conditions on *gina* and *karpef* beyond the size limit. Tosafot reads the question more narrowly, focusing on why Rabbi Akiva restates the figure of seventy and two-thirds when it has already been stated.

### Precision Difference

The *gemara* resolves this: *ika beinaihu davar mu'at* — the difference lies in whether the measurement is precisely 70 and two-thirds or 70 and two-thirds plus a small additional amount. As noted, 70 and two-thirds (*amos*) equals approximately 70.67, while the true square root of 5,000 is approximately 70.71. The *Tanna Kamma* allows the small difference between those two figures, permitting anything up to the full *beit satayim* including that fractional remainder. A *braitta* is then cited: Rabbi Yehuda says there is a slight additional amount beyond 70 and two-thirds, and the *chachamim* did not specify the precise figure — understandably so, since the true square root of 5,000 is irrational and cannot be expressed as a simple fraction. Rabbi Akiva insists on precisely 70 and two-thirds, nothing more.

### Mishkan Source

The *gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — from where is the size of *beit satayim* derived? Rav Yehuda says the verse states: *orech hachatzer meah ba-amah ve-rochav chamishim ba-chamishim* — the length of the courtyard is 100 *amot* and the width is 50 *amot*, yielding a total of 5,000 square *amot*. This is the courtyard of the *Mishkan*, and it serves as the halakhic benchmark for *beit satayim*. It should be noted that applying this measure as a limit on *lo hukaf l'dira* spaces is a rabbinic enactment; the verse is likely cited as *asmachta*.

### Math Derivation

The verse's phrasing raises a question: it says *chamishim ba-chamishim* — 50 within 50 — yet the courtyard was 50 by 100, not 50 by 50. The *gemara* explains: *tul chamishim ve-sovev chamishim* — take the 50 and surround it by 50. This encodes a geometric construction for approximating the square root of 5,000 without the benefit of positional notation or decimal arithmetic. Rashi explains the procedure as follows: begin with a 50-by-50 square. Take a second 50-by-100 rectangle — the other half of the courtyard — and cut it into strips of 10 by 50. Place four such strips along the four sides of the original 50-by-50 square, adding 10 to each side, expanding it to a 70-by-70 square. There are small square corners left unfilled; take the remaining strip material, cut it to fill those corners, repeat the process with what remains, and one arrives at approximately 70 and two-thirds. This elegant construction is how the ancients identified the side length of a square equal in area to the 50-by-100 courtyard. Rabbi Akiva's insistence on precisely 70 and two-thirds, the *gemara* notes, is also reinforced by the square nature of this construction.

### Pasuk Meaning

A further question arises: in its plain sense, why does the verse say *chamishim ba-chamishim* if the courtyard was 50 by 100? Abaye answers: *ha'ameid Mishkan al sfat chamishim* — position the *Mishkan* at the far end of the 50-*amah* boundary of the courtyard. If one imagines the full 100-by-50 courtyard and draws a line across the middle, the front half — the open approach area before the *Mishkan* — is a perfect 50-by-50 square. The *Mishkan* structure itself, measuring 30 by 10 *amot*, stands symmetrically behind that line, centered with 20 *amot* on each side and 20 *amot* behind it. The verse's *chamishim ba-chamishim* thus highlights the 50-by-50 open forecourt that constituted the primary functional space of the *Mishkan*'s courtyard.

---

## Square vs. Rectangle

### Contradiction Noted

The *mishna* records that Rabbi Eliezer holds: *im haytah orkhah yeter al rochbah afilu amah achat, ein metaltelin betokhah* — if the length exceeds the width by even one *amah*, one may not carry within it; the space must be a perfect square. Yet a *braitta* attributes to Rabbi Eliezer an apparently contrary position: if the length exceeds the width by more than double, even one *amah* more than a two-to-one ratio, it is forbidden — implying that up to a two-to-one rectangle is permitted. This sounds precisely like Rabbi Yosi's view. The contradiction between the *mishna* and the *braitta* attributed to Rabbi Eliezer requires resolution.

### Text Emendation

Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye proposes reading the *mishna* as the *braitta* reads it — namely, that even the *mishna*'s text should be understood as referring to excess beyond a two-to-one ratio. If so, however, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosi appear identical, which the *gemara* rejects.

---

## Square vs. Rectangle (II)

### Akiva vs. Yosi

The *gemara* resolves the apparent identity between the positions by pointing to a distinction: *ika beinaihu ribuah de-ribuah de-rabbanan* — they differ regarding the square of the rabbanic square. Rashi explains this as a question of preference: one position prefers a square configuration (allowing rectangles only reluctantly), while the other prefers a rectangle modeled on the *Mishkan*'s courtyard dimensions, permitting squares as well but regarding the two-to-one rectangle as the ideal.

### Tosafot Practical

Tosafot raises a pointed objection: what can "prefer" possibly mean in this context? This is not a *mitzvah* with a *lechatchila* — is one supposed to redesign an actual courtyard to conform to the preferred shape? If the space is permitted, it is permitted; if forbidden, it is forbidden. One cannot tell a person to reconfigure his yard from a rectangle to a square or vice versa. Tosafot therefore reinterprets the distinction more technically: one position reads "twice as long" in terms of the diagonal measurement rather than the simple linear dimension, making it a more stringent standard. This at least yields a genuine legal difference without the absurdity of prescribing courtyard renovations.

---

## Lenient Ruling

### Both Lenient

The *gemara* records two rulings transmitted by Rav Yosef and Rav Bibi respectively, both in the name of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: the *halakha* follows Rabbi Yosi (permitting a two-to-one rectangle), and the *halakha* follows Rabbi Akiva (requiring no additional feature beyond *beit satayim*). The *gemara* notes: *ve-tarvaihu le-kula* — both rulings represent the lenient aspect of each authority's position taken together.

### Why Both Stated

Both rulings must be stated explicitly. Had one ruled only like Rabbi Yosi, one might have supposed that Rabbi Yosi addresses shape but still requires a guardhouse or dwelling, since he does not explicitly address that condition. The ruling like Rabbi Akiva clarifies that no such additional feature is needed. Conversely, had one ruled only like Rabbi Akiva, one might have inferred that since his formulation emphasizes the *beit satayim* square, the space must literally be a square. The ruling like Rabbi Yosi clarifies that a two-to-one rectangle is equally permissible. The combined ruling thus establishes a fully lenient position: no additional qualifying features are required, and the space may be rectangular up to a two-to-one ratio, provided the total area does not exceed *beit satayim*.

---

## Garden in Lot

### Lot to Garden

The *gemara* now cites a *braitta* introducing a more complex case. A *karpef* — an open lot — that is larger than *beit satayim* but was enclosed *hukaf l'dira*, meaning the original intention was residential use (one might think of it as a campground or the like). Subsequently, *nizra rubo* — the majority of the space was planted as a vegetable garden. The question is how this mixed space is categorized. A *gina* is considered *lo hukaf l'dira* by definition; a *karpef* designated for habitation is *hukaf l'dira*. What happens when one contains a majority portion of the other?

This raises a broader and striking principle: the identity of such a space is not fixed by its original designation. Even if the enclosure was made with residential intent, subsequent use as a garden can transform its character. If it has been fully converted, the transformation is complete. But what if only a majority has been converted?

### Majority Rules

The *braitta* rules: *harei hu ke-gina* — if the majority is planted as a vegetable garden, the entire space takes the identity of a garden. Since the original *karpef* was larger than *beit satayim*, and now the whole space is treated as a *gina*, it is *lo hukaf l'dira* and larger than *beit satayim*, and therefore one may not carry within it.

### Trees Exception

However, if the majority of the space was planted not with vegetables but with trees — *nata rubo* — the ruling is different: *harei hu ke-chatzer u-mutar*. Trees do not undermine the residential character of a space. A park planted with trees remains a place where people walk, rest, and spend time; it is an amenity of habitation, not a departure from it. Therefore the space retains its status as the equivalent of a *chatzer* and carrying remains permitted. This yields two significant insights: first, trees do not diminish *hukaf l'dira* status; second, and more broadly, the identity of an enclosed space can shift with changes in its dominant use, and that majority use is what determines the applicable category.

---

## Minority Garden

### R. Huna Limit

The *gemara* now examines the converse of the *braitta*'s ruling regarding a majority-planted garden. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua qualifies the *braitta*: *lo amran ela yoter mi-beit satayim* — the ruling that the planted majority renders the entire space forbidden applies only if the planted portion itself exceeds *beit satayim*. If the garden portion is less than *beit satayim*, even if it constitutes the majority of the space, it does not render the surrounding area forbidden.

The logic is as follows: when the planted area itself exceeds *beit satayim*, it becomes an independently forbidden space — a *gina* that is *lo hukaf l'dira* and too large to be permissible. That forbidden space is then open into the remainder of the *karpef* with no dividing wall, and the principle of *patuach le-makom ha-assur lo* — being open to a forbidden area — causes the entire space to become forbidden as well. But if the garden is under *beit satayim*, it does not itself carry independent forbidden status, and so the surrounding lot is not affected.

### Beit Sasayim Threshold

The *gemara* recasts this principle more directly in a subsequent formulation: if the planted portion is a *minority* of the space, it is permissible — *miuta shari*. Yet Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua applies his qualification in reverse as well: *lo amran ela de-lo havei beit satayim* — that leniency holds only as long as the minority garden has not itself reached *beit satayim*. Once the garden portion reaches *beit satayim*, even as a minority, it becomes a problem, because at that threshold it gains an independent identity as a *gina*. Even though a *gina* of exactly *beit satayim* is itself permissible according to Rabbi Akiva's ruling, the problem is now different in character: one now has a *gina* that is open into a *karpef* with no wall between them. Those are categorically distinct types of *reshut hayachid*, and carrying from one to the other raises its own concerns.

### Opening Rule

This brings the *gemara* to an important general principle: if a space is *patuach le-makom ha-assur lo* — open to a domain where carrying is forbidden — the space itself becomes forbidden even if it would otherwise be permissible. When the garden portion exceeds *beit satayim*, it is itself a forbidden space, and by being open into the *karpef*, it renders the *karpef* forbidden as well. This explains Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's original qualification: the majority-planted garden creates a problem only because and when the planted area itself rises above *beit satayim* and becomes forbidden.

### R. Shimon

The *gemara* then asks: *ke-man* — according to whom is this position? The analysis of the minority case, where the space is permissible as long as the garden is under *beit satayim*, requires that a *gina* opening into a *karpef* is not itself treated as a problem when both are permissible. This implies the ruling of Rabbi Shimon. The *mishna* records Rabbi Shimon's position: *echad gagot ve-echad chatzerot ve-echad karpifot, reshut achat hen le-keilim she-shavtu be-tokhan* — rooftops, courtyards, and lots are all considered a single domain with respect to items that were within them at the onset of Shabbat, though not for items that were in a house. Rabbi Shimon thus holds that these distinct types of *reshut hayachid* — rooftop, courtyard, lot, garden — are not treated as separate domains requiring further demarcation between them; they are collectively one domain.

The *chachamim* disagree and hold that each such space has a distinct enough character that one cannot carry freely between them without an *eruv*, even when each is independently permissible. The *gemara*'s final formulation goes like Rabbi Shimon: when the garden portion is a minority of under *beit satayim*, the whole space is permissible because a *gina* opening into a *karpef* presents no difficulty (per Rabbi Shimon). But once the garden reaches even *beit satayim* — gaining full independent identity as a *gina* — the problem arises according to the *chachamim*, and even according to Rabbi Shimon, because within an otherwise *hukaf l'dira* enclosure one now has a sub-space of *beit satayim* that is *lo hukaf l'dira* and therefore forbidden, which by its opening into the surrounding area renders the whole space forbidden.

---

## Eruv Application

### Eruv Challenge

This analysis carries immediate and substantial implications for practical *eruvin*. One might construct an *eruv* enclosing an entire neighborhood or city, but if within that enclosed area there exists a space larger than *beit satayim* that is *lo hukaf l'dira*, the principle of *patuach le-makom ha-assur lo* threatens to render the surrounding area forbidden as well. Ensuring that no such unqualified space exists within an *eruv* is therefore one of the central practical challenges in *eruvin* construction.

### Lakes & Parks

What types of spaces might qualify as *lo hukaf l'dira* within an urban *eruv*? A park planted with trees, as the *gemara* established, is permissible — people walk there, rest there, and use it as an extension of residential life, so it retains *hukaf l'dira* status. But consider a lake within that park. People do not inhabit a lake. Does a lake constitute a *lo hukaf l'dira* space larger than *beit satayim*? Some authorities argue that if people actually use the lake — rowing boats, floating toy boats, engaging with the water's edge — then the lake is also part of human activity and may qualify as *hukaf l'dira*.
