There are in fact lakes in Central Park where boats are taken out, and that use may be relevant to the analysis. But the precise boundaries of what constitutes *hukaf l'dira* in such cases remain a matter of careful halakhic determination. What emerges clearly from the *gemara* studied today is that this question — the definition of *lo hukaf l'dira* and the consequences of such a space being open within a larger *eruv* — is not merely theoretical. It is one of the primary concerns that arises in the practical construction and validation of an *eruv*, and the principles learned here on 22b are directly operative in contemporary halakhic practice.

---

---

# Eiruvin 27

## Eruv Types & Mishna

### Mishna Review

The *daf* opens with the beginning of a new *perek*, and the *mishna* at the bottom of 26b sets the stage for the entire chapter. *Bechol me'arvin u'mishtatfin* — one may make an *eruv* and a *shituf* with any food. The *shituf* refers to the joining of the different *chatzerot* — the various courtyards or streets onto which houses open — to form a unified domain for carrying purposes within the *mavoi*, the alleyway. This is the higher-level structure. The more basic building block is *eruv chatzerot* itself, by which the houses opening into a common courtyard are unified so that one may carry freely between them. Both mechanisms require participants to contribute a quantity of food that symbolizes shared ownership and residence.

### Tosafos Reading

Rashi reads *bechol me'arvin* as encompassing *eruvei chatzerot* as well as *eruvei techumin*. Tosafos, however, argues that the *gemara* subsequently makes clear that *eruv chatzerot* may only be performed with bread — *b'pat* exclusively. Therefore, Tosafos understands *me'arvin* in this *mishna* as referring specifically to *eruvei techumin*, while *mishtatfin* covers *shitufei mevo'ot*. The practical upshot is striking: *eruv chatzerot*, which is the counterpart to *shitufei mevo'ot*, is limited to bread, whereas the broader category of food that may be used for any purpose applies to *shitufei mevo'ot* and *eruvei techumin*. One should be attentive to this distinction throughout the chapter.

### Water & Salt

Both uses of food enumerated in the *mishna* — *eruv* and *shituf* — exclude water and salt: *chutz min hamayim u'min hamelach*. The same exclusion recurs in two further *halakhot* stated in the *mishna*: *v'hakol nikach b'kesef ma'aser chutz min hamayim u'min hamelach* — one may redeem *ma'aser sheni* funds to purchase anything except water and salt — and *hanoder min hamazon mutar b'mayim u'melach* — one who vows to abstain from food remains permitted to drink water and eat salt. The shared thread is that water and salt do not carry the legal status of *mazon*, food. This is paradoxical in a sense, since water and salt are among the most essential substances for sustaining life, yet the *halakha* declines to classify either as food proper.

### Techumin Definition

The *mishna*'s emphasis on *eruvei techumin*, in light of Tosafos's reading, calls for a brief orientation to that institution. One is ordinarily prohibited from traveling beyond 2,000 *amot* — approximately a kilometer — outside city limits on *Shabbat*. There is a dispute among the *rishonim* whether this restriction has a biblical basis. According to the Rambam, there is an underlying biblical prohibition, but it applies only to a far greater distance; the 2,000-*amot* limitation is in any case a rabbinic enactment. *Al yetzei ish mimkomo b'yom hashabbat* is cited by some as the biblical source, though its precise application is debated.

### Eruv Placement

The *eruv techumin* operates by depositing food — sufficient for two meals, and comprising any foodstuff except water or salt — at a designated location outside the city before *Shabbat* begins. That location then functions as the person's virtual place of residence for purposes of *Shabbat* travel, so that his 2,000-*amot* radius is measured from there rather than from the city. Critically, this does not merely extend one's range in the desired direction; it shifts one's entire starting point. One gains distance in one direction but loses it in the other, since the city itself may now lie at the far edge of one's 2,000-*amot* boundary. The technicalities of how the 2,000 *amot* are measured — how overlapping city boundaries interact, what constitutes a qualifying placement, and precisely how the shift operates — will occupy much of the subsequent discussion in this *perek*.

### Eruv Protection

One might reasonably ask: since the food must be placed outside the city, in what is by definition an unoccupied area, is it not vulnerable to loss or consumption by animals before *Shabbat*? This is indeed a concern addressed by *halakha*, and the answer is that the food must be deposited in a protected location. The details of what constitutes adequate protection will be treated more fully in the *gemara* ahead.

### Special Cases

The *mishna* continues with a set of cases that sharpen the definition of the food requirement. *Me'arvin le-Nazir be-yayin u'le-Yisrael bi-Trumah* — one may make an *eruv* for a *nazir* using wine, even though a *nazir* is prohibited from drinking it, and for a non-*kohen* using *trumah*, even though a non-*kohen* may not eat it, since in both cases the food is fit to be consumed by someone — a non-*nazir* may drink the wine, and a *kohen* may eat the *trumah*. Sumchus disagrees, holding that the food must be fit for the person on whose behalf the *eruv* is made; it must represent a potential meal for him specifically, making *chullin* the required standard.

The *mishna* further states that one may place an *eruv* for a *kohen* in a *beit ha-pras* — a field in which graves have been plowed, creating a rabbinic concern of bone-contamination — since the prohibition is only rabbinic and the food remains accessible. Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may even place it in a graveyard, since a *mechitzah* can be constructed enabling the *kohen* to enter without transgressing.

Tosafos raises a pointed question in this context. Given that the *mishna*'s dominant opinion permits food the person himself cannot eat — as in the case of wine for a *nazir* — why should the location of the food matter? Why not say: even if the *kohen* personally cannot access the food because it lies atop a grave, someone else could eat it, and the rule of accessibility should be no stricter than the rule of personal edibility? Tosafos concludes that there is in fact a meaningful distinction: while the food need not be personally edible by the individual, it must at minimum be personally accessible. The *stam* of the *mishna* permits food the person cannot eat, but it maintains that the food must be retrievable by the person making the *eruv*. This distinction will be developed further in the *gemara*.

---

## Ein Lomedim Principle

### Rabbi Yochanan's Rule

At the top of 27a, Rabbi Yochanan states a foundational principle of *halakhic* methodology: *ein lemedin min haklalos va'afilu b'makom shene'emar bo chutz* — one cannot draw legal conclusions from general rules, even in cases where the rule explicitly enumerates its exceptions. When a *mishna* or *beraita* declares *zeh haklal* — this is the rule — one cannot assume that the rule is exhaustive and iron-clad, even if exceptions are spelled out. There may always remain additional, unenumerated exceptions.

The *gemara* notes the precision of Rabbi Yochanan's language. The fact that he said "even where it states *chutz*" implies that he originally formulated this principle in a context where no exceptions were listed at all — since that would be the more obvious case. This prompts the question: in what context did Rabbi Yochanan first say this?

### Mitzvot Asei Exceptions

The *gemara* answers that Rabbi Yochanan's primary reference was the well-known rule: *kol mitzvot asei shehazman grama anashim chayavim venashim peturos* — all positive time-bound commandments obligate men but exempt women; and correspondingly, those that are not time-bound obligate both equally. This formulation contains no enumerated exceptions — it is a pure *zeh haklal* — and it is precisely here that Rabbi Yochanan's caveat applies most forcefully.

### Torah Obligation Examples

The *gemara* challenges both halves of the rule with concrete counterexamples. Against the claim that women are exempt from all time-bound positive commandments: *harei matzah, simchah, ve-hakhel* — *matzah* is time-bound, yet women are obligated, derived from the juxtaposition of the prohibition of *chametz* with the obligation to eat *matzah* (*lo tochal alav chametz — shivat yamim tochal alav matzot*), which applies to anyone bound by the *chametz* prohibition. *Simchah* — the obligation of festive joy — derives from *vesamachta ata u'veitecha*, "you and your household," which includes women. *Hakhel* — the septennial assembly — explicitly enumerates *anashim, venashim, vehataf*.

Against the claim that women are obligated in all non-time-bound positive commandments: *harei Talmud Torah, peru urvu, u'Pidyon HaBen*. Women are exempt from *Talmud Torah*, derived from *velimaditem otam et beneichem* — "your sons," implying not your daughters. Women are exempt from *peru urvu* — procreation — derived from the concluding phrase of the commandment, *umilu et ha'aretz vechivshuha*, "and conquer," which implies the verse addresses men. And women are exempt from *Pidyon HaBen*, derived from a principle connecting the obligation to redeem with the theoretical capacity to have been redeemed — an obligation structured around a paternal relationship.

### Rule Paradox

This lengthy catalogue of exceptions invites genuine reflection on the explanatory power of the rule. Rabbi Saul Berman, in a well-known article on women and *mitzvot*, observed that when one counts the total number of positive commandments that are actually time-bound and those that are not, the exceptions on each side approach, and perhaps equal, the number of cases that actually conform to the rule. If the exceptions are approximately as numerous as the conforming cases, one must ask: in what sense is the rule truly explanatory? The rule *mitzvot asei shehazman grama* is often invoked as though it provides a principled reason for why women are exempt from particular *mitzvot* — but if the exceptions are equally numerous, the rule loses much of its descriptive and normative force. This does not render Rabbi Yochanan's principle incorrect; rather, it illustrates precisely his point that *klalos* are never to be trusted as exhaustive.

The *gemara* then restates Rabbi Yochanan's conclusion: *ein lemedin min haklalos va'afilu b'makom shene'emar bo chutz* — even in cases where exceptions are explicitly listed, one cannot be certain the list is complete. The more obvious case (a *klal* with no exceptions listed) having been demonstrated, the *gemara* now turns to demonstrate the rule in the context of an explicit *chutz*.

### Zavim Merkav Case

Abaye — or, as the *gemara* alternatively attributes, Rabbi Yirmiya — cites a further example: *od klal echad amru* — another general rule was taught — in *Zavim*. *Kol she'nisa al gabei hazav tamei* — anything that a *zav* carries becomes *tamei*. *Vekol hazav nisa alav tahor* — anything that carries a *zav* is *tahor*.

Some background is necessary here. The ordinary rules of *tumah* involve *tumas massa* — contracting impurity by carrying a *tamei* object. In the case of a *zav*, an unusual dynamic obtains: the *zav* is himself the *tamei* entity, yet he is a person capable of the act of carrying. Accordingly, the Torah establishes a special category — *elyono shel zav*, "what is above the *zav*" — whereby objects the *zav* carries or wears themselves become *tamei*. Rashi notes this is derived from the verse *vekol asher yihyeh tachatav*, which is read creatively to mean "anything beneath which the *zav* is" — i.e., anything that the *zav* is carrying.

The converse rule — that what carries a *zav* is *tahor* — has important qualifications. A human being who carries a *zav* contracts *tumas massa* in the ordinary way. And if the object beneath the *zav* is designed for sitting or lying — a *mishkav* or *moshav* — it becomes an *av hatumah*, even without direct contact, since its *halakhic* identity is determined by its function as the *zav*'s designated seat or bed. But an object not made for sitting or lying that happens to support a *zav* does not become *tamei*. These are the stated exceptions.

The *gemara* then asks: *v'tov leka* — are those the only exceptions? What about *merkav* — a saddle, something one rides on? The *gemara* responds that a saddle upon which the *zav* sits is itself in the category of *moshav* and would already be included. The real question concerns *gavva de'ukfa* — the pommel of the saddle, the raised front horn. The pommel supports the act of riding but is not the surface directly sat upon. The *gemara* establishes that the saddle itself (*ha'ukaf*) has the *tumah* of *moshav*, while the pommel (*hatapus*) has the *tumah* of *merkav* — a parallel but slightly lesser category. This distinction suggests that even the part of an object not directly sat upon may carry a form of *tumah* if it functionally enables the riding, which was not enumerated in the original general rule. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *shema mina ein lemedin min haklalos va'afilu b'makom shene'emar bo chutz*.

### Fungi Exception

Ravina — or, alternatively, Rav Nachman — then adduces the case closest to the present *daf*: *af anan nami tanina* — we too have taught this in our *mishna*. The *mishna* states one may use any food for *eruv* and *shituf*, *chutz min hamayim u'min hamelach* — yet there are additional exceptions. *Ve'ika kmeihim u'pitriot* — what about fungi and mushrooms? Those too cannot be used, yet they are not listed among the exceptions. Thus, *ein lomedim min haklalos va'afilu b'makom shene'emar bo chutz*.

Two distinct understandings emerge regarding why fungi are excluded, and they differ on which category the exception applies to. Tosafos reads the *gemara* as excluding fungi from *eruvei chatzerot*, *shitufei mevo'ot*, and *eruvei techumin*, on the grounds that fungi are not fit to be eaten in their raw state. This, Tosafos argues, reflects an important distinction: while *ma'aser* money may be used to purchase raw meat that is not yet fit for consumption, the *eruv* requirement demands that the food be presently edible, since the *eruv* functions to establish a legal residence and the food must plausibly represent an actual meal. Mushrooms in their raw state do not meet that standard, at least in Tosafos's view.

The *Gra*, however, reads the *gemara* differently. Noting a textual annotation (*nichtav batziddo ve-chulu* — "written alongside: etc.") indicating that the full text of the *mishna* is being referenced, the *Gra* argues that the exception applies specifically to *ma'aser sheni*, not to *eruv*. His comment on *ve'ika kmeihim u'pitriot* cites *Torat Kohanim*, *perek* 1, *piska* 8, in the context of the *ma'aser* rules. The reason fungi are excluded from *ma'aser* is that they are not *gidulei karka* — they do not genuinely grow from the ground in the manner required by the verse governing *ma'aser sheni* purchases. Thus, while Tosafos locates the exclusion in *eruv* and grounds it in a standard of present edibility, the *Gra* locates it in *ma'aser* and grounds it in the criterion of *gidulei karka*. The significance of this distinction will carry into the discussion of *ma'aser* that follows.

---

## Kesef Ma'aser

### Eruv vs. Ma'aser

The *gemara* now turns directly to the *halakhot* of *kesef ma'aser* — what may be purchased with the redeemed funds of *ma'aser sheni*. A dispute is recorded between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina. *Chad masni a'eruv* — one transmits the following clarification as pertaining to *eruv* — *vichad masni a'ma'aser* — and the other transmits it as pertaining to *ma'aser*.

### Salt Water Dip

The clarification in question is: *lo shanu ela mayim bifnei atzman u'melach bifnei atzman* — the prohibition against using water or salt applies only when each is used alone. *Aval bemayim u'melach me'arvin yachad* — but salt water, water and salt combined, one may use. The combination, functioning as a dipping condiment, acquires the status of food in a way that neither ingredient does on its own.

### Scope Comparison

The one who applies this ruling to *ma'aser* implies an even broader permission for *eruv*: *kol shekein a'eruv* — if combined salt water qualifies even for the stricter category of *ma'aser*, it certainly qualifies for *eruv*. The one who applies it to *eruv* does not necessarily extend it to *ma'aser*, since *ma'aser* may have more restrictive criteria. What are those criteria? *Pirei ba'inan* — by *ma'aser*, we require something in the conceptual category of *peri*, a fruit or product, meaning something generated by another living thing, whether animal or plant. Water and salt, as minerals and liquid, do not meet this standard, even when combined. Thus, the *ma'aser* category may be narrower: not merely any food, but specifically food that qualifies as a *peri* in the abstract sense.

Tosafos introduces a nuance that runs in the opposite direction: there is one area in which *eruv* is actually more demanding than *ma'aser*. As noted above, the food for an *eruv* must be presently edible — fit to be eaten in its current state — whereas *ma'aser* money may be used to purchase raw meat and other foods not yet ready to eat. This is the foundation of Tosafos's understanding of why fungi are excluded from *eruv* but not from *ma'aser*. Setting this aside, the general pattern holds: *ma'aser* is the narrower category, defined by the requirement of *peri*, and possibly by *gidulei karka* as well.

### Fish Brine Testimony

Rav Yitzchak, upon returning from *Eretz Yisrael*, transmitted this ruling as applying to *ma'aser*. The *gemara* challenges him with a *beraita*: Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish testified before Rabbi Eliezer that in his father's household, *tzir* — fish brine — was purchased with *ma'aser* money. The *gemara* responds to the challenge:

### Fish in Brine

*Shema lo shamata ela k'she'irvei dagim me'uravin bahen* — perhaps what Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish testified was only valid when actual pieces of fish were mixed into the brine. Plain brine, without fish, would not qualify. Even Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish's permission extends only to *tzir*, and he grounds it in *shumnah depeirah hu* — the brine carries the "fat" of the fish, understood as a product of the fish itself. Fish, as a living creature producing offspring, qualifies as a *peri* in the abstract sense, and the brine that exudes from the fish partakes of that status. But plain salt water, with no fish component, would not.

### Oil Addition

Rav Yosef offers a resolution at the top of 27b: *lo nitzrecha ela shenasan lesochan shemen* — the permission to use salt water for *ma'aser* applies specifically when oil has been added to the mixture. In that case, it is the oil — a legitimate *ma'aser* product — that grounds the permission, and the salt water is permitted along with it.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye immediately objects: *vetifok lei mishum shemen* — if the entire basis of the permission is the oil, why mention salt water at all? Simply say one may spend *ma'aser* money on oil. What is the *chiddush* of including the salt water in the discussion?

### Havla'ah Principle

The *gemara* answers: *tzricha* — it is indeed necessary, because the case teaches the principle of *havla'ah*: *shenasan dmei mayim u'melach b'havla'ah* — that one may pay for salt water using *ma'aser* money when it is absorbed (*bilvua*) into the larger purchase. If one spends ten coins of *ma'aser sheni* funds on a composite dip consisting of oil, water, and salt, part of the purchase price is factually going toward the salt water. The principle of *havla'ah* holds that when a non-qualifying ingredient is acquired as part of a unified purchase whose primary component is legitimate, the portion of the price attributable to the non-qualifying element is absorbed and permitted along with the rest.

The *gemara* confirms this from a *beraita*: Ben Bag Bag says that the verse *vekol asher tishalkha nafshecha*, in its context alongside *bakar, tzon, yayin, u'shechar*, teaches through each word that *havla'ah* applies to various composite units. When one buys cattle, some of the cost goes toward the hide, which is not food; when one buys sheep, some goes toward the wool; when one buys wine, some goes toward the bottle; and when one buys *temed* — a fermented mead made by soaking grape lees in water — the primary ingredient is water, with only a trace contribution from the grape product. In each case, *ma'aser* money may be used for the entire purchase. This is the *halakhic* principle of *havla'ah* — secondary and otherwise non-qualifying components are absorbed into, and covered by, the primary legitimate purchase.

---

## Ben Bag Bag Exegesis

### Cattle Example

Ben Bag Bag derives *havla'ah* from the verse *babakar* — cattle. *Melamed shelokchin bakar agav oro* — one may purchase cattle with *ma'aser* money even though some of the cost goes toward the hide, which is not food. The justification is *mishum degufei hu* — the hide is literally part of the same body. It is physically inseparable from the animal and constitutes a genuine unity with it.

### Bakar Necessity

Rabbi Yochanan famously declares: *man de'mitargem li b'vakar aliba d'Ben Bag Bag* — whoever can explain to me why Ben Bag Bag requires the word *bakar* in the verse, *movilna manei avatrei l'vei masuta* — I will carry his clothes after him to the bathhouse. In other words, why is *bakar* necessary at all? Given that *tzon* — sheep — already teaches *havla'ah* in a harder case (since wool, unlike skin, can be detached), does not *bakar* follow all the more readily? The *gemara* develops this challenge carefully.

### Sheep Example

*Bakar* could not have been inferred from *tzon* alone. Had the Torah only mentioned sheep, one might have thought the permission regarding *gizatah* — its wool — applied only because the wool is still physically attached to the body at the time of purchase (*mishum de'mechubar*). From *tzon* alone, one might not have inferred that cattle's hide may be included, since the hide might be treated as a mere *tofel* without even the argument of *guf echad* — one unified body — which does apply to the skin of cattle in a way distinct from wool. Therefore, *bakar* is needed to teach the paradigmatic case of skin as literally part of the body.

### Wine Example

*Tzon* could not have been inferred from *yayin* alone. Wine comes with a bottle — *agav kankanno* — which is clearly a separate object from the contents it contains. One might have thought *havla'ah* applies only because the bottle is the container without which the wine cannot exist or be transported — *hainu netiruteih*, that is its means of preservation. But extending this to wool, which is not necessary for the sheep's continued existence, would not follow. Hence *tzon* must be stated separately.

### Mead Example

*Shechar* — mead or the fermented *temed* — teaches the most extreme application of *havla'ah*. *Temed mishehichmitz*: wine lees were soaked in water until the mixture became slightly sharp, and then the water was poured off and drunk. In this preparation, the actual grape contribution is minimal — *dikpaya d'alma hu* — it is essentially just the sharpness, a faint trace of fruit character in what is fundamentally water. One might have thought *ma'aser* money could not be spent on something so predominantly water-based. Therefore *shechar* must be stated: even this qualifies.

### Each Word Distinct

The *gemara* works through the logic in both directions, demonstrating that no word in the list could have been omitted. Had only *shechar* been written, one might have understood it to mean *dveilah ke'ilit* — a particular type of intoxicating date-product, which is genuine fruit — and derived nothing about wine with its bottle or sheep with its wool. Had only *yayin* been written, one would know the bottle is included because of *netirutei*, but not have extended *havla'ah* to wool. Had only *tzon* been written, one might have read *agav gizatah* as referring to a sheep already shorn — meaning only the skin qualifies — and not to the wool as such. Therefore *bakar* is needed: from *bakar* we derive the skin, from *tzon* we derive the wool, from *yayin* the bottle, and from *shechar* the case of a predominantly non-food component. Each word performs irreplaceable work.

The ultimate resolution to Rabbi Yochanan's challenge, then, is as follows: *aval tzon agav gizoteiha mishteban, bakar agav ora miba'ei?* — if we know that sheep may be purchased together with their wool, is there any question that cattle may be purchased together with their skin? The answer is that without the word *bakar*, we would have misread *tzon* as referring only to a shorn sheep, leaving the skin of cattle unaddressed. *Tzon* is needed to teach wool; *bakar* is needed to establish that the skin-inclusion principle exists so that *tzon* can be read to include the wool. Each word is thus indispensable, and the system is fully coherent.

The *chiddush* of the entire passage for the *halakha* of *ma'aser sheni* is therefore: *havla'ah* is a genuine principle. The composite salt-water-and-oil dip may be purchased with *ma'aser sheni* funds, even though part of the price is going toward water and salt that could not be purchased alone, because those elements are absorbed into the primary legitimate purchase. The same principle underlies every composite acquisition — the animal with its hide, the sheep with its wool, the wine with its bottle, the mead with its water base.

---

## Hermeneutical Approaches

### Ribbuy U'Miu'ut Method

The *gemara* now turns to a foundational question: on what hermeneutical basis do the *tannaim* disagree about what may be purchased with *ma'aser sheni* funds? *B'mai kamiflagi Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish v'Rabbi Eliezer v'hani tannai d'lekaman?* — what is the methodological dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish and Rabbi Eliezer on one side, and the other *tannaim* on the other?

The answer is that they employ different hermeneutical schools. Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish and Rabbi Eliezer interpret the verse using *ribbuy u'mi'ut* — the method of inclusive and exclusive language. The relevant verse is: *V'nasatah hakesef b'chol asher te'aveh nafshecha* — *riba*, inclusive; *babakar uvatzon uvayayin uvashechar* — *mi'et*, limiting terms; *uvechol asher tishalkha nafshecha* — *chazar v'riba*, returning to inclusion. This produces a structure of *ribbuy, mi'ut, ribbuy*.

### Three-Term Rule

Under the *ribbuy u'mi'ut* methodology, the structure *ribbuy–mi'ut–ribbuy* yields the conclusion *riba hakol* — virtually everything is included. The limiting middle term (*mi'ut*) does not narrow the category to items similar to the list; rather, it serves only to exclude that which is most dissimilar from all the items mentioned. *U'mai mi'et?* — what does the limiting term exclude? For Rabbi Eliezer, it excludes *tzir* — fish brine alone; for Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish, it excludes *mayim u'melach* — plain water and salt. Fish is certainly included by both, since fish, as a living creature producing offspring, qualifies as a *peri* in the abstract sense, and the brine is arguably a product of the fish as well.

### Klal U'Prat Method

*V'hani tannai darshi klal u'prat* — the other *tannaim* employ the school of *klal u'prat*. The identical verse is now read as: *bechol asher te'aveh nafshecha* — *klal*, a general term; *babakar uvatzon uvayayin uvashechar* — *prat*, specific terms; *uvechol asher tishalkha nafshecha* — *chazar v'klal*, a return to the general. This three-part structure — *klal, prat u'klal* — yields the conclusion *ein ata dan ela k'ein haprat* — you may only include items similar to the specific terms.

### Inclusion Criteria

What makes the specific items in the *prat* distinctive? Two criteria are identified: *pri mi'pri* — they are a product produced from another product, in the sense of a fruit or living-generated item — and *gidulei karka* — they grow from the ground. *Af kol pri mi'pri v'gidulei karka* — anything that satisfies both criteria falls within the scope of the verse.

### Fish Exclusion

The consequence of the *klal u'prat* method is that fish are excluded. Fish do not grow from the ground — they live in water and reproduce in water. However clearly they satisfy *pri mi'pri* (since fish are born from other fish), they fail the criterion of *gidulei karka*, and under *klal u'prat u'klal* both criteria must be met. Fish brine, accordingly, also falls outside the permitted category.

### Tomorrow Preview

The *gemara*'s analysis of these hermeneutical approaches bears directly on the question, raised earlier, of mushrooms and fungi under the *Gra*'s reading. If fungi are excluded from *ma'aser sheni* because they are not *gidulei karka* — as the *Gra* argues from *Torat Kohanim* — then their exclusion fits neatly within the *klal u'prat u'klal* methodology: they fail the criterion of growth from the ground. This will be developed further in the following *daf*, where the *Gra*'s understanding of fungi as *ein lomedim min haklalos* exceptions will receive fuller treatment alongside the broader debate about what qualifies under the *klal u'prat* approach.

---

# Eiruvin 28

## Mishnah & Global Stateme…

### Mishnah Overview

Today's daf is 28, and we pick up from the bottom of 27b. The *mishnah* had established two parallel rules: one may use virtually anything for *eruv*, and virtually anything for *maaser sheni*, with the exception of *maaser sheni* money, water, and salt. The structure of today's discussion follows from those two broad permissions, and the bulk of the daf is devoted to qualifying and limiting them — adding, case by case, to the list of exceptions.

### Reb Yochanan's Warning

Rabbi Yochanan had already cautioned that one should not rely on global statements of this kind, even when they are accompanied by explicit exceptions. His point is that such formulations are inherently imprecise: the "except" clause does not exhaust the exclusions, and the day's learning will bear this out repeatedly. We begin with *maaser sheni* and then circle back to *eruv*.

---

## Maaser Sheni Fish Brine

### Fish Brine Debate

The *Gemara* opens with a *tannaim* dispute concerning fish brine. Two *tannaim* both exclude plain salt water but debate whether fish brine is included within the scope of *maaser sheni* purchases. Both, however, agree that actual fish are permissible. A third view holds that fish are excluded entirely. The *Gemara* traces this disagreement to a fundamental difference in hermeneutical method applied to the *pasuk* in Devarim: *venatata hakesef bechol asher te'aveh nafshecha babakar uvatzon uvayayin uvashichar uv'chol asher tish'alcha nafshecha* — "you shall give the money for whatever your soul desires: cattle, sheep, wine, or strong drink, or whatever your soul asks." The structure of this verse is: a general statement, a specific list, and another general statement.

### Hermeneutical Schools

The question is how to apply hermeneutical principles to this three-part structure. The school of Rebbi Yishmael employs the rule of *klal u'prat u'klal* — general, particular, general — which yields a category defined by similarity to the specific middle list. The school of Rebbi Akiva, by contrast, applies *ribuy u'mi'ut u'ribuy* — inclusion, exclusion, inclusion — which produces a considerably broader category. Under *ribuy u'mi'ut u'ribuy*, once there is a *ribuy* and a *mi'ut*, the second *ribuy* implies that virtually everything is included except what is most dissimilar from the list — which would mean only things like water and salt, substances that belong to neither the animal nor the plant world. Under *klal u'prat u'klal*, however, the derived category must be *ke'ein ha'prat*, similar to the specific items enumerated, and the analysis becomes considerably more restrictive.

### Pri Mipri & Mushrooms

The *Gemara* now asks: what, precisely, is "similar" to the *prat* according to those who apply *klal u'prat u'klal*? The answer given is *mah ha'prat meforash pri mipri ve'gidulei karka* — just as the specific items in the list are a "fruit from a fruit" and grow from the ground, so too anything derived from such a category is included. The term *pri mipri* is not limited to literal fruit in its natural state; as Rashi in Bava Kamma explains, it encompasses things produced from fruit — wine, for instance, is the product of grapes and qualifies as *pri mipri*. The requirement of *gidulei karka* means the item must derive from something that grows from the ground.

This formulation excludes mushrooms on two grounds: first, a mushroom does not come from another mushroom in the ordinary reproductive sense; second, and more compellingly, mushrooms grow from decomposing matter and do not draw their nutrients from the ground the way ordinary plants do. They are not truly *gidulei karka*. Rashi in Bava Kamma states this explicitly, and notably, the *braita* that appears at the beginning of the *Sifra* — the *braita* of Rebbi Yishmael's thirteen hermeneutical principles — uses precisely this case, *maaser sheni* and the exclusion of mushrooms, as the paradigmatic illustration of *klal u'prat u'klal*.

### Vlad Vladot & Fish

A second *braita* formulates the same rule differently: *mah ha'prat meforash vlad vladot aretz* — just as the specific items are "descendants of the descendants of the land," so too the full category must satisfy that description. One might assume that *vlad vladot aretz* and *pri mipri* are simply two ways of expressing the same idea, but the *Gemara* asks whether there is a practical difference between them.

Abaye answers: *dagim*, fish, constitute the point of difference. According to the formulation *pri mipri ve'gidulei karka*, fish might be included, since one could argue that they live off of things that ultimately draw their nourishment from the ground. Tosafot notes in multiple places that *gidulei karka* can be understood in either a narrow sense — things that literally spring from the earth, like plants — or in a broader sense — things whose nutritional chain traces back to the ground. If the broader reading is intended, fish, which feed on vegetation in the water or on other fish that do so, might qualify. The *Gemara* will proceed to challenge this.

According to the formulation of *vlad vladot ha'aretz*, however, the critical question is not how the creature currently sustains itself but how it was created in *maaseh bereishit*. Land animals were fashioned from the ground; fish, *dagim mi'maya ivru*, were created from the water. Accordingly, fish are excluded under *vlad vladot ha'aretz* in a way they might not be under *pri mipri ve'gidulei karka*.

The *Gemara* then questions Abaye's premise. Would Abaye truly classify fish as *gidulei karka*? Abaye himself has a famous statement at the top of 28a: one who eats a *putita* — a water insect — receives four lashes, corresponding to four distinct prohibitions. The count depends on the creature being classified as a water creature rather than a land creature. If fish and water insects were considered *gidulei karka*, a water insect would also fall under the prohibition of *sheretz ha'shoretz al ha'aretz* and the lash count would increase. Since Abaye does not include that prohibition in his count, he evidently does not treat water creatures as *gidulei karka*. Ravina therefore proposes a different answer.

### Birds & Creation

Ravina suggests that *ofos*, birds, are the true point of difference between the two formulations. Under *pri mipri ve'gidulei karka*, birds are included: they currently live off of what grows from the ground and satisfy the criterion of *gidulei karka* in the broader sense. Under *vlad vladot ha'aretz*, however, the question is how they were created, and here the *Gemara* invokes a well-known textual difficulty. In the first chapter of Bereishit, birds appear to have been created from the water: *yishretzu hamayim sheretz nefesh chaya ve'of ye'ofef al ha'aretz*. Yet in the second chapter, the verse states: *vayitzer Hashem Elokim min ha'adama kol chayat ha'sadeh ve'et kol of ha'shamayim* — He formed from the ground all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the heavens. How can birds be said to have been formed from the ground if the earlier account created them from the water?

The *Gemara*'s resolution is that birds were created from *rakak* — mud, a mixture of water and earth. Mud is not simply ground, and therefore birds do not qualify as *vlad vladot ha'aretz* in the full sense. Accordingly, the practical difference between the two formulations is this: *pri mipri ve'gidulei karka* includes birds but excludes fish; *vlad vladot ha'aretz* excludes both. On fish, both approaches agree on exclusion.

### Abstraction Debate

This leaves an important question. Both formulations belong to the *klal u'prat u'klal* school — they agree that the derived category must resemble the *prat*. Why then does one formulation yield a broader category (including birds) while the other yields a narrower one (excluding birds)? The *Gemara* asks: *man de'amar be'ofos mai ta'ama u'man de'miat ofos mai ta'ama* — what is the underlying reasoning of each position?

The *Gemara*'s answer is subtle. Even within the framework of *klal u'prat u'klal*, one can ask which building block is primary. One approach takes the first *klal u'prat* as the foundational unit: that unit, in isolation, yields only the *prat* — a very narrow list. The subsequent *klal* then broadens it, but only moderately, because one is expanding something small. The result is a list that requires resemblance in three characteristics — *pri mipri*, *gidulei karka*, and *vlad vladot ha'aretz*. This is the position of *klala kamma davka*: the first *klal* is the operative anchor.

The other approach takes the *prat u'klal* as the primary building block. That unit, in isolation, yields the *klal* — a very expansive list. The first *klal* then contracts it, but one is contracting something already very large, so the final list remains broad. The result requires resemblance in only two characteristics. This is *klala basra davka*: the final *klal* is the operative anchor. The former position excludes birds; the latter includes them.

The overall upshot of this entire hermeneutical analysis is that the *mishnah*'s sweeping statement — that one may use *maaser sheni* money for anything — is far more limited than it first appears. Even granting the most expansive reading within *klal u'prat u'klal*, mushrooms and fish are excluded. On the view of *klala kamma davka*, birds are excluded as well. The *tanna kamma* of the *mishnah* who said "anything" may well have been operating according to the Rebbi Akiva school of *ribuy u'mi'ut u'ribuy*, for whom only water and salt fall outside the category — which is why the exception he listed was so limited.

---

## Eruv Edibility Rules

### Eatable vs. Uneatable

The discussion now shifts to *eruv*. Rav Yehuda, in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat, in the name of Rav, states: one may make an *eruv* with *papuin* (cress), with *chalgoogloit* (purslane), and with *gud gadaniyot* (sweet clover). One may not make an *eruv* with *chaziz* (green corn or green wheat, the immature stalk of grain cut before it has fully developed) or with *chafniyot* (unripe dates). The criterion implicit in this list is fitness for human consumption: things that are genuinely edible qualify, while things used primarily as animal fodder, or that are insufficiently ripe, do not.

### Clover Sterilization

The *Gemara* immediately questions the inclusion of sweet clover. A *braita* teaches that sweet clover promotes sterility in men. The recommendation is that those who have many children may eat it — *gud gadaniyot marbe banim, merube banim yochlu* — while those who have no children should not — *chashuchei banim lo yochlu*. And if the plant has hardened into seed, even those with many children should avoid it for general health reasons. How then can sweet clover be classified as fit for human consumption and therefore usable for *eruv*?

The *Gemara* offers three responses. First, the statement permitting its use for *eruv* refers specifically to before the plant has hardened into seed, and to individuals who are not concerned about its reproductive effects. Second — and this is the more conceptually significant answer — even a person who cannot eat something may use it for *eruv* if it is food for others. The *mishnah* itself provides the precedent: one may make an *eruv* for a *nazir* using wine, and for an Israelite using *terumah*, even though the *nazir* may not drink wine and a non-*kohen* may not eat *terumah*. The principle is *af al gav de'lo chazi le'hai chazi le'hai* — even if it is not fit for this one, it is fit for that one, and that suffices to define it as food. The same logic applies here: sweet clover is fit for those without fertility concerns. Third, Rav's original statement permitting its use for *eruv* refers specifically to the Median variety of sweet clover, which poses no health concerns at all.

### Green Corn in Bavel

The *Gemara* then turns to *chaziz*, green corn, which was listed as impermissible for *eruv*. Yet Rav Yehuda himself, in the name of the same Rav, states elsewhere that *kshuta ve'chaziz* — hops and green corn — may be used for *eruv*, and one recites *borei pri ha'adama* over them, since they grow from the ground and are fit for eating. There is thus a direct contradiction within Rav's own rulings.

The *Gemara* resolves this: the statement prohibiting *chaziz* was issued before Rav came to Bavel, when he was living in Eretz Yisrael, where green corn was not consumed by humans and was considered animal fodder. Once he arrived in Bavel and observed that people there do eat it, he revised his position. The *Gemara* objects to this resolution: is Bavel the majority of the world? Why should local Babylonian practice override the general human norm?

### Intention Changes

The objection draws on a *braita* about *pul* (beans), *se'ora* (barley), and *tilson* (fenugreek). These plants are ordinarily cultivated for their seeds. If one planted them with the intention of harvesting them as vegetables — eating their leaves and stalks — *batla da'ato etzel kol adam*: the individual's idiosyncratic intention is voided by the universal norm. The legal consequence is that *ma'aser* obligation attaches to their seeds but not to their vegetable portion, regardless of what the planter intended. One cannot redefine what something is by deciding to use it differently than everybody else does.

By contrast, *shachalayim* (cress) and *gargir* (arugula) are plants that people commonly eat both as vegetables and for their seeds, so intention does matter for them. If one planted them as vegetables, the vegetable character is primary; if for seed, the seed character is primary. But for the grains that are universally understood as seed crops, the individual who plants them as vegetables is simply ignored.

The implication for *chaziz* is sharp: if the majority of the world considers it animal food, the fact that people in Bavel eat it should be dismissed the same way idiosyncratic individual intentions are dismissed. The *Gemara* does not fully resolve the tension here. The answer ultimately given is that when Rav permitted *chaziz* in Bavel, he was referring to a specific cultivated variety — *digunaisa*, the garden variety of *chaziz* — which is universally eaten and unambiguously considered human food. That resolves the contradiction: the prohibition applied to the wild variety; the permission applies to the garden variety.

The question of whether Bavel's widespread practice suffices to alter the legal category is left somewhat open. Tosafot notes the difficulty: Bavel is not a few individuals but an entire large region, and it is counterintuitive to dismiss an entire country's food culture as *batla da'ato*. The distinction the *Gemara* seems to draw is between something whose basic definition is animal food — where even a whole country of human consumers cannot redefine it — and something whose basic definition is human food, where secondary reasons that prevent certain individuals from eating it (allergies, religious restrictions, health concerns) are irrelevant because the item's fundamental character remains edible.

### Child's Teaching

While on the topic of hops and green corn, the *Gemara* relates a charming episode. Rabbi Zeira, when he needed a break from learning and wanted to accumulate *s'char* even during his rest, would sit by the doorway of Rav Yehuda bar Ami and rise in honor of the rabbinic students passing in and out of the *beis medrash*. On one such occasion, a schoolchild emerged. Rabbi Zeira asked what his teacher had taught him. The child said: for *kashus* (hops), one recites *borei pri ha'adama*; for *chaziz* (green corn), one recites *shehakol nihiyeh bidvaro*. This accords with what we have seen: *chaziz* is not fully fit for eating and therefore warrants only *shehakol*, while hops are fit and warrant *borei pri ha'adama*.

Rabbi Zeira challenged the ruling: *adaraba ipcha mistabra* — the opposite seems more logical. Green corn grows directly from the ground and should therefore merit *borei pri ha'adama*. Hops, by contrast, grow as a parasitic plant, drawing their nourishment from a host plant rather than directly from the soil, and should therefore receive only *shehakol*.

The *Gemara* rules: *ve'hilchata k'yanuka d'vei Rav* — the law follows the schoolchild. *Hai gmar peira* — hops are a completed, ripened fruit, and therefore receive *borei pri ha'adama*. *Lav gmar peira* — green corn at this stage is not a completed fruit; it is not only unripe but, as established earlier, not even considered human food at this stage, meriting only *shehakol*. As for Rabbi Zeira's objection that hops grow from the air rather than the ground: the *Gemara* rejects this. *Keshuta nami me'ara ka'rabei* — hops also grow from the ground, indirectly. We can see this empirically: if you cut down the host bush, the hops die. This demonstrates that the hops are drawing real nourishment from the host plant, which in turn draws it from the ground — and that chain is sufficient to call them *gidulei karka* and to warrant *borei pri ha'adama*. This is also what distinguishes hops from mushrooms, which can grow on decaying wood entirely disconnected from the ground.

### Unripe Dates Issue

The *Gemara* returns to *chafniyot*, unripe dates, which were listed as impermissible for *eruv*. A *braita* complicates this: *kore* (heart of palm) may be purchased with *maaser sheni* money, but does not contract the ritual impurity of foodstuffs (*tum'at ochlin*). Unripe dates, by contrast, may also be purchased with *maaser sheni* money and *do* contract *tum'at ochlin* — they are therefore considered food. If they are food, why can they not be used for *eruv*?

Rabi Yehuda in the same *braita* adds his position: *kore* is like wood in all respects except that it may be purchased with *maaser sheni* money. As for unripe dates, they are fully a fruit in all respects except that they are exempt from *ma'aser* — because they have not yet reached the stage of full ripeness that triggers *ma'aser* obligation.

The *Gemara* initially suggests that the *braita*'s statements about unripe dates refer to the male palm variety, which never ripens and is therefore always in the same state. For that variety, even the unripe stage is the final and consumable form, and it is unambiguously food. The *Gemara* rejects this: if the male variety were meant, Rabbi Yehuda would never have exempted it from *ma'aser*, because for a variety that never develops further, whatever stage it has reached is its maximum — and Rabbi Yehuda himself explicitly rules elsewhere that the unripe dates of certain specific locations, such as the dates of Tuvina, are *chayav* in *ma'aser*.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes that both the *braita* and our original ruling refer to the ordinary female palm variety. The resolution rests on an important distinction introduced by Rabbi Yochanan: *ho'il ve'ra'uy l'matkan al yedei ha'ur* — since they can be sweetened by cooking them over fire, they qualify as food for purposes of *tum'at ochlin* and for redemption with *maaser sheni* money. But *eruv* imposes a stricter standard: the food must be fit for eating in exactly the state it is in right now, without requiring any preparation. Unripe dates that need to be cooked before they are palatable fail this test. Raw meat provides a parallel: one may certainly use *maaser sheni* money to purchase raw meat, but one may not use raw meat for *eruv*, because it is not currently fit for immediate consumption.

The context for Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is a *braita* about *shkedim ha'marim*, bitter almonds. When small and unripe, bitter almonds are still edible and are therefore obligated in *ma'aser*; when large and ripe, they are bitter and inedible and are therefore exempt. Sweet almonds follow the opposite pattern: large ones are obligated; small, unripe ones are exempt. Rabbi Shimon bar Yossi in the name of his father says both sizes of the bitter variety are exempt. Others say both are obligated. Rabbi Yochanan's statement responds to the latter position: how can the large, bitter almonds be obligated if they are inedible? *Ho'il ve'ra'uy l'matkan al yedei ha'ur* — since they can be made palatable by cooking, they count as food for *ma'aser* and *tum'at ochlin* purposes. But that leniency does not extend to *eruv*, where immediate edibility is required.

---

## Heart of Palm

### Kore as Wood

Having addressed unripe dates, the *Gemara* returns to the statement about *kore*, the heart of palm. Rabbi Yehuda's ruling was: *kore* is like wood in all respects, except that it may be purchased with *maaser sheni* money. This appears to say exactly what the first *tanna* said — namely, that it is purchasable with *maaser sheni* money but not considered food for *tum'at ochlin* purposes.

### Boiling & Frying

Abaye explains the difference between them: *shulka ve'tigna ika beinaihu* — boiling and frying. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who categorically declares *kore* to be wood, even boiling and frying it would not change its status. It would be, as it were, fried wood. According to the first *tanna*, who does not make such a categorical declaration, perhaps once the heart of palm has been sufficiently prepared and rendered genuinely edible, it would acquire the status of food for *tum'at ochlin* purposes.

### Rava on Bracha

Rava challenges Abaye's distinction. Would anyone truly say that boiling and frying fails to confer food status? A *braita* explicitly addresses the case of animal hide and placenta: hide is not food and does not receive *tum'at ochlin*; but hide that has been boiled, or a placenta that one intended to eat, does receive *tum'at ochlin*. Even hide — something that no one thinks of as food in its ordinary state — becomes food once sufficiently prepared. It strains credulity to say that boiled and fried heart of palm would not be food for anyone.

Rava therefore proposes a different resolution: *ika beinaihu bracha* — the operative difference between the two opinions is the blessing one recites over *kore*.

### Rav Yehuda vs. Shmuel

The debate over the *bracha* on *kore* is attributed to Rav Yehuda and Shmuel. Rav Yehuda holds that one recites *borei pri ha'adama*, because *kore* is food. Shmuel holds that one recites *shehakol nihiyeh bidvaro*, because *kivan shesofo lehakshot* — since the heart of palm will eventually harden into the trunk of the tree, it is considered part of the tree and therefore not a fruit of the ground in the relevant sense. Shmuel himself conceded to Rav Yehuda's reasoning, saying *kevatech mistabra* — your opinion is more logical — pointing to the analogy of a radish, which will also eventually harden yet still receives *borei pri ha'adama*.

### Final Ruling on Kore

The *Gemara* rejects the analogy. A radish is planted expressly to be eaten as a radish; it is inherently the "fruit" the farmer seeks. A palm tree, by contrast, is not planted for its heart of palm — *lo nati inash ada'ata d'kora*. The heart of palm is an incidental byproduct of a tree planted for its dates. Since the heart of palm was never the intended product, and since it will inevitably become part of the wooden trunk, it retains its identification with the tree and is not reclassified as food. Accordingly: *hilchata kevasei de'Shmuel* — the law follows Shmuel. Despite Shmuel's own expressed admiration for Rav Yehuda's position, the ruling is *shehakol nihiyeh bidvaro* over *kore*.

---

---

# Eiruvin 30

## Food Quantities

### Sheshisa/Kisoni

The daf begins at the bottom of 28b, dealing with various items and their use in an *eiruv techumin*. To recall the framework: while *eiruv chatzeiros* requires bread specifically, *eiruv techumin* may be established with any type of food sufficient to constitute two meals. The Gemara proceeds to address specific foods whose quantities require clarification.

*Sheshisa* is a preparation made from roasted grain combined with honey and other ingredients — a kind of sweet food. Since there is no question that it qualifies as human food, the only issue is the required amount. Rav Acha bar Pinchas rules: two scoops (*trei sargushi*), whatever that measure entails locally.

*Kisoni* is similar but simpler — roasted grain without the mixture. Abaye rules: two measures of Pumbedisa (*trei bunei de-Pumbedisa*), the local standard of that city. Abaye then adds a medical note in the name of the woman who raised him, whom he calls his *em* — his nursemaid, who served as his mother after his own mother died. She taught him that *kisoni*, roasted grain, is good for the heart (*ma'ali le-libba*) and dispels anxious thoughts (*mevatli machshavta*). Abaye further quotes her regarding a remedy for weakness of the heart: take meat from the right thigh of a ram, burn dried dung of grazing animals from the month of Nissan to make coals, roast the meat over them, eat it, and drink mixed wine afterward. Abaye frequently cited his nursemaid's guidance on such medical matters.

### Condiment vs. Main

Returning to the quantitative standards for *eiruv techumin*, Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel, five lines from the bottom of 28b: anything that functions as a condiment (*liftan*) requires the amount that one would eat *with* other food during two meals (*kedei le-echol bo*), while anything that is not a condiment requires the amount one would eat of it straight to constitute two meals (*kedei le-echol mimenu*).

There is a certain irony here: something less central to the meal — a condiment — requires a smaller quantity to count as two meals' worth for *eiruv techumin*, since one only uses a little of it per meal. As was discussed previously, even a small quantity of vinegar — the amount one would put on a salad — suffices, and according to one opinion it counts even if the salad was not the main dish.

### Raw/Roasted Meat

The Gemara turns to raw meat (*basar chai*). One might have thought raw meat could not be used for an *eiruv* at all — who eats raw meat? — yet the Gemara proceeds on the assumption that raw meat is edible and classifies it as *kedei le-echol mimenu*: one needs the amount one would eat of it straight, not as a condiment on bread. This is already quite surprising, since raw meat eaten as a stand-alone food is hardly a common practice.

*Basar tzelui*, roasted meat, generates a dispute. Rabba holds that roasted meat is a condiment (*kedei le-echol bo*) — you eat it together with bread, not straight. Rav Yosef disagrees and rules *kedei le-echol mimenu*, holding that roasted meat is eaten straight. Rav Yosef then asks: how do I know this? Because the Persians (*parsa'ei*) eat chunks of meat (*tavhikei*) without bread. Hence roasted meat is a stand-alone food, not merely a condiment.

### Persian Standard

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef: are Persians the majority of the world (*ruba de'alma*)? He demonstrates from a *baraita* that we do not allow a subgroup's practice to define the standard for everyone. The *baraita* teaches that the minimum size that constitutes a garment differs based on whether the owner is poor or wealthy. Clothing of the poor (*bigdei ani'im*) is classified as a garment at three finger-widths by three finger-widths, while clothing of the wealthy (*bigdei ashirim*) requires three *tefachim* by three *tefachim*. A piece of fabric that a poor person would use as a patch or small covering counts as a garment for him; the wealthy would discard anything of that size. These categories are therefore applied separately to each social group. One does not take the poor person's lower threshold and extend it to classify rags as garments for everyone; equally, one does not demand the wealthy person's standard of the poor.

The implication is clear: Persians' eating customs may define the *halacha* for Persians, but one cannot project that standard onto the rest of humanity. Each subgroup is assessed by the criteria relevant to it.

## Standards Debate

### Clothing Sizes

The discussion of Persian standards leads directly into a broader question about universal versus subjective or group-specific measures, and the Gemara introduces the clothing analogy as the governing precedent. As already noted, *bigdei ani'im la-ani'im* and *bigdei ashirim la-ashirim*: each group's garment-size threshold applies within that group only. The principle is that when different groups genuinely use objects differently, the relevant measure is determined by the practices of the group in question, not by some externally imposed uniform standard.

### Stringency/Leniency

The Gemara then raises a possible counter-principle: perhaps the criterion for applying a group-specific standard is whether it results in a *chumra* or a *kula*. In the clothing case, using the smaller standard for the poor person is a *chumra* applied to that group — a small scrap is enough to become *tamei*, which is the stringent result. So perhaps the rule is: we apply the subgroup's standard only when it produces a *stringency* for that subgroup.

By contrast, in the roasted meat case, invoking the Persian standard would produce a *chumra* for everyone — classifying roasted meat as a main dish requires a larger quantity for *eiruv*, making it harder to establish the *eiruv*. The Gemara seems to be suggesting that we could at least apply the Persian custom as a *chumra* for all. The way Rashi frames the issue is that perhaps the default assumption ought to be that a food is a main dish rather than a condiment, and that assumption should stand until there is evidence to the contrary that is relevant for the general population.

A *baraita* is then cited that complicates this *chumra*/*kula* framework considerably. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules: when establishing an *eiruv* for a sick person (*choleh*) or an elderly person (*zaken*), one uses the amount sufficient for *their* two meals — a subjective, reduced standard. But for someone who is ravenous (*ravtan*), one does not use his outsized meal as the measure; instead one applies the average standard (*seudah beinonis shel kol adam*).

This is striking. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar applies the subjective standard only in the lenient direction: when a person's particular circumstances call for a smaller quantity, we accommodate that. But when a person's exceptional appetite would call for a larger quantity, we revert to the universal average. The Gemara notes this is the exact opposite of what the *chumra*/*kula* framework might have predicted, and concludes: *kashya* — this is difficult. It is not straightforward to reconcile the various cases using a simple stringency-leniency principle.

It should be noted that the parallel is also imperfect on its own terms. In the case of the poor and the wealthy, each group's relevant standard is applied specifically to that group. The Gemara's attempt to use the Persian custom to establish a universal *chumra* does not fit that model cleanly: the issue there was not about applying Persians' own standard to Persians, but about extending it to everyone. And Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling is even more individualized — not a subgroup but a particular person — which is a greater *chiddush* than the *ani'im* and *ashirim* distinction.

### R. Shimon Standard

The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is truly consistent in applying subjective standards. It asks: did Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar really say one can go leniently based on individual capacity?

A *baraita* is cited: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules regarding Og Melech ha-Bashan — *pitcho k'milo'o*, his doorway must match his full size.

The context requires some background. There is a *halacha* known as *sof tumah latzes*: when a corpse lies in a house, the doorway through which the body will ultimately be removed is treated as if already opened, and *tumah* exits through it. If a specific exit is designated, only that exit transmits *tumah* to the outside; this spares the other exits. But a doorway can only serve as the designated exit if it is of minimal halachic size — at least four *tefachim* wide.

Now imagine the corpse of Og Melech ha-Bashan, the giant of Bashan, lies in a house. If one wishes to designate a specific exit so as to protect the other openings from *tumah*, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that the door must be large enough to actually extract the giant. A standard four-*tefachim* doorway would not suffice; one needs a doorway that matches the enormous body. This is subjective measurement in the stringent direction — applying a larger-than-normal standard because the particular object (in this case, the body) demands it.

This seems to contradict the leniency-only application of subjective standards that characterized Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's *eiruv* ruling. The Gemara asks: and did Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar really say this?

The Gemara cites Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: regarding Og Melech ha-Bashan's doorway, the standard four *tefachim* suffices (*pitcho b'arba*). This would mean we do not go by the giant's subjective size in the stringent direction after all — which would vindicate the claim that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar only applies subjective standards leniently.

The Gemara deflects this proof: perhaps Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies only where there are *multiple* openings in the house, one of which is four *tefachim*, and one could designate that one as the exit since it is the most likely candidate for expansion — *de'ika chad de'hava arba'ah, de'vada'ei ki ka marvach behu ka marvach*. One expands the opening that is already at the minimal qualifying size. But if all openings are equally sub-standard for a body the size of Og's, none of them is a proper doorway for him at all, and then Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar might indeed hold that all are *tamei*.

The practical question of how Og came to be inside the house in the first place is left to the imagination.

Abaye then answers the challenge from Og's door more directly: *hasam heichi liyaved* — what do you want to do there, chop him up into pieces and carry him out? There is no alternative. With the ravenous person, by contrast, one could still manage with a standard two-meal quantity; it would merely be insufficient to fully sate him. The two cases are therefore not parallel. For Og's door, there is no way to call an undersized doorway his exit because physically he cannot fit through it. For the *ravtan*, the Gemara can still maintain the universal standard of two average meals.

### Og's Door

The Gemara then explores a further question: *ibaya lehu* — they raise the issue of whether the *rabbanan* dispute Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar or whether all agree with him. The Gemara brings a proof from Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan regarding Og's doorway — as just discussed, Rabbi Yochanan rules four *tefachim* suffices — and then deflects it on the grounds discussed above, that this could be a case where there is already one opening of four *tefachim* and one would expand that one.

The Gemara then returns to raw meat, having earlier assumed without discussion that it may be used for an *eiruv*. Rav Chiya bar Abba says in the name of Rav: one may indeed establish an *eiruv* with raw meat. Rav Shimi bar Chiya adds: one may establish an *eiruv* with raw eggs. How much raw egg constitutes two meals' worth? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak — identified as *Sinai*, a title given to Rav Yosef for his encyclopedic mastery — said: two raw eggs, one per meal.

It is worth pausing on the strangeness of the underlying assumption. The Gemara takes it entirely for granted that raw meat is eaten straight, and that the only question about roasted meat is whether it is eaten straight or as a condiment. More people eat raw eggs than raw meat, to be sure. But the prior discussion's casual acceptance that raw meat is consumed *kedei le-echol mimenu* — as a straight food — remains puzzling.

The broader conceptual landscape emerging from this entire discussion is that there are at least three distinct axes along which standards may be set: (1) a single universal measure for all people; (2) a group-specific measure, such as for *ani'im* and *ashirim*, or for Persians; or (3) an individual-specific measure, as Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar applies for the *choleh* and *zaken*. And across these axes, there is a further distinction between what determines whether a food qualifies at all versus how much of it counts as two meals versus whether the food is a staple or a condiment. Different questions may call for different standards, and it is not always clear which axis governs which question.

## Neder/Shebuah

### Mazon/Zan

The Gemara shifts to a new topic introduced by the *Mishnah*: one who vows not to have *mazon* — *ha-noder min ha-mazon* — is nonetheless permitted water and salt. The implication is that water and salt are not called *mazon*, but everything else apparently is. The Gemara asks whether this poses a difficulty for Rav and Shmuel, who both hold that the blessing *borei minei mezonos* is recited only over the five grains (*chameshet ha-minim*) and not over other foods.

The question is pointed: if for *neder* purposes *mazon* encompasses virtually everything edible, how can Rav and Shmuel restrict *mezonos* to the five grains only? The Gemara notes that Rav and Shmuel have already been challenged on this point elsewhere in Berachos, and asks whether the present *Mishnah* constitutes yet another contradiction to their position.

Rav Huna resolves the difficulty by reframing the *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* should be read not as *ha-noder min ha-mazon* — one who vows from *mazon* — but rather as *be-omer kol ha-zan alai*, one who declares forbidden anything that *zan* — that sustains — him. There is a conceptual distinction between *mazon*, which connotes that the item is a nutritive staple (its very identity is as a filler), and *zan*, which merely means that the item provides some degree of sustenance as one of its properties. Rav and Shmuel use *mazon* in the strict sense, limiting it to the five grains, which are the archetypal staple foods. The *Mishnah*, by contrast, uses the broader concept of *zan* — anything that fills to some degree — and therefore encompasses virtually all foods.

### Ginosar Fruits

The Gemara challenges even Rav Huna's reformulation. The claim is that water and salt don't *zan* — don't sustain — but everything else does. But does everything else truly provide satiation? The Gemara cites Rabbah bar bar Chana's account of following Rabbi Yochanan to eat the fruits of Ginosar in Eretz Yisrael — a passage that also appears in Berachos. The fruits of Ginosar were so extraordinarily delicious that quantities were gathered in enormous amounts: when a party of a hundred people went, each person gathered ten fruits; when a party of ten went, each gathered a hundred. Every hundred fruits would fill a basket holding three *se'ah*, an enormous volume. Yet after eating all of them, they would say — by way of a *shvua* — that they had not tasted enough to feel genuinely sated (*de-lo ta'amna zizuna*). The fruits were so pleasurable that the experience of fullness remained elusive. One is reminded of the popular observation about Chinese food.

The Gemara then clarifies the precise term used. The phrase is *zizuna* — a feeling of satiation — not *mazuna*, which would mean a staple food. This reinforces the distinction. The fruits of Ginosar do not fail to *zan* one; they merely fail to produce the feeling of being *mazuna*, of having consumed a staple. The distinction is between subjective satiation and the objective status of a food as a sustaining staple.

The Gemara concludes: according to Rav and Shmuel, *borei minei mezonos* is recited only over the five grains (or, in the view that extends the blessing, over rice as well). The *Mishnah* is broader because it uses *zan* rather than *mazon*. That resolves the apparent contradiction.

### Eat vs. Forbidden

Since the discussion has touched on *shvua* and *neder*, the Gemara proceeds to examine a related ruling. Rav Huna says in the name of Rav: if someone takes an oath that he will not eat a particular loaf of bread (*shvua she-lo ochel kikar zo*), one may nevertheless use that loaf for an *eiruv*. But if someone declares that this loaf is *forbidden to me* (*kikar zo alai*), one may not use it for an *eiruv*.

What distinguishes these two formulations? Rashi explains: the oath *she-lo ochel* — I will not eat — is personal and specific. The person has restricted his own act of eating, but the loaf itself retains its normal status; others may eat it freely. Since others can eat it, it qualifies as food, and one may use it for an *eiruv*. By contrast, *kikar zo alai* — this loaf is forbidden to me — is more generic and object-directed. The person has placed a broad prohibition on any benefit from this item, and using it for an *eiruv* constitutes a form of benefit that falls within that prohibition.

This raises a point flagged by Tosafos: according to a significant position in the Gemara, *eiruv techumin* may only be established as a *dvar mitzvah*. If so, does not the principle of *mitzvot lav le-hanot nitnu* — that commandments are not given for personal benefit — apply here, allowing one to use even a forbidden loaf? The standard application of *mitzvot lav le-hanot nitnu* is that the spiritual reward for fulfilling a commandment does not count as *hana'ah*. Here, however, one is gaining a concrete practical benefit — the ability to travel an additional distance — and so the principle may not apply straightforwardly. This tension is left open.

Tosafos makes an additional observation of significance for those who study Shvuos and Nedarim: there is a fundamental distinction between a *shvua* and a *neder* that underlies this entire discussion. A *shvua* is a first-person commitment — the person binds himself: *I* will not eat, *I* will not taste, *I* will not derive benefit. A *neder* operates on the object itself: *this item* is forbidden to me, as if the object has been rendered prohibited. This distinction appears almost explicitly in the final *baraita* under discussion: the emphasis on whether *I* am forbidden versus whether *the food* is forbidden captures the *shvua*/*neder* axis, not merely the difference between eating specifically and benefit generically.

### Baraita Disputes

The Gemara now examines a *baraita* that challenges Rav Huna's ruling. The *baraita* states: *ha-noder min ha-kikar, me'arvin lo bah* — if one vows not to eat from a loaf, one may use it for an *eiruv*. The Gemara initially reads this as the case where one has declared the loaf generically forbidden (*alai*), in which case Rav Huna's ruling would be contradicted. The Gemara deflects: no, the *baraita* means only the case where one said *I will not eat this* (*deamar zo*), which is consistent with Rav Huna.

The end of that *baraita* specifies: when is the loaf usable? When one said *shvua she-lo et'amenu* — an oath not to taste it. But if one said *alai* generically, what then? And the *baraita* concludes that if one declares *kikar zo hekdesh* — this loaf is consecrated — one may not use it for an *eiruv*, because *ein me'arvin be-hekdesh*. One cannot make an *eiruv* with consecrated property.

The problem is that the *baraita* seems to permit everything short of *hekdesh*, including the generic *alai* formulation. If *alai* were also forbidden, the *baraita* should have drawn that distinction rather than leaping to *hekdesh* as the only disqualifying case. The Gemara proposes reading the *baraita* as *chasurai mechasra* — incomplete as written — and reconstructing it to say: the *noder min ha-kikar* case is always permitted, even if one said *alai*; for *alai* is treated like *she-lo et'amenu* and is effective. Only *hekdesh* invalidates.

This reconstruction, however, creates difficulty for Rav Huna, whose ruling explicitly distinguishes *alai* from the oath not to eat. The Gemara concludes: that *baraita* follows Rabbi Eliezer (*d'amar ke-Rabbi Eliezer*), for we find in another *baraita* that Rabbi Eliezer himself makes precisely Rav Huna's distinction: *shvua shelo ochel kikar zo, me'arvin lo bah; kikar zo alai, ein me'arvin lo bah*.

But then the Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer was consistent, for yet another *baraita* in Rabbi Eliezer's name reads the opposite way — permitting everything except actual *hekdesh*. The resolution: *trei tanna'ei aliba de-Rabbi Eliezer* — there is a dispute among *tannaim* as to what Rabbi Eliezer's position was.

The net result is that there are two coherent positions: (1) the distinction lies between a personal oath not to eat and a generic object-directed prohibition, where the latter precludes using the loaf for an *eiruv* even though others may eat it; (2) everything is permitted until one actually sanctifies the loaf as *hekdesh*, which removes it from the category of permissible food for anyone, and only at that point is it disqualified.

## Who Cannot Eat

### Nazir/Wine Debate

The Gemara returns to the *Mishnah*'s ruling that an *eiruv* may be established with wine for a *nazir*. The assumption of the *tanna kamma* is that even if the person for whom the *eiruv* is placed cannot eat the food — since others can — it qualifies. A *nazir* is forbidden to drink wine, yet wine can be used for his *eiruv* because others can drink it. The *Mishnah*'s ruling is then identified as not following Beit Shammai.

### Yom Kippur Case

A *baraita* is cited: Beit Shammai say one may not make an *eiruv* for a *nazir* with wine nor for a *Yisrael* with *terumah*. Beit Hillel say one may do both. Our *Mishnah* follows Beit Hillel.

Beit Hillel press Beit Shammai with a challenge: do you not agree that one may establish an *eiruv* for an adult on Yom Kippur? On Yom Kippur no one may eat at all — the food is perfectly fit food, but the person for whom the *eiruv* is made cannot consume it on that day. Yet it is accepted that an *eiruv* may be placed. The food is fit to be eaten by Jews at other times, and it is food that was valid at the onset of Shabbos or Yom Kippur.

Beit Shammai respond: *aval* — they acknowledge the point — and Beit Hillel press the analogy: just as an *eiruv* may be made for an adult on Yom Kippur, so too for a *nazir* with wine, since others can drink it.

Beit Shammai might distinguish the cases: on Yom Kippur, the food was fit to be eaten by that very person a moment before Yom Kippur began — it was fit at the time of establishing the *eiruv*, when the boundary is set by being in the place as it becomes Yom Kippur. By contrast, wine for a *nazir* was never fit for him on the day the *eiruv* is placed. *Hacha leika seudah re'uyah mibod yom* — here there is no meal fit for him from the outset of that day.

The Gemara then asks: whose position is this debate following? *De-lo ke-Chananya*: not like Chananya. A *baraita* teaches that Chananya holds Beit Shammai categorically rejected the entire institution of *eiruv* as insufficient to establish the presence of a person in a location. For Beit Shammai, according to Chananya, a genuine establishment of one's location requires physically bringing all of one's possessions — one's bed, one's belongings — to that place. The debate about wine for a *nazir* presupposes that Beit Shammai accepts the general institution of *eiruv*; hence the dispute about wine for a *nazir* cannot be following Chananya's version of Beit Shammai.

The Gemara then asks who follows another *baraita* about one who made his *eiruv* wearing black clothes: if the next day he needs to go out wearing white clothes, he has not validly left (*lo yatza*). Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak identifies this as Chananya's formulation of Beit Shammai: since establishing one's presence requires bringing all one's possessions, needing different clothing the next day demonstrates that not everything was present at the time of the *eiruv*. The Gemara refines the ruling: the case is one who made the *eiruv* in white clothes and discovered he needs black — even the white clothes he had there are insufficient. One should appreciate that our normative practice follows Beit Hillel, and that considerably more stringent alternatives — including Chananya's Beit Shammai — were considered and rejected.

### Sumchus/Terumah

Sumchus dissents from the *tanna kamma*. He holds that a *Yisrael* cannot use *terumah* for an *eiruv*; the food must be fit for the person himself. The Gemara asks why Sumchus does not equally object to using wine for a *nazir* — there too the food is not fit for the person making the *eiruv*.

The answer: a *nazir* can in principle have his *nezirut* undone through *hatarat nedarim*. *Nezirut* is a verbal commitment, a species of *hekflaah*, and just as other verbal vows can be dissolved by a *chacham*, so can *nezirut*. Critically, *hatarat nedarim* is permitted even on Shabbos when done for the needs of Shabbos (*le-tzorech Shabbos*). Since he could — even during *bein ha-shmashos* — dissolve his *nezirut* in order to use the wine, the wine is theoretically fit for him. Hence Sumchus concedes that wine for a *nazir* qualifies.

But the same logic, argues the Gemara, would apply to *terumah*: the status of *terumah* is also produced by a verbal act of designation, itself a form of *haflaah*, and verbal designations can be undone. Why, then, can't a *Yisrael* theoretically undo the *terumah* status of the food during *bein ha-shmashos*, rendering it *chulin* and thus fit for him?

The Gemara proposes: undo it and re-designate *terumah* from other grain. But that grain is back at the house, not adjacent to the *eiruv* food — and *chaverim* do not separate *terumah* unless the grain is all together (*min ha-mukaf*). What about undoing it and re-designating from within the same portion? The problem is that the *eiruv* food contains exactly two meals' worth.
