The classic example of *chokekin lehashlim* involves an arched doorway that has the required four-*amah* width at the bottom but narrows toward the top: Rabbi Meir permits us to envision the archway as if the requisite rectangular space were carved into it, thereby treating it as meeting the dimensional requirement for a *mezuzah*. Similarly here: even though the branch is only four by two, we envision the remaining space as carved out of the branch, so that together with the basket, a four-by-four *tefachim* space is conceptually present.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Space Req

The second principle is that of Rabbi Yehuda: *ba'inan eruv al gabei makom arba'ah* — an *eruv* must rest on a space of four by four *tefachim* to be valid. If the *eruv* rests on a space smaller than four by four, it is not considered to occupy a real, significant location and therefore cannot function as an *eruv*. Without *chokekin lehashlim*, the basket case would fail on this ground: the basket sits in a space of four by two, which is below the threshold. But precisely because we apply *chokekin lehashlim*, we envision the full four by four, and Rabbi Yehuda's requirement is satisfied.

The *chiddush* of the basket case thus emerges: (a) the basket completes the four-by-four dimension; (b) *chokekin lehashlim* allows us to treat the completed dimension as halachically real; (c) the *eruv* thereby meets Rabbi Yehuda's space requirement. But a question immediately surfaces — if we have just established a four-by-four space above ten *tefachim*, haven't we recreated the *reshus hayachid* problem?

## Base vs. Top Question

### Rashi Base Requirement

Rashi resolves this difficulty by introducing a crucial distinction. A *reshus hayachid* requires four by four *tefachim* not only at the top of the structure but at the base. If the base of the structure — the column or trunk supporting the elevated platform — is not four by four, the elevated platform does not constitute a *reshus hayachid*, even if the top surface is four by four.

In the basket case, the branch from which the basket hangs is four by two. Even after *chokekin lehashlim* conceptually completes the space to four by four at the top, the base of the structure remains four by two. Because the base is not four by four, the space does not qualify as a *reshus hayachid*. The *eruv* can therefore sit in a space that is virtually four by four for purposes of Rabbi Yehuda's placement requirement, without that space simultaneously constituting a *reshus hayachid* that would make the *eruv* inaccessible.

### Pole Analysis

This distinction becomes clearest when the *gemara* introduces the case of a pole. The *baraita* cited in the name of Rabbi Yehuda reads: *na'atz koreh bi'reshus harabbim ve-hinnicho eiruv aleha, gavo'ah yud ve-rochavo arba'ah eruvo eruv* — one drove a post into the *reshus harabbim* and placed an *eruv* on top of it; if the post is ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* wide, the *eruv* is valid. If not — *ein eruvo eruv*.

This initially seems backwards. Ten high and four by four usually means *reshus hayachid*, which should be a problem. The *gemara* clarifies the reading: *gavo'ah asarah tzarich she-ye-hei be-rosho arba'ah* — if the post is ten *tefachim* high, it must have four by four at the top. *Ein gavo'ah asarah, ein tzarich she-ye-hei be-rosho arba'ah* — if it is not ten *tefachim* high, it need not be four by four.

The logic proceeds as follows. Below ten *tefachim*, the airspace of the *reshus harabbim* extends to that height, and the *eruv* on the post is effectively within the same domain as the person standing below — at least for *eruv* purposes. The post need not have its own four-by-four designation because it is, conceptually, continuous with the ground-level domain. But above ten *tefachim*, the post protrudes beyond the *reshus harabbim* airspace. At that height, the *eruv* only "counts as being somewhere" if it occupies a genuine space of four by four *tefachim*. Without that, it is a *makom patur* — too insignificant to be a valid location for an *eruv*.

And what of the concern that ten high and four by four is a *reshus hayachid*? Here Rashi again invokes the four-*amos* principle: within four *amos* of where the *eruv* is placed, everything is considered unified space. One does not worry about the domain distinction between the *reshus hayachid* on top of the pole and the *reshus harabbim* at ground level, because they are within four *amos* of each other and treated as the same space for *eruv* purposes.

### Rabbi Yosi Position

At this point the *gemara* raises the question: *keman?* — whose position does the basket case reflect? The *gemara* answers that it does not accord with the opinion of Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda.

The *baraita* records: Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda says, *na'atz kaneh bi'reshus harabbim ve-hiniach be-rosho terraskal* — one drove a pole into the *reshus harabbim* and placed a basket on top — *ve-zorak ve-nach le-gabav, chayav* — if one threw an object that landed in that basket, one is liable. This means that a basket atop a pole, even with no four-by-four base, constitutes a *reshus hayachid* sufficient to generate liability. Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda does not require the base to be four by four; the four-by-four dimension at the top alone is sufficient.

If so, the basket in our case — which sits above a two-by-four branch — would also constitute a *reshus hayachid* according to Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda, recreating the problem of the person standing in a *reshus harabbim* while the *eruv* sits in a *reshus hayachid*.

### Mechitza Descent Diff

The *gemara* deflects this challenge: *afilu teima Rabbi Yosi be-Rabbi Yehuda* — even according to Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda, the basket case works. Why? *Hatam hadra mechitzta, hacha lo hadra mechitzta* — there, in the pole-and-basket case, the walls of the basket descend and surround the space below, creating a genuine enclosed domain down through the pole. Here, in our tree-and-basket case, the walls do not descend in the same way. Because the branch is four by two and the basket adds only two more on one dimension, envisioning the walls descending creates not an open enclosed space but rather a column in which the branch itself occupies much of the interior. The *gud achit* principle — envisioning walls as extending downward — cannot produce a clean four-by-four enclosed space below, and therefore even Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda would not classify this as a *reshus hayachid*. Rebbi's basket case therefore works even on Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda's view.

## Tilting Basket Access

### Tilt Mechanism

Rebbi Yirmiyah offers an entirely different explanation for why placing the *eruv* in a basket suspended from the tree works, even when the basket is above ten *tefachim*. His approach sets aside entirely the analysis of *reshus hayachid*, *chokekin lehashlim*, and base-versus-top distinctions. Instead, he focuses on a practical mechanism of access: *shani kalkala, ho'il ve-yachol le-hatotah u-le-havi'ah le-toch asarah* — the basket is different, because one can tilt it, bringing its contents to within ten *tefachim* of the ground.

When the basket is tilted, the food inside slides or shifts downward, and the *eruv* — now at a position below ten *tefachim* — is no longer in the *reshus hayachid*. At that lowered position, it occupies a *karmelis*, not a *reshus hayachid*.

### Two-Stage Method

The access, according to Rebbi Yirmiyah, thus proceeds in two stages. First, by tilting the basket, one moves the *eruv* from the *reshus hayachid* down into the *karmelis* (below ten *tefachim*). This first movement involves only a rabbinic violation — transferring from *reshus hayachid* into *karmelis* — which Rebbi permits at *bein hashmashos*. Second, from the *karmelis*, one takes the *eruv* to oneself in the *reshus harabbim* — again only a rabbinic violation.

The elegance of Rebbi Yirmiyah's explanation is that it avoids entirely the complex theoretical apparatus of the previous explanation. One does not need to invoke *chokekin lehashlim*, analyze the dimensions of base versus top, or distinguish between the basket's walls descending or not. The reason the basket case works is simply that the basket is tiltable, and tilting it provides a two-step path to the *eruv* that never requires a biblical violation.

This is, as the lecturer notes, a considerably simpler explanation than Ravina's. The reason a basket works, and a bare branch does not, is not because of dimensional analysis but because a basket can be physically tilted — something a fixed branch cannot replicate.

## Physical Placement Q

### Radical Access Q

Rav Pappa was sitting and presenting this entire discussion when Rav Shava challenged him with a question that takes all of the preceding theoretical arguments to their logical — and troubling — conclusion. If the principle is that theoretical accessibility suffices — if the *gemara* has been permitting various indirect, multi-step, or hypothetical methods of reaching the *eruv* — then why does one ever need to physically place the *eruv* anywhere at all?

The question can be stated as follows: *naima, keivan d'ee bei lei matzi mati lei* — since in theory one could bring the *eruv* to oneself, *af al gav d'lo mati lei* — even if one did not actually bring it, *ke-man d'mati lei dami* — it is as if one had brought it. If the reasoning that "one could get there in stages" justifies an *eruv* on a branch six *amos* away, then surely "one could hypothetically travel to retrieve any *eruv*" justifies leaving the *eruv* wherever it happens to be.

### Yom Tov/Shabbat Case

The scenario that frames Rav Shava's challenge involves a case where *Yom Tov* falls immediately after *Shabbos* — that is, *Shabbos* leading into Sunday which is *Yom Tov*. One wants to make an *eruv techumin* that will be valid both for *Shabbos* and for the subsequent *Yom Tov*. The problem is that the *eruv* must remain in place through both days, yet the *eruv* food might get eaten or spoiled. The *baraita* prescribes: *molicho ba-rishon* — bring it out to the required location on the first day (*Erev Yom Tov*, Thursday); then take it back home; then on the second day (Friday, which is *Yom Tov*), bring it back to the same location at dusk, *machshich alav* — remain there as darkness falls, and *ochlo* — eat it.

Rashi notes that this scenario assumes the person does not personally go to the destination; rather, he relies on an agent, invoking the principle of *chazakah shliach oseh shelichuso* — we presume an agent completes his mission. Since the agent's presence substitutes for the food, not for the person himself, the food must actually be placed at the destination.

### Rabbi Zeira Answer

Rabbi Zeira supplies the answer to the radical challenge. The only reason one ever needs to physically place an *eruv* at its destination is because of the case of *Yom Tov* that falls after *Shabbos*: *gezeirah mishum Yom Tov she-chal lihiyot achar Shabbos*. When *Yom Tov* falls on Sunday, one must have the *eruv* physically present at the destination as darkness falls on *Shabbos* Friday night leading into Saturday. During that *bein hashmashos*, one cannot even hypothetically bring the *eruv* to the destination, because *Shabbos* is already in effect — one cannot carry on *Shabbos*. There is no theoretical path by which the *eruv* could be brought there. In that case, physical placement is genuinely necessary.

### Theory vs. Practice

In every other standard case — a Friday leading into *Shabbos* — one could, in theory, say: at *bein hashmashos*, I could have brought the *eruv* there through a series of steps involving only rabbinic violations, which Rebbi permits. If that theoretical accessibility is legally sufficient, then physical placement should never be required in the standard case.

The implication is far-reaching: according to this analysis, the entire requirement to physically place one's *eruv* at the desired location may exist only as a *gezeirah* — a rabbinic safeguard — driven by the edge case of *Yom Tov* following *Shabbos*. For the standard *eruv techumin* on an ordinary Friday, the theoretical availability of access may be all that is halachically required.

This is a striking conclusion, and it represents the *gemara*'s own moment of stepping back from all the preceding cases — the branch, the basket, the four-*amos* zone, the theoretical multi-step access — and asking what follows if we take all of these principles seriously. The *gemara* does not reject the logic; it channels it into a specific ruling about physical placement and the *Yom Tov* case, and signals that the fuller implications remain to be worked out in the discussion that continues on the following *daf*.

# Eiruvin 33

## Eruv in Tree Basics

### Tree Placement Rules

The *mishnah* under discussion presents the case of placing an *eruv* in a tree. The question is: what happens when the base of the tree stands in a *reshus harabbim*, and the *eruv* is placed in the tree itself? If the branch or platform is higher than ten *tefachim* and is four *tefachim* by four *tefachim* in area, then the tree constitutes a *reshus hayachid*. This creates a fundamental problem: you are standing in a *reshus harabbim* while your *eruv* is in a *reshus hayachid*, meaning you and your *eruv* are not in the same halachic space. For an *eruv techumin* to function, you must be able to access your *eruv*.

Compounding this difficulty is the rabbinic prohibition against using a tree on *Shabbos* — the tree is *mechubbar lekarka*, attached to the ground, and therefore forbidden to handle. This prohibition, however, is only rabbinic in nature. The entire discussion that follows proceeds according to the position of Rebbi, who holds that rabbinic violations are not a concern during *bein hashmashos*, the twilight period when the *eruv* takes effect.

### Two Domains Problem

The core tension is between two categories of domain. When your *eruv* sits in a tree more than ten *tefachim* off the ground on a platform of four by four *tefachim*, it occupies a *reshus hayachid*, while the person seeking to rely on it stands in a *reshus harabbim*. Moving an object between these two domains constitutes a biblical violation. Even granting Rebbi's leniency regarding rabbinic prohibitions at *bein hashmashos*, a biblical obstacle cannot be waived in this manner.

### Rava's Four Amot

Into this difficulty steps Rava, whose principle is introduced at the bottom of 32b. Rava states: *lo shanu ella be-ilan ha-omed chutz le-ibura shel ir* — this restriction applies only when the tree stands outside the *ibura shel ir*, the environs of the city. But if the tree stands within the *ibura shel ir*, then even if it is higher than ten *tefachim*, the *eruv* is valid, as the *gemara* states: *demasa keman demalya damya* — a city is considered as if it were filled. This echoes the earlier principle of *beisa keman demalya damya* — a house is considered as if it is filled — which we encountered at the beginning of *maseches Shabbos*.

### Ibura Shel Ir

The *ibura shel ir* is the halachic concept that the outer boundary of a city extends an additional 70⅔ *amos* beyond its outermost structures. This figure, equivalent to the square root of 5000 and connected to the dimensions of a *beis se'ah*, represents the zone within which all houses are treated as continuous with the city itself. Within this zone, any two locations are treated as part of one unified space for purposes of *hilchos eruv*.

Rashi explains why one might even need to place an *eruv techumin* within this zone. If a person's city is at point A and another city is at point B, and the two cities are within 2000 *amos* of each other, someone starting *Shabbos* in city A might still lack enough range to reach a desired destination beyond city B. Such a person might place an *eruv* within the *ibura* of city B in order to extend their range. It is in precisely this scenario that Rava's principle applies.

Rava's underlying claim is striking: although the *eruv* may be located in a *reshus hayachid* and the person stands in a *reshus harabbim*, if both are within the *ibura shel ir*, it is as if they occupy the same space. This is not a statement about the normal laws of carrying — one may still not carry from the tree to the street — but rather a conceptual determination that for purposes of the *eruv*, the person and the *eruv* are considered collocated. The city's domains are treated as compressed into a single unified space for *eruv* purposes, much as the city itself is considered to occupy no distance when calculating *techumin*.

## Gemara Questions Rava

### Challenge Formulated

The *gemara* immediately presses Rava's logic: *ei hachi* — if this is true, if the reason the *eruv* is valid within the *ibura shel ir* is because everything within the city environs is considered one compressed space, then the same reasoning should apply even outside the *ibura shel ir*. Why? Because Rava himself articulates another principle: *hanosen eiruvo yesh lo daled amos* — wherever a person places his *eruv*, he is granted four *amos* in every direction.

### Rava's Defense

This four-*amos* principle means that even if the *eruv* rolled slightly beyond the permitted boundary just before *bein hashmashos* — say, to 2003 *amos* from the city instead of 2000 — Rava would hold that within those four *amos* surrounding the *eruv*, everything is considered the same space, as if the *eruv* has not actually traveled. The four *amos* around the *eruv* are treated like a small enclosed domain: *havei lei reshus hayachid*, and *reshus hayachid ola ad l'rakia* — a *reshus hayachid* extends upward without limit.

### All-or-Nothing Logic

The *gemara* therefore frames a sweeping challenge: given that the four *amos* around the *eruv* are treated as a unified space regardless of domain distinctions, why should it ever matter whether the *eruv* is in a tree that is a *reshus hayachid*? Just as we compress the entire city into one space for *eruv* purposes, and just as we compress the four *amos* around the *eruv* into one space, the *eruv* in the tree should always be considered accessible, wherever it is placed.

This challenge drives the *gemara* toward a highly constrained reading of the *mishnah*. Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Mesharshiya proposes — at the top of 33b — that the *mishnah*'s problematic case involves a tree whose branch extends *outside* the four-*amos* zone: *hacha be-ilan hanoteh chutz le-arba amos askinan*. The branch curves outward and upward, so that the *eruv* placed upon it is situated both more than four *amos* from the person and more than ten *tefachim* above the ground.

## Branch Extension Case

### Rav Yitzchak's Fix

Rav Yitzchak's resolution reframes the *mishnah* entirely. The tree in question is not a straightforward case of an *eruv* placed directly above the person's position. Rather, the branch extends laterally beyond the four-*amos* zone, and then curves upward. The critical variable — whether the *eruv* is above or below ten *tefachim* — is now reread: *u'mai l'ma'ala u'mai l'mata, d'hadar zakif* — what does it mean for the *eruv* to be "above" versus "below" ten? It refers to the point at which the branch bends upward.

### Branch Height Problem

The diagram this generates is as follows. The tree has a branch that extends horizontally beyond four *amos*, and then curves upward. The portion of the branch at or below ten *tefachim* off the ground constitutes a *karmelis* — a rabbinically prohibited domain. Carrying from there to the *reshus harabbim* is only a rabbinic violation. Above ten *tefachim*, if the branch is four by four *tefachim*, it becomes a *reshus hayachid*, and transferring from there to the *reshus harabbim* where the person stands is a biblical violation.

So the rule of the *mishnah* can now be stated precisely: if the *eruv* is placed on the branch at or above ten *tefachim*, it sits in a *reshus hayachid*, and since the person is in a *reshus harabbim* and the *eruv* is more than four *amos* away, there is no access without a biblical violation — the *eruv* is invalid. If it is placed below ten *tefachim*, even though the branch extends outside the four-*amos* zone, accessing the *eruv* requires only a rabbinic violation (carrying through a *karmelis*), which is permissible according to Rebbi at *bein hashmashos*.

### Multi-Step Access Theory

One might object: even if the *eruv* is at the ten-*tefachim* level in a *reshus hayachid*, cannot the person retrieve it in stages without any biblical violation? Tosafot's approach to this question is that one could first move the *eruv* from the upper portion of the branch (the *reshus hayachid*) down to the lower portion of the branch (the *karmelis*), and from there bring it to the *reshus harabbim*. Each individual transfer involves only a rabbinic prohibition. Rashi's approach similarly allows multiple small movements, each within four *amos*, to accomplish the transfer incrementally.

This is precisely the *gemara*'s internal question: *d'ha i ba'ei meisi lei derech alav* — if one wanted, one could bring it down by moving it across the branch in stages. If this is true, why does placement above ten *tefachim* invalidate the *eruv* at all?

### Tosafot Suspension Q

Tosafot raises an independent question at this point. If the branch is ten *tefachim* off the ground — elevated and suspended — we would normally not treat it as a *reshus hayachid* simply by virtue of its height and dimensions, because a suspended *mechitza* does not typically create a valid enclosed domain. A platform suspended more than three *tefachim* off the ground, through which animals or people can pass beneath, does not generally function as a *reshus hayachid*. Why should such a branch constitute a *reshus hayachid* here?

Tosafot's answer is that the case involves a branch that is itself ten *tefachim* tall — meaning the branch has height in its own right, not merely elevation off the ground. Because the branch itself possesses the requisite height of ten *tefachim* as a structure, it constitutes a *reshus hayachid* in its own right, independently of any consideration about the space beneath it.

## Branch Usage Effect

### Ulla's Platform Rule

The *gemara*'s answer to the multi-step access theory invokes a principle of Ulla. Ulla teaches: *amud tisha bi'reshus harabbim, rabbim mekatfin alav, ve-zorak ve-nach al gabei, chayav* — if there is a platform nine *tefachim* high in a *reshus harabbim*, and the public regularly uses it as a resting place for their burdens, and one throws an object from a *reshus hayachid* that lands on it, one is liable. This is counterintuitive: ordinarily, airspace above three *tefachim* in a *reshus harabbim* is a *karmelis*, not part of the *reshus harabbim* itself. But because this platform is at a usable height and is actively used by the public, it is absorbed into the *reshus harabbim*.

### Public Usage Bars Access

Applying Ulla's principle to the branch: since the lower portion of the branch — the section below ten *tefachim* — is at a height regularly used by the public for resting packages, it too becomes part of the *reshus harabbim*. There is therefore no intermediate zone through which the *eruv* could be brought step by step without a biblical violation. Moving the *eruv* from the *reshus hayachid* (above ten *tefachim*) down to the branch (which is *reshus harabbim* by virtue of public use), and then to the person standing in the *reshus harabbim*, constitutes a direct transfer between *reshus hayachid* and *reshus harabbim* at every stage. There is no *karmelis* stopping point available.

This is why, in this particular configuration, placement above ten *tefachim* is genuinely problematic: every potential intermediate step is itself *reshus harabbim*. Below ten *tefachim*, the *eruv* is no longer in a *reshus hayachid*, and so the transfer problem disappears.

It must be acknowledged that this entire reading of the *mishnah* is, as the *gemara* itself suggests, a *dachak* — a strained construction. *Eichpal tanna lashmi'inan kol hai* — would the *tanna* really go to such lengths to teach us this unusual scenario? The answer, honestly, is that this reading is necessitated entirely by the need to preserve Rava's position. If one were to ask whether this is the straightforward *peshat* of the *mishnah*, the answer is clearly no.

## Rabbi vs. Chachamim

### Baraita Cases

Having established the framework of Rava's position and the branch case, the *gemara* now asks: what precisely is the dispute between Rebbi and the *Chachamim*? The answer is drawn from a *baraita*: *nasno be-ilan lemala me-asara tefachim ein eruvo eruv* — if one placed the *eruv* in the tree above ten *tefachim*, it is invalid. *Lemata me-asara tefachim eruvo eruv* — below ten *tefachim*, it is valid. However: *ve-asur litlo* — it is forbidden to remove it from the tree on *Shabbos* itself, because doing so would constitute using something *mechubbar lekarka*.

Additionally, if the *eruv* is within three *tefachim* of the ground — even if technically on the tree — it is treated as though it is on the ground, and one may even take it. Within three *tefachim*, the halachic principle of *lavud* treats it as ground-level. Between three and ten *tefachim*, the *eruv* is valid but may not be physically retrieved on *Shabbos*.

### Rabbi Permits Rabbinic

Rebbi's position is that even though one cannot remove the *eruv* from the tree — because doing so would violate the rabbinic prohibition against using *mechubbar lekarka* — the *eruv* nevertheless counts. Rebbi holds that a rabbinic obstacle does not render the *eruv* inaccessible in the relevant halachic sense. An *eruv* that can only be reached by incurring a rabbinic violation is still considered a reachable *eruv*.

Furthermore, regarding the basket: *nasno be-kalkala, afilu lemala me-asara tefachim eruvo eruv* — if the *eruv* was placed in a basket suspended from the tree, even above ten *tefachim*, it is valid. This is Rebbi's position: *divrei Rabbi*.

### Chachamim Require Access

The *Chachamim* disagree: *kol makom she-asur litlo ein eruvo eruv* — wherever it is forbidden to take the *eruv*, it does not count as an *eruv*. The *gemara* clarifies which case the *Chachamim* are disputing. If they are arguing about the basket case specifically, this would imply they hold *tzedadin asurin* — that using an item connected to a tree even indirectly is forbidden. Since we do not want to lock the *Chachamim* into that position, the *gemara* concludes that they are disputing the middle case: the *eruv* placed between three and ten *tefachim*, which may not be removed from the tree. Rebbi says this counts; the *Chachamim* say it does not, because if you cannot take it, it is not considered accessible.

### Generalization to Bein H…

What is remarkable about how the *gemara* processes this dispute is its degree of abstraction. The *baraita* seems, on its face, to be presenting a narrow halachic ruling within *hilchos eruvin*: in this specific scenario, does a rabbinic obstacle prevent the *eruv* from counting? One might have thought this was purely an internal principle of *eruv* law — that within the conceptual framework of *eruvin*, we evaluate accessibility in a particular way.

But the *gemara* generalizes Rebbi's position to a broad halachic principle: according to Rebbi, one may perform rabbinic prohibitions during *bein hashmashos*. This is not merely a rule about what counts as an accessible *eruv*; it is a general ruling that rabbinic *issurim* are suspended during the twilight period. It should be noted that we rule like Rebbi, but with two important qualifications. First, many *poskim* hold that this leniency applies only *l'tzorech mitzvah*, in the context of a mitzvah need such as making an *eruv*. Second, if one has already accepted *Shabbos* through *Kabbalas Shabbos*, or on the outgoing end has not yet made *Havdalah*, the subjective declaration of *Shabbos* or the continuation of *Shabbos* applies, and the leniency does not help.

## Suspended Basket Case

### Why Basket Works

The *gemara* now presses a question about the basket case. We have established that when the *eruv* is on a branch more than four *amos* away and above ten *tefachim*, it is in a *reshus hayachid* and inaccessible without a biblical violation. But the *baraita* states that placing the *eruv* in a basket suspended from the tree — even above ten *tefachim* — is valid according to Rebbi. Why? The same problems should apply. The basket above ten *tefachim* would constitute a *reshus hayachid*, and the person stands in a *reshus harabbim*.

The *gemara* first asks the diagnostic question: *hai ilan heichi dami?* What exactly are the dimensions of this tree? If the branch or platform lacks four by four *tefachim*, it is a *makom patur* — an insignificant space — and one may carry freely from it to any domain. If it does have four by four *tefachim*, then it is a *reshus hayachid* and we have the problem. Since the entire discussion presumes a problem exists, we must be dealing with the case where the branch is four by four. Then why does the basket make a difference?

### Ravina's Dimensions

Ravina resolves this by distinguishing the two cases on grounds of dimension. In the problematic case — where the *eruv* on the branch above ten *tefachim* is invalid — the branch itself is four by four *tefachim*, and that is why it constitutes a *reshus hayachid*. In the basket case, however, the branch itself is not four by four — for example, it is four by two — and only together with the basket does the combined space reach four by four *tefachim*: *ve-kalkala mashlimta le-arba* — the basket completes it to four. So in the basket scenario, the branch alone is insufficient to constitute a *reshus hayachid*, and the combined measurement requires a separate legal mechanism to be meaningful.

### Chokekin Lehashlim

This is where the *gemara* invokes two tannaitic principles simultaneously, attributing them both to Rebbi in a famous formulation: *ve-Rebbe savar lah ke-Rabbi Meir, ve-savar lah ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — Rebbi holds like Rabbi Meir in one respect and like Rabbi Yehuda in another.

The first principle is that of Rabbi Meir: *chokekin lehashlim* — we envision a space as though it has been carved out in order to complete the required measurement. The classic example of *chokekin lehashlim* involves an arched doorway that has the required four-*amah* width at the bottom but narrows toward the top: Rabbi Meir permits us to envision the archway as if the requisite rectangular space were carved into it, thereby treating it as meeting the dimensional requirement for a *mezuzah*. Similarly here: even though the branch is only four by two, we envision the remaining space as carved out of the branch, so that together with the basket, a four-by-four *tefachim* space is conceptually present.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Space Req

The second principle is that of Rabbi Yehuda: *ba'inan eruv al gabei makom arba'ah* — an *eruv* must rest on a space of four by four *tefachim* to be valid. If the *eruv* rests on a space smaller than four by four, it is not considered to occupy a real, significant location and therefore cannot function as an *eruv*. Without *chokekin lehashlim*, the basket case would fail on this ground: the basket sits in a space of four by two, which is below the threshold. But precisely because we apply *chokekin lehashlim*, we envision the full four by four, and Rabbi Yehuda's requirement is satisfied.

The *chiddush* of the basket case thus emerges: (a) the basket completes the four-by-four dimension; (b) *chokekin lehashlim* allows us to treat the completed dimension as halachically real; (c) the *eruv* thereby meets Rabbi Yehuda's space requirement. But a question immediately surfaces — if we have just established a four-by-four space above ten *tefachim*, haven't we recreated the *reshus hayachid* problem?

## Base vs. Top Question

### Rashi Base Requirement

Rashi resolves this difficulty by introducing a crucial distinction. A *reshus hayachid* requires four by four *tefachim* not only at the top of the structure but at the base. If the base of the structure — the column or trunk supporting the elevated platform — is not four by four, the elevated platform does not constitute a *reshus hayachid*, even if the top surface is four by four.

In the basket case, the branch from which the basket hangs is four by two. Even after *chokekin lehashlim* conceptually completes the space to four by four at the top, the base of the structure remains four by two. Because the base is not four by four, the space does not qualify as a *reshus hayachid*. The *eruv* can therefore sit in a space that is virtually four by four for purposes of Rabbi Yehuda's placement requirement, without that space simultaneously constituting a *reshus hayachid* that would make the *eruv* inaccessible.

### Pole Analysis

This distinction becomes clearest when the *gemara* introduces the case of a pole. The *baraita* cited in the name of Rabbi Yehuda reads: *na'atz koreh bi'reshus harabbim ve-hinnicho eiruv aleha, gavo'ah yud ve-rochavo arba'ah eruvo eruv* — one drove a post into the *reshus harabbim* and placed an *eruv* on top of it; if the post is ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* wide, the *eruv* is valid. If not — *ein eruvo eruv*.

This initially seems backwards. Ten high and four by four usually means *reshus hayachid*, which should be a problem. The *gemara* clarifies the reading: *gavo'ah asarah tzarich she-ye-hei be-rosho arba'ah* — if the post is ten *tefachim* high, it must have four by four at the top. *Ein gavo'ah asarah, ein tzarich she-ye-hei be-rosho arba'ah* — if it is not ten *tefachim* high, it need not be four by four.

The logic proceeds as follows. Below ten *tefachim*, the airspace of the *reshus harabbim* extends to that height, and the *eruv* on the post is effectively within the same domain as the person standing below — at least for *eruv* purposes. The post need not have its own four-by-four designation because it is, conceptually, continuous with the ground-level domain. But above ten *tefachim*, the post protrudes beyond the *reshus harabbim* airspace. At that height, the *eruv* only "counts as being somewhere" if it occupies a genuine space of four by four *tefachim*. Without that, it is a *makom patur* — too insignificant to be a valid location for an *eruv*.

And what of the concern that ten high and four by four is a *reshus hayachid*? Here Rashi again invokes the four-*amos* principle: within four *amos* of where the *eruv* is placed, everything is considered unified space. One does not worry about the domain distinction between the *reshus hayachid* on top of the pole and the *reshus harabbim* at ground level, because they are within four *amos* of each other and treated as the same space for *eruv* purposes.

### Rabbi Yosi Position

At this point the *gemara* raises the question: *keman?* — whose position does the basket case reflect? The *gemara* answers that it does not accord with the opinion of Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda.

The *baraita* records: Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda says, *na'atz kaneh bi'reshus harabbim ve-hiniach be-rosho terraskal* — one drove a pole into the *reshus harabbim* and placed a basket on top — *ve-zorak ve-nach le-gabav, chayav* — if one threw an object that landed in that basket, one is liable. This means that a basket atop a pole, even with no four-by-four base, constitutes a *reshus hayachid* sufficient to generate liability. Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda does not require the base to be four by four; the four-by-four dimension at the top alone is sufficient.

If so, the basket in our case — which sits above a two-by-four branch — would also constitute a *reshus hayachid* according to Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda, recreating the problem of the person standing in a *reshus harabbim* while the *eruv* sits in a *reshus hayachid*.

### Mechitza Descent Diff

The *gemara* deflects this challenge: *afilu teima Rabbi Yosi be-Rabbi Yehuda* — even according to Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda, the basket case works. Why? *Hatam hadra mechitzta, hacha lo hadra mechitzta* — there, in the pole-and-basket case, the walls of the basket descend and surround the space below, creating a genuine enclosed domain down through the pole. Here, in our tree-and-basket case, the walls do not descend in the same way. Because the branch is four by two and the basket adds only two more on one dimension, envisioning the walls descending creates not an open enclosed space but rather a column in which the branch itself occupies much of the interior. The *gud achit* principle — envisioning walls as extending downward — cannot produce a clean four-by-four enclosed space below, and therefore even Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda would not classify this as a *reshus hayachid*. Rebbi's basket case therefore works even on Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda's view.

## Tilting Basket Access

### Tilt Mechanism

Rebbi Yirmiyah offers an entirely different explanation for why placing the *eruv* in a basket suspended from the tree works, even when the basket is above ten *tefachim*. His approach sets aside entirely the analysis of *reshus hayachid*, *chokekin lehashlim*, and base-versus-top distinctions. Instead, he focuses on a practical mechanism of access: *shani kalkala, ho'il ve-yachol le-hatotah u-le-havi'ah le-toch asarah* — the basket is different, because one can tilt it, bringing its contents to within ten *tefachim* of the ground.

When the basket is tilted, the food inside slides or shifts downward, and the *eruv* — now at a position below ten *tefachim* — is no longer in the *reshus hayachid*. At that lowered position, it occupies a *karmelis*, not a *reshus hayachid*.

### Two-Stage Method

The access, according to Rebbi Yirmiyah, thus proceeds in two stages. First, by tilting the basket, one moves the *eruv* from the *reshus hayachid* down into the *karmelis* (below ten *tefachim*). This first movement involves only a rabbinic violation — transferring from *reshus hayachid* into *karmelis* — which Rebbi permits at *bein hashmashos*. Second, from the *karmelis*, one takes the *eruv* to oneself in the *reshus harabbim* — again only a rabbinic violation.

The elegance of Rebbi Yirmiyah's explanation is that it avoids entirely the complex theoretical apparatus of the previous explanation. One does not need to invoke *chokekin lehashlim*, analyze the dimensions of base versus top, or distinguish between the basket's walls descending or not. The reason the basket case works is simply that the basket is tiltable, and tilting it provides a two-step path to the *eruv* that never requires a biblical violation.

This is, as the lecturer notes, a considerably simpler explanation than Ravina's. The reason a basket works, and a bare branch does not, is not because of dimensional analysis but because a basket can be physically tilted — something a fixed branch cannot replicate.

## Physical Placement Q

### Radical Access Q

Rav Pappa was sitting and presenting this entire discussion when Rav Shava challenged him with a question that takes all of the preceding theoretical arguments to their logical — and troubling — conclusion. If the principle is that theoretical accessibility suffices — if the *gemara* has been permitting various indirect, multi-step, or hypothetical methods of reaching the *eruv* — then why does one ever need to physically place the *eruv* anywhere at all?

The question can be stated as follows: *naima, keivan d'ee bei lei matzi mati lei* — since in theory one could bring the *eruv* to oneself, *af al gav d'lo mati lei* — even if one did not actually bring it, *ke-man d'mati lei dami* — it is as if one had brought it. If the reasoning that "one could get there in stages" justifies an *eruv* on a branch six *amos* away, then surely "one could hypothetically travel to retrieve any *eruv*" justifies leaving the *eruv* wherever it happens to be.

### Yom Tov/Shabbat Case

The scenario that frames Rav Shava's challenge involves a case where *Yom Tov* falls immediately after *Shabbos* — that is, *Shabbos* leading into Sunday which is *Yom Tov*. One wants to make an *eruv techumin* that will be valid both for *Shabbos* and for the subsequent *Yom Tov*. The problem is that the *eruv* must remain in place through both days, yet the *eruv* food might get eaten or spoiled. The *baraita* prescribes: *molicho ba-rishon* — bring it out to the required location on the first day (*Erev Yom Tov*, Thursday); then take it back home; then on the second day (Friday, which is *Yom Tov*), bring it back to the same location at dusk, *machshich alav* — remain there as darkness falls, and *ochlo* — eat it.

Rashi notes that this scenario assumes the person does not personally go to the destination; rather, he relies on an agent, invoking the principle of *chazakah shliach oseh shelichuso* — we presume an agent completes his mission. Since the agent's presence substitutes for the food, not for the person himself, the food must actually be placed at the destination.

### Rabbi Zeira Answer

Rabbi Zeira supplies the answer to the radical challenge. The only reason one ever needs to physically place an *eruv* at its destination is because of the case of *Yom Tov* that falls after *Shabbos*: *gezeirah mishum Yom Tov she-chal lihiyot achar Shabbos*. When *Yom Tov* falls on Sunday, one must have the *eruv* physically present at the destination as darkness falls on *Shabbos* Friday night leading into Saturday. During that *bein hashmashos*, one cannot even hypothetically bring the *eruv* to the destination, because *Shabbos* is already in effect — one cannot carry on *Shabbos*. There is no theoretical path by which the *eruv* could be brought there. In that case, physical placement is genuinely necessary.

### Theory vs. Practice

In every other standard case — a Friday leading into *Shabbos* — one could, in theory, say: at *bein hashmashos*, I could have brought the *eruv* there through a series of steps involving only rabbinic violations, which Rebbi permits. If that theoretical accessibility is legally sufficient, then physical placement should never be required in the standard case.

The implication is far-reaching: according to this analysis, the entire requirement to physically place one's *eruv* at the desired location may exist only as a *gezeirah* — a rabbinic safeguard — driven by the edge case of *Yom Tov* following *Shabbos*. For the standard *eruv techumin* on an ordinary Friday, the theoretical availability of access may be all that is halachically required.

This is a striking conclusion, and it represents the *gemara*'s own moment of stepping back from all the preceding cases — the branch, the basket, the four-*amos* zone, the theoretical multi-step access — and asking what follows if we take all of these principles seriously. The *gemara* does not reject the logic; it channels it into a specific ruling about physical placement and the *Yom Tov* case, and signals that the fuller implications remain to be worked out in the discussion that continues on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Eiruvin 34

## Eruv Accessibility

### Tosafos on Eruv Placement

The discussion on *daf* 34 opens by reviewing the *Gemara*'s extended treatment of whether an *eruv* must be physically and halachically accessible at the moment of *bein hashmashot* in order to be valid. The *Gemara* had been exploring a series of theoretical scenarios — what if the *eruv* is in a *reshut hayachid* and the person is in a *reshut harabim*? According to Rebbe, rabbinic restrictions (*derabbanan*) are not enforced during *bein hashmashot*, so even a configuration that would otherwise be problematic on a rabbinic level is still considered accessible. The *Gemara* had also discussed the possibility of staged transfers — taking the *eruv* from a *reshut hayachid* through a *karmelit* and then into a *reshut harabim* — and the case of a basket in a *reshut hayachid* that could be tipped so that its contents descend into a *karmelit*, thereby rendering the *eruv* accessible. After following this chain of what-ifs to its logical extreme, the *Gemara* threw up its hands: if one can always conjure a theoretical reconfiguration, why must one ever physically place the *eruv* at its intended location at all?

*Tosafot* raises a pointed objection to Rashi's reading of this passage. According to Rashi, the *Gemara*'s question applies even to a standard Friday *eruv* for *Shabbos*. *Tosafot* rejects this: in the ordinary case of an *eruv* placed on *Erev Shabbos*, the entire question of accessibility is measured at *bein hashmashot*, and at that moment the person is two thousand *amot* outside the city while the *eruv* is in the house. There is simply no way to bring it — it would take longer than *bein hashmashot* lasts, and the act of carrying would in any case constitute a biblical prohibition, not merely a rabbinic one. Rebbe's dispensation for *derabbanan* violations during *bein hashmashot* does not help when the problem is a *d'oraisha*. So *Tosafot* argues that the *Gemara*'s question never applied to a standard *Shabbos eruv* in the first place. The question pertains exclusively to a *Yom Tov eruv*: if one wishes to establish an *eruv* for a weekday *Yom Tov*, why does the *eruv* need to be physically placed anywhere? Since carrying is permitted on *Yom Tov*, one could always, even during *bein hashmashot Yom Tov*, have brought the *eruv* from wherever it was to wherever it needed to be.

### Yom Tov After Shabbat

This reframing renders the *Gemara*'s question and answer considerably more intelligible. The *Gemara*'s answer, attributed to Rabbi Zeira, is that the *eruv* must in fact be physically placed in its proper location — but the only reason this is ever required is for the case of *Yom Tov* that falls on Sunday, immediately following *Shabbos*. In that scenario, even though carrying would otherwise be permitted on *Yom Tov*, the *eruv* could not have been brought to its location during *Shabbos*, and by the time *Yom Tov* begins it is too late. To ensure the *eruv* is in place for that one case, the requirement to physically lay the *eruv* was established across the board.

The *Gemara* thus arrives at a somewhat remarkable conclusion: the general requirement to actually place one's *eruv* in the designated location is anchored in a single edge case — a *Yom Tov* that follows immediately after *Shabbos*. The *Gemara* does not shy away from this implication; rather, it articulates it directly.

---

## Wall Height & Access

### Eruv on Wall

The *Gemara* now takes up a series of cases from the *Mishnah* in order to test the theoretical framework that had been established. The first: one wished to begin *Shabbos* in the *reshut harabim* and placed the *eruv* on a wall. If the wall is less than ten *tefachim* high — *lemata me'asara tefachim* — the *eruv* is valid. If the wall is higher than ten *tefachim* — and we also assume four by four *tefachim* wide, making it a *reshut hayachid* — the *eruv* is invalid, because the person is in a *reshut harabim* and the *eruv* is in a *reshut hayachid*.

### Tower/Coop Case

A second case: one wished to begin *Shabbos* on the roof of a chicken coop (*shovach*) or on the roof of a tower (*migdal*). In such a case, the rule is reversed: if the wall alongside it is higher than ten *tefachim*, the *eruv* placed on that wall is valid — both the person and the *eruv* are in a *reshut hayachid*, and the *eruv* is accessible. If the wall is lower than ten *tefachim*, the *eruv* is not valid.

Rashi offers two explanations for why the low-wall configuration fails. The first is that a wall lower than ten *tefachim* that is usable by the public becomes part of the *reshut harabim*, so the *eruv* would be in a *reshut harabim* while the person on the elevated roof is in a *reshut hayachid* — a prohibited configuration. The second explanation, which Rashi also advances, is more conceptual: the airspace of the *reshut harabim* extends up to ten *tefachim*. Anything above that threshold belongs to a different conceptual domain. If the person is above ten *tefachim* and the *eruv* is below ten *tefachim*, they are considered to occupy different zones, and the *eruv* is therefore not accessible. It should be noted that this second explanation does not fit easily with all the *Gemara*'s other discussions, and the *Mishnah* about the pole — to be discussed shortly — appears to contradict it.

The *Gemara* then asks: given the logic established earlier about tipping the basket, why should the lower-wall case be a problem at all? In theory, could one not simply tip the *migdal* over, bringing the *eruv* below ten *tefachim* and thus into the same zone as the person? The *Gemara* is using this as a *reductio ad absurdum*: the theoretical reconfiguration argument, which was accepted in the basket case, would seem to apply here as well.

### Nailed vs. Tall

Two answers are given. Rabbi Yirmiah says: here we are dealing with a *migdal* that is nailed into the ground — *migdal mesumares* — and therefore physically cannot be tipped. Rava offers a second answer: even if it is not nailed down, we are dealing with a tall *migdal* — *migdal aroch* — such that if one were to tip it even slightly, the *eruv* would wind up outside of four *amot* from where the person intended to begin *Shabbos*. And that creates two problems: one cannot bring the *eruv* from four *amot* away in a *reshut harabim*, and moreover, one's intended location for *shevitah* would itself be displaced, since the tipped configuration would place it four *amot* from the original position.

The broader point the *Gemara* is making is that the theoretical-reconfiguration argument has real limits. It was accepted in the basket case, but here, in both of Rabbi Yirmiah's and Rava's scenarios, something prevents the reconfiguration from working. The *Gemara* is not withdrawing the principle; it is confining it to cases where the reconfiguration is actually workable.

### Window & Rope

The *Gemara* continues pushing on this theme. It asks: what if there is a window and a rope? Could one not thread the rope through the window and pull the *eruv* out that way, making it accessible without tipping? The *Gemara* responds: the case we are discussing is precisely one where there is no window and no rope. But the *Gemara*'s willingness to entertain the rope scenario is itself instructive. *Tosafot* explains that if a rope were already attached to the *eruv*, the object would be considered partially extended toward the person even before it was fully retrieved, so that drawing it in fully would not constitute a complete biblical act of carrying — analogous to the principle of *eged kli* discussed elsewhere in *Shabbos*. The *Gemara* is not dismissing the what-if; it is simply ruling it inapplicable to the case at hand.

The overall conclusion of this entire section is that the principle of theoretical accessibility is real but bounded. Yes, one can invoke reconfiguration — tipping a basket, threading a rope — to establish that an *eruv* is accessible. But those considerations only apply when the reconfiguration is actually feasible: the tower is not nailed down, the reconfiguration does not push one outside of four *amot*, and there is actually a rope in place.

---

## Well Case

### Well Domains

The *Gemara* turns to the *Mishnah*'s case of an *eruv* placed in a well, even one a hundred *amot* deep, and rules it valid. The *Gemara* asks where this well is located, in order to determine what the *chiddush* actually is.

If the well is in a *reshut hayachid* — that is, surrounded by a private domain — the ruling is obvious. Just as a *reshut hayachid* extends upward to the heavens, it extends downward into the earth. The well is a *reshut hayachid*, and if the person is also in a *reshut hayachid*, the *eruv* is in the same domain and is clearly valid. No novelty there.

If the well is in a *reshut harabim*, then the bottom of the well, by virtue of being ten *tefachim* deep and enclosed, constitutes a *reshut hayachid*. If the person intends to begin *Shabbos* at ground level — above the well in the *reshut harabim* — the *eruv* is in a different domain and is inaccessible. If the person intends to begin *Shabbos* at the bottom of the well, then obviously the person and the *eruv* are in the same place, and again there is no novelty.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: the *chiddush* arises specifically where the area surrounding the well is a *karmelit*. The bottom of the well is a *reshut hayachid*, and the person intends to begin *Shabbos* at a normal height just above the well, within the *karmelit*. The problem is that retrieving the *eruv* from the *reshut hayachid* while standing in a *karmelit* would involve a rabbinic violation. The *Mishnah*'s ruling that it is valid follows the position of Rebbe — *ve-Rabbi hi* — who holds that rabbinic prohibitions are not enforced during *bein hashmashot*, and therefore the *eruv* is considered accessible even across this domain distinction.

This case rounds out the *Gemara*'s treatment of the *Mishnah* cases from the previous *amud*. The underlying thread is consistent: accessibility is determined halachically, not merely physically. Rebbe's position that *derabbanan* restrictions do not apply during *bein hashmashot* transforms the halachic calculus of what counts as "accessible," with substantial ramifications across all of these cases.

---

## Pole & Reed

### Pole vs. Reed

The *Gemara* moves to a new *Mishnah*: if one placed the *eruv* on top of a tall pole (*kaneh*) or a tall reed (*kundas*), the ruling depends on whether the object is *talush vena'utz* — cut and then thrust back into the ground — or whether it is still growing from the earth. If it is a detached pole replanted in the ground, the *eruv* is valid even if the pole is a hundred *amot* tall. This case is notable because it appears to contradict Rashi's earlier position that anything above ten *tefachim* is in a different conceptual zone from someone standing in the *reshut harabim* below — yet the *Mishnah* has no difficulty with an *eruv* atop a flagpole of any height. The *Mishnah* thus seems to take for granted that the person could, at least in theory, shake the pole until the *eruv* falls, and that there is no halachic barrier to doing so.

Rav Adda bar Masna then challenges Rava: the *Mishnah* specifies *talush vena'utz* — meaning if the reed is still attached to the ground, the *eruv* is not valid. Whose position does this reflect? It reflects the *Rabbanan* who disagree with Rebbe and hold that rabbinic restrictions *are* enforced during *bein hashmashot*. Since using something attached to the ground (*mechubar l'karka*) is rabbinically prohibited on *Shabbos*, the *eruv* placed on a growing reed would not be accessible.

But this immediately raises a difficulty: the first *Mishnah* in the chapter explicitly discussed placing the *eruv* on a tree — which is also *mechubar l'karka* — and apparently validated it. Can the beginning of the *Mishnah* reflect Rebbe's more lenient position and the end reflect the *Rabbanan*'s stricter one? Rava responds that Rami bar Chama had already posed this exact question to Rav Chisda, and Rav Chisda answered that yes, the beginning of the *Mishnah* follows Rebbe and the end follows the *Rabbanan*. While this answer might seem weak at first glance, it is historically defensible: the *Mishnayos* were collated and redacted by Rebbe from diverse sources, and different sections may well originate from different schools of thought.

Ravina, however, offers a more unified reading: the entire *Mishnah* follows Rebbe — *kula Rabbi* — and yet Rebbe would prohibit placing the *eruv* on a reed. The reason is not simply the rabbinic concern about *mechubar l'karka* that Rebbe otherwise overrides at *bein hashmashot*, but rather a more acute concern: one might come to cut the reed — *shema yiktom*. Since reeds are easily snapped, there is a realistic concern that one will break one off, which would constitute a biblical violation. This concern is severe enough that even Rebbe would not permit it, even though he would permit a comparably minor rabbinic restriction. The tree case and the reed case are therefore distinguishable, and the *Mishnah* is internally consistent on Rebbe's own terms.

### Rav Nachman Story

An incident further illuminates the distinction. When a military detachment was quartered in Nehardea, the students had to vacate the study hall and needed somewhere to gather on *Shabbos*. Rav Nachman instructed them: before *Shabbos*, go out to the marshy field and flatten (*kvushey kavshey*) some of the reeds, so that on *Shabbos* there will be a place to sit and learn. Rami bar Chama — and some attribute the challenge to Rav Ukva bar Abba — challenged Rav Nachman: the *Mishnah* implies that reeds attached to the ground are problematic, so how could one sit on flattened reeds on *Shabbos*, which would be using something *mechubar l'karka*?

Rav Nachman replied: *hatam be'ozardin* — that rule applies when the reeds have hardened. It is the hardened reeds, *ozardin*, that are categorized like trees and therefore subject to the rabbinic prohibition of *mechubar l'karka*. Soft, pliable reeds are more like grass or vegetables, and they are not subject to that prohibition. The *Mishnah*'s stringency about reeds applies to hardened reeds only. Moreover, the concern that one will snap off a piece — the concern underlying the prohibition — is more acute with hardened reeds, which snap easily, than with soft reeds, which are difficult to break off cleanly.

### Reeds in Kilayim

The *Gemara* then seeks a source for the distinction between hardened and unhardened reeds in terms of categorical classification. It turns to the laws of *kilayim*. One *baraita* states that stalks, thornbushes (*atadim*), and brambles (*higim*) are all *min ilan* — they belong to the tree category — and therefore do not constitute *kilayim* with a vineyard, since trees may be planted alongside vines. A separate *baraita*, however, lists reeds (*kanim*) together with other plants and classifies them as *min yerakin* — the vegetable category — in which case planting them near vines would constitute *kilayim*.

### Soft vs. Hard

The two *baraitot* appear to contradict one another. The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction by applying exactly the distinction Rav Nachman had invoked: hardened reeds (*ozardin*) belong to the tree category and are therefore not *kilayim* with a vineyard; soft reeds belong to the vegetable category and are subject to *kilayim* restrictions when planted near vines. The resolution — *kan be-zardin kan she-eino zardin* — confirms that the formal category of a reed as tree or vegetable depends on its state of hardness.

This is a methodologically significant moment in the *sugya*. The concern that motivates the prohibition of *mechubar l'karka* on *Shabbos* is that one might snap off a branch. In principle, one could ask whether the category of "tree" for *Shabbos* purposes should be defined by that motivating reason — whatever is likely to be snapped off — or by a formal, cross-halachic definition. The *Gemara* here takes the formalist approach: it imports the definition of "tree" from *kilayim* and applies it to *Shabbos*. This reflects the broader question of whether halachic categories are local (*din mesuyam*) or universal (*din klali*), a *chakira* that runs throughout the literature. Here the *Gemara* clearly treats the category as universal, drawing the definition from an entirely different area of *halacha*.

The *Gemara* also notes a further refinement regarding *kida*: one *baraita* lists it in the vegetable category, while the *Mishnah* treats *kida levana* (white *kida*) as belonging to the tree category, such that grafting rue — a vegetable — onto it would constitute *kilayim* of vegetable with tree. Rav Papa resolves the apparent contradiction: plain *kida* and white *kida* are distinct varieties, one in each category. The broader point is reinforced — classification as tree or vegetable can vary even within what appears to be a single species, whether by variety or by developmental stage.

---

## Locked Wardrobe

### Mishna Position

The final *Mishnah* of the *daf* addresses a scenario that shifts the question of accessibility from the halachic to the purely practical: one placed the *eruv* in a *migdal* — understood here as a wardrobe or chest — locked it, and then lost the key. The *Tanna Kamma* rules it valid. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees: if one does not know that the key is in its place (*im eino yodea she-ha-mafteiach bimkomo*), the *eruv* is invalid.

The *Tanna Kamma*'s position raises an immediate conceptual question. All of the earlier discussion about accessibility presupposed that halachic barriers are what render an *eruv* inaccessible, while Rebbe's dispensation for *derabbanan* violations at *bein hashmashot* is what restores accessibility. But in this case, there is no halachic barrier at all — the wardrobe is simply locked and the key is gone. It is a purely physical problem. Yet apparently even a physical barrier can be sufficient to render an *eruv* inaccessible. The *Tanna Kamma*'s ruling that it *is* valid seems to suggest that only a halachic barrier matters — that physical inaccessibility does not transform the two locations into separate *makomot* the way a domain boundary does.

### Brick & Yom Tov

The *Gemara* declines to accept this reading and instead offers an explanation: *hacha bemigdal shel leveinim askinan* — the *Mishnah* is speaking of a wardrobe constructed from bricks laid without plaster. And the ruling follows the opinion of Rabbi Meir, who permits dismantling such a structure.

### Rabbi Meir on Bricks

The underlying principle derives from a *Mishnah* in *Beitzah* about a storehouse sealed with bricks that then sustained a breach: Rabbi Meir rules that one may even deliberately dismantle such a wall *lechatchilah* to retrieve the contents inside — *pocheis ve-notel lechatchilah*. Since the bricks are laid without mortar or plaster, there is no binding agent, and Rabbi Meir holds that undoing such a structure does not constitute the prohibited labor of *soser* — demolishing.

The application to the wardrobe case is as follows: since the brick construction can be taken apart, the *eruv* is considered physically accessible after all, and the *Tanna Kamma* is therefore justified in ruling it valid. However, Rav Zeira notes that Rabbi Meir's dispensation applies specifically on *Yom Tov* — *be-Yom Tov amru* — but not on *Shabbos*. The difference is likely connected to the *Yom Tov* value of *simchat Yom Tov* and the *Torah*'s special dispensation regarding food preparation on *Yom Tov*. Consequently, the *Mishnah*'s case of the locked wardrobe is specifically a *Yom Tov eruv* scenario: on *Shabbos*, even according to Rabbi Meir, the brick construction could not be dismantled, and the *eruv* would be inaccessible.

### Key Location

Once this framework is established, the *Gemara* turns to a *baraita* that elaborates on Rabbi Eliezer's position. Rabbi Eliezer states: if the key was lost in the city (*ba'ir*), the *eruv* is valid; if the key was lost in the field (*basadeh*), the *eruv* is invalid. The criterion Rabbi Eliezer applies is not the mere fact of loss but the practical consequence: if the key were found in the city, one could theoretically carry it through a series of *reshut hayachid* configurations — through walled courtyards, via rooftops — and eventually get it to the *eruv*. If the key is lost in the field, there is no way to get it to the *eruv* even once found, and so the *eruv* cannot be considered accessible.

### Found Key

The *Gemara* notes, however, that this *baraita* cannot be describing the same scenario as the *Mishnah* if the *Mishnah* is a *Yom Tov* case. On *Yom Tov*, carrying is generally permitted — so whether the key is lost in the city or the field, one could carry it directly. The distinction between city and field would be irrelevant. The *Gemara* therefore concludes that the *Mishnah* and *baraita* must be restructured, and offers a reading in which they address different aspects of the problem.

In the *Gemara*'s revised reading, the *Tanna Kamma*'s ruling that the locked wardrobe is a valid *eruv* applies when it is *Yom Tov* and the wardrobe is constructed of un-plastered bricks — which is why it is considered accessible. On *Shabbos* under those conditions, it would not be valid. And once the key is actually found, it is not automatically valid even in the city, because getting the key from one *reshut hayachid* to another is itself complicated: there is a dispute among authorities as to whether one can transfer an object from a rooftop to a courtyard or vice versa, since those are considered distinct sub-domains within the broader *reshut hayachid* category. Rabbi Eliezer, then, draws his city/field distinction not on the basis of whether the key was *lost* there, but on whether — once found — it can be gotten to the *eruv* through a chain of *reshut hayachid* transfers. The *Chachamim* hold that even finding it in the city is insufficient to establish accessibility, given the practical difficulties of executing such a transfer across different types of *reshut hayachid*. The *Gemara* leaves the full elaboration of this dispute to continue on the following *amud*.

---

---

# Eiruvin 35

## Migdal & Key Review

### Tanna Kamma vs Eliezer

We pick up at the very top of 35a, though it is worth reviewing the ground covered previously, as the conclusion of the prior session was somewhat rushed. The *mishna* on our *daf* addresses a situation where one places an *eiruv* inside a *migdal* — a wooden wardrobe or chest — and then loses the key. The *tanna kamma* rules that the *eiruv* remains valid, while Rabbi Eliezer rules that it does not. The underlying question is straightforward: if you lack the key, how can you access the *eiruv* on *Shabbos*? Presumably one cannot simply break the wardrobe open, though we will see that this assumption itself becomes the subject of debate.

The *gemara* initially explored a special case — a *migdal* constructed from *liveini* bricks laid without cement — where, according to one opinion, dismantling the structure would not constitute a violation. However, this leniency was applicable only on *Yom Tov*, not *Shabbos*, and so the *gemara* proposed that the *mishna*'s case is confined to *Yom Tov*. That was the first answer.

### Yom Tov Exception

Within that framework, the *gemara* quoted an additional *braisa* presenting a position of Rabbi Eliezer that introduces a further distinction: the validity of the *eiruv* depends on where the key was lost. Even when Rabbi Eliezer rules that the *eiruv* is invalid, that ruling applies only when there is no realistic possibility of retrieving the key. If there is a genuine possibility of finding the key and bringing it to the *eiruv*, Rabbi Eliezer would concede that the *eiruv* is valid — even if the key has not yet been found.

The operative question is therefore the location of the loss. If the key was lost in the city, and the intervening spaces between the finder and the wardrobe consist entirely of *reshuyos hayachid*, then it would theoretically be possible to retrieve the key and carry it through those domains. In that case, Rabbi Eliezer would validate the *eiruv*. If, however, the key was lost in the *sadeh* — the open field — retrieval is practically impossible, and Rabbi Eliezer would invalidate it. The *gemara* notes that the introduction of the carrying question indicates the case is being discussed in the context of *Shabbos*, not *Yom Tov*, since carrying is only a concern on *Shabbos*.

The *chidush* of this *braisa* is remarkable: Rabbi Eliezer does not require that the key actually be found — only that finding it is a realistic possibility. The mere theoretical accessibility of the key, at the moment *Shabbos* begins, is sufficient to validate the *eiruv*.

### Key Location Logic

The *braisa* as quoted by the *gemara* frames the question not in terms of where the key was lost, but in terms of where it was found — specifically, found on *Shabbos* itself. Rashi explains that the finding must have occurred on *Shabbos* because if the key had been found before *Shabbos* began, the scenario of *Shabbos* commencing without the key would not apply. One might then ask: why should finding the key on *Shabbos* matter, if the validity of the *eiruv* is determined by conditions at the moment *Shabbos* begins?

The answer, which the *rishonim* appear to accept without lengthy discussion, is that the location where the key is found on *Shabbos* is simply evidence of where it was located when *Shabbos* began. If found in the city, it was in the city on *erev Shabbos*; if found in the *sadeh*, it was in the *sadeh* on *erev Shabbos*. One might also suggest, in the spirit of *yesh bereirah*, that the act of finding the key retroactively confirms that it was findable all along — and since this is a rabbinic matter, *yesh bereirah* would apply. Regardless, the *gemara*'s emphasis is squarely on the question of where the key was lost at the onset of *Shabbos*, and the finding is simply probative of that fact.

### Three Positions

Reading the *mishna* and *braisa* together yields three distinct positions. The *tanna kamma* of the *mishna* rules that the *eiruv* is valid even when there is no possibility of accessing the key — but this, according to the *gemara*'s first answer, is limited to the special case of a brick-constructed wardrobe on *Yom Tov*, where dismantling is permissible. In the general case — a wooden wardrobe, on *Shabbos* — the *tanna kamma* would also concede that the *eiruv* is invalid.

Rabbi Eliezer, who in the *mishna* appears to be the strict opinion, turns out on examination to be more lenient than the general position of the *chachamim*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that even setting aside the special case of bricks and *Yom Tov*, the *eiruv* is valid on *Shabbos* as long as the key was lost within the city, since it could theoretically have been retrieved via the interconnected *reshuyos hayachid* — relying on the principle, attributed to Rabbi Shimon, that rooftops, courtyards, and enclosed fields all share a single *reshus hayachid* status for objects that spent *Shabbos* within them. Thus one could carry the key from domain to domain without transgression.

The *rabbanan*, by contrast, are unmoved by the theoretical possibility of finding and retrieving the key. Even if the key was lost in the city, they do not share Rabbi Eliezer's view that the various *reshuyos hayachid* constitute a unified domain for this purpose, and they therefore rule the *eiruv* invalid in all cases other than the special brick-and-*Yom Tov* scenario.

---

## Kli vs Ohel Debate

### Ohel Status

Rabbah and Rav Yosef propose an entirely different approach to the *mishna*, cutting through the complexity of the first answer. They argue: *hacha b'migdal shel etz askinan* — the *mishna* is speaking of an ordinary wooden wardrobe, not a brick structure. The reason the *tanna kamma* considers the *eiruv* accessible has nothing to do with *Yom Tov* or the special properties of unbonded bricks. Rather, it turns on the fundamental question of what halakhic category the wardrobe belongs to: is it a *kli* — a vessel — or an *ohel* — a structure?

If the wardrobe has the status of a *kli*, then the principle that there is no *binyan b'keilim* — no prohibition of building that applies to vessels — would mean that there is correspondingly no *stirah b'keilim*, no prohibition of destroying vessels either. One could therefore break open the wardrobe with a hatchet, just as the *gemara* in *Shabbos* permits breaking a wine barrel to access the wine inside. Destroying the wardrobe would not constitute the *melacha* of *soter*, and the *eiruv* would accordingly be considered accessible.

### Destruction of Vessels

The *tanna kamma* holds precisely this view: the wardrobe is a *kli*, and one may break it open. The second opinion — that of Rabbi Eliezer — holds that the wardrobe is not a *kli* but an *ohel*. A sufficiently large wardrobe, one that functions like a freestanding structure with a roof, takes on the character of a tent or small building. The roof is halakhically significant: creating a roofed enclosure is the paradigm of *boneh*, even when the structure is not permanent. If the wardrobe has *ohel* status, then breaking it open would constitute *soter*, and the *eiruv* would be inaccessible — hence Rabbi Eliezer's stringency.

It is worth noting in this context that Tosafot takes a more expansive view of *soter b'keilim*, arguing that even genuine vessels can be subject to *soter* under certain conditions. Tosafot therefore would say that even a smaller wardrobe — one that would not qualify as an *ohel* — could not simply be smashed open on *Shabbos*, since destroying a complete, fully formed vessel may itself constitute *soter*. This has implications for the familiar question of opening packaging on *Shabbos*: the wine barrel case involves an object designed to be opened, whereas a full-fledged *kli* that is not intended for destruction might stand differently. According to Tosafot, it would then follow that the *gemara*'s case necessarily involves a wardrobe bound with a string — but more on that shortly.

### Tum'ah Connection

Having articulated the *kli*-versus-*ohel* dispute, the *gemara* suggests that this disagreement between Rabbah and Rav Yosef maps onto an earlier *tannaitic* dispute. The *mishna* in *Maseches Zavim* teaches that a *zav* — whose mode of transmitting *tum'ah* includes moving objects even without direct contact — who strikes a *shida*, *teiva*, or *migdal*, renders them *tamei*. The *tanna kamma* rules them *tamei*; Rabbi Nechemiah and Rabbi Shimon rule them *tahor*.

The *gemara* suggests that their dispute may hinge on the same question: if the *migdal* is a *kli*, it is susceptible to *tum'ah* through the *zav*'s action; if it is an *ohel*, it is not. This would make the *tanna'im*'s debate in *Zavim* a direct parallel to Rabbah and Rav Yosef's dispute in our *sugya*.

### Tremor Debate

Abaye, however, rejects this parallel. He adduces a *braisa* that makes clear that the *ohel* status of the *migdal* is irrelevant to the *tum'ah* question. The *braisa* states: if an *ohel* was actually moved — *nisa* — by the *zav*, it becomes *tamei*; if a *kli* was not actually moved — *eino nisa* — it remains *tahor*. The classification as *ohel* or *kli* does not determine the outcome; what matters is whether genuine displacement occurred. Furthermore, the *mishna* in *Zavim* itself states in its closing clause that Rabbi Nechemiah and Rabbi Shimon concede that if the object was actually moved — *nisutin* — it would be *tamei*. So there is no dispute about the principle.

What, then, is their dispute? Abaye explains: *ve-hacha be-re'adah machmat kocho askinan* — they are debating a case where the *zav* strikes the wardrobe and it shakes in place, vibrating without being displaced. The rule of *nisa machmat kocho* — moved through direct force — renders it *tamei*; *machmat re'adah* — moved through vibration — renders it *tahor*. Everyone agrees on this rule. The debate is whether causing an object to shake in place without displacing it constitutes *hesset*, genuine movement, or not. One opinion holds that shaking counts as movement; the other holds it does not. In any event, Abaye has shown that the *kli*-versus-*ohel* distinction is not what the *tanna'im* in *Zavim* are arguing about.

As Rashi frames it, the practical upshot for our *eiruv* question is as follows: if the wardrobe is small enough to be a genuine *kli* — below the threshold of *arbaim se'ah* volume — then everyone agrees one can break it, and the *eiruv* is accessible. If it is large enough to fall into a non-*kli* category — above *arbaim se'ah* — then everyone agrees it cannot be broken. The middle ground that generates debate must lie elsewhere.

---

## String & Knife Issue

### String Binding

Both Abaye and Rava resolve the problem together. The *mishna* must be discussing a case of *migdal kashur b'matna* — a wardrobe bound with a string. Rashi's understanding is that we are dealing with a large wardrobe that is too big to qualify as a *kli* and therefore cannot be broken open without transgressing *soter*. That rules out simply smashing it. However, the wardrobe is secured not only by a lock but also by a rope or string wrapped around it. The key to the lock may be missing, but the string is accessible. Could one simply cut the string and open the wardrobe that way, without touching the lock?

The answer requires a knife, and here the entire dispute of the *mishna* resolves itself into a *muktzah* question: may one use a knife on *Shabbos* to cut a rope?

### Rabbi Yosei Lenient

The *tanna kamma* of the *mishna* rules the *eiruv* valid because he holds like Rabbi Yosei, *de-amar kol ha-kelim nitlin b'Shabbos* — that all vessels may be handled on *Shabbos* except for the great saw and the plow-peg. In other words, any ordinary vessel may be used even for purposes beyond its primary function, without concern for *muktzah*. On this view, one may take a kitchen knife and use it to cut the rope binding the wardrobe. The *eiruv* is therefore considered accessible, and it is valid.

### Rabbi Nechemiah Strict

Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, holds like Rabbi Nechemiah, *de-amar afilu tallis ve-afilu tarvad ein nitlin ella le-tzorech tashmishan* — that even a cloak or a ladle may only be handled for their own specific, intended purpose. A kitchen knife is intended for cutting food; using it to cut a rope is outside its designated function, and therefore the knife is *muktzah* for that purpose. Since one cannot use the knife, the rope cannot be cut, the wardrobe cannot be opened, and the *eiruv* is inaccessible.

It is striking that what appears in the *mishna* as a fundamental dispute about the validity of an *eiruv* in a locked wardrobe resolves, on this reading, into a narrow and technical *muktzah* question: whether Rabbi Yosei or Rabbi Nechemiah's position on handling vessels governs.

---

## Nitgalgal & Destruction

### Rolling Away

The next *mishna* addresses what happens when the *eiruv* itself is removed from its intended location before *Shabbos* begins. *Nitgalgal chutz la-techum* — if it rolled outside the *techum*, it started *Shabbos* beyond the two-thousand-*amah* boundary that the *eiruv* was meant to extend, and it can no longer serve its function. The *mishna* proceeds to enumerate additional cases: *nafal alav gal* — rubble fell on top of it; *nisraf* — it was burned; or, if it was *terumah*, it became *tamei*. The rule is: if any of these occurred while it was still *b'od yom* — on Friday before *Shabbos* — the *eiruv* is invalid. If they occurred only after nightfall — *mishe-chashechah* — it is valid, since at the moment of *Shabbos* the *eiruv* was in proper order.

Rava adds a qualification to the *nitgalgal* case: *lo shanu ela she-nitgalgel chutz le-arba amot* — the rule of invalidity applies only when the *eiruv* rolled more than four *amot* beyond the two-thousand-*amah* mark.
