Within four *amot* it remains valid, since the place where one deposits an *eiruv* is treated halakhically like one's home, and within four *amot* of that location is considered to share that space. This is the source cited earlier in the *masechta* for the four-*amah* rule.

The most consequential case is the *safek* — doubt. If one does not know whether the disqualifying event occurred before or after *Shabbos* began, the *mishna* records a dispute. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah rule *harei zeh chammar gamal* — it is like being both a donkey-driver and a camel-leader simultaneously. The donkey-driver walks behind and pushes the animal forward; the camel-leader walks in front and pulls the animal forward. If one is somehow positioned between a donkey and a camel moving in opposite directions, one is pulled both ways at once and can go nowhere. The idiom captures the halakhic predicament precisely.

If the *eiruv* was valid, the person acquired a *techum* extending two thousand *amot* to the north of where he placed it, but he forfeited the corresponding two thousand *amot* to the south of his starting point. If the *eiruv* was invalid, he never acquired the extended northern range but retains the full two thousand *amot* in every direction from where he spent *Shabbos*. Not knowing which, he cannot travel the full four thousand *amot* north — because maybe the *eiruv* was valid, in which case he gets only two thousand from the *eiruv*'s location — and he cannot travel freely to the south — because maybe the *eiruv* was valid, in which case he surrendered his southward range. He is left with only two thousand *amot* to the north of his starting point, the minimum guaranteed to him in either scenario.

### Building Falls

Concerning the case of *nafal alav gal* — where rubble falls onto the *eiruv* — the *gemara* initially assumes that the case is one where the stones are merely *muktzah*, a rabbinic prohibition, and could in principle be removed. If so, one might expect the *mishna*'s ruling that the *eiruv* is inaccessible to conflict with the opinion of Rabbi — Rebbe — who holds that rabbinic prohibitions (*shevut*) were not in force *bein ha-shemashos*, during twilight. If the *eiruv* was already covered as *Shabbos* began, but the only impediment is a rabbinic *muktzah*, should Rabbi not consider it still accessible?

The *gemara* resolves this: the *mishna* could accord with Rabbi, but the case must involve a situation where a shovel or hoe is required to uncover the *eiruv* — and that would constitute a biblical violation. The *rishonim*, including the Ritva, explain that digging through rubble with implements could constitute either *boneh* — if it improves the floor of a structure — or *choresh* — plowing, if it disrupts and prepares ground in a field context. Either way, the prohibition is biblical, not merely rabbinic.

The *gemara* then explains why each scenario in the *mishna* is necessary. If the *mishna* had only stated *nitgalgal*, one might think the invalidity follows only because the *eiruv* is no longer physically present at the right location — but *nafal alav gal* would be different since the *eiruv* remains in place, merely covered. Conversely, if only the *nafal alav gal* case were given, one might say it fails because the *eiruv* is hidden and invisible — but for *nitgalgal* one might think it valid, since one can see where it went and a wind could theoretically blow it back. By stating both cases, the *mishna* teaches that any form of inaccessibility — regardless of the specific mechanism — disqualifies the *eiruv*.

### Burned & Impure

The *mishna* then gives two further cases: *nisraf* — the *eiruv* was burned — and *terumah nitme'et* — it was *terumah* that became *tamei*. Why are these cases necessary once the previous ones have established the principle? The *gemara* answers at the top of 35b: *tana nisraf le-hodia kocho de-Rabbi Yossi* — the case of burning is cited to reveal the full extent of Rabbi Yossi's leniency. Rabbi Yossi holds that when the *safek* arises, one may assume the *eiruv* was valid. One might have thought this assumption is plausible only when the *eiruv* still exists in some form — perhaps it deteriorated or was partially destroyed — and one can extend the presumption of its prior valid status. When the *eiruv* has been completely destroyed by fire, can one still invoke the prior good status? Rabbi Yossi says yes — even in that extreme case.

The case of *terumah nitme'et* teaches the opposite lesson: *le-hodia kocho de-Rabbi Meir* — to reveal the full extent of Rabbi Meir's stringency. Here the *eiruv* is physically present, entirely intact, unchanged in form. The only question is a halakhic one: did its status change before or after *Shabbos*? One might expect that since nothing physical has changed, even Rabbi Meir would allow reliance on the prior good status. He does not. Even in this most minimal scenario, where the *eiruv* is present before one's eyes and only its halakhic status is in doubt, Rabbi Meir rules that the *safek* leaves one in the *chammar gamal* predicament.

---

## Safek Eiruv

### Chammar Gamal

With those boundaries established, the *mishna* turns to the core dispute about *safek eiruv* — a doubtful *eiruv*. The *chammar gamal* image captures the halakhic paralysis with vivid precision. A person who left his *eiruv* at point B, two thousand *amot* north of where he will spend *Shabbos*, intended to extend his *techum* northward to four thousand *amot*. If the *eiruv* was valid, he effectively started *Shabbos* at point B, giving him two thousand *amot* north of B but surrendering free movement south of his actual sleeping location. If it was invalid, he started at his own location and has two thousand *amot* in every direction.

Not knowing which scenario applies, he cannot commit to either. He cannot walk the full four thousand *amot* north — because if the *eiruv* failed, he has only two thousand from his starting point. He cannot walk freely to the south — because if the *eiruv* succeeded, he forfeited that range. He is left with the bare two thousand *amot* north of himself, the minimum guaranteed under either outcome. That is the chammar gamal.

### Meir & Yehudah

Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah adopt the stringent position. When the status of the *eiruv* is unknown, they do not allow any reliance on its prior good standing. The person is left in the *chammar gamal* position: restricted to two thousand *amot* north, and cut off from his full southern range. There is no basis, in their view, for defaulting to the favorable assumption that the *eiruv* remained intact when *Shabbos* began.

### Yosei & Shimon

Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Shimon take the lenient position: *safek eiruv kasher* — a doubtful *eiruv* is valid. Since the entire institution of *eiruv* is rabbinic, a doubt is resolved leniently. Moreover, the *gemara* will develop the point that in addition to the general principle of leniency in rabbinic doubts, there is a *chazakah* at work: since the *eiruv* was properly in place before *Shabbos*, one may presume that it remained in that valid state when *Shabbos* began. Rabbi Yossi bolsters this further by citing the testimony of Aftolmus in the name of five elders that a doubtful *eiruv* is indeed *kasher* — an ancient tradition confirming the lenient position.

---

## Meir Consistency Q

### Tum'ah Comparison

The *gemara* now poses a sharp challenge against Rabbi Meir. His stringency in the *safek eiruv* case seems surprising given that the *gemara* assumes *techumin* might be rabbinic — and Rabbi Meir is generally lenient on rabbinic doubts. The *gemara* supports this from a well-known *mishna* concerning *tum'ah*: someone who was *tamei* went to immerse in a *mikvah*, and is uncertain whether he immersed, or uncertain whether the *mikvah* contained the requisite *arbaim se'ah*, or chose between two *mikvaos* one of which was *kasher* and one of which was not, without knowing which he entered — all of these constitute a *safek* regarding his *taharah*. When the underlying *tum'ah* is biblical in severity, the rule is *sefeko tamei*: he remains presumed *tamei*, since he began in that status and cannot confirm its removal. But when the underlying *tum'ah* is a rabbinic one — such as eating *tamei* food, drinking *tamei* liquids, or immersing in drawn water (*mayim she'uvin*) — the ruling is *sefeko tahor*. On a rabbinic *tum'ah*, the *safek* is resolved leniently.

This is presumed to reflect the opinion of Rabbi Meir, since the *stam mishna* is attributed to him. And it raises an obvious difficulty: if Rabbi Meir is lenient on doubts in rabbinic *tum'ah*, why is he strict on a *safek eiruv*, which is likewise rabbinic?

### Bird Flies Measure

A further challenge arises from a *mishna* regarding the measurement of *techumin* when the path crosses a mountain. The standard approach is to measure as the bird flies, treating the terrain as flat. The *gemara* describes this as *yachol le-havli'o* — one can "swallow" the mountain using fifty-*amah* measuring strings: one measurer stands on one side, another on the other, the string is held taut at the appropriate horizontal level, the position is marked, and measurement continues. When the mountain is wider than fifty *amot* — *eino yachol le-havli'o* — a more complex method is employed, *mekadrin beharim*, which still attempts to approximate horizontal measurement using a four-*amah* string held at chest and foot level.

Cited in the name of Rabbi Meir — specifically transmitted by Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai in the name of Rabbi Meir — is the ruling that one does indeed pierce through the mountain with measurements as the bird flies even in the *eino yachol le-havli'o* case. This is significant because Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Abbuha rules that *ein mekadrin* — one does not measure by piercing through — *lo be-arei miklat* and *lo be-eglah arufah*. For *arei miklat*, the cities of refuge, the 2000-*amah* buffer zone is measured along the actual ground, not as the bird flies; similarly, *eglah arufah* requires measuring which city is closest by walking distance, not aerial distance. The *gemara* infers from these cases a principle: biblical measurements are made as the dog walks, not as the bird flies. If *techumin* were biblical, one would not measure them as the bird flies.

### Techumin D'Rabbanan

The *gemara* therefore concludes: since the ruling attributed to Rabbi Meir permits measuring *techumin* as the bird flies, Rabbi Meir must hold that *techumin* are *d'rabbanan*. But then why is he strict in the *mishna* about *safek eiruv*?

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *ha didei ha de-rabbeih* — the leniency is his teacher's view, not Rabbi Meir's own. The language of the ruling makes this clear: Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai does not cite the bird-flies measurement as Rabbi Meir's personal position, but rather says *shamati she-makkilin* — "I heard a tradition that one is lenient." Rabbi Meir is transmitting what he received, not endorsing it as his own *pesak*. The *gemara* notes that the precise phrasing — *shamati* — supports this inference. Rabbi Meir personally holds that *techumin* are *d'oraisa*, which is why he is strict by *safek eiruv*, and he would not permit measuring as the bird flies for a biblical *halacha*.

---

## Meir Strictness

### Started Bad

With that reconciliation in place, the *gemara* launches a second challenge against Rabbi Meir: a *d'oraisa* versus *d'oraisa* inconsistency. The *gemara* cites a *mishna*: someone who touched a person at night without knowing whether that person was alive or dead at the time of contact — *eino yodeia im chai im meit* — and then discovered in the morning that the person had died sometime during the night. Rabbi Meir rules *tahor*; the *chachamim* rule *tamei*, reasoning *shekol tumos ke-sha'at metziatam* — one assesses *tum'ah* statuses as of the moment of their discovery. Since the person is now found to be dead, the presumption runs backward, treating the corpse as having already been dead at the time of contact. But Rabbi Meir is lenient, even though touching a corpse is a biblical *tum'ah*. This appears to contradict his stringency in the *mikvah* case.

The distinction is crucial. In the *mikvah* case, the person *began* in a state of *tum'ah*. His initial status was bad. The doubt is whether that bad status was removed; and when one cannot confirm removal, the rule is to remain with the prior bad status. The logic is unimpeachable: you were *tamei*, you don't know if you became *tahor*, remain *tamei*.

### Two Chazakos

The touching case is structurally different. The person began the night in a state of *taharah* — he was *tahor* before he reached out in the dark. Moreover, he himself began as *tahor*. So there are two *chazakos* of good status: the person being touched was alive and the one doing the touching was *tahor*. When there are two *chazakos* operating in the direction of leniency, Rabbi Meir is willing to be lenient even in a *d'oraisa* case. He resolves the doubt in favor of those two presumptive statuses and rules *tahor*.

The *chachamim*, by contrast, disagree with this approach and instead apply the principle of *ke-sha'at metziatam* — assessing as of the time of discovery — which overrides the prior good status.

### Witnesses Weaken

How does this framework apply to the *safek eiruv* case, where the *eiruv* also *began* in a good state? Rava and Rav Yosef propose that the case in the *mishna* involves two contradictory sets of witnesses. One set testifies that the *eiruv* was disqualified before *Shabbos* began; another set testifies that it was disqualified only after nightfall. Each set of witnesses undermines the other, leaving the question unresolved. But crucially, the very existence of witnesses testifying to the bad outcome — even if contradicted — erodes the *chazakah* of the *eiruv*'s initial good status. The prior good status is weakened not merely by uncertainty but by affirmative testimony to its failure. The *chazakah* is undermined, leaving Rabbi Meir unable to rely on it, and so he rules stringently.

### Two Chazakos Rule

Rava offers a cleaner formulation of the entire principle. *Hasam trei chazakei le-kula, ve-hacha chada chazakah le-kula* — in the touching case there are two *chazakos* supporting leniency; in the *eiruv* case there is only one. In the touching case: first, the person being touched started the night alive; second, the person doing the touching started the night *tahor*. Two independent presumptive statuses, both pointing toward leniency — and Rabbi Meir allows them to prevail even over a *d'oraisa* doubt. In the *eiruv* case there is only one *chazakah*: that the *eiruv* was in good order before *Shabbos*. One *chazakah* alone is insufficient for Rabbi Meir when the stakes are *d'oraisa*, and he rules stringently.

This distinction between a single *chazakah* and a double *chazakah* as the determining factor in Rabbi Meir's approach to *safek d'oraisa* represents one of the deeper conceptual tensions in the *sugya*, and the discussion will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Eiruvin 44

## Boat Landing & Techum

### Setup & Rabban Gamliel

The daf opens still in the context of the boat scenario introduced on 43b. The *mishna* considers a case in which a boat failed to enter port before *Shabbat* began — *paam achat lo nichnasu la-namal* — and the passengers found themselves more than two thousand *amot* from the shore when *Shabbat* commenced. Under ordinary circumstances, having traveled *chutz la-techum*, they would be restricted to four *amot* from wherever they stood. The question is whether they could disembark at all. Rabban Gamliel resolved the matter by reporting that he had been watching as they approached and confirmed that the vessel was already within two thousand *amot* of the port when *Shabbat* began. That being so, the passengers could disembark, even if walking home remained a separate question.

### Disembark Question

The *gemara* presses the point: can they in fact disembark? Given the uncertainty inherent in the exact moment *bein hashmashot* transitions into *Shabbat* — "like the blink of an eye," one moment outside and one moment inside, impossible to pinpoint precisely — any claim about the boat's precise position at that instant is inherently precarious. The assumption is that Rabban Gamliel's observation was made from the outset of *bein hashmashot*, and the *braita* now cited explains how he was confident in his measurement.

### Shfoferet Device

The *braita* records: *shfoferet hayta lo le-Rabban Gamliel* — Rabban Gamliel possessed a *shfoferet*, a tube, through which *she-haya mabit ve-tzofeh bah alpayim ama ba-yabashah* — he would look and ascertain two thousand *amot* on dry land, *u-k'negdo alpayim ba-yam* — and correspondingly two thousand *amot* on the sea. By means of this device, he could determine whether the boat was within the permitted boundary even while at sea.

### Rashi's Focus Theory

The instrument sounds like a telescope, but Rashi explains it differently. Rashi says it was not designed to see farther; in fact, it shortened the distance of vision. By narrowing the aperture at the far end of the tube — collapsing or extending it to open or close that opening — the device limited how far one could see. Once calibrated through actual measurement on flat ground to correspond to exactly two thousand *amot*, anything visible through the tube fell within that distance, while anything beyond it would not be visible. The device could then be applied at sea to make the same determination.

The difficulty with Rashi's explanation is apparent: a narrow aperture limits one's *field* of vision but does not restrict the *distance* one can see. It is hard to understand technically how this would work as described. One suggested reading of Rashi — proposed during the *shiur* — is that the tube was focused at a fixed focal length of two thousand *amot*, so that an object at exactly that distance would appear sharply in focus, while anything further would not. That may be a defensible way of reading Rashi.

### Surveying Methods

The *Steinsaltz* edition cites the *Geonim* and others who understand the *shfoferet* not as an optical device at all but as a surveying instrument of the kind used even today — something like a theodolite or a sextant — employing angular measurements and mathematics to estimate distances. Surveyors are familiar with such instruments, typically mounted on tripods, which use angular geometry to calculate distance without needing to traverse it physically. This would explain how Rabban Gamliel could determine distances across water using measurements previously taken on land.

### Valley & Tree Measuring

The *gemara* proceeds to describe two further applications of the same device. *Ha-rotzeh leida kama omko shel gei* — if one wishes to know the depth of a valley — one brings the *shfoferet* and uses it there as well. Assuming the device has been calibrated by actual measurement on flat ground, one uses that same calibration to determine the distance at the bottom of the valley, or alternatively, one first sights down to the valley floor and then applies that same calibration along flat ground to derive the depth.

For measuring the height of a palm tree, the *gemara* offers an even more elegant method. *Moded komato ve-tzilo* — one measures one's own height and the length of one's shadow, then measures the length of the shadow cast by the palm tree on the same day. Since the shadows are proportional to the objects casting them, a simple ratio yields the palm tree's height. If one's shadow is twice one's height, then the palm tree's height is half the length of its shadow; if one's shadow is half one's height, one multiplies the shadow's length by two. The logic is straightforward and mathematically exact.

### Grave Shadow Remedy

The *gemara* then introduces a case that, while related to the theme of shadows and measurements, seems somewhat unexpected in this context. *Ha-rotzeh she-lo tishre chaya ra'ah be-tzel kever* — one who does not wish poisonous or biting animals, such as scorpions, to take shelter in the shadow of a tombstone. Such creatures seek shade when the day grows warm. The method is as follows: at four hours into the day — approximately 10:00 AM, when warmth begins in earnest — one inserts a stick into the ground near the grave and observes where its shadow falls. That shadow marks exactly where the dangerous creatures will congregate. One then builds a mound at that location so that no shaded area remains at that time of day. Rashi explains that since the animals do not find shade there at 10:00 AM, they will not bother coming to that spot at all during the rest of the day. One might wonder whether they would simply find another nearby spot — but that is the *gemara*'s practical solution.

---

## Nechemya & Wall

### Nechemya's Story

The *gemara* now presents a narrative. *Nechemya brei de-Rav Chanilai* — Nechemya the son of Rav Chanilai — became so deeply absorbed in his learning, *mashchatya shmata*, literally, his *sugya* drew him away, that he walked without awareness of his surroundings and found himself *nafak chutz la-techum* — outside the boundary. He was now stranded, unable to return to the city.

### People Wall Solution

Rav Chisda reported the situation to Rav Nachman: Nechemya, your student, *shari be-tza'ar* — is sitting in distress out there. Rav Nachman replied: *asu lo mechitza shel bnei adam ve-yikanes* — make a wall of people and let him enter. The plan was to assemble a group of people, surround Nechemya with them in a circle, and thereby create an enclosed space. This is significant because the ruling follows the position of Rav, who rules like Rabban Gamliel in the *mishna*: even someone who has gone *chutz la-techum* and is limited to four *amot* may traverse an entire enclosed space if those four *amot* bring him within it. If the enclosure, moreover, brings him back within the original two thousand *amot*, he can return home.

The obvious question is how the people making the wall could themselves reach Nechemya without violating their own *techum*. Rashi suggests they had made some form of *eiruv*, or alternatively they had not gone so far — they were closer to the boundary to begin with, with the houses near the edge of the *techum*.

### Rabban Gamliel Rule

This entire solution depends on ruling like Rabban Gamliel: that an enclosed space, even one created on the spot, allows a person who was stranded *chutz la-techum* to move freely within it. Rava had already established — *halacha ke-Rabban Gamliel be-dir ve-sahar ve-safina* — that the law follows Rabban Gamliel with respect to a fold, a corral, and a boat. Though one might question whether this principle applies straightforwardly to a newly improvised enclosure rather than a pre-existing one, the *gemara* proceeds on that assumption.

### Question on Solution

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak was sitting behind Rava, who was sitting before Rav Nachman, when this exchange took place. After it concluded, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak turned to Rava and asked: what exactly was Rav Chisda's question? What difficulty prompted him to seek Rav Nachman's guidance? Surely the answer seemed clear. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak formulates the possibilities. If the situation was *bi-dmalu gavrei* — that there were enough people to form an enclosure reaching back within the two thousand *amot* — then the only question would have been whether we rule like Rabban Gamliel, and that has already been settled by Rava's ruling. So evidently Rav Chisda's question must have been something more subtle.

### Two Cubit Problem

The true problem, concludes the *gemara*, was *bi-de-lo milu gavrei* — there were not enough people to form a continuous enclosure from Nechemya's position back to within the original two thousand *amot*. They could only bring the enclosure to within two *amot* of the boundary. And that raises the question of whether we rule like Rabbi Eliezer.

Rabbi Eliezer holds two positions: first, a stringency — one's four *amot* are measured as two *amot* in each direction from one's position rather than four in any direction. But second, a leniency — if after stepping outside the boundary one's four *amot* overlap with the original two thousand *amot*, one is considered still within the *techum*, effectively receiving two thousand and two *amot*. The *Chachamim* disagree: once one has crossed the line, even if one's four *amot* would reach back across it, that provides no benefit. So the question was whether Nechemya could benefit from this leniency of Rabbi Eliezer to bridge the remaining two *amot*.

The *gemara* confirms this reading from the precise language Rav Nachman used: *yikanes* — "let him enter." That phrasing implies a gap, that he would leave the enclosure and then *enter* the *techum*, suggesting they could only bring him to within two *amot* of it. The *gemara* thus infers: *peshita bi-de-lo milu gavrei askinan* — it is clear the case involved insufficient people. *Tosafot* raises the natural question: why not simply move the circle of people in successive steps, gradually bringing Nechemya back? The *gemara*'s answer to this will emerge from the discussion that follows — namely, that the people forming the wall must be unaware of their role.

---

## Wall Contradiction

### First Braita Prohibition

At this point Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak raises a more fundamental challenge to the entire solution of surrounding Nechemya with people: is it even permitted to create a wall out of people on *Shabbat*? A *braita* rules: *nafal dofenah* — if a wall of one's *sukkah* fell down — *lo ya'amid bah adam behema ve-kelim* — one may not use a person, an animal, or vessels to reconstitute that wall, even temporarily. And not only with new construction materials is this forbidden — even these improvised substitutes are prohibited. *Ve-lo yizkof et ha-mitah li-fros aleha sadin* — and one may not upturn a bed and spread a sheet over the frame to serve as a wall. *Le-fi she-ein osim ohel arai ba-rishona be-Yom Tov* — because one may not create a temporary *ohel* de novo on *Yom Tov*. *Ve-ein tzarich lomar be-Shabbat* — and certainly not on *Shabbat*. This *braita* would seem to forbid the solution proposed for Nechemya entirely.

### Second Braita Permission

Against this, a second *braita* permits exactly what the first forbids. *Oseh adam et chavero dofen* — one may use one's friend as a wall for a *sukkah* — *kedei she-yochal ve-yishte ve-yishan* — so that one can eat, drink, and sleep in the *sukkah*. And further: *ve-yizkof et ha-mitah ve-yifros aleha sadin kedei she-lo tilke chama al ha-met* — one may upturn a bed and spread a sheet to shade a corpse from the sun; and similarly to protect food from spoiling. So a wall made from a person for the *sukkah* is permitted, and a temporary structure for shade is permitted.

### Reconciliation Attempt

These two *beraitot* directly contradict one another. The *gemara* first attempts to resolve the contradiction by assigning one to Rabbi Eliezer and the other to the *Rabbanan*, based on a dispute recorded in a *mishna* concerning a window stopper (*pekak ha-chalon*). Rabbi Eliezer holds that a window stopper may be used only if it is tied and suspended — essentially already part of the wall's structure, like a shutter. If not, he forbids it, treating even a temporary addition as prohibited. The *Rabbanan* permit it in either case. On this reading, the debate about people and animals serving as walls for a *sukkah* would map onto this dispute.

However, the *gemara* — citing Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — rejects this framing. *Ha-kol modim she-ein osim ohel arai be-Yom Tov* — everyone agrees that one may not create a temporary structure de novo on *Yom Tov*, and certainly not on *Shabbat*. The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Rabbanan* is only about *adding* (*mosif*) to an existing structure. Rabbi Eliezer forbids even adding on *Yom Tov*; the *Rabbanan* permit adding even on *Shabbat*. But creating something entirely new — building a first-time wall — is universally forbidden. Since the fallen wall of a *sukkah* represents the third wall, replacing it is not an addition but a creation, and that is forbidden according to everyone. The contradiction between the two *beraitot* therefore cannot be resolved by attributing them to Rabbi Eliezer and the *Rabbanan*.

### Animal Wall Debate

The *gemara* then proposes resolving the contradiction through the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda. A *braita* teaches: *asah le-vehema dofen le-sukkah* — if one used an animal as a wall for a *sukkah* before *Yom Tov* — Rabbi Meir invalidates it (*posel*) and Rabbi Yehuda validates it (*machshir*). Whether Rabbi Meir's invalidation stems from concern that the animal might wander off, or from a categorical position that a living creature cannot halakhically constitute a wall, the *gemara* proposes the following reading: the *braita* that permits using a person as the third wall goes according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that an animal — and by extension a person — does not constitute a halakhic wall. Therefore, the argument runs, using a person to stand as the third wall on *Shabbat* is not really doing anything halakhically significant, and hence not prohibited.

This *hava amina* is admittedly strained, as Rashi himself acknowledges. The *gemara* quickly dismantles it. First: even granting Rabbi Meir's position about animals, one cannot extend it to people and certainly not to vessels — the prohibition cited in the first *braita* covered all three, and there is no source for saying Rabbi Meir would regard vessels as non-halakhic walls. Second, and more structurally: *Rabbi Meir aliba de-man* — under whose authority is Rabbi Meir operating? If under Rabbi Eliezer, even *adding* is forbidden on *Yom Tov*, which makes the question of whether it is halakhic irrelevant. If under the *Rabbanan*, then the *Rabbanan* only permit *adding* to an existing structure; creating the third wall from scratch — *oseh le-khatechila* — remains forbidden even to them, regardless of whether the new wall is halakhically significant.

### Third vs. Fourth Wall

The *gemara* arrives at the true resolution. *Ela ha va-ha Rabbanan* — both *beraitot* reflect the position of the *Rabbanan*. The contradiction is not a dispute at all; the two *beraitot* address different situations. The first *braita* — which prohibits everything — speaks of the *third* wall of the *sukkah* (*dofen shlishit*), the wall whose creation constitutes the de novo construction of a halakhically functional enclosure. Creating this is forbidden on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* because it is the equivalent of building an *ohel* afresh. The second *braita* — which permits everything — speaks of the *fourth* wall (*dofen revi'it*), or of a wall erected separately that serves no formal halakhic definition of an enclosure — such as providing shade for a corpse or protecting food. This distinction can be inferred from the language of the first *braita* itself, which says *nafal dofenah* — *its* wall fell — implying the wall that was halakhically constitutive. The second *braita* simply says *oseh dofen* — making *a* wall — without that definite possessive force.

---

## Halachic Distinction

### Halachic Wall Defined

The resolution of the *braita* contradiction turns on a fundamental distinction that the *gemara* here articulates and that has far-reaching practical implications. A halakhic wall (*mechitza*) is one that serves a formally recognized halakhic function: defining the boundaries of a *reshut*, completing the required walls of a *sukkah*, or establishing an enclosed space within which movement is permitted on *Shabbat*. Creating such a wall on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* is prohibited, even if it is entirely temporary, because it constitutes the act of building — *oseh ohel arai* — in a halakhically significant sense.

### Non-Halachic Allowed

A wall that serves only a practical or incidental function — providing shade, blocking wind for comfort, protecting a corpse or food — does not rise to the level of an *ohel arai* in the prohibited sense. Such a wall may be erected on *Shabbat* even if it is newly created. The distinction is not merely formal; it reflects a substantive halakhic category. Only when a wall is *doing something* in the halakhic sense — defining a *reshut*, completing a *sukkah* — is its creation treated as an act of building.

### Mechitza Example

This principle has practical application in the laws of the *mechitza* in a synagogue. The *Mordechai* records that when women came to hear the rabbi's *derasha*, a *mechitza* could be erected — at the time of the *Rishonim*, women typically prayed in a separate room or building, but the rabbi did not wish to deliver the *derasha* twice, so the women would gather in the main space and a partition would be put up between them and the men. This was permitted because the *mechitza* served a practical purpose of modesty and separation, not a formal halakhic function of dividing *reshuyot* or defining an enclosure. It was therefore not considered a halakhic wall.

This connects to a broader dispute among later authorities regarding the nature of the *mechitza* in a *shul*. Rav Henkin cites his grandfather, Rav Yosef Eliyahu Henkin, who argued that the fundamental role of the *mechitza* is to halakhically designate the men's and women's sections as separate domains — not primarily to obstruct physical interaction. Under that view, a *mechitza* of *asara tefachim* — approximately thirty inches — would suffice, since it accomplishes the formal halakhic function of separation. Indeed, some synagogues, even within the OU, historically maintained *mechitzot* of that height. Rav Moshe Feinstein strongly disagrees with this position.

Importantly, Rav Henkin's approach carries its own stringency: if the *mechitza* must serve as a formal halakhic wall, it must come within three *tefachim* of the ground (*lavud*). In one of his *teshuvot*, he critiques a particular kibbutz where the *mechitza* was a suspended fabric screen that began more than three *tefachim* off the floor — which would be halakhically invalid on that understanding. The practical consequence for our *sugya* is direct: if the *mechitza* serves a formal halakhic function, it cannot be erected on *Shabbat*, because creating a halakhic wall is prohibited. If it serves only a practical function of modesty or visual separation, it may be erected on *Shabbat*.

### Unaware People Rule

With the distinction between halakhic and non-halakhic walls established, the *gemara* returns to the contradiction regarding people. The first *braita* forbids using a person as the third wall of a *sukkah*; the second permits it. The *gemara* resolves: *kan la-da'at kan she-lo mi-da'at* — here the person is aware he is serving as the wall; there, he is not. When the person standing as a wall knows he is functioning as a formal halakhic division, the wall has been consciously constructed and is treated as a prohibited act of building. When he is unaware — when he is simply standing there, and another person has arranged the scenario without informing him of his halakhic role — the wall is not considered to have been formally erected in the prohibited sense.

The underlying logic seems to be that a human being is not simply an object. The idea that a person can be designated as a halakhic wall has something inherently tenuous about it. If the person himself is unaware, the designation lacks the consciousness that would transform him into something formally defined. He is still just a person standing there. Yet paradoxically — and this is a striking feature of the halakha — he is simultaneously *sufficient* to function as a wall for the *sukkah*, permitting eating, drinking, and sleeping. The halakha thus plays both sides: he counts enough to function as a wall, but not enough for his placement to constitute a prohibited act of construction.

### Unaware Examples

The *gemara* illustrates the principle with several cases. A group of gardeners used a circle of people as a *mechitza* to carry water — apparently from a well in the field into a domain where carrying was otherwise prohibited — and Shmuel had them flogged, because the people forming the wall were aware of their role. Subsequently, when Rava was leaving the *beit midrash* surrounded by his students — as was typical, the disciples walking around him — someone exploited the moment: while the entourage moved through the street of Mechuza, he retrieved some flasks that had been lying in the thoroughfare and carried them within the moving circle of students. The students were unaware they were functioning as a *mechitza*, and so this was permitted. The following *Shabbat*, when the same trick was attempted again, Rava forbade it — *de-hayu yadei* — because by then everyone knew what was being done, and awareness had been established.

Similarly, Levi's household used surrounding people to bring in *tivna* — straw; Zeiri's for *asfasta* — some variety of fodder; Rav Shimi bar Chiya's for water. In each case the people involved were presumably unaware of their halakhic role.

### Awareness Prohibition

This leads to the broader conclusion: awareness of halakhic purpose converts the act of using people as a wall into a prohibited act of building on *Shabbat*. This is why *Tosafot*'s solution — moving the circle of people in successive steps to gradually bring Nechemya back — would not have worked. Each successive repositioning, done deliberately to extend a *mechitza*, would necessarily involve awareness, and the prohibition would apply.

---

## Techum Above Ground

### No Techum Aloft

The *gemara*'s treatment of the boat scenario rests on a crucial halakhic premise: *ein techum le-mala me-asara tefachim* — there is no *techum* obligation above ten *tefachim* off the ground. Since *techumim* are in any case rabbinic in nature — and on the sea or in the air even the opinion that a *techum* of twelve *mil* might be biblical does not apply, as all authorities agree that *techumin d'oraita* pertains only to travel on dry land — the prohibition of *techum* above ten *tefachim* is at most a rabbinic question, and given the dispute, the rule is resolved *le-kula*.

### Plane Landing

This principle applies equally to air travel. If a plane lands on *Shabbat* and throughout its approach and taxiing the aircraft remains above ten *tefachim* off the surface — which is typically the case during flight and much of the landing roll — the passenger's *techum* begins only from the point where the plane effectively comes to ground level contact with a four-by-four *tefach* base. Precisely when during taxiing this occurs — whether the aircraft's contact with the tarmac while still in motion constitutes grounding in the halakhic sense, given that the body of the plane is still elevated — is a question worth examining further. But the basic principle is that so long as the aircraft remains above ten *tefachim*, no *techum* has been established.

### Boat Passenger Ruling

The *Shulchan Aruch* addresses this directly. One who travels by boat on *Shabbat* and arrives at port: *im mi-she-nichnas ha-Shabbat ad she-higia la-namal le-olam hayata le-mala me-asara mi-karka ha-yam o ha-nahar* — if from the moment *Shabbat* began until arrival at port the vessel was always above ten *tefachim* from the floor of the sea or river — *yored ve-aino nimnah ve-yesh lo alpayim ama mi-makom she-paga bo le-mata me-asara* — the passenger disembarks and is not counted as having a prior *techum* location, and receives two thousand *amot* from the point where the vessel first came within ten *tefachim* of the ground.

### Cruise Ship Case

This ruling applies to cruise ships and any other vessel that travels in waters deep enough to remain above ten *tefachim* throughout the voyage. Wherever such a ship docks on *Shabbat*, the passengers receive two thousand *amot* from the landing point. They do not carry a *techum* established from some distant home port, having spent *Shabbat* above ten *tefachim* for the duration.

---

## Mitzvah Departure Case

### Mitzvah Permission

The *gemara* now turns to a new *mishna*. *Mi she-yatza bi-reshut* — one who went out *chutz la-techum* with halakhic permission. The cases paradigmatically cited in *Masechet Rosh Hashanah* include one who went to give testimony regarding the new month, a midwife going to assist at a birth, or one going to rescue a person in mortal danger. When a person leaves the *techum* to perform a *mitzvah*, the rabbis granted a leniency: upon arrival at the destination, one receives two thousand *amot* in every direction from that new location, even without having made an *eiruv*.

### Services Unneeded

The *mishna* now addresses a complication: *ve-amru lo k'var na'asa ma'aseh* — and they told him, the situation has already been resolved. The midwife arrives and learns that another midwife delivered the baby. The witness arrives and learns that enough other witnesses have testified. At that point, the *mitzvah* purpose of the journey has evaporated. What is this person's status? *Yesh lo alpayim ama le-chol ruach* — he has two thousand *amot* in every direction from wherever he stands when he receives that information. He does not get to continue to the destination city and receive two thousand *amot* from there. He may be stuck in the middle of a road, two thousand *amot* from neither his home nor his destination — a potentially uncomfortable situation, and one that *Hatzolah* volunteers and emergency responders must navigate in practice.

### Original Techum Reversion

The *mishna* then adds: *im haya be-soch ha-techum ke-ilu lo yatza* — if he was still within his original *techum* when he received this information, it is as if he never left. Rava clarifies what this means: *ke-ilu lo yatza mi-toch beito* — it is as if he never left his house. That is, he does not receive a new two thousand *amot* centered on his current position within the *techum*. He reverts entirely to his original *techum* from home. The *gemara* notes that one might have thought *ho'il ve-akar akar* — since he uprooted himself halakhically and was granted the traveler's two thousand *amot*, perhaps that grant persists even upon return. The *mishna* teaches otherwise.

### Overlapping Techumim

Rachumi bar Chiya offers a more expansive reading of the *mishna*'s ruling. He reads *im hayu techumim she-nasnu lo chachamim muvla'in be-soch techumo ke-ilu lo yatza mi-techumo* as follows: if the two thousand *amot* granted to him from his current position — wherever he received the news — *overlap* with his original *techum* from home, then he is treated as if he never left his original *techum*. The practical consequence is significant: since both *techumim* are operative and they overlap, he may travel from his home two thousand *amot* in one direction and from his current position two thousand *amot* in the other direction, with free movement throughout the overlapping zone. In one reading, Rashi indicates that the two *techumim* effectively merge into a single enlarged *techum* — allowing movement from the home's far boundary all the way to the position's far boundary in the opposite direction, potentially close to eight thousand *amot* in total.

### Overlap Debate

The underlying dispute is whether *havla'at techumim* — the absorption of one *techum* within another, or their overlap — *milsa hi*, constitutes something significant, or whether it is halakhically inconsequential. According to the position that it is significant, the overlap creates a merged *techum* from which one may benefit in both directions. According to the opposing view, the two *techumim* remain independent, and overlap does not extend one's rights.

### Cave Example

Abaye challenges Rava: surely you must agree that *havla'at techumim milsa hi*. He proves it from the case of one who began *Shabbat* at the bottom of a cave (*shavat bi-me'ara*). If the interior of the cave at ground level is four thousand *amot* wide, and the cave narrows toward the top so that the opening at each end is less than four thousand *amot* across, the person at the bottom — surrounded by the cave's walls — has established his *techum* in an enclosed space. He exits either opening and receives two thousand *amot* in that direction. But since the cave bottom is four thousand *amot* wide, and both exits feed from the same enclosed space, he effectively has two thousand *amot* beyond each exit — even though the total distance from one outer boundary to the other exceeds four thousand *amot*. This appears to be a case where the two *techumim* overlap and merge into one enlarged domain.

Rava's response is that the cave case is categorically different: there, the person *began Shabbat* surrounded by *mechitzot* — the walls of the cave enclosed him on all sides from the start of *Shabbat*. The two exits are not two separate positions but two openings of a single enclosed space. It is the cave's enclosure, present from the outset, that generates the two directional *techumim*; they are not two independent *techumim* that happen to overlap. The case of the traveler whose *techum* from his current position overlaps his *techum* from home is structurally different — those are genuinely two distinct *techumim* — and their overlap does not necessarily produce the same merger.

---

## Coerced Departure

### Coercion Restriction

The *gemara* moves to the final *mishna* of the *daf*. *Mi she-hotziu'uhu nochrim o ruach ra'ah* — one who was taken out of his *techum* by gentiles or by a *ruach ra'ah* — typically understood as a spirit of insanity or some compulsion that removed him involuntarily — *ein lo ela arba amot*. He has only four *amot* from wherever he was deposited. He had no agency in the departure; the exit was entirely coerced. The halakha therefore does not grant him any extended *techum* beyond the bare minimum.

### Return Clause

If, however, the gentiles or the spirit returned him to his original place — *ke-ilu lo yatza* — it is as though he never left. His original *techum* is fully restored.

### Fold/Corral Dispute

The *mishna* then presents a dispute regarding a specific subcase: *netanuhu be-dir o be-sahar* — if they placed him in a *dir* (a fold or pen for animals) or a *sahar* (a corral or enclosure). Within such an enclosed space, does he have the right to walk throughout the entire area, or is he still limited to four *amot*?

### Rabban Gamliel Position

Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah rule: *mehalech et kulah* — he may walk the entire enclosure. Even though he was brought *chutz la-techum* by coercion and receives only four *amot*, if those four *amot* bring him within a pre-existing enclosed space, he may traverse the entire space. This follows the logic of Rabban Gamliel's broader position on enclosed spaces and *techum*.

### Rabbi Yehoshua Position

Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva disagree: *ein lo ela arba amot* — even within the fold or corral, he is limited to four *amot*. The coercive nature of his removal, in their view, restricts him to the absolute minimum regardless of the physical structure he finds himself in.

### Brindisi Ship Case

The *mishna* records a historical incident that maps directly onto this dispute. *Ma'aseh she-ba'u mi-Prundisin* — there was an episode involving travelers coming from Brindisi, the Italian port — *ve-hifligah sefinatam ba-yam* — and their ship was sailing at sea on *Shabbat*. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah *halchu et kulah* — walked through the entire ship, treating the vessel as an enclosed space in which they were free to move. Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva *lo zazu me-arba amot* — did not move beyond four *amot*, *ela she-ratzu le-hachmir al atzmam* — because they chose to be stringent upon themselves. The phrasing is notable: the *mishna* does not say they ruled the halakha required it, but rather that they voluntarily adopted the stringent position. Both pairs of *Tannaim* were on the same ship, and each acted in accordance with his own ruling.

---

---

# Eiruvin 45

## Overlap & Techum

### Intro: Chutz L'Techum

Today's *daf* is 45, and we pick up at the bottom of 44b dealing with the issue of somebody who goes *chutz l'techum*. The first *mishna* of the chapter addressed going *chutz l'techum* because of an *ones* — one was forced outside the *techum*. This *mishna*, by contrast, speaks about going out for a *mitzvah* purpose, and also mentions going out *b'reshut* — by permission or choice — without yet specifying what that entails. The *halacha* established there is that one receives 2,000 *amot* from where one currently stands.

### Rabba vs. Rav Shimi

The question now debated in the *Gemara* between Rabba and Rav Shimi bar Chiya concerns what happens when one went out, found that one's services were no longer needed, and has 2,000 *amot* from one's current location. How does that relate to the original *techum* from home? If one has stepped beyond one's original 2,000 *amot* from home — if the new position lies outside the circle one began with — does the new 2,000 *amot* get one back to one's house, or does it simply define a new, independent *techum*?

The first position holds that if one is still within 2,000 *amot* of one's original *techum*, the overlap allows one to revert to one's old *techum*. But if one has left those 2,000 *amot*, one is confined to the new *techum* alone. The second position holds that even if one has left the original 2,000 *amot*, because the two *techumin* overlap, that overlap is sufficient to allow one to return home. And according to one reading in Rashi, the overlap does not merely restore the original *techum* — it grants both simultaneously. One could traverse all the way back through one's original *techum* and all the way forward through the new one, effectively having the combination of both.

### Rabbi Eliezer & Overlap

The *Gemara* picks up at the last line of 44b and raises a challenge. If without the special circumstance of a walled enclosure one would not invoke the principle of *havlaat techumin* — overlap of *techumin* — then how do we account for what we learned in the *mishna* at the top of 45a? Rabbi Eliezer says: *shtayim yikanes, shalosh lo yikanes* — if one steps over the 2,000-*amah* line by up to two *amot*, one may return; if by three *amot*, one may not. The reasoning is that Rabbi Eliezer holds one stands in the middle of one's four *amot*, meaning two *amot* extend in each direction. If one stepped over the 2,000-*amah* line by two *amot*, one's two *amot* in the backward direction will still overlap with the 2,000 *amot*, permitting re-entry. At three *amot*, one is completely outside — even one's two *amot* no longer create any overlap — and so one cannot return.

The *Gemara* asks: is not the explanation here that *Rabbi Eliezer l'teimei* — Rabbi Eliezer follows his own reasoning — since he holds one stands at the center of one's four *amot*, and the four *amot* granted by the Rabbis are *k'man d'mivlu damu*, as if absorbed into or overlapping the 2,000 *amot*, allowing one to re-enter one's original *techum* and travel all the way back home? This demonstrates that *havlaat techumin* — overlap — is indeed a significant and operative principle, permitting one to restore, at minimum, the original *techum*.

### Rabba bar bar Chana

Rabba bar bar Chana challenged this proof, saying to Abaye: Are you citing Rabbi Eliezer against the master — that is, against Rabba? Perhaps the Rabbis disagree precisely because they hold that *havlaat techumin* is not operative; that is the very point of their dispute with Rabbi Eliezer, and we may well rule like the *chachamim*.

The response was: yes, I am bringing my proof from Rabbi Eliezer, because I heard from the same master, Rabba himself, the following tradition: *ad kan lo pligi Rabbanan alei d'Rabbi Eliezer ela l'dvar reshut* — the Rabbis only disagree with Rabbi Eliezer in a case of *devar reshut*, where one overstepped the *techum* without any permissible cause. In such a case, since one should not have been *chutz l'techum* to begin with, the Rabbis refuse to allow the overlap to restore one's original *techum*. But *l'dvar mitzvah* — when one went *chutz l'techum* for a *mitzvah* purpose, as in our *mishna*, where one receives a full 2,000 *amot* rather than the usual four — in that case, even the Rabbis would agree that the overlap permits one to return home, and according to one version of Rashi, potentially to have both *techumin*.

### Practical Halacha

Before moving on, several practical *halachic* implications of the preceding discussion deserve attention. First, regarding Rabban Gamliel's ruling on *dir u'sohar* — a walled enclosure — the *Gemara* on yesterday's *daf* took for granted that we rule like Rav, who holds that we rule like Rabban Gamliel, meaning that even if one did not begin *Shabbat* inside the walled enclosure, one is given the entire enclosure upon entering it after going *chutz l'techum*. This is brought by the *Rishonim* as proof that the rule of Rabban Gamliel is accepted *halacha*.

A highly relevant modern application concerns someone whose flight is delayed on *Shabbat*: upon landing and stepping into the jetway or terminal, one finds oneself in a walled enclosure — and on this basis one would be granted the full space of that enclosure.

A second and equally important issue concerns the *mishna*'s listing of cases where one was placed *chutz l'techum* — including being forcibly transported to another city, *holichuhu l'ir acheres*, alongside the case of *dir u'sohar*. What constitutes "another city" here? The *Shulchan Aruch* and a number of *Rishonim* hold this refers specifically to a walled city, making it simply another instance of a walled enclosure. But the Rambam and other *Rishonim* — and some permit relying on this *b'shas hadechak* — understand it to mean even an unwalled city. Just as one who begins *Shabbat* within a city is given the entire city as a single unit without it counting against one's 2,000 *amot*, so too, if one is brought *chutz l'techum* and deposited in an unwalled city, one receives the full city. The practical implication is significant: if one's plane was delayed and one had no control over the situation, one may be given the full city in which the airport is located, entirely aside from any question about walled enclosures.

A further question raised concerns the case where one willfully chose to fly over *Shabbat* and land. There it is a *machlokes Rishonim* whether one who voluntarily left one's *techum* and finds oneself in a walled enclosure may walk the full space — the debate of the *mishna*'s emphasis on *ones* cuts in different directions among the *Rishonim*, and the practical question about delayed flights turns on exactly this distinction.

---

## Saving & Weapons

### Contradiction

The *mishna* concludes: *v'chol hayotzim l'hatzil chozrin limkoman* — and all who go out to save may return to their original place. The *Gemara* is troubled: the earlier part of the *mishna* established that one going out for a *mitzvah* has 2,000 *amot* from the new position — yet the conclusion seems to offer a blanket permission to go home regardless of distance. If one entered a new city in the course of the mission, one has the whole city plus 2,000 *amot* from its edge. But one is still defined by the new position. So which is it: 2,000 *amot*, or an unlimited return home?

### Rav Yehuda Answer

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers: *shechozrin bichlei zayin limkoman* — the *mishna*'s statement is not primarily about the distance one may travel. It comes to teach an additional and distinct leniency: that those who went out to save may return *carrying their weapons*. The permission to carry arms on *Shabbat* is the novel ruling — not necessarily an extension of travel beyond 2,000 *amot*.

Why is carrying weapons permitted? This is not a case of *heter sofo mishum techilaso* — the end permitted on account of the beginning. Rather, as will be seen, the reason is that even once the battle appears to have concluded, depositing one's weapons immediately exposes one to renewed attack. Therefore one may remain armed until safely home, as a matter of *pikuach nefesh*.

One might ask: why does the *mishna* say *limkoman* — back to their place — implying travel all the way home? Practically speaking, the *halacha* as ruled is that when one goes out to fight the enemy, one may go all the way home, not merely 2,000 *amot*, because the entire situation is one of *pikuach nefesh*. The 2,000-*amot* limit applies to those who went out for other permissible purposes. The *Gemara* at this stage does not emphasize this point, but *l'halacha* that is how it is understood.

### Rosh Hashanah Mishna

The *Gemara* then reconsiders: was there even a question to begin with? Perhaps *l'hatzil shani* — saving from attack is obviously different from other permitted departures, and so the blanket return makes self-evident sense without any contradiction. The *Gemara* replies: *ela ha kashya ha kashya* — it is a different difficulty that drove the question and its answer, namely the *mishna* in *Rosh Hashanah*.

That *mishna* recounts that originally, when witnesses came on *Shabbat* to testify about the new moon and went *chutz l'techum* to do so, they were confined to the courtyard where they had arrived — no special leniency yet existed for those who departed for a *mitzvah*. Rabban Gamliel the elder then enacted a *takana* that these witnesses receive 2,000 *amot* in every direction. The *mishna* then broadens this: *v'lo elu bilvad amru* — and they did not say this only for the witnesses, but also for a midwife coming to assist a birth, and for *ha'ba l'hatzil min hagayis umin hanahar umin hamapolet umin hadeika* — one who comes to save people from an attacking army, from a flooding river, from a collapsing building, or from a fire. All such individuals become like the inhabitants of the city they entered and receive 2,000 *amot* in every direction from its edge.

Now the difficulty becomes sharp: the *Rosh Hashanah mishna* explicitly includes saving from an army among the cases granted 2,000 *amot* — yet our *mishna* says those who go out to save may return home without any stated limit. So there are now two cases of *l'hatzil* — one capped at 2,000 *amot* and one apparently uncapped — and one cannot simply say *l'hatzil* is categorically different. This is the contradiction that produced the answer of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: the return-home clause speaks not to distance of travel but to carrying weapons.

### Weapons Braita

The *Gemara* elaborates by citing a *braita*: *barishonah hayu manichin klei zaynam b'veit hasamuch lachomah* — originally they used to leave their weapons in a house near the city wall after repelling an attack. On one occasion, *hikiru vahen oyvim* — the enemy recognized that they had disarmed, chased them, and the soldiers rushed to retrieve their weapons from the armory. In the ensuing crush, *hargu zeh et zeh yoter mimah shehargu oyvim* — they killed one another more than the enemy had killed them. This episode has the quality of moral instruction — a recurring motif in rabbinic literature — that internal disorder can cause us more damage than the enemy.

*B'osa shaah hitkinu* — at that moment they enacted that soldiers may keep their weapons on them until they have returned safely to their homes. This is the *takana* referred to in the *mishna*'s ruling. According to the approach of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, one's permitted distance of travel remains 2,000 *amot*, but the carrying of weapons is sanctioned for the full journey home as a *pikuach nefesh* measure.

One additional observation about calling this a *takana*: there is merit to the point that framing the law as a public enactment serves the purpose of broadcasting the rule — which is itself important for the safety of those returning, as the enemy would know not to expect the soldiers to disarm prematurely.

### Rav Nachman

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an independent resolution to the question of distance — setting aside the weapons issue entirely. He holds: *lo kashya* — there is no contradiction. *Kan shenitzchu Yisrael et umot haolam* — where the Jews won the battle, they have only 2,000 *amot*, since they are presumably in a position of strength, especially if permitted to remain armed. *Kan shenitzchu umot haolam* — when the non-Jews prevailed, the soldiers may travel all the way home, since remaining at a fixed point 2,000 *amot* from the city would leave them dangerously exposed. The need to return home in that case is itself a *pikuach nefesh* concern, and no distance limit applies.

---

## Siege & Pikuach Nefesh

### Siege Categories

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches: *nochrim shetzaru al ayarot Yisrael* — if non-Jews lay siege to Jewish towns, *ein yotzim aleihem bichlei zaynam v'ein mechalelin aleihem et haShabbat* — one may not go out to fight them with weapons or violate *Shabbat* on their account. This is a striking ruling, since one might assume any siege implicates *pikuach nefesh*.

A *braita* explains: *bameh devarim amurim* — when does this apply? *Sheba'u al iskei mamon* — when the siege concerns monetary matters, such as a dispute over tribute. In that case, one does not violate *Shabbat*; the remedy is to pay. But *ba'u al iskei nefashot* — if they have come for matters of life, where actual killing is intended, *yotzim aleihem bichlei zayin umechalelin aleihem et haShabbat* — one must fight and may violate *Shabbat*.

It is worth noting that the earliest documented instance of *Torah Sheba'al Peh* — of applying reasoned legal analysis to yield a novel practical ruling — appears to be the episode in *Sefer Chashmonaim* where soldiers, after being slaughtered because they refused to fight on *Shabbat*, concluded that God intends for them to fight back in self-defense. The principle that *pikuach nefesh docheh Shabbat* and that one may fight the enemy on *Shabbat* traces its earliest narrative expression there.

### Border Cities

There is a further and more expansive rule: *uve'ir hasmucha lasefar* — in a city near the border, *afilu lo ba'u al iskei nefashot* — even if the attackers came only over monetary matters, such as straw and stubble, *yotzim aleihem bichlei zayin umechalelin aleihem et haShabbat* — one may go out armed and violate *Shabbat*. A border city under siege is treated as a situation of *pikuach nefesh* in its own right, because allowing a border city to be overrun — even over a property dispute — poses an existential threat.

Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Nachman states: *uveBavel ke'ir hasmucha lasefar damya* — Babylonia as a whole is treated as a city near the border. The *Gemara* clarifies that what is meant is *Nehardea* specifically, which was on the border of the Persian Empire and was in fact overrun by the Romans on multiple occasions. The mention of Nehardea thus serves as a concrete illustration of a border city in the relevant geopolitical context — the frontier between Rome and Persia.

This raises a genuinely interesting question: is the *Gemara* presenting this as a theoretical illustration, or is it ruling practically that Jews living in Nehardea would be obligated to defend the Persian frontier against Rome? There are documented cases of Jews serving in foreign armies, sometimes by conscription and sometimes by choice. If a Jew were a citizen of Nehardea during an attack, it is a real question whether the *Gemara* intends to say he could take up arms in defense of the Persian Empire on *Shabbat* — not merely as a matter of protecting his own life, but as a participant in the broader defense of the city.

### David & Keilah

Rav Dostai from Biri expounds the verse in Shmuel 1, chapter 23: *Vayagidu l'David lemor, Hinei Plishtim nilchamim b'Keilah v'heima shosim et hagranot* — they told David that the Philistines were fighting in Keilah and attacking the granaries. A *braita* teaches that Keilah was a city near the border — *ir hasmucha lasefar* — and the Philistines came only over monetary matters, *iskei teven v'kash*, straw and stubble. This aligns precisely with the rule about border cities, where even a monetary dispute triggers the obligation to fight on *Shabbat*.

David then asks God — through the *Urim v'Tumim* — whether to go and strike the Philistines. The *Gemara* pauses: what exactly was David asking? If the question was whether it was permitted or forbidden — a *halachic* question about *Shabbat* — he had no need to consult the *Urim v'Tumim*, for *Beit dino shel Shmuel ha'Ramati kayam* — the court of Shmuel the Ramathite was active. One does not ask *halachic* questions of the *Urim v'Tumim*. Rather, *i mazlach i lo mazlach* — he was asking whether he would succeed. This is confirmed by the divine response: *v'hoshat et Keilah* — you will save Keilah — which speaks to outcome, not to legal permissibility. The *Gemara* notes that this interpretation means the Keilah episode does not directly prove the rule about border cities on *Shabbat*, though the *braita* itself establishes that rule independently.

---

## Sleeping Traveler

### Mishna Setup

The next *mishna* introduces a distinct category: *mi she'yashan baderech* — one who was traveling and fell asleep before *Shabbat* began, encamping wherever one happened to be. Upon waking — presumably the next morning — one sees that one is near a city. *Harei hu samuch l'ir* — the city was within 2,000 *amot* of where one slept. *Ho'il v'lo haita kavanato l'kach* — since when *Shabbat* began, one was not intending to join that city, indeed was entirely unaware of its proximity, *lo yikanes* — one is not treated as an inhabitant of that city. One may travel toward the city but only up to one's 2,000-*amah* limit. If one camped 1,999 *amot* from the city's edge, one can enter one *amah* into it and no further.

This ruling requires appreciation of the underlying leniency that is being withheld. Ordinarily, if one begins *Shabbat* inside a city, the entire city is treated as a single unit and does not count against one's 2,000 *amot*. A further leniency allows that even if one is outside the city but within 2,000 *amot* of it, one may be treated as an inhabitant of the city — one's notional starting point is extended to the city itself. This is an unusual concession, since ordinarily one's *techum* begins from where one physically stands, not from a separate location one did not occupy. The *mishna* is debating whether this secondary leniency requires at minimum that one was aware of and intending toward the city when *Shabbat* began.

### Rabbi Meir & Yehuda

Rabbi Meir holds that without the requisite *kavanah* — intention or awareness — one is not considered to have begun *Shabbat* in the city, and one has only one's 2,000 *amot* from the point of encampment. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and holds that one may enter the city as if one had begun *Shabbat* there.

### Rabbi Tarfon

Rabbi Yehuda supports his position with a *ma'aseh*: *ma'aseh b'Rabbi Tarfon shehayah mahalech baderech v'chashchah lo* — it once happened that Rabbi Tarfon was traveling and darkness overtook him on Friday. He slept outside the city, unaware of its proximity. In the morning, some cowherds found him and told him: *Harei ha'ir l'fanecha* — the city is right before you. He rose, entered, went to the *beit medrash*, and taught there the entire day — treating himself as an inhabitant of the city he had not knowingly camped near.

Rabbi Meir dismisses this proof on two grounds. First: *shema b'libo hayta* — perhaps Rabbi Tarfon was not truly unaware; just because the cowherds told him does not mean he had no prior knowledge of the city's location. Second: *beit hamedrash muvla b'toch tchomav hayah* — perhaps the *beit medrash* itself was within his personal 2,000 *amot*, and he simply traveled there without invoking the city-inhabitant status at all. So the story proves nothing about the broader principle.

### Sleep Onset

A related but distinct case concerns one who sat down on the road and *lo yada shechashchah* — did not know that *Shabbat* was beginning, falling asleep before dark and remaining unconscious when *Shabbat* commenced. This goes beyond the prior question. The earlier debate concerned whether awareness of the city matters; this debate concerns whether consciousness at the moment *Shabbat* begins is necessary at all to establish one's *techum*.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds: *yesh lo alpayim amah l'chol ruach* — one has 2,000 *amot* in every direction from where one slept. Even without consciousness at the moment *Shabbat* began, one's physical presence at a location is sufficient to establish it as one's *makom* — one's place — for *techum* purposes.

The *chachamim* disagree: *ein lo ela arba amot* — one has only four *amot*. The *chachamim* apparently hold that some measure of conscious establishment of place is required, and an unconscious person has not done so.

The sub-disputes of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehuda about *how* to measure the four *amot* apply here as they do elsewhere. Rabbi Eliezer holds one stands at the center, so two *amot* extend in each direction. Rabbi Yehuda holds one may choose in which direction to deploy the four *amot*, though once one has committed to a direction one cannot retract.

---

## Multiple People

### Two People

A further case: if two people found themselves *chutz l'techum*, each with only four *amot*, and the four *amot* of one overlapped with the four *amot* of the other — *miktzat amotav shel zeh b'toch amotav shel zeh* — they may bring food and eat together in the shared middle space. However, *uvlevad shelo yotzi zeh mishelo l'toch shel chaveiro* — neither may bring objects from the portion of space that is exclusively one's own into the other's space. The reason is that one's vessels and possessions are also limited by one's *techum*, and carrying them from one's exclusive zone into the other's exclusive zone would take them outside their *techum*. The shared, overlapping zone is available to both; one's exclusive zone is not.

### Three People

When there are three such people, with the middle person overlapping with both neighbors but the two outer persons not overlapping with each other: *ha-emtzai muvla benehem* — the middle one is swallowed between them. He may eat with either of the two outer persons; they may eat with him. But *shnayim hachitzonim asurim ze im ze* — the two outer persons may not share with each other, as they have no overlapping space.

### Three Courtyards

Rabbi Shimon illustrates this with an analogy to three courtyards, each opening both into the others and into the *reshut harabbim*. If two of the courtyards each made a joint *eruv* with the middle courtyard — but not with each other — the middle courtyard may carry with either neighbor, and each neighbor may carry with the middle, but the two outer courtyards may not carry between themselves, as they made no *eruv* with each other.

The reason it matters that each courtyard has an opening to the *reshut harabbim* is significant: if the only access to an inner courtyard were through an outer one, it would compel all three to make a single combined *eruv*, since independence would be impossible. Where each has independent street access, they can each act independently in their *eruv* arrangements, producing this scenario of partial mutual permission.

---

## Rava's Question

### Cheftzei Hefker

Rava poses the foundational question about Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position: *mai kasavar Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri?* What is the conceptual basis for holding that a sleeping person establishes a *techum* where he lies? There are two possible ways to understand him.

The first possibility: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds *cheftzei hefker konim shevita* — that even ownerless, inanimate objects establish their *shevita* — their resting place for *Shabbat* — wherever they happen to be when *Shabbat* begins. No consciousness is required; physical presence at a location suffices. Under this view, the *Gemara* notes, *uvedin hu deliflu bekelim* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri could just as well have stated his position by the case of inanimate vessels. He chose to debate it by a sleeping person in order to *lehodia'acha kochan derabbanan* — to reveal the far-reaching position of the Rabbis: that even a sleeping person — who after all *could* have been awake and consciously established his place — does not, in the Rabbis' view, establish his *techum* where he sleeps. Conversely, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds it works even for ownerless objects.

It should be noted that by inanimate objects the question of *koneh shevita* is a *chumra*: if an ownerless object establishes its own *techum*, one is limited in how far one can carry it. If it does not, one's possession of it on *Shabbat* causes it to follow one's own *techum* — which is how one wants it defined, since one can take it wherever one goes.

The second possibility: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds *cheftzei hefker ein konim shevita* — ownerless objects do not establish their own *techum*. Consciousness is in principle required. Nevertheless, a sleeping person is different: *ho'il venir'or kanei, yashen nami kanei* — since had he been awake he would clearly have established this as his place, even while asleep it is considered established. Under this reading, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri requires at least potential intention — the capacity for consciousness — and a sleeping person satisfies that condition in a way an inanimate object does not.

The *Gemara* thus leaves open which of these two rationales underlies Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position.

### Rain Case

Rav Yosef attempts to resolve the question. He cites the case of rain: *geshamim sheyardu me'erev Yom Tov* — rain that fell on *erev Yom Tov*, before *Yom Tov* commenced. The ruling is *yesh lahem alpayim amah l'chol ruach* — the rain water has 2,000 *amot* from wherever it fell. Since the water was physically present at that location when *Yom Tov* began, it is defined by that location. By contrast, rain that fell *b'Yom Tov* itself — meaning it did not exist at any location when *Yom Tov* commenced — *harei hen k'raglei kol adam*, it follows the person who takes possession of it.

This appears to be direct evidence that an inanimate, ownerless substance — rain water — is *koneh shevita* wherever it lies when *Yom Tov* begins, supporting the first reading of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri.

Rav Safra challenges: *dilma begeshamim hasmuchim l'ir askinan* — perhaps the case concerns rain falling near a city whose inhabitants knew it was about to rain and had it in mind. Under that reading, the rain is not truly ownerless *hefker* — the people's anticipatory awareness effectively constitutes a quasi-intentional designation of where it fell. The rain therefore goes by where they expected it to fall, not because inanimate *hefker* establishes its own *techum*. One cannot extract a principle about *cheftzei hefker* from a case where human intention was implicitly present.

### Wells Case

The *Gemara* dismisses this objection and adduces clearer evidence from a *braita* about wells. A privately owned well — *bor shel yachid* — goes by the *techum* of its owner. A well owned by an entire city — *shel osa ha'ir* — goes by the *techum* of the city as a whole, even if individual inhabitants made their own private *eiruvi techumin* extending in different directions. So far there is no novelty.

The instructive case is *shel olei Bavel* — a well belonging to the travelers, meaning an ownerless public well on the highway used by anyone passing. The ruling is *k'raglei hamemalei* — it goes by the person who draws from it. This indicates that an ownerless object does *not* establish its own *techum*; it follows the one who takes possession.

But a second *braita* presents the case of *bor shel Shvatim* — a well owned by the *Shvatim*, meaning by all of *Klal Yisrael*. Although *Klal Yisrael* does own this well, the ownership is so diffuse — all of Israel has no single *techum* — that it is effectively equivalent to *hefker*. Yet the ruling here is *yesh lahem alpayim amah l'chol ruach* — it has 2,000 *amot* from the well itself. This well, despite its effectively ownerless status, *does* establish its own *techum*.

### Mapping Debate

These two *braitot* contradict each other directly on the question of ownerless objects. One holds *cheftzei hefker ein konim shevita* — they do not establish their own *techum*, and the *olei Bavel* well follows whoever draws from it. The other holds *cheftzei hefker konim shevita* — the *Shvatim* well establishes its own 2,000-*amah* radius. The *Gemara* concludes: *ela shma mina tannaim hi* — this is necessarily a dispute among *Tannaim*. *Ha Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, ha Rabbanan* — one *braita* follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position, and the other follows the *chachamim*. The debate about the wells maps precisely onto the debate of our *mishna* concerning the sleeping traveler.

### Rav Yosef

Abaye reported this entire exchange to Rav Yosef — including Rav Safra's attempt to dismiss the rain case by invoking the city-dwellers' anticipatory awareness, and Abaye's counter that the wells *braita* provides independent Tannaitic evidence of the dispute. Rav Yosef then points out that one could have refuted Rav Safra's objection from the rain case itself, without needing to invoke the wells at all. If the reason the rain establishes its *techum* from where it fell were only because the city's inhabitants had it in mind, then the *braita* should have stated *k'raglei anshei osa ha'ir* — it goes by the *techum* of the people of the city, since it would effectively be as if they placed it there. Instead, the *braita* says it goes 2,000 *amot* from where the rain fell — a point that would only make sense if the rain itself is *koneh shevita* at the location of its fall, independent of any human intention. Rav Safra's explanation thus collapses from within the rain case before one even reaches the wells.

The upshot of the entire discussion is that there is Tannaitic evidence for both positions. There are *Tannaim* who hold *cheftzei hefker konim shevita* — as expressed in the *Shvatim* well and arguably in the rain case — and *Tannaim* who hold *cheftzei hefker ein konim shevita* — as expressed in the *olei Bavel* well. The *Gemara* maps this dispute onto the debate between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the *chachamim* about whether a sleeping person establishes a *techum*, suggesting that the deeper question is not specific to human consciousness but concerns the general principle of whether physical presence at a location — without active awareness or intention — suffices to establish *shevita* there. The discussion will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Eiruvin 46

## Sleeping & Eruv

### Mishna: Falling Asleep

Today's daf is 46, and we pick up from the bottom of 45b. The *mishna* addresses the case of somebody who falls asleep: if a person is not conscious, can he establish that location as the place of his *eruv*?
