According to *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*, he can; according to the *Chachamim*, he cannot. Interestingly, if he cannot, where is the place of his *eruv*? The *mishna* gives him the same status as someone who has gone outside the *techum* — he is not defined as being in any particular place and has only his four *amos*.

Some *Rishonim* ask why this is different from the case discussed later in the *Gemara* of rain that falls on *Shabbos* or a boat that lands on *Shabbos* when it was higher than ten *tefachim* — in those cases the object can at least acquire two thousand *amos* from where it lands. Here, however, the *Chachamim* are not so lenient: they reason that in those other cases the object was never yet situated within the zone, whereas here the person was in the zone but simply was not conscious. The distinction is not entirely clear, but the consequence is plain: without an established place, the sleeping person is left with only four *amos*.

### R. Yochanan vs. Chachamim

The *Gemara* then raises the possibility that this debate runs even deeper — that it is not merely about a person who is unconscious but may extend to inanimate objects as well. The question becomes: does an inanimate object that normally follows its owner — but which is currently ownerless — establish its place for *Shabbos* as two thousand *amos* from where it began *Shabbos*, or is it defined by the person who subsequently finds it? The sleeping person serves as an analogy: does he establish his place for two thousand *amos*, or does he lack any place for *Shabbos* and remain limited to four *amos*?

### Hefker Objects

With this framework in place, the *Gemara* turns to examine both the case of ownerless objects and the case of the unconscious person in tandem, setting the stage for the extended discussion that follows.

---

## Rain & Techumin

### Rain on Yom Tov

The *Gemara* continues: *ki ata lekamei deRav Yosef* — when Abaye came before Rav Yosef, he reported over this entire discussion about the *braisa* regarding rain. The foundational principle being explored is that *chafzei hefker* — ownerless objects — are *koneh shvisa* where they are at the onset of *Shabbos*, and this is treated as parallel to the position of *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*.

The *Gemara* now reads: *amar mar* — if rain fell on *Yom Tov*, then clearly its place was not established when *Yom Tov* began (since it was still in the sky and not yet on the ground), and therefore *harei hen ke-ragli kol adam* — it is defined by the person who takes possession of it.

### Ocean & Water Cycle

The *Gemara* then asks: *v'amai* — why is this so? *Likni lei shvisa be-Okianos* — why doesn't the rainwater acquire its *shvisa* in the ocean? The *Gemara* is working with the understanding that there is one great ocean surrounding the world and that, based on the water cycle, all rainwater ultimately originates there. If that is so, when *Yom Tov* began the water was in the ocean — why not say that is where it establishes its two thousand *amos*, such that by the time it has evaporated, condensed, and fallen as rain, it is already far outside its *techum* and would be forbidden to use?

The *Gemara* raises the possibility: *lema d'lo ke-Rebbi Eliezer* — perhaps this contradicts Rabbi Eliezer, since *ha-amar kol olam kulo mi-mei Okianos hu shoteh* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that the entire world drinks from the waters of the ocean. The *Gemara* assumes this process occurs within twenty-four hours, so rain falling on *Shabbos* or *Yom Tov* would have originated in the ocean on *erev Shabbos*. That we permit the use of such rain may indicate that this ruling does not follow Rabbi Eliezer.

Rav Yitzchak responds: *hacha b'avim shenitkashru m'erev Yom Tov askinan* — we are dealing here with a case where the clouds had already darkened before *Yom Tov* began. The water was already up in the clouds at the onset of *Yom Tov*; it was not on the ground and was not *koneh shevitah* in the ocean.

### Clouds & Movement

The *Gemara* immediately challenges: *v'dilma hanei azlei v'hanei achrinei ninhu* — perhaps those original dark clouds blew away, and the rain that actually fell on *Yom Tov* came from different clouds, formed from water that had evaporated during *Yom Tov* itself? The *Gemara* responds: *d'it lehu simana b'gavaihu* — the clouds bear an identifying mark, so we can establish that it is the same clouds.

A second, more principled answer then follows: *v'iba'it eima safek d'rabbanan l'kula*. We simply do not know for certain whether the water came from those pre-existing clouds or from newly evaporated water. But since the entire institution of *techumin* is rabbinic in nature, a *safek* in a rabbinic matter is resolved leniently.

The *Gemara* then poses a further question: even granting that the water was in the clouds when *Yom Tov* began, *v'likni shevitah b'avim* — why doesn't it establish its *shevitah* in the clouds? If so, *tifshot minah d'ein techumin l'ma'ala m'asara* — we could derive from here that there are no *techumin* above ten *tefachim*, since otherwise the cloud-water would already have established its zone in the sky. The *Gemara* declines to accept this inference: *le'olam eima lach yesh techumin* — in truth, *techumin* do apply even above ground level. Rather, *u'maya b'avei mivla blei'i* — the water is absorbed within the cloud. It does not yet exist as a discrete entity; it is merely vapor and therefore has no *techum* of its own.

The *Gemara* then raises a further objection: *kol sheken d'havu lehu nolad* — if the water does not yet truly exist, it should certainly be a problem of *nolad* and forbidden on *Yom Tov* entirely. The *Gemara* responds: *ela maya b'avei mida nayedi* — it is not that the water is completely non-existent; it is present in the cloud but is not stationary. Since it is constantly in motion as water vapor, it cannot be *koneh shevitah*. The decisive factor is non-stationarity, not non-existence.

It is worth noting how striking this treatment of *nolad* is. We are generally quite stringent in our definition of *nolad* — some opinions hold that changing water to ice or ice to water constitutes *nolad*, even though the substance itself has not changed, only its state. Yet rain and snow are not considered *muktzeh* or *nolad*. This inconsistency would seem to argue for a more relaxed definition of *nolad* across the board, though the *Gemara* does not address this tension directly.

### Rivers & Flowing Water

The *Gemara* then draws the full conclusion: *hashta d'ateit l'hachi, v'd'Okyanus nami lo tikshei lach* — now that we have established the principle that non-stationary objects cannot be *koneh shevitah*, there is no difficulty even from the starting position of the ocean. *Miha b'Okyanus nami maya nayedi* — the water in the ocean is also in motion. This is now a fully general principle: something that is moving when *Shabbos* begins does not establish a fixed place.

This is confirmed by a *braita*: *neharot hamoshchin u'mayyanot hanovim, harei hen k'raglei kol adam* — rivers that run and springs that flow do not have a fixed place for *Shabbos* and are therefore defined by the person who draws from them, not by where the water happened to be at the onset of *Shabbos*. Notably, in the case of a boat that has not yet docked and is still moving — bracketing the separate issue of ten *tefachim* — it too would not be *koneh shevitah* by reason of motion. Once the boat stops, its place would then be defined by where it docked.

---

## Lenient in Eruvin

### Psak: R. Yochanan

The *Gemara* now shifts to the question of *psak*. *Amar Rav Yakov bar Idi amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: halacha k'Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* — we rule like *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* that a person who falls asleep establishes *Shabbos* where he is, with two thousand *amos* in every direction, and is not treated like someone deposited outside the *techum* with only four *amos*.

### Explicit vs. Inferred

*Rabbi Zeira* then asked Rav Yakov bar Idi: *befeirush shemia lach* — did you hear this ruling explicitly from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, *o m'chlala shemia lach* — or did you infer it from a more general statement he made? Rav Yakov bar Idi replied: *befeirush shemia li* — I heard it explicitly.

Why did Rabbi Zeira think it might have been inferred? Because Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had also stated a general principle: *halacha k'divrei hameikel b'eiruv* — we rule like the lenient position in *eruv*. One might have thought that Rav Yakov bar Idi applied that general principle to the case of *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* on his own, since *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*'s ruling is indeed the lenient one: he permits two thousand *amos* rather than restricting the sleeper to four. But Rav Yakov bar Idi clarified that no inference was necessary — the explicit ruling was transmitted directly.

### General Leniency Rule

The *Gemara* then asks: *v'taryeihu lama li* — why were both statements necessary? Why say both the general principle (*halacha k'divrei hameikel b'eiruv*) and the specific ruling (*halacha k'Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*)? *Amar Rabbi Zeira tzrichi* — both were necessary.

### Person vs. Object

Had Rav Yakov bar Idi stated only *halacha k'Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*, we might have thought that this applies not only where *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*'s position is lenient but even where it is strict. When would that be? The *Gemara* earlier suggested that *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*'s ruling may be grounded in the principle that inanimate objects are *koneh shevitah* where they are when *Shabbos* begins. Applied to ownerless objects, however, that principle is actually a *chumra* — it restricts the object to its own two thousand *amos* rather than allowing the finder to use it within his own *techum*. Had we simply ruled like *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* across the board, we might have extended his ruling to inanimate objects as well, to their detriment.

*Ka mashma lan halacha k'divrei hameikel b'eiruv* — the additional statement that we always rule leniently in *eruv* tells us that we go leniently in both directions: for the sleeping person, we follow *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* (two thousand *amos* rather than four), and for the ownerless object, we rule that it is not *koneh shevitah* on its own but follows the finder.

Both *Rashi* and *Tosafos* raise the obvious objection: earlier in this *masechet* we established that one cannot adopt two contradictory *kulot* — one must be consistent. How can we be lenient in both directions, saying the object establishes its *shevitah* when a person is involved but does not when an object is involved? Both *Rashi* and *Tosafos* resolve this by reverting to an answer proposed earlier in the *Gemara*: *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*'s ruling regarding a sleeping person is not based on the analogy to ownerless objects. Rather, his reasoning is that since a conscious person would have been *koneh shevitah* where he stood, the sleeping person — who is still a person — retains that status. An inanimate object, by contrast, is a categorically different entity, and even *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* may concede that it is not *koneh shevitah*. There is therefore no contradiction: the person establishes his place even while asleep, while the ownerless object follows its finder.

### Minority Opinion

*Ela v'leima halacha k'divrei hameikel b'eiruv* — conversely, had Rav Yakov bar Idi stated only the general principle of leniency in *eruv*, we might have assumed that this principle applies only where it is one opinion against one opinion (*yachid bimkom yachid*). But *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* stands alone against the *Chachamim*, who represent multiple opinions — *yachid bimkom rabbim*. Under normal rules of *psak* one follows the majority. Therefore, had only the general principle been stated, we might have said it does not apply to a case as lopsided as *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* against the majority. Hence the explicit ruling was necessary: even in this asymmetric fight, we rule like *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*.

This has broad implications for the entirety of *hilchos eruvin*: across virtually all of its discussions, we adopt the lenient position — and, as the *Gemara* will shortly establish, this holds even when the lenient position is a single opinion against many.

---

## General Psak Rules

### Rava's Challenge

*Amar lei Rava l'Abaye* — Rava raised a challenge. He did not find this a surprising *chiddush* at all. Since *eruvin* is rabbinic in origin, what difference should it make whether it is *yachid bimkom yachid* or *yachid bimkom rabbim*? In matters of rabbinic law one should always follow the lenient position, even against a majority. Rav Pappa responded that this assumption is simply incorrect.

### Niddah Example

*U'vidrabonon lo shani lan bein yachid bimkom yachid l'yachid bimkom rabim?* — Do you really think that in all rabbinic matters it makes no difference whether it is one against one or one against many? *V'ha tnan* — consider the following *mishna* in *niddah*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that any woman — not only an elderly woman — who goes three periods (ninety days) without bleeding attains the status of *mesuleket damim*, one whose blood is effectively removed. This is a lenient position, for such a woman need not be concerned that she bled prior to the moment she actually observed blood. This is a *yachid bimkom rabbim* — Rabbi Eliezer stands alone against the majority of *Chachamim*.

A *braita* then records: *maaseh v'asah Rabbi k'Rabbi Eliezer* — there was an actual case in which *Rabbi* (Yehudah HaNasi) ruled like Rabbi Eliezer. A woman who was not elderly had gone three months without bleeding and had handled *trumah*, and *Rabbi* permitted it. *Rashi* explains that this was a period of famine — which also provides a physiological rationale, since malnutrition is itself a cause of amenorrhea. *Tosafos* alternatively suggests that a very large quantity of *trumah* was involved, making the potential loss significant.

### Sha'as HaDchak

The *braita* continues: *l'achar shenizkar, amar, kedai hu Rabbi Eliezer lismoch alav b'sha'as hadachak* — after he remembered something, *Rabbi* said: Rabbi Eliezer is worthy of being relied upon in a time of exigency. This is a critically important halachic principle: one may rely on a *da'as yachid* that has not been definitively rejected *b'sha'as hadachak*.

What did *Rabbi* remember? The *Gemara* considers whether he remembered that the *halacha* had been explicitly ruled against Rabbi Eliezer — but if so, *b'sha'as hadachak heichi avid k'vasei*? How could he have relied on a position that had been formally rejected? Rather, *d'lo itmar hilchesa lo k'Rabbi Eliezer v'lo k'Rabbanan* — no explicit ruling had been issued either way. What *Rabbi* remembered was that Rabbi Eliezer is nonetheless a *da'as yachid* against the majority, and the ordinary rules of *psak* should therefore have directed him toward the *Rabbanan*. The ruling in favor of *trumah* was not reversible since it was already done, but *Rabbi* acknowledged that under normal circumstances he should have followed the majority. Nevertheless, *kedai Rabbi Eliezer lismoch alav b'sha'as hadachak* — in a time of genuine need one may rely on him, since his position has never been formally and definitively silenced.

This principle carries enormous practical weight in later halachic literature. The question of when a *da'as yachid* may be relied upon *b'sha'as hadachak* involves several layers of analysis: how authoritative must the minority position have been to begin with? And, critically — at what point has a position been so thoroughly displaced by subsequent *psak* that it can no longer function as a legitimate *da'as yachid* at all? This question bears directly on the role of the *Shulchan Aruch*: when it first appeared it was one opinion among many, becoming authoritative only gradually. Can one rely on a view in the *Rishonim* that the *Shulchan Aruch* did not adopt? What of authorities the *Shulchan Aruch*'s author was unaware of entirely, such as the *Meiri*? These are all live questions whose answers depend on exactly the same conceptual framework the *Gemara* is developing here.

Rav Kook engages this entire framework at length in his introduction to *Shabbos Aretz*, laying the groundwork for *heter mechirah* by examining the parameters of relying on a *da'as yachid b'sha'as hadachak* in *shemitah*. Those who oppose *heter mechirah* argue that Rav Kook himself framed the leniency as contingent on *sha'as hadachak* — raising the question of whether, if that emergency no longer obtains, the reliance on those minority positions lapses entirely.

Determining what constitutes *sha'as hadachak*, and when a minority opinion has been effectively silenced, are ultimately judgment calls belonging to the *posek*. They are informed by precedent and responsa literature, but the evidence is often contradictory, and the art of weighing it is precisely what distinguishes one *posek* from another.

### Aveilus Leniency

The *Gemara* now draws the broader conclusion from this discussion. *Kol makom she-ata motzei yachid meikel v'rabbim machmirim, halacha k'divrei hamachmirim* — the general rule is that whenever a single opinion is lenient and the majority is stringent, we follow the majority. This applies even in rabbinic matters. However, there are two famous exceptions: *halacha k'divrei hameikel b'eiruv* and *halacha k'divrei hameikel b'avel* — in both *eruvin* and *aveilus* we always rule like the lenient position.

The *aveilus* case emerges from the ruling of *Shmuel: d'amar Shmuel halacha k'divrei hameikel b'avel*. The specific case concerns *shemua kerova* — hearing of a relative's death within thirty days — versus *shemua rechoka* — hearing more than thirty days after the death. Rabbi Akiva holds that a *shemua rechoka* requires only one day of *aveilus*, while the *Chachamim* require *shiva* and *sheloshim* even for old news. *Rabbah bar bar Chana* rules in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* that we follow the majority (*Chachamim*) in general, but makes an explicit exception: *halacha k'divrei Rabbi Akiva* — here we rule like the lenient minority, in accordance with *Shmuel*'s principle of *halacha k'divrei hameikel b'avel*.

Thus the *Gemara* on today's daf establishes a clear and important framework: the default rule, even in rabbinic matters, is to follow the majority over the minority. The two exceptions — *eruvin* and *aveilus* — are categorical departures from this default, in which we always follow the lenient position regardless of the numerical weight of the opposing views.

---

## Eruv Chatzerot vs. Techu…

### Chatzerot vs. Techumin

Rav Pappa now adds a further reason why both statements — the general principle of leniency in *eruv* and the specific ruling like *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* — were necessary. *Salka daitach amina hani mili be-eiruv chatzeiros* — one might have thought the rule of leniency in *eruv* applies only to *eruv chatzerot*, but *aval be-eiruvi techumin, eima lo* — perhaps it would not apply to *eruvi techumin*. Both statements were therefore needed to establish that the leniency covers *eruvi techumin* as well.

*U-mena teimra de-shani lan bein eiruv chatzeiros ve-eiruv techumin?* — What would have led one to think there is a meaningful distinction between the two? One might naturally suggest that *eruvi techumin* has a *de-oraisa* dimension, making it stricter — but that is not the *Gemara*'s reasoning.

### Alleyway Courtyards

Instead, the *Gemara* cites a *mishnah* that demonstrates a structural difference. *Bameh devarim amurim be-eiruvi techumin* — by *eruvi techumin* one may not establish an *eruv* on behalf of another person without their knowledge, since doing so benefits the person in one direction while restricting them in another. It is a trade-off, not a pure benefit, and therefore requires explicit consent. *Aval be-eiruvi chatzeiros me-arvin bein le-daas bein she-lo le-daas* — by *eruv chatzerot*, by contrast, one may establish the *eruv* on behalf of another even without their knowledge, because *zakin le-adam she-lo be-fanav* — one may act to another's benefit in their absence.

*Tosafos* notes that this reasoning is somewhat strained: there is in fact a minor loss involved in *eruv chatzerot* as well, since one takes a portion of the other person's bread for the *eruv* without their explicit consent. Nevertheless, *Tosafos* reads the *Gemara* as ruling that in *eruv chatzerot* the benefit predominates, while in *eruvi techumin* the trade-off is genuine and therefore requires consent. This structural asymmetry is what might have led one to treat the two types of *eruv* differently for purposes of the leniency principle — hence the necessity of specifying that the principle applies to both.

---

## Beginning vs. Remnant

### Techillas vs. Shiyurei

Rav Ashi offers yet another reason why both statements were necessary. *Hani mili be-shiyurei eiruv* — one might have thought the leniency applies only to the *remnant* of an existing *eruv*, where the question is whether what remains is sufficient to preserve the *eruv*'s validity. *Aval bi-techillas eiruv, eima lo* — but at the *outset*, when one is first establishing the *eruv*, perhaps we would not apply the leniency.

*U-mena teimra de-shani lan bein shiyurei eiruv le-vein techillas eiruv?* — What grounds would there be for such a distinction? From a *mishnah* that records Rabbi Yose's ruling: *bameh devarim amurim bi-techillas eiruv* — the minimum food requirement applies at the outset of placing the *eruv*. *Aval be-shiyurei eiruv, afilu kol she-hu* — once an *eruv* was valid and the food subsequently diminished, even a minimal remnant suffices to maintain it. One is demonstrably more lenient once the *eruv* was established than at its inception — and one might therefore have thought that the general principle of leniency applies only in the *shiyurei* context.

### Food Minimum

The explicit ruling like *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* — which concerns the initial establishment of one's place — clarifies that the leniency applies *b'techillas eruv* as well.

The *mishnah* appends: *v'lo amru l'arev chatzeros ella k'dei shelo lishkach toras eruv min hatinokos* — the Rabbis required *eruv chatzeros* in order that children (and by extension the community) not forget the laws of *eruv*. This remark addresses a specific configuration: three courtyards, each feeding into the next, with all of them opening into a shared alleyway. If the courtyards all made a joint *eruv* with one another through their interconnecting doors, they would technically not need to make a separate *shituf mavos* in the alleyway. Nevertheless, the Rabbis required it in order to prevent a misleading inference. If people saw the residents of those courtyards carrying freely in the alleyway without any *shituf*, they might conclude that a *shituf mavo'os* is never required. The concern is not about teaching children incorrectly but about the community inferring a wrong principle from observed practice. Demanding a *shituf mavo'os* even where it is not technically necessary avoids the more consequential error of assuming it is never needed.

---

## Tannaitic Hierarchy

### Standard Authorities

Having established the general principles of *eruvin* leniency, the *Gemara* now turns to a broader discussion of *klalei psak* — the general principles governing how *halacha* is decided when *Tannaim* disagree. *Rabbi Yaakov v'Rabbi Zrika amru*: we rule like *Rabbi Akiva* when he disputes a single colleague (*mechavero*), but not when he disputes multiple colleagues. We rule like *Rabbi Yose* even when he disputes multiple colleagues (*mechaverav*). And we rule like *Rabbi* (Yehudah HaNasi) when he disputes a single colleague, but not when he disputes multiple colleagues.

### Three Levels

The *Gemara* then asks *l'mai hilchesa* — when we say we "rule like" one of these authorities, what precisely do we mean? Three *Amoraim* offer different formulations. *Rabbi Yochanan amar halacha* — we rule definitively. *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba amar matim* — we incline in that direction. *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina amar nir'im* — it appears that way, or seems to us to be correct.

*Tosafos* explains the distinctions in a way that illuminates the underlying structure. To say *halacha* means the opposing view is entirely illegitimate — if someone ruled in accordance with the rejected position, the ruling would have to be reversed. *Matim* means we incline toward the favored position, but the other view remains a valid *da'as yachid*; a ruling based on it would stand. *Nir'im* is weaker still — the preferred position appears more correct, and one should ideally rule accordingly, but it is fully legitimate to rule *l'chatchila* like the other view as well. These three levels thus represent a hierarchy of exclusivity: from absolute displacement of the opposing view, to its demotion to secondary status, to its retention as a fully equal alternative.

### Tannaitic Ranking

*Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi* then transmits in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* a hierarchy of *Tannaitic* authority relevant to specific pairings. When *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* dispute one another, *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* — we follow *Rabbi Yehuda*. When *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Yose* dispute one another, *halacha k'Rabbi Yose* — we follow *Rabbi Yose*.

### Transitive Logic

*Pshita* — this would seem to make obvious by transitive logic that when *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yose* dispute, we also follow *Rabbi Yose*, without needing an explicit statement. The *Gemara* confirms: *ain tzorich lomar Rabbi Meir v'Rabbi Yose halacha Rabbi Yose* — since *Rabbi Meir* cannot prevail against *Rabbi Yehuda*, and *Rabbi Yehuda* cannot prevail against *Rabbi Yose*, it is self-evident that *Rabbi Yose* prevails over *Rabbi Meir*. *Hashta b'makom Rabbi Yehuda leisa, b'makom Rabbi Yose mibaya* — if *Rabbi Meir*'s position is set aside in the presence of *Rabbi Yehuda*, is there any question whether it falls before *Rabbi Yose*?

Rav Assi adds that the same transitive reasoning extends to *Rabbi Shimon*. *D'amar Rav Abba amar Rav Yochanan*: when *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* dispute, *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda*. Since *Rabbi Yehuda* beats *Rabbi Shimon* and *Rabbi Yose* beats *Rabbi Yehuda*, it follows by transitivity that *Rabbi Yose* beats *Rabbi Shimon* as well. Both *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Shimon* emerge as the weakest positions in this ranking. One is then left to ask: when *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Shimon* dispute each other directly, what is the *psak*? The *Gemara* leaves this as *teiku* — unresolved.

---

## Challenge to Rules

### Mesharshiya Dissent

The *Gemara* now challenges the universality of these *klalei psak*. *Amar Rav Mesharshiya: leisnehu l'hanei klalei* — we do not hold of these rules. Where does Rav Mesharshiya get this?

### Three Courtyards Case

From the following *mishnah*. The *mishnah* records *Rabbi Shimon*'s ruling about three courtyards opening into one another and also opening to the public domain. If the outer courtyards each made an *eruv* with the middle courtyard, then the middle courtyard may carry with either outer courtyard, and vice versa — but the two outer courtyards are forbidden to one another. *Rav Chama bar Guriya* then states in the name of Rav: *halacha k'Rabbi Shimon* — we rule like *Rabbi Shimon*.

But who is the opposing position? The *Gemara* identifies it as *Rabbi Yehuda*, even though no explicit dispute appears in this *mishnah* (Rashi clarifies how the *Gemara* knows this). The difficulty is immediate: we just established that when *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* dispute, *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* — yet here we rule like *Rabbi Shimon*. *V'ha amart Rabbi Yehuda v'Rabbi Shimon halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* — does this not contradict the *klal*?

### Conditional Rules

The *Gemara*'s resolution is fundamental: *dilma heicha d'itmar itmar, heicha d'lo itmar lo itmar* — perhaps the answer is that these rules were never intended to be universal. When a specific tradition exists about how to rule in a particular case, that tradition governs — regardless of what the general *klal* would suggest. The *klalei psak* are not absolute rules; they are default principles to be invoked precisely when we lack a specific tradition or explicit determination. *Heicha d'lo itmar* — where no such specific ruling exists, these principles provide guidance. But they cannot override a direct, transmitted *psak* in a given case. The *klalim* fill the gaps; they do not supersede specific knowledge.

---

---

# Eiruvin 47

## Principles of Psak

### Lenient Opinion Rule

The daf before us — 47a — continues a discussion that occupied much of the previous daf regarding foundational principles of *psak halacha*. The dominant principle, already familiar, is that in matters of rabbinic law (*derabanan*) one follows the lenient opinion (*le-kula*). A critical qualification, however, is that this principle applies specifically when the decisor has genuinely exhausted his analysis and finds himself unable to determine the correct ruling. As the Rambam frames it, when one does not know toward which direction the law leans — *eini yodea le-heichan hadin noteh* — the first obligation is to apply one's own judgment. Only when genuinely stymied does the principle of *halacha divrei ha-meikel* take effect. Furthermore, even in rabbinic matters, this leniency does not apply when it would mean following a lone opinion against many (*yachid bi-mkom rabbim*) — with one notable exception: in matters of *eruvin* and *aveilus*, the lenient view is followed even against the majority, without the Gemara specifying why.

### Minority Opinions

A related principle discussed on the previous daf concerns relying on a minority opinion in a time of pressing need (*sha'at ha-dechak*). This raises two questions: first, whether such reliance is permitted even in Torah-level prohibitions (*de'oraita*) or only in rabbinic ones — the context of the preceding discussion was specifically rabbinic; and second, what makes a minority opinion a legitimate *da'at yachid* that retains its standing as a viable minority view rather than one that has been effectively rejected by tradition. The authority of the *Shulchan Aruch* and its contemporary application to these principles was also addressed.

### Tannaitic Disputes

The Gemara then reviewed the established rules for adjudicating *machloket tannaim*: when Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir dispute, the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda; when Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda dispute, the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda; and there are parallel rules regarding Rabbi Akiva *me-chavero* and Rabbi Yosi *me-chavero*.

### Rav Mesharshya

The Gemara concluded the previous daf with a challenge from Rav Mesharshya, who sought to demonstrate that these principles are not actually in force by citing cases where we rule contrary to them. The Gemara's response was the principle of *heicha d'itmar itmar, heicha d'lo itmar lo itmar*: where an explicit ruling exists, that ruling stands — but that does not undermine the general principles, which govern precisely those cases where no explicit ruling has been given and one needs guidance on how to decide. The existence of exceptions, whether explicit rulings that go against the general principle or cases where we have *paskined* otherwise for particular reasons, does not mean the principles lack force in cases where they are the only available guidance.

---

## Testing Principles

### Exception Cases

The Gemara on 47a now turns to an extended examination of the principles by running through a series of *mishnayot*. This daf is notably sparse in *Tosafot*, for good reason: it consists almost entirely of a long chain of cases. The Gemara's method is twofold. First, it attempts to prove the principles are not operative by citing cases where we rule against them. The ready answer in each such case is that the existence of explicit rulings or recognized exceptions does not invalidate the general principle — these rules apply when nothing else determines the outcome.

### Cases Requiring Ruling

The Gemara then presses from the opposite direction: if the principles genuinely hold, why would an Amora ever need to issue an explicit ruling in a case where the principles already determine the outcome? The very act of issuing such a ruling seems to imply that the principles alone are insufficient — that without the explicit statement, one might not have known how to rule. This forms the core tension the Gemara will work to resolve across the cases that follow.

---

## Private/Public City

### Reshut Status

The first case is drawn from a *mishnah* the Gemara introduces with the words *ela mei-ha*. The *mishnah* discusses a city that was private (*shel yachid*) and became public (*shel rabbim*), or vice versa. The interpretation of "private" and "public" here depends on one's broader understanding of *reshut ha-rabbim*. Rashi ties this to his position that a true *reshut ha-rabbim* requires 600,000 people: a public city is one large enough to constitute a genuine *reshut ha-rabbim*, and a private city is one that is not. Most *Rishonim* hold that ownership is irrelevant to this determination — what matters is use and traffic. The Ramban, however, takes a distinctive view that ownership is relevant, and reads the *mishnah* literally as addressing the question of whether a city is publicly or privately owned.

### Transition Cases

The *mishnah* presents two scenarios. In the first, a privately owned or insufficiently populous city becomes a public city — and the *mishnah* rules that one may still make an *eruv* for the entire city, a ruling that itself requires explanation given the public character now assumed by the city. The second scenario, which is the Gemara's focus here, involves the reverse: a city that was public and has now become private, meaning that in principle an *eruv* should now be permitted. Nevertheless, the *mishnah* rules that one may not make an *eruv* for the entire city. One must leave a portion outside the *eruv* as a *zecher* — a memorial reminder — lest people come to think that one may make an *eruv* over a genuinely public city. The *mishnah* specifies the minimum size of the excluded area: it must be at least the size of a new city in Yehudah, which the *mishnah* defines as containing fifty residents — a figure that reflects a very different scale of settlement than our own.

### Yehuda vs Shimon

Rabbi Yehuda requires that the excluded area contain fifty residents. Rabbi Shimon, at the top of 47a, takes a far more lenient position: the excluded area need only consist of three *chatzeros*, each containing two houses — that is, three courtyards with two houses each. This is a considerably smaller area than what Rabbi Yehuda requires.

### Rav's Ruling

Rav Chama bar Guria reports in the name of Rav that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara immediately raises the difficulty: the one who disputes Rabbi Shimon here is Rabbi Yehuda, and one of the established principles is that when Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon dispute, the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda. Why then did Rav rule like Rabbi Shimon? The Gemara dismisses this as a problem by invoking the principle of *heicha d'itmar itmar, heicha d'lo itmar lo itmar*: the existence of an explicit ruling in favor of Rabbi Shimon is precisely the kind of case where the rule is overridden. The rules apply by default; explicit rulings stand on their own.

---

## Absent Householder

### Eruv Participation

The Gemara moves to the next case with *ela mei-ha*. The background principle is that all residents of a *chatzer* — a courtyard surrounded by walls whose houses open onto a common yard — must participate together in an *eruv* in order to be permitted to carry in that shared space. Although technically *reshut ha-yachid*, the common courtyard is used by multiple residents whose domains remain in some sense distinct, and rabbinic law requires collective unification through the *eruv*. If even one resident refuses to participate, his distinct claim to the shared space frustrates the unification and invalidates the *eruv* for everyone.

### Absence Issue

The question the *mishnah* addresses is what happens when a resident is not present for *Shabbat* at all — he left to spend *Shabbat* in another city. Since he is not actively using the *chatzer*, perhaps his theoretical ownership of a distinct portion is irrelevant in practice, and the remaining residents can proceed with their *eruv* without him. The *mishnah* asks this both for a Jew and a non-Jew who have left: does either of them still prevent the *eruv*?

### Rabbi Meir

Rabbi Meir's position is that both a Jew and a non-Jew who have left still prevent the *eruv* from taking effect. Their ownership of a distinct portion in the *chatzer* remains legally relevant regardless of their physical absence.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees entirely: neither the absent Jew nor the absent non-Jew prevents the *eruv*. Since they are not present for *Shabbat*, their portion is treated as effectively ownerless for this *Shabbat*, and the remaining residents may proceed.

### Rabbi Yosi

Rabbi Yosi draws a distinction: an absent non-Jew still prevents the *eruv*, but an absent Jew does not. The reasoning for the distinction is that a non-Jew can travel on *Shabbat* — he might ride out and return even on *Shabbat* itself — and therefore his potential presence on *Shabbat* cannot be discounted. A Jew, by contrast, does not travel on *Shabbat*; if he has left the city, he will not return. Rabbi Shimon goes further still: even if a Jew has merely gone to spend *Shabbat* at his daughter's house within the same city, he does not prevent the *eruv*, because *hisiyach da'ato* — he has mentally disengaged from his own home. When one goes to spend *Shabbat* elsewhere, even locally, the entire framework of *Shabbat* — the meals, the presence, the plans — is organized around that other place. For a non-Jew, by contrast, *Shabbat* is no different from any other day, and physical departure does not imply the same mental disengagement. (The *mishnah*'s choice to specify his daughter's house rather than his son's house likely reflects the social reality that married daughters live with their husbands and a father going there would not return home, whereas sons might continue living in the same household, making the disengagement less complete.)

### Rav Rules

Once again, Rav Chama bar Guria reports in the name of Rav that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara raises the difficulty in doubled form: not only do we have the principle that Rabbi Yehuda beats Rabbi Shimon, but here we also have the principle that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi *me-chavero*. Both principles point away from Rabbi Shimon, yet Rav rules like him. As Rashi notes, one could have raised both objections together. The Gemara again answers with *heicha d'itmar itmar*: these are exceptions where an explicit ruling exists, and the existence of such explicit rulings does not undermine the principles in cases where no explicit ruling has been given.

---

## Presence vs Bread

### Poor Person

The Gemara presses once more with *ela mei-ha*, this time turning to the *mishnah*'s teaching: *ha-ani me'arev be-raglav* — a poor person makes his *eruv techumin* with his legs rather than with bread. The mechanism of *eruv techumin* establishes one's permitted *Shabbat* boundary by positioning food or oneself at a point up to 2000 *amot* from the city before *Shabbat* begins. Normally the *eruv* is established with bread placed at that point; but one may also establish it with one's own physical presence, simply being at that location when *Shabbat* begins.

### Only Poor

Rabbi Meir's position is that this option — making an *eruv techumin* through personal presence rather than food — is available only to a poor person who has no bread to spare. The general rule requires bread, and only the economic necessity of the poor person justifies the departure from that requirement.

### All Can Use

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, saying the option is available to anyone, whether poor or wealthy: *echad ani ve-echad ashir*. His reasoning is that the institution of *eruvin* with bread was itself a *leniency* introduced for the wealthy — to spare them the trouble of going out and standing at the boundary until *Shabbat* begins. They can instead send someone to place their bread there, or place it before *Shabbat* without remaining. This means that making an *eruv* with personal presence is the more basic and universally available option, and the bread *eruv* is the facilitation that was added for convenience. Any person who prefers to use his physical presence may do so.

### Rav's Teaching

Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi was teaching this *mishnah* to Chiya bar Rav in the presence of Rav, presenting Rabbi Yehuda's view that the option is available to all. Rav instructed Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi that when he teaches this *mishnah*, he should append the ruling: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — we rule like Rabbi Yehuda.

### Challenge

This produces the second direction of the Gemara's challenge. Now we are not dealing with an exception to the rules; we are dealing with a case that the rules already resolve. The rule is that when Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda dispute, the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda. So *pshita* — why did Rav need to say so? As *Tosafot* phrases the underlying tension: *tarti lama li* — why do we need both the general principle and an explicit ruling to the same effect? The *Gemara* asks *u-mai koshya*: is this really difficult?

---

## Mishnah vs Baraita

### Rav vs Yochanan

The Gemara's answer is that perhaps Rav himself does not hold of these general principles at all. It was Rabbi Yochanan who articulated the *klalim*, and perhaps they reflect only his approach. When Rav explicitly ruled like Rabbi Yehuda, he did so because without his statement there would be no way to know where the *halacha* fell — since the general principles are not operative from his perspective. What Rav Mesharshya was therefore saying, the Gemara now clarifies, is not that these principles never apply, but that they are not universally held. Rabbi Yochanan may hold of them; Rav does not. The rules are thus not a consensus position, and knowing that Rabbi Yochanan formulated them does not mean one can rely on them in all contexts or according to all authorities.

---

## Three Month Wait

### Paternity Concern

The Gemara continues to the next *mishnah* with *ela mei-ha*. The new topic is the *halacha* requiring women to wait three months after widowhood or divorce before remarrying. The case of the *yevamah* is presented first: a woman whose husband died childless, leaving a surviving brother who must perform either *yibum* or *chalitzah*. The *mishnah* rules that neither *yibum* nor *chalitzah* may be performed until three months have elapsed from the husband's death. The concern is determining whether the widow is pregnant. If she is, *yibum* would constitute the grave prohibition of *eishas ach* — the biblical prohibition of a brother's wife — since *yibum* is mandated only in the absence of children, and a pregnant widow is not childless. Performing *chalitzah* when pregnant would be similarly problematic: the *chalitzah* would not have been necessary, yet someone might later see that she married a *kohen*, not knowing that the *chalitzah* was nullified by the subsequent discovery of her pregnancy, and draw the false conclusion that a *chalutzah* is permitted to a *kohen*.

### Blanket Rule

The *mishnah* then generalizes: *ve-chen shaar kol ha-nashim* — so too all other women whose marriages ended through death or divorce must not enter into *nisuin* or even *eirusin* until three months have elapsed. The stated concern in these cases is paternity: if a woman remarries quickly and a child is born, it may be unclear whether the child belongs to the first or second husband — a matter of enormous *halachic* significance. Understanding *nisuin* as the concern is natural, since it is through *nisuin* that husband and wife begin living together and the possibility of pregnancy arises. The extension to *eirusin* — the formal betrothal that does not yet involve cohabitation — is a *lo plug*: the Rabbis did not want to permit *eirusin* lest it lead to permitting *nisuin*.

The *mishnah* applies this rule without distinction: *echad betulot ve-echad be-ulot* — whether or not the woman is known to have had marital relations; *echad almanot ve-echad gerushot* — whether she is a widow or a divorcee; and even *echad arusot ve-echad nesuot* — whether her prior relationship was one of *nisuin* or merely *eirusin*. This last category is where the blanket rule becomes most striking: if she was only an *arusah* to her first husband — betrothed but never having lived with him or had relations — there is no logical basis for concern about pregnancy from the first husband. Similarly, if the second relationship is only *eirusin* with no intention of immediate *nisuin*, the paternity concern does not apply. Yet the *mishnah*'s blanket formulation covers all cases alike. This is the *lo plug* principle at its most sweeping: rather than require courts and communities to navigate complex distinctions, a uniform rule is imposed even where its underlying rationale does not apply. The practical implications are serious — a seventy-year-old woman receiving a *get* is still told she must wait three months — and the Gemara will engage with how far this blanket rule actually extends.

### Rabbi Yehuda Logical

Rabbi Yehuda takes the logically differentiated position. He holds that *nesuot yisarsu ve-arusot yinaseu*: a woman who had *nisuin* with her first husband may have *eirusin* with the second — since the two are not yet cohabitating — and a woman who had only *eirusin* with the first husband may have *nisuin* with the second — since there is no possibility of pregnancy from the first. Rabbi Yehuda adds one exception: *arusa she-bi-Yehuda* — an *arusah* in Yehudah is treated with greater stringency, because in Yehudah it was customary for the *chatan* and *kallah* to spend time alone together even before *nisuin*, creating the possibility of relations having occurred after betrothal.

### Rabbi Yosi

Rabbi Yosi goes further in the lenient direction: *kol ha-nashim yisarsu* — all women may have *eirusin* immediately, without waiting three months. He agrees with Rabbi Yehuda that *eirusin* poses no genuine concern for any of these women. His sole exception is the widow who is still in the period of *aveilus* for her first husband: *chutz min ha-almana mipnei ha-eivel* — a widow should not enter into *eirusin* during her mourning period. This is a distinct concern, rooted not in paternity but in the integrity of mourning. Whether obligations of *pru u-rvu* or other considerations might in some circumstances override the concern of *aveilus* is a matter explored at length in *Tosafos* and by Rabbeinu Tam, but that discussion lies beyond our present focus.

### Yochanan Rules

Rabbi Elazar had been absent from the *beit midrash* on the day this ruling was discussed. He encountered Rabbi Assi and asked him for a summary of what had been taught. Rabbi Assi reported that Rabbi Yochanan had ruled: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yosi* — we rule like Rabbi Yosi. The Gemara notes that implicit in this explicit ruling is the assumption that the position opposing Rabbi Yosi is a *da'at yachid* — a lone opinion. Both Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Yehuda agree that *eirusin* is permitted immediately; the only opposing voice is the anonymous *stam* of the *mishnah* that prohibits it. The question of whether the *stam* represents a *da'at yachid* or a *da'at rabbim* is thus significant in evaluating how widely the opposing position reaches.

### Challenge

Now the challenge runs in the other direction. Rabbi Yochanan was himself the one who articulated the general principle that when Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi dispute, the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi. The *stam* of the *mishnah*, which forbids *eirusin*, has been identified as representing a *lo plug* position — precisely the kind of categorical decree (*gezeira*) characteristically associated with Rabbi Meir. Why then did Rabbi Yochanan need to issue an explicit ruling? The principle already dictates the outcome: Rabbi Yosi against Rabbi Meir — follow Rabbi Yosi.

---

## Mishnah vs Baraita (II)

### Baraita Uncertainty

Abaye provides the resolution. He explains: *itztarich* — the explicit ruling was necessary. One might have thought that the principle by which Rabbi Yosi's position prevails over Rabbi Meir's applies only when the dispute is recorded in a *mishnah* — since *mishnayot* were edited with great care and the attribution of positions to named Tannaim can be relied upon with confidence. A *baraita*, however, was not edited with the same precision, and there is room to doubt whether the attributed positions are correctly recorded. As Rashi explains, when it comes to a *baraita*, even if the *klalim* would otherwise apply, there is insufficient certainty that we have the names right to rely on the principle alone. The Gemara's earlier cases were all drawn from *mishnayot*; the case of the three-month wait and Rabbi Yosi's position in the *baraita* requires an explicit ruling because one cannot automatically extend the *klalim* to *baraitot* with the same confidence.

This answer also explains why one might have been uncertain about whether to follow Rabbi Yosi here even though the general principle would seem to apply: the *klalim* may not apply to *baraitot* with the same certainty as to *mishnayot*.

### Shmuel's Rule

There is an additional reason why Rabbi Yochanan's explicit ruling was needed. Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules: *halacha ke-Rabbi Meir bi-gzeirotav* — we follow Rabbi Meir specifically when he is making a *gezeira*, a categorical preventive decree. This is precisely what is happening here: Rabbi Meir's insistence on a uniform three-month rule regardless of circumstances is not a substantive argument about the likelihood of pregnancy in any particular case. It is a *lo plug* decree — a *gezeira* designed to keep the rule simple and universally applicable. According to Shmuel's principle, this is exactly the type of ruling where we follow Rabbi Meir.

### Contradiction

This creates a direct conflict between two operative principles: the *klal* that we follow Rabbi Yosi against Rabbi Meir, and Shmuel's principle that we follow Rabbi Meir in his *gezeirot*. Both principles apply here, and they point in opposite directions. It was therefore essential for Rabbi Yochanan to state explicitly that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi — because without that explicit ruling, one might have applied Shmuel's competing principle instead. The explicit statement is thus not redundant but necessary precisely because two rules are in tension and only a direct ruling can resolve the conflict.

---

## Pagan Markets

### Permitted Items

The Gemara introduces the next case with *ela mei-ha*, now turning to a *baraita*. The *baraita* teaches that one may attend non-Jewish market days (*yarid shel nochrim*) for the specific purpose of purchasing certain categories of items that we prefer to see under Jewish ownership: servants, animals, houses, fields, and vineyards in the Land of Israel. Normally, participation in such market days raises concerns because these markets were organized in connection with pagan festivals. Yet the *baraita* permits attendance when the purpose is acquiring items that bring important resources under Jewish control — servants and animals who are thereby brought under the wings of the *Shechina* in a Jewish household, and real estate in *Eretz Yisrael* which Jewish ownership helps preserve. Furthermore, the *baraita* permits registering such transactions in non-Jewish courts — *ke-chotev u-ma'aleh be-arkaot shelahem* — even though Jews are generally discouraged from using non-Jewish legal forums. The justification in both cases is *ke-matzil mi-yadam*: one is effectively rescuing these resources from non-Jewish hands, which overrides the usual concerns.

### Kohen Exception

The *baraita* continues with a further allowance: if the person seeking to acquire land in Israel is a *kohen*, he may travel to *chutz la'aretz* for the purpose of defending the acquisition in non-Jewish courts, even though *chutz la'aretz* carries the status of *tumah* and *kohanim* are normally forbidden from leaving *Eretz Yisrael* and thereby becoming *tameh*. He may even enter what is classified as a *beit ha-pras* — a field with rabbinic-level grave *tumah* — though the *baraita* clarifies that entering a full *beit ha-kevarot* with biblical *tumah* would not be permitted for this purpose.

### Marriage Torah

The *baraita* adds two further circumstances under which a *kohen* may leave *Eretz Yisrael* and become *tameh* in *chutz la'aretz*: to get married, and to learn Torah. These correspond to the two purposes for which one may sell even a *Sefer Torah* — the two supreme personal obligations that override otherwise operative restrictions.

### Yehuda Restricts

Rabbi Yehuda qualifies the allowance to travel to *chutz la'aretz* for Torah study: *eimatai? bi-zman she-ein motze lilmod* — this is permitted only when no adequate *yeshiva* exists in *Eretz Yisrael*. If a sufficiently good *yeshiva* can be found in the Land, there is no justification for leaving. Notably, Rabbi Yehuda does not apply this same restriction to marriage — presumably he accepts that the consideration of finding a suitable spouse is not bounded by the same geographic logic.

### Yosi Allows

Rabbi Yosi disagrees: *af bi-zman she-motze lilmod nami yitameh* — even if there is a good *yeshiva* in *Eretz Yisrael*, the *kohen* may still go to *chutz la'aretz* to learn Torah. His reasoning is *she-ein min ha-kol zocheh lilmod* — not everyone merits to learn from just any teacher. Even if the *yeshiva* in Israel is excellent by any objective standard, a student has the right to seek out the particular *rebbe* from whom he personally can best learn, and he cannot be told that the presence of other teachers nearby is sufficient. Rabbi Yosi then cites a precedent: the story of Yosef ha-Kohen, who traveled to his teacher in Sidon — which is in *chutz la'aretz* — for the purpose of Torah study.

### Yochanan Explicit

Rabbi Yochanan rules: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yosi* — we follow Rabbi Yosi. The challenge is immediately apparent: this is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi, and the established principle is that when they dispute, the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi. Why did Rabbi Yochanan need to state the ruling explicitly? Abaye's answer is the same as before: the principle applies with confidence to *mishnayot*, where the editorial care of Rabbi Yehuda ha-Nasi ensures that the names and positions are correctly attributed. A *baraita*, however, was not edited with the same rigor — as Rashi explains, the concern is not that the *baraita* is unreliable in a wholesale sense, but that it is not reliable enough to automatically apply the *klalim* without additional confirmation. Therefore, Rabbi Yochanan's explicit ruling was necessary to establish that we follow Rabbi Yosi even in this *baraita*.

---

## Non-Jewish Objects

### Shmuel Position

The Gemara now shifts to a separate topic that will occupy the remainder of the daf: the *techum* status of objects owned by non-Jews. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states: *cheftzei nochri ein konim shevita* — objects owned by non-Jews do not acquire a fixed place. This means that such objects, when they come into a Jew's possession or vicinity on *Shabbat*, are not limited to the 2000 *amot* that objects owned by Jews are restricted to. They have no *techum* limit.

### No Owner Techumin

The reasoning emerges from the general principle that owned objects acquire their *Shabbat* rest in accordance with the *techum* of their owner. The owner of these objects is a non-Jew, who has no *Shabbat techum* restriction at all — a non-Jew may travel wherever he wishes on *Shabbat*. Therefore, objects owned by a non-Jew, being defined by their owner's *techum*, are similarly without limit.

The Gemara sharpens the point by asking according to whom Shmuel's ruling must be directed. If according to the Rabbis — who hold that ownerless objects (*cheftzei hefker*) do not acquire a fixed place — then Shmuel's ruling seems obvious. If ownerless objects, which have no owner to define their *techum*, have no 2000-*amot* limit, then objects owned by a non-Jew, whose owner's *techum* is unlimited, should *a fortiori* have no limit. The Gemara therefore concludes that Shmuel's statement must be directed according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that ownerless objects *do* acquire a fixed place, with a 2000-*amot* limit measured from where they were when *Shabbat* began. Shmuel comes to teach that even Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri would agree that objects owned by a non-Jew are different: since they have an owner, and that owner's *techum* is unlimited, the objects themselves are not restricted to 2000 *amot*.

### Baraita Contradiction

The Gemara raises a challenge from a *baraita*. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules regarding two scenarios: one where a vessel was borrowed from a non-Jew during *Yom Tov* — meaning the object began *Yom Tov* in the non-Jew's possession — and one where a vessel was lent to a non-Jew before *Erev Yom Tov* and returned during *Yom Tov*, again meaning it began *Yom Tov* in non-Jewish possession. In both cases, the *baraita* states: *yesh lahem alpayim amah le-chol ruach* — they have 2000 *amot* in every direction from where they began *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*. The *baraita* continues: a non-Jew who brought fruit from outside the *techum* — meaning the fruit began *Shabbat* more than 2000 *amot* outside the city — may not be moved from its place. This strongly implies that objects owned by a non-Jew at the onset of *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* do have a *techum* of 2000 *amot*, contrary to Shmuel's ruling.

### Positions Analysis

The Gemara works through the implications. If one follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position that *cheftzei hefker* acquire a fixed place — 2000 *amot* from where they are — then the *baraita*'s ruling that non-Jewish objects are similarly limited makes sense: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri extends the same logic from ownerless objects to objects owned by a non-Jew, treating them as analogously fixed. The *baraita* would then reflect Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's view. But if one holds, following the Rabbis, that *cheftzei hefker* do not acquire a fixed place, then the *baraita*'s ruling that non-Jewish objects have 2000 *amot* fits neither the Rabbis nor Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri in the way Shmuel described him. The Gemara therefore says: according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, this *baraita* is readily understood. And Shmuel's ruling — that non-Jewish objects have no *techum* limit — was issued according to the Rabbis, but was nonetheless necessary because one might have thought there is a reason to treat non-Jewish-owned objects more like Jewish-owned objects due to possible confusion.

### Confusion Concern

This brings the Gemara to a third position. Rav Chiya bar Avin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states: *cheftzei nochri konim shevita* — objects owned by non-Jews do have a 2000-*amot* limit. The reason is *gezeira ba'alim de-nochri atu ba'alim de-Yisrael* — a rabbinic decree that we treat ownership by a non-Jew analogously to ownership by a Jew, out of concern that people will confuse the two situations. Once an object is known to be owned — rather than ownerless — people might not stop to ask whether it is Jewish-owned or non-Jewish-owned, and allowing non-Jewish-owned objects to travel without restriction might lead to the erroneous conclusion that Jewish-owned objects can similarly be brought from beyond the *techum*. Rabbi Yochanan therefore decrees a 2000-*amot* limit even for non-Jewish objects.

The result is two reasons to hold that non-Jewish objects have a *techum* limit: the approach of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who treats such objects like *cheftzei hefker* with a 2000-*amot* limit measured from the object itself; and Rabbi Yochanan's approach, which is grounded in the rabbinic concern about confusion with Jewish-owned objects and presumably measures the 2000 *amot* from where the owner was when *Shabbat* began, since the logic is based on analogy to Jewish-owned objects.

---

## Rams Case

### Rava Allows

Against this background the Gemara presents a practical incident. Rams were brought to a city called Mavrakhta, having come from outside the *techum*. Rava permitted the residents of Mechuza to purchase them — presumably on *Yom Tov*, since rams would be *muktzeh* on *Shabbat*, and there are recognized allowances for purchasing food items on *Yom Tov* in an indirect fashion, such as taking the object and settling accounts afterward.

### Ravina Challenges

Ravina challenged Rava: what is the basis for the permission? If Rava's ruling relies on Shmuel's position that *cheftzei nochri ein konim shevita* — that non-Jewish objects have no *techum* limit — that would justify the purchase. But the established rule is that when Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan dispute, the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yochanan. And Rabbi Yochanan holds that non-Jewish objects do have a 2000-*amot* limit, as a *gezeira* paralleling Jewish-owned objects. These rams were brought from outside the *techum* and should be forbidden to be moved or purchased because they have traveled beyond their permitted 2000 *amot*.

### City as Four Amot

Rava's response draws on the foundational rule established at the very beginning of this *perek*: an object that was taken *chutz la-techum* and placed within a city is treated as having the entire city as its four *amot*. Once an object that originated outside the *techum* is brought within a walled city, it may be moved throughout the entire city — the city functions as an equivalent of the four *amot* that any person or object retains even when it has gone *chutz la-techum*. Rava therefore says: grant Ravina's premise entirely, and accept that these rams have gone *chutz la-techum* under Rabbi Yochanan's ruling. Nonetheless, once they have entered Mavrakhta — *dekula Mavrakhta ke-arba amot damya* — the entire city of Mavrakhta counts as their four *amot*, and anyone within the city may use them. Rashi specifies that this rule presupposes Mavrakhta was a walled city, and *Tosafot* concurs. Several *Rishonim*, however, raise the question of whether an unwalled city might similarly function as a unified domain for this purpose — a question with practical implications for cases such as being stranded in a city when *Shabbat* begins unexpectedly.

---

## Fishnet Boundary

### Fishnet Setup

The Gemara presents its final case. Imagine a body of water positioned exactly at the boundary between the *techumin* of two different cities — so that the water on one side belongs to the *techum* of city A, and the water on the other side belongs to the *techum* of city B. A fishnet is laid across the middle of the water, marking the boundary line. The net itself creates no legal separation; it merely makes visible the problem that exists regardless.

The problem is this: the water of the lake is owned by the residents of the respective cities, and just as their personal movement is limited to 2000 *amot* from the city, so too their water — being owned — is limited to the *techum* of the city. The water on city A's side should not mix with the water on city B's side, because taking water from one side to the other would be moving it *chutz la-techum*. Yet water flows freely, and the net does nothing to stop it.

### Iron Wall

Rabbi Chiya says: *cherem shebein techumei Shabbat tzarich mechitza shel barzel lehafsika* — a fishnet dividing *techumin* requires an iron wall to create a meaningful separation. In other words, without such a wall, the waters are hopelessly mixed, and neither city can use the water freely.

### Yosi Laughs

Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina laughed at this ruling. The Gemara asks why. One possibility is that he was mocking Rabbi Chiya for holding a strict position — requiring an iron wall — when by contrast Rabbi Yosi himself holds a lenient position, perhaps treating the water as analogous to *cheftzei hefker* without a *techum* limit. The Gemara pushes back on this: just because you hold a lenient position does not mean you may laugh at someone who holds a stricter one. A lenient position is legitimate, but so is a strict one, and ridicule is not warranted. And this is indeed a striking moment in the *sugya*, because the entire discussion earlier in the daf emphasized *halacha ke-divrei ha-meikel be-eruv* — that in *eruvin* we follow the lenient view. Yet here we see that there are indeed positions within the domain of *eruvin* that rule strictly, and mockery of such positions is rejected.

### Water Leniency

The real reason Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina laughed, the Gemara explains, is different. There is a *baraita* that teaches: *naharot ha-moshchin u-ma'yanot ha-novim harei hen ke-raglei kol adam* — flowing rivers and springs have no *techum* limitation; they belong to everyone. And while the Gemara considers whether perhaps the waters in question were stationary rather than flowing, the deeper point is that the Rabbis adopted a general policy of leniency in matters involving water. This emerges from the famous exchange between Rav Tabla and Rav: Rav Tabla asked whether a *mechitza teluyah* — a suspended wall that does not reach the ground — may serve as a valid *mechitza* on dry land. Rav answered that a suspended wall is valid only over water (*ba-mayim*), not on dry land. As the Gemara puts it: *ela kal hu she-hikilu chachamim ba-mayim* — this is a special leniency the Rabbis introduced specifically for bodies of water. They were willing to treat a non-continuous wall as legally sufficient over water in a way they would not accept on land, precisely because the alternative would deny communities access to water entirely.

By this same logic, Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina laughed at the requirement for an iron wall: given the Rabbis' established leniency regarding barriers and water, one should be able to use even an imperfect division — such as a fishnet or a reed wall — to serve as a sufficient *mechitza* between the two *techumin*. The fact that water passes through the net is no objection, because the Rabbis apply a fictional-wall standard over water; what matters is the defined separation, not its physical impermeability. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina's point is thus that Rabbi Chiya's iron-wall requirement is not merely strict, but fails to account for the established rabbinic leniency in this domain — and that is what he found worthy of challenge.

---

---

# Eiruvin 48

## Ownerless Objects & Tech…

### 2000 Amah Debate

Today's *daf* is 48, and we begin by revisiting the closing discussion of 47b, which was covered somewhat hastily at the end of the previous session. The *gemara* there had been framing a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the Rabbis concerning whether ownerless objects — *cheftzei hefker* — are subject to the 2,000-*amah* limit of *techum Shabbat*, or whether, having no owner, they may be carried without restriction.

### Non-Jewish Property

Closely related to this is the question of objects owned by non-Jews. Since non-Jews have no *techum* of their own, one might argue that their property likewise carries no *techum* restriction. The *gemara* considers a case in which objects are brought from beyond the *techum* — presumably on *Yom Tov* — and then potentially acquired by Jews within the *techum*. The very mention of acquisition on *Yom Tov* requires a brief clarification: when necessary for *simchat Yom Tov*, a purchase may be transacted without the actual transfer of money. Once that is established, the remaining question is whether the objects themselves are permitted to be moved — and that turns entirely on whether objects owned by a non-Jew are defined by a *techum*.

### Melacha by Non-Jew

Beyond the *techum* question, there is a further consideration: ordinarily, the *halacha* prohibits benefiting from *melacha* performed by a non-Jew on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* on a Jew's behalf. The case under discussion presumably sidesteps this concern by positing that the non-Jew brought the goods for the majority of the city's population, which was non-Jewish. When a non-Jew performs *melacha* for a predominantly non-Jewish population, a Jew may benefit incidentally from that activity.

### Walled vs. Open Cities

A further point arising from that case is that the objects, even if brought from beyond the *techum*, could be carried throughout the entire city. *Rashi* and *Tosafot* understand this to mean it was a walled city — analogous to the barn discussed in the first *mishnah* of the tractate, where the wall creates a defined enclosed space. Other *rishonim*, however, maintain that any location within the city is considered a single contiguous space regardless of walls. This dispute carries significant practical relevance: when an object arrives *mechutz latechum*, is its movement restricted to a walled enclosure, or does the entire city constitute one unified domain?

---

## Net Dividing Techum

### Rabbi Chiyya's Net

With that review complete, we turn to the passage that opens our *daf* — the last line of 47b: *Tani Rabbi Chiyya* — "Rabbi Chiyya taught." The case involves a net (*cherem*) stretched across a body of water situated precisely at the boundary between the *techum Shabbat* of two adjacent cities. Rabbi Chiyya rules that in order to draw and use the water on either side of the net, a *mechitza shel barzel* — an iron wall — would be required to separate the domains. The reasoning is that the water is considered communally associated with the inhabitants of each respective city; once the water crosses the net, it has passed beyond the city's *techum*. Accordingly, residents of city A cannot use the water on city B's side, and vice versa, unless an iron wall physically demarcates the boundary.

### R. Yose Laughs

*Mechayech alei Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina* — Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina laughed at this ruling. The *gemara* inquires: *mai ta'ama kamechayech* — what was the reason for his laughter? One possible reading is that Rabbi Yose holds like the Rabbis *lekula* — that *cheftzei hefker* have no *techum* restriction — and he was mocking Rabbi Chiyya for ruling stringently like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. But the *gemara* rejects this reading: the mere fact that one holds the lenient position is no grounds to ridicule one who holds the strict position. That remains a perfectly legitimate stance, and it is worth noting here that the principle *halacha kedivrei hameikel be-eruv* — that the law follows the lenient opinion in matters of *eruv* — was not stated as a universal consensus; the *gemara* clearly does not assume that every authority must accept it.

There is also a subtler difficulty worth pausing over. If the water is truly *hefker*, its *techum* should be measured from where it physically sits — 2,000 *amot* from the water itself — not 2,000 *amot* from where the city's residents are. The *gemara*'s framing, which ties the water's *techum* to the city's inhabitants, occupies a strange middle ground: technically ownerless, yet somehow defined by those who wish to use it. The *gemara* acknowledges this tension but nonetheless proceeds with the framework as given.

A second possible reason for the laughter is rejected as well. Perhaps Rabbi Yose was mocking the ruling because a *braita* teaches that *neharot hamoshchin u-mayanos hanovim* — flowing rivers and natural springs — are *keraglei kol adam*, available to everyone without restriction. If so, water should never be subject to a *techum* at all. But the *gemara* deflects this too: how do we know the body of water in question was flowing? Perhaps Rabbi Chiyya was speaking of a stationary (*mechunas*) body of water, which does *koneh shevita* and is subject to the *techum* restriction. A ruling about still water is perfectly reasonable, and there is nothing there to mock.

### Water Leniency

The *gemara* then identifies the true basis for Rabbi Yose's laughter. Even granting that there is a genuine *techum* problem, Rabbi Yose found it absurd to suppose that an iron wall would solve it. *Mishum dekalushei hikelu chachamim bemayim* — the Sages were broadly lenient regarding bodies of water in order to enable their use, and that general leniency ought to apply here. The classic illustration of this principle is the case of drawing water from the sea on *Shabbat* while aboard a boat. Since the boat is a *reshut hayachid* and the sea is a *karmelit*, one may not draw water directly over the side. The halachic solution is to construct a box-frame on the side of the boat before *Shabbat* — four walls with no floor — and lower the bucket through it. The *mechitza* of this frame is treated as if it descends to the bottom of the sea, thereby creating a *reshut hayachid* below, even though ordinarily a *mechitza teluyah* — a suspended partition that does not reach the ground — would not halachically constitute a valid *mechitza*.

This principle is made explicit through a related teaching: *Rabbi Tavla* once asked *Rav* whether a *mechitza teluyah* would be effective to permit use of a ruin on dry land. *Rav* replied: *ein mechitza teluyah materet ela bemayim* — a suspended partition is effective only over water. It is a specific leniency, *kalushei hikelu chachamim bemayim*, granted uniquely in the context of bodies of water. Accordingly, Rabbi Yose's point was that even if one grants Rabbi Chiyya's concern, the netting itself — already present in the water — should qualify under this leniency as a sufficient *mechitza*, rendering it no different in principle from the boat frame. The demand for an iron wall is therefore not a solution; it is beside the point.

### Netting Problem

The *gemara* presses the question further: why would an iron wall be any better than the netting already there? The water passes through the netting — *de'ayli behu maya* — so the netting does not physically stop anything. But the *gemara* responds: *shel barzel nami ayli behu maya* — an iron wall likewise does not stop the water from passing beneath it, assuming the wall does not extend to the very floor of the body of water. A standard halachic wall of ten *tefachim* presents the same problem regardless of material. 

One possible resolution is that Rabbi Chiyya was not actually proposing the iron wall as a practical remedy. Rather, *tzricha ve-ein lah takanah ka'amar* — he was using it as a rhetorical device, a hyperbolic way of expressing that the problem is insoluble: if you wanted a real fix, you would need an iron wall sunk all the way to the floor, and since no such thing exists, the water simply cannot be used across the boundary. This too is a reasonable reading. But Rabbi Yose's objection stands regardless: given the *gemara*'s established leniency for water, even an imperfect partition such as the netting should suffice, and there is no need for any iron wall at all.

### Boat Water Example

The boat example, already introduced to illustrate the principle of *mechitza teluyah* over water, bears emphasis. The reason the box-frame on the side of the boat works is not that it literally encloses a column of water — it manifestly does not go to the sea floor — but that the Sages treated it as though it did, as a specific dispensation to make bodies of water practically usable on *Shabbat*. It is precisely this dispensation that Rabbi Yose invokes: once you accept that the Sages created such a leniency, the netting across the river should benefit from the same logic.

---

## Four Amot Debate

### Mishnah Positions

We now return to the *mishnah* and the question of the four *amot* granted to a person who finds himself outside the *techum* — whether because he intentionally left, or because he fell asleep before *Shabbat* and had not *kana shevita*. The *mishnah* presents a range of views on how those four *amot* are measured. The *chachamim* rule that a person has four *amot*, but once he chooses a direction — how much he takes in front of him versus behind him — he is committed to that choice. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees, holding that the person is fixed at the center of a four-by-four box, with two *amot* in each direction. It is noteworthy that the *chachamim*'s position permits a degree of subjectivity unusual in *halacha*: one may choose to take all four *amot* in front, zero behind, or any combination, and that choice is binding.

### Box Dimensions

The *gemara* raises an apparent redundancy: Rabbi Yehuda's position — that one has four *amot* with the freedom to choose one's placement within them — seems identical to the *tanna kamma*, who also says four *amot*. *Amar Rava: shmona al shmona ika beinaihu* — Rava resolves the difficulty by pointing out that the *tanna kamma*'s statement of "four *amot*" follows the convention used throughout the tractate for measurements like 2,000 *amot*, which always means four *amot* in each direction. The *tanna kamma* therefore grants a box of eight by eight *amot*, with the person at the center. Rabbi Eliezer reduces this to a four-by-four box, also centered. Rabbi Yehuda accepts the four-by-four box but allows the person to choose where within it he stands.

*Tanya nami hachi* — a *braita* corroborates this: *yesh lo shmona al shmona — divrei Rabbi Meir*, explicitly stating that the person occupies the center of an eight-by-eight box, consistent with the *tanna kamma*.

*Rava* adds an important qualification: *machlokes lehalech* — the dispute between the eight-by-eight and four-by-four positions concerns movement. When it comes to *letalteil* — carrying in a *reshut harabim* — all agree that one may carry only four *amot* from where one picked up the object. Even Rabbi Meir, who grants eight *amot* for walking, would not permit carrying an object the full eight *amot* across the box.

### Biblical Source

The *gemara* asks: *ve-hani arba amot hecha ksiva* — where in the text are these four *amot* found? The answer comes from a *braita* citing the verse *shevu ish tachtav* — "let each person remain in his place" — which serves as the *asmachta* for the concept of *techum*. The phrase *tachtav*, "beneath him," is understood to denote the physical space a person occupies.

### Body Measurement

The *braita* elaborates: *gufo shalosh amot* — a person's body occupies three *amot* — plus one additional *amah* for a total of four. Rabbi Meir describes this extra *amah* as *kedei lifshot yadav ve-raglav* — room to stretch out one's arms and legs while lying down. Rabbi Yehuda agrees on the total of four *amot* but describes the extra *amah* differently: it is *kedei she-yitol chefetz mi-tachas margelosav u-maniach tachas merashosav* — sufficient space to take an object from beneath one's feet and place it beneath one's head. This evokes, perhaps intentionally, the imagery of *Yaakov* lying down with something beneath his head.

The *gemara* then asks *mai beinaihu* — what is the practical difference between these two formulations?
