If Rabbi Yehuda holds universally, as Rav Chisda claims, that even an *ashir* may designate a distant spot, why would the traveler have any advantage over the city residents? They should be able to designate a distant spot too, regardless of their status. The fact that the *Mishna* assigns the traveler a distinct privilege — allowing him to reach city B when others cannot — implies that even for Rabbi Yehuda, there remains a meaningful distinction between the person who is genuinely stuck outside and the person who is not. The case of distant designation must, after all, be limited to the true *ani* — even in Rabbi Yehuda's view. This inference supports Rav Nachman's reading: the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerns only the case where one begins *Shabbos* at the spot where one stands.

---

## Rabbah Case

### Rabbah's Practice

The *Gemara* reports that Rabbah bar bar Chana was accustomed to traveling regularly from Artivna to Pumbedita over *Shabbos*. Rather than going out on Friday afternoon to place bread or to be physically present at the midpoint, he would simply sit at home and declare: *tehei shvisasi be-Tzinza* — "Let my *Shabbos* be in Tzinza" — designating that particular location from the comfort of his home.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenged him: *mai datchach* — what are you thinking? He was apparently relying on the combination of two positions: the ruling that we follow Rabbi Yehuda, together with Rav Chisda's interpretation that Rabbi Yehuda permits even an *ashir* to designate a distant spot. Abaye rejected this reliance.

### Nachman Restated

Against Rav Chisda's reading, Rav Nachman's position stands: when it comes to designating a specific distant location, the rule is *ani* — yes, *ashir* — no. This is not merely one opinion among equals; it is supported by the *beraita* cited earlier in the sugya, which clearly establishes that the mechanism of remote designation was a limited exception for the person caught outside with no alternatives, and that the debate of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerned only the case of beginning *Shabbos* at the spot where one physically stands.

### Retraction

Abaye's point struck home. Rabbah bar bar Chana replied: *hadar bi* — I retract. He acknowledged that he could no longer rely on Rav Chisda's reading of Rabbi Yehuda and that he would henceforth need to schlep out on Friday afternoons to be physically present at the designated location.

### Final Resolution

The *Gemara* thus concludes firmly in accordance with Rav Nachman's position. The *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda — one may begin *Shabbos* at the spot where one physically stands, whether *ani* or *ashir* — but this applies only to the case of starting *Shabbos* where one is present. To designate a distant spot without being there, without placing bread there, and without any physical connection to that location — that remains exclusively the provision of the person who is genuinely stuck outside the city with no other options. The attempt to invoke this mechanism from one's easy chair at home, designating a faraway space by declaration alone, is rejected by the *Gemara* as a misapplication of the leniency. The *ani* exception is precisely that: an exception born of necessity, not a general license to designate *Shabbos* locations at will.

---

---

# Eiruvin 52

## Four Amot & 2000

### Meir vs. Yehuda

We pick up several lines into the daf with the statement of Rami bar Chama. By way of review: the preceding discussion had established the terms of the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the designation of *shvisas Shabbat* — the declaration of where one intends to begin Shabbat. Rabbi Meir holds that one may establish Shabbat at one's current physical location without bread only if one is an *ani*, meaning one who is not beginning from home. Rabbi Yehuda holds that even an *ashir* — someone starting from home, with food readily available — may rely on physical presence alone, without requiring a loaf of bread. An *ani*, in this technical sense, is one who begins his Shabbat designation not from his own home, and thus has no accessible bread; an *ashir* is one who does have that access.

That debate, the Gemara clarified, applies specifically when one is physically present at the spot one wishes to designate. But in the special case of the mishnah — where one designates a *makom shvisah* at a spot one is not physically standing — both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree that this is permitted only for the *ani*, only for the person who did not begin the eruv process from home. This principle will bear directly on the mishnayot that follow.

### Distance Eruv

Rami bar Chama raises a question arising from these discussions. When one is physically present and declares *tehei shvisasi bimkomi* — let my Shabbat rest be in this place — it is established that one receives a square of four *amot* surrounding oneself, plus 2000 *amot* extending outward from the edges of that square, yielding in practice 2004 *amot*. The question is whether the same geometry applies when one designates an eruv through a loaf of bread placed at a distant location. Does one measure a four-*ama* square around the bread and then 2000 *amot* beyond it — just as one measures the city first and then extends 2000 *amot* beyond the city's boundary — or does one simply measure 2000 *amot* from the bread itself, without any preliminary square?

### Bread Leniency

Rava responds: *ta shma* — come and hear from the language of the mishnah itself. The mishnah states that the use of bread was instituted not as a requirement but as a *kula* — a leniency — for the *ashir*, so that he would not need to go out in person (*shelo yeitzei beraglav*). This being so, if using bread meant that one would receive only 2000 *amot* without the additional four-*ama* square, the supposed leniency would carry a hidden cost, rendering it in some respects a *chumra* rather than a *kula*.

The Gemara, however, deflects this argument. Even if bread comes with a slight disadvantage in terms of total *techum*, it is still overwhelmingly beneficial: one need not go out personally, one need not wait near the spot as darkness falls, and a representative may deposit the eruv without personal effort. The convenience outweighs the marginal geometric cost. The Gemara therefore leaves unresolved whether bread-placement generates a surrounding four-*ama* square. What is clear is that physical presence at a spot does generate that square, in precise parallel to the way a city generates its own area first, before the 2000 *amot* are measured outward.

### Squaring & Compass

Before turning to the next mishnah, it is worth consolidating some of the arresting conclusions introduced on the previous daf. We ordinarily speak of 2000 *amot* as if that is simply a distance measured from where one stands. But we have now learned that: (a) even when one starts outside a city, the 2000 *amot* begins from the edge of a four-*ama* square centered on the person, not from the person's precise point; (b) it remains debated whether that square is four-by-four with the person at its center, or eight-by-eight; and (c) the square is oriented to the compass points, not simply to whatever direction one happens to be facing.

This squaring principle will be central to the fifth perek which we are about to begin. The Gemara also raised, in the context of carrying four *amot* in a *reshut harabim* and the minimum size of a *reshut hayachid* of four *tefachim* by four *tefachim*, the possibility that these measurements are also always understood relative to compass-aligned squares. One opinion — attributed to Rabbeinu Tam — holds that the four-by-four space of an object is always conceived as a compass-aligned square, so that carrying an object due north constitutes carrying it four *amot*, while carrying it at a 45-degree angle to the compass would involve the diagonal of that square, approximately 5.6 *amot*. A related view holds that an object occupying a space that is larger than four-by-four but is rotated relative to the compass may not qualify as a *reshut hayachid* if no compass-aligned four-by-four square can be inscribed within it. Rashi's position is that a square is required, full stop. These are striking departures from the way we ordinarily think about carrying and spatial definitions.

---

## Traveler Case

### Setup

The mishnah introduces the following case: someone left City A on Friday afternoon, intending to spend Shabbat in City B. Before he reached City B, his friend persuaded him to turn around and return home to City A. His intention, however, remained to reach City B the following day. The question is whether his eruv designation is effective.

The mishnah rules: *hu mutar* — he himself is permitted to travel toward City B on Shabbat — *ve'chol bnei ha'ir assurim* — but all the other residents of City A are forbidden to do so. The reason the townspeople cannot travel is not merely that they failed to make an eruv. Even if they had explicitly stayed home and announced their intention to designate a distant tree as their eruv, it would not have worked. This is because designating a distant spot — being physically absent from the eruv location and using no bread — is, as we established, permitted only for an *ani*. The residents of City A are each an *ashir*; they began the process from home. Only the traveler, who began his Shabbat designation in the course of an actual journey, is treated as an *ani* and may designate a distant spot.

### Ani Status

Rav Huna clarifies the precise conditions: the case involves someone who owns a house in City A and a house in City B, with the two cities separated by two *techumei Shabbat* — that is, 4000 *amot* — and a landmark (such as a tree) at the midpoint. Since this traveler had already set out on his journey (*keivan d'nafik lei l'orcha*), he is considered an *ani* for these purposes. He did not begin the process of eruv-making from his home; he was already in motion. The act of beginning a journey, *hechezik baderech*, removes him from the category of one whose eruv starts at home.

### Ashir Cannot

The other residents of City A, by contrast, never left home. They remain *ashirim* in the halachic sense — they have access to bread, they are rooted at their point of departure — and therefore they cannot designate a distant spot without bread or physical presence. Their verbal declarations of intention, however sincere, are legally ineffective.

### Chamor Gamal

Rabbi Meir's position introduces a significant complication. He says: *kol she'hu yachol le'areiv velo eireiv* — anyone who could have made a valid eruv and failed to do so — *harei zeh chamor gamal*, is like a donkey being pulled by a camel driver in both directions at once. What does this mean in practice?

Consider the geography: City A on one side, City B on the other, with 2000 *amot* in each direction to a central landmark. According to Rabbi Yehuda, our traveler is an *ani* and his eruv designation works. He gains the 2000 *amot* toward City B on Shabbat. According to Rabbi Meir, however, this traveler is considered an *ashir* — he started his journey from his home in City A, and therefore he had the ability to make a proper eruv with bread. Having failed to do so effectively, he forfeits the benefit of his home base in City A without gaining the benefit of a valid eruv at the landmark. What remains to him? Only the 2000 *amot* of overlap — the stretch he would have access to regardless.

Rashi illustrates a simpler version of this principle: if one placed an eruv at the 2000-*ama* marker and it was eaten or rolled away before Shabbat, the eruv failed. Rabbi Meir holds that the mere attempt to make an eruv in a given direction is itself costly — it constitutes a forfeiture of the equivalent 2000 *amot* in the opposite direction — regardless of whether the eruv ultimately succeeded. The person paid the price of attempting the eruv in terms of lost mobility, even when the eruv itself brought no benefit. This is a striking and, as we shall see, far-reaching position.

One might be tempted to explain Rabbi Meir's ruling in terms of *safek* — since we are uncertain whether the eruv worked, we apply a conservative approach and grant only the intersection of the two possible ranges. But the language of the mishnah — *kol she'hu yachol le'areiv velo eireiv* — does not point to uncertainty; it speaks of a case where the eruv definitively failed. We will return to this below.

---

## Rav Huna Analysis

### Journey Begins

We have already quoted Rav Huna's explanation above, in context: *keivan d'nafik lei l'orcha havei lei ani* — once the traveler departed on his journey, he acquires the status of *ani* and may designate a distant spot. This is the key halachic mechanism: the journey itself transforms his status. The eruv designation that follows is therefore legally effective, in contrast to the designation made by a townsperson who never left home.

### Baraita

A *baraita* confirms this ruling directly: in the case of one who has houses in two cities separated by two *techumei Shabbat*, *keivan she'hechezik baderech kana eruv divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — once he has begun his journey, his eruv is acquired, in the words of Rabbi Yehuda. The phrase *hechezik baderech* — literally, grasped the road, or established oneself on the road — is the operative criterion: having taken those first steps of the journey, one is no longer considered to be eruv-making from home.

### Rabbi Yosi

Rabbi Yosi the son of Rabbi Yehuda (*Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda*) adds a further ruling: *afilu matza'o chaveiro v'amar lo lin po* — even if his friend found him and said, do not travel tonight, it is too cold or too hot, sleep here — *lemachar mashkim ve'holech*, the following morning he may still travel on Shabbat. This is presented as *yitir al ken*, a step beyond Rabbi Yehuda's position. But this requires explanation: it appears at first glance to be the same scenario as the mishnah itself, and moreover, it is not clear wherein the novelty lies relative to what Rabbi Yehuda already said.

---

## Rabbah vs. Yosef

### Rabbah View

Rava explains the nature of the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda. Following one reading of Rashi, he states: *kuli alma lo pligi de'tzarich* — everyone agrees that verbal designation (*lomar*) of the specific location is necessary. One cannot rely on the Gemara "reading one's mind" to determine where precisely one intended to establish Shabbat. We have seen throughout this masechet that the designation must be precise; one cannot merely say "somewhere near the wall" or "somewhere near the tree." So verbal designation is universally required.

The debate, according to Rava, is over *lehachzik* — whether one must actually begin the journey (*hechzik baderech*) or whether mere intention suffices. Rabbi Yehuda requires at minimum the single step out the door. The journey of a thousand miles, so to speak, begins with that first step; without it, one is still an *ashir*. Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda holds that even if one's friend found one still at home — not yet having taken a single step — the mere fact that one was planning the journey and had designated a spot verbally is sufficient to grant the status of *ani* and render the eruv effective. This is the genuine *chiddush*.

The question of verbal designation, on this reading, is settled: everyone requires it. What remains contested is the threshold of physical departure.

### Yosef View

Rav Yosef reads the dispute in precisely the opposite way. He says: *lehachzik, kuli alma lo pligi de'tzarich* — everyone agrees that one must actually begin the journey; mere planning without stepping outside is insufficient. The debate, according to Rav Yosef, is over *lomar* — verbal designation. Rabbi Yehuda requires it; one must explicitly declare the spot. Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda holds that once the journey has begun, no verbal designation is needed; we may infer the intended location from the traveler's evident purpose. This is a striking position, given how much emphasis the preceding mishnayot placed on precision of designation.

Thus the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef concerns which of the two components — beginning the journey and verbal designation — is universally required and which is the subject of the tannaitic debate. Rabbah says: verbal designation is universally required, and the debate is about whether physical departure is also necessary. Rav Yosef says: physical departure is universally required, and the debate is about whether verbal designation is also necessary.

### Ulla

The Gemara asks: *ke'man azla ha de'amar Ulla?* — Whose view is consistent with the statement of Ulla? Ulla states: one who *hechzik baderech* and was turned back by his friend is *mutar u'muchzar u'muchzak* — permitted, turned back, and established. The Gemara notes the apparent tension: if he is *muchzar* — turned back and restored to his home base — why is he *muchzak*, still considered to have established an eruv? And conversely, if he is *muchzak*, meaning his status as one on a journey persists, why is he *muchzar*?

The Gemara resolves this: *af al pi she'muchzar muchzak* — even though he has been turned back, his eruv status is intact. Now, whose position does this align with? The Gemara concludes it follows Rav Yosef's reading of Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda: physical departure (*hechzik baderech*) is the universal requirement — hence the explicit mention that he began his journey — and verbal designation is not required — hence the fact that no mention is made of any declaration. Ulla's statement thus endorses the view that what matters is the journey, not the words.

### Ishtata Story

The Gemara supports this further with a narrative. Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata brought a basket of fruit to Rav Natan bar Oshaya on *erev Shabbat* and was about to return home. Rav Natan bar Oshaya waited deliberately until Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata had taken one step down from the upper level — *ad d'nachit darga* — thereby establishing *hechzik baderech*, having begun his journey. At that moment, Rav Natan bar Oshaya said to him: *beitkha* — make this your home tonight, stay here, go home tomorrow on Shabbat itself. The story thus deliberately recreates the scenario of the mishnah: departure followed immediately by a reversal prompted by another's invitation.

The notable feature of this account is that there appears to have been no verbal designation by Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata. The Gemara therefore asks: *ke'man?* — whose view does this reflect? It answers: Rav Yosef's reading of Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda, who requires the journey but not verbal designation. The Gemara adds, however, that it is also consistent with Rava's reading of Rabbi Yehuda — because perhaps Rav Natan bar Oshaya did, in fact, verbally instruct Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata to designate a particular spot at the moment he invited him to stay. The story does not exclude this possibility.

### Conclusion

In sum, the operative criteria for the *ani* who may designate a distant eruv location are: (a) that the journey has genuinely begun — one has stepped out of one's home — and (b) the question of verbal designation remains contested. What seems clear is that the journey is essential. Whether designation may be waived is left somewhat open. It is worth noting how conceptually strange it would be to dispense with verbal designation entirely, given the precision the Gemara has consistently demanded in specifying the location of the *makom shvisah*.

---

## Meir Penalty

### Parallel

The Gemara notes that Rabbi Meir's *chamor gamal* ruling has already appeared in an earlier mishnah, and asks why it must be restated here. The earlier case involved one who placed an eruv at the 2000-*ama* marker and the eruv was then destroyed *bein hashmashos* — in the twilight period between Friday and Shabbat — leaving a genuine *safek* as to whether the eruv took effect. In that case, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda both rule *chamor gamal*: since one does not know which of the two 2000-*amot* ranges applies, one receives only their intersection, the middle 2000.

That is a straightforward application of the *safek* principle. But the present case in the mishnah — the traveler who tried to designate a spot and failed — is not framed as a *safek*. The mishnah says *kol she'hu yachol le'areiv velo eireiv*: anyone who could have made an eruv and did not. This sounds not like uncertainty but like certain failure.

### Sheshet

Rav Sheshet draws the distinction explicitly: *lo teima ta'ama de'Rabbi Meir safek eireiv safek lo eireiv hu de'havei chamor gamal* — do not say that Rabbi Meir applies *chamor gamal* only when there is a doubt whether the eruv took effect. *Aval vadai lo eireiv lo havei chamor gamal* — one might have thought that if the eruv definitely failed, there would be no *chamor gamal*. Not so. *Ella afilu vadai lo eireiv havei chamor gamal* — even when it is certain the eruv failed, one still receives only the overlap range. The language of the mishnah — *yachol le'areiv velo eireiv*, he could have made an eruv and did not — reflects a case of certain failure, and Rabbi Meir's penalty applies nonetheless.

### Cost

The implication of this position is sharp. According to Rabbi Meir, the mere attempt to create an eruv in a given direction is itself costly, regardless of outcome. By reaching toward the eruv location, one forfeits the 2000 *amot* in the opposite direction. Even if the eruv is later known with certainty to have failed before Shabbat began, the person is still left with only the middle 2000 *amot*. This is not a *safek* calculus yielding an intersection; it is a penalty for having tried. It is, as Rashi reads it, a particularly rigorous ruling, and the Gemara makes clear that we do not rule this way.

---

## Exiting Techum

### One Step Out

The mishnah states: *mi sheyatza chutz la'techum* — one who stepped outside the *techum* — *afilu ama achat lo yikanes* — even one *ama*, he may not reenter. This echoes the earlier mishnayot regarding the traveler who walked outside the *techum* and was thereby limited to four *amot*. The present mishnah makes clear that there is no tolerance whatsoever: a single step over the *techum* boundary locks one out. One now has four *amot* from wherever one is standing outside, but the 2000 *amot* of the *techum* from one's city are inaccessible.

### Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer disagrees: *shtayim yachol likhanes, shalosh lo yikanes* — if one has overstepped by up to two *amot*, one may reenter; if by three, one may not. His reasoning: the moment one steps outside the *techum*, one immediately acquires four *amot* of personal space. If one has stepped only one or two *amot* beyond the boundary, those four *amot* extend back across the *techum* line, creating an overlap. Since one's allocated space straddles the boundary, one may step back. The *chakhamim* hold that notwithstanding any such overlap, having crossed the line at all precludes reentry.

### One Foot

Rabbi Chanina extends the analysis to an even more granular case: one foot inside the *techum* and one foot outside — *raglo achat betokh ha'techum ve'raglo achat chutz la'techum*. According to the *chakhamim*'s strict rule that even one step outside locks one out, it follows that one may not pull the outside foot back in. The Gemara supports this from the verse *im tashiv mishabbat raglecha* (Isaiah 58:13), stressing *raglecha* in the singular — even one foot that has crossed must be stopped.

A *baraita*, however, states that in this scenario one may reenter. The Gemara explains: *ha manni acherim hi* — this follows the minority opinion of *Acherim*, who hold *lemakom she'rubo nizdaker* — one is drawn toward wherever the majority of one's body is located. Since one foot is still inside, one's bodily center of gravity and weight remain within the *techum*, and one has not yet truly crossed the line.

A parallel tradition then reports that Rabbi Chanina himself stated this leniency, citing the same verse but reading *raglayich* in the plural — only when both feet have crossed does the restriction apply. This reading yields the lenient ruling: one foot out is not yet a full crossing.

The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction: a *baraita* attributes to Rabbi Eliezer both the position of his mishnah (two *amot* permissible) and an apparently stricter position (even one *ama* impermissible). The Gemara resolves this: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. The ruling of one *ama* permissible and two *amot* impermissible reflects the distinction between having just lifted one foot into the second *ama* versus having fully planted oneself in the second *ama*. "You can go back" means you are still in the first *ama* zone; "you cannot go back" means you have genuinely stepped into the third *ama*.

### Measurement

There is a further *baraita* in which Rabbi Eliezer says *afilu ama achat lo yikanes* — even one *ama*, one may not go back in — identical to the *chakhamim*'s position in the mishnah. Is this not contradictory to his mishnah ruling? The Gemara answers: *ki tanya hahi lemoded* — that *baraita* addresses an entirely different scenario: the measurer. The mishnah rule — two *amot* are permissible — addresses *bedi'avad*, where someone inadvertently stepped across the *techum* boundary. The *baraita* addresses the one who is deliberately measuring off his 2000 *amot* from a point outside the city. When one starts outside the city, one measures 2000 and stops precisely there — even if the end point falls inside a cave, inside a building, or inside a city. One does not gain the right to enter that structure. The mishnah (*detnan*) makes clear: *notnim lo alpayim ama afilu sof midato kala bime'arah* — we give him his 2000 *amot* even if his measurement ends in the middle of a cave, meaning he gets the 2000 *amot* but nothing further.

So the two rulings address distinct situations: one is the *lechatchila* instruction to a measurer not to step one *ama* beyond the calculated 2000, and the other is the *bedi'avad* situation of someone who has already crossed and wonders whether reentry is possible.

---

## Forced Outside

### Forced Stay

The final mishnah of the fourth perek: *mi shehotzi'uhu chutz la'techum afilu ama achat lo yikanes* — one who was forced or found himself outside the *techum* when Shabbat began, even if only one *ama* outside, may not reenter. The practical meaning: if one ends up outside the city as Shabbat falls, and one's personal 2000-*ama* allotment from that point does not reach the city limits, one cannot enter the city. Even if one's house is just beyond that line, one is restricted to the 2000 *amot* from one's current location.

### Shimon Buffer

Rabbi Shimon dissents: *afilu chamesh esrei ama yikanes* — even if one is fifteen *amot* outside the *techum*, one may enter. His reason: *she'ein hamshuchot mamtzi'ot et hamidot mipnei hato'im* — the measuring ropes do not yield perfectly accurate measurements, on account of errors. The result is that the formal markers placed at the *techum* boundary are already set fifteen *amot* short of the actual boundary, as a built-in buffer to account for human imprecision. Therefore, if one finds oneself within fifteen *amot* of the marker at the onset of Shabbat, one is in reality still within the *techum*.

### Buffer Rationale

The Gemara explains the precision of the fifteen-*ama* figure. The measuring rope used for *techum* measurements is fifty *amot* long. Two people hold the rope — one at each end — and they walk forty repetitions to measure 2000 *amot*. But each person, at each measurement, occupies a *tefach* of the rope with his grip. Since both ends of the rope are held, two *tefachim* are lost per measurement. Over forty measurements, that is eighty *tefachim* of total rope that are not actually measured as distance. Since there are six *tefachim* per *ama*, eighty *tefachim* equals just over thirteen *amot*. Rashi adjusts slightly — accounting for a *tefach* and a bit per grip — and arrives at the full fifteen *amot*. The upshot: the measurer consistently understates the true distance by this margin, and therefore everyone has an effective buffer of fifteen *amot* beyond the marked boundary before they have actually crossed the real *techum*.

---

## Perek 5 Intro

### City Boundaries

We now begin the fifth perek — *Keitzad me'abrin et he'arim* — How does one extend the boundaries of a city? The word *me'abrin* (from *ubar*, embryo) evokes the image of giving a city an expanded, pregnant form: one takes the inhabited core and surrounds it with a structured, squared-off perimeter from which the 2000 *amot* are then measured. The perek will deal at length with how precisely to define and square off a city's dimensions, a topic directly relevant to everything we have been discussing.

### Structures

The mishnah begins by enumerating the types of features that complicate a city's outline. *Beit niknas beit yotzei* — houses that jut inward or outward from the general city wall, creating irregular lines. *Pogum niknas pogum yotzei* — indentations or protrusions in a fortification or structure. *Gedudiyot gevohot asarah tefachim* — destroyed structures that are still ten *tefachim* high; Rashi explains these as ruins of buildings or turrets. *Gesharim* — bridges. *Nefashot* — tombstones and funerary structures. All of these are included in the city's measured area, provided that each has a *beit dira* — some form of habitation associated with it. By "habitation," the mishnah means some ongoing human use: the cemetery example is explained by the presence of the caretaker's booth within which he sleeps and keeps watch. The dead bodies themselves, needless to say, do not count toward habitation.

### Outermost Points

The method for measuring the city begins with identifying the outermost inhabited points. One surveys the city and marks every location — including the structures enumerated above — where there is some form of genuine habitation. The most distant such points in every direction define the outer perimeter of the city. From these furthest inhabited points, *motzi'in et hamida kenegdan* — one extends the measuring line outward, opposite those points. This yields a rough perimeter of the city's actual extent.

### Squaring Off

Once the outermost inhabited points have been identified, the mishnah prescribes: *ve'osin ota ke'min tablo meruva'at* — one fashions the city's boundary into a square tablet, *kedei shenishtaker et hazaviyot* — so that one gains the benefit of the corners. Squaring off the city means that rather than tracing a jagged, irregular outline around all the inhabited points, one draws a rectangle — or, more precisely, a square aligned to the compass points — that encompasses all those points. The corners of that square extend beyond the inhabited area, and the 2000 *amot* are measured outward from each side of that square.

The practical consequence is significant. A city like Manhattan, for example, which runs at roughly a 45-degree angle to true north, would if squared off along the compass axes yield a much larger base area than if one simply inscribed a rectangle along the city's own axis. The rules of *techum* measurement follow the compass, not the city's natural orientation. We rule that the squaring-off is performed according to the compass points, and we will continue to examine the implications of this in the material ahead.

# Eiruvin 53

## Me'abrin Overview

### Me'abrin/Me'arvin

We open on 53b, the beginning of a new *perek*. The *mishnah* that opens this chapter will serve primarily as a jumping-off point for several pages of *aggadeta*. The *mishnah* introduces the concept of *keitzad me'abrin* — how do we extend the boundaries of a city — not to be confused with *me'arvin*, which relates to *eiruv*. The term *me'abrin* derives from *ibbur*, like a pregnant woman, because the process involves squaring off the protrusions of the city to generate additional space, so that the city, as it were, "juts out" beyond its natural perimeter. That is the conceptual backdrop against which the *gemara* proceeds.

### Alef vs. Ayin

The *gemara* opens with a dispute between Rav and Shmuel. One of them (*chad tani*) has the version of the *mishnah* spelling *me'abrin* with an *ayin* — *ibbur*, the root connoting pregnancy — while the other (*ve'chad tani*) reads *me'avrin* with an *alef*, connoting *eiver*, a limb, since the process adds limbs to the city's outline. The *gemara* explains both readings: the *alef* version relates to the extension of the city limb by limb, while the *ayin* version compares the process to a pregnant woman, whose form extends outward in an irregular shape that is then squared off.

### Guttural Loss

It is worth noting here that other *gemarot* reflect the phenomenon that in the more Hellenized, Greek-Roman cities of the Land of Israel, the distinction between *ayin* and *alef* was being lost — a direct consequence of the difficulty speakers of a non-Semitic language have with guttural consonants. In a fully oral culture, one would expect that the audible difference between *ayin* and *alef* would be immediately apparent. Yet the very fact that this dispute arises suggests that in certain communities, the guttural capacity was eroding — making these two letters effectively indistinguishable in pronunciation. They were, as one might quip, the first *Ashkenazim*.

## Me'arat HaMachpelah

### Machpelah Structure

The *gemara* proceeds to a series of related disputes between Rav and Shmuel touching on biblical geography and etymology. The first concerns *Me'arat HaMachpelah*: what does the name *Machpelah* — "the doubled one" — actually mean? One opinion holds that *Machpelah* refers to the cave's physical structure: two chambers, one behind the other (*shenei batim zeh lifnim mizeh*). The other holds that it refers to two stories, a house built atop another (*bayit al gabav*).

The *gemara* notes that the two-story interpretation explains the name *Machpelah* straightforwardly: it is doubled because it has two roofs, and in *halachah*, a house is defined by its roof. But for the view that it is two chambers side by side, the doubling of roofs does not apply — so what is the meaning of *Machpelah*? The answer given is *she'kfulah b'zugot*: the cave is "doubled" in the sense that it contains multiple pairs (*zugot*) of the buried — Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah, and Adam and Eve. The *Maharsha* notes, however, that from a *pshat* perspective this is clearly a *drash*, since the *pesukim* refer to the field as *S'dei HaMachpelah*, suggesting that *Machpelah* is simply the name of the place rather than a description of the cave's configuration — unless one says the field was named after the cave. In any case, the *gemara* treats this as an aggadic interpretation.

### Four Couples

The same theme of four pairs leads the *gemara* to address *Kiryat Arba* — the city of Hebron. Rav Yitzchak is quoted: *Kiryat Ha'arba* means the city of four pairs — Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, and Jacob and Leah (*arba zugot*). The *Maharsha* observes that in *Sefer Yehoshua*, Arba appears as a proper name, but that in one passage in *Bereishit* the text reads *Kiryat Ha'arba* — with the definite article *heh* — and a *heh hayedi'ah* would not be attached to a proper noun. This grammatical observation grounds the *gemara*'s *drasha* that *arba* here is a number, not a name.

### Amraphel/Nimrod

A further dispute between Rav and Shmuel concerns *Amraphel*, king of Shinar, mentioned at the opening of the war of the four kings against five. The *midrash* identifies Amraphel with Nimrod, since Nimrod is described as *gibor tziyad lifnei Hashem* and the first major war in the *Torah* is fought under Amraphel's leadership. The dispute is over which name is primary and which is the descriptive epithet. One view holds that his real name was Nimrod, and Amraphel was descriptive: *she'amar ve'hipil* — "he said and caused to fall" — referring to his decree that Abraham be cast into the furnace (*kivshan ha'esh*). The other holds that Amraphel was his actual name, while Nimrod was the epithet: *she'himrid et kol ha'olam b'malchuto* — that he caused the entire world to rebel against God, associating him with the leadership of the *Migdal Bavel* insurrection, consistent with his role as *Melech Shinar*.

## New King Egypt

### New King Debate

The *gemara* then turns to another famous dispute — one that *Rashi* cites in his commentary on the *Torah*. The verse states *vayakom melech chadash al Mitzrayim*, "a new king arose over Egypt." Rav and Shmuel disagree: one holds *chadash mamash* — he was literally a new king — while the other holds *she'nitchadesh gezeirotav* — the same king renewed his decrees and changed his policies toward Israel.

The *gemara* supports the "literally new" position from the text itself: the *Torah* says *chadash*. And it supports the "renewed decrees" position from what is absent: the text does not say *vayamot vayimloch* — it never tells us that the previous king died and a new one reigned. The *gemara* then raises an objection against the latter view: the verse says *asher lo yada et Yosef* — "who did not know Joseph" — which implies he was a different person entirely, since surely the same king who had ruled during Joseph's time would have known him. The *gemara* resolves this: the phrase means he acted *as if* he did not know Joseph — he deliberately chose to ignore Joseph's legacy and behave as though it were unknown to him.

## Rabbi Yochanan/Oshaya

### Eighteen Days Learning

Rabbi Yochanan makes a statement that at first appears to be a digression, but will circle back directly to the question of *me'abrin* with *alef* or *ayin*. He says: *yud-chet yamim gidalti etzel Rabbi Oshaya b'rebi* — I spent eighteen days in the presence of Rabbi Oshaya the Great. And note the verb *gidalti* — "I grew" — an unusual formulation for merely spending time. *Ulo lamadti mimenu ela davar echad b'mishnatenu* — and the only thing I learned from him relating to the *mishnah* was: *keitzad me'avrin et ha'arim b'aleph* — that the word in the *mishnah* is spelled with an *alef*.

This sounds, on its surface, like a rather deflating statement — both about the value of the eighteen days spent and about Rabbi Oshaya himself. One might ask: is Rabbi Yochanan diminishing the importance of Rabbi Oshaya by suggesting that after eighteen days, only a single textual point could be learned from him? And is the point itself — merely an orthographic variant with no halakhic consequence — so trivial as to make the whole encounter seem underwhelming?

It is worth noting that this is entirely consistent with Rabbi Oshaya's broader scholarly enterprise. Rabbi Oshaya, together with Rabbi Chiya, was instrumental in establishing the authoritative texts of the *Tannaic* literature. As the *gemara* elsewhere states, a *baraita* that was not taught in the academy of Rabbi Oshaya or Rabbi Chiya cannot be fully relied upon — they performed for the *baraitot* and *Tosefta* the same editorial work that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi performed for the *mishnah*. Precision of text was precisely Rabbi Oshaya's domain. So it is perhaps not surprising that what Rabbi Yochanan learned from him in connection with the *mishnah* was a textual clarification.

The *gemara* then questions the statement itself: *ini?* Can this really be so? It immediately contrasts it with another statement of Rabbi Yochanan: there were twelve prize students of Rabbi Oshaya, and Rabbi Yochanan spent eighteen days among them — *v'limadti lev kol echad ve'echad* — he came to understand the heart of each one of them, *ve'chachmat kol echad ve'echad* — and the wisdom of each one. *Rashi* explains that this means he grasped their individual methods of learning, their ways of thinking, their particular approaches to *derech* and analysis, as well as their accumulated knowledge.

### Lev and Chochmah

So was it really the case that he only learned one thing? The *gemara* qualifies. *Lev kol echad ve'echad ve'chachmat kol echad ve'echad gemar* — he did indeed learn their approaches and methodologies — *gemara lo gemar* — but he did not actually acquire new material from them. A first resolution: *mineihu dideihu gemar* — what he learned, he learned from the students; *minei didei lo gemar* — he did not learn new material from Rabbi Oshaya himself. A second resolution: *davar echad b'mishnatenu gemar* — he may have learned other things, but in relation to the *mishnah* specifically, only one thing was clarified for him by Rabbi Oshaya. Perhaps he learned much else, but the single contribution Rabbi Oshaya made to his understanding of the *mishnah* was this orthographic point.

This tension — between learning methodology on the one hand and acquiring new material on the other — is instructive. Learning a *rebbe*'s *derech*, understanding how he thinks, grasping what each student carries — that is arguably more valuable than any single piece of information. The adage about teaching a man to fish rather than giving him a fish captures something of this distinction. And yet the *gemara* acknowledges both dimensions as real and distinct.

There is an additional passage that sheds light on Rabbi Oshaya's stature. Rabbi Yochanan elsewhere states: Rabbi Oshaya in his generation was like Rabbi Meir in his generation — *mah Rabbi Meir bedoro lo yachlu chaveirav la'amod al sof da'ato*, just as no one in Rabbi Meir's time could fully follow him to the depth of his thinking, so too with Rabbi Oshaya. Rabbi Yochanan's remark that he learned only one *mishnaic* point from Rabbi Oshaya may in fact reflect this: Rabbi Oshaya's analysis was of a depth that Rabbi Yochanan himself could not fully access, and so the one thing he could confirm and carry away was a textual correction.

### Four in One Amah

Rabbi Yochanan adds: when we were learning *Torah* by Rabbi Oshaya, *hayinu yoshvim arba arba be'ama* — four of us would sit, pressed together, within a single *amah*. If an *amah* is roughly a cubit — something on the order of a foot and a half — this represents an extraordinarily tight fit. *Rashi* explains that everyone was crowding around Rabbi Oshaya to hear what he said. This implies that the full student body was considerably larger than twelve; the twelve were the prize students, while the others pressed in as best they could.

The *mishnah* records a parallel: *amar Rebbi*, when we were learning *Torah* by Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua — the famous student of Rabbi Akiva and teacher of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — *hayinu yoshvim shisha shisha be'ama*, six of us would squeeze into a single *amah*. The *Maharsha* observes that this is either miraculous or hyperbolic, but either way, both accounts convey the same essential image: the pressing, crowded, almost physical intensity of learning in the presence of a true master.

## Yeridas HaDoros

### Opening Comparison

The discussion of the great *gedolim* of preceding generations leads Rabbi Yochanan to one of the most celebrated passages in this section. *Liban shel rishonim kepitcho shel ulam* — the heart, meaning the intellectual capacity and depth of understanding, of the earlier generations was like the opening of the *ulam*, the great hall that preceded the *heichal* of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *ulam* was twenty *amot* wide. *Ve'shel acharonim kepitcho shel heichal* — the later generations had a capacity only like the opening of the *heichal* itself, which was ten *amot* wide — half as large. This goes back to the very first *perek* of *Eruvin*, where these measurements were established.

The *gemara* specifies who these generations are. According to one view, the *rishonim* with the understanding of the *ulam*'s opening refers to Rabbi Akiva, and the *acharonim* with the *heichal*'s opening refers to Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, his student. According to another view, the *rishonim* already includes Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, and the decline began only with Rabbi Oshaya. Either way, the generation from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi onward represents a further and steeper drop — represented by the image of a needle's point.

One student raised an intriguing counterpoint: since the *acharonim* are closer to the *heichal*, might the spatial metaphor also suggest proximity to the sacred core — that later generations, while diminished in raw capacity, are in some sense drawing nearer? This is a beautiful thought, and resonates with the well-known image of dwarfs standing on the shoulders of giants. Later generations may understand less in absolute terms, but they build on everything that preceded them and can therefore sometimes see further. Whether this is the *pshat* of the metaphor is uncertain, but it is a striking observation.

### Needle/Wax Metaphors

*Ve'anu*, continues Rabbi Yochanan — and we, the *Amoraim* as compared to the *Tannaim* — *kemale nekev machat sidkit* — our capacity is like the opening of a very fine needle. The drop from twenty *amot* to ten is significant; the drop from ten *amot* to a needle's eye is catastrophic. This may also serve as the *gemara*'s own internal explanation for the principle that an *amora* cannot argue with a *tanna*. Why not? Because the *Tannaim*, even at their latest stage, operated with the understanding of the *heichal*'s opening; the *Amoraim* are left with a needle's point. The transitional generation of Rav — about whom the *gemara* says *Rav tanna hu u'palig* — is the exception that proves the rule.

Abaye, speaking from the later *Amoraic* period, adds: *ke'sikhtsa be'guda le'gemara* — we are like a peg being driven into a stone wall when it comes to *gemara*, meaning the mastery and transmission of received material. The further one gets from the source, the greater the loss of the chain of transmission, and the harder it becomes to drive that peg through. Rava adds a parallel formulation: *ke'etzbeta be'kira le'sevara* — we are like a finger in wax when it comes to *sevara*, analytical reasoning. Abaye speaks of *gemara* — the acquisition of tradition; Rava speaks of *sevara* — independent intellectual capacity. Both are diminished, but perhaps in different ways. If one pressed the wax metaphor slightly, one might note that a finger pressed into soft wax does leave some impression; it does not pass all the way through, but something sticks. Nonetheless, the *gemara*'s intent is clearly to describe limitation. And Rav Ashi, the latest of these voices, concludes: *ke'etzbeta be'bira le'shikhcha* — we are like a finger plunged into a well when it comes to forgetting. There is no resistance at all; information passes through us without leaving a trace.

As the total body of *Torah she'be'al peh* grows with each generation, so too does the challenge of retaining it. More information, less retention — and in an oral culture, the combination is particularly acute.

### Rabbinic Authority

This extended treatment of *Yeridas HaDoros* deserves some broader reflection, though only along the lines that the *gemara* itself suggests. The theology of declining generations — while certainly rooted in statements like the ones here, as well as *im rishonim kemalachim anachnu kivnei adam, im rishonim kivnei adam anachnu kachamorim* — is not the only posture that *chazal* adopt. The principle of *halacha k'basrai*, going by the later authorities, reflects a competing intuition: that later generations, having the benefit of all prior learning, can in some respects see further than their predecessors, like the dwarfs on the shoulders of giants.

The book *Maimonides and the Descent of Generations* by Menachem Kellner addresses precisely this tension and argues, among other things, that the *Rambam* took a fundamentally different view of the nature of rabbinic authority. For the *Rambam*, the authority of the *Talmud Bavli* — and of *halachic* norms generally — rests not on the assumption of superior wisdom or infallibility, but on canonization: the acceptance by *Klal Yisrael* of a body of literature and a system of practice. The *Bavli* is more authoritative than the *Yerushalmi* not because the *Bavli*'s sages were wiser, but because it was the *Bavli* that was canonized and accepted throughout the Jewish world. Similarly, the *Kesef Mishneh* argues that the rule against *Amoraim* disputing *Tannaim* derives not from an assumption about intrinsic superiority but from an implicit consensus — a canonization of the *Tannaic* corpus that occurred after the closing of the *Mishnah*.

This distinction has significant practical implications. If rabbinic authority rests on claims of intrinsic wisdom and near-infallibility, then any acknowledgment of error in *chazal* is profoundly threatening. If it rests on canonization — on *Klal Yisrael*'s acceptance — then it is the fact of acceptance itself that confers authority, independently of questions about superior knowledge. The *Chazon Ish* famously took this latter approach: *rishonim* whose works were not part of the *mesorah* of *Klal Yisrael* — those discovered late and never incorporated into the living tradition — carry no *halachic* weight, not because he doubted their intelligence or their *pshat*, but because what gives a work *halachic* authority is its integration into the accepted system. By extension, as the *Meiri* and similar works become increasingly cited by *poskim*, they can begin to acquire that standing organically.

Those who hold the alternative view — that authority flows from intrinsic truth — tend to account for the *Shulchan Aruch*'s authority through a different lens: the fact that *Klal Yisrael* accepted it demonstrates *siyata d'shmaya*, Divine assistance, which would not have been granted unless the *Shulchan Aruch* embodied the true *halachah*. The question of manuscript variants, textual corruptions through censorship, and the *halachic* weight of newly discovered *rishonim* all turn, in part, on which of these two foundational positions one adopts.

## Judea vs. Galilee

### Judean Precision

The *gemara* transitions back toward the theme of *me'abrin* with *alef* or *ayin* through a teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *bnei Yehuda she'hikpidu al leshonam, nitkayma Toratam be'yadam* — the people of Judea, who were precise and exacting in their language, held on to their *Torah*. The *gemara* then contrasts this with *bnei Galil she'lo hikpidu al leshonam, lo nitkayma Toratam be'yadam* — the Galileans, who were careless in speech, did not hold on to their *Torah*.

### Galilean Looseness

The *gemara* asks: *midi be'kfeida talya milta?* Is the preservation of *Torah* really dependent on carefulness of speech? The explanation is as follows. *Bnei Yehuda de'dayki lishna* — those who are precise in language, when they learn a *mishnah* in an oral culture, establish a fixed, exact text. *U'matni lehu simana* — and with a precise, fixed text, one can devise *simanim*, mnemonics, to remember the material. *Nitkayma Toratam be'yadam* — the tradition is thus preserved. *Bnei Galil de'lo dayki lishna* — those who are imprecise have a moving target: the text shifts from person to person and occasion to occasion. *Ve'lo matni lehu simana* — without a fixed text, you cannot build reliable mnemonics. *Lo nitkayma Toratam be'yadam* — and so the tradition is lost.

*Rashi* adds a further dimension: it is not only each individual *mishnah* that requires precision, but also the order in which one *mishnah* follows another. If that order is carefully maintained, one can use the sequence itself as a mnemonic — the opening of one *mishnah* triggers the memory of the next. But if the ordering is loose or inconsistent, that entire associative chain collapses.

### One vs. Many Teachers

The *gemara* continues with a further contrast. *Bnei Yehuda gamru mi'chad raba, nitkayma Toratam be'yadam* — the Judeans learned from a single *rebbe*, and their *Torah* was preserved. *Bnei Galil de'lo gamru mi'chad raba, lo nitkayma Toratam be'yadam* — the Galileans learned from many different teachers, and their tradition was not preserved. *Tosafot* clarifies: this is specifically about the transmission of material. When you learn a *mishnah* from one teacher, you receive one precise *girsa* — one version of the text. If you go from teacher to teacher, each gives you a slightly different version, and the result is confusion and instability.

However — and *Tosafot* is careful to note this — for the purposes of analytical learning, *sevara* and methodology, learning from many teachers is in fact a *mitzvah*. Already in the first *perek* the *gemara* states that one who learns *Torah* before only a single *rebbe* will never see a sign of blessing — the implication being that exposure to multiple approaches is essential for intellectual development. The resolution is that these are two distinct tasks: mastering the text requires one stable *girsa* from one consistent source, while mastering analysis requires exposure to many minds and approaches.

### Text Analysis

A related insight: Chaim Soloveitchik once observed that *Tosafot* as a genre was only possible after *Rashi*. Not because the *Baalei Tosafot* could not understand the *gemara* without *Rashi*, but because *Rashi* established a default interpretation — a fixed reading — that became the standard starting point. Before *Rashi*, the *gemara* was, in a sense, a moving target: with multiple possible readings of every line, how does one formulate a precise critical question? Once *Rashi* establishes what a passage means, one has a fixed text against which to push. The question becomes sharp and the analysis becomes possible. This is precisely the model the *gemara* is articulating: first establish a single, precise text; then, from that stable foundation, undertake the broader analytical work.

*Ravina* adds a final point: *bnei Yehuda degalu masechta, nitkayma Toratam be'yadam* — the Judeans revealed a *masechta*, meaning, according to *Rashi*, either that they taught it to others or that they analyzed it in depth. *Bnei Galil delo galu masechta, lo nitkayma Toratam be'yadam*. This is a fitting counterpart to what came before: if precision of text and learning from a single teacher are about retention, then going deep into the material and revealing it — whether through teaching or through analysis — is about understanding. And understanding, in turn, reinforces memory. Memorization and comprehension are not separate enterprises; each supports the other.

## David/Shaul Paradigm

### David/Shaul

This observation about *galui masechta* — revealing a *masechta* — is then illustrated through the contrast between David and Shaul. *David degali masechta* — David revealed his *masechet*; *Shaul lo gali masechta* — Shaul did not. By David it is written: *yereiecha yiruni veyismachu* — those who fear You will see me and rejoice. The *gemara* reads this as those who come to David with *halachic* questions are happy with his answers, knowing that he understands what he is talking about. This connects with the *midrashim* in *Berachot* portraying David as a *posek*, immersed in questions of *Tannaic* law, going to *Mephibosheth* with his rulings.

### Shaul's Evil

By contrast, of Shaul it is written: *uv'chol asher yifneh yarshia* — wherever he turned, he would do wrong, or cause evil. The *gemara* reinterprets this: it does not mean that Shaul was a wicked person in the conventional sense, but rather that he would *pasken* incorrectly. Because he had not fully revealed his *masechta* — had not fully analyzed and transmitted his learning — his *halachic* judgments were unreliable, and harm would follow from them. This is, notably, a significant softening of what the verse says on its surface. The entire weight of Shaul's moral failure is recast as a failure of *halachic* competence.

### Shaul's Forgiveness

Consistent with this more sympathetic reading, Rabbi Yochanan asks: *minayin she'machal lo HaKadosh Baruch Hu al oto avon?* How do we know that God forgave Shaul for that sin — the sin of destroying Nov, the city of the priests? The proof is from Shmuel's message to Shaul when he was summoned from the dead: *machar atah u'vanecha imi* — tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The word *imi*, with me *bimchitzati*, in my portion — meaning Shaul would share in *Shmuel*'s *mechitzah* in the *olam haba*. The implication is that Shaul merited a share in the world to come alongside *Shmuel*, which the *gemara* reads as Divine forgiveness.

## Asking Judeans

### Which Version

Having established the superior precision of *bnei Yehuda* in matters of language and textual transmission, the *gemara* now makes the connection explicit. Rabbi Abba says: if there is someone who can ask the *bnei Yehuda*, those who are careful with their language, they should be asked: *ma'avrin tnan o me'abrin tnan?* Is the *mishnah*'s word spelled with an *alef* or with an *ayin?* Similarly, with respect to a *mishnah* in the laws of *mumim* in a *bechor* — where the text describes an animal sitting on its haunches — is it *achuzu* with an *alef* or *achuzu* with an *ayin?* In both cases, the question hinges precisely on the distinction between *alef* and *ayin*, which in the more Hellenized communities of the Galilee had become blurred. The Judeans, being *daykei lishna*, would know the difference.

It is worth noting parenthetically that the Galilee was the more cosmopolitan, Hellenistically influenced region, while Judea was more rural. The loss of guttural consonants — *ayin*, *alef*, *chet* — was precisely a feature of the Greek-influenced urban centers. So *bnei Yehuda*'s precision was not merely a cultural disposition; it was tied to the fact that their language had not been assimilated into a non-Semitic phonological framework. The instruction to ask the *bnei Yehuda* is therefore specifically appropriate for questions that turn on *alef* versus *ayin*.

### Both Versions Exist

*Shailunhu* — they were asked. *Va'amru lehu* — and they replied: *ika de'tanni me'avrin ve'ika de'tanni me'abrin* — there are manuscripts with one version and manuscripts with the other. Similarly, *ika de'tanni achuzu ve'ika de'tanni achuzu*. Both variants exist.

## Green Textile

### Tardin Example

What is a concrete example of *bnei Yehuda*'s linguistic precision? A certain Judean was going about telling people: *talit yesh li limkor* — I have a *talit* to sell. They asked him: *mai gavan talitecha?* What color is it? He replied: *ke'tardin alei adama* — like the leaves of beets growing from the ground. He gave not just a color but a precise shade and hue — the particular green of beet leaves as distinct from the beet itself.

The *Maharsha* explains the point more sharply: why not simply say *yarok*, green? Because in the *mishnah*, *yarok* spans a range from green to yellow — it covers what we would call the green-yellow continuum — and is therefore ambiguous. Rather than risk misunderstanding, the Judean merchant described the color by comparison to a specific, recognizable natural object. That is precision of language.

## Galilean Errors

### Chamar Confusion

What is an example of *bnei Galil*'s imprecision? A Galilean was going about asking: *chamar leman, amar leman?* — looking for someone who had *chamar* or *amar*. Those who heard him responded: *galila shota* — stupid Galilean, what are you asking for? Are you asking for a *chamor lemirkav*, a donkey to ride? Or *chamar limishti*, wine to drink? And continuing: *amar lemilbash*, wool to wear? Or *imar le'iksa*, a lamb to slaughter? All four words — donkey, wine, wool, lamb — are rendered nearly identical by someone who cannot distinguish between *alef*, *ayin*, and *chet*. The story illustrates precisely how the loss of gutturals produces communicative chaos.

### Woman's Slips

A woman wanted to say to her friend: *ta de'ochlich chalba* — come, let me feed you milk. But she garbled it. First she said *shiluchti* — a mispronunciation of *shaluvti*, a term of endearment meaning something like "my companion" or "my friend." And then, instead of *de'ochlich chalba*, she said *tochlich lavi* — which means "a lion should eat you." A Freudian slip of the most dramatic kind, and again, one rooted in the imprecise handling of guttural consonants.

### Judge's Woman

A woman came before a judge. Instead of addressing him respectfully with *kiri* spelled with a *kuf* — an honorific — she said *kiri* with a *chaf*, meaning slave. She wanted to say she had a *tavla* — a plank or tablet — but said *tifla*, a senseless thing, a beam perhaps. She said it had been stolen from her — *vigenovach min* — but the phrasing meant that it was *the judge* who had been stolen. And then, to make it worse, she explained that if the tablet were laid out flat, a person's legs would not reach the floor — an image of the judge being stretched across it. The last part was not a mispronunciation but simply crude and inappropriate — and yet somehow the entire speech collapsed into something deeply disrespectful despite her apparent intention to make a legitimate claim. The combination of mispronunciation and poor word choice produced results the speaker never intended.

## Wise Speech

### Maidservant's Wisdom

Having illustrated the failures of imprecise speech, the *gemara* turns to positive exemplars of *leshon chachma* — wise, refined, and circumspect expression. The first is the maidservant of Rabbi's household. When she wished to speak *bileshon chachma* — in a tasteful, indirect way — she would say: *alat nakfast bechad* — the ladle has struck the bottom of the barrel, meaning there is no wine left. *Yadu nishra lekineihem* — let the eagles fly back to their nests — time for the scholars gathered there to go home, as there is nothing left to drink.

And when she wished to convey the opposite — that they should stay, that there was wine aplenty — she would say: *ya'adi batar chaverta* — let it be removed from its companion, meaning let the stopper be pulled from the barrel. *Ve'tishkufi alat bekad* — and let the ladle float in the barrel. *Ke'ifa de'azla beyama* — like a ship sailing on the sea. Both messages — come and go — are delivered with dignity, metaphor, and a kind of poetic restraint appropriate to her station. It was not her place to directly invite or dismiss guests; so she expressed herself through images that conveyed the message without overstepping.

### Riddles

Rabbi Yossi bar Asyan, when he wished to speak in this same refined and indirect mode, would use riddles. Wanting beets with mustard, he would say: *asu li shor bamishpat, be'tur misken* — make me an ox in judgment, in a poor mountain. Translated: *shor bamishpat* in Aramaic becomes *tor din*, i.e., *tordan* — *tardin*, beets. *Tur misken*, a poor mountain, is *har dal* — *chardal*, mustard. Beets with mustard.

When he wished to inquire about an innkeeper, he would ask: *gvar pum din chai* — this man, mouth, judgment, live. *Gvar* is *ish*, *pum* is *peh*, *din* is *zeh*, *chai* is *na*: *ushpizachna* — my innkeeper.

### Abbahu's Riddle

Rabbi Abbahu's riddle language: wanting coals to be lit, he would say *asrigu lepachamim* — turn them into coals resembling *esrogim*, reddish-yellow. *Arkiu lezehavim* — spread them out like gold. *Ve'asu li shney magidei ba'alata* — and make for me two speakers in the night — two roosters that crow as the night ends. That is: light the coals, spread them out, and put up two roosters as an alarm. Some say the phrasing is *veyasu li bahen shney magidei ba'alata* — make with them two speakers of the night — a slight variant that does not substantially change the meaning.

## Word Games

### Hide-and-Seek

The rabbis said to Rabbi Abbahu: *hatzpinenu heichan Rabbi Elai tzafun* — play on words: *hatzpinenu* (show us, or perhaps conceal us) and *tzafun* (hidden) — tell us where Rabbi Elai is hiding. The *gemara* presents this as a kind of game they were playing among themselves, in which questions about one another's whereabouts were posed in riddle form — a pastime of wit and wordplay among people for whom precise and elegant language was itself a form of recreation.

### South Journey

Rabbi Abbahu responded with a carefully composed riddle: *alatz bena'arah — aharonit, acharonit, iranit — vehinehartehu*. He rejoiced in a young woman — one of Aaron, or the last, or the lively one — and she kept him awake. The play runs through *aharonit* (of Aaron, suggesting priesthood or sanctity), *acharonit* (last, perhaps a later wife), *iranit* (wakeful, lively), and *vehinehartehu* (she illumined him or kept him up). One reading of this is the literal one — he was up late with his wife. The other reading, which some prefer, is metaphorical: the *masechta* was his "other woman," a well-established metaphor for *Torah* as an intimate companion, and he spent the night absorbed in learning. Rabbi Abbahu's riddle is considerably more artful than the reply Rabbi Elai gave in turn, when asked about Rabbi Abbahu's whereabouts: *nisya'etz be'machtir* — he took counsel from the crown-giver, meaning he received *semichah* from the *Nasi* — *ve'henguiv l'Mefivoshet* — and he went south to Mephibosheth, meaning to Eretz Yisrael to learn *Torah*, since Mephibosheth is held up as the *rebbe* of David. It is a functional answer, but it lacks the elegance of what came before.

## Three Encounters

### Woman/Pe'ah

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya is quoted: *miyamai lo nitzachani adam chutz me'ishah, tinok, ve'tinoket* — in all my days, no one has ever bested me except for a woman, a young boy, and a young girl.

The woman: once I lodged with a certain innkeeper. On the first day she made me lentils, and I ate them completely — I left nothing over. The second day, same dish, and again I finished everything on my plate. On the third day, she added excessive salt, ruining the dish. When I tasted it, I pushed it aside and could not eat. She asked: *Rebbi, why are you not eating?* I said I had already eaten earlier and was not hungry. She replied: if you truly were not hungry, you should have left over some bread and saved your appetite for the main dish. That explanation does not hold.

But then she pressed the real point: *shema lo hinachta pe'ah barishonim* — perhaps you failed to leave *pe'ah* on your plate on the previous days? There was a *minhag*, referred to here by the same term as the agricultural *pe'ah*, of leaving a small portion of food on one's plate. *Rashi* explains the purpose: so that the servant who clears the plates has something to eat. The *chachamim* said: *ein meshayrin pe'ah be'ilpas* — one does not leave it in the serving pot — *aval meshayrin pe'ah be'kara* — but one does leave it on the plate. Rabbi Yehoshua had not done this. The woman's pedagogical method — deliberately salting the dish too heavily on the third day in order to create the occasion for the lesson — was itself a form of wisdom.

### Girl/Field Path

The young girl: once I was walking along a road, and there was a path that cut through a field. I was walking on it. A young girl said to me: *Rebbi, lo sadeh hi zo?* Is this not a field? I replied: is this not an established path? She said back: *listim k'moscha kevashuha* — robbers like you made it into a path. Each person who crosses the field thinking it is permissible because others have done so before them participates in the creation of an illicit path. The path was made by trespassers, and the fact that it is now well-trodden does not legitimate the trespass. The observation is as practically acute today as it was then — many a shortcut through someone's property becomes a sidewalk in precisely this fashion, each person justifying himself by the path already worn.

### Boy/Crossroads

The young boy: once I was walking and I came to a crossroads. A young boy was sitting there. I asked him: which road leads to the city? He replied: *zo ktzara va'arucha* — this one is short and long — *ve'zo arucha u'ktzara* — and this one is long and short. I took the road he described as short and long. When I reached the city, I found it ringed by gardens and orchards, and it took me a very long time to work my way around them and inside. I went back to the boy and said: did you not tell me it was short? He replied: did I not also tell you it was long? *Nashakti al rosho* — I kissed him on his head. *Ashreichem Yisrael* — praised are you, Israel — *she'kulchem chachamim gedolim atem, migdolchem ve'ad ketanchem* — for you are all great and wise, from your greatest to your smallest.

The image of *arucha she'hi ktzara, ktzara she'hi arucha* — the long road that proves to be short, the short road that proves to be long — is a metaphor with wide resonance, deployed elsewhere in *chazal* as well. What appears to be the direct path may in fact cost you more; what appears to be the longer route may in the end bring you there faster and more securely. The boy said exactly what he meant, with complete precision, and Rabbi Yehoshua's haste to take the seemingly shorter path led him astray. The lesson in *Derech Eretz* — not to rush, to listen carefully, to understand what is being told to you before acting — is delivered by a child.

---

---

# Eiruvin 54

## Bruriah & Language

### Yosi & Bruriah

The *aggadeta* of Eruvin 54 opens in the midst of a thematic discussion that grew out of the very first word of the *mishnah* — a discussion about language, precision, and economy of expression. The *gemara* picks up four lines from the bottom of 53b. Rabbi Yosi HaGlili was traveling on the road (*hava ka'azil be'orcha*) when he encountered Bruriah, the wife of Rabbi Meir, a figure renowned not only for her erudition but for her characteristic sharpness of mind.

He asked her: *be'eizeh derech nelech le'Lud* — "which path should we go to get to Lud?" It is worth noting, as an alert listener pointed out, that he phrased his question in the plural, *nelech*, which carried its own impropriety — implying that they might travel together. But Bruriah's rebuke focused on a different excess.

### Bruriah's Critique

*Glili shoteh* — stupid Galilean, she called him. The epithet is pointed: the tractate has already established that the Galileans were known for imprecision and carelessness with language, and Rabbi Yosi HaGlili was himself a Galilean. She then asked: did the sages not say *al tarbeh sichah im ha'ishah* — one should not speak excessively with a woman? (The statement appears in *Pirkei Avot*, Perek 1, Mishnah 5, attributed to Yosi ben Yochanan of Jerusalem, one of the *Zugot* — predating Rabbi Meir's era considerably.) You should have simply said *be'eizeh le'Lud* — "which way to Lud?" Two words instead of seven. You wasted words.

There is an obvious irony here that the *gemara* seems to leave deliberately unspoken: Bruriah is the one citing the prohibition against speaking excessively with women — and she is a woman whose intellectual stature makes her a peer of the sages. The ironic deployment of that statement by Bruriah herself feels intentional, a kind of witty self-awareness about her own anomalous position.

---

## Learning Aloud

### Whisper Student

Bruriah then encountered a certain student (*ashkachatih le'hahu talmida*) who was learning in a whisper (*de'hava ka garis belachisha*) — quietly, murmured, as one might study in a library. She kicked him (*batsha beih*) and rebuked him: does the verse not say *arucha vakol ushmura* — "it is arranged with everything and protected"? If the Torah is *arucha be'ramach evarim shelcha* — laid out within your 248 limbs, meaning if you engage your entire body in the act of study, then *mishtameret* — it will be retained. And if not, it will not be retained.

The specific emphasis on vocalizing — saying Torah out loud — will be developed more explicitly in the *baraitot* that follow. But Bruriah's formulation is perhaps broader: what enables Torah to be retained is a kind of full-bodied engagement, where not just the mind but the entire physical self is enlisted in the process of learning. The *shoklen*, the movement, the voice — all of it is part of how Torah becomes truly internalized.

### Undertone Student

A *tanna* taught: Rabbi Eliezer had a student who would learn in an undertone (*shehayah shoneh belachash*). Three years later, he had forgotten everything he had learned. This confirms Bruriah's point and connects directly to the earlier discussion about precision of language as a means of preserving Torah in memory: how one physically engages with learning is determinative of whether that learning endures.

### Deserving Death

A second *baraita* reports that Rabbi Eliezer had another student who was considered deserving of divine death by burning (*shenitchayav bisreifah la'Makom*). It is not entirely clear from the text how this was known. The *Maharsha* suggests the connection to a teaching that one who causes himself to forget something he has learned is liable to a form of heavenly death — so this student's failing was presumably in that domain. Nevertheless, *amru* — it was said in heaven — *hinichu lo*, give him a pass: *adam gadol shimesh*, he had attended upon and served a great rabbi, Rabbi Eliezer. The principle seems to be that serving *talmidei chachamim* carries its own profound merit, sufficient to outweigh serious spiritual liability. Whether the liability was understood as death at the hands of heaven or at the hands of man, the phrasing *nitchayev srefa la'Makom* — liable to burning before God — points clearly to the former.

### Open Your Mouth

Shmuel said to his student Rav Yehuda, whom he affectionately addressed as *Shinena* — "O sharp one" — *petach pumach ukrei*: open your mouth and read the verses. And again: *petach pumach tani* — open your mouth and speak the *mishnah*, so that it should be established within you (*ki heichi detitkayem bach*) and your life should be lengthened. The instruction is not metaphorical: do not learn in your head, do not mumble — speak it aloud. The benefit Shmuel promises is both mnemonic and metaphysical, as the *gemara* now elaborates.

### Words of Life

The verse cited is from Mishlei: *ki chayim hem lemotzeihem ul'chol besaro marpe* — "for they are life to those who find them and healing to all their flesh." The *gemara* applies a *al tikrei* reading: do not read *lemotzeihem*, "to those who find them," but *lemotzi'eihem bepeh* — "to those who bring them out through the mouth." When one actually speaks words of Torah, they become a source of life — retained in memory and productive of longevity. The movement here is from what Bruriah said about embodiment and retention all the way to the metaphysical dimension: articulating Torah with the mouth is itself a life-giving act.

---

## Enjoying Life

### Grab & Eat

Since the *gemara* has now assembled a series of things Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda, it continues with another teaching from that pair. Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda: *Shinena* — *chatof ve'echol, chatof ve'ishti* — grab and eat, grab and drink, *de'alma de'azlinan minei ke-hilula dami* — for this world that we are leaving is like a wedding party. Rashi does not soften this. What it means, Rashi says, is: do not be an ascetic. Do not deny yourself pleasure. There will be no physical pleasure in the World to Come. The opportunity to enjoy this world is here and now, like a party that eventually ends. This does not mean hedonism or the unbridled pursuit of pleasure; it means one should not adopt a life of self-denial and asceticism. The echo of *Kohelet* — "eat, drink, and be merry" — is unmistakable, and here it is presented not as a philosophical blind alley but as a genuine teaching about how to live.

### Do Good

Rav said to his student Rav Hamnuna: *beni, im yesh lecha heitiv lach* — my son, if you have the means, do good for yourself. Buy yourself nice clothing, good food, pleasant furnishings. Don't deny yourself. *She'ein bish'ol ta'anug* — there is no pleasure waiting in the depths, and *ein lamaves hitmahmeha* — death does not tarry. You may not have the opportunity later; do not defer gratification on the assumption that tomorrow will come.

And if one argues: *aniach livni choki* — I want to leave my wealth to my children — Rav responds: *bish'ol mi yagid lecha* — who will tell you in the depths whether your children made use of it? *Bnei adam domim le'isvei hasadeh* — people are like the grass of the field, *halalu notzetzim vehalalu novlim* — some sprout and some wither. Who knows whether one's children will live to benefit?

This is a notably frank teaching, and the lecturer rightly observes that it resonates with several passages in *Kohelet* — passages we typically read as Shlomo's philosophical explorations of paths eventually abandoned. Here, however, the same themes are presented as positive guidance: do not go to the extreme of total self-denial, neither for the sake of the World to Come nor for the sake of an inheritance. *Chazal* speak elsewhere of the importance of leaving something to one's children; the point here is not to abandon that value but to guard against the opposite excess of denying oneself everything present.

---

## Torah Medicine

### Body Cures

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught: if one is walking on the road with no companion (*ein lo levayah*), which is dangerous, one should engage in Torah study, for the verse says *ki livyat chen hem* — they are a gracious accompaniment. If one has a headache, one should study Torah — *ki livyat chen hem l'roshecha*, they are like an ornament for your head. If one has a sore throat — Torah, for *va'anakim l'gargerotecha*, like a necklace around your throat. If one has a stomachache — Torah, for *rif'ut tehi l'sharecha*, healing for your navel. If your bones are weary — Torah, for *v'shikui l'atzmotecha*, strengthening for your bones. If your whole body aches — Torah, for *ul'chol besaro marpe*, it heals all your flesh.

The *Maharsha* notes some tension between this *gemara* and the principle elsewhere stated that *ein mitrap'in b'divrei Torah* — one may not use Torah as a medical remedy. He suggests that this passage should be understood either as a metaphysical statement — Torah protects and heals through a supernatural mechanism — or as a more psychological one: when a person immerses fully in Torah study with whole-body engagement, as Bruriah described, the focus becomes so complete that headaches and bodily discomforts cease to register. The practical or metaphysical mechanism is not made explicit. What is clear is that the theme continues: Torah is meant to permeate the entire body, not to remain a merely cerebral activity.

### Human vs Divine

Rabbi Yehuda the son of Rabbi Chiya elaborated: *bo ure'eh shelo k'middat haKadosh Baruch Hu middat basar vadam* — come and see that the way of God differs from the way of flesh and blood. A human physician gives a patient medicine that may help one ailment but harm another — what is good for the liver may be bad for the eye. But God gave Israel the Torah as *sam chayim l'chol gufo* — a medicine of life for the entire body, as the verse says *ul'chol besaro marpe*. It is not a remedy effective for one part and dangerous for another; it is beneficial throughout.

### Belly & Lips

Rabbi Ami asked: what is the meaning of the verse *ki na'im ki tishmerem bevitcha, yikonu yachdav al sefatecha* — "for they are pleasant when you keep them in your belly; they shall be established together on your lips"?
