When are words of Torah pleasant? When you keep them in your belly — when you internalize them. And when do you succeed in keeping them in your belly? When they are arranged on your lips — when you speak them aloud. Again the pattern: verbalization is not the goal in itself but the means by which Torah becomes genuinely internal, truly part of one's body.

### Joy in Speaking

Rabbi Zeira derived a similar principle from a different verse: *simcha le'ish bema'aneh fiv, vedavar be'ito mah tov* — "a joy to a person is in the response of his lips, and a matter spoken in its time, how good is it." When does a person have joy? When there is response on his lips — when the Torah is expressed through his speech, which both internalizes it and brings genuine satisfaction. An alternative formulation (*lashon acher*) takes the first half of the verse as a unit: joy comes when something is said in its proper time. Rashi offers two readings of this: either that one's learning is appropriate to the season of the year (studying *Hilchos Pesach* on Pesach, etc.), or more broadly that the learning is somehow fitting for the moment.

Rabbi Yitzchak derived the same principle from yet another verse: *ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od, beficha uvelevavecha la'asoto* — "for the matter is very close to you, in your mouth and in your heart to do it." When is it close to you — when do you truly own it? When it is on your lips and in your heart to act upon it. The addition here goes slightly beyond verbalization: it includes the commitment to act, the *uvelevavecha la'asoto*, which is itself a dimension of how Torah becomes embodied.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava raised a contradiction within a single verse: *ta'avat libo natata lo, va'areshet sefatav bal manata selah* — "You have given him the desire of his heart, and the expression of his lips You have not withheld, forever." The first half implies that it is sufficient to desire something internally — God gives it. The second half implies that one must express it through the lips. These appear to conflict.

Rava's resolution: *zacha* — if one merits it, then *ta'avat libo natata lo* — the desire of his heart is given even without verbal expression. *Lo zacha* — if one does not merit it, then one must reach *va'areshet sefatav bal manata selah* — one must actually verbalize and exert effort to receive what is desired. Rashi, notably, does not read this in the context of *tefilla* but in purely this-worldly terms: some fortunate people have good things fall into their lap without effort, while others must labor strenuously for what they seek. Why one person merits the former and another the latter is left unexplained — that is simply how it is.

The *gemara* here adds a teaching from the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: wherever the Torah uses the words *netzach*, *selah*, or *va'ed*, it connotes absolute permanence — *ein lo hefsek olami*, no cessation whatsoever. This is demonstrated through verses where each of these words appears in parallel with *olam*, confirming that all three carry the meaning of "forever."

---

## Student Virtues

### Necklace

Rav Elazar asked: what is the meaning of the verse *va'anakim legargrotacha* — "and a necklace around your throat"? If a person makes himself like a necklace — *sharaf al hatzavar*, loose around the neck rather than a choker — and *venireh ve'eino nireh*, sometimes visible and sometimes not, then *talmudo mitkayem beyado* — his Torah learning will be established in his hand. And if not, it will not.

What does it mean to be visible and not visible? Rashi offers an interesting reading: a man wearing a necklace may have his beard cover it, so it is not always prominently on display. Applied to the Torah scholar, the point seems to be twofold: be easy and undemanding in your interactions with others, not choking those around you, and spend much of your time sequestered in the *beit midrash* rather than constantly out in public. The person who is relaxed and not always demanding to be seen is the one whose Torah will endure.

### Flowerbed

Rav Elazar continued: what is the meaning of *lechayav ka'arugat habosem* — "his cheeks are like a flowerbed of fragrance"? If a person makes himself like a flowerbed (*arugah*) upon which *shehakol dashim bah* — everyone walks, everyone tramples — and like fragrance, *shekol mitbashmim bah* — everyone wants to be near it and enjoy its scent — meaning: if you are not haughty, not demanding of your own honor (*kavod*), not *makpid*, and you are genuinely pleasant and desirable to those around you — then *talmudo mitkayem*, your learning will be established. And if not, it will not.

The lecturer flags this as a genuinely puzzling connection. Unlike the straightforwardly practical advice about speaking aloud or reviewing what one has learned, the link between humility and *talmudo mitkayem* is not self-evident on a practical level. There are surely haughty scholars who sit alone in their rooms and retain their Torah. The *gemara* seems here to be framing this more as a dimension of divine reward — that the quality of character one brings to learning is itself part of what sustains it — rather than as a mechanistic causal claim.

### Stone

Rav Elazar again: the verse *luchot even* — the tablets of stone — if one reads *luchot* as *lechayav*, one's cheeks (or more broadly, one's manner of speech in Torah), and makes those *ke'even zu she'eina nimcheit* — like stone that is not worn away — meaning one constantly speaks in Torah, one's learning is never eroded, never interrupted — then *talmudo mitkayem beyado*. Rashi confirms: the point is constant engagement in speaking and reviewing Torah, so that it never fades from one's lips and is therefore never worn away.

### Broken Tablets

The same Rav Elazar extended the verse in a more sweeping direction: *charut al haluchot* — engraved on the tablets. *Ilmalei lo nishtabru luchot harishonot, lo nishtachacha Torah miYisrael* — had the first tablets not been broken, Torah would never have been forgotten. The tablets as stone are a symbol of permanence, and Rav Elazar understands them symbolically: when they were engraved, Torah was meant to be permanently inscribed — not only in stone but in the minds and souls of Israel. The breaking of the tablets introduced, in some metaphysical sense, the reality of forgetting. This does not refer merely to individual students who forget their learning, as one listener noted; Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds that had the tablets not been broken, *ein kol uma u'lashon sholetet bahen* — no other nation would ever have had dominion over Israel. The breaking of the tablets was the first great national sin, and as this week's *parasha*, *Behar-Bechukotai*, makes clear, sin leads to *galus*. The possibility of exile entered history precisely at the moment the tablets shattered — indeed, the tablets were broken at the very moment the Torah was first given, so that fallibility and its consequences arrived together with the gift itself.

The *gemara* adds: *al tikrei charut ela cheirut* — do not read "engraved" (*charut*) but "freedom" (*cheirut*). Had the tablets never been broken, the Torah would have represented complete freedom from subjugation by other nations.

---

## Wilderness Gift

### Rav Matna

Rav Matna asked: what is the meaning of the verse *umimidbar matana* — "and from the wilderness, a gift" — from the song of the well? If a person makes himself like the wilderness, *shehakol dashim bo* — that everyone tramples upon it, for the wilderness is open to all and no one honors it or protects it — then *talmudo mitkayem beyado*, his Torah learning will be established in his hand, and moreover the Torah will be given to him as a *matana*, a gift. Humility — the willingness to be like open, trampled ground — is the condition under which Torah is truly received.

### Rava Explains

On *Erev Yom Kippur*, Rava — the son of Rav Yosef bar Chama — went to appease Rav Yosef, with whom he had a quarrel. Finding Rav Yosef's attendant preparing a cup of wine, Rava took over and mixed it himself, exactly as Rav Yosef preferred. Rav Yosef, who was blind, recognized the mixture and said: it tastes just like the way Rava the son of Rav Yosef bar Chama used to mix it. Rava revealed himself — *ana hu*, it is I — and Rav Yosef told him: don't sit down until you explain these verses to me. What is the meaning of *umimidbar matana, umimatana Nachaliel, umiNachaliel Bamoth, umiVamoth Hagai*?

Rava explained: if a person makes himself like the wilderness that everyone tramples, the Torah is given to him as a gift — *umiMidbar Matana*. Once it is given as a gift, God becomes his inheritance — *umiMatana Nachaliel*. Once God is his inheritance, he rises to greatness — *umiNachaliel Bamoth*. But if he then becomes haughty — *ve'im megis libo* — God brings him low, *umiVamoth Hagai*, from the heights to the valley. And if he then does *teshuvah*, God raises him up again — *kol ge yinnase*, all the valleys will be lifted.

The lecturer observes that there is likely a subtext running beneath this exchange. Was Rava confessing that he himself had acted with excessive pride and was now doing *teshuvah* — and was that the meaning of the reconciliation? Or was he perhaps subtly directing the interpretation toward Rav Yosef, suggesting that one who holds a grudge may be too *makpid* on his own *kavod*? The text leaves this deliberately open. What is clear is that Rav Yosef himself invited the interpretation, so the conversation is doing double work: reconciling a personal dispute while expounding a teaching about humility and its consequences.

---

## Torah Metaphors

### Fig Tree

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: what is the meaning of *notzer te'ena yochal pirya* — "one who tends a fig tree will eat its fruit"? Why is Torah compared to a fig tree? Because figs do not all ripen simultaneously: anytime you reach into a fig tree and feel around, you will find ripe figs — perhaps hidden, requiring searching, but always there. So too Torah: *kol zman she'adam hoge bahen motze bahen ta'am* — the more one immerses in Torah, deeply contemplating and analyzing it, the more one finds reason and meaning.

This marks a subtle shift in the *gemara*'s emphasis. The bulk of the discussion until this point has concerned *talmudo mitkayem* — retention and memory. What you do to internalize Torah, to keep it from being forgotten. Here the *gemara* moves toward a different dimension: understanding. The more you delve into Torah, the more it yields. It is not merely a matter of remembering what you learned; it is an inexhaustible source of insight for those who search it.

### Doe

Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani asked: why is Torah compared to a doe (*ayelet ahavim v'ayelet chen*)? Because the doe (*rachmah tzar*) — and the *gemara* uses physiological language here quite explicitly — is always desired by its mate. So too, *divrei Torah chavivin al lomdeihem bechol sha'ah v'sha'ah kisha'ah rishonah* — words of Torah are beloved to those who study them at every moment just as at the first moment. Torah does not grow stale or tiresome for the devoted learner; every encounter with it is like the first.

The lecturer acknowledges that the metaphor is striking — even jarring — in its physicality, and notes the student observation that this is exactly the kind of image Bruriah might have objected to. But the point being illustrated is a serious one, connecting back to the teaching *asher anochi metzavecha hayom* — that each day Torah should feel as fresh as the day it was given (*bechol yom vayom yihyu b'einecha kachadashim*). The earlier discussion spoke of how one retains what one has learned; here the *gemara* speaks of how, if one truly throws oneself into Torah, it never loses its freshness or power.

The verse continues: *va'ayelet chen* — and she who lifts favor — meaning that Torah *shemaalet chen al lomdeha*, it causes those who study it to find favor in the eyes of others.

### Breast

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba continued with the next part of the verse: *dadeha yeravucha bechol et* — "her breasts will satisfy you at all times." Why is Torah compared to a breast? Just as an infant who nurses on a breast — who handles it and suckles from it — always finds milk, so too with Torah: *kol zman she'adam hoge bahen motze bahen ta'am* — every time a person immerses in Torah, he finds nourishment. The same principle as the fig tree, now expressed through a different natural image — this one shifting from the erotic register to the maternal, to the nourishment of an infant by its mother.

---

## Torah Metaphors (II)

### Elazar Passion

The verse concludes: *be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid* — "in its love you will constantly be intoxicated." What does this passionate attachment look like in practice? The *gemara* cites Rabbi Elazar ben Padat as its example. They used to say about him: he would sit and engage in Torah in the lower marketplace of Tzippori while his cloak lay forgotten in the upper marketplace. He was so consumed by his learning — so *meshugah* for Torah — that he was entirely oblivious to his surroundings and possessions. And a *baraita* adds: once someone came along and found the cloak, thinking to take it for himself, and found a serpent (*saraf*) inside — God was protecting the garment so that it would be there when Rabbi Elazar eventually returned for it.

---

## Scholars Classes

### White Donkeys

A *tanna* from the school of Rav Anan taught: what is the meaning of the verse from *Shirat Devorah* (*Shoftim*): *rochvei atonot tzechorot, yoshvei al midin, veholechi al derech sichu* — "those who ride on white donkeys, who sit upon *midin*, and those who walk on the road have spoken"?

*Rochvei atonot* — those who ride on donkeys — these are *talmidei chachamim* who travel from city to city and from province to province to learn Torah. *Tzechorot* — white — they make Torah as clear as the noon-day sun (*katzahorayim*); through their effort and dedication, Torah is clarified and illuminated. *Yoshvei al midin* — reading *midin* as *din* — these are those who sit in judgment and render a true ruling (*din emet la'amito*): Torah is not merely learned but applied. *Holechi al derech* — those who walk on the path — these are *ba'alei mikra*, masters of the written text; they are on the right path. *Sichu* — those who speak — these are *ba'alei Talmud*, masters of Talmud, *shekol sichatan divrei Torah* — for whom all conversation consists of words of Torah.

The progression here is significant. *Mikra* is the foundation; *mishnah* is knowing and transmitting the law; *Talmud* — meaning not the compiled tractate but the enterprise of analysis — is the capacity to penetrate and investigate. And the mark of a true *ba'al Talmud* is that the analysis has permeated his entire being, so that *kol sichato divrei Torah*: there is no idle speech, because his mind is always engaged in the substance of Torah. This is the culmination of the *gemara*'s long discussion about embodying Torah in the whole body — the person whose entire verbal life is Torah.

---

## Repetition

### Hunter Metaphor

Rav Shizbi said in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: what is the meaning of *lo yachroch remiyah tzeido* — the sly one will not char his catch? Reading *yachroch* as a combination of *lo yichyeh velo ya'arich yamim* — the deceptive hunter will not live long and will not have length of days. And who is the deceptive hunter? Rashi understands this as someone who learns a great deal but does not review (*chazer*). All that accumulation is deceptive — perhaps even self-deceptive — if it is never consolidated. It will not pay off.

### Break Wings

Rav Sheshet reads the same verse more positively: the crafty hunter — *tzeid haramai* — if he is truly clever about his catch, *yachroch* — he will be able to preserve it. And how is one crafty about retaining what one has learned? When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael* he offered a parable: it is like a hunter who catches birds. If after catching the first one he immediately breaks its wings — does something to fix it in place — then when he pursues the second bird, the first one stays. *Ve'im lav ein mishtamer* — if he does not, it will not be kept. After learning a piece of Torah, do something to break its wings — review it, repeat it — so that it cannot fly away before you go on to the next thing.

### Bundles Warning

Rav Sachora said in the name of Rav Huna: what is the meaning of *hon mehevel yimat, vekoveitz al yad yirbeh* — "wealth gathered by vanity will be diminished, and one who gathers hand by hand will increase"? Reading *hevel* as *chavila* — a bundle: if a person makes his Torah into bundles upon bundles, piling on more and more without pausing to internalize what he has already accumulated, *mitma'et* — it will diminish, it will be lost. But *vekoveitz al yad* — if one gathers slowly, hand by hand, piece by piece — *yirbeh*, it will increase and be retained.

### Rava's Critique

Rava stated: *yad'u rabanan lehai milta ve'avru alah* — the rabbinic students know this principle and ignore it anyway. It is always more appealing to press forward to the next page than to slow down and review what has just been learned. The observation drew a pointed remark from the room about the *Daf Yomi* cycle — if any context makes this critique vivid, it is that one. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, however, testified: *ana avidtah* — I actually did it the right way, learning slowly with review, *vekayma beyadai* — and it was established in my hands. The method works.

---

## Sinai Transmission

### Order at Sinai

The *gemara* asks: *keitzad seder mishnah* — what was the order of the *mishnah*, meaning how was the Torah transmitted when God gave it at *Har Sinai*? Moshe received the Torah from God. Aaron then entered and Moshe taught him his portion (*shanah lo Moshe pirko*). Aaron then sat to Moshe's left — not to his right, because sitting on someone's right when there is no one at his left implies a degree of presumptuousness. Aaron's sons then entered, and Moshe taught them; Elazar sat to Moshe's right (since Aaron was at his left) and Itamar to Aaron's left. Rabbi Yehuda maintains that once there was someone to sit at Moshe's left, Aaron moved to Moshe's right. The elders then entered and Moshe taught them. Finally all of Israel entered and Moshe taught them as well.

The result: Aaron heard the material four times, Aaron's sons three, the elders twice, and all of Israel once. Moshe then stepped back, and Aaron repeated the teaching; Aaron's sons then taught it; then the elders taught it to everyone. By the end of the day, everyone had heard the material at least four times.

### Four Times Rule

From this, Rabbi Elazar derived: *chayav adam lishnot letalmido arba pe'amim* — a person is obligated to teach his student four times. The *kal vachomer* is straightforward: if Aaron, who learned from Moshe, who learned from God (*mipi ha-Gevurah*), required four repetitions before the material was truly his — how much more so an ordinary student learning from an ordinary teacher?

### Akiva Teaching

Rabbi Akiva adds a further dimension: *minayin she-chayav adam lishnot letalmido ad she-yilmadennu* — how do we know that one must teach until the student actually learns, however many repetitions that requires? From *ve-lamdah et bnei Yisrael* — "teach it to the children of Israel," without limit. The *Maharsha* understands Rabbi Akiva as rejecting the idea that four repetitions is a fixed, fulfillable obligation; rather, you teach until they know it.

Moreover: *minayin ad she-tehei sedurah befihem* — how do we know the material must be *arranged* in the student's mouth, not merely vaguely known? From *simah befihem* — "place it in their mouths." And: *minayin she-chayav le-har'ot lo panim* — how do we know one must not only transmit the text but explain and illuminate it, which is the function of the *gemara* relative to the *mishnah*? From *ve-eleh hamishpatim asher tasim lifnehem* — "these are the judgments which you shall place before them," like a set table, as the famous Rashi reads it. Teaching is not complete with four recitations. The student must be able to say it back; must be able to articulate it clearly; and must understand it.

### Moshe's Method

A question arises: why did Moshe not simply teach each group four times himself, so that Aaron would hear it four times directly from Moshe, the sons four times from Aaron, and so on down the chain? The *gemara* answers: *kedei lachlok kavod le-Aaron* — to give honor to Aaron, to the sons, and to the elders. By stepping back and allowing each tier to teach the next, Moshe ensured that the transmission of Torah carried dignity for all of its transmitters.

But a further question presses: why not have Aaron enter and hear it four times straight from Moshe, then the sons enter and hear it four times straight from Aaron? The *gemara* responds: *keivan deMoshe mipi hagevurah gamar, mistayeia milta* — since Moshe himself had received the Torah directly from God, there is a *siata d'shmaya*, a divine assistance, that accompanies Moshe's teaching. The people benefit from hearing it from Moshe himself; the very fact that he received it from the mouth of the Almighty lends his transmission a quality that carries through to those who receive it from him directly.

---

---

# Eiruvin 55

## Teaching & Repetition

### Aharon's Position

The daf opens by picking up a discussion from the bottom of 54b concerning the transmission of Torah from Moshe to Aharon and the broader question of how many times one must repeat a teaching. Having established the view of Rabbi Akiva — that the obligation is not limited to a fixed number but extends until the student actually knows the material — the *gemara* now asks: *keman azla ha detanya*, whose position does the following *baraita* accord with?

The *baraita* in question concerns the seating arrangement of Aharon relative to Moshe. Rabbi Yehuda had maintained that *le'olam Aharon limin Moshe chozer* — Aharon always returned to Moshe's right whenever another person was available to occupy the left. The *gemara* now asks whether a related teaching about walking arrangements reflects the view of Rabbi Yehuda exclusively, or whether the Sages agree as well. The *baraita* states: *sheloshah she'hayu mehalchim baderech* — three people walking together should arrange themselves so that the teacher (*rav*) is in the middle, the more senior student on his right, and the less senior on his left. The logic assumes that the right side connotes greater honor.

The *gemara* asks: *leima Rabbi Yehuda velo Rabbanan* — is this the view of Rabbi Yehuda alone? After all, the Sages maintained that Aharon remained on Moshe's left even after another person was present. The *gemara* responds: *afilu teima Rabbanan* — even the Sages agree in principle that the more important person belongs on the right. Their leniency with Aharon was *mishum tircha de-Aharon* — so as not to inconvenience him by requiring him to get up and switch sides once he had already settled on the left. The normative rule, however, is that the right side is the place of honor. The basis for this arrangement is rooted in the verse *lev chacham liyemino velev kesil lismolo* — "the heart of the wise is to his right, and the heart of a fool to his left." These positional conventions function as social signifiers of respect — not unlike other *halakhic* expressions of *kavod* such as *lifnei seiva takum* — and while they may appear to be mere etiquette, once established, they carry genuine normative weight.

### Rav Preida's Story

The *gemara* then relates the celebrated story of Rav Preida and his student. Rav Preida had a particular student whom he had to teach every lesson *arba mea zimnei* — four hundred times — before the material was retained. One day, a messenger arrived informing Rav Preida that he was needed for a *mitzvah* matter. He told the messenger to wait, and proceeded to teach the lesson the requisite four hundred times — yet this time the student still could not absorb it.

Rav Preida asked him: *mah idna maishana* — why is today different? The student replied that from the moment he heard Rav Preida had been called away for a *mitzvah*, he could not concentrate: *ascha lei da'ati* — his mind was distracted, and every moment he thought, *hashta kai mar* — "he is about to leave." Rav Preida reassured him — set aside that concern, I am here — and then taught him the lesson another four hundred times, *arba mea zimnei achrinei*, until the student finally mastered it.

### Heavenly Voice

Upon completing this second set of four hundred repetitions, *nafka bat kol* — a heavenly voice went forth — and offered Rav Preida a choice: either he would be granted four hundred additional years of life, *deleispu lach arba mea shani*, or he and his entire generation would merit *olam haba*. This is, in a sense, a question with only one correct answer. Rav Preida chose the latter: *de-nizku ana ve-darai l'alma de-atei* — "let me and my generation merit the World to Come." The *gemara* concludes that the Holy One, Blessed be He, then granted him both — *tenu lo zu ve-zu* — because he had chosen the more selfless option. This narrative powerfully illustrates the theme of the entire passage: the extraordinary self-sacrifice a teacher must be prepared to make to ensure his students truly acquire what they are taught.

---

## Signs & Memory

### Simanim Concept

Rav Chisda teaches: *ein Torah niknet ela be-simanim* — Torah is acquired only through *simanim*, signs or mnemonics. The support he cites is the verse *simah be-fihem* — "place it in their mouths" — read not as *simah* but as *simanah*, "its signs." The principle is that the retention of Torah depends on the active construction of memory aids and associative markers. This connects naturally to the foregoing discussion about the need to repeat a lesson many times: repetition and *simanim* are two sides of the same pedagogical coin.

### Rav Tachlifa

Rav Tachlifa from the west — that is, from *Eretz Yisrael* — heard Rav Chisda's teaching and reported it to Rabbi Abbahu. Rabbi Abbahu replied: in Babylonia you derive this idea from that verse; we derive it from a different one: *hatzivi lach tziyunim* — "set up markers for yourself." The word *tziyun* is understood in the sense of a sign or signpost, as it appears in the verse *ra'ah etzem adam u-vanah etzlo tziyun* — "they saw a human bone and built a marker by it." Rabbi Elazar derives the same principle from yet another verse: *emor la-chochmah achoti at* — "say to wisdom: you are my sister" — reading *moda* as a *muda*, an informer or sign: *asu moda'im la-Torah*, make signs for the Torah.

Rava then adds a reading of his own: *asu mo'adim la-Torah* — make fixed times for Torah, reversing the letters of *muda* to yield *mo'ed*. Rashi explains this as an instruction to the teacher: *kiv'u itim l'talmideichem she-yihyu yode'im et lavo ve-lishnot* — establish fixed times so that students know when to come and review. The analogy is precisely that of *Daf Yomi*: a fixed, predictable schedule creates the focused mindset necessary for proper learning.

### Fixed Times

This theme of fixed times flows into a teaching of Rav Dimi bar Chama (found at the top of 55a), which expounds the verse *lo va-shamayim hi ve-lo me-ever la-yam hi* — "it is not in the heavens, nor is it across the sea." The literal meaning implies that Torah is accessible and need not be sought in remote places. But Rav Dimi reads the verse as teaching the *extent* of one's obligation: *she'im ba-shamayim hi, atah tzarich la-alot achareha* — were it in the heavens, you would be required to ascend after it; *ve-im me-ever la-yam hi, atah tzarich la-avor achareha* — were it across the ocean, you would be required to cross after it. The point is one of absolute commitment: even in the most extreme hypothetical, the pursuit of Torah would be obligatory. Rashi frames this as *l'harim be-tachbulot kedei she-yitkayem ha-Torah be-lomdeha* — to be crafty and resourceful in every device to ensure that Torah is retained by those who study it.

Rava then offers a homiletical reading of the same verse directed at a different failure mode: *lo timtza be-mi she-magbi'ah da'ato aleha ka-shamayim* — Torah will not be found among those who elevate themselves as high as the heavens in arrogance; *ve-lo timtza be-mi she-marchiv da'ato aleha ka-yam* — nor will it be found among those who spread themselves as broadly as the sea, rushing over more and more ground without proper review (*chazarah*). Rabbi Yochanan adds: *lo timtza begassei ruach* — it will not be found among the haughty; *lo timtza lo be-sachranin ve-lo be-tagrin* — nor among merchants, whether local traders or those who travel from city to city, whose professional demands leave them without the time and focus Torah requires.

What is distinctive about this entire passage — more so than other passages on the importance of *talmud Torah* — is its sustained practical focus: how do you remember what you learn? The answers given are repetition, oral recitation, *simanim*, fixed times, and the cultivation of humility. The moral dimension — that haughtiness and restlessness are incompatible with Torah retention — is woven into the same discussion as the practical pedagogical advice.

---

## City Boundaries

### Baraita Overview

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishnah* and the *halacha* of *me'avrin et ha'arim* — how one extends or expands the effective boundaries of a city for purposes of *eruvin* and *Shabbat tchumin*. The *gemara* introduces a *baraita* that systematically addresses various city configurations:

If the city is *arucha* — long — you leave it as it is. If it is *agula* — circular — *osim la zaviyot meruba*, you square it off and give it corners. If it is *meruba'at* — already square — you do not add corners. If it is wide on one side and narrow on the other (a trapezoid), *ro'in otah k'ilu hi shaveh* — you treat it as though it were uniform, converting it to a rectangle. If one house juts out (*pagum*), or two houses jut out, *ro'in otam k'ilu chut matuach aleihem* — you treat it as though a string were stretched from them — and measure the 2,000-*amah tchum* from that extended line. If the city is shaped like a bow (*keshet*) or like a *gam* (the Greek letter gamma), *ro'in otah k'ilu hi mele'ah batim u-chatzeirot* — you treat the open interior space as though it were filled with houses and courtyards — and then measure 2,000 *amah* outward.

### Long Cities

The *gemara* notes that the ruling about a long city seems obvious — of course you leave it as it is. The *gemara* responds: *lo tzricha de'aricha u-ktina* — the point addresses a city that is not merely long but long and very narrow, like a thin rectangle. One might have thought that in such a case the city should be made square by giving it width equal to its length. The *baraita* therefore teaches that one does not go that far: you make a rectangle around the city, not a square.

### Square Cities

Similarly, the ruling that a city already square needs no further adjustment seems obvious. The *gemara* explains: *lo tzricha de-murbaat ve-lo merabaat be-ribua olam* — the case is one where the city is indeed rectangular but its sides do not align with the compass points. One might have thought that in such a case the city should be rotated or adjusted to align with *ribua olam* — the four cardinal directions — and in so doing gain additional corner area. The *baraita* therefore teaches that since the city is already the right shape, no such adjustment is made. The benefit of squaring off according to the compass points applies only when the city needs to be squared off in the first place; a city that is already rectangular does not get to re-square itself by the compass points.

The practical implication is significant. A city whose rectangle happens not to align with the cardinal directions would still have its *tchum* measured outward from its actual walls, without the benefit of the corner areas that would be gained by rotating the square to the compass. Conversely, a city that requires squaring off — say, a circular city — gets squared off according to the compass points and thereby gains those corners.

### Jutting Houses

The *baraita*'s mention of one and then two jutting houses is analyzed by the *gemara*. One jutting house makes sense as a case; why add two? The *gemara* explains: *lo tzricha mishtei ruchos* — the case of two houses addresses houses jutting in *opposite directions*. One might have thought that a single jutting house in one direction is sufficient to extend the *tchum* in that direction, but two small houses jutting in opposite directions — neither of which is the main city proper — would not both be honored as extensions. The *baraita* teaches that both extensions are recognized, even though each jutting house is only a single structure at the periphery.

### Bow-Shaped Cities

The rule about *keshet*- and *gam*-shaped cities treats the entire open interior space as if it were filled with houses. This is essentially an extreme generalization of the jutting-house rule: in the bow-shaped city, there are so many effective "jutting outs" that the entire concave interior is treated as built-up. One draws the bounding rectangle from the outermost points and measures 2,000 *amah* from there in each direction. One might ask whether the interior space needs to be buildable — whether, for instance, a mountain or body of water in the center would affect the analysis. The *gemara* does not address buildability per se, focusing instead on the critical question of how large the interior space may be before the city loses its unified character.

---

## Unifying Cities

### Rav Huna's Rule

Rav Huna now introduces a critical limiting principle for the *keshet* configuration. *Im yesh bein shenei rosheha pachas me-arba'as alafim amah* — if the distance between the two tips of the bow is less than 4,000 *amah*, then *modidin la min ha-yeter* — the *tchum* is measured from the chord (the *yeter*), treating the interior as filled. If the gap between the tips exceeds 4,000 *amah*, then the city cannot be treated as unified in this way, and each house must be measured individually.

The logic of 4,000 *amah* as the threshold is that for two points to be considered within a single unified city, it must be possible for a resident of one endpoint to reach the other within the standard *Shabbat tchum* of 2,000 *amah*. Each tip of the bow contributes its 2,000 *amah*, and if they overlap, the interior is treated as one. If the tips are more than 4,000 *amah* apart, no overlap is possible and the unified treatment fails.

Tosafot raises the question of what happens when the distance at the outermost tips exceeds 4,000 *amah* but at some point closer to the apex of the bow the distance between the two arms narrows to less than 4,000. Tosafot rules that one begins measuring from the point at which the gap first reaches 4,000 or less, and from that point downward the city is treated as unified. Others disagree.

### Broken Walled City

A seemingly contradictory ruling of Rav Huna is then adduced. Rav Huna had also stated: *chomas ir she-nifretza be-me'ah arba'im ve-achas ve-shlish* — if the wall of a city broke and there is a gap in the middle of 141 and one-third *amah*, the city can still be considered unified. This figure of 141 and one-third is far smaller than 4,000, raising an apparent contradiction.

The *gemara* resolves this through Rabbah bar Ulla: *kan be-ruach achas kan mishtei ruchos* — here the gap is on one side, there the separation is from two sides. In the case of the broken walled city, the city was originally unified and remains connected on three sides; the gap affects only one aspect of its continuity. In the *keshet* case, the two arms of the bow are entirely separate from each other — there is no built-up connection between them whatsoever. Because the *keshet* presents a far more radical form of disconnection, the standard for unification is set much higher, at 4,000 *amah*.

### Karpaf Buffer

The *gemara* then clarifies what Rav Huna is actually teaching with the 141-and-one-third figure, which derives from the concept of *karpaf* — the buffer zone around a city. The standard distance for determining whether an outlying house is considered part of a city is 70 and two-thirds *amah*. This figure derives from the *beit se'atayim* measurement — the area required to plant two *se'ah* — which, when expressed as a square, has a side of approximately 70 and two-thirds *amah* (the square root of 5,000 square *amot*). A house within 70 and two-thirds of the city limit is considered part of the city; beyond that distance, it is not.

When two cities are to be unified, Rav Huna rules *karpaf la-zu ve-karpaf la-zu* — each city receives its buffer of 70 and two-thirds *amah*, and if these buffers overlap (meaning the gap between the cities is 141 and one-third *amah* or less), the cities are considered unified. Chiyya bar Rav disagrees, ruling *ein notnim ela karpaf echad li-shneihem* — only a single *karpaf* of 70 and two-thirds is shared between them; the cities must be within 70 and two-thirds of each other to be combined. The *gemara* explains why Rav Huna found it necessary to state this rule in both contexts — the broken walled city and the two separate cities — since each case might have been treated differently on its own terms. In the broken-walled city one might have been more lenient (because it once was unified); in the separate-cities case one might have been more strict (because each city needs breathing room). Both rulings are therefore necessary.

### Arc to Apex Distance

Beyond the question of the distance between the two tips of the bow, the *gemara* now asks: *ve-chama havi bein yeter la-keshet* — is there also a maximum permitted distance between the chord (the *yeter*, the straight line connecting the two tips) and the apex of the arc? Even if the tips are within 4,000 *amah* of each other, could the arc extend so far outward that the city effectively loses its unified character?

Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules: *alpayim amah* — the distance from the chord to the apex may not exceed 2,000 *amah*. His reasoning is that the houses at the tips of the bow each extend 2,000 *amah* into the interior, and if the apex is more than 2,000 *amah* from the chord, those houses cannot reach the apex, and the apex cannot be considered part of the same city as the tips.

His son Rava disagrees: *afilu yeter me-alpayim* — even if the distance exceeds 2,000 *amah*, there is no limit once the two tips are considered unified. Abaye concurs with Rava's position: *d'ee bei hadar asit derech patzin* — because one can always travel from the apex back through the built-up portions of the arc to reach any other part of the city. No point in the city is truly isolated; one can always traverse the city's actual built-up areas to get from one part to another. Once the two tips are connected at the chord level, the entire structure is unified, regardless of how far the arc extends outward.

---

## Habitation Structures

### Gedudiyot

The *gemara* introduces *gedudiyot* — ruined or partially destroyed structures — and asks whether these count as part of the city. The question is: *mai gedudiyot*? Rav Yehuda answers: *shalosh mechitzot she-ein aleihen tikrah* — three walls without a roof. Even a roofless three-walled ruin counts, because as Rashi explains, the criterion is not whether the structure is currently inhabited but whether it was built for habitation and retains the potential for habitation. The *gedudiyot* satisfy this standard.

This leads immediately to the question: what about *shtei mechitzot ve-yesh aleihen tikrah* — two walls *with* a roof? Does the presence of a roof compensate for the absence of a third wall?

### Inclusive List

To address this question, the *gemara* turns to a comprehensive *baraita* listing those structures that are *mitabrim imah* — included within the city's extended boundary — and those that are not.

The inclusive list begins with a *nefesh* — a funerary structure adjacent to a grave — provided it measures at least four *amot* by four *amot*, which is the minimum size for a habitable space (*beit dirah*). Also included: a bridge or a cemetery, provided *she-yesh bahem beit dirah* — they have a place for someone to live there; a *beit knesset* (synagogue), provided *she-yesh bah beit dirah le-chazzan* — it has a dwelling for the *chazzan* or sexton; and — strikingly — even *beit avodat kochavim*, a pagan temple, provided *she-yesh bah beit dirah le-komerim* — the priests who serve there have living quarters. The point is entirely functional: the religious character of the building is irrelevant; what matters is whether human beings live there.

The list continues: *urvot ve-otzarot she-ba-sadot* — stables and storehouses in the fields — with living quarters; *burganin she-betochah* — little huts out in the fields; and *ha-bayit she-ba-yam* — a house on the water, which Rashi understands as a house on a small island. All of these, if within 70 and two-thirds *amah* of the city, are considered part of it.

The common thread throughout is *beit dirah* — human habitation. Structures that serve functions other than dwelling — storing goods, marking graves, conducting worship — qualify only when they also contain a residential component. A cemetery is not part of the city by virtue of being a cemetery; it is part of the city by virtue of the caretaker who lives within it.

### Exclusive List

The exclusive list is, as noted, a near-perfect mirror image of the inclusive list. A *nefesh* whose walls were breached from two opposite sides does not count. A bridge or cemetery without living quarters does not count. A *beit knesset* without a *chazzan*'s residence does not count. A pagan temple without priests' quarters does not count. Stables and storehouses without living quarters do not count. A well, a ditch, a cave (*me'arah*), a wall (*geder*), a pigeon coop — all are excluded regardless of their size or structural significance. The principle is consistent: without *beit dirah*, a structure is merely a structure, not a habitation node capable of extending the city boundary.

One case that requires particular attention: *ha-bayit she-ba-sefinah* — a house on a boat. This is excluded not because no one lives in it — someone may well live aboard — but because it lacks a fixed location. The requirement is not merely habitation but habitation that is geographically anchored. A dwelling that moves cannot serve as a fixed extension of a city's boundary.

### Wall Requirements

The *gemara* now returns to the question raised by *gedudiyot*: two walls with a roof versus three walls without. The *baraita*'s exclusive list mentions *nefesh she-nifretza mishtei ruchoteha* — a structure with two walls breached on opposite sides — as insufficient. The *gemara* asks: *mai lav de-ika tikra* — does this mean that even with a roof, two walls are not enough? The *gemara* deflects: *lo, de-leika tikra* — it refers to a structure that also lacks a roof. The *gemara* thus leaves open the possibility that two walls *with* a roof would qualify. The question is not fully resolved from this passage alone.

### Water & Caves

The *bayit she-ba-yam* raises a further question: *le-mai chazi* — what purpose does such a house serve? If it is a tiny island, presumably no one actually lives there. Rav Pappa answers: *bayit she-asui lifnot bo kelim she-ba-sefinah* — a structure used to offload cargo from boats. Even this functional use — facilitating the activity of those passing on the water — can qualify as a form of *beit dirah* in context, provided the structure is built for human use and occupancy.

Finally, the *gemara* confronts an apparent contradiction regarding caves. The *baraita*'s exclusive list includes *me'arah* — a cave is not included in the city. Yet Rabbi Chiyya taught in a *baraita*: *me'arah mitaberet imah* — a cave is included. Abaye resolves this: *ki she-yesh binyan al piha* — Rabbi Chiyya is speaking of a cave that has a structure built at its entrance. But if so, the structure itself would suffice — why mention the cave at all? *Lo, tzricha le-hashlem* — the cave is needed to supplement. Rashi understands this to mean that even if the built structure is less than the minimum four *amot* by four *amot*, the cave completes the measurement, and together they constitute the required *beit dirah*. Tosafot goes further and rules more significantly: once a built structure stands at the cave entrance, the entire cave — however deep — is considered part of the city boundary, since the presence of a *beit dirah* at the entrance transforms the whole space into a habitable unit.

This principle has striking practical implications. The same logic, as discussed, appears to apply to cemeteries and bridges: once there is a dwelling within that space, the entire space — the whole cemetery, the full length of the bridge — is drawn into the city boundary. Whether this would extend to, for example, a modern tunnel with a guardhouse at its entrance, or a bridge with toll booths that function as habitable structures, are questions that remain to be explored.

---

---

# Eiruvin 56

## Permanent Structures

### City Boundary Structures

The daf begins at the bottom of 55b, continuing the discussion of which types of structures can be considered part of the boundaries of a city for purposes of *eruv techumin*. The basic principle, which Rashi reiterates consistently throughout, is that any structure made for habitation and fit for habitation counts — even if it is not currently being inhabited.

### Thatched Huts Rule

The Gemara records a ruling of Rav Huna: *yoshvei tzerifim ein modedin lahem ela mi-petach bateihem* — those who live in huts made of thatch do not have their dwellings counted as part of the city. Even if an entire settlement consists of such huts, it is not defined as a city; rather, each inhabitant is treated as an isolated individual household. The underlying assumption is that these structures are entirely non-permanent and therefore can never constitute a city, nor can they extend an existing city's boundaries.

### Desert Encampment

Rav Chisda raises an objection from the verse: *va-yachanu al ha-Yarden mi-Beit ha-Yeshimot* — "and they encamped on the Jordan from Beit ha-Yeshimot." Rabba bar bar Chana testified that he had personally seen that location by the Jordan River, and it measured three *parsaot* by three *parsaot*. Since a *parsa* is four *mil* and a *mil* is 2,000 *amot* — which is itself the measure of *techum Shabbat* — the encampment extended twelve *mil* by twelve *mil*. (This calculation is also the basis for the Rambam's position that the biblical *techum Shabbat* is twelve *mil*, not merely 2,000 *amot*.)

A *Baraita* further describes the practices of the encampment: when the people needed to relieve themselves, they would not go in front of the camp or to its sides, only behind it — since they knew the camp would not retrace its path, and they did not wish to later walk over areas they had used. The relevance to Rav Huna's ruling is clear: the Israelites lived in tents in the wilderness, structures no more permanent than thatched huts, and yet the entire encampment was considered their *machaneh* — their established settlement. How can Rav Huna say that non-permanent dwellings form no city?

### Divine Command Permanence

Rava resolves the contradiction: *diglei midbar kaamrat* — "you are speaking of the encampments in the desert." Since the Torah states *al pi Hashem yachanu ve-al pi Hashem yisau* — they encamped and traveled by God's word — their settlements are considered permanent, *ke-man de-kavi'a dami*. As long as God declared "remain," they remained, and the encampment therefore had the full legal status of a permanent settlement. This principle has a parallel in other areas of *hilchot Shabbat*, where the Gemara discusses why the *mishkan*'s construction can serve as a model for *melachot* despite the fact that it was constantly dismantled and reassembled — and the same logic applies: whenever God said "stay," it was permanent.

### Courtyards Exception

Rav Chinana bar Rav Kahana citing Rav Ashi adds an important qualification: *im yesh sham shalosh chatzerot o shenei battim, hu kevuah* — if within a settlement of thatched huts there exists a nucleus of three courtyards, each containing two permanent houses, the entire settlement acquires the status of a city. Rashi explains that the word *bayit* here, as opposed to *tzerif*, specifically denotes a permanent structure. The problem Rav Huna identified was exclusively when the entire settlement consisted of non-permanent dwellings; if even a portion of the city meets the standard definition of urban permanence — three courtyards with two permanent houses — then the thatched huts around it are also incorporated into and serve as an extension of that city.

---

## Nomadic Critique

### Nomadic Life Quality

The Gemara continues with a broader set of observations about the nature of city life, prompted by the discussion of thatched huts and nomadic existence. Rav Yehuda citing Rav declares: *yoshei tzerifin ve-ochelei midbarot, chayeihem einam chayim* — those who live in thatched huts and those who eat and travel in the wilderness, their lives are not real lives. The statement captures the sense that a nomadic existence, lacking the amenities and social stability that constitute genuine civilized life, does not qualify as genuine living.

### Fidelity Concerns

The statement continues with a harsher dimension: *nesheihem u-veneihem einam shelahem* — their wives and children are not truly theirs. The Gemara will go on to explain the concern, but the thrust of the remark is that those living nomadic lives must entertain serious suspicions about fidelity. The remark is directed primarily from the perspective of the man's concerns — his anxiety about his wife and the paternity of his children — though as the subsequent discussion makes clear, the moral exposure cuts in multiple directions.

### Graveyard Comparison

A *Baraita* corroborates and intensifies this view: Elazar Ish Birayah says that those who dwell in *tzerifin* are like those dwelling in graveyards — not a life at all. And regarding their daughters — meaning the women of such communities — he invokes an extreme verse: *arur shochev im kol behemah*, "cursed is he who lies with any animal." This is a strikingly harsh statement, and the Gemara will now seek to explain the underlying concern that motivates these judgments.

### Bathhouse Absence

The Gemara asks: *mai taama* — what is the reason for these concerns? Ulla answers: *she-ein lahem merchata'ot* — they have no bathhouses. A properly functioning city, particularly in the Roman-influenced world of the Talmud, would have public bathhouses. Without access to such facilities, people in nomadic or semi-nomadic settings have no private, regulated space for bathing.

### Mikvah Encounters

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different explanation: *mipnei shemargishim zeh lazeh bitvila* — because they become aware of one another during immersion in the *mikvah*. Rashi explains the mechanics of each concern. Regarding the absence of bathhouses: when people must bathe, they go out to the river alone, far from the settlement and without supervision — a circumstance that enables illicit encounters. Regarding the *mikvah*: because immersion is not conducted privately, it becomes known publicly that a woman has immersed, and an unscrupulous man may seize upon that knowledge to attempt seduction immediately after she emerges.

The Gemara notes that the practical difference between Ulla's and Rabbi Yochanan's views is the case of *nahara de-samich la-birta* — a river situated close to the city. In that scenario, there would still be a *mikvah* concern (Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning would apply), but not the concern about isolation and lack of privacy that grounds Ulla's explanation, since proximity to the settlement reduces the danger. The overall picture that emerges from this section is a sharp critique — from at least some *Tannaim* — of the moral consequences of nomadic or semi-nomadic life.

---

## Urban Components

### Vegetables Required

The Gemara now offers additional criteria for what constitutes a livable city. Rav Huna states: *kol ir she-ein bah yerek, ein talmid chacham rashai ladur bah* — any city that does not have vegetables available is not a place where a Torah sage should reside. The reasoning is that vegetables are an inexpensive and readily available form of sustenance, important for *talmidei chachamim* who devote the bulk of their time to study and require accessible, affordable food.

### Vegetable Health Debate

This raises an immediate question: does the Gemara mean to imply that vegetables are beneficial? A *Baraita* seems to contradict this, listing three things that increase excrement, cause one to become bent over, and diminish one's eyesight by one five-hundredth. The three items are *pat kibar* (coarse bran bread), *shechar chadash* (new mead or beer), and *yerek* (vegetables). Vegetables, then, would appear to be harmful, not beneficial.

### Specific Vegetables

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya* — it is not difficult. One teaching refers to *tuma ve-charti* — garlic and leeks — while the other refers to other vegetables. Garlic and leeks are beneficial; other vegetables may not be. Rashi initially presents the assignment one way and then reverses himself, concluding that garlic and leeks are indeed the healthful ones — which accords with the general reputation of garlic as one of the most beneficial foods.

The Gemara then cites a *Baraita* elaborating on specific cases. Garlic is a vegetable of full standing. *Krishin* (leeks) count as half a vegetable. And then there is a dispute about the radish: one tradition says *nira tzenon nira sam chayim* — seeing a radish is like seeing the elixir of life; another says *nira tzenon nira sam mavet* — it is the draught of death. The Gemara resolves this as well: *lo kashya* — one refers to the leaves, the other to the bulb itself, and additionally the effects differ depending on whether it is summer or winter.

### Topography Effects

Returning to the conditions of a livable city, Rav Yehuda citing Rav states: *kol ir she-yesh bah ma'alot u-mordot* — any city with steep inclines, a very hilly terrain, *adam u-veheimah she-bah meitim ba-chatzi yemeihem* — the people and animals in it die in the middle of their days. The Gemara immediately qualifies the hyperbole: *meitim salka daatach?* — can they literally die at half their age? Rather, *mizkinim ba-chatzi yemeihem* — they age prematurely, they become old while still in their middle years, because of the constant physical exertion demanded by the terrain. One might note the irony that contemporary sensibility would reverse this judgment entirely, viewing hilly terrain as conducive to exercise and health.

### Personal Testimony

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua provides personal testimony in corroboration: *hanei milyata de-vei Beiri ve-de-vei Narash azkunun* — the hills of Beiri and Narash, two towns, made him old. This is consistent with the principle just stated.

---

## Compass Directions

### Constellation Method

The Gemara now returns to the laws of *techumin* and addresses the procedure for squaring off a city to the cardinal directions. The ruling is: *ba le-reivah, mereiva be-reibua olam* — when squaring off a city, one aligns it to the compass points of the world. The practical significance of squaring off a city to the cardinal directions is substantial: instead of simply measuring a circle around the city, one draws a rectangle aligned to north, south, east, and west, gaining the corners and thereby extending the effective boundary considerably. A visual illustration makes this vivid — take Manhattan, square it off to the directions, and the additional area captured includes portions of Queens, Brooklyn, and New Jersey.

The directions are established by the formula *notin tzafonah le-tzafono shel olam, deromah le-deromo shel olam* — the northernmost point is set to true north, the southernmost to true south, and so forth.

### Constellation Guide

The way to identify the directions before magnetic compasses was by the constellations: *ve-simanach, egla be-tzafon* — the mnemonic is that *agala* (Ursa Major, or according to some sources Ursa Minor) is in the north, and *ve-akrav be-darom* — the scorpion constellation is in the south. According to the Soncino commentary, the scorpion is not due south but is situated in the southern sky as seen from *Eretz Yisrael*, and unlike the north star it is not always visible.

The names of the directions carry their own etymological interest: *Tzafon* (north) may derive from a root meaning "hidden," because the sun never appears there; *Darom* (south) may be read as *dar ram*, "where the sun dwells in its height," since the sun always moves toward the south for those in the Northern Hemisphere.

### Solstice Method

Rabbi Yosi offers an alternative method for those who do not know the constellations: *mereivah ke-min ha-tekufah* — one can establish the directions by means of the season and the rising and setting of the sun. *Chama yotza be-yom aroch ve-shoka'at be-yom aroch, zehu pnei tzafon* — when the sun rises on a long day (the summer solstice) and sets on a long day, the direction it comes from indicates the north. *Ve-chama yotza be-yom katzar ve-shoka'at be-yom katzar, zehu pnei darom* — on the shortest day (the winter solstice), the direction of sunrise and sunset indicates the south.

### Sun's Path

The underlying astronomical reality is as follows. At the vernal and autumnal equinoxes, the sun rises due east and sets due west. On the longer days — approaching the summer solstice — it rises from the northeast and sets in the northwest; on the shorter days — approaching the winter solstice — it rises from the southeast and sets in the southwest. If one thinks about this carefully: since the sun always moves toward the south (for those in the Northern Hemisphere), a longer path means it starts further north, hence the sunrise is more northerly on long days.

The Gemara corroborates this from the verse: *holech el darom ba-yom, ve-sovev el tzafon ba-lailah* — the sun moves toward the south during the day and circles back toward the north at night, tracing an elliptical path. The verse in *Kohelet* then says *sovev sovev holech ha-ruach* — "round and round goes the wind" — which the Gemara reads as a reference to the east and west faces, *pnei mizrach u-pnei ma'arav*, the directions that the sun sometimes traverses and sometimes goes around.

The Gemara also notes that *tekufat Tishrei* — the autumnal equinox — offers the clearest orientation: *chama yotza b'chatzi mizrach ve-shoka'at b'chatzi ma'arav* — the sun rises exactly due east and sets exactly due west. One might wonder why the tradition emphasizes the solstice method rather than the simpler vernal or autumnal equinox approach, where due east and due west are directly observable and a right angle immediately yields north and south.

### Sun Limits

Rav Mesharshaya objects that these directional methods based on the solstices are not reliable rules. A *Baraita* states: *lo yatza chama me'olam mi-keren mizrachit tzfonit* — the sun has never truly risen from the exact northeast, nor has it ever set in the exact northwest; likewise it has never risen from the exact southeast nor set in the exact southwest. This is precisely the point noted above: while the sun moves northward in summer and southward in winter, it never reaches a full 45 degrees from due east. The maximum deviation is approximately 23 degrees. Therefore, one cannot use the solstice sunrise or sunset to determine true north or south with precision, since the sun never actually reaches the northeast or southeast positions that would be required for that calculation to work.

---

## Seasonal Timing

### Four Tekufot

Shmuel, who was particularly distinguished in matters of astronomy, now presents his astronomical calculations. He states: *ein tekufat Nissan nofelet ela b'arba'ah rivei ha-yom* — the vernal equinox, *tekufat Nissan*, only ever falls at one of the four quarters of the day: either at sunrise (*tchilas ha-yom*), or at the beginning of night (sunset), or at noon (*chatzi ha-yom*), or at midnight (*chatzi ha-lailah*).

To understand this, one must grasp the four *tekufot* and their structure. The four seasonal turning points are: *Nissan* (vernal equinox), *Tammuz* (summer solstice), *Tishrei* (autumnal equinox), and *Tevet* (winter solstice). *Tevet* is the winter solstice — hence *Chanukah* always falls in the cold — and *Tammuz* is the summer solstice — hence *Shiva Asar B'Tammuz* always falls in the heat.

### Annual Shift

The reason for Shmuel's rule is the following calculation. The solar year, by the Julian reckoning that Shmuel uses, is 365 and one-quarter days. Therefore, the shift from one year's vernal equinox to the next year's vernal equinox is one day and six hours beyond exactly 52 weeks. If the vernal equinox occurred on Monday at sunrise one year, then the following year it will occur on Tuesday at noon (sunrise plus six hours). The year after that, it will fall on Wednesday at sunset. The year after that, on Thursday at midnight. And then on Friday at sunrise again. Consequently, the *tekufa* can only ever fall at sunrise, noon, sunset, or midnight — cycling through these four points year after year. This same 28-year cycle is the basis for *Birkat HaChammah*, which returns to its starting point after 28 years.

It is worth noting that Shmuel's value of 365 and one-quarter days is the Julian figure. The actual solar year is slightly less than this, which is why the Gregorian calendar introduced the correction of omitting the leap year in three out of every four century years (years divisible by 100 but not by 400). The Jewish permanent calendar, meanwhile, achieves a closer approximation of the true solar year over the 19-year cycle than the Julian calendar — a remarkable achievement.

### Tammuz Times

Having established the pattern for *tekufat Nissan*, the Gemara moves to *tekufat Tammuz*. From one *tekufa* to the next is a quarter of a year. The annual shift is one day and six hours; therefore the quarterly shift between consecutive *tekufot* is one-quarter of that, namely seven and a half hours. So *tekufat Tammuz* will always fall seven and a half hours after the corresponding *tekufat Nissan* slot. If *tekufat Nissan* can fall at midnight, then *tekufat Tammuz* can fall at midnight plus seven and a half hours, which is seven-thirty in the morning — one and a half hours into the day. The Gemara therefore states: *ein tekufat Tammuz nofelet ela o b'achat u-mechtza o b'sheva u-mechtza, bein ba-yom bein ba-lailah* — it falls either at one and a half hours or seven and a half hours, whether into the day or into the night.

### Other Tekufot

Continuing the pattern, *tekufat Tishrei* adds another seven and a half hours to the *Tammuz* slots, yielding: *nofelet o b'shalosh sha'os o b'teisha sha'os, bein ba-yom bein ba-lailah* — it falls at either three hours or nine hours into the day or night. And *tekufat Tevet* adds yet another seven and a half hours: *nofelet o b'arba u-mechtza o b'eser u-mechtza, bein ba-yom bein ba-lailah* — at four and a half or ten and a half hours into the day or night. The pattern is straightforward: each successive *tekufa* shifts by an additional hour and a half in its starting point.

### Tekufa Distances

The Gemara explicitly states the distance between one *tekufa* and the next: *tish'im ve-echad ve-sheva sha'ot u-mechtza* — 91 days, seven hours, and thirty minutes. The arithmetic confirms this: 91 times four equals 364, and seven and a half hours times four equals 30 hours, which is one day and six hours. The total is therefore 365 days and 6 hours, i.e., 365 and one-quarter days — exactly the Julian solar year.

### Tekufa Precision

Shmuel adds an astronomical observation: *ein lecha tekufat Nissan she-nofelet be-tzedek she-einah meshaberet ilanos* — whenever the vernal equinox falls under the influence of *Tzedek* (Jupiter, in the seven-planet reckoning familiar to the Talmudic sages), it invariably causes trees to be broken — presumably by severe winds. Similarly, *tekufat Tevet* never falls under *Tzedek* without the seeds drying up. These observations apply specifically when the moon or sun is in ascendancy in relation to Jupiter — a framework that belongs to the astronomical and astrological system of the Talmudic period.

---

## Squaring Method

### Square Tableaux

The Gemara now sets out the full procedure for squaring the city and the *techumin*. The *Baraita* teaches: *ha-merubeia et ha-ir, oseh otah ke-min tavla meruba'at* — when one squares off the city, one makes it into a square tableau, aligned to the cardinal directions. Then, *ve-chozer u-merubeia et ha-tchumin, ve-oseh otan ke-min tavla meruba'at* — one squares off the *techumin* as well, creating a larger square around the inner square of the city.

### Diagonal Benefit

The *Baraita* then specifies: *lo yimdod me-emtza ha-keren alpayim amah, mipnei she-hu mafsid et ha-zaviyot* — one must not measure the 2,000 *amot* at an angle from the corner, because doing so would cause one to lose the corners. The key geometric insight is this: if one measured 2,000 *amot* diagonally from a corner rather than squaring off, the resulting area would be far smaller than what one gains by squaring. Measuring straight out from each face and then completing the square captures far more territory. The additional reach afforded by the corner of a square — relative to a circle of the same radius — is the square root of two times the radius, approximately 1.4 times, which means that going diagonally one can travel some 1,200 *amot* further than going straight.

### Manhattan Example

The visual illustration captures this vividly. Take Manhattan as the city. When it is squared off to the cardinal directions rather than simply surrounded by a circle, the resulting rectangle captures significant portions of what would otherwise lie outside the boundary — parts of Queens, Brooklyn, and New Jersey. Then when the 2,000-*amot* *techum* is squared off around that rectangle, still more territory is included.

### City Gain

The *Baraita* states: *nimtzet ir mishtakeret arba me'ot amah le-kan ve-arba me'ot amah le-kan* — the city itself, by virtue of being squared off, gains 400 *amot* on each side in the corners. This assumes a city of 2,000 *amot* across, meaning a radius of 1,000 *amot*. The diagonal of a square with a side of 1,000 is 1,000 times the square root of two, approximately 1,400 *amot* — a gain of 400 over the circular measurement.

### Tchumin Gain

For the *techumin*, the gain is larger: *nimtzu tchumin mishtakerin shmonah me'ot amah le-kan u-shmonah me'ot amah le-kan* — the *techumin* gain 800 *amot* on each side. Here the full span from center to the edge of the *techum* is 1,000 (city radius) plus 2,000 (*techum*) = 3,000 *amot*. The square's diagonal at that scale is approximately 4,200 *amot*, a gain of 1,200. But accounting for the inner city's own 400-*amot* gain, the net gain attributed specifically to the *techum* squaring is 800 *amot*.

### Total Diagonal Gain

The Gemara synthesizes: *nimtza ir u-tchumeha mishtakrin elef u-matayim le-kan ve-elef u-matayim le-kan* — taken together, city and *tchumin*, one can travel 1,200 extra *amot* when walking diagonally at a 45-degree angle. Traveling straight in any cardinal direction, one covers 1,000 (city) plus 2,000 (*techum*) = 3,000 *amot*. Traveling diagonally, one covers 3,000 times the square root of two, approximately 4,200 *amot* — an excess of 1,200 *amot*. Abaye confirms that this calculation applies when the city is 2,000 by 2,000.

---

## Levitical Cities

### Torah Measures

The Gemara now turns to a *Baraita* on the cities of the *Levi'im*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi states: *tchum arei Levi'im alpayim amah* — the boundary of the Levitical cities is 2,000 *amot*. The Torah specifies two figures in proximity: one verse mentions 2,000 *amot* around the city; another mentions 1,000 *amot*. The Sages understood these two figures as follows: of the 2,000 *amot*, the inner 1,000 constitutes the *migrash* — an open, unplanted area, essentially parkland — and the outer 1,000 constitutes *sadot*, fields for grain and vineyards. The *migrash* is thus the inner ring and the *sadot* the outer ring, already suggesting that the *sadot* cover far more area than the *migrash*, since they form a much larger square.

### Quarter Claim

The *Baraita* asserts: *nimtza migrash revia* — the *migrash* turns out to be one-quarter of the whole, with the remainder being fields and vineyards. The Gemara immediately asks: where does this figure come from? Rava cites the verse: *mikir ha-ir va-chutzah elef amah saviv* — one thousand *amot* outside the city all around. This is the basis for the *migrash* being 1,000 *amot*. But the question of whether the *migrash* is truly one-quarter of the whole remains to be demonstrated.

### Square City Model

Rava bar Rav Adda reports: *meshu'acha asbara li* — the measurers (those who professionally calculate *techumin*) explained this to me. Rashi identifies these *meshu'ach'in* as the men who measure out the *techumin* for communities. Their explanation begins: *mishkachat lah be-mata d'hava trei alfi a-trei alfi* — take a city that is 2,000 by 2,000 *amot*. The *techum*, extending 2,000 *amot* in every direction, makes the entire area — including city and everything surrounding it — 8,000 by 8,000. To calculate areas conveniently, divide the total space into units of 1,000 by 1,000 each. The entire span is eight units across in each direction, giving 64 such units in total. But the relevant counting proceeds differently: the city itself occupies a 2,000 by 2,000 square, giving four units. The band of *migrash* (1,000 *amot* thick) surrounds the city, giving eight more units on the four sides (two per side), plus four corner units — twelve units for the *migrash*. The *sadot* and the remaining *techum* occupy the rest.

### Math Problem

The problem is immediate: twelve out of thirty-six (the total of city units plus surrounding units, before considering the outermost *techum* corners) is not one-quarter but one-third. Even when the four units of the city are added to yield a total of thirty-six units, twelve out of thirty-six is still one-third — *tilsha havei*, not *revia*. So how can the *Baraita* claim it is a quarter?

### Circular City Solution

The Gemara provides the resolution: *mi savrat be-rivua kamart? be-igula kamart* — who said we are talking about a square city? We are talking about a circular city. The crucial distinction is that only the *techum* — the outermost boundary — is squared off. The city itself and the *migrash* surrounding it are circular. The squaring applies only to the final 1,000 *amot* of *sadot* and *techum*. This is a significant *chiddush*: the presumption that squaring applies at every level is incorrect; it is applied only at the outermost stage.

### Square-Circle Ratio

The Gemara then invokes the geometric ratio: *ve-kamma meruba yeter al ha-igul? revia* — how much larger is a square than a circle inscribed within it? One-quarter larger. This follows from the approximation that *pi* equals three. If the diameter of the circle is two (making the radius one), the area of the circle is *pi r²* = three. The area of the circumscribed square is four. The ratio is three to four — the square is one-quarter larger than the circle. The same ratio holds for circumference to perimeter: the circumference is 2*pi*r = six, while the perimeter of the square is eight. Thus the square exceeds the circle by one-quarter in both area and linear measure.

Applying this to the calculation: the city circle has a radius of 2,000 *amot* (since the city is 2,000 by 2,000 in diameter). Its area is *pi* times four million — approximately twelve million square *amot* (using *pi* = three). The inner city circle alone (radius 1,000) has area three million. The *migrash* circle, then, has area twelve minus three = nine million. But the outer square of everything is thirty-six million (6,000 by 6,000). Reducing the *migrash* from nine to nine times three-quarters (since a circle is three-quarters of the square that contains it) yields a *migrash* of effectively nine units out of thirty-six — but wait, the Gemara's calculation proceeds as follows: take the thirty-six units of the full square, remove one-quarter (nine units) because the city and *migrash* are circular rather than square, leaving twenty-seven; but the *migrash* portion before that reduction was twelve, reduced by a quarter to nine. And nine out of thirty-six is exactly one-quarter. *Dal revia mina-ihu, pashu lei tisha, ve-tisha mi-telatin ve-shisha revia havya* — remove a quarter from the thirty-six, you get nine, and nine out of thirty-six is one-quarter.

### Smaller City

Abaye confirms that the same result holds when the city has a radius of only 1,000 *amot* (a city 1,000 by 1,000). *Tchumim kama havay? Temanya* — the *techum* squares yield eight units. *Kranot kama havay? Shitsar* — the corners yield sixteen. The total outside the city is twenty-four units; the *migrash* portion, before the circular correction, is eight of those. But twenty-four minus the circular correction: *dal revia mina-ihu, pashu lei shita, ve-shita mi-kaf-dalet revia havay* — remove one-quarter from twenty-four, you get six, and six out of twenty-four is one-quarter. Thus whether the city is 1,000 or 2,000 *amot* in radius, the same ratio holds.

The upshot of the entire discussion is a ruling of considerable geometric subtlety: the squaring of the *reibua olam* applies only to the *techum* — the outermost layer. The city and the *migrash* retain their circular form. It is only when computing the extended *techum* boundary that we impose the square and gain the corners. This is what makes the *migrash* exactly one-quarter of the whole.

---

---

# Eiruvin 58

## Fifty-Amah Rope

### Mishkan Source

The *gemara* opens with the question *mina hani mili* — from where do we derive that the measuring rope used for *techumim* must be fifty *amot* in length? *Rav Yehuda* cites *Shmuel*, who points to the *pasuk* describing the courtyard of the *mishkan*: *orech hachatzer meah ba'amah v'rochav chamishim b'chamishim* — the length of the *chatzer* was a hundred *amot* and its width was fifty by fifty. The phrase "fifty by fifty" is admittedly unusual. The *gemara* elsewhere explains the simple meaning: the first fifty *amot* of the courtyard did not contain the *ohel mo'ed*, which was situated only in the rear fifty. But the peculiar formulation *b'chamishim* — with the *bet* prefix — invites further attention.

### Two Principles

The *gemara* asks: surely that phrase *b'chamishim* is already needed to teach something else — *litol chamishim v'lisaveiv chamishim*, to take fifty and surround fifty. That is, if one has a city plot of a hundred by fifty *amot*, one takes the second fifty and distributes it equally around the first fifty, effectively squaring the rectangle. The result is a square with a side equal to the square root of five thousand, which equals seventy and two-thirds *amot* — a figure that recurs throughout this tractate as the critical measurement for determining whether structures outside the city boundary are still considered connected to it. If so, does this use of the *pasuk* leave nothing over for deriving the fifty-*amah* rope?

The *gemara* responds: had the *Torah* intended only the squaring principle, it would have written simply *chamishim chamishim*. What does the additional *bet* — *b'chamishim* — teach? *Shema mina tarti* — you learn both. This is characteristic of how the *gemara* throughout this tractate treats *eruv techumim*: it consistently grounds these laws in *psukim*, even though the dominant view is that *eruv techumim* is *d'rabanan*. The tension between *drashot* of this kind and the rabbinic character of the law is itself notable.

### Rope Length Limits

A *baraita* teaches: *lo phachot v'lo yoter* — not less and not more than fifty *amot*. Not less, because a shorter rope can be held very taut, causing the measurement to stretch beyond its true length. Not more, because a longer rope will sag, causing it to fall short of measuring the full distance. The practical logic underlying these reasons is worth noting: if the rule were truly derived from a *pasuk*, one would not expect functional justifications to be offered. This *baraita* thus lends the rule a pragmatic character that sits somewhat in tension with the scriptural derivation above.

### Rope Materials

*Rabbi Assi* states: *ein modedin ela b'chevel shel afaskima* — you may only measure with a rope made of *afaskima*. The *gemara* then proceeds through two stages of translation. *Rav Abba* says *afaskima* is *nargila*. *Rav Yaakov* says *nargila* is *dikla de-chad navra* — a palm tree with a single vine wrapped around it. According to Steinsaltz, this refers to the coconut palm, and the relevant material is the fiber of the coconut husk, which is prized for making ropes that do not absorb water and therefore do not expand or contract with moisture. This property would allow the rope to maintain a consistent length regardless of conditions — exactly what is required for accurate measurement.

An alternative version of the tradition holds that *Rav Abba* and *Rav Yaakov* were not offering a chain of translation but two competing opinions: *Rav Abba* said *afaskima* is *nargila*, while *Rav Yaakov* said it is *dikla de-chad navra*, each being a distinct material, with the meaning of *nargila* itself left unclear. This second reading leaves even more uncertainty about what, precisely, one was supposed to use.

### Iron vs. Rope

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya* states: *ein lecha she-yafeh l'medidah yoter mi-shalshela'ot shel barzel* — there is nothing better for measuring than iron chains. Iron chains do not sag and do not stretch, making them in principle the most reliable tool. Surveyors historically did indeed use iron — and later steel — chains for precisely this reason. But, he asks, *aval mah na'aseh* — what can we do? The *Torah* (or more precisely *Nach*, from *Zechariah*) says *u-vyado chevel midah* — in his hand was a rope of measurement — indicating that a rope is the prescribed instrument. The *gemara* then notes that *Yechezkel*, when describing the measurements of the *Mikdash Shelishi*, refers to *kneh ha-midah*, a measuring reed, which is also rigid. The *gemara* answers: that was for measuring the gates, which were short enough to be measured with a reed. For the longer distances involved in *techumim*, a rope is necessary since repeating many short reed-lengths would be impractical.

One might also ask: if a rope must be used, why hold it in the air rather than lay it on the ground? If the rope were truly a rigid chain, measuring along the ground might suffice.
