The answer, as will emerge from a later *gemara*, is that when the ground slopes at an angle, one measures the horizontal distance rather than the walking distance along the slope — and holding the rope at chest height facilitates taking the horizontal.

### Three Rope Types

*Rav Yosef* teaches that three types of rope appear in various *mishnayot*, each used for a different purpose. The rope of *megag* — identified by Rashi as a material not susceptible to *tumah* — was used for the *parah adumah*. As the *mishnah* in that tractate records, after the cow was slaughtered it was bound with a *chevel ha-megag* and placed on the wood pile to be burned. *Tosafot* notes that ropes generally are not *mekabel tumah* since they are twisted rather than woven; nevertheless, the preference was for a material that had never been susceptible to *tumah* at all, consistent with the general concern for purity in the *parah* procedure.

The rope of *netzer* — identified by Rashi as *sivei dedikla*, fibers of palm — was used for the *sotah*. The *mishnah* there records that after her garment was torn, a *chevel mitzri* (an Egyptian rope, understood here as this palm-fiber rope) was tied above her breasts to prevent her from standing exposed. Finally, *pishtan* — flax — was used for measurement. This stands in contrast to the earlier discussion that identified the measuring rope as being made from a type of palm. The basis for assigning flax to measurement is not explained; it is simply asserted. Flax, of course, is quite absorbent, which would seem to make it less ideal than a non-absorbent material, and the *gemara* does not address this tension.

---

## Valley Crossing

### Absorbing Valleys

The *gemara* now turns to a *baraita* that elaborates on the measuring procedure. *Haya moded vehigi'a hamidah lege* — if you were measuring and you reached a valley, the procedure depends on its width. If the valley is narrow enough — less than fifty *amot* — you can throw the rope across while two people stand on either side and hold it taut: *im yachol lehavli'o bechevel shel chamishim amah meval'o*, you absorb it within the fifty-*amah* rope. This is the simplest case.

*Rashi* explains that the phrase *chozer lemidato* — returning to one's measurement — which appears in the *mishnah*, implies the more complex case: when you cannot absorb it in a single rope-length because the valley is wider than fifty *amot*, you go to the side where the valley is narrow enough to cross, do your crossing there, and then sight back parallel to where you had been measuring: *vetzofeh keneged midato, vechozer lemidato* — you look to where you were and return to that line.

### Parallel Measurement

The requirement to return to the same measurement line raises an immediate practical difficulty: how does one ensure that the detour is made along a precisely parallel line and that one returns to exactly the correct spot? This is a genuine surveying problem. Any slight deviation from a true perpendicular during the detour will compound into an error in the final measurement. Moreover, if one walks due north for any significant distance, the curvature of the earth means that the distance along the ground from east to west actually varies, introducing small but real discrepancies. For the purposes of the *gemara*'s discussion, the goal of returning to one's line is simply assumed to be achievable, and no mechanism for verifying the parallel is specified.

### Bent Valleys

The *baraita* continues: *im haya gai me'ukam* — if the valley is bent, you do *makdir ve'oleh makdir veyored*, the piercing. *Rashi*'s simpler explanation of "bent" is that the valley curves in such a way that by the time you have gone far enough to the side to find a crossing point, you have already gone *chutz letchum* — outside the *techum* — in the lateral direction. If the surveyors are seen that far out, onlookers will mistakenly assume that the *techum* extends to where the surveyors are standing, when in fact it ends much closer. *Tosafot* adds a further consideration: even if the lateral displacement would not technically take the surveyors outside the *techum*, if the detour is so long that they cannot reliably find their way back to the same line, the method is no longer viable. In either case, when moving to the side is not an option, one must resort to the piercing technique.

---

## Piercing Technique

### Four-Amah Rope Method

The piercing technique — *makdir ve'oleh makdir veyored* — is a method for measuring horizontal distance when a valley is too wide to cross with a rope and too awkward or far to circumvent. The basic principle is this: instead of using a fifty-*amah* rope, one uses a rope of only four *amot*, as *Abaye* states: *naktinan ein mekadrin ela bechevel shel arba amot* — we have received the tradition that one only pierces with a rope of four *amot*. One person stands at a lower position and holds the rope at the level of his heart; the person above holds it at the level of his feet. This places the rope as close to horizontal as possible, minimizing the vertical component of the measurement. By repeating this process in successive steps up or down the slope, one accumulates a total that approximates the horizontal distance rather than the walking distance along the incline. The reason for using a short rope rather than the standard fifty-*amah* rope is precisely to reduce the angle: a longer rope held between two people at different heights would capture far more of the vertical than the horizontal.

This is, of course, a technological solution constrained by the instruments available. Since this procedure is not based on any *pasuk* and is simply a pragmatic approximation technique, it follows that if better methods were available — satellite imaging, for instance, or modern surveying equipment — one would presumably use them to obtain a more accurate horizontal measurement.

### Walls and Estimation

The *gemara* then addresses a qualitatively different obstacle. *Higia le-kotel, ein omrim yikof ha-kotel* — if you arrive at a wall, we do not say you should pierce through it. *Tosafot* suggests this means one should not try to hold the rope up over the wall on poles, i.e., attempting to engineer a straight-line measurement over an impassable obstacle. Instead: *ela omdo ve-holech lo* — you estimate it and move on.

The *gemara* then asks: but we just said that in the valley case you absorb it and return to your measurement — why do we allow simple estimation here? The answer is *nicha tashmishtei* versus *lo nicha tashmishtei*: in the valley case, the terrain is usable, meaning accessible enough to do successive measurements; in the wall case, it is not. *Rashi* explains this distinction in terms of gradient. A relatively gradual slope or descent — one that can be traversed — permits either crossing with the rope directly, moving off to the side, or doing the successive measurements. A nearly vertical face — a steep mountain or a wall — cannot reasonably require the surveyors to climb it. In such a case, estimation is the appropriate response.

It should be noted that this asymmetry between valley and mountain treatment — that mountains admit estimation while valleys require more careful treatment — will persist as the *gemara* develops further rules. It is also worth noting the halakhic implication for the measurer's experience: the *techum* is measured horizontally, not by walking distance. Thus a person could in principle climb an enormous mountain on *Shabbat* without violating the *techum*, provided the horizontal distance does not exceed two thousand *amot*, since vertical climbing does not count against the *techum*.

### Plumb Line Test

*Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel* introduces an important qualification regarding valleys. *Lo shanu ela she'ein chut hamishkolet yored kenegdo* — the rule that you do successive measurements applies only when the plumb line does not fall directly beneath your feet, i.e., when the valley wall is not purely vertical. *Aval chut hamishkolet yored kenegdo* — if the plumb line does fall straight down, indicating a sheer vertical drop — *modedo medida yafa*, you do a proper measurement. And what is that proper measurement? You go down to the bottom of the valley and measure the flat ground there.

The logic is as follows: if the drop is perfectly vertical, there is no horizontal component to the valley wall itself, and therefore the piercing technique (which measures horizontal distance in successive steps) is neither necessary nor applicable. The horizontal distance is simply the width of the valley floor, and one measures that directly. If however the plumb line does not fall straight down — meaning the valley is inclined at an angle — then measuring the floor would give you a shorter figure than the true horizontal span at the top, and you must use the successive measurements to capture that horizontal distance.

---

## Valley Depth Rules

### Hundred-Amah Limit

The *gemara* now turns to the question of how deep a valley may be before different rules apply. *Ve-chama omko shel gai* — how deep is the valley for which we permit you to absorb it? *Abaye* states: *omek kuf ve-rochav nun mavlio* — if it is a hundred *amot* deep and fifty *amot* wide, you can absorb it. If not — presumably meaning deeper than that — *ein mavlio*, you cannot absorb it in the simple sense, and you must use successive measurements. This is the position of the *tanna kama* as the *gemara* understands it.

### Two-Thousand-Amah Limit

The *gemara* then cites an alternative view. *Acherim omrim*: even if the depth is two thousand *amot* and the width is fifty, you absorb it. This implies that beyond two thousand, one cannot absorb it. *Rav Yosef* goes further still, saying *afilu yatir me-alpayim* — even more than two thousand *amot* deep makes no difference in the absorbability. The *gemara* then asks: *keman* — who does *Rav Yosef* follow? *Lo k'tanna kama v'lo k'acherim* — it fits neither the *tanna kama* who limits it to a hundred *amot*, nor the view of *Acherim* who permit up to two thousand. *Rashi* explains the consequence of *Rav Yosef*'s view: even if the valley is deeper than two thousand *amot*, if you could otherwise absorb it within a single fifty-*amah* rope, you may still do so. Yet this explanation in *Rashi* is not explicit in the *gemara* itself.

One might ask: why should depth matter at all? The whole purpose of the measurement is to determine horizontal distance. Whether the valley is a hundred or two thousand *amot* deep, as long as it is narrow enough to throw the rope across or to circumvent, the technique seems the same. The *gemara* does not resolve this difficulty fully, and it remains genuinely puzzling — particularly since the practical scenario of someone walking through a two-thousand-*amah* chasm on *Shabbat* seems remote. Perhaps the intent is that when the valley is extraordinarily deep, doing the successive measurements involves so much effort — and covers so much distance — that it becomes effectively impossible, and the ruling adjusts accordingly.

### Plumb Line Standards

The *gemara* reconciles the seemingly conflicting standards — one hundred *amot* versus two thousand *amot* — by invoking the plumb line distinction introduced earlier. When the *tanna kama* and *Acherim* debate at what depth you can no longer absorb the valley, they are referring to a valley that is *she'ein chut hamishkoles yored kenegdo* — where the plumb does not fall straight down, i.e., the valley has inclined walls. In such a case it is possible to do the piercing and successive measurements, and the debate is about how deep a valley can be before we require you to do so rather than simply absorbing it with a rope. *Rav Yosef*, by contrast, is referring to the case *bechut hamishkoles yored kenegdo* — where the plumb falls straight down, meaning the walls are sheer. In that case, there is no way to perform the successive measurements on the wall at all, and so he says that no matter how deep it is, you simply go to the bottom and measure: depth is irrelevant to that calculus.

### Four-Amah Deviation

The *gemara* then asks: when we say the plumb line does not fall straight down, indicating the valley is inclined — *ad kama*, how much of a deviation constitutes that condition? *Avimi* states: four *amot*, and *Rami bar Yechezkel* teaches the same. That is, if when you drop a plumb line from the top of the valley wall, the weight lands four *amot* away from directly beneath you when it reaches the ground, that constitutes a non-vertical incline, and the successive-measurement procedure is required.

This raises a natural concern: four *amot* of deviation is a function of both the angle and the depth of the valley. Four *amot* of horizontal displacement over a very shallow valley would indicate a very gentle slope, while the same four *amot* over a deep valley would indicate a nearly vertical one. The *gemara* does not address this geometric ambiguity directly. The overall picture of valley measurement — when to absorb, when to pierce, when to go to the bottom, and what depth thresholds apply — is complex, and as *Tosafot* recognized, requires a systematic framework to understand in its totality.

---

## Mountain Slopes

### Ten-in-Four Slope

*Rava* introduces the central qualification for mountains. *Lo shanu ela behar hamitlaket asara mitoch arba* — the rule that you move off to the side of a mountain applies only when the mountain rises ten *tefachim* within four *amot* of horizontal distance. An *amah* is six *tefachim*, so four *amot* equals twenty-four *tefachim*, and the slope is therefore ten over twenty-four, which works out to an angle of approximately 22.6 degrees. This is the standard threshold used in *halacha* to define a slope so steep that it is treated as a wall rather than mere inclined ground. It is roughly five times the maximum slope permitted under the Americans with Disabilities Act (one in twelve), which is itself already a fairly challenging incline. A slope that rises at this rate has the visual character and practical effect of a wall rather than a passable hillside.

### Rava's Distinction

An alternative version of *Rava*'s statement is presented *lekula* — in the more lenient direction. *Aval behar hamitlaket asara mitoch chamesh* — but if the mountain rises ten *tefachim* within five *amot*, a more gradual slope, *modedo medida yafa* — you do a proper measurement. *Rashi* explains that *medida yafa* here means measuring as you walk: you simply treat the gradual slope as ordinary ground and measure along it, without trying to correct for the incline by moving off to the side or doing successive measurements.

Conversely, when the slope is sharper — ten in four — *omdo ve-holech lo*, you estimate and proceed. This is the statement *Rav Huna son of Rav Natan* taught in the lenient formulation. The overall logic is consistent with the general approach: when a mountain or slope is sufficiently gradual that walking it is straightforward, you measure the walking distance and treat it as ordinary terrain. When it is steep enough to be wall-like, you do not demand that the surveyors deal with it through precise measurement techniques; you simply estimate.

This represents a systematic leniency toward mountains relative to valleys. By valleys, elaborate measurement techniques — successive piercings, bottom measurements — are required in many scenarios. By mountains, once the slope reaches the threshold of a wall, the *gemara* simply says: estimate and move on.

### Techum Boundary

The rule that when moving to the side, the surveyors may not go *chutz latchum* in the other direction — *u-bilvad shelo yetzei chutz lat-techum* — is given its rationale by *Rav Kahana*: *gezeira shema yomeru midat techumin ba'ah lechan* — a rabbinic decree lest people say the *techum* boundary reaches that far. If surveyors are seen measuring in a particular location, observers will naturally assume that location falls within the *techum*, even if the surveyors are only there because they had to detour around an obstacle. To prevent that false impression, the surveyors must stay within the *techum* when making their lateral detour.

It follows that when the valley or obstacle is so broad that even moving off to the side would push the surveyors outside the *techum*, the only option is the piercing technique. And as *Abaye* states: *naktinan ein mekadrin ela bechevel shel arba amot* — the tradition is that this is done with a four-*amah* rope, the lower person holding it at his heart, the upper person at his feet. The short rope and the height differential work together to capture horizontal distance rather than the diagonal or vertical.

---

## Experts & Testimony

### Expert Measurers

The *mishnah* states: *ein modedin ela min hamumche* — you may only measure from an expert. *Tosafot* offers a surprising reading: *mumche* here does not mean an expert measurer but rather the *middle point* of each side of the city, connecting the word to the expression *macha al ketef yam kinneret*. This is a minority reading. The straightforward understanding is that the *mishnah* requires trained, qualified individuals to perform the measurements.

### Conflicting Measures

*Riva bimakom echad u-mi'et bimakom acher* — if one measurement comes out longer and another shorter at different points along the same side of the city, *shomin limakom sheriva* — you accept the longer measurement. Since the entire institution of *techumim* is *d'rabanan*, we adopt the more lenient position, which in this context means the greater distance. The *gemara* notes a second formulation: *riva l'echad u-mi'et l'echad* — if different measurers produced different results, again you follow the more expansive result. The *gemara* will clarify the distinction between these two formulations, but the underlying principle — following the longer distance — is uniform.

### Slave Testimony

*Va'afilu eved va'afilu shifcha ne'emanim lomar ad kan techum Shabbat* — even a male or female slave is believed to testify as to where the *techum Shabbat* ends. The *mishnah* notably does not mention women separately, which is presumably because this is not formal *edut* at all — it is the kind of everyday informational statement governed by the principle of *eid echad ne'eman b'issurin*, under which even ordinarily disqualified witnesses are relied upon for practical matters of *issur*. Women are already trusted in such contexts; the novelty here is extending that trust to slaves, who might otherwise be considered less reliable. If a slave says that a marker has fallen but that the *techum* always ended at this particular spot, that testimony is accepted.

### Leniency Principle

The *mishnah* concludes: *shelo amru chachamim et hadavar l'hachmir ela l'hakel* — the Sages did not establish this matter in order to be strict but rather to be lenient. The principle of leniency pervades the laws of *techumim*: conflicting measurements resolve in favor of the greater distance, slave testimony is accepted to expand the *techum*, and — as has been noted at various earlier points in the tractate — when there is doubt in *eruv* matters, we generally rule *lekula*. This is the appropriate posture for a rabbinic ordinance: having established the framework, the Sages built into it a consistent tilt toward leniency rather than stringency.

---

---

# Eiruvin 59

## Overlapping Squares

### NYC Tchumim Problem

Before turning to the daf itself, a practical question arising from the preceding sugya on measuring *tchumim* deserves attention — one with direct relevance to contemporary metropolitan life. Consider the geography of New York City: a sprawling, multi-borough urban area whose irregular shape poses a genuine challenge for the laws of *tchumim*. If one squares off Manhattan, the resulting rectangle may extend into New Jersey or Queens but still fail to encompass Riverdale in the Bronx. And even squaring off the Bronx separately may not bridge the gap to lower Manhattan. How, then, do people routinely travel across these distances on Shabbos without violating the *tchumim*?

### Brooklyn Bridge Tshuva

The most obvious theoretical solution — though one stated nowhere explicitly in the *Gemara* — is that if the squared-off areas of two cities overlap, they should be treated as a single city. This would resolve the geometric problem elegantly: the process of squaring off (*ibbur*) occurs before the 2,000 *amos* are even measured, and if two squares overlap, the cities merge into one for the purpose of *tchumim*. Whether this is actually the *halacha*, however, is not self-evident. A number of *teshuvos* in the responsa literature address this question in the specific context of the Brooklyn Bridge — asking whether a *beis dira* located on the bridge, particularly a toll booth or some small habitable structure situated not immediately adjacent to the city but somewhere in the middle of the bridge, suffices to connect the two shores for purposes of *tchum* measurement. It seems from Rashi that as long as there is a functional residential presence near the bridge, it would count. Several of these *teshuvos* conclude, however, somewhat cryptically, that when you look at a map, "it all works out" — a phrase that presumably points to the overlapping-squares principle as the operative rationale.

### Chazon Ish Overlap

There is in fact an explicit source for this principle. The Chazon Ish, in his commentary on *Eruvin* (at the beginning of siman 16), writes: *im yesh shivim amos v'shiyayrim oseh karpaf l'shnayim l'hiyot k'echad* — if there are 70-and-a-fraction *amos* between two settlements, the *karpaf* measurement joins them as one. He then raises the further question: *yesh l'ayein im yesh ibbur hapgumim hayotzim dimotzi es hamidah k'negdam v'ose oso k'min tavla* — one must examine whether, when the irregular protrusions of a city are squared off, and *v'avir hazeh shemitaber ima pogea b'ir acheres* — the air of that squared-off area impinges upon another city — *mahu sheibbur hazeh yaaseh shteihen k'ir achas* — whether that overlapping squared area causes both cities to be treated as one. Drawing on Rashi, the Chazon Ish argues affirmatively: if squaring off one city causes its squared area to overlap with another city, the two are treated as a single city for purposes of *tchumim*.

### Contemporary Practice

This ruling of the Chazon Ish is not extensively discussed in the classical *poskim* and *teshuvos*, yet it is evidently assumed in contemporary *eruv* and *tchum* practice. No authority appears to dispute it. Its practical significance is considerable: it is presumably the reason why people travel without concern from one New York borough to another on Shabbos, relying on the principle that once the respective squares overlap, all the boroughs constitute a single continuous city. This is a striking case where a ruling of the Chazon Ish quietly shapes widespread practice without having generated significant formal debate.

---

## Competing Markers

### Greater Measurement

Turning now to the top of 59a: the *Mishna* had established that when there are competing measurements of a *tchum* — one marker extending further than another — we follow the more lenient, i.e., the greater, measurement. The *Gemara* opens by parsing the language of the *Mishna*: *b'makom she'ribu hein b'makom she'miatu lo* — in the place where they gave more, that is where you are limited by the lesser. Then the *seifa* adds: *af l'makom she'ribu* — you may even go to the further marker.

### Rashi v. Tosafos

Rashi and Tosafos differ sharply on what question is being asked and answered here. According to Rashi, the *Gemara*'s question is somewhat trivial: if you are going toward the further marker, you obviously pass the nearer one along the way. The principle of *yesh bichlal masayim maneh* applies — the greater includes the lesser — so the answer is obvious. You may go to the further one, and certainly to the nearer one along the same path.

Tosafos rejects this reading and identifies a more substantive question. Recall that the preceding material dealt at length with the complications of measuring *tchumim* over hills, valleys, and uneven terrain. Tosafos therefore understands the *Gemara* as asking about two markers on the same side of a city — say, the western side — but at different positions: one marker here, and another further along the same side but at a different point. The question is whether one must respect the nearer marker when traveling in one direction, even if the further marker is legitimate for a different position along that side, owing to different topographical conditions. Perhaps the more sloped terrain in one area accounts for a closer marker, while flatter terrain elsewhere justifies a farther one. The *Gemara*'s answer — *af l'makom she'ribu* — means that yes, you may go to the further marker from your current position, but from the other position you must stop at the nearer marker. Both markers are legitimate, each reflecting the topography at its location, and both must be respected. This reading, Tosafos notes, connects directly to the preceding discussion of how terrain affects measurement.

### Two Surveyors

The *Gemara* then continues: *ribu l'echad u'miatu l'echad* — one measurement was greater, the other lesser — and the ruling is to follow the greater one. This sounds identical to the earlier case in the *Mishna*, and the *Gemara* itself asks: *hainu hach* — is this not exactly the same thing? The *Gemara* answers: *hachi ka'amar* — the intent is different. Here we are speaking not of a single surveyor who produced different markers at different points along the same side, but of two different surveyors whose measurements conflict. One surveyor's marker falls further out; the other's falls closer in. Even according to Rashi, the novelty here is that these are competing measurements from different people. According to Tosafos, the case is even more pointed: the two competing markers are for the exact same location — one surveyor placed his marker here, the other placed his there, on precisely the same side and roughly the same spot. In that case you might think each marker's legitimacy is simply negated by the other, yet the ruling is still to follow the greater one.

It is worth noting a difference in the *girsa*: the *Gemara* here reads *ribu echad miat echad* — one person gave more, one gave less — while the *Mishna* reads *ribu l'echad*, which Rashi reads as referring to one of the measurers. The grammatical variation supports Rashi's understanding that the novelty lies in the two-surveyor scenario.

### Diagonal Limit

Abaye adds a qualification: *u-vilvad shelo yarbeh yoter mi-midat ha-ir be-alakhsonah* — provided that the further marker does not exceed the diagonal of the city. The logic of squaring off a city means that instead of 2,000 *amos* in each direction, one can potentially reach up to 2,828 *amos* along the diagonal. If the further surveyor's marker falls within this expanded range, it retains legitimacy. If it extends beyond even this, it is simply too far off to be credited.

This raises an interesting question: if we are now capable of remeasuring and can see that the further marker is significantly off, why follow it at all? Why not simply remeasure and discard the erroneous marker? The *Gemara* seems to envision a scenario in which established signposts carry authority so long as they retain some plausible basis — as long as the error is not so gross as to exceed even the diagonal. Tosafos appears to read this as specifically addressing the case where the two competing markers are themselves located at the diagonal, which makes the reference to the diagonal measurement pointed. A simpler reading of the *Gemara*, however, would be that the markers are not necessarily at the diagonal, and the *Gemara* is simply saying that any marker within 2,800 *amos* has a residual claim to legitimacy even if we now know it may not be perfectly precise.

One might ask why the *Gemara* allows established markers to override a current remeasurement. This seems to be one of those cases where a *halakhic* reality is maintained even when it may not align perfectly with physical reality — and the rationale for this leniency is stated explicitly at the close of the *Mishna*: *lo amru chakhamim et ha-davar le-hachmir ela le-hakel* — the Sages said this matter only to be lenient, not to be strict. Since *eruvin* and *tchumim* are rabbinic, a degree of leniency in their administration is not only permitted but intended.

---

## Informal Witnesses

### Why Rabbinic

A *Baraita* now seems to contradict the *Mishna*: while the *Mishna* said the Sages spoke *le-hakel*, the *Baraita* says *lo amru chakhamim et ha-davar le-hakel ela le-hachmir* — they said it only to be strict, not lenient. Ravina resolves the contradiction: the Sages were not being lenient with respect to a Torah obligation. Rather, the entire institution of *tchumim* was itself a rabbinic *chumra* imposed where the Torah did not require it. Once established as rabbinic, however, the administration of *tchumim* proceeds with leniency — including the acceptance of testimony from those who do not qualify as formal witnesses.

The *Mishna* at its close trusts even a male or female slave to testify about where the *tchum* marker was. Normally, slaves are excluded from formal *edus*. The *Gemara*'s emphasis that *techumim derabbanan* — the Sabbath boundary laws are rabbinic in origin — functions here not only to explain why we follow the more lenient marker, but also to explain why we trust categories of testimony that would otherwise be inadmissible.

### Ed Echad Principle

This prompts Tosafos to raise a broader question: if the reason we trust slaves (and, by extension, women and children, since Tosafos includes them in this discussion) is specifically because *tchumim* are rabbinic, would we *not* trust them for a matter that is biblical? What about everyday reliance on women for matters of biblical prohibition?

### Women Beyada

Tosafos notes — as the first line of that *Tosafos* makes explicit — that *mashma i havei de-oraita lo mehumni*: it sounds like that if *tchumim* were biblical, these informal witnesses would not be believed. Yet in practice, *ma'aseh be-khol yom she-ma'aminim nashim* — every single day we trust women: *bi-shechitah u-venikkur* — we eat meat that our wives or household members tell us was properly slaughtered and *nikkured* of *chelev*, and we trust them that *challah* was separated. How is this consistent?

The answer lies in the principle of *beyada* — control over outcome. When something carries a *chezkat issur*, as a live animal does before *shechita*, a person is trusted to report that it was rendered permissible only if they were in a theoretical position of control — *beyada* — to have effected the permissible outcome. A woman is believed about *shechita* not because she necessarily performed it herself, but because she could theoretically have done so or arranged for it to be done. Women are indeed eligible to perform *shechita*, as the opening *Mishna* of *Chullin* establishes: *hakol shochtin*. Even if this particular woman does not know how, she could in principle have brought the animal to a *shochet*. The theoretical control is sufficient.

### Tosafos Women

Tosafos then goes further and asks about cases where *beyada* may not apply — where the woman is not in a position of theoretical control. The case of *eruvin* itself is given as an example: one cannot control where a *tchum* boundary falls, so the *beyada* framework does not apply there. This is why the *Gemara* must fall back on the rabbinic nature of *tchumim* as the justification for trusting informal witnesses.

The remainder of Tosafos extends this analysis to *bedikat chametz* and to the question of whether women are trusted for it because of the rabbinic status of the obligation or because of *beyada* — a discussion that becomes increasingly complex and somewhat less straightforward. The broader point that emerges from Tosafos is that there are at least two distinct grounds on which informal witnesses may be trusted: (1) the principle of *ed echad ne'eman be'issurin*, which does not require formal *edus* and under which women are generally believed, especially when *beyada* applies; and (2) the rabbinic status of the underlying law, which independently permits reliance on testimony that would not suffice for a Torah obligation. By *tchumim*, the *Gemara* appears to rely on the second ground, since the first may not cleanly apply.

---

## Private/Public Cities

### Mishna Rule

The next *Mishna* introduces a new topic: the *halakhic* significance of a city's history — whether it began as private (*shel yachid*) or public (*shel rabbim*) — and how that history affects the permissibility of making an *eruv* for the entire city. The rule is as follows: *ir sheyachid vena'asit shel rabbim* — a city that was private and became public — *me'arvin et kullah* — one may make an *eruv* for the entire city. But *shel rabbim vena'asit shel yachid* — if it was public and became private — *ein me'arvin et kullah* — one may not make an *eruv* for the whole city. Rather, one must leave out a section equivalent to a small city — the *Mishna* uses the example of *Ir Chadashah*, an actual town in Judah (not "new city" as a description, but a proper name) which Rabbi Yehuda says had 50 residents. That is the minimum that must be left off. Rabbi Shimon is more lenient: three courtyards of two houses each is sufficient.

### 600,000 Criterion

Rashi uses this *Mishna* as the anchor for the principle — which originates with the *Ge'onim* rather than being stated explicitly in the *Gemara* — that 600,000 people are required for a street to constitute a *reshus harabbim* from the Torah. For Rashi, "public city" (*shel rabbim*) means one with 600,000 inhabitants, and "private city" (*shel yachid*) means one without. This gives the history-of-the-city criterion a concrete meaning: a city that once had 600,000 residents had the *potential* for a Torah-level *reshus harabbim*, even if no actual street met all the formal criteria; one that never reached that population did not.

Within this framework, Rashi introduces an important nuance: what does 600,000 mean? Does it mean 600,000 people living in the city, or 600,000 people actively using a particular road on a daily basis? Rashi here says it means 600,000 *living in the city*, not necessarily using the road. He also raises another possibility: that a city becomes "public" not through permanent residents but through the influx of 600,000 on market days — a city that becomes a major commercial hub. This matters considerably for contemporary *eruv* discussions, since the definition of the 600,000 criterion significantly affects which streets in modern cities might theoretically qualify as a *reshus harabbim*.

With this framework, Rashi's explanation of the *Mishna* runs as follows. If a city started private — fewer than 600,000 — and now has become public — 600,000 — it nonetheless never actually had a functioning *reshus harabbim* even now, since a *reshus harabbim* requires not only population but a street of 16 *amos* wide running through the full length. Given that it started private, we permit making an *eruv* over the entire city. This seems counterintuitive — the city is *now* public, and surely that should be more restrictive — but Rashi's logic is that since it started private, there is no concern that people will mistake the *eruv* for a permissible enclosure of an actual *reshus harabbim*. Conversely, if the city started as public, even though it is now private, we require leaving over a section. The reason: people remember the city's former grandeur and may still think of it as a large public city, so we create a *heker* — a reminder — lest someone come to make an *eruv* around an actual *reshus harabbim*.

### Ownership Model

The Ramban reads the *Mishna* very differently, and is notably skeptical of the 600,000 criterion altogether. For the Ramban, "public" and "private" mean precisely what they say: ownership. A *shel yachid* is a city literally owned by one person; *shel rabbim* is a city owned by the public. This is not a demographic question but a proprietary one. The Ramban holds that one of the formal requirements for a Torah-level *reshus harabbim* is that the thoroughfare be publicly owned. A privately owned road, however busy, cannot constitute a *reshus harabbim*. Accordingly, a city that starts private — owned by one person — and then becomes public — ownership transfers to many — presents one set of concerns, while the reverse presents another.

### Logical Problem

Both Rashi and the Ramban, however, struggle with the same logical problem: why should we be *more lenient* when the city is now public than when it is now private? Intuitively, we should be governed by current conditions: if the city is now public, now is when a *reshus harabbim* might exist, and now should be more restrictive. The *Mishna* seems to invert this expectation.

Rashi's answer, as noted, appeals to historical perception: people recall the former status of the city and may confuse it with its current one. A city that was once great but is now diminished still carries its former identity in the public consciousness, and we must account for the possibility that someone will treat it as if it still has a *reshus harabbim*. A city that started small and is now large presents less risk — people are aware of the growth and will be appropriately careful.

The Ramban's answer is more technical. When the *Mishna* says the city "became public," this need not mean it became *fully* publicly owned. Perhaps the inhabitants are renting the land while the owner retains title, or perhaps the residential plots were sold while the major thoroughfares remained in private ownership. In that case, the roads — the potential *reshus harabbim* — are still privately owned, and the *reshus harabbim* concern is mitigated. This is admittedly not the simple reading of the *Mishna*, but the Ramban is deliberately drawing the *Gemara*'s subsequent discussion into the analysis to address the logical problem.

The *Gemara* then asks: *heichi dami yachid vena'aseh rabbim* — what is the actual scenario? Rav Yehuda gives the example of *Iskurta*, the city of the *Resh Galuta* — the exilarch — which was presumably once his private domain and has now become public. Rav Nachman challenges this: if the reason the city qualifies as public is that many people come to it, say, to receive authorization from the *Resh Galuta*, then the same logic should apply to any city where Jews gather on Shabbos morning — *deshabta shchichi ahadadi lishmo'a drasha*, as Rashi explains: they gather to hear the weekly *drasha*, at which point they will all remind one another not to carry. If that is the reason we are lenient, then we should be lenient in every city. The Gemara then revises the example to a city of *Natzu'ei*, a private individual — suggesting, as the Ramban reads it, that the point is that the city, while nominally public, retains enough private character (the owner still holds the major roads, or inhabitants are renters) that the leniency is justified. This answer is not entirely satisfying as *pshat* of the *Mishna*, and the Ramban acknowledges it, but at minimum he brings this logical tension explicitly into the *Gemara*'s discussion.

---

## Eruv in Reshus

### Rabbi Yehuda Lechi

Having established the rules about private and public cities, the *Gemara* now examines a *Baraita* that pushes the analysis further. The *Baraita* says: *ir shel yachid vena'asit shel rabbim* — a city that was private and became public — *reshus harabbim overes besochah* — and a real *reshus harabbim* passes through it — *keitzad mearvin osah* — how does one make an *eruv* for it? *Oseh lechi mikan ulechi mikan o korah mikan vekorah mikan venoise u'nosein be'emtza* — one places a *lechi* on each end of the street, or a *korah* on each end, and one may then carry in the middle.

A word on terminology: the *Gemara* here uses the verb *le'areiv* to refer to the construction of the physical enclosure, not merely the combining of domains through the bread loaf. This represents an evolution in the use of the word *eruv* — from its original, technical meaning of joining through the loaf, to encompassing the structures that permit carrying. It is worth noting this semantic development, as it reflects how the term entered the broader vocabulary of the *halacha*.

Now, *keitzad mearvin osah* — making an *eruv* around a *reshus harabbim* with a mere *lechi* or *korah* — is a striking claim. The *Gemara* immediately asks: who is the *Tanna* that permits this? The answer given by Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua is: *Rabbi Yehuda hi* — it is Rabbi Yehuda. A *Baraita* is cited in which Rabbi Yehuda says: *mi sheyesh lo shenei batim mishenei tziddei reshus harabbim* — one who has two houses on opposite sides of a *reshus harabbim* — *oseh lechi mikan ulechi mikan o korah mikan vekorah mikan venoise u'nosein be'emtza* — places a *lechi* or *korah* on each end, and may carry in the middle. The language is identical to the *Baraita* above, confirming the attribution.

The *Baraita* then records the Sages' rejection: *ein me'arvin reshus harabbim bekach* — one cannot use this method to close off a *reshus harabbim*. A *lechi* or *korah* is insufficient to transform a *reshus harabbim* into a domain where carrying is permitted. We do not rule in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda on this point.

This explains a great deal about the structure of contemporary *eruv* discussions. Those *Rishonim* and *poskim* who require 600,000 for a *reshus harabbim* are effectively saying that almost no modern city ever has a genuine *reshus harabbim*, and therefore the question of enclosing one with a *lechi* or *korah* never arises. This is crucial, because if there were a real *reshus harabbim*, we rule like the Sages — *ein me'arvin reshus harabbim bekach* — and no amount of *lechin* or *koros* would suffice. The entire practical edifice of the contemporary *eruv* depends on the position that the streets being enclosed do not qualify as a *reshus harabbim* at the Torah level to begin with.

Furthermore, the *Baraita* adds: *ve'ein me'arvin osah lachatza'in* — one may not make an *eruv* for only half the city. Either the whole city is enclosed as one *eruv*, or each individual alleyway (*maboi*) makes its own. This raises further questions, addressed immediately below.

### Sages Reject

Before turning to the question of partial *eruvin*, it is worth pausing to absorb the significance of the *Baraita*'s structure. The entire distinction between starting *shel yachid* and starting *shel rabbim* — which the *Mishna* presented as a rule about leaving a portion off — is here shown to have a deeper implication: when it started *shel yachid*, one may (according to Rabbi Yehuda) make a full *eruv* even around a genuine *reshus harabbim*, placing *lechin* or *koros* at the two ends of the through-street. When it started *shel rabbim* and remains *shel rabbim*, Rabbi Yehuda himself is more limited: the city may be enclosed only if the major street is a dead-end — that is, only if the street does not pass fully through the city from one end to the other, so that it is not a true *reshus harabbim*. A street with two open ends that begins and ends *shel rabbim* cannot be enclosed under even Rabbi Yehuda's lenient view.

What emerges is that the history of the city's status confers a kind of *halakhic* identity. A city's origin, whether private or public, shapes how the *halacha* categorizes its current configuration, even when the current conditions have changed. This is admittedly counterintuitive from a purely logical perspective — the *halacha* typically focuses on present conditions — yet both Rashi and the Ramban acknowledge this feature and offer their respective explanations for it.

### Length v. Width

The *Baraita*'s prohibition against making an *eruv* for half the city — *ve'ein me'arvin osah lachatza'in* — is now analyzed. Rav Pappa distinguishes between length and width. *Lo amru ella le'orkah* — this prohibition applies only lengthwise, i.e., splitting the city into an eastern half and a western half along the length of the through-street. *Aval lerachvah me'arvin* — but one may divide it widthwise, i.e., splitting the city into a northern half and a southern half across the width of the street.

The scenario is as follows. The city has a major through-street running, say, east to west. The courtyards line up on either side of the street. If one attempts to make an *eruv* for the eastern half of the city as one unit and the western half as another, the problem is that both halves are competing for the same road. Since the entire city was once *shel yachid*, there is a presumption that it is all unified, and any division that creates competing claims over the same stretch of road is untenable. One person cannot use the eastern portion of the road under one *eruv* while another uses the western portion under a different *eruv*, especially when the road is the single artery serving both — or when there is no way to draw a dividing line across the road without both communities needing to cross it.

But if the division is widthwise — say, the north side of the street makes its own *eruv* and the south side makes its own — the problem is less acute, because in principle the north can exit through the northern end of the road and the south through the southern end. They are not competing over the same stretch of road in the same direction.

### Rabbi Akiva Rule

The *Gemara* now asks: according to whose view is this? *Dlo ke-Rabbi Akiva* — this must not be according to Rabbi Akiva, because Rabbi Akiva states in another context: *regel hamutteres bimkomah oseres afilu shelo bimkomah* — a foot that is permitted in its own place can nonetheless make forbidden even a place where it is not normally located. What is Rabbi Akiva's case? If two courtyards are arranged with courtyard B interior to courtyard A — meaning the only way out of B is through A — and each makes a separate *eruv*, Rabbi Akiva says A cannot carry, even though B is *mutteres* in its own domain, because B's presence in A's space (which B must traverse to exit) renders A's domain forbidden.

By analogy, one might think that in our case of the city divided widthwise, the northern half and the southern half each effectively intrude into one another's territory by both needing the through-street, such that Rabbi Akiva would forbid even the widthwise division.

The *Gemara* responds: *afilu teima Rabbi Akiva* — one may explain this even according to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva's ruling applies specifically to *shtei chatzerot zu lifnim mizu* — two courtyards one interior to the other — where *dipnimit leit lei pitcha achrina* — the inner courtyard has no other exit. In that case there is no alternative, and B must inevitably traverse A. Here, however, *hani nafki be'hai pitcha vehani nafki be'hai pitcha* — the north can exit one way and the south another. They are not forced into one another's space, and therefore even Rabbi Akiva would permit the widthwise division.

A second version of Rav Pappa's position is then cited, more stringent than the first: not only may one not divide the city lengthwise, one may not divide it widthwise either. Even the widthwise division is forbidden. The *Gemara* asks: is this like Rabbi Akiva? The answer again is no — even the Sages who disagree with Rabbi Akiva can explain the stringency. The Sages' leniency in the courtyard case rests on the fact that there is a door between the courtyards that can be conceptually closed — *achdi ledasha umishtamsha* — the inner courtyard could shut its door, and it is therefore viewed as if they are fully separate. Here, however, where the dividing line runs across the middle of a public street, *mi matzit mesalekat reshus harabbim mehacha* — one cannot simply remove the *reshus harabbim* from the middle. There is no door to shut, no partition to interpose. The two halves of the city remain interconnected by the open street, and any attempt to treat them as separate *eruv* domains is undermined by their unavoidable shared access to that road. According to this version of Rav Pappa's ruling, the only options are to enclose the whole city under one *eruv*, or to designate each alleyway individually with additional measures.

---

## Alleyways v. City

### Daka Barrier

The *Baraita* had permitted, as an alternative to a citywide *eruv*, making each *maboi* its own *eruv* — *mavoi mavoi bifnei atzmo*. But the *Gemara* asks: if the problem with dividing the city in half is that the two halves compete for the through-street, how do individual alleyways avoid the same problem? After all, each *maboi* opens onto the common through-street, and they would seem to be competing with one another for that shared space just as much as any two halves of the city would.

The answer: *hacha bamai askinan kegon de'avad daka* — the case here is where each *maboi* constructs a *daka*, a small physical barrier at its opening. This is supported by a ruling cited in the name of Rav Chisda: *echad mibnei maboi she'asa daka lepitcho eino oser bnei maboi* — one of the residents of an alleyway who constructs a small barrier (*daka*) at his opening does not thereby create a problem for the rest of the alleyway's residents. The *daka* here is not a full *lechi* or *korah* — it is an actual, even if small, physical barrier — and it signals that this household has effectively withdrawn from the shared domain of the alleyway.

### Courtyard Analogy

This ruling illuminates the mechanics by analogy. In a standard *maboi* configuration, all the *chatzeros* open into the alleyway, and all must join in the *eruv*. If one *chatzer* refuses to participate, it renders the entire alleyway's *eruv* problematic, because its residents remain in a separate domain that impinges on the shared alleyway space. However, if that *chatzer* constructs a *daka* — a real, if modest, physical barrier — it effectively signals that it is not participating in the alleyway's shared space at all. It has removed itself, and the remaining residents of the alleyway may carry without interference.

The same principle applies here. Since the city started *shel yachid*, there is a presumption of unity that causes all domains within it to be treated as if they pull together — meaning each *maboi* is viewed as sharing in the common through-street, and therefore competing with every other *maboi* for it. Under ordinary conditions, of course, individual *maboyim* make their own *eruvin* without difficulty. The problem here is specifically the *shel yachid* origin, which imposes an artificial unity. To overcome this, each *maboi* must make a *daka* at its opening — a real physical barrier — to signal its separation from the common street and from the other *maboyim*. Only then can it make its own independent *eruv* without the concerns that otherwise arise from the city's private origins.

---

## Garbage Dump Case

### Rabbi Zeira Case

The *Gemara* now presents a case study. Rabbi Zeira made an *eruv* for the city of Rabbi Chiyya — *areiv lemasa devei Rebbi Chiyya* — and did not leave over any portion of the city. Abaye questioned him: why did you not leave a section off, as required for a city that started *shel rabbim*? Rabbi Zeira replied that the elders of the city told him that Rav Chiyya bar Ashi used to make an *eruv* for the entire city without leaving anything over. Rabbi Zeira reasoned from this precedent: the only way one can make an *eruv* for the whole city without leaving a section is if the city started as *shel yachid* — private. Therefore, this city must be *shel yachid*, and I followed suit.

### Ashpa Dump

Abaye corrected him. The elders had not told Rabbi Zeira the full story. What they had told *Abaye* was different: *hai ashpa hava lei michad gisa* — on one side of the city there used to be a garbage dump (*ashpa*). A garbage dump is not a proper opening; it effectively closes off one end of the through-street, rendering it a dead-end rather than a full *reshus harabbim*. With only one functional opening, the street was not a genuine *reshus harabbim*, and therefore Rav Chiyya bar Ashi could make an *eruv* for the whole city without difficulty, regardless of whether it started *shel yachid* or *shel rabbim*.

But *vahashta de'afneiyeh le'ashpa* — now the garbage dump has been cleared away. *Havei lei kishnei pesachim va'asir* — the street now has two open ends, constituting a genuine *reshus harabbim*, and making an *eruv* for the whole city is therefore problematic. Rabbi Zeira responded: *lav ada'atai* — I had not considered that; you make a good point.

### Opening Definition

The case thus illustrates that the requirement to leave a section off the *eruv*, and indeed the entire question of whether one may make an *eruv* for the whole city, is not primarily driven by whether the city historically was *shel yachid* or *shel rabbim*. It is driven by whether there is an actual, genuine *reshus harabbim* within the city — a street open at both ends, 16 *amos* wide, through which the public passes. When a garbage dump closed off one end, the street lacked the requisite second opening and was not a *reshus harabbim* at all. Only when both ends are open does the problem arise in earnest. The history of the city's public or private character compounds or mitigates this concern, but the existence of a genuine *reshus harabbim* is the foundational question.

---

## Wall & Ladder

### Rav Nachman Dual

The case of Rabbi Zeira raises the broader question: what constitutes a genuine opening for purposes of *reshus harabbim*? This brings us to a question posed by Rav Ami bar Adda to Rabbah: *sula mikan ufesach mikan mahu* — what is the law if there is a wall on one side and a regular opening (*pesach*) on the other? If the wall effectively closes one end, the street might not be a true *reshus harabbim*. But what if the wall has a ladder (*sulam*) leaning against it — does the ladder count as an opening, making it as if both ends are open?

One view reported in Rav's name is that *sulam torat petach alav* — a ladder has the legal status of an opening. If so, the wall-with-ladder functions like a full opening, the street has openings at both ends, and it is a genuine *reshus harabbim* — with all the attendant stringencies.

Rav Nachman rejected this. He cited a more complete tradition in Rav's name: *sulam torat petach alav vetorat mechitzah alav* — a ladder functions both as an opening and as a partition. It is simultaneously a *petach* and a *mechitzah*. How can it be both? The two functions apply in different contexts.

*Torat mechitzah alav* — it counts as a partition: for purposes of determining whether the street has genuine openings at both ends, the wall with a ladder counts as a wall, not an opening, because the ladder does not remove the wall's status as a physical barrier. Therefore, a street that ends in a wall — even one with a ladder — does not have two open ends, and is not a genuine *reshus harabbim*. This makes it *easier* to make a full-city *eruv*, since the street is treated as a dead-end.

### Two Courts Ladder

*Torat petach alav* — it counts as an opening: this function applies in the context of two courtyards separated by a wall, where the question is whether the two courtyards may optionally join in a single *eruv* or must remain separate. *Ratzu echad me'arev ratzu shenayim me'arvin* — if the residents prefer to treat the two courtyards as one, they may make one *eruv*; if they prefer to treat them as separate, they make two *eruvin*. The ladder allows passage between the two courtyards, and because of this possibility of access, it is treated as an opening — which means the courtyards are legally connected enough to join in one *eruv* if they choose, yet also separate enough to maintain independent *eruvin* if they prefer. The ladder grants the residents this choice.

The elegance of Rav Nachman's ruling lies in its recognition that the *sulam* with a *lechi* serves a dual function simultaneously, and the applicable function depends entirely on the legal question being asked. When the question is: does this constitute a thoroughfare that creates a *reshus harabbim*? — the wall (even with a ladder) counts as a *mechitzah*, closing off the street. When the question is: may these two courtyards join in one *eruv*? — the ladder counts as a *petach*, connecting them. The ladder thus yields the most lenient possible ruling in both directions: it is a *mechitzah* when being a wall helps, and a *petach* when being an opening helps. The *Gemara* will continue to develop this principle further on the next *daf*.

---

---

# Eiruvin 60

## Overlapping Cities & Sta…

### Chazon Ish Squares

Before engaging with the new material on daf 60, it is worth consolidating the key principles established in the preceding discussion. The Chazon Ish addresses the practical consequence of squaring off adjacent cities: if the squared-off boundaries of two cities overlap, they are treated as a single unified area. This has dramatic real-world implications, effectively merging what might appear to be geographically separate municipalities into one contiguous halachic zone.

### 600K Criterion

The broader discussion of cities turning from private to public status, and vice versa, revolves around the question of *reshut harabim*. Rashi holds that the operative criterion is whether the city has the potential to contain 600,000 people, which is the threshold for a biblical *reshut harabim*. The Ramban agrees that the issue is fundamentally about *reshut harabim*, but reads the criterion far more narrowly: it must pertain to actual public ownership of the streets, and he is deeply skeptical of the 600,000-person standard as a halachic measure.

### Leaving Off Sections

The *mishna* established two rules. First, if a city began as a city of the *rabim* — a public city — that identity remains even if its character subsequently became more private. As a result, to signal that this city retains the character of a *reshut harabim*, one cannot make a single unified *eruv* encompassing the entire city. A section must be left off. One explanation is symbolic: the exclusion of a portion reflects the fact that this is not a unified private domain but rather a space belonging to the masses. A related rationale is that it reminds people of the prohibition of carrying — just as some communities once annually suspended their *eruv* on a given day so that people would not forget the underlying *melacha*.

### Unified or Multiple

The second rule in the *mishna* cuts in the opposite direction. If a city began as privately owned — an *ir shel yachid* — even if it has since grown and become more public, the requirement is to make a unified *eruv*, not multiple separate ones. The underlying logic is that such a city retains its identity as a private space, and any shared areas could be halachically problematic without a unified *eruv*. Additionally, the *mishna*'s prior discussion raised the complication of whether one can even make an *eruv* around a genuine *reshut harabim* using only a *tzurat hapetach* or *lechi* and *kora*, since the Gemara had discussed the need for at least one closed end. These distinctions — whether to unify or leave off, and whether an *eruv* can be constructed at all — together frame the opening context of daf 60.

---

## Ladder/Wall Status

### Rav Ami Query

The Gemara now presents a question posed by Rav Ami bar Ada to Rabba. The scenario involves a *reshut harabim* that has a wall on one side with a ladder leaning against it — *sulam mikan u-fetach mikan*, a ladder on one side and an opening on the other. The question is whether this configuration is treated as a genuinely open-ended *reshut harabim* — which would make it impossible to encircle with an *eruv* — or whether the ladder-wall constitutes a sufficient closure. Rav, as reported to Rabba, is said to have ruled that *sulam torat petach alav*: a ladder confers upon the wall the status of an opening, rendering the *reshut harabim* open-ended and problematic for *eruv* purposes.

### Dual Function

Rav Nachman intervenes with a correction, telling the questioner not to accept that account of Rav's position. The accurate tradition, transmitted by Rav Ada bar Ahava in the name of Rav, is more nuanced: *sulam torat petach alav v'torat mechitza alav* — a ladder on a wall functions sometimes as an opening and sometimes as a barrier, depending on which leniency is needed. As a *mechitza*, it renders the wall-plus-ladder sufficient to close off a *reshut harabim*, enabling the construction of an *eruv*. As a *petach*, it operates differently, and the Gemara proceeds to explain when that function applies.

### Two Courtyards

The *petach* function of a ladder is illustrated in the case of *besulam shebein shtei chatzerot* — a ladder positioned between two courtyards separated by a wall. In that context, the ladder functions like a doorway: *ratzu echad me'arvin ratzu shnayim me'arvin* — if the residents wish, they may treat themselves as one courtyard and make a single unified *eruv*; if they prefer, they may treat themselves as two distinct courtyards and each make their own *eruv*. This is precisely the halachic flexibility afforded by an actual doorway. A fully open boundary would force unity; a solid wall would require separation; a doorway — or a ladder functioning as one — permits choice.

This raises a pointed question from the Gemara. Rav Nachman himself had previously cited a ruling from Shmuel regarding *anshei chatzer ve-anshei mirpesset* — the residents of a courtyard below and the residents of a balcony above who share access to that courtyard, and who forgot and did not make a unified *eruv*. The ruling there is that if the people of the balcony placed a small barrier — a *daka* of four *tefachim* — in front of their ladder-access to the courtyard, they are considered legally separate and do not create a prohibition for one another. Without such a barrier, they do forbid one another.

Now, if a ladder has the dual function described — capable of serving as either a *petach* or a *mechitza* — why should such a barrier be necessary at all? If the residents of the balcony wish to treat the ladder as a *mechitza*, they should simply be able to do so and thereby exempt themselves from the *eruv* requirement without constructing any additional barrier. And even if they treat it as a *petach*, a *petach* allows for the choice of separate *eruvin*, so they should still be independent without a *daka*. Why, then, does the *baraita* require the extra barrier?

### Low Balcony

The Gemara resolves this by limiting the *baraita* to a highly specific case: *bidlo gavoah mirpeset asarah* — the balcony is less than ten *tefachim* off the ground. If the balcony is below ten *tefachim*, the concept of a wall-with-ladder is inapplicable, because nothing below ten *tefachim* constitutes a valid *mechitza* in the first place. The balcony residents are effectively considered to be on the ground level, meaning there is no wall and no ladder for halachic purposes — they are simply part of the courtyard.

This immediately generates a follow-up difficulty: if they are considered flush with the ground and the balcony is below ten *tefachim*, then what does the small *daka* of four *tefachim* accomplish? The Gemara answers: *bimgufefet ad eser amot* — the case involves a balcony that is surrounded by a wall on all sides except for a gap of up to ten *amot*. An opening of ten *amot* or more is not legally a *petach* — it is treated as a complete break, not a doorway. Therefore, even though the balcony is low and the residents are treated as being on ground level, the ten-*amah* opening prevents them from being considered separate. Once they place even a small barrier at the top of the ladder access, they effectively narrow that opening below ten *amot*, transforming it back into a valid *petach* — and a *petach* permits separation. The barrier achieves precisely this narrowing, and that is why it helps. The *baraita*, then, is not a general case but a very particular configuration, and it poses no challenge to Rav's position that a ladder on a wall can function as either a *petach* or a *mechitza*.

---

## Continuous Ladders

### Rav Yehuda Position

Rav Yehuda rules in the name of Shmuel: *kotel sheritzo b'sulamot* — a wall that has been covered continuously with ladders, *afilu b'yeter me'eser* — even if it spans more than ten *amot* — still retains the status of a *mechitza*. This requires explanation. The Gemara had established earlier that a gap of more than ten *amot* in a wall is not considered a *petach* but a complete breach, rendering the structure not a wall at all, and two areas separated by such a gap are therefore considered a single space, requiring a unified *eruv*. One might think that a series of ladders covering a continuous eleven-*amah* stretch would operate the same way as a break of eleven *amot*, since the people can cross over freely. Rav Yehuda rules otherwise: the physical presence of the wall itself, even adorned with continuous ladders throughout its entire length, preserves the status of a *mechitza*. The ladders do not transform the wall into an open breach, because the wall remains structurally intact.

### Challenge/Resolution

Rav Bruna challenges Rav Yehuda with a contradiction from the same *baraita* about *anshei chatzer ve-anshei mirpesset* — the people of the courtyard and the balcony who forgot to make a unified *eruv*. The *baraita* states that if there is a *daka* of four *tefachim*, they do not create a prohibition for one another; otherwise they do. The implication seems to be that without the *daka*, the ladder alone — even in a wall — does not suffice to establish separation. But if a wall with ladders is a proper *mechitza*, the ladder on the wall between the balcony and the courtyard should already be sufficient to render them separate without needing any *daka*.

The resolution is the same as before: *hachi asinan delo gavah mirpeset asarah* — the *baraita* is addressing the case where the balcony is less than ten *tefachim* high, so the wall-with-ladder framework is irrelevant. And the further question of why the *daka* helps in that case is answered, again, by the *megufefet ad eser amot* scenario: the *daka* narrows a ten-*amah* gap into a valid *petach*, enabling separation. This is a repetition of the earlier resolution, demonstrating that the *baraita* presents no obstacle to Rav Yehuda's position. Rashi notes in passing that the general principle operative here — that a ladder on a wall can function as either a *petach* or a *mechitza*, whichever is more lenient — reflects the broader principle that in matters of *eiruvin* we apply leniency.

---

## Kakunai Story

### Abaye's Task

The Gemara now relates an instructive narrative. The people of Kakunai came before Rav Yosef and asked him to send them someone who could arrange an *eruv* for their city. Rav Yosef directed Abaye to go, with a specific instruction: *zil eirev lehu*, go and make an *eruv* for them, *ve-chazi delo metzavchu alach be-bei midrasha* — but be careful that they do not have grounds to complain about you in the *beis medrash*. The charge is thus twofold: do the job correctly, but do not impose unnecessary stringencies that would leave people without a proper *eruv* or impose undue burdens upon them. The term *eirev* here clearly encompasses the entire enterprise of halachically preparing a city to permit carrying — far more than simply placing bread.

### River Houses

Abaye arrived and observed that some houses on the edge of the city opened only onto a river — *ptichi le-nahara* — and did not have openings into the public space of the city itself. Since this was an *ir shel rabim*, Abaye needed to identify a section of the city to leave off from the *eruv*. These river-facing houses seemed like an ideal candidate: since their residents accessed the river but not the city's interior, leaving them out of the *eruv* would impose minimal disruption on them. Abaye's initial instinct was to designate them as the *shiyur* — the excluded portion.

### Includability Concern

Abaye then reconsidered. The *mishna* states that one cannot make an *eruv* for the entire city of an *ir shel rabim* — implying that a section must be left off that, in principle, *could* have been included. *Ein me'arvin et kullah* implies *de-va'alei eruvi matzi me'arvei* — that the residents excluded are ones who could theoretically have been part of the *eruv*. The river-facing houses, however, had no openings into the city whatsoever. Since they did not open onto any shared public space, they could not be incorporated into the *eruv* even if one wanted to include them. Leaving off a section that was never includable in the first place does not satisfy the requirement. The *shiyur* must be a section one is choosing to exclude, not a section that was already excluded by circumstance.

### Window Solution

Abaye therefore proposed a solution: *avid lehu kivei* — have them cut windows into their back walls, opening onto the public space of the city. If such windows exist, then in theory these residents *could* access the city and *could* be included in the *eruv* — they would simply have to use the window rather than the river entrance. Their theoretical includability would be established, and Abaye could then legitimately designate them as the excluded portion. The practical reality that they would likely never use the windows, and thus lose little by the exclusion, made them still the most convenient section to leave off.

### Mechuza Model

Abaye then reconsidered again, because requiring residents to break windows into their back walls was exactly the kind of unnecessary burden Rav Yosef had warned him to avoid. He recalled a precedent: Rav bar Avuha had made an *eruv* for all of Mechuza — the Babylonian city — by arranging separate *eruvin* for each neighborhood individually, *arisyata arisyata*, because of the large ditches filled with animal fodder (*peira de-vei tori*) that ran between the neighborhoods and effectively separated them. The principle articulated there was *de-kol chada ve-chada havei shiyur le-chavertah* — each neighborhood's *eruv* serves as the excluded portion for every other neighborhood's *eruv*, so that no single *eruv* encompasses the entire *ir shel rabim*.

The crucial point, Abaye reasoned, is that those ditches would have prevented a unified *eruv* in any case — the neighborhoods could not halachically have been merged. Yet each neighborhood's *eruv* still counted as the required *shiyur* for the others. This suggested that a *shiyur* need not be a section that *could* have been included. By analogy, the river-facing houses — which also could not have been incorporated — could still serve as the legitimate *shiyur* for Kakunai's *eruv*.

However, Abaye immediately challenged this analogy as well: *hadar amar lo dami* — upon reflection, it is not comparable. The Mechuza neighborhoods were separated by ditches, but there was rooftop overhang connecting them — *ibai lei eruvei derech gagot* — meaning one could theoretically have made a unified *eruv* by routing it across the rooftops. The ditches did not represent a complete and total impossibility of inclusion; the rooftops provided an alternative avenue. Consequently, each neighborhood retained theoretical includability, and therefore qualified as a *shiyur*. The river houses, with no window and no rooftop connection, were simply outside the system entirely.

### Grain Storage

At this point Abaye concluded that the windows would after all have to be constructed. But then he recalled yet another precedent: *de-hahu beit tivna de-hava lei le-Mar bar Papidutsa bi-Pumbedita ve-shavyei shiyura li-Pumbedita* — there was a grain storage facility belonging to Mar bar Papidutsa in Pumbedita that was designated as the *shiyur* for the entire city's *eruv*. A grain storage facility is not a residence; it is not the kind of dwelling that could ordinarily be part of a residential *eruv*. Yet it was accepted as a valid *shiyur*.

Tosafot and other *rishonim* address the obvious difficulties: one would need to posit that there was some small domicile attached to the structure (as is required for bridges and graveyards in analogous cases), and regarding the minimum shiur requirement — which Rabbi Shimon sets at three *chatzerot* of two houses each — one would have to say either that the grain facility was one of the three, or that we follow the opinion (to be discussed momentarily) that one house in one courtyard suffices. In any case, the precedent established that a section not naturally part of the residential *eruv* enterprise could nonetheless constitute a valid *shiyur*. Abaye concluded that the grain storage case resolved his problem: the river houses could serve as the *shiyur* for Kakunai without any windows being required. Rav Yosef's instruction — that they should not be yelling about this in the *beis medrash* — was fulfilled: the *eruv* was valid, the excluded section was legitimate, and no resident was burdened unnecessarily.

---

## Shiur Amount

### Chadashah Model

The Gemara now cites a *baraita* establishing the required size of the *shiyur*. Rabbi Yehuda states: *ir achat hayetah bi-Yehuda ve-Chadashah shemah* — there was a city in Judea named Chadashah (this city is explicitly mentioned in Sefer Yehoshua in the inheritance of Judah, as Tosafot notes). *Ve-hayu vo nun diyorin anashim ve-nashim ve-taf* — it had fifty residents, counting men, women, and children together (unlike the count of 600,000, which tallies only adult males). *U-vah hayu misha'arim chachamim* — this city was the model the Rabbis used to define the minimum size of the section that must be left off from the *eruv* of an *ir shel rabim*.

### Chadashah Problem

This immediately raises a striking question: *Chadashah mahu*? What would the city of Chadashah itself do if it needed to make an *eruv* as an *ir shel rabim*? If fifty people is the minimum *shiyur*, and Chadashah has exactly fifty, there is no one left to designate as the excluded portion. One might note in passing that this *baraita* itself is quite difficult to reconcile with Rashi's approach equating *ir shel rabim* with the 600,000 criterion — Chadashah has fifty residents and the Gemara straightforwardly treats the question of its *eruv* as an *ir shel rabim* concern.

The Gemara first assumes that the question concerns not the city of Chadashah as a standalone entity, but a fifty-person neighborhood within a larger city. In that case, the answer is elegant: *Chadashah ke-heichi de-havei shiur le-gedolah, gedolah nami havei shiur le-ktanah* — the same way the fifty-person section is the *shiyur* for the large city, the large city is the *shiyur* for the fifty-person section. Each serves as the other's excluded portion. No unified *eruv* covers everything; each makes its own *eruv* while excluding the other.

### Reciprocal

The Gemara then sharpens the question: *ke-ein Chadashah mahu* — what about a city that is itself like Chadashah, meaning a standalone city of only fifty people? If it must leave off fifty people as its *shiyur*, there is nobody remaining. A city of fifty-one could theoretically have one person left off while fifty make their *eruv* — but even that would require the *shiyur* to be fifty, leaving the excluded party alone and unable to have their own meaningful *eruv*. The question sharpens further as the numbers get tighter.

Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda disagree: one holds that even such a small city requires a *shiyur* in the technical sense, meaning the *eruv* simply cannot be made in full if there is no viable portion to leave off; the other holds that in such a case, no formal *shiyur* is required, presumably because a city so small does not truly carry the character of an *ir shel rabim* to the same degree.

### R. Shimon

Rabbi Shimon disagrees with the premise that fifty people must be left off. In his view, the required *shiyur* is far more modest: *gimmel chatzerot shel shnei batim* — three courtyards, each containing two houses. Rav Chama bar Gurya rules in the name of Rav that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon.

### R. Yitzchak

Rav Yitzchak goes further still: *afilu bayit echad ve-chatzer achat* — even one house within one courtyard suffices as the *shiyur*. The Gemara initially reads this as a courtyard without any house, which would make no sense, since a courtyard without a residential structure has no halachic significance in this context. The Gemara therefore corrects the reading to *bayit echad be-chatzer achat* — one house situated within one courtyard.

### Gemara or Reasoning

Abaye asks Rav Yosef: *ha de-Rav Yitzchak, gemara o sevara* — is Rav Yitzchak's position a received tradition, or did he derive it through independent reasoning? Rav Yosef replies: *mai nafka minah* — what practical difference does it make? Abaye's famous rejoinder: *gemara gmur zmoreta hi* — should we just learn and chant our rulings like a song? The question of whether a ruling derives from tradition or reasoning matters enormously: a position arrived at by independent *sevara* is more open to challenge and debate, while a transmitted tradition carries greater authority.

Tosafot engages with the question of whether Abaye was actually challenging the *halacha* — which would be difficult, since Rav Yitzchak is an *amora* arguing on a *tanna* (Rabbi Shimon), which requires either a tradition or extraordinary reasoning — or merely raising a theoretical point. Tosafot suggests the exchange was more theoretical, while the *Ramo* maintains that even in theoretical terms the distinction between *gemara* and *sevara* has importance. Some *rishonim* do in fact incline toward accepting Rav Yitzchak's position *le-ma'aseh*.

---

## Eruv Techumim

### Two Scenarios

The *mishna* now returns to the topic of *eruv techumim*, after the preceding discussion of *ir shel rabim* and *eruv chatzerot* which had been interpolated within this *perek* — itself a somewhat puzzling arrangement that invites further study. The *mishna* presents two scenarios. In the first: a person is in the east, sends his son to place an *eruv* in the west, and the result is that from him to his house is 2,000 *amot*, but to his *eruv* it is more than that. The ruling is *mutar le-beiso ve-asur le-eiruvo* — he may walk to his house but not to his *eruv*. The *eruv* is ineffective because at the moment *Shabbos* begins, he is more than 2,000 *amot* away from it, making him *chutz la-eruv* relative to the *eruv* itself. Since the *eruv* cannot take effect — one explanation being that a valid *eruv* requires the ability to access it at the onset of *Shabbos* — he reverts to his natural residence as his starting point. Rashi and Tosafot note that this is preferable to certain other failure modes: when an *eruv* fails under some conditions, the person is left with only four *amot*; here, however, since the *eruv* is simply null, his home serves as his default, and he retains the full range of movement centered on his house.
