In the second scenario: to his *eruv* is 2,000 *amot*, but to his house it is more. In this case, *asur le-beiso u-mutar le-eiruvo* — he cannot reach his house, but his *eruv* is effective and he may travel to it.

### Relative to Son

The second scenario raises an immediate geometric puzzle. If the person is in the east, his house is to the west, and he placed his *eruv* even further west, how can he be closer to the *eruv* than to the house? On a straight east-west line, the house must always be closer to him if it lies between him and the *eruv*. The Gemara resolves this by reinterpreting the directional terms: *lemizrach lemizrach beno, lemaarav lemaarav beno* — "east" and "west" in the *mishna* refer to the son's position, not the house's. The person was somewhere, and he told his son to place an *eruv* "to the west" — meaning west of where the son was standing. The *eruv* thus ends up in a location that happens to be closer to the father than the house is, because the geometry is defined by the son's position.

### Diagonal Solution

Rava bar Rav Shila offers a more elegant geometric solution. *Afilu seima lemizrach lemizrach beiso lemaarav lemaarav beiso* — the directional terms may indeed refer to the house. The *eruv* is placed to the west of the house, and the person is to the east. What makes the *eruv* closer than the house? *De-kai beiso be-alkhsona* — the house is positioned diagonally. The person and the *eruv* lie on a straight east-west line, but the house is far off to the side, at an angle. In that geometry, the straight-line distance from the person to the *eruv* is 2,000 *amot*, while the diagonal distance from the person to the house, which lies far to the north or south, exceeds 2,000 *amot*. This is an entirely coherent reading of the *mishna* that requires no reinterpretation of terms.

### Within Extension

The *mishna* then rules: *ha-noten et eruvo be-iburah shel ir lo asah velo klum* — if one places his *eruv* within the squared-off extension of the city (*ibbur ha-ir*), it is entirely ineffective. Since the *eruv* is within the extended city boundaries, and a person who begins *Shabbos* in the city already receives the benefit of all those boundaries plus 2,000 *amot* from the edge, placing the *eruv* within those confines gains nothing. It is already included in the city's base measurement.

### Outside Limits

The *mishna* continues: *nasno chutz la-tchum afilu amah achas, mah she-niskar hu mafsid* — if he placed the *eruv* even one *amah* outside the city's squared-off boundaries, whatever he gains on one side he loses on the other. If the city counts for zero (as the person's *arba amot* of residence), then one *amah* outside the city gives him 2,000 *amot* in one direction but only 1,999 in the other, for a net gain of one *amah* and a loss of one *amah*. Tosafot notes the question of whether the city counts for exactly zero or for four *amot*, and whether the position outside the city similarly counts for four *amot*, and works through the arithmetic at length — the rough principle holds either way.

---

## City Counts Query

### Baraita Position

The *mishna*'s formulation — that placing the *eruv* one *amah* outside the city causes only a one-*amah* net loss — assumes that the city itself counts for zero against the *techum*. But a *baraita* teaches something strikingly different: *hanoten et eruvo betoch ibburah shel ir lo asah velo klum; nasno chutz le-ibbura shel ir, afilu amah achas, mistaker osa ama u-mavsid et kol ha-ir kulah, mipnei she-midas ha-ir olah lo be-midas ha-techum* — if the *eruv* is placed even one *amah* outside the city, one gains that one *amah* but loses the entire city, because the city now counts against one's *techum*. This is a far more severe ruling than the *mishna*, which implies only a one-*amah* exchange.

### Midway vs. Complete

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, kan she-kaltah midato ba-chatzi ha-ir, kan she-kaltah midato be-sof ha-ir* — the two rulings address different situations. If one's 2,000-*amah* measurement ends in the middle of the city — meaning the city is large enough that 2,000 *amot* from one's position does not carry one to the far side — then the city counts against the *techum*, and the loss is the entire city. If, however, the 2,000 *amot* carries one completely through the city to its far end, then the city is entirely contained within the *techum* and counts as nothing — only four *amot* — and one gains 2,000 *amot* in the other direction. The *mishna* speaks of the latter case (a small city fully traversable within 2,000 *amot*); the *baraita* speaks of the former.

### Rav Idi's View

This distinction is attributed to Rav Idi, who cites it in the name of Rav Yehoshua ben Levi. Rav Idi formulates it as follows: if one is measuring off one's *techum* and finds oneself approaching a city, and *kaltah midato be-chatzi ha-ir* — the 2,000 *amot* runs out in the middle of the city — *ein lo ela chatzi ha-ir*, one receives only that half of the city within the 2,000 *amot* and no more. But *kaltah midato be-sof ha-ir* — if the 2,000 *amot* reaches the far end — *na'asit lo ha-ir kulah ke-arba amot u-mashlimin lo et ha-shar*, the entire city is treated as merely four *amot*, and one receives the balance of the *techum* beyond the city.

### Prophecy Debate

Rav Idi himself responds to his own ruling with a striking comment: *ein elu ela divrei nevi'os* — this is nothing but words of prophecy. *Mah li kaltah ba-chatzyah mah li kaltah be-sofah* — what difference does it make whether the 2,000 *amot* ends in the middle or at the end of the city? Either the city counts or it doesn't; why should a distinction that hinges on whether one's measurement ends three steps earlier or later produce such dramatically different outcomes?

Rashi interprets *divrei nevi'os* as a sharp criticism — the phrase is equivalent to saying the ruling has no rational basis, that it is being pronounced ex cathedra without any logical foundation, like a prophet who speaks without offering reasons. In *Torah she-be'al peh*, such arbitrary-seeming distinctions carry no weight unless backed by tradition. Rashi concludes that Rav Yehoshua ben Levi must have had a received tradition for this ruling, because on purely logical grounds he never would have articulated so counterintuitive a distinction.

Tosafot takes a diametrically opposite reading: *divrei nevi'os* here is a compliment, an expression of awe — as if to say, this is such a precise and illuminating insight that it is almost prophetic in quality. The debate between Rashi and Tosafot here is thus about the valence of the phrase, with Rashi reading it as rebuke and Tosafot as admiration. Both agree that the substantive distinction itself is non-obvious; they differ only on whether Rav Idi was criticizing or praising it.

### Rava Response

Rava responds to Rav Idi's challenge — the claim that the distinction is arbitrary — by arguing that in fact both positions are inferable from *mishnayos*, not merely from Rav Yehoshua ben Levi's independent ruling. *Atu Braisa tanya?* — as if this is only from a *baraita*? It follows from our own *mishnayos*. Rava thus defends the distinction not as prophetic intuition but as grounded in standard *mishnaic* reasoning.

### Large/Small Cities

The *mishna* in question states: *anshei ir gedolah mahalchin et kol ir ketanah, ve-ein anshei ir ketanah mahalchin et kol ir gedolah* — the people of a large city can traverse the entire small city adjacent to it, but the people of the small city cannot traverse the entire large city. Rava argues that this *mishna* implicitly encodes exactly the distinction Rav Idi articulated. The people of the large city begin in their city — which, being large, encompasses their full *techum* and more — and when they reach the small adjacent city, their 2,000 *amot* carries them through the entire small city. Since the small city is fully within their *techum*, it counts as nothing and they receive 2,000 *amot* beyond it. The people of the small city, by contrast, begin in their city and their 2,000 *amot* runs out somewhere in the middle of the large city — they do not get through it, so it counts against them and they are stuck. This is precisely the midway-versus-complete distinction.

### Alternative Reading

However, this inference from the *mishna* is not accepted by all. An alternative reading of the *mishna* about large and small cities is proposed — that it is not addressing measurement endpoints at all, but rather the scenario of *nesuyin*, where a person wishes to affiliate his *Shabbos* residence with the other city by placing his *eruv techumim* there. Under this reading, the *mishna* is saying that a resident of either city may choose to place his *eruv* in the neighboring city and thereby walk throughout that city on *Shabbos*. The asymmetry between large and small cities would then reflect different practical constraints of that scenario, not anything about where one's 2,000-*amah* measurement ends. Under this alternative reading, the *mishna* is entirely irrelevant to the midway-versus-complete distinction, and Rava's proof collapses. The Gemara will continue to examine this question in the following daf, pressing further to establish whether the fundamental distinction of Rav Yehoshua ben Levi can be sustained and proven from standard *mishnaic* sources.

---

---

# Eiruvin 61

## City in 2000 Amot

### Mishnah Contradiction

The daf opens with an apparent contradiction between two *mishnayot*. The first *mishnah* teaches that when one places an *eiruv* outside of a city, what one gains on one side one loses on the other — meaning the city does not count against one's 2000 *amot* at all. Yet a second *mishnah*, appearing at the bottom of today's *amud*, states that when a person begins measuring from outside a city and his measurement reaches into the city, he must stop where his 2000 *amot* end, even in the middle of the city. This implies that the city does count against him. The two *mishnayot* thus appear to flatly contradict one another on the question of whether a city is counted within the 2000 *amot* boundary.

### Rav Yehoshua Solution

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction through a distinction introduced by Rav Idi in the name of Rav Yehoshua ben Levi: if the city is completely contained within the 2000 *amot*, it does not count against the traveler at all — he traverses the entire city and continues from its far edge. But if his 2000 *amot* end in the middle of the city, the city does count against him and he may go no further. This distinction reconciles the two *mishnayot* by showing they address different geometric scenarios.

### Divrei Neviyut

Rav Idi himself, having transmitted this teaching in Rav Yehoshua ben Levi's name, then described it as *divrei neviyut* — words of prophecy. The force of this remark is that this crucial distinction was nowhere made explicit in the *Mishnah* itself; it required inspired inference to identify it.

### Gemara Demonstration

The *Gemara* then attempts to demonstrate whether this distinction is in fact derivable from the *mishnayot*. It quotes the *mishnah* at the bottom of today's page: *ulmodeh she'amru nosnin lo alpayim amah, she'afilu sof midato kalah bim'arah* — one who measures from outside is given 2000 *amot*, and even if his measurement ends in the middle of a cave, he stops there. The *Gemara* concedes that it is indeed clear from the text that a city counts against you when your 2000 end in its interior. What was not explicit in the *mishnayot*, and what thus merited the designation *divrei neviyut*, is the converse principle — that when the entire city falls within the 2000 *amot*, it does not count against you at all. That positive half of the distinction was Rav Yehoshua ben Levi's original contribution. And it is this ruling that governs how we *pasken*.

## Big & Small Cities

### Two Girsaot

The *Gemara* now turns to the next *mishnah*, which concerns the relationship between a large city and a small city when they are within range of one another. Rav Nachman notes that there are two textual versions — *girsaot* — of the *mishnah*, and he argues that neither version is necessarily in error. One version reads *anshei ir ketanah* — people of the small city can traverse the big city. The other reads *ein anshei ir ketanah* — the people of the small city cannot traverse the big city. He proceeds to explain how each reading can be correct, depending on which scenario the *mishnah* is describing.

### Measuring Scenario

The version that reads *ein anshei ir ketanah* — the small city cannot go through the big — describes a scenario where each person begins measuring from his own native city. Take as an example a big city of 3000 *amot* and a small city of 1000 *amot* with 900 *amot* between them. The people of the big city travel 900 *amot* to the small city and then traverse its entire 1000 *amot*, all of which falls within their 2000 *amot*, so none of it counts against them, leaving them another 1100 *amot* beyond. The people of the small city, however, travel the 900 *amot* across and then continue 1100 *amot* further — stopping exactly at the middle of the big city, since their 2000 *amot* end there and the big city was not fully contained within them. Hence, *ein anshei ir ketanah mahalchin et kol ir gedolah* — the small city cannot traverse the entirety of the big city.

### Eiruv Membership

The version that reads *anshei ir ketanah* — the people of the small city can go through the big — describes an entirely different scenario: a person who places his *eiruv* in the other city effectively becomes a member of that city. Under this reading, the *mishnah* is not about measuring from one's home city at all, but about the power of the *eiruv* to transfer one's legal affiliation. If the person from the big city places his *eiruv* in the small city, he becomes a member of the small city and is entitled to traverse it entirely and 2000 *amot* beyond. Conversely, a person from the small city who places his *eiruv* in the big city becomes a member of the big city and similarly gets the whole city plus 2000 *amot*. Both can thus traverse each other's cities — not because of their geographic relationship, but because of their *eiruv*-based membership.

### Textual Reconstruction

The *Gemara* notes that the *mishnah* text is incomplete — *chisurai mechasra* — and must be supplemented to make the full contrast explicit. The reconstructed reading inserts a *bameh devarim amurim* clause: when is it that the small city cannot traverse the big? *Bimdud* — when one is simply measuring from one's native city without having placed an *eiruv* in the other. But — and this is how the *mishnah* actually continues — *mi she-hayah b'ir gedolah v'hiniach et eruvo b'ir ketanah*, one who was in the big city and placed his *eiruv* in the small, or was in the small and placed his *eiruv* in the big, may travel the whole of it and 2000 *amot* beyond. The version that reads *ein anshei ir ketanah* thus sets up a contrast: without an *eiruv* in the other city, you are limited; with one, you gain full membership and the complete range of that city.

## Retaining Walls

### Wadi Cities

Rav Yosef, quoting Rami bar Abba quoting Rav Huna, introduces a new principle: a city built at the edge of a river or *wadi* — *ir she-yoshevet al sfat ha-nachal* — requires a *dakah* of four before it is treated as a city for purposes of *techum* measurement. If such a barrier exists, the city is measured from the edge of the wadi as any other city. If it does not, *ein modedin lah ela mipetach beito* — the city is not treated as a unified entity, and each individual must measure from the doorway of his own house. Rashi explains this by analogy to an earlier *sugya* about temporary dwellings: if the settlement is too precarious or impermanent, it cannot be considered a city. A community perched at the edge of a wadi, with no retaining wall to stabilize it, is not considered a sufficiently stable settlement, and so it lacks the legal status of a city.

### Functional vs Symbolic

One might ask why the barrier must be four *amot* rather than four *tefachim*, as is standard in other contexts where a *dakah* or minimal partition suffices. Abaye raises precisely this question with Rav Yosef — you told us originally that the barrier must be four *amot*, not four *tefachim*. Why the difference? Rav Yosef explains: in other cases, *hatam lo bi'ita tashmishta* — one is not afraid to use the space, and so a minimal symbolic barrier suffices to achieve the needed legal separation. Here, however, *hacha bi'ita tashmishta* — without a serious wall, residents are genuinely afraid to use the space at the edge of the wadi. The barrier is therefore not merely symbolic but must be a genuinely functional structure. The requirement of four *amot* reflects this practical, rather than formal, purpose.

### Slope Cities

Rav Yosef then adduces a *baraita* to support this principle. The *baraita* records that *Rebbi* — Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi — permitted the people of Gadgader to descend to Chamtan, but did not permit the people of Chamtan to ascend to Gadgader. Rashi provides a helpful illustration: the two cities sit on a slope, with Gadgader at the top and Chamtan below. Both were within the *techum* of the other, so in principle travel in either direction should have been permitted. Yet *Rebbi* allowed only one direction. The *baraita* offers no explanation, leaving considerable room for interpretation.

### Wall Explanation

Rav Yosef himself proposes the following explanation: *lav mishum dehani avdu dakah v'hani lo avdu dakah* — Gadgader built a retaining wall while Chamtan did not. As a result, Gadgader has the status of a stable city, and its outer edge serves as the point from which its *techum* is measured, bringing it within range of Chamtan. Chamtan, lacking a retaining wall, does not have city status, and its residents must each measure from their own doorways. Only those whose houses happen to be within 2000 *amot* of Gadgader can actually reach it — and those who can benefit from the rule of squaring off can extend their range further. But because Chamtan has no city status, its people do not uniformly reach Gadgader the way Gadgader's people uniformly reach Chamtan. This is how *Rebbi*'s asymmetric ruling reflects the asymmetric physical and legal situation of the two cities.

## Slope Explanations

### Political Takana

Rav Dimi, when he came from Eretz Yisrael, offers a completely different explanation — one that has nothing to do with retaining walls or city status. He explains that the people of Gader were attacking (*mitatrogi*) the people of Chamtan. *Rebbi*'s ruling was therefore not a *pesak* in *hilchos Shabbat* at all, but rather a *takana* — a political decree — issued in his capacity as communal leader to prevent a dangerous situation.

### Power Dynamics

This raises an immediate question: if *Rebbi* feared violence, why did he only restrict travel on *Shabbat*, and why only forbid movement in one direction? The *Gemara* answers the first question by explaining *de'shchichi beshichrus* — on *Shabbat*, when people drink more wine, aggression is more likely to be acted upon. As for the directionality: *kalba belo mataye shev shanin lo navach* — a dog not on its own turf will not bark for seven years. Even though the people of Gader are the aggressors, when they are visitors in Chamtan they will not act out. But when the people of Chamtan enter Gader's territory, they place themselves in genuine danger, since Gader's people on their home ground, drinking on *Shabbat*, become a serious threat. The *Gemara* then anticipates a further question: should we not also be afraid that the people of Chamtan would attack Gader's visitors on their own territory? The answer is *kulei hai lo kaifi lehu* — the people of Chamtan are not powerful enough to harm the stronger Gadgerites even on home turf. The asymmetry of power explains the asymmetry of the ruling.

### Rainbow City

Rav Safra proposes a third explanation, dispensing with the retaining wall and the political considerations alike. He says it was a case of *ir ha'asuya k'keshet* — a city shaped like a rainbow, which creates a complex geometric situation affecting who can reach whom based on where they start.

### Squaring Off

Tosafot's explanation of Rav Safra's view is considerably clearer than Rashi's. Imagine a rainbow-shaped city and a second city nearby. Because the arc of the rainbow is within 4000 *amot* from end to end, the entire arc is treated as a single city. For those who reside within the rainbow city, the rule of squaring off applies — the city is treated as one unit, and from its far side they gain the full benefit of measuring outward. Residents of the upper arc can thus reach the neighboring city and traverse it entirely, all within their 2000 *amot*. But the residents of the neighboring city, starting from outside the rainbow, do not benefit from the same squaring off. When they travel toward the rainbow city, they end up somewhere in its interior — their 2000 *amot* run out before they reach the upper arc. They do not gain access to the full extent of the rainbow city. This is, in essence, a variant of the same underlying principle established at the outset: if the entire city is contained within your 2000 *amot*, it does not count against you; if your 2000 end in the city's interior, it does count against you.

### Simple Big/Small

Rav Dimi bar Chinnena offers the simplest explanation of all: it was a straightforward case of a big city and a small city, where the big city was not fully contained within the *techum* of the small city. Those starting in the big city could traverse the small city entirely since it fit within their 2000 *amot*. Those starting in the small city ended up stranded in the middle of the big city. No retaining walls, no political tensions, no unusual geometry — just the standard rule applied to an ordinary size disparity.

The *Gemara* then records a dispute about attribution: Rav Kahana and Rav Tavyumi disagree about who said which of the final two explanations, whether it was Rav Safra who spoke of the rainbow city and Rav Dimi bar Chinnena who gave the big-city-small-city explanation, or the reverse. What emerges from the full discussion is that *Rebbi*'s asymmetric ruling in the *baraita* about Gadgader and Chamtan admits of multiple readings — a dispute about walls, a political decree, an unusual city geometry, and a simple size disparity — and that the *baraita* itself is sufficiently open-ended to sustain all of them.

Tosafot also notes a textual curiosity: some had the *girsa* in the *Gemara* of *v'od hitir Rebbi* — "and furthermore *Rebbi* permitted." Tosafot explains this as a misreading. The original context, reflected in the *Tosefta*, had an elder testifying before *Rebbi*: *zakhur ani she-hayu bnei Migdal yordim l'Chamtsan ad hachatzer hachitzonah hasmucha l'gesher v'od* — I remember that the people of Migdal would descend to Chamtsan until the outermost courtyard near the bridge and a bit further. The word *v'od* properly belonged to the end of that testimony, indicating they could go slightly beyond. It was subsequently misread as the opening of the next sentence, *v'od hitir Rebbi*, suggesting a new ruling. According to Tosafot's reading, the elder's testimony about how far people previously traveled served as the evidentiary basis upon which *Rebbi* then established the parameters of who could go where.

## Eiruv Membership

### Eiruv Integration

The *mishnah* that we now reach — and which we have already encountered in fragments throughout the preceding discussion — states its rule directly: one who was in a big city and placed his *eiruv* in a small city, or was in a small city and placed his *eiruv* in a big city, may travel the entire city in which his *eiruv* was placed and 2000 *amot* beyond it. The principle is that placing one's *eiruv* in a city makes one, in a meaningful legal sense, a member of that city. This is what allows the person to treat the entire city as his base of operations for *Shabbat*, gaining the full benefit of city membership including the rule that a city completely within one's 2000 *amot* does not count against the measurement.

### Rabbi Akiva

Rabbi Akiva disputes this. He holds that placing one's *eiruv* — one's bread — in another city does not transform one into a member of that city. *Ein lo ela mimakom eiruvo alpayim amah* — he receives only 2000 *amot* from the location of the *eiruv*, not the full extent of the city and 2000 *amot* beyond. To benefit from complete city membership, one must actually have been present in the city when *Shabbat* began. The leniency whereby an entire city within 2000 *amot* does not count against the measurer was stated for actual residents of that city — real city-dwellers — not for those who have only nominal or virtual membership through the placement of an *eiruv*. Rabbi Akiva thus draws a sharp distinction between *me'arev beraglo* — one who establishes his *Shabbat* location through his own physical presence — and one who relies solely on the placement of bread.

### Cave Precedent

Rabbi Akiva then attempts to secure agreement from the *Chachamim* by citing the case of a cave: *ei atem modim li benoten eruvo beme'arah she'ein lo mimakom eruvo alpayim amah* — don't you agree that if one placed his *eiruv* in a cave, he does not receive the whole cave, only 2000 *amot* from the point of placement? The *Chachamim* respond: *eimatai* — when is that so? Only *bezman she'ein bah diyurin* — when there are no inhabitants in the cave. But if people actually live there, *mahalech es kullah vechutzah lah alpayim amah* — one traverses the entire cave and 2000 *amot* beyond it. The logic of the *Chachamim* is that an inhabited space, whether cave or city, functions as a city, and placing one's *eiruv* among its residents makes one legally part of that community.

### Physical Presence

The *Gemara* draws a striking corollary: *nimtza kaltah mima'al gabah* — it is more lenient to place one's *eiruv* inside the cave than on top of it. If one's *eiruv* is placed inside the cave where people live, one gains the entire length of the cave and 2000 *amot* in all directions. If it is placed on the ground above the cave, one is not within any inhabited space, and the benefit of city-like membership does not apply — only 2000 *amot* from that point. This is a clean illustration of the principle: it is inhabited space, not walls alone, that confers the advantage of collective membership.

The final line of the *mishnah* then restates the principle established at the beginning of the daf: one who starts measuring from outside a city receives 2000 *amot*, and even if his measurement ends in a cave — and now we understand why the *mishnah* chose the cave example, since the discussion immediately above involved a cave — he stops precisely where his 2000 *amot* end, regardless of whether anyone lives in the cave. This is the uncontested rule, agreed upon by both Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim*. What divides them is the intermediate case: one who places his *eiruv* in an inhabited city but does not himself begin *Shabbat* there.

## Desolate Cities

### Physical Presence Requir…

Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel now introduces the case of a *ir chareiva* — a desolate, formerly inhabited city, a ghost town. The question is whether such a place retains enough of its former status to confer the benefits of city membership. Shmuel rules: if someone actually began *Shabbat* physically present in a desolate city, *mehalech es kullah vechutzah lah alpayim amah* — he may traverse the entire city and 2000 *amot* beyond it. Physical presence in the ghost town, when *Shabbat* begins, is sufficient to invoke city-level entitlements — even though nobody else lives there.

### Eiruv Insufficient

However, if one merely places one's *eiruv* in a desolate city without being personally present, *ein lo mimakom eruvo ela alpayim amah* — he receives only 2000 *amot* from the location of his *eiruv*. Unlike an inhabited city, where the *Chachamim* hold that placing one's *eiruv* among the residents is sufficient to confer membership, a desolate city has no residents among whom to join. The *eiruv* thus cannot anchor one's membership in a community that no longer exists.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer disputes this limitation. He holds that *echad Shabbat ve'echad heiniach* — whether one physically rested in the desolate city when *Shabbat* began, or merely placed one's *eiruv* there, *mehalechet kullah vechutzah lah alpayim amah* — one receives the entire city and 2000 *amot* beyond. For Rabbi Eliezer, the walls of the former city are sufficient to confer its benefits regardless of current habitation or personal presence.

### Scope Dispute

The *Gemara* raises a challenge from the *mishnah*'s earlier exchange between Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim*. Rabbi Akiva had asked: don't you agree that placing one's *eiruv* in a cave yields only 2000 *amot* from that spot? The *Chachamim* replied: only if the cave is uninhabited; if it is inhabited, one gets the whole cave. The *Gemara* infers: *ha be'eina bat diyurin modi leh* — the *Chachamim* concede that when a place is not fit for habitation, the *eiruv* alone does not suffice. Is a desolate city not in exactly the same position? The *Gemara* distinguishes: *ein re'uyah lediyurah* — the cave is not fit for habitation at all. A ghost town is different; it was once a city, its walls still stand, and it remains in principle habitable. Whether that distinction is sufficient to bring a desolate city within the rule of the inhabited city, or whether it is assimilated to the uninhabited cave, is precisely the question the *Gemara* presses.

### City-Cave Analogy

The *Gemara* then introduces a *baraita* to test this question. The *baraita* states: if one spent *Shabbat* in a city — *afilu hi gedolah k'Antiocha*, even as large as Antioch — or in a cave — *afilu hi k'me'arat Tzidkiyahu*, even as vast as the cave of Tzidkiyahu, the underground tunnels through which the last king of Yehudah attempted to flee — one traverses the entire space and 2000 *amot* beyond. The *Gemara* notes that the *baraita* juxtaposes city and cave: *katani ir dumya d'me'arah* — a city is stated analogously to a cave. Just as a cave is desolate, so too the city is desolate. And it specifies *shavat* — that you must actually begin *Shabbat* there; *aval hiniakh lo* — merely placing one's *eiruv* there does not suffice.

The *Gemara* then asks: *mani* — whose opinion is this *baraita*? If it reflects Rabbi Akiva's view, there is no particular novelty in requiring personal presence in a desolate city, since Rabbi Akiva requires personal presence even in an inhabited city. The *baraita* must therefore reflect the position of the *Rabbanan*, for whom this is a genuine *chiddush*: even though the *Rabbanan* ordinarily allow an *eiruv* to confer membership in an inhabited city, a desolate city is different — only personal presence works there. At this point the *Gemara* challenges the identification of the cave as desolate, since the *baraita* compared it to the cave of Tzidkiyahu, which was hardly inhabited. The *Gemara* resolves this: *k'me'arat Tzidkiyahu v'lo k'me'arat Tzidkiyahu* — the comparison is only to the size of the cave of Tzidkiyahu, not to its desolate character. The cave in the *baraita* is, like the city, assumed to be inhabited; it is comparable to Tzidkiyahu's cave only in its enormous dimensions.

The upshot of the full discussion: according to the *Rabbanan*, one who is personally present in a walled space — inhabited or desolate — at the onset of *Shabbat* gets the full benefit of that space. One who places only an *eiruv* in an inhabited city also gets the full benefit, because the *eiruv* anchors one among real residents. But placing an *eiruv* alone in a desolate city, where there are no residents among whom to join, does not suffice. Whether to extend the *halacha k'divrei hameikel* principle to resolve this last case in the lenient direction is left somewhat open.

## Synagogue Eiruv

### Mar Yehudah Case

A practical case is now related. Mar Yehudah found the people of Mafrachta placing their *eiruv* — *eruvai-hu* — in the synagogue of the house of Agogva. He advised them: *gavu batfei ki hechi di-lish-ru le-chu tfei* — place it further inside, so that more will be permitted to you. The idea is that by placing the *eiruv* deeper into the synagogue — further in the direction of the city they wished to reach — they would gain a greater range of permitted movement into that direction. Mar Yehudah was concerned about Rabbi Akiva's position, under which placing an *eiruv* in a location where one is not physically present does not make one a full member of that space. If that view is taken seriously, the placement of the *eiruv* at the near edge of the synagogue would be less advantageous than placing it deeper inside.

### Inhabited Synagogue

One might ask why the synagogue in this case is treated as a city-like space at all, rather than as bare walls surrounding an uninhabited area. The answer, apparent from Rashi, is that people actually live or regularly gather in this synagogue — *dayarei*, residents. Because the space is inhabited, placing one's *eiruv* there functions like placing it in a city: it makes one a legal member of the community of inhabitants. The key distinction from the desolate city case is precisely this: an inhabited space, whatever its form, allows the *eiruv* to work. It is the desolate, uninhabited space — like the empty cave — for which the *eiruv* alone is insufficient and personal presence is required.

### Lenient Ruling

Rava, however, objects to Mar Yehudah's counsel. *Pag'a ba-eiruvin* — he was acting contrary to the established practice regarding *eruvin*. *Leit lach l'had d'Rabbi Akiva* — we do not give weight to Rabbi Akiva's stringent position in the domain of *eruvin*. Rashi states this explicitly: *d'kaima lan halacha k'divrei hameikel be'eruv* — the established ruling is that we follow the lenient view in all matters of *eruv*. Tosafot similarly affirms this principle. The practical consequence is that Mar Yehudah's instruction to move the *eiruv* deeper inside — motivated by solicitude for Rabbi Akiva's view — was unnecessary. The majority position, and the operative *halacha*, allows an *eiruv* placed in an inhabited location to fully confer membership, without requiring physical presence in that space.

## Non-Jews in Courtyard

### Mishnah Rule

With the conclusion of *Perek Keitzad Me'arvin* — which dealt with *eruv techumin* — the *Gemara* turns to the opening *mishnah* of the next *perek*, which returns to the domain of *eruv chatzeros*, the communal *eiruv* of the courtyard. This topic is more legally intricate, and the *mishnah* opens with a striking rule: *hadar im ha'akum bechatzer* — if one lives in a courtyard with a non-Jew, *o im mi she'eino modeh be'eruv* — or with a Jew who does not accept the validity of *eruv*, *harei zeh oser alav* — that person renders it forbidden. The effect is that the other residents of the courtyard cannot make a valid *eruv chatzeros*.

The underlying logic of *eruv chatzeros* is worth pausing on. The institution is fundamentally about creating a unified community: all the residents of a courtyard join together, pooling their symbolic ownership of the shared space, and are thereby permitted to carry within it on *Shabbat*. The *eiruv* creates a sense of communal cohesion. When a non-Jew or a Jew who rejects the premise of *eruv* shares that courtyard, the possibility of full communal unification is broken. They cannot be meaningfully incorporated into the *eiruv* community — the non-Jew because he is not Jewish, the dissident because he excludes himself. Their presence therefore makes the *eiruv* invalid and carrying in the courtyard forbidden.

### Rabbi Eliezer Exception

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disagrees with a partial exception. He holds that *le'olam eino oser ad she'yehu shnei Yisraelim osrim zeh al zeh* — the prohibition applies only when there are two Jews in the courtyard who are each restricting the other. A single Jew, even when cohabiting with non-Jews or with those who reject *eruv*, does not create a problem. This is somewhat counterintuitive: one might have assumed that the more Jews present, the better the prospects for a valid *eiruv*, and that reducing the number of Jewish participants to one would make things worse, not better. The *Gemara* will explore this further, but the premise appears to be that if there is only one Jewish householder with legal standing over the courtyard, there is no conflict of membership to resolve — the issue only arises when at least two Jews are in a position to obstruct one another.

### Sadducee Story

Rabban Gamliel then reports a case that he saw his father handle. There was a Sadducee — a *Tzeduki*, one who did not accept rabbinic authority and its institutions, including *eruv* — who lived with them in the same *mavoi* in Jerusalem. Rabban Gamliel's father instructed his household: *maharu vehotziu et hakelim lamavoi ad shelo yotzi veye'aser aleichem* — hurry and bring your vessels out into the *mavoi* before he comes out and makes it forbidden to you.

### Waiving Rights

Rashi explains the legal logic underlying this instruction. A *Tzeduki* is treated differently from a non-Jew. A non-Jew, as the *Gemara* will develop, must have his portion formally rented from him in order for the *eiruv* to function — the rental effectively removes his legal standing in the shared space for that *Shabbat*. But a *Tzeduki*, because he is Jewish, can instead be *mevattel reshut* — he can waive or renounce his rights in the shared space. He cannot be an active participant in the *eiruv*, but he can voluntarily surrender his claim over his portion, thereby removing the obstacle his presence creates.

The problem is that *bitul reshut* — the waiver of rights — is revocable. Unlike a formal rental, which transfers rights definitively for the duration of the agreement, a waiver can be retracted. The *Tzeduki* might change his mind and reclaim his portion, at which point the *eiruv* would again be invalid. The strategy Rabban Gamliel's father employed was therefore to assert the community's rights over the shared space *before* the *Tzeduki* could reclaim his — going out and using the *mavoi* first, thereby establishing the others' possession of the space for that *Shabbat*. Once they had used it, his subsequent reclamation could not undo what had already been established for this *Shabbat*.

### Retractable Waiver

Rabbi Yehudah presents an alternative version of the story. In his account, the instruction was: *maharu ve'asu tzorcheichem bamavoi ad shelo yotzi veye'aser aleichem* — hurry and attend to whatever you need to do in the *mavoi* before he comes out and makes it forbidden. The *Gemara* explains the difference: according to Rabbi Yehudah, the *Tzeduki*'s waiver is always retractable. At any moment, he may reassert his rights, and once he does, the *eiruv* is gone. The advice is therefore not to secure the space permanently for the *Shabbat*, but simply to make use of it for as long as he has not yet objected. The practical implication is that there is no mechanism for the other residents to lock in the benefit of the waiver — they must simply act quickly and make whatever use of the *mavoi* they can before he changes his mind.

What emerges from this final *mishnah* and its accompanying narrative is a richly layered set of issues: the distinction between a non-Jew and a Jew who rejects *eruv* with respect to the remedy available; the nature of *bitul reshut* and its revocability; the asymmetry between one Jewish dissenter and two; and the practical legal maneuvering that the rabbis employed to navigate a shared courtyard with a non-cooperative neighbor. The *Gemara* will continue to develop all of these themes in the *dappim* ahead.

# Eiruvin 62

## Eruv Chatzeros Setup

### Perek Overview

The new *perek* marks a transition in the tractate from *eruv techumin* to *eruv chatzeros*, and with it comes an entirely new set of questions: who may participate in the eruv, who renders the courtyard problematic, and what sense of community is being constructed through the institution of *eruv chatzeros* itself. The *perek* addresses the full and fascinating issue of participation, exclusion, and the social reality created when Jews attempt to establish a unified domain in a shared courtyard.

### Mishnah Problem

The opening *mishnah* establishes that if a non-Jew — or someone who does not accept the *eruv*, such as a *Kuti* or *Tzaduki* — resides in the courtyard, that person renders the courtyard forbidden to the Jewish residents. Strikingly, the *mishnah* offers no solution whatsoever; it does not suggest any mechanism by which the problem might be remedied. The non-Jew's presence simply creates a prohibition, and the *mishnah* leaves matters there.

## Abaye's Challenge

### Scene Setup

The *gemara* opens on 62a with a vignette: *Abaye bar Avin* was sitting together with *Rav Chanina bar Avin* — brothers — and *Abaye* was sitting alongside them. The brothers were engaged in a discussion about the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov concerning the effect of non-Jewish residents on the courtyard.

### Meir vs. Eliezer

The dispute under discussion is as follows. Rabbi Meir holds that the presence of non-Jews in the courtyard creates a problem regardless of how many Jews reside there — whether one Jew or two. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, by contrast, holds that the non-Jews pose a problem only when there are two or more Jews in the courtyard. If there is only one Jew — even if he shares the courtyard with ten non-Jews or ten *Kutim* — he may carry freely: from the courtyard into his house, from his house into the courtyard, and even from the courtyard into the non-Jews' houses and back, all without an *eruv*.

### Abaye's Logic

Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chanina bar Avin were reasoning as follows: *bishlama* Rabbi Meir — we understand Rabbi Meir. He holds *diras akum shema dira*: the domicile of a non-Jew is legally considered a domicile. His presence in the courtyard registers as a distinct domain, and since he is not part of the unified community, he disrupts the shared space. Therefore, *velo shna chad velo shna terei* — it makes no difference whether there is one Jew or two; the non-Jew's presence is always problematic.

But what does Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov hold? *Mai kasavar?* If he holds *diras akum shema dira* — that the non-Jew's domicile counts — then *afilu chad nami nitzur*: even with one Jew it should be forbidden. And if he holds *lo shema dira* — that the non-Jew's domicile is legally irrelevant — then *afilu terei nami lo nitzur*: even with two Jews it should be permitted. What, then, is the significance of the distinction between one Jew and two? Make up your mind: either the non-Jew is relevant or he is not.

## Gezeirah Framework

### Non-Jews Not Relevant

Abaye responds by challenging the brothers' foundational assumption about Rabbi Meir. They had assumed that Rabbi Meir's position — that non-Jews are always problematic regardless of how many Jews reside in the courtyard — rests on the principle that *diras akum shema dira*. Abaye rejects this. He says: and does Rabbi Meir truly hold that the non-Jew's domicile is a domicile? The *gemara* then invokes a *baraita* — which will be quoted in full later in the *daf* — stating: *chatzeros shel oved kochavim harei hu ke-diras shel behema*. The courtyard of a non-Jew is like a stable.

This is, as the *gemara* acknowledges, a deeply striking formulation. Steinsaltz suggests that the point is simply that the non-Jew's courtyard is not relevant for *halachic* purposes — that it does not carry the legal weight of a residential domain. Even granting that interpretive charity, the metaphor remains jarring. But the *halachic* point is clear: according to Rabbi Meir, as expressed in this *baraita*, the non-Jew's presence has no effect. It is not as though another person is living in the courtyard for purposes of *hilchot eruvin*; they are simply not part of the Jewish community being legally constituted.

And yet Rabbi Meir says they create a problem. How can one hold simultaneously that the non-Jew's domicile is irrelevant and that their presence makes it forbidden to carry? The resolution, Abaye explains, is that this is not a formal, principled *halachic* problem. It is a *gezeirah* — a rabbinic decree — and a matter of policy.

*De-kulei alma diras akum lo shemei dirah* — everyone agrees, Abaye says, that a non-Jew's domicile is not considered a domicile for these purposes. *Hecha be-gezeirah shema yilmedu mima'asav kamiflegi* — the entire dispute about whether and when non-Jews make the courtyard problematic is a dispute about a rabbinic decree, enacted out of concern that Jews not become accustomed to living among non-Jews.

### Rabbinical Policy

This is quite a remarkable reading of the *mishnah*. The entire structure of the laws governing non-Jews in the courtyard — the prohibition on carrying, the demand for *sechirut*, the various distinctions between one Jew and two — is not rooted in any formal *halachic* category about domain or residence. It is social policy, enacted through the vehicle of *hilchot eruvin*, designed to make it difficult for Jews to establish themselves in mixed courtyards. The rabbis chose *Shabbat* as the point of pressure: they would not tell you what to do during the week, but they would make carrying on *Shabbat* difficult if you chose to live among non-Jews, thereby creating a counter-incentive.

### Community Coherence

This raises a broader point about what *eruvin* actually does. The modern scholar Charlotte Fonrobert has written extensively about *eruvin* and its role in creating coherent Jewish communities — not merely as a matter of architecture or *hilchot reshuyot*, but as a social institution that shapes urban patterns. When an *eruv* is established, property values shift, Jewish families concentrate, and a dense communal reality takes shape. The *eruv* creates a space; people want to carry on *Shabbat*; and so they come together within that space.

One can observe this phenomenon in cities around the world. The contrast is instructive: in Paris, for instance, where no *eruv* exists, Jews are dispersed throughout the city, and the formerly dense Jewish neighborhood that existed before the Second World War — when there was an *eruv* — has dissipated. The *eruv* creates community in a very concrete and measurable sense.

With this in mind, the *gemara*'s explanation of the *mishnah* takes on additional resonance. The rabbis, by making *eruv* more difficult to establish in the presence of non-Jews, were not merely regulating *Shabbat* carrying; they were shaping the social geography of Jewish life, encouraging a concentrated and coherent Jewish community rather than a diffuse, mixed one. The *mishnah*'s silence about any solution — it offers no mechanism for overcoming the non-Jew's presence — may itself reflect this intention. Perhaps, at the level of the *mishnah*, there was no solution at all.

## Eliezer's Logic

### Safety Rationale

Given this *gezeirah* framework, the *gemara* now works out how each *tanna* applies it. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds: *kivan de-oichal imach chashud ashfichut damim* — since a non-Jew who eats with you may be suspected of murderous intent. This reflects the reality of the period in which the *mishnah* was written, when Roman persecution was a genuine and documented danger, and when concern about the intentions of non-Jewish neighbors was not merely theoretical.

Against this background, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov reasons: *trei d'shchichi d'dayri* — two Jews might realistically choose to live together in a courtyard shared with non-Jews, because together they feel less vulnerable. Two Jews would feel secure enough to remain in such a situation. *Gazru behu* — therefore the rabbis made a decree applying to that scenario.

### One Jew Rare

*Chad lo shchiach* — but one Jew living alone in a courtyard full of non-Jews? That is rare. Who would do that? And because that scenario is sufficiently uncommon, *lo gazru bei rabbanan* — the rabbis did not extend the decree to cover it. Therefore, one Jew among non-Jews may carry freely; as soon as there are two Jews, the decree takes effect.

This explanation is admittedly strange. The rabbis are effectively sending a signal — even if unintentionally — that one Jew may live in such a situation but two may not. It is a paradoxical message: we will restrict the more common case and leave the rarer one unrestricted. One might also ask: what about the opposite scenario? If ninety-nine Jews live in a courtyard with one non-Jew, is the non-Jew still problematic for all of them? These difficulties with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position remain, and the *gemara* does not fully resolve them. Nevertheless, what is significant is the underlying framework: this is fundamentally a *takkana* — a policy determination — not a principled ruling about the nature of domains.

## Meir's Position

### Meir's Case

Rabbi Meir's position is now explained within the same *gezeirah* framework. He holds: *zimnin d'mikri v'dayri* — sometimes it happens that one Jew ends up living among non-Jews. The scenario occurs, even if infrequently. And therefore *v'amru rabbanan ein eruv mo'il bimkom oved kochavim* — the rabbis declared that an *eruv* will not be effective in the presence of non-Jews, even though in principle, as established, the non-Jew's domicile is not a domicile. *V'ein bitul reshut mo'il bimkom oved kochavim* — and similarly, even the mechanism of *bitul reshut* — waiving one's rights in the domain — will not solve the problem. Both potential remedies are closed off.

### Sechirut Solution

The one and only remedy, according to this approach, is *sechirut* — rental. *Ad sheyaskir* — only if the Jew rents the non-Jew's domain can the problem be resolved. The *mishnah*, which mentions no solution at all, may reflect a position that nothing works. The *gemara*, however, introduces *sechirut* as a theoretical solution — while simultaneously explaining why it remains practically difficult.

## Rental Problem

### Fear of Rights

*V'oved kochavim lo mugar* — the non-Jew will not want to rent. Why? *Mai taama?* The *gemara* proposes: *ei neima mishum d'savar dilma ati l'achzukei b'reshuso* — perhaps he fears that if he rents his space to the Jew every *Shabbat*, the Jew will eventually come to claim real, ongoing rights in the courtyard. What begins as a formal religious arrangement might be leveraged into a permanent claim of possession. The non-Jew will therefore be reluctant to cooperate.

### Bria vs. Reua'a

But this explanation, the *gemara* notes, works only *haniicha l'man d'amar sechirut bria ba'inan* — if we require a "healthy rental," one with genuine legal substance. *Ela l'man d'amar sechirut reu'a ba'inan* — but if all we require is a "shaky rental," a pro forma arrangement with no real transfer of rights, *mai icha lemeimar* — why would the non-Jew resist? If the entire transaction is obviously a ritual with no practical legal consequences, what does he stand to lose?

The *gemara* here introduces a debate between *Rav Chisda* and *Rav Sheshet*. Rav Chisda holds *sechirut bria* — you need a healthy rental. Rav Sheshet holds *sechirut reu'a* — a shaky rental suffices. The question of what precisely distinguishes the two positions will be explored shortly. The parallel to *mechiras chametz* is apt: how real is the transaction, and which legal system — Jewish or non-Jewish — governs its validity when the two parties operate under different frameworks?

## Bnei Noach Laws

### Pruta Threshold

The *gemara* initially considers whether the distinction between *bria* and *reu'a* concerns the monetary amount involved: perhaps *bria* means giving at least a *pruta* — the minimum halachically recognized coin — and *reu'a* means giving something worth less than a *pruta*. The *gemara* immediately challenges this interpretation with a pointed question: *mi ika l'man d'amar me-akum pachos mishavei pruta lo?* — is there anyone who would say that when dealing with a non-Jew, less than a *pruta* is legally insignificant?

This question is genuinely surprising, since the standard assumption throughout *halachah* is that less than a *pruta* is legally meaningless. Yet the *gemara* asserts that when non-Jews are involved, even less than a *pruta* carries legal weight.

The basis for this is a teaching transmitted by Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *she-sochrim min ha-akum afilu b'pachos mishavei pruta* — one may rent from a non-Jew even with an amount less than a *pruta*. And the conceptual foundation for this principle is supplied by another statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, transmitted by Rabbi Chiya bar Abba: *ben Noach neherag al pachos mishavei pruta* — a *ben Noach* is liable to capital punishment for theft of less than a *pruta*.

### Pruta for Rental

This invokes the broader framework of *sheva mitzvot Bnei Noach*. In that framework, punishment for any violation is in principle *chayav misa* — there are no graduated penalties as there are in Jewish law (restitution, *malkot*, and so on); the single category of liability is capital. But beyond the severity of punishment, the *gemara* is drawing attention to a distinctive structural feature of the *Bnei Noach* laws: the concept of *shiurim* — minimum thresholds — does not apply to them. Any amount of theft constitutes *gezel*. Any portion of *eiver min hachai* constitutes a violation. Any degree of life — including a fetus — is considered life for purposes of the prohibition against *retzicha*.

There is a pattern here: the minimum thresholds that Jewish law carefully calibrates do not operate in the *Bnei Noach* framework. A *kezayis* of *eiver min hachai*, a *pruta*'s worth of *gezel* — these minimum measures are Jewish legal constructs that do not transfer. One might speculate that the *Bnei Noach* laws function on a more categorical level: all stealing is prohibited, full stop, without the nuanced gradations that Jewish jurisprudence developed. The consequence — that liability is triggered by amounts that would be irrelevant under Jewish law — could be understood as reflecting a deliberate policy of categorical simplicity, even if that simplicity carries its own complications regarding the relative stringency of the two systems.

The *gemara* in Sanhedrin does make the assertion that nothing should be permitted to a non-Jew that is forbidden to a Jew. The *rishonim* engage seriously with this principle alongside the apparent discrepancies in threshold and punishment, and the tension is genuine. But the operative point here is that since less than a *pruta* is legally significant in transactions involving non-Jews — because the non-Jew is *makpid* even on the smallest amount — such a minimal payment constitutes a valid rental even by rigorous standards.

### Pruta Debate

This point is explained differently by Rashi and Tosafot. Rashi's explanation, interestingly, inverts the common stereotype: it is not Jews but non-Jews who are *makpid* on the smallest amounts of money. Jews, by contrast, are accustomed to being *mochel* — to forgoing — trivial sums. Therefore, from the non-Jew's perspective as the recipient, even the most minimal payment is genuinely meaningful and sufficient to finalize a transaction. Since the non-Jew takes even a fraction of a *pruta* seriously, such a payment constitutes a valid consideration for the rental.

Tosafot offers a different reading of *v'lo nitan le-hishavon* — the phrase stating that there is no requirement to return the stolen amount. Rashi understands this as a positive commandment: Jews have a *mitzvah* to return stolen objects, while non-Jews do not. Tosafot reads it differently: it means that if a non-Jew steals less than a *pruta* from a Jew, there is no obligation of return — because from the Jew's perspective, less than a *pruta* is not *makpid*-worthy, and the loss is not legally cognizable.

## Bria/Reua'a Detail

### Rashi: Use Rights

Having established that the distinction between *bria* and *reu'a* is not about the amount paid, the *gemara* turns to what it actually means. *Ela bria bimuharki ve-aburgini, re'uah belo muharki ve-aburgini.* Rashi explains that *muharki* and *aburgini* refer to chairs and benches. A *sechirut bria* — a healthy rental — means that the Jew, having rented the space, may fill the entire courtyard with his furniture and effectively exercise physical dominion over it on *Shabbat*; the non-Jew cannot object, because he has rented out his domain. A *sechirut reu'a* — a shaky rental — means the Jew acquires no practical use rights at all; the transaction is purely formal, and he cannot do anything on *Shabbat* he could not have done the day before.

### Tosafot: Registration

Tosafot and the *Aruch* explain these terms differently. *Muharki* and *aburgini* refer to official registration — the degree to which the transaction is formally documented before authorities, something like notarization. A *bria* rental is one that is officially recorded and legally formalized; a *reu'a* rental is informal, unregistered, and legally thin. One might ask whether any rental arrangement between Jews requires such formal documentation — a standard Jewish contract requires witnesses, not notarial records. The question of why a non-Jew's involvement would change this requirement is a fair one, and the answer likely lies in the intent to make the transaction practically difficult.

### Witchcraft Fear

This brings the *gemara* back to its original question: if the rental is purely a *reu'a* — a pro forma ritual with no real transfer of rights — why would the non-Jew refuse to cooperate? The answer: *chashish akum lechshafim* — the non-Jew fears witchcraft, and therefore *velo mogir* — he will not rent.

What does this mean? The *gemara* has a kind of self-awareness here: non-Jews observe Jews performing strange rituals — wires on telephone poles, formal rental agreements for spaces they do not actually use, mysterious weekly transactions — and they do not understand what is happening. The concern about witchcraft reflects the non-Jew's perception of an incomprehensible religious practice. If the entire transaction is obviously not a real rental, then from the non-Jew's perspective it is something else entirely — some form of ritual manipulation of his space, perhaps intended to give Jews mystical power over it. He wants no part of it. The *gemara*'s observation captures something true: if the transaction cannot be explained as a straightforward commercial arrangement, it looks, from the outside, like something uncanny.

## Non-Jew Stable

### Stable Metaphor

The *gemara* now turns to the *baraita* invoked earlier: *chatzeros shel oved kochavim harei hu ke-dir shel behema* — the courtyard of a non-Jew is like a stable. The *halachic* content of this statement, bracketing the troubling metaphor, is that the non-Jew's presence does not create a legally distinct domain for purposes of *hilchot eruvin*. It is not considered a separate *reshut* requiring unification.

### No Jew Present

Therefore, the *baraita* continues, *mutar lehachnis ulehotzi min hachatzer labatim umin habatim lachatzer* — it is permitted to carry from the courtyard into the houses and from the houses into the courtyard. The scenario envisioned here is one in which no Jew is living in the courtyard. A Jew may be visiting his non-Jewish neighbors on *Shabbat* — he is present, but not resident. In that case, since the non-Jews' presence has no *halachic* status as creating a distinct domain, the entire space is treated as a unified area, and carrying is freely permitted.

The underlying principle, again, is that in the absence of any Jew establishing residence in this courtyard, the *takkana* designed to discourage such living arrangements has no occasion to operate. The non-Jews' houses do not, in and of themselves, create the *eruv*-related problems that Jewish houses would create. They are, for these purposes, treated as though they were not separate residential units at all.

### Jew Arrives

The situation changes entirely the moment a Jew moves in. *V'im yesh sham Yisrael echad, oser* — if one Jew takes up residence, carrying becomes forbidden. This is the position of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, as noted, holds that the problem arises only when there are two Jewish residents: *l'olam eino oser ad she'yehu shnei Yisraelim osrim zeh al zeh* — it is never forbidden until there are two Jews who forbid one another.

What is striking about this formulation is how dramatically it illustrates the *takkana* nature of the prohibition. In principle, the non-Jews' presence is entirely irrelevant. The courtyard remains freely usable. The moment a Jew arrives — not because of any change in the non-Jews' status, not because of any new *halachic* reality regarding domains — the entire courtyard becomes forbidden. The prohibition is triggered by the Jew, and its rationale is entirely rooted in the rabbinic policy of discouraging Jewish residence among non-Jews.

## Mishnah Harmony

### Contradiction

The *gemara* now raises a textual difficulty. The *mishnah* states: *hadar im akkum b'chatzer harei zeh oser alav* — one who lives with a non-Jew in the courtyard: the non-Jew renders it forbidden to him. This formulation suggests that it is the non-Jew who imposes the restriction on the Jew. But the *baraita* states: *v'im yesh sham Yisrael echad, oser* — if there is a Jew there, he makes it forbidden. This formulation suggests the opposite: it is the Jew who imposes the restriction, presumably on the ability to carry into the non-Jews' houses. Who is making it forbidden to whom?

### Present vs. Absent

The resolution: *lo kashya — ha d'isa, ha d'leisa*. The two cases differ based on whether the non-Jew is actually present. When the non-Jew is living in the courtyard — *d'isa*, he is there — it is the non-Jew who makes it forbidden to the Jew: the Jew cannot carry freely from his house to the courtyard and back, because of the *gezeirah* against living among non-Jews. When the non-Jew is absent — *d'leisa*, he is not there — it is the Jew who imposes a restriction: specifically, the Jew's presence makes it forbidden to carry into the non-Jews' houses.

## Presence Matters

### Jews Always

The *gemara* now draws out the full implications of this distinction. By Jews, the rule is different: a Jewish resident creates a *halachic* problem even when he is not home. If five Jews live in a courtyard and four of them go away for *Shabbat*, the absent four still require their rights to be addressed in the *eruv*. Jewish residents create a real, formal *halachic* issue — a genuine problem of *reshuyot* — and therefore even their absence does not eliminate the need to include them.

### Non-Jews When Home

By non-Jews, the situation is different. Since the entire problem is rooted in a *gezeirah* — a policy concern about the reality of Jews living among non-Jews — the problem only applies when the non-Jews are actually present. *De-chi ita assar, de-chi leita lo assar* — when he is home, the decree applies; when he is not home, it does not. The concern that motivated the decree — the reality of cohabitation in a mixed courtyard — does not exist when the non-Jew is simply away. Therefore the rabbis did not extend the decree to that scenario.

### Left House Case

A challenge to this principle: does the *mishnah* not teach that one who leaves his house and goes to spend *Shabbat* in another city — *ha-maniach et beito ve-halach lo lishbot be-ir acheret* — is still considered to make the courtyard forbidden? And the case of *echad akum ve-echad Yisrael oser divrei Rabbi Meir* — the *mishnah* seems to indicate that even an absent non-Jew continues to impose a restriction. If so, how can we say that a non-Jew who is not present creates no problem?

### Same-Day Return

The *gemara* resolves this: *hatam de-ati beyomei* — that case concerns a situation where the non-Jew has not gone far and might realistically return on the same day. Since there is a genuine possibility that he will be present during *Shabbat*, the rabbis treated his status as though he were still there. But if he has genuinely gone away and cannot return that day, the decree does not apply and he does not render the courtyard forbidden.

## Rulings Summary

### Shmuel Rules

Having established the theoretical framework, the *gemara* turns to *pesak*. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel halachah ke-Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* — Rav Yehuda rules in the name of Shmuel that the *halachah* follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. This is a leniency: the problem arises only with two Jewish residents, not one.

## Paskening Before Reb (II)

### Abaye Asks

Abaye poses a question to Rav Yosef: *kaima lan mishnat Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov kav ve-naki* — it is a standing principle that the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is like a sifted measure of grain: compact, precise, and authoritative. Furthermore, Rav Yehuda explicitly rules in the name of Shmuel that the *halachah* follows him. One might add that the principle *halachah ke-divrei ha-meikel be-eruv* — in matters of *eruvin*, we follow the lenient opinion — points in the same direction. Given all this, Abaye asks: *mahu le-oruyei bimkom rabbo* — is it permitted to render this ruling in the presence of one's *rebbe*?

## Rulings Summary (II)

### Minhag View

Before turning to Rav Yosef's response, the *gemara* notes two additional positions. Rav Huna says *minhag* — accepted practice is in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. According to Rashi, this means that we do not make a public pronouncement about it, but if anyone asks a *shaila*, that is how we *pasken*. The *minhag* is operative but not loudly proclaimed.

### People Practice

Rabbi Yochanan formulates it differently: *nahagu* ke-Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — people practice in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. This is a weaker endorsement: Rabbi Yochanan might personally prefer a different *psak*, but since the practice has become widespread, he does not intervene to overturn it. If asked directly for a ruling, he would give a stricter answer; but he accepts the established practice as a fait accompli.

## Paskening Before Reb (II)

### Yosef Answers

Rav Yosef responds to Abaye's question with a vivid example. *Afilu be'ata be-kutcha ba'u minei mi-Rav Chisda kol shenei de-Rav Huna ve-lo ori* — even the question of whether one may eat an egg dipped in a milk-based condiment (*kutcha*), the students would pose to Rav Chisda throughout all the years that Rav Huna was alive, and Rav Chisda would refuse to rule. Even so obvious and elementary a question — one that any child would know the answer to — Rav Chisda would not answer in the presence of his *rebbe* Rav Huna. The implication is unambiguous: when your *rebbe* is present, you do not issue rulings, regardless of how self-evident the answer may be.

### Written Law

Rav Yaakov bar Abba then poses a further challenge to Abaye: *kegon Megillat Taanit* — what about a case involving *Megillat Taanit*? This is a book that lists the days on which fasting and eulogies are prohibited. If someone asks: may I fast today, or may I deliver a *hesped* today — and the answer is written explicitly in the book, right there on the shelf (*de-ketiva u-mancha*) — is stating that answer considered *paskening*? Is it not merely reading from a text? And yet *mahu le-oruyei be-atra de-rabbeih* — is it permitted even to do that in the locale of one's *rebbe*, even if not in his immediate physical presence?

## Tosafot Qualifies

### Prevent Sin

Tosafot qualifies the sweeping prohibition against *paskening* before one's *rebbe* in several important ways. The first qualification: one may rule that something is *assur* in order to prevent an actual transgression. If a person asks a question and there is a real possibility that, without receiving an answer, he will proceed to do something forbidden, the student may step in and declare the act *assur*. The duty to prevent an *issur* from being committed overrides the prohibition against *paskening* before the *rebbe*.

### Hypothetical OK

Tosafot's second qualification: if the question is not a practical *shaila* — if the person is not asking for a ruling to govern his immediate conduct but is raising the matter as a hypothetical, as part of *talmud Torah* discussion — then responding is permitted. The prohibition against *paskening* applies to actual *pesak halachah*; academic engagement with *halachic* questions, even in the form of "how would you rule in such a case," does not cross that line. Tosafot acknowledges that many people frame practical questions as hypotheticals, but the principle stands: a genuinely theoretical discussion is not *paskening*.

### Novel Issue

Tosafot's third qualification pushes against what the *gemara* seems to say on its face: even in cases of actual *pesak*, the prohibition applies only when there is a real *chiddush* involved — a novel point of law or interpretation. If the answer is genuinely and completely obvious, it is not really *paskening*. Tosafot reads the cases cited in the *gemara* not as examples of self-evident law but as cases that contain a genuine *chiddush*.

### Examples

On this reading, the case of the egg in *kutcha* is not the trivial question it appears to be. What was actually asked, Tosafot argues, was a more complex case: a chicken was slaughtered (*shecht*) and an egg was found still inside it. The question — is that egg *fleishig*? — involves a genuine *chiddush*, not an obvious answer. Similarly, the question about *Megillat Taanit* involved some non-obvious *halachic* nuance about the scope or application of that document's provisions. In both cases, the *chiddush* is what makes it a genuine act of *paskening* — and therefore something that Tosafot holds must involve a *chiddush* in order to be prohibited before one's *rebbe*. Tomorrow's discussion will continue to explore the precise contours of this prohibition: what exactly the concern of *kvod rav* entails, how it applies when so much of *halachah* is now codified in writing, and where exactly the line falls between *talmud Torah* and *pesak*.

---

---

# Eiruvin 63

## Ruling b'Makom Rav

### Non-Jewish House Debate

The daf begins against the backdrop of a dispute in the *Mishnah* concerning whether a non-Jewish house situated in a *chatzer* creates a halachic problem for *eruvin*. According to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, such a house is only problematic when there are two Jews in the *chatzer*; a single Jew presents no difficulty. The *Gemara* rules in accordance with his position, and this ruling immediately raises a sensitive question: may a *talmid* issue this ruling *b'makom rav* — in the presence of, or within the jurisdiction of, his teacher? The *Gemara*'s instinct is that even an apparently obvious *psak* creates a problem. Even something as clear-cut as an egg cooked in milk, or a ruling recorded in *Megillat Taanit*, cannot be decided by a student in his teacher's presence. The prohibition, it seems, is categorical.

### Tosafot's Qualifications

Tosafot, however, introduces three significant qualifications that soften this categorical picture. The first is the case of *afrushe mei'issura*: if someone is about to commit a prohibition and is asking whether something is *assur*, the student must answer. Tosafot understands that even framed as a *shaila*, if the answer is *assur*, responding falls within the obligation to prevent another from sinning — a category the *Gemara* will address explicitly in a later passage. The second qualification is that purely theoretical Torah discussion is permitted; only issuing a practical ruling to a practical question is restricted. The third, and perhaps most consequential, qualification concerns cases where the ruling genuinely requires no judgment whatsoever — where the answer is truly self-evident and involves no real weighing of factors. Tosafot suggests that in such cases there is no prohibition, though this sits in some tension with the *Gemara*'s apparent absolutism.

### Perception & Kavod

What, then, is the underlying concern? Tosafot makes clear that the prohibition is fundamentally about *kavod ha-rav* — respect for one's teacher — and that perception plays a central role. Reading from the relevant passage in Tosafot on 62b, four lines from the bottom of the long *tosafot* beginning *v'amar Rav Chisda*: *v'amar Ri d'davka b'davar shenirei chiddush l'shoel* — the Ri explains that the issue is specifically when the ruling appears to the questioner as a *chiddush*, as something novel and authoritative. Even *Megillat Taanit*, though written down, is not known to everyone, and someone who does not know the *Shulchan Aruch* may experience even a well-established ruling as a *chiddush* when a student pronounces it in the teacher's presence.

The key line follows: *v'lo naktinu ela l'ashmi'inan d'afillu b'hanei shehatalmid be'atzmo yodea she'ino toeh* — even in a case where the student himself knows with complete certainty that he is not making an error, it is still *assur l'horos* if the questioner perceives it as a *chiddush*. The prohibition, in other words, is not merely about the epistemological status of the ruling — it is about whether the act of ruling carries the appearance of a student assuming authority in his teacher's presence. That perception itself constitutes a breach of *kavod ha-rav*.

### Tosafot Examples

Tosafot continues: *aval davar shehashoel yodea sheyadu'a minhago shel davar* — but something that even the questioner himself essentially already knows, such as *nosein ta'am lifgam*, is different. When a person asks about a pot that hasn't been used for days and is really just seeking reassurance rather than a genuine ruling, and the answer is not experienced as a *chiddush* when pronounced — *k'shomoreh lo heter ein zeh karui davar chiddush* — that is permitted. Tosafot thus draws the line not around the difficulty of the question per se, but around whether the act of answering will be experienced as an exercise of independent rabbinic authority. The examples of *megillat taanit* and *beita b'chutcha* are understood not as cases of genuinely trivial rulings but as cases where, for at least some questioners, the ruling carries the weight of a novel determination.

---

## Historical Cases

### Rav Chisda & Hamnuna

The *Gemara* at the bottom of 62b and the top of 63a records a series of historical cases that illuminate the practical scope of this prohibition. Rav Chisda issued rulings in Kafri during the lifetime of Rav Huna, his teacher — but Kafri was a different city. Then Rav Hamnuna issued rulings in Charsa de'Arga during the lifetime of Rav Chisda. The symmetry is pointed: what Rav Chisda did to his teacher, Rav Hamnuna did to him. This raises the question of what geographic scope the prohibition covers. Is it limited to the same room, the same city, or does it extend across an entire country?

### Ravina's Knife

The question becomes sharper with Ravina. The *Gemara* reports that *Ravina sar skina be'Bavel* — Ravina inspected knives in Bavel — during the lifetime of Rav Ashi, who was also in Bavel, though not in the same city. Rav Ashi challenged him: *mai ta'ama avid mar hachi* — why are you doing this? I am still alive.

It is important to understand what knife inspection (*sar skina*) represented. When a new rabbinic figure arrived in a city, the *shochtim* would present their knives for inspection. This was not primarily about the technical halachic question of whether the blade was acceptable; it was a symbolic gesture that declared who held rabbinic authority over the community's *kashrut*. The *Gemara* later makes this explicit: *lo amru le'harot sakin le'chacham ela mipnei kvodo shel chacham* — the reason for showing a knife to a sage is precisely on account of the sage's honor, as a demonstration of authority. This is why the act raised the issue of *kavod ha-rav* even more starkly than a routine ruling might: it was a public claim to institutional authority, not merely an answer to a *shaila*.

### Rav-Talmid Chaver

Ravina defended himself by citing the case of Rav Hamnuna ruling in a different city during Rav Chisda's lifetime. Rav Ashi corrected him: two versions of that story circulate — one in which Rav Hamnuna ruled and one in which he did not. In fact, both versions are accurate and refer to different periods. When Rav Huna was alive, Rav Hamnuna did not rule even in another city, because Rav Huna was his full *rav*. After Rav Huna died, Rav Hamnuna did rule in Rav Chisda's lifetime — *de'talmid chaver dilei hava* — because by that point his relationship with Rav Chisda was that of a *talmid chaver*, a student-colleague, not a full subordinate student. As a *talmid chaver*, he had greater latitude, at least when operating in a different city.

Ravina then applied this logic to himself: *ve'ana nami talmid chaver de'mar ana* — I too am your student-colleague. Since their relationship had matured beyond the strict *rav-talmid* dynamic, the latitude afforded a *talmid chaver* should apply to him as well, permitting the knife inspection at least when conducted in another city.

### Authority Gesture

The *Gemara* then confirms what was implicit throughout: the act of showing a knife to a sage was never about a *psak shaila* in any technical sense — it was entirely about the gesture of rabbinic authority. This is why Ravina's act raised the problem in the first place and why the discussion turns on the nature of the relationship between the parties rather than on any halachic complexity of the knife itself.

---

## Modern Framework

### Shulchan Aruch

The *Gemara*'s treatment of this topic finds its halachic codification in the *Shulchan Aruch* under *Hilchot Kavod Rav* in *Yoreh De'ah*. The *Shulchan Aruch* states plainly: *ve'assur le'adam le'horot lifnei rabbo* — it is forbidden to issue rulings in one's teacher's presence. The prohibition extends beyond the teacher's literal physical proximity: *aval likvo'a atzmo le'hora'ah lashevet le'horot afilu besof ha'olam assur le'horot ad sheyamut rabbo o ad sheyiten lo reshut* — even to establish oneself as a decisor anywhere in the world is forbidden until the teacher dies or explicitly grants permission. That permission — *reshut* — is a substantive halachic concept, not merely a courtesy.

### Semicha

This brings into focus the halachic function of *semicha* in the modern period. Contemporary *semicha* serves two distinct roles. The first is sociological: it functions as a form of licensing, informing the community that this individual has demonstrated the knowledge and competence to render halachic decisions and can be relied upon. The second, and halachically operative, role is that it constitutes a *reshut hora'ah b'makom rabbo* — the teacher's explicit authorization for the student to rule even in his presence.
