The *Shulchan Aruch*'s formulation *o ad sheyiten lo reshut* encompasses precisely this: the *yoreh yoreh* that appears on a *semicha* certificate is not merely an honorific but a formal grant of halachic permission to rule even where the teacher is present. Without such permission, absent the teacher's death, issuing rulings would constitute a violation of this prohibition.

### Disagreement

One might ask how this framework coexists with the give-and-take of *Torah she-be'al peh*, in which students and later authorities regularly dispute and disagree with their predecessors and teachers. The *Rema* addresses this directly, noting that *mutar lachlok alav be'eizeh psak o hora'ah im yesh lo re'ayot ve'hochachot le'devarav she'hadin imo* — one may dispute even a teacher's ruling if one can bring evidence and proof that the law is otherwise.

The *Pitchei Teshuva* on *siman* 242 takes up a related concern. He cites the *Teshuvat Chut HaShani*, in which a complaint was lodged against an authority for disagreeing with earlier *poskim* — and worse, for suggesting that those *poskim* had overlooked a *Gemara*. The *Chut HaShani* responds that there is nothing objectionable about this: *she-kol dor va-dor lo nimnu le'hasig al gedolim she-lifneihem* — every generation has always argued with and critiqued the authorities that preceded it, and this is the very nature of *Torah she-be'al peh*. Indeed, framing a disagreement as "perhaps they did not have access to this *Gemara*" is itself a form of respect — it attributes the divergence to circumstance rather than error. The distinction the *Pitchei Teshuva* preserves is between the free discourse of *Torah she-be'al peh*, which is unrestricted, and the specific act of assuming practical decisory authority in one's teacher's presence, which the prohibition addresses.

---

## Ravina & Innkeeper

### Ravina Declines

The *Gemara* presents a further case involving knife inspection. Rava had taught: *tzurba me'rabanan chazi l'nafshei* — a *talmid chacham*, even a student, may inspect his own knife before slaughtering his own meat. This is categorically different from the symbolic act of inspecting a *shochet*'s knife as an assertion of communal authority; inspecting one's own knife for one's own purposes is simply managing one's own *halachic* life and carries none of the authority-laden implications of the formal inspection ritual.

Ravina came to Mechuza — Rava's city, where Rava was the recognized rabbinic authority. His host, an innkeeper, brought him a knife before slaughtering an animal, showing it to him for inspection. Ravina declined: *zil amteih l'Rava* — go bring it to Rava. This is Rava's city and Rava is the authority here.

### Pre-Purchase Issue

The innkeeper pressed back, citing Rava's own ruling that a *talmid chacham* may inspect for himself. Ravina's response was precise: *ana mizban zavina* — I am going to be purchasing this meat from you. At the moment of inspection, the animal has not yet been slaughtered and the meat is not yet his. Because he would only acquire it after the fact, inspecting the knife now is not inspecting for himself but for someone else — it is an exercise of authority over the *shechita* of meat that is not yet his. The permission to inspect for oneself does not extend to this case.

---

## Two Visiting Rabbis

### Respect for Elder

The *Gemara* presents another scenario involving knife inspection that turns on a more subtle point. Rabbi Eliezer mi-Gronya and Rav Abba bar Tachlifa came as guests to the home of Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika, in the locale where Rav Acha bar Yaakov — a different figure — was the established halachic authority. The host wished to prepare a fine calf (*igla tilsa*) for his guests and brought out a knife, showing it to the two visiting rabbis for inspection. Rav Abba bar Tachlifa raised an objection: *lo lachush lei l'saba* — should one not show concern for the elder, meaning Rav Acha bar Yaakov, the local authority? Ought the knife not be brought to him, as the one whose rabbinic jurisdiction covers this locale?

### Eliezer's Citation

Rabbi Eliezer mi-Gronya dismissed the concern. He cited Rava's ruling — *tzurba me'rabanan chazi l'nafshei* — and reasoned that since the two visiting rabbis were going to eat this meat, they were effectively inspecting for themselves as guests who would be consuming it.

### Punishment & Resolution

The *Gemara* then reports: *chazi v'ianash* — they inspected the knife, and Rabbi Eliezer mi-Gronya was punished. Something befell him, understood as divine retribution for proceeding with the inspection. The *Gemara* challenges this outcome: had not Rava himself taught that a *talmid chacham* may inspect for himself? The resolution is pointed: *shani hasam d'atchilu bichvoda* — the case is different here because they had already introduced the question of showing it to the local authority. Once Rav Abba bar Tachlifa raised the idea of deferring to Rav Acha bar Yaakov, the matter of his honor was on the table. To then dismiss that consideration — to say "never mind, we'll go ahead anyway" — transformed the act from a neutral inspection into an affirmative rejection of the elder's honor. Had the question never been raised, proceeding would have been unproblematic. But once it was raised and then set aside, the inspection became an act of disrespect rather than a permissible exercise of self-interest.

### Rav Acha Muflag

An alternative explanation is offered: *shani Rav Acha bar Yaakov d'muflyag* — Rav Acha bar Yaakov was exceptional. Rashi explains *muflyag* as meaning he was *harbeh me'od zaken ve'chacham* — exceptionally old and wise, a *gadol* of singular stature. When the authority in question is of such exceptional distinction, the ordinary permission for a *talmid chacham* to inspect for himself may not apply; the standards of deference are correspondingly elevated.

---

## Afrushe Mei'Issura

### Rava's Teaching

The *Gemara* now records Rava's explicit ruling on the exception carved out for preventing sin: *l'afroshe mei'issura afilu bifnei rabbo shafir dami* — to stop someone from committing a prohibition, even in one's teacher's presence, is entirely permissible. This was already anticipated by Tosafot's first qualification. What the *Gemara* now adds is a formal, named principle: *afrushe mei'issura* is not merely a practical concession but a recognized category that overrides the ordinary restrictions of *b'makom rav*.

### Ravina's Niddui

The *Gemara* presents a dramatic case. Ravina was sitting before Rav Ashi — in his immediate presence — when he observed a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on *Shabbat*. Using a tree that is attached to the ground (*mechubar*) on *Shabbat* is prohibited. Ravina called out to the man to stop; the man ignored him. Ravina then declared: *lehavyei hai gavra b'shamsa* — this man should be placed in *niddui*. Having done so, Ravina turned to Rav Ashi and asked: *ki hai gavna mi chazai k'apikorsus* — does this seem like *apikorsus*? The term *apikorus*, as the *Gemara* in Sanhedrin explains in the famous *Mishnah* of those who have no share in the *olam ha-ba*, refers to one who is *m'vazeh talmid chacham* — who flagrantly demeans Torah authority. Ravina was asking whether his own act of imposing *niddui* in Rav Ashi's presence might itself constitute that kind of affront — an act of rabbinic authority exercised in the presence of the greater authority, and thus a form of disrespect.

### God's Honor Override

Rav Ashi's response draws on a principle from elsewhere in the *Gemara*: *ein chochma v'ein tevuna v'ein eitzah l'neged Hashem* — there is no wisdom, understanding, or counsel in the face of God. *Kol makom she-yeish bo chillul Hashem ein cholkin kavod l'rav* — wherever there is a desecration of God's name, one does not defer to the honor of the teacher. This ruling goes further than simple *afrushe mei'issura*. In this case, the man had already ignored Ravina's verbal intervention and was not being stopped. Imposing *niddui* was not about preventing the act — the act was proceeding — but about publicly defending the honor of God and of the Torah. To allow that act to pass without consequence, in that society, would have been understood as a failure to stand up for divine authority. In such a case, the teacher's honor is entirely displaced by the imperative to defend God's honor, and the student is not only permitted but obligated to act.

---

## Consequences

### Rava's Statement

Having established the nature and exceptions of the prohibition, the *Gemara* now turns to its consequences. Rava formulates the graded framework: one who rules *halacha* literally in the teacher's physical presence — *befanav* — deserves heavenly death. One who does so outside the teacher's physical presence — *shelo befanav*, meaning perhaps the same city or same country, depending on the analyses above — commits a prohibition, but is not deserving of death.

### Bnei Aharon

The *Gemara* immediately challenges the second part of this statement. The *Tanna* Rabbi Eliezer teaches: *lo mesu Bnei Aharon ad she-horu halacha bifnei Moshe Rabbeinu* — the sons of Aharon died specifically because they issued a ruling in the presence of Moshe, not merely because of the *eish zarah* they brought. The *drasha* is from the opening of *Tzav*, where the *pasuk* states that the sons of Aharon should place fire on the altar. They derived from this that despite the heavenly fire that descended when the *Mishkan* was inaugurated, it is still a *mitzva* to bring fire from an ordinary source. That act of independent legal derivation — *darash* — in Moshe's presence was the sin. The problem was not the fire itself but the assumption of decisory authority in the presence of the supreme authority. Tosafot notes a minor difficulty — those *pesukim* refer to the outer altar, while Nadav and Avihu brought the *ketoret* on the inner altar — but the *Gemara*'s point stands that the death was a consequence of ruling *befanav*.

### Eliezer's Student

A second proof follows. Rabbi Eliezer had a student who issued a halachic ruling in his presence. Rabbi Eliezer said to his wife Ima Shalom: *tamiah ani im yotzi zeh shenaso* — I would be astonished if this person lived out the year. And indeed he did not. When Ima Shalom marveled at what seemed like prophecy, Rabbi Eliezer replied: *lo navi anochi velo ben navi anochi* — I am no prophet. *Ela kach mekubalni* — I have received this as a tradition: *kol hamoreh halacha bifnei rabbo chayav mita* — whoever rules halacha in the presence of his teacher deserves death.

### Three Parsaos

The *Gemara* then cites Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: that student was Yehuda ben Guria, and he lived three *parsaot* from Rabbi Eliezer — twelve *mil* away. This seems to prove that even *shelo bifanav*, even at a meaningful distance, the punishment of death applies, which would undermine Rava's distinction.

The *Gemara* responds: *bifanav havay* — it was actually considered "in his presence." The three *parsaot* referred to where Yehuda ben Guria lived, not where he issued the ruling relative to Rabbi Eliezer. But why mention where he lived at all? *Shelo tomar mashal haya* — so that one does not dismiss this as a *mashal*, a parable rather than a real event. The biographical detail — his name, his father's name, his place of residence — establishes the historicity of the account. The *Gemara* therefore resolves the challenge: Rava's distinction between *befanav* and *shelo befanav* stands, and the consequence of heavenly death is limited to one who rules literally in the teacher's presence.

---

## Snake Bite & Sinner

### Snake Bite

Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan offers a parallel formulation: *kol hamoreh halacha lifnei rabbo ra'uy lehakhisho nachash* — whoever rules halacha before his teacher is deserving to be bitten by a snake. This echoes the gravity of *chayav mita* but expresses it through a somewhat different image.

### Biblical Verses

The *Gemara* derives this from *Iyov*, where Elihu ben Barkhel ha-Buzi says: *tza'ir ani l'yamim ve'atem yeshishim al ken zachalti* — I am young in years and you are elders, therefore I *zachalti* — held back. The word *zachalti* evokes *zochel*, to slither, as in a snake; and this is linked to the *pasuk* *im chamat zochelei afar* — with the venom of those who slither in the dust. One who does not restrain himself in the presence of his elders deserves precisely what he evoked by failing to *zachal*.

A further formulation, cited by Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina, tones the consequence down further: such a person is simply called a *chotei* — a sinner. The *pasuk* is from *Tehillim*: *belibi tzafanti imratecha l'ma'an lo echta lach* — I have stored your words in my heart so that I not sin against You. Holding back one's words in the presence of a greater authority is itself the fulfillment of this verse; speaking when one should remain silent is the sin.

### David & Ira

Rav Hamnuna observes a contradiction between two verses attributed to David. One verse says *belibi tzafanti imratecha* — I have held your words in my heart — suggesting David kept Torah wisdom to himself. Another says *bisarti tzedek b'kahal rav* — I have proclaimed your righteousness to a great congregation — suggesting David taught publicly and freely. The resolution: *lo kashya*. The first verse describes the period when Ira ha-Yairi was alive — Ira ha-Yairi, in the rabbinic reading, served as David's teacher — and during that time David refrained from teaching in his presence. The second verse describes the period after Ira ha-Yairi was no longer living, when David was free to teach. The case of David and Ira ha-Yairi thus provides a biblical paradigm for the entire discussion: the restriction applies only during the teacher's lifetime, and with the teacher's passing, the student's full authority is unlocked.

---

## Yehoshua

### Responding Lose Children

Rabbi Levi introduces a further and sharper consequence: *kol ha-mosif mila lifnei rabbo* — whoever adds a word in the presence of his teacher — meaning whoever responds to a question asked of the teacher, interjecting before the teacher has an opportunity to answer — *ozil li-she'ol be-lo banim* — goes to his grave without children. This is a severe consequence, more visceral in its nature than death by divine decree, and it signals that the problem of responding to another's question in the teacher's presence carries distinct weight.

### Numbers Verse

The *Gemara* derives this from the episode in *Bamidbar* where Yehoshua bin Nun responds to the report that Eldad and Medad are prophesying within the camp: *va-ya'an Yehoshua bin Nun mesharet Moshe mi-bechurav va-yomar adoni Moshe kela'em* — Yehoshua rose up and said, my master Moshe, restrain them. The irony is profound: Yehoshua was acting out of zeal for Moshe's honor, seeking to protect his teacher's unique prophetic authority. Yet the very act of interjecting his own response — of answering a situation that was presented to Moshe — was itself a breach of the deference he owed. The subsequent genealogical record lists: Nun, his son Yehoshua — and stops. Nowhere in *Tanach* do we find that Yehoshua had children.

### Jericho Siege

The *Gemara* notes that this conflicts with the view of Rabbi Abba bar Pappa, who provides an entirely different explanation for Yehoshua's childlessness: *lo ne'enash Yehoshua ela bishvil she-bitel et Yisrael laila achat mi-pirya ve-rivya* — Yehoshua was punished for having prevented the Jewish people from engaging in procreation for one night. This explanation is grounded in the episode at Jericho. The *pasuk* states: *va-yhi bi-hyot Yehoshua bi-Yericho* — when Yehoshua was at Jericho — and describes an encounter with an angelic figure standing with a drawn sword. Yehoshua asked: *ha-lanu ata im le-tzareinu* — are you with us or against us? The angel replied: *ani sar tzva Hashem ata bati* — I am the commander of God's army; I have come now.

The *Gemara* fills in the dialogue. The angel charged Yehoshua on two counts: the afternoon *tamid* sacrifice had not been brought the previous evening, and now, during the siege of Jericho, the people were neglecting *Talmud Torah*. Yehoshua asked which failure was more serious; the angel answered that it was the neglect of *Talmud Torah*. Tosafot notes the difficulty of knowing how the *Gemara* derives these details, and offers an interpretation based on the language of Yehoshua's original question — *ha-lanu ata im le-tzareinu* — reading *ha-lanu* as an allusion to *Torah tziva lanu Moshe* and *le-tzareinu* as an allusion to the sacrifices that protect from *tzarot*. The angel's answer, *ata bati* — I have come now — signals that the current, pressing failure is *Talmud Torah*, not the sacrifice.

The *Gemara* then adds: *mi-yad va-yalen Yehoshua ba-laila ha-hu be-toch ha-emek* — and Yehoshua immediately went and spent that night in the depths of *halacha*, learning Torah, correcting the failure. Rabbi Yochanan comments: *melamed she-halach be-omka shel halacha* — this teaches that he immersed himself in the depths of *halacha*.

### Wrong Ark

Having presented the account of Yehoshua's neglect of *Talmud Torah* — which in its original form concludes there — the *Gemara* now grafts onto it the explanation for Yehoshua's childlessness invoked by Rabbi Abba bar Pappa. A tradition is cited: *de-gmiri de-chol zman she-aron u-shchina shruyim shelo bi-mkomam asurim be-tashmish ha-mita* — whenever the Ark and the divine presence were not in their proper place, marital relations were prohibited. Since Yehoshua brought the Ark to the Jericho campaign, the people were forbidden to engage in *tashmish ha-mita* during that period.

Tosafot addresses the difficulty: the Ark was regularly brought to war — we know this from David's era and the case of Uriah — and yet there is no general prohibition on marital relations during wartime campaigns. Tosafot resolves this by distinguishing between two Arks. After Moshe descended from Sinai and broke the *luchot*, he fashioned a wooden Ark to house the fragments; a second, gold-inlaid Ark was constructed for the *Mishkan* to hold the whole *luchot*. Normally the wooden Ark with the broken *luchot* would be brought to war, and in that case marital relations remained permitted. On a few occasions — including the episode when the Ark was captured by the *Plishtim* — the gold Ark was taken instead, and that is when the prohibition applied. Tosafot suggests that Yehoshua's error was precisely this: he took the wrong Ark to war, thereby imposing the prohibition on the entire camp. The childlessness then follows as *midah keneged midah*: he prevented an entire night of legitimate marital intimacy, and so he himself was left without children.

As Tosafot notes, these two explanations — responding to a question in Moshe's presence, and taking the wrong Ark — are two independent *midrashim* that the *Gemara* has joined together. The primary *drasha* of the Jericho passage, as it circulates elsewhere, is about *Talmud Torah*, and the material about *tashmish ha-mita* is appended to it here to serve the explanation of Yehoshua's childlessness.

### Talmud Torah Priority

With this episode as its springboard, the *Gemara* arrives at a sweeping general principle, cited by Shmuel bar Ina in the name of Rav: *gadol Talmud Torah yoter me'hakravat temidin* — *Talmud Torah* is greater than offering the daily sacrifices. The proof is the angel's own declaration: *ata bati* — I have come now, on account of this — referring to the neglect of *Talmud Torah*, not of the *korbanot*. This principle deserves to be appreciated in its full cultural weight: the *Gemara* is addressing an audience that understood the *Beit ha-Mikdash* and its sacrificial service as the apex of religious life. To assert that *Talmud Torah* supersedes even the *tamid* offering is a bold statement of rabbinic values, one that helped define the character of Jewish religious experience in the absence of the Temple.

---

## Marital Intimacy

### Rav Huna

The discussion of *tashmish ha-mita* leads naturally to a cluster of teachings about the sanctity of marital intimacy and the obligations that flow from it. Rav Huna states in the name of Rav: *kol ha-yashan be-kila she-ish ve-ishto shruyin bah* — whoever sleeps in a tent, meaning a room, in which a husband and wife are dwelling — *alav ha-katuv omer n'shei ami te-gareshun mi-beit ta'anugeha* — of him the *pasuk* says: the women of my people you have driven from the house of their pleasure. By inserting himself into the couple's private space, a person effectively drives husband and wife apart, preventing the intimacy they are entitled to. The *pasuk* applies to such a person as though he had forcibly separated them.

### Rav Yosef

Rav Yosef extends this further: *va-afilu be-ishah niddah* — even if the wife is a *niddah*, and physical relations are in any case prohibited, the presence of a third person in the room still violates the couple's intimacy. This is a striking ruling. Even when there is no possibility of sexual relations, the couple is entitled to emotional closeness and private space, and a person who intrudes on that space is held accountable by the same *pasuk*.

### Rava Disagrees

Rava takes a different view: *im ishah niddah hi, tavo alav berachah* — if she is a *niddah*, one should actually sleep in that room, as a kind of guardian to prevent any potential transgression. Rava then immediately deflates this suggestion: *v'lav hi, de-ato idi man natra* — but actually, this does not hold. Who keeps them apart on all the other days of the year? They keep themselves apart. The *halacha* of *niddah* is observed by the couple themselves, without the need for external supervision. To post oneself in their room as a chaperone is to show distrust where trust is owed, and the ruling stands with Rav Yosef: one does not enter the couple's space, even when she is a *niddah*.

---

## Modern Framework (II)

### Written Rulings

The *Shulchan Aruch* preserves a notable position on how the prohibition of *hora'ah b'makom rav* adapts to a world in which Torah law is comprehensively codified in written texts. The *Shulchan Aruch* records: *yeish mi she-kasav she-kol ha-kasuv be-sfarim mi-piskei ha-geonim yachol le-horot bi-mei rabbo* — there is an opinion that anything written in the books of the *Geonim* may be ruled upon even during one's teacher's lifetime. The limitation is equally clear: *rak lo yoreh davar mi-libo ve-lo yismach al ha-ketav li-lmos milsa le-milsa me-atzmo* — but one may not rule from one's own judgment, and may not rely on written texts to reason independently from case to case on one's own. The permission to convey what is already written does not extend to the exercise of independent judgment even with written texts as one's basis.

### Consulting Books

The *Shevut Yaakov* draws out the full implications of this shift. Since we live in a world where Torah law is written down, and since the written books are the repositories of transmitted wisdom in a way that previously only living teachers were, the *Shevut Yaakov* teaches: *oy le-chol mi she-higia le-hora'ah she-lo yoreh shum hora'ah bilti iyun techilah ba-sefer* — woe to anyone who has reached the status of a decisor and issues any ruling without first consulting the books. The reason: *ki raboseinu hein hein ha-sfarim asher nispashtu be-kerev Yisrael* — our teachers are the books that have spread among the Jewish people. The living teacher has, in a meaningful sense, been succeeded by the codified tradition. The obligation of *b'makom rav* — not to rule in the teacher's presence — now primarily expresses itself as an obligation not to rule without consulting the *sfarim* that embody the accumulated authority of all previous generations.

---

---

# Eiruvin 65

## Drunkenness & Kavana

### Non-Jew Ownership

The daf begins in the middle of a digression that arose from the discussion of how to handle a non-Jew's ownership in a shared courtyard. The *Gemara* had noted that if a non-Jew has Jewish hired hands working on his property, those workers may be treated as owners and can thereby participate in an *eruv*. This observation prompted Rav Nachman to remark approvingly about the quality of the *psak*, which in turn opened a lengthy digression about the conditions under which a ruling may or may not be issued — and specifically about the problem of issuing rulings while drunk.

### Rav Nachman on Psak

The digression was set in motion by Rav Nachman's observation connecting the pleasure of a fine *psak* with the warning against *paskening* while drunk. The *Gemara* had already established that issuing *halachic* rulings in a state of intoxication is inappropriate, and that observation serves as the launching point for the extended discussion that follows throughout this section of the daf.

### Drunk & Liability

As reviewed from the previous session: a drunk person remains fully liable for his actions and any business transaction he enters into is binding — unless he has reached the extreme state of intoxication comparable to Lot, where he has literally no awareness of what he is doing. At the same time, even a lesser degree of drunkenness suffices to exempt a person from *davening*, because prayer requires the capacity to stand before God as one would stand before a king — a standard of composure that intoxication undermines.

### Magein Avraham

The *Gemara* now presents a statement by Rabbi Chanina: *kol hamaphsik magein b'sha'at ga'ava, sogrin v'chosmin tzarot ba'ado* — anyone who *maphsik* (passes over, or alternatively, does not reveal) *magein* at the time of *ga'ava*, his enemies are handed over and sealed away from him.

Rashi explains that *magein* here refers to *Magein Avraham*, the first *berachah* of the *Amidah* — the one for which *kavanah* is most essentially required. The word *ga'ava* is understood in connection with drunkenness, carrying the connotation of self-indulgence or self-absorption. Rashi draws support from a *Gemara* in *Berachot* that interprets the *pasuk* *v'oti hishlachta acharei gevecha* — "you have cast Me behind your back" — with the play *al tikrei gevecha ela ge'echa*, meaning: after a person has attended to his own bodily needs through eating and drinking, turning to *daven* is an act of placing God second. The concept of *ga'ava* is thus set in opposition to the proper disposition for prayer. The reward for passing over *Magein Avraham* under such circumstances is, fittingly, that the protection promised in that *berachah* — the divine shielding of Avraham from his enemies — is instead granted to the one who abstains. The *pasuk* cited is *ga'ava afikei m'ginim, sagur chotam tzar* — the *ga'ava* of shields, with the enemy closed and sealed.

### Afik Etymology

The *Gemara* now subjects the key word *afik* to linguistic scrutiny. On what basis does the term *aphik* mean "to pass over"? The proof is from the *pasuk* *k'aphik nechalim ya'avoru* — "like the rushing channels of wadis they will pass by." The *afikim* here are those dramatic seasonal watercourses familiar from *Shir HaMa'alot*'s image of *k'aphikim ba'Negev*: dry gulches in the Negev that erupt into powerful flash floods when rain falls. The term *aphik* is thus connected lexically to *ya'avoru*, the root meaning to pass over or through.

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different reading. He agrees that the one who is drunk should not say *Magein Avraham*, but he understands *maphsik* in the opposite etymological direction: not "passes over" but "reveals." Thus according to Rabbi Yochanan, the phrase means that one does not *reveal* or *articulate* *Magein Avraham* — one does not say it aloud. His proof text is *vayeira'u afikei mayim* — the *afikim* of water were *revealed* — where the cognate word *afikei* is linked to the verb *vayiglu*, "and they were revealed." The practical upshot, however, is the same in both readings: the person who is drunk should not recite *Magein Avraham*. The *Gemara* itself acknowledges this near-equivalence: *michdi, kra mashma bein lomar bein lomar* — the *pasuk* implies more or less the same thing either way. So what, then, is the practical difference between the two formulations?

### Rav Sheshet Sleep

The *Gemara* answers: *ika beinaihu d'Rav Sheshet* — the practical difference emerges in the case of Rav Sheshet. When Rav Sheshet was drunk, he would hand over his sleep to his attendant — that is, he would instruct his attendant to wake him after a set amount of time, such as an hour, so that he could sleep off the intoxication and then proceed to *daven*.

Rashi explains the dispute as follows. If the obligation is framed in the positive — one must *pass over* the drunkenness, allowing it to fully run its course — then merely setting an alarm, so to speak, is insufficient. One must wait until one wakes naturally. But if the obligation is framed in the negative — one must simply refrain from *actively revealing* (i.e., reciting) *Magein Avraham* while consciously intoxicated — then one need not proactively wait out every last effect. Waking after a period of sleep arranged in advance is sufficient. The difference between stating the rule in the positive (pass it over) versus the negative (do not reveal it) thus translates precisely into this question about whether Rav Sheshet's practice is valid.

The *Maharsha* further notes the connection to an earlier discussion in which the *Gemara* distinguished between drinking a *revi'it* of wine versus more: a small amount of wine might be ameliorated by a little sleep, while a larger amount is worsened by exertion. Now the question is refined further — does waking naturally differ from waking by an attendant's call? These are subtle but internally consistent distinctions.

### Chananel & Yetzer

*Tosafot* cites Rabbeinu Chananel, who offers a strikingly different reading of the entire passage. He explains that *ga'ava* here does not refer to drunkenness at all, but to the *yetzer hara* — the evil inclination. On this reading, the *Gemara* is raising a classic question in the psychology of moral struggle: when battling one's *yetzer hara*, should one attempt to sublimate and suppress it (the "pass over" approach, in which the desire is pushed down without being directly confronted), or should one expose and confront it directly (the "reveal" approach)? This is a question of moral strategy — do you deal with inner drives by suppression or by direct engagement?

*Tosafot* then works to connect this alternative framing back to the question about Rav Sheshet: if the issue at stake is how to handle the state of drunkenness itself, does one sleep it off passively (an act of suppression, allowing the condition to resolve on its own), or does one actively work through it, as the *Gemara* earlier suggested by the strategy of walking? Rabbeinu Chananel's reading opens the *Gemara* to a broader discussion of how human beings should deal with their various drives and distractions — not only the specific case of *Magein Avraham*.

### Unsettled Mind

The *Gemara* now transitions from drunkenness to a related but broader concern: the requirement of *da'as meyushevet* — a settled mind — as a precondition for *davening*. Rav Chiya bar Ashi said in the name of Rav: *kol she'ein da'ato meyushevet alav al yitpalel* — anyone whose mind is not settled upon him should not pray. The proof text offered is *batzar al yoreh* — in anguish, do not rule. This is a striking application: the *pasuk* speaks of issuing legal rulings, yet the *Gemara* maps it onto prayer. Rashi himself notes that he searched for this *pasuk* throughout all of Scripture and could not find it, suggesting it may originate in *Sefer Ben Sira*, which the *Gemara* sometimes quotes with the formula *dechtiv*, treating it with a quasi-canonical standing. *Tosafot* offers a series of alternative suggestions, including the possibility that it is a paraphrase of another *pasuk* rather than a verbatim quotation.

The connection between *paskening* and *davening* is itself worth examining. The requirement to stand before God in prayer presupposes an awareness of Whom one is addressing, and there are at least two distinct components to this awareness: the appropriateness of one's general state (as with drunkenness, where one's very condition is unseemly before God), and the more cognitive requirement of being able to focus on the words one is saying. The *Gemara* does not formally subdivide these, but the transition from drunkenness to *da'as meyushevet* suggests a movement from the former concern toward the latter.

The *Gemara* also notes, earlier in the amud, the expression *shikhura v'lo miyayin* — drunk but not from wine — as a description of the entire period since *galut* began. This had already introduced the idea that distractedness, not only literal intoxication, is the operative concern. That theme now becomes explicit.

Rav Chanina, we are told, would not *daven* on a day when he became angry — *beyoma dertach lo matzli*. He too cited *batzar al yoreh*: in anguish, do not rule — and again translating the language of *psak* into the context of *davening*. The *Gemara* notes the curiosity of applying a formulation about *paskening* to the act of prayer, particularly given that the source text may not even be canonical Scripture.

Mar Ukva, for his part, would not go to the *beit din* to serve as a *dayan* on days of *shusah* — a hot, dry, windswept day that made concentration difficult. Here, uniquely, the concern is explicitly about *paskening*, not about *davening*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak crystallizes the principle: *hilchasa ba'ya tzilusa* — halachic ruling requires clarity, like a day of northern wind, a cool, clear, focused day. Rashi adds that the *Maharsha* understands *k'yoma d'istana* not necessarily as a literal north wind but as a metaphor for an ideal, cloudless spring day: the kind of mental clarity that one should bring to the seat of judgment.

### Clarity for Rulings

This observation about *hilchasa ba'ya tzilusa* points to a genuine asymmetry between the standards for *davening* and for *paskening*. One might initially suppose that judgment demands more rigorous clarity than prayer — and in terms of consequences, that may well be true. But prayer, unlike a postponable court case, carries a time-bound obligation: if one does not *daven*, one may forfeit the *mitzvah* entirely. The *Gemara* nonetheless indicates, consistently across this entire passage, that the preferred course of action when one lacks the required state of mind is to refrain from *davening* rather than to *daven* improperly.

A further asymmetry worth noting is that *paskening* can be delegated or postponed — another *dayan* can hear the case, or it can wait for a better day. The forfeiture of prayer, by contrast, is final. Yet the *Gemara* maintains that an improper *tefillah* is worse than no *tefillah*. At the same time, there is a *machlokes* among the *Rishonim* — the *Rambam* maintains a biblical obligation to pray daily, while the *Ramban* holds that the only biblically mandated prayer is *be'eis tzarah*, in a time of affliction. Interestingly, the *Gemara* here says the opposite: it is specifically in a state of anguish or agitation that one should *not* pray. The resolution is that the *Ramban* refers to external affliction that generates a desire to turn toward God in supplication, whereas the *Gemara*'s exemption concerns internal distraction or agitation that prevents focused *davening*. The former is the condition par excellence for meaningful prayer; the latter is its enemy.

### Distractibility Tales

The *Gemara* now moves from institutional standards to personal anecdotes, offering a series of vivid illustrations of the distractibility of even the greatest *Amoraim*. Abaye said: if his mother — the nursemaid who raised him, frequently quoted in the *Gemara* on matters of healing and medicine — would say to him in the middle of learning, *karei kucha* (bring me the dip), *lo tanoei*: he could no longer learn. Whether the interruption threw him entirely off his stride or left him too preoccupied until the request was fulfilled, the point is the same: even a minor external demand shattered his concentration.

Rava said — and some say it was Ravina — *itratztin kina, lo tanoei*: if a louse bit him, he could not learn. It is difficult not to find this humanizing. These are figures of towering intellectual achievement, and yet a mosquito bite — or its ancient equivalent — was enough to derail them entirely. The *Gemara* is making a serious point about the conditions required for genuine learning: distraction is not a minor inconvenience to be pushed through but a substantive impediment to the kind of clarity that the tradition demands.

The *Gemara* then adds that the mother of Mar the son of Ravina — and if the previous statement was attributed to Ravina, perhaps it is no coincidence — made for him seven garments, one for each day of the week. Fresh garments, being less likely to harbor lice, would remove that particular source of distraction from her son's learning.

### Night Learning

The discussion of optimal conditions for learning naturally raises the question of timing. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *lo ivri leilya ela leshinta* — the night was created for nothing other than sleep. The implication is that serious learning belongs to the daylight hours, and attempting to learn at night is working against the natural order. Reish Lakish takes the opposite view: *lo ivri saira ela legirsa* — the moon was created for nothing other than study. Night, illuminated by the moon, is itself an invitation to learn.

*Tosafot* is troubled by the absolute formulation of Rav Yehuda's position and qualifies it: the statement refers specifically to the long summer nights, when sixteen or more daylight hours are available for learning and sleep can reasonably fill the nighttime. But in winter, when nights are long and days short, nighttime learning is not only permitted but expected. The *Maharsha* suggests a harmonization: the two opinions are not really in dispute, since moonlit nights are well-suited for learning while pitch-dark nights favor sleep. He also notes, with some wit, that Reish Lakish — who had spent part of his earlier life as a bandit — may have been more naturally at home in the night hours.

### Learning Examples

Rabbi Zeira was asked why his teachings were so sharp and penetrating. He replied: *deymamei ninhu* — those are things I learned during the day. He did not claim to learn exclusively by day, but he attributed his depth of insight specifically to his daytime study.

The daughter of Rav Chisda once asked her father whether he did not need to sleep at all, given that he learned straight through the night. He replied: *hashta atu yomei de'arichi veketini veninum* — soon enough, the days that are long and short will come, and there will be plenty of time to sleep. Rashi explains that these are the days of death, which are long for sleeping and which offer no opportunity whatsoever for *mitzvot*. The exchange is reminiscent of the famous story of the Vilna Gaon, who, upon a rare visit from his sister after twenty years of separation, greeted her briefly and returned to his learning, saying they would have time to talk in *Olam HaBa*. This *Gemara* is arguably the source of that ethos. It is worth noting, however, that here Rav Chisda is simply declining to sleep — he is not neglecting a person to whom he has concrete obligations. The *Gemara* elsewhere does engage with the tension between total immersion in learning and one's responsibilities to family and community, a tension that different authorities resolve quite differently.

### Day Workers

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak declares: *ana poalei d'yimami anan* — we are day workers. The phrase evokes the teaching of *Pirkei Avot*: *hayom katzar v'hamelacha merubah v'hapoalim atzelim u'va'al habayit dochek* — the day is short, the work is great, the workers are lazy, and the Master of the house is pressing. Here the emphasis falls on the day: we work when there is daylight, and the night is our time off — for sleep.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov took a more pragmatic approach: *yazif u'para* — he would borrow and pay back. The *Maharsha* explains that his primary learning was conducted during the day, but if something came up and disrupted his daytime schedule, he would make up the lost time at night. Nighttime study was not his preferred mode but served as a reserve against unavoidable interruptions to his daytime regimen.

---

## Prayer Conditions

### Travel Recovery

The *Gemara* turns from internal states to external circumstances as conditions affecting prayer. Rabbi Elazar rules: *haba min haderech al yitpalel shelosha yamim* — one who returns from a journey should not pray for three days. For the *Amoraim*, a journey was an arduous undertaking, far removed from the minimal inconvenience of modern travel. The proof text is from Ezra: *va'ekbetzem el hanahar haba el Ahua vanachana sham yamim shelosha va'avina ba'am* — I gathered them by the river and we rested there for three days, and then I understood. The *Maharsha* notes that the very next *pasuk* references prayer, implying that only after three days of recovery does one attain the clarity needed to pray properly.

Practical application: the father of Shmuel, *avuha d'Shmuel*, would not pray for three days after returning from a journey — *lo matzli tlata yomei* — following this ruling precisely.

### Environmental Avoidance

Shmuel himself would not pray in a house in which drinking had been taking place — *lo matzli b'veita d'is bei shichra*. Whether the smell of alcohol, the ambient atmosphere, or some other associative quality made such a setting incompatible with prayer, this was Shmuel's personal standard, though the *Gemara* does not present it as an objective *halachah* applicable to all.

Rav Pappa would not pray in a house containing *harsana* — a particularly pungent fried-fish dish — *lo matzli b'veita d'is bei harsana*. The overpowering odor made concentration impossible for him. This example is perhaps easier to relate to than the drinking case, as a truly noxious smell is an immediate and visceral impediment to *kavanah*. One might note the anecdote of a student who asked a *rabbi* whether it was permissible to pray near the smell of cattle on a *kibbutz*, only to receive the reply: "What smell?" — a reminder that what constitutes a distraction is, at least in part, a function of habituation.

---

## Wine Aggada

### Wine & Appeasement

Rabbi Chanina opens the *aggadic* passage on wine with the following teaching: *kol hamitpateh b'yaino yesh bo midas kono* — anyone who can be appeased through wine possesses a quality of his Creator. The proof text is *vayaryach Hashem es reiach hanichoach* — God smelled the pleasing aroma of the sacrifice and declared that He would no longer curse the earth. It is, as the *Gemara* presents it, a strikingly anthropomorphic *pasuk*, one of the more unusual *pesukim* in this regard. The idea seems to be that when a person waits for an opportune moment — when his counterpart is relaxed and in good spirits — and at that point seeks reconciliation, he is engaged in a kind of *imitatio Dei*.

The *Maharsha* adds a nuance: the key phrase is *b'yaino*, in his own wine. If someone takes you out and wines and dines you in order to soften you up, that is a different matter. But if a person is drinking his own wine, and you approach him at that moment seeking to make amends, and he is generous enough to be appeased — that parallels the divine acceptance of a sacrifice. After all, when one brings a sacrifice, one is offering back to God what is already God's. Yet God accepts it graciously. So too here: the one drinking his own wine who allows himself to be appeased is demonstrating a generous spirit that mirrors the divine quality.

---

## Prayer Conditions (II)

### Modern Thresholds

The *Gemara*'s extended discussion of conditions that excuse one from *davening* — travel, environmental distraction, anger, distractedness — raises the question of how these exemptions apply in later generations. Many *Rishonim* take the position that these exemptions are effectively moot in practice, because we no longer have the *kavanah* even under ideal conditions that would justify such a high standard. Our threshold for what counts as acceptable *kavanah* has been substantially lowered over the generations — *yeridas hadoros* — and therefore we do not apply these exemptions. The *halacha* as *paskened* in the *Shulchan Aruch* reflects this position.

This approach does raise a genuine question: if someone truly is in a state of extreme distraction — grieving, overwhelmed, unable to focus at all — should we in fact advise them not to *daven*? The *Gemara* is unambiguous that an improper *tefillah* is worse than no *tefillah*. Yet we do not, as a practical matter, apply these exemptions today, on the theory that our baseline *kavanah* is already sufficiently minimal that the gap between our normal state and an agitated state is not significant enough to trigger the exemption.

The case of a *chatan* on his wedding day is instructive here as well: the *Gemara* debates whether his exemption from *Shema* is a function of *tirda* (distraction) or *osek b'mitzvah* (engagement in a *mitzvah*). These are distinct conceptual categories, and the *Rishonim* who limit the distraction-based exemptions still acknowledge the *osek b'mitzvah* category as operative.

---

## Wine Aggada (II)

### Wine & Wisdom

Rabbi Chiya teaches: *kol hamisyashev b'yaino yesh bo da'as ayin zekeinim* — anyone who is settled and composed when he drinks wine possesses the wisdom of the seventy elders. The reasoning is *gematriah*: *yayin*, wine, has a numerical value of seventy (*yud-yud-nun* = 10+10+50), and *sod*, secret, likewise has a value of seventy (*samech-vav-dalet* = 60+6+4). Hence the saying: *nichnas yayin yatza sod* — wine enters, secrets emerge. A person who can drink and yet remain composed — who does not let secrets spill out — has demonstrated the self-possession associated with the wisdom of the Sanhedrin.

Rashi reads this as: one who holds his secrets in is as weighty as the *Sanhedrin*. There is also a complementary reading: *sod* here carries the sense of wisdom and *Torah* depth, and one who drinks and yet retains the *Torah*'s wisdom within him — who does not lose his inner world to the wine — is himself a repository of that seventy-fold wisdom.

### Wine Purpose

Rabbi Chanin teaches: *lo nivra yayin ela lenachem avelim u'leshalem sachar la'resha'im* — wine was created only to console mourners and to pay back the wicked. In a world in which wine has so many potential negative effects, one might ask what justifies its existence. The answer: it has a legitimate therapeutic role in comforting those in mourning — and for the wicked, it functions as their reward in this world (since they will receive none in the next). The *Maharsha* notes a play on words between *shechar* (strong drink) and *sachar* (reward): *tenu shechar la'oved* — give *shechar* to the one who is lost — is the reward (*sachar*) of the *rasha* in this world. The verse concludes *v'yayin l'marei nafesh* — and wine to those who are embittered of soul — affirming its consolatory function.

### Wine Abundance

Rabbi Chanin bar Pappa offers yet another perspective: *kol she'ein yayin nishpach betoch beito kemayim eino bichlal bracha* — anyone whose wine is not as plentiful in his house as water is not in the category of blessing. The proof text is *u'verach et lachmecha v'et meimecha* — He will bless your bread and your water. The *Gemara* asks: in what sense could wine be described as water? The answer: the same way that bread in this *pasuk* refers to items purchased with *Ma'aser Sheni* money, so too *meimecha* (your water) must refer to a liquid that can be purchased with *Ma'aser Sheni* money — which rules out literal water and points to wine. The verse calls wine "water" to convey that when wine is as freely available in one's home as water, *that* is the sign of true blessing.

### Character Revelation

The famous teaching of Rabbi Ilai closes this *aggadic* passage: *bishlosha devarim adam nikar* — a person's character is revealed through three things: *b'choso u've'chiso u've'chaso* — in his cup, in his purse, and in his anger. When drunk, a person's self-control is reduced and more of his true self emerges — *nichnas yayin yatza sod*. In business dealings, money is at stake, and how a person behaves when there is genuine financial pressure says much about who he really is. And in anger, as with drunkenness, the usual restraints weaken and character is exposed.

*Ve'amrei lah af bischoko* — some add: and in his joking around. Much truth is said in jest, and the content and manner of a person's humor can reveal aspects of character that more guarded social interaction conceals.

---

## Two Courtyards Eruv

### Configuration Setup

The *Gemara* returns to *halacha*, specifically the question of two connected courtyards — an inner and an outer — in which both Jews and a non-Jew reside. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *Yisrael ve'nochri bifnimit, Yisrael bechitzona* — a Jew and a non-Jew in the inner courtyard, and only a Jew in the outer courtyard. This case was brought before Rebbe, who ruled it forbidden (*asar*), and before Rabbi Chiya, who likewise ruled it forbidden.

The basic structure of the problem: the inner courtyard (call it A) is accessible only through the outer courtyard (B). Anyone wishing to exit from A to the street must pass through B. The question is: does A's presence affect B? And specifically, given that a non-Jew lives in A, does this create a situation in which B faces a *eruv* problem?

### Rav's Position

When Rav was asked about the inner courtyard standing alone — *penimi bi'mkomo* — he ruled: *mutar* — it is permitted. The problem lies in the outer courtyard, B. Why? Because in B, the configuration effectively brings together the Jew from A, the Jew of B, and the non-Jew of A — all three interacting in B's space. It is this aggregation in B, not A's internal configuration, that creates the *eruv* problem. A by itself contains only one Jew and one non-Jew, and where there is only one Jewish resident, the non-Jew does not generate an *eruv* issue.

### Rabbi Eliezer & Akiva

After Rav's ruling is established, a discussion breaks out at the end of Rav Sheshet's *shiur*, where Rabbah and Rav Yosef had remained to continue the analysis. Rav Sheshet suggested that Rav's ruling follows the position of Rabbi Meir, who holds that even a single Jew creates an *eruv* problem when sharing space with a non-Jew. Rav Yosef objected sharply: *trei gavrei ravrevei ke'rabbanan lito behai milta?* — would two great scholars make such an elementary error? If this were Rabbi Meir, who holds one Jew is already problematic, then why mention the Jew in the outer courtyard at all? The outer courtyard detail would be entirely superfluous. Moreover, the *Gemara* records explicitly that when asked about the inner courtyard by itself, Rav said it is *mutar* — permitted. That ruling is incompatible with Rabbi Meir's position, since Rabbi Meir would find a problem even in A alone (one Jew with a non-Jew).

The better attribution, therefore, is to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds that *two* Jews with a non-Jew create a problem, but *one* Jew with a non-Jew does not. His formulation: *ad she'yesh sheni Yisrael osrin zeh al zeh* — the prohibition applies only where two Jews are making one another forbidden (i.e., where they are effectively in the same shared space). This is consistent with Rav's ruling that A alone is fine.

### Akiva's Rule

If the operative position is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — two Jews with a non-Jew is a problem, one Jew with a non-Jew is not — then why is B a problem? B has its own Jew, and A has a Jew and a non-Jew. The Jew of A is not literally living in B. The answer lies in the position of Rabbi Akiva: *regel ha'muteret bi'mkomah oseret she'lo bi'mkomah* — a *regel* (foot, or presence) that is permitted in its own domain nonetheless creates a prohibition in a domain where it is not located.

This principle operates as follows: according to Rabbi Akiva, because A must pass through B to reach the street, A's residents are in a meaningful sense also present in B. If this were an all-Jewish scenario, B would therefore be required to make an *eruv* together with A — it cannot make an independent *eruv* that ignores A. The *Rabbanan* disagree: since A is *mutar bi'mkomo* (permitted in its own space), it does not impose any obligation on B, and B can make its own *eruv* independently.

The *chiddush* in the case before us is not simply that Rabbi Akiva requires B to include A in its *eruv* — that would apply even in an all-Jewish scenario. The *chiddush* is that once B is required (per Rabbi Akiva) to make an *eruv* together with A, the combined configuration now consists of two Jews (B's Jew and A's Jew) together with A's non-Jew. That constitutes the problematic two-Jews-plus-non-Jew configuration of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, which is forbidden. The ruling against B thus flows from the combination of Rabbi Akiva's rule (B must include A) and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's rule (two Jews with a non-Jew is a problem).

### Reversed Setup

The *Gemara* now considers the reverse scenario: *Yisrael ve'nochri be'chitzona, Yisrael be'pnimis* — a Jew and a non-Jew in the outer courtyard, and only a Jew in the inner one. By the same logic, since B (now the outer courtyard containing the Jew and the non-Jew) is the passage through which A's resident must travel, the analysis should be symmetrical: A must make an *eruv* together with B, creating the two-Jews-plus-non-Jew configuration.

The *Gemara* asks whether the two cases are truly equivalent or whether some distinction might apply. The argument for a distinction: perhaps the first case (Jew and non-Jew on the inside) is more common, because the Jew in the outer courtyard would be more likely to intimidate the non-Jew. The non-Jew, aware that the Jew from the outer courtyard could at any moment pass through and demand to know the whereabouts of the Jew from the inner courtyard — *Yisrael dehavi gabach heicha?* — would be deterred from any act of violence. In the reversed configuration, the non-Jew might calculate that he could simply claim his neighbor had gone out to the market, since the outer courtyard opens directly to the street and no one would necessarily know otherwise. On this reasoning, the concern about the non-Jew's presence (which underlies the *eruv* regulation) is less acute when the Jew is in the inner courtyard.

The *Gemara*, however, rejects this distinction: *o dilma hacha nami mirsas* — perhaps here too the non-Jew is deterred, reasoning that the Jew from the inner courtyard might pass through at any moment and witness any wrongdoing. The response of the *Gemara* is: *ten le'chacham ve'yechkam od* — give to the wise person and he will grow wiser still. The same *halacha* applies in both directions. In both configurations, the conclusion is the same.

---

## Landlord Rental

### Inn Scenario

The *Gemara* presents a practical case that has direct implications for the construction of *eruvin* in later times. Reish Lakish and the students of Rabbi Chanina arrived at a certain inn. The inn had multiple rooms, one of which was rented by a non-Jew. The group needed to make an *eruv* for the inn, which would normally have required renting the rights from the non-Jew tenant. However, that tenant was absent.

### Landlord Authority

The question posed: *mahvei lei minei* — can we rent from the landlord, even though the one who actually holds the current lease on the room, and therefore has rights to it, is not present?

### Eviction Power

The *Gemara* structures the question carefully. If the landlord has no power to move or reassign the tenant — if the tenant could not be displaced even by the landlord — then clearly the landlord has no meaningful authority over the room and cannot transfer any rights. In that case, there is no question: one cannot rent from the landlord, *d'lo agrinan*. The operative question arises only where the landlord *does* have the power to remove or reassign the tenant. Even in that case, one might argue: right now the tenant has not been removed, and he currently holds rights to the room. Can a merely potential power to remove him translate into a presently actionable right to rent from the landlord?

### Practical Decision

As Shabbat approached with the question unresolved, Reish Lakish decided to act: *niskor* — let us rent from the landlord. He added: *u'keshenagia etzel raboteinu shebadarom nishal lahem* — and when we reach our masters in the south, we will ask them. Rashi explains that this approach was reasonable because the matter is *de-rabbanan* in character, and the general principle *halacha kedivrei hameikel b'Bavel be'eiruv* — that in cases of *eruv*, we rule leniently — justified acting on the assumption that the rental would prove valid, with the intention of seeking confirmation afterward.

### Rav Afes Approval

When Reish Lakish's group came before Rav Afes, one of the masters of the south, they reported what they had done. *Rav Afes amar lahem: yafe asitem shesechartem* — Rav Afes said to them: you did well to rent from the landlord. The ruling is thus confirmed: where a landlord retains the power to remove or reassign a tenant, that power is sufficient to enable the landlord to serve as the party from whom one rents *eruv* rights — even if the tenant is currently in place and present in his lease.

The implications of this ruling extend well beyond the immediate case. The foundational principle that one can rent *eruv* rights from a landlord who has the power to displace a tenant — rather than necessarily from the tenant himself — underlies the structure of many communal *eruvin* in later periods, including urban *eruvin* that involve renting rights from municipal authorities rather than from every individual property owner. The case of the inn is thus not a curiosity but a precedent of considerable practical consequence, to be developed further in the *sugyot* that follow.

---

---

# Eiruvin 66

## Inn Scenario & Renting

### Landlord & Rental

The present daf picks up at the bottom of 65b with the case of Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef. The discussion from the previous daf concerned a scenario where the landlord was present and the renter was absent. The principle established was that as long as the landlord retains the right to relocate the renter from one room to another, he maintains sufficient presence and control over the space, allowing the other residents to perform *sechirus* — a rental arrangement — from him. The relevant authorities made their practical decision without having confirmed the *halacha* in advance, and only afterwards received confirmation that they had acted correctly — a situation somewhat reminiscent of the episode of *tekias shofar* at Yavneh, where the precedent was set before the legal question was formally resolved.

These principles carry significant practical implications for the laws of *eruv*. They bear directly on how one rents from a city authority rather than from individual homeowners, and on questions such as whether an *eruv* is needed in an apartment building — given that a landlord may be unable to physically displace a tenant yet retains ownership of major appliances and shared spaces. Such questions of presence and control are at the heart of these laws and have ongoing relevance to contemporary *halacha*.

### Non-Jew Arrives Shabbat

The *gemara* now turns to a new episode. Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef, Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, and Rabbi Assi found themselves at a certain inn — *ikle'u l'hahu pundak* — together with various rented rooms. On *shabbos* itself, the non-Jewish owner of the inn arrived. The problem this created requires some background.

### Eruv Voided

The *gemara* had previously established, through a dispute among *tanna'im*, that if a non-Jew is absent from a shared space before *shabbos* begins, he does not create a *halachic* problem for those who share that space. It is only when the non-Jew is actually present before *shabbos* that his presence voids the *eruv*. Accordingly, the assumption here is that the guests at the inn had made an *eruv* before *shabbos* on the basis that the non-Jewish owner was not present — a perfectly sound arrangement. But when the owner arrived on *shabbos*, his presence retroactively rendered the *eruv* invalid. The assessment is made as if he had been present from before *shabbos*, and *sechirus* — renting the non-Jew's domain — would therefore have been required.

There is a lengthy *Tosafos* that labors over the question of precisely when a situation that was valid before *shabbos* began remains valid and when it is reversed by a problem that arises afterward. The *gemara* here operates on the assumption that it is reversed.

### Rent on Shabbat?

This raises an immediate practical question: *amru mahu l'meigar minei* — can we rent from the non-Jew on *shabbos* itself and thereby remedy the problem? The *gemara* frames the question as a comparison between two legal mechanisms: *socher k'me'arev dami* — is renting analogous to making an *eruv*? If so, just as an *eruv* must be established before *shabbos* begins, so too *sechirus* must be effected before *shabbos*. Or, *o dilma socher k'mevatel reshut dami* — perhaps renting is more akin to *bitul reshut*, the annulment of domain rights, which may be performed on *shabbos* itself when a problem arises.

*Sechirus* from a non-Jew and *bitul reshut* from a Jew are the two remedial strategies available when a standard *eruv* cannot function as intended. The *eruv* must be in place before *shabbos*; *bitul reshut* classically addresses situations discovered on *shabbos* itself. The question is therefore which of these two categories *sechirus* belongs to.

One might ask whether performing a rental transaction on *shabbos* itself is not inherently problematic as a prohibited commercial act. The relevant *Tosafos* on 66a addresses this directly, stating: *lo dami l'mikach u'mimkar de'asur b'Shabbos de'lo havei ela k'matanah b'alma she'ein asin ela l'hatir tiltul* — it is not comparable to a commercial transaction forbidden on *shabbos*, since this arrangement functions merely as a symbolic gift, performed solely to permit carrying. There is no genuine commercial exchange involved; indeed, it was already established earlier in the *masechta* that the *sechirus* may be performed for less than a *shaveh perutah*. The question, then, is not whether the act is permissible on *shabbos*, but whether it will be *halachically* effective.

---

## Sechirus Comparison

### Timing Question

The *gemara* formulates the central question precisely: *socher k'me'arev dami* — does *sechirus* follow the same timing requirement as *eruv*, demanding that it be accomplished before *shabbos*? Or does it follow the rules of *bitul reshut*, which may be performed even on *shabbos* itself?

### Two Models

The narrative proceeds: Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef said *niscor* — let us rent. Rav Yosef, citing Rav Assi, said *lo niscor* — let us not rent. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba then resolved the impasse: *nismoch al divrei zaken v'niscor* — let us rely on the elder, Rabbi Chanina, and proceed to rent. This echoes the logic of that famous *mishna* in Rosh Hashanah, where Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai proceeded to sound the *shofar* at Yavneh on *shabbos* and only afterward sought formal confirmation.

After *shabbos*, they brought the question to Rabbi Yochanan. He replied: *yafeh asitem she-sechartem* — you did well to rent. As in the case from the previous daf, they either were genuinely confident in their judgment, or, since the matter is *derabanan* and the rule is *halacha k'divrei ha'meikel b'eruv*, they felt sufficiently grounded to rely on the lenient position.

The *gemara* then records that the scholars of Nehardea were astonished: *ve-chi amar Rabbi Yochanan hachi* — did Rabbi Yochanan truly say this? For it was known that Rabbi Yochanan had himself declared *socher k'me'arev dami* — that renting is like making an *eruv*! Does this not imply that *sechirus*, like an *eruv*, must be performed before *shabbos*?

### Lenient Comparisons

The *gemara* rejects that reading: *lav ma me'arev afilu b'pachos mi'shaveh perutah af socher afilu b'pachos mi'shaveh perutah*. When Rabbi Yochanan compared *sechirus* to *eruv*, he was making a lenient comparison, not a strict one. The parallel is being drawn for the purpose of leniency, not stringency, and *Rashi* emphasizes this point: *d'kulah akshinu m'Rabbi Yochanan v'lo l'chumra d'kol b'eruv l'hakel* — all the comparisons being drawn from Rabbi Yochanan are toward leniency; everything in *eruvin* we interpret favorably.

The *gemara* then marshals three such lenient parallels. First: just as an *eruv* is valid even when the bread contributed is worth less than a *perutah*, so too *sechirus* may be performed for less than a *perutah*. Second: *u'ma me'arev afilu sochir v'lakito* — just as an *eruv* may be effected even by the hired laborer or gleaner of a non-Jew (a Jew employed on the property who may act in lieu of the owner), so too *sechirus* may be effected even through the non-Jew's hired hand rather than only from the owner himself. This extends the ease with which the non-Jew's domain can be brought within the *eruv* arrangement. Third: just as when five people share a courtyard, one person may deposit the *eruv* on behalf of all of them, so too one person may perform the rental from the non-Jew on behalf of all residents of the courtyard, since the *sechirus* is not directed at any individual member but at the collective. All three comparisons point in the same direction — toward making the *eruv* arrangement easier to accomplish, not harder.

### Sechirus Works Shabbat

The conclusion is that *sechirus* operates according to the rules of *bitul reshut*, not *eruv*. It may be performed on *shabbos* itself. Rabbi Yochanan's statement that *socher k'me'arev dami* was never intended as a timing restriction; it was a statement about leniency, that wherever *eruv* law is applied, we apply it generously. With this, the practical question raised by the scenario at the inn is resolved: the *sechirus* performed on *shabbos* was entirely valid.

---

## Shmuel's Principle

### Osrin & Mearvin

It would seem that once the *sechirus* was performed, the problem should be fully resolved. However, *Rashi* and *Tosafos* both point out that renting from the non-Jew does not, by itself, restore the *eruv* that was made before *shabbos* — that *eruv* was already nullified by the non-Jew's arrival and cannot be retroactively revived. What the *sechirus* accomplishes is removing the non-Jew from the equation. But the courtyard is now in the position of a group that has no valid *eruv* in place. The remedy for that situation — a problem arising on *shabbos* itself when an *eruv* was not made or was nullified — is *bitul reshut*.

This implicit understanding is what animates the following discussion. The *gemara* now identifies what was troubling a certain Rabbi Eliezer about this case. The term used is *tohi bah* — he was probing it, trying to smell out what was going on. Rav Sheshet responds with some emphasis: could a great scholar like Rabbi Zeira not understand what was bothering Rabbi Eliezer? He was troubled by the statement of Shmuel, his teacher. For Shmuel stated: *kol makom she'osrin u'me'arvin m'vatlin* — in any place where the residents create a forbidden situation for one another and they are able to make an *eruv* together, they may also perform *bitul reshut*.

The logic behind this principle is as follows. An individual's presence in a shared space creates a problem for every other resident — this is the concept of *osrin*, the capacity to forbid. If they choose to work together, they can all unify the space through an *eruv* — this is *me'arvin*, the capacity to join. Where both these conditions exist, the residents are in a fundamental sense already one unit. It is because they are recognized as one unit that *chazal* permitted the fiction of *bitul reshut* — the waiving of domain rights on *shabbos* — as a remedy when the proper *eruv* arrangement failed. The flip side is equally clear: *me'arvin v'ein osrin, ein m'vatlin* — if they could make an *eruv* but their individual presence does not create a problem for one another, *bitul reshut* does not apply. And *osrin v'ein me'arvin, ein m'vatlin* — if their presence creates a problem but an *eruv* is not possible, *bitul reshut* likewise does not apply.

Both conditions must be present simultaneously.

### Nested Courtyards

The *gemara* illustrates the case where both conditions are met with the example of *shtei chatzeiros zo lifnim mi'zo* — two courtyards, one nested inside the other. In this configuration, which figured prominently in the previous daf's discussion, the residents of the inner courtyard (A) must pass through the outer courtyard (B) to access the street. This means that A's presence is inherently a concern for B — A is *oser* on B. At the same time, they are capable of unifying their space through a joint *eruv*. Therefore, if one person forgot to participate in the *eruv*, they satisfy both conditions and *bitul reshut* is available as a remedy.

This ruling is a *chiddush*, because one might have said that *bitul reshut* is only available within a single courtyard and cannot operate between two separate courtyards. The alternative opinion, to be discussed shortly, will indeed take that more restrictive view. Shmuel's logic here is that since the two courtyards are fundamentally one unit — they create problems for each other and could unify under one *eruv* — the fiction of *bitul reshut* can function across them.

### Separate Access

The contrasting case is *shtei chatzeiros u'fetach echad beineihen* — two courtyards each with its own independent access to the public domain. In this configuration, neither courtyard imposes itself upon the other. Each has its own separate space. While they could, if they chose, make a joint *eruv*, they are under no obligation to do so, and the presence of residents in one courtyard does not create a problem for residents in the other. Here *osrin* does not apply, even though *me'arvin* does. Since they are not inherently bound together, they are not truly one unit, and the fiction of *bitul reshut* — which only functions when there is an underlying unity — cannot bridge the gap between them. If one courtyard failed to make an *eruv*, *bitul reshut* toward the other courtyard is not available. They would require an actual *eruv* to permit carrying between them.

### Non-Jew Exception

The case of *osrin v'ein me'arvin* — where the presence of a party creates a forbidden situation but an *eruv* together with them is not possible — is identified as the scenario of the non-Jew. In the normal case, a non-Jew's presence is a problem because he cannot be incorporated into an *eruv* directly; *sechirus* is required. Yet if he was present before *shabbos*, the potential for *sechirus* existed — that potential is considered the functional equivalent of *me'arvin* — and therefore *bitul reshut* would remain available for the Jews who share the courtyard, should one of them fail to make an *eruv*.

The *gemara* clarifies: *d'ata me'etmol lo garmi me'etmol* — if the non-Jew came yesterday, we could have rented from him yesterday. That possibility classifies him in the *me'arvin* category, and consequently *bitul reshut* among the Jewish residents remains effective in principle. It is important to note the asymmetry here: the non-Jew does not perform *bitul reshut*, nor is *bitul reshut* directed at him. His presence creates a problem for the Jews, and the question is whether the Jewish residents may use *bitul reshut* amongst themselves. But if the possibility of *sechirus* existed, the answer is yes.

The scenario that does *not* allow *bitul reshut* is precisely the case at hand — *d'ata b'shabsa* — the non-Jew arrived on *shabbos* itself. He is *oser*, yes — his arrival on *shabbos* created the problem. But he is *ein me'arvin* — since he was not present before *shabbos*, the option of renting from him to bring him into the *eruv* framework never existed. Therefore, by Shmuel's principle, the case falls into the category of *osrin v'ein me'arvin* and *bitul reshut* cannot be used. A *baraisa* is cited confirming exactly this: *osrin v'ein me'arvin v'ein m'vatlin*.

The implication is striking. Even after the *sechirus* was performed on *shabbos* — which the *gemara* has already validated — the *bitul reshut* that would be needed to reconstitute carrying rights in the courtyard cannot be performed. Shmuel's principle stands in apparent tension with Rabbi Yochanan's approval of how the scholars at the inn acted.

The *gemara* then records that Rav Yosef said: *lo shemi'a li ha shema'ta* — I never heard this teaching of Shmuel about the two criteria. Abaye immediately corrected him: *at amrat neilan* — you yourself taught us this position of Shmuel. Abaye reminds him that Rav Yosef had cited it in connection with a further statement of Shmuel: *ein bitul reshut mi'chatzer l'chatzer v'ein bitul reshut b'churba* — there is no *bitul reshut* from one courtyard to another, and there is no *bitul reshut* in a *churba*, a back alley.

The prohibition on *bitul reshut mi'chatzer l'chatzer* directly corresponds to the case of two separate courtyards discussed above. The prohibition on *bitul reshut b'churba* rests on a distinct consideration: *bitul reshut* is a fiction that *chazal* permitted only for a *chatzer*, where the need for carrying is greatest and most practically significant. They did not extend this fiction to a back alley, even though houses may open into it. These are distinct restrictions, though both reflect the same underlying principle that *bitul reshut* has defined limits and cannot be applied universally wherever it would be convenient.

Abaye then corrects another of Rav Yosef's recollections. When Rav Yosef had cited Shmuel's statement that *ein lanu b'eruvin ela l'shon mishnatenu* — in matters of *eruvin* we follow the precise language of our *Mishna* — this was not a universal interpretive principle. Shmuel was applying it specifically to one *Mishna* that reads *ha'mavo'in l'chatzerot k'chatzer l'battim*, drawing an analogy between the relationship of houses to courtyards and courtyards to an alley (*mavoi*). From the plural *chatzerot*, Shmuel derived that a valid arrangement for *shituf mavo'os* requires at least two courtyards each containing at least two houses. That *diyuk* was local to that *Mishna*, not a general rule foreclosing *bitul reshut* across courtyards whenever the *Mishna* uses the singular *chatzer*. When it comes to *bitul reshut* in the case of nested courtyards where *osrin* applies, Shmuel himself would permit it under the right conditions.

With this, Shmuel's various statements are rendered consistent with one another, and Rav Yosef is set back on track.

---

## Shmuel vs. Yochanan

### Shmuel Restricts

The *gemara* returns to examine Shmuel's double ruling directly: *amar Shmuel ein bitul reshut mi'chatzer l'chatzer v'ein bitul reshut b'churba* — Shmuel holds that *bitul reshut* does not function from one courtyard to another, and does not function in a back alley.

### Yochanan Permits

Rabbi Yochanan takes the opposite position on both counts: *yesh bitul reshut mi'chatzer l'chatzer v'yesh bitul reshut b'churba* — he permits *bitul reshut* both between courtyards and in a back alley. The notational marking on both of Rabbi Yochanan's rulings signals that this is the operative *halacha*, consistent with the principle of *halacha k'divrei ha'meikel b'eruv*.

### Usage vs. Space

The *gemara* explains why both cases must be stated independently rather than deriving one from the other. One might have thought that Shmuel's restrictiveness is particularly intuitive in the case of two courtyards with separate access to the street, where *vadah tashmishta l'chud v'ha tashmishta l'chud* — each one has its own distinct and separate space for use. Where each courtyard functions entirely independently, there is no compelling need for *bitul reshut* and no meaningful shared framework to which the fiction can attach. But perhaps in the *churba*, a back alley that both sets of residents use jointly — *tashmishta chada l'tarvaihu* — where it is more like a shared courtyard, Shmuel might have conceded to Rabbi Yochanan. Conversely, one might have said Rabbi Yochanan's leniency is most intuitive in the *churba*, where the shared usage makes it function practically like one space, but that he might have deferred to Shmuel regarding separate courtyards. Since neither direction of inference is certain, the *gemara* establishes that both authorities maintain their respective positions across both cases, making it necessary to state each ruling explicitly.

The underlying conceptual tension between the two positions reflects two different understandings of when *bitul reshut* can function as a meaningful legal fiction. For Shmuel, the critical element is genuine unity — *bitul reshut* works only where the parties are already one unit in the relevant sense, which requires both *osrin* and *me'arvin*. For Rabbi Yochanan, *bitul reshut* is a broader remedy and need not be so tightly constrained.

---

## Abaye & Rava

### Abaye's View

The *gemara* now brings Abaye's formulation of Shmuel's position: when Shmuel said *ein bitul reshut mi'chatzer l'chatzer*, this applies only to *shtei chatzeiros she'petach echad beineihen* — the case where the courtyards have separate access and are not in a relationship of mutual dependence. But *aval zo lifnim mi'zo* — where one courtyard is nested inside the other and A is *oser* on B, since in that configuration one person's presence creates problems for others and they can make a joint *eruv*, the conditions of *osrin u'me'arvin* are met and *bitul reshut* functions. Abaye is here restating what had been attributed to Shmuel earlier in the discussion as the basis for reconciling Shmuel's various rulings.

### Rava Objects

Rava sharply qualifies this conclusion: *afilu shtei chatzeiros zo lifnim mi'zo, pa'amim mevatlin u'pa'amim ein mevatlin* — even in the case of nested courtyards, there are times when *bitul reshut* is effective and times when it is not. The mere fact that they are in a nested configuration and create problems for each other is not sufficient, in Rava's view, to make *bitul reshut* automatically available across the two courtyards. The details of how the *eruv* was arranged and which person failed to participate determine whether the remedy is available at all.

---

## Shared Eruv Scenarios

### Eruv in Outer

Rava proceeds to spell out the scenarios in full. The case under discussion involves two courtyards — inner (A) and outer (B) — that have made a joint *eruv*, depositing it in one or the other courtyard. The key variables are: where the *eruv* was placed, and who forgot to participate.
