When the joint *eruv* was placed in the outer courtyard (B), and any member of either courtyard — whether inner or outer — forgot to join the *eruv*: *shteihen asuros* — both courtyards are forbidden, with no available remedy.

The *gemara* works through why this must be so. If one of the inner residents (A) forgot, to whom can he perform *bitul reshut*? If he says *levatel livnei pnimis* — I will do *bitul* to my fellow inner residents — that does not help, because *leis lei eruva gabaihu* — the *eruv* is not located with them. The inner courtyard cannot be considered functionally independent from the outer one, since the outer courtyard holds the *eruv* and the inner residents must go through the outer to benefit from it. Any meaningful *bitul* would have to encompass the outer courtyard as well. But *ein bitul reshut mi'chatzer l'chatzer* — *bitul* from one courtyard to the other is precisely what Rava (following Shmuel's restrictive reading) disallows, even in nested courtyards.

If one of the outer residents (B) forgot, the analysis is symmetrical but no more hopeful. If he says *levatel livnei chitzona* — I will do *bitul* to my fellow outer residents — *ika pnimis d'asru aleih* — the inner courtyard is also creating a problem for the outer one. The inner residents go through the outer courtyard and are inherently part of its domain; one cannot simply ignore them. To make the *bitul* effective, the outer resident would need to also do *bitul* to the inner courtyard, which again runs into *ein bitul reshut mi'chatzer l'chatzer*. There is no path forward in either scenario, and both courtyards remain forbidden.

### Inner Eruv, Inner Forgot

When the joint *eruv* was placed in the inner courtyard (A), and a member of the inner courtyard forgot: *shteihen asuros* — both are again forbidden.

The analysis follows the same logic. The forgetting inner resident might try *bitul* to his fellow inner residents. But *ika chitzona d'asra aleih* — the outer courtyard is part of this arrangement, since the inner courtyard's *eruv* was made jointly with them. Since B is incorporated into A's *eruv*, one cannot treat them as irrelevant. To make the *bitul* work, it would have to extend to B, which is *bitul mi'chatzer l'chatzer* — and that is unavailable.

### Inner Eruv, Outer Forgot

The one case where a remedy is available: the *eruv* was placed in the inner courtyard (A), and a member of the outer courtyard (B) forgot. In this case, *pnimis muteres v'chitzona asura* — the inner courtyard is permitted and the outer is forbidden.

The *gemara* states the reason succinctly: *de'achad dasha u'mishtamsha* — A closes its door and uses its own space. The inner courtyard, holding the *eruv*, can simply seal itself off from the outer courtyard and proceed as though it were independent.

### Why It Works

The question is pointed: in this scenario, it appears that the inner courtyard is simply closing its door and benefiting from its own *eruv* without anyone performing *bitul reshut* at all. Where is the *bitul* in this case?

*Rashi* at the top of 67a addresses this precisely. He explains that what the outer residents (B) do is *bitul* of a very specific and limited kind: *de'ha modeh Shmuel de'mevatlin benei chitzona livnei pnimis osah reshut she'ba'ah lahen l'tochan al yedei hergel eruvan* — Shmuel concedes that the outer courtyard performs *bitul* to the inner courtyard of that particular *reshus* that had come to them through the circuit of the joint *eruv*. When B joined A's *eruv*, they acquired a stake in A's *eruv* arrangement. When B withdraws — is *mochel* on — that stake, they remove themselves from the *eruv* and allow A to use it for itself alone.

This is a narrow and specific form of *bitul*: not a transfer of domain rights from one *chatzer* to another, which would be *bitul mi'chatzer l'chatzer* and therefore prohibited even by Shmuel's restrictive view. Rather, it is the outer courtyard relinquishing the claim it had acquired to A's *eruv*. Since B can be sealed off, and since B is merely withdrawing a right it had previously taken on rather than conferring rights in its own domain upon A, the arrangement is acceptable.

In every other scenario — where either an inner resident forgot or where the *eruv* was placed in the outer courtyard — the *bitul* that would be required involves genuine cross-courtyard transfer of domain rights, and that Rava, following the restrictive understanding of Shmuel, will not permit. The architecture of the *eruv* and the identity of the party that failed to participate thus determine, with considerable precision, whether any remedy is available at all.

---

---

# Eiruvin 67

## Bittul & Joint Eruv

### Osrin & Me'arvin

The *gemara* here on 67a continues to examine the conditions under which *bittul* can operate effectively. The foundational principle, at least in *Shmuel*'s initial position, is that *bittul* requires two concurrent criteria: first, that the individual in question is *osrin* — that is, he creates a problem for the others by virtue of his presence — and second, that he is *me'arvin*, meaning he could in theory have joined the *eruv*. Both of these must be satisfied before *bittul* can function.

A further question then arises: what if both criteria are technically met, but the relationship between the parties is characterized as *mechatzar lechatzar* — one courtyard to another, rather than members of a single, unified domain? According to one version of *Shmuel*'s position, as represented by *Abaye*, even a *mechatzar lechatzar* configuration can suffice. According to another view associated with *Rava*, however, as long as the parties stand in a *mechatzar lechatzar* relationship, *bittul* cannot function between them. And there is also the position of *Rabbi Yochanan*, who rejects *Shmuel*'s framework entirely and holds that one can never perform *bittul me'reshut lereshut* — that is, *bittul* cannot operate across distinct domains at all.

### Eruv in A, Problem in B

Against this backdrop, the *gemara* presents a scenario in which the parameters converge in a specific and instructive way. Imagine two courtyards, designated here as A (the inner courtyard) and B (the outer courtyard). A joint *eruv* has been made, with the *eruv* physically placed in A. One of the residents of B then forgot to participate. In this case, A can simply disregard B: it has its *eruv*, B is the source of the problem, and A can function independently. As the *gemara* states at the very opening of 67a: *shachach echad min hachitzonah velo eirev* — if one of the outer courtyard's residents forgot and did not join the *eruv* — *vadai pnimis muteres* — the inner courtyard is certainly permitted. *De'achda dasha umishamsha* — it effectively closes its door and operates within its own domain.

The reason this works even for those who resist *bittul me'reshut lereshut* is that in this scenario, *bittul* is not really being used to bridge two distinct domains. What is happening, rather, is that B as a whole waives its participation in the *eruv*. So long as B maintains its participation, the presence of a problematic member in B contaminates A as well; but once all of B performs *bittul* — waives its share in the *eruv* — A is free to function on its own. *Vachitzonah asurah* — and B remains forbidden.

### B Waives Rights

If, however, the problem is located in A — that is, one of the members of A forgot — the situation is far more complicated. Since the *eruv* is housed in A, and since B is part of the *eruv* arrangement together with A, one cannot simply cut B off. For the *bittul* to be effective, the forgetful member of A would need to be *mevatel* not only to his fellow residents of A, but also to the members of B. And that is precisely what is prohibited according to those who hold *ein bittul me'reshut lereshut* — one cannot perform *bittul* across separate domains.

### Gal'u Dasha

This is the conclusion the *gemara* arrives at, and it encapsulates the most restrictive position on *bittul*: the mechanism functions reliably only when the parties constitute a single, coherent domain. The case where it works is effectively one in which B is simply excised — and what is labeled *bittul* is little more than a formal waiver that achieves the conceptual exclusion of the problematic party.

---

## Problem in Inner Court

### Huna's Challenge

*Amar leh Rav Huna brei deRav Yehoshua leRava* — Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua posed a challenge to Rava. He questioned the ruling that if a member of A forgot, both courtyards are forbidden. The *gemara* had explained that this is because the *eruv* encompasses B, and therefore *bittul* by the forgetful member of A would require him to be *mevatel* to B as well — which constitutes *bittul me'reshut lereshut* and is impermissible. But Rav Huna argued: why can't it work?

### Huna's Solution

His proposed solution: *livatel bar pnimis lipnimis* — let the member of A be *mevatel* only to his fellow residents of A, and *vetipoki chitzonah vetishtari bahadeihu* — let B automatically become permitted along with them. The logic is that once the forgetful member performs *bittul* to one member of his group, it takes effect for the entire group. Since the *eruv* is in A and the problem is in A, he directs his *bittul* to his own courtyard, and B gets drawn in automatically without requiring any direct *bittul* across domains.

### Eliezer vs Rabbanan

The response is: *ke'man* — according to whom are you saying this? *Ke'Rabbi Eliezer.* Rav Huna's proposed mechanism aligns with Rabbi Eliezer's view, *de'amar eino tzarich levatel reshus le'chol echad ve'echad* — that one need not be *mevatel* to every individual separately; a single act of *bittul* directed at one can be effective for all. But the *gemara* responds that when it was said that the case of A forgetting presents a problem, the ruling follows *lerabbanan* — *de'amri tzarich levatel le'chol echad ve'echad* — the Rabbis hold that one must be *mevatel* to each individual. Since B's members are residents of a separate domain, one would need to be directly *mevatel* to each of them, which is *bittul me'reshut lereshut* and cannot be done.

### Restrictive Position

This is therefore the most restrictive approach: *bittul* requires not merely *osrin u'me'arvin* — it demands that the parties be effectively one domain. The mechanism works only when B can simply be cut off, which is the case when the problem originates in B and B waives its participation. When the problem is in A, no clever workaround can circumvent the requirement, under the Rabbis' view, that each individual must be addressed directly.

One might ask what precisely *bittul* is, since it seems as though waiving one's rights to one member of an *eruv* group should carry over to the whole. The difficulty here is that at the moment *bittul* is needed, the *eruv* is not functioning — the outlier's presence has disrupted it. So the cohesion of the group cannot yet be assumed as a basis for the *bittul* to spread automatically. Furthermore, *bittul* is inherently weaker than an *eruv*: once one performs *bittul*, one cannot carry from one's own house into the courtyard, because doing so would reassert one's property rights and annul the *bittul*. This is why *bittul* is primarily a Shabbos emergency measure rather than a preferred arrangement, and why the parameters for its operation are so carefully delimited.

---

## Chisda & Sheshes

### Their Relationship

The *gemara* introduces a celebrated vignette: *Rav Chisda ve-Rav Sheshes, ki paguei bahadi hadadi* — when Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshes would encounter one another, *Rav Chisda martzin sifvosei mi-matneisa d'Rav Sheshes* — Rav Chisda's lips would tremble on account of Rav Sheshes' mastery of *beraisos*. Rav Sheshes was a consummate *baki*, a repository of *mishnayos* and *beraisos*, and whenever a halachic exchange was in the offing, Rav Chisda feared being outmaneuvered by a well-placed citation. On Rav Sheshes' side, *marta kulei gufei mi-pilpulei d'Rav Chisda* — his entire body would tremble from Rav Chisda's sharpness of analysis.

This is the classic *gemara* dichotomy between *Sinai* and *oker harim* — one who holds the tradition in its entirety and one whose analytic power can move mountains. In an era without books, where access to information depends entirely on what is stored in a scholar's memory, these two types represent complementary and mutually intimidating forms of mastery.

### Two Houses Setup

*Ba'ei minei Rav Chisda me-Rav Sheshes* — Rav Chisda, the analytically sharp one, posed a question to Rav Sheshes. *Shnei batim mishnei tzidei reshus harabbim* — two houses on opposite sides of a *reshus harabbim*, which can never be joined by an *eruv*. *Ubau nochrim vehikkifum mehitzah beshabbos* — non-Jews came on Shabbos and built a wall enclosing the *reshus harabbim*. A *mechitza* erected on Shabbos is halachically valid, so the enclosed space is now a *reshus hayachid*. However, no *eruv* was in place between the two houses when Shabbos began. The question: can *bittul* be performed now?

### Bittul Without Eruv

The question is posed specifically according to the view that *ein bittul reshus mechatzar l'chatzar* — *bittul* cannot operate from one courtyard to another unless there is sufficient unity between the parties. On that view, *lo tiba'i lach* — there is no question, it obviously cannot work. The argument runs as follows: if even in a case where the two courtyards *could* have joined together in an *eruv* — where *me'arvin* is satisfied — and yet we say *ain bittul mechatzar l'chatzar* because there is no *osrin*, then certainly in this case, where when Shabbos began the two houses had no possibility of making an *eruv* between them — the enclosed space not yet existing — there is no basis for unity and *bittul* cannot function.

The genuine question arises, Rav Chisda explains, *aliba d'man d'amar yesh bittul reshus mechatzar l'chatzar* — according to Rabbi Yochanan, who permits *bittul* even across separate domains. On Rabbi Yochanan's view, one might ask whether the reason *bittul* functions is because the parties had the potential of forming an *eruv* together (*me'arvin*), or whether Rabbi Yochanan holds that *bittul* is always available regardless of prior capacity. The former reading would mean that even Rabbi Yochanan could not allow *bittul* here, since there was no possibility of forming an *eruv* before Shabbos. The latter would mean Rabbi Yochanan allows *bittul* universally whenever it would be helpful. *O dilma lo shna* — or perhaps the distinction makes no difference.

This question is particularly resonant because Rabbi Yochanan was also the one who permitted *bittul* in a *churva* — a courtyard or ruin — a context with no relation to the conceptual unity question. This suggests Rabbi Yochanan's leniency on *bittul* may be categorical, not contingent on potential *eruv* formation. So the question is whether his position allows *bittul* even in this new and entirely unprecedented scenario.

### Sheshes Dismisses

*Amar lei ein m'vatlin* — Rav Sheshes responded simply: it does not work. Even according to Rabbi Yochanan, there is not enough here to constitute a unit, and *bittul* cannot function. A further question followed: what if the non-Jew who had appeared on Shabbos and disrupted the *eruv* then died on Shabbos? According to *Tosafos*, the scenario is that a non-Jew arrived on Shabbos, rendering the *eruv* inoperative and requiring both rental from him and *bittul*, and then died. Now that he has died, can *bittul* alone suffice? Rav Sheshes' response: *ani omer mevatlin, veHamnuna omer ein mevatlin* — I hold it works, and Rav Hamnuna holds it does not.

What is striking about this exchange is that it does not quite bear out the introduction's promise of a clash between analytic brilliance and encyclopedic tradition. Rav Sheshes does not deploy a *mishna* or *beraisa* in response; he simply gives bottom-line rulings. Perhaps this is itself the point. Rav Sheshes, knowing he cannot best Rav Chisda in a conceptual debate, declines to engage on that terrain. He offers no *shakla vetarya*, no discursive reasoning — only apodictic conclusions. Here is how I hold, here is how Rav Hamnuna holds, end of discussion. Avoiding the arena where Rav Chisda would have the advantage may be precisely what the story is meant to illustrate.

---

## Nochri Back Door

### Valley Opening OK

The *gemara* transitions to a series of cases involving a non-Jew whose presence in the courtyard creates a problem because he cannot participate in an *eruv*. The principle introduced is: *nochri sheyesh lo pesach arba'ah al arba'ah patuach lebik'ah* — a non-Jew who has a back door of four *tefachim* by four *tefachim* opening into a valley. Even if he uses his front door the entire day — *afilu machnis umotzi gemalim vekeronos kol hayom kulo derech mavoi* — bringing camels and wagons in and out through the front — *eino oser pnei mavoi* — he is not considered a problem for the *mavoi*. The reason: *bepsitcha demayachad lei bah nicha lei* — because of his private back door opening into a secluded space, we say that is his preferred domain.

This is, on its face, a remarkable legal fiction. The man is plainly using the front door all day long. Yet the halacha says that since he possesses a private opening to a private space, he effectively does not inhabit the courtyard in the legally relevant sense. His rights are considered to be exercised in his backyard, not the *chatzer*, and so he poses no problem there. The rationale is that a non-Jew whose legal footprint lies elsewhere — whose domain is conceptually elsewhere — does not assert rights over the courtyard, and therefore the *eruv* of the other residents remains intact.

### Karpef Question

*Ibaia lehu: patuach lekarpef mahu?* — the question was raised: what if the back door opens not into a wide valley but into a *karpef* — a walled enclosure, an open space that is bounded rather than unlimited? Does the same fiction apply? *Amar Rav Nachman bar Ami mishmei d'Ulla* — in the name of Ulla: *afilu patuach l'karpef* — even if it opens to a *karpef*, the principle holds.

The inquiry itself is revealing. The *gemara*'s willingness to question whether a *karpef* suffices suggests some underlying assumption that the fiction tracks something real: perhaps the idea is that a sufficiently large and private space genuinely draws the non-Jew's use away from the courtyard. When the space is smaller and more enclosed, the fiction becomes harder to sustain.

### Beit Sa'atayim Limit

*Rava v'Rav Yosef d'amri tarvaihu* — Rava and Rav Yosef jointly place a limit on this ruling: *beit satayim nochri beit satayim oser* — if the non-Jew's back enclosure is only a *beit satayim* or smaller, he does create a problem. If it is larger than a *beit satayim* — more than five thousand square *amos*, roughly a hundred feet by a hundred feet — then we maintain the fiction and say that is his domain, and he is not a problem.

The logic turns on the *beit satayim* threshold's halachic significance. A walled enclosure that is *yoter mibeit satayim* and was not enclosed for the purpose of habitation (*lo hukaf l'dirah*) is treated rabbinically as a *karmelit* — a domain in which carrying is prohibited. As a *karmelit*, it is not usable space for the non-Jew on Shabbos. His effective domain therefore remains the courtyard, and he is a problem there. If, however, the enclosure is *beit satayim* or smaller, it functions as a proper *reshus hayachid* — a genuinely private space — and we can say the non-Jew uses that space as his primary domain. *Tosafos* sharpens this: if the enclosure is *beit satayim* or smaller, it is halachically part of his house, which makes the fiction less sustainable in one direction but more coherent in another — it is all simply his private space.

### Jew Reverse Case

Interestingly, the reverse applies when the party with the back opening is a Jew who forgot to participate in the *eruv*. *Beit satayim eino oser yoter m'beit satayim oser* — a *beit satayim* enclosure does not make the Jew a problem; more than a *beit satayim* does. The inversion is striking. When the backyard is *yoter mibeit satayim* and is therefore a *karmelit* — prohibited for carrying — the Jew cannot use it on Shabbos. His only viable space is the courtyard, and so he genuinely asserts his presence there and becomes a problem. When the backyard is *beit satayim* or smaller and functions as a *reshus hayachid*, the Jew has a private space he can carry within, and we say he prefers it to the courtyard.

*Rashi* explains the asymmetry between the Jew and the non-Jew: for the Jew, Shabbos is Shabbos, and he wishes to carry in whatever private space is available to him; for the non-Jew, who does not observe Shabbos in the same sense, he requires more expansive space before we say it constitutes his primary domain. Whatever the precise rationale, the practical picture is that for the non-Jew the larger the space the better, while for the Jew the reverse is true — the fiction runs in the opposite direction.

---

## Reshus Status

### Yochanan's Teaching

*Amar Ulla amar Rabbi Yochanan* — the *gemara* now shifts into a more foundational discussion of *reshus* classification. The teaching: *karpaf yoter mibeit satayim shelo hukaf ledira* — a walled enclosure larger than a *beit satayim* that was not enclosed for purposes of habitation. The question of what constitutes *hukaf ledira* — enclosed for habitation — is itself a major issue with real-world implications for *eruv* construction; generally, any space that people regularly traverse or use is considered *ledira*, while spaces that go entirely unused, such as a large lake within the walls, raise genuine concerns.

Rabbi Yochanan's teaching continues: *ve'afilu kor ve'afilu korayim* — even if this enclosure is vast, the size of a *kor* or even greater, *hazorek letocho chayav* — one who throws an object into it is biblically liable. That is: biblically, no matter how large a walled enclosure is, it remains a *reshus hayachid*. Rabbinically it is treated as a *karmelit* and one may not carry within it — but that is only a rabbinic restriction. The biblical status is *reshus hayachid* in all cases where walls are present. *Mai ta'ama mechitza hi* — because it is genuinely walled. *Ela she-mechuseret diyurin* — it is simply that no one inhabits it, which is a rabbinic deficiency, not a biblical one.

### Rock in Sea

*Metiv Rav Huna bar Chinana* — Rav Huna bar Chinana challenged this position with a *beraisa*. The case: *sela she-bayam gavoah asara* — a rock in the sea that is ten *tefachim* tall and four by four *tefachim* wide. The sea is a *karmelis*. Given the rock's dimensions, it is a *reshus hayachid*, and accordingly: *ein metaltelin lo mitocho layam velo mehayam letocho* — one may not carry from the rock to the sea or from the sea to the rock, because this constitutes crossing from *reshus hayachid* to *karmelis*. *Pachus mikan metaltelin* — if the rock is smaller or lower, one may carry, because then it too is a *karmelis*, and crossing from one *karmelis* to another is rabbinically treated more leniently than crossing the *reshus hayachid* boundary.

Now, the *beraisa* then adds: *ad beit satayim* — this applies until a certain size. The question is on which clause does the *beit satayim* qualifier fall. *Ileima aseifa* — if it falls on the latter clause, the case where the rock is low and therefore a *karmelis*, that makes no sense: if the rock is a *karmelis* regardless of size, why would it matter whether it exceeds *beit satayim*? Moving from one *karmelis* to another is not a problem irrespective of the size of either. Therefore, *ella lav areisha* — it must apply to the first case, where the rock is tall enough to be a *reshus hayachid*. The *beraisa* is saying: the restriction on crossing the line from the rock to the sea applies only when the rock is *beit satayim* or smaller — that is, when it expresses itself as a genuine *reshus hayachid*. But once it is *yoter mibeit satayim*, one may carry across. The implication: at that point, it is no longer functioning as a *reshus hayachid* but as a *karmelis* — from which Rav Huna bar Chinana deduces a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan. If a space larger than *beit satayim* truly remains a biblical *reshus hayachid*, why does the prohibition on crossing the line dissolve?

### Rava Dismisses

*Amar Rava* — Rava responded sharply: *man d'lo yada litaratzei masnisa tiyuvta motiv lei* — a person who does not know how to properly explain a *beraisa* should not use it as a challenge. Learn the *beraisa* first, then deploy it. Rava's reading: the *beraisa* does indeed apply to the first clause, but the *beit satayim* reference does not mean that beyond that threshold one is permitted to cross the line. Rather, implicit in the prohibition on crossing the line is the permission to carry *on* the rock. The *beraisa* is noting that this permission to carry on the rock applies only up to *beit satayim*; beyond that, one may not carry on the rock. There is no implication that crossing the line becomes permitted — only that carrying within the larger space becomes prohibited as a *karmelis*. Whether this reading of the *beraisa* is fully persuasive is debatable; the text's plain structure does not obviously support it, and Rava's dismissive tone perhaps overreaches his interpretive case.

### Hen Amru Vehen

Rav Ashi offers a different and more compelling resolution. *Amar Rav Ashi le'olam areisha* — Rav Ashi agrees that the *beraisa* applies to the first case and that once the rock exceeds *beit satayim*, one is indeed permitted to cross the line. He does not dispute Rav Huna bar Chinana's reading. His answer is: *hein amru vehein amru* — they said, and they said. The Rabbis who enacted the rabbinic restrictions are the same Rabbis who defined their scope. The prohibition on crossing from *reshus hayachid* to *karmelis* is itself rabbinic. The classification of a *yoter mibeit satayim* enclosure as a *karmelis* is likewise rabbinic. When the Rabbis designated a large walled space as a *karmelis*, they simultaneously and consistently permitted crossing the line into it from the surrounding *karmelis*, because to do otherwise would be internally contradictory.

### Carrying Priority

The *gemara* presses further: *u'mai shna* — why do the Rabbis favor one restriction over the other? When facing a *yoter mibeit satayim* space, why do they maintain the prohibition on carrying within it while waiving the prohibition on crossing the line, rather than the reverse? The answer: *tocho shchi'ach* — carrying within the space is the more frequent concern, the more common scenario. *Mitocho leyam umiyam letocho lo shchi'ach* — crossing the line between the rock and the sea, in contrast, is uncommon; one can only go a distance of less than four *amos* in any case before being back over the line. The Rabbis' *gezeirah* targets what is most practically significant. If they had maintained the crossing-the-line prohibition while waiving the carrying restriction, the public would observe that one is permitted to carry in this large enclosed space and might conclude that it is a full *reshus hayachid*, leading to carrying throughout its entirety — *ve'asi letaltulei dechulei*. To prevent that inference, they prioritize the restriction on internal carrying. Keeping the crossing-the-line prohibition would paradoxically undermine their message, so they let it go in order to hold the more important line.

---

## Brit Milah Water

### Spilled Water

The *gemara* moves to a vivid practical episode involving *Rabba*. *Hahu yanuka de'ishtapich chamimei* — there was a child for whom a *bris milah* was to be performed, and the hot water prepared for post-operative care was spilled. It was Shabbos, and hot water was needed — held in one house, required in the courtyard or another location. *Tosafos* notes that this scenario pertains specifically to before the *bris milah* was performed; once the *bris* takes place, the situation becomes one of *pikuach nefesh* and the analysis changes entirely.

### Rabba's Plan

*Amar lei Rabba* — Rabba told those present: *naisu lei chamimei migov beisai* — go bring the hot water from my house; I have hot water we can use.

### Abaye Objects

*Amar lei Abaye: veha lo arvinnan* — but Abaye pointed out that no *eruv* had been made. This observation is itself remarkable on two levels. First, that Rabba apparently did not know they had failed to make an *eruv*. Second — and more puzzling — why had they not made an *eruv* at all? Establishing an *eruv chatzeros* requires minimal effort; it can be set up with something as simple as a *matzah* and left in place for an entire year. Why would a courtyard go without one?

### Rabba's Rejoinders

Rabba replied: *nismoch achituf* — we can rely on the *shituf mevo'os*. There is an opinion that a *shituf mevo'os* — the joining of the alleyway, done at the broader level encompassing multiple courtyards — can, *bedieved*, substitute for individual *eruv chatzeros*, permitting carrying within the individual courtyards. *Amar lei: veha lo shaftinnan* — Abaye informed him that the *shituf* had not been done either. The exchange has a certain wry humor: Rabba is spending his Shabbos absorbed in learning, entirely removed from the logistical realities of the courtyard.

Rabba then suggested: *namelei lenochri leiselei* — tell a non-Jew to bring the hot water. It was at this point that Abaye wished to raise a challenge, but *Rav Yosef* — who was present, and who was both Abaye's and Rabba's teacher — stopped him. *Veloch shavkan Rav Yosef* — Rav Yosef would not let him raise the objection.

### D'Rabbanan vs Torah

*De'amar Rav Yosef amar Rav Kahana: ki havinnan bei Rav Yehuda, havi amar lan* — for Rav Yosef cited a principle he had received from Rav Kahana in the name of Rav Yehuda: when we were in the study house of Rav Yehuda, he taught us the following. *Bide'oraisa* — in a matter of biblical law, when there is a debate about permissibility, *mosvinnan tiyuvta vehadar avdinan ma'aseh* — we first raise all challenges before acting. A biblical prohibition demands that we exhaust our doubts before proceeding. *Biderabbanan* — in a matter of rabbinic law, where someone has articulated a position permitting a given action, *avdinan ma'aseh vehadar mosvinnan tiyufta* — we act first and raise challenges afterward. If a competent authority has stated a position and you have a question about it, hold your question; when the pressing need is rabbinic in nature, act on the ruling and debate it later.

This principle is less radical than it might first appear. It does not mean one presumes leniency in rabbinic matters without any basis. The scenario is that an authority has actually ruled, and a student wishes to challenge that ruling. Rav Yosef's point is: in a *d'rabbanan* context, do not let the challenge stand in the way of action.

### Hazah vs Amira

After the episode concluded, Rav Yosef turned to Abaye and invited him to share what he had wanted to ask. *Amar lei: detanya — hazah shevus, ve'amirah lenochri shevus* — from a *beraisa*: sprinkling (*hazah*) the ashes of a *parah adumah* is a *shevus* — a rabbinic prohibition — and instructing a non-Jew (*amira lenochri*) is also a *shevus*. The *beraisa* deals with a case where *erev Pesach* falls on Shabbos and a person is *tamei*. His only path to bringing the *korban Pesach* is through sprinkling the ashes of *parah adumah* on Shabbos. Yet we do not do so — we do not override the rabbinic prohibition of *hazah* even to enable the *korban Pesach*, a *mitzvah she'yeish bo kares*. If so, Abaye argued, by the same logic we should not override *amira lenochri* for the *bris milah*. Let the *bris* be delayed rather than violate a rabbinic prohibition.

The comparison carries force: both *bris milah* and *korban Pesach* are *mitzvos asei she'yeish bo kares*, positive commandments whose violation incurs *kares*. If we forego *korban Pesach* rather than perform a rabbinic violation, ought we not forego the timely *bris milah* rather than instruct a non-Jew? The *bris*, after all, can be performed the next day — it will be *shelo bizmano*, not at the appointed time, but it will be done. *Korban Pesach Sheini* is a makeup option as well, though perhaps a more significant deferral.

### Ma'aseh Distinction

*Amar lei Rav Yosef: velo shani lach bein shvus d'is beih ma'aseh l'shvus d'leis beih ma'aseh?* — Rav Yosef replied: do you not distinguish between a rabbinic prohibition that involves an *act* and one that does not? Sprinkling — *hazah* — is a *shvus d'is beih ma'aseh*: the person performing it is executing a physical action, a genuine act. *Amira lenochri* — instructing a non-Jew — is *shvus d'leis beih ma'aseh*: the speaker merely speaks; the physical act is performed entirely by the non-Jew. This removes the Jewish actor one significant step from any violation, making *amira lenochri* a categorically weaker rabbinic prohibition.

The *gemara* then adds a further clause: *d'ha'amar lo amar lenochri zil achim lei* — and he did not even tell the non-Jew to heat the water. Rabba instructed the non-Jew only to carry — and carrying is itself only a rabbinic prohibition in this context. Thus the *amira* was directed at a *d'rabbanan*, not a *d'oraisa*. This creates what is termed *shvus dishvus* — a double-layered rabbinic prohibition: the instruction itself (*amira lenochri*) is *d'rabbanan*, and the act being performed (carrying through an unenclosed space) is also *d'rabbanan*. This double remove from biblical prohibition is what permits the action, at least in a case of *tzorech mitzvah*.

This small response of Rav Yosef carries enormous halachic weight, and it is worth noting that its interpretation is contested. One reading is that Rav Yosef's primary point is the *d'leis beih ma'aseh* distinction — that *amira lenochri* is inherently weaker because it involves no act, and this lower threshold makes it permissible in circumstances of need. On this reading, other rabbinic prohibitions that do involve an act would require a higher threshold. The second reading focuses on the *shvus dishvus* element — that the specific permissibility here rests on the doubling of rabbinic removes, and that even *amira lenochri* would not be permitted if the act being commissioned were a *d'oraisa*.

These two readings undergird a wide range of practical *halachos*, including the parameters for *amira lenochri* for a *choleh she'ein bo sakanah* and the thresholds for *tzorech mitzvah* on Shabbos. The broad consensus follows the more lenient reading, under which *amira lenochri* is a sufficiently attenuated rabbinic act that it can be permitted across a meaningful range of pressing needs — a consequence that is, as the *gemara*'s own framing suggests, a considerable relief.

*Chag sameach* to all.

---

---

# Eiruvin 70

## Recent Issues: Labor & S…

### Non-Jew Labor, Mitzvah

Before turning to the *mishna* proper, it is worth summarizing two significant halachic issues that arose over the course of the preceding days, as not everyone may have been present for those discussions.

The first concerned the heating of water for an infant on *Shabbos* and the attendant question of whether a non-Jew may be instructed to perform such an act. This naturally opens onto the broader question of what categories of need or purpose can justify *amira l'goi* — instructing a non-Jew to perform a *melacha*. Where there is *sakanas nefashos*, the matter is clear. Similarly, for a *choleh kol gufo* — a genuinely ill person, not merely someone with a minor complaint, though without mortal danger — one may have a non-Jew perform a *melacha*. The question of whether one may directly perform a *derabonon* oneself in such circumstances is debated separately. Instructing a non-Jew is generally easier, since one is not personally performing any act. When the purpose is the performance of a *mitzvah*, however — such as facilitating a *bris milah* — a range of opinions comes into play.

### BaHaG & Opinions

The spectrum of *poskim* on this question extends from the *BaHaG*, who permits instructing a non-Jew to perform even a *d'oraisa* for the sake of a *mitzvah*, to the more restrictive view that *amira l'goi* may be employed only for a *derabonon* — or more precisely, only for a double *derabonon* — or that the leniency is limited specifically to *milah* rather than extending to every *mitzvah*. The practical tendency adopted in many communities is to permit even a direct performance of a double *derabonon* for the sake of any *mitzvah*, and under certain circumstances *poskim* do rely on the position of the *BaHaG* as well. This also bears on what is permissible on *Yom Tov* in analogous situations.

### Mechallel Shabbat Status

The second major issue from the preceding day concerned the status of a *mechallel Shabbos* — a habitual public violator of *Shabbos* — with respect to participation in the *eruv* process through *bittul reshous*. The *Gemara* addressed this initially through the case of a *Tzedoki*, and there is reason to think the *Tzedoki*'s disqualification might stem from a very local cause: since a *Tzedoki* does not accept the rabbinic framework of *eruv* altogether, he cannot be part of a system he categorically rejects. The *Gemara* then explored whether the disqualification of a *mechallel Shabbos* might be limited to matters pertaining specifically to *Shabbos* laws, or whether it extends universally. This was in fact a disputed question among *tannaim*, and it was only the final position of the *Gemara* that treats it as excluding the *mechallel Shabbos* across all areas.

### Rambam & Rav Moshe

Even that final conclusion in the *Gemara* is framed in terms of *mumar* — an apostate — rather than the categorical formulation that follows in the *Rambam*, who states that a *mechallel Shabbos* is *harei hu kegoy l'chol davar*, equivalent to a non-Jew in every respect. Rav Moshe questions whether that degree of absolute universality is actually supported by the *Gemara*, both in terms of its categorical nature and in terms of the specific comparison to a non-Jew.

### Tzedoki & Habitual

Within this discussion, an important distinction was noted regarding the *Tzedoki* and, by extension, the Karaites and analogous groups in our own time. The question is whether someone who operates within an entirely different halachic or theological system — rather than simply transgressing the accepted one — should be treated the same as an ordinary *mechallel Shabbos*. Additionally, it was emphasized that the disqualification of a *mechallel Shabbos* requires habitual violation, not a single act, and the question of whether this applies even to violations of rabbinic law tends toward inclusion.

### Chashad Distinction

Finally, a crucial conceptual distinction was drawn between the question of *status* exclusion — whether the *mechallel Shabbos* is categorically excluded from certain legal frameworks — and the separate question of *chashad*, untrustworthiness. The latter concerns whether a person can be relied upon to testify or be believed regarding certain matters, and this is an independent consideration that should not be conflated with the question of categorical status.

---

## Forgotten Eruv & Waivers

### Forgotten One: Private H…

We now turn to the *mishna*, which begins on 69b. The *mishna* states: *anshei chatzer sheshachach echad mehem v'lo eirev* — the residents of a courtyard, one of whom forgot and did not make an *eruv*. The consequence is *beiso assur le'hachnis u'lehotzi lo v'lahem* — his house is forbidden for carrying in and out, both for him and for them.

The reason he himself cannot use his house in connection with the *chatzer* is, as we have been discussing, that doing so would constitute a reassertion of his rights in the *chatzer*. The reason the others cannot carry in and out of his house requires elaboration, and the *Gemara* will address it shortly. The operating assumption — which frames the *mishna* as following the position of the *Rabbonon* rather than Rabbi Eliezer, a debate discussed earlier — is that he waived only his rights in the *chatzer*, not in his house. His house remains a separate, private domain, and therefore neither he nor anyone else can carry between his house and the *chatzer*. The *mishna* continues: *veshelachem mutarim lo v'lahem* — their houses they may all carry in and out of freely, as these form one collective domain together with the *chatzer*.

### All Waive to One Person

The *mishna* then presents a reverse scenario: *natnu lo rishusan* — the other residents waived their rights to him. Perhaps he had a particular pressing need to use the *chatzer*, and so the others transferred their rights to him. Now the entire *chatzer* is effectively his; he alone has rights, without having made an *eruv*, but with everyone else having waived to him. In this case, *hu muttar* — he may carry in and out of his house — *v'hen asurin* — but they are forbidden to carry from his house into the *chatzer*. The *Gemara* will explain the reasoning: while one person can be considered a guest in the collective domain of many, the many cannot plausibly be considered guests in the domain of one. The fiction that the entire *chatzer* belongs to a single individual is tenuous enough; once the others begin carrying from his house, they are effectively reasserting their own presence.

### Two Receivers Problem

The *mishna* continues: *hayu shnayim osrin zeh la'zeh* — if there were two people who both failed to make an *eruv*, and all the other residents waived their rights to these two, the courtyard remains problematic. These two individuals are not a unified collective; they are two separate people with competing and unresolved domains within the *chatzer*. Their presence continues to prohibit carrying.

### Give & Receive Rules

The *mishna* then articulates the governing principle: *she'echad noten reshut v'notel reshut* — one person can both give rights and receive rights. *Shnayim notnim reshut* — two people can give rights. *V'ein notlin reshut* — but two people cannot receive rights, since two non-participants remaining in the *chatzer* still leaves unresolved domains.

### Shammai vs. Hillel

The *mishna* also addresses the timing of *bittul reshut*: *Beis Shammai omrim miba'od yom* — Beis Shammai holds that the waiver must be performed while it is still day before *Shabbos* begins. The logic is that if you intend to create a new status for the *chatzer*, it must be done before *Shabbos* takes effect — though one might wonder why the person couldn't simply participate in the *eruv* in the first place. *U'Beis Hillel omrim mishe'chashechah* — Beis Hillel permits the waiver even after nightfall, after *Shabbos* has already begun, which is the assumption operative throughout the surrounding discussions.

### Reassertion Debate

Finally, the *mishna* addresses what happens if a person waives his rights and then carries out from his domain. *Bein b'shogeg bein b'mezid harei zeh oser divrei Rabbi Meir* — whether he did so intentionally or unintentionally, he has thereby reasserted his rights and has now made carrying forbidden for everyone else, in the view of Rabbi Meir. *Rabbi Yehuda omer: b'mezid oser, b'shogeg eino oser* — Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between intentional and unintentional reassertion: only a deliberate act of carrying reclaims his rights, while an inadvertent one does not.

It was noted earlier in the *Gemara* that all of this is only a concern if the other members of the *chatzer* had not already established their own claim. Once they have staked their claim in the *chatzer*, one person's subsequent reassertion does not undo what they have already acquired. One might also raise the question of whether, having reasserted rights by carrying out, the person could then perform a second *bittul* — whether *mevattelin v'chozrin u'mevattelin* applies here as well. The further question of whether, according to the opinions that permit reassertion, a *bittul* after a reclaiming of previously-waived rights would be effective remains open.

---

## Gemara: House vs. Courty…

### Separate Domains

The *Gemara* opens by asking what seems like an obvious question but turns out to require careful analysis. The *mishna* states that when one person forgets the *eruv* and waives his rights to the *chatzer*, his house remains forbidden even to the other residents. The *Gemara* asks: *beiso hu d'asar* — his house is what is forbidden — *ha chatzeiro sharei* — the *chatzer* itself is permitted; that is explicit in the *mishna*. So what exactly is the case?

The *Gemara* frames this as a dilemma: *heichi dami* — what are the circumstances? If he waived his rights to his house entirely, then why is his house forbidden to the others? And if he did not waive his rights to the *chatzer* at all, why is the *chatzer* permitted? The resolution — *hacha b'mai askinan* — is that the case involves someone who waived his rights to the *chatzer* but did not waive his rights to his house. He waived the *chatzer reshut* alone, so the *chatzer* is open to all; but his house retains its separate status as his private domain, and therefore neither he nor the others may carry between his house and the *chatzer*.

### House Independence

This leads to a more general principle. *Kasavari rabbanan*, the position of the *Rabbonon* is that *hamvattel reshus chatzeiro* — one who waives his rights to the *chatzer* — *reshus beiso lo bitel* — has not thereby waived the rights to his house. The reason, as the *Gemara* explains, is *dedayri inshi beveita belo chatzer* — people can and do live in houses without a *chatzer*. Since a house can exist as an independent dwelling independently of a courtyard, when someone waives rights over the *chatzer*, the natural assumption is that he was focused solely on the *chatzer* and retains his house as his own domain. It is not that he must have explicitly stated he was keeping his house; the implication is simply that nothing he said touched upon his house.

The *Gemara* then turns to the reverse scenario from the *mishna*: *veshelhen muttar lo u'lahem* — their houses are permissible for him and for them. The question is: *mai taama* — what is the reason that he, the one who forgot the *eruv*, may carry in and out of their houses? The *Gemara* answers: *dehavei oreiach legabeihu* — he has the status of a guest relative to them. Since the *chatzer* and their houses form one collective domain, and he has waived his own rights, he enters their shared space as a guest. A guest may carry in and out of a host's house without thereby asserting proprietorial rights.

### Guest Status Asymmetry

This reasoning then forces a closer examination of the reverse scenario: *nasnu lo reshusan* — when they all waived their rights to him — *hu muttar v'hen asurin* — he may carry, but they cannot, even from his house. The question is: *venihavu inhu legabeih ke-orchin* — why cannot they also be treated as guests relative to him? The *Gemara*'s answer is: *chad legabeih chamisha havei oreiach* — one person can be a guest relative to a collective of many people; *chamisha legabeih chad lo havei oreiach* — but many people cannot be guests relative to one. The numbers here are illustrative rather than precise; the point is that when a large group is treated as belonging to the domain of a single individual, the fiction becomes too tenuous. The moment those many people start carrying from his house into the *chatzer*, they are effectively reasserting their presence, because it is simply implausible that a large group could genuinely be subsumed under the single domain of one person the way one person can disappear into the collective domain of many.

The *Gemara* briefly considers whether the *mishna*'s two scenarios — he waives to them, and then they waive to him — represent a single sequential case, from which one could infer that *mevattelin v'chozrin u'mevattelin* is permitted. The *Gemara* rejects this reading: *hachi kaamar*, the *mishna* is presenting two independent cases. The first, *nasnu lo reshusan me-ikara*, is simply the scenario where they waived to him from the outset — not as a sequel to a prior waiver in the other direction.

### Conditional Waiver Fails

Returning to the problem of two people neither of whom made an *eruv* — if everyone in the *chatzer* waives their rights to both of them, the *chatzer* remains forbidden, as two unresolved domains persist. The *Gemara* notes that this might seem obvious — *peshita* — but the ruling is needed for the following case: *de-hadar chad mineihu bittel lei le-chavreih* — what if after everyone waives to the two, one of them then turns and waives to the other? You might think — *mahu de-teima lishteri* — that now it should be permissible, since effectively one person is the sole rights-holder. *Ka mashma lan*: it does not work. The reason is that *be-idna de-vittel* — at the moment the others performed their waiver — the *chatzer* was not yet usable by those two, since they constituted two separate unresolved domains. The initial waiver was therefore ineffective from the very first moment. Since the fiction of *bittul reshut* operates not by genuine transfer but by a legal relinquishment, it must be effective immediately. If the waiver did not take effect at the moment it was performed, nothing was actually conferred, and there is nothing that one of the two can then pass along to the other.

Similarly, a proposal involving a stipulated condition — *knei al menat lehaknot* — acquiring on condition to subsequently transfer — also fails. Even if the others specified that they were waiving to one person on condition that he would then transfer the rights to the second, this does not work. At the initial moment, two people still had unresolved rights, so the waiver was ineffective, and no subsequent transfer can remedy what was never validly established.

---

## Braita Scenarios

### Case 1: Non-Participant

The *Gemara* now turns to a *braita* that presents a series of cases governing who may give and receive *bittul reshut*. The *braita* is admittedly intricate — there are a great many cases — but the underlying logic, once traced through, is coherent.

Case 1: *echad she-lo eirev noten reshuto le-echad she-eirev* — one person who did not make an *eruv* may give his rights to one person who did make an *eruv* (that is, one member of the *eruv* collective). This case, as we will see, immediately raises difficulties in how it is to be understood.

### Case 2: Two Give to One

Case 2: *shnayim she-eirvu notnim reshusan le-echad she-lo eirev* — two people who made an *eruv* together can give their rights to one person who did not make an *eruv*. Since there will then be only one person with unresolved rights in the *chatzer*, the situation is resolved. The *braita* uses the plural *notnim* — they give — which the *Gemara* will take as indicating that each of them must individually perform the waiver.

### Case 3: Both Give & Rece…

Case 3: *shnayim she-lo eirvu notnim reshusan li-shnayim she-eirvu* — two people who did not make an *eruv* may give their rights to two people who did make an *eruv*. Alternatively — a sub-case — those two non-participants may give their rights to one non-participant, since then only one person's rights remain unresolved.

### Case 3b: Two Give to Non…

This sub-case — two people who did not make an *eruv* giving their rights to one person who also did not make an *eruv* — is important. One might have thought that since nobody in this scenario made an *eruv*, the entire arrangement should be prohibited as an inducement to abandon *eruv* practice altogether. The *Gemara* will return to this concern below.

### Case 4: Participant Cannot…

Case 4: *aval ein echad she-eirev noten reshuto le-echad she-lo eirev* — but one person who made an *eruv* cannot give his rights to one person who did not make an *eruv*. The implicit reasoning is that the others who also made the *eruv* are still present and have not waived their rights; only one of them is acting, and all members of the *eruv* must give individually. Since only one person is waiving rather than all of them, the act is insufficient.

### Case 5: Cannot Give to T…

Case 5: *v'ein shnayim she-eirvu notnim reshusan li-shnayim she-lo eirvu* — two people who made an *eruv* cannot give their rights to two people who did not make an *eruv*. Even if they both waive, two non-participants remain in the *chatzer* with competing unresolved domains, and the problem persists.

### Case 6: Two to Two Failu…

Case 6: *v'ein shnayim she-lo eirvu notnim reshusam li-shnayim she-lo eirvu* — two people who did not make an *eruv* cannot give their rights to two other people who also did not make an *eruv*. Again, two unresolved domains remain at the conclusion of the act. This is the mirror image of case 3, and like case 5 it fails because one cannot be left with two people whose rights have not been resolved.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava Debate

### Rava: Deaths Hypothesis

The *braita* generates an immediate tension. Case 1 — one non-participant giving to one participant — seems to imply that a single member of the *eruv* collective can receive the waiver on behalf of the whole group. But case 3 — two non-participants giving to two participants — uses the language *li-shnayim*, to two, which seems to require that both members of the receiving collective individually receive.

Rava resolves the difficulty by positing that in Case 1, *de-havu u'meit* — the other members of the *eruv* collective had died. That is why only one remains: the *chatzer* at the time of the *bittul* had a single surviving member of the *eruv* group. This is admittedly a significant qualification to leave unstated, but Rava holds it is the only way to read the *braita* consistently.

The *Gemara* challenges Rava by pointing out that the cases in the *braita* appear to be consistent scenarios, not isolated edge cases requiring each to be understood under different circumstances. If the latter cases of the *braita* clearly assume the *eruv* members are alive — since the language *li-shnayim* requires two receivers — then consistency demands the same for Case 1. Rava responds that the cases need not be read as internally consistent — *hachi isa v'hachi isa* — each is an independent scenario and may obtain under different circumstances.

The *Gemara* then notes that Rava can adduce positive support from Case 3 itself: the fact that the *braita* says *li-shnayim she-eirvu* — to the two who made an *eruv* — using the plural, implies that *li-shnayim in, le-echad lo* — giving to two is permitted but giving to only one of the two is not. This, argues Rava, demonstrates that everyone in the receiving group must individually receive.

### Abaye: Collective Repres…

Abaye disagrees. He argues that when Case 3 says *li-shnayim she-eirvu*, this should be read as *le-echad mi-shnayim* — to one representative of the two, one person acting on behalf of the collective. The *braita* is not requiring that both receive individually; it is simply specifying that the rights go to the collective, which is adequately represented by one of its members.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges Abaye: *i hachi* — if so — *lisni le-echad she-eirev o le-echad she-lo eirev* — then why does the *braita* say "two"? Why not simply say "one"? This remains a *kashya* against Abaye's reading. However, the difficulty against Rava's reading — requiring the implausible assumption that four people died in Case 1 — is arguably greater.

### Case Analysis

The *Gemara* then proceeds case by case, explaining how each reading — Abaye's and Rava's — accounts for the *chiddush* of each scenario.

Case 1, according to Abaye: the other members of the *eruv* are still alive, and the *chiddush* is precisely that one need not waive to every individual member of the collective — giving to one suffices. According to Rava: the others died, and the *chiddush* is that we are not concerned (*delo gozrinan*) that allowing a waiver in a case where others happened to die will lead people to mistakenly think they can give to only one member of a living collective.

Case 2: the *chiddush* according to Rava and Abaye alike is that we do not penalize the non-participant by refusing to allow him to be the recipient. One might have thought — *mahu de-teima* — that the person who failed to make an *eruv* should be disqualified from receiving rights as a form of fine. *Ka mashma lan* that no such fine applies.

Case 3: according to Rava, the *chiddush* is that the receivers must be both of the *eruv* participants — *li-shnayim* is read literally — making explicit what Case 1 left implicit. According to Abaye, the *chiddush* of Case 3 is not about the receivers but about the givers: one might have thought that since neither of the two giving parties made an *eruv*, we should prohibit the entire arrangement, either to penalize them or out of concern that allowing *bittul* where nobody made an *eruv* will cause *torat eruv* to be forgotten altogether. *Ka mashma lan* that we do not apply this concern.

Case 3b — two non-participants giving to one non-participant — according to Abaye, the *chiddush* is the same: we are not concerned that permitting *bittul* in a case where nobody participated in an *eruv* will lead to the abandonment of *eruv* practice.

Case 4: according to Abaye, this case is the mirror of Case 1, and its *chiddush* is to clarify what Case 1 said: when we said in Case 1 that one could give to one member of the collective, we meant one receiver is sufficient — but one giver is not. A single member of the *eruv* collective cannot give on behalf of all the others, because each giver must act individually. According to Rava, this case simply parallels Case 1 in structure and its logic is self-explanatory given the framework already established.

Case 5: the *chiddush* is that even if one of the two receivers subsequently waives his share to the other — producing what looks like a single effective recipient — this still does not work, because at the moment of the original waiver, the *chatzer* was not usable by those two. The initial act was therefore ineffective, and no subsequent act can repair it.

Case 6: the *chiddush* is the same as Case 5 but with the added stipulation — *knei al menat lehaknot* — that even a conditional waiver (receiving on condition of passing along) fails, because the initial transfer was not immediately effective.

### Givers Individual, Recei…

The conclusion that emerges from this entire analysis is striking: there is, in fact, broad agreement on one side of the question. All agree that when the *eruv* collective is giving away rights, every individual member of that collective must personally perform the *bittul* — no one person can represent the group as a giver. The practical analogy offered is that when people give away property, one person cannot relinquish what belongs to another. The disagreement between Abaye and Rava centers exclusively on the receiving end: must every individual member of the receiving collective personally receive, or can one representative of the collective receive on behalf of all?

---

## Heir's Bittul Reshut

### Rava's Question

The *Gemara* now shifts to a question posed by Rava to Rav Nachman. The question involves an *yoresh* — an heir. Consider the case where a father owned a house in a *chatzer* but did not make an *eruv* with the other residents. The father then dies on *Shabbos*, and the son inherits the house at that point. The question is: *yoresh mahu she'yevatel reshus* — may the heir perform *bittul reshut*?

At the onset of *Shabbos*, the son was not a member of the *chatzer* and had no stake in it. He was not in a position to participate in an *eruv*, nor could he have performed *bittul*. Now that he has inherited the property mid-*Shabbos*, can he waive his newly acquired rights?

### Continuation vs. New

Two framings present themselves. On one reading, the heir is simply a newcomer who acquired a house on *Shabbos* — someone who had no connection to the *chatzer* when *Shabbos* began, and therefore cannot do *bittul*, just as any other newcomer who acquires a stake in a *chatzer* after *Shabbos* begins cannot retroactively regularize the situation. On the other reading, *yoresh kera d'avuha hu* — an heir is the legs of his father, a continuation of the father's identity and ownership. Under this conception, the heir is not a new legal entity at all; he is the same abstract owner, merely in a different person, and therefore what his father could have done he may also do.

### Rav Nachman Answer

Rav Nachman answers: *ani omer mevatel* — I would say he can perform *bittul*. However, a *braita* from the school of Shmuel states the opposite: *ein mevatel* — he cannot perform *bittul*. So there is a genuine dispute on the question, turning on whether the heir is to be seen as a continuation of the father or as an independent legal personality.

---

## Status at Shabbat Start

### Begin Permitted

The *Gemara* now introduces a broad principle, which is brought as a challenge to the preceding discussion. The principle states: *kol shehutar lemiktzas Shabbos hutar lechol haShabbos* — anything that was permissible for any part of *Shabbos* remains permissible for all of *Shabbos*. Conversely: *kol sheneesar lemiktzas Shabbos neesar lechol haShabbos* — anything that was forbidden at any part of *Shabbos* remains forbidden throughout *Shabbos*. The operative principle is the status at the beginning: what begins as permitted continues as permitted; what begins as forbidden remains forbidden.

### Sealed Openings

The *Gemara* illustrates the permissive side of the principle. *Eruv derech pesach* — an *eruv* made through a door connecting two courtyards, *venistam hapetach* — and then the door was sealed on *Shabbos*. One might have thought the *eruv* is now broken, since the connection has been severed. But since the *eruv* was valid when *Shabbos* began, it remains valid and carrying between the two courtyards continues to be permitted. The same applies to *eruv derech chalon venistam chalon* — an *eruv* made through a window, with the window subsequently sealed on *Shabbos*. Since it was valid at the start, it remains valid.

### Walls Fall

The principle extends further. *Mavoi shenitlu korosav o lechayav* — an alleyway whose beam (*korah*) or side-post (*lechi*) was removed on *Shabbos*. This is actually a significant *chiddush*: one might have thought that the removal of these structural markers — which in the first chapters of the tractate were shown to be what defines the alleyway as a domain permitting carrying — would fundamentally alter the legal status of the space. But the principle holds: since the *eruv* was valid and carrying was permitted when *Shabbos* began, the removal of the *lechi* or *korah* does not retroactively invalidate the *eruv*. Carrying may continue. One need not check on *Shabbos* whether the physical markers are still in place if they were verified before *Shabbos*. (This, of course, does not extend to actual walls: if two walls of an alleyway fall, there is nothing left to carry in, and no principle can save that.)

### Begin Forbidden

The converse is stated with equal force: *kol sheneesar lemiktzas Shabbos neesar lechol haShabbos kullah* — anything that was forbidden at the outset of *Shabbos* remains forbidden throughout. Again, the key is the status at the moment *Shabbos* begins.

### Wall Built on Shabbat

The illustration offered for the forbidden side of the principle is the following: two houses on opposite sides of a *reshus harabbim*, and non-Jews who, on *Shabbos* itself, surrounded the public domain with a *mechitza* — a partition — thereby converting it halachically into a *reshus hayachid*. One might think that now the two homeowners should be able to perform *bittul reshut* to each other and regularize their domains. The *Gemara* says this is not so. Since at the beginning of *Shabbos* they were not in a position to make an *eruv* or perform *bittul* — the *reshus hayachid* did not exist yet — the status that began as forbidden does not change, and they may not now do *bittul*. (Rashi notes an important caveat: if only one person were involved, the wall built by the non-Jews on *Shabbos* would genuinely create a *reshus hayachid*, and that individual would be the sole occupant — a different matter altogether. The issue of two unresolved parties is what blocks the remedy here.)

### Bittul Exception

The principle as stated, however, carries a crucial exception: *chutz mimvatel reshus* — except for the case of waiving rights. *Bittul reshut* is the one case in which *Shabbos* began in a state of prohibition — the *chatzer* was forbidden because someone sat out of the *eruv* — and yet a subsequent act of *bittul* in the middle of *Shabbos* converts that forbidden status into permission. This is precisely what makes *bittul reshut* singular: it is the exceptional mechanism that operates against the general principle.

---

## Heir Death Timing

### Dies Before Shabbat

The *Gemara* now applies these principles to the question of the heir through a series of scenarios. First: *echad mibnei chatzer shemeis vehiniach reshusso leachad min hashuk* — one of the residents of the *chatzer* dies and bequeaths his property to a stranger, someone from outside, who had no connection to this *chatzer*. If the resident died *mibe'od yom* — before *Shabbos* began — then the stranger enters the *chatzer* on *Shabbos* as a new party who never made an *eruv* and never had the opportunity to regularize his status before *Shabbos*. The stranger's presence makes carrying forbidden, and *bittul reshut* is not available to him, because the status began forbidden.

### Dies on Shabbat

In contrast: *mishe'chashecha eino osser* — if the same courtyard member died after *Shabbos* began, his property passes to the stranger mid-*Shabbos*. But since the *chatzer* was already in a permitted state when *Shabbos* began — the deceased was a member of the *eruv* — the principle *kol shehutar lemiktzas Shabbos hutar lechol haShabbos* applies. The status of permission is locked in from the beginning of *Shabbos* and continues; the stranger inheriting mid-*Shabbos* does not disrupt what was already established as permitted.

### Marketplace to Courtyard

The *Gemara* presents the inverse scenario: *echad min hashuk shemeis vehiniach reshusso le-echad min hachatzer* — a person from outside the *chatzer* who did not participate in the *eruv* dies and bequeaths his property to one of the *chatzer* residents. Here, whether he died before or after *Shabbos*, the practical question is whether the inheriting *chatzer* resident can now do *bittul* on behalf of what he has inherited. If the outsider died before *Shabbos*, the *chatzer* resident may acquire before *Shabbos* and the question is cleaner. If he died after *Shabbos* began, the problem of that unresolved domain persists into *Shabbos*, and the principle *kol sheneesar lemiktzas Shabbos neesar lechol haShabbos* would seem to block any remedy.

### Forbidden Until Bittul

The *Gemara* then clarifies what *osser* — forbidden — means in this context. It does not mean irreparably forbidden for all of *Shabbos* with no exit. Rather, *mai osser nami d'tani ad she'yevateil* — it means it is forbidden *until* the person performs *bittul reshut*. Once he does perform *bittul*, the status changes. This is, of course, the exception already identified — *chutz mimvatel reshus* — *bittul reshut* is precisely the mechanism that uniquely permits a change from forbidden to permitted mid-*Shabbos*.

One might note that the *Gemara* here does not draw an explicit distinction between the case of a direct heir — someone who is *kera d'avuha*, a continuation of the father — and a stranger who receives a bequest. That distinction, which lay at the heart of Rava's original question, would seem to argue powerfully in favor of the heir's ability to perform *bittul*: unlike a pure stranger, the heir carries a kind of continuity of identity with the original owner. It is notable that the *Gemara* does not press this distinction, and the question of whether the heir may perform *bittul* will continue to be examined.

---

---

# Eiruvin 72

## Shituf vs. Eruv Debate

### Intro: Shituf & Eruv

Eruvin 72 — the two-thirds mark of the tractate — opens in the midst of a crucial *halacha l'maiseh* discussion. The question at stake is whether a *shituf mevo'ot*, the combining together of the various courtyards that open into a shared street, obviates the need for a separate *eruv chatzeirot* — or, conversely, whether courtyards that collectively perform an *eruv* still require a *shituf mevo'ot* in addition.

The structural distinction between the two institutions is as follows. An *eruv* is performed specifically with bread, whereas a *shituf* may be performed with virtually anything — wine being the paradigmatic alternative discussed here. Furthermore, an *eruv* is placed in a house within the courtyard, while a *shituf* is placed in the courtyard itself. The courtyard stands in relation to the *mavoi* as the house stands in relation to the courtyard. Rashi holds that the *shituf* may also be placed in a house, whereas Tosafot maintains it may only be placed in the courtyard — a distinction that matters for Tosafot because it provides the only unambiguous indicator of whether a collective *eruv* of all the courtyards is being labeled an *eruv* or a *shituf*. According to Rashi, where it is placed does not always resolve that question.

The overarching dispute is between Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim. Rabbi Meir holds that one must always perform both — the *eruv chatzeirot* and the *shituf mevo'ot* — while the Chachamim rule that one may serve as a substitute for the other.

### Bread vs. Wine

Picking up from the bottom of 71b, the Gemara records a dispute between Rav Nechumi and Rava about precisely when Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim disagree.

*Pligi bah Rav Nechumi v'Rava* — one of them says: *b'pat d'chulei alma lo pligi d'bachada sagi* — when bread is used for the *shituf mevo'ot*, everyone agrees that one suffices. By choosing bread — a medium that would have been valid for the *eruv chatzeirot* as well — one has already done something that signals the higher standard, and there is therefore no debate. *Ki pligi b'yayin* — the dispute arises only when wine is used for the *shituf*. Wine could not have served for an *eruv chatzeirot*, and so the question is whether such a *shituf* can nonetheless substitute for one.

The other opinion inverts this entirely: *b'yayin d'chulei alma lo pligi d'beina tartei* — when wine is used, everyone agrees that it is insufficient and both are required. *Ki pligi b'pat* — the debate is about bread. Even there, Rabbi Meir insists that both must be performed — though the Gemara noted earlier that his reason is not a conceptual one but a secondary concern, lest the institution of *eruv chatzeirot* be forgotten if *shituf* can always substitute for it.

### Resolving the Dispute

The Gemara then challenges whichever reading places the debate in the case of wine, by citing the language of the Chachamim: *o meiarvin o mishtatfin* — either one performs an *eruv* or a *shituf*. The apparent implication is that each institution operates according to its normal parameters — *eruv* with bread in the courtyards, *shituf* with wine in the *mavoi* — and the Chachamim hold that either one suffices. This would suggest that the wine case is precisely what they are permitting, and what Rabbi Meir disputes.

### Rav Giddel's Reading

Rav Giddel, citing Rav, offers a reinterpretation: *hachi ka'amar* — this is what the Mishnah means. Either one performs an *eruv* in the courtyard with bread, and one is then permitted both there and in the street, or one performs a *shituf* in the *mavoi* — but also with bread — and one is permitted both there and in the individual courtyards. On this reading, the phrase *o meiarvin o mishtatfin* does not invoke wine at all; the word *shituf* here refers to an act performed with bread. Consequently, it remains unclear from the Mishnah whether the dispute concerns wine or bread.

---

## Practical Rulings

### Three Levels

The Gemara now turns to the practical ruling. Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, declares: *halacha k'Rabbi Meir* — the law follows Rabbi Meir, and one must perform both. Rav Huna says: *minhag k'Rabbi Meir* — the accepted practice follows Rabbi Meir. And Rabbi Yochanan says: *nahagu am k'Rabbi Meir* — the people conduct themselves in accordance with Rabbi Meir.

These three formulations represent distinct levels of legal force, a distinction the Gemara has addressed earlier in the tractate. *Halacha* means the ruling is publicly declared and everyone should know it. *Minhag* means the position is accepted but need not be actively imposed; if someone comes with a *shaila*, one rules accordingly, but one does not make a public announcement to correct those who act otherwise. *Nahagu* is the most attenuated: it means that the underlying *halacha* does not actually follow Rabbi Meir, but the people have adopted the practice, and one need not go out of one's way to correct them.

### Tosafot's Challenge

This third level raises an obvious difficulty, which Tosafot addresses directly. If Rabbi Meir's position is merely a *chumra*, why would one ever imagine correcting someone who follows it? The entire concept of *nahagu* implies that there exists a level below it — practices that people adopt but that must be corrected. What possible harm could come from requiring both an *eruv* and a *shituf*?

Tosafot, in the first wide line of his commentary, states: *v'im tomar mah mecha'ah shayach kan im machmirim k'Rabbi Meir* — if people are simply being stringent, why would we stop them? He then gives two answers. First, *d'lo havei bracha l'vatala* — one recites a *bracha* when performing the *eruv* and when performing the *shituf*; if in fact only one is required, making a *bracha* on the unnecessary second act constitutes a *bracha l'vatala*. Second, *im nimna'im al kach l'havi sakin v'chamin l'tzorech mila* — if one mistakenly believes both are required, one may refrain from carrying something urgently needed, such as a knife or hot water for a *bris mila*, because one incorrectly concludes that without both an *eruv* and a *shituf* one cannot carry.

### Tradeoffs of Chumra

This Tosafot captures a broader principle of considerable importance: there is almost no such thing as a purely unadulterated *chumra* with no downside. Every stringency entails a leniency somewhere else. Here, acting like Rabbi Meir when the *halacha* does not require it leads to *brachos l'vatala* on one side, and to failing to fulfill genuine obligations on the other. In this particular case the tradeoff is not simply between *bein adam l'chavero* and *bein adam la'Makom* — it is largely within *bein adam la'Makom* itself, since performing a *bris mila* in its proper time is also a religious imperative. The lesson is that trade-offs of this kind must always be considered when adopting a stringent position.

### How We Pasken

Given that the Gemara concludes *halacha k'Rabbi Meir*, the further question is which version of Rabbi Meir's position we adopt. The dispute in the *rishonim* turns on whether Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim debate the case of wine or the case of bread. If the debate concerns only wine, then performing the *shituf* with bread resolves the issue and one need not perform both separately. Many *rishonim* rule this way.

The *Shulchan Aruch* in *Orach Chaim* 387 states: *hamishtatfin bamavoi tzrichin le'arev bechatzerot* — those who perform a *shituf mevo'ot* must also perform an *eruv chatzeirot*, so that children not forget the institution of *eruv*, since, as Rabbi Meir's language has it, people do not pay attention to what is done in the *mavoi* and may not realize that the *mavoi shituf* was intended to substitute for the courtyard *eruv*. However: *lefikach im nishtatfu bamavoi bepat somchin alav ve'ein tzrichin le'arev bechatzerot* — if the *shituf mevo'ot* was performed with bread, one may rely on it and is not required to also perform an *eruv chatzeirot*. Bread carries the combined significance of both institutions and satisfies both requirements.

### Box of Matzah

This ruling explains the widespread contemporary practice in city-wide *eruvin*. The rabbi takes a single box of *matzah*, transfers ownership through a *kinyan* on behalf of the entire city, and thereby makes everyone partners in that *pat*. Because it is bread — *bepat* — it functions as both *shituf* and *eruv*, and there is no need to perform a separate *eruv* for every individual street or courtyard. As for the quantity of bread required: once one has two meals' worth, the quantity suffices regardless of how many people are involved — even a city of a hundred thousand. The box of *matzah* thus covers the entire population.

One practical consequence is that if one forgot to purchase bread for *Shabbos*, one could in principle obtain a couple of pieces of *matzah* from the rabbi's box, since one is already a partner in it. This also illustrates that the question of *hilchata k'divrei hameikel* — whether we always rule leniently in cases of doubt — is not absolute. The Gemara's last three rulings here all trend toward the stringent position, though within that there is a push to say that at least everyone agrees the bread case is resolved, which is indeed what we rule.

---

## Apartment Buildings

### Mishna: Five Groups

The next Mishnah introduces a scenario that is, in essence, the question of an apartment building. Five groups (*chamishah chavurot*) all spent *Shabbos* in one large building (*traklin echad*) — one great hall or castle, with different groups in different sections. Rashi notes that the case assumes each group also has its own individual exit into the courtyard, which makes even clearer that from the courtyard's perspective these are separate units. But even apart from the question of the courtyard, the question of the shared internal space — the hallways and common areas — is the apartment building question in its essential form.

### Beit Shammai vs. Hillel

*Beit Shammai* rules: *eruv lechol chavurah vechavurah* — each group must contribute separately to the *eruv*. Each is a separate unit, both for purposes of participating in the courtyard *eruv* and for using the common internal space. *Beit Hillel* rules: *eruv echad lechulam* — one *eruv* suffices for all. The reason one suffices, according to *Beit Hillel*, is that internally they are seen as a single coherent unit. If they are one unit internally, they need no *eruv* among themselves to use the common space; and when contributing to the courtyard's *eruv*, one contribution represents them all.

The Mishnah then records agreement: *umodim bizman shemiktzasan sheruyin bachadarim o va'aliyot shetzrichin eruv lechol chavurah vechavurah* — both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* agree that if they are in truly separate rooms, or if some are upstairs and some down, each group requires its own separate *eruv*.
