This signals that there is a degree of physical separation which even *Beit Hillel* concedes renders them distinct units — and the Gemara must now determine what that threshold is.

For the practical question of apartment buildings: the last line of the Mishnah, describing fully separate rooms, represents our case. When people live in genuinely separate units, they are distinct, and if they wish to use common space, they must make an *eruv*. One need not knock on every door; one may take a box of *matzah* and effect a *kinyan* on behalf of all residents — though the presence of non-Jewish residents raises a separate complication to be addressed below.

### Agreement: Separate Units

The distinction established by the Mishnah — that some forms of division render the groups entirely separate even in *Beit Hillel*'s view — is the key to understanding where the two schools' debate is located. The Gemara proceeds to analyze what type of physical division triggers universal agreement, and what type falls into the zone of dispute.

---

## Walls & Barriers

### Low Barriers Debate

Rav Nachman offers one account of the dispute. *Machloket bemespis* — the debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* concerns a *mespis*, a low or flimsy barrier. *Aval bemechitza asara* — if a genuine halachic wall of ten *tefachim* divides them, then *divrei hakol eruv lechol chavurah vechavurah* — everyone agrees they are separate units. On this reading, *Beit Hillel*'s leniency applies only in the marginal case of minimal separation, while any proper *mechitza* produces agreement that the groups are distinct.

### Both Types Debated

A second version of Rav Nachman's position: *af bemespis machloket* — even the *mespis* case is debated, and the debate extends to the *mechitza* of ten *tefachim* as well. On this reading, *Beit Hillel* holds that even a full ten-*tefach* wall that does not reach the ceiling leaves the groups as one unit, while *Beit Shammai* considers them separate in both cases. This version leaves open the question of what would finally lead *Beit Hillel* to concede that the groups are genuinely distinct.

---

## Wall Height Dispute

### Reaching Ceiling

Bar Rabbi Chiya and Bar Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbe disagree about how to frame the debate. One says: *machlokes bemechitzot hamigi'ot letikra* — the dispute concerns walls that reach all the way to the ceiling. When walls do not reach the ceiling, *divrei hakol eruv echad lechulam* — everyone, including *Beit Shammai*, agrees it is one unit. The debate is only when the wall goes all the way up, where *Beit Hillel* says it remains one unit and *Beit Shammai* says it is separate.

### Not Reaching Ceiling

The other says the opposite: *machlokes bemechitzot she'ein migiot letikra* — the debate is specifically when the wall does not reach the ceiling. When walls do reach the ceiling, *divrei hakol tzrichim eruv lechol chaburah vechaburah* — everyone agrees these are separate units requiring individual participation.

### Analysis & Reconciliation

To lay out the full range of scenarios: at one extreme is the *mespis*, the low flimsy barrier; next is a *mechitza* of ten *tefachim* that does not reach the ceiling; then a wall that approaches but does not quite reach the ceiling; and finally a wall that fully reaches the ceiling (*magias latikra*). The question is where along this spectrum *Beit Hillel* acknowledges separation and where *Beit Shammai* might acknowledge unity.

On the question of what distinguishes "separate rooms" (*chadarim mamash*) in the Mishnah from the cases under debate, Rashi and Tosafot differ. Rashi holds that separate rooms means units originally constructed as distinct, as opposed to one large space subsequently divided. Tosafot holds the distinction is between permanent real walls and non-permanent or improvised partitions. Either way, if the rooms are genuinely separate — whether by original construction or by full permanent walls — everyone agrees they are distinct units, and that is the apartment building case. The debate falls somewhere in the intermediate range of ad hoc or non-permanent divisions that do not quite constitute full separate rooms.

---

## Rav Yehuda Resolution

### Ceiling Rule

Rav Yehuda Hassavar — a name Rashi explains as connoting analytical sharpness, while Tosafot suggests it may indicate his profession, a place name, or possibly a connection to hat-making — issues an authoritative ruling that resolves the competing versions: *lo nechleku Beit Shammai u'Veit Hillel al mechitzot hamigi'ot latikra shetzrichin eruv lechol chaburah vechaburah* — both schools agree that walls reaching the ceiling create separate groups. *Al mah nechleku? Al mechitzot she'ein migiot latikra* — the dispute is about walls that do not reach the ceiling. *Beit Shammai* says those too make them separate groups requiring individual *eruv* participation; *Beit Hillel* says that where the wall does not reach the ceiling they remain one group.

### Testing Interpretations

This statement of Rav Yehuda Hassavar constitutes a challenge — *tiyuvta* — to the version that holds *Beit Hillel* maintains the groups are one even when the wall reaches the ceiling. If Rav Yehuda Hassavar rules that everyone agrees walls to the ceiling produce separate groups, then the version claiming *Beit Hillel* permits even that case is directly contradicted.

Conversely, it provides support — *siyata* — to the version that locates the debate specifically in walls that do not reach the ceiling.

As for the first version of Rav Nachman — that the debate concerns only the *mespis* while any *mechitza* of ten *tefachim* produces universal agreement on separation — this too is contradicted. Rav Yehuda Hassavar's ruling shows that even a genuine *mechitza* that does not reach the ceiling is still debated; *Beit Hillel* says even that scenario is one unit.

For the second version of Rav Nachman — that the debate encompasses both the *mespis* and the full *mechitza* — the Gemara raises the question of whether this also is contradicted.

### Rav Nachman's Response

Rav Nachman responds: *pligi bimchitza vehu hadin bimispes* — they debate the *mechitza* case, and the same law applies by logical extension to the *mespis* case. The reason the ruling cites a *mechitza* rather than a *mespis* is *lehodiacha kochan deBeit Hillel* — to demonstrate the reach of *Beit Hillel*'s leniency. It is easy to be stringent; it is the leniency that is the *chidush*. By showing that even in the case of a tall wall that nearly reaches the ceiling *Beit Hillel* still considers the space unified, the ruling reveals how far *Beit Hillel* is willing to extend the principle of shared domain. To have debated only the *mespis* case would have shown *Beit Shammai*'s stringency — even a tiny barrier suffices for *Beit Shammai* to call them separate — but the Gemara's principle is *koach deheteira adif*: it is always a greater *chidush* to reveal the extent of the leniency.

Thus, on this reading, the two cases — *mespis* and *mechitza* that does not reach the ceiling — are halachically equivalent, both falling within the zone of debate. In both cases *Beit Hillel* holds one unit, *Beit Shammai* holds two. Only when the wall reaches the ceiling does universal agreement emerge: it is then two groups.

The version holding that even walls to the ceiling leave *Beit Hillel* saying one unit remains flatly contradicted and does not survive.

### Mishnah's Language

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that this resolution can also be inferred from a close reading of the Mishnah itself. The Mishnah says *umodim* — both schools agree — when they are in *chadarim* or *aliyot*, separate rooms or upper stories, that each requires its own *eruv*. If *chadarim mamash* meant simply rooms with any walls at all, the ruling would be obvious and the Mishnah would be saying nothing new. It must therefore mean something *ke'ein chadarim* — resembling separate rooms — and what does that mean? *Mechitza hamaga'at latikra* — an after-the-fact or non-permanent wall that nonetheless reaches all the way to the ceiling. Since that case produces universal agreement, one can infer that the debate applies to the range of partitions below that threshold. *Shma mina* — this is a valid inference from the Mishnah's precise language.

The upshot for the apartment building: once there are full walls reaching the ceiling — the standard case of any real apartment — both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* agree these are separate units. Each unit must independently participate in the *eruv* of the courtyard, and if the residents wish to carry in the common hallways, they must create an *eruv* among themselves. One practical solution is a box of *matzah* with a *kinyan* effected on behalf of all Jewish residents, though the presence of non-Jewish residents raises a distinct challenge.

---

## Receive vs. Contribute

### Contributing Separately

The Gemara introduces a *baraita* that draws an important distinction based on whether the groups in the large building are contributing to an *eruv* or receiving one. *B'meh devarim amurim k'she'molichin et eruvam le'makom acher* — when is the rule that each group must contribute separately? When they are bringing their *eruv* out to another location — that is, when they are the ones contributing to the unified *eruv* of the courtyard, placing their food in someone else's house outside the group.

### Receiving Exception

*Aval im hayah eruvam ba etzlan dei'hen eruv echad le'kulan* — but if the *eruv* comes to them — if they are the ones receiving the *eruv*, meaning the communal food is placed in one of their spaces — then even according to the more stringent opinions, one *eruv* suffices for all of them. Their shared space, however imperfectly unified, is coherent enough to receive as one.

### Two Interpretations

The Gemara offers two ways of understanding this asymmetry. The first version holds that *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* fundamentally agree that these groups are somewhat distinct yet have been unified — like separate units in a courtyard that have combined through a shared *eruv*. They are, as it were, five that have become one. The debate between the schools is not about their fundamental status but about what happens when this unified group wants to contribute outward: *Beit Hillel* says one representative can contribute on behalf of all, while *Beit Shammai* says that even a group that has become internally unified must contribute separately when linking with others, because the act of contributing outward expresses their individual identities.

When receiving, however, even *Beit Shammai* agrees. Since when the *eruv* is received it is simply placed in the space and no active contribution is required from each unit individually, even *Beit Shammai* accepts that the unified group receives as one.

The Gemara challenges this reading from a *baraita*: five houses in a courtyard that collectively made an *eruv* — when they send their *eruv* to link with another courtyard, one person contributing on their behalf suffices. The Gemara asks: whose position does this reflect? On the first version, it follows *Beit Hillel*, since *Beit Shammai* would require separate contributions even when giving. That much is consistent.

The second version of the interpretation holds that the fundamental debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* is precisely about whether these groups constitute a single unit at all — and the asymmetry between giving and receiving is total. When receiving, *Beit Hillel* says they are one unit and one reception suffices; *Beit Shammai* says they remain separate and each must receive individually. When contributing outward, even *Beit Hillel* concedes that the individual identities re-emerge and each must contribute separately. On this reading, the *baraita* about five houses contributing as one goes like no one's position — it is consistent with neither *Beit Shammai* (who requires separate contributions even when receiving) nor *Beit Hillel* (who, on this version, would require separate contributions when giving).

On the broader question of apartment buildings and non-Jewish residents: the concept of *tfisas yad* — the owner's presence in each unit through ownership of major appliances or infrastructure — can unify the building into a single domain, obviating the need for an *eruv* altogether. If the building owner retains ownership of the stove or refrigerator in each unit, the owner's presence creates a unified domain. In cooperative buildings where residents own only shares rather than discrete units, the analysis may similarly support a unified domain, since no resident has exclusive ownership of a particular space. Condominium arrangements require separate analysis, turning on whether the condominium association retains ownership of elements within each individual unit.

---

## Brothers Scenario

### Mishna: Brothers

The next Mishnah presents a related scenario. *Ha'achim shehayu ochlim al shulchan avihem* — brothers who all eat at their father's table, being supported by and taking their meals with their father, *veshenim bevateihen* — but who sleep each in his own home. The Mishnah rules: *tzrichin eruv lechol echad ve'echad* — they are considered separate units, and each must contribute independently to the *eruv*.

### Separate Contributions

The practical consequence follows: *ulefikach im shachach echad mehem velo eirev mevatel es reshuso* — if one of the brothers forgot to participate in the *eruv*, he must relinquish his rights in the courtyard to allow the others to carry. The asymmetry noted in the previous discussion appears here as well. *Bizman shemolichin eruvam bemakom acher* — this stringency applies when they are contributing their *eruv* elsewhere, meaning the *eruv* is placed in another household in the courtyard. *Aval im hayah eruv ba'etzlan* — but if the *eruv* comes to them, or if there are no other residents sharing the courtyard, *einam tzrichin le'arev* — they need not each contribute separately. The same logic applies: their individual identities become more salient when they are actively contributing outward, while their shared identity is sufficient when they are merely receiving or when there is no external group to interact with.

### Place of Sleeping

The Gemara draws a significant inference from this Mishnah: *shema mina makom lina gorem* — one learns that it is the place of sleeping, not the place of eating, that determines one's halachic domicile. The brothers all eat at their father's table, yet they are treated as separate units because each sleeps in his own home. This principle recurs throughout the halachic literature — for questions of *ner Chanukah*, for yeshiva students who eat communally but sleep in separate dormitory rooms, the operative question is where one sleeps.

Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, qualifies this inference: *be-mikablei pras shanu* — the Mishnah refers to brothers who receive a portion from their father, meaning the father sends them food to eat in their own homes; they are not literally eating at the father's table in the father's house. On this reading, the Mishnah does not actually prove that eating together in one place is irrelevant; perhaps if they ate at the father's house itself, the ruling might differ. The Gemara thus leaves open the theoretical question of whether shared meals in a shared location could define domicile, even as the practical ruling from the Mishnah applies to the case of separately dwelling brothers who receive their food portions separately.

---

## Valid Domicile

### Gatehouses & Porches

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: *mi she-yesh lo beit sha'ar achsadra u-mirpeset be-chatzer chaveiro* — if someone has a gatehouse, a covered porch, or an open colonnade in another person's courtyard, *harei zeh eino oser alav* — this does not create an obligation; such a person need not participate in the *eruv*. These structures are not domiciles, and even if one happens to spend *Shabbos* there, one's presence does not generate the *eruv* obligation.

### Granaries & Stables

However, *beit ha-teven beit ha-bakar beit ha-etzim u-veit ha-otzarot* — a granary, a stable, a woodshed, or a storehouse — *harei zeh oser alav*: these do create an obligation. Although one does not typically reside in such structures, they have four walls, a ceiling, and a certain fitness for use that generates halachic significance. Their owner must therefore participate in the *eruv* of the courtyard they open into.

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *eino oser alav ela makom dira bilvad* — only a genuine place of domicile creates an obligation. A structure that is merely four walls and a ceiling, without being actually fit for human habitation, does not suffice.

### Ben Napcha Case

Rav Yehuda cites a case in support: *ma'aseh be-ven Napcha she-hayu lo chamesh chatzerot be-Usha* — a certain man, Ben Napcha, owned parcels of property in five different courtyards in Usha, and the case came before the Sages. They ruled: *eino oser ela beit dira bilvad* — he does not create an obligation in those courtyards, because the property he holds in each is not a domicile. The Gemara notes that the formulation should be corrected: rather than *beit dira* — a house of dwelling — the proper phrase is *makom dira* — a place of dwelling. The distinction points toward the question, taken up in the following discussion, of what precisely qualifies as a *makom dira*: whether it is defined by sleeping, by eating, or by some other indicator of genuine habitation.

---

---

# Eiruvin 73

## Sleep vs. Eating

### Brothers' Eating vs. Sle…

The discussion resumes at the bottom of 72b, picking up a theme introduced in the *mishna*: brothers who eat at their father's table but sleep in separate homes are considered distinct units for *eruv* purposes, each required to contribute separately. The *mishna* had also drawn a distinction based on the direction of the *eruv*'s movement — when brothers are the recipients rather than the contributors, they may be treated as a single household. The *gemara* now probes the underlying principle: does the definition of primary domicile follow where one sleeps or where one eats?

This question has broad practical implications beyond *eruv chatzeros* alone. It recurs in laws of *ner Chanukah*, and it arises regularly in contemporary settings — dormitory students who sleep in individual rooms but eat in a common dining hall, for instance, face precisely this ambiguity. The *mishna*'s plain reading seems to privilege sleep: the brothers eat together yet are still classified as separate units, implying that where one sleeps is the operative factor. However, the *gemara* challenges this reading by suggesting that the *mishna* may not describe brothers literally eating together but rather brothers who receive their food from the father and eat separately. The debate thus remains open.

### Rav Yehuda's Position

Six lines from the bottom of the page, the *gemara* cites a ruling of Rav Yehuda: *eino osel ela mekom dira bilvad* — only a place of actual habitation creates a problem for *eruv*. A granary, a stable, or similar structures do not. Rav Yehuda further illustrates this with a precedent: Ben Nafcha had five separate properties in Usha, and when the matter came before the Sages, they ruled that his ownership of those properties did not impede the residents from making an *eruv*, since those properties were not places of domicile.

The *gemara* then refines the terminology. The phrase *beis dira* — literally "a house of dwelling" — might be read too literally, as if any place where someone happens to sleep or eat would qualify. One of the commentaries explains that the *gemara*'s concern is with fitness for habitation: a gatehouse, for example, does not count even if someone happens to be sleeping there, because it is not designed as a place of human dwelling. The *gemara* therefore emends the formulation to *mekom dira* — a place suited for habitation. This sets the stage for the central debate about what constitutes such a place.

### Rava vs. Shmuel

The *gemara* now frames the core dispute explicitly. *Mai mekom dira?* — What is the place of domicile? *Rava amar: mekom pita* — Rava says it is the place where one eats one's bread. *Shmuel amar: mekom lina* — Shmuel says it is the place where one sleeps.

It is worth noting that two distinct questions are in play here. The first is whether a given location qualifies as a *beis dira* at all. If someone sleeps in one courtyard but takes all his meals in another, does the eating-location rise to the level of a *beis dira* that requires participation in the *eruv*? The second question concerns priority: when two locations are in competition — one where a person sleeps and one where he eats — which takes precedence in determining his primary domicile? Both questions may be answered by the same principle, but they are conceptually distinct.

### Shepherds' Domicile

The *gemara* raises a challenge from a *baraita*: shepherds, harvesters, wanderers, and fruit-watchers — people who spend their days out in the fields — if they customarily return to the city to sleep, *harei hen k'anshei ha'ir*, they are considered city dwellers. For purposes of *eruv techumin*, the 2,000-*amah* Sabbath boundary is measured from the city's edge, giving them the full benefit of the city's expanse. However, if they customarily sleep in the field, *yesh lo alpayim l'chol ruach*, the 2,000 *amah* is measured from their sleeping location in the field — a far less advantageous starting point. This *baraita* appears to settle the question decisively in favor of Shmuel: domicile follows where one sleeps.

### Eating Preference

The *gemara* deflects the challenge: *anan sahadi* — it is self-evident — that these field workers, had they been brought their bread where they sleep, would have preferred to eat there. In other words, the *baraita* does not actually disprove Rava's position that domicile follows the place of eating. Rather, since the workers eat in the field only out of necessity — because they work far from home and have no practical alternative — their field eating does not define their genuine *mekom pita*. Where one would choose to eat, given full freedom of choice, is the operative criterion, not where one is compelled to eat by circumstance.

This introduces a notably abstract dimension to the concept of *mekom pita*. The place of eating is no longer simply where one in fact eats, but where one would prefer to eat in an idealized situation. The *gemara* thus makes it difficult to pin down a clean, empirical rule. Both Rava and Shmuel can accommodate most cases by appealing to what the person would choose if circumstances were otherwise. The pattern continues in subsequent passages as the *gemara* applies this contextual reasoning to further scenarios.

---

## Household Units

### Five Wives & Servants

The *gemara* now turns from the question of what constitutes a *mekom dira* to the related question of household unity: when are multiple individuals considered a single domestic unit for *eruv* purposes? A *baraita* presents a case of a man married to five wives, each living in her own home within the courtyard and receiving her food from her husband — *mekablot pras miba'aleihen* — and five servants similarly living in separate quarters and receiving food from their master — *mekablim pras mirabeihen*. Crucially, the *baraita* explicitly states that each party receives food, corresponding precisely to Rav's interpretation of the *mishna* regarding the brothers: the father provides food, but they eat separately. Neither sleeping together nor eating together in the same house occurs. The question is whether wives or servants in this situation constitute a single unit with the head of household or are independent units requiring separate participation in the *eruv*.

### Ben Beseira's View

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira rules that wives are one unit with the husband and do not require separate participation (*matir benashim*), but servants must participate separately (*oser ba'avadim*). This position is intuitive: husband and wife form a family unit even when occupying separate quarters on the estate, and marital unity is sufficient to subsume the wife's dwelling into the husband's household. Servants, however, are a distinct category — employees rather than family — and their separate quarters constitute separate *batim*.

### Ben Baba's View

Rabbi Yehuda ben Baba takes the opposite position: servants are considered united with their master (*matir ba'avadim*) and do not require separate participation, while wives living in separate homes are considered independent units (*oser benashim*). This is the more surprising ruling and requires explanation.

### Rav's Reasoning

Rav provides the rationale for Rabbi Yehuda ben Baba's position. A *pasuk* states that Daniel was always present at the king's gate — *deDaniel bitra malka* — signifying that a servant-attendant is conceptually always in attendance upon the master, never truly separate. The servants' quarters are therefore an extension of the master's domain; they are always his, as it were, in a functional sense. Wives, by contrast, are independent persons. Even within a patriarchal structure, a wife who has her own home is considered to have established her own domain, and the marital bond alone does not subsume her residence into his.

Tosafot notes a play on words here: *tira* means a gate, and the name *Baba* likewise means a gate, making it fitting that it is Rabbi Yehuda ben Baba who derives his ruling from this verse about the gate.

A question arises as to why the analysis is framed with the husband as the center and the wives as satellites. Women bear independent obligations in *halacha*, so why should a wife not simply be viewed as responsible for her own *eruv*? The answer lies in the nature of the question: the issue is not personal obligation but household classification. A household, however large, requires only one contribution to the *eruv*. If the wife's home is an extension of her husband's household, the single household-unit is obligated once. If she is an independent unit, she — or rather, her dwelling — creates a separate obligation. In a context where one man is the head of a household providing food for multiple dwellings, the question of whether all those dwellings constitute one *reshus* is the operative inquiry.

### Distinctions

The *gemara* draws together the different categories. A son vis-à-vis his father — *pita ben etzel aviv* — is the case established in the *mishna*: adult children are separate units, as stated explicitly. The relationship of a wife to her husband and a servant to his master — *isha etzel ba'alah ve'eved etzel rabo* — is the debate between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira and Rabbi Yehuda ben Baba: one of these relationships creates a tighter unit than a father and adult children, but which one is disputed. Interestingly, the *gemara* does not include the case of the man with five wives in this list, perhaps because the father-children case was established explicitly in the *mishna* at one extreme, and the Rav-student relationship — apparently agreed upon — represents the other.

### Students at Yeshiva

This brings the *gemara* to ask: *talmid etzel rabo mai?* — What is the status of a student in relation to his Rebbe? A student boarding on the same courtyard, dependent on the Rebbe's household for sustenance, might be expected to form a tighter unit than an adult child, since the relationship of dependence persists rather than diminishing with maturity.

The *gemara* cites a precedent: when Rav studied in the *yeshiva* of Rabbi Chiya, he declared that the students need not make their own *eruv*, since they all relied on Rabbi Chiya's table — *she'anu somchin al shulchano shel Rabbi Chiya* — even if they did not physically eat there. And Rabbi Chiya himself, when studying with Rebbi, similarly declared that the students need not make an *eruv* because they relied on Rebbi's table. The chain of precedent indicates that students at a *yeshiva* whose sustenance is provided by the Rebbe are considered extensions of the Rebbe's household, forming a single unit that does not require a separate *eruv*.

---

## External Contributions

### Five Contributors

The *gemara* now shifts to a related question posed by Abaye to Rava. If five people in a courtyard have already collected an *eruv* — *chamisha she'gavu es eruvon* — and now wish to contribute their *eruv* to another courtyard, can they do so as a single collective unit, or must each person contribute separately? Rava answers: one *eruv* suffices for all of them — *eruv echad lekulan*.

### Brothers' Role

The *gemara* challenges this from the case of the brothers in the *mishna*. The brothers, when the *eruv* remains in their home, are treated as a single unit and need not contribute separately. This resembles a situation in which they have already made an *eruv* among themselves. Yet the *mishna* states that when they go out to contribute their *eruv* elsewhere, they must each contribute separately. Should the same not apply to the five people in Rava's case?

### Strangers' Effect

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty: *hacha bemai askinan kegon de'ika diyarin bahadeihu* — the *mishna*'s case involves strangers also living in the courtyard. It is precisely the presence of these outsiders that compels separate contribution. The *gemara* articulates the principle: *demigo dehanei asri hanei nami asri* — because the strangers create a prohibition for the brothers' side, this in turn establishes the brothers as a distinct unit as well. Once a stranger's presence demands that the courtyard be treated as composed of multiple units, the brothers can no longer claim to be a single cohesive household. They too become individual units, and thus must contribute separately when going out.

### Receiving vs. Contributi…

By contrast, when they are receiving the *eruv* — when the bread is simply deposited in their home — they are not actively asserting anything about the structure of the courtyard. There is no active participation that underscores the multiplicity of units. The *gemara* therefore permits them to be treated as a single unit in that context. But when they actively contribute, they are acknowledging and participating in a system that recognizes separate units, and that very act of participation makes them individually distinct. This asymmetry — the same brothers being one unit when receiving and separate units when contributing — is explained entirely by the presence of strangers, which creates the condition in which active participation forces individual accountability.

In Rava's case, by contrast, everyone actively made an *eruv*, uniting them into a genuine single unit. Nothing disrupts that unity. When they go to contribute, there is no stranger's presence to disaggregate them, so one contribution on behalf of the whole suffices. The *gemara* confirms this reasoning: *shma mina* — we derive from here that it is the introduction of strangers that creates the disruption. Without them, the active *eruv* holds them together as one.

---

## Techumin Shabbos

### Students' Location

The *gemara* now presents a question from Rav Chiya bar Avin to Rav Sheshet. The case concerns *bnei bei Rav* — *yeshiva* students — who eat their bread in a house or hall some distance away (*baguei*) and return to sleep in the *beis medrash* of the *yeshiva*. The question is where to measure the *techum Shabbos* for these students: from the *yeshiva* where they sleep, or from the place where they eat — the classic scenario of dormitory and dining hall in different locations.

### Bread Location Priority

Rav Sheshet answers: *mishchina mi-bei Rav* — measure from the *yeshiva* itself, i.e., from where they sleep. The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: this seems to contradict the very logic of *eruv techumin*. When one deposits an *eruv techumin* — placing bread at a designated point to establish a Sabbath domicile there — one measures from where the bread is, not from where one returns home to sleep that night. Does this not demonstrate that the place of eating (or at least the place of the bread) takes priority over the place of sleep?

### Contextual Preference

The *gemara* resolves this with the same contextual reasoning deployed earlier: *anan sahadi* — it is self-evident — in each case what the person would prefer. Regarding *eruv techumin*: someone who places the *eruv* to the north, intending to travel in that direction on Shabbos, demonstrably would prefer his domicile to be there. He has to schlep out to the *eruv* location in any case, and he would rather begin from there. So it is evident that given full choice, he would prefer to eat and live at the *eruv* location — his effective preference places him there.

In the case of the *yeshiva* students, by contrast, *anan sahadi de-maisu le-rifta le-bei Rav nicha lehu* — it is self-evident that they would rather have their food brought to them where they sleep in the *yeshiva*. The fact that the dining hall is elsewhere is a circumstantial arrangement, not a reflection of genuine preference. Therefore, the *yeshiva* — their sleeping place — is their true domicile. The *gemara* thus continues to resist any rigid rule of "always follow sleep" or "always follow eating," instead calibrating each case according to where the person would genuinely prefer to be located.

---

## Father & Children

### Rami's Question

The *gemara* records a further question posed by Rami bar Chama to Rav Chisda: *av u-veno, ha-Rav ve-talmido* — a father and his son, or a Rav and his student — what is their status in *eruv* law? This appears at first glance to be a recapitulation of the discussions already conducted. According to Rashi, it largely is. Tosafot suggests the new question may involve a scenario where they eat at separate tables rather than together, which would constitute a slight variation on the earlier cases. In either reading, the question touches on the same essential inquiry about household unity.

### Unit Classification

The question is posed in two parts: *tzrichim eruv o ein tzrichim eruv* — do they need an *eruv* at all? And a second question: are they classified as many or as one? The first question presupposes that if they are the sole occupants of a courtyard, perhaps no *eruv* is required at all. The second question concerns how they are treated vis-à-vis others.

### Mavoi Requirements

The second part of the question takes on particular halachic significance with respect to *lechi* and *kora*. A *mavoi* — a dead-end alleyway — does not require a full wall to permit carrying. A *lechi* (side post) or *kora* (crossbeam) suffices. However, this leniency applies only to a structure that qualifies as a genuine *mavoi*, and the definition of *mavoi* requires at minimum two *chatzeros* each containing at least two *batim*. If the father and sons, or the Rav and students, constitute a single household, then their collective dwellings might be classified as one *bayit* rather than multiple *batim*, which would mean the courtyard fails to meet the minimum threshold of a proper *chatzer*, and the *mavoi* would not qualify for the *lechi*-and-*kora* leniency.

### No Strangers Rule

Rav Chisda responds by citing a *baraita*: *av u-veno, ha-Rav ve-talmido, bizman she'ein imahem diyurin* — a father and his son, or a Rav and his student, when there are no other residents in the courtyard with them — *harei hen ke-yachidim* — they are considered like a single individual. This directly parallels what was established earlier: it is the introduction of strangers that fragments the unity. Without strangers, they are a coherent single unit, and *ein tzrichim le'arev* — they need not make an *eruv* among themselves.

### Lechi & Kora Leniency

Nevertheless, the *baraita* continues: *u-mavoi shelahen nitar be-lechi ve-korah* — their *mavoi* is still permissible with a *lechi* or *kora*. This is the crucial resolution: although they are classified as one unit for purposes of *eruv* requirements, they retain enough of a distinct character that their courtyard counts as a legitimate *chatzer* and their *mavoi* qualifies for the lesser leniency. The answer, in effect, is that these categories resist a clean binary. The father-and-children or Rav-and-student household is one unit in some respects and several in others. When strangers enter, they fully fragment into distinct units; in their absence, they function as one — yet even then, they retain enough structural distinctness to support the *lechi*-and-*kora* leniency for the *mavoi*.

---

## Eruv vs. Shituf

### Five Courtyards

The *gemara* now turns to a new *mishna* concerning five *chatzeros* that are open to one another and open into a common *mavoi*. The *mishna* explores the interplay between *eruv chatzeros* and *shituf meva'ot*, asking whether each can substitute for the other.

### Eruv Alone

If the residents of the courtyards made an *eruv* among their *chatzeros* but did not make a *shituf* in the *mavoi* — *eirvu ba-chatzeros velo nishtatfu ba-mavoi* — then the *chatzeros* are permitted for carrying but the *mavoi* remains forbidden. Making an *eruv* has unified the courtyards into a coherent residential unit, but that unification has not extended to the street. The *mavoi* remains a separate domain with no mechanism to permit carrying within it.

### Shituf Alone

Conversely, if they made a *shituf* in the *mavoi* without making *eruv chatzeros* — *ve'im nishtatfu ba-mavoi mutarin kan u-van* — then carrying is permitted both in the courtyards and in the *mavoi*. The logic here is that when the residents unify at the level of the street, emerging from their respective courtyards and sharing the *mavoi*, that unification radiates inward and encompasses the courtyards as well. The *shituf* thereby accomplishes what the *eruv* could not do in reverse.

### Asymmetry

The *mishna* thus presents a clear asymmetry: *shituf* can substitute for *eruv*, but *eruv* cannot substitute for *shituf*. The lecturer notes that this asymmetry is intuitively compelling. The *eruv chatzeros* is an inward-facing act of unification; it consolidates the private domain of the *chatzer* but does not engage the street. The *shituf*, by contrast, operates at the level of the *mavoi*, the quasi-public corridor through which all the courtyards communicate — and so it naturally draws together both the street and the courtyards feeding into it. The asymmetry flows from the structural relationship between the domains.

### Gemara's Objection

The *gemara*, however, refuses to accept this asymmetry. It argues that the *mishna* must be internally consistent: either one can always substitute for the other, or neither can substitute. The *gemara* raises a further complication from the *mishna*'s own continuation: if everyone made both an *eruv* and a *shituf* and then one person from a *chatzer* forgot to contribute to the *eruv*, it is still permitted. And if one person forgot to contribute to the *shituf*, carrying in the *mavoi* is forbidden. The *gemara* proceeds to test whether ביטול *bitul* (nullification of rights) can explain these outcomes under a single, internally consistent rule — whether that of Rabbi Meir or the *rabanan* — and finds that no such clean explanation resolves the apparent contradictions. It attempts to attribute the beginning and end of the *mishna* to Rabbi Meir and the middle to the *rabanan*, then rejects this patchwork as untenable.

---

## Rabbi Meir's Rule

### Need Both

Having failed to resolve the *mishna* by splitting it between authorities, the *gemara* asserts that the entire *mishna* follows Rabbi Meir — *kulla Rabbi Meir* — who holds that one always needs both an *eruv* and a *shituf*: *ba'inan eruv u-va'inan shituf*.

### One Forgot Eruv

Under this reading, the first clause of the *mishna* — stating that a *shituf* permits both the courtyards and the *mavoi* — means that they performed both a *shituf* and an *eruv*, and it was the combination of the two that achieved full permission. The apparently asymmetric statement was not about *shituf* alone sufficing but about the case where both were in place. Then the *mishna* moves to the scenario where everyone made an *eruv* and a *shituf* but one person forgot to contribute to the *eruv*: the result is still permitted. The *gemara* explains that in this case the *shituf* serves as a backup.

### One Forgot Shituf

By contrast, if one courtyard's residents forgot to participate in the *shituf* of the *mavoi*, then while carrying within the courtyards (covered by the *eruv*) remains permitted, the *mavoi* is forbidden. Here, the *eruv* cannot serve as a backup for the missing *shituf*. The problem exists even though everyone has an *eruv*, because the *eruv* does not encompass the *mavoi*.

### Shituf Backup Logic

The *gemara* explains the asymmetry between these two cases under Rabbi Meir's framework. Rabbi Meir's reason for requiring both *eruv* and *shituf* is not that each is independently necessary in principle, but that he wishes to prevent people from forgetting that two distinct *halachos* exist — *shelo lishakeach toras eruv min ha-tinokos*. In a case where most or nearly all participants actively made both an *eruv* and a *shituf*, and only a single person inadvertently forgot the *eruv*, the *halacha* of *eruv* is not at risk of being forgotten. Therefore Rabbi Meir tolerates the *shituf* functioning as a backup in that narrow circumstance. This is a strikingly situation-dependent ruling, assessing each case on the basis of how likely the underlying *halacha* is to be forgotten. The lecturer acknowledges that the ruling has an ad hoc quality to it, and notes that the plain reading of the *mishna* — simple asymmetry between *shituf* and *eruv* — remains the more natural interpretation. The *gemara* does not appear to even consider this possibility, which is itself a striking feature of the sugya.

---

## Rav's Text

### Text Variant

The *gemara* records that Rav Yehuda reports: Rav did not have the phrase *petuchot zu la-zu* — "open to one another" — in his text of the *mishna*. Rav Kahana corroborates this: Rav's version of the *mishna* described five courtyards open into a *mavoi*, without specifying that the courtyards were also open to each other.

### Why Eruv Fails

This textual variant has a substantive halachic payoff. If the courtyards are not open to one another, then an *eruv* made among their residents is not a joint *eruv chatzeros* in the ordinary sense but rather a collection of individual *eruvin* made separately by each household. Individual *eruvin* that have not merged the courtyards into a unified domain cannot substitute for a *shituf* of the *mavoi*, because they have not achieved any collective unification. The *shituf*, which does unify at the *mavoi* level, can then substitute for the *eruv* — because it draws everyone together — but not vice versa. Rav's *girsa* thus resolves the asymmetry that troubled the *gemara*: it is not that *shituf* is inherently more powerful in some abstract sense, but that separate individual *eruvin* simply have no capacity to unify anyone for purposes of the shared street.

---

## Shituf Requirements

### Entry & Exit

The *gemara* now introduces a different approach, attributed to Rav Kahana. He holds that a valid *shituf* for a *mavoi* requires that residents physically enter and exit each courtyard through the *mavoi* — *machniso u-motzio derech ptachim ba-mavoi* — in the course of making the *shituf*. The act of traversing the street while gathering or depositing the *eruv* bread is what gives the *shituf* its unifying quality. The street must actively be used as the conduit through which the partnership is forged.

### Direct Passage Problem

This requirement creates a problem when the courtyards are open to one another. If residents can pass directly from one courtyard to another without ever entering the *mavoi*, they can complete the entire process of assembling the *shituf* without using the street at all. Under Rav Kahana's view, such a *shituf* would be defective.

### Not a True Shituf

If the collection is conducted through internal passageways rather than through the *mavoi*, then even though bread has been gathered and shared, *lo shmeh shituf* — it is not called a *shituf* in the halachic sense. The act of physically unifying the parties through the shared public space is constitutive of the *shituf*, not merely incidental to it.

### Business Partner Case

The *gemara* tests this principle against an earlier *mishna* about a homeowner who was in a wine partnership with his neighbor — each having contributed to a shared barrel. The *mishna* had treated that business partnership as constituting a *shituf*. But surely, the *gemara* objects, those business partners did not go in and out of each other's courtyards through the *mavoi* as part of their commercial arrangement. The *gemara* responds that they did in fact do so — *d'afkei ve'ayeilei* — when transporting the wine. This is a strained *ukhimta*, and the *gemara* presses further.

### Shared Meal Bread

A similar challenge arises from the rule that bread shared at a communal meal — where a group was eating together when Shabbos arrived unexpectedly — can serve as an *eruv* or, according to some, as a *shituf*. Surely these people did not traverse the *mavoi* together while eating their meal. Once again, the *gemara* insists that they did go in and out through the street.

### Location Matters

Rabbah offers a resolution that sidesteps the question of street-traversal entirely. The debate over whether the shared meal bread constitutes an *eruv* or a *shituf* depends simply on where the meal was held. *Kan be-mesubin ba-bayis* — if they were eating in a house, the bread serves as an *eruv chatzeros*, the deposit being in the house. *Ve-kan be-mesubin ba-chatzer* — if they were eating in the courtyard, the bread serves as a *shituf* of the *mavoi*, the deposit being in the *chatzer*. Crucially, in neither case did the participants walk through the *mavoi* during the course of their meal. Rabbah's resolution thus effectively refutes the premise of Rav Kahana's requirement: since a shared meal can constitute a valid *shituf* without any traversal of the street, street-traversal cannot be the operative factor. The *gemara* concedes: the approach requiring active passage through the *mavoi* must be abandoned.

---

## Rav's Alternative

### One Courtyard Result

Having set aside Rav Kahana's traversal requirement, the *gemara* returns to Rav's actual reason for excluding the phrase *petuchot zu la-zu* from the *mishna*. The issue is not the manner of making the *shituf* but a consequence of making the *eruv*. If all five courtyards make an *eruv* together, they are transformed into a single unified *chatzer*. What had been five separate courtyards becomes, legally, one.

### Lechi Ineligibility

This transformation creates a problem. A *mavoi* is only eligible for the leniency of *lechi* or *kora* if it services at least two *chatzeros*, each containing at least two *batim*. If the five courtyards have merged into one through the *eruv*, the *mavoi* now opens onto a single *chatzer* — and a single *chatzer* does not satisfy the minimum threshold. The *mavoi* therefore loses eligibility for the *lechi*-or-*kora* leniency and would require a full wall to permit carrying.

### Transformation Problem

This is the reason Rav excises the phrase "open to one another" from his text. If the courtyards are open to each other and the residents make a combined *eruv*, they genuinely unify into one courtyard — and that unification, while achieving permission within the courtyards, undermines the *mavoi*'s status. Rav's concern is structural: the very success of the *eruv* destroys the prerequisite for the *mavoi*'s leniency. There is a paradox here — getting things right in one domain creates a problem in another — and Rav resolves it by insisting that the *mishna*'s case not involve courtyards open to each other at all.

---

---

# Eiruvin 74

## Eruv vs. Shittuf

### Asymmetry Resolution

This daf, 74a, picks up at the very bottom of 73b. To recapitulate: the *mishna* had raised the question of whether a *shittuf* can substitute for an *eruv* among courtyards, and conversely, whether an *eruv* can substitute for a *shittuf* in a *maboi*. The *mishna* seemed to reflect an asymmetry — a *shittuf* can work in place of an *eruv*, but not an *eruv* in place of a *shittuf*. There is a certain logic to this, since the *eruv* of courtyards does not directly incorporate the *maboi*. Nevertheless, the *gemara* was unwilling to accept the asymmetry at face value and worked to resolve it, whether according to Rabbi Meir or according to the *Rabbanan*.

### Rav's Definition

The *gemara* then turned to Rav's statement that the *mishna* was speaking of a case where the courtyards did not open into one another — they were separate from each other. This observation may originally have been intended to resolve the asymmetry problem, but the *gemara* redirected it toward a different issue entirely: the question of when it suffices to use only a *lechi* or *kora* — a vertical or horizontal beam — for the fourth wall of a *maboi*. Ordinarily, a *maboi* requires four walls, but the Rabbis were lenient and permitted a *lechi* or *kora* — provided the alleyway has the formal status of a *maboi*, which is normally defined as having two *chatzerot*, each with at least two houses. Rav's point was that if the courtyards open into one another and could theoretically all form a single unified *eruv*, they are considered one *chatzer* rather than two, and the leniency of the *lechi* or *kora* is therefore unavailable.

---

## Maboi Requirements

### Rav vs. Shmuel

With that background established, the *gemara* now takes up the relevant passage directly — *gufa* — beginning at the top of 74a. Rav states: *ein maboi nitar b'lechi v'kora ad she-yihiyu batim v'chatzerot petuchim l'tocho* — a *maboi* cannot be rendered permissible with a *lechi* or *kora* unless it has houses and courtyards opening into it, meaning at least two houses in each *chatzer* and two *chatzerot* opening into it. That is the threshold that qualifies it as a *maboi* for which the Rabbis granted the leniency.

Shmuel disagrees: *afilu bayit echad v'chatzer achat* — even one house and one courtyard suffice. Rashi explains this carefully. Shmuel does not mean a single house standing alone or a bare yard. Rather, his picture is that one house opens directly into the *maboi* and one *chatzer* opens into the *maboi* as well — and for a space to qualify as a *chatzer*, it must of course have at least one house attached to it. So whereas according to Rav, each of the two *chatzerot* requires two houses, according to Shmuel, a single house opening directly into the *maboi* combined with a *chatzer* containing at least one house is sufficient. There is much that Shmuel's brief formulation leaves unstated; the explanation just offered is Rashi's reading of the passage.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan goes even further: *afilu horva* — even a ruin or desolate unbuilt lot qualifies. Not even a house is required on the second side. Rashi, however, supplies an important assumption that is not explicit in the text: everyone agrees that at least one *chatzer* must be present. What is being debated is only what can stand on the other side. According to Rashi, Rabbi Yochanan holds that the second element need not be a house at all — even a *horva* will do. But all authorities agree that one *chatzer* is required as a baseline.

### Horva vs. Path

The *gemara* raises a further question. Abaye asks Rav Yosef: does Rabbi Yochanan's leniency extend even to a *bishya shel keramim* — a path running through a vineyard? If almost nothing suffices, perhaps even a footpath through a forest or vineyard would do. The *gemara* answers: No. Rabbi Yochanan limited his ruling to a *horva* — a ruin or desolate lot — *d'chazi l'dira*, something that is fit in principle to be built up and inhabited. A *shevil shel kramim*, a path through a vineyard that is not fit for habitation and cannot be built into a dwelling, does not qualify.

### Rav Huna's Link

Rav Huna bar Chinana then observes that Rabbi Yochanan is being consistent with his own broader reasoning: *v'azda Rabbi Yochanan l'ta'amei*. The *gemara* connects this to a *mishna* in which Rabbi Shimon articulates a far-reaching principle — and it is to that principle that we now turn.

---

## Rabbi Shimon

### Unified Domains

The *gemara* cites the teaching: *Rabbi Shimon omer — echad gagot, v'echad karpifot, v'echad chatzerot — reshut achat hein l'keilim she-shavtu l'tochan, v'lo l'keilim she-shavtu b'toch ha-bayit*. Rabbi Shimon says: roofs, enclosed lots, and courtyards are all one domain with respect to vessels that began Shabbat within them — but not with respect to vessels that began Shabbat inside a house.

### Vessel Identity

To understand this, it is worth pausing to think carefully about what an *eruv* actually accomplishes and what the underlying problem is when no *eruv* is made. When residents of a courtyard have not made an *eruv* together, each house and the courtyard itself are all *reshuyot hayachid* — private domains. The prohibition is not simply carrying in general but specifically the act of moving an object from one type of domain into another. A vessel that begins Shabbat inside a particular house may not be taken from that house into the courtyard. Conversely, a vessel that began Shabbat in the courtyard may be carried within the courtyard — because the problem is not carrying per se, but crossing from one domain-type into a distinct domain-type. When the residents make an *eruv*, these separate units merge into one collective domain, and free movement among them becomes permitted.

### Carrying Between Domains

Rabbi Shimon now applies this logic across a broader set of spaces. Suppose there are multiple courtyards — call them A1, A2, A3 — that open into one another but whose residents have not made a joint *eruv*. The standard assumption would be that without an *eruv* among them, one cannot carry from the courtyard of A1 into the courtyard of A3, because they are distinct *reshuyot hayachid*. Rabbi Shimon disagrees. He holds that courtyards, rooftops, and enclosed lots all belong to the same fundamental category of *reshut hayachid* — they are all spaces that are not actual places of habitation. Because they share this character, a vessel that begins Shabbat in one of them may be carried into any other, without an *eruv*. One still cannot take a vessel from inside a house of A1 into the courtyard of A3, because the house is a qualitatively different type of domain. But among courtyards, rooftops, and enclosed lots, Rabbi Shimon sees one unified domain.

This is a striking position, and it is worth reiterating because it is essential to everything that follows. The Rabbis' requirement of an *eruv* to carry from house to courtyard reflects the fact that these are distinct domain-types, even though both are technically *reshut hayachid*. Rabbi Shimon says the same logic applies across courtyards: since a vessel that started in a courtyard carries the identity of that courtyard, and since all courtyards share the same essential character, no special unification is needed.

### Rashi's Expansion

Rashi actually goes even further with Rabbi Shimon's principle, noting that according to Rabbi Shimon, one may carry not only from one courtyard to another but also from a rooftop in A1 into the courtyard of A2 and from there into an enclosed lot — because all three categories (*chatzer*, *gag*, and *karpaf*) are treated as one single abstract domain. They are all spaces that are not actual homes. One can therefore traverse from one to another freely, provided a vessel began Shabbat within this category. This is not immediately apparent from the text itself, and the *gemara* does explore it later — there is indeed a debate between those who hold that each subcategory constitutes its own unit and those who, like Rashi's reading of Rabbi Shimon, treat them all as one large unified domain. The questions of adjacency also apply: one cannot cross a *reshut ha-rabbim* to get from one of these spaces to another; the discussion assumes they are all adjacent to one another.

---

## Gezeirah Concern

### Rav's Gezeirah

Given Rabbi Shimon's principle, the *gemara* now reports: *amar Rav halacha k'Rabbi Shimon* — Rav rules in accordance with Rabbi Shimon. But then Rav adds a critical qualification: *v'hu she-lo eirvu* — this leniency applies only if the courtyard residents did not make an *eruv*. The irony is striking. Rav says: if A1 made an *eruv* internally, so that its residents can carry freely between their houses and their courtyard, then the rule of Rabbi Shimon — that a vessel from A1's courtyard may be carried into A3's courtyard — no longer applies.

Why? Because as soon as A1 makes an *eruv*, it becomes permissible to take a vessel from inside a house of A1 into the courtyard of A1. Once that happens, the *gemara* explains, we are concerned — *gazrinan d'atei l'apukei manei d'vatim l'chatzer* — that people will come to take vessels that began Shabbat in a house of A1 into A1's courtyard and from there carry them into A3's courtyard. The vessel that made it from the house to the courtyard has now been carried in from a qualitatively different domain-type, and yet it continues traveling into other courtyards. This would be a prohibited carrying, and Rav imposes a *gezeirah*: when an *eruv* has been made, the leniency of Rabbi Shimon is suspended entirely, lest people fall into this error.

### Shmuel Rejects Gezeirah

Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan both reject this *gezeirah*. Shmuel rules: *bein eirvu bein lo eirvu* — whether or not the residents made an *eruv*, the principle of Rabbi Shimon stands and one may carry a vessel from A1's courtyard into A3's courtyard. Rabbi Yochanan states the same: *halacha k'Rabbi Shimon bein eirvu bein lo eirvu*. Neither of them is concerned that permitting cross-courtyard carrying will lead people to mistakenly take vessels that originated in a house.

### True Concern

At this point the *gemara* shifts course, and it is worth pausing to appreciate that this is genuinely a change of direction. Until now, the dispute between Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan about the minimum requirements for a *maboi* seemed to be a purely formalistic question: how many *chatzerot* does a *maboi* need, and how many houses does a *chatzer* need? Now the *gemara* introduces a different concern entirely. The concern is not only formal but functional: even if we recognize a *maboi* as valid, the fact that a *horva* has no residents means that no one has made an *eruv* or *shittuf* incorporating it. It therefore remains a conceptually separate zone — a distinct space that has not been unified with the rest. If we permit carrying in the *maboi*, people may come to carry from the *maboi* into the *horva*: *lo gazrinan dilma atei l'apukei manei d'chatzer l'chorva*.

The *gemara* concludes that Rabbi Yochanan is consistent with his broader reasoning precisely here. Since Rabbi Yochanan does not make such a *gezeirah* in the context of Rabbi Shimon's principle — he is untroubled by the concern that permitting something will lead people to extend it improperly — so too here he is not troubled by the fear that permitting carrying in the *maboi* will lead people to carry into the *horva*. That is why Rabbi Yochanan *azda l'ta'amei* — his ruling about the *maboi* flows naturally from his general refusal to impose *gezeirot* of this type.

One might note an additional irony: since nobody inhabits the *horva*, no *shittuf* is needed to cover it — there is only one party in this entire alleyway. But since the *horva* is not part of any *eruv* and remains a conceptually distinct type of space, one cannot actually carry into it. According to Rabbi Yochanan, however, this residual concern does not prevent us from recognizing the *maboi* as valid for the purpose of the *lechi* and *kora* leniency.

---

## Eivu Bar Ichi Case

### Rav Bruna Challenge

The *gemara* now returns to the earlier dispute about the minimum requirements for a *maboi*. Rav Bruna was sitting and relating Shmuel's lenient ruling — that even one house and one courtyard suffice — when Rabbi Elazar bar Bei Rav challenged him: did Shmuel really say this? Rav Bruna confirmed that he did. Rabbi Elazar bar Bei Rav was not satisfied and insisted on going to Shmuel himself to verify the report.

When Rabbi Elazar bar Bei Rav came before Shmuel and asked whether he had truly ruled this way, Shmuel confirmed it. Rabbi Elazar then pressed Shmuel with a challenge: *ein lanu b'eiruvin ela k'lashon mishnateinu* — we follow exactly the language of the *mishna*, and nothing more. Which *mishna* is he invoking? The *mishna* that states: *she-ha-maboi la-chatzerot k'chatzer la-batim* — the *maboi* is to the courtyards as the *chatzer* is to the houses. This is an analogy: just as units of houses constitute a *chatzer*, so units of *chatzerot* constitute a *maboi*. And since the *mishna* uses the plural — *chatzerot* for the *maboi* and *batim* for the *chatzer* — a *maboi* requires two *chatzerot* and a *chatzer* requires two houses. How then can Shmuel permit a *maboi* with only one house and one courtyard?

### Mishna's Language

In the face of this challenge, the *gemara* reports: *ishtik* — Shmuel was silent. The *gemara* then asks: did he accept the refutation and reverse his ruling, or did he not? *Kiblah minei o lo kiblah minei?*

### Chazan Case

To resolve this, the *gemara* cites a case. There was a certain *maboi* in which a person named Eivu bar Ichi was living. He placed a *lechi* and Shmuel permitted it. The assumption is that this *maboi* had only one *chatzer* and one house — which would be the minimum Shmuel originally permitted. Rabana then came and threw down the *lechi*, declaring that the arrangement was invalid because the *maboi* lacked two *chatzerot*.

Eivu bar Ichi protested: this is the *maboi* in which he lives, and he has been carrying in it in the name of Shmuel — is Rabana bar Rav now going to throw down his *lechi*? The *gemara* infers from the fact that Shmuel maintained his original ruling despite Rabana's challenge that Shmuel had not reversed his position in the face of the earlier *kashya* about the *mishna*'s language.

### Resolution

But the *gemara* immediately offers an alternative reading. Perhaps Shmuel did accept the refutation and did reverse his position. In that case, what was actually happening in the case of Eivu bar Ichi? The *gemara* explains: *v'hacha chazana hu d'hava achil nahma b'veiteih v'ati bayit b'veit kenishta* — there was a *chazan*, a synagogue sexton, who ate his meals in his own home but slept in the synagogue, and the synagogue was located in this *maboi* and courtyard.

Now the question becomes: does the synagogue count as a second house for purposes of the *eruv*? This depends on a broader debate about what constitutes a person's primary residence. Eivu bar Ichi thought that Shmuel was permitting the *lechi* because he held that where a person eats determines his dwelling place — *makom pita goreim* — and since the *chazan* ate elsewhere, he was not considered a resident of the *maboi*, and Shmuel was permitting it even with only one actual dwelling. But in fact, Eivu bar Ichi had misunderstood Shmuel's ruling. Shmuel's actual view is *makom linah goreim* — the place where a person sleeps determines his residence — and since the *chazan* slept in the synagogue, he was deemed a resident of the *maboi*. The synagogue thus counted as a second house, giving the *maboi* the two houses and two *chatzerot* it needed.

This reading allows the *gemara* to bring the entire discussion full circle: even Shmuel, in the end, may have reversed himself and agreed with the requirement of two houses and two *chatzerot*, and the case of Eivu bar Ichi turns not on a lenient minimum threshold but on the question of what determines a person's legal place of habitation.

---

## Non-Jew Maboi

### Case Setup

The *gemara* continues with a new ruling transmitted in the name of Rav: *mavoi she-tzido echad oved kochavim v'tzido echad Yisrael* — a *maboi* in which one side is inhabited by non-Jews and the other side by Jews. Rashi provides a helpful diagram of the arrangement: the *maboi* is the alleyway, one *chatzer* on one side is occupied by non-Jews, and the *chatzer* on the other side has Jewish residents.

### Rav's Prohibition

Rav rules: *ein me'arvin oto derech chalonot l'hatiro derech petachim la-maboi* — one may not make an *eruv* through windows between the houses in order to permit carrying through the doorways into the *maboi*. The Jews cannot solve the problem of the non-Jewish presence by making an internal *eruv* among themselves through windows connecting their houses, and then use that to enable carrying into the *maboi*.

### Abaye's Question

Abaye asked Rav Yosef: would Rav say the same even if instead of a *maboi* between them, it was a *chatzer*? That is, does this prohibition apply equally when the obstruction is a courtyard rather than a *maboi*?

### Non-Jew Domain

Rav Yosef replied in the affirmative: yes, Rav would say the same even by a *chatzer*. And this response is necessary, because without it one might have misunderstood the entire force of Rav's ruling. If Rav had spoken only about a *maboi*, one would have said that his concern is simply the formalistic one: you do not have two valid *chatzerot* here, because the non-Jew's *chatzer* does not count as a proper *chatzer*. That would merely restate his earlier requirement of two *chatzerot* with two houses, with the added note that a non-Jew's dwelling does not qualify. But then there would have been no need to articulate this ruling separately at all — it would have been fully subsumed by the earlier statement. The fact that Rav applies this ruling even to a *chatzer* — where the issue of the *lechi* and *kora* is irrelevant — shows that there is something more at stake.

---

## Yachid Issue

### Unified Household

What, then, is the real concern? The *gemara* explains Rav's reasoning: *ta'ama d'Rav d'kasavar asur la'asot yachid bimkom ovdei kochavim* — Rav holds that it is prohibited to constitute oneself as a single unified household in the presence of non-Jews. The Jews in this courtyard were attempting to solve the problem by making an *eruv* among themselves through the windows connecting their houses — essentially merging into one household without going through the courtyard at all. The intention was to bypass the non-Jewish presence entirely. But Rav rules that this very maneuver — creating a *yachid* in the presence of a *nochri* — is itself prohibited.

### Rav Yosef Understanding

Rav Yosef then adds a striking observation. Now, he says, I understand something that had previously puzzled him. Rav Tavla, when transmitting this teaching of Rav, repeated the phrase *ovdei kochavim* — non-Jews — twice in the course of a single short ruling: *mavoi she-tzido echad ovdei kochavim, tzido echad Yisrael, ein me'arvin oto derech chalonot l'tzorech derech petachim la-maboi*. Rav Yosef had not understood why Rav Tavla emphasized the non-Jewish element twice — *ovdei kochavim, ovdei kochavim, trei zimnei*. It seemed redundant.

### Yachid Summary

But now it is clear. The repeated emphasis on the non-Jew is not stylistic redundancy but the very heart of the ruling. The reason the *eruv* through windows is prohibited is not a formalistic concern about the count of *chatzerot* — it is because what the Jews are trying to create is a *yachid bimkom nochri*, a single unified household in the presence of a non-Jew, and that is independently forbidden. By stressing the non-Jewish presence twice, Rav Tavla was flagging that the non-Jew is not incidental background detail but the operative legal factor. The entire ruling turns on it.

To summarize the arc of this final section: what at first appears to be a ruling about the technical structure of a *maboi* with a mixed neighborhood reveals itself, upon closer examination, to be driven by the principle of *yachid bimkom nochri*. The attempted solution — forming one household through windows while ignoring the non-Jewish courtyard — is precisely what Rav prohibits. And the need to state this ruling both for the *maboi* and for the *chatzer* was necessary in order to make clear that the concern is not about the count of *chatzerot* required by the *lechi* and *kora* leniency, but about the independent prohibition of constituting a *yachid* in the presence of a non-Jew.

---

---

# Eiruvin 75

## Yachid Bemakom Nochri

### Rav vs Rashi/Tosafot

Before turning to the new *mishnah*, it is worth clarifying how the previous daf concluded. The final case on 74 involved a chain of houses opening into one another, which in turn opened into a courtyard shared with a non-Jew. The *gemara* there framed the difficulty as a problem of *yachid bemakom ovdei kochavim* — a single Jew finding himself alone in a courtyard with a non-Jewish resident. The way that concern was expressed in the lecture was that treating the chain of houses as a single unit effectively created such a scenario.

Rashi and Tosafot, however, understand the issue differently. In their reading, the problem is not one that arises from the consolidation of the houses; rather, the situation already presents itself as a case of *yachid bemakom nochri* from the outset. The concern is that allowing the other Jews — those whose houses open into one another but not directly into the courtyard — to join in an *eruv* would actively encourage the lone Jew to remain there, dwelling in isolation with the non-Jew. Since only one Jew has immediate access to the courtyard, the others' participation would validate and entrench an undesirable arrangement.

### Lechi/Kora Requirements

Connected to this is the broader question of what constitutes a *chatzer* for the purpose of permitting it through a *lechi* or *kora*. Rav's position is that a courtyard requires at least two houses opening into it for a *lechi* or *kora* to suffice. Tosafot develops this point at considerable length — the size of that *tosafot* reflects not the usual effort of reconciling cross-tractate *sugyot*, but simply the difficulty of making coherent sense of the case itself. Tosafot's essential question is: when do multiple houses that open into one another, rather than directly into the courtyard, become considered a single house? The answer has implications for whether there are truly "two houses" sufficient to permit the courtyard via *lechi* or *kora*. That is the underlying structural issue Tosafot is working through in his several explanations.

---

## Shtei Chatzerot Structure

### B Through A Layout

The *mishnah* on 75a opens with the case of *shtei chatzerot zo lifnim mizo* — two courtyards, one situated behind the other. The physical setup is that courtyard B, the inner one, has no direct exit to the street; its only access is through courtyard A, the outer one. Each courtyard has its own residents with their respective houses. The practical consequence of this arrangement is that the people of B must necessarily pass through A at all times.

The central question this arrangement raises is whether the constant movement of B's residents through A — what the *mishnah* calls *drisat haregel*, the "trampling of the foot" — has any halachic significance for A's *eruv*. It must be clarified that the concern is not about the act of walking itself; one may walk anywhere within the *techum* without restriction. The issue is that because the residents of B are perpetually present in A and carry their objects there, they are, in a certain sense, conceptually members of A's courtyard. The question, then, is whether that virtual presence disrupts A's *eruv*, given that B and A have not made an *eruv* together.

### B Eruv, A No Eruv

The first case: the inner courtyard, B, made an *eruv*, but the outer courtyard, A, did not. The ruling is *hapnimis muteret vehachitzonit asurah* — B is permitted and A is forbidden. B can ignore A entirely, since A's traffic flows only outward, toward the street, and never inward through B. A, however, has not made an *eruv*, and so carrying there is prohibited.

### A Eruv, B No Eruv

The second case: A made an *eruv* but B did not. Here, *shteihem asurot* — both are forbidden. B is obviously forbidden, having made no *eruv*. But A is also forbidden because the residents of B, who are in a state of prohibition in their own zone, are constantly present in A. Their ongoing presence there means that A's *eruv* cannot be effective, since A is, conceptually, a courtyard whose members include B — and B has not participated.

### Both Eruv Separately

The third case: both A and B each made their own *eruv* independently. The *mishnah* states *zu muteret bifnei atzmah vezu muteret bifnei atzmah* — each is permitted in its own right. This appears entirely logical: B is fine on its own terms, and A is fine on its own terms. It is here that Rabbi Akiva intervenes. He rules *oser hachitzonit* — A is nonetheless forbidden — *she'drisat haregel osartah*: because B's constant trampling through A makes A's *eruv* deficient.

Rabbi Akiva's reasoning is formulated as *regel hamuteret bimkomah oseret shelo bimkomah*: even though B is permitted in its own place — it has its own valid *eruv* — it still renders A forbidden, because since B is always physically moving through A, B is considered a virtual member of A's courtyard. Since B has not made an *eruv* together with A, A's *eruv* is incomplete: it does not include all of A's effective "members." The *chachamim* disagree and state *im muteret bimkomah einah oseret shelo bimkomah*: if B is permitted in its own domain, it does not create a problem in a domain that is not its own.

### Shachach One Member

The *mishnah* then transitions to a parallel set of cases, not where a courtyard entirely failed to make an *eruv*, but where one member forgot to participate — *shachach* — which produces the same functional result of an invalid *eruv*. If one resident of A forgot, *hapnimis muteret vehachitzonit asurah* — B is fine, A is forbidden. If one resident of B forgot, *shteihem asurot* — both are forbidden, for the same reason as before: a defective B compromises A.

The *mishnah* then introduces the case of *natnu eiruvam bemakom echad* — they placed their *eruv* in a single location, meaning A and B made a unified *eruv* together. In this case, *bein min hapnimis bein min hachitzonit*, whether the one who forgot was from B or from A, *shteihem asurot* — both are forbidden. Normally, if A and B had made separate *eruvin*, a problem in A would leave B unaffected. But once they have formed a unified *eruv*, they constitute one entity, and any single member's failure to participate compromises the whole. The usual solutions of *bitul* are theoretically available, but the point is that combining into one unit removes the insulation that separate *eruvin* would have provided.

### Two Yechidim

The final scenario: *ve'im hayu shenei yechidim einam tzerichin le'eruv* — if each courtyard has only a single resident, no *eruv* is needed. A single person in A has no need for an *eruv*, and a single person in B has no need for one either. Crucially, according to the *chachamim*, B's presence does not affect A regardless of what is happening in B. Each is simply independent.

This final ruling, however, applies only according to the *chachamim*. According to Rabbi Akiva, even a single resident of B creates a problem for A, because the conceptual principle remains: B is always present in A. The debate is, at bottom, about whether the act of physically passing through A renders B's residents conceptual co-members of A's courtyard — Rabbi Akiva says yes, always; the *chachamim* say the extent to which B creates a problem for A depends on whether B itself is in a state of prohibition.

---

## Gemara Positions

### Rav Dimi Interprets

The *gemara* opens its analysis with a statement brought by Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yannai: *zu divrei Rabbi Akiva* — this is entirely the position of Rabbi Akiva. The claim is striking: the *entire mishnah* is to be read as the view of Rabbi Akiva, not as a debate between a *tanna kama* and Rabbi Akiva. The purpose of this reading is to carve out space for a third position, attributed to the *chachamim*, that is even more lenient than the middle position the *mishnah* appears to articulate.

Rabbi Yannai's formulation of Rabbi Akiva's position is: *afilu regel hamuteret bimkomah oseret shelo bimkomah* — even when B is fully permitted in its own place, it nonetheless creates a problem for A. And the *chachamim*, in this reading, say something far more radical than the *mishnah*'s apparent middle ground: *keshem she'regel muteret einah oseret, kach regel ha'asura einah oseret* — just as when B is permitted it does not create a problem for A, so too even when B is forbidden it does not create a problem for A. On this view, B is entirely irrelevant to A in all circumstances.

### Gemara Challenges Reading

The *gemara* immediately presses on this reading. The *mishnah* states plainly that when A made an *eruv* and B did not, both are forbidden. The *gemara* asks: *mani*? Whose view is this? If it is Rabbi Akiva's, why specify the case where B is *asur*? Rabbi Akiva holds that B creates a problem for A even when B is *mutar* — so the case of an *asur* B creating problems tells us nothing distinctive about Rabbi Akiva's position. The *gemara* therefore suggests this must represent the *rabbanan* — the middle position, which holds that B creates a problem for A only when B is itself forbidden.

The *gemara* then attempts to preserve the reading of Rav Dimi by interpreting the *mishnah* as using the rhetorical device of *velo zo af zo* — not only in the case where B is *asur* does B create a problem, but even when B has made its own *eruv* and is *mutar*, B still creates a problem for A. In this reading, the *mishnah* builds from the less surprising to the more surprising case, and the whole is Rabbi Akiva's view.

### Gemara Rewrites

The *gemara*, however, is still not satisfied. The line of the *mishnah* stating *eiru zu le'atzmah vezu le'atzmah, zu muteret bifnei atzmah vezu muteret bifnei atzmah* — when both made separate *eruvin* each is permitted — implies that it is specifically *because* B made its *eruv* and is *mutar* that A is also *mutar*. The logical corollary is that had B not made an *eruv*, A would be forbidden. This is the middle position, not Rabbi Akiva's extreme.

The *gemara* responds by invoking the principle of *chasorei mechasra vehachi katani* — the *mishnah* is missing words and must be read as follows: when both made their respective *eruvin*, each is permitted — and this is specifically when B also constructed a *dakah*, a small partition, separating itself from A. Without such a partition, even if B made its own *eruv*, A would still be forbidden according to Rabbi Akiva, because *drisat haregel* still renders B conceptually present in A.
