The underlying logic seems to be that when the underlying configuration is a ditch — something that by its nature divides — one needs something more than a temporary fill to redefine that configuration. A wall of straw, by contrast, is not fighting against a pre-existing dividing structure; it is simply asserting itself as a new partition, and for that purpose straw is sufficient.

### Dirt & Rocks

The gemara now presses further on the case of dirt and rocks. Our mishna implies that dirt filling a ditch suffices without any special designation — it is, in the default (*stam*) case, enough to neutralize the ditch. But the gemara cites a contradiction from the tractate of Oholot. That mishna states: if a house is filled with straw or rocks (*teven o tzerorot*) and one has been *mevatel* them — designated them as permanently remaining — then they are *batel* and alter the halachic configuration of the house for purposes of the laws of *tumah*. The concern there is whether a corpse buried under such fill is treated as buried in the ground (in which case the *tumah* passes upward through the fill directly rather than spreading throughout the house via the intervening airspace beneath the ceiling). The implication of *uvitlo batel* — that it is only effective when one has performed *bitul* — is that even rocks, without such designation, do not suffice on their own. This appears to contradict our mishna, which treats dirt as automatically effective.

### Rabbi Yose View

Rav Huna suggests that the author of the mishna in Oholot is Rabbi Yose, whose position is more demanding. The gemara immediately objects: from what we know of Rabbi Yose's actual view, he demands *less*, not more. The gemara then cites a *baraita* that articulates Rabbi Yose's position with precision and elegance. Rabbi Yose says: *teven de-ein asuy le-pnoto harei hu ke-stam afar u-vattel* — straw that one does not intend to remove is treated like ordinary undesignated dirt, and is *batel*, altering the configuration. Conversely, *afar ve-asuy le-pnoto harei hu ke-stam teven ve-lo battel* — dirt that one intends to remove is treated like ordinary undesignated straw, and does not alter the configuration.

The key to remembering this position is that Rabbi Yose makes intent the decisive variable. The default (*stam*) case for dirt is that it alters the landscape — one does not need *bitul*; the only exception is if one explicitly plans to remove it. The default case for straw is that it does not alter the landscape — it is assumed to be temporary and removable; the only exception is if one has explicitly designated it as permanent. This three-way matrix — *bitul*, *stam*, and *asuy le-pnoto* — maps neatly onto the cases in our mishna, which describes the undesignated (*stam*) case: straw does nothing, dirt does everything.

Thus our mishna is entirely consistent with Rabbi Yose. The initial suggestion — that Rabbi Yose is the author of the ruling in Oholot that demands *bitul* even for dirt — was mistaken. Rav Assi corrects the attribution: *man tanna Eruvin Rabbi Yose hi* — Rabbi Yose is the author of our mishna in Eruvin, not of the more stringent position in Oholot. As Tosafot observes, what this exchange reveals is that the amora'im knew that Rabbi Yose was the key figure in resolving the contradiction between Eruvin and Oholot, but initially got confused about which mishna he authored.

---

## Domains

### Tumah/Shabbat

Setting aside the dispute between *tanna'im*, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua offers a structural resolution that does not require attributing the two mishnas to different authorities: *tuma Shabbat karamsi* — *tumah* and *Shabbat* are simply different halachic categories, and different standards legitimately apply to each. Why, specifically, does dirt not require *bitul* in the context of Shabbat? Because on Shabbat, one would never remove the dirt anyway — dirt is *muktzeh*, and one does not handle *muktzeh* on Shabbat. Therefore, even if the standard halachic rule requires *bitul* to treat dirt as permanently neutralizing a space, on Shabbat the dirt is effectively treated as *batel* by default, since no one will disturb it. *Afilu arneki nami mivatel inshi* — even something as valuable as a wallet, if it happened to be sitting in the dirt, one would leave it there on Shabbat rather than move the dirt.

### House vs Ditch

Rav Ashi offers yet another angle of resolution, one that returns to the contrast between a house and a ditch rather than invoking the distinction between *tumah* and Shabbat. *Bishlama charitz limitamei khei* — a ditch exists in order to be filled; that is, one naturally fills a ditch to restore level ground, and therefore dirt in a ditch is naturally read as having restored the ground to its unfilled state. *Aval bayis* — but a house? Who fills a house with dirt and leaves it that way? The default assumption when dirt is found in a house is that it will be removed, and so without explicit *bitul*, one does not assume the configuration has been permanently altered. The question, in other words, is not just about the substance filling the space but about what we naturally assume regarding that substance given the nature of the space it is filling.

---

## Plank Mechanics

### Rava Plank

Having established the mishna's general framework, the gemara turns to the specifics of the plank. Rava clarifies: *lo shanu ella shenasan le-rochvo* — the requirement that the plank be four *tefachim* wide applies specifically when the plank is laid across the width of the ditch — that is, the four *tefachim* of the plank span the gap from one bank to the other. In that configuration, the plank must be wide enough to walk across, hence the four-*tefach* minimum. *Aval le-orkho afilu kol shehu nami sharei* — but if one lays the plank lengthwise along the ditch, so that it runs along the edge rather than bridging the gap, even a very thin plank may suffice — provided it reduces the actual gap to less than four *tefachim*.

### Gap Options

This raises a conceptual question: if one lays the plank lengthwise, must it run the entire length of the ditch? The gemara's discussion suggests that what matters is whether there exists some point at which the gap is reduced below four *tefachim*. If the ditch is itself only four *tefachim* from end to end, then a lengthwise plank — even a narrow one — placed along its edge reduces the crossing distance to less than four *tefachim* at that point, which may be sufficient to consider it traversable and thereby give the two courtyards the option of combining. The logic is that just as a natural narrowing of the ditch below four *tefachim* creates an optional connection, an artificial narrowing achieved by placing a plank can serve the same function. This is, admittedly, a somewhat counterintuitive result — that a lengthwise plank of minimal width could accomplish what a crosswise plank of less than four *tefachim* cannot — and the precise mechanics of the scenario invite further analysis.

---

## Balconies Revisited

### Opposition/Height

Returning to the case of the two balconies, Rava establishes several limiting conditions. *Ha de'amrat zu keneged zu in zu shelo keneged zu lo* — the leniency of treating two balconies as potentially connected applies only if they directly face one another. If one balcony is offset horizontally from the other, they are not considered accessible to one another even if the gap between them is less than four *tefachim*. Similarly, *vezu lemala mizu nami* — if one balcony is at a higher elevation than the other, that too disqualifies the connection, even if the horizontal distance between them is minimal.

### Three Tefach

Rava then adds: *lo amran ela sheyesh bein zeh lezeh shelosha tefachim* — even the requirement of direct opposition and equal height applies only when the gap between the balconies is more than three *tefachim*. *Aval ein bein zeh lezeh shelosha, gezustra akuma hi* — but if the gap is less than three *tefachim*, the two balconies are considered a single bent balcony. In that case, the principle of *lavud* — the halachic rule that treats a gap of less than three *tefachim* as though it were closed — applies automatically, rendering them connected regardless of whether they are at exactly the same height or in perfect alignment. The interplay here is subtle: when the gap is between three and four *tefachim*, the balconies are considered disconnected, and the conditions of direct opposition and equal height are necessary for the optional connection to apply; when the gap is less than three *tefachim*, *lavud* makes the question of traversability moot, and they are considered joined in any event.

---

## Straw Walls

### Wall Specs

The next mishna introduces the case of a *matben* — a large mound of straw — serving as a wall between two courtyards. Unlike the ditch scenario, the mishna does not specify that this wall must have any particular width; it need only be ten *tefachim* high. This reflects the general principle that a wall, however thin, serves as a divider — the width requirements that arose earlier concerned the ditch itself, not the wall. *Gavoha asarah tefachim — me'arvin shnayim ve'ein me'arvin echad*: the straw wall at this height functions as a full halachic partition, and the two courtyards are necessarily treated as separate. There is no option to combine them.

Importantly, this is straw that is designated as animal fodder, not the construction straw we encountered in an earlier discussion of *muktzeh*. Because it is intended for feeding animals, it is not *muktzeh*, and one may draw from it on Shabbat.

### Rav Huna Restrict

Having established that the straw wall is a legitimate *mechitza* and the straw is not *muktzeh*, one might conclude that one may freely draw from this wall to fill a basket and then feed one's animals from the basket. Rav Huna rules otherwise: *uvilvad shelo yiten le-toch kupato ve-yachil* — one may not directly fill a basket from the straw wall. The concern is practical: if one stands there filling a basket, one is liable to remove large quantities without carefully monitoring the wall's height. The wall may drop below ten *tefachim* on Shabbat itself, at which point the two courtyards — which had separate *eruvin* — become merged into one without a unified *eruv*, creating a violation.

Rashi adds a second rationale: since the straw is designated as a wall, it has the character of *muktzeh* in the sense that one has mentally removed it from the category of animal fodder for Shabbat purposes. It has been assigned a structural role, and treating it as simply available fodder conflicts with that designation. This second rationale, as we will see, explains why the gemara requires the same caution even when one's animal is feeding directly from the wall.

### Animals Feed

One might assume that since one cannot personally fill a basket from the straw, at least one's animals may feed directly from the wall. The gemara probes this. It cites a ruling of Rav Huna in the name of Rav Chinana: *mamid adam et behemto al gabei asabim be-Shabbat* — one may cause one's animal to stand over grass and eat it on Shabbat, by walking behind the animal and guiding it there. However, *ve-ein mamid adam et behemto al gabei muktzeh be-Shabbat* — one may not cause one's animal to stand over and eat *muktzeh*, because one might come to pick up the *muktzeh* oneself and feed it to the animal.

Why the asymmetry between grass and *muktzeh*? Picking up grass would involve a *melachah de-oraita*, and we are not concerned that someone will inadvertently perform a biblical violation. But picking up *muktzeh* is only a rabbinic prohibition, and since the animal is already eating from it — which somewhat diminishes the sense that it is off-limits — one might come to take it with one's own hands. This is exactly the concern with the straw wall: if you are standing there while your animal eats, you might yourself reach in and take some.

The gemara therefore limits the permissibility of animal feeding from the straw wall. *De-kaim lei be-apa ve-azla ve-achla* — what is permitted is to guide the animal toward the wall and let it go eat on its own, without standing over it. One may not personally supervise the animal's feeding at the wall, lest one come to fill a basket directly.

---

## Oholot Case

### Baraita

The gemara now confronts Rav Huna's restriction with a *baraita* that appears to contradict it directly. The *baraita* describes a house situated between two courtyards, serving as the connective passage from one to the other, and filled with straw. *Me'arvin shenayim ve-ein me'arvin echad* — like the straw wall in the mishna, this configuration forces them to be separate. But then: *ve-noten le-toch kupato ve-ochel* — one may go ahead and directly fill one's basket from this straw house and feed one's animals. This is precisely what Rav Huna forbade. The *baraita* not only permits direct basket-filling but seems to take it for granted as the normal mode of use.

Furthermore, the *baraita* proceeds: *nismat ha-teven me-asara tefachim — shenehem asurin* — if the straw drops below ten *tefachim*, both courtyards become forbidden, since they are now merged without a unified *eruv*. And it then describes the remedy: *no'el beito u-mevatel et reshuso* — one locks one's house and performs *bitul reshut*, renouncing one's rights in the courtyard.

---

## Wall Collapses

### Collapse Problem

The scenario of a straw wall dropping below ten *tefachim* on Shabbat raises a fundamental problem. If the two courtyards had been set up with separate *eruvin* for the very reason that the straw wall divided them, and the straw wall then collapses — whether gradually through animal feeding or otherwise — the two courtyards become merged into a single space that has no valid *eruv* at all. Both courtyards are now forbidden for carrying, since each had established its eruv in anticipation of the continued existence of the wall.

The gemara also raises whether this change in halachic status takes effect on Shabbat itself — that is, whether a wall that falls on Shabbat immediately alters the *eruv* status of the courtyards for that very Shabbat — or whether the status established at the onset of Shabbat persists throughout, with the problem only manifesting the following Shabbat. This question has a bearing on how urgent the situation is and what remedies are available.

### Solutions

The *baraita*'s proposed remedy is twofold: *no'el beiso u-mevatel reshuso* — one locks one's house and performs *bitul reshut*. The scenario as described involves three houses: house one, house two, and the straw-filled house in the middle. Once the straw wall falls below ten *tefachim*, the courtyards merge. A resident of one house, wishing to help the other courtyard maintain usability, locks the door connecting his house to the now-merged space, thereby effectively reconstituting a barrier, and simultaneously performs *bitul reshut*, renouncing his own rights to the courtyard so that the others may freely use it. He himself is then forbidden — the one who performs *bitul reshut* loses his own carrying rights — but his neighbors are permitted.

---

## Oholot Case (II)

### House Interior

The gemara now explains why the *baraita* permits direct basket-filling from the straw-filled house, while the mishna's straw wall — Rav Huna's case — does not permit it. The difference lies in the visual cue provided by an enclosed space. *Bayit, keivan de-ika tikrah, ki mifchat, minkara lei milta* — in a house, because there is a ceiling, when the pile of straw diminishes, the growing gap between the top of the pile and the ceiling makes the shrinkage immediately apparent. One will notice that the pile is getting lower before it drops below ten *tefachim*. *Hacha lo minkara milta* — in the open field, with no ceiling overhead, the gradual reduction from eleven *tefachim* to ten to nine is far less perceptible. There is no visual reference point to alert one to the danger. Accordingly, when filling one's basket from an enclosed straw house, one can trust that one will notice the diminution in time; when filling from an outdoor straw wall, one cannot.

This resolution raises a further halachic complication. The *baraita* states that as long as the pile remains at ten *tefachim*, both courtyards are permitted — *ha asara shari* — even if the ceiling is very high above the pile. This might seem to suggest that a ten-*tefach* partition inside a house is sufficient even when it does not approach the ceiling. But this is in tension with a principle established elsewhere that partitions within an enclosed structure must reach the ceiling to be effective; a ten-*tefach* partition in a room is not the same as a partition between two fully separate spaces.

Abaye resolves this by saying that the case in the *baraita* involves a very low ceiling: specifically, a house that is thirteen *tefachim* and a fraction high — *beiveit sheloshah asar chasar mashehu*. The pile of straw at ten *tefachim* is then within three *tefachim* of the ceiling, and by the principle of *lavud*, the gap is treated as closed. The partition is thus considered to extend all the way to the ceiling, making it a full *mechitza*.

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua offers an even more compressed scenario: the entire house is only ten *tefachim* high — perhaps it is really more of a storage space than a dwelling — and the pile of straw is seven *tefachim* and a fraction. Since there is less than three *tefachim* between the top of the straw and the ceiling, *lavud* completes the partition and it is treated as a full wall of ten.

The gemara notes the asymmetry between these two resolutions: according to Abaye, "less than ten" means the pile has dropped below the threshold where *lavud* can still bridge the gap; according to Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, "less than ten" is measured *mi-toras asarah* — it means the pile is no longer functioning as the equivalent of a ten-*tefach* partition once the *lavud* contribution is subtracted.

This discussion has a fascinating practical ramification noted in a *teshuvah* of Rav Henkin. There is longstanding debate among the *poskim* about whether an *ezrat nashim* — a women's section — possesses the same *kedusha* as the men's section of a synagogue, a question that arises, among other contexts, when considering whether one may reconfigure a synagogue by converting the men's section to women's use. Many of those responsa were written in the context of synagogues where the women's section was a genuinely separate room, with the dividing *mechitza* reaching the ceiling. Rav Henkin argues that as soon as the *mechitza* does not reach the ceiling, the space is halachically a single room regardless, and the entire framework of those discussions becomes moot. Whether or not one accepts his conclusion — and there are certainly *poskim* who would not — the underlying principle is directly rooted in discussions such as this one, where a partition that fails to reach the ceiling, even if ten *tefachim* high, does not genuinely divide the space it occupies.

---

## Wall Collapses (II)

### Lock vs Bitul

The gemara now returns to the question of whether both remedies — locking the door and performing *bitul reshut* — are required, or whether either one alone suffices. *Tarti?* the gemara asks: why both? Normally, *bitul reshut* is effective on its own to resolve the problem of an unjoined resident in a courtyard. And locking the door should, at least in principle, reconstitute a barrier. The gemara resolves: *o no'el beiso o mevatel reshuso* — it is one or the other; either remedy independently suffices. Locking the door is presumably most useful before Shabbat, while *bitul reshut* is the available solution once Shabbat has begun. Alternatively, the gemara entertains the possibility that both really are required: *le'olam tarti, keivan dedash bah asi letaltulei* — since one is accustomed to traversing between the spaces, one is liable to forget and carry, and therefore a double measure is needed.

### Rashi/Tosafot

Rashi explains the requirement for both as follows: locking the door is for the resident's own benefit — as a *heikera*, a reminder — so that he does not accidentally carry from his house into the now-merged courtyard. The *bitul reshut* alone makes the other courtyard's residents permitted, but without physically locking the door, the resident who performed *bitul* might forget his own restrictions and violate Shabbat. Rashi's position implies that the locking requirement is ongoing throughout Shabbat: when one leaves the house, one locks it behind oneself; when one re-enters, one locks the door again. One need not remain inside the house all of Shabbat, but the door must be locked whenever one is inside.

Tosafot is dissatisfied with this explanation. Tosafot argues that the double requirement of locking and *bitul* applies only to this particular unusual case — where everything was fine at the start of Shabbat and an unexpected event midday forced a change in status. In such a circumstance, because one has not mentally prepared for a changed halachic reality, one requires a double safeguard to prevent accidental violation. Under ordinary circumstances, a single remedy would be sufficient.

---

## Grain Techumim

### Grain Pile

The mishna adds a parallel case: *gov shel teven she-bein shtei techumei Shabbat* — a pile of grain straddling two Shabbat boundaries. Each city has a *techum* of two thousand *amot*, and if a pile of grain lies exactly at the boundary between two communities' *techumim*, each side may take from its own portion of the pile — *zeh noten le-toch kupato ve-zeh noten le-toch kupato* — but must be careful not to take from the other side's portion, which would constitute carrying beyond one's *techum*.

### Rabbi Akiva

The gemara notes that this ruling requires explicit statement specifically according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that *techumim* is a biblical prohibition. One might have thought that since the risk of reaching across and taking from the wrong side is a biblical violation, Rabbi Akiva would require a protective rabbinic *gezeira* — forbidding one from taking from one's own side of the pile at all, lest one come to mistakenly take from the other side as well. *Kamashma lan* — the ruling teaches that no such gezeira is imposed. Each person may take from his own portion, and we do not add a preventive layer to guard against biblical transgression in this context.

---

---

# Eiruvin 80

## Shituf Mevo'os Setup

### Shituf Intro

The *mishna* on the middle of 79b opens with the question *keitzad mishtatfin bamavoi* — how does one perform a *shituf* of the *mavoi*? The mechanics begin with *maniach es hachavis*, setting down a barrel of wine, or alternatively dates, figs, or any other food, because unlike *eruv chatzeiros*, a *shituf mevo'os* does not require bread. Once the food is designated, one declares: *harei zu lechol bnei hamavoi* — this is for all the residents of the *mavoi*.

The underlying mechanism involves a shortcut available to anyone willing to act: one takes one's own food, declares it to be the *shituf*, and in doing so transfers partial ownership to every resident of the *mavoi*. The result is that each resident now holds a share in the barrel. This same requirement — of actually transferring ownership to others — applies, as we will see, to the other forms of *eruvin* as well, but the *mishna* introduces it here in the context of *shituf*.

### Zikui Requirement

The *mishna* states *umizakeh lahen* — and one must transfer ownership to the others. The requirement of *zikui* (transfer of ownership) rests on a basic principle of *kinyan*: you cannot transfer an object from your own possession to another without a second party. Even though the rule of *zachin le'adam shelo befanav* — one may do something meritorious on behalf of another even in that person's absence — permits the transfer without the recipient's knowledge or consent, it does not permit a transfer without any second party at all. Removing something from one hand and placing it in the other is not an act of transfer. A third party is required to serve as the receiving agent.

The practical illustration is straightforward: if one wishes to give a gift to someone who is absent, one may appoint a second individual to take possession on behalf of the intended recipient. The recipient need not know, because the transfer is purely to her benefit. But without any second party, the act of *zikui* is incomplete.

### Valid Recipients

Who may serve as this second party? The *mishna* enumerates the options: *umizakeh lahen al yedei bno u'vito hagedolim* — through one's adult sons or daughters, who are the most conveniently available persons in a household. This is precisely why, in practice, the community *rav* who establishes an *eruv* for an entire city will hand the food to a designated individual and declare it possessed on behalf of all residents — the congregants themselves need never be individually solicited.

Also valid are Jewish male and female servants — *avdo ve'shifchaso ha'ivrim* — because their Jewish status makes them legally independent persons. One may have a lien on their labor, but their capacity for ownership is their own; they constitute a separate *yad*, a separate domain of ownership. Likewise, one's wife — *al yedei ishto* — may serve as the receiving party.

What is excluded? *Ein m'zakeh lo al yedei bno u'vito haktanim* — one's minor children may not serve, because they are treated as an extension of the parent's legal domain rather than as independent owners. Nor may one's non-Jewish slaves serve — *lo al yedei avdo ve'shifchaso hakena'anim* — because, as the *mishna* states, *yadan k'yado*, their hand is like his hand. Placing the object in their possession is legally equivalent to keeping it in one's own hand.

### Age vs. Dependency

A question arises — and *Tosafos* engages with it directly — about whether the relevant distinction in the *mishna* is truly one of literal age (adult versus minor) or rather one of practical and financial dependence. This question is rooted in discussions in other passages of *Gemara*. The *sugya* at hand takes the *mishna* at face value: it is a question of adulthood, even if the adult child still lives in the parental home.

Another *Gemara*, however, suggests that what is truly decisive is not age per se but practical financial dependence. Under that view, a minor who is financially independent might, in unusual circumstances, be treated as a separate domain. *Tosafos* raises a difficulty with this: since when can a minor legally take possession of an object? In response, *Tosafos* notes that *shituf* occupies a hybrid position — it is partly a genuine *kinyan* but also partly a quasi-ritual act. The standards for the *kinyan* dimension may therefore be lower than they would be in a purely commercial context. Moreover, this is a case of *da'as acher makneh oso* — the transfer is driven by the active will of the one transferring, not by the initiative of the recipient. Since the recipient may be more passive in such a scenario, perhaps a minor could suffice even where one normally could not.

The conclusion of this *Gemara*, however, is not to pursue that complexity. The *mishna* is read straightforwardly: adulthood versus minority is the operative criterion.

### Erev Shabbat Apps

A related application arises in practice on *Erev Shabbos*. There is a *halacha* prohibiting *kinyan* on *Shabbos* — one may not formally transfer ownership on *Shabbos* itself. This creates a challenge when one wishes to bring a gift to a host: if the item is *letzorech Shabbos*, needed for *Shabbos* use, the transfer is permitted. But if the item is not clearly for *Shabbos* use — a book one might not read until after *Shabbos*, or a bottle of wine when the host already has an open one — the issue becomes more complicated.

A practical solution is to call over one's spouse or a *bar* or *bat mitzvah* child before *Shabbos* and say: take possession of this on behalf of the people we are visiting. Once possession is transferred *before Shabbos*, the item already belongs to the recipients, and there is no issue with carrying it on *Shabbos*. Alternatively, one may bring the item and declare explicitly that ownership will not transfer until after *Shabbos* — or until the item is actually consumed, whichever comes first.

The question is also raised: can the wife or other valid recipients serve not merely as passive receiving agents but as the active party initiating the *eruv* — for example, by knocking on neighbors' doors and collecting food? The answer is yes, and the *Gemara* addresses the matter in greater detail. The more nuanced question, to which the *Gemara* will return, is whether a wife acting as the active party may contribute food that legally belongs to her husband, without his knowledge or consent — a question rooted in the standard property arrangements of the Talmudic period, where the husband owned the assets and the wife was supported from them.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Hagba'ah Tefach

*Amar Rav Yehuda*: when transferring ownership of the barrel used for *shitufei mevo'os*, the receiving party must lift it off the ground a minimum of one *tefach*. This is the *kinyan* of *hagba'ah* — the formal act of acquisition through lifting — and a *tefach* is both the minimum and, apparently, the sufficient amount.

One might infer from this ruling that *hagba'ah* in general requires only a *tefach*. *Tosafos* cautions against that inference. There is in fact contradictory evidence elsewhere in the *Gemara* suggesting that *hagba'ah* may require three *tefachim* in other contexts — a significant amount, given that three *tefachim* is also the threshold below which *lavud* applies. *Tosafos* explains that no general rule should be derived from this case, because the *kinyan* here is, once again, partly genuine acquisition and partly ritual. The lower standard of one *tefach* may apply specifically here without setting a broader precedent.

### Pumbedita Rulings

*Amar Rava*: the following two rulings were both transmitted by the elders of *Pumbedisa* — *Shmuel*'s *yeshiva* — and specifically attributed to *Rav Yehuda*, the principal disciple of *Shmuel*'s leading students. The first is the ruling just mentioned regarding *hagba'ah* of a *tefach*.

The second ruling: *ham'kadesh im ta'am melo lugmav yatza, ve'im lav lo yatza* — one who recites *Kiddush* must drink a mouthful that fills one cheek; if one takes only a negligible sip, one has not fulfilled the obligation. *Tosafos* notes a difficulty here: it is known that the *kos shel Kiddush* must hold a *revi'is*, and another *Gemara* seems to suggest that *melo lugmav* exceeds a *revi'is*, which would create a problem — how can one be required to drink more than the cup contains? *Tosafos* resolves that *melo lugmav* is in fact less than a *revi'is*. The fuller treatment of this question belongs to the discussion in *Pesachim*.

A further statement attributed to the elders of *Pumbedisa*: *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel* — *osim medura l'chaya b'Shabbos* — one may kindle a bonfire for a woman who has just given birth on *Shabbos*. She is considered a *chola* with a *sakana*, and the fire is deemed medically necessary. The *Gemara* initially infers from this that the permission applies only to a *chaya* (a woman post-partum) and not to a regular *chola*, even one who is *yesh bo sakana*, and only in winter rather than summer. However, *Amar Rav Chiya bar Avin amar Shmuel* introduces a qualification: if someone has undergone bloodletting and feels chilly, one may make a bonfire on *Shabbos* even during the summer month of *Tammuz*. The concern for a sick person who feels cold overrides all seasonal considerations, and one does not hesitate.

### Asherah Debate

*Amar Ameimar*: another ruling was also transmitted by the elders of *Pumbedisa*. The question: *eizu hi ashera stam* — what type of tree can be presumed to be an *ashera* (an idolatrously worshipped tree, mentioned repeatedly in the *Torah* in contexts such as *ashiroteihen tisrefun ba'esh*) without explicit confirmation that it was used for idol worship?

*Rav* says: any tree *kol she'mishamshei avoda zara shomrim osah ve'ein to'amin mipiroseha* — that is guarded by the attendants of idol worship and whose fruit they refuse to eat. The combination of protective custody and refusal to consume the produce is a strong indicator of cultic veneration.

*Shmuel* takes a different approach: a tree whose fruit the worshippers designate for a specific cultic purpose — for example, if they say, we are using the dates of this tree to brew beer *de'Bei Netzarphei* (apparently a reference to a Zoroastrian fire-temple, as *Steinsaltz* suggests, connecting *netzarphei* to the root meaning *fire*) — and the beer is to be drunk on a religious festival. Here the tree is not itself worshipped, but its produce is consecrated to serve a cultic function.

Some *Rishonim* note that according to *Shmuel*'s criterion, the tree might constitute only a rabbinic extension of *ashera* rather than a full Biblically prohibited *ashera*, since a true *ashera* by strict definition must be an object of worship, not merely a provider of materials for religious rituals. In any case, the elders of *Pumbedisa* — whose sympathy for *Shmuel*'s positions is acknowledged, given *Rav Yehuda*'s connection to that tradition — conclude: *hilcheta k'vatei d'Shmuel*, the *halacha* follows *Shmuel*.

### Baraita Shituf

Returning now to the main topic, the *Gemara* raises an objection from a *baraita*: *keitzad mishtatfin be'mavoi?* — How does one make a *shituf* for a *mavoi*? One brings a barrel of wine, oil, dates, figs, or any other produce, since *shituf* (unlike *eruv chatzeiros*) does not require bread.

The *baraita* then draws a critical distinction: *im mishelo, tzarich lezakot* — if one is using one's own food, one must perform an act of transfer of ownership. *Ve'im mishelahen, tzarich lehodiya* — if the food happens to belong to the other residents (for example, stored in one's possession), one must at minimum inform them and obtain their awareness and agreement before using their food for the *shituf*.

As for the mechanics of transfer: *u'magbihah min ha'karka mashehu* — one lifts it slightly from the ground. The *Gemara* explains that *mashehu* (a little bit) here means a *tefach*, consistent with what was said earlier. The *Gemara* also notes that the lifting seems to be performed even in the case where the food already belongs to the others, suggesting that the lifting is not purely about *kinyan* — it also carries a ritual dimension, a formal designation of the material as belonging to the *shituf*.

### Rav No Transfer

With that *baraita* on the table, the *Gemara* now presents the famous dispute: *itmar, shitufei mevo'os — Rav amar ein tzarich lezakot*. Contrary to what the *mishna* explicitly states, *Rav* holds that one need not perform an act of *zikui* — a formal transfer of ownership — when establishing a *shituf mevo'os*. One may simply take one's own wine, designate it for the *shituf*, and be done.

*Rashi* explains the logic: the person initiating the *shituf* has a compelling personal interest in making it work, because without the *shituf* no one will be able to carry in the *mavoi* or *chatzer*. This high degree of *gemirat da'at* — of genuine and total commitment — is powerful enough that his intention alone can effect the transfer without a second party. The blocking of that outcome by others who are unavailable is precisely what grants his unilateral will sufficient legal force. *Tosafos* suggests an alternative framing: one might argue that the entire mechanism of *shituf* has been so thoroughly ritualized that the formal *kinyan* requirements are simply inapplicable. *Rashi*, however, does not go that far; he grounds the leniency in the heightened *gemirat da'at* of the initiator.

This position is explicitly against the *mishna*, which states *tzarich lezakot* — transfer is required. The *Gemara* will need to address how *Rav* can stand against the *mishna*.

### Shmuel Position

*Shmuel* takes the position consistent with the *mishna*: by *shituf mevo'os*, one does require a formal act of *zikui*. However, the debate between *Rav* and *Shmuel* involves a striking inversion when it comes to *eruv techumin*.

For *eruv techumin* — where one deposits food beyond the city limits on behalf of another person, allowing that person to extend their *Shabbos* walking boundary two thousand *amos* in that direction — *Rav* holds that *tzarich lezakot*: one must formally transfer the food to that person. *Shmuel* holds the opposite: by *eruv techumin*, *ein tzarich lezakot*, no formal transfer is needed.

The inversion is striking. Why would *Rav* demand transfer for *eruv techumin* but not for *shituf mevo'os*, and *Shmuel* demand it for *shituf mevo'os* but not for *eruv techumin*?

*Rav*'s reasoning: when establishing a *shituf mevo'os*, the initiator has a powerful personal stake — without the *shituf* the entire street is unusable — so his *gemirat da'at* alone is sufficient. But when doing an *eruv techumin* for someone else, as a favor, there is no equivalent personal urgency, and so the food must actually belong to the beneficiary through a formal transfer.

*Shmuel*'s reasoning (as *Tosafos* explains): *eruv techumin* is typically done *l'dvar mitzvah* — for a religious purpose — and this heightened motivation either substitutes for or mitigates the need for a formal *maaseh kinyan*. Alternatively, *eruv techumin* is less about creating a shared ownership structure (as *eruv chatzeiros* is) and more about designating a location — so the transfer requirements may be inherently lower. *Shmuel* agrees with the *mishna* that by *shituf* (and by implication *eruv chatzeiros*) transfer is required, and by *eruv techumin* it is not.

The *Gemara* notes that *Shmuel*'s position is internally coherent and consistent with the sources: where the *mishna* mentions *zikui*, *Shmuel* requires it; where the *mishna* is silent (as with *eruv techumin*), he does not. *Rav*'s position, however, contradicts the *mishna* directly on *shituf mevo'os*. The *Gemara* responds: *tannai hi* — this is in fact a *tannaitic* dispute, and *Rav* has a *tanna* to rely upon.

*Tosafos* also observes, in the course of this discussion, that there is no general principle making *eruv techumin* consistently stricter or more lenient than *eruv chatzeiros*. By some measures *eruv techumin* is stricter — for example, by *eruv techumin* each participant must contribute two meals' worth, whereas by *eruv chatzeiros*, if there are many residents, two meals' worth for all of them combined suffices, and if there are few, the size of a pressed fig per person. By other measures *eruv techumin* is more lenient. The two categories simply have different parameters, with no overarching hierarchy.

### Daughter-in-Law

To demonstrate that *Rav*'s position has a *tannaitic* basis, the *Gemara* cites a story: *maaseh be'kallasa shel Rabbi Oshaya* — an incident involving the daughter-in-law of *Rabbi Oshaya*. She had gone to the bathhouse on *Erev Shabbos* and was detained there as *Shabbos* fell. In her absence, her mother-in-law took care of the *eruv* on her behalf. The case came before *Rabbi Chiya*, who ruled it invalid.

*Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yossi* challenged that ruling, invoking the name of his father *Rabbi Yossi*: *kol she'ata yachol lehakel b'eiruv hakel* — wherever possible to be lenient in matters of *eruvin*, one should be lenient. This is a principle we have encountered repeatedly in the *masechet*: *halacha k'divrei hameikel b'eiruv*.

Two questions surround the story: What exactly was the problem? Was it that the mother-in-law used her own food but failed to perform an act of *zikui* on behalf of the daughter-in-law? Or was it that the mother-in-law used the daughter-in-law's own food but did so without the daughter-in-law's knowledge?

*Rashi* understands this as a case of *eruv techumin*: the daughter-in-law was stranded outside the city, and the mother-in-law established an *eruv techumin* for her. On that reading, the dispute concerns whether *zikui* is required for *eruv techumin*.

*Tosafos* disagrees. *Rav*'s position is that *zikui* is unnecessary for *shituf mevo'os* — but this is against the explicit *mishna*. To demonstrate that *Rav* has *tannaitic* support, the story must be one about *shituf mevo'os* or *eruv chatzeiros*. Therefore *Tosafos* understands the story as follows: the daughter-in-law was at home for *Shabbos* but simply absent at the moment the *shituf* was being established, and the mother-in-law stepped in on her behalf. The question is whether the mother-in-law's unilateral action — without performing a formal *kinyan* transferring the food to the daughter-in-law — was valid. *Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yossi* says yes, reflecting the lenient position that *zikui* is not required.

The *Gemara* records a further chain of inquiry to resolve the ambiguity. A certain rabbinic student named *Rabbi Yaakov* reports that he heard from *Rabbi Yochanan* that the food was the mother-in-law's own food, and the issue was her failure to perform *zikui* on behalf of the daughter-in-law. *Rabbi Zeira* then sends a message to *Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi*, taking the roundabout coastal route through Tyre (as *Steinsaltz*'s maps illustrate), to determine which version of the story is historically accurate. *Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi* confirms: it was the mother-in-law's food, and the dispute concerned whether she had to transfer ownership — thereby establishing that *Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yossi* held that *zikui* was not required, giving *Rav* his *tannaitic* precedent.

*Tosafos* adds a parenthetical note on the apparent inconsistency in strictness between *eruv techumin* and *eruv chatzeiros*: if *Rashi*'s reading is correct and this story concerns *eruv techumin*, then the lenient opinion (*Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yossi*) may reflect the view that *techumin* is *derabbanan*, while the stricter opinion (*Rabbi Chiya*) may reflect the view that it is *de'oraita*.

### RN Conclusion

Following this extended discussion, the *Gemara* arrives at a clear and authoritative conclusion. *Amar Rav Nachman*: *naktinan* — we take as our established position — *echad eiruvei techumin, ve'echad eiruvei chatzeiros, ve'echad shitufei mevo'os, tzarich lezakot*. Whether the issue is *eruv techumin*, *eruv chatzeiros* (now explicitly named for the first time in this discussion), or *shituf mevo'os* — in all three cases, a formal act of transfer of ownership is required.

This conclusion is more demanding than either *Rav* or *Shmuel* individually required. Each of them held that at least one category did not need *zikui*; *Rav Nachman* adopts the stringent position of each where applicable and requires *zikui* across the board. *Tosafos* confirms: *v'chein halacha* — this is the ruling we follow.

---

## Eruv Tavshilin

### Tavshilin Query

With the conclusion that *zikui* is required for all three types of *eruvin*, the *Gemara* raises one further question. *Ba'ei Rav Nachman*: what about *eiruvei tavshilin*? When a *rav* establishes an *eruv tavshilin* with the intention that it should serve as a *halachic* umbrella for all the residents of a city — formulating the intention *l'chol b'nei ha'ir*, as the familiar language of the *beracha* indeed states — must he perform a formal act of *zikui* to the residents, or is his declaration alone sufficient?

*Eruv tavshilin* differs fundamentally from the *eruvin* previously discussed — it involves permitting cooking on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbos* rather than establishing carrying domains — and its detailed analysis properly belongs to *Beitzah*, where it is treated at length. The *Gemara* here raises it only in connection with the *zikui* question.

### RY Challenge

*Amar Rav Yosef*: I don't understand the question. Has *Rav Nachman* not heard the teaching transmitted as *amar Rav Nachman bar Adda amar Shmuel* — that *eiruvei tavshilin* does require *zikui*? *Shmuel* already addressed this, and if so, what is the basis for *Rav Nachman*'s uncertainty?

*Amar lei Abaye*: obviously he hadn't heard it — *peshita d'lo shmei leh*. If he had heard it, he would not have asked. The question itself demonstrates ignorance of the prior ruling.

*Rav Yosef* responds: not necessarily. Perhaps *Rav Nachman* did hear it, and his question is whether to follow it. After all, *Shmuel* also said that *eruv techumin* does not require *zikui* — and *Rav Nachman* just ruled against that, requiring *zikui* for *eruv techumin* as well. Perhaps he is prepared similarly to deviate from *Shmuel* here.

The *Gemara* rejects this comparison. *Bishlama hatam* — there, by *eruv techumin* and *eruv chatzeiros*, there was a full debate: *Rav* and *Shmuel* both articulated explicit positions on both issues. *Rav Nachman*, in ruling that *zikui* is required across the board, did not reject either authority; he adopted the stringent ruling of each on its respective issue. *V'ka mashma lan k'chumrei d'mar u'k'chumrei d'mar* — he teaches us to apply the more stringent position of each *amora*. But regarding *eruv tavshilin*, *Shmuel* stated that *zikui* is required, and no one disputes it. Had *Rav Nachman* known of that uncontested ruling, he would simply have followed it. There is no competing opinion to navigate and no reason to deviate. The *Gemara* concludes, therefore, that *Shmuel*'s ruling stands: *eruv tavshilin* also requires *zikui*.

This will be revisited when we reach *Beitzah*. For now, the operative conclusion is: if one wishes the *eruv tavshilin* to function on behalf of the entire community, one must perform a formal act of transfer.

### Weapons Officer

The *Gemara* then introduces two parallel narratives. There was a certain *turzina* — a weapons officer, head of the municipal armory — living in the neighborhood of *Rabbi Zeira*. The residents asked him to rent his property to them, as required to permit carrying when a non-Jew's domain is part of the shared *reshus*. He refused. They came to *Rabbi Zeira* and asked: what about going to his wife? Can we rent from her?

A second, nearly identical story is told about a *turzina* in the neighborhood of *Rabbi Yehuda bar Oshaya*. Again the non-Jew refused to rent. The question again went to *Rabbi Yehuda bar Oshaya*, who did not know the answer. It was then brought to *Rav Masna*, who also did not know. Finally it reached *Rav Yehuda*, who answered in the name of *Shmuel*: *ishto shel adam me'arreves shelo mida'ato* — a man's wife may establish the *eruv* without his knowledge.

### Wife Authority

The ruling of *Reish Lakish*, cited in the first story, and the ruling of *Shmuel* cited by *Rav Yehuda* in the second, are consistent: the wife may act *shelo mida'ato* — without the husband's awareness. Notably, the language used is *me'arreves*, not *sokheres* — this applies not merely to the *sekhirus* of the non-Jew's property (which is itself a somewhat formal legal construct) but to contributing food directly to the *eruv* or *shituf*.

This creates an apparent tension with the *mishna*'s requirement of *zikui*. *Shmuel* himself insists on *zikui* — a formal transfer of ownership through a second party — when using one's own food to establish a *shituf*. Yet here, when going in the opposite direction — taking food from another person's household without their explicit consent — *Shmuel* seems to permit it. The point of reconciliation is that the wife in this context is not transferring ownership but rather contributing the household food, which is understood ultimately to be in the husband's interest as well. There is no genuine loss to him, and therefore his explicit consent is not required.

### Women Baraita

A *baraita* appears to contradict this ruling: *nashim she'eirvu venishtatfu shelo mida'at ba'aleihen — ein eiruvah eruv ve'ein shitufah shituf*. If women contributed to an *eruv* or *shituf* without their husbands' knowledge, the *eruv* is invalid and the *shituf* is invalid. This seems to flatly contradict the ruling that the wife may act without the husband's knowledge.

### Mandatory Status

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, ha de'assar, ha de'lo assar* — the cases are not the same. The key distinction is whether the household's non-participation would render the *eruv* forbidden for the other residents. There are configurations — the *Gemara* alluded to such cases earlier in the *masechet* — where a household opens onto two streets, and its participation or non-participation may be decisive for one street but not the other. For the street where their abstention creates no halachic problem for others, the residents cannot demand their participation, and the wife therefore cannot contribute without the husband's consent, since he has no stake in the matter that compels him. But where their non-participation would prevent other residents from using the *mavoi* or *chatzer*, then the household can be pressed to participate, and the wife's contribution without his explicit consent is valid — because at that point the husband is, in effect, blocking the community, and his abstention is not merely passive.

### Force Limits

This principle — that participation may be compelled when a household's abstention creates a communal halachic problem — leads the *Gemara* to a further question. *Leima msaye'a lei: kofin oto la'asot lechi ve'kora le'mavoi* — one may even compel a person to contribute to the construction of a *lechi* or *kora* for the *mavoi*. This resembles the principle in *Bava Batra* of compelling residents to contribute to communal needs. If we can force participation in the construction of the physical structures of the *mavoi*, perhaps the same principle applies to forcing participation in the *eruv* itself.

The *Gemara* rejects the parallel. *Shani hasam* — there it is different. *Rashi* explains: the absence of walls (*deleika mechitzos*) represents a more concrete, practical concern for the residents of the *mavoi*, not merely a halachic technicality. *Tosafos*, however, reports a different *girsa* from earlier manuscripts: *de'ika mechitzos* — because the walls are already there. Once physical walls exist, it does not matter whether anyone was forced to contribute to their construction — their halachic efficacy is determined by physical reality, not by the voluntariness of the participants. An *eruv*, by contrast, is conceptually about shared participation and partnership; it may therefore require more genuine consent than a physical structure does. On either reading, compelling contribution to the *eruv* may not follow straightforwardly from compelling contribution to the *lechi* or *kora*.

*Tosafos* adds that even the ruling of *bene mavoi nichnasim le'toch beito ve'notlin shitufan mimeno ba'al karcho* — that the residents may enter a person's home and take his contribution against his will if he normally participates but failed to do so — should be understood as meaning that they obtain it through his wife. The *Gemara* may sound more radical in its literal wording, but *Tosafos* tones it down to mean that the wife provides the food rather than that the residents break in and seize it.

### Asherah Materials

After these discussions, the *Gemara* records three words — *lashon acher mitzad sheni* — that the marginal commentators flag as entirely incomprehensible. A gloss printed in the margin notes: *shalosh teivos hallalu meshulalei havana lim'od* — these three words are utterly without meaning — and observes that in certain early printed editions of the *Gemara*, including the Venice printing and the Salonika printing, these words are entirely absent.

The *Gemara* then turns to a brief related ruling: *Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi* says one may fashion a *lechi* (an upright post) from an *ashera* — a tree that has been worshipped as an idol. Although an *ashera* is *assur b'hana'ah*, forbidden from benefit, obtaining the *halachic* ability to carry in a *mavoi* is not considered direct physical benefit, and the *lechi* therefore remains technically valid.

*Reish Lakish* goes further: one may even fashion a *kora* (the horizontal beam) from an *ashera*. If so, *man de'amar kora kol shekein lechi* — whoever permits the beam certainly permits the post. But *man de'amar lechi aval kora lo* — whoever permits only the post but not the beam — does so because of the principle *kisusei michsas shiureih*: since there is a *mitzvah* to destroy an *ashera*, it is treated as if already destroyed, and its *shiur* is considered burnt up and unavailable. A *kora* must be wide enough to support a brick (*aris leveinah*), and if its effective *shiur* is deemed annulled, it cannot meet that standard. A *lechi*, by contrast, has no minimum width requirement — though *Tosafos* notes it does have a minimum height — and so the problem of *kisusei michsas shiureih* may be less acute or at least differently applied. *Tosafos* concedes that the precise distinction is not fully clear.

---

## Quantities Rules

### Self Replenish

The *mishna* states: *nismait ha'ochel* — if the food of the *eruv* or *shituf* became depleted below the required minimum — *mosif u'mezakeh, ein tzarich lehodiya* — one may add to it and perform *zikui* without informing the other residents. The reasoning is straightforward: the person replenishing is using their own food and performing a *zikui* to the others. Since it is one's own food being given as a gift, there is no need to obtain the recipients' prior awareness; the transfer works unilaterally in their favor.

### New Residents

If new residents joined the *mavoi* or *chatzer* after the *eruv* was established — *nitosefu aleihen, mosif u'mezakeh* — one must add food to account for the new participants. *Rashi* explains that if the replenishment comes from the initiator's own food, it again requires no prior notification, since one is simply performing *zikui* of one's own assets. But if the new residents' own food is to be drawn upon, then *tzarich lehodiya* — one must inform them, because using their food without their awareness is not permitted when, as in this case, they are not yet part of the existing *eruv* structure.

### Min Quantities

How much food is needed? *Biz'man she'hen merubin, mazon shtei se'udos lekulam* — when the number of participants is large, two meals' worth of food for all of them combined is sufficient. This is the principle underlying the practice of many community *rabbis* who set aside a single box of *matzos* before *Pesach* as the *eruv* for an entire city of thousands — two meals' worth collectively is enough. *Biz'man she'hen mu'atin, kegrogeret lechol echad va'echad* — when the number of participants is small, each person must contribute the equivalent of a pressed fig (*grogeret*).

### RY Distinction

*Amar Rabbi Yosi*: these minimum quantities apply specifically to the initial establishment of the *eruv* — *bitechilat eruv*. But once an *eruv* has been properly established and some food remains — *bishiyurei eruv*, a leftover *eruv* — even the smallest amount, *kol shehu*, is sufficient to maintain its validity. One need not reconstitute the minimum amounts.

### Reason Waived

The rationale for this leniency: *lo amru le'arev bachatzerot ela kedei shelo tishkach et hatinokot* — the *eruv chatzeiros* requirement (even alongside a *shituf mevo'os*) exists primarily so that children do not forget the practice and the concept of *eruvin*. Since a *shituf mevo'os* using bread already covers the carrying requirements in most cases — rendering the separate *eruv chatzeiros* technically superfluous — the latter's minimum quantities need not be rigorously maintained as long as some food remains. The *eruv chatzeiros* in that context serves a pedagogical rather than strictly operative function.

This is also the basis for the ruling, followed in practice, that if one uses bread for the *shituf mevo'os*, there is no need to separately establish an *eruv chatzeiros* — the *rav* takes a single quantity of bread, two meals' worth for the entire city, and the matter is concluded.

### One vs. Two Types

The *Gemara* then examines what type of scenario the *mishna* is actually addressing when it says the food was "depleted" (*nismait*). If the *eruv* originally consisted of one type of food — say, wine — and one wishes to replenish it with the same type, the *Gemara* asks: why does the *mishna* mention depletion at all? Even if the wine were completely gone, one could presumably take more wine from the same contributors, since they already agreed to participate with wine. Conversely, if one wishes to replace the wine with oil — a different type — even a small depletion might be problematic, since the contributors consented to wine specifically, not oil.

### Depletion Baraita

A *baraita* clarifies: *kala ha'ochel mimin echad, ein tzarich lehodiya* — if the food was completely consumed and one wishes to replenish with the same type, no notification is required; the prior agreement covers the replenishment. *Mishnei minin* — if one wishes to replenish with a different type, *tzarich lehodiya* — notification is required. The prior consent covered the original food type, not a substitution.

This *baraita* makes the distinction between single-type and dual-type replenishment explicit for the case of complete depletion — a case that the *mishna* itself did not directly address, having spoken only of partial depletion.

### Two Interpret

The *Gemara* offers two ways of reading the *mishna* in light of the *baraita*. *Ibba'is eima min echad*: perhaps the *mishna* is discussing the case of a single food type, and when it says *nismait* (depleted), it actually means the food was completely used up — *mai nismat nismat* — rather than merely reduced. The *mishna* then teaches that even when fully depleted, if you replenish with the same type, no notification is needed.

*Ibba'is eima shnei minin*: alternatively, the *mishna* is discussing a case where one wishes to replenish with a different type, and *nismait* means genuinely diminished rather than entirely gone. Here the question is whether, when there is still some of the original food left, one may add a different type without notification. The answer, in that case, may be that partial remaining supply constitutes a kind of continuation of the original arrangement, so no new consent is needed. But *kalu shani* — once the original food is fully exhausted, the prior arrangement may be considered concluded, and a fresh contribution of a different type would require explicit agreement.

The practical upshot: once residents have agreed to participate in a *shituf* or *eruv*, replenishment is largely self-executing. As long as one is restoring the same arrangement — same food type, same parties — one need not reopen the matter. It is only when introducing something genuinely new — a new food type, or a completely fresh start after total depletion with a different substance — that renewed notification and consent are required.

---

---

# Eiruvin 81

## Replenishing & Informing

### Replenishing with Same/D…

The daf begins at 81b, precisely at the passage of *nitosfu alehem mosif u'mezake* — the case of replenishing a depleted *eruv*. The context is one in which food had been collected for an *eruv* or *shituf* and then became depleted — eaten, lost, or otherwise consumed. If one is replenishing with the same type of food as was originally used, the Gemara indicates that one need not seek the participants' permission anew. If, however, one wishes to replenish with a different type of food — say, the original was wine and one now wishes to add oil — then depending on circumstances, particularly if the original supply had been entirely consumed and one is effectively starting from scratch, consultation may be required.

An underlying ambiguity runs through this entire discussion: whose food is being used for the replenishment? If one is contributing from one's own stores and simply conferring the benefit upon the courtyard's residents, why should their permission be necessary at all? One is merely doing them a benefit. If, however, one is drawing upon the participants' own food to which one happens to have access, then any significant new action might well require their authorization, since they had initially consented to participate but not necessarily to this new arrangement. The Gemara does not address this distinction directly, and the ambiguity persists.

### New Residents & Notificati…

The Mishnah adds that if new residents have moved into the courtyard between one Shabbat and the next, one must add food to the *eruv* and *tzarich lehodiya* — one must inform the newcomers. Again, it is not entirely clear whether the obligation to inform arises because one is taking from their food, or whether even when using one's own food there is still a requirement to notify them. The Gemara leaves this ambiguous as well.

### R. Yehuda: No Notificati…

In response to this Mishnah, Rav Shizbi said in the name of Rav Chisda: *zot omeret chalukin alav chaverav al Rabbi Yehuda* — this teaches that Rabbi Yehuda's colleagues disagree with him. The Rabbi Yehuda in question is the one who appears in the upcoming Mishnah: *bameh devarim amurim be-eruvei techumin* — when is it that a person's awareness and buy-in are required? It is specifically by *eruv techumin*, where making an *eruv* in one direction benefits the person in that direction but curtails his range in the opposite direction. There, one clearly needs the person's participation from the outset. *Aval be-eruvei chatzerot* — but when it comes to a courtyard *eruv*, which only benefits everyone involved, *me'arvin ben l'daato ben shelo l'daato* — one may make the *eruv* whether or not the person is aware, since it is an unqualified benefit.

The Gemara thus assumes that our Mishnah, which requires informing new residents even when doing something beneficial for them, conflicts with Rabbi Yehuda's position. The Gemara does not entertain the possibility that the cases differ based on whose food is being used — it simply assumes that the question of notification applies equally in both scenarios. The Gemara notes: *peshita de-chalukin* — obviously they disagree! Our Mishnah requires notification; Rabbi Yehuda does not.

### Two-Alleyway Courtyard I…

But then the Gemara reconsiders. One might have thought that our Mishnah requiring notification applies only to the case of *chatzer she-bein shtei mavo'ot* — a courtyard situated between two alleyways, as discussed the previous day, where the courtyard has a choice of which alleyway to affiliate with. In such a case, joining alleyway A is not obviously to one's benefit over alleyway B, and the courtyard's participation may not even obstruct other courtyards. There, naturally, one would need the residents' buy-in. But *aval chatzer she-bemavoi echad* — if the courtyard has only one alleyway it can join, where the benefit is clear and non-participation would obstruct others, *eima lo* — perhaps even our Mishnah would agree that no notification is needed, or one could even compel participation. *Kama shma lan* — so the Gemara tells us that our Mishnah speaks even of the single-alleyway case, and still requires notification.

The conclusion of this passage is therefore that there is a genuine dispute between our Mishnah and Rabbi Yehuda: our Mishnah holds that even a courtyard with only one alleyway — where the benefit of participation is unambiguous and where non-participation creates a problem for others — nonetheless must have its residents informed. Rabbi Yehuda holds that no notification is required under these circumstances. And the Gemara, for its part, does not resolve the question of whose food is being used, making it genuinely difficult to understand why our Mishnah would require notification if one is using exclusively one's own food to benefit others.

---

## Shiur: Seudot vs. Groger…

### Large Number Threshold

The Mishnah concludes with the question of *kama shiuro* — what is the minimum quantity of food required for a valid *eruv*? The answer is: *shtei seudot* worth of food for the entire group when the group is large; but when the group is small, each person must contribute a quantity the size of a *grogeret* — a dried fig. One might ask: what constitutes a "large" number?

### Eighteen-Person Threshold

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *shmonah asar bnei adam* — eighteen people. The Gemara immediately asks: *shmonah asar v'tu lo* — only exactly eighteen, and no more? The clarification follows: the intent is *mishmonah asar v'eilach* — eighteen and above. Any group of eighteen or more is considered a "large number," and *shtei seudot* worth suffices for everyone.

### Grogeret to Seudot Calcu…

The Gemara then asks: why specifically eighteen? Rav Yitzchak the son of Rav Yehuda explained it in the name of his father: *kol she'ilu mechalko le'mazon shtei seudot beineihem ein magia k'grogeret le'chol echad v'echad* — if you were to divide two meals' worth of food among all the participants and each person would receive less than a *grogeret*, that is a large group and two meals' worth applies. The logic is that the required quantity is the lesser of the two standards: either a *grogeret* per person or *shtei seudot* for everyone. For seventeen people, each contributing a *grogeret* amounts to a total less than *shtei seudot*; therefore one still goes by a *grogeret* per person. But once there are eighteen people, eighteen *grogeros* exceeds the value of *shtei seudot*, so the *shtei seudot* figure becomes the operative standard. And in passing, the Gemara notes: *d'shtei seudot havyan shmonah asar grogerot* — two meals' worth of food equals eighteen dried fig portions in volume.

This is precisely why, practically speaking, a rabbi making an *eruv* for an entire city — whether ten thousand residents or more — can satisfy the requirement with a single box of *matzos*, since *shtei seudot* worth suffices for any number of participants.

---

## Types of Food for Eruv

### Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

The next Mishnah addresses what type of food may be used for an *eruv*. *Bechol me'arvin u'mishtatfin* — one may use any food for an *eruv* or *shituf*, *chutz min hamayim u'min hamelach* — with the exception of water and salt, which are not considered real foods in the relevant sense. This is the position of Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Yehoshua, however, says: *kikar hu eruv* — only a loaf of bread constitutes a valid *eruv*. Moreover, even the form matters: *afilu maafeh se'ah vehu prusa ein me'arvin bah* — even if one has a gigantic loaf, large enough to be the baking of an entire *se'ah* of flour, if it is not whole, one cannot use it. Conversely, *kikar ke'issar vehu shalem me'arvin bah* — if one has a tiny roll no larger than a small coin but it is whole and intact, one may use it.

Rashi explains that this means each individual participant must contribute a whole loaf, not that the combined *eruv* as a whole must consist of whole loaves. Rashi adds at the end of his commentary: one must still satisfy both conditions — each person's contribution must be in the form of a whole loaf, and the total quantity must reach at least a *grogeret* per person in volume. If there are a thousand participants, one would theoretically need a thousand tiny whole rolls. How this interacts with the rule of *shtei seudot* for large groups is left somewhat open by Rashi, though a reasonable reading is that once the group exceeds eighteen, two large loaves — or one whole loaf of sufficient size — suffice for everyone, while for smaller groups each individual must provide a whole loaf.

### Whole Loaf Definition

The operative principle emerging from Rabbi Yehoshua's position is not the distinction between bread and other foods per se, but rather the requirement of wholeness: *shalem* versus *prusa*. A loaf the size of a coin qualifies if it is whole; a loaf as large as a wedding bread does not qualify if it is broken.

### Whole vs. Broken Bread

This gives rise to the question: does the Tanna Kamma — the first, anonymous position in the Mishnah that permits all foods — also require that the bread be whole? Or is the debate between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehoshua purely about whether bread is required at all? The Gemara proceeds to examine this question in detail.

---

## Two-Place Enumeration

### Why State Twice?

The Gemara at the top of 81a notes: *tanina chada zimna* — we have already taught this rule! The formulation *bechol me'arvin u'mishtatfin, chutz min hamayim u'min hamelach* — that one may use any food except water and salt — appeared earlier in the *perek* called *bechol me'arvin*, which discussed *eruvei techumin*. Why is it being stated again here by *eruvei chatzerot*?

Rabba answers: *la'apukei mi-deRabbi Yehoshua d'amar kikar in midei achrinei lo* — to exclude the position of Rabbi Yehoshua, who says that only bread qualifies. By stating the rule twice, the Mishnah underscores that we do not rule like Rabbi Yehoshua — in both contexts. Rashi explains that one might have thought Rabbi Yehoshua voiced his bread requirement only in the context of *eruvei chatzerot*, and that by *eruv techumin* he would concede that any food is acceptable. By repeating the *bechol me'arvin* formulation in both places, the Mishnah implies that Rabbi Yehoshua in fact held his position in both cases, and that the Tanna Kamma is therefore responding to him in both contexts. Hence the need for the double statement.

### Girsa and Scope

Abaye then challenges this with a *braita*: *bechol me'arvin eruvei chatzerot uvechol mishtatfin shitufei mevo'ot, velo amru le'arev bepat ela bechatzer bilvad* — one may use any food for *eruvei chatzerot* and *shitufei mevo'ot*, and the requirement of bread applies only in the chatzer setting. This raises an immediate problem: first the *braita* says one may use anything, then it says bread is required — which is it?

Here the *girsa* becomes critical. Tosafot's version of the *braita* omits the phrase *eruvei chatzerot* from the opening clause. Without that phrase, the *braita* reads: one may use anything for an *eruv* — meaning *eruv techumin* — and anything for *shituf mevo'ot*, but when it comes to *eruvei chatzerot*, there one requires bread. Under this reading, the *braita* actually demonstrates that Rabbi Yehoshua agrees that for *eruv techumin* any food is acceptable; his bread requirement applies only to *eruvei chatzerot*.

### R. Yehoshua's Positions

With this reading, the implication is significant: the first *bechol me'arvin* stated in the earlier chapter about *eruvei techumin* was in fact *divrei hakol* — a position everyone, including Rabbi Yehoshua, agreed to. The debate between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehoshua only emerges in the context of *eruvei chatzerot*. Given this, the earlier *bechol me'arvin* statement was uncontested, and the question is: what does restating *bechol me'arvin* here accomplish? The Gemara's answer is that in this context the phrase does not mean all types of food — since by *eruvei chatzerot* even the Tanna Kamma may agree that bread is required — but rather all forms of bread: *la'apukei mi-deRabbi Yehoshua d'amar shleima in prusa lo kama shma lan bechol* — to exclude Rabbi Yehoshua's position that only a whole loaf qualifies and a broken piece does not. The word *bechol* here thus teaches that any form of the bread is acceptable, whole or broken, and not that any type of food is acceptable.

The conclusion is striking: by *eruv techumin* everyone agrees any food works; by *eruvei chatzerot* the Gemara seems to be converging on a reading where even the Tanna Kamma agrees it must be bread, and the debate between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehoshua is only about whether it must be a *whole* loaf. The Gemara then proceeds to take this question of wholeness as its central concern.

---

## Whole Loaf & Eivah

### Broken Loaves & Competit…

*U-frusa mai ta'ama lo* — why does Rabbi Yehoshua disqualify a broken loaf? Rabbi Yosi ben Shaul said in the name of Rabbi: *mishum eivah* — because of enmity or social rivalry. The concern is that if broken loaves were permitted, participants would begin comparing contributions: one person gives a whole loaf while another gives a partial loaf, and this gives rise to ill-feeling and competition. Just as there is a takkanah that on Tu B'Av all the young women should dress uniformly so as to eliminate the embarrassment of the less wealthy, so too by the *eruv* one requires a uniform standard — everyone gives a whole loaf — in order to prevent this sort of invidious comparison.

### Escalation Concern

### Deterioration of Practice

Rav Acha the son of Rava asked Rav Ashi: what if everyone agreed to give broken loaves? If the concern is only comparison between participants, and everyone brings the same broken piece, what objection remains? Rav Ashi responded: *shema yachzor davar le-kilkulo* — we fear that once one permits broken loaves even as a uniform practice, someone will then choose to demonstrate generosity by bringing a whole loaf, prompting others to respond in kind with even larger loaves, and the entire standardization unravels. Therefore, even a collective arrangement of broken loaves is disqualified, because it is inherently unstable and leads to the deterioration of the practice.

There is also a beautiful dimension here, beyond the legalistic concern about *eivah*. The Gemara earlier emphasized that the very name *eruv* — meaning mixture or joining — captures the essential idea of creating community. Bread itself symbolizes this: flour, water, and other ingredients come together into something unified. The whole loaf embodies the aspiration of the *eruv* — smaller contributions joining into a coherent whole — even if this is not the Gemara's explicit reasoning here.

---

## Defining Wholeness

### Challah & Dimua Amounts

Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of ben Shaul: *nitla heimena k'dei challah u-k'dei dimua me'arvin bah* — if from a loaf there was removed an amount equivalent to *challah* or an amount equivalent to *dimua*, one may still use it for the *eruv*. This addresses the question of how much material must be missing before a loaf is no longer considered whole. *Challah* refers to the portion of dough that must be separated and given to a *kohen* when baking above the minimum quantity. *Dimua* refers to a mixture in which forbidden material — such as *terumah* or *challah* — fell into a loaf, and one must then remove one one-hundredth of the mixture; that one one-hundredth is the *dimua* amount.

The question then arises from a *braita*: *k'dei dimua me'arvin bah k'dei challah ein me'arvin bah* — if the missing amount equals the *dimua* portion one may use the loaf, but if the missing amount equals the *challah* portion, one may not! This contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that both amounts are acceptable.

### Homeowner vs. Baker

The resolution is: *lo kashya ha be-challas nachtom ha be-challas ba'al habayit* — no difficulty; one case refers to a baker's *challah* and the other to a homeowner's *challah*, because the percentage differs between them. As the Mishnah teaches: a homeowner baking for private consumption — even if he bakes a hundred loaves for his son's wedding — separates one twenty-fourth as *challah*. A baker (*nachtom*) who bakes to sell in the marketplace, as well as a woman who bakes at home for sale, separates only one forty-eighth. The rationale for the baker's reduced percentage is either that it reflects a rough estimate of large-quantity production, or more compellingly, that the rabbis showed a measure of consideration for the baker's profit margin and did not demand as large a portion.

Accordingly, when a homeowner's *challah* is removed — one twenty-fourth of the loaf — that is a substantial portion, large enough to render the loaf no longer whole and therefore disqualified for use as an *eruv*. When a baker's *challah* is removed — one forty-eighth, a mere two percent — the loaf remains substantially intact and is still considered *shalem*.

Tosafot raises a further refinement: why does the passage speak of *k'dei challah* — "the amount of *challah*" — rather than simply saying *challah nitalah* — "the *challah* was taken"? This phrasing suggests that perhaps the ruling applies not only when the *challah* was formally separated, but even when a piece broke off accidentally, so long as the missing piece is equivalent in size to the *challah* portion. Tosafot ultimately does not favor this reading — preferring to limit the ruling to actual *challah* removal — but acknowledges that a straightforward reading of the Gemara could support the broader application, namely that even accidental breakage of a certain size disqualifies the loaf.

### Sewn Bread & Visibility

Rav Chisda rules: *tafra bekisam mearvin bo* — if a loaf broke in two and was then "sewn" back together with a splinter or toothpick, holding the halves in place, one may use it for the *eruv*. A *braita*, however, contradicts this: one may not use such a loaf. The resolution: *lo kashya ha d'yedia tafra ha d'lo yedia tafra* — if the repair is visibly apparent it is disqualified, but if the repair is concealed and the loaf appears whole, it is valid. Throughout this discussion, the Gemara operates under the assumption that we rule like Rabbi Yehoshua on the requirement of wholeness, and the entire analysis is aimed at defining what "whole" means for practical purposes.

---

## Grain Varieties for Eruv

### Rice vs. Millet Bread

Rav Zeira said in the name of Shmuel: *me'arvin be-pas orez* — one may use rice bread for an *eruv*. However, Mar Ukva adds a clarification received directly from Shmuel: *pas orez me'arvin pas dochen ein me'arvin* — rice bread is valid, but millet bread is not. The distinction is not about the halakhic category of *hamotzi*, since rice is well-known not to carry the obligation of *hamotzi* in the normative sense. The *chiddush* here is precisely that even food not classified as *lechem* for the purposes of *birkat ha'mazon* may qualify for *eruv* if it is sufficiently staple-like and satiating. The question is therefore one of relative edibility and adequacy as a food.

### Edibility Standard

The implicit principle is that what qualifies for *eruv* must be something a person would genuinely eat as sustenance. Rice, despite its halakhic status, is sufficiently edible and satiating to meet this standard. Millet, apparently, is not — it is less palatable and less nourishing in the relevant sense, and therefore does not qualify.

### Lentil Bread & Yechezkel

Rabbi Chiya bar Abin said in the name of Rav: *me'arvin be-pas adashin* — one may even use bread made from lentils for an *eruv*. The Gemara immediately challenges this. Was there not a person in the time of Shmuel who made such a lentil-bean bread and threw it to his dog to test its edibility, and even the dog would not eat it? If lentil bread is so unpalatable that a dog refuses it, how can it qualify for the *eruv*?

The Gemara responds: *hahi de-shar minim hava* — that was not pure lentil bread; it was a multi-grain mixture.
