# Eiruvin 83

## Mazon Shtei Seudot

### R. Yochanan: Half Kav

The daf opens with a deceptively simple question: how much bread constitutes *mazon shtei seudot*, the two meals' worth of food that determines the minimum size of an *eruv*? The answer requires close attention to the coin-based pricing system by which the Mishnah defines loaf size.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka's position is this: the relevant loaf is the kind that can be purchased for one *pundion* when four *se'in* of flour are going for one *sela* on the market. To unpack the arithmetic — one *se'ah* equals six *kav*, so four *se'in* equal twenty-four *kav*. A *sela* contains forty-eight *pundion*. Therefore, for every two *pundion* spent, one *kav* of bread is obtained. A single *pundion* thus buys half a *kav*. According to Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, a half *kav* is the size of the loaf — and since the Mishnah is discussing two meals' worth, each *seuda* in his view is a quarter of a *kav*.

### R. Shimon: One-Third Kav

Rabbi Shimon's position, stated as *shtei yodot l'kikar mi-shalosh l'kav*, holds that a *kav* yields three loaves, so a single loaf is one-third of a *kav*. However, Rabbi Shimon specifies that *shtei yodot* — two-thirds — of that loaf constitutes the *eruv* measure. Two-thirds of one-third is two-ninths of a *kav*, and since this represents two *seudot*, a single *seuda* in his system equals one-ninth of a *kav*.

### Four vs. Nine Meals

The *Gemara* then cites a *Tannaitic* source stating *ukrovin divreihem l'hiyot shavin* — that their positions are approximately equal. The *Gemara* immediately objects: *mi dami*? How can this be? According to Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, a half *kav* equals two *seudot*, so there are four *seudot* per *kav*. According to Rabbi Shimon, two-ninths of a *kav* equals two *seudot*, so there are nine *seudot* per *kav*. The gap between four and nine is not trivially close, and the *Gemara* presses on how the *Braita* could claim otherwise.

### Baker's Profit Margin

Rav Chisda resolves the difficulty by introducing the profit margin of the *chanvani*, the baker or retailer. The prices cited in the Mishnah reflect the wholesale cost of flour. A baker, however, does not sell at wholesale rates; he marks up the price. Rav Chisda's first formulation holds that the *chanvani* takes a one-third profit margin — meaning that for the same *pundion*, he sells only two-thirds of what the wholesale price would suggest. Applying this to Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka: the nominal amount was a half *kav*, but the actual bread sold for a *pundion* is two-thirds of a half, which is one-third of a *kav*. One-third of a *kav* for two *seudot* means one *seuda* equals one-sixth of a *kav*, yielding six *seudot* per *kav*. Yet Rabbi Shimon still gives nine — so six and nine remain far apart.

The *Gemara* therefore invokes a second teaching of Rav Chisda: *tfei mehen palga l'chanvani*, the baker actually charges a fifty-percent markup. At a fifty-percent margin, the baker sells only half of the wholesale quantity for the same price. Half of a half *kav* is a quarter of a *kav* for two *seudot*, making one *seuda* one-eighth of a *kav*, or eight *seudot* per *kav*. Now eight and nine are genuinely close — and this, the *Gemara* explains, is what the *Braita* means when it says their positions are approximately equal.

The *Gemara* then asks: is there a contradiction between Rav Chisda's two statements — one-third markup versus fifty-percent markup? The resolution is that it depends on who supplies the wood for baking. If the homeowner provides the firewood, the baker's labor alone is compensated, and a one-third margin suffices. If the baker must supply the wood himself, his costs are higher and he charges a fifty-percent margin. In both cases, the Mishnah's stated price reflects the wholesale flour cost, not the retail bread price, and accounting for the baker's margin is essential to understanding how much bread actually changes hands.

---

## Pras & Tumat Ochlim

### Loaf to Eggs Conversion

Having established the size of two *seudot* in terms of *kav*, the *Gemara* now translates these quantities into *beitzim* — eggs — the standard sub-unit of volume measurement. A *kav* contains twenty-four *beitzim*. According to Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, the loaf (representing two *seudot*) is a quarter of a *kav*, so one *seuda* — the *pras* — is one-eighth of a *kav*, which equals three *beitzim*. According to Rabbi Shimon, the loaf is one-third of a *kav* (the two-thirds measure being specific to the *eruv* context), so one *seuda* is one-sixth of a *kav*, which equals four *beitzim*.

One important clarification belongs here: Rabbi Shimon's *shtei yodot* — the two-thirds reduction — was applied only in the context of *eruv*. For all other halachic purposes, including the measurements that follow, the full loaf size is used. So the operative debate is whether the loaf itself is a quarter of a *kav* (Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka) or a third of a *kav* (Rabbi Shimon), and correspondingly whether a *pras* — half a loaf, one *seuda* — is three or four *beitzim*.

### Pras Measurement

The *Gemara* now extends this framework to several other halachic domains. The text reads: *chetzi l'veit hamenuga, v'chatzi chetziyah lifsol et hageviyah*. Half of the loaf — one *seuda*, the *pras* — is the relevant measure for the *beit hamenuga*, the house afflicted with *tzara'at*: the time it takes to eat a *pras* determines how long one must remain inside before becoming *tamei*. This is the *kedai achilat pras* measure that appears across many areas of halachah.

Half again — half of the *pras* — is the measure for *pissul hageviyah*, rendering oneself invalid through eating forbidden food. This would be one-and-a-half or two *beitzim* depending on the position. And half of that — one-quarter of a *pras* — is the threshold for *tumat ochlin*, food impurity.

The *Gemara* at the top of 83a then introduces one further subdivision: *v'chatzi chatzi chetziyah l'tamei tumat ochlin* — a half of the half of the half is the measure for rendering food susceptible to or transmitting *tumah*. Working through the arithmetic, this yields either three-quarters of a *beitza* (following Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka's three-*beitzim pras*) or one full *beitza* (following Rabbi Shimon's four-*beitzim pras*). The standard ruling of one *beitza* for *tumat ochlin* aligns with Rabbi Shimon's position.

The practical halachic stakes of this three-versus-four debate are significant. If one rules that *tumat ochlin* is one *beitza*, then by working backward, *kedai achilat pras* is four *beitzim* — Rabbi Shimon's position. Rashi understands two *zeitim* per *beitza*, making *kedai achilat pras* eight *kezayitim*. Rambam, however, in at least one formulation, rules by Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka's three-*beitzim* measure, yet holds three *zeitim* per *beitza*, yielding nine *kezayitim*. The practical question of how quickly one must eat *matzah* on Pesach, or how much constitutes a halachically significant eating, turns on this unresolved debate between eight and nine *kezayitim*.

### Precision Argument

Having laid out the full chain of subdivisions, the *Gemara* raises a pointed question: *u'tana didan mai ta'ama lo tana tumat ochlin*? Why did our *Tanna* stop before reaching *tumat ochlin*? If the subdivisions are this neat, why not carry them all the way through?

The answer is *mishum d'lo shavu shiuraya l'hadadi* — because the sizes do not precisely match up with one another. A *Braita* then demonstrates the imprecision: *bei beitzim chasar kima divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — Rabbi Yehuda says the relevant measure is two *beitzim* minus a little. The loaf size was never defined with the precision of a fixed number of eggs; it was defined by how much bread people actually eat, which is inherently approximate. The *tumat ochlin* measure, by contrast, is exact — it is defined as precisely one *beitza* (or three-quarters, depending on position), and is not derived from these meal-based calculations. Mixing an imprecise chain of subdivisions with a precise benchmark would be misleading, and that is why the *Mishnah* did not include *tumat ochlin* in this sequence.

### Egg with/without Shell

The *Gemara* proceeds to lay out the range of positions regarding the size of this *chatzi pras*. Rabbi Yehuda says two *beitzim* minus a little; Rabbi Yossi says *bei beitzim sochakos* — two *beitzim* measured loosely, a slightly larger amount. Rabbi, Judah the Prince, estimated by physically measuring a *se'ah* and working downward; he came out with *bei beitzim v'od*, two *beitzim* and a little extra, which the *Gemara* specifies as one-twentieth of a *beitza*. So where Rabbi Yehuda gives roughly 1.98 and Rabbi Yossi gives roughly 2.1, Rabbi gives 2.05. The root of this imprecision is that a *kav* — twenty-four *beitzim* — is not an exactly precise number of eggs when one actually measures out the volume.

A separate dispute recorded in a *Braita* and cited by Rabbah bar Papa in the name of Rav Chisda addresses a related question: when the Sages said *kebeitza* for *tumat ochlin*, did they mean an egg including its shell or without? Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Dosa say with the shell; the Sages say without. This is a dispute about a precise measurement, not a derived one — which is precisely the *Gemara*'s point. *Tumat ochlin* is defined by the egg itself, exactly, while all the meal-based measures are approximations.

The *Gemara* then notes that in Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka's system, the *chatzi pras* comes out to one-and-a-half *beitzim sochakos* — also slightly larger than a bare number — and this too is slightly imprecise in the same direction as Rabbi's formulation.

---

## Se'ah Measurement

### 217 Eggs Puzzle

The *Gemara* reports that when Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he transmitted an account: Bunios sent Rabbi a *se'ah* measure from the town of Ni'usa, and Rabbi estimated that it held 217 eggs. This figure demands explanation, because the straightforward calculation gives a very different result. One *se'ah* equals six *kav*, and one *kav* equals twenty-four *beitzim*, so six times twenty-four yields 144 eggs. How does one arrive at 217?

### Three Se'ah Types

The *Gemara* resolves the starting confusion by asking *ha se'ah deheicha* — which *se'ah* are we talking about? Three distinct measures went by the name *se'ah* in different eras and locales: the *se'ah midbarit* (the Wilderness measure from the Torah's time), the *se'ah Yerushalmit* (the Jerusalem measure from the period of the kings), and the *se'ah Tziporit* (the measure used in the Rabbinic period, associated with Tzippori). Each successive measure was larger than the previous one.

The *se'ah midbarit*, with the simple calculation of six *kav* at twenty-four *beitzim* each, yields 144 eggs. The *se'ah Yerushalmit* is one-sixth larger — that is, twenty percent larger — than the *midbarit*, so it contains 144 plus approximately 28.8, which rounds to 173 eggs. The *se'ah Tziporit* is in turn one-sixth larger than the *Yerushalmit*, another twenty percent increase, bringing it to approximately 207.6 eggs, which the *Gemara* rounds to 207. Even so, 207 is not 217. The *Gemara* is aware of this gap.

### Math Reconciliation

The *Gemara* offers two additional factors that, combined, account for the remaining difference. First, *aiti chalta shadi aleihu* — add the *challah* portion. When baking bread from this quantity of flour, one must separate *challah*, which is one twenty-fourth of the dough. Adding one twenty-fourth of 207 gives approximately 8 more, bringing the total to roughly 215. This is still short of 217.

The second adjustment draws on Rabbi's own teaching that the *beitza* as a sub-unit is not perfectly divisible into larger measures — every *beitza* in this system is actually a *beitza* plus one-twentieth. That is, the *se'ah Tziporit* measured in terms of real eggs contains not 207 eggs but 207 eggs each of which is one-twentieth larger than a nominal *beitza*. One-twentieth of 207 is approximately 10, and adding this to 207 yields approximately 217. The *Gemara* notes that the result is slightly more than 217, but since the remainder is less than a full *beitza*, it is not counted, and 217 is the rounded figure.

### Growth Ratios

A *Braita* addresses the growth relationships among the three *se'ah* types directly: the *se'ah Yerushalmit* exceeds the *midbarit* by one-sixth (*shtos*), and the *se'ah Tziporit* exceeds the *Yerushalmit* by a further one-sixth. The *Braita* then states that the *Tziporit* therefore exceeds the *midbarit* by a full third — *shelish*.

The *Gemara* subjects this claim to careful scrutiny. *Shelish de'man* — a third of which measure? If a third of the *midbarit* (144), that gives a difference of 48. But the actual difference between the *Tziporit* (207) and the *midbarit* (144) is 63, not 48. If a third of the *Yerushalmit* (173), that is approximately 57 and a fraction — still not 63. If a third of the *Tziporit* itself (207), that is approximately 69 — too large. No interpretation of the *Braita*'s "third" produces the actual difference of 63.

Rav Yirmiah proposes a qualified reading: the *Braita* should be understood as saying the *Tziporit* exceeds the *midbarit* by *approximately* a third of its own size — *karov l'shelish*. A third of the *Tziporit* (approximately 69) is indeed in the vicinity of the actual difference. He further notes that this one-third of the *Tziporit* is itself *karov l'machtza d'midbarit* — approximately half of the *midbarit* measure. Ravina objects to the word *karov* being read into a *Braita* that does not contain it. He therefore offers a different resolution: taking a third of the *se'ah Tziporit* as corrected by Rabbi's *v'od* adjustment — a third of 217 — yields approximately 72, which is very close to half the *midbarit*'s 144. This is the *Gemara*'s best reconciliation of the *Braita*, though it requires incorporating Rabbi's fractional correction to make the numbers work.

---

## Challah & Meal Size

### Omer Conversion

The *Gemara* now turns to a *Braita* with direct practical implications for the *mitzvah* of *challah*. The verse says *reshit arisoteichem* — the first of your kneading — and the *Braita* asks: how large a quantity of dough is subject to the obligation of *challah d'orayta*? The answer is *kedei isat midbar*, the size of the dough prepared in the wilderness — meaning the amount of the *omer*.

The *omer* is defined by the Torah as one-tenth of an *ephah*, and an *ephah* is three *se'in*. So the *omer* equals three-tenths of a *se'ah midbarit*. Since the *se'ah midbarit* equals 144 *beitzim*, three-tenths of 144 yields 43.2 *beitzim*. This is the minimum quantity of dough that obligates one in *challah* according to Torah law — forty-three and one-fifth *beitzim*, a figure familiar to anyone who has looked into the practical laws of *challah* separation.

### Measure Conversion

The *Braita* then expresses this same threshold in the larger measures of *kav*: *zayin reva'im kemach v'od chayevet b'challah* — seven quarter-*kav* portions of flour plus a little obligates in *challah*. A *reva* is one-quarter of a *kav*, and one *kav* equals twenty-four *beitzim*, so one *reva* is six *beitzim*. Seven *reva'im* is therefore forty-two *beitzim*, and the "little" extra accounts for the remaining 1.2, bringing the total to 43.2.

The *Braita* adds: *shehen vav shel Yerushalmiyot, shehen hey shel Tziporiyot* — this quantity is equivalent to six *reva'im* in the *Yerushalmit* measure and five *reva'im* in the *Tziporit* measure. The conversion is consistent: since the *Yerushalmit se'ah* is one-fifth larger than the *midbarit* in effective ratio, seven-and-change *reva'im midbariyim* convert cleanly to six *reva'im Yerushalmiyim*, and those in turn to five *reva'im Tziporiyim*.

### Health Blessing

The *Braita* closes with a remarkable statement about the significance of this 43.2-*beitzim* measure beyond its legal context. *Ha-ochel k'middah zo harei zeh bari u'mvorach* — one who eats this amount is healthy and blessed. *Yaser kahn ra'avtan* — one who eats more is considered ravenous. *Pachos mikan mekukul b'mayav* — one who eats less will have digestive troubles.

Whether this refers literally to eating 43.2 *beitzim* worth of bread in a single meal or rather to consuming an amount proportional to one's *seuda* measure — the precise interpretation is not entirely clear. What the *Gemara* is expressing is the idea that there is a perfect, divinely calibrated quantity of bread for a meal, and that both excess and deficiency depart from that ideal.

---

## Courtyard vs. Balcony

### Physical Setup

The *Gemara* now pivots to the new *Mishna*, which introduces a scenario familiar in structure but novel in geometry: *anshei chatzer v'anshei mirpeset* — the residents of a courtyard and the residents of a balcony. The physical arrangement envisions a ground-level courtyard with residents below, a *mirpeset* — a balcony — above, and access between the balcony and the courtyard by means of a ladder. Each group made its own *eruv* but they did not establish a joint *eruv* together. The question that follows is which group has rights to the intermediate spaces — mounds, rocks, or structures — that occupy the space between the two levels.

### Ten-Tefachim Rule

The *Mishna* states: *kol shegavoha asarah tefachim l'mirpeset, pachos mikan l'chatzer* — anything ten *tefachim* or more in height belongs to the balcony; anything less than ten *tefachim* belongs to the courtyard. The same rule applies to a well-surround (*chuliyat habor*) or a rock (*sela*): if ten *tefachim* high, it is associated with the *mirpeset*; if less, with the *chatzer*.

The logic is that in halachic spatial reasoning, ten *tefachim* marks the boundary between what is part of the ground domain and what is elevated above it. Once a structure reaches ten *tefachim*, it is no longer considered part of the ground-level domain and is instead treated as belonging to the elevated domain of the balcony. This may seem counterintuitive — a mound of three feet in height would seem perfectly accessible from below — but the halachic threshold is fixed at ten *tefachim* regardless.

### Proximity Requirement

The *Mishna* adds an important qualification: *bameh devarim amurim bismucha* — this rule applies only when the mound is close to the balcony. The *Gemara* specifies how close: *kol she'eina rechoka arba'a tefachim* — it must be within four *tefachim*, approximately one foot. If the mound is further than four *tefachim* from the balcony, it cannot be associated with the balcony's domain regardless of its height, and it reverts to the *chatzer*. The combination of height (ten *tefachim* or more) and proximity (within four *tefachim*) must both be satisfied for the mound to belong to the *mirpeset*.

---

## Equal vs. Unequal Access

### Equal Easy Access

The *Gemara* now abstracts the underlying principles by working through a series of cases. *L'zeh b'petach ul'zeh b'petach* — if one courtyard has easy access to an intermediate space and the other also has equally easy access — *hainu chalon shebein shtei chatzerot*, this is analogous to the well-known case of a window between two courtyards. In that case, neither courtyard can use the space for its own purposes, because each is an equal competitor. Both parties are forbidden from transferring objects through that space into their own domain.

### Equal Hard Access

The same logic governs equally difficult access. *L'zeh b'zirika ul'zeh b'zirika* — if both courtyards can only reach the space by throwing — *hainu kotel shebein shtei chatzerot*, this is the case of a wall between two courtyards that is equally hard to access from both sides, ten *tefachim* or more for both. Again, equal difficulty means equal competition, and neither side may use the space. *L'zeh b'shilshul ul'zeh b'shilshul* — if both must stoop down, as in a trench — *hainu charitz shebein shtei chatzerot*, this is the case of a ditch between two courtyards, and the same conclusion applies. Equality in either direction — equally easy or equally hard — yields mutual prohibition.

### Unequal Access

When access is unequal, the result changes. *L'zeh b'petach ul'zeh b'zirika* — easy access for one, access only by throwing for the other — *hainu d'Rabbah bar Rav Huna amar Rav Nachman*, this is the ruling of Rabbah bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav Nachman about a wall that is less than ten *tefachim* on one side and more than ten on the other. The space goes to the one for whom access is easy. Similarly, *l'zeh b'petach ul'zeh b'shilshul* — easy access for one, stooping required for the other — *hainu d'Rav Shizbi amar Rav Nachman*, the case of a ditch that is less than ten deep on one side and ten or more on the other. Again, the space goes to the side for which it is more accessible.

### Shmuel vs. Rav

The genuinely novel case is *l'zeh b'shilshul ul'zeh b'zirika* — one side can access the space by stooping down into it, the other only by throwing up to it. Both are forms of difficult access, but they are different in kind. Is one more connected to the space than the other?

Rav rules *shneihem asurin* — both are forbidden, because the access is equally difficult in both directions. Shmuel rules *nosnim oso l'zeh sheb'shilshul* — we assign it to the one who must stoop down, reasoning that *tashmisho b'nachas* — access by lowering oneself is easier — while access by throwing is harder: *tashmisho b'kasha*. The general principle Shmuel derives is: whenever it is easy for one and hard for the other, we give the space to the one for whom it is easier.

### Application to Case

The *Gemara* now applies this dispute to our *Mishna*. The ruling that a mound of ten *tefachim* belongs to the *mirpeset* — rather than to neither party — would seem to support Shmuel. The mound is more than ten *tefachim* up from the courtyard level (so the courtyard residents must throw to reach it — *zirika*), while for the balcony residents it is below their level (they must lower something to reach it — *shilshul*). Giving it to the *mirpeset* is consistent with Shmuel's principle that *shilshul* beats *zirika*.

Rav, however, is not contradicted by this *Mishna*. Rav Huna clarifies: *le'osam hadarim b'mirpeset* — the *Mishna* is speaking of the people who actually live on the balcony itself, not the residents of an upper story. For the balcony residents, the mound may actually be within less than ten *tefachim* of their floor level — within easy reach. In that case, the mound is simply less than ten *tefachim* away from them and more than ten away from the courtyard below, which is the ordinary case of unequal access that both Rav and Shmuel agree goes to the more accessible party. Rav's position — that when both sides face equally difficult access the space belongs to neither — remains intact. The *Mishna* does not force a contradiction, because the *Mishna*'s case is one of genuinely unequal access, not the ambiguous *shilshul-versus-zirika* scenario that divides Rav and Shmuel.

---

---

# Eiruvin 84

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Framework

The entirety of Eruvin 84a is devoted to working out the debate between Rav and Shmuel, which had been introduced in the preceding daf. The underlying question concerns competing access to a shared space by two different domains. The Gemara had established three basic configurations. First, when both parties have equally easy access — *lazeh bapetach u'lazeh bapetach* — the object or space in question is considered jointly relevant to both domains, and without an *eruv*, neither party may use it. Second, when both parties have equally difficult access — whether *lazeh bizrika u'lazeh bizrika* (both must throw upward) or *lazeh beshilshul u'lazeh beshilshul* (both must lower downward), also expressed as *lazeh bekasha u'lazeh bekasha* — the same principle applies: equal difficulty means equal status, and the space remains forbidden to both. Third, when access is easy for one party and difficult for the other, the space is attributed to the party with easy access.

### Shmuel's Preference

The debate between Rav and Shmuel concerns a fourth configuration: what happens when both parties have difficult access, but the difficulty is of different kinds? Specifically, when one party's access requires *zrika* (throwing upward) and the other's requires *shilshul* (lowering downward). Shmuel holds that *shilshul* — lowering something down, or bending down into a depression — represents easier access than *zrika*. Accordingly, when access to a shared space is difficult in both directions, but one direction is downward and the other is upward, Shmuel attributes the space to the party for whom the approach is downward. It should be noted that while the height under discussion is ten *tefachim* — a perfectly manageable vertical distance when approached from above — Shmuel's reasoning turns on the comparative ease of the downward direction rather than on any absolute measure.

### Rav's Equal Status

Rav disagrees. In his view, when both parties face difficult access — regardless of whether one goes up and the other goes down — they are considered equally situated with respect to the space. Neither side has a dispositive advantage, and the space is therefore forbidden to both, just as in the case of equally easy access. The remainder of the daf consists of the Gemara's sustained effort to resolve the tension between this dispute and various cases in the *Mishnah*, testing whether those cases support Rav or Shmuel.

## Mound Case Analysis

### Initial Question

The Gemara opens with a challenge from the *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* describes a mound (*tel*) situated in a courtyard (*chatzer*), with a *mirpeset* — a balcony or elevated porch — positioned above. The *Mishnah* rules that if the mound is ten *tefachim* or higher, it belongs to the people of the *mirpeset*; if it is less than ten, it belongs to the *chatzer*. The Gemara asks: does this not constitute a case of competing difficult access — the *chatzer* residents must climb up to reach the top of the mound, while the *mirpeset* residents must descend — and yet the *Mishnah* assigns the mound to those above? Does this not vindicate Shmuel, who gives preference to the party whose access is downward (*shilshul*)?

### Rav's Answer

Rav's response reframes the scenario entirely. The *Mishnah*, Rav explains, is not describing the situation of people living one full story above in an *aliyah* (upper story), for whom the descent to the mound would be considerable. Rather, we are speaking of people who live on the *mirpeset* itself. For them, the mound is within ten *tefachim* of their position — perhaps only nine *tefachim* away. That proximity constitutes easy access. The mound is therefore attributed to the *mirpeset* residents not because of a preference for downward access, but because for them the access is formally easy, falling within the ten-*tefach* threshold. This reading eliminates any proof for Shmuel from the *Mishnah*.

### Seifa Resolution

The Gemara immediately presses on: if Rav's reading is correct, consider the *seifa* — the concluding clause of the *Mishnah*, which states that if the mound is less than ten *tefachim*, it belongs to the *chatzer*. The Gemara asks: *amai* — why? If the *mirpeset* residents are close to the mound and enjoy easy access, and if the mound is now lower than ten, then the *chatzer* residents also enjoy easy access. This creates a case of equally easy access for both parties, in which case both should be forbidden the use of the mound — not just granted to the *chatzer*. The Gemara resolves this by reading the *Mishnah*'s phrase *lachatzer* not as "exclusively to the *chatzer*" but as *af lachatzer* — "even to the *chatzer*." When the mound is lower than ten, it falls within easy access of the *mirpeset* residents (for whom it was always accessible) and now also of the *chatzer* residents. Both parties have easy access, and therefore neither may use it without an *eruv*: *ushnayhem asurim*.

The Gemara adds that this reading is linguistically supported by the *seifa* of the *Mishnah*'s later clause concerning the *mupleget* case, where the same logic of *af lachatzer* applies. This parallel confirms Rav's interpretive approach.

### Mupleget Distance

A further distinction arises from the *Mishnah*'s teaching that when the mound is *mupleget* — set at a distance of more than four *tefachim* from the *mirpeset* — even if the mound is ten *tefachim* high, it belongs to the *chatzer*. The Gemara raises the obvious difficulty: if the mound is very high, it is difficult for the *chatzer* residents to climb it, and if it is far from the *mirpeset*, it is also difficult for the *mirpeset* residents to reach it. Why should the mere fact of distance beyond four *tefachim* automatically consign the mound to the *chatzer*, even when it stands, say, a hundred *amot* high? In such a case, the access seems equally difficult for both parties, and Rav would say they are equal — and therefore both should be forbidden.

The Gemara addresses this by once again applying the reading *af lachatzer*: when the *Mishnah* says the mound belongs to the *chatzer* in the *mupleget* case, it means it belongs *even* to the *chatzer* — i.e., since the *mirpeset* residents can no longer be said to have easy access (they must traverse a gap exceeding four *tefachim* and then climb), and the *chatzer* residents are always within reach of the base, the mound is equally difficult for both, and therefore *asur* to both. The *Mishnah*'s language is consistently read through this lens: attribution to the *chatzer* signals a state of mutual forbiddenness, not exclusive ownership.

## Well Case

### Well Introduction

The Gemara now turns to the *Mishnah*'s next clause: *chulyat habor v'hasela* — the mound of earth surrounding a well (*bor*) and a bare rock (*sela*). The *Mishnah* applies the same basic rule: if these are ten *tefachim* or higher, they belong to the *mirpeset*; if less, to the *chatzer*. The case of the simple *sela* (rock) poses no new difficulty — it follows the same logic as the mound case already analyzed. But the well introduces a genuine complication.

### Gemara Dilemma

Pictured concretely: there is a well sunk into the ground, surrounded by a raised earthen wall (the *chulyah*). The *chatzer* residents on the ground floor wish not only to stand on top of the mound around the well, but more practically to draw water from the well's depth. For the *mirpeset* residents, reaching the water requires only a downward motion — lowering a bucket. For the *chatzer* residents, reaching the water requires going *up* over the mound and then *down* into the well: both *zrika* and *shilshul* combined. Shmuel has no difficulty here: he always prefers the party whose access is purely downward, so the well belongs to the *mirpeset* residents. But for Rav, the question is acute. Rav's entire justification for assigning the mound to the *mirpeset* in the earlier case was that the top of the mound was within ten *tefachim* of the *mirpeset* residents — that is, it was easy access for them. But the relevant access here is to the water at the bottom of the well, which lies more than ten *tefachim* below the *mirpeset* and more than ten *tefachim* below the *chatzer*. By Rav's logic, access is equally difficult for both, and the well should be *asur* to both — a difficult conclusion when one party may have constructed and relies upon the well.

### Rav Huna's Answer

Before the Gemara reaches its resolution, Rav Huna clarifies a preliminary point that parallels the mound discussion. When the *Mishnah* says the mound or well belongs to the *mirpeset*, it does not mean the people of the *aliyah* — residents of a full upper story, who would be far above. Rather, *mirpeset* refers specifically to those who live on the balcony level itself, for whom the distance to the top of the surrounding mound remains within ten *tefachim*.

### Filled Well

Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda proposes the first resolution: the case in the *Mishnah* concerns a well filled with water — *bor melei'ah mayim*. If the well is completely full to the brim, then reaching the water does not require descending more than ten *tefachim*; the water's surface is effectively at the top of the mound, within easy reach. This restores the scenario to one of straightforward proximity. The Gemara objects: *v'ha chasra* — once people begin drawing the water, the level will drop, and what was once within ten will soon be more than ten below the *mirpeset*. The Gemara replies: *keivan d'ki malya shari, ki chasra nami shari* — since when it is full it is permitted, even when it is not quite full it remains permitted. But the Gemara immediately inverts the reasoning: *aderaba*, one should argue the opposite — *keivan d'ki chasra asira, ki malya nami asira* — since when it is depleted it is problematic, even when it is full it should be treated as problematic from the outset. This objection is not easily dismissed and stands against the water-filled resolution.

### Fruit-Filled Well

Abaye offers an alternative: *hacha b'vor melei'ah peiros askinan* — the case concerns a well filled with fruit. Solid fruit filling the well to the top converts what is functionally a hole in the ground into what is effectively a mound: there is no depth to descend into, and access is simply to the flat top surface, identical in character to the *sela* case. The Gemara again raises the same *v'ha chasri* objection — the fruit will eventually be removed, and access will again require descending. Abaye's answer: *b'tivla* — the fruit is *tevel*, untithed produce that is forbidden for consumption on Shabbat. Since the fruit cannot be eaten or removed on Shabbat, it remains in place indefinitely, and the well functions exactly as a mound for these purposes.

The Gemara notes *deika nami* — this reading is also supported by the *Mishnah*'s phrasing, which presents the well case in parallel with the *sela*, suggesting a structural similarity. On the surface this parallel actually seems more naturally to favor Shmuel's reading — that both the rock and the well simply go to the *mirpeset* because access is downward. But for Rav, the necessity of presenting both cases is explained as follows: had the *Mishnah* mentioned only the *sela*, one might have thought that a well could never go to the *mirpeset* because one might decree against permitting it — fearing that the well might be filled with proper, permitted fruit (*peiros metukanim*) that residents would remove, thereby eventually lowering the accessible surface below ten *tefachim*. The separate mention of the well teaches that when it is in fact filled with *tevel*, there is no such concern and it is treated exactly like the rock.

## Airspace Division

### Airspace Setup

The Gemara now introduces a new category of proof. The case concerns residents of a *chatzer* and residents of an *aliyah* — a full upper story — who forgot to make an *eruv* together. Despite the absence of an *eruv*, the Gemara maintains that the *chatzer* residents may use the lower ten *tefachim* of the shared airspace, and the *aliyah* residents may use the upper ten *tefachim*. The question the Gemara raises is a practical one: the relevant space is entirely air — how can one "use" airspace in a way that renders these formal divisions operative?

### Ziz Protrusion

The Gemara explains by reference to a *ziz* — a protrusion or ledge extending from the shared wall between the two domains. If a *ziz* protrudes from the wall within the lower ten *tefachim* (measured from the ground), it falls within easy access of the *chatzer* residents and belongs to them. If it protrudes above ten *tefachim*, it lies within easy access of the *aliyah* residents and belongs to them. Any protrusion in the middle space — between the lower ten and the upper ten — is *asur* to both. This middle-space ruling is presented as direct proof for Rav: when access is equally difficult for both parties (neither within their respective ten-*tefach* easy-access zone), the Gemara does not give preference to the party who must descend. It simply forbids both, exactly as Rav would predict.

### Rav Nachman's Wall

The Gemara, sensitive to the obvious implication of the proof — that there appears to be a "middle" zone inaccessible to either party — introduces Rav Nachman's clarification. He states: *hacha b'kotel tish'asar askinan* — the case concerns a wall that is exactly nineteen *tefachim* high. With such a wall, there is no middle space between the lower ten and the upper nine. Any point on the wall is either within the lower ten (easy access for the *chatzer*, difficult for the *aliyah*) or within the upper nine (easy access for the *aliyah*, difficult for the *chatzer*). The *ziz* at any given point therefore always sits squarely in one domain's easy-access zone and the other domain's difficult-access zone, cleanly assigning it to one party rather than creating a contested middle ground. The division is exhaustive: below ten belongs to the *chatzer*; above ten — which in a nineteen-*tefach* wall means within nine *tefachim* of the top — belongs to the *aliyah*. There is no gap.

## Two Gazuztraot

### Gazuztraot Intro

The Gemara continues with another *ta shema* — come and hear — and introduces the case of two *gazuztraot* (ledges or protrusions) extending from different apartments over a body of water. The scenario is that two households, living at different heights, both have ledges projecting outward over the sea or a river. Each household might wish to use the water below — either to draw water or to dispose of waste — and the question is whether the vertical and horizontal configuration of the two ledges creates a situation of competing access, analogous to the *chatzer*-and-*mirpeset* cases discussed throughout the daf.

### Ledges & Partition

The *Mishnah* rules that if a *mechitza* (partition) was made for the upper ledge (*elyonah*) but not for the lower ledge (*tachtonah*), both are *asur* until they make an *eruv* together. This at first appears puzzling: the upper ledge has its partition and is technically set up for proper use; why should the lower ledge's failure to have a partition disable both? The answer lies in the principle of competing access. Even though the upper household has done everything structurally necessary to use the water, the lower ledge is considered to be within the access range of both parties — and since they have not made an *eruv* with one another, the shared access of the lower household disqualifies the upper household's use as well.

### Rava bar Avin

Rava bar Avin addresses a subtlety in the case. He explains: *bevo'im bnei tachtonah derech elyonah lemalaot* — the case is specifically one in which the residents of the lower ledge actually walk up through the upper ledge's space in order to draw water. This is not merely a theoretical claim of access; the lower residents are in practice passing through the upper residents' area to reach the water. This practical overlap of access, Rava bar Avin explains, is what renders both ledges mutually forbidden.

### Abaye's Formal Rules

Abaye offers a different reading that cuts to the heart of the formal-versus-practical debate. He says: *kigon d'kaiman betoch asara dehadadi* — the case concerns two ledges that are within ten *tefachim* of each other. The formal distance between the two ledges is less than ten *tefachim*, and that single fact establishes that they are in each other's domain of easy access. There is no need to invoke actual foot-traffic between the ledges.

Abaye then presents the teaching as a *lo mibaya* — a fortiori — construction. It goes without saying (*lo mibaya*) that if the lower ledge had its partition and not the upper, both would be forbidden, because the access is identical in direction for both parties: both must lower (*shilshul*), and they are within ten of each other. That is the obvious case of equal access. The novel ruling — *afilu asu le'elyona velo asu letachtona* — is that even when the partition was made for the upper ledge and not the lower, both remain forbidden. One might have thought to say that in practice, the lower residents must travel upward slightly to reach the water — they must cross the gap of the ledge heights and then lower — while the upper residents lower directly. This practical advantage ought to favor the upper residents, assigning the water to them exclusively. Abaye teaches that this practical consideration is entirely overridden by the formal rule: *keivan d'begov asara kaiman, asrin ahadadi* — since they are formally within ten *tefachim* of each other, both are treated identically, and neither may use the water without an *eruv*. Whether in practice one party has a somewhat easier approach than the other is irrelevant; formal proximity within ten *tefachim* places both in the same legal category.

This ruling is, as the Gemara implies, a genuinely significant *chidush*. It crystallizes a principle that has been operating implicitly throughout the entire daf: the Gemara does not evaluate access on a case-by-case practical basis. It defines "easy" and "difficult" by reference to a single formal threshold — ten *tefachim* — and applies that threshold uniformly. If two parties are both within ten *tefachim* of a space, they are considered to have equal access, full stop, regardless of whether one's path is in fact more physically demanding than the other's.

## Roof Case

### Roof Scenario

The Gemara now cites a ruling of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel that further illustrates this principle. The case is *gag hasamuch l'reshut harabim* — a roof situated near a public domain (*reshut harabim*), also accessible from an adjacent private courtyard (*chatzer*). The question is whether the roof may be considered part of the *chatzer*'s *reshut hayachid*, allowing the *chatzer* residents to use it on Shabbat, or whether its proximity to the *reshut harabim* creates a competing access that disqualifies it.

### Fixed vs. Temporary

Rav Nachman rules: *tzarich sulam kavua l'hatira* — to render the roof permissible for the *chatzer* residents, a fixed ladder (*sulam kavua*) is required. A fixed ladder, yes; a temporary ladder (*sulam arai*), no. The distinction is sharp and, on first reading, counterintuitive. If anything, a temporary ladder physically present in the *chatzer* actually makes access to the roof easier for the *chatzer* residents — they can climb up whenever they like. Why should the presence of a movable ladder fail to establish the roof as part of the *chatzer*'s domain?

### Formal vs. Practical

The Gemara's answer is precisely the principle Abaye articulated in the *gazuztraot* case: the Gemara does not ask practical questions when the parties fall within the same formal category. The roof is within ten *tefachim* of the *reshut harabim* and is also accessible (via ladder) from the *chatzer*. In formal terms — the only terms the Gemara applies — both parties stand within ten *tefachim* of the roof, placing both in the category of "easy access." At that point, neither party has a dispositive advantage over the other, and without a *sulam kavua* that structurally and permanently anchors the roof to the *chatzer*, the roof is treated as jointly accessible and therefore forbidden to the *chatzer* residents. The temporary ladder makes things practically easier for the *chatzer* residents, but that practical consideration is categorically set aside in favor of the formal rule.

### Rav Papa's Objection

Rav Papa raises an objection to the Gemara's proof structure. The Gemara had cited the *sulam kavua* ruling as a demonstration that the ten-*tefach* formal rule overrides practical assessment. Rav Papa asks: how do we know the ruling is motivated by the formal rule at all? Perhaps the roof is simply easy access for the *reshut harabim* people as well — they lean over, rest packages on the roof, place their hats there (*miktafei alei b'kumsa v'sudra*). If the *reshut harabim* residents genuinely and practically use the roof's surface, then the case isn't about abstract formal rules at all; it is just a straightforward case of practical equal access, which would be forbidden on those grounds alone. The *sulam kavua* ruling would then not prove anything about the primacy of formal over practical reasoning. This objection is left unresolved by the Gemara at this point, and the proof remains less than fully established.

## Formal vs. Practical

### Principle

The objection of Rav Papa does not, however, undermine the broader principle the Gemara has been building toward throughout the daf. The principle itself — that formal legal rules defined by the ten-*tefach* threshold take absolute precedence over case-by-case practical assessment — has been stated and restated in multiple contexts. Whether the question involves a mound within four *tefachim* of a *mirpeset*, two *gazuztraot* within ten *tefachim* of each other, or a roof reachable from both a *chatzer* and a *reshut harabim*, the Gemara consistently applies the same logic: the formal category governs. If two parties are within the same formal threshold, they are treated as equal — even when one's practical access is plainly more convenient than the other's. The Gemara has no interest in adjudicating access empirically. It wants an exact, objective rule.

### Irony

There is an undeniable irony in this approach. The drive toward formal precision — rooted in the Gemara's preference for objective, verifiable legal categories over subjective practical judgments — generates precisely the complexity and apparent arbitrariness that makes these laws so difficult for ordinary people to navigate. As Abaye's ruling makes vivid: even if in practice it is easier for one party to reach the space than for the other, as long as both fall within ten *tefachim*, the law treats them identically and forbids both. A legal system motivated by the desire to provide clear, consistent, and predictable rulings ends up producing intricately differentiated outcomes that depend on measurements down to fractions of a *tefach*. Yet the Gemara's commitment to this methodology is unwavering. Formal rules, however demanding, provide a stable framework; practical assessments, however intuitive, introduce subjectivity that a legal system cannot easily administer. The entirety of Eruvin 84a is, in a sense, a sustained demonstration of that jurisprudential choice.

# Eiruvin 86

## Eruv & Shituf Placement

### Eruv vs Shituf

The daf begins, technically at the bottom of 85b, with a ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel concerning the placement of an *eruv* and a *shituf*. The underlying framework is already established: an *eruv chatzerot* must be placed in a *bayit*, a house within the *chatzer*, while the *shituf mevo'ot* can — and according to Tosafot, must — be placed in the *chatzer* rather than in a *bayit*. What types of spaces qualify as a *bayit* is itself a subject of discussion in the *mishna*, where the *Tanna Kamma* holds that even a barn or storage shed constitutes a sufficient *bayit* for purposes of *eruv*, since it constitutes a form of edifice related to habitation, even if no one actively lives there.

### Bread as Eruv

Into this framework, Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel introduces a striking practical case: if a group of people — *bnei chaburah* — were reclining together at a meal on Friday afternoon, and *Shabbat* entered before they had established an *eruv*, the bread already on the table before them can serve as their *eruv*. The phrasing is significant: it does not seem to require that anyone formally acquire the bread on behalf of all participants, nor that anyone explicitly designate it *leshem eruv*. The simple reality of shared participation in the meal appears to be sufficient.

This raises interesting questions. First, does the bread need to be a whole loaf? Various *mishnayot* suggest that a full, unbroken loaf is required. Since *Shabbat* entered while they were already eating, it is possible the loaf had already been broken. One might resolve this by assuming the ruling follows the view that a whole loaf is not strictly required, or perhaps the consideration is that the loaf was whole at the moment *Shabbat* began — though this deserves further investigation in the *posekim*.

The *Gemara* adds: *ve'amri lah mishum shituf* — some say the same bread can count as a *shituf* for the *mavoi*. This formulation, rather than contradicting the first, sets the stage for Rava's resolution.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava clarifies that these two opinions are not in dispute: *velo pligi*. The difference is purely situational. If the group is dining inside the *bayit*, the bread counts as an *eruv chatzerot*, since the *eruv* must be located within a *bayit*. If they are eating outside in the *chatzer* — a picnic of sorts — it cannot qualify as an *eruv* (since it is not in a *bayit*) but it can qualify as a *shituf* for the *mavoi*. The resolution is elegant and preserves both formulations.

### Baraita Support

Abaye then tells Rava that a *tanya* supports this position: *eiruvi chatzerot bachatzer veshitufai mevo'ot bemavoi*. But this support is immediately complicated, because the *baraita* as stated seems to place the *eruv chatzerot* in the *chatzer* itself — which contradicts the *mishna* that invalidates an *eruv* placed even in a gatehouse (*beit sha'ar*), porch (*achsadra*), or balcony (*mirpeset*), places that fall short of a proper *bayit*. Certainly the *chatzer* itself does not qualify.

The *Gemara* therefore amends the *baraita*: *ela eima eiruvi chatzerot bebayit shebachatzer veshitufai mevo'ot bachatzer shebamavoi* — the *eruv chatzerot* goes in a *bayit* that belongs to the *chatzer*, and the *shituf mevo'ot* goes in a *chatzer* that opens into the *mavoi*. What begins as a seeming support turns out to require textual emendation, yet even after that emendation, the amended reading does provide genuine support for Rava's position.

The upshot of this whole discussion: an *eruv chatzerot* must be placed in a *bayit* — a genuine domicile or structure associated with habitation — that belongs to the *chatzer* in question. Whether the owner must be actively present, or whether absentee ownership also creates a *halachic* problem, is a separate question taken up in the next *mishna*.

---

## Tfisat Yad

### Tfisat Yad Doctrine

Rabbi Yehuda introduces a qualification of great practical importance: *im yesh sham tfisat yad* — if the owner retains a "holding of the hand" in the space. The *halacha* is this: if someone rents out a barn or apartment, the tenant would ordinarily be considered a new, independent presence in the *chatzer*, obligating his participation in the *eruv*. However, if the owner retains objects in that unit — maintains a *tfisat yad* there — the unit is considered to remain fundamentally the owner's domain even while it is occupied by another. Consequently, it does not constitute a separate *reshut* requiring independent participation in the *eruv*.

### Ben Bunyas Example

The *Gemara* illustrates this with the paradigm of Ben Bunyas — a wealthy individual identified by Rashi as someone who rented out all the houses in his *chatzer* but furnished each one, keeping his own equipment and objects in every unit. Because he retained a *tfisat yad* throughout, all the units remained, in effect, a single unified domain belonging to one owner. No *eruv* was required among them.

### Honoring Wealthy

The *Gemara* digresses around this figure. Ben Bunyas came before Rebbi, who instructed his attendants to clear a place of honor for him — *pnu makom l'ven me'ah maneh*, for a man of great wealth. A second, apparently more distinguished visitor arrived, and Rebbi similarly directed his servants to honor him. Rabbi Yishmael b'Rebbi Yosi then informed Rebbi that the first visitor's father, the patriarch Bunyas himself, possessed a thousand ships at sea and a thousand villages on dry land — far greater wealth than his son's appearance suggested. Rebbi's response was instructive: he told Rabbi Yishmael b'Rebbi Yosi to convey to the father that when he sends his son to visit, he should dress him in a manner befitting his station, so that he receives his proper honor.

The episode may initially appear to reflect an unbecoming preoccupation with wealth. The *Gemara* directly addresses this by noting that both Rebbi and Rabbi Akiva made a point of honoring the wealthy. The verse cited is *yeshav olam lifnei Elokim chesed v'emes man yintzruhu* — the world endures before God when *chesed* and *emes* sustain it. Rava bar Mari expounds that wealthy individuals who support society through philanthropy, employment, and material sustenance are worthy of recognition. The juxtaposition of *chesed v'emes* may also carry a deeper resonance: *chesed* represents material benevolence, while *emes* often refers to *Torah*. The implication is that rabbinic leadership should not cultivate disdain for wealth or for those who pursue it, particularly when those individuals sustain both the poor and the institutions of *Torah* study.

### Tfisat Yad Definition

Returning to the *halacha*, Rabbah bar bar Chana specifies what constitutes a *tfisat yad*: even something as seemingly minor as the spike of a plow left in a rented barn is sufficient to maintain the owner's presence there.

Rav Nachman then transmits a principle from the school of Shmuel that sharpens the definition considerably: *davar hanitil b'Shabbat osser, davar she'eino nitil b'Shabbat eino osser*. An object that can be moved on *Shabbat* does not constitute a *tfisat yad* — because it is entirely possible that the owner could come and retrieve it on *Shabbat* itself, meaning it creates no permanent, binding presence. An object that cannot be moved on *Shabbat*, however — whether because it is *muktzah machamat chisron kis* (set aside due to monetary concern), or *tevel* (untithed produce), or some other category of *muktzah* — does constitute a *tfisat yad*, because its presence there is effectively immovable on *Shabbat* and thereby establishes an ongoing claim. A *baraita* confirms this principle.

### Modern Applications

This *halacha* is of striking practical importance. In cities without an *eruv*, the question of whether one may carry within an apartment building, a hotel, or a cruise ship often turns on this very principle. All of these structures are in a sense the modern equivalent of a *chatzer* with multiple separate units opening onto a shared space — precisely the paradigm case of *eruv chatzerot*. Yet in nearly all of these scenarios, the owner retains a *tfisat yad* of one kind or another.

In a hotel or on a ship, the guest typically has no absolute right to a specific room; management can reassign the guest to a different room if necessary. This means the guest never truly possesses an independent *reshut* — the owner's claim over each room is not displaced. In an apartment building, the owner may retain the major appliances in each unit, which would typically qualify as items not movable on *Shabbat*, and thereby establish a *tfisat yad* throughout the building. The result is that in many such cases, the entire structure is treated as a single owner's domain, and the *eruv chatzerot* concern does not arise. There are extensive contemporary *teshuvot* on the application of these principles to modern settings.

---

## Presence Requirements

### Absent Owner Case

The next *mishna* addresses the question of what level of presence is required for an owner's house to count as a problematic, independent domain in a *chatzer*. The case: *hamaniach beiso v'halach lishbot b'ir acheret* — a person left his house and went to spend *Shabbat* in another city. Does his house in the *chatzer* still create a *halachic* obstacle requiring participation in the *eruv*?

### Rabbi Meir View

Rabbi Meir says: yes, regardless of whether the absent owner is Jewish or non-Jewish, his house is a problem — *harei zeh osser*. For Rabbi Meir, ownership of a domicile within the *chatzer* is sufficient to create an obligation; active presence is irrelevant.

### Rabbi Yehuda View

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *eino osser*. If the owner is not actively present, his house does not create a problem. Presence itself is the operative criterion.

### Rabbi Yosi View

Rabbi Yosi agrees in principle with Rabbi Yehuda but introduces a crucial distinction: *nochri osser, Yisrael eino osser*. A non-Jew who has left his house is still a problem, because a non-Jew might return on *Shabbat* — there is no *halachic* inhibition preventing him from traveling. His potential, imminent return keeps him effectively "present." A Jew, however, would not normally travel back on *Shabbat*, and therefore — even if he is technically within *techum* and could theoretically return — his return is sufficiently unusual that we do not consider him imminently present. The relevant standard, for Rabbi Yosi, is not physical presence but imminent presence.

### Rabbi Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon refines and extends Rabbi Yosi's position. He rules that even if a Jew did not go to another city but merely went to spend *Shabbat* with his married daughter in the same city, he is nevertheless not considered present in his home: *shekvar hisiyach milibo* — he has already mentally and practically disengaged from his house for *Shabbat*. He is spending *Shabbat* elsewhere; his original home is, for this *Shabbat*, effectively unoccupied. Physical proximity does not substitute for presence.

### Rav Ruling

Rav rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Shimon*. Even a Jew who has merely gone a few blocks to his daughter's house for *Shabbat* is not considered present in his original dwelling.

However, Rav adds a qualification: *v'davka bito* — this applies specifically when he is staying with his daughter. If he is staying with his son, *lo* — we cannot be equally confident that he will not return. The *Gemara* captures this in a folk expression: if a male dog barks at you, you can still enter the house; if a female dog barks, you had better leave. The point is that the relationship with a son-in-law is typically more fraught than with a daughter-in-law, and a man spending *Shabbat* at his son's home might feel compelled to leave if friction with his daughter-in-law becomes acute, making his return to his own home a live possibility.

### Conceptual Discussion

This raises a broader conceptual question: what is the underlying logic of the entire *eruv* framework? Halachically, the *chatzer* and all of its constituent spaces already form a single *reshut hayachid* — it is all walled, it is all private domain. The Rabbinic requirement of *eruv chatzerot* is not a biblical necessity but a Rabbinic enactment, driven by the experiential reality that even within a single *reshut hayachid*, multiple separate households create a fragmented sense of domain. The *eruv* reestablishes the unified character of the space at a practical and experiential level.

Given this, it makes considerable sense that an owner who is simply not present for *Shabbat* does not generate the friction or the sense of competing, separate domains that the *eruv* was designed to address. He is not an outlier; his absence removes any experiential disruption. If one can establish the *eruv* once for the year — as is standard practice, using a preserved food item that will not spoil — then the question of re-establishing it weekly only arises in unusual circumstances, and can in any case be arranged communally, with one individual taking formal responsibility each week on behalf of the others.

---

## Well Division

### Mishnah Setup

The *mishna* now introduces a new topic with its own distinct geometry: *bor shebein shtei chatzerot* — a well situated between two courtyards. The *mishna* rules: you may not draw water from it on *Shabbat* unless a *mechitza* ten *tefachim* high has been constructed — *bein milmata bein mitoch ogno*, whether lower in the well or at its lip.

### Physical Scenario

The physical scenario requires some visualization. Two separate, fully walled courtyards share a common wall between them. That shared wall runs directly over a well — the wall passes above the well at ground level, but the well itself is below, and the wall does not extend down through the water. Each courtyard thus has access to the same well from its own side. The problem: drawing water from one side effectively draws water that is shared with the other courtyard, making it a transfer of objects across courtyard boundaries in the absence of a joint *eruv*. A *mechitza* within the well itself is therefore required.

### Below vs Above

The *mishna* speaks of the *mechitza* being *milmata* or *lemala*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reports that this is actually a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: Beit Shammai requires it to be below (*milmata*) and Beit Hillel allows it to be above (*lemala*). But what do "below" and "above" actually mean within the well?

### Rav Huna Reading

Rav Huna explains: *lamata mamash* and *lemala mamash* — both positions refer to locations entirely within the well itself, not above ground level. "Below" means near the waterline; "above" means near the lip of the well. Both are inside the well, differing only in their elevation within it.

### Rav Yehuda Reading

Rav Yehuda reads differently: "below" (*lamata min hamayim*) means within the water itself, and "above" (*lemala min hamayim*) means above the waterline. Notably, what Rav Yehuda calls "above" corresponds roughly to what Rav Huna calls "below."

Rashi understands Rav Yehuda's "within the water" to mean a *mechitza* constructed from the very floor of the well upward through the water, protruding at the top. Tosafot modifies this: the *mechitza* need not go to the floor, but must be substantially within the water and protrude slightly above the surface.

### Water Mixture Challenge

A pointed question follows. Rabbah bar bar Chana asks Rava: granted that Rav Yehuda requires the *mechitza* to be within the water — but what does that accomplish? The water still flows on both sides of the wall; the water intermingles regardless of where the partition is placed. And conversely, if the water mixes anyway, what is the advantage of placing the *mechitza* within the water as opposed to above it?

### Protrusion Requirement

The answer invokes a tradition cited by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, which Rav Yehuda traces through to Rabbi Hiyya: *tzarich she-yiru rosho kanim l'mala min hamayim tefach* — the *mechitza* must protrude a *tefach* above the waterline so that it is visible. According to Rashi, this means the *mechitza* must run the entire height of the water column and emerge above it — an imposing structure that actually does prevent water from mixing. According to Tosafot, the requirement of protruding a *tefach* above the water is not about preventing mixing but about visual symbolism: the *mechitza* must be substantially in the water (to symbolize the division of the water) and must also be seen above the water (to serve as a visual marker). On this view, the water continues to mix in practice, but the partition is considered symbolically effective.

A parallel formulation, cited by Yaakov Karchina, holds that even the "above the water" position of Rav Yehuda requires the partition to dip a *tefach* into the water. The logic is consistent: a *mechitza* that floats entirely above the waterline without touching the water does not symbolize a division of the water at all; it must at minimum make contact with the water to discharge its symbolic function.

---

## Beam Division

### Pi Tikra Principle

The *Gemara* turns to an alternative means of dividing the well — one that, counterintuitively, turns out to be more permissive than a physical *mechitza*. The relevant principle is *pi tikra yored v'soteim* — the edge of a ceiling is viewed as descending and sealing the space below it. The irony is significant: ordinarily, a suspended wall that does not reach the ground is *halachically* invalid, because we do not apply *gud achit* (the principle of imagining the wall extending downward) once the gap exceeds three *tefachim*. Yet a ceiling — which is not a wall at all — is treated as generating virtual walls from its edges, precisely because its horizontal surface communicates an enclosure more powerfully than a partial wall does. This principle applies when the beam is at least four *tefachim* wide and has straight, smooth edges.

### Beam Alternative

Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuha, rules: *kora arba mataret bamayim* — a beam four *tefachim* wide placed over the well allows both courtyards to draw water from the well. By *pi tikra*, the edges of the beam are viewed as extending downward through the well, effectively dividing it. Each side may draw water from beneath "its" edge of the beam.

### Bucket Confinement

An obvious practical objection arises: even if the virtual wall is *halachically* effective, a bucket lowered into the well will float freely across to the other side. There is no physical barrier to keep it in place. The *Gemara* responds: the rabbis established that a bucket does not travel more than four *tefachim* laterally from where it is lowered — and since the beam itself is four *tefachim* wide, the bucket will remain within the confines of the beam's virtual wall.

### Water Leniency

Still, the question remains: in what sense is the well "divided" when the water itself mingles freely below? We have already seen that even the *mechitza* opinions concede that water mixing is not a complete disqualification. The *Gemara* invokes a broader principle: *hikilu chachamim bamayim* — the rabbis were lenient with regard to water. Access to drinking water is a pressing need, and the rabbis calibrated their standards accordingly.

Tosafot understands this leniency as specific to the beam case: the standard for a beam (*pi tikra*) is simply less demanding than the standard for a *mechitza*, particularly with respect to whether the divider must actually penetrate the water. Rashi draws a broader *posekim* conclusion: since the beam clearly works without any contact with the water, the opinion that a *mechitza* must be placed in the water cannot be the normative ruling. We rule like the more lenient position — the *mechitza* need not reach the water. This has significant practical implications regarding the permissibility of structures built over bodies of water, a question directly engaged by Tosafot in reference to the practice of constructing outhouses over rivers in medieval France and Germany.

### Wall Sufficiency

Rav Yehuda then goes further: the wall that already runs *above* the well at ground level is itself sufficient — there is no need for any additional *mechitza* within the well at all. *Lo tehei mechitza gedolah min hakotel shebeineihem* — the dividing wall between the courtyards is already a greater *mechitza* than anything placed inside the well. The *Gemara* subsequently characterizes this position as aligning with the view of Rabbi Yosi regarding suspended walls, a connection explored in the following section.

---

## Suspended Walls

### Position Separation

Rabbah bar bar Chana, citing Rabbi Yochanan, equates Rav Yehuda's leniency about the wall above the well with the position of Rabbi Yosi: *Rav Yehuda b'shitas Rabbi Yosi amra* — because Rav Yehuda relies on a wall that is suspended above the well (not penetrating it at all), and Rabbi Yosi, in the context of *Sukkah*, permits suspended walls to extend their effect downward even without touching the ground. The *Gemara* therefore identifies Rav Yehuda's ruling as an application of Rabbi Yosi's broader principle.

The *Gemara* immediately pushes back: *v'lo hi* — these positions are not necessarily identical, and one does not necessarily commit to the other.

### Rabbinic vs Biblical

The distinction the *Gemara* draws is one of *halachic* domain and gravity. Rav Yehuda's leniency about the wall above the well operates in the realm of *eruv chatzerot*, which is entirely Rabbinic — the underlying space is already a *reshut hayachid* biblically, and the entire *eruv* framework is a Rabbinic enactment. One might be lenient with suspended walls in a context that is *derabanan*. Rabbi Yosi's leniency in *Sukkah*, on the other hand, involves the biblical *mitzvah* of *Sukkah* — yet at worst, an invalid *sukkah* violates a positive commandment (*issur assei*), which is categorically less severe. One cannot automatically extend either position to the other's domain. The *Gemara* therefore holds: Rav Yehuda's permissiveness about the well does not commit him to Rabbi Yosi's position about *Sukkah*, and Rabbi Yosi's position about *Sukkah* does not commit him to leniency in the realm of *hilchot Shabbat* — where the underlying transgressions, at the biblical level, carry the gravest penalties. Even if Rabbi Yosi believes suspended walls are genuinely effective, he might impose stricter standards in a *halachic* domain whose severity warrants additional caution.

### Tzippori Case

An objection is raised: we know of a famous incident in Tzippori — Rabbi Yosi's own city — in which sheets were spread over pillars to create an ad hoc enclosure on *Shabbat* itself, enabling a *Sefer Torah* to be transported. This would suggest that Rabbi Yosi did apply his leniency regarding suspended walls to *Shabbat*, not merely to *Sukkah*.

The *Gemara* responds: that incident was not performed on the authority of Rabbi Yosi himself but on the authority of his son, Rabbi Yishmael b'Rebbi Yosi. The son may have extended the father's ruling from *Sukkah* to *Shabbat* — but the father's own position in the domain of *Shabbat* remains unstated, and one cannot automatically attribute to him a leniency he never explicitly applied there.

---

## Suspended Walls (II)

### Sefer Torah Case

The full account of the Tzippori incident: Rav Dimi reports that on one occasion, the community forgot to bring the *Sefer Torah* to the *shul* before *Shabbat*, and it remained in a private house. The following day — on *Shabbat* itself — they spread sheets over pillars, creating an improvised enclosure, and carried the *Sefer Torah* to the *shul* and read from it. Rashi notes that the purpose of the enclosure was not simply to create a *reshut hayachid* out of a *karmelit*, but specifically to address an *eruv chatzerot* concern: by constructing a walled corridor between the house and the *shul*, they effectively blocked the access of other houses to the shared *chatzer* space, thereby circumventing the need for a formal *eruv chatzerot* for that corridor.

### Creation on Shabbat

This raises an immediate question: how could they erect *halachic* partitions on *Shabbat* at all? It is universally agreed that one may not construct a temporary *ohel arai* on *Shabbat*, and a fortiori one may not create a new *halachic mechitza* on *Shabbat* for the purpose of defining a new domain.

### Repositioning Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves this: *matzau sadinim pursuim al amudin* — they found sheets already hanging on pillars. The structure was not newly created on *Shabbat*; it pre-existed in folded or compressed form, and they simply repositioned it — moved the pillars, spread the sheets — on *Shabbat*. There was no act of construction, only the repositioning of an already-existing *mechitza*. The resulting enclosure was *halachically* effective because it was pre-formed, not newly made.

---

## Lenient Authorities

### Rava Connection

Rava draws an explicit connection between two lenient authorities: Rav Yehuda — whose position about the wall over the well we have already examined — and Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya, presenting them as essentially aligned in their treatment of virtual or suspended walls over water on *Shabbat*.

### Platform Rule

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* to establish Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya's position. A *gezustra* — a platform or protruding structure — that extends over a body of water and measures four *amot* by four *amot* (24 *tefachim* by 24 *tefachim*) poses a question of how one may draw water from below it on *Shabbat*. Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya rules: one opens a hole of four *tefachim* by four *tefachim* exactly in the center of the platform and draws water through it.

### Virtual Walls

The geometric reasoning is as follows. If the platform is 24 *tefachim* wide and the opening is four *tefachim* in the center, then there are ten *tefachim* of platform on each side of the opening. Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya holds that those ten *tefachim* on each side are viewed as bending downward — creating four virtual walls, each ten *tefachim* high, descending from the edge of the platform to the water. This establishes a *reshut hayachid* at the water's surface, permitting one to draw water through the opening.

This is a remarkable leniency: no physical wall exists at all. The entire structure of the domain is virtual, constructed entirely from the platform's own edges extended downward by *halachic* imagination. Rava's identification of this position with Rav Yehuda's ruling about the wall over the well underscores the common thread: both authorities are prepared, at least in the realm of water access on *Shabbat* — a domain treated with Rabbinic leniency — to rely on virtual or constructively extended walls where a physical *mechitza* would normally be required.

---

---

# Eiruvin 87

## Mechitza Over Well

### Dividing Well

The eighty-seventh daf opens by returning to a *mishnah* concerned with a well situated between two courtyards. Since the water itself cannot be physically divided, what is required symbolically to permit each courtyard to draw from its own side? According to the *chachamim*, some form of *mechitzah* must be placed inside the well itself, and the precise depth and extent of that partition into the water was the subject of debate. According to Rabbi Yehuda, however, the wall running over the top of the well suffices — we view it as though it extends downward and effectively divides the water below, even though it does not physically penetrate the well. The *gemara* notes that this position is analogous — if not identical — to the lenient approach of Chananya ben Akavya, who is remarkably permissive when it comes to *mechitzos* situated over bodies of water.

### Chananya Leniency

This general leniency with virtual partitions over water is not arbitrary. *Chazal* recognized the critical importance of access to water and were correspondingly more accommodating when it came to drawing water, as opposed to other uses. The baseline leniency, accepted by all, is that if one constructs booth-like *mechitzos* around a hole in a platform extending over a body of water — whether above or below — we treat those walls as extending all the way into the water, even though *mechitzos* ordinarily must be connected to the ground. Chananya ben Akavya goes further still: if the platform itself is four *amos* by four *amos* — that is, twenty-four *tefachim* in each direction — and the hole cut into it is four by four *tefachim*, which is the minimum required to constitute a *reshut hayachid*, then no actual walls need be built at all. Each side of the platform is imagined as bending downward around the hole, providing ten *tefachim* of virtual wall in each direction, and one may lower a bucket through the hole and draw water without any physical construction.

## Bent Plank Math

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye challenges the equation between Rabbi Yehuda's position in the *mishnah* and that of Chananya ben Akavya. He argues that the two may in fact differ in important respects. Rabbi Yehuda's ruling — that the wall above the well is treated as extending downward — involves only a linear extension (*gud*). But bending a wall and then extending it (*kuf ve-gud*) is a more complex fictional move, and Rabbi Yehuda may not have countenanced that. Conversely, Chananya ben Akavya may have articulated his leniency only in the specific context of Tiberias, over the Lake Kinneret, and not as a general principle applicable to all bodies of water.

### Tiberias Exception

The reason Chananya ben Akavya's ruling applied specifically to Tiberias, the *gemara* explains, is that the Kinneret has banks (*agnaim*), surrounding towns (*ayarot*), and enclosed yards (*karfifot*) encircling it. Precisely how these features translate into a halachic distinction is not entirely clear. Rashi emphasizes that the banks themselves constitute the beginnings of a *mechitzah*, giving the water a quasi-enclosed character. Others suggest that the combination of geographic features and the concentrated need of the local population together justified a more expansive ruling. But whatever the precise logic, Chananya ben Akavya's leniency is to be understood as particular to the Kinneret; he would not extend it to ordinary bodies of water.

### Plank Configs

Having established the principle of imaginarily bending a plank, the *gemara* proceeds to explore — with considerable mathematical creativity — what various physical configurations of the plank would actually require in practice.

Abaye begins with the case of a plank suspended horizontally within three *tefachim* of a wall. Since the gap between the plank and the wall is less than three *tefachim*, the principle of *lavud* applies — the gap is treated as closed, as if the plank reaches the wall. In this configuration, the plank need not span the full four *amos* in both directions. Because one side of the virtual enclosure is supplied by the wall itself (treated via *lavud* as contiguous with the plank), the plank only needs to be four *amos* in one direction and eleven *tefachim* and a small additional amount (*mashehu*) in the other. The logic is as follows: the hole must be four by four *tefachim* to constitute a *reshut hayachid*. The bend down each long side provides ten *tefachim* of wall height. In the short direction, the bend provides 1.1 *tefachim* of actual plank, and *lavud* closes the remaining 2.9 *tefachim* to the wall. Hence the plank's width need only be 11.1 *tefachim* — ten for the bend on one side, 1.1 for the portion to be bent on the other, with *lavud* completing the fourth wall.

The *gemara* then considers a plank positioned vertically — standing upright rather than lying flat — and suspended within three *tefachim* of the wall. Here the plank must be ten *tefachim* high and seven *tefachim* and two *mashehus* wide. The wall of the building already provides one full side, and the upright plank, with its edges bent in and *lavud* closing the gap to the wall on each side, supplies the remaining three walls.

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua then addresses the case where the plank is positioned at the corner of the building — *keren zavit*. In this configuration, two walls of the required enclosure are already provided by the intersecting walls of the building. Only two more corners are needed. If the plank is ten *tefachim* high and measures 1.1 *tefachim* in each direction — for a total width of just over two *tefachim* — it can be folded into an L-shape and placed within 2.9 *tefachim* of each wall. *Lavud* closes the remaining gaps, and the four-walled enclosure is complete.
