The *gemara* thus states that in the corner case, the plank need only be ten *tefachim* high and two *tefachim* and two *mashehus* wide.

### Four-by-Four

Having established all these creative configurations through which one can construct the required enclosure with a plank far smaller than four by four *amos*, the *gemara* returns to ask: when does Chananya ben Akavya's original formulation — that the platform must be four *amos* by four *amos* — actually apply?

One straightforward answer is that it applies simply when the plank is not suspended in a position that allows exploitation of *lavud* — for example, when it is attached flush to the wall in the ordinary case. Rashi, however, understands the *gemara* differently: the requirement of four *amos* by four *amos* applies when the plank is suspended far out from the wall — more than three *tefachim* away — so that *lavud* cannot be invoked and the plank must generate all four walls entirely on its own. In that case, each side must provide a full ten *tefachim* of bend, requiring the full four-*amah* span in each direction. Either way, the *gemara* appears to have enjoyed the exercise of imaginatively bending planks and calculating the savings that *lavud* provides.

## Aqueduct Divider

### Karmelit Status

The *mishnah* turns to a new case: an *ama hamayim* — an aqueduct or canal — that passes through a courtyard. The *mishnah* rules that one may not draw water from it on *Shabbat*, because such a waterway has the status of a *karmelit*.

This requires explanation. If the aqueduct is less than ten *tefachim* deep or less than four *tefachim* wide, it does not constitute its own domain and is simply treated as part of the *reshut hayachid* of the surrounding courtyard; in that case, drawing from it poses no problem. The issue arises only when the aqueduct is both ten *tefachim* deep and four *tefachim* wide — at which point it is a domain unto itself. But why, then, is it a *karmelit* rather than a *reshut hayachid*? A well of identical dimensions would be a *reshut hayachid*.

The answer lies in the structure of the aqueduct's walls. Several explanations are offered. One holds that the slope of the aqueduct's banks is too gradual to qualify as halachic walls. More compellingly, as one of the students observes, the aqueduct passes through and connects to the outside world — it enters from elsewhere and exits elsewhere — meaning it functionally has only two walls where it runs through the courtyard. The *Meiri* makes a similar point. Even if one might ordinarily argue for *reshut hayachid* status despite the absence of two full walls, the rabbinic authorities treated such a waterway, at minimum rabbinically, as a *karmelit*, because as encountered within the courtyard it lacks the requisite four walls.

The goal, therefore, is to construct *mechitzos* at the two open ends — where the aqueduct enters and exits the courtyard — thereby enclosing it on all sides and transforming it into a *reshut hayachid*, from which one may draw water on *Shabbat*.

### Wall Above

The *mishnah* states: one may not draw water from an aqueduct passing through a courtyard on *Shabbat* unless one has erected a *mechitzah* ten *tefachim* high at the entry and at the exit of the courtyard — and this partition must penetrate into the depth of the aqueduct itself. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: the wall of the courtyard that passes over the aqueduct already counts as the required *mechitzah*. This is the same position Rabbi Yehuda took regarding the well — just as the wall atop the well may be viewed as extending downward into the well, so too the courtyard wall passing over the aqueduct may be viewed as extending downward into the water channel.

A further *baraita* reinforces the basic ruling of the *chachamim*: a *mechitzah* at the entry but not the exit, or at the exit but not the entry, does not suffice — both are required.

### Abel-Tzipori

Rabbi Yehuda adduces a practical precedent. He cites the case of the aqueduct that ran from Abel to Tzipori — two towns in close proximity — from which the residents would draw water on *Shabbat* with the approval of the elders, apparently relying on the wall that passed over the aqueduct rather than a specially constructed partition within the channel itself.

The *chachamim* dismiss this proof. That aqueduct, they explain, was not ten *tefachim* deep and four *tefachim* wide. It therefore did not constitute its own domain at all and was simply part of the surrounding *reshut hayachid*. No *mechitzah* of any kind was required, and the conduct of the residents of that town proves nothing about cases where the aqueduct genuinely constitutes a *karmelit*.

## Three-or-Four

### Threshold Question

A further *baraita* introduces a new scenario: an aqueduct running between two buildings, with the householders' windows opening onto it from either side. The *baraita* rules that if the gap between the buildings above the aqueduct is less than three *tefachim*, one may lower a bucket and fill it; if it is three *tefachim* or more, one may not. Rabbi Shimon dissents, placing the threshold at four *tefachim*: less than four permits drawing water, four or more does not.

The *gemara* seeks to understand what, precisely, is measured by this three-or-four *tefachim* threshold. The scenario involves a *karmelit* — the aqueduct — and a *reshut hayachid* — the house — and the question is under what circumstances the householder may lower a bucket into the water below. What role does the specific measurement of three or four *tefachim* play in this determination?

### Karmelit Width

One possible explanation: the debate concerns the minimum width that renders the aqueduct a *karmelit* in the first place. Recall that if the aqueduct is less than four *tefachim* wide, it is not its own domain but part of the *reshut hayachid*. Perhaps according to the *tanna kamma*, the minimum width for a *karmelit* is three *tefachim*, and only when the gap reaches three does it become a prohibited *karmelit*; according to Rabbi Shimon, the threshold remains the standard four.

However, this explanation runs into a difficulty: when Rav Dimi transmitted teachings from Eretz Yisrael in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, he stated explicitly that a *karmelit* requires a minimum width of four *tefachim*. If that is indeed universally accepted, it is strange to suggest that any *tanna* would hold the minimum to be three.

### Makom Patur

A second explanation: the debate does not concern the width of the *karmelit* itself but rather the width of the banks — the *agappah* — alongside the aqueduct. If those banks are narrow enough, they constitute a *makom patur*, an exempt domain lacking the minimum four-by-four *tefachim* required for any defined domain. In that case, the procedure under discussion would work as follows: one lowers the bucket from the *reshut hayachid* of the house down onto the bank below, where someone fills it from the *karmelit* waters; the filled bucket is then raised back through the *makom patur* into the house. The question is whether this bank is a *makom patur* when it is less than three *tefachim* wide or less than four.

### Yochanan Rule

This explanation also faces a challenge. Rav Dimi reported in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a space lacking four-by-four *tefachim* is a *makom patur*, and that both those of the *reshut harabbim* and those of the *reshut hayachid* may set down their burdens upon it — but they may not use it as a transit point to transfer between the two domains. If one may not use a *makom patur* as a way station between a *reshut hayachid* and a *reshut harabbim*, how can one use the bank — assuming it is a *makom patur* — to ferry water between the house and the *karmelit*?

### Rabbinic Transfer

The *gemara* answers: the prohibition against using a *makom patur* as a transit point applies when the two domains on either side are biblical domains — *reshut hayachid* and *reshut harabbim* — where a direct transfer would constitute a Torah-level violation of *Shabbat*. Here, however, the *karmelit* is a rabbinic domain; a direct transfer between a *reshut hayachid* and a *karmelit* would only be a rabbinic transgression. In such a case, the *makom patur* may be used as an intermediary.

The *gemara* then re-examines this resolution. The prohibition attributed to Rabbi Yochanan against using a *makom patur* as a transit point — as transmitted by Ze'iri — appears to apply even to rabbinic domains. The *gemara* recalls a *mishnah* studied approximately ten days earlier: a wall ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* wide standing between two courtyards constitutes its own *reshut hayachid*. Fruit sitting on top of such a wall belongs to neither courtyard and may be eaten there, but may not be transferred down into either courtyard without a proper *eruv*. The *gemara* had already asked: if the wall is ten *tefachim* high but less than four *tefachim* wide, what is its status?

Rav held that since the wall is less than four *tefachim* wide, it is a *makom patur* but one that is simultaneously claimed by both courtyards; the airspace of both domains governs it, and nothing may be moved upon it at all — not even a hairsbreadth. Rabbi Yochanan disagreed: it is simply a standard *makom patur*, and just as a *makom patur* in the middle of a *reshut harabbim* may be used by those of both the *reshut harabbim* and the *reshut hayachid*, so too this wall may be used by those of both courtyards — but with the crucial limitation that items may not be transferred *through* it from one courtyard to the other.

The *gemara* then notes: Rabbi Yochanan goes according to his own reasoning, as Rav Dimi transmitted in his name: a space lacking four by four *tefachim* is a *makom patur*, and people from both the *reshut harabbim* and the *reshut hayachid* may use it — *ubilvad shelo yachlifu* — as long as they do not exchange items through it from one domain to the other.

The upshot is that the prohibition against transiting through a *makom patur* applies even in this rabbinic context — between two *reshuyot hayachid* without an *eruv* — according to Ze'iri's transmission of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling. Hence Ze'iri would presumably also prohibit using the bank of the aqueduct as a *makom patur* transit point to the *karmelit* waters. The *gemara* concludes that this second explanation — the debate concerns the size of a *makom patur* — is consistent with the position of Rav Dimi, who would permit using a *makom patur* to access a rabbinic domain, but creates difficulty for Ze'iri. The *gemara*'s resolution at this stage is to bifurcate the two transmissions: Ze'iri's version of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling remains internally consistent and would locate the dispute about three or four in the width of the *karmelit* itself; Rav Dimi's version maintains that the dispute concerns the *makom patur* and that transit through a *makom patur* into a rabbinic domain is permitted.

### Holes Debate

The *gemara* raises a further question, setting up the third explanation. Even granting that the aqueduct is a *karmelit* when it runs through the open world, once it narrows as it passes between the buildings, why is it still a *karmelit*? Should it not be treated like the *chorei reshut harabbim* — the holes or recesses of a public domain — which retain the domain status of the larger space they serve? If the aqueduct is a *karmelit* in the broader waterway, should that status not extend even to the narrowed section between the buildings?

Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chanina bar Avin answer jointly: *ein chorin le-karmelit* — a *karmelit* does not have "holes" in the same way that biblical domains do. By a Torah-level domain such as the *reshut harabbim*, we say that attendant or adjacent spaces partake of the domain's status. But for the rabbinic *karmelit*, the rabbis were more lenient: once the waterway narrows below the threshold width, it loses its *karmelit* status even if a full-fledged *karmelit* continues downstream.

Rav Ashi adds a qualification: even if one holds that a *karmelit* does have "holes" — that is, that attendant spaces partake of its status — that applies only where those spaces are directly adjacent (*smucha*) to the main body. Here, by contrast, the full *karmelit* may be quite distant from the narrowed section between the buildings; at such a remove, the narrow passage cannot be considered a "hole" of the *karmelit*.

### Lavud Gap

Ravina proposes what the *gemara* presents as the most straightforward resolution. The debate is not about the minimum width of a *karmelit*, nor about the minimum size of a *makom patur*, nor about access via a *makom patur*. Rather, it is a simple dispute about *lavud*. In order to draw water, one constructed partial *mechitzos* — small walls — at the points where the aqueduct passes between the buildings, but left a gap between the walls and the banks. The question is: how large a gap does *lavud* close, rendering the walls halachically complete? Is a gap of less than three *tefachim* treated as closed, or must it be less than four?

This, Ravina notes, is precisely the well-established dispute between the *rabanan* and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel elsewhere in the *gemara*: the *rabanan* hold that *lavud* applies when the gap is less than three *tefachim*, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that *lavud* applies when the gap is less than four. Each *tanna* here simply follows his standard position on *lavud*. This reading avoids the need to challenge the universally accepted minimum size of a *karmelit* or the definition of a *makom patur*, and is accordingly far more straightforward than the preceding explanations.

## Balcony Walls

### Balcony Mishna

The *mishnah* addresses the *gezustra* — a balcony or platform projecting over a body of water — and the conditions required to draw water from it on *Shabbat*. One may not lower a bucket through a hole in the balcony unless walls ten *tefachim* high have been constructed, either above or below the level of the platform. The reason is that while the balcony, being attached to the building, is part of the *reshut hayachid*, the water below is a *karmelit*, and the walls — whether constructed above the platform or extending downward below it — are viewed as continuing all the way into the water. This creates an enclosed *reshut hayachid* in the space directly beneath the hole, permitting the drawing of water.

### Two Balconies

The *mishnah* adds a further case: if there are two balconies, one above the other but not directly stacked — one set out further than the other — and the upper balcony erected walls while the lower balcony did not, neither may draw water. Even the upper balcony, which did construct its *mechitzos*, is forbidden. This is because both balconies are competing for the same space: there is some form of access — whether a ladder between them or sufficient proximity to jump — that renders them as sharing the zone below. Since they have not made a joint *eruv*, neither can claim exclusive use of that space.

### Imaginary Walls

The *gemara* notes that this *mishnah*, which requires actual physical walls around the hole in the balcony, does not accord with the position of Chananya ben Akavya. A *baraita* records his view: if the *gezustra* is four *amos* by four *amos*, one may simply cut a hole of four by four *tefachim* in its center and draw water — no walls are needed, because the surrounding platform is imaginarily understood as bending downward around the hole on all sides. The *mishnah*'s requirement of real walls reflects the position of the *chachamim*, not Chananya ben Akavya.

## Tiberias Leniencies

### Water Drawing

Rabbi Yochanan, in the name of Rabbi Yose ben Zimra, clarifies the scope of Chananya ben Akavya's ruling: he only permitted this arrangement over the Kinneret, the Sea of Tiberias, because it has banks, surrounding towns, and enclosing yards that give it a special character. Over other bodies of water he would not have made this allowance.

Since the *gemara* is now discussing a ruling specific to Tiberias, it digresses to enumerate three leniencies that Chananya ben Akavya granted to the people of that city. First, he permitted drawing water from a *gezustra* on *Shabbat* even without constructing real *mechitzos*, relying instead on the imaginary bending of the platform's edges — this is the ruling already discussed. Second, he permitted burying fruit in legume pods without concern for ritual impurity. Third, he permitted drying oneself with towels on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* without fear that one might come to wring them out. The *gemara* notes this third leniency and will take it up subsequently.

### Fruit Burial

The second leniency — burying fruit in the pods of legumes — requires explanation. A *baraita* teaches: if a person rises early in the morning to gather the leftover husks or pods of legumes from the yard, and does so because he wants them moist, this constitutes a deliberate desire for the moisture on them. As a result, the dew that has fallen upon them is considered wanted, and the produce becomes susceptible to *tumah* — *ki yutan* — since susceptibility to ritual impurity requires both that liquid has come into contact with the food and that the owner desired that contact.

### Intent Doctrine

If, however, the person rose early not because he wanted the pods moist but simply because he had a full day of work ahead of him and wished to complete this task early, then his desire for the dew is immaterial — *eino be-ki yutan* — and the produce does not become susceptible to *tumah* as a result.

The *gemara* notes that the people of Tiberias were known for their industriousness: rising early was standard practice among them not out of any desire for moist produce but simply because of the press of the workday. Chananya ben Akavya's leniency, as Rashi explains it, was therefore the following: if one buried fruit in those pods — perhaps to keep it warm — the fruit would not become susceptible to *tumah*, because the dew on the pods was not desired by the people of Tiberias for any purpose related to the food. Their characteristic motivation was work, not moisture, and so the legal trigger for susceptibility was simply not present. The discussion of the third leniency — drying with towels — will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Eiruvin 88

## Chananya's Tiberias Leni…

### Intro & Chananya Overview

Daf 88 opens by wrapping up a brief digression that occupied the close of the previous daf. The Gemara had been discussing the remarkable leniencies granted by Chananya ben Akavia to the people of Tiberias in connection with the problem of drawing water from a balcony that protrudes over a body of water. Ordinarily, the halachic fiction of suspended walls (*mechitzos taluyos*) is not employed to create a valid *reshut hayachid*. Chananya went considerably further than even those who would permit suspended walls: he ruled that a flat extension over the water could itself be treated as though all of its edges were bent downward around the hole through which a bucket is lowered, thereby creating virtual walls without requiring any actual physical walls at all. This extraordinary leniency was confined to the people of Tiberias (*anshei Tveryah*), either because of the acute practical need arising from the dense population living along the shores of the Kinneret, or because the natural banks of the Kinneret already constituted a partial wall that made the additional leniency more defensible.

### Walls & Extensions

The nature of this first leniency — the wall-like treatment of the flat extension and the downward projection of walls — has already been analyzed. The Gemara now turns to present the second and third rulings Chananya issued in connection with the people of Tiberias, both of which appear at the opening of daf 88, amud 1, beginning with the words *u'mistapkin b'aluntit*.

### Legume Refuse

The second ruling concerned the refuse of legumes — perhaps the pods or outer casings — and the question of whether they were susceptible to *tumah*. In brief, Chananya ruled that they were not, because the people of Tiberias gathered them early in the morning not out of any interest in keeping them moist — which would be the operative consideration for *tumah* susceptibility — but simply because they needed to clear them away before beginning the workday. It should be noted that this was not a leniency particular to the people of Tiberias in any meaningful sense; it was the straightforward application of a general principle to their specific circumstances. This raises a broader reflection on what we even mean by *kula* and *chumra*: such terms are always relative to one's baseline assumption about the *halacha*. Someone doing what is actually required by the law is neither lenient nor stringent — they are simply following the *halacha* as they understand it.

### Towel Drying on Shabbat

The third ruling is the one introduced by the phrase *u'mistapkin b'aluntit*: Chananya permitted the people of Tiberias to dry themselves with towels. The Gemara asks: what exactly does this mean? A *baraita* is cited that clarifies: a person may dry himself with a towel after bathing in cold water on *Shabbat*, leave the towel in the window to dry — the prohibition against squeezing (*sechitah*) being understood throughout — and must not hand the towel over to the bathhouse attendants, because those attendants are suspected of wringing out towels. The concern is *lifnei iver* or a form of facilitating a violation: even if the attendants are themselves acting improperly on *Shabbat*, one should not contribute to the situation by placing the towel in their hands.

This raises a natural question about the scenario: if the bath in question was in a bathhouse, how were the bathers permitted to be in a bathhouse at all on *Shabbat*? The Gemara's discussion assumes cold water, which sidesteps the prohibition against bathing in hot water on *Shabbat*, but exactly how this plays out in an actual bathhouse setting — and what the attendants were doing there on *Shabbat* — remains somewhat unclear. The concern articulated is not that the bather should rebuke the attendants for working on *Shabbat*, but rather the narrower point that one should not place a wet towel in their hands.

The *baraita* continues: *divrei Rabbi Shimon*, this is Rabbi Shimon's view. And Rabbi Shimon further adds — *af meivi beyado letoch beito* — that one may even carry the towel home. The concern that one might come to squeeze the towel while carrying it is dismissed. The practical upshot is that this ruling about towel-drying is not a specialized enactment for the people of Tiberias; it is a general *halacha* that happened to come up frequently in their context, presumably because they regularly bathed in or near the Kinneret. The distinction between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon is that the *tanna kamma* requires leaving the towel at the bathhouse (placing it in a window to dry), while Rabbi Shimon permits carrying it home.

---

## Drawing vs. Pouring

### Rav Huna's Ruling

The Gemara now returns to the central topic with a ruling from Rabbah bar Rav Huna: *lo shanu ela lemallot* — the permission discussed in connection with the balcony over the water applies only to drawing water (*mallot*) from the water below. *Aval lishpoch assur* — to pour water downward from the balcony is forbidden.

One might initially suppose the distinction is based on need: there is greater necessity for drawing water than for disposing of it, and therefore the leniency applies only where necessity warrants it. But the Gemara will not take that path. The distinction will instead be grounded in the directionality and behavior of the water itself.

When one draws water up through the hole in the balcony, the water, at the moment of drawing, is contained within the virtual *reshut hayachid* created by the fictional walls extending downward. It stays there. But when one pours water down, the water strikes the surface below and flows outward — out of the virtual *reshut hayachid* and into the surrounding body of water, which has the status of a *karmelis*. Essentially, the act of pouring down results in transferring the water from a *reshut hayachid* to a *karmelis*, and even if unintended, that flow is the predictable and regular consequence of the action.

### Rav Shizvi's Challenge

Rav Shizvi raises a challenge: *vechi mah bein zeh le-ukkah* — what is the difference between this case and the case of the pit (*uka*) that we will encounter in the Mishnah at the bottom of this daf? The Mishnah there deals with a small courtyard from which waste water threatens to run off into the *reshut harabim*. The remedy prescribed is to dig a pit in the courtyard: one pours the water into the pit, and even if the pit is already somewhat full and water will run off into the *reshut harabim* regardless, the act is permitted — because one's intention was to put the water into the pit, not into the *reshut harabim*, and the diversion of water from there is incidental.

The parallel seems to undercut Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling. Why should pouring water from the balcony be forbidden on the grounds that it will flow out into the *karmelis*? If we permit pouring into a pit in the courtyard even when we know the water will flow from the pit into the *reshut harabim*, the same logic should apply here: one's act is directed at the virtual *reshut hayachid* below, and whatever flows from there into the *karmelis* is incidental.

### Resolution: Absorption v…

The Gemara's answer is captured in the phrase *hani tayeimi vehani lo tayeimi* — the waters in the one case cease and the waters in the other do not. In the case of the courtyard pit, the fundamental design of the pit is that the water absorbs into the earth. Even if there is currently water standing in the pit, that is a temporary state; the ground will eventually absorb it. Therefore, the pit regularly and typically has available capacity, and one's act of pouring into it is genuinely an act of putting water into a receiving vessel that will hold it. By contrast, when water is poured down from the balcony onto the open surface of the Kinneret, there is no such absorption. The water flows outward continuously and immediately. There is never a state of rest within the virtual *reshut hayachid*. The water's movement out into the *karmelis* is not an occasional overflow but the constant, predictable reality. It is therefore treated as though one is pouring directly into the *karmelis*, even if technically the water passes through the *reshut hayachid* first.

### Alternative: No Distinct…

The Gemara then presents an alternative version of Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling: *lo teima lemalos hu deshari lishpoch assur* — do not say that drawing is permitted and pouring is forbidden. Rather, *lishpoch nami shari* — pouring too is permitted. Rav Sheshes remarks that this is obvious — *hainu uka*, this is simply the case of the pit. The Gemara then notes: one might have thought the distinction *hani tayeimi vehani lo tayeimi* applies — that the pit case is better because the water is eventually absorbed, and the balcony case is worse because it is not — and therefore, *kamashmalan*, the ruling comes to teach us that we do not draw that distinction. According to this second view, there is no meaningful difference between drawing and pouring, and the balcony case is treated the same as the pit: once the act is directed at a valid receptacle within the *reshut hayachid*, what subsequently happens to the water is not the actor's concern.

---

## Two Balconies & Ownership

### Rav Huna on Proximity

The Mishnah now introduces the case of two balconies (*gezustraos*), one above the other, where the upper balcony has constructed the proper apparatus and the lower has not. The Gemara had previously established that in such a configuration, because the lower balcony can access the upper one — the occupants can come up, or perhaps jump across — the territory is considered contested, and neither may use the well without an *eiruv*.

Rav Huna, citing Rav, rules: *lo shanu ella bismucha* — the ruling that the lower balcony creates a problem for the upper applies only when the two are within four *tefachim* of each other horizontally. If the lower balcony is more than four *tefachim* away horizontally (*mupleges*), the upper one is unaffected and may use its apparatus freely. This reflects the principle Rav articulated elsewhere: *ein adam oser al chaveiro derech avir* — one cannot restrict another's domain through access that requires traversal of open air alone. A gap of four or more *tefachim* is considered effectively impassable for practical purposes, and therefore the lower balcony's occupants are not considered to have meaningful access to the upper one.

### Gezel & Churvah

A new principle is now introduced, cited in two versions attributing it either to Rabbi Chiya or to Rabbi Oshaya (with Rabbah citing Rav in one version and Rabbi Yosef citing Rabbi Oshaya in another): *yesh gezel beshabbos, vechurva machzir lebaalim* — there is (as it were) *gezel* on *Shabbat*, and a ruin returns to its owners.

What does this mean? Rashi explains the context as follows. Imagine two courtyards — belonging to A and B respectively — without a shared *eiruv*, and between them an abandoned lot (*churva*) belonging to B. In practice, during the week, B allows A to use the lot. On *Shabbat*, can A carry within it as though it were part of A's courtyard? This question engages the intersection of *Choshen Mishpat* and *hilchos eiruvin*: does A's habitual use — their quasi-possession — give them enough of a foothold to treat the lot as part of their *reshut* for purposes of *Shabbat* carrying?

The phrase *yesh gezel beshabbos* — meaning, as the Gemara will clarify, *yesh din gezel beshabbos* — suggests that the laws of *gezel* remain operative on *Shabbat*. This is not to say that one is prosecuted for *gezel* in a monetary court; rather, it means that even on *Shabbat*, A's use of the lot is not treated as a valid acquisition (*kniyas*) of the space. The lot is still legally B's, and A's informal use does not transform it into part of A's domain. And *churva machzir lebaalim* — the ruin returns to its true owner — completes the point: regardless of who is practically using it, it belongs to B, and therefore A cannot carry in it without a proper *eiruv*.

### Resolving Contradiction

At first glance, *yesh gezel beshabbos* and *churva machzir lebaalim* appear to contradict each other. The first phrase seems to say A acquires the lot (*kanya*), the second seems to say A does not (*lo kanya*). The Gemara resolves this: *hachi kaamar* — what it really means is *yesh din gezel beshabbos*, the *din* (law) of *gezel* applies. That is, A's use of the lot is considered a form of *gezel* — in the sense that it is not a genuine acquisition — and therefore *churva machzir lebaalim*, the lot is treated as reverting to its true owner, B. The two phrases are thus consistent: the law of *gezel* applies on *Shabbat*, meaning the informal use creates no valid ownership, and so the lot returns, in legal contemplation, to its actual owner. A cannot carry in it as though it were part of A's courtyard.

The introduction of this principle represents a significant conceptual shift. Up to this point, the entire analysis of contested space had been framed around questions of practical access — who can reach the space, how easily, at what cost. Now the Gemara introduces the criterion of ownership and asserts that, in at least some contexts, ownership overrides practical access entirely.

### Balconies & Walls

The Gemara now applies this principle back to the case of the two balconies: *umotvinan ashmatin* — we challenge the ruling just stated. If *yesh din gezel beshabbos* — if ownership is what matters — why does the Mishnah say the lower balcony's presence restricts the upper? Even if the lower occupants regularly access the upper balcony's apparatus, that access is merely de facto use. It does not give them ownership. The upper balcony belongs to its owner. Why should the lower occupants' use create a restriction on what is unambiguously the upper owner's property?

Rav Sheshes answers: *hacha bemai askinan kegon she'asu mechitza beshutfus* — we are speaking of a case where the lower balcony's occupants contributed to the construction of the walls that enable the apparatus to function. The walls are therefore jointly owned. It is not merely that the lower occupants use the upper space; they have a genuine proprietary interest in the walls that make the space valid. This co-ownership of the walls is what creates the contested status.

This is admittedly a somewhat *heichi timtza* — a technically constrained — answer. The Mishnah itself does not mention shared construction of the walls, and one would have expected it to do so if that were the operative fact. But the Gemara accepts this as the reading of the Mishnah necessary to reconcile it with the principle of *yesh din gezel beshabbos*.

### Challenge: Own Balcony

The Gemara now raises a difficulty: *ihachi ki asu letachtona nami*? If the problem in the Mishnah is that the lower balcony has co-ownership of the walls, why does the Mishnah imply that the problem is resolved when the lower balcony constructs its own apparatus? The straightforward understanding of the Mishnah is that once each party has made their own setup, there is no competition — A will use A's apparatus and B will use B's — and therefore both may use freely. That reasoning makes sense if the issue is practical competition. But if B has a proprietary stake in the walls of A's apparatus, then even after B makes their own, B still has a co-ownership interest in A's walls. Why should B's making of their own apparatus dissolve that ownership claim?

### Renunciation of Interest

The Gemara's answer: *kivan de'asu letachtona, gilluy gallia deitei de-hana bahadach lo nichle* — once the lower party constructs their own apparatus, they have made a clear and manifest declaration of intent (*gilluy da'at*) that they are no longer interested in the upper one. By investing in their own facility, they effectively renounce whatever interest or claim they had in the upper party's walls. The co-ownership is thereby dissolved by the act of construction itself.

The broader significance of this entire discussion should not be lost. The Gemara spent considerable time — the better part of the preceding week's learning — developing a framework based entirely on practical access and competition. Now, at the conclusion of that discussion, the Gemara introduces ownership as an independent and overriding criterion. A space that is owned by one party belongs to that party for purposes of *Shabbat* carrying, regardless of who else uses it in practice. This reframing requires a complete re-reading of the Mishnah: what appeared to be a question of who uses the balcony is revealed to be a question of who owns the walls. Ownership, not use, is the determinative criterion — at least where the ownership question is real.

---

## Water Disposal & Pits

### Mishnah on Pits

We now arrive at the final Mishnah of the eighth *perek*, which deals with the disposal of waste water. It is worth noting, as a preliminary matter, that the entire subsequent discussion proceeds without any concern about *zoreia* — the prohibition against sowing — even though pouring water onto a dirt surface might seem to implicate agricultural *melachos*. In practice, if one is pouring onto bare, hard-packed dirt in a courtyard where nothing is growing, there is no issue of *zoreia*. The concern about adding water to loose particulate matter — which might constitute *lisha* (kneading) by binding separate particles into a unified mass — does not apply when the surface is hard earth rather than sand or loose soil. The Mishnah's silence on these concerns is therefore understandable.

The Mishnah states: *chatzer shepichusa me'arba amos ein shofchin betocha mayim beShabbos* — a courtyard that is less than four *amos* may not have water poured into it on *Shabbat*. The reasoning is as follows. When a courtyard is of sufficient size, one pours waste water into the courtyard and the bulk of it is absorbed into the ground; whatever small amount runs off into the *reshut harabim* is entirely unintended and statistically improbable. But when the courtyard is very small — less than four *amos* in the relevant dimension — the water will almost certainly run from the courtyard into the *reshut harabim*, and even though one did not intend to pour into the *reshut harabim*, it is treated rabbinically as though one effectively did.

One might ask whether this should depend on how many households are disposing water and how much water each uses. The Gemara does not pursue that line of analysis; it treats the four-*amah* threshold as a fixed standard. In any case, a courtyard of less than four by four *amos* — roughly six feet by six feet — is unlikely to serve many households to begin with.

If the courtyard is too small, the Mishnah prescribes a remedy: *ella im kein asu lah uka machazeket sasayim* — one must construct a pit (*uka*) capable of holding two *se'ah* of water. Two *se'ah* is assumed to be the normal daily water disposal of a single household. According to Rav Chaim Na'eh, a *se'ah* is 8.29 liters, so two *se'ah* is approximately 16.58 liters — equivalent to roughly eight of the standard two-liter bottles. This is not a particularly large volume; the cavity in question would be perhaps a foot by a foot by a foot in rough approximation.

### Pit Measurement

The Mishnah specifies: *asu lah uka machazeket sasayim min hanekev ulemattah* — the pit must be capable of holding two *se'ah* measured from the opening (*nekev*) downward. Even if the pit currently contains standing water that has not yet been absorbed, as long as the cavity itself — the total volume from the rim downward — is sufficient to hold two *se'ah*, the condition is met. The key measurement is the size of the cavity, not the available empty space at any given moment.

The Mishnah further specifies: *bein mibachutz bein mibifnim* — the pit may be located either inside the courtyard or outside it. However, *ella shebachutz tzarich likmor* — if the pit is located outside the courtyard, in the *reshut harabim*, it must be covered (*kamur*), whereas a pit inside the courtyard does not need to be covered.

### Covering & Debris

This provision — that a pit in the *reshut harabim* must be covered — requires explanation. The most obvious scenario is that one situates the pit inside the courtyard, near or adjacent to the boundary with the *reshut harabim*, and the cavity extends underground beneath the *reshut harabim*. The water enters the pit from within the courtyard and drains underground into the larger cavity beneath the public domain. If left open — that is, if the pit were uncovered — it would appear as though one were pouring directly into the *reshut harabim*, since the visible opening in the *reshut harabim* would obviously be receiving water. Covering the pit resolves this appearance problem: from the surface of the *reshut harabim*, nothing is visible, and whatever occurs below the surface is hidden.

A second and related explanation, attributed to Rashi as cited by the *Beis Meir*, focuses on the status of the pit as a *makom patur*. A depression in the ground that is more than three *tefachim* deep and less than four by four *tefachim* in area constitutes a *makom patur* — an exempt space that is neither a *reshut hayachid* nor a *reshut harabim* and from which carrying is Biblically neutral. If such a pit is located in the *reshut harabim*, it may serve as an intermediate stopping point for the water, thereby eliminating the concern about pouring from a *reshut hayachid* into a *reshut harabim*. However, if the pit is uncovered, debris from the *reshut harabim* — stones, dirt, refuse — may fall in and gradually raise the floor of the pit to less than three *tefachim* below ground level. At that point, the pit loses its *makom patur* status and becomes part of the *reshut harabim* around it. Covering the pit prevents this accumulation and ensures that the *makom patur* status is maintained.

Both explanations have merit, and it is somewhat striking that the *rishonim* do not elaborate more fully on this point. There is also a broader conceptual question: a covered underground tunnel or cavity — to use a modern analogy, something like a utility vault beneath a public street — is it considered part of the *reshut harabim* at all, given that it is covered and has no direct public access from above? If access to a space is primarily from below or from the side rather than from the surface of the *reshut harabim*, the question of its domain classification becomes genuinely complex. The covering of the pit may work precisely by severing any visual or functional connection to the *reshut harabim* above, thereby allowing the cavity to function independently as a *makom patur*.

In any event, the principle is ironic and worth noting: the Mishnah effectively prefers that one construct a drainage channel that goes underground beneath the *reshut harabim* rather than simply pour water into a large open courtyard and let it run off naturally. The former, with appropriate covering, is permitted; the latter, if the courtyard is too small, is not.

### R. Eliezer ben Yaakov

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov now offers a different standard: *biv hakamurarba amos bireshus harabim shofchin lesocho mayim beShabbos* — a drainage pipe (*biv*) that is covered and extends four *amos* into the *reshut harabim* suffices to permit pouring. On its face, this sounds similar to the previous ruling about covered pits, but Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov specifies four *amos* rather than the two-*se'ah* standard of the Mishnah's first ruling. Four *amos* is a substantially larger space than a cavity holding two *se'ah* — the latter being roughly the size of a half-*amah* cube, whereas four by four *amos* is a sizable expanse. The Gemara will analyze what lies behind this discrepancy.

### Chachamim on Drainage

The Sages (*Chachamim*) then state: *afilu gag o chatzer meiah amah lo yishpoch al pi habiiv* — even if one has a roof or a courtyard a hundred *amos* in size, one may not pour water directly into the drainage pipe. This is because the drainage pipe channels water directly into the *reshut harabim*, and pouring into the mouth of the pipe is functionally equivalent to pouring into the *reshut harabim* regardless of the distance the water travels before reaching its outlet. The mere fact that there is a hundred-*amah* expanse of roof between the person pouring and the street does not matter; the act is directed at the pipe, and the pipe is directed at the *reshut harabim*.

However, *aval shofech hu legag vehamayim yordim labiiv* — one may pour the water onto the roof itself, and the water will then run on its own into the drainage pipe. As long as one's act is directed at the roof surface — a valid domain — and the subsequent flow into the pipe is incidental and not the immediate result of one's pour, the Sages permit it.

### Courtyard & Portico

The Mishnah then adds two further provisions. First: *hachatzer veha'achsadra mitztarfin learba amos* — a courtyard and an adjacent *achsadra* (a covered portico or colonnade) may be combined to meet the four-*amah* threshold. If neither alone is four *amos* but together they total the requisite area, the combination suffices.

Second: the Mishnah addresses the case of two balconies facing each other, some of whose occupants have made a pit and some have not — *miktzasan asu uka umiktzasan lo asu uka*. Those who made the pit may pour; those who did not may not. This is relatively straightforward: the entitlement to pour water into the courtyard is contingent on having satisfied the pit requirement, and it is determined on an individual basis. One party's compliance does not extend to cover another.

---

## Intent vs. Absorption

### Rava: Intent & Dust

The Gemara now probes the underlying rationale for the four-*amah* standard. Rava explains: *adam asuy l'histapek sa'atayim mayim bechol yom* — a person typically uses two *se'ah* of water per day that require disposal, *u've'arba amot adam rotzeh le-zalfan* — and if one's courtyard is four by four *amos*, one actually wants the water to remain there. Why? Because a dirt courtyard generates dust, and one periodically sprinkles water on the ground precisely to suppress the dust. In a courtyard of four by four *amos*, the water serves a useful purpose and the owner genuinely wishes to retain it. Therefore, disposing of water into such a courtyard is not an act of getting rid of it; it is an act of using it. There is no concern that it will run into the *reshut harabim* in a problematic way, because the owner is content for it to remain.

In a courtyard smaller than four by four *amos*, by contrast, either the dust problem is minimal or the volume of water becomes excessive for the available surface area, and the owner simply wants to get rid of the water. The act of disposal is therefore directed at removing the water from one's domain, and the likelihood of it running into the *reshut harabim* becomes the operative concern. According to Rava, then, the four-*amah* threshold is fundamentally a matter of *intent*: does the owner want the water in the courtyard or not?

### R. Zeira: Absorption

Rabbi Zeira disagrees. The four-*amah* standard has nothing to do with whether the owner wants the water. It is a question of whether the courtyard can physically absorb the water. *Arba amot ta'amei* — four *amos* is the threshold because a surface of that area has sufficient capacity to absorb two *se'ah* of water. *Pachot me'arba amot lo taimei* — less than that, it will not absorb fully, and the water will inevitably run off. For Rabbi Zeira, the determinative consideration is physical reality — the absorption capacity of the ground — not the owner's subjective intention.

### Abye's Nafka Mina

Abaye identifies the practical difference (*nafka mina*) between the two positions: *arikh v'katin ika beinaihu* — a courtyard that is long and narrow rather than square. If the operative criterion is total area (Rabbi Zeira's view), then a courtyard with a total area of sixteen square *amos* — whether it is four by four or eight by two — has the same absorption capacity, and the *halacha* should be the same in both cases. If, however, the criterion is whether the owner wants to sprinkle the water and keep it in the courtyard (Rava's view), then a long narrow courtyard, even if its area equals sixteen square *amos*, is not the type of space for which one would sprinkle water to suppress dust. Rashi notes simply that a long narrow space is not suited for sprinkling, though the reason is not fully articulated.

The Gemara then attempts to prove the matter from the Mishnah and a *baraita*. The Mishnah that combines a courtyard with a *portico* seems to favor Rabbi Zeira: combining two spaces of different shapes to achieve a threshold of sixteen square *amos* is a matter of total area, not square dimensions. Rav Zeira defends Rava by explaining that the *portico* runs the full length of the courtyard, so when combined they produce a shape that is four by four — a proper square — and therefore no challenge to Rava's position results.

The *baraita*, on the other hand, explicitly states: *chatzer she'ein ba arba amot al arba amot* — a courtyard that is not four *amos* by four *amos*, using the standard formulation that specifies dimensions in both directions. This seems to support Rava, for whom proportions matter, and to challenge Rabbi Zeira, for whom total area is all that counts.

### Rava's Proof

Rava then offers a proof from the language of the Mishnah itself. The Mishnah uses the phrasing *chatzer shepachuta me'arba amos* — a courtyard less than four — rather than the standard *chatzer she'ein ba arba amot al arba amot* (a courtyard that is not four by four). This is notable. If the Mishnah intended to require minimum dimensions in each direction — a proper square of at least four by four — it would have used the familiar formulation. Instead, it simply says "less than four," which most naturally refers to total magnitude rather than specific dimensions in each direction. From this, Rava argues, one may infer that the Mishnah is concerned with area rather than proportions, and therefore the Mishnah aligns with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's absorption-based approach.

### Drainage Pipe Debate

The Gemara draws together the discussion by connecting it explicitly to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *Chachamim* regarding pouring into the drainage pipe. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov permits pouring directly into a covered drainage pipe of four *amos* in the *reshut harabim*, because for him the operative question is whether there is sufficient capacity for absorption. Once there is enough space — whether in the ground of a courtyard or in the volume of an underground pipe — absorption is theoretically possible, and that suffices. It does not matter that one is pouring directly into the mouth of the pipe; what matters is the physical reality of what can be absorbed.

The *Chachamim*, by contrast, prohibit pouring directly into the drainage pipe even when the roof is a hundred *amos* long. For them, the operative question is intent and the direction of one's act. Pouring into the pipe is pouring toward the *reshut harabim*, because the pipe's function is to carry water there. The theoretical possibility of absorption along the way is irrelevant to how we classify the act. Only by pouring onto the roof — a space where one can genuinely wish for the water to remain — does the act become permitted.

The Gemara thus elegantly maps the abstract dispute between Rava and Rabbi Zeira onto the concrete disagreement between the *Chachamim* and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: the *Chachamim* hold that intent and the direction of one's action are determinative (Rava's approach), while Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that physical absorption capacity is what matters (Rabbi Zeira's approach).

---

## Rainy vs. Dry Season

### Baraita: Rainy Season

A *baraita* is cited that introduces a significant relaxation of all the foregoing requirements: *bameh devarim amurim* — when do all these requirements apply? *Bi'ymei hachama* — in the summer, the dry season. *Aval bi'ymei hageshamim* — but in the rainy season, *shofech veshoneh ve'eino nimna* — one may pour as much water as one wishes and need not refrain at all, without any pit requirement whatsoever.

### Rava Explains

Rava explains the reason for this blanket dispensation in the rainy season along two lines. First, the concern that one wants to remove the water from the courtyard — because a small courtyard becomes too wet and the owner wishes to expel the water — dissolves entirely during the rainy season, when the courtyard is already saturated from rainfall. One does not particularly care whether the additional water stays or goes. Second, the concern that it will appear as though one is deliberately sending water into the *reshut harabim* — that observers will say "his drainage pipe is discharging into the street" — also dissolves, because in the rainy season all drainage pipes are discharging into the street. Water in the *reshut harabim* is unremarkable; it is there from the rain regardless. Neither the subjective intent concern nor the objective appearance concern is operative in the rainy season.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rava's explanation. Rava said that in normal circumstances, when one has a four-by-four courtyard and pours water in, the act is permitted because the owner wants the water there — he wants it to suppress the dust. If so, one could ask: even when the courtyard is too small, why should overuse be a concern? In the Mishnah's framework, even with a pit, there is a maximum amount one may pour corresponding to the pit's capacity. Why does that limit exist at all, if in principle one simply wants the water to stay in the courtyard and absorb?

Rava's answer is implicit in the structure: in the summer, when a courtyard is less than four *amos*, the owner does not want the water there — the space is too small and it becomes a nuisance — so the water runs out, and that creates the appearance problem. The pit is the prescribed solution, and its size (two *se'ah*) is calibrated to the maximum reasonable daily disposal. In the rainy season, as Rava explained, neither the desire to expel nor the appearance problem applies, and therefore no pit is necessary at all.

### Rav Nachman's View

Rav Nachman takes a more measured position. He does not concede that the rainy season eliminates all requirements; he maintains that even then some standard of proportionality applies. *Ukma machzik sasayim notnim lo sasayim* — if the pit holds two *se'ah*, one may pour in two *se'ah* of water. *Machzik seah* — if the pit holds only one *se'ah* — normally, in the dry season, a pit of only one *se'ah* would be entirely insufficient and one could pour nothing at all. But in the rainy season, that smaller pit suffices: *notnim lo seah* — one may pour in one *se'ah*. The leniency of the rainy season manifests not in eliminating the pit requirement altogether but in allowing smaller pits to suffice proportionally. 

The inverse question naturally arises: in the dry season, if one has a pit of only one *se'ah*, should one at least be permitted to pour in that one *se'ah*? No, rules Rav Nachman: *gezeirah dilma ati leiten lah sasayim* — we are concerned that one will pour the full two *se'ah* of the typical daily usage, exceeding the pit's capacity. In the dry season, where the risks are real and the standards are strict, we do not permit partial use of an undersized pit, lest one become accustomed to using it and eventually overuse it.

And why, Abaye asks, do we not apply the same precautionary logic in the rainy season — why not prohibit even the proportional use of a small pit lest one overuse it? The Gemara returns to the same dual rationale: *ee mishum kilkul chatzeiro, ha mekulkal veka'ei* — if one were concerned about the courtyard being ruined by excess water, the courtyard is already ruined by the rain. *Ee mishum gezeirah shema yomru tzinoro shel ploni mekaleach mayim, stam tzinorot mekalachim hem* — if one were concerned about the appearance of one's pipe discharging into the street, all pipes are discharging in the rainy season. There is simply no occasion for either concern to take hold.

### Abaye: Large Pits OK

Abaye draws a final conclusion: *hilkach* — therefore — the dispensation in the rainy season is not merely about the minimum thresholds but about any amount whatsoever. *Afilu kor va'afilu korayim* — even a *kor* or two *korim* of water — vastly exceeding the two-*se'ah* standard — may be poured in the rainy season, because the foundational concerns that generated all the requirements of pits and dimensions and covered drainage pipes simply do not apply when it is raining. Whatever variation exists among the Amoraim — whether no pit is needed at all (the *baraita*'s position), or a smaller proportional pit suffices (Rav Nachman's position) — they all agree that the rainy season significantly relaxes the standard, and Abaye's conclusion is that the relaxation is effectively unlimited once the underlying rationale has dissolved.

The *perek* is not completed in this shiur and will, God willing, be concluded in the next session.

---

---

# Eiruvin 89

## Water & Pit Issue

### Intro & Review

Daf 89 begins with a brief return to the close of the preceding *perek*, picking up from 88b. The discussion there concerned the disposal of waste water on *Shabbat*: if one pours water into a courtyard that measures at least four by four *amot*, the water will be absorbed and there is no concern; but if the courtyard is smaller, the water will run off, creating an appearance — or an actuality — of pouring directly into the *reshut harabim*. The remedy established by the Gemara was that one must prepare a pit (*bor*) into which the water can drain. The *mishna* at the end of that *perek* then introduced a case involving two second-story balconies overlooking a shared courtyard, one of which had made such a pit and one of which had not. The ruling was that only the balcony adjacent to the pit may pour water into the courtyard; the other may not.

### Two Balconies

The case requires closer examination. On the surface, one might expect that since both balconies overlook the same courtyard and the courtyard contains a pit, either party should be able to pour into the yard — after all, there is a pit there. The *mishna*'s asymmetry, granting rights to one and not the other, calls for explanation. To visualize the scenario in plan view: House One and House Two share a *chatzer*, and it is House One that arranged the pit. The Gemara will probe why the presence of that pit does not extend its benefit to the other party as well.

### Rava's Position

Four lines from the bottom of 88b, Rava opens the discussion: *amar Rava v'chein shtei diyutos — afilu ervu*, even if the two households made an *eruv*, one remains unable to use the pit. Before arriving at the Gemara's ultimate resolution, it is worth understanding what Rava is introducing. The scenario, drawn flat, is simply two houses opening onto a shared *chatzer*. When two such houses share a *chatzer*, they are required to make an *eruv chatzerot* with one another. Rava is going to assert that even when they have done so, the problem of the *mishna* persists. The Gemara will later clarify that the real issue concerns a case where no *eruv* was made, but Rava begins by framing the problem more broadly.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rava: *amar Abaye mai ta'ama* — what exactly is the problem, even if they made an *eruv*? Abaye proposes that Rava may be bothered by a concern about water quantity — *nefisha demaya*. Perhaps a small courtyard with a pit was only ever permitted when a single household uses it. Once two households pour into the same pit, there may simply be too much water for the pit to handle, and thus neither should be permitted. This would explain why the *mishna* assigns usage to only one party: we give it to the one who arranged the pit and tell the other one that they have now exceeded the threshold.

Abaye rejects this interpretation, however, by citing a *baraita*: *achad uka ve-achad gistera breicha va-areiva* — whether the receptacle is an underground pit, a pottery vessel (*gistera*), a furrow, or a kneading trough (*areiva*), all of these are valid solutions. Crucially, the *baraita* adds: *af al pi she-nitmalu mayim me-erev shabbat, shofchin letocho mayim be-shabbat* — even if they were already filled from *erev shabbat*, it remains permitted to pour into them on *Shabbat*. This demonstrates that once one has satisfied the formal criterion — possessing a pit or equivalent receptacle — the actual capacity of the vessel is irrelevant. The pit may already be full and incapable of receiving more water, yet halachically the requirement is satisfied. It follows logically that the same criterion applies regardless of how many people are using the yard; if the pit's practical capacity is irrelevant in one direction, it is irrelevant across the board. And additionally, if the concern were simply about excessive water, the *mishna* would have forbidden both parties rather than permitting one and forbidding the other.

Abaye's reading of Rava's own position, reconstructed: Rava himself read the *mishna* as saying that a single pit was only instituted for a single household. Once two households use the yard, the one-pit arrangement is insufficient. Rather than forbid both, we assign the pit's benefit to the one who made it, restoring the single-household premise and permitting that party to pour. Abaye, however, demonstrates from the *baraita* that practical capacity is simply not the operative concern, and therefore the real issue must lie elsewhere.

### Rava Clarified

The Gemara then re-presents Rava's view with a correction: *ela i itmar hachi itmar — amar Rava lo shanu ela shelo eirvu*. The problem in the *mishna* arises specifically when the two households did not make an *eruv*. Without an *eruv*, neither party may carry objects from their dwelling into the *chatzer*. The party whose pit is nearby can avoid this prohibition: he pours his waste water onto his own balcony, it runs off naturally, and flows into the yard. He has not carried anything into the *chatzer* directly. The other party, whose balcony is more distant, cannot accomplish the same. If he wishes to use the pit, he would have to carry his vessel down into the yard — precisely what is forbidden without an *eruv*. We are therefore concerned (*gezeira dilma ati l'apukei mimani debatim lehatam*) that permitting him to use the pit will lead him to carry his household vessels out into the *chatzer*. But with an *eruv* — *aval eirvu mutarin* — both parties may freely use the pit, since there is no longer any concern about carrying in the *chatzer*. This concludes the discussion of the final *sugya* of *perek* "Keitzad Mishtatefin."

---

## Domains & No Eruv

### Objects & Movement

The penultimate *perek*, "Kol HaGagot," opens with a focused examination of what follows from the absence of an *eruv*. When a group of households sharing a *chatzer* fails to make an *eruv chatzerot* among themselves, certain movements of objects become prohibited. Specifically: one may not carry an object from one's house into the *chatzer*, nor from the *chatzer* into any house, nor consequently from one house to another, even by a route that passes through the *chatzer*. Even if the houses were somehow directly connected, their being separately owned makes them distinct *reshuyot*, and carrying between them is prohibited.

What does remain permitted is movement within a single *reshut*: one may carry within one's own house freely, and objects that began *Shabbat* in the *chatzer* may be moved throughout the *chatzer*. The *chatzer* remains a *reshut hayachid* by virtue of its *lechi* or *korah* and its enclosed walls; the only prohibition is the crossing of domain boundaries.

### Object Identity

The crucial halachic principle governing these cases is that an object's identity — the domain to which it belongs for purposes of *Shabbat* — is fixed by its location when *Shabbat* begins. An object that began *Shabbat* in the *chatzer* may circulate throughout the *chatzer*. An object that began in one's house and was then improperly carried into the *chatzer* does not acquire a new *reshut* identity; it retains its association with the house, and moving it further within the *chatzer* remains prohibited. Conversely, a *chatzer* object that began there legitimately may be moved freely within the *chatzer*, but not into any of the houses. Domain identity is a fixed attribute, not a floating one.

### Multiple Courtyards

A further question arises: if there are multiple courtyards that open into one another, and no *eruv* has been made among them — or even if an *eruv* was made within each courtyard separately but not between them — may one carry from one courtyard into the next? Are all courtyards considered, even without an *eruv*, a single domain? The reasoning that might support this: courtyards are used less intensively and less personally than houses. Houses are the primary locations of household objects and personal domain; they are distinctly owned and felt as distinct *reshuyot*. Courtyards, being more general and communal spaces, might be treated as a single undifferentiated category, such that an object starting in any courtyard could freely move to any other courtyard. This is the analytical question the *perek* will address — beginning with the specific case of rooftops.

---

## Rooftops Mishna

### Mishna Text

The *mishna* opens: *kol ha-gagot ir reshut achat* — all the rooftops of a town are one domain — *u-vilvad shelo yehei gag gavo'ah asarah o namuch asarah* — provided that no one rooftop is ten *tefachim* higher or lower than its neighbor. A height differential of ten *tefachim* would apparently classify it as a distinct domain. Since all rooftops are already more than ten *tefachim* above the ground (by virtue of the walls below), this qualification — that one rooftop not be ten higher or lower than another — is puzzling, and the Gemara will address why such a height difference should matter at all. This is the position of Rabbi Meir.

### Three Positions

The *mishna* then presents two additional positions. The *Chachamim* reject Rabbi Meir's leniency: *kol echad ve-echad reshut bifnei atzmo* — each and every rooftop is its own distinct domain, and one may not carry from one to another. Rabbi Shimon is the most lenient of the three. He declares that *achat gaghot ve-achat chatzerot ve-achat karpifot* — whether rooftops, courtyards, or *karpifot* (enclosed lots surrounded by a fence) — *reshut achat hen* — they are all a single domain — *le-keilim she-shavtu letokan* — for vessels that began *Shabbat* within them — *ve-lo le-keilim she-shavtu betoch habayit* — but not for vessels that began *Shabbat* inside a house. Objects that begin in a house cannot be carried into any of these spaces even if they are accidentally brought out; they retain their house identity. But objects that began in any of these spaces — rooftop, courtyard, or *karpef* — may be moved freely among all of them.

### Rabbi Shimon

A natural question arises about Rabbi Shimon's formulation: does he mean that rooftops are one category among themselves, courtyards one among themselves, and *karpifot* one among themselves — i.e., each type is internally unified — or does he mean that all three types together form a single unified domain? The Gemara reads him in the most expansive sense: all three types are one single *reshut*. The reasoning is that all of these spaces are technically *reshut hayachid* and none of them is a home. Homes are the primary locus of personal domain; they carry a sharp and distinct identity. All other spaces — rooftops, courtyards, and *karpifot* — share the character of being *reshut hayachid* without being living spaces, and therefore constitute one broad, undifferentiated category. Under Rabbi Shimon's view, one may carry from a courtyard to a rooftop (via a ladder, since one cannot pass through a house), from that rooftop into a *karpef*, and from one *karpef* into another, as long as none of it began in a house.

The *Tanna Kamma* — Rabbi Meir — says only that all rooftops are one; whether he extends the same principle to courtyards among themselves or to *karpifot* among themselves is left open by the *mishna*. The Gemara will clarify this. As for the *Chachamim*, they dispute even the basic premise.

---

## Height Difference

### Height Problem

The Gemara at this point engages the two sons of Rav Avin — Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin — who were sitting with Abaye and raising the following analytical difficulty. The *Chachamim*'s position is easy to understand: just as the inhabitants below are distinct (*keshem she-diyuran chalukin lemata kach diyuran chalukin lemala*), so too their rooftops are considered distinct domains above. But what does Rabbi Meir hold? He must hold one of two things.

If he agrees that the rooftops follow the divisions below — that they are distinct because the inhabitants are distinct — then why does he permit carrying from one rooftop to another? And if he holds the opposite: that above, these spaces are not differentiated by the separate inhabitants below, because no one actually *lives* on the rooftop, and anything above ten *tefachim* is in any case a unified *reshut* — then why does the *mishna* in Rabbi Meir's name require that no rooftop be ten *tefachim* higher or lower than its neighbor? If the distinguishing factor between rooftops is not the separate inhabitants below but simply height, why should one height within an already-elevated space be treated differently from another? Both are well above the ground-level threshold of ten *tefachim* that would classify them as *reshut hayachid*. What is the halachic significance of a difference in elevation between one roof and another?

### Pillar Teaching

Abaye answers by invoking a principle in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Adimi: *amar haya Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir used to teach — that wherever one finds two *reshuyot*, specifically a *reshut hayachid* within a *reshut hayachid* — for example, a pillar standing in a *reshut hayachid* that is ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* wide, which would itself constitute a *reshut hayachid* even were it standing in a *reshut harabim* — *asur le-katef alav*, one may not place objects on top of that pillar. The reason: *gezeira mishum tel bi-reshut harabim* — a rabbinic decree lest one come to do the same when such a pillar stands in a *reshut harabim*, which would constitute a biblical violation (transferring between a *reshut harabim* and a *reshut hayachid*).

This is a striking *chumra*. It cannot apply indoors in all cases, or one would be prohibited from placing objects on furniture or a *shtender*. The Gemara is clearly applying it in outdoor contexts. And even then, it is an extreme position — one effectively cannot, in one's own *reshut hayachid*, place objects atop a fixed elevated structure, for fear that one will confuse the case with an identical-looking structure standing in a *reshut harabim*.

### Rooftop Application

This teaching of Rabbi Meir is then applied to explain the height-difference restriction in the *mishna*. When one rooftop is ten *tefachim* higher than an adjacent one, the person standing on the lower roof is in a *reshut hayachid*, and the higher roof is itself a *reshut hayachid* elevated above the lower. Placing objects on the higher roof from the lower would be analogous to placing objects on a pillar within a *reshut hayachid* — and Rabbi Meir therefore prohibits it by the same *gezeira*. The Gemara notes that this explanation is somewhat surprising: the plain reading of the *mishna* in Rabbi Meir's name sounds as though the height difference categorically creates a distinct domain. The Gemara, however, is internally compelled to explain it as a collateral concern of Rabbi Meir — the *gezeira* regarding pillars in a *reshut harabim* — rather than as a fundamental domain distinction, because normally once something exceeds ten *tefachim* in height, further differences in elevation do not create new domain categories.

### Limitation

Having proposed this principle, the Gemara considers how far it extends. One might initially suppose that Rabbi Meir's prohibition applies to any elevated structure in a *reshut hayachid* — even a barrel (*gigis*) or a mortar (*machteshet*). The Gemara clarifies: *lo amar Rebbi Meir ela amud va-amasa de-rechayim* — Rabbi Meir only said this about a pillar and the large fixed stone configuration of a millstone. The criterion is *ho'il v'adam koveia lahem makom* — because a person fixes a permanent place for these structures. The prohibition applies only to structures that are truly fixed in the landscape, part of the permanent topography. A barrel or other movable vessel does not trigger the same concern.

### Wall Between

The Gemara then pushes further: *v'harei kosel shebein basei chatzeiros* — what about the wall between two courtyards? Such a wall is certainly *kavu'a*, fixed. According to Rabbi Meir's principle, one should be prohibited from placing objects from one's courtyard onto the top of such a wall, since the wall functions like a pillar within the *reshut hayachid*. This is a significant implication: the entire discussion in the preceding *perek* about who may use the top of a wall separating two courtyards — with all its analysis of *eruv* arrangements and competing claims — was framed as an *eruv* question, with nobody suggesting that placing objects on a wall is intrinsically prohibited. According to Rabbi Meir, one could apparently never use a wall top at all. The Gemara will now turn to resolving this tension.

---

## Categories

### Rabbi Meir

The Gemara uses the wall question to clarify an important point about Rabbi Meir's position. Rabbi Yehuda states: *k'she-timtza lomar l'divrei Rebbi Meir — gagin reshus l'atzman, chatzeiros reshus l'atzman, karpifos reshus l'atzman*. Rabbi Meir holds that rooftops form their own unified domain, courtyards form their own unified domain, and *karpifot* form their own unified domain — but these three categories remain distinct from one another. One may carry within any given category but not between categories. This is the distinction between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon: Rabbi Shimon unifies all three into a single domain, while Rabbi Meir maintains their categorical separateness while unifying each category within itself. This clarification is independent of the pillar discussion and illuminates the logical structure of the three-way debate.

### Doorways

Now the Gemara resolves the wall question. If Rabbi Meir holds that all courtyards form a unified domain and one may carry from one courtyard to another, but also holds that one may not use a wall as a platform (due to the *gezeira* regarding pillars), how does one actually transfer objects between courtyards? The Gemara answers by citing Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rav Sheshet: *lo lehachnis ulehotzi derech p'tachim* — one carries between courtyards not over the wall but through doorways. If there is an opening in the wall between the courtyards, one simply walks the object through. The top of the wall is never implicated. The implication, which the Gemara notes, is that according to Rabbi Meir, the wall top is indeed entirely unavailable — one may never place objects on a fixed wall within a *reshut hayachid*. This is a more radical position than the preceding *perek* assumed, but it follows coherently from Rabbi Meir's *gezeira* regarding pillars.

---

## Chachamim & Rav

### Chachamim View

The Gemara now turns to the *Chachamim*'s position. The *Chachamim* rule: *kol echad ve-echad reshut bifnei atzmo* — every individual rooftop is its own separate domain. Their reasoning, articulated by Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin, is that just as the inhabitants below are distinct (*keshem she-diyuran chalukin lemata kach diyuran chalukin lemala*), so are the rooftops above. The rooftop of Building A is an extension of the distinct identity of Building A, and it may not mix with the rooftop of Building B. Given this, one cannot carry between rooftops. But may one carry freely on one's own rooftop?

### Rav Four Cubits

Rav rules: *ein metalatelin bo ela be-arba amot* — one may carry on a given rooftop only within four *amot*. The reasoning will become clear through the principle of *parutz bimlo'o*, discussed below. Rav holds that the absence of an effective partition between Roof A and Roof B compromises Roof A's status sufficiently that even carrying within Roof A is restricted to the *Shabbat* limit of four *amot* applicable in an open public-like space.

### Shmuel Allowed

Shmuel disagrees and rules: *mutar letaltel b'kulo* — one may carry throughout one's own rooftop without restriction. Shmuel applies the principle of *gud asik mechitzta* — the walls of Building A are considered to extend upward, creating virtual *mechitzot* around Roof A. Those virtual walls, though invisible at roof level, suffice to define Roof A as a fully enclosed *reshut hayachid* in which free carrying is permitted.

### Parutz Principle

The debate between Rav and Shmuel is anchored in the principle of *parutz bemilo'o lemakom ha'asur lo* — if a domain is completely open on one side toward a domain into which carrying is forbidden, that exposure renders the otherwise-permitted domain forbidden as well. In the rooftop scenario, Roof A and Roof B are adjacent, and one may not carry from A to B. If there is no effective partition between them — if A is completely open toward B — then A is considered *parutz bemilo'o* and one may not carry freely in A itself. Rav holds that this principle applies here, because when the buildings are attached, the wall below is invisible at roof level and cannot effectively divide A from B. Shmuel holds that the wall's extension upward via *gud asik* provides a sufficient division, and *parutz bemilo'o* therefore does not apply.

### Walls Visible

The Gemara clarifies the scope of their disagreement. When the walls between the two buildings are *nikarot* — visible — there is no dispute. Detached buildings have visible walls, and those visible walls define the boundaries of each rooftop clearly. Even if the gap between rooftops is physically small, the visual presence of the wall creates the division, and Roof A is not considered to be *parutz bemilo'o* toward B. Both Rav and Shmuel agree that in such a case, carrying on one's own rooftop is fully permitted.

The dispute is specifically *b'mechitzot she'einam nikarot* — when the walls between the buildings are invisible at roof level, i.e., the buildings are attached. In this case, is the concealed wall sufficient to divide A from B? Rav rules: *lo amrinan gud asik mechitzta* — in this configuration, one does not apply *gud asik* to extend the invisible wall upward so as to create a meaningful partition. This does not mean Rav entirely denies *gud asik*; as Rashi notes on the final line of the Gemara, the wall certainly extends enough to make the rooftop a *reshut hayachid* in general. But it does not extend sufficiently to effect a meaningful *separation* between A and B when it is invisible below. Therefore, A is considered *parutz bemilo'o* toward B, and carrying is restricted to four *amot*. Shmuel holds that *amrinan gud asik mechitzta* — the invisible wall's upward extension is fully operative, A and B are effectively separated above, and A is therefore a complete *reshut hayachid* in which free carrying is permitted.

The simple reading of the *mishna* — *kol echad ve-echad reshut bifnei atzmo*, each rooftop is its own domain — strongly implies that one may carry freely on one's own rooftop, which aligns with Shmuel's position. The Gemara acknowledges this (*bishlama l'Shmuel nicha*) and notes the difficulty for Rav. Rav's school responds by re-reading the *mishna*: the statement that each rooftop is its own domain means only that one may carry four *amot* on one's own rooftop, and categorically may not carry from A to B — not even a step that spans both. The language "its own domain" does not imply unlimited carrying; it implies four *amot* on the home rooftop and zero from rooftop to rooftop. The *baraita* from Shmuel's school (*ein lahen ela gagan* — they have only their own rooftop) is similarly re-read by the Gemara to permit only four *amot*, not full carrying — the same explanatory move applied to the language of the *mishna* itself.

---

## Large & Small

### Scenario

The Gemara now introduces the case of a large rooftop (*gag gadol*) adjacent to a small rooftop (*gag katan*).
