This case arises when the buildings are of different sizes — Building A is larger, Building B is smaller — such that the two buildings share a portion of wall (the connected section) but Building A's wall extends visibly beyond that connection. The ruling: *hagadol mutar vehakatan asur* — the large rooftop is permitted and the small is forbidden.

### Why Difference

Why the asymmetry? The small rooftop is *parutz bemilo'o* — it is completely exposed to the adjacent space without any visible wall demarcating it. The large rooftop, by contrast, has a partial visible wall: its extended section is bounded by a visible wall, even though the portion shared with the small building has no visible divider at roof level. This partial wall suffices to prevent A from being classified as *parutz bemilo'o*, and A therefore retains its status as a permitted domain. B, lacking any such visible boundary, is fully exposed and forbidden. This case therefore appears to support Rav's position, since it demonstrates that the invisible connecting wall is not treated as a partition — if it were, B would also have a wall and would also be permitted.

### Shmuel Habitation

Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel an alternative reading of this case. Shmuel says: *lo shanu ela sheyesh diurin al zeh vediurin al zeh* — this ruling (that the large is permitted and the small forbidden) applies only when people are actually regularly residing on both rooftops. In that case, the dividing line between A and B is constantly being walked over (*mechitza nidreset*), and by virtue of that regular trampling, the line is shown to be no line at all. When people habitually cross that boundary, they demonstrate its non-existence, and therefore A is exposed to B as if the wall did not exist. In this specific circumstance, B is *parutz bemilo'o* (completely exposed, since even the connecting section is effectively abolished by regular use), and A is only partially bounded (its extended section being visible). Hence the large is permitted and the small is forbidden.

But if people do not regularly use the rooftops and do not walk over that line — *aval ein diurin al zeh veal zeh shneihem mutarin* — then both rooftops are fully permitted, because the invisible wall, unviolated by actual use, does retain its status as a division. This reading aligns with Shmuel's general position: *gud asik* applies, and the invisible wall is effective unless actively undermined by habitual crossing.

### Rav Yosef

Rav Yosef initially states he has no recollection of this *shemata* — this teaching — at all. Abaye informs him that he himself taught it, and that he did so in the context of this very case of the large and small rooftop. One finds this recurring motif in *Eruvin*: Rav Yosef, following his illness, frequently requires his students to restore his own teachings to him. Abaye's reading of what Rav Yosef had taught was that the operative factor was habitation — whether people were actually living up on the roof — and that the question of whether the boundary line was being walked over or not determined the ruling.

Rav Yosef, however, corrects Abaye's understanding. He says: *ana hachi amri lechu* — this is what I actually said. *Lo shanu ela sheyesh mechitza al zeh umechitza al zeh — de-gadol mishtari be-gifufei ve-katan nifrat bimlo'o*. Rav Yosef's position is more stringent than either Rav or Shmuel. He holds that the only reason A is permitted is that A has actual physical *mechitzot* surrounding it — even partial walls (*gifufei*) — whereas B is *parutz bemilo'o* by virtue of being entirely exposed. But if neither A nor B has any real *mechitza* at all — *aval ein mechitza lo le-zeh velo le-zeh, sheneihem asurin* — both are forbidden. One cannot rely on the wall below, visible or otherwise, to constitute a division above. A real *mechitza* at rooftop level is required. This is more stringent than Rav, who at least accepts the visible wall below as sufficient to permit the rooftop.

---

## Dwelling Mechitza

### Mechitza Definition

Abaye, however, pushes back, insisting that the concept of *diurin* — habitation — which he remembers Rav Yosef introducing is not about whether people habitually walk over the line (Shmuel's reading) but refers to something else. Rav Yosef then refines his position further: *hachi amri lechu — lo shanu ela sheyesh mechitza re'uya le-dira al zeh u-mechitza re'uya le-dira al zeh*. What is required is not merely any halachic *mechitza* but specifically a *mechitza re'uya le-dira* — a partition suited for habitation. The definition of *mechitza re'uya le-dira* is a genuinely permanent constructed wall, the kind around which one could realistically decide to inhabit the rooftop space. A curtain, a canvas partition, or any halachically valid but physically impermanent *mechitza* does not qualify. Only a permanent wall constitutes a *mechitza re'uya le-dira*.

### Contrast Effect

This leads to a subtle and consequential ruling. The contrast between permanent and temporary *mechitzot* on adjacent rooftops is not merely a matter of degree; it generates an active legal effect. If Building A has permanent walls — *mechitzot re'uyot le-dira* — around its rooftop, this signals that the occupants of A have genuinely established their presence and domain on the rooftop. Building B, which may have halachically valid but temporary and impermanent partitions, signals that its occupants have not made any serious claim to the rooftop space. The reality of A's presence above *contrasts* with B's absence, and this contrast actively diminishes B's standing as a separate domain.

### Result

The ruling that follows: *aval yesh mechitza re'uya le-dira al hagadol ve-ein re'uya le-dira al hakatan — afilu katan shari livnei gadol*. If A has permanent *mechitzot* and B has only impermanent ones, then even B's rooftop is permitted for the residents of A. Why? *Keivan d'lo avad mechitza, silukei silikei nafshei meihacha* — since B's occupants did not erect a permanent wall, they have effectively withdrawn their presence from the rooftop. The rooftop above B is no longer a genuinely contested domain; from the perspective of someone who has truly established themselves on the roof (Building A), B's rooftop has been vacated of any competing claim. A may therefore carry into B's rooftop as well, treating the combined rooftop as a single domain under A's control. B, for its part, remains restricted in the usual way and may not freely carry even on its own rooftop, since its *mechitzot* do not assert a genuine presence.

---

## Ladder & Habitation

### Fixed Ladder

The Gemara closes with a statement of Rav Nachman that generalizes this logic into a practical tool: *asu sulam kavua l'gago* — if one installs a fixed ladder to one's rooftop, *hutar b'chol hagagin kulan* — one becomes permitted to carry across all the rooftops.

The reasoning follows directly from the principles developed above. According to the *Chachamim*, all rooftops are in principle distinct domains, each corresponding to the separate ownership of the building below. But this distinctness is, in an important sense, virtual: no one actually lives on any rooftop, and the differences are projected upward from the reality below rather than grounded in genuine habitation above. When one installs a permanent ladder to one's rooftop, one does more than gain physical access — one establishes *real*, actual habitation above. One has made a genuine claim to the rooftop space, as opposed to a merely constructive one.

### Total Use

Once genuine habitation is established — by fixed ladder, by permanent walls, or by any comparable means — that real presence trumps all the competing virtual claims of the other rooftop owners, none of whom have made a comparable investment in the space above. The person who has established real habitation may therefore treat all the rooftops as a single domain under his effective control, carrying freely across all of them. The other rooftop owners, lacking that genuine presence, do not acquire symmetric rights; they remain restricted in the ways their *mechitzot* and presence — or absence thereof — determine.

### Summary

By way of summary: the *Chachamim* hold that each rooftop is a distinct domain, since the separate inhabitants below generate separate domains above. Whether one may carry freely on one's own rooftop — even without crossing to another — depends on the debate between Rav and Shmuel. Rav holds that when buildings are attached and the wall between them is invisible at rooftop level, *parutz bemilo'o* applies and carrying is limited to four *amot*; *gud asik* is not operative in this configuration. Shmuel holds that *gud asik* does apply even for invisible walls, and one may carry freely on one's own rooftop. Rav Yosef goes further than either, holding that not even visible walls below are sufficient; only real *mechitzot* at rooftop level enable full carrying on that rooftop. And across all these positions, the one overriding leniency is the principle of establishing genuine habitation above: once a person makes a real and fixed presence on the rooftop — by permanent ladder or permanent wall — that presence overrides all virtual distinctions and grants full rights over the entire expanse of connected rooftops.

---

---

# Eiruvin 90

## Second Story Access

### Abaye's Second Story

The *gemara* picks up at the bottom of 89b, continuing its analysis of what constitutes a sufficiently serious residential presence on a rooftop to dissolve the distinctions that the *chachamim* draw between separately owned rooftops. Recall the broader context: the *chachamim* hold that adjacent rooftops are considered distinct domains because the homes beneath them are under distinct ownership, and therefore carrying from one rooftop to another would require an *eruv*. However, the *gemara* had established that if one creates a genuinely substantial presence on one rooftop — such as constructing permanent walls or a fixed ladder — that presence dominates and the other rooftops, lacking any comparable habitation, lose their status as competing domains.

With this framework in place, Abaye introduces a new case. He states: if one built a second story atop his house — thereby transforming his rooftop into a genuine place of habitation — and then fashioned before it a *daka* of four, he is thereby permitted to access all the surrounding rooftops. The logic is continuous with what preceded: by constructing a second story, one has made the rooftop into a genuine dwelling place. The *daka*, on Rashi's reading, is a small doorway — an opening of four — that provides direct access from this second story out onto the adjoining rooftops. Without such an opening, the second story might be accessed only from inside the building, without any passage onto the roof itself; the doorway creates that connection, confirming that the rooftop is not merely a building top but an extension of a real living space. Since only this one person has done this, and the others have not made any competing claim of habitation on their own rooftops, the real dwelling presence here dominates, and there is no meaningful distinctiveness left in the surrounding rooftops.

### Daka Interpretation

The meaning of *daka* is itself a point of dispute between the *rishonim*. Rashi explains it here as a small opening or doorway — a departure from its usage elsewhere, where *daka* refers to a small barrier or partition. Tosafot, seeking consistency with the earlier usages of the term, attempts to retain the meaning of a barrier rather than an aperture. The practical implications of this disagreement are significant: on Rashi's reading, the key feature is the access created by the doorway; on Tosafot's reading, the small barrier plays a different structural role in defining the space.

### Rooftop Access

On Rashi's reading of the case, once the doorway is in place, *hutrah bechol hagagin kulan* — one is permitted access to carry across all the surrounding rooftops. The doorway opening outward onto the other rooftops establishes the second story's connection to them, effectively dissolving whatever distinctiveness those other rooftops might otherwise have had. One might ask whether this leniency extends to everyone, not merely to the person who built the second story — and indeed, this is an interesting question that the *gemara* itself does not explicitly address. The logic, however, points toward a broader permission: the real dwelling presence on the second story removes the distinctiveness of all the other rooftops as domains in their own right, regardless of who seeks to carry there. And since all these buildings already have four walls below, no *lechi* or *korah* is needed to frame the space — the walls of the buildings themselves provide all the necessary enclosure.

### Rava's Restriction

Rava then introduces a counterpoint: *pe'amim shehadaka le'issur* — sometimes this very doorway can generate a prohibition rather than a leniency. Rashi explains that this applies even according to Rabbi Meir, who in the normal case holds that all rooftops constitute a single domain. The scenario Rava describes is one in which the doorway is fashioned facing a garden below, and it is understood that this configuration was created in order to oversee and guard that garden area. By orienting the rooftop toward the garden in this way, one has effectively defined this rooftop as serving the space below rather than participating in the community of rooftops. Even Rabbi Meir, who would normally group all rooftops together, would concede that this rooftop has been given a distinct identity — it is categorized together with the garden below, not with the surrounding rooftops.

---

## Roof vs. Platform

### Rami's Question

The *gemara* transitions to a question posed by Rami bar Chama at the top of 91b. The question is framed within Rav's position — namely, that when the *chachamim* say each rooftop is a distinct domain, not only can one not carry from rooftop A to rooftop B, one also cannot carry more than four *amot* within rooftop A itself, because the exposure to the forbidden domain of rooftop B undermines the carrying capacity within A. Rami bar Chama accepts this as the operative framework and then poses his question: *shtei amot bagag u-shtei amot ba'amud mahu* — what is the rule if one carries two *amot* on a rooftop and two *amot* on a platform (*amud*)? One remains within four *amot* total, so the distance itself is not the concern. The question is whether the roof and the platform constitute distinct domains — and if so, even a movement of less than four *amot* that crosses from one into the other would be forbidden, just as crossing from rooftop A to rooftop B is forbidden even for short distances.

The motivation for the question is clear: rooftops are deemed distinct because different people live in the houses below. A platform, however, does not have someone living beneath it in the same way. Is it therefore to be treated differently, or is the experiential similarity of moving from one elevated surface to another enough to prohibit it?

### Rava Responds

Rava dismisses the question as improperly formulated: *mai kamibaya lei — karmelit u-reshut hayachid kamibaya lei?* What kind of question is that? One of these spaces is a *karmelit* and the other is a *reshut hayachid* — of course they are distinct. Rashi explains that Rava understands the rooftop to be, in effect, a *karmelit* — not in its strict technical definition, but functionally, because one cannot carry on it in the manner of a true *reshut hayachid* given the exposure to the neighboring rooftop. The platform, by contrast, is a genuine *reshut hayachid* of the standard kind. Tosafot reverses the assignments: the platform is the *karmelit* — being less than ten *tefachim* high — and the rooftop is the *reshut hayachid*. Either way, Rava's point stands: the two spaces are obviously distinct in domain-status, so the question answers itself.

The *gemara* adds a memorable characterization: *VeRami bar Chama agav churpeih lo iyein bah* — because of his sharpness, Rami bar Chama did not slow down enough to think it through. This is a striking observation about a certain type of intellectual temperament: the question sounds incisive precisely because it was posed quickly, but a moment's reflection reveals that the categories had not been properly sorted. The *gemara* then proceeds to reconstruct what Rami bar Chama's question must have actually been — or at least, what it should have been. Whether this represents what he truly meant, or a sympathetic reformulation of an imprecise question, is itself an interesting methodological point about how the *gemara* handles such cases.

### Roof vs. Portico

The *gemara* reconstructs the question as follows: *bein amot begag u-vein amot be-achsadra mahu* — what is the rule if one carries partially on a rooftop and partially on a portico (*achsadra*)? The *achsadra* is not a mere pillar; it is a structure with a roof but open on its sides, like a columned porch. This is meaningfully different from the pillar of the original question. The *achsadra* can be understood as a technical *reshut hayachid* — if we count its roof-edge or some form of virtual wall as adequate — yet it shares with the rooftop the quality that no one genuinely lives in it as a primary dwelling. The two spaces may both be, in effect, non-primary habitation zones, giving rise to the genuine question of whether they should be treated as a single domain or as distinct ones.

### Domain Analysis

The *gemara* frames the question in two directions. On one hand: *keivan dehai chazi ledira vehai lo chazi ledira, chada reshuta hi* — since neither space is truly fit for habitation in the primary sense, perhaps they are functionally a single domain and movement between them is permitted. The rooftop is distinct from other rooftops only because of different ownership below; the *achsadra* has no such competing ownership at all. On the other hand: *keivan demigag legag assar, migag le'achsadra nami assar* — perhaps the experiential similarity between moving from one rooftop to another and moving from a rooftop onto the roof of an *achsadra* is close enough that the same prohibition applies, even though technically no distinct ownership is in conflict.

Rashi offers two possible understandings of why the *achsadra* might share the quasi-*karmelit* status of the rooftop: either it is an exceptionally large space that exceeds *beit satayim* and was not enclosed for habitation, or it simply lacks proper walls altogether — being open on all sides beneath its roof, it may not qualify as a *reshut hayachid* at all and is straightforwardly a *karmelit*. The question then becomes whether carrying from a space that is *de facto* a *reshut hayachid* but functionally restricted like a *karmelit* to a space that is simply a *karmelit* is permissible. The *gemara* leaves this as an open question.

---

## Roof vs. Ruin

### Bibi's Question

Rav Bibi bar Abaye poses a related question: *bayis she-begago u-vayis she-bachurvah mah* — what is the rule regarding a rooftop of a standing house and a *churvah*, a ruin or vacant lot? This is a step removed from the *achsadra* case. Rashi understands the *churvah* here as a ground-level open structure — not even a roof, just an empty lot. The question is whether one may carry from the rooftop into this space.

Importantly, the *gemara* has been assuming — and will make this explicit later — that the *chachamim*'s concern is specifically about *different ownership* creating distinct domains. The *churvah*, being vacant, does not have an active competing owner. So the question is not one of competing ownership; it is a question of whether the difference in kind between a rooftop and a ruined lot is itself a sufficient barrier. Rashi adds that this particular *churvah* has three walls but one side is open to a *reshut harabim*, rendering it a *karmelit*. We thus have, once again, a question of moving between two spaces that are each effectively restricted in a similar way — yet the physical and categorical difference between a rooftop and a ground-level ruin may itself generate a prohibition.

One might note that this raises the deeper question, left somewhat unresolved in the discussion of the *chachamim*'s position, of whether carrying from a rooftop to a *chatzer* below is inherently problematic. The *chachamim* focus on distinct ownership as the operative factor; Rabbi Meir focuses on the physical category of rooftops as similar to one another. It is possible, then, that Rabbi Meir — who permits movement from rooftop to rooftop — might actually be stricter than the *chachamim* about moving from a rooftop to a structurally different space like a *chatzer*, while the *chachamim* might be more lenient about that transition since their concern is ownership rather than physical category. The two authorities may be looking at different things entirely.

### Kahana's Response

Rav Kahana dismisses Rav Bibi bar Abaye's question by saying it is essentially the same as Rami bar Chama's earlier question — implying it has already been posed and left unresolved, so there is nothing new to deliberate.

### Portico vs. Ruin

Rav Bibi bar Abaye pushes back sharply: *de-khi me-acher atzei u-mitnatzei* — am I pilfering someone else's questions just to make trouble? He insists his question is genuinely distinct. The difference is this: *achsadra lo chazya ledira, churva chazya ledira* — the *achsadra* is not suitable for habitation, whereas the *churvah* is, at least in theory. The *achsadra* is by nature a porch or a colonnade; the ruin is a structure that, if repaired, could serve as a dwelling. This potential habitability may be enough to give the *churvah* a latent status of distinct ownership — perhaps the absentee owner's theoretical claim to the space matters even when he is not present.

### Habitability Debate

The *gemara* reformulates this as a conditional question: *im timtzei lomar achsadra lo chazya ledira* — if you rule that the *achsadra* case is permissible (because neither the rooftop nor the *achsadra* constitutes a truly distinct dwelling, so they are treated as one domain), the *churvah* still presents a further question. Even if we look past the ownership issue when no one is actively present, the *churvah*'s fitness for potential habitation may mean we treat it as having a notional distinct ownership. On the other hand: *hashta miha leit bah diyurin* — right now, at this moment, no one lives there; and we have seen in the context of *eiruvin* that a person absent from home on *Shabbat* does not create a domain conflict. Perhaps the same principle should apply here.

The *gemara* concludes: *teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

The broader implication, which the *gemara* makes visible but does not state explicitly, is that the *chachamim*'s framework is essentially ownership-focused, and the *gemara*'s entire line of questioning has been probing the limits of that framework: what happens when ownership is absent, theoretical, or ambiguous? What happens when the difference is not one of ownership at all but of structure or habitability? These questions will continue to reverberate throughout the subsequent discussions.

---

## Equal Roofs Debate

### Rav Permits

The *gemara* now introduces a new debate, this time operating within the position of Rabbi Meir — who holds that all equal-height rooftops together constitute a single domain — and within the position of the *rabbanan* regarding a single standalone rooftop. In both scenarios the basic premise is that there is no competing ownership creating domain conflicts. The question is how freely one may carry in these spaces.

Rav states: *mutar letaltel bekulo* — one may carry throughout the entire combined space of connected equal-height rooftops, or on the single standalone rooftop. This is the intuitive position: if all the rooftops form one domain per Rabbi Meir, one should be able to traverse the entire expanse.

### Shmuel Restricts

Shmuel disagrees: *ein metaltelin bo ela be-arba* — one may carry no more than four *amot*. This seems counterintuitive to the point of being bizarre. Shmuel was the lenient voice in the earlier debate between Rav and Shmuel about the *chachamim*'s position, holding that even within the framework of competing ownership one may carry fully within one's own rooftop. Yet here, in a scenario where Rabbi Meir has eliminated the problem of competing ownership entirely, Shmuel says one may carry only four *amot*?

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* notes the apparent contradiction in Shmuel's position directly: *kashya de-Shmuel le-Shmuel*. The *gemara* first addresses the parallel tension in Rav's position, but quickly notes that Rav's position is easily explained. One might have thought that the rooftops, being exposed to the street below where a *reshut harabim* runs, should lose their *reshut hayachid* status — just as rooftop A, exposed to the forbidden domain of rooftop B, was compromised in the earlier discussion. But the *gemara* deflects this: *hatam lo minkara mechitza, hacha minkara mechitza* — in the earlier case the virtual walls between adjacent rooftops were invisible from below, creating a domain problem; here, however, the walls of the buildings are fully visible to anyone standing in the street below. The roof retains its distinct *reshut hayachid* character because the enclosure is visible and recognizable. This is a relatively easy resolution, and indeed the *gemara* treats it as such.

### Wall Visibility

The principle emerging here is significant: it is not merely the existence of walls but their *visibility* to those below that determines whether the rooftop is sufficiently distinguished from the surrounding domain. When the walls are invisible — as in the case of virtual partitions between adjacent rooftops — the domain is compromised. When they are visible — as with the actual walls of buildings seen from street level — the rooftop remains a recognizable and distinct *reshut hayachid*.

### Shmuel Explained

The harder question is Shmuel's position. The *gemara* explains: *hasam lo havya yoser mi-beis sa'atayim, hacha havya yoser mi-beis sa'atayim* — in the earlier case of the *chachamim*, where each rooftop was treated as a distinct domain, no single rooftop ever became larger than *beit satayim*; each building's roof is a bounded space. Therefore, even according to Shmuel, one could carry freely within that individual rooftop. But according to Rabbi Meir, who declares all the connected equal-height rooftops to be one unified domain, combining them all may easily produce a space that exceeds *beit satayim*. And a space greater than *beit satayim* that was not *hukaf ledira* — enclosed for the purpose of habitation — acquires the status of a *karmelit*, limiting carrying to four *amot*.

The crux is whether the walls of the buildings below render the rooftop above *hukaf ledira*. Shmuel says no: *ve-hani mechitsos lemata avidun, lemala lo avidun* — the walls down below were built for the sake of those living inside the houses; they were not built for the sake of the rooftop above. The roof therefore is not *hukaf ledira* and, when it exceeds *beit satayim*, becomes like a *karfaf* that was not enclosed for habitation — a *karmelit* in which one may carry only four *amot*.

Rav, by contrast, maintains that since the walls below and the rooftop above share the same physical structure — the same walls — the *hukaf ledira* status of the interior extends upward and renders the rooftop *hukaf ledira* as well.

The *gemara* confirms this understanding in its language: *ve-havei ke-karfap yoser mi-beis sa'atayim shelo hukaf ledira — ve-chol karfap yoser mi-beis sa'atayim shelo hukaf ledira ein metaltelin bo ela be-arba* — it is like an enclosed field exceeding *beit satayim* that was not walled in for habitation, and in any such space one may carry only four *amot*.

---

## Boats & Vessels

### Rava on Boats

The *gemara* next applies the same conceptual framework to a boat. The question is whether one may carry freely throughout a large boat on *Shabbat*, or whether the boat's interior — if it exceeds *beit satayim* — is restricted to four *amot* as a space not *hukaf ledira*. Rava rules: *mutar le-taltel be-kula* — one may carry throughout the entire boat. The walls of the boat constitute an enclosure, and Rava holds that this enclosure qualifies as *hukaf ledira*.

### Shmuel on Boats

Shmuel, consistent with his earlier reasoning, rules: *ein metaltelin bo ela be-arba* — one may carry only four *amot*. His explanation: *mechitsos le-avruchi maya avidun* — the walls of a boat are constructed primarily to keep out water and allow the vessel to float, not to create a habitable enclosed space. The purpose of the walls, in Shmuel's analysis, is structural and nautical rather than residential, and therefore they do not confer *hukaf ledira* status.

This is admittedly a difficult position to sustain, and the *gemara*'s discussion acknowledges as much. People do in fact live on boats, sleep in them, and use them as residential space. One might argue that the reason one wants the boat not to take on water is precisely so that one will have a vessel in which people can dwell — making habitation the ultimate end even if water-resistance is the proximate means. The difficulty of Shmuel's position is particularly acute for the enclosed hull of a boat where people sleep, rather than the open deck. If individual cabins or rooms have been constructed within the hull, those walls would clearly be *hukaf ledira*. The debate may be most coherent when applied to an open galley-style hull with no internal partitions — a large undivided space in which one might argue that the walls were built purely as a nautical structure rather than as a residential enclosure.

---

## Boats & Vessels (II)

### Rava's Exception

Even Rava, who permits carrying throughout the boat in its normal configuration, agrees that there are cases where the boat is restricted. Rav Gidal citing Rav Chiya bar Yosef reports: *u-modeh Rava* — Rava concedes that if one overturned the boat — *im kapa pi-ha* — and sought to use the hull space underneath as a shelter, carrying would be restricted to four *amot*. The logic is that when a boat is flipped upside down, typically the purpose is repairs — applying tar (*le-zufta*) or caulking the hull — not creating a place of habitation. Although the overturning creates a new enclosed space with walls, those walls were not fashioned *le-dirah*: they came into being for a repair function. Since the enclosure was not created for habitation, Rava agrees that it does not qualify as *hukaf ledira*, and the space is restricted.

The *gemara*'s question about whether one might flip the boat to live inside it is resolved by noting that in practice the purpose of overturning is repair, not residence. The analogy with a boat in its normal orientation is instructive: in normal use, even if water-resistance is the primary engineering motivation for the walls, people do live inside — so Rava considers it *hukaf ledira*. When overturned, no one lives in it and no one intends to; the new wall configuration is incidental to a non-residential function.

### Boat Ruling

The *halachic* ruling is stated explicitly: Rav Chiya bar Yosef asked Shmuel directly — *hilchosa kevassach o hilchosa ke-Rava* — do we rule like you or like Rava? Shmuel replied: *hilchosa ke-Rava* — the law follows Rava. This exchange is itself noteworthy: Shmuel, who held his own position, nonetheless readily endorsed the accepted ruling in favor of the opposing view when asked directly. He did not attempt to leverage his authority as the questioner's interlocutor to promote his own *psak*. The law therefore follows Rava: one may carry freely throughout a boat in its normal configuration.

---

## Portico Walls

### Rav Virtual Walls

The *gemara* now records a dispute — cited in two different versions by Rav Ashi and by Rav Acha son of Rava, each claiming that Shmuel's ruling in favor of Rava applied to a different debate — concerning an *achsadra b'vikah*, a portico standing in a valley. Rav rules: *mutar le-taltel bekula* — one may carry throughout the entire portico. His reasoning is that we apply the principle of *pi tikra yored v'sotem* — the edge of the roof descends and seals, creating virtual walls. Even though the portico has no actual walls — only supporting columns or posts — the edge of the roof is treated as if it extended downward, producing virtual partitions that enclose the space beneath.

### Shmuel No Walls

Shmuel rules: *ein metaltelin bah ela be-arba* — one may carry only four *amot* in the portico. He rejects the application of *pi tikra yored v'sotem* in this case: *lo amrinan pi tikra yored v'sotem* — we do not invoke this principle here. Without actual walls, and without virtual walls generated by *pi tikra yored v'sotem*, the portico is a *karmelit* and carrying is restricted.

### Wall Interpretation

This dispute has implications beyond the immediate case, and it surfaces in the *gemara* in Tractate *Sukkah* as well. The precise scope of *pi tikra yored v'sotem* — under what conditions the roof-edge is sufficient to create virtual walls — is the underlying question. Rashi and Tosafot interpret the debate differently. Rashi understands the distinctive feature of this case to be that one would need to invoke *pi tikra yored v'sotem* on all four sides simultaneously — that is, in the complete absence of any actual walls, one is relying on the roof-edge to generate the entire enclosure. It is this application on all four sides that Shmuel rejects. Tosafot, however, understands the dispute as concerning even a single virtual wall created by *pi tikra yored v'sotem*; Rav and Shmuel disagree about the principle as such, not merely about its extension to multiple sides.

It is worth noting the interesting contrast with the rule of *mechitza teluyah* — a suspended partition that does not reach the ground. There, we say that a gap of more than three *tefachim* between the bottom of the partition and the ground invalidates the partition, since small animals could pass through. The edge of a roof descending by perhaps only one *tefach* would seem far less effective than even a suspended partition. Yet *pi tikra yored v'sotem* claims that this thin roof-edge is sufficient to create a virtual wall. The reason appears to be that the roof-edge is not merely a partition but part of a roofed structure — it carries the connotation of an enclosed house or domicile — and this implicit sense of enclosure generated by a roof structure is what allows even a minimal downward projection to be treated as a wall. That conceptual rationale is precisely what Rav and Shmuel are debating.

---

## Roof to Courtyard

### Rav's Position

The *gemara* now turns to a series of positions in which the major *amora'im* are aligned with the *tanna'im* on specific questions. The first concerns Rav according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir, as established, holds that all equal-height rooftops constitute a single domain — one may carry from any rooftop to any other. But what about carrying from a rooftop to a *chatzer* below? Even granting that the rooftops form one unified domain, a *chatzer* is a categorically different kind of space: it is at ground level, it is physically distinct from the elevated rooftop plane. Does the *hukaf ledira* quality shared by both a rooftop (as Rav reads it) and a *chatzer* make them sufficiently similar that one may carry between them?

The *gemara* states that Rav according to Rabbi Meir would prohibit carrying from a rooftop to a *chatzer*: *gezeira mishum deRabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi*. This is a *gezeira* — a rabbinic precautionary measure — based on the principle articulated by Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi: one must not confuse a *reshut hayachid* elevated above the ground with a pillar standing in the middle of a *reshut harabim*. The fear is that if one becomes accustomed to moving objects from a rooftop down to a ground-level space, one might come to carry from a pillar in a *reshut harabim* to the *reshut harabim* itself. More simply stated: the physical difference between a rooftop and a *chatzer* — one high, one low — is itself sufficient to categorize them as distinct for these purposes, even if their abstract domain qualities are similar.

### Gezeira Logic

The reasoning here is more than just technical domain-categorization. Even if one could argue that both the rooftop and the *chatzer* are *reshut hayachid*, or that both are equally *hukaf ledira* in a non-primary residential sense, the physical reality of ascending and descending creates a recognizable transition that the rabbis treated as categorically significant. The *gezeira* of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi provides the formal halachic articulation of this intuition.

---

## Roof to Field

### Shmuel Status

The *gemara* concludes with Shmuel according to the *rabbanan*. Shmuel holds, as established, that the rooftop is *lo hukaf ledira* — the walls built for the house do not render the rooftop above as *hukaf ledira*. With this in view, the *gemara* asks: why can one not carry from a rooftop to a *karfaf*, an enclosed field? A *karfaf* is technically a *reshut hayachid* — it has walls — but it is not *hukaf ledira*, because it was enclosed for agricultural or animal-keeping purposes, not for habitation. According to Shmuel, the rooftop also lacks *hukaf ledira* status. The two spaces thus share the same defining qualities: real *reshut hayachid* status in principle, but non-*hukaf ledira* in character.

### Why Prohibited

Given this symmetry, one might expect that carrying between them would be permitted — or at least that the question would be no harder than any other case of two similar spaces. Yet the *chachamim* do not permit carrying from a rooftop to a *karfaf*. Why not?

### Roof Collapse Fear

Rava bar Ula provides the answer: *gezeira shema yipaches hagag* — a rabbinic precautionary measure lest the roof become smaller. Rashi clarifies the specific scenario: we are speaking of a very large roof, one that exceeds *beit satayim*. Because it exceeds *beit satayim* and lacks *hukaf ledira* status, the rooftop is in effect a *karmelit*. Similarly, the *karfaf* in question is large and not *hukaf ledira*, making it also a *karmelit*. Both are therefore *karmelit*. The question is why one cannot carry from one *karmelit* to the other.

The concern is that part of the roof might deteriorate and collapse, reducing the rooftop's area to below *beit satayim*. A rooftop smaller than *beit satayim* that is not *hukaf ledira* would then be a genuine *reshut hayachid*, not a *karmelit*. If people continued to carry as before — from the now-*reshut hayachid* rooftop to the *karmelit* field — they would be violating a prohibition that had been created by the structural change, without realizing it.

### Field vs. Roof

The *gemara* anticipates the obvious challenge: why not apply the same concern to carrying from one *karfaf* to another? If part of one enclosed field's walls collapsed, it too could become smaller than *beit satayim* and transition from *karmelit* to *reshut hayachid*, creating the same problem. Why do we not issue the same *gezeira* for field-to-field carrying?

The *gemara* answers: *hasam ei mipachas minkara milsa, hacha ei mipachas lo minkara milsa* — in a field, if the walls change, the change is visible. The walls of a *karfaf* are actual physical structures surrounding a visible space; if a wall collapses or shifts, the change in the enclosed area is readily apparent to anyone using the space. But on a rooftop, the walls are invisible — they are the virtual extensions of the building walls below, perceived by convention rather than observed directly. If the roof area changes — say a section deteriorates — the change in the effective domain boundary is not obvious. A person standing on the roof would have no easy way of knowing that the space has become smaller than *beit satayim* and has thereby changed its domain status. The *gezeira* is therefore applied specifically to rooftops, where invisible boundaries create genuine risk of unwitting violation.

This discussion serves as the conceptual bridge to the material that will follow: the *gemara* is setting up an analysis not merely of competing ownership but of the similarity and difference between various types of spaces — rooftops, courtyards, fields, ruins — and what makes two spaces close enough in kind that movement between them is treated as unproblematic, or different enough that it generates a prohibition even when ownership conflicts are absent.

---

---

# Eiruvin 91

## Intro: Three Positions

### Opening remarks

We begin at the very bottom of 91b, continuing the discussion that has occupied this *perek*: which domains, in the absence of an *eiruv*, are considered sufficiently unified that a vessel originating in one may be carried freely throughout them all? The underlying assumption throughout is that all the spaces in question — rooftops, courtyards, enclosed yards, balconies, alleys — are each individually a *reshut hayachid*. The question is not their basic legal status, but rather how to define the groupings that govern inter-domain movement on Shabbos when no *eiruv* has been made.

### Three positions explained

*Rav Yehuda* opens with the phrase *keshetimtzei lomar* — "when you find yourself to say," a locution meaning something like "upon reflection you will realize." Reflecting carefully on the debate, he articulates three distinct positions.

*Ledivrei Rabbi Meir*: rooftops (*gagin*) constitute their own domain, courtyards (*chatzerot*) constitute their own domain, and enclosed yards (*karpifot*) constitute their own domain. Each genre is internally unified but externally separate. You may carry from one rooftop to another rooftop, from one courtyard to another courtyard, from one *karpaf* to another *karpaf* — but you may not carry from a *gag* to a *chatzer* or from a *chatzer* to a *karpaf*.

*Ledivrei Rabbi Shimon*: all three combined — *gag*, *chatzer*, and *karpaf* — form a single unified domain. One might initially read Rabbi Shimon's language in the *Mishnah* — *echad gagot ve'echad chatzerot ve'echad karpifot reshut achat* — as meaning that each category is its own respective unit. The *Gemara* clarifies, and will shortly confirm from a *baraita*, that Rabbi Shimon means all three together form one unified *reshut*. Vessels that originate in any of these spaces may be carried freely into any of the others.

The *Chachamim* represent a position that the *Gemara* will develop in greater detail. Their disagreement with Rabbi Meir in the *Mishnah* concerned rooftops of different ownership: Rabbi Meir holds that all rooftops form one collective domain regardless of ownership, while the *Chachamim* hold that different ownership creates different domains — *kol echad ve'echad reshut bifnei atzmo*. By extension, the *Gemara* understands that the *Chachamim* occupy a middle position between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon, one that will be elaborated as the *sugya* progresses.

### Practical implications

The practical stakes of this debate concern vessels: which objects may be carried between which spaces, and under what conditions? The working assumption is that we are speaking of vessels that began Shabbos — *shavtu* — within one of the outdoor domains, not inside a house. House vessels present an entirely different problem, one tied directly to the *eiruv* question. The three-way debate governs only which outdoor *reshuyot* are considered sufficiently unified to permit free movement of vessels originating within them.

### Yards A & B example

To make this concrete: consider two courtyards, A and B, which did not make a joint *eiruv* with each other. If the residents of A *did* make an *eiruv* among themselves, house vessels may be brought out into A's courtyard. But the rule is that from courtyard A to courtyard B, one may only carry *chatzer* vessels — items that began Shabbos in the courtyard itself, not in the house. This raises an immediate difficulty: if A made an *eiruv*, house vessels can legitimately appear in A's yard. Now there are two kinds of vessels sitting side by side in the same courtyard — one that began in the house and one that began in the yard — and one is permitted to be carried to B while the other is not. How is one supposed to remember which is which?

This is precisely the concern the *Gemara* will now turn to examine. The underlying question is: does the permissibility of carrying yard vessels from A to B depend on whether A has made an internal *eiruv* or not?

---

## Baraita: Rav & R. Meir

### Baraita: roofs vs. courts

The *Gemara* announces *tanya k'vasei d'Rav* and simultaneously *tanya k'vasei d'Rabbi Yehuda* — a *baraita* has been taught that supports both Rav's ruling and Rabbi Yehuda's interpretation of the *Mishnah*'s positions.

The *baraita* states: *kol gagot ha'ir reshut achat hen* — all the rooftops of the city are one domain. This is the position of Rabbi Meir: the rooftops collectively form a single unified *reshut*. But the *baraita* immediately qualifies: *v'assur l'ha'alos u'lehorid min ha'gag la'chatzer* — it is forbidden to carry up or down between the rooftop and the courtyard, and correspondingly, from the courtyard to the rooftop. Vessels that began Shabbos in the *chatzer* may be carried within the *chatzer*; vessels that began on the roof may be carried across the rooftops. But the two genres do not communicate with each other. This elegantly confirms Rabbi Yehuda's formulation: all rooftops are one, all courtyards are one, and the two categories are mutually distinct.

The *baraita* adds: *uvilvad shelo yehei gag gavoah asarah o namuch me'chatzer* — provided that no rooftop is ten *tefachim* higher or lower than the adjacent one, which replicates the *Mishnah*'s own qualification and grounds the ruling in the earlier discussion.

### Chachamim: 4 amot limit

*Vachachamim omrim*: the *Chachamim* say *kol echad ve'echad reshut le'atzmo* — each individual rooftop is its own domain. One may not carry from rooftop A to rooftop B. And crucially: *ve'ein metaltelin bo ella be'arba* — even within a single rooftop, one may not carry more than four *amot*. This is exactly the position Rav articulated earlier in explaining the *Chachamim*: once a rooftop is fully exposed to an adjacent rooftop to which carrying is forbidden, the space is treated as compromised, and even movement within it is limited to four *amot*.

This *baraita* thus provides clean textual confirmation of both Rav's interpretation of the *Chachamim* and Rabbi Yehuda's account of Rabbi Meir.

---

## Oil & Towels Story

### Tekoa bathing story

The *Gemara* now says *tanya k'vasei d'Rabbi Yehuda* — a *baraita* supports Rabbi Yehuda's reading of Rabbi Shimon's position specifically, demonstrating that Rabbi Shimon means not that each genre is internally unified but that all genres together are one.

Rabbi states: *keshehayinu lomdim Torah etzel Rabbi Shimon biTkoa* — when we were studying Torah with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa. On Shabbos they would bathe — with cold water or natural hot springs, which is permitted, since the prohibition on bathing in hot water stems from concern that one will come to heat the water on Shabbos. *Hayinu ma'alin shemen ve'aluntit* — they would carry oil and towels. And they would carry them *migag legag, umigag lechatzer, umichatzer lechatzer, umichatzer lekarpef, umikarpef lekarpef acher* — from roof to roof, from roof to courtyard, from courtyard to courtyard, from courtyard to *karpaf*, from one *karpaf* to another — *ad shehayinu magi'im etzel hama'ayan shehayinu rochtzin bo* — until they reached the spring where they would bathe.

This account demonstrates unmistakably that in Rabbi Shimon's academy and by his ruling, *gag*, *chatzer*, and *karpaf* were treated as a single unified domain. One may move freely between all of them. Notably, the account begins *migag* — from the rooftop — because the items must begin Shabbos within one of the outdoor domains. One cannot take something from inside the house; the oil and towels were presumably stored on the rooftop before Shabbos began.

### Torah scroll danger story

Rabbi Yehuda then offers an additional story: *ma'aseh bish'at hasakanah* — there was an incident in a time of danger in which a *Sefer Torah* was carried *michatzer legag, umigag lechatzer, umichatzer lekarpef* — from courtyard to rooftop to courtyard to *karpaf* — in order to read from it. The *Sefer Torah* presumably could not be left in the synagogue lest it be seized, and so it was moved on Shabbos itself from one outdoor domain to another to reach the place where it was needed.

The response is immediate: *ein sha'at hasakanah re'ayah* — a time of danger cannot serve as a legal proof. When lives or sacred objects are at stake, authorities may permit what they would otherwise forbid, and one cannot derive ordinary *halacha* from emergency practice.

A notable detail: in the bathing story, the oil and towels begin *migag* — from the rooftop — underlining that the items must originate in one of the permitted outdoor domains. The *Sefer Torah* story is somewhat less clear on this point, which may be precisely why it is dismissed: one cannot be certain the movement was technically licit rather than an emergency accommodation.

The broader discussion in the *baraita* at this point touches on the question of oil and rubbing on Shabbos — *sicha* (anointing) is prohibited on Yom Kippur but not on Shabbos, and oil with the viscosity of typical oil may be rubbed on the body freely. Similarly, the question of towels and squeezing (*sechitah*) had been addressed earlier in the *masechet*.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Rav's ruling

*Amar Rav, halacha k'Rabbi Shimon* — Rav rules in accordance with Rabbi Shimon. The most expansive position prevails: *gag*, *chatzer*, and *karpaf* are all one domain, and vessels originating in any of them may be carried freely throughout all of them.

### Rav's confusion concern

But Rav immediately qualifies: *vehu shelo eirvu* — and this applies only if they did not make an *eiruv*. Not merely that A and B did not make a joint *eiruv* with each other — that would render the entire discussion moot — but that A did not even make an internal *eiruv* among its own residents.

Why does this matter? *Degazrinan dilma ati l'apokei manei debatim lechatzer* — because we are concerned that if A made an internal *eiruv*, house vessels can legitimately be brought out into A's courtyard. Now the courtyard of A contains both yard vessels (which may be carried to B) and house vessels (which may not). Rav fears that one will lose track of which vessel started where and will carry a house vessel to B in the mistaken belief that it is a yard vessel.

There is a genuine tradeoff here: if you make an *eiruv* in A, you gain the ability to bring house vessels out into A's yard, but you forfeit the ability to carry yard vessels from A to B, because the risk of confusion is too great. If you forgo the *eiruv* in A, you cannot bring house vessels out at all, but yard vessels remain mobile across all the unified domains. It is not that one option is simply better than the other — they are genuinely different modes of carrying permission, and one must choose.

### Shmuel: no confusion fear

*U'Shmuel amar: bein eirvu bein shelo eirvu* — Shmuel disagrees. Whether A made an internal *eiruv* or not, yard vessels may still be carried from A to B. Shmuel is not afraid that people will confuse house vessels with yard vessels.

*Vechein amar Rabbi Yochanan* — and Rabbi Yochanan concurs with Shmuel. Tosafot notes the phrase used here — *mi lachshacha*, roughly "who whispered this distinction to you?" — is not common in the Talmud but appears a number of times in the *Torat Kohanim* (the *Sifra* on *Vayikra*). In context it conveys something like: on what basis do you draw this distinction between made-an-*eiruv* and did-not-make-an-*eiruv*? The allowance to carry yard vessels between courtyards is categorical, regardless of whether A has made an internal *eiruv*.

### Rav Chisda's challenge

*Metiv lei Rav Chisda le'Shmuel* — Rav Chisda raises an objection to Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan. *Yehyu shnei keilim be'chatzer achat* — you will have two vessels sitting in the same courtyard, *ze mutar ve'ze assur* — one permitted to be carried to the adjacent yard and one not. The practical impossibility of enforcing this distinction makes the ruling unworkable. If A has made an *eiruv* and both a house vessel and a yard vessel are now sitting together in A's courtyard, who can realistically remember which is which?

---

## R. Shimon's logic

### No gezeirah principle

The *Gemara* responds: *Rabbi Shimon le'taameih* — Rabbi Shimon acts consistently with his own broader reasoning. Rabbi Shimon does not issue a *gezeirah* out of concern for eventual confusion. This is not merely an assertion; it is demonstrated from a *Mishnah* we have seen earlier in the *masechet*.

### Three courtyards case

*Amar Rabbi Shimon: lamah hadavar domeh? Leshalosh chatzerot hapetuchot zo l'zo* — Rabbi Shimon compares his position to the case of three courtyards open to one another and each also opening into the *reshut harabim*. In this scenario, A made an *eiruv* with B, and C made an *eiruv* with B, but A and C did not make an *eiruv* with each other. The result is: B may carry freely with A, and B may carry freely with C, but A and C are forbidden to each other.

Now consider what this looks like in practice: vessels from A may enter B, and vessels from C may also enter B. Courtyard B now contains three types of vessels — its own, A's, and C's — with different rules applying to each. A's vessels may return to A or stay in B but not go to C. C's vessels may return to C or stay in B but not go to A. B's own vessels may go anywhere. Yet Rabbi Shimon, in that *Mishnah*, was not concerned that this complexity would lead to confusion and error.

By precise analogy: if Rabbi Shimon is unconcerned that people will confuse A-vessels, B-vessels, and C-vessels in the multi-courtyard case, he will similarly be unconcerned that people will confuse house vessels with yard vessels in the A-and-B case. The *gezeirah* Rav invokes — the fear of confusion — is one Rabbi Shimon simply does not invoke.

### Conclusion: R. Shimon

The upshot is that according to Rabbi Shimon himself, it would make no difference whether A made an internal *eiruv* or not. Even if A's yard contains both house vessels (carried out via the *eiruv*) and original yard vessels, Rabbi Shimon trusts that people will keep track. He permits yard vessels to move between the unified domains — *gag*, *chatzer*, *karpaf* — regardless. The *gezeirah* against confusion is not part of his legal reasoning.

---

## Balcony/Courtyard Ba (II)

### Height ownership test

The *Gemara* brings a new *baraita* concerning a *mirpeset* (balcony) and a *chatzer* (courtyard) that did not make an *eiruv* with one another. There is a structure — a mound or post — in the shared space, and the question is whether it "belongs" to the balcony level or the courtyard level for purposes of who may use it. The rule: *kol shegavoah asarah tefachim lemirpeset, pachot mikan lachatzer* — anything higher than ten *tefachim* belongs to the *mirpeset*; anything lower belongs to the *chatzer*. The *Gemara* earlier in the *masechet* had discussed the various ways to read this rule, but the principle itself is what matters here.

### Many people, no eruv

When does this height-based ownership rule apply? When there are many people living on each level and they each made their own internal *eiruv* — A's people made an *eiruv* among themselves, B's people made an *eiruv* among themselves — but they did not make a joint *eiruv* between the two levels. In that scenario the distinction between their spaces is meaningful, and the ownership of the mound matters.

But the *baraita* then states: if there were many people on each level and nobody made any *eiruv* at all — not even an internal one — then *gag, chatzer, achsadra, umirpeset kulan reshut achat hen* — rooftop, courtyard, *achsadra* (portico), and balcony are all one unified domain. The ownership question dissolves, because anything originating in any of these spaces may move freely among all of them.

### Listed vs. omitted spaces

Strikingly, the *baraita*'s list — *gag, chatzer, achsadra, umirpeset* — does not include *karpaf* or *mavoi*. This is not an accident. All four listed spaces share a characteristic: they are areas of regular or at least routine use. The *chatzer* is the yard directly in front of the house, used daily; the rooftop is accessible and functional; the *achsadra* is a portico or hallway through which people regularly pass; the *mirpeset* is a balcony in regular use. The *karpaf*, by contrast, is a more remote enclosed space, less frequently used, more like a vacant lot. The *Gemara* understands this omission as principled: the *karpaf* belongs to a different legal-functional category.

---

## Balcony/Courtyard Ba (II)

### Baraita is Chachamim

The *Gemara* draws the inference: this *baraita* cannot represent Rabbi Shimon's position, because Rabbi Shimon — as we know from the bathing story and from the three-courtyards *Mishnah* — includes *karpaf* along with *gag* and *chatzer* in the unified domain, and does not draw a line that excludes less-frequented spaces. The *baraita*, by omitting *karpaf*, must represent the *Chachamim*. This confirms that the *Chachamim* hold a genuine middle position: they unify the regularly-used outdoor spaces (*gag, chatzer, achsadra, mirpeset*) but treat *karpaf* and *mavoi* as distinct genres.

---

## Five courts & alley

### Setup: no eruv

The *Gemara* now introduces a case involving five courtyards open to one another and all opening into a *mavoi* (alley): *chamesh chatzerot hapetuchot zo l'zo ufetuchot lemavoi, veshachachu kulam velo eirvu* — all of them forgot and did not make an *eiruv*, not even an internal one among themselves.

### Chachamim: distinct doma…

The ruling that follows: *assur lehachnis ulehotzi mechatzer lemavoi umin hamavoi lechatzer* — it is forbidden to carry from courtyard to *mavoi* or from *mavoi* to courtyard. This is assumed to represent the position of the *Chachamim*, who, as we have now established, treat *mavoi* (like *karpaf*) as a domain categorically distinct from the regularly-used outdoor spaces. Even though nobody made any *eiruv* — so there is no concern of confusing house vessels with yard vessels — the *Chachamim* still prohibit movement between *chatzer* and *mavoi* because these are different *genres* of domain, not merely different individual spaces.

### Within each domain

*Aval kelim sheshavtu bechatzer mutar letaltelam bechatzer* — but vessels that began Shabbos in the courtyard may be carried within the courtyard freely. The *chatzer* is internally unified. However — and here is something striking — *uvemavoi assur*: vessels in the *mavoi* may not be freely carried even within the *mavoi* itself. Why the *mavoi* should be worse in this respect than the *chatzer* is a question the *Gemara* will take up shortly.

### R. Shimon adds karpef

*Rabbi Shimon omer* — Rabbi Shimon allows carrying from *chatzer* to *mavoi*. His formulation: *kol zman shehen shel rabbim veshachachu velo eirvu* — as long as many people live there and none of them made an *eiruv* — then *gag, chatzer, achsadra, mirpeset, ve'karpaf umavoi* — all of these, including *karpaf* and *mavoi*, *kulan reshut achat hen*, are one domain. This confirms the full reach of Rabbi Shimon's position: nothing is excluded. The *Chachamim*'s categorical distinction between the regularly-used spaces and the less-used *karpaf* and *mavoi* does not feature in Rabbi Shimon's reasoning at all.

---

## R. Shimon's concession

### Why 'no eruv'?

The *Gemara* immediately questions Rabbi Shimon's formulation. He specifies *velo eirvu* — and they did not make an *eiruv*. Does this mean that his leniency applies *only* if no *eiruv* was made? The implication would be that if A did make an internal *eiruv*, Rabbi Shimon would be more restrictive — which seems inconsistent with the position we have established for him.

### Meaning of 'no eruv'

The *Gemara* offers a first resolution: *mai lo eirvu? Lo eirvu chatzerot bahadi hadadi* — what does "they did not make an *eiruv*" mean? It means they did not make the grand collective *eiruv* — the *shituf* — that would have unified all the courtyards and the *mavoi* into a single shared space. It does *not* mean that no individual *eiruv* was made within courtyard A. In other words, Rabbi Shimon is saying: even in the scenario where the big collective *eiruv* was not made — a scenario that requires a ruling about what may be done — I will tell you that yard vessels may still move freely between all these spaces.

### Concession to opponents

The *Gemara* offers an alternative interpretation: *Rabbi Shimon ledivreihemdeRabbanan ka'amar* — Rabbi Shimon is formulating his ruling in terms that concede a premise to those who argue with him. From Rabbi Shimon's own perspective, *lo shena eirvu velo shena lo eirvu* — it makes no difference whether an *eiruv* was made in A or not; he is not afraid of vessel confusion regardless. But he addresses his opponents on their own terms: even if you, the *Rabbanan*, would be concerned about confusion when an *eiruv* exists in A and house vessels mix with yard vessels in the courtyard — *aval odu li mihat d'heicha d'lo eirvu* — at least concede to me that where no *eiruv* was made, where there is simply no possibility of a house vessel having entered the courtyard, you should agree that yard vessels may move freely from *chatzer* to *mavoi*.

### Chachamim: genre differe…

*Ve'amru lei Rabbanan*: the *Rabbanan* respond — *lo*. Even that concession we will not make. We are not restricting movement from *chatzer* to *mavoi* out of fear of vessel confusion. We restrict it because *shear reshuyot bamavoi asurin* — the *mavoi* is a categorically different type of domain from the courtyard. The prohibition is not remedied by the absence of an *eiruv*; it is structural. The *Chachamim*'s middle position does not rest on confusion concerns at all — it rests on a principled taxonomy of domain types.

---

## Mavoi vessel status

### Mavoi-origin vessels

The *Gemara* now focuses on an unexplained element of the *baraita*: *uvemavoi assur* — vessels originating in the *mavoi* may not be freely carried even within the *mavoi* itself. This is asymmetric with the *chatzer*: courtyard vessels may be carried freely throughout the courtyard even without an *eiruv*, but *mavoi* vessels apparently cannot be carried freely within the *mavoi*. The *Gemara* asks whether this supports the position of Rabbi Zeira.

### Rabbi Zeira: 4 amot limit

*De'amar Rabbi Zeira amar Rav*: Rabbi Zeira stated in the name of Rav — *mavoi shelo nishtatfu bo, ein metaltelin ella be'arba amot* — a *mavoi* in which no *shituf* (the alley-level communal contribution) was made allows carrying only four *amot*. This parallels the ruling about the rooftop according to the *Chachamim*: just as the *Chachamim* limit carrying on a single rooftop to four *amot* because the roof is exposed to adjacent forbidden space, so too the *mavoi* without a *shituf* is restricted to four *amot*.

The *Gemara* then reinterprets the *baraita*'s phrase *uvemavoi assur*: it does not mean that vessels originating in the *mavoi* may not be carried within the *mavoi*. Rather, *u-lemavoi assur* — one may not carry *to* the *mavoi* from the *chatzer*. The *baraita* is restating, for emphasis, the point already established: that the *Chachamim* categorically forbid movement between *chatzer* and *mavoi* regardless of whether an *eiruv* existed.

### Why mavoi is stricter

Why should the *mavoi* without a *shituf* be more restricted than the *chatzer* without an *eiruv*? The *Gemara* suggests one possible explanation: a *mavoi*, as a street-like passage, has some of the qualities of a *carmelit* — the semi-public intermediate domain — and therefore receives correspondingly stricter treatment. Other *sugyot* in the *Gemara* ground this restriction differently, invoking concerns about confusion of vessel types. The *Gemara* here does not fully resolve the question, but the *carmelit* analogy stands as a reasonable account.

The *Gemara* then adds a further note: the *Rabbanan* genuinely mean their categorical position. One might think that when they prohibit movement from *chatzer* to *mavoi*, they do so only because an *eiruv* was made in the courtyard and they fear confusion about house vessels. *Kama'shma lan* — the *baraita*'s reiteration comes to teach us that is not so. Even where no *eiruv* was made at all and there is no conceivable confusion, the *Chachamim* still hold that *chatzer* and *mavoi* are distinct domains, and one may not carry between them.

### Three-position summary

The full three-position framework can now be stated clearly. Rabbi Meir: each domain type — *gag*, *chatzer*, *karpaf* — is internally unified but externally separate from the others. The *Chachamim*: the regularly-used outdoor spaces (*gag*, *chatzer*, *achsadra*, *mirpeset*) are unified with one another, but *karpaf* and *mavoi* are categorically separate. Rabbi Shimon: all outdoor spaces — *gag*, *chatzer*, *achsadra*, *mirpeset*, *karpaf*, and *mavoi* — are one unified domain, and vessels originating in any of them may move freely throughout all of them. The further debate between Rav and Shmuel — whether Rabbi Shimon's leniency applies even when an internal *eiruv* has been made in one of the courtyards — turns on whether Rabbi Shimon is concerned about confusion between house vessels and yard vessels. The answer is that he is not: consistent with his position in the three-courtyards case, Rabbi Shimon makes no *gezeirah* against such confusion.

---

---

# Eiruvin 93

## Large & Small Yards

### Two-Directional Model

Today's daf is 93, and we pick up at the bottom of 92b with an important discussion that carries ramifications well beyond the immediate topic of *hilchos Shabbos*. The central configuration under discussion involves a large courtyard (A) and a small courtyard (B), where B is entirely open to A but A is not entirely open to B. This asymmetry gives rise to two distinct legal consequences, which the *gemara* treats together but which are worth distinguishing analytically.

### Disassociation & Walls

The first consequence concerns the ability to disassociate. Because B is completely open to A, there is no way for B to divorce itself from what is happening in A. The reverse, however, is not true: A can disassociate itself from B. A concrete illustration of this appears in the preceding discussion about reciting *shema* in proximity to excrement. If one is reciting *shema* in A and excrement is located in B, B need not be considered relevant to A — A sees B as a partially separate space, accessible only through a distinct opening. But if one is reciting *shema* in B and excrement is in A, B cannot disassociate from A, because from B's perspective the two spaces form one continuous expanse. This is the same logic underlying the *mishna* itself: if one is not permitted to carry in A and finds oneself in B, one cannot carry in B either, precisely because B is *parutz bimlo'o* — completely breached into A.

### Primary & Adjunct

The second consequence concerns the relationship of primary and adjunct space. B is an adjunct to A, but A is not an adjunct to B. This has practical implications for the laws of *minyan*. If the majority of a *minyan* is in A and the *shliach tzibbur* is in B, that arrangement is valid, because B as the adjunct space follows A as the primary space. However, the reverse does not work: if the *minyan* is in B and the *shliach tzibbur* is in A, the arrangement fails. The secondary element must be in the adjunct space, not the primary one. A cannot be pulled after B; only B can be pulled after A.

### Perceptual Perspective

A useful way to understand these two principles as a unified whole is to consider the perspective of a person standing in each yard. If you are standing in A and look around, you see your own space with a smaller yard off to one side — something clearly distinct, requiring you to pass through a doorway to reach it. The walls of B are visible; B registers as a separate room. But if you are standing in B and look around, you see no interior walls demarcating a boundary. The far wall of A is simply the far wall of your visual field, and the entire expanse appears as one undivided space. This is precisely why, from B, one cannot disassociate and why A functions as the encompassing primary domain.

---

## Wall Paradox

### Vineyard & Walls

Abaye, who was seated among three senior colleagues during this discussion, posed a sharp challenge: *im kein matzinu mechitza le-issur* — if so, we find that a *mechitza* creates a prohibition. The context for this observation draws on the laws of *kilayim* in vineyards. The standard *halakha* is that if one has a row of grapevines and wishes to plant wheat nearby, it suffices to distance oneself four *amot* from the vines. Now consider what happens when a wall is added around the vineyard: from the perspective of B, the enclosed vineyard is treated as a *kerem*, extending into B's space. The prohibition of *lo tizra karemcha kilayim* — do not sow your vineyard with mixed species — now applies within B. Even if one is more than four *amot* from the vines, if the wall has effectively incorporated the space, planting anything there becomes forbidden.

### Mechitza Le-Issur

Abaye's challenge is thus: the presence of walls should, if anything, demarcate and separate. Yet what we are being told is that by configuring B as an adjunct to the *kerem*, the walls make things *more* forbidden, not less. Is it possible that a *mechitza* — something that should create separation — actually produces greater association and, consequently, a greater *issur*?

### Rav Zeira Answer

Rav Zeira responded to Abaye: *velo matzinu mechitza le-issur?* — are you really claiming we find no such precedent? He cited our very *mishna*: *chatzer gedola shenifretzah liketana, gedola muteres ketana asura* — the large courtyard that is breached into the small one leaves the large permitted and the small forbidden. And furthermore, *v'ilu hishveh et kipifeha gedola nami asura* — if one levels the overhang of the small yard, creating a new wall that effectively extends the boundary, the large yard also becomes forbidden. Here, adding a *mechitza* made something that was formerly permitted into something forbidden. This is a case of *mechitza le-issur*, and it is familiar *halakha*.

---

## Wall Removal Cases

### Mikveh & Roof

Abaye, however, was not satisfied. He noted that in Rav Zeira's example, the act of adding a wall did not simply add a wall — it removed other walls. The new partition effectively eliminated the existing walls that had defined A as its own distinct space. By adding this wall, those defining walls were rendered irrelevant, causing A to collapse into the same status as B. So what looks like an addition of a wall is really a removal of walls, and it is the *siluk mechitzot* — the removal of those walls — that creates the prohibition, not the mere act of building a new one.

This same response applies to the next attempted counterexample, brought by Rabba bar bar Chana, involving a house half of which has a roof and half of which does not. If grapevines are planted under the roofed section and one wishes to plant seeds under the open section, the roofline serves as a type of *mechitza* — a demarcating edge akin to *pi tikra yored v'sotem*, the conceptual principle that the edge of a roof descends and closes the space. If one then extends the roof to cover the entire house, the division disappears and planting seeds anywhere in the house becomes forbidden. Once again, Abaye responds: this is not a case of adding a wall and thereby making things worse — it is a case of adding a roof that effectively removes the wall created by the partial roofline. The answer is the same: *hasam siluk mechitzot hu*.

### Distinguish Removal

Abaye's sustained point across all these exchanges is precise: every counterexample offered involves a scenario where building something new has the effect of dismantling an existing *mechitza*. None of these examples, therefore, address his original question, which concerns a *mechitza* that is purely additive — one that does not eliminate any prior partition but that nonetheless produces greater association rather than greater separation.

### Sukka & Posts

Rava then offered another attempted counterexample, drawn from the laws of *sukka* (79a). The case involves placing *s'chach* on top of a portico (*achsadra*) that has *patzimim* — a type of structural shoulder or partial wall extending inward at the corners, creating what functions as a partial third wall. Such a *sukka* is *keshera*, because two full walls and a minimal third wall suffice for *sukka* validity. However, if one levels the *patzimim* — by adding a wall between them — the *sukka* becomes *pesulah*. Adding a wall made the *sukka* invalid.

### Pi Tikra Yored

Abaye responds on two levels. First, for his own position, the case is not a question at all: *lididi keshera* — according to me, it is already *keshera* even after the modification, because I hold *pi tikra yored v'sotem*, that the edge of the roof descends and closes the space, providing the needed third wall regardless of what is done to the *patzimim*. Second, addressing the position of those who do hold the *sukka* becomes *pesulah*: that is once again a case of *siluk mechitzot*. By adding the new wall between the *patzimim*, one has effectively removed the *patzimim* themselves as halakhically significant walls. The addition caused the disappearance of prior valid walls. This is the same dynamic as all the earlier cases, and therefore it still does not constitute a genuine proof that a *mechitza* can create prohibition purely through addition.

---

## Vineyard Solution

### Mechitzot Rules

The *gemara* then turns to a *braita* sent to Abaye by Rava through the intermediary of Shmaya bar Zeira. The *braita* teaches: *yesh b'mechitzos hakerem lehakeil ulehachmir* — there are ways in which the walls of a vineyard can be both lenient and stringent.

### Leniency: Opposite

The leniency is as follows. If a vineyard is planted right up to the edge of a wall — *kerem hanatu'a ad ikkar mechitza* — one may plant other species beginning immediately on the other side of the wall, *zorei'a mei'ikkar mechitza v'eilaich*. Without the wall, one would have been required to distance four *amot* from the vines. The wall effectively substitutes for that distance, allowing planting right against the wall's opposite face. This is *mechitzos hakerem lehakeil*.

### Stringency: Same Side

The stringency is the inverse. If there is open space between the vineyard and a wall, and that space is only eleven *amot*, one may not plant anything there — *lo yehei zorei'a l'sham*. Without the wall, four *amot* of distance from the vines would have been sufficient. With the wall present and one on the same side as the vineyard, the requirement is now twelve *amot* rather than four. This is *mechitzos hakerem lehachmir*, and this, says Rava, is the clear precedent for Abaye's concern: a *mechitza* that, rather than separating, requires far greater distance and is therefore stringent.

To complete the picture: the *mishna* in *Kilayim* records that a *karachas hakerem* — a bald spot in the middle of a vineyard, surrounded by vines on all sides — must be at least sixteen *amot* wide according to Beis Hillel (Beis Shammai requires twenty-four) for it to be treated as an independent space in which one may plant. A *machol hakerem* — the band of space between the vines and the surrounding wall — must be at least twelve *amot* wide according to Beis Hillel (Beis Shammai requires sixteen). In both cases, the surrounding vines or walls pull the space into the orbit of the vineyard, requiring a minimum threshold before the space is considered independent. Once that threshold is met, one must still maintain four *amot* from the vines themselves — *kedei avodaso*, the working space needed to tend the vine — and may plant only in the remainder.

### Workspace Forfeit

The *gemara*, however, ultimately concludes that this is not the reason the wall creates a stringency. Abaye responds: *ela hasam lav hainu taama* — the reason there is not what you think. The wall does not pull the space together in some abstract halakhic sense. Rather, the explanation is practical: the four *amot* immediately adjacent to the wall are, in effect, already forfeit. Since one cannot plant against the wall — both because the roots would undermine the wall's foundation and because a plow cannot operate in that narrow strip — those first four *amot* along the wall are treated as if one has already renounced ownership of them: *afkurei mafkir lehu*. They are simply unavailable. Therefore, for the remaining space between the vine and the wall to be considered independent — significant enough to plant in — it must be four *amot* on its own, beyond the already-forfeited strip. That yields a total of twelve *amot*: four forfeit at the wall, four of *kedei avodaso* at the vine, and four of independent space in the middle. This is not because the wall integrated the space into the vineyard; it is because the wall practically eliminated a portion of the available space. Abaye insists that a *mechitza* pulling disparate spaces together into a single unified domain — without any such practical mechanism — remains conceptually troubling.

---

## Caravans & Space

### Three Overhang Setup

Rav Yehuda now applies the framework of primary and adjunct space to a different context, drawing on the *halakha* of *eruv* boundaries for encamped groups. The scenario involves three spaces — A, B, and C — arranged side by side, where the two outer ones (A and C) have overhangs and the middle one (B) does not. There is one person in each space. The question concerns whether these three individuals qualify as a *shayara* — a caravan — which would permit them to enclose a space larger than *beis sasayim* using even minimal (*lavud*-based) wall structures.

The ruling is that they do qualify: *na'asah keshayara v'nosnim lahem kol tzorchan*. From B's perspective, A and C are entirely open to it; all three individuals are effectively present in B. Since three people constitute a *shayara*, B's enclosure can be as large as needed. According to Rashi's reading, it is specifically B's space that may be unlimited, since all three are treated as residents there.

### Opposite Setup

The reverse configuration changes matters considerably. Here B (the middle space) has the overhang and is the larger space, while A and C (the outer spaces) are smaller and lack overhangs. Again there is one person in each.
