In this arrangement, B sees A as an adjunct and C as an adjunct, but A and C each see only one person associated with themselves — the single person in B can be said to extend toward A, but from C's perspective that same person also extends toward C. No single space accumulates three individuals. The ruling is *ein nosnim lahem ela beis shesh* — they are given a combined total of six *se'ah*, which is simply three times the standard individual allotment of *beis sasayim*, one for each person. No *shayara* status is achieved.

### Ambiguous Cases

The *gemara* then raises a series of uncertain configurations. The first: what if there are two people in B and one in each of A and C, using the second (opposite) configuration? One might reason that from A's perspective, both people in B are associated with A, yielding three people — *shayara* status. From C's perspective the same logic would apply. Or perhaps one person from B is associated with A and the other with C, leaving each side with only two — no *shayara*. A further scenario: two in A, two in C, and one in B. From A's perspective, the single B-resident joins them for three; from C's perspective the same. Or perhaps the one person in B can go in only one direction, and since we do not know which, neither A nor C can count on having three.

### Leniency Ruling

The *gemara* resolves all these open questions with a single ruling: *v'hilchasa ba'ayan lekula* — the *halakha* for all the unresolved cases is lenient. This is consistent with the general posture of *eruvin* toward permissibility in doubtful cases.

---

## Mound & Wall

### Five & Five Setup

Rav Chisda raises a new question directly relevant to the laws of *reshus hayachid*: if there is a *giddur* — a raised platform or mound — of five *tefachim*, and atop it stands a wall of five *tefachim*, do the two combine to constitute a valid enclosure? A full *reshus hayachid* requires a height of ten *tefachim*. If the entire elevation were in the ground itself, or entirely in a wall, the answer would be straightforward. But here, five comes from the raised ground and five from a wall built upon it.

### Tosafot Problem

Tosafot raises a searching difficulty with this scenario. The *gemara* suggests that such a combination might function as a *mechitza* from one side but not from the other: a person standing on the far side would see a wall of ten and would treat the space as *reshus hayachid*, while a person on the near side — standing at ground level looking at a five-*tefach* mound with a five-*tefach* wall atop it — might not. Tosafot asks whether it is coherent to say that something is a *reshus hayachid* in only one direction. He notes that if this were true, throwing an object from the far side into the enclosure would be *chayav*, while throwing from the enclosure outward would be *patur* — a striking asymmetry that seems halakhically untenable.

### Two Yards Brayta

The *gemara* then cites a *braita* that appears to bear directly on the question: two courtyards, one elevated above the other by ten *tefachim*, or alternatively one elevated five *tefachim* with a five-*tefach* wall on top — *me'arvin shnayim v'ein me'arvin echad*. They make two separate *eruvin* and cannot make a single unified one. This implies that the five-and-five configuration constitutes a genuine separation between the two courtyards. Conversely, if the wall is lower — *pachot mikan* — the ruling reverses: *me'arvin echad v'ein me'arvin shnayim*, they must make one unified *eruv* and cannot make two.

The problem this *braita* poses is immediate. Rav Chisda's initial ruling is that five-and-five do *not* combine. If so, from the upper courtyard's perspective there is no genuine wall of ten separating it from the lower courtyard — in which case why can the two not simply make one unified *eruv*? And yet the *braita* says they must make two separate ones, which implies a genuine separation exists.

---

## Weak Answer

### Lower Perspective

Rava addresses the difficulty: *modeh Rav Chisda betachtonah haoveret al pnei asara* — Rav Chisda concedes that with respect to the lower courtyard, which looks up at what appears to be a full ten-*tefach* wall, a genuine separation exists. From the lower courtyard's vantage point, the combined height of mound and wall presents a complete barrier. The lower courtyard is therefore genuinely separated and must make its own independent *eruv*.

### Upper Dilemma

The difficulty, however, is with the upper courtyard. From above, the wall is only five *tefachim*, which — on Rav Chisda's reading — does not suffice to create a separation. The upper courtyard therefore cannot make its own separate *eruv*, since from its perspective no genuine wall divides it from the lower courtyard. Nor can it make a unified *eruv* with the lower courtyard, because from the lower courtyard's perspective a full separation does exist. The upper courtyard is entirely stuck — unable to make either a separate or a joint *eruv*: *lo tearav lo echad velo shnayim*.

### Special Case

To resolve this, Rabbah bar Ulla proposes a constrained reading of the *braita*: *kegon shehayta elyonah megufefet ad eser amot* — we are dealing with a special case in which the upper courtyard is itself enclosed on its other sides by walls that reach the full ten *tefachim*. In such a case, the upper courtyard has an independent halakhic enclosure by virtue of those other walls, allowing it to make its own separate *eruv* regardless of the ambiguous status of the shared boundary. The five-and-five wall that faces the lower courtyard need not itself constitute a full *mechitza*, because other walls of the upper courtyard supply the necessary enclosure independently.

### Below Five Rule

The second clause of the *braita* — that when the wall drops below five, the two must make a single *eruv* — is explained as follows. Once the wall falls below five *tefachim*, the total height from the lower courtyard's perspective also drops below ten. The lower courtyard is now *parutz bemilo'o* — completely open to the upper courtyard — and can no longer maintain an independent *eruv*. Both must therefore join together. The upper courtyard, meanwhile, retains the option to separate itself by means of its other walls, but the lower courtyard loses its independent standing entirely. This is a labored and technically constrained explanation of the *braita*, and its complexity signals that the *gemara* is not fully satisfied with it.

---

## Mareimar Solution

### Five Amot Combine

The resolution comes from Mareimar, who rules directly and cleanly: *gidud chamisha u'mechitza chamisha mitztarfin* — a mound of five and a wall of five do combine to form a valid *mechitza*. This position cuts through all the difficulties generated by the weak answer, because it accepts the plain reading of the *braita*: the five-and-five scenario genuinely constitutes a full partition on both sides, not merely from one direction.

### Ravina Confirms

Ravina encountered Rav Acha brei de-Rava and asked whether he had heard any teaching on the question of *mechitza* in this context — specifically, whether there was an alternative ruling on the five-and-five combination. The answer was no: *amar lei lo*. No competing position on this question was in circulation.

### Final Ruling

The *halakha* is therefore stated explicitly: *v'hilchesa gidud chamisha u'mechitza chamisha mitztarfin* — a raised mound of five *tefachim* combined with a wall of five *tefachim* atop it does form a complete *mechitza*, constituting a valid enclosure of *reshus hayachid* on both sides. The asymmetric reading — *reshus hayachid* from one direction but not the other — is rejected. The simple sense of the *braita*, which treats the five-and-five combination as producing a genuine separation requiring two separate *eruvin*, is affirmed as the *halakha*.

---

## Shabbat Changes

### Wall Falls Case

Rav Hoshaya raises an independent question: *diyorin habaim b'Shabbos* — what is the law when the configuration of a courtyard changes on *Shabbos* itself, so that parties who were previously considered separate become, in effect, combined? The question is specifically whether such a mid-*Shabbos* change renders carrying forbidden where it had previously been permitted.

Rav Chisda brings a proof from our *mishna*: *chatzer gedolah shenifretzah liketanah, hagedolah muteres vehaketanah asurah* — the large courtyard that is breached into the small one; the large is permitted and the small is forbidden. He reads *shenifretzah* — "that was breached" — as referring to a wall that fell during *Shabbos*. On this reading, B was permitted when *Shabbos* began because the wall was intact, but once the wall fell, B became forbidden. This would demonstrate that changes occurring during *Shabbos* can retroactively alter the *halakhic* status of a space.

### Raba Interprets

Raba challenges this reading. He suggests that *shenifretzah* does not necessarily imply the wall fell during *Shabbos*: *eimar mibod yom nifretzah* — one may equally read it as the wall having already fallen before *Shabbos* began. In that case, the *mishna* describes a static situation present at the onset of *Shabbos* and says nothing at all about mid-*Shabbos* changes.

### Abaye Insists

Abaye, however, insists on a definitive reading: *ela vaday mibod yom nifretzah* — it must mean the wall fell before *Shabbos*, not during *Shabbos*. And critically, this is not merely a textual preference. Abaye reminds Raba that the principle at stake is Raba's own established position — one that Raba himself had applied in an earlier context when he directed Abaye to query both Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah about the following case: if an *eruv* was established through an opening — *eruv derech hapetach* — and that opening was subsequently sealed on *Shabbos*, or an *eruv* was established through a window that was then sealed during *Shabbos*, what is the *halakha*?

### Shabbat Haturah

The response that came back — attributed in the text with some ambiguity of singular and plural — was: *Shabbos keivan shehutar hutar* — since *Shabbos* began in a state of permissibility, it remains permitted. Whatever configuration was in place at the onset of *Shabbos* governs the entire day. A change that occurs *during* *Shabbos* does not alter the status that was established at *Shabbos'* beginning. Abaye presses this principle: if the wall fell before *Shabbos*, then B's status was already fixed as forbidden when *Shabbos* started, and the *mishna* simply describes that. But if the wall fell during *Shabbos*, the principle of *Shabbos keivan shehutar hutar* would apply — and B, which began *Shabbos* in a permitted state, should remain permitted throughout. The *mishna* therefore cannot be describing a mid-*Shabbos* collapse, for if it were, B should still be permitted. This is where the daf concludes.

---

---

# Eiruvin 95

## Wall Breaches & Pi Takra

### Keivan De'hutra Hutra

We pick up on the bottom of 94b, four lines from the bottom. By way of review, the *mishnah* established that if a wall falls down on *Shabbos*, one may still carry in that zone, because the space was *mutar* when *Shabbos* began. This was the position of the *tanna kamma*, Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yosi, by contrast, insists on consistency: either the space is valid for future *Shabbosos* or it is not valid for this *Shabbos*.

This connects directly to the principle of *keivan de'hutra hutra* — once something begins *Shabbos* in a permitted state, *hutra le'oho Shabbos*, it remains permitted for the entire *Shabbos*: *hutra lechol ha'Shabbos kulo*. Things continue in the condition in which they began. There is, of course, a limit to this principle. If the situation deteriorates to the point of a genuine biblical violation — such as a true *reshus ha'rabim* — one cannot invoke mere rabbinic leniency to sustain it.

### Maintaining Initial Stat…

This is precisely why the *gemara* labored to explain that the *mishnah*'s case of two walls falling down does not really mean that the space has been reduced to an open field. Rather, we are dealing with something like two corners of a wall having crumbled, while the structure retains mostly intact walls on three sides in various configurations. The *gemara* explored why the *mishnah* needed to specify two walls when even one wall falling would suffice to compromise the *reshus ha'yachid* status and generate the scenario under discussion.

### Rav vs. Shmuel Debate

Within that broader discussion, we encountered the debate between Rav and Shmuel regarding the principle of *pi takra yored vesosem* — the notion that the edge of a roof descends conceptually and seals off that side, creating a wall. According to Rashi's reading of the *gemara*, Shmuel holds that one cannot invoke *pi takra* for all four walls, while Rav permits invoking it even for a full four walls. That debate over how broadly one may apply *pi takra* is the backdrop against which the *gemara* now examines several further parameters.

---

## Pi Takra Parameters

### Ten Amos Consensus

The *gemara* opens this analysis with the statement *b'eser kulei alma lo peligi* — if the breach is ten *amos* or fewer, everyone agrees that one invokes *pi takra yored vesosem*. There is no dispute in that case.

### Larger Than Ten Amos

The disagreement arises when the breach is *beyaser me'eser* — larger than ten *amos*. An opening wider than ten *amos* is not treated as a normal doorway and therefore requires correction. It is precisely here that Rav and Shmuel diverge: according to Rashi, Shmuel will not invoke *pi takra* for four walls, while Rav will do so even in that scenario.

The *gemara* then presents an alternative formulation — *ika de'amri* — which inverts the premise: *beyaser kulei alma lo peligi*, meaning that for openings larger than ten *amos*, everyone agrees that *pi takra* does not apply. The debate, on this reading, concerns openings of ten *amos* or smaller: *ki peligi b'eser*. That is, it is only within the ten-*amah* range that Rav and Shmuel differ over whether *pi takra* may be invoked.

One might ask: if the breach is ten *amos* or smaller, what is the need for *pi takra* at all? A gap that size would ordinarily be treated like an ordinary doorway. The answer is that there are scenarios where it matters — most notably where there are too many openings such that *parutz meruba al ha-omed* becomes a concern, and in the extreme case Rashi describes of a portico situated in the middle of a valley with no walls at all. In those situations, the question of whether *pi takra* can function for an opening of a given size becomes critical. One could also imagine an analogous vertical limit — whether *pi takra* applies when the roof is higher than twenty *amos*, which connects to the beginning of the *masechet*, though this specific question is not taken up explicitly here.

### Beam in Field Case

The *gemara* next cites a ruling of Rav Yehuda: *kora arba matya b'churva* — a beam four *tefachim* wide positioned in the middle of an open field creates a *reshus ha'yachid* beneath it. The mechanism is *pi takra* applied to all four sides: the edges of the beam descend and form four conceptual walls, enclosing a space four by four *tefachim*. This is an extreme application of *pi takra*, relying on it to generate all four walls simultaneously.

### Water vs. Dry Land

Rav Nachman, citing Rabba bar Avuha, qualifies this ruling: *kora arba matya b'mayim* — the beam case applies only over water, not over dry land. We have seen elsewhere that the *halachos* of walls over water involve special leniencies, such as permitting the drawing of water. The question of who this ruling follows — *mani* — is then addressed in light of the two formulations of the Rav-Shmuel debate. According to the first reading (*leima*), where everyone agrees for openings of ten *amos* or smaller, *de'eser ve'divrei hakol*, even Shmuel could accept the beam case, provided the opening is less than ten *amos*. According to the second reading (*ve'idach lishana*), where the debate extends even to ten *amos* or smaller, the beam case reflects the position of Rav alone.

### Sukkah S'chach Debate

The *gemara* then asks whether the debate between Abaye and Rava regarding *s'chach* on a portico parallels the dispute between Rav and Shmuel. The case: *sekhakha gabei achsadra she'yesh lah petzimim* — *s'chach* placed on a portico that has posts at its open edges. When such posts exist, they constitute at least two and a half walls, which suffices for a *sukkah*, and everyone agrees it is *keshera*. The difficulty arises when *ein lah petzimim* — there are no posts, meaning the portico lacks the requisite walls. Here the debate turns entirely on *pi takra*: Abaye says it remains *keshera* because *pi takra yored vesosem*, while Rava says it is *pesulah* because we do not invoke *pi takra* in this configuration.

The *gemara* asks whether this means Abaye follows Rav and Rava follows Shmuel. The answer is more nuanced: the debate of Abaye and Rava, on this reading, is *aliba d'Rav* — both are working within Rav's framework, which ordinarily permits invoking *pi takra* on all four sides. Abaye holds that this applies to the *sukkah* case as well. Rava disagrees.

### Permanent vs. Ad Hoc Roo…

Rava's position is that Rav's permission to invoke *pi takra* on four sides was stated specifically where *hani mechitzos l'achsadra avidi* — the roof was built as part of the portico structure itself, and so the roof defines and encloses the space beneath it. In that case, the logic of *pi takra* is compelling: a permanent roof suggests the existence of walls and creates a sense of enclosed space. But in the *sukkah* case, one simply set up posts and laid *s'chach* on top — an ad hoc arrangement made for a specific purpose. Rava holds that such a roof, *lav l'sukka avidi* in the relevant sense, lacks the structural character necessary to invoke *pi takra* on all four sides. The underlying logic, as one might frame it, is that *pi takra* derives its force from the way a roof naturally implies an enclosed structure beneath it; a purely temporary covering arranged for *Sukkos* does not carry that implication strongly enough to generate four conceptual walls.

---

## Rabbi Yosi's Position

### Past vs. Future Shabbosos

The *gemara* now returns to the central question of the *mishnah*: what is Rabbi Yosi's ruling, and in which direction does it cut? *Ibayu lehu*: Does Rabbi Yosi's principle apply *l'issura* — meaning the wall's compromise renders the space forbidden for this *Shabbos* as well as future ones — or *l'hetera* — meaning its permitted status now carries forward to future *Shabbosos*?

### Ruling Like Rabbi Yosi

Rav Sheshet rules *l'issura*, and so does Rabbi Yochanan. The logic is straightforward: it would be anomalous for an accident that occurs on *Shabbos* to generate more leniency going forward. The normal rule should govern. This is corroborated by a *beraita*: *amar Rabbi Yosi k'shem she'asura l'asid lavo kach asura l'osa Shabbos* — just as it is forbidden going forward, so too it is forbidden for this very *Shabbos*.

### Rabbi Yehuda in Eruvin

On the question of practical *psak*, Rav Chiya bar Yosef rules like Rabbi Yosi, while Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yehuda, maintaining that the space retains its permitted status. This latter ruling appears consistent with the broader principle cited in Rav Yehuda's name from Shmuel: *kol makom sheshana Rabbi Yehuda b'Eruvin halacha k'moso* — wherever Rabbi Yehuda rules in *Eruvin*, we follow him.

### Shmuel's Qualified Posit…

However, the *gemara* challenges whether Shmuel truly maintains this position across the board. Rav Chana Bagdata'ah asks Rav Yehuda: does Shmuel mean to rule like Rabbi Yehuda even in the case of our *mishnah* — where the beam or post of a *mavoi* fell down, eliminating the requisite wall configuration — and say that carrying there remains permitted? This is the case of *b'mavoi shenitla koraso o lechayav*.

### Eruvin vs. Mechitzos

Shmuel clarifies: *b'Eruvin amri lach, v'lo b'mechitzos* — his ruling in favor of Rabbi Yehuda applies to *halachos* of *eruvin* proper, not to questions of wall requirements. The distinction is significant: while we often discuss both under the heading of *Eruvin*, the laws of *mechitzos* are technically *Shabbos* laws that define the character of a *reshus ha'yachid*, while *eruvin* in the narrow sense concerns the joining together through bread or food to create communal unity permitting carrying. Shmuel will follow Rabbi Yehuda on the former, not the latter.

### Karmelis vs. Reshus Hara…

Rav Abba offers a further precision, reporting what was explained to him directly from Shmuel: the ruling depends on what domain the wall opens to. *Kan shenifretzu l'karmelis, kan shenifretzu l'reshus ha'rabim*. If the breach exposes the *chatzer* to a *karmelis*, there is less cause for concern — even if one carries from the *chatzer* into the *karmelis*, it is only a rabbinic transgression, and so the space may remain in its initial permitted status over *Shabbos*. But if the breach opens to a *reshus ha'rabim*, one risks a biblical transgression, and Shmuel would not permit the space to continue in its permitted status.

Crucially, the leniency of the *mavoi* case involving the *korah* or *lechi* that fell — distinct from our *mishnah*'s concern about the number of walls — brings in an additional dimension: the function of the *korah* or *lechi* is partly to serve as a *heker*, a reminder that one is entering a different zone. When that marker falls, the severity of the concern depends on what zone is exposed. So Shmuel's position emerges as quite narrow: he would rule like Rabbi Yehuda only when three full walls remain intact and the breach opens only to a *karmelis*.

Tosafot's conclusion on the practical *halacha* is that we rule like Rav against Shmuel in prohibitions, and therefore even in the case of a breach to a *karmelis*, the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi who is stringent: *v'afilu b'nifretza l'karmelis halacha k'Rabbi Yosi d'machmir*.

---

## Bridge & Portico Cases

### Second Story Case

The *mishnah* with which we close this *perek* presents two related cases. The first: *haboneh aliyah al gavi sheni batim* — someone builds a second story over two houses situated on opposite sides of a *reshus ha'rabim*, connected like a bridge overhead. The practical image is vivid: two houses flanking a public thoroughfare, with a walkway or room built above spanning the gap between them, open at both ends below. Rabbi Yehuda rules that *metaltelin tachteihen b'Shabbos* — one may carry underneath the bridge on *Shabbos*. The *chachamim* forbid it.

The second case: *me'arvin l'mavoi mefulash* — Rabbi Yehuda further holds that one may make an *eruv* for an open-ended street, a *mavoi mefulash*, that has walls on its two long sides but is open at both ends. The *chachamim* forbid this as well.

### Rabba's Pi Takra View

Rabba cautions against misreading Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning in the first case. *Lo teima hainu ta'ama d'Rabbi Yehuda mishum d'kasvar shtei mechitzos d'oraita* — do not assume that the permission in the bridge case rests on Rabbi Yehuda's principle that two walls suffice biblically. Rather, says Rabba, *mishum d'kasvar pi tikra yored vesosem* — the bridge case relies on *pi takra*: the edges of the overhead structure descend and create four effective walls, leaving the two actual house walls on the sides and the two conceptual walls generated by *pi takra* at the open ends.

### Two Walls Sufficing

Abaye challenges this interpretation. He demonstrates from a different *sugya* that Rabbi Yehuda's principle that two walls suffice is independently established: *yeter al ken amar Rabbi Yehuda* — Rabbi Yehuda further ruled that a person with houses on two sides of a *reshus ha'rabim* need only add a *lechi* or *korah* at each open end in order to carry in the enclosed stretch, even though it traverses an actual *reshus ha'rabim*. This is an extreme position — a minimal post or beam alongside two existing walls is sufficient to create a *reshus ha'yachid*. The *chachamim* responded that one cannot make an *eruv* in a *reshus ha'rabim* with so few structural elements. But the point for Abaye is that Rabbi Yehuda's view that two walls suffice is clearly established from this independent source.

Abaye's response to Rabba is therefore: *me'ha leka l'mishma minah* — I do not claim you are wrong about Rabbi Yehuda's position; I know full well he holds two walls suffice. I am only saying that the first case in the *mishnah* does not make that principle clear, since the bridge itself provides *pi takra* on the remaining sides. So the debate between Rabba and Abaye is largely academic.

### Two Principles Analysis

Rav Ashi, however, observes that the *mishnah* itself points toward Rabba's interpretation. Since the *mishnah* adds a second case with the words *ve'od amar Rabbi Yehuda* — *and further* Rabbi Yehuda said one may make an *eruv* in an open-ended street — this formulation implies that the second case adds something beyond the first. *Ei amart bishlama mishum de'kasvar pi tikra yored vesosem* — if the first case is about *pi takra*, then *ve'od* makes perfect sense: the second case goes further and shows that Rabbi Yehuda does not even need *pi takra*, for he relies on two walls alone. But if the first case were itself already about two walls, there would be no escalation in the second case and the *ve'od* would be superfluous. *Shma mina*.

### Chachamim Disagree

This analysis also raises a noteworthy question about the *chachamim*'s position. It is understandable that the *chachamim* reject the principle that two walls suffice — that is the second case's dispute. But since everyone, including the *chachamim*, has been working with some form of *pi takra* throughout this *sugya*, why do the *chachamim* forbid the bridge case where *pi takra* is in play? The answer, presumably, is that the bridge case involves *pi takra* being invoked in the middle of an active *reshus ha'rabim* — a space being constantly traversed by the public. Invoking invisible conceptual walls in a thoroughfare through which people are continually passing is a different matter from invoking *pi takra* over a quiet courtyard or valley. This, evidently, is where the *chachamim* draw the line.

With that, the *perek* concludes. *Hadran alach kol ha'gagos.*

---

## Tefillin Transport Case

### Finding Tefillin

The new *perek*, *Hamotzi Tefillin*, opens a significantly different kind of discussion. The scenario: one finds *tefillin* lying in the street on *Shabbos* — not *chutz la'tchum*, but simply outdoors with no *eruv*, no walls, no valid enclosure. What is one to do?

### Pair-by-Pair Transport

The *mishnah* rules *machnisan zug zug* — one brings them in pair by pair. One dons a complete pair — both the *shel yad* and the *shel rosh* — wears them while walking home, removes them, and returns for the next pair, repeating as needed.

### Two Pairs Option

Rabban Gamliel goes further: *shnayim shnayim* — one may wear two complete pairs simultaneously, corresponding to the view of Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam. We will analyze the basis of this debate in detail shortly.

### Used vs. New Tefillin

The *mishnah* then qualifies the first ruling. *Bameh devarim amurim b'yashanot* — this applies to old, used *tefillin*. If the *tefillin* are brand new, one is not only exempt from this procedure but actually forbidden to employ it. The concern is that at that time it was common to fashion amulets housed in containers that resembled *tefillin* and worn on the body. A new, unworn set of *tefillin* could plausibly be mistaken for such an amulet. One cannot be certain they are genuinely *halachic tefillin* and therefore may not carry them in this manner.

This raises an obvious question: how does age resolve the concern? Rashi explains that *yashanot* in practice means that the knots have been tied — the *dalet* of the *shel rosh* and the *yud* of the *shel yad* are visibly formed. Since no one would go to the trouble of creating an amulet with the proper *kesher* of *tefillin*, the presence of these knots establishes that one is dealing with genuine *halachic tefillin*. A further question arises: one might think amulets too are worn, so why would wearing not raise the same concern? The answer is that the wearing here is a device for transport, not a straightforward act of donning an amulet in the normal sense. The concern is whether the items are genuine, not how they are being used.

### Bundled Tefillin Case

If the *tefillin* are found *tzvatim o kerichot* — tied in bundles — a different regime applies. One cannot simply don them, so *machshikh aleihem u'meviyan*: one remains with them until nightfall and brings them in at *Motzaei Shabbos*. The reason one cannot simply unbundle them and wear them is not stated explicitly here and will be addressed in the *gemara*. The *mishnah* is clear, however, that guarding them is an obligation — one who encounters *tefillin* lying exposed has a duty to remain there all day if necessary to protect them from mistreatment or theft.

### Danger Override

If remaining poses a *sakkanah* — a danger to oneself, whether from human threat or simple vulnerability of being left in an exposed field until dark — then *mekhasan ve'holekh lo*: one covers the *tefillin* and is exempt from staying. At *Motzaei Shabbos* one returns, and hopefully they will still be there. The *tefillin* matter greatly, but the danger to the person overrides.

### Daisy Chain Method

Rabbi Shimon offers a practical alternative for situations where wearing the *tefillin* is not possible. *Noten le'chavero ve'chavero le'chavero ad she'magia la'chatzer ha'chitzonah* — a chain of people is formed; each person passes the *tefillin* to the next, with no individual carrying them more than *arba amos*, thereby avoiding any prohibited act even in a *reshus ha'rabim*. The *tefillin* are thus brought to an outer yard where they can be protected.

The *mishnah* extends this principle to an infant — Rashi understands this to refer to a newborn delivered in the field — and the same daisy-chain method may be employed to transport the child.

### Object Techumim Rule

The *mishnah* returns to the theme of *Eruvin* by way of Rabbi Yehuda's position, which introduces the *halacha* that objects are bound by their owner's *techumim*: *lo teileich zo yoter me'raglei be'aleha* — an object cannot travel further than its owner may go.

### Property Outside Tehum

Rabbi Yehuda extends the daisy-chain principle even further, ruling that one may employ it not only for *tefillin* and infants but even for property — *noten adam chavilo le'chavero* — and crucially, even property that is *chutz la'tchum*, beyond the owner's *techum*. This is a significant leniency: not merely permitting the transport of personal possessions but allowing one to move property across a *techum* boundary to protect it, provided one does not carry it into an enclosed *reshus ha'yachid*.

### Tosafot's Reasoning

Tosafot explains why this *perek* belongs in *Eruvin*: it is precisely this final *halacha* of *techumim* that anchors it here. One can also see a thematic connection to the preceding *perek*, which dealt with scenarios where there is no *eruv* yet carrying is still necessary — asking how one navigates a world without proper wall configurations. This *perek* continues that inquiry: when there are no walls at all and something sacred or vulnerable needs to be transported, what tools does *halacha* provide?

---

## One vs. Two Pairs

### Mishnah Positions

The *mishnah* establishes the base positions: the *tanna kamma* permits only one pair at a time, while Rabban Gamliel permits two. The *gemara* now proceeds to analyze these positions carefully, asking first whether our *mishnah* is simply in tension with a more permissive *tanna*.

### Rabbi Meir Comparison

Perhaps the *mishnah*'s restriction to one pair is inconsistent with Rabbi Meir, who in another context — a fire that threatens property on *Shabbos* — rules that one may wear as many layers of clothing as possible: *lovesh kama sheyachol lilvosh, ve'otef kama sheyachol la'atof*. If Rabbi Meir permits piling on garment after garment as a device for saving property, why does our *mishnah* limit the transport of *tefillin* to one pair? The *gemara* establishes that the fire *mishnah* is indeed attributed to Rabbi Meir by way of a *beraita* that makes this explicit: *lovesh umotzi ufoshet velovesh umotzi ufoshet afilu kol ha'yom kulo, divrei Rabbi Meir* — one may wear, bring out, remove, and repeat the entire day.

### Rava's Distinction

Rava resolves the apparent contradiction. Even if our *mishnah* were consistent with Rabbi Meir, *tefillin* are categorically different from clothing. In the fire case, *hatam devachol kama d'ba'ei lavish* — during the weekday one may choose to wear as many layers as one wishes; wearing many layers, however eccentric, remains within the range of normal wearing. Therefore, even for the purpose of rescue, the Rabbis permit it, since it does not constitute an abnormal or prohibited act. But with *tefillin*, the position is *hacha devachol nami zug echad in, tefei lo* — even during the week, only one pair is *halachically* acceptable; more than one is not. This is not a matter of being unusual; it is a matter of being prohibited. Therefore, *le'inyan hatzalah nami zug echad in, tefei lo* — for the purpose of rescue as well, only one pair may be worn.

### Shabbos as Zman Tefillin

The *gemara* now reaches the heart of the analysis, framing the debate as hinging on a fundamental question: is *Shabbos* a *zman tefillin* — a time when one is obligated to wear *tefillin*? The accepted practice is that *tefillin* are not worn on *Shabbos*, rooted in the understanding that *Shabbos* itself bears the character of an *ot*, a sign of the covenant, and wearing *tefillin*, which is also an *ot*, would be superfluous or even incongruous. But this is not immediately obvious from the text of the Torah, and the theoretical question of whether *Shabbos* is *zman tefillin* has genuine *halachic* implications.

### One Pair If Zman

If *Shabbos* is *zman tefillin*, then wearing *tefillin* on *Shabbos* is subject to the normal laws governing the *mitzvah*: one pair, worn properly, is the obligation. Wearing a second pair would then constitute *bal tosif* — the prohibition against adding to a commandment — and would be entirely unacceptable. The consequence for transport is stark: one pair may be worn as fulfilling or simulating the *mitzvah*; more than one renders the additional pairs forbidden, which in turn means they are not being worn in any legitimate sense, and carrying them would be prohibited.

### Tefillin as Accessory

If *Shabbos* is *not zman tefillin*, the analysis shifts. Since one is not obligated to wear *tefillin* on *Shabbos*, the *tefillin* one carries are not being viewed through the lens of the *mitzvah* at all. They function more like an accessory — an object donned on the body in a manner that happens to resemble *tefillin*-wearing but is not framed as a *mitzvah* act. In that case, multiple pairs need not be seen as an impermissible expansion of the commandment.

### Normal Wearing Location

Nevertheless, Rabban Gamliel does not permit unlimited pairs even on the view that *Shabbos* is *lav zman tefillin*. The Rabbis permitted this form of transport only when it constitutes *derech malbush bimkom tefillin* — wearing in the normal place that *tefillin* are worn. One cannot, say, tie *tefillin* around one's ankle and call it wearing. So even on the permissive view, the constraint is that the *tefillin* must be placed where *tefillin* actually go. This places an upper bound on how many may be worn simultaneously.

### Space for Two

Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak provides the anatomical grounding: *makom yesh ba'rosh le'haniach bo shtei tefillin* — the head has sufficient space to accommodate two sets of *tefillin*, one behind the other. Similarly, the arm has adequate space for two *shel yad* placements. This is the basis for Rabban Gamliel's position that two pairs — no more — are acceptable.

### Head Placement

Tosafot raises the question of the precise size of *tefillin*, noting that the Ri found in a *midrash* that the minimum width of *tefillin* is two fingers. Tosafot connects this to the *tzitz* worn by the *Kohen Gadol*, which Tosafot believes was positioned in the location of the *shel rosh* rather than on the forehead. The *tzitz* was two fingers wide, and with the *Kohen*'s head covering above it, there was exactly enough room for the *tefillin* to fit in the proper space. The place of the *shel rosh* is defined by the *gemara* through the ruling of *d'vei Rav Yannai*: *makom she'mocho shel tinok rofes* — the place where an infant's skull is still soft, the fontanelle or crown of the head.

### Zman Tefillin Resolution

The *gemara* settles the matter: *dkulei alma is lehu de'Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak* — everyone would agree that there is physical space for two pairs. The debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabban Gamliel is not about anatomy but about the *zman tefillin* question: *d'Tanna Kamma savar Shabbos zman tefillin hu, v'Rabban Gamliel savar Shabbos lav zman tefillin hu*. The *tanna kamma* holds *Shabbos* is a *zman tefillin*, which means only one pair is ever acceptable; any second pair is *bal tosif*. Rabban Gamliel holds *Shabbos* is not *zman tefillin*, which means the *tefillin* are not being treated as a *mitzvah* act and so the *bal tosif* framework does not apply. Given that, the only constraint is whether one is wearing them in the normal place — which, as Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak establishes, accommodates precisely two pairs.

### Bal Tosif Principle

Tosafot adds a further dimension to this analysis that deepens the logic considerably. *Bal tosif* — the prohibition of adding to a commandment — is most easily violated when one is in the *zman* of that *mitzvah*, because then one is genuinely expanding an obligatory act. If it is not the *zman* of the *mitzvah*, adding to it is not a meaningful expansion of the commandment — it is simply doing something unnecessary. Tosafot's illustration is instructive: were one today, outside of *Sukkos*, to take a *lulav va'esrog* and shake it with the appropriate formula, one would likely not be transgressing *bal tosif*, because the *mitzvah* season has not begun and one is not expanding any active obligation. Accordingly, if *Shabbos* is *zman tefillin*, wearing a second pair falls directly within the prohibition of *bal tosif*; if *Shabbos* is not *zman tefillin*, there is no *bal tosif* concern, and the only question becomes one of what constitutes normal wearing. This is the principle that will carry the discussion forward into the next *gemara*.

---

---

# Eiruvin 96

## Two Tefillin Pairs Debate

### Finding Tefillin Mishna

The daf begins at the bottom of 95b, picking up from a *mishnah* concerning one who finds *tefillin* on the street without an *eruv* — no walls, no enclosure — and must bring them indoors. The solution the *mishnah* contemplates is wearing them. But the question then becomes: may one wear a single pair at a time, or two pairs simultaneously? That is the debate the *gemara* has been unpacking.

### Shabbat as Zman Tefillin

The *gemara* has been presenting the debate through two lenses. The first concerns whether *Shabbat* is a *zman tefillin* — a time when *tefillin* properly apply. Ironically, if *Shabbat* is indeed a *zman tefillin*, one is limited to wearing a single pair, because the act is viewed through the lens of the *mitzvah* itself, and the *mitzvah* calls for one pair. If *Shabbat* is not the time of the *mitzvah*, however, two pairs becomes theoretically permissible — not because of any special dispensation, but because wearing *tefillin* at that point is regarded as something closer to wearing an unusual garment than to performing a *mitzvah*. More than two pairs, even on this view, would not work: there is only a proper anatomical place for two pairs of *tefillin* to sit, and wearing them anywhere else would be like tying a tie around one's leg — not considered wearing at all.

The second dimension is *bal tosif*, the prohibition against adding to a *mitzvah*. Adding to a *mitzvah* is most potent when one does so during the *mitzvah*'s own time and alters its parameters — taking two *lulavim* simultaneously on *Sukkos*, for instance. If one were to take a *lulav* on an ordinary weekday, it would be hard to call that *bal tosif*; it would be strange, but without the core *mitzvah* as a foundation, there is nothing to expand. Accordingly, if *Shabbat* is not the time of *tefillin*, wearing two pairs is less likely to constitute *bal tosif*, since one is not building upon the *mitzvah* at all. If it were *bal tosif*, and if *Shabbat* were the *zman tefillin*, the extra pair would be clearly superfluous — creating not only a *bal tosif* problem but presumably a *Shabbat* violation as well, since the second pair would be rendered obviously extraneous.

### Kavanah in Mitzvot

Continuing from two lines at the bottom of 95b, the *gemara* now offers an alternative framing: *dekhulei alma Shabbos zman tefillin hu* — suppose everyone agrees that *Shabbat* is indeed the time for *tefillin*. How then could wearing two pairs ever be permitted? The *gemara* says: *vehakha bemitzvos tzrichos kavanah kamiflgi* — the debate here concerns whether *mitzvos* require *kavanah*, intention, in order to be fulfilled. *Tanna Kamma* holds that to be *yotzei* a *mitzvah* one needs *kavanah*, and here *kavanah* is absent. *Rabban Gamliel* holds that *kavanah* is not required.

### Rashi on Kavanah

*Rashi* explains the underlying logic: the assumption at this stage is that what is required to *fulfill* the *mitzvah* is also what is required to *transgress* the prohibition of *bal tosif*. If *kavanah* is not needed to fulfill the *mitzvah*, then the act is defined as a *mitzvah* act even without intention — and that same definition would apply to a second pair of *tefillin* as well. Wearing two pairs would then mean one is expanding the *mitzvah*, constituting *bal tosif*. But if *mitzvos tzrichos kavanah* — if the *mitzvah* is only defined as such with intent — then without intent, the second pair is also not classified as part of the *mitzvah* act. Since one is wearing two pairs not for the purpose of the *mitzvah* but simply to transport them indoors, one cannot be said to be expanding the *mitzvah*, and there is no *bal tosif*. Whatever defines the fulfillment of the *mitzvah* likewise defines what constitutes the *mitzvah* act — and therefore, where *kavanah* is required, one would not be *over* on *bal tosif* without it.

## Bal Tosif Transgression

### Bal Tosif Without Intent

At the top of 96a, the *gemara* sharpens the analysis with yet another framing. One could say: *dekhulei alma latzet lo ba'ei kavanah* — everyone agrees that fulfilling the *mitzvah* at the right time in the right way does not require *kavanah*. The act, properly done at the proper moment, more or less defines itself as the *mitzvah* act. But perhaps more is needed to be *over* on *bal tosif*, because there one is doing something wrong — incorporating an additional element into the *mitzvah* that does not naturally belong there — and that incorporation requires an active intention to bring it within the scope of the *mitzvah*.

### Tanna Kamma vs Gamliel

With this framing, *vehakha la'avor mishum Bal Tosif kamiflgi* — the debate is specifically about what is needed to transgress *bal tosif*. *Tanna Kamma* holds that to be *over* on *bal tosif* one does not need *kavanah*. Since the *mitzvah* itself is fulfilled without *kavanah*, and the additional element is performed alongside it, that element too becomes incorporated into the *mitzvah* act without any intent being necessary. Extra *tefillin*, or a *lulav* held in addition to one's own, becomes part of the *mitzvah* framework regardless of intention — and so wearing two pairs of *tefillin* would constitute *bal tosif* and presumably a *Shabbat* violation as well.

*Rabban Gamliel* holds that even though the base *mitzvah* is fulfilled without *kavanah*, an additional element does not become part of the *mitzvah* unless one intends it to be so. When one picks up one's *lulav* without thinking about the *mitzvah*, one is still *yotzei* — that is the *mitzvah* itself. But a second *lulav* held at the same time does not become incorporated into the *mitzvah* without an active intention. Similarly, a second pair of *tefillin* worn only to carry them indoors does not, absent such intent, become part of the *mitzvah* act — and without that, there is no *bal tosif*, and presumably no *Shabbat* violation either. The second pair can be regarded as an unusual garment, nothing more.

### Two Pairs No Bal Tosif

The underlying point across all these approaches is consistent: how can one wear two pairs of *tefillin* without violating *bal tosif*? Either because *Shabbat* is not the *zman* of the *mitzvah* at all, or because even if it is, the *mitzvah* requires *kavanah* which is absent here, or — the sharpest version — because even if *mitzvos* generally do not require *kavanah* for fulfillment, incorporating an additional element into the *mitzvah* act does require active intention, and without such intention, the second pair remains entirely outside the scope of the *mitzvah*.

## Bal Tosif Shelo BiZmano

### Transgressing Out of Sea…

The *gemara* now raises a further possibility. Perhaps the debate is not about *kavanah* at all, but about something even more basic: *vekhakha be-la'avor shelo bizmano kamiflgi* — can one even be *over* on *bal tosif* when performing an act *shelo bizmano*, outside the time when the *mitzvah* applies? The earlier reasoning assumed that if *Shabbat* is not the *zman tefillin*, one is entirely safe, because the act is not even viewed through the *mitzvah* lens — comparable to taking a *lulav* during an ordinary weekday. But the *gemara* now questions whether that is actually so. Is it possible to violate *bal tosif shelo bizmano*?

### Intent Outside Appointed…

The *gemara* suggests that this is precisely what *Tanna Kamma* and *Rabban Gamliel* disagree about. *Tanna Kamma* holds that even outside the *mitzvah*'s proper time, one can be *over* on *bal tosif* without *kavanah* — the mere act of wearing two pairs of *tefillin* on *Shabbat*, even if *Shabbat* is not the *zman tefillin*, suffices to constitute a transgression. *Rabban Gamliel* holds that outside the *mitzvah*'s time, *kavanah* is specifically required to be *over* — and since there is no such intent here, two pairs may be worn freely.

### Sukkah Evidence

The *gemara* immediately challenges the position that one could violate *bal tosif shelo bizmano* without *kavanah*: *ee hakhi*, if that were so, *ve-Rabbi Meir zuga chada nami lo* — according to *Tanna Kamma* (associated here with Rabbi Meir), one should not even be permitted to wear a single pair of *tefillin* on *Shabbat*. If transgressions of *bal tosif shelo bizmano* require no *kavanah*, then even the one pair would be problematic.

Furthermore: *ha-yashen bi-shmini be-sukka yelakeh* — one who sleeps in the *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret* should be liable. Biblically, the *mitzvat sukkah* ends after the seventh day of *Sukkos*. Yet the *gemara* elsewhere assumes that one may dwell in the *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret* because of *sefeika de-yoma* — the doubt about which day is the final day of the holiday — and also because *Chazal* explicitly ordained it. Could one be *over* on *bal tosif* under those circumstances? After all, one lacks any intention to add to the *mitzvah*: one is dwelling in the *sukkah* because one was told to, or because of calendar uncertainty — not because one wishes to expand the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* from seven days to eight. If *bal tosif shelo bizmano* required no *kavanah*, there would be no way to avoid the violation.

The *gemara* concludes from this that clearly, *shelo bizmano*, one cannot be *over* on *bal tosif* without *kavanah*. Without the intention to add — whether one is wearing *tefillin* on *Shabbat*, sitting in the *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret*, or taking a *lulav* on an ordinary day — there is no *bal tosif* violation whatsoever.

This discussion also raises an interesting question about a case where one does have *kavanah*: if one sat in the *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret* with the explicit intention that the biblical *mitzvah* of *sukkah* should apply for eight days, that would indeed be *bal tosif*. Similarly, if one put on *tefillin* on *Shabbat* with the intention that the *mitzvah* applies seven days a week, one would be *over*. But if one took a *lulav* today — many months removed from *Sukkos* — and declared it a *mitzvah* on its own terms, that might not be *bal tosif* at all, since one has not expanded the base *mitzvah* from its natural scope; one has simply created an entirely new and separate ritual. *Bal tosif*, as *Chazal* understand it, is defined narrowly as expanding a *mitzvah* from its base — not inventing a new observance entirely unmoored from the original. If, however, one were to do it on the day immediately following *Sukkos*, or on each successive day until it connected back, then one would be expanding the *mitzvah*'s scope and might indeed be *over*.

### Original Approach Confir…

The *gemara* concludes: *ela mehvarta keshaninan mei'ikara* — it is better to understand the matter as originally stated. If *Shabbat* is definitively not the *zman tefillin*, one is entirely safe with no *bal tosif* concerns whatsoever. All the debates reduce to: either *Shabbat* is not the *zman tefillin* — in which case wearing two pairs carries no *bal tosif* risk — or *Shabbat* is the *zman tefillin*, in which case the question is what is required to constitute *bal tosif* and whether the second pair without intent triggers it.

## Finding the Tanna

### Rabbi Akiva Position

Having established the debate's framework, the *gemara* turns to identify which *tanna* holds which position with respect to *Shabbat* and *zman tefillin*. The *gemara* asks: *u'man shamat lei Shabbos zman tefillin* — who is it that holds *Shabbat* is the time of *tefillin*? The first candidate raised is Rabbi Akiva.

The *gemara* cites a *braita*: *v'shamarta es hachukah hazos l'mo'adah miyamim yamimah*. This verse appears at the close of one of the four *parshiyos* of *tefillin* — specifically the *parsha* at the end of *Parashas Bo*. In context, the *peshat* of the *pesukim* refers to the *korban Pesach*, but since it is one of the four places in the *Torah* where the text introduces the language of a sign on one's hand and a memorial between one's eyes, it is also read as referring to *tefillin* themselves. The *braita* derives from the words *miyamim yamimah*: *yamim* — days and not nights, thus excluding nighttime from the *mitzvah* of *tefillin*; *miyamim yamimah* — some days and not all days, thus excluding *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* from the *mitzvah*. That is the position of Rabbi Yosei HaGlili.

Rabbi Akiva disputes this reading entirely: *lo ne'emar chukah zo ela l'inyan Pesach bilvad* — this ordinance, the word *chukah*, is said only with respect to the *korban Pesach*. The verse is not speaking about *tefillin* at all. Consequently, according to Rabbi Akiva, there is no scriptural basis to exclude *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* from the *zman tefillin* — and no basis, from this verse, to exclude nighttime either.

The *gemara* then digresses briefly onto a related point: the *mishnah* in another context states that *Pesach* and *milah* are the only positive commandments for which one incurs *karet* without the transgression of a *lo ta'aseh*. The question is raised whether this is consistent with Rabbi Akiva, since according to him, the verse *v'shamarta es hachukah hazos* — which ordinarily introduces a negative prohibition (*hashamer* connoting a warning not to transgress) — would apply to *Pesach*, creating a *lav*. The *gemara* answers by invoking the principle of Rabbi Avin citing Rabbi Ila'i: *kol makom she'ne'emar hashamer pen v'al, eino ela b'lo ta'aseh* — wherever the *Torah* says "guard yourself lest" or "you shall not," it is a negative prohibition; but *hashamer* in the context of a positive command functions as a positive exhortation. Guarding oneself not to transgress is a negative prohibition; guarding oneself to perform is a positive commandment. This resolves the side issue and returns the discussion to the main question.

### Shabbat Not Zman Tefillin

The *gemara* now presses further: does Rabbi Akiva really hold that *Shabbat* is a *zman tefillin*? A *braita* is cited in which Rabbi Akiva himself addresses the question directly: *yachol yaniach adam tefillin b'shabatot u'v'yamim tovim?* — perhaps one should put on *tefillin* on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*? Rabbi Akiva answers with a *drashah* on the verse *v'hayah l'cha l'os al yadecha*: *tefillin* are to be a sign on one's hand — and this applies to *mi she'tzrichin os*, those who need a sign. *Yatz'u elu she'hen gufan os* — excluded are those days that are themselves a sign. *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, being themselves an *os*, do not require the additional sign of *tefillin*; not only is one not required to wear *tefillin* on those days, but one is actually prohibited from doing so. Wearing *tefillin* as a sign on a day that is itself a sign would seem to imply that the day's own *os* is insufficient — and that is treated as an actual prohibition, perhaps a kind of *bal tosif*, perhaps an undermining of the sanctity of *Shabbat* as an *os* in its own right.

*Rashi* offers a striking description of what the *os* of *tefillin* signifies: *yamim sheYisrael tzrichin le'amid os al atzmam lehakir shehem machazikim b'Toraso shel haKadosh Baruch Hu* — these are days on which Israel needs to establish a sign upon themselves to demonstrate that they embrace God's commandments. There is something active and powerful in that formulation: wearing *tefillin* is not merely a mark of chosenness but a physical demonstration of one's embrace of God's *mitzvos*, done *al yadecha*, directly on one's body.

The question naturally arises: how does the exclusion extend to *Yom Tov*? The verse *ki os hi beini uveineichem* speaks most explicitly of *Shabbat*. The extension to *Yom Tov* is more difficult to ground textually, though *Rashi* simply states that *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* are themselves a sign between God and Israel, citing that verse. The question of *Chol HaMoed* is even more disputed, and notably the *gemara* never resolves it directly — a silence that became the opening through which a major *machlokes Rishonim* developed, one in which *Kabbalah* played a significant role.

*Tosafos* addresses *Chol HaMoed* at the top of the page. Their initial instinct is that *tefillin* should not be worn on *Chol HaMoed*, since the day carries its own markers of special status — the prohibition of certain *melacha*, and the active rituals of *sukkah* during *Sukkos* and the prohibition of *chametz* during *Pesach* — all of which render the day recognizably distinct without the *os* of *tefillin*. Yet *Tosafos* also cites a *Yerushalmi* whose plain meaning seems to support wearing *tefillin* on *Chol HaMoed*, and he notes *vekhen ama davar* — that this was the common practice. *Tosafos* himself acknowledges the tension: logical analysis would suggest not wearing them, yet the practice was to wear them. This became one of the most consequential divergences between Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities — with the *Zohar*'s position subsequently tipping the balance decisively for many communities away from wearing *tefillin* on *Chol HaMoed* altogether.

So the conclusion emerges clearly: Rabbi Akiva himself holds that *Shabbat* is *lav zman tefillin* — not the time for *tefillin* — based on the principle that *Shabbat* is itself an *os*. We have thus not yet identified the *tanna* who holds that *Shabbat* is the *zman tefillin*.

### Rabbi Natan Night Tefill…

The *gemara* turns to another candidate: *ela hai tanna hu* — perhaps it is the following *tanna*. A *braita* teaches: *haneior balayla*, one who is awake at night while wearing *tefillin* — *ratza choletz ratza maniach*, if one wishes one may remove them, and if one wishes one may keep them on. This is the opinion of Rabbi Natan. And since Rabbi Natan permits actively wearing *tefillin* at night, this implies that *layla zman tefillin* — nighttime is a time for *tefillin* according to his view, which in turn implies that the verse of *miyamim yamimah* is not applied to exclude nighttime from the scope of the *mitzvah*.

It must be noted that there is a major debate about nighttime and *tefillin*. Everyone agrees that the practice is not to wear *tefillin* at night — but the reason is disputed. Is it because nighttime is biblically excluded by *miyamim yamimah*, making it simply not a *zman tefillin*? Or is it that biblically the *mitzvah* could apply at night, but *Chazal* were concerned one might fall asleep while wearing them and pass gas in an undignified manner? The position of Rabbi Natan, which permits putting them on *lechatchila* at night for one who is wide awake, reflects the view that nighttime is biblically the *zman tefillin* — the concern is only practical, and if one is fully alert, that concern is removed. The *gemara* therefore reasons: *mi'd'layla l'tanna kamma zman tefillin hu, Shabbos nami zman tefillin* — if nighttime is included in the *zman tefillin* for this *tanna*, then presumably the verse of *miyamim yamimah* plays no limiting role at all, and *Shabbat* too would be the *zman tefillin*.

The *gemara* rebuts this: perhaps one can hold that nighttime is the *zman tefillin* without holding that *Shabbat* is. We know that Rabbi Akiva himself held *layla zman tefillin* — since he rejected the verse of *miyamim yamimah* as applying to *tefillin* entirely, reading it instead as referring to the *korban Pesach*, nighttime is implicitly included. And yet Rabbi Akiva explicitly ruled that *Shabbat* is *lav zman tefillin* based on the principle of *os*. The two exclusions are thus independent: nighttime is excluded only by *miyamim yamimah* — a ground Rabbi Akiva does not accept — while *Shabbat* is excluded by the *os* principle, which is distinct and which Rabbi Akiva does accept. The two positions do not travel together as a package.

We therefore still have not identified the *tanna* who holds that *Shabbat* is the *zman tefillin*.

## Women Tefillin Status

### Michal and Yona Stories

The *gemara* introduces yet another candidate. A *braita* is cited: *Michal bas Kushi haysa menachas tefillin*, Michal the daughter of Kushi was accustomed to wearing *tefillin*, *v'lo michu bah chachamim* — and the Sages did not object. *Rashi* explains that Kushi here refers to Shaul — there is a *pasuk* that uses the term *Kushi* to describe Shaul — making this the famous Michal, daughter of the king. Additionally: *v'ishto shel Yona haysa ola la-regel*, the wife of the prophet Yonah would make the pilgrimage to Yerushalayim for the *regel*, and the Sages likewise did not object.

### Women Obligated Problem

The *gemara* attempts to infer from these two stories: *mi'd'lo michu bah chachamim* — since the Sages did not object, presumably these women were performing a *mitzvah* they were obligated to perform. *Alma kasavri mitzvas asei she-lo ha-zman grama hi* — this implies that *tefillin* is not a time-bound *mitzvah*, since if women are fully obligated, that obligation must apply even on *Shabbat*, meaning *Shabbat* is indeed *zman tefillin*. If so, we have found our *tanna*.

The problem, of course, is that if women were genuinely obligated, the *gemara* would expect not merely *lo michu bah*, but an affirmative statement that women are required to wear *tefillin* — with every woman doing so as a matter of course. The phrasing of non-objection already begins to suggest something more like permissive tolerance than obligatory fulfillment.

### Women Exempt Resolution

The *gemara* resolves this by pointing to the case of Yonah's wife and the *regel*. *Regel* is clearly a time-bound *mitzvah* — indeed, the Torah explicitly says *yeira'eh kol zechurcha*, "all your males shall appear," making the obligation explicitly gendered. No one would suggest that women are obligated in *aliyah la-regel*. And yet the Sages did not object to Yonah's wife making the pilgrimage. Why not? Because being exempt does not necessarily mean one is forbidden — one may choose to fulfill a *mitzvah* from which one is exempt, and the Sages would not object.

*Dekhulei alma lo ba'ei kavanah* — if this is true of *aliyah la-regel*, it is equally true of *tefillin*. Michal and Yonah's wife were both exempt from time-bound *mitzvos*, and both chose to fulfill them anyway. *Lo michu bah chachamim* does not mean they were obligated; it means the Sages permitted their voluntary performance. This resolves the story: *tefillin* is time-bound, *Shabbat* is *lav zman tefillin*, and women are exempt — but the Sages did not object to their choosing to perform the *mitzvah* regardless.

### Exempt Woman Perform

The *gemara* then raises the question that has been lurking beneath the surface throughout: does being exempt simply mean one is not required, or does it mean one is actually prohibited from performing the *mitzvah*? The *mishnah* under consideration in the broader context — which is attributed by convention to Rabbi Meir, as an unattributed *mishnah* reflects his position — states: *ein m'akvin es hatinokos mil'itkoa*, one does not prevent children from blowing a *shofar* on *Rosh Hashana*, as part of their *chinuch*. The *diyuk* is: by implication, *nashim m'akvin* — women one would prevent. This suggests that a *mitzvah* from which women are exempt is not merely optional but actually impermissible for them.

Similarly, the *braita* from the *Sifra* on *Vayikra* states: *b'nei Yisrael somchin v'ein b'nos Yisrael somchos* — Israelite males perform *smicha* on their *korbanos*, but women do not. Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Shimon add: *nashim somchos reshus* — women may nonetheless do so if they choose. The *tanna kamma* who does not offer this qualification, and whose *Sifra* position is attributed to the school of Rabbi Yehuda (*stam Sifra* follows Rabbi Yehuda), appears to hold that exempt women are not merely excused but actually barred. The *gemara* concludes from these sources that neither Rabbi Meir nor Rabbi Yehuda follow the position of Rabbi Yosi — both hold that a woman exempt from a *mitzvah* is also prohibited from performing it.

This creates a powerful inference regarding *tefillin*: since both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda nevertheless rule that a woman who finds *tefillin* on *Shabbat* may wear them — the first permitting it regardless of whether old or new, the second permitting it for old pairs — they cannot be treating it as something a woman is merely tolerated in doing despite her exemption. If they held that exempt women are prohibited, and yet they allow women to wear *tefillin*, it must be because women are not exempt at all. Women must be fully obligated in *tefillin*. And if women are obligated in *tefillin*, then *tefillin* is not a time-bound *mitzvah* — and *Shabbat* is *zman tefillin*. So we have finally found our *tanna*: both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda hold *Shabbat* is *zman tefillin* and women are *chayav*. This is a striking conclusion — effectively half of the canonical Tannaitic all-star team.

### Exempt Woman Perform

The *gemara* continues to press whether *lo michu bah chachamim* can itself bear the weight of the inference. Could one not simply say that even Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda — despite generally prohibiting exempt women from performing *mitzvos* — simply tolerated it here? The *gemara* says *lo salka datchach*: it is untenable to read the cases that way, because we have explicit evidence that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda both hold that exempt women are prohibited. The *mishnah* about *shofar* and the *Sifra* on *smicha* make their positions clear. Knowing that, the fact that they still permit women to wear *tefillin* can only mean they regard women as *chayavos* — obligated.

### Rashi Niros Mosifos

The broader question of whether exempt women may perform *mitzvos* they are not obligated in generates a major debate between *Rashi* and *Tosafos* with significant *halachic* ramifications. *Rashi*, in the relevant passage, explains that the problem with exempt women performing such *mitzvos* is that they *niros k'mosifos* — they appear to be adding. Even though it is not technically *bal tosif* (since an exempt person has no base *mitzvah* to begin with), the act of someone performing something outside their obligation creates the appearance of expanding the *mitzvah*'s scope. According to *Rashi*, this would be a global concern: women should refrain from performing any *mitzvah* from which they are exempt, because in every case it would look like an improper addition.

### Tosafot Context Problems

*Tosafos*, followed by the great majority of the *Rishonei Ashkenaz*, rejects this global approach. The concern is not uniform; rather, each case of a *mitzvah* that exempt women are said to be prohibited from involves a *specific contextual problem* that would not exist if the woman were obligated but emerges precisely because she is not.

Consider *tekias shofar*: producing sound from a musical instrument on *Yom Tov* is ordinarily prohibited. The only reason it is permitted on *Rosh Hashana* is because of the *mitzvah*. If a woman is exempt from the *mitzvah*, that justification evaporates — and the playing of the *shofar* on *Yom Tov* becomes problematic in its own right. The prohibition is not based on *niros k'mosifos* in the abstract, but on a specific prohibition that the obligation would otherwise override.

Similarly with *smicha*: leaning one's weight upon the *korban* in the *azarah* carries the appearance of *shevus b'kodshim* — using a sacred animal as a support — which is at least rabbinically problematic. When one is obligated in *smicha*, this concern is overridden. When one is exempt, the local problem resurfaces.

By this approach, *mitzvos* that have no such attendant problems are entirely unaffected by a woman's exempt status. Sitting in a *sukkah*, hearing *tekias shofar* when men are in any case blowing, taking a *lulav*, wearing *tzitzis* — none of these carry the kind of local issue that would become activated by the woman's exemption. According to *Tosafos*, a woman may freely perform these *mitzvos*, and there is no general principle barring her from doing so.

### Tefillin Guf Naki

This brings us to *tefillin*. What is the specific contextual problem that *Tosafos* identifies for exempt women who wish to wear *tefillin*? The issue is *guf naki* — the requirement to maintain bodily cleanliness and to avoid passing gas while wearing *tefillin*. As is well known, this concern is the reason why *tefillin* are no longer worn throughout the entire day as they once were: the *gemara* itself treats *tefillin* as an exceptionally demanding *mitzvah* in this regard, which is also why the practice of starting *chinuch* for *tefillin* begins only a short time before *Bar Mitzvah*, far later than for other *mitzvos*. When one is obligated in *tefillin*, this challenge is an obligation one accepts and works to meet. When one is exempt, the difficulty remains but the obligation that would justify confronting it is absent — and therefore, according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda as read by *Tosafos*, the exempt woman should not take on the challenge.

This is not a gender-specific concern in *Tosafos*'s framing: it is the same concern that applies to everyone, overridden for obligated men but not available to override for exempt women. That said, it should be acknowledged that in later *Ashkenazic* practice — particularly in the *Rema* — the notion of *guf naki* in the women's context expanded well beyond the original concern about passing gas, becoming entangled with questions of *niddah* and a broader culture of women maintaining distance from certain holy activities during their menstrual cycle. This expansion, while influential in shaping communal practice, goes considerably beyond the *gemara*'s original framing.

It is worth noting that the entire debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on one hand and Rabbi Yosi on the other — about whether exempt women are prohibited or merely excused — maps directly onto the contemporary question of women and *tefillin*. Rabbi Yosi's position, that women may perform *mitzvos* from which they are exempt, permits women to wear *tefillin*. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's position prohibits it — but on the narrower *Tosafos* reading, the prohibition is specifically because of *guf naki*, which raises the further question of whether that concern is sufficient to bar a woman who is genuinely careful in this regard.

### Bracha Exempt Women

The question of *tefillin* and *bracha* is directly addressed by *Tosafos* in the first note at the bottom of 96a. *Tosafos* cites Rabbeinu Tam: *de-mutar le-nashim le-varech al kol mitzvat asei she-hazman gerama af al gav de-peturot* — it is permitted for women to make a *bracha* on all time-bound positive commandments even though they are exempt. The proof from the stories of Michal and Yonah's wife is that they were clearly performing the *mitzvah*, and by implication, making the appropriate *bracha* — *ke-ama de-hachi she-osa mi-stama ka-mevarechet*. This is the classic Ashkenazi position: women recite the *bracha* on *mitzvos* from which they are exempt.

Sephardi practice, following the *Rambam*, is that women do not make a *bracha* on such *mitzvos*, since one cannot say *asher kiddishanu bemitzvosav vetzivanu* — that He has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us — if one has not in fact been commanded.

The Ashkenazi position offers two explanations for why a woman may say *vetzivanu*. The first is collective: *vetzivanu* refers to *Klal Yisrael* as a whole; even if I personally was not commanded, we as a people were, and I speak within that collective framework. The second and more substantive explanation is that women were in fact obligated but were given an exemption — and there is a meaningful difference between never having been obligated and having been obligated with an exemption available. One who is obligated but chooses not to take the exemption re-enters the category of the obligated, and may therefore say *vetzivanu* with full force. This understanding also gives greater weight to the religious act itself: the woman performing a *mitzvah* under this conception is not doing something optional in a casual sense, but is taking on an obligation that has real standing — and that in turn reduces the force of arguments that *guf naki* or other concerns should categorically override her choice to perform.

The practical consequences of the Sephardi position are significant. When no *bracha* is made, the entire cultural investment in the act diminishes. An exchange is noted in which a Sephardic woman of the household, during *Sukkos*, was offered the opportunity to take the *lulav* and responded with complete incomprehension — *why would I do that?* — having no framework within which the act carried meaning. This stands in contrast to the Ashkenazi approach, where the *bracha* expresses and reinforces the genuine religious value of the woman's voluntary performance of the *mitzvah*.

## Blue Threads Evidence

### Marketplace Techeiles

The *gemara* shifts to a related evidentiary question. Rabbi Elazar rules: *ha-motzei techeiles ba-shuk* — one who finds blue threads in the marketplace. The governing question is whether these threads were dyed *lishmah* — for the sake of the *mitzvah* of *tzitzis* — since *techeiles* must be so prepared to be valid. How much evidence of proper preparation does one need before relying upon what one finds?

### Thread Preparations

Rabbi Elazar establishes a graduated standard. Simple strips or lengths of fabric — *leshonos* — are *pesul*, invalid, since one might reasonably assume they were dyed to make a blue garment. Twisted threads — *chutim* — are *kasher*, valid for *tzitzis*, since it takes more effort to produce twisted threads, and one would presumably not bother unless intending them for the *mitzvah*.

The *gemara* challenges this reasoning: perhaps twisted threads too were made for some other purpose — perhaps for sewing a blue garment? The *gemara* responds: *bishzurin* — the standard of the strings is that of fully twisted cords, like our *tzitzis*. But even twisted cords could have been made as decorative trim along the edge of a garment. The *gemara* answers: *bimfaksikin* — if the strings have already been cut to the precise length appropriate for *tzitzis*, that resolves the matter.

### Effort Standard

*Dechulei hai vadai lo tarchai inshi* — to that full extent of effort, people simply do not bother unless they are producing them specifically for the sake of the *mitzvah*. Dyeing, spinning into a twisted cord, and cutting to the precise right length — each step adds specificity; together they constitute sufficient evidence that the object was prepared *lishmah*.

### New Tefillin Problem

Rava then raises an obvious question: if that graduated effort is the evidential standard, why can one not apply the same logic to a brand new pair of *tefillin*? Surely the effort involved in producing a pair of *tefillin* — assembling the boxes, inserting the *parshiyos*, tying the straps — vastly exceeds that involved in cutting blue threads to length. *Vechi adam tore'ach la'asot keme'a kemin tefillin?* Would anyone go to the trouble of fabricating an amulet that looks exactly like *tefillin*?

And yet the *mishnah* itself states: *bame de'amru, biyeshanot* — the ruling that one may carry them in applies specifically to old *tefillin*, implying that new-looking *tefillin* do not carry the same presumption. Rav Zeira dispatches his son Ava to cite a *braita* in the *beit midrash* that explicitly states the principle — cut strings are *kasher* because *ein adam tore'ach*, no one would bother — as a way of asserting the foundational rule. Rava is unimpressed: *umishum detani lei Ava brei deRav Zeira, kifenan lei?* — just because Rav Zeira's son recites a *braita*, should we simply capitulate? The *braita* may establish the principle for *techeiles*, but it does not answer why that same principle cannot be applied to brand new *tefillin*.

The answer, and the resolution of why new-looking *tefillin* cannot be presumed genuine despite the considerable effort involved in their production, is left as a *cliffhanger* — to be continued on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Eiruvin 97

## Tefillin New vs. Old

### New Tefillin Concern

Today's daf is 97, and we pick up at the very bottom of 96b. The *mishnah* had been discussing the case of finding new *tefillin* on *Shabbat*, and the ruling that one cannot bring them home — the concern being that new *tefillin* might not actually be *tefillin* at all, but rather some form of amulet. "New," as will become clear shortly, means that the knots have never been tied on them, or at least it is visibly apparent that no knots were ever formed.

The *gemara* raises an obvious challenge: we have an entire discussion elsewhere about finding blue strings of *techeilet* in the marketplace, and the ruling there is that if they were cut at the right length and prepared in the right way, we can assume they were done correctly. Why should the case of *tefillin* be any different?

### Torach/Effort Debate

To this, the *gemara* answers — *ella amar Rava* — that the underlying question of whether we say "nobody would go to such an effort unless this were the real thing" (*torach*) is actually itself a *tannaitic* dispute. As the *baraita* teaches: *hamotzei tefillin machnisam zug zug, echad ish v'echad isha, echad chadashot v'echad yeshanot* — if you find *tefillin* you may bring them in one pair at a time, whether men's or women's, and whether new or old. That is the position of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehudah, however, forbids the new but permits the old.

So we see that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah are debating precisely this principle. A new *tefillin* is a black square leather box — it has the form. Rabbi Meir holds that nobody would go to the effort of producing such an object if it were not genuine *tefillin*, and therefore we do not suspect it is an amulet. Rabbi Yehudah remains concerned that it might be, and the debate is precisely over whether the effort invested in producing such an object is itself proof of authenticity: *mar savar torach inish, u'mar savar lo torach inish* — one holds a person would go to such effort even for a counterfeit, the other holds they would not. This also resolves the earlier question about the blue *tzitzit* strands — that position, that we assume proper preparation from the appearance of proper preparation, is the view of Rabbi Meir.

### Definitions of Old/New

At this point the *gemara* introduces a teaching that fundamentally shifts the entire analysis. The father of Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak — that is, Rav Yitzchak, the grandfather of Shmuel — teaches a *baraita* that defines old and new *tefillin* in concrete terms: *elu hen yeshanot, kol she-yesh ba-hen retsuot u'mekusharot* — old *tefillin* are those that have straps, and the straps have been knotted. *Chadashot* — new ones — are those that may have straps but the straps have not yet been knotted.

### Wearing Problem

This teaching transforms the analysis entirely. The *gemara* now says: *de-kulei alma lo torach inish* — everybody agrees in principle that nobody would construct these *tefillin* boxes if they were not genuine. The concern about new *tefillin* is therefore not that they might be amulets. Rather, the problem with new *tefillin* is: how can you wear them home on *Shabbat* if no knot has been tied? The *dalet* on the head *tefillin* keeps it in place; the loop on the *shel yad* allows it to be tightened. Without those knots, there is no way to wear the *tefillin* home, and tying a knot on *Shabbat* is itself a violation. The *amulet* concern was never the real issue — the question is one of practical wearability on *Shabbat*.

---

## Knot vs. Bow

### Bow Forbidden

The immediate question this raises is: if the only problem is the absence of a knot, why not simply make a bow? After all, one ties one's shoes with a bow rather than a knot. So could one not wear the *tefillin* home by fastening them with a bow?

*Amar Rav Chisda*: *zos omeres aniva psulah b'tefillin* — this demonstrates that a bow is invalid for *tefillin*. A bow cannot substitute for a knot in fulfilling the *mitzvah* of wearing *tefillin*. The permission to wear *tefillin* on *Shabbat* — even when *Shabbat* is generally not *zman tefillin* — is based on the fact that wearing them constitutes a normal mode of dress, *derech malbush*.
