But just as one may not wear *tefillin* on a part of the body where they are not normally worn, because that would not constitute *derech malbush*, similarly, if the normal mode of wearing *tefillin* requires a knot, then wearing them with a bow is not *derech malbush*, and such wearing would not be valid either for the *mitzvah* or as a legitimate mode of carrying on *Shabbat*.

### Bow = Shabbat Knot

*Abaye* then says: *Rav Yehudah l'taamei*, Rabbi Yehudah goes according to his own reasoning, for Rabbi Yehudah holds that a bow in the laws of *Shabbat* counts as a proper knot — *aniva kshira maalya hi*. Therefore, making a bow is not a solution to the problem. One cannot bind the *tefillin* onto one's arm, *Shabbat* has begun, one cannot make a knot — and the proposed alternative of a bow is equally problematic for Rabbi Yehudah, since for him a bow is halachically equivalent to a knot with respect to *Shabbat*.

This also perfectly explains the structure of the debate between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir presumably holds that a bow does *not* constitute a *Shabbat* violation, and therefore one could wear new *tefillin* home by means of a bow. Rabbi Yehudah holds the bow is itself a *Shabbat* problem, so no solution exists, and new *tefillin* without knots cannot be worn home at all.

The *gemara* then draws out the implication: *taama d'aniva kshira maalya hi* — the reason Rabbi Yehudah prohibits it is precisely because a bow equals a knot for *Shabbat*. But *ha lav hachi aniv lehu* — if not for the *Shabbat* concern, using a bow would have been a viable solution in principle. This brings the *gemara* back to whether a bow could ever serve as a legitimate knot for *tefillin*.

### Knot Form

Rav Yehudah son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas says in the name of Rav: *kesher shel tefillin halacha l'Moshe miSinai hu* — the knot of *tefillin* is a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. And Rav Nachman adds: *v'noyehem l'var* — their beauty must be on the outside. That is, when one forms the knot at the back of the head in the shape of a *dalet*, or the knot on the *shel yad* in the shape of a *yud*, the shape must be visible and exposed so that one who looks at it can see it.

This generates two distinct questions: first, what constitutes a valid knot — can a bow qualify? And second, what must the knot look like? The *gemara* now presses the point: according to Rabbi Meir, who permits wearing new *tefillin* home on *Shabbat*, he must be permitting some form of bow since one cannot make a full knot. But how could a bow ever be a legitimate knot for *tefillin*, given that it would not form the required shape of a *dalet* or a *yud*?

### Bow Solution

The *gemara* answers: *d'aniv lehu k'ein kshira dideyhu* — one makes the bow so that it resembles the required knot, shaping it to look like a *dalet* or like a *yud*. Whether such a bow would fully constitute fulfillment of the *mitzvah* of *tefillin* on a regular weekday remains ambiguous in the *gemara's* formulation. But at minimum, it means the *tefillin* look normal enough that wearing them on *Shabbat* would be considered a legitimate mode of dress — not something bizarre or unprecedented — and therefore would not constitute carrying but rather wearing.

This is the *gemara's* answer for Rabbi Meir's position: one makes a bow, which for Rabbi Meir is not a *Shabbat* violation, and one shapes it to resemble the required knot form. For Rabbi Yehudah, in theory such a bow would be possible in terms of appearance, but the *Shabbat* problem with the bow prevents it.

On the question of what exactly constitutes a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* with respect to the knot: Rashi holds that all three letters are included — the *shin* on the *tefillin* (though it is not quite a knot in the conventional sense), the *dalet*, and the *yud*. Tosafos, in the first line, takes issue with this and argues that the *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* applies only to the *shin* itself. The *dalet* and *yud*, by Tosafos' reading, are derived from the structure of the knots and straps, not from the *Sinaitic* tradition as such. In either case, the *gemara* is clear that the knots must visibly resemble the *dalet* and *yud*, and the solution of a bow shaped accordingly is what enables wearing on *Shabbat* according to Rabbi Meir.

A further question naturally arises: beyond the knot and the letters, *tefillin* are typically wound around the arm seven times and then around the finger. If one were to wrap the *tefillin* around the arm only once, would an observer even recognize it as wearing *tefillin*? The principle seems to be that there is a range of tolerance — what counts as a legitimate wearing of *tefillin* need not be perfectly identical to the standard weekday practice, but at a certain point it ceases to be recognizable as wearing them at all. The precise limits of that range are not spelled out in the *gemara*.

---

## Buying Tefillin

### Two-One Check

*Amar Rav Chisda amar Rav*: if one purchases *tefillin* from someone who is not a *mumcheh* — not an expert with proven credentials — one must verify their *kashrus* before relying on them. The term *mumcheh* here does not simply mean "skilled"; it means someone whose reliability has been established and certified. In the scenario the *gemara* envisions, a wholesaler collects *tefillin* from various *sofrim* and sells them to retailers. Since this wholesaler's reliability is not independently established, the buyer must conduct spot checks. The rule: *bodek shtayim shel yad v'achas shel rosh*, or *shtayim shel rosh v'achas shel yad* — check two of one type and one of the other type, for a total of three.

### Why Two-One?

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *ma nafshach* — make up your mind. If this wholesaler purchased all his *tefillin* from a single supplier, then why not simply check three of the same type? The principle of *chazaka* — that three instances establish a presumption — would apply here, and if all the *tefillin* come from one *sofer*, the type distinction should not matter. Conversely, if the wholesaler buys from multiple suppliers — two or three different *sofrim* — then checking three pieces total is clearly insufficient; every individual pair would require its own verification, since each might have come from a different, unvalidated source. Under neither scenario does the "two of one and one of the other" formula make intuitive sense.

### One Supplier

The *gemara* resolves this: *le'olam michad gavra zavnin* — indeed, the wholesaler purchases from a single supplier. But the purpose of the mixed sampling is this: one needs to ensure that this *sofer* is validated, *mitmachei*, with respect to both *shel yad* and *shel rosh*. A *sofer* might write a beautiful *ksav* yet make a systematic error specific to one type. For example, he might not arrange the *parshiyos* in the *shel rosh* in the correct order, or he might fail to make the proper separation between the *parshiyos* in the *shel yad*. Therefore, three samples are sufficient to establish a *chazaka* of reliability — but among those three, one must ensure that both types have been examined. It is not enough to check three *shel yad* pieces and extrapolate to the *shel rosh*.

The logic is thus: three samples from a single supplier establishes reliability, but the sample must cover both types, so as to validate the supplier's practice with respect to each. That is why two of one and one of the other suffices — not three of the same, and not three of each.

### Rav Kahana

A *baraita* of Rav Kahana then states: *b'tefillin bodek shtayim shel yad u'shtayim shel rosh* — check two of the *shel yad* and two of the *shel rosh*, for a total of four. This does not fit neatly into either a "total of three" framework or a "three of each type" framework.

### Rebbi Position

The *gemara* identifies this position as that of *Rebbi*: *ha mani Rebbi hi, d'amar bitrei zimnei hvei chazakah* — Rebbi holds that a *chazaka* is established after two instances, not three. This is the well-known dispute between Rebbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding how many occurrences are required to establish a presumption. Here, applied to spot-checking, Rebbi holds that two samples from each type suffice to establish confidence in the supplier's practice for that type — hence two of *shel yad* and two of *shel rosh*.

### Multiple Bags

The *gemara* then turns to a *seifa* in that same *baraita*: *v'chein batzeves hashaini, v'chein batzeves hashlishi* — and similarly for the second group and the third group. This seems to say that after verifying two bags, one can extrapolate to all remaining bags. But this contradicts Rebbi's own principle: if two instances establish a *chazaka*, then after verifying two bags, one should already be able to stop.

The *gemara* resolves: *modeh Rebbi bitzvatim d'mitrei tlata gavra zavnin* — Rebbi concedes that when it comes to separate bags, each bag comes from a different supplier, and therefore no cross-bag extrapolation is possible. The principle of two establishing a *chazaka* applies within a single bag from a single source; it cannot bridge across multiple bags sourced from multiple suppliers. The mention of a third bag in the *baraita* is therefore not to say "after three bags you are done" — rather, it is *lafukei michizkei*, to negate the normal *chazaka* rule: do not think that verifying two bags allows you to extrapolate to all subsequent bags. Each bag requires its own inspection. As the *gemara* confirms: *ein hachi nami* — indeed, even a fourth and fifth bag must be checked.

This discussion has practical resonance well beyond *tefillin*, touching on how *halakha* treats sampling in contexts where large quantities of goods are examined — such as the checking of produce for insects, where a similar question arises about how many units from a given batch must be inspected.

---

## Bundles/Bags

### Bundle Types

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* rules that if one finds *tefillin* in bundles — *tzfashim* or *krichot* — one waits until nightfall and brings them home after *Shabbat*. The *gemara* first asks what distinguishes *tzfashim* from *krichot*. *Amar Rav Yehudah amar Rav*: they are essentially the same thing in different configurations. *Tzfashim* — *zuzei zuzei* — are paired sets of *tefillin*, a *shel yad* and *shel rosh* wrapped together as pairs, multiple such pairs collected together. *Krichot* — *de'krichu tuvah* — are bundles where all the *tefillin* are wrapped together without being separated into pairs. The functional difference between them is limited; they simply describe different physical arrangements.

### Single vs. Multiple Trips

The *gemara* then asks why one cannot simply carry the *tefillin* home pair by pair, wearing each pair in turn for the duration of the trip, and making multiple trips until all are safely brought in.

### Completion Test

*Amar Rav Yitzchak berei de'Rav Yehudah*: his father Rav Yehudah explained to him the following principle — *kol she'ilu machnisan zug zug ve'chlot kodem shkiat hachamah, machnisan zug zug*. If the number of *tefillin* is small enough that making individual trips, one pair at a time, could realistically be completed before the end of *Shabbat*, then one should indeed make all those trips. But if the quantity is so large that even after dozens of trips there will still be pairs remaining when *Shabbat* ends, then one should not begin the process at all — *machshich aleihem u'mivian*, one waits there until nightfall and brings them all home at once.

The logic: if one cannot in any case remove all of them within *Shabbat*, then leaving some behind is unavoidable regardless. In that case, it is better not to engage in the piecemeal rescue at all, and simply remain with the *tefillin* until *Shabbat* ends. This reasoning, of course, assumes that waiting there is a viable option — the *mishnah's* next case will address the scenario where it is not.

---

## Danger Scenarios

### Cover & Leave

When waiting is not possible — *u'v'sakana michasan ve'holech* — if there is genuine danger, one covers the *tefillin* and leaves. The scenario envisioned is one where remaining to guard them through nightfall poses a risk, whether from attack, theft, or another threatening circumstance. In such a case, if wearing one pair home is possible, one would presumably do so; the rest are covered and left. The question of what happens to the *tefillin* left momentarily unguarded during the back-and-forth of individual trips is a genuinely difficult one — *Chazal* appear to have exercised a degree of practical leniency here, perhaps because an item visibly in the process of being tended to is treated somewhat differently by passersby. More importantly, the character of *tefillin* as *kisvei kodesh* means the effort to rescue as many as possible is obligatory, on the model of a *sefer Torah* in a burning synagogue: one saves what one can.

### Small Trips

The *gemara* now introduces a competing solution from a *baraita*: *besakanah molichan pachos pachos me'arba amot* — in a case of danger, one may carry them in increments of less than four *amot* at a time. If one can recall the *mishnah* at the end of *Masechet Shabbat*, this is the same technique described there for a person caught outside the city with belongings at nightfall. The suggestion is that rather than leaving the *tefillin* behind and simply covering them, one could take the entire bundle and inch it home in multiple segments, each less than four *amot*, thereby avoiding a biblical violation while still rescuing all of the *tefillin*. Why, then, does the *mishnah* say simply "cover them and leave"?

### Two Danger Types

*Amar Rav lo kashya* — Rav resolves the apparent contradiction: these two rulings address two entirely different types of danger. *Ha besakanas nochri, ha besakanas listin* — one ruling pertains to danger from non-Jews, the other to danger from robbers.

### Rashi's View

Rashi initially understands the distinction as follows. When the danger is from non-Jews who will mistreat the *tefillin* — desecrate their *kedushah* — one cannot simply cover and leave, since an enemy who finds them will handle them disrespectfully. However, when the danger is from Jewish robbers who are motivated by the monetary value of the *tefillin*, one need not carry them at all using the less-than-four-*amot* method, since if the robbers find them they will at least treat the *tefillin* with appropriate reverence, being Jews themselves who recognize their sanctity. The less-than-four-*amot* method is therefore unnecessary for the *kedushah* concern, but one should not carry them openly due to the personal danger of being attacked for their monetary value. Rashi's comment on *besakanas listin* — that Jewish robbers *dekatlei lei mishum mamona*, would kill for money, but *vetfillin lo mevazu lehu*, would not disrespect the *tefillin* — is a striking formulation.

### Revised: Edict

Rashi himself, however, ultimately rejects this reading in light of the continuation of the *gemara*, and offers a revised understanding. *Sakanas nochri* refers to a *sha'as hashmad* — a period of persecution in which Jews are forbidden by decree from wearing or handling *tefillin*. In such a circumstance, one cannot wear the *tefillin* or be found in possession of them at all; the only recourse is to cover them and leave. *Sakanas listin*, by contrast, refers to the risk that the *tefillin* will be stolen by robbers who covet them for their value — there is no edict, no prohibition on being found with them. In that case, the concern is the risk of being physically attacked while carrying them, but not of being caught with them by an authority. Therefore, the solution is to carry them in increments of less than four *amot*, avoiding a biblical violation while keeping them in one's possession.

The distinction is thus clean: if the danger is that *tefillin* cannot be found on one's person, cover and leave. If the danger is merely the risk of robbery, carry in small increments.

---

## Tanna Kamma vs. R. Shimon

### Quiet Approach

*Abaye* then presses on the *mishnah*: having established that the *mishnah* speaks of a case of *sakanas ovdei gilulim* — danger from non-Jews enforcing a prohibition — how does Rabbi Shimon's position fit in? Rabbi Shimon says *nosein l'chaveiro v'chaveiro l'chaveiro* — pass the *tefillin* from person to person in a daisy chain. But in a case where the non-Jews are enforcing a decree against *tefillin*, such a large public operation would only attract attention: *kol shekein d'avsha milsa* — it would make the matter far more conspicuous.

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *chasuri mechasra v'hachi kasani* — the *mishnah* is to be read as if a distinction is embedded within it. *Bameh devarim amurim besakanas ovdei kochavim* — when there is a non-Jewish edict, cover and leave. *Aval besakanas listim* — but when the danger is merely robbery, carry in small trips of less than four *amot*. And it is on *this* case — the robbery case — that Rabbi Shimon disagrees and advocates the daisy chain method instead.

### Daisy Chain

So the debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon applies specifically to the robbery scenario, where one may handle and carry the *tefillin*. The *tanna kamma* says: carry in segments of less than four *amot*, doing so quietly and individually. Rabbi Shimon says: use the daisy chain — *nosein l'chaveiro v'chaveiro l'chaveiro* — passing the *tefillin* from person to person down a line of people.

### Philosophy

The *gemara* articulates the underlying logic of each position. *Mar savar pachos m'arba amot adif* — the *tanna kamma* holds that individual small trips are preferable, because *d'ei amart nosein l'chaveiro v'chaveiro l'chaveiro, avsha milsa d'shabbos* — the daisy chain creates a large public commotion on *Shabbat*, which is in itself disrespectful of the day's character, setting aside any concern about non-Jews. Better to handle the matter quietly.

Rabbi Shimon holds the opposite: *nosein l'chaveiro adif* — the daisy chain is preferable, because *d'ei amart molichan pachos pachos m'arba amot, zimnin d'lav adateih* — if you rely on a person to carry in segments shorter than four *amot*, there will be moments of inattention where one takes a few extra steps without thinking, and one will come to carry four *amot* in *reshus harabim* — a biblical violation.

This is a conceptually rich debate, touching on what one might describe as the tension between the quality of *Shabbat* as a public experience and the protection of the individual from personal transgression. The *tanna kamma* is willing to accept a modest risk of inadvertent personal violation if it preserves the texture of *Shabbat* for the community. Rabbi Shimon prioritizes eliminating the risk of individual transgression even at the cost of some disruption to the public experience of *Shabbat*. This debate also resonates with a larger dispute among the *rishonim* — both Rambam and Ramban maintain that there is a biblical *mitzvah* of *tishbos*, of resting on *Shabbat*, that extends beyond the thirty-nine *melachos*. Ramban understands *tishbos* to mean that *Shabbat* must be experienced as a day of genuine rest and appropriate quality, independent of technical violation of the *melachos*. Rambam understands *tishbos* as a prohibition on activities that might lead one *to* transgress a *melachah*. The *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon can be read as anticipating precisely this dispute.

---

## Newborn Child

### Scenario

The *mishnah* then introduces an analogous case involving a child. *Bno mai ba'ei hasam* — what is a child doing out in the field? A *baraita* of the school of Menashya clarifies: *be-she-yeldato imo ba-sadeh* — the child was born in the field just before *Shabbat*, and there was no opportunity to bring the newborn home before *Shabbat* began.

The *mishnah* extends the same daisy-chain method to the case of the child: pass the infant from person to person to bring it home. The *gemara* notes: *u'mai afilu hen me'ah* — even if a hundred people are needed to form the chain, *de-af al gav de-kashya lei yada* — even though the repeated handoffs are uncomfortable and unpleasant for the infant — *afilu hachi, hadi* — even so, this is the preferred approach.

This is a striking formulation. The *gemara* elsewhere is unequivocal that *pikuach nefesh* overrides virtually all of *halachah*. One must therefore assume that the *gemara* is working with the understanding that in this particular scenario, the daisy-chain method does not increase any actual risk to the newborn — the difficulty is described as discomfort, not danger — and that if bringing the child home via this method would in any way endanger it, the *pikuach nefesh* principle would obviously take precedence and one would simply carry the child home directly.

### Barrel Analogy

Rabbi Yehudah then extends the principle: *nosein adam chavit* — Rabbi Yehudah says one can do the same daisy-chain method with a barrel. Before even reaching the *halachic* questions about *tchum*, one might ask: since when may one use this technique for a barrel, which is simply a monetary object? The case of *tefillin* involves *kisvei kodesh*; the case of a child involves life. A barrel of wine or oil raises a different kind of question. The answer may lie in the precedent of the *mishnah* at the end of *Masechet Shabbat*, where the *gemara* permitted the less-than-four-*amot* technique for personal belongings in situations of significant distress.

### Tchum Problem

The *chakhamim* object to Rabbi Yehudah's barrel case on a different ground entirely: *ha'behema v'hakeilim k'raglei ha'bealim* — animals and vessels are subject to their owner's *tchum*. If the barrel would need to be transported beyond the owner's *tchum* to reach safety, that is a separate and independent *halachic* problem. How does Rabbi Yehudah address the *tchum* issue?

---

## Water & Tchum

### Pour Method

*Amar Reish Lakish mishum Levi Saba*: the scenario being described is not one in which anyone physically moves the barrel. Rather, *d'meara m'chavis l'chavis* — one pours from barrel to barrel. Everyone along the line has their own barrel, and the liquid is transferred by pouring, each person pouring into the next person's barrel. This way, no barrel crosses the *tchum* — only the liquid moves. The question then becomes whether the liquid itself has a *tchum* issue.

### Water Insignificant

*Rabbi Yehuda l'taamei d'amar mayim ein bahen mamash* — Rabbi Yehudah applies his own principle that water lacks legal substance. The source: a *baraita* teaches that Rabbi Yehudah rules that water and salt are *beteilim* — nullified — in dough and therefore do not have the laws of *tchumin*. The water borrowed from a neighbor to make *challah* does not impose the neighbor's *tchum* on the dough, because Rabbi Yehudah holds that water absorbed into dough is insignificant. If water lacks *tchum* relevance, then moving it raises no *tchum* problem.

### Water in Pot

The *gemara* immediately challenges this extrapolation. *Eima d'shamas lei l'Rabbi Yehudah heicha d'belian b'isa* — Rabbi Yehudah said water is insignificant specifically when it is absorbed into dough and has become invisible as an independent substance. But *aval heicha d'isneihu b'einihu* — when the water exists in its own state, as free liquid, has Rabbi Yehudah ever said it lacks *tchum* significance?

The *gemara* proceeds to demonstrate the opposite: *hashta b'kdeira amar Rabbi Yehudah lo betili* — Rabbi Yehudah explicitly says that water in a pot — the liquid component of a stew — is *not* nullified and *does* carry *tchum* laws. The same *baraita* cited above continues: *v'ein betilim b'kdeira, mipnei rotva* — water and salt are not nullified in a pot, because the sauce retains its independent character. If water in a pot has *tchum* significance for Rabbi Yehudah, then surely water in its free state does as well. The Reish Lakish / water-insignificance approach therefore cannot stand.

### Rava: Drawn

*Ela amar Rava*: the case must be understood differently. *Hacha b'chavis she'kansah shevisa u'mayim she'lo kanu shevisa askinan* — the barrel acquired its *shvisa* — established its resting place — at the onset of *Shabbat*, but the water did not. Rashi explains: the water was drawn from a river on *Shabbat* itself, or it is rainwater collected on *Shabbat*. Water drawn from a flowing river during *Shabbat* never had an established location at the onset of *Shabbat* and therefore was never subject to a *tchum* boundary.

Once the water has no *tchum*, the barrel — which is merely the container for the water — is secondary to it. *D'vateil hachavis l'gabei mayim* — the barrel is subordinate to the water it contains, just as the *gemara* rules in related contexts: *hamotzi chai b'mita patur af al hamita* — if one carries a living person on a stretcher, one is exempt not only regarding the person — since *chai nosei es atzmo*, a living person bears his own weight — but also regarding the stretcher itself, since the stretcher is subordinate to its contents. Similarly, *hamotzi ochlin pachos mikishiur b'kli, patur af al hakli, mipnei shehakli tafel lo* — if one carries food below the minimum quantity in a vessel, one is exempt even for the vessel, since it is secondary to the food. The same principle applies here: the barrel is secondary to the water, and if the water has no *tchum*, neither does the barrel.

### Caravan Need

*Masiv Rav Yosef*: a *baraita* states — *b'shayara, nosein mayim v'chavis l'chaveiro v'chaveiro l'chaveiro* — in a caravan, one passes the water and the barrel from person to person. *B'shayara in, shelo b'shayara lo* — in a caravan yes, otherwise no. This implies the permission is limited to a caravan context, whereas the *mishnah* appears to speak without that restriction.

*Ela amar Rav Yosef*: read the *mishnah* too as referring to a caravan. And this resolves the *tchum* problem not through the technical mechanism of water drawn on *Shabbat*, but through *pikuach nefesh*: in a caravan without access to water, the need for water is a genuine life-threatening emergency. Rabbi Yehudah therefore sets aside the *tchum* concern entirely in such a circumstance.

### Two Cases

*Abaye* then draws a careful distinction between the two scenarios. In the caravan case: *b'shayara afilu chavis shekansah shvisa u'mayim shekanu shvisa* — even if the barrel and the water both established their *shvisa* at the onset of *Shabbat*, the *tchum* concern is overridden because of the life-threatening need for water in the caravan context. Outside the caravan: *shelo b'shayara, chavis shekansah shvisa u'mayim shelo kanu shvisa* — the case is specifically where the water did not establish a *shvisa*, i.e., it was drawn on *Shabbat* and therefore never acquired a *tchum* boundary. Abaye's contribution is thus to maintain both cases as distinct: the caravan case is governed by *pikuach nefesh* and dispenses with the *tchum* question entirely; the non-caravan case is the one Rava described, where the water was drawn on *Shabbat* and technically lacks a *tchum*.

### Ownerless

*Rav Ashi amar*: the case involves an ownerless barrel and ownerless water — *chavis d'hefker askinan u'mayim d'hefker askinan*. Ownerless objects are not subject to their owner's *tchum*, since they have no owner. The objection that *chakhamim* raise regarding *tchum* — *v'man amru lah, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri hi* — belongs to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that even ownerless objects acquire their own *shvisa*, defined by 2000 *amah* from wherever they happened to be at the onset of *Shabbat*, and are therefore not entirely free of *tchum* concerns. The *chakhamim's* objection — *lo yehalechu elu yoser mi'keilim sheyesh lahem baalim* — is therefore not to say these objects are limited by their owner's *tchum*, but rather to say that ownerless objects are no more permissive than owned objects; they too carry *tchum* limitations, just derived differently.

---

## Fallen Scroll

### Scenario

The *mishnah* now turns to a case that continues the theme of special dispensations for *kisvei kodesh*. *Haya kore b'sefer al ha-iskopa* — one was reading from a scroll on the porch, and *v'nisgalgal ha-sefer mi-yado* — the scroll rolled out of one's hand and began to fall, leaving half of the scroll hanging over the edge of the balcony, with the *reshus hayachid* above and the *reshus harabim* below. Can one roll it back up?

### Porch Case

In the *iskopa* case — reading from a porch or covered area — *v'gololo etzlo* — one may always roll the scroll back up toward oneself. No restriction applies.

### Within Ten

On a roof: *ad she-lo higia l'asara tfachim, gololo etzlo* — as long as the hanging portion has not descended into the ten-*tefach* airspace of *reshus harabim*, one may roll it back up. Above ten *tefachim* from the ground, the airspace is a *makom p'tor* — an exempt domain — not a *reshus harabim*. Rolling the scroll up from there does not constitute removing it from *reshus harabim*, and the action is therefore permitted.

### Beyond Ten

Once one end of the scroll is hanging within the ten *tefachim* of *reshus harabim* — *mishe-higia l'asara tfachim* — one may no longer roll it up. The scroll is now effectively present in *reshus harabim*, and rolling it up would constitute an act of transferring from *reshus harabim* to *reshus hayachid*. What does one do instead? *Hofcho al ha-ksav* — one turns the script-side of the scroll toward the wall, so that the text is at least somewhat protected from the elements. One is still holding one end of the scroll; the turning is possible without rolling it up.

The difference between the *iskopa* and the roof cases — why the porch carries no limitation while the roof must distinguish between within and beyond ten *tefachim* — is a point the *gemara* addresses separately.

### R. Yehudah

Rabbi Yehudah extends the permission: *afilu eino mesulak min ha-aretz ela k'mlo machat* — even if the hanging end is only a needle's width above the ground — a millimeter — as long as it is not actually resting on the ground of *reshus harabim*, one may roll it back up. Even within the ten-*tefach* zone, the hair's breadth of elevation is sufficient.

### R. Shimon

Rabbi Shimon goes further still: *afilu ba-aretz, gololo etzlo* — even if one end of the scroll is actually resting on the ground of *reshus harabim*, one may roll it up. One end remains in one's hand in *reshus hayachid*, and even though the other end is touching the ground of *reshus harabim*, the scroll may be retrieved.

### Principle

Rabbi Shimon grounds this ruling in a general principle: *she-ein l'cha davar mishum shvus omed bifnei kisvei kodesh* — there is no rabbinic prohibition that may stand in the way of protecting *kisvei kodesh*. While the earlier sections of this *daf* involved techniques and workarounds that did not require formally overriding any rabbinic decree, here — at least according to Rabbi Shimon's most expansive position — we are explicitly told that rabbinic restrictions yield before the imperative to protect holy scriptures. The biblical prohibition of *Shabbat* is not abrogated; but rabbinic enactments do not prevail when *kisvei kodesh* are at stake. We will continue from there.

---

---

# Eiruvin 98

## Ogdo BeYado & Porch

### Principle Intro

As we enter the final week of *Masechet Eruvin*, the last *perek* represents a significant thematic shift — away from the laws of *eruvin* proper and toward the broader laws of carrying in *reshut hayachid*, along with special exceptions for *kitvei kodesh*. This parallels the end of *Masechet Shabbat*, where we encountered special dispensations for one who was caught outside the *techum* with a *lulav*.

The principle that anchors the opening discussion is known as *ogdo beyado* — literally, "the knot is in his hand." The idea is that if one holds one end of a long object while the other end extends into a different domain, one has not performed a complete act of *hotza'ah*, because the entire object did not begin fully within one domain and transfer fully into another. The whole object is physically one unit; the papers or parchment cannot be divided. Accordingly, even if a *sefer* rolls from a *reshut hayachid* into a *reshut harabim*, and the reader is still holding one end, the act of rolling it back would at most constitute a rabbinic violation. The animating question, then, is whether we permit such a rabbinic violation for the sake of protecting *kitvei kodesh*.

### Porch vs Rooftop

The *Mishnah* addresses two distinct scenarios. In the case of the porch (*iskopa*), the ruling is unqualified: if one is reading on a porch and a *sefer* rolls away, one may roll it back without restriction. In the case of the rooftop, however, the *Mishnah* introduces a three-way debate that turns on how close the fallen end of the scroll is to the ground of the *reshut harabim*.

The first opinion holds that once the scroll enters the airspace of *reshut harabim* — that is, once it descends within ten *tefachim* of the ground — one may not roll it back. At that point, even a rabbinic violation is impermissible, and one must instead turn the scroll so that the writing faces the wall, protecting it from the elements. Rabbi Yehuda is more lenient: even if the scroll is only a hair's breadth (*melo hachut*) off the ground, one may roll it back — the *Gemara*'s version of the measurement is *melo hachut*, a string's breadth, rather than the needle's breadth sometimes cited. As long as the scroll has not actually touched the ground, Rabbi Yehuda permits rolling it back. Rabbi Shimon is the most permissive: even if the scroll has hit the ground, one may roll it back, since the entire prohibition is rabbinic, and rabbinic prohibitions yield before the need to protect *kitvei kodesh*.

This immediately raises a structural question: why is the porch case stated without debate, as a simple ruling, while the rooftop case generates a three-way *machloket*?

### Reconciling Opinions

The *Gemara* (top of 98a) opens by analyzing the porch case: *hai iskopa heichi dami* — what exactly are we dealing with? If the porch is a *reshut hayachid* — ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* wide — and the *reshut harabim* lies before it, and we are told without qualification that one may roll the scroll back, this implies we have no concern even if the scroll has made contact with the *reshut harabim*. As the *Gemara* notes: *velo gazrinan dilma nafal ve'ati le'atuyei* — we are not concerned that once he rolls it back up, the scroll might fall entirely and he will then go out and retrieve it from the domain. Given that conclusion, the unqualified porch ruling corresponds precisely to Rabbi Shimon's position in the rooftop debate: even if the scroll rests in the *reshut harabim*, it may be retrieved because the entire *issur* is rabbinic, and rabbinic prohibitions do not stand in the way of protecting *kitvei kodesh*.

The *Gemara* asks: *mani* — whose opinion is this? *Rabbi Shimon hee* — it is Rabbi Shimon, *d'amar kol davar shehu mishum shvus ein omeid bifnei kisvei hakodesh*, who holds that anything that is merely a *shvus* — a rabbinic prohibition — will not stand in the way of protecting holy scriptures.

This creates a structural puzzle: *reisha v'seifa Rabbi Shimon, metziata Rabbi Yehuda* — the opening case (the porch) follows Rabbi Shimon, the closing position (in the rooftop debate) is Rabbi Shimon, yet the middle of the *mishnah* presents the debate including Rabbi Yehuda's view. How can the *mishnah* proceed in this manner? Rav Yehuda answers: this is not, in fact, a problem. The porch case was stated as an unattributed *stam* position reflecting Rabbi Shimon's view; the rooftop debate then records the range of opinions, the last of which is Rabbi Shimon — the same view as the opening case. The difference between porch and rooftop is not substantive; it is merely a matter of literary presentation.

---

## Karmelis vs Reshut

### Rabba's Trampled

Rabba, however, is dissatisfied with this answer. He prefers to establish a *substantive* distinction between the porch and the rooftop. He says: *hacha b'iskopa hanidreset askinan* — we are dealing with a porch that has heavy foot traffic. Although such a porch may technically be a *reshut hayachid*, the constant trampling creates a situation where the scroll, once fallen, is in genuine danger of being trodden upon. In that case, *umishum bizayon kisvei hakodesh sharu rabbanan* — because of the concern for the degradation (*bizayon*) of holy scriptures, the *rabanan* permit overriding even a rabbinic prohibition. According to Rabba, this leniency would be agreed upon by all opinions, since the concern is not merely an abstract rabbinic violation but an imminent *bizayon* to *kitvei kodesh*. The porch case is therefore not specifically a ruling of Rabbi Shimon; it is a consensus position grounded in the special urgency of preventing physical disrespect to sacred texts.

### Abaye's Four Amot

Abaye challenges Rabba's explanation. There is a *braisa* which refines the porch case: if the scroll rolled within four *amot*, one may roll it back (*golelo etzlo*); if it rolled further than four *amot*, one turns it face-down (*hofcho al hakasv*). Abaye's challenge is as follows: *v'ee amarta b'iskopa hanidreset askinan* — if we are dealing with a trampled porch, and the entire leniency is grounded in the urgency of preventing *bizayon* to *kitvei kodesh*, then *ma li toch arba amos ma li chutz l'arba amos* — what difference does it make whether it is within or beyond four *amot*? If a rabbinic prohibition is overridden because of the danger of degradation, it should be overridden regardless of distance. The four-*amot* distinction is therefore inexplicable on Rabba's terms.

Abaye therefore offers his own explanation: *hacha b'iskopa karmelis askinan v'reshut harabim overet l'faneha* — we are dealing not with a *reshut hayachid* but with a porch that is less than ten *tefachim* high, making it a *karmelit*, and a *reshut harabim* runs before it. This is the key distinction. Because the porch is a *karmelit*, when the scroll rolls from the porch into the *reshut harabim*, the violation involved in rolling it back is doubly attenuated. First, it is only rabbinic because of *ogdo beyado* — one is holding one end of the scroll. Second, it is only rabbinic because one is moving an object from a *karmelit* to a *reshut harabim*, which is itself only a *derabbanan*. The *issur* is thus a *derabbanan* layered upon a *derabbanan* — what one might call a *d'rabbanan* of a *d'rabbanan* — and it is this compounded attenuation that explains the porch ruling.

### No Torah Risk

The four-*amot* distinction then becomes intelligible. If the scroll fell within four *amot*, *d'ee naflu u'maisi lah lo asi lidei chiyuv chatas* — even in the worst case, if the scroll fell entirely out of one's hand and one walked over and retrieved it, one would never reach the threshold of a Torah violation. The distance is too short to carry four *amot* in *reshut harabim*, and one is in any case moving from *reshut harabim* to *karmelit*. In this scenario, *sharu lei rabbanan* — the *rabanan* permit the rolling. But once the scroll is beyond four *amot*, *d'ee maisi asi lidei chiyuv chatas* — if it fell entirely and one carried it back, one could potentially incur a Torah violation. In that case, *lo sharu lei rabbanan* — the *rabanan* do not permit it.

According to Abaye, the porch case is therefore not premised on *bizayon kitvei kodesh* overriding rabbinic prohibitions. Rather, it reflects the principle that when the prohibition is already doubly attenuated — both *karmelit* and *ogdo beyado* — and there is no risk of a Torah violation, the *rabanan* simply permitted the rolling from the outset. This is categorically different from a case where rolling up the scroll would risk even theoretically leading to a *de'oraita* transgression.

It is worth clarifying the phrase "double *d'rabbanan*" used here. This does not mean two *rabbinic* prohibitions committed simultaneously — one can transgress two independent *derabbanans* at once, and that simply means one has violated two rabbinic rules. A *d'rabbanan* of a *d'rabbanan*, by contrast, means that the prohibition is only rabbinic insofar as it operates within a domain that is itself only rabbinically problematic. It is a kind of structural or hierarchical weakness in the *issur*, not a mere accumulation of separate violations. It is somewhat analogous to the concept of *gezeira l'gezeira*, though that term refers to a deliberate double fence-building, whereas here the layering arises from the intersection of two independently applicable rabbinic categories.

### Carrying Concern

The *Gemara* raises a further objection: *toch arba amos nami nigzar dilma maisi me'reshut harabim l'reshut hayachid* — even within four *amot*, should we not be concerned that one will pick up the scroll from the *reshut harabim* and carry it all the way into the house, which is a *reshut hayachid*? After all, most porches stand in front of a house, and one would naturally bring a fallen book inside. If that is a real concern, then even within four *amot* there is a risk of a Torah violation — not by carrying in the *reshut harabim*, but by transitioning from *reshut harabim* through the *karmelit* and into the house.

The *Gemara* first suggests that perhaps the *karmelit* interposes as a break: *keivan d'mafseka karmelit leit lan bah* — since the *karmelit* separates the *reshut harabim* from the house, we are not concerned, because one would have to consciously execute two separate transitions rather than one fluid act of carrying. The *Gemara* then raises a challenge from a ruling of Rava: *hamavir chaifetz mitchillat arba l'sof arba v'he'eviro derech alav chayav* — if one takes an object and carries it from the beginning of four *amot* to the end of four *amot*, passing it over a neutral zone along the way, one is still liable. Rashi explains this ruling as addressing a case where one carried the object above ten *tefachim* — through airspace that is technically not *reshut harabim* — and yet remained liable. Thus, passing through a neutral zone such as a *karmelit* does not break the act of *hotza'ah*. If one picked up the scroll from the *reshut harabim* and deposited it in the house, one would be liable, regardless of having passed through the *karmelit*.

### Long Porch Memory

The *Gemara* resolves the difficulty by offering two alternatives. The first: *hacha b'askupa arucha* — we are dealing with a very long porch, oriented not along the *reshut harabim* but extending deeply away from it, like a pier. If the scroll fell near the edge of such a long porch, and one went down to retrieve it, by the time one had walked all the way back through the length of the porch to reach the house, *adeihachi v'hachi midkar* — in the meantime, one would remember that one is carrying on *Shabbat* and would set the scroll down on the porch rather than continuing into the house. The length of the porch itself serves as a cognitive buffer that makes the concern of inadvertently carrying into the house sufficiently remote.

The second alternative: *ee ba'it eima de-ulam b'shipufa she'eina arucha, v'stam kitvei kodesh iyunei me'aynei behu u'manach lehu* — even if the porch is not particularly long, one must consider what the person was doing on the porch in the first place: reading. The natural thing for someone who retrieves a scroll from the *reshut harabim* and places it back on the porch is to resume reading, not to carry it inside. Once the scroll is back on the porch, the reader's own engagement with the text provides the stop — one sits down and continues reading, rather than walking inside. The concern that one might carry it the entire way into the house is therefore treated as sufficiently attenuated.

The overall resolution, then, is that the porch case operates on a distinct principle: it is a *karmelit*, yielding a doubly attenuated *d'rabbanan*, and within four *amot* there is no realistic concern of reaching a Torah violation. For that reason, everyone — even Rabbi Yehuda, who disputes Rabbi Shimon in the rooftop case — would agree that rolling the scroll back is permitted. Outside of four *amot*, however, the risk of inadvertently incurring a *de'oraita* violation reasserts itself, and the *rabanan* do not allow it.

---

## Rooftop Proximity

### Suspension Issue

Returning now to the rooftop case — which is a *reshut hayachid* — the *Gemara* asks: *v'ha lo nach* — but the scroll hasn't come to rest! When the scroll tumbles from a rooftop and hangs suspended in midair, with the reader holding one end at the top and the other end dangling, there is no *hanacha* — no resting — in the *reshut harabim*. Without *hanacha*, there is no act of carrying at all, not even a rabbinic one. If so, there should be no issue with rolling it back regardless of whether it is within or beyond ten *tefachim*. Why does the *mishnah* establish distinctions based on proximity to the ground?

This is the *Gemara*'s opening challenge on the rooftop case: if the scroll is merely suspended — not resting on anything — then the debate about ten *tefachim*, a hair's breadth, or touching the ground seems to address a non-problem, since a suspended object has neither *akirah* nor *hanacha* in any meaningful sense.

### Slanted Wall

Rava answers: *amar Rava b'kosel meshupa* — the *mishnah* is dealing with a slanted or angled wall, meaning a wall with a protrusion or ledge jutting out at some point along its face. When the scroll falls from the roof, it does not hang freely; it lands on this ledge and comes to rest. The ten *tefachim* question then becomes live: if the ledge on which it rests is within the ten-*tefachim* airspace of *reshut harabim*, the scroll is considered to have come to rest within *reshut harabim*, making rolling it back a genuine rabbinic act — which is precisely the question the *mishnah* debates. If the scroll were simply suspended with no resting point, there would be no prohibition to discuss.

### Two Scenarios

Abaye challenges Rava's interpretation: *bemai okimta l'masechtein b'kotel meshupa* — if the entire *mishnah* operates on the assumption of a slanted wall where the scroll actually rests, then look at Rabbi Yehuda's position: *afilu eino mesulak min ha'aretz ela melo chut golelo etzlo* — even if it is only a hair's breadth off the ground, one may roll it back. Now, how can there be a platform or ledge a hair's breadth off the ground? The *Gemara* grants that such a scenario might exist in principle, but then pushes further: if the scroll is resting on a platform that is a hair's breadth above the ground of *reshut harabim*, it is effectively *within* three *tefachim* of the ground and governed by the principle of *lavud* — it is halachically as though it is resting on the ground itself. Given that, how does Rabbi Yehuda permit rolling it back?

The *Gemara* responds: *chasorei mechasra v'hachi katani* — the *mishnah* is actually incomplete as stated, and must be read as containing two sub-cases rather than three opinions about a single scenario. *Bameh devarim amurim* — in what circumstances do we apply the rule of ten *tefachim*? When the wall is slanted (*kotel meshupa*) and the scroll actually landed on a protrusion — in that case, if the protrusion is within ten *tefachim*, the scroll has genuinely rested in the airspace of *reshut harabim*, and whether one may roll it back is the subject of debate. But *aval b'kotel she'eino meshupa* — if the wall is straight and the scroll is simply suspended in midair, then the calculation shifts entirely: the relevant threshold is three *tefachim*, not ten.

### R. Yehuda Rest

With this reconstruction in place, what is Rabbi Yehuda's position and what is its rationale? The *Gemara* explains: *de'ba'inan hanacha al gabei mashehu* — Rabbi Yehuda requires an actual physical resting on something, however minimal. Even if the scroll is within three *tefachim* of the ground — which would normally be treated as *lavud* and halachically equivalent to resting on the ground — that is not sufficient for Rabbi Yehuda. He holds that unless the scroll is actually in physical contact with a surface, there is no *hanacha* and therefore no *issur* even in the rabbinic sense. Accordingly, as long as the scroll remains a hair's breadth above the ground, it has not physically rested, and one may roll it back. Only once it touches the ground and achieves actual *hanacha* does the restriction engage — and even then, Rabbi Shimon disagrees, as will be seen.

The *Gemara* then notes that Rava himself had articulated a similar principle in a different context: *keluta betoch shelosha l'rabbanan tzarich hanacha* — even according to the *rabbanan* in the debate surrounding *keluta k'mi she'huncha* (a concept going back to the beginning of *Masechet Shabbat*), an object within three *tefachim* of a surface still requires actual physical placement to constitute a *hanacha*. The *Gemara* asks whether Rabbi Yehuda's position in the *mishnah* is essentially a *tannaitic* parallel to Rava's *amoraic* ruling — *leima k'tannai amrah l'shma'atetah* — and whether Rava and the tannaim are debating the same underlying question.

### Final Positions

The *Gemara* ultimately consolidates the positions as follows. Remove the intermediate "within three *tefachim*" scenario from the debate of the suspended scroll — *ella kulei Rabbi Yehuda hi*, it is all Rabbi Yehuda's framework. The *mishnah* reconstructed contains two cases:

First, when the wall is slanted (*kotel meshupa*) and the scroll rests on a ledge: the relevant threshold is ten *tefachim* — that is the airspace of *reshut harabim* — and the first opinion holds that once the scroll is within that airspace and at rest, one may not roll it back.

Second, when the wall is straight and the scroll is suspended in midair: *afilu pacho mishlosha tefachim golelo etzlo* — even within three *tefachim*, Rabbi Yehuda says one may roll it back, because *be'inan hanacha al gabei mashehu* — physical resting on something is required, and mere suspension, even within three *tefachim*, does not constitute *hanacha*. The hair's-breadth formulation expresses this principle: as long as the scroll has not actually touched the ground, it has not rested, and rolling it back involves no *issur*.

Rabbi Shimon then stands as the final opinion: even if the scroll has physically touched the ground and achieved actual *hanacha* in *reshut harabim*, the act of rolling it back is only rabbinic — because *ogdo beyado* — and rabbinic prohibitions yield to protect *kitvei kodesh*. The two primary opinions in the suspended scenario thus debate the threshold of *hanacha*: does mere proximity within three *tefachim* constitute *hanacha* sufficient to prohibit rolling back (the first position), or is actual physical contact with a surface required (Rabbi Yehuda)? Rabbi Shimon does not enter this debate about *hanacha* thresholds — he simply holds that even actual *hanacha* does not prohibit, given the rabbinic nature of the *issur* and the imperative to honor *kitvei kodesh*.

---

## Window Ledge

### Fragile Vessels

A new *mishnah* introduces the case of *ziz she'lifnei chalon* — a ledge or protrusion extending outward from a window. The *mishnah* states that one may place objects on it and remove objects from it on *Shabbat*. The *Gemara* immediately asks: *hai ziz demafik leheicha* — into what domain does this ledge extend? If it juts out over *reshut harabim*, we should be concerned — *leichush shema nafal v'ati l'asuyei* — that an object placed on the ledge will fall to the ground below, and the owner will go out to retrieve it, thereby carrying from *reshut harabim* to *reshut hayachid*. On the other hand, if the ledge extends over a *reshut hayachid* such as a private courtyard (*chatzer*), then the entire ruling is trivially obvious — *peshita* — and requires no elaboration.

Abaye resolves the tension: *le'olam demafik l'reshut harabim* — indeed, the ledge extends over *reshut harabim*, but the *mishnah*'s permissive ruling is limited. When it says one may place objects on the ledge, this refers specifically to *keilim hanishbarim* — fragile vessels, things that would break upon falling. If an object would break upon landing in *reshut harabim*, one will not bother going down to pick it up, so the concern of retrieval is eliminated. Sturdy objects, by contrast, may not be placed on the ledge, since if they fell one would likely retrieve them.

### Permitted Objects

A *braisa* confirms and elaborates this position: *ziz she'lifnei chalon hayotzei l'reshut harabim noten alav katarot v'khossot, kitoniyot v'tzelochiyor* — on a ledge extending over *reshut harabim*, one may place plates, cups, pitchers, and similar vessels. Rashi understands these items as implicitly being breakable — the *braisa* is listing characteristic fragile objects, consistent with Abaye's interpretation. The *braisa* also adds: *u'mishtamesh b'chol hakotel* — one may also make use of the entire wall surface, including holes or recesses within it, for storage or placement purposes. However, this use of the wall is limited to those portions above ten *tefachim*; anything done within the ten *tefachim* airspace of *reshut harabim* constitutes a problematic transfer from *reshut hayachid* into *reshut harabim* airspace.

### Ledge Rules

The *braisa* then introduces an additional distinction that requires explanation: *v'im yesh ziz echad lemata heimenu mishtamesh bo* — if there is a second, lower ledge beneath the first, one may use it. *U've'elyon ein mishtamesh bo ela kineged chalono* — but the upper ledge may only be used in the space directly opposite one's window, not along its entire length. This asymmetry is puzzling. Why should a lower ledge be usable anywhere, while an upper ledge is restricted to the area facing the window?

The *Gemara* presses: *hai ziz heichi dami* — what are the dimensions of this *ziz*? If it does not have four *tefachim* of width, then even directly opposite the window one should not use it, since objects placed on so narrow a ledge will inevitably fall. Conversely, if it has four *tefachim*, then one should be able to use it anywhere along the wall without restriction.

### Width & Stability

Abaye offers the resolution: *tachton d'it bei arba'ah* — the lower ledge that may be used anywhere is one that has four *tefachim* of width, making it a stable surface. Objects placed there are unlikely to fall, so there is no concern of retrieval from *reshut harabim*. *Elyon leit bei arba'ah v'chalon mashlimo l'asarah* — the upper ledge, however, has less than four *tefachim* of width, but the window itself adjoins it and provides the additional depth needed to create a functional resting surface. *Keneged chalon mishtamesh* — opposite the window, where the ledge is stabilized by the window opening that completes its width, one may use it; *dehai gisa u'dehai gisa asur* — but on either side of the window, where the ledge stands alone without the window's supplementary width, it is too narrow to be relied upon, and objects placed there are liable to fall. The apparent rule about upper versus lower ledges is therefore not really about height at all — it is about width. A narrow ledge is usable only where the window stabilizes it; a wide ledge may be used anywhere along the wall.

---

## Cross-Domain Motion

### Standing & Moving

The next *mishnah* moves from special cases involving *kitvei kodesh* and architectural features to a broader analysis of *hotza'ah* — specifically, what it means to move an object across domains when the person doing so is not fully within either domain. *Omed adam b'reshut hayachid u'metaltel b'reshut harabim* — a person may stand in *reshut hayachid* and move objects within *reshut harabim*. Likewise, one may stand in *reshut harabim* and move objects within *reshut hayachid*. The caveat is *u'bilvad shelo yotzi chutz m'arba amot* — one must not move the object more than four *amot* within the *reshut harabim*, since that would replicate the full prohibited act of carrying, regardless of where one's body is standing.

This is a striking ruling. Throughout *Masechet Eruvin* and *Masechet Shabbat*, the *rabanan* erected numerous rabbinic fences against situations far less likely to lead to a *de'oraita* violation. Yet here, where the person is standing in *reshut hayachid* and actively moving an object in *reshut harabim* — a scenario that, intuitively, seems quite likely to result in the object being brought back into *reshut hayachid* — the *mishnah* permits it without restriction beyond the four-*amot* limit. The ruling is indeed a *chiddush*, and the *Gemara* will take it up further.

### Bodily Waste

The *mishnah* then introduces a related prohibition: *lo ya'amod adam b'reshut hayachid v'yashtin b'reshut harabim* — a person may not stand in *reshut hayachid* and urinate into *reshut harabim*, nor stand in *reshut harabim* and urinate into *reshut hayachid*. Similarly, *v'chein lo yarok* — one may not spit across domains. The logic is straightforward: the liquid or spittle originates in one domain and travels to another, making the bodily function itself an act of cross-domain transfer. In an era without indoor plumbing, when urination in the street and spitting were common, these prohibitions had immediate practical application.

### R. Yehuda Spit

Rabbi Yehuda adds a further dimension specifically regarding spitting: *af mishenitlash ruko befiv* — from the moment that the spittle becomes distinctly separated within one's mouth, one is halachically treated as carrying it. The phenomenon is experiential: when one gathers saliva in preparation to spit, the spit feels like a discrete object, no longer simply part of the mouth's moisture. At that point, says Rabbi Yehuda, *lo yehalech arba amot ad sheyirok* — one may not walk four *amot* without spitting, because one would be carrying a liquid for that distance. Moreover, one may not spit into a *reshut hayachid*. The only permissible option is to spit directly in front of oneself, where one stands. This ruling has a parallel on *Yom Kippur*, where the question of whether separated saliva in the mouth may be swallowed raises analogous concerns about what counts as a distinct object within the body.

### Text Dispute

The *Gemara* records a textual variant. Rabbi Chinana bar Shelmaya taught this *mishnah* to Chiya bar Rav in the presence of Rav, but his version read *lo ya'amod adam b'reshut hayachid v'yashtin b'reshut harabim* — a prohibition — rather than the *mishnah*'s permissive framing of the opening case (standing in one domain and moving in another). In other words, his version of the earlier *mishnah* about moving objects appeared to prohibit what our *mishnah* permits.

Rav reacted: *shavkta rabbanan v'avdata k'Rabbi Meir* — you have abandoned the view of the *rabanan* and are acting like Rabbi Meir. The implication is that Rabbi Chinana bar Shelmaya's version of the earlier *mishnah* tracked Rabbi Meir's stricter position, which will appear in a subsequent *mishnah* explicitly prohibiting cross-domain movement.

### Rabbanan vs R. Meir

The *Gemara* explains Rabbi Chinana bar Shelmaya's reasoning: *mid'seifa Rabbi Meir, reisha nami Rabbi Meir* — since the end of the *mishnah* presents Rabbi Meir's view prohibiting these acts, he assumed the opening of the *mishnah* was simply the same opinion restated. He therefore read the whole *mishnah* as Rabbi Meir's position.

The *Gemara* corrects this: *v'lo hi* — this is not so. *Seifa Rabbi Meir, reisha rabbanan* — the end of the *mishnah* belongs to Rabbi Meir, but the opening belongs to the *rabanan*. They represent a genuine *machloket*, not a repetition. Our *stam mishnah* — the unattributed ruling permitting a person to stand in one domain and move objects in the other — follows the *rabanan*, while Rabbi Meir's more stringent position appears explicitly as a named opinion in the later *mishnah*. The two are not to be harmonized; they reflect a real dispute between the *rabanan* and Rabbi Meir.

---

---

# Eiruvin 100

## Trees & Carrying

### Branches & Three Tefachim

The daf opens with the *mishnah* at the bottom of 99b. The *mishnah* states: *ilan*, a tree, *shemesach al ha'aretz* — that was overhanging the ground, its branches extending outward like a willow — if the foliage, the branches, are less than three *tefachim* removed from the ground, then by the principle of *lavud* they are considered as if connected to the ground and thereby create walls. Consequently, *metaltelin tachtav* — one may carry underneath such a tree on *Shabbos*, since the overhanging branches function as enclosing walls.

### Roots & Ground

The *mishnah* then turns to a second *halacha* concerning trees, this one not about carrying but about use and contact. The question is: at what point is something considered part of a tree, and at what point is it simply part of the ground? If roots protrude from the ground but remain within three *tefachim* of the ground, they are treated as part of the ground itself — one may sit on them freely. If, however, roots extend higher than three *tefachim*, they are considered part of the tree. The same principle applies to a tree stump: if it remains within three *tefachim* of the ground, it is treated as ground. The distinction of tree versus ground is therefore defined by whether something rises more than three *tefachim* above the earth.

### Rav Huna's Ruling

The *gemara* then records the ruling of Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua: *ein metaltelin bo yoter mibeit sa'atayim* — even if overhanging branches create walls and a valid enclosed space, if that space exceeds *beit sa'atayim* (approximately one hundred by one hundred feet), one may not carry throughout the full area; one is limited to carrying within four *amot*. Rashi notes that this applies even if the tree was planted specifically for that purpose. Normally, a space larger than *beit sa'atayim* that was enclosed *l'dirah* — for the purpose of habitation — would permit carrying throughout. Why then does this case differ?

### Tashmishah L'Avir

The *gemara* at the top of 100a explains: *mishum dehavi dirah she'tashmishah l'avir* — because this is a habitation whose function is oriented toward the air. Any such habitation, even if enclosed *l'dirah*, does not permit carrying beyond *beit sa'atayim*. The phrase *tashmishah l'avir* is deliberately ambiguous, and Rashi elaborates at the opening of 100a: *eino ladur bah tamid ela lehistofef bah shomrei hasadeh* — it is not a space for permanent dwelling, only for temporary shelter, such as when field-watchmen duck under the tree for shade. Rashi suggests two dimensions to this: first, it is not genuine habitation but merely temporary refuge; and second, those who use it are the *shomrei hasadeh*, whose attention is directed outward, toward the field they are guarding, rather than inward toward the space itself. Whether Rashi means to emphasize the temporariness of the shelter or the outward orientation of its occupants — or both — is not entirely resolved.

---

## Prohibit Climbing

### High Roots

The *mishnah* continues: *shorshav gvohin min ha'aretz gimmel tefachim lo yeshev aleihem* — if the roots of a tree are higher than three *tefachim* off the ground, one may not sit on them, because they are considered part of the tree and are subject to the *gezeirah* against using a tree on *Shabbos*.

This raises a more intricate question. Suppose a root begins below three *tefachim* — within ground-level range — then rises above three *tefachim*, and then curves back down below three *tefachim* again. One might draw the situation as follows: the first portion of the root, running along the ground and below three *tefachim*, is unproblematic. The root then rises past the three-*tefachim* threshold, becoming classified as tree. But what of the portion that continues downward after having crossed that threshold? Is it still considered tree, because it emerged from a part already classified as tree? Or does the fact that it is now below three *tefachim* render it ground again?

The underlying concern with climbing a tree, as the *gemara* explains, is that one may come to break off a branch — a *melachah* on *Shabbos*. Yet once a *gezeirah* is enacted, the rabbis typically do not calibrate it case by case. Rather, a formal definition is established: anything above three *tefachim* is tree; anything below is ground. The practical question, then, is purely technical: what is the status of the descending portion of the root?

### Rava vs. Sheshet

On this question, Rava and Rav Sheshet disagree. Rava rules *muttar lishhtamesh bahen* — one may use those portions of the root that dip back below three *tefachim*, because *kol pachos migimmel de'ara ara hi* — anything below three *tefachim* is treated as the ground itself, regardless of where it came from. Rav Sheshet rules *assur lishhtamesh bahen* — it is forbidden, because *keivan demikoach issur ka'ati* — since that descending portion emerges from what was already classified as tree, it carries the forbidden status with it. *Issur ka'ati assuri.*

The *gemara* then introduces the case of *damu kemashunita* — something resembling a crag — which Rashi explains as a root that protrudes not only upward and downward but also laterally in multiple directions. The analysis proceeds: those portions that go up above three *tefachim* (*desalkin le'eila*) are forbidden; those that descend below three *tefachim* before ever having crossed the threshold (*denachtin letattai*) are permitted. Those that shoot off to the side (*litzdadin*) and then arc downward — this is the *pelugta de-Rava ve-Rav Sheshet*, the same dispute as before. The lateral offshoot emerges from a portion that was above three *tefachim* and thus classified as tree; according to Rav Sheshet, anything proceeding from that forbidden portion retains the forbidden status, even if it ultimately descends below three *tefachim*.

### Furrows & Corners

The *gemara* then proceeds to two analogous cases, which it treats as subject to the same dispute. The first is *anigra* — a tree growing within a furrow. Here the ground level around the tree is at one height, but the tree's base sits in a depression below that level. A person standing on the ordinary ground level might be at a point on the tree that appears to be only one *tefach* above the floor of the furrow. Should one measure from the furrow itself, or from the level at which the person is standing? The *gemara* holds that this falls under the same dispute: the portion of the tree at which the person stands is technically less than three *tefachim* from the furrow floor, but it emerged from a segment of the tree that, from the perspective of the surrounding ground level, stands more than three *tefachim* high. Rav Sheshet would forbid it as *issur ka'ati*; Rava would permit it.

The second case is *b'keren zavit* — a corner. Here the tree grows in a corner formed by two walls. Someone standing atop the walls sees only one face of the tree, the rest being enclosed by the structure on two sides. From the perspective of the person on the wall, it is almost as if the tree begins afresh at that point. And yet the visible portion of the tree above the wall is continuous with what lies below, which from the perspective of the outside is already more than three *tefachim* high. This, too, is the same dispute. The *gemara* acknowledges the conceptual peculiarity that the same segment of tree could simultaneously appear permitted (from above the wall) and forbidden (from below it), depending on where one is standing.

### Abaye's Palm Tree

From these cases the *gemara* moves to a story. There was a palm tree growing in Abaye's house — *dahu dikla dahavi lei b'Abaye* — that grew upward through his skylight. Abaye wished to know whether, standing on the roof on *Shabbos*, he could use the first three *tefachim* of the tree that protruded above the roof level. He came before Rav Yosef.

The situation is similar to the corner case: for someone standing on the roof, the tree seems to emerge fresh from the rooftop. And yet below, inside the house, it was already more than three *tefachim* of tree. Rav Yosef permitted it. Rav Acha bar Tachlifa observed that this ruling follows Rava, who holds that one begins counting afresh when the geometry changes.

The *gemara* objects: *peshita* — is this not obvious? The answer is that one might have thought that even Rav Sheshet would agree here, because of the principle that *beita k'man d'mali dami* — the interior of a house is considered as if completely filled. Since the tree passes through solid space inside the house, perhaps even Rav Sheshet would treat the portion above the roof as entirely new. The *gemara* therefore teaches that one may not use even the three *tefachim* immediately above the roof (*lishhtamesh b'pachot mi'gimmel samuch l'gagga*), and that Rav Sheshet's position applies here as well.

### Mishnah's Case

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishnah* to clarify its precise scenario. The *mishnah* states that roots higher than three *tefachim* may not be sat upon. The *gemara* asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If the roots simply project upward without bending back down, that seems obvious — we know the prohibition against using a tree, and roots more than three *tefachim* off the ground are clearly part of the tree. The *gemara* therefore concludes that the *mishnah* must be speaking of a case where the roots do bend back down, and is coming to support Rav Sheshet's position: even though the roots return below three *tefachim*, they are forbidden.

The *gemara* pushes back: perhaps the *mishnah* always speaks of roots that do not bend back down, and its *chiddush* is different. It teaches *af al gav d'tzido echad shaveh la'aretz* — even if one side of the root is level with the (higher) ground. In other words, even if one is standing on high ground such that from one's vantage point the root appears to be less than three *tefachim* above the surface, and even three sides of the root are exposed and high, the prohibition still applies. Even Rava, who would normally permit use once the geometry suggests the root starts afresh, would agree here: only when a segment is enclosed on two, three, or all four sides does one begin counting anew. When only one side is at a higher ground level and three sides are fully exposed and more than three *tefachim* above the earth, one does not count afresh.

A *baraita* then elaborates: roots that are three *tefachim* above the ground (*shorashai ilan shegvoim min ha'aretz gimmel tefachim*), or under which there is a hollow of three *tefachim* (*shechalal tachteihem gimmel tefachim*) — even if one side is level with the ground — may not be sat upon. The first formulation may refer to a root that is itself physically thick enough to rise three *tefachim*, while the second refers to an arching root with a gap beneath it; in either case the three-*tefachim* threshold determines status.

The *baraita* then restates the broader prohibition: one may not climb a tree (*ein olim be'ilan*), hang from a tree (*ein nitlin be'ilan*), lean on a tree (*ein nish'anin be'ilan*), nor ascend a tree on Friday afternoon and sit there when *Shabbos* begins — for sitting in the tree is itself a prohibited use. Significantly, the prohibition is not limited to the effort involved in climbing; it is about using the tree at all. This is why the *baraita* draws a parallel: just as one may not ride an animal on *Shabbos* (lest one break off a branch to guide it), the same structure applies to trees. But one may scale a wall or climb in and out of a pit of even a hundred *amot*, because there is no specific *gezeirah* about such structures.

The *gemara* then presents two *beraitot* that appear to contradict each other. One states that if one has climbed a tree before *Shabbos*, one may descend once *Shabbos* begins. The other states that one may not descend. The *gemara* resolves this in several ways: the first distinction is between having gone up before nightfall (*mib'od yom*), in which case the initial act was permitted and we show leniency by allowing descent, versus having gone up after nightfall (*misheshachashachah*), in which case the initial act was itself forbidden and we do not permit further activity. An alternative resolution: both cases involve going up after nightfall, but one was done *beshogeg* — unknowingly — and the other *bemeizid* — intentionally. When done unknowingly, we allow descent out of compassion; when intentional, we do not. A third resolution: both cases are *beshogeg*, and the dispute is whether we penalize unintentional violators because of intentional ones — a familiar question of *kansinan shogeig atu meizid*.

At this point Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua notes that this debate mirrors a dispute among *tanna'im* regarding a completely different subject — the mixing of sacrificial bloods — and it is to this comparison that the *gemara* now turns.

---

## Marital Relations (III)

### Active vs. Passive

The *gemara* invokes a well-known dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua concerning the case of sacrificial bloods requiring one application that became mixed with bloods requiring four applications (*matan arba b'matan achat*). If the blood of a *bechor*, which requires a single application, becomes mixed with the blood of an *olah*, which requires application at two opposite corners — effectively four sides — what should be done with the mixture?

Rabbi Eliezer says *yinasnu b'matan arba* — apply four times, to ensure that the blood of the *olah* receives its full treatment. Rabbi Yehoshua says *yinasnu bematana achat* — apply only once, doing the minimum. Rabbi Eliezer charges that doing only one application violates *bal tigra* — the prohibition against diminishing a commandment. Rabbi Yehoshua retorts that doing four violates *bal tosif* — the prohibition against adding to a commandment. Each one then dismisses the other's objection: Rabbi Eliezer argues that *bal tosif* only applies when one is performing the extra application with the blood of the offering that requires only one; Rabbi Yehoshua responds symmetrically, that *bal tigra* only applies when one is diminishing the offering with its own blood, not when the situation is complicated by a mixture.

It is worth pausing on the rarity of *bal tigra* as an operative prohibition. The verse states: *lo tosif alav v'lo sigra mimenu* — do not add and do not diminish. *Bal tosif* requires that one begin with the base of a *mitzvah* and augment it; one cannot violate *bal tosif* by simply performing an act outside the *mitzvah* context. Similarly, *bal tigra* is difficult to transgress in practice, because the moment one performs less than required, one simply has not fulfilled the *mitzvah* at all — one cannot be said to have diminished the *mitzvah* if one never completed it. This case is therefore unusual: because *bedi'eved* one is considered to have fulfilled the obligation with even a single application, there is a biblical substrate of the *mitzvah* against which a deliberate reduction can be measured. That is what makes *bal tigra* operative here.

Rabbi Yehoshua adds a decisive point: *keshenatata avarta al Bal Tosif ve'asita ma'aseh beyadecha* — if you go ahead and apply four times, you have actively committed *bal tosif* with your own hands. Whereas if you apply only once, you may have passively transgressed *bal tigra* by not completing the *olah*'s requirement, but *velo asita ma'aseh beyadecha* — you have not done so through an active deed. Better to transgress passively than to transgress actively.

This is precisely the principle the *gemara* invokes to illuminate the tree debate. Staying in a tree on *Shabbos* is a continuing passive transgression; climbing down stops the long-term violation but involves an active transgressive act in the process of descending. Rabbi Eliezer, who says in the blood case that one should actively apply four times — *kum aseh adif*, the active course is preferable — would correspondingly say here: *yered*, get down from the tree. Rabbi Yehoshua, who says in the blood case that passive omission is preferable to active transgression — *shev v'al ta'aseh adif* — would correspondingly say: *lo yered*, remain in the tree rather than actively violate in the process of descending.

However, the *gemara* immediately qualifies this parallel. Perhaps the comparison does not hold in either direction. When Rabbi Eliezer said the active course is preferable, that was because the active element — applying four times — was itself a *mitzvah* act, fulfilling part of the blood service. Climbing down a tree, by contrast, is not a *mitzvah* act; it is only a means of preventing ongoing transgression. *Aval hacha delo avid mitzvah* — here the active part is not a *mitzvah*, so even Rabbi Eliezer might say *lo yered*. Similarly, when Rabbi Yehoshua said passive omission is preferable, that was because remaining passive meant not actively transgressing *bal tigra* — the passive option truly involved no active wrong. Sitting in a tree, however, is a form of continuous active use of the tree — one's sitting is itself the forbidden act. *Deka avid issura* — even the passive option here involves ongoing transgression. Consequently, perhaps even Rabbi Yehoshua would say *yered* — descend.

The *gemara* thus concludes that the parallel to the blood dispute illuminates the conceptual structure of the tree question without definitively resolving it. The positions on whether to descend correspond to intuitions about whether active or passive transgression is preferable, but the analogy has limits in both directions.

---

## Live & Dead Trees

### Moist vs. Dry

One *baraita* states that the prohibition against using a tree applies equally whether the tree is moist (*lach*) or dry (*yavesh*). A second *baraita* states that the prohibition applies only to a moist tree; a dry tree may be used. The tension between these two positions requires resolution.

### Regrowing Trees

Rav Yehuda resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya* — the cases are not in conflict. *Kan shegezo machalif* — when the prohibition applies to a dry tree, it is because *gezo machalif*, the stump will regrow. A tree that will regenerate is not truly dead, even if it currently appears dried out, and therefore the prohibition remains in force. *Kan she'ein gezo machalif* — when a dry tree is permitted, it is because the tree is genuinely dead and will not regrow.

The *gemara* challenges this resolution: *gezo machalif yavesh karisu lei?* — if the tree will regrow, can you call it *yavesh*? *Yavesh* implies dead. A dormant but living tree would not normally be called dry.

The *gemara* therefore offers an alternative resolution: *lo kashya* — both *beraitot* deal with a genuinely dead tree. The difference is seasonal. *Kan biyemos hachamah kan biyemos hageshamim* — one *baraita* speaks of summer and the other of winter. A dead tree in summer is obviously dead — it is bare while everything around it blooms — and there is no concern that people will mistake it for living and permit themselves to use live trees.
