A dead tree in winter, however, looks no different from any dormant tree; people cannot tell whether it is dead or merely seasonally bare, and so there remains a concern that permitting its use will lead people to use live trees.

The *gemara* then asks: even a dead tree in summer — if one climbs it, fruit will fall. Rashi explains that this does not mean one transgresses *kotzer* — since the tree is dead, nothing is being severed from a growing plant — but the concern is that allowing one to climb a dead tree bearing remnant fruit from the previous season may lead one to climb live fruit-bearing trees. The *gemara* responds: suppose there is no fruit. It then asks: even so, small chips and twigs (*kintzi*) will fall. The *gemara* ultimately limits the permitted case to *geduda* — a tree that has been stripped bare, with no remaining twigs or protrusions, so that nothing can fall or be dislodged.

### Rav's Fence

Yet even this fully stripped dead tree was forbidden in practice by Rav in a specific context. The *gemara* reports: *rav ikla l'aspatya ve'asar begeduda* — Rav arrived in the town of Aspatya and forbade using even a stripped dead tree. The *gemara* explains this with the famous phrase: *rav bika matza vegadar bah gader* — Rav found an open valley and built a fence around it. Technically, using a stripped dead tree was permitted, but Rav observed that the population in that locale was apparently too casual about these distinctions, and he imposed a stricter standard than the letter of the law required, judging that these people needed a firm boundary rather than the nuanced case-by-case analysis that the *gemara* had just constructed.

---

## Grass on Shabbat

### Grass Prohibition

Rav Assi teaches, as quoted by Rabbi bar Abba: *assur l'adam sheyehaleich al gabi asavim b'Shabbos* — it is forbidden to walk on grass on *Shabbos*. The reason: one will inevitably uproot blades of grass, thereby violating *kotzer*. The source offered is the verse *v'atz beraglayim chotei* — one who hastens with the feet is a sinner; by the mere act of walking one can commit a transgression.

### Seasons & Grass

Two *beraitot* again appear to contradict each other: one permits walking on grass, the other forbids it. The first resolution: *ha belachim ha biyaveshim* — moist, growing grass is forbidden (since uprooting it constitutes *kotzer*); dry, dead grass is permitted (since there is nothing growing to uproot). An alternative resolution: both *beraitot* refer to moist grass, and the distinction is again seasonal. *Kan biyemos hachamah kan biyemos hageshamim* — in summer versus winter. Rashi suggests that in summer there are seeds in the grass stalks that become scattered, creating an additional concern; in winter this does not apply, or alternatively the grass in winter is not actually pulled up by walking. Precisely why the season makes the operative difference is not entirely clear from Rashi's formulation.

### Shoes & Details

The *gemara* offers further alternative resolutions, each more granular than the last. Perhaps both cases involve moist grass in summer, and the distinction is whether one wears shoes: *d'siyamei masanei* — shoes with flat soles do not pull up grass as easily as bare feet. Or both cases involve shoes, and the difference is whether the shoes have cleats (*uktzei*): cleated shoes will catch and tear up grass, flat-soled shoes will not. Or both cases involve cleated shoes, and the distinction is whether the grass is long enough to become entangled in the cleats (*sircha*) or short enough that it will not.

### Rabbi Shimon

Having offered all these distinctions, the *gemara* concludes with a sweeping practical ruling: *ve'idna d'kaima lan k'Rabbi Shimon d'davar she'eino mitkavein mutar* — in contemporary practice we rule like Rabbi Shimon that an unintentional act (*davar she'eino mitkavein*) is permitted, provided it is not a *psik reisha* — an inevitable consequence. Walking on grass, even moist summer grass with cleated shoes, does not inevitably uproot every blade underfoot; it is not a *psik reisha*, and since one does not intend to uproot, it is therefore entirely permitted under Rabbi Shimon's ruling.

One might ask: if so, why is leaning on a tree still forbidden, given that one does not intend to break off a branch? The answer is that leaning on a tree is an *issur derabbanan* — a rabbinic prohibition enacted as a *gezeirah* against coming to use a tree deliberately. That prohibition does not turn on the *davar she'eino mitkavein* analysis; the rabbis forbade the act categorically lest one proceed to intentional violation, quite apart from what one's actual intention in the moment happens to be.

---

## Marital Relations (III)

### Forcing Wife

The *gemara* now takes up the verse *v'atz beraglayim chotei* — one who hastens with the feet is a sinner — in a very different context. Rami bar Chama teaches in the name of Rav Assi: *assur l'adam sheyakof ishto l'dvar mitzvah* — a man may not compel his wife to have sexual relations. *Dvar mitzvah* here refers to the conjugal obligation. The source is the same verse: *v'atz beraglayim chotei*, where *raglayim* is understood as a reference to the sexual domain — hastening toward the wife before she is ready constitutes a sin.

It is worth pausing to note the historical context. Marital coercion was not legally recognized as a wrong in most Western legal systems until roughly the last fifty years. The *gemara*'s framing, while genuine in its moral concern, positions the prohibition primarily as a question of proper conduct rather than as a formal crime — the topic appears in Rambam under *Hilchot De'ot* rather than in the laws of prohibited acts. This framing is itself neither entirely progressive nor entirely traditional by contemporary standards; it reflects the complex position of the *gemara* on this question, which is frankly mixed. On one side, the *gemara* clearly says one may not force one's wife. On the other, a wife who refuses conjugal relations may lose her *ketubah*, and the asymmetry is never resolved. The dual nature of the situation should not be smoothed over.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds: *kol hakofer ishto l'dvar mitzvah havayan lo banim she'einam mehuganim* — whoever forces his wife to have sex will have children who are not fitting, not well-formed in character. This formulation situates the prohibition squarely within the *gemara*'s broader concern that the moral conditions surrounding conception influence the nature of the children conceived. The precise scope of the term *yakof* is not fixed by the *gemara*; whether it covers only physical compulsion or also subtler forms of psychological pressure is left open.

Rav Ika bar Chanina locates the proof text in the rest of the same verse: *gam belo daat nefesh lo tov* — also without knowledge the soul is not good. When the act of relations occurs without the wife's *daat* — not mere awareness, but genuine assent and acquiescence — the souls that result will not be good. A *baraita* confirms this: *ze hakofeh et ishto ledvar mitzvah* — this refers to one who compels his wife.

### Woman Demands Sex

The *baraita* continues: *va-atz beraglayim chotei — ze haboel veshoneh* — one who hastens is also the man who has relations and then, after completing the act, immediately has relations a second time. The assumption is that after the first act the wife is satisfied and no longer interested, and therefore pressing for a second act resembles the same form of imposition. The *gemara* challenges this from Rava's ruling: *harotzeh laasot kol banav zecharim yivol veyishneh* — one who wishes all his children to be male should have relations and then have relations a second time. How can the second act be simultaneously condemned and recommended?

The *gemara* resolves: *lo kashya — kan ledaat kan shelo ledaat* — the two rulings speak to different situations. The second act is condemned when the wife is no longer interested and the husband persists anyway; it is commended when the wife in fact desires to continue. Rashi illuminates the physiological reasoning embedded in the ruling: the first act of relations arouses the wife, who may not have been fully aroused at the outset, and it is at this point that she desires the second encounter. When a second act occurs with her full desire — *bishaat ta-avah* — she gives forth seed first (*hi mazra-at techilah*), which the *gemara* elsewhere associates with the conception of male children.

### Second Intercourse

This leads to a broader observation. The rabbinic teaching that a male child results when the woman achieves arousal and seed before the man is a principle that, whether or not one accepts its medical premises, creates a practical imperative for the husband to attend to his wife's arousal. A man who proceeds entirely according to his own timeline risks not satisfying the conditions for the outcome the tradition prizes. Whether the *gemara* consciously intended this as an endorsement of the wife's pleasure or arrived at it incidentally through a different set of concerns, the practical effect is to orient marital intimacy toward the wife's experience in a way that is quite striking in its context.

Rashi's reading makes explicit what the *gemara* implies: after the first act, *shemachamat biah rishonah nitavah ha-ishah*, it is the first act that awakens the woman's desire, and it is at this point that the second act, if she wants it, fulfills the conditions for male offspring. This framing, Rivka notes, carries a sharp inverse risk: if a daughter is born, the logic of the teaching implies that the mother desired relations and the father held back, which can produce a deeply harmful stigma attached to the birth of a daughter. The *gemara*'s teaching does not resolve this tension.

---

## Eve's Curses

### Seven Curses

The teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — that a woman who initiates and demands sex produces exceptional children — seems to be in tension with what follows. The *gemara* introduces a counterpoint: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi teaches that Chava received ten curses at the time of the sin in the garden, derived from the verse *el ha'ishah amar* — to the woman He said. The curses are enumerated as follows.

*Harbeh arbeh* — I will greatly increase — is taken as a doubled expression, indicating two separate curses: *dam niddah*, the blood of menstruation, and *dam besulim*, the blood of the hymen. These are two forms of bleeding associated specifically with the female body. *Itzvonech* — your anguish — refers to *tza'ar gidul banim*, the anguish of raising children. *V'heronech* — your pregnancy — refers to *tza'ar ha'ibur*, the suffering of pregnancy itself. *Be'etzev teldi vanim* — in pain shall you give birth to children — is taken *k'mashma'o*, at face value, as the pain of childbirth. That accounts for five.

*V'el ishech teshukasech* — to your husband shall be your longing — teaches that a woman longs for her husband precisely *b'sha'ah shehu yotzei laderech*, when he goes away on a journey. The curse is not that she desires him in his presence, but that she feels his absence acutely when he is gone and she cannot fulfill that longing. *V'hu yimshol bach* — and he shall have dominion over you — teaches that *ha'ishah tova'as balev v'ha'ish tove'a bapeh*: when a woman wants to have relations, she keeps that desire within her heart and cannot bring herself to express it openly, while the man is able to voice his desire without inhibition. He controls the verbal expression of their sexual dynamic. These seven constitute the initial enumeration.

### Three More Curses

When Rav Dimi arrived from the Land of Israel, he added three further curses. *Atufah ke-avel* — she wraps herself like a mourner — refers to a woman covering her hair, as if in a state of *avel*, mourning. It is striking that the *gemara* here frames the requirement of hair-covering explicitly as a curse, not as an expression of modesty or sanctity. *Umenudah mikol adam* — she is set apart from all people — means that she is forbidden to two men simultaneously: she can be married to only one husband, while he may take multiple wives. This asymmetry in the exclusivity of marriage is identified as a curse. *Vachavushah be-veit ha-assurim* — she is imprisoned — refers to *kol kevudah bat melech pnimah*, the woman's place being inside the home, away from the public sphere.

Notably, the language the *gemara* uses for these conditions is the language of curse, confinement, and mourning — not the language of virtue or ideal. With a single exception to be addressed shortly, the *gemara* does not present these conditions as praiseworthy; it presents them as aspects of an existence marked by loss and constraint.

---

## Marital Relations (III)…

### Woman's Modesty

This creates a tension with the earlier teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who praised the woman who demands sex from her husband. How can that be a virtue if *v'hu yimshol bach* — the curse that she cannot openly demand sex — is itself being enumerated as a bad thing? And how can the *gemara* add *zo hi middah tovah banashim* — this is a good character trait in women — regarding the woman who does not verbally express her sexual desire?

The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between verbal demand and active initiation through signal and persuasion. *Ki ka'amrinan d'mirtzia artzuyei kameih* — what we mean when we say a woman initiates or makes her desires known is that she communicates through gestures, approach, and non-verbal cues, not through explicit verbal command. A woman may do everything up to the point of explicit verbal insistence, and that is not only permissible but praiseworthy. What is considered immodest is the stark verbal demand — in the manner, one might say, of Leah, who said *elai tavo*, you will come to me, as a flat declaration. At least one *posek* reads Leah's statement as nonetheless still within the bounds of permissibility, since it could be read as descriptive rather than commanding; on this reading, the line is crossed only by something even more openly imperative than Leah's words.

The tension between the two approaches — one holding that female initiative produces extraordinary children, the other holding that restraint in verbal expression is a praiseworthy trait — is real and is not fully dissolved by the *gemara*'s reconciliation. It reflects two genuinely different orientations toward female agency in the sexual domain. In practical *halacha*, the question of where exactly the line falls has significant consequences. Women who are taught that they may never initiate sometimes develop real difficulties in the marriage, and it is important to understand that there are two serious approaches in the *gemara*, with the line between them being far less clear than either side sometimes acknowledges.

---

## Eve's Curses (II)

### Blessings Not Curses

A *baraita* teaches that the three curses added by Rav Dimi are not the right candidates for the additional three; other elements should replace them, and moreover those elements are in fact not curses at all but positive attributes. *Hani shvach haviyan* — those are actually praiseworthy things. Rabbi Chiyya teaches, drawing on the verse *malefenu mi-behemot aretz, ume'of hashamayim yachakmenu* — the earth's animals teach us, and the birds of the sky make us wise — that we learn proper conduct by observing animals.

### Animal Lessons

The things attributed in this alternative *baraita* to women — growing long hair, urinating in a seated position, and lying beneath her husband during relations — are each aligned with animal behavior and reinterpreted as dignified or modest. *Malefenu mi-behemot aretz — zu predah*, a donkey crouches when urinating. For a woman to urinate in this fashion is therefore more modest: the genitals are less exposed and the act is less visible. *Ume'of hashamayim yachakmenu — ze tarnigol*, this is the rooster, *she-mifayes achar boel*, who appeases his mate and then has relations. The rooster's courtship behavior, approached with tenderness and prior attention to the hen's disposition, is held up as a model.

Rabbi Yochanan adds the famous teaching: *ilmalei lo nitnah Torah, hayinu lemadim tzniut me-chatul* — had the Torah not been given, we would have learned modesty from the cat, *gezel mi-nemalah* — the prohibition of theft from the ant who toils in summer and stores for winter, *arayot mi-yonah* — the prohibition of forbidden sexual relations from the dove, who mates faithfully with only one partner, *ve-derech eretz mi-tarnigol* — and proper conduct in relations from the rooster, *she-mifayes ve'achar kach boel*, who first appeases and only then mates.

### Rooster Courtship

The *gemara* then gives a richly symbolic account of what exactly the rooster communicates through his courtship display. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: the rooster flaps his wings around the hen, and this is his way of saying, *zavinna lach ziga dematu lach ad karayich* — I will buy you a garment that will reach to your feet. After relations, he hangs his head as if ashamed, and this gesture means: *lishmatay seya lekarbala*, let my comb be removed — that is, if I have the money and did not buy you that garment, I deserve to be disgraced. And then he adds the poignant qualification: *i is li velo zavinna lach* — if I had it I would certainly have bought it for you; he acknowledges that he has made a promise he cannot quite keep, but at least he tried.

This aggadic passage closes the daf on a note that ties together several threads. The concern throughout — about forcing one's wife, about the second act of relations, about who initiates, about the curses and conditions of women's lives — finds a kind of culmination in the image of the rooster who appeases before acting. And crucially, the *gemara* throughout this section, particularly in the enumeration of Chava's curses, does something that is far from obvious: it surfaces these inequities, names them openly, and labels them as curses — as departures from an ideal, not as ideal conditions themselves. The one exception, that a woman's not verbally demanding sex is a *middah tovah*, is carefully carved out, and even that exception is immediately qualified. The overall posture of the *gemara* here, for all its complexity and internal tension, is one of acknowledging that the conditions of women's lives represent a diminishment — something to be recognized and, perhaps, worked against, not celebrated.

---

---

# Eiruvin 101

## Doors & Structures

### Hadeles shebe-muktza

The *mishna* at the top of daf 101 opens with the case of *hadeles shebe-muktza* — a door in a *muktza*, meaning not a door that renders objects *muktzeh*, but rather a door that opens into a back alley, an underused and largely neglected entrance to a building. At first glance this seems a surprising turn for *Masechet Eruvin*, since we appear to have left behind the domain-related questions of *eruvin* and carrying, finding ourselves instead in what looks like a random collection of *hilchos Shabbos* — not unlike the final chapter of *Masechet Shabbos*, to which there are striking parallels. Just as that tractate concluded with the *pkak hachalon*, the temporary window-stopper, this chapter addresses temporary door-like structures and the degree to which closing or opening them constitutes *boneh*, the prohibited act of construction.

The *mishna* presents several cases: *hadeles shebe-muktza*, the back-alley door; *chadakim shebepirtza*, bundles of thorns or sticks used to fill a breach in a wall; and *machatzalos*, mats similarly used to plug a hole. The principle governing all these cases is: *ein no'elin bahen* — one may not use them to close on *Shabbos* — *ella im kein gevohin min ha'aretz*, unless they are elevated off the ground. If such an object is dragging along the ground, it looks less like operating a door and more like adding a new component to the wall — an act that resembles *boneh*.

### Rashi on Back Doors

*Rashi* explains in the third line of his commentary that because this is a back door to a back alley, the homeowner does not bother to fashion a proper, hinged door for it. Rather, as *Rashi* puts it: *ein baal habayis choshesh laasos lo deles teluya kera'uy ukevua ella kefefa keneged hapessach* — the owner simply props a large plank against the opening. Such an object resembles more a construction addition to a wall than the operation of a genuine door, which is why the *mishna* demands it be elevated off the ground.

### Dragging Doors

The *gemara* opens with a challenge: *remini* — there is a contradiction. A *braita* discusses *deles hanigreret*, a dragging door; *machatzeles hanigreret*, a dragging mat; and *kankan hanigrar*, a dragging implement used to fill a hole. In each case, the *braita* states that *bizman shekshurim utluyim* — when they are tied and suspended — *no'elin bahen bein be-Shabbat bein be-Yom Tov*, one may close with them on both *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*.

The apparent contradiction with the *mishna* is this: the *braita* requires only that the item be tied and suspended, without explicitly demanding it be elevated off the ground. The *mishna*, by contrast, demands *gevohin min ha'aretz*. One can imagine an object tied by a rope to the doorframe but still lying flat on the ground — connected, like the pens chained to a bank counter, but not in any meaningful sense suspended. That distinction is not the same as *lavud*, which concerns physical proximity creating structural continuity; it is rather a question of whether the object appears genuinely integrated into the door or merely appended to the wall.

### Abaye's Hinge Rule

*Abaye* resolves the contradiction: *be-she-yesh lahem tzir* — the *braita*'s leniency applies when the door has an actual hinge. The presence of a *tzir* visually and functionally signals that the object is a genuine part of the building's door structure, removing the concern that one appears to be adding to the wall. As *Rashi* notes, *ve-lo mechezi ke-boneh* — it no longer looks like construction. This incidentally suggests that the prohibition in question is rabbinic in character, since the entire concern turns on visual appearance. Once there is a hinge, the additional requirement of being off the ground falls away; without a hinge, both conditions — tied and suspended, *and* elevated — are required.

### Rava on Former Hinges

*Rava* goes further: *be-she-hayah lahem tzir* — it suffices that there *was* once a hinge, even if the door has since fallen off its hinge and the hinge structure alone remains. So long as the remnant of the former hinge is visible, people understand that this object is conceptually a replacement door rather than a novel construction. In such a case, *Rava* holds that elevation off the ground is likewise unnecessary.

### Braita Contradiction

The *gemara* then raises *meitivi* — a further challenge from a *braita* that appears to combine all three criteria: *bizman she-kshurim u-tluyim u-gevohim min ha-aretz* — tied, suspended, *and* elevated off the ground, even if only *afilu melo nima*, a hair's breadth — *no'elin bahen*; if not, one may not. This seems to require all three conditions simultaneously, directly contradicting the positions of both *Abaye* and *Rava*.

The *gemara* resolves this by noting that *Abaye metaretz le-ta'ameh ve-Rava metaretz le-ta'ameh* — each authority reconciles the *braita* according to his own reasoning. According to *Abaye*: *o she-yesh lahem tzir o she-gevohim min ha-aretz* — either there is a hinge, or it is elevated. According to *Rava*: *o she-hayah lahem tzir o she-gevohim min ha-aretz* — either there formerly was a hinge, or it is elevated. The *braita*'s triple requirement thus applies only to the case where the item lacks any hinge, past or present.

A subsequent *braita* — *tanu rabbanan* — discusses *sochei kotzim ve-chavilin*, bundles of thorns or wood set aside to fill a breach in a courtyard wall. When these are *kshurim u-tluyim*, tied and suspended, one may close with them on *Shabbos*, and *ve-ein tzarich lomar be-Yom Tov*, needless to say on *Yom Tov*. This case presumably involves a *tzir* as well, which is why it does not separately invoke the requirement of elevation.

### Widowed Door

*Rabbi Chiyya* taught: *delet almanah ha-nigeret* — a widowed door that drags — *ein no'elin bah*, one may not close with it. The question is: what qualifies a door as "widowed"? Given that this ruling introduces an additional disqualification beyond dragging, the door is presumably otherwise compliant — it is tied, suspended, and perhaps even has a *tzir* — yet something about its "widowed" character renders it deficient.

The *gemara* offers two explanations. *Ika de-amri de-chad sheifa*: some say it means the door consists of a single plank of wood. Even if tied and suspended, a bare plank looks more like a construction material being installed than a fashioned door being operated. *Ika de-amri d'leit lei gashma*: others say it lacks a *gashma* — some structural feature. *Rashi* suggests this may refer to a bar or handle, though that reading fits awkwardly with the cases of thorn bundles and mats. A more compelling interpretation is that the door lacks a proper threshold or frame recess below, missing the structural element that would anchor it and mark it as a genuine door rather than a makeshift partition. In all interpretations, the "widowhood" of the door signals an absence — something once integral to its door-nature is missing — even if the object otherwise meets the other criteria.

---

## Binyan Hierarchy

### Fire Piles

*Rav Yehuda* teaches: *hai medurta* — a fire pile — *mimalla l'mata shari*, from top down is permitted; *mimatta l'mala assur*, from bottom up is forbidden. This teaching, connected to our *mishna*'s discussion of construction-like acts, launches a remarkable sequence of cases in which actions one would never expect to be problematic on *Yom Tov* turn out to carry a prohibition because they resemble *boneh*.

The principle at stake is *derech binyan* — the manner of building. When one stacks wood for a fire in the classic fashion, progressively building walls upward from the ground in a crisscross structure, that assembly-from-the-bottom constitutes *boneh* and is forbidden. The permitted alternative is to begin from the top and build downward — placing upper elements first and inserting lower ones beneath, rather than stacking upward. This is the general rule that will govern all subsequent cases: construction *derech binyan*, from the ground up, is prohibited; inverting that sequence removes the prohibition.

### Eggs & Grills

Similarly, *vchein beiza* — and so too with eggs. *Rashi* explains the case not as stacking eggs atop one another but as positioning eggs on a fire: one wishes to place eggs over a crisscross of twigs. The prescribed method is to hold the egg and construct the crisscross of twigs beneath it, rather than building the twig structure first and setting the egg on top. The structural act — creating the supportive framework — must follow, not precede, the placement of the item being supported.

### Pots & Beds

*Vchein kedira* — and similarly a pot. On *Yom Tov*, when one places a pot over a fire, the typical method employs two barrels as side walls with the pot resting in the hollow between them. The correct procedure is to hold the pot in position and bring the barrels to either side of it, rather than first setting up the barrels and then lowering the pot between them. Likewise, *vchein purya* — a collapsible bed: one must hold the mattress and place the frame structure beneath it, not first assemble the frame and then lay the mattress on top. And *vechen chavita* — barrels: placing two barrels on the ground and then a third atop them in a pyramidal arrangement constitutes building a structure from the ground up and is forbidden by the same logic.

### Tosafot Qualifications

One might ask — taken at face value, does this prohibition mean that any act of placing objects in a bottom-up sequence is forbidden on *Shabbos* or *Yom Tov*? Could one not pile books on a table, or arrange produce in a basket? *Tosafot* here provides essential qualifications that give the rule workable limits.

*Tosafot* begins by questioning *Rashi*'s interpretation of the egg case. To place an egg on an existing griddle — a prefabricated structure — does not constitute *boneh* at all, since one is not building walls but merely placing an object on a pre-existing implement: *ein derech binyan bekach*. The critical element, *Tosafot* argues, is not simply that items are placed bottom-up, but that one is building the walls themselves from the ground up: *lo damu lemchitzot upuraya demesader zu etzel zu*. This is the first criterion: the prohibition applies when one is constructing the enclosing walls of a structure in sequence, not merely placing objects in a stacked arrangement.

*Tosafot* further notes that it is universally accepted as straightforwardly permitted to place a pot on a tripod, and uses this as a springboard for his broader interpretation of the egg case: the forbidden act involves building up the enclosing walls *and* positioning an item within them. This leads to his second criterion: the prohibition applies when one intends to *use the space created beneath*, such as for a fire. When the space between the walls is functional — trapping heat, providing ventilation, serving the fire — the assembly has the character of constructing a functional enclosure. If one is merely piling objects with no intention of using the space between them, the resemblance to *boneh* dissipates.

*Tosafot* offers an additional, independent ground for leniency: *aval im machmirim machamat taut* — *ee nami lo damu lebinyan ela keshe'oseh al gabei karka velo al hashulchan* — the prohibition applies only when building on the ground, not when piling objects on a table. Piling books on a table, therefore, raises no concern, since it lacks the quality of ground-level construction that defines *binyan*.

### Piling Objects

The question of whether piling objects generally — including books arranged on a table — constitutes a forbidden act is thus squarely addressed by *Tosafot*'s qualifications: such acts are unproblematic because they lack both the wall-building character and the creation of an intentionally used enclosed space, and because they occur on a table rather than on the ground.

### Sadducee Debate

The section concludes with an interchange between a certain *Tzadoki* — likely a *min*, a sectarian or early Jewish-Christian — and *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya*. The *Tzadoki* cites a verse: *tovam kechedek* — "their best are like thorns" — as a contemptuous description of the Jewish people, connecting *chedek* to the *chadakim* (thorns) mentioned in our *mishna*. *Rabbi Yehoshua* replied: *tipsha* — you have not read the end of the *pasuk*. The verse continues *yashar mi-mesukah* — "the most upright is more straight than a hedge." Just as *chadakim* — thorn bundles — protect a breach in a wall, so too the best among Israel protect their people, as a *sukkah* provides shelter. A further interpretation: *tovam kechedek she-machadikin et ha-resha'im l'Gehennom* — the righteous of Israel will ultimately trample the wicked, as expressed in the verse *kumi v'dushi bat Tziyon* — "Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion," with the promise of iron horns and copper hooves to trample the nations. The connection to our *mishna* is thus not merely textual wordplay but a pointed halakhic and polemical exchange rooted in the specific terminology of the chapter.

---

## Cross-Domain Issues

### Rabbi Meir's Rule

The next *mishna* returns to domain-related concerns: *lo yaamod adam bi-reshut ha-yachid veyiftach bi-reshut ha-rabim* — a person may not stand in the private domain and use a key to open a door into the public domain, nor vice versa. The underlying issue is *Rabbi Meir*'s well-known position, encountered in previous discussions, that one may not stand in one domain and manipulate objects in another. Here is a concrete expression of that ruling: if one's front porch is enclosed and constitutes a *reshut ha-yachid*, and the key lies there, one may not lean in from the *reshut ha-rabim* to retrieve it and open the lock. The solution the *mishna* provides is to have a wall of ten *tefachim* — *ella im kein asa mechitzah gevohah asara tefachim* — so that one is standing within a *reshut ha-yachid* and the entire operation occurs within a single domain.

### Patamin Marketplace

The sages challenge *Rabbi Meir* with a precedent: *maaseh be-shuk shel patamin she-hayu b'Yerushalayim* — there was an established practice in the marketplace of the fat-sellers (*patamin* — dealers in fattened fowl or other goods) in Jerusalem, where the shopkeepers would lock up and leave the key in the window above the doorway, retrieving it on *Shabbos* to open their shops. *Rabbi Yose* adds a point of precision: it was in fact a wool marketplace, not a poultry market — but the principle is the same. Presumably these keepers were standing in what appeared to be a *reshut ha-rabim* while manipulating an object in the *reshut ha-yachid* zone of the lock and windowsill — a direct challenge to *Rabbi Meir*'s position.

### Jerusalem Status

The *gemara* responds that *Rabbi Meir* can deflect this evidence: *rabbanan amru Rabbi Meir reshut ha-rabim, u-mahadar inhu karmelis?* The sages are citing a *karmelis* in response to a ruling about a biblical *reshut ha-rabim*. Even the marketplaces of Jerusalem were at most a *karmelis*, not a true *reshut ha-rabim*, because Jerusalem was surrounded by walls with gates locked at night.

The basis for this is the statement of *Rabba bar bar Chana* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *Yerushalayim ilmalei daltoteha nin'alot balailah chayavin aleha mishum reshut ha-rabim* — Jerusalem would otherwise be a *reshut ha-rabim*, but since its gates were locked at night, it was not. This implies that at the time the gates were intact and locked, the marketplaces were at most a *karmelis*; and so the precedent cited by the sages does not address *Rabbi Meir*'s concern about a true *reshut ha-rabim*.

*Rav Pappa* refines this further: *kan kodem she-nifretzu bo pratzot, kan l'achar she-nifretzu bo pratzot* — the distinction turns on whether Jerusalem's walls had yet been breached. Before the breaches — that is, in the period of the intact walls before the *churban* — the marketplaces were a *karmelis*. After the walls were breached by the enemy, the walls ceased to function as genuine enclosures, and the marketplaces reverted to the status of a true *reshut ha-rabim*. The *mishna*'s ruling thus pertains to the post-*churban* reality in which *Rabbi Meir* could indeed encounter real *reshut ha-rabim* conditions in what had been Jerusalem's markets.

*Rava* then draws out an additional implication: *seifa asya l'sharei gina* — the *mishna*'s closing clause actually extends *Rabbi Meir*'s ruling to a *karmelis*. The fuller reading of the *mishna* is: *lo yaamod adam bi-reshut ha-yachid veyiftach b'karmelis, b'karmelis veyiftach bi-reshut ha-yachid* — one may not stand in a *karmelis* and open into a *reshut ha-yachid*, or vice versa — unless one has erected a wall of ten *tefachim*, placing oneself entirely within a *reshut ha-yachid*. This is the evidence the sages are bringing from the Jerusalem marketplace — since that marketplace was a *karmelis*, they demonstrate that *Rabbi Meir* prohibits even standing in a *karmelis* and manipulating into a *reshut ha-yachid*.

### Garden Gates

The *gemara* then presents a *braita* about *pitchai shaarei gina* — the gates of a garden, which are typically a *karmelis* scenario. The governing rule is: *bizman sheyesh lahem beis shaar mipifnim* — when there is a gatehouse on the inside, one opens and closes from the inside; when on the outside, from the outside; and when gatehouses exist on both sides, one may operate from either direction. The reason in all these cases is that the gatehouse — itself a *reshut ha-yachid* — allows the person to be physically located within a *reshut ha-yachid* when performing the operation, so that everything occurs within a single domain.

*Ein lahem lo kan v'lo kan asurin* — if there is no gatehouse on either side, the operation is forbidden in both directions. *Rashi* explains: the lock mechanism on the door is itself a *reshut ha-yachid*, and the key placed upon it is therefore located in a *reshut ha-yachid*. What *Rabbi Meir* prohibits is standing in a *karmelis* — even a garden, not even a *reshut ha-rabim* — and taking a key from the *reshut ha-yachid* lock and operating it. Even though the key moves from *reshut ha-yachid* to *reshut ha-yachid* (lock to keyhole), *Rabbi Meir* is concerned that the person standing in the *karmelis* is engaged in manipulating objects across domains. In the absence of a gatehouse, the person unavoidably stands in the *karmelis*, and that is forbidden according to *Rabbi Meir*.

### Store Locks

A parallel case follows: *ve-chen chanuyos ha-petuchos li-reshut ha-rabim* — stores that open onto a *reshut ha-rabim*, where the lock mechanism is a contraption attached to or recessed into the door. The *braita* distinguishes based on the height of the lock mechanism:

*Bizman she-hamanul lemata me-asara* — when the lock is below ten *tefachim* in height, it is not a *reshut ha-yachid*. In this case one may bring the key from *erev Shabbos* and leave it on the *iskopa* — the porch or threshold — which is a *karmelis*. The next day one opens the lock and returns the key to the *iskopa*, all within the *karmelis* zone. This is permissible even according to *Rabbi Meir*.

*Bizman she-hamanul lemala me-asara* — when the lock is above ten *tefachim* and thus a *reshut ha-yachid*, *Rabbi Meir* says: bring the key from *erev Shabbos* and place it *in the lock itself*. The next day open and re-lock and return it to its place. This is counterintuitive at first — *Rabbi Meir* who objects so strenuously to cross-domain manipulation now appears to allow standing in a *karmelis* and using a key planted in a *reshut ha-yachid* lock. The *gemara* will need to address this.

*Ve-Chachamim omrim* — the sages say that even when the lock is above ten *tefachim*, one may bring the key from *erev Shabbos* and leave it on the *iskopa* (a *karmelis*), and the next day open and either return it to the *iskopa* or place it in the window above the doorway — *o be-chalon she-al gabei ha-petach* — provided the window is less than four by four *tefachim*. If the window is four by four, it is *assur*, because it constitutes a *reshut ha-yachid*, and taking the key from the *karmelis* into the window would be taking from a *karmelis* to a *reshut ha-yachid*.

*Rashi* notes that store lock mechanisms, unlike house gates, vary in height — sometimes low, sometimes high — which is precisely what makes them a useful vehicle for illustrating the full range of this ruling.

### Abaye's Lock Solution

The *gemara* presses the difficulty: if the *iskopa* is a *karmelis*, and if the lock mechanism — even when above ten *tefachim* — could theoretically be a *reshut ha-yachid*, how can the sages permit taking the key from the *iskopa* and inserting it into the lock? That would be *kamitaltel mi-karmelis li-reshut ha-yachid* — taking an object from a *karmelis* to a *reshut ha-yachid*, which is rabbinically prohibited.

*Abaye* resolves this: *le'olam d'leit bei arba'ah* — in fact the lock mechanism does not have the full four-by-four dimensions required for a *reshut ha-yachid*. However, *yesh bo lachok u-lehashlimo l'arba'ah* — it is the kind of recess in the wall that could in principle be carved out to reach the four-by-four threshold. This is a familiar *gemara* consideration: does theoretical capacity for four-by-four dimensions confer *reshut ha-yachid* status?

*B'ha pligi* — this is the precise point of dispute: *Rabbi Meir savar chokekim lehashlim* — *Rabbi Meir* holds that we treat a space that can be enlarged to four-by-four *as if* it already were, giving it *reshut ha-yachid* status. *Rabbanan savri ein chokekim lehashlim* — the sages hold that we do not apply this principle, and since the recess does not presently measure four by four, it is not a *reshut ha-yachid*, and the entire operation remains within a *karmelis* or *makom patur* zone, free of any transfer prohibition.

This analysis also resolves the apparent reversal in *Rabbi Meir*'s position. He does not in fact permit a *karmelis*-to-*reshut ha-yachid* manipulation in the case of the high lock; rather, he treats the lock as a *reshut ha-yachid* and requires that the key be placed there from *erev Shabbos*, so that the operation on *Shabbos* takes place entirely within the *reshut ha-yachid*. The sages, not treating the lock as a *reshut ha-yachid*, permit leaving the key on the *karmelis* and operating from there.

### Window Restrictions

The final clause of the *braita* concerns the window above the doorway. After opening the store, one may return the key either to the *iskopa* or to the window — but only if the window is less than four by four *tefachim*. If the window is four by four, placing the key there is *assur* — *mipnei she-hu ke-motzi me-reshut li-reshut* — because it would constitute carrying from the *karmelis* to the *reshut ha-yachid*.

The principle at work here is that even passing through a *makom patur* does not sanitize a transfer between two incompatible domains. So while one may move an object from the *karmelis* to the *makom patur* lock, and separately from the *makom patur* lock to the *karmelis* or to another *makom patur* window, one may not use the *makom patur* as a relay station to move an object from the *karmelis* to a *reshut ha-yachid* window.

### Rav Dimi Teaching

*Rabbi Bibi bar Abba* notes that three distinct conclusions (*shma mina telat*) emerge from this *braita*. First, *chokekim lehashlim* — we accept this principle as operative, at least according to *Rabbi Meir*. Second, *Rabbi Meir* has reversed himself from his earlier ruling about garden gates: here he permits standing in a *karmelis* and operating a key in a *reshut ha-yachid*, which is consistent only if one understands that *Rabbi Meir* restricts his prohibition to a true *reshut ha-rabim*, not a *karmelis*. Third, we accept the teaching of *Rav Dimi*.

*De-ki asa Rav Dimi amar Rabbi Yochanan*: when *Rav Dimi* came from *Eretz Yisrael* he reported that *Rabbi Yochanan* taught — *makom she-ein bo arba al arba, mutar li-bnei reshut ha-rabim u-li-bnei reshut ha-yachid le-katef alav* — a space that is less than four by four *tefachim* is a *makom patur* and may be used by people of either the *reshut ha-rabim* or the *reshut ha-yachid* — *u-bilvad she-lo yachlifu* — provided they do not use it as an exchange point between the two. One may not take something from the *karmelis*, set it down on the *makom patur*, and then take it into the *reshut ha-yachid*; that chain of transit violates the prohibition even though each individual step is technically permissible. This is confirmed by the *braita*'s ruling that returning the key to a window that is four by four is forbidden: moving from *karmelis* to *makom patur* to *reshut ha-yachid* is a prohibited sequence, even via the intermediate exempt space.

---

## Nagar & Glustra

### Rabbi Eliezer's Rule

The final *mishna* of the daf introduces the case of a *nagar she-yesh be-rosho glustra* — a locking bar with a bulbous head. The scenario is familiar in structure to the suspended-door cases that opened the daf: one wishes to use this bar to bolt the door on *Shabbos*, but the question is whether inserting it constitutes *boneh*. The bar hangs from the door, and in this regard it parallels the discussion of *neger ha-talui* from earlier in the tractate. The additional element here is the *glustra* — the bulbous protuberance at the head of the bar, which resembles a pestle and theoretically qualifies the bar as a *kli*, a vessel in its own right (something one could, for instance, use to pound spices).

*Rabbi Eliezer oser* — *Rabbi Eliezer* forbids using it unless it is *kashur ve-talui* — tied to the door and suspended — which, as established in the opening section of the daf, is what integrates the object into the door structure and removes the appearance of *boneh*.

### Rabbi Yose Lenient

*Rabbi Yose matir* — *Rabbi Yose* permits it even without being tied and suspended. His reasoning: since the bar has a *glustra* and thus the character of a *kli*, using it to bolt the door is clearly an ad-hoc, temporary act — as if one took a spoon and lodged it in the door brackets as a makeshift bolt. No one considers this the installation of a structural component; the object's vessel-nature makes its temporary use self-evident. According to *Rabbi Yose*, the *kli* character of the bar eliminates the concern that one is doing anything resembling *boneh*.

### Tiberias Synagogue

*Rabbi Eliezer* then cites a historical precedent: *maaseh bi-chneset she-be-Tverya* — a story from the synagogue in Tiberias. The community there had maintained a practice of permitting this bar (*she-hayu noghim bo heter*), until *Rabban Gamliel* and the elders came and declared it forbidden. This is *Rabbi Eliezer*'s evidence that the permissive practice was ultimately overturned by rabbinic authority.

*Rabbi Yose* disputes the facts: *issur nahagu bo* — they had actually been treating it as forbidden, and *Rabban Gamliel* and the elders came and declared it permitted. The same event, the same synagogue, but the opposite narrative. Both authorities invoke Tiberias; each claims that the final ruling of *Rabban Gamliel* and the elders supports his own position.

### Rope Lifting Test

The *gemara* resolves the dispute by introducing a functional criterion. *Bi-nittol be-agdo kulei alma lo pligi* — if the bar can be lifted by its rope (i.e., the rope is strong enough to bear it and raise it), all agree it is permitted, since it is clearly and functionally integrated into the door structure. *Ki pligi be-she-eino* — the dispute concerns the case where the rope cannot bear the bar's weight and would break if used to lift it.

In that case: *mar savar keivan de-ika berosha glustra torat kli aleiha* — one authority holds that since it has a *glustra* and the character of a *kli*, it retains its vessel-identity and its use is clearly temporary and non-constructive. *U-mar savar keivan de-la nital be-agdo lo* — the other holds that since it cannot be lifted by its rope, it is not genuinely integrated into the door mechanism, and inserting it into the bolt-brackets has the appearance of adding to the structure.

### Tosafot Chumra

*Tosafot* raises a question on the *Rabbi Yose* side of the Tiberias case. The *gemara* in *Nedarim* teaches that if a community has adopted a stringent practice regarding something otherwise permitted — *devarim hamutarim ve-chen nahagu bahen issur* — one may not come and declare it permitted in their presence, lest they come to treat forbidden things lightly. How, then, could *Rabban Gamliel* and the elders come and permit what the Tiberias community had been observing as forbidden?

*Tosafot* answers with a crucial distinction: *dehaynu keshe-yod'im she-mutar u-machmirim al atzman* — that rule applies only when the community *knows* the practice is permitted but has voluntarily adopted a stringency. In that case, you do not override their accepted *chumra*, because doing so risks training people to dismiss self-imposed stringencies indiscriminately, potentially leading to the violation of genuine prohibitions: *shelo yargilu bnei adam lehakeil veyavo'u lehatir issur*.

But *aval im machmirim machamat taut* — if they are observing the stringency because of a mistake, because they believe it to be genuinely required when it is not, then *mutar lehatir bifneihem* — it is not only permitted but appropriate to correct the error. One need not and should not buy into the ignorance of others. This principle extends beyond the Tiberias case: *Rav Moshe* articulates a parallel rule regarding *marit ayin* — the concern about appearances applies when people might misread the facts, not when they have a mistaken understanding of the law itself. Where the error is one of law, the correct response is correction and education, not accommodation of the misconception.

---

---

# Pesachim 5

## Timing of Chametz Removal

### Previous Discussion Cont…

The discussion on this daf flows directly from the previous day's analysis of *hashbata* and *biur*. The central question concerns the precise timing of *biyur chametz*: when exactly must one eliminate *chametz* before *Pesach*?

### Why Not Night Before

The answer emerges from a chain of interconnected obligations. The removal of *se'or* is linked to the prohibition of *chametz*, which is in turn linked to the eating of *matzah*. Since we know that when one begins eating *matzah* one must already have been rid of *chametz*, the elimination must precede that moment. This rules out the night before — but it equally rules out doing it a full twenty-four hours prior, since the relevant *pesukim* indicate the removal occurs during the day.

### Why Not Early Morning

If the removal must happen during the day, why not first thing in the morning, in keeping with the principle of *zerizin makdimin*? The answer lies in the word *ach*. The particle *ach* functions as a limiting term — *mechaleik* — dividing the day. It indicates that only a portion of the day is the relevant time for this act, not the entirety of it.

### Biyur After Six Hours

Drawing together all these elements — the *hekesh* linking *se'or*, *chametz*, and *matzah*, the requirement that removal occur during the day rather than the night before, and the limiting force of *ach* — the *gemara* concludes that *biyur chametz* is performed after six hours of the day have passed.

---

## Dvar Bei R. Ishmael

### Rishon Interpretation

A different approach to the same question is introduced by a teaching from the school of Rabbi Ishmael. The central question is what *rishon* refers to in the verse *ach bayom harishon tashbitu se'or mibateichem*. Does it mean the first day of *Pesach* itself, or does it mean a different day entirely?

### 14th of Nisan = Rishon

The school of Rabbi Ishmael teaches: *matzinu yud-daled shenikra rishon* — we find that the fourteenth of Nisan is explicitly called *rishon* in a *pasuk*. The verse *barishon b'arba'ah asar yom lachodesh* demonstrates that the term *rishon* can refer to the fourteenth of the month. When the Torah therefore commands *ach bayom harishon tashbitu se'or mibateichem*, the *rishon* does not refer to the first day of *Pesach* but rather to the fourteenth of Nisan, the day preceding the *chag*.

### Textual Parallels

The broader textual context in Parshat Bo reinforces this reading. Several *pesukim* in close proximity employ the term *rishon*. The verse *ki kol ochel chametz venichreta hanefesh hahi miyom harishon ad yom hashvi'i* uses *harishon* to describe the first day of the *chag*. Immediately following: *ubayom harishon mikra kodesh uvayom hashvi'i mikra kodesh yihyeh lachem*. Then, one *pasuk* further: *barishon b'arba'ah asar yom lachodesh baerev tochlu matzot* — where *barishon* clearly refers to the first month of the year, not the first day of the festival. This last usage is admittedly *pshat*, not the school of Rabbi Ishmael's intended *drash*, but the point stands that *rishon* carries multiple referents across the *pesukim*.

---

## Rav Nachman's View

### Rishon = Prior

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an independent interpretation. He proposes that *rishon* in biblical usage can inherently mean "prior" or "beforehand" — not merely "first." His proof is a *pasuk* outside the Torah: *harishon adam tivaled* — "were you born prior to the first man?" This usage establishes that *rishon* can indicate temporal priority rather than sequential position. Accordingly, when the Torah commands *ach bayom harishon tashbitu se'or mibateichem*, *rishon* means the day prior to the *chag*.

### Sukkot Counterexample

The *gemara* immediately challenges this position. If *rishon* invariably means "prior," what is one to make of the verse *ul'kachtem lachem bayom harishon* — the commandment to take the *lulav* on the first day of *Sukkot*? Would we conclude that one must take the *lulav* the day before *Sukkot* begins? That is plainly not the practice, and no one suggests it. Thus *rishon* cannot categorically mean "prior."

### Seventh = First (Chag)

The *gemara* responds that *Sukkot* presents a different case. The *pasuk* states *u'semachtem lifnei Hashem Elokeichem shivat yamim* — you shall rejoice before Hashem for seven days. Within this framework, the comparison is explicit: *ma shevii shevii lachag*, just as the seventh day of rejoicing plainly means the seventh day of the *chag*, *af rishon rishon lachag* — so too the first day means the first day of the *chag*. This parallel locks the *rishon* in *Sukkot* to the festival itself and prevents it from meaning "the day before."

But then the same logic could be applied to *Pesach*: the verse *shivat yamim matzot tochelu ach bayom harishon tashbitu se'or mibateichem* similarly situates *harishon* within the framework of seven days of eating *matzah*. By the same reasoning, *bayom harishon* in this verse would refer to the first day of *Pesach*, not the day before.

### Mikra Kodesh Parallel

The difficulty intensifies when one considers *ubayom harishon mikra kodesh uvayom hashvi'i mikra kodesh yihyeh lachem kol melacha lo ye'aseh bahem*. Here *harishon* and *hashvi'i* stand in precise parallel: the first day is a *mikra kodesh* and the seventh day is a *mikra kodesh*. If the seventh day unambiguously refers to a day of the festival, the parallelism makes it extremely difficult to argue that *harishon* means anything other than the actual first day of *Pesach*. The *pesukim* are so symmetrical that the interpretation strains credulity.

### HaRishon Excludes Chol H…

The *gemara* then pivots to a grammatical observation. The text could have written simply *ach bayom rishon* — but instead it writes *ach bayom harishon*, with the definite article *heh*. The extra *heh* is the critical textual element. The question is: *harishon lama li* — why is the definite article needed? The answer is *shema mina lechde'amran* — it signals that *rishon* here does not mean the first day of the *chag*, but rather something prior to it. Meanwhile, the *harishon* in the *Sukkot* context serves a different purpose: *lemiyutei cholo shel moed* — to exclude *Chol HaMoed*. Only the first and seventh days are days on which *melacha* is forbidden, not the intermediate days of the festival.

### Grammar: Vav and He

This answer generates its own difficulty. The reason one might have thought *Chol HaMoed* was included is because of the verse *uvayom hashmini shabaton* — the *vav* of *uvayom* invokes the principle *vav mosif al inyan rishon*, meaning the conjunctive *vav* adds the eighth day to what came before and might suggest that the intermediate days are included as well. It is therefore necessary to use *harishon* — with the *heh* — to teach that only the first day and the eighth day carry the *issur melacha*, not *Chol HaMoed*.

But the *gemara* then asks: if the only reason we need the *heh* in *harishon* is because of the *vav* in *uvayom hashmini*, why not simply write *bayom shemini* without the *vav*, thereby eliminating the need for the *heh* in *harishon* in the first place? The *gemara* answers that this move is blocked by the verse *ubayom harishon mikra kodesh*, which itself uses *harishon* with the definite article. If *rishon* there means the actual first day of the *chag*, which seems unavoidable given the context, then the attempt to use *harishon* in the *hashbata* verse to mean "the day before" runs into an almost inescapable parallel that argues against it. The structural parallels between the *pesukim* are so close that the argument of *rishon* meaning "prior" has largely reached its limits.

---

## Three Rishonim

### Rishon for Derash

At this point, the *gemara* takes a step back and acknowledges the difficulty. On its face, the attempt to read *rishon* as "the day before" cannot be sustained against the full weight of the parallel *pesukim* in *Sukkot* and *Pesach*. The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between *peshat* and *drash*: the three instances of *harishon* in the *Sukkot* and *Pesach* contexts — the *issur melacha* on *Pesach*, the *issur melacha* on *Sukkot* together with the *mitzvah* of *lulav* — are each used for their plain meaning in context, referring to the actual first day of the *chag*. The only reason one might have thought otherwise is to serve the *drasha* of *rishon* meaning "prior" — but that *drasha* is not needed for *peshat* purposes in those verses.

Instead, the *gemara* says: *ella hanei shelosha rishon miba'ei lei kedatanya devei Rabbi Yishmael*. These three instances of *rishon* are required for a specific *drasha* taught by the school of Rabbi Ishmael, and it is precisely because they are "used up" for this *drasha* that the *harishon* in the *hashbata* verse can be understood as meaning "prior." The argument is not that *rishon* always means "the day before" everywhere — it is that in the specific context of *hashbata*, once the other *harishon* instances are accounted for, this one remains available to mean something different.

### Merit of Rishonim

The teaching of the school of Rabbi Ishmael is: *bisechar shelosha rishon zachu leshelosha rishon* — in the merit of three *rishonim*, Israel merited three other *rishonim*. The three rewards are: the destruction of the seed of Esau, the building of the *Beit HaMikdash*, and the name of *Mashiach*.

### Esau's Seed

The first of the three *rishonim* for which Israel receives reward corresponds to the destruction of the seed of Esau. The *pasuk* cited is *vayeitzei harishon admoni kulo keaderet se'ar* — Esau emerged first, red all over like a hairy garment. The *Maharsha* elaborates: *Pesach* celebrates the *geulah* from Egypt, and just as God redeemed Israel from that subjugation, so too will Israel be redeemed from the subjugation of the seed of Esau. The parallel between past and future redemption is the animating logic here.

### Se'or & Yetzer Hara

The *Maharsha* also develops a homiletic dimension: the *se'or* that one removes is understood to represent the *yetzer hara*, identified with the *koach* of Esau. The ability to overcome the *yetzer hara* — to eliminate the *se'or* — prefigures the ultimate elimination of the evil it represents. The future redemption will bring the eradication of the desire to do evil, corresponding to the removal of the *yetzer hara* entirely.

### Beit HaMikdash

The second *rishon* for which Israel is rewarded corresponds to the building of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *pasuk* cited is *kissei kavod marom merishon mekom mikdashenu* — a throne of glory, exalted from the very beginning, is the place of our sanctuary. The festival of *Sukkot* and the verse *ki vasuccot hoshavti et b'nei Yisrael behotzi'i otam me'eretz Mitzrayim* also commemorates the redemption from Egypt. Just as God spread the *ananei hakavod* over Israel in the wilderness — which *Sukkot* recalls — so too will God restore the *shechina* through the rebuilding of the *Beit HaMikdash*.

### Mashiach

The third *rishon* for which Israel is rewarded corresponds to the name of *Mashiach*. The *pasuk* cited is *rishon leTziyon hinei hinam* — the first one to Zion, here they are. The connection runs through the *mitzvah* of *lulav*, which the verse introduces with *ul'kachtem lachem bayom harishon*, and which is associated with *Sukkot* as *zman simchatenu*. Because of this *rishon* of rejoicing, Israel merits the *rishon* who is *Mashiach*.

The *gemara*'s resolution thus works as follows: the three *harishon* instances elsewhere are legitimately occupied by this *drasha* and do not function as proofs that *rishon* means the first day of the festival in the *hashbata* verse. It must be said, though, that this is not the most straightforwardly convincing of readings — and indeed, several other, more direct answers were already provided earlier and will be developed further.

---

## Rava's Proof

### Lo Tishchat Al Chametz

Rava offers an independent and more direct source for the prohibition. The verse states *lo tishchat al chametz dam zivchi* — do not slaughter the Pesach offering while *chametz* still exists in your possession. Rava reads this as a temporal command: one cannot perform *shechitat haPesach* so long as one still has *chametz*. Since *shechitat haPesach* takes place from midday of the fourteenth of Nisan onward, it follows that *chametz* must be eliminated before that point. This provides a clear *asmachta* for the timing of *biyur chametz*.

### Individual Shifts Problem

The *gemara* raises a difficulty. The verse literally addresses each individual at the moment of *shechita*. But in the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *bnei Yisrael* were divided into three *katim* — three shifts — for the *shechita*. Each individual performs *shechita* at a slightly different time. If the prohibition means that each person cannot have *chametz* at the precise moment he slaughters, then one person's *zman* might fall later than another's, just as one who accepts *Shabbat* early is bound from that moment while others are not yet bound. The person slaughtering in the third shift could theoretically still be eating *chametz* while someone in the first shift has already slaughtered. Why should the prohibition apply uniformly to everyone from the same moment?

### Zman Shechita Begins

The *gemara* resolves this by explaining that *zman shechita amar Rachmana* — the Torah is referring not to each individual's personal moment of slaughter but to the *zman shechita* as a collective institution: the moment when *shechita* begins for people generally. Unlike the individual acceptance of *Shabbat*, which genuinely operates on a personal timeline, the *zman shechita* of the *Pesach* is a fixed communal threshold. From the point when *shechita* becomes possible for anyone, *chametz* must already have been eliminated.

---

## Tanya Interpretations

### Three Meanings

A *baraita* addresses the same verse — *ach bayom harishon tashbitu se'or mibateichem* — and considers three possible readings: does the commandment apply *me'erev Yom Tov*, from the eve of the festival the night before; does it apply *beyom Yom Tov atzmo*, on the festival day itself; or does it refer to some division of the day?

### Cannot Slaughter with Ch…

The *baraita* resolves the question by citing the prohibition of *lo tishchat al chametz*: one cannot slaughter the Pesach offering while *chametz* remains. This demonstrates that *chametz* must be eliminated before the *shechita* of the Pesach, which occurs on the fourteenth from midday — and therefore the commandment to remove *se'or* cannot be referring to the festival day itself.

---

## Rabbi Akiva's Answer

### Melacha Objection

Rabbi Akiva offers yet another independent argument. He cites two verses in proximity: *ach bayom harishon tashbitu se'or mibateichem* — on the first day eliminate *se'or* from your homes — and the adjacent verse *kol melacha lo ta'asu* — no work shall be done. If *harishon* referred to the first day of *Pesach*, and if eliminating *chametz* requires burning, there would be a direct contradiction: one cannot perform the *melacha* of burning on a *Yom Tov* when *melacha* is forbidden. The only way to resolve the contradiction is to read *harishon* as referring to the day before *Yom Tov* — the fourteenth of Nisan — when *melacha* is still permitted. Thus, Rabbi Akiva derives from the internal tension between the two verses that *biyur chametz* must occur prior to *Yom Tov*.

---

## Rabbi Yossi's Answer

### Ach Divides Day

Rabbi Yossi returns to the limiting force of *ach*. The word *ach* in *ach bayom harishon tashbitu se'or mibateichem* functions as *chalak* — it divides the day, indicating that only part of the day is meant. And if *harishon* refers to the first day of *Pesach*, *ach* would be meaningless, since one cannot have *chametz* at all during any part of that day. The verse must therefore be speaking of a day during which one is permitted to have *chametz* for part of the time and must eliminate it during another part — which can only be *erev Pesach*.

### Hekesh to Matzah

Rabbi Yossi's argument, when unpacked, relies on the same chain of *heikeshim* established earlier. The prohibition of *hashbatat se'or* is linked by *hekesh* to *achilat chametz*, which is itself linked to *achilat matzah* — *itkash hashbatat se'or la'achilat chametz, vechol chametz la'achilat matzah*. On the first day of *Pesach* one cannot have *chametz* at any point; it is therefore impossible to read *harishon* in the *hashbata* verse as referring to that day. Rabbi Yossi thus arrives at the same conclusion as the earlier discussion, but via the *ach* rather than through the *heikesh* alone.

---

## Rabbi Akiva's Answer (II)

### Matzah on Erev Pesach

An implicit assumption in Rabbi Akiva's argument requires clarification. One might ask: if *erev Pesach* is a day during which one may still have *chametz* for part of the time, why is it that one does not eat *matzah* on that day? After all, if the *hekesh* ties together *se'or*, *chametz*, and *matzah*, one might think *matzah* eating begins from the same point that *chametz* must cease. The answer is that the practice of not eating *matzah* on *erev Pesach* is rabbinic in origin — the concern being *lete'avon*, that one should approach the *seder* night with appetite and enthusiasm for the *matzah*. Some extend this practice even further, refraining from *matzah* for thirty days before *Pesach*. This practice, however, is distinct from any biblical prohibition.

---

## Three Lessons from R. Ak…

### Biyur = Sreifah

Rava observes: *shema mina midivrei Rabbi Akiva telat* — three distinct *halachot* can be derived from Rabbi Akiva's position. The first: *ein bi'ur chametz ela sereifah* — the proper method of *biyur chametz* is specifically burning. How does this follow from Rabbi Akiva? Rabbi Akiva's entire argument rests on the premise that eliminating *chametz* constitutes a *melacha*. There are many ways one might conceivably eliminate *chametz* — eating it beforehand, throwing it into the ocean, disposing of it otherwise — none of which involve a *melacha*. If Rabbi Akiva says that performing *biyur* on *Yom Tov* would be problematic because of *melacha*, he must be holding that *biyur* specifically means *sereifah*. Indeed, even according to opinions that eating one's *chametz* beforehand is a valid form of elimination, the prevailing practice is still to preserve a small amount specifically to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *sereifah*. Rabbi Akiva's argument thus implicitly establishes *sereifah* as the required form of *biyur*.

### Sreifah Melacha

The second lesson: *havara l'chalek yatza* — the *melacha* of burning is a distinct and independent *melacha*. This connects to a well-known debate regarding the verse *lo tivaru eish b'chol moshvoteichem b'yom hashabat* — you shall not kindle a fire in any of your dwellings on *Shabbat*. The question raised by this verse is: given that *melacha* is already prohibited on *Shabbat* by the verse *lo ta'aseh kol melacha*, what does the prohibition on kindling fire add? The two positions are: *l'chalek yatza* — it emerges as a distinct *melacha*, meaning it is counted separately among the 39 *melachot*, such that one who performs it receives a distinct punishment independent of other *melachot*; or *lav yatza* — it does not emerge as a *melacha* but rather as a *lav*, a negative prohibition, meaning it is not subject to the same *issur melacha* framework that carries *kareth*. Since Rabbi Akiva grounds his argument in the impossibility of performing *sereifah* on *Yom Tov* due to its being a *melacha*, he must hold *l'chalek yatza* — that *havara* is indeed counted as a full and distinct *melacha*.

### Not Permitted on Yom Tov

The third lesson: *lo amrinan ho'il v'hutchra havara l'tzorech hutchra nami shelo l'tzorech* — one does not apply the principle that since burning is permitted on *Yom Tov* for *ochel nefesh* purposes it is thereby permitted for other purposes as well. On *Yom Tov*, the general permission to cook — to use fire *l'tzorech* — is sometimes extended to other uses of fire that are not strictly for food preparation, on the grounds that once a category of *melacha* is permitted, it is permitted broadly. Rabbi Akiva's position demonstrates that this principle does not apply to burning *chametz*. Eliminating *chametz* provides no tangible personal benefit; it is purely destructive in nature. Since one does not stand to gain from burning the *chametz* in the manner one gains from cooking food, the leniency of *ochel nefesh* does not carry over to this act. Therefore, even if one has a fire burning on *Yom Tov* for legitimate purposes, one may not use it to burn *chametz* on *Yom Tov* — this must be done beforehand.

---

## Seven Days Chametz Not F…

### Yimatzei vs. Yeira'eh

The *gemara* returns to the *pesukim* in Parshat Bo. The *baraita* opens by citing two distinct verses: *shiv'at yamim se'or lo yimatzei bevateichem* — seven days *se'or* shall not be found in your homes — and *lo yeira'eh lecha chametz velo yeira'eh lecha se'or bechol gevulecha* — *chametz* and *se'or* shall not be seen anywhere within your borders. Why do we need both verses? Each teaches something the other does not.

It is worth noting that these verses come from different contexts within the Torah. The first is the instruction given by Hashem to Moshe; the second is Moshe's transmission of those instructions to the people, to which Moshe added additional elements — *tefillin*, the commemoration of the exodus, and other matters. This is why Moshe's account does not simply restate the divine command verbatim. Nevertheless, the *gemara* treats both verses as independently operative sources and asks what each contributes.

The *gemara*'s operative principle emerges from the verse *lo yeira'eh lecha se'or*. The word *lecha* — "to you" — is read as *shelcha*, "yours." The verse therefore teaches: *shelcha ee atta ro'eh aval atta ro'eh shel acheirim veshel gavo'ah* — your own *se'or* cannot be seen, but you may look upon *se'or* belonging to others, whether to other Jews or to *hekdesh*. The prohibition of *bal yeira'eh* applies only to one's own *chametz*.

### Your Own vs. Others'

This distinction between one's own *chametz* and others' *chametz* is fundamental. One is prohibited from possessing or seeing *chametz* that belongs to oneself; the property of others is not one's concern. This is why the verse says *lecha* — *shelcha* specifically cannot be seen.

### Hiding & Deposits

One might think that if visibility is the standard, one could satisfy the prohibition simply by hiding the *chametz* — burying it in a pit or concealing it in some other fashion. Furthermore, one might think one could accept a *pikadon* — a deposit — of *chametz* from a non-Jew and keep it over *Pesach* without violation, since it does not belong to oneself. The *gemara* addresses both scenarios by invoking the other verse: *lo yimatzei* — it shall not be found. This prohibition extends beyond visibility to actual possession. Even if *chametz* is hidden and cannot be seen, *lo yimatzei* prohibits its very presence. And even if *chametz* deposited by a non-Jew is not technically one's own, *lo yimatzei* in your homes prohibits maintaining such possession.

### Houses vs. Borders

The two verses serve complementary and non-redundant functions. The verse *lo yimatzei bevateichem* — in your houses — covers *se'or* that is in the domestic sphere and adds the prohibition of possession even when hidden, and the prohibition of accepting deposits from non-Jews. The verse *lo yeira'eh lecha se'or bechol gevulecha* — in all your borders — extends the prohibition beyond the house to all of one's property: pits, cisterns, caves, and fields. Neither verse alone would cover both categories. *Lo yimatzei bevateichem* would not cover property outside the home; *lo yeira'eh bechol gevulecha* would not prohibit hidden *chametz* or deposits, since one might think that what is not visible is not subject to this verse. Both are therefore necessary.

---

## Gezeirah Shava Se'or

### Se'or Equivalence

The *gemara* then establishes a *gezeirah shava* between the two verses. Both employ the word *se'or*: *shiv'at yamim se'or lo yimatzei bevateichem* uses *se'or* in the context of houses, and *lo yeira'eh lecha se'or bechol gevulecha* uses *se'or* in the context of borders. The verbal parallel creates the basis for drawing equivalence between the two domains.

### House Rules to Borders

From the *gezeirah shava*, what is said of *se'or* in houses applies to *se'or* in borders. Specifically: just as one transgresses in one's house regarding *bal yeira'eh*, *bal yimatzei*, hidden *chametz* (*tamun*), and deposits from non-Jews (*pikadonot*), so too one transgresses on all these grounds with respect to *chametz* or *se'or* anywhere within one's broader property.

### Border Rules to Houses

Conversely, what is derived from the borders verse applies to houses as well. The ruling that *shelcha ee atta ro'eh aval atta ro'eh shel acheirim veshel gavo'ah* — one's own *chametz* is prohibited but others' is permitted — is derived from the borders verse. Via the *gezeirah shava*, this principle extends to houses as well. Thus, one does not violate any prohibition by having the *chametz* of others in one's home, provided it genuinely belongs to someone else and not to oneself.

---

## Non-Jewish Chametz

### Uncontrolled Non-Jews

The *gemara* turns to the question of chametz belonging to a non-Jew in one's possession. The *baraita* initially frames the permission to have another's *chametz* as applying to a non-Jew who is *shelo k'vashatuhu ve'eino sharui imcha b'chatzer* — not under one's control and not dwelling in one's courtyard. Such a non-Jew is entirely independent of the Jew's household, and his *chametz* is clearly his own.

### Controlled Non-Jews Prob…

But what about a non-Jew who *is* under one's control (*kavush*) or who does live in one's courtyard (*sharui imcha b'chatzer*)? How can a Jew have that individual's *chametz* in the home? One might think that the closer a non-Jew's connection to the Jew's household, the more his property would be considered the Jew's own for purposes of the prohibition. It would seem, on this reasoning, to be a greater *chiddush* to permit *chametz* from a non-Jew who has no connection to the household than to permit it from one who is entirely integrated into it.

### Abaye's Reversal

Abaye suggests *ipecha* — reversing the formulation. In his view, the greater *chiddush* is the permission regarding the non-Jew who is *not* under one's control and does not live with one. This should be the case requiring explicit license.

### Rava Maintains Reisha

Rava disagrees: *lo teipecha*, do not reverse it, and *reisha ka'ei* — the *reisha* of the *baraita* stands as stated. The initial permission regarding the uncontrolled, non-resident non-Jew is the *chiddush* that requires derivation, and the ruling regarding the controlled or resident non-Jew follows from an additional source.

### Shelcha Twice = Ribui

The textual basis for the permission regarding even the non-Jew who is under one's control is derived from a *ribui*. The word *shelcha* — "yours" — appears twice in the relevant verses: once in Shemot and once in the repetition in Parshat Re'eh (*velo yeira'eh lecha se'or bechol gevulecha shivat yamim*). The doubling of *shelcha* functions as a *ribui*, an inclusion. The *gemara* derives that the repeated *shelcha* comes to expand the scope of the permission: it includes *chametz* belonging even to a non-Jew who is under one's control and living in one's courtyard. The greater *chiddush*, in Rava's reading, is precisely this: even in that situation of apparent integration, the non-Jew's *chametz* remains his own and does not become the Jew's for purposes of *bal yeira'eh* and *bal yimatzei*.

---

---

# Pesachim 6

## Bal Yera'eh Bal Yimatze

### Extension outside house

We begin at the point on 5b where the lines widen. Yesterday's discussion established the scope of the *issur* of *bal yera'eh bal yimatzei*: it applies to one's *chametz* whether or not it is in one's house, because one *pasuk* speaks of *bevateichem* and another of *bigvulecha*, and both are required. Each *pasuk* independently is insufficient — from one alone, one might have thought it permissible to bury the *chametz*, or that while it cannot be found in one's house, it may remain in a field, cave, or cistern. The two *pesukim* together close off those possibilities entirely.

### Hiding & deposits issue

The *Gemara* now turns to a seeming contradiction embedded in a lengthy passage reviewed at the close of the previous session. The position was advanced there that one might have thought it permissible to hide one's *chametz* or to accept a *pikdon* from a *nochri* — reasoning that the *chametz* deposited by the non-Jew is not one's own, and therefore not subject to the prohibition. Yet the *Gemara* responds: *talmud lomar lo yimatzei* — the *pasuk* says it cannot be found, and that suffices to forbid it.

But this creates an immediate tension: did we not just say from *lo yera'eh lecha* that one is prohibited from seeing only one's *own* chametz, but that *chametz* belonging to others — even *hekdesh chametz* — is permitted? If so, why should accepting a deposit of non-Jewish *chametz* be a problem at all? The *nochri* is asking you to watch his Oreo cookies, so to speak. Either that is a problem or it is not.

### Responsibility principle

The *Gemara* resolves this by drawing a distinction: *ha de-kibbel alei achrayut ha de-lo kibbel alei achrayut* — it depends entirely on whether one has accepted responsibility for the deposit. If something happens to the non-Jew's *chametz* while it is in your possession and you are obligated to compensate him, it is as if the *chametz* is yours. The logic of *shomer chinam* and *shomer sachar* applies: once you accept financial responsibility, the object acquires the legal character of your own property. If you did not accept such responsibility, it remains the non-Jew's *chametz* — the kind one is permitted to "see" because it is not *shelcha*.

### Mechuza soldiers case

This principle finds expression in a parallel ruling: *ha de-amar lehu Rava livnei Mechuza* — just as Rava instructed the residents of Mechuza regarding the soldiers quartered in their homes. The objection to housing soldiers is not a new one — colonial-era America had similar grievances — but the *halachic* point Rava makes is that the residents of Mechuza were obligated to remove the *chametz* of the soldiers billeted with them. Why? *Keivan di-illu migna ve-illu mitabed birshuteichun kai ve-bayitu lishalumei* — because if that *chametz* were stolen or lost, it would be within their domain and they would be required to pay for it. Therefore, *kedilchon dami ve-assur* — it is treated as theirs and is forbidden.
