It is worth noting the interesting asymmetry in this case: the residents are not voluntarily accepting responsibility — they are being *held* responsible by the soldiers' presence. Yet the *halachic* consequence is identical.

### Svara vs. pasuk

The *Gemara* now questions the very premise of this analysis. *Hanicha leman de-amar davar hagorem lemamon kemamon dami* — this entire construction works smoothly according to the view that something which will cause a person to pay money is itself treated as their property. But what of the view that holds *lav kemamon dami* — that such indirect financial exposure does not render an object legally one's own?

According to that view, *shani hacha de-amar lo yimatzei* — in the case of *chametz*, it is different, because the Torah itself says *lo yimatzei*. The *pasuk* functions as an independent *chumra*, rendering the *chametz* forbidden even where general principles would not do so.

A second formulation reverses the emphasis. *Ika de-amri*: for the view that *davar hagorem lemamon lav kemamon dami*, the *pasuk* of *lo yimatzei* is precisely what is needed — *hainu de-itztrich lo yimatzei* — that is why the special *pasuk* is required. For the view that *kemamon dami*, however — that indirect financial liability does render the object one's own — the *pasuk* appears superfluous. Why would I need the *pasuk* if a *svara* already establishes the same conclusion?

This raises a broader point, and a striking one. *Svarot* are apparently as powerful as *pesukim* — yet the *Gemara*'s treatment of when a *pasuk* is rendered unnecessary by a *svara* is not entirely consistent. Sometimes they invoke *lavo alav bishnei lavin*, deriving two separate prohibitions from what might seem redundant. Other times, when a *svara* exists, the *pasuk* is redirected to serve a different *inyan* entirely. The tension is real, and both possibilities are alive here.

### Returned chametz case

The *Gemara* concludes that even for the view that *kemamon dami*, the *pasuk* is still needed, and for a specific reason: *salka da'atcha amina ho'il vechi ityei hadar be'einei lav birshutei kai kamashma lan*. One might have thought that in a case where the *chametz* will ultimately be returned to the non-Jew — where, for example, the soldiers pack up and leave and one simply hands back their *chametz* — it is never truly in one's possession. After all, it was given to you, you never wanted it, it is his, and when he leaves you give it back. One might reason: *beinei* — it is intact, it remains his throughout, and it was never mine at any moment. Therefore, comes the *pasuk* to teach that even then, one transgresses *bal yera'eh uval yimatzei*.

This is quite a stringent ruling. The *pasuk lo yimatzei* extends the prohibition even to *chametz* one never intended to acquire, never exercised dominion over, and that will be returned whole to its rightful owner.

---

## Non-Jewish ownership

### Bechor ownership issue

Having discussed the concept of non-Jewish ownership over *chametz*, the *Gemara* transitions to a related category: cases where a non-Jew holds partial ownership in an animal that would otherwise be subject to *bechorah*. As we know from *Kodashim*, an animal must be entirely in Jewish ownership to be subject to the obligation of *bechor* — partial non-Jewish ownership exempts it.

The question now becomes: what if the non-Jewish government has not a proprietary share in a specific animal, but rather a general tax claim against one's livestock? The government, after all, demands a tenth of one's cattle — but it does not have a *tefisah* in this particular animal. One can give them a different animal, not the *bechor*. Does the government's general tax lien nonetheless constitute enough of an ownership interest to exempt the *bechor*?

### Arnona tax case

This is the question posed in *ba'ei Rava behemot arnona* — the case of the *arnona* tax. Is such an animal *chayevet bivchorah* or not? The *Gemara* specifies: *kol heicha de-matzi mesalek lei b'zuzi lo kamiba'aya lan de-chayav* — where you can pay off the government in money, there is no question. If the government is content with cash and has no specific interest in taking animals, then there is clearly no partial ownership in any particular beast, and the animal is certainly subject to the *bechor* obligation.

The question arises only *heicha de-lo matzi mesalek lei b'zuzi* — where you cannot pay them off, where they specifically insist on a tenth of your actual herd. Does that specific demand create a lien sufficient to be considered an ownership stake in the *bechor* and thereby exempt it? Or is it still more abstract — a general claim against the herd that does not attach to any individual animal, leaving the *bechor* subject to its own separate obligation?

### Rava's exemption

Rava was asked, and he responded: *peturah* — exempt. Where you cannot pay them off and they specifically demand animals, the tax lien is considered substantial enough to constitute a degree of non-Jewish ownership that exempts the animal from *bechorah*.

### Behemah vs. isah

*Ika de-amri* introduces an alternative formulation. Here Rav Pappa states that there is a *matnita* that actually declares the animal *patur* from *bechorah* — but then draws a distinction with the case of *isat ha'arnona*, dough subject to the same tax: *chayevet be-challah*, it is still subject to the *challah* obligation, *ve-af al gav de-lo matzi mesalek lei* — even where one cannot pay them off. If we are saying the animal is exempt, why is the bread subject?

### Public knowledge

*Behemah it lei kala, isah leit lei kala* — for livestock, the matter is well known; for bread, it is not. The reasoning is as follows: tax collectors coming to take cattle is a matter of public knowledge — everyone in a community is aware that the government has an interest in the herd, and that this claim effectively constitutes a partial ownership stake. The *bechor* is therefore understood by all to be exempt. Bread, by contrast, is not subject to the same public awareness. The government's interest in the baker's output may not be widely known, and people who observe the baker not taking *challah* will not understand the reason. The result is a concern of *marit ayin* — it will appear that *challah* is simply not being taken, giving rise to a problematic appearance of neglecting a Torah obligation. Therefore, even where the government technically has a claim over the dough, the obligation of *challah* remains in force.

The precise mechanics of who would observe whether *challah* was taken is admittedly puzzling — how public can the baker's practice actually be? One possible resolution: in a town with a single baker, the government's tax policy on cattle is general knowledge, but the specific implications for bread may not be. In any event, that is the principle: *it lei kala* versus *leit lei kala* drives the distinction between the two cases.

---

## Non-Jew in house

### Non-Jew's chametz entry

The *Gemara* now turns to a *beraita* addressing the non-Jew who enters a Jewish home with *chametz* in hand: *nochri shenichnas lechatzeiro shel yisrael ve-chamtzo beyado* — a non-Jew who enters the courtyard of a Jew with his *chametz*. The ruling: *ein ze zakuk leva'er* — one is not obligated to have it removed. It is not your *chametz*; you have no obligation to tell him to leave or to dispose of it immediately.

### Designated space

However, *hifkido etzlo zakuk leva'er* — if he deposits it with you, you are obligated to remove it. This, as established, follows from the principle of *achrayut*: accepting the deposit makes it legally yours.

The *beraita* then introduces a third case: *yicheid lo bayit* — if one designates a space for the non-Jew's *chametz*, *ein ze zakuk leva'er* — one is again not obligated. Rashi explains that by designating a space and saying, essentially, put it wherever you like, one is not thereby accepting *achrayut*. That is the entire point: the obligation to remove flows from acceptance of responsibility, and by designating a space without formally accepting a deposit, one makes clear that the *chametz* remains entirely the non-Jew's.

### Tosafot view

Tosafot disagrees with Rashi's framing. According to Tosafot, even if one *has* accepted *achrayut*, if one nonetheless designates a specific space for the non-Jew, that suffices to exempt from the obligation. The two positions — Rashi's, that designating a space signals *non-acceptance* of responsibility, and Tosafot's, that it operates as an independent factor even alongside accepted responsibility — lead to meaningfully different frameworks.

### Lo yimatze scope

The *beraita* concludes with the phrase *shene'emar lo yimatze*. The question then arises: to which case does this *pasuk* attach? Rav Pappa says it refers back to the first case — *areisha ka'i* — specifically to the case of the formal deposit, *hifkido etzlo zakuk leva'er*. The *pasuk lo yimatzei* is the reason one must remove it in that case: by accepting the deposit and its attendant responsibility, the *chametz* becomes one's own and falls under *lo yimatzei*. According to Rashi's view, the second case — designating a space without accepting responsibility — would not implicate *lo yimatzei* at all, since the *chametz* never became one's own.

### Rav Ashi's view

Rav Ashi reads it differently: *l'olam aseifa ka'i* — the *pasuk* actually refers to the second case, the designated space. How does that work? *Ke-shene'emar lo yimatze b'vateichem* — because the Torah says it cannot be found *in your homes*, and this *chametz* is not considered to be in your home at all. *V'hai lav dideih hu* — it is not yours. And why is it not yours? Because *nochri ki ka ayil l'veitei d'nafshei ka ayil* — when the non-Jew enters and retrieves his *chametz*, he is entering what is, in the relevant sense, *his* space. He has rights to that designated area such that when he goes into it, he goes into his own domain.

The *pasuk* thus comes to *permit* the second case, not to *prohibit* it. *Lo yimatzei* teaches that only *chametz* which is genuinely *matsui beyadcha* — readily accessible to you — is prohibited. This designated space, which the non-Jew enters as if it were his own, does not meet that threshold.

### Sekhirus kanya

This, however, raises a sharp question: *lemeimra de-shkhirut kanya* — does this mean that designating a space for the non-Jew effectively constitutes a rental? Has the non-Jew thereby acquired the area as a *shkhirut*? If so, one needs to account for the broader *halachic* principle regarding renting to non-Jews.

### Idolatry concern

*Ve-tenan af bemakom she-amru lehaskhir lo leveit dira amru mipnei she-makhnisin le-tocho avodat gilulim* — the *Mishnah* teaches that even in cases where it is permitted to rent property to non-Jews, it was said not for a *beit dira* — a dwelling — because they will bring their idols into it. If designating a chametz-storage space within a Jewish home operates as a *shkhirut* and thereby renders it the non-Jew's domain, we have effectively created a *beit dira* arrangement — precisely what is prohibited because of the concern about idolatry being brought into what might be understood as one's own home.

So the question presses: if *shkhirut kanya* and the non-Jew has effectively acquired this space within the Jewish house, how can we permit designating such a space?

### Torah exclusion

The resolution is: *shani hacha de-afkei rahmana bilshon lo yimatzei* — it is different here because the Torah expressed the prohibition in the language of *lo yimatzei*. The *pasuk* itself defines the scope of what is forbidden.

### Matsui beyadecha

*Mi she-matsui beyadekha, yatsei zeh she-eino matsui beyadekha* — only that which is readily accessible to you, in your control and at your disposal, falls under the prohibition. That which is not *matsui beyadekha* is excluded. The designated space given to the non-Jew for his *chametz* is, in the relevant sense, not readily accessible to the Jew: he did not accept responsibility for it, he does not exercise dominion over it, and when the non-Jew enters to retrieve it, he enters what has been assigned to the non-Jew's use. Therefore *lo yimatzei* does not apply.

The bottom line, at least according to Rashi, is that the exemption does not rest on the non-Jew having formally *acquired* the space — which would raise the *beit dira* problem — but rather that the Jew has not accepted responsibility for the *chametz*, and consequently it is not *matsui beyado*. The designation of a space signals and effects this non-acceptance of responsibility. The particulars of whether the non-Jew has some right of use short of ownership, or whether the space technically remains in the Jew's domain while still not being *matsui*, are somewhat difficult to work out precisely — but the operative principle is clear: the absence of *achrayut* means the absence of the *matsui beyadcha* relationship that *lo yimatzei* requires.

This ruling has real practical implications. A non-Jew who simply walks into a Jewish home with *chametz* on *Pesach* — without a deposit arrangement and without a designated space — raises no obligation on the Jew's part. One need not order him out or demand he remove his food. And if a space is designated for non-Jewish workers or maintenance staff in a building over *Pesach*, the *chametz* they bring to their designated area is not the Jew's concern under this *issur*. This is what the *Gemara* is saying — though practical *peskening* on such matters belongs to one's own *posek*.

---

## Covering on Yom Tov

### Muktzeh covering

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: if one finds *chametz* in one's home on *yom tov* — having searched and thought everything was gone, yet opening a cabinet and discovering something — what does one do? *Chametz* on *yom tov* is *muktzeh*: one has no permitted use for it, and one cannot burn it either, since lighting a fire for this purpose is not permitted on *yom tov*. The ruling is *kofeh alav keli* — one covers it with a vessel and deals with it after *yom tov*.

### Hekdesh exception

*Amar Rava: im she-hekdesho eino tzarich* — if one declares the *chametz* to be *hekdesh*, one need not cover it at all. *Mivdal bedili minei* — one knows to stay well away from *hekdesh*. It is off-limits in a serious sense, and one will naturally maintain distance from it without the need for a physical cover to serve as a reminder or barrier.

### Non-Jewish separation

*Ve-amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: non-Jewish *chametz* found in one's home requires a *mechitzah* of ten *tefachim* to separate it — *mishum heker*, for purposes of recognition and distinction. It must be clearly set apart so that it is evident that this *chametz* is not the Jew's. *Ve-shel hekdesh eino tzarich* — *hekdesh chametz*, by contrast, does not require a physical partition, for the same reason as before: *mivdal bedil inish minei* — people know to keep away from *hekdesh* and will not approach it carelessly.

---

## Timing of bi'ur

### 30-day rule

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: one who sets out on a sea voyage or joins a caravan more than thirty days before *Pesach* — *ein zakuk leva'er*. No obligation to perform *bi'ur* before departing. This operates on the understanding that *min ha-Torah*, *bitul* alone suffices; and if one has already performed *bitul* and is not returning, the need for physical *bi'ur* does not arise. One is not here for *Pesach*, one is not going to eat the *chametz*, and one has already nullified it in one's heart.

Within thirty days of *Pesach*, however — *toch sheloshim yom zakuk leva'er* — one is obligated to perform *bi'ur* before departing.

### Abaye's intent

Abaye qualifies this: even the ruling that within thirty days one is obligated to perform *bi'ur* — *lo amaran ella sheda'ato lachzor* — applies only when one intends to return for *Pesach*. But if one does not intend to return, *ein zakuk leva'er* — even within thirty days one is not obligated. One might wonder whether "return" means returning before *Pesach* ends, and the answer is yes — the question is whether one will be home during *Pesach* itself.

### Rava's principle

Rava sharpens the formulation: if you are going to return, then *afilu meRosh HaShanah nami* — even if you are leaving six months before *Pesach*, you must perform *bi'ur*. The controlling factor is not temporal proximity to *Pesach* but rather intent. *Da'ato lachzor* means you will come back to your *chametz* — and therefore the obligation applies regardless of when you leave. Conversely, the exemption before thirty days applies only *ella she-ein da'ato lachzor* — where one truly has no intention of returning for *Pesach*. Within thirty days, the obligation applies in any case.

### Storehouse case

The same principle appears in a related ruling: *de-amar Rava oseh beito otzar* — if one turns one's house into a storehouse with both *chametz* and other items packed together. *Kodem sheloshim yom ein zakuk leva'er, toch sheloshim yom zakuk leva'er* — outside thirty days, no obligation; within thirty days, obligated. And even before thirty days, the exemption applies only *ella she-ein da'ato lefanoto* — if one has no intention of clearing out the storehouse before *Pesach*. If one does intend to access and clear it, then *afilu kodem sheloshim yom nami zakuk leva'er*. The principle is consistent: intent to engage with the *chametz* over *Pesach* triggers the obligation; genuine separation from it removes it.

### Issur hana'ah

Rashi makes a striking observation. Why is it that if one intends to return, one is obligated even from *Rosh HaShanah*? *Deki hadar bei b'yemei haPesach avar alei* — because when one returns during *Pesach*, one transgresses *bal yera'eh uval yimatzei*. And once *Pesach* has arrived, *sheharei issur hana'ah hu ve-eino shelo* — the *chametz* is *issur hana'ah* and is no longer legally his. One cannot perform *bitul* at that point because the Torah has removed it from one's *reshut* in the relevant sense. And so one will find oneself faced with *chametz* one cannot nullify, and the moment one sees it and does not immediately remove it, one transgresses. Hence the obligation to perform *bi'ur* before leaving — so that one does not return to find *chametz* that one is powerless to address.

---

## Bitul after bedika (II)

### Issur hana'ah paradox

This raises what is truly a striking conceptual difficulty. On *Pesach* itself, *chametz* is *issur hana'ah* and, in a meaningful legal sense, is out of one's possession — the Torah removes it from one's *reshut*. Yet one remains liable for *bal yera'eh uval yimatzei* as if it were one's own. The Torah simultaneously removes the *chametz* from one's possession (in the sense that one cannot benefit from it or perform *bitul* over it) and retains it in one's possession (in the sense that one remains *over* on the prohibition). This paradox is essential for understanding the structure of the obligation and will continue to bear on the discussion that follows.

---

## Timing of bi'ur (II)

### Lav hanitak la'aseh

Tosafot on a different *daf* offers an intriguing position: *lav hanitak la'aseh*. Even if one keeps *chametz* in one's house for the entire duration of *Pesach* without removing it — even for several days — one does not violate the *lav* as long as one burns it before *Pesach* ends. The reasoning is that the *lav* of possessing *chametz* is *nitak la'aseh*, linked to the positive commandment of *tashbitu*: *ach bayom harishon tashbitu*. Since *tashbitu* is an *aseh* that can redeem the situation, the *lav* does not fully crystallize until the *aseh* becomes impossible to perform — that is, until *Pesach* is over.

One might ask: does this mean that *lav hanitak la'aseh* operates not merely to exempt from *malkut* but to prevent violation of the *lav* altogether? Apparently so, at least according to Tosafot's position. The *lav* has not been transgressed until the window for performing *tashbitu* closes.

If so, one might further ask: given that burning suffices, why must one perform *bitul* before *Pesach*? Tosafot would agree that *bitul* cannot be performed on *Pesach* itself — the Torah removes the *chametz* from one's *reshut* for purposes of *bitul* — but the concern is practical: to burn *chametz* one needs wood and fire, and the process takes time. The *Rabbanan* feared that one would procrastinate, delay gathering what is needed, and ultimately fail to burn the *chametz* before *Pesach* ends altogether. *Bitul* before *Pesach*, therefore, is a safeguard against that failure — ensuring that even if the physical *bi'ur* is not performed, the *chametz* has already been addressed.

---

## 30-day origin

### Pesach Sheini source

Why thirty days? *Ke-detanya sho'alin ve-dorshin be-hilchot Pesach kodem la-Pesach shloshim yom* — as the *beraita* teaches, one inquires into and expounds the laws of *Pesach* within thirty days of *Pesach*. Within that window, one is already in the ambit of *Pesach* and its concerns. The thirty-day period itself derives from the interval between *Pesach Rishon* and *Pesach Sheini*: Moshe stood at *Pesach Rishon* and warned regarding *Pesach Sheini* — *shene'emar ve-ya'asu venei Yisrael et ha-Pesach*. Those who were *tamei* came to Moshe at *Pesach Rishon* and were then told about the *Pesach Sheini* that would take place a month later.

### Pesach context

The principle is that within thirty days of *Pesach*, a person is already engaged in *Pesach* matters. The halakhic world of *Pesach* has begun to bear on him, and so the obligations associated with *bi'ur* properly take hold from that point.

### Two-week option

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: *shtei shabbatot* — two weeks suffice. The appearance of thirty days in the story of *Pesach Sheini*, he argues, is incidental. The people came to Moshe at *Pesach Rishon* asking about their situation, and since they were already discussing *Pesach*, Moshe addressed all *Pesach*-related matters, including the institution of *Pesach Sheini*. But that is a function of the specific circumstance — the *Pesach Sheini* teaching did not require thirty days of lead time; Moshe could have waited and told them two weeks later, just before *Pesach Sheini*. The thirty-day figure is therefore not normative. For everyone else, two weeks is the appropriate threshold.

Where does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel get two weeks? *Sheharei Moshe omed be-Rosh Chodesh u-mazhir al ha-Pesach* — because Moshe stood on *Rosh Chodesh Nisan* and warned about *Pesach*, which falls fourteen days later. The *pasuk* in *Parshat Bo*: *ha-chodesh hazeh lachem rosh chodashim*, and then, *dabru el kol adat benei Yisrael lemor be-asor la-chodesh hazeh veyikechu lahem ish seh* — Hashem tells Moshe on *Rosh Chodesh* to instruct the people about the *korban Pesach* that begins on the tenth and is brought on the fourteenth. Two weeks thus anchors the obligation.

The *Gemara* immediately asks: *mimmay de-vereish yarcha ka'i* — how do we know that Moshe actually taught the people on *Rosh Chodesh*? Perhaps Hashem spoke to Moshe on *Rosh Chodesh*, but Moshe transmitted the instruction to the people on the fourth or fifth of the month — which would give less than two weeks. *Dilma be-arba'ah be-yarcha o be-chamishah be-yarcha ka'i*? The two-week calculation depends on Moshe telling the people on *Rosh Chodesh* itself.

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak mishmeih de-Ravina*: another *pasuk* is brought. *Vayedabber Hashem el Moshe be-midbar Sinai ba-shanah ha-sheniyah ba-chodesh ha-rishon* — Hashem spoke to Moshe in *Midbar Sinai* in the second year, in the first month, and then *ve-ya'asu venei Yisrael et ha-Pesach bemo'ado*. Here too the question: how do we know this was *Rosh Chodesh*? It says only "in the first month."

The answer comes through *gezeirah shavah*: *atya midbar mimmidbar* — the word *be-midbar* appears here in the context of the *Pesach* instruction, and it also appears at the opening of *Sefer Ba-Midbar*: *vayedabber Hashem el Moshe be-midbar Sinai be-Ohel Moed be-echad la-chodesh ha-sheni* — on the first of the second month, which is *Rosh Chodesh*. Just as the *midbar* statement in *Sefer Bamidbar* was delivered on *Rosh Chodesh*, so too the *midbar* statement regarding *Pesach* was delivered on *Rosh Chodesh* — specifically *Rosh Chodesh Nisan*, two weeks before *Pesach*. That is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's source.

### Chronological order

The *Gemara* then notes that the opening of *Sefer Ba-Midbar* — which took place in the second month — appears *before* the *Pesach* passage — which took place in the first month. Why is the Torah presenting events in the second month before events in the first month? *Amar Rav Menashia bar Tachlipa mishmeih de-Rav*: *zot omeret ein mukdam u-meuchar ba-Torah* — from here we learn that the Torah is not bound by chronological order.

### Single topic order

Rav Pappa immediately qualifies: *lo amran ela be-trei inyanei* — we say this only when two separate *inyanim* are involved. The beginning of *Bamidbar* concerns the census of the Jewish people; the *Pesach* passage concerns the *korban Pesach*. When two distinct topics are in play, the Torah may present them in any order. *Aval be-chad inyana mai de-mukdam mukdam ve-mai de-meuchar meuchar* — but within a single *inyan*, what comes first is first and what comes later is later. There is chronological integrity within a unified topic.

### Hermeneutics

And if one does not accept this limitation, the entire system of hermeneutical derivation would collapse. *Ve-ee lo tema hachi, klal u-frat ein bi-chlal ela mah she-bi-frat* — consider: the rule of *klal u-frat* depends on identifying which phrase is the *klal* and which is the *prat*, and this identification rests on order of appearance. The *klal* comes first, the *prat* second, and the *klal* is then understood to be limited to what the *prat* specifies. But if there is no chronological integrity within an *inyan*, then for all we know the *prat* came first and the *klal* came second — in which case the rule of *prat u-chlal* applies instead, and the *klal* is understood as *expanding* beyond the *prat* rather than being limited by it. The entire basis for choosing between these hermeneutical rules would evaporate. *Dilma prat u-chlal hu*?

The same problem applies in reverse: *ve-tu prat u-chlal na'asa klal mosif al ha-prat* — a *prat* followed by a *klal* means the *klal* adds onto the *prat*. But without order, how do you know which is which?

The *Gemara* then presses: could one not say the same thing even about *trei inyanei* — two separate topics? If we invoke *ein mukdam u-meuchar* for two separate topics, why doesn't that also disrupt the *klal u-frat* rules that appear across different passages? The answer: *hanicha leman de-amar klal u-frat meruchakin zeh mi-zeh ein danin oto be-klal u-frat* — according to the view that a *klal* and *prat* widely separated from one another do not generate *klal u-frat* derivation at all, the question does not arise. *Ela le-man de-amar danin* — but according to the view that even widely separated *klal* and *prat* do generate the derivation, the response is: *afilu le-man de-amar danin, hanei milei be-chad inyana, aval be-trei inyanei ein danin* — even that view limits the derivation to a single *inyan*. Across two separate topics, *klal u-frat* simply does not operate regardless.

What runs beneath this entire discussion is a striking intellectual honesty about the nature of textual interpretation. The *Gemara* is implicitly acknowledging that the Torah's text could in principle be read in many ways — that the assignment of *klal* and *prat*, the determination of chronological order, the identification of which passage governs which — all of these could theoretically go differently. The *Rabbanan* know the text admits multiple readings, and they are here establishing the rules of engagement: within a single *inyan*, order is binding. Across *inyanim*, it is not. This is not presented as though the rules derive self-evidently from the text — it is presented as a set of disciplined hermeneutical commitments, and the intellectual tension underneath that commitment is very much alive in the *sugya*.

---

## Bitul after bedika (II)

### Bitul necessity

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: *ha-bodek tzarich she-yevatel* — one who searches for *chametz* must nonetheless still perform *bitul*. Having done a thorough *bedika*, one might think the *bitul* is superfluous — after all, one has found and removed everything. Why is *bitul* still required?

The first suggested answer is: perhaps there are still crumbs (*perurin*) remaining. But this is immediately rejected — *ha ninhu lo chashivi*, crumbs are *batel* and do not constitute a violation of *bal yera'eh*. A few crumbs are simply not significant enough to trigger the prohibition. Nor does the general significance of one's house impart significance to the crumbs — *keivan de-minter lehu agav beiteih chashivi* is proposed and then set aside. The *beraita* demonstrates: when a field-owner watches his land during one harvest season while the previous season's remnants sit untended, those remnants are not considered significant. If the owner is *makpid* on them, they become significant; if not, they are *hefker* and *patur* from *ma'aser*. Since one certainly does not care about a few crumbs after a thorough *bedika*, they achieve no significance.

### Gluska yafa concern

*Amar Rava*: the true reason one who performs *bedika* still requires *bitul* is a *gezeirah* — a rabbinic precaution. *Gezeirah shema yimtza gluska yafa* — lest one find a beautiful, choice roll (*gluska yafa*) that one did not discover during the search. If there is no prior *bitul*, one's attention becomes arrested by this discovery — *da'ateih ilaveih* — one's mind is drawn to it. And then? One might hesitate to destroy it.

The further difficulty is that if one finds this *gluska yafa* on *Pesach* itself, one cannot simply perform *bitul* at that point: *dilma mashkachat lah batar issura* — perhaps one discovers it after the *issur* has taken effect. And *lav birshuteih kayma, de-lo matzi levatlei* — it is no longer in one's legal *reshut* in the sense required for *bitul*; one cannot nullify it.

### Rav Elazar

*Amar Rav Elazar*: there are two things not in a person's *reshut*, yet the Torah treats them as if they were: *bor birshut ha-rabim* — a pit dug in the public domain, and *chametz mi-shesh sha'ot ul-maalah* — *chametz* from the sixth hour onward. In both cases, the person does not own the relevant domain or object in the ordinary sense, yet the Torah holds them liable as owners. Regarding *chametz*: once the sixth hour arrives and the *issur* of *chametz* takes effect, the *chametz* is *issur hana'ah* and has in a meaningful sense left one's possession — yet *ve-chaschan ha-katuv k'ilu birshutu*, the Torah treats it as if it remained in one's *reshut*, and one transgresses *bal yera'eh uval yimatzei*. One cannot perform *bitul* at this stage, and one is liable for what one cannot legally exercise dominion over. This is why the *bitul* must be performed *before* that threshold is crossed.

---

## Bitul mechanics

### Rashi's ke'afra

How precisely does *bitul chametz* work? Rashi's formulation of the *bitul* text is instructive: *ha-bodek tzarich she-yevatel be-libo samuch la-bedika miyad*, and what one says is *kol chamira de-ika be-veita hadein livatel*. Notably, Rashi makes no mention of *hefker*. He says *livatel* — that it be nullified. And the language associated with *bitul* is *ke-afra de-ara* — like the dust of the earth. This is not a declaration of ownerlessness; it is a declaration of insignificance, of non-existence as an object of value.

### Tosafot hefker

Tosafot, on the *mishnah*, reads *bitul* as an act of *hefker* — rendering the *chametz* ownerless. If it is ownerless, it is no longer one's own, and the prohibition of *bal yera'eh* cannot apply. The mechanism, on this view, is divestiture of ownership.

### Ran's objection

The Ran objects strongly to this position. His critique appears at the opening of his commentary on the first *daf*. First, the textual objection: the formulation of *bitul* is *ke-afra de-ara*, with no mention of *hefker* — the language does not support reading *bitul* as *hefker*. Second, and more fundamentally, *hefker* is ineffective in this context. *Hefker* means that one has relinquished ownership and anyone may now acquire the object. But ownership under *hefker* passes fully to another party only when that party takes possession. Until someone else acquires the *chametz*, it remains, in a relevant sense, the original owner's. And on *Pesach*, no one is permitted to acquire *chametz* — it is *issur hana'ah* for everyone — meaning no one will ever take it. If *hefker* is only fully effective upon acquisition by another, and no acquisition can occur, the *hefker* of *chametz* on *Pesach* is a legal nullity. Furthermore, *bitul* is performed *be-libo*, in one's heart — and *devarim she-ba-lev einan devarim*, unexpressed mental intentions have no legal force. *Hefker* performed purely mentally, without verbal declaration, would be ineffective on those grounds as well.

### Ran's alternative

The Ran's own understanding of *bitul* is more subtle. When *Pesach* arrives, as established, the Torah's law of *issur hana'ah* effectively displaces the *chametz* from one's *reshut* — it is removed from one's possession in the sense that one can derive no benefit from it. Yet the Torah simultaneously holds one liable for *bal yera'eh uval yimatzei* as if it were fully in one's possession. The Torah, in effect, *returns* the *chametz* to one's possession for purposes of this prohibition. What *bitul* accomplishes is not making the *chametz* ownerless but rather *preventing it from returning to one's possession* through the Torah's mechanism. By performing *bitul* — by mentally treating the *chametz* as destroyed, as non-existent, as mere dust — one preempts the Torah's act of re-attribution. Since *bitul* does not need to be effective as an act of acquisition or transfer to another party, it can operate purely *be-libo*. One is not divesting ownership; one is foreclosing the re-establishment of a connection that would otherwise be imposed by the Torah's own framework.

### Both positions

Given the range of positions — Rashi and the Ran understanding *bitul* as mental negation or destruction rather than *hefker*, and Tosafot understanding it as *hefker* — the practical formulation adopted is inclusive: both *yibatil* and *lihyot hefker ke-afra de-ara*. By including both elements — the declaration of nullification and the language of *hefker* cast as dust-like insignificance — one is covered according to all the major views. If *bitul* works as *hefker*, the declaration accomplishes that. If it works as mental destruction and non-attribution, the *ke-afra de-ara* language accomplishes that. The formulation is thus structured to satisfy the requirements of the full range of *rishonim* on the question.

---

---

# Pesachim 7

## Bitul & Bedika Intro

### Rashi: Bitul & Tashbitu

The opening discussion of our *daf* centers on a foundational principle stated earlier in the *masechet*: *habodek tzarich sheyevatel* — one who performs the search for *chametz* must also perform *bitul*, nullification. To understand why, it is worth surveying the range of opinions about how *bitul* functions in the first place.

In several places the *gemara* states that *bitul b'alma sagi* — mere *bitul* suffices. Rashi explains this by grounding *bitul* in the biblical command of *tashbitu*: the Torah's instruction to destroy *chametz* is fulfilled, according to Rashi, by the psychological act of negation. When one genuinely regards one's *chametz* as nothing — as worthless, as non-existent from one's own perspective — that mental act constitutes a fulfillment of *tashbitu*. The implication follows naturally: once *tashbitu* has been performed in this manner, one cannot be in violation of *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh*, even though, technically speaking, one might still be said to "own" the *chametz* in some sense.

### Tosafot: Hefker Model

Tosafot finds this approach unsatisfying. For Tosafot, the only way to avoid transgressing *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh* is to ensure that the *chametz* is genuinely no longer one's own. The *chametz* must cease to belong to the person. Accordingly, Tosafot understands *tashbitu* as operating essentially as a form of *hefker* — a declaration of ownerlessness. When one performs *bitul*, one is in effect saying: this is not mine, I renounce it, it is hereby *hefker*. This position does create certain difficulties — there is a view that *hefker* requires three people present to take effect — but that is the thrust of Tosafot's position.

### Ran: Torah Non-Ownership

The Ran offers what might be characterized as a synthesis, or at least a significant variation on the Tosafot approach. He agrees that *bitul* works because the *chametz* is rendered not one's own — but the mechanism by which this occurs is not an act of *hefker*. Rather, the Ran points to a *gemara* learned earlier in the *masechet* which establishes that the Torah itself does not ascribe ownership of *chametz* to a person, at least in a meaningful sense. The underlying reasoning is that *chametz* during Pesach is *asur b'hana'ah* — forbidden to derive benefit from — and objects from which no benefit may be derived are, in principle, not owned in any legally cognizable sense. This is a broader question in halakha: do *issurei hana'ah* admit of *ba'alut*, of ownership at all? The straightforward reading of the *gemara* is that they do not.

And yet, the *gemara* also says that if one was holding *chametz* at the moment it became forbidden, one is liable. How does the Ran reconcile this? He explains that if a person actively possesses or implicitly holds onto *chametz* — if he has not in any way detached himself from it — then even though technically he does not "own" it, the Torah holds him responsible as if he did. The transgression of *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh* reflects that continued, implicit possession.

*Bitul*, then, on the Ran's view, works as follows. Since *chametz* will automatically become *asur b'hana'ah* and thus not truly "owned," all one needs to do is indicate — at the moment *yom tov* begins — that one has no interest in it. By signaling that detachment, one ensures that the automatic non-ownership operates in one's favor. One is not making an active *hefker*; rather, one is simply removing the one factor — implicit possessive intent — that would have caused one to be held responsible despite the technical non-ownership. The moment one withdraws one's hands, so to speak, one is no longer responsible.

### Why Bedika After Bitul

Having established that *bitul* in principle suffices to avoid *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh*, a natural question arises: why does the *gemara* institute *bedika* at all? This question is more pointed than it might first appear. The first Rashi on the *mishna* explains that one performs *bedika* precisely in order not to transgress *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh* — one doesn't want *chametz* remaining in the house. Tosafot challenges this: the *gemara* itself says *bitul* suffices to avoid that violation, so once *bitul* is performed, Rashi's reason for *bedika* collapses.

The real answer to Rashi is that, from the *mishna*'s perspective, he is entirely correct. Scanning the *mishnayot*, one finds that *bitul* is almost never mentioned as a general practice — the sole exception is the case of someone on his way to bring a *korban Pesach* or to perform a *bris milah* for his son who suddenly realizes he left *chametz* at home. In that emergency scenario, the *mishna* permits *bitul* as a fallback. Beyond that, the *mishnayot* treat *bedika* as the primary, and indeed only, obligation. *Bitul* is a *bedi'eved* option for when circumstances prevent one from doing it properly.

It was Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav — *amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav, habodek tzarich sheyevatel* — who introduced the now-standard practice of combining *bedika* with *bitul* as belt-and-suspenders. The logic is: if somehow one missed a piece of *chametz* during the *bedika*, the *bitul* covers it. Once this belt-and-suspenders principle is established, Tosafot's question emerges with full force: if the suspenders (*bitul*) are already in place, why do we still need the belt (*bedika*)? Tosafot gives two reasons. First, even if one is not technically in violation of *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh*, having *chametz* around the house creates a real risk of accidentally eating it. *Chametz* is not like *chazir*, which one knows at all times not to eat; *chametz* is food one normally consumes, and one might simply forget that it is Pesach. Second, beyond that practical concern, the Torah's language of *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh* demonstrates that the Torah itself objects intrinsically to the presence of *chametz* — not merely because one might eat it, but because there is something inherently problematic about its being there at all. The rabbis therefore maintained the *bedika* requirement even after *bitul* was introduced.

### Bal Yera'eh Approaches

These two reasons Tosafot offers for *bedika* — the safeguard against accidental eating, and the intrinsic objection to the presence of *chametz* — actually map onto two distinct approaches to understanding the *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh* prohibition itself. One might ask: why does the Torah state *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh* at all? For every other prohibition, the Torah simply says: don't eat this. Why, with *chametz*, does it add: don't even have it visible, don't even have it found?

One approach holds that this is a safeguard. *Chametz* is so common, so familiar as a food, that simply prohibiting its consumption is insufficient — people will forget, they will slip. *Bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh* therefore operates as a hedge around the eating prohibition. On this view, Tosafot's first reason for *bedika* — the concern about accidental eating — precisely parallels the Torah's concern.

The second approach inverts the logic entirely. The focus is not on *chametz* as a food that must not be consumed. The focus is on Pesach as *Chag HaMatzot* — the Festival of Matzot. On this reading, the very presence of *chametz* is antithetical to the nature of the *chag*. It is a reenactment of the primal experience of *Bnei Yisrael* leaving Egypt with no *chametz* whatsoever. The prohibition on eating *chametz* is therefore a consequence of this more fundamental reality, not the other way around. And so the very presence of *chametz*, even when there is no risk of eating it, is itself a violation of what the *chag* demands. This parallels Tosafot's second reason: the rabbis objected intrinsically to *chametz* in the house, not only because one might come to eat it.

This interpretive duality is further reflected in the distinction between the two *pesukim* underlying *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzeh*. The *gemara* — which was the subject of the previous *daf* — treats *lo yimatzeh b'vateichem* and *lo yera'eh lecha b'chol gevulecha* as a unified prohibition. But the *pshat* of the two verses reflects the two different concerns independently. *Lo yimatzeh b'vateichem* carries no limit of *lecha* — it is not about my ownership or my seeing it; it is about the possibility that *chametz* could be uncovered and found in my home, regardless of whose it is or whether it is buried. Proximity creates risk. By contrast, *lo yera'eh lecha b'chol gevulecha* — out in the wider world beyond one's home — the concern shifts to one's personal connection: it is mine (*lecha*) and I am encountering it. Even absent any risk of eating, my being connected to *chametz* in the public domain is itself the problem. So the two reasons Tosafot gives for *bedika* may indeed correspond to the two different emphases of the Torah's language, which the *gemara* has unified into one *issur*.

### Da'ateih Iluyei Debate

The *gemara* justifies the combined practice of *bedika* and *bitul* by noting: if one searches but does not also perform *bitul*, one might find a loaf of *chametz* on Pesach and *da'ateih illuyeih* — one's mind will fix upon it — and one will thereby transgress. The question is what exactly *da'ateih illuyeih* means, and here Rashi and Tosafot diverge significantly.

For Tosafot, *da'ateih illuyeih* does not require any special affirmative act of wanting to keep the *chametz*. It simply means the opposite of *perurin* — crumbs. The *gemara* elsewhere establishes that crumbs are automatically *batel*, considered insignificant by default. *Da'ateih illuyeih* is merely saying: unlike crumbs, a proper loaf is not automatically *batel*. If you missed it during *bedika* and did not do *bitul*, that loaf is still fully significant and you have transgressed by having it there. No new act of positive desire is needed.

Rashi, however, makes the term carry more weight. For Rashi, *da'ateih illuyeih* implies an active desire — one finds the loaf and actively wants it, fixes one's intention upon it. This connects to the Ran's framework in an interesting way. One who performed *bedika* has been actively searching to rid the home of *chametz*, and that very act of searching signals a general detachment from all *chametz* in the house. The *chametz* was technically never one's own to begin with, and one was actively trying to eliminate it. So one exists in a grey zone: not having pushed the *chametz* actively away through *bitul*, but also clearly not possessing it with any affirmative intent. Perhaps, in that grey zone, if upon discovery one immediately acts to destroy the *chametz*, one would be safe — because it was never truly one's own, and one never intended to keep it. The moment one *wants* the loaf, however — that is an act of possession. And that, according to Rashi's understanding of *da'ateih illuyeih*, is what triggers the transgression. *Bitul* prevents this by preemptively eliminating even the possibility of such possessive intent arising.

---

## Bitul Timing Rules

### Fourth/Fifth Hour

The *gemara* now raises a seemingly simple question: given that *bitul* must accompany *bedika*, why not simply defer the *bitul* to the daytime on *erev Pesach* — say, the fourth or fifth hour of the day? Why connect it to the nighttime *bedika* at all?

The *gemara* answers: *keivan d'lav zman issura hu v'lav zman biyura hu* — the fourth and fifth hours are neither the time when *chametz* becomes forbidden nor the recognized time of its destruction. If *bitul* is not anchored to a defined, meaningful moment in the *chametz*-removal process, *dilma pasha v'lo mivatel lei* — one will be negligent and fail to perform it. The rabbis understood human psychology well: attaching *bitul* to the *bedika* ritual gives it a clear moment and ensures it will be performed. A diffuse obligation with no defined hook will be forgotten.

### Sixth Hour Limit

The *gemara* then considers whether *bitul* should instead be performed at the sixth hour — 11 o'clock on a standard day — when *chametz* becomes rabbinically prohibited. This moment has clarity and significance; surely it would be an appropriate time for *bitul*? The *gemara* answers: *keivan d'issura d'rabbanan it lei, k'd'oraisa damya* — since the rabbinic prohibition has taken effect, it operates functionally like the biblical prohibition in this context. Once *chametz* is rabbinically forbidden, it is *lav birshutei kayma* — it is no longer in one's legal domain — and therefore *v'lo matzi mevatel lei*, one can no longer perform *bitul* over it. Just as one cannot perform *bitul* once it is 12 o'clock and the biblical prohibition has set in, so too one cannot perform *bitul* at 11 o'clock once the rabbinic prohibition has set in.

### Kiddushin Analogy

The *gemara* grounds this principle in a teaching: *d'amar Rav Gidel amar Rav Chiya bar Yosef amar Rav, hamekadesh mishesh sha'os ul'ma'la afilu b'chitei kordneisa ein choshashin l'kidushin*. If one betroths a woman from the sixth hour onward using *chitei kordneisa* — a variety of hard wheat from a certain region that will not ferment even if water touches it, and thus constitutes only rabbinic *chametz* (*chametz nuksha*) — there is no concern whatsoever for the validity of the *kiddushin*. The wheat is *asur b'hana'ah* and therefore effectively worthless; one cannot effect a betrothal with it.

The structure of the analogy is instructive. The case involves the biblical time period — from midday onward — but rabbinic *chametz*. The parallel case for our purposes involves biblical *chametz* but the rabbinic time period — from the sixth hour, meaning 11 o'clock. In both configurations, the *chametz* is rendered legally without value, and therefore *bitul* — like *kiddushin* — cannot take effect.

Rashi, it should be noted, attempts to read *mishesh sha'os ul'ma'la* as meaning from 11 o'clock onward — that is, from the beginning of the sixth hour rather than from its end at midday. Almost all the *Rishonim* disagree, maintaining that the phrase always means from midday onward. The analogy therefore, in their view, involves *chametz nuksha* at the biblical time, standing in for biblical *chametz* at the rabbinic time period. What motivates Rashi's reading is the very need to make the analogy work directly, without the transposition — a reading that the other *Rishonim* find linguistically unpersuasive.

This raises a broader question about rabbinic authority over *d'oraisa* statuses. One could argue that the rabbis are not directly declaring a *d'oraisa* status to be altered; rather, since in practice no benefit may be derived from the *chametz* within the normative framework of rabbinic law, it is effectively worthless in practice, and therefore worthless for *kiddushin* purposes as well — regardless of whether the disqualification is rabbinic or biblical in origin. A parallel question arises regarding a witness who is disqualified only rabbinically: does a *kiddushin* in which he served as witness have *d'oraisa* validity, or does the practical reality of his non-acceptance in rabbinic courts undermine even the *d'oraisa* status of the *kiddushin*? That, too, is debated, and the structure of the question is the same.

### Braita: Yom Tov Exception

The *gemara* now faces a challenge from a *braita*. The *braita* states: *ha-yoshev b'veis ha-midrash v'nizkar she-yesh chametz b'soch beiso, mevatlo b'libo* — if one is sitting in the *beis midrash* and recalls that there is *chametz* in one's home, one may simply perform *bitul* in one's heart. And this applies equally to *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*.

The *gemara* accepts the *Shabbat* case without difficulty — that refers to when the fourteenth of Nisan falls on *Shabbat*, so one performed *bedika* on Thursday night and now finds oneself on *erev Pesach* which is *Shabbat*, with *chametz* one forgot to eliminate. *Yom Tov*, however, is startling: if it is *Yom Tov*, then Pesach has already begun. This appears to directly contradict the principle just established — *bitar issura*, once the prohibition has taken effect, *bitul* is no longer possible. Yet the *braita* seems to permit *bitul* even after Pesach has commenced.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov resolves the difficulty: *hacha b'issos ha-yoshev lifnei rabbo askinan* — the *braita* is speaking of a specific case. The person sitting in the *beis midrash* is a student sitting before his teacher, and what he recalls is not that he left finished *chametz* behind, but that he left behind *issos megulgalos* — dough that had not yet been put in the oven. On *Yom Tov* one could have baked it; the student is sitting before his teacher and realizes he left the dough, and *u-misyara shema tachmitz* — he fears it will become *chametz*. But it has not yet become *chametz*. Therefore, *kodem hu u-mevatlah mikamei de-tachmitz* — he can perform *bitul* before it becomes *chametz*, because at this moment it is still not forbidden.

The *gemara* finds support for this reading in the very language of the *braita*: it says *ha-yoshev* — the one who is *sitting* in the *beis midrash*. The specific scenario of sitting before one's teacher explains why he cannot simply leave and resolve the problem directly. The implication is that if he could leave, he would have done so and prevented the dough from becoming *chametz* in the first place. *Shema mina* — this is a valid inference.

The overall picture that emerges from this section is that the *gemara*'s introduction of *bitul* as a standard accompaniment to *bedika* represents a significant shift from the *mishna*'s framework. Where the *mishna* treated *bedika* as the primary obligation and *bitul* as an emergency fallback, the *gemara* transforms the picture: *bitul* becomes a standard and important practice, with careful rules governing when it can and cannot be performed.

---

## Moldy Bread Case

### Bread Basket Rov

The *gemara* now transitions to a case brought by Rabbah bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav: *ha-pach she-ipash* — a bread basket in which a moldy piece of bread is found. *Keivan she-rubah matzah, muteres* — if the majority of use of that basket has been for *matzah*, the moldy bread is permitted.

Some preliminary clarification is in order. This discussion presupposes a world in which *matzah* looked very different from the flat, cracker-like *matzah* we know today. Sefardi *matzah* gives a better approximation — something closer to a pita. When a piece of bread goes moldy in a basket, it can be impossible to determine at that stage of decomposition whether the original item was a flat *matzah* or a regular loaf of *chametz*. In that state of uncertainty, the *gemara* says one may rely on *rov* — majority usage — and the bread is *muttar*. This is a striking ruling: on Pesach, where we might expect extreme stringency, the *gemara* is prepared to apply ordinary halakhic decision-making principles rather than simply requiring one to discard the item.

### Jerusalem Money Parallel

The *gemara* immediately questions this approach. Why rely on *rov* at all? Even if the majority of usage was for *chametz*, surely we should rather follow *batar basra* — the most recent use. If the basket was last used for *matzah*, that should be the operative assumption. Isn't that the stronger principle?

The *gemara* supports this intuition by citing a *mishna* concerning money found near the animal-sellers in Jerusalem. Money found in front of those who sell animals for slaughter in Jerusalem must always be assumed to be *ma'aser sheni* money — regardless of the time of year — because the predominant use of funds in that vicinity is *ma'aser sheni* money, which pilgrims brought to spend, often on meat or *shelamim* sacrifices. Money found on the Temple Mount itself (*Har HaBayis*) is assumed to be *chulin* — ordinary money — because people did not typically bring animals there for purchase; Tosafot adds that even if one might carry money there, that location does not generate the same presumption of *ma'aser sheni* usage.

The more interesting case is money found in the streets of Jerusalem generally. *B'sha'as ha-regel* — during the festival period — such money is assumed to be *ma'aser sheni*, because the entire city is filled with pilgrims and the majority of currency circulating is *ma'aser sheni* money. *B'she'ar yemos ha-shana* — the rest of the year — such money is assumed to be *chulin*. But why? One might think that even after the *regel*, there could still be leftover *ma'aser sheni* money that had been in circulation.

Rav Shmaya bar Zeira explains: *ho'il u-shukei Yerushalayim asuyim lehiskaibed bechol yom* — the marketplaces of Jerusalem were swept daily. Therefore one can always assume that the money found on the ground fell recently — within the last day. After the *regel*, the most recent money circulating would be ordinary *chulin* money, so that is what one assumes. The principle at work here is *kamai kamai azlu lei, v'hanei achrinei ninhu* — the earlier money has been swept away, and what remains is from the most recent usage.

The *gemara* then asks: why not apply this same principle to the bread basket? Even if one used the basket for *chametz* in the weeks prior, that older *chametz* usage is gone, and the most recent use was for *matzah*. Why rely on *rov* rather than *batar basra*?

### Mold Evidence

The *gemara* answers: *lo, shani hacha d'ipusha mochach iluyei* — no, here it is different, because the mold is itself evidence. If the bread is moldy, it is clearly not from the last few days. Therefore the principle of *azlinan batar batra* cannot be invoked, since the mold demonstrates that this is not a recent item.

The *gemara* then pursues this further. If the mold proves the bread is old, then one might say the *rov* is also irrelevant: the mold demonstrates the bread is from a time before Pesach, when *chametz* was certainly being used — so what does it help that the majority use was *matzah* if the item demonstrably predates the *matzah* period?

### Fresh Baking Theory

Rava resolves this by reinterpreting the case. The operative factor is not merely that the majority use of the basket was *matzah*, but rather that *rabu yemei matzah iluyeih* — most of Pesach has already passed. Given that most of Pesach has elapsed, one can account for the heavy mold not by assuming the bread is from before Pesach, but by applying the following reasoning: *amrinan kol yoma v'yoma nami chamimei afu* — each day fresh *matzah* was baked and placed in the basket, piling on top of the small remaining piece, and the accumulation of fresh, warm bread on top is what caused the mold to develop so extensively. In other words, the mold is explained not by the item's pre-Pesach origin but by the continuous process of fresh *matzah* being added daily throughout Pesach.

The *gemara* presses: if it is merely very moldy, one might have thought — *keivan d'ipusha meruba iglai milta d'vadai chametz mealya hu* — that such extensive mold proves definitively that this is pre-Pesach *chametz*. The *gemara* teaches: no, *keivan sherabu yemei matzah iluyeih*, since most of Pesach has passed, we can account for the mold through the daily baking theory, and therefore the bread remains permitted.

### Practical Leniency

The underlying conceptual issue is significant. One might have assumed that in the context of Pesach — where we are extraordinarily careful about even the slightest possibility of *chametz* — we would never rely on *rov* or *batar basra* to permit something that could conceivably be *chametz*. Yet the *gemara* shows no such hesitation. Standard halakhic tools of probability and presumption apply. This reflects an important baseline: the *gemara* does not treat Pesach *chametz* as categorically different from other halakhic uncertainties when it comes to applying evidentiary principles. The stringency that characterizes our contemporary practice — where any possibility of *chametz* leads to immediate disposal — is not the *gemara*'s default posture.

The principle of *azlinan batar batra* — follow the most recent use — and *rov* each have their domain. When the most recent use is clear, one follows it. When it is not clear (because one does not remember which use was most recent, or because one used the vessel for both simultaneously, or because the item found was in a crevice that would have escaped any emptying), one follows *rov*. This emerges from the *gemara*'s further analysis of the money-box case, where Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda rules by *rov* rather than *batar basra*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains this is where one does not remember which use was most recent; Rav Zevid explains it as a case where both uses occurred simultaneously; Rav Pappa explains it as a case where the coin was found in a crevice, meaning it could not be assumed to have come from the most recent deposit.

---

## Brachot on Bedika

### Bracha Requirement

The *gemara* returns to the ritual of *bedika* itself with the statement of Rav Yehuda: *ha-bodek tzarich she-yivarech* — one who performs the search for *chametz* must recite a blessing. The *mishna* discusses using candlelight for *bedika*, but the *mishna* does not cast *bedika* as a formal ritual with a required blessing. It is the *gemara* — and specifically this ruling of Rav Yehuda — that transforms *bedika* into a ritualized act demanding a *bracha*. Once *bitul* has been introduced as a standard accompaniment to *bedika*, the *bedika* itself takes on greater ritual significance, and that significance demands a blessing.

### Le-Va'er vs. Al Biyur

The *gemara* then poses the natural follow-up: *mai mivarech* — what blessing does one recite? Here there is a dispute between two of Rava's students. Rav Pappi, citing Rava, says: *le-va'er chametz* — "who has commanded us to destroy *chametz*." Rav Pappa, also citing Rava, says: *al bi'ur chametz* — "upon the destruction of *chametz*."

Both agree on the conceptual content — this blessing relates to the *d'oraisa* mitzva of *bi'ur chametz*, of *tashbitu*. The dispute is purely linguistic: should the blessing use the infinitive *le-va'er* (to destroy), or the prepositional phrase *al bi'ur* (upon the destroying)? The *gemara* frames this as follows. *Be-le-va'er kulei alma lo peligi d'vadai le-haba mashma* — regarding *le-va'er*, all agree it unambiguously refers to the future, to something about to be done. The phrase "to destroy," formulated as an infinitive, clearly speaks of an imminent action. *Ki peligi be-al bi'ur* — the dispute is specifically about *al bi'ur chametz*. One view holds that *al* intrinsically implies a past action — "upon the destroying" means "in response to destroying that has already occurred" — and therefore using *al* before the act is linguistically problematic. The other view holds that *al* can equally refer to the future and poses no difficulty.

### Al for Future Tense

The *gemara* now proceeds to test whether *al* can legitimately refer to a future action, by examining instances where *al* appears in established blessings that clearly precede the act they accompany.

The first example: *baruch asher kiddishanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu al ha-mila* — the blessing recited at *mila*, which uses the *al* formulation. Is this not a case of *al* referring to a future act? The *gemara* deflects the proof: in the context of *mila*, using *le-mul* (to circumcise) would be problematic, because "You have commanded *me* to circumcise" implies a personal obligation to perform the act — yet it is typically the *mohel* who performs *mila*, not the father. *Al ha-mila* is therefore a more general formulation — "upon the *mila*" — which does not imply personal agency. The *al* formulation was chosen not because *al* refers to the future but because the personal *le* formulation was unavailable. The *gemara* then asks: what would the father say if he himself performs the *mila*? The answer: in that case, one could say *la-mul*, and presumably that would be correct. This opens the possibility that the blessing's formulation varies based on circumstance — a fluidity that was characteristic of the Tannaitic period, before blessings were fully standardized.

Tosafot draws an important observation from this exchange: the very fact that the *gemara* permits *al ha-mila* when there is a need, even though *al* might suggest the past, proves that everyone agrees *al* is capable of referring to the future. Otherwise, it would never have been permitted even in cases of necessity. What the position opposed to *al* maintains is not that *al* is incapable of future reference, but that *le* is more naturally forward-looking, and therefore *le* is preferable when available.

The second example: *baruch asher kiddishanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu al ha-shechita* — the blessing upon *shechita*, which also uses *al*. Again the *gemara* deflects: *shechita* as a command is not personal to any particular individual — the *shochet* is not uniquely commanded to perform it, others could do so — and therefore a *le-shechot* formulation would be inappropriate. *Al ha-shechita* is the general, non-personal formulation required by the circumstances. The *gemara* asks about one who brings a *korban Pesach* and could personally be said to be commanded to perform the *shechita* — and again the answer is that in such a case, *li-shchot* would be appropriate.

The third example concerns the blessing upon taking the *lulav*: *al netilat lulav*. Here the *gemara* offers a different explanation for the use of *al*. *B'idana d'agbei nafik bei* — at the moment one lifts the *lulav*, one has already fulfilled the obligation. The act of lifting constitutes fulfillment. Therefore the blessing upon taking the *lulav* can be said to come, in practice, after the moment of fulfillment, and thus *al* — which suggests response to something that has occurred — is actually apt. Tosafot qualifies this: one cannot truly say the obligation is completely fulfilled the moment the *lulav* is lifted, because then making a *birchat ha-mitzva* after fulfillment would be improper. Rather, the continued holding and shaking of the *lulav* constitutes an ongoing *ma'aseh mitzva*, so even once the initial act of lifting has been performed, the person is still in the midst of the mitzva. The *al* formulation reflects the slightly-after-the-fact character of the blessing relative to the initial moment of fulfillment.

The *gemara* further notes that the *braita* formulating the *lulav* blessing uses the language *latzet bo* — "to go out with it" — rather than *yatza bo* — "having gone out with it." This might suggest the act has not yet occurred. The *gemara* explains the choice of *latzet* as a function of literary parallelism with the *succah* blessing that follows: the *succah* case involves sitting in the *succah* to fulfill the obligation, using the formulation *leishev ba-succah*, a clearly future-oriented *le* formulation. To maintain parallel structure, the *braita* uses *latzet* for *lulav* as well, even though in fact the *lulav* obligation is already being fulfilled at the moment of lifting.

### Halakha: Al Biyur

The *gemara* rules: *v'hilchasa al biyur chametz* — the *halacha* follows the view of *al bi'ur chametz*. This ruling, combined with the discussion above, effectively endorses the position that *al* poses no difficulty when used in reference to a future act. Rashi concludes from this that all the distinctions drawn in the preceding discussion — whether the father performing *mila* himself should say *la-mul* rather than *al ha-mila*, whether the one bringing a *korban Pesach* should say *li-shchot* — dissolve. Now that the *gemara* has affirmed *al bi'ur chametz* as the standard and non-problematic formulation, there is no longer a need to craft special formulations for edge cases.

This leaves unresolved, however, a broader question: why do some blessings use *le* and others use *al*? The Ri (cited by Tosafot) attempted to identify a consistent principle governing when each formulation is used, and could not. The Ran devotes a substantial discussion to surveying all *birchat ha-mitzva* formulations and mapping them against the *le* vs. *al* distinction. One significant factor is personal obligation: when the blessing-maker is specifically and personally commanded to perform the act, *le* is natural. When the obligation is more general or the person is not the uniquely mandated agent, *al* fits better. Another possible factor — which does not perfectly account for all cases — is whether the blessing focuses on the act itself or on an end result to be achieved. *Al bi'ur chametz* and *al ha-mila* focus on an outcome: the *chametz* being gone, the child being circumcised. *Leishev ba-succah* and *lehaniach tefillin* focus more directly on the act of performance. This distinction captures something real even if it does not fully resolve every case.

One additional observation from Tosafot concerns the blessing *lehachniso bi-vriso shel Avraham Avinu* — "to bring him into the covenant of Abraham our father" — which uses a *le* formulation. One might think this blessing, being future-oriented (*le-haba mashma*), must be recited before the *mila*. Tosafot argues otherwise: *lehachniso bi-vriso shel Avraham Avinu* is not a *birchat ha-mitzva* on the act of *mila* — it is a *birchat ha-shevach*, a blessing of praise by the father, expressing gratitude that the Jewish people have been commanded this covenant. A *birchat ha-shevach* need not precede the act; it responds to the experience. Therefore this blessing comes after the *mila*, notwithstanding its *le* formulation.

Tosafot further notes that the question of whether *birchat eirusin* precedes or follows the *kiddushin* is a *machloket Rishonim*. The text of that blessing — *asar lanu et ha-arayot v'hitir lanu et ha-arusos* — reads much more as a *birchat ha-shevach* than as a standard *birchat ha-mitzva*. If it is fundamentally a *shevach*, it should follow; if it is a *birchat ha-mitzva*, it should precede. Contemporary practice uniformly recites it before the ring is given, but the underlying question reflects a genuine dispute about the category of that blessing.

---

## Brachot on Mitzvot

### Bracha Before Mitzva

The *gemara* now establishes the universal principle underlying the entire preceding discussion: *kol ha-mitzvot mevarech aleihen over la'asiyastan* — for all *mitzvot*, the blessing is recited prior to performing them. This statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel is itself taken as a given, but the *gemara* pauses to ask how we know that *over la'asiyastan* means *prior to* doing them, rather than during or after.

### Over L'Asiyatan Proof

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains through *pesukim*. The root *avar* — to pass — is demonstrated from biblical usage to mean going in front of, preceding. The verse recounting *Achimaatz* running by way of the plain (*vayaratz Achima'atz derech ha-kikar*) and passing the *Kushi* — *vaya'avor et ha-Kushi* — shows that *avar* here means he went ahead, he preceded. Abaye adds: *v'hu over lifnehem* — "and he passed before them," meaning he went in front of them. A further source: *vaya'avor malkam lifnehem v'Hashem berosham* — "their king passed before them, and God at their head" — which again means the king went ahead of the people. Through these prooftexts, the *gemara* demonstrates that *over la'asiyastan* means to precede the act of performance.

The underlying logic of this rule, while not stated explicitly by the *gemara*, connects to the nature of *birchat ha-mitzva*. The blessing functions to frame the act — to identify, label, and direct consciousness toward the mitzva about to be performed. As such, it must precede the act, much as framing a picture necessarily precedes placing the picture in the frame. This is in contrast to *birchat ha-shevach*, which responds to experience and therefore comes after, and *birchat ha-nehenin*, which serves a different function altogether.

### Three Blessing Types

The *gemara*'s discussion illuminates a fundamental taxonomy of blessings. *Birchat ha-mitzva* — the blessing on performance of a commandment — always precedes the act. Its function is to frame the performance, and by reciting it, one in effect declares: I am about to perform a mitzva. *Birchat ha-nehenin* — the blessing recited before deriving benefit, such as eating or drinking — also precedes, but for a different reason: one must acknowledge the divine source of one's pleasure before being permitted to enjoy it. *Birchat ha-shevach* — the blessing of praise, such as *asher yatzar* after using the bathroom, or *borei me'orei ha-eish* at *Havdalah* — comes after, because it is a response to an experience, not a preparation for one.

The example of *borei me'orei ha-eish* is instructive. Everyone visually demonstrates the practice by holding their hands to the flame and looking at them before reciting the blessing. But this is in fact the wrong order — or at least, not what the *gemara* requires. The *gemara* states *ad she-ye'osu l'oro* — one must first benefit from the light, and only then recite the blessing. *Borei me'orei ha-eish* is a *birchat ha-shevach* responding to seeing fire; it comes after the experience of benefit, not before. If one is going to perform this act of looking at one's fingernails, one should see the reflection of the light before making the blessing, not after.

### Tevilah Exception

The *gemara* notes an exception to the rule of *bracha* before the act. In the school of Rav they taught: *chutz min ha-tvila v'shofar* — the exceptions are *tvila* (immersion in a *mikvah*) and *shofar*, in which the blessing is recited afterward. The *gemara* immediately accepts *tvila* but challenges *shofar*: *shofar mai ta'ama* — what is the reason for making the blessing after *shofar*? If the reason is that one might blow improperly and then the blessing would have been made in vain — *v'chi teima mishum dilma mekalkel tekiya* — then the same concern applies to *shechita* and *mila*, where one could also err. The *gemara* therefore concludes with Rav Chisda: *chutz min ha-tvila bivad* — the only exception is *tvila*. *Shofar* is removed from the list.

### Tevilah Explanations

The reason *tvila* is an exception is stated as: *d'achti gavra lo chazi* — the person is not yet fit to recite the blessing. Why not? Two explanations are offered.

Rashi explains that the *braita* speaks of a *ger* — a convert — who immerses as part of the conversion process. Before immersion is complete, the *ger* has not yet become part of *Klal Yisrael* and is not yet obligated in *mitzvot*. One who is not yet commanded cannot recite *asher kiddishanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu* — "who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us." The blessing can only be recited after one has emerged from the water and entered the covenant.

Tosafot disagrees and explains the exception differently: it refers to *takanas Ezra*, the ordinance that a man who was a *ba'al keri* — who had experienced a seminal emission — must immerse before being permitted to recite blessings or study Torah. For such a man, he cannot recite the blessing before immersing because he is specifically prohibited from doing so in his current state. The blessing therefore must wait until after he emerges.

The practical question that follows from this debate is significant for women. Neither a *ger* nor a *ba'al keri* account for a woman immersing in a *mikvah* after her period of *niddah*. If the exception for *tvila* is exclusively due to one of those two specific circumstances, then a woman immersing for *tahara* purposes would not fall into the exception and should recite the blessing *before* immersion. Some *Rishonim* hold precisely this. Others hold that once the *gemara* establishes that for *tvila* the blessing is recited after, this becomes the rule regardless of the specific reason, and it applies to all cases of *tvila*. The resulting difference in practice is well known: *Sefardi* women recite the blessing before immersion; *Ashkenazi* women immerse, emerge, recite the blessing, and then immerse again — thereby covering both possibilities while ensuring the blessing is in close proximity to the act of immersion regardless of which timing is correct.

---

---

# Pesachim 11

## Intro & Overview

### Course Intro

Daf 11 of Pesachim spans amudim 11a and 11b, with the bulk of the *sugya* occupying 11a and the top of 11b. After this extended discussion, the daf introduces a new *mishnah* and opens a separate inquiry into how much error people can reasonably be expected to make in assessing the time — a topic that flows from that *mishnah*'s discussion of the deadline for deriving benefit from and consuming *chametz*. But the dominant *sugya* of the daf, the one that commands the most sustained attention, has its launching point in a debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* in the *mishnah* on 10b.

### Gezeira Framework

What begins as an exegetical question about that *mishnah* quickly becomes something considerably broader: a conceptual investigation into when, as a general legal matter, one makes a *gezeirah* to prevent a person from coming to violate an *issur d'Oraita*. Several interlocking factors emerge over the course of the *sugya*: whether one naturally interacts with and is at ease around a given item (the concept of *badil minei* and *lo badil minei*); whether a particular domain of *halacha* generates a heightened general caution that substitutes for a specific *gezeirah*; and whether the very mindset of the person engaged in the relevant activity can be expected to protect against violation. Along the way, the *sugya* surveys a range of *halakhic* domains — *chametz*, *chadash* and grain offerings, *bechor*, and *hilchot Shabbat* — using each as a test case for refining the framework. It amounts to a kind of mini-survey of the concept of *assu syag laTorah*, of building fences around the Torah, examined through the lens of when such fences are necessary and when they are superfluous.

---

## Mishna Bedika Chametz

### Three Times for Bedika

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 10b records a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* regarding *bedikat chametz*. Rabbi Yehuda identifies three distinct time periods during which the *bedika* may be performed: the night of the fourteenth of Nisan, the morning of the fourteenth, and around the time when *chametz* must be destroyed — roughly midday. The *Chachamim* articulate a different formulation: if one did not perform *bedika* on the night of the fourteenth, one should do so on the fourteenth itself; if not then, during *Chol HaMoed*; if not during *Chol HaMoed*, then after *Yom Tov*. There is a significant dispute among the *Rishonim* — between Rashi and Tosafot — about whether the three stages of the *Chachamim* essentially parallel Rabbi Yehuda's three times, with the sole difference being that the *Chachamim* extend the window through the remainder of *Erev Pesach*, or whether, as Tosafot appear to read more literally, the *Chachamim* permit *bedika* all the way through *Pesach* itself if it was not done earlier — a position Tosafot explicitly link to their broader disagreement with Rashi about the fundamental purpose of *bedikat chametz*. The *mishnah* also records what seems to be an uncontested ruling: whatever *chametz* remains after the *bedika* should be set aside securely so that no further searching is required.

### When Bedika Ends

The *Gemara*'s initial question concerns what Rabbi Yehuda actually means by listing three distinct times. An early proposal — that Rabbi Yehuda derives three separate biblical obligations from three different *pesukim* referring to the removal of *chametz* — is ultimately rejected. The *Gemara* concludes that Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* fundamentally agree: these are not three mandatory moments but three sequential opportunities, each available if the prior one was missed. The real point of contention, the *Gemara* now clarifies, is what happens once the time of prohibition has arrived. On this the two positions are: *mikamei issura in, batar issura la* — before the time of prohibition one may perform *bedika*, but after the prohibition takes effect, one may not. This is the position attributed to Rabbi Yehuda.
