And the reason: *gezeirah dilma ati l'meichal minei* — we are concerned that in the course of performing *bedika* after the prohibition has taken effect, a person might come to eat the *chametz*, which is prohibited by Torah law. The *Chachamim*, by contrast, hold that no such decree is warranted — *lo gazrinan* — and therefore *bedika* may continue even after *chametz* becomes forbidden.

---

## Gezeira & Consumption

### Dilma Ati L'Meichal

This characterization of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning — that he makes a *gezeirah* whenever one might come to consume something prohibited by Torah law — appears to be a general principle. And the *Gemara* immediately presses that assumption by pointing to a conflicting source.

### Chadash Counterexample

The contradiction comes from a *mishnah* in Menachot. The *mishnah* there records that when the *omer* offering was brought on the sixteenth of Nisan, people would go out and find the markets of Jerusalem already filled with *kemach v'kali* — flour and roasted or popped grain — prepared in advance. According to Rabbi Meir, who represents the majority position, this was *shelo birtzon Chachamim*, contrary to the wishes of the sages. But Rabbi Yehuda says: *birtzon Chachamim hayu osim* — this was done with the approval of the sages. The implication is striking. If Rabbi Yehuda holds the general principle that we make a *gezeirah dilma ati l'meichal minei*, why does he here permit the preparation of grain products before the *omer* has been offered and before *chadash* becomes permitted for consumption? The marketplace workers are interacting with grain that remains prohibited — should not Rabbi Yehuda decree against this, lest they come to eat it?

---

## Rava: Shinuy & Zachor

### Shinuy in Harvesting

Rava proposes that *chadash* is categorically different, and that Rabbi Yehuda's general principle can be maintained. The key is the concept of *shinuy* — a modified or altered method of performing the activity. As Rashi explains: *shelo hitarta lo ketzira k'derech kol hashana ela b'yadayim kotfin hamililot min hakarka* — you were not permitted to harvest grain in the normal fashion before the *omer* was brought, since the *omer* was to be *reishit k'tzirchem*, the first of the harvest. Instead, the grain for pre-*omer* preparation was gathered by hand, *kotfin hamlilot*, plucking the stalks from the ground rather than cutting them with a scythe. This deviation from standard harvesting practice constitutes a *shinuy*, and Rashi articulates its function precisely: *zachor hu et issur hachadash al yedei shinuy hama'aseh v'lo ati l'meichal* — the altered method of preparation causes the worker to remember that *chadash* is generally prohibited, and that awareness itself prevents him from coming to eat it. The *shinuy* serves as the mechanism of *zachor*, of keeping the prohibition cognitively present, and because it performs that function, an additional *gezeirah* prohibiting all interaction with the grain becomes unnecessary. This is the *syag* in a different register: not a blanket prohibition, but a required modification that keeps the person alert to the underlying prohibition.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges this resolution. He concedes that at the moment of harvesting a *shinuy* was present. But once the grain moved to subsequent stages of preparation — specifically *t'china*, grinding, and *harkada*, sifting — there is no indication that any *shinuy* was employed. Those who received the grain for further processing would have worked in the ordinary manner. At that stage, the reminder function of the *shinuy* would be absent, and one might therefore come to eat from the grain. If Rabbi Yehuda's principle is that we make a *gezeirah* wherever someone might come to consume something prohibited, the absence of *shinuy* in grinding and sifting should trigger that decree. How, then, does Rabbi Yehuda permit the grain to appear in the marketplace in its final processed form?

### Shinuy Resolved

The *Gemara* responds: *ha lo kashya* — this is no problem at all. In fact, *shinuyim* were employed at each of these later stages as well. The grinding was done *b'reichaya d'yad*, with a hand millstone rather than a water-powered mill, which as Rashi notes was the standard grinding apparatus: *lo hayu tochnin oto b'reichayim shel mayim ela b'reichayim shel yad d'hava shinuy l'zikaron* — they did not grind with a water mill but with a hand mill, which constituted a change that served to keep the prohibition in memory. The hand mill is not only a different tool but a less efficient one, and both the difference and the difficulty heighten the grinder's awareness that something out of the ordinary is occurring. Similarly, the sifting was done *al gabay naffa*, on the reverse side of the sifter — turned upside down and used in an inverted manner, again a less effective and deliberately altered procedure. With *shinuyim* present at every stage of preparation, the original resolution holds: Rabbi Yehuda did not need to decree against this preparation because the altered methods at each step ensured that the workers would remain aware of the prohibition and not come to eat from the grain. One note worth flagging: it is not clear that this answer about *shinuyim* in grinding and sifting appears elsewhere in the Talmud — it may be offered only here, in the context of this *sugya*'s effort to map Rabbi Yehuda's position, perhaps generated by the pressure of this local question rather than as a freestanding tradition from Menachot.

---

## Harvesting Non-Omer Fiel…

### Ella Hadetnan Kashya

With the *shinuy*-based resolution apparently in hand, the *Gemara* surfaces a further difficulty. A different *mishnah* states: *kotzrin beit hashlachim v'shebe'amakim* — one may harvest from irrigated fields and from valley fields before the *omer* is brought. As Rashi explains, these are fields whose produce is environmentally inferior and from which the *omer* would never be taken; the conflict between two *pesukim* about the *omer* — one implying some pre-*omer* harvesting is permitted, the other indicating the *omer* must be the first of the harvest — is resolved by limiting the prior rule to fields of this category. Critically, this *mishnah* was established elsewhere in Menachot as reflecting the position of Rabbi Yehuda. And here there is no mention of any *shinuy* in the harvesting. This is ordinary harvesting, simply of fields that are categorically ineligible to supply the *omer*. If Rabbi Yehuda's principle is that a *gezeirah* is avoided only when a *shinuy* is present to remind the person of the prohibition, this case — harvesting without any *shinuy*, of grain that remains prohibited for consumption until the *omer* is brought — should require a *gezeirah*. Rava's *shinuy*-based framework cannot account for it.

### Abaye: Badil Minei

This objection effectively demolishes Rava's approach, and Abaye now offers a fundamentally different answer. *Chadash badil minei, chametz lo badil minei* — with *chadash*, people naturally separate from it and are on guard about it; with *chametz*, they do not. *Chadash* is a category of prohibition that operates across virtually the entire year — all grain from the prior year's crop is forbidden until the sixteenth of Nisan. People have an ingrained consciousness of *chadash* as something from which they must remain separate. This categorical wariness, this being *badil minei*, means that a person working with *chadash* grain will not simply eat it; the very nature of the item, as something from which one perpetually maintains distance, provides sufficient protection against inadvertent consumption. Therefore Rabbi Yehuda needs no additional *gezeirah* — neither of the blanket-prohibition type nor of the *shinuy* type — when it comes to *chadash*. The protection is already built into the person's relationship with the category of food.

*Chametz*, by contrast, is ordinary food. It is perfectly permitted for consumption for the vast majority of the year. A person's normal, comfortable, unreflective relationship with *chametz* as food — *lo badil minei* — means that when one encounters it even in a context involving prohibition, the instinct of familiarity remains. There is nothing in the nature of *chametz* itself that would cause a person to pause. That is precisely why Rabbi Yehuda enacts the *gezeirah* in the case of *bedikat chametz* after the time of prohibition: the item is not one from which people naturally separate, and without an external legal constraint, the person doing *bedika* might simply eat what is at hand.

This exchange also illuminates the apparent contradiction that Rava had raised about the positions of the *Rabbanan* themselves. In Menachot, Rabbi Meir — representing the *Chachamim* — indicated that the *Chachamim* were unhappy with grain preparation before the *omer*, suggesting they do hold a concern of *dilma ati l'meichal minei*. But in our *mishnah*, the *Chachamim* allow *bedika* even after *chametz* becomes prohibited, apparently without such concern. The *Gemara* resolves this: *hu atzmo mechazer alav le-sorfo, meichal ka-achil minei?* — the person performing *bedika* is actively engaged in collecting the *chametz* for destruction. The entire mindset and motivation of the activity is elimination, not consumption. Given that context, the rabbis hold that one simply will not come to eat the *chametz* in the middle of the *bedika*. The activity itself provides the cognitive protection.

---

## Rav Ashi Rejected

### Technical Non-Edibility

Rav Ashi enters with a different approach, attempting a more technical resolution of the contradiction between the two *mishnayot* — the one in Pesachim about *bedika* and the one in Menachot about grain in the marketplace. He proposes: *kemach v'kali tnan* — what the *mishnah* tells us was found in the marketplace is flour and roasted grain, and these items, as Rashi notes — *v'ein elu reuyin l'achilah* — are simply not edible in the form in which they appeared. If the grain products in the marketplace were never in an edible state at the time of preparation, there is no concern that one might come to eat them, and therefore Rabbi Yehuda had no occasion to make a *gezeirah*. The prohibition of *dilma ati l'meichal minei* presupposes that eating is a live possibility; if the item on hand is not ready for consumption, the premise of the concern does not arise.

### Beduta Hi Rejection

The *Gemara* dismisses this answer: *ha d'Rav Ashi beduta hi* — what Rav Ashi said is a fabrication. The term *beduta* is a strong form of rejection used when a position is so untenable that it is attributed not to the named authority himself but to a student's misunderstanding or misreport. The *Gemara* itself supplies the evidence: *lechem v'kali v'karmel lo tochlu* — the Torah explicitly lists *kali* among items one may not eat until the *omer*, implying it is in principle edible. Beyond that, the *Gemara* presses: even if *kali* in its final roasted form might be considered not fully edible, *ha teinach mi'kali va'eilach mei'ikara v'ad kali mai ika l'meimar* — at some point in the process of roasting the grain, before it reached its final form, the grain passed through a stage when it was edible, and at that moment the concern of *dilma ati l'meichal minei* should have applied. Rav Ashi cannot account for that intermediate stage. The *Gemara* then briefly considers whether one might rescue Rav Ashi by combining his approach with Rava's *shinuy* argument — perhaps the *shinuyim* in harvesting applied through those intermediate stages — but this too is rejected, because the problem of fields not eligible for the *omer* being harvested without any *shinuy* remains unresolved. *Ela d'Rav Ashi beduta hi* — Rav Ashi's position is definitively set aside. We are left with Abaye's framework of *badil minei* and *lo badil minei* as the operative organizing principle.

---

## Badil Minei Framework

### Lo Badil Minei Question

With Abaye's framework now established, the *Gemara* subjects it to a pair of probing questions. The first: *v'chi heicha d'lo badil minei migzar Rabbi Yehuda?* — is it truly the case that everywhere one is *lo badil minei*, not naturally separated from an item, Rabbi Yehuda makes a *gezeirah*? The presumption being tested is that Rabbi Yehuda's rule is exceptionless in the *lo badil minei* direction — that any item with which a person is comfortable and unreflective automatically generates a rabbinic decree when Torah-level violation is possible.

### Shfoferet Shel Beitza

The counterexample comes from the second chapter of tractate Shabbat, the chapter of *Bameh Madlikin*. The *mishnah* there states that a person may not puncture a hole in a *shfoferet shel beitzah* — an eggshell — fill it with oil, and position it beside the Shabbat lamp so that oil drips steadily from the shell into the lamp, feeding it additional oil as the lamp burns. The prohibition applies even if the shell is made of earthenware. Rashi clarifies the setting: a *ner* in this context means an oil lamp with a wick floating in it, not a wax candle; and the concern is that the oil feeder is positioned above or beside the lamp so that oil drips through a tiny puncture into the flame. The worry is that the person will take some of that oil for use at the Shabbat table — perhaps for food — and in doing so will draw oil away from the lamp, thereby hastening its extinction, which constitutes the prohibited *melacha* of *mechabeh*, extinguishing. The concern was heightened by the fact that the Shabbat lamp in antiquity typically stood at the table where the meal was served, making the oil physically proximate to food. The *mishnah* specifies that even earthenware was not exempt — one might have thought that the grosser material would be *ma'us*, repugnant enough that a person would not help themselves to it for food, but the *mishnah* says this concern overrides even that consideration. And Rabbi Yehuda — *Rabbi Yehuda matir* — permits the eggshell feeder arrangement entirely.

This is surprising. Oil is quintessentially a *lo badil minei* substance — people are entirely at ease with oil, it is ordinary food, there is nothing about oil that naturally puts one on guard. If Rabbi Yehuda makes a *gezeirah* whenever one is *lo badil minei*, he should make a *gezeirah* here against using the feeder, lest one take oil from the lamp for food. And yet Rabbi Yehuda allows it, while the *Chachamim* prohibit it. This seems to invert what we would expect: it is the *Chachamim* who are making the stricter *gezeirah*, and Rabbi Yehuda who is lenient.

### Chumra d'Shabbat

The resolution is formulated as a new principle: *hatam mishum chumra deShabbat mivdal badilei* — there, in the context of Shabbat, because of the *chumra d'Shabbat*, the weight and strictness of Shabbat, people are *mivdal badilei*, they are naturally in a separated and cautious posture. Rabbeinu Chananel phrases it similarly: *shanei Shabbat dechamir lei* — Shabbat is different because it is strict to the person. The key to understanding *chumra d'Shabbat* is not simply that Shabbat carries severe punishment — *karet* is no less severe for other violations — but rather something about the phenomenology of Shabbat as it is experienced: the density of its prohibitions, the many *gezeirot* and *syagim* layered upon it, the sense that one is always near the edge of potential transgression. Shabbat generates a pervasive personal wariness, an internal *chumra*, that keeps people alert. Because of this, even a *lo badil minei* substance like oil becomes, on Shabbat, something one handles with caution. That caution functions as a substitute for a specific *gezeirah*, and therefore Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a *gezeirah* is unnecessary when one is already *badil minei*, does not need to make a decree about the oil feeder. The *Chachamim*, by contrast, do not accept *chumra d'Shabbat* as a sufficient substitute and therefore maintain their prohibition.

---

## Kesher vs. Aniva

### Bucket Rope Dispute

A tangential but structurally important sub-discussion now arises. Having established that the *Chachamim* and Rabbi Yehuda have opposite positions on the oil feeder (*Chachamim* strict, Rabbi Yehuda lenient), the *Gemara* raises a *baraita* about a different Shabbat case that appears to reverse their roles. The *baraita* states: if the rope of a bucket has snapped on Shabbat, one may not tie it back together — tying a *kesher shel kayama*, an enduring knot, is a prohibited *melacha* on Shabbat — but one may make an *aniva*, a loop, which is a temporary configuration rather than a true knot. Rabbi Yehuda, however, says one may take a *punda* or *piskiya* — a sash, belt, or some third cord — and wrap it around the broken ends, even tying it with some form of temporary tie, but one may *not* make a plain loop using only the two ends of the original rope.

This seems to be a contradiction within each camp. The *Chachamim*, who were stricter about the oil feeder, here appear lenient: they permit the loop. Rabbi Yehuda, who was lenient about the oil feeder on the grounds that *chumra d'Shabbat* provides adequate caution, is here strict: he forbids even the loop using the original rope. The *Gemara* frames this explicitly: *kashya d'Rabbi Yehuda ad Rabbi Yehuda, kashya d'Rabbanan ad Rabbanan* — there is a contradiction within Rabbi Yehuda's position and within the Rabbis' position.

### Shemen vs. Aniva

The resolution offered is elegant and operates differently for each camp. Regarding the *Rabbanan*: *shemen b'shemen michlaf, aniva b'keshira lo michlaf* — oil is interchangeable with oil; a person looking at oil for the lamp and oil for the table is looking at the same substance, and it is easy and natural to transfer from one use to the other. That is why the *Chachamim* were concerned enough to prohibit the oil feeder. But an *aniva* — a loop — is not the same activity as a *kesher* — a knot — and the transition from one to the other is not natural or easy. *Aniva b'keshira lo michlaf*: one making a loop will not be led by that action to make a knot. Hence the *Chachamim* have no concern about permitting the loop; there is no realistic path from the permitted act to the prohibited one.

Regarding Rabbi Yehuda: *ta'ama d'Rabbi Yehuda lav mishum d'gazar aniva atu keshira, ella mishum d'kasavar aniva gufa keshira hi* — Rabbi Yehuda's reason for prohibiting the loop is not that he worries it will lead to a knot. Rather, Rabbi Yehuda holds that an *aniva* is itself, by its legal nature, a form of *keshira* — it is a binding, and he treats it with the same stringency as a proper knot. His strictness here has nothing to do with the logic of *gezeirot* at all; it reflects his substantive position about what constitutes a forbidden tying. The two cases are therefore not actually in tension: Rabbi Yehuda is lenient about the oil feeder because *chumra d'Shabbat* renders the *gezeirah* unnecessary, and he is strict about the loop because he categorically considers a loop a form of knot.

The *Gemara* also explores a further internal question within the *Rabbanan*'s position — *verami Rabbanan ad Rabbanan* — raised by another *mishnah* which states that one may tie a bucket with a *piskiya* but not with a rope. The resolution there similarly turns on *michlaf*: ropes are interchangeable with other ropes, so using a weaver's rope (*chevel d'gardi*, a cord used professionally and expected to be removed promptly) could lead to using ordinary rope, and therefore the *Rabbanan* extend the prohibition to all rope. But this does not conflict with their leniency toward the loop, since *aniva b'keshira lo michlafa* — looping and knotting remain categorically distinct activities that do not naturally lead one to the other.

---

## Badil Minei Question

### Bechor Bloodletting

The *Gemara* now turns to the other side of the *badil minei* framework. Having confirmed, through the resolution of the oil-feeder case, that *chumra d'Shabbat* means even a *lo badil minei* substance does not require a *gezeirah* in the Shabbat context, the *Gemara* now asks: *v'chol heicha d'badilei minei lo gazar Rabbi Yehuda?* — is it truly the case that everywhere one *is* naturally separated from something, Rabbi Yehuda feels no need to decree? This is the other flank of the principle, and the *Gemara* brings a *baraita* that appears to undermine it.

The *baraita* concerns a *bechor* — a firstborn animal that belongs to the *kohen* and may not be used for ordinary purposes or caused to have a *mum*, a blemish. If a *bechor* is afflicted with an excess of blood — a medical condition requiring bloodletting — there is in principle a permissible way to treat it: one may bleed the animal in a location where the bloodletting will not create a permanent *mum*, since a minor puncture in such a location will heal without trace. Rabbi Yehuda, however, says: *afilu hu met, ein makizin lo dam* — even if the animal is going to die, we do not perform bloodletting. The *Chachamim* say: *yakiz, u'vilvad shelo yatil bo mum* — one may perform bloodletting, as long as one takes care not to create a *mum*.

A *bechor* is paradigmatically a *badil minei* item — it is hedged about with restrictions, it cannot be used by a non-*kohen*, one must not cause it a *mum*, people are cautious around it. And yet Rabbi Yehuda makes a *gezeirah* even here, prohibiting even the permissible form of bloodletting. This contradicts the principle that *badil minei* renders a *gezeirah* unnecessary.

### Adam Bahul al Mamono

The *Gemara* explains: *hatam mishum she'adam bahul al mamono* — this case invokes the principle that a person is *bahul al mamono*, anxious and agitated about their financial assets. Rashi on 11b specifies: *kohen zeh bahul al bechor shelo yamut* — the *kohen* is intensely worried that the animal will die, because once it dies it has no monetary value to him, whereas even a *bechor* with a *mum* can be slaughtered and eaten. That financial anxiety — the *bahul* quality, the worked-up, barely-contained worry about money — overrides the *badil minei* protection. Why? *Ei sharit lei b'makom she'ein osin bo mum, ati l'me'evad b'makom she'osin bo mum* — if you permit the *kohen* to do bloodletting in the location that does not create a *mum*, he is so anxious that when the permissible method proves insufficient or uncertain, he will simply bleed the animal wherever it takes, including locations that would create a permanent *mum*. His anxiety will erode his capacity to maintain the line between the permitted location and the prohibited one. *Adam bahul al mamono* thus constitutes a separate factor that can override *badil minei*: when financial anxiety is at such an acute level that it undermines the normal capacity for self-regulation, even a *badil minei* situation requires a *gezeirah*.

### Chachamim Pragmatism

The *Chachamim* counter with a pragmatic argument that is both legally and psychologically interesting: *kol sheken de-i lo sharit lei klal, ati l'me'evad* — all the more so, if you do not permit him anything at all, he will act anyway. The *Chachamim*'s position reflects a kind of legal realism: when someone is genuinely *bahul al mamono*, total prohibition may be less effective than a targeted permission. Give the *kohen* a lawful outlet for his anxiety — the permissible form of bloodletting — and the relief it provides makes it more likely, not less, that he will restrain himself from the forbidden form. The logic resembles the principle that a *gezeirah she'ein ha-tzibur yakhol la-amod bah* — a decree the community cannot abide — is itself invalid. Here, a decree that does not actually address the underlying anxiety may generate worse outcomes than a permission that channels the behavior in a lawful direction. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, holds that the anxiety is too destabilizing to trust that the *kohen* will maintain even the distinction between permitted and prohibited forms of bloodletting, and therefore the total *gezeirah* is the only effective protection.

---

## Kidur vs. Kartsuf

### Combing Methods

A final test case is drawn from the laws of *Yom Tov* and animal care. A *mishnah* and *baraita* discuss combing animals — specifically, removing fleas, dirt, or embedded matter from an animal's coat. The concern is that the combing might create a *chaburah*, a bruise or wound, which would be prohibited on *Yom Tov*. The *baraita* defines the two implements: *kidor* refers to a fine-toothed comb — small, closely set teeth — which is likely to cause a bruise; *kartsuf* refers to a wide-toothed comb — large, widely spaced teeth — which does not cause a bruise. Rabbi Yehuda holds that *kidor*, the fine-toothed comb, is prohibited on *Yom Tov*, but one may use the *kartsuf*. The *Chachamim* prohibit both: *ein mekadrin v'af ein mekartsfin*.

### Comparative Gezeirot

This raises a question that brings the discussion full circle back to *chametz*. With *kartsuf*, one is in a *lo badil minei* relationship with the animal — this is one's regular livestock, a familiar creature one handles constantly. If Rabbi Yehuda makes a *gezeirah* whenever one is *lo badil minei* and there is potential for a Torah-level violation, why does he not make a *gezeirah* against using the *kartsuf* as well, lest one reach for the *kidor*? The comparison to *chametz* makes the question sharp: Rabbi Yehuda prohibits *bedika* after the time of *chametz* prohibition, but here he permits the wide-toothed combing method, even though the potential violation — using the fine-toothed comb and causing a *chaburah* — is real.

### Lechem vs. Kidur

The resolution: *lechem b'lechem michlaf, kidor b'kartsuf lo michlaf* — bread is interchangeable with bread; *kidor* and *kartsuf* are not interchangeable with each other. When a person is handling *chametz* during the period of prohibition, and *chametz* looks and smells and feels exactly like the bread they eat every day of the year, the transition from handling to eating is frictionless — *lo badil minei* in the most concrete sense, because the object is identical in kind and appearance to permitted food. The *gezeirah* is required because the forbidden and the permitted are phenomenologically indistinguishable. But *kidor* and *kartsuf* are distinct implements: they look different, they feel different in the hand, the teeth are different. *Lo michlaf* — one simply does not confuse them. A person using the wide-toothed *kartsuf* will not inadvertently reach for the fine-toothed *kidor* instead. Since the transition from the permitted to the prohibited act requires a deliberate change of implement, there is no realistic path from one to the other, and no *gezeirah* is required.

---

## Summary & Framework

### Abaye's Synthesis

With this final case, the *sugya* completes its traversal of the conceptual landscape. Abaye's principle — that a *gezeirah* against interaction with a prohibited item is required when one does not naturally separate from that item, and is unnecessary when one does — emerges as the organizing framework for Rabbi Yehuda's position. The burden of the *sugya* has been to test this principle from both directions, and to identify the factors that complicate its application.

### Multiple Factors

What the *sugya* ultimately yields is not a single clean rule but an array of interlocking considerations. The base principle is *badil minei* and *lo badil minei*: when a person naturally separates from a category of item — because it is habitually prohibited, like *chadash*, or because it is classified as sacred and restricted, like *bechor* — the separation itself provides the protection that a *gezeirah* would otherwise supply. When a person does not naturally separate from an item — as with *chametz*, an ordinary food prohibited only at a particular time of year — a *gezeirah* is needed to supply that protection externally.

But the principle interacts with other factors. *Chumra d'Shabbat* — the general wariness and heightened alertness that characterizes a person's orientation toward Shabbat — can substitute for *badil minei* even with respect to a *lo badil minei* substance, rendering a *gezeirah* unnecessary. *Adam bahul al mamono* — a person's acute financial anxiety — can override *badil minei* by eroding the self-regulation that would ordinarily protect against violation, making a *gezeirah* necessary even in a *badil minei* context. And *michlaf* — the interchangeability or distinguishability of the permitted and prohibited items or activities — determines whether the concern that one will slide from a permitted act to a prohibited one is realistic enough to require legal intervention. Where items or actions are easily confused (*lechem b'lechem, shemen b'shemen, chevel b'chevel*), a *gezeirah* is warranted; where they are categorically distinct (*kidor b'kartsuf, aniva b'keshira*), no *gezeirah* is needed. The entire discussion is, at its depth, an inquiry into the conditions under which the institution of *assu syag laTorah* is both necessary and sufficient.

---

---

# Pesachim 14

## Levels of Tumah

### Six Levels of Tumah

The *mishnah* at the top of 14a opens a discussion about the various levels of *tuma* and whether one may mix items of different *tuma* levels when burning them. Before turning to the specific cases, it is worth reviewing the structure of *tuma* transmission. The highest level is the *avi avot hatuma* — the granddaddy of *tuma* — which is the dead body itself. There is a special extension of this category: metal that comes into contact with a corpse attains the same status as the corpse itself, as we will see later. Something that touches the dead body becomes an *av hatuma*. Something that touches the *av hatuma* becomes a *rishon letuma* — also called by the *mishnah* a *vlad hatuma*, the "child" of the higher level. From there the chain continues: *sheni*, *shlishi*, and *revi'i*. Not everything, however, can reach each of these lower levels. Generally speaking, only *ochlin u'mashkin* — food and liquids — transmit *tuma* at these lower levels, and at the further degrees perhaps only *teruma* or *kodshim* are affected at all.

The overarching problem the *mishnah* is addressing is this: when *kodshim*, *teruma*, or *chametz* must be burned and destroyed, is it permitted to mix items of different *tuma* levels together — thereby either increasing the *tuma* of one item or, in some cases, conveying *tuma* to something *tahor* in the first place? Because these items are being destroyed, perhaps the usual concern about increasing *tuma* does not apply.

### Rabbi Chanina Case

Rabbi Chanina *Sgan HaKohanim* — the vice *kohen gadol* — states: *mi-yemeihem shel kohanim lo nimneu milisrof et habasar she-nitma bivlad hatuma im habasar she-nitma be-av hatuma* — in all the days of the *kohanim*, they never refrained from burning meat that became *tamei* through a *vlad hatuma* (i.e., a *rishon letuma*, rendering it a *sheni letuma*) together with meat that became *tamei* through an *av hatuma* (i.e., a *rishon letuma*). This is permitted *af al pi she-mosifin tuma al tumato* — even though one is thereby increasing the *tuma* level — because the items are in any case being destroyed.

### Rabbi Akiva Case

Rabbi Akiva added a further case: *mi-yemeihem shel kohanim lo nimneu milahadlik et hashemen she-nifsal bitvul yom bener she-nitma betmei meit* — they also never refrained from lighting oil that had become *nifsal* through contact with a *tvul yom* together with a lamp that had become *tamei* through a person who was *tamei* through the dead body.

The word *pasul* rather than *tamei* is used for levels below *rishon letuma* because at those levels *tuma* is generally not transmitted onward to other objects. The oil that touched a *tvul yom* — a person who has immersed in a *mikvah* and is awaiting nightfall — is a *shlishi letuma*. The lamp that was made *tamei* by contact with a person who had touched a *tamei meit* is a *sheni letuma*. Rabbi Akiva similarly permits mixing these while burning, *af al pi she-mosifin tuma al tumato*.

## Rabbi Meir Inference

### Meir's Deduction

From the practices described by Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Meir draws a practical ruling: *she-sorfin teruma tehora im hatmeia b'Pesach* — on *Erev Pesach*, when *chametz* that is *teruma* must be burned, one may burn the *tahor* portion together with the *tamei* portion, without concern about conveying *tuma* to the *tahor teruma* in the process. The rationale is that since the items are being burned, we are unconcerned with increasing or transmitting *tuma*.

### Yossi Objection

Rabbi Yossi disagrees: *ein hi hamidda* — this is not a valid analogy. One cannot derive the rules governing *chametz* from the rules governing the burning of *teruma* or *kodshim*. The *gemara* will elaborate on why the two contexts are not comparable.

### Eliezer/Yehoshua

The *mishnah* notes that despite their broader dispute, both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree with Rabbi Yossi's position that one must burn the *tamei* portion of *chametz teruma* separately from the *tahor* portion — *sorfin zo le'atzmah vezu le'atzmah*. Where do Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua themselves disagree? Their dispute concerns *teruma* in a state of *safek tumah* — doubtful *tuma* — and whether it may be burned together with *teruma* that is definitely *tamei*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that even the *safek* must be burned separately; Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the *safek* and the definitely *tamei* may be burned together.

## Levels Analysis

### First Case Levels

The *gemara* now proceeds to analyze the precise *tuma* levels in each case of the *mishnah*. Regarding the first case — meat that became *tamei* through a *vlad hatuma* — the *gemara* asks: *mah havei*? What level is that? It is a *sheni letuma*. And the meat that became *tamei* through an *av hatuma* — what is that? That is a *rishon letuma*. When you burn them together, the *rishon* makes the *sheni* — a *sheni*. But the *sheni* was already a *sheni*. So in what sense is one adding *tuma* to the other? The novelty the *mishnah* is teaching appears elusive.

### Sheni Transmission

One might wonder whether the problem the *mishnah* is addressing concerns the *rishon* being elevated in some way by contact with the *sheni*, or vice versa. The deeper issue the *gemara* is probing is whether *sheni letuma* can transmit *tuma* to other food at all — and if it cannot, then what precisely is the *chiddush* of burning them together?

A *baraita* is cited: *yakhol yiheyeh ochel metamei ochel* — one might think that at the level of *sheni letuma* food can make other food *tamei*. The *pasuk* teaches: *ve-chi yutan mayim al zera ve-nafal mi-nivlatam alav tamei hu* — when water falls on a seed and a *neveilah* comes in contact with it, it becomes *tamei*. The *derasha* drawn from the word *hu* is: *hu tamei ve-ein oseh kayotzei bo tamei* — that food itself becomes *tamei* but does not transmit its *tuma* to other food. Rather, at that level it can only make liquids *tamei*.

### Rav Yehudah View

Rav Yehudah offers an emendation to the *mishnah*: *hacha bivlad vlad askinan de-havei lei shlishi* — the case actually involves not a *vlad hatuma* but a *vlad vlad hatuma*, meaning a *shlishi letuma*, and the ruling is that *shlishi mutar la'asoto sheni* — it is permitted to make a *shlishi* into a *sheni* when burning, since these items are being destroyed in any case.

The *gemara* challenges this: *veha ein ochel metamei ochel* — but does not the principle that food does not transmit *tuma* to food apply here? At the level of *shlishi letuma*, food cannot make other food *tamei* — it can only affect liquids.

### Ochel Transmission

Two Amoraic positions address this difficulty. Abaye holds: *lo shanu ela be-chulin* — the rule that food does not transmit *tuma* to food applies only to *chulin*. But with *teruma* and *kodshim*, food does transmit *tuma* to food. According to Abaye's view, the *mishnah* is discussing *kodshim*, and the *chiddush* is that even in this context — where the transmission is real and significant — one is permitted to burn them together. Rav Adda bar Ahava (citing Rava) goes one step further: this limitation applies to *chulin* and *teruma*, but *kodshim* food can transmit *tuma* to other *kodshim* food. Either way, the *mishnah* is dealing with *kodshim*.

### Liquid Resolution

A further position is attributed to Ravina, also citing Rava: *mikra malei divrei ha-kasuv* — the verse is comprehensive, and food does not transmit *tuma* to food regardless of category — whether *chulin*, *teruma*, or *kodshim*. According to Ravina, the *mishnah* cannot be explained by reference to food-to-food transmission at all. The *gemara* answers: *hacha mai askinan de-ika mashkin bahadi basar* — the *mishnah* is discussing meat that has liquid on its surface. The rule that food does not transmit *tuma* to food does not apply to liquids; food transmits *tuma* to liquids readily. Therefore, the *chiddush* is that even though by burning the meat together one is making the liquid *tamei* at a higher level, it is permitted because they are being destroyed.

The *gemara* raises a stylistic question: if the case depends on the presence of liquid on the meat's surface, why does the *mishnah* not mention the liquid explicitly? The *gemara* ultimately resolves this by proposing: *ella nehi de-ein ochel mitamei ochel mi-de-oraita, aval mi-derabbanan mihu mitamei* — granted that *mi-de-oraita* food does not transmit *tuma* to food at the *sheni* level, nonetheless *mi-derabbanan* such transmission does exist. It is this *de-rabbanan* concern that the *mishnah* is addressing, and it is telling us that because these items are being burned, we need not be concerned even with that *de-rabbanan* transmission.

## Oil & Lamp Case

### Oil/Lamp Levels

The *gemara* now turns to analyze the second case in the *mishnah* — that of Rabbi Akiva. The oil that became *nifsal* through a *tvul yom*: *mah havei*? It is a *shlishi letuma*. The *tvul yom* is himself a *sheni letuma*, and what he touches becomes a *shlishi*. And the lamp *she-nitma betmei meis* — that became *tamei* through a person who had contact with the dead: *mah havei*? Here the *mishnah* means that the lamp touched someone who had himself touched a *tamei meit* — that person is a *rishon letuma*, and the lamp he touched is a *sheni letuma*. So Rabbi Akiva's case involves oil that is a *shlishi* and a lamp that is a *sheni*. The apparent *chiddush* would be that *shlishi mutar la'asoto sheni* — one may elevate a *shlishi* to a *sheni* in the process of burning. But the *gemara* asks: *hainu hach* — is this not the same as what we already learned from the meat case? What does Rabbi Akiva add?

### Metal Lamp Status

Rabbi Yehudah explains: *hacha bener shel matechet askinan* — here we are dealing with a metal lamp. And metal has a special halakhic status that changes the calculus entirely.

### Metal Rule

The *gemara* explains immediately: *drachmana amar bechalal cherev, cherev harei hu kechalal* — the Torah, in describing the *tuma* of the dead, uses the phrase "through a sword," and from this we derive that the sword and the *chalal* (the corpse) are on the same level. Metal that touches a corpse does not descend a level — it attains *av hatuma* status in its own right. By extension, this principle is generalized to all metal: metal attains the same *tuma* level as what it touches, rather than descending one level as food or vessels ordinarily do.

In Rabbi Akiva's case, a person who touched the dead body is a *rishon letuma*. The metal lamp that this *rishon* touched becomes — not a *sheni* as one might expect — but itself a *rishon letuma*, because metal jumps up a category. With the oil being a *shlishi letuma*, burning the two together does not merely jump one level — it jumps two levels. That is the *chiddush* Rabbi Akiva adds over Rabbi Chanina's case.

### Rava Alternative

Rava proposes an alternative approach that does not require specifying a metal lamp. One could explain the *mishnah* as dealing with an ordinary clay lamp, and the *chiddush* of Rabbi Akiva would then be different: *deilu hatam tamei vetamei* — in Rabbi Chanina's first case, both items are in the category of *tamei* — one is a *rishon* and the other is a *sheni*. *Veilu hacha pasul vetamei* — but here in Rabbi Akiva's case, one is *pasul* (the *shlishi*) and one is *tamei* (the *sheni*). Even though the jump is only one level, it crosses a qualitative category — from the realm of *pasul*, which does not transmit *tuma* to other things, into the realm of *tamei*, which does. That categorical crossing is itself a *chiddush*.

### Meis Specification

However, Rava notes that this alternative reading runs into a difficulty from the *mishnah* itself: *matnitin kashya lei*. The *mishnah* specifies *ner she-nitma betamei meis* — a lamp that became *tamei* through a *tamei meit*. Why specify *tumas meit* in particular? Let the *mishnah* have used *tumas sheretz* — impurity from a creeping creature — which would work equally well if we were only talking about a one-level categorical jump. The fact that the *mishnah* specifically chooses *tumas meit* indicates that something unique about *tumas meit* is at play. And what is uniquely different about *tumas meit* as opposed to *tumas sheretz*? Metal — since metal uniquely attains *av hatuma* status when it touches a corpse, but not when it touches a *sheretz*. Therefore, *ela eizehu davar she-chaluka tumato bein tumas meit le-sheretz hevei omer zeh mateschet* — the distinction between *tumas meit* and *tumas sheretz* points to metal. This confirms Rabbi Yehudah's reading: the *mishnah* is discussing a metal lamp, and Rabbi Akiva's *chiddush* is the two-level jump.

### Liquids Transmission

Rava draws a further inference from this: *shma mina kasvar Rabbi Akiva tumas mashkin letamei acherim de-oraita* — from this case we can conclude that Rabbi Akiva holds the *tuma* of liquids to transmit *tuma* to other objects is *de-oraita*. The reasoning: what exactly is the metal lamp doing to the oil in this case? If the lamp's function were merely to render the oil *pasul* — unfit for temple use — the oil is already *pasul* and the lamp adds nothing. The lamp must therefore be conveying genuine *tuma* to the oil, elevating it from *shlishi* to *sheni*. This transmission would have to pass through the liquid surface of the oil, and for that to be significant it must be *de-oraita*.

The *gemara* interjects: perhaps the transmission is only *de-rabbanan*, not *de-oraita*? The response: *im miderabbanan mai irya be'av hatumah afilu berishon uvesheni nami* — if we were dealing entirely with *de-rabbanan* concerns, why would the *mishnah* need to specify a case involving the *av hatuma* derived from *tumas meit*? The entire structure of *rishon* and *sheni* is *de-rabbanan* in the first place, so if Rabbi Akiva's case were also *de-rabbanan*, the specific choice of *av hatuma* would be unmotivated. The *gemara* confirms this from a *mishnah* elsewhere: *kol ha-posel et ha-teruma metamei mashkin lihyot techila* — anything that renders *teruma* unfit can make liquids *tamei* as a *rishon*, *chutz mi-tvul yom* — except for a *tvul yom* which is an exception. Therefore, we must be speaking of *de-oraita* transmission, and Rava's conclusion stands.

## Chametz Learning

### Meir from Chanina

The *gemara* now returns to Rabbi Meir's attempt to derive a ruling about *chametz* from the cases of Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Akiva. From which case does Rabbi Meir learn? If one suggests it is from Rabbi Chanina's case of the meat — *mi domei*? — is it analogous? *Hasam tamei vetamei, hacha tahor vetamei* — there, both items were *tamei*, merely at different levels; here, one item is *tahor* entirely and one is *tamei*. The case of the meat cannot serve as the source, because Rabbi Chanina speaks only of changing *tuma* levels, not of conveying *tuma* to something *tahor* in the first place.

### Meir from Akiva

What then of Rabbi Akiva's case of the oil and lamp? Again — *mi domei*? *Hasam pasul vetamei, hacha tahor vetamei*. Rabbi Akiva's case similarly involves changing the degree of *tuma* — from *pasul* to *tamei* — not the introduction of *tuma* to something that was *tahor*. That too cannot directly prove Rabbi Meir's point.

### Meir Position

The *gemara* therefore proposes a way to salvage Rabbi Meir's inference: *neima kasavar Rabbi Meir matnitin be-avi tumah de-oraita ve-vlad ha-tumah de-rabbanan* — perhaps Rabbi Meir holds that the *av hatuma* discussed in the *mishnah* is a genuine *de-oraita* level of *tuma*, while the *vlad hatuma* — the *rishon letuma* — is only *de-rabbanan*. On this reading, *de-midoraita* the corresponding piece of *teruma chametz* that is a *vlad hatuma* is essentially *tahor* — the *de-rabbanan* status does not constitute real *tuma* in a *de-oraita* sense. And it is from Rabbi Chanina's case that Rabbi Meir learns: just as the *kohanim* would burn meat that is *av hatuma* together with what is, in *de-oraita* terms, *tahor* (*vlad hatuma* being only *de-rabbanan*), so too one may burn *chametz teruma* that is genuinely *tamei* together with *chametz teruma* whose *tuma* is only *de-rabbanan* — and in *de-oraita* terms is *tahor*.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish, citing Bar Kappara, takes a different position: *matnitin be-avi tumah de-oraita ve-vlad ha-tumah de-oraita* — the *mishnah* discusses levels of *tuma* that are both *de-oraita*, and Rabbi Meir learns from the end of the *mishnah* — from the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. Those *tanna'im* agree that definitely *tahor* and definitely *tamei* *teruma* must be burned separately on *Erev Pesach*; their dispute is only about *safek tumah* burned together with definite *tamei*. Reish Lakish reads Rabbi Meir as learning from the position adopted by Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

### Which Yehoshua

Which Rabbi Yehoshua does Reish Lakish have in mind? The *gemara* raises the possibility that it is the Rabbi Yehoshua of a *mishnah* elsewhere, who rules that if one has a barrel of *teruma* in a state of *safek tumah*, one should place it in the open and allow it to become definitely *tamei* — rather than continuing to protect it. This implies that it is better to give the *teruma* a definite *tuma* status so that it can be properly burned. However, the *gemara* objects: *hasam grama b'alma* — there, Rabbi Yehoshua is speaking of only indirect causation, placing the barrel where it is likely to contract *tuma* rather than actively conveying *tuma*. *Hacha b'yadayim* — here we are speaking of actively mixing *tahor* and *tamei* together by hand. The two cases are not analogous. The question of precisely which statement of Rabbi Yehoshua Reish Lakish intends will require further analysis in the continuation of the *gemara*.

---

---

# Pesachim 15

## Witness Testimony & Cham…

### Rav Ashi's Position

The daf opens near the bottom of 12b, where the Gemara presents the ruling of Rav Ashi. The broader sugya has been examining how much latitude witnesses are permitted in their determination of time — specifically, whether differing testimony by several hours, or testimony that spans the distinction between day and night, constitutes a contradiction that invalidates the witnesses altogether. The context motivating this entire discussion is, of course, the laws of *chametz*: when must one stop eating *chametz*, and does the imprecision of ordinary people's timekeeping bear on that determination?

Rav Ashi articulates a clean principle: *kamachloket b'edus kach machloket b'chametz* — whatever the rule is regarding the permissible discrepancy in *edus*, the same rule applies to *chametz*. If witnesses may be off by an hour, then one must stop eating *chametz* an hour before the prescribed time.

The Gemara immediately objects: *peshita* — this is obvious! That is precisely why the entire preceding discussion took place. The Gemara answers that the novelty lies in the following clarification: one might have supposed that there is a *machloket tannaim* as to whether the witness testimony rules can even be applied to the *chametz* context at all — perhaps the analogy is contested. Rav Ashi therefore comes to inform us that this is not a dispute about whether to apply the rule, but rather that the application is accepted by all. The *machloket* concerns only what the rule itself is — how far off may witnesses be before their testimony is discredited — and that same rule maps directly onto *chametz*.

### Witness Discrepancy Rules

The discussion of how much divergence in witness testimony is tolerable now sharpens through the contribution of Rav Shimi bar Ashi. He rules: *lo shanu ela b'shaos* — the leniency regarding discrepancy applies only when the disagreement is a matter of hours within the same part of the day. However, if one witness says the event occurred before *hanetz hachama* — before sunrise — and another says it occurred after sunrise, their testimonies are mutually contradictory and are *bateilah*.

The Gemara interjects: *peshita* — surely this is self-evident? One witness says nighttime, the other says daytime. What novelty is there here?

### Applying to Chametz

The Gemara therefore reformulates the case: what if one witness says the event occurred before sunrise and the other says it occurred *b'toch hanetz hachama* — during the sunrise itself? Here too, Rav Shimi bar Ashi rules that the testimonies are contradictory and invalid.

Again the Gemara objects that this seems obvious. The answer is that one might have thought the two witnesses are actually saying the same thing — that the one who says *b'toch hanetz hachama* means only that he saw the glow on the horizon, the *giluya*, the atmospheric light preceding the actual cresting of the sun, and not the sun itself. In that reading, both witnesses would be describing pre-dawn conditions and would be in agreement. Rav Shimi therefore comes to inform us that this is not so: the expression *b'toch hanetz hachama* is interpreted to mean that the sun had already begun to rise, and that creates a genuine contradiction with the testimony of the first witness who places the event before any sunrise at all.

### Day vs. Night

This ruling raises a natural methodological question. If the concern is ambiguity in how a witness phrases his description of the time, why not simply ask him to clarify? One might distinguish between a city dweller and a farmer or shepherd, who would be far more attuned by eye to the precise stages of dawn and would use this language with greater precision.

### Sunrise Terminology

A closer look reveals that the Gemara may be establishing principles for a structured context of inquiry — the formal *chakiros* and *derishos* applied to witness testimony — rather than purely abstract rules. At a certain point in the examination, once a witness has expressed himself using the phrase *b'toch hanetz hachama*, that formulation is treated as carrying a definite meaning, and one does not probe further lest one put words in his mouth and introduce uncertainty in the opposite direction. In other words, the rule is not about abstract testimony in a vacuum, but about the fixed legal weight assigned to particular formulations once they have been uttered in the context of formal examination. Two witnesses independently producing the same formulation lend one another precision. Whatever ambiguity might theoretically attach to the phrase is resolved by the legal convention that assigns it a single fixed meaning.

---

## Chametz Fifth Hour

### Rav Nachman's Psak

The Gemara now records that Rav Nachman rules in the name of Rav: *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that one may eat *chametz* until the beginning of the fifth hour, that the fifth hour is a suspended period of *toleh* — neither eating nor burning — and that one burns the *chametz* at the end of the fifth hour.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges Rav Nachman: why rule like Rabbi Yehuda? One should instead rule like Rabbi Meir, since there is a *stam mishna* that accords with Rabbi Meir's view. The principle is well established that the *halacha* follows the *stam mishna*, and the Mishnah states *kol sha'ah she-mutar le-ekhol ma'akhil* — as long as one is permitted to eat *chametz*, one may feed it to one's animals and derive benefit from it — implying that there is no intermediate suspended period at all, which is consistent with Rabbi Meir's position.

### Stam Mishna Analysis

The Gemara rejects this argument. That Mishnah is not in fact a *stam mishna* in the relevant sense, because it contains a difficulty in its own language: *mishum de-kashi mutar*. The Mishnah says *kol sha'ah she-mutar le-ekhol* — as long as it is permitted to eat — rather than the simpler formulation *kol sha'ah she-okhel* — as long as one eats. The Gemara in the chapter *Kol Sha'ah* explicitly raises this linguistic difficulty: the word *mutar* implies "as long as some other person is permitted to eat it," meaning as long as there exists someone for whom it remains permitted. This would refer to a *kohen*, who is the third opinion in the Mishnah — one who can eat *chametz* longer than an ordinary Israelite. Since the language points in the direction of the third view rather than resolving the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, the Mishnah cannot serve as a *stam* ruling in favor of either.

### Rabban Gamliel Not Machr…

One might then suggest: rule like Rabban Gamliel, whose view might serve as a *machria* — a tiebreaker tilting toward one of the other positions. The Gemara rejects this as well: Rabban Gamliel is not a *machria* at all. He does not tip the balance between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda; rather, he presents a third, independent opinion entirely his own — *ta'ama denafshei ka'amar*. Rabban Gamliel's position of *toleh chullin kol arba, terumah kol chamesh* operates according to its own logic and cannot be used to adjudicate between the other two views.

Alternatively, the Gemara suggests, *i ba'it eima*: Rav, in ruling like Rabbi Yehuda, was following a different *tanna* as his authority for determining the *halacha*, as will now be established from a *baraita*.

---

## Pre-Pesach Terumah Rules

### 13th Erev Shabbat Burning

The *baraita* presents the following case: when the fourteenth of Nisan falls on Shabbat — so that one cannot perform *bi'ur chametz* on Shabbat itself — one destroys all *chametz* on the thirteenth. The *baraita* adds that on this thirteenth, one also burns *terumah* that is *tamei*, *terumah* that is *taluy* (whose status is doubtful), and *terumah* that is *tahor* (ritually pure). However, one leaves over from the *terumah tehorah* enough food for two meals — for Friday night and for Shabbat morning — sufficient to eat until the fourth hour on Shabbat *erev Pesach*. This is the opinion of Rabbi Elazar ben Yehuda of Bartota, stated in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua.

It is worth noting that this *baraita* applies specifically to a *kohen* who possesses *terumah*. The underlying question — whether to leave over provisions for Shabbat or destroy everything early — is framed entirely around *terumah*, since for a non-*kohen* the question of leaving over *terumah* for a meal would not arise.

### Terumah Burning Objection

The Sages object to Rabbi Elazar's ruling: *tehoros lo yisarefu shema yimtzu lahen ochlim* — you should not burn the *terumah tehorah* early, because perhaps *kohanim* will come in the morning who can eat it, and you will have destroyed it prematurely, before any prohibition required it. Rabbi Elazar responds: *kvar bikshu v'lo matzu* — we have already investigated and found that no *kohanim* in the area will come to eat it.

The Sages push back further: *shema chutz la-choma lanu* — what of those who have lodged outside the city walls and will come in the morning? Rabbi Elazar's opponents argue that the possibility of such visitors should prevent premature burning.

### Eliyahu Safek Argument

Rabbi Elazar then turns the argument back on his interlocutors: if one is going to reason from speculative possibilities, then even the *taluy* — the *terumah* of doubtful status — should not be burned, because *shema yavo Eliyahu v'yitaharem* — perhaps Eliyahu HaNavi will arrive on the morning of *erev Pesach* and declare all the doubtful cases to be *tahor*, at which point the *terumah* could have been eaten. Since the opponents insist that no opportunity for consumption should be foreclosed, they cannot consistently permit burning the *taluy*.

### Eliyahu Won't Come Erev…

The Sages respond with a striking ruling: *kvar muvtach lahen l'Yisrael she'ein Eliyahu ba lo b'arvei Shabbatot v'lo b'arvei yamim tovim mipnei ha-torach* — it has already been assured to Israel that Eliyahu will not come on the eve of Shabbat or on the eve of Yom Tov, because of the *torach*, the burden of preparation that the nation is engaged in. This is a remarkable statement. It reflects the principle that the legitimate demands of daily life and sacred preparation take precedence over the immediacy of redemption — the people are occupied building their lives as God has given them, and Eliyahu will not disrupt their Shabbat preparations. It bears noting that Eliyahu *could* come on *erev Pesach* itself; the restriction applies only to *erev Shabbat* and *erev Yom Tov*. The discussion here concerns the thirteenth of Nisan, which falls on a Friday in this scenario.

Following this exchange, the Gemara records: *lo zazu misham ad she-kav'u halacha k'Rabbi Elazar ben Yehuda ish Bartota* — they did not leave that place until they established that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Elazar, namely that one should not burn the extra *terumah tehorah* prematurely, because someone might yet come to eat it.

One might ask: does this ruling pertain to eating — that one may eat until the fourth hour — or only to the question of *bi'ur*, when one must destroy? Rashi clarifies: the ruling in favor of Rabbi Elazar concerns only the *bi'ur*, the timing of destruction on the thirteenth versus waiting until the fourteenth. Regarding the question of eating, *l'olam eima lach k'dei le'ekhol ad chamesh sha'os* — in truth one leaves over enough to eat until the fifth hour, and the *halacha* that we follow Rabbi Elazar does not imply that the eating deadline is the fourth hour.

The Gemara adds that *Rebbi* himself also holds with Rav Nachman's ruling — that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda — as evidenced by the following *ma'aseh*.

---

## Lost Chametz Case

### Yochanan Chakuka Story

The case involves a certain individual who deposited a bag full of *chametz* with Yochanan Chakuka. Mice chewed through the bag and the *chametz* began leaking out. It was *erev Pesach*, and the man came before Rebbi seeking guidance — caught between the prohibition against destroying another person's property and the spreading presence of *chametz* as the deadline approached.

### Fifth Hour Deadline

Rebbi's response was hour by hour: at the first hour he said, wait — the owner may yet come and retrieve it. At the second hour, the same. Third hour: wait. Fourth hour: wait. At the fifth hour, Rebbi said: *tze u-mchor ba-shuk* — go out and sell it in the marketplace. The moment the fifth hour arrived, Rebbi instructed that the *chametz* be sold, representing the last possible moment at which value could still be salvaged on the owner's behalf. This *ma'aseh* demonstrates that Rebbi held the fifth hour is indeed the final deadline — consistent with the ruling like Rabbi Yehuda.

### Rav Yosef Interpretation

The Gemara asks: *mai lav l'nochrim* — presumably this sale is to non-Jews? This would accord with Rabbi Yehuda's position that during the fifth hour one may no longer eat *chametz* but may still derive *hana'ah* from it — which could take the form of selling it to a *nochri*. Rav Yosef, however, suggests that perhaps *lo l'Yisrael* — Rebbi's instruction could be interpreted as permitting sale to a Jew as well, in accordance with Rabbi Meir's view that *chametz* remains fully permitted until the end.

### Abaye's Question

Abaye immediately raises a difficulty with Rav Yosef's interpretation: if one may sell to a fellow Jew, why go to the marketplace at all? The guardian could simply take twenty dollars from his own pocket, pay it into an account on behalf of the owner, and consume the *chametz* himself. What is the purpose of going out to the *shuk*?

### Chashda Principle

The answer is: *mishum chashada* — because of the concern for suspicion. A guardian cannot transact with himself over property entrusted to him, as it creates the appearance of self-dealing. He might underpay, pocketing the difference, and no one would be the wiser.

---

## Charity Oversight Rules

### Charity Fund Rules

The Gemara cites a *baraita* establishing the same principle in a parallel domain. *Gabbai tzedakah* — charity administrators — who have money in the communal fund and no poor recipients available at the moment, may exchange the coins for bills through a third party, but may not make the exchange with themselves. They cannot, for example, pocket the quarters from the collection box and replace them with their own dollar bill.

### Soup Kitchen Rules

Similarly, the administrator of a *tamchui* — a communal soup kitchen — who has leftover food and no recipients to give it to, must sell the surplus to others. He may not purchase it for himself, even at fair market value, and keep the proceeds for the institution.

### Nekyim Source

The source for both rulings is the verse *v'heyitem nekiyim me'Hashem u-mi-Yisrael* — "you shall be clean before God and before Israel." This is a striking demand: one must not only be honest before God, but must also appear honest before one's fellow human beings. One's conduct must withstand scrutiny from both directions.

### Corruption Prevention

This principle is worth pausing over. It is not simply *marit ayin* — the rabbinic concern that onlookers might be led to erroneous conclusions about what is permitted. *Marit ayin* functions when observers might mistakenly infer that a forbidden act is allowed. Here the concern is different and in some ways more serious: the worry is not that people will imitate the act, but that they will suspect the actor of genuine wrongdoing. These are positions of institutional trust, and the temptation for self-dealing is inherent in the structure. The rabbis therefore impose procedural safeguards — and, as the *Rambam* records as *halacha* based on *Masechet Pe'ah*, communal charity administration must be carried out by at least two or three individuals together, never by one person alone.

---

## Fifth Hour Debate

### Rav Adda Clarification

Returning to the *ma'aseh* of Yochanan Chakuka, Rav Adda bar Mattana clarifies the matter directly: he tells Rav Yosef that Rav Yosef had himself explicitly stated — *befarush amrat lan* — that the instruction was *tze u-mochran l'nochrim k'Rabbi Yehuda*, to go and sell the *chametz* to non-Jews, consistent with Rabbi Yehuda. There is therefore no ambiguity about whether the sale was to Jews or non-Jews.

### Following Rabban Shimon

The clarification resolves the earlier question. Rav Yosef then asks: according to whose view does this ruling of Rav proceed? He answers: it goes according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

### Entrusted Fruit Mishna

The Mishnah governing deposited produce is cited: *ha-mapkid peirot etzel chaveiro afilu hen avudin lo yiga bahen* — if one deposits fruit with a friend, even if they are rotting and going to be lost, the guardian should not touch them. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees and rules: *mochrin b'veit din mipnei hashavat aveidah* — one sells them through *beit din* in order to restore value to the owner, treating the situation as analogous to *hashavat aveidah*, returning a lost object.

### Spoilage Standards

Abaye adds a refinement from a ruling of Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *lo shanu ela bi-khdei chesronah* — the general rule that one must leave deposited produce alone applies only when the spoilage is proceeding at the normal expected rate. Every farmer knows that a certain percentage of produce will go bad; that is accepted and the guardian bears no responsibility to intervene. However, *aval yoter mi-khdei chesronah* — if the spoilage is advancing faster than would ordinarily be expected, then one sells through *beit din*, for at that point genuine loss is being inflicted.

### Chametz Complete Loss

And certainly, *v'chol sheken hacha de-aveida legamrei* — all the more so in the case of *chametz*, where the loss is total and absolute. Once the sixth hour arrives, the *chametz* has no value whatsoever and cannot be transferred or consumed by anyone. This is not ordinary spoilage proceeding at some rate; it is a cliff edge. The case of *chametz* is therefore a fortiori stronger than even the case of produce spoiling faster than expected, and the instruction to sell through *beit din* — or, in this practical case, in the marketplace — is entirely justified.

---

## Todah Signal System

### Two Loaf Signal

The Gemara now turns to the Mishnah that provides the subject matter for the remainder of the daf. The Mishnah records that the public signal for when to stop eating *chametz* and when to burn it was based on two loaves of *todah* — thanksgiving offering bread — placed *al gabei ha-itztaba*, on a platform or bench in the *Beit Hamikdash*. *Kol zman she-munachos kol ha-am ochlin* — as long as both loaves remained in place, the public knew they could still eat. *Nitlah achas* — when one was removed, the signal for *toleh* had arrived: no more eating, but not yet burning. *Nitlu shteihen hischilu kol ha-am sorfin* — when both loaves were removed, everyone began burning their *chametz*.

This is a striking system. The obvious question is how widely the signal could be perceived. The assumption appears to be that word travels quickly, particularly during the *regel* when Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims and the *Beit Hamikdash* was at the center of communal life. The signal presumably reached those who were either in direct sight of the platform or close enough to hear from those who were. The Mishnah's system was evidently considered adequate for its purpose, even if it did not reach every individual simultaneously.

A *tanna* who recited the Mishnah before Rabbi Yehuda had the text reading *al gav ha-itztaba* — on the bench itself. Rabbi Yehuda objected: do you put it there to keep it hidden? The whole point is that it serve as a visible signal. The correct reading is *al gag ha-itztaba* — on the *roof* of the *itztaba*, the elevated platform, so that it could be seen from a distance.

Rav Ashi then adds that Rabbi Yehuda taught that *Har Habayit istav kaful hayah* — the Temple Mount precinct had a double row of covered colonnades, in the style of a Roman *stoa* or basilica. A *baraita* confirms this, adding that Rabbi Yehuda referred to it by the term *istavanit*, reflecting the architectural form common in Roman urban design where columns line a main street and support a covered walkway above. The loaves were placed on the roof of this structure — high, visible, and open to view from across the *Har Habayit*.

### Why Todah Pesulin

The Mishnah specifies that the two *todah* loaves used as the signal were *pesulot* — disqualified. The Gemara investigates why. Rabbi Chanina explains: *mitoch she-hayu merubos nifsalos be-linah* — because so many people brought *korban todah* at the time of the *regel*, there was far more bread than could be eaten within the allotted time period. A *todah* must be consumed within a day and a night; bread left over beyond that time becomes *linah* — leftover — and is disqualified. The congregations of pilgrims who brought their *todah* offerings typically did so on the thirteenth, and the sheer volume of forty-loaf sets accompanying each offering meant that inevitably some bread went uneaten and became *pesul*.

The Gemara cites a *baraita* supporting the timing: *ein mevi'im todah be-Chag HaMatzos mipnei chametz she-ba* — one does not bring a *korban todah* on Pesach itself because the offering involves leavened loaves. The Gemara notes this seems obvious, but Rav Adda bar Ahava clarifies: the *baraita* addresses the fourteenth of Nisan specifically, where one cannot bring a *todah* because even though the bread is still edible at the time of offering, it will become prohibited before the *korban* can be completed and consumed — a principle of *ein meviim kodshim le-beit ha-psul*, one does not bring sacred offerings into a situation where they will inevitably become disqualified. The *baraita* thus explains why everyone's *todah* obligations accumulated until the thirteenth, at which point the volume of bread overwhelmed the capacity for consumption, generating the *linah* that rendered the loaves *pesulot*.

### Rabbi Yannai Kosher

Rabbi Yannai dissents and argues: *kesherot hayu* — the loaves used as the signal were in fact perfectly *kasher*. They should not be described as *pesulot* at all. The reason they are called *pesulot* is not because they were inherently disqualified, but rather *she-lo nishchat aleihen ha-zavach* — because the *todah* animal had not yet been slaughtered over them. Until the *shechitah* is performed and the blood is sprinkled, the loaves, though baked and ready, have not yet been formally sanctified as part of the *todah* offering and therefore cannot be eaten. They are called *pesulot* only loosely — they are not yet *kasher* for consumption, not because of any defect but because the process has not been completed.

### Pre-Shechitah Bread

This raises the question of why the loaves were placed on the platform in an incomplete state rather than being used after the offering was completed. The Gemara suggests they were placed there because they served as a public signal, not as part of ordinary consumption. The bread in this state — before *shechitah* — was understood by everyone to be inedible, and its presence and removal served the signaling function without creating any halachic confusion.

---

## Bread Sanctification

### Rava Redemption

Rava raises a question about the *kasher*-but-incomplete loaves: if the *todah* animal is subsequently lost and the *shechitah* can no longer be performed on it, can the bread be redeemed? The Gemara works through the implications: if one explicitly designated *zot todah v'elu lachma* — "this is the *todah* and these are its loaves" — then the loaves are linked to that specific animal, and if the animal cannot be slaughtered the loaves cannot be transferred to another *todah*. However, Rava rules: *avad ha-lechem mevi lechem acher* — if the bread is lost, one may bake new bread. But *avdat todah ein mevi todah acher* — if the *todah* animal itself is lost, one may not bring a different *todah* animal to complete the offering with the original loaves. The reasoning: *lechem glal todah* — the bread exists on account of the *todah*, the offering is primary and the bread is its accessory, not the reverse.

The Gemara then asks: why not simply redeem the bread and free it from its *kodesh* status, making it *chullin*? This would resolve the problem of bread that can neither be used nor consumed. The Gemara sets that possibility aside and redirects the discussion.

### Two Acts Required

The Gemara then pivots to the underlying question of sanctification: what is the mechanism by which bread acquires its *kodesh* status in the context of a *todah* or *shtei ha-lechem*? The Gemara establishes that there are two required acts: *shechitah* and *zerika* — slaughter and sprinkling of blood. The question is whether performing only one of these two acts confers any intermediate status on the bread, or whether the bread is fully in or fully out depending on whether both acts have been completed.

### Shtei Halechem

A *baraita* addresses this in the context of the *shtei ha-lechem* brought on Shavuot. The *shtei ha-lechem* are accompanied by two lambs, and the *shechitah* of those lambs is what initiates the sanctification of the loaves. The *baraita* records: *shachtam lishman v'zarak daman lishman kidash ha-lechem* — if both the *shechitah* and *zerika* were performed with proper intent for the *shtei ha-lechem*, the bread is sanctified. *Shachtam shelo lishman v'zarak daman shelo lishman lo kidash ha-lechem* — if both acts were performed for the wrong purpose, the bread acquires no sanctification at all.

### Intermediate Status

The more complex case: *shachtam lishman v'zarak daman shelo lishman* — the *shechitah* was done properly but the *zerika* was done for the wrong purpose. The ruling is *lechem kadosh v'eino kadosh* — the bread is in a suspended state: it has acquired some sanctity through the *shechitah*, yet it is not fully sanctified and cannot be eaten. This is the opinion of *Rebbi* — that the two acts together confer full sanctification, each act independently confers partial status, and the combination of a valid *shechitah* with an invalid *zerika* produces this intermediate condition.

### All-or-Nothing Status

Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *l'olam eino kadosh ha-lechem ad she-yishchat lishman v'yizrok daman lishman* — the bread is simply not sanctified unless both acts are performed correctly. There is no intermediate state; the bread is either fully sanctified or it has no special status at all. For Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, the system is all-or-nothing.

### Spilled Blood Application

The Gemara resolves how to apply these positions to the case at hand — *todah* bread placed on the platform where the *shechitah* has been done but the blood has spilled before *zerika*. Even according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, one might argue that the bread here does have a degree of sanctification, because *kol ha-omed lizrok ke-zarak dami* — whatever stands ready to be sprinkled is considered as if already sprinkled. Once the blood was collected in the bowl and the *zerika* was imminent, that moment of readiness was legally equivalent to the *zerika* itself. The subsequent spilling is therefore a retroactive undoing of what had already been accomplished in legal terms. On this reading, even Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon would agree that such bread holds an intermediate status — at the moment it was placed on the platform, it was in a condition that was the equivalent of post-*zerika* — and thus the *baraita*'s description of the bread as occupying a distinct status is consistent across opinions.

---

## Signal Systems

### Loaf Signal Restatement

Returning to the Mishnah's signal system, the Gemara recapitulates: two *todah* loaves — whether *pesulot* through *linah* or in an intermediate state through incomplete *shechitah* and *zerika* — were placed on the elevated roof of the *itztaba* on the *Har Habayit*. Their placement, removal of one, and removal of both provided the three-stage public signal for *erev Pesach* chametz disposal.

### Cow Plowing Signal

A *baraita* records that Abba Shaul describes an alternative signal system: *shtei parot hayu chorshos be-Har ha-Mishcha* — there were two cows plowing on *Har ha-Mishcha*, which is identified with *Har ha-Zeitim*, the Mount of Olives. The same three stages applied: *kol zman she-shteihen chorshos kol ha-am ochlin* — as long as both were plowing, eating was permitted. When one cow was removed, it signaled *tolein*. When both were removed, everyone began burning.

The logic of visibility is appealing here: *Har ha-Zeitim* is visible from much of Jerusalem and from the *Beit Hamikdash*, and two large animals plowing in a field would be observable from a considerable distance — arguably more broadly than a loaf of bread on a platform.

### Cow Signal Problems

This signal, however, raises its own difficulties. Identifying from a distance which cows are *the* signal cows — as opposed to any number of other cows that might be plowing in fields around the city — presents a real problem of visibility and recognition. One would need to know exactly where on *Har ha-Mishcha* to look, and distinguish these particular cows from any others. Moreover — and this is a point worth noting on its own — cows do not plow; oxen do. The Mishnah's term *parot* (cows) is technically imprecise, and one might have expected the text to read *parim*. Whether this reflects a loose usage of terms or some other consideration, the Gemara does not address directly here.

---

---

# Pesachim 17

## Haggai's Questions

### Rav's Position Intro

The sugya opens at the close of the discussion of Rav's interpretation of Yosi ben Yoezer. Rav's position was that Yosi ben Yoezer's famous testimony established that liquids are exempt from *tumah* as a matter of biblical law — *tumat mashkin* does not apply *mi-d'oraita*. Before the Gemara brings its final proof on this question, it pauses to examine the passage in Haggai, which the Gemara quotes as a *tashma* — a potential challenge or support to the discussion at hand.

### Haggai Pasuk Intro

The prophet Haggai addresses the *kohanim* in the post-exilic period, posing what appears to be a parable framed as a series of legal questions about *tumah* and *taharah*. The relevant verses read:

> *Ko amar Hashem Tzeva'os: sha'al na es ha-kohanim Torah leimor: hein yisa ish b'sar kodesh bichnaf bigdo, v'naga bichnafo el ha-lechem v'el ha-nazid v'el ha-yayin v'el ha-shemen v'el kol ma'achal, ha-yitkadash? Va-ya'anu ha-kohanim va-yomru lo.*

The literal translation: if a person carries holy meat in the corner of his garment, and that corner touches bread, stew, wine, oil, or any food — does it become holy? The *kohanim* answered: no. Haggai then asked a second question:

> *Im yiga t'mei nefesh b'chol eileh, ha-yitma? Va-ya'anu ha-kohanim va-yomru yitma.*

If someone who is *tamei* by contact with a corpse touches any of these things, do they become *tamei*? The *kohanim* answered: yes. To this Haggai responded:

> *Ken ha-am ha-zeh v'chen ha-goy ha-zeh lefanai ne'um Hashem, v'chen kol ma'aseh yedeihem, v'asher yakrivu sham tamei hu.*

Haggai's apparent aim was to draw an analogy: he elicited the answer *tamei* so that he could apply it metaphorically to the nation and everything they bring upon the *mizbeach*.

### Sheretz Chain

The Gemara, however, interprets the opening verses quite differently from their plain sense. Following Rashi's reading — which is really the only way to make sense of the Gemara's analysis — the passage is reread as describing a chain of *tumah* transmission. A *sheretz* (a dead creeping thing) is present in the corner of the man's garment. The *sheretz* in the corner touches the bread; the bread touches the stew; the stew touches the wine; the wine touches the oil. Each successive item contracts a progressively more distant level of *tumah* from the original source.

It should be noted that the verse also mentions *v'el kol ma'achal* — "and any food" — as a fifth item in the sequence, yet the Gemara entirely ignores this fifth element in its chain analysis, which is puzzling. Likewise, the plain sense of the verse has the *garment* touching the food items, not the *sheretz* inside it, but the Gemara reinterprets the possessive *bichnafo* to refer to the *sheretz* lodged in the corner.
