These interpretive moves are admittedly difficult, but the Gemara's purpose is not to read the verse peshat — it is to extract a halakhic question about the chain of *tumah*.

On this reading, the *kohanim* answered that the sequence posed no problem — and Rav says: *ishtabesh kahanei* — the *kohanim* made a mistake. This is initially surprising. Rav holds that *tumat mashkin* does not exist *mi-d'oraita*. How can Rav say the *kohanim* were wrong to declare these liquids *tahor*?

The Gemara resolves this directly: there is no contradiction for Rav, because Rav's exemption applied only to *mashkeh beit mitbachaya* — the liquids of the slaughterhouse, i.e., blood and water. Here, Haggai is asking about wine and oil — *mashkeh beit midbachaya*, the liquids of the *mizbeach* (the *dalet* and *zayin* are interchangeable in Aramaic, yielding *midbachaya* from *mizbe'ach*). Wine accompanies most *korbanot* as a *nesach*, and oil is mixed into the *minchah* offering. These are categorically different from slaughterhouse liquids, and Rav holds they are fully subject to *tumah*. Hence the *kohanim* erred when they declared the chain *tahor*.

### Revii vs. Chamishi

The Gemara now develops the argument in a formal dispute between Rav and Shmuel:

*Rav amar ishtabesh kahanei* — Rav says the *kohanim* were wrong. Why? *Revii bakodesh ba'u mineihu va-amru lei tahor* — Haggai was asking about a *revii*, a fourth-level *tumah*, and they wrongly declared it *tahor*. Working through the chain: the *sheretz* is the source (*av ha-tumah*); the bread it touches becomes a *rishon*; the stew becomes a *sheni*; the wine becomes a *shelishi*; and the oil is a *revii*. In the domain of *kodshim*, a *revii letumah* is still *tamei* — the *kohanim* should have said so, but they said *tahor*. That was their error.

*U-Shmuel amar lo ishtabesh kahanei* — Shmuel says the *kohanim* were not wrong. According to Shmuel, Haggai was asking about a *chamishi*, a fifth-level *tumah*. Since there is no *chamishi letumah* even in *kodshim*, the *kohanim* were correct to say *tahor*.

But where does Shmuel find the fifth level? The Gemara notes that the verse counts only four food items after the *sheretz*: bread, stew, wine, oil — which fits Rav's four-level chain perfectly. *Bishlama le-Rav, hainu deksiv arba'ah* — for Rav, four items, four levels, all works out. *Ella le-Shmuel, chamisha menaslan?* — from where does Shmuel derive the fifth level?

The Gemara's answer turns on the word *bichnafo* — "in his corner." Shmuel reads this to mean that it was not the *sheretz* itself that directly touched the bread, but rather something that had itself touched the *sheretz* — an unmentioned intermediary, which is implied by the prefix *be-* (indicating contact *through* the corner rather than *by* the corner itself). This introduces an additional step at the beginning of the chain, yielding five levels total: *sheretz* → garment-corner → bread (*rishon*) → stew (*sheni*) → wine (*shelishi*) → oil (*revii*) — wait, even with the intermediary, the chain as presented in the verse still terminates at a *revii* for oil. The Gemara's point is that Haggai's question, by Shmuel's reckoning, was really aimed at a *chamishi* — whether anything touched after all these intermediaries would be *tamei* — and the *kohanim* correctly said no, there is no *chamishi*. This reading of *bichnafo* is conceded to be a stretch, but it is the only way to make Shmuel's position cohere.

### Why Kohanim Erred

The Gemara then raises a difficulty for Rav. In the second part of Haggai's exchange, where a *tamei nefesh* (one who has contacted a corpse) touches the same sequence of foods, the *kohanim* answered correctly — *yitma*. But according to Rav, the *kohanim* were wrong in the first case. If they are ignorant enough to err once, why didn't they err in the second case as well?

Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuha, answers: the *kohanim* were expert in the laws of *tum'at met* (corpse-impurity) but not in the laws of *tum'at sheretz* (impurity from creeping things). Hence they got the *tamei nefesh* question right and the *sheretz* question wrong.

Ravina offers a different resolution: the two questions are not actually parallel cases of the same level of *tumah*. In the second question, when the *tamei nefesh* (an *av ha-tumah*) directly touches the bread, the chain runs: *tamei nefesh* → bread (*rishon*) → stew (*sheni*) → wine (*shelishi*) → oil (*revii*). The *kohanim* knew the rule of *revii letumah* and answered correctly. In the first case, according to Rav, there was also a *revii* — but the *kohanim* had never properly internalized that a *sheretz* chain can produce a *revii letumah*. So the asymmetry is between their mastery of *revii* arising from *tum'at met* versus *revii* arising from *tum'at sheretz*, not between a *revii* and a *chamishi*.

### People as Tamei

Turning to Haggai's conclusion — *ken ha-am ha-zeh... tamei hu* — the Gemara considers how each position makes sense of this statement. For Rav, it is straightforward: Haggai was asking a case where the correct answer was *tamei*, the *kohanim* said *tahor*, and then Haggai declares the people are like this — *tamei*. The flow of the passage coheres naturally.

For Shmuel, however, the first question yielded a *tahor* answer — and the *kohanim* were correct. So when Haggai says "so too the nation is *tamei*," what does that mean? The Gemara suggests that Haggai is posing a rhetorical question — *atmuhei ka matma* — he is asking in astonishment: are the people really *tamei*? The implication would be a compliment: the people are as pure as the *tahor* answer you just gave. But the Gemara immediately rejects this, noting that the *nevi'im acharonim* are not in the business of flattering the people, and the verse continues: *v'chen kol ma'aseh yedeihem* — "so too all that they do" — clearly implying censure.

The Gemara therefore concludes, in the name of Zutra (and some say Rav Ashi): *mitoch she-kilkelu et ma'aseihem, ma'aleh aleihem ha-katuv k'ilu hikrivu b'tumah* — because the people's deeds were corrupt, Scripture reckons it as though they had sacrificed in a state of *tumah*. In other words, Haggai is not drawing a strict halakhic equivalence but rather a moral-metaphorical one: the people are behaviorally so defiled that it is *as if* they are *tamei*. Rashi adds a striking nuance: *l'achar zman she-kilkelu ma'aseihem b'Bayit Sheni b'sha'ar aveirot* — Rashi places this rebuke prophetically in the future, referring to future corruptions in the era of the Second Temple. Just as Moshe rebuked the people for what he knew they would do after his death, Haggai's words carry a forward-looking dimension — a remarkable interpretive move.

---

## Mitbachaya vs. Midbachaya

### Rav v. Levi

The Gemara now turns *gufa* — to the substance of the dispute itself — regarding which liquids Yosi ben Yoezer's ruling exempts from *tumah*. *Rav tanei mashkei beit mitbachaya* — Rav's version of the text has Yosi ben Yoezer ruling about *beit mitbachaya*, the slaughterhouse. *V'Levi tanei mashkei be-mitbachaya* — Levi's version reads *be-midbachaya*, the *mizbeach*, which encompasses not only blood and water but also wine and oil.

### Levi's Braisa

The Gemara examines Levi's position. If Levi reads Yosi ben Yoezer as exempting *mizbeach* liquids broadly — including wine and oil — this works out well if Levi agrees with Shmuel's interpretation of Yosi ben Yoezer, namely that the liquids themselves can become *tamei* but cannot be *metamei* other things (*dachun mi-letamei tumas acheirim, aval tumas atzmam yesh lahem*). Under that reading, all four *mizbeach* liquids — blood, wine, oil, and water — could have contracted *tumah* when they touched a *rishon letumah*, even if they cannot then pass *tumah* further.

A *braisa* is cited in support of Levi, enumerating these four liquids — *ha-dam, ha-yayin, ha-shemen, ve-ha-mayim* — as *mashkei beit midbachaya*. The *braisa* states: if these liquids became *tamei* inside the *mikdash* and were then taken outside, they are *tehorin* — meaning, as Rashi clarifies, *tehorin mi-letamei acheirim*: they themselves remain *tamei*, but they cannot render other things *tamei*. However, if they became *tamei* outside the *mikdash* and were then brought inside, they are *tmei'im* — they do have the power to transmit *tumah*.

### Rav's Braisa

A corresponding *braisa* supports Rav's narrower reading. It specifies only *ha-dam ve-ha-mayim* — blood and water — as *mashkei beit mitbachaya* (slaughterhouse liquids). These, whether they became *tamei* in vessels or while still in the ground, are *tehorim* — they cannot be *metamei* other things. Rabbi Shimon dissents within this *braisa*, ruling that if these liquids are in vessels (*keilim*), they are *tamei*, but if they are still in the ground, they are *tahor*. The *braisa*'s identification of only two liquids — blood and water — rather than four clearly supports Rav's reading of Yosi ben Yoezer.

The Gemara also notes a tension: if Levi holds like Rav (rather than Shmuel) — that is, if even *mizbeach* liquids are exempt from *tumah* entirely — then the Haggai passage involving wine and oil creates no problem of a *revii* or *chamishi* at all, and Levi would be forced to say the *kohanim* were wrong for different reasons. Working through the permutations, the Gemara concludes that *al karchach ke-Shmuel sevira lei* — Levi must hold like Shmuel, that *mizbeach* liquids can themselves become *tamei* but cannot be *metamei* other things. And by parallel logic, Shmuel's view of the *kohanim*'s error must align with Rav's version of the text — *mashkei beit mitbachaya* — since if Shmuel accepted Levi's version (wine and oil are categorically exempt even from contracting *tumah*), there would be no need to invoke the *revii/chamishi* analysis at all.

### Halacha L'Moshe MiSinai

Rav Pappa introduces a new framework for understanding the exemption of slaughterhouse liquids. Even if one holds, as a general proposition, that *tumat mashkin* applies *mi-d'oraita*, Rav Pappa says: *mashkei beit mitbachaya hilchata gemiri la* — the exemption of slaughterhouse liquids from *tumah* is a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, a transmitted tradition from Sinai, not a deduction from logic or an extension of general principle. The exemption thus floats free of the broader debate about whether *tumat mashkin* is biblical or rabbinic.

### Challenge to Rav Pappa

Rav Huna the son of Rav Natan immediately challenges this. If the exemption of blood and water is only a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* applying specifically to slaughterhouse liquids, how could Rabbi Elazar in our Mishnah derive from it the sweeping rule *ein tumah le-mashkin kol ikkar* — that no liquid whatsoever can contract *tumah*? Rabbi Elazar's proof was: look, Yosi ben Yoezer testified that slaughterhouse liquids are *tahor*, which shows that liquids in general have no *tumah*. But if the slaughterhouse exemption is merely a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, it is self-contained and cannot be extrapolated to other liquids. *Halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* applies only to its specific domain — one cannot reason *kal va-chomer* or *binyan av* from it to generate new rulings. This objection is substantial.

Ravina raises a second challenge from the *braisa* cited above, in which Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between liquids in vessels (*tamei*) and liquids in the ground (*tahor*). If the exemption were a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* with no qualifications, why would there be any difference between the two? A *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* either exempts or it does not — the vessel-versus-ground distinction suggests we are not dealing with a blanket traditional exemption but rather with some principled analysis that can accommodate internal distinctions. The Gemara concludes simply: *kashya* — this stands as an unresolved difficulty against Rav Pappa.

### Reviyit Threshold

Rav Pappa continues with a clarification of the *braisa*'s ruling about water in the ground. When the *braisa* says that water in the ground is *tahor*, this is limited to a specific case. First, it applies only to water, not blood — blood originates in the animal, not the ground, so the "in the ground" consideration is irrelevant to blood. Second, even for water, the ground-based *taharah* applies only when there is at least a *reviyit* of water collected there. The reason: a *reviyit* of water is sufficient — apparently as a matter of law — to immerse needles and small metal implements (*tzinorot*) and render them *tahor*. Water of that volume in the ground has the character of a valid *mikveh*-like body and is therefore not susceptible to *tumah*. But if the collected water is less than a *reviyit*, it loses that status and is *tamei*. The Gemara stops here without resolving all the questions raised against Rav Pappa — the matrix of positions is laid out, but a definitive ruling is not issued.

---

## Rabbi Yehudah's Liquids

### Cushion Cases

Returning now to the larger *braisa* with which the Gemara had been occupied — the four-way dispute about *safek mashkeh tamei* — the Gemara focuses on Rabbi Yehudah's position. Rabbi Yehudah had said *lakol tamei*: in all cases of doubt about whether a *tamei* liquid touched something, we rule *tamei*. This seems to indicate that Rabbi Yehudah holds *tumat mashkin le-tamei keilim de'oraita* — that *tamei* liquids rendering vessels *tamei* is a biblical prohibition. That would explain why a *safek* is treated strictly, since the rule for a *safek d'oraita* is to be stringent.

The Gemara challenges this from a Mishnah. The Mishnah rules: a vessel that has an inside and an outside — cushions (*karim*), pillows (*kisasot*), sacks (*sakin*), leather bags (*martzufin*) — follows this rule: if the inside contracted *tumah*, the outside also becomes *tamei*; but if only the outside contracted *tumah*, the inside remains *tahor*. Rabbi Yehudah qualifies: *bameh devarim amurim she-nitme'u machmas mashkin* — this asymmetric rule (outside *tamei* does not render inside *tamei*) applies only when the *tumah* arrived through liquids. *Aval nitme'u machmas sheretz* — but if the cushion came into direct contact with a *sheretz*, then regardless of which side was touched, the entire object — inside and outside alike — becomes *tamei*.

### Logical Problem

This distinction creates an internal tension in Rabbi Yehudah's position. If *tumat mashkin* is *de'oraita* — as his ruling of *lakol tamei* seems to imply — then why should it matter whether the *tumah* reached the vessel through a liquid or directly through a *sheretz*? If anything, liquid *tumah* should generate the same or stricter results, not more lenient ones. The leniency Rabbi Yehudah grants to liquid-transmitted *tumah* of the vessel (outside does not affect inside) appears to contradict a *de'oraita* premise.

### Yehudah Changed Mind

Rav Yehudah, citing Shmuel, resolves this by asserting: *chazar bo Rabbi Yehudah* — Rabbi Yehudah retracted his position. The statement that *lakol tamei* — that *safek mashkeh tamei* renders everything *tamei* — was an earlier view. After encountering the difficulty posed by the cushion cases, Rabbi Yehudah reconsidered and backed away from the claim that *tumat mashkin* of vessels is *de'oraita*. Under his revised position, the strict ruling of *lakol tamei* no longer stands as stated.

### Hands vs. Sheretz

Ravina disagrees. He says: *le'olam lo hadar* — Rabbi Yehudah never retracted at all. There is no contradiction in his two rulings because they address categorically different types of liquid *tumah*. *Ha b'mashkin ha-ba'im machmas yadayim, ha b'mashkin ha-ba'im machmas sheretz* — one case involves liquids that became *tamei* by virtue of contact with *yadayim* (hands), while the other involves liquids contaminated by direct contact with a *sheretz*.

The status of ordinary hands is a *rabbinic* presumption of *tumah* — unless one has been careful about them, hands are assumed *tamei*. Liquid rendered *tamei* through such hands is thus *tamei mi-d'rabbanan*. Rabbi Yehudah's leniency for liquid-transmitted *tumah* of the cushion applies in this case: the *tumah* being rabbinic, the lenient asymmetric rule (outside does not render inside *tamei*) is appropriate.

When the liquid, however, contracted *tumah* by direct contact with a *sheretz*, that *tumah* is *de'oraita*. In such a case, Rabbi Yehudah would agree that the resulting *tumah* of the vessel is full and bilateral — touching any part of the cushion renders the whole thing *tamei* — matching the *sheretz* rule entirely. On Ravina's reading, Rabbi Yehudah's two statements are not contradictions but applications to different categories, requiring no retraction.

### Mishnah's Silence

The Gemara responds to Ravina by pointing to the language of the Mishnah itself. The Mishnah draws its distinction between two cases: *tumah* arriving through liquids versus *tumah* arriving through a *sheretz*. If Ravina is correct that the real operative distinction is between liquids contaminated by hands (rabbinic) and liquids contaminated by a *sheretz* (biblical), the Mishnah should have stated *that* distinction explicitly. It should have said: when does the asymmetric leniency apply? When the *tumah* came through liquids that were contaminated by hands. But when the *tumah* came through liquids contaminated by a *sheretz* — then the object is *tamei* in full. The fact that the Mishnah did not frame the distinction this way, instead presenting it simply as liquid versus *sheretz*, indicates that no such sub-category distinction was intended. The implication is that Rabbi Yehudah's original position was stated without qualification — and therefore the Gemara concludes that Rav Yehudah's report in the name of Shmuel is correct: *chazar bo Rabbi Yehudah* — Rabbi Yehudah did indeed retract.

---

---

# Pesachim 18

## Prior Dispute Review

### Rabbi Meir Position

The daf under discussion opens by returning to a dispute that had been established on 17b, concerning a case of *safek* — doubtful status — involving *mashkin tmayim*, defiled liquids, and whether those liquids then impart *tumah* to whatever they subsequently contact. Rabbi Meir takes the most lenient position: since *tum'at mashkin* is *mid'rabbanan* in his view, a *safek* arising from a rabbinic prohibition is treated leniently, and the item in question is *tahor*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Reversal

Rabbi Yehuda initially occupies the opposite pole. In his opinion, *mashkin* are *metam'im mid'oraita*, and therefore a *safeika mid'oraita* is treated *l'chumra* — the item is *tamei*. If Rabbi Meir represents an extreme in leniency, Rabbi Yehuda represents an extreme in stringency. At some point, however, Rabbi Yehuda was said to have reversed himself — *chazar bah* — and the question now is the extent of that reversal.

### R. Yose & Shimon Split

Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon occupy a middle position, splitting their ruling between categories. They hold that in a case of *safek*, items of food (*ochlin*) are *tamei*, while vessels (*kelim*) are *tahor*. The implication of their position is that *mashkin* are *metam'im ochlin mid'oraita* — which is why they rule stringently regarding *ochlin* — while *tum'at kelim* through *mashkin* is only *mid'rabbanan*, and therefore *safek* is treated leniently when it comes to *kelim*.

### Extent of Reversal

With this framework in place, the question sharpens: when Rabbi Yehuda reversed himself, did he retreat only one step — aligning with Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon, meaning he now holds that *kelim* are *tahor* in a case of *safek* but *ochlin* remain *tamei* — or did he reverse himself entirely, becoming as lenient as Rabbi Meir and holding that these *mashkin* cannot render anything *tamei* at all? This question, *ibayu lehu mi-kelim hu d'hadar beh o b'ochlin k'Rabbi Yose v'Rabbi Shimon sevirah leh — o dilma legamrei hadar beh k'Rabbi Meir*, drives the analysis forward.

---

## Cow & Mei Chatat Case

### Mei Chatat Setup

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes to resolve the question by examining a specific case. The case involves *mei chatat* — the waters prepared from the ashes of the *parah adumah*, the Red Heifer — which carry a well-known paradox: they purify the *tamei* and render *tamei* the *tahor*. These waters represent a rare and highly regulated substance. Under ordinary circumstances, *mei chatat* carry the status of *av hatumah* — a primary source of *tumah* — not merely a *rishon* or any secondary derivative.

### Slaughter Scenario

The constructed case is the following: a cow — an ordinary, non-consecrated animal — wanders to the vessel containing *mei chatat* and drinks from it. The cow is then slaughtered (*shechita* is performed) before the water has passed through its digestive system, so the liquid remains inside the animal. The question is: what is the status of the meat of this cow, which now contains within it what was, prior to being swallowed, an *av hatumah*?

### Meat Status Dispute

The ruling recorded is *besarah tamei* — the flesh is *tamei*. Rabbi Yehuda then offers a dissenting position: *batlu b'me'eha* — they were nullified within its intestines — implying that the meat is *tahor*. This appears to be a *machloket* between a *tana kama* and Rabbi Yehuda. Since this is a case in which *mashkin tmayim* are now in contact with food — namely, the flesh of the slaughtered animal — and Rabbi Yehuda says the flesh is *tahor*, this would seem to answer the earlier question about his *chazarah*: it appears he holds that *mashkin tmayim* cannot render *ochlin tamei* at all, which would place him entirely in the camp of Rabbi Meir.

### Chazarah Analysis

The *gemara* examines this reasoning carefully. If Rabbi Yehuda's reversal was only partial — that is, if he aligned with Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon and still holds that *mashkin* can render *ochlin tamei* — then why does he say *batlu b'me'eha* with no qualification? The objection is framed: *nehi d'tumah chamura lo metamu — tumah kala miha nitamu*? Even granting that the severe dimension of *tumah* might be nullified, surely some lighter degree of *tumah* should still apply?

### Tumah Gravity Levels

The *gemara* responds by reinterpreting the word *batlu*. Rather than meaning the *tumah* is completely annihilated, *batlu b'me'eha* means the liquid is no longer an *av hatumah* — the *tumah chamura*, the severe grade, is gone. However, it still retains *tumah kalah*, a lighter grade of *tumah*. So the meat is indeed *tamei* in the sense of *tumah kalah* — the water, once inside the animal, has been downgraded from an *av* to something more like a *rishon*, and a *rishon* can still render flesh *tamei*. The flesh becomes *tamei* through *tumah kalah*, but the liquid can no longer function as an *av hatumah* to render *kelim tamei*.

### Reconciling Positions

This reinterpretation raises a further question about the *tana kama*. If Rabbi Yehuda — the lenient one — still holds the meat is *tamei* by virtue of *tumah kalah*, then the *tana kama*, who is apparently the more stringent opinion, should hold that *tumah chamura* still applies — that the water remains an *av hatumah* even inside the animal. But if it is a full *av hatumah*, then why does the *tana kama* say only *besarah tamei*? An *av hatumah* would render *kelim tamei* as well, so why is the ruling limited to the flesh?

The *gemara* answers: *kula Rabbi Yehuda hi* — the entire passage reflects Rabbi Yehuda's opinion alone. There is no independent *tana kama* here; the text requires the principle of *chasorei mechasra*, meaning the passage as it stands is incomplete and must be supplemented. Reading it fully: the case of *parah she'shat'tah mei chatat* — *besarah tamei* — refers only to *tumah kalah*. The qualification *bameh devarim amurim* applies: this is specifically not *tumah chamura*, since Rabbi Yehuda himself says *batlu b'me'eha* — nullified with respect to *tumah chamura*, but retaining *tumah kalah*. It is all Rabbi Yehuda's own elaboration of his position.

Rav Ashi, however, offers an alternative reading. Rather than reinterpreting *batlu*, he maintains the plain meaning — *le'olam batlu b'mayim legamrei*, it truly is fully nullified. But this case does not resolve the question of Rabbi Yehuda's general position regarding *mashkin tmayim*, because this situation is categorically different: *mishum dehavai lei mashkeh saruach* — once the liquid has been swallowed by the animal and sits within its digestive tract, it is no longer considered a proper *mashkeh* at all. It has become disgusting, *saruach*, and just as a food that has become putrefied beyond the point of being *raui l'achilat kelev* loses its status under various laws, this liquid too loses its *tumah*-status. The *parah* case is therefore a special case, and Rabbi Yehuda's position in ordinary cases of *mashkin tmayim* remains unresolved.

---

## Yitma Yitma Derashah

### R. Yose Intro

The *gemara* now turns to Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon's position — *l'ochlin tme'in ul'kelim tehorin* — that *mashkin* render *ochlin tamei* but not *kelim*. Rabbah bar bar Chana reports in the name of Reish Lakish that Rabbi Yose arrived at his position by following the *shitat* his teacher, Rabbi Akiva: *Rabbi Yose b'shitat Rabbi Akiva rabo amrah*. This attribution is significant: Rabbi Yose is presenting the underlying method of Rabbi Akiva, though he may not follow it to all of its conclusions. The *limmud* — the textual derivation — is from the doubled form *yitma yitma*.

### Torah Verses Setup

The *gemara* turns to the relevant *pesukim* in *Parshat Shmini* (Vayikra). The first passage discusses what happens when a dead *sheretz* — one of the eight ritually unclean crawling creatures — falls upon various objects. The Torah states: *mikol kli eitz o veged o or o sak v'chol kli asher yeiaseh melachah bahem — bamayim yuva v'tamei ad haerev v'taher*. An object that a dead *sheretz* lands upon becomes *tamei* and requires immersion.

### Clay Vessel Case

The next *pasuk* presents a distinct scenario: *v'chol kli cheres asher yipol meihem el tocho — kol asher b'tocho yitma*. When a dead *sheretz* falls into a *kli cheres* — a clay vessel — everything inside it becomes *tamei*. The mechanism here is distinctive: a *kli cheres* conveys *tumah* through its airspace (*mei'aviro*). One need not have the *sheretz* touch the food directly; even dangling it within the interior of the clay vessel renders everything inside *tamei*. The clay vessel, unlike other vessels, cannot be purified — it must be broken. The food within it, however, must previously have been made susceptible to *tumah* through contact with liquid (*hechsher*); it need not be wet at the moment of contact, but it must have been wet at some prior point after being detached.

### Food vs. Liquid

The *gemara* then reads the next pair of verses: *mikol ha'ochel asher ye'achel asher yavo alav mayim yitma — v'chol mashkeh asher yeshateh b'chol kli yitma*. Two categories are presented: *ochel* — food upon which *mayim* have come — and *mashkeh* — liquid in a vessel. In each case the word *yitma* appears. The critical observation is that the Torah, which is written without vowel markings, uses *yitma* twice — once for *ochel* and once for *mashkeh*.

### Yitma Vocalization

The word *yitma* as vocalized is passive: "shall become *tamei*." But the same consonantal text can be vocalized as *yetamei*, meaning active: "shall render *tamei*," i.e., shall make something else *tamei*. Rabbi Akiva's method — and Rabbi Yose's adoption of it — exploits this ambiguity. By reading *yitma* as *yetamei*, one derives that both the *ochel* and the *mashkeh* do not merely become *tamei* themselves but also impart *tumah* to other things.

### R. Yose Derashah

The question then becomes: what precisely can the *mashkeh* render *tamei* — other *mashkin*, *ochlin*, or *kelim*? Rabbi Yose's conclusion — derived through the *yitma yitma* reading in the *shitat* Rabbi Akiva — is that *mashkin* can render *ochlin tamei* but cannot render *kelim tamei*. The *pasuk* uses the doubled *yitma* precisely to capture this asymmetry: the active dimension (*yetamei*) is present, but it is bounded. This is Rabbi Yose's *derashah*: *mashkin metame ochlin* but not *kelim*. That is the basis for his split ruling in the *safek* case — *l'ochlin tme'in, l'kelim tehorin*.

---

## Can Liquid Metame Liquid?

### Same Type Principle

Having established that *mashkin* can render *ochlin tamei*, the *gemara* raises a further question: can *tamei mashkin* render other *mashkin tamei*? The Talmud's answer is no, and the reasoning is articulated in two ways.

### Rav Papa Explanation

Rav Papa states the principle: *lo matzinu tumah osah kayotzei bah* — we have never found a case in which a *tumah* renders something of its own kind *tamei*. An *ochel* does not make another *ochel tamei*; a *mashkeh* does not make another *mashkeh tamei*. Only entities of different categories act upon one another. This principle is striking and far-reaching. It implies that when *tamei* and *tahor* items of the same category become mixed — as in numerous earlier cases involving *terumah teme'ah* falling into *terumah tehorah* — the issue is not that the entire mixture becomes *tamei* through transmission; rather, the individual items retain their own status, and the *halachic* difficulty is simply one of *bitul* — one cannot identify which item is which. The *tamei* items do not actively render the *tahor* ones *tamei*. This reading of Rav Papa's principle, though surprising, appears to be uncontested in the *gemara*.

### Ravina Textual Proof

Ravina adds a textual proof from the very *pesukim* under discussion. If one were to claim that *mashkin* render other *mashkin tamei*, then the *yitma* of the *seifa* — applied to *mashkeh* — would mean: liquid renders liquid *tamei*. But then what would the *yitma* of the *reisha* — applied to *ochel* — mean? It could only mean: food renders liquid *tamei*. The result would be that both the *reisha* and the *seifa* are teaching the same thing — that some substance renders *mashkeh tamei*. If so, the Torah could have collapsed them into a single *pasuk*: whether food or liquid, it renders liquid *tamei*. The fact that the Torah uses *yitma* separately in each clause — once for *ochel* and once for *mashkeh* — demands that they be teaching two different things.

### Two Yitmas Explained

The two *yitmas* therefore teach two distinct *dinim*: the first *yitma*, applied to *ochel*, means that food renders *mashkin tamei* (*yitma de'reisha letamei tumah de'mashkin*); the second *yitma*, applied to *mashkeh*, means that liquid renders *ochlin tamei* (*yitma de'seifa letamei tumah de'ochlin*). Each *yitma* conveys an asymmetric relationship: food acts on liquid, and liquid acts on food. Neither acts on its own kind.

---

## Liquid & Vessels

### Why Not Vessels?

Having resolved that *mashkin* render *ochlin tamei* but not other *mashkin tamei*, the *gemara* now asks why *mashkin* cannot also render *kelim tamei*. Why should *kelim* be excluded?

### Kal Vachomer

The attempt to include *kelim* proceeds by way of a *kal vachomer*. The original scenario involves a *sheretz* dangled in the airspace of a *kli cheres*: the *kli* becomes *tamei*, and as a result the *mashkin* inside it become *tamei*. These *mashkin* — which became *tamei* through the *kli* — are called *mashkin haba'in machmat kli*. Now, we know that a *kli* itself cannot render another *kli tamei*. If so, these *mashkin*, which derive their *tumah* from the *kli*, certainly should not be able to render a *kli tamei*: *eino din shelo yetamei et hakeilim*.

However, the *gemara* raises a second scenario: what if the *sheretz* does not fall into the airspace of the *kli* but falls directly into the *mashkeh* itself, touching the liquid? In that case, the *mashkin* derive their *tumah* directly from the *sheretz* (*mashkin haba'in machmat sheretz*), not through the *kli*. Should a *kal vachomer* not apply — if *mashkin haba'in machmat kli* cannot render *kelim tamei*, surely *mashkin haba'in machmat sheretz* — which are more severely *tamei*, since they were directly contaminated by an *av hatumah* — can render *kelim tamei*?

### Sheretz Direct Case

The *gemara* thus considers whether the case of a *sheretz* falling directly into water creates a *halachic* difference. The question is pointed: if a *sheretz* is floating in a pool of water and the water touches a *kli*, what is the status of that *kli*? The case where the *sheretz* itself is in the liquid — rather than in the airspace of the vessel — is not explicitly covered by the *pesukim*; one would have to derive it. The *kal vachomer* suggests it should be *metame* the *kli* a fortiori from the case where the *kli* itself is the source.

### Dayo Principle

The *gemara* responds with the principle of *dayo l'va min hadin lihyot kenidon* — it is sufficient for the conclusion of a *kal vachomer* to equal the *din* of its source, and one may not extend it beyond. The Torah's case established that whatever is inside the *kli* — food or liquid — becomes *tamei*. The maximum that the *kal vachomer* may derive in the case of a *sheretz* directly in the water is exactly what was established in the original precedent: the liquid can render *ochlin tamei*. It cannot, by extension of the *kal vachomer*, be made to render *kelim tamei*, because the original case never established *tumah* for *kelim* through this mechanism. The *dayo* principle blocks the inference at that point.

---

## R. Akiva Derashah

### First Yitma Food

Returning now to Rabbi Akiva's own *derashah* on the *yitma yitma*, the *gemara* examines how he himself reads each of the two instances. The first *yitma*, from *mikol ha'ochel asher ye'achel asher yavo alav mayim yitma*, Rabbi Akiva reads as teaching: the food renders *mashkin tamei* — *yitamei letamei et hamashkin*.

### Second Yitma Liquid

The second *yitma*, from *v'chol mashkeh asher yeshateh b'chol kli yitma*, he reads as teaching: the liquid renders *ochlin tamei* — *yitamei letamei et ha'ochlin*. These are the two directions of transmission established by the doubled language: *ochel* to *mashkeh*, and *mashkeh* to *ochel*.

### Food Cannot Metame Food

One might ask: if *ochel* is *metame mashkin*, why should we not say it is also *metame kelim*? Rabbi Akiva establishes this via *kal vachomer* in the negative. A *mashkeh* renders *ochlin tamei* but does not render *kelim tamei* — this was established above. An *ochel*, which cannot even render another *ochel tamei* (since like cannot make like *tamei*), is certainly not going to render *kelim tamei*: *ochel she'ein metamei ochel — eino din shelo yetamei kli*. The logic cuts in the negative direction: the weaker party (*ochel*, which cannot act on its own kind) certainly cannot exceed what the stronger party (*mashkeh*, which can act on a different category) is permitted to do.

### Mishkin Severity

The *gemara* anticipates an objection: perhaps *ochlin* should be considered more severe than *mashkin* — after all, *ochel* is *metame mashkin*, and perhaps that greater capacity warrants a conclusion that *ochel* should also be *metame kelim*. The *gemara* rejects this: the apparent severity of *ochlin* is not intrinsic to food itself. It is *chumra demashkin hu* — it is a stringency that flows from the nature of *mashkin*.

### Chumra Mishkin

The explanation is as follows: *mashkin* are more susceptible to receiving *tumah* than *ochlin* because *mashkin* can receive *tumah* without any prior *hechsher* — without any preparatory act. A food item must first have liquid come upon it (*hechsher b'mayim*) before it can receive *tumah*; without this preparation, even direct contact with an *av hatumah* leaves the food *tahor*. A *mashkeh*, by contrast, requires no such preparation — by its very nature it is susceptible to *tumah*. This greater receptivity of *mashkin* to *tumah* is what gives them their apparent force, so that when they contact *ochlin*, they render them *tamei*. But this *chumra* belongs to the *mashkeh*, not to the *ochel*. The *ochel*'s ability to render *mashkin tamei* is therefore a reflection of the *mashkeh*'s own susceptibility — *mishum demashkin dekabel tumah shelo behechsher* — not a sign that *ochlin* themselves occupy an elevated position in the hierarchy of *tumah*. Consequently, the *kal vachomer* that would have extended *ochel*'s reach to *kelim* is without foundation.

---

---

# Pesachim 19

## Ein Oseh Tumah

### Mashkin Rule

By way of review: the premise established in prior discussion is that *mashkin* cannot be *metame* *mashkin*, and *ochlin* cannot be *metame* *ochlin*. The cross-contamination is permitted — *mashkin* can be *metame* *ochlin* and vice versa — but the rule of *ein oseh tumah kayotze bah*, "does not create like," prevents like from contaminating like. This does not extend to *keilim*, as was established through a series of *kal va'chomers*, the application of the principle of *dyo*, and the double usage of *yitamei* in a relevant *pasuk*. That double formulation was understood to refer to *mashkin*, given their inherent predisposition to receive *tumah*, and through them the contamination works its way into *ochlin* — not directly because *ochlin* contaminate *ochlin*, but because *mashkin* serve as the enabling agent, the *makhshir*, for everything else.

### Seeds & Sheretz

The *Gemara* now raises a challenge: is the principle of *ein oseh tumah kayotze bah* really derived from the double *yitamei*, as we have been assuming? Surely, it is derived from elsewhere entirely — from the *pasuk* dealing with seeds and a *sheretz*: *v'chi yutan mayim al zera* — if water had been placed on seed — *v'nafal mivlatam alav*, and then the carcass of the *sheretz* falls upon it — *tamei hu*. The Torah says *tamei hu*, and the *Gemara* darshens the word *hu* as a limiting particle: it is *tamei*, and it does not create *tumah* in the manner of itself. The seed becomes *tamei*, but it cannot make another object of the same type *tamei*.

To clarify what becomes *tamei* in this case: the water falls on produce — seeds, kernels of wheat — and renders them susceptible to *tumah*; then the dead *sheretz* falls upon them and they become *tamei*. But those *tamei* seeds cannot in turn render other food *tamei*. They can render *mashkin* *tamei*, since *ochlin* can contaminate *mashkin* and *mashkin* can contaminate *ochlin*, but *ochlin* cannot contaminate *ochlin de-oraita*. Given that we already derive *ein oseh tumah kayotze bah* from *tamei hu*, why do we need the double *yitamei* at all?

### Direct vs. Indirect

The answer is that the two *pesukim* are addressing two distinct cases. One — *chad* — speaks of *mashkin ha-ba'im mechamat sheretz*: liquid that became *tamei* through direct contact with a *sheretz*. The other speaks of *mashkin ha-ba'im mechamat kli*: liquid that became *tamei* not because the *sheretz* touched the liquid directly, but because the *sheretz* touched the *kli* containing the liquid, and through that vessel the liquid became *tamei*. In the second case, the *sheretz* touched the *kli*, the *kli* contained the *mashkeh*, and the *mashkeh* became *tamei* via the vessel — a more indirect path.

### Two Verses Purpose

Even though both cases involve a *sheretz* and both arrive at the same *halachic* outcome — *ein oseh tumah kayotze bah* — both *pesukim* are necessary, and neither can be inferred from the other alone.

If we had only the *pasuk* about *mashkin* coming through a *kli* — the indirect case — one might have thought the rule applies only there, *mishum delo chamiri*: precisely because that route is less direct, the *tumah* is weaker. By the time the contamination travels from *sheretz* to *kli* to *mashkeh*, the *mashkeh* is already a *sheni*, and being a *sheni*, it is less powerful. One might therefore say that such a weakened *tumah* cannot create like — but that a more direct *tumah*, where the *sheretz* touches the *mashkeh* itself, would be powerful enough to do so. Hence the necessity of the other *pasuk*, which addresses the direct case and teaches that even there — *ein oseh tumah kayotze bah*.

Conversely, had we only the direct case — *mashkin ha-ba'im mechamat sheretz* — and from it derived that even strong, direct *tumah* cannot create like, one might conclude *kal va'chomer* that certainly the weaker, indirect case cannot create like either. So in principle, one *pasuk* could have sufficed and the other inferred logically.

### Svara vs. Mikra

This brings us to a striking tension. The *Gemara* acknowledges the principle of *milta d'atya b'kal va'chomer tarach v'chtav lah kra*: sometimes the Torah goes to the trouble of writing out explicitly what could have been derived through logical reasoning. This is essentially another way of saying *ein hachi nami* — yes, you could have inferred it, but the Torah chose to state it explicitly anyway.

This highlights a genuine tension in *halachic* methodology between learning a *din al pi svara* — through human reasoning — and learning it *al pi hamikra* — from an explicit scriptural source. The *Gemara* here takes the position that even where a logical derivation would suffice, an explicit *pasuk* is preferred. This is perhaps especially true in the domain of *tumah v'taharah*, which is sufficiently abstruse that explicit textual grounding is more desirable than relying on human creativity alone — even very sophisticated creativity.

---

## Rabbi Akiva/Yosei

### Ravina's Question

Ravina now challenges Rav Ashi by invoking a statement of Rava: *lo Rabbi Yosei savar ke-Rabbi Akiva v'lo Rabbi Akiva savar ke-Rabbi Yosei* — Rabbi Yosei does not hold like Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Akiva does not hold like Rabbi Yosei. This requires unpacking.

Recall that among the *Tannaim*, there were multiple positions regarding how far *tumos* extend. Rabbi Meir rejected any rabbinic extension of *tumah* altogether. Rabbi Yehudah accepted a more expansive position, though the question arose as to how far he ultimately retracted. Rabbi Yosei occupied a middle position — *ochlin* yes, *keilim* no — citing Rabbi Akiva's methodology while not endorsing his conclusions. And Rabbi Akiva himself pushed the categories further, maintaining that one can reach a *shlishi be-chullin*.

The question now is: how exactly do Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Akiva diverge? Rav Ashi formulates this for Rav Kahana.

### Yosei's Position

*Bishlama* — it is understandable why Rabbi Yosei does not hold like Rabbi Akiva. The proof comes from a *baraita* in which Rabbi Yosei himself teaches: *minayin li-revii ba-kodesh she-hu pasul* — from where do we know that a *revii* in *kodesh* is *pasul*? He then reasons as follows.

Everyone agrees that a *revii be-kodesh* is *pasul*. In the standard framework, *chullin* extends only to a *sheni*; *terumah* extends to a *shlishi*; *kodesh* extends to a *revii*. Rabbi Yosei establishes the *shlishi be-kodesh* as *min ha-Torah*, derived explicitly from the verse *ve-ha-basar asher yiga be-chol tamei lo ye-akhel* — the meat that touches anything *tamei* shall not be eaten. The *Gemara* reasons: *mi lo askinan di-nega be-sheni* — are we not dealing with a case where this flesh of *kodesh* touches a *sheni*? The flesh then becomes a *shlishi*, and the Torah says it may not be eaten. Since a *sheni* is called *tamei* — as established by the double *yitamei* discussed earlier — the verse teaches explicitly that a *shlishi be-kodesh* is *pasul min ha-Torah*.

From there, Rabbi Yosei derives the *revii be-kodesh* through a *kal va'chomer*: a *mechusar kippurim* — one who has immersed in a *mikvah* but not yet brought the required *korban*, and who may eat *terumah* but not *kodesh* — is *pasul* from *kodesh* though permitted in *terumah*. A *shlishi* is *pasul* from *terumah*. *Kal va'chomer*: if *mechusar kippurim*, who is less restricted in *terumah*, is excluded from *kodesh*, then a *shlishi* that is *pasul* in *terumah* should certainly produce a *revii* that is *pasul* in *kodesh*. The *kal va'chomer* derives the *revii* as *min ha-Torah* — not that a *kal va'chomer* automatically makes something *de-rabbanan*, but rather that the logical deduction draws its force from the implications of the underlying *pesukim* and thus carries *de-oraita* weight.

Now, if Rabbi Yosei were actually operating on Rabbi Akiva's framework — which extends *chullin* one further level to a *shlishi be-chullin* — he should logically have also taught that there is a *revii be-terumah* and a *chamishi be-kodesh*. But he does not. He stops at *revii be-kodesh* and *shlishi be-terumah*. This proves that Rabbi Yosei does not hold like Rabbi Akiva.

### Akiva's Position

The reverse — that Rabbi Akiva does not hold like Rabbi Yosei — is established differently. Rav Ashi argues: if Rabbi Akiva's position implied the further extension that Rabbi Yosei's *kal va'chomerim* would logically entail, then surely some *tanna* would at some point have come forward and taught explicitly in Rabbi Akiva's name that there is a *revii be-terumah* and a *chamishi be-kodesh*. The fact that no such teaching exists anywhere suggests that Rabbi Akiva's position does not generate that conclusion.

This is, however, immediately questioned: *v'anan hachi nekum v'nismach* — can we really rely on this? Is absence of evidence evidence of absence? Is the fact that no *tanna* ever formulated such a teaching sufficient proof that Rabbi Akiva would have rejected it? This is a striking methodological moment: the later Amoraim are openly debating whether silence in the tradition can constitute positive proof of a rejected position.

### Kli Metzaref

To resolve the question, Rav Ashi — or, as the *Gemara* says, *v'isayma* Rav Kahana — investigated and found an explicit teaching. *Dak v'ashkach*: he searched and discovered. *Hachi tnan*: the following is a *Mishnah*: *ha-kli m'tzaref es mah she-b'tocho l'kodesh aval lo l'terumah* — the vessel combines everything contained within it for purposes of *kodesh*, but not for *terumah*. And accordingly, a *revii be-kodesh* is *pasul* and a *shlishi be-terumah* is *pasul*.

This teaching requires explanation, particularly to distinguish it from the case of apples lined up in a row. If one apple touches the next, and the next touches the next, the *tumah* would theoretically extend without limit — or rather, it would reach whatever level of depletion *halakha* recognizes, but the point is that the contamination would flow through sequential contact, not through the vessel itself. The principle of *kli metzaref mah she-b'tocho* is different: it is not the sequential touching that matters, but the fact that all the contents share a common vessel that unites them as one. The *kli* acts as an encompassing entity, and through its containing power, everything inside it is treated as a unit — and the *tumah* of that unit extends as far as the *kli metzaref* concept carries it, reaching to *revii be-kodesh* but no further.

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba then says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *me'iduto shel Rabbi Akiva nishnit mishna zu* — this *Mishnah* was taught based on the testimony of Rabbi Akiva.

### Revii Limitation

The attribution to Rabbi Akiva is confirmed from a *Mishnah* in *Eduyot*. The case involves a *tvul yom* — one who has immersed but for whom the sun has not yet set, and who therefore has not yet achieved full *taharah*. Rabbi Akiva added to the standard list of items susceptible to contamination: not only food items like *soles*, but also *ketores*, *levonah*, and *gechalim* — the coals used to burn the *ketores*, which are certainly not food. All of these, Rabbi Akiva taught, are subject to the rule that if a *tvul yom* touches part of them — *im naga tvul yom be-miktzatam* — the entire contents are rendered *pasul*. This is precisely because they are in a *kli* together: the vessel unites them, and the *tvul yom* touching one of the coals on the *mizbei'ach* renders all the coals in that vessel as one unit.

The crucial point is that Rabbi Akiva's teaching goes only as far as a *revii*. *Ve-amar Rabbah bar bar Chanah amar Rabbi Yochanan me'eiduto shel Rabbi Akiva nishnit mishna zu* — and the *Mishnah* reaches only to *revii be-kodesh*. If Rabbi Akiva had accepted the *kal va'chomer* logic that Rabbi Yosei employed, he should have extended the chain further — to a *revii be-terumah* and a *chamishi be-kodesh*. He did not. The explicit teaching attributed to him reaches only as far as *revii be-kodesh* and *shlishi be-terumah*, thereby confirming that Rabbi Akiva does not hold the *kal va'chomer* that would extend things further. The absence-of-evidence argument is thus vindicated, but now backed by explicit textual support: we have a positive teaching from Rabbi Akiva that stops precisely where it should stop if he rejects the further extension.

### Tziruf Status

The *Gemara* then notes that this entire principle of *tziruf* — of the vessel combining its contents — is, in Rabbi Akiva's view, *de-rabbanan*, and he therefore disagrees with Rabbi Chanin.

Rabbi Chanin holds that *tziruf de-oraita* — the combining power of a vessel is a Torah-level concept — and he derives this from the *korbanot* of the *nesi'im*: *kaf achas asara zahav meleia ketores* — one ladle of ten [*shekalim*] weight, full of *ketores*. The verse says *kaf achas* — one cup — and the *Gemara* reads this *derashah*: the *kaf* makes everything within it *achas*, one unified entity. From this, Rabbi Chanin derives that the combining power of a vessel is *min ha-Torah*.

Rabbi Akiva, however, holds that *tziruf d'rabbanan* — the concept is rabbinic in nature, since the Torah-level discussions of *tumah* concerned *ochlin* and *mashkin*, and extending it to *keilim* and their combining power requires rabbinic enactment.

---

## Needle Case

### Needle Rule

The *Gemara* transitions to a new topic with the teaching *tenan hasam*: a *Mishnah* cited from elsewhere. *Ha-machat she-nimtzet ba-basar* — a needle that was found in meat. The case is that an animal of *kodshim* was slaughtered and a needle was discovered inside the flesh. The ruling: *ha-sakin ve-ha-yadayim tehorot* — the knife and the hands remain *tahor*. We do not assume that the knife, used in cutting the meat, necessarily struck the needle; nor do we assume the hands came into contact with it. However, *ve-ha-basar tamei* — the meat itself is *tamei*. And if the needle was found in the excrement of the animal rather than in the flesh, *ha-kol tahor* — everything, including the meat, is *tahor*.

### No Hand Tumah

Upon this, Rabbi Akiva comments: *zachinu she-ein tumas yadayim ba-Mikdash* — we have gained, we are fortunate, that there is no *tumat yadayim* in the *Mikdash*. The point requires context. *Tumat yadayim* is fundamentally a rabbinic enactment — hands are presumed *shniyot le-tumah* by rabbinic decree, and there was no corresponding *gezeirah* imposed within the *Mikdash* itself. Rabbi Akiva's comment reflects that outside the *Mikdash* we are more *machmir* in this regard, while the *Mikdash* was deliberately left free of this particular rabbinic imposition.

### Kli Logic

One might ask: the *Mishnah*'s case mentions that the *sakin* was *tahor* — yet Rabbi Akiva speaks only of *yadayim*. Why does he not also say that we have gained that there is no *tumat keilim* in the *Mikdash*?

A first answer suggested is that of Rav Yehudah citing Rav: the laws of *tumat yadayim* and *tumat keilim* were enacted at different times, and Rabbi Akiva's comment was made after the *gezeirah* on *yadayim* but before the *gezeirah* on *keilim* had been enacted — hence no need to mention what did not yet exist.

Rava rejects this: both *gezeirot* were enacted on the same day. The *Gemara* cites the *Mishnah* listing the famous eighteen decrees issued in the *aliyah* of Chananya ben Chizkiya ben Garon, in a session in which *Beis Shammai* prevailed. That list mentions *ha-sefer*, *ha-yadayim*, *ha-tvul yom*, and *ha-ochlin ve-ha-keilim she-nitme'u be-mashkin* — all together, in one sitting. *Yadayim* and *keilim* are part of the same decree. One cannot say Rabbi Akiva was commenting before one but after the other.

The true answer, Rava explains, is simpler: *hanach l'tumas sakin de-afilu be-chullin nami lo metamei*. Leave aside the *tumah* of the *sakin* entirely — even in *chullin*, the knife would not have been *tamei*. Why not? *Hai sakin d'naga b'mai* — what did the knife touch that would make it *tamei*? If it touched the meat — *ein ochel metamei kli*: food cannot render a vessel *tamei*. If it touched the needle — *ein kli metamei kli*: a vessel cannot render another vessel *tamei*. The *machat* is a *kli* and the *sakin* is a *kli*, and we have established that like does not contaminate like in this sense either. Therefore there was nothing to say: even in *chullin*, the knife would never have been *tamei* from this situation, and so there was no gain specific to the *Mikdash* worth announcing.

### Safek in Jerusalem

This brings the *Gemara* to a new question: what exactly makes the needle *tamei* in the first place? The ruling is that the meat is *tamei* because of the needle, but why should we assume the needle is *tamei*? One might say it is a *safek* — an uncertainty — and surely there is a principle at work: the *Gemara* cites a *baraita* in which Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Chanina all hold that no *gezeirah* of *tumah* was enacted upon *safek*-cases in Jerusalem. One version of the teaching is *lo gazru al safek ha-rukin she-bi-Yerushalayim* — we do not rule *tamei* regarding doubtfully *tamei* spit found in Jerusalem. Since Jerusalem is populated by people striving toward *taharah*, and since those with *zav*-status would presumably avoid spitting publicly, the *rov* of spit found there may be presumed *tahor*.

Another version of the teaching states: *lo gazru al safek ha-keilim she-bi-Yerushalayim* — we do not rule *tamei* regarding vessels of uncertain status found in Jerusalem, since people are generally careful to maintain *taharah* of their vessels in the holy city. If the needle is at most a *safek* as to whether it was rendered *tamei*, and if *safek keilim bi-Yerushalayim* are presumed *tahor*, then the needle should be *tahor* — and the meat should be *tahor* as well. Why, then, does the *Mishnah* rule the meat *tamei*?

### Vadai Case

Rav Yehudah citing Rav resolves this: *hacha lav be-safek* — this is not a *safek* case at all. The case of the *Mishnah* is a *vadai*: specifically, *kegon she-ivad lo machat temei met ve-hikkirah ba-basar* — a person who was *tamei met* had lost a needle, and now he recognizes it in the meat. He is a *tamei met*, he touched this needle, and here it is — found in the animal that was slaughtered. The needle is definitively *tamei*, not doubtfully so, and therefore the meat it was embedded in is *tamei*. The tailorer who was *tamei met* lost his needle; it was swallowed by the animal; the needle is now recovered from the flesh. The principles regarding *safek keilim bi-Yerushalayim* simply do not apply, since there is no *safek* here.

### Muzzled Cow

Rabbi Yosei bar Avin offers an alternative construction of the case, one that preserves the *safek* framework while still explaining why the meat is *tamei*. The case is *kegon she-haytah parah chasumah u-va'ah michutz li-Yerushalayim* — a cow that was muzzled and came from outside Jerusalem. Since the cow was muzzled, it could not have ingested anything while in Jerusalem; therefore any needle found inside it must have been swallowed before it arrived — that is, from outside Jerusalem. And outside Jerusalem, the principle of *lo gazru al safek* does not apply: *safek* *tumah* in the public domain is resolved as *tamei* in the normal way. The needle came from outside, its *safek* status is therefore *tamei*, and accordingly the meat is *tamei*. The muzzled cow thus establishes that the needle could not have come from within Jerusalem, removing any benefit of the special leniency that applies to *safek keilim* within the city.

---

---

# Pesachim 25

## Derech Hana'ah

### Practical Parameters

The daf opens by turning from the theoretical question of *how* we derive that certain objects are forbidden in benefit to the practical parameters governing that prohibition. The preceding discussion had established two distinct conceptual models for the source of *issur hana'ah*: the model rooted in *achilah* (eating), associated with Chizkiyahu's and Rabbi Abbahu's derivations from *lo yochal*, and the model rooted in *kodesh* — something completely taboo and off-limits, akin to consecrated property. As we will see, this distinction between the *achilah* world and the *kodesh* world turns out to have significant practical consequences.

### Rabbi Abbahu

Rabbi Abbahu, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, had already made two interconnected statements. First, for things one is forbidden to eat, one is liable only if one consumes them in the normal way of eating — eating raw forbidden fat, for example, would not constitute a transgression, since eating in a normal fashion involves a certain kind of pleasurable engagement with the act. Second — and this is a considerably more radical claim — even with respect to things that are forbidden in *hana'ah* (benefit), one must derive that benefit in a normal way. If one were to apply the fat of a *shor haniskal* (an ox condemned to be stoned) to a wound in order to heal it, one would not transgress, even though healing a wound is a recognizable and legitimate benefit. The reason is that just as eating is defined by a process with specific parameters — including the requirement that it be a normal, pleasurable act — so too deriving benefit, particularly insofar as it is conceptually linked to eating, must follow a normal process. The end result of having received benefit is insufficient; the manner in which the benefit was obtained must itself be a recognized form of *hana'ah*.

### Orlah Proof

Rav Zeira proposes a proof for this principle from a teaching about *orlah*. The rule is that one receives lashes for *orlah* only for juice that comes from olives and grapes — not for juice pressed from strawberries, figs, or pomegranates. The inference Rav Zeira draws is that one would not transgress by drinking pomegranate juice from *orlah* fruit, because drinking the juice of a pomegranate is not the normal way in which people derive pleasure from that fruit. In the period of the Gemara, only olive oil and wine were recognized as authentic fruit juices; all other fruit liquids were not considered a normal form of enjoying the fruit. This, Rav Zeira argues, demonstrates that at least by eating, one must act in the normal, pleasure-deriving manner.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges whether this constitutes a valid proof. He notes that if the case had involved the fruit itself — if someone had eaten the pomegranate in some abnormal fashion and thereby failed to derive normal pleasure from the act — that would indeed prove that the act of eating requires a normal mode of benefit. But the case of pomegranate juice is different. The reason one does not transgress is not that the process of deriving benefit was abnormal. The reason is a problem with the *object* itself.

### Zei'ah Be'alma

The term Abaye uses is *zei'ah be'alma* — it is merely like sweat, a runoff of the fruit that does not carry the legal status of the fruit itself. Halacha does not recognize fruit juices other than olive oil and wine as a genuine expression of the fruit. The Gemara elsewhere illustrates this: when one squeezes an olive before the true oil has separated, what runs off first is a watery liquid called *mohal*, which is not yet considered olive oil and does not legally represent the fruit. Similarly, on *Shabbos*, the melachah of squeezing fruit and extracting its juice is a biblical transgression only for olives and grapes; squeezing an orange or lemon is not biblically prohibited, because the extracted liquid is not considered a substance of significance — it is, in halachic terms, nothing.

The question, then, is not whether the person derived benefit in a normal way, but whether what they extracted is even legally considered "the fruit" at all. If the object is not the forbidden thing, there is no transgression, regardless of how one benefited from it.

### Taam Ke'ikar

Tosafot sharpens this difficulty considerably by raising the principle of *taam ke'ikar* — that the taste of a forbidden substance is treated as equivalent to the substance itself. If one cooks *chazir* with a potato, the potato absorbs the taste of the *chazir* and becomes forbidden. Why, then, should the liquid pressed from an *orlah* orange not be forbidden as the *taam* of the *orlah* fruit, even if it lacks the full legal status of the fruit? Tosafot acknowledges this is a genuine difficulty without a fully satisfying resolution. One possibility is that *taam ke'ikar* creates a secondary, derivative prohibition rather than the primary prohibition of the fruit itself — one may not transgress the specific *issur* of *orlah*, but one might still violate a secondary *taam* prohibition. The practical stakes of this question are real: one of the disputes among the *acharonim* regarding grain alcohol on *Pesach* turns precisely on this axis. Some hold that since it is derived from grain and water and constitutes a form of *chametz*, it is fully forbidden. Others argue, based on reasoning parallel to this Gemara, that it is *zei'ah be'alma* — it lacks the legal status of *chametz* since it is not olive oil or grape juice — and is therefore permissible on *Pesach*. The tension between *zei'ah be'alma* and *taam ke'ikar* is thus a live and unresolved issue with significant halachic consequences.

---

## Kilayim & Basar

### Kilayim Exception

The Gemara now records a statement of Abaye: everyone agrees that with respect to *kilayim* (diverse kinds planted together in a vineyard), one receives lashes even if one derived benefit in an abnormal way — *afilu shelo k'derech hana'atan*.

### Kodesh Model

The reason Abaye gives is precisely the conceptual distinction established earlier: *mishum d'lo ktiv behu achilah* — the Torah does not prohibit *kilayim* through the language of eating. What the Torah says is *pen tikdash* — lest it become sanctified. This language invokes the *kodesh* model, the world of something completely taboo and off-limits, rather than the *achilah* model of a normal act of eating extended to benefit. When a prohibition is rooted in *achilah*, it inherits the process-parameters of eating: the benefit must be derived in a normal fashion. When a prohibition is rooted in the *hekdesh* framework — something categorically forbidden and set apart — there are no such process parameters. Any benefit, however derived, violates the taboo. A straightforward illustration of the *achilah* framework's process-dependence is the case of an intravenous drip on Yom Kippur: one does not transgress the prohibition of eating, because eating is defined by a specific process, and an IV does not constitute that process.

### Basar Proof

The Gemara now tests Abaye's assertion by examining a *baraita* that attempts to derive the prohibitions of *basar bechalav* through a *kal vachomer*. The *baraita* opens with the view of Issi ben Yehuda: how do we know that *basar bechalav* is forbidden to *eat*, given that the Torah only explicitly prohibits *cooking* meat and milk together? The *baraita* establishes this through a *gezeirah shavah*: the prohibition of *basar bechalav* is introduced with the phrase *ki am kadosh atah l'Hashem Elokecha* — "for you are a holy nation to the Lord your God" — and another verse uses similar language introducing the prohibition of *treifah*: *v'anshei kodesh tihyun li uvasar basadeh treifah lo tocheilu* — "you shall be holy people to Me, and flesh torn in the field you shall not eat." The parallel implies that just as the *kodesh* formulation by *treifah* means you must abstain from eating it, so too by *basar bechalav*. Having established that *basar bechalav* is forbidden to eat, the *baraita* then asks: from where do we know that *hana'ah* (benefit) is also forbidden? A *kal vachomer* is proposed: *mah orlah shelo ne'evdah bah aveirah asurah bahana'ah* — *orlah*, for which no transgression was committed in its production, is nonetheless forbidden in benefit. *Basar bechalav*, for which a transgression was actually committed (the act of cooking), should certainly be forbidden in benefit.

### Orlah vs Chametz

The Gemara challenges the *kal vachomer* on two fronts. First, *orlah* may be more severe in one respect: *sha'at hachosher* — *orlah* never had a permissible state. From the moment the fruit grew it was forbidden. *Basar bechalav*, by contrast, begins with permitted meat and permitted milk; perhaps that prior permitted status mitigates the severity of the resulting prohibition, and therefore one cannot derive a *kal vachomer* from *orlah* to *basar bechalav*. The rejoinder is to invoke *chametz b'Pesach* as a comparison point: here is something that begins as permitted, becomes forbidden, and is nonetheless forbidden in benefit. But *chametz b'Pesach* is itself vulnerable to a counterargument: it carries the penalty of *kares*, making it uniquely severe, and thus cannot serve as a *kal vachomer* basis for *basar bechalav*, which carries no such penalty. The Gemara then turns to *kilayim* from the vineyard (*kilayei hakerem*, the only variety that is *assur bahana'ah*) as a possible model: it carries no *kares*, and one has committed a transgression in its production. This appears to be a valid comparison to *basar bechalav*, allowing the inference that *basar bechalav* is likewise forbidden in benefit.

### Abaye Responds

But this is precisely where Abaye's assertion about *kilayim* becomes problematic for the *kal vachomer*. If *kilayim* is *assur bahana'ah* even *shelo k'derech hana'ah* — even in an abnormal mode of benefit — then *kilayim* is more severe than an ordinary *issur hana'ah*. The challenge would then be: how can we learn a *kal vachomer* to *basar bechalav* from *kilayim*, if *kilayim* is uniquely stringent in this regard and *basar bechalav* would presumably be limited to normal modes of benefit? The response attributed to Abaye is striking: *atu b'vasar bechalav achilah kesivah bei?* Is the word *achilah* written in connection with *basar bechalav* itself? It is not. The Torah says nothing about eating *basar bechalav*; it speaks only of cooking it. We infer the prohibition of eating from other sources, but the Torah does not use the act-language of *achilah* directly with *basar bechalav*. Therefore, Abaye argues, the same logic that applies to *kilayim* applies here: because the Torah does not ground the prohibition in the language of eating, *basar bechalav* also is transgressed even when one derives benefit in an abnormal way. This is in fact the *halacha*: both *kilayim* and *basar bechalav* are transgressed *shelo k'derech hana'ah*, provided the object still retains its status as food. At some point, if the food becomes so altered or contaminated that it is no longer recognizable as food, one would not transgress — but as long as it remains food, the prohibition applies regardless of the mode of benefit.

### Kodesh Framework

The opposing view — that *basar bechalav* should be limited to normal benefit — had been grounded in the argument that we learn the prohibition of *basar bechalav* from *neveila* or *treifah*, and those prohibitions do use the language of *achilah*. What is prohibited vis-à-vis *treifah* is an act of eating, so by extension what is prohibited vis-à-vis *basar bechalav* should also be defined as an act — normal *derech hana'ah*. Abaye's rejoinder is that even though we may derive the *issur* of *basar bechalav* from *treifah*, the Torah itself never uses the language of *achilah* directly in connection with *basar bechalav*. The Torah formulates *basar bechalav* as something generically off-limits, not as a prohibited *act* of eating. What one learns from *treifah* is the category of the prohibition, but the specifics — whether it must be a formal act with process-parameters — one does not derive from *treifah*. Because *basar bechalav* is formulated as categorically forbidden rather than as a prohibited act, the prohibition does not require a normal mode of benefit. This is the same principle at work in *kilayim*, and the conceptual parallel between the two is thus complete. A practical illustration of this principle is discussed in the *Shulchan Aruch*, where the *Rema* addresses the use of ashes from a fire on which meat and dairy pots had been used, for purposes such as washing one's hair — a case where the question of *shelo k'derech hana'ah* of *basar bechalav* arises as a genuine halachic concern.

---

## Object Transformation

### Flower Pot Case

With the foregoing analysis of *kilayim* and *basar bechalav* established, the Gemara turns to a new challenge bearing on the scope of *kilayim*. Rav Shemaya raises a difficulty from a *mishna*: the case of *hamavir atzitz nakuv b'cherem* — one who passes a flower pot with a hole through a vineyard. A flower pot with a hole is treated halachically as if the plant within it is planted in the ground, since the only separation between the soil in the pot and the ground below is air, and the hole establishes a kind of legal continuity. If one places such a flower pot containing, say, a growing stalk of grain, on the floor of a vineyard, one has effectively brought grain into contact with grapevines — the classic configuration of *kilayei hakerem*.

### Bitul 1:200

The *mishna* rules: *im hosif matayim, assur* — if the grain stalk grew by one two-hundredth of its prior volume, it is forbidden. The underlying principle is that *kilayim* is subject to *bitul* (nullification) at a ratio of one in two hundred — more stringent than ordinary *bitul* at one in sixty and even more stringent than *terumah* at one in one hundred, reflecting the severity of *kilayim* as a prohibition that is *assur bahana'ah*. The practical application: suppose the grain in the flower pot had a volume of 199 units before placement in the vineyard, and upon removal it had grown to 200 units. The one unit of new growth is *kilayim*. One unit of *kilayim* against 199 units of *heter* is a ratio of one to 199 — insufficient to achieve *bitul*, which requires at least one to 200. Therefore the mixture is forbidden. If less than one unit had grown, *bitul* would be achieved and there would be no prohibition.

### Two Kilayim Forms

Crucially, the structure of this *mishna* implies that only the new growth is *kilayim* — not the original stalk of grain that was already growing before the flower pot was placed in the vineyard. The original stalk is treated as pure *heter*, and only what grew while situated in the vineyard carries the status of *kilayim*. This appears to directly contradict the earlier discussion, in which it was suggested that when seeds are crossed and planted together, even the original seed becomes forbidden. The *mishna* here seems to say the opposite: the original material retains its permissible status, and only the new growth is forbidden.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between two forms of *kilayim*, supported by a close reading of the relevant verse, which contains two distinct expressions: *hazera* (the seed) and *hamlei'ah* (the fullness, i.e., the growth). The verse thus encompasses both the original seed and the new growth, but applies each to a different case. *Zaru'a mei'ikaro* — something that was planted together from the outset, where both seeds were placed in the ground at the same time — in that case, *behashrasha*, as soon as the seeds take root together, the original seed itself becomes forbidden. *Zaru'a uva* — something that was already planted and was subsequently brought near the other plant, as in the flower pot case, where the grain stalk was already growing and was merely moved into the vineyard — in that case, *hosif in, lo hosif lo*: only what grows subsequently becomes forbidden; the original material does not take on *kilayim* status. The logic reflects the act emphasized by the Torah: *lo tizra karmecha kilayim* — "do not plant your vineyard with diverse kinds." When one plants two kinds together, the very act of planting creates the forbidden entity, and the original seeds are transformed by that act. When, however, one plant already exists and is simply brought into proximity with the other, no single act of joint planting occurred, and therefore the original material is not implicated — only the subsequent growth, which actually grew in the condition of *kilayim*, acquires that status. An interesting edge case left open by the Gemara is what happens when one seed is already growing and one plants a new seed next to it — neither the pure case of joint planting nor the pure case of the pre-existing flower pot. The Gemara does not resolve this.

---

## Healing & Martyrdom

### Healing Exception

Rabbi Yaakov, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, states: *b'khol mitrappin chutz me-atzei Asherah* — one may heal oneself using all types of things, even those that are otherwise forbidden in benefit, with the sole exception of wood from an *asherah*, a tree that has been worshipped as *avodah zarah*. The Gemara immediately asks: what is the case? If there is a genuine risk to life, then even *asherah* wood should be permissible — one may transgress any prohibition to save one's life. If there is no risk to life, then even ordinary forbidden objects should not be permissible for use in healing, since their benefit remains biblically prohibited. The Gemara resolves: we are speaking of a case where there is genuine *sakanah* (risk to life), and even so, *asherah* wood may not be used. All other prohibitions yield to *pikuach nefesh*; this one does not.

### Love Midrash

The basis for this exception is a *baraita* of Rabbi Eliezer interpreting the verse commanding love of God *b'khol nafshekha* (with all your soul) and *b'khol me'odekha* (with all your might). Rabbi Eliezer asks: if the Torah says love God with all your soul, why does it add all your might? And if it says all your might, why add all your soul? The answer: for a person whose body is more precious to him than his property, the Torah says *b'khol nafshekha* — you must be prepared to sacrifice even your life for God. For a person whose money is more precious to him than his body, the Torah says *b'khol me'odekha* — you must be prepared to sacrifice even your wealth. From this we derive the principle that one is obligated to give up one's life rather than violate certain categories of prohibition — the principle of *yehareg v'al ya'avor*.

### Three Sins

When Ravin transmitted the teaching of Rabbi Yochanan, he formulated it as follows: one may heal oneself with all things except *avodah zarah*, *gilluy arayot*, and *shfikhut damim* — idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and murder. These are the three categories for which one must give up one's life rather than transgress. The principle is bidirectional: just as one cannot violate these three even when coerced at the cost of one's life, one cannot violate them even when doing so would cure an illness or save one from disease. Saving one's own life does not override these three prohibitions.

### Avizrayhu Debate

The case of *asherah* wood raises a pointed question: using *asherah* wood is a transgression of the prohibition against deriving benefit from *avodah zarah*, but it is not itself an act of *avodah zarah*. Should it be treated as equivalent to actual idol worship for purposes of *yehareg v'al ya'avor*? Tosafot argues that in principle the prohibition on deriving benefit from *asherah* wood would not in itself require martyrdom. What the Gemara prohibits, says Tosafot, is specifically the case where the healing power attributed to the *asherah* tree is bound up with belief in its sacred or supernatural properties — where the tree is worshipped precisely because of its reputed powers, and one is seeking to harness those same powers. In that situation, using the wood for healing is a gateway to genuine belief in the *avodah zarah*, and therefore one must give up one's life rather than do it. If, however, the *asherah* tree merely happens to provide useful bark or fruit, and the benefit sought is entirely incidental to its status as a worshipped object, Tosafot would permit it even under *sakanah*, despite the technical *issur hana'ah*. The Ran takes a fundamentally different position. He holds that any prohibition that belongs to the constellation of *avodah zarah* — even if it is not itself an act of worship and does not lead to worship — carries the status of *yehareg v'al ya'avor*. This is the principle of *avizrayhu d'avodah zarah*: the appurtenances of idolatry share in the severity of idolatry itself. The Ran's position extends this framework to the other two capital prohibitions as well: *avizrayhu d'gilluy arayot* — prohibitions within the constellation of forbidden sexual relations — are likewise *yehareg v'al ya'avor*. This principle, it should be noted, is the basis on which some authorities have argued that certain sexual prohibitions short of outright *gilluy arayot* also carry this status, though Tosafot explicitly disagrees with the broader extension. The Rosh was asked a related question during the Crusades, when Jews sought refuge inside churches to escape violent mobs. The Rosh ruled that entering a church for protection was permitted, since the Jews were using the walls of the building, not seeking salvation through any religious power — precisely the distinction Tosafot draws.

---

## Murder & Rape

### Torah Comparison

The Gemara now examines how each of the three categories is derived. *Avodah zarah* has already been established through the verse of *b'khol nafshekha*. For *gilluy arayot* and *shfikhut damim*, the Gemara cites a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi. The *baraita* begins from the verse discussing a *na'arah me'orasah* (a betrothed young woman) who was raped: *ki ka'asher yakum ish al re'ehu u'retzacho nefesh ken hadavar hazeh* — "for just as a man rises against his fellow and murders him, so is this matter." The Torah is declaring that the woman bears no guilt — she is like a murder victim, not a perpetrator. The Torah's point is moral and exculpatory, but the Gemara notes that the comparison, *hekesh*, also teaches law bidirectionally.

### Kill Rapist

From the case of the *na'arah me'orasah*, we learn that one may — indeed must — intervene to save her, even at the cost of the attacker's life. This is derived from the verse stating that she called out and no one came to save her: the implication is that had rescue been possible, it would have been not merely permitted but obligatory. Thus: *nitnah lehatzilah benafsho* — she may be saved through the life of the attempted rapist. Correspondingly, from the case of the murderer, one learns the same: *nitan lehatzilo benafsho* — one may save the intended murder victim through the life of the attempted murderer.

### Extension to Acts

The *hekesh* also runs in the other direction: from murder to the case of forbidden sexual relations.
