Just as *shfikhut damim* requires *yehareg v'al ya'avor* — one must be killed rather than commit murder — so too *gilluy arayot*: a woman being coerced into a forbidden sexual act must, in principle, allow herself to be killed rather than comply. The grammatical form of the ruling (*tehareg v'al ta'avor*) is significant, and the Rishonim debate its precise reading.

### Rava's Case

The basis for the *yehareg v'al ya'avor* of murder itself is not a verse but a *sevara* — pure logic — as illustrated by the famous episode of the man who came before Rava. The local authority had commanded him: go kill so-and-so, or I will kill you. What should he do? Rava answered: let him kill you — *likatlukha v'lo tiktol*. Why? *Mai chazit dedama didakh sumak tfei?* — What makes you think your blood is redder? *Dilma dama de'ahu gavra sumak tfei?* — Perhaps this other person's blood is redder than yours? There is no basis in logic or morality to privilege one's own life over an innocent person's such that one would be licensed to commit the sin of murder. Rashi emphasizes: the act of choosing to murder constitutes the sin itself. One might imagine that the principle of *chayecha v'chayei achikha* — the general rule that one's own life takes precedence over another's — could apply here. But that principle governs cases of passive competition for limited resources, not the active commission of murder. No license to commit the sin exists merely because one's own life is at stake.

### Unresolved Issues

Several significant questions are left open. First, regarding the case of the woman: some Rishonim read the relevant *girsa* as *tehareg v'al ta'avor* — she must allow herself to be killed — while others read it as *yehareg v'al ya'avor* referring to a man commanded to commit a forbidden sexual act. Connected to this is the Gemara's discussion elsewhere about *Esther* and the concept of *karka olam* — passivity. The Ramban makes a pointed observation: in a case of rape, even if a woman were willing to give up her life rather than submit, she might be physically unable to prevent the act. Her choice to sacrifice her life would not necessarily prevent the violation. This introduces a fundamental asymmetry that may affect how the rule applies to her case. Second, there is the question of what exactly is included in *gilluy arayot* for purposes of *yehareg v'al ya'avor*. The Gemara derives this law from the case of rape of a betrothed woman, which involves both violence and a violation against another person (the woman's betrothed). The question of whether less obviously "victimizing" prohibited sexual acts — such as a prohibition of *niddah* — would equally require martyrdom is not fully settled. The general assumption among the Rishonim is that anything classified as *arayot* is included, but the issue is worth noting. Third, on the question of *shfikhut damim*: Rava's logic rests on the inability to establish whose blood is "redder" — that is, whose life is objectively more valuable. But this raises the further question of whether, if killing one person would save multiple lives, the calculus changes. The Talmud's framework treats each life as infinite in value, making such arithmetic impossible — but the question of whether *yehareg v'al ya'avor* admits of any exception when one murder prevents many murders is left as a profound open question.

---

## Fever Healing

### Orlah Application

The final case on the daf involves Mar bar Rav Ashi, who encountered Ravina rubbing his daughter with *guharki de'orlah* — some form of juice or liquid from *orlah* fruit, perhaps unripe olives with their sediment intact, applied externally for what is understood to be a health purpose. The case raises immediate questions, since *orlah* is forbidden in *hana'ah*, and *orlah* does use the language of *achilah* — meaning, as established earlier in the daf, that the prohibition ordinarily requires *derech hana'ah*, the normal way of benefiting.

### Fever as Sakanah

Mar bar Rav Ashi challenges: when did the Rabbis say one may derive benefit from forbidden objects? Only in a situation of *sakanah* — genuine risk to life. When there is no such risk, deriving benefit from *orlah* remains prohibited. Ravina responds with the first answer: *hai ishta tzamirta nami ke-sha'at sakanah damya* — this high fever is itself the equivalent of *sakanah*. It is not merely discomfort; high fevers carry the potential for serious danger, and therefore this situation falls within the category of life-threatening conditions that permit use of otherwise forbidden items.

### Not Derech Hana'ah

A second answer is offered: *midi derech hana'ah ka avidna?* — Am I doing this in the normal way of benefit? The juice being applied is from unripe olives, or perhaps mixed with sediment, and is being rubbed onto the skin rather than consumed. This is not *derech hana'ah* for *orlah*. Since *orlah* prohibitions are tied to the language of *achilah* and therefore require a normal mode of benefit, using *orlah* fruit in this unripe, sediment-laden, externally applied form does not constitute a biblically prohibited act of benefit.

### Refuah Exception

The Rishonim note that the absence of a biblical transgression does not mean the act is entirely without restriction — a rabbinic prohibition may still apply. But the key ruling that emerges is that for purposes of *refuah* — healing — using something *shelo k'derech hana'ah* is permissible. This provides a fitting closure to the arc of the daf: the discussion opened with the principle that *shelo k'derech hana'ah* does not incur lashes, and concludes with the practical ruling that such abnormal use of forbidden objects is permissible in a medical context. The shiur will continue after the break with further discussion of these themes of *hana'ah* and *refuah*.

---

---

# Pesachim 27

## Oven & Forbidden Woo (II)

### Setup: Orlah/Kilayim

The previous daf concluded with a rich discussion of *hana'ah* — specifically the question of whether benefit that comes upon a person passively, without any deliberate action, constitutes forbidden *hana'ah*, and the related question of what categories of sensory experience even qualify. Auditory pleasure (*kol*) and visual pleasure (*mareh*) are not considered biblically significant forms of *hana'ah*, though they may be rabbinically restricted; olfactory pleasure (*rei'ach*), by contrast, is treated as more substantive and physical, and is indeed considered a genuine concern.

We continue now on 27a with a *sugya* that is closely related to these *hana'ah* themes. The *mishna* had stated that one may not use *chametz* to heat up an oven — burning *chametz* to bake bread or cook food constitutes a forbidden form of benefit. The *Gemara* broadens this discussion by citing a *Tosefta* (*tanu rabbanan*) that applies analogous reasoning to other items that are *assur be-hana'ah*.

The case is: *tanur she-hisiko bi-klipei orlah* — an oven that was fired using shells or wood from *orlah* (fruit from a tree's first three years, which is forbidden in benefit), *o be-kashim shel kilei ha-kerem* — or with stalks from *kilayei ha-kerem* (a forbidden mixture of grain sown in a vineyard). Both *orlah* and *kilayim* are classic categories of *issurei hana'ah*, and the *Tosefta* applies to them the same concerns raised by the *mishna* regarding *chametz*.

### New Oven Hardening

The *Tosefta* distinguishes between a new oven (*chadash*) and an old oven (*yashan*). If the oven is new, the initial firing serves as a kind of kiln process: it hardens the pottery and permanently transforms the vessel. By using wood of *issurei hana'ah* for this purpose, one has derived a concrete and lasting benefit — the oven itself has been fashioned and completed through the forbidden material. The *Tosefta* therefore rules *chadash yutzat* — the new oven must be destroyed.

One might have argued otherwise: the prohibited act of firing occurred once and is over; going forward, one is merely using the oven, not the *issurei hana'ah* themselves. But this position rejects that reasoning. The continued use of the oven is viewed as a continued, indirect derivation of benefit from those *issurei hana'ah* — one would never be cooking in this oven today were it not for the fact that the forbidden wood hardened it in the first place. The wood accomplished a *gmar ma'aseh*, a completed constructive act, and every subsequent use remains connected to that initial benefit.

### Old Oven Treatment

If the oven is old (*yashan*), the analysis differs. An old oven does not require that initial kiln-firing; it is already functional. The current fire, however, is itself derived from *issurei hana'ah*, and one may not benefit from that active fire. The ruling is therefore *yutzan* — let it cool. Once the fire has gone out completely, the oven may be used again, provided that any subsequent fire comes from permitted wood. The oven itself, having not been fundamentally altered or constituted by the forbidden fire, does not require destruction.

---

## Bread Dispute

### Rebbi: Bread Assur

The *Tosefta* continues: *afah bo et ha-pat* — suppose one went ahead and baked bread in this oven while the forbidden fire was still active. *Rebbi omer: ha-pat asurah* — Rebbi holds that the bread is forbidden. This seems intuitive: if one cannot derive benefit from an oven hardened by *issurei hana'ah*, one certainly cannot eat bread baked through them.

### Chachamim: Bread Mutar

*Ve-Chachamim omrim: ha-pat muteret* — the Sages, however, rule that the bread is permitted. Their position is that although an act of transgression may have occurred in the baking, once the bread has been baked, eating it does not constitute a new or ongoing act of *hana'ah* from the *issurei hana'ah*. The forbidden benefit has already been derived; continuing to eat the bread is not a further violation.

### Continued Benefit Logic

The underlying conceptual question is whether eating the bread constitutes a *continued* deriving of benefit from the *issurei hana'ah*, or whether the moment of baking was the singular act of *hana'ah* and what follows is simply using bread. Logically, one might assume that the Sages would apply the same reasoning to the oven — if the benefit was exhausted in the act of hardening, then continued use of the oven should similarly be permissible. The *Gemara* will indeed draw this connection.

---

## Oven & Forbidden Woo (II)

### Coals Permitted

The *Tosefta* contains a further provision: *bishra agavi gechali* — if the wood has already turned to coals before the bread is baked, then *divrei hakol mutar* — everyone agrees the bread is permissible. Once the wood has fully combusted into charcoal, it is no longer considered *orlah* or *kilayei ha-kerem*; the forbidden material has been destroyed and no longer exists as such. At that stage, it may even be permitted *le-chatchilah* to bake the bread.

### Nisrafim Principle

This ruling is not as self-evident as it might appear. The *Ran* notes that the question of when *issurei hana'ah* lose their status is a substantive one, and the *Gemara* articulates the governing principle at the close of today's *daf*: *kol ha-nisrafim afaran mutar* — anything that the *halacha* prescribes to be burned, its ashes are permissible; *kol ha-nikbarim afaran assur* — anything for which burial is the designated mode of disposal, its ashes remain forbidden even after burning.

The logic is tied to the concept of *na'aseit mitzvato* — once the prescribed *mitzvah* has been performed upon an object, it loses its forbidden status. For *kilayei ha-kerem*, the *Gemara* derives from the verse *pen tikdash* (Devarim 22:9) the requirement to burn it — *tukad aish* — and therefore, once burned, the *mitzvah* has been fulfilled and the object becomes permissible. The same principle applies to *orlah*.

By contrast, a *shor ha-niskal* (an ox condemned to be stoned) has no prescribed act of burning; even if one chooses to burn it, the act does not trigger *na'aseit mitzvato*, and the ashes remain forbidden. The *Ran* explicitly limits the ruling about coals to *kilayim* and *orlah*, where burning is itself the commanded act. Other *issurei hana'ah* — including *chametz be-Pesach*, whose method of destruction is a separate discussion — may not share this leniency.

It should be noted that *na'aseit mitzvato* can operate even without a complete physical transformation. By analogy: *zerikat ha-dam* at the *mizbe'ach* does not visibly alter the blood, yet it renders the offering permissible because the *mitzvah* has been fulfilled. In principle, even if the prescribed act were accomplished before the substance became fully unrecognizable, *na'aseit mitzvato* would be sufficient to permit it.

The distinction between *kilayei ha-kerem* specifically — and not *kilayei zera'im* — should be noted; it is the former to which the *drasha* of *pen tikdash* / *tukad aish* applies.

---

## Zeh V'Zeh Gorem

### Oven & Fire Join

The *Gemara* now considers whether the two positions in the *Tosefta* regarding the oven — one requiring the destruction of a new oven, the other permitting continued use — map onto the dispute between Rebbi and the *Chachamim* regarding the bread. The *Gemara* suggests: *ha Rebbi, ha Rabbanan* — one position reflects Rebbi's view and the other the Sages'.

But the *Gemara* resists this too quickly. *Eima de-shamat lei le-Rabbi* — when did we actually hear Rebbi say the bread is forbidden? *Mishum de-yesh shevach eitzim be-pat* — because the benefit of the wood remains present in the bread. The wood baked the bread, and that contribution (*shevach etzim*) is still considered to inhere in the bread; eating it is therefore still a form of deriving benefit from the *issurei hana'ah*.

But that reasoning applies cleanly to the bread, where the only contributor is the wood. The oven case is more complex: *zeh va-zeh gorem mi-shamat lei* — did we ever hear that Rebbi holds that *zeh va-zeh gorem* — two things jointly contributing — constitutes a problem? When one bakes bread in an oven, two things are contributing to the baking: the oven and the fire. The benefit being derived is not traceable exclusively to the *issurei hana'ah*; it is a joint product. Perhaps even Rebbi would not say that a dual-contributor scenario creates a prohibition.

This introduces the central conceptual question of *zeh va-zeh gorem*: when two things jointly bring about a result and one of them is forbidden, does the forbidden element's participation make the outcome prohibited? Or does the presence of the permitted contributor sufficiently dilute the problem?

### Sourdough: Eliezer

The *Gemara* therefore looks for a *Tanna* who explicitly rules that *zeh va-zeh gorem* is forbidden. *Ela lo kashya: ha Rabbi Eliezer, ha Rabbanan* — let us say the debate about the oven reflects the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages.

*D'tnan* — the *mishna* presents the following case: *seor shel chullin ve-shel terumah she-naflu le-toch issah* — sourdough starter of ordinary produce (*chullin*) and sourdough starter of *terumah* both fell into a batch of dough. *Ve-ein be-zeh ke-dei le-hachmitz ve-ein be-zeh ke-dei le-hachmitz* — neither on its own contains enough to cause the dough to ferment. *Ve-nitztarfu ve-chimtzu* — but together they caused fermentation. The analogy to *davar ha-mamid* (a substance that gives form or structure) is instructive: even a small quantity that has a transformative effect may retain its forbidden status regardless of its proportional insignificance.

*Rabbi Eliezer omer: achar acharon ani ba* — Rabbi Eliezer says one follows the last element added. His reasoning is sequential: whatever fell in first had no effect on its own; the dough was non-fermenting until the final element was added, and therefore that final element is the operative cause. If the last element added was *chullin*, the *terumah* is not considered to have caused the fermentation, and the bread is permissible. *Ve-Chachamim omrim* — the Sages say it makes no difference whether the *issur* fell in first or last; in neither case did the forbidden element cause the fermentation alone, and therefore *zeh va-zeh gorem* is permissible.

### Abaye: Issur Present

The *Gemara* notes, however, that Rabbi Eliezer's position is ambiguous. His formulation of "following the last" could mean something other than a ruling on *zeh va-zeh gorem*. Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer would agree that simultaneous contribution (*bat achat*) is permissible, and his concern is only about sequential contribution — specifically, whichever element was last is considered the operative cause, and if that last element was the *issur*, it is problematic. But if the *issur* acted simultaneously with the *heter*, or if the *issur* came first and the *heter* came last, it might be fine — not because of *zeh va-zeh gorem*, but simply because of the "last one" principle.

Abaye therefore proposes a reinterpretation: *lo shanu ela she-kadam ve-silek et ha-issur* — Rabbi Eliezer is lenient only where the *issur* fell in first and was then removed before the *heter* fell in. In that case, the *issur* was no longer present when fermentation occurred, and one can say it contributed nothing to the outcome. But if the *issur* was not removed — if it was still present — then even if it was not the last element added, it is still forbidden, because it is present while the fermentation occurs. On this reading, Rabbi Eliezer's position is that whenever the *issur* remains present, it is a problem — which would mean he holds that *zeh va-zeh gorem* is *assur*.

*U-mimai de-ta'amei de-Rabbi Eliezer ke-d'Abaye* — but the *Gemara* immediately pushes back: what makes us confident that Abaye's interpretation is correct? The *Gemara* notes, strikingly, that it is prepared to question whether an *Amora*'s reading of a *Tanna* is accurate — a move that is itself unusual. Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer means exactly what he says: follow the last element, regardless of whether the *issur* is still present. *Dilma ta'amei de-Rabbi Eliezer mishum de-achar acharon ani ba* — maybe his entire principle is simply "the last one counts," and if the last one was *heter*, there is no problem even if the *issur* is still present in the dough. The *Gemara* therefore concludes that Rabbi Eliezer in the sourdough case cannot definitively establish that *zeh va-zeh gorem* is forbidden.

---

## Asherah Wood Case

### Avodah Zarah Mishna

The *Gemara* therefore turns to a different Rabbi Eliezer — *Rabbi Eliezer de-atzei Asherah* — the Rabbi Eliezer of the *Asherah* wood case.

The *mishna* in Avodah Zarah teaches: *natal himenah etzim* — if one took wood from an *Asherah* tree (a tree worshipped as part of idolatry), *assurin be-hana'ah* — that wood is forbidden in benefit. *Hisik ba-hen et ha-tannur* — if one used those sticks to fire up an oven: *chadash yutatz, yashan yutzan* — a new oven must be destroyed; an old oven must simply be allowed to cool. *Afa bo et ha-pat* — if one baked bread in the oven, whether new or old, *assurin be-hana'ah* — the bread is forbidden in benefit.

The *mishna* then addresses a case of commingling: *nitarva be-acherot ve-acherot be-acherot* — the forbidden loaf became mixed with other loaves, and those then mixed with still others. Despite the possibility of invoking *rov*, *bittul*, or *sfeik sfeika*, by *Avodah Zarah* the rule is one of complete stringency: *kullan assurin be-hana'ah* — all the loaves are forbidden in benefit.

Rabbi Eliezer offers a more lenient option in the commingled case: *yolichet hana'ah le-Yam Ha-Melach* — one may cast into the sea a coin equivalent in value to the benefit one would have derived from the bread, and this symbolic renunciation of profit renders the bread permissible. The Sages respond: *ein pidyon le-Avodah Zarah* — there is no redemption for *Avodah Zarah*. (The full discussion of this position belongs to tractate Avodah Zarah; what is relevant here is the underlying *mishna* and its ruling about the oven.)

### Attributing Position

What is relevant to the current *sugya* is that this *mishna* in Avodah Zarah — bracketing the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Tanna Kamma* regarding the coin — reflects a unanimous position that a new oven must be destroyed and the bread is forbidden. This is precisely the strict position we needed to identify for the oven case in our *Tosefta*. Since Rabbi Eliezer's name appears in this *mishna*, the *Gemara* attributes the strict position to him — and to the *Tanna Kamma* alongside him.

The *Gemara* immediately raises an objection: *eimur de-shamat lei le-Rabbi Eliezer be-Avodah Zarah* — we heard this stringency in the context of *Avodah Zarah*, which is *d'chamir issura* — known for its exceptional strictness. By *Avodah Zarah*, commingled bread is never *batel*, and a host of additional stringencies apply. *Aval be-sha'ar issurin she-ba-Torah mi-shamat lei* — but regarding other *issurin* of the Torah, did we ever hear Rabbi Eliezer apply this position?

This point has direct practical relevance. The question of *zeh va-zeh gorem* as it might apply to *Pesach* — for instance, the concern raised by some about purchasing milk and eggs produced from animals that consumed *chametz* feed — is addressed explicitly by Rav Moshe Feinstein. Rav Moshe notes that the stringencies motivating this *chumra* derive from discussions rooted in the laws of *Avodah Zarah*, where the *Gemara* is peculiarly strict. One cannot assume that stringencies applicable to *Avodah Zarah* carry over to *chametz*; in principle, the distinction the *Gemara* is drawing here precludes that transfer, and Rav Moshe rules that the concern is not applicable to *chametz*.

### Braita Authority

The *Gemara* responds with two points. First, as a practical matter: if we do not use this *mishna* in Avodah Zarah to identify the *Tanna* who holds the strict oven position by *orlah*, we are left without any named *Tanna* to attribute it to. We therefore must associate it with Rabbi Eliezer and the *Tanna Kamma* of Avodah Zarah, and assume that the distinction between *Avodah Zarah* and other *issurin* does not hold.

Second: *ha tanya be-hedya* — there is a *Braita* that states it explicitly. The *Braita* records that Rabbi Eliezer (together with the *Tanna Kamma*) applies the strict position *be-chol issurin she-ba-Torah* — to all categories of things forbidden in benefit, not only *Avodah Zarah*. The *Gemara* acknowledges an interesting textual wrinkle: in the *mishna* in Avodah Zarah, it is actually Rabbi Eliezer who is *matir* relative to the *Tanna Kamma* — he is the more lenient one, allowing the coin-throwing ritual — while the *Tanna Kamma* is stricter. So the attribution of the strict oven position to "Rabbi Eliezer" requires a nuanced reading: it is really the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer together on the oven question, even as they diverge on the commingling question.

---

## Zeh V'Zeh Gorem (II)

### Pots vs. Ovens

Abaye now articulates the logical structure of the dispute more precisely. *Im timtzei lomar zeh va-zeh gorem assur* — if we accept that *zeh va-zeh gorem* is forbidden, then Rebbi, who rules the bread forbidden because *yesh shevach eitzim be-fat*, would also rule that the oven is forbidden, since the oven-plus-fire scenario is simply a *zeh va-zeh gorem* on top of the already problematic *shevach etzim* concern. *Ve-im timtzei lomar zeh va-zeh gorem mutar* — and if *zeh va-zeh gorem* is permissible, then even Rebbi would say that the oven is permissible, because the oven's contribution is jointly made with the fire, and Rebbi's concern (*yesh shevach eitzim be-fat*) would only apply to the bread, not to the dual-contributor scenario of the oven.

This framing opens a further question about intermediate cases. *Hani kderot ve-khosot ve-tzluchiyot assiri* — what about plates, cups, and bowls? If forbidden wood was used to fire pottery in a kiln, and those ceramic vessels are now used, are they like the bread or like the oven?

The answer is that plates and cups are treated like the bread: using them is a single-contributor *hana'ah*. The vessel derived its form from the forbidden fire, and when one uses it, one is deriving benefit from that vessel alone, with no other contributor at that moment. The oven, by contrast, is only ever used *together with* a new fire; the benefit of baking bread comes from both the oven and the fire jointly, making it a *zeh va-zeh gorem* scenario.

The case of a pot (*kedeirah*) is subtler and is the subject of a dispute within the *Gemara*. *Ki pligi be-tannur u-ve-kedeirah* — the debate between Rebbi and Rabbi Eliezer, or between those who permit and those who forbid in the *zeh va-zeh gorem* scenario, concerns specifically the oven and the pot. *Le-man de-amar zeh va-zeh gorem assur* — if *zeh va-zeh gorem* is a problem, both the oven and the pot are forbidden. *Le-man de-amar zeh va-zeh gorem mutar* — if it is permissible, both are allowed.

But *ika de-amrei* — an alternative formulation holds that even according to the opinion that *zeh va-zeh gorem* is permissible, the pot may still be forbidden: *de-kablah bishulah mi-kamei de-nitan etzim de-heteira* — because one places the food into the pot before lighting the fire. At the moment the food enters the pot and begins to be affected, the pot is acting alone, without any other contributor. Only an oven receives the food *after* the fire is already burning, so that from the first moment of baking, two things are contributing. A pot that is placed empty onto the fire first and only then filled, everyone would agree, is permissible — since the food is never placed into the pot without the fire already being present as a joint contributor.

---

## Shmuel's Girsa

### Two Text Versions

*Amar Rav Yosef amar Rav Yehudah amar Shmuel*: The *Braita* as Shmuel transmitted it reads: *tanur she-hisiko be-klifei orlah o be-kashim shel kilei ha-kerem: chadash yutzat, yashan yutzan. Afah bo et ha-pat: Rebbi omer ha-pat muteret; ve-Chachamim omrim ha-pat asurah*. According to this *girsa*, it is Rebbi who permits the bread and the *Chachamim* who forbid it — the reverse of our *Tosefta*, in which Rebbi forbids and the *Chachamim* permit.

### Shmuel's Problem

*Ve-hatanya ipcha* — but our *Tosefta* has the positions reversed: Rebbi forbids and the *Chachamim* permit. The *Gemara* acknowledges: *Shmuel ipcha tani* — Shmuel taught the *Braita* in the inverted form.

*Ve-iba'it eima: be-alma kasavar Shmuel halacha ke-Rabbi me-chaveiro* — Shmuel generally holds that the *halacha* follows Rebbi when he argues with a single colleague, but not when he argues against many colleagues (*me-haveirav*). In our case, Rebbi is arguing against the *Chachamim* — a majority — and so Shmuel's ordinary rule would lead him to rule like the *Chachamim*, i.e., that the bread is permissible. But Shmuel in fact holds that the bread is *forbidden*, agreeing with Rebbi on the merits.

### Reversing Text

This creates a problem of presentation. If Shmuel were to rule openly that the bread is forbidden — citing a *Braita* in which Rebbi is the minority — his colleagues would object: according to Shmuel's own principle (*halacha ke-Rabbi me-chaveiro, ve-lo me-haveirav*), he should be ruling leniently. So Shmuel *ashniye ipcha* — he deliberately inverted the *girsa* of the *Braita* so that in his version, the *Chachamim* (the majority) are the ones who forbid. This way, *d'nigmaru Rabbanan le-issura* — the majority position in the text aligns with the stringent ruling, and Shmuel can rule stringently without appearing to contradict his own principle.

This is, as the *Gemara* presents it, a striking and genuinely troubling passage. Whatever happened to intellectual honesty? Is this not a misrepresentation of *Torah*? It is worth noting a partial parallel: the *Gemara* elsewhere records that Rebbi himself would sometimes take a *da'at yachid* and incorporate it as the *stam* (anonymous) position in the *Mishna*, thereby giving it greater weight. But that is a question of editorial presentation, not falsification — the minority view is being elevated, not reversed. Here the *Gemara* says plainly that Shmuel would actually reverse the *girsa* so that people would accept his *psak*. The *Gemara* itself does not soften this; it presents it without apology.

---

## Coals vs. Flames

### Whispering Coals

We return now to the provision in the *Tosefta* that when bread is baked over *gechalim* — coals — rather than active flames, *divrei hakol* the bread is permitted. The *Gemara* cites a dispute between *Rav Yehudah amar Shmuel* and *Rav Chiya bar Ashi amar Rabbi Yochanan* about the exact scope of this leniency.

*Chad amar: lo shanu ela be-gechalim omemot* — one opinion holds that the unanimous leniency applies only to coals that are *omemot*, essentially extinct — fully black charcoal with no remaining combustion. *Aval gechalim lochashot* — but if they are *lochashot*, "whispering" coals — still glowing, still smoldering — *assurin*: still forbidden, because there remains active burning of the wood, and the bread is still being baked with wood of *issurei hana'ah*.

*Ve-chad amar: afilu gechalim lochashot nami mutarot* — the other opinion holds that even glowing, whispering coals are permissible, and that even Rebbi would agree at this stage that the bread is permitted.

### Raging Flame

This second opinion creates a puzzle. *Bishlama le-man de-amar lochashot assurin* — the position that whispering coals are forbidden is coherent: there is still some unburned wood contributing to the baking, and therefore *yesh shevach eitzim be-fat* applies. *Ela le-man de-amar afilu lochashot mutarot* — but if even whispering coals are permissible, what case remains where Rebbi would say the bread is forbidden? If the threshold for leniency is that low, when is there ever a case of *yesh shevach eitzim be-fat*?

*Amar Rav Pappa: ke-she'avuka ke-negdo* — Rav Pappa answers: the case where Rebbi forbids is when there is a full, raging flame directly opposite the bread. That is when the wood is actively burning and visibly contributing to the baking; at that stage, the *shevach etzim* is present and operative.

The conceptual distinction being drawn here is somewhat elusive. If whispering coals are permissible because the wood is essentially charred and no longer contributes as wood, then the question is whether *lochashot* still contains some unburned wood or not. If there is still some wood burning in *lochashot*, then the distinction from *avuka ke-negdo* is one of degree — 2% unburned wood versus 100% — and it is not obvious why the former is permissible and the latter forbidden, unless one invokes *zeh va-zeh gorem*: in the *lochashot* case, most of the contribution comes from the charcoal (which is already transformed and permissible), and only a minimal share from the remaining wood.

### Chachamim Logic

*Michlal* — from this one can infer the *Chachamim*'s reasoning. *De-Rabbanan de-pligi alei: shari afilu ke-she'avuka ke-negdo* — the Sages who disagree with Rebbi would permit even when there is a full raging flame opposite the bread. Their reasoning, as the *Gemara* understands it, is more radical than a simple *bedi'avad* leniency: they hold that fire is itself already-destroyed wood. When wood burns, what is produced — the flame itself — is generated from the consumption and destruction of the wood. The flame you see is not the wood; it is the product of the wood's annihilation. Therefore, from the moment the fire exists, it is already a product of destroyed material, and cooking over it is never in the category of deriving benefit from *issurei hana'ah*.

If this is so, the *Chachamim* would say not merely that the bread baked with forbidden fire is permissible *bedi'avad*, but that one may *le-chatchilah* cook using such fire. This seems a far-reaching conclusion, and the *Gemara* itself acknowledges the tension with the *stam mishna* that states *ve-lo yasik bo tannur ve-khirayim* — one may not fire an oven with *chametz*. That ruling appears to assume that everyone agrees one may not use forbidden wood to fire an oven, which does not fit easily with the *Chachamim*'s position as the *Gemara* has now framed it. The *Gemara* is aware of this difficulty.

*Ela etzim de-issura Rabbanan heichi mashkachat lehu* — so how, according to the *Chachamim*, could one ever transgress with forbidden wood? If fire already represents destroyed wood, making a fire with forbidden wood is never a transgression. *Amar Rami bar Chama: be-shashifa* — Rami bar Chama answers with a single word: with a stool. One transgresses with forbidden wood not by burning it, but by fashioning an object from it — a chair, a table, some artifact — and deriving use from that object directly. Only then is one benefiting from the *issurei hana'ah* as such. Burning it, by the *Chachamim*'s logic, always transforms it into something other than itself.

---

## Hekdesh Wood

### Hekdesh Non-Batel

The *Gemara* now introduces a new question: *tanur she-hisiku be-atzei hekdesh* — what if the oven was fired with consecrated wood (*hekdesh*), and then bread was baked in it? *De-Rabbanan de-sharu bi-kamaita* — the Sages who normally permit the bread in the *orlah*/*kilayim* cases: what would they say when the wood is *hekdesh*?

*Amar lei: ha-pat asurah* — the bread is forbidden even according to the Sages, in the case of *hekdesh*. Why should *hekdesh* differ? *Hachi hashta* — the comparison is not apt, answers Rava. *Orlah beteilah be-matayim* — *orlah* becomes *batel* at a ratio of one in two hundred. *Hekdesh afilu be-elef lo batil* — *hekdesh* is never *batel* at any ratio. Since *hekdesh* is subject to uniquely severe rules of non-*bittul*, we apply correspondingly greater stringency across the board, including to the question of whether the bread retains forbidden status. The logic parallels what the *Gemara* said earlier about *Avodah Zarah*: where a category is inherently more severe, we are more strict even in cases where the direct reasoning might not compel it.

### Me'ilah Doctrine

*Ela amar Rava: ei kashya li ha kashya* — Rava says the more pressing question is not whether the bread is forbidden but how it could be forbidden at all given the laws of *me'ilah*. *Ve-halo maal ha-masik* — the moment one takes consecrated firewood and places it in the oven, one has committed *me'ilah* — unauthorized benefit from sacred property. And the operative rule is: *kol heicha de-maal ha-masik, nafku lehu le-chullin* — wherever the one who lit the fire is guilty of *me'ilah*, the object loses its consecrated status and becomes *chullin*. So by the time the bread is baked, the wood has already ceased to be *hekdesh*, and the bread should be entirely permissible.

The *Gemara* is careful to specify: this applies to objects sanctified for their monetary value (*kedushat damim*), which lose their *hekdesh* status through *me'ilah*. Objects whose sanctity is intrinsic — *korbanos*, *keilei shareit* — retain their identity. But firewood sanctified for the *Beit Ha-Mikdash* treasury is the former category and should, on this analysis, become *chullin* the moment it is misappropriated.

### Shelamim Exception

*Amar Rav Pappa: hacha be-atzei shelamim askinan* — Rav Pappa answers: we are discussing wood that has been consecrated with the sanctity of a *shelamim* offering — specifically, wood that one declared: with the proceeds of the sale of this wood, I will purchase a *shelamim*.

The reason this matters is that *shelamim* is unique among *korbanos*: there is no *me'ilah* on a *shelamim*, because a *shelamim* is considered essentially the property of the owner who brings it. The *imurin* (fatty portions) are God's portion, and those become off-limits after *zerikat ha-dam*, but the bulk of the *shelamim* is eaten by the owner and his household. The *shelamim* is therefore not considered fully *mish-ulchan gavoah* — from the table of the Most High — in the same sense that a *chatat* is. A *chatat*, by contrast, is described as *mi-shulchan gavoah ka zachu*: the *kohanim* who eat it are eating from God's meal; they are considered part of the *Beit Ha-Mikdash* apparatus, not independent recipients.

Since there is no *me'ilah* on a *shelamim*, misusing wood consecrated with the sanctity of a *shelamim* does not trigger *me'ilah*, and therefore the wood does not become *chullin*. It remains *hekdesh* even after misuse.

The *Gemara* adds: *ve-aliba de-Rabbi Yehuda* — this follows the position of Rabbi Yehuda. *De-amar hekdesh be-shogeg mitchalel* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that *hekdesh* is desecrated (becomes *chullin*) through inadvertent *me'ilah* (*be-shogeg*). *Be-mezid eino mitchalel* — but deliberate misuse (*be-mezid*) does not desecrate it. The reason, counterintuitive as it may seem, is that *me'ilah* as a legal category applies only where one can bring a *korban* of *me'ilah*, and a *korban* of *me'ilah* is only brought for inadvertent (*shogeg*) violations. *Mezid* misuse, however serious as a prohibition, does not carry the *korban* and therefore lacks the full legal trigger that would render the object *chullin*. *Lo nafik le-chullin* — it does not exit its sanctified status.

By analogy: *shelamim nami* — *shelamim* likewise does not qualify for *me'ilah* as a legal category, because one does not bring a *korban me'ilah* for misusing a *shelamim*. *Lo nafik le-chullin* — therefore, even when misused, it retains its *hekdesh* status. It is not the act of misuse that discharges *hekdesh*; it is the specific legal mechanism of *me'ilah*. Where that mechanism is absent — whether because the transgressor acted *be-mezid*, or because the object is *shelamim* — the *hekdesh* endures.

### Ashes Forbidden

The *Gemara* closes with the *Braita* mentioned at the outset: *kol ha-nisrafim afaran mutar* — all objects that are prescribed to be burned, their ashes are permissible — *chutz me-atzei Asherah ve-afar hekdesh* — with the exception of *Asherah* wood and the ashes of *hekdesh*.

*D'afar hekdesh le-olam assur* — the ashes of *hekdesh* wood remain forbidden permanently. But this raises the same question again: once the wood is burned, hasn't *me'ilah* been committed, rendering the ashes *chullin*?

*Amar Rami bar Chama: ke-gon she-nafal deleka me'eleha be-atzei hekdesh* — who said any *me'ilah* was committed? Perhaps a fire broke out on its own, spontaneously consuming the consecrated wood. *De-leka inish de-nimal* — no human committed *me'ilah*, and yet the ashes remain. This establishes that the ashes of *hekdesh* are forbidden even in the complete absence of *me'ilah*.

*Ve-Rav Ashi amar: be-osam she-te'unim gniza* — Rav Ashi offers a different case: ashes that require *gniza* (burial/preservation), specifically the *terumas ha-deshen* — the ashes removed from the *mizbe'ach* each morning, which the *Torah* requires to be placed carefully beside the *mizbe'ach* and not scattered. *D'tanya: ve-samo benachas, ve-samo kulo, ve-samo she-lo yefazer* — these ashes were never the product of any *me'ilah*; they were created through the legitimate service of the *mizbe'ach* itself. They therefore retain their sacred status permanently.

The *Gemara*'s conclusion is that *hekdesh* and *Avodah Zarah* represent the two categories subject to heightened stringency throughout this entire *sugya*. As a general rule, burning destroys forbidden status (*nisrafim afaran mutar*), and benefiting from the product of the burning — whether in the form of baked bread or coal — follows from that leniency. But in the exceptional categories of *Avodah Zarah* and *hekdesh*, the ashes remain forbidden, the bread remains problematic, and the principles of *zeh va-zeh gorem* that would otherwise relax the analysis are held to a stricter standard.

# Pesachim 28

## Sreifah Requirement

### Debate Overview

The daf opens at the midpoint of 27b with a *mishnah* that encapsulates one of the central practical disputes of *hilchot Pesach*: *Rabbi Yehuda omer ein biyur chametz ela sreifa* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that the only valid method of destroying *chametz* is burning. The *chachamim*, by contrast, rule that one may crumble and scatter the *chametz* to the wind, or cast it into the sea.

This debate arrives after several dapim of sustained analysis concerning *issurei hana'ah* — the category of objects from whose use one may derive no benefit — and the various questions attending that category: whether the prohibition is connected to *achilah*, whether it extends to *shelo kederach hana'atan*, and what precisely counts as *hana'ah* in the first place. The discussion of benefit derived from wood and from ashes led naturally to the principle that the residue of objects subject to a *mitzvas sreifah* becomes permitted once burned, unlike most other prohibited items whose ashes remain forbidden. With that background in place, the *Gemara* now turns to the question of *chametz* itself: is it subject to a *mitzvas sreifah* like *nosar* and *kodshim*, or is the Torah's directive more broadly construed?

It is worth pausing on the company *chametz* keeps here. The things one burns — primarily *kodshim* and *avodah zarah* — belong to a paradigm of complete *issur*, total taboo. *Shor haniskal*, by contrast, one buries; burning is reserved for objects surrounded by an especially dense web of prohibition. *Chametz*, as we know, is *assur behana'ah* based on a prohibition of *achilah*, which would seem to place it in a less severe category. And yet Rabbi Yehuda maintains it belongs with the things one burns — that it too partakes of this quality of radical detachment, of something one must utterly eliminate rather than merely cease to use.

### Kal Vachomer Argument

Rabbi Yehuda's first derivation, preserved in a *braita*, takes the form of a *kal vachomer*. The argument runs: *u-mah nosar she'eino be-val yeira'eh u-val yimatze, ta'un sreifa* — *nosar* (sacrificial meat left past its permitted time), which does not trigger the prohibition of *bal yeira'eh u-val yimatze* (the prohibition against *chametz* being found in one's possession), must nonetheless be burned. *Chametz*, which does trigger *bal yeira'eh u-val yimatze*, should all the more so require burning.

The internal logic deserves scrutiny. The connection being drawn is between the gravity of an object's prohibited status and the requirement to destroy it by fire. If something as "merely" prohibited as *nosar* must be burned, surely something as deeply taboo as *chametz* — which one may not even own — should require the same treatment. There is, however, a complication. By *nosar*, one has already transgressed by leaving the sacrifice over; the act of burning follows upon an established violation. With *chametz*, Rabbi Yehuda's own position (as *Rashi* notes explicitly) is that the *mitzvah* is to burn it *before* one transgresses *bal yeira'eh*, so as to prevent the transgression in the first place. The logic of the *kal vachomer* — connecting the requirement to burn to the severity of the *bal yeira'eh* violation — is therefore somewhat strained when the burning is meant to forestall rather than respond to that very violation.

### Chachamim Rebuttal

The *chachamim* challenge Rabbi Yehuda's *kal vachomer* with a pointed counter-principle: *kol din she'ata dan techilato le-hachmir ve-sofo le-hakel eino din* — any *kal vachomer* that begins as a stringency but ends as a leniency is no valid *kal vachomer* at all. What leniency emerges from requiring *sreifah*? *Lo matza etzim le-sarfo, yehei yoshev u-vatel* — if one cannot find wood with which to burn the *chametz*, one would simply be exempt from doing anything at all, since one is an *oness*. But the Torah says *tashbitu se'or mi-bateichem* — destroy the leaven from your houses — implying any means of disposal will do. By insisting on one specific method, you paradoxically relieve a person of responsibility when that method is unavailable. The *chachamim*'s ruling, they argue, is the true stringency: demanding that one exhaust every possible means of removal, with no escape through the unavailability of any single method.

This argument points toward something important beyond its immediate dialectical purpose. The *chachamim* are not simply proposing a different technique for the same underlying obligation. They are articulating a different conception of what the obligation *is*. This distinction will bear fruit in the conceptual discussion later.

It is also worth noting the broader *hashkafic* point raised in connection with this exchange: *chumros* carry real costs and often generate *kulos* in unexpected places. The assumption that being *machmir* is always without downside is precisely what the *chachamim* are disputing here — the *chumra* of requiring *sreifah* produces the *kula* of exempting someone who lacks wood entirely.

### Heikesh from Nosar

Rebuffed on the *kal vachomer*, *chazar Rabbi Yehuda ve-danu din acher* — Rabbi Yehuda returned and offered a different derivation, this time framed as an analogy rather than a logical inference. *Nosar assur be-achilah ve-chametz assur be-achilah* — both *nosar* and *chametz* are forbidden in eating. *Ma nosar be-sreifa af chametz be-sreifa* — just as *nosar* requires burning, so too *chametz*.

This derivation is structured as a *heikesh*, drawing an analogy between two cases that share the quality of being forbidden in *achilah*. The *chachamim* immediately counter: *neveila tochiach* — a *neveila* (an animal that died without proper *shechita*) is similarly forbidden in eating, yet no one suggests it must be burned. Rabbi Yehuda responds: *hefresh* — there is a distinction. *Nosar* is not merely *assur be-achilah*; it is *assur be-achilah u-va-hana'ah*. I am not proposing a rule that anything forbidden in eating must be burned; I am proposing that things totally off-limits — forbidden both to eat and to derive benefit from — require *sreifah*.

### Nosar Distinctions

The *chachamim* come back with another counterexample: *shor haniskal yochiach* — the ox that gored and killed a person is *assur be-achilah u-va-hana'ah*, and yet it is not burned; it is buried. So the combination of *issur achilah* and *issur hana'ah* alone cannot be what generates the *sreifah* requirement.

Rabbi Yehuda refines his position once more: *nosar assur be-achilah u-va-hana'ah v'yesh bo karet* — *nosar* carries the added dimension of *karet*. The combination of *issur hana'ah* and *karet* marks it as categorically taboo, something completely excised from permissible existence. And *chametz* likewise is *assur be-achilah u-va-hana'ah v'yesh bo karet*. *Ma nosar be-sreifa af chametz be-sreifa*. This seems like a compelling formulation.

The *chachamim* try once more with *chelbo shel shor haniskal* — the fat of a gored ox. The fat carries *karet* on account of being *chelev*, and the entire animal is *assur behana'ah* on account of being *shor haniskal*, yet there is no *sreifah* requirement. To this, Rabbi Yehuda does not directly respond, and the discussion moves in a different direction. The counterargument is somewhat artificial in structure — the *karet* and the *issur hana'ah* here inhere in two separate *isurim* that happen to coincide in one object rather than belonging to a single unified prohibition — which may explain why Rabbi Yehuda treats it as less than fully compelling.

It is worth pausing to note the unusual literary character of this extended exchange. It is all in Hebrew, and consists of a sustained back-and-forth between *tanna'im* debating not the *halacha* itself but the derivations that underlie it. This is different from a standard *mishnah* or *braita*, which typically states the law apodictically. It also differs from classic *midrash halacha*, which anchors itself in a *pasuk* and derives from there. Here, the disputants are working from the *halacha* and seeking to establish or undermine its derivations, which gives the passage a distinctive texture. It may well originate as a *midrash halacha* on *tashbitu se'or mi-bateichem*, subsequently transposed and embedded in its current context — the *mechilta* may well contain a parallel.

### Bal Totireu Parallel

At the top of 28a, Rabbi Yehuda attempts a third derivation. *Nosar yeshno b'val toisiru ve-chametz b'val toisiru* — both *nosar* and *chametz* share the prohibition of *bal totireu*, the injunction not to leave things over. The prohibition against leaving *nosar* past its time and the prohibition of possessing *chametz* past its permitted point reflect a shared conceptual structure: both involve a categorical imperative not to allow a certain thing to persist. This commonality, added to the previous shared features of *issur hana'ah* and *karet*, reinforces the analogy. *Ma nosar be-sreifa af chametz be-sreifa*.

### Asham Talui Challenge

The *chachamim*'s response to this third derivation is unexpected and comes from a surprising direction. *Asham talui ve-chatat ha-of haba al hasafek l'devarecha yochichu* — the *asham talui* and the *chatat ha-of* that is brought under conditions of doubt, according to your own position, serve as a counterproof.

To understand the force of this: an *asham talui* is the offering brought when one suspects but cannot confirm that one has committed an inadvertent sin warranting a *chatat* — the classic case being two pieces before one, one forbidden fat and one permitted, and one was eaten without knowing which. A *chatat ha-of haba al hasafek* arises in the context of purification, as when a woman has a miscarriage and is uncertain whether the fetus was viable enough to obligate her to bring a bird *chatat*; since without that offering she can never again eat *kodshim*, she brings it, but the *kohanim* do not eat the bird because its status is uncertain.

Now, both of these objects are *assur be-achilah u-va-hana'ah* and carry the weight of *karet* — they are *kodshim* and thus subject to *me'ila* — and they would seem to fall squarely within the framework Rabbi Yehuda has constructed. One would expect, by his reasoning, that if they become invalid (*nosar*, *tamei*, etc.) they must be burned like all other *kodshim*. Yet Rabbi Yehuda himself holds that these are buried rather than burned. The *chachamim* say: by your own logic, you have created an exception that undermines your general rule.

*Shatak Rabbi Yehuda* — Rabbi Yehuda was silenced. He had no response.

*Rav Yosef* captures the moment with a folk saying: the ladle the carpenter carved out burned his own tongue on mustard — he was undone by his own work. *Abaye* offers another formulation: the one who made the stockade must sit in it himself. And *Rava* adds: the arrowmaker is killed by his own arrows — *midlei yadei mishtalem*, he is paid back by the work of his own hands. These are not expressions of gloating so much as a kind of wry, teasing appreciation of the irony that one's own carefully constructed position has become the instrument of one's defeat.

The practical *halachic* upshot is significant: there is a major *machlokes rishonim* about whether we rule like Rabbi Yehuda or the *chachamim*. Had it not been for Rabbi Yehuda's unusual position on the *chatat ha-of*, his argument would have been considerably stronger. The very position that created a problem for his opponents' counterargument is the one that silenced him.

---

## Chachamim Methods

### Multiple Options

The *mishnah*'s formulation of the *chachamim*'s position is: *mefareir ve-zoreh la-ruach* — one crumbles and scatters to the wind — *o matil la-yam* — or one throws it into the sea. The word *zoreh* here should be noted: it means to winnow or scatter, not to sow, and is spelled without an *ayin*.

### Parsing Ambiguity

An *ibaya* is raised: how exactly is the *chachamim*'s ruling to be read? The question is whether the requirement to crumble (*pirur*) applies to both methods of disposal or only to the first. One reading would have it: crumble and scatter to the wind — or crumble and cast into the sea. The alternative reading: crumble and scatter to the wind — or simply cast it into the sea as it is, without crumbling. The first reading makes *pirur* a prerequisite for both methods; the second makes *pirur* necessary only when throwing to the wind (since otherwise it will fall to the ground and be found by others), while throwing into the sea suffices without preliminary crumbling.

The practical question is immediate and very concrete: if one finds *chametz* in one's house, does one need to crumble it before flushing it down the drain? That is precisely the modern instantiation of *matil la-yam*, and whether *pirur* is required first is what the *Gemara* is working toward.

A parallel *mishnah* in the context of *avodah zarah* surfaces here. Rabbi Yosei rules that one who wishes to dispose of an idol should grind it (*shocheik*) and scatter it to the wind or cast it into the sea. The same ambiguity applies: does *shechika* (grinding) accompany both options or only the first?

### Rabbah's Distinction

*Rabbah* proposes that the two cases — *chametz* and *avodah zarah* — may operate under different rules. With *avodah zarah*, when the *mishnah* speaks of casting into the sea, it means the *Yam HaMelach* (the Dead Sea), which no one traverses and from which no one draws. Even a pristine, intact idol floating in the Dead Sea poses no real danger of retrieval or use, and therefore *shechika* is not required before casting it there. *Chametz*, by contrast, when it says cast into the sea, means any body of water — and people do encounter those. A floating loaf of bread in an ordinary river could easily wash up and be found. Therefore, *pirur* is required before casting *chametz* into the water.

### Rav Yosef Response

*Rav Yosef* inverts this reasoning entirely. *Avodah zarah delo mami'isa* — an idol does not dissolve or become disgusting when submerged in water; it remains intact and recognizable wherever it ends up. Therefore *shechika* is required regardless of where one throws it. *Chametz de-mami'is* — bread, by contrast, becomes soggy, dissolves, and renders itself effectively unrecognizable and unappetizing wherever one throws it. Therefore *pirur* is never required for *chametz* since the natural process of submersion accomplishes the same thing.

### Conflicting Braitot

The *Gemara* then produces *braitot* supporting each position. In support of *Rava*: a *braita* states explicitly that one traveling in the wilderness should crumble and scatter his *chametz* to the four winds, and one traveling by ship should crumble and cast it into the sea — the verb *mefareir* appearing in both cases, explicitly requiring crumbling for *chametz* in all situations. In support of *Rav Yosef*: a *braita* states that for *avodah zarah*, one traveling in the wilderness grinds and scatters, and one traveling by ship grinds and casts into the sea — *shechika* required in both cases, with no apparent distinction between bodies of water.

Taking these *braitot* at face value would seem to favor neither *Rabbah* nor *Rav Yosef* but rather to suggest that crumbling is always required for *chametz* and grinding always required for *avodah zarah*. But that is not the conclusion the *Gemara* draws.

### Resolution via Geography

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradictions as follows. *Shechika kashya le-Rava* — the *braita* requiring grinding of *avodah zarah* into the sea seems to challenge *Rabbah*, who said no grinding is needed when throwing into the *Yam HaMelach*. *Pirur kashya le-Rav Yosef* — the *braita* requiring crumbling of *chametz* before casting into water seems to challenge *Rav Yosef*, who said *chametz* dissolves on its own. The resolution: *shechika le-Rava lo kashya* — for *Rabbah*, the *braita* requiring grinding of *avodah zarah* refers to ordinary bodies of water, not the *Yam HaMelach*. Into the *Yam HaMelach* no grinding is required; into other seas it is. *Rabbah* never disputed the latter. *Pirur le-Rav Yosef lo kashya* — the *braita* requiring crumbling of *chametz* refers to wheat kernels (*chitei*), not to bread (*nahama*). Bread dissolves readily when submerged and requires no crumbling. Scattered wheat kernels, however, may not dissolve and therefore do require dispersal — though the practical meaning of "crumbling" wheat is simply ensuring the kernels are scattered rather than bundled together in a sack, as *Rashi* explains. There is no practical concern about *gebrochts* in this context, it should be said, since that is a much later *minhag*.

### Conceptual Framework

With this analysis in hand, a deeper conceptual point emerges — one articulated by *Rav Chayim HaLevi* on the *Rambam*. The *chachamim*'s willingness to allow disposal by methods short of burning — including throwing an intact idol into the *Yam HaMelach* without any destruction of the object itself — reveals that their understanding of the obligation is fundamentally different from Rabbi Yehuda's. For the *chachamim*, the concern is not that a specific act of destruction be performed upon the object. The concern is that the *chametz* be removed from human access and possession. Throwing something into the *Yam HaMelach* without grinding it does not destroy it in any technical sense; it merely renders it inaccessible. That suffices according to the *chachamim* because their operative category is not *hashchatah* (destruction) but *bi'ur* in the sense of removal from one's domain and from people's reach.

*Rabbi Akiva Eiger* raises a related question: the *Tur* rules that if one burned one's *chametz*, the ashes are *mutar behana'ah*. This is based on the principle of *na'aseh mitzvato* — one has fulfilled the *mitzvah* associated with the object, and so the object's prohibited character is exhausted. But why should the ashes be *mutar* even according to the *chachamim*, who permit other means of destruction? There is still a *mitzvas tashbitu* — so one has fulfilled the *mitzvah* through burning. *Rav Chayim* answers that the distinction is precisely this: if the *mitzvah* is *sreifah* — a specific act of burning performed upon the object — then the *Torah*'s concern is focused on the object and on what was done to it. When that act is performed, the object's *mitzvah* has been fulfilled, and the resulting ashes are free. But if the *Torah*'s directive is to get the *chametz* out of one's possession and away from people, then the *Torah* is not focused on the object at all. There is no concept of doing something *to* this object; there is only the concept of getting rid of it. Burning, under this conception, does not release the ashes, because the *Torah* never focused on the object to begin with. The ashes of burned *chametz*, according to the *chachamim*'s conceptual framework, would remain *assur behana'ah*.

---

## Chametz Shel Nochri

### Mishnah Ruling

The next *mishnah* presents a clean contrast: *chametz shel nochri she-avar alav ha-Pesach mutar behana'ah* — *chametz* owned by a non-Jew over which Pesach has passed is permitted for benefit. No *aveira* was committed; the prohibition did not apply to the non-Jew; once Pesach ends, the *chametz* is simply *chametz* again and may be used. *Ve-shel Yisrael assur behana'ah* — *chametz* that was owned by a Jew throughout Pesach, however, remains *assur behana'ah* even after Pesach ends. The *mishnah* derives this from *she-ne'emar lo yeira'eh lecha se'or* — since you as a Jew transgressed by owning it, it remains forbidden as a consequence. Whether this post-Pesach prohibition is *mi-de'oraisa* or *mi-derabbanan* is a matter of dispute, and the *Gemara* will address it.

---

## When Chametz Forbidden

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

The *Gemara* opens its analysis of this *mishnah* by asking: *mani matnitin* — whose position does our *mishnah* reflect? The answer, striking in its directness, is: *lo Rabbi Yehuda ve-lo Rabbi Shimon ve-lo Rabbi Yossi HaGlili* — it fits none of the three *tanna'im* we know to have debated the question of when *chametz* is *assur behana'ah*. The *Gemara* then cites a *braita* that lays out all three positions.

Rabbi Yehuda's position: *chametz bein lifnei zemano u-vein le-achar zemano over alav be-lav* — eating *chametz* before its time (meaning from the sixth hour of *Erev Pesach*, when there is already an obligation to destroy it) and after its time (after Pesach ends) both constitute a violation of a *lav*. *Toch zemano, over alav be-lav ve-charet* — during Pesach itself, one transgresses both a *lav* and incurs *karet*. So for Rabbi Yehuda, there is a biblical negative prohibition in all three periods; the difference is only that the prohibition during Pesach carries *karet* as well.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon holds the opposite: *chametz lifnei zemano u-le-achar zemano eino over alav be-lav klum* — before and after Pesach, one transgresses nothing at all. *Toch zemano, over alav be-lav ve-charet* — during Pesach, one transgresses both the *lav* and *karet*.

This requires clarification, since we have operated throughout these dapim with the assumption that eating *chametz* from midday of *Erev Pesach* is at minimum biblically prohibited. *Tosafot* clarifies that Rabbi Shimon does not mean one may blithely eat *chametz* during the sixth hour. He holds that there is a *mitzvah* of *tashbitu*, and eating *chametz* during that period would be a corollary violation of that *mitzvah* — but it is not a formal *lav* in its own right, and there is certainly no *issur hana'ah*. What we take for granted — *issur hana'ah* from midday of *Erev Pesach* — is the position of Rabbi Yehuda, not a universal assumption.

### Rabbi Yossi Position

Rabbi Yossi HaGlili's position is the most radical. *Temah alecha* — you should be astounded at yourself — *he chametz assur behana'ah kol shivah?* Who told you that *chametz* is even *assur behana'ah* during the seven days of Pesach? He disputes what we take as the most basic premise of *hilchot chametz*. It is a striking *Gemara*.

### Shimon Rebuttal

What does Rabbi Shimon do with the *pesuk* Rabbi Yehuda cites — *lo tochal alav chametz* — which Rabbi Yehuda reads as establishing a prohibition from the time of the *korban Pesach*, i.e., from midday of *Erev Pesach*? Rabbi Shimon responds: *ve-chi efshar lomar kein?* Can you really read the *pasuk* that way? The very same *pasuk* continues: *shivat yamim tochal alav matzot* — seven days you shall eat *matzot*. If *alav* refers to the *korban Pesach* brought from midday, then the parallel clause about eating *matzah* for seven days makes no sense as a temporal reference. The end of the *pasuk* clearly anchors the prohibition of *chametz* to the seven days of the holiday.

Therefore Rabbi Shimon inverts the *derashah*: *be-sha'ah she-yeshno be-kum echol matzah, yeshno be-bal tochal chametz* — the moment when there is an obligation to eat *matzah*, there is a prohibition of *chametz*; *u-ve-sha'ah she-eino be-kum echol matzah, eino be-bal tochal chametz* — when there is no obligation to eat *matzah*, there is no prohibition of *chametz*. The *chametz* prohibition begins when the *matzah* obligation begins: on Pesach night, not on *Erev Pesach*. And correspondingly, when Pesach ends, both end together.

### Three Pesukim Derivation

What is the source for Rabbi Yehuda's position? *Tilsa kra'ei ksivi* — three *pesukim* are written: *lo ye'achel chametz*, *kol machmetzes lo tocheilu*, and *lo tochal alav chametz*. Rabbi Yehuda reads these three formulations as addressing three distinct periods: one establishes the prohibition before Pesach (*lifnei zemano*), one during (*toch zemano*), and one after (*le-achar zemano*). *Tosafot* further notes that since one of the three uses the formulation *lo ye'achel* — even according to the position of *Chizkiya* that *lo ye'achel* establishes the *issur hana'ah* for similar prohibitions — all three carry the implication of *issur hana'ah*.

What does Rabbi Shimon do with these three *pesukim*, since for him only the during-Pesach prohibition exists? He must redirect each of the other two. One he uses to derive that the prohibition applies throughout all seven days. A second he redirects to the derivation discussed below.

### Kol Machmetzes

Rabbi Shimon uses *kol machmetzes lo tocheilu* not to establish a temporal prohibition but to teach a substantive *halacha*: *ein li ela shenischametz me-elav* — I might have thought only *chametz* that fermented on its own is prohibited. *Machmat davar acher* — if it fermented due to an external fermenting agent — *minayin?* — how do I know that is included? *Talmud lomar kol machmetzes lo tocheilu* — the word *machmetzes* (in the *hif'il* causative form) teaches that even something that was *caused* to become *chametz* by an external agent is included.

*Tosafot* clarifies that the case is not bread leavened with sourdough, which is the paradigmatic *chametz* and could never have been thought to be excluded. Rather, the question arises when the fermenting agent is something other than sourdough — a different type of fermenting substance, such as the kind produced from grape peels with their natural sugars. *Tosafot* describes how such fermenting agents were produced in the context of bread-making. In modern terms: baking powder or packets of non-sourdough yeast would fall into this category. The yeast or baking powder itself is not *chametz*. But bread that fermented because of such an agent — even if it fermented in less than eighteen minutes — is *chametz* by virtue of this *derashah* from *kol machmetzes*.

There is an implicit principle at work here worth noting: when a *derashah* rests on redundancy — the fact that a *pasuk* is "extra" and must therefore be teaching something new — once that redundancy is expended to teach one thing, it cannot simultaneously be expended to teach another. This is why, for Rabbi Shimon, the *pasuk* of *kol machmetzes* teaches the law of externally-fermented *chametz* rather than a separate temporal period of prohibition.

For Rabbi Yehuda, who uses *kol machmetzes* to derive the prohibition *le-achar zemano*, the teaching about external fermentation is derived differently: from the combination of the extra *pasuk* and the distinctive use of the word *machmetzet*, which allows him to learn two separate things from one *pasuk* — the temporal prohibition from the redundancy of the *pasuk* itself, and the law of external fermentation from the unusual choice of language.

### Pesach Mitzrayim

Rabbi Shimon's third *pasuk*, *lo ye'achel chametz*, is used to derive an entirely different category of *halacha*: the law of *Pesach Mitzrayim*. Rabbi Yossi HaGlili asks: *minayin le-Pesach Mitzrayim she-ein chimutzo noheig ela yom echad?* — how do we know that at the original Pesach in Egypt, when the holiday of *Chag HaMatzot* had not yet been established, the prohibition of *chametz* applied for only one day? The answer comes from *lo ye'achel chametz*, which appears in the context of the first *korban Pesach* and is followed by *hayom atem yotzim* — today you are going out from Egypt. The rabbinic reading is: do not eat *chametz* today, implying a one-day prohibition only.

This is a purely historical *halacha* with no practical application to subsequent generations. It is striking that a *pasuk* would be "used up" to establish a fact about a one-time event in *Pesach Mitzrayim* rather than to derive an ongoing *halachic* rule. But that is precisely what Rabbi Yossi HaGlili does with this *pasuk*, and Rabbi Yehuda — who does not employ *smuchin* (the principle of derivation from juxtaposed *pesukim*) in the same way — disputes this reading.

---

## Matzah Obligation

### Rabbi Yehuda on Matzah

Having established his reading of Rabbi Shimon's *derashah*, the *Gemara* now examines how Rabbi Yehuda uses the *pasuk* that Rabbi Shimon employed. Rabbi Shimon read *lo tochal alav chametz shivat yamim tochal alav matzot* as teaching that *chametz* is prohibited only when *matzah* is obligatory — i.e., during Pesach itself, not before or after. Rabbi Yehuda, who has three other *pesukim* for before, during, and after, cannot accept that reading. He therefore reads the linkage in the opposite direction.

*Hahu le-kavoa chova afilu bi-zman ha-zeh hu de-asa* — that *pasuk* comes to establish that there is a *mitzvah* of *matzah* even nowadays, even after the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*. The logic: as long as there is a prohibition of *chametz*, there is an obligation of *matzah*, and the prohibition of *chametz* applies in every generation. Therefore the obligation of *matzah* also applies in every generation.

This derivation addresses a real and substantial question. The *peshat* of most *pesukim* concerning *matzah* speaks either of seven days of *matzah* as a dietary alternative to *chametz*, or of eating *matzah* together with the *korban Pesach*. In neither formulation is there an obvious source for a specific *mitzvah* to eat *matzah* on *leil ha-seder* in the absence of a *korban*. If the seven-day *matzah* obligation is an alternative to *chametz* and not an independent *mitzvah* on each night, and if the *matzah* accompanies only the *korban Pesach*, then in a post-*Mikdash* world without a *korban* and without a daily eating-obligation, why should there be a *mitzvah* to eat *matzah* on the first night at all? Rabbi Yehuda answers: the linkage between *chametz* and *matzah* in this *pasuk* establishes that wherever there is a prohibition of *chametz*, the *mitzvah* of *matzah* follows. Since *chametz* applies in every generation, *matzah* applies in every generation, at minimum on the first night.

### Rabbi Shimon on Matzah

If Rabbi Yehuda uses the linking *pasuk* to derive *matzah*'s applicability post-*Mikdash*, and Rabbi Shimon uses it to limit *chametz* to Pesach itself, then the question is: where does Rabbi Shimon derive the obligation of *matzah* nowadays? The *Gemara* answers: *nafka lei mi-ba'erev tochelu matzos* — he learns it from the *pasuk*, *ba-rishon be-arba'ah asar la-chodesh ba-erev tochelu matzos* — on the first day, on the fourteenth of the month, in the evening you shall eat *matzot*.

This might seem obvious — does the *pasuk* not say plainly "in the evening eat *matzot*"? The difficulty is that the *pasuk* continues: *ad yom ha-echad ve-esrim la-chodesh ba-erev* — until the night of the twenty-first. Reading the *pasuk* in full, it appears to establish a seven-day obligation of eating *matzah*, from the evening of the fourteenth to the evening of the twenty-first. If one takes the *pshat* that this is an independent seven-day *mitzvah* to eat *matzah*, then all seven nights would require eating *matzah*. Since we do not hold that, we must be reading the *pasuk* differently — and Rabbi Shimon focuses on the first clause alone, *ba-erev tochelu matzos*, as establishing the first-night obligation.

### Arel and Ben Nochri

Rabbi Yehuda, for his part, also has a use for *ba-erev tochelu matzos*. He employs it not to establish the first-night *matzah* obligation in general (which he derives from the linkage *pasuk* as explained above), but to teach that the *matzah* obligation applies even to those who are not eating the *korban Pesach* — specifically the *tamei* and those who were *be-derech rechokah* (in a distant place) and were therefore exempt from bringing the *korban*. Without this *pasuk*, one might have thought: *ho'il u-ve-Pesach lo yochal matzah u-maror nami lo neichol* — since such a person does not eat the *korban Pesach*, perhaps the associated *matzah* and *maror* also do not apply. *Ka mashma lan* — this *pasuk* teaches that they do. This establishes the first stage of *matzah*'s independence from the *korban* — it applies even in the presence of a *Mikdash* to those not eating the *korban*. But Rabbi Yehuda maintains that a second *pasuk* is needed to extend this to the post-*Mikdash* world entirely.

Rabbi Shimon, however, does not need the *tamei* and *be-derech rechokah* case as a separate derivation. *Lo gara me-arel u-ven neichar* — they are no different from an uncircumcised person or a *ben neichar* (here meaning one who is a *mumar* in certain respects), whose exclusion from the *korban Pesach* is stated explicitly: *ve-chol arel lo yochal bo, ve-chol ben neichar lo yochal bo* — they shall not eat *in it*, meaning the *korban Pesach*, but they still eat *matzah u-maror*. From this *pasuk*, Rabbi Shimon already knows that *matzah* applies to those not eating the *korban*. Therefore *ba-erev tochelu matzos* is free for him to use toward the larger derivation — establishing the obligation of *matzah* in the post-*Mikdash* era entirely.

The upshot: Rabbi Yehuda requires two *pesukim* to reach the conclusion that *matzah* applies post-*Mikdash* — one for the *tamei* and *be-derech rechokah* in the presence of the *Mikdash*, and a second to extend this to our own times. Rabbi Shimon needs only one, having derived the prior step from an independent source. What is clear from both positions, and what the *Gemara* leaves us with, is that the obligation to eat *matzah* on *leil ha-seder* is not at all straightforward from the *pesukim* on their own — it requires careful and deliberate derivation, and the independence of *matzah* from *korban Pesach* is a conclusion that had to be established, not assumed.

---

---

# Pesachim 31

## Intro: Collateral & Pesa…

### Welcome & Overview

Today's material constitutes a somewhat standalone *sugya* — a self-contained legal unit — that spans nearly the entirety of the *daf*. By way of introduction, it is worth noting that this discussion is moderately complex, dealing with the intersection of financial law and the laws of *chametz* over *Pesach*. Those around the table will inevitably be a collaborative resource as we make our way through.

### Scope & Framework

The material runs from the *mishna* at the bottom of 30b through the *mishna* at the bottom of 31b, with the bulk of 31a constituting an elaborate discussion of the relationship between creditors, debtors, and collateral. The central question is: when is a creditor considered to have possession of the collateral placed against a loan, and when can the default presumptions governing that relationship be altered by the specific language used at the time of the loan? Along the way, the *sugya* examines implications for cases involving inheritance, all of which ultimately serves to clarify the positions articulated in the *mishna*.

### Mishnah: Two Cases

The *mishna* at the bottom of 30b presents two cases. The first: a *nochri* who lends money to a Jew and takes the Jew's *chametz* as collateral — *achar haPesach mutar behana'ah*, after *Pesach* that *chametz* is permitted to the Jew to derive benefit from. The essential inference is that the *chametz* must have been sufficiently considered in the possession of the *nochri* — the creditor — already from the moment the loan was made, such that the Jew is not considered to have violated *bal yera'eh u'bal yimatze* over *Pesach*.

The second case is the converse: a Jew who lends money to a *nochri* and takes the *nochri*'s *chametz* as collateral — *achar haPesach asur behana'ah*, after *Pesach* that *chametz* is prohibited for the Jew to derive benefit from. The operative principle is the same: if the creditor has sufficient claim on the collateral to be considered its possessor, then the Jew who holds the *nochri*'s *chametz* as collateral is treated as if that *chametz* was in his domain over *Pesach*, rendering it *chametz she'avar alav haPesach*.

By way of background, the rabbis enacted a decree that *chametz she'avar alav haPesach* — *chametz* over which *Pesach* has passed — is prohibited not merely for eating but even for deriving any benefit, in accordance with the view of Rabbi Shimon. This prohibition serves in some sense to add teeth to the biblical prohibitions of *bal yera'eh u'bal yimatze* even after the fact.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Lemafrea vs. Mikan

Three lines from the bottom of 30b, the *Gemara* introduces an *itmara* — a transmitted Amoraic dispute: *ba'al chov: Abaye amar lemafrea hu goveh, veRava amar mikan ulehaba hu goveh*. That is, with respect to a creditor's acquisition of collateral: Abaye holds that the creditor acquires the collateral *lemafrea* — retroactively — meaning the item is considered to have been in the creditor's possession all along from the inception of the loan. Rava holds that the creditor acquires *mikan ulehaba* — prospectively — meaning the collateral only officially passes into the creditor's possession at the moment the borrower defaults and repayment becomes impossible.

### Scope of Dispute

The *Gemara* proceeds to clarify the precise circumstances in which this dispute applies. Where the *borrower* is the one who took action with the collateral — consecrating it (*hikdish* it) to the *Beit HaMikdash* or selling it — all agree (*kulei alma lo pligi*) that the lender may come and seize it from whoever now holds it, or redeem it. In the case of *hekdesh*, the *Gemara* notes in passing (citing the *mishna* in *Arachin*) that the lender would add a nominal *dinar* and use that to redeem the item — out of a degree of deference to sanctified property not accorded to an ordinary third-party buyer.

The dispute between Abaye and Rava applies specifically where it is the *lender* — not the borrower — who sold or consecrated the collateral item. In that situation alone does the question of when acquisition takes effect become critical.

### Svara: Both Sides

The *Gemara* articulates the internal reasoning (*svara*) of each position. Abaye reasons: *keivan demata zamnei velo parei, iglai milta lemafrea deme'ikara bireshutei hava ka'ei* — once the time for repayment arrived and the borrower did not pay, it was retroactively revealed that from the very beginning the collateral had been in the lender's possession. The lender therefore acted entirely properly in selling it or consecrating it.

Rava reasons: *keivan de'ilu hava lei zuzei hava mesalek lehu bizuzei, ishtakhakh dehashta ka kaneh* — given that throughout the entire duration of the loan, had the borrower possessed the funds he would have been able to repay and reclaim the collateral, it follows that until the moment of actual default, the collateral was never truly the lender's. It is only now, when it becomes definitively clear that repayment is impossible, that the collateral passes into the lender's possession. Up to that point, the theoretical possibility of repayment precluded any firm claim.

---

## Reuven & Shimon

### The Sale Setup

At this point the *Gemara* raises a challenge from a case cited by Rami bar Chama: *Reuven she'machar sadeh leShimon b'achrayut*. Reuven sold a field to Shimon *b'achrayut* — with a warranty. *Achrayut* here means that Reuven stipulated that if his own creditor were to come and seize the field from Shimon on account of a debt Reuven owed, Reuven would repay Shimon whatever Shimon was required to pay. As Rashi explains, this is the sort of provision a buyer might insist upon when acquiring property from a seller who carries outstanding debts.

At the same time, *vezakfan alav bemilveh* — Shimon did not actually have the funds to pay for the field at the time of purchase. He therefore wrote Reuven a promissory note obligating himself to pay the price of the field, effectively seller-financing the transaction. The field passed to Shimon, and Reuven held a note for the purchase price.

### Creditor Arrives
