Reuven then dies. His creditor arrives and seeks to seize the field from Shimon on account of Reuven's outstanding debt. Shimon, rather than surrendering the field, pays off Reuven's creditor directly in money, thereby preventing the seizure.

The heirs of Reuven now approach Shimon and argue: our father left behind a debt — the purchase price of the field — which you owe us. Moreover, they contend, *metaltlei d'yatmi leba'al chov lo mishtabdei* — the personal property (in this case, the monetary debt owed to the estate) that orphans inherit cannot be subjugated to their father's creditor. Consequently, Shimon finds himself in the position of having paid Reuven's creditor once with money, and now being compelled to pay the value of the field a second time to Reuven's heirs. He has, in effect, been made to pay twice.

### Rava's Solution

Rava intervenes with a practical suggestion: *ee pike'ach Shimon, magbei lehu ara vehadar gabei lah minaihu* — if Shimon were shrewd, he would give the field to Reuven's heirs as payment of his debt to them, and then turn around and reclaim the field from them in order to pay Reuven's creditor.

The mechanism for this is a principle cited in the name of Rav Nachman: *yetomim shegavu karka bechovot avihem, ba'al chov chozer vegoveh otah mehen* — when orphans have collected land in satisfaction of their father's debts, the father's creditor may come back and collect that same land from them. By this route, Shimon would surrender the field to the heirs (satisfying his debt to them) and then recover the field from the heirs via the *achrayut* stipulation in order to pay the creditor — ending up with the loss of only the field rather than twice the field's value.

### Challenge to Rava

The *Gemara* now presses on Rava's own position. *Ei amart bishlama lemafrea hu goveh* — had this been Abaye's position, Rav Nachman's ruling would be perfectly coherent: since the lender acquires retroactively, the field is considered as though it was in the creditor's possession already during Reuven's lifetime, and therefore the heirs who received it are holding something that was already effectively the creditor's. *Ela ei amart mikan ulehaba hu goveh, amai chozer vegoveh otah mehen* — but if you hold that the creditor only acquires from the time of default onward, how can the creditor reach back and collect from the heirs? The heirs, at the time they received the field, appear to have acquired it as a fresh transaction; *havei keman dezavin yatmi nichsei dami* — it is as though the orphans themselves purchased the property, and if they had purchased property, it would not be subjugated to their father's creditor. This is a pointed difficulty for Rava.

### Stipulation resolves

The *Gemara* resolves the difficulty: *shani hatam*, this case is different, *de'amar lehu: ki heichi demishtabdina leh le'avuchon, mishtabdina nami leba'al chov de'avuchon* — because Shimon explicitly said to the heirs: just as I am obligated to your father, so too am I obligated to your father's creditor. This explicit stipulation creates a chain of obligation that operates independently of the general rule of *mikan ulehaba*.

The basis for this is the principle of Rabbi Natan, cited in a *braita*: *minayin lenoseh bechavero maneh vechavero bechavero maneh, shemotzi'in mizeh venotnin lazeh* — how do we know that when A is owed a *maneh* by B, and B is owed a *maneh* by C, we may extract from C and give to A? The *pasuk* teaches: *venatan la'asher asham lo* — he shall give to the one to whom he is indebted. This creates a recognized chain of debt through which an original creditor may reach a later obligor, provided the requisite stipulation was made. The present case thus works for Rava not because of the general principle of retroactive acquisition, but because of this specific and explicit undertaking that created a direct link between Shimon and Reuven's creditor.

---

## Back to Mishnah

### Problem for Rava

Having worked through the implications of Rava's position in the case of Reuven and Shimon, the *Gemara* returns to the *mishna* and challenges Rava directly. The *mishna* states that when a *nochri* loans to a Jew with *chametz* as collateral, the *chametz* is *mutar behana'ah* after *Pesach* — implying that the *chametz* was considered in the *nochri*'s possession during *Pesach*. *Ei amart bishlama lemafrea hu goveh* — for Abaye, this is perfectly understandable: the creditor acquired retroactively, and so the *chametz* was in the *nochri*'s domain throughout *Pesach*. *Ela ei amart mikan ulehaba hu goveh, amai mutar behana'ah?* — but for Rava, how can this be permitted? *Bireshuta deYisrael hava ka'ei* — during *Pesach* the *chametz* was in the Jew's possession, rendering it *chametz she'avar alav haPesach*.

### Okimta: Deposit

The *Gemara* resolves this with an *okimta*: *hacha bemai askinan? Keshehirhino etzlo* — the case in the *mishna* must be one where the Jew physically deposited the *chametz* with the *nochri*. Even if Rava holds that in general the creditor does not acquire the collateral until default, in this particular situation the Jew transferred the *chametz* into the *nochri*'s physical domain. That act of deposit, even without a formal *kinyan*, is sufficient to remove the item from the Jew's *reshut* in a meaningful enough sense that the Jew does not violate *bal yera'eh u'bal yimatze*, and the *chametz* is therefore *mutar behana'ah* after *Pesach*.

As Rashi explains, the rationale combines the formal collateral arrangement (*torat mashkon*) with the principle that *ba'al chov koneh mashkon* — a creditor acquires the collateral. The practical upshot is that when the item is physically in the lender's domain, even under Rava's view, the combination of physical transfer and the collateral relationship is sufficient to render it not in the Jew's possession for *chametz* purposes. The prohibition of *lo yera'eh lecha velo yimatze lecha* is understood as requiring presence in one's domain (*reshut*), not merely legal ownership — and here the *chametz* is genuinely out of the Jew's *reshut*, even if ownership remains technically ambiguous until default.

It is worth noting that this entire prohibition — *chametz she'avar alav haPesach* — is *derabbanan*. The rabbis, who enacted the decree, have the authority to delineate precisely under what circumstances it applies and under what circumstances it does not, including calibrating it according to the degree of physical and legal control a Jew exercises over the *chametz* in question.

---

## Tannaim: Meir & T.K.

### Braita: Jew→Nokhri

Having established the positions of Abaye and Rava, the *Gemara* attempts to trace a Tannaic precedent for this debate: *leima ketannai*. A *braita* is cited: *Yisrael shehilvah lenochri al chametzo, le'achar haPesach, eino over* — a Jew who loans to a *nochri* with the *nochri*'s *chametz* as collateral, after *Pesach*, does not transgress *chametz she'avar alav haPesach*, according to the *Tanna Kamma*. But *mishum Rabbi Meir amru over* — Rabbi Meir holds that the Jew does transgress.

### Explain via A/R?

One might naturally propose that this Tannaic dispute maps directly onto the Abaye/Rava debate: the *Tanna Kamma*, who says the Jew does not transgress, holds *mikan ulehaba* — the creditor only acquires upon default, and so during *Pesach* the *chametz* remained in the *nochri*'s possession; Rabbi Meir holds *lemafrea* — retroactively the Jew already owned the collateral throughout *Pesach*. However, the *Gemara* questions this alignment: *vetisbra?* Can this really be so? *Eima seifa* — we must look at the second half of the *braita*.

### Braita: Nokhri→Jew

The *seifa* states: *aval nochri shehilvah leYisrael al chametzo, le'achar haPesach, divrei hakol over* — but when a *nochri* loans to a Jew with the Jew's *chametz* as collateral, everyone agrees the Jew transgresses. This is a problem for a simple mapping onto Abaye and Rava. If the *Tanna Kamma* in the *reisha* holds *mikan ulehaba* (creditor does not acquire until default), and Rabbi Meir holds *lemafrea* (creditor acquires retroactively), then in the *seifa* — where it is now a *nochri* lending to a Jew — the *Tanna Kamma* should say the *nochri* acquires the collateral retroactively (freeing the Jew from the prohibition) and Rabbi Meir should say *mikan ulehaba* (keeping it in the Jew's *reshut*). The *seifa* should present reversed positions. Instead, both agree the Jew transgresses — meaning the alignment with Abaye and Rava is not straightforward, and a different explanatory framework is needed.

---

## Rabbi Yitzchak

### Biblical Derivation

The alternative framework is introduced through the position of Rabbi Yitzchak. The *Gemara* asks: *minayin leba'al chov shekoneh mashkon* — from where do we know at all that a creditor acquires the collateral? Rabbi Yitzchak derives it from the *pasuk* in *Devarim* (24): *hashev tashiv lo et ha'avot kevo hashemesh veshachav besalmato uverachecha* — you must return the collateral garment to the borrower at night so he can sleep in it and bless you — *ulecha tihyeh tzedakah lifnei Hashem Elokecha* — and this shall be an act of charity before God. The innovative interpretation of Rabbi Yitzchak is: *im eino koneh mashkon, tzedakah minayin?* — if the garment truly belongs to the borrower all along, how is returning it to him an act of *tzedakah*? One only performs *tzedakah* by giving something of one's own. The very fact that the *Torah* calls the return of the collateral *tzedakah* proves that the creditor actually owns the collateral — *mikan leba'al chov shekoneh mashkon*.

### T.K.: Jew-Jew only

The *Tanna Kamma* accepts Rabbi Yitzchak's principle but limits its application: *hani milei Yisrael miYisrael hu dekarina beih ulecha tihyeh tzedakah* — this principle of *ba'al chov koneh mashkon* applies only where both parties are Jewish, because only in a Jew-to-Jew loan does the concept of *tzedakah* as commanded in the *Torah* apply. The *mitzvah* of *tzedakah* in this context is specifically to one's Jewish brother (*achicha*). Therefore, in a Jew-to-*nochri* loan, where there is no operative *mitzvah* of *tzedakah* from Jew to non-Jew, the derivation of *ba'al chov koneh mashkon* falls away, and the Jew does not acquire the *nochri*'s collateral.

### R. Meir: Kal Vachomer

Rabbi Meir disagrees, applying a *kal vachomer*: if a Jew acquires collateral from another Jew (*Yisrael miYisrael kani*), then in a Jew-to-*nochri* loan, *lo kol sheken* — how much more so should the Jew acquire the *nochri*'s collateral. The reasoning of the *kal vachomer* is not made fully explicit, but the direction is clear: Rabbi Meir sees the Jew-Jew acquisition as the baseline, and the Jew-*nochri* case as stronger rather than weaker.

### Nokhri never acquires

This framework resolves the *seifa* of the *braita*. When a *nochri* lends to a Jew — *aval nochri shehilvah leYisrael al chametzo, divrei hakol over* — everyone agrees the Jew transgresses. The reason is: *vadai nochri miYisrael lo kani* — it is certain that a *nochri* taking collateral from a Jew never acquires that collateral at all. There is no *pasuk* of *ulecha tihyeh tzedakah* applying to a *nochri* creditor, and there is no *kal vachomer* that would extend acquisition to the *nochri* side. Therefore, even if the Jew deposited the *chametz* with the *nochri*, the *nochri* never truly becomes its owner, and the *chametz* remains legally in the Jew's domain throughout *Pesach* — a fact about which both *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Meir agree. The debate between them pertains only to the Jew-to-*nochri* direction.

---

## Me'achshav Principle

### Okimta: Stipulation

Having established that a *nochri* lending to a Jew never acquires the collateral, the *Gemara* must now revisit the *mishna*, which states that when a *nochri* loans to a Jew with *chametz* as collateral, the *chametz* is *mutar behana'ah* after *Pesach*. But we have just concluded that a *nochri* never acquires the collateral — so how can the *chametz* be *mutar*? If it remained the Jew's throughout *Pesach*, it should be *chametz she'avar alav haPesach*.

The *Gemara* answers with a new *okimta*: *lo kashya — ha de'amar leih me'achshav, ha delo amar leih me'achshav* — there is no contradiction. The case in the *mishna* where the *chametz* is *mutar* must be one where the *nochri* explicitly said to the Jew *me'achshav* — from now, this is yours — explicitly stipulating at the time of the loan that the *chametz* is transferred into the Jew's possession immediately. In such a case, even under the framework of Rabbi Yitzchak and the *Tanna Kamma*, the explicit declaration overrides the default rule and does cause the *chametz* to transfer. The case where no such stipulation was made follows the default rule and the *chametz* remains the *nochri*'s (or more precisely, remains not-the-Jew's).

### Braita: Deposit

In support of the distinction introduced by the *me'achshav* stipulation, the *Gemara* cites a *braita*: *nochri shehirhin patporni eitzel Yisrael, eino over* — a *nochri* who deposits a *patporni* (a significant or fancy loaf of bread — presumably used as an example of collateral worth pledging) with a Jew does not cause the Jew to transgress *chametz she'avar alav haPesach*. *Ve'im amar lo higaticha, over* — but if the *nochri* said to the Jew *higaticha* — "it has arrived in your possession," meaning it is now yours — then the Jew does transgress.

### Inference: Words matter

The *Gemara* draws the obvious inference: *mai shna reisha umai shna seifa?* — what is the difference between the first clause and the second clause? The only difference is that in the second clause, the *nochri* explicitly declared *higaticha* — a statement of immediate transfer equivalent to *me'achshav*. This confirms that explicit verbal stipulation at the time of collateral transfer has legal effect, changing the ownership status of the pledged item. *Shma mina* — this may be derived from here.

---

## Stores & Presumption

### Jewish store

The *sugya* concludes with a *braita* establishing practical presumptions of ownership where chametz is found after *Pesach* in ambiguous circumstances. The first case: a store belonging to a Jew, with inventory belonging to a Jew, into which non-Jewish workers enter and exit. If *chametz* is found there after *Pesach* — *asur behana'ah*, it is prohibited to derive benefit from it, and certainly prohibited for eating. The presumption is that any *chametz* found there was the Jew's *chametz* that was not disposed of before *Pesach*, rather than the lunch brought in by a non-Jewish worker. The non-Jewish workers' occasional presence does not create sufficient doubt to override the presumption that the contents of a Jewish-owned store with Jewish inventory belong to the Jewish owner.

### Non-Jewish store

The converse case: a store belonging to a *nochri*, with inventory belonging to a *nochri*, into which Jewish workers enter and exit. If *chametz* is found there after *Pesach* — *mutar be'achilah*, it is permitted even for eating, and certainly permitted for benefit. Here the presumption runs the other way: the contents of a *nochri*-owned store with *nochri* inventory are presumed to belong to the *nochri*, and the Jewish workers' entry does not raise sufficient suspicion that the *chametz* found there was brought in and left by a Jewish worker — which would itself involve a transgression. We follow the default presumption of the store's ownership, and the *chametz* is therefore treated as the *nochri*'s throughout *Pesach*, rendering it entirely permissible after *Pesach*.

---

---

# Pesachim 32

## Chametz Under Rubble

### Buried Chametz Status

The daf opens by picking up the *mishnah* on 31b. The case is *chametz shenaphlah alav mapolet* — leavened bread that has been buried under rubble. The *mishnah* rules *harei hu kimevuar*: the chametz is considered as though it has already been destroyed, since it is inaccessible. Rabban Gamliel, however, applies a more demanding criterion: mere burial is insufficient. What matters is whether *kol she'ein hakelev yakhol lachapes acharav* — a dog would be unable to dig it up. Only if the chametz is buried deep enough that a dog cannot unearth it is it considered *mevuar*.

### Bitul Despite Burial

Rav Chisda adds a critical qualification: even in the case where the chametz is buried and considered destroyed, *tzarich sheyevatel belibo* — one must still perform *bitul* in one's heart. Rashi explains the reasoning: *shema yipaka'ach hagal be-Moed* — perhaps the rubble will be cleared away during *Chol ha-Moed*, and the chametz will then be found intact. At that point, one would be in violation of *lo yeira'eh lekha velo yimatzei lekha*, since the chametz would again be *matzui* — accessible and present. This is why *bitul* remains necessary: since *min ha-Torah* *bitul* alone suffices, performing it in advance provides the essential legal protection.

### Three Tefach Standard

A *tanna* teaches: *kama chapisat hakelev* — how deep can a dog dig? The answer is *sheloshah tephachim*, three *tephachim*, according to the view of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. The *tephach* is roughly three to four inches, placing the total depth at somewhere between nine and twelve inches. This is the operative standard: if the chametz is buried beneath three *tephachim* of rubble, a dog will not be able to reach it.

### Chametz & Money Storage

Rav Acha the son of Rav Yosef poses a question to Rav Ashi by drawing in a different ruling. Shmuel teaches that *kesaphim ein lahen shemirah ela be-karka* — the proper way to safeguard money that has been entrusted to you is to bury it in the ground. Given that we have now introduced the standard of three *tephachim* in the context of chametz, the question arises: *mee ba'inan sheloshah tephachim alav* — must one also bury money three *tephachim* deep in order to fulfill this requirement?

### Smell vs. Visibility

Rav Ashi distinguishes sharply between the two cases. *Hacha mishum reicha ba'inan sheloshah tephachim* — in the case of chametz, the reason three *tephachim* are required is specifically because of smell. A dog will dig only where it detects a scent; below three *tephachim*, the chametz cannot be smelled and therefore will not be sought. But *hatam mishum ikhsoyyei me-ayna hu* — for money, the concern is entirely different: it is simply a matter of concealing it from view. Once it is buried even slightly and the surface is smoothed over, it is considered hidden. *Ve-lo ba'inan sheloshah* — there is no need for three *tephachim*. Indeed, Rav Afram bar Pappa, from Sikhra, rules that for money, a single *tephach* suffices.

---

## Terumah Chametz Laws

### Terumah Status

The *gemara* transitions to a new topic, introducing the *mishnah* concerning one who eats *terumah* that is *chametz* on Pesach. By way of background: *terumah* is not *hekdesh* — it is not Temple-consecrated property — but it occupies a related sanctified domain. As the *gemara* has already established, one is permitted to maintain in one's possession *chametz* that belongs to *nokrim* and *chametz* that belongs to *hekdesh*, since *shel'cha i atta ro'eh aval atta ro'eh shel acherim veshel gavoah* — the prohibition is against seeing *your* chametz, but you may see the chametz of others or of *gavoah*. The question now is what happens when a non-*kohen* eats, on Pesach, chametz that had the status of *terumah* belonging to a *kohen*.

### Payment & Intent

The intuitive expectation might be that no obligation of restitution would arise, for two distinct reasons. First, one might invoke *kim lei b'drabbah minei*: eating *chametz* on Pesach is an *issur karet*, and when one has incurred a grave spiritual penalty, the accompanying monetary obligation is set aside — the more severe punishment supersedes the lesser one. Second, one might argue that the chametz is simply worthless — *assur be-hana'ah* on Pesach — so what is there to repay?

Nonetheless, the *mishnah* rules otherwise. *Ha'ochel terumat chametz be-Pesach be-shogeg meshalem keren ve-chomesh* — one who eats *terumah chametz* on Pesach unintentionally must pay the principal and an additional fifth, just as with any other inadvertent consumption of *terumah*. However, *be-mezid patur mi-tashlumin u-mi-d'mei etzim* — if done intentionally, he is exempt from payment — and also exempt from payment of the value of the wood (i.e., whatever fuel value the *terumah chametz* might have had). The ruling is thus precisely parallel to the general law of *terumah*: *shogeg* obligates, *mezid* exempts.

### Rashi's Rationale

Rashi's explanation helps clarify what is at stake. The case of *shogeg* that triggers the *keren ve-chomesh* obligation is defined as *shagag bi-terumah* — one who was unaware of the *terumah* status of the food, even if he knew it was *chametz* and knew it was Pesach. *Ve-af al gav d'la havei shaveh midei* — and even though the chametz may not be worth anything in monetary terms, since *chametz shel Pesach assur be-hana'ah*, nonetheless the *terumah* restitution laws still apply. The obligation is grounded in the *terumah* dimension of the transaction, not in the market value of the item consumed.

The verse underlying this law reads: *uve-chamishito yosef alav ve-natan la-kohen et ha-kodesh* — with its fifth he shall add to it and give it to the *kohen* as *kodesh*. Rashi notes that restitution is made not in money but in kind — in produce that itself has *terumah* status. And the *gemara* elsewhere further specifies that repayment must be in something *hara'uy lihyot kodesh*, fit to be sanctified, which already begins to hint at why chametz itself, given its legal status on Pesach, raises complications.

### Atonement Principle

If we ask why the *mezid* is exempt, the answer emerges from two complementary angles. On one level, it is *kim lei b'drabbah minei*: intentional consumption of *terumah* carries *misah bi-yedei shamayim*, death at the hands of Heaven, and the principle holds that the graver penalty displaces the monetary one. On a more conceptual level, the payment of *keren ve-chomesh* functions as an act of atonement — *kaparah* — for the violation of *terumah*'s sanctity. The *mezid*, one who violates deliberately, is not considered worthy of that path of atonement. Paradoxically, then, the *shogeg* incurs monetary liability while the *mezid* does not — the *mezid* avoids financial obligation but forfeits the spiritual rectification that payment would represent.

A nuance worth noting: *karet* and *misah bi-yedei shamayim* are distinct categories of Heavenly punishment, with *karet* carrying additional dimensions, including potential effects on one's descendants. Intentional eating of *chametz* on Pesach is *karet*; intentional eating of *terumah* by a non-*kohen* is *misah bi-yedei shamayim*. The *gemara* does not elaborate on these distinctions here, but they bear on the general question of how broadly *kim lei b'drabbah minei* applies — a matter that will be taken up shortly through the ruling of Harkonus ben Hakanas.

---

## Measure vs. Value

### Core Question

Having established the basic *mishnah*, the *gemara* now raises a fundamental question about the mechanics of *terumah* restitution generally: *keshe-hu meshalem, lefi midah meshalem o lefi damim meshalem* — when one pays back, does he pay according to quantity or according to monetary value? To make this concrete: suppose someone consumed a liter of *terumah* olive oil. Does he owe back a liter of olive oil, regardless of price fluctuation? Or does he owe back the monetary equivalent of what he took — say, six dinars' worth — even if that now buys only half a liter?

### Hekdesh Principle

Before analyzing the upside scenario, the *gemara* dispenses with one direction of the question. Where the value has decreased — *d'heicha d'me'ikara shavya arba'a, u'levasof shavya zuza* — where it was originally worth four and is now worth only one — the answer is unambiguous: *vadai k'me'ikara meshalem*, he certainly pays at the original value. This follows from the general principle that applies also to *hekdesh*: the sanctified party never loses out due to depreciation. Furthermore, the minimum standard is that of an ordinary *gazlan*, of whom the *mishnah* rules *kol ha-gazlanim meshalmim k'sha'at ha-gezeilah* — all robbers pay the value as of the time of the theft. Terumah restitution cannot be more lenient than ordinary robbery.

The question, therefore, pertains only to the reverse: *d'me'ikara shaveh zuza u'levasof shaveh arba'a* — where it was worth one at the time of consumption and is worth four now. Does one pay the quantity (one liter, now worth four) or only the original value (one zuz's worth of oil, perhaps now only a quarter liter)?

### Figs & Dates Example

Rav Yosef attempts to resolve this from a teaching: *achal grogerot ve-shileim lo tmarim, tavo alav bracha* — one who ate dried figs and repaid the *kohen* with fresh dates, a blessing should come upon him. Dried figs are worth less than fresh dates; the restorer has thus given back something more valuable. *Tavo alav bracha* indicates he has exceeded his obligation.

Now, says Rav Yosef, this works out well if payment is *lefi midah* — by quantity. I consumed a *kor* of figs worth one zuz, and I returned a *kor* of dates worth four. Since I only needed to return the same quantity, returning something more valuable is praiseworthy. *Ela ei amrat lefi damim meshalem* — but if payment is by value, then I took one zuz's worth of figs, and I return one zuz's worth of dates, which is merely a quarter *kor*. I have given back the same monetary value, just in a different form. Why would there be *tavo alav bracha*? The *kohen* receives precisely what was taken, in terms of value.

This appears to constitute proof that repayment is *lefi midah*.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye, however, resolves the question without conceding to that conclusion. *Le'olam lefi damim meshalem* — payment is indeed by monetary value. Yet *tavo alav bracha* still applies, not because the restorer gave more value in absolute terms, but because *d'ka meshalem leh midi d'lo kafeitz aleh zabina v'ka meshalem leh midi d'kafeitz aleh zabina* — he repaid something that is difficult to sell (dried figs) with something that is much easier to sell (fresh dates). The *kohen* benefits practically: even if the absolute value is identical, he can liquidate the dates far more readily than the figs. That practical advantage to the *kohen* is what earns the restorer the blessing. The question of *midah* versus *damim* thus remains formally unresolved by this *sugya*, to be further engaged through the lens of *terumah chametz* specifically.

---

## Chametz Value Debate

### Worthlessness Problem

The *gemara* circles back to *terumah chametz* with fresh force. The *mishnah* obligates payment of *keren ve-chomesh* for the *shogeg* who eats *terumah chametz* on Pesach. But if payment is *lefi damim* — by value — and if *chametz shel Pesach* has no monetary value because it is *assur be-hana'ah*, then what is there to repay? The value is zero; a fifth of zero is zero. The obligation seems to collapse under its own logic.

### Rabbi Yosi Position

The *gemara* offers an initial resolution: *hah mani, Rabbi Yose HaGelili hi* — this *mishnah* accords with the opinion of Rabbi Yosi HaGelili, who holds *chametz be-Pesach mutar be-hana'ah*, that chametz on Pesach is not prohibited from benefit and therefore retains monetary value. According to his view, there is no problem: the chametz does have value, one can pay *lefi damim*, and the *mishnah* works smoothly. The mainstream ruling that chametz is *assur be-hana'ah* is a separate matter; this *mishnah* may simply reflect the minority position.

### Akiva-Yochanan Dispute

The *gemara* then presents a *tannaitic* dispute that sharpens the analysis. *Ochel terumat chametz be-Pesach — patur min ha-tashlumim u-mi-d'mei etzim, divrei Rabbi Akiva* — one who eats *terumah chametz* on Pesach is exempt from repayment and also from paying for the fuel value of the wood; this is the ruling of Rabbi Akiva. *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri mechayev* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri obligates payment.

Rabbi Akiva challenges: *ve-chi ma hana'ah yesh lo bah* — what benefit does one derive from chametz on Pesach that would justify an obligation to repay? Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri counters: *ma hana'ah yesh le'ochel terumah temeiah bi-sh'ar kol ha-shanah shemeshaleim lo* — and what benefit does one derive from eating *terumah temei'ah* during the rest of the year, yet one must still pay? The rest of the year, *terumah temei'ah* is also forbidden to eat, and yet restitution is obligated.

### Harkonus Equation

Rabbi Akiva deflects this challenge: the cases are not parallel. With *terumah temei'ah* during the year, *she'af al pi she'ein lo bah heter achilah yesh lo bah heter hasakah* — even though it may not be eaten, it may still be used as fuel. There is some permissible use. But for *terumah chametz* on Pesach, *she'ein lo bah lo heter achilah ve-lo heter hasakah* — according to the position that chametz is *assur be-hana'ah*, there is no permitted use whatsoever. He compares it to *terumah* of strawberries and grapes that became *tamei*: neither edible nor useful as fuel, and thus entirely without value.

The *gemara* then asks: even granting all this, why would the *mezid* be exempt from paying even *d'mei etzim* — the fuel value — according to Rabbi Yose HaGelili, who holds that chametz retains value on Pesach? The answer lies in the principle articulated by Harkonus ben Hakanas. *Harkonus ben Hakanas haya oseh et Yom ha-Kippurim ke-Shabbat le-tashlumim* — he equated Yom Kippur with Shabbat for purposes of *kim lei b'drabbah minei*. The point is this: one might have thought that *kim lei b'drabbah minei* applies clearly in cases of *karet* (as for Shabbat violation) but not necessarily in cases of *misah bi-yedei shamayim* (as for Yom Kippur), since they carry different levels of severity. Harkonus ben Hakanas rules that *kim lei b'drabbah minei* applies in all such cases equally — whether the Heavenly penalty is *karet* or *misah bi-yedei shamayim*, it displaces the accompanying monetary obligation. Therefore, the *mezid* who ate *terumah chametz* on Pesach, having incurred the graver penalty, is exempt from financial restitution even according to Rabbi Yose HaGelili.

### Kedushah of Chametz

A further distinction is introduced: *bamah devarim amurim be-mafresh terumah ve-himtzi'ah* — the foregoing discussion applies specifically where one separated *terumah* from wheat and it subsequently became *chametz*, or where the *terumah* was separated before Pesach from already-leavened dough, at a time when the transaction could be valid. *Aval mafresh terumat chametz* — if, however, one separates *terumah* from chametz at a time when it is forbidden, *divrei ha-kol einah kedushah* — by all opinions the *terumah* does not attain sanctified status at all.

This is derived from the verse *ve-natan la-kohen et ha-kodesh* — *davar ha-ra'uy lihyot kodesh*, the item given must be of a type fit to attain *kedushah*. Chametz that is *assur be-hana'ah* cannot become sanctified, and therefore cannot become *terumah* if separated as such *ab initio*. This is the position of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov, who on this basis rules that one who eats *terumah chametz* on Pesach is *patur min ha-tashlumim u-mi-d'mei etzim* — the underlying *kedushah* was never established. Rabbi Elazar Chisma disagrees and holds one liable.

Rabbi Elazar Chisma then reproduces, nearly verbatim, the exchange between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva: what about *terumah temei'ah* the rest of the year, where one still pays? Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov responds in kind: the rest of the year, *terumah temei'ah* retains fuel value — *yesh lo bah heter hasakah* — whereas *terumah chametz* on Pesach does not. Rabbi Elazar Chisma, however, contends: *af zo yesh lo bah heter hasakah* — even this has fuel value, citing *she'im matza'o kohen mereita fney k'vo'o masikah tachat tavshilo* — if a *kohen* found it, he may feed it to his dog or use it to heat his cooking pot. He holds that some *hana'ah* remains permissible, and therefore value exists and restitution is owed.

### Joint Chamutz View

On *amud bet*, Abaye provides a sweeping clarification of where all these opinions actually stand. *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri — kulam sevira lehu chametz shel Pesach assur be-hana'ah* — all of them hold that chametz on Pesach is forbidden from benefit. Their dispute is not about whether chametz has value. They all agree it does not. The dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri concerns a different question entirely.

### Abaye's Clarification

*U've-ha plagei: d'Rabbi Akiva savar lefi damim meshalem, ve-Yochanan ben Nuri savar lefi midah meshalem* — their dispute is precisely about whether *terumah* restitution is calculated by value or by quantity. According to Rabbi Akiva, one pays *lefi damim*. Since chametz on Pesach has no value, and since payment is by value, there is nothing to pay — hence *patur*. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds one pays *lefi midah*: I consumed a particular quantity, and I must return that quantity regardless of its market value. Since I took a *kor* of chametz *terumah*, I must return a *kor* of equivalent *terumah* produce — and value is irrelevant.

One might have supposed otherwise — that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri obligates payment because he holds, like Rabbi Yose HaGelili, that chametz on Pesach is *mutar be-hana'ah* and thus retains value even *lefi damim*. Abaye rules this out: *ka mashma lan* that this is not his reasoning. All these authorities reject Rabbi Yose HaGelili's position. The dispute is purely structural — *midah* versus *damim* — and Abaye establishes that as the correct framing of the entire *tannaitic* debate.

---

## Terumah Minimums

### Kezayit vs. Perutah

A *baraita* is now introduced to address the general law of *terumah* restitution: *ochel kezayit terumah meshalem keren ve-chomesh* — one who eats a *kezayit* of *terumah* must pay principal and fifth. This is the view of the *Tanna Kamma*. Abba Saul, however, qualifies: *ad she-yehei bo shaveh perutah* — not so fast; the obligation does not apply unless the item consumed is worth at least one *perutah*, the smallest recognized unit of monetary value. The question now becomes whether these are two independent conditions — one requiring a minimum *kezayit* in size, the other requiring a minimum *perutah* in value — or whether one supersedes the other.

### Tanna Kamma Source

The *Tanna Kamma*'s position is derived from the verse: *ve'ish ki yochal kodesh bi-shgagah* — if a man eats *kodesh* (here referring to *terumah*) inadvertently. The operative word is *yochal*, eating. The minimum measure of *achilah* recognized by *halacha* is a *kezayit* — an olive's volume. The *Tanna Kamma* therefore anchors the restitution obligation in the act of eating, setting the quantity threshold accordingly. Value, on this view, is not the operative factor.

### Abba Saul Source

Abba Saul derives his position from a different clause of the same verse: *ve-natan la-kohen et ha-kodesh* — and he shall give to the *kohen* the *kodesh*. The word *ve-natan*, giving, appears in multiple contexts where the *halacha* has established that an act of giving is legally meaningful only when it involves something worth at least a *perutah* — *ve-ein netinah pachos mi-shaveh perutah*. Giving something worthless is not a *netinah* in any legally cognizable sense. Abba Saul therefore holds that if the *terumah* consumed was not worth a *perutah*, no restitution obligation arises, regardless of how large a quantity was consumed.

### Tanna Kamma Response

Abba Saul's *perutah* requirement would seem to raise a difficulty for the *Tanna Kamma*: the verse also says *ve-natan*, and yet the *Tanna Kamma* does not require a minimum value of a *perutah*. The *Tanna Kamma* resolves this: *ve-natan* teaches something else entirely — *davar ha-ra'uy lihyot kodesh* — the item given in repayment must be of a type that can attain *kedushah*. This is what excludes, for example, paying back *terumah* with chametz on Pesach, or with anything else that cannot become sanctified. The verse's giving-language establishes a qualitative requirement on the repayment, not a minimum monetary floor.

### Abba Saul Response

Abba Saul, for his part, must contend with the *Tanna Kamma*'s reading of *yochal* as setting a *kezayit* threshold. Abba Saul reads *yochal* as *prat le-mazik* — eating is specified to exclude the case of one who damages or destroys the *terumah* without consuming it. A destroyer pays the principal but not the additional fifth, since the verse specifies *achilah*. The *yochal* clause does not, for Abba Saul, establish a minimum quantity for the eating-based obligation; it simply carves out the case of destruction from the *chomesh* requirement. The minimum quantity threshold, therefore, does not follow from this verse at all on Abba Saul's reading, and his sole operative criterion remains the *perutah* of value.

---

## Sub-Kezayit Cases

### Sub-Kezayit Rule

A further *baraita* addresses an intermediate scenario: *ha'ochel terumah pachos mi-kezayit meshalem et ha-keren ve-eino meshalem et ha-chomesh* — one who eats less than a *kezayit* of *terumah* pays the principal but is not required to pay the additional fifth.

### Value & Size

The *gemara* immediately asks: how is this case to be understood? If the item consumed is not worth a *perutah*, the principal should not be owed either. And if it is worth a *perutah*, why is the fifth not owed as well? The *gemara* resolves: *le'olam d'it beh shaveh perutah* — the case involves an item that is indeed worth a *perutah* in value. Nevertheless, since it lacks the minimum *kezayit* in size, one pays only the principal and is exempt from the *chomesh*. The logic is that the *chomesh* requirement is tied to the eating-act threshold, which demands a *kezayit*, while the basic principal obligation follows simply from having taken something of value.

### Dual Requirement?

This ruling raises a pointed question regarding Abba Saul's position. Abba Saul holds that the operative factor is value — a *perutah*. Does he also require, in addition, that the consumed item meet the *kezayit* size threshold? Or does he hold that value alone is sufficient, in which case even a sub-*kezayit* item worth a *perutah* would trigger the full *keren ve-chomesh* obligation?

### Rav Papa Position

Rav Papa initially rules that even Abba Saul requires both conditions: *Abba Saul tarti ba'ei* — Abba Saul requires both value and size. Thus, even according to Abba Saul, consuming less than a *kezayit* — even if it is worth a *perutah* — would result in the same ruling as the *baraita*: principal yes, *chomesh* no. Under this reading, both the *Tanna Kamma* and Abba Saul converge on requiring both a *kezayit* and a *perutah* in order for the full obligation to apply; they differ only in which of these two conditions generates the affirmative obligation, and which functions as an additional limiting criterion.

### Refutation

This position is immediately challenged. The *mishnah* explicitly quotes Abba Saul: *et she-yesh bo shaveh perutah chayav be-tashlumim, et she-ein bo shaveh perutah eino chayav be-tashlumim* — if it is worth a *perutah*, one is liable; if not, one is not liable. The criterion presented is solely *shaveh perutah*, with no mention of *kezayit*. If Abba Saul truly required both, the *mishnah* should have said *keivan she-yesh bo kezayit* — since it has a *kezayit* — rather than framing the obligation purely in terms of *perutah*.

The *gemara* concludes: *tiyuvta* — this is a decisive refutation of Rav Papa's position. And indeed, *af Rav Papa hadar bei* — Rav Papa himself retracted his view. The upshot is that the *Tanna Kamma* and Abba Saul represent genuinely competing, mutually exclusive positions. The *Tanna Kamma* requires a *kezayit* — size alone is the operative criterion. Abba Saul requires a *perutah* — value alone is the operative criterion. Each condition is sufficient on its own view and neither opinion demands both simultaneously.

---

---

# Pesachim 33

## Terumah: Size vs. Value

### Yesterday's Debate

The discussion opens with a brief review of the preceding day's material. The fundamental question was: when one must repay *terumah* that he ate inadvertently — since one who ate it *b'meizid* (deliberately) is not considered worthy of the atonement afforded by paying the principal and an added fifth — is the obligation to repay governed by size or by value? If it is size-based, one who ate a requisite volume repays that volume. If it is value-based, the amount consumed must be worth at least a *pruta*, even if it is what would normally constitute the requisite measure.

### Rav Pappa's Theory

Into this debate, Rav Pappa introduced the possibility that according to Abba Shaul — who had articulated a value-based criterion — the standard is actually a dual one: both the requisite size *and* a minimum value of a *pruta* are required. This position, and the *pasuk* that was subsequently cited to challenge it, forms the backdrop for the discussion that follows.

---

## Rav Pappa Retraction

### Rav Pappa Retracts

The Gemara states *v'af Rav Pappa hadar bei* — Rav Pappa also retracted his position. The mechanism of this retraction, and the proof that he indeed reversed himself, emerges from the extended analysis of a *baraita* that follows.

### Me'ilah: Intentional

The *baraita* opens with the verse *ve-cheit at bishgagah* — the Torah's requirement that one who commits *me'ilah* (misappropriation of consecrated property) brings an *asham* korban only when the act was done *bishgagah*, in error, *prat l'meizid* — thereby excluding one who acted deliberately from the obligation to bring this offering.

### Why Need Verse?

The Gemara immediately questions whether this exclusion required an explicit verse at all. Could it not have been derived by *kal va-chomer*? The reasoning would run: by other *mitzvot* where one incurs *karet* for an inadvertent transgression, the deliberate transgressor is exempt from a *korban*. *Me'ilah*, which carries no *karet* but rather *mita b'yedei shamayim*, should certainly exempt the deliberate transgressor — if anything, *mita b'yedei shamayim* is a more severe punishment than *karet*, so the argument for exemption seems even stronger.

### Karet vs. Mita

The Gemara immediately reverses this logic. Perhaps *mita b'yedei shamayim* is actually the more severe punishment. In that case, from the other *mitzvot* — where the punishment is "only" *karet* — one cannot draw a *kal va-chomer* to *me'ilah*, where the intentional violator might face something worse. The discussion thus produces what Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak points out is a troubling circularity: at one moment the analysis treats *karet* as the more severe standard, and at the next it treats *mita b'yedei shamayim* as more severe — and it flip-flops between the two without resolution.

### Kezayit Distinction

The resolution offered reframes the entire argument. The *kal va-chomer* does not founder on uncertainty about which punishment is worse; rather, one should set aside the punishment entirely and focus on the crime — specifically, on the minimum measure required for liability. By other *mitzvot*, one is not liable for *mita* on less than a *kezayit*. *Me'ilah*, by contrast, makes one liable even for an amount less than a *kezayit*. This is why *me'ilah* cannot be derived by *kal va-chomer* from other *mitzvot*: the other *mitzvot* are in fact more lenient (they require a *kezayit*), making them the *kal*, not the *chomer*. Therefore, a verse is genuinely necessary.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, upon receiving this explanation from Rav Chiyya bar Avin, responds warmly: *tanu'ach da'at'cha she-hinachta et da'ati* — may your mind be at ease, for you have put my mind at ease. This had been a genuinely troubling matter.

### Verse Teaches Korbanot

The verse is thus necessary precisely because without it one would have no way of knowing, via *kal va-chomer*, that the deliberate transgressor of *me'ilah* is exempt from the *asham*. The *kal va-chomer* fails because *me'ilah* is actually the more stringent case (liability on less than a *kezayit*), making it impossible to derive leniency for the deliberate transgressor from less stringent categories.

### Rabba & Rav Sheshet

This resolution, however, is undermined. Rabba and Rav Sheshet throw an axe into it — *shadu bah narga*. The problem: who exactly holds that the deliberate transgressor of *me'ilah* is liable to *mita b'yedei shamayim*? That view is attributed to Rebbi, as we shall see. But Rebbi, who derives *me'ilah*'s punishment from a *gezeirah shavah* with *terumah*, would also be bound by the *kezayit* standard of *terumah* — and if that is so, the very distinction the Gemara used (that *me'ilah* applies even below a *kezayit*) collapses entirely, taking the resolution with it.

---

## Rebbi on Me'ilah

### Who Holds Mita?

The Gemara now focuses: *man shamat lei de-amar meizid be-me'ilah be-mita?* — who is it that holds that deliberate *me'ilah* results in *mita b'yedei shamayim*? The answer emerges from a *baraita*: *meizid be-me'ilah Rebbi omer be-mita va-chachamim omrim be-azharah* — Rebbi says the deliberate transgressor is liable to death, while the Sages say he violates only a *lav*, a prohibition, without incurring death. Clearly, only Rebbi holds the position that underlies the entire prior analysis.

### Rebbi's Derivation

The Gemara then asks: *mai ta'ama de-Rebbi* — what is Rebbi's reasoning? He derives the punishment for deliberate *me'ilah* via a *gezeirah shavah* of *cheit-cheit* from *terumah*: just as *terumah* carries a penalty of *mita* (the verse *metu vo ki yechalelu'hu* and related *psukim* establish this), so too *me'ilah* carries a penalty of *mita* for the deliberate transgressor.

### The Problem

Precisely here lies the difficulty that Rabba and Rav Sheshet have raised. If Rebbi learns *me'ilah* from *terumah* via *gezeirah shavah*, then just as *terumah* requires a minimum measure of a *kezayit* for liability, so too *me'ilah* — according to Rebbi — should require a *kezayit*. The entire resolution of the *kal va-chomer* problem depended on saying that *me'ilah* is more stringent than other *mitzvot* because it applies even below a *kezayit*. But for Rebbi, who derives *me'ilah*'s law from *terumah*, the same *kezayit* standard applies. The distinction collapses, and so does the reason why a verse was deemed necessary.

### Rav Pappa's Challenge

At this point Rav Pappa raises a challenge: *mimay d'Rebbi k'rabanan svira leh* — how do we know that Rebbi holds like the *rabanan* (rather than like Abba Shaul) regarding the measure of *terumah*? The *machloket* between the *rabanan* and Abba Shaul was precisely about whether the operative criterion is size or value. Rebbi says the minimum for *me'ilah* is a *kezayit* — a size. That aligns him with the *rabanan*. But perhaps, Rav Pappa suggests, Rebbi holds like Abba Shaul, who requires a *shaveh pruta* — a monetary value — even without a *kezayit*.

### Abba Shaul Question

The force of Rav Pappa's challenge is that if Rebbi holds like Abba Shaul, then Rebbi's standard for *me'ilah* (derived from *terumah*) would be value-based rather than size-based. On that reading, the *kezayit* distinction — which was essential to the prior resolution — would not exist within Rebbi's framework, and the *kal va-chomer* problem remains unresolved even under the proposed answer.

### Pappa's Retraction Proof

The Gemara responds: but Rav Pappa himself is the one who originally said that Abba Shaul requires *tartei* — both a *kezayit* and a *pruta*. If that were correct, then even if Rebbi held like Abba Shaul, a *kezayit* would still be required, and the challenge would dissolve. The very fact that Rav Pappa poses the question — treating Abba Shaul's position as purely value-based, with no *kezayit* requirement — demonstrates that he must have retracted his original theory. *Ela shema mina hadar bei* — from this we infer that Rav Pappa reversed his earlier position.

---

## Baraita Analysis

### Intent Distinction

The Gemara now explores additional ways of explaining why the *kal va-chomer* fails — and thus why the verse is indeed necessary. A further basis for distinguishing *me'ilah* from other *mitzvot* concerns the role of intent. By other *mitzvot*, there is a meaningful difference between an act performed with intent and one performed without intent. By *me'ilah*, this distinction does not operate in the same way.

### Shabbat & Me'ilah

The classic case: regarding *Shabbat*, if one intends to take an already-detached fruit (*talush*) but by mistake takes one that is still attached (*mechubar*) — *she'eino miskaven lachtoch et hatallush ve-chatech et hamechubar* — one is exempt, because the act of severing was entirely unintentional. The two cases are distinct, and acting on the wrong one incurs no liability.

*Me'ilah* is far more demanding. If someone wanted to warm himself with a cloak of ordinary *chullin* material but inadvertently wrapped himself in the skin of an *olah* — *she'eino miskaven lehischamem begizei chullin ve-nischamem begizei olah* — he has committed *me'ilah*. The fact that he had no intention of benefiting from consecrated property affords him no protection. Because *me'ilah* makes one liable even without the requisite intention that other *mitzvot* demand, it is more stringent — and therefore the *kal va-chomer* from other *mitzvot* would not work. Hence the verse was necessary.

### Mis'asek

Rav Chama bar Yitzchak formulates this in terms of *mis'asek* — an act that is entirely incidental to one's purpose. The principle is: *lo mis'chayev bahen she'ein mis'asek ke-mis'asek* — by other *mitzvot*, one who performs an act in the manner of *mis'asek* is not liable as if he had acted fully intentionally. *Mis'asek* refers to a case where the act occurs entirely as a byproduct of doing something else: the classic example is one who is juggling knives and inadvertently performs *shechitah* on an animal that happened to be in the path, or one who is blowing a *shofar* as a musical exercise and happens to produce the requisite *kolos* on Rosh Hashanah — the action is performed with no awareness of its legal significance.

Similarly: if one intended to lift a *talush* fruit but severed the *mechubar* instead — *she'eino miskaven lehagbi'ah et hatallush ve-chatech et hamechubar* — one is exempt.

### Me'ilah Stringent

*Me'ilah* operates differently. If one reached into a vessel to retrieve an object and in doing so coated one's hand with consecrated olive oil — oil designated for *menachot*, for example — that is *me'ilah*, even though using the oil was entirely incidental to one's purpose. One wanted only to retrieve the object; one's hand passed through the oil; yet the benefit from *kodesh* property constitutes *me'ilah*. This is the quintessential *mis'asek* scenario, and yet liability attaches. *Me'ilah* therefore cannot be derived by *kal va-chomer* from other *mitzvot* in which *mis'asek* does not generate liability.

### Rav Chama's View

Rav Chama bar Yitzchak's formulation thus parallels the first explanation (focused on *kezayit*) in structure but differs in substance: rather than distinguishing the minimum measure of the transgression, it distinguishes the role of intention. In both formulations, the conclusion is the same — *me'ilah* is more stringent than other *mitzvot*, the *kal va-chomer* cannot be constructed in the way initially proposed, and therefore the explicit verse *bishgagah prat l'meizid* was indeed necessary.

---

## Terumah from Chametz

### Original Question

The Gemara now returns to an earlier topic: is it possible to separate *terumah* from *chametz* on *Pesach*? A *baraita* cited previously (on 32a) established that one cannot do so — but the question of sourcing and mechanism remained. The Gemara revisits this: *mafrish terumah ve-hichmitzah* — perhaps the produce was kosher grain at the time of separation and subsequently leavened; or alternatively, one separated *terumah* from *chametz* before *Pesach*, when chametz was still permitted. The most problematic case, however, is when one attempts to separate *chametz* as *terumah* on *Pesach* itself — in that case, *einah kedoshah*, it does not attain the status of *terumah* at all.

### Titen Lo

The source for this ruling is derived from the verse *reshit degancha tiroshcha ve-yitzharecha u-reshit gez tzonecha titen lo* — the obligation to give *terumah* to the *kohen* encompasses grain (*dagan*), wine (*tirosh*), and oil (*yitzhar*). The operative phrase is *titen lo* — you must give it *to him*, ולא לאורו — and not for his fire. The principle is that what one separates as *terumah* must constitute a full and usable gift to the *kohen*, not something that can only be burned.

### No Benefit

If *chametz terumah* on *Pesach* is separated and given to a *kohen*, the *kohen* cannot eat it (it is *chametz* on *Pesach*) and, even granting the view of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili that one may derive *hana'ah* from *chametz* on *Pesach*, the only *hana'ah* available is burning it. It is not a full giving — not a *titen lo* in the complete sense — and therefore fails to qualify as *terumah* at all.

### Rav Huna Challenge

Rav Huna berei de-Rav Yehoshua raises an objection. The rule is: *ein tormin min ha-teme'ah al ha-tehorah* — one may not separate *terumah* from *tamei* produce for *tahor* produce. Yet, if one did so inadvertently, *terumato terumah* — the separation is effective *b'dieved*. The challenge: if the same verse (*titen lo ve-lo le'oro*) applies to *terumah teme'ah* — since *terumah teme'ah* can only be burned and cannot be eaten — why does the separation work at all, even *b'dieved*?

### Terumah Teme'ah

The resolution: *lo kashya, hatam hayta lo sha'at kosher, hacha lo hayta lo sha'at kosher* — the cases differ fundamentally. *Terumah teme'ah* had a *sha'at kosher* — a moment when it was *tahor* and could have been properly separated. At that prior moment, the produce was fully within the framework of *terumah*. Even though it is now *tamei* and cannot be eaten, the fact that it once had eligibility means that the retroactive *b'dieved* separation is still recognized. *Chametz* on *Pesach*, by contrast, never had a *sha'at kosher* within the operative framework.

### No She'at Kosher

How can one arrive at a case where *chametz* genuinely never had a *sha'at kosher*? The Gemara acknowledges the apparent difficulty: the wheat grew as ordinary grain, which was certainly fit for *terumah* separation. The only way to construct a genuine case of no *sha'at kosher* is *k'gon de-achmetz bi-mechubar* — if the grain fermented while still attached to the ground (*mechubar*). *Terumah* does not apply to produce that is still *mechubar* — the obligation only arises once the grain is harvested, brought in, and the *kri* (the heap) is properly formed. If the grain became *chametz* while still *mechubar*, it was never within the scope of *terumah* obligation at any point, and thus had no *sha'at kosher* whatsoever.

### Rav Huna Disagrees

The follow-up question is natural: *aval achmetz b'talush* — but what if the grain became *chametz* only after it was harvested, when it was *talush*? At that point it was, in principle, within the *terumah* framework. Would we then say the separation works *b'dieved*, just as *terumah teme'ah* works *b'dieved*? The response is: yes, if it became *chametz* while *talush* — after it was harvested and subject to *terumah* — it would indeed have had a *sha'at kosher*, and the separation would work *b'dieved*.

Rav Huna berei de-Rav Yehoshua, however, disagrees with this conclusion and holds that even *chametz talush* does not work. His reasoning is not based on *sha'at kosher* but on a separate analysis of the word *reishit* in the verse.

### Reishit Analysis

Rav Huna's argument proceeds from the word *reishit* in the verse *reshit degancha... titen lo*. The word *reishit* — "the first" or "the beginning" — implies, by its very nature, that there is something that follows after it. One cannot have a beginning without something coming after it; the "beginning" presupposes a remainder. Applied to *terumah*: *reishit* implies that by separating the *terumah*, one creates a recognizable distinction between what was taken and what remains — *she-shiyareiha nikkarin le-Yisrael*, that the remainder should be recognizably distinct and permitted to Israel. The separation of *terumah* from *tevel* is what renders the rest of the pile permissible to eat. The *terumah* functions as the *reishit* that enables the *shiyarim*, the remainder, to be *muttar*.

### Yatzah Zo

*Yatza zo she-ein shiyareiha nikkarin* — this case is excluded. When one separates *terumah* from *chametz* on *Pesach*, the remainder does not become permitted to the Israelite who owns it. The *chametz* remains *chametz*, and the Israelite still cannot eat it. The separation accomplishes nothing by way of *hetter* for the rest of the pile. Since the defining characteristic of *reishit* — that it renders the *shiyarim* permissible — is entirely absent, this separation cannot be considered a valid *terumah* at all. On this basis, Rav Huna holds that even if the grain became *chametz* while *talush* (with what might otherwise have been a *sha'at kosher*), the separation remains invalid.

---

## Tamei Grapes Wine

### Ruling Introduced

The Gemara now presents a striking ruling transmitted by Rav Acha bar Avya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan. *Anavim she-nitme'u* — grapes that have become *tamei*. One would naturally assume that such grapes are entirely disqualified from any use in the *Beit HaMikdash*. Yet the ruling states: *darchan pachot pachot mi-kebeitzah ve-yeinan kasher le-nesachim* — if one presses them in increments of less than an egg's volume at a time, the resulting juice is *kasher* for *nesachim*, the wine libations offered on the altar. The reaction to this ruling is one of genuine surprise: how is this possible?

### Kebeitzah Limit

The ruling specifies *pachot pachot mi-kebeitzah* — less than a *kebeitzah* at each pressing — as the operative condition for validity. The Gemara adds that while *lechatchilah* only less than a *kebeitzah* is permitted, a *baraita* establishes that even *b'dieved*, if a *tamei meit* pressed exactly a *kebeitzah* of olives or grapes, *tehorim* — the result is still *tahor*. The reason only less than a *kebeitzah* is permitted *lechatchilah* is a *gezeirah* — a rabbinic precaution lest one come to press more than a *kebeitzah*, which would clearly be problematic. So the full picture: less than a *kebeitzah* is permitted *lechatchilah*; up to a *kebeitzah* is valid *b'dieved*; more than a *kebeitzah* is not acceptable under any circumstances.

### Juice Separation

To understand how this is possible at all, the Gemara articulates a conceptual distinction: *mashkin mifkad pikidi* — the juice is considered a separate, contained entity within the grape, not simply an aspect of the grape itself. The analogy is to water in a cup: the water and the cup are distinct entities, even though one contains the other. So too, the juice exists inside the grape as a separate entity. When the grape becomes *tamei*, the juice does not automatically become *tamei* along with it.

### Shiur for Tumah

This conceptual separation leads to a further point. Even if the juice were to be considered at risk, the *tamei* status of *food* (*ochel*) can only convey *tumah* to a liquid (*mashkeh*) if the food meets a minimum measure — a *kebeitzah*. If the *ochel* is less than a *kebeitzah*, it lacks the *shiur* necessary to make the liquid *tamei*. Combined with the pressing method described: the presser does not touch the juice directly; the pressing implement is made of plain wood (*pshutei klei eitz*) that is not *mekabel tumah*; and the grapes being pressed are always less than a *kebeitzah* — which means they lack the *shiur* to convey *tumah* to the juice as it emerges. Furthermore, the juice becomes susceptible to *tumah* through *hukshra* — preparation via liquid — only when it exits the grape; but by that point there is no longer sufficient *ochel* to convey *tumah* to it. The result, under this framework, is juice that is *tahor* and fit for *nesachim*.

### Rav Chisda Object

Rav Chisda is dismissive: *man tza'it lakh u-le-Rabbi Yochanan rabakh* — who is going to listen to you and to Rabbi Yochanan your teacher? This is a stark challenge, reflecting that the ruling is genuinely difficult to accept. The implicit concern: if the grape is *tamei*, how does one simply say the juice is untouched?

### Counter Challenge

A counter-challenge is then raised from the case of *terumah* berries, olives, and grapes that became *tamei* (*terumat tutin zeitim va-anavim she-nitme'u*). Of such produce the rule is that it has neither *heter achilah* — it may not be eaten, being *tamei* — nor *heter hasaka* — it cannot even serve as fuel, being too moist. The question: if the juice is indeed a separate entity that can emerge *tahor*, why not simply press the *tamei terumah* fruit in increments of less than a *kebeitzah* and thereby obtain usable *tahor* juice? The fact that we do not do this seems to imply that the juice is not considered a separate entity at all — it is regarded as part of the fruit and therefore equally *tamei*.

### Never Hukhshar

The response: *hakha be-mai askinan be-anavim she-lo hukhsharu* — the case of the Mishnah deals with grapes that were never rendered susceptible to *tumah* (*hukhshar*) in the first place. This introduces the requirement of *hukshra*: food does not become *tamei* automatically upon contact with an *av ha-tumah*; it must first be rendered susceptible through one of the seven liquids. Until food has been *mukhshar*, it is not in the *parsha* of *tumah* for food.

### Hukshra Needed

The Gemara elaborates. A person who is *tamei meit* can make other people and vessels *tamei* through contact, without any prior preparation being necessary on their part. But for *food* to become *tamei*, it must first be prepared — *mukhshar* — through contact with one of the seven liquids (*shivah mashkin*). Plain grapes that have never had any liquid on them are not *mukhshar* and thus cannot become *tamei* as *ochel* through contact with a *tamei meit*.

When, then, might the grapes become *mukhshar*? Only when the juice is pressed out, since *ve-eimat mechashrei de-chi sachatei de-hu* — they become susceptible at the moment of pressing, when the juice flows. But at that very moment, *batsir lei shiura* — the volume remaining has been compressed to less than a *kebeitzah*, and there is no longer sufficient *ochel* to convey *tumah* to the liquid. The *tumah* chain is thus broken at precisely the point where *hukshra* would have occurred.

This response also addresses why the *terumah* berry case is different: those berries *were* already *mukhshar* and *tamei*, so the juice cannot escape the *tumah* that pervades the fruit as an integrated unit. The resolution is thus that Rav Chisda's challenge from that *baraita* does not undermine Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, which is limited to a specific and carefully constructed case.

### Rava: Takala

Rava offers an alternative explanation for why the *terumah* berry case does not work — not because the juice shares the *tumah* of the fruit as an integrated whole, but as a *gezeirah*: *de-dilma ati ba de-takala* — lest it lead to a dangerous precedent. If one were permitted to press the berries and use the juice, one might reason that if the juice is acceptable, so too is the fruit itself — and then come to eat the *tamei* fruit, which is forbidden. The prohibition on using the pressed juice from *tamei terumah* berries is thus a protective *gezeirah*, not a statement about the intrinsic *tumah* of the juice.

### Abaye Counter

Abaye challenges Rava's position: *umi khaishinan le-takala* — are we really concerned about *takala*? A *baraita* explicitly permits using *terumah* oil that has become *tamei* as fuel, burning it for light. If we were genuinely concerned about *takala*, we should not permit this either — for one might reason that if the oil is usable, perhaps the olive it came from could be consumed as well.

### Kli Ma'us Solution

The response: we do indeed take *takala* seriously, and the permission to use *tamei terumah* oil or bread as fuel is only granted under conditions that prevent *takala* from materializing. *Pat zarik lei beina eitzim* — the bread is thrown into the woodpile, where it becomes dirty and disgraceful; one will not come to eat it. *Shemen shel terumah ramei lei bi-khli ma'us* — the oil is placed in a disgusting vessel; one will not come to consume it under those circumstances. The *takala* is averted by rendering the *terumah* object repugnant, so that no one would think to eat it.

The concern with the *tamei* berries is different: if one presses the juice and sees it emerge seemingly *tahor*, one may well reason that the fruit itself is fine — there is no parallel mechanism of *kli ma'us* to prevent that inference. The *gezeirah* against pressing thus stands. Rav Chisda's dismissal of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and Rava's *takala* concern together frame the parameters within which the ruling of *anavim she-nitme'u* must be understood — a carefully bounded halakhic ruling that stands, according to those who accept it (and remarkably, the Rambam *paskens* in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan), only where every element of the protective framework is in place.

---

---

# Pesachim 34

## Trumah & Chametz Issues

### Trumah Payment Review

The daf begins six lines from the bottom of 33b, at the word *gufa*. The broader sugya has been occupied with a series of interconnected discussions arising from the question of how *trumah* payment works: specifically, whether the obligation is defined by the *damim* — the monetary value of what was destroyed — or by *mida*, the replacement of the fruit itself in terms of quantity. This question connects directly to the case of *chametz b'Pesach*: if the item is essentially worthless, does one return it at all? That question led the *gemara* into a debate among *tannaim* about whether the threshold for payment is measured by a *kezayit* or a *perutah*, which appears to bear directly on the underlying issue.

### Chametz B'Pesach

The *gemara* then moved to the question of whether one can be *mafrish trumah* from *chametz*, and the answer was no, because one cannot separate *trumah* from something that is *assur b'hana'ah* — it gives the *kohen* nothing of value and does not improve the remainder. This, in turn, opened the broader question of *trumah temei'ah* and what use can be made of it.

### Tamei Grapes Extraction

The discussion arrives at the case of *tamei* grapes: is there a way to press them such that the juice that emerges is not *tamei*? This seems directly relevant because in the back-and-forth over whether *trumah* without value creates an obligation, the example of *tamei trumah* arose, and with it the question of why one cannot simply press the grapes in a manner that keeps the juice pure. One answer offered by the *gemara* is that even if there exists a technically acceptable method of extraction, the concern of *atei l'yidei takalah* prevents it — we do not permit the method because one might come to eat the *tamei* grapes in the process.

---

## Tamei Terumah & Takalah

### Bread & Oil as Fuel

The *gemara* now cites the *gufa* of the ruling: *madlikin b'pas u'b'shemen shel trumah she'nitme'it* — one may use *tamei* bread or *tamei* oil of *trumah* as fuel. This is the standard disposition of *trumah teme'iah*: a *kohen* is permitted to burn it and derive benefit from it in the course of its destruction. As soon as bread is thrown into the fire it becomes inedible immediately, so there is no concern that one will come to eat it. Similarly, oil can be placed in a disgusting vessel, ensuring that no one would want to consume it after the process has begun.

### Abaye & Rava on Grain

Both Abaye, transmitting in the name of Chizkiyah, and Rava, transmitting from the school of Rav Yitzchak bar Marta, report the following ruling of Rav Huna: *lo shanu ela pat* — this permission applies only to bread. But by grain — *chiti*, wheat kernels — one may not do so, *shema yavo lidei takalah*, lest one come to eat from it. The same principle that prevents pressing *tamei* grapes applies here: if the grain does not immediately become disgusting in the course of being burned, we are concerned one might eat from it.

### Rabbi Yochanan's View

Rabbi Yochanan, however, permits even grain: *afilu chiti*. The *gemara* immediately questions this: should we not be concerned about *takalah*? Is Rabbi Yochanan not bothered by this principle?

### Rav Assi: Boiled Grain

The *gemara* resolves the question by citing Rav Assi's formulation from the top of 34a: *b'shlikta u'mista* — Rabbi Yochanan's permissive ruling refers specifically to grain that has already been boiled and is therefore revolting. Once boiled, the grain is soft and unappetizing, and as soon as it is thrown into the fire it will become disgusting instantly, just like bread. The concern of *takalah* is simply absent in this circumstance. Had the grain not been boiled — had it remained hard and palatable — Rabbi Yochanan would agree that it would be forbidden.

The *gemara* here also revisits Rabbi Yochanan's earlier statement about *tamei* grapes — the ruling that one may press them a little at a time to produce juice that is *kasher* for *nesachim*. The *gemara* clarifies that this earlier statement was not addressing *trumah* grapes at all; it concerned ordinary *tamei* produce where the fruit itself is not *trumah*. In the *trumah* scenario, even if the technical method would keep the juice pure, *atei l'yidei takalah* prevents it.

---

## Abba Shaul's Terumah

### Abba Shaul & Firewood

The *gemara* asks: where was the ruling of Rav Ashi — that the *takalah* concern is resolved when the grain is boiled — actually stated? It was stated in connection with the following: Rav Avin bar Rav Acha, in the name of Rav Yitzchak Abba, citing Rav Yitzchak the elder, reports that Abba Shaul was the dough-maker in the household of Rebbi. They would heat the water for his baking using the grain of *trumah teme'iah* as firewood. Rashi notes that *trumah teme'iah* sold for a very low market price, since few could make use of it, and so it was purchased cheaply for use as firewood — which is entirely permitted, as burning *trumah teme'iah* and deriving benefit from it in the course of its destruction is the standard permitted use.

Rashi adds that part of the *chiddush* is that Rebbi was *ochel chullin b'taharah* — he ate *chulin* in a state of ritual purity — yet he was not concerned that the handlers might inadvertently touch the *tamei* grain below and thereby contaminate things above. Tosafot, however, raises the issue from other *gemaros* that only *kohanim* may derive benefit from burning *trumah teme'iah*, just as only *kohanim* may eat *trumah*. According to Tosafot, then, one may have to say that the bread being baked from this process was intended to feed the *kohanim* of Rebbi's household.

### Takalah Concern Here

The *gemara* raises the obvious question: why is Abba Shaul permitted to do this at all? *Neichosh shema yavo lidei takalah* — perhaps in the process of throwing grain down to serve as firewood one might pop a kernel in one's mouth? This is precisely the concern that Rav Huna articulated: by grain, unlike bread, the *takalah* problem is real.

### Rav Ashi's Resolution

Rav Ashi resolves it: *b'shlikta d'mista* — the grain had already been boiled and was therefore disgusting. Once boiled grain is thrown into the fire it is revolting, and no one would think to eat it. The *takalah* concern therefore does not apply. The *gemara* at this point is working with the assumption that the principle of *shema yavo lidei takalah* is universally accepted — it was not merely one optional answer among several, but a genuine operative rule that requires an answer whenever the circumstances seem to trigger it.

---

## Learning Terumos Dispute

### Rava bar Masnah's Q

The *gemara* now introduces a new narrative. Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chanina bar Avin — apparently two brothers — were studying the tractate *Terumos* in the house of Rava. Rava bar Masnah encountered them and asked what *chiddushim* they had encountered in their learning. Sensing that he had a specific difficulty in mind, they turned the question around: what was bothering him? What issues did he have with *Terumos*?

### Planted Terumah Mishnah

He responded by citing a *mishnah* in *Terumos*: *shtilei Terumos she'nitme'u* — plantings of *trumah* that had become *tamei*. The case is: one had *trumah* produce — grain, onions, or the like — which became *tamei*. Rather than burn it, one chose to plant it in the ground. The *mishnah* rules that *tehorim mil'tamei* — once planted, the produce ceases to be *tamei*. This follows from the principle that things attached to the ground, or more precisely things that take root and grow within the ground, lose their *tumah*. However, the *mishnah* continues: *asurin mil'echol* — they remain forbidden to eat.

### Rava's Problem

This split ruling is puzzling. The reason the produce could not be eaten was that it was *trumah teme'iah*. If the *tumah* is removed by planting, why does the prohibition to eat remain? This is what troubled Rava bar Masnah, and he asked whether they had come up with a satisfactory explanation.

---

## Removing Tumah, Keeping…

### Rabbah: Asurin L'Zarim

They reported that Rabbah had resolved the *mishnah* as follows: *mai asurin? asurin l'zarim* — what does it mean they are forbidden? It means they are forbidden to non-*kohanim*. In other words, the *mishnah* is not saying that the *kohanim* themselves cannot eat it; rather, it is simply reaffirming that the produce retains its *trumah* status. Planting removes the *tumah* but does not remove the *kedushah* of *trumah*.

### Gidulei Terumah

This prompts the obvious question: if that is the *chiddush*, what is novel about it? Rava bar Masnah said precisely this: *mai kamashma lan* — what is the *mishnah* teaching us? And the response was: *gidulei Terumah Terumah* — things that grow from *trumah* retain the status of *trumah*. The *mishnah* is not merely saying that planting does not change the status of the planted item itself; it goes further and teaches that the growth that emerges from a *trumah* seed also carries *trumah* status. If one plants a grain of *trumah* and a full stalk of wheat grows from it, that wheat is *trumah*.

Rava bar Masnah pushes back: but we already know this — *tanina*, we have also learned that *gidulei Terumah Terumah* in another *mishnah*. So this is not a *chiddush* either.

### Gidulei Gidulin & Seeds

Perhaps the *chiddush* is *gidulei gidulin* — a second generation. According to Tosafot, this means: one plants a *trumah* grain, the resulting stalk grows, one takes a kernel from that stalk and plants it again, and the wheat that grows from that second planting is also *trumah*. According to Rashi, the scenario is slightly different — an onion bulb is planted and additional bulbs cluster around it as an outgrowth, and those secondary bulbs are the *gidulei gidulin*.

The *gemara* specifies that this rule applies *b'davar she'ein zar'o kalah* — in cases where the original seed is not destroyed in the course of growth. When a wheat grain is planted, the original kernel ceases to exist as it transforms into the stalk; there is nothing left. But when an onion bulb is planted, the original bulb remains present throughout as the additional bulbs develop. In the latter case, where the original remains present, even a second-generation growth retains *trumah* status.

Rava bar Masnah says this too is already known — *ha nami tanina* — because the *mishnah* elsewhere teaches a parallel rule about *tevel*.

### Tevel vs. Terumah

The *mishnah* states regarding *tevel* — produce from which *terumos u'maasros* have not yet been separated: *ha'tevel gidulav mutarin b'davar she'zar'o kalah* — the growth of *tevel* is permitted when the original seed has been destroyed. Rashi explains why this should matter at all: the original grain of *tevel* had already been threshed and processed, and once *gemar melachah* was performed on it, one may not even eat from it *achilas arai* — casually, before formal separation. But new grain that grows and has not undergone *gemar melachah* may be eaten casually. If the new growth is considered a continuation of the original *tevel*, it cannot be eaten *achilas arai*; if it is considered an entirely new entity, it may be. By *tevel*, the *gemara* is lenient, and the growth is treated as new.

However, the *mishnah* continues: *aval b'davar she'ein zar'o kalah* — but when the original seed is not destroyed, *afilu gidulei gidulim assurim b'achilah* — even second-generation growth is forbidden. This is a stringency even by *tevel*. Certainly by *trumah* the rule would be at least as strict. This comparison actually suggests that the entire restriction of *gidulei trumah* is rabbinic in origin, since the same logic of continuation versus new growth would apply equally to both — and yet the *halachah* treats them differently without an obvious *d'oraita* basis for the distinction.

In sum, Rava bar Masnah's point stands: all of this is already known from other *mishnayos*, and the *mishnah* in *Terumos* adds nothing new. The two brothers had no response and admitted he had stumped them. They asked if he himself had heard a good explanation. He said: here is what Rav Sheshet says.

---

## Rav Sheshet & Hesech

### Asurin L'Kohanim

Rav Sheshet offers a fundamentally different reading of the *mishnah*: *mai asurin? asurin l'kohanim* — what does it mean they are forbidden? It means they are forbidden even to *kohanim*. The *mishnah* is saying exactly what it sounds like: the planting removes the *tumah*, and yet even *kohanim* cannot eat the produce. The first answer — that *asurin* merely means *asurin l'zarim*, forbidden to non-*kohanim* — collapses the *mishnah*'s statement into something already known. Rav Sheshet insists the *mishnah* is saying something genuinely striking: despite the *tumah* being gone, a *kohen* still cannot eat it.

### Hesech Hadaat Psul

Why not? *Ho'il ve'ifsalu lehu b'hesech hada'as* — because the produce has become *pasul* not through *tumah* but through *hesech hada'as*, lack of attention. *Kohanim* are commanded to guard their *trumah* from becoming *tamei* — *mishmeret terumati*. Once the produce became *tamei*, they ceased paying attention to it. They reasoned: it is already *tamei*, there is nothing left to protect. This neglect itself constitutes an independent *psul* called *hesech hada'as*. Even after the *tumah* is removed by planting, the *psul* of *hesech hada'as* remains, because it is not a *psul* that depends on the *tumah* — it is its own category of invalidity.

This is a striking claim.
