One would naturally assume that the entire point of guarding *trumah* is to prevent *tumah*, and so once *tumah* is addressed, there is nothing left for *hesech hada'as* to do. Rav Sheshet's position is that *hesech hada'as* has become an independent *psul* in its own right.

---

## Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish

### Yochanan: Psul Tumah

The *gemara* immediately notes that this answer only works according to one view in an established dispute. *Hanicha l'man d'amar hesech hada'as psul hagoof havei* — this works if *hesech hada'as* is an intrinsic invalidity, independent of whether *tumah* actually occurred. But *ela l'man d'amar hesech hada'as psul tumah havei* — if *hesech hada'as* is merely a *tumah* concern, then once the *tumah* is removed by planting, any prior *hesech hada'as* dissolves along with it, and the produce should be permitted.

The *gemara* identifies this as an explicit dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says *psul tumah havei* — it is a *tumah*-type concern. The entire problem of *hesech hada'as* is that inattention raises the possibility that the produce became *tamei*; it is not an independent category. *She'im yavo Eliyahu v'yitaharena, shomin lo* — if Eliyahu the Prophet were to come and establish with certainty that nothing had in fact happened to the produce during the period of inattention, we would accept his testimony, the produce would be declared *tahor*, and there would be no problem.

### Reish Lakish: Psul Hagoof

Reish Lakish disagrees: *psul hagoof havei* — *hesech hada'as* is an intrinsic invalidity, entirely independent of whether *tumah* occurred. *She'im yavo Eliyahu v'yitaharena, ein shomin lo* — even if Eliyahu were to come and testify that nothing happened, we would not accept it. The *kohen* was supposed to pay attention, and the failure to pay attention is itself the problem — regardless of outcome. According to Reish Lakish, the *mishnah* about planted *trumah* is perfectly intelligible: planting it is like Eliyahu coming to declare it *tahor*, but that makes no difference, because *hesech hada'as* remains as an independent *psul* even when the *tumah* itself has been removed.

### Bird Offerings Evidence

Rabbi Yochanan challenged Reish Lakish with a *mishnah*. Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka taught: there was a small funnel-like recess (*lul*) between the ramp and the altar, on the western side of the ramp, in the southwest corner where *kohanim* would perform *chatas ha'of* — bird sin-offerings. When a bird offering became invalid, it would be placed in this recess. *V'ta'avor tzuratan* — one would wait until its appearance passed over, a term meaning that nightfall would arrive and the offering would become *pasul* as *notar* (leftover sacrifice). It would then be taken out to *beit hasreifah* to be burned.

The assumption of the *gemara* is that the only invalidity that is not sufficient to permit immediate burning — and therefore requires waiting until nightfall — is *hesech hada'as*. If something has a full intrinsic *psul*, the *mishnah* elsewhere rules *yisaref miyad* — burn it immediately. The only reason to wait for *notar* to develop is that the current *psul* is not intrinsic enough. And the only *psul* that is not intrinsic but prevents bringing the offering is *hesech hada'as* — we are uncertain whether it became *tamei*, cannot bring it, but also cannot burn it. So we wait for nightfall, and then the *psul* becomes intrinsic through *linah* (remaining overnight), and we burn it.

Rabbi Yochanan's argument: if *hesech hada'as* were an intrinsic *psul* as Reish Lakish maintains, one should be able to burn the bird immediately upon the *hesech hada'as* occurring, without waiting for nightfall. The fact that one must wait shows that *hesech hada'as* is not intrinsic — it is merely a *tumah* concern.

### Notar & Linah

Tosafot presses a sharper version of this argument: even if we granted that the invalidity in the bird case arose from an external cause such as the blood spilling (*dam*) or the *ba'alim* dying, once the bird is placed in the recess and the *kohen* walks away, *hesech hada'as* has occurred. If *hesech hada'as* were an intrinsic *psul*, one could turn around immediately and burn the bird right then, without needing to wait for nightfall. The fact that the procedure requires waiting until morning shows that *hesech hada'as* alone is never sufficient to permit immediate burning.

Reish Lakish responds: *hai tanna tanna devei Rabba bar Avuha hu* — the author of this *mishnah* is the *tanna* from the school of Rabba bar Avuha, who holds that *even* intrinsically invalid offerings require *ibur tzurah* — one must wait for nightfall before burning them. According to this *tanna*, the rule of *yisaref miyad* for intrinsic *psul* does not apply; everything requires waiting. The argument would only work if one accepted the majority position that intrinsic *psul* permits immediate burning. Reish Lakish concedes that according to that majority position, the argument would indeed hold, but the *mishnah* cited here follows a different school.

---

## Korban Psul Types

### Psul B'Gufo Rule

The *gemara* now articulates the general *mishnah* framework for the two categories of invalidity. *Zeh haklal: kol shepsulo b'gufo, yisaref miyad* — this is the rule: anything whose invalidity is intrinsic — located in the body of the *korban* itself — is burned immediately. No waiting, no *ibur tzurah*; the status is clear, and the burning proceeds at once.

### Dam & Baalim

By contrast, *v'dam u'va'alim ta'avor tzuratan v'yotzin l'veit hasreifah* — if the problem was with the blood or with the owners, one must wait for the appearance to pass before burning. These are cases where the invalidity is external to the meat itself. With *dam*, the blood became *tamei* or was spilled, so *zerikat hadam* cannot be performed, and the meat cannot be eaten — but nothing happened to the meat. With *ba'alim*, the situation is similar: the owner died, for instance in the case of a *chatas* where the owner's death terminates the offering — but again the meat itself is intact. In these cases, the meat cannot be eaten and cannot be burned yet, because its own *psul* is not intrinsic. One waits until the following morning, when the meat becomes *notar*, acquires an intrinsic *psul*, and can then be burned.

This framework is the backdrop for the debate about *hesech hada'as*: Rabbi Yochanan argues that *hesech hada'as* belongs in the second category — external, *tumah*-related — which is why it requires waiting. Reish Lakish's position, that it is *psul hagoof*, would require placing it in the first category and burning immediately, which the *mishnah*'s procedure does not support.

---

## Tamei Meat & Zrika

### Rabbi Eliezer: Perform

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita* raising the related question of *zerikat hadam* when the meat is invalid. The *baraita* states: if the meat became *tamei*, or became otherwise invalid, or was taken outside the *kla'im* (the Temple precincts, for *kodshei kodashim* that may only be eaten on the Temple grounds), what does one do about *zerikat hadam*? The meat can no longer be eaten; should one still perform the blood-sprinkling?

Rabbi Eliezer says: *yizrok* — yes, perform *zerikat hadam* even without valid meat.

### Rabbi Yehoshua: Don't Do

Rabbi Yehoshua says: *lo yizrok* — do not perform it. Nevertheless, *umodi Rabbi Yehoshua she'im zarak hurtzah* — Rabbi Yehoshua concedes that if one did perform *zerikat hadam* in this situation, the *korban* is accepted *b'dieved*.

### Tzitz Atonement

Rabbi Yochanan uses this passage in his argument against Reish Lakish. The *baraita* lists three scenarios making the meat invalid: *nitma*, it became *tamei*; *yatza chutz laklaim*, it left the Temple precincts; and *nifsal*, it became *pasul*. The third scenario is the crux. Rabbi Yochanan argues: *nifsal* presumably refers to the *psul* of *hesech hada'as*, and Rabbi Yehoshua concedes that *b'dieved* the *korban* is accepted. Why? Because the *tzitz*, the golden plate worn by the *Kohen Gadol*, atones for *tumah* problems — *nosei avon hakodashim*. The *Kohen Gadol*'s wearing of the *tzitz* retroactively validates *kodashim* that were compromised by *tumah*. This makes sense if *hesech hada'as* is purely a *tumah* concern — the *tzitz* covers it *b'dieved*. But if *hesech hada'as* were an intrinsic *psul*, why should the *tzitz* help? The *tzitz* atones for *tumah*, not for intrinsic invalidity.

Reish Lakish responds: *mai nifsal? nifsal b'tvul yom* — when the *baraita* says *nifsal*, it does not mean *hesech hada'as* at all. It means the meat was touched by a *tvul yom* — someone who had immersed in a *mikvah* but was awaiting nightfall to complete their purification. This is an extremely low level of *tumah*, insufficient to transmit further *tumah* in most cases but sufficient to disqualify *kodashim*. This is technically a variation of *tumah* — *terei gavnei tamei*, two types of *tumah* — and therefore the *tzitz* covers it *b'dieved*. Reish Lakish thus maintains that *hesech hada'as* never appears in this *baraita* at all.

The *gemara* notes that while it is somewhat redundant to list both *nitma* and *nifsal b'tvul yom* since both are *tumah*, the *mishnah* often lists multiple variations of the same category. The *b'dieved* rule regarding *chutz laklaim* — which is not a *tumah* problem — is addressed by both Rashi and Tosafot as derived from a separate source establishing that this external invalidity also falls under the *tzitz*'s protective reach in some manner.

The *gemara* concludes this section by noting that all the evidence marshaled favors Rabbi Yochanan's position that *hesech hada'as* is merely a *tumah* concern, not an intrinsic *psul*. Reish Lakish's position, while conceptually striking, finds no clear support in the sources. And this returns us to the original problem: if *hesech hada'as* is only a *tumah* concern, then planting *tamei trumah* should restore its permitted status fully, and the *mishnah*'s ruling that the planted produce remains *assur* is left unexplained.

---

## Water Sanctification Pro…

### Mei Chag Hashaka

When Ravin went up to Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted this entire unresolved discussion to Rabbi Yirmeya. Rabbi Yirmeya responded sharply: *Bavla'ei tipshai* — foolish Babylonians. Because you dwell in a dark land (*ar'a d'chashoka*), you transmit discussions that lack light. You tried to explain this *mishnah* without having the key piece of information, so you invented explanations. Rashi makes the point explicit: when one does not know the true reason for something, one constructs a reason from one's own reasoning. These answers — that it is still *trumah*, that it is *hesech hada'as* — were improvised because the crucial teaching of Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yoshia had not reached Babylonia.

The teaching is this: *mei chag she'nitme'u* — the water used for *nisuch hamayim* on *Sukkot* that became *tamei*. Suppose it is *Shabbat* and new water cannot be drawn. The only recourse is *hashaka* — literally "kissing" — a process that works specifically for liquids: if *tamei* water is placed in a vessel and that vessel is submerged in the *mikvah* so that the waterline of the vessel's opening is level with and effectively merges into the *mikvah* water, the *tamei* water becomes part of the *mikvah* and loses its *tumah*. This process is called *zri'ah* in the *gemara*'s idiom, by analogy to planting in the ground — both involve the *tamei* item becoming absorbed into something that is inherently *tahor*.

### Sanctify Then Hashaka

*Hishikun v'achar kach hikdishan, tehorin* — if one first performed the *hashaka* and then sanctified the water for *nisuch hamayim*, the water is *tahor* and valid. The process worked.

### Hashaka Then Sanctify

*Hikdishan v'achar kach hishikun, tme'in* — but if one first sanctified the water and then performed the *hashaka*, the water remains *tamei* and is not valid.

### Ein Zri'ah L'Hekdesh

The question is obvious: in both cases the exact same physical process was performed. Why should the order of sanctification relative to *hashaka* make any difference? The answer Reish Lakish derives: *ein zri'ah l'hekdesh* — planting, or its liquid analog *hashaka*, does not work for *kodesh*. Once something has been sanctified and then becomes *tamei*, the process of *zri'ah* cannot restore it. The underlying principle is: when a mundane item becomes *tamei*, its status is simply a neutral condition to be rectified. Remove the *tumah* and you return to square one. But when a *kodesh* item becomes *tamei*, the holiness itself has been violated. To then run a purification process and have the item return to its prior *kodesh* status involves something the *halachah* will not allow. Once *kodesh* has been violated, it remains compromised. *Ein zri'ah l'hekdesh*.

---

## Terumah Like Kodesh

### Terumah Zri'ah

This principle now provides the long-sought explanation for the *mishnah* about planted *tamei trumah*. The parallel is direct: *hacha nami ein zri'ah l'trumah* — just as *zri'ah* does not restore *kodesh* to its pre-violation status, so too *zri'ah* does not restore *trumah* to the status of *trumah tehorah*. The produce is *trumah*, it became *tamei*, the *kedushah* of *trumah* was violated. Planting it in the ground may technically remove the *tumah* in the sense that it will no longer transmit *tumah* to other items, but it does not undo the violation of its sacred status.

### Zri'ah Effect Limited

This is the *pshat* of the *mishnah*: *tehorim mil'tamei* — yes, planting makes it *tahor* in the sense that it will not render other things *tamei*; *asurin mil'echol* — but it remains forbidden to eat, because the *trumah* status has been irrevocably compromised. There is no need to invoke *gidulei trumah*, no need to invoke *hesech hada'as*. The simple explanation is: once *trumah* becomes *tamei*, planting cannot restore its usable status, because *ein zri'ah l'trumah* just as *ein zri'ah l'hekdesh*. And had the Babylonians possessed this teaching of Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yoshia, they would never have needed to construct the other explanations.

The *gemara* continues with Abaye pressing further. He asked Rav Dimi: does this principle — that *zri'ah* does not work once something is sanctified — apply when the sanctification was performed merely *b'peh*, verbally, before the item was placed in a *kli sharet*? Or does it apply only once the item has been formally sanctified through a vessel? This is a question specific to the world of *korbanos* and the *Beit Hamikdash*, where sanctification of liquids and produce becomes fully operative only when placed in a *kli sharet*. Perhaps prior to that stage, verbal sanctification alone does not give the item sufficient status to trigger the rule of *ein zri'ah*.

Rav Dimi replied: *zu lo shamati, kiyotzei vah shamati* — I have not heard a ruling specifically on that point, but I have heard something analogous.

---

## Tamei Grapes Pressing

### Grapes Before Sanctify

Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *anavim she'nitme'u* — grapes that became *tamei*. *Drachan v'achar kach hikdishan, tehorim* — if one pressed them and then sanctified the resulting wine, they are *tahor*. This is the connection back to the original discussion of *tamei* grapes. The ruling mirrors the water case exactly: press first, sanctify afterward, and the product is valid.

### Sanctify Before Press

*Hikdishan v'achar kach drachan, tme'im* — but if one sanctified the grapes first and then pressed them, the resulting juice is *tamei*. Same reasoning applies: once the grapes have been sanctified, they have *kodesh* status, and the *zri'ah*-like process of pressing — which under ordinary circumstances would yield juice that is not *tamei* — no longer works, because *ein zri'ah l'hekdesh*.

Rav Yosef challenges this reading. He questions whether Rabbi Yochanan's statement about grapes involves *Beit Hamikdash* sanctification at all: *hacha b'anavim shel trumah askinan* — perhaps the entire case concerns *trumah* grapes, not *hekdesh*. And by *trumah*, verbal sanctification is the only mode — it is the full and complete sanctification, equivalent to the *kli sharet* stage in the *Beit Hamikdash*. If so, the grape case teaches nothing new about whether verbal-only sanctification in the *Beit Hamikdash* context triggers the restriction. It only confirms what was already established about *trumah*, where verbal sanctification is the operative act. The question about *beit hamikdash* and *kdushat peh* specifically therefore remains open.

### Pressing Kezayit Limit

The *gemara* raises a further question: when Rabbi Yochanan permitted pressing *tamei* grapes and yielding *tahor* juice, did he mean pressing without restriction? *Dorchan v'afilu tuva* — does he permit pressing even a large amount?

The *gemara* answers: *umi amar Rabbi Yochanan hachi?* — but did Rabbi Yochanan not himself say elsewhere that *tamei* grapes can be pressed to yield *tahor* juice only if one presses *pachot pachot mi-kabi'tzah* — less than the volume of a *kezayit* at a time? This is the statement that connects back to the very beginning of the daf's discussion, and it is precisely why this entire extended passage was developed — to arrive at this statement of Rabbi Yochanan, that *anavim she'nitme'u* can be pressed to yield *tahor* juice if one presses less than a *kezayit* at a time.

The *gemara* offers two possible reconciliations. The first is the straightforward one: *ibayit eima hacha nami pachot pachot mi-kabi'tzah* — the statement here that permits pressing also assumes the rule of less than a *kezayit* at a time, and the two rulings are consistent.

The second resolution is more technical: *hatam denagu lehu b'rishon d'havu lehu inhu sheni, hacha denagu b'sheni d'havu lehu shelishi* — in the case there, the grapes were touched by a *rishon l'tumah*, making the grapes themselves *sheni*; here, the grapes were touched by a *sheni*, making the resulting juice only *shelishi*. The difference in the degree of *tumah* involved may explain why different rules apply in the two scenarios. The full elaboration of this second resolution, however, is left for the following daf.

---

---

# Pesachim 35

## Tamei Grapes & Sanctity

### Tamei Grapes Overview

Our discussion picks up at the very bottom of 34b, where we need a few lines to wrap up the previous sugya before proceeding to the new chapter. By way of reminder: the Gemara had been building toward a statement of Rabbi Yochanan that if one has *tamei* grapes, it is possible to extract the grape juice in a way that does not render the juice *tamei* — by pressing less than a *kebeitzah* at any given moment, so that at no point does sufficient mass exist to transfer *tumah* to the liquid. An entire daf had been devoted to the buildup toward that ruling.

The other central discussion of 34b concerned a Mishnah teaching that if one plants *tamei terumah*, the *tumah* departs but the *terumah* status remains problematic. The difficulty is obvious: if the *tumah* is gone, why should the *terumah* remain an issue? The Gemara offered several answers, ultimately settling on a teaching attributed to Reish Lakish — or presented as something known in Eretz Yisrael but not in Bavel — that we maintain different standards for holy items and non-holy items. For non-holy items, the principle of *zreia* applies: plant it in the ground and the *tumah* departs, or immerse it in a *mikveh* (the same conceptual language is used), and similarly the *tumah* is removed. But if the item was holy and became *tamei*, this "trick" does not apply. Hence, *terumah*, which possesses sanctity, does not shed its problematic status merely through planting, even though the *tumah* technically departs for other purposes.

### Zreia & Mikveh Tricks

This same distinction — that certain purification mechanisms do not apply to sanctified items — was stated regarding water designated for *nisuch hamayim*: once such water became *tamei* after being sanctified, it cannot be immersed in a *mikveh* to become *tahor*. The principle, then, is that the "tricks" which work for ordinary *chulin* do not function for items possessing sanctity.

### Nisuch Hamayim Status

The question now before the Gemara is whether this elevated status — which prevents the use of such purification mechanisms — applies only to items at the highest level of *kedushah*, such as water that has been placed into a *kli sharet*, or whether it extends even to items that have been sanctified verbally but not yet placed in a *kli sharet*, which represents a lower level of *kedushah*.

### Oral vs Vessel Sanctity

The Gemara pursues this question by examining what exactly was sanctified and at what level. Items designated for *korbanot* that have been sanctified verbally but not yet placed in a *kli sharet* have not attained their full level of *kedushah*. Would we still say that even such items are treated with the special stringency that bars these purification tricks?

### Rabbi Yochanan Grapes

To address this, the Gemara introduces a statement of Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: if grapes that were *tamei* were pressed *first* and then sanctified, the resulting juice is *tahor*. But if they were sanctified first and then pressed, the juice is *tamei*. The Gemara notes that these grapes must be *kedushat peh* — sanctified only verbally, not yet through a *kli sharet* — and yet the Rabbis maintained the stringency. This would suggest that even oral sanctification suffices to trigger the special restrictions.

However, Rav Yosef objects: when Rabbi Yochanan spoke of grapes that were sanctified, he was not referring to grapes designated for altar wine. Rather, he was referring to grapes of *terumah* — and by *terumah*, the only mode of sanctification is verbal, which is already the *highest* available level of *kedushah* for *terumah*. Hence we do not allow tricks to undo *tumah* once *terumah* has been sanctified. But for items designated for the altar that have not yet been placed in a *kli sharet* — perhaps even there we would not extend the stringency. The question thus remains unresolved at that level.

### Kebeitzah & Tumah Levels

The Gemara then turns back to Rabbi Yochanan's statement that one may press grapes with the juice remaining *tahor*, and asks: did he not limit this to doing less than a *kebeitzah* at any moment? How can the earlier statement speak without such a qualification? The Gemara offers two resolutions. The first: here too the rule is that one must press less than a *kebeitzah* at any time. The second resolution is more illuminating: when Rabbi Yochanan said that one must press less than a *kebeitzah* at a time, that was addressing a situation where the grapes had touched a *rishon* and were therefore a *sheni*. A *sheni* that contacts liquid elevates that liquid to *rishon* — hence the need for caution. But in the other statement, where the grapes had touched only a *sheni* and were therefore a *shlishi*, if those grapes are unsanctified *chulin*, the liquid they produce cannot be elevated beyond a *sheni* even in the worst case, and in fact non-sanctified food cannot become a *shlishi* at all. So the concern about the juice is entirely absent, and the distinction between pressing before and after sanctification has nothing to do with the *kebeitzah* trick — rather, it turns on the much simpler point that unsanctified *shlishi* grapes cannot render liquid problematic at all, whereas once sanctified, by *kodshim* one can go all the way to *revi'i*, so the entire calculus changes.

### Rava's Comparisons

Rava then offers a series of comparisons to demonstrate that we regularly find the Torah imposing heightened standards on *kodesh* items — and that this principle therefore supports the ruling that such purification tricks are unavailable once an item is sanctified.

His first comparison involves the *parah adumah*: the verse states that live spring water must be placed into the vessel (*el keli*), indicating that the water must be drawn directly into the mixing vessel. Yet another verse uses language suggesting the water was already drawn and then placed. Rava resolves the tension by noting that the requirement to draw directly into the vessel is a *ma'alah* — a special stringency — imposed because of the item's sanctified character.

Rav Shimi bar Ashi adduces another comparison: one who immerses in a *mikveh* while in a state of *tumah* becomes *tahor* at nightfall for the purpose of *terumah*, but remains unfit to eat *kodshim* until the following morning and the bringing of a *korban*. Why, if one is already *tahor*? The answer again is *ma'alah* — the Torah imposes a stricter standard for *kodshim* than for *terumah*.

Rav Ashi adds yet another comparison: the verse's use of *ve-habasar* (and the meat) is expounded to include *etzim* and *levonah* — wood and frankincense — within the category of things that can receive *tumah* when sanctified, even though ordinarily *tumah* does not adhere to wood or incense. This is possible, the Gemara concludes, because *ma'alah* — *tumah* adheres more strongly to sanctified items.

These comparisons are admittedly loose. They range from the question of whether *zreia* removes *tumah* from *terumah*, to whether a *kebeitzah* trick works, to whether a *korban* is needed to complete *tahara*, to whether wood can receive *tumah*. The Gemara is drawing broad analogical support for the general proposition that *kodesh* items operate under heightened rules — and that this principle underlies the various restrictions under discussion. With that, the lengthy excursus on *tumah*, *terumah*, and the related topics that arose from a Mishnah discussing the eating of *chametz terumah* on Pesach comes to a close.

---

## Transition to Matzah

### Topic Shift

We now encounter a radical shift in the tractate. Until this point — for the first thirty-odd pages — the discussion has centered almost entirely on the *issur* of owning *chametz*: the obligation of *bedikah*, the prohibition of owning *chametz* from *chatzot* onward, the requirement to destroy *chametz* and by what method, the time from which eating is forbidden, and the status of *chametz she-avar alav ha-Pesach*. Even the discussions about a non-Jew who owns *chametz* and the permissibility of benefit after Pesach were all about ownership of *chametz*. The entire first section of the tractate has revolved around that theme.

Now we shift — and it is a very radical shift — to the positive *mitzvot* of Pesach: the obligations of *matzah* and *maror*. We will return to *chametz* later, but for now a new chapter begins.

### Mishnah Grains

The Mishnah states: *Elu devarim she-adam yotzei bahen yedei chovato be-Pesach* — these are the things with which one fulfills his obligation on Pesach. With *chitim* (wheat), with *se'orim* (barley), with *kusmin*, with *shifon*, and with *shibolet shual*. One may also fulfill the obligation using *demai*, and with *maaser rishon* from which *terumah* has been taken, and with *maaser sheni* and *hekdesh* that have been redeemed. *Kohanim* may use *challah* and *terumah* for their *matzah*. One does not fulfill the obligation with *tevel*, with *maaser rishon* from which *terumah* has not been taken, or with *maaser sheni* and *hekdesh* that have not been properly redeemed.

---

## Five Grains Identified

### Five Species Listed

The Gemara immediately explains the relationship among these five grains. *Kusmin*, it says, is *min chitin* — a type of wheat. *Shibolet shual* and *shifon* are *min se'orim* — types of barley. The Gemara also provides Aramaic equivalents: *kusmin* is called *gulba*, *shifon* is *dishra*, and *shibolet shual* is *shivile ta'ala* — literally "fox-paths," a direct rendering of the Hebrew *shibolet shual*, evoking the image of the rows along a fox's tail.

### Rashi Identification

The standard translations given for these three secondary grains, largely following Rashi, are: *kusmin* as spelt, *shifon* as rye, and *shibolet shual* as oats. These are the identifications that have shaped traditional practice and popular understanding for centuries.

However, a closer examination reveals that these identifications are not without difficulty.

### Felix's Identification

Dr. Yehuda Felix, the author of the comprehensive study of flora and fauna in the Mishnah, subjects these identifications to modern botanical analysis, with significantly different conclusions. Regarding *shifon*, which Rashi translates as rye (*sigla*), Dr. Felix notes that rye was unknown in the land of Israel in antiquity and therefore cannot be correct. He concludes that *shifon* is rather *Triticum spelta* — spelt — which resembles barley in many respects and has historically been used as an alternative to barley for animal feed, and which the Gemara itself characterizes as a type of barley.

That shifts the identification of *kusmin*, which Rashi had translated as spelt. Since spelt is now assigned to *shifon*, *kusmin* must be something else. Dr. Felix concludes that it is *kusemet* — emmer wheat — one of the earliest cultivated forms of wheat, well attested in the land of Israel from the First Temple period onward. The Gemara's characterization of *kusmin* as *min chitin* (a type of wheat) fits this identification very well.

That leaves *shibolet shual*. Rashi translates it as oats. Under Dr. Felix's system, since spelt and emmer wheat have already been assigned, and rye cannot be included because it was unknown in ancient Israel, *shibolet shual* is identified as a form of two-row barley.

The result is that according to Dr. Felix, the three secondary grains are emmer wheat, spelt, and two-row barley — and neither rye nor oats belongs on the list.

### Celiacs & Oats Issue

The practical stakes of this disagreement are significant, particularly regarding oats. Oats do not contain gluten — the protein that gives dough its elasticity, allows it to be kneaded and shaped, and is present in all the other grains on the list. The absence of gluten from oats provides a structural basis for Dr. Felix's conclusion that oats do not belong among the five grains: the common denominator of all five species appears to be the presence of gluten, which also underlies the capacity to produce genuine *chametz* in the sense of dough that rises and releases gas.

The consequence for practice is acute. People suffering from celiac disease who cannot tolerate gluten rely on oat-based *matzah* to fulfill their Pesach obligation, precisely because oats — following Rashi's identification — are included among the five grains. If Dr. Felix is correct and oats are not actually one of the five grains, celiacs would have no grain with which to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah* and would be exempt altogether.

### Auerbach vs Elyashiv

Hebrew Wikipedia, under the entry on *chamisha minei dagan*, records a telling episode. Professor Felix relates that on the basis of his botanical identification, Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach began reciting *shehakol* — rather than *mezonot* — on his morning oatmeal, treating oats as a non-grain food much as one would treat rice or corn. He maintained this practice for two years. Rav Shlomo Elyashiv then objected sharply, arguing that one cannot overturn a Jewish custom stretching back to the time of the *Rishonim* simply on account of a single scholar's academic findings.

This episode crystallizes a fundamental tension in *halacha*: to what degree may scientific discovery revise legally canonized meanings? The Gemara's understanding of the Mishnah — even if it may not have been the Mishnah's original intent — becomes binding through the process of *psak*. *Halacha* operates within legal realities that do not automatically recalibrate in response to botanical or archaeological evidence, however compelling. There is also an eminently practical dimension: *paskening* that oats are a valid grain enables celiacs to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah* on Pesach. The normative conclusion remains that oats are included among the five grains.

---

## Rice & Hamitz Defined

### Rice Excluded

The Gemara states: *hani in, orez ve-dochen lo* — these five grains yes, but rice (*orez*) and millet (*dochen*) are not included. From where is this derived?

### Biblical Source

Rav Shimon ben Lakish cites a verse from Devarim, and the same teaching is attributed to the school of Rabbi Yishmael and the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. The verse reads: *lo tochal alav chametz, shivat yamim tochal alav matzot* — do not eat *chametz* on it; for seven days eat *matzot*. The exegetical principle is *devarim habaim lidei chimutz adam yotzei yedei chovato b'matzah* — only things that are capable of becoming *chametz* can serve as *matzah* when they are not allowed to ferment. Rice and millet are excluded because *she-ein ba'in lidei chimutz ela lidei sirchon* — they do not arrive at *chimutz* (fermentation/rising), but rather at *sirchon* (decomposition or spoilage).

### Chimutz Definition

This raises an immediate question: rice does ferment. Its sugars break down, and in fact rice vinegar exists as a product of that process. So what precisely does the Gemara mean when it says rice does not come to *chimutz*?

Commentators and scholars point to two possible distinctions. The first is gluten: the five grains contain gluten, which binds and elasticizes the dough, enabling it to be kneaded and shaped. Rice lacks gluten. The second — and perhaps more intuitive — explanation relates to what *chimutz* means from a practical, experiential standpoint: not simply the biochemical process of fermentation, but the visible leavening of dough — the release of gas, the puffing and rising that occurs when water is combined with flour. This is what *chametz* means to the lay observer, and this is what does not happen with rice. If you prepare a dough from rice flour and leave it on the table, you do not observe the same dramatic rising that occurs with wheat flour dough. That seems to be the line the Gemara is drawing. It does not mean that no chemical decomposition occurs in rice; it means that the characteristic *machmitz* phenomenon — the rising of dough — is not replicated.

This distinction also underlies the broader *Ashkenazi chumra* of *kitniyot*. While that is a separate discussion, it developed in part because rice and grains are easily confused (both can be milled into flour and formed into dough), and because rice sold in the market was sometimes adulterated with actual grain. That gave rise to the Ashkenazi practice of avoiding *kitniyot* — but the underlying *halacha* as established by the Gemara is that rice is not one of the five grains and does not produce genuine *chametz*.

### R. Yochanan Nuri

The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not accord with the position of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that *orez min dagan hu* — rice is a type of grain. According to him, one is liable to *karet* for eating leavened rice on Pesach, and one may fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah* with rice. A *braita* confirms: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri forbids rice and millet dough that has not been baked immediately, because *she-karov l'hachmitz* — it is close to becoming *chametz*. He further rules that one who lets it become *chametz* is liable to *karet*, and if one bakes it in time, it can be used for *matzah*. The Mishnah, and normative *halacha*, do not follow this view.

### Karov vs Gamur

The Gemara raises a further question about Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's use of the phrase *karov l'hachmitz* (close to fermenting). Does this mean that rice ferments even faster than regular flour — making it *more* stringent — or does it mean that rice comes close to *chametz* but does not reach the status of *chametz gamur* (full *chametz*), placing it instead in the category of *chametz nukshah* (incompletely leavened)? The *braita*'s explicit statement that one incurs *karet* and may use rice for *matzah* resolves the question: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regards rice as producing full *chametz*, not merely a quasi-*chametz*. The phrase *karov l'hachmitz* means that it ferments quickly, not that it falls short of full fermentation.

---

## Fruit Juices

### Reish Lakish Liquids

We now arrive at another major category directly relevant to contemporary practice. Rabbah bar bar Chana cites Reish Lakish: *issa she-nilsha be-yayin u-ve-shemen u-ve-devash* — dough that was kneaded with wine, oil, and honey — that is, with *mei peiros* (fruit juices) rather than water — *ein chayavin al chimutza karet*. Even if such dough is left and allowed to sit, one does not incur *karet*, because it does not produce genuine *chametz*. The characterization *matzah ashira* (rich matzah) enters here as well.

### Matzah Capability

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua poses the question to Rav Pappa: what is Reish Lakish's reasoning? The answer offered initially draws on the verse *lo tochal alav chametz, shivat yamim tochal alav matzot*. The argument is framed in the reciprocal direction from the one used earlier: not only can only things capable of becoming *chametz* serve as *matzah*, but conversely, only things capable of serving as *matzah* become full *chametz* carrying the penalty of *karet*. In formula: *devarim she-adam yotzei yedei chovato ba-hem be-matzah, chayavin al chimutzan karet* — only things from which one can fulfill the *mitzva* of *matzah* carry the full penalty for *chametz*.

### Matzah Ashirah

Why can dough kneaded with fruit juices not serve as *matzah*? Because one of the defining criteria of *matzah* is *lechem oni* — the bread of poverty. A dough enriched with wine, oil, and honey is no longer poor person's bread; it is *matzah ashira*, rich matzah. Since it cannot fulfill the *mitzva* of *matzah*, the argument runs, its becoming leavened does not carry the full severity of *chametz*.

This is a striking argument. It implies that the extra criteria of *matzah* — criteria added on top of the basic requirement that it be made from fermentable grain — somehow retroactively affect whether the leavened version of that dough constitutes serious *chametz*. That is a counterintuitive claim.

### Dissolved Bread

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua challenges this reasoning. He cites a case: *ha-mechahu u-gema'o* — if one takes *chametz* and dissolves it completely in water and then swallows it, one is still liable to *karet* for eating *chametz*. Yet this dissolved *chametz* cannot possibly fulfill the *mitzva* of eating *matzah* — there is no *akhila* (eating) that would count for the *mitzva*, and the Gemara elsewhere would likely apply the principle that one who dissolves *matzah* and swallows it does not fulfill *achilas matzah*. So here we have a case where the very same substance is full *chametz* with *karet*, and yet cannot serve as *matzah*. The logical framework — that only things capable of *matzah* can be full *chametz* — is thereby refuted.

### Mei Peiros Resolved

At this point, Rav Idi bar Avin, who had been dozing during the exchange, wakes up and addresses the two students: *dardekei* — children. The true reason for Reish Lakish's ruling, he explains, is altogether different: *mishum de-havei lei mei peiros, u-mei peiros ein machmitzin* — because the dough was kneaded with fruit juices, and fruit juices simply do not cause *chimutz*. The ruling has nothing to do with the logical reciprocity between *matzah* and *chametz*. It is a straightforward empirical-halakhic principle: *mei peiros* do not ferment dough in the manner that produces *chametz*. This appears to have at least partial empirical support: the presence of sugars and other compounds in fruit juices alters the fermentation process and may inhibit the gas-releasing, dough-rising phenomenon that characterizes *chimutz*.

### Rishonim Positions

The question then becomes: what precisely does *mei peiros ein machmitzin* mean? Reish Lakish said one is not liable to *karet* — which could mean either that the dough becomes only *chametz nukshah* (quasi-*chametz*) and not *chametz gamur*, or that it does not become *chametz* at all. There is contradictory evidence across various sugyas, which gave rise to two basic positions among the *Rishonim*.

One position holds that fruit juices without water produce at least quasi-*chametz* (*chametz nukshah*), and therefore one must still be careful — baking immediately avoids the problem, but if the dough sits, it becomes at least rabbinically problematic *chametz*, perhaps even more quickly than standard dough. A second, very prominent position — that of Tosafot — distinguishes between two scenarios: fruit juices with water added, and fruit juices without water. When no water is added, the dough simply does not become *chametz* at all, and one need not rush to bake it. When water is added alongside the fruit juice, the dough does become *chametz* — and possibly even faster than usual.

### Shulchan Aruch Ruling

The *Shulchan Aruch* rules in accordance with the second position: dough kneaded with pure fruit juice and no water does not become *chametz*, there is no urgency to bake it, and it may be eaten on Pesach without restriction. This is analogous to the status of rice according to the *ikkar halacha* — permissible, though it cannot fulfill the *mitzva* of *matzah* because it does not meet the criterion of *lechem oni*.

The *Rama*, predictably given the broader *Ashkenazi* approach to Pesach stringencies — the same approach that produced the *kitniyot* practice — rules that the *minhag* is to be *machmir*: even without water added, fruit juices may produce quasi-*chametz*, and therefore the practice among *Ashkenazim* is to avoid dough made with fruit juices on Pesach except for the sake of a *choleh* (someone who is ill) or very young children.

### Egg Matzot

Eggs raise a separate but related question: some *Rishonim* suggested that eggs might be subject to stricter rules than other fruit juices, because egg-based dough becomes considerably thicker and therefore might be more prone to *chimutz*. The normative consensus, however, is to treat eggs exactly as other fruit juices. Egg *matzot* are therefore in the same category as *matzah ashira*: the *Shulchan Aruch*'s ruling would permit them, but the *Ashkenazi minhag* following the *Rama* restricts them to the sick and to very young children — and in practice, even baked egg *matzot* are avoided by *Ashkenazim* except in those circumstances.

The irony is worth noting. The entire question of *mei peiros ein machmitzin* concerns whether the dough, if left unbaked, becomes *chametz*. Once it is actually baked into *matzah*, that concern does not apply in the same way. In principle, baked egg *matzah* should be no more problematic than water-based *matzah*. And yet, just as plain corn is forbidden to *Ashkenazim* on Pesach while plain wheat is obviously not, the stringency has taken on a life of its own such that even baked egg *matzot* are avoided except by those with special need.

---

## Technical Cases

### Demai Status

The Mishnah ruled that one fulfills the obligation of *matzah* using *demai* — grain purchased from an *am ha-aretz* about which there is doubt whether *terumos u-maasros* have been separated. The difficulty is obvious: if one may not eat *demai* (at least rabbinically), how can grain that cannot be eaten fulfill an eating-based *mitzva*?

The Gemara resolves this with a striking argument. In theory, one could renounce all one's possessions, become a pauper, and then be fully permitted to eat *demai* — because the Rabbis were lenient with regard to paupers, given that the prohibition of *demai* is only rabbinic, and the biblical presumption (*rov*) is that *terumos u-maasros* have in fact been separated. The Mishnah elsewhere confirms: *ma'achilin et ha-aniyim demai* — one may feed paupers *demai*, and similarly one may feed quartered soldiers (*achsanya*) *demai*, even according to Beit Hillel. Beit Shammai disagreed, but the normative ruling follows Beit Hillel.

The deeper conceptual point may be this: where do we ever find a category of *ma'achalos assuros* — forbidden foods — that paupers are specifically permitted to eat? We would never say, for instance, that a rabbinically forbidden meat-and-milk mixture is permitted for the poor. The fact that the Rabbis made such a specific leniency for paupers with *demai* indicates that *demai* does not have the character of genuinely forbidden food. It is technically restricted but not in the same qualitative category as *issur*, and therefore it does not disqualify *matzah* made from it.

### Ma'aser First

The Mishnah also permits *maaser rishon* from which *terumas ma'aser* has been taken. The Gemara objects: this is obvious — once the Levite has given the tenth-of-a-tenth to the Kohen, the remaining *maaser rishon* is fully *chulin* and anyone may eat it. Why state it?

### Levi Beat Out

The *chiddush* applies to a special case: where the Levite "beat out" the Kohen by approaching the grain's owner while the grain was still in the sheaves (*shibbolim*) — before it had been threshed, winnowed, and processed into a pile. At that stage, the grain has not yet reached the point of full obligation in *terumot u-maasros* (the stage known as *miruach* — the smoothing over of the pile — has not occurred). The owner gave the Levite his *maaser* at that early stage. The Levite then took *terumas maaser* — the tenth-of-a-tenth — from his portion and gave it to the Kohen. But *terumah gedolah* was never taken from this grain, either before or after the Levite received his portion.

One might think that since *terumah gedolah* was never separated, the grain remains *tevel*. But Rabbi Abbahu cites Reish Lakish: *maaser rishon she-hikdimo be-shibbolim, patur mi-terumah gedolah*. When the Levite takes his *maaser* while the grain is still in the sheaves — before it has become fully obligated — he is exempt from *terumah gedolah*. The verse states *ma'aser min hama'aser amarti lach* — I told you to take a tenth of a tenth, and not also *terumah gedolah u-terumas maaser min hama'aser*. Once the Levite received his portion before full obligation set in, he escapes the requirement of *terumah gedolah* entirely.

The Gemara then poses a challenge. Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if the Levite escapes the *terumah gedolah* obligation by beating the Kohen to the grain, why limit this to the case where the grain was in sheaves? Even if the Levite came after the grain had already been piled and processed (*bikari*) but still before the Kohen arrived, should he not similarly be exempt? Abaye responds by citing a second verse: *mi-kol matnoséichem tarimu et kol terumat Hashem* — from all your gifts you shall give all of the *terumos*. This verse indicates that sometimes the Levite must give all *terumos* from his *maaser*, including *terumah gedolah*.

The resolution: the distinction is whether the grain had already reached the point of full obligation. When the Levite takes his *maaser* while the grain is in sheaves — *lo idgan*, not yet fully processed — no obligation in *terumah gedolah* ever attached to the portion he received. But if he received his *maaser* after the grain had been winnowed, threshed, and piled — *idgan*, it has already become grain subject to *ma'aser* — the obligation in *terumah gedolah* had already taken effect, and the Levite cannot escape it merely by collecting his portion before the Kohen does.

The Mishnah's ruling that *maaser rishon* from which *terumah* has been taken is valid for *matzah* therefore applies even to this unusual case where the Levite escaped *terumah gedolah* by collecting his portion while the grain was still in sheaves.

### Ma'aser Sheni Redeemed

The Mishnah permits *maaser sheni* and *hekdesh* that have been redeemed. Again the Gemara asks: is this not obvious? Once redeemed, the sanctity is removed and the item is ordinary *chulin*. The *chiddush*, the Gemara explains, lies in a case where the redemption was technically deficient — specifically, where one gave the principal value (*keren*) without adding the extra fifth (*chomesh*) that is normally required when redeeming *maaser sheni* or *hekdesh*. The Mishnah teaches that the absence of the *chomesh* does not invalidate the redemption: *ein chomesh me'akev* — the fifth does not block the removal of sanctity. As long as the principal was paid, the *maaser sheni* or *hekdesh* is sufficiently redeemed to be treated as *chulin* and may be used for *matzah*.

### Kohanim Challah

The Mishnah's ruling that *kohanim* may use *challah* and *terumah* for their *matzah* obligation might also have been questioned: perhaps *matzah* must be universally edible — *shaveh le-chol adam*. The Gemara rejects this requirement. The verse uses the plural *matzot*, which serves to include even items not edible by all. As long as the item is edible by the one eating it, that is sufficient. Since *challah* and *terumah* are fully edible for *kohanim* — indeed, that is precisely what they are designated for — *kohanim* may use them to fulfill the *mitzva* of *matzah*.

### Forbidden Cases

The Mishnah then lists the items with which one cannot fulfill the obligation. One cannot use real *tevel* — untithed grain. The Gemara notes that this is obvious. The *chiddush* applies to *tevel de-rabbanan* — specifically grain grown in a flowerpot without a hole in the bottom (*atzitz she-eino nakuv*), which is only rabbinically obligated in *maasros* since it is not truly connected to the ground. Even this rabbinic *tevel* disqualifies *matzah*, since it cannot be eaten by anyone — not even paupers, unlike *demai* — and therefore lacks the quality of edible food required.

One cannot use *maaser rishon* from which *terumah* has not been taken. The Gemara again: this is obvious — it is *tevel*. The *chiddush* is the mirror image of the permitted case above: here the Levite collected his *maaser* after the grain had already been piled (*bikari*), and therefore after the obligation in *terumah gedolah* had already attached. Even though the Levite beat the Kohen in the sense of collecting his portion first, the prior attachment of the *terumah gedolah* obligation means the grain remains *tevel* until *terumah gedolah* is separated. As Abaye explained to Rav Pappa, the verse *mi-kol matnoséichem tarimu et kol terumat Hashem* requires full separation in such a case.

Finally, *maaser sheni* and *hekdesh* that have not been properly redeemed cannot be used. The cases of deficient redemption here are: *maaser sheni* redeemed on an unminted coin (*asimon*), which the verse *ve-tzarta ha-kesef* — bind the money — excludes (only properly minted coins with an image suffice); and *hekdesh* redeemed on land rather than on moveable property, which the verse *ve-natan ha-kesef ve-kam lo* requires.

The overall principle that emerges from these cases is coherent: if the food is edible — even if only by a specific group, like *kohanim*, or only in a technical or contingent way, like *demai* — then it may be used for *matzah*. If it is forbidden to eat, even rabbinically, it cannot fulfill the *mitzva* — and this even in cases where the prohibition is technical or the redemption merely deficient. The further question of *why* forbidden food cannot fulfill the *mitzva* of *matzah* — whether it is derived from a verse or from the general principle of *mitzva ha-ba'ah be-aveirah* — will be addressed as the discussion continues.

# Pesachim 36

## Review & Overview

### Prior Topics

The previous daf was devoted to the question of what is necessary to produce *matzah* and what causes *chametz*, focusing on the five grains — to the exclusion of rice and millet — which is the heart of the *kitniyos* issue. The shiur considered whether oats belong among those five grains, a question with particular relevance for those with celiac disease and gluten concerns. Central to that discussion was the precise meaning of *machmitz*: even rice ferments to some degree, and so the term must refer specifically to the release of gases and the puffing up of dough, a process that does not occur to any comparable degree in rice or similar grains.

The discussion also touched on *mei peiros* — fruit juices — and whether they cause *chametz*. Two opinions were considered: one holding that *mei peiros* produces no *chametz* at all, and another holding that it produces an intermediate category called *chametz nuksha*, which does not carry liability for *kares* but is nonetheless prohibited. The dominant position among the *Rishonim*, as codified in the *Shulchan Aruch*, is that *mei peiros* without the addition of water presents no problem, while the addition of water can render the mixture *chametz*. The *Rema*, however, takes the more stringent view that even pure fruit juices are problematic — except in cases of illness or for children, which is why egg matzah is certified *kosher l'Pesach* for such individuals. One important clarification: the *Rema*'s stringency applies only when the dough is left unattended. The classic rule is that eighteen minutes is the limit only for unattended dough; as long as one is actively working the dough, there is no fixed time constraint. Thus, if the dough is kneaded with fruit juices and placed in the oven immediately, the *Rema* has no additional stringency beyond what he holds with water.

### Mishnah Overview

The remainder of the previous daf addressed the *Mishnah*'s distinction between *matzah* that is halachically valid and *matzah* that, while edible in ordinary circumstances, carries some other legal problem. *Matzah* of *demai*, *terumah*, or *ma'aser* from which *terumah* has already been taken — these fall into a gray area. But *matzah* of genuine *tevel*, or *ma'aser* that has not yet been redeemed, cannot be eaten. The question the Gemara now turns to is a sharper one: granted that eating such *matzah* is forbidden — but why should that mean one does not fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah* as well? That is the inquiry that opens Daf 36.

## Tevel & Terumos

### Tevel Definition

The Gemara picks up at the bottom of 35b and cites a *Tanu Rabbanan*: one might think a person fulfills the obligation of *matzah* with *tevel* that has not been fixed — *tevel shelo nitkan*. The Gemara immediately notes that this phrasing is redundant: by definition, all *tevel* has not been fixed. The *Baraita* therefore must be speaking of *tevel shelo nitkan kol tzorcho* — grain that has not been fully rectified. Several graduated cases are enumerated. One took *terumah gedolah* from the grain but did not take *terumas ma'aser*. Or one took *maaser rishon*, which carries within it the *terumas ma'aser*, so that only *maaser sheni* remains outstanding. Or the year is the third or sixth year and the only thing not yet separated is *maaser ani*.

The gradation matters for the following reason. When *terumah* or *terumas ma'aser* has not been taken, the grain contains within it something that, if consumed by a non-*kohen*, carries liability for *misah bidei shamayim*. The severity of the *tevel* status is, one might suppose, a function of the severity of what has not yet been extracted. But when the only thing remaining is *maaser ani*, the prohibition is not that of a forbidden food at all — it is a form of *gezel*, theft from the poor. One might therefore reason that eating such grain is no worse than a monetary transgression, not a food prohibition, and that the *tevel* status has effectively lapsed. The *Baraita* rejects this: even if the only thing not separated is *maaser ani*, the *tevel* status remains and one does not fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah*. Whether the severity is equivalent — whether eating this attenuated form of *tevel* still carries *misah bidei shamayim* — is a separate question left open.

### Tevel Source

The *Baraita* derives this from the verse: *lo sochel alav chametz* — do not eat *chametz* on it — followed by *shivas yamim tochal alav matzos*. The juxtaposition of *matzah* to the prohibition of *chametz* has been established previously: it tells us that *matzah* can only be made from things that are capable of becoming *chametz*, i.e., the five *minim*. But the verse is now extended further: one fulfills the *mitzvah* of *matzah* only with something whose sole potential prohibition is that of *chametz* — *mi she-issuro mishum bal tochal chametz*. The case of *tevel* is thereby excluded: *she-ein issuro mishum bal tochal chametz ella mishum bal tochal tevel* — its prohibition is not from eating *chametz* but from eating *tevel*. The underlying logic is that *matzah* of *tevel*, even if left to ferment, would never result in a prohibition of *chametz*, because the prevailing prohibition is that of *tevel*.

But this raises an obvious difficulty: why shouldn't the *chametz* prohibition also apply? Even if the grain is *tevel*, if it ferments it seems one should transgress *chametz* as well.

### Ain Issur Chal

The Gemara answers: *ha-mani Rabbi Shimon hi* — this entire teaching follows the position of Rabbi Shimon, who holds *ein issur chal al issur*: one prohibition cannot take effect upon an object that already carries another prohibition. Since the grain already carries the prohibition of *tevel*, the *chametz* prohibition cannot attach to it, even if it ferments. Thus, *matzah* of *tevel* can never become prohibited on account of *chametz*, and is therefore excluded from fulfilling the *mitzvah*.

The paradigmatic illustration of Rabbi Shimon's principle is the *Baraita* cited: if one eats a *neveilah* on *Yom HaKippurim*, Rabbi Shimon says one is *patur* for the *Yom HaKippurim* violation, because the animal was already forbidden as *neveilah* before *Yom HaKippurim* arrived. This is a striking example, not only because it means one could eat *treifas* on *Yom HaKippurim* without incurring the additional *Yom HaKippurim* liability, but also because the conceptual structure is somewhat unusual: the prohibition of *Yom HaKippurim* does not attach to the meat itself in the way that *tevel* attaches to grain. Rather, it is a personal obligation to fast. Nonetheless, Rabbi Shimon's position is consistent: once an object carries one prohibited status, a second prohibition does not take effect.

One might ask whether *chametz* should be considered an *issur mosif* — an additional prohibition that adds something the prior prohibition did not — since *chametz* carries *issur hana'ah* while *tevel* does not prohibit all forms of benefit equally. Whether *issur hana'ah* constitutes an *issur mosif* in this context is genuinely questionable, and the Gemara proceeds on the assumption that it does not.

The conclusion, then, is that the entire *Mishnah*'s ruling — that one does not fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah* with *matzah* that is forbidden for another reason — reflects the position of Rabbi Shimon alone. According to the *Chachamim*, who hold that one prohibition *can* take effect atop another, the *chametz* prohibition would indeed attach even to *tevel*, and one would presumably fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah* even with such bread.

This is a remarkable conclusion: the *Mishnah* as a whole would not be the normative *halacha*. A number of *Rishonim*, while acknowledging that this appears to be the Gemara's conclusion, nevertheless rule otherwise — that even according to the *Chachamim* one does not fulfill the *mitzvah* with forbidden *matzah*. One compelling reason, raised by *Rashi* in multiple places but notably absent from the Gemara itself, is the principle of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* — a *mitzvah* fulfilled through the commission of a transgression. The *Rishonim* grapple with why this consideration is entirely absent from the Gemara's discussion, and several attempt to narrow the definition of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* to account for this omission. *Rashi* nonetheless insists that it is operative here as well, and several *Rishonim* conclude that the *Mishnah* holds even according to the *Chachamim*, with *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* as a possible underlying rationale.

One distinction worth noting: the classic case of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* — a stolen *esrog* — involves an object upon which a transgression was previously committed, which then becomes, as it were, stigmatized. The Gemara in *Sukkah* compares such an object to one with a *mum*, a blemish. In the case of *tevel matzah*, however, the transgression and the *mitzvah* occur simultaneously — at the moment of eating. The object has not had a transgression previously performed upon it. This temporal distinction is cited by several *Rishonim* as a reason to question whether *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* applies in precisely the same way here.

### Ravina's View

Ravina offers an alternative reading of the *drasha* that avoids limiting the *Mishnah* to Rabbi Shimon entirely. According to Ravina, the verse means: one fulfills the *mitzvah* of *matzah* only with something whose *sole* additional potential prohibition is *chametz* — *mi she-issuro mishum bal tochal chametz bilvad*. The case of *tevel* is excluded not because it lacks the *chametz* prohibition, but because it carries an *additional* prohibition of *tevel* alongside *chametz*. The *drasha* thus operates even according to the *Chachamim*: any grain that carries another prohibition beyond *chametz* cannot be used for *matzah*.

The Gemara, however, is dissatisfied: *mi-di bilvad ktiv* — does the verse actually say "only"? The verse speaks of things that can become prohibited as *chametz*; it does not say the *chametz* prohibition must be the *sole* prohibition. The Gemara therefore concludes: *ela mivarta k'Rav Sheshet* — the better reading is that of Rav Sheshet, and the *Mishnah* does indeed follow Rabbi Shimon.

That said, as noted, the *Rishonim* do not simply accept that the entire *Mishnah* is unrepresentative of normative *halacha*, and the principle of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* remains a serious and independently grounded reason why one cannot fulfill the *mitzvah* with *matzah* that was forbidden.

## Fruit Juices & Additives

### Lechem Oni Drasha

The Gemara introduces another *Tanu Rabbanan*: could one fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah* with *maaser sheni* in *Yerushalayim*? One is permitted — indeed obligated — to eat *maaser sheni* in *Yerushalayim*; why not use it for *matzah*? The verse teaches: *lechem oni* — "bread of affliction." Reading with a play on the word *oni*, repointing it as *avon* (related to *aninut*), one learns that valid *matzah* must be the kind that can be eaten in a state of *aninut* — by one who has just lost a close relative and not yet buried them, the *onen*. The case of *maaser sheni* is then excluded: *shene'eno ne'echal b'aninut* — *maaser sheni* cannot be eaten by an *onen*, since the verse explicitly states *lo achalti b'oni mimenu*. The play on words *b'oni* / *b'avon* is deliberate. This is the position of Rabbi Yose HaGalili.

There is a deeper thematic dimension here: *matzah*, symbolizing affliction, cannot be composed of *maaser sheni*, which is associated entirely with *simcha* — the joy of eating before God in *Yerushalayim*. The contrast is pointed: the *matzah* of the *Seder* is meant to evoke profound humility and sorrow, while *maaser sheni* is eaten in a spirit of festival rejoicing.

### Akiva: Fruit OK

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. He reads *matzot matzot* — the repetition of the word *matzot* in the Torah — as an inclusive *ribui* that specifically permits the use of *maaser sheni* in *Yerushalayim* for the *matzah mitzvah*. If so, what work does *lechem oni* do for Rabbi Akiva? In all likelihood, it excludes dough kneaded with wine, oil, and honey — enriched bread that is too flavored and sweet to qualify as "poor man's bread" for the purpose of the *mitzvah*.

The dispute then turns on how to read the word itself. Rabbi Akiva asks: *mi ksiv lechem oni*? The word is written as *ani* — without the *vav* — which means simply "poor person's bread." That reading excludes sweetened, enriched *matzah*. Rabbi Yose HaGalili, by contrast, reads it as *oni* with the *vav*, connecting it to *aninut*, and uses this to exclude *maaser sheni*. Rabbi Akiva counters that we do read it as *oni* — but, following Shmuel's teaching, *lechem she-onin alav devarim harbeh*: bread over which one recites many things, i.e., the *Haggadah* and the *Hallel*. The *matzah* of the *Seder* must be embedded within the narrative context of the *Haggadah*; that is what *oni* teaches. It does not exclude *maaser sheni* through a comparison to *aninut*.

It is worth noting *Rashi*'s comment on *she-onin alav devarim harbeh*: *Rashi* states *she-gomrin alav es ha-Hallel v'omrim alav Haggadah* — one completes the *Hallel* over it and recites the *Haggadah* over it. Notably, *Rashi* mentions *Hallel* first, which may seem surprising to us. Yet early records from the *Bayis Sheni* period — in Philo and Josephus and similar sources — emphasize above all that on *Pesach* night the people ate the *Korban Pesach* and sang songs of praise to God. The story-recounting aspect, while certainly present, was not always the primary emphasis. *Rashi*'s formulation echoes something of that earlier sensibility.

### Kosher vs. Seder

The Gemara resolves the apparent tension in Rabbi Akiva's position. He says one may knead dough with fruit juices — and indeed attests that he did so in the presence of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, who raised no objection. Yet he also seems to say that *matzah* kneaded with wine, oil, and honey does not fulfill the *mitzvah*. Is this a contradiction?

The Gemara answers: *lo kashya* — it is not difficult. These are two entirely separate questions. *Yom Tov rishon* — the Seder night — requires *lechem oni*, which cannot be enriched or sweetened. But for the remaining days of Pesach (*yom tov sheni* here meaning the other days of the festival, not specifically the second *Yom Tov* of the diaspora), such *matzah* is perfectly valid. Fruit-juice *matzah* is not *chametz* — it may be eaten throughout *Pesach* — but it does not fulfill the specific obligation of the first night's *mitzvah* of *matzah* because it is not *lechem oni*.

Thus both aspects of *ani* / *oni* apply specifically to the Seder night. The word *ani* without the *vav* teaches that the *Seder* night *matzah* must be plain and unadorned. The word *oni* with the *vav*, as read by Rabbi Akiva following Shmuel, teaches that the *matzah* must be accompanied by *devarim harbeh* — the *Haggadah* and *Hallel*. Both requirements pertain only to the first night. The other days of *Pesach* have no such restriction on what may constitute kosher, non-*chametz* bread.

### Milk Exception

The Gemara illustrates this distinction with a teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua to his son: on the first night of *Pesach*, do not knead the dough with milk; thereafter, you may knead it with milk. The implication is clear — *matzah* kneaded with milk is not *chametz* and is permissible on the other days of *Pesach*, but does not fulfill the *Seder* night *mitzvah* because it is not *lechem oni*.

The Gemara immediately challenges this: is it not taught in a *Baraita* that one may never knead dough with milk, and that if one did so, the entire bread is forbidden? This is because bread is eaten with everything, and *milchig* bread will inevitably lead one to eat it together with meat. This is the principle of *mipnei hergel aveira*. If *milchig matzah* is categorically forbidden, how could Rabbi Yehoshua permit it after the first night?

The Gemara offers two resolutions. First, perhaps he was speaking of honey rather than milk: do not knead with honey on the first night; thereafter, do so. Second, *ve-iba'is eima*, one may indeed maintain that he was speaking of milk, in accordance with Ravina's ruling: *milchig* bread is permitted when made *ke-ein tura*. *Rashi* understands this phrase to mean small, bite-sized loaves — each portion is consumed in a single sitting, eliminating any concern of mixing with meat afterward. Others read *ke-ein tura* as meaning that the loaves are shaped distinctively, like an ox, so that they are immediately recognizable as *milchig* — a visible *siman* that prevents confusion. The Gemara concludes that this applies here as well: Rabbi Yehoshua was permitting *milchig matzah* when produced in small individualized portions that would be entirely consumed without remainder. The broader principle is established: the first night of *Pesach* imposes heightened criteria for the *matzah* itself, above and beyond what is merely required to avoid *chametz*.

### Lukewarm Water

The *Mishnah* concludes with a point on which all opinions agree: one may not knead *matzah* dough with *poshrin* — lukewarm water — since warmth accelerates fermentation. This consensus is then compared to the laws of *minchos* in the *Beis Hamikdash*, since *minchos*, like *matzah*, are subject to the prohibition of *chametz* and must be made as *matzos*.

## Minchos & Sisah

### Kneading vs. Sisah

The Gemara asks: *mai sh'na mi-minchos* — how is the rule about lukewarm water different from the law of *minchos*? The *Mishnah* in *Menachos* explicitly teaches that *all minchos are kneaded with lukewarm water* — and one watches them so that they should not become *chametz*. The *Mishnah* in *Menachos* thus acknowledges the risk of lukewarm water causing *chametz*, yet permits its use provided proper vigilance is maintained. The standard method of vigilance is continuous kneading: as long as the dough is being actively worked, fermentation is prevented.

Why, then, is this not the rule for ordinary *matzah* baking at home? The Gemara answers: *im amru bi-zerizin yomru b'she-ein zerizin* — just because we are lenient for the meticulous, highly trained priests in the *Beis Hamikdash*, we cannot extend that leniency to every householder. Not everyone will maintain the necessary vigilance. The *Kohanim* in the *Beis Hamikdash* are entirely focused on this work; the general population baking at home cannot be assumed to exercise comparable care.

The Gemara then asks: if that is the reasoning, why do we not similarly permit *sisah* — the practice of soaking grain in water to soften the husk and facilitate the removal of bran, thereby producing fine white flour — in the *Beis Hamikdash* as well? This process was not done for *minchah* flour, since contact with water at that early stage risked *chametz*, but the argument of *zerizin* should apply.

The Gemara cites a teaching of Shmuel transmitted through Rav and Rabbah bar Yirmiyah: the wheat used for *minchos* may not undergo *sisah*. Why not? The distinction is precise: *lisha bi-zerizin isa* — the kneading of dough is done by *zerizin*, either by the *Kohanim* themselves or, at minimum, within the *Beis Hamikdash*. But *sisah*, the soaking to remove bran, is *lav bi-zerizin isa* — it is not done by those same meticulous individuals. A person could bring finished flour to the *Beis Hamikdash* and the *Kohanim* would take it from there. The preparation of fine flour — including *sisah* — was done at home, by laypeople, outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. We cannot assume that everyone processing grain at home will be sufficiently careful.

The Gemara questions whether kneading is truly performed only by *Kohanim*, noting that a verse in the Torah describes the *minchah* preparation — the pouring of oil and the mixing — as being done before the *kohen* is involved: *mi-kemitza va-eilach mitzvas kehunah* — only from the *kemitza* onward is priestly participation required. The pouring of oil, the *belila*, the kneading, the baking — all of these are valid when performed by a non-*kohen*.

The Gemara responds: *nehidu bi-zerizin leisa* — it is true that the kneading need not be done by *Kohanim* specifically. Nevertheless, *bemakom zerizin isa* — it is done in the *Beis Hamikdash* itself. Processing grain into fine flour happens at home; kneading the dough happens inside the *Beis Hamikdash*. And regarding the *belila*: while the *belila* may technically be valid when performed by a non-*kohen*, it is invalid if performed outside the walls of the Temple precinct — *chutz le-chomas ha-azarah pesulah*. *Rashi* and *Tosafos* both note, independently, that the kneading must in any case be done inside the *Beis Hamikdash* because the dough must immediately be placed in a *kli shares*, a sacred vessel, which is only found within the Temple. *Tosafos* further adds that the dough must go directly from kneading into the oven; it cannot be kneaded at home and transported, as it would become *chametz* in transit. For whatever precise reason, the Gemara's conclusion stands: kneading is done within the *Beis Hamikdash* and thus benefits from the atmosphere of *zerizus* that prevails there; *sisah* is done outside and therefore may not be performed even for *minchos*.

### Minchas Omer

The Gemara raises one further case. The *Minchas HaOmer* — the first barley offering, the *omer* — did in fact undergo *sisah*, the soaking to remove bran. How does this square with the general prohibition on *sisah* for *minchos*?

The Gemara answers: *tsibur shani* — a communal offering is different. The *Minchas HaOmer* is a *korban tsibur*, a communal sacrifice. Because it is centrally organized and supervised by those responsible for the entire community's offering, one may assume that the process will be carried out with complete vigilance, even at the earlier stages of grain preparation. There is no individual householder who might be careless. A single coordinated authority oversees the entire process from beginning to end, and the concern that motivates the general prohibition — that some individual will not be careful enough — simply does not apply.

The Gemara notes an elegant verbal echo: the word *tsover osah* — "you pile it up" — which describes a step in the *sisah* process, sounds similar to *tsibur*, the community. Some read *tsibur shani* as meaning the *pile* makes a difference, not the communal nature. *Rashi* firmly rejects that reading, insisting that *tsibur* refers unambiguously to the communal character of the sacrifice.

## Ma'aser & Bikkurim

### Yose: Ma'aser OK

The Gemara opens a new *Tanu Rabbanan*: one might think a person fulfills the obligation of *matzah* with *bikkurim* in *Yerushalayim*. The comparison to *maaser sheni* is natural — both are eaten in *Yerushalayim*, both have a festive character. Can one use *bikkurim* flour for the Seder night *matzah*?

The verse teaches: *be-chol moshvoseichem tochlu matzos* — "in all your dwelling places you shall eat *matzos*." This phrase establishes a criterion: valid *matzah* must be the kind that *can* be eaten in all dwelling places. The case of *bikkurim* is thereby excluded — *she-einan nekhalin be-chol moshvoseichem ela bi-Yerushalayim* — *bikkurim* can only be eaten within *Yerushalayim* and nowhere else. Even if one is presently in *Yerushalayim*, the *matzah* must in principle be capable of being eaten anywhere. This is the position of Rabbi Yose HaGalili.

There is something conceptually striking here. The paradigmatic setting for eating *matzah* in the Torah era was *Yerushalayim* — the entire nation would be in *Yerushalayim* for *Pesach*, eating the *Korban Pesach* together with *matzah*. Yet the *halacha* is that valid *matzah* must have the potential to be eaten outside of *Yerushalayim*. The universal accessibility of *matzah* is a halachic requirement even in a context where the actual eating was entirely localized.

### Akiva: Both?

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. He derives from the juxtaposition of *matzah* and *maror* — *al matzos u-m'rorim* — that just as *maror* cannot be *bikkurim* (since the *shivas haminim* do not include the bitter herbs used for *maror*), so too *matzah* cannot be *bikkurim*. He agrees with the practical *halacha* — one cannot use *bikkurim* — but learns it from a different verse.

The Gemara challenges Rabbi Akiva's *drasha*. If the comparison to *maror* is taken strictly, it would imply not merely that *matzah* cannot happen to be *bikkurim*, but that *matzah* must be made from species that *cannot even in principle* become *bikkurim*. This would exclude wheat and barley from use for *matzah* entirely — since wheat and barley are among the *shivas haminim* and are precisely the species from which *bikkurim* are brought. One would be left using only the other three of the five *minim*. Rabbi Akiva invokes *matzos matzos riba* to prevent this overly restrictive reading. But the Gemara then turns the argument against him: if the repetition of *matzos* is inclusive, why does it not include *bikkurim* themselves?

### Redemption Logic

The Gemara concludes: *hadar beih Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva reversed himself, not in the practical ruling, but in the *drasha* from which it is derived. He ultimately accepted the *drasha* of Rabbi Yose HaGalili — *be-chol moshvoseichem* — as the source. A *Baraita* confirms this explicitly, giving the verse *be-chol moshvoseichem tochlu matzos* as the source for excluding *bikkurim*, in the name of a ruling that allows *maaser sheni* — which we know to be Rabbi Akiva's position.

The question then becomes: why does Rabbi Akiva include *maaser sheni* but exclude *bikkurim*, given that both can only be eaten in *Yerushalayim*? The answer is a crucial distinction: *maaser sheni* has a path to being eaten outside *Yerushalayim* — it can be redeemed. Under ordinary circumstances, once *maaser sheni* is brought into *Yerushalayim* it cannot be redeemed. But there is an exception: if *maaser sheni* becomes *tamei*, the verse says *ki lo tuchal se'eto* — "if you cannot carry it up" — and *Rashi* reads *se'et* through a play on words, connecting it to a verse about Yosef's gifts to his brothers where *mas'ot* refers to food portions. If you cannot eat it, you may redeem it. Therefore, even *maaser sheni* that has already entered *Yerushalayim* can theoretically be redeemed and carried out if it becomes *tamei*. This theoretical accessibility means *maaser sheni* qualifies under the criterion of *be-chol moshvoseichem*. *Bikkurim*, by contrast, have no such release mechanism; they can never be eaten outside *Yerushalayim* under any circumstances, and are therefore excluded.

### Yose Like Shimon

The Gemara then asks why Rabbi Yose HaGalili needed the *drasha* of *be-chol moshvoseichem* to exclude *bikkurim* at all. He already excludes *maaser sheni* on the grounds that it cannot be eaten *b'aninus* — invoking *lechem oni*. The same consideration — that *bikkurim* are also eaten *b'simcha* and not by an *onen* — should equally exclude *bikkurim*. Why does he need an additional verse?

The Gemara answers: *savar lah ke-Rabbi Shimon* — Rabbi Yose HaGalili holds in accordance with Rabbi Shimon's view on *bikkurim* and *onenin*.

### Onen & Bikkurim

A *Baraita* records the dispute directly: the majority view holds that *bikkurim* may not be eaten by an *onen*, linking *bikkurim* to *maaser sheni* through the verse *lo suchal le-echol bi-sharecha* — which enumerates things that must be eaten in *Yerushalayim*, mentioning *maaser degancha* (i.e., *maaser sheni*) and *trumas yadecha* (identified as *bikkurim*) together. Since *maaser sheni* cannot be eaten by an *onen*, neither can *bikkurim*, because the two are linked by the verse.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees. He reads the phrase *trumas yadecha* — the gift of your hands — as identifying *bikkurim* with the category of *terumah*.
