Just as *terumah*, though sacred, can be eaten by an *onen* (since *terumah* is not eaten in *Yerushalayim* but anywhere among *kohanim*, and the *onen*-restriction is associated with the Temple's sphere of sanctity rather than with holiness per se), so too *bikkurim* can be eaten by an *onen*.

Rabbi Shimon's position requires a response to the clear association of *bikkurim* with *simcha* — the verse says *ve-samachta be-chol ha-tov* — "and you shall rejoice in all the good." How can an *onen*, who is in acute mourning, eat something tied to *simcha*? The Gemara answers: *hahu l'zman simcha hu d'ata* — that verse is not establishing a legal condition for the eating of *bikkurim*; it is describing the time of year in which *bikkurim* are brought.

### Bikkurim Season

The *Mishnah* in *Bikkurim* specifies: from *Shavuos* until *Sukkos* — the harvest season — one brings *bikkurim* and recites the *mikra bikkurim* declaration (*ve-ata heiveiti et reishit pri ha-adama*). This is the true *zman simcha*, the time of joyous harvest. After *Sukkos* and until *Chanukah*, one may still bring *bikkurim* but no longer recites the declaration, because the season of harvest joy has passed and a different season has begun. The reference to *Chanukah* as the terminal date is a matter of the seasonal calendar, not a reference to the holiday itself; the question of whether this outer limit is rabbinic in character is noted.

The reason *bikkurim* begin only after *Shavuos* is that *Shavuos* marks the offering of the *shtei ha-lechem* — the two loaves — which is itself called *bikkurim*, serving as the first Temple-offering of the new produce. Only after this inaugural offering may the new produce be brought as individual *bikkurim*. The period thus runs from after *Shavuos* through *Sukkos*, when the final ingathering is complete, and *Sukkos* itself stands as the apex of that harvest joy — *zman simchateinu*.

Thus the verse *ve-samachta be-chol ha-tov* describes the setting in which *bikkurim* are brought — the season of rejoicing — but does not create a legal barrier preventing an *onen* from eating them. According to Rabbi Shimon, *bikkurim* are halachically identified as *terumah*, and the *onen* restriction does not apply. It follows that Rabbi Yose HaGalili, who aligns with Rabbi Shimon on this point, cannot use *lechem oni* to exclude *bikkurim* from the *matzah mitzvah* — since, in his view, *bikkurim* may be eaten by an *onen* and therefore do not conflict with the criterion of *matzah* eaten *b'aninus*. He must instead rely on the separate *drasha* of *be-chol moshvoseichem* to make the exclusion.

The larger thematic irony remains. *Matzah* on *Seder* night is *lechem oni* — the bread of affliction, poverty, and sorrow. *Bikkurim* are the paradigm of joyful harvest, *simcha*, and gratitude. That these two should be in such sharp halachic tension — that the most exuberant expression of agricultural thanksgiving cannot serve as the vehicle for the most solemn expression of historical memory — is itself a telling commentary on the layered meanings the Torah encodes in a single shared food.

---

---

# Pesachim 38

## Maaser Sheni & Challah

### Intro: Matzah/Challah

The daf opens at the bottom of 37b, continuing the sustained comparison between *matzah* and *challah* that occupied much of the preceding discussion. Both the *mitzvah* of taking *challah* and the *mitzvah* of eating *matzah* turn on the Torah's use of the word *lechem* — bread — and a great deal of the previous analysis explored what qualifies as *lechem* in each context. The discussion encompassed the requirement that *matzah* have the capacity to become *chametz*, that it be *lechem oni* (poor person's bread), and that it remain plain in certain respects, even while fine flour is permitted. The word *lechem* functions similarly across *challah* and *matzah*, and yesterday's discussion examined that comparison in depth — touching on bagels, *sufganiyot*, and the *beracha* of *Hamotzi Lechem Min Ha'aretz*.

Now the Gemara turns to a more arcane dimension of the same question: what happens when *matzah* carries an additional halachic status — such as *maaser sheni*, *bikkurim*, or other sanctified designations — and how does that affect its fitness for the *mitzvah*? We re-enter a discussion that began two days ago and continues here in a different register.

### Rav Assi's Ruling

Rav Assi's statement appears at the bottom of 37b: *issa shel maaser sheni le-divrei Rabbi Meir patur min ha-challah* — dough of *maaser sheni*, according to Rabbi Meir, is exempt from the obligation of *challah*. According to the *Chachamim*, however, such dough is obligated in *challah*. The *challah* context is distinct from the earlier *matzah* discussion; here the question is not the criterion of *bechol moshvoteichem* (all your dwelling places) but rather a different issue entirely regarding the ownership status of *maaser sheni* dough.

The Gemara then extends the ruling: *matzos shel maaser sheni* — according to Rabbi Meir — do not fulfill one's obligation on Pesach, because the *matzah* is not considered the person's own. According to the *Chachamim*, one does fulfill the obligation. Similarly, an *esrog shel maaser sheni*: according to Rabbi Meir one may fulfill the obligation on *Yom Tov*, while according to the *Chachamim* one may not. The reversal between *matzah* and *esrog* is deliberate — in each case the direction of the ruling follows from who holds the *maaser sheni* to be *mammon gavoah* or *mammon baalim*.

### Ownership Status

The conceptual foundation of this debate is the famous dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* over the ownership of *maaser sheni*. When *maaser sheni* is brought to Jerusalem and eaten there, who is the owner? The parallel case is *kodshim kalim* — *shelamim* and the like — which must also be eaten in Jerusalem. One who brings a *korban* has certain rights: the *korban* is credited to him, he is entitled to eat from it, and yet he cannot sell it or dispose of it in other ways. Is it then *mammon baalim* — truly his — or *mammon gavoah* — ultimately belonging to God?

The same question applies to *maaser sheni*. One separates it and brings it to Jerusalem, but the conceptual framing is that it has been given over to God — yet the owner still eats it. Do the restrictions (it may only be eaten in Jerusalem, it may only be used in specified ways) mark it as *mammon gavoah*, or do the practical rights of ownership — control, consumption, designation — mark it as *mammon hedyot*, belonging to the owner?

Rabbi Meir holds *maaser sheni* is *mammon gavoah* — God's produce, not the owner's. The *Chachamim* hold it is *mammon baalim* — it remains the owner's. This dispute, the Gemara explains, directly determines both the *challah* obligation and the *matzah* obligation, under the assumption that both require the item to belong to the person performing the *mitzvah*.

### Rav Pappa's Question

Rav Pappa raises a sharp question. He grants the *challah* case: the verse says *arisoteichem* — "your kneading troughs" — a possessive form that clearly demands the dough be yours. He grants the *esrog* case: the verse says *u-lekachtem lachem* — "you shall take for yourselves" — explicitly requiring ownership. But regarding *matzah*, he asks: *mi ketiv matzatechem*? Is there anywhere a verse that says "your *matzah*"? There is no such verse. So why should the ownership question matter for *matzah* at all? Even if the *matzah* is theoretically God's under Rabbi Meir's view, as long as one is permitted to eat it and is not stealing it, why should one not fulfill the obligation?

This question implicitly challenges the symmetry Rav Assi assumed across all three cases. The *challah* and *esrog* cases rest on explicit textual pegs; *matzah* has no comparable peg. What entitles us to import the ownership requirement there?

### Rava's Gezeirah Shavah

Rava — and some attribute this to Rav Yeimar bar Shalamya — answers with a *gezeirah shavah*: *lechem lechem*. The verse regarding *matzah* uses the phrase *lechem oni* — poor person's bread. The verse regarding *challah* uses the phrase *ve-hayah be-acholchem mi-lechem ha-aretz* — when you eat from the bread of the land, you shall separate *challah*. Since both use the word *lechem*, we draw an analogy: just as *challah* must come from *your* dough — *mishalchem* — so too *matzah* must come from *yours* — *mishalchem*.

This *gezeirah shavah* does more than link a definitional quality of bread (as was discussed the day before); it imports the ownership requirement from *challah* into *matzah*. The conceptual comparison made throughout the chapter now acquires a technical halakhic edge: whatever "yours" demands in the *challah* context, it demands equally in the *matzah* context.

One might note a related unaddressed question lurking in the background: the issue of *matzah ha-gezulah* — stolen *matzah* — and *mitzvah ha-ba'ah ba-aveirah* — a *mitzvah* performed through or intertwined with a transgression. These are prominent concerns in the third *perek* of Masechet Succah when discussing a stolen *lulav*, yet they are not raised directly in this *perek* in connection with either *gezel* or *matzah*. The focus here remains squarely on the *lechem* linkage and the ownership question it generates.

### Double 'Ariso'teichem'

The Gemara then considers whether the *baraita* that records the Rabbi Meir/*Chachamim* debate about *challah* of *maaser sheni* serves as support for Rav Assi's broader position. The Gemara deflects: that *baraita* only establishes the *challah* case directly — it does not automatically extend to *esrog* and *matzah*. The question is whether we can infer from the *challah* debate that the same dispute plays out across all three cases.

Here the Gemara introduces an important distinction. The Torah uses the word *arisoteichem* — "your kneading troughs" — twice in connection with *challah*. This double expression reinforces the ownership demand: not merely "yours" in the practical sense that you possess and control it, but "yours" in a more exacting technical sense, such that even *maaser sheni*, which you do practically control and are entitled to eat, is still excluded under Rabbi Meir because theoretically it is God's. Perhaps this doubled demand is unique to *challah*. If so, *esrog*, where *lachem* appears only once, and certainly *matzah*, where there is no *lachem* at all (before the *gezeirah shavah* is applied), might have a more lenient standard — and even Rabbi Meir might concede that *maaser sheni* suffices there.

Rav Assi's position, then, is that the ownership requirement does apply across all three cases. The *chiddush* is specifically in extending it to *matzah* by way of the *gezeirah shavah*.

---

## Matzah of Maaser Sheni

### R. Shimon ben Lakish

The Gemara now shifts to a creative question posed by Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: *mahu she-yeitzei adam yedei chovaso be-challah shel maaser sheni bi-Yerushalayim*? Can a person fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah* with *challah* that is also *maaser sheni*, eaten in Jerusalem?

The scenario: one brings *maaser sheni* grain to Jerusalem, makes it into dough, and separates *challah* from it before baking. The *challah* is given to a *kohen* (or the questioner is himself a *kohen*). This piece of dough now carries two halachic identities simultaneously — it is *challah* and it is *maaser sheni*. We established two days ago (based on the view of Rabbi Akiva) that *matzah* of plain *maaser sheni* can in principle fulfill the obligation, because were the *maaser sheni* to become *tamei*, it could be redeemed and eaten outside Jerusalem — meaning it has latent capacity to be eaten anywhere. We established elsewhere in the *Mishnah* that a *kohen* can fulfill the *matzah* obligation with *matzah* made from *challah*. If *challah* alone is fine and *maaser sheni* alone is fine, why should their combination be problematic?

### Tamei Status Problem

The Gemara first dispenses with the simpler case. According to Rabbi Yose HaGalili, who disputes Rabbi Akiva and holds that *maaser sheni matzah* can never fulfill the obligation, there is no question: if plain *maaser sheni* does not work, *challah* of *maaser sheni* certainly does not. The question only arises according to Rabbi Akiva.

According to Rabbi Akiva, plain *maaser sheni matzah* is permissible because, were it to become *tamei*, it could be redeemed and eaten outside Jerusalem — granting it theoretical accessibility to all dwelling places, as the verse requires. But the problem surfaces specifically when the *maaser sheni* is also *challah*. What happens when *challah* becomes *tamei*? It cannot be redeemed — it must be burned, like *terumah tme'ah*. The very scenario that makes *maaser sheni* workable (the possibility of *tumah* leading to redemption and broader availability) is blocked by the *challah* status. *Challah* that becomes *tamei* is consumed in fire, not consumed by a person. So perhaps this combination disqualifies the *matzah* after all.

### Hypothetical Arguments

Yet the Gemara entertains the opposing argument: *hoil ve-ilu lo kara aleha shem* — had one never designated it as *challah*, and had it become *tamei*, there would have been *heter be-moshavos*, permission to eat it anywhere. Since that hypothetical obtains, perhaps even now one fulfills the obligation.

This is a striking move: the argument essentially says, ignore the *challah* status, because in the abstract, without that designation, the *matzah* would be valid. Rashi explains the logic as follows: the *challah* status by itself does not disqualify something from the *matzah* obligation — a *kohen* may use *challah* for *matzah*. The *maaser sheni* status by itself also does not disqualify — Rabbi Akiva permits it. Neither status independently creates a problem. Therefore, the fact that they happen to converge should not create a disqualification. It is as though each status can be "bracketed" because on its own it causes no harm to the *matzah* obligation. Whether this line of reasoning is persuasive is precisely the Gemara's question.

The Gemara adds a complicating variant: *ikka de-amri* — some say the above case (original *maaser sheni* that is also *challah*) is in fact obviously permissible, and the real question is the next case.

### Purchased w/ Maaser Money

The more complex scenario involves *challah halakuach bekesef maaser sheni* — *challah* that was purchased with *maaser sheni* money rather than being originally *maaser sheni* produce. The mechanism: one redeems *maaser sheni* produce onto coins and brings the money to Jerusalem. There, one purchases *challah* from a *kohen* using those coins. The *challah* now carries *maaser sheni* status not because it originated as *maaser sheni* grain, but because it was acquired with *maaser sheni* money.

The question of what one may do with such food if it becomes *tamei* is disputed. The *Rabbanan* hold that food purchased with *maaser sheni* money may be redeemed if it becomes *tamei*, just like original *maaser sheni*. According to them, this case reduces to the earlier question and there is no new difficulty. But Rabbi Yehuda holds — as recorded in a *Mishnah* in Masechet Maaser Sheni — that food purchased with *maaser sheni* money that became *tamei* must be buried; it cannot be redeemed. His reasoning appears to be that derivative *kedushah* — the sanctity that attaches to something purchased with *maaser sheni* money — is weaker than the original *kedushah* of *maaser sheni* produce itself, and cannot transfer out through redemption the way the original can.

According to Rabbi Yehuda, then, even setting aside *challah*, one might simply ask: can *matzah* purchased with *maaser sheni* money fulfill the obligation at all? The problem of *maaser sheni* — its restriction to Jerusalem — is alleviated for Rabbi Akiva by the possibility of redemption following *tumah*. But if Rabbi Yehuda denies that possibility for purchased items, the *matzah* would be permanently restricted to Jerusalem and could never gain the theoretical universal accessibility the verse demands. And now add the *challah* status on top: if it becomes *tamei*, both its *challah* status and its derivative *maaser sheni* status independently block any resolution.

The Gemara frames this as: do we say *hoil ve-ilu lo lakuach hava* (had it not been purchased with *maaser sheni* money) *ve-hoil ve-lo kara lah shem* (and had it never been designated *challah*) — two hypothetical disregards — then it would be fine, and therefore even now it is fine? Or do we say *chad hoil amrinan u-trei hoil lo amrinan* — we can posit one counterfactual, but not two? Rashi's explanation of each *hoil*: the *challah* designation by itself is no problem for *matzah*; and the *maaser sheni* money origin, while problematic in Rabbi Yehuda's view, is only because it is derivative — had it been original *maaser sheni*, Rabbi Akiva would permit it. Bracketing each status individually, neither independently causes disqualification; only their intersection does. Whether both may simultaneously be bracketed is the open question.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava resolves: *shem maaser chad hu* — the identity of *maaser sheni* is a single unified category. Whether the *maaser sheni* status attaches because the item is original *maaser sheni* produce or because it was purchased with *maaser sheni* money, it is all one *maaser sheni* designation. Since *maaser sheni* as a category is permissible for the *matzah* obligation under Rabbi Akiva, the derivative form is no different, and the combination does not create a disqualification.

In summary, the Gemara explored three conceptual layers: (1) whether *maaser sheni matzah* can fulfill the obligation due to the restriction to Jerusalem; (2) whether the ownership question (*mammon gavoah* vs. *mammon baalim*) creates an additional problem; and (3) whether combining *maaser sheni* with *challah* — or with derivative *maaser sheni* — creates a compound problem greater than either part alone. Rava's inclination is that since each status independently does not obstruct the *matzah* obligation, their combination likewise does not.

---

## Chalos Todah & Nazir

### Mishnah Introduction

The final case in the *Mishnah* regarding unusual *matzah* statuses involves *chalos todah* and *rekikei nazir* — the loaves brought with a *korban todah* (thanksgiving offering) and the wafers brought with a *nazir*'s completion offering. A *korban todah* is accompanied by forty loaves, ten of which are *chametz* and thirty of which are *matzah*. A *nazir* who completes his term brings wafers that are also *matzah*. Both types are therefore *matzah* in form.

By way of context: on account of the *korban todah* requiring *chametz* loaves, the *Mizmor L'Todah* prayer is omitted from *Pesukei D'Zimra* throughout Pesach — including *erev Pesach* — since one cannot bring the *todah* bread then. The *matzah* portion of the *todah* bread, however, is what concerns us here.

The *Mishnah*'s ruling: if one made these *matzah* loaves for oneself (intending to use them as one's own *korban*), one cannot fulfill the *matzah* obligation with them. If one made them to sell in the marketplace (to potential buyers who would later bring the *korban*), one may fulfill the obligation with them. Crucially, the *Mishnah* is speaking of bread that has not yet been sanctified — it was prepared for the purpose of a *korban* but has not been formally consecrated. Once the buyer sanctifies it, the seller can no longer use it. But at the moment of making, the status is defined by intent, not yet by actual consecration.

### Rava's Derasha

The Gemara asks: *mena hanei milei* — what is the source for this disqualification? Rava derives it from the verse *u-shmartem et ha-matzos* — "you shall guard the *matzot*." This verse, he argues, requires that the guarding be *leshem matzah* — for the purpose of [the *mitzvah* of] *matzah*. *Matzah hamishtameres leshem matzah* — only *matzah* watched for the purpose of the *matzah* obligation qualifies. *Yatza* this case — which is watched to ensure it does not become *chametz* for the sake of the *korban*, not for the sake of the *matzah mitzvah*. Even though the bread is technically being protected from fermentation — because the *korban* requires *matzah* and not *chametz* — the intent of the guarding is directed toward the *korban*, not toward the *mitzvah* of *matzah* on the *seder* night.

This requires attention. Rashi, at the top of 38b, explains: *kol shimur she-ata mishamrah shelo tachmitz* — any guarding you perform to prevent fermentation — *hitkaven leshem matzah shel mitzvah* — must be directed toward its being *matzas mitzvah*. Preventing fermentation is necessary but not sufficient; the intent must be explicitly for the *mitzvah*.

This is a striking principle, and one might wonder why it is unique to *matzah*. Many *mitzvah* objects do not carry a *lishmah* requirement. A *sukkah* need only be built for shade; it need not be built for the purpose of the *mitzvah*, and it need not even be built by a Jew. A *lulav* and *esrog* have no such intent requirement. The answer is that this is not a general rule of *mitzvah* objects but a specific requirement derived from the particular verse *u-shmartem et ha-matzos*, which the Gemara reads as embedding a purposive demand into the guarding itself.

### Rav Yosef's Derasha

Rav Yosef offers a different derivation, from a different verse: *shivat yamim matzot tochelu* — "seven days you shall eat *matzah*." From the fact that the verse specifies seven days, Rav Yosef derives that the *matzah* must be of a type that *can* be eaten for seven days. *Matzah nechelet le-shiva yamim* qualifies; *yatza* this bread — which, once consecrated as part of a *korban todah* or *nazir* offering, can only be eaten for one day and the following night before becoming *notar* (leftover that may not be consumed) — does not qualify.

Both Rashi and Tosafot are compelled to clarify, in light of the later Gemara's treatment of the marketplace case, that we are speaking of bread not yet sanctified. The dough, at the time of its preparation, has not yet been formally consecrated. So how can one say it "can only be eaten for one day"? Rashi and Tosafot explain that Rav Yosef's criterion applies to the *intent* at the time of preparation: if the bread is made with the intent that it will ultimately only be usable for one day (because the maker intends it to become a *korban*), that intent-governed limitation disqualifies it — even before sanctification. If one makes the bread without that limiting intent (i.e., to sell in the marketplace, knowing it might not sell and might be kept for one's own use over the seven days of Pesach), then the bread is not disqualified on this ground.

This second approach is significant: it does not require that the *matzah* be prepared *leshem matzas mitzvah* — for the explicit sake of the *matzah* obligation. The problem is rather the negative intent of one-day limitation. Absent that negative intent, the *matzah* is permissible, without any affirmative requirement to have directed the guarding specifically toward the *mitzvah*.

The Gemara notes that a *baraita* can be adduced in support of each position: one *baraita* employs the *u-shmartem* verse in the manner of Rava, and another *baraita* employs the *shivat yamim* verse in the manner of Rav Yosef. Both derivations are thus supported by *tannaitic* sources.

### Kol Moshavos Query

Having established these reasons, the Gemara raises a challenge: *ve-teipok lei* — why not simply invoke the *bechol moshvoteichem* principle? The same criterion invoked earlier in the chapter — that *matzah* must be capable of being eaten in all dwelling places — should exclude *chalos todah* and *rekikei nazir* directly. Once consecrated as part of a *korban*, these breads can only be eaten in Jerusalem. Why do we need the novel derivations about *shimur* or *shivat yamim*?

### Nov & Givon History

Reish Lakish answers: from the very fact that the Gemara sought other reasons and did not simply invoke the *bechol moshvoteichem* criterion, we can derive that *chalos todah* and *rekikei nazir* are in fact *ne'echalim be-Nov u-ve-Givon* — they may be eaten in Nov and Givon. This requires explanation.

When the *Bnei Yisrael* entered *Eretz Yisrael*, there was an extended period before a permanent central sanctuary was established. During the fourteen years of conquest and division of the land, there were private altars (*bamot*). Then the *Mishkan* was established at Shilo, which functioned analogously to what Jerusalem would later become: a central location to which *korbanot* were brought, with the surrounding area serving as the designated eating zone. Then Shilo was destroyed, and there was a transitional period. The quasi-central places of worship during this period were Nov — the city of priests, familiar from the narratives of Shaul and David — and later Givon.

During the periods of Nov and Givon, the status was less formalized than at Shilo. Unlike Shilo, where eating of *korbanot* was geographically delimited, at Nov and Givon one could bring a *korban* at the central altar but eat the resulting meat and bread anywhere in Eretz Yisrael — *bechol arei Yisrael*. Therefore, the bread of a *korban todah* and the wafers of a *nazir* brought during the Nov and Givon periods could be eaten anywhere. Since there existed a period in Jewish history when these breads could be eaten in any location, they retain a theoretical classification as potentially universally edible — and therefore the *bechol moshvoteichem* criterion does not exclude them.

Tosafot acknowledges the tension: if we can reach back a millennium to the time of Nov and Givon to neutralize the *bechol moshvoteichem* concern, why could we not do the same for the earlier discussions about *maaser sheni* and its restriction to Jerusalem? Reish Lakish's answer is specific to the *todah* and *nazir* breads on account of their particular historical status during those transitional periods. The answer is admittedly somewhat far-reaching, but the Gemara requires it in order to preserve the marketplace/personal-use distinction — for if the *bechol moshvoteichem* criterion were operative, it would disqualify the bread regardless of who it was made for, and the distinction could not be maintained.

---

## Eliezer & Yehoshua

### Baraita: R. Ilai Query

A *baraita* records the following exchange. Rabbi Ilai related: I asked Rabbi Eliezer whether one may fulfill the obligation of *matzah* with *chalos todah* and *rekikei nazir*. Rabbi Eliezer replied: *lo shamati* — I have not received a tradition on this matter. This response is characteristically Rabbi Eliezer: he would not say anything he had not received by tradition, and absent a received tradition, the discussion was closed.

### R. Yehoshua's Tradition

Rabbi Ilai then went and asked before Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Yehoshua did have a received tradition: *harey amru* — they have said — that *chalos todah* and *rekikei nazir she-asa l'atzmo* — which one made for oneself — *ein adam yotzei bahem*, one does not fulfill the obligation. But *limkor ba-shuk* — if one made them to sell in the marketplace — *yotzei bahem*, one does fulfill the obligation.

### R. Eliezer's Acceptance

Rabbi Ilai returned and reported this tradition to Rabbi Eliezer. Upon hearing it, Rabbi Eliezer said: *Brit* — by covenant — *hen hen ha-devarim she-ne'emru le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — these are the very words transmitted to Moses at Sinai. He embraced the tradition as a genuine and authoritative *mesorah*, even though he himself had not possessed it. His response is notable: he did not independently hold the tradition, but once it was brought to him from Rabbi Yehoshua, he affirmed it as authentically *Halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*.

*Ikka de-amri* — some say — his response was in fact not a positive affirmation but a sharp critique. According to this reading, his statement was: by oath, these may be words *ne'emru le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — but *ve-lo ta'ama bah* — without any reason to them. He was questioning whether this could be a genuine transmitted tradition given that it makes no apparent sense. Why should it matter whether the bread was made for oneself or made for sale? What rational principle could account for such a distinction? If it were Rabbi Eliezer's own tradition, the absence of an apparent rationale would not matter — a tradition is a tradition. But receiving it from elsewhere, without a reason to validate it, gave him pause.

### Rava's Intent Explanation

The Gemara presses: *ve-ta'ama mai* — what is the reason? Rava explains. When one makes the bread *le-shuk* — for the marketplace — *imluchi memlach* — one has second thoughts. One says to oneself: if it sells, it sells; and if it does not sell — *eipuk bei ana* — I will use it for myself for the *matzah* obligation on Pesach. This inner reservation, this hedging of intent, means that even when the bread is made, the maker has in the back of his mind the possibility that it will ultimately be used for the *mitzvah* of *matzah*. Some level of intent toward *matzat mitzvah* is present from the outset.

This resolution also explains why the Gemara had to rule out other reasons — the oil, the restriction to Jerusalem — as the primary grounds for disqualification. If the oil content made it intrinsically *matzah ashirah*, or if the geographic restriction were the operative concern, then intent would be irrelevant — the bread would be disqualified regardless of whether it was made for personal use or for sale. Only if the problem is purely one of intent — specifically, the intent behind the guarding (Rava's derivation) or the intent behind the one-day limitation (Rav Yosef's derivation) — can the marketplace scenario serve as a corrective. When selling in the marketplace, one's intent is not unidimensionally directed toward a *korban*; the possibility of personal use for the *mitzvah* is held in mind, and that latent intention is sufficient.

The converse: if one made the bread explicitly for oneself — intending to use it personally as a *korban* — that unambiguous intent directed toward the *zevach*, without any reservation about possibly eating it as *matzas mitzvah*, disqualifies it. The relevant point for practical purposes is the question of whether protecting *matzah* from becoming *chametz* is sufficient on its own, or whether explicit intention directed toward the *mitzvah* of *matzah* is additionally required. That question does not receive a final definitive ruling here, but at minimum one of the positions in the Gemara — Rava's derivation from *u-shmartem* — clearly establishes that intent toward *matzas mitzvah* is indispensable, and that intent directed only toward avoiding *chametz* for the sake of a *korban* does not suffice.

---

---

# Pesachim 39

## Five Vegetables

### Intro to Maror

Having spent several pages on *matzah* — its special status regarding *ma'aser sheni*, the question of what constitutes *lechem*, the specifics of *lechem oni*, comparisons to *challah*, and what substances are capable of becoming *chametz* — the Gemara now turns to a more focused discussion: *maror*. We open at the top of 39a.

### Mishnah: Five Plants

The Mishnah opens: *ve'eilu yerakot she'adam yotzei bahen yedei chovato bapesach* — these are the vegetables with which one fulfills the obligation of *maror* on Pesach. The five are: *chazeret*, *tamcha*, *charchavina*, *ulshin*, and *maror*. It is worth noting at the outset that the Torah uses the term *merorim* (Numbers 9:11) — bitter herbs in the plural — which is not a reference to any particular species but rather to a category of things that are bitter. The Mishnah's identification of precisely five varieties is therefore itself a subject for the Gemara to explore.

The Mishnah continues: *yotzin bahen bein lachin bein yeveshim* — one fulfills the obligation whether the vegetables are moist or dry. However, if they are pickled (*kevusha*), that is not acceptable — pickling overwhelms the plant's own taste and presumably eliminates whatever bitterness it had. Nor does one fulfill the obligation with *shelukin* (double-cooked, almost dissolved) or *mevushalim* (cooked), all of which significantly alter the taste. The Mishnah also states that one can combine smaller amounts of different species to make up a *kezayit*, and that the obligation can be fulfilled with the stalk (*klach*) of the plant, not only with its leaves.

### Ma'aser Status

The Mishnah closes by noting that *maror* of *demai* status (produce from which one is uncertain whether *terumot u'ma'asrot* have been separated), or *ma'aser rishon* from which *terumah* has been taken, or *ma'aser sheni* and *hekdesh* that have been redeemed, all satisfy the obligation — paralleling what we saw by *matzah*. One point worth flagging: the obligation of *terumot u'ma'asrot* for vegetables is entirely rabbinic in nature, meaning that whatever *ma'aser* status attaches to these plants is rabbinic at most. That distinction will become significant later.

---

## Plant Identifications

### Chazeret & Ulshin

The Gemara begins identifying the five plants. *Chazeret hi chasa* — *chazeret* is *chasa*, ordinarily understood to be a type of lettuce. Rashi gives the Old French *letuga*, which clearly corresponds to the Latin *Lactuca sativa*, the standard botanical term for lettuce. The Gemara then identifies *ulshin* as *hindivi*. Rashi describes it as a type of weed or herb, while the resemblance between *hindivi* and the word "endive" is itself suggestive. Indeed, Cichorium endivia — endive, chicory, and escarole are all of the same species — is the identification offered by modern commentators on the basis of both Rashi's language and the Gemara's term.

### Tamcha & Charchavina

For *tamcha*, Rabba bar Bar Chana simply says *tamchata shemah* — that is its name — which is not especially illuminating. Rashi's identification (*maruvya*) has led some to understand *tamcha* as horehound, while others identify it as horseradish. The distinction matters: horseradish is a root vegetable, while horehound is an herbaceous plant with a bitter, pungent flavor.

*Charchavina* is identified by Rabbi Shimon Lakish as *atzvata d'dikla* — a type of vine that grows around a palm tree. Modern botanical commentators have suggested Eryngium creticum, a perennial plant found in Israel, though this identification does not obviously match the description of something climbing a palm.

As for the fifth plant, *maror* (or *meririta*), Rashi offers *ampurya* or *vipupres*, and various modern translations suggest common sow thistle (Sonchus oleraceus) or a species of wild lettuce. The honest assessment is that none of these identifications is certain.

This uncertainty has real historical and practical implications. For many generations, the Ashkenazic practice was to use horseradish for *maror* — likely reflecting both the unavailability of the more ancient plants in northern Europe and a preference for something with an unmistakable sharpness. In more recent decades, rabbinic authorities have increasingly stressed that Romaine lettuce — as a form of *chazeret* — is actually the preferred vegetable according to the Gemara itself. Today, many fulfill the obligation with both.

### Tannaim on Plants

The Gemara introduces several tannaitic traditions that expand the list. Bar Kappara teaches a list of vegetables that includes *ulshin*, *tamcha*, *charchalin* (not *charchavina* as in our Mishnah), and *chazeret* — omitting *maror* by name but apparently substituting *charchalin* as a variant. Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may fulfill the obligation with both wild endives (*ulshei sadei*) and cultivated endives (*ulshei gina*) — the innovation being that even the wild variety is acceptable, equivalent to the cultivated form and to *chazeret*.

Rabbi Meir adds three further plants: *atzvata*, *tura*, and *mar yeruar*. Rabbi Yose responds that *atzvata* and *tura* are actually the same plant, and that *mar* is itself *yeruar* — so Rabbi Meir's three reduce to two. The Gemara cites a textual variant on the side suggesting the words mean something sharp or singular, but in any reading, Rabbi Yose is reducing the apparent additions.

Rabbi Ila reports in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that even *arkavalim* — which Rashi describes as some kind of vine — is acceptable. Significantly, Rabbi Ila adds that he searched through all of Rabbi Eliezer's students to find corroboration for having heard this ruling, and found none. He then approached Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov, who conceded the point — though it is not entirely clear whether he was conceding that Rabbi Eliezer had said so, or merely that he agreed the ruling was correct.

### Shmuel's List

The school of Shmuel (*tana d'vei Shmuel*) offers yet another list: *chazeret*, *ulshin*, *tamcha*, *charchavina*, *charginnim* (identified by some as oregano — a plant whose Aramaic name bears resemblance to the word), and *hardofnin* (which Rashi describes as a kind of wormwood; the *Arukh* identifies it as oleander). Rabbi Yehuda adds two subspecies of *chazeret*: *chazeret yulin* and *chazeret galin*, noting that these too count as valid — the novelty being the inclusion of these particular variants, which are on par with the standard *chazeret* already listed.

---

## Criteria: Bitter Herbs

### Sap Criterion

The proliferation of tannaitic opinions raises a fundamental question: what principle underlies all of these identifications? Without a clear criterion, one cannot determine whether a given plant is valid for *maror*. The Gemara now turns to this.

Rabbi Yehuda states: *kol sheyesh lo saraf* — any plant that, when cut, exudes a type of sap. If you cut open a lettuce leaf, for instance, you can see a milky liquid along the spine. The difficulty is understanding why this criterion is significant. Does the presence of sap necessarily indicate a bitter taste? The Gemara will address this, but even before that, the question stands: what exactly are we trying to identify here? If the criterion is ultimately bitterness, why not simply say so?

Part of the answer may lie in the imprecision of taste as a subjective experience. The categories of bitter, sour, sharp, and pungent overlap considerably. Horseradish, for instance, would be described by most people as sharp or hot, not bitter in the way that black coffee or grapefruit peel is bitter. Given these difficulties of classification, it is understandable that the Gemara seeks more objective, measurable criteria.

### Pale Face

Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka adds a different criterion: *kol she-panav makhsifin* — any plant whose face (surface) is pale. Rashi explains that this means not a dark green but a lighter, more washed-out shade. A leek, for instance, would exemplify this. Again, the connection to bitterness is not immediately obvious, but the criterion is at least more visually verifiable than taste alone.

### Both Criteria

*Acherim* then say: *kol yerek mar yesh lo saraf u-fanav makhsifin* — any bitter herb has both features: it exudes sap and has a pale face. This formulation synthesizes the two individual opinions and claims that bitter herbs are characterized by the conjunction of both properties.

### Halakhic Ruling

Rabbi Yochanan draws the conclusion: from all of these views, we learn that bitter herbs (*yerek mar*) have sap and a pale face. He presents this as something that follows from the totality of the opinions, reading them as complementary rather than contradictory. The logic, however, requires care: showing that all valid *maror* plants share these two features does not by itself prove that every plant with these features is valid *maror*. The inference runs in one direction. Nevertheless, the practical thrust is that these criteria help identify eligible plants more reliably than relying on subjective taste assessments alone.

Rav Yehuda rules: *halakha ke-Acherim* — we follow the view of *Acherim*, meaning both criteria together define the eligible category.

---

## Chazeret Preferred

### Ravina & Rav Acha

With the criteria established, the Gemara turns to a brief but instructive episode. Ravina found Rav Acha the son of Rava searching for *marisa* — the fifth item on the list, which may correspond to something more pungent or sharp in character. Ravina challenged him: why specifically that one? Because it is more bitter (*meririn tfei*)? But the Mishnah lists *chazeret* first, and primacy in a tannaitic list typically signals preference. Moreover, both the teaching of the school of Shmuel and the explicit ruling of Rabbi Oshaya place *chazeret* at the top and identify it as the preferred species for the *mitzvah*.

### Symbolism: Chasa

Rava then provides an explanation for why *chazeret* is preferred that goes beyond technical eligibility. *Mai chazeret? — mai chasa?* — what is the significance of *chasa*? *De-chas Rachmana alan* — that God (*Rachmana*) had compassion (*chas*) on us. The name *chasa* evokes *chesed* or compassion, and so using it at the Seder carries a symbolic resonance beyond its botanical properties. Since all valid *maror* species are in principle equivalent in fulfilling the obligation, choosing one that also conveys meaningful symbolism adds an additional dimension. This kind of symbolic layering is, of course, fundamental to the *Seder* — indeed, it is what the *Seder* is built upon.

### Maror Symbolism

The Gemara deepens the symbolism further. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: why were the Egyptians compared to *maror*? The verse does not explicitly compare the Egyptians to *maror*; the language is *va-yimararu et chayeihem* — they embittered their lives — and it is the actions of the Egyptians that are described as embittering. The teaching, then, is this: *ma maror zeh she-tchilato rach ve-sofo kasheh* — just as *maror* begins soft and ends hard, so too the Egyptians: *af Mitzrim tchilatan rakah ve-sofan kashah* — at first they were softer toward the Israelites, and in the end they were harder.

Rashi understands this to refer to the physical plant itself: the stalk begins soft and gradually hardens as the plant matures. Others read it as referring to taste — that lettuce begins mild and becomes more bitter as the leaves mature. Either way, the symbolism is apt: the Egyptian enslavement did not begin overnight. The process was gradual, moving from welcome to exploitation to brutal oppression, in the manner of a slow tightening — not unlike the way the Nuremberg laws and similar mechanisms historically have worked, drawing their targets in incrementally before the full weight of subjugation becomes apparent.

This observation reinforces the preference for *chazeret* over something like the fifth, sharper plant: the symbolism of *chazeret* — a soft beginning that becomes harder — captures the nature of Egyptian oppression more faithfully than something that simply overwhelms with immediate sharpness. Following this exchange, Rav Acha conceded: *hadri bi* — I retract; I will use the lettuce.

---

## Maror Definition

### Is Maror Plant?

Rav Chumi raises a foundational question to Abaye: *mimai de-hai maror min yerak hu?* — what makes us assume that *maror* must be a vegetable at all? The Torah says *merorim*, which simply means something bitter. Perhaps, he suggests, one could even use *merirta de-chufya* — the bitter part of a fish called *chufya*. Who says it must come from a plant?

### Kal Vachomer

The Gemara answers through an analogy to *matzah*: *dumya de-matzah* — just as *matzah* must come from something that grows from the ground (*gidulei karka*), so too *maror* must come from the ground. The Gemara then asks: even granting that it must come from the ground, perhaps it could be from a tree — specifically from something like *hirdof*, a plant (Rashi notes it may be toxic to animals) that grows as bark or timber? Again the answer is *dumya de-matzah*: just as *matzah* comes from *min zera'im* — from something planted and harvested as a crop rather than a multi-year tree — so too *maror*. And finally: even granting all of that, perhaps the bitter thing could come from something like *hirzifu*, a plant that may be mildly toxic and not normally considered edible? Again: *dumya de-matzah* — just as *matzah* is something one would purchase with *ma'aser* money, i.e., a food considered ordinarily edible, so too *maror* must be something that qualifies as a normal food, purchasable with *ma'aser* money.

Through this chain of *kal va-chomer*-style reasoning, the Gemara delimits the category: *maror* must be a plant, not a tree, and must be ordinarily edible.

Rava bar Bar Chana then asks Abaye: even granting that *maror* is a plant, perhaps only one species is meant? The Torah says *merorim* in the plural — does that give us two, or many? *Dumya de-matzah*: just as *matzah* may be made from many types of grain, so *maror* encompasses many types of plants, not a single species.

### Planted in One Bed

Rav Huna in the name of Rav adds: all the vegetables eligible for *maror* can be planted together in a single bed (*aruga achat*) without violating *kilayim*. The implication is that since they all share the designation *maror*, they are treated as a related category. The Gemara, however, pushes back immediately.

### Kilayim Objection

The Gemara cites a Mishnah in tractate Kilayim: *chazeret* and *chazeret galim* may be planted together; *ulshin* and *ulshei sadeh* may be planted together; *kerishin* and *kerishei sadeh* similarly; and so on with *kusbar*, *chardal*, and certain gourds. Each pair may be planted together because the two members of each pair are the same species. But the Mishnah is clearly structured in pairs — and the inference is unmistakable: *chazeret* and *ulshin* may *not* be planted together. Rav himself confirmed that the Mishnah is to be read as pairs (*zugot zugot*), not as a blanket permission to combine everything.

### Vegetables Allowed

So what did Rav mean when he said all the *maror* vegetables can be planted in one bed? The Gemara resolves this: *nizra'im ke-hilchatan* — they may be planted in accordance with the general rule for diverse species, namely the well-known arrangement of five species in a six-by-six *tefach* bed. In such an arrangement, four species occupy the four sides or corners and a fifth occupies the center (or similar configurations), with sufficient visual separation that *kilayim* is not violated.

But this rule is already stated explicitly in the Mishnah in Kilayim — so what does Rav add? The *chiddush* is that one might have thought this rule applies only to grain (*zera'im* in the sense of crops like wheat), while vegetables, being larger and drawing more nutrients from the soil, might require additional separation. Rav teaches that vegetables are no different — they can be arranged in the same five-in-a-bed configuration. In fact, a Mishnah in Kilayim explicitly states the opposite concern: that *all types of seeds* (*kol minei zra'im*) cannot be in one bed, while *all types of vegetables* (*kol minei yerakot*) can be, following the proper arrangement. So vegetables are actually more lenient than grains in this regard, and Rav's statement confirms that the *maror* vegetables fall into this lenient category.

### Chazeret Space

The Gemara raises one remaining complication specific to *chazeret*. One might have thought that *chazeret* requires more space than other vegetables, because of the property already noted in connection with the symbolism of *maror*: *sofo lehakshot* — it eventually hardens and thickens as it matures. As it grows larger, it takes up more room, potentially creating a *kilayim* problem that other vegetables do not. Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Chanina had stated that a cabbage stalk, once it thickens and hardens, requires the space of a *beit rova* — considerably more than a standard planting. Perhaps *chazeret*, which similarly hardens over time, would require comparable extra space. The Gemara concludes that it does not — though the precise reason for distinguishing *chazeret* from cabbage in this regard is not fully spelled out and remains somewhat difficult.

---

## Moist vs. Dry

### Rav Chisda: Dry

The Mishnah had stated that one fulfills the obligation with *maror* whether it is moist or dry, and also with the stalk (*klach*). Rav Chisda draws a distinction: *lo shanu ela be-klach* — the rule permitting dry *maror* applies only to the stalk that has dried out. But if it is the leaves that are dried, then only moist leaves fulfill the obligation, not dry ones — because a dried-out leaf has essentially lost its taste.

### Meir vs. Chachamim

The Gemara cites a *braita* that stages the dispute more explicitly. Rabbi Meir says: one fulfills the obligation with them and with their stalks, whether moist or dry — applying the permission for dryness to both leaves and stalks. The *Chachamim* say: moist, yes; dried, no. The plain reading of both the Mishnah and the *braita* seems to address leaves, since stalks are introduced separately — making Rav Chisda's reading, which confines the "dry is permitted" rule to the stalk, somewhat forced. The Gemara defends it nonetheless, reading the Mishnah as structured so that "moist or dry" is a description of the stalk that follows, not of the leaves mentioned earlier.

One observation worth noting: dried herbs — oregano being the classic example — actually concentrate flavor. Whether drying intensifies the bitterness of something like lettuce specifically is another matter, and an open empirical question.

### Wilted Permitted

Both Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* agree on one middle category: *kemushin* — wilted. If the *maror* has wilted (begun to lose moisture but not fully dried out), it remains acceptable. This is clearly a category that applies to leaves, which further complicates the attempt to confine the moist/dry discussion entirely to stalks. The agreement also extends in the negative direction: pickled (*kevusha*) and double-cooked (*shelukin*) and boiled (*mevushalim*) are all invalid according to both.

### Must Retain Taste

The *braita* concludes with a general principle: *kol sheyesh bo ta'am maror yotzin bo* — anything that retains the bitter taste fulfills the obligation; *kol she'ein bo ta'am maror ein yotzin bo* — if the bitter taste has been lost, whether through processing or drying, one does not fulfill the obligation. This formulation places taste at the center — the various processing modes (boiling, pickling, drying) are problematic precisely because they eliminate or overwhelm the characteristic bitterness.

---

## Ma'aser Sheni

### Question Posed

Rami bar Chama raises a question: *mahu sheyeitzei adam yedei chovato be-maror shel ma'aser sheni bi-Yerushalayim?* — can one fulfill the obligation of *maror* with produce that has the status of *ma'aser sheni* while in Jerusalem? The issue parallels the earlier discussion about *matzah*: *ma'aser sheni* may be eaten in Jerusalem, but its consumption is restricted to that location. By contrast, the verse *bechol moshvoteichem* (Exodus 12:20) requires *matzah* to be something that can in principle be eaten anywhere.

### Rabbi Akiva View

The question is posed against the background of two tannaitic positions we have already encountered. According to Rabbi Akiva, who permitted *ma'aser sheni matzah* in Jerusalem, there is no question about *maror*: *aliba de-Rabbi Akiva lo tiba'i lach* — for Rabbi Akiva, if *ma'aser sheni* is acceptable for *matzah*, which is a biblical obligation (*d'oraisa*), then certainly it is acceptable for *maror*, which — as the Gemara will explain — carries a rabbinic status (*derabbanan*).

### Yosi HaGlili View

The genuine question arises according to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, who held that *ma'aser sheni matzah* in Jerusalem does *not* fulfill the obligation. The question is whether the same stringency applies to *maror*. Two possibilities present themselves: either the disqualification of *ma'aser sheni* applies specifically to *matzah* because *matzah* is a biblical obligation, and the weaker status of *maror* means it is not subject to the same restriction; or, conversely, whatever standards the rabbis enacted for rabbinic obligations were modeled after the biblical ones — *kol de-tikkun rabbanan ke-ein d'oraisa tikkun* — and so *maror* would be treated the same as *matzah*.

### Rava's Ruling

Rava rules: *mistavra matzah maror* — the logical connection between *matzah* and *maror* holds. Just as we derived numerous properties of *maror* from *matzah* (it must be a plant, must be edible, etc.), so here: if *matzah* of *ma'aser sheni* is invalid in Jerusalem according to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, then *maror* of *ma'aser sheni* is likewise invalid.

### Rashi Explains

The phrase "matzah is *d'oraisa*; maror is *derabbanan*" invites interpretation. One reading — which Rashi rejects — is that the contrast refers to the current state of the obligations: nowadays, the *mitzvah* of *matzah* is biblical while *maror* is only rabbinic (since *maror* is tied to the *korban pesach* and therefore no longer obligatory on a biblical level). Rashi rejects this reading because if that were the meaning, the Gemara should have said so explicitly. Moreover, the case of *ma'aser sheni* in Jerusalem is inherently a Temple-era scenario, so the discussion is set at a time when both *matzah* and *maror* were biblically operative.

Rashi therefore reads *matzah d'oraisa* and *maror derabbanan* as referring not to the level of the eating-obligation but to the level of the *ma'aser* obligation itself. *Matzah* is made from grain, and the obligation to tithe grain (*terumot u'ma'asrot*) is biblical. *Maror* consists of vegetables, and the obligation to tithe vegetables is entirely rabbinic. Thus the *ma'aser sheni* status of the grain used for *matzah* is a more serious biblical-level restriction, whereas the *ma'aser sheni* status of the *maror* vegetables is only rabbinic — and perhaps, on that basis, Rabbi Yosi HaGlili might be more lenient about *maror* even while being stringent about *matzah*.

### Conceptual Issue

This raises a striking conceptual point. According to Rashi, we are discussing a Temple-era scenario: one is in Jerusalem eating the *korban pesach* together with *matzah* and *maror*. The *matzah* of *ma'aser sheni* cannot be taken out of Jerusalem; neither can the *maror*. The *korban pesach* itself must be eaten in Jerusalem. Yet the Gemara — following the argument that the *matzah* must be something eligible to be eaten *bechol moshvoteichem*, anywhere — holds that even in the Temple-era context, *ma'aser sheni matzah* may not satisfy the obligation. And now, following Rava, the same applies to *maror*.

This is a striking formulation: one is eating one's *korban pesach* in Jerusalem, which by definition can only be eaten in Jerusalem, and yet the *matzah* and *maror* eaten alongside it must in principle be edible outside Jerusalem. The requirement of *bechol moshvoteichem* governs the *matzah* even when the *matzah* is being eaten together with something that is itself Jerusalem-restricted.

A further conceptual question emerges from the Mishnah itself. Our Mishnah discusses a *kezayit* of *maror*, implying it is treated as an independent *mitzvah* requiring a standard measure of eating. But biblically, *maror* is not an independent obligation — it is an accompaniment to the *korban pesach*: *al matzot u-merorim yochluhu* (Numbers 9:11) describes the *korban pesach* as the primary act, with *matzah* and *maror* as its accompaniments. Several *Rishonim* hold that biblically one does not need a *kezayit* of *maror* to fulfill that verse — the presence of any *maror* alongside the *korban pesach* suffices. The independent *mitzvah* of *maror* with its *kezayit* requirement is a rabbinic enactment for post-Temple life. The fact that our Mishnah discusses *maror* and its *kezayit* measure as a standalone topic — without a corresponding Mishnah about the *korban pesach* eating — is itself consistent with the understanding that the Mishnah is addressing the rabbinic, post-Temple obligation rather than the biblical accompaniment to the *korban*.

---

## Soaking Bran

### Mishnah: Soaking

The Gemara now pivots back to *chametz* concerns — interrupting what had been a lengthy discussion of *matzah* and *maror* to return to the broader tractate topic. The Mishnah states: *ein shorin et ha-mursan la-tarnagolim* — one may not soak bran in water to use as feed for chickens, since contact with water will cause it to become *chametz*. The *chametz* concern is not limited to intentional bread-making; any grain left in contact with water is subject to fermentation.

### Chalut Permitted

However, *chalut* is permitted: if one scalds the bran with already-boiling water, the heat arrests the fermentation process. This was discussed earlier in the context of the general rules about *chametz*: *chalut* — grain or flour poured into or covered with actively boiling water — is cooked before fermentation can begin.

The Mishnah similarly prohibits a woman from soaking bran to take to the bathhouse for cosmetic use as a skin treatment. However, if her skin is already dry, she may rub dry bran directly against the skin — the prohibition is specifically against soaking it in water first.

### Chewing Wheat

A person may not chew wheat and apply the resulting paste as a poultice on a wound, since the chewing process introduces moisture and warmth that would promote fermentation. All of these cases illustrate the same underlying principle: any combination of grain and water, left without immediately applying heat sufficient to stop fermentation, creates *chametz*.

---

## No Chametz: Baked

### Three Methods

A *braita* now lists three processes that prevent *chametz* formation: if the grain has been baked (*afuy*), cooked (*mevushal*), or scalded (*chalut*) — specifically with boiling water (*shechalato be-rotchin*) — it cannot become *chametz*.

### Baking vs. Cooking

The Gemara challenges the inclusion of *mevushal*: if you place grain in water before it reaches a boil and cook it slowly, fermentation has time to begin before the cooking is complete — *ad de-mivashil lei machma* — by the time it is cooked, it has already fermented. This seemingly undermines the claim that cooking prevents *chametz*.

### Gebrochts

Rav Pappa resolves this: the *braita* is not describing slow-cooking of raw grain. Rather, it is describing the case of *ha-afuy she-bishlo* — something already baked that is subsequently cooked in water. Once grain has been baked, it cannot ferment; cooking it afterward poses no *chametz* risk. Rav Pappa identifies this as the subject of the entire *braita*: baked goods immersed in liquid — the phenomenon known as *gebrochts*. The halakhic conclusion is that this is permitted.

### Dripping Water

A further *braita* cites Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda: flour upon which water drips continuously — *kol ha-yom kulo* — does not become *chametz* as a result. The constant agitation or contact prevents the fermentation process from taking hold, analogous to the principle that continuously kneaded dough does not ferment. Rav Pappa adds: this applies only when the dripping is truly continuous, *tip la-chad tip* — drop immediately following drop, with no pause.

### Vatika

Regarding *vatika* — a food item made from flour — a dispute emerges. One source permits it; a *braita* prohibits it. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the permissive ruling applies when *vatika* is prepared with oil and salt, with no water involved (*de-avdi be-mishcha u-milcha*), since oil does not cause fermentation (*mei peirot ein machmitzin*). The prohibition applies when it is prepared with water (*de-avdi be-maya u-milcha*).

### Gebrochts Concern

Mar Zutra adds a practical caution that reveals the underlying concern behind *gebrochts* restrictions. One should not thicken a pot of soup with roasted grain (*kimcha d'avishna*), even though we have established that already-baked grain cannot become *chametz*. The reason: *dilma lo bishal shapir* — perhaps the grain was not roasted sufficiently. If some flour was undercooked, placing it in warm liquid could cause those insufficiently roasted particles to ferment. This is precisely the logic behind the *gebrochts* concern: the *halakha* is that baked goods in liquid do not become *chametz*, but the practical worry is that not every piece was thoroughly baked, and residual raw flour in contact with liquid could ferment. The actual *halakha* does not prohibit *gebrochts*, but Mar Zutra's caution — that one should not rely on roasting being complete — shows exactly where the concern originates.

---

---

# Pesachim 40

## Chalitah & Chametz

### Gebrochts Overview

Today's daf is Pesachim 40, and we begin at the very bottom of 39b. The preceding discussion had moved from *matzah* and *maror* back to concerns about *chametz*: specifically, the practice of putting grain in water to feed chickens, and the various worries about fermentation that arise from bringing grain into contact with liquid. The *gemara* established the important principle that once grain has been baked, roasted, or even scalded, it can no longer become *chametz*. At the same time, the *gemara* closed with a ruling that a certain type of roasted grain should not be added as a thickener to soup, because it may not have been roasted thoroughly enough and could still ferment — and that concern is precisely the concern that underlies *gebrochts*. The *gebrochts* custom extends even to baked *matzos*, reflecting an anxiety that perhaps the process was not one hundred percent effective and some residual concern remains. This is the theme the *gemara* now continues.

### Rav Yosef's Scalding

*Amar Rav Yosef*: a person should not scald — that is, submerge grain in boiling hot water as a means of cooking it rapidly before it has a chance to become *chametz* — two kernels of wheat simultaneously. Why? *Dilma azla chada v'yatva b'tzira'ei d'chaverta v'lo salik lehu dikula d'maya* — perhaps one kernel will lodge itself in the crack of the other, and the stream of boiling water will fail to penetrate that area, leaving part of a kernel exposed to water that never reached the temperature needed to prevent fermentation. In other words, the two overlapping kernels create a kind of *chatzitza*, a barrier, that defeats the very mechanism on which *chalitah* relies. This makes it clear that *chalitah* demands that every kernel be completely separate from every other — and one can readily understand, in light of such concerns, why later authorities became reluctant to permit *chalitah* at all.

Indeed, the *Shulchan Aruch* rules that nowadays we cannot trust anyone to perform *chalitah* correctly, and therefore we may not rely on it as a method of avoiding *chametz* — if one performed *chalitah*, one must still assume the grain became *chametz*. It is worth noting, however, that one of the later *Acharonim* — the *Chai Adam*, if memory serves — discusses the exceptional historical circumstance in which Jews were required to prepare food for quartered troops over *Pesach* and had virtually no alternatives. In such straits, he recommends relying on *chalitah*. This is not a routine leniency; it is an acknowledgment that in the absence of any other option, one may fall back on what the *gemara* considered theoretically sound, even if current practice rejects it. The underlying issue, it seems, is not a genuine uncertainty about technique — it does not take great expertise to ensure that water is boiling — but rather a heightened sensitivity to *chametz* that later generations adopted as a matter of religious temperament rather than technical incapacity.

### Abaye's Roasting

*V'amar Abaye*: Abaye adds a related caution regarding dry roasting. One should not roast two ears of wheat — two stalks with the kernels still on them — next to one another simultaneously, even without the involvement of any external water. Why? *Dilma nafik maya mehai u'ba l'idach* — perhaps there will be water runoff from one, since grain has an inherent moisture content, and that runoff will be absorbed by the other. *V'ati lidei chimutz* — and it may come to ferment.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenged this position sharply. *Ei hachi afilu chada nami* — if that is the concern, then one should not even be able to roast a single stalk. Why? *Dilma nafik mehai reisha u'ba l'idach reisha* — the water will run off from the top of the stalk and be absorbed by the bottom, or from one end to another within the same ear. If moisture content is the problem, there is no obvious reason why even a single ear of grain should be safe. Rava's point is that Abaye's concern, taken seriously, renders any roasting of wheat kernels impossible — a conclusion that seems untenable.

### Mei Peirot Doctrine

*Ela amar Rava* — Rava resolves the problem differently. He says: *mei peirot ninhu* — the water runoff from grain kernels is *mei peirot*, the liquid intrinsic to a fruit or grain, and *mei peirot einan machmitzin* — *mei peirot* does not cause fermentation. The overwhelming consensus of the *Rishonim* and *Poskim* is that grain mixed only with its own intrinsic liquid, without the addition of water, does not become *chametz* at all. Reading Rava through that lens, his argument is that water running off from wheat kernels during roasting is not water in any problematic sense — it is the grain's own juice, and it cannot produce *chametz*. The concern Abaye raised simply does not exist.

What, then, was Abaye's position? The deeper question may be what qualifies as *mei peirot*. Fruit juice — orange juice, for example — contains water as a component, but is fundamentally something other than water. Grain moisture, by contrast, is largely H₂O that was absorbed from rain and the environment and is now being released. Whether absorbed water that exits the kernel retains the character of *mei peirot* or reverts to plain water is, arguably, the crux of the debate between Abaye and Rava.

### Flow vs. Absorption

*V'hadar beh Abaye* — the *gemara* records that Abaye reversed his position. He does not, however, accept Rava's *mei peirot* reasoning. His reversal rests on a different principle: *d'chol agav madleihu* — as long as water is still flowing and running off, *lo machmitz*, it does not ferment. The key distinction is between water that flows across or off a surface and water that is absorbed and sits in contact with the grain. This principle has a useful parallel in the laws of *kashring* meat: one salts meat on an incline precisely so that the blood drawn out runs off rather than pooling beneath it. Even if the runoff from an upper piece strikes a lower piece, as long as it continues flowing away, we do not assume it is absorbed. Abaye applies the same logic here: even if the water released during roasting drips onto adjacent parts of the same ear or neighboring kernels, as long as it is in motion and draining away, it will not be absorbed and will not produce *chametz*.

### Pot Orientation

How do we know Abaye reversed himself? Because Abaye himself subsequently taught: *hai chatzva de'avishna* — a pot used for roasting grain: if it is placed upside down in the oven (*sechifa*), it is permitted, because whatever moisture runs off the grain drains away freely. If placed right-side up (*zekifa*), it is forbidden, because the released moisture will collect at the bottom of the pot and pose a *chametz* concern.

The very fact that Abaye permits the upside-down configuration reveals that he has changed his mind — after all, even in an inverted pot with multiple kernels, the moisture drips from one kernel onto another as it flows downward. Since Abaye permits this, he must now accept that flowing water does not cause absorption. What evidently prompted the reversal was Rava's challenge: if you cannot roast two stalks together you cannot roast even one stalk, and since nobody has ever questioned the basic permissibility of roasting grain, the concern must not operate as Abaye initially feared.

Rava, for his part, rules that even an upright pot is permitted — *mei peirot ninhu*, *mei peirot ein machmitzin* — because whatever collects at the bottom is still *mei peirot* and cannot ferment. The practical upshot is that Abaye permits the upside-down configuration for reasons of flowing water, while Rava permits even the upright configuration on the grounds of *mei peirot*.

---

## Lesisa (Bran Removal)

### Lesisa Prohibition

*Tanu rabbanan*: the Rabbis taught — *ein losesim se'orim be-Pesach* — one may not perform *lesisa* with barley on *Pesach*. *Lesisa* refers to the practice of moistening the outer shell of a grain kernel and rubbing or working it to remove the bran, thereby producing a cleaner, finer grain. This process inevitably brings water into contact with the grain and creates a *chametz* concern. Before proceeding, it is worth clarifying what actually defines *chametz*: from the moment flour comes into contact with water, if it is not baked within the requisite time — quantified for practical purposes as eighteen minutes — it becomes *chametz*. That eighteen-minute figure derives from a *gemara*, but the *gemara* itself acknowledges that fermentation is not so neatly quantifiable. The visual signs the *gemara* uses to detect fermentation — whether the dough has expanded, whether cracks have appeared — reflect a more nuanced reality. Moreover, a kernel of wheat or barley is very different from flour: water applied to a kernel's surface does not necessarily penetrate it and initiate fermentation in the same way it would with ground flour.

### Cracking Test

*Ve'im latat* — if one did perform *lesisa*, how does one determine whether a *chametz* problem has resulted? *Nitbaku asurot* — if the kernel has cracked, it is forbidden, because cracking indicates that water penetrated sufficiently to cause expansion. *Lo nitbaku, mutarot* — if the kernels have not cracked, they are permissible, because either the water did not penetrate or it did not penetrate enough to be consequential.

### Rabbi Yosi's Vinegar

*Rabbi Yose omer*: Rabbi Yosi offers an additional solution. Even in cases where the kernels are beginning to expand, or perhaps even after they have cracked — the text is not entirely clear on this point, and Rashi's reading suggests it may extend even to after cracking — one can throw them into vinegar, and the vinegar will impede the fermentation process, causing the kernels to contract. Rabbi Yosi is operating in a realm of practical intervention: fermentation is not an instantaneous or irreversible process, and under certain conditions it can be arrested. Whether Abaye would agree with this approach in the case where *nitbaku* has already occurred is not explicitly addressed, though it raises a fair question.

### Stringency Debate

The *gemara* then introduces a further stringency. *Lo nitbaku mamash* — when the ruling says the kernels have not cracked, this does not mean they must literally crack before becoming forbidden. *Ella kol she-ilu menicham al pi chavit ve-hein nitbaku me-aleihen* — anything that, if placed over the mouth of a barrel (Rashi understands this as a wine barrel whose vapors would interact with the kernels and cause them to crack), would crack on its own — that too is already forbidden, even before any visible cracking occurs. *Tosafot* has a different reading of the text: not *al pi chavit* but *al pi avuv*, a metal tube used for roasting grain — so that the criterion is whether applying heat to the kernels would cause them to crack. According to *Tosafot*'s reading, the test is whether the kernels have absorbed enough water that heat would split them; if so, they are already too compromised, even if no crack is yet visible.

### Shmuel's Position

Against this stringent reading, Shmuel states: *nitbaku mamash* — it is only a problem if they have literally cracked. Shmuel's father in fact rendered a practical ruling in the village of Bar Chashush consistent with this position — grain had been subjected to *lesisa* and he ruled it permissible on the grounds that the kernels had not literally cracked, without concern that they might yet do so.

### Rabbah vs. Rava

*Amar Rava*: Rava introduces the category of the *baal nefesh* — one who is particularly punctilious in religious observance (Rashi glosses this as a *chasid*, and some versions of Rashi read *yarei shamayim ha-chared al nafsho*, one who is earnest about his spiritual well-being). Such a person, Rava says, *lo yilsos* — should not perform *lesisa* at all. The *gemara* immediately challenges this: why speak of a *baal nefesh*? Even ordinary people are prohibited from doing this — the *braita* just said *ein losesim se'orim be-Pesach*! The *gemara* explains that Rava means something more: *ba'al nefesh afilu chitin* — a truly punctilious person will apply this prohibition even to wheat, not only to barley. The *braita* mentioned barley specifically; wheat, having a harder kernel, is presumably less susceptible to water penetration and is technically permitted. Rava says that someone who wishes to be particularly careful will refrain from *lesisa* even with wheat.

Rav Nachman is unimpressed. *Man detzayis lei l'Abba* — whoever listens to Rabbah (a respectful form of address) will wind up eating *nahama de'ipusha*, spoiled bread — that is, whole wheat *matzah* — on *Pesach*. If one takes seriously the concern about *lesisa* even with wheat, the result is that no one can ever eat fine flour *matzah*; everyone must make do with coarsely milled whole wheat. To demonstrate that this was never the practice, Rav Nachman notes that the households of Rav Huna and Rava bar Avin routinely performed *lesisa* on their wheat. Rava himself then goes a step further than Rabbah: he states outright that *lesisa* is actually prohibited — not merely something a *baal nefesh* would avoid, but categorically *assur*.

### Rav Nachman's Critique

One might ask: if *lesisa* is truly prohibited even with wheat, why did the *braita* single out barley? Rava answers with a *lo mibaya* construction: it goes without saying that wheat is forbidden — wheat, despite its harder exterior, has internal cracks in the kernels (*tzirya*), and the water may work its way in through those fissures. The *braita* mentions barley precisely because one might have supposed that barley, though softer-shelled, is smooth enough on its exterior that water would not penetrate — so the *braita* comes to teach that barley too is forbidden. According to Rava, then, *lesisa* is prohibited with both barley and wheat, leaving no path to fine flour *matzah* on *Pesach*.

---

## Rava's Reversals

### Permit Lesisa

*Hadar amar Rava* — Rava then reversed himself and declared: *mutar lilsos* — *lesisa* is actually permitted. His proof is a *braita* stating that one fulfills one's *matzah* obligation whether the *matzah* is made from fine flour (*pas nekiya*) or whole wheat (*hadra'ah*) — Rashi would add even bran bread. The question is simple: fine flour matzah evidently fulfills the obligation. But how does one obtain fine flour? *V'ee efshar nekiya belo lsisah* — it is impossible to produce fine flour without performing *lesisa*. If the *braita* presupposes that fine flour *matzah* is a valid option, then the process required to produce fine flour must be permitted. One cannot say "you can use it but you can't make it." Since *lesisa* must have been performed before *Pesach* rather than during it, and since that pre-*Pesach* use would still have produced flour susceptible to *chametz* concerns once it reached the stage of dough, this is not simply a *ta'aroves* question — it is a *chametz* question. The permissibility of the result implies the permissibility of the process.

### Rav Pappa Challenge

*Eitzeivei Rav Pappa leRava* — Rav Pappa challenged this proof. He cites a *braita* dealing with *tumah* and *taharah*: flour and fine flour (*kamchim ve-hasaltos*) purchased from non-Jews in villages (*kefarim*) are *tahor* — not susceptible to *tumah* — whereas the same products purchased in cities (*krachim*) are *tamei*. What makes food susceptible to *tumah*? Contact with liquid, including water. The implication is that fine flour from villages was produced *without* water — and yet it is still called *soles*, fine flour. This would suggest that one can produce *soles* without *lesisa*, which would undermine Rava's proof that the permissibility of fine flour matzah entails the permissibility of *lesisa*.

### Flour Susceptibility

The *gemara* attempts to deflect this by suggesting that the *braita*'s statement about *tahor* status applies only to ordinary flour (*kemach*), not to *soles* — only *soles* from cities, where higher-quality processing occurred, would have involved water. This answer is, as even the *gemara* seems to acknowledge, somewhat strained, since the *braita* explicitly mentions both *kamchim* and *saltos*. Rava resists the proof and maintains his position. After Rava departed, Rav Pappa remarked that he should have pressed a stronger challenge: the wheat used for *menachos* (Temple meal-offerings) must be *soles* — the Torah explicitly requires it — yet Shmuel rules that one should not perform *lesisa* on wheat designated for a *mincha*, precisely because *chametz* is forbidden in that context. The implication is clear: one can produce *soles* without *lesisa*. This would constitute a more decisive counter-proof to Rava's argument. Nevertheless, Rava's final ruling — that *lesisa* is permitted — stands.

### Mitzvah to do Lesisa

*Hadar amar Rava* — Rava reverses himself yet again, this time in a more striking direction: *mitzvah lelisos* — it is actually a *mitzvah* to perform *lesisa*, to use water to remove the bran before making *matzah*. This reversal is connected to the concept of *shimur* and is explained in the subsequent discussion.

---

## Shimur Concept (III)

### Ushmartem Etymology

The basis for Rava's claim that *lesisa* is a *mitzvah* lies in the verse *ushmartem et ha-matzos* — "you shall watch/guard the matzos." The *gemara* interprets this as a directive to guard the *matzah* against becoming *chametz*. Rava argues: *ilo d'va'i lesisa* — if it were not that *lesisa* is performed at an earlier stage when water first contacts the grain, *shimur lemai* — what exactly is one guarding? The *gemara* will explore this question in detail.

### Non-Jewish Dough

The *gemara* invokes a teaching of Rav Huna: *betzikot shel nochrim adam memalei kriso mehen* — one may eat one's fill from dough prepared by non-Jews, provided that a visual inspection reveals the dough has not fermented. This demonstrates a striking principle: one need not have been present at the kneading to be confident the dough is not *chametz* — a visual inspection suffices to establish that. *Uvilvad she-yochal kezayis matzah b'achronah* — but in order to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah*, one must ensure the final piece eaten is *matzah* that was specifically watched, from an earlier stage, by Jews. This is clearly not a *chametz* concern — after all, the non-Jewish dough is permissible to eat throughout *Pesach* based on visual inspection alone.
