It is rather a *kavana*, or *lishmah*, concern: the *matzah* of *mitzvah* requires a form of intentional guarding that goes beyond merely confirming the absence of fermentation.

### When Shimur Begins

This raises the question of when such *shimur* must begin. One might think that *shimur* at the kneading stage — when water is added to flour — would be sufficient. But Rav Huna's ruling implies otherwise: if *shimur* could begin at kneading, why couldn't one simply purchase the non-Jewish dough at that point and declare one is now performing *shimur*? *V'li'avad lei shimur me'afiyah va-eilach* — why not do *shimur* from the point of baking onward? The *gemara* concludes: *ella lav shema mina shimur me'ikara ba'inan* — evidently, *shimur* must begin from the very outset of the relevant process. *Shimur* at a midpoint is insufficient.

### Early Shimur Requirement

Rava develops this argument. If *shimur* at baking is too late, and *shimur* at kneading is also too late, then the earliest stage at which water contacts the grain — namely *lesisa* — is where *shimur* must commence. That is why Rava says it is a *mitzvah* to perform *lesisa*: not for the intrinsic value of the bran-removal process, but because doing so establishes the *shimur* at the earliest possible stage of water contact. One might reasonably object — as the *gemara* does — that this does not actually compel one to perform *lesisa*. Perhaps the *halacha* is simply that *shimur* must begin whenever water first contacts the grain, at whatever stage that occurs. If one skips *lesisa* and adds water only at kneading, then *shimur* from kneading suffices. *Lesisa* is not obligatory; it is simply one path to an earlier starting point. The *gemara* acknowledges this as a valid challenge to Rava's proof, yet notes that Rava did not reverse himself.

### Bundle Intent

*De'amar lehu l'hanu de-mahepkhei kifi* — Rava instructed those workers who were binding the bundles of grain in the fields: *ki mahephkhei hapeikhu l'shem mitzvah* — when you bind these bundles, do so *l'shem mitzvah*, with the intention that this is for the *matzah* of the *mitzvah*. Rava thus pushed *shimur* back even further — to the binding of the sheaves in the field, before any water has been applied at all. *Alma kasavar shimur me'ikara mit'chilato v'ad sofo ba'inan* — one sees that Rava holds *shimur* must span the entire process from its very beginning to its end.

---

## Shimur Positions (III)

### Shmura Label

The practical consequence of Rava's position is reflected on the label of every box of *shmura matzah* available today: *shamur mishat ktzira* — guarded from the time of cutting. This follows directly from Rava's ruling that *shimur* must begin at the very earliest stage of the grain's processing.

---

## Shimur Concept (III)

### Mar's Mother Example

*Mar breih de-Ravina* — Mar the son of Ravina: his mother would collect sheaves of grain stalks and place them in a container, watching over them and protecting them from the moment of cutting until it was time to make *matzah*. This is offered as a practical illustration of the position that *shimur* from cutting is the appropriate standard — and it is noteworthy that this practice was carried out by women as a matter of course.

---

## Shimur Positions (III)

### Machine Matzah

The question of what *shimur* actually requires has significant contemporary relevance in connection with machine *matzah*. The issue turns on the nature of *shimur*: is it fundamentally a *lishmah* or *kavana* requirement — that is, a requirement of conscious human intent directed toward producing *matzah* for the sake of the *mitzvah* — or is it simply a requirement of practical vigilance, ensuring the grain is protected from water contact throughout the process?

If *shimur* is purely a matter of practical protection and prevention of *chametz*, then the question is only whether the machinery accomplishes that protection, and a human operator who turns on the machine with the requisite intention might arguably satisfy the requirement even if the machine then runs unattended. But if *shimur* is a *lishmah* requirement, something closer to the *l'shem matzas mitzvah* declared by bakers before kneading, then continuous human engagement at each stage of the process may be necessary — and a machine running autonomously for hours, regardless of what intention the operator had at the outset, may not satisfy it.

---

## Shimur Concept (III)…

### Shimur Distinction

It is important to distinguish between two types of *shimur* that appear in this discussion. The first is *shimur* to prevent *chametz*: ensuring the grain or dough does not ferment. This form of *shimur* can apparently be accomplished by visual inspection — as we saw with the case of non-Jewish dough, where one simply confirms no fermentation has occurred. The second is *shimur l'shem matzah*, guarding the grain specifically so that the resulting *matzah* qualifies as *matzas mitzvah*. These are distinct requirements. The first is a *chametz* concern, addressed by any adequate monitoring. The second is a *kavana* or *lishmah* concern, requiring intentional, dedicated attention from the beginning of the process. Even where one can satisfy the first by visual inspection — as with purchased non-Jewish dough — one cannot satisfy the second without prior dedicated *shimur*.

---

## Shimur Positions (III)…

### Rishonim Timeline

The *Rishonim* debate precisely when the obligation of *shimur* begins. Some rule in accordance with the end of the *gemara*'s discussion, requiring *shimur* from the time of cutting (*mishas ketzira*). Others read the subsequent narratives — particularly the story of Mar's mother — as reflecting a praiseworthy *chumra* adopted by especially pious individuals, not as normative *halacha*, and do not require *shimur* from so early a stage. A third position holds that *shimur* is required, but not necessarily from cutting — rather, from the point at which serious exposure to water becomes a realistic concern.

### Rosh's Position

The Rosh, for example, holds that *shimur* should begin at the grinding stage, when grain is taken to the mill. His reasoning is twofold: flour is considerably more susceptible to *chametz* than whole kernels, and more critically, where did one grind wheat in the Talmudic period? At a water mill. The environment of the mill itself represents the first serious point of water exposure, and therefore that is where the obligation of *shimur* begins. This position is a middle path — earlier than the kneading stage, but not as early as the cutting of the grain.

---

## Submerged Trough

### Rava Permits Sale

*Hahu arva d'chiti d'tava b'chishta* — a certain trough containing wheat kernels that fell into and was submerged in a river. This is a graver situation than *lesisa*, which involves brief and controlled water contact; submersion in a river is prolonged, unmonitored, and presumably quite thorough. *Sharei Rava l'zabuni l'nochrim* — Rava permitted selling the wheat to non-Jews before *Pesach*. Since the wheat cannot be safely used and there was no intention to acquire *chametz*, the practical solution is to divest oneself of it.

### Kilayim Analogy

*Ava bar Livai* challenged Rava from the laws of *kilayim*. If one has a wool garment in which a linen thread has become embedded somewhere and cannot be located, one may not sell it to a non-Jew — *harei zeh lo yimkerenu l'nochri* — nor use it as a saddle blanket for a donkey. The concern is not that the non-Jew will wear it — it is generally understood that the prohibition of *shatnez* applies only to Jews — but that the non-Jew may eventually resell the garment to a Jew who will not realize it contains *shatnez* and will wear it. Similarly, the non-Jew who acquires the wheat may sell it back to a Jew before *Pesach*, and that Jew will not know the wheat is problematic.

### Shrouds Solution

The same *braita* dealing with the *kilayim* garment offers a solution: *aval osin oto tachrichin l'meit* — one may use the garment as burial shrouds. Once a garment has been designated and used as shrouds for the dead, it becomes *assur b'hana'ah* — forbidden for any benefit — taking on, as it were, the status of the corpse itself, and cannot reenter general use. The *kilayim* analogy raises a tangential point noted by *Tosafot*: the practice of removing *tzitzit* from the *tallit* of the deceased before burial, despite the *gemara*'s concern about *lo'eg la-rash* — mocking the dead who can no longer perform *mitzvot* — by displaying the fringes. *Tosafot* notes that contemporary practice relies on a line in *Masechet Semachot* in which Abba Shaul ben Batnis instructed his sons to remove his *techelet* — understood as his *tzitzit* — and bury him at the feet of his father. This leads *Tosafot* to observe that in a number of instances Ashkenazic practice follows non-Talmudic sources — *Yerushalmi*, *midrash*, or the minor tractates — in ways that diverge from the *Bavli*. This is likely connected to the historical transmission of Ashkenazic practice through Italy from *Eretz Yisrael* culture, as opposed to Sephardic tradition, which derives more directly from Babylonian Jewish culture. Sometimes *Eretz Yisrael* practices survived in Ashkenazic *minhag* in tension with, or contrary to, Babylonian rulings.

### Sell in Portions

*Hadar amar Rava* — Rava accepted the critique and reversed himself again. *L'zabninhu kava kava l'Yisrael* — sell the wheat in small quantities to Jews before *Pesach*, in such a way that each individual buyer will use up their portion before *Pesach* arrives. *Ki haychi d'kalya kamei Pischa* — so that it will be consumed before *Pesach*. The logic is that people in that environment did not stockpile grain; if someone was buying wheat, they would be baking with it within days. By selling in small amounts to multiple individuals, one ensures that the problematic wheat is consumed and does not survive into *Pesach* in any Jewish household.

---

## Mollel (Thickening)

### Mollel Prohibition

*Tanu rabbanan*: the Rabbis taught — *ein molin et ha-kederah be-Pesach* — one may not *mollel* the pot on *Pesach*. *Mollel* refers to adding flour as a thickening agent to a pot of soup or stew. The concern is obvious: flour added to a hot liquid is in contact with water under conditions that could promote fermentation, or at minimum represents an unnecessary and risky introduction of flour to a liquid environment on *Pesach*.

### Flour-then-Vinegar

*Ve-ha-rotzeh she-yimlo mah ya'aseh* — what should one who wishes to thicken the pot do? The first opinion: *nosen et ha-kemach ve-achar kach nosen et ha-chometz* — put the flour in first, then add the vinegar. One might think it would be preferable to add the vinegar first, so that the flour never contacts water unprotected. But this first opinion holds that adding the vinegar afterward is better, because at that moment the vinegar arrives undiluted and thus with its full potency to arrest any incipient fermentation.

### Vinegar-then-Flour

*Ve-yesh omrim* — there is another opinion: add the vinegar first, then the flour. *Man yesh omrim* — the *gemara* identifies this view as that of Rabbi Yehudah.

### Vinegar Power

Why Rabbi Yehudah? *De-tenan*: a *mishnah* in the context of *Shabbat* laws teaches that if one removed a boiling pot or pan from the flame, one may not add spices to it on *Shabbat* because the vessel — a *kli rishon* — retains sufficient heat to cook the spices even off the flame. However, one may add spices to the soup or stew once it has been poured into a serving bowl — a *kli sheni* — which does not cook. Rabbi Yehudah adds an exception: *chutz mi-davar she-yesh bo chometz va-tzir* — except for something that contains vinegar or fish brine. Even in a *kli sheni*, the pungency of the vinegar maintains its power to act upon food. Rabbi Yehudah thus holds that vinegar retains its active properties even within a cooked mixture. It follows that if one adds vinegar to the pot first, the vinegar's power persists even after other ingredients are introduced, and placing the flour into an already-vinegar-infused environment would protect against fermentation.

The *gemara* asks: why attribute this opinion to Rabbi Yehudah rather than to Rabbi Yosi, who already said that vinegar arrests fermentation in grain? The answer is that Rabbi Yosi's position addressed undiluted vinegar applied directly to kernels — *de'isa be'inei*, when it is present in its pure form. *Aval al yedei ta'aroves* — but once the vinegar is mixed into the pot with other ingredients, diluted and blended, it may no longer retain the power to prevent fermentation. Rabbi Yosi's ruling does not necessarily extend to vinegar already incorporated into a dish. Rabbi Yehudah, by contrast, holds explicitly that vinegar maintains its potency even within a mixture — hence it is his view that supports the practice of adding vinegar first.

### Undiluted Vinegar

The critical limitation that emerges is that vinegar's power to prevent fermentation is contingent on its being undiluted and directly applied. Once mixed into the liquid environment of the pot, it may lose that capacity. This distinction governs the entire debate about which ingredient should go into the pot first.

### Ulla's Stricture

*Ulla amar echad ze ve'echad ze assur* — Ulla holds that it makes no difference whether vinegar goes in first or last: both procedures are forbidden. One should not add flour to a pot on *Pesach* under any circumstances. His reasoning reflects a principle the *gemara* expresses with the maxim: *lech lech amrinan nezira, sechor sechor, le-karma lo tikrav* — we tell the *nazir*: go away, go around, do not come near the vineyard. A *nazir* is technically forbidden only from grapes and grape products, not from entering a vineyard per se — but we instruct him to keep his distance entirely, to put safety margins around the prohibition. The same logic applies here: the theoretical possibility of managing flour in a pot on *Pesach* using vinegar is precisely the kind of risky proximity to prohibition that we should avoid categorically, rather than parsing the technique to find a permissible pathway.

### Rav Pappi Roasted

*Rav Pappi shari lehu le-bordakei devei Reish Galusa* — Rav Pappi permitted the cooks or bakers in the household of the *Reish Galusa* to thicken the pot with *chasisi*, which Rashi understands as roasted grain. Presumably Rav Pappi reasoned that once grain has been properly roasted, it can no longer become *chametz* — as the *gemara* established at the outset of today's daf. *Tosafot* understands *chasisi* differently, reading it as lentil flour, which would pose no *chametz* concern at all. In any event, the question is whether one can rely on proper roasting to render the thickener safe.

### Rava Practical

*Amar Rava*: Rava questioned whether one could really sanction such a practice in a household staffed by servants — *ika de-shari ki hai milsa be-duchta de-shchichi avdei*? Who can trust servants to ensure the grain is thoroughly roasted? We opened today's daf with precisely this concern: if grain is not roasted well enough, the *chametz* risk remains. Using roasted grain as a thickener, in an environment where the roasting may have been carelessly executed, seems to recreate the very problem the roasting was meant to solve.

Yet the *gemara* closes with a striking counter-note: *ika de'amri Rava gufa machi leh kedeira bechasisi* — some say that Rava himself would thicken his pot with this grain. And so the *gemara* ends as it began: moving back and forth between stringency and leniency, between those who say one must keep one's distance from any such practice and those who say that careful, attentive use of the relevant techniques is entirely permissible. The tension between these poles is not a failure of the *gemara* to reach a conclusion — it is the honest reflection of a legal system grappling with practical reality.

---

---

# Pesachim 41

## Flour + Charoset/Mus (II)

### Mishna Overview

The daf opens at the bottom of 41a with a *mishna* that continues a running series of discussions about *chametz* concerns arising from the mixing of flour or grain with various liquids. The *mishna* states: *ein notnim kemach letoch charoset* — one may not place flour into *charoset*. This *charoset* need not refer specifically to the *Seder* night preparation; as Rashi explains, it refers to a vinegar-based dipping sauce used with meat, into which flour might be added as a thickening agent. The *mishna* extends the same prohibition to mustard — *o letoch chardal* — which in its ancient form was a preparation made from mustard seed, vinegar, and other ingredients, into which flour might similarly be incorporated.

Both cases raise the same underlying question: does the presence of vinegar prevent or accelerate the process of fermentation? The vinegar in question throughout the *Gemara* is wine vinegar — not a wheat product itself — but the question remains whether its acidic character stalls or promotes the leavening of any flour mixed into these preparations.

### Vinegar Role

The concern is not abstract. If vinegar neutralizes fermentation, then mixing flour into these preparations may be essentially harmless from a *chametz* standpoint. If, however, vinegar does not inhibit fermentation — or worse, actively promotes it — then the addition of flour creates an immediate *chametz* problem. The *mishna*'s formulation does not resolve this question directly; it simply prohibits the addition of flour to either preparation and then addresses what happens if one goes ahead and does so anyway.

### Eat Immediately

The *mishna* rules: *v'im natan yochal miyad* — if one did add flour, one should eat the mixture immediately. The assumption is that fermentation will not occur instantaneously, so immediate consumption avoids any *chametz* violation. However, *Rabbi Meir* dissents: *Rabbi Meir oser*. In his view, the mixture poses a *chametz* risk from the very moment the flour is added, and one cannot rely on eating it quickly. According to Rabbi Meir, the mixture must be destroyed immediately.

With that, the *mishna* sets aside this theme momentarily and — in an organizational move that will require comment — pivots to discuss the *korban Pesach* and then returns to a baker's working water. The structural peculiarity of these *mishnayot* is noted by Tosafot and will be addressed below.

---

## Korban Pesach Prep

### Roasting Only

The *mishna* states: *ein mevashelin et hapesach* — one may not cook the *korban Pesach*. The Torah's prohibition (Shemot 12:9) reads: *al tochlu mimenu na uvashel mevushal bamayim* — do not eat from it rare, or cooked in water. The *korban Pesach* must be *tzeli esh*, fire-roasted. The *mishna* extends this to all liquids: *lo bemashkin* — not in any liquids — and *velo bemei peirot* — not even in fruit juices. The prohibition of cooking encompasses every liquid, not only water.

### Basting vs. Cooking

The *mishna* qualifies this prohibition: *aval sachin umatbilin oto bahen* — however, one may baste the *korban Pesach* as it roasts over the fire, applying liquids to the surface for flavor, and one may also dip the meat in liquids when eating it. The prohibition is specifically against cooking it *in* liquid — one may not prepare a *Pesach* stew or boiled *Pesach*. The question of pan-roasting will be addressed when the *Gemara* explores the precise contours of the prohibition.

### Baker's Water

The *mishna* then transitions abruptly to yet another *chametz* topic: *mei tashmisho shel nachtom* — the working water of the professional baker. A baker kneading dough keeps a bucket of water nearby to rinse his hands between batches. That water accumulates residual dough and, as it sits, begins to ferment. The *mishna* rules that this water must be poured out — *yishfechu* — because *mipnei shehein machmitzin*, it causes *chametz*.

The organizational structure here is, as the lecturer observes, genuinely puzzling, and Tosafot explicitly raises the question. One moment the *mishna* deals with flour in *charoset* and mustard; then it pivots to the laws of the *korban Pesach*; then it returns to a *chametz* concern involving a baker's water. A partial answer may be that the unifying thread is the interaction of flour or grain with liquids — the *charoset* and mustard cases involve flour with liquid, the *korban Pesach* case involves the prohibition of cooking in liquid, and the baker's water involves dough residue in liquid — but even granting this, the insertion of the *korban Pesach* material into what is otherwise a sequence of *chametz* discussions remains structurally jarring.

---

## Flour + Charoset/Mus (II)

### Rav Kahana's View

The *Gemara* now returns to the *mishna*'s ruling about flour in *charoset* and mustard, beginning with a distinction drawn by Rav Kahana: *machlokes letoch hachardal* — the debate between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* about whether one can eat the mixture immediately or must destroy it applies specifically to the mustard case. *Aval letoch hacharoset, divrei hakol yisaref miyad* — but if flour was mixed into the vinegar-based *charoset* dip, everyone agrees it must be burned immediately. Rashi explains that mustard, being more pungent, may retard fermentation sufficiently to permit immediate consumption according to the *Chachamim*, whereas the *charoset* dip does not have this property, and all opinions agree it must be destroyed.

This position is corroborated by a *braita*: *ein notnin kemach letoch hacharoset, v'im natan yisaref miyad* — you may not add flour to *charoset*, and if you did, it must be burned immediately. By contrast, in the mustard case, Rabbi Meir rules it must be burned while the *Chachamim* permit immediate consumption.

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehuda then transmits a ruling in the name of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *halacha k'chachamim* — the ruling follows the *Chachamim* that immediate consumption is permitted. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then challenges Rav Huna: when you say we rule like the *Chachamim*, does that apply even to the *charoset* case, or only to the mustard case as Rav Kahana maintained? Rav Huna responds: *lemay nafka mina* — in the sense of asking what practical difference the distinction would make, and implicitly expressing skepticism about Rav Kahana's differentiation. He concludes: *lo shamia li* — I have not heard that teaching.

As the *Gemara* notes in a pointed phrase, *lo shamia li* here means *lo sevira lei* — "I haven't heard it" is idiomatic for "I don't accept it." Rav Huna thus rules that even in the *charoset* case, the *Chachamim* would permit immediate consumption, and the *halacha* follows the *Chachamim*.

### Vinegar Neutral

Rav Ashi, however, sides with Rav Kahana's distinction: *kevastei de-Rav Kahana mistavra* — Rav Kahana's differentiation makes logical sense. His proof is from a ruling of Shmuel himself: *ein halacha ke-Rabbi Yosi* — we do not rule like Rabbi Yosi. Rabbi Yosi had argued on an earlier daf that if grain soaking in water begins to crack and ferment, one can immerse it in vinegar to halt the process, since vinegar prevents fermentation. Shmuel rejected this view. The question then is: what precisely does Shmuel's rejection mean? Does it mean (*mai lav*) that vinegar does not merely fail to prevent fermentation, but actually *accelerates* it — *hachmei machme* — because it functions as a liquid that promotes *chametz* formation? If so, the vinegar in the *charoset* would make it ferment faster than mustard, and Rav Kahana's distinction would be well-supported.

The *Gemara* rebuts this inference: *dilma lo matzmit tzamit velo hachmei machme* — perhaps vinegar neither retards fermentation nor hastens it. When Shmuel says we do not rule like Rabbi Yosi, he may simply mean that vinegar provides no protective benefit — it does not shrivel or arrest the fermentation process — but this does not imply that vinegar actively causes fermentation faster than other substances. If so, the presence of vinegar in the *charoset* does not make it more problematic than mustard, and Rav Kahana's distinction loses its logical grounding.

The *Gemara* thus leaves the resolution incomplete: the argument that *charoset* is categorically more problematic than mustard is not clearly established, because rejecting Rabbi Yosi's view does not necessarily entail that vinegar accelerates fermentation.

---

## Other Liquids

### Kal Vachomer

The *Gemara* now turns to the broader question of whether liquids other than water are included in the biblical prohibition against cooking the *korban Pesach*. The verse (Shemot 12:9) specifies *uvashel mevushal bamayim* — cooked in water. A *braita* asks: *ein li ela bamayim, she'ar mashkin minayin?* — I know only that water is prohibited; how do I derive the prohibition of other liquids?

The answer offered is a *kal vachomer*: water, which does not mask the taste of the meat — it does not introduce a competing flavor — is nevertheless prohibited. Other liquids, such as fruit juices or wine, which do mask and overlay the meat's taste, should certainly be prohibited. The *kal vachomer* thus draws the following inference: if even the more neutral substance is prohibited, the more transformative substances are certainly included.

This application of a *kal vachomer* raises a technical concern, since we generally hold *ein mazhirin min hadin* — one does not derive prohibitions from logical inference in a way that would generate lashes for the derived case. Additionally, making a *kal vachomer* argument presupposes that we understand the *reason* the Torah prohibited cooking in water — namely, that it affects the meat's taste and character. If there were some other, unarticulated rationale for the prohibition, the *kal vachomer* to other liquids would not hold. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* uses the *kal vachomer* as a way of understanding that the word *bamayim* in the *pasuk* is not meant precisely — it functions as a paradigmatic example, with the *kal vachomer* establishing that the prohibition encompasses any liquid.

### Rabbi's Drasha

Rabbi (Rebbi, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) derives the same extension through a different exegetical route. Rather than a *kal vachomer*, he reads the double language of the verse — *uvashel mevushal* — as doing independent exegetical work. The doubling of the root expands the prohibition beyond what a single usage would indicate, encompassing cooking in any substance, not only in water.

### Pan-Roasting

The *Gemara* identifies the *nafka mina* between the two approaches: *tzeli kedeirah* — pan-roasting. Pan-roasting involves placing the meat in a pan directly over fire without adding any external liquid; the meat's own juices accumulate in the pan as heat is applied, and the meat essentially cooks in those internal juices. There is no external liquid introduced, only the meat's own exudate.

According to the *kal vachomer*, pan-roasting would not be included in the prohibition, since the *kal vachomer* only addresses external liquids — one derives from water that other external substances are likewise prohibited. The absence of any external liquid means the *kal vachomer* generates no prohibition for pan-roasting. By contrast, Rabbi's reading of *uvashel mevushal* as an expansive double language would include pan-roasting as a form of cooking, even in one's own juices.

Tosafot is careful to note, however, that this does not mean pan-roasting would be *permitted* according to the view that uses the *kal vachomer*. Even without a negative prohibition derived from *uvashel mevushal*, the end of the verse — *ki im tzeli esh* — requires fire-roasting. Pan-roasting does not qualify as *tzeli esh*, and therefore it remains impermissible regardless of whether it falls within the *bishul* prohibition. The practical difference between the two approaches is therefore not about permissibility but about whether pan-roasting violates a *lav* specifically.

The Rambam, it is worth noting, rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's position, such that pan-roasting would constitute a violation of a negative commandment.

---

## Before/After Roasting

### Cook Then Roast

Having established that the double language of *uvashel mevushal* carries additional exegetical weight beyond extending the prohibition to other liquids, the *Gemara* now identifies what the *Rabbanan* — who derive other liquids from the *kal vachomer* rather than from the double language — do with that double language. The answer is found in a *braita*: *bishlo v'achar kach tzla'o* — if one first cooked the *korban Pesach* and then roasted it, one transgresses. Similarly, *o shetzla'o v'achar kach bishlo* — if one first roasted it and then cooked it, one also transgresses. The double language of *uvashel mevushal* conveys that even a partial or secondary act of *bishul* is sufficient to render the *korban* transgressed — it need not be exclusively cooked; even if it was also roasted at some point, the cooking violates the prohibition.

The case of cooking first and then roasting is straightforward: *deha bashlei bashlei* — the initial cooking defines the meat's identity, and the subsequent roasting does not undo that status. The identity as a cooked item was established at the outset.

### Roast Then Cook

The reverse case — roasting first and then cooking — is more analytically challenging. *Ha tzeli esh hu* — might one not say that since the meat was originally fire-roasted, that original act stamps its identity as *tzeli esh*, and the subsequent cooking is merely incidental? Perhaps it should retain the status of *tzeli* even after having been cooked?

### Rabbi Yosi Matzah

The *Gemara* resolves this by invoking the position of Rabbi Yosi, via Rav Kahana: this case follows Rabbi Yosi's ruling in an analogous context involving *matzah*. The *braita* records a dispute about whether one can fulfill the obligation of *matzah* with a baked wafer that was subsequently cooked. Rabbi Meir holds that one may fulfill the obligation with such a *matzah* — *uvimvushal* — provided it has not dissolved, since it was originally baked. Rabbi Yosi disagrees: while he agrees that a baked wafer that has been soaked in water (*rakik hashurui*) remains valid — because merely soaking it does not constitute a second act of cooking — he maintains that a baked *matzah* that has been subsequently cooked does not fulfill the obligation, even if it has not dissolved: *aval lo b'mevushal, af al pi shelo nimoach*.

The *Gemara* understands Rabbi Yosi's reasoning not as resting on the requirement that *matzah* be *lechem oni* (poor person's bread), since that rationale would be specific to *matzah* and irrelevant to the *korban Pesach*. Rather, the *Gemara* reads Rabbi Yosi as articulating a formal principle: when a second process is applied to an object, that second process attaches a new label to it. The baked *matzah*, once cooked, is no longer simply "baked bread" — it has now also become "cooked," and that new designation strips it of its exclusive *lechem* identity. Analogously, the *korban Pesach* that was roasted and then cooked acquires the label of *mevushal* through the secondary act of cooking, even though it was originally *tzeli*.

This discussion has significant implications beyond *korban Pesach*. The *Yeraim* (Rabbi Eliezer of Metz, a student of Rabbeinu Tam) cites this *Gemara* as proof for a principle in *hilchot Shabbat*: while *ein bishul achar bishul* — one cannot "cook" something already cooked, so reheating cooked food on *Shabbat* raises no *bishul* concern — the same is not true for *bishul achar afiyah* (cooking after baking). Taking baked bread and placing it into boiling liquid on *Shabbat* is a change of process category, not a repeat of the same process, and the *Yeraim* argues this constitutes a genuine act of cooking. His proof is precisely from this *Gemara*, where Rabbi Yosi and the *korban Pesach* discussion demonstrate that a secondary process of a *different* type changes the item's halakhic status. The *Shulchan Aruch* is stringent in accordance with the *Yeraim*'s position.

### Apply to Pesach

Ulla adds a further dimension: *afilu teima Rabbi Meir* — even according to Rabbi Meir, who rules that cooking after baking does not disqualify *matzah*, one could maintain that cooking after roasting *does* disqualify the *korban Pesach*. Why? *Shani hatam, de'amar kra uvashel mevushal mikol makom* — the *korban Pesach* is different because the Torah's double language of *uvashel mevushal* explicitly teaches that even a secondary act of *bishul* is enough to create a violation, regardless of what other processes were applied. The double language thus functions as a specific textual override for the *korban Pesach* context, ensuring that even those who would not extend Rabbi Yosi's principle globally must accept it here.

---

## Extremes

### Charred

Having established the parameters of the prohibitions governing the *korban Pesach*, the *Gemara* explores two extreme cases that lie outside those categories. The first: *yachol tzala'o kol tzorko yehei chayav* — one might think that if the *korban* was roasted completely — meaning charred beyond recognition — one would still transgress. The *Gemara* derives from the verse (*al tochlu mimenu na uvashel mevushal bamayim*) that only *na* and *mevushal* are included in the prohibition, but not *tzala'o kol tzorko* — completely roasted through. Rav Ashi explains: *de-shavei charucha* — the case refers to one who turned the meat into something resembling a piece of charcoal. Such an extreme state of overcooking is not included in the prohibitions of *na* or *mevushal*. One should note that this does not mean charring the *korban Pesach* is otherwise acceptable — presumably one has not fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *korban Pesach* by eating charcoal, and there may be other concerns — but the specific transgression of *al tochlu mimenu na* does not apply to it.

### Completely Raw

The second extreme: *yachol achal kezayit chai yehei chayav* — perhaps eating from the *korban* when it is completely raw, without any application of heat whatsoever, would constitute a transgression. The *Gemara* again derives from *na uvashel mevushal* that *na* and *mevushal* are included, but *lo chai* — not completely raw. The prohibition of *na* refers to undercooked or rare meat, as the *Gemara* will shortly clarify, not to meat that has never touched heat at all.

The irony is notable: one who eats a completely raw *korban Pesach* or one that has been charred to ash has not fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *korban Pesach* — the requirement of *tzeli esh* has obviously not been met — yet these extreme cases fall outside the specific biblical prohibitions enumerated in the verse. They are governed, as the *Gemara* goes on to explain, by the second half of the *pasuk*: *ki im tzeli esh*.

---

## Na and Tzeli Esh

### Definition Na

The *Gemara* now addresses a terminological question: *heichi dami na?* — what exactly is *na* as used in the *pasuk*? Rav explains that it corresponds to the Persian word *avarnim*, which denotes meat that has been subjected to heat but remains substantially undercooked — what we might today describe as rare or very underdone. It is not completely raw, but it has not been adequately roasted either. This is the specific state prohibited by *al tochlu mimenu na*.

### Hot Springs

Rav Chisda raises a distinctive case: what if one cooked the *korban Pesach* in the hot springs of Tiberias (*chamei Tveryah*), which are naturally heated by underground geothermal forces rather than by fire? In the context of *Shabbat*, cooking in the hot springs of Tiberias is exempt from the *bishul* prohibition — *beShabbat patur* — because *toldot esh ba'inan velieka*, one needs fire or its derivative (*toldot esh*), and geothermally heated water does not qualify. The *Shabbat* prohibition of cooking requires that the heat source trace back to fire. The hot springs draw their heat from the earth, not from a fire that was kindled, and therefore they do not constitute *toldot esh*.

One might expect the same definition to apply to *korban Pesach*: since geothermal heating is not *bishul* by *Shabbat* standards, perhaps cooking the *korban* in *chamei Tveryah* would similarly not fall under *uvashel mevushal*. Yet Rav Chisda rules: *pesach shebishlo bechamei Tveryah, chayav* — if one cooked the *korban Pesach* in the hot springs, one has transgressed.

The *Gemara* could have resolved this by arguing that for *korban Pesach*, what matters is the result — whether the product is functionally "cooked" — rather than the precise character of the process, as in *Shabbat*. But the *Gemara* does not take this route. Instead, Rava explains: *mai chayav, d'ka avar mishum tzlui* — what does "transgressed" mean here? Not that one has violated *uvashel mevushal*, since *bishul* for *korban Pesach* purposes, like for *Shabbat*, requires fire-based heating. Rather, the transgression is that the meat is *not tzeli esh*: it was subjected to a liquid environment in the hot springs without fire, and therefore it fails to satisfy *ki im tzeli esh*. The violation is the failure of the positive requirement of fire-roasting, which the *Gemara* reads as also carrying a negative dimension.

Rav Chiya the son of Rav Nachman confirms that this is the explicit teaching: the transgression in the *chamei Tveryah* case is *mishum tzlui* — it pertains to the *ki im tzeli esh* half of the *pasuk*, not to *uvashel mevushal*.

### Two Halves

This leads to a conceptual clarification about the structure of the *pasuk*. The *pasuk* (Shemot 12:9) has two halves: the first, *al tochlu mimenu na uvashel mevushal bamayim*, prohibits eating it rare or cooked in water (extended to all liquids); the second, *ki im tzeli esh*, commands that it be fire-roasted. The *Gemara* has now demonstrated that several categories of preparation fall outside the first half: completely raw meat (*chai*), charred meat (*charucha*), and — according to Rava's reading — meat cooked in *chamei Tveryah*. Yet all of these still fail to satisfy *ki im tzeli esh*. The question, then, is whether *ki im tzeli esh* functions as a positive commandment (*aseh*) or whether it carries the force of a negative prohibition (*lav*) as well — a question to which the *Gemara* now turns.

---

## Lashes Debate

### Rava Position

Rava articulates the view that *ki im tzeli esh* generates actual negative prohibitions that carry lashes. If one ate from the *korban* rare (*na*): *lokeh shtayim* — two sets of lashes. One set is for violating *al tochlu mimenu na*, and the second is for violating the implicit prohibition of *ki im tzeli esh* — since it was not roasted, one has violated the negative dimension of that clause. If one ate from it cooked (*mevushal*): again *lokeh shtayim*, one for *uvashel mevushal* and one for *ki im tzeli esh*. If one ate it both rare and cooked: *lokeh shalosh*, three sets of lashes — one for *na*, one for *mevushal*, and one for *ki im tzeli esh*.

### Abaye Position

Abaye disagrees: *ein lokin al lav shebichlalus* — one does not receive lashes for a *lav shebichlalus*, an umbrella prohibition. The phrase *ki im tzeli esh* does not specify a particular act to avoid; it is a catch-all that encompasses anything other than roasting. Such a generalized prohibition that does not identify a specific, narrowly defined act does not generate lashes. The prohibition of muzzling an ox (*lo sachsom shor b'disho*) serves as the paradigm for the kind of specific, action-defined *lav* that generates lashes, and *ki im tzeli esh* does not share that character.

### Abaye Dispute

There are two versions of Abaye's position. According to the first, Abaye says that when the *lav shebichlalus* appears together with a specific prohibition — for instance, one ate rare *and* it was not roasted — *tarti hu d'lo laki*, one does not receive two sets of lashes because the generic prohibition is subsumed under the specific one. But *chada meiha laki*, one still receives one set for the specific violation. According to the second version, Abaye goes further: *chada nami lo laki* — even one set of lashes for the generic prohibition is unavailable, since the prohibition is not sufficiently defined, like *lav d'chasimah*.

### Rashi Solution

Rashi offers a careful reading to reconcile these two versions within Abaye's position. Abaye, Rashi explains, would of course agree that one receives lashes for eating *mevushal* — the prohibition of *uvashel mevushal bamayim* is a perfectly specific *lav*. The question is only about the umbrella of *ki im tzeli esh*. When a specific *lav* is already operative (eating cooked or rare), adding lashes for the generic *ki im tzeli esh* on top of it is redundant and improper — one does not punish for the title of a category when one is already punishing for the specific act within that category. But what about a case where no specific *lav* applies — for example, one ate the *korban* completely raw (*chai*), which falls outside *na* and *mevushal*? In that case, might the generic *ki im tzeli esh* operate on its own to generate lashes? The first version of Abaye says yes; the second version says no, since even when it stands alone, an umbrella prohibition lacking the specificity of the *chasimah* paradigm never generates lashes.

### Nazir Example

The same dispute is played out in a parallel context involving a *nazir*. Rava holds that if a *nazir* ate the pit of a grape (*zag*): *lokeh shtayim* — two sets of lashes, one for the specific prohibition of *mechartzanim v'ad zag* (from the skin to the pit), and one for the general prohibition of *mikol asher yei'aseh migefen hayayin* (anything made from the grapevine). Similarly, eating the skin (*chartzan*) yields two lashes. Eating both yields *lokeh shalosh*, three sets. Abaye, consistent with his position, rules that the generic umbrella of "anything from the vine" does not generate independent lashes alongside the specific prohibitions. Whether the umbrella prohibition can ever stand alone to generate a single set of lashes — when one consumes some other grape derivative that does not fall under a specific prohibition — is subject to the same two versions as in the *korban Pesach* discussion.

---

## Timing Issue

### When Cooked

The *Gemara* now addresses a question about the timing of the transgression: at what point does the prohibition of eating the *korban Pesach* in an improper manner attach? One dimension of this question concerns when the *korban* was *cooked* — must the improper preparation have occurred after nightfall, or does it suffice that the cooking occurred on *Erev Pesach*? A *braita* teaches: if one cooked the *korban Pesach* on *Erev Pesach* during the day and then ate it on the night of the 15th, does one transgress? One might think the prohibition only applies if the cooking itself occurred at night, when the *mitzvah* of the *korban Pesach* takes effect. Rabbi derives from the double language of *uvashel mevushal* — *bashel mevushal mikol makom* — that the prohibition applies regardless of when the cooking was done. Whether the *korban* was cooked earlier in the day or at night, if one eats it improperly prepared, one has transgressed.

The *Gemara* acknowledges an objection: we already explained on 41a that Rebbi uses the double language of *uvashel mevushal* to derive the prohibitions against other liquids and pan-roasting. How can he simultaneously use it to derive this timing ruling? The *Gemara* responds with the standard answer that the double language, being genuinely redundant from a grammatical standpoint (*im kein leima kra o bashel bashel o mevushal mevushal*), can support multiple *drashos* simultaneously.

### When Eaten

The more fundamental timing question concerns when the *eating* must occur for the prohibition to apply. A *braita* teaches: *achalo kezayit na be-od yom, patur* — if one ate a *kezayit* of rare *korban Pesach* during the day of the 14th, before nightfall, one is exempt. *Kezayit na mishechasheicha chayav* — but if one ate it rare after nightfall, one has transgressed. The prohibition of eating it improperly applies only from the time the *mitzvah* of the *korban Pesach* takes effect — at nightfall on the 15th.

A related ruling distinguishes between eating improperly prepared meat before nightfall and eating properly roasted meat before nightfall. The *braita* teaches: *achalo kezayit tzali be-od yom, lo pasal atzmo mibenei chavurah* — if one ate a *kezayit* of properly roasted *korban Pesach* during the day of the 14th, one does not disqualify oneself from membership in the *chavurah* (the group with whom one is obligated to eat the *korban* at night). Eating the *korban* before nightfall lacks the halakhic significance of eating it at the designated time; it does not count toward the *mitzvah* and does not define one's *chavurah* affiliation. By contrast, once nightfall arrives and one has consumed a *kezayit* of roasted *korban* — *kezayit tzali mishechasheicha, pasal atzmo mibenei chavurah* — one has fulfilled the designated eating and may not then transfer to another group.

### Pasuk Contrast

Having established that the prohibitions only apply at nightfall, the *Gemara* considers a strikingly counterintuitive argument that the *braita* raises and then refutes. The *braita* entertains the possibility that Erev Pesach — when one is not yet permitted to eat the *korban* roasted — might be the time of greater stringency: since even roasting is forbidden during the day, perhaps eating it rare is *also* forbidden during that period. The argument goes further: one might even claim that the prohibition of eating rare applies *only* on Erev Pesach, and paradoxically that on the night of the 15th, when one is commanded to eat it roasted, one would not transgress if one ate it in a prohibited manner. This is admittedly a startling conclusion, and the *Gemara* acknowledges it: *al titema* — do not be amazed, since one could argue that when the *mitzvah* of eating roasted is permitted and indeed commanded, perhaps those prohibitions become inoperative.

The *Gemara* resolves this by appealing to the structure of the *pasuk* itself: *al tochlu mimenu na uvashel mevushal bamayim ki im tzeli esh*. Why does the Torah conclude by contrasting these prohibitions with the command to eat it roasted? This juxtaposition teaches: *besha'ah sheyeshno bekum echol tzli yeshno beval tochal na* — at the time when one is obligated to eat it roasted, that is precisely when the prohibition of eating it rare applies. *Besha'ah she'eino bekum echol tzli, eino beval tochal na* — when one is not yet obligated to eat it roasted, the prohibition of eating it rare does not yet apply. The *pasuk*'s contrast between the prohibited modes and the commanded mode of roasting is not a contradiction but a synchronization: the prohibitions and the positive obligation are coextensive in time, all taking effect at nightfall on the 15th.

---

## Early Consumption

### Eat Day Before

Returning to the case of eating roasted *korban Pesach* on the day before the 15th, the *Gemara* confirms: *achalo tzli mib'od yom chayav* — one who eats the *korban* roasted during the day has transgressed something. The question is what. The *braita* further notes that *kezayit nami mishechasheicha chayav* — eating it rare at nightfall also constitutes a transgression. The *Gemara* observes that the two cases are presented in parallel: *katani tzli dumya de-na* — the case of eating roasted prematurely is formulated analogously to the case of eating rare. This suggests that just as eating rare is a *lav* — a negative prohibition — so too eating roasted prematurely should be a *lav*. *Ma na belav, af tzli belav* — just as rare carries a *lav*, so should premature eating of the roasted *korban*.

### Negative from Positive

But where is this *lav* derived? For the case of *na*, the verse explicitly states *al tochlu mimenu na* — a clear negative prohibition. For premature consumption of roasted *korban*, there is no explicit *lav* in the text. The verse that establishes the timing of the *mitzvah* is *v'achlu et habasar balaila hazeh* — they shall eat the meat on this night — which is a positive commandment. From the positive command to eat at night, one infers *balaila in beyom lo* — at night yes, during the day no. But this inference is derived from an *aseh*, a positive commandment.

### Lav M'Klal Aseh

This is the principle of *lav haba mikhlal aseh*: a negative prohibition inferred from the implication of a positive commandment. The *Gemara* raises the question: *v'chol lav haba mikhlal aseh, aseh* — any "do not" that is derived from "do," is treated halakhically as a positive commandment, not as a negative prohibition. The practical consequence is significant: a *lav* that is inferred from an *aseh* carries the force of an *aseh*, which does not generate lashes.

If so, eating roasted *korban Pesach* before nightfall would not generate lashes — one has violated the *aseh* of *v'achlu et habasar balaila hazeh* by consuming it prematurely, but not a *lav* in the full sense. Yet the *braita* presents the case as parallel to *na*, which does carry a *lav*. How then are they truly analogous?

Rav Chisda resolves this: *ha mani Rabbi Yehuda hi* — this ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda, who maintains that a *lav haba mikhlal aseh* is treated as a genuine *lav*, not merely as an *aseh*. According to Rabbi Yehuda, when a negative is inferred from the implication of a positive command, it retains the full force of a negative prohibition. The details of Rabbi Yehuda's position and its textual grounding will be the subject of the next day's learning.

---

---

# Pesachim 42

## Raw/Roasted & Timing

### Na vs. Tzali Esh

The daf begins with a review of the previous discussion concerning the Korban Pesach. The Torah prohibits eating the *korban pesach* in a manner described as *na uvashel mevushal* — that is, raw, cooked in liquid, or in any form other than *tzali esh*, roasted over fire. The Gemara had previously interpreted *na* not as completely raw meat, but rather as undercooked or rare — a distintion from *tzali esh* proper. It is worth noting that a check of a concordance reveals this is the only instance in all of Tanakh where the word *na* appears in the sense of a manner of cooking. No other verse uses it in this context, though the concordance does not dispute the Gemara's interpretation. Beyond the prohibition of *na*, the question arises whether eating the *korban pesach* in any manner other than *tzali esh* — even if it is neither rare nor boiled — constitutes the violation of a positive commandment, a negative prohibition, or one that would incur lashes. These are the issues examined in the preceding discussion.

### Eating Before Erev

The final matter carried over from the previous amud concerns one who ate the *korban pesach*, properly roasted as *tzali esh*, on *Erev Pesach* itself rather than at the designated time that evening. The Gemara states that such a person has transgressed. The difficulty is identifying the nature of that transgression. There is a positive commandment — *ve-achalu et habasar balaila hazeh*, they shall eat the meat on this night — which implies eating it that night and no earlier. But nowhere is there an explicit negative prohibition against eating it before that time. Negating a positive commandment is itself a violation, but it does not rise to the level of a negative prohibition. The question with which the Gemara closed on 41b is therefore: where does the negative prohibition come from?

## Rabbi Yehuda Drasha

### Blemished Animals

The Gemara answers by citing *Rav Chisda*: the view that eating the *korban pesach* before its designated time involves a negative prohibition follows the opinion of *Rabbi Yehuda*. A *baraita* is brought in support. The verse states regarding a blemished ox or sheep — one that is *sarua* or *kalut*, meaning disfigured in a limb or with improperly split hooves — that it may be brought as a *nedavah* but not as a *neder*. The rabbinic interpretation of this verse is that such a blemished animal may be consecrated for *bedek habayit*, donated to the Temple treasury for its monetary value, but may not be brought as a *korban* in the full sense.

The *baraita* then draws out the parallel implication: just as a blemished animal may be donated for its proceeds but not used as a *korban*, so too an unblemished animal — *temimim* — may not be donated for its monetary value to *bedek habayit*. The reasoning is that an unblemished animal consecrated to the Temple ought to be used as a *korban* directly, since that constitutes a higher elevation of the animal itself, rather than merely selling it and using the proceeds. The verse *nedavah ta'aseh oso* — you shall make of it a donation — thus implies that this type of animal, a blemished one, may be given as a donation, but an unblemished one may not. One who consecrates an unblemished animal for the temple treasury accordingly violates a positive commandment, *over be-aseh*: the positive commandment that blemished animals are what are donated implies that unblemished ones are not.

### Vayedaber Drasha

Having established that one who consecrates an unblemished animal for *bedek habayit* transgresses a positive commandment, the *baraita* asks: from where do we know that a negative prohibition is also incurred? The verse introducing this entire passage begins *vayedaber Hashem el Moshe lemor* — God spoke to Moses saying. *Rabbi Yehuda* derives from this introduction that everything stated in this *parsha* carries the force of a negative prohibition as well.

When *Rabbi* pressed *Bar Kappara* — *mai mashma*, what exactly does that phrase teach? — *Bar Kappara* replied that the word *lemor* itself encodes the derivation. *Lemor* is read as *lo ne'emar*, a prohibition is stated. *Rabbi bei Rav* articulate this as *lemor lav emor* — the word *lemor* itself announces that a prohibition is being declared. Thus, according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, the introductory formula *vayedaber Hashem el Moshe lemor* converts the implications of the positive commandment in that *parsha* into a full negative prohibition as well. *Tosafot* clarifies that this does not apply to absolutely every implication, but specifically to things that are forbidden by virtue of what the positive commandment implies.

### Universal Application

The Gemara assumes that *Rabbi Yehuda*'s principle can be applied more broadly to explain why eating the *korban pesach* before its time constitutes a negative prohibition — the *parsha* of the *korban pesach* similarly opens with *vayedaber Hashem el Moshe lemor*. However, this universalization gives pause. If one takes the *drasha* globally, then any four-cornered garment worn without *tzitzit* would not merely negate a positive commandment but would constitute a full negative prohibition as well — since the passage concerning *tzitzit* also contains *lemor*. The implications, once broadly applied, become quite sweeping. The Gemara appears to assume the principle operates generally in order to answer its question about the *korban pesach*, yet limiting its application in a principled way remains a challenge. One possible constraint is that the principle applies only where the introductory formula includes *vayedaber* specifically, since *vayedaber* is *lashon kasha*, a term connoting severity, but this too remains uncertain.

## Baker's Water

### Water Disposal Rules

The final *mishnah* of the second *perek* turns to a different concern: the water that a baker uses to wash the sticky dough from his hands. This water, which contains dough residue, will itself become *chametz* and must therefore be disposed of. A conflict arises between two *baraitot*. One teaches that the water must be spilled on an incline — *bemakom midron* — so that it flows downward and is absorbed into the ground. Spilling it on flat, level ground — *bemakom ha'ishborn* — is prohibited, since it will pool and remain *chametz* in place. The other *baraita*, however, permits spilling it on level ground. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: when there is a large quantity of water that will pool and not be quickly absorbed, it must be spilled on an incline; when there is only a small amount, it will be absorbed readily even on level ground.

### Mayim Shelannu Pun

*Rav Yehuda* rules that a woman may not knead *matzah* dough except with *mayim shelannu* — water that has slept overnight. The concern is that in the month of Nissan, at the onset of spring, well water drawn from underground tends to be warm, and warm water accelerates fermentation and the onset of *chametz*. Allowing the water to rest overnight lets it cool, making it suitable for use the following morning.

*Rav Matna* went and publicly taught this ruling in the town of Pappunya. The very next morning, he opened his door to find the entire town assembled outside his house holding their jugs, calling out *hav lan mayya* — give us your water! The townspeople had understood *mayim shelannu* not as "water that has slept," from the root *linah*, but as *our* water — water belonging to the rabbi who had taught them. *Rav Matna* was obliged to clarify: he meant water that had rested overnight, not water from his household. This stands as one of the more memorable puns in the Gemara, the Hebrew *shelannu* carrying both meanings simultaneously.

## Rava's Requirements

### Water Heat Concerns

*Rava* extends the concern about warm water into a set of stringent requirements for women kneading dough on Pesach. She may not knead dough out in direct sunlight, *bachama*, since the sun will heat the water in the vessel she is using. She may not use water already warmed by the sun, *bechamei chama*. She may not use water drawn from a *mulyar* — a metal cooking pot — since even after being removed from the fire, the metal retains heat and the water sitting at its bottom will remain warm. All of these restrictions flow from the same underlying principle: warm water speeds the fermentation process and poses a heightened risk of *chametz*. Furthermore, she may not lift her hand from work at the oven until all the dough has been formed and baked — *ad shetigmor et kol hapat* — since continuous working of the dough prevents it from having the opportunity to become *chametz*.

### Two Vessels

In addition to the above requirements, *Rava* rules that a woman kneading dough requires two separate vessels. One vessel is used for actually working the dough — for rolling and slapping it in the process of kneading. The second vessel is for cooling her hands between portions. The concern here is not merely cleanliness or hygiene: as her hands are actively pounding and working the dough, they become warm. Warm hands in contact with the dough create the same risk as warm water — accelerating fermentation. Therefore, the woman must periodically cool her hands by dipping them into the second vessel, ensuring that the heat of her hands does not contribute to the onset of *chametz*.

### Warm Water B'Diavad

A question is then raised: what if a woman transgressed and kneaded with warm water — what is the law *b'diavad*, after the fact? *Mar Zutra* rules that the dough is permitted. His reasoning draws on a *baraita* cited earlier in the tractate: one does not remove bran from barley on Pesach using water, but if one did, the status of the result depends on observation — if the kernels cracked, the grain is forbidden as *chametz*; if not, it is permitted. This demonstrates that even where the initial act was prohibited, the resulting product may be evaluated by direct observation to determine whether *chametz* has actually formed. The same principle should apply here: if observation shows the dough has not become *chametz*, it should be permitted.

*Rav Ashi* disagrees. He rejects *Mar Zutra*'s analogy on the grounds that a ruling stated in one context does not automatically extend to all analogous cases: *heicha d'itmar itmar, heicha d'lo itmar lo itmar* — where it was said, it was said; where it was not said, it was not said. In the case of the barley, leniency *b'diavad* was explicitly stated; here it was not.

*Rashi*'s understanding of *Rav Ashi*'s position is particularly instructive. *Rashi* maintains that observation genuinely can determine whether dough has become *chametz* — this is not in doubt. Indeed, the Gemara elsewhere permits purchasing dough from non-Jews and evaluating it by inspection. *Rav Ashi*'s stringency is therefore not rooted in skepticism about the reliability of observation. Rather, because the woman disregarded a rabbinic ruling by using warm water, *Rav Ashi* holds that there must be consequences for that disregard — even if the dough is demonstrably not *chametz*. This understanding importantly reinforces the broader Talmudic assumption that physical inspection of dough genuinely can reveal whether *chametz* has formed.

## Third Perek Intro

### Mishnah Items

With the conclusion of the second *perek* — *hadran alach Kol Sha'ah* — we enter the third *perek*, the last of the three chapters devoted primarily to the laws of *chametz* and *matzah* as objects, before the tractate moves to the *korban pesach* and ultimately to the *Seder* night in the tenth *perek*. The *mishnah* opens with the words *v'eilu ovrin b'Pesach* — the following things you transgress regarding on Pesach. The *mishnah* lists: *kutach ha'Bavli*, Babylonian *kutach*, a dairy-based dip containing sour milk and molded bread; *sheichar ha'Madi*, Median beer or mead, which uses barley rather than date honey as other varieties might; *chometz ha'Adomi*, Edomian vinegar, which unlike ordinary vinegar has a grain or barley basis rather than a wine basis; *zeisom ha'Mitzri*, Egyptian *zeisom*, a mixture to be described shortly; *zoman shel tzavaim*, some type of mixture used in the dyeing of leather; *amilan shel tavachim*, a dough used by butchers, placed on pot rims to absorb froth during cooking; and *kolan shel sofrim*, the glue used by scribes. *Rabbi Eliezer* adds women's ornaments — cosmetic preparations containing a flour component.

### Rabbi Eliezer Klal

*Rabbi Eliezer* states the general principle: *kol she'hu mi'min dagan*, anything that has a grain component, *harei ze over b'Pesach* — you transgress on Pesach. The concluding line of the *mishnah* then states: *harei eilu b'azhara v'ein bo mishum karet* — these carry a negative prohibition but not the full *karet* penalty.

Two significant questions arise from this *mishnah*. First, what exactly does *harei ze over b'Pesach* mean in the opening clause? *Rashi* understands it to mean that one transgresses by owning these items — the prohibition of *bal yira'eh u'val yimatzeh*, the biblical prohibition against possessing *chametz* — and additionally transgresses a *lav* by eating them, though without incurring *karet*. A *ba'al Tosafot* goes further, reading *eilu ovrin b'Pesach* as meaning these items must be *removed* — *ma'avir* — from one's possession. *Rabbeinu Tam* disagrees with both readings. In his view, *bal yira'eh u'val yimatzeh* applies only to *chametz* for which one would incur *karet* if eaten. These items, being of a lesser category, do not trigger the biblical ownership prohibition at all. According to *Rabbeinu Tam*, the requirement to remove them is at most rabbinic in origin, and the phrase *harei eilu ovrin* refers solely to the prohibition incurred by eating them. This dispute among the *Rishonim* — whether *bal yira'eh u'val yimatzeh* applies to these lesser forms of *chametz* — is thus embedded in the very reading of the *mishnah*.

## Zeisom & Dyers

### Three Categories

Why do these items carry a *lav* but not *karet*? There are essentially three categories of explanation. The first is *ta'aruvet* — mixture. Some of these items contain a *chametz* component but only as a minority ingredient, diluted among other substances. Normal rules of *ta'am* and *rov* might still establish a biblical prohibition in mixtures, but a minority chametz ingredient in a compound may reduce the severity from *karet* to a *lav*. The *kutach*, the beer, the vinegar, and the *zeisom* all appear to fall into this category, each containing grain or barley as only one component among others.

The second category is *chametz nuksha* — quasi-leavened product. This refers to a substance that has undergone some fermentation but not the complete process that constitutes full *chametz*. The precise definition of *chametz nuksha* requires further development as the Gemara proceeds.

The third category is *ra'ui l'kelev* — fit for a dog but not for human consumption. A substance that is not genuinely fit for human eating may still incur a *lav* if eaten but not the full penalty of *karet*, which is reserved for *chametz gamur* that a person would actually eat. The professional items at the end of the *mishnah* — the dyers' paste, butchers' dough, and scribes' glue — seem more naturally to fall into this third category or possibly the second, since they are not themselves foods consumed by people. The butchers' dough, for example, is placed on pot rims to absorb cooking froth, not eaten, and may not have fully fermented; the dyers' paste and scribes' glue are craft materials. The task remaining for the Gemara is to precisely identify which of these three rationales applies to each item.

## Kutach & Wine

### Kutach Effects

The Gemara now turns to a detailed description of the items listed in the *mishnah*, beginning with *kutach ha'Bavli*. A *baraita* states that three things are said about Babylonian *kutach*: it *metamtem et halev* — stops up the heart, apparently due to the harmful effects of the sour whey it contains; it *mesame et ha'einayim* — blinds the eyes, owing to the large quantity of salt in it, which makes its way to the eyes; and it *machlish et haguf* — generally weakens the body, on account of the moldy, fermented bread — *kumnitsa* — that it contains. These three ingredients — sour milk, salt, and molded bread — thus each contribute a distinct harmful effect.

The Gemara then cites two parallel *baraitot* cataloguing categories of foods that affect the body. The first lists three foods that increase excretion, bend one's posture, and diminish eyesight by one five-hundredth: bran bread (*pat kibar*), new beer (*sheichar chadash*), and raw vegetables (*yerek chai*) — *Rashi* noting that this applies when one consumes them frequently and in large quantities. In direct parallel, three foods are listed that decrease excretion, straighten one's posture, and illuminate the eyes: fine white bread (*pat nekia, samnid*), fatty meat (*basar shamina*) — specifically from a young goat that has never given birth — and aged wine (*yayin yashan*). *Rashi* identifies "old" wine as three years aged, though the basis for that figure is unclear. Finally, the Gemara notes a general principle: most foods that are beneficial to one part of the body are harmful to another, and vice versa. Exceptions to this rule include moist ginger (*mizangavila retivta*), long peppers (*pilpili arichta*), fine white bread, fatty meat, and old wine — all of which benefit the entire body without corresponding harm elsewhere.

### Wine Quality Change

The Gemara proceeds to describe the Median beer and Edomian vinegar. The beer — *sheichar ha'Madi* — is identified as having barley water added to it, distinguishing it from varieties made purely from date honey. The Edomian vinegar — *chometz ha'Adomi* — is identified as having barley added to what would otherwise be a wine base.

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* then offers a striking teaching that illuminates why the Edomian vinegar carries this barley additive. He states that originally, when wine libations — *nesachim* — were brought from Judea at the time of the *Beis Hamikdash*, the wine of Judea was of such extraordinary quality that it would never spoil on its own and turn to vinegar. If one wished to produce vinegar from it, one had to introduce barley as a catalyst to initiate the souring process. This vinegar was simply called *chometz stam* — plain vinegar. Now, however, since the destruction of the Temple, the wine of Judea has declined in quality and spoils naturally without any additive. In its place, *Rav Nachman* notes, it is the Edomian wine that is now of this high quality, not turning to vinegar unless barley is added — and that product is therefore called *chometz ha'Adomi*, Edomian vinegar.

Looking back at the Gemara's formulation for the beer and vinegar — *deramu bei mei sa'ari, deshadu bei sa'ari* — they put into it barley water, they added to it barley — it is evident that these were not beverages made entirely of barley, but ones with a barley additive, consistent with *Rav Nachman*'s account. The Edomian vinegar had a wine base to which barley was added to induce souring.

*Rav Nachman* grounds this historical reversal in the verse *imaleh hacharava* — I will fill the desolate places — understood through the *drasha* that when one rises the other falls: *ule'om mile'om ye'ematz*, nation will prevail over nation. The Judean wine was preeminent when the Temple stood; once the *Churban Habayis* came, Judean wine declined and Edomian wine rose. *Rashi* adds that the merit of using Judean wine specifically for *nesachim* was itself what sustained its exceptional quality.

It is worth pausing over the historical identification involved here. When the *mishnah* refers to *Adomi* wine, it most plausibly refers to Idumaea — the region to which Herod's family belonged, whose inhabitants were forcibly converted by the Hasmoneans, and which was geographically in the Negev and southern regions. This is distinct from the biblical *Edom*, descendants of *Esav*, on the other side of the Jordan. The Gemara, however, maps *Adomi* onto *Edom*, which rabbinic tradition in turn identifies with Rome. There are thus two layers of historical identification at work: the general rabbinic mapping of *Edom* to Rome, and the identification of the *mishnah*'s Idumaea with that same *Edom*. Both identifications carry their own complexities.

### Temet & Separations

The Gemara next cites *Rav Yehuda* teaching that in Judea in former times, one who purchased vinegar from an *am ha'aretz* — an ordinary person of the field, generally suspected of not observing *ma'aser* — did not need to tithe it. The reason: since Judean wine was of such high quality, sellers would never make vinegar from actual wine. They would only make vinegar from *temed* — water in which grape lees had been soaked, producing a weak, grape-flavored liquid — and one need not tithe *temed*. Now, however, since the quality of Judean wine has declined, vinegar may well be made from actual wine, and one who purchases it from an *am ha'aretz* must indeed tithe it.

This raises a difficulty: *Rav Yehuda* himself holds elsewhere — as the *mishnah* records — that *temed* does in fact require the separation of *terumah* and *ma'aser*. How then can he say that in earlier times one need not worry about the vinegar coming from *temed*? The Gemara resolves this in two ways. First, *Rav Yehuda* may hold that even though *temed* technically requires *ma'aser*, it is of such negligible value that even *amei ha'aretz* who ordinarily neglect *ma'aser* would not bother skipping it here — the loss would be too trivial to evade. Second, the question of whether *temed* requires *ma'aser* may itself depend on how it is produced: if the grape lees are merely soaked in water, yielding only flavor with no actual juice, it is exempt; if the pressing is more thorough and actual juice is extracted along with the water, *Rav Yehuda* would require *ma'aser*. These are two distinct modes of preparation, and the rulings differ accordingly. The broader point, however, reinforces the theme that *after the Churban Habayis* the quality of our wine declined.

## Zeisom & Dyers (II)

### Zeisom Composition

The Gemara now identifies the composition of *zeisom ha'Mitzri*. *Rav Yosef* teaches that it consists of one-third barley (*sa'ari*), one-third saffron (*kurtami*), and one-third salt (*milcha*). *Rav Pappa* disputes the first ingredient, substituting wheat (*chiti*) for barley. A mnemonic preserves who said which: the double-*sin* sound in *sisni* stands for *Yosef sa'ari* — Yosef's version uses barley. The preparation involves soaking the ingredients, roasting them, grinding them, and then drinking the resulting mixture — presumably after adding water to create a drinkable suspension. This was consumed from Pesach until *Shavuot*, the spring season during which it was relevant. Its principal use was medicinal: it could loosen the bowels for those who were constipated, and conversely constipate those who suffered from loose bowels. For a sick person or a pregnant woman, however, it posed a danger.

### Dyers' & Scribes'

*Zoman shel tzavaim* is interpreted locally in the Gemara as a kind of whitening liquid used in the dyeing or treatment of leather, though its precise composition — beyond the evident grain component — is not specified. *Kolan shel sofrim* is first explained as *perufa de'ushchafi* — a type of adhesive used by cobblers and leatherworkers. A second explanation is offered by *Rav Shimi miChozna*, who identifies it as a skin plaster used by wealthy women, with any leftover donated to the wives and daughters of scribes and *cheder* teachers — hence the name. However, *Rav Chiyya*'s *baraita* distinguishes between the first four items in the *mishnah* as *minei medina* — foodstuffs consumed by people — and the last three as *minei omanut* — items used in professional or craft contexts. If *kolan shel sofrim* were a cosmetic skin plaster used in private households, it would not qualify as a *minei omanut*. This objection rejects *Rav Shimi*'s interpretation. The Gemara then asks: if it is indeed *perufa de'ushchafi*, a craft adhesive used by leatherworkers, why is it called the *kolan* of scribes rather than of leatherworkers? *Rav Oshaya* resolves this: it is indeed the leatherworkers' adhesive, but scribes also use it to glue papers together — hence it came to be known by their name.

### Butchers' Dough

*Amilan shel tavachim* — the butchers' dough — is identified as bread made from grain that had not yet reached even one-third of its full ripening, *shelo hevi shlish*. This immature grain dough is placed along the rim where the pot and its cover meet, where it absorbs the froth and overflow produced during cooking. Since this dough is not a foodstuff consumed by people, the question of why it incurs a prohibition without *karet* must be understood differently from the food mixtures earlier in the *mishnah*. It is not *chametz b'ta'aruvet* — the grain here is not diluted by other ingredients in the way the *kutach* or *zeisom* are. Rather, the reason it falls short of *chametz gamur* must lie either in the fact that it did not fully ferment — since it is placed on the pot lip and not baked in the normal fashion — or in the fact that it is not fit for human consumption. The underlying rationale for this last category remains to be fully worked out as the Gemara continues.

---

---

# Pesachim 43

## Two Chametz Categories

### Intro: Chametz Categories

The *daf* opens by situating us within a broader classification of non-standard *chametz* — forms that are prohibited on Pesach yet fall short of the full prohibition that incurs *karet*. The *Mishnah* presents two conceptually distinct categories. The first is *chametz betaarovet*: items that are genuine foods, yet contain *chametz* as one ingredient within a larger mixture. The paradigmatic case is *kutach*, a sour-milk-based dip into which moldy bread has been dissolved. Similarly, barley placed into wine to produce vinegar, or into mead to produce beer, generates a fully fermented grain product — but one subsumed within a larger liquid medium. The *chametz* is real; what renders it a lesser category is its role as a constituent within a mixture rather than as a food unto itself.

The second category, which the *Gemara* will shortly label *chametz nuksha*, comprises items that may indeed have a high grain content, yet are not truly edible in the ordinary sense and were not produced for human consumption. The *Mishnah* lists items such as glues and plasters — preparations applied to the skin for cosmetic or depilatory purposes — which may be flour-based yet are not foods in any meaningful sense. Both categories share the same halachic status: there is a negative prohibition (*lav*) against eating them on Pesach, but no *karet*.

It is worth pausing on this point, which the *Gemara* itself will probe at length. That *chametz betaarovet* — real, fully fermented grain dissolved into a mixture — carries only a *lav* and not *karet* is, on its face, striking. The *Rishonim* debate whether this middle category also violates the biblical prohibition of *bal yera'eh bal yimatze* (owning *chametz* over Pesach), though that question lies at the margin of today's discussion.

### Women's Cosmetics

The *Mishnah* concludes with a position attributed to *Rabbi Eliezer*: *af takhshitei nashim* — even women's cosmetics. The *Gemara* immediately flags the literal translation, "women's jewelry," as incoherent in this context, and clarifies that the reference is to *tipulei nashim*, women's cosmetic preparations. The context for this is provided by a teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, which describes the depilatory practices used by young Jewish women who had reached physical maturity before the socially expected age, presenting unwanted hair growth as a social concern.

Three tiers of practice are described, corresponding to economic class. Poor women (*bnos aniyim*) would apply *sid*, a plaster, to their skin and then peel it away along with the hair. Wealthy women (*bnos ashirim*) would use *soles*, a fine-flour-based paste — a dough preparation, and notably more expensive. The daughters of kings (*bnos melachim*) used *shemen hamor*, an aromatic oil — the same substance, the *Gemara* notes, used by Esther, as attested by the verse describing her six-month preparation with *shemen hamor* and six months with fragrant spices.

The *Gemara* inquires into the precise identity of *shemen hamor*. Rav Yehuda bar Yirmyah calls it *satachet*, a substance Rashi acknowledges is uncertain. Rav Yirmyah bar Abba identifies it as olive oil pressed from olives that have not yet reached a third of their ripening (*shemen zayit shelo hevi'a shalish*). A *baraita* confirms that Rabbi Yehuda identifies this with *anpikanon*, which in the tractate Menachot is similarly described as *shemen zayit shelo hevi'a shalish*. Its use was twofold: it causes hair to fall away (*mashir et hase'ar*) and softens the skin (*me'aden et habasar*). The relevance to Pesach is that some of these cosmetic preparations — specifically the dough-based paste used by wealthier women — are flour-based and thus raise the question of *chametz*. Why *Rabbi Eliezer* mentions them separately, and what he is adding beyond what the *Chachamim* already prohibit, is a question left for the subsequent analysis.

### Grain Principle

Having enumerated specific cases, the *Mishnah* offers a generalization: *ze haklal kol shehu mi-min dagan* — the principle is that anything containing a grain component is problematic on Pesach.
