The *mishnah* provides a practical solution: *im yesh kayotzei bo she-hichmitz harei zeh assur* — if there are comparable doughs that were prepared at the same time and those doughs have fermented, then this hardened dough is presumed to have fermented as well and is forbidden. This marks a significant methodological shift: rather than direct observation of the dough itself, one infers its status from the behavior of analogous doughs prepared under the same conditions and at the same time.

### Eighteen-Minute Standard

The *gemara* then raises the next case: *im ein sham kayotzei bo mahu* — what if there are no comparable doughs available for reference? One has no basis for comparison. The *gemara* answers in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, as transmitted by Rabbi Abba: *kedei she-yeilech adam mi-Migdal Nunia le-Tverya mil* — one goes by the time it takes a person to walk from Migdal Nunia to Tiberias, which is one *mil*. If that amount of time has elapsed since the dough was last worked, one assumes fermentation has occurred.

### Mil Measurement

The *gemara* asks: why give the reference of Migdal Nunia to Tiberias? Why not simply say one *mil*? The answer is that it teaches us the concrete measure of a *mil*: *de-shiur de-mil ke-Migdal Nunia le-Tverya* — the distance from Migdal Nunia to Tiberias defines the *mil* as a unit of measurement. Based on other *gemarot*, the minimum time assumed for walking one *mil* is eighteen minutes. A modern mile takes roughly twenty minutes on flat paved roads, and a *mil*, being approximately one kilometer, should theoretically take somewhat less. The eighteen-minute figure appears to presuppose a slower pace — roughly a half-hour mile — which may reflect variations in terrain, physical condition, or the gait of different walkers, including, as the *gemara* elsewhere notes, a pregnant woman.

What is historically significant here is the move from observation to quantification. The entire *gemara* up to this point has assumed that *chametz* is determined by direct observation of fermentation. This *gemara* introduces a temporal standard — eighteen minutes — as a substitute when observation is unavailable. That standard has subsequently been codified as the definitive outer limit for leaving dough unattended during the Pesach baking process, regardless of whether the original context of *batzek hacherish* fully accounts for all the practical circumstances.

---

## Four-Mil Standard

### Kneading Dough

The mention of the *mil* as a measure prompts a broader discussion. Rav Abbahu cites Resh Lakish: *legabul u'letfilla u'li'netilat yadayim arba'ah mil* — for kneading dough *betaharah*, for prayer, and for washing hands before eating, the operative standard is four *mil*. The case of kneading dough *betaharah* envisions a traveler who normally prepares his dough in a state of *taharah* but is on the road without access to *tahor* vessels. If a baker who works *betaharah* is located within four *mil* ahead in the direction of travel — approximately seventy-two minutes of walking — one must wait until reaching that baker rather than preparing the dough in a state of *tumah*. If the baker is further away than four *mil*, one need not wait indefinitely and may prepare the dough where one is.

### Prayer Timing

The four-*mil* standard applies similarly to prayer. If one is traveling and it is time to *daven*, but a *beit knesset* lies within four *mil* ahead, one must wait and *daven* there rather than praying on the side of the road. *Rashi* frames this in terms of the significance of the *beit knesset* as a location, while *Tosafot* understands the concern as reaching a *minyan* — if a *minyan* is available within four *mil*, one must wait for it. These two readings reflect a broader question in the *gemara* in Berakhot about the relative halakhic weight of *davening* in a *beit knesset* as opposed to *davening* with a *minyan*.

### Hand Washing

The same four-*mil* standard governs *netilat yadayim* before eating. A traveler who is hungry but has no access to water for washing — the familiar predicament of a long car journey with packed food — must wait for the next opportunity to wash hands if it lies within four *mil* in the direction of travel. If the nearest water source is more than four *mil* away, one need not wait. Since the measure is fundamentally one of time and effort rather than bare distance, the practical application scales with how far one has to go.

### Leather Processing

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that it was actually Aivo, not Rav Abbahu, who transmitted this teaching, and that Aivo cited four matters, not three — the fourth being the *ibud* of hides, the processing of animal skins into leather. This connects back to the earlier *baraita* about *areivas ha'avdanim*. Certain animals have hides that are soft enough to be considered edible and therefore food-like, capable of receiving *tumah* as *ochlin*. Once such a hide is properly processed into leather, it loses its food status and can no longer become *tamei*. The *mishnah* states: *v'chullan she'ibdan o shehilach bahen kedei avodah tehorim* — all such hides, if one processed them chemically or walked on them for the duration required for leather-working, become *tehorim* and are no longer subject to *tum'at ochlin*. *Chutz me'or ha'adam* — with the exception of human skin, which remains exceptional for reasons the *mishnah* does not elaborate. Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yannai specifies: *kedei hiluch arba mil* — the walking required to process the leather is four *mil*.

### Direction Qualifier

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina qualifies the entire four-*mil* standard: *lo shanu ela lefanav* — this applies only when the relevant destination lies ahead in the direction one is already traveling. *U'le'achorav afilu mil eino chozer* — but if one has already passed the location, even a *mil* of backtracking is not required. The obligation is to delay forward progress, not to reverse course. The *gemara* draws an implication from this formulation: *mil hu de'eino chozer, ha'pachos mimil chozer* — the fact that even a *mil* of backtracking is not required implies that less than a *mil* would require backtracking. If the nearest *shul* with a *minyan*, or the nearest rest stop with water, lies less than a *mil* behind, one should in principle turn back.

---

## Challah on Yom Tov

### The Dilemma

A new *mishnah* poses a challenging practical problem: *keitzad mafrishim challah be'tumah be'Yom Tov?* — how does one separate *challah* when the dough has become *tamei* on *Yom Tov*? The setting is a household preparing *matzot* on *Yom Tov* — baking on *Yom Tov* is permitted. The dough has become *tamei*, perhaps through contact with a *sheretz* that fell into the kneading trough. One must still be *mafrish challah*, but the *challah teme'iah* cannot be given to a *kohen* to eat, nor can it simply be left out, since it will become *chametz*. The obvious solution — burning it — is also unavailable on *Yom Tov*, because burning *challah teme'iah* is fundamentally an act of destruction rather than a constructive use of fire, even if one incidentally benefits from the fuel. Baking it in the oven is similarly prohibited, since one may not bake on *Yom Tov* food that one cannot eat, and *challah teme'iah* is inedible. The situation thus presents a genuine impasse: one cannot burn it, cannot bake it, and cannot simply leave it.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer proposes a solution: *lo tikra lah shem ad shete'afeh* — do not designate any loaf as *challah* until after all the loaves are baked. While the loaves are in the oven, none of them has yet been designated as *challah*, and any one of them is theoretically edible. Therefore, the baking of all the loaves is entirely permissible on *Yom Tov* — one is baking potentially edible food. Once the baking is complete, one designates one loaf as *challah*. At that point, the *challah* is already baked and hard; it is no longer at risk of becoming *chametz*, and no prohibited labor remains to be performed.

### Ben Beteira

Ben Beteira offers a different approach: *tateih betzonen* — submerge the dough in cold water. Cold water prevents fermentation, and so one can set aside the raw *challah* dough in cold water and leave it there until *Yom Tov* is over, at which point it can be dealt with normally. The practical difficulty of this approach in a Pesach context — deliberately leaving raw dough outside the oven — is self-evident.

### Rabbi Yehoshua

Rabbi Yehoshua takes a more expansive position: *lo zehu chametz shemuzeharin alav beval yera'eh uval yimatzeh* — this is not the kind of *chametz* regarding which one is warned by the prohibitions of *bal yera'eh* and *bal yimatzeh*. The *challah* has already been sanctified; it belongs to *kohanim*, even if no specific *kohen* has yet received it. It is not the owner's property. One therefore does not transgress by leaving it in one's possession. *Ella mafrisha u'manicha ad ha'erev* — one separates it, leaves it until the evening, and lets it become *chametz* if it will. *V'im hechmitza hechmitza* — and if it becomes *chametz*, so be it. No one transgresses.

### Tovat Hana'ah Debate

The *gemara* explores the underlying debate. The disputants appear to disagree about *tovat hana'ah* — the right of the one who separated the *challah* to direct it to a *kohen* of his choosing. Even though the *challah* does not belong to the owner in a full proprietary sense, the owner possesses the right to determine which *kohen* receives it. This right — analogous to a government official who does not personally receive a contract but controls who does — may constitute a form of concrete monetary interest in the object. *Rabbi Eliezer savar tovat hana'ah mamon* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that this right of distribution constitutes monetary ownership, and therefore the owner does transgress *bal yera'eh* with respect to the *challah*. *Rabbi Yehoshua savar tovat hana'ah einah mamon* — Rabbi Yehoshua holds that this right does not rise to the level of monetary ownership, and therefore no transgression occurs.

### Ownership Theory

The *gemara* then proposes an alternative framework for the dispute, one that does not require taking a position in the broader *tovat hana'ah* controversy. *De'kulei alma savri tovat hana'ah einah mamon* — perhaps both opinions agree that *tovat hana'ah* is not monetary ownership. The dispute instead turns on the principle of *ho'il* — theoretical possibility. *Rabbi Eliezer savar amrinan ho'il v'i ba'ei mitshil alah mamona hu* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that since one could theoretically reverse the designation of *challah* — the act of separation, like a vow, can be retroactively annulled — the *challah* is still sufficiently in one's possession. The theoretical ability to reclaim it makes it enough of one's property to trigger *bal yera'eh*. *Rabbi Yehoshua savar lo amrinan ho'il* — Rabbi Yehoshua does not accept this reasoning. Theoretical reversibility does not constitute ownership.

The *gemara* notes that of the two frameworks, *tovat hana'ah* intuitively seems the stronger basis for considering the *challah* one's property — the right to direct the benefit is a concrete, ongoing interest. The reason the *gemara* avoids locking in that framework is that the *tovat hana'ah* question recurs in broader contexts throughout the *gemara*, and the current discussion is better served by the more local principle of *ho'il* and retroactive annulment.

---

## Cooking on Yom Tov

### Baking for Tomorrow

The *gemara* now turns to what is arguably the most conceptually central discussion on the *daf*: the permissibility of cooking or baking on *Yom Tov* for a purpose other than *Yom Tov* itself. *Ha'ofeh miyom tov lechol* — one who bakes on *Yom Tov* explicitly stating that the food is intended for the following weekday.

### Rav Chisda

Rav Chisda rules: *lokei* — one receives lashes. The Torah permitted cooking and baking on *Yom Tov* solely for the benefit of *Yom Tov*. If one explicitly intends the food for the following day, the cooking is not *le'tzorech Yom Tov* and the prohibition against *melacha* on *Yom Tov* is violated. The hypothetical argument that guests might arrive and benefit from the food on *Yom Tov* itself does not factor into the analysis: what matters is the actual intention, and the actual intention is for the following day.

### Rabbah

Rabbah rules: *ein lokei* — one does not receive lashes. Rabbah's position is based on the principle of *ho'il* — since (*ho'il*), theoretically, if guests were to arrive, this food could be eaten on *Yom Tov* itself. The food is objectively edible on *Yom Tov*; it is present and available. The cooking therefore has the character of being for *Yom Tov* in an objective sense, even if subjectively one intended it for the following day. *Tosafot* adds a qualification to Rabbah's position: if the baking occurred in the very last moments of *Yom Tov* — so close to nightfall that there was literally no time remaining to benefit from the food on *Yom Tov* — then even Rabbah would concede to Rav Chisda, since there is no objective possibility of benefit on *Yom Tov* itself, not merely a subjective lack of intention.

### Yom Tov to Shabbat

Rabbah then challenges Rav Chisda: *hei ofei miyom tov leShabbat* — according to your position, how is it ever permitted to cook on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat*? We know that one may do so with an *Eiruv Tavshilin*, but according to Rav Chisda, any cooking not intended for *Yom Tov* itself should be a biblical violation. How does *Eiruv Tavshilin* resolve a *de'oraita* prohibition?

### Shared Kedusha

Rav Chisda responds by citing Rav Yitzchak: *mi de'oraita tsorkhei Shabbat na'asin b'Yom Tov* — biblically, cooking on *Yom Tov* for a *Shabbat* that immediately follows is permitted. When *Yom Tov* and *Shabbat* are contiguous, they share a single *kedushah*; the *Shabbat* is, in a sense, an extension of the *Yom Tov*, and cooking for it is tantamount to cooking for the *Yom Tov* itself. One could not, by contrast, cook on a *Yom Tov* in Tishri for *Shabbat* in Tishri two weeks later; contiguity is essential. The Rabbis added a prohibition against cooking from *Yom Tov* to *Shabbat* without preparation, as a *gezeirah* lest people conclude that one may also cook from *Yom Tov* for an ordinary weekday — *gezeirah shema yomru ofin miyom tov af lechol*. *Eiruv Tavshilin* was then instituted as a rabbinic mechanism to permit what the Torah allows while providing a *hekeira* — a recognizable signal — that makes clear to all that the general rule forbids cooking from *Yom Tov* for the weekday, and that cooking for *Shabbat* is only possible under specific conditions. The *Eiruv Tavshilin* thus navigates between biblical permission and rabbinic restriction.

### Sick Animal Case

Rabbah then presses Rav Chisda with another challenge: *behema hamesukhenet* — a sick animal that is about to die. The rule is *lo yishchot ela k'dei sheyochal heimena k'zayit tzali mib'od yom* — one may only slaughter such an animal on *Yom Tov* if there is enough time to roast a *kezayit* of its meat and eat it before the day ends. Roasting is specified because it is the fastest cooking method and requires no *kashering* through salting, since the blood drips out during the roasting process. The implicit rationale for the condition is that the slaughter is only *le'tzorech Yom Tov* — for the purpose of *Yom Tov* — if there is time to actually benefit from it on *Yom Tov*. Rabbah argues that this supports his position: *bishlama ledidi de'amri ho'il* — according to me, who says *ho'il* — since in principle you could eat from it on *Yom Tov*, the slaughter is permitted even if in practice you do not intend to eat the meat. The *mishnah* requires only that there be enough time, not that one actually intend to eat it.

### Financial Loss Objection

Rav Chisda objects: how can this be permitted according to his own view? If one is not planning to eat the meat, then the slaughter is not for the purpose of *Yom Tov*, and it should constitute a biblical violation. Financial loss — however significant — does not override a *de'oraita* prohibition. *Umishum hefsed mamon sharina issur d'oraita?* The question is stark.

### Financial Loss Resolution

Rabbah resolves the difficulty in a way that fully preserves Rav Chisda's framework rather than overriding it. Because the alternative is the complete financial loss of the animal — a thousand-dollar cow dying and becoming *neveilah* — the owner is strongly motivated to eat some of the meat on *Yom Tov*. We therefore tell the owner: you may slaughter the animal *on condition* that you genuinely commit to eating a *kezayit* of it today. *Gamar belibo le'echol kezayit v'i efshar li'kzayit basar belo shechita* — if he sincerely resolves to eat a *kezayit* today, then the slaughter of the whole animal is a necessary precondition for eating that *kezayit*, and the entire *shechita* is considered *le'tzorech Yom Tov*. Financial loss does not override the Torah — it merely provides the practical incentive that makes genuine intention credible and forthcoming. The *de'oraita* prohibition is not overwritten; rather, the owner navigates through it by genuinely forming the requisite intention.

This debate between Rav Chisda and Rabbah — one requiring actual intention for *Yom Tov* benefit, the other permitting *melacha* wherever objective benefit on *Yom Tov* is theoretically possible — is the conceptual pivot around which much of the later *Yom Tov* cooking discussion turns. The *gemara* will continue to develop its implications in the *daf* that follows.

---

---

# Pesachim 47

## Challah b'Tumah

### Opening

Today's daf is 47, and we pick up at the very last line of 46b — literally the final three words. The broader context is a *mishna* that asks the question of *keitzad mafrishin challah b'tumah*: how does one separate *challah* from a *tamei* dough on the *yom tov* of Pesach, when one faces a seemingly inescapable bind? One cannot bake the *challah* because it is *tamei* and one will not eat it. One cannot leave it unbaked because it will become *chametz*. And one cannot simply burn it, because burning things unnecessarily on *yom tov* is itself prohibited.

### Mishna Debate

The *mishna* records a three-way debate about how to resolve this dilemma. One opinion holds that the dough should be placed in cold water so that it does not ferment. A second opinion holds that one need not worry at all, since the *challah* is *kodesh* — it belongs to the *kohen*, not to the owner — and therefore no transgression occurs. A third opinion holds that one should bake the entire dough first, and only afterward designate one of the loaves as *challah*, thereby separating it in its already-baked form. These three positions will be returned to in due course, but in order to furnish the necessary background, the *gemara* at this point is in the middle of a heated and wide-ranging debate between Rava and Rav Chisda.

---

## Rava v. Rav Chisda

### Ho'il Principle

The question Rava and Rav Chisda are debating is whether one who bakes on *yom tov* for a weekday purpose actually incurs lashes. Prima facie, it would seem that he should, since the biblical dispensation of *ochel nefesh* — the license to perform food-related labor on *yom tov* — applies only when one is cooking for the sake of *yom tov* itself. Nevertheless, Rava maintains that such a person does not receive lashes. His reasoning is the principle of *ho'il*: since theoretically, if guests were to arrive unexpectedly, the food one cooked would serve *yom tov* purposes, the cooking retains at least a hypothetical *yom tov* character. It is a type of cooking that *could* serve the day, even if that was not the cook's actual intent.

### Intent Requirement

Rav Chisda disagrees sharply. In his view, intent is decisive. The cooking must specifically be for a *yom tov* purpose; absent that intent, one does receive lashes. The disagreement between them thus turns on whether a hypothetical permissibility — the mere possibility that the food could have been eaten today — is sufficient to license the act.

### Eruv Tavshilin

This raises a natural question: how, according to Rav Chisda, does one cook from *yom tov* to *Shabbos*? Rav Chisda's answer is that cooking from *yom tov* to *Shabbos* is fundamentally permitted — one has a license to do so — and the institution of *eruv tavshilin* is what gives practical expression to that license. The prohibition Rav Chisda is targeting is specifically the case of cooking on *yom tov* for a plain weekday, where there is no such license and where intent to cook only for that weekday purpose would render one liable. With this backdrop established, the *gemara* proceeds with its analysis.

---

## Lechem HaPanim

### Showbread Challenge

Rava now challenges Rav Chisda with a *braita* concerning *lechem hapanim*, the showbread that was placed on the *shulchan* in the *Beis HaMikdash* each week. The *lechem hapanim* was baked and then replaced every *Shabbos*, sitting on the table for an entire week before being eaten the following *Shabbos*. The *braita* teaches that the *lechem hapanim* could be eaten on the ninth, tenth, or eleventh day from its baking — no fewer than nine and no more than eleven — and explains the three possibilities as corresponding to different calendar configurations.

### Day Counting

In a normal week, the *lechem hapanim* would be baked on *erev Shabbos* — that is, Friday — and eaten the following *Shabbos*. Counting inclusively from the day of baking, this makes Friday day one and the following *Shabbos* day nine. That is the scenario of *ne'echal l'tishah* — eaten on day nine.

If Friday happened to fall on *yom tov*, one could not bake the *lechem hapanim* on *yom tov* to be eaten a week later — and this is precisely the crux of the *braita*'s significance, as we will see. Accordingly, the baking would be pushed back to Thursday. The bread would then be replaced on *Shabbos* and eaten the following *Shabbos*, arriving at day ten. That is the case of *ne'echal l'asarah* — eaten on day ten.

If both Thursday and Friday were the first two days of Rosh Hashanah, one could bake neither on the first day of Rosh Hashanah nor on the second. The baking would be pushed back to Wednesday, and the bread would be eaten the following *Shabbos*, arriving at day eleven. That is the scenario of *ne'echal l'echad asar* — eaten on day eleven.

### Rosh Hashanah Issue

Here a sharp difficulty emerges — one that Rashi already raises explicitly. If Thursday and Friday are the first and second days of Rosh Hashanah, and the *lechem hapanim* is baked on Wednesday, then it is replaced on *Shabbos* and eaten the following *Shabbos*. But if Rosh Hashanah falls on Thursday and Friday, then the following *Shabbos* is the 8th of Tishrei — and day eleven from Wednesday's baking would land precisely on the 10th of Tishrei. That is Yom Kippur. How can the *kohanim* eat the *lechem hapanim* on Yom Kippur?

### Counting Resolution

The resolution lies in a crucial difference between how Rosh Hashanah was observed in the era of the *Beis HaMikdash* and how we observe it today. In our calendar, when Rosh Hashanah falls on two days, it is the *first* day that is treated as the 1st of Tishrei. Today, for example, is Rosh Chodesh Elul — the second day of a two-day Rosh Chodesh — yet it is this second day that is the actual first of Elul, while yesterday was still the thirtieth of Av. Rosh Hashanah is the one exception to this pattern in our fixed calendar, where the first of the two days is counted as the 1st of Tishrei.

In the era of the *Beis HaMikdash*, however, there was no fixed calendar. The month was determined by the testimony of witnesses who came before the court to testify that they had seen the new moon. If witnesses arrived after *mincha* on the thirtieth of Elul, it was too late to formally accept their testimony for that day. The court would declare the remainder of that day as a second day of Rosh Hashanah — retroactively, as it were — but the *actual* first of Tishrei would be the *following* day. In other words, in this scenario, just as with every other two-day Rosh Chodesh, the second of the two days is the genuine first of the month.

This changes the calendar entirely. If the witnesses arrived after *mincha* on Thursday and the court declared Thursday and Friday as the two days of Rosh Hashanah, the actual first of Tishrei would be Friday, not Thursday. Accordingly, the following *Shabbos* would be the 2nd of Tishrei, and the *Shabbos* on which the *lechem hapanim* is eaten — eleven days from Wednesday's baking — would be *erev Yom Kippur*, the 9th of Tishrei, not Yom Kippur itself. The problem dissolves.

One might ask further: if the baking took place on Wednesday, it was done in anticipation of the possibility that witnesses would arrive after *mincha* on Thursday. The Kohanim could not bake Thursday morning, because they were afraid the witnesses might arrive at any moment and it would turn out to be Rosh Hashanah — and then, retroactively, they would have baked on *yom tov*. Baking Wednesday was the only safe option, given the scenario of witnesses arriving *min hamencha ul'mala*.

---

## Shvut Debate

### No Override

The *braita* continues: *she-eina dokha lo es ha-Shabbat v'lo es Yom Tov* — the *lechem hapanim* cannot override either *Shabbos* or *yom tov*. This is the premise from which Rava now launches his challenge to Rav Chisda.

### Distant Shabbos Q

Rava's question runs as follows. You, Rav Chisda, maintain that the reason one may cook from *yom tov* to *Shabbos* is because there is a fundamental license to cook from *yom tov* for *Shabbos* — *tzorkhei Shabbat na'asin b'Yom Tov*. It is not because of *ho'il*, the hypothetical possibility of eating it today; it is simply that cooking on *yom tov* for *Shabbos* is permitted as a matter of principle. Very well. But then why can one not bake the *lechem hapanim* on a *yom tov* that falls on Friday for the *Shabbos* a week later? If the license to cook from *yom tov* to *Shabbos* is a genuine, freestanding license — not contingent on the food being theoretically edible today — why does that license not extend to baking for a *Shabbos* eight days away?

Rava's point is that his own position — *ho'il* — actually explains the *braita* neatly. He says: you cannot bake *lechem hapanim* on *yom tov* because the bread cannot theoretically be eaten today. No matter what scenario one imagines — even unexpected guests — the *lechem hapanim* cannot be eaten until the following *Shabbos*. The *ho'il* justification is simply unavailable. But Rav Chisda, who says the license is not about hypothetical eating but about having a recognized *Shabbos*-purpose, cannot explain why the license would not extend to a *Shabbos* a week later.

### Shvut Distinction

Rav Chisda's response is: *shvut krovah hitiru, shvut rechoka lo hitiru* — the Rabbis permitted the nearby *shvut*, but not the distant *shvut*. Rav Chisda holds that cooking from *yom tov* to *Shabbos* is, at the biblical level, permitted. Rabbinically, it requires an *eruv tavshilin* or some recognized rabbinic license. But even granting that the biblical principle would allow cooking from *yom tov* for any *Shabbos* — even a distant one — the Rabbis only permitted this when the *Shabbos* is immediately adjacent to the *yom tov*. They did not permit it when the *Shabbos* is separated by many days.

Two ways of understanding this rabbinic distinction present themselves. One could say that when cooking for the next day and that day is *Shabbos*, the special character of the act is evident — one will not mistake it for cooking from *yom tov* to a weekday. But if one is cooking on *yom tov* for a *Shabbos* eight days later, the purpose is far less transparent, and one might come to cook for an ordinary weekday under the same logic. Alternatively, one could frame it more conceptually: the Rabbis allowed the license to cook from *yom tov* to *Shabbos* only when the two days function as an extended *yom tov*, a single extended period of sanctity. When there is a temporal gap between them, the days cannot be seen as one continuous entity, and the rabbinic license does not apply.

Either way, Rav Chisda's position is: you are right in principle — there is a fundamental license to cook from *yom tov* for *Shabbos*. But rabbinically, that license was granted only for the immediately adjacent day, not for a distant *Shabbos*.

### Rabban Gamliel

The *gemara* then introduces the position of Rabban Gamliel, who cites Rabbi Shimon ben ha-Sgan and who actually holds — unlike the anonymous first opinion — that one *may* bake the *lechem hapanim* on *yom tov* for a *Shabbos* a week later. He would permit it even for a *Shabbos* that is not adjacent. However, he would *not* permit baking it on Yom Kippur, just as one would not bake on *Shabbos* itself for a future *Shabbos*.

### Dispute Explained

The *gemara* identifies the crux of the dispute clearly: the first opinion holds *shvut krovah hitiru, shvut rechoka lo hitiru* — the rabbinic dispensation applies only to adjacent days. Rabban Gamliel holds *shvut rechoka nami hitiru* — even a distant *shvut* was permitted.

Returning now to the overall debate: Rava maintains that the problem with baking *lechem hapanim* on *yom tov* is precisely that there is no *ho'il* — no theoretical possibility of eating it today. That is his consistent position, and it fits the *braita* seamlessly. Rav Chisda says the license has nothing to do with theoretical edibility; it is a principle of *tzorkhei Shabbat na'asin b'Yom Tov*. The *braita*, on his account, reflects the rabbinic limitation that this license does not apply to a distant *Shabbos*. Rabban Gamliel, according to Rav Chisda's framework, simply holds that even the distant-*Shabbos* limitation was not adopted by the Rabbis in practice.

---

## Shtei HaLechem

### Shtei HaLechem Braita

Rav Mari now raises a question from a different *braita*, this one concerning the *shtei halechem* — the two loaves brought as a communal offering on Shavuos. The *braita* states: *einam ne'echalos lo pachos mishnayim v'lo yoseir al shlosha* — the two loaves may not be eaten fewer than two days or more than three days from the day they were baked. How do these scenarios arise?

In a normal case, the loaves are baked on *erev Shavuos* and brought and eaten on *Shavuos* itself — counting inclusively, that is day two: *ne'echalos lishnayim*. If *yom tov* followed *Shabbos* — that is, if Shavuos fell on Sunday — then the loaves could not be baked on *Shabbos*, so they would be baked on Friday, held through *Shabbos*, and brought on Sunday. Counting from Friday, Sunday is day three: *ne'echalos lishlosha*. And the *braita* specifies: *she-eino doche lo es ha-Shabbat v'lo es Yom Tov* — one may not bake them on *Shabbos* or *yom tov*.

### Korban Issue

The *braita*'s statement that one cannot bake the *shtei halechem* on *yom tov* requires explanation. Unlike *lechem hapanim*, which is to be eaten a full week later and thus cannot be hypothetically eaten today, the *shtei halechem* are eaten on *yom tov* itself. One might therefore have expected that they *could* be baked on *yom tov* — if not for *Shabbos*, then at least for *yom tov* that same day.

### Rashi Explanation

Rashi's explanation runs as follows. According to Rava's *ho'il* principle, one may bake on *yom tov* only when the food is, at least theoretically, edible immediately upon coming out of the oven. The *shtei halechem*, however, cannot be eaten the moment they are baked, even if baked on *yom tov* itself. To eat them, one must first *shecht* the accompanying *korban*. Until the *korban* is brought, the loaves remain forbidden. At the very moment of baking, they are not theoretically edible — there is a further required act standing between baking and eating. Therefore, according to Rava, *ho'il* cannot justify baking them on *yom tov*.

But Rav Chisda presents a difficulty. He maintains that the license to cook on *yom tov* is not about the food being theoretically edible at this moment. The license is about having a recognized *yom tov* or *Shabbos* purpose. On that account, baking the *shtei halechem* for later consumption on *yom tov* itself should certainly be permitted — the purpose is *yom tov*, and the later-day obstacle of the *korban* should not undercut a license that does not require present theoretical edibility to begin with. If anything, baking for *yom tov* later that day is an even stronger case than baking for a subsequent *Shabbos*.

### Lachem Exclusion

The *gemara*'s answer is: *shani hatam d'amar kra lachem* — this case is different because the Torah says, *ach asher ye'achel l'chol nefesh hu levado ye'aseh lachem* — food preparation on *yom tov* must be done *lachem*, for yourselves. *Lachem v'lo l'Gavoha* — for your own purposes, not for the purpose of bringing a sacrifice to God. The *shtei halechem* are fundamentally a *korban*. Even though the *kohanim* ultimately eat the meat, the primary act is one of bringing an offering. The eating is derivative; the *korban* is primary. Therefore, even though the license to cook for a future *Shabbos* would in principle apply here, baking the *shtei halechem* falls outside that license entirely because the act is not one of preparing food for oneself — it is an act of offering a *korban*.

### Rabban Shimon View

However, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, citing Rabbi Shimon ben ha-Sgan, permits baking the *shtei halechem* on *yom tov* for Shavuos. How does he navigate the *lachem* exclusion? The *gemara* answers: *savar lah k'Abba Shaul* — he holds in accordance with Abba Shaul, who interprets *lachem* on *yom tov* as excluding only cooking done for non-Jews. Cooking for the sake of God — for a *korban* — is not excluded, both because it represents an elevated purpose and because, ultimately, the *kohanim* do eat from the *shulchan Gavoha* and thus derive personal benefit, however indirect.

This parallels the famous dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the bringing of *shelamim* on *yom tov*. One winds up eating all the meat of the *shelamim*, yet the fundamental act is one of bringing a *korban*; the eating of the meat is only a derivative benefit. The same logic applies here: whether the derivative personal benefit is sufficient to bring the baking within the scope of *lachem* is precisely what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the *chachamim* disagree about.

To summarize the overall picture: Rava says the problem with both *lechem hapanim* and *shtei halechem* is that *ho'il* is unavailable — neither can be theoretically eaten right now. According to Rav Chisda's position, which does not require present theoretical edibility, one would in principle expect both to be permissible. The *gemara* limits Rav Chisda's license by the *lachem* exclusion — baking may not be done as an act of bringing a *korban* rather than as an act of preparing one's own food. And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, following Abba Shaul, holds that cooking for the sake of a *korban* from which one ultimately benefits is still within the *lachem* license.

---

## Plowing Challenge

### Challenge Sent

Having established Rava's position through multiple exchanges, the *gemara* now turns the tables. Rav Chisda sends a challenge to Rava — not directly, but *biyad Rav Acha bar Rav Huna*, through the hand of Rav Acha bar Rav Huna, as though dispatching a question in what amounted to a correspondence debate. The question Rav Chisda sends is aimed squarely at the *ho'il* principle.

### Eight Prohibitions

The vehicle for the challenge is a *mishna* in Makkos, which discusses how a single act can accumulate multiple violations. The *mishna* states: *yesh choresh telem echad* — one who makes a single furrow can violate eight prohibitions simultaneously. What are the eight? The person is plowing with an ox and a donkey yoked together — that is one, the prohibition of *lo tacharosh beshor uvachamor yachdav*. The animals happen to be sanctified *kodashim* — two, the prohibition of *me'ilah* (misappropriating Temple property). Rashi adds a third: there is a distinct prohibition against performing labor with animals that are *kodshei korban* — animals sanctified as sacrificial offerings. The donkey, though not itself a valid *korban*, can be sanctified for its monetary value as *bedek habayis*, constituting *me'ilah* as a separate violation — and that is the third, the way Rashi reads it. The field they are plowing happens to contain mixed seeds and grapevines — four, the prohibition of *kilayim be'cherem*. It happens to be *shemittah* — five. It happens to be *yom tov* — six. And the one doing the plowing happens to be both a *kohen* and a *nazir*, and he is plowing in a graveyard — seven for the *kohen*'s entry into a graveyard, and eight for the *nazir*'s. One might note that the last two are somewhat less organically connected to the act of plowing than the first six, since they depend on who the person is and where he happens to be rather than on the act itself — but those are the eight.

### Ho'il to Plowing

The challenge now becomes clear. If Rava says one does not receive lashes for cooking on *yom tov* for the weekday because of *ho'il* — because theoretically the food could be eaten today — then by the same logic, should one not be exempt from lashes for plowing on *yom tov*? After all, the plowing, too, might have a theoretically valid *yom tov* purpose.

### Blood Coverage

What would that purpose be? The dirt produced by the plowing could theoretically be used for *kisuy hadam* — covering the blood of a slaughtered bird, which is a *mitzvah* requiring loose earth. If one could point to this hypothetical use, then by Rava's logic — *ho'il v'chazi lechisuy dam tzippor* — the *ho'il* principle would render the act of plowing non-actionable, and the sixth lash, for plowing on *yom tov*, should not apply.

This challenge is, in truth, a surprising one. Rava's *ho'il* principle was articulated specifically in the context of cooking — an act that is explicitly licensed on *yom tov* by *ach asher ye'achel l'chol nefesh*, and which requires only a justifying *yom tov* purpose to be fully permitted. The point of *ho'il* was that the hypothetical possibility of eating counts as a sufficient *yom tov* purpose to justify the cooking. That is very different from plowing, which is a fundamentally prohibited *melachah* on *yom tov*, and from which a far-fetched alternate scenario — covering bird blood — is being invoked to escape liability. These are conceptually quite different cases. Nevertheless, Rav Chisda understood Rava's principle more broadly — as saying that whenever a hypothetical scenario could justify an act, one cannot receive lashes for it — and challenged him accordingly.

---

## Resolving Plowing

### Clumps Answer

The *gemara* does not record Rava answering this himself. Instead, other *amora'im* step in to answer on his behalf, which itself is telling. Rav Papa bar Shmuel offers the first answer: the case involves *b'vanei mekurzalos* — hard, compacted clumps of earth. When one plows through such soil, what is produced are clumps, not loose dirt. Compacted clumps cannot be used for *kisuy hadam*, which requires loose earth. Therefore, *ho'il* does not apply — there is no hypothetical valid use for this particular dirt — and lashes for plowing on *yom tov* stand.

### Back and Forth

The *gemara* immediately challenges this. The clumps could be ground up — *re'uyos lekotesh* — so what difference does it make that they are hard? To that, the *gemara* responds: grinding up dirt on *yom tov* is itself forbidden — *v'ketisha b'Yom Tov mi shari?* — so the clumps cannot realistically be made usable. But the *gemara* pushes back: one could grind them up with a *shinui*, an irregular technique — *re'uyos lekotesh kela'achar yad* — and a *shinui* renders the act permissible. So the answer of hard clumps fails.

The *gemara* then proposes: the case involves *tzunma* — actual rocks. Rocks certainly cannot be used for *kisuy hadam*. But the *gemara* rejects this as well, for a different reason: if one is plowing through rocks, how is one simultaneously violating *kilayim* and *shevi'is*? One cannot plant in rocks. So the *gemara* revises the picture: *tzunma mil'ala v'afar tichucha mil'mata* — rocks on the upper layer and loose, tillable soil below. One is plowing in order to reach the plantable soil beneath. But now the problem returns: if there is loose soil beneath, one could use that very soil for *kisuy hadam*, and *ho'il* would seem to apply after all.

### Mud Resolution

The final resolution, offered by Mar bar Rav Ashi, is: *bitina* — the soil in question is mud. It is wet enough and thick enough that it can be planted in, satisfying the conditions for *kilayim* and *shevi'is* violations, but it is not usable for *kisuy hadam*, which requires dry, loose earth. Mud, by its nature, cannot cover blood in the manner required. This is the case in which *ho'il* is unavailable, and lashes for plowing on *yom tov* accordingly stand.

It must be acknowledged that this entire exchange is analytically strange, and for two distinct reasons. First, as noted above, Rava's *ho'il* principle was never meant to apply to acts that are fundamentally forbidden on *yom tov* — it was specifically about cooking, which has an explicit license and merely needs a *yom tov* justification. Second, even if one were to accept the broader reading of *ho'il*, it is not at all clear that plowing in order to obtain dirt for *kisuy hadam* would itself be permitted on *yom tov* to begin with — the first *mishna* in Beitzah deals precisely with the availability of loose earth for *kisuy hadam* and the restrictions that apply. As the *gemara* appears to have accepted Rav Chisda's framing of the question, subsequent *amora'im* engaged with it on those terms — and, as one might say, sometimes the first mistake is simply responding to the question as posed.

---

## Gid HaNasheh

### Braita Overview

Abaye now poses a further challenge, framed similarly to Rav Chisda's plowing question but more intuitively grounded in the *halakha* of *yom tov*. A *braita* states: *ha'mevashel gid hanasheh b'chalav b'yom tov v'ochlo lokeh chameish* — one who cooks the *gid hanasheh* in milk on *yom tov* and eats it receives five lashes. The enumeration is as follows. Cooking on *yom tov* for something one is forbidden to eat constitutes cooking *lo l'tzorech* — without a valid *yom tov* purpose — that is one lash. Cooking *gid hanasheh* in milk constitutes cooking *basar b'chalav* — two. Eating *gid hanasheh* — three. Eating *basar b'chalav* — four. And making the fire — *havarah* — five.

### Fire Question

Here is Abaye's challenge. If *ho'il* grants a license for cooking even when one's intent was not for *yom tov*, the same *ho'il* should surely apply to making the fire — *havarah*. The fire, after all, is usable for any legitimate purpose on *yom tov*. Even if this particular fire was made to cook a forbidden mixture, theoretically the fire itself could serve any number of *yom tov* needs. This is, in fact, a much more intuitive version of Rav Chisda's challenge, because fire on *yom tov* is not simply analogous to cooking — it has an even more basic and fundamental license. The prohibition of *melacha* on *yom tov* applies to fire; yet we know from other *sugyot* that fire and carrying enjoy something close to a blanket license on *yom tov*, and cooking a somewhat more conditional but still broadly applicable license. The *gemara* here treats all three as formally parallel, each requiring some *yom tov* justification, with *ho'il* supplying that justification wherever a hypothetical use is available.

It is worth pausing to note the broader significance. Among the *melachos*, fire (*havarah*), carrying, and cooking occupy a distinctive status on *yom tov*. Fire is the only *melachah* mentioned explicitly in the Torah in the context of *Shabbos* — *lo tivaru esh bechol moshveichem* — and there is a *tannaic* opinion that *havarah* carries only a *lav* and not *chiyuv misa*, since *lav yatza* — it is singled out to teach the principle of individual liability. Carrying is what the *rishonim* describe as a *melachah gru'ah* — a diminished *melachah*, the one non-creative *melachah* in the entire list. And cooking has an explicit *yom tov* license from *ach asher ye'achel l'chol nefesh*. Come *yom tov*, these three acquire something close to a blanket allowance. We would never spontaneously wonder whether making a fire on *yom tov* requires a specific justification. Yet this *gemara* treats fire on the same plane as cooking, and asks: if *ho'il* gives you latitude on cooking, should it not equally give you latitude on fire?

### Fire Answer

Given the strength of that question, the *gemara* accepts it. One should indeed not receive lashes for *havarah*; *ho'il* applies. Accordingly, the fifth lash in the *braita* cannot stand as stated. The fire violation must be removed from the list and replaced with something else.

---

## Muktza Wood

### Muktza Proposal

The proposal is to amend the *braita* text: *eipcha havarah v'ayeil gid hanasheh shel neveila* — perhaps take out the fire violation and replace it with a different element. One option floated is to change the *gid hanasheh* to one from an animal that was not properly *shechted* — a *neveila* — so that eating it constitutes an additional violation of eating *neveila*, making up the fifth lash through eating rather than cooking. But this is rejected, because Rabbi Chiya's version of the *braita* specifies that two of the five lashes are for eating and three are for cooking-related acts. If we replace the fire violation with a *neveila* violation, we would have three lashes for eating and two for cooking, which contradicts Rabbi Chiya's breakdown.

Therefore, the replacement must be a cooking-related violation, not an eating one. The *gemara* proposes: *v'ayeil atzei muktza* — replace the fire violation with the use of *muktza* wood to make the fire. The fire itself is fine — *ho'il* applies. But the violation was using *muktza* wood. Since there is no *ho'il* for *muktza* wood — there is no theoretical permitted use for *muktza* items on *yom tov* — the lash for that act would stand.

### Muktza Biblical

This proposal immediately raises the objection: *v'muktza de'oraisa hu?* — is *muktza* a biblical prohibition? One only receives lashes for biblical violations. The *gemara* answers: yes, there is a biblical basis. The verse says *v'haya bayom ha-shishi v'heichinu es asher yaviu* — on the sixth day they shall prepare that which they bring. This is the principle of *hachana de-Rabbah* discussed in the beginning of Beitzah: the idea that what is to be used on *Shabbos* or *yom tov* must be prepared beforehand, and that using items that were not set aside — *muktza* — is biblically disfavored. The *azharah*, the biblical warning, comes from *lo ta'aseh kol melachah* — the general prohibition of labor.

### No Permitted Use

But if *muktza* is biblical, one might then ask: why does *ho'il* not apply to *muktza* as well? The answer is that *ho'il* requires at least a theoretical scenario in which the act would be permitted. A fire made from non-*muktza* wood is theoretically permissible at any moment. But *muktza* wood has no theoretical permitted use on *yom tov* — there is simply no scenario in which one can legitimately use it. Therefore, *ho'il* is unavailable, and the violation stands.

---

## Muktza Biblical?

### Gazelle Question

The claim that *muktza* is biblical is immediately subjected to scrutiny. The *gemara* recalls a question that was posed to Rav Chisda — or according to some versions, to Rav Huna: if one caught a wild gazelle on *yom tov* and wanted to bring it as a *korban tamid*, may one do so, given that the animal was *muktza* — it was grazing in the wilderness when *yom tov* began?

### Mutar Principle

The answer given draws on a *pasuk* in Yechezkel: *seh achat min ha-tzon min ha-masa'yim mimashke Yisrael* — one sheep from the flock, from two hundred, from the drink of Israel. This verse in Yechezkel is expounded to teach several conditions for valid *korbanos*: not a *bechor*, not *ma'aser*, not a *pilgas* (an animal between one year and thirteen months old, between the category of *seh* and *ayil*). And the concluding phrase, *mimashke Yisrael*, is read as *min ha-mutar le-Yisrael* — from that which is permitted to Israel. *Mikan amru ein mevi'in nesachim min ha-tevel* — just as one cannot bring wine that is *tevel* (untithed) as a libation offering, so one cannot bring as a *korban* anything that is intrinsically forbidden to eat.

### Not Intrinsic

One might then ask: perhaps one also cannot bring a *korban* from an animal that is *muktza*? The answer given is no — the exclusion applies only when *issur gufo garam lo*, when the prohibition is intrinsic to the object itself, as with *tevel*, whose untithed status is an inherent legal disability. *Muktza*, by contrast, is an example of *issur davar acher garam lo* — the prohibition arises not from the animal itself but from an external circumstance, namely the fact that *Shabbos* or *yom tov* began while the animal was out in the wilderness. The animal itself is perfectly permissible; only the circumstance renders it *muktza*.

### Not Like Tevel

But this distinction raises a sharp question. If *muktza* is truly a biblical prohibition, what difference does it make whether the prohibition is intrinsic or circumstantial? *Tevel* is forbidden; *muktza* is forbidden. Why should one be treated differently from the other when it comes to bringing a *korban*? The *gemara* presses this point: *v'i amarta issur muktza de'oraisa* — if *muktza* is really a biblical prohibition, then *mah li issur gufo, mah li issur davar acher* — what difference does it make whether the source of the prohibition is the object itself or the circumstances? Both are biblical prohibitions; both should disqualify a *korban* equally. The fact that one *can* bring a *korban* from a *muktza* animal therefore constitutes strong evidence that *muktza* is *not* a biblical prohibition at all.

### To Be Continued

This leaves the *gemara* at an impasse. The proposal to replace the fire violation in the *braita* with *muktza* wood collapses, because *muktza* does not appear to be a biblical prohibition. But the fire violation cannot stand either, since *ho'il* applies to fire and should exempt it from lashes. If neither fire nor *muktza* can serve as the fifth cooking-related violation in the *braita*, what biblical prohibition *does* the fifth lash correspond to? This question remains open, and the *gemara* will continue to address it in the following daf.

---

---

# Pesachim 48

## Rava vs Rav Chisda

### Cooking Yom Tov Setup

The daf opens in the midst of an ongoing discussion that has occupied nearly two full pages of Gemara. By way of orientation: the *mishna* earlier addressed the question of how one separates *challah* from *tamei* dough on *Pesach*. The predicament is well-defined — one cannot bake the dough because it is *tamei* and therefore inedible, yet one cannot leave it unbaked because it will become *chametz*. Two opinions emerged. *Rabbi Eliezer* held that one bakes the dough and only afterward designates one loaf as *challah*, so that at the moment of baking no loaf has yet been formally rendered *challah* and the act of baking is therefore not yet a problem. *Rabbi Yehoshua* countered that there is in any case no concern about violating *bal yera'eh* and *bal yimatzei*, since the *challah* is *hekdesh* — a form of consecrated property — and does not belong to the owner in a way that triggers those prohibitions.

Before returning to that debate directly, the Gemara has been engaged with a foundational disagreement between *Rava* and *Rav Chisda* about cooking on *Yom Tov* for a weekday meal. The connection will shortly become apparent, but the discussion of *Rava* and *Rav Chisda* must first be understood on its own terms.

### Rava's Ho'il Principle

The practical question is whether someone who cooks on *Yom Tov* intending to eat the food on a weekday receives *malkot*. *Rava* holds that he does not, on the basis of the principle of *ho'il* — literally "since," functioning here as a kind of hypothetical sufficiency. The argument is: since, if a large number of guests were to arrive unexpectedly, the food could in fact be consumed on *Yom Tov* itself, the act of cooking is classified as *tzorech Yom Tov* — cooking for the holiday's needs — even though that was not the cook's actual intention. The theoretical permissibility suffices to render the act legitimate.

### Rav Chisda's Intent Rule

*Rav Chisda* disagrees sharply. For him, *ho'il* is not a valid basis for permitting the act. What is required is actual intention to eat the food on *Yom Tov* itself; cooking with the plan to eat on a weekday constitutes a genuine violation and subjects the person to *malkot*. The theoretical possibility of consuming the food now does not transform the nature of the act.

### Furrow Challenge

A challenge to *Rava's* position is raised — though the Gemara presents it without recording *Rava's* own response. If *ho'il* is sufficient to exempt cooking because the food could hypothetically be eaten now, then by the same logic, one who digs a furrow on *Yom Tov* should also be exempt, since the dirt could theoretically be used to cover the blood of a freshly slaughtered bird — a legitimate *Yom Tov* purpose. Yet digging a furrow is a quintessential prohibited labor with no culinary character, and it stretches the principle of *ho'il* beyond the domain of food preparation into acts that are fundamentally not *ochel nefesh*. The Gemara engages with this tension, and we proceed from there.

---

## Five Lashes Mishna

### Gid Hanasheh Lashes

The more immediately pressing issue is a *beraita* that presents a scenario in which one can incur five separate sets of *malkot* through a single act of cooking on *Yom Tov* — for example, cooking the *gid hanasheh* of an animal. The list of five includes the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* itself, *basar bechalav*, and other forbidden categories, along with — according to the *beraita* as initially read — making a fire on *Yom Tov* without a legitimate purpose. The question pressed against *Rava* is immediate: according to his principle of *ho'il*, one should never incur *malkot* for making a fire on *Yom Tov*, since hypothetically the fire could always serve some legitimate function. Why then does the *beraita* list it as a separate category meriting *malkot*?

This is a particularly resonant challenge because we do in practice grant considerable latitude for making fire on *Yom Tov* even without a specific food-preparation purpose in mind. The Gemara's answer to this challenge is direct: *Rava* is correct, and the fire entry must simply be removed from the list. The *beraita* cannot be counting *hav'ara* as a distinct lashing category — and something else must be substituted in its place.

### Ein Chiluk Melachot

Before arriving at the replacement, the Gemara introduces an independent and powerful reason why *hav'ara* cannot appear in that list regardless of the *ho'il* debate. The principle is *ein chiluk melachos* on *Yom Tov*. On *Shabbos*, the thirty-nine categories of *melacha* are each treated as distinct for the purpose of *korbanot*: one who violates multiple categories *beshogeg* may be liable for up to thirty-nine separate sin-offerings. The categories are meaningful because of their relevance to atonement.

On *Yom Tov*, however, there is no *karet* and no *mita* for forbidden labor — *Yom Tov* carries only a *lo ta'aseh* and an *aseh*. Since there is no *karet*, there is no *korban chatat*, and therefore the entire framework of distinct labor categories has no purchase. The only practical consequence of intentional *melacha* on *Yom Tov* in this world is *malkot*, and for *malkot* there is no distinction among the thirty-nine categories. It is a single prohibition — performing *melacha* on *Yom Tov* — that one either violates or does not, regardless of which specific labor is involved.

### Fire Not Separate

The implication is decisive. If one dug thirty-nine furrows on *Yom Tov* — or performed one of each of the thirty-nine categories — one receives only a single set of *malkot*, not thirty-nine. The *beraita*'s project of identifying five qualitatively distinct lashing categories is therefore not served by listing *hav'ara* alongside cooking; they are both violations of the same prohibition of *melacha* on *Yom Tov* and do not generate separate *malkot*. Even before the *ho'il* argument is invoked, *hav'ara* simply does not belong in the list.

### Nazir Wine Example

One might ask whether the problem could be solved by separate *hatra'ot* — independent warnings — rather than by categorically distinct prohibitions. The Gemara alludes to the well-known *mishna* regarding a *nazir* who drinks wine throughout the day: if separate warnings are administered between each act of drinking, separate sets of *malkot* are incurred. The same principle could in theory apply here. But the Gemara dismisses this: the *beraita*'s purpose is to enumerate qualitatively different *isurim* that produce separate *malkot* in a principled way, not to describe the same prohibition triggered multiple times through repeated *hatra'ot*. A *beraita* could construct any number of such scenarios by simply counting repeated warnings; what makes the five-lashes *beraita* interesting and instructive is that it identifies five genuinely distinct prohibitions. *Hav'ara* does not satisfy that criterion, and the attempted substitution of *muktza* wood likewise fails, since *muktza* is not *de-oraita* and therefore cannot generate its own independent lashing category.

---

## Replacing Fire Category

### Muktza Solution

The first proposed replacement for *hav'ara* in the *beraita*'s list of five is *muktza* wood. If one uses wood that was *muktza* — set aside and designated for a use other than burning — to make the fire, that might constitute a separate prohibited act distinct from the *melacha* of cooking. This would circumvent the *ho'il* problem, since *muktza* wood has no theoretical alternative use; one cannot invoke *ho'il* to say it could hypothetically have served another purpose, because as *muktza* it is precluded from any other use. The proposal fails, however, because the Gemara concludes that *muktza* is not *de-oraita*. Without biblical standing, it cannot anchor an independent category of *malkos de-oraita*, and the attempt is rejected.

### Avoda Zara Wood

The Gemara then proposes *atzei ashera* — wood from a tree that had been worshipped as an object of *avoda zara*. If one uses such wood to fuel the fire with which one cooks the *gid hanasheh*, one incurs a separate prohibition of deriving benefit from *avoda zara*, derived from the verse *velo yidbak beyadecha me'uma min hacherem* — nothing from the banned material shall cleave to your hand. This seems a promising candidate: it is a qualitatively distinct *issur* that is unrelated to the *melacha* of cooking, and the *ho'il* argument does not apply because the prohibition is categorical, not contingent on purpose.

However, the Gemara raises a further objection: there are in fact *two* separate prohibitions associated with *avoda zara* wood — the prohibition of benefiting from it, and the distinct prohibition of *velo tavi to'evah el beisecha*, do not bring an abomination into your house. If both apply, then using *atzei ashera* contributes not one but two sets of *malkot* to the count, pushing the total beyond five. The proposal overachieves, and a different replacement is needed.

### Hekdesh Wood Solution

The final solution offered is *atzei hekdesh* — wood belonging to the Temple treasury, i.e., property of *hekdesh*. Using such wood to fuel the fire constitutes a violation derived from the verse *lo ta'asun kein l'Hashem Elokeichem*, understood homiletically to prohibit the destruction or improper use of that which is consecrated to God. This reasoning — which is also foundational to the prohibition against erasing *Shem Hashem* — provides a single, distinct prohibition tied to the sanctity of *hekdesh* property.

One might wonder why the prohibition of *me'ila* — misappropriating *hekdesh* — is not invoked as an additional category, which would again push the count beyond five. The Gemara does not fully resolve this, though one possible direction is that the benefit derived is attenuated given that the cooking itself is forbidden and the result cannot lawfully be consumed. Regardless, the Gemara appears satisfied with *hekdesh* wood as the fifth category, and the discussion of the fire-and-lashes *beraita* concludes with *hekdesh* wood replacing *hav'ara*.

---

## Rami bar Chama's Link

### Same Debate Theory

With the extended discussion of *Rava* and *Rav Chisda* now concluded, the Gemara circles back to tie that debate to our *mishna*. *Rami bar Chama* proposes that the dispute of *Rav Chisda* and *Rabba* is in fact the same debate as that of *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* in the *mishna* about *challah teme'ah*. The equation is intellectually elegant: both debates turn on the principle of *ho'il*, and *Rami bar Chama* offers a framework for understanding what separates the two Tannaitic opinions.

### Eliezer's Ho'il

According to *Rami bar Chama*, *Rabbi Eliezer*, who permits baking the dough and subsequently separating *challah*, operates on a principle of *ho'il*. At the moment the loaves are placed in the oven, every single loaf is theoretically edible. The baker does not yet know which loaf will be designated as *challah*; any particular loaf could be the one he eats. Since no specific loaf is definitively forbidden at the time of baking, and since in theory one could even separate *challah* from each loaf individually and thereby render every loaf edible, there is sufficient theoretical permissibility to classify the baking as *tzorech Yom Tov*. This is the structure of *ho'il*: the act is deemed legitimate because it could, under the right conditions, be entirely permissible.

### Yehoshua Rejects Ho'il

*Rabbi Yehoshua*, who would prohibit the baking, rejects *ho'il* as a basis for permission. For him, it is dispositive that one of the loaves will certainly be inedible — that much is guaranteed by the obligation of *hafrashat challah*. The identity of that loaf may be unknown, but its existence is certain. The argument that any *particular* loaf is theoretically edible does not resolve the fact that one loaf *definitely* cannot be eaten. This parallels *Rav Chisda's* position: theoretical possibility does not suffice; what matters is whether the food will actually be eaten on *Yom Tov*.

### Rav Pappa's Distinction

*Rav Pappa* immediately qualifies *Rami bar Chama's* equation, pointing out that the two debates are not symmetrical. The cases differ in at least two significant respects, and conflating them may produce false conclusions about what each disputant would hold in the other's scenario.

In the *challah* case, *Rabbi Eliezer* says *ho'il* because at the moment of placing the loaves in the oven — *be-idana de-ka-ayeil le-tanura* — every single loaf is genuinely fit for the baker's own consumption. The baker wants to eat all of this *matzah*; the only reason one loaf will be forbidden is the subsequent act of designation, which has not yet occurred. The *ho'il* here is grounded in a situation where the person is fundamentally baking *for himself* and *for today*, with the limitation being a single unknown loaf.

This is structurally different from the case of *Rava* and *Rav Chisda*, where the cook has no intention whatsoever of eating the food on *Yom Tov*. The only basis for invoking *ho'il* there is the hypothetical scenario of unexpected guests — *de-orchim hu de-chazei lei, le-didei lo chazi* — for the cook himself it is not fit at all. It is possible that even *Rabbi Eliezer*, who accepts *ho'il* when one is fundamentally baking for personal consumption today, would not accept *ho'il* when one has no intention of eating today and relies solely on the theoretical possibility of guests.

Conversely, the *challah* case has a feature that makes *ho'il* harder to invoke: one loaf is objectively, certainly going to be forbidden, even if its identity is unknown. In the cooking-for-weekday case, everything is theoretically edible — *d'chazi mihat l'orchin* — the only deficit is the absence of actual guests. *Rav Pappa* suggests that this might lead *Rabbi Yehoshua* to actually be *more* lenient in the Rava-Rav Chisda scenario than in his own, since there no loaf is structurally foreclosed.

The upshot is that the two debates have overlapping features but are not identical, and one cannot straightforwardly read the positions of *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* as direct precedents for *Rava* and *Rav Chisda*.

### Sheshet's Challenge

*Rav Sheshet brei de-Rav Idi* presses the point further from the opposite direction. Just as *Rav Pappa* argued that *Rabbi Eliezer's ho'il* in the *challah* case does not necessarily extend to *Rava's* position, *Rav Sheshet* argues that *Rabbi Yehoshua's* rejection of *ho'il* in the *challah* case does not necessarily correspond to *Rav Chisda's* position either. *Rabbi Yehoshua* refuses to permit the baking because, despite the baker's overall intention to eat most of the loaves, one loaf will definitively be off-limits to anyone — not merely to the baker himself, but to *le-didei* and *le-orchin* alike. That categorical objective prohibition is what drives *Rabbi Yehoshua's* stringency.

In the case of cooking for potential guests, by contrast, the food is theoretically edible by everyone — guests included. The only problem is their hypothetical nature. *Rav Sheshet* suggests it is possible that *Rabbi Yehoshua* would be more willing to accept *ho'il* in that scenario, since nothing is categorically foreclosed. The debates are thus distinguishable in both directions: the *challah* case has a feature that makes *ho'il* easier to invoke (the baker is personally intending to eat most of the food today) and a feature that makes it harder (one loaf is certainly forbidden). Neither *Rabbi Eliezer* nor *Rabbi Yehoshua* can be read as simple stand-ins for *Rava* and *Rav Chisda*.

---

## Yirmiyah-Zeira Dispute

### Yirmiyah Accepts

The question of whether the debates are identical was also discussed before *Rabbi Yirmiyah* and *Rabbi Zeira*. *Rabbi Yirmiyah* enthusiastically accepts *Rami bar Chama's* equation. He describes how for many years the scholars had struggled to identify the core logic underlying the debate of *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* — why exactly *Rabbi Eliezer* permits the baking and on what grounds *Rabbi Yehoshua* would object. Now *Rami bar Chama*, a great authority, has provided a compelling framework: the debate is about *ho'il*. *Rabbi Yirmiyah* sees no reason to reject this powerful explanatory proposal.

### Zeira's Silence Proof

*Rabbi Zeira* disagrees and presents a textual argument. A *baraita* records an exchange in which *Rabbi Yehoshua* confronts *Rabbi Eliezer* with the challenge: *harei over mishum lo ta'aseh kol melacha* — by baking this dough you are transgressing the prohibition of *melacha* on *Yom Tov*, since part of the food cannot be eaten. In the *baraita*, *Rabbi Eliezer* says nothing in response — *v'shatik lei*. *Rabbi Zeira* argues that this silence is telling. If *Rabbi Eliezer's* position were indeed grounded in *ho'il*, he would have responded: "I do not consider this a prohibited *melacha* because *ho'il* — since theoretically every loaf could be eaten." The absence of this defense in the *baraita* suggests that *ho'il* is not actually his reasoning, and therefore *Rami bar Chama's* equation cannot be sustained.

### Yirmiyah's Response

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* counters with a parallel argument that undermines *Rabbi Zeira's* methodology. The same *baraita* continues with *Rabbi Eliezer* turning the charge back on *Rabbi Yehoshua*: if you tell me I am transgressing *melacha* by baking it, then according to you, who says to leave the dough and let it become *chametz*, you are causing a violation of *bal yera'eh* and *bal yimatzei*. And *Rabbi Yehoshua* is equally silent — *v'shatik lei*. Does *Rabbi Zeira* conclude from that silence that *Rabbi Yehoshua* has no answer?

Of course not — *Rabbi Yehoshua's* answer is recorded elsewhere: the *mishna* itself states explicitly that *lo zehu chametz she-muzharan alav mishum bal yera'eh* — consecrated *challah* of this kind does not implicate those prohibitions, since it is a form of *hekdesh* and does not belong to the owner in the relevant sense. *Rabbi Yehoshua* is silent in the *baraita* not because he has no answer, but because the *beraita*'s literary form presents the competing arguments dramatically without recording every rejoinder. The answer exists; it simply appears in the *mishna* rather than in the *baraita*.

By parity of reasoning, *Rabbi Eliezer's* silence when challenged about *melacha* does not mean he has no defense. His defense — namely, *ho'il* — may be recorded in another collection of Tannaitic material, *be-mechilta achriti*, even if it does not appear in this particular *baraita*. The absence of a recorded response in any one source does not constitute evidence that the response does not exist. *Rabbi Yirmiyah* therefore maintains that *Rami bar Chama's* equation stands, and *Rabbi Zeira's* proof from silence fails.

---

## Halacha Bakah Minimum

### Halacha Eliezer

The Gemara concludes the debate between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* with a *baraita*: "*Rabbi* says the *halacha* is like *Rabbi Eliezer*." A second authority, *Rav Yitzchak*, is cited as ruling like *Ben Betaira*, whose position involves placing the dough in cold water. The practical *halacha* is a matter that the *Rishonim* engage with seriously, particularly *Tosafos*, which notes that we follow *Rabbi* given the principle that *halacha* follows him against his colleagues. *Rashi* similarly addresses the question. This is practically significant because when *matzah* is baked on *Yom Tov* itself — which involves dough that is by definition *tamei* given that we all presume ourselves to be in a state of *tumah* today — the question of how to handle *hafrashat challah* remains operative.

### Dough Size Question

The Gemara now pivots to a related but distinct question: *kama shiur issah* — what is the maximum amount of dough that a person may work with at one time when baking *matzah* on *Yom Tov* or on *Chol HaMoed*, or in principle even on *Erev Yom Tov*? The concern is that if one kneads an excessively large mass of dough, portions of it that are not being actively worked may begin to ferment and become *chametz* before the baker can attend to them. The question therefore has a ceiling defined by practical safety against *chimutz*.

The question also intersects with a minimum: there is a minimum amount of dough required to obligate *hafrashat challah*. The question of whether these two measurements — the maximum safe for *matzah* baking and the minimum for *challah* obligation — are compatible is genuinely significant. If the maximum safe dough size falls below the *challah* minimum, one could never both bake *matzah* safely and fulfill the obligation of *challah*.

### Yishmael Measurements

*Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka* provides the following measurements for the maximum safe dough size: for wheat flour, two *kavim*; for barley flour, three *kavim*. These are substantial quantities — two *kavim* of wheat corresponds to approximately eighty egg-volumes, which is significantly more than the minimum *shiur challah* of roughly forty-three eggs. The differentiation between wheat and barley presumably reflects different rates of fermentation.

### Natan Reversal

*Rabbi Natan* citing *Rabbi Elazar* reverses the figures: barley ferments more quickly than wheat, and therefore the barley maximum is lower — two *kavim* for barley and three for wheat. A *beraita* appears to contradict both positions by citing *Rabbi Yishmael* as giving three *kavim* for wheat and four for barley. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between inferior-grade and superior-grade flour. A larger quantity of inferior grain is required to yield the same effective amount, so the higher figures apply to *chasichta* — lower-quality grain — while the lower figures apply to *maalyusa* — refined grain.

*Rav Pappa* draws a further inference from these numbers: the degradation ratio of inferior to superior wheat is greater than the degradation ratio of inferior to superior barley. For wheat, three units of inferior yield two of superior — a loss of one third. For barley, four units of inferior yield three of superior — a loss of only one quarter. The difference in processing loss between the two grains is thus measurable from these very figures.

### Rav's One Kab

*Rav* states: the *kav de-melugna* — the *kav* of a particular locale called *Melugna* — is the relevant measure for *Pesach* dough, and likewise for the minimum *shiur challah*. This seems considerably smaller than the figures just cited, and the Gemara notes the apparent contradiction with the *mishna*'s requirement of five *reva'im* of flour.

### Five Revaim Min

The *mishna* establishes that *chamisha reva'im kemach va'od* — five *reva'im* of flour plus a small additional amount — obligates *challah*. A *reva* is one quarter of a *kav*, equivalent to a *log*, which is approximately fourteen ounces by volume. Five *reva'im* thus equals one and a quarter *kavim* — a quantity greater than the single *kav* that *Rav* cited. The Gemara resolves this by explaining that *Rav* was referring to the *kav de-melugna*, a locally larger unit of measurement that in fact corresponds to the one-and-a-quarter *kav* standard for *challah*. The practical equivalence is maintained: the maximum safe dough size for *matzah* baking is the same as the minimum dough size that obligates *challah* separation.

### Combination Solution

*Rav Yosef* raises a practical difficulty. In the domestic setting, women baking *matzah* for *Pesach* would customarily work with very small quantities — he describes the practice as *kaphiza kaphiza*, tiny batch by tiny batch, with *Rashi* explaining that each batch was approximately three *lugim*, or three quarters of a *kav*. This was deliberately conservative, designed to eliminate any risk of *chimutz* through careful portion control.

*Abaye* objects sharply: this *chumra* becomes a *kula*. By keeping each batch below the *challah* minimum, the women exempt themselves from the obligation of *hafrashat challah* entirely — a significant practical leniency achieved through what was intended as a stringency. *Rav Yosef* responds that the problem is resolved by following *Rabbi Eliezer's* ruling — not the *Rabbi Eliezer* of our *mishna*, but the *Rabbi Eliezer* cited in the tractate of *Challah* — who holds that if separate loaves, each below the minimum, are baked and then placed together into the same basket, *hasal metzarfan le-challah* — the basket combines them into a single quantity sufficient to obligate *challah*. The women bake their small individual batches and keep each one safe from *chimutz*, but by collecting all the finished loaves in the same basket upon removing them from the oven, they aggregate to the required minimum and the *chiyuv challah* is created.

---

## Basket Combining

### No-Rim Question

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* raises a question about this combining mechanism: what if the basket has no rim — *tavlah she'ein lah levazbezin*? The operative principle, according to *Rabbi Eliezer* (of *Challah*), is that the basket (*sal*) combines the loaves. But does this require that they be held within the walls of a vessel — *tokh kli* — or is it sufficient that they occupy the *airspace* of a vessel — *avir kli* — even without enclosing walls? A flat board with no rim allows the loaves to rest together without being surrounded on any side. Whether such a surface qualifies as a combining vessel remains unresolved — the Gemara leaves this as *teiku*.

### Basket vs Oven

A *baraita* records the foundational dispute among the *Tannaim*: *Rabbi Eliezer* holds that the basket (*sal*) is what combines the loaves for *challah* purposes; *Rabbi Yehoshua* holds that it is the oven (*tanur*). The precise relationship between these two positions — whether the one who says basket requires the oven as well, or whether the one who says oven excludes the basket — is not fully unpacked by the Gemara. The *beraita* does raise the additional question of whether baking in the same oven is a prerequisite in addition to placement in the same basket, or whether the basket alone suffices regardless of whether the loaves shared an oven.

### Babylonian Breads

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* introduces a third position: the loaves must actually touch one another as they expand in the oven — *shenoshkhot zo mizo*, literally biting one another — as is characteristic of *kikarot shel Bavel*, Babylonian-style round loaves that are placed close together so that they press into each other as they rise. Only under those conditions, where the loaves physically merge during baking, does the combination become effective. The Gemara notes the irony that the *matzah*-baking context makes this condition particularly difficult to satisfy, since *matzah* by definition does not rise and expand and therefore will not naturally press into adjacent loaves. *Rabbi Chanina* subsequently rules that even the elongated, non-expanding type of bread — *kakhin*, the *beraita's* term for loaves that do not touch — can combine through the basket even without physical contact in the oven.

---

## Multi-Woman Baking

### Gamliel Lenient

The *mishna* now introduces the question of how multiple women sharing a single oven may bake *matzah* without risk of *chimutz*. *Rabban Gamliel* takes the most lenient position: three women may all knead their dough simultaneously — *lashot k'echat* — and then bake sequentially in the same oven, one after another — *v'ofot b'tanur echad zu achar zu*. Under this arrangement, two women may be waiting while the third bakes, and *Rabban Gamliel* is not concerned that the waiting dough will ferment in the interim.

### Assembly Line Model

The *Chachamim* reject this arrangement as insufficiently protective. For them, three women working simultaneously is permissible only if they operate as a continuous assembly line — *shalosh nashim oskot bebatzek k'echat* — so that no woman is ever in a position of simply waiting with idle dough. The structure must be sequential and continuous: at any given moment, each woman is actively engaged in a different stage of production.

### Station Rotation

The *Tanna kama* articulates the assembly line in detail. There are three stations. The first woman kneads at station A; she then moves to station B to shape and pat the dough, and the second woman enters station A to begin kneading.
