The first woman moves from station B to station C — the oven — to bake; the second woman moves from A to B; the third woman enters station A to knead. Then the first woman, having finished baking, returns to station A to begin a new batch; the second moves from B to C; the third moves from A to B. The cycle continues in this rotation — *v'chozeret chalilah* — so that every station is occupied at all times and no dough waits unattended. The governing principle underlying this arrangement is stated explicitly: *kol zman she'oseket babatzek, eino ba lidei chimutz* — as long as dough is being actively worked, it cannot ferment. The danger of *chimutz* arises only during intervals of inactivity.

### Akiva No Rules

*Rabbi Akiva* rejects the possibility of any fixed rule. *Lo kol hanashim velo kol ha'etzim velo kol hatannurim shavim* — not all women work with the same efficiency, not all wood burns with the same heat or speed, and not all ovens behave identically. A rule that works under one combination of conditions may be dangerously inadequate under another. The variables are too numerous and context-dependent to admit of quantification. This is a striking methodological position: *Rabbi Akiva* refuses to validate either *Rabban Gamliel's* permissive arrangement or the *Chachamim's* assembly-line model as reliable in the abstract. The only valid standard is observation of the dough itself.

### Inspection Principle

A *baraita* records that *Rabbi Akiva* pressed this point directly before *Rabban Gamliel*: are we speaking of efficient women or less efficient ones? Of wet wood or dry wood? Of a hot oven or a cold one? With each question, the inadequacy of any fixed rule becomes more apparent, since the answer would determine how quickly *chimutz* might set in. The *baraita* indicates that *Rabban Gamliel* ultimately conceded *Rabbi Akiva's* point. The one principle both agree upon is expressed in the formula: *tapach* — if the dough begins to expand — *v'tiltosh betzonen* — apply cold water to arrest the process. The inspection of the dough itself, rather than any fixed time-interval or structural arrangement, is the authoritative standard.

---

## Chametz Stages

### Tapach Expanding

The beginning of fermentation is visible as expansion — *tapach*. At this stage the process has begun but has not yet crossed any threshold of prohibition. The dough can still be saved: applying cold water — *tiltosh betzonen* — arrests the fermentation and returns the dough to a workable state. This is the window of intervention, and both *Rabban Gamliel* and *Rabbi Akiva* agree that it is the operational criterion.

### Se'or Blanching

The *mishna* defines the intermediate stage — *se'or* — as dough that has progressed beyond the expanding phase. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, *se'or* at the stage described in the *mishna* is characterized by blanching of the surface — *k'sheyichsifu panav* — a change in color likened to the face of a person whose hair stands on end in fright. Small, initial cracks — *k'karnei chagavim*, like the antennae of grasshoppers — begin to appear. This stage is rabbinically forbidden: the *se'or* must be burned — *yisaref* — but one who eats it is *patur*, exempt from *karet*, indicating that it has not yet reached biblical *chametz* status.

### Siduq Cracking

*Siduq* is the stage of full biblical *chametz*. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, this is identified by crisscrossing cracks — *shenitarvu sdekim zeh bazeh* — visible on the surface of the dough. At this stage, *yisaref v'ochlo chayav karet*: the dough must be burned, and one who eats it incurs *karet*. The progression is thus: expanding (arrested by cold water), blanching with minor cracks (rabbinic prohibition only), and crisscrossed cracks (biblical *chametz* with *karet*).

### Yehuda-Meir Dispute

The *mishna* and the *baraita* present the debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Meir* in inverted form. In the *mishna*, the anonymous *Chachamim* state *zeh v'zeh ha'ochlo chayav karet* — both the intermediate and final stages incur *karet* — which the *baraita* identifies as *Rabbi Meir's* position. For *Rabbi Meir*, the grasshopper-antennae crack stage is already biblical *chametz*; *se'or* at this degree of development is not merely rabbinically forbidden but carries *karet*. *Rabbi Meir's* definition of the rabbinic-only *se'or* stage accordingly refers to the earlier blanching stage, without visible cracks.

*Rabbi Yehuda*, whose position is explicitly named in the *mishna*, draws the biblical threshold higher: only the crisscrossing cracks constitute biblical *chametz*, while the grasshopper stage remains at the level of rabbinic prohibition only — *ochlo patur*. The earlier blanching constitutes the *se'or* that is rabbinically forbidden without *karet*.

### Rava's Explanation

The Gemara asks: what is *Rabbi Meir's* reasoning for treating even the small grasshopper-stage cracks as biblical *chametz*? *Rava* explains: *ein l'cha kol sedek v'sedek milma'ala she'ein lo kama sedakim milmata* — any crack visible on the surface of the dough necessarily reflects a far more extensive network of cracks developing within the dough below the surface. What appears to the eye as a modest surface crack is in reality an indicator of advanced internal fermentation. *Rabbi Meir* therefore holds that the visible grasshopper crack is not a superficial sign of early-stage leavening; it is evidence that the dough has already fermented deeply, and biblical *chametz* status applies.

This closes the daf with the three-stage model of *chimutz* formation clearly in view. The stages — expansion, surface blanching or minor cracking, and visible crisscrossed cracks — map onto the practical-halachic categories of no prohibition, rabbinic prohibition, and biblical *chametz* with *karet*, though *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* disagree about where precisely along that continuum the biblical threshold falls. It is also worth noting that an earlier discussion in the Gemara touched on the possibility of a middle category — *chametz nuksha* — that might carry biblical prohibition without *karet*, though our *mishna* does not surface that intermediate tier explicitly.

---

---

# Pesachim 49

## Arba'asar b'Shabbat

### Intro: 14th on Shabbat

The third *perek* draws toward its close, and we open daf 49a with the *mishnah* addressing *arba'asar she'chal lihyot b'Shabbat* — the 14th of Nisan falling on *Shabbat*. This is a recognized subspecialty within *hilchot Pesach*, significant enough that entire *sefarim* have been written on *arba'asar she'chal lihyot b'Shabbat* and *erev Pesach she'chal lihyot b'erev Shabbat*. The core difficulty is layered: you cannot perform *bi'ur* on *erev Pesach* itself in the usual way, and there are additional questions the *mishnah* does not address — how to fulfill *shalosh seudot*, how to handle the prohibition against eating *matzah* on *erev Pesach*, and whether one may make *Hamotzi* on *matzah ashirah*. These are questions that stand, as the expression goes, *b'rumo shel olam*. The *mishnah* addresses what it addresses, and the *Gemara*'s treatment is worth examining closely.

### Rabbi Meir: Erev Shabbat

*Arba'asar she'chal lihyot b'Shabbat* — if the 14th falls on *Shabbat*, *m'va'arin et hakol milifnei haShabbat*, we destroy everything the day before *Shabbat*. These are the words of Rabbi Meir. The concern motivating his position is real: one cannot be certain an opportunity to destroy the *chametz* properly will present itself on *Shabbat*. The complication is that some of what must be destroyed may be *terumah*, which ordinarily could be consumed. Destroying *terumah* before absolutely necessary involves a genuine waste, yet Rabbi Meir holds that the concern about *chametz* overrides. It is also worth noting that Rabbi Yehudah, who holds *bi'ur chametz* must be specifically through burning — *sereifah* — would presumably agree with Rabbi Meir's conclusion, since waiting until *Shabbat* forecloses the option of *sereifah* altogether. This raises an interesting question: who are the *chachamim* who disagree with Rabbi Meir? It cannot be Rabbi Yehudah, precisely because of the *sereifah* requirement. Rabbi Meir's insistence on doing everything *erev Shabbat* is thus particularly pointed.

### Chachamim: Bizmano

The *chachamim* say *bizmano* — wait and do everything on the 14th, on *Shabbat* itself. The assumption is that one will find some way to handle it, some person available to consume the *terumah*, some arrangement. The difficulty, of course, is that waiting until *Shabbat* both risks *chilul Shabbat* and makes destruction more difficult — one cannot burn on *Shabbat*, and more indirect means of destruction are harder to arrange than simply throwing *chametz* into a fire.

### R. Eliezer b. Tzadok

Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok offers a differentiated position: *terumah milifnei haShabbat v'chullin bizmana* — destroy the *terumah* before *Shabbat*, but the *chullin* on *Shabbat* itself. This is initially counterintuitive. One might expect the reverse — surely *terumah* is the more precious item we wish to preserve as long as possible. But the logic is the opposite: *terumah* can only be eaten by a *kohen*, so the pool of people available to consume it before it must be destroyed is small. *Chullin*, by contrast, can be eaten by anyone, so there is far greater confidence that the *chametz chullin* can be handled on *Shabbat* itself — whether by eating or by some other means. *Terumah* presents the greater practical difficulty, and therefore should be dealt with *erev Shabbat*.

One might add a qualification: the calculus would shift depending on one's circumstances. If one is a *kohen* with many *kohanim* in the household, or has relatively little *terumah* and much *chullin*, the picture changes accordingly — *lo kol anashim shavot*.

### Yavneh Precedent

A *tanna* taught in support of Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok's position: *pa'am achat shabat Abba b'Yavneh* — once my father spent *Shabbat* in Yavneh, and that *Shabbat* happened to coincide with *erev Pesach*, the 14th falling on *Shabbat*. Yavneh was at that time the seat of the *nasi*. *Zonin*, an officer of Rabban Gamliel, came and made an announcement throughout the city: *higia et l'va'er et hachametz* — the time to destroy the *chametz* has arrived. The son relates: *v'halachti achar Abba u'viarnu et hachametz* — I followed my father and we destroyed the *chametz*.

The phrase *biarnu et hachametz* is admittedly a bit strange in a *Shabbat* context, since it conjures the image of burning, which one cannot do on *Shabbat*. Perhaps the more accurate way to have told the story would have been *v'achalnu et hachametz*. The *mishnah* itself uses the verb *mevaarim* even when describing what happens on *Shabbat*, and presumably *mevaarim b'Shabbat* in that context means consuming it. The precedent is thus cited to support Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok's view that *chullin bizmanan* — destroying the *chullin* on *Shabbat* itself — is the correct approach, though one would have hoped for greater specificity in how that destruction was accomplished.

---

## Holech Lishchot

### Multiple Mitzvot Crisis

The next *mishnah* shifts to a different scenario: *haholech lishchot et hapesach* — a person is on his way to perform *shechitah* of the *korban Pesach* on the 14th. The *mishnah* compounds the picture: *u'lamol et bno* — perhaps his son's *bris milah* is also today; *v'le'echol seudat eirusin b'veit chamiv* — or he is going to his father-in-law's house for a *seudat eirusin*. Some context is needed here: *eirusin* in the Talmudic sense means *kiddushin* — one is legally married but has not yet entered into *nissuin* and the couple is not yet living together. The post-*kiddushin* celebration at the father-in-law's house was a recognized practice with legal standing in other areas of *halachah*.

A brief digression: while *ein mearvin simcha b'simcha* applies to *nissuin* on *Chol HaMoed*, *kiddushin* is permitted on *Chol HaMoed*, partly because *shema yikadmenu acher* — one fears another may come and take her — and partly because *kiddushin* technically does not yet carry the quality of lived *simcha* that *sheva brachot* celebrate. The *seudas eirusin* at the father-in-law's house, however, was treated as carrying a special character of *simcha* and *mitzvah* in its own right.

Now comes the complication: *v'nizkar she-yesh lo chametz b'toch beito* — he suddenly remembers he has *chametz* in his house that he forgot to destroy. What should he do?

### Bittul: Last Resort

If he can return and destroy the *chametz* and still return to perform his *mitzvah* — *lachzor u'lvaer v'lachzor l'mitzvato* — then *yachzor v'yvaer*, he goes back and destroys it. If not, *mevatlo b'libo* — he nullifies it in his heart, performing *bittul*.

This is a significant moment in the *mishnah*: for anyone who has been following since the beginning of the *perek*, this is the first appearance of *bittul chametz* in the *mishnah*. Throughout the earlier *mishnayot*, the *mishnah* discusses only burning and physical destruction of *chametz*. *Bittul* appears here, at the close of the third *perek*, as a last resort in extenuating circumstances.

### Osek b'Mitzvah

This connects to a broader principle worth examining: *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah*. One might ask how that principle applies here. The complication is that this is not simply a conflict between two *mitzvot*, where we resolve that one who is engaged in a *mitzvah* is exempt from another. Here, owning *chametz* involves a *lav* — the prohibitions of *bal yira'eh uval yimatzei* — and a *lo ta'aseh* carries more serious implications than simply not performing a positive commandment. The *mishnah* therefore frames the question as: can you return and still do your *mitzvah*, or not? If you can, go back. If you cannot, *bittul* is available.

This context illuminates the broader development of *bittul* as a halachic tool. The first *Rashi* in the *masechet* explains that *bedikat chametz* is performed to avoid violating *bal yira'eh u'val yimatzei*. Tosafot objects: the *Rav* rules that one who performs *bedikah* must also do *bittul*, and if *bittul* is effective, how can the *bedikah* alone be serving the function of preventing the violation? Tosafot's question, however, reflects the *amora'ic* period. In the era of the *mishnah*, *bittul* was not routinely practiced — precisely because allowing it universally would turn the whole enterprise into a farce. One could simply declare mental nullification and never actually rid oneself of *chametz*. So *chazal* in the *mishnaic* period permitted *bittul* only in exceptional circumstances, while the standard obligation was to perform *bedikah* and *bi'ur*. The rule *habodek tzarich sheyivatel* — that one who searches must also nullify — was introduced in the *amora'ic* period, adding *bittul* as a backup measure even for one who performs a thorough search, in case something was missed. That later development then raised Tosafot's question, but the historical progression clarifies why the *mishnah* presents *bittul* as the exceptional last resort rather than the primary tool.

### Pikuach Nefesh

The *mishnah* then considers a different kind of situation: *lehatzil min hanochri, umin hanahar, umin halistin, umin hadeleikah, umin hamapolet* — one is going not to perform a standard *mitzvah* but to save lives: people are being attacked by hostile forces, a river threatens to flood, bandits are present, a fire is spreading, or a building has collapsed. In such cases, *yevatel belibo* — simply do *bittul* immediately, without any calculation about whether one might return in time. There is no *cheshbon* about whether the fire might not have spread too far, or whether the river will have risen too much. When lives are at stake, one does not weigh the *mitzvah* of *bi'ur* against the urgent need for rescue. Act immediately on the life-threatening situation, and rely on *bittul*.

### Reshut: Must Return

The final case in this sequence inverts the logic entirely: *v'lishbot shevitat hareshut* — one is traveling not to perform a *mitzvah* at all, but simply to spend *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* somewhere for discretionary reasons. Rashi understands this as placing an *eruv techumin*; Tosafot reads it more simply as going to spend *Yom Tov* with family — at one's parents' home, or visiting one's children. One is already on the road, already packed and gone, and one suddenly remembers: *bi'ur chametz* was not done. In that case, *yachzor miyad* — turn around immediately and go back. There is no calculation about whether you can still make it to your destination in time. Since what you were doing is only a *reshut*, the obligation of *bi'ur chametz* takes full precedence. Even *bittul*, which is technically available, is not sufficient to excuse you from returning when what you were pursuing was discretionary.

This is a striking feature of the *mishnah*: it demonstrates how seriously the physical destruction of *chametz* was demanded at a time when *bittul* was viewed as a true last resort. The obligation to actually perform *bi'ur* was pressed even at real personal cost, set aside only when a *mitzvah* or danger to life made return genuinely impossible.

---

## Yetza mi-Yerushalayim

### Meat Spoilage Case

The *mishnah* continues: *mi she-yatza mi-Yerushalayim v'nizkar she-yesh b'yado basar kodesh* — someone who left Jerusalem and realized he was still carrying meat from *shelamim* that had not been consumed in time. *Kodshim* that leave Jerusalem become *pasul* and must be destroyed. The question is: must one go back to Jerusalem to burn it there, or may one burn it wherever one finds oneself?

### Tzofim Boundary

*Im avar Tzofim* — if one has passed Tzofim, one burns it *bimkomo*, wherever one stands. Rashi understands *Tzofim* as a proper place-name. Tosafot, however, understands it as a descriptive term: any point outside Jerusalem from which Jerusalem is no longer within line of sight. According to Tosafot, the operative moment is when one can no longer see Jerusalem. If one has not yet passed that boundary — if one is still within line of sight — one must turn back.

### Line of Sight Rule

If one is still within the *Tzofim* boundary — still within line of sight of Jerusalem — *chozer v'sorfo lifnei ha-birah* — one returns and burns the meat in the presence of the *birah*, the royal court, presumably on or near the *Beit HaMikdash*, using wood dedicated to the *ma'arachah*, the altar's woodpile.

Tosafot raises an important difficulty here. Rashi, citing an earlier *Gemara*, notes that *kodesh she-psulah b'kodesh teunah sereifah* — consecrated items that become *pasul* must be burned in a sacred place. If so, how could the *mishnah* ever permit burning the meat outside Jerusalem? At least for *chametz* there is a backup — *bittul* — but if there is a genuine obligation to burn the *kodesh* within the *Beit HaMikdash*, how can we release someone from that obligation simply because of the distance?

Tosafot resolves this by distinguishing categories: the requirement to burn *kodesh* within the *Beit HaMikdash* applies specifically to *kodshei kodoshim*, the most sacred class of offerings. *Shelamim* are *kodshim kalim* — offerings of lesser sanctity, which may be eaten by any Jew throughout Jerusalem. *Kodshim kalim* that are taken outside Jerusalem do not technically carry the same requirement to be burned within the *Beit HaMikdash*. Therefore, *chazal* instituted the practice of returning to burn them near the *Beit HaMikdash* so as not to generate confusion, but when the burden of returning becomes excessive, they were lenient.

### Size Thresholds

For how large a quantity must one return — whether to destroy *chametz* or to return meat that has become *pasul*? Rabbi Meir says *zeh v'zeh k'beitzah* — both require returning if the amount is at least a *beitzah* (an egg's bulk). Rabbi Yehudah says *zeh v'zeh k'zayit* — both require returning for an olive's bulk. The *chachamim* distinguish: *basar kodesh b'khazayit v'chametz k'beitzah* — for the sacred meat the threshold is a *zayit*, but for *chametz* it is a *beitzah*.

The *Gemara* explains the positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah but does not explain the *chachamim*. Tosafot supplies the reasoning: *chametz* has the backup mechanism of *bittul*, and because of that backup option, the *chachamim* set the threshold at the more lenient *beitzah* rather than the *zayit*. For *basar kodesh*, no comparable backup exists, so the stricter *zayit* threshold applies.

One sharp observation deserves mention: in the *chametz* case, when one is leaving for a purely discretionary purpose (*reshut*), one is always required to return regardless of how far one has gone. Yet in the *basar kodesh* case — where one is also presumably leaving for a *reshut* — the *mishnah* allows leniency depending on how burdensome the return would be. The apparent asymmetry is striking. One might have expected the *chametz* case, given the availability of *bittul*, to be treated more leniently — and yet it is precisely there that the *mishnah* demands return even when what one was doing was purely discretionary. The resolution may be that the two cases operate by different considerations, though this question deserves further analysis.

---

## Marriage Hierarchy

### Seudas Eirusin Debate

The *Gemara* now raises a difficulty against the *mishnah*'s classification of the *seudat eirusin* as a *mitzvah*. A *baraita* is cited: *haholech le'echol seudat eirusin b'veit chamiv v'lishbot shevitat hareshut* — one who goes to eat the *seudat eirusin* at his father-in-law's house, or who travels merely for discretionary purposes — in both cases *yachzor miyad*, one must turn back immediately. This *baraita* groups the *seudat eirusin* together with *reshut* — apparently treating it as not a *mitzvah* at all. This stands in apparent contradiction to the *mishnah*, which presents the *seudat eirusin* as a *mitzvah* that affects whether one must or need not interrupt to return.

### First vs Second Meal

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction: it is a *machlokes* between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yosei. A *baraita* teaches — *seudat eirusin reshut divrei Rabbi Yehudah*: Rabbi Yehudah holds it is purely discretionary. *Rabbi Yosei omer mitzvah*: Rabbi Yosei holds it is a *mitzvah*. This is a somewhat curious debate — in what precise sense is such a celebration a *mitzvah*? Presumably in the *rabbinic* sense, like many institutions that *chazal* elevated and formalized.

Rav Chisda sharpens the picture: the debate between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yosei is specifically about the *seuda shniya* — the second meal — which involved the sending of *sivlonot*, gifts, to the father-in-law's house, followed by a second celebratory meal in which those gifts were consumed. *Aval b'seuda rishona divrei hakol mitzvah* — but regarding the first meal, everyone agrees it is a *mitzvah*. The *mishnah* refers to the first meal; the *baraita* refers to the second. And even holding by Rabbi Yehudah, one can resolve the apparent contradiction: the *mishnah* speaks of the first meal (*mitzvah*), the *baraita* of the second (*reshut*).

A *baraita* is then cited in direct support of Rav Chisda's clarification: *amar Rabbi Yehudah ani lo shamati ela seudat eirusin* — I have only heard of the first *seudat eirusin* as having this status, *aval lo sivlonot* — but not the *sivlonot* meal. Rabbi Yosei disagrees: *ani shamati seudat eirusin v'sivlonot* — I heard that both carry the status of *seudat mitzvah*.

### Talmid Chacham Restricti…

The discussion of *seudat eirusin* transitions into a broader teaching. A *baraita* cites Rabbi Shimon: *kol seudah she-einah shel mitzvah, ein talmid chacham rashai l'henot mimena* — any meal that is not a *seudat mitzvah*, a *talmid chacham* may not derive pleasure from it. The scope of this prohibition requires clarification. Presumably it does not apply to ordinary meals shared with friends or to the ordinary rhythms of daily life. It seems to address more specifically meals to which the *talmid chacham* is invited by virtue of his status, or grand celebrations in which his presence lends a certain cachet. Two concerns may be at play: the danger of personal indulgence in physical pleasure, and the more specific concern about the *talmid chacham* allowing his Torah standing to function as social currency — a kind of *kardom lachpor bah*, leveraging one's Torah status for personal benefit. On the other hand, there are *Gemarot* that speak strongly about the responsibility of wealthy people to support *talmidei chachamim*, so the concern here seems to be about something more than simple hospitality.

The *Gemara* asks: *kegon mai* — what would be a concrete example of a meal that is *not* a *seudat mitzvah* in this sense? Rabbi Yochanan answers: *kegon bat kohen le-Yisrael u'vat talmid chacham le-am ha'aretz* — for example, the wedding feast of a *bat kohen* marrying a *Yisrael*, or the daughter of a *talmid chacham* marrying an *am ha'aretz*. The *Gemara* thus identifies these specific matches as the paradigmatic cases of a *seudah she-einah shel mitzvah*. Technically, *kiddushin* is a *mitzvah* — but it is not something the *Rabbanan* view as appropriate, and therefore the celebration does not carry the character of a true *seudat mitzvah*. The word *mitzvah* is being used normatively, not technically. One sees this appropriation of terminology in other contexts as well.

### Bad Match Examples

Rabbi Yochanan further teaches: *bat kohen le-Yisrael ein zivugan oleh yafeh* — the marriage of a *bat kohen* to a *Yisrael* does not turn out well. Rav Chisda specifies what this means, drawing on adjacent *psukim* in the Torah: *o almanah o gerushah o zera ein lah* — either she becomes a widow, or divorced, or they have no children. The *baraita* adds even more starkly: *kovrah o koverato* — either he buries her or she buries him. Rashi explains this means one of them dies before their time. Or, the *Gemara* adds, *mevi'ato lidei aniyut* — it brings him to poverty. One practical explanation for the poverty concern: the *kohanim* represented the aristocracy, and a *bat kohen* accustomed to that standard of living may strain the household's resources.

The *Gemara* challenges this with a statement also attributed to Rabbi Yochanan: *ha-rotzeh she-yitasher yidbak b'zaro shel Aharon* — whoever wishes to become wealthy should cleave to the descendants of Aharon. Indeed, *kol she-ken she-Torah u'khunah measheran* — all the more so if one combines Torah learning with a priestly lineage through marriage, both will contribute to wealth. Does this not contradict the earlier pessimism about such marriages?

The *Gemara* resolves: *lo kashya — ha b'talmid chacham, ha b'am ha'aretz*. The positive outcome attaches to a *talmid chacham* marrying a *bat kohen*; the negative outcome describes an *am ha'aretz* doing so. The two aristocracies — priestly lineage and Torah scholarship — are natural partners. The match becomes problematic when someone crosses out of both aristocratic categories: a *bat kohen* marrying an *am ha'aretz*, or a *bat talmid chacham* marrying an *am ha'aretz*. The original formulation of *bat kohen le-Yisrael* must therefore be understood as *bat kohen le-am ha'aretz* — a *Yisrael* who is an *am ha'aretz*.

### Good Match Examples

The *Gemara* proceeds to positive examples. Rabbi Yehoshua married a *kohenet* — note the shift from the construct *bat kohen* (a daughter defined by her father) to the feminized Aramaic *kohenet*. He fell ill and feared this was divine displeasure — *lo nicha leh l'Aharon d'idbak b'zarei d'havei leh chasna ki ana?* — Does Aharon not want me to cleave to his descendants? Am I not worthy to be his son-in-law? The complaint itself implies that a *talmid chacham* marrying a *bat kohen* is considered a proper match.

Rav Idi bar Avin married a *kohenet*, and the *Gemara* records: *nafak minei trei b'nei smichi* — from him came two sons who achieved full *semikhah*, two prominent rabbinic authorities: Rav Sheshet b'rei d'Rav Idi and Rav Yehoshua b'rei d'Rav Idi. Rav Pappa states: *ilu lo nasivna kahanta, lo itat'ri* — had I not married a *kohenet*, I would not have become wealthy. Rav Kahana, by contrast: *ilu lo nasivna kahanta, lo galai* — had I not married a *kohenet*, I would not have gone into exile. His going into *galut* from Bavel to Eretz Yisrael was not voluntary; he was forced to flee. When his students pointed out that he went to a place of Torah, he acknowledged it, but insisted this was not a *galut* in the ordinary sense — *lo galai k'degali inshi* — it was not the exile one chooses.

Tosafot makes an interesting observation: from the fact that Rav Kahana attributes his exile to having married a *kohenet*, it seems he was not himself a *kohen* — otherwise one would not expect punishment for marrying within the *kehunah*. This is corroborated by the linguistic point that *Kahana* is a first name in the Talmudic period, not a patronym or family designation, so bearing it carries no presumption of priestly lineage.

### Marriage Obligation

The *Gemara* now states the positive obligation more explicitly. *Tanu Rabbanan: le'olam yimkor adam kol mah she-yesh lo v'yisa bat talmid chacham* — a person should always sell everything he owns and marry the daughter of a *talmid chacham*. The reasoning: *she-im met o goleh yafeh* — if he dies or is compelled to travel, who will ensure the Torah education of his children? A *bat talmid chacham* carries those values as core commitments, not merely as external aspirations. *Im asah ken muvtach lo she-banav talmidei chachamim* — if he does so, he can be confident his children will carry those values forward. Conversely: *v'al yisa bat am ha'aretz* — do not marry the daughter of an *am ha'aretz*, for *banav amei ha'aretz* — if you are not present to invest in their education, no one else will ensure it, and they will become *amei ha'aretz*.

The *Gemara* then introduces the complementary principle: not only should one seek a *bat talmid chacham* for oneself, but *v'yasi bito l'talmid chacham* — one should also ensure one's daughter marries a *talmid chacham*. The parable given captures the ideal: *mashal l'invei hagefen b'invei hagefen davar na'eh u'mitkabel* — it is like grapes of the vine with grapes of the vine, a beautiful and pleasing combination. By contrast, *l'invei hagefen b'invei hasneh, davar ka'ur v'eino mitkabel* — grapes of the vine with berries of the thornbush is ugly and finds no favor.

A hierarchy is then laid out for cases where no *bat talmid chacham* is available. After a *talmid chacham*, one should seek *bat gedolei hador* — the daughter of the prominent leaders of the generation, presumably figures of civil authority. If not them, then *bat rashei kenesiyot* — the daughter of synagogue heads, a position of recognized communal prestige. Failing that, *bat gaba'ei tzedakah* — overseers of charitable funds, positions of both rectitude and public trust. Then *bat melamdei tinokot* — the daughter of those who teach children in the schools, people deeply invested in Torah transmission even if not themselves great scholars. The hierarchy reflects a combination of Torah commitment, public responsibility, and communal standing. Notably, the *melamdei tinokot* appear at the bottom rather than the top of the list even though the practical concern about ensuring children's education might seem to favor them — this reflects that the *Gemara* is tracking a prestige hierarchy alongside the purely educational concern. In every case, the clear bottom line is: *v'lo yisa bat am ha'aretz*.

It is worth stepping back to appreciate what motivates this passage. The language of selling everything one owns to ensure the right match is not mere rhetoric. It is an acknowledgment of what the right match costs — financially, logistically, and personally — and a statement that ensuring Torah continuity across generations is worth that cost. The concern is not primarily about social hierarchy for its own sake, but about the concrete transmission of Torah values within the home.

---

## Am Ha'aretz Rhetoric

### Sheketz Designation

Now comes the most challenging portion of the daf. The *Gemara* assigns stark characterizations to the *am ha'aretz* and his household: *mipnei she-hein sheketz v'nshoseihem sheretz* — because they are an abomination, and their wives are like vermin. And regarding their daughters the verse is invoked: *arur shochev im kol behemah* — cursed is one who lies with any animal. Rashi understands this as referring to their ignorance — they are treated as animals, as beings devoid of intellectual or spiritual distinction. But the verse is applied broadly, and as the *Gemara* continues the language only intensifies.

### Extreme Violence

Rabbi Elazar states: *am ha'aretz mutar l'nochro b'Yom HaKippurim she'chal l'hiyot b'Shabbat* — it is permitted to stab an *am ha'aretz* even on Yom Kippur that falls on *Shabbat*, meaning one may violate both Yom Kippur and *Shabbat* to do so. His students question the choice of language: why *nochro* — stabbing? Should he not say *shochto* — slaughtering, *shechitah*? He responds: *zeh ta'un berachah v'zeh eino ta'un berachah* — *shechitah* requires a *berachah*, and he does not wish any *berachah* to be associated with killing a person. This is an extraordinarily extreme statement. We can hope it is hyperbolic in the extreme, but it is in the text.

Rabbi Eliezer teaches: *am ha'aretz assur l'hitlavot imo baderech* — one may not accompany an *am ha'aretz* on a journey, as the verse says *ki hi chayecha v'orech yamecha* — Torah is your life and the length of your days. The reasoning: *al chayav lo chas* — he does not care about his own life, since he never invests in Torah learning; *al chayei chaveiro lo kol sheken* — all the more so will he not care about yours. Rabbi Yochanan adds: *am ha'aretz mutar l'kor'o k'dag* — one may tear him like a fish. Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak specifies: *u'migavo* — from his back, as one guts a fish by cutting along the spine, quickly and without the fish resisting.

### R. Akiva Confession

*Tanya*: Rabbi Akiva himself testifies — *k'she-hayiti am ha'aretz, amarti: mi yiten li talmid chacham v'anshchenu k'chamor* — when I was an *am ha'aretz*, I said: if only I could get hold of a *talmid chacham*, I would bite him like a donkey. His students ask: why a donkey rather than a dog? He explains: *zeh noshech v'shover etzem v'zeh noshech v'eino shover etzem* — a donkey bites and breaks the bone, while a dog bites but does not break bones. So fierce was his hatred. Rabbi Akiva's testimony here is remarkable: the violent animus was not one-directional. The *am ha'aretz* harbored equivalent — or greater — hatred toward *talmidei chachamim*, at least as reported here. This mutual contempt is a cycle that the *Gemara* clearly regards as a communal pathology even as it participates in it.

### Behavioral Claims

The *Gemara* continues with a teaching of Rabbi Meir: *kol hamashi bito l'am ha'aretz k'ilu kaftah u'minichtah lifnei ari* — whoever marries his daughter to an *am ha'aretz* is as if he bound her and left her before a lion. The *Gemara* explains the analogy: *mah ari dores v'ochel v'ein lo boshes panim, af am ha'aretz makeh u'bo'el v'ein lo boshes panim* — just as a lion tramples and eats without any shame (and Tosafot notes without even waiting for the prey to die), so too an *am ha'aretz* will smite and engage in sexual relations without any sense of privacy or restraint. The characterization is that an *am ha'aretz*'s approach to sexuality is violent and animalistic, without the modesty and self-restraint that Torah cultivation produces.

A *baraita* teaches: *Rebbi omer, am ha'aretz assur l'echol basar* — an *am ha'aretz* is forbidden to eat meat, because the verse says *zot torat habehemah v'ha'of* — this is the Torah of animal and bird. Torah is connected to animal and bird; therefore, *kol ha'osek baTorah mutar l'echol basar behemah v'of* — one who engages in Torah may eat meat, while *kol she'eino osek baTorah assur l'echol basar behemah v'of* — one who does not engage in Torah is forbidden to eat it. The implication: consuming animal flesh is a privilege granted to those whose Torah study elevates them above the merely animal. Eating meat without that spiritual framework may only deepen the animalistic orientation.

### Mutual Hatred

*Amar Rebbi: gedolah sinah she'sonim amei ha'aretz l'talmid chacham yoser mi'sinah she'sonim ovdei kochavim et Yisrael* — the hatred that *amei ha'aretz* bear toward *talmidei chachamim* is greater than the hatred non-Jews bear toward Jews. *V'neshoseihem yoter mehem* — and their wives hate even more virulently than the men. One might observe that at least part of this reflects projection — the *Gemara* itself has expressed extraordinarily hostile attitudes toward the *am ha'aretz*, and it should not surprise us that those attitudes generated reciprocal hostility.

The *Gemara* adds: *shana u'peireish yoter mi'kulam* — one who studied Torah and then left that world is worse than all of them, more virulent in his hatred than someone raised entirely as an *am ha'aretz*. Rashi's explanation is psychologically acute: he has heard everything that *chazal* say about *amei ha'aretz*, and therefore he hates the rabbinic community with particular intensity born of intimate knowledge.

### Practical Restrictions

*Tanu Rabbanan: shisha devarim ne'emru b'amei ha'aretz* — six practical rules were stated regarding an *am ha'aretz*. First, *ein mosrim lahem edut* — one does not call them as witnesses for a document. Second, *ein mekabelim mimenu edut* — one does not accept testimony from them when they come forward. The distinction between these two: the first is that you would not invite them to serve as witnesses for a transaction; the second is that even when they volunteer testimony — saying they witnessed Reuven lend money to Shimon — their testimony is not accepted. Third, *v'ein megalim lahem sod* — one does not share secrets with them. Fourth, *v'ein memanim osam apitropus al yesomim* — one does not appoint them as guardians over orphans' estates. Fifth, *v'ein memanim osam apitropus shel kupas tzedakah* — one does not appoint them as overseers of charitable funds. Sixth, *v'ein mitlavim imahem baderech* — one does not accompany them on the road. The common thread is untrustworthiness in matters of money and personal safety.

Some add a seventh: *af ein machrizim al aveidato* — one does not even announce their lost object so as to return it. Tosafot notes the practical question: how would one even know whose lost object it is? Tosafot answers: one found the object in a neighborhood of *amei ha'aretz*, so it is presumable that the owner is an *am ha'aretz*. The basis for not returning it seems to relate to a general suspicion that their property may not be honestly acquired.

The first *tanna* who holds that one does return the *aveida* of an *am ha'aretz* gives the following reason: *zimnin d'nafik minei zera ma'alya v'achal leh* — sometimes from him will come worthy offspring who will deserve to benefit from the wealth. As the verse says: *yachin tzaddik yilbash* — the righteous man prepares, and another righteous man will wear it.

### Tosafot Nuance

Tosafot registers an important qualification regarding the entire arc of this *Gemara*. Elsewhere in the Talmud there are many passages that take a far more measured, accepting attitude toward *amei ha'aretz* — far less harsh, far more nuanced. Tosafot explains that there are distinct categories of *am ha'aretz*, and the most extreme rhetoric in this *Gemara* addresses a specific category: those who were actively and even violently hostile to rabbinic authority. Tosafot invokes the ruling *ein machzirin lo aveidato* — not returning his lost object — and clarifies in that context: *v'nir'eh li d'la mairi b'makir v'kofer l'hach'is d'havei lei k'mo pikuach nefesh d'listim v'chashud al hadamim* — this refers specifically to someone who consciously rejects rabbinic authority in a provocative way, making him like a bandit, suspect regarding bloodshed. Tosafot further notes: *d'ika harbe inyanei am ha'aretz* — there are many different categories of *am ha'aretz*, and by later periods, testimony from an *am ha'aretz* was accepted in practice.

By the *Gemara*'s own close, the rhetoric has moderated. The final concern is no longer murder or gutting like a fish but questions of trust in monetary matters and whether one returns a found object. Even there, a voice within the *Gemara* itself insists one should return the *aveida*, because worthy descendants may benefit from it. This trajectory — from extreme violence to measured practical restrictions, with a dissenting voice arguing even for the return of lost property — offers some evidence that we are dealing throughout with hyperbole, with a specific and hostile sub-category of *am ha'aretz*, and with a historical moment of sharp communal conflict that must be read carefully and not generalized. Tosafot makes exactly this point, and it remains an essential hermeneutic for approaching this *Gemara*.

# Pesachim 50

## Kezayis vs. Kibeitzah

### Returning for Chametz

Today's daf is 50, and we wrap up the third *perek* before beginning the fourth. We continue from the bottom of 49b, picking up seven lines from the bottom at the two dots, beginning with the word *she'yatza*.

The preceding Mishna had established two parallel scenarios in which a person might need to turn back and destroy something: the case of *chametz* left at home, and the case of meat from a *korban shelamim* taken out of Jerusalem. With respect to *chametz*, the principle is clear — one must destroy *chametz* before *Pesach*. Where turning back is not feasible, either because one is occupied with a *mitzvah* and lacks time, or because one is rushing to save lives (in which case no calculation is made at all), then *bitul* is performed instead. As noted in the previous session, *bitul* appears only once in all the *Mishnayos* of Masechet Pesachim — as a last resort. It was only in the Amoraitic period that the *Gemara* ruled *ha'bodek tzarich she'yevatel*, expanding *bitul* into a standard backup practice, which then raised the question of why *biyur* remains necessary at all. In the Mishnah, however, *bitul* was the fallback when *biyur* was impossible, reflecting the primary focus on physically destroying *chametz*.

The parallel case of the *shelamim* meat involves a *korban* that becomes *pasul* the moment it is taken beyond the walls of Jerusalem. The Rabbis ruled that one must return it and burn it in Jerusalem or in the Beit HaMikdash. Tosafos notes that had it been *kodshei kodashim*, such as a *chatas*, the biblical requirement would be to burn it specifically in the Beit HaMikdash; since it is *kodshei kalim*, the obligation is rabbinic, and the Rabbis accordingly ruled that if one has already passed the point from which Jerusalem is no longer visible, one need not turn back. But if Jerusalem can still be seen, one must return and burn the meat there.

### Mishna Debate

The Mishna then addresses the threshold question: how much *chametz* or *korban* meat must remain for the obligation to turn back to apply? This is where the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda enters. Rabbi Meir holds that one returns only for a *kibeitzah* of either substance, while Rabbi Yehuda holds that even a *kezayis* obligates return.

### Reversal Question

The *Gemara* notes the apparent implication of these positions: Rabbi Meir considers a *kibeitzah* the significant minimum, while Rabbi Yehuda considers even a *kezayis* significant. This seems internally consistent — until the *Gemara* raises a contradiction from the Mishna concerning *zimun*. There, the question is the minimum amount of bread required for a *zimun* obligation: the first opinion holds a *kezayis*, which is presumably Rabbi Meir's view, while Rabbi Yehuda states a *kibeitzah* is required. Thus in our Mishna, Rabbi Meir requires a *kibeitzah* and Rabbi Yehuda a *kezayis*, but in the *zimun* Mishna their positions appear precisely reversed. How is this to be explained?

(It is worth noting the curious use of the word *ad* — "until" — in the *zimun* Mishna, which implies a downward direction rather than a minimum threshold. The Vilna Gaon apparently offers a brilliant reading of this language involving the size of a loaf divided among the *mezamnim*, though the precise details of his reading are not at hand.)

### Texts Switched

Rabbi Yochanan's response is *muchlefet hashitah*: one of the texts has the names of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda switched, and the apparent contradiction is simply a scribal transposition.

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye, however, resists this approach: *l'olam lo teipoch* — do not reverse the texts. The contradiction is only apparent because the two debates operate on entirely different grounds. *Hasam bikra pligi* — there, in the *zimun* Mishna, they debate based on a scriptural verse. *Hacha bisvara pligi* — here, in our Mishna, they debate based on a different principle altogether.

### Rabbi Meir's Ketubim

In the *zimun* debate, Rabbi Meir draws on the verse *v'achalta v'savata u'veirachta* (Devarim 8:10). He reads *v'achalta* as referring to the act of eating and *v'savata* as referring to drinking — not literal satiation — so that the act triggering the obligation of *Birkat Hamazon* is *achila*, and the standard measure of *achila* is a *kezayis*. Tosafos notes this reflects the principle of *achila k'moshehi*, that eating by definition is measured in *kazayis*.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Sevia

Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, reads the verse in its plain sense — *pshat*: *achila she'yesh bo sevia*, an eating that brings about satiation. The act that triggers *Birkat Hamazon* must be the kind of eating that satiates, and that minimum is a *kibeitzah*. It admittedly does not sound like a very large amount to produce satiation, which would imply that most people would rarely be biblically obligated.

### Tosafos Asmachta

Tosafos clarifies that at the biblical level both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree that true satiation is required. The measures of *kezayis* and *kibeitzah* are not strictly biblical thresholds; rather, they function as *asmachta* — rabbinic standards that are anchored to scripture, as Rashi explains elsewhere in a reference to Perek Kama of Mi She'meiso. At the rabbinic level, when a more objective and accessible minimum is needed, Rabbi Meir holds one *kezayis* is sufficient as a symbolic act of eating, while Rabbi Yehuda insists on a *kibeitzah* as at least symbolically evocative of satiation.

### Hazarah Significance

In our Mishna, the debate concerns not *Birkat Hamazon* but *hazarah* — when one is obligated to return and destroy. The two Tannaim apply different frameworks for determining what amount renders an object significant enough to warrant the effort of returning.

### Rabbi Meir Tumah

Rabbi Meir holds *hazartu k'tum'atu* — the threshold for return mirrors the threshold for *tumah*. The minimum measure for transmitting *tumah* is a *kibeitzah*. Whether *kibeitzah* is the minimum for an object to *receive* *tumah* or the minimum to *transmit* it is itself a matter of debate, but in either case it is the measure associated with the significance of food as a substance. Therefore, one returns for a *kibeitzah*. This applies equally to the *chametz* case and the *korban* case: even though the *korban* meat did not become *tamei* but merely *pasul* by leaving Jerusalem, the relevant framework is still the significance of *okhel* as food, and that significance is measured by *kibeitzah*. It is admittedly not immediately transparent why *tumah* thresholds apply to the *chametz* case, but the underlying logic seems to be that *kibeitzah* represents when an object attains substantial status as food.

### Rabbi Yehuda Issurah

Rabbi Yehuda's position is more directly intuitive: *k'issuro hazartu k'issuro* — the threshold for return mirrors the threshold for prohibition. The minimum amount of *chametz* one transgresses by eating is a *kezayis* — though *chametz* carries an *issur* for any amount (*kol shehu*), the standard *shiur* of significance is a *kezayis*. Likewise, the meat of a *pasul korban* becomes forbidden in the measure of a *kezayis*. Therefore one must return for a *kezayis*.

### Object vs. Act

One way of framing this debate: Rabbi Meir focuses on the significance of the *object itself* — at what point is this food considered a meaningful object? That is determined by *kibeitzah*, the threshold at which food acquires or transmits *tumah*. Rabbi Yehuda focuses on the significance of a problematic *act* one could perform with it — at what amount does eating it constitute a genuine violation? That is determined by *kezayis*. Rabbi Meir thus asks: when is this considered a meaningful *amount of food*? Rabbi Yehuda asks: when does this amount pose a meaningful *risk of transgression*?

### Rabbi Natan

A *braisa* adds a third opinion: Rabbi Natan says the threshold is *shtei beitzim* — two eggs' worth. One returns for neither a *kezayis* nor a *kibeitzah* but only for two *beitzim*. The *Gemara* records simply that the Sages did not agree with him, and the source of this measure is left unexplained.

---

## Aggada Future World

### Light Yikaros

Having concluded the analytical discussion of *hazarah*, the *Gemara* transitions into an extensive *aggadic* section. Rashi notes this connects thematically to the references to Jerusalem, and it also serves as a fitting close to the first three *prakim* of the *masechta*, which form a unified thematic unit focused on the laws of *chametz*. The verse from Zechariah (14:6–7) provides the opening: *v'haya bayom hahu lo yihiye or yikaros v'kipaon* — on that day there will no longer be the light of *yikaros* and *kipaon*. The precise translation of these two words is not obvious, and the *Gemara* proceeds to offer competing interpretations.

### Rabbi Elazar Light

Rabbi Elazar reads the verse as a statement about relative weight and weightlessness. *Yikaros* — from the root *yakar*, "heavy" or "precious" — refers to the light that is precious and weighty in this world, meaning the strong, brilliant sunlight we currently value highly. *Kipaon* — from an Aramaic word meaning to float — describes that same light as it will be in the world to come: featherweight, trivial, inconsequential by comparison. The divine light of *olam haba* will be so overwhelming that the light of this world, for which we now have such regard, will seem like nothing at all. The metaphor of heavy and light runs throughout this passage in a striking way.

### Negaim Oholos

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different reading. The *yikaros* — the weighty and precious things of this world — are the tractates of *Negaim* and *Oholos*, universally regarded as the most challenging portions of the entire *Shas*. When Rabbi Akiva was once drawn toward *aggadata*, the retort directed at him was: *Akiva, mah lecha etzel agadata? Kelach lecha etzel Negaim v'Oholos* — go occupy yourself with *Negaim* and *Oholos*, implying they were his true domain. These tractates are *yikaros* — enormously weighty — in this world. But in the world to come they will be *kappuyin* — lightweight, accessible to all. The level of Torah knowledge in the world to come will be so exalted that even schoolchildren will know *Negaim* and *Oholos*.

### Weighty People

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi applies the verse to people: the *yikaros* of this world — those given great honor and prestige — will be *kappuyin* in the world to come, reduced to nothing. This refers to the powerful and wealthy who are not righteous, who command great respect in this world but will have no standing in the next.

### Rav Yosef Vision

This teaching is illustrated by the famous story of Rav Yosef, the son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rav Yosef became gravely ill — *chalash* — and *isnagid*: he fainted or, in the more dramatic reading, his vital signs briefly ceased and he was brought back. When he revived, his father asked: *mai chazit?* — what did you see? The assumption was that the brief brush with death had afforded him a vision of the world to come, much as is reported by people today who describe such experiences.

### Olam Hafuch

Rav Yosef answered: *olam hafuch ra'iti* — I saw a topsy-turvy world. *Elyonim l'mata v'tachtonim l'ma'ala* — those who are at the top in this world are at the bottom in the next, and those who are at the bottom here are elevated there. The powerful, the prestigious, those who command status in this world — there they are at the bottom. The quiet *tzaddik*, perhaps one of the *lamed-vavniks*, who receives no recognition here — in the world to come, such a person is elevated.

### Father Response

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's response is striking: *olam barur ra'ita* — you saw the *clear* world, the world as it truly is. It is *this* world that is upside down. The world to come sets things right. He then asks the natural question: *heichi hasam?* — what is the status of Torah sages like us there? The answer: *ki heichi d'isinnan hacha hachi isinnan hatam* — the same way we are here, we are there. The Rabbis, who are given respect in this world, also have that respect in the world to come.

### Talmudo B'Yado

Rav Yosef further reports: *v'shamati shehayu omrim, ashrei mi sheba l'khan v'talmudo b'yado* — blessed is the one who arrives there with his learning in hand. Entering *olam haba* with a rich store of Torah knowledge is a most distinguished entrance. This is notable because the earlier focus was on the *tachtonim* — the *tzaddikim* and *chasidim* outside the rabbinic class who are elevated in the next world — yet the narrative consistently returns to Torah scholarship as a distinct and prized form of merit, reflecting an ongoing counterpoint: while recognizing the tremendous value of personal righteousness and piety, the *Gemara* is careful not to minimize the extraordinary standing of *talmidei chachamim*.

### Harugei Malchut

A second report: *harugei malchut* — those martyred by the Roman government, killed for their faith — occupy the highest *madrega* of all. *Ein adam yachol la'amod bimechitzatam* — no one else can stand in their section.

### Harugei Lod

The *Gemara* immediately asks: who are these *harugei malchut*? If one says it means Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues, the great sages persecuted in the Hadrianic persecutions — would Rabbi Akiva require martyrdom to achieve this standing? His stature as a Torah sage would alone place him at the summit of *olam haba*. The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ella harugei Lod* — it refers to those killed in Lod. The Talmud elsewhere records that when the Roman government sought to hold the entire city of Lod accountable for a killing, two individuals came forward and accepted blame upon themselves to save the entire city. Such selfless martyrdom — sacrificing oneself to redeem an entire community — places those individuals at a level where no one else can stand alongside them.

This raises a broader question that the discussion implicitly gestures toward: why does the *Gemara* limit *harugei malchut* at this highest level to so specific a group rather than extending the category to all who died rather than renounce their faith? The very phrase *ein adam yachol la'amod bimechitzatam* implies a select, almost singular subset. And there is something telling in how the *Gemara* consistently situates the rabbinic voice as observing all of this from a slight distance — noting who achieves the highest standing, reaffirming its own stable position, but treating these extremes of selfless martyrdom and unknown piety as objects of admiration from the outside.

### Metzilot Hasus

The *Gemara* proceeds to the verse later in Zechariah 14: *bayom hahu yihiyeh al metzilot hasus kodesh l'Hashem* — on that day the words *kodesh l'Hashem* will be inscribed on the *metzilot hasus*, the ornaments or bells of horses. What is the meaning of *metzilot hasus*?

### Jerusalem Expansion

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — and this, says Rashi, is the thematic connection to the preceding *aggadata* about Jerusalem — understands *metzilot* through the root *tzel*, shade. The verse describes Jerusalem's future expansion: the city will grow until it reaches as far as a horse can run while still casting its shade, meaning for half a day, approximately six hours. The city will be so vast as to span the distance a horse travels in half a day, which by rough reckoning could be thirty miles or more. Jerusalem today, while considerably larger than in the time of the *Gemara*, does not yet approach such dimensions, though the *Gemara*'s contemporaries would have found even present-day Jerusalem fantastically large.

### Horse Ornaments

Rabbi Eliezer reads *metzilot* as the ornamental decorations — beads and adornments — hung between horses' eyes. *Kol metzilot shetola'im lasus bein einav yihiyeh kodesh l'Hashem* — all such ornaments will be consecrated to God. Everyone will donate their horses' decorations to the Temple.

### War Booty

Rabbi Yochanan reads the verse as referring to the booty of war: *kol biza shebozin Yisrael ad shehasus ratz umatzil* — all the booty that Israel captures in the time it takes a horse to run and cast its shade, half a day, presumably during the war of *Gog u'Magog*, will be consecrated to God.

### Verses Resolved

The *Gemara* then examines how the interpretations connect to the continuation of the verse: *v'haya hasirot b'veit Hashem k'mizrakim lifnei hamizbeach* — even the pots in the House of God will be like the sacred vessels used for casting blood by the altar, meaning everything will be made of purest gold. This continuation fits naturally with Rabbi Yochanan's reading: if all war booty is consecrated, there will be immense wealth, and even ordinary vessels will be fashioned from gold. But for the other two interpretations — whether about the expansion of Jerusalem's boundaries or the donation of horse ornaments, neither of which implies enormous wealth — how does the next verse follow? The *Gemara* answers: *milta achrita ka'amar* — it is simply an additional, separate point. Another element of the messianic era is that Israel will be very wealthy, will donate generously, and even the pots in the Temple will be of gold.

Similarly, the verse concludes *v'lo yihiye Kna'ani od b'veit Hashem Tzeva'ot* — there will no longer be a *Kna'ani* in the House of God. According to Rabbi Yochanan's reading about booty, *Kna'ani* is understood as a trader, meaning there will no longer be any commercial activity in the precincts of the Temple. In the Temple era, there was significant transactional activity around the Beit HaMikdash — people purchasing animals for *korbanot*, money-changers, merchants — which was always viewed with a certain unease, famously evoked by Jesus's expulsion of the money-changers. In the messianic era, with such abundance, none of that will be necessary.

### Kena'ani Trader

The *Gemara* establishes this reading of *Kna'ani* as trader from elsewhere: the verse in Bereishit states *vayar sham Yehuda bat ish Kna'ani u-shmo Shua* — Yehuda saw there the daughter of a *Kna'ani* man. The *Gemara* asks: could this literally mean a Canaanite woman? *Efshar?* Abraham had charged his servant not to take a wife for Yitzchak from the inhabitants of Canaan; Yitzchak charged Yaakov *al tikach isha mibnot Kna'an* — do not marry a Canaanite woman. Would Yehuda then go and marry one? *V'Yehuda azil v'nasiv?* Rather, says Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, *bat gavra tagra* — the daughter of a *trader*. Support for this reading comes from Hoshea: *Kna'an beyado mozney mirma* — in his hand are deceitful scales — which explicitly associates the *Kna'ani* with commerce.

### No Kena'ani

For the other two interpretations of *metzilot hasus*, the *Gemara* reads *v'lo yihiye Kna'ani* differently. Rabbi Yirmiyah says: *ein kan ani* — there will be no poor person there. Either way, the verse speaks of a future era of prosperity in which neither commerce nor poverty will mar the sacred space. The word *Kna'ani* thus supports two distinct readings: a trader, or a person in material need, and both are taken to describe a reality that will be absent in the messianic era.

### God's Name Echad

The *Gemara* turns to the theological climax of the passage: *vehaya Hashem l'melech al kol ha'aretz; bayom hahu yiheyeh Hashem Echad u'shmo Echad* — on that day God will be One and His name will be One. The *Gemara* immediately asks: is God not One now? God's unity is eternal. One straightforward reading would be that all peoples will come to recognize God as One — but the *Gemara* presses further, looking specifically at the Jewish experience of God.

Rabbi Acha bar Chanina explains: it is not that God will become One — He is always One — but rather that our *experience* of God will become unified. In this world, when good things happen one recites *Baruch Hatov ve'hametiv*; when bad things happen one recites *Baruch Dayan ha'emet*. These are two different *brachot*, reflecting two very different modes of encountering God: God as the source of good, and God as the true Judge whose decrees, though just, are experienced as painful. In the world to come, *kulo Hatov ve'hametiv* — there will only be *Baruch Hatov ve'hametiv*. No one will ever need to say *Baruch Dayan ha'emet*. God will be *Echad* in the sense that our experience of God will be undivided — only goodness, only blessing, no longer the duality of joy and grief that characterizes life in this world.

### Experience God

This raises a further difficulty: if the point is about our *experience* of God rather than some objective theological change, why not simply say that all peoples will recognize God as One? The *Gemara* seems to be addressing something more internal, more specifically Jewish — a change in how the Jewish people encounters the divine. Even granting this, the question of why the verse needed to say *Echad* to express this experiential unity is not fully resolved.

### Name Pronunciation

The *Gemara* then turns to the second half: *u'shmo Echad* — His name will be One. Is God's name not one now? Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: in this world, God's name is written one way — *yud-heh* (the Tetragrammaton) — but read another way — *alef-dalet* (*Adonai*). The written form and the pronounced form are different, introducing a kind of disunity into even how we refer to God. In the world to come, *nichtav be'yud-heh ve'nikra be'yud-heh* — God's name will be both written and read the same way. The barrier between the true name and the spoken name will dissolve, reflecting a closeness and directness of relationship with the divine that is not available in this world.

There is further support for this hiddenness being intentional in our current state: the verse *zeh shemi le'olam* ("this is My name forever") is written *le'alem* — without a *vav* — which can be read as *le'alem*, meaning "to conceal." The name is to be hidden. *Veze zichri ledor dor* — the way I am *remembered* and evoked across generations is not through my true name, but through the substitute name *alef-dalet*. The two halves of the verse thus complement each other: the true name (*yud-heh*) is *ze shemi*, hidden *le'alem*; the way of evoking God in this world is *ze zichri*, the pronounced name *alef-dalet*. The imperfection of this world is manifest even in how we name God — we experience divinity through a filter, unable in this state to encounter it directly.

### Rava Pronunciation

Rava once thought to teach the proper pronunciation of the divine name publicly, at his regular lecture.

### Name Hidden

An old man in the audience immediately cautioned him: *le'alem ktiv* — it is written to be concealed. The very spelling of the verse instructs that the name must remain hidden. This is not merely a practice but something close to a divine directive embedded in the text itself, and even in discussing it publicly one must observe a limit. With that, the *Gemara* concludes with *Hadran alach Eilu Overin*, marking the end of the third *perek*.

---

## Perek III-IV Transition

### Masechta Structure

With the conclusion of *Hadran alach Eilu Overin*, the third *perek* closes. As noted, the first three *prakim* of Masechet Pesachim form a coherent unit entirely devoted to the laws of *chametz* — how to find it, ensure that dough does not become *chametz*, how to dispose of it, and all related concerns. The final *perek* of the *masechta* addresses the *leil seder*, and the middle section is devoted to *korbanot*. The fourth *perek*, which we now begin, is something of a standalone unit: it opens with certain practices of *Erev Pesach* that are not *chametz*-related, and then develops into an extensive treatment of *minhagim* and the binding nature of local custom — a topic that becomes genuinely fascinating. The conclusion of the first three *prakim* with an extended *aggadic* passage is, in this light, particularly fitting.

---

## Work Erev Pesach

### Mishna Work

The fourth *perek* opens: *makom shenahagu la'asot melacha b'arvei pesachim ad chatzot osim* — in a place where the custom is to perform *melacha* on the eve of *Pesach* until midday, one may do so. Implicit in the Mishna is that from midday onward, no one does *melacha* on *Erev Pesach* — the *korban pesach* is slaughtered in the afternoon, and everyone must be ready. The question the Mishna addresses is whether *melacha* is permitted in the *morning* hours. The answer varies by community. *Makom shenahagu shelo la'asot ein osim* — where the custom is not to work, one does not work.

This is significant on two levels. First, it powerfully recognizes the binding nature of *minhag*, which raises a serious question — since when does *minhag* carry the force of an obligation? Second, it implicitly embraces the principle of *eilu va'eilu* — the possibility of legitimately different practices coexisting in different communities without one being simply right and the other wrong.

### Rashi Explanation

Rashi explains the rationale for the stricter custom: *kedei shelo yehei tarud bemelacha veyishkach* — so that one not become absorbed in work and forget the things that must be done. What must be done on *Erev Pesach*? *Biyur chametz*, the final disposal of *chametz*; *shechitat hapesach*, the slaughtering of the *korban pesach* after midday; and *tikkun matzah*, the preparation of *matzot* for the *leil seder*. And underlying all of this is a further principle: *demitzvah litro'ach mibe'od yom kedei lehaseiv maher* — it is a *mitzvah* to complete one's preparations before nightfall so as to begin the *Seder* as early as possible. This desire to start early, driven partly by the famous practice of *chalukat matzah be'leil pesachim bishvil tinokot shelo yishanu* — distributing *matzah* at the Seder to keep the children awake — is evidently ancient. The concern about children falling asleep before the Seder was just as real then as now.

### Travel Stringency

The Mishna then addresses the case of one who travels between communities with differing practices: *hahoilech mimakom she'osim lemakom she'ein osim o mimakom she'ein osim lemakom she'osim* — whether going from a place that permits work to one that does not, or vice versa. The ruling is *notnin alav chumrei makom sheyatza misham v'chumrei makom shehalach lesham* — one adopts the stringencies of both the place one left and the place one is going. One receives the worst of both worlds. This principle recurs prominently in the context of the second day of *Yom Tov* for travelers and will be well familiar from that discussion.

### Avoid Machlokes

The Mishna adds: *v'al yishaneh adam mipnei hamachloket* — a person should not change his practice in a way that will cause controversy. The Mishna thus holds two apparently competing values in tension: on the one hand, it embraces legitimate diversity between communities; on the other hand, it insists that within a given community, one should conform to local practice to avoid *machloket* and preserve *shalom*.

The natural question is whether these values can always be harmonized. When someone arrives from a community that does not permit work and enters one that permits it, is that person *violating* the local convention by refraining from work? Not necessarily — the permissive practice *allows* work; it does not *require* it. Refraining from work does not openly contradict local practice, and therefore there is no *machloket*. This distinguishes *Erev Pesach* from cases like wearing *tefillin* on *Chol HaMoed*, where different practices are visibly incompatible: one either wears *tefillin* or does not, and the difference is immediately apparent to everyone around. In a more heterogeneous community — which, it is worth noting, was not the reality in the time of *Chazal* — the very norm of uniformity may be inherently inapplicable.

### Shevi'it Produce

The Mishna presents a parallel case involving *shevi'it* produce: *hamolich peirot shevi'it mimakom shekalu lemakom shelo kalu* — one who transports *shemita* produce from a place where it is no longer available in the fields to a place where it still is, or vice versa. The law of *biur* — the requirement to destroy *shevi'it* produce once it is no longer accessible to animals in the wild — depends on local availability. When produce is still available to animals outdoors, one need not destroy what one has indoors; when it is no longer so available, one must destroy it. In both directions of travel, the traveler must apply the more stringent standard: *chayav leva'er* — he is obligated to destroy the produce.

### Rabbi Yehuda Shevi'it

Rabbi Yehuda offers his own position, saying *tzei vehavei lecha af ata* — "go out and bring even for yourself," a somewhat enigmatic phrase. The *Gemara* will need to clarify what Rabbi Yehuda means by this.

---

## Mai Irya Erev Pesach

### Why Pesach

The *Gemara* opens with a question: *mai irya arvei pesachim?* — why specify *Erev Pesach* in particular? The prohibition on doing *melacha* in the latter part of the day is not unique to *Erev Pesach*; it applies to other *erev* occasions as well. The question seems to press on the idea that since there is evidently a broader principle at work, what *chiddush* is the Mishna introducing by specifying *Erev Pesach*?

### Braisa Mincha

A *braisa* establishes the general principle: *ha'oseh melacha b'arvei shabbatot v'yamim tovim min hamincha ulemala* — one who performs *melacha* on *Erev Shabbat* or *Erev Yom Tov* from *Mincha* onwards — Rashi clarifies this means *Mincha Ketana*, i.e., from approximately 3:30 in the afternoon — *eino ro'eh siman beracha* — will never see a sign of blessing in that work.

### Threshold Difference

The *Gemara* now delineates why *Erev Pesach* is genuinely distinct. There are two differences. First, the *Erev Shabbat* prohibition begins only at *Mincha Ketana* — 3:30 in the afternoon — while the *Erev Pesach* prohibition begins at midday (*chatzot*), a substantially earlier point in the day. Second, the consequence differs: on *Erev Shabbat*, working after *Mincha* means one *eino ro'eh siman beracha* — one will see no blessing in the work, but it is not technically prohibited. On *Erev Pesach*, the situation is categorically different.

This *siman beracha* teaching deserves more attention than it typically receives. How many people are aware that performing *melacha* after 3:30 on *Erev Shabbat* will deprive them of blessing in that work? Rav Soloveitchik once observed that while America had produced genuinely *shomer Shabbat* Jews, it had not produced *shomer Erev Shabbat* Jews — people who devoted *Erev Shabbat* itself to the preparations and spirit of *Shabbat*, an idea deeply connected to the insight that the experience of any sacred time is inseparable from how one prepares for it. Practically, of course, not everyone has the latitude to leave work at 3:30 on a Friday afternoon, but the principle remains largely unacknowledged.

### Noon Cherem

On *Erev Pesach* the stakes are higher. *Hacha shamutei nami meshamtinan lei* — here, one who does *melacha* after midday would actually be subject to *cherem*, to excommunication. This is not merely a loss of blessing; it is an actual violation. The *Gemara* thus establishes that *Erev Pesach* is a genuine *chiddush* compared to the general *erev* prohibition, differing both in when the restriction begins and in the severity of the consequence for violating it. Given this, the question of how seriously the *issur melacha* of *Erev Pesach* afternoon is observed in practice is, to say the least, pointed.

---

## Zariz Shafel Rewards

### Four Types

A *braisa* is cited presenting a taxonomy of four character types defined by the combination of diligence or laziness with their resulting gain or loss: the *zariz veniskar* (diligent and rewarded), the *zariz venifsad* (diligent and harmed), the *shafel veniskar* (lazy and rewarded), and the *shafel venifsad* (lazy and harmed). All four cases are framed around the practice of *Erev Shabbat*.

### Zariz Niskar

The *zariz veniskar* — the diligent person who gains — is one who works productively throughout the week but refrains from work on *Erev Shabbat*. Such a person is rewarded for their industry while properly honoring the approach of *Shabbat*.

### Zariz Nifsad

The *zariz venifsad* — the diligent person who loses — is one who works hard throughout the entire week including *Erev Shabbat*. In the end, that overreach will come back to harm them; the failure to stop before *Shabbat* undoes the blessing of the week's labor.

### Shafel Niskar

The *shafel veniskar* — the lazy person who gains — is one who does no work at all during the week, nor on *Erev Shabbat*. Through sheer idleness, they accidentally achieve the proper observance of *Erev Shabbat*. Like the proverbial stopped clock that is right twice a day: by not working at all, they succeed in not working on *Erev Shabbat*.

### Shafel Nifsad

The *shafel venifsad* — the lazy person who loses — is one who does nothing the entire week, but then specifically chooses to work on *Erev Shabbat*. This is the worst outcome: all the idleness of the week brings no benefit, and the one time action is taken, it is taken at the wrong moment.

### Mechuza Women

Rava applies this framework with characteristic sharpness to the women of Mechuza. Even though they do not work on *Erev Shabbat* — not out of any religious motivation, but purely out of their pampered, indulgent lifestyle, since they do not work any day of the week either — *afillu hachi shafel veniskar karinan lehu*: even so, they are classified as *shafel veniskar*. They receive the reward of not working on *Erev Shabbat*, regardless of the reason. Rava's critique of the overly cosmopolitan ways of Mechuza is subtly embedded even in the compliment.

### Kindness Height

Rava then notes a contradiction between two verses. One verse states *ki gadol ad shamayim chasdecha* — God's kindness reaches up to the heavens. Another states *ki gadol me'al shamayim chasdecha* — God's kindness reaches *above* the heavens. Which is it?

### Lishma Intent

The resolution: *kan be'osim lishma vekan be'osim shelo lishma* — one verse describes those who perform *mitzvot lishma*, for the right reason, and the other describes those who perform them *shelo lishma*, for the wrong reason. When one acts *lishma*, God's kindness extends above the heavens; when one acts *shelo lishma*, it extends only to the heavens — still a vast and remarkable reward, but less than the highest. This connects back to Rav Yehuda's famous teaching in the name of Rav: *le'olam ya'asok adam be-Torah u-mitzvot af al pi shelo lishma, she-mitoch shelo lishma ba lishma* — one should always engage in Torah and *mitzvot* even if not for the right reason, because from acting *shelo lishma* one will eventually come to *lishma*. Even doing the right thing for the wrong reason carries great reward — and may ultimately lead to doing it for the right reason.

---

## Work Blessing Teachings

### Wife Millstone

A *braisa*: *ha-metzapeh li-sechar ishto ve-reichayim eino roeh siman beracha le-olam* — one who hopes to profit from the earnings of his wife or from a millstone will never see a sign of blessing. Rashi explains that the wife's earnings refer to her use of *matkolta* — a type of measuring scale — which she rents out, apparently a low-yield enterprise. Tosafos suggests it refers to a woman doing knitting or weaving in public, which poses other concerns.

### Work vs. Rent

With respect to the millstone: *agarta* — if one is simply renting it out, that apparently yields no blessing. But *aval avda u-mezavna* — if one actually produces and then sells, that is another matter entirely: *ishtabuchi mishtabach ba kera* — Scripture itself praises this. The connection is to *Eshet Chayil*.

### Eshet Chayil

The verse cited is *sadin asta va-timkor... de-chagor natna la-Kena'ani* — she made linen garments and sold them, she gave a girdle to the trader. The *Eshet Chayil* passage in Mishlei, as noted here and as we will encounter again shortly, uses *Kna'ani* in the sense of a merchant or trader, consistent with what the *Gemara* established earlier. The point of the contrast is the difference between active production and selling (which is blessed) versus passive rental of tools or equipment (which is not).

### Large Volume

Another *braisa*: *ha-mistacher be-kanim u-ve-kankanim eino roeh siman beracha le-olam* — one who deals in rods or large vessels will never see a sign of blessing. The reason: *keivan de-nafish ap-chazeihu* — because their bulk is very large, *shalta beihu eina* — the *ayin hara* takes hold. The sheer visibility of large quantities of merchandise attracts the evil eye. The recommendation is therefore not to be in a business of highly visible, voluminous goods.

### Market Vendors

*Tagrei simta* — market stall vendors; *megadlei beheima daka* — those who raise small animals, i.e., sheep, known for grazing in fields not their own, which constantly drew complaint; *kotzei ilanos tovos* — those who cut down beautiful trees for timber, an act that drew the ire of onlookers; *ve-nosnin eineihem be-chelek yafe* — and those who always grab the nicer portion — all of these will never see a sign of blessing.

### Nicer Portion

The common thread is public grievance: *de-tohu inshi* — people are astounded and upset. The market vendors are constantly exposed to the public; the shepherds were notorious for their animals grazing where they should not; those who destroy beautiful trees provoke the outcry of passersby; those who always claim the best portion for themselves generate resentment. All such activities draw negative attention and, with it, the absence of divine blessing.

### Four Prutos

Another *braisa*: *arba prutos ein bahem siman beracha le-olam* — four types of payment, associated with small earnings, will never yield a sign of blessing: *schar kosvin*, the fees paid to scribes; *schar meturgamin*, the pay of translators or the *meturgeman* who repeated the *rav*'s words loudly for the audience; *schar yesomim*, fees earned from managing orphans' estates; and *ma'ot ha-ba'ot mi-medinat ha-yam*, returns on overseas investments.
