### Scribes Translators

The case of the translators is understandable: *mishum demechzei k'sechar Shabbat* — it looks like payment for work performed on *Shabbat*, which is inherently problematic even when technically permitted. The case of orphans' money: *lav bnei mechila ninhu* — minors cannot grant forgiveness; if one misuses their funds, even unwittingly, there is no pardon available, as there would be with an adult who might be *mochel*. Overseas investments: *mishum delo kol yoma misrachesh nisa* — one cannot rely on a miracle every day; ships sank regularly in those waters, and building an enterprise on such unpredictable risk will not yield lasting blessing.

### Why Scribes Specifically

The case of scribes requires more explanation: why should writing *Sifrei Torah*, *tefillin*, and *mezuzot* not be a well-rewarded enterprise? The answer comes from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *chaf daled taaniyot yashvu Anshei Knesses Ha-Gedolah al kosvei Sfarim Tfillin u-Mezuzos* — the Men of the Great Assembly sat in twenty-four fasts, directed at God, for the scribes who write sacred texts.

### Scribes Profitability

What were they praying for? *Shelo yisasheru* — that the scribes should never become wealthy. And why? *Sheilmalei misaashrin ein kosvin* — because if writing these texts were too profitable an enterprise, the scribes would stop writing. If the work became so lucrative that it attracted people who would then move on to more profitable ventures, or if the cost became prohibitive, the supply of *Sifrei Torah*, *tefillin*, and *mezuzot* would dry up. It was therefore a kind of divine decree, emerging from the prayers of the greatest sages, that this work remain modestly compensated — affordable and constantly available.

### Sacred Text Sellers

The *braisa* extends the category: *kosvei Sfarim Tfillin u-Mezuzos, hein ve-tagreihen ve-tagrei tagreihen* — the scribes themselves, their wholesalers, and their retailers. And *kol ha-oskim bimelechet Shamayim* — all who occupy themselves in this heavenly work, with *laasuyei mochrei Techeiles* — including those who sell *techeiles*, the sacred blue dye used for *tzitzit*. All of these, like the scribes, will never see a sign of blessing — not because they are doing something wrong, but because the enterprise is, by divine design, kept from becoming too profitable.

### Lishma Exception

The *braisa* concludes with a redemptive qualification: *ve-im oskin lishma, ro'im* — if they engage in this work *leshem Shamayim*, for the sake of Heaven rather than for profit, then they *will* see a sign of blessing. The reason there is no *siman beracha* for those who do it for the money is precisely so they will not stop producing these sacred objects. But one who does it *lishma* — whose motivation is not financial gain but genuine devotion to making Torah, *tefillin*, *mezuzot*, and *techeiles* available — such a person will, even if they become successful, continue to do it. For them, prosperity need not undermine the work, and so for them the divine concern that inspired the twenty-four fasts does not apply. With this observation — that *lishma* transforms not only the spiritual value of an act but even its material outcomes — the fourth *perek* begins.

---

---

# Pesachim 52

## Minhagim Review

### Binding Nature of Minhag…

Today's *daf* is 52. We pick up in the middle of 51b to review some of the highlights from the previous session, which raised a number of important issues regarding *minhagim*, even if it lacked a certain systematic quality. One foundational question that arose was the very nature of what makes *minhagim* binding upon later generations. The *pasuk* of *shma bni musar avicha* was cited as a way of giving expression to the idea that being bound by tradition is a fundamental, core operating principle of a religious traditional society — indeed more than a core value. That at least begins to open the question of the source and nature of that binding force.

### Minhag Avot vs. Hamakom

An important distinction that emerged was between *minhag avot* — custom inherited through one's forebears — and *minhag hamakom*, the custom of a particular place. The dominant concept throughout this section of Gemara is *minhag hamakom*: *makom shenhagim*, *makom she-eino nohagim*, and so forth. Yet the earlier story introduced the question of what your fathers accepted upon themselves. Nowadays the common claim that "we follow *minhag* Ashkenaz" or "we are *Sefardim* who have *minhag* Sfarad" represents an interesting hybrid of both categories: we do not actually live in Ashkenaz or Sfarad, and yet we view ourselves as people of that place in a virtual, extended sense, even though we are not literally of that place.

### Personal Minhag vs. Local

This distinction becomes especially pressing when *mekomot* ceased to be uniform and became instead a mixture of different practices — as happened in Amsterdam after the *Gerush Sfarad*, when many different types of communities converged, producing the more cosmopolitan realities we recognize today. A further issue arising from the previous session was the question of keeping one's own *minhagim* even when they conflict with the current reigning practice. This sits in sharp tension with the *Mishnah*'s principle of *chumrei makom shehalach l'sham*, yet the *Gemara* seemed to allow that under certain circumstances — particularly where there was no concern of a slippery slope — a visitor might at least observe his own *minhag*, and perhaps even actively maintain it.

### Eretz Yisrael Authority

By the end of the previous *daf*, the *Gemara* suggested that special circumstances may govern the case of a visitor from *Eretz Yisrael* to *Bavel*: because of the inherent authority of *Eretz Yisrael*, such a visitor retains the right to keep his own *minhag* without surrendering it to the norms of *Bavel*. We will touch on this momentarily. Other issues discussed included the role of *da'ato lachazor* — one's intention to return — as an independent factor, and how much weight it carries.

### Conceptual Distinctions

Among the *Rishonim* there are important conceptual distinctions worth recalling. First, there is the difference between *minhag* — a custom consciously adopted as such, with awareness that the law does not strictly demand it — and *nihug*, a practice that people follow without necessarily understanding it as a matter of choice. People often confuse these categories: when someone says "it is my *minhag* to use *chalav Yisrael*," they may actually mean that *chalav Yisrael* is the *psak* they follow, not a mere custom they have adopted beyond the strict requirement. These distinctions matter. If someone follows a practice because they believe it to be the *halakhah* when in fact it is not, that is a practice *b'ta'ut*, and one might be more licensed to actively negate and overturn it. There is also the concept of *minhag shtut* — though not explicitly articulated as a term in the *Gemara* itself — referring to a custom that is not merely discretionary but is arguably nonsensical, and which might even generate other *halakhic* problems, such as an improper *d'oraisa*-level concern. Who gets to determine that something qualifies as a *ta'ut* or a *shtut* is, of course, its own fascinating question.

### Psak & Tradition

The final point from the previous session touched less on *minhag* and more on *psak*: the idea that when someone follows a more innovative *psak*, there may be reason to rest on that authority only if one heard it directly from the authority in question. If it was not received through direct transmission, it may be harder to regard oneself as genuinely part of that chain of tradition. This represents a conception of tradition applied to the world of *psak* that is quite different from how we normally operate, since ordinarily we rely on a *posek*'s written ruling even generations later.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Mishnah Case

We now continue in the *Mishnah* with the principle that when a person travels from one place to another, he carries the *chumros* of where he came from — and yet, out of respect for the local practice, he should not deviate from local norms *mipnei hamachlokes*. The *Gemara* identifies a tension between these two principles by examining the following case: *holech mimakom she'osim l'makom she'ein osim* — if you go from a place where they perform *melacha* on *Erev Pesach* to a place where they do not, *nosnim alav chumrei makom shehalach l'sham*, you adopt the practices of the place you are now visiting and therefore refrain from *melacha*. In this case, both principles align perfectly: you are keeping the *chumra* of your current location, and you are also avoiding conflict with local practice. No tension exists.

### Contradiction

The difficulty emerges in the reverse case: *mimakom she'ein osim l'makom she'osim* — you come from a place that does not do *melacha* and you travel to a place that does. If the principle of *mipnei hamachlokes* were applied strictly, you would do *melacha* along with the locals. But the *Gemara* has also told you that you are bound by the *chumros* of the place you came from — *nosnim alav chumrei makom sheyatza misham*. These two principles are directly contradictory: you cannot both keep the *chumros* of your hometown and avoid acting differently from your current location when those are in conflict.

### Abaye Position

*Amar Abaye ha'reisha*: Abaye resolves this by saying that the principle of keeping the peace applies only in the first case — where you have traveled to a more stringent place. When you respect the *chumros* of where you are visiting, that is indeed *mipnei hamachlokes*, and in that case the two principles coincide. But if your own hometown is the place with *chumros*, then those *chumros* take priority. According to Abaye, when there is a conflict between preserving your personal *chumros* and keeping the peace in your current location, your *chumros* win out. To use a vivid example: if you are *Sefardi* and you are visiting an *Ashkenazi* community during *Pesach*, you are not truly bound by their practice of not eating rice — but the reason you refrain is *mipnei hamachlokes*. That is respecting the *chumros* of the place you are visiting. However, if you are *Ashkenazi* visiting *Sefardim*, what matters more is preserving your own practice.

### Rava Position

*Rava amar l'olam haseifa*: Rava disagrees fundamentally. He says that even in the second case — where you have traveled from a stringent place to a lenient one — the principle of keeping the peace can still be operative and can still reign. The question is *why* we assumed that not doing *melacha* when others are doing it would be contentious in the first place.

### Rava's Logic

Rava's answer is striking: *ha'roeh omer melacha asura?* — are we worried that onlookers will conclude that you believe *melacha* is forbidden? No. *Eimar, kama batlanei havi bishuka* — there are plenty of lazy people in the marketplace. If you stay home on *Erev Pesach*, no one will conclude that you regard *melacha* as prohibited; they will simply assume you are taking the day off. Therefore, there is no real conflict of appearances and no cause for *machlokes*. The practical *halakhic* implication is important: if you go from a place that does not do *melacha* to a place that does, you should refrain from *melacha* — but you must be careful not to make it obvious that you are doing so on account of your *minhag*. If someone asks you to help with a task, you cannot say "that is not my *minhag*"; you need some other ordinary excuse. According to Rava, then, the principle of *mipnei hamachlokes* is actually the more important principle, one that can override *chumrei makom sheyatza misham* — with the recognition that it must be done in a way that does not visibly signal your departure from local practice.

### Halakha Application

Tosafot states Rava's position explicitly as the operative *halakhah*. And the *halakhah* follows that if you go from a place with certain *minhagim* to another place, the more important principle is keeping the peace. This is true even in cases that are not a matter of *chumra* versus *kula* — for instance, a question about *nusach hatefilla*: if a *Sefardi* serves as *shliach tzibbur* in an *Ashkenazi* shul, the reigning principle is to respect the practice of the place, not to insist on one's own *nusach*. The difficult question is what to do when one's own *minhag* is genuinely more *machmir* but performing it publicly would visibly conflict with local norms. According to Rava, when you cannot maintain your own *chumros* without it being obvious that you are doing so in defiance of local practice, you are actually supposed to give more weight to the *minhagim* of the place you are in.

This naturally raises the question of what happens with something like *kitniyot* on *Pesach* — an *Ashkenazi* visiting *Sefardim* for an entire *Pesach*. *Poskim* make distinctions here: *minhagim* that function as safeguards against genuine *issurim* are given significantly greater weight than those that are purely customary in nature. For most *Ashkenazim*, refraining from rice on *Pesach* does not feel like a mere *minhag* — it feels constitutive of *Pesach* itself, almost a violation of the holiday. The *poskim* try to draw the line by saying that practices rooted in *chashash issur* carry greater weight than *stam minhagim*, such as the difference between *kapparot* and the *kitniyot* prohibition. But it is genuinely difficult to quantify, and these distinctions operate more as guidelines than as hard-and-fast rules.

### Modern Communities

A further complication is how much the principle of *mipnei hamachlokes* applies in today's cosmopolitan communities. If one is visiting a *Sefardi* household in a multi-practice neighborhood, one cannot straightforwardly invoke *al yishaneh mipnei hamachlokes*, because the very nature of such a community is that it encompasses multiple practices. There is no single reigning norm against which deviation creates offense. The offense that *machlokes* is meant to prevent presupposes a relatively uniform community where divergent practice stands out — a reality that is increasingly rare. In certain places, however — particularly tightly knit communities where a single practice truly dominates — these considerations apply with full force. Even the question of awareness matters: in a community where everyone knows that *Ashkenazim* have their particular *minhagim*, no one will be offended by a visitor maintaining them; they may regard it as eccentric, but it will not generate real conflict.

### Consistency Tension

One might observe that there is a broader tension at work throughout all of these discussions — a tension between consistency and creativity. As one attempts to apply these principles across new situations, the principles themselves frequently pull in opposite directions. The *Rishonim* grapple with this, and subsequent *poskim* continue to do so. *Poskim* will attempt to categorize — if it is *mipnei issura*, if it involves *chashash issur*, it carries more weight and cannot be easily set aside. But even that categorization is contested in practice, and many of these cases end up governed by guidelines rather than rules. *Minhagim* are given different types of emotional and religious weight at the grassroots level, and that lived weight does not always track the formal *halakhic* categories neatly.

---

## Rav Safra Example

### Rav Safra's Question

*Amar lei Rav Safra le-Rabbi Abba: kegon ana, d-yidana b-kavia d-yarcha* — like me, who knows when *Rosh Chodesh* is fixed: why should I have to keep two days of *Yom Tov*? The question is posed against the backdrop of *Yom Tov sheni*, the second day of festivals observed in the diaspora. Rav Safra is raising the issue of someone who has direct knowledge of when *Rosh Chodesh* falls: what is the basis for requiring him to observe *Yom Tov sheni* when he knows the calendar precisely?

### Rabbi Ami Response

The answer reported is *b'yishuv assur, u-vamidbar mutar*: in a settled town, one may not perform *melacha* on *Yom Tov sheni*, but out in the wilderness one is permitted. The distinction thus turns not on abstract knowledge but on context — on whether one is situated within a community where the second day is the reigning practice.

### Tosafot Reread

Tosafot raises an important challenge: the *Gemara* elsewhere explicitly states that we all know when *Rosh Chodesh* is and we nonetheless keep two days. So what makes Rav Safra's knowledge exceptional? Tosafot therefore reinterprets the passage, acknowledging that this is a somewhat forced reading of the *Gemara*'s language, but arguing that Rav Safra was not merely someone who happened to know the calendar. Rather, he was actually from one of the places near *Eretz Yisrael* that had always been informed of *Rosh Chodesh* in time — and such places traditionally kept only one day. In effect, Tosafot reads Rav Safra as saying: I am from a one-day place.

### One vs. Two Days

This leads to the deeper question. The dividing line between one day and two days in the *Gemara* is not simply *Eretz Yisrael* versus *chutz la'aretz*. It is rather *Eretz Yisrael* and all places close enough to have been reached by the messengers announcing *Rosh Chodesh* within the relevant timeframe — roughly fourteen to fifteen days. Those places keep one day; those that could not have been reached in time keep two. On this reading, Rav Safra is saying he is from a one-day place, and he is now visiting a two-day location. What must he do? The *Gemara*'s answer is: *b'yishuv assur, bamidbar mutar* — in a settled Jewish community, he must observe two days; in the wilderness, he need not. The operative principle is *mipnei hamachlokes*: in a community where two days is the norm, he cannot publicly deviate from that practice.

This generates a rich practical debate among *poskim*: what about someone from *Eretz Yisrael* visiting a *Yom Tov* community in *chutz la'aretz*, who is indeed in a *yishuv* — can he at least perform *melacha be-tzina*, privately, where no one will see? Some *poskim* say yes, some say no. The key point is that the operative concern here is *mipnei hamachlokes*, not *maris ayin*. *Maris ayin* is the concern that an observer will conclude one is doing something *assur*; but no one will think the Israeli is doing something forbidden — they know he is Israeli. The offense, rather, is a matter of communal sensibility. Many Israelis in practice are indeed *makpid* to perform *melacha be-tzina* on *Yom Tov sheni*, while others simply do *melacha* openly. The strong reaction this often provokes — "you're not supposed to do that, you have to keep two days" — reflects how deeply *chutz la'aretz* Jewry has internalized *Yom Tov sheni*. It is worth recalling, moreover, what was established in the previous *daf*: a visitor from *Eretz Yisrael* to *Bavel* does not need to weigh the *mipnei hamachlokes* consideration as heavily, precisely because of the inherent authority of *Eretz Yisrael*. And in the case of *Yom Tov sheni* specifically, there is an additional dimension: everyone knows that one day is the original practice. An Israeli keeping one day is, in a certain sense, a reminder of the authentic standard.

### Flip Case Scenario

The flip case — an American visiting *Eretz Yisrael* for *Yom Tov* — raises the question of *chumrei makom sheyatza misham*. The older consensus was clearly that one keeps two days, with certain Zionist *poskim* arguing one should keep one day as an expression of hope that one would remain. More recently, however, the *pesak* has been shifting. Some say one keeps a "day and a half" — no *melacha*, but one *davens* *chol*. Increasingly, *poskim* are ruling that one keeps only one day. Whatever the driving factors — more frequent travel, greater numbers of visitors, or changed communal realities — the logic deserves examination. What happened to *chumrei makom sheyatza misham*?

---

## Chacham Tzvi

### Bal Tosif Concern

The Chacham Tzvi addressed precisely this question in a brief but beautiful *teshuvah*. He ruled that with respect to the *nusach* of *davening*, one certainly says *nusach chol* — not *shel Yom Tov*. To *daven shel Yom Tov* when it is genuinely a weekday in *Eretz Yisrael* is not a *chumra*; it is actually the wrong *davening*. Similarly, if the question involves *tefillin* on a day when one is obligated to wear them, failing to wear them is not a *chumra* — it is a failure to fulfill the obligation. These cases are straightforward. But what about refraining from *melacha*? The Chacham Tzvi argued that this too is not permitted as a *chumra*. His reasoning: when do you keep your *chumros* in a place you are visiting? Only when, if you were living there, those *chumros* would constitute an acceptable practice. An Israeli who refuses to perform *melacha* on what is, in *Eretz Yisrael*, an ordinary weekday — or on the day after *Yom Tov* — is not being *machmir*. He is committing *bal tosif*: adding to the *mitzvah* in a context where the rabbinically mandated second day does not apply. The obvious question this raises — why is keeping *Yom Tov sheni* in *chutz la'aretz* not itself *bal tosif*? — is that there, at minimum, the rabbis mandated it. But where no such mandate exists and one is choosing to treat an ordinary day as *Yom Tov*, the violation of *bal tosif* is real.

### Temple Period Logic

A clarifying reformulation of the Chacham Tzvi's position makes it even more compelling. The reason we keep two days in *chutz la'aretz* today is *minhag avoseinu b'yadeinu* — we follow our ancestors' practice. Had we been living in the time of the *Beis Hamikdash* in *chutz la'aretz*, we would have kept two days because we would not have known when *Rosh Chodesh* was declared. Now imagine that same scenario: you are a visitor from America to *Eretz Yisrael* during the time of the *Beis Hamikdash*. What would you have done? You would have kept one day — because in those circumstances, being in *Eretz Yisrael*, you would have known when *Rosh Chodesh* was. Therefore, the *minhag avoseinu* is not to observe two days everywhere regardless of circumstance; it is to do what your ancestors would have done in the period of the *Beis Hamikdash* given their actual situation. A visitor to *Eretz Yisrael* in that era would have kept one day, and that remains the proper practice.

### Modern Application

This argument is genuinely persuasive, and increasingly widely applied. Many people visiting *Eretz Yisrael* now receive *pesak* to keep one day. At the same time, there is an interesting parallel to the *kitniyot* question: many Americans who will readily keep one day *Yom Tov* when visiting Israel would nevertheless not dream of eating *kitniyot* there. This reflects the broader reality that not all *minhagim* are treated equally at an emotional and religious level. For many, the two days of *Yom Tov* carry a weight of *issur melacha* and *kedushah* that transcends the legal category of *minhag*, making it difficult to simply set aside — regardless of the *psak*. Whether *Yom Tov sheni* is best understood as a *takkanah* or as a *minhag* is itself a separate debate across different *gemarot*, and that characterization affects how one weighs all of these questions.

---

## Rav Natan Story

### Story Setup

*Rav Natan bar Asya azal m'bei Rav l'Pumbedita* — Rav Natan bar Asya traveled from the house of Rav to Pumbedita on *Yom Tov sheni shel Atzeret*, the second day of *Shavuot*. In doing so, he was in violation of *Yom Tov sheni* — at minimum there is a *techum* issue, and potentially direct violations of *Yom Tov* observance as well. *Shamsay Rav Yosef* — Rav Yosef placed him in *cherem*.

### Cherem Choice

Abaye challenged this: *velingdeh mar nigidei* — why *cherem*? You should have given him lashes. Rav Yosef responded: *d'tav lei avidti lei* — I did something better for him, meaning more stringent. Why? *D'vema'arava, minu a-nigidei d'bar bei rav, v'lo minu a-shamta* — in *Eretz Yisrael*, they take a formal vote before administering lashes to a member of the rabbinic class, but they do not take a vote before placing someone in *cherem*. The explanation, following Rashi, is that *cherem* is reserved for violations that are so pressing and severe that there is no time to deliberate; one acts immediately. The gravity of the offense is such that the response bypasses the ordinary deliberative process. Hence *cherem* is the more stringent punishment.

### Alternate Reading

*Ika d'amri* — there is an alternate version of the story in which Rav Yosef actually administered lashes, not *cherem*. In that version, Abaye asks the opposite question: *v'lishamteih mar* — why did you not put him in *cherem*? The response is: *d'Rav u'Shmuel d'amri t'vayu, meshomtinan a-shnei yamim tovim shel galuyos* — both Rav and Shmuel rule that one is placed in *cherem* for violating *Yom Tov sheni shel galuyot*.

### Rabbinic Leniency

Rav Yosef's answer: *hani mili inish d'alma* — that is the rule for an ordinary person. *Hacha tzurba miderabanan hu* — here he is a member of the rabbinic class. *D'tav lei avidti lei* — I did something better for him, meaning in this version, more lenient. And the same asymmetry applies: *d'vema'arava minu a-nagiduta d'bar bei rav v'lo minu a-shamta* — in *Eretz Yisrael*, they take a vote before lashing a *bar bei rav*, but not before placing him in *cherem*. Since lashes require a vote and *cherem* does not, lashes — counterintuitively — represent the lesser and more careful punishment, and Rav Yosef administered that out of leniency toward a fellow member of the rabbinic academy.

### Unequal Treatment

The larger lesson of this story deserves emphasis. We have been speaking throughout this *daf* about *Yom Tov sheni* as a *minhag* maintained *mipnei hamachlokes* — a custom upheld to preserve communal harmony. And yet here we see that violating *Yom Tov sheni* warrants either lashes or *cherem*, depending on the reading. This is a striking *Gemara*. Whatever the precise characterization of *Yom Tov sheni* — *minhag*, *takkanah*, or *d'rabanan* obligation — its violation is treated with a severity that is simply not comparable to violating most ordinary *minhagim*. If someone performs *melacha* on *Erev Pesach* in a place where that is the local *minhag* not to do so, one would not expect lashes or *cherem* as the consequence. This demonstrates concretely that not all *minhagim* are treated in the same way — a point that runs through the entire discussion but is rarely illustrated so vividly. Nor, it turns out, are all Jews treated the same: the rabbinic class receives somewhat different treatment, whether in the direction of greater stringency or greater leniency depending on which version of the story one reads.

---

## Shemita Produce

### Mishnah Setup

We now turn to a *Mishnah* that appears to digress thematically but introduces an entirely new application of the principles we have been discussing — this time in the domain of *Shemita*. The basic law of *bi'ur* is as follows: during the *Shemita* year, produce that one has gathered may be kept in the house as long as the same type of produce is still available in the field for wild animals to forage. Once that produce is no longer available in the field, one is obligated to remove it from the house and distribute it — to the poor, to animals, to anyone — rather than holding it privately. The *Mishnah* addresses the case of someone who carries *Shemita* produce from one region to another, where the availability status of that produce differs between the two regions.

### Tanna vs. Yehuda

The *Tanna Kamma* takes the position that whenever produce must be removed by the laws of either place — where one came from or where one is — one must perform *bi'ur*. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.

### Rabbi Yehuda Analogy

Rabbi Yehuda's argument, as explained by Rashi, is powerful and direct. He says: this is not a matter of *chumrei makom shehalach l'sham v'chumrei makom sheyatza misham*. If I am visiting a place where there are no longer apples available in the field, but I have brought my apples from a place where apples are still on the trees — Ohio, let us say — then my continuing to eat those apples is not a failure to respect the local *chumra*. I can say to the local residents: if you were to import Ohio apples, you would not have to perform *bi'ur* on them either, because the produce follows the rules of where it was picked. These are Ohio apples, and Ohio apples are still permitted. This is an argument about the status of the *food*, not about the *minhag* of the place. And that seems like a reasonable position.

### Gemara Objection

The *Gemara* is nonetheless troubled by Rabbi Yehuda's ruling. *Uleis lei leRebbi Yehuda haditnan* — does Rabbi Yehuda not hold by the principle that one follows the *chumros* of both the place one came from and the place one is traveling to? How can he simply say, "my apples are from Ohio," when the local practice requires *bi'ur*?

### Rav Sheshet Read

*Amar Rav Sheshet brei deRav Idi milsa achrita kaamar Rebbi Yehuda*: Rav Sheshet argues that Rabbi Yehuda is not addressing the simple case at all. He would fully agree that one must perform *bi'ur* when the produce's status requires it at either location. What Rabbi Yehuda is addressing is a more particular case — one in which the status changed in the interim — and the *Mishnah* must be read accordingly, with an implicit scenario that the straightforward text does not spell out.

---

## Produce Status

### Abaye Reading

Abaye offers a more straightforward reading of the *Mishnah*, without the forced insertion of an additional case. *Vehachi kaamar* — this is what the *Mishnah* means: the debate concerns a situation in which the produce was taken from a place where it was still available in the field, brought to a place where it is no longer available, and then brought back.

### Three-Stage Case

To make the case concrete: one takes apples from Ohio, where they are still on the trees. One brings those apples to New York, where apples are no longer on the trees. One then returns those same apples to Ohio, where apples are still on the trees.

### Tanna Allow

The *Tanna Kamma* rules: *eino chayav leva'er* — you need not perform *bi'ur* when you return to Ohio. When you took the apples from Ohio, eating them was permitted; now that you have returned to Ohio, it is again permitted. The intermediate sojourn in New York does not retroactively alter the status of these apples.

### Yehuda Status

Rabbi Yehuda says otherwise: *tze v'havi lach apatza meheicha d'aytinu* — go try to obtain apples from New York now. You cannot, because New York apples are subject to *bi'ur*. And these apples, having been in New York, became New York apples. Even now that they have been returned to Ohio, they retain their New York status and must be treated accordingly.

### Rav Ashi Challenge

*Matkif lah Rav Ashi*: Rav Ashi finds this entirely unconvincing. *Atu agaba d'chamra kaltinhu?* — did they get absorbed into the city while riding on the back of the donkey? Because the apples spent some time in New York, they magically transformed into New York apples? They are still Ohio apples, grown from Ohio trees, and when returned to Ohio they plainly follow Ohio law. *Ela amar Rav Ashi* — rather, Rav Ashi reframes the entire debate. The dispute between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda does not actually hinge on some theory of produce changing its geographic identity. Instead, *b'plugta d'hanei tanna'ei* — it follows the lines of a dispute among *Tanna'im* found in a separate *Mishnah*, to which we now turn.

---

## Rav Papa Connect

### Rabbi Eliezer

The *Mishnah* referenced by Rav Ashi concerns the following case: *hakoveish shlosha kvashin b'chavit achat* — one pickles three different types of vegetables together in a single barrel. Imagine a mixture of cauliflower, cucumbers, and tomatoes, all pickled together. During the *Shemita* year, one or two of those types may no longer be available in the field while the third is still available. What is the law? There is also a question of *ta'am* — the transfer of taste — since all three types are pickling together in the same barrel. *Rabbi Eliezer omer ochlin al harishon*: one may eat only as long as every single type in the barrel is still permitted to be eaten. The moment any one type can no longer be eaten — because it is no longer available in the field — the taste of that type has permeated the entire barrel, and one must perform *bi'ur* on the whole mixture. No type remains edible once any single type has become subject to *bi'ur*.

### Rabbi Yehoshua

*Rabbi Yehoshua omer af al ha'acharon*: one may keep eating from the barrel as long as even one of the types is still available. Tosafot notes that this is an approach we would never apply to ordinary *issurim*: if three things are pickling together and one of them is *chametz*, we would never say the other two remain permitted simply because they are still present. But *Shemita* produce is categorically different — it is not *assur* in the sense of forbidden food. If one performs *bi'ur* and distributes the produce publicly, others may eat it, and even the original owner may eat alongside them. The food is not intrinsically *assur*; the obligation is about possession and distribution, not about the inherent status of the produce. Therefore, as long as one does not yet need to distribute one of the types, one may treat the whole barrel as a single unit and continue eating.

### Rabban Gamliel

*Rabban Gamliel omer: kol shekala mino min hasadeh yeva'er mino min hachavit* — anything that is no longer available in the field must be removed from the barrel. However, once you remove, say, all the cucumbers because cucumbers are no longer in the field, you may continue eating the pickled tomatoes — even though they have absorbed the taste of the cucumbers — because the concern of taste transfer does not apply here. You must physically remove the vegetables that have become subject to *bi'ur*, but what remains in the barrel is not disqualified by the absorbed taste. *V'halakha k'divarav* — and we rule in accordance with Rabban Gamliel.

### Shemita Parallel

Rav Papa now applies this to the dispute of the *Mishnah* about Rabbi Yehuda and the *Tanna Kamma*. The operative question in both contexts is: what determines whether produce is still considered "available in the field"? Is it the status at the current location? At the original location? And what happens when those statuses diverge? The debate between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda about fruit brought between regions maps onto the debate between the *Tanna'im* about the barrel — both turn on the same underlying question of when field availability controls what you may eat.

### Pickling Mishnah

The *Mishnah* on pickling further illustrates the point: *ochlim betmarim ad she-yichleh ha-achron she-be-Tzoar* — one may eat dates until the very last date is no longer available anywhere on the palm trees in *Tzoar*, the city of dates. Even if dates are no longer accessible in one's immediate locale, as long as they remain available somewhere in the region, one continues to eat. This connects directly to the broader regional framework for *bi'ur*, which the *Gemara* now elaborates.

---

## Shemita Regions

### Three Regions

*Shalosh aratzot le-vi'ur: Yehuda ve-Ever HaYarden ve-haGalil* — there are three regions for the law of *bi'ur*: Judea, Transjordan, and the Galilee. The principle is *she-ochlim be-chol achat ve-achat ad she-yichleh ha-achron she-bah*: one may eat within any one of those regions as long as there is still produce anywhere within that same region. So long as there are dates somewhere in Judea, one may eat dates anywhere in Judea. So long as there are dates somewhere in the Galilee, one may eat dates anywhere in the Galilee. One does not go by the immediate locale but by the entire region — as illustrated by the earlier example of *Tzoar*, where availability in a distant corner of the region suffices.

### Scriptural Source

*Mena hani mili?* — where does this whole framework come from? *Amar Rav Chama bar Ukva amar Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina amar k'ra: ve-livhemtecha ve-lachaya asher be-artzecha* — the *pasuk* says that the *Shemita* produce is for "your animals and the wild animals in your land." The operative principle is: *kol zman she-chaya ochelet min ha-sadeh ha'achel li-vhema she-be-bayit* — as long as wild animals can eat the produce in the field, you may feed the domesticated animals in your home. *Kalyah la-chaya she-ba-sadeh, kalyah li-vhemtecha min ha-bayit* — once the produce is no longer available to the wild animals foraging in the field, you must remove it from your home as well. Your domesticated animal's access to the produce must remain on the same footing as the wild animal's.

### Animal Boundaries

The three-region framework — why Judea is one unit and the Galilee another, rather than treating the whole land as a single unit — is derived from a received tradition: *de-ein chaya she-bi-Yehuda gedela al peirot she-ba-Galil ve-da-ein chaya she-ba-Galil gedela al peirot she-bi-Yehuda* — animals in Judea do not range over to feed on the produce of the Galilee, and animals in the Galilee do not range over to feed on the produce of Judea. Animals observe, in effect, the political boundaries of the regions. Therefore, as long as there are dates somewhere in Judea, the animals of Judea can access them, and one may eat throughout Judea. But the availability of dates in the Galilee provides no benefit to Judea, because Judean animals do not cross into the Galilee. The regional unit is defined by where the relevant wild animals actually forage.

### Sub-divisions

What are the three sub-areas mentioned within each region? Rashi suggests they are mentioned but do not affect the *halakhah* in a meaningful practical sense — the controlling principle remains that the whole of Judea functions as one unit and the whole of the Galilee as another. Tosafot, however, says that the three sub-areas — mountains, valleys, and fields — do in fact matter additionally. The principle that one goes by the entire region applies only within the same terrain type: mountain to mountain, valley to valley, field to field. One cannot say that because there are dates available in the valley, one may continue eating while living on a hill. These sub-area distinctions are operative alongside the larger regional framework.

### Rabbi Shimon

*Peirot sheyatze'u me'eretz yisrael lechutz la'aretz mitbar'im bechol makom* — produce that leaves *Eretz Yisrael* for *chutz la'aretz* must be subjected to *bi'ur* wherever one is, even in *chutz la'aretz*. One distributes them in Cincinnati if that is where one finds oneself. *Sheyei bechol makom shehem sham* — the obligation follows the produce wherever it goes. *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar omer yachzeru limkomam*: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that one must bring the produce back to *Eretz Yisrael* and distribute it there. His reasoning: *mishum shene'emar be'artzecha* — the *pasuk* says *asher be'artzecha*, specifically within the land. Making the produce available to the animals of *Eretz Yisrael* in particular is the requirement, not simply relinquishing private possession abroad. The *Gemara* asks how this *pasuk* can carry two separate lessons — both the regional framework and the requirement to distribute in *Eretz Yisrael*. The answer is that the extra word *asher* in *asher be'artzecha* yields both principles.

---

## Rav Saphra Wine

### Saphra Situation

*Rav Saphra nafik me'eretz yisrael lechutz la'aretz* — Rav Saphra was departing from *Eretz Yisrael* to *chutz la'aretz*. *Hava ba'ahadei garba dechamra deshivita* — with him he had a flask of *Shemita* wine. He suddenly realized the halakhic question his departure created: does he have to return to *Eretz Yisrael* to distribute the wine there, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, or may he distribute it wherever he ends up in *chutz la'aretz*?

### Two Traditions

He turned to his two companions, Rav Huna brei deRav Ika and Rav Kahana, and asked them whether they had heard from Rabbi Abbahu the ruling: *halacha keRabbi Shimon ben Elazar o lo* — do we rule like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar or not? Rav Kahana reported: *hachi amar Rabbi Abbahu, halacha keRabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — we rule like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar; you must return to *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Rav Huna Precision

Rav Huna brei deRav Ika then said: *hachi amar Rabbi Abbahu, ein halacha keRabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — I have a different tradition: Rabbi Abbahu ruled that we do *not* follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. The difference between the two traditions hinges on the single word *ein* — a word that can easily be dropped or swallowed in transmission.

### Saphra's Choice

*Amar Rav Saphra: nakit klala deRav Huna beyadcha* — Rav Saphra declared that they should follow Rav Huna's tradition. Why? *Dedaik agmra shamata mipumei derabeih* — because Rav Huna is scrupulously precise in receiving and transmitting teachings directly from the mouth of his teacher. He is as precise as *Rachta* from Pumbedita, who transmitted from Rav Yehuda the tradition that *har habayit istav kaful hava* — the Temple Mount had a double *istav*, a portico within a portico — capturing that exact unusual phrasing *istav kaful* with evident precision. Just as *Rachta* heard and transmitted distinctive wording precisely, so too Rav Huna is the kind of transmitter who would not drop a word like *ein*.

### Rav Yosef Critique

When Rav Yosef heard this story, he applied to Rav Saphra the verse *ami be'etzo yishal umaklo yagid lo* — "my people ask their wooden stick, and their staff tells them" — a reference to the practice of seeking omens through divining rods. *Kol hameikel lo magid lo* — whoever will tell you the lenient ruling, that is who you ask. It is a sharp critique: Rav Saphra, confronted with two conflicting traditions from Rabbi Abbahu, conveniently found a principled-sounding reason — Rav Huna's precision — to follow the one that spared him the inconvenience of turning around and returning to *Eretz Yisrael*. Rav Yosef's pointed remark suggests that the chosen criterion for preferring one tradition over another was not truly principled but was driven by the desired outcome. It is a fitting note on which to end the *daf*: a reminder that even within the world of *psak* and transmission, the human tendency to seek the lenient ruling — *kol hameikel lo magid lo* — is never far from the surface.

---

---

# Pesachim 53

## Shemita & Biur

### Ownerlessness Principle

The daf begins in the middle of a discussion concerning several aspects of *shemita*, specifically the obligations that flow from the fundamental ownerlessness of *shemita* produce. During the *shemita* year, all food is treated as ownerless: it is a free-for-all, and both the poor and the wealthy alike are free to collect it from the fields. One may bring produce home, but keeping it stored for an extended period contradicts the essential ethos of *shemita*. Hoarding food in one's home — treating it as exclusively one's own — runs counter to the principle that this produce belongs to everyone.

### Biur Requirement

The Rabbis therefore understood that once a particular type of produce is no longer available out in the field, one may no longer keep it stored at home. The verse states *v'lachaya asher b'artzecha* — "for the wild animal that is in your land" — which is read as the governing principle: as long as there are, say, apples out in the field for any animal to take, one may maintain apples at home. But once nothing of that type remains available in the field, one must perform *biur* — removing the produce from one's possession. Rashi understands *biur* as putting the produce out for the animals, while Tosafot cites other sources indicating that *biur* means distributing the produce equally among the poor and among all comers. One may place one's stored produce outside, declare it available to all, allow everyone to take from it — and then take back a portion for oneself. What one cannot do is continue to hoard it alone.

### Geographic Regions

The Gemara had established by the end of the previous daf that *biur* operates according to three distinct geographic regions: Yehuda, Galil, and Ever HaYarden — Judea, the Galilee, and the Transjordan. So long as any produce of the relevant type remains available somewhere within one's region — even if not in one's immediate locale — one need not perform *biur*. Only when the produce has disappeared from the entire region does the obligation take effect.

### Transporting Produce

This question of regional availability had served as the backdrop for the prior discussion of a traveler leaving Israel with *shemita* produce. If one departs the Land with, for instance, apples, and the time of *biur* arrives while one is abroad, what does one do? A debate ensued: some hold that one distributes the produce wherever one happens to be, while others maintain that the verse *b'artzecha* — "in your land" — requires one to return to the Land of Israel and distribute the produce there. The Gemara had concluded with a memorable story: Rav Safra was leaving Israel when he realized he had a *miflakh* of wine with him. He asked the two students traveling with him how to rule. One cited a tradition requiring return to Israel; the other cited a tradition to the contrary. Rav Safra declared that he would follow the second, more lenient ruling — claiming it was because that student had the more reliable tradition. Rav Yosef then offered a pointed remark, quoting the verse *ami b'atzo yishal umaklo yagid lo* — "My people ask their stick, and their staff tells them" — a verse associated with necromancy and divination. The wordplay: *kol hamekel magid lo* — whoever gives him the lenient ruling, that is the one he wants to tell him the *halacha*.

---

## Rabbi Ilai & Fruit Status

### Unripe Dates Case

The Gemara now introduces a new episode. Rabbi Ilai cut down a palm branch during *shemita*, and that branch bore *kasnisa* — unripe dates that were not yet edible and were going to go to waste. The question immediately arises: *heichi avid hachi* — how could he do this? The Torah states that *shemita* produce is designated *l'ochla* — for eating — *v'lo l'hefseid* — and not for destruction. By cutting down the branch with unripe dates still on it, was he not wasting the produce?

One might suggest that the prohibition against waste applies only once the item *nachis l'peira* — has descended to the status of fruit, that is, once it is recognizable and developed as fruit. If the dates are still at such an early, unripe stage that they have not yet attained the legal status of fruit, then perhaps there is no issue with cutting down the branch even if those immature dates are discarded. This is a plausible reading — and, as will emerge, ultimately the correct one — but the Gemara does not accept it immediately, first exploring other angles.

Rashi makes explicit what might otherwise be left implicit: Rabbi Ilai cut the palm branch in order to use it for firewood, leaving behind the unripe dates. The question, therefore, is not one of *bal tashchit* with respect to the wood — using branches for firewood is a perfectly legitimate purpose — but rather what one does about the fruit on those branches.

### Protective Shell

The Gemara introduces the teaching of Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: these *matchli* — the shell-like protective coverings that grow around unripe dates — are subject to the laws of *orlah*. The reason: *hoil v'nasu shomer l'pira* — since they serve as a protective covering for the fruit, they are treated as an extension of the fruit itself and thus bear *orlah* status. The Gemara then observes that this protective function is operative specifically *bekufri* — when the dates are still in their unripe stage, for it is then that the shell exists; as the fruit ripens, the shell falls away. The implication is striking: if the *matchli* qualifies as a *shomer l'pira* and thereby falls under the laws of *orlah* — which apply only to fruit — then the unripe date itself must already be considered a fruit, even at this early stage. Since *orlah* only applies to fruit, and since the shell is treated as an extension of the fruit, the Gemara concludes that *v'ka kari lehu peiri* — he is treating even the unripe date as fruit. If this is true regarding *orlah*, one would presume it should apply equally to *shemita*.

### Fruit Definition

However, this position is attributed to a specific authority: *hi d'amar k'Rabbi Yosi* — this follows the view of Rabbi Yosi, who holds that *smadar* — the very earliest emergence of the grape, before it has developed into anything recognizable — is already forbidden as *orlah* because it is already considered fruit: *smadar assur mipnei shehu peiri*. But *u'pligi rabbanan alei d'Rabbi Yosi* — the Rabbis dispute Rabbi Yosi. According to the Rabbis, produce is not considered fruit for purposes of *orlah* or *shemita* until a later stage of development. This would then explain how Rabbi Ilai could cut down that branch — he follows the more lenient position that the unripe dates have not yet attained legal fruit status, and therefore there is no issue with allowing them to go to waste.

### Beit Shammai/Hillel

The Gemara then asks: do the Rabbis really dispute Rabbi Yosi across the board, including by trees other than grapevines? The answer is found in a Mishnah that addresses precisely the case at hand. *Me'eimatai ein kotzetzin es ha'ilanos bishvi'is* — from when is it prohibited during *shemita* to cut down branches because of the fruit on them? Beit Shammai say: *kol ha'ilanos misheyotziu* — for all trees, as soon as any fruit emerges at all. Beit Hillel say: the carob from the time *misheyishaleshalu* — they begin to form into a chain-like cluster; the grapevines from *misheyagri'u* — a somewhat later stage of development; olives from the time they flower; and all other trees from when the fruit emerges. Thus Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree only with respect to carob, grapevine, and olive. For all other trees, both agree that once the fruit emerges, it is considered fruit and may not be wasted.

### Smadar vs. Boser

Rav Assi then draws an explicit connection: *hu boser, hu girua* — the stage called *boser*, the intermediate unripe grape that is nonetheless somewhat developed, is the same stage referred to by Beit Hillel's phrase *misheyagri'u*. Furthermore, *hu pul halavan* — this corresponds in size to the white bean, a standard halakhic measurement. The Gemara asks, somewhat incredulously: can a grape really be compared to a white bean? The answer is that the comparison is to size: *shehu kepul halavan* — it is the size of the white bean.

This then clarifies the positions. Beit Shammai, who says even *smadar* constitutes fruit, parallels Rabbi Yosi. Beit Hillel, who says not until the *boser* / *girua* stage, parallels the Rabbis who argue on Rabbi Yosi. And crucially, for all other trees — those not in the carob-grapevine-olive group — Beit Hillel agrees with Beit Shammai that the fruit is considered fruit from the moment it emerges.

### Male Palms Resolution

This leads back to the difficulty: how could Rabbi Ilai cut down that palm branch? For palm trees, which are not among the three trees in dispute, everyone — including Beit Hillel — agrees that once the fruit emerges, it is considered fruit. So how could he discard the unripe dates without concern?

The Gemara's answer: *ella Rabbi Ilai bediniskhani katz* — Rabbi Ilai cut down male palm trees, or branches from male palm trees. Palm trees do in fact come in male and female varieties, and the fruit on male palms never fully ripens on the tree. Rashi explains that if one wishes to ripen the dates from male palms, one picks them and places them in baskets woven from palm fronds, where they then ripen off the tree. This is entirely analogous to fruits such as pears, which also fully ripen only after being picked. Thus Rabbi Ilai's action involved no waste at all: he cut down the branch for firewood, and the fruit from the male palm — which would not ripen on the tree in any case — could be picked and brought to ripen separately. There was no destruction of fruit, and the resolution precisely mirrors the intuition that had been suggested earlier in the discussion.

A related question was raised concerning *bal tashchit* more broadly. The halakhic parameters of *bal tashchit* are worth clarifying: the prohibition applies to wanton destruction without any constructive purpose. Using a branch for firewood — where there is a legitimate need and no waste of the wood itself — does not constitute *bal tashchit*, because the act serves a genuine purpose. The *bal tashchit* prohibition looks at the macro question of whether the use is legitimate, not at whether every incidental item in the transaction is maximally preserved. The concern about the unripe fruit, by contrast, was a more focused, micro-level question about *kedushat shevi'it* — the sanctity of *shemita* produce and whether that produce was fulfilling its purpose. These are distinct concerns, and the resolution of the second (that male palm fruit can ripen off the tree) addresses the *shemita* difficulty directly.

---

## Consumption Seasons

### Grapes & Avel

The Gemara now returns to the central theme of *biur* and the question of how long one may continue consuming stored *shemita* produce of various types. A *baraita* teaches: *ochlin ba'anavim ad sheyichlu dalyos shel* Avel — one may eat grapes as long as there are still grapes on the trellises in the place called Avel, which was apparently known as the region where grapes could be found latest in the season. The underlying principle is the one established earlier: as long as produce of a given type remains available somewhere within the region — even if not in one's own locale — one may continue to keep and consume it at home.

But the *baraita* makes an important qualification: *im yesh me'ucharos meihem, ochlin aleihem* — if there are grapes that remain available even later than those in Avel, one relies on those later grapes. The name of the place is not a limit; it is a rule of thumb. The true governing principle remains subjective observation — as long as something is actually still available out in the field. These geographic names serve as practical shorthand, not as absolute cutoff points.

### Olives/Figs/Dates

The *baraita* continues: *ochlin bazayisim ad sheyichleh acharon shebiTkoa* — one may eat olives until there are no more olives in Tekoa. Rabbi Eliezer says: until there are none left in Gush Chalav, since he holds that olives were available there even later. A quantitative standard is also provided: *kedei she'ani yotzei v'eino motzei lo benofo v'lo be'ikaro rova* — once a poor person going out could not find even a *rova* (roughly a quart) of olives, neither on the branches nor fallen to the ground, olives are considered to have ceased being available.

For *grogeros* — pressed or dried figs — one may eat them until those in Beit Hini are no longer available.

### Dried Figs

A subtle difficulty: the *baraita* speaks of eating dried figs, yet what remains in the field are fresh figs, not dried ones. Why is the rule for dried figs determined by the availability of fresh figs in the field?

The answer lies in a distinctive characteristic of figs: unlike most fruits, which ripen all at once within a single season, figs ripen progressively over an extended period. As a result, one might have dried figs at home from figs picked months earlier, and those dried figs might still be edible long after the main season has passed. The *baraita* therefore finds it necessary to specify the rule for dried figs — because figs alone present the scenario where one is eating preserved produce from one harvest period while figs continue ripening in the field through a much later season. The clock for *biur* of those dried figs runs until the fresh figs of Beit Hini are no longer available.

### Small Figs Debate

Rav Yehuda then raises a challenge: *lo hutru pagei Beit Hini* — the small figs of Beit Hini were only deemed relevant in the context of *ma'aser*, not *shemita*. The original ruling had been *pagei Beit Hini v'ahini deTuvina chayavin b'ma'aser* — the small figs of Beit Hini and the dates of Tuvina are obligated in *ma'aser* despite their small size. One might have inferred that since these small figs are halakhically significant as fruit (sufficient to require *ma'aser*), their presence in the field extends the period during which one may continue eating one's stored larger figs at home. Rav Yehuda rejects this inference: the small figs of Beit Hini may be large enough to be considered fruit for *ma'aser* purposes, but that determination in the domain of *ma'aser* does not carry over to establish that their continued availability in the field extends the *shemita* eating window for the larger varieties one has stored at home. The two categories — *ma'aser* and *shemita biur* — are governed by distinct criteria.

### Holiday Markers

A second *baraita* presents the same rules in terms of calendar dates rather than geographic markers: *ochlin be'anavim ad haPesach* — one may eat grapes until Pesach; olives until Shavuot; dried figs until Chanukah; and dates until Purim. It is notable, and not without pedagogical value, that these seasonal cutoffs align conveniently with the major holidays — a natural mnemonic.

The tension between these two *baraitot* — one giving geographic markers, the other giving calendar dates — is apparent. What, for instance, is the relationship between "until the last olive in Tekoa" and "until Shavuot"? The Gemara resolves: *idi v'idi chad shiura hu* — both formulations are describing the same measure. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who spoke descriptively ("until there are none left in Tekoa"), and the second *baraita*, which translates that into a calendar date, are both expressing the same practical reality: that is approximately when the olives of Tekoa run out.

### Rav Bibi's Alternative

Rav Bibi reports that Rabbi Yochanan reversed the last two items: he held that dried figs could be eaten until Purim and dates until Chanukah — a striking difference, given the large gap of time between the two holidays. The Gemara takes note but does not resolve the discrepancy by distinguishing between the positions. Rather, since the *baraita* itself had already acknowledged that the calendar dates are only approximations — *im yesh me'ucharos meihem, ochlin aleihem* — the discrepancy may simply reflect the inherent imprecision in translating observation-based rules into fixed calendar markers.

### Observation Principle

This pattern raises a broader halakhic question about the tension between subjective observation and fixed, quantifiable standards. The most rigorous standard is direct observation: is this produce still available in the field? But people want measurable, calendar-based rules. The Gemara here, as in other contexts — the parallel case of the eighteen-minute standard for *chametz* being one prominent example — acknowledges both the practical utility of fixed markers and the ultimate primacy of the observational principle. The fixed dates on the calendar are heuristics; the underlying rule is always whether produce of that type is still genuinely available somewhere in the field.

---

## Geographic Characteristi…

### Mnemonic Markers

The Gemara cites a teaching of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *siman leharim milin* — the characteristic of mountains is *milin* (a type of gallnut); *siman la'amakim dkalim* — the characteristic of valleys is palm trees, as anyone who has traveled to the low-lying areas near the Dead Sea can observe; *siman lenachalim kanim* — the characteristic of wadis is bullrushes; *siman lishfela shikma* — the characteristic of the lowlands (*shfela*) is the sycamore tree. A Scriptural support is adduced: *vayiten hamelech et hakesef biYerushalayim ka'avanim v'et ha'arazim natan kashikmim asher bashfela* — Solomon made silver in Jerusalem as plentiful as stones, and cedar trees as plentiful as the sycamores in the *shfela*. From this verse one sees that the *shfela* is identified by its sycamore trees. Although Rabban Shimon acknowledges that this verse is not a formal proof but a *zecher ladavar* — a textual hint or allusion — it supports the mnemonic association.

### Bikurim Application

The practical significance of these geographic identifications is spelled out. With respect to *bikurim*: *ein mevi'im bikurim ela mishivat haminim* — one brings *bikurim* only from the seven species. Even when bringing dates, one may not bring from palm trees that grow in the mountains — *v'lo midkalim shebeharim* — because those are not the paradigmatic palm trees. The true date palms, yielding the finest fruit, grow in the valleys. Conversely, the finest grains do not grow in the valleys. Each species must come from its optimal natural habitat, and these geographic markers identify which trees and crops qualify as the finest exemplars of their kind for *bikurim* purposes.

Similarly, the wadi (*nachal*) identification by bullrushes has relevance for the law of *egla arufa*: the *nachal eitan* to which the heifer of *egla arufa* is brought must be a wadi in the halakhic sense, and a wadi without bullrushes does not fulfill the criteria of a paradigmatic wadi.

### Business Application

The *shfela* identification by sycamore trees has relevance for commercial transactions: *nafka mina lemikach umimkar* — if one contracts to sell property described as being in the *shfela*, and the land lacks sycamore trees, it may not halakhically qualify as *shfela* at all. Once this business application is raised, the Gemara generalizes: *kulhu nami lemikach umimkar* — all of these geographic identifiers could similarly be relevant to commercial law. If a seller represents land as "mountain" and it has no *milin* trees, one might question whether it truly meets the halakhic definition of mountain. These botanical-geographic markers thus serve not merely as mnemonics but as legal definitions of terrain types, with consequences across multiple areas of *halacha*.

---

## Animal Sales Customs

### Custom Variations

The Gemara now returns to the broader theme of place-based customs, presenting a Mishnah that is treated more extensively in Masechet Avodah Zarah: *makom shenagu limkor behema daka lenochrim mocherin* — in a place where the custom was to sell small grazing animals (sheep and goats) to non-Jews, one may sell them; *makom shenagu shelo limkor, ein mocherin* — in a place where the custom was not to sell even these, one does not sell them.

The Bavli understands the primary concern underlying these restrictions to be a *Shabbat* concern: if a cow or horse is loaned or rented to a non-Jew and that non-Jew uses it for labor on *Shabbat*, the Jewish owner has permitted his animal to perform *melacha* on *Shabbat* — a violation of *behemtecha* ("your animal" shall rest). Selling creates a risk that the transaction might devolve into a lending arrangement before the sale is finalized, and one's animal would then be performing *melacha* on *Shabbat* while still halakhically in Jewish ownership. Small grazing animals present somewhat less of this concern, which is why some communities permitted their sale while restricting large animals.

However, one might also read these restrictions through a different lens — not purely *Shabbat*-based, but connected to broader concerns about maintaining Jewish control over the agricultural assets of the Land of Israel: who owns the land and who controls the animals that work it.

The Mishnah concludes with a rule that applies in all places universally: *behema gassa* — large animals such as cows and horses — may not be sold to non-Jews. This restriction extends even to *agalim vesiyachin* — calves and foals — even though they cannot yet perform labor. Once the Rabbis established the prohibition, they applied it to the entire category. Nor does it matter whether the animal is *shalem* (uninjured) or *shavur* (with a broken limb), since the entire category was prohibited. Rabbi Yehuda permits the sale of an injured animal, reasoning that it will be slaughtered immediately and will never be used for *melacha*. Ben Beteira permits the sale of horses specifically, on the grounds that riding an animal does not constitute *melacha* in the halakhic sense — because of the principle *chai nosei et atzmo* (a living being supports its own weight), such that one does not technically violate the *Shabbat* prohibition by having a non-Jew ride one's horse, since the horse's living body provides its own balance and support. The Gemara in Avodah Zarah develops these positions in full.

---

## Roasted Meat on Pesach

### Eating Custom

The Mishnah now arrives at a topic of direct relevance to Pesach: *makom shenagu le'echol tzali beleilei Pesachim ochlim* — a place where the custom is to eat roasted meat on the night of Pesach, one eats it; *makom shenagu shelo le'echol, ein ochlim* — where the custom is not to eat roasted meat, one does not.

This passage presents a striking ambiguity about what the normative baseline is and what constitutes the special *minhag*. From an Ashkenazic perspective, the familiar practice is not to eat roasted meat on the *Seder* night, lest it appear that one is eating a *korban* outside of Yerushalayim — *shelo yochlu d'mechzi ke'ochel Pesach bachutz*, as Rashi frames the concern. On this reading, the *minhag* is restraint, and those who eat roasted meat are following a place-based exception. But Sephardic practice runs in the opposite direction: many Sephardic communities eat roasted meat — some specifically roasted lamb or goat — *davka* on the *Seder* night, as a *zecher lePesach*. On that reading, the *minhag* is to have roasted meat as a commemorative act, and the restraint is the departure from the norm.

Both orientations find expression in the Mishnah, and both are grounded in the same underlying tension: there is a push toward commemorating the *korban Pesach* through roasted meat, and simultaneously a push to keep one's distance from anything that too closely resembles the actual *korban* being brought outside its proper context. This tension plays out directly in the Gemara that follows.

### Rav Yehuda Restriction

Rav Yehuda Amar Rav: *assur le'adam sheyomar basar zeh lePesach* — it is prohibited for a person to designate meat on the *Seder* night by saying "this meat is for the *Pesach*," because *mipnei shenireh kemakdish behemato v'ochel kodshim bachutz* — it appears as though he has sanctified his animal and is eating consecrated meat outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. This is why at the *Seder*, when we recite *Pesach matzah maror*, we say *Pesach shehayu avoteinu ochlim* — "the *Pesach* offering that our ancestors ate" — rather than pointing to the meat and calling it *Pesach zeh* — "this Pesach."

### Rav Pappa Clarification

Rav Pappa refines the prohibition: *davka basar* — this applies specifically to meat. *Aval chitey lo* — but one may say "this wheat is for *Pesach*," because wheat cannot be construed as a *korban Pesach* in any sense. The word *lePesach* in connection with wheat is immediately understood as referring to the festival, not the offering. Meat is different precisely because it is capable of being interpreted as a reference to the *korban Pesach*, and that ambiguity is what the prohibition targets.

### Theodosius Case

The Gemara now cites a *baraita* that introduces Theodosius of Rome. Rabbi Yosi (or, in an alternate version, Rabbi Shimon) reports: *Tudos Ish Romi hinhig et bnei Romi le'echol gedayim mekulasin beleilei Pesachim* — Theodosius of Rome instituted the practice for the Jews of Rome to eat whole roasted goats on the nights of Pesach. *Mekulasin* means the goats were roasted whole over an open flame, exactly as the *korban Pesach* was prepared — *rosho al kra'av v'al kirbo* — with the head over the legs and the innards, precisely replicating the form of the offering. The Rabbis sent him a message: *ilmaleh Tudos attah, gazarnu alecha niduy* — were you not who you are, Theodosius, we would place you in *cherem* — *she'atah ma'achil et Yisrael kodshim bachutz* — for causing Israel to eat *kodshim* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*.

The Gemara immediately clarifies: *kodshim salta da'atach?* — could it literally be *kodshim*? Obviously not; these are ordinary animals. *Ella eima karov le'hachil Yisrael kodshim bachutz* — rather, it is as if he was causing them to eat *kodashim* outside, because the whole-roasted form so closely resembles the actual *korban Pesach* that the distinction becomes dangerously blurred.

From here the Gemara draws a distinction: *mekulas in, she'eino mekulas lo* — if the animal is roasted whole (*mekulas*), the prohibition applies regardless of whether one verbally designates it, because the form alone already creates an impermissible resemblance to the *korban*. If it is not roasted whole, the prohibition is triggered only by explicit verbal designation — *pireish in, lo pireish lo*. Thus, either the visual resemblance alone (whole roasting) or the verbal declaration alone (saying "this is for the Pesach") creates the problem; absent both, there is no issue with roasted meat per se.

It is worth noting that while this Gemara presents Theodosius as having been censured, one should not conclude too quickly that the practice of eating roasted meat was universally rejected. The Mishnah itself attests to communities that maintained the custom, and other Tannaitic sources indicate that some *tanna'im* were specifically careful to have roasted meat on Pesach. The *minhag Sefardim* of eating roasted meat — and in some communities specifically roasted lamb — reflects a legitimate reading of the same Mishnah that the Ashkenazic tradition reads in the opposite direction.

### Rav Sheshet Challenge

The Gemara then reports that Remi bar Chama taught this *baraita* — the criticism of Theodosius — in the name of Rabbi Shimon (rather than Rabbi Yosi). Rav Sheshet challenges this attribution. If the *baraita* is reported in the name of Rabbi Yosi, the criticism is intelligible. But if it is in the name of Rabbi Shimon, there is a difficulty: *v'hatnan, Rabbi Shimon poter shelo hitnadev kederech ha-mitnadvim* — we have a Mishnah in which Rabbi Shimon exempts a person who made a vow that does not conform to the normal manner of vowing. The case involves someone who declares an obligation to bring a *mincha* from barley. Since vowed *minchot* can only be of wheat (barley *mincha* is the *sotah* offering, not a vowed offering), the statement is self-contradictory. Some authorities would truncate the statement and treat it as a valid vow to bring a wheat *mincha*. Rabbi Shimon says: we take the complete statement as it was spoken, and because the whole statement is internally contradictory and meaningless, the person is exempt — he need not bring anything.

How is this relevant to Theodosius? Because, according to Tosafot's understanding of the issue, the concern with Theodosius was that his followers might be thought to have sanctified their animals as *korban Pesach* offerings and then consumed them outside Yerushalayim. But according to Rabbi Shimon, such a declaration would be legally meaningless — there is no such thing as a *korban Pesach* brought outside of Yerushalayim, just as there is no such thing as a vowed *mincha* of barley. A statement that is inherently impossible to fulfill is not a valid declaration at all. If one explicitly says "I am consecrating this animal to bring as a *korban Pesach* here in Rome," the animal acquires no *kedusha* — the declaration is void. Note: there is an *issur* in bringing a *korban* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* (*makriv bachutz*), but if the consecration itself is void *ab initio* because the stated purpose is impossible, the concern evaporates. And if we cannot even construct a scenario in which Theodosius's practice constituted a real violation, why would Rabbi Shimon have criticized him?

### Rava's Resolution

Ravina then turns the question around: even if it is taught in the name of Rabbi Yosi, is it unproblematic? The same challenge should apply — if the declaration is impossible to fulfill, why is any criticism warranted?

Rava resolves this: *Reb Shimon b'shitat Reb Yosi amrah* — Rabbi Shimon's ruling draws on a position of Rabbi Yosi. There is a broader debate about what to do when someone makes a statement that contains an internal contradiction: do you truncate the statement at the point where it first becomes coherent, or do you accept the full statement including its final words? Rabbi Yosi holds *bi-gmar devarav adam nitpas* — a person is bound by the full conclusion of his words. In the case of an *olah shelamim* — where someone says an animal is simultaneously an *olah* and a *shelamim* — Rabbi Yosi accepts the whole statement and resolves it by dividing the proceeds between both types of offering. Rabbi Shimon goes even further: he too accepts the full statement (agreeing with Rabbi Yosi that one does not truncate), but unlike the *olah shelamim* case — which can be satisfied by a splitting of proceeds — the *mincha* of barley cannot be satisfied in any way, and so Rabbi Shimon is prepared to throw out the entire statement and exempt the person entirely.

Thus the relationship between the two authorities: *Reb Shimon savar lah k'Rebbi Yosi* — Rabbi Shimon holds like Rabbi Yosi, that one looks at the full statement. *V'Rebbi Yosi lo savar lah k'Reb Shimon* — but Rabbi Yosi does not hold like Rabbi Shimon; Rabbi Yosi, when the full statement can be partially satisfied, seeks to make it work rather than void it entirely. Only Rabbi Shimon is willing to void an impossible statement in its entirety.

It follows that according to Rabbi Shimon, even a verbal declaration consecrating an animal as a *korban Pesach* in Rome would be entirely void — and therefore Rabbi Shimon, consistently, should have had no problem with Theodosius's practice. According to Rabbi Yosi, by contrast, there is no analogous principle voiding the declaration, and the criticism stands.

---

## Theodosius Identity

### Derasha on Martyrdom

Having raised the question of whether Theodosius was a great scholar or merely a powerful patron, the Gemara adduces evidence. A *baraita* records: *od zu darash Tudos Ish Romi* — Theodosius of Rome expounded the following additional *derasha*. (The "additional" implies he was known for multiple teachings.) What was his *drasha*?

*Mah rau Chananiah Mishael va-Azariah she-masru atzmam al kedushat ha-Shem le-kivshan ha-eish?* — What moved Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah to give up their lives and allow themselves to be thrown into Nevuchadnezzar's fiery furnace? *Nas'u kal va-chomer b'atzman mi-tzfarde'im* — they reasoned by *kal va-chomer* from the frogs of the plague of Egypt. The logic: *u-mah tzfarde'im she-ein mitzuavin al kedushat ha-Shem* — frogs are not commanded to sanctify God's name, yet the verse says *u-vau b'tanurecha u-v'misharosecha* — they came into the ovens and the kneading troughs. *Eimasai misharos metzuyot eitzel tannur* — when are kneading troughs found next to an oven? *B'sha'ah she-ha-tannur cham* — when the oven is hot. So the frogs threw themselves into a burning oven simply because God commanded them to enter it. *Anu she-mitzuavin al kedushat ha-Shem, al achas kamma v'khamma* — we who are commanded to sanctify God's name, how much more so must we be prepared to give our lives.

Rashi understands the question as how they knew they should give their lives rather than bow to an idol. Tosafot raises a more nuanced reading: perhaps the bowing demanded by Nevuchadnezzar was not technically *avoda zara* — perhaps it was merely bowing to a statue without real idolatrous intent — and even so, Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah chose to sanctify God's name by entering the fire. Or, according to Tosafot's second suggestion, perhaps they could have escaped — and they chose not to. In either case, they went beyond the strict *yehareg v'al ya'avor* requirement.

This reading of the story is historically and intellectually significant. As scholars such as Chaim Soloveitchik have noted, Tosafot's reading cannot be divorced from the historical realities of the Crusades, during which Ashkenazic Jews martyred themselves — sometimes for acts that were not halakhically among the three cardinal sins that require one to die rather than transgress, and sometimes when escape was possible. Tosafot reads into the story of Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah a model for this kind of voluntary *kiddush Hashem*: that there exists a category of optional *kiddush Hashem*, a willingness to give one's life for God's honor even when not strictly commanded to do so. Whether such voluntary martyrdom is permitted or is equivalent to suicide is itself a subject of halakhic debate, but Tosafot's position is that such a category exists and is laudable.

The very fact that Theodosius could formulate and transmit this sophisticated *drasha* — one with deep halakhic, aggadic, and existential dimensions — establishes his credentials as a serious Torah scholar, not merely a wealthy patron.

### Financial Support Reason

Having established his scholarship, the Gemara now explains why the Rabbis held back from actually placing him in *cherem*: *matya malya le'kisa de'talmidei chachamim havah* — Theodosius was someone who filled the wallets of Torah scholars. He provided financial support for the *talmidei chachamim*, managing investments on their behalf and securing their economic wellbeing. One does not publicly censure one's major benefactors, even when they cross a line halakhically.

### Reward for Support

The Gemara closes with a teaching of Rabbi Yochanan that provides the theological underpinning for the high regard in which such a supporter is held: *kol hamatil melai le'kis talmidei chachamim, zoche v'yoshev bi'yeshiva shel ma'ala* — whoever places "filler" into the wallet of Torah scholars — that is, whoever invests in their financial wellbeing — merits to sit in the *yeshiva shel ma'ala*, the heavenly academy, in the world to come. The wealthy person who supports Torah scholars will ultimately sit alongside them and learn Torah together with them in the realm above. The Scriptural support: *ki betzel ha-chochma betzel ha-kesef* — "in the shade of wisdom is the shade of money." Provide the shade of money, and you will ultimately dwell in the shade of wisdom.

# Pesachim 54

## Yom Kippur Candles

### Mishnah: Candles on Yom…

We are at the *mishnah* on *amud bet* of daf 54, still within the fifth *perek* — a *perek* that has become genuinely rich and interesting. Its opening engaged the core meta-question that so many of us want to understand more deeply: what makes *minhagim* binding, and under what circumstances can they or cannot they be changed?
