No definitive black-and-white answers emerged, but what followed was a wide-ranging collection of particular practices: *shemita* issues, *Pesach* questions such as working on *erev Pesach* and eating roasted meat at the *leil seder*, *Avoda Zara* questions about selling to non-Jews, matters touching *Nezikin*, *Tahara*, and *Zeroim*. Now we arrive at a *Yom Kippur* issue.

The *mishnah* opens: *makom she-nahagu le-hadlik et ha-ner be-leil Yom ha-Kippurim, madlikin* — in a place where the custom is to light candles on the night of *Yom Kippur*, one lights. *Makom she-nahagu shelo le-hadlik, ein madlikin* — in a place where the custom is not to light, one does not light.

### Why Light Candles?

Why do we light candles on *erev Shabbat*? Because there is light present when one is eating — the connection to *shalom bayit* is specifically realized through the meal and the preference that one light in the place where one will eat. On *Yom Kippur*, however, one is not eating. So should candles be lit at all?

That is precisely the question. If one has a *minhag* to light, one does; if one has a *minhag* not to light, one does not. One might ask whether the default assumption is that one lights and some communities have a *minhag* not to, or the reverse. As the *Gemara* will make clear — in a manner analogous to the earlier discussion about roasted meat on *Pesach* — there appear to be active *minhagim* in both directions, each grounded in its own reasoning, not simply one practice that exists and one that is the absence of practice.

### Public Lighting

The *mishnah* continues: *u-madlikin be-vatei kenesiot u-vatei midrashot* — one lights in the synagogues and study halls, *u-mevo'ot ha-afelim* — in dark alleyways, *ve-al gabei ha-cholim* — and beside the sick. In these contexts, lighting is essentially equivalent to turning on the lights for safety or basic function, or in the case of the *beit knesset*, perhaps carrying a dimension of *kavod beit ha-knesset* as well. Occasionally the sick person needs light, and occasionally needs darkness — the *mishnah* elsewhere notes that one may extinguish a candle before a *choleh*. The practical lighting in public spaces and for the infirm is not in dispute; the question concerns domestic lighting.

### Shammai vs. Hillel

A *baraita* is then cited: *Beit Shammai le-hadlik* — those who say one should light — and those who say one should not light — *sheneihem le-davar echad nitkavenu* — both had one thing in mind. What was that one thing? According to *Rashi*, and as alluded to in the *Gemara*, the concern underlying both positions is the prohibition of marital relations on *Yom Kippur*. One school holds that one should *davka* have the lights burning so that there is no *yetzer ha-ra* that might lead to transgression — since one typically does not engage in relations in a lit room. The other school holds that one should *davka* extinguish the lights, because seeing one's spouse could arouse desire and lead to violation.

Rav Yehoshua reports that Rava expounded the *pasuk* *netzer mata'ai ma'aseh yadai le-hitpa'er*, applying to this case the verse *ve-amech kulam tzaddikim* — all of your people are righteous. Whether one lights or one does not, both sets of communities are pursuing the same goal by two different theories of human psychology and *yetzer ha-ra*.

---

## Fire Blessing Debate

### Blessing Only Motzaei Sh…

From the discussion of candles on *Yom Kippur*, the *Gemara* transitions to an associated matter: the blessing over fire. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* — Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *ein mevarachin al ha-or ela be-motzaei Shabbat*, one recites the blessing *borei me'orei ha-esh* only on *motzaei Shabbat*, *ho'il u-techilat beriyato hu* — because that is when fire was originally created.

One might assume the reason we light the *havdalah* candle on *motzaei Shabbat* is simply to mark the transition from a period when one could not use fire — essentially as a celebration of restored access to flame. The *Gemara*, however, is now pointing toward a different, or at least primary, rationale.

### Fire and Creativity

Note first that *borei me'orei ha-esh* contains within it an ambiguity: is it about *or* — light — or about *esh* — fire itself? In either case, the blessing is understood here not as a reaction to the *Shabbat* prohibition on fire, but as a commemoration of the original creation of fire.

To appreciate the weight of this claim, consider the ancient significance of fire-making. The image of Prometheus stealing fire from the gods captures something universal about the cultural depth of this act. For *Chazal*, fire is the necessary foundation of civilization. The moment God completes Creation and *Shabbat* arrives, the world is, in a sense, handed over to human beings: *u-milu et ha-aretz ve-khivsuha*, conquer the earth and subdue it — build your society, take creative control. And the first profound creative act, the foundational one, is the making of fire. So for *Chazal*, that moment of human creativity occurred precisely on *motzaei Shabbat*, as the first moment after *Shabbat* ended. The entire week begins by recalling that first human creative act.

This is why, according to this statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, one does *not* recite *borei me'orei ha-esh* on *motzaei Yom Kippur*. The blessing is not about what was prohibited on *Yom Kippur* any more than we go out and plow a field on *motzaei Shabbat* simply because plowing was forbidden. The blessing is about the symbolism of the creation of fire, and that symbolism is specific to *motzaei Shabbat*.

A question naturally arises about whether an electric light could fulfill the requirement. Electricity is, in a meaningful sense, the most astonishing instance of humanity harnessing fire — clean, efficient, universally accessible. As long as electricity is categorized as *esh*, it would be sufficient. There is a historical note worth mentioning: when the question of electricity first arose, some rabbis who wished to demonstrate that electric lights constituted *esh* and therefore could not be used on *Shabbat* would *davka* recite *havdalah* over electric lights. Other considerations might make this *lechatchila* suboptimal — such as the traditional preference for a mingling of flames — but *bidi'avad* a single flame suffices, and the classification as *esh* is what matters.

### Ulla's Inquiry

Now a narrative enters the *Gemara*. A certain elder — in one version identified as Rabbah bar Bar Chana — heard Rav Yehuda's teaching and responded *yasher koach*, affirming it. And *ve-chen amar Rabbi Yochanan* — Rabbi Yochanan, it is reported, said the same thing.

The transmission of this teaching is then complicated by a scene: Ulla was riding on a donkey, with Rabbi Abba on his right and Rabbah bar Bar Chana on his left — an arrangement that already hints at the relative standing of the participants. Rabbi Abba addressed Ulla: is it truly the case that you said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one does not recite the blessing on *or* except on *motzaei Shabbat* because that is when fire was originally created — implying that one does *not* recite it on *motzaei Yom Kippur*?

Ulla turned and gave Rabbah bar Bar Chana a *bisha* — a dirty look. He assumed it was Rabbah bar Bar Chana who had attributed this position to Rabbi Yochanan (via Ulla), since that is precisely what one version of the story above recorded. Rabbah bar Bar Chana quickly defended himself: *ana lav ha amri* — I never said that. I never claimed Rabbi Yochanan said one does not recite the blessing on *motzaei Yom Kippur*. What I said was something different entirely.

### Yom Kippur Shabbat Case

What Rabbah bar Bar Chana actually reported was the following. A *tanna* taught before Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says that when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*, even in a place that has the custom not to light candles on *erev Yom Kippur*, one nevertheless lights — *mipnei kvod ha-Shabbat*. Even without the eating component, the dimension of *kvod Shabbat* — distinct from *oneg Shabbat* though often intertwined with it — demands that candles be lit. And Rabbi Yochanan responded to that teaching by saying: *va-chakhamim osrin* — the rabbis disagree. Even when *Yom Kippur* falls on *Shabbat*, communities that maintain the custom not to light on *erev Yom Kippur* do not light.

So the statement attributed to Rabbi Yochanan relating to *Yom Kippur* and lighting was not about *motzaei Yom Kippur* at all. It was about the case of *Yom Kippur* that falls on *Shabbat*, and whether communities that don't light on *erev Yom Kippur* would override their *minhag* for the sake of *kvod Shabbat*. Rabbi Yochanan rules they do not. That is the teaching Rabbah bar Bar Chana had reported, and it was entirely consistent with Rabbi Yochanan separately holding that one *does* recite *borei me'orei ha-esh* on *motzaei Yom Kippur*.

Ulla, upon hearing the clarification, responded with the expression *adatahei* — meaning, in effect: that is indeed the right thing to say; that is a proper report of Rabbi Yochanan's position. Rabbi Yosef then applied a verse to this exchange: *mayim amukim etzah be-lev ish, ve-ish tevunah yidlenah* — deep waters is the counsel within a person's heart, and a person of understanding will draw them out. *Ze Ulla* — Ulla represents the deep waters, as it was his unstated assumption, communicated only through a sharp glance, that something had been misattributed to him. *Ve-ish tevunah yidlenah — ze Rabbah bar Bar Chana*, who was perceptive enough to understand why Ulla was angry, to figure out exactly what was being alleged, and to defend himself by clarifying what he had actually said.

Meanwhile, the broader question remains: did Rabbi Yochanan say one recites *borei me'orei ha-esh* on *motzaei Yom Kippur* or not? The tradition reported by Rabbi Binyamin bar Yephet in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states: *mevarachin al ha-ner bein be-motzaei Shabbat bein be-motzaei Yom Kippurim* — one blesses over fire both on *motzaei Shabbat* and on *motzaei Yom Kippur*. And *ve-chen ama devar* — that is indeed the widespread practice of the people.

---

## Fire Contradiction

### Conflicting Sources

The *Gemara* now raises a direct contradiction. Against the tradition that one recites *borei me'orei ha-esh* on *motzaei Yom Kippur*, there stands an opposing teaching: *ein mevarachin al ha-ner ella be-motzaei Shabbat ve-hi techillat beriyato hu* — one does not bless over fire except on *motzaei Shabbat*, for that is when it was originally created. This is word for word identical to the formulation of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel. Moreover, a statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that we rule like Rav Yehuda — that all the blessings should be recited together *al ha-kos* — appears in the context of this very *baraita*, suggesting Rabbi Yochanan may well be endorsing the position that the blessing belongs only to *motzaei Shabbat*.

So we appear to have conflicting reports. One tradition in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says the blessing is recited on *motzaei Yom Kippur* as well; another body of teaching implies it is not.

### New vs. Old Fire

*Lo kashya* — the *Gemara* resolves the contradiction with a crucial distinction: *kan be-or she-shavat, kan be-or ha-yotze min ha-etzim u-min ha-avanim* — here we speak of fire that has "rested" (i.e., was burning through *Shabbat*), and there we speak of fire newly produced from wood and stones.

The practical application of this distinction is well known, even if its underlying logic often eludes people. On *motzaei Shabbat* one recites the blessing specifically over newly created fire — fire freshly struck from flint or kindled from scratch — because the entire purpose of the blessing is to commemorate the original creation of fire by human hands. On *motzaei Yom Kippur*, by contrast, the tradition is to recite the blessing only over a flame that was burning *through* Yom Kippur — a *yahrtzeit* candle or similar.

This is genuinely counterintuitive and confuses nearly everyone who encounters it. If the idea on *motzaei Yom Kippur* were to signify that we now can make fire after a day when we could not, one would expect the symbol to be a *newly* created fire. The answer is that this is precisely the point: we do *not* want to create that association on *motzaei Yom Kippur*. The symbolism of newly created fire belongs exclusively to *motzaei Shabbat* — to that first human creative act. To avoid any confusion between the two occasions, the rule on *motzaei Yom Kippur* insists on old fire. The term *nur she-shavat* — fire that "rested" — is somewhat misleading, since the candle was burning the entire day; the operative point is not anything positive about an old flame but rather the deliberate exclusion of a newly struck flame, so as not to blur the symbolism of *motzaei Shabbat*.

This same principle resolves a second apparent contradiction between two *braitot*: one teaching that one *does* recite the blessing over fire newly produced from wood and stone, and another teaching that one does *not*. *Lo kashya* — *kan be-motzaei Shabbat, kan be-motzaei Yom Kippur* — on *motzaei Shabbat* one specifically uses new fire; on *motzaei Yom Kippur* one specifically uses old fire.

### Blessing Order

A brief additional note on the ordering of *havdalah* blessings: the *Gemara* mentions that Rabbi — Rabbeinu HaKadosh — *mefarzeran*, he scattered them, reciting the blessings separately rather than as a unit. For instance, upon seeing fire on the way home from *shul*, he would immediately recite *borei me'orei ha-esh* even before reaching the cup. Rabbi Chiyya, by contrast, *mechanseran* — bundled them all together to be recited *al ha-kos*. Rabbi Yosef bar Abdimi clarifies: even though Rabbi scattered them in practice, he would nonetheless *return* and arrange them all *al ha-kos* as well — *chozer ve-sodran al ha-kos*. The practical ruling is that everything is recited *al ha-kos*, though it is important to know that conceptually the components are not inseparably bound to one another, and if circumstances require, *borei me'orei ha-esh* and *besamim* may be recited independently of *havdalah*.

---

## Fire Creation

### Ten Things Created

*Ve-ha-or be-motzaei Shabbat nivra* — the *Gemara* has just stated that fire was created on *motzaei Shabbat*. But is that so? A *baraita* challenges this: *asarah devarim nivru be-erev Shabbat bein ha-shmashot* — ten things were created on *erev Shabbat bein ha-shmashot*. This list is also found in *Pirkei Avot*, with slight variation. The items are: the well of Miriam, the *man*, the rainbow, *ktav u-michtav* — script and writing (Rashi understands *ktav* as the alphabet and *michtav* as the implements of writing, though the distinction is not entirely clear), the *luchot*, the burial place of Moses, the cave in which Moses and Elijah each stood when the divine Presence was revealed to them, the opening of the donkey's mouth in the Bilaam episode, and the opening of the earth to swallow the wicked in the episode of Korach.

If fire is among the things created on *erev Shabbat bein ha-shmashot*, that contradicts the claim that it was created on *motzaei Shabbat*.

### Liminal Space

This list is a fascinating and somewhat heterogeneous collection. Most items are miraculous events or objects, yet a few — such as the written alphabet — seem to reflect profound human innovation. What principle unites them?

The key is the concept of *erev Shabbat bein ha-shmashot* itself. The six days of *Bereishit* established the natural order of things. *Shabbat* then arrived as a kind of seal upon Creation — a closing of the natural order, after which everything is fixed for eternity. But this raises a challenge: where in this schema is there room for human creativity? Where is there room for things that partially violate the natural order — whether genuine miracles like the opening of the earth, or quasi-miraculous things like the invention of writing, or the human mastery of fire?

If all such things were assigned to *motzaei Shabbat*, they would seem entirely external to the natural order, something grafted onto it from outside. If they were simply part of the six days, they would lose their distinctive character. *Chazal*'s solution is the liminal space of *erev Shabbat bein ha-shmashot*: that gray zone between the closing of the natural order and the arrival of *Shabbat* which seals it. In this twilight, the seeds of human creativity and of certain departures from the natural order were planted. They belong neither fully to the natural order of the six days nor fully to the sealed world of *Shabbat* and after. This framework allowed the world to function according to consistent laws of nature and yet also to contain creativity and events that appear to transcend those laws.

This also explains why the list does not include *Keri'at Yam Suf* or the great wilderness miracles. The *Rambam* raises this question in his *Peirush ha-Mishnayot*, and a compelling answer is that those events represent a *total* violation of the natural order — miracles that come from entirely outside the way God set the world in motion. The items on this list, by contrast, are embedded within the natural order even as they stretch it. Some, like the *man*, are closer to miraculous; others, like writing, are genuinely human achievements that nonetheless carry a dimension of the extraordinary. It is not the same degree of rupture as the splitting of the sea.

### Creativity vs. Miracle

Now another tradition is cited alongside the established list. *Rabbi Nechemia omer mishum aviv* — Rabbi Nechemia says in the name of his father: even *ha-or ve-ha-pered* — fire and the mule — were created at that liminal moment. *Rabbi Yehoshua omer mishum aviv* — Rabbi Yehoshua says in the name of his father: even *ha-ayil ve-ha-shamir* — the ram that Abraham found at the *Akeidah* and the *shamir* worm used to cut stone for the *Beit ha-Mikdash* without metal tools.

Rabbi Yehuda adds: even the *tzevet* — the tongs. He was accustomed to say: *tzavta be-tzavta mit'abda* — tongs are made using tongs. You need to hold metal in a fire with tongs in order to shape it. So who made the first tongs? *Birya bidei shamayim hi* — it must be a heavenly creation, said Rabbi Yehuda. The *hakhamim* responded: perhaps the first tongs were cast in a mold and set correctly — *ya'asena be-dfus ve-yichavenena kiven* — poured as molten metal, requiring no prior tongs. In that case, *birya bidei adam hi* — it is a human creation entirely. (The formula *ya'asena be-dfus* is in fact the same language used earlier in *Pesachim* by Beisos ben Zunin in his proposal to make matzah in a mold — likely borrowed from precisely this passage.)

The philosophical issue of the tongs is the classic problem of lifting oneself by one's bootstraps: how does human civilization develop the tools necessary to transcend its current level of development? At some point there must have been a first, miraculous leap — a first tool made without the preceding tool — and that is what this discussion tries to capture.

### Gehennom Fire

The *Gemara* now reconciles the contradiction about when fire was created. *Ha lo kashya: ha be-nur didan, ha be-nur de-Gehennom* — there is no difficulty. The fire that concerns us — the fire of human civilization — was made on *motzaei Shabbat*. The fire of *Gehennom* was made on *erev Shabbat bein ha-shmashot*. So the *baraita*'s listing of fire among the *erev Shabbat* creations refers to the fire of *Gehennom*, not to the fire of human civilization.

But the *Gemara* immediately asks: was the fire of *Gehennom* really created on *erev Shabbat bein ha-shmashot*? A different *baraita* teaches that *shiva devarim nivru kodem she-nivra ha-olam* — seven things were created *before* the world was created — and among them is *Gehennom*. This is a completely different category from *erev Shabbat bein ha-shmashot*. These seven things are not liminal creations squeezed between the natural order and *Shabbat*; they are the foundational metaphysical prerequisites for a world of religious meaning to exist at all.

What are the seven? *Torah* — without God's message and direction there is no meaningful world. *Teshuva* — the possibility of repentance, the capacity for human beings to go astray and return, to change who they are and repair their relationship with the divine. This is utterly foundational to any conception of a meaningful human life. *Gan Eden ve-Gehennom* — the reality that actions have ultimate consequences, that how we live results in reward or punishment; in another reading, the concept of a possible utopia and a possible dystopia, the poles within which human history operates. *Kisei ha-kavod* — God's heavenly throne — and *Beit ha-Mikdash*, its earthly counterpart, representing together the principle that God is not a remote first cause but a king with a throne, whose presence can be experienced in this world: *ha-shamayim kisi ve-ha-aretz hadom raglai*. And *shemo shel Mashiach* — the name, or concept, of the Messiah.

The phrase *shemo shel Mashiach* is deliberately chosen over simply *Mashiach*. The Messiah himself was not created before the world; what was established was the concept. The idea of a Messiah removes Jewish civilization from a consciousness of myth. Greek thought understood history as cyclical, endlessly repeating. Jewish thought contains a cyclical element — the reliving of *yetziat Mitzrayim* each *Pesach*, the application of old frameworks to new historical configurations, the sense that Rome is *Edom* is Christianity — but it is also fundamentally linear and directional. History is moving toward a redeemed reality. The best description of the Jewish concept of history may in fact be a corkscrew: cycling, but also vectored toward ultimate redemption. *Shemo shel Mashiach* anchors this, rooting communal life not only in the reliving of ancient archetypes but in orientation toward a future that is genuinely different from the present.

The *Gemara* then provides *pesukim* for each of these seven pre-Creation concepts. *Torah*: *Hashem kanani reishit darko* — "God acquired me at the very beginning of His way" (Proverbs 8:22). *Teshuva*: *beterem harim yuladu* — before the mountains were born — followed by *tashev enosh ad daka va-tomar shuvu benei adam* — "return, O people" (Psalms 90:2–3). *Gan Eden*: *va-yita Hashem Elokim gan be-Eden mi-kedem* — "God planted a garden in Eden from before" (Genesis 2:8). *Gehennom*: *ki aruch me-etmol tofeth* — "for *tofeth* was arranged from yesterday" (Isaiah 30:33). *Kisei ha-kavod* u-*Beit ha-Mikdash*: *kisei kavod marom me-rishon mekom mikdasheinu* — "a throne of glory, exalted from the beginning, the place of our sanctuary" (Jeremiah 17:12). *Shemo shel Mashiach*: *yehi shemo le-olam lifnei shemesh yinon shmo* — "may his name endure forever; before the sun, *yinon* is his name" (Psalms 72:17).

So the *Gemara* resolves: *chalalo hu she-nivra kodem she-nivra ha-olam* — the *space* of *Gehennom* was established before the world was created. *Ve-or didei be-erev Shabbat ivrei* — and the *fire* of *Gehennom* was created on *erev Shabbat bein ha-shmashot*.

But now a further complication: is it really true that the fire of *Gehennom* was created on *erev Shabbat*? Another *baraita* is brought: Rabbi Yosei says that the fire which the Holy One created on the *second day* of Creation — *yom sheini* — is a fire that will never be extinguished, as the verse says: *ki tolatam lo tamut ve-esham lo tichbeh* — "their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be quenched" (Isaiah 66:24). And Rav Bana'ah son of Rav Ulla adds: this explains why the phrase *ki tov* does not appear in the account of the second day of Creation — because that is the day when the fire of *Gehennom* was created.

Rabbi Eliezer adds a coda: even though *yom sheini* was not graced with *ki tov*, it was retroactively included on the sixth day when the Torah says *va-yar Elokim et kol asher asah ve-hineh tov me'od* — "and God saw all that He had made and behold it was very good." Rashi notes that the existence of the fire of *Gehennom* is ultimately good, as it gives human beings reason to remain on the right path and ensures that justice is realized in the world.

So the complete resolution is: *chalalo* — the hollow, the conceptual space of *Gehennom* — was before the world was created. Its fire was created on *yom sheini*. And what then of the *baraita* that listed fire among the *erev Shabbat* creations? That must refer to a different dimension of the fire of *Gehennom*, or the *Gemara* adjusts its reading accordingly. Our fire — human fire — requires its own accounting, which the *Gemara* now provides.

### Our Fire Created

*Ve-or didan* — and as for human fire — *be-machshava alah le-hibarot be-erev Shabbat, ve-lo nivra ad motzaei Shabbat* — it arose in God's mind to be created on *erev Shabbat*, but was not actually created until *motzaei Shabbat*. This resolution is not merely technical. It is profound.

The concept of *machshava techila* — divine thought preceding actualization — appears elsewhere in the tradition, most famously in *Lecha Dodi*: *sof ma'aseh be-machshava techila*, the last thing made was first in thought. Here the distinction between *machshava* and *beri'ah* is doing something beautiful and specific: the divine component, the spark of inspiration that would be implanted in the human being, was already present in the *erev Shabbat* moment — embedded within the natural order, in that liminal space. But the actual creative act, the human execution, took place only when Adam was given the world to work with, beginning on *motzaei Shabbat*.

A *baraita* makes this explicit: *Rabbi Yosei omer — shnei devarim alu be-machshava le-hibarot be-erev Shabbat ve-lo nivre'u ad motzaei Shabbat*. Two things were in God's plan on *erev Shabbat* but were only created on *motzaei Shabbat*. And on *motzaei Shabbat* what happened? *Natan ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu de'ah be-Adam ha-Rishon me'ein dugma shel ma'alah* — God gave Adam a spark of wisdom, an echo of something truly heavenly. And with that divine spark, Adam brought two stones, ground them against each other, and fire came forth — *va-yatza mehem or*. And the second thing: he brought two animals — a horse and a donkey — crossbred them — *ve-hirkhiv zu be-zu* — and from them came the mule — *va-yatza mehem pered*.

What this captures is the unity of the divine and human dimensions of creativity. The divine component was present in the *erev Shabbat* liminal space. But the human creative act — fire, the mule — required human beings to actually be given the world and to work in it, beginning from *motzaei Shabbat*. This is the meaning of the verse *va-yashev Hashem Elohim et ha-adam ba-gan le-ovdah u-le-shomrah* — and it is why the image of fire as the first human creative act has always carried civilizational weight. It is, in every sense, a spark from the divine.

---

## Adam's Creations

### Fire and Mule

The *baraita* just cited establishes that both fire and the mule were among the things God planned on *erev Shabbat* and that Adam actually created on *motzaei Shabbat* through the divine spark of wisdom placed in him. As noted, crossbreeding a horse and a donkey to produce a mule is prohibited as *kilayim*, and yet the mule was an essential beast of burden without which the foundations of ancient civilization would have been impossible. The creative act is censured and yet also recognized as having been divinely inspired — a nuanced and characteristically *talmudic* way of holding two truths in tension.

### Ana's Genealogy

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers a different tradition: *pered bimei Ana hu she-haya* — the mule was first produced in the days of Ana. The verse states: *hu Ana asher matza et ha-yeimim ba-midbar* — "he is Ana who found the *yeimim* in the wilderness" (Genesis 36:24). The term *yeimim* here is read not as its more literal meaning — perhaps watercourses or springs — but as mules: Ana discovered, or more precisely invented, them. *Ve-dorshei chamurot hayu omrim* — those who interpret difficult passages would say — *Ana pasul haya*, Ana himself was born of an illicit union. *Lefichach hevi pasul la-olam* — therefore he brought a *pasul* creature into the world. There is an element of moral censure here: the one who engaged in transgressive breeding was himself a product of illicit breeding.

Where do we know Ana was *pasul*? The verse in *Bereishit lamed-vav* lists *va-elu venei Se'ir ha-Chori: Tzi'veon ve-Ana* — listing Tzi'veon and Ana as brothers. But another verse says *ve-elu venei Tzi'veon: Aya ve-Ana* — listing Ana as the *son* of Tzi'veon. Is Ana Tzi'veon's brother or his son?

The answer must be: both. *Alma ba Tzi'veon al imo ve-holid mimenah Ana* — Tzi'veon had relations with his own mother and fathered Ana. Thus Ana was simultaneously Tzi'veon's son and, through the shared mother, his brother. This genealogical scandal explains both the *pasul* designation and the *midrashic* appropriateness of Ana being the inventor of hybrid breeding.

### Ana Question

The *Gemara* raises an objection: *dilma trei Ana havu* — perhaps there were simply two different people named Ana, one Tzi'veon's brother and one Tzi'veon's son? This is not inherently impossible.

Rava responds: *amina milta de-Shavur Malka lo amrah* — I will say something that even the Persian king did not say. (*Shavur Malka* is the Persian king, and calling Shmuel by that title was a way of honoring his authority in monetary law and jurisprudence. *U-mano Shmuel* — and who is meant? Shmuel.) The solution: *amar kra hu Ana asher matza et ha-yeimim* — the verse says *hu Ana* — *he* is Ana. The repetition *hu Ana de-me'ikara* — he is the same Ana mentioned earlier — establishes that the Ana who found the mules is identical with the Ana who was Tzi'veon's son and also his brother. There were not two people named Ana; there was one, and the biblical text signals this through the emphatic *hu*.

Rav Papa uses the same formulation — *amina milta de-Shavur Malka lo amrah* — attributing the clever reading to Rava (or in some versions, to Rabbah).

---

## Hidden Things

### Seven Hidden Things

*Tanu rabbanan — shiva devarim mechusin mi-bnei adam* — the Rabbis taught: seven things are hidden from human beings, and these are they.

*Yom ha-mita* — the day of one's death. The *Maharsha* and *Rashi* both observe that this concealment serves a purpose: if a person knew when they would die, they would not live their days in a meaningful way. Knowing the precise endpoint of life might either lead to reckless living earlier (since "there is still time") or to paralysis and despair. The uncertainty keeps each day potentially significant.

*Ve-yom ha-nechama* — the day of consolation. Rashi understands this as: when one is in the midst of suffering and anguish, one does not know when relief will come. The *Maharsha* offers a somewhat different reading that is not fully recalled here.

*Ve-omek ha-din* — the depth of judgment. On one reading this means the profound difficulty of rendering proper legal judgment. Rashi also suggests it means one is never fully aware of the degree to which one will be held accountable for one's actions — which again serves a moral function: if the full weight of divine accounting were known, it might either terrify into paralysis or, conversely, if known precisely, enable a kind of cynical calculation.

*Ve-ein adam yodea ma be-libo shel chavero* — one does not know what is in the heart of one's friend. A person may appear friendly and well-disposed, while their inner thoughts are something altogether different.

*Ve-ein adam yodea ba-meh mishtaker* — one does not know how one will ultimately earn a living.

*U-malkhut beit David matai tachazoer* — one does not know when the Davidic kingdom will be restored, i.e., when a more perfect world will come into being. *U-malkhut chayevet matai tichleh* — and when the wicked empire will finally cease.

What binds these together into a single list is not entirely transparent, but the first cluster relates to judgment, mortality, and accountability in personal life, while the final pair relates to the trajectory of history and redemption. All are things one might desperately wish to know, and all remain hidden.

### Three Necessary Evils

A *tanna* teaches: *gimel devarim alu be-machshava le-hibarot* — three things came up in God's plan to create — *im lo alu din hu she-ya'alu* — and even if they had not come up in the plan, the logic of things would have demanded them. These are things that seem at first glance painful or undesirable, yet serve an essential function.

*Al ha-met she-yasriach* — that a dead body would decompose. *Al ha-met she-yishtakach min ha-lev* — that the memory of the dead would fade from the heart. *Ve-al ha-tevua she-tarkiv* — and that grain would rot.

### Life's Necessities

Each of these "necessary evils" enables human life to continue. If a dead body did not decompose, Rashi observes, people would not bury their dead; they would remain in the constant presence of the corpse, unable to move forward. The second follows directly: even apart from physical decomposition, the natural fading of grief from the forefront of consciousness — without ever fully forgetting the person — is what allows the bereaved to re-engage with life. One does not decompose emotionally alongside the deceased.

The third — that grain rots — serves an economic function. Rashi explains that if grain could be hoarded indefinitely without loss, those who controlled the supply could manipulate markets without limit, holding grain off the market forever. The perishability of grain creates pressure to sell, which keeps prices accessible and prevents indefinite monopolistic hoarding. Currency is mentioned in some versions as a related item: the *Gemara* notes that the prevalence of money serves those who do not make their living from agriculture, and currency is a far from trivial invention — its availability profoundly affects who can survive in a complex economy.

What is striking about the framing *din hu she-ya'alu* — the logic of things demands them — is the acknowledgment that these are things about which one has a *ta'anah*, a genuine complaint. Decomposition is horrifying. Forgetting loved ones feels like a betrayal. Grain rotting is a loss. The formulation validates the protest even while insisting that these realities are not accidents or cruelties but necessities embedded in the structure of a livable world. One need not pretend they are pleasant. One only need recognize that without them, life could not go on.

---

---

# Pesachim 55

## Tisha B'Av Melacha

### Tisha B'Av Customs

The daf begins by picking up from the *mishna* on 54b, which addresses regional *minhagim* surrounding *melacha* on *Tisha B'Av*. The *mishna* states: *makom shenahagu laasot melacha b'Tisha B'Av osin* — in a place where the custom is to permit *melacha* on *Tisha B'Av*, one may do it; *makom shenahagu shelo laasot melacha ein osin* — where that is not the custom, one does not do it. This is striking, because in certain respects *Tisha B'Av* carries the character of *aveilut*, and indeed the mourning intensifies as the day itself approaches. We might have expected a uniform prohibition. Yet we find different practices, and *melacha* is not strictly forbidden across the board.

### Talmidei Chachamim

The *mishna* continues: *uv'chol makom talmidei chachamim batelim* — in all places, *talmidei chachamim* do not perform *melacha*. They devote the day to *kinnot*, learning, and matters connected to the mourning. This reflects a reality both ancient and contemporary: there are those who make a point of treating *Tisha B'Av* as a day fully devoted to mourning, even when it falls on a weekday that would otherwise demand professional obligations.

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* adds: *l'olam yaaseh adam atzmo talmid chacham* — a person should always regard himself as a *talmid chacham* in the sense that he adopts greater stringencies upon himself. The word *talmid chacham* here means a disciple of the sages — not necessarily a towering *gadol*, but one from the class of *Torah* students whose entire orientation and time are devoted to religious pursuits. Such people tend naturally toward *chumra* and, practically speaking, often have the opportunity to observe it as well.

### Shmuel & Babylon

The *gemara* opens with a teaching of *Shmuel*: *ein ta'anit tzibur b'Bavel ela Tisha B'Av bilvad* — there is no *ta'anit tzibur* in *Bavel* except for *Tisha B'Av* alone. *Ta'anit tzibur* in its technical sense — as developed in *Masechet Ta'anit* — refers to the full-blown public fast declared in response to a drought, which, after a series of escalating cycles, becomes a complete day-fast accompanied by public prayer, additional *brachot* in the *Shmoneh Esrei*, *slichot*, and the prohibition of *melacha*. *Rashi* explains that *Bavel* is a water-rich region not dependent on rain in the way that *Eretz Yisrael* is. Therefore, either the need for such a fast will never arise there, or categorically, *Bavel* does not warrant that status even if rain were somehow needed. In either reading, the historical fasts — such as *Tzom Gedaliah* and *Shiva Asar B'Tammuz* — will never achieve the weight of a full *ta'anit tzibur* in *Bavel*. The one exception is *Tisha B'Av*, which is not rain-based and which alone is observed there as a complete fast with all the stringencies of *ta'anit tzibur*.

### Bein Hashmashos

The *gemara* initially assumes that *Shmuel*'s equation of *Tisha B'Av* with *ta'anit tzibur* implies that the *bein hashmashot* period — the twilight transition — is forbidden on *Tisha B'Av*, just as we treat *bein hashmashot* stringently for *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*. However, *Shmuel* himself also stated that one may eat during *bein hashmashot* of *Tisha B'Av*. The *gemara* attempts to resolve this by suggesting that perhaps *Shmuel* holds that *bein hashmashot* is permitted on every full-day *ta'anit tzibur*, since they are all *drabbanan*. But this is challenged from a *mishna* in *Ta'anit* that states *ochlin v'shotin mib'od yom* — eating and drinking must cease from the day before — implying that *bein hashmashot* is excluded from the permitted eating period.

The *gemara* deflects this challenge: *lo, l'me'utei mishechashicha* — the *mishna* is not emphasizing the *bein hashmashot* boundary but rather contrasting the full-blown fast from the earlier rain-based fasts, where eating the prior night was permitted. The key distinction is whether the fast begins at night or only in the morning — not whether *bein hashmashot* specifically is forbidden. Thus the *gemara* reconciles *Shmuel*'s statements: both for *ta'anit tzibur* and for *Tisha B'Av*, eating during *bein hashmashot* may be permitted according to *Shmuel*.

---

## Three Fast Types

### Full-Day Fasts

The *gemara* now attempts to support *Shmuel*'s position that *bein hashmashot* of *Tisha B'Av* is permitted. It cites a *braita*: *ein bein Tisha B'Av l'Yom HaKippurim ella shezeh sefeiko assur v'zeh sefeiko mutar* — the only difference between *Tisha B'Av* and *Yom Kippur* is that the doubtful period of one is forbidden and the doubtful period of the other is permitted. The immediate inference is that this *safek* refers to *bein hashmashot* — directly supporting *Shmuel*'s position that *bein hashmashot* is permitted on *Tisha B'Av*.

### Safek Comparison

The *gemara*, however, does not accept this inference straightforwardly. It invokes an alternative interpretation in the name of *Rav Sheshet brei d'Rav Idi*: *lo, l'kavia d'yarcha* — the *safek* referred to is not *bein hashmashot* but a genuine calendrical doubt about which day is *Rosh Chodesh*. In the era of the *Beis HaMikdash*, if one genuinely did not know which day was *Rosh Chodesh*, a real doubt would arise as to the date of *Yom Kippur*, and one would be required to fast both days. No such obligation applies to *Tisha B'Av* — one would never be required to keep two days. *Tosafot* makes clear that the general practice of *sfeika de'yoma* — keeping two days due to doubt — does not apply to *Yom Kippur*, and indeed there is an obvious reason: who would fast for two full consecutive days? The *gemara* acknowledges the reference to the extraordinary circumstances of the *Mir Yeshiva* in Shanghai during the Second World War, where a handful of students, uncertain about where to draw the international date line, were indeed stringent and fasted two full days of *Yom Kippur*. But this is a remarkable exception, not a general practice.

The *gemara* thus deflects the proof from the *braita*: the *safek* referred to is the calendrical doubt, not *bein hashmashot*. Admittedly, this is a somewhat strained reading, since the calendrical doubt is an unusual hypothetical — particularly so in the context of *Tisha B'Av*, where the presence of the *Beis HaMikdash* would itself dissolve the fast.

The *gemara* now shifts focus. If the *braita* implies that *Tisha B'Av* and *Yom Kippur* are otherwise equivalent in all their practices, this supports *Rabbi Elazar*, who ruled: *assur lo l'adam she'yoshit etzba'o b'mayim b'Tisha B'Av* — it is forbidden to extend even one's finger into water on *Tisha B'Av*, just as on *Yom Kippur* — *k'derech she'assur lo l'hoshit etzba'o b'Yom HaKippurim*. This is more stringent than the bathing rules of *ta'anit tzibur*, where face, hands, and feet — *panav yadav v'raglav* — are permitted.

### Pregnant Women

*Rava* expounds: *uberos umenikot mit'anot umashlimot bo* — pregnant and nursing women must fast and complete the full fast on *Tisha B'Av*, just as they do on *Yom Kippur*. This differs from the minor historical fast days, where even a generally healthy pregnant woman is exempt. On *Tisha B'Av*, the threshold is significantly higher — though whether one must reach a level of actual *sakana* or whether some intermediate threshold applies is a separate question not fully resolved here. What is clear is the basic rule: the fast is complete, parallel to *Yom Kippur*.

### Rava's Position

*Rava* concludes his exposition by stating that *bein hashmashot* of *Tisha B'Av* is forbidden — *u'vein hashmashot shelo assur*. This places *Rava* in direct disagreement with *Shmuel*, holding that *Tisha B'Av* resembles *Yom Kippur* in that the twilight period is prohibited.

### Rabbi Yochanan

The *gemara* reports that the same position — that *bein hashmashot* of *Tisha B'Av* is forbidden — was also stated in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*. But this prompts a challenge: *Rabbi Yochanan* himself stated that *Tisha B'Av eino k'ta'anit tzibur* — *Tisha B'Av* does not have the weight of a *ta'anit tzibur*. If the initial assumption of the *gemara* was that equating *Tisha B'Av* with *ta'anit tzibur* signaled that *bein hashmashot* is forbidden, then *Rabbi Yochanan*'s statement distancing *Tisha B'Av* from *ta'anit tzibur* should imply the opposite — that *bein hashmashot* is permitted.

The *gemara* therefore asks: *mai lav l'bein hashmashot* — does *Rabbi Yochanan* not mean that the distinction between them is precisely the *bein hashmashot* issue? The *gemara* rejects this: *lo, l'melacha* — no, the distinction *Rabbi Yochanan* draws concerns *melacha*. On *ta'anit tzibur*, *melacha* is forbidden; on *Tisha B'Av*, it is in principle permitted, as the *mishna* established. But this, responds the *gemara*, adds nothing new — the *mishna* already told us that *melacha* on *Tisha B'Av* is a matter of regional *minhag* and not strict prohibition. *Aval meitsar lo assar* — no one actually prohibited *melacha* on *Tisha B'Av*. So the statement of *Rabbi Yochanan* must mean something else.

The *gemara* offers two liturgical explanations. First: *l'tefillat ne'ila* — on a full-blown *ta'anit tzibur*, an additional prayer of *ne'ila* was recited, as we know from *Masechet Ta'anit*. *Tisha B'Av* does not carry this obligation. One might object that *Rabbi Yochanan* himself said *ul'vai sheyitpalel adam veholech kol hayom kulo* — would that a person would pray the entire day — implying no restriction on additional *tefillah*. But the *gemara* resolves this: *hatam chova, hacha reshut* — there, in *ta'anit tzibur*, *ne'ila* is an obligatory part of the liturgy, a formal fourth *tefillah*; here, on *Tisha B'Av*, additional prayer is merely voluntary.

A second explanation is offered: *l'esrim v'arba* — on a full *ta'anit tzibur*, six additional *brachot* of petition and supplication are inserted into the *Shmoneh Esrei*, bringing it to twenty-four. This too is not practiced on *Tisha B'Av*. The underlying distinction makes sense: the *ne'ila* and the twenty-four *brachot* belong to the structure of rain-based petitionary fasting, where the entire community stands together before God in urgent collective *bakasha*. *Tisha B'Av* is historical and mourning-based in character — not the same kind of pressing petition.

*Rav Pappa* then offers yet another reading: *ino k'rishonot ella k'achronot* — *Tisha B'Av* is not like the earlier, smaller rain-based fasts, but it is like the final, full-blown stage of the rain cycle. This effectively reinterprets *Rabbi Yochanan* to align him with *Rava*: *Tisha B'Av* is as severe as the last stage of *ta'anit tzibur*, and *bein hashmashot* is forbidden.

The *braita* is then cited again as a challenge: *ein bein Tisha B'Av l'Yom HaKippurim ella shezeh sefeiko assur v'zeh sefeiko mutar* — and the question recurs whether *safek* means *bein hashmashot* or the calendrical doubt of *Rav Sheshet brei d'Rav Idi*. The *gemara* returns to the same answer: *lo, l'kavia d'yarcha* — it refers to the genuine calendar doubt, not *bein hashmashot*. In sum: there is a genuine debate among the *rishonim* as to how we rule on eating during *bein hashmashot* of *Tisha B'Av* upon its entry, and this debate is rooted in the unresolved tensions of this *sugya*.

The *gemara* then raises a broader inference from the *braita*: if *Tisha B'Av* and *Yom Kippur* are alike in all other respects, and *Rabbi Elazar*'s ruling is supported, then a further comparison becomes relevant. A second *braita* states: *ein bein Tisha B'Av l'ta'anit tzibur ella shezeh assur b'asiyat melacha v'zeh mutar b'asiyat melacha* — the only difference between *Tisha B'Av* and *ta'anit tzibur* is the question of *melacha*: on *ta'anit tzibur*, *melacha* is forbidden; on *Tisha B'Av*, it is technically permitted. This establishes a way in which *ta'anit tzibur* is stricter than *Tisha B'Av*.

### Bathing Rules

*Rav Pappa* resolves the apparent tension between the two *baraitot* — one equating *Tisha B'Av* to *Yom Kippur*, the other to *ta'anit tzibur*: *tana kulei kulei katani* — the *tanna* is enumerating the leniencies of *Tisha B'Av* relative to each comparison point. *Tisha B'Av* is more lenient than *Yom Kippur* with respect to *safek*. It is more lenient than *ta'anit tzibur* with respect to *melacha*. But in terms of bathing, *Tisha B'Av* is actually more stringent than *ta'anit tzibur*: on *ta'anit tzibur*, *lo amru ela kol gufo* — only full-body immersion is prohibited; *aval panav yadav v'raglav lo* — washing one's face, hands, and feet is permitted. On *Tisha B'Av*, even extending a finger into water is forbidden, as *Rabbi Elazar* ruled, aligning *Tisha B'Av* with *Yom Kippur* in this regard.

The picture that emerges is not a simple continuum. *Ta'anit tzibur* prohibits *melacha* and is likely stricter regarding *bein hashmashot*, but is more lenient in bathing. *Tisha B'Av* prohibits *melacha* only as a matter of regional *minhag*, is debated regarding *bein hashmashot*, but is as strict as *Yom Kippur* in bathing. Each fast type has its own character and its own logic. The prohibition of *melacha* on *ta'anit tzibur* serves the urgent communal dimension — everyone gathered in the streets, petitioning together for rain. *Tisha B'Av*'s *aveilut* dimension is weighty and real, yet lacks the same pressing urgency, and hence *melacha* is treated differently. The bathing restriction, by contrast, has an *aveilut* component that intensifies *Tisha B'Av*'s stringency beyond what *ta'anit tzibur* demands.

### Work Restrictions

The *gemara* returns to the *mishna*'s statement that *talmidei chachamim* refrain from *melacha* everywhere, and that *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* says everyone should adopt this practice. The *gemara* infers that *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* holds *lo chashinan l'yuhara* — we are not concerned that such behavior will appear ostentatious — while the Rabbis who restrict this to *talmidei chachamim* hold *chashinan l'yuhara* — we are concerned about the appearance of sanctimony.

The *gemara* then notes a tension with another context. In the *mishna* concerning a *chassan* on his wedding night: the *tanna kamma* says that if he wishes to recite *krias shema* he may do so, despite being exempt due to distraction; *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* says *lo kol harotzeh litol es hashem yitol* — not everyone who wishes to take upon himself the reputation of piety should be entitled to. There, *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* is the one concerned about religious ostentation — the reverse of his position in our *mishna*.

---

## Yuhara Concept

### Self-Stringency

The *gemara* thus finds the positions apparently reversed. *Rabbi Yochanan* responds: *muchelefes hashita* — reverse the attributions in our *mishna*. If *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* in the *chassan* case is worried about *yuhara*, then logically the Rabbis are the ones in our *mishna* who say everyone should refrain from *melacha*, and *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* is the one who limits it to *talmidei chachamim*.

### Context Matters

*Rav Sheshet brei d'Rav Idi* disagrees: *lo tehafech* — do not reverse the positions. There is no contradiction, and both can be resolved as originally stated. *D'rabbanan ad'rabbanan lo kashya*: the Rabbis here and the Rabbis there adopt different positions without inconsistency. The key is context. In the case of *Tisha B'Av*, if everyone in the city is performing *melacha* and you alone refrain, *mechazi k'yuhara* — it looks like you are displaying piety ostentatiously. But in the case of *krias shema*, everyone else is also reciting it. If you recite it as well, you are doing exactly what everyone else does, and there is nothing conspicuous about it — *lo mechazi k'yuhara*.

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* similarly presents no contradiction. In the *krias shema* case, the *chassan* needs *kavanah* and it is well known that he cannot achieve it on his wedding night. Everyone watching knows he is a *chassan* tonight. If he recites *krias shema*, people will say he is acting as though he has *kavanah* when demonstrably he does not — that is a visible act of *yuhara*. By contrast, in the *melacha* case, if someone simply sits and does not work, no one can know the reason. He might simply have no work today.

### Idle Workers

This final point is made explicit: *amar melacha hu d'leis lei* — people will assume he simply has no work. *Puk chazi kamma batlanei ika b'shuka* — go outside and look at how many people in the marketplace are idle, not because of piety but simply because they have nothing to do at that moment. He does not stand out as someone making a show of religious stringency.

The *sugya* raises a broader question about the concept of *yuhara* in *halacha*: on one hand, religious striving and *chumra* can encourage genuine growth and aspiration; on the other hand, the concern is twofold — the communal problem of standing out in a way that alienates others or invites resentment, and the personal problem of using visible *chumrot* as a substitute for working on genuine deficiencies. The *gemara* does not resolve this tension abstractly but addresses it case by case, distinguishing when context makes behavior conspicuous and when it does not.

---

## Erev Pesach Work

### Judea/Galilee

The *gemara* now transitions back to the main topic of the *mishna* concerning *minhag* and *melacha* on *Erev Pesach* in the morning. *Chatzot* is the boundary after which no *melacha* may be done, and this applies universally. The question is the morning period. *V'Chachamim omrim* — the Sages say: *bi-Yehudah hayu osim melachah be-arvei Pesachim ad chatzot u-va-Galil lo hayu osim kol ikar* — in *Yehudah*, the practice was to perform *melacha* on *Erev Pesach* up until *chatzot*; in the *Galil*, they did not do it at all.

### Shammai/Hillel

As for the night before: *Beit Shammai* forbids it, while *Beit Hillel* permits it until sunrise. The language here is striking — *osrim* and *matirin*, the vocabulary of prohibition and permission, rather than the *minhag*-language that has governed the discussion until this point.

### Minhag or Halacha

The *gemara* notes this shift: *me-ikara tani minhaga, u-ve-sof tani issura* — initially the text speaks of custom, and then suddenly it speaks in the language of halachic prohibition. Is this a *minhag* or an actual *din*? *Rabbi Yochanan* answers: *lo kashya, ha Rabbi Meir, ha Rabbi Yehuda* — no difficulty. It is a dispute between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* about the very nature of the practice.

### Meir vs. Yehuda

A *braita* is cited in which *Rabbi Yehuda* presents the *Yehudah/Galil* distinction, and *Rabbi Meir* responds: *mah re'ayah Yehudah ve-Galil le-kan* — why should I care what they do in *Yehudah* or *Galil*? The rule is simply that you follow the *minhag* of your locale, wherever you are. The *gemara* infers from this exchange that while *Rabbi Meir* treats the entire matter as purely *minhag*, *Rabbi Yehuda*'s invocation of regional practice implies something more: an actual *psak* that differs between regions. *Minhag* does not require you to cite regional precedent to validate it — you simply follow your locale. But if *Rabbi Yehuda* is presenting *Yehudah* and *Galil* as evidence of how one should rule, he must understand this as a question of *halacha*, where different authoritative *psakim* apply in different regions. Hence it is *Rabbi Yehuda* who is the author of the *mishna*'s *Yehudah/Galil* formulation, and he who leads into the *Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel* debate, which is framed in properly halachic language.

The *gemara* then challenges whether *Rabbi Yehuda* could ever hold that *melacha* is permitted at all on the morning of the fourteenth. A *braita* teaches that if one is weeding a wheat field on the thirteenth of *Nisan* and accidentally pulls up a stalk, one may replant it in muddy soil — where it will take root — but not in hard ground. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that any planting that does not take root within three days will not take root at all. The *gemara* asks: since the stalk needs only the fourteenth, fifteenth, and part of the sixteenth to take root, why does the *braita* specify the thirteenth? If *melacha* were permitted on the fourteenth, one could simply replant on the fourteenth. This implies *Rabbi Yehuda* holds *melacha* is forbidden on the fourteenth.

*Rava* answers: *bi-Galil shanu* — the *braita* speaks of the *Galil*, where no *melacha* is done, so naturally it specifies the thirteenth. *Rav Sheshet brei d'Rav Idi* adds: and as for the night before, *Beit Shammai* prohibits it as well, so the *braita* reflects the most stringent position. *Rav Ashi* responds: even assuming *Beit Hillel*, it is simply not the practice of people to weed their fields at night — a practical observation rather than a halachic one. *Ravina* offers a further resolution: even in *Yehudah*, where some do *melacha* in the morning, the principle of *miktzas hayom kekulo* — a partial day counting as the whole — only applies once; one cannot apply it to two partial days simultaneously, and therefore the thirteenth is specified regardless.

The broader tension underlying the *Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel* dispute concerns how formally to treat the day. *Beit Shammai* treats the entire day including the night as a unit requiring preparation-mode from the outset. *Beit Hillel* takes a more practical view: the morning hours before *chatzot* are the pressing time for *hachanos*, and that is where the focus should be. The question of how to balance the formal dimension of sanctifying the entire day against the practical urgency of the morning is genuine and unresolved by neat formula.

The *gemara* also touches on the broader phenomenon by which *minhag* becomes *halachisized* — a process visible in *Erev Pesach* work restrictions, in *kitniyot*, and in the customs of *sefira*. Some practices remain clearly in the domain of *minhag* without acquiring formal halachic status; others are subjected to the full apparatus of *psak halacha*. What determines which category a practice falls into is itself an interesting question.

---

## Completing Work

### Two Conditions

The *mishna* now states: *Rabbi Meir omer kol melacha she-hitchil bah kodem le-arba'ah asar gomra b'arba'ah asar* — any *melacha* that one began before the fourteenth may be completed on the fourteenth. *Aval lo yatchil bah betchilah b'arba'ah asar* — but one may not begin something new on the fourteenth, even if there would be time to complete it. This allowance to finish previously started work holds even in locales where *melacha* is otherwise not done on the morning of *Erev Pesach*. Then the *mishna* states that the *Chachamim* identify three crafts — *chayatin* (tailors), *saparim* (barbers), and *kovsin* (launderers) — who may work on *Erev Pesach* regardless of *minhag*.

### Tzorech Hamoed

The *gemara* raises a question: does *Rabbi Meir*'s allowance to finish previously started *melacha* apply only when the work is *l'tzorech hamoed* — in service of the festival — or even when it is not? And conversely, does *l'tzorech hamoed* alone, without having started earlier, suffice to permit beginning anew? Three logical possibilities emerge: first, that both criteria — *l'tzorech hamoed* and having started earlier — are required; second, that either one is sufficient; third, that *l'tzorech hamoed* is irrelevant and the only operative factor is whether one began earlier, in which case finishing is always permitted.

### Small Objects

A *braita* is cited: *aval lo yatchil betchilah b'arba'ah asar afilu tzilzul katan, afilu shvacha ktana* — one may not begin anew on the fourteenth, even something as small as a little belt or a tiny woven cap that takes only minutes to complete. The *gemara* probes what the word *afilu* — "even" — is emphasizing. Is it saying that even these small *l'tzorech hamoed* items may not be started? The *gemara* considers but rejects this reading. The *chiddush* of the *braita* is different: one might have thought that for such tiny items, starting them is effectively the same as finishing, since the whole *melacha* is completed so quickly. The *braita* teaches that even so, beginning counts as beginning — *l'chatchila matchil bahen nami l'chatchila* — and does not receive the finishing exemption. The *braita* thus does not resolve the *l'tzorech hamoed* question.

### Both Required

A clearer *braita* is then cited: *Rabbi Meir omer kol melacha shehi l'tzorech hamoed gomra b'arba'ah asar; eimatai, bizman shehit'chil bah kodem arba'ah asar; aval lo hit'chil bah kodem arba'ah asar, lo yatchil bah b'arba'ah asar* — any *melacha* that is *l'tzorech hamoed* may be finished on the fourteenth, but only if it was begun before the fourteenth; if it was not begun before the fourteenth, it may not be started anew even though it is *l'tzorech hamoed*. This would seem to establish clearly that both criteria are required.

The *gemara* attempts to escape this conclusion by suggesting that the *braita*'s mention of *l'tzorech hamoed* is incidental — that even *shelo l'tzorech hamoed* one could finish, and *l'tzorech hamoed* is mentioned only to teach that even so, one cannot begin afresh. But this reading is strained. A final, unambiguous *braita* settles the matter: *kol melacha shehi l'tzorech hamoed gomra b'arba'ah asar, v'sheino l'tzorech hamoed assur* — any *melacha* that is *l'tzorech hamoed* may be finished; anything not *l'tzorech hamoed* is forbidden. Both criteria are required: the work must have been started before the fourteenth and must serve the purpose of the *moed*. This applies specifically in locales where *melacha* is not generally permitted in the morning — in places where the *minhag* allows it, no special license is needed.

---

## Permitted Professions

### Three Crafts

The *mishna* states that the *Chachamim* permit three crafts to work on *Erev Pesach* regardless of local *minhag*: tailors, barbers, and launderers. Separately, *Rabbi Yossi bar Yehudah* adds shoemakers.

### Other Contexts

A *braita* provides the rationale, not by directly invoking *l'tzorech hamoed* for *Erev Pesach*, but by pointing to leniencies extended to these crafts in other halachic contexts. Tailors: *sheken hedyot tofer k'darko b'cholo shel moed* — a layperson is permitted to sew in the ordinary fashion on *Chol Hamoed*, so there is precedent for treating sewing as permissible even in restricted periods. Barbers and launderers: *sheken habaim mimedinat hayam v'hayotzim mibeit ha'asurim mesaprim umachavsin b'cholo shel moed* — those who return from overseas travel or emerge from prison are permitted to get a haircut and launder their clothes on *Chol Hamoed*, clearly based on the principle of *kvod haregel*. Since these leniencies exist in contexts that are halachically restricted — namely *Chol Hamoed*, where the *Masechet Moed Katan* treats these very activities as *assur* except for specific exceptions — the *gemara* takes those exceptions and generalizes them as the basis for permitting these professions on *Erev Pesach* even in places where *melacha* is otherwise not done.

### Shoemakers

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Betira* adds shoemakers: *sheken olei regalim metaknim man'aleihem b'chol hamoed* — pilgrims ascending to *Yerushalayim* are permitted to repair their sandals on *Chol Hamoed*, since they have been walking throughout their journey and have had no opportunity to do so.

### Inference Method

The dispute between the Sages and *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Betira* over whether to include shoemakers turns on an inferential principle: *mar savar lemedin techilat melacha misof melacha* — one position holds that we may learn the permissibility of making shoes (the beginning of the craft) from the permission to repair shoes (the end of the craft). *U'mar savar ein lemedin techilat melacha misof melacha* — the other position holds that one may not generalize in this way: the fact that we allow repair under certain circumstances does not mean we allow the full craft of shoemaking, and therefore the profession as a whole does not receive the general exemption. The entire framing in terms of analogical reasoning from other contexts is notable — rather than a direct *l'tzorech hamoed* analysis, the *gemara* grounds the leniency in the logic of existing exceptions elsewhere in the halachic system.

---

---

# Pesachim 56

## Work on Erev Pesach

### Intro & Chatzos

The daf begins mid-*mishna*, picking up from 55b, in the context of the prohibition of *melachah* on *Erev Pesach*. The discussion is transitioning from the realm of *minhag* — regional custom — into more formally defined *halachic* territory. It is possible that the *mishna* is also addressing the period after *chatzos*, when the prohibition is universally agreed upon and no longer merely a matter of custom.

The previous *mishna* had dealt with the concept of *tzorech hamoed* and completing *melachah* in ways that warranted leniency. This *mishna* turns to analogous activities that are permitted, presumably on account of *hefsed* — the concern for financial loss.

### Hens on Eggs

The *mishna* states: *moshivin shovchin letarnigolim b'yod daled*, that one may have hens sit on eggs on the fourteenth of Nisan, and if a hen ran away, *vetarnigolet shebarchah machzirin otah limkomah* — one may return it to its nest. Rashi offers two readings of *moshivin shovchin*: either it is a single phrase referring to setting hens upon eggs, or it refers to two distinct acts — settling doves in a dovecote and having chickens sit on eggs. In either case, the practical point is that one may arrange for hens to sit on eggs on the fourteenth so that the eggs will be fertilized and hatch, thereby preventing loss. The *mishna* adds that if a hen dies, one may substitute another in its place — *ve-im metah moshivin acheret tachteiah*. All of these acts are permitted in order to guard against possible loss.

### Sweeping Dung

The *mishna* continues: *gorfin mitachat raglei behemah b'yod daled ubamoed mesalkin litzedadin* — one may sweep the dung from beneath the legs of animals on the fourteenth, removing it entirely from the barn, while on *Chol HaMoed* one may only sweep it to the sides. One observes here that the *melachah* under discussion is emphatically not *melachah* in the sense of the thirty-nine prohibited labors; it refers, rather, to the kind of ordinary physical work one would associate with going about one's daily occupation.

### Vessels from Uman

The *mishna* states further: *molichin kelim umevi'im mibeit ha-uman af al pi she'einam letzorech hamoed* — one may bring vessels to and take them back from the craftsman's house, even if they are not needed for the festival. The precise basis for this leniency is less immediately clear. It does not appear to involve *hefsed* in the same straightforward sense as the preceding cases, and the *mishna* itself emphasizes that it applies even when the vessels are not required for the *moed*.

---

## Returning Hens Debate

### Abaye on Returns

The *Gemara* opens with a pointed question: *hashta otuvei motvinan* — the *mishna* permits one to set hens upon eggs in the first place, so *ahadorei mibaiya*? Is it even a question that one may return them once they have already been sitting? Returning them would seem to involve an even clearer concern for *hefsed*. Abaye resolves this by explaining that *seifa atan l'cholo shel moed* — the latter clause of the *mishna* is in fact addressing *Chol HaMoed*. On the fourteenth, one may even place hens on eggs *lechatchilah*; on *Chol HaMoed*, one may not do so *lechatchilah*, but one may return a hen that has wandered.

### Rav Huna 3 Days

Rav Huna then qualifies the scope of the allowance to return a hen on *Chol HaMoed*: *lo shanu ela betoch sheloshah l'mirdah* — the permission applies only within three days of the hen's rebellion and flight, because *dekarir uparash chamimuta minah* — within this window, its warmth has not yet entirely dissipated and there remains a natural inclination for it to return to the eggs. Beyond this, the hen will neither be willing nor useful. In addition, Rav Huna restricts the allowance to *betoch sheloshah l'yeshivatah* — only after the hen has already been sitting for three days, *de-pseida de-bei'ei*, because by that point the eggs have begun to fertilize and their loss would be total if the hen does not continue. If the hen rebelled more than three days ago, *deparach uparash chamimuta minah*, its warmth has fled entirely. Or if it is within the first three days of sitting, the eggs have not yet substantially fertilized and one may still simply use them as ordinary eggs — in either such case, *lo mahadrinan*, one may not force the hen to return, since the justification of *hefsed* is insufficient.

### Hefsed Merubah

Rabbi Ami disagrees: *afilu betoch shlosha liyeshivata mahadrinan* — even within the first three days of the hen's sitting, when the eggs have only begun to fertilize, one may nevertheless return the hen. That degree of loss is already sufficient justification. The *Gemara* identifies the crux of their dispute: *mar savar hefsed merubeh chashashu, hefsed muat lo chashashu* — one authority holds that the rabbis permitted intervention only for major loss, not minor loss, while the other holds *hefsed muat nami chashashu* — even minor loss is sufficient grounds. It is worth noting the relative scale involved: we are speaking of the difference in value between a fertilized egg that fails to hatch and one that does not — sums that in absolute terms are quite small, yet they are nonetheless treated as meaningful gradations of *hefsed merubeh* and *hefsed muat* relative to the value of the object at stake.

---

## Dung Removal

### Chatzer Contradiction

The *Gemara* turns to the second clause of the *mishna* regarding sweeping dung. A *baraita* is cited: *hazeval shebachatzer mesalkin oto latzedadim* — dung in the *chatzer* (the shared courtyard, familiar from the discussions in Eruvin) may be swept to the sides. The *baraita* then states *shebarefet ushevachatzer motzi'in oto le'ashpah* — dung in the barn or in the *chatzer* may actually be carried out to the garbage dump entirely. The internal contradiction regarding the *chatzer* is immediately apparent: *hagufa kashya* — does one sweep it to the sides, or remove it to the dump? The initial distinction between barn and courtyard — that a barn contains far more dung and thus warrants greater leniency — does not resolve the problem, since the *baraita* states contradictory things about the *chatzer* itself.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye resolves the contradiction by applying the same principle he articulated earlier: *kan beyod-daled vekan becholo shel moed* — one clause addresses the fourteenth and the other *Chol HaMoed*. In this case the order is inverted from what might be expected: the first statement — that one may only sweep to the sides — applies to *Chol HaMoed*, while the second — that one may remove entirely to the dump — is the more expansive allowance granted on the fourteenth. The same logic operates throughout: the fourteenth permits more than *Chol HaMoed*.

### Rava Alternative

Rava offers an alternative resolution: *ha veha becholo shel moed* — both statements may be referring to *Chol HaMoed*, and there is no contradiction. *Ve-hakhi ka'amar*: the general rule for the *chatzer* is that one may only sweep to the sides. However, *ei na'aseh chatzer kerefet* — if the quantity of dung in the *chatzer* has grown so great that it resembles a barn, then *motzi'in oto le'ashpah* — one may remove it entirely to the dump. The allowance thus tracks not the time period but the quantity of the dung. One notes also the parallel to *geraf shel rei* in the laws of *muktzeh*, where the presence of excrement creates exceptional leniency because of the profound discomfort it causes.

---

## Vessels Trust

### Rav Papa Question

Rav Papa reports that Rava once tested his students with the following difficulty. The *mishna* states *molichin umevi'im kelim mibeit ha-uman af al pi she'eino letzorech hamoed* — one may bring vessels to and from the craftsman even when they are not needed for the festival. Against this, a *baraita* states *ein mevi'in kelim mibeit ha-uman* — one may not retrieve vessels from the craftsman. The *baraita* adds that *ve-im choshesh lahen shema yignavu* — if one fears that the vessels may be stolen, one may place them in another nearby courtyard, but one may not bring them home directly. The tension with the *mishna* is clear: one source permits retrieval outright, the other forbids it even when there is concern for the safety of the vessels.

### Gemara Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction in the standard manner: *kan bearba'ah asar vekan becholo shel moed* — the blanket permission belongs to the fourteenth, the restricted allowance applies on *Chol HaMoed*. Alternatively, *ve-i ba'it eima*, both may be addressing *Chol HaMoed*, and the distinction is *kan bema'amino vekan beshe'eino ma'amino* — in one case one trusts the craftsman, in the other one does not. Rashi explains that "trusting him" means one is not concerned that the craftsman will either demand re-payment or sell the vessels if they are not promptly retrieved. When one does trust him in this sense, one is afforded less latitude, since the urgency is lower. When one does not trust him — fearing either that he will sell the item or demand additional payment — a broader allowance is granted.

### Zilzul Yom Tov?

A question arises as to whether the underlying concern is *zilzul yom tov* — the concept known from Moed Katan, whereby one is pressed to complete such errands before the festival so as not to treat *Chol HaMoed* as an opportunity to catch up on ordinary business. The issue of *melachah* on *Chol HaMoed* encompasses two distinct categories: certain prohibitions, such as those involving haircuts and laundering, are specifically designed to ensure that matters are attended to before the festival; others reflect the principle that *Chol HaMoed* is *mikzat yom tov* and thus certain labors are simply forbidden. Which category governs the case of vessels from the craftsman is not entirely clear. It is possible that the entire framework here is about ensuring one takes care of these matters beforehand — which would explain why the fourteenth carries a blanket allowance, a structure parallel to the allowances regarding haircuts already discussed in prior material.

### Baraita Vessels

A *baraita* is cited in support of these distinctions. It permits one to retrieve items like a pitcher from the potter or a glass vessel from a glassblower — things that have immediate *tzorech hamoed* utility — but not dyed wool or ordinary vessels that have no particular use during the festival. If the craftsman needs his fee and has no other means of support, one may go and pay him, but still may not take the vessels home. If one does not trust the craftsman to hold the item securely, one may transfer the vessels to a nearby house. If one fears even that location is vulnerable to theft, *mivi'an betzina betoch beito* — one may bring them home quietly. The *Gemara* then notes that this *baraita* addresses the case of retrieval but does not resolve the question of *molichin* — dropping the vessels off. The *mishna* permits this while the *baraita*'s formulation implies it is forbidden, and explaining one direction of the transaction does not automatically account for the other.

---

## Jericho Practices

### Jericho Intro

The *Gemara* now presents a *baraita* describing six practices of the people of Jericho (*anshei Yericho*): three regarding which the Sages did not protest, and three which they did protest. The thematic connection to the preceding discussion is twofold: one of the practices relates to *melachah* on the fourteenth, and the broader subject — variation in local practice and the rabbinic response thereto — continues the discussion of *minhag* and deviation from standard norms.

### No Protest

The three practices regarding which the Sages did not protest are as follows. First, *markivin dekalim kol hayom* — they would graft palm trees the entire day of the fourteenth, even in the afternoon when *melachah* would ordinarily be forbidden. This was apparently tolerated because of *hefsed* concerns. Second, *vekorchin et shema* — they would "wrap" the *Shema*, reading straight through without the appropriate separation; the meaning of this will be elaborated below. Third, *vekotzrin vegodshin lifnei ha'omer* — they would cut their grain and bind it into sheaves before the *Omer* offering was brought. This would seem to violate the principle of *reishit ketzirchem*, the biblical prohibition on harvesting before the *Omer*. However, the grain of Jericho — growing as it did in the valley — was not considered of sufficient quality for use as the *Omer*, which required grain from higher ground. Since it could not be brought for the *Omer*, there was no biblical prohibition on harvesting it beforehand. There might have been a rabbinic concern that one could inadvertently come to eat from it, but the Sages did not protest.

### With Protest

The three practices against which the Sages did protest are as follows. First, *matirin gamziyot shel hekdesh* — they would permit the additional growths that sprouted from sycamore trees after these trees had been consecrated as *hekdesh*. Once a tree is sanctified, the later growth that emerges after one trims it and new shoots proliferate should retain its sanctified status; the people of Jericho held that this subsequent growth was permitted. Second, *ve'ochlin mitachat hanesharim beShabbat* — they would eat on *Shabbat* from produce that had fallen off trees, which raises a *muktzeh* concern or another *Shabbat* problem. Third, *venotnin pe'ah leyarak* — they would designate *pe'ah*, the corner of the field left for the poor, from vegetables. The difficulty with this seemingly generous practice is that *pe'ah* is exempt from *terumot u'ma'asrot*. Since vegetables are ordinarily not subject to the obligation of *pe'ah*, the people of Jericho's designation of *pe'ah* from vegetables did not actually exempt the produce from tithes — meaning the poor were consuming *tevel*, untithed produce. This is why the Sages protested.

---

## Hezekiah Actions

### Actions Approved

The *Gemara* continues with a parallel *baraita* concerning King Hezekiah (*Chizkiyahu HaMelech*): *shisha devarim asah Chizkiyahu haMelech, al shlosha hodu lo ve'al shlosha lo hodu lo* — six things Hezekiah did, three of which the Sages approved and three of which they did not. The three they approved: first, *girer atzmot aviv al mita shel chavalim* — he dragged his father's bones in the street on a bier of ropes rather than carrying them in a coffin with proper honor. His father was Achaz, who had led the people into idolatry. Despite the obligations of *kibbud av va'em* and respect for the dead, this act of public dishonor was considered necessary for *Kiddush Hashem* — to express condemnation of Achaz's idolatrous reign and to help restore the people to the proper religious path. The Sages agreed. Second, *ve-khitet nekhash ha-nekhoshet* — he ground up the copper serpent that Moses had made, because people had begun to worship it or employ it in healing rituals, treating it as a magical object. Destroying it was similarly an act of religious restoration. Third, *ganaz Sefer Refuot* — he hid the book of healing, and the Sages agreed with this as well.

### Rambam & Medicine

The nature of the *Sefer Refuot* is a matter of significant debate. One view is that it was simply a straightforward medical text, and Hezekiah hid it because he wished to encourage people to pray to God when ill, rather than turning to human remedies. The Rambam famously and forcefully rejects this interpretation. He argues that the use of rational faculties to address illness and physical hardship is not only permitted but expected. In his view, one thanks God for healing not because one expects miraculous intervention but because God has endowed the human intellect with the capacity to develop medicine, and has given the physician the skill to heal — and this is itself *yad Hashem*. One need not forgo natural means of healing in order to acknowledge divine providence. The Rambam therefore suggests that the *Sefer Refuot*, analogous to the copper serpent, contained magical or incantation-based healing methods — the type of quasi-idolatrous practice that warranted suppression — and that it was this, not legitimate medicine, that Hezekiah sought to eradicate.

### Actions Disapproved
