The three actions the Sages did not approve: first, *kitzetz daltot shel Heikhal ve-shigar le-melekh Ashur* — he cut off the golden doors of the *Heikhal* and sent them to the king of Assyria as tribute. The Sages held that he should have placed greater trust in God. Second, *setam mei Gichon ha-elyon* — he sealed the upper waters of the Gichon spring, so that a besieging army could not benefit from them. Again, the Sages felt this reflected insufficient faith. Third, *ve-ibar Nisan be-Nisan* — he intercalated the year and declared an additional month of Adar while Nisan had already begun. The halacha requires that a leap year be declared before Nisan commences; a *leap year* intercalation cannot be effected once Nisan has already begun. The Sages did not agree with this action. The Talmud notes that while all three disapproved actions find some textual basis in *pesukim*, the first two are more explicitly grounded there.

---

## Palm Grafting

### Rav Yehuda Method

Having introduced the practice of *markivin dekalim* in the Jericho *baraita*, the *Gemara* now inquires *heikhi avid* — what exactly does this grafting procedure involve? Rav Yehuda describes the following method: one takes a moist myrtle branch (*asa dara*), combines it with a resinous sap from a particular tree (*shikhla de-dafna*), and barley flour that has been sitting in a vessel for fewer than forty days since grinding (*kimcha de-sa'arei de-rami be-mana de-lo khalfei aleih arba'in yomin*). This mixture is then heated and poured into the heart of the palm tree. Rav Yehuda adds that any palm trees standing within four *amot* of the treated tree that do not receive a similar treatment will immediately wither. This procedure, then, is less a conventional graft than a medicinal or restorative treatment applied to the tree.

### Rav Acha Method

Rav Acha the son of Rava offers a different description: *manchi kufra dikhra le-nukveta* — one takes a branch from a male palm and inserts it into a corresponding hole bored into a branch of a female palm. This is a genuine graft in the more familiar sense of the term. One might ask whether this constitutes *kilayim* — the forbidden crossbreeding of species — but since both trees are palm trees, no such prohibition applies.

---

## Wrapping Shema

### Shema V'ahavta

The *Gemara* now turns to the second practice of the people of Jericho: *korchin et shema* — wrapping the *Shema*. The concern is the transition between *Shema Yisrael* and *Ve'ahavta*. These two passages are fundamentally different in character: the *Shema* is a declaration of faith, an assertion, while *Ve'ahavta* is a commandment — not a statement of belief but a statement of obligation. A break between them is therefore required. The practice of the people of Jericho was to run from one directly into the other without such a break.

### Rashi Break

Rashi explains that the break is necessary because the two sections are qualitatively distinct. The *Shema* functions as a kind of *ani maamin*, an affirmation addressed to oneself and to one's fellow Jews. *Ve'ahavta*, by contrast, returns to the standard language of Torah obligation. The transition from one mode to the other demands a pause.

### Rava Pause

Rava offers a different reading of the *korchin* practice. He maintains that the people of Jericho did in fact pause between *Shema* and *Ve'ahavta* — *mafsikin hayu*. Their error, however, lay elsewhere: *ella shehayu omrim hayom al levavecha* — they combined the phrase *asher anochi metzavecha hayom al levavecha* in a way that implied "today it shall be upon your heart, but not tomorrow," distorting its meaning by an irregular break in the verse.

### Tannaim Debate

A *baraita* is cited that maps this dispute back to a *tannaic* debate. Rabbi Meir holds that the practice of *korchin* meant *velo hayu mafsikin* — they would recite *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* and flow straight into *Ve'ahavta* without any pause whatsoever. Rabbi Yehuda holds *mafsikin hayu* — they did pause — *ella shelo hayu omrim Baruch Shem kevod malchuto l'olam va'ed* — but they did not insert the *Baruch Shem* as the break. Both *tannaim* agree that *korchin* denotes an insufficient separation between *Shema* and *Ve'ahavta*; they differ on whether the deficiency was a complete absence of any break or merely the omission of *Baruch Shem*.

### Jacob Midrash

The *Gemara* then asks why we ourselves recite *Baruch Shem kevod malchuto l'olam va'ed* at all, given that it does not appear in the text of the Torah. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish expounds the following *midrash*: the verse states *vayikra Yaakov el banav vayomer he'asvu ve'agidah lachem et asher yikra etchem be'acharit hayamim* — Jacob called his sons and said, "Gather, and I will tell you what will befall you at the end of days." Yet what follows in the Torah is not a prophecy of the end of days but a series of blessings, descriptions, and pronouncements. The *Gemara* understands this gap by saying that *bikeish Yaakov legalot le-vanav keitz hayamin* — Jacob sought to reveal the end of days to his sons, but *venistalkah mimenu Shechinah* — the divine presence departed from him at that moment, preventing the revelation.

Jacob was seized by anxiety: *shema chas ve-shalom yesh be-mitati pasul* — perhaps, God forbid, one among his descendants is unworthy, as had been the case with Abraham, from whom Ishmael had come forth, and with his father Isaac, from whom Esau had emerged. In response, his sons declared: *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* — "Hear, O Israel" — addressing Jacob by his name Israel — "the Lord is our God, the Lord is one." They were assuring him: just as for you there is only one God, so too for us — we are entirely faithful. Upon hearing this, Jacob responded: *Baruch Shem kevod malchuto l'olam va'ed* — blessed is the name of His glorious kingdom forever, an expression of relief and gratitude that all his sons were true believers.

### Resolution Softly

The Sages then faced a practical dilemma: *heikhi na'avid* — what should we do with *Baruch Shem*? If we recite it, *lo amaro Moshe Rabbeinu* — Moses did not include it in the Torah text. If we omit it, *amaro Yaakov* — Jacob said it, and it has this powerful responsive function in the context of the *Shema*. The resolution was *hitkinu sheyehu omrim oto bechashai* — they ordained that it be recited quietly. In this way, it fulfills its function as a break and a response to the declaration of *Shema*, while maintaining the integrity of the Torah text as it flows from *Shema* to *Ve'ahavta*. A *mashal* is offered: it is like a princess who caught the scent of a pot of humble stew and desired it. To give it to her openly would be beneath her dignity; to refuse her would cause her distress. So her servants brought it to her quietly. Similarly, *Baruch Shem* is recited — because it belongs there and serves an important purpose — but it is said in a whisper, so as not to visibly disrupt the flow of the Torah's text.

### Minim Challenge

Rabbi Abbahu adds a further historical note: *hitkinu sheyihyu omrim oto bekol ram mipnei taromet ha-minim* — at some point an ordinance was issued to recite *Baruch Shem* aloud, on account of the provocations of the *minim*, the heretics. Rashi explains that the *minim* would mock the practice of whispering, accusing the Sages of inserting words into the liturgy and then being embarrassed by them. To counter this charge, the practice in some communities was to say *Baruch Shem* loudly, demonstrating that there was no shame in the recitation. The *Gemara* notes that in Nehardea, where there were no *minim*, the practice remained to say it quietly. Over time, of course, the universal practice returned to reciting it in a whisper, as we do today — except on *Yom Kippur*, when it is said aloud.

---

## Jericho Mishna

### Mishna No Protest

The *Gemara* now presents a parallel *baraita* that restates the Jericho practices with some variation from the *mishna*, and the *mishna* itself then provides a summary. Both agree on the three practices against which the Sages did not protest: *markivin dekalim kol hayom* — attending to the palm trees the entire day; *korchin et shema* — wrapping the *Shema*; and *vekotzrin vegodshin lifnei ha'omer* — both the cutting and the bundling of grain before the *Omer*. The *baraita* separates the cutting from the bundling and treats only the cutting as unprotested; the bundling (*godshin*) is listed among the disputed practices, on the grounds that binding grain into sheaves creates greater concern that one will come to eat from it before the *Omer* is brought. The *mishna*, however, groups both cutting and bundling together among the practices the Sages did not protest.

Rabbi Yehuda raises a structural objection to the *baraita*'s formulation: if the Sages truly acquiesced in these practices, *kol adam osim ken* — why was it only the people of Jericho who followed them? If the Sages endorsed the practice, everyone should have adopted it. He therefore maintains *ella eilu ve'eilu shelo birtzon chachamim hayu osim* — in truth, the Sages disapproved of all six practices. The distinction in the *mishna* is not between approval and disapproval, but between active protest and silence: *al sheloshah miche b'yadam ve'al sheloshah lo miche* — three they formally protested, three they did not.

### Mishna Protest

The *mishna* lists the three practices the Sages did formally protest. First, *matirin gamziyot shel hekdesh shel charuv veshel shikma* — permitting the new growths from sanctified carob and sycamore trees; these should remain *hekdesh* and may not simply be declared permitted. Second, *portzin pratzot begannotayhen u'fardesayhen le'ha'achil nesher la'aniyim bishabbatot ve'yamim tovim bishnei batzoret* — breaching the fences of their gardens and orchards so that the poor could enter on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* in years of famine to eat from produce that had fallen. While the motivation was charitable, consuming fallen produce on *Shabbat* raises concerns of *muktzeh* or other *Shabbat* prohibitions, and accordingly the Sages protested. Third, *notnim pe'ah leyarak* — designating *pe'ah* from vegetables. As discussed, vegetables are not biblically subject to *pe'ah*, and the unilateral designation of *pe'ah* from them does not exempt the produce from *terumot u'ma'asrot*; the poor thus consume *tevel*, and for this reason the Sages protested.

---

---

# Pesachim 59

## Tamid & Pesach Order

### Tamid Timing

The fifth *perek* of *Pesachim*, *Tamid Nishchat*, opens a vast central section of the tractate — roughly fifty *daf* in length, equal in size to all the rest of *Pesachim* combined — that deals almost exclusively with *korbanos* and the bringing of the *korban pesach*. One could easily imagine this material having been placed in *Seder Kodashim*.

The *gemara* picks up from where the previous *daf* concluded, at the bottom of 58b, two lines from the end. The *korban tamid* — the daily afternoon sacrifice — is ordinarily slaughtered at 8.5 halachic hours (2:30 PM) and offered on the *mizbe'ach* at 9.5 hours (3:30 PM). On *erev Pesach*, however, it was brought earlier to allow sufficient time for the *korban pesach*, and when *erev Pesach* fell on *erev Shabbat*, it was moved even earlier still — as early as 6.5 hours (12:30 PM), the earliest permissible time for *mincha* and therefore the earliest the afternoon *tamid* can be brought. The underlying assumption is that the *korban pesach* comes after the afternoon *tamid*, even though the general rule is that no *korban* follows the afternoon *tamid* — it is the last of the day's *korbanos*.

### Erev & Bein Arbayim

The *baraisa* cited at the top of 59a articulates the hierarchy: *tamid kodem l'Pesach* — the *tamid* comes before the *korban pesach*; *Pesach kodem l'ketores* — the *pesach* precedes the afternoon *ketores*; and *haketores kodemes l'neiros* — the *ketores* precedes the lighting of the *menorah*. These two final services — burning the incense and lighting the *neiros* — were performed not in the outer *azarah* but in the inner *heichal*, the roofed interior of the *Beit Hamikdash*. The question is how we know any of this ordering, and the *gemara* proceeds to derive it.

*Ye'achar davar shene'emar bo ba'erev u'vein ha'arbayim* — something is placed later when the *Torah* describes it using both the term *erev* and the term *bein ha'arbayim*. By the *korban pesach*, the *Torah* uses both: *tishchat es haPesach ba'erev* (Deuteronomy 16:6) and *v'shachatu oso kol kehal adas Yisrael bein ha'arbayim* (Exodus 12:6). This double language of the afternoon period signals that the *pesach* comes as late as possible in the day. By contrast, the *tamid* uses only the single term *bein ha'arbayim*: *es hakeves hasheni ta'ase bein ha'arbayim* (Numbers 28:4). Therefore the *korban pesach*, marked by the double afternoon language, comes later than the *tamid*, which carries only the single term.

### Erev Definition

The terms deserve clarification. *Erev* does not mean night — it means the darkening, the waning of the day, the late afternoon. The word shares a root with *ma'arav*, the west, because the sun begins to set toward the west as the afternoon progresses. *Bein ha'arbayim* — literally "between the two *erevs*" — spans from the moment the sun passes its midday zenith and begins its descent to the moment it actually dips below the western horizon. The entire afternoon period thus constitutes *bein ha'arbayim*, while *layla* proper begins only with nightfall.

This is also the occasion to note the important *Rashbam* at the very beginning of the *Torah* on *vayehi erev vayehi voker yom echad*. The *Rashbam* argues that the *pshat* is not that the day begins with the night. Rather, *vayehi erev* means the sun set at the end of the day of creation, and *vayehi voker* means it rose the following morning, completing the previous day. In this reading, *erev* and *boker* demarcate the natural day — from sunrise to daybreak — rather than the halachic day that begins at nightfall.

### Pesach Double Language

Returning to the *gemara*'s argument: the double language of *erev* and *bein ha'arbayim* by the *korban pesach* establishes that it comes later than something that carries only the single term *bein ha'arbayim* — which is the *tamid*. This derives the first element of the ordering.

The *gemara* then raises an immediate question: if that is the logic, why shouldn't the *ketores* and *neiros* also precede the *korban pesach*? Those services likewise use only the single term *bein ha'arbayim*, not the double language. By the same reasoning, the *pesach* — with its double language — should come even after the *ketores* and *neiros*. This is precisely the question the *gemara* takes up.

### Menora & Incense

The *gemara* answers: *shani hasam dimi'at Rachmana oso* — there it is different, because the *Torah* excludes by the word *oso*. A *baraisa* is cited: the verse says *yaaroch oso Aharon u'vanav me'erev ad boker* — Aaron and his sons shall arrange *it*, the *menorah*, from evening until morning (Exodus 27:21). From *me'erev ad boker* we derive that one must provide enough oil for the *menorah* to burn through even the longest winter night. But a second teaching is derived as well: *ein lecha avoda shekesheira me'erev ad boker ela zo bilvad* — this is the only *avoda* in the *Beit Hamikdash* that runs from evening until morning. Why? Because the verse says *yaaroch oso* — *it*, and only *it*, spans the entire night. Nothing else runs from evening through morning.

### Menora Night Service

The force of the word *oso* is understood on two levels. It limits the nighttime duration to the *neiros* alone, but it also implies something about when the *hadlakas neiros* begins: precisely because the *menorah* is meant to burn throughout the entire night, starting from *me'erev*, it must be lit as late as possible in the afternoon, right at the threshold of nightfall. *Oso* therefore teaches that only the *neiros* begin at the very end of the afternoon and extend through the night — nothing else shares that property. This is how the *gemara* establishes that the *neiros* occupy the absolute latest slot in the daily sequence of *avodot*.

A student raises the intuitive point that one lights candles when it begins to grow dark precisely so they can be seen and tended before full darkness sets in — especially since the *avodah* in the *Beit Hamikdash* was fundamentally a daytime service. Nighttime activity in the *mikdash* was generally limited to completion work, such as burning leftover fats; active *avodah* was a daytime enterprise. Lighting the *neiros* at the very last moment of the day, while one can still see, makes practical sense on both grounds.

---

## Ketores & Neiros

### Ketores Linked

The *gemara* adds: *v'ikish ketores l'neiros* — the *ketores* is linked to the *neiros* through a shared verse. The verse in Exodus 30:8 reads: *u've'haalos Aharon es ha-neros bein ha'arbayim yaktirenah* — and when Aaron raises the flames of the *menorah* in the afternoon, he shall burn the incense. Because the two services appear together in a single verse, they are understood to occur at or near the same time, both toward the end of the afternoon.

### Pesach Before

The first opinion — which the *gemara* ultimately endorses — holds that the *korban pesach* comes before the *ketores* and *neiros*. The sequence is: *tamid*, then *pesach*, then *ketores*, then *neiros*.

### Neiros Last

The *gemara* then introduces a *baraisa* that actually sides with the position the questioner raised: *tamid kodem l'ketores, ketores kodemes l'neiros, v'neiros kodmin l'Pesach* — the *tamid* comes first, then the *ketores*, then the *neiros*, and only then the *korban pesach*. The *baraisa*'s reasoning is precisely the double-language argument: since *pesach* says both *erev* and *bein ha'arbayim*, it should come last of everything.

### Oso Exclusion

The *gemara* challenges this *baraisa*: but the verse said *oso* — only the *neiros* extend from evening to morning, and from that exclusion we derived that the *neiros* come at the very latest. How can the *pesach* then come even after the *neiros*?

The answer is that the word *oso* is needed for a different limitation: *le'mi'utei avoda she'bifnim* — to tell us that the *neiros* come last only among the services performed *bifnim*, inside the *heichal*. The *heichal* housed the *menorah*, the *shulchan*, and the golden *mizbe'ach* — all under a roof, as distinct from the outdoor *azarah*. The word *oso* therefore says: of the interior services, the *neiros* come absolutely last. Between the two interior services — *ketores* and *neiros* — the *neiros* come after.

### Ketores First

But why would one have thought the *ketores* should come after the *neiros*? Because the verse reads *u've'haalos Aharon es ha-neros bein ha'arbayim yaktirenah* — when Aaron raises the *menorah*, he shall burn the incense. Taken at face value, this sounds as though you first light the *menorah* and then burn the *ketores*. The *gemara* therefore needed *oso* to teach otherwise: *yaktirenah* — he shall be burning the incense, meaning the *ketores* is already burning at the time he lights the *menorah*. The *ketores* precedes the *neiros*. The preposition *be'haalos* functions as a temporal marker — while he is lighting, the *ketores* should already be underway — not as a sequential indicator.

Thus the *gemara* has accounted for both pieces: the *neiros* come last of the interior services because of *oso*; the *ketores* precedes the *neiros* because of the verse *u've'haalos*; and the *korban pesach* comes before both *ketores* and *neiros* according to the primary opinion, while coming after the *tamid* because of its double afternoon language.

---

## Morning Ketores

### Ketores Earliest

A new *baraisa* is introduced: *ein lecha davar she'kodem l'Tamid shel shachar ela ketores bilvad* — nothing precedes the morning *tamid* except the *ketores* alone. The morning *ketores* and the afternoon *ketores* thus bracket the entire day's service from both ends, just as the morning and afternoon *tamid* bracket the *korbanos*. The *ketores* frames the day even more broadly.

The derivation: by the *ketores* the verse says *baboker baboker* — morning, morning — a double language of morning (Exodus 30:7). This parallels the logic of *erev* and *bein ha'arbayim* for the afternoon: double language means that service comes at the most extreme point of the time period. The morning *tamid* says only *baboker* once (*es hakeves echad ta'ase vaboker*, Numbers 28:4), so the *ketores* — with its double *baboker* — precedes even the morning *tamid*.

### Complete Order

The *baraisa* concludes: *v'ein lecha davar she'mit'akev achar Tamid shel bein ha'arbayim ela ketores v'neiros — u'Pesach* — nothing is held back, nothing is postponed until after the afternoon *tamid* except the *ketores*, the *neiros*, and the *pesach*. The complete daily order is therefore: *ketores* (morning), morning *tamid*, [other *korbanos* throughout the day], afternoon *tamid*, *korban pesach*, *ketores* (afternoon), *neiros*.

The word *mit'akev* is notable. In halachic terminology *me'akev* denotes something that is indispensable — without it the requirement is not fulfilled. Here it carries the meaning of being held back or postponed, indicating that these three services alone are performed after the afternoon *tamid*.

---

## Mechusar Kippurim

### Tahara Scenario

The *baraisa* now introduces a case not yet discussed: *mechusar kippurim b'erev haPesach* — someone who has not completed the purification process on *erev Pesach*. A *zav* or *metzora*, for instance, cannot eat *korbanos* until the final stage of *tahara* is complete, which requires bringing a *korban*. On the fourteenth of Nisan, such a person would want to bring that final *korban*, achieve *tahara*, and be able to eat the *korban pesach* that night.

The scenario that arises: the person has failed to bring the *korban* before the afternoon *tamid*. Normally, it is too late. But not bringing it means being unable to eat the *korban pesach* that evening. Should an exception be made?

### Tanna Kamma Allow

The *tanna kamma* says yes: *she'tovel v'shoneh v'ochel pesach l'erev* — on *erev Pesach*, a *mechusar kippurim* who has missed the window may still bring the *korban* after the afternoon *tamid*, immerse once more, and eat the *korban pesach* that night. The weight of the *korban pesach* obligation justifies the exception.

### Rabbi Yishmael Expand

*Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka* goes further: *af mechusar kippurim b'she'ar yemot hashanah she'tovel v'ochel b'kodashim l'erev* — even on an ordinary day, if a *mechusar kippurim* has already brought some other *korban* that day and now realizes too late that he cannot eat from it without completing his *tahara* process, he may bring the completing *korban* after the afternoon *tamid* in order to eat from the *korban* brought earlier that day. The concern here is the obligation to eat *korbanos* — there is a *mitzvah* of eating them.

### Hashlama Question

The *gemara* asks: *bishlema l'tanna kamma* — the *tanna kamma* is understandable. The positive *mitzvah* of *korban pesach*, which carries *kares* for its violation, can override the positive *mitzvah* of *hashlama* — the obligation to complete all *korbanos* before the afternoon *tamid*, derived from the verse *v'hiktir aleiha chelvei ha'shlamim* at the beginning of *Tzav*. The word *hashlamim* is read as *hashlama* — completion — teaching that all *korbanos* should be completed around the morning *tamid*, and certainly before the afternoon *tamid*.

This analysis involves a striking move: what the *Torah* presents as an indication of the *seder hayom* — the ordered sequence of Temple services — is treated by the *gemara* as a genuine *mitzvat asei*. One might have thought the *Torah* was merely describing procedure, leaving open questions about the *kashrus* of things done out of order. But the *gemara* frames the orderly completion of *korbanos* as a positive commandment, such that the weightier *mitzvat asei* of *korban pesach* — reinforced by *kares* — can displace it.

But according to *Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka*, who allows this even for ordinary *korbanos*: what makes the *mitzvat asei* of eating a *korban* stronger than the *mitzvat asei* of *hashlama*? Why should we set aside the rule governing the order of Temple services merely so someone can eat their *shelamim*?

### Bird Chatas Only

*Ravina* answers in the name of *Rav Chisda*: *hacha be'chatat ha'of tanan* — we are speaking specifically of a bird *chatat*. By a bird *chatat*, there is no burning on the altar; only blood is applied. And the entire prohibition against performing *avodah* after the afternoon *tamid* is derived from a verse about burning on the altar — specifically the passage at the beginning of *Tzav* (*zot torat ha'olah... v'hiktir aleiha chelvei ha'shlamim*), which speaks throughout about what is burned on the *mizbe'ach*. If the only act performed is sprinkling blood — with nothing burned on the altar — the prohibition has not technically been violated. *Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka*, on this reading, permitted only the narrow case where all that remained was a bird *chatat*, requiring no burning.

### Tomorrow Burning

*Rav Pappa* disagrees and offers a different resolution: *afilu teima be'chatat behemah* — even a regular animal *chatat* can be accommodated. His solution: *ma'aleinan b'rosh ha'mizbe'ach* — after sprinkling the blood, you do not burn the *emurim* that night. Instead, you lift the fat and innards up and place them on top of the *mizbe'ach* — not on the fire, but on the surrounding ledge. The rule of *lina* — invalidation due to being left overnight — does not apply to offerings already resting on the *mizbe'ach* itself. Then the following morning, after the morning *tamid*, you burn the fat. The critical act of the *korban* — throwing the blood on the altar — has been performed; the owner's obligation is essentially effected thereby. The burning of the *emurim*, while required, is deferred without invalidating the *korban*.

### Other Korbanos

The *gemara* then asks: *v'ha'ika asham* — what about the *asham*? A *metzora*, for instance, must bring not only a *chatat* but also an *asham* and an *olah*. *Rav Pappa*'s solution extends naturally to all these: in each case, sprinkle the blood and defer the burning until the next morning via placement on top of the *mizbe'ach*. But for *Ravina*, who limited the allowance to the bird *chatat* — which has no burning component — the *asham* poses a serious problem, since an *asham* cannot be brought as a bird.

*Ravina* would have to say that we are speaking of a scenario where the *asham* and *olah* had already been brought earlier in the day, leaving only the bird *chatat* outstanding. But the *gemara* challenges this: could you really say the *olah* was brought before the *chatat*? A *baraisa* teaches explicitly from the verse *v'hikriv es asher la'chatat rishona* (Leviticus 5:8) — and it shall bring the *chatat* first — that this is a *binyan av* applying to all cases: whenever a *chatat* and an *olah* come together, the *chatat* precedes. The *chatat* cleanses — whether from sin or from *tumah* — and only once cleansed can the person draw close to God through the *olah*. The *olah* cannot precede the *chatat*.

### Chatas Before Olah

The principle is emphatic: *le'chol chatos she'kodemes le'chol olos haba'os imahen* — every *chatat* precedes every *olah* that comes together with it. This is stated as a universal rule derived from the *binyan av*. Moreover, *kayma lan* — it is established — that *afilu chatat ha'of kodemes l'olat behemah* — even a bird *chatat*, inexpensive as it is, precedes an animal *olah*. So there is no way to describe a scenario where the *olah* was already brought before the bird *chatat*.

### Olat Metzora

*Rava* resolves this by noting a special leniency for the *olat metzora* specifically. The verse in Leviticus 14 reads *v'he'elah ha'Kohen et ha'olah* — using the *hif'il* perfect form rather than the future imperfect *ya'aleh*. The *drasha*: *she'he'elah kevar* — even if the *olah* had already been brought up, that is acceptable. For a *metzora*, uniquely, the *olah* may precede the *chatat*, because the *Torah*'s formulation implies that even a situation in which the *olah* already happened is accommodated. This resolves the *gemara*'s challenge to *Ravina*: one can construct a valid scenario where the *olah* was brought before the *chatat* — but only in the case of a *metzora*, owing to this special verse.

---

## Emurim Overnight Risk

### Kohanim Risk

The discussion now turns to a practical challenge against *Rav Pappa*'s solution. *Rav Shemen bar Abba* asks *Rav Pappa*: *le'didach*, according to your approach — that you lift the fats onto the top of the *mizbe'ach* (*ma'alu u'melina be'rosho shel mizbe'ach*) and leave them there overnight to be burned the next morning — are we going to arrange a situation that leads the *kohanim* to stumble? A *kohen* ascending the *mizbe'ach* at night to tend the fire will see meat and fat resting there. He will naturally assume it is leftover material from *korbanos* brought earlier in the day — which is precisely what is burned during the overnight hours. He will not realize this was placed there intentionally to be left until morning, and he will burn it, thereby causing a violation of the principle that nothing brought after the afternoon *tamid* may be burned on the altar.

The *gemara* treats this potential violation as a genuine *takalah* — a stumbling, a transgression — reflecting how seriously it takes the rule of *hashlama* and the prohibition against burning something on the altar that derives from a *korban* offered after the afternoon *tamid*.

### Kohanim Careful

*Rav Pappa* responds: *kohanim zerizim hein* — *kohanim* are scrupulous and careful. They will inform one another: the material in that corner is not to be touched; it waits until morning. Their diligence and mutual oversight ensure no inadvertent violation.

### Meat Eating Rule

*Rav Huna bar Rav Nasan* then raises a different and deeper challenge. As long as the *emurim* have not been burned — *kol zman d'lo niskatru emurim* — the *kohanim* cannot eat the meat: *kohanim lo matzi achli basar*. The source: a *baraisa* asks whether *kohanim* might eat the breast and thigh of a *shelamim* before the fats have been burned. The verse teaches: *v'hiktir ha'Kohen es hachelev ha'mizbeicha* — only after the *kohen* has burned the fat on the altar does the *Torah* say *v'hayah hachazeh l'Aharon u'l'vanav* — the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons. The sequence is fixed: burn the *emurim* first, then the *kohanim* may eat.

This generates a cascade: if the *kohanim* cannot eat the meat, the owners are not atoned. The source for this: *v'achlu osam asher kuppar bahem* — they shall eat them, those through whom atonement is made. This is the basis for the concept of *mishulchan gavo'ah kacha'u* — the *kohanim* eat from God's table, as it were; their consumption in the sacred precincts is an extension of the altar's consumption. First God's portion — the *emurim* — is offered; then the *kohanim* eat their portion; and through that entire process the owners' atonement is complete.

The difficulty is now acute: the whole purpose of *Rav Pappa*'s scheme was to enable the person to achieve *tahara* and eat the *korban pesach* that night. But if the *emurim* cannot be burned until morning, the *kohanim* cannot eat the meat that night, and therefore the owner's atonement — which was the prerequisite for *tahara* — is not complete.

### Lost Meat Rule

The *gemara* resolves this with a principle of *de facto* impossibility. *Kivan d'lo efshar* — since it is not possible to burn the fat tonight — the Rabbis treat it as if the meat were lost. A *baraisa* supports this: *yachol nitmu imurin o she'avdu lo yiheyu kohanim zochin ba'chazeh v'shok* — one might think that if the fats became *tamei* or were lost, the *kohanim* cannot eat their portion. The verse teaches otherwise: *v'hayah hachazeh l'Aharon u'l'vanav* — the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons regardless. *Mikol makom* — in any case, even without the burning of the *emurim*, the *kohanim* eat and the owners are atoned.

The principle that emerges is that when burning is impossible, the Rabbis declare the situation equivalent to lost *imurim*, and in that case the *kohanim* may eat immediately — their eating effects the owner's atonement even without the burning having taken place. At the deepest level, the *gemara* acknowledges that *b'diavad*, it is all about the blood. If the meat and fat became *tamei* or lost entirely, no one says the owner must bring another *korban*. What the *gemara* explores here is the *lechatchila* process by which atonement is fully realized — and it concludes that when circumstances prevent the full process, the blood alone suffices.

---

## Night Burning

### Yolin Question

*Rav Kahana* raises a new tension from a different set of verses. One verse states *lo yalin chelev chagagi ad boker* — the fat of my festival sacrifice shall not remain overnight until morning. The implication of the verse: *ad boker hu d'lo yalin* — only until morning is it prohibited to leave it; but *kol halailah kulo yalin* — throughout the entire night it may remain, i.e., the fat can and should be burned throughout the night. Yet another verse — *v'hiktir aleha chelvei ha'shlamim* — is the very verse from which we derived *hashlama*, that all burnings must be completed in connection with the morning *tamid*, before the afternoon *tamid*. How can these be reconciled? How can the fat be burned through the night if everything must be completed before the afternoon *tamid*?

### Pesach Yolin

*Rav Kahana* himself raises the question and provides the answer. The resolution is that the burning of fat through the night refers to *korbanos* whose blood was sprinkled before the afternoon *tamid*. For those, the nighttime burning is simply the completion of a *korban* that was already properly brought — it is wrap-up, not a new initiation. What is forbidden is burning on the *mizbe'ach* something that belongs to a *korban* whose blood was sprinkled after the afternoon *tamid*. The restriction is about the initiation of a *korban* after the *tamid*, not about completing one that was validly begun earlier.

### Weekday on Yom Tov

A further challenge is posed by *Rav Safra* to *Rav* — some say *Rava*. One verse states *lo yalin laboker zevach chag haPesach* — do not leave the sacrifice of *Pesach* until morning. On the simple reading this refers to the meat, which must be eaten before morning. But on the reading being discussed here, it implies that the fat of the *korban pesach* may be burned throughout the night. The difficulty: that night is the fifteenth of Nisan — *Yom Tov*. The *korban pesach* was brought on the fourteenth. Another verse establishes *olat Shabbat b'Shabbato* — the *Shabbat olah* in its *Shabbat* — and from this is derived *v'lo olat chol b'Shabbat* and *v'lo olat chol b'Yom Tov* — you may not burn the fat of a weekday *korban* on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*. How then can the fat of the *korban pesach*, which was brought on the fourteenth, be burned on the fifteenth?

### Shabbat Solution

*Rav Abba bar Chiyya* had already posed this question to *Rabbi Abbahu*, and *Rabbi Abbahu* answered: *hacha b'arba'asar she'chal liyos b'Shabbat askinan* — here we are dealing with the special case where the fourteenth of Nisan falls on *Shabbat*. When *erev Pesach* is *Shabbat*, the *korban pesach* brought that *Shabbat* is considered *chelvei Shabbat* — fat of a *Shabbat korban*. And the rule that permits burning yesterday's fat on *Yom Tov* applies when yesterday was *Shabbat*, since the verse permits *olat Shabbat* to be offered on the following day. Thus the fat of the *pesach* — a *Shabbat korban* — may be burned on the night of the fifteenth.

### Pasuk Self-Limit

The questioner presses: is it really acceptable to constrain an entire verse to such a narrow case — when *erev Pesach* coincides with *Shabbat* — simply to resolve this technical conflict? Why not simply take the verse at its plain meaning and allow the burning?

The response: *shavkineihu l'kra d'hu dachik u'moki anafshei* — leave the verse alone; it is the verse itself that is under pressure and forces itself into this narrow interpretation. The Artscroll renders this: it forces itself to be interpreted this way. The Soncino: it is compelled to establish its own particular case.

This is a conceptually significant moment. The plain sense of the verse seems to permit burning the *pesach* fat throughout the night of the fifteenth. But because that plain sense conflicts irreconcilably with the established rule — derived from another verse — that one cannot burn a weekday *korban*'s fat on *Yom Tov*, the *gemara* concludes that the verse must be confining itself to the extraordinary case where the fourteenth fell on *Shabbat*. The verse does not establish a new leniency overriding existing rules; rather, the internal pressure of the halakhic system forces the verse into its only coherent application.

This illustrates something fundamental about *Torah she'ba'al peh* and its relationship to the *psukim*. When the plain meaning of a verse conflicts with our understanding of the broader halakhic framework as derived from other verses and principles, the Rabbinic reading — grounded in consistency and systemic coherence — prevails. The verse does not override the system; the system compels the verse into its narrow, self-defined meaning. *Moki anafshei* — it establishes itself, within the constraints the system imposes on it.

---

---

# Pesachim 60

## Shechita Shelo Lishmo

### Pesach Scheduling

The daf begins at the very bottom of 59b, with the *mishnah* that addressed the schedule of *Erev Pesach*: when the afternoon *tamid* is normally brought, and how it is adjusted on *Erev Pesach* to allow time for the *korban Pesach*. Although the general rule prohibits bringing any *korbanot* after the afternoon *tamid*, the *Pesach* was the exception, brought later in the afternoon — though care was still taken to leave sufficient time for everyone to bring their *korban Pesach*.

The *mishnah* now turns away from scheduling and toward the question of how the *korban Pesach* was slaughtered — specifically, the effect of improper intention during the slaughter.

### Zevachim Analogy

This discussion is closely parallel to the very opening *mishnah* of *Zevachim*, which is fitting, given that the next several *prakim* of *Pesachim* could easily belong to *Seder Kodashim*. *Zevachim* opens with the question of what happens when one slaughters a *korban shelo lishmo* — not for its intended purpose — whether because one thought it belonged to a different owner, or, more commonly, because one thought it was a different type of *korban* than it actually was.

### Shelo Lishmo Rule

The general rule stated in that *mishnah* is: *kol hazvachim sheshchatan shelo lishman ksheirin ela shelo alu labaalim lesheim chovah* — any *korban* slaughtered for the wrong purpose is still valid as an object, but does not count toward the owner's obligation. If the *kohen* had in mind the wrong type of *korban*, the sacrifice itself may proceed — the blood may be sprinkled, the meat eaten, the fats burned — but the owner has not discharged his obligation. The *korban* as an object is legitimate; the owner's personal fulfillment is not.

### Chatat Exception

The *chatat* presents a more severe case. The entire purpose of the sin offering is to atone for a specific sin of a specific owner; the *chatat* is inseparable from its owner's relationship to the transgression. Once *shelo lishmo* severs that relationship, there is no longer any valid *chatat* at all. A *chatat shelo lishmo* is therefore completely invalid, not merely insufficient for the owner's obligation.

### Pesach Strictness

Our *mishnah* will show that the same stringent rule applies to the *korban Pesach*. Although the *Pesach* is in many ways a lighter *korban* — akin to a *shelamim*, eaten by the owners — it shares with the *chatat* the principle that *shelo lishmo* renders it completely invalid, not merely unhelpful for the obligation. The reason for this will become clearer as the discussion unfolds, but it is connected to the unique centrality of eating in the *korban Pesach*.

### Pigul vs Shelo Lishmo

One might ask whether this is the same as *pigul*. It is not. *Pigul* arises when one intends to eat the *korban* at the wrong time — or in a variation, in the wrong place — and that too invalidates. But *shelo lishmo* is distinct: it refers to thinking in one's mind that the *korban* is a different type altogether — a *chatat* instead of a *shelamim*, or an *olah* instead of a *chatat*. Both *pigul* and *shelo lishmo* depend on the *kohen*'s intentions, but they are conceptually separate categories.

### Articulated Thought

It is worth noting at this stage — as it arises at the very beginning of *Zevachim* as well — that when the *halachah* speaks of intention (*machshavah*) invalidating a *korban*, a significant view among the *Rishonim* holds that this means articulated thought, that is, thought which was verbalized. Whether silent, purely internal thought has any legal effect is itself a subject of debate. The discussion below proceeds in terms of stated intentions, which makes the analysis more tractable, though the underlying question of silent thought carries its own implications.

### Four Avodot

The *mishnah* reads: *hapesach sheshchatan shelo lishmo* — if one slaughtered the *korban Pesach shelo lishmo*, for a different purpose. The next *mishnah* will address the case of wrong owners; here the concern is a different type of *korban*. *Vekibel vehilach vezarak shelo lishmo* — or if one caught the blood, walked it to the altar, or threw it *shelo lishmo*. The *vav* here clearly functions as "or," not "and."

There are four primary *avodot* involved from *shechitah* through the application of the blood: (1) *shechitah*, the slaughter; (2) *kabbalah*, catching the blood in a vessel; (3) *holachah*, carrying the blood to the altar; and (4) *zrika*, throwing the blood on the altar. An improper intention at any one of these four acts can invalidate the *korban*.

### Mishnah Structure

The *mishnah* goes on: *o lishmo veshelo lishmo* — or if one had a mixed intention, partly for the correct purpose and partly for the wrong one. This is the formulation the *Gemara* will focus on closely. The rule stated is: at any of the four *avodot*, whether the intention was entirely *shelo lishmo* or was a hybrid of the two, if any part of the intention was for the wrong *korban*, the *Pesach* is invalid — just as with the *chatat*.

### Mixed Intentions

The *mishnah* then asks: what is the case of *lishmah u'shelo lishmah*? The example given: *leshem Pesach u'leshem shelamim* — one slaughtered it thinking it was a *Pesach* and then thinking it was a *shelamim*. And the reverse: *shelo lishmah u'lishmah* — thinking it was a *shelamim* and then a *Pesach*. The *mishnah* clearly states both hybrid orderings as invalidating. How and when these two intentions occurred — simultaneously, sequentially during one *avodah*, or across two separate *avodot* — is precisely the question the *Gemara* now takes up.

---

## Rav Pappa's Query

### One Act or Two?

Before entering the *Gemara*'s formal question, it is worth pausing on why *shelo lishmo* is particularly strict by the *korban Pesach*. The *korban Pesach* is unique among all *korbanot* in that its primary purpose is eating. In most *korbanot*, the focal moment is the *zrikat hadam* — the throwing of the blood. The eating by the *kohanim* or by the owners is a secondary dimension. By the *korban Pesach*, however, everything is *leshem achilah* — oriented toward the eating. This will emerge in several important *halachot* as the *masechta* continues.

Furthermore, the *pasuk* states *ish lefi ochlo tachosu al haseh* — one counts the group that will eat from it and slaughters accordingly. The designated eaters are bound up with the act of *shechitah* itself. Just as the *chatat* cannot exist without an owner — because its entire purpose is the owner's atonement — so too the *korban Pesach* cannot exist without designated eaters, because its entire purpose is the eating by the designated group. *Shelo lishmo* severs the relationship between the *korban* and its owners, and without that relationship the *Pesach* has no purpose. Hence it is invalid entirely, not merely insufficient for the obligation.

With this context established, the *Gemara* presents the question of *Rav Pappa*: *ba'ei Rav Pappa* — does our *mishnah* speak of a case where the two thoughts occurred *b'avodah achat*, during one *avodah*, or *bishtei avodot*, during two separate *avodot*?

The four *avodot* — *shechitah*, *kabbalah*, *holachah*, and *zrikat hadam* — each constitute a distinct act. The question is whether the hybrid statement of "for a *Pesach* and for a *shelamim*" was made as a single composite utterance during one act, or whether it represents two separate statements at two different acts.

### Rabbi Meir vs Yose

To understand the stakes of Rav Pappa's question, the *Gemara* invokes a *machlokes* between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose that was already discussed earlier in the tractate. If a person says *harei ze tmuras olah tmuras shelamim* — this is a substitute for an *olah* and a substitute for a *shelamim* — the statement is self-contradictory. Something cannot simultaneously be both. How does one interpret such a hybrid utterance?

Rabbi Meir holds *tfos lashon rishon* — one grabs hold of the first part of the statement, reads the sentence as ending after the first clause, and disregards the remainder as incoherent. Rabbi Yose holds *af bigmar devarav adam nitpas* — a person is held accountable even for the conclusion of his words. Even if the end of the sentence creates a contradiction with the beginning, one must grapple with the entirety of what was said, not truncate it.

### Shechita Debate

If our *mishnah*'s hybrid case — where one said both *leshem Pesach* and *leshem shelamim* — refers to a single act of *shechitah*, then we are dealing with a single contradictory statement during one *avodah*. In that case, Rabbi Meir would say: simply read only the first part. If the first part was *lishmo* — for the sake of a *Pesach* — then the *korban* stands, and the trailing *shelamim* is disregarded. If the first part was *shelo lishmo*, it invalidates immediately. Rabbi Yose, by contrast, would hold the person accountable to the entirety of the hybrid statement, and since part of it was *shelo lishmo*, the *korban* is invalid.

### Two Acts Agreement

If, however, the two thoughts were expressed at two separate *avodot* — say, *lishmo* at *shechitah* and *shelo lishmo* at *zrika* — then there is no single contradictory sentence to parse. Each act stands alone. The *shechitah* was valid, and the *zrika* was *shelo lishmo*, which invalidates the *korban*. In this scenario, even Rabbi Meir would agree that the *korban* is invalid, because the rule of *tfos lashon rishon* applies to a single contradictory utterance; it does not rescue an entirely separate act performed with a wrong intention.

### Mishnah Interpretation

The *Gemara*'s interest, then, is not in what the *halachah* is — that is clear. If two separate *avodot* are involved with separate improper intentions, everyone agrees the *korban* is invalid. If a hybrid thought occurs during one *avodah*, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose disagree. The question is simply: which scenario does our *mishnah* actually describe? The *Gemara* will now attempt to resolve this through careful reading of the *mishnah* itself.

### Shelo Lishmo First

Before analyzing the hybrid case, the *Gemara* first clarifies a simpler matter. If the *mishnah*'s hybrid refers to *shelo lishmo u'lishmo* — where the wrong intention came *first* — then there is no need for any debate at all. Everyone agrees, regardless of whether it is one *avodah* or two, and regardless of whether one follows Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yose, that the *korban* is invalid from the moment the first word — *shelamim* — is out of one's mouth. After all, both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose agree that the beginning of a statement binds; Rabbi Yose merely adds that even the end of the statement binds. So *shelo lishmo* first invalidates immediately and comprehensively. The interesting case — and the one Rav Pappa's question targets — is the hybrid where the *kosher* intention comes first: *lishmo u'shelo lishmo*.

---

## First vs Hybrid Case

### Mishnah First Case

The *Gemara* now reads the *mishnah* carefully to determine which scenario it describes. The *mishnah* opens: *hapesach sheshachto shelo lishmo, vekibel vehilach vezarak shelo lishmo* — the *Pesach* that one slaughtered *shelo lishmo*, or caught the blood, or walked it, or threw it *shelo lishmo*.

### Vav Reading

The *vav* connecting these acts cannot mean "and" — as if one had to commit all four *avodot shelo lishmo* to invalidate the *korban*. That reading is untenable: if the first *avodah* was already *shelo lishmo*, the *korban* was invalidated at that point. Why would the *mishnah* require all four? Rather, the *vav* here means "or." The *mishnah* is saying: if any one of these acts was performed *shelo lishmo*, the *korban* is invalid.

### Different Avodot Proof

Reading it this way, the *mishnah*'s first clause actually covers the case of different intentions at different *avodot*. The *mishnah* is saying: whether you did the *shechitah shelo lishmo* (with the rest performed correctly), or the *kabbalah shelo lishmo*, or the *holachah*, or the *zrika* — any single act *shelo lishmo* invalidates. This includes the case where, say, the *shechitah* was *lishmo* but the *zrika* was *shelo lishmo*: a case of one correct *avodah* followed by one incorrect *avodah*.

### One Avodah Conclusion

If that is so, then when the *mishnah* subsequently discusses the hybrid of *lishmo u'shelo lishmo* and *shelo lishmo u'lishmo*, it cannot again be referring to different thoughts at different *avodot* — that was already covered. The hybrid case at the end of the *mishnah* must therefore describe two thoughts occurring during a *single avodah*: a composite intention at the moment of, say, the *shechitah*. And that case reflects the position of Rabbi Yose — *af bigmar devarav adam nitpas* — that even when both thoughts are expressed in one utterance, the *shelo lishmo* component invalidates.

### Alternative Reading

The *Gemara* considers a rebuttal. Perhaps the *mishnah* in its entirety addresses only cases where the wrong intention and the right intention occur at *separate* acts — and the hybrid at the end is not truly a single compound intention at one act.

### Thought During vs Future

To sustain this reading, the *Gemara* distinguishes between two ways of having different intentions at different *avodot*. In the first case — covered by the *mishnah*'s opening — the *kohen* has a *machshavah* about the act he is currently performing. When he slaughters, he thinks: "I am slaughtering this *shelo lishmo*." Or when he throws the blood, he thinks: "I am throwing this blood as a *shelamim*." Each act is accompanied by a *machshavah* about that act.

### Hybrid Example

The second way — which would correspond to the *mishnah*'s hybrid case — is that the *kohen* during one act harbors an intention about a *different, future* act. In this reading, the hybrid statement is: *hareini shocheit es haPesach lishmo lizrok damo shelo lishmo* — "I am slaughtering this *korban Pesach* for its proper purpose, with the intention that I will throw its blood for the sake of a *shelamim*." Here, the *shechitah* itself is designated correctly, but the *kohen* articulates a *machshavah* that the future *zrika* will be *shelo lishmo*. These are not contradictory statements about a single act; they are two distinct, self-consistent statements. There is no incoherent hybrid sentence that would prompt Rabbi Meir to truncate it. Both statements stand independently, and even Rabbi Meir would hold the *kohen* accountable to both.

### Machshavah Transfer

This reading also teaches an important principle: *machshevina me'avodah le'avodah* — a *machshavah* expressed during one *avodah* regarding a future *avodah* is halachically significant and can invalidate the *korban*. One does not need to entertain the wrong intention precisely at the moment of the disqualifying act; having the wrong intention during the *shechitah* about the *zrika* is sufficient.

### Unresolved Question

On this reading, Rav Pappa's question can be rephrased as follows: does the *mishnah*'s hybrid case describe a single contradictory utterance at one *avodah* — in which case the *mishnah* reflects Rabbi Yose's position — or does it describe a non-contradictory compound statement at one *avodah* about a future *avodah* — in which case even Rabbi Meir could accept it? The *Gemara* at this stage leaves the question open.

---

## Owners Case

### Second Mishnah

The *Gemara* now turns to the next *mishnah*, which concerns intention regarding the wrong owners rather than the wrong type of *korban*. The basic distinction here is important.

### Owners Rule

When one slaughters the *Pesach* with the sole intention of the wrong group of owners — the wrong *le'ochlav* — the *Pesach* is invalid, much as it would be if the wrong type of *korban* was intended. However, when the intention is a mixture — partly for the right owners and partly for the wrong ones — the *Pesach* is *kasher*. This stands in direct contrast to the rule for wrong-*korban* intention, where even a hybrid thought is sufficient to invalidate. The next *mishnah* thus teaches an asymmetry: hybrid intention regarding the type of *korban* invalidates; hybrid intention regarding the *eaters* does not.

### Wrong Owners Case

The *mishnah* states: *shachto shelo le'ochlav ushelo limnuyav* — one slaughtered it for those who cannot eat it, or for people registered to a different group. In both cases the *Pesach* is *pasul*.

### Owners Definitions

*Shelo le'ochlav* may refer to those who, though they are part of the designated group, are physically incapable of eating — they are ill, elderly, or unable to consume the requisite amount. *Shelo limnuyav* refers more straightforwardly to those belonging to an entirely different group — men who are uncircumcised for whatever reason, or those who are *tamei*. In either case, a pure intention directed at the wrong eaters invalidates.

### One Avodah Clear

Crucially, the text frames this case entirely in terms of *shachto* — the *shechitah* alone. This is clearly a case involving one *avodah*, not a spread of intentions across multiple acts.

### Proof from Seifa

The *Gemara* attempts a proof: since the *seifa* — the *mishnah* about eaters — is unambiguously about one *avodah*, we might infer that our *mishnah* about *shelo lishmo* is also about one *avodah* when it describes the hybrid case.

### Separate Mishnas

The *Gemara* rebuts: *ha kede'ita veha kede'ita* — each *mishnah* operates according to its own parameters. The fact that one *mishnah* discusses a single *avodah* tells us nothing about the scope of a different *mishnah*. The question about our first *mishnah* remains unresolved.

---

## Machshevet Ochlim

### Two Avodot Case

The *Gemara* now attempts a stronger proof from the same *mishnah* about owners. It focuses on the *mishnah*'s positive case: *le'ochlav ushelo le'ochlav kasher* — if one slaughtered with intention both for those who can eat and for those who cannot, the *Pesach* is *kasher*. If this refers to two separate *avodot* — the *shechitah* with intention for the right eaters and the *zrika* with intention for the wrong eaters — why is it *kasher*? Surely *zrika shelo le'ochlav* would be a problem.

### Ein Machshevet

The answer is a striking principle: *ein machshevet ochlin b'zrika* — the thought about the eaters is not legally relevant during the act of throwing the blood.

### Pesach Uniqueness

This is distinctive to the *korban Pesach*. By all other *korbanot*, the *machshavah* of the officiating *kohen* during any of the four *avodot* can affect the *korban's* status. By the *Pesach*, when it comes to the question of *who* will eat it, only the *shechitah* matters. The other three *avodot* are simply irrelevant for purposes of this particular form of *machshavah*.

### Torah Source

The reason traces back to the *pasuk*: *ish lefi ochlo tachosu al haseh* — one counts the eaters and slaughters accordingly. The *Torah* links the designated eaters specifically to the act of *shechitah*. The *shechitah* is what transforms the animal into meat; it is the moment most intimately connected to eating. Hence it is at *shechitah* — and only at *shechitah* — that one's thoughts about the eaters carry legal weight.

### Hybrid at Shechita

Given this principle, if the *mishnah*'s case of *le'ochlav ushelo le'ochlav* were a hybrid thought during the *shechitah* itself — both the right and wrong eaters in mind simultaneously during the one *avodah* where eater-related thought is relevant — it would indeed be *pasul*. The *machshavah* about wrong eaters during *shechitah* would invalidate.

### Mixed Valid Only If

This means the reason the *mishnah* declares the hybrid case *kasher* cannot be that hybrid thoughts about eaters are generally permissible. Rather, it must be *kasher* specifically because the bad thought about wrong eaters occurred at an *avodah* other than *shechitah* — for example, at the *zrika* — where that thought is entirely irrelevant.

### Eaters Leniency

We do have a received tradition that a mixed thought regarding eaters is not problematic in the same way that a mixed *shelo lishmo* thought is. But the *Gemara* reasons that this leniency only operates when the bad thought about eaters does not occur during *shechitah*.

### Seifa One Avodah

Consequently, when the *mishnah*'s case of *le'ochlav ushelo le'ochlav* is declared *kasher*, it can only be referring to one *avodah*: a mixed thought during *shechitah* itself. Only there does the thought about eaters matter at all. And there, the tradition is that a partially-wrong thought about eaters is acceptable.

### Reisha One Avodah

The *Gemara* draws the inference: since the *seifa* of the owners' *mishnah* is necessarily discussing a hybrid thought during one *avodah* — the *shechitah* — we can argue that the *reisha* of our *mishnah* about *shelo lishmo* is similarly discussing a hybrid thought during one *avodah*. The parallel structure supports the reading that the entire discussion concerns single acts, not sequences of separate *avodot*.

### No Final Answer

However, the *Gemara* once again resists this inference: *ha kede'ita veha kede'ita*. Each *mishnah* stands by its own internal logic. The owners' *mishnah* necessarily refers to one *avodah* because only *shechitah* is relevant for eater-related *machshavah*. That tells us nothing definitive about whether the *shelo lishmo* *mishnah* describes one *avodah* or two. Rav Pappa's question is left unresolved.

What is never in doubt is the *halachah* itself: if two separate intentions were expressed at two separate *avodot*, the *korban* is invalid and everyone agrees. If a single *avodah* was performed with a hybrid intention, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose disagree, with the *mishnah* lending itself more naturally to Rabbi Yose's reading. The sole unresolved issue is which scenario the *mishnah* actually addresses.

---

## Pesach Other Days

### Pesach Transformed

The *Gemara* now raises a fascinating new question. There is a well-known *halachah*: a *korban Pesach* that was slaughtered not on *Erev Pesach* — but at another time of year — takes on the status of a *shelamim*. If *Pesach* has already passed and the animal was designated but never slaughtered, it can no longer be held until the following year (since a *korban Pesach* must be under one year old), so its status is automatically reassigned as a *shelamim* even without any particular intention.

But consider a different scenario: it is still before *Pesach* — say, around *Purim* — and one slaughters the designated *Pesach* at that time. Its natural status remains a *korban Pesach* because it could yet be brought as such in a few weeks. However, if one slaughters it *with intentional* intention of a *shelamim*, the animal is transformed into a *shelamim* by that designation.

### Mixed on Purim

The *Gemara* now poses the question: what if on *Purim* one slaughtered the designated *Pesach* with a *mixed* intention — *lishmo ushelo lishmo* — partly for a *Pesach* and partly for a *shelamim*? Which intention governs?

### Conflicting Thoughts

The situation is the inverse of the *mishnah* we have been studying. In the *mishnah*, *shelo lishmo* is the bad thought and *lishmo* is the good thought; *shelo lishmo* wins, invalidating the *korban*. Here, on *Purim*, *lishmo* is the bad thought — thinking of it as a *Pesach* being brought at the wrong time is what would make it invalid as a *Pesach* — while *shelo lishmo* (thinking of it as a *shelamim*) is what validates it. The question is: does the *shelo lishmo* thought still win out even when it is the validating thought? Or is it always the *bad* component of a hybrid thought that wins?

### Which Wins

The question cuts to the heart of what the principle really is. If the rule is simply that in any hybrid thought the *shelo lishmo* component always dominates — regardless of whether it is the validating or invalidating element — then on *Purim* the *shelo lishmo* thought should validate the *korban* even in a hybrid. If, on the other hand, the rule is that a bad thought always spoils — and on *Purim* the *lishmo* thought is the bad one — then the hybrid would leave the *korban* invalid as both a proper *Pesach* and a proper *shelamim*.

### Rav Dimi Argument

When *Rav Dimi* came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported the following reasoning that he had presented to Rabbi Yirmiyah. He argued: *hoil ulishmo machshiro bizmano ushelo lishmo machshiro shelo bizmano* — since *lishmo* validates on *Erev Pesach* and *shelo lishmo* validates the rest of the year. Now, on *Erev Pesach*, when a hybrid thought is present — *lishmo* combined with *shelo lishmo* — the good thought of *lishmo* is not strong enough to overcome the bad thought of *shelo lishmo*. That is the principle established by our *mishnah*: the *shelo lishmo* wins and invalidates. By the same logic, he argued, on the rest of the year when *shelo lishmo* is the validating thought: just as *lishmo* could not overcome *shelo lishmo* on *Erev Pesach*, so too *shelo lishmo* cannot overcome *lishmo* on *Purim*. In both cases, the presence of a bad thought is what ruins the hybrid, regardless of which element of the hybrid is bad. The *korban* on *Purim* with a mixed intention would therefore be invalid.

This seems like the straightforward extension of the principle. Rabbi Yirmiyah, however, disagreed: *lo*. He argued that the two cases are not symmetric. *Shelo lishmo* on *Erev Pesach* is a universal invalidity — *sheken noheig bechol hazvachim*. The rule that *shelo lishmo* is problematic applies to every *korban*; it is a pervasive, powerful disqualification. That is why it wins out even in a hybrid. But *lishmo* is almost never an invalidating thought. The only *korban* for which thinking of it as what it actually is could ever be a problem is the *Pesach* brought at the wrong time — *sheken eino noheig bechol hazvachim ela bePesach bilvad*. Such a weak and context-specific disqualification does not carry the force to overcome the validating *shelo lishmo* thought in a hybrid.

### Rava's Turn

The question is left open at this point, and the *Gemara* now turns to *Rava* for a resolution.

---

## Rava's Position

### Rava Kosher

*Rava* rules: *Pesach sheshachto bish'ar yemot hashana lishmo ushelo lishmo* — a *korban Pesach* slaughtered at another time of year with a mixed intention is *kasher*. The *shelo lishmo* component prevails and validates it as a *shelamim*.

### Normal Analogy

*Rava* grounds this ruling in an analogy. In the normal case — on *Purim*, without any hybrid thought — when one slaughters the designated *Pesach* as a *shelamim*, this is *kasher*. The *shelo lishmo* thought transforms it. But note: the animal was already designated as a *korban Pesach*. It carries that identity.

### Pesach Status

The designated *Pesach* on *Purim* represents, in effect, a *lishmo* status: it is a *Pesach* in waiting, sanctified as such, with no other identity. When one slaughters it and thinks *shelamim*, the *shelo lishmo* thought overcomes the *korban*'s own entrenched status as a *Pesach* — *stamei dePescha ushemo ka'ei*, its standing designation is that of a *Pesach* — and the *shelamim* thought wins out and validates it.

### Rava's Logic

Now, *Rava* reasons, if *shelo lishmo* can overcome even the *korban*'s own standing identity as a *Pesach* — not just a competing verbal intention, but the *korban*'s very designation — then surely when one says both *lishmo* and *shelo lishmo* aloud, the *shelo lishmo* will prevail. After all, saying "this is a *Pesach*" is no more weighty than the *korban*'s own inherent designation, which *shelo lishmo* already overcomes in the normal case.

### Shelo Lishmo Trumps

The implication is that *shelo lishmo* carries an inherent dominance — it trumps even in the direction of validation, not only in the direction of invalidation. Just as on *Erev Pesach shelo lishmo* wins and invalidates a hybrid thought, on *Purim shelo lishmo* wins and validates a hybrid thought.

### Mixed Irrelevant

Therefore, the mixed intention does not leave the *korban* in an indeterminate state. *Shelo lishmo* still determines the outcome: the *korban* is *kasher* as a *shelamim*.

---

## Rav Adda Objection

### Speaking Weakness

*Rav Adda bar Ahava* challenges *Rava*. He distinguishes between a scenario where one *says* a hybrid thought and a scenario where one *says nothing* and the *korban*'s own standing status fills in the other half. When one says *shelamim* alone and the *korban* represents *Pesach*, one's explicit statement of *shelamim* contends against the *korban*'s status — and wins. But when one says both *Pesach* and *shelamim*, one's own statement is internally divided and weakened. Perhaps a compromised, self-contradicting utterance does not carry the same force as a clean, unambiguous declaration.

### Shelo L'Ochlav Proof

*Rav Adda* supports this from the eaters case. We know that if one thinks *shelo le'ochlav* alone — only of the wrong eaters — the *Pesach* is invalid. Yet the *korban Pesach* naturally represents its designated eaters: *stamei le'ochlav ka'ei*. Why does the *korban*'s inherent association with the right eaters not combine with the wrong-eaters thought to create a valid hybrid? Logically, one might think: the *korban* represents the right eaters; the *kohen* said the wrong eaters; together it is a hybrid, and by the principle we have seen, a hybrid in the eaters case is *kasher*.

### No Combination

This does not happen. One's explicit statement of wrong eaters does not get rescued by the *korban*'s natural association with the right ones. The *korban*'s status cannot supplement one's stated intention to create a hybrid.

### Said vs Silent

The distinction is between what one *says* and what one leaves implicit. When one says nothing and the *korban*'s status supplies the *lishmo*, one's explicit *shelo lishmo* can overcome it. But when one has *said* only the wrong thing, one cannot invoke the *korban*'s status as an unspoken addition to one's own declaration to construct a valid hybrid retroactively.

### Here Too Weak

The same logic applies here. When one says *shelamim* alone and says nothing else, one's clear declaration of *shelamim* wins against the *korban*'s identity. But when one says both *Pesach* and *shelamim*, one's own utterance is compromised — it no longer presents a clean, decisive declaration of *shelamim*. A divided statement is weaker than a unified one.

### Can't Supplement

Therefore, *Rav Adda* concludes, one cannot invoke what the *korban* naturally represents to shore up one's own hybrid statement. The situations are genuinely different: when one says one thing, the *korban*'s status is irrelevant because one's own clear statement determines the outcome. When one's own statement is already mixed, the *korban*'s status does not rescue it.

---

## Rava Responds

### Different Cases

*Rava* rejects the comparison. The eaters case and the *Purim* case are fundamentally different, and the asymmetry explains why the *korban*'s status can supplement one's declaration in the *Purim* scenario but cannot do so in the eaters scenario.

### Mutable Group

By the eaters case, the *korban* does not have a fixed, fully determinate identity with respect to who its eaters are. The *Torah* itself provides for fluidity: *nimnin umoshchin yadeihem mimenu ad sheyishachet* — one may be added to the group or withdraw from it until the moment of *shechitah*. The membership of the group is a moving target, variable right up to the final moment.

### Status Not Fixed

Precisely because the identity of the eaters is not locked in and can change, the *korban Pesach* does not fully and immutably represent a specific set of eaters. It therefore cannot supply the other half of a hybrid thought about eaters by itself. When one's statement refers to wrong eaters, there is no sufficiently firm counter-designation standing behind the *korban* to create a meaningful hybrid. To express the right owners, one must articulate them explicitly; the *korban* cannot do it for you.

### Fixed Status

On *Purim*, however, the situation is entirely different. The *korban*'s identity is fully fixed and immutable: it is a *korban Pesach*, sanctified as such, and nothing about that designation fluctuates. There is no way for its status to change except through an intentional act of the *kohen* at the time of *shechitah*. *Stamei dePascha ushemo ka'ei* — its standing designation is that of a *Pesach*, completely and unambiguously.

### Full Status Loss

When one declares *shelamim* and nothing else, this single, clear declaration overcomes the *korban*'s fully committed identity as a *Pesach* and transforms it. This is remarkable: a simple statement of *shelo lishmo* wins against the *korban*'s entire, entrenched, immutable status.

### Rava Final

If *shelo lishmo* is powerful enough to overcome the *korban*'s fully committed *Pesach* status when nothing else is said, then adding the word *Pesach* to one's own utterance — thereby creating a hybrid — cannot make things worse. The *korban*'s own designation already provided a *lishmo* element against which *shelo lishmo* already wins. Saying *lishmo* explicitly adds nothing beyond what the *korban*'s status already supplied. Therefore *shelo lishmo* still wins, and the *korban* is *kasher* as a *shelamim*.

### Debate Ends

The debate between *Rava* and *Rav Adda bar Ahava* thus turns on a precise and elegant distinction. *Rav Adda* argues that there is a meaningful difference between saying something and saying nothing — that one's own hybrid statement is weaker than a clean unilateral declaration, and that the *korban*'s status cannot make up the difference. *Rava* responds by distinguishing between the eaters case, where the *korban*'s status with respect to its designated group is genuinely mutable and therefore cannot supply a fixed counterweight, and the *Purim* case, where the *korban*'s *Pesach* identity is fully immutable and the *shelo lishmo* declaration already prevails against it in the simple case — making the addition of an explicit *lishmo* statement by the *kohen* carry no additional weight against the *shelo lishmo* that was already dominant.

---

---

# Pesachim 61

## Shelo Lishmo Overview

### Pesach Shelo Lishmo Intro

The daf opens at the bottom of 60b, where the Gemara is completing its treatment of the *mishnah* dealing with the *korban pesach* slaughtered *shelo lishmo* — not for its proper designation. The *korban pesach* is one of only two *korbanot* for which *shelo lishmo* renders the sacrifice invalid; the other is the *chatat*. The Gemara has not yet, at this point in the sugya, provided the derivation for why *shelo lishmo* creates this invalidity, but the conceptual logic is apparent: the entire purpose of the *korban pesach* is to be eaten by its designated owners, and — similar to the *chatat*, which is bound up with the personal atonement of its bringer — the identity of the sacrifice is inextricably tied to the intention with which it is brought. Whatever its theoretical underpinnings, it is established that *shelo lishmo* invalidates, and the Gemara has been working through a series of associated questions, including the ruling that even a partial *shelo lishmo* intention suffices to invalidate.

### Pesach Off-Season Q

The Gemara now raises a new question: *Pesach sheshachto bish'ar yemot hashanah bishinuy be'alim mahu?* — If one slaughtered a *korban pesach* during the rest of the year — say, on Purim — with a *shinuy be'alim*, a change of owners, what is the law?

To appreciate the question, some background is necessary. We have already learned that what invalidates the *pesach* on the fourteenth of Nisan can, paradoxically, validate it when brought at the wrong time of year. If one brings a *korban pesach* on Purim for the sake of a *shelamim*, designating it as a different type of offering altogether, it becomes valid as a *shelamim*. If, however, one brings it on Purim still intending it as a *pesach*, it remains a *pesach* and is therefore invalid — a *korban pesach* has no place outside its proper time.

We have also learned that, as will be developed in the next *mishnah*, slaughtering the *pesach* for the wrong owners — *shelo limnuav*, not for the group counted on it — is itself an invalidity. By other *korbanot*, a change of owners (*shinuy be'alim*) does not invalidate the *korban* outright; it merely fails to provide atonement or credit to the rightful owner. By the *korban pesach*, however, it invalidates entirely.

The question, then, is whether this parallel holds in the off-season as well: just as *shinuy kodesh* — slaughtering it as a different type of *korban* — transforms the *pesach* into a valid *shelamim* on Purim, does *shinuy be'alim* — slaughtering it for the wrong owners — similarly transform it into something valid? There is, as the Gemara immediately senses, an obvious conceptual difficulty: it is one thing to designate a *pesach* as a *shelamim* and thereby actively alter its *korban* identity; it is quite another to claim that intending different owners somehow performs the same transformation.

### Rav Papa Analogy

*Amar Rav Papa* — Rav Papa reports that he presented this discussion before Rava. Notably, he says he "told over the *shema'ta*" — the discussion — not merely the question, implying the matter had been under active debate, though no definitive answer had yet emerged. Rav Papa's own proposal was as follows: *hoil veshinuy kodesh posel bizmano veshinuy be'alim posel bizmano* — since *shinuy kodesh* invalidates the *pesach* on the fourteenth and *shinuy be'alim* likewise invalidates it on the fourteenth, perhaps the same parallel holds in the positive direction. Just as *shinuy kodesh* which invalidates on the fourteenth *machshir shelo bizmano* — validates when it is not the fourteenth — so too *shinuy be'alim* which invalidates on the fourteenth should validate *shelo bizmano*, on Purim. By this reasoning, intending the wrong owners on Purim would transform the *pesach* into a valid offering.

---

## Rava vs Rav Papa

### Identity vs Ownership

Rava rejected Rav Papa's analogy outright. *Im amarta beshinuy kodesh* — if you wish to say this of *shinuy kodesh*, the reason it has the power to transform the *pesach* into a *shelamim* off-season is *sheken poslo begufo* — it strikes at the very identity of the *korban* itself. When the *kohen* declares or intends a different type of sacrifice, he is making a statement about what this offering fundamentally *is*. That intention, because it is so directly constitutive of the *korban*'s identity, carries the power to reshape it when brought at a time when a *pesach* has no place. *Shinuy be'alim* — the owners — is by contrast more tangential to the *korban*'s essential nature. Ownership is secondary; the identity of the sacrifice as a *pesach*, a *shelamim*, or a *chatat* is primary. This is Rava's first distinction.

### Four Avodos Debate

Rava's second distinction: *yeshno be-arba avodos* — *shinuy kodesh* creates invalidity at any of the four *avodos*: *shechita*, receiving the blood, conveying the blood, and *zerika*. The concern about what type of *korban* is being offered is relevant from the very first act of service, because the identity of the *korban* is at stake from the moment it is slaughtered. *Shinuy be'alim*, by contrast, is only relevant at *zerikat hadam*. The reason for this limitation will be developed further below, but the point here is structural: *shinuy kodesh* is pervasive across all stages of the *avodah*, whereas *shinuy be'alim* is restricted to one. This asymmetry reflects that *shinuy kodesh* is a more deeply rooted invalidity.

### After Death Analysis

Rava's third distinction: *ve-yeshno le-achar misa* — *shinuy kodesh* applies even after the owner's death, whereas *shinuy be'alim* does not. This requires some unpacking.

It is a remarkable *halacha* that if an individual obligated himself to bring a *korban* — saying *harei alai*, committing to bring, say, a *shelamim* — and he dies before fulfilling that obligation, the obligation survives him. The *Beis Hamikdash*, as it were, holds a lien against his estate, much like an unpaid creditor. His heirs must bring the *korban* from the estate. This is one of those areas of *halacha* where the relationship between a person and God is translated into concrete legal-financial obligations — the *Beis Hamikdash* operates not merely as a spiritual institution but as an entity capable of holding real claims on property.

Now, if the *kohen* slaughters that posthumous *shelamim* with an intention of the wrong *korban* type — thinking *chatat* rather than *shelamim* — this constitutes *shinuy kodesh* and invalidates even though the owner is dead. The estate will be liable to bring a replacement. The identity of the *korban* type is so fundamental that it remains relevant regardless of whether the person for whom it is brought is alive.

By contrast, according to the mainstream position, *shinuy be'alim* does not apply after the owner's death. If someone dies and leaves behind a *shelamim*, and the *kohen* performs the *zerika* thinking about different owners than the deceased, there is a position that this does not invalidate. Why? Because the concept of *shinuy be'alim* — whose *korban* this is, who receives the personal credit — is less meaningful once the owner has died.
