# Pesachim 63

## Shelo L'Ochlav

### Intro: Shelo L'Ochlav

We pick up at the very bottom of 62b and turn to the issue of *shelo l'ochlav* — the invalidity created when one *shechts* the *korban Pesach* with the intention of offering it for the sake of people who are owners yet are unable to eat. This is a *pasul* unique to the *korban Pesach*, and it applies specifically at the moment of *shechita*.

### Arelim v. Mulim

The *gemara* resumes four lines from the bottom of 62b with a *tanya*. The *baraita* states in the name of *Acherim* — understood to be Rabbi Meir — that if one first mentions *mulim* (circumcised) and then *arelim* (uncircumcised), the *shechita* is *kasher*. But if one says *arelim* before *mulim*, it is *pasul*. The *gemara* sets out to unpack this ruling.

### Mixed Thought Analysis

The *gemara* asks: *mai shna mulim l'arelim de-kasher* — why is it valid if one says *mulim* and *arelim*? Because, as the preceding discussion established, *shelo l'ochlav* is only invalid when the entire intended group is an ineligible group. A mixed group — partly *mulim*, partly *arelim* — does not constitute that kind of fully invalid designation. But that reasoning applies equally when the words are said in reverse order. Whether one says *arelim l'mulim* or *mulim l'arelim*, one is still referring to a mixed group. So why does the order matter? The *gemara* turns to the top of 63a to resolve this.

### Yeshna L'Shechita

The *gemara* proposes: *leima kasavri Acherim — eina lishchita ela besof*, and invokes a ruling of Rava, noting that it remains a standing dispute. An enormous amount is packed into these few words, as they reference two distinct and expansive *sugyot* in *Shas*.

The first is the question of *yeshna lishchita mitchila v'ad sof* versus *eina lishchita ela l'besof* — whether the act of *shechita* is considered to be performed continuously throughout the entire cutting process, or whether it is treated as taking legal effect only at its conclusion. The second is the debate of *tchilas devarav adam nitpas* versus *besof devarav adam nitpas* — whether, when a person makes a statement whose components are in tension, we hold him to the first part he uttered or the last.

### Process vs. Moment

The question of *yeshna lishchita mitchila v'ad sof* is fundamentally about whether *shechita* should be understood as a continuous process or as a discrete point in time. It is not simply a question of identifying at which precise instant the act legally occurs — everyone agrees that the cut must be completed — but rather whether the entire duration of the cutting constitutes the act, or whether the act is defined solely by its final moment, with that final moment then incorporating everything that preceded it.

This question has wide application across the laws of *korbanot*. An invalidating *machshava* — whether *shelo lishmah*, *shelo l'shem ba'alim*, or *shelo l'ochlav* — does not become irrelevant simply because one stops thinking it at the precise last instant. The question is rather: when did that thought take legal effect? If *shechita* is a process, then a thought present at any point during the cutting took effect during the act of *shechita* itself. If *shechita* is only at its end, then the question becomes what thoughts are operative at that final moment, which then absorbs all that preceded.

### Timeline Model

To make this concrete: imagine the *shechita* begins at one point and concludes when both the trachea and esophagus have been cut. If *yeshno lishchita mitchila v'ad sof* — that the entire process constitutes *shechita* — then at some point during the cutting one might have thought *mulim*, and a split second later *arelim*, or vice versa. Since both thoughts are present during the act of *shechita*, the designation is mixed, and a mixed designation is *kasher*. On this view, both orderings should be equally valid.

If, on the other hand, *eino lishchita ela basof* — only the final moment counts — then one would think that both thoughts, having been expressed sequentially, are effectively absorbed into that single final moment and are simultaneously operative. This should also produce a mixed designation, which would also be *kasher*. So on either view, the order should not matter. What changes everything is the introduction of the second *sugya*.

### Rav Papa's Position

If *eino lishchita ela basof* — if everything takes legal effect at the end — then the two statements of *arelim* and *mulim*, although uttered sequentially, are combined into a single moment of effect. This is where the debate of *tchilas devarav adam nitpas* becomes operative. Rabbi Yosi holds *batchilat devarav adam nitpas* — one is bound by the first part of a compound or seemingly contradictory statement. If both *arelim* and *mulim* take effect simultaneously at the conclusion, it is as though they were said at once, and according to that principle, only the first part would govern.

Rava addresses a case where this principle is applied not retroactively but prospectively — if one says "I want this animal to be an *olah-shelamim* starting at noon." Here one cannot argue that the person first said *olah* and then changed their mind, since both are being designated for a future moment. Abaye holds that Rabbi Yosi would not apply *tchilas devarav* in such a case, since there is no sequence of reconsideration. Rabbah, however, says *adayin hi machloket* — the debate persists even then. Even when the two designations are intended to take effect together at a later point, Rabbi Yosi would still hold that only the first governs.

### Tchilas Devarav

The *gemara* now reads this into the case of *arelim* and *mulim*. The *shochet* is performing the cut and intends to say *l'mulim v'l'arelim*, but the *shechita* takes effect at the final moment, meaning both statements are combined into that single point. Rabbah says *adayin hi machloket*, meaning: even in such a case, the debate about *tchilas devarav adam nitpas* still applies. According to the position that one is bound by the first thing said, the entire designation reduces to whichever word came first. Hence the *gemara*'s conclusion follows:

*Hilcha hikdim mulim l'arelim* — if *mulim* was said first, *mulim chaili arelim lo chaili*: only *mulim* takes legal effect at that final moment, not *arelim*, and the *shechita* is valid. *Heicha d'amar arelim l'mulim* — if *arelim* was said first, *arelim chaili mulim lo chaili*: only *arelim* takes effect, and it is *pasul*.

This is then stated explicitly in the text: *hilcha hikdim mulim l'arelim* — if *mulim* was said first — *mulim chaili arelim lo chaili*, and it is valid. Reversed, *arelim chaili mulim lo chaili*, and it is invalid. The key word *chaili* means the designation *chal* — takes legal effect.

Now Rabbah (some have the *girsa* of Rava; the *gemara* will address this) responds: *le'olam kasavar Acharin yeshna lishchita mit'tchila v'ad sof*. One need not invoke the *eino lishchita ela basof* position at all. Even if we say *shechita* is a continuous process throughout, there is still a reason the order matters — but for a completely different reason.

### Mulim First Case

Rabbah's answer redirects the analysis entirely. *Dehacha b'mai askinan* — the case under discussion is one where the *shochet* intended in his mind to designate the *korban* for both *mulim* and *arelim*, but what he actually articulated during the *shechita* was only one of them — and the second word came out only after the *shechita* was complete.

If he said *mulim* first, then while the *shechita* was ongoing, he had said *l'mulim*, and he finished the *shechita* before he could complete the phrase *v'l'arelim*. At the critical moment of *shechita*, what was said was *l'mulim*, and the *arelim* was added only afterward. The designation at the time of the act was therefore for *mulim*, which is valid.

### Arelim First Case

Conversely, if he said *arelim* first and then completed the *shechita* before getting to *mulim*, then at the critical moment of the *shechita* only *arelim* had been articulated. The subsequent utterance of *mulim* does not help, since it came after the act was already complete. What matters is what was said during the *shechita*, and what was said was only *arelim*, which is *pasul*.

This is the ruling as the *gemara* states it: *vegamar belivo l'travaiyu* — in his mind he intended both — *vehotzi b'piv l'arelim* — but what he said aloud was *arelim*, *velo hispik lomar l'mulim ad shenigmara shchita* — and he did not manage to say *mulim* before the *shechita* was complete.

### Piv v'Libo Shavin

The *gemara* then raises a fundamental objection from a different direction. If the reason we dismiss the second half of the statement is that it came too late, the implicit assumption is that we go by what was said — and specifically what was said at the critical moment — even if it does not reflect what was in the speaker's mind. After all, in his mind he was thinking of both *mulim* and *arelim* throughout. But one might ask: does Rabbi Meir really hold that one's speech need not reflect one's inner intention?

The *gemara* challenges this from the following ruling: if a person intended to say *terumah* and accidentally said *maaser*, or intended to make a *neder* about one house but misspoke and said another — *lo amar klum*, the statement has no effect, *ad sheyehei piv uleevo shavin* — until one's mouth and heart are aligned. This appears to be a universal principle. Why then would Rabbi Meir not require *piv v'libo shavin* here?

The *gemara* answers: *deRabbi Meir savar lo ba'inan piv v'libo shavin* — Rabbi Meir holds that we do not require the mouth to match the heart. *Rabbanan savri ba'inan piv v'libo shavin* — the Rabbis hold that we do. The Rabbis would therefore say: since the *shochet* was thinking of *mulim* and *arelim* as a mixed group throughout, and his speech at the critical moment was only a partial expression of that full intention and did not match what he was thinking in its entirety, we cannot reduce his designation to just the first word.

### Articulated Thought

This leads to a conclusion of broad importance. We have been speaking throughout this *sugya* and the preceding ones as though the *psulei machshava* of *shelo lishmah*, *shelo l'shem ba'alim*, and *shelo l'ochlav* are purely about what one thinks. Here the *gemara* makes clear that the operative category is what one articulates. Rashi states explicitly — commenting on *ve-hacha bemai askinan* — that *kol machshava de-kodshim motzi befiv*: whenever the *gemara* speaks of an invalid *machshava* by *kodshim*, it means an expressed, articulated thought — not a silent intention held in the mind alone.

Tosafot makes the same point even more directly. From the *gemara*'s discussion here, Tosafot derives that what is called *machshava* throughout the *sugya* in all cases of *pigul* and *shelo lishmah* does not mean pure mental intention — *eino pigul ad she-yotzi befiv* — it is not *pigul* unless one has expressed it verbally.

The reason Tosafot gives for distinguishing this from the principle of *devarim shebalev einam devarim* is significant. The principle that unexpressed thoughts have no legal force applies when a person harbored a silent condition or intention that they simply never stated — in that case, since you did not say it, we cannot give it legal effect. But here, the *shochet* did speak. The problem is not that he was silent about part of his intention but that he misspoke, or that the second part of what he was saying came out too late. When speech does not reflect intent because of error or mistiming, we can set aside the spoken word. When speech reflects a deliberate silent reservation one chose not to articulate, we cannot import that reservation.

### Two Siman Model

Abaye offers a different resolution entirely. *Reisha d'amar siman rishon lemulin vesiman sheini af lareilin* — the case where the order is *mulim* first is one where the *shochet* said, while cutting the first *siman* (the trachea), that this is for *mulim*, and when cutting the second *siman* (the esophagus), he added that it is also for *arelim*. Since the *arelim* designation was attached to the second *siman* and came after the *mulim* had already been stated, the *mulim* is embedded in the context of the second *siman* as well — *nami ptichi be-mulin*, it opens into the *mulim* — and the thought is therefore mixed throughout.

In the reverse case — *siman rishon lareilin siman sheini lemulin* — he designated the first *siman* for *arelim* alone. Even though he later said *lemulin* during the second *siman*, the first *siman* stood entirely on its own as a designation for *arelim*, with no admixture of *mulim* at that point. That isolated designation of *arelim* for the first *siman* creates a *psul machshava* that cannot be remedied by what was added later.

### Mefalgin Bachatzi

Abaye's resolution leads the *gemara* to an explicit connection: *veRabbi Meir letaimei de-amar mefalgin be-chatzi matir, verabbanan letaimei de-amri ein mefalgin be-chatzi matir*. Can one produce *pigul* — or any *psul machshava* — by means of an invalid thought applied to only half of the *matir*, i.e., only one of the two *simanim*? Rabbi Meir holds *mefalgin be-chatzi matir*: an invalid thought attaching to half the *matir* is sufficient to create the *pasul*. Therefore, when one says *arelim* during the first *siman* alone, that creates a *psul* independent of what was said during the second. The Rabbis hold *ein mefalgin be-chatzi matir*: you cannot generate an invalid designation from only half the *matir*, so we assess the thought only when both *simanim* are complete — at which point the designation is mixed, and therefore *kasher*.

This debate of *mefalgin be-chatzi matir* is larger than the case at hand. It applies, for example, to a *mincha* where both the *kometz* and the *levonah* must be offered, and one has an invalid thought by only one of them. The question of whether one can create *pigul* with half the *matir* is a broad *sugya* in *Shas*, and here the *gemara* roots the *arelim-mulim* dispute directly within it. There is also a conceptual relationship to the question of *yeshna lishchita mitchila v'ad sof*, since treating *shechita* as two discrete acts — each of the two *simanim* — presupposes that we are willing to analyze each act separately, which is itself the underlying logic of *yeshna lishchita*.

---

## Lo Tishchat Al Chametz

### Intro: Chametz Prohibiti…

We now shift to a distinct but related topic — the prohibition of *lo tishchat al chametz dam zivchi*, the prohibition against *shechting* the *Pesach* while *chametz* is present. The *pasuk* does not say *Pesach* explicitly, but says *dam zivchi* — the blood of my sacrifices. As we will see, this generates significant debate about the scope of the prohibition and about who must own the *chametz* for the violation to apply.

### Mishna & R. Yehuda

The *mishna* opens: *hashochet et hapesach al hachametz over belo taaseh* — one who *shechts* the *korban Pesach* while *chametz* is present transgresses a negative commandment. Rabbi Yehuda adds: *af hatamid* — even the afternoon *tamid* on *erev Pesach*. He understands the prohibition to extend beyond the *korban Pesach* itself, applying to other *korbanot* offered during the *zman shechitat chametz* as well.

### R. Shimon Principle

Rabbi Shimon's position introduces a major new principle. *Hapesach bearba asar lishmo* — if one *shechts* the *korban Pesach* on the fourteenth properly in its name, and one has *chametz*, *chayav* — one has transgressed. *Veshelo lishmo* — if the *shechita* was done *shelo lishmo*, *patur* — one is exempt. The reason, according to Rabbi Shimon, is the principle of *shchita she'eina reu'ya lo kriya shchita* — a *shechita* that did not achieve the effect of rendering the meat permissible or of constituting a valid *korban* is not called an act of *shechita* at all. It is as though the animal was simply stabbed. Since *shelo lishmo* rendered the *Pesach* invalid, there was no act of *shechita* in the relevant sense, and therefore the prohibition of *lo tishchat* was not violated.

### Pesach Still Kosher

A striking ruling emerges from the Tosafot Riva: *depesach kashar* — the *korban Pesach* itself remains *kasher* even if one transgressed the prohibition of *lo tishchat al chametz*. The *Tosefta* in the *Mechilta* states explicitly: *hashochet et hapesach al hachametz be-yud-daled over belo taaseh, vehapesach atzmo kashar, veyotzei bo yedei chovato bapesach* — one violates the *lav* but fulfills the *mitzvah* of eating the *korban Pesach*. The transgression of *lo tishchat al chametz* does not invalidate the *Pesach*. This is distinct from the *shelo lishmo* case, which addresses the validity of the *korban*, not the *lo tishchat* prohibition.

### Chattat Exception

Rabbi Shimon then continues with his taxonomy of *shelo lishmah*. For all other *korbanot*, if done *shelo lishmo* on the fourteenth, whether or not they are *kasher*, he holds *patur*, because *erev Pesach* is the time designated for *korban Pesach* — the prohibition can only be violated by *shechting* a *korban Pesach*, not by *shechting* other *korbanot*. For the *chag* itself, the picture changes: if one *shechts* a *Pesach lishmo* on the fifteenth, it is *pasul*, and therefore *patur* by Rabbi Shimon's principle; if *shelo lishmo* — which renders it a *kasher shelamim* — then *chayav*. All other *korbanot*, whether *lishmo* or *shelo lishmo*, are *kasher* and therefore *chayav*, with one exception: *chatat sheshachto shelo lishmah*, which is invalid, and therefore by Rabbi Shimon's principle is again *patur*.

### Invalid Shechita Logic

The logic driving all of Rabbi Shimon's exemptions is consistent: *shechita she'eina reu'ya lo kriya shechita*. Wherever the *shechita* did not produce a valid *korban*, it does not legally qualify as an act of *shechita*, and the prohibition of *lo tishchat* does not apply. Where the *shechita* produced a valid *korban* — even if it was not the intended *korban Pesach* — the prohibition does apply. This principle is at work throughout Rabbi Shimon's position and will recur in subsequent analysis.

### Ownership Requirement

The *gemara* turns to the *amora'im* to address the question of whose *chametz* is relevant. Reish Lakish states: one does not transgress the prohibition unless the *chametz* belongs either to the *shochet* or to the *zorek* — the one who performs the sprinkling of the blood — or to one of the members of the *chaburah*, the group of owners who will eat the *korban*. This is a critical structural distinction: the *shochet* is the one who transgresses, but the relevant *chametz* need not be his own — it suffices that any member of the *chaburah* owns *chametz*. Conversely, owning *chametz* does not in itself cause a member of the *chaburah* to transgress the *lo tishchat* prohibition. Only the one performing the *shechita* or the *zerika* can transgress, and only if someone within the relevant circle owns *chametz*. Additionally, the *chametz* must be *im'o ba'azarah* — present with him in the *azarah*. This last requirement flows from the language of *al chametz*, which Reish Lakish understands to require physical proximity.

That the *zorek* is included at all is not obvious from the *pasuk*, which says *lo tishchat*. Rashi refers to a *Mechilta* from which we learn that *zrikat hadam* is also included, derived from a related *pasuk* of *vedam zvachecha yishapech*.

### Al Samuch Debate

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees with Reish Lakish's requirement of physical proximity: *af al pi she'eino imo ba'azarah* — even if the *chametz* is not present in the *azarah*, the prohibition applies. The *gemara* asks: *bemai kamiflagi* — what exactly do they dispute? The most natural reading is that they disagree about whether the word *al* in *lo tishchat al chametz* requires physical proximity — *al besamuch* — or merely conceptual connection. Reish Lakish holds *al besamuch*; Rabbi Yochanan holds *lo beinan al besamuch*.

The *gemara* notes that this same pair has apparently debated this question in another context, and wonders whether their dispute here is the same one restated, or whether there is an additional dimension — specifically, the question of *hatra'at safeik*, a doubtful warning. If the *chametz* is not in the *azarah*, the *kohein* performing the *shechita* cannot see it and may well doubt that the warning being given — do not *shecht*, one of the owners has *chametz* — is accurate. Reish Lakish holds, in another context, that *hatra'at safeik lav shma hatraa* — a doubtful warning is not a valid warning, and without a valid warning one cannot receive *malkot*. That would provide an independent reason for exemption separate from any question about *al besamuch*.

### Toda Bread Case

The *gemara* identifies the prior context in which Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish already argued about *al besamuch*: *hashochet todah lifnim velachmah lachutz* — one who *shechts* a *korban toda* inside the *azarah* while the accompanying bread is outside. The *toda* is accompanied by bread, and the *pasuk* connects them with the word *al* — *al zevach hatoda* — implying that the *shechita* of the *toda* sanctifies the bread when they are properly connected. If the bread is outside the *azarah* when the *toda* is *shechted*, does the bread become sanctified?

Rabbi Yochanan holds: *chutz lachoma Beit Pagi* means outside the wall of Jerusalem — if the bread is outside Jerusalem, it is not sanctified, but if it is merely outside the *azarah* but still within Jerusalem, it is sanctified. *Al besamuch* is not required for the bread. Reish Lakish holds: *afilu chutz lechomat azara lo kadish* — even one step outside the *azarah* and the bread is not sanctified. *Al besamuch* is required.

### Issura v. Kedushat Lechem

The *gemara* concludes that both disputes are necessary, despite their apparent overlap. *U-tzricha* — both cases must be stated, because each one alone might have led to a different inference about the other.

Had the dispute been stated only in the context of *chametz*, one might have thought: Rabbi Yochanan only says *lo beinan al besamuch* there because it involves a *transgression* — wherever the *chametz* is and however it is connected, the *issur* is present in full. But when it comes to *sanctifying the bread*, one might have supposed that even Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Reish Lakish that the bread must be within the *azarah*, since the *shechita*'s power to sanctify it is analogous to the power of a *kli shareit* — and a *kli shareit* can only sanctify what is placed within it. Rashi understands the *azarah* itself as functioning in a manner analogous to a *kli shareit*: what is within it is amenable to sanctification, and what is outside is not. Tosafot makes a more technical version of this point: a *kli shareit* can only sanctify things placed into it when the *kli shareit* itself is in the *azarah*; similarly, the sanctifying power of the *shechita* extends only to what is present within the *azarah*. Therefore, had the dispute appeared only by *chametz*, we might have said Rabbi Yochanan would agree to Reish Lakish for the bread case.

Conversely, had the dispute appeared only by the bread, one might have thought: Reish Lakish insists on *al besamuch* there because sanctification requires physical proximity — *de-i ika gavai kadish, i lav lo kadish* — but for *chametz*, which is about a prohibition and not about conferring sanctity, even Reish Lakish might agree with Rabbi Yochanan that physical proximity is not required. Therefore, both cases must be stated.

It is also worth noting what all opinions agree upon: physical proximity alone, even if necessary according to Reish Lakish, is never sufficient. The *chametz* must be owned by the *shochet*, the *zorek*, or a member of the *chaburah*. Stranger's *chametz* in the *azarah* creates no liability whatsoever.

### Ownership Scenario

Rav Oshaya posed a question to Rabbi Ami: *ein lo la-shochet ve-yesh lo le-achad mi-benei ha-chaburah mahu* — what if the *shochet* himself has no *chametz*, but one of the members of the *chaburah* does? Is the *shochet* liable?

### Lo Yalin Connection

Rabbi Ami responded: it does not say *lo tishchat al chamtzecha* — do not *shecht* on your *chametz*. The *pasuk* says *lo tishchat al chametz* — with *chametz*, meaning *chametz* that is in some relevant sense connected. The connection is established not by ownership specifically, but by the juxtaposition within the *pasuk* itself: *lo tishchat al chametz dam zivchi velo yalin chelev chagi ad boker*. The prohibition of *lo tishchat* is linked to *lo yalin* — the prohibition against leaving the fat unburned overnight. Those who are subject to the obligation of *lo yalin* with respect to this *korban* — i.e., those whose connection to the *korban* is such that its overnight neglect would concern them — are the ones whose ownership of *chametz* renders the *shochet* liable. This definitively includes the members of the *chaburah*.

### Rav Papa Extension

Rav Papa draws an additional inference. If the category of those subject to *lo yalin* is what determines whose *chametz* is relevant, then: *kohein hamaktir et hachelev* — a *kohein* who burns the fats of the *korban Pesach* — *over belo taaseh* — transgresses the *lav* of *lo tishchat* — *hoil veyeshno bichlal halanat imurin* — because he is within the category of those subject to *halanat imurin*, the prohibition against leaving the *eimurin* unburned overnight.

This is a significant analytical leap. Until this point, the *lo yalin* connection was used to identify whose *chametz* ownership is relevant for the *shochet's* liability. Rav Papa now uses it to create liability for an entirely new act — *haktarat imurin* — that is nowhere mentioned in the *pasuk*. We already knew from Reish Lakish that *zerika* is also an act that triggers liability, derived from a separate *pasuk*. Rav Papa adds *haktarat imurin* on the basis of the *kohein*'s relationship to *lo yalin*, reasoning that one subject to *lo yalin* who performs an *avoda* on this *korban* is brought within the scope of the prohibition.

### Braita: Who Transgresses

The *gemara* cites a *braita* in support of Rav Papa. The *braita* states: *hashochet et hapesach al hachametz* — one who *shechts* the *Pesach* with *chametz* present — *over belo taaseh* — when it is: *lashochet, o lazorek, o leachad mibnei chaburah* — belonging to the *shochet*, the *zorek*, or one of the members of the *chaburah*. If the *chametz* belongs to some stranger — *hayah leachad besof haolam, ein zakuk lo* — it does not matter. The *braita* then confirms the scope of Rav Papa's ruling: *ve'echad hashochet ve'echad hazorek ve'echad hamaktir chayav* — whether one performed the *shechita*, the *zerika*, or the *haktara*, one is liable.

### Melikat Exception

The *braita* adds one further ruling: *aval hamolek et ha'of bearba'ah asar eino over belo klum* — one who performs *melikat ha'of* — the neckpinching that substitutes for *shechita* in bird-offerings — on the fourteenth of Nisan is not liable at all. The surface reading might suggest the reason is that *melika* is not an act of *shechita*, and therefore falls outside the prohibition of *lo tishchat*. However, Rashi explains that the actual reason is different: on *erev Pesach*, the prohibition only applies to *shechting* a *korban Pesach*, and *melika* is done for a bird, not a *korban Pesach*. The most common reason to bring a bird at this time is for *mechuserei kippurim* — those completing the *taharah* process — who would bring such a bird even after the *tamid* in order to become *tahor* in time to eat the *korban Pesach*. Since the bird is not a *korban Pesach*, the prohibition of *lo tishchat al chametz* simply does not apply to it on the fourteenth.

# Pesachim 64

## Chametz during Shechita

### Lo Tishchat Al Chametz

The daf opens by wrapping up the prohibition of *lo tishchat al chametz dam zivchi* — the prohibition against *shechting* the *Korban Pesach*, or *korbanot* generally, while one still owns *chametz*. The scriptural basis is the verse *lo tishchat al chametz dam zivchi v'lo yalin chelev chagi ad boker*, which prohibits both the slaughter while *chametz* is present and the leaving over of the fats.

### Who Transgresses

The Gemara introduces a *baraita* from the bottom of 63b: *ha-shochet et ha-Pesach al ha-chametz over b'lo ta'aseh* — one who *shechts* the *Pesach* while *chametz* is owned transgresses a negative prohibition. Rabbi Yehuda extends this to include even the *tamid* on *erev Pesach*, while the Sages respond that the prohibition applies only to the *Korban Pesach* alone. The *baraita* then specifies whose *chametz* is relevant: that of the *shochet*, the *zorek*, or any member of the *chaburah*. If some stranger owns *chametz* at the other end of the world, that is not the group's concern. As for which act triggers the transgression, the *baraita* states: *v'echad ha-shochet v'echad ha-zorek v'echad ha-malik v'echad ha-mazeh chayav* — whether one performs *shechita*, *zerika*, *melika*, or the sprinkling of the blood in the context of a bird offering, one is liable. However, the *kometz* of a *minchah* does not trigger the prohibition — the verse says *al dam*, which excludes a *minchah* — and, according to this *baraita*, neither does *haktarah*.

### Melika vs. Haktarah

This *baraita* stands in tension with the earlier discussion. The earlier source had excluded *melika* but included *haktarah*; this *baraita* does the reverse, including *melika* and excluding *haktarah*. The Gemara observes: *kashya melika a-melika kashya haktara a-haktara* — there is a contradiction regarding *melika* and a contradiction regarding *haktarah*. But before resolving the inter-*baraita* conflict, the Gemara notes that this *baraita* is already internally problematic. It begins by declaring *lo amru ela b'Pesach bilvad* — the prohibition applies only to the *Korban Pesach* — yet immediately proceeds to discuss *melika*, which is the method of slaughter for birds, not an act performed in connection with the *Korban Pesach* at all. The Gemara answers: *ela ha v'ha Rabbi Shimon* — both *baraitot* reflect the position of Rabbi Shimon.

### Erev Pesach vs. Pesach

The resolution turns on Rabbi Shimon's distinctive position as stated in the *mishnah*: on the fourteenth, only the *Korban Pesach* triggers the prohibition — not the *tamid* and not any other *korban*. On *Pesach* itself, from the fifteenth through the end of *Yom Tov* including *Chol HaMoed*, any *korban* triggers the prohibition. With this in mind, the *melika* contradiction dissolves: *kan b'arba'ah asar kan b'cholo shel moed* — one *baraita* speaks of *erev Pesach*, where only the *Korban Pesach* is relevant, and the other speaks of *Chol HaMoed*, when all *korbanot* including bird offerings — which involve *melika* — are included. The first *baraita*'s statement that it applies only to the *Korban Pesach* addresses the question of which type of *korban* triggers liability on the fourteenth, while the second *baraita*'s enumeration of acts, including *melika*, concerns what acts trigger liability during the *chag* itself. The two *baraitot* are not addressing the same question, which explains why their conclusions appear to diverge. As for the *haktarah* contradiction — one *baraita* includes it and one excludes it — the Gemara resolves this simply as a debate among *tannaim*: *de'ika de-makish haktara li-shechita ve-ika de-man de-lo makish*. Whether the act of burning the *emurim* is included in the prohibition is a *machloket*, depending on whether one draws the analogy between *haktarah* and *shechita* from the second half of the verse, *v'lo yalin chelev chagi ad boker*.

### Zevach vs. Zivchay

Rabbi Yehuda's inclusion of the *tamid* rests on his reading of *mai zivchi* — "my sacrifice" — as referring to the sacrifice uniquely associated with the *mizbe'ach* at all times, which is the *tamid*: *olat tamid asuyah be-Har Sinai*. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, derives his position from the fact that the verse *lo tishchat al chametz dam zivchi* appears twice in the Torah — once in *Mishpatim* and again following the episode of the *eigel*, when the *Aseret HaDibrot* and portions of *Mishpatim* are repeated. Rabbi Shimon reads the two appearances together: *kari beih zevach zivchay* — by moving the *yud* from one occurrence to the other, one instance is read as *zevach* (singular) and the other as *zivchay* (plural). *Zevach* — singular — refers to the single *korban* that matters on *erev Pesach*, namely the *Korban Pesach*. *Zivchay* — plural — refers to all *korbanot* brought during the *chag* itself. The Torah's deliberate doubling of the verse, rather than simply writing *zivchay* outright, signals a partition: *b'zman d'ika zevach lo mechayev a-zivchay* — when the singular *zevach* is in force (*erev Pesach*), one is liable only for that one; *b'zman d'leika zevach mechayev a-zivchay* — when that singular *zevach* is no longer in force (the *chag* itself), one becomes liable for all *korbanot*.

### Pesach Shelo Lishmo

Rabbi Shimon's position generates a further ruling: *u-b'moed lishmo patur* — if one *shechts* a *Korban Pesach* on the *moed* in its proper name as a *Pesach*, one is exempt from the prohibition. The reason is that a *Korban Pesach* slaughtered *lishmo* as a *Pesach* after the fourteenth is *pasul*, because *Pesach she-lo bi-zmano* is invalid. And Rabbi Shimon holds that *shechitah she-einah re'uyah lo shemai shechitah* — an act of *shechita* that is inherently unfit does not even register as a valid *shechita*, and therefore carries no liability. Conversely, if one *shechts* the animal *shelo lishmo* — designating it as a *shelamim* — it becomes a valid *zevach* and one would be liable.

This leads to a question: why does the *mishnah* say one needs to actively slaughter it *shelo lishmo* in order to make it a *shelamim*? The principle is that a *Pesach* in the rest of the year automatically becomes a *shelamim* — *pesach bi-sh'ar yemot ha-shanah shelamim havei*. If so, why is an active change of designation necessary? The Gemara entertains the inference that even after the fourteenth, a *Pesach* retains a submerged status as a *Pesach* and requires active uprooting — *akira* — to convert it. Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda reports that this question was resolved by the group in discussion: the ruling applies specifically to a case where the owners were *tumei meitim* and were therefore deferred to *Pesach Sheni*. In that case, the animal still genuinely awaits its proper time — the fourteenth of *Iyar* — and so it does not automatically convert to a *shelamim* during *Chol HaMoed*. An active *akira* is required. But where the owners have already fulfilled their obligation and this animal is simply a leftover, it automatically converts.

*Tosafot* reads the Gemara's question somewhat differently. According to *Tosafot*, the question is not merely why an active change is needed, but why *shechting* it *lishmo* as a *Pesach* would make it *pasul* at all. If after the fourteenth it is simply a *shelamim*, then *shechting* it in the name of a *Pesach* should merely render it a *shelamim shelo lishmo*, which is *kasher*. The only reason it would be *pasul* is if the *korban* retains some underlying *Pesach* identity that can be reawakened — so that *shechting* it *lishmo* as a *Pesach* actually does something, and that something is invalid. The Gemara's answer — that this is a special case involving animals held over for *Pesach Sheni* — explains why that dormant *Pesach* status persists and can be reactivated.

---

## Three Groups & Shechita

### Three Groups

The Gemara now turns to the *mishnah* describing the procedure of bringing the *Korban Pesach*, a welcome shift from abstract prohibition analysis to vivid Temple reality. *Ha-Pesach nishchat bi-shlosh kitot* — the *Pesach* is slaughtered in three groups. The scriptural basis is the verse *ve-shachatu oto kol kehal adat Yisrael bein ha-arbayim* — the three terms *kehal*, *edah*, and *Yisrael* each indicate a distinct group, and so the *Korban Pesach* is brought in three separate rotations throughout the afternoon of the fourteenth.

### Locking the Azarah

*Nichnesah kat rishonah* — the first group enters. *Nitmal'ah ha-azarah* — the *azarah* fills with those bringing their *korban*. At that point, *na'alu daltot ha-azarah* — the doors of the *azarah* are locked, signaling that the space is at capacity and the rest must wait for the next round. The *kohanim* then sounded *tekiah teruah tekiah* — a set of three *shofar* blasts — to mark the beginning of the service.

### Gold & Silver Bowls

*Ha-kohanim omdim shurot shurot* — the *kohanim* stand in rows. *U-veyadeihem bezichei chesef u-vezichei zahav* — in their hands are bowls of silver and bowls of gold. A row of silver bowls is entirely silver; a row of gold bowls is entirely gold. *Velo hayu me'uravim* — the two types are not intermingled within a row. And all of these bowls, *velo hayu la-bezichim shulayim*, have no base — they are rounded at the bottom and cannot be set down. The reason: *shema yanichum ve-yikaresh ha-dam* — lest the *kohanim* put a bowl down and forget it, allowing the blood to congeal and rendering *zrikat ha-dam* impossible. By making the bowls impossible to set down, the procedure ensures the blood is always in motion.

### Shechita & Blood Pass

The physical arrangement was a conveyor of sorts: *shachat Yisrael ve-kibel ha-Kohen* — a *Yisrael* performed the *shechita*, and a *Kohen* received the blood in a bowl. The Gemara will clarify that the *mishnah* is not saying a *Yisrael* must perform the *shechita* to the exclusion of a *Kohen*, but rather affirms that *shechita* by a non-*Kohen* is valid. However, the *Tosefta* quoted by *Tosafot* — *Yisrael shochtim et pischeihem u-Leviyim korim et ha-Hallel* — does suggest that in practice the owners themselves would perform the *shechita* while the *Leviyim* recited *Hallel*. The *mishnah* continues: *nosno l'chavero ve-chavero l'chavero* — the first *Kohen* passes the bowl to the next, who passes it to the one behind him. *U-mekabel et ha-male u-machazir et ha-reikan* — as one receives the full bowl coming toward the *mizbe'ach*, he simultaneously returns an empty bowl going back toward the point of *shechita*. This is a bucket brigade — a long line of *kohanim* passing blood forward and empty vessels backward in continuous motion, engaging as many *kohanim* as possible in the sacred service.

### Zrika Location

*Ha-Kohen ha-karov etzel ha-mizbe'ach zorko zrika achat keneged ha-yesod* — the *Kohen* nearest the *mizbe'ach* throws one *zrika* against the wall of the *mizbe'ach* opposite the base. This specification is meaningful because the *yesod* — the protruding base — did not run along all four sides. The *yesod* protruded only along the northern and western walls, not the southern and eastern ones. For a standard *korban*, blood is thrown at the two corners where two sides with a *yesod* meet — *shtayim she-hen arba*, two throws covering four walls. For the *Korban Pesach*, a single throw suffices, but it must be against one of the walls from which blood can run down to the *yesod*. The blood is thrown against the wall itself, and from there it runs down to the protruding base below.

### Hallel Recitation

While the *shechita* is underway, *Hallel* is being recited — as the *Tosefta* states, the *Leviyim* read *Hallel* while *Yisrael* perform the *shechita*. If the *Leviyim* completed *Hallel* and the group had still not finished bringing all their *korbanot*, they began *Hallel* a second time; if that too was completed, they began a third time. *Af al pi she-lo shilshelu mi-yemeihem* — in all of history, it never came to a third recitation. Rabbi Yehuda adds an observation about the third group in particular: *mi-yemeihem shel kat shlishit lo higu le-Ahavti ki yishma Hashem* — the third group was so small that they never even reached the passage *Ahavti ki yishma Hashem* in a single recitation of *Hallel*.

---

## Shabbat Pesach Procedure

### Flaying on Shabbat

*Ke-ma'aseihu be-chol kach ma'aseihu be-Shabbat* — the same procedure performed on a weekday is performed on *Shabbat*. One difference, however, involved the rinsing of the *azarah*. On a weekday, the *kohanim* would dam up the water channel flowing through the *azarah*, causing it to overflow and wash away the blood from the floor, after which the floor was squeegeed into the drainage holes. On *Shabbat* they would do this as well, *ella she-ha-kohanim madichin et ha-azarah she-lo birtson chachamim* — but the *chachamim* objected to this practice on *Shabbat*. The grounds for the objection will be discussed in the Gemara.

### Hooks & Poles

*Keitzad tolin u-mafshitin* — how did they suspend and flay the *Korban Pesach*? *Unkelyot shel barzel hayu kevi'im ba-ktalim u-va-amudim* — iron hooks were fixed into the walls and posts of the *Beit HaMitbachayim*, the slaughterhouse area of the *Beit HaMikdash*, and the carcasses were hung from these hooks for *hafshata* (flaying). The *emurim* needed to be removed and burned on the *mizbe'ach*, and since this constituted the *avodah* of the *korban* rather than mere meat preparation, the *hafshata* was permitted even on *Shabbat*. For those who could not find an available hook, *maklot dakkim ve-chalakim hayu sham* — thin, smooth poles were kept on hand. *Meniach al ktefo ve-al ktef chaveiro* — one person would put the pole on his shoulder and his friend's shoulder, creating a human post from which the carcass was suspended for flaying.

### Rabbi Eliezer's Ruling

Rabbi Eliezer rules that when the fourteenth falls on *Shabbat*, even the smooth poles should not be used, and instead one uses human arms directly: *meniach yado al ktef chaveiro ve-yad chaveiro al ktefo* — placing one arm on his companion's shoulder and his companion's arm on his, forming a living crossbeam from which to suspend and flay the offering. The apparent concern is something akin to *muktzah* regarding the poles, even in the midst of all the other *Shabbat*-permitted *avodah*. The precise mechanics of how the carcass could be adequately supported by arms rather than poles remain somewhat difficult to picture given the weight of the animal.

### Innards & First Group

*Kar'o* — they split the carcass. *Hotzi et emurav* — the innards and fats were removed. *Netano ba-magis* — placed in a pan. *Hiktiru al gabbe ha-mizbe'ach* — and burned on the *mizbe'ach*. This completed the *avodah* of that group.

### Groups' Locations

On a weekday, after completing their *korbanot*, the first group simply went home. On *Shabbat*, however, carrying is prohibited and one cannot leave *Yerushalayim* with the carcass until nightfall. The *mishnah* therefore describes where each group waited. *Yatz'ta kat rishonah ve-yashvah lah b'Har HaBayit* — the first group went out and sat on *Har HaBayit*, which was enclosed by the outer wall. *Shniyah ba-cheil* — the second group waited in the *cheil*, the narrow corridor between the outer *soreg* barrier and the *azarah* walls. *Ha-shlishit bi-mkomah omedet* — the third group remained standing in the *azarah* itself. *Chashecha* — when darkness fell, they all went out and roasted their *Korban Pesach* at their lodgings in *Yerushalayim*.

---

## Minimum Pesach Size

### 30 per Group Rule

Rabbi Yitzchak teaches: *ein ha-Pesach nishchat ela bi-shlosh kitot shel shloshim shloshim bnei adam* — the *Pesach* may not be slaughtered unless there are three groups of thirty people each. The reasoning derives from the same verse: the three terms *kehal*, *edah*, and *Yisrael* each imply a minimum quorum of ten, yielding thirty. Rabbi Yitzchak is uncertain whether the Torah means thirty people must be present simultaneously, or whether it requires three separate groups of ten brought in sequence. *Hilkhakh ba'inan shalosh kitot shel shloshim shloshim bnei adam* — to satisfy both possibilities, he requires three groups of thirty each. However, the Gemara points out that this need not mean ninety people altogether. *Chamishim nami sagi* — fifty suffice. The first group of thirty enters and performs the *shechita*, satisfying the requirement of thirty at one time. Then ten of them leave and ten newcomers enter, forming a second group of ten at a new time — but the twenty remaining from the first group still make up a group of thirty alongside them. Then another ten of those original thirty exit and the final ten newcomers enter, again reaching thirty with the lingering members. This overlapping arrangement covers both possibilities with only fifty individuals.

### Miracle vs. Manual Lock

The *mishnah* says the doors of the *azarah* were locked once the first group entered and filled the space. A dispute between Abaye and Rava concerns the nature of this locking. Abaye holds *ninalu* — the doors locked themselves, miraculously, of their own accord. The procedure was to allow people to continue entering for as long as they could, and one relied on the miracle that the doors would seal themselves when capacity was reached: *d'samchinan a-nisa*. Rava holds *no'alin* — human beings actively monitored the incoming crowd and locked the doors manually: *v'lo samchinan a-nisa*.

### Akavya Story

This same debate is applied to the story of Akavya ben Mahalalel. In a separate context in the Gemara, there is a claim that Akavya was placed in *niduy* after he disputed a ruling of Shemaya and Avtaliyon regarding whether a freed slave woman would undergo the *Sotah* process. Rabbi Yehuda responds: *chas v'shalom she-Akavya ben Mahalalel nitnade* — God forbid that Akavya ben Mahalalel was ever put in *niduy* — for *she-ein azarah nin'elet al kol adam b'Yisrael* — when the doors of the *azarah* were sealed on *erev Pesach* with all of Israel packed within, there was not to be found among all those people anyone equal *b'chokhmah u-v'yirat cheit* to Akavya ben Mahalalel. The phrase *azarah nin'elet* is thus read as an expression of the totality of Israel assembled.

Abaye and Rava each explain this phrase in accordance with their respective positions: Abaye reads *nin'elet* as the doors locking themselves — in that miraculous moment when the *azarah* sealed itself, there was no one within equal to Akavya. Rava reads *no'alim otah* — when they locked the *azarah* actively, among all those assembled there was no one his equal. The *masorah* does not decisively favor one reading over the other.

---

## Agrippas' Census

### Crushing Incident

The Gemara states: *me'olam lo nitma'eikh adam ba-azarah* — no one was ever crushed in the *azarah* despite the extraordinary crowding. The one exception: *chutz mi-Pesach echad she-hayah bi-ymei Hillel* — except for one *Pesach* in the time of Hillel, when an elderly person was crushed. That event was remembered and the *Pesach* of that year was called *Pesach Me'uchin* — the crushed *Pesach*. The Gemara notes that the report of this single exception actually strengthens the claim that it otherwise never happened.

### Kidney Count

Another *baraita* reports that King Agrippas — one of the kings at the close of the *Bayit Sheni* period — wished to gain a sense of the vast numbers of the Jewish people he ruled. He instructed the *Kohen Gadol* to count the *Pesachim* as a means of census. *Natlu kulya mi-kol echad* — a kidney was taken from each *Pesach* offering as a marker. *Ve-nimtze'u sham shishim ribo zugei kelyot* — six hundred thousand pairs of kidneys were found, meaning 1.2 million *Pesachim*. Since each *Pesach* was shared by at minimum ten people, this implies a population of twelve million — *kiflayim ke-yotzei Mitzrayim*, double those who left Egypt. The *baraita* notes that this count excluded those who were *tamei* or who were on a distant journey and therefore did not bring a *Pesach*. That year's gathering was called *Pesach Me'uvin* — the thick or dense *Pesach* — in contrast to the *Pesach Me'uchin* of Hillel's day.

### Capacity Analysis

This figure invites scrutiny. The *azarah* in front of the *mizbe'ach* — the *ezrat Yisrael* — was 135 *amot* long by 11 *amot* wide, yielding approximately 1,400 to 1,500 square *amot*. Even allowing two or three people per square *amah* in extremely crowded conditions, the space could hold at most several thousand people at a time. With three groups rotating, the total might reach fifteen thousand individuals at the outside. The figure of twelve million adult males is plainly beyond any physical capacity the *azarah* could accommodate — even accounting for the well-known principle of *omdim tzefufim u-mishtachavim b'revach*. The story is clearly not intended as a precise census.

### Kidney Marking

The Gemara raises a technical difficulty with Agrippas' method. The kidney must be burned on the *mizbe'ach* — *ha-ketiv haktarah*. How could it be removed and used as a counting token? The Gemara answers: *de-hadar maktru lehu* — after the count, they were returned and burned. But a further difficulty arises: the verse *ve-hiktiram* implies all the *emurim* of a single *korban* must be burned together, not separately. And another source says *she-kulan k'achat* — all together. How then can a kidney be temporarily separated and later returned? The Gemara resolves: *ella tefisa b'alma* — the kidney was not actually removed, but merely grasped and held up as a marker, *de-shakil mineihu*, while another indicator was used for the count, and then the kidney was immediately released back with the rest of the *korban*'s *emurim*.

---

## Practical Details

### Bowls Without Bases

A *baraita* clarifies that the practice of making bowls without a base was not unique to the blood-collection procedure of the *Korban Pesach* but was universal in the *Mikdash*: *kol ha-bazichin she-ba-Mikdash lo hayu lahem shulayim* — all the bowls in the *Mikdash* had no base, always for the same reason of preventing blood from congealing if set down. The sole exception: *chutz mi-vazichei levonah shel lechem ha-panim* — the spoons used to hold the *levonah* (frankincense) placed on the *shulchan* alongside the *lechem ha-panim*. Those needed to lie flat on the *shulchan* for an entire week. If they had no base, they would have to lean against the bread, and *v'yipresu ha-lechem* — they would crack the delicately made loaves.

### Aesthetic Arrangement

The question of why the gold and silver bowls are not intermingled within a single row is addressed by the Gemara. One might suggest that the concern is a kind of inequitable exchange — a *Kohen* might hand back a gold bowl and receive a silver one, or hand back one worth two hundred *zuz* and receive one worth only a hundred. But the Gemara dismisses this: that imbalance is always possible regardless of arrangement, since any two bowls of the same material can differ in value. Rather, *ella de-hachi shapir tefei* — the reason is simply aesthetic. A row of uniform silver and a row of uniform gold is more beautiful and dignified than a mixed arrangement.

### Transport Without Feet

The *mishnah*'s description of the bucket-brigade procedure — *nosno l'chavero ve-chavero l'chavero* — raises a significant *halachic* question. One of the *avodot* of blood service is *holacha*, the act of transporting the blood to the *mizbe'ach*. But in this procedure, no individual *Kohen* actually walks anywhere. Each stands in place and merely passes the bowl to the next person. Does *holacha she-lo be-regel* — transport without the use of one's feet — constitute a valid *holacha*? The Gemara offers the possibility that *dilma dahani purta* — perhaps the last *Kohen* in the line, the one adjacent to the *mizbe'ach*, took a small step before performing the *zrika*, which would satisfy the requirement of *holacha* through actual movement.

### Honor in Procedure

But if the question of *holacha* is resolved so simply, what is the *mishnah*'s purpose in elaborating the entire bucket-brigade procedure at all? The Gemara answers: *ha kamashma lan b'rov am hadrat melech* — it teaches us the principle that in the presence of a multitude, there is glory to the King. The point of involving so many *kohanim* in the passage of the blood is not to solve a *halachic* problem of transport but to maximize the honor and beauty of the sacred service by engaging as many participants as possible. The greater the number of *kohanim* involved in even a single act of *avodah*, the more magnificent the event becomes.

---

---

# Pesachim 66

## Pesach on Shabbat

### Intro & Debate

Daf 66 opens immediately after the *mishnah*, which had catalogued what aspects of *shabbat* may be overridden when the fourteenth of Nisan falls on *shabbat*. The *mishnah* had framed this primarily as a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer on one side, who took the radical position that virtually anything necessary to enable the *korban pesach* may be done even if it could have been prepared the day before, and Rabbi Yehoshua together with his student Rabbi Akiva on the other. At the end of the *mishnah*, Rabbi Akiva had cited the word *b'moado* — "in its appointed time" — as the scriptural basis for bringing the *korban pesach* on *shabbat* regardless of when the fourteenth falls.

The *gemara*, however, does not begin by analyzing that dispute. Instead it steps back to a more fundamental question: how do we know in the first place that *pesach* overrides *shabbat* at all? The answer emerges through a remarkable historical narrative.

### B'nei Beteira Forget

*Tanu rabbanan* — our Rabbis taught: *halacha zu nitalma mi-B'nei Beteira* — this *halacha* that *pesach* may be brought on *shabbat* was lost to *B'nei Beteira*. *B'nei Beteira* were the major authorities at the *Beit HaMikdash* at the time of Hillel. Rashi identifies them as *nesi'im*. They appear elsewhere in the tradition as well — most famously in the story involving Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai at Yavneh, where *shabbat* fell on Rosh Hashanah and *B'nei Beteira* argued that the *shofar* could only be blown on *shabbat* in the *Beit HaMikdash*, which no longer existed.

One might wonder how such a basic *halacha* could have been forgotten, given that *pesach* falls on *shabbat* on average once every seven years. It is possible that the leaders of that era found ways to manipulate the calendar to avoid the situation; in any case, the *gemara* states plainly that when the fourteenth fell on *shabbat* that year, they had simply forgotten — *shachachu v'lo yadu im pesach doche et hashabbat im lav* — whether *pesach* overrides *shabbat* or not.

They asked around: does anyone know whether *pesach* overrides *shabbat*? They were told: there is a certain man who has recently come up from Bavel — *Hillel HaBavli* — who spent time attending upon the two great leaders of the generation, Shemaya and Avtalyon, and he would know. The designation *Hillel HaBavli* is striking, since we do not normally know him by that name; Hillel's family was connected to the *nesi'im* and the *Reish Galuta*, yet the tradition here identifies him as coming from Bavel. They sent for him and summoned him.

They asked: do you know whether *pesach* overrides *shabbat*? His opening response is unforgettable: *v'chi pesach echad yesh lanu bashanah shedoche et hashabbat* — what, do we have only one *korban pesach* in a year that overrides *shabbat*? We have more than 200 sacrifices each year that override *shabbat*! The arithmetic is simple: two *tamid* offerings every day times roughly fifty *shabbatot* is one hundred, plus the *musaf* of *shabbat* — two additional animals — is another hundred. Add the *musaf* offerings of *yamim tovim* that fall on *shabbat* and you already exceed 200. The point is that the overriding of *shabbat* by fixed-time obligations is a thoroughly established principle in *avodah*.

### Hillel's Proof

Hillel then proceeded to lay out his formal proofs. He said: *ne'emar moado b'Pesach v'ne'emar moado b'tamid* — the word *mo'ado*, "in its appointed time," appears both by the *korban pesach* and by the *tamid* daily offering. Just as *mo'ado* by the *tamid* indicates that it overrides *shabbat*, so too *mo'ado* by the *pesach* indicates the same.

But there is an immediate difficulty: where do we know that *tamid* itself overrides *shabbat*? The word *mo'ado* appears there too, so if *mo'ado* alone established the override, we would not need to derive *pesach* from *tamid* — *pesach* has its own *mo'ado*. The *gemara* will address this in detail later, but for now, Hillel is presenting both a *gezerah shavah* — a verbal analogy linking the shared word — and, additionally, a *kal vachomer*: if the *tamid*, for which there is no punishment of *karet* if one fails to bring it, overrides *shabbat*, then certainly the *pesach*, for which neglect carries the penalty of *karet*, should override *shabbat*. This *kal vachomer* added independent logical weight beyond the verbal link.

### Hillel Becomes Nasi

The reaction was immediate: *miyad hoshivuhu b'rosh u'minuhu nasi aleihem* — they placed him at their head and appointed him *nasi* over them. He then spent the entire day expounding the laws of *pesach*, both to educate the people and to demonstrate his newly established authority.

Then, pointedly, he began to taunt them: *mi garam lachem she'e'eleh miBavel v'ehyeh nasi aleihem* — what caused this, that I, an outsider, had to come from Bavel to be your leader? *Atzlut shebachem* — your laziness. You did not do as I did; you did not devote yourself to attending upon and truly learning from the great masters of the generation, Shemaya and Avtalyon.

At that moment — and as the narrative makes clear, this is where the element of *comeuppance* enters — they turned to him with a practical question. *Rabbi*, they now called him, deferentially: what is the law if someone forgot to bring his slaughtering knife to the *Beit HaMikdash* before *shabbat*? Could he bring it on *shabbat* itself? This was, as the *gemara* will later connect, precisely the question debated by Rabbi Eliezer — whether preparatory acts for the *korban pesach* override *shabbat*.

Hillel's answer is arresting: *halacha zo shamati v'shachachti* — I heard this *halacha*, and I have forgotten it. There it is — the man who had just mocked the leaders for their failure to learn properly from Shemaya and Avtalyon now cannot remember what he himself heard from Shemaya and Avtalyon.

But Hillel did not leave them without guidance. *Hanach lahem l'Yisrael*, he said — leave it to the Jewish people. *Im einam nevi'im hem b'nei nevi'im hem* — if they are not themselves prophets, they are at least the descendants of prophets. They will have the religious intuition to work it out correctly.

The following day — which was the fourteenth itself, a *shabbat* — this is precisely what the people did. Those whose *pesach* was a sheep embedded the knife in the animal's wool; those whose *pesach* was a goat stuck it between the animal's horns. The animal would then walk itself to the *Beit HaMikdash* carrying the knife, without the person having performed the act of carrying. When Hillel saw what they were doing, he remembered the *halacha*: *kach mekublani mipi Shemaya v'Avtalyon* — this is exactly the tradition I received from Shemaya and Avtalyon.

There is something striking and beautiful about this episode. The *gemara* elsewhere employs the principle of *puk chazei mai ama davar* — if you do not know the *halacha*, go and see what the people are doing, and take your cue from established popular practice. But that principle relies on an existing practice already being observed. Here no one knew what to do; there was no established practice. Hillel was trusting not existing practice but the people's forward-looking religious intuition — *im einam nevi'im hem b'nei nevi'im hem*. That is a considerably stronger statement. There are *teshuvot* that invoke this phrase, though typically in the sense of "since they have been doing it, we may assume they are right" — a kind of retroactive validation of existing practice. The use of the phrase here, to mean "let us see what they will do and trust they will arrive at the truth," is rarer and more arresting.

One might also note how *B'nei Beteira* address Hillel here: *rebbi*. We do not normally encounter the title "Rabbi Hillel." The *zugot*, the pairs of leaders, were not called *rabbis* in the technical sense; the title had not yet come into that usage. When *B'nei Beteira* say *rebbi*, they mean it as a deferential honorific — "my master" — not as a formal designation.

---

## Knife on Shabbat

### Animal Carries Knife

The *gemara* now returns to examine the *halacha* of the knife more carefully. The *baraita* had described how the animal was made to carry the knife — embedded in the wool of the sheep or between the horns of the goat. But an immediate objection arises: *beha ka avid avodah b'kodashim* — by doing this, you are using your consecrated animal to perform labor for you, which is itself prohibited. The verse *lo ta'avod b'bechor shorecha* establishes that one may not perform labor with a consecrated animal.

In response, the *gemara* cites a *baraita* about Hillel's own practice: *miyamav lo ma'al adam b'olato* — never once did anyone have the opportunity to commit *me'ilah* through Hillel's *olah* offering. How was this possible? Because Hillel's practice was to bring his animal into the *azarah* while it was still *chullin* — unsanctified — and only to sanctify it at the very last possible moment. He would then perform *semicha*, lay his hands on the animal, and immediately *shochet* it. By sanctifying the animal only at the moment of *shechita*, there was never a window during which misuse could occur.

This explains the knife situation: if the owner had not yet sanctified his animal, having the animal carry the knife on *shabbat* would not involve using a consecrated animal for labor. But this immediately raises a new problem: *pesach v'shabbat heichi matzi makdish lei* — how could you sanctify your *korban pesach* on *shabbat* itself? A *mishnah* teaches explicitly that one may not perform acts of *hekdesh* — consecration — on *yom tov*, and certainly not on *shabbat*. The prohibition encompasses sanctifying, assigning monetary valuations (*ma'arich*), *hacharama*, and the separation of *terumah* and *ma'aser*.

The *gemara* resolves this: *hani mili b'chovah she'ein kavua lahem zman* — that prohibition applies to obligations that do not have a fixed time. But an obligation with a fixed time — *chovah she'kavua lahem zman* — such as the *korban pesach*, which must be brought specifically on the fourteenth, may be sanctified even on *shabbat* itself. This is derived from the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan: *makdish adam et pischo b'shabbat* — a person may sanctify his *pesach* on *shabbat*, and similarly may sanctify his *chagigah* on *yom tov* itself.

---

## Gemara Analysis

### Gezerah Shavah Analysis

The *gemara* now steps back to analyze the structure of Hillel's argument. *Amar mar* — we return to the text of the *baraita*: *ne'emar moado b'Pesach v'ne'emar moado b'tamid* — it says *mo'ado* by *pesach* and it says *mo'ado* by *tamid*.

The *gemara* asks: where do we actually know that *tamid* overrides *shabbat*? If we say the source is simply the word *mo'ado* written in connection with the *tamid*, the same word appears in connection with *pesach* — so why would we need to derive *pesach* from *tamid* at all? The *gemara* concludes: *mo'ado lo mashma lei* — to the author of this derivation, i.e., Hillel, the word *mo'ado* by itself does not carry the implication of overriding *shabbat*. He required an independent source for *tamid*. And that source is the verse *olat Shabbat b'shabato al olat hatamid* — the *olah* of *shabbat* is brought alongside the regular *tamid*, which means the *tamid* is itself brought on *shabbat*. Since the verse describing *shabbat* uses the word *mo'ado*, and we know the *tamid* is brought on *shabbat*, we can make the *gezerah shavah* linking the *mo'ado* of *pesach* to the *mo'ado* of *tamid*.

The *gemara* then turns to the *kal vachomer*: if the *tamid*, which carries no punishment of *karet* for its neglect, overrides *shabbat*, then certainly the *pesach*, which carries *karet*, should override *shabbat*. The *gemara* immediately identifies a challenge to this *kal vachomer*: *mah l'tamid sheken tadir v'chalil* — the *tamid* has the additional factors of being offered daily (*tadir*) and being entirely consumed (*chalil*). Perhaps these factors are what enable it to override *shabbat*, and the *pesach*, which is brought only once a year and from which people eat the meat, should not be compared. The *kal vachomer* is therefore *paricha* — contradicted; it does not hold.

The *gemara* then asks: if Hillel had a valid *gezerah shavah* available, why did he first present the *kal vachomer* that turns out to be contradicted? *Kal vachomer amar lehu b'reisha* — he tried the *kal vachomer* first, and when they successfully challenged it, *hadar amar lehu gezerah shavah* — he then fell back on the *gezerah shavah*. But this raises the question: if he had the *gezerah shavah* all along, why lead with the *kal vachomer*?

The answer the *gemara* gives is: *ella l'didehu ka'amar lehu* — he was speaking for their benefit. A *gezerah shavah* is only valid if it is your received tradition; *she'ein adam dan gezerah shavah me'atzmo* — one may not independently construct a *gezerah shavah* without having received it as a *mesorah*. Clearly *B'nei Beteira* did not have this *gezerah shavah* as their tradition — if they had, the *halacha* would not have been lost to them in the first place. So Hillel first presented the *kal vachomer* because a *kal vachomer* is something *adam dan me'atzmo* — it may be derived independently through reason. He was giving them a proof they could have worked out for themselves. When they successfully rebutted it, he offered the *gezerah shavah* as his own tradition.

This leads to a striking observation: in the end, Hillel did not actually prove anything to *B'nei Beteira* by logical necessity. The *kal vachomer* was successfully refuted; the *gezerah shavah* is only as good as the tradition behind it, and they had no such tradition themselves. They were, in the end, simply accepting his word that he had received this tradition. Whether a *gezerah shavah* transmitted by one authority in one locale is universally binding is itself a debated question. The *Ramban* in fact argues that *gezerah shavah* was never a tradition about which specific words could be linked; the tradition was the *halacha* itself — that *pesach* is brought on *shabbat* — and the *gezerah shavah* was the way one could find a support or peg for it in the *pesukim*. This touches on a deeper question about the nature of *Torah she-be'al peh*, which the *gemara* will explore through a comparison with the *Yerushalmi*.

---

## Knife on Shabbat (II)

### Melacha Ba-Kodashim

Having resolved the question of how one sanctifies the *pesach* on *shabbat* itself, the *gemara* returns to the remaining *shabbat* problem with the knife. If the animal was unsanctified when it carried the knife, there is no violation of *melacha b'kodashim* — using a consecrated animal for labor. But there is still the prohibition of *mechamer* — using an animal to carry loads, as one would use a donkey (*chamor*). Having an animal carry something for you on *shabbat* is a form of prohibited *melacha*, even when the animal itself is not consecrated.

### Sanctification on Shabbat

As discussed, the resolution to the *hekdesh* problem — the prohibition against consecrating on *shabbat* — is that an obligation with a fixed time (*chovah she'kavua lahem zman*) such as the *korban pesach* may be sanctified on *shabbat* itself. Rabbi Yochanan states explicitly: *makdish adam et pischo b'shabbat* — a person may sanctify his *pesach* on *shabbat*, and similarly may sanctify his *chagigah* on *yom tov*.

### K'Le'Achar Yad

The remaining problem is *mechamer*. Here the *gemara* offers an important resolution: *mechamer k'le'achar yad* — the animal is carrying in an unusual manner. If one truly intended to use a sheep as a beast of burden, one would not embed the knife in its wool. If one wanted a goat to carry something, one would not attach it between its horns. The animal is performing the function of carrying, but doing so via a *shinuy* — a significant deviation from normal procedure. This reduces the act from a biblical prohibition to a rabbinic one.

But the *gemara* acknowledges that even a rabbinic prohibition remains: *issur d'Rabbanan miha ika*. And as our *mishnah* established — against the position of Rabbi Eliezer — one may not violate a rabbinic prohibition that is merely *hechsher* for the *korban pesach*, i.e., preparatory rather than the act of sacrifice itself. So how was this permitted?

Tosafot explains that two mitigating factors together made it permissible to override this *d'rabanan*. First, the act was done *k'le'achar yad* — in an unusual manner — which signals clearly that this is not normal procedure and renders the violation less severe. Second, it was not the person performing the carrying but the animal. Even though using an animal inappropriately is itself prohibited, the prohibition is less direct when the person is not personally the one performing the *melacha*. A *d'rabanan* that is indirect and performed in an unusual manner is more susceptible to being overridden for the sake of the *korban pesach* than a straightforward *d'rabanan* of the kind that our *mishnah* does not permit.

### People's Intuition

The *gemara* now ties this back to the narrative: *hainu d'ka ba'a minei* — this is precisely the question they were asking Hillel when they asked about the knife. The question was whether something that has a biblical *heter* — i.e., could in principle be done in a permitted way — but is rabbinically problematic in the manner being contemplated (*davar shevut omed l'fanav*) may be overridden in a *k'le'achar yad* fashion for the sake of the *mitzvah*. And Hillel's answer, as we saw: *halacha zo shamati v'shachachti* — I heard this and I have forgotten it. *Ela hanichu lahem l'Yisrael im einam nevi'im hem b'nei nevi'im hem* — leave it to Israel; if they are not prophets, they are descendants of prophets, and they will arrive at the truth through their own religious intuition.

---

## Gemara Analysis (II)

### Bavli vs. Yerushalmi

The *Yerushalmi* contains a parallel version of this entire story, but with significant differences that illuminate a much deeper dispute about the nature of *Torah she-be'al peh* itself. It is worth comparing the two carefully.

The *Yerushalmi* opens similarly: this *halacha* was lost to the elders of *Beteira* (*ziknei Beteira*, not *B'nei Beteira*). They are told there is a certain Babylonian — simply *Bavli echad*, not even named at first — who studied under Shemaya and Avtalyon, and perhaps there is hope to be had from him. They summon him, he gives the same dramatic opening about there being more than one *pesach* that overrides *shabbat*, and the elders respond approvingly: yes, indeed we said there might be hope from you.

But what follows is entirely different. The *Yerushalmi* explicitly states that Hillel then proceeded to prove his case *mehekesh umikal vachomer umigzeirah shavah* — from an analogy, a *kal vachomer*, and a *gezerah shavah*. And critically, the *Yerushalmi* identifies all three *before* presenting the content, deliberately foregrounding the hermeneutic tools being deployed. The *hekesh* — a conceptual analogy rather than a verbal link — runs as follows: just as the *tamid* is a *korban tzibur*, a communal offering, and the *pesach* is likewise a *korban tzibur*, they are analogous and the *tamid*'s override of *shabbat* applies equally to the *pesach*. Then comes the *kal vachomer* as in our *gemara*, and finally the *gezerah shavah* of *mo'ado mo'ado*.

Now notice the *Yerushalmi*'s response to all three arguments: *yesh lo teshuvah* — each one can be answered. The *hekesh* has a rebuttal; the *kal vachomer* has a rebuttal; and the *gezerah shavah* — *she'ein adam dan gezerah shavah me'atzmo* — you cannot construct that on your own. Every argument he offered, they dismissed.

In the *Yerushalmi*'s account, Hillel then spent the entire day — *kol hayom kulo* — not teaching *halachot* and holding court as the new *nasi*, but trying to convince them. *Lo kiblu mimenu* — they refused to accept anything he said. Finally, at the end of the day, he said: *yavo alay kach shamati miShemaya v'Avtalyon* — let it come upon me, this is what I received as a tradition from Shemaya and Avtalyon. The moment they heard this — *keivan shesham'u mimenu ken amdu u'minuhu nasi aleihem* — they immediately stood and appointed him *nasi*.

This is a completely different story. In the *Yerushalmi*, all the logical derivations, all the hermeneutics, meant nothing to them. What mattered was the *mesorah* — do you have this as a received tradition from an authoritative teacher? The moment he invoked the direct chain of transmission from Shemaya and Avtalyon, they accepted him entirely. The story ends the same way — with him mocking them and then forgetting the *halacha* about the knife, and being forced to say *kach shamati v'shachachti*. Even there, the resolution comes through the invocation of tradition.

This contrast between the *Bavli* and the *Yerushalmi* versions is not merely a narrative variation. It encodes a fundamental dispute about what *Torah she-be'al peh* is. In the *Yerushalmi*'s telling, *Torah she-be'al peh* is primarily about *mesorah* — the transmission of a received tradition from teacher to student, generation to generation. Logical proofs and hermeneutic derivations, however sophisticated, are not authoritative in themselves. What is authoritative is: who taught you, and can you trace your teaching back to an unbroken chain of transmission?

In the *Bavli*'s telling, by contrast, what impressed *B'nei Beteira* was Hillel's ability to derive the *halacha* through logic and hermeneutic principles. The *kal vachomer* alone ultimately failed, but the *gezerah shavah* was accepted, and the whole framework of logical derivation was treated as genuinely probative.

Hillel comes from Bavel. In Bavel, the tradition had always leaned more toward the creative, intellectually generative model of *Torah she-be'al peh* — the *yud-gimmel middot*, the hermeneutic principles, the derivation of *halacha* from first principles. The chain of direct transmission from teachers in *Eretz Yisrael* was more attenuated in Bavel; necessity itself drove a more derivation-based approach. *B'nei Beteira* represent the *Mikdash*-centered, tradition-bound model — this is how we have always done it, and we need to know that it is what was always done.

What Hillel brought to *Eretz Yisrael* was precisely the Babylonian *Torah she-be'al peh* — and this was the founding moment of the rabbinic leadership that would define the tradition going forward, from Hillel's own dynasty through Rabbi Akiva's school and ultimately to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the redaction of the *mishnah*. The whole subsequent rabbinic project — a *Torah she-be'al peh* grounded in derivation, interpretation, and the creative application of hermeneutic principles — has its symbolic origin in this encounter.

There is also a thread worth noting within the story itself that complicates a pure *mesorah*-only view: the story begins precisely because something was *forgotten*. The whole problem is that even received traditions can be lost. And in the resolution, Hillel says: trust the people's intuition. *Im einam nevi'im hem b'nei nevi'im hem*. They are not using the *yud-gimmel middot*; they are not applying *gezerah shavah*; and they do not have a tradition. Yet they arrive at the correct answer through religious intuition. This too is a form of arriving at truth that is neither pure derivation nor pure *mesorah* — and Hillel, the arch-proponent of the derivation model, endorses it.

There is an important *tosefta* in Sanhedrin that illuminates this further. It describes seven things Hillel expounded before *B'nei Beteira* — and the seven things are precisely his seven hermeneutic principles: *kal vachomer*, *gezerah shavah*, *binyan av mikatuv echad*, *binyan av mishnei ketuvim*, *kelal u'frat*, *prat u'chelal*, and *davar halamed me'inyano*. What he was expounding was not merely the *halacha* about *pesach* on *shabbat* — he was teaching them the very methodology by which *halacha* is derived. He was, in effect, presenting a manifesto for a new kind of *Torah she-be'al peh*.

### Seven Principles

The *tosefta* in Sanhedrin states: *shiv'ah devarim darash Hillel haZaken lifnei B'nei Beteira* — seven things Hillel the Elder expounded before *B'nei Beteira*. The seven are enumerated as: *kal vachomer*, *gezerah shavah*, *binyan av mikatuv echad*, *binyan av mishnei ketuvim*, *kelal u'frat*, *prat u'chelal*, *davar halamed me'inyano* — and also *kayyotzei bo mimakom acher*, a case similar to another case from elsewhere. That accounts for all seven.

The significance of the *tosefta*'s phrasing is the word *darash* — he was expounding, teaching them actively. What was he teaching them? Not just the specific *halacha* about *pesach* and *shabbat*, but the framework: here are the authorized principles of derivation by which *halacha* is legitimately determined. This is the deeper revolution that Hillel represented. *B'nei Beteira* operated in a world where authority meant transmission; Hillel was introducing — or formalizing and championing — a world in which authority could also mean disciplined, principled derivation.

The profound question this raises — whether *Torah she-be'al peh* is primarily a repository of transmitted laws or primarily an authorized interpretive process given to human beings — is one that runs throughout the entire *talmud*. The *Rambam* in his *Perush HaMishnayot* addresses this directly in response to the Karaite challenge: if everything was transmitted, how can there be debates on every page of the *talmud*? His answer is that what was transmitted directly — what we call *halacha l'Moshe m'Sinai* — is a tiny fraction of the tradition. The overwhelming majority was given to human beings to derive through the application of authorized principles; and because derivation by human beings is inherently not predetermined, different scholars can and do arrive at different conclusions. The debates are not a sign of confusion but of the system working as intended. The *Ramban*'s view on *gezerah shavah* — that it was never a tradition of which words to link, but rather a tradition of the *halacha* for which one then found textual support — represents a mediating position between pure derivation and pure *mesorah*.

Both of these positions are embedded in this story. The *Bavli*'s Hillel champions derivation; the *Yerushalmi*'s *B'nei Beteira* insist on *mesorah*. And the resolution — in both versions — ultimately involves both: Hillel had a tradition, which he was able to express and support through hermeneutic reasoning, and the people's intuition arrived at the same place.
