The episode becomes a founding narrative not just for a specific *halacha*, but for the nature of *Torah she-be'al peh* itself.

---

## Aggadic Stories

### Hillel's Pride Falls

After these passages, the *gemara* shifts into an *aggadic* register with a series of morally instructive narratives connected to the themes of pride and anger. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: anyone who conducts himself with haughtiness — if he is a wise person, his wisdom departs from him; if he is a prophet, his prophecy departs from him.

The proof that a wise man's wisdom departs from him on account of haughtiness is drawn directly from Hillel himself. We just saw: he mocked *B'nei Beteira* for their laziness, exalted himself for having attended upon Shemaya and Avtalyon, and was immediately made to say *halacha zo shamati v'shachachti* — I heard this and I forgot it. The very thing he boasted about — his superior learning from the great masters — was the thing he was then shown to have forgotten. The narrative works as a precise and pointed comeuppance.

### Moshe's Anger

*Reish Lakish amar*: anyone who gets angry — if he is wise, his wisdom departs from him; if he is a prophet, his prophecy departs from him. The proof that anger causes wisdom to depart comes from Moshe. The verse says *vayiktzof Moshe al pekudei hachayil* — Moshe became angry at the officers of the army when they returned from the war against Midian. After that anger, when there was a *halacha* to be transmitted — regarding the purification of vessels captured in war — it was Elazar the *kohen* who transmitted it, not Moshe: *vayomer Elazar hakohen el anshei hatzava... zot chukat hatorah asher tziva Hashem et Moshe* — this is the statute of the Torah that God commanded Moshe. The verse specifies it was commanded to Moshe, yet it was Elazar who transmitted it. The conclusion is that Moshe had forgotten it on account of his anger.

### Prophecy & Anger

The proof that anger causes prophecy to depart comes from Elisha. After expressing anger at Yehoram, Elisha said: *lulei p'nei Yehoshafat melech Yehudah ani nosei im abit elecha v'im ereka* — were it not for my regard for Yehoshafat king of Judah, I would not even look at you. He was venting his anger openly. Then immediately the verse says: *ve'ata k'chu li menagen* — and now bring me a musician — *vehaya kenagen hamenagen vatehi alav yad Hashem* — and it was only when the musician played that the spirit of God rested upon him again.

The contrast between these two examples is worth noting. The case of Elisha and music has a naturalistically comprehensible quality: extreme anger disturbs the inner equilibrium that prophecy requires; calming music restores it. This reads as something close to cause and effect in a psychological sense. The case of Hillel's haughtiness reads differently — more as divine *comeuppance*, a measure-for-measure correction.

The proof that anger caused prophecy to depart comes also from Devorah, who in her song said: *ad shekamti Devorah ad shekamti em b'Yisrael* — until I arose, Devorah, until I arose as a mother in Israel. This self-aggrandizement on her part led to her then having to push herself to prophecy: *uri uri Devorah uri uri dabri shir* — rouse yourself, Devorah, rouse yourself, speak your song — implying that prophetic inspiration did not come easily to her and she had to prod herself to attain it.

### Eliab's Story

*Amar Rav Mani bar Patish*: anyone who gets angry — even if greatness was decreed for him from heaven, he is brought down from it. This is derived from Eliab, the brother of David. The verse says *vayichar af Eliab beDavid* — Eliab became angry at David when David came to the battle camp before the confrontation with Goliath. Eliab accused David of abandoning his flock and coming out of idle curiosity or impudence: *ani yadati et zedonecha v'et roa levavecha ki lemaan re'ot hamilchama yaradta* — I know your willfulness and the evil of your heart; you came just to see the battle.

When Shmuel came to anoint the new king from among the sons of Yishai, God's response to each son he considered was: *lo beze bachar Hashem* — this is not the one God has chosen. But for Eliab specifically, the verse reads differently: *vayomer Hashem el Shmuel al tabet el marehu v'el geva komato ki me'astihu* — God said, do not look at his appearance or his height, for I have despised him. Not merely "not chosen" — *despised*.

The *gemara* reads this as follows: Eliab had indeed *been* chosen — *michlal dehavah rachim lei* — he had been selected for greatness by heaven, but was subsequently rejected. The anointing episode occurred before the scene of his anger at David, which the *gemara* acknowledges. Rashi explains that Eliab's anger in that scene was simply the latest expression of a deep-seated anger that had been there all along, and that it was this character trait that led to his rejection even prior to the Goliath episode. The language of the verse — *me'astihu*, I have despised him — echoes the language used of Saul's rejection, creating a deliberate parallel between two figures who were chosen and then removed on account of inner flaws.

---

## Pesach & Tumah

### Pesach Overrides Tumah

The *gemara* now pivots back to *halachic* analysis. We have established that *tamid* and *pesach* override *shabbat*. The next question is: how do we know they override *tumah*? The *gemara* reasons as follows: the same way we derived the override of *shabbat* for *pesach* from *tamid* — knowing that *tamid* overrides *shabbat* and applying that to *pesach* — we can reverse the reasoning for *tumah*: knowing that *pesach* overrides *tumah*, we can derive the same for *tamid*.

But this immediately invites the question: *pesach gufeih minlan* — where do we know that *pesach* itself overrides *tumah*? *Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: the verse states *ish ish ki yiheyeh tameh la-nefesh* — if any individual is *tamei* due to contact with the dead, he is pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*. The *drasha* is: an individual is pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*, but the entire congregation is not pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*. If the majority of the congregation is *tamei*, they do not wait — *ella avdi be-tumah* — they perform the *korban pesach* while *tamei*. This is derived from the fact that the Torah provides an alternative (*Pesach Sheni*) only for an individual, signaling that no such alternative operates when it is the congregation as a whole.

### Reish Lakish's View

Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan's derivation. Why read this *drasha* as a leniency for the congregation? One could equally read it as a stringency: an individual is pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*, but if the entire congregation is *tamei*, they have no recourse at all — neither *Pesach Rishon* nor *Pesach Sheni*. The derivation cuts in the opposite direction: the Torah's provision of an alternative is granted only to individuals, not to congregations — meaning the congregation is actually worse off, not better. Reish Lakish rejects the leniency reading as insufficiently grounded.

### Three Categories

Reish Lakish therefore offers an alternative source for the principle that *pesach* overrides *tumah*, and specifically derives from it an important limitation. The verse in Bemidbar states: *vishalchu min hamachaneh kol tzarua v'chol zav v'chol tamei la-nefesh* — send out of the camp all who are *tzarua*, all who are *zav*, and all who are *tamei* through contact with the dead. Why enumerate all three categories? The most severe are the *tzarua* and the *zav*, whose *tumah* arises intrinsically from their own bodies. The least severe is the *tamei meit*, whose *tumah* comes from an external source. Logic alone would have told us: if even the *tamei meit* — the least severe — must be sent away, certainly the *zav* and *metzora* must be as well. The explicit enumeration of all three must therefore be teaching something that could not have been derived by logic alone.

Reish Lakish's answer: the verse is telling us that there is a time of year when only the *zav* and *metzora* are sent out, but *tamei meitim* are not. That time is *pesach* celebrated in a state of *tumah* — *zeh pesach haba b'tumah*. The *halacha* that *pesach* overrides *tumah* applies only to *tamei meit* — the person rendered impure through contact with a corpse. It does not apply to those whose *tumah* is intrinsic, arising from their own bodies, such as the *zav* and the *metzora*. For the congregation's *tumah* to be overridden and the *korban pesach* brought, it is necessary that the *tumah* be *tumat meit* — externally contracted impurity — not the more severe, intrinsic impurities of *zivah* or *tzara'at*. For those, even a congregation must wait until they are able to bring the *korban* in purity.

The *gemara* will continue this analysis on the following daf.

---

---

# Pesachim 67

## Mesorah vs. Interpretati…

### Hillel/Bnei Beteira

We begin with a recapitulation of a theme that dominated the preceding daf, because it is too critical to pass over without emphasis. Much of the previous session was devoted to the *drasha* establishing that the *korban pesach* overrides *Shabbat*, introduced through the famous narrative of the *Bnei Beteira*. The story is set on an *erev Pesach* that fell on *Shabbat* — an occasion that, logically, should recur once every seven years, though the calendar may have been manipulated so that it had not been seen in some time. The *Bnei Beteira* did not know the *halacha*, and someone suggested summoning Hillel, who had studied under Shemaya ve-Abtalion and had come from Bavel. According to the *Bavli*, Hillel presented a series of *drashot* — *kal va-chomer*, *gzeirah shava*, and others — and conclusively demonstrated that *Pesach* overrides *Shabbat*, after which he spent the remainder of the day teaching *halacha*.

### Bavel vs. E.Y.

The *Yerushalmi*'s version of this story is, in many key respects, quite different, and the contrast is illuminating. The *Yerushalmi* opens with skepticism about whether Hillel, as someone from Bavel, would be of any use at all. When Hillel proceeds to derive the *halacha* through hermeneutic principles — *gzeirah shava*, *hekesh*, *kal va-chomer* — the *Bnei Beteira* counter every one of his arguments. They have a response to each derivation. Hillel does not spend the rest of the day in triumph; he spends it struggling to prove his point. Only when he gives up on argumentation entirely and declares, "This is the *mesorah* I received from Shemaya ve-Abtalion," do they accept.

The Netziv, in his extended introduction to the *She'iltos*, highlights precisely this contrast. He argues that the Torah of *Eretz Yisrael* was closer to the source and therefore primarily about transmission — *mesorah* to *mesorah*. The Torah of Bavel, more distant from that source, necessarily relied more heavily on creative intellectual engagement with the *pesukim*, on the hermeneutic process of interpretation and derivation. The clash with the *Bnei Beteira* was not merely personal or regional — it was a fundamental disagreement about the nature of *Torah she-ba'al peh* itself: is it a matter of what you received and pass on, or is it a matter of how you interpret and derive?

### Public Intuition

The end of the story reinforces this theme. When Hillel is asked about someone who forgot to bring a sheep or a knife on *erev Pesach*, and it is now *Shabbat*, he admits he does not remember the *halacha*. But rather than conceding defeat, he says: trust *Bnei Yisrael* — *inam nevi'im hem, bnei nevi'im hem* — if they are not themselves prophets, they are sons of prophets; their intuition can be trusted. The next day, people stuck their knives in the wool of their sheep and let the animals carry them to *Har ha-Bayit*. Hillel then recalled that this was indeed what Shemaya ve-Abtalion had told him, though he had forgotten.

The *Bavli* reads this conclusion as Hillel receiving a measure of comeuppance — after making himself so important, he had to admit he forgot something. But there is another dimension worth appreciating. The *Yerushalmi*'s account has the *Bnei Beteira* accept Hillel only when he invokes *mesorah*. The very next moment demonstrates that *mesorah* is fragile — it can be forgotten. If Hillel had not been present, no one would have remembered. What restores the *mesorah* is not another chain of transmission but the intuition of the people. Hillel, in this reading, does get the final word: he shows that trusting the intuition of *Bnei Yisrael*, and the ability to engage the *pesukim* creatively, is itself another legitimate path to accessing and reconstructing the *mesorah*. The process is not mechanical — there is an irreducible role for judgment, for intuition, for how one reads the *pesukim* in the first place.

### Rambam Model

One might ask whether this is a matter of "creating" *Torah she-ba'al peh* — and that framing requires nuance. The Rambam, in defending *Torah she-ba'al peh* against the Karaites, was confronted with the following problem: if the entire Oral Torah is simply a chain of transmission, then the existence of so many debates reveals a broken pipeline, undermining the claim to reliable tradition. The Rambam's response is that *mesorah* in the strict sense — *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — is actually a small portion of the whole. The overwhelming majority of *Torah she-ba'al peh* is not pure transmission; it is the empowerment given to *Chazal* to operate within hermeneutic principles, to interpret and derive within certain parameters. The process is one of finding the best understanding of what the text actually means — revelation through interpretation, not invention. Different *poskim* arriving at different conclusions through that process are not one right and others wrong; all are legitimate expressions of *Torah she-ba'al peh*. And that, ultimately, is exactly what the clash between Hillel and the *Bnei Beteira* is about.

---

## Three Impurity Categ (II)

### Pesach/Tumah Override

We now pick up from the final lines of 66b. The *Gemara* states: *ashkhichan tamid u-pesach de-dachu Shabbat* — we know that the *tamid* and the *Pesach* override *Shabbat*. But *de-dachu tumah minalan* — where do we know that they override *tumah*? The *Gemara* answers by analogy: just as we derived that *Pesach* overrides *Shabbat* by learning from the *tamid*, we reverse the direction and derive that the *tamid* overrides *tumah* by learning from *Pesach*. But this presupposes we already know that *Pesach* itself overrides *tumah* — and for that we need a source.

### Ish Ish Drasha

Rabbi Yochanan provides the source: the *pasuk* states *ish ish ki yihyeh tameh l'nefesh* — if any person is *tamei* through corpse-*tumah* and cannot bring the *korban Pesach*, he may bring it on *Pesach Sheni*. From this, Rabbi Yochanan derives: *ish nidcha l'Pesach Sheni v'ein tzibur nidchin l'Pesach Sheni* — an individual is pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*, but the *tzibur* is not pushed off. If the entire community is *tamei meit*, they bring the *Pesach* even in a state of *tumah* — *tumah hutrah b'tzibur*.

### Reish Lakish Challenge

Reish Lakish challenges this reading. He argues: perhaps you should read the *pasuk* *l'chumra* — an individual gets pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*, and the *tzibur* gets no accommodation at all, neither in *Pesach Rishon* nor in *Pesach Sheni*. On that reading, the *pasuk* about *ish ish* cannot be the basis for the *halacha* of *pesach habah b'tumah*.

Reish Lakish therefore proposes a different *pasuk* as the source: *v'yishalchu min hamachaneh kol tzarua v'chol zav v'chol tamei lanefesh* — send out of the camp everyone with *tzara'at*, everyone with a *zav* flow, and everyone who is *tamei* for a corpse. This *pasuk* identifies three categories. Now, the *Gemara* notes, the *pasuk* could have said only *tamei meit* — the most lenient category — and derived the others by *kal va-chomer*: if the lightest category is sent out, certainly the heavier ones are. The fact that the *pasuk* names all three separately implies there is something to learn from each. According to Reish Lakish, there are times when some categories are not sent out even though others are — and that time is *pesach habah b'tumah*, when *tamei meit* are permitted to remain inside while *zav* and *metzora* are not.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye objects to Reish Lakish's derivation. If the logic is that the *pasuk* divides categories to teach that sometimes some groups stay while others leave, then one might equally read the *pasuk* as teaching that *metzora* gets sent out while *zav* and *tamei meit* stay — or any other combination. There is no internal basis in Reish Lakish's reading for specifying precisely which groups gain access during *pesach habah b'tumah*.

More decisively, we already have a *mishna* that settles the question empirically: *pesach habah b'tumah lo yochlu mimenu zavim v'zavot niddot v'yoldot* — when the *Pesach* is brought in *tumah*, those with *zav*-type *tumah*, women who are *niddot*, and women who are *yoldot* may not eat from it. The license to eat extends only to those who are *tamei meit*. If Reish Lakish's reading implied that *zavim* might also receive license — since the *pasuk* could just as easily be read to allow them as well — and we know from the *mishna* that they do not, then Reish Lakish's derivation cannot be sustained.

Therefore, Abaye concludes, we return to the original *pasuk* of Rabbi Yochanan: *ish ish*. The remaining difficulty with that *pasuk* — that the *tzibur* might simply receive no accommodation at all — is resolved as follows. Had the *Torah* intended only to address the individual case, it would have written simply *ish ish ki yihyeh tamei*, with no qualification. The specification *tamei lanefesh* — *tumah* of a corpse — is doing additional work. One might have thought to read it *l'chumra*: only if you are *tamei meit* do you get a *Pesach Sheni*; if you are *tamei* for other reasons such as *zav* or *metzora*, you do not. But that is contradicted by a *braita*: *yachol lo yi'u osim Pesach Sheni ella tmei meitim* — could it be that only *tamei meit* bring *Pesach Sheni*? *Zavin u'metzora'im u'vo'alei niddot minayin?* How do we know *zavim*, *metzoraim*, and men who have had relations with a *niddah* are also included? *Talmud lomar: ish ish* — the inclusive phrasing *ish ish* broadens the category to include anyone who is *tamei* for any reason.

Given this *braita*, the word *lanefesh* — corpse — cannot be functioning to limit the individual case. It must be functioning for the *tzibur* implication. The *Torah* says *tamei lanefesh* to teach: when an individual is *tamei meit*, he goes to *Pesach Sheni*; when the *tzibur* is *tamei meit*, they bring the *Pesach* now. And critically, the *heter* for the *tzibur* applies specifically to *tumat meit* — the lightest category — and not to *zav* or *metzora*.

### Pesach B'Tumah Limits

The practical scope of *pesach habah b'tumah* now emerges with precision. When the *Pesach* is brought in *tumah*, the *tzibur* that receives license is specifically *tamei meit* — those whose *tumah* was contracted from the outside, not generated from within their own bodies. The *Gemara* will elaborate at length on why *tumat meit* is categorically distinct from *zav* and *metzora* in this regard.

The *mishna* cited by Abaye had stated that *zavim*, *zavot*, *niddot*, and *yoldot* may not eat from the *pesach habah b'tumah*, but if they did eat, they are *pturim* — exempt from *karet*. Normally, a *tamei* person who eats from a *korban* is liable for *karet*; during a period of *pesach habah b'tumah*, even those who had no license to eat are not subject to that penalty *bedi'avad*. The same principle will emerge with respect to entering the *Mikdash* — *zavim* and *metzoraim* have no license to enter, but if they did during such a period, they are exempt from the usual liability.

It is worth noting, parenthetically, that the list appearing in the *braita* — *zavin*, *metzora'im*, and *vo'alei niddot* — is a list exclusively of men, whereas the *mishna*'s list included *zavot*, *niddot*, and *yoldot* as well. This is because the *braita* is addressing the *chiyuv* to bring *Pesach* and thus *Pesach Sheni*, and it is presumably assumed that the obligation falls upon men. Whether women are obligated in *korban Pesach* is a question the *Gemara* will address elsewhere.

What emerges from the full discussion is: the source for *pesach habah b'tumah* is the *pasuk* of *ish ish*, which teaches that an individual is pushed off while the *tzibur* is not. The license for the *tzibur* is limited to *tamei meit*, and neither *zav* nor *metzora* may eat or enter — though if they do, they bear no liability during that period.

---

## Three-Camp Division

### Camp Hierarchy

Rav Chisda now introduces a ruling that occasions a broad discussion of the three-camp division and the respective exclusion zones that apply to each category of *tumah*. He states: *metzora shenichnas lifnim mimchitzato* — a *metzora* who enters the zone beyond his permitted boundary — *patur* — is exempt from lashes.

To understand this, it is necessary to lay out the tripartite spatial structure. In the time of the *Midbar*, there were three concentric zones. At the center was the *Mishkan* itself, the dwelling of the *Shechinah*. Surrounding it was the *Machaneh Leviyah* — the camp of Moshe, Aharon, and the *Levi'im*. Surrounding that was the *Machaneh Yisrael* — the camp of the rest of *Bnei Yisrael*. Each category of *tamei* person is excluded from a progressively inner zone. A *tamei meit* may not enter the *Mishkan* itself but may remain in the *Machaneh Leviyah*. A *zav* may not enter even the *Machaneh Leviyah* but may remain in the *Machaneh Yisrael*. A *metzora* is excluded even from the *Machaneh Yisrael* — he must sit in solitude outside all three camps.

### Yerushalayim Zones

When this framework is transposed onto the geography of *Yerushalayim*, the correspondences are as follows. *Machaneh Shechinah* becomes the *Beit HaMikdash* itself — specifically the *Azarah*. *Machaneh Leviyah* becomes *Har HaBayit*. *Machaneh Yisrael* becomes *Yerushalayim*. And *Chazal* extend this further, understanding that the status of *Yerushalayim* as *Machaneh Yisrael* applies to all walled cities — which is why the *metzora'im* in the *haftarah* are found sitting outside the city gate, even though the city is not *Yerushalayim*.

Practically speaking, a *tamei meit* may ascend *Har HaBayit* — which is the basis for those tours that take place on the *Har HaBayit* today. What such tours must be careful about is ensuring that participants do not walk on any ground that was once part of the *Azarah*, the *Ezrat Yisrael*, or the area near the *Mizbe'ach*, since a *tamei meit* is excluded from *Machaneh Shechinah*, which corresponds to that inner space. The *Gemara* also makes explicit that the category of *zav* includes a *ba'al keri* — a man who has had a seminal emission — as well as a *niddah* and a *yoledet*. These individuals may not ascend *Har HaBayit*. This has obvious contemporary implications: those who lead tours on *Har HaBayit* must ensure that participants are aware that a *ba'al keri* who has not immersed, or who has immersed but has not yet reached *ha'arev shemesh*, remains in a prohibited category for the *Machaneh Leviyah* zone. It is not clear that sufficient stringency is applied to this issue in practice.

### Metzora Lashes

Returning to Rav Chisda's ruling: the *metzora* who enters *Yerushalayim* is *patur* — exempt from lashes. This might seem paradoxical. If the *metzora* is the most severe category, why does he not receive lashes while presumably the others do? The answer lies in the *pasuk*: *badad yeshev michutz lamachaneh moshavo* — he shall sit alone outside the camp. This *pasuk* introduces what the *halacha* calls a *lav hanitak l'asei* — a negative prohibition that is connected to a remedying positive command.

Rashi reads this as follows: the *metzora* who enters *Yerushalayim* has violated the *lav* of *velo yitamu et machanehem*, but the transgression can be corrected by going back outside — the *asei* of *badad yeshev* provides the remedy. Because the *lav* is rectifiable through an *asei*, it does not carry lashes. Tosafot reads it differently: for the *metzora*, entering *Yerushalayim* is governed only by an *asei*, not a *lav* at all — the *pasuk* transformed the prohibition for the outermost zone into a positive command to remain outside. If the *metzora* were to enter a more interior prohibited zone — such as *Har HaBayit* or the *Azarah* itself — that would be a *lav* carrying lashes. But for the specific crossing of the *Yerushalayim* boundary, it is only an *asei*.

A *braita* is then cited that seems to contradict Rav Chisda's ruling, stating that a *metzora* who enters beyond his *mechitza* does receive lashes. The *Gemara* resolves this as a *tannaitic* dispute, which it then elaborates through a *braita* that also establishes the three-camp structure itself.

### R. Yehuda Derivation

The *braita* presents two *tannaitic* positions on how to derive the three distinct exclusion zones. Rabbi Yehuda derives it from two *pesukim*. First, from *badad yeshev* — the *metzora* sits alone, meaning no other *tamei* people share his zone, establishing that the *metzora* has a distinct and more distant zone from all others. Second, from *machanehem* — "their camps," in the plural — which teaches that *zavim* and *tamei meitim* do not share a single zone either, but each occupies a different camp. The word *machanehem* rather than *machanam* is read as implying multiple distinct camps for multiple distinct categories.

### R. Shimon Kal V'Chomer

Rabbi Shimon disagrees not on the *halacha* but on the derivation. He argues that there is no need for the *pesukim* of *badad* and *machanehem* to establish the three camps. It emerges directly from the structure of the *pasuk*: *v'yishalchu min hamachaneh kol tzarua v'chol zav v'chol tamei lanefesh*. As the *Gemara* has already established, this *pasuk* could have stated only *tamei meit*, the most lenient category, and derived the others by *kal va-chomer*: if the lightest category is sent out, how much more so the heavier ones. The *Torah* stating *zav* in addition to *tamei meit* can only be to teach that a *zav* is sent even further — to a second camp. And stating *metzora* in addition to *zav* can only be to teach that a *metzora* is sent yet further still — to a third camp. The three-camp structure is embedded in the very necessity of mentioning all three categories when one would have logically sufficed.

According to Rabbi Shimon, then, *badad yeshev* is not needed for the *camp* derivation. What, then, does it teach? That is where *badad yeshev* does its work in the *halacha nitak l'asei*: it teaches that the *metzora* entering *Yerushalayim* does not receive lashes.

---

## Three Impurity Categ (II)

### Severity Comparison

With the three-camp structure established, the *Gemara* now examines the hierarchy of severity that underlies it. The assumed order is: *tamei meit* is most lenient, then *zav*, then *metzora*. But the *Gemara* subjects each step of this hierarchy to challenge.

*Mai chumrei dezav mitmei meit?* — Why is a *zav* considered more severe than a *tamei meit*? The answer given is *tumah yotza alav migufo* — the *tumah* emerges from his own body. It is intrinsic to him, not contracted from an external source.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: perhaps *tamei meit* is more severe. After all, *tamei meit* requires *haza'ah* on the third and seventh days using the ashes of the *Parah Adumah* — a uniquely burdensome purification process that does not apply to a *zav*. Should that not indicate greater severity?

The resolution lies in a close reading of the *pasuk*: *v'chol tamei lanefesh* — "and anyone *tamei* for a person" — interpreted as *kol tamei lanefesh*, anyone with a *tumah* similar to that of a corpse. This broadens the *tamei meit* category to include *tamei sheretz* — someone who touched a dead rodent or similar creature. *Tumah* contracted by contact from the outside is, in the *Gemara*'s framework, categorically less intrinsic than *tumah* that flows from within the body. Once the *tamei meit* category is understood to encompass even *tamei sheretz* — the most lenient form of *tumah* conceivable — the entire category is understood as the lightest tier. If even a *tamei sheretz* must leave the *Mikdash*, then certainly a *zav* must be sent even further, because the *Torah* still found it necessary to say so explicitly.

The *Gemara* then challenges the next step: *ve-zav chamur mitmei sheretz* — is a *zav* genuinely more severe than a *tamei sheretz*? The obvious case for severity is *tumah yotza migufo*, the internal origin of *zav*-*tumah*, and its seven-day duration. But the counterargument is: *shekein mitamei be'ones* — a *tamei sheretz* renders one *tamei* regardless of whether it was accidental. If one accidentally came into contact with a *sheretz*, one is nonetheless *tamei*. A *zav*, by contrast, is only classified as a full *zav* after a second flow; if the flow is attributable to external causes — something he ate, for instance — it may not count as a *zav* flow at all. This suggests a leniency in how the *zav* category is contracted.

The *Gemara* responds by citing Rav Huna, who states on 69b that the *ra'iyah rishonah shel zav* — the first flow of a *zav* — renders him *tamei* even *be'ones*. On his first flow, a *zav* has the same one-day *tumah* status as a *ba'al keri*, and a *ba'al keri* is *tamei* regardless of how the emission occurred. So even by *ones*, the *zav* category is not entirely exempt. The counterargument from *ones* therefore fails to establish the superiority of *tamei sheretz*, and the hierarchy stands: *tamei meit* (including *tamei sheretz*) is the most lenient, and *zav* is more severe.

### Zav/Ba'al Keri/Metzora

The category of *zav* is itself broader than the name implies. The *pasuk* reads *v'chol zav* — interpreted as encompassing anyone with a *zav*-like *tumah*: *lerabot ba'al keri* — this includes a man who has had a seminal emission. A *ba'al keri* is included within the *zav* category for purposes of the *machanot* exclusion, meaning a *ba'al keri* is likewise excluded from *Machaneh Leviyah* — from *Har HaBayit*. The same zone would apply to a *niddah* and a *yoledet*, who are parallel to the *ba'al keri* in this context.

The *Gemara* now asks: *mai chumrei de'metzora mi'zav* — what makes the *metzora* more severe than the *zav*? Several *chumrot* are enumerated: the *metzora* must let his hair grow wild (*peri'ah*), rend his garments (*perimah*), and is prohibited from marital relations — derived from *vayeshev michutz le'ohalo*, "and he sat outside his tent," understood as separation from his wife. All of these indicate a uniquely severe personal status.

The *Gemara* challenges this too: perhaps *zav* is actually more severe in a critical dimension. *Shekein metamei mishkav u'moshav u'metamei kli cheres be'heseit* — a *zav* renders *tamei* whatever he sits or lies upon, and this *mishkav u'moshav* is an *av hatumah* — a primary source of *tumah* — not a derivative *tumah*. Even through ten cushions of separation, whatever constitutes a seat of the *zav* is *tamei* at the highest level. This category of *mishkav u'moshav* does not apply to a *metzora*. Additionally, a *zav* renders an earthen vessel (*kli cheres*) *tamei* through mere displacement (*heseit*), without direct contact — another stringency absent by *metzora*.

The resolution again turns on the broader scope of *kol zav*. Once the *zav* category includes a *ba'al keri* — a one-day *tumah* of the most lenient kind — and if even a *ba'al keri* must leave *Machaneh Leviyah*, then by *kal va-chomer* a *metzora* must be sent even further. The *Torah* explicitly naming *metzora* is to say that it is sent to a third, still more distant zone.

One final step of the hierarchy is examined: *u'metzora chamur mi'ba'al keri* — and clearly a *metzora* is more severe than a *ba'al keri*. The counterargument offered is *shekein metamei be'mashehu* — a *ba'al keri* is *tamei* from even the smallest quantity of emission, while a *metzora*'s *tzara'at* must reach a minimum size of a *gris* (the area of a bean). The *Gemara* resolves this by citing the position of Rabbi Natan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael: a *zav*'s flow must be of sufficient volume to seal the opening of the reproductive organ. Since *ba'al keri* is connected to *zav* by analogy (*hekesh*), the same minimum applies. The *Gemara* acknowledges that Tosafot finds this comparison difficult — the opening in question seems smaller than a *gris* — but in any case the hierarchy is maintained: *tamei meit* at the base, then *zav*, then *metzora*.

At the conclusion of the analysis, the *Gemara* notes that *kol tzarua* — the corresponding expansion formula for the *metzora* category — does not in fact include any additional category. Having used *kol* with *tamei lanefesh* to include *tamei sheretz*, and *kol* with *zav* to include *ba'al keri*, the *Torah* wrote *kol tzarua* simply for stylistic parallelism — *aidi dechtav kol zav, uch'tav nami kol tzarua* — but no additional category is thereby included.

---

## Zav/Metzora in Pesach B'…

### R. Eliezer Query

The *Gemara* now turns to a question raised by Rabbi Eliezer that returns us to the topic of *pesach habah b'tumah*. Rabbi Eliezer asks: suppose *zavim* and *metzoraim* pressed forward and actually entered the *Azarah* during a *Pesach* brought in *tumah* — would they be liable? The question is whether the general *heter* of *pesach habah b'tumah*, which suspends the usual prohibition for *tamei meit*, also extends in any way to *zavim* and *metzoraim*.

### Conditional Exemption

The resolution comes from the same *pasuk* that drove the earlier discussion: *v'yishalchu min hamachaneh kol tzarua v'chol zav v'chol tamei lanefesh*. The *Gemara* reads this as encoding a conditional relationship among the three categories. The principle is: *besha'ah she'tamei meitim mishtalchim, zavin u'metzoraim mishtalchim* — at the time when *tamei meitim* are subject to being sent out of their respective zones, then *zavin* and *metzoraim* are also subject to their respective exclusions. *Aval ein tamei meitim mishtalchim* — but at the time when the rule of exclusion is suspended for *tamei meitim*, as during *pesach habah b'tumah*, then *ein zavim u'metzoraim mishtalchim* — the *zavim* and *metzoraim* also do not transgress *bedi'avad* if they enter. They have no license to enter; they still may not do so *lechatchila*. But if they did enter during such a period, they are *patur*. The exemption is not an affirmative permission but a suspension of liability that follows logically from the exceptional status of the entire period. This is what Rabbi Yehuda, in his derivation, learns from the *pasuk* that lists all three categories — not the three-camp structure, which he derives elsewhere, but this conditional exemption that links all three categories together.

---

## Ba'al Keri Issues

### Ba'al Keri Status

Having established that *v'chol zav* includes *ba'al keri*, the *Gemara* notes that this supports Rabbi Yochanan's position. A *braita* had stated *ba'al keri ke'maga sheretz* — a *ba'al keri* is like someone who touched a *sheretz*. One might read this as placing a *ba'al keri* in the most lenient category, equivalent to *tamei meit* (which includes *tamei sheretz*), and therefore permitting him on *Har HaBayit* just as a *tamei meit* is permitted. But the *Gemara* argues that the comparison is not about the *machanot* exclusion zones but about the nature of the *tumah* itself — specifically, that just as *tamei sheretz* applies even *be'ones* (regardless of intent or circumstance), so too a *ba'al keri* is *tamei be'ones*. The *pasuk* itself already specifies that each carries a one-day *tumah* (*tumat erev*), so the comparison is not needed for that purpose. The comparison must therefore be about the *be'ones* rule, not about the exclusion zones. This leaves Rabbi Yochanan's position intact: a *ba'al keri* is sent out from two camps — from *Machaneh Shechinah* (the *Mikdash*) and from *Machaneh Leviyah* (*Har HaBayit*).

### Tunnels Not Sanctified

Rabbi Yochanan himself states two related *halachot*: *mechilos lo niskadshu* — the underground tunnels beneath the *Beit HaMikdash* were not sanctified — and *u'ba'al keri mishtalei'ach chutz lishtei machanos* — a *ba'al keri* is sent out from both camps, from *Machaneh Shechinah* and from *Machaneh Leviyah*, that is, not only from the *Mikdash* itself but from *Har HaBayit* as well. The connection between these two statements may be that the first — the unsanctified tunnels — provides a practical avenue for *tamei* individuals to navigate beneath the *Har HaBayit* without violating the exclusion; and the second clarifies just how extensive the exclusion for *ba'al keri* is within the upper zones.

The ruling that underground tunnels were not sanctified has obvious relevance to contemporary discussions about *Har HaBayit*. Someone who is *tamei* could theoretically pass through tunnels beneath the walls without transgressing the *kedushah* of the *Machaneh Leviyah* zone.

### Priests' Ba'al Keri

This raises a pointed practical question about life in the *Beit HaMikdash* period. The *Kohanim* and *Levi'im* lived within or adjacent to *Machaneh Leviyah* — the zone corresponding to *Har HaBayit*. A man who has marital relations with his wife becomes a *ba'al keri* and is excluded from *Machaneh Leviyah*. How, then, did the *Kohanim* and *Levi'im* manage? Would a man have to leave his home in the middle of the night and travel outside the *machaneh* boundary after relations with his wife? The practical logistics seem deeply difficult, and the *Gemara* does not provide a resolution here. This is a question worth further investigation, but for now it is left open, and the *daf* concludes on this note.

---

---

# Pesachim 68

## Ba'al Keri Status

### Three Levels Tumah

Today's *daf* is 68, and we begin with literally the last word on 67b. The discussion concerns the *ba'al keri*, and we arrive at it through a chain of digressions: the *korban Pesach* brought on *Shabbat* led us to the question of the *Pesach* brought *bi-tumah*, which in turn brought us to the *pasuk* of *ish ish ki yiheyeh tamei la-nefesh* — that an individual who is *tamei* from corpse-*tumah* brings *Pesach Sheni*, while a *tzibur* in that state brings the *Pesach Rishon*. That discussion then opened into an analysis of the different levels of *tumah* and their corresponding camp restrictions.

The fundamental structure is a three-way hierarchy. *Tamei meis* is the most familiar form of *tumah*, yet paradoxically it is the least severe for purposes of camp exclusion. More severe are the *zav* and the *metzora*, whose *tumah* emanates from their own bodies — *tumah yotzei mi-gufo* — and it is this quality, not mere severity, that governs how far they must be distanced from the *Beis HaMikdash*. The resulting division: a *tamei meis* must leave the *Mikdash* precincts but may remain on *Har HaBayit*, which corresponds to *Machaneh Leviyah*; a *zav* must leave *Machaneh Leviyah* entirely but may remain within *Yerushalayim*, which is *Machaneh Yisrael*; and a *metzora* must be expelled even from there.

### Ba'al Keri Classification

Against this backdrop, the *Gemara* asks: where does the *ba'al keri* fit? On one hand, his *tumah* issues from his own body, making him qualitatively similar to the *zav*. On the other hand, his *tumah* lasts only one day, making him far more lenient. The question is whether he belongs in the *zav* category — and is therefore excluded from *Har HaBayit* — or whether he is treated like a *tamei meis* and permitted on *Har HaBayit*. *Rabbi Yochanan* had stated that a *ba'al keri* is like a *zav* for this purpose, but this ruling is now subjected to challenge.

### Boel Niddah Equation

The *Gemara* raises a *meitivei* from the conclusion of a *braita*: *boel niddah ke-tamei meis* — a man who has relations with a *niddah* is equated to one who has contracted corpse-*tumah*. The *Gemara* asks: for what *halacha* does this equation apply? If the intent is merely to equate their degree of *tumah*, that point is superfluous, since both already carry a seven-day *tumah* by explicit Torah law. The equation must therefore be teaching something about their camp restrictions: a *boel niddah* shares the same camp status as a *tamei meis*. Since his *tumah* does not originate within his own body but is contracted through external contact, he belongs in the least restrictive category and may even enter *Machaneh Leviyah* — he is only excluded from the *Mikdash* itself.

From this conclusion about the *seifa* of the *braita*, the *Gemara* reasons: since the end of the *braita* speaks about camp restrictions, the beginning of that same *braita* — which equated the *ba'al keri* to a *zav* — must also be speaking about camps, meaning the *ba'al keri* must leave *Machaneh Leviyah* and is forbidden on *Har HaBayit*. A sharp question immediately arises: if a *boel niddah* is in the least-restrictive category, but one who is *boel niddah* has presumably also become a *ba'al keri*, would that not place him in the more restrictive *zav* category as well? The answer is that it is possible in principle to be a *boel niddah* without becoming a *ba'al keri*, and the *braita* presumably addresses that case.

The *Gemara* rejects this line of reasoning with *midi irya*: the two halves of the *braita* need not serve the same legal function. Just because the *seifa* addresses camp restrictions does not compel us to read the *reisha* as doing the same. Each clause stands on its own.

### Ba'al Keri Exception

The *Gemara* presses further. A second *braita* states: *metzora chamur mi-zav*, *v'zav chamur mi-tamei meis* — the *metzora* is stricter than the *zav*, and the *zav* is stricter than the *tamei meis* — clearly articulating the camp hierarchy. The *braita* then adds: *yatzah ba'al keri*, the *ba'al keri* is excluded, because *tamei meis chamur mimenu* — a *tamei meis* is even stricter than he is.

The *Gemara* asks what this exclusion means. One reading: *yatza mikhlal zav* — the *ba'al keri* is excluded from the *zav* category entirely. Although his *tumah* issues from his own body, he should not be grouped with the *zav*. Instead, *u'va l'klal tamei meis* — he enters the *tamei meis* category. The rationale is that a *tamei meis* is already stricter than he is, carrying a seven-day *tumah* while his lasts only one day, so he should be placed in the most lenient group. According to this reading, the *ba'al keri* may enter *Machaneh Leviyah* and is permitted on *Har HaBayit*.

### Qualitative Classification

The *Gemara* rejects this reading and proposes an alternative. The word *yatzah* need not mean he is excluded from the *zav* category into a more lenient one; it can mean he is excluded from the *tamei meis* category despite being even more lenient than a *tamei meis*. The exception runs in the other direction: your instinct would have been to place him with *tamei meis* since he is so mild, but the *braita* tells you no — *bnichnas lemachaneh zav*, he enters the *zav* category. Why? *Ve'af al gav detamei meis chamur mimenu* — even though a *tamei meis* is more severe in terms of duration, the *ba'al keri* is nonetheless an exception to the severity-based hierarchy, because the operative principle is *le-mai de-dami lei midaminan lei* — we categorize him according to what he is most similar to qualitatively, not according to where he falls in the severity ranking. Since his *tumah*, like that of the *zav*, issues from his own body, he is classified with the *zav* — and is therefore forbidden on *Har HaBayit* — regardless of the fact that in terms of duration his *tumah* is far milder.

This leaves the *Gemara* without a clean resolution, since the argument about classification based on qualitative similarity rather than severity is offered as a possible reading but not unanimously established.

### Rav Yitzchak Braita

A *tana* taught before *Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi*, still addressing the question of which camps the *ba'al keri* must leave. The relevant *pasuk*, *ish asher lo yiheyeh tahor mikreh laylah*, explicitly concerns a *ba'al keri*. The verse continues: *veyatza michutz lamachaneh* — he goes out of the camp — *lo yavo el toch hamachaneh* — he shall not enter inside the camp. The *braita* reads these two clauses as referring to two different camps: *veyatza michutz lamachaneh, zo machaneh Shechinah* — he must leave the camp of the *Shechinah*, meaning the *Mikdash* precinct; *lo yavo el toch hamachaneh, zo machaneh Leviyah* — and he must not enter *Machaneh Leviyah* either. The conclusion: *mikan le-va'al keri she-yatza chutz li-shtei machanot* — the *ba'al keri* must be outside both camps, supporting *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position.

### Ejection Paradox

When the *tana* presented this *braita*, *Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi* challenged him: *akti lo ayiltei apiktei* — you haven't even brought him in yet, and you're taking him out? The point of the challenge is this: if the first clause says he must leave *Machaneh Shechinah*, then the second clause — "do not enter the camp" — cannot logically refer to *Machaneh Leviyah*, because he has only been ejected from *Machaneh Shechinah*. He has not yet been expelled from *Machaneh Leviyah*, so there is nothing to prohibit him from re-entering. For a prohibition of entry to make sense, he must first have been ejected from that very camp. The *braita* as originally read is therefore internally incoherent.

### Two Camps Reading

The resolution proposed is to reverse the order in which the clauses are matched to the camps. *Michutz lamachaneh, zo machaneh Leviyah* — the first clause, the positive obligation to leave, applies to *Machaneh Leviyah*; *lo yavo el toch hamachaneh, zo machaneh Shechinah* — the prohibition of entry applies to *Machaneh Shechinah*. This reading is both logically coherent and halachically significant. Once he has left *Machaneh Leviyah*, the prohibition of not entering applies specifically to *Machaneh Shechinah*, the more interior precinct. The practical consequence: remaining in *Machaneh Leviyah* transgresses the positive commandment of *veyatza*, while actually entering *Machaneh Shechinah* additionally violates the negative prohibition of *lo yavo*. Thus the *ba'al keri* is subject to two distinct prohibitions corresponding to two different camps.

### Ravina Position

*Ravina* objected to this entire framework. In his view, both clauses of the *pasuk* refer to the same camp — *Machaneh Shechinah* — and the reason the Torah states the matter twice is not to identify two different camps but to establish both a positive and a negative commandment applying to the single prohibition of entering *Machaneh Shechinah*. This minimalist reading is consistent with the principle of *tafasta merubah lo tafasta*: when in doubt, read the *pasuk* as narrowly as possible.

The *Gemara* responds that the word *hamachaneh* appears twice in the verse. If the intent were only to establish a positive and negative commandment regarding one camp, the Torah could have written *veyeitzei el michutz lamachaneh velo yavo el tokhah* — using a single instance of the word. The repetition of *hamachaneh* as a full noun implies that a second, distinct camp is being invoked. The conclusion: the *ba'al keri* is at minimum forbidden in *Machaneh Leviyah* by virtue of the positive commandment of *veyatza*, with the additional negative prohibition applying to *Machaneh Shechinah*.

### Har HaBayit Practice

It should be noted that the only *chiyuv karet* applies when any *tamei* individual — regardless of which category of *tumah* — actually enters *Machaneh Shechinah*, meaning the *azarah* precinct of the *Mikdash*. All of the other restrictions are of lesser severity. A *metzora* entering *Yerushalayim* violates at most a *lo ta'aseh*, according to some opinions only an *asseh*. A *zav* ascending *Har HaBayit* violates a *lo ta'aseh* without *karet*. And the *ba'al keri*'s status on *Har HaBayit* is itself debated: whether he is prohibited at all, as *Rabbi Yochanan* holds, and if so, whether the prohibition is a *lo ta'aseh* or merely an *asseh*, remains unresolved by the *Gemara*.

These questions carry direct practical relevance for those who ascend *Har HaBayit* today. Even those who believe they can navigate around the approximate location of the *makom hamikdash* — and are therefore unconcerned about the *chiyuv karet* that applies to a *tamei* entering the *azarah* — must still contend with these questions. A woman who is a *niddah* is certainly in the more stringent category and is forbidden. For a man who is a *ba'al keri*, the *Gemara*'s unresolved debate means that tour organizers would need to ensure participants either refrained or immersed in a *mikvah* beforehand. But even immersion creates a further complication: the status of a *tvul yom* of a *ba'al keri* — one who has immersed but whose *tumah* does not end until nightfall — may not be fully equivalent to taharah, and thus the prohibition may persist even after immersion. Beyond that, there is a further question of *bi'ah bemiktzat* — whether partial entry, such as extending a hand into the wall, constitutes a prohibited act — and disagreement about precisely where *Har HaBayit* begins, whether at the inner or outer face of the surrounding wall. These compounding uncertainties make the practical *halacha* of ascending *Har HaBayit* considerably more complex than is sometimes appreciated.

One broader question that the *Gemara* does not address is worth noting. If a *ba'al keri* is forbidden in *Machaneh Leviyah*, it is difficult to understand how the *Kohanim* and *Levi'im* in the *midbar*, who resided within *Machaneh Leviyah*, could have maintained conjugal relations with their wives. Any seminal emission — whether through relations or otherwise — would have immediately required them to exit the camp until they could immerse in a *mikvah* and wait out the day. Given the further question of whether a *tvul yom* of a *ba'al keri* may re-enter, it is not obvious how they could have returned home even after immersing.

---

## Shabbat Acts Pesach

### Michui Kreivim

Returning now to the *Mishnah* concerning what may be done on *Shabbat* for the sake of the *korban Pesach*, one of the permitted acts is the cleansing of the intestines — *michui kreivim* — the removal of fecal matter from the intestinal lining. This is required because the *eimurim*, the sacrificial portions, cannot be offered in a state of contamination from their contents. The *Gemara* asks: what exactly does this *michui kreivim* involve, and where lies the boundary between the permitted cleansing and the prohibited rinsing in water?

### Rav Huna vs Chiyya

*Rav Huna* says the method involves making a hole in the intestine with a knife — *shemenakvin be-sakin* — and through that incision squeezing out the digested contents. *Chiyya bar Rav* describes it differently: *shirka damei aya d'nafka agav duchka d'sakina* — the liquids and matter of the intestines that come out through the pressure exerted by the knife, without necessarily puncturing through. The practical difference is subtle but significant. According to *Rav Huna*, the knife is used as a cutting instrument to create an opening; according to *Chiyya bar Rav*, it is used as a pressing implement, with the knife's edge or flat providing the force needed to expel the contents. The reason rinsing in water remains forbidden while this mechanical method is permitted is presumably that the cleansing by knife pressure is the minimum necessary act of *tzorech hakravah* — preparation required for the *korban* itself — whereas rinsing would constitute an additional, separable *melacha* that could have been performed before *Shabbat*.

### Isaiah Proof

*Rabbi Elazar* asks: what is the source that lends support to the view of *Chiyya bar Rav*, that it is specifically the pressure of a knife that forces out the contents? He cites the *pasuk* in *Yeshayahu*: *v'charvot mechim garim yocheilu*, and explains it using the *targum* of *Rav Yosef*: *u-nichsei d'rasha'aya tzadika ya-achasnun* — the property of the wicked the righteous will inherit. The word *garim* is thus read as referring to the righteous, and *charvot mechim* — the sword of the *mechim* — identifies the disgusting material driven out by the blade. *Rashi* explains that *garim* evokes *Klal Yisrael* as sojourners in this world, somehow identifying them with the righteous who will inherit the substance of the wicked.

---

## Techiyat HaMetim

### Righteous Power

The discussion of that verse in *Yeshayahu* draws the *Gemara* into a substantial *excursus* on *techiyat ha-metim* and the power that will be granted to the righteous in the future. The *pasuk* continues: *v'ra'u kvassim k'dabram* — the flock will graze as has been spoken of them. *Rav Nachman bar Yirmeya* in the name of *Rav* interprets *k'medubar bam* — "as has been spoken about them" — as a reference to the second half of that very verse. *Abaye* elaborates: the flock, which is *Yisrael*, will receive what has been spoken to them, namely the inheritance of the wealth of the wicked described in the *seifa*.

*Rava* objects. If the word had been written *charvot* without a *vav*, one could read the second half of the *pasuk* as completing the thought of the first half. But since it is written *v'charvot* — with a *vav* — it introduces an independent new statement: *milta chadta hi deka'amar*, the second clause is a separate point entirely. The first clause must therefore be interpreted independently.

*Rava* therefore invokes the tradition of *Rav Chananel* in the name of *Rav*: *atidin tzadikim sheyichyu et hametim* — in the future, the righteous will have the power to resurrect the dead. The verse *v'ra'u kvassim k'dabram* is read by means of a *gezeira shava* connecting *vera'u* here to *yir'u Bashan vegilad kimei olam* in the prophet *Micah* — that *Bashan* and *Gilad* will shepherd as in the days of old. *Bashan* is identified as *Elisha*, *haba min ha-Bashan*, who came from the locale of *Bashan*, as established by the connection between the *pasuk* in *Melachim* placing *Shafat* in *Bashan* and the identification of *Elisha ben Shafat* as the attendant who poured water over the hands of *Eliyahu*. *Gilad* is *Eliyahu*, as the verse says *Eliyahu ha-Tishbi mi-toshavei Gilad*. The verse in *Micah* therefore promises that as *Eliyahu* and *Elisha* shepherded — meaning as they brought back the dead in the days of old — so will this power be restored.

### Resurrection Power

*Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani* in the name of *Rabbi Yonatan* extends this further: *atidin tzadikim sheyichyu metim* — not only *Eliyahu* and *Elisha*, but the *tzadikim* in general will in the future have the power to resurrect the dead. The source is the *pasuk* in *Zechariah*: *od yeshvu zkenim u-zkenot birchovot Yerushalayim, v'ish mishanto beyado merov yamim* — elder men and women will sit in the streets of *Yerushalayim*, each one with a staff in hand from great old age. The connection: we know from the episode of *Elisha* — *v'shamta mishanti al pnei ha-na'ar* — that a staff can serve as the instrument of *techiyat ha-metim*. Since the *pasuk* in *Zechariah* says every *zaken* and *zkenah* will hold such a staff, the implication is that every *tzadik*, or at least every elder, will possess this power to resurrect the dead.

### Death Contradiction

*Ulla* raised a contradiction between two verses. One verse states *bila hamavet la-netzach* — death will cease forever in the future time. A second verse states *ki ha-na'ar ben me'ah shanah yamut* — that even a young death will occur at a hundred years, implying that death continues to exist, merely postponed to very old age.

### Israel vs Nations

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction: *kan be-Yisrael, kan be-ovdei kochavim* — the verse promising the cessation of death applies to *Yisrael*, while the verse describing death at a hundred years describes the fate of the nations. The *Gemara* then asks: what are non-Jews doing in the *Olam HaBa* at all? The answer is drawn from the *pasuk* in *Yeshayahu*: *v'amdu zarim v'ra'u tzonechem, u-vnei nechar ikareichem v'charmeichem* — the foreigners will shepherd the flocks of *Yisrael* and tend their fields and vineyards. The non-Jews will be present in a functional, servile capacity in that future world, and while they will live extremely long lives, it is *Yisrael* that will live forever.

This is a striking *Gemara*, and it is worth pausing on its broader implication. When the *Gemara* says that the *tzadikim* will perform *techiyat ha-metim*, it is making a remarkable claim about agency. Whether this means that the event we call *techiyat ha-metim* — the general resurrection — will be executed by the *tzadikim*, or whether it means that after the initial resurrection, the ongoing power over life and death will reside with the righteous, is not entirely clear. It may mean that following the resurrection, death will no longer be absolute — if someone dies, a *tzadik* can restore them. The *Gemara*'s claim in either case is arresting: the ultimate mastery over life and death will pass into human hands, or at least into the hands of the righteous. In one reading, this is a statement about the fullness of reward that the *tzadikim* will receive; in another, it carries the more radical implication that even *techiyat ha-metim*, which we associate entirely with divine power, will in some sense come from within. The connection to the earlier discussion is beautiful: where the earlier portion of the *daf* dealt with bodily *tumah* creating distance from the *Mikdash* and from the divine presence — where access to God is constrained by circumstances beyond one's control — here we arrive at a vision in which even life and death become subject to human agency.

### Luminaries Brightness

*Rav Chisda* raised a further contradiction. One *pasuk* states *v'chafra ha-levana u-vosha ha-chama* — the moon will be embarrassed and the sun ashamed, their light rendered meaningless before the radiance of God in the future time. A second *pasuk* states *v'haya or ha-levana k'or ha-chama, v'or ha-chama yiheyeh shivtayim k'or shivat ha-yamim* — the moon will shine with the strength of the sun, and the sun will be seven times as powerful as the light of the seven days of creation. *Rashi* understands this as forty-nine times the power of each individual day, yielding light many hundreds of times more intense than now. These two visions are in direct conflict: one depicts luminaries outshone into irrelevance, the other depicts them blazing with unprecedented brilliance.

### Mashiach vs Olam HaBa

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction: *kan l'Olam HaBa, kan le-Yemot HaMashiach* — the verse depicting the embarrassed luminaries refers to *Olam HaBa*, while the verse depicting their extraordinary brightness refers to *Yemot HaMashiach*. The distinction is fundamental. Messianic times will be miraculous but will still involve a form of normal earthly life — people will eat, there may still be death of some kind, nature will be transformed but not transcended. The *Olam HaBa* that follows Messianic times is the complete utopia in which only the divine light obtains and the luminaries are altogether eclipsed.

This distinction is significant because for a contemporary audience the term *Olam HaBa* typically evokes the world of souls after death. Much of that reorientation was due to the *Rambam*, who emphasized the eternal life of the soul and deliberately de-emphasized miraculous earthly transformation as the content of the eschatological promise. But in the plain meaning of this *Gemara*, *Olam HaBa* is a future state of existence on this earth — the sequence runs from this world, to Messianic times, to *Olam HaBa*.

For *Shmuel*, who held that the only difference between this world and *Yemot HaMashiach* is *shibbud malkhuyot* — the end of subjugation to foreign powers — with no miraculous transformation of nature, the resolution cannot appeal to Messianic times as the referent of the verse about brilliant luminaries. The *Gemara* therefore says: for *Shmuel*, both verses refer to *Olam HaBa*, and the contradiction is resolved differently.

### Rambam Approach

In this connection it is worth noting the *Rambam*'s famous treatment of these questions, which he discusses in his *hakdamah le-Peirush ha-Mishnayot*. The *Rambam* was deeply troubled by the amount of religious energy people invested in speculating about the details of *Yemot HaMashiach* — who one's spouse would be after resurrection, whether one would be resurrected at the age and with the infirmities one had at death, and similar questions. His view was that such speculation is religiously unproductive: we simply do not know, nobody has been there, and our obligations lie in this world.

At the same time, in *Hilchos Melachim* the *Rambam* writes — attributing it to the consensus of *Chazal* — *ein bein olam hazeh li-Yemot HaMashiach ela shibbud malkhuyot*, that the only difference between this world and Messianic times is the end of foreign domination. This is in fact the minority opinion of *Shmuel* in the *Gemara*, yet the *Rambam* presents it as the authoritative consensus, precisely because he wished to discourage miraculous expectations of Messianic times and redirect attention to present obligations.

The irony, as *Dr. David Berger* observed in an article written approximately twenty years ago, is that this attempt to demystify Messianic times had the exact opposite of its intended effect. By insisting that the *Mashiach* need perform no miracles and that the only distinguishing criterion is the end of political subjugation, the *Rambam*'s formulation made it far easier for subsequent messianic movements to advance their claims. When challenged — "the world looks exactly the same, how can this be the true redemption?" — a follower could simply reply: according to the *Rambam*, nothing miraculous is required. *Dr. Berger* identifies three major movements that exploited this dynamic: the followers of *Shabbetai Zevi*, certain elements within *Chabad*, and the religious Zionist concept of *aschalta di-ge'ulah* — the idea that the establishment of the State of Israel represents the beginning of the redemption, with *shibbud malkhuyot* progressively diminishing.

### Resurrection Healing

The *Gemara* then turns to another verse. *Rava* raises a contradiction. One verse says *ani amis va-achayeh* — I will bring death and I will bring life. A second says *machatzti va-ani erpa* — I have struck down and I will heal. The challenge: if God already told us He will bring life, is it not self-evident that He can heal? Why add the anti-climactic assurance of healing after promising resurrection?

The *Gemara* answers: God is saying *mah she-ani memis ani mechayeh* — the very person whom I cause to die, I will resurrect. It is not a general statement about death and life as separate events but a promise that the identical individual who died will be restored. The parallel with the end of the verse clinches this: when the verse says "I struck down and I will heal," *healing* obviously refers to healing the same person who was struck — so too, "I will bring life" refers to restoring life to the very person who died. This is an affirmative scriptural basis for the doctrine of *techiyat ha-metim*.

A *braita* elaborates on this point. One might have thought *ani amis va-achayeh* means I will cause one person to die and bring new life to a different person — the ordinary workings of the natural world, where some die and others are born. Therefore the verse adds *machatzti va-ani erpa*: just as wounding and healing refer to the same person, so do death and life. *Mikan teshuvah la-omrim ein techiyas ha-meitim min ha-Torah* — this is the Torah-level refutation of those who deny that resurrection of the dead is grounded in the Written Torah.

An alternative reading of the verse is then offered: *betechilah mah she-ani memis ani mechayeh* — first God will resurrect the dead; *ve-hadar mah shemachatzti va-ani erpa* — and subsequently, He will heal all the wounds and physical afflictions with which they were resurrected. The sequence is first resurrection, then healing — those who return to life bearing old wounds or missing limbs will afterward be made whole. According to this reading, the two halves of the verse describe two sequential stages of the eschatological process, both occurring in Messianic times.

---

## Shabbat Acts Pesach (II)

### Blemish Removal

Returning to the *Mishnah* on what may be done on *Shabbat* for the *korban Pesach*: a *braita* in *Eruvin* teaches that for any *korban* brought to the *Mikdash* on *Shabbat*, one may cut off a blemish — a *mum* such as a wart or hanging piece of skin — on *Shabbat*, because the principle *ein shevut ba-Mikdash* applies: rabbinic prohibitions are not observed when they conflict with the needs of the *Mikdash* service. The same *braita* continues: *aval lo ba-medinah* — but outside the *Mikdash*, this is not permitted. And if done with a vessel — a knife or similar implement — it is forbidden in both locations.

The *Mishnah* under discussion prohibits cutting off such a blemish in terms that appear to be absolute. This creates an apparent contradiction with the *braita* that allows it within the *Mikdash* by hand.

### Hand vs Vessel

Two *Amoraim*, *Rabbi Elazar* and *Rabbi Yose bar Chanina*, each offer a resolution, and they disagree with one another.

The first opinion holds: *idi ve-idi beyad* — both the *Mishnah* and the *braita* are speaking about doing the act by hand, without a vessel. The difference is *ha belacha ha beyavesha* — the *braita* permits it when the blemish is dry, no longer physiologically integrated into the body, while the *Mishnah* prohibits it when the blemish is still moist and genuinely part of the body. According to this view, two criteria must be met to permit the act even within the *Mikdash*: using one's hand rather than a vessel, and the blemish being dried out.

The second opinion holds: *idi ve-idi belacha* — both are speaking about a moist blemish. The difference is *ha beyad ha be-kli* — the *braita* permits it when done by hand within the *Mikdash*, while the *Mishnah* prohibits it when done with a vessel, inside or outside the *Mikdash*. According to this view, only one criterion governs: if done by hand, it is permitted even when moist; if done with a vessel, it is forbidden everywhere.

The *Gemara* then challenges the first opinion. If the blemish is dried out — *mifrach parich*, it is merely crumbling — why would there be any prohibition even with a vessel, and why would there be any prohibition outside the *Mikdash*? If it is no longer genuinely part of the body, removing it should present no halachic difficulty under any circumstance. The second opinion escapes this difficulty: according to it, the dried-out case is indeed entirely unproblematic, and both the *Mishnah* and the *braita* deal only with the moist case.

### Mishnah Repetition

The *Gemara* turns to a further question: according to the second opinion — that the distinction is between hand and vessel, and that the *braita* already explicitly states *im be-kli, kan ve-kan assur* — if done with a vessel, it is forbidden in both locations — why does the *Mishnah* need to repeat this prohibition? It is already stated explicitly in the *braita*.

The *Gemara* answers: *pulgeta de-Rabbi Eliezer ve-Rabbi Yehoshua ata leashmienan* — the *Mishnah* repeats the prohibition in the specific context of the *korban Pesach* in order to address the position of *Rabbi Eliezer*, who holds that preparatory acts which could have been done before *Shabbat* may nonetheless be performed on *Shabbat* for the sake of the *korban Pesach*. Since *Rabbi Eliezer* is lenient even about certain *melacha* for *hechsher mitzvah*, one might think he would certainly permit rabbinic prohibitions in this context. The *Mishnah* therefore needs to state explicitly, even in the context of this great obligation, that cutting a *mum* with a vessel remains forbidden — even *Rabbi Eliezer* does not extend his leniency to permit that.

---

## R. Eliezer vs R. Yehoshua

### Eliezer Shechita

The dispute between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* now comes into focus. *Rabbi Eliezer* argues: *umah im shechita* — if the *shechita* of the *korban Pesach* overrides *Shabbat*, it is certainly the case that preparatory acts of a rabbinic character should also be permitted. If the Torah overrides *Shabbat* for the core act, surely rabbinic restrictions that merely facilitate the performance of that core act should be set aside as well.

### Yehoshua Yom Tov

*Rabbi Yehoshua* counters with an analogy from *Yom Tov*. On *Yom Tov*, cooking is permitted — yet even so, one may not chop wood on *Yom Tov* that could have been chopped the day before, even though the wood is needed for the cooking. This demonstrates that the permission to perform the core act does not automatically license all preparatory acts that could have been completed earlier, including those that are only rabbinically prohibited.

### Reshut vs Mitzvah

*Rabbi Eliezer* responds: the analogy from *Yom Tov* fails because cooking on *Yom Tov* is a *reshut* — a permitted but optional act — not a true obligatory *mitzvah*. The license to override *Shabbat* or to set aside other restrictions flows from the nature and gravity of the underlying obligation. A *reshut* provides very limited license; a genuine *mitzvah* like *korban Pesach* provides far more. Therefore, what we see on *Yom Tov* — that a *reshut* does not license preparatory acts done before — tells us nothing about what a true *mitzvah* can license.

### Simchat Yom Tov

*Rabbi Yehoshua* responds by invoking the obligation of *simchat Yom Tov*. The *Gemara* introduces a *braita* that reflects this same debate in a different context: *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* dispute the nature of *Yom Tov* itself. *Rabbi Eliezer* holds that *Yom Tov* presents a binary: one may spend it entirely in divine service — *yoshev ve-shoneh* — or entirely in physical pleasure — *ochel ve-shote* — but the two are not mixed. *Rabbi Yehoshua* holds one must split the day: *chetzyo le-achilah, chetzyo le-Beis HaMidrash* — half for eating and physical enjoyment, half for Torah study.

The significance for the dispute is this: *Rabbi Yehoshua* maintains that *simchat Yom Tov* — specifically the physical enjoyment of eating and drinking — is itself a genuine *mitzvah*, not a mere *reshut*. Since even for this genuine *mitzvah* we do not permit preparatory acts on *Shabbat* that could have been done before, the same should apply to the *korban Pesach*. *Rabbi Yehoshua le-ta'amei* — this is entirely consistent with his position that physical *simchat Yom Tov* is an obligatory *mitzvah*, and therefore his analogy holds: since even a *mitzvah* like *simchat Yom Tov* does not license the performance on *Shabbat* of acts that could have been done before, the *korban Pesach* provides no greater license.

### Atzeres Source

*Rabbi Yochanan* observes that both *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* derive their positions from the same verse. The Torah uses the word *atzeres* — a holding back, an assembly — twice in adjacent contexts: once *Atzeres l'Hashem Elokecha* — the *atzeres* is for God — and once *Atzeres yiheyeh lachem* — the *atzeres* is for you.

### All or Nothing

*Rabbi Eliezer* reads these two formulations as alternatives. Either the day is entirely dedicated to God — *kulo l'Hashem* — or it is entirely for oneself — *kulo lachem*. There is no mandated mixture. One may choose a path of total spiritual engagement or total physical enjoyment, and either constitutes a valid fulfillment of *Yom Tov*. On this reading, the physical enjoyment of *Yom Tov* is not obligatory — it is merely one option — and therefore constitutes a *reshut* rather than a *mitzvah*.

### Half and Half

*Rabbi Yehoshua* reads the two formulations not as alternatives but as instructions to divide: *chalkeihu*, split it — *chetzyo l'Hashem, chetzyo lachem* — half the day for God, half for oneself. On this reading, the physical dimension of *Yom Tov* is not optional but mandatory, and thus constitutes a genuine *mitzvah*. Both Sages derive their entire halachic framework from the tension within this single verse, reading it in opposite directions.

---

---

# Pesachim 69

## Preparatory Acts

### Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

The daf picks up in the middle of 69b with a dispute found in the *mishnah* between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua concerning *machshirei mitzvah* — preparatory acts — for the *korban Pesach* when *erev Pesach* falls on Shabbat. Rabbi Eliezer holds that one may perform even *d'rabanans* — rabbinic prohibitions — that could have been done beforehand, in order to bring the *korban Pesach*, even on Shabbat. Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees.

### Firewood & Reshus

Rabbi Yehoshua draws a proof from the prohibition against chopping firewood on *Yom Tov* to make a fire for cooking: even though cooking on *Yom Tov* is permitted, the preparatory act of chopping wood that could have been done from beforehand is not. To this, Rabbi Eliezer responds that chopping wood for cooking is a *reshus* — an optional act — whereas the *korban Pesach* is a *mitzvah*, and there is therefore no valid comparison. Notably, in taking this position, Rabbi Eliezer implicitly characterizes having good food on *Yom Tov* as a *reshus* rather than a *mitzvah*.

### Simchat Yom Tov

The *Gemara* connects this to a broader dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Yehoshua holds that *simchat Yom Tov* — the physical pleasure of the holiday — is itself a *mitzvah*. Accordingly, preparing food for *Yom Tov* is comparable to preparatory acts for the *korban Pesach*, and the analogy is apt. Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, holds that one may devote the entire *Yom Tov* to *l'Hashem* — to purely spiritual *simcha* — and therefore physical enjoyment is not necessarily a *mitzvah* at all. The *Gemara* reads back into the first dispute: what made it obvious that Rabbi Yehoshua's proof was legitimate was precisely *his own position* that *simchat Yom Tov* carries the force of a *mitzvah*.

---

## Atzeret Division

### All or Nothing

A *baraita* elaborates on the underlying dispute. Rabbi Eliezer says: a person has nothing on *Yom Tov* except one of two choices — either *ochel v'shoteh*, eating and drinking, or *yoshev v'shoneh*, sitting and learning. There is no hybrid. The dedication must be total: either fully physical or fully spiritual.

### Half and Half

Rabbi Yehoshua says *chelkeihu* — divide it. Half should go to *achila v'shtiya*, eating and drinking, and half to the *beit hamidrash*. This is not simply a pragmatic compromise; it reflects a principled view about the nature of *Yom Tov* and what is demanded of a person on such days. One might observe that *t'filla* is conspicuously absent from the discussion — this is consistent with the rabbinic orientation in which the primary mode of religious expression is *talmud Torah*, not prayer.

### Samach Lifnei

Rabbi Yochanan teaches that both *tannaim* derive their positions from a single juxtaposition of verses: one verse reads *Atzeret l'Hashem Elokecha* — the *atzeret* is for Hashem — while another reads *Atzeret tihyeh lachem* — it is for you. Rabbi Eliezer reads the two verses as presenting a choice: *o kulo l'Hashem o kulo lachem*, either entirely for God or entirely for yourself. Rabbi Yehoshua reads them as complementary: *chetzyo l'Hashem v'chetzyo lachem*, half for God and half for yourself.

It is worth noting that the Torah's description of *simchat Yom Tov* frequently emphasizes *sameach lifnei Hashem* — rejoicing in the presence of God. The *Gemara* elsewhere teaches *ein simcha ela b'vasar shelamim* — there is no *simcha* without the meat of a *shelamim*. The physical pleasure and the act of bringing a sacrifice were once integrated experiences, with the physical *simcha* serving as a manifestation of one's joy in the *mikdash*. In the post-*mikdash* reality, however, that integrated experience has fractured, and what was once a unified expression of *simcha lifnei Hashem* now requires some deliberate allocation between the spiritual and the physical.

### Shavuot Agreement

Rabbi Elazar — an *amora* — adds a striking qualification: *hakol modim b'Atzeret d'ba'inan nami lachem* — everybody agrees that on *Shavuot*, even Rabbi Eliezer concedes that we require an element of *lachem*, of physical pleasure. This is notable precisely because one would have expected the opposite: on the day the *Torah* was given, one might assume that everyone would agree we need *l'Hashem* — an expression of purely spiritual engagement, especially since, as noted, the primary expression of *l'Hashem* for the rabbis is *talmud Torah*, not *t'filla*. Rashi explains that the day carries such intense joy that it must find expression in *achila u'shtiya*.

A different approach suggests itself. On other days of the year, one may express one's religious life through purely spiritual pursuits without any risk of misrepresenting the nature of *Torah*. But on the day the *Torah* was given, to engage exclusively in spiritual *limud* would risk conveying the wrong message — that the *Torah* belongs to heaven, that it is the exclusive domain of the spiritual, as the *malachim* argued it should remain. It was Moshe Rabbeinu who replied to the angels: does the *Torah*'s prohibition of *kibbud av va'em* apply to you? Does *lo tirtzach* speak to your situation? The *Torah* was given to human beings living in the physical world. On *Yom shenitna bo Torah*, we must demonstrate that the *Torah* finds its fullest expression precisely in how we live our lives in this world — that even *achila u'shtiya* can become the expression of a *mitzvah*. On other days, there is no risk of this message being lost; on *Shavuot*, there is.

---

## Oneg Shabbat

### Shabbat Lachem

Rava extends the principle further: *hakol modim be'Shabbat d'ba'inan nami lachem* — everyone agrees, as a regular weekly matter applying far more broadly than the once-or-twice-yearly *Yomim Tovim*, that Shabbat requires *lachem*, physical pleasure. The source is the verse *vekarata l'Shabbat Oneg* — you shall call Shabbat a delight, a day of *oneg*.

### Oneg vs. Simcha

There is an important distinction between *oneg* and *simcha*. *Simcha* — joy — is a capacious category: it can arise from a fine meal, but equally from an enriching conversation, an inspiring experience, or an elevated *limud*. Joy is an inner state of elevation and completeness that can be reached through many paths, and it is therefore plausible that for some people *kulo l'Hashem* is itself a path to *simcha*. *Oneg*, by contrast, connotes specifically physical pleasure and enjoyment. The Torah does not say *vekarata l'Shabbat simcha*; it says *oneg*.
