This is why, on *Yom Tov*, it is *simcha* that is emphasized, whereas on Shabbat, the concept foregrounded is *oneg* — and why the specific *halachot* of Shabbat, from *shalosh seudot* to the preparation of the Shabbat meal, are so precisely oriented around this quality of physical delight.

### Yom Kippur Shabbaton

Why must Shabbat in particular emphasize physical *oneg*? One consideration emerges from a comparison with *Yom Kippur*. The Rambam explains that we fast on *Yom Kippur* not primarily as a form of self-affliction for purposes of *teshuva*, but because *Yom Kippur* is *Shabbat Shabbaton* — a complete *Shabbat*, meaning *Shabbat mimlacha u'Shabbat mei'achila v'shtiya*. It is a full cessation of our physical engagement with the world, both in terms of creative action and in terms of sustaining our bodies. The ideal of *Yom Kippur* is a day of total withdrawal from the physical dimension of existence. That is the meaning of *Shabbat Shabbaton*.

### Shabbat Rest

The other *Shabbatot*, by contrast, must ensure that *oneg* is present — and this is important on at least two levels. First, one must not overextend the idea that the highest Jewish religious ideal is the complete renunciation of the physical world. But second, and equally, one must not allow Shabbat to become associated in the mind — particularly in the minds of children — with deprivation. When a day defined by cessation from weekday activities becomes experienced primarily as a day of *what you can't do*, it invites dread rather than delight. The antidote is precisely the *lachem*: the beautiful Shabbat table, the fine food, the warmth of the experience — these ensure that the day of rest from the world is associated with *oneg* rather than with its absence. On Shabbat there is a special imperative to cultivate that association.

---

## Purim & Erev YK

### Purim Celebration

Rav Yosef adds that *hakol modin b'Purim d'ba'inan nami lachem* — everyone agrees that *Purim* requires physical pleasure. The source is explicit in the *megilla*: *yemei mishteh v'simcha* — days of feasting and rejoicing — where the *mishteh*, the drinking and feasting, is written directly into the text.

### Fasting Exceptions

The *Gemara* then relates that Mar bar Ravina would fast the entire year — presumably maintaining a pattern of daytime fasting with eating at night, a kind of year-round regimen of ascetic practice. The three exceptions to his fasting were *Atzarta*, *Shavuot*; *Puraya*, *Purim*; and *ma'alei Yoma d'Kippuri*, *erev Yom Kippur*. Reading this carefully, the *Gemara* seems to indicate that even *Yom Tov* and Shabbat were included in his year-round fast — though there is a known concept of a *ta'anit chalom* on Shabbat, the plain reading here does seem to extend further. In any event, three days stood apart: *Shavuot*, because it is *yom shenitna bo Torah*; *Purim*, because *yemei mishteh v'simcha* is written explicitly; and *erev Yom Kippur*, as the *baraita* of Chiya bar Rav mi-Diftei explains.

### Erev YK Eating

That *baraita* teaches: *v'innitem et nafshoteichem b'tish'a lachodesh* — you shall afflict your souls on the ninth of the month. But surely we fast on the tenth, not the ninth? The *Gemara* derives: *kol ha'ochel v'shoteh b'tish'a bo*, one who eats and drinks on the ninth — on *erev Yom Kippur* — it is counted as though one had fasted both the ninth and the tenth.

Several explanations are offered for this striking formulation. One approach: since one cannot observe *simchat Yom Tov* and *kavod Yom Tov* on *Yom Kippur* itself, those observances are displaced to *erev Yom Kippur*, which is why people set a festive table and make a proper meal on that day. A second approach, consistent with the Rambam's understanding of the purpose of the *Yom Kippur* fast — that it is not meant as self-affliction but as a day of complete separation from the physical — suggests that one eats on the ninth precisely so that the fast does not become an act of undue hardship; the fasting would then be done for the right reasons rather than as a form of self-flagellation.

A third approach parallels the argument made regarding *Shavuot*: on the day that is entirely devoted to divorcing oneself from the physical world, it is equally important, on the day before, to demonstrate that serving God through *achila u'shtiya* is no less an act of *avodah*. It is genuinely challenging to experience eating as *avodas Hashem* — but *davka* on *erev Yom Kippur*, when the following day will be entirely about cessation from the physical, we are called upon to demonstrate that serving God in our embodied, eating-and-drinking lives is also *mitzvah*. There is a story of an elderly rabbi, a *talmid* of the Chofetz Chaim who had survived the *Mir Yeshiva*'s years in Shanghai, who in his nineties was told by his doctor that he could no longer fast on *Yom Kippur*. He was devastated. The doctor said to him: the same way you served God all these years by fasting on *Yom Kippur*, now you will serve God by eating on *Yom Kippur*. A profound formulation of the same principle.

### Ninth vs. Tenth

The Rav offers an additional explanation for the emphasis on eating on the ninth: it serves to make a demonstrative distinction between the ninth and the tenth. Just as we do not blow *shofar* on *erev Rosh Hashana* so as to mark the distinction between the day before and the *Yom Tov* itself, similarly eating robustly on the ninth creates a clear demarcation from the fast of the tenth. This connects as well to the *Rashi*-influenced reading that just as by *Atzeret* we demonstrate our joy at having received the *Torah*, so on *erev Yom Kippur* the eating expresses the *rishuma de'chapara* — the imprint of the atonement that is coming. Indeed, the *Gemara* elsewhere teaches *lo hayu yamim tovim b'Yisrael k'chamisha asar b'Av u'k'Yom HaKippurim* — no days were as joyous for Israel as the fifteenth of Av and *Yom Kippur*, which is *yom slicha u'mechila u'chapara*. Since that joy cannot be expressed on *Yom Kippur* itself, it finds its expression on *erev Yom Kippur*.

---

## Egla Talita

### Yosef's Feast

The *Gemara* relates that Rav Yosef, on *Shavuot*, would instruct his household: *avdi li egla tlata* — make for me a choice calf. The *egla tlata* was a particularly fine and luxurious dish, reserved for occasions of genuine celebration. And he would explain his reasoning: *ei lav hai yoma d'ka garim, kama Yosef ika b'shuka* — were it not for this day that brought about everything it brought about, there would be plenty of Josephs in the marketplace. Meaning: without *yom shenitna bo Torah*, without the day the *Torah* was given and the world it created, he would be just another unremarkable person. It is the *Torah* and the day it was given that gives his life its entire meaning and religious purpose. Therefore, on this day above all, he expresses profound *simcha*.

### Sheshet's Joy

A parallel story is told of Rav Sheshet, whose regimen was to review all of his learning every thirty days — *kol taltin yomin mahader lei letalmudei* — and then go stand by the river bank and say: *chadai nafshai chadai nafshai* — my soul rejoices, my soul is glad. *Lach karai, lach tanai* — for you have I studied *mikra*, for you have I learned *mishna* and the rabbinic corpus. What Rav Sheshet is expressing is the profound personal pleasure he takes in his *Torah* learning — a joy so complete that it finds expression in this outburst of personal delight.

### Torah's Role

The *Gemara* challenges this: *ini*? Is that really so — that one takes personal pleasure in one's learning as if for oneself? Did not Rav Elazar teach: *ilmalei Torah lo nitkaymu shamayim va'aretz* — were it not for *Torah*, the heavens and earth would not be sustained? As the verse says, *im lo briti yomam valaila, chukot shamayim va'aretz lo shamti* — were it not for my covenant of day and night, I would not have established the laws of heaven and earth. Torah keeps the world going. It is not about personal pleasure; it is about God and the cosmos. So what is this sense of private joy and personal satisfaction?

### Personal Investment

The *Gemara* responds: *meikara ki avid inish ada'ata denafshei ka'avid* — initially, when a person throws himself into something, he does it based on his own *da'at*, his own mind, his own personal investment. What drives people initially into a life of *Torah* is not a philosophical understanding of *chukot shamayim va'aretz*; it is personal resonance, personal pleasure, the sense that this speaks to me. The joy of a *rebbe* who approaches learning with delight and enthusiasm; the experience of *Torah sha'ashua* — Torah as a source of pleasure and play — these are what generate the initial love and investment. Obviously one comes to understand, over time, that there is an infinitely larger dimension — *chukot shamayim va'aretz lo shamti* — but the personal investment is what motivates and sustains the engagement from the outset.

### Joy Expression

These two stories together illustrate something important: the greatest *talmidei chachamim* experienced their *Torah* learning as a source of profound personal joy, and that joy translated into the full expression of *simcha* — including its physical dimension. The *ba'inan nami lachem*, the requirement that even on *Shavuot* there be physical celebration, is not merely a concession to human nature. It is the full expression of what *simcha* looks like when a person's *Torah* life is genuinely one of joy and love.

---

## Eliezer's Position

### Machshirei Argument

The *Gemara* now returns to the substantive halachic dispute with which the daf opened. Rav Ashi clarifies: even according to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that cooking on *Yom Tov* is a *reshut*, one could challenge his position from a different direction. Even granting that cooking is a *reshut*, on *Yom Tov* one may perform *melacha* for the *reshut* purpose of cooking — and yet *d'rabanans* that could have been done beforehand are not permitted even to enable that cooking. If so: on Shabbat, where only *melacha* of *mitzvah* — such as the *korban Pesach* — is permitted, should it not be *a fortiori* that even the preparatory *d'rabanans* are prohibited? Rabbi Eliezer's response is that this *kal v'chomer* fails: it is true that Shabbat is more restrictive than *Yom Tov*, but what makes the *shevut* permissible here is that it is a *shevut d'mitzvah* — a rabbinic prohibition being overridden for the sake of a *mitzvah*. And *shevus d'mitzvah adif lei* — the weight of a *shevut* being performed for the sake of a *mitzvah* is sufficiently powerful to override even Shabbat.

A *baraita* then elaborates Rabbi Eliezer's position directly. Rabbi Eliezer reasons: *uma im docha machshirei mitzvah she-le'achar shechita et ha-Shabbat* — if preparatory acts performed *after* the *shechita* override Shabbat, then certainly preparatory acts *before* the *shechita* should override Shabbat.

### Burning Fats

What are the *machshirei mitzvah* performed after *shechita* that override Shabbat? According to Tosafot, this refers to burning the *chalavim* — the fats — of the *korban Pesach* on Shabbat itself. One could theoretically wait until *motzei Shabbat* to burn the fats — the *korban* has already been brought, the *mitzvah* in its essential form is done — and yet we permit burning the fats on Shabbat. If even these post-*shechita* acts override Shabbat despite being deferrable, then *a fortiori*, the pre-*shechita* acts that are necessary to *enable* the bringing of the *korban Pesach* — removing a *mum*, carrying the animal — should certainly override. This is the logical structure of Rabbi Eliezer's argument.

---

## Haza'ah Proof

### Haza'ah Prohibited

Rabbi Akiva responds with a counter-proof. He invokes *haza'ah* — the sprinkling of purification waters — for a *tamei meit* whose seventh day of *tumah* falls on Shabbat which is *erev Pesach*. This is a person who, without *haza'ah*, cannot become *tahor* in time to bring the *korban Pesach*. The *haza'ah* itself is only *d'rabanan* — it is a *shevut*. And yet everyone agrees: *haza'ah* is not performed on Shabbat even to enable the *korban Pesach*.

### Act vs. Preparation

Here is Rabbi Akiva's logic. Rabbi Eliezer argues that things enabling the *korban* should be permitted because they remove obstacles to the *mitzvah*. But Rabbi Akiva draws a categorical distinction: it is the *shechita* itself — the *hakrava* of the *korban* — that overrides Shabbat, not the enabling of one's personal obligation to bring it. Once the *shechita* has overridden Shabbat, everything flowing from that act — the post-*shechita* activities — is carried along in the same *hetter*. But before the *shechita* has overridden Shabbat, there is no basis to override preparatory acts, because it is not your personal need to be in a position to bring the *korban* that does the overriding — it is the act of *hakrava* itself. One should not confuse the two.

There is something genuinely attractive about Rabbi Eliezer's position — the idea that if the *mitzvah* obligation overrides, everything standing in the way of its fulfillment should yield. Nevertheless, we do not *pasken* like him.

### Psul Concern

A second counter-argument is introduced: *shema yimatzei zevach pasul v'nimtza mechallel Shabbat l'mafrei'a* — perhaps the *shechita* will turn out to be invalid, and then everything done beforehand to enable it will retroactively be a *chilul Shabbat* without justification. The *Gemara* immediately rejects this concern on logical grounds: by that reasoning, one should not perform the *shechita* at all, since it too might be *pasul*. Clearly, we do not void a *hetter* due to the mere possibility of *psul*. The *Gemara* notes that this weaker argument was recorded first, and the stronger argument — Rabbi Akiva's categorical distinction — came second, even though in the actual exchange it was the first argument given. The written version records the more powerful reasoning first.

### Eliezer's Response

Rabbi Eliezer responds to Rabbi Akiva: the case of *haza'ah* is different from all the other *machshirei mitzvah*. He acknowledges the question but maintains that *haza'ah* falls into a separate category — it is not simply a *shevut d'mitzvah* comparable to carrying the *korban* or removing a *mum*. As we will see, his exact reasoning for distinguishing *haza'ah* becomes the subject of sustained *Gemara* analysis.

---

## Akiva Reminds

### Inverse Logic

A *baraita* records the following exchange in greater detail. Rabbi Akiva offers what sounds at first like a foolish argument: just as *haza'ah* does not override Shabbat, so too *shechita* should not override Shabbat. Rabbi Eliezer responds indignantly: obviously *shechita* overrides — it says *bemo'ado*, implying even on Shabbat. He dismisses the comparison in sharp terms: *bishchita heshivatani, bishchita tehei mitato* — you challenge me with *shechita*? Your argument will be slain by *shechita*. The response is mock-contemptuous: it is self-evident that *shechita* overrides; the argument is absurd.

### Akiva's Tradition

Rabbi Akiva then reveals what he was actually doing. He says to Rabbi Eliezer: *Rebbi*, do not dismiss me in the middle of a legal argument — *al tikpacheini bishat hadin*. Do you really want to engage me head-on? Because *kach mekublani mimcha* — this is a tradition I received *from you*: *haza'ah shevut v'einah dochah et ha-Shabbat* — *haza'ah* is a *shevut* and it does not override Shabbat.

The structure of Rabbi Akiva's argument is now clear. By saying something apparently foolish — that *shechita* should not override just as *haza'ah* does not — he was not actually making a logical argument. He was signaling that he was treating the prohibition of *haza'ah* on Shabbat as axiomatic. What you hear when he makes that argument is: I am taking it as given — as a first principle — that *haza'ah* does not override. So certain was he of this that he built it into the premise of an *a fortiori* argument, not as a conclusion to be argued, but as something too obvious to require proof. And the reason he was so certain is that Rabbi Eliezer himself had transmitted this tradition to him.

### Eliezer Forgot

The *Gemara* asks: but if Rabbi Eliezer himself taught Rabbi Akiva that *haza'ah* does not override Shabbat, why was Rabbi Eliezer now backtracking, challenging the principle, and suggesting that perhaps one *would* do *haza'ah* for the *korban Pesach*? Ulla initially offers a reinterpretation: perhaps the tradition Rabbi Eliezer had transmitted concerned only *haza'ah* for the purpose of eating *terumah*, not *haza'ah* for the *korban Pesach* — and Rabbi Akiva had misunderstood. On this reading, they were simply talking past each other.

But Rava rejects this reading. He cites the *baraita* explicitly: *hazat tmei meis tochaich, shechal shvi'i shelo lihyot be'Shabbat u've'erev Pesach* — the *haza'ah* for a *tamei meit*, whose seventh day falls on Shabbat which is *erev Pesach* — that is the explicit case in which, despite it being a *mitzvah* and only a *shevut*, it does not override Shabbat. This is unambiguously about the *korban Pesach*, not about *terumah*. So *ella vadai haza'ah d'Pesach agmrei* — clearly the tradition Rabbi Eliezer transmitted to Rabbi Akiva was precisely this case. And yet Rabbi Eliezer was now challenging it.

The *Gemara* concludes: *Rabbi Eliezer gmara itaker leh* — Rabbi Eliezer forgot. He was ill or aged, and the tradition had slipped from him. *V'ata Rabbi Akiva l'azkurei gmareh* — Rabbi Akiva came to remind him of his own teaching. But he could not do so directly, for *lav orach ara* — it is not *derech eretz* to tell one's teacher to his face that he has forgotten. So Rabbi Akiva reminded him indirectly, by making a statement so bizarre in its apparent logic — you can't do *shechita*! — that Rabbi Eliezer would hear from it: this student is treating the non-overriding of *haza'ah* as so axiomatic that he is prepared to make an absurd argument from it. And perhaps Rabbi Eliezer would then recall: yes, I did teach him that.

### Mesorah Irony

There is a striking and beautiful irony here. Rabbi Eliezer is described elsewhere as a *bor sud she'eino me'abeid tipah* — a plastered cistern that loses not a drop. He is the consummate guardian of received tradition; his entire *Torah* persona is organized around the faithful transmission of the *mesorah*. And it is precisely him who forgets — and it is Rabbi Akiva, the master of analysis and intellectual creativity, who restores the lost tradition to its rightful owner. The one who prided himself on never having said a word he did not receive from his teachers needed his student to give him back his own *Torah*.

---

## Obligation Status

### Tiltul Question

Having established that *haza'ah* does not override Shabbat even for the *korban Pesach*, the *Gemara* asks a more fundamental question: why can't one simply do *haza'ah* on Shabbat in general? After all, *haza'ah* is *tiltul be'alma* — it is merely moving water from one place to another. What makes it a *shevut* of such weight that it cannot be overridden for the *korban Pesach*?

### Carrying Concern

Rava provides his standard answer: *gezeirah shema yitlena v'ya'virena arba amot bi'reshut ha'rabim* — a rabbinic decree lest one pick up the water and carry it four *amot* in the public domain. This is the same reasoning Rava applies to explain why one does not blow *shofar* on Shabbat and why one does not take *lulav* on Shabbat — practices already codified in the *Mishnah* whose original reasoning may not have been this concern about carrying, but which Rava consistently explains through this lens. The fear of incidental carrying thus explains why *haza'ah* was given the status of a significant *shevut*.

But this raises the question for Rabbi Eliezer's position: if carrying would itself be *mutar* to enable the *korban Pesach* according to Rabbi Eliezer — since *machshirei mitzvah dochin et ha-Shabbat* — how could *Rava's* concern about carrying explain why even Rabbi Eliezer would prohibit *haza'ah*? The *Gemara* therefore must look for a different reason why *haza'ah* stands apart even for Rabbi Eliezer.

### Obligation Override

The answer emerges from a conceptual distinction: only those things that place a person in a state of *chiyuv* can override Shabbat. The *mitzvat korban Pesach* overrides Shabbat because one is *obligated* — and everything that is an obstacle to that obligated person performing the *mitzvah* can yield. But in the case of a *tamei meit* waiting for his seventh-day *haza'ah*, the person is not currently obligated to bring the *korban Pesach*. He could, by performing the *haza'ah*, put himself into the category of obligation — but right now, *gufei lo chazi*, he is not fit, and therefore *lo rami chiyuva alei*, the obligation is not upon him. Since his current status places him outside the sphere of *chiyuv*, he cannot invoke the principle that a *mitzvah* obligation overrides preparatory obstacles — because the obstacle is not in the way of his *chiyuv*; the obstacle is what stands between him and *having* a *chiyuv* at all.

### Infant Milah

Rabba draws out the logical implications of this principle with an application to *bris milah*. For a healthy infant on the eighth day, one may heat water to prepare him for the *milah* on Shabbat — *mechaminin lo chamim lehavroso u'lemolo be'Shabbat* — because *de'chazi lei katan*, the child is fit and the obligation is upon him; the hot water is merely an obstacle-removal for someone who is already obligated. For a sick infant, however, one may not heat up water to nurse him to health so that he can then receive the *milah* on Shabbat — *de'ha lo chazi lei*, right now he is not fit, and one cannot perform a *Shabbat* violation to bring someone *into* the category of obligation.

Rabba then challenges this distinction. In the case of the healthy infant, he asks: if he is so healthy, why does he need the hot water prepared for him at all — *lamah lei chamim lehavroso*? Rabba then resolves the difficulty: *akol cholim heim etzel milah* — all infants are considered ill relative to *milah*; even a healthy baby needs some preparation before he is genuinely fit for *bris milah*. But this actually *collapses* the distinction rather than preserving it. If even the healthy baby requires preparation before he is fit, then even the healthy baby is currently not fit — and by our principle, one cannot perform Shabbat violations to bring him into fitness. The conclusion is surprising: *echad katan bari v'echad choleh, ein mechaminin lo chamim lehavroso u'lemolo be'Shabbat* — whether the infant is healthy or sick, one does not heat water on Shabbat to prepare him for *milah*. One must prepare the water beforehand. This is a significant limitation even within Rabbi Eliezer's permissive approach: the permission to override Shabbat applies only when one is already obligated; it does not extend to actions that *generate* the obligation.

---

## Arel vs. Tamei

### Arel Karet

Abaye challenges this framework with a sharp question. Rabbi Eliezer holds that an *arel* — an uncircumcised man who was capable of receiving a *bris milah* — is liable for *karet* if he fails to bring the *korban Pesach* on *erev Pesach*. He could have found a *mohel*, undergone *bris milah* that day, and brought his *korban*. His failure to do so is culpable, and he receives *karet*. But one can only be liable for *karet* if one is *obligated* to bring the *korban Pesach*. If the principle we established says that someone who is currently not fit — like the *tamei meit* before *haza'ah* — is not considered obligated, then the *arel*, who currently cannot eat the *korban* and is therefore not fully fit, should also not be considered obligated. How then can he be liable for *karet*?

### Tumah Hutra

Rava responds: *arlus* and *tumah* are fundamentally different categories, and the difference is rooted in the principle of *tumah hutra b'tzibur*. For *arlus*, there is no such principle. If the entire *tzibur* were *arelim*, we would not say that they may bring the *korban* in a state of *arlus* — we would say *kumu mehul*, go circumcise yourselves. There is no *arlus hutra b'tzibur*. Therefore, our basic approach to *arlus* is: you are obligated, and *arlus* is an obstacle — go remove the obstacle. The obligation is upon you, the *arlus* stands in the way, and you must deal with it. This is why an *arel* who fails to address the obstacle is *chayav karet*.

For *tumah*, however, the principle of *tumah hutra b'tzibur* means that our fundamental approach to the *tzibur* in a state of *tumah* is not to insist they become *tahor* — it is to permit them to bring the *korban* in their current state. This fundamentally reframes the nature of *tumah* relative to the *korban*: it is not simply an obstacle to be removed before one can be obligated; it is a state that may in some circumstances be accommodated.

### Tzibur Principle

The *tzibur* principle reshapes the *yachid* case as well. *V'chol milsa d'leisa b'tzibur leisa b'yachid* — whatever is not demanded of the *tzibur* is not demanded of the *yachid* either. Since we would not insist that the *tzibur* become *tahor* if they are all *tamei* — we would invoke *tumah hutra b'tzibur* and let them bring the *korban* in their state — we similarly do not insist that the *yachid* who is *tamei* become *tahor* before bringing his *korban*. His *tumah* is, in effect, accommodated. He is redirected to *Pesach Sheni*, but he is not considered presently obligated in the same way the *arel* is. And since he is not presently obligated in the same categorical way, there is no basis for overriding Shabbat to enable his *haza'ah*.

---

## Braitah Proof

### Both Liable

A *baraita* is cited to challenge this framework: *yachol lo yei'einosh karet ella she'hayah tahor v'she'lo hayah b'derech rechokah* — one might think that only someone who was *tahor* and not far away is subject to *karet* for failing to bring the *korban Pesach*. *Arel u'tmei sheretz u'she'ar kol ha'tmei'im minayin* — from where do we know that even an *arel*, even someone *tamei* from contact with a *sheretz*, and all other *tmei'im* who could have corrected their status — are liable? The *baraita* derives it from a verse — *ve'ha'ish* — which broadens the category. The implication is clear: both the *arel* and the *tmei sheretz* are considered *obligated*, and their inability to currently bring the *korban* is treated as an obstacle they were required to remove.

### Status Fix

This *baraita* appears to demonstrate that even someone in a state of *tumah* — someone who could have jumped into the *mikvah* that day and become *tahor* — is considered *chayav* and must fix his status. This challenges the claim that *tumah* places a person outside the category of obligation. If the *tmei sheretz* is considered obligated and subject to *karet*, he seems to be in the same position as the *arel* — obligated, with an obstacle, required to address it.

---

## Braitah Proof (II)

### Sheretz Alternative

Rava, however, reinterprets the *baraita*. He argues that the *baraita* actually presupposes that one cannot bring the *korban Pesach* for a *tmei sheretz* in his current state — *ein shochtin v'zorkin al tmei sheretz* — meaning that the *baraita* is treating his situation as parallel to the *arel*: he is obligated, he has an obstacle, and he must remove it. The *baraita* is not describing the generally accepted *halacha* for *tumah*; rather, it is establishing that even in this case where his state prevents the bringing of the *korban*, the obligation still rests upon him.

---

## Final Answer

### Tamei Yotzei

Rava now articulates a complete reorientation. Rabbi Eliezer actually holds *shochtin v'zorkin al tmei sheretz* — one *does* bring the *korban Pesach* on behalf of a person who is *tamei* from *sheretz*, even before he has gone to the *mikvah*. And similarly, *ve'hu ha'din le'tmei meit be'shivii shelo* — the same applies to a *tamei meit* on his seventh day. Even without having done *haza'ah*, the *korban* may be brought for him.

### Eating Optional

This completely inverts the earlier analysis. The earlier framework assumed that *haza'ah* is prohibited because the person is too far outside the category of obligation. Rava now says the opposite: the reason *haza'ah* is not done is that it is *unnecessary*. The person is so thoroughly within the category — the *korban* can be brought for him even in his current state — that the only reason he would ever need *haza'ah* is so that he can *eat* the *korban* that night. And on this point, *achilat pesachim lo me'akva* — eating the *korban Pesach* is not indispensable. One can be *yotzei* the *mitzvah* of *korban Pesach* without eating it, at least in circumstances such as this. Therefore, since *haza'ah* is needed only to enable eating, and eating is not strictly required, there is no basis to permit *haza'ah* on Shabbat even according to Rabbi Eliezer. Not because he is too *outside* the obligation — but because he is already so *inside* it that *haza'ah* adds nothing to the core *mitzvah*.

### Shelo Lochlav

Rav Adda bar Ahava raises an objection to Rava: if a person cannot eat the *korban* — because he has not yet done *haza'ah* and remains *tamei* — then the *shechita* was performed *shelo le-ochlav*, for one who cannot eat it, which is a *psul* that invalidates the *korban*.

### Theoretical Fitness

Rava responds: *shelo le-ochlav* refers to cases like a *choleh* or *zaken* — someone who is truly unable to eat, whose incapacity is fixed or at least not immediately remediable. *Aval hai*, this *tamei* person — *mechazi chazi*, he is theoretically fit. His inability to eat is not an intrinsic incapacity; it is merely the result of his not having taken the available steps to make himself fit — *tikunei hu delo metaken*. Since in principle he is capable of eating, he retains his status as a theoretical *ochal*, and the *shechita* is not *shelo le-ochlav*. The *korban* is valid.

The same reasoning would presumably apply to an *arel* as well — since he could theoretically have had a *bris milah*, he too would be considered a theoretical *ochal* rather than someone who falls into the category of *shelo le-ochlav*. This final resolution thus redraws the entire landscape of who is considered *fit* and who is not: fitness is determined not by one's current state but by one's theoretical capacity. And it is this theoretical fitness — not any achieved status — that keeps a person within the frame of the *mitzvah*.

---

---

# Pesachim 70

## Prep Acts Debate

### Tumah Recap

Today's *daf* is 70. We pick up on 69b, just before the *mishnah* of *klal amar Rabbi Akiva*. The previous discussion had centered on the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua concerning whether *de'oraita* acts — and even *derabbanan* acts — that could have been performed the day before, yet now stand as obstacles to the *Korban Pesach*, may be carried out on Shabbat. Rabbi Eliezer permits this, both for *Pesach* and for *milah*, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva do not.

The *Gemara* had just concluded by noting that even according to Rabbi Eliezer's tradition — which he himself had forgotten — *haza'ah*, the sprinkling of the ashes of the *Parah Adumah*, was the one act he would not permit. Two reasons had been offered: the first, ultimately rejected, was that the *tamei* person has fallen so far outside the category of obligation that he cannot perform acts necessary to become obligated. The second, and more striking, was the radical possibility that a person who is *tamei* for only a single day — and who will therefore become *tahor* by evening — can have a *Korban Pesach* brought on his behalf even if he does not ultimately eat it. His obligation of bringing the *korban* is thereby fulfilled even in his *tamei* state, and there is consequently no warrant to perform any violation on his behalf. This is a quite fascinating and radical conclusion: that someone who theoretically could be *tahor* that evening can be *yotzei* through the *Pesach* being brought for him, even if he does not in the end become *tahor* and does not eat it.

### Akiva's Principle

We now turn to the opposing opinion and the question of *p'sak*. The *mishnah* states: *klal amar Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva articulated a general principle: anything that could have been done the day before cannot override Shabbat today. It should be emphasized that *haza'ah*, while it technically cannot be performed the day before, is nevertheless not mandated to be done specifically today. It is therefore not merely the question of whether something could have been done earlier; the operative principle is whether there is an affirmative mandate to perform it today. Since no such mandate exists for *haza'ah*, it does not override Shabbat even if it is an obstacle to bringing the *korban*.

The same debate is recorded in the context of *milah*. Rabbi Akiva states there as well: *kol melachah she'efshar la'asotah me'erev shabbat einah dochah et hashabbat* — any act that could have been performed before Shabbat does not override Shabbat. Even if, for example, no *mohel* was available and one became available only on Shabbat in a neighboring city, the fact that the *milah* does not carry a mandate to be performed specifically today means that traveling to fetch him — even though it prevents the *milah* — may not be done on Shabbat. On the other hand, *milah she-iy efshar la'asotah me'erev shabbat* — a circumcision that could not have been performed before Shabbat and that is mandated to be performed today — does override Shabbat.

### Rav's Ruling

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav ruled, on 69b, *halachah k'Rabbi Akiva* — we rule like Rabbi Akiva. One may perform the act of *milah* or the slaughter of the *Pesach* on Shabbat, but not the preparatory acts that serve as obstacles to those acts.

### Two Rulings Needed

*V'tzricha*: it was necessary to state this ruling in both contexts. Had the ruling been stated only for *Pesach*, one might have said that it was only there that Rabbi Akiva applied his principle, since preparatory acts do not override Shabbat — *mishum d'lo nichretu aleha shelosh-esrei britot* — because *Pesach*, for all its stringencies, is not the subject of a *brit*, a covenant, repeated thirteen times, as is the case with *brit milah*. Perhaps *milah*, with its thirteen covenants sealed upon it, carries greater weight and would permit a broader override. Conversely, had the ruling been stated only for *milah*, one might have inferred that it was only there that preparatory acts are restricted, since there is no *karet* for failing to perform *milah* specifically today — whereas *Pesach* carries *karet* for non-performance today, and one might therefore have thought it should override. Hence both rulings are necessary.

### 13 Covenants

The argument that thirteen covenants ought to carry halachic weight — to the point of determining whether one may override Shabbat — might seem more in the realm of *aggadata* than of technical *halachah*. Indeed, Tosafot explains that what is at stake is the *derabbanan* dimension of the override, where there is somewhat more discretion as to whether we permit it or not. On that level, the additional weight of thirteen covenants might have tipped the balance differently for *milah* than for *Pesach*. Tosafot therefore understands these considerations as bearing on the *derabbanan* question and not on overriding a *de'oraita* prohibition. The word *brit* appears thirteen times in the *parashah* of the covenant with Abraham — *ve'et brisi tishmor*, *zot brisi asher tishmeru*, *vehayesah le'os bris beini uveineichem* — and if one counts them, indeed thirteen instances of the word appear, underscoring the depth of that covenant.

---

## Chagigah Overview

### Chagigah Definition

Having concluded the discussion of preparatory acts, the *Gemara* turns to other aspects of bringing the *Korban Pesach*, and specifically to the *chagigah*. There is ordinarily a *chagigah* brought on *Yom Tov*. When the Torah states *vechagosem oto chag la'Hashem shivat yamim bashana*, the word *chag* according to the Sages does not simply mean to celebrate: it refers to a *korban* classified as a *Korban Chagigah*, which is a *shelamim* specifically designated as such. This is how one fulfills *vechagosem oto chag* — by bringing a *Korban Chagigah*. Ordinarily it should be brought on the first day of *Yom Tov*, but if not brought then, it may be brought on any of the remaining days of the festival.

### Chagigat 14th

By *Pesach*, however, there is a specific institution known as *chagigat arba'ah asar* — a *Korban Chagigah* brought on *Erev Pesach*, the fourteenth of Nisan. As we shall see in the *Gemara*, this is derived from the verse *zevach chag hapesach* — a *zevach* of the *chag* accompanies the *Pesach*. The word *chag* in the idiom of the Sages denotes a *Korban Chagigah* that comes together with the *Korban Pesach*.

### Al HaSova

There is a debate in the *Gemara* as to whether there is a genuine obligation to bring this *chagigah* at all. According to some, it is not strictly obligatory; it is brought in order to fulfill the concept that the *Pesach* must be eaten *al hasova* — while one is already satiated. This connects to the institution of the *afikoman*, which for some authorities is the eating that most directly represents the *Korban Pesach*: not the earlier eating of *matzah*, which fulfills *mitzvas matzah*, but the eating that comes at the end of the *seder*, after one is already full. How does one become full? There may not be sufficient meat from the *Pesach* itself, depending on the size of the group relative to the animal. One therefore eats a substantial meal first — the meat of the *Korban Chagigah* — and then eats the *Pesach* at the end, *al hasova*, when already sated. According to this view, there is no strict obligation to bring the *chagigah*; it is appropriate when and if necessary so that the *Korban Pesach* is eaten *al hasova*.

Other opinions hold that there is an independent *chiyuv* to bring the *chagigah* regardless of these considerations. We will see that debate unfold through the *pesukim* and their interpretation.

---

## Mishnah Parameters

### When Brought

The *mishnah* asks: *eimasai mevi'in chagigah imo* — when does one bring a *chagigah* together with the *Korban Pesach*? The *mishnah* specifies conditions, reflecting the view that it is not strictly obligatory:

*Bizman shehu ba bechol* — when the *Pesach* falls on a weekday; *betahara* — when the people are in a state of *taharah*; and *u'b'muat* — when the portion of meat from the *Pesach* is small relative to the number of people in the group. It is worth noting that "small" here means a small amount of meat per person — a large group sharing a single animal — and not a small group. In that case, the meat of the *chagigah* is needed to supplement what each person receives from the *Pesach*.

### When Not Brought

Correspondingly, the *mishnah* states that when the *Pesach* falls on Shabbat, or when the portions are large, or when the people are *tamei*, one does not bring the *chagigah*. Just as *Pesach* overrides Shabbat, and similarly overrides *tumah*, the *chagigah* overrides neither. The ordinary *halachah* is that a *korban* is not brought in a state of *tumah*, and so if the community is *tamei* and brings the *Pesach* in *tumah*, the *chagigah* does not follow. Any one of these conditions — Shabbat, *tumah*, or a large portion of meat — is sufficient to preclude bringing the *chagigah*.

### Chagigah Properties

The *mishnah* continues to distinguish the *chagigah* from the *Pesach* in its very nature. The *chagigah* may come *min hatzon* from sheep, or *min habakar* from cattle — cattle being a more practical option for feeding a large group. Furthermore, it may come *min hazacharim u'min hanekevot* — from both males and females — which is explicitly not the case for the *Korban Pesach*, which is restricted to males.

### Eating Rules

The *chagigah* is eaten *ne'echelet l'shnei yamim v'layla echad* — for two days and the intervening night, like a standard *shelamim*. This contrasts sharply with the *Korban Pesach*, which must be consumed entirely that night, as derived from the verse *v'lo yalin min habasar* — none of the flesh shall remain until morning. As we shall see, there is an opinion that departs sharply from all of this.

---

## Why Discuss

### Context

The *Gemara* asks: *man tanna, mai ta'ama d'katani chagigah* — what is the *tanna*'s context for discussing the *chagigah* here? The *mishnah* plunges directly into a discussion of when the *chagigah* is and is not brought, without first establishing that such a *chagigah* exists at all. The answer offered by the *Gemara* is that the preceding discussion established that certain preparatory acts do not override Shabbat. The *mishnah* therefore transitions naturally to another item that also does not override Shabbat — the *chagigah* — and that is how one discussion led to the other. The *mishnah* is, in effect, parenthetically noting: there is also a *chagigah* that does not override Shabbat, and here are the conditions under which it is brought.

### Not Obligatory

Rav Ashi draws a significant conclusion from the structure of the *mishnah*: *shma mina* — we learn from this that *chagigat arba'ah asar lav chovah hi* — the *chagigah* of the fourteenth is not a strict obligation. It is brought to serve the function of *ne'echal al hasova*, but there is no absolute requirement to bring it. The proof is decisive: *d'ee salka da'atach chovah hi* — if you thought it were a strict obligation, *teitei b'Shabbat* — it should be brought on Shabbat, as any *korban* with a fixed time overrides Shabbat. *V'teitei b'merubeh* — it should be brought even when the portions are large, since an obligation is an obligation. *V'teitei b'tumah* — it should be brought even in a state of *tumah*, as any *korban* with a fixed time and a strict obligation is brought even in *tumah*. Since all of these exceptions apply, the *chagigah* clearly is not a strict obligation.

The *Gemara* then asks: granted that it is optional and therefore does not come on Shabbat or in *tumah* — but what is the connection to the amount of meat? The answer comes from a *braisa*: *chagigas haba im hapesach ne'echeles techila kidei sheyehei hapesach ne'echeles al hasova* — the *chagigah* that accompanies the *Pesach* is eaten first, so that the *Pesach* is eaten while one is already full. The *Gemara* understands this *braisa* as revealing the entire rationale for bringing the *chagigah*: it is brought not because of an independent obligation but solely so that the *Korban Pesach* is eaten *al hasova*.

---

## Chagigah Overview (II)

### Full Eating

One might ask: if the goal is simply to be full when eating the *Pesach*, why not simply bring sandwiches? Why must this be done in the context of a *korban* at all? The answer is that there is indeed some concept of a *chagigah*, but not a strictly obligatory one — it occupies a middle ground where the form of a *korban* is appropriate, but no absolute mandate exists.

Two reasons are given for the requirement of eating the *Pesach al hasova*. The first is symbolic: one should not eat the *Pesach* in a state of ravenous hunger, as though eating simply to satisfy one's appetite. The *Pesach* is eaten for its symbolic and religious significance. There is an interesting balance here — one is not supposed to eat excessively before *Erev Pesach* and must approach the *seder* with some appetite, yet one must not arrive at the *Korban Pesach* famished. The *Pesach* is eaten with desire but not desperation.

The second reason is offered in the *Yerushalmi* and endorsed by Tosafot as a genuinely rabbinic concern: there is a prohibition against breaking the bones of the *Korban Pesach*. If a person is truly hungry while eating the *Pesach*, the temptation to crack the bones and suck out the marrow becomes very real. One must therefore arrive at the *Pesach* already sated, so that there is no *yetzer hara* to break the bones — a far more technical, practical concern. Both reasons reflect the importance of the *chagigah*'s role, even within the framework of a non-obligatory *korban*.

---

## Ben Teima View

### Identical to Pesach

Having established the position of our *mishnah* — which treats the *chagigah* as independent from and considerably more lenient than the *Korban Pesach* — the *Gemara* announces: *matnisin delo ke'Ben Teima* — our *mishnah* does not follow Ben Teima.

*Detanya*: Ben Teima says in a *braisa* that *chagigah haba'ah im hapesach harei hi ke'Pesach* — the *chagigah* that accompanies the *Pesach* is treated exactly like the *Pesach* itself. It may be eaten only *leyom velailah* — the day and the following night — and may not be eaten the next morning. There is a subtle question worth noting here: the *Korban Pesach* itself is brought on the fourteenth but not eaten until the night of the fifteenth. If so, when Ben Teima says *yom velailah*, does he mean the night of the fifteenth only, or might the *chagigah* actually be eaten beginning on the fourteenth? That question deserves attention and was not resolved here.

Ben Teima continues: *vachagigas chamisha asar ne'echeles lishnei yamim velayla echad* — the *chagigah* of the fifteenth, the standard *Yom Tov chagigah*, is eaten for two days and the intervening night, as normal. And regarding the *chagigah* of the fourteenth: *yotzei bah mishum simcha ve'ein yotzei bah mishum chagigah* — one fulfills one's obligation of *simcha* through it, but not one's obligation of the standard *chagigah* of the festival.

The meaning of this last clause requires clarification, and the *Gemara* understands it differently from what might seem to be the straightforward reading. One might have thought Ben Teima is saying that eating the *chagigah* meat on the *leil haseder* satisfies *mitzvas simcha* but cannot substitute for the *chagigah* of the fifteenth. The *Gemara*, however, understands the case differently: the animal was sanctified for *chagigat arba'ah asar* but was not brought on the fourteenth. The owner now wishes to bring it on the fifteenth. In that case, it may function as *shalmei simcha* — animals sanctified for one purpose may be brought on *Yom Tov* and used to fulfill *mitzvas simcha* — but it cannot fulfill the obligation of *chagigat hachag*, which requires an animal sanctified specifically for that purpose, not one previously designated for another *korban*.

### Baraita Proof

What is Ben Teima's reasoning? *Ki dematni Rav Chiyya bar Abba* — as Rav taught his son Chiyya: the verse states *lo yalin laboker zevach chag hapesach* — the offering of the *chag* of the *Pesach* shall not remain until morning. The verse contains both the word *chag* and the word *pesach*: as Dov correctly noted, *zevach chag* refers to the *chagigah*, and the Torah instructs that this too — like the *Pesach* itself — may not remain until morning. Ben Teima thus learns from this verse that the *chagigah haba'ah im hapesach* is in all respects like the *Pesach*: it is a strict obligation and may be eaten only that night.

### Questions

The *Gemara* then poses a series of questions: according to Ben Teima, can the *chagigah* come from cattle, or only from sheep? Can it come from female animals? Can it be older than one year, as the *Pesach* is limited to its first year of life?

### Roasted Only

The *Gemara* addresses the question of roasting. It asks: *le'Ben Teima ne'echelet tzali o ne'echelet tzali* — must the *chagigah* be eaten specifically roasted, as the *Pesach* must be? Perhaps the verse connects it to the *Pesach* only for the *halachah* of not remaining until morning — that being related to the act of eating — but not for the manner of preparation. Or perhaps *chag hapesach* means the *chag* and the *Pesach* are entirely assimilated, and all the *halachot* of the *Pesach* apply. *Ta shema*: the *mishnah* elsewhere records among the four questions the phrase *halailah hazeh kulo tzali* — on this night everything is roasted. Rav Chisda explains: *zu divrei Ben Teima* — this question is formulated according to Ben Teima's view. This serves as a clear proof that according to Ben Teima the *chagigah* must also be eaten roasted.

### Full Requirements

A *braisa* settles the broader questions decisively: *chagigah haba'ah im hapesach harei hi ke'Pesach* — the *chagigah* is entirely like the *Pesach*. *Ba'ah min hatzon ve'eina ba'ah min habakar* — it comes from sheep and not from cattle, just like the *Pesach*. *Ba'ah min hazacharim ve'eina ba'ah min hanekevot* — from males and not females. *Ba'ah bas shnatah ve'eina ba'ah bas shtei shanim* — it must be within its first year and cannot be in its second year. *Ve'eina ne'echelet ela leyom velailah* — it may be eaten only day and night. *Ve'eina ne'echelet ela tzli* — it may only be eaten roasted. *Ve'eina ne'echelet ela leminuyav* — it may only be eaten by those who have been formally enrolled in its group, exactly as one must be enrolled for the *Korban Pesach*.

The *Gemara* notes: *man shamsat leh d'is leh hai sevara* — who holds this entire position? Ben Teima. *Shma mina kulhu milamdinan* — and we see that Ben Teima takes the equation to its logical extreme: the *chagigah* must be identical to the *Pesach* in every particular.

This raises a striking question. If the *chagigah* must come from sheep, must be male, must be under a year old, must be eaten roasted, and must be eaten by enrolled members — how does one even distinguish experientially between the *chagigah* and the *Pesach*? Both animals look identical. One is brought before the other, but practically speaking, the only distinguishing features at the table would be the *matzah* and *maror* that accompany the *Pesach*. One might further ask: when is the *chagigah* slaughtered relative to the afternoon *Korban Tamid*? What is done with its blood? Does one group formation suffice for both, or must each have a separate enrollment? These questions, while not explicitly addressed in the *Gemara*, underscore just how far-reaching and in some ways challenging Ben Teima's position is in practice.

One could argue the opposite: rather than undermining the uniqueness of the *Pesach*, the identity of the *chagigah* with it serves to transform *Erev Pesach* into a kind of miniature *chag* — *chag haPesach* — emphasizing the festive dimension of the fourteenth itself. Already there are aspects of *Erev Pesach* that mark it as semi-sacred: restrictions on labor from midday, prohibition of *chametz* from midday, and according to Beit Shammai's view, even from the night before. The *chagigah* as an obligation identical to the *Pesach* fits naturally into this picture. But making the two animals practically indistinguishable pushes the equation further than one might expect.

---

## Bone-Breaking

### Bones Question

The *Gemara* now asks whether, according to Ben Teima, there is a prohibition of *sheviras etzem* — breaking bones — that applies to the *chagigah* as well. The verse states *kol etzem lo tishberu bo* — you shall not break any bone *bo*, in it, with the word *bo* being very specific. Perhaps *bo* limits the prohibition to the *Pesach* itself, not to the *chagigah*. Or perhaps *bo* means only that the prohibition applies to a valid *korban* and not to a *pasul* one — in which case it would apply equally to the *chagigah*.

### Knife/Cleaver

A *mishnah* is cited to explore this question. If one finds a *shechita* knife on the fourteenth of Nisan, one may use it immediately — one can assume it is *tahor*. The reasoning: in Jerusalem on *Erev Pesach*, everyone is preparing their *Korban Pesach* and has already immersed their utensils. Since a *kli* immersed in a *mikveh* requires nightfall to become fully *tahor*, anyone who needed a knife for *shechita* on the fourteenth would have immersed it on the thirteenth. Therefore a knife found on the fourteenth may be assumed to have been immersed the previous day and is now *tahor*.

If the knife is found on the thirteenth, however, one must immerse it again — or at least ensure it has been immersed — since the owner may not yet have done so, or may have dropped it on the way to the *mikveh*.

A *kofit* — a meat cleaver — is treated differently. Whether found on the thirteenth or the fourteenth, one must immerse it. Why? Because one does not need a cleaver for the *Korban Pesach* — one may not break bones, and the cleaver's function is to chop through meat and bone. At most, one would need a cleaver starting on the fifteenth of Nisan, when other *korbanot* are brought. A person planning to use the cleaver on *Yom Tov* would only need to immerse it by the fourteenth — not earlier — so finding it on the fourteenth provides no assurance that it has been immersed.

### Cleaver Use

The *Gemara* now asks: *mani* — whose position is this *mishnah* reflecting? If it reflects the view of the Rabbis — *rabanan* — then why do they not assume that the cleaver has been immersed because the owner would need it today for his *chagigah*? One can chop the meat of the *chagigah* with a cleaver even if one cannot use it on the *Pesach*! If so, by the reasoning that everyone prepares their slaughtering knife the day before, everyone should also have prepared their cleaver the day before for use on their *chagigah*. The only one who would have no need for a cleaver on the fourteenth would be Ben Teima — because according to Ben Teima, one cannot break the bones of the *chagigah* either, making the cleaver useless on the fourteenth just as it is useless for the *Pesach*. This appears to yield a compelling proof: *shma mina yesh bah mishum sheviras etzem* — even the *chagigah* is subject to the prohibition of breaking bones according to Ben Teima.

### Resolution

The *Gemara* resists this conclusion and attempts alternative explanations. *Le'olam rabanan* — perhaps the *mishnah* follows the Rabbis after all — and the case is one where the *Pesach* falls on Shabbat, when there is no *chagigah* brought at all. Since there is no *chagigah*, there is no reason anyone would have needed the cleaver on the fourteenth, and so one cannot assume it has been immersed.

The *Gemara* objects: this cannot be the case in the first half of the *mishnah*, because the end of the *mishnah* teaches explicitly: *chal arba'ah asar* — if the fourteenth falls on Shabbat, one may use both the knife and the cleaver immediately. Why? Because when *Erev Pesach* is Shabbat, *Erev Yom Tov* was Friday, and one cannot immerse a *kli* on Shabbat. To use the cleaver on *Yom Tov* one would have had to immerse it on Thursday. Therefore anything found on Shabbat the fourteenth has certainly already been immersed, and both knife and cleaver may be used immediately.

The *Gemara* then attempts: perhaps the case involves *sheba bimrubeh* — a group with sufficient meat, meaning the household has no need for a *chagigah* at all. But the *Gemara* challenges this too: one never knows in advance how large one's group will be. The membership of a *Pesach* group may be changed until the last moment. Therefore one could never be sure in advance whether a *chagigah* would be needed, and one would presumably always bring the cleaver to the *mikveh* just in case. Even people with small groups might find at the last minute that additional members join, and so everyone would have prepared their cleaver.

The *Gemara* then tries: *sheba betumah* — perhaps everyone became *tamei*, eliminating the need for a *chagigah*. But this raises the question: if you knew everyone was going to be *tamei*, why did you bother immersing the *shechita* knife? And if you immersed the knife because you did not yet know, why did you not also immerse the cleaver for the same reason?

The *Gemara* introduces a complex scenario: *demet nasi* — the *nasi* died, causing mass *tumah* as everyone was obligated to attend his burial. When did he die? If on the thirteenth, the knife question dissolves — you would have known you were going to become *tamei* and would not have immersed anything. If on the fourteenth, you were already immersing on the thirteenth, before his death, so again you should have treated knife and cleaver equally.

The *Gemara* resolves this with the scenario of *nasi goseis b'shlosha asar* — the *nasi* was dying on the thirteenth, near death but not yet deceased. In that case: the knife involves only one *safek* — perhaps he will die, perhaps not. Given this single doubt, you prudently immerse the knife in case he recovers and you bring the *Pesach* in *taharah*. The cleaver, however, involves *terei safeika* — a double doubt: maybe the *nasi* will die and there will be no *chagigah* due to *tumah*, and even if he does not die, perhaps you will have a large enough portion of meat that you will not need a *chagigah* anyway. Given this compound uncertainty, you do not bother immersing the cleaver.

This is an intricate resolution, and while it does explain the distinction between knife and cleaver without relying on Ben Teima's prohibition of bone-breaking, it must be acknowledged that the initial and simpler reading of the *mishnah* seemed to support the conclusion that even the *chagigah* is subject to *sheviras etzem* according to Ben Teima.

---

## Ben Dortai

### Complaint

The *Gemara* now introduces a new figure and a striking episode. *Yehuda ben Dortai* separated himself from the Rabbis — he and his son Dortai went to live in the south, away from Jerusalem. He did not want to be in Jerusalem when the *Korban Pesach* was being brought in a year when *Erev Pesach* fell on Shabbat. His reason: *amar — im yavo Eliyahu ve-yomar lahem l'Yisrael: mipnei mah lo chagagtem chagigah be-Shabbat* — he said: if Elijah the Prophet were to come and ask the Jewish people why they did not bring their *chagigah* on Shabbat, what would they answer him?

Ben Dortai's position was that the *chagigah* must be brought even on Shabbat, and he was scandalized that it was not. He declares: *tameihani al shnei gedolei ha-dor, Shemaya ve-Avtalyon* — I am astounded by the two great leaders of the generation, Shemaya and Avtalyon, who are great sages and great expositors of Scripture, *ve-lo amru lahem l'Yisrael: chagigah docha et ha-Shabbat* — and they did not tell the Jewish people that the *chagigah* overrides Shabbat. This is particularly striking in context: it was Shemaya and Avtalyon who were the source of the teaching that the *Pesach* overrides Shabbat — the very ruling that Hillel invoked. Ben Dortai is saying that in his view that principle should have been extended to the *chagigah* as well.

### Rav Defends

*Amar Rav: mai ta'ama d'Ben Dortai* — Rav explains his reasoning. The verse states *ve-zavachta Pesach la-Hashem Elokecha tzon u-vakar* — you shall slaughter the *Pesach* for God, sheep and cattle. But the *Pesach* does not come from cattle — it comes only from *kevasim* and *izim*, sheep and goats. Ben Dortai therefore reads the verse as follows: *tzon zeh Pesach, bakar zo chagigah* — the sheep refers to the *Pesach*, the cattle refers to the *chagigah*. The Torah thus presents both together under the same verb *ve-zavachta*, implying that the *chagigah* carries the same obligation as the *Pesach* — including the requirement to bring it on its fixed time, even on Shabbat.

### Ashi Objects

Rav Ashi objects sharply: *anan ta'ama d'perushim nekum u-nefaresh* — are we going to stand up and expound Scripture according to these separatists? There is no obligation on our part to defend or explain a reading advanced by those who broke from the rabbinic tradition. The word play here is pointed: the same root *p-r-sh* that means "to expound" also means "to separate," and Ben Dortai's group had separated themselves — *peireish* — from the community. Rav Ashi refuses to engage with the exegesis of *perushim* who are themselves *mafrish* themselves from the fold.

There is also a broader intertextual resonance that should not be missed. Ben Dortai went south of Jerusalem and separated himself. The word *perushim* — those who separate — recalls the Pharisees, but the act of going south to form a separate community recalls other known sectarian movements of the period. It would be very interesting to examine whether the Essene community — whose solar calendar was engineered so that the fifteenth of Nisan always fell on Wednesday — had any position on whether a *chagigah* accompanied the *Pesach* or whether it overrode Shabbat. The connection was not fully explored here, but it is a suggestive line of inquiry, particularly given the loaded use of *perushim* and *nefaresh* in Rav Ashi's formulation. Rashi himself notes the rhetorical weight of this phrase: *chazei heichi ka'amar — itztarich l'midrash mikra k'da'ateihu d'hanech muvdalin* — see how he phrases it: must we expound the verse according to the view of those who have separated themselves?

---

## Surplus Money

### Money Use

*Ella kra* — what then does the verse *ve-zavachta Pesach la-Hashem Elokecha tzon u-vakar* actually teach? The *Gemara* answers: *kra l'chi'd'Rav Nachman*. *D'amar Rav Nachman amar Rabbah bar Avuha*: the verse teaches what happens to surplus *Pesach* money. If one designated money for a *Korban Pesach* and ultimately used only part of it, what is done with the remainder? From the verse — which mentions cattle alongside the *Pesach*, yet the *Pesach* cannot come from cattle — we derive: *motar ha-Pesach yehei l'davar ha-ba min ha-tzon u-min ha-bakar* — the surplus money may be used to purchase a *shelamim*, which may come from either sheep or cattle, without restriction as to sex or species. The mention of cattle in the verse is thus not a reference to the *chagigah* at all, but a source for the law of surplus *Pesach* funds.

---

## Why No Override

### Core Question

The *Gemara* now takes up the fundamental question: *l'rabanan mai ta'ama lo dachi Shabbat* — according to the Rabbis, why does the *chagigah* not override Shabbat? Even setting aside Ben Teima's extreme position — even if one does not require the *chagigah* to be sheep, or roasted, or restricted to enrolled members — if the *chagigah* is an obligation fixed to the fourteenth, any fixed-time obligation should override Shabbat. What is the Rabbis' reasoning?

### Corporate Answer

One answer offered is: *chovat korban tzibbur hu* — it is a corporate communal obligation. This framing requires some care. The *chagigah* is not brought by the community as a single entity in the way that, say, the daily *Tamid* is. Every individual brings his own. Yet the *Gemara* applies the terminology *korban tzibbur* when all Israel brings something simultaneously. More importantly, as Tosafot notes, this framing does not actually explain the exemption from overriding Shabbat. The real question is not whether it is a *korban tzibbur* or *korban yachid* — there are cases of individual *korbanot* that do override Shabbat because they have a fixed time. The operative criterion is whether the *korban* must be brought specifically today. If it is a strict obligation with a fixed time — *bemo'ado* — it overrides Shabbat regardless.

### Seven Days Proof

*Amar Rav Ulla mishum Rabbi Yehuda ben Safra*: a verse-based proof is offered. The Torah states *ve-chagosem oto chag la-Shem shivat yamim bashana* — you shall celebrate it as a *chag* for seven days. This verse, which pertains to the *chagigah* of *Sukkot*, specifies seven days. But the full festival has eight days — *shmona havuh*! Why then does the verse say seven? *Ela mikan la-chagigah she'einah dochah et ha-Shabbat* — from here we derive that the *chagigah* does not override Shabbat: one of the eight days will inevitably be Shabbat, during which the *chagigah* is not brought, leaving seven days available for it.

### Tosafot Caveat

Tosafot raises a critical qualification: this proof establishes only that the *chagigah* of *Yom Tov* — the *chagigah* of the fifteenth onward — does not override Shabbat, precisely because there are other days on which to bring it. The fact that the Rabbis gave you seven days instead of requiring you to bring it on a specific single day is itself the reason it does not override Shabbat. But this proof says nothing about *chagigat arba'ah asar*, which has no such flexibility — it must be brought specifically on the fourteenth. Tosafot therefore suggests that the separatist Ben Dortai was not even arguing about *chagigat arba'ah asar*; he was arguing that even the *chagigah* of *Yom Tov* overrides Shabbat — which is why the Rabbis were so indignant. Ben Dortai's position, on Tosafot's reading, was the obviously untenable one that the *Yom Tov chagigah* overrides Shabbat even when it can be brought on other days.

### Ravin Challenge

*Ki ata Ravin amar*: when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael he reported having posed a challenge to his teachers. You say the *chagigah* may be brought over seven days and not eight because Shabbat is excluded — but sometimes there are only six available days: *kegon she-chal Yom Tov rishon shel chag be-Shabbat* — if the first day of *Sukkot* falls on Shabbat, then the last day of *Sukkot* also falls on Shabbat, leaving only six days on which the *chagigah* may be brought.

### Abaye Answer

*Amar Abaye* — and Abaye did not receive this objection kindly, addressing Ravin with the phrase *avin tichla*, a pointed expression — you will never find eight days on which to bring the *chagigah*. *Shivah ita be-rov shanim* — in most years you will have seven days. The Torah is not stating the absolute minimum; it is stating the standard. Seven days is the ordinary situation; occasionally there will only be six, and so be it. The verse reflects the norm.

### Conclusion

The conclusion of this *Gemara* is therefore as follows. The *chagigah* of *Yom Tov* does not override Shabbat because there are other available days on which to bring it — the seven-day proof. Whether this reasoning applies equally to *chagigat arba'ah asar*, which has no such alternative days, is left with Tosafot's caveat. But the *Gemara* at the outset, immediately after the *mishnah*, already established the most direct answer: the *chagigah* does not override Shabbat because it is not a strict obligation — *lav chovah hi*. It exists solely to ensure that the *Korban Pesach* is eaten *al hasova*, and a *korban* that is not strictly obligated does not override Shabbat or *tumah*. The discussion of *korban tzibbur* and the seven-day verse are additional frameworks, but the foundational answer is the one the *Gemara* introduced first: the *chagigah* is not strictly obligatory, and therefore it yields to Shabbat.

---

---

# Pesachim 71

## Chagigah Status

### Ben Tema

The daf begins at the bottom of 71b, picking up the ongoing discussion of the status of the *korban chagigah*. We have already encountered the position of Ben Tema, who holds that the *chagigah* is nearly identical to the *korban Pesach* in its essential features: it must be a sheep in its first year, roasted, and eaten during the day and night — so similar to the *korban Pesach* that the two are difficult to distinguish. For Ben Tema, the *chagigah* carries the force of a strict obligation.

### Chachamim Dispute

The *chachamim* disagree. In their view, the *chagigah* follows the normal rules of a *shlamim*, retaining its independent identity — cattle, two years old, and so forth — while remaining unique in that it is brought on the fourteenth together with the *korban Pesach*, rather than at the onset of *yom tov* when a *chagigah* would ordinarily be brought. Within this disagreement lies a further question: even if one rejects Ben Tema's view on the essential character of the *chagigah*, one might still hold that it constitutes a strict obligation. The practical consequence of that question is significant.

### Kvua Lo Zman

Anything that is a strict obligation tied to a specific time is brought even on *Shabbat* and even in a state of *tumah*. The *gemara* uses the phrase *korban tzibur*, but as noted in earlier sessions, the truly operative criterion is that it is a *korban she-kavua lo zman* — an offering whose time is fixed. It is therefore possible, on the view that the *chagigah* is a real *chiyuv*, that it could override *Shabbat*. As for the *chagigah* brought on the *chag* itself — although the ideal occasion is the first day of *yom tov*, it may be made up on any subsequent day of the *chag*, and for that reason it does not override *Shabbat*.

### Ben Dortai

The *chachamim* dispute the stringent position on this point as well. This was also the subject of a heated controversy involving Yehuda ben Dortai, who separated himself from the *chachamim* over the question of whether the *chagigah* could be brought on *Shabbat* or in a state of *tumah*. Two questions thus run through the entire discussion: first, whether the *chagigah* is a strict obligation or merely a means of ensuring that the *korban Pesach* is eaten in a state of satiety; and second, how closely its identity tracks that of the *korban Pesach* itself.

---

## Holiday Korbanot

### Three Korbanot

Before proceeding further, it is worth pausing to survey the *korbanot* that *chazal* require on every *yom tov*. On *Pesach*, of course, one brings the *Pesach* on the fourteenth — it bears noting that *Pesach* is not the name of the *yom tov*, which is properly called *Chag HaMatzot*; *Pesach* refers specifically to the *korban Pesach* and the day of its offering. Alongside the *korban Pesach* comes the special *korban chagigah* called *chagigat arba'ah asar* — a *chagigah* brought even before the *chag* itself begins. As already discussed, there is debate as to whether this serves as a strict obligation or merely a practical measure to ensure the *korban Pesach* is eaten in satiety. To the extent the *chagigah* connotes the status of the day as a *chag*, one might infer that even the fourteenth carries something of that character — a point reflected in the discussions about refraining from *melachah* on *erev Pesach*. The *beitzah* on the Seder plate also recalls the *chagigah*; we do not rule like Ben Tema, and so we use something visually distinct from the *zroa* to make that difference clear.

### Olat Re'iyah

The first of the three standard obligations on every *yom tov* is the *mitzvah* of *olat re'iyah*. The Torah commands that all males appear before God — *yera'eh kol zchurecha* — and adds: *ve-lo yer'u panai reikam*, "do not appear before Me empty-handed." From this the *poskim* derive a positive obligation to bring an *olah* when appearing at the *Beit HaMikdash* on *yom tov*. If one does not appear at all, one has merely failed to fulfill the positive obligation of *re'iyah*. But if one does appear without a *korban* in hand, one additionally transgresses the negative prohibition of *ve-lo yer'u panai reikam*. This *olat re'iyah* is discussed in the first *mishnah* of Masechet Chagigah.

### Chagigah Offering

The second *korban* is the *chagigah* itself. When the Torah uses the word *chag* — as in *chag la-Shem* or *chag ha-Sukkot* — *chazal* understand the term *tachogu* to mean that one marks the day as a *chag* through the bringing of a *korban chagigah*, which takes the form of a *shlamim*. The owners eat the meat in Jerusalem over two days and the intervening night. The primary obligation falls on the first day of *yom tov*; if not fulfilled then, one may make it up on any other day of the *chag*. On Sukkot, one may even make it up on *Shemini Atzeret*. On Shavuot, although it is a single-day *chag*, the principle of equating the *chagim* allows for six days of makeup, parallel to Pesach.

### Shlamei Simcha

The third *korban* is the *shlamei simcha*. The Torah's command *ve-samachta lifnei Hashem Elokecha* is understood by *chazal* as mandating *simcha* through the bringing of *korbanot*. This is a separate obligation from the *chagigah*, yielding a third *korban* of *shlamim* brought for the purpose of *simcha*, whose meat is eaten in the context of the *Mikdash* and Jerusalem. When *chazal* say *ein simcha ella be-vasar shlamim*, the original formulation referred specifically to these *shlamim*; the joy achieved through bringing and eating a *korban* in connection with God is itself the *simcha*. The derived practice of eating meat on *yom tov* in our day reflects this principle in its post-*mikdash* form.

### Korban Shutafin

One might consider whether one could fulfill the obligations of *olat re'iyah*, *chagigah*, or *shlamei simcha* collectively, pooling resources across a group. These are not *korbanot tzibur* — they remain in the category of *korban yachid*. The broader question of *korban shutafin* — a partnership *korban* — remains somewhat unsettled as a category, and when and how it applies is not straightforwardly resolved.

---

## Slaughter Timing

### Ulla/R. Elazar

Four lines from the bottom of the daf, the *gemara* records: *amar Ulla amar Rabbi Elazar* — Ulla says in the name of Rabbi Elazar the *Amora* — that *shlamim she-shachtan me-erev Yom Tov*, if one slaughtered a *shlamim* on *erev Yom Tov* and then ate it that night, one does not fulfill one's obligation either of *simcha* or of *chagigah*. This applies whether it is *erev Pesach*, *erev Sukkot*, or *erev Shavuot*: if the *korban* was brought the day before and the meat was consumed that night — or even over the following day, since *shlamim* may be eaten for two days and the intervening night — neither obligation is discharged.

### Zvicha B'Sha'at Simcha

Why does slaughtering *erev Yom Tov* fail to fulfill the *simcha* obligation? The reason given is *mishum simcha de-chtiv ve-zavachta ve-samachta* — because the verse says "you shall slaughter and you shall rejoice." Although that verse concerns the offerings brought at Har Eival and is not directly about *simchat yom tov*, *chazal* derive from it a relationship: *be'inan zvicha be-sha'at simcha ve-leka* — the *shechita* must be connected to the joy. The fulfillment of *simcha* is achieved not merely through eating the meat of a *korban*, but through the act of bringing it. Joy in this sense is not mere physical pleasure; it is the specific *simcha* that arises from the connection with God through the act of offering. The *shechita* must therefore occur on *yom tov* itself, not the day before.

### Davar Shebechova

The reason slaughtering *erev Yom Tov* fails for *chagigah* is more fundamental. The *gemara* states: *havei davar she-be-chovah* — the *chagigah* is an obligatory *korban*, and *kol davar she-be-chovah eino ba ela min ha-chulin* — any obligatory offering may only be fulfilled from *chulin*, from an animal not previously sanctified and not already designated for another purpose. One may not bring an animal already sanctified as a *shlamim* — even as a *neder* one intended to fulfill — and have it do double duty as one's *chagigah*. The *chagigah* demands a fresh designation. As Tosafot points out, this problem is independent of timing: even had the animal been brought on the fifteenth rather than the fourteenth, the pre-existing sanctification would still disqualify it from serving as one's *chagigah*.

### Simcha Exception

One might ask: if *shlamei simcha* is itself an obligation, why does the same rule not apply — why can a previously sanctified animal be used for *shlamei simcha*? Rashi quotes the *midreshei halacha* that establish *shlamei simcha* as the single exception to this rule. Although it is an obligation, one may use an animal already sanctified for a different purpose — say, a *shlamim* set aside to fulfill an old *neder* — and have it count for *shlamei simcha* as well. This exception makes conceptual sense if the emphasis of *shlamei simcha* lies in the eating of the meat rather than the act of bringing. The bringing of that particular *korban* serves its original purpose; the eating of the meat in the context of *yom tov* constitutes the *shlamei simcha* — the two functions are not truly in conflict.

### Tosafot

Tosafot clarifies that the *gemara*'s emphasis on the animal having been slaughtered on the fourteenth is somewhat curious. The disqualification of the *chagigah* arises from the pre-existing sanctification, not from the timing — and therefore even had the animal been brought on the fifteenth, it still could not have counted toward the *chagigah* obligation. Tosafot's point is simply to ensure this is understood clearly. The case of *shlamei simcha*, by contrast, carries a separate timing problem: according to the opinion under discussion, the *shlamim* must be slaughtered on *yom tov* itself; bringing it before *yom tov* disqualifies it for *simcha* regardless of when the meat is eaten.

---

## Timing Dispute

### V'Hayita Ach Samei'ach

The *gemara* now attempts to find support for the claim that *shechita* must occur on *yom tov* itself. The verse regarding Sukkot — *ve-hayita ach same'ach* — concludes a passage that speaks of seven days of *simcha* (*v'samachta be-chagecha shivat yamim tachog*). The addition of *ve-hayita ach same'ach* is taken to include something beyond the seven days: *lerabot leilo Yom Tov ha'acharon le-simcha* — it extends the *simcha* even to the night of the last *yom tov*, the night of *Shemini Atzeret*, allowing one to eat the meat of a *chagigah* then and thereby fulfill the obligation.

### Ach Division

The *gemara* challenges: you say this verse includes the night of *Shemini Atzeret* — but perhaps it should include the first night of Sukkot, the night of the fifteenth, so that one who slaughtered on the fourteenth could eat that night and be *yotzei*? The verse answers with the word *ach*: *chilek* — it divides, it limits. The extension adds one night only, not both.

### Last Night Reason

The *gemara* asks: given that we may include only one of the two nights, why do we choose the last night of the *chag* rather than the first? The answer offered is: *lav mishum de'ein lo be-ma yismach* — because on the first night of Sukkot, there is nothing with which to perform *simcha*. Since *shechita* must occur on *yom tov*, one cannot have slaughtered the day before; therefore the first night is excluded. The *simcha* obligation has nothing available to activate it the first night, whereas the last night is preceded by a full period of *yom tov* during which *korbanot* may have been slaughtered.

### Daytime Focus

The *gemara* immediately deflects this reasoning. Perhaps, it suggests, one could slaughter before *yom tov* and still fulfill the obligation — and yet the last night would still be preferred over the first. Why? Because the *baraita* itself gives its own reason: *mah ra'ita lerabot leilo Yom Tov ha'acharon u-lehotzi leilo Yom Tov ha'rishon* — why include the last night and exclude the first? *Marbeh ani leilo Yom Tov ha'acharon she-yesh simcha lefanav* — I include the last night because *simcha* precedes it; *u-motzi ani leilo Yom Tov ha'rishon she-ein simcha lefanav* — I exclude the first night because it is not preceded by *simcha*. This reasoning does not require that *shechita* be on *yom tov* — it only explains the preference for the last night on independent grounds. The logic appears to rest on a *chazal*ic tendency to read *yom* as literally daytime.
