Beginning from the assumption that *shivat yamim* means seven days rather than seven nights, the nights must be included by extension — and the natural night to include is the night that follows the day, not the night that precedes it. That explains why the night of *Shemini Atzeret* is preferred: it follows the seventh day, whereas the night of the fifteenth precedes the first day rather than following it.

### Rashi/Tosafot

Rashi holds that the verse includes only the night of *Shemini Atzeret*, not its daytime. Given the framework just described — starting from seven days, then extending to include the following nights — the night of *Shemini Atzeret* is included, but the day of *Shemini Atzeret* is not drawn in by this logic. Tosafot disagrees. Based on other considerations, Tosafot holds that once the night of *Shemini Atzeret* is included, the day of *Shemini Atzeret* follows as well — since a *shlamim* is canonically eaten for a day and the following night, if the seventh day is the basis and its night is included, the day following that night should also be included. The practical conclusion remains that one could, strictly speaking, slaughter on the fourteenth and eat the meat on the day of the fifteenth and be *yotzei* — the attempt to prove that *shechita* must be on *yom tov* from this verse has not succeeded. The *gemara* treats it only as a *mesayea*, a supporting indication for a claim that requires further examination.

---

## Rav Yosef Challenge

### 14th Chagigah

The *gemara* records: *mativ Rav Yosef* — Rav Yosef challenges the claim that *shechita* must occur on *yom tov*. The *baraita* quoted earlier in connection with Ben Tema states that the *chagigah* brought on the fourteenth fulfills the obligation of *simcha* but does not fulfill the obligation of *chagigah* of *yom tov*. According to Rav Yosef's reading, one slaughters this *chagigah* on the fourteenth alongside the *korban Pesach* and eats it that night — the night of the fifteenth — thereby satisfying the *simcha* obligation. This appears to be a direct contradiction: here is a case where the *shechita* occurred on the fourteenth and the *simcha* is nonetheless fulfilled.

### Zvicha Timing

The difficulty is sharp: according to the requirement of *zvicha be-sha'at simcha*, the *shechita* must occur at the time of *simcha* — on *yom tov* itself. Here the *shechita* was on the fourteenth, yet the *baraita* says the *simcha* obligation is discharged. This seems to refute the rule entirely.

### Rav Idi Bar Avin

Rav Idi bar Avin resolves the difficulty: *she-ikvei ve-shachta* — the animal was held over. The *baraita* does not mean the animal was slaughtered on the fourteenth and the *simcha* was fulfilled by eating it that night. Rather, the animal was designated for the *chagigah* of the fourteenth but was not actually slaughtered then; it was held over and slaughtered on the fifteenth. On that reading, the *shechita* did occur on *yom tov*, and the *simcha* is fulfilled on *yom tov*. The animal's original sanctification for the *chagigah* of the fourteenth does not disqualify it for *shlamei simcha*, since *shlamei simcha* is the one obligatory category that permits this form of double duty.

Rav Ashi adds corroboration: *hachi nami mistabra* — this reading is indeed more reasonable. For if you assume the animal was slaughtered on the fourteenth, you immediately run into an insurmountable problem. When exactly would one eat this *chagigah* in fulfillment of *simcha*? Not at night — the *mitzvah* of *simcha* through *korbanot* begins with the day, not the preceding night, as established earlier. And by the daytime of the fifteenth, according to Ben Tema — who holds this *chagigah* is like the *korban Pesach* — the meat is already *pasul*, since Ben Tema holds it expires at daybreak. There is thus no window in which the meat is both fit for consumption and subject to the *simcha* obligation. This confirms that the *baraita* must be speaking of an animal slaughtered on the fifteenth, not the fourteenth.

---

## 8-Day Challenge

### Rava Objection

*Mativ Rava* — Rava now challenges the requirement that *shechita* occur on *yom tov*. The *mishnah* in Sukkah establishes that *hallel* and *simcha* over Sukkot span eight days — including *Shemini Atzeret*. If *shechita* must occur on *yom tov* itself, then *ve-im amarta ve-i'nan zvicha be-sha'at simcha*, one will frequently find oneself with only seven days of *shlamei simcha* rather than eight.

### Shabbat Problem

The problem arises when the first day of Sukkot falls on *Shabbat*. *Shlamei simcha* are not brought on *Shabbat*. If one could slaughter on *erev Yom Tov* and eat the meat the following day, there would always be a remedy: even when the day itself is *Shabbat*, one could have slaughtered the day before and eaten the meat that *Shabbat*. But if the *shechita* must be on *yom tov* — and that *yom tov* is *Shabbat* — there is no permissible day to slaughter, and the first day of *simcha* is lost. One would then have only seven days available, contradicting the *mishnah*'s statement of eight.

### Se'ir Chatat

The *gemara* proposes a resolution in the name of Rav Huna son of Rav Yehuda: *misamcha be-sei'rei ha-regalim* — one fulfills *simcha* by eating the meat of the *se'ir ha-chatat*, the goat sin-offering that accompanies each *musaf*. Since the *musaf* includes a *chatat* whose meat is available, perhaps eating that meat constitutes *simcha* even when no *shlamim* can be brought.

### Two Objections

Rava raises two objections. First: when the *se'ir ha-chatat* is brought on *Shabbat*, cooking it for consumption would require performing *melachah* — and one does not perform *melachah* on *Shabbat* to facilitate eating the *musaf korbanot*. The meat would therefore have to be eaten raw. *Ve-simcha be-chai leka* — there is no joy in eating raw meat. Second: *kohanim ochlin, Yisrael lo masmchan* — only *kohanim* eat the *chatat*; the rest of the people have no access to it. It cannot therefore provide a general basis for *simcha*. Both objections together dispose of the proposed solution.

### Rav Papa

With Rav Huna's solution eliminated and the difficulty left standing, Rav Papa offers an alternative: *ella amar Rav Papa misamcho bi-ksut nekiya ve-yayin yashan* — one achieves *simcha* through fine clothes and aged wine. This is precisely the alternative we rely upon today in the absence of *korbanot*: without *shlamei simcha*, one uses wine and new clothing to mark the joy of *yom tov*. The answer is admittedly weak — if the fundamental obligation is a *chiyuv korban*, a substitution of wine and clothing is a thin replacement — but it is the *gemara*'s conclusion in this context.

---

## Simcha Nature

### Korban Joy

Two broader points emerge from this sugya regarding the nature of *simcha* and how it is experienced through *korbanot*. First, within the framework of the *mikdash*, the emphasis of *simcha* lies in the bringing of the *korban*, not merely in the eating — the joy of connection with God achieved through the act of offering.

### Modern Practice

In our time, without *korbanot*, the obligation of *simcha* operates differently. Some are careful to eat meat on *yom tov* in honor of the principle of *ein simcha ella be-vasar* — and some observe this by eating *milchigs* on Shavuot and then serving a meat meal afterward. However, a closer look at the sources reveals that when the *gemara* considers the absence of *korbanot*, it does not even mention meat — it mentions wine and fine clothing. Other *gemarot* list *basar va-yayin* among the alternatives, but the strict requirement of meat is not as clearly mandated as is sometimes assumed. The meat referred to by *ein simcha ella be-vasar* was specifically the meat of *shlamim*; in the absence of that context, the obligation takes different forms.

### Context Matters

A second point concerns the starting point of *simcha* during the *chag*. Within the *korban* framework, the *simcha* obligation begins on the day of the fifteenth, not the preceding night — a conclusion emerging from all the foregoing analysis. It would be absurd, however, to say that a guest arriving on the first night of the *chag* need not be welcomed with a proper meal because *simcha* does not technically begin until the following morning. The timing rules developed in the *gemara* are specific to the *korban* context, with its halakhic emphasis on the *yom* as the primary unit and the night as derivative. In the non-*korban* context, *simcha* plainly begins at the onset of the *chag*.

### Rambam One

A final question concerns the extent of the obligation: must one bring a *korban* every single day to satisfy *simcha*, or every other day since the meat can be eaten over two days, or is a single *korban* for the entire *chag* sufficient? The Rambam appears to hold that the *mitzvah* of *simcha* in the context of a *korban* requires bringing at least one additional *korban* over the course of the *chag* — not necessarily one per day or one per two days. When the *gemara* extends *simcha* to the last night, the Rambam understands this to mean that if one has not yet had opportunity to fulfill the *mitzvah*, even the final night remains available — not that there is a recurring daily or two-daily obligation.

---

## Rava Response

### Rabin Report

The *gemara* now turns to a contrasting tradition: *ki ata Rabin amar Rabbi Elazar* — when Rabin came from Eretz Yisrael, he brought a different version of what Rabbi Elazar had said. This stands in direct opposition to what Ulla had reported in Rabbi Elazar's name.

### Eating as Key

According to Rabin's version: *shlamim she-shachtan me-erev Yom Tov yotzei ban mishum simcha* — if one slaughtered a *shlamim* on *erev Yom Tov* and eats the meat on *yom tov*, one does fulfill the obligation of *simcha*. The *simcha* is not contingent on the *shechita* occurring on *yom tov*; what matters is when the meat is eaten. *Lo be'inan zvicha be-sha'at simcha* — there is no requirement that the *shechita* occur at the time of *simcha*. Furthermore, the exception for *shalmei simcha* applies: even an animal sanctified for a prior *korban* and slaughtered before *yom tov* can count for *simcha*, as long as its meat is eaten on *yom tov*. This view strongly emphasizes the eating rather than the bringing — in a manner somewhat analogous to the *korban Pesach*, which is brought entirely for the purpose of *achila*.

### Chagigah Separate

This more lenient view regarding *simcha* does not extend to *chagigah*. *V'lo mishum chagigah — havei davar she-be-chovah, v'chol davar she-be-chovah eino ba ella min ha-chulin*: the *chagigah* remains an obligatory *korban*, and the rule that obligatory *korbanot* must come from *chulin* — from animals not previously sanctified — is not waived. Tosafot further notes that even had the animal been brought on the fifteenth itself, the pre-existing sanctification would disqualify it for *chagigah*. The two obligations — *simcha* and *chagigah* — thus diverge sharply: one is governed primarily by when the meat is eaten, the other by the status of the animal at the time of designation.

### Rambam Ruling

The Rambam rules in accordance with this opinion of Rabin. The *halacha* follows the view that *shlamim* slaughtered before *yom tov* fulfill the *simcha* obligation as long as the meat is eaten on *yom tov* — and that *zvicha be-sha'at simcha* is not required.

---

## Imurim Expiry

### Rav Kahana Q

The *gemara* transitions to a new question raised by Rav Kahana: *minayin le-imurei chagigas chamisha asar she-nifsalim be-lina* — from where do we know that the *imurim*, the fats and internal portions of the *chagigah* of the fifteenth, become invalid by lingering overnight? In a normal *shlamim*, the meat may be eaten over two days and the intervening night. But the *imurim* — the portions that must be burned on the *mizbe'ach* — have an earlier expiration: they become *pasul* by the following night, before the meat itself expires. The *hakrava* portion of the *korban* closes sooner than the *achila* portion. This is true not only of the *chagigah* but of all *shlamim*, as Tosafot notes — the *chagigah* is merely the vehicle for the discussion.

### Lo Yalin

The source is the verse: *ve-lo yalin chelev chagi ad boker* — do not let the fat of My *chag* remain until the morning. This verse prohibits leaving the *imurim* overnight. But which morning? The question is whether the verse means the morning immediately following the offering or some subsequent morning.

### Boker Rishon

Rav Kahana's derivation proceeds as follows: the verse immediately following is *reshit bikurei admatecha* — the firstfruits of your soil. Reading *boker* and *reshit* together yields *boker reshit* — the first morning. The *imurim* thus become *pasul* at the first morning following the offering, not some later point. This establishes that the *hakrava* expiration precedes the *achila* expiration by an entire day.

### Yosef Challeng

Rav Yosef challenges this derivation: *ta'ama de-chtiv reshit* — the only reason we know it means the first morning is because the verse contains the word *reshit*. *Ha lo katav reshit, hava amina mai boker, boker sheni* — had the Torah not written *reshit*, one might have thought that *boker* refers to the second morning rather than the first. But how could that possibly have been entertained as a reading? *Mi ika midi de-vasar ipsalei me-orta ve-imurin ad tzafra* — is there any case in which the meat becomes *pasul* that very night, and yet the fats remain valid until the following morning? That would mean the fats receive *more* time than the meat — a seemingly impossible inversion, given that the *imurim* are the *hakrava* component, which must logically expire before, not after, the *achila* component.

### Abaye Response

Abaye responds: *almah la* — why is that impossible? *Harei Pesach le-Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah* — consider the *korban Pesach* according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, who holds that the *Pesach* may only be eaten until midnight. According to this view, *de-vasar ipsalei me-chatzot* — the meat's time expires at midnight — *ve-imurin ad tzafra* — yet the fats may still be burned until morning. So there is a genuine precedent for the fats having more time than the meat. Rav Yosef's challenge was therefore not unreasonable: it was at least conceivable that *boker* might mean the second morning, since fats can in principle outlast the meat.

Rava then clarifies what was really troubling Rav Yosef. Although the precise formulation does not match his stated words, Rashi notes that the *gemara* here reconstructs what was actually bothering him. The deeper concern is this: *mi ika midi de-ilu tanna le-vasar lo ba'ei reshit, Rav Kahana le-imurin ba'ei reshit* — is there something for which, when the Torah restricts the *meat*, it does not use the word *reshit*, yet when restricting the *imurim*, Rav Kahana requires *reshit* to determine the morning? The word *boker* on its own, as we will see, already means the immediate next morning — and a *baraita* about the meat itself confirms this, assuming *boker* to mean the immediate morning without needing *reshit*. If *boker* automatically defaults to the first morning, why does Rav Kahana need *reshit* at all to establish this for the *imurim*?

---

## Baraita Unpack

### Repetition

The *gemara* turns to a *baraita* that appears to repeat itself in puzzling fashion. The verse states: *lo yalin min ha-basar asher tizbach ba-erev ba-yom ha-rishon la-boker* — do not let the meat that you slaughter that evening remain until morning, on the first day, until morning. The doubling is immediately striking. The *baraita* sets out to interpret this and in doing so appears to loop back on itself: it poses a question, offers a reading, then reintroduces what seems like the same question.

### Two Chagigot

The *baraita* teaches: *limed al chagigat arba'ah asar she-ne'echelet li-shnei yamim ve-laila echad* — this verse teaches that the *chagigah* of the fourteenth is eaten for two days and the intervening night. But that reading requires unpacking. The phrase *tizbach ba-erev* identifies the *korban* as one slaughtered in the afternoon — and the only *korban* other than the *Pesach* slaughtered in the afternoon is *chagigat arba'ah asar*. The phrase *ba-yom ha-rishon*, "on the first day," indicates that the eating continues through the fifteenth; and *la-boker*, "until morning," tells us it does not extend past the morning following the fifteenth, i.e., the morning of the sixteenth.

But initially, one might have read the verse differently: perhaps *la-boker* refers to the morning of the fifteenth — meaning the *chagigah* of the fourteenth may only be eaten for one day and one night. The *baraita* then re-poses this possibility: perhaps the verse means the first morning, and the *chagigah* of the fourteenth expires at the morning of the fifteenth. The *baraita* also raises the possibility of reading the verse as referring to two *chagigot* — one slaughtered *ba-erev* (the fourteenth) and one slaughtered *ba-yom ha-rishon* (the fifteenth) — with each expiring at its own respective next morning.

### Two-Day Problem

But this reading generates an impossible result. We have a firm tradition that some *chagigah* in the world is eaten for two days and the intervening night — *chagigah ne'echelet li-shnei yamim ve-laila echad*. If both the *chagigah* of the fourteenth and the *chagigah* of the fifteenth each expire at their own next morning, then neither is eaten for two full days. Every *chagigah* that exists would be limited to one day and a night. That contradicts the established principle.

### Neder Solution

The resolution is found in a separate verse: *im neder o nedava zevach korbano ba-yom zivcho ye'achel u-mi-macharat ve-ha-notar mimenu ba-esh yisaref* — if it is a *neder* or *nedava*, one eats the *korban* on the day it is slaughtered and the day after, and what remains is burned. From this verse, *chazal* derive — through an extra textual element, which Rashi identifies as the word *im* — that the *chagigah* of the fifteenth is eaten for two days and the intervening night. Once the *chagigah* of the fifteenth is relocated to this verse for its two-day span, the original verse — *lo yalin min ha-basar asher tizbach ba-erev ba-yom ha-rishon la-boker* — is now read as referring exclusively to the *chagigah* of the fourteenth.

### Fourteenth Proof

With the entire verse now speaking of the fourteenth's *chagigah*, the phrase *ba-yom ha-rishon* tells us that the eating extends through the fifteenth, and *la-boker* means the morning following the fifteenth — the morning of the sixteenth. So the *chagigah* of the fourteenth is also eaten for two days: the fourteenth and the fifteenth. And the word *boker* in this context refers to the *boker* that follows *ba-yom ha-rishon* — the second morning from when the *korban* was slaughtered. This is only because the verse itself establishes that eating continues through the fifteenth; *boker* is then naturally read as the morning that ends that extended period.

---

## Boker Meaning

### Bayom Context

This analysis yields a crucial methodological conclusion. The only reason *boker* in this verse refers to a morning two days removed from the slaughter is because the verse itself — through the phrase *ba-yom ha-rishon* — establishes that the eating period extends to the fifteenth. Given that context, *boker* means the morning that follows *yom ha-rishon*. Remove that context, and *boker* would revert to its default meaning.

### Default Meaning

The default meaning of *boker* is always the immediate next morning. *Ha kol heicha de-chtiv boker stam, boker rishon* — wherever the Torah writes *boker* without further context, it means the first morning, the morning immediately following. This holds *af al gav de-lo ktiv beih rishon* — even without the word *reshit* or *rishon* appearing explicitly. The word *boker* on its own already implies immediacy. The lesson of *reshit* in the verse *ve-lo yalin chelev chagi ad boker* is thus not to restrict *boker* to the first morning — that would be its meaning regardless — but rather to confirm it in a context where one might otherwise have been confused by the parallel to the meat's longer window.

### Imurim Rule

Applying this conclusion to the *imurim*: the fats of the *chagigah* — and of any *shlamim* — expire at the end of the night immediately following the *hakrava*. The *lo yalin* prohibition means that the *imurim* must be entirely burned on the *mizbe'ach* by the morning following the day of offering. This morning comes before the meat itself expires — the meat may be eaten through the following day — establishing a clear asymmetry: the *imurim* deadline is the night, the meat deadline extends further. The *hakrava* closes with the first morning; the *achila* continues beyond it.

---

---

# Pesachim 73

## Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

### to'eh b'dvar mitzvah

We begin on 72b, in the midst of the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua concerning one who is *to'eh b'dvar mitzvah* — who errs while in the course of performing a *mitzvah*, particularly one that carries a license to override Shabbat, such as *brit milah* or the *Korban Pesach*. Rabbi Yehoshua holds that under the right circumstances — an honest mistake, properly understood — the person is *patur*. The Gemara now picks up with a scene: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak were sitting on the porch of Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak, and they were discussing the following statements.

### Notar & Niddah

Reish Lakish says: if the spits became confused — the spit bearing *notar*, leftover sacrificial meat whose willful consumption incurs *kares*, was mixed up with the spit bearing properly roasted *korban* meat that one is obligated to eat — and one ate from the wrong spit, one is *chayav*. This is not a case involving Shabbat; it is a case of attempting to perform a *mitzvah* and, through a factual error, committing an *aveira* that would ordinarily require a *korban* if done *b'shogeg*.

Rabbi Yochanan adds a related case: if a man attempts to have marital relations with his wife — a *mitzvah* — and it turns out she is a *niddah*, he is *chayav*. However, if a man performs *yibum* with his *yevama* — his widowed sister-in-law, where the act of *yibum* is itself a *mitzvah* — and she too turns out to be a *niddah* at that moment, he is *patur*.

The Gemara then considers how these cases relate to one another. One version says: *kol shekein b'hi mechayev* — all the more so Rabbi Yochanan would hold the one who ate *notar* is *chayav*, since by eating *notar* there is no *mitzvah* element at all. When the husband had relations with his wife, at least he also fulfilled the *mitzvah* of marital intimacy, even though he transgressed the prohibition of *niddah*; there is a dual dimension to the act. But eating *notar* yields nothing but the *aveira*.

Another version inverts this: by the *notar* case, he is actually *patur*, because there he could not have asked the spit whether it was *notar*. The liability in the *niddah* case of his wife flows precisely from the fact that he *could* have asked her. This reading recognizes the personhood of the wife — she is someone he could and should have consulted. *Aval hacha*, where inquiry was impossible, there is greater grounds for exemption.

What remains somewhat open is exactly how these cases map onto Rabbi Yehoshua's framework. Presumably the discussion takes place within Rabbi Yehoshua's position, which does allow for exemption in certain cases. Yet here, liability is affirmed in most instances — either because the person could have asked, as in the wife case, or perhaps because, as in the *notar* case, the person did not ultimately perform a *mitzvah* at all. The Gemara does not fully unpack why the *notar* case yields liability vis-à-vis Rabbi Yehoshua; it can be surmised that accomplishing a *mitzvah* in the end is a relevant factor that has been somewhat underplayed here but is more explicit elsewhere.

### Yevama Exception

The Gemara then asks: Rabbi Yochanan, what is the difference? By the *yevama* he performed a *mitzvah* — but by his wife he was also attempting, and at least arguably accomplishing, a *mitzvah*. Marital relations is a *mitzvah* for husband and wife. So why is one *chayav* and the other *patur*?

The Gemara's initial response is *me'uberet* — the wife is pregnant. Since pregnancy precludes *pru u'revu*, perhaps marital relations in that context carry no *mitzvah*. The Gemara immediately rejects this: *ve'ika simchat onatah* — the *mitzvah* of marital intimacy is not confined to procreative contexts. There is a *mitzvah* of giving one's wife pleasure, *simcha*, through regular conjugal relations, independent of whether children will result.

The Gemara then proposes: *she'lo bish'at onatah* — it was not the time of her scheduled *onah*. There is a regularity, discussed in Ketubot, based on the husband's occupation, and the *mitzvah* applies at those scheduled intervals. Outside of them, perhaps it is not a *mitzvah*. To this the Gemara raises Rava's statement: *chayav adam lesameach ishto bidvar mitzvah* — a man is obligated to give his wife pleasure even outside the fixed schedule, whenever it would be welcome and pleasurable to her. So there seems to be a *mitzvah* at virtually any time.

## Marital Mitzvah

### Pregnant Wife

This passage in the Gemara is striking in its own right, quite apart from the primary question of *to'eh b'dvar mitzvah*. The Gemara moves through a progression of views on when marital relations constitute a *mitzvah*: first, only when procreation is possible; then, at scheduled intervals; and finally, from Rava's statement, at essentially any time it would be pleasurable to the wife. This is a significant broadening of the concept.

### Rava's Ruling

Rava's ruling — that a man is obligated to give his wife pleasure, even outside the formal *onah* schedule, as a *mitzvah* — represents the Gemara's most expansive position on this question. The Gemara's apparent refusal to accept that marital relations are ever *not* a *mitzvah* (at least whenever they would be welcome) carries weight. Rashi, drawing on another Gemara, qualifies this somewhat: the *mitzvah* applies when she is signaling her interest. The Gemara here, however, may not have wanted to rely on that qualification — perhaps because it did not wish to assume that the absence of such signals implies unwillingness, which would approach coercion. A middle position is conceivable: she is not overtly initiating, but nor would she decline. The simple reading of this Gemara suggests that whenever relations would be welcomed or appreciated, there is a *mitzvah*. This Gemara thus stands as a significant source on the scope of *onah* as a *mitzvah*.

### Samuch Levistah

Given this, when would it not be a *mitzvah*? The Gemara answers: *samuch levistah* — when it is close to the time of her expected period. Relations are prohibited at that time, since she may become a *niddah* during the act itself. Whether the prohibition is *d'Oraita* or *d'Rabbanan* is a debate among the *Rishonim*, but the point is that proximity to the expected onset renders relations not only non-obligatory but actively prohibited. Therefore, in that specific context, there is no *mitzvah* — and the husband is *chayav* because he was not performing a *mitzvah* at all.

The Gemara then asks: if so, the same should apply to the *yevama* — she too would presumably be *samuch levistah* at the relevant moment, so he was not performing a *mitzvah* with her either. Why then is he *patur* in that case?

### Embarrassment Factor

The Gemara answers: *yevamto baziz mina* — with his *yevama*, he is embarrassed. They have never been intimate before. He is not comfortable asking her whether she is approaching her period, even as they are about to have their first act of *yibum* together. *Ishto lo baziz mina* — with his wife, by contrast, he has no such embarrassment, and he should have asked.

The Gemara thus shifts from what initially appeared to be a substantive distinction — that *yibum* is a *mitzvah* while relations with a *niddah* wife are not — to a procedural one: the determinative factor is whether it was reasonable to expect him to inquire. In the case of the *yevama*, inquiry was not reasonably expected; in the case of his wife, it was. One might observe that the Gemara completely leaves aside the question of the woman's own liability — whether the *yevama* herself was *meizid*, *shogeg*, or *ones* — focusing entirely, as is its consistent practice, on the man.

The larger point emerging from all of this is that these cases — not Shabbat cases, but cases of attempting a *mitzvah* and committing an *aveira* through error — result in liability in most configurations, except where inquiry was genuinely impracticable. The Gemara has also not unpacked why Reish Lakish holds the *notar* case to be *chayav* within Rabbi Yehoshua's framework; one plausible answer is that there the person did not wind up performing a *mitzvah* in any meaningful sense, and that is what Rabbi Yehoshua requires for exemption. But the Gemara does not articulate this explicitly here.

## Rabbi Yehoshua Position

### Following Which Opinion

The Gemara now asks: *Rabbi Yochanan k'man* — who exactly is Rabbi Yochanan following? He applies the principle of *to'eh b'dvar mitzvah* to the *yevama* case, which lacks urgency. The Gemara considers whether he follows Rabbi Yosi, Rabbi Yehoshua of the *Mishnah* regarding the *Korban Pesach*, Rabbi Yehoshua of the *brit milah* cases, or Rabbi Yehoshua of *trumah*. Each possibility is examined.

### Urgency Cases

If Rabbi Yochanan follows Rabbi Yosi — as we learn in a *Mishnah*: if the first day of *Sukkot* falls on Shabbat and one forgot and carried the *lulav* into the *reshut harabbim* while attempting to perform the *mitzvah*, he is *patur mipnei she'hotzi birshut*, because he carried with license, trying to fulfill a *mitzvah*. The Gemara objects: *dilma shani hatam zmano bahu* — perhaps that case is distinct because of the urgency. If you want to perform the *mitzvah* of *lulav* on the first day of Sukkot, you must do it today. That urgency — *zmano bahu* — provides grounds for exemption that do not apply to *yibum*, which can be performed today or next week.

The same objection applies to Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling in the *Mishnah* of our tractate: when one makes a mistake while bringing the *Korban Pesach*, there too there is urgency — *zmano bahu* — the *korban* must be brought today. And similarly for the *brit milah* cases discussed yesterday: the circumcision must be performed on its designated day. All of these cases of exemption share the feature of temporal pressure. Rabbi Yochanan's application of the principle to *yibum*, where no such urgency exists, therefore represents a *chidush*, an extension beyond what was previously established.

### Trumah Exception

The Gemara then considers Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling in the case of *trumah*: *detnan*, as we learned in a *Mishnah*, someone was eating *trumah* and in the middle of the meal was informed that he is, in fact, a *ben grushah* or *ben chalutzah* — the son of a *kohen* who married a divorcée or a woman released from *levirate* marriage — and therefore lacks the sanctity of a *kohen* and is a *challal*. Rabbi Eliezer holds him *chayav* to pay the *keren v'chomesh* — principal and an additional fifth — for having eaten *trumah* as a non-*kohen*. Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him.

Now, eating *trumah* carries no urgency tied to a particular day. There is no *zmano bahu* here — a *kohen* may eat *trumah* on any day. Yet Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him. This seems to be exactly the kind of precedent Rabbi Yochanan needs for extending the exemption to the non-urgent *yevama* case.

The Gemara pushes back: *dilma k'Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye* — perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling in the *trumah* case was specifically where the *trumah* was eaten on *Erev Pesach*, and on that day there *was* urgency: the *trumah* bread was about to become *chametz* and forbidden, so it had to be consumed that day. On any other day, he would be *chayav*. The urgency factor persists even here.

### Trumah Avodah

Alternatively, the Gemara offers a distinct rationale for the *trumah* ruling that has nothing to do with urgency: *shani trumah d'ikrei avodah* — eating *trumah* is categorized as an act of *avodah*, divine service. *Avodah rachmana achsher* — and where a *kohen* performed *avodah* without knowing he was disqualified, the Torah itself validates that *avodah* retroactively.

This is demonstrated from a *Mishnah*: if a *kohen* was standing at the altar bringing a *korban* and it was then revealed that he is a *ben grushah* or *ben chalutzah*, Rabbi Yehoshua holds that all the *korbanot* he brought throughout his life as a *kohen* are *kasher*. The Scriptural basis, as derived by the Gemara, is the verse *barech Hashem cheilo u'fo'al yadav tirtzeh* — "bless, O Lord, his valor, and accept the work of his hands" (Devarim 33:11), read in conjunction with the preceding verse about the *kohen* bringing incense and *korbanot*. The *drashah* understands this as divine approbation of the *kohen*'s service performed in good faith, even if he was retroactively discovered to be disqualified.

The source for treating *trumah* as *avodah* is established through a *Tosefta*-style teaching involving Rabbi Tarfon, who once told Rabban Gamliel that he had not come to the study hall the previous night because he had been performing *avodah* — priestly service. Rabban Gamliel was puzzled: *vechi avodah bizman hazeh minayin* — how is there temple service nowadays? Rabbi Tarfon replied by citing the verse *avodat matanah eten et kehunatchem*, in the context of *trumah*, which uses the language of service and declares that those who draw near improperly shall die. From this the *Gemara* derives a *hekesh*: eating *trumah* in the provinces is analogous to performing *avodah* in the Temple. Therefore, just as a *kohen* who served unknowingly while disqualified is not required to bring a *korban* — indeed, his *avodah* stands — so too a *kohen* who ate *trumah* while unknowingly disqualified is exempt.

The Gemara's conclusion, then, is that Rabbi Yochanan's extension of the *patur* principle to the *yevama* — a non-urgent case — represents a genuine *chidush* relative to the established *Tannaitic* precedents. All the prior cases either involved urgency (*zmano bahu*) or a special status of *avodah* applicable only to *trumah*. Rabbi Yochanan has gone a step further.

## Productive Acts

### Tiken Principle

The Gemara now transitions to 73a, to the *Mishnah*'s cases of *shechitah* performed on Shabbat for the *Korban Pesach* in various invalid configurations, and the question of why each results in liability — specifically, why each constitutes a productive *melachah* on Shabbat.

The background principle: on Shabbat, *kol hamikalkelin peturin* — any act that is destructive rather than constructive carries no liability. The *chiyuv* for a *melachah* requires a productive act. This creates a difficulty for the cases in the *Mishnah*: if one slaughters a *Korban Pesach* incorrectly — *shelo lishmah*, for the wrong owners, or in other disqualifying circumstances — the result is a *pasul korban*, a piece of meat that must be burned. In what sense was the *shechitah* a productive, constructive act?

Rav Huna bar Chinena posed this question to his son to bring before Rav Zreika, working from the premise that *makalkel bechabura patur* — that wounding, like any other *melachah*, is only culpable when productive. If you slaughter an animal *shelo lishmah* on Shabbat, what did you *tiken* — what did you fix or improve?

The Gemara answers: *tiken im alu lo yerdu* — you produced at least this benefit: a *pasul korban*, even though invalid, if its fats were placed on the *mizbe'ach* would not be removed. The act of *shechitah*, even invalid, creates a minimal legal improvement in the animal's status. That small positive consequence is sufficient to categorize the act as constructive and impose liability.

### Treifa Beseter

The *Mishnah* then addresses the case where the animal was slaughtered and was subsequently found to be a *treifa* with an internal defect — *treifa beseter*, a hidden *treifa*. In that case, one is *patur*. The implication of the *Mishnah*, as the Gemara reads it, is that had the *treifa* been evident externally — *begaluy* — one would be *chayav*. The Gemara asks: *mai tiken*? What was improved? A *treifa* slaughtered as a *korban* would have to be removed from the altar.

The Gemara answers: *tiken lehotzi midei gezeila* — the *shechitah* accomplished something. Had the animal died without *shechitah*, it would have been a *neveilah* — ritually impure and possibly subject to the prohibition of *gezeila* (theft) if taken by others. By performing *shechitah*, even of a *treifa*, one removed it from the status of *neveilah*. That is a sufficient productive dimension to establish liability on Shabbat.

### Avodah Zarah

Rav Avina then raises a more challenging case from a *Braita*: one who slaughtered a *chatas* on Shabbat, outside the Temple, and for *avodah zarah* — three separate violations, each *chayav kares* if done willfully, each *chayav* a *chatas* if done *beshogeg*. The Gemara thus says one would bring three sin offerings. But Rav Avina's question is: *mai tiken*? What constructive act was performed?

The answer of *lehotzi midei neveilah* does not apply here. Something slaughtered for *avodah zarah* is treated as *tamei*, indeed bearing *tumah b'ohel* according to the Gemara in Shabbat — a severity beyond that of ordinary *neveilah*. The *shechitah* did not remove the animal from *tumah*; it replaced one severe status with another, arguably worse one.

The Gemara answers through Rav Avira: *shemotzi'o midei eiver min hachai* — the *shechitah* at least removed the prohibition of *eiver min hachai*, the limb of a living animal. Before *shechitah*, anyone consuming a limb of that animal — certainly a *ben Noach* — would have violated *eiver min hachai*. After *shechitah*, that specific prohibition no longer applies. Even if what remains is *neveilah*, *tamei*, and *tikroves avodah zarah*, it is no longer *eiver min hachai*. This minimal improvement suffices to render the act productive and impose *chiyuv*.

Notably, Rashi points out explicitly that this benefit is relevant to the *ben Noach*. This raises an interesting implication: a *ben Noach* is prohibited in *eiver min hachai*, yet apparently is not prohibited in *tikroves avodah zarah* — since if trading one for the other provided no benefit, the answer would fail. Although a *ben Noach* is certainly warned against *avodah zarah* itself, perhaps the status of *tikroves avodah zarah* — the offering of *avodah zarah* — does not carry the same prohibition for a *ben Noach*.

Tosafot also notes that the *tumah* status of *tikroves avodah zarah* that the Gemara here treats as *d'Oraita* appears elsewhere to be *d'Rabbanan*, and addresses that tension.

## Akirah Debate

### Asham to Olah

Having addressed the Shabbat liability questions, the Gemara returns to one final matter arising from the last case of the *Mishnah*: you slaughtered the *Pesach* and it was discovered that the owners had already withdrawn. You are *patur* because you were *onus* — you could not have known. This opens a broader discussion about *akirah* — the question of whether a *korban* that can no longer be used for its original purpose requires an active redefinition to become valid for another purpose, or whether it is automatically redefined.

Rav Huna reports in the name of Rav: if you have an *asham* — a guilt offering — that was set out to *reiyah* (pasture), because the owners had died and the *halacha* is to let it graze until it acquires a *mum*, at which point it is redeemed and the money used for a communal *olah* — and before acquiring a *mum* you slaughtered it *stam*, without specifying its purpose, it is *kasher l'olah*. It automatically counts as an *olah*, since that was its intended destination all along. The money, and therefore the identity, was already heading toward an *olah*.

### Rav's Position

From this, the Gemara infers: *almah kasavar lo ba'ei akirah* — Rav holds that once a *korban* can no longer be used for its original purpose and is in the pipeline toward another use, it requires no active redefinition. It is automatically transformed.

The Gemara immediately challenges: if that is so — *ki lo nitak nami* — why confine this ruling to after the animal was put out to pasture? The moment the owners die, the only possible destination for this animal is an *olah*. The *halacha* of *lo ba'ei akirah* should apply even before it was put out to pasture. The Gemara answers: *gezeirah l'achar kaparah atu lifnei kaparah* — it is a rabbinic enactment. Biblically, the same would apply even before *reiyah*. But rabbinically, if we permit using the animal as an *olah* immediately — before the visible, public act of setting it out to pasture — people who see an *asham* become an *olah* will think that *korbanot* can simply be switched at will. The act of *reiyah* serves as a visible marker signaling that this is a special category case.

The Gemara then attempts to prove this ruling from another *Mishnah*: an *asham* whose owners died or who were atoned for through another animal — the *Mishnah* says it grazes until it acquires a *mum*, is sold, and the money goes into the donation box for communal *olot*. Rabbi Eliezer holds it must die, treating it like a *chatas*. Rabbi Yehoshua holds it is sold and the money used for a personal *olah*. The Gemara notes: *bidamav in, aval gufo lo* — only the money may be used for an *olah*, not the animal itself directly. Why not use the animal directly? The Gemara applies the same rationale: *d'gazar l'achar kaparah atu lifnei kaparah*. Tosafot finds this proof somewhat circular — the explanation simply restates the same principle without independently demonstrating it — but the point is affirmed: Rav's position of *lo ba'ei akirah* is supported, with the *reiyah* requirement being a rabbinic fence.

### Pesach Challenge

Rav Chisda challenges Rav Huna: the *Mishnah* says that if the owners withdrew from the *Pesach* and this was discovered after *shechitah*, the *Pesach* is *pasul*, and a *Braita* teaches it must be burned immediately. If Rav is correct that no active redefinition is needed — that the moment the owners withdrew, the *Pesach* automatically became a *shelamim* — then why is it *pasul* at all? It is a *kasher shelamim*. The worst one could say is that it was slaughtered after the *tamid shel bein ha-arbayim* — somewhat out of sequence — but that would not be an intrinsic *psul*. One would simply wait overnight and burn it. It would not be burned immediately.

The Gemara's initial response is to suggest reversing Rav's ruling: perhaps Rav's formulation should not be read as *shachato stam kasher l'olah* — slaughtered it without designation and it is automatically an *olah* — but rather *shachato l'shem olah kasher* — it is valid only if one actively slaughtered it for an *olah*. Under this reading, Rav holds *ba'ei akirah*, that active redefinition is required. That would explain the *Mishnah*: since the owners withdrew and no one actively redefined it as a *shelamim*, it remains a *Pesach pasul*.

## Akirah Resolution

### Rabbi Chiya Bar Gamda

The Gemara now introduces Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda, who formulated a position that preserves the original reading of Rav — *lo ba'ei akirah* — while resolving the difficulty from the *Mishnah*. His view emerged as a consensus from a group: *nizreka mipi chabura*. The distinction is as follows. When does a *Pesach* require active redefinition to become a *shelamim*? Only when the *Pesach* still has a viable future as a *Pesach* — specifically, when the owners were *temei meit* and are therefore in line for a *Pesach sheini*. In that case, the *korban* has not lost its *Pesach* trajectory; it might yet be used as a *Pesach* on the 14th of Iyyar. Such an animal must be actively redefined to become a *shelamim*; it will not transform automatically.

But when the owners have simply withdrawn entirely — they have no future claim on any *Pesach* — the animal has no remaining *Pesach* pipeline to remain in. In that case, *lo ba'ei akirah*: it automatically becomes a *shelamim*, with no need for active redefinition.

This maps neatly onto Rav's original ruling. The *asham* set out to pasture is likewise not in any remaining *asham* pipeline — there is no residual use for it as an *asham* — and it therefore becomes an *olah* automatically. Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda's formulation vindicates that original position. The principle is: *ba'ei akirah* only when the *korban* remains in its original pipeline; *lo ba'ei akirah* when that pipeline is closed.

The Gemara then restates the principle cleanly: *hayinu d'ba'ei akirah, hu d'ba'ei akirah; ha b'alma lo ba'ei akirah* — the type of *Pesach* that requires *akirah* is specifically that type; in a general case it does not.

The question then remains: how does this resolve the difficulty from the *Mishnah* regarding the *Pesach* whose owners withdrew? According to *lo ba'ei akirah*, it should automatically have become a *shelamim*. The Gemara notes that Rav himself cannot use the *nireh venidcha* answer — that it was once fit and then rejected — because Rav holds *ba'alei chayim einan nidchin*: living animals cannot be permanently rejected. This is a resonant principle: the possibility of change inheres in living things; they cannot be labeled and discarded as irrevocably invalidated.

### Nireh Venidcha

A further resolution is offered by Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua: the case in the *Mishnah* is specifically where the owners separated the animal before *chatzos* and then died after *chatzos*. This is significant because *chatzos* is the operative moment for the *Korban Pesach*. At *chatzos*, the animal was fully valid — the owners were alive and enrolled. Then it became unfit. This constitutes *nireh venidcha*: it was once fit (*nireh*) at the critical moment, and then was pushed away (*nidcha*). The principle *kol ha-nireh venidcha, shuv eino chozer venireh* — once something was fit and was rejected, it cannot be reinstated — applies here. The *Pesach* cannot revert to become a *shelamim*, because it has the stigma of having been valid and then rejected. This is why the *Mishnah* treats it as an intrinsically invalid *Pesach pasul*, burned immediately.

But the Gemara immediately notes: this answer works only within Rav's framework on the condition that Rav does not hold *ba'alei chayim einan nidchin*. Since Rav does hold that living animals cannot be permanently rejected, the *nireh venidcha* principle does not help him. The question therefore remains for Rav.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

Rav Pappa proposes: *ha mani Rabbi Eliezer hi* — the *Mishnah* follows Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Eliezer holds: *keivan sheshochet leshem Pesach pasul* — slaughtering another *korban* in the name of a *Pesach* is intrinsically invalid. Apply this here: once the owners withdrew, the animal automatically became a *shelamim* per *lo ba'ei akirah*. The *shochet*, not knowing this, continued slaughtering it as a *Pesach*. He was therefore slaughtering a *shelamim* for the purposes of a *Pesach*. According to Rabbi Eliezer, *hashochet acheirim leshem Pesach pasul* — slaughtering another *korban* for the purposes of a *Pesach* is *pasul* with an intrinsic *psul* — and that is why it must be burned immediately.

This is an elegant solution, but the Gemara objects: *ve'i Rabbi Eliezer hi, chatas nami mechayev* — if the *Mishnah* follows Rabbi Eliezer, why does the end of the *Mishnah* hold that one who slaughtered the *Pesach* without knowing the owners had withdrawn is *patur*? Rabbi Eliezer does not accept *to'eh b'dvar mitzvah* as grounds for exemption. He should hold one *chayav* a *chatas*. This is the very debate we began with.

One could respond that the *patur* at the end of the *Mishnah* rests on *ones* rather than on *to'eh b'dvar mitzvah* — how was the *shochet* to know the owners had withdrawn? Rashi makes this point. But the Gemara apparently understands that *to'eh b'dvar mitzvah* is at least a contributing factor in the exemption, and Rabbi Eliezer would not recognize it. The Rabbi Eliezer solution therefore cannot accommodate the *Mishnah* in its entirety.

### Yosef Ben Choni

The resolution comes through Rav Yosef the son of Rav Sala Chasida, before Rav Pappa: *ha mani Yosef ben Choni hi* — the *Mishnah* follows Yosef ben Choni, a *tanna* whose opinion we seldom encounter. Yosef ben Choni says: *hanishchatim leshem Pesach uleshem chatas pesulin* — things slaughtered for the purpose of a *Pesach* or a *chatas* are *pasul*. Just as a *Pesach* or *chatas* slaughtered for another *korban* is invalid, so too other *korbanot* slaughtered for the purposes of a *Pesach* or *chatas* are invalid.

This is substantially the same ruling as Rabbi Eliezer's on this point, but without the broader position of Rabbi Eliezer on *to'eh b'dvar mitzvah*. The *Mishnah* can therefore hold that the *shelamim leshem Pesach* is intrinsically *pasul* — *pasul b'gufo* — burned immediately, while separately holding, on the question of the *shochet*'s liability, like Rabbi Yehoshua: *to'eh b'dvar mitzvah patur*. *Alma psulah b'gufo hi, umishum hachi yisaref miyad* — it is intrinsically invalid, and therefore burned immediately. *Uvi'pturei, savar lah k'Rabbi Yehoshua* — and regarding exemption from a *korban*, it follows Rabbi Yehoshua. This is a fully coherent and internally consistent reading of the *Mishnah*.

### Investigation Factor

Rav Ashi offers a final answer: *Rav de'amar k'Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka*. This tanna adds a dimension of investigation as a factor in liability and exemption. He says: if there was time during the day to investigate and discover whether the owners had withdrawn, or whether they had died, or whether they had become *tamei*, then one is *chayav* — the failure to investigate is actionable. If there was no such time, one is *patur*.

This tanna also holds — and this is what is relevant for the *akirah* question — *ute'ubar tzurah vetatze leveit hasereifah*: you wait for its appearance to change overnight before burning it. This indicates that according to him, the *Pesach* whose owners withdrew is not intrinsically *pasul* as a *Pesach*. It is a *shelamim* automatically, it is simply *pasul* because it was brought after the *tamid*, and therefore one waits for it to become *notar* overnight before burning. This is entirely consistent with *lo ba'ei akirah* — automatic redefinition, without intrinsic *psul*.

### Burning Timeline

The Gemara asks: how do we know this reflects *lo ba'ei akirah* rather than reflecting the position of the school of Rabba bar Avuha, who holds that *even pigul* and all other invalid *korbanot* require waiting overnight before burning — derived through a *gezeirah shavah* of *avon avon* from *notar*? Under that position, even an intrinsically *pasul Pesach* would require waiting overnight, and no inference about automatic *shelamim*-status could be drawn.

The Gemara answers: the school of Rabba bar Avuha cannot be the basis here, because among the cases where Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka requires waiting overnight is the case where the owners became *tamei*. But if the owners are *tamei*, the *Pesach* is in line for *Pesach sheini* — and as Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda established, that case certainly requires *akirah*. So that *Pesach* is *pasul* intrinsically as a *Pesach* (without *akirah* it remains a *Pesach pasul*). Why then would one wait overnight? Only if we say that our tanna follows *lo ba'ei akirah* for the withdrawal case, treating it as a *shelamim* with only an extrinsic *psul*, while for the *tamei* case, since it needs *akirah* and lacks it, it is also intrinsically *pasul* — yet both cases share the rule of waiting overnight. That consistency can only be explained by the school of Rabba bar Avuha's blanket rule that *all* invalid *korbanot* wait overnight. Which means our tanna might be following that rule rather than reflecting *lo ba'ei akirah*.

The Gemara concludes: *ela mivarta k'deshanin meikara Yosef ben Choni hi* — the clearest answer remains the one already given. The *Mishnah* follows Yosef ben Choni regarding the intrinsic invalidity of *shelamim leshem Pesach*, and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the exemption from a *korban* for the *to'eh b'dvar mitzvah*. The *akirah* debate itself remains a dispute among *tannaim*: some hold that a *korban* whose original purpose has lapsed must be actively redefined for another purpose (*ba'ei akirah*); others hold it transforms automatically (*lo ba'ei akirah*), with the *reiyah* requirement for the *asham* being only a rabbinic fence and not a substantive condition.

# Pesachim 74

## Intro: Roasting Pesach

### Overview & Intro

With today's daf, 74a, we begin the seventh *perek*, *Keitzad Tzolin* — "How does one roast?" It is worth briefly situating this chapter within the broader arc of the masechta. The fifth *perek* focused heavily on the *shechita* of the *korban pesach* — issues of *shelo lishmah*, its timing relative to the *tamid*, and the intentions required for *korbanot* generally. It concluded with the actual bringing of the *korban pesach*, dividing the people into three groups, the recitation of *Hallel*, and the prohibition against owning *chametz* at the time of *shechita*. The sixth *perek* then addressed bringing the *pesach* on *Shabbat* — which preparatory acts override *Shabbat*, the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, and the question of the *chagiga* that accompanies the *pesach* and whether its preparations similarly override *Shabbat*. The *perek* also treated the case of one who erred and brought the *korban* incorrectly on *Shabbat* — whether that constitutes *to'eh b'davar mitzvah* or requires a *korban chatat*.

Now, with the *korban* already brought — whether on *Shabbat* or a weekday — the seventh *perek* turns to the preparation and eating of the *pesach*: the *mitzvah* to roast it and the mechanics of how that roasting is to be carried out.

## Spit Material Rules

### Pomegranate vs Metal

The *mishnah* opens: *Keitzad tzolin et hapesach?* — How would one roast the *korban pesach*? The answer: *mevi'in shfud shel rimon* — one would take a spit made of pomegranate wood. *Tochuv letoch piv* — one would insert it through the mouth of the animal, *ad beit nikuvato* — until it emerged from the opening at the other end. Then *v'noten et kra'av v'et b'nei me'av letocho* — one would place the legs and inner organs inside the cavity of the animal. This is the position of Rabbi Yose HaGelili.

It should be noted that by this point the fats — the *chelev* — have already been separated and burned on the *mizbe'ach*. What remains are the inner organs, which Rabbi Yose HaGelili says are reinserted into the cavity and roasted there.

Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *kemin bishul hu zeh* — placing them on the inside is like cooking. As the animal roasts, the juices accumulate inside the cavity and effectively cook the organs within — like a pot over a fire. His ruling is therefore *ella talin chutz lo* — one hangs the organs on the outside. As Rashi explains, one would insert them onto the spit itself above the animal's mouth, so that they are directly exposed to the fire and roasted independently, not enclosed within the cavity.

The *mishnah* then rules: *Ein tzolin et hapesach lo al hashfud v'lo al ha'askala* — one does not roast the *pesach* on a [metal] spit nor on a metal grate. The reason, as the *gemara* will explain, is that metal conducts heat: the portion of the spit exposed to the fire heats up, transfers that heat throughout the metal, and the animal ends up being partially roasted by the hot metal rather than directly by the fire. This violates the requirement of *tzli eish* — roasting by fire — and not by the medium of another object.

Rabbi Tzadok then cites a story: Rabban Gamliel instructed his servant Tevi to roast the *pesach* on a grate (*askala*). This is problematic on two counts — first, we just ruled against using a grate; second, the Rabban Gamliel who had a servant named Tevi lived after the *churban habayit*. That second tension is genuinely interesting and will need to be addressed, though we will leave it for now.

The *gemara* explains the rejection of the metal spit: *aidi dechami miktzaso cham kulo* — because if any part of it heats up, the entire thing heats up. The result is *v'kamtvei lei mei'achmas hashfud* — the animal gets roasted through the spit — whereas *rachmana amar tzli eish* — the Torah requires *tzli eish*, roasting by fire, *v'lo tzli mei'achmas davar acher* — not roasting mediated through something else.

### Other Woods Rejected

If the concern with metal is heat transfer, why not simply use a wooden spit of a different variety? The *gemara* works through the alternatives systematically. A palm branch: *aidi d'is lei shivi mafik maya* — because palm wood has grooves, and the moisture absorbed in the wood seeps out through those grooves. The result is *v'hava lei k'mevushal* — the water that collects against the *pesach* as it roasts creates something akin to cooking, which is less than ideal even if not a formal biblical violation of *bishul*.

What about fig wood? *Aidi d'mechalkhal mafik maya* — fig wood has sap that seeps out and similarly produces the effect of having liquid in contact with the roasting *pesach*. And what of oak, carob, or sycamore? *Aidi d'is bei kitrei mafik maya* — these species have knots. In order to use a branch as a spit, one must smooth it, which means cutting away the knots and exposing the interior wood beneath the bark. Once that inner wood is exposed, moisture and sap will seep out — again producing the liquid-contact problem.

But does pomegranate wood not also have knots? The *gemara* offers two answers. First, *she'ei kitrei* — pomegranate knots are smoother and do not require cutting away; they can be left as is. Alternatively, *binavga bar shata d'leis bei kitrei* — one uses a one-year-old sapling, which has not yet developed knots. As for the cut ends of the spit — one end protrudes from the animal's mouth and the other from the opposite end, so any moisture that seeps from the cut ends does not come into contact with the *korban*. The case for pomegranate wood is thus established through systematic elimination.

### Metal Spit Debate

The *gemara* notes that our *mishnah* does not follow the view of Rabbi Yehuda. A *baraita* records that Rabbi Yehuda argued: just as a wooden spit does not burn when inserted inside the animal — since it is protected from the flame — so too a metal spit inserted into the animal will not get hot and transfer heat, since it too is mostly interior. The Rabbis responded by drawing a fundamental distinction: *zeh cham miktzato cham kulo, zeh cham miktzato eino cham kulo* — with metal, if any portion heats up, the entire thing does; with wood, heat does not transfer along the length of the material. The *mishnah* therefore rules in accordance with the Rabbis: only a wooden spit, and specifically one of pomegranate wood, may be used.

## Organ Placement

### Organ Inside/Outside

Having established the mechanics of the *shfud*, the *mishnah* itself records the dispute about the inner organs. As noted, Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds they are placed inside the cavity, based on the verse *al kra'av v'al kirbo* — it is roasted together with its limbs and intestines. Rabbi Akiva counters that this arrangement creates a cooking effect inside the cavity, and therefore the organs must be placed outside, directly on the spit.

### Gadi Mekulas Term

A *baraita* elaborates on the terminology. Rabbi Yishmael calls the arrangement of organs inside the cavity *tuch tuch* — evoking the bubbling, pot-like sound of the juices as the animal roasts, which simultaneously highlights why Rabbi Akiva objects to it. Rabbi Tarfon refers to the whole-roasted animal, presumably with organs on the outside as per Rabbi Akiva's position, as a *gadi mekulas* — a helmeted kid. Rashi explains the etymology: *mekulas* derives from the word for a bronze helmet (*kova nechoshet*), since the organs, placed on the spit above the head of the animal, resemble a helmet atop a warrior's head. Rabbi Yishmael, then, was describing the inner-cavity arrangement, while *gadi mekulas* as Rabbi Tarfon uses it envisions the organs hanging above the head — the outer arrangement of Rabbi Akiva.

## Gadi Mekulas Rules

### Gadi Mekulas Defined

The *gemara* now connects this term to a practical prohibition in the present day. A *baraita* asks: *eizehu gadi mekulas de'assur le'echol b'leilei pesach bizman hazeh* — what constitutes the *gadi mekulas* that is forbidden to eat on the night of *pesach* nowadays? The answer: *kol shetzla'o kulo ke'echad* — anything roasted entirely as a whole. Roasting a whole goat or lamb in the manner of the *korban pesach* is prohibited because it too closely mimics what was done with the *korban*, and such mimicry is inappropriate in the absence of the *Beit Hamikdash*.

### Gadi Exceptions

Two exceptions will remove the prohibition. *Nechtach mimenu ever* — if even one limb was cut off from the animal — or *nishlak mimenu ever* — if one limb was cooked separately — then *ein zeh gadi mekulas* and the whole-roast does not constitute a *gadi mekulas*, and it is permissible.

The *gemara* probes these two cases. Regarding the case where a limb is cut off: even if that separated limb is then roasted together with the rest of the animal on the same spit, it is still not considered a *gadi mekulas* and is permissible. The cutting itself is sufficient to break the resemblance to the *korban*. As for the case where a limb was boiled — *nishlak mibaya?* — is there even a question? Should we need a special ruling for a limb that was cooked rather than merely cut? Rav Sheshet explains: the ruling refers to a limb that was cooked while still attached to the body — *deshalkia bimchubar* — for instance if a leg was somehow immersed in water and boiled while still connected to the rest of the roasting animal. Even in that unusual circumstance, the combination of a cooked limb, though still physically attached, suffices to distinguish the preparation from the *korban pesach*.

### Whole Roasting Query

Before moving on, it is worth pausing at a *Tosafot* near the top of the *amud*. Given that today one is permitted to roast the animal if it is not entirely whole, one might ask: what would the *halacha* be with respect to the *korban pesach* itself if it were roasted in pieces rather than as a whole unit? Tosafot writes that while *lechatchila* there is a *mitzvah* to roast it whole, *bediavad* if it was not roasted whole the *korban* is not rendered *passul*. The proof is drawn from a later passage in the *gemara*. This is a meaningful distinction: the whole-roasting is obligatory as an ideal but does not define the validity of the offering after the fact.

## Blood Removal Rules

### Mulyasa Problem

The *gemara* now transitions into a lengthy discussion that reads, as the lecturer observes, as though it could have come straight from the pages of *Chullin* — a detailed treatment of blood removal from meat. The occasion is the *mulyasa*: a bird stuffed with ground meat, to be roasted without prior salting. The question is whether the roasting process will adequately draw out the blood both from the bird itself and from the ground meat stuffed inside it.

Before entering the specifics of the *mulyasa*, it is essential to understand the underlying principles of blood removal. Blood is prohibited only when it has left the meat and returned to it. Blood that remains in its natural state within the flesh — not pooled, not released — is not forbidden in that form. One could, in theory, eat raw unsalted meat, since the blood within it has not undergone the forbidden process of leaving and returning.

The primary method of preparing meat is salting: salt draws out the blood, which then runs off the meat, and the meat can subsequently be placed in a pot for cooking. However, roasting over fire is also an accepted method of blood removal. The critical distinction between salting and roasting is this: when one salts meat, the goal is complete blood extraction, after which the meat may be placed in a pot — since there is no blood left to come out and re-enter. With roasting, even if not all the blood is extracted, the blood that remains is not problematic as long as the meat is not subsequently placed in a pot, because whatever blood came out fell away from the fire and whatever remains inside never underwent the forbidden cycle. Roasting well enough will extract all the blood and permit subsequent cooking; roasting less thoroughly is still acceptable as long as no pot is involved.

Now, with the *mulyasa*: the ground meat is stuffed inside the bird, and neither has been salted. As the bird roasts, blood is drawn from the ground meat stuffing. But to exit the bird, that blood must first pass through the walls of the bird's body. There is a genuine concern that the blood from the stuffing, on its way out, gets absorbed by the bird's flesh — in which case the bird's flesh has absorbed blood that came out of another piece of meat, which would render it forbidden.

### Rava vs Abaye

Rava rules: *hai mulyasa sharya* — this stuffed bird is permissible. Abaye challenges him: *v'ha kabla dama?* — but the bird absorbs the blood from the stuffing! Rava replies with the principle *ke-volo kach polto* — as it absorbs, so it releases. The same heat that drives the blood from the stuffing into the walls of the bird continues to drive it outward and out of the bird entirely. The absorption and release are part of a single continuous process driven by the fire.

### Pesach Proof

The *gemara* attempts to bring a proof for Rava's position from the *mishnah*'s ruling that one places the inner organs of the *pesach* inside the animal's cavity. Why is there no concern that the blood from the organs gets absorbed by the surrounding flesh? Is it not because we apply *ke-volo kach polto* — the blood drawn out by the heat from the organs likewise exits through the surrounding flesh? The *gemara* rejects this proof, however. *Shani hatam, kivan d'ika bei shechita d'mechalchel* — there it is different, because the place of the *shechita* is open, and that exposed incision — with its severed veins — creates a continuous flow of blood downward, which draws out all blood in the system with greater force. In the case of the *mulyasa*, we cannot assume this same facilitated drainage is present, particularly if the bird is not oriented with the *bei shechita* pointing downward.

### Heart Exception

The *gemara* next attempts another proof, this time from the *halacha* of the heart. When preparing a heart for consumption, one is required to cut it open and remove the pooled blood from the cavity before cooking or roasting. If one did not cut it open — *lo kora'o* — one may cut it open *after* cooking (*bishulov*) and it remains permissible. Rashi notes that *bishulov* here is not to be taken literally as cooking; it means after roasting. The case then would seem to support *ke-volo kach polto*: the blood in the cavity is drawn into the walls by the heat and then drawn back out again. 

The *gemara* rejects this proof as well, though with a striking claim: *shani lev d'shia* — the heart is different, because its walls are smooth. Rashi goes further — the walls of the heart are so smooth that they do not even absorb the blood at all: *v'lo bala*. According to this answer, *ke-volo kach polto* is not operative here, because there is no absorption in the first place. Indeed, Rashi suggests that on this reading, *bishulov* can be taken literally — even if the heart was actually cooked in a pot, since the walls never absorbed the blood from the cavity, there is nothing forbidden that re-entered the flesh. This is a striking position, difficult to intuit, though the physiological observation that the blood pooled in the heart cavity originates from elsewhere in the circulatory system rather than from the heart muscle itself may be relevant context — though that distinction would not, from a *halachic* standpoint, change the concern about absorption.

### Clear Liquids Test

The *gemara* records a related incident involving Ravina. Ravina was served a coated pigeon (*bar gozla*) that had been prepared for Rav. Rav said: *ei ma'ali taphlei havu li v'achilna* — if the outer coating has taken on good flavor from the bird, give it to me and I will eat it. Ravina ate it himself. The point is that Rav expressed interest in the juices absorbed by the coating as an indicator of good roasting, and showed no concern that the coating had trapped blood.

More instructive is an incident involving Rava at the home of the *Reish Galuta*, where he was served a coated goose. Rava said: *ilo de-hazisei de-zig ke-zuza chivra* — had I not seen the juices flowing off clear, like a white coin, *lo achli minei* — I would not have eaten from it. The implication is that once Rava observed entirely clear liquids flowing from the roasting bird, he was satisfied that all blood had been expelled. Only after that evidence of complete blood removal was he willing to eat.

This raises the question: if we accept *ke-volo kach polto* universally, why should clear liquids be necessary? If whatever is absorbed is always released, why should the color of the flowing liquids matter? The *gemara* answers that Rava's case involved a coating of *chivarta de-shari* — a dense white flour — which actively traps juices and blood. For such a coating, the principle of *ke-volo kach polto* cannot simply be assumed; direct evidence of clear liquids is required.

### Flour Coating Rules

The discussion of coatings yields a tripartite *halacha*. If the coating is *smida* — a fine, loose flour, like scattered breadcrumbs with gaps between them through which liquids can freely escape — then *bein asmik bein lo asmik sharya*: whether or not the flowing liquids appear red, the coated meat is permissible. Even if blood is still visible, whatever came out of the meat has fallen away, and what remains inside never underwent the forbidden process.

If the coating is the dense white flour that traps juices, then *i zig ke-zuza chivra sharya* — only if one observes clear liquids flowing off is it permissible; *i lo assira* — if clear liquids have not been observed, it is forbidden, since one cannot assume complete blood removal.

If the coating is something intermediate — a medium flour — then *asmik assur, lo asmik sharya*: if the flowing liquids appear red, the coating has absorbed blood and it is forbidden; if they do not appear red, it is permissible, since the absence of red in the flowing liquids is sufficient evidence that no blood is being trapped.

### Mulyasa Final Rule

Having surveyed all the related cases, the *gemara* arrives at its *halacha* for the *mulyasa* itself. The debate between those who forbid it and those who permit it corresponds to the question of orientation: does it matter whether the *puma* — the opening of the bird, presumably where the neck was cut — is facing downward toward the fire, facilitating drainage, or upward, impeding it? The strict position would forbid the *mulyasa* even when the mouth faces down; the lenient position would permit it even when the mouth faces up. The final *halacha*: *mulyasa sharya afilu puma le'eil* — the stuffed bird is permissible even with the mouth pointing upward. This is a notably lenient conclusion, resting on confidence that the heat of the fire draws out all blood regardless of orientation.

## Red Meat Debate

### Umtsa & Coals

The *gemara* now turns to three related cases, all involving items with unusually high blood content, and in each case the question is whether placing them directly on coals — rather than salting or mounting on a spit over an open flame — adequately draws the blood out. The three items are *umtsa* (a piece of red meat), *bei* (testicles), and *mizraki* (what Rashi identifies as blood vessels — veins or arteries). In all three, the debate is between Rav Acha and Ravina. This is notable because a general principle applies throughout *Shas*: *Rav Acha l'chumra v'Ravina l'kula* — Rav Acha is characteristically strict and Ravina lenient — and we rule like Ravina leniently. These three cases are among the rare exceptions: *l'var mehani tlata d'Rav Acha l'kula* — in these three, Rav Acha takes the lenient position and Ravina the strict one — and we nonetheless rule like Rav Acha leniently in all three.

For the *umtsa*: if one cuts it and salts it, *afilu l'kdira shari* — it may even be placed in a pot afterward, since the salting has fully extracted all blood. If one places it on a spit (*b'shipuda*), it is permissible — *meidiv diyah*, the blood flows out. If one places it directly on coals (*atchei agumrei*): *pligi bah Rav Acha v'Ravina*. The one who forbids holds *mitzmat tzamit* — the coals cause the meat to contract and trap the blood within. The one who permits holds *mishav shaiv* — even coals draw the blood out. The *halacha* is like the lenient opinion: the coals draw out the blood.

One might ask: even if the coals trap the blood, why should that be forbidden? As we have established, blood that remains inside meat and never comes out is not problematic — only blood that exits and re-enters creates a prohibition. The concern here therefore likely pertains to the question of whether one may subsequently place the meat in a pot after using coals — if the coals did not fully extract the blood, cooking it afterward would cause blood to exit and re-enter.

### Testicles Rules

The ruling for *bei* (testicles) is identical in structure. If cut and salted, the meat may be placed even in a pot. If placed on a spit, it is permissible — *meidiv diyah*, the blood flows out. If placed on coals, Rav Acha and Ravina debate: one holds *mitzmat tzamit* (contraction traps the blood), the other *mishav shaiv* (the coals draw it out). The *halacha* follows the lenient view that the coals draw it out.

### Arteries & Shechita

The same structure applies to *mizraki*. If cut and salted, permissible even for a pot. On a spit — permissible. Then the *gemara* specifies: *beisa d'shchita l'tata* — the section of the neck where the *shechita* was performed should be oriented downward, so that the exposed veins and arteries at the cut allow blood to drain freely. When this condition is met, *meidiv diyah* — the blood flows out. On coals: the same debate between contracting and drawing, with the same lenient conclusion.

### Liver on Coals

The *gemara* adds a parallel case for the liver (*kavda*) placed on coals. Here the debate is between Rabba and Rav Yosef: one forbids on the grounds that the coals cause contraction and trap the blood; the other permits because the coals draw the blood out. The *halacha* is again: *mishav shaiv* — the coals draw the blood, and the liver is permissible.

## Vinegar Pickling

### Meat & Vinegar

The final sugya of the daf concerns meat placed in vinegar. The scenario: one takes a piece of meat (*umtsa d'atmik* — that has become very red) and places it in *chala* — vinegar. The meat's redness is the key indicator. When meat becomes red in vinegar, what does that signify? Did the blood get trapped inside, making the meat appear very red? Or did blood come out of the meat into the vinegar and then re-enter, producing the redness? If the latter, then both the meat and the vinegar are forbidden — the blood that exited and returned renders the meat forbidden, and the blood that is now in the vinegar renders it forbidden as well.

Following the *girsa* of Tosafot (based on the Bahag): *hi v'chalyie assur* — when the meat turns red, both the meat and the vinegar are forbidden. The blood came out of the meat, entered the vinegar, and returned to the meat — a complete forbidden cycle. *Lo asmit* — if the meat did not turn red, then *hi v'chalyie shari* — both the meat and the vinegar are permissible, since there is no evidence that blood left the meat and returned.

### Ravina's Vinegar

Ravina disagrees with this latter ruling. *Afilu lo asmit nami chalyie assur* — even when the meat did not turn red, the vinegar is still forbidden. His reasoning: *iy efshar d'leis bei shiriki d'dama* — it is impossible that the vinegar contains no strands of blood at all. Some blood must have exited the meat into the vinegar, even if not enough returned to cause the meat to change color. Therefore, even if the meat itself remains permissible — since it evidently did not re-absorb blood — the vinegar is minimally forbidden because it contains blood that came out.

### Vinegar Reuse

Mar bar Ameimar reported to Rav Ashi: his father (*abba*) would drink (*maglei gimei*) — that is, would freely use — the vinegar after pickling meat, as long as the meat had not turned red. According to an alternate version, Rav Ashi himself would drink such vinegar without concern.

Mar bar Ameimar then raised a further point to Rav Ashi: his father would never reuse vinegar a second time to pickle meat (*hai chala d'chalifei chada zimna, tu lo tanni chalifei chalifei*). This prompts a question from the *gemara*: how is reused vinegar any different from weak vinegar that we are permitted to use for pickling in the first place? If weak vinegar is acceptable, why should strong vinegar that has been used once be rejected?

### Fresh Vinegar Power

The *gemara* resolves the distinction: *hasam issa le-keifa de-peiri be-aneih* — in the case of fresh weak vinegar, even if it is weak, it retains the original power of the fruit (*keifa de-peiri*) in its natural, unspent form. *Hacha leisa le-keifa de-peiri be-aneih* — here, in reused vinegar, the original power of the fruit is no longer intact, since it has already been expended in the first round of pickling. The pickling efficacy of vinegar depends not merely on its current strength but on whether its natural properties remain intact. Once spent, it is qualitatively different from fresh vinegar of equivalent concentration, and therefore unsuitable for reuse.

With this, the *gemara* concludes its extended discussion — one that, as noted, reads very much like *Chullin* — of the principles governing blood removal from meat through salting, roasting, and pickling in vinegar.
