# Pesachim 75

## Rabban Gamliel & Grate

### Grate Paradox

The *daf* opens two lines from the top of the page, within a *perek* that has been focused on the proper manner of roasting the *korban pesach*. The earlier discussion treated the type of wooden spit required — one that does not exude moisture, so the roasting is not akin to cooking — and the prohibition of a metal spit, which heats up and thereby roasts the meat through the heat of the metal rather than the direct heat of the fire. The *gemara* now turns to a line in the *mishna* that had prohibited roasting on a metal grate, immediately following which the *mishna* itself records a story: Rabban Gamliel instructed his servant Tavi to go and roast the *pesach* on a grate. The difficulty is glaring. The *gemara* asks: *maaseh listor?* — is this story being brought in order to contradict the very *halacha* just stated?

### Chasuri Mechasra

The *gemara* resolves the problem by invoking the principle of *chasuri mechasra vehachi katani* — the *mishna* is missing some words, and it must be read as follows: *ve'im askala menukevet mutar* — if the grate has perforations, it is permitted. A standard grate has a criss-cross pattern creating a solid surface; a *menukevet* grate, by contrast, has wide enough gaps between its bars that the meat can be suspended between them, resting over the fire directly rather than on the metal. In such a case, the meat is not genuinely roasting on the grate at all but is supported by it while the fire roasts it from below. Only then is it permissible. Rabbi Tzadok's account of Rabban Gamliel and Tavi is accordingly read as referring to this perforated variety. As with any *chasuri mechasra*, the reading is admittedly difficult, since once the meat is truly suspended between the bars, one wonders whether one is meaningfully roasting on the grate at all.

### Rashash Solution

There is, however, a far more compelling reading of the *mishna* — one that is both closer to the *pshat* and historically illuminating. The *Rashash*, a nineteenth-century commentator whose sharp and incisive notes appear in the back of the *gemara* (he was a wealthy businessman who paid to have his commentary included, a phenomenon that might appear to be a modern invention of the vanity press, though clearly it is not), offers the following observation. The Rabban Gamliel associated with Tavi the servant is, by all evidence, the Rabban Gamliel who lived after the *churban habayis*. What, then, is he doing instructing his servant to roast the *pesach*? The *Rashash* notes that in the *mishna* in *Beitzah*, this same Rabban Gamliel is recorded as permitting the preparation of a *gedi mekulas* — a fully roasted goat — on the eve of *Pesach*, and furthermore that he would refer to this dish as a *pesach*. This connects directly to the earlier story of Todos Ish Romi, who had the people of Rome prepare a *gedi mekulas* on *erev Pesach* and who similarly *v'hayu korin lo psachim* — called it *pesach* — provoking the strong objection of the Sages, who felt it resembled an actual *korban pesach* offered outside its proper context.

### Todos & Shinuy

According to the *Rashash*, Rabban Gamliel — living after the *churban* — was indeed maintaining this quasi-*pesach* ritual, preparing a fully roasted goat and calling it a *pesach*. But in order to create a *heiker*, a recognizable distinction from the actual *korban*, he deliberately introduced a *shinuy*: he had it roasted on a grate, something that would never have been done with a genuine *korban pesach*. This reading answers all of the difficulties simultaneously: the post-*churban* context of this Rabban Gamliel, the *mishna* in *Beitzah* attesting to his practice of *gedi mekulas*, the connection to the Todos Ish Romi narrative, and the purpose of the grate as a marker of difference.

This reading carries considerable weight beyond the immediate exegetical question. It speaks to the broader tension that existed after the *churban* around how much of a pseudo-*pesach* ritual should be preserved. We Ashkenazim tend to be deeply cautious — indeed, there are real questions about whether one may even eat pan-roasted chicken on *Pesach* night — yet the *gemara* makes clear that there were those who were *davka makpid* to eat fully roasted meat, and that the *minhag makom shenahagu* may have been precisely to do so. Here it was not merely the practice of Todos Ish Romi but arguably of someone as great as Rabban Gamliel himself. The *Rashash*'s reading is thus not only the better *pshat* of the *mishna* but illuminates an entire dimension of post-*churban* religious life.

A student raised the question of what exactly *chasuri mechasra vehachi katani* claims to accomplish — is it a genuine reconstruction of an alternative text, or something more modest? The answer is that it is a working assumption: given a problem, the *gemara* must conclude that something is contextually missing, without necessarily asserting that an alternative manuscript existed. Some authorities hold that even the "missing" material may refer not to actual absent words but to implicit context that was never spelled out. As for the *halachic* authority of a reading arrived at through *chasuri mechasra* — once the *gemara* adopts that reading, it carries the weight of the *bavli*'s canonization, the same weight as any other interpretation the *gemara* endorses.

---

## Orlah & Fire Debate

### Orlah Setup

The *gemara* continues with a new question. Rav Chanina bar Idi poses the following to Rava bar Avuh: if one heats an oven using the shells of *orlah* fruit — from which one may not derive *hana'ah* — the *halacha* is that bread baked in that oven while the fire is burning is forbidden. But what if one heats the oven with such shells, then *vegarfo* — sweeps out the oven, removing all the wood — and then bakes bread in the retained heat, without the actual prohibited wood being present? According to the authorities who forbid baking in the *orlah* fire, what is the rule when only derivative heat remains?

Rava bar Avuh answers directly: *hapat muteret* — the bread is permitted. Since the bread is not deriving benefit directly from the wood, but only from the secondary retained heat, it does not constitute forbidden *hana'ah*.

### Category Distinction

His interlocutor challenges this from a tradition in the name of Rav Chanina Saba, who cited Rabbi Yoshiyah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: if one heats an oven, sweeps it out, and then roasts a *korban pesach* in the retained heat — without any fire — *ein zeh tzli esh*, that does not constitute roasting by fire, as required by the *pasuk*, which uses the phrase *tzli esh* twice, teaching that it must literally be over an open fire. The implication is striking: *ta'ama degallei Rachmana tzli esh tzli esh shtei pe'amim* — the only reason retained heat is excluded is because the Torah repeated the phrase. Had it said *tzli esh* only once, retained heat would have sufficed, meaning that the ordinary definition of *tzli esh* would naturally encompass derivative heat. If so, derivative heat should similarly be considered as coming from the fire — and bread baked by it in an *orlah* oven should be forbidden.

### Direct Contact

The response to this challenge is twofold. The first answer: *gali Rachmana hatam v'yalfinan minah* — once the Torah teaches explicitly by the *pesach* that only direct fire counts, that principle becomes a paradigm applicable across *halachot*, and derivative heat carries no significance. The second and more analytically rigorous answer distinguishes the two categories entirely. By *pesach*, the *pasuk* says *tzli esh* twice because otherwise one would have thought that retained heat of a fire *is* fire-roasted — since the heat originates in fire. The Torah thus teaches that the heat must remain anchored to the actual fire. But by *orlah*, the operative question is entirely different: *a'atzim d'isura kapid Rachmana* — what the Torah prohibits is benefit derived from the forbidden *wood*. Once the wood is no longer present, one is at best receiving benefit at two removes — the heat came from the wood, and the bread is benefiting from the heat. The nature of forbidden *hana'ah* requires a direct relationship with the prohibited object; when the wood is absent, that directness is broken.

One might note that this is the most obvious of the distinctions: in one case the question concerns the *quality* of the cooking process, and in the other it concerns the *source* of prohibited benefit. These are simply different categories governed by different definitions.

### Fire Definition

With the *orlah* question resolved, the *gemara* transitions to a broader conceptual inquiry into what constitutes *tzli esh* as a general matter, leaving behind the issue of forbidden wood and moving toward a sustained analysis of the definition of fire itself.

---

## Tzli Esh Definition

### Rebbi's Coals

A *braisa* is introduced: *chatcho u'netano al gabei gechalim* — if one cut up the *korban pesach* and placed it directly on coals without an exposed flame. Before addressing the central question, it is worth noting that *Tosafot* infers from this and other *gemarot* that *bedi'avad*, even if the *pesach* was not roasted whole, it remains *kasher* and may be eaten. *Rashi*, by contrast, reads "cut" not as actual dismemberment but as partial cuts made to lay the meat flat, without fully separating the pieces. Either way, the *halacha* regarding the requirement of wholeness is that it applies *lechatchila*, not as an absolute invalidating condition.

Returning to the main question: *Rebbi omer, omer ani shezeh tzli eish* — Rebbi declares that roasting over coals, even without an exposed flame, constitutes *tzli esh*. No other authority explicitly disagrees in this *braisa*, but Rebbi's position is stated prominently enough to invite challenge.

### Tzara'as Challenge

Rav Acha bar Ami raises a contradiction to Rav Chisda: does Rebbi really maintain that coals are considered fire? A *braisa* treating the laws of *tzara'as* is cited. The *pasuk* speaks of a *michvat eish*, a burn caused by fire, and the *braisa* asks: what if the skin was burned not by a flame but by a coal (*gachelet*), by hot ashes (*remetz*), by boiling plaster (*sid roteach*), by hot tiles (*gafsit rotachat*), or by anything else that derives its heat from fire, including water heated by a fire underground? How do we know these are included in the category of *michvat eish*? The answer is that the Torah uses the word *michvah* twice, *michvah michvah ribah*, the repetition serving as an inclusion of cases beyond direct flame.

The implication is pointed: *ta'ama di-ribei Rachmana michvah michvah* — the only reason a coal-burn qualifies as *michvat eish* is the doubled word. *Ha lo ribei Rachmana michvah michvah, gechalim lav eish ninhu* — without that doubling, a coal would not be considered fire. This suggests that the baseline definition of fire requires an exposed flame, not merely glowing coals. If so, how can Rebbi say that coals constitute *tzli esh* for the *korban pesach*?

### Wood vs Metal

Rav Chisda responds: *gachelet shel etz lo itzterich lei ribuya* — when the *braisa* needed a *pasuk* to include a coal-burn under *michvat eish*, it was not speaking about a coal derived from burning wood. A wood coal is clearly fire, even without an exposed flame, and requires no special derivation. *Ki itzterich kra le-gachelet shel matechet* — the inclusion was needed only for a piece of burning-hot metal, which is categorically different.

Why is heated metal different from a wood coal? Two reasons present themselves. First, a burning piece of wood can in principle be fanned into an exposed flame; its coal-state is simply a diminished stage of fire. Metal, by contrast, can never spontaneously generate a flame. Even when metal glows incandescently — and this is directly relevant to incandescent electric lighting, which is essentially *gachelet shel matechet*, a glowing metal filament — it does not produce a flame in the sense that wood does. Second, a related consideration in *hilchot Shabbat* is that the act of *kibui*, extinguishing, is defined partly by whether what remains after the fire is extinguished constitutes a coal — a transformed residue of the burning process. Wood becomes coal; metal that cools simply returns to inert metal.

This *sugya* bears directly on the question of whether turning on an incandescent light on *Shabbat* is a *de-oraita* violation and whether turning it off constitutes a *de-oraita* act of *kibui*. Some authorities, in order to underscore that incandescent lights are genuinely *eish*, deliberately used them for *havdalah* and recited *borei meorei ha-eish* over them. The question of *kibui* remains genuinely complex, as the metal filament does not produce a coal when extinguished. Fluorescent lights, which function through excited molecules rather than a glowing filament, are generally not considered *de-oraita* by anyone. For any practical ruling on these matters, one should consult a *posek*.

Returning to the *sugya*: the answer is satisfying. Rebbi's position that wood coals constitute *tzli esh* for the *korban pesach* stands unchallenged, since the *tzara'as braisa*'s derivation concerned only the anomalous case of heated metal, not ordinary wood coals.

### Bat Kohen Case

The *gemara* now pivots in the opposite direction, raising a case that would seem to push the definition of fire *beyond* even what Rebbi claims. The *pasuk* in the Torah states that a *bat kohen* who commits adultery is put to death *ba-esh tisaref* — she shall be burned in fire. Rav Masna explains: *psila shel avar hayu osim lah* — a strip of lead was heated until molten and poured down her throat. This, then, is the method of *sereifa* — the court-imposed death by fire. Yet molten metal is clearly not fire itself; it is only heated by fire. If so, it would seem that even metal heated by fire is included in the category of *eish*, going further even than Rebbi's position on wood coals.

The *gemara* responds: *shani hatam* — that case is different. The *pasuk* states *ba-esh tisaref*, with *ba-esh* preceding *tisaref*. The word *tisaref* appearing last is the operative term: *lerabot kol srefot haba'ot min ha-eish* — it includes any burning that derives from fire, even if not fire itself. It is the word *tisaref*, not *ba-esh*, that does the work. *Ve-kol she-ken eish atzmah* — actual fire itself certainly suffices, but that is not the limiting principle.

One might then ask: if anything that derives from fire counts for *sereifa*, why not simply surround the condemned with bundles of wood and burn her on a pyre? The *gemara* answers with a *gezeirah shavah* of *sereifa-sereifa* from the death of the sons of Aharon: just as their death involved *srefat neshama ve-guf kayam* — the soul destroyed but the body left intact — so too the court's *sereifa* must leave the body intact. Only the inner burning, the life, is extinguished; the body is not consumed. This explains why actual fire is excluded and why molten lead poured into the body serves as the method.

It is worth pausing on this principle. Contemporary scholarship has debated the *halachic* and philosophical basis for *Chazal*'s insistence on this mode of execution. Yair Loberbaum, in his work *Tzelem Elokim*, argues that *Chazal* treated the physical body as bearing the image of God and therefore prohibited its mutilation. Dvorah Steinmetz, in what may be a more persuasive argument based on a consistent reading of the *arba misos beis din* in *Sanhedrin*, argues differently: the court derives its license to take human life precisely from its role as the arm of divine justice, and therefore the execution must most closely approximate a natural death — one in which the soul departs while the body remains. The mutilation of a body by a pyre would be inconsistent with this framework. Whichever reading one finds more compelling, both agree that the practical requirement is a death in which *neshama nisrefet ve-guf kayam*.

### Rav Nachman

Given the constraint that the body must remain intact, why use molten lead specifically rather than, say, boiling water or another heated liquid poured down the throat? The *gemara* answers: *mishum de-Rav Nachman* — because of the principle articulated by Rav Nachman. *D'amar Rav Nachman amar kra, ve-ahavta l'rei-acha kamocha* — the *pasuk* commands love of one's fellow as oneself — *beror lo misa yafa*, choose for him a pleasant death. Even at the moment of execution, the obligation of love toward one's fellow requires choosing the most merciful, quickest means available. Molten lead, however horrific it sounds, presumably causes nearly instantaneous death. Boiling water, by contrast, would not.

But the *gemara* then asks: if the principle of *beror lo misa yafa* already suffices to mandate the quickest method, why do we need the *gezeirah shavah* from *bnei Aharon* at all? The answer: without the *gezeirah shavah*, one would never have known that pouring molten lead constitutes *sereifa*. One might have thought that *ba-esh tisaref* required actual flame, and that to make it as quick and merciful as possible, one should simply make a very large pyre — as in the harrowing account of Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon, who was wrapped in a Torah scroll, surrounded by bundles of wood (*chavilei zemoros*), and ignited by the Romans. The *gezeirah shavah* teaches that such a method is not the required — or permitted — form of court-imposed *sereifa*, and once we know that molten lead qualifies, *beror lo misa yafa* directs us to that method as the most merciful.

### Parim Restriction

The *gemara* now challenges from the opposite direction. The *pasuk* regarding the *parim hanisrafim* — the cows that are burned outside the *Beis HaMikdash* when their blood has been sprinkled within the *Kodesh Kodashim* — states *u-srafo oto al ha-etzim ba-esh*. A *braisa* teaches: *ba-esh ve-lo be-sid ve-votach* — this burning must be with actual fire, not with boiling plaster, hot tiles, or other materials heated by fire. So here, unlike the case of the *bat kohen*, derivative heat is excluded. How does one account for the asymmetry?

The *gemara* answers with a close reading of word order. By the *bat kohen*, the *pasuk* reads *ba-esh tisaref* — *ba-esh* first, *tisaref* last. The final word determines the operative category: *tisaref*, burning in any form, is what matters, and the word *ba-esh* merely indicates the source. By the *parim hanisrafim*, the *pasuk* reads *u-srafo oto al ha-etzim ba-esh* — the word *ba-esh* appears last. *U-le-vasof esh* — fire is the final and defining word, *de-esh in midai achrinei lo* — only fire, not derivative heat. This hermeneutical principle — that the final term in a *pasuk* carries definitional weight — is striking, though as *Tosafot* notes, one might ask why standard principles such as *klal u-frat u-klal* are not applied instead. The underlying logic, however, is intuitive: what is stated last receives the emphasis.

The *gemara* then anticipates a further question: another *pasuk* by the *parim hanisrafim* states *al shefech ha-deshen yisaref*, ending with *yisaref*, a form of *sereifa* — should this not then include derivative heat? The *gemara* responds: *hahu yisaref mibaei lei le-khid-tanya* — that second *yisaref* serves an entirely different function. A *braisa* derives two teachings from it: first, that the burning is performed even if there are no ashes currently at the designated location outside the Temple grounds; and second, *yisaref af al pi she-hitzisu or be-rubo* — even once the majority of the animal has caught fire, the obligation to actively attend to the burning continues. One may not simply walk away and allow it to finish on its own.

The overall structure of this extended *sugya* can now be summarized. Rebbi holds that wood coals constitute *tzli esh* for the *korban pesach*. The *tzara'as* case, which seemed to require an exposed flame, in fact speaks only of heated metal, not wood coals. The case of the *bat kohen*, which seemed to include even heated metal in the *eish* category, does so only through the word *tisaref*, not *ba-esh* — so it does not reflect the ordinary definition of fire. The *parim hanisrafim* requires literal fire because *ba-esh* is the final word of the relevant *pasuk*. The case of *tzara'as* requires real fire — or, at minimum, the doubling of *michvah* is needed to include derivate heat. Rebbi's position — that wood coals constitute *tzli esh* for the *korban pesach* — thus remains intact.

---

## Gachlei Esh

### Ravina Reorder

As a further defense of Rebbi's position, Ravina offers an alternative reading of the *tzara'as braisa* itself. Rather than saying the *braisa* was discussing heated metal, Ravina proposes *kroch u-teni* — rewrap the text, meaning reorganize the categories. In his reading, the opening clause — "I know only that one burned by fire is included" — should encompass both a flame and a coal, since a wood coal is obviously fire. The doubled *michvah* is then needed only to extend the category to the further cases: hot ashes, boiling plaster, hot tiles, and water heated by underground fire. This reading places the coal firmly in the baseline fire category without any need for a special derivation, directly supporting Rebbi. While *kroch u-teni* does not add entirely new words as *chasuri mechasra* does, it does reorganize the structure of the *braisa* — it is a recategorization rather than a wholesale reconstruction.

### Whisper Coals

Rava now raises a fresh challenge. *Mi amar Rebbe gechalim ikru eish* — did Rebbi really say that coals are fire? A *midrash halacha* is cited dealing with the *kohen*'s taking of *gechalei eish* from the outer *mizbeach* on *Yom Kippur*. This is the central act of the *Yom Kippur avoda* involving the *ketores*: the *kohen* takes fire-coals (*gechalei eish*) from the outer altar into a fire pan, carries them into the *Kodesh Kodashim*, and deposits the *ketores* on top of them, filling the inner sanctum with incense smoke. The term *gechalei eish* occupies a precise intermediate space: it is neither pure *gechalim* — coals — nor pure *eish* — fire. What exactly does it require?

The *braisa* teaches: *yachol omemos* — perhaps even smoldering coals would suffice. *Talmud lomar eish* — the word *eish* teaches that the coals must be more than merely smoldering. *I eish, yachol shalheves* — if it had only said fire, perhaps an exposed flame would be required. *Talmud lomar gechalei* — the word *gechalei* teaches that it need not be a full flame. *Ha keitzad? Meivi min ha-lochashos* — the resolution: one brings from the *lochashos*, the whispering coals, the coals that still carry the living sound of fire within them.

### Braisa Logic

The *gemara* immediately notes an internal contradiction in this *braisa*. From the *reisha*: the possibility of smoldering coals sufficing was rejected by the word *eish*, implying that *lochashos* — one step above smoldering — are themselves considered *eish*. But from the *seifa*: the possibility of an exposed flame was rejected by the word *gechalei*, implying that even *lochashos* — which are below a flame — are not in the *eish* category. So which is it? Are whispering coals *eish* or not?

The *gemara*'s difficulty is that it assumes a strictly binary system: something is either a coal or a flame, with no intermediate category. The simple reading of the *braisa* — that whispering coals occupy a middle ground — is rejected as conceptually incoherent. The *gemara* therefore demands: in which of the two binary categories do whispering coals naturally belong?

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet reads the *braisa* as follows: *gechalei* — coals — might have been taken to include both smoldering and whispering coals. *Talmud lomar eish* — the word fire then tells you that whispering coals are *not* in the coal category. *I eish*, had it only said fire, one might have required an exposed flame. *Talmud lomar gechalei* — the word coals brings you back, teaching that even whispering coals — which are below an exposed flame — count. In this reading, whispering coals are situated within the *gechalim* category as their baseline classification; they are included in the composite term *gechalei eish* only because both words together bracket them in. *Eish* alone would have meant only a flame; *gechalei* alone would have meant only fully extinguished, smoldering coals. The combination yields: whispering coals.

The critical implication is that whispering coals are, on their own, not *eish*. They are coals. This directly contradicts Rebbi, who said that roasting on coals constitutes *tzli esh*. *Mi kol makom, gechalim lo ikrei eish* — in any event, coals are not called fire; even whispering coals gain inclusion here only through the dual formulation, not because they are independently in the fire category.

### Abaye Counter

Abaye offers the opposite reading. *Yachol omemos velo lochashos* — the initial supposition was that "coals" meant only smoldering coals, not whispering coals — because whispering coals, being closer to an active fire, would naturally fall in the *eish* category. *Talmud lomar eish* — the word fire confirms: yes, even whispering coals are included. *I eish, yachol ratza shalheves yavi ratza gacheles yavi* — had the text only said fire, one might have thought there was a choice: bring either an exposed flame or whispering coals. *Talmud lomar gechalei* — the word coals tells you there is no such choice; it must be coals, not a free-burning flame.

In this reading, whispering coals are naturally in the *eish* category, and the word *gechalei* serves not to include them but to exclude the large exposed flame. This is consistent with Rebbi's position that coals — at least whispering coals — are *eish*. The *braisa*'s simple meaning, that the whispering coals occupy the intermediate space between two poles and are drawn in by the combination of both words, is thus what Abaye is also essentially recovering, though framing it in the binary terms the *gemara* demands.

### Rava Final

Rava then raises a difficulty against Abaye's reading. If the word *eish* alone would have permitted bringing either a flame or whispering coals at one's choice, that implies a flame could come *without* a coal. But *shalhevet belo gechelet heichi mashkachat lah* — how would one find a flame without any coal attached to it? Any flame burning from wood necessarily has coals.

The *gemara* answers: one might have taken a vessel, smeared it with oil, and lit it, producing a flame with no coal. Rava then dismisses even the need for a *pasuk* to exclude this: *hahu lav orach ara* — that method is simply not appropriate. Before an earthly king one would never carry a burning oil vessel to burn incense; *kol she-ken* before the King of Kings it would be unthinkable. No *pasuk* would be necessary to exclude it.

Rava therefore reformulates the reading: *gechalei* — coals — might have meant only smoldering coals, not whispering coals. *Talmud lomar eish* — fire tells you that whispering coals are included. *I eish, yachol yavi mechtza gechalim u-mechtza shalhevet* — had it only said fire, one might have thought one could bring something half flame and half coal, meaning coals with a very large and active exposed flame rather than quietly glowing coals. *Talmud lomar gechalei* — coals: it must be a coal-dominated form, not a blazing fire.

But if one might bring something with a large flame, does that not create the problem of appearing disrespectful before the King? The *gemara* resolves this: *de'aylei legavai havei kulei gechelet* — by the time one carries the coals from the outer altar into the *Kodesh Kodashim*, what began as a larger flame will have diminished to coals. One might therefore have supposed that the act of *taking* the coals from the altar (*lekicha*) could be with a larger flame, even if it subsides by the time of entry. *Talmud lomar, v'lakach melo ha-machta gechalei eish me'al ha-mizbeach* — the *pasuk* says that even at the moment of taking, it must already be *gechalei eish*, coals, not a large flame.

The bottom line of the entire *sugya*: Rebbi holds that at least whispering coals are *eish*, and roasting on such coals constitutes *tzli esh* for the *korban pesach*. Rava's final construction defends this position. Heated metal falls outside even Rebbi's definition of fire, though the *bat kohen* case extends further through a different *pasuk*. And the *yom kippur* ritual of *gechalei eish* — the very coals that the *kohen* would take from the outer *mizbeach* in the fire pan, carrying them while they were neither smoldering nor blazing but *lochashos*, whispering — illustrates precisely the category Rebbi has in mind.

---

## Pottery/Flour

### Oven Wall

The *gemara* now moves to the next *mishna*, which addresses practical problems that arise when roasting the *korban pesach* in an oven. One should picture not an open-air spit over a barbecue, but rather an oven with the fire burning inside and the *pesach* suspended directly over the fire within it — a more effective method, since the oven contains and concentrates the heat. The *Yerushalmi* does ask why this is permissible, since part of the cooking effect comes from the retained heat of the oven walls rather than the direct flame. The answer is that the oven walls contain but do not generate heat; they are an extension of the fire, not an independent source.

A problem nonetheless arises. As the *pesach* roasts, it may accidentally touch the pottery wall of the oven. That spot on the meat has now been roasted by the hot pottery — derivative heat — rather than directly by the fire. The ruling is: *yiklof es mekomo* — peel away the area of contact. That portion is not considered *tzli esh* and must be removed.

### Gravy Bounce

A further case: *nataf me-rutvo al ha-cheres ve-chazar alav* — drippings from the roasting meat fall onto the pottery wall or floor of the oven and then bounce back, being reabsorbed into the meat. Those juices were roasted by the pottery, not directly by the fire, and are therefore invalid. Since they have now been absorbed into the meat, peeling the outer surface is insufficient; the absorbed material must be extracted. The ruling is *yitol es mekomo* — one must dig in and remove the affected area where the juice was absorbed, not merely peel the surface.

### Flour Removal

A further complication: *nataf me-rutvo al ha-solet* — the drippings fall onto flour placed at the base of the oven. The flour, sitting in a hot oven, is itself extremely hot. When the juices hit the flour, they are roasted by the heat of the flour rather than directly by the fire. Those juices are therefore invalid, having not been subjected to *tzli esh* directly. Since one presumably wishes to eat the flour, the ruling is *yikmotz et mekomo* — one must remove a *kmitza*, a hand-grasp, of the flour at the point of contact, ensuring that none of the flour containing those juices is eaten.

### Pre-Roast Oil

Moving to a different type of problem: *sacho beshemen terumah* — one smears the *pesach* with *terumah* oil before or after roasting. Before addressing the post-roasting case, the *mishna* first treats the pre-roasting scenario. If the oil was applied while the meat was still raw, *yidichenu* — it may simply be rinsed off, since the oil has only adhered to the surface and has not been absorbed into cold raw meat. After rinsing, the group may eat it. If this is a group of *kohanim*, even without rinsing they may eat it, since they are permitted to eat *terumah*.

### Post-Roast Oil

If the oil was applied after the meat was already roasted — *im tzeli hu* — the situation is more serious. Roasted meat is absorbent, and even cold *terumah* oil applied to the surface is presumed to have been absorbed into the outer layer. *Yiklef et ha-chitzon* — one must peel off the outer layer, since that is where the oil is presumed to have penetrated. Deeper absorption is not assumed, so peeling the surface layer suffices.

### Maaser Sheni

The final case of the *mishna* shifts to a different *issur*. If one used *maaser sheni* oil rather than *terumah* oil — *sacho beshemen maaser sheni* — the group may eat the *pesach* with the absorbed oil, since *maaser sheni* is not forbidden to non-*kohanim* in the way *terumah* is; it must simply be consumed in Jerusalem. However, *lo yaasenu damim livnei chabura* — one may not charge the other members of the *chavura* for the oil, because *she'ein mochrin maaser sheni bi-Yerushalayim* — one does not sell or redeem *maaser sheni* in Jerusalem. The particulars of this prohibition will be addressed when the *gemara* treats that topic directly.

This final group of cases in the *mishna* thus represents the intersection of two bodies of law: the requirements of *tzli esh* and the proper roasting of the *korban pesach* on one side, and the laws of *kashrut* and *terumah* regarding absorption and the peeling of surfaces on the other. The practical question underlying each case is how deeply a foreign substance penetrates and how much of the meat must be removed to ensure that what is eaten has been properly subjected to *tzli esh* and contains nothing forbidden.

---

# Pesachim 76

## Ila'ah Gavar / Tata'ah G…

### Cham L'toch Cham / Tzone…

Daf 76 opens on the very last line of 75b, resuming from the *mishnah* studied the previous day. That *mishnah* addressed the case of a *pesach* that touches the pottery walls of the oven: if those walls are hot, the *pesach* is being roasted not directly by fire but by something that has absorbed heat, and the affected spot must be cut away. Similarly, if juices drip from the *pesach* and bounce back after being heated by the pottery walls, those juices cannot be eaten and the area they re-entered must be removed.

The *gemara* now introduces two foundational principles of *kashrus* — one on 76a and one on 76b — that are central well beyond the context of *Pesachim*. It is striking that they appear here in the middle of this tractate, but there they are.

*Itmar* — it was stated. The *gemara* begins with a tripartite framework for heat transfer between prohibited and permitted substances. *Cham l'toch cham, divrei hakol assur*: if something hot falls into something hot — say, a hot piece of meat falling into hot milk, or a hot piece of *chazir* falling into a stew — everyone agrees it is forbidden. The heat causes a transfer of taste. The operative threshold is *yad soledes bo*, commonly understood as approximately 110–115 degrees Fahrenheit, hot enough that one could not hold a finger in the liquid for more than a few seconds without pulling away. Some *rishonim* associate this threshold with cooking, but for *kashrus* the operative concern is heat sufficient to cause taste transfer, which is technically a lower standard — nonetheless, the ruling is *yad soledes bo*.

At the opposite pole: *tzonen l'toch tzonen, divrei hakol mutar* — cold into cold, everyone agrees it is permitted. If, for example, a cold apple falls into cold milk or cold *chazir*, rinsing suffices. There is at most a surface film; nothing penetrates. This assumes non-absorbent materials — an absorbent substance can complicate matters — but as a baseline, cold-into-cold poses no problem.

### Rav: Ila'ah Gavar

The difficult case is when one substance is hot and the other is cold: *cham l'toch tzonen v'tzonen l'toch cham* — something hot into something cold, or something cold into something hot. A hot piece of meat falling into cold milk; a cold piece of meat falling into hot milk. What governs?

*Rav amar ila'ah gavar* — Rav says the upper one wins out. According to Rav, the thermal outcome is determined by the substance on top. If the top substance is hot, it heats the bottom, and there is a transfer of taste — forbidden. If the top substance is cold, it cools everything down, and there is no transfer — permitted.

### Shmuel: Tata'ah Gavar

*V'Shmuel amar tata'ah gavar* — Shmuel says the lower one wins out. The bottom determines the result. If the bottom is hot, it heats everything upward — forbidden. If the bottom is cold, everything cools — permitted. This is the direct inverse of Rav's position.

### Heat Rises Physics

One might pause to note that from the standpoint of physics, Shmuel's position has a certain intuitive support: heat rises. If the hot substance is on top and the cold is on the bottom, much of the heat from above dissipates upward into the air rather than conducting downward. The ruling, of course, was reached before modern thermodynamics, but it is at least consistent with our understanding — *baruch Hashem*, as the lecturer observes, the halachic ruling and physical reality are not at odds here.

---

## Nataph Merutvo Al HaCher…

### Pesach Juice on Pottery

The *gemara* now attempts to derive proof from the *mishnah* itself. *Tnan* — we taught: *nataph merutvo al hacheres v'chazar elav* — if some of the juices of the *pesach* drip down onto the pottery and then bounce back, one must cut away the area of the *pesach* where the juice was reabsorbed — *yitol mekomo*. The *gemara's* initial assumption is *becheres tzonenet* — the pottery was cold to begin with.

### Rav's Explanation

*Bishlama le-Rav* — the *mishnah* works well according to Rav, who says the upper substance wins. The hot gravy drips from above onto the cold pottery. Since the upper is hot, *ila'ah gavar*, the pottery becomes heated. *Meratach lei lacheres* — the pottery gets hot. And then: *vehadar cheres umeratach lei lerutva* — the now-hot pottery turns around and roasts the gravy. When that gravy — which has now been heated by something other than fire — bounces back into the *pesach*, *kamatli lei lePesach machmas chamimusa decheres*: the *pesach* is being roasted by the heat of the pottery, or more directly, the gravy that was improperly heated is being reabsorbed. *Rachmana amar tzeli esh v'lo tzeli machmat davar acher* — the Torah requires roasting by fire, not by some other medium that itself absorbed fire. That explains why one must cut away the affected part.

### Challenge to Shmuel

*Ela l'Shmuel d'amar tata'ah gavar* — but according to Shmuel, who rules that the bottom wins: if the pottery is cold and the hot gravy falls onto it from above, the bottom is cold. *Akorei meikar lei lerutva* — the cold pottery should be cooling off the gravy. *Amai yitol mekomo* — why then must anything be cut away? The gravy was never heated by the pottery; it was simply cooled. It should be just as if the gravy remained in contact only with the fire, and there should be no problem.

### Pottery Was Hot

The *gemara* resolves this by anticipating an answer that Rav Yirmeyah will state explicitly in Shmuel's name regarding the flour case below: *hacha nami becheres rotachat* — here too, the pottery was not cold; it was hot. If both the gravy and the pottery are hot, then regardless of whether one follows Rav or Shmuel, there is unambiguously a problem. The debate between *ila'ah gavar* and *tata'ah gavar* is relevant only when one substance is hot and one is cold. When both are hot, the *mishnah* cannot serve as proof for either position.

---

## Nataph Al HaSolet

### Gravy Into Flour

The *mishnah* continues: *nataf merotevo al hasolet* — some of the gravy drips not onto hard pottery but into flour. The flour absorbs it rather than bouncing it back, but the problem is similar: if the *pesach's* gravy is heated by something other than the fire, it may not be eaten, and the affected area of the flour must be removed.

### Rav's Flour Explanation

*Ka salka daitakh besolet tzonenet* — the initial assumption is that the flour was cold. *Bishlama le-Rav d'amar ila'ah gavar*: according to Rav, the top wins. The hot gravy falls from above, heats the cold flour — *demartach lah lasolet* — and once the flour is heated, it turns around and roasts the gravy inside it. *Veka mitvei rotev machmat chamimuta desolet* — the gravy is now being roasted by the heat of the flour. *V'Rachamana amar tzli esh v'lo tzli machmat davar acher* — the Torah says fire-roasting, not roasting by a secondary medium, even one that was itself heated. Exactly the same structure as the pottery case.

### Shmuel Challenge Flour

*Ela l'Shmuel d'amar tata'ah gavar*: but according to Shmuel, the bottom wins. The flour is on the bottom and it is cold; the hot gravy falls in from above. The cold bottom wins, everything cools down — *ikorei ka meikar lei* — why must anything be removed? It makes no sense according to Shmuel's position if we assume the flour was cold.

### Hot Flour Resolution

*Amar Rav Yirmeyah amar Shmuel: besolet rotachat* — Rav Yirmeyah, citing Shmuel directly, resolves it: the *mishnah* is speaking of boiling hot flour, not cold. The flour was already hot. And it is from this ruling that the *gemara* extends the answer retroactively to the pottery case — *hacha nami becheres rotachat* — the pottery was also hot. In both cases, since both substances were hot, there is no challenge to either Rav or Shmuel.

It is worth noting in passing that *Tosafot* raises the question of *ein bishul achar bishul* — the principle that once something has been fully cooked, additional cooking has no halachic effect. The *mishnah* would presumably be speaking of a *pesach* that has not yet been fully roasted, so additional "roasting" by the pottery or flour does constitute a change in its status. *Tosafot* engages with this and attempts to fit it into the *mishnah's* cases.

One might also ask: if the gravy drips into a large quantity of flour, could *bitul* apply? In theory, yes — but *bitul* would not apply to the immediate area where the gravy fell, where there is a concentrated and identifiable taste of meat juice. One would focus the removal on that localized spot.

---

## Sach BaShemen Shel Terum…

### Oil on Pesach Rules

The *gemara* now seeks proof from a different part of the *mishnah*: *sach ba'shemen shel terumah* — if one rubbed *terumah* oil onto the *pesach*. If the group eating the *pesach* is a *chavurat kohanim*, no problem — *kohanim* may eat *terumah* and the *pesach* together. But if the group consists of non-*kohanim*:

### Raw Pesach Rinsing

*Im chai hu, yadi'chenu* — if the *pesach* is raw, simply rinse off the oil. This is the cold-into-cold case: a cold oil on a cold raw surface, and rinsing is sufficient.

### Roasted Pesach Peeling

*Im tseli hu, yiklof et hachitzon* — if the *pesach* is roasted, one must peel off the outer layer. Even if the roasted *pesach* is now cold, roasted meat is absorbent — unlike a hard smooth surface, it is porous and soft, comparable to a sponge rather than a stone. One cannot simply rinse off the surface of an absorbent material.

### Rav: Oil on Hot Pesach

*Bishlama le-Rav d'amar ila'ah gavar*: the *mishnah* works well according to Rav. The oil is on top, and the oil is cold. Since the upper wins, even if the *pesach* is hot, everything cools down — the oil does not penetrate deeply. Only the outermost surface absorbs the oil through natural contact, hence *yiklof et hachitzon* — peeling the outer layer is sufficient. There is no concern that the oil penetrated throughout.

### Shmuel's Oil Problem

*Ela l'Shmuel d'amar tata'ah gavar*: but if the *pesach* is hot and the bottom wins, the hot *pesach* should heat up the cold oil and cause it to be absorbed throughout — *mivla bala* — not merely in the outer layer. Why then does the *mishnah* say peeling is enough? If we follow Shmuel, the entire *pesach* should be forbidden to non-*kohanim* because the oil should have penetrated throughout.

### Oil Amount Limited

The *gemara* responds: *shani sicha de-mashu be'alma hu* — rubbing oil is different; it is only a minimal, surface-level application. Even if the *pesach* is hot and the bottom wins in principle, there simply is not enough oil to penetrate deeply. It remains limited to the outer shell. The *gemara* notes further that this is retained heat in the meat — the *pesach* is not sitting directly over a fire — which also limits how deeply the oil can penetrate.

One might wish this were a general *kashrus* principle — that a small amount of a forbidden substance need not be treated as absorbed more than superficially — but that is not how *halacha* generally operates. The *gemara* is making a specific, limited point about the mechanics of rubbing oil.

### No Proof From Mishna

The conclusion is that the *mishnah* cannot prove either Rav or Shmuel correct. In the pottery and flour cases, both substances were hot and the debate is irrelevant. In the oil-on-roasted-*pesach* case, the limited quantity of oil means the *mishnah* is consistent with both positions. The dispute between *ila'ah gavar* and *tata'ah gavar* remains unresolved from the *mishnah*.

---

## Baraita: Tata'ah Gavar

### Baraita Text

*Tanya kivsei d'Shmuel* — a *beraita* was taught in accordance with Shmuel. *Cham l'toch cham assur, v'chein tzonen she-nasan l'toch cham assur* — hot into hot is forbidden, and likewise cold into hot is forbidden. In both cases, the bottom is hot, and the bottom wins — that is Shmuel's position. *Cham l'toch tzonen v'tzonen l'toch tzonen, madiach* — hot into cold, or cold into cold, since the bottom is cold, simply rinsing suffices. This *beraita* is a direct ruling like Shmuel, and it is the basis for ruling *l'halacha* like *tata'ah gavar*.

### Objection to Hot Into Co…

But the *gemara* resists accepting the *beraita* as stated. *Cham l'toch tzonen madiach?* — hot into cold and you merely rinse it off? *Keivan d'cham hu*, since the upper substance is hot, *ad mekar lei* — while the cold bottom is in the process of cooling it down, *ee efshar d'lo bala purta* — it is impossible that nothing at all is absorbed in the interim. Heat transfer takes time; during that cooling process, some minimal absorption must occur. *Klipah miha nibei* — at the very least, a *klipah*, an outer layer, should be required.

### Amended Baraita

The *gemara* accordingly revises the *beraita*: *ela eima* — say instead: *cham l'toch tzonen, kolef* — hot into cold requires peeling off an outer layer. *Tzonen l'toch tzonen, madiach* — cold into cold, just rinse. This amendment now captures the nuance: even if the cold bottom wins and cools everything down, during the process of cooling, the hot upper substance causes some minimal absorption at the point of contact.

### Meat and Milk Baraita

A second *beraita* makes the identical point in the domain of *basar b'chalav*: *basar rote'ach she-nafal l'toch chalav rote'ach* — hot meat that fell into hot milk, *v'chein tzonen she-nafal l'toch cham* — or cold meat that fell into hot milk: *assur*, forbidden. The bottom is hot, the bottom wins. *Cham l'toch tzonen, tzonen l'toch tzonen, madiach* — if the bottom is cold, whether the falling substance is hot or cold, merely rinse.

### Second Objection

Again the *gemara* objects: *cham l'toch tzonen madiach?* — hot meat into cold milk and one need only rinse? *Keivan d'cham hu, ad m'karei lei, ee efshar d'lo bala purta* — while the cold milk is cooling off the hot meat, some absorption must occur. *Klipah miha ba'ei* — a *klipah* is at minimum required.

### Second Amendment

*Ela eima*: here too the *beraita* must be corrected. *Cham l'toch tzonen, kolef* — hot into cold, remove an outer layer. *Tzonen l'toch tzonen, madiach* — cold into cold, rinse.

### Kleipah Consensus

The upshot of both emended *baraitot* is this: the practical difference between Rav and Shmuel lies in which hot substance "wins." For Shmuel, the bottom wins when hot; for Rav, the top wins when hot — and whichever wins, it is as if both are hot, producing a full absorption requiring more than *klipah*. But both Rav and Shmuel would agree that when the "winning" side is cold, there is still a minimal transfer during the cooling process — and therefore at least *klipah* is required whenever one substance is hot, even if it is on the "losing" side.

*Tosafot* raises a practical question: when hot meat falls into cold milk, we require *klipah* from the meat — but how does one perform *klipah* on a liquid? *Tosafot* records two approaches. One is to estimate the volume of milk that would correspond to a *klipah*-thickness at the point of contact, and then require *shishim* against that amount in the remaining milk. *Rabbeinu Tam*, however, holds that the *klipah* requirement in this cold-bottom scenario is entirely *d'rabbanan* — a rabbinic stringency introduced at the end of the *sugya*, since fundamentally Shmuel's principle is that the cold bottom nullifies any concern. Consequently, where *klipah* is structurally impossible — as with a liquid — the rabbinic requirement does not apply, and the liquid is entirely permitted.

A related question concerns *iruy* — pouring boiling liquid in a stream onto something. One might reason: Shmuel says *tata'ah gavar*, so an uninterrupted stream of boiling milk poured onto cold meat would be cooled by the cold bottom and require only *klipah* at most. *Tosafot* addresses this and the resolution drawn from their discussion distinguishes between an uninterrupted stream — one that remains attached to the boiling source — and a broken stream. An uninterrupted pour is treated as an extension of the boiling vessel; the full force of the heat applies and *tata'ah gavar* does not apply for the duration of the stream. A broken stream, by contrast, falls under the standard analysis.

---

## Maliach K'Rotach

### Rav Huna Salted Exception

The *gemara* returns to the rule that cold-into-cold requires only rinsing. *Amar Rav Huna: lo shanu ela she-lo malcho* — this leniency applies only to unsalted meat. The rule that cold-on-cold merely requires rinsing assumes the meat has not been salted.

### Shmuel: Salted Like Hot

*De-amar Shmuel: maliach harei hu ke-rote'ach* — Shmuel teaches that something salted is halachically equivalent to something boiling. Just as heat causes absorption, so does salt. Accordingly, salted meat that falls into milk, even if everything is cold by temperature, behaves as if it were hot and cannot be resolved by mere rinsing.

### Rava: Heavy Salt Only

*Amar Rava*: not every degree of salting triggers this rule. *Lo amran ela she-eino ne'echal machmat malcho* — Shmuel's principle of *maliach k'rotach* applies only when the meat is so heavily salted that it is unfit to eat in that state. Rashi understands this as salted somewhat beyond the edible threshold, as one would salt meat for short-term preservation. *Tosafot* takes an even more stringent view, describing the level as the extreme salting used for long-term preservation, requiring substantial soaking to remove. *Avel ne'echal machmat malcho* — if the meat is still fit to eat despite the salt, it does not carry the status of *rotach* and remains in the category of cold, requiring only rinsing.

### Pigeon Case

The *gemara* relates a practical incident: *hahu bar gozala de-nafal le-khadda de-kamcha* — a pigeon that had been salted for the purpose of removing blood fell into *kamcha*, a dairy dip resembling sour cream or cottage cheese. *Sherayei Rav Chinana berei de-Rava mi-Pashrunya* — Rav Chinana permitted it and ruled that rinsing was sufficient.

### Rava's Praise

*Amar Rava: man chakim le-mishra milta ki hai, ilav Rav Chinana berei de-Rava mi-Pashrunya, de-gavra rabba hu* — Rava praised him: who but such a great scholar would have the wisdom to permit this? *Ki amar Shmuel maliach harei hu ke-rote'ach* — when Shmuel said that salted is like boiling, that was only when *she-eino ne'echal machmat malcho*, the meat is inedibly oversalted. But this pigeon, *ne'echal machmat malcho*, was still edible despite its salt, and therefore did not carry the stringent status of *rotach*. Rinsing was sufficient.

---

## Roasted / Porous / Spice…

### Roasted Cold Exception

The *gemara* now catalogues additional exceptions to the rule that cold-on-cold requires only rinsing. *V'hani milei, chai* — the leniency of rinsing applies to raw meat. *Aval tseli, ba'ei klipah* — if the meat is roasted, even if it is cold, a *klipah* must be removed. Roasted meat, even cold, is absorbent by its nature. A roasted piece of meat is soft and porous; one cannot assume that a foreign substance remains only on the surface, the way one might with a smooth non-absorbent material. It must be treated with the same removal of the outer layer that one would apply in a case of minimal heat transfer.

### Porous Meat Exception

*V'lo amrinan, ela deleit bei peila* — and even the *klipah* rule for roasted meat assumes the meat has no deep cracks or crevices. *Aval it bei peila* — if the meat does have significant cracks and fissures, even *klipah* is insufficient, because the foreign liquid can penetrate deeply into the interior through those openings. In that case the prohibition is more extensive.

### Spiced Meat Exception

*U-metubal betavlin* — similarly, if meat is heavily spiced, even cold, it is *assur*. Heavy spicing creates an absorbency analogous in effect to heavy salting: the surface becomes particularly receptive to drawing in foreign substances, even without heat.

### Absorbency Principle

The broader principle emerging from these exceptions is that absorbency — not just heat — drives halachic concern. The basic rule is that heat causes transfer and cold does not; hence cold-into-cold requires only rinsing. But that baseline assumes the cold substance is not independently absorbent. Where the substance has structural or chemical properties that cause it to absorb even in the absence of heat — roasting, spicing, cracking — the cold-rinsing rule no longer applies.

---

## Reicha Debate: Rav vs. L…

### Rav: Reicha Transfers

The *gemara* now introduces the second major principle of the daf, shifting from the question of contact-based heat transfer to the question of *reicha* — taste transfer through aroma without physical contact. *Amar Rav: basar shechuta shemena, she-tzla'o im basar neveila kechusha* — Rav states that if fatty *shechted* kosher meat is roasted alongside lean *neveila* meat, with no contact between them, the kosher meat becomes forbidden. *Maptemi mehadadi* — they fatten one another; the fatty kosher meat, through its vapor and aroma, draws out the flavor of the lean *treif* meat and absorbs it back. Rav holds that *reicha milsa hi* — aroma has halachic status and constitutes a transfer of taste. The case is striking: even the lean *treif* meat, which emits less aroma, still contributes enough through the fatty kosher meat's drawing power that the result is forbidden.

### Levi: Reicha Irrelevant

Levi goes to the opposite extreme: *afilu basar shechuta kachush she-tzla'o im basar neveila shamen* — even if the kosher meat is lean and the *treif* meat is fatty, so that the entire atmosphere is laden with *treif* aromas, the kosher meat remains permitted. *Reicha be'alma hu, v'reicha lav milta hi* — it is mere smell, and smell has no halachic status. Levi's position may carry a further implication: even if some aroma does in fact penetrate the kosher meat and alters its taste, *reicha* as such does not constitute the halachically operative concept of *ta'am* — taste. Only contact produces genuine *ta'am*; smell alone does not.

### Levi Practical Ruling

*Amar avid Levi uvda be-Reish Galuta be-gedi v'davar acher* — Levi actually rendered a practical ruling in the house of the *Reish Galuta*, permitting a goat that had been cooked in the same oven as a pig. Whatever the pig was doing in the *Reish Galuta's* household is left unaddressed, but the ruling was clear: according to Levi, the goat was entirely permitted.

---

## Two Pesachim Together

### Baraita Text

*Meitivei* — the *gemara* challenges. A *beraita* states: *ein tzolin shnei pesachim k'echad mipnei ha-ta'arovot* — one may not roast two *korban Pesach* animals side by side, because of *ta'arovot* — mixing.

### Mixing Question

What does *ta'arovot* mean here? Either the actual bodies of the two *pesachim* will become physically confused — one group might eat from the wrong animal — or the concern is that tastes will be exchanged through aroma transfer in the air. The second reading would present a direct challenge to Levi.

Consider: if one *pesach* absorbs the aroma and flavor of another, the result is that someone is eating from the flavor of another group's *pesach*. The Torah specifies *ish kefi achlo* — each person eats from their own *pesach*; one may not eat from another *chaburah's pesach*. Accordingly, if flavor transfer through *reicha* is halachically significant, roasting two *pesachim* side by side could cause each to absorb the other's taste, thereby making the meat forbidden to its rightful owners.

### Problem for Rav

If *ta'arovot* in the *beraita* refers to taste-mixing through aroma, this supports the concern about *reicha* — but it presents a difficulty for Rav. The *beraita* continues: *v'afilu gedi v'taleh* — one may not even roast a goat and a sheep side by side. If the concern is taste transfer through aroma, why specify "even a goat and a sheep"? A goat-and-goat and a goat-and-sheep are equally subject to *reicha* transfer — there would be nothing novel about adding the goat-and-sheep case. The word "even" implies that the goat-and-sheep case is a *chiddush*, a surprising stringency.

### Two Pots Resolution

*Hachi nami mistabra* — the *gemara* accepts this: the *beraita's* concern is for *ta'arovot gufin* — mixing of the actual bodies. If two goats are roasted side by side, one might serve a piece from the wrong one; with a goat and a sheep they are easily distinguishable by appearance, yet the *beraita* still prohibits it — because even then, if they are adjacent, physical confusion remains possible, and that is the *chiddush*.

The *gemara* then asks: does this disprove Rav, since the *beraita* apparently dismisses the concern of taste-mixing through aroma? *Amar Rav Yirmiyah: hacha b'mai askinan — kegon she-tzla'o bi-shtei kedeirot* — the *beraita* speaks of a case like two covered pots, where the smells are contained and cannot transfer between them. In that configuration, there is no *reicha* concern, and the only remaining concern is physical body-mixing — hence the focus on *ta'arovot gufin*.

### Rav Reinterpreted

This reading of the *beraita* actually clarifies Rav's position. *V'hachi ka-amar*: according to Rav, the *beraita* should be read as follows. The primary prohibition on roasting two *pesachim* together is because of *ta'arovot ta'amim* — the smells will intermingle, and this happens in virtually every case. *V'afilu ke-ein shtei kedeiros* — and even if one sets up the scenario like two separate pots, with a dividing mound or separation that blocks scent transfer, it remains forbidden — *mishum ta'arovot gufin* — because the bodies might still get confused. *V'afilu gedi v'taleh* — and for that concern, even a goat and a sheep is prohibited. Rav's original concern for *reicha* stands, and the *beraita* adds the further point that even without *reicha* transfer, the physical mixing concern alone would forbid it. The phrase *ke-ein shtei kedeiros* — like two pots, meaning a covered or separated arrangement — emerges here as an important category that will recur.

---

## Bread and Wine Tannaim D…

### Bread Wine Case

*Amar Rav Mari: ke-tana'ei* — Rav Mari states that this debate between Rav and Levi parallels a *tannaic* dispute. *Ha-rodeh pas chamah u-nesanah pi chavis yayin shel terumah* — one takes a hot loaf of bread fresh from the oven and places it over the opening of a barrel of *terumah* wine. The question is whether the aroma of the wine, drawn out by the heat of the bread, penetrates the bread to the extent that the bread must now be treated as *terumah* — forbidden to non-*kohanim*.

### Three Opinions

Three *tannaitic* opinions are recorded. *Rabbi Meir osser* — Rabbi Meir forbids the bread in all cases; the heat draws the wine's aroma into the bread. *Rabbi Yehuda mattir* — Rabbi Yehuda permits in all cases; no halachically significant transfer occurs. *Rabbi Yossi mattir be-shel chittin v'osser be-shel se'orim* — Rabbi Yossi distinguishes by grain type: wheat bread is not particularly absorbent and is permitted; barley bread is absorbent — *mipnei she-ha-se'orim sho'avot*, barley draws in the wine — and is forbidden.

### Is It a Reicha Debate?

*Mai lav tana'ei? De-mar savar reicha lav milsa hi* — is this not simply a *tannaic* debate over the halachic status of *reicha*? Rabbi Yehuda holds *reicha lav milsa* — smell has no effect; Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yossi (at least for barley) hold *reicha milsa hi*.

*Le-Levi vadai tana'ei* — for Levi, who rules that *reicha* is irrelevant, he must concede that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yossi disagree with him. He holds like Rabbi Yehuda. *Le-Rav neima tana'ei* — must Rav similarly concede that Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with him?

### Rav's Synthesis

*Amar lach Rav* — Rav responds that in principle, everyone agrees with him: *de-kulei alma reicha milsa hi* — the *reicha* itself, when it actually transfers, is halachically significant. The debate among the *tannaim* is not about *whether* transferred aroma matters, but about *when* the circumstances produce actual transfer. As *Rabbah bar bar Chana* cited in the name of *Reish Lakish*:

### Consensus Cases

*Be-pas chamah ve-chavis pesuchah, divrei ha-kol assur* — hot bread and an open barrel: everyone agrees this is forbidden. The heat draws out the aroma, the open barrel releases it — everyone would agree that significant transfer occurs. *Be-pas tzonenes ve-chavis megufah, divrei ha-kol muttar* — cold bread and a sealed barrel: everyone agrees this is permitted, regardless of one's principle, because there is no mechanism for transfer. *Lo nechelku ela be-pas chamah ve-chavis chasumah, i nami be-pas tzonenes ve-chavis pesuchah* — the *tannaic* debate concerns only the intermediate cases: hot bread over a sealed barrel, or cold bread over an open barrel. In those cases, whether enough transfer occurs to be halachically significant is debated among Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yossi.

Rav's synthesis is thus: *reicha milsa hi* is agreed upon by all; the disagreement concerns only the factual threshold of when *reicha* is substantial enough to trigger halachic concern.

### Pesachim Application

*De-hahi* — and accordingly, the case Rav discussed — fatty kosher meat roasted alongside lean *treif* meat — *ke-pas chamah ve-chavis petucha damya* — is like hot bread over an open barrel. Everyone, even Rabbi Yehuda, would agree this is forbidden. The *pesach* roasting scenario, by extension, is one where all would agree that *reicha* transfer is occurring at a meaningful level.

---

## Bread/Fish With Meat Rul…

### Bread with Meat Ruling

*Tani Rav Kahana berei d'Rav Chinena Sava*: bread baked together with roasted meat in an oven — *assur l'ochla b'kutach* — may not be eaten with a dairy dip.

### Rav or Levi?

One might ask whether this ruling proves that the *halacha* follows Rav. After all, the bread is being treated as *fleishig* by virtue of having absorbed meat aroma in the oven. However, it is equally possible that even Levi would agree that *lechatchila* one should not eat such bread with dairy — not because *reicha* has created a genuine *basar b'chalav* concern, but as a precautionary rabbinic measure. And if we rule like Levi, then *b'di'eved* — after the fact — if such bread were mixed with dairy, it would not be forbidden. The ruling of Rav Kahana does not conclusively decide the question.

### Fish with Meat Ruling

A parallel case: *ha'i binisa d'itvava b'hadai bisra* — a fish that was roasted together with meat in the same oven. *Assar Rava mifarzika l'meichla b'kutcha* — Rava from Farzika forbade eating that fish with a dairy dip, again treating the fish as having absorbed meat aroma. The same ambiguity applies: whether this reflects ruling like Rav on *reicha*, or whether even Levi would agree to a *lechatchila* stringency, remains unresolved.

### Health Concern Reason

*Mar bar Rav Ashi amar: afilu b'melcha nami assur* — Mar bar Rav Ashi goes further: such fish — and here he is speaking of fish and meat combined — may not even be eaten with salt alone, meaning they may not be eaten together at all. *Mishum d'kashya l'reicha v'davar acher* — because it causes bad breath and leprosy. According to this view, the prohibition of fish and meat together is rooted not in *reicha* or *ta'am* considerations, but in a health concern.

---

## Rambam / Shulchan Aruch…

### Rambam on Health

Rambam never codifies the prohibition of eating fish and meat together. His general approach was that medical and health-related guidance embedded in the *gemara* reflects the medical knowledge of its time, and does not carry the force of halachic ruling. Accordingly, the Rambam did not treat this as an *issur*.

### Shulchan Aruch Issur

Nevertheless, the *gemara's* language — *assei*, he forbade — is that of a prohibition, and the *Shulchan Aruch* does rule it as an *issur*, regardless of the underlying rationale. The health origin of the prohibition does not prevent it from being codified as a halachic rule.

### Extended Practice

The practical stringency extends considerably beyond what the *gemara* itself describes. The *gemara* addresses fish roasted together with meat in the same oven. Our practice, however, is to avoid eating cold fish and cold meat together — chewing them simultaneously even when cooked separately. This is a significant extension of the *gemara's* ruling, though it has become normative practice.

---

## Modern Oven Applications

### Unresolved Ruling

The *sugya* leaves unresolved which position governs as a matter of practical *psak*: *ila'ah gavar* (Rav) or *tata'ah gavar* (Shmuel), and similarly whether *reicha milsa hi* (Rav) or *reicha lav milta hi* (Levi). Both debates have support in both directions from the sources discussed.

### Shtei K'deirot Exception

Regardless of how the *ila'ah/tata'ah* debate is resolved, the *sugya* has established that the case of *ke-ein shtei kedeiros* — two separate covered arrangements — eliminates the *reicha* concern even according to Rav. If the substances are covered so that steam cannot escape and mingle, there is no transfer of aroma and no prohibition on that ground.

### Wrapping Practice

This is the basis for the practice of wrapping *kosher* airline food. The *kosher* meal can be heated in the same oven as non-*kosher* food, provided it is wrapped. There is no *halacha* that requires double-wrapping as such; the reason double-wrapping is sometimes used is purely practical — if the outer wrap is torn or compromised, the inner wrap still protects. The *halacha* requires one layer of coverage sufficient to prevent escape of steam and aroma.

### Ventilation Leniency

*Tosafot* extends the *shtei kedeiros* principle further. If the oven is a large, well-ventilated space where aromas dissipate and do not concentrate between items, that too may suffice to eliminate the *reicha* concern — even without explicit covering. The logic is that the *reicha* prohibition depends on the actual concentration and transfer of aroma; in a sufficiently airy space, the conditions for transfer do not obtain.

### Rabbeinu Tam Modern Oven

*Tosafot* cites *Rabbeinu Tam* as ruling in accordance with Rav on *reicha* — and yet permitting the baking of bread together with *fleishig* food in large ovens, *ho'il mechusos heitev havei k'shnei kedeiros*, since covered items are treated as if in separate vessels. *Tosafot* adds that even in a case without covering, *ein nira l'rabbi she'yehei assur she'yeish avir merubeh b'tanur v'hahevel mitpashet* — if the oven has abundant airflow and the vapors disperse widely, it does not appear that there would be a prohibition. This is the halachic underpinning for relying on coverage and ventilation when cooking different categories of food in close proximity — a question that extends beyond *reicha* to the broader issue of cooking *kosher* and non-*kosher* items sequentially in the same oven, a topic treated at length in *Yoreh De'ah*.

---

---

# Pesachim 80

## Rav vs Rav Kahana

### 50-50 Status

The daf opens, continuing from 79b, with a fundamental debate between Rav and Rav Kahana concerning the case where the *tzibur* is divided exactly fifty-fifty between *tahor* and *tamei* individuals. The question is whether such a split counts as a *rov* — a majority — for purposes of determining whether the *korban pesach* is brought as a *pesach b'tumah*.

### Rav's View

Rav holds that *palga u-palga* — an exact fifty-fifty split — is treated as a *rov*. His ruling is: *hallalu osin le-atzmam ve-hallalu osin le-atzmam* — each half acts independently. The fifty percent who are *tahor* bring on their own, and the fifty percent who are *tamei* are not pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*. The *tamei* half constitutes a sufficient *kahal* to bring *Pesach Rishon* on its own, even though it is not large enough to pull the *tahor* half into a *pesach b'tumah* framework.

### Rav Kahana View

Rav Kahana disputes this, holding that *machetza al machetza* does not qualify as a *rov*, though his position comes in two versions. The precise implications of that disagreement will be developed below.

### Mishnah Analysis

The *Gemara* attempts to derive support from the *mishnah*, noting the classic problem that many *mishnayot* present: they address the case of a *rov* and a *miut* but pass over the intermediate case of fifty-fifty entirely. The *mishnah* states that if the entire congregation or its majority — *nitmah hakahal o rubo* — became *tamei*, or if the *kohanim* were *tamei* while the congregation was *tahor*, then *ya'aseh b'tumah*, the offering is brought in a state of *tumah*. The implication appears to be that only a majority of *tamei* suffices — *rubo hu de-avdi bi-tumah* — and that a fifty-fifty split would not trigger the *pesach b'tumah* dispensation. This would seem to pose a difficulty for Rav, who treats the fifty percent *tamei* as independently entitled to bring on *Pesach Rishon*.

### Mishnah Supports Rav

Rav responds that the *mishnah* is entirely consistent with his position, provided one reads it carefully. When there is a *rov tamei*, the entire community does *pesach b'tumah* together — *avdi kulu bi-tumah*. In a fifty-fifty split, *hallalu osin le-atzmam ve-hallalu osin le-atzmam*: each half does it by itself. The *mishnah*'s silence on fifty-fifty is not an implicit rejection of this arrangement; the *mishnah* simply did not address it. The *Gemara* affirms that this reading is indeed plausible — *hachi nami mistabra* — pointing to the *seifa* of the *mishnah*, which states that if a *miut* became *tamei*, the *tahor* people bring on *Pesach Rishon* while the *tamei* people bring on *Pesach Sheni*: *tehorin osin et ha-rishon u-tme'im osin et ha-sheni*. The implication is *miut hu de-avdi be-sheni* — only a minority is pushed off to *Pesach Sheni* — whereas in a fifty-fifty case, according to Rav, the *tamei* half does not get pushed off at all but rather brings *Pesach Rishon* on its own. The *mishnah* works cleanly according to Rav: a majority means everyone does *pesach b'tumah* together; a minority means the *tamei* do *Pesach Sheni*; and the unmentioned fifty-fifty case is the one where each group acts independently.

### Rav Kahana Versions

The *Gemara* notes that this same analysis poses a difficulty for Rav Kahana, since the *mishnah*'s *seifa* implies that a *miut* is specifically what triggers the *Pesach Sheni* obligation — yet Rav Kahana, in at least one version of his position, holds that even a fifty-fifty split sends the *tamei* people to *Pesach Sheni*. The *Gemara* therefore distinguishes between Rav Kahana's two formulations.

According to Rav Kahana's second version (*lishna batra*), in a fifty-fifty case the *tamei* people bring neither *Pesach Rishon* nor *Pesach Sheni* — *einan osin lo et ha-rishon ve-lo et ha-sheni*. They are not a majority and therefore cannot bring on the first; they are not a *miut* and therefore cannot bring on the second. On this reading, the *mishnah* poses no difficulty: when the *tamei* people are a *miut*, they do *Pesach Sheni*; when they are precisely fifty percent, they fall between the two categories and lose out entirely. The *mishnah*'s formulation highlights the *miut* case precisely because it is the favorable one — the fifty-fifty case is the one in which the *tamei* people are excluded from both.

### Mishnah Reconciled

The difficulty is with Rav Kahana's first version (*lishna kama*), which holds that even in a fifty-fifty case the *tahor* people bring on *Pesach Rishon* and the *tamei* people bring on *Pesach Sheni* — *tehorin osin et ha-rishon u-tme'im osin et ha-sheni*. On this view, the *mishnah* should have illustrated its rule using the fifty-fifty case, not just the *miut* case. Rav Kahana's response is that the rule stated in the *seifa* is equally true in the fifty-fifty case — *ihu ha-din de-afilu palga u-palga nami* — but the *mishnah* chose to formulate it using the *miut* case in order to parallel the *reisha*, which speaks of a majority. Just as the *reisha* requires a *rov tamei* to trigger *pesach b'tumah* for all, the *seifa* correspondingly speaks of a *miut tamei* as the condition for *Pesach Sheni*. The middle case of fifty-fifty was omitted by the *mishnah* for stylistic reasons of contrast, but in truth even fifty percent *tamei* would do *Pesach Sheni* according to this version of Rav Kahana. On this reading, all three positions — Rav and the two versions of Rav Kahana — can be reconciled with the *mishnah*.

---

## Three Baraitot

### Baraita for Rav

The *Gemara* now observes that we possess three *baraitot*, each of which supports a different one of the three positions just laid out. The first *baraita* is introduced as *tanya kevata de-Rav* — a *baraita* that accords with Rav's ruling. It states: if the Jewish people were exactly half *tahor* and half *tamei* — *harei she-hayu Yisrael mechetza tehorin u-mechetza tme'im* — then *hallalu osin le-atzmam ve-hallalu osin le-atzmam*, each group brings on its own. The fifty percent *tamei* are sufficient to constitute a *kahal* for purposes of *Pesach Rishon*, but do not define the *tahor* half.

### Baraita for RK1

The second *baraita* supports Rav Kahana's first version: in a fifty-fifty case, the *tahor* people bring on *Pesach Rishon* and the *tamei* people, since they are not a majority, are treated as a *miut* and bring on *Pesach Sheni* — *tehorin osin et ha-rishon u-tme'im osin et ha-sheni*.

### Baraita for RK2

The third *baraita* supports Rav Kahana's second version, which represents the more novel ruling. In a fifty-fifty case, the *tahor* people bring *Pesach Rishon*, while the *tamei* people — being neither large enough to constitute the *kahal* nor small enough to qualify as a *miut* — fall precisely between the two categories: *einan osin lo et ha-rishon ve-lo et ha-sheni*, they bring neither.

---

## Reconciling Baraitot

### Explaining RK1 Baraita

The *Gemara* will not rest content with simply noting that each position has a supporting *baraita* while two *baraitot* oppose it. Since each *Amora* is committed to a single ruling, they must find a way to reconcile all three *baraitot* with their respective positions. The *Gemara* therefore undertakes this exercise systematically.

The first challenge: according to Rav and according to Rav Kahana's second version, what is to be done with the *baraita* that says that in a fifty-fifty case the *tamei* people bring *Pesach Sheni*? According to Rav they should be bringing *Pesach Rishon*; according to Rav Kahana's second version they should be bringing neither. How do these two positions explain away (*heichi matretzei lah*) the *baraita* that places them in *Pesach Sheni*?

### Women's Role

The *Gemara* answers: *kegon she-hayu Yisrael mechetza tehorim u-mechetza tme'im* — it looks like a fifty-fifty case — *ve-nashim mashlimot le-tme'im*, but what creates the appearance of fifty percent *tamei* is that women's votes were included in the count. This introduces an important distinction regarding women's obligation in the *korban pesach*. The *baraita* in question operates according to the view that women's participation in *Pesach Rishon* is *reshut* — optional, not obligatory — *nashim be-rishon reshut*. If women are not obligated, then when determining the composition of the *tzibur* for purposes of this calculation, one looks only at those who bear a genuine obligation: the men.

### Recounting Without Women

Once women are removed from the count — *dal nashim mi-tme'im* — and correspondingly removed from both columns, the true numbers emerge: among the men alone, the *tamei* group constitutes a *miut*. Thus, *havu lehu tme'im miyuta* — the *tamei* people are in fact a minority — *u-miyuta yidchu le-Pesach Sheni*, and it is on account of this minority status that they bring *Pesach Sheni*. The *baraita* is therefore not a genuine fifty-fifty case at all; it only appears that way because the women's count was initially included. In reality, among those actually obligated, the *tamei* group is a minority, and the *baraita* is fully consistent with the positions of Rav and Rav Kahana's second version.

### Rav on RK2 Baraita

The *Gemara* turns to the more difficult challenge. According to Rav and according to Rav Kahana's first version, what is to be done with the *baraita* that says in a fifty-fifty case the *tamei* people bring neither *Pesach Rishon* nor *Pesach Sheni* — *tehorim osin et ha-rishon ve-tme'im ein osin lo et ha-rishon ve-lo et ha-sheni*? According to Rav, the *tamei* half should be doing *Pesach Rishon*; according to Rav Kahana's first version, they should be doing *Pesach Sheni*. Neither position accommodates a total exclusion from both. The *Gemara* asks: *heichi mitartzei lah* — how do they explain it away?

Rav's explanation again manipulates the numbers by distinguishing between which population is counted at which moment. The scenario: it appears to be fifty-fifty, but this time — *ve-nashim odfot al ha-tehorim* — the women's presence is what makes it look like fifty-fifty on the side of the *tahor* people. Without the women, the men's vote would yield a majority *tamei*. This *baraita* operates according to the view that women are obligated in *Pesach Rishon* — *nashim be-rishon chovah* — so they are counted for that calculation. But women are not obligated in *Pesach Sheni* — *u-ve-sheni reshut* — and so are excluded from that calculation.

### Retroactive Census

This generates a striking and genuinely unusual result. For the purposes of *Pesach Rishon*, women are counted. With women included, the *tahor* side constitutes a majority and the *tamei* side a minority. Therefore the *tamei* people, being a *miut*, cannot bring *Pesach Rishon* — *rishon lo avdi de-havu lehu miuta* — and are pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*. But when *Pesach Sheni* arrives, the question becomes: who is now obligated, and what were the relevant numbers a month ago? For *Pesach Sheni*, women are not obligated, so one looks back at the composition of the community through the male-only lens. And looking back through that lens, the *tamei* people were a majority — *dal nashim minaihu, havu lehu tme'im ruba* — and *ruba lo avdi be-sheni*, a majority cannot bring *Pesach Sheni*.
