The result is deeply counterintuitive. At the time of *Pesach Rishon*, the *tamei* people were counted as a *miut* because women were included in the census; so they were denied *Pesach Rishon*. At the time of *Pesach Sheni*, one looks back at the same community but now counts only the men — and through that retroactive male-only lens, the *tamei* group turns out to have been a *rov*, disqualifying them from *Pesach Sheni* as well. The numbers are genuinely the same underlying reality, but the applicable census methodology differs depending on which *Pesach* one is assessing, since women's obligation differs between the two. The result is that the same community ends up excluded from both — not because they fall between two categories, but because the category they belong to shifts depending on which obligation is being measured.

### RK on RK2 Baraita

Rav Kahana's explanation of the same *baraita* is structurally parallel but employs the inverse scenario. In this version, *ve-nashim mashlimot le-tehorim* — the women's count is what makes the *tahor* side appear to constitute fifty percent. Without the women, the men's count alone would show a minority *tahor* and a majority *tamei*. The *baraita* operates according to the view that women are obligated in *Pesach Rishon* but optional for *Pesach Sheni* — the same *sevara* as before.

For *Pesach Rishon*, counting women, the *tamei* side constitutes exactly fifty percent — *de-havu lehu palga u-palga*. For Rav Kahana, fifty percent *tamei* does not qualify for *Pesach Rishon* — *be-rishon palga lo avdi*. For *Pesach Sheni*, one looks back through the male-only lens, and now the *tamei* side turns out to have been a majority of the men — *dal nashim mineihu, havu lehu tme'im ruba* — and a majority cannot bring *Pesach Sheni*. The *tamei* people are thus excluded from both. The mechanism is the same: the census methodology changes between *Pesach Rishon* and *Pesach Sheni* because women's obligation changes, and this shifting methodology produces a double exclusion.

### RK's Challenge

The third *baraita* — the one supporting Rav's position, which allows each group to bring independently — now poses a challenge to Rav Kahana. However one adjusts the numbers using the women's count, the *baraita* explicitly envisions a scenario in which half the community brings as one *kahal* and the other half brings separately. Rav Kahana fundamentally rejects the idea that *Klal Yisrael* can be split in this way, such that one group brings *Pesach Rishon* in one mode while another group simultaneously brings in a different mode. No number manipulation can explain away a *baraita* that directly endorses that very possibility.

### RK Concedes

Rav Kahana therefore concedes that this *baraita* represents a genuinely opposing *tannaic* view — *tanna'ei hi*, it is a dispute among *Tannaim*. There is a *Tanna* who holds *mechetza al mechetza ke-rov* — that a fifty-fifty split is treated as a *rov* — which produces the result of each half acting as its own independent community. Rav Kahana himself holds *mechetza al mechetza eino ke-rov*, which leads, in his two versions, either to *Pesach Sheni* for the *tamei* half or to exclusion from both. He can reconcile the two *baraitot* that align with his position through the manipulation of the women's census; the third he must acknowledge as representing the *tannaic* view that he disputes.

---

## Detailed Baraita

### Majority Tamei

The *Gemara* proceeds to examine the full text of one of the *baraitot* in detail. It begins with the straightforward case: if the *tamei* people outnumbered the *tahor* — *hayu tme'im odfim al ha-tehorim* — then even if the margin was a single individual — *afilu echad* — everyone brings *pesach b'tumah*: *ya'asu be-tumah*.

### No Splitting Korban

The *baraita* grounds this rule in the principle *she-ein korban tzibbur chaluk* — a communal offering cannot be divided. This principle now carries greater logical weight in context than it did when first introduced. In the fifty-fifty case discussed above, splitting was tolerated because there was no majority to unify the *tzibur* in a single direction. But once a majority — even by one — exists, one cannot try to protect the *tahor* minority by separating them from the *tamei* majority. The principle of *ein korban tzibbur chaluk* demands that everyone proceed together, and therefore everyone brings *pesach b'tumah*.

### RE ben Matya

Rabbi Eliezer ben Matya dissents from the rule that a single individual tips the scales: *ein ha-yachid machria et ha-tzibbur le-tumah*. He derives this from the *pasuk* (cited at the beginning of 80a): *lo tuchal lizbo'ach et ha-pesach be-achad bishe'arecha* — one person cannot determine that the entire *tzibur* will bring *pesach b'tumah*.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon introduces a further dimension. Even if the *tamei* group does not constitute a majority of the entire people, if they constitute an entire *shevet* — a tribal unit — they are entitled to bring *Pesach Rishon* on their own, while the remaining *shevatim*, who are *tahor*, bring in *taharah*: *hallalu osin le-atzmam ve-hallalu osin le-atzmam*. The reason is *kasavar shevet echad ikrei kahal* — Rabbi Shimon holds that even a single *shevet* qualifies as a *kahal*, consistent with the discussion in *Horayot* regarding the *par helam davar shel tzibbur* and whether a single tribe can constitute the *kahal* that triggers that communal atonement. One *shevet* is sufficient to constitute a *kahal* that may bring *Pesach Rishon* independently, but it is not large enough to impose *pesach b'tumah* on everyone else. The arrangement therefore parallels the fifty-fifty case: each unit functions as its own *tzibur*.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda takes this logic in the opposite direction. Even if only a single *shevet* is *tamei* while all the remaining *shevatim* are *tahor*, everyone brings *pesach b'tumah*: *ya'asu be-tumah* — because *she-ein korban tzibbur chaluk*. Rabbi Yehuda agrees with Rabbi Shimon that one *shevet* constitutes a *kahal*, and therefore that *kahal* is entitled to bring *pesach b'tumah*. But Rabbi Yehuda adds the principle that once any *kahal* brings *b'tumah*, the prohibition against dividing the *korban tzibbur* applies to all of *Klal Yisrael*: once one group has activated the *tumah* dispensation, the entire community must bring together in *tumah*.

---

## Tipping Scales

### Rav's Method

Having established that a fifty-fifty split allows each group to act independently, the *Gemara* considers what should be done practically to avoid such a split. Rav proposes that when the community is exactly evenly divided, one of the *tahor* individuals should be made *tamei* — *metam'im echad mehem be-sheretz* — thereby tipping the balance to a majority *tamei* and enabling everyone to bring together in *tumah*.

### Gemara Challenge

The *Gemara* immediately presses the question: why bother? Rav himself holds that in a fifty-fifty case *hallalu osin le-atzmam ve-hallalu osin le-atzmam* — each group brings on its own. Why go to the trouble of artificially creating a majority *tamei*? Let each half do what it does and leave it at that.

The *Gemara* initially attempts to say that perhaps the case is not perfectly fifty-fifty but rather has one extra person in the *tamei* column already — *de-hayu tme'im odfim al ha-tehorim echad* — but that one individual's vote is insufficient to tip the scales per the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer ben Matya. The *Gemara* rejects this: if there is one extra, the *tamei* are already a *rov*; simply bring *pesach b'tumah*. And if one person doesn't count, the situation is effectively fifty-fifty again — so again, why not simply split?

### Reconciliation

The *Gemara* resolves the matter by positing a specific combination of opinions. If one holds, like Rav, that *machetza al mechetza* is treated as *ke-rov* — such that the fifty percent *tamei* is in principle entitled to bring *Pesach Rishon* — but simultaneously holds, like Rabbi Yehuda, that *ein korban tzibbur chaluk* — that the *tzibur* cannot be divided under any circumstances — then one arrives at a genuine impasse. The fifty percent *tamei* cannot be pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*, since they are treated as a *rov* entitled to bring on the first; yet they are also not large enough to draw the *tahor* half into a *pesach b'tumah*; and the principle of *ein korban tzibbur chaluk* precludes any split. The only available resolution is to engineer an actual majority: make one more person *tamei*, thereby producing an unambiguous *rov tamei* and enabling everyone to bring *pesach b'tumah* together. Once that majority is established, *ein korban tzibbur chaluk* takes full effect and the entire community brings together without difficulty.

The underlying tension is also worth noting: there is an extensive body of discussion about *tumah dechuya b'tzibur* — the view that *tumah* in the *tzibur* is tolerated rather than permitted outright — which would suggest a preference to minimize exposure to *tumah*. Yet once the decision is made to bring *pesach b'tumah*, the *Gemara* here appears to assume without further qualification that everyone may become *tamei*, without requiring any effort to minimize it. How that sits alongside the *dechuya/hutra* framework is left unexplored in this context.

### Ulla's Method

Ulla offers an alternative to Rav's approach. Rather than rendering one *tahor* person *tamei*, Ulla proposes sending one of the *tahor* individuals away on a distant journey — *meshalechin echad mehem le-derech rechoka* — thereby removing that person from the calculation. With one fewer *tahor* person in *Yerushalayim*, the remaining *tamei* group constitutes a majority, and the community brings *pesach b'tumah* as a unit.

### Ulla's Problem

The *Gemara* challenges Ulla on two grounds. First, it asks: why not simply follow Rav's solution of making a *tahor* person *tamei be-sheretz*? The *Gemara* explains that Ulla holds *shochtin ve-zorkin al tamei sheretz* — that one who is *tamei sheretz* may still have the *korban pesach* slaughtered and its blood sprinkled on his behalf, since he will become *tahor* by nightfall. In other words, making someone *tamei sheretz* does not genuinely remove them from the *tahor* side of the calculation, since they will be able to eat the *pesach* that night. To create a genuine *tamei* person who cannot bring, one would need to make them *tamei* through a *meit*, but that would prevent them from bringing their *korban chagigah* on the first day of *Yom Tov*.

The *Gemara* asks: why not simply let this person bring the *chagigah* later in the *Yom Tov* week, since there are seven days during which it may be offered? To this the *Gemara* responds: then the same objection applies to Ulla's solution — send the person away, and he can bring *Pesach Sheni*; make him *tamei be-meit*, and he can bring the *chagigah* on the seventh day of *Pesach*, when he will have completed seven days of *tumah* and become *tahor*. The *Gemara* therefore notes that making someone *tamei be-meit* is actually preferable to sending them away, since the person made *tamei* still participates in the communal *pesach b'tumah*, whereas the person sent away misses the *korban pesach* entirely.

Ulla's rationale for nevertheless preferring his solution rests on his view regarding the *chagigah*: *kullan tashlumin de-rishon ninhu* — all the subsequent days of *Yom Tov* on which the *chagigah* may be brought are understood as makeup opportunities for the first day. This means that only someone who was genuinely obligated and capable on the first day may bring on subsequent days. Someone who was *tamei* on *Rosh Yom Tov* — the first day of the festival — is, in Ulla's view, not in the category of those who could have brought that day, and therefore cannot avail themselves of the makeup days: *kol de-lo chazi be-rishon, lo chazi be-kulhu* — whoever was not fit on the first day is not fit on any subsequent day. Therefore, making someone *tamei be-meit* would permanently deny them the *chagigah*, which Ulla considers a graver consequence than simply delaying their *pesach* to *Pesach Sheni*.

### Practical Reality

Rav Nachman dismisses Ulla's solution on entirely practical grounds. He instructs his students: *zilu ve-imru lei le-Ulla* — go tell Ulla — *man tzayit lach de-akar shichei ve-masganei be-rahi* — who is going to listen to you and uproot his tent pegs and run out of *Yerushalayim* on *Erev Pesach*? Someone who has made the pilgrimage to *Yerushalayim* for the *korban pesach* is not going to simply walk away on the eve of the holiday on the strength of a theoretical legal solution. Rav Nachman regards the suggestion as impractical regardless of its theoretical validity.

---

## Zavin & Tamei

### Rav on Zavin Case

A new case is introduced: *hayu ruban zavin u-mi'utan tmei meitim* — the majority of the community were *zavin* and the minority were *tamei meitim*. This scenario requires some background. The dispensation of *tumah be-tzibur* — whereby *tumah* in the community overrides the normal prohibition against bringing a *korban* in *tumah* — applies specifically to the type of *tumah* that could, in principle, permit a communal offering to be brought *b'tumah*. *Zavin* — individuals with *tumah* rooted in bodily flux — represent a category of *tumas ha-guf* that is not subject to the *tumah be-tzibur* dispensation even if they constitute a majority. Their *tumah* is too severe; one does not say *tumah hutra b'tzibur* for *zavin*. Consequently, *zavin* do not count in the *tamei* column when calculating whether the *tzibur* is majority *tamei* in the operative sense. Only *tamei meitim* count, since only that category of *tumah* is potentially subject to the communal dispensation.

In this scenario, Rav rules: the *tamei meitim* bring neither *Pesach Rishon* nor *Pesach Sheni* — *ein osin lo be-rishon ve-lo be-sheni*.

### No First Pesach

The *tamei meitim* cannot bring on *Pesach Rishon* because they are a *miut* — *b'rishon lo avdi de-havu lehu miuta*. Since *zavin* are excluded from the *tamei* column, the *tamei meitim*, who constitute only a minority of the total community, do not reach the threshold of a majority that would enable a *pesach b'tumah*.

### No Second Pesach

The *tamei meitim* cannot bring on *Pesach Sheni* because *Pesach Sheni* is only available when a *tzibur* brought *Pesach Rishon* — *k'heicha de-avdi tzibur b'rishon, avdi yachid be-sheni*. In this case, no *tzibur* brought *Pesach Rishon*: the *zavin* can never bring *Pesach Rishon*, and the *tamei meitim* were unable to because they were a *miut*. Since no *tzibur* brought on the first *Pesach*, there is no *Pesach Sheni* framework into which individuals can step: *kol heicha de-lo avdi tzibur be-rishon, lo avdi yachid be-sheni*.

One might ask whether a *tzibur* need constitute a full majority of *Klal Yisrael*, or whether a smaller group — such as a *shevet* — might suffice to trigger the *Pesach Sheni* option for individuals who missed the first. In the present case, however, there was no such group at all, and so the question does not arise. The *tamei meitim* are simply a *chavura* with no *tzibur* framework behind them.

### Shmuel Challenge

Shmuel challenges Rav's ruling: *zilu amru lei le-Abba* — go tell Rav — *ve-ya'asu Bnei Yisrael et ha-Pesach be-mo'ado* — what do you do with the verse requiring the Jewish people to bring the *pesach* in its appointed time? Can Rav truly accept a scenario in which the entire applicable population brings no *korban pesach* whatsoever on the fourteenth of Nisan?

### Rav Response

Rav responds in kind: *zilu amru lei* — go tell Shmuel — *ki havu kulhu zavin, mai avdit lei* — what would Shmuel do if a hundred percent of the community were *zavin*? In that case, nobody could bring at all. Yet surely one cannot argue from the *pasuk* that they must bring regardless. *Ella keivan de-lo efshar lo efshar* — when it is genuinely impossible, it is impossible, and the *halakha* accepts that outcome. *Hacha nami lo efshar* — here too, when the applicable population is a minority incapable of bringing, and the majority cannot bring *b'tumah* under the *tzibur* dispensation, the *pasuk* cannot override that reality.

---

## Tamei & Zavin

### Zavin Pesach Sheni

The *Gemara* now presents the inverse case: *hayu ruban tmei meitim u-mi'utan zavin* — the majority were *tamei meitim* and the minority were *zavin*. Here the *tamei meitim*, constituting the majority, bring *pesach b'tumah* on *Pesach Rishon*. The straightforward question is whether the *zavin*, who cannot participate in a *pesach b'tumah*, may bring *Pesach Sheni* — since the *tzibur* did in fact bring *Pesach Rishon*, just in a state of *tumah*.

### Rav Huna

Rav Huna rules: *ein tashlumin le-pesach ha-ba be-tumah* — there is no makeup offering (*tashlumin*) for a *pesach* that was brought in *tumah*. For individuals to be entitled to bring *Pesach Sheni*, the *tzibur* must have brought *Pesach Rishon* in a state of *taharah*. A *pesach* brought *b'tumah*, even when permitted for the *tzibur*, does not generate the entitlement to *tashlumin* for those who were unable to participate.

### Rav Adda

Rav Adda bar Ahava disagrees: *yesh tashlumin le-pesach ha-ba be-tumah* — even when the *tzibur* brought *pesach b'tumah*, there is still a *tashlumin* framework that allows individuals who could not participate to bring *Pesach Sheni*.

### Tumah Status

The *Gemara* identifies the underlying conceptual dispute. Rav Huna holds *tumah dechuya hi be-tzibur* — the *tumah* of the *tzibur* is tolerated under duress, meaning the *pesach* brought *b'tumah* remains essentially problematic; it is not the normative *Pesach Rishon* that generates the classic framework entitling individuals to a makeup. Rav Adda bar Ahava holds *tumah hutra be-tzibur* — the *tumah* of the *tzibur* is fully permitted, meaning the *pesach* brought *b'tumah* is treated as though it were a fully valid *Pesach Rishon* for all purposes, including the entitlement to *tashlumin*. If it is as though the *tzibur* brought in *taharah*, then those who could not participate are entitled to their individual *Pesach Sheni*.

---

## Three-Way Split

### Rav Mani Analysis

The final case of the daf is the most intricate: *hayu shelishtan zavin u-shelishtan tehorim u-shelishtan tmei meitim* — one third *zavin*, one third *tahor*, and one third *tamei meitim*. Rav Mani bar Patti rules: *tmei meitim ein osin lo be-rishon ve-lo be-sheni* — the *tamei meitim* bring neither *Pesach Rishon* nor *Pesach Sheni*. The *tahor* third brings *Pesach Rishon*, as they are always entitled to do. The *zavin* bring neither, which goes without saying. The analysis focuses on why the *tamei meitim* are also excluded from both.

### No First Pesach

On *Pesach Rishon*, the *tamei meitim* cannot bring because the situation does not qualify as a *pesach ha-ba be-tumah*. Why not? Because *higdilu zavin al tehorim de-lo avdi be-tumah* — the *zavin* are added to, or rather shift the weight of, the *tahor* side, in the sense that they are not counted in the *tamei* column. Since *zavin* are never entitled to bring *Pesach Rishon* even in a *pesach b'tumah* scenario, they do not figure in the *tamei* count. The operative census, for purposes of determining whether the *tamei* side constitutes a majority, excludes the *zavin*. When only the *tamei meitim* are counted in the *tamei* column, they constitute only one third of the entire *Klal Yisrael* — a clear *miut*. A *miut tamei* does not bring *Pesach Rishon b'tumah*.

### Zavin Recounted

One might question whether the *zavin* ought simply to be removed from the calculation entirely, leaving a fifty-fifty split between the *tahor* third and the *tamei meitim* third. The *Gemara* does not adopt this framing. The *chiddush* of Rav Mani bar Patti is precisely that the entire *Klal Yisrael* — including the *zavin* who cannot bring — constitutes the denominator for the census. The *tamei meitim*, being one third of that total, are unambiguously a *miut*, not a fifty-fifty, and there is therefore no question of treating them as a *rov* or as equal to the *tahor* population.

### No Second Pesach

On *Pesach Sheni*, the *tamei meitim* are also excluded. The reason is that for *Pesach Sheni* to be available, the majority of the *tzibur* must have brought *Pesach Rishon*. In this case, two thirds of the community — the *zavin* and the *tamei meitim* together — did not bring *Pesach Rishon*: *nitztarfu zavin im tmei meitim de-lo avdi be-rishon, de-havu lehu ruba*. Since the majority of the *kahal* did not bring *Pesach Rishon*, there is no *Pesach Sheni* framework. The only third that did bring was the *tahor* group — and that is not a majority of the community. Therefore *rova lo maytu le-pesach sheni* — a majority that did not bring cannot bring *Pesach Sheni*, and the minority who actually did bring was too small to generate a *Pesach Sheni* entitlement for those who missed it.

---

---

# Pesachim 80b

## Tzitz & Tamei Meat

### Pesach Tamei Overview

The *mishnah* near the top of 80b introduces a principle that has been building throughout the preceding discussion: the *tzitz* — the golden forehead-plate worn by the *Kohen Gadol* — has the power to render acceptable a *korban* that would otherwise be invalidated by *tumah*. The specific case here is that of an individual's *korban Pesach*, a *korban yachid*, where the *pesach* itself became *tamei* while the owner remained *tahor*. The *mishnah* states: *hapesach shenizrak damo v'achar kach noda shehu tamei — hatzitz meratzeh* — if the blood of the *pesach* was sprinkled and only afterward did it become known that the offering had been *tamei*, the *tzitz* renders it acceptable.

The underlying assumption here, following the view that we do not rule like *Rebbi Natan*, is that if the meat is *tamei* the owner does not fulfill his obligation of *korban Pesach*. Ordinarily — and certainly *lechatchila*, and likely even *b'di'eved* — if the meat or blood is *tamei* and one is aware of this, the *pesach* is invalid. But when the person was ignorant of the *tumah* at the time, the *tzitz* operates to make it acceptable. The condition of ignorance, as we will see, is central to the entire discussion that follows.

### Tzitz: Objects vs. Person

The *mishnah* draws a sharp distinction between two types of *tumah*. The *tzitz* is effective when the objects involved — the meat or the blood — became *tamei*. These are the *kodshim* themselves, and the *tzitz* atones, so to speak, for the *avon hakodashim*, the sin inherent in the *tumah* of the sanctified matter. However, if it is the *guf* — the person himself — who became *tamei*, the *tzitz* does not apply: *nitma haguf ein hatzitz meratzeh*. This is stated in the *mishnah* as an established tradition: the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* for the *tumah* of the blood and meat in the case of the *nazir* and the one bringing the *korban Pesach*, but it does not render acceptable *tumat haguf*.

It is worth pausing on why the *mishnah* specifically mentions the *nazir* alongside the one bringing the *pesach*. The reason will become clearer as the discussion proceeds, but the common thread is that these are the two *korbanot* for which the *tumah* of the person is uniquely consequential: with other *korbanot*, a *tamei* owner can simply arrange for someone else to perform the *zerikat hadam*, and the *korban* remains valid. With the *pesach* and the *nazir*, however, the person's own *tumah* undermines the very possibility of bringing the *korban* at all.

### Tumat HaTehom

The *mishnah* then introduces a remarkable exception: *nitma tumat hatehom — hatzitz meratzeh*. Even with respect to *tumat haguf*, where the *tzitz* normally does not operate, if the *tumah* is of the category known as *tumat hatehom* — literally the *tumah* of the depths — the *tzitz* does render it acceptable.

*Tumat hatehom* is not merely a situation where the person happened to be unaware. It refers to a *tumah* that is objectively unknowable — a doubt that exists not simply in the mind of the individual but in the very nature of the situation. The paradigmatic case is a corpse buried underground, unknown to anyone, whose *tumah* one inadvertently incurred. The *halacha* accepted here, transmitted as *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, is that such an unknowable *tumah* does not disqualify the individual when the *tzitz* is present, even though ordinarily *tumat haguf* would not be remedied by the *tzitz*.

### Pesach & Nazir Rules

This special dispensation — that the *tzitz* works even for *tumat haguf* in a case of *tumat hatehom* — is specifically limited to the *pesach* and the *nazir*. These are precisely the two cases where personal *tumah* is most consequential. A *tamei* person seeking to bring the *korban Pesach* is entirely displaced to *Pesach Sheini*. A *nazir* who becomes *tamei* must restart his *nezirut* from the beginning and cannot complete his *korban* to conclude the *nezirut*. In both cases, the person's *tumah* fundamentally prevents the *korban* from being brought at all.

For other *korbanot*, the question of the owner's *tumah* is largely irrelevant — someone else can perform the *zerikat hadam* regardless. But for *pesach* and *nazir*, we have a special tradition (*halacha l'Moshe miSinai*) that if the *tumah* was truly unknowable — *tumat hatehom* — then the *tzitz* makes it acceptable even for *tumat haguf*. The *mishnah*'s pairing of *pesach* and *nazir* is thus not incidental; they represent the only two cases where this particular dispensation is even relevant.

---

## Ignorance Requirement

### Timing of Ignorance

The *gemara* opens by analyzing the precise condition of ignorance required for the *tzitz* to operate in the case of *tamei* blood or meat. The *mishnah*'s phrasing — *nizrak damo v'achar kach noda*, the blood was sprinkled and then it became known — implies that what matters is the state of awareness at the moment of *zerikat hadam*. From this the *gemara* derives: *ta'ama d'nizrak v'achar kach noda* — the *tzitz* works because one sprinkled while still unaware. The corollary is clear: *aval noda v'achar kach nizrak — lo meratzeh* — if one already knew the *dam* was *tamei* before the *zerikat hadam* was performed, the *tzitz* does not help.

### Ravina vs. R. Shila

This straightforward reading of the *mishnah* is immediately challenged by a *beraita*. The *beraita* asks: for what does the *tzitz* render things acceptable? For blood, meat, or fat that became *tamei* — *bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid*, whether unintentionally or intentionally; *bein b'oness bein b'ratzon*, whether against one's will or willingly; *bein b'yachid bein b'tzibur*, whether an individual's *korban* or a communal one. The *beraita* seems to say explicitly that the *tzitz* operates even if the *tumah* or the *zerikat hadam* was done *b'meizid* — deliberately and knowingly.

*Ravina* resolves the contradiction as follows. When the *beraita* says *bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid*, it is referring to how the *dam* or *basar* became *tamei* in the first place. Whether the *tumah* of the object came about intentionally or unintentionally is irrelevant — the *tzitz* works either way. What does matter, however, is the state of mind at the time of *zerikat hadam*: *zrikato b'shogeg hurtzah, b'meizid lo hurtzah* — if the *zerikat hadam* itself was performed in ignorance, it is accepted; if it was performed with full knowledge of the *tumah*, it is not.

*Rabbi Shila* takes the opposite position. He accepts the *beraita* at face value and argues that even if one knew about the *tumah* and proceeded to perform the *zerikat hadam* deliberately, the *tzitz* still makes it acceptable: *zrikato bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid hurtzah*. What matters for *Rabbi Shila* is not the intentionality of the *zerikat hadam* but the manner in which the *tumah* itself occurred. If the *tumah* came about *b'shogeg* — unintentionally — then the *tzitz* works regardless of how the *zrika* was performed. But if the *tumah* itself was *b'meizid* — if the object was deliberately rendered *tamei* — then the *tzitz* does not help.

The logic of *Rabbi Shila*'s position, while striking, has a certain internal coherence: an object that was deliberately made *tamei* bears a qualitative stain that makes it undeserving of the *tzitz*'s atonement. An object that became *tamei* inadvertently can more naturally be "papered over" by the *tzitz*, even if one subsequently proceeds knowingly with the *zerikat hadam*. This is admittedly a counterintuitive reading and not the simple sense of the *mishnah*, but it is how *Rabbi Shila* understands the law.

### Braita Reconciliation

The *gemara* then confronts the question of how to reconcile each position with the other's primary text. For *Rabbi Shila*, who holds that the *tumah* must have arisen *b'shogeg* and that the *zrika* may be *b'meizid*, how does he read the *beraita*'s statement *bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid*? The *gemara* explains that, according to him, the *beraita* should be read as: when the *tumah* arose *b'shogeg*, I do not care whether the subsequent *zrika* was *b'shogeg* or *b'meizid* — the *tzitz* works either way.

The more pressing question is how *Ravina* — who holds that the *zrika* must be *b'shogeg* — can accommodate the *mishnah*'s seemingly restrictive phrasing. After all, the *mishnah* says *nizrak v'achar kach noda*, implying that one must have been unaware at the time of *zrika*. The *gemara* offers an elegant resolution: the *mishnah* chose to present the case of ignorance at the time of *zrika* not because that is the only scenario where the *tzitz* works, but because of the *mishnah*'s literary structure. The *mishnah* needed to contrast the first clause — where the *tzitz* works — with the second clause, where *nitma haguf* and the *tzitz* does *not* work. In the second clause, the *gemara* tells us, the *tzitz* fails to operate *even* when one was ignorant at the time. So to maintain the parallel structure, the *mishnah* presented the first clause using the case of ignorance at the time of *zrika* as well — *tani reisha nami nizrak v'achar kach noda* — even though in reality, according to *Ravina*, one could know of the *tumah* at the time and the *tzitz* would still be effective, as long as it was the *tumah* of the object and not the person.

In summary, the *gemara* yields two positions. *Ravina* focuses on the *act* of *zrika*: it must be performed without knowing the *dam* is *tamei* for the *tzitz* to work. *Rabbi Shila* focuses on the *origin* of the *tumah*: if the *tumah* arose inadvertently, the *tzitz* operates regardless of how the *zrika* was performed. Both agree that some degree of unintentionality is required — they disagree about where that unintentionality must be located.

---

## Tumat HaTehom Query

### Kohen vs. Owner

Having clarified the *tzitz*'s operation for *tamei* objects, the *gemara* turns to the domain in which the *tzitz* does work for *tumat haguf* — namely, *tumat hatehom*. *Rami bar Chama* poses the following question: when we say that *tumat hatehom* is permitted, that the *tzitz* renders the *korban* acceptable even for *tumat haguf* in cases of unknowable *tumah* — does this dispensation extend only to the *baalim*, the owners of the *korban Pesach* or the *nazir*, or does it extend as well to the *kohen* who performs the *avodah*?

The question has obvious practical significance. For most *korbanot*, it matters greatly whether the *kohen* performing the service is *tamei*. For the owner of a *pesach* or a *nazir*'s *korban*, the unique concern is that their personal *tumah* disqualifies them from having the *korban* brought at all. But is the *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* of *tumat hatehom* formulated around the *baalim* specifically — because they are the ones whose *tumah* uniquely prevents the *korban* — or is it formulated around the *korban* itself, such that any person involved, including the *kohen*, benefits from the dispensation?

Put differently: *mi amrinan ki gmeiri tumat hatehom b'baalim* — perhaps the tradition was transmitted specifically for the owners — *b'kohen lo gmeiri* — and we have no such tradition for the *kohen*? Or *dilma b'zivcha gmeiri* — the tradition was transmitted with reference to the offering itself, and therefore applies equally to the *kohen* and the *baalim*?

### Braita Proof

*Rava* attempts to resolve this question by citing the *beraita* of *Rabbi Chiya*, which states: *lo amru tumat hatehom ela l'meis bilvad* — the principle of *tumat hatehom* was said only with respect to a corpse, not to other forms of *tumah*. The *gemara* then asks: *le-mes l'mautei mai* — what is this exclusion designed to rule out? The most natural candidate is *tumat hatehom d'sheretz* — a case where a dead rodent was buried underground, unknowable to anyone, and someone inadvertently incurred its *tumah* in a way that could not have been known.

If such a case were to arise, *Rabbi Chiya*'s *beraita* tells us that the *tzitz* would *not* render it acceptable. But the *gemara* immediately asks: in what scenario would this exclusion even be necessary? For whom would it matter?

### Owner or Kohen

The *gemara* works through the possibilities. If the person who stepped on the buried rodent was the owner bringing his *pesach*, the question becomes: does being *tamei sheretz* even prevent one from bringing a *korban Pesach*? This depends on a dispute in the *gemara* elsewhere. According to the view that *ein shochtin v'zorkin al tmei sheretz* — that one may not perform the *shechita* and *zerikat hadam* while the owner is *tamei* even with a one-day *tumah* — the case is meaningful. The *chiddush* would be that even though the *tumah* was of the *tumat hatehom* variety, since it arose from a *sheretz* rather than a corpse, the *tzitz* does not save the *pesach*. But according to the view that *shochtin v'zorkin al tmei sheretz* — that one *may* bring the *korban Pesach* even while the owner has a one-day *tumah* — then the owner does not need the *tzitz* at all. Even if we *knew* he had touched a *sheretz*, the *pesach* would still be valid. *A fortiori*, if the *tumah* was unknowable, there would be no reason to speak of the *tzitz* at all.

Similarly, if the owner were a *nazir*, there would be no issue. A *nazir* is only concerned with *tumas meis* — *tumah* from a human corpse. Touching a *sheretz* has no bearing on his *nezirut* whatsoever: *ki hames mealoto amar Rachmana*. So the *nazir* case does not require the *tzitz* in a *sheretz* scenario either.

That leaves the *kohen* as the only person for whom the exclusion would be practically relevant. For every *korban*, the *kohen* performing the *avodah* must be *tahor*. If the *kohen* unknowingly touched a dead rodent buried in a manner consistent with *tumat hatehom* — a truly unknowable *tumah* — the *beraita* tells us the *tzitz* would not remedy this. But the fact that we need to *exclude* this case implies that for the *tumat hatehom* of a corpse, the *tzitz* would indeed work for the *kohen*. As the *gemara* puts it: *u-shma mina hutrah lo tumat hatehom* — we may infer from this that *tumat hatehom* operates to permit the *kohen* as well, not only the owner.

*Rav Yosef*, however, objects that this inference is not proven. The proof rests on two unstated assumptions: first, that the excluded case involves a *sheretz*; and second, that there is no scenario involving the *baalim* in which the *sheretz* exclusion would be necessary. But if the excluded case is something entirely different — namely, *tumat hatehom d'ziva*, the unknowable *tumah* of a *zav* or *zava* flow — then the *beraita*'s exclusion could still be referring entirely to the owners, and no inference about the *kohen* can be drawn. *Rav Yosef* therefore says: *le'olam b'baalim* — we are always talking about the owners — and the excluded case is not *sheretz* but *ziva*.

---

## Ziva & Unknowable Status

### Shomeres Yom k'Neged Yom

The abstraction of *tumat hatehom* beyond its literal meaning of "buried underground" is essential to understanding *Rav Yosef*'s counter-proposal. *Tumat hatehom* is not a topographical concept; it refers to any *tumah* whose status is genuinely unknowable at the time the *korban* is brought. And *Rav Yosef* proposes that it includes the *tumah* of a *zava* — a woman experiencing irregular uterine bleeding — in the following scenario.

A woman had a vaginal flow on the first day — let us say Monday. Under the laws of *ziva*, having bled once, she must observe the following day, Tuesday, without any further bleeding; this is the *shomeres yom k'neged yom*. If she does not bleed on Tuesday, she is *tehorah*. If Tuesday happens to be *Erev Pesach*, she arises in the morning, has not yet bled, and is currently *tehorah*. She brings her *korban Pesach*. But later on Tuesday she bleeds again.

At this point the question arises: was she *tamei* retroactively from the beginning of Tuesday, meaning she was *tamei* when her *korban Pesach* was brought? Or does the new bleeding only create *tumah* from the moment it begins? At the time of bringing the *korban*, her status was genuinely unknowable — it would only be determined by whether she bled later in the day. This is the *tumat hatehom* of *ziva*: not a buried corpse, but an objectively unknowable *tumah* at the time of the *korban*.

*Rav Yosef* says that this is what *Rabbi Chiya*'s *beraita* is excluding when it says *tumat hatehom* applies only to a corpse. It is excluding this case — *tumat hatehom d'ziva* — and saying the *tzitz* does not work for that. And since the excluded case is one involving the *baalim* of the *pesach* (not the *kohen*, who is entirely unaffected by *ziva* in this context), the *beraita* proves nothing about whether the *kohen* is included in *tumat hatehom* at all.

The *gemara* challenges this by citing *Rabbi Yosei*'s ruling in a *beraita*: a *shomeres yom k'neged yom* for whom the *korban Pesach* was slaughtered and sprinkled on her second day, and who subsequently bled — she may not eat the *korban Pesach* that evening (she is now *tamei*), but she is *patur* from the obligation to bring a *Pesach Sheini*. This suggests that the *korban* was retroactively acceptable. And the most natural explanation would be that the *tzitz* operated — because at the time of the *korban* it was a genuine *tumat hatehom*, and the *tzitz* rendered it acceptable.

### New vs. Retroactive Tumah

The *gemara*, however, pushes back: perhaps the reason *Rabbi Yosei* exempts her from *Pesach Sheini* is not because the *tzitz* worked, but because of a completely different principle regarding the nature of her *tumah*. Specifically, the *gemara* proposes that *Rabbi Yosei* holds *mikan u'l'haba hi mitameia* — her *tumah* operates only from this point forward, not retroactively.

The scenario unfolds as follows: the woman bled on Monday, immersed in a *mikvah* Tuesday morning, and began her day of watching in a state of *tahara*. The *korban Pesach* was brought during the daytime on Tuesday. Later on Tuesday, she began bleeding again. According to *Rabbi Yosei*, that new bleeding makes her *tamei* from that moment onward — it is a new *tumah*, not a continuation of Monday's. Therefore, when the *korban* was brought earlier in the day, she was genuinely *tehorah*, and the *pesach* was fully valid. The reason she cannot eat the meat that evening is simply that she has since become *tamei* again. And the reason she is exempt from *Pesach Sheini* is not that the *tzitz* covered over some retroactive *tumah*, but that there was no *tumah* at the time of the *korban* at all.

If this is *Rabbi Yosei*'s reasoning, then his ruling provides no proof that *tumat hatehom d'ziva* is a genuine category recognized by the *tzitz*. The *gemara* thus leaves the original question of *Rami bar Chama* — whether *tumat hatehom* extends to the *kohen* as well as the owners — unresolved, to be continued in the discussion on the following *daf*. The deeper question of what precisely constitutes *tumat hatehom* in the case of *ziva*, and whether the *tzitz* operates for such cases, remains the axis around which the *gemara* will continue to turn.

---

---

# Pesachim 81

## Ritzuy Tzitz Principle

### Ritzuy Tzitz Basics

The *mishna* on this *daf* builds upon the concept of *ritzuy tzitz* — the mechanism by which the *kohen gadol*'s golden forehead plate renders acceptable a *korban* that would otherwise be invalid on account of *tumah*. The Torah states *venasa Aharon et avon hakodashim asher yakdishu bnei Yisrael* — that Aaron shall bear the sin of the sanctified objects consecrated by the children of Israel. The *halacha* understands this to mean that *korbanot* which contracted *tumah* are rendered acceptable through the presence of the *tzitz*, provided the *tumah* was contracted without awareness at the time of the *zerikah*, the throwing of the blood. This is the technical meaning of *ritzuy*: making the *korban* acceptable despite the *tumah*.

One background issue is whether this principle is needed in concert with the concept of *tumah hutrah b'tzibur* — that *tumah* is entirely permitted when the community is *tamei* — or only when *tumah* is merely *dechuya*, overridden but still present. Our discussion, however, shifts to the case of the individual. The *mishna* teaches that the *tzitz* works when the *korban's* blood or meat is *tamei*, not when the person offering it is *tamei*. The *tzitz* is *meratze* only for *avon hakodashim*, the sin pertaining to the sanctified objects themselves, and not *avon hamakrivim*, the sin pertaining to those who bring the offering.

### Object vs. Person Tumah

In most circumstances, the *tumah* of the owner of the *korban* is immaterial — the owner need not be present in the *Beit Hamikdash*. But two *korbanot* are exceptional in this regard: the *korban pesach* and the *korban* of the *nazir*. If the owner of a *korban pesach* is *tamei*, he cannot participate in the *Pesach* offering and must instead bring a *Pesach Sheni*. If the *nazir* is *tamei*, his *nezirut* must begin again from the start. In these two cases, *tumah* of the person is critically determinative, and the *tzitz* does not assist even if the person was entirely unaware of the *tumah*.

### Tumat HaTehom Exception

There is, however, a remarkable exception. The *mishna* teaches that the *tzitz* does work for *tumat hatehom* — a *tumah* of the depths — even when the person himself is *tamei*. *Tumat hatehom* refers not merely to a *tumah* that was unknown to the person, but to a *tumah* that was unknowable at the time. This is treated as a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, a received tradition from Sinai, that in such a case the *tzitz* renders the *korban pesach* or the *korban* of the *nazir* acceptable. The question then follows from the preceding *gemara*: does this *halacha* apply exclusively to the owner (*be'alim*) of the *korban*, or does it extend also to the *kohen* performing the *avodah*?

---

## Zavah & Rabbi Yose

### Shomeret Yom Scenario

To address this question, the *gemara* introduces the position of *Rabbi Yose*, and before analyzing how his position bears on the question of the *kohen*, it is necessary to understand the underlying scenario. The case involves a woman who is a *shomeret yom kineged yom* — she observed one clean day opposite a day of *tumah*.

The relevant *halacha* is as follows. A woman who experiences uterine bleeding outside her regular menstrual period is subject to the laws of *zavah*. If she bleeds on Sunday, she is *teme'ah* that day. She then immerses in the *mikveh* Monday morning and must observe Monday without further bleeding. If she successfully remains clean through Monday, she is *tehorah*. If, however, she bleeds at some point during Monday, that becomes a second day of *tumah*, and she must observe Tuesday as well; should she bleed again on Tuesday, it becomes three consecutive days, rendering her a *zavah gedolah* who must count seven clean days.

The scenario the *gemara* highlights is this: a woman bleeds on Sunday, immerses on Monday morning, and they then bring a *korban pesach* on her behalf during Monday — since *Erev Pesach* falls on that day — while she is apparently *tehorah*. Later on Monday she bleeds again. Retroactively, it turns out she was in an ambiguous state during the entire period from Monday morning until the renewed bleeding. The *gemara* identifies this as a paradigmatic case of *tumat hatehom* — a *tumah* that was unknowable at the time of the offering. The question is whether the *tzitz* works for such a case of *zavah* or only for *tumas meis*, corpse *tumah*.

### Rabbi Yose's Baraita

A *baraita* is cited: *Rabbi Yose* states that in exactly this case — a *shomeret yom kineged yom* for whom the *korban pesach* was slaughtered and the blood thrown, and who then bled later that same day — she may not eat the *korban pesach* that night, since she is now *teme'ah*, but she is exempt from bringing a *Pesach Sheni*. The *korban* was accepted. The *gemara* initially suggests the reason must be *ritzuy tzitz* — the *tzitz* worked for her because her *tumah* was unknowable at the time of the *zerikah*.

### Rami's Objection

*Rami* objects. The exemption from *Pesach Sheni* need not be attributed to *ritzuy tzitz* at all. Perhaps *Rabbi Yose* holds the position that a *zavah* who bleeds on the second day does not thereby create a retroactive continuous *tumah*. Rather, the renewed bleeding constitutes a new and independent onset of *tumah*, commencing only from the moment it occurs. Under this reading, the woman was genuinely *tehorah* from the time of her *mikveh* immersion on Monday morning until she bled again that afternoon. The *korban pesach* was therefore brought in a state of actual *taharah*, and no *tzitz* was needed. The reason she cannot eat that night is that she became *teme'ah* after the offering was completed, but the *korban* itself was entirely unimpeachable.

### Zav & Zavah Cases

The *gemara* then cites a *baraita* to push back on *Rami*'s interpretation. A *zav* — a man who experiences an abnormal penile flow (distinct from semen) — follows a similar but not identical structure of *tumah* to the *zavah*. Whereas a *zavah* is defined by three consecutive days of bleeding, the *zav* is defined by the number of flows. If he has two flows he is a *zav*, and must count seven clean days before bringing his *korbanot* and ending his *tumah*.

The *baraita* describes a case in which a *zav* who has had two flows reaches day seven, and they bring his *korban pesach* on that day. He then has another flow just before nightfall. Similarly, a *shomeret yom kineged yom* has her *korban pesach* brought on her second day, and she then bleeds again that afternoon. The *baraita* states that retroactively they are *tamei* with *tumat mishkav u'moshav* — the unique *tumah* which a *zav* or *zavah* transmit to that which they sit or lie upon, which carries an especially severe degree of *tumah* as an *av hatumah*. Retroactively, anything they had sat upon during that period is rendered *tamei*. Yet despite this retroactive *tumah*, the *baraita* states they are exempt from *Pesach Sheni*. The *korban* was good.

If *Rabbi Yose*'s position is that there is no retroactive *tumah* at all and the second day's bleeding is an entirely new onset, then why does the *baraita* explicitly invoke the language of *lemafrea* — retroactively? The *baraita* seems to say there *was* retroactive *tumah*, and yet the *korban pesach* was valid. This suggests the *korban* was saved not by the absence of any *tumah* but by the *tzitz* working for an unknowable *tumah*.

---

## Retroactive Tumah Debate

### Retroactivity Challenge

The *gemara* presses further. The language of the *baraita* — *metamei mishkav u'moshav lemafrea*, that one renders *mishkav* and *moshav* retroactively *tamei* — seems to directly contradict *Rami*'s interpretation that there is simply no retroactive *tumah* according to *Rabbi Yose*. If it is truly a new *tumah* from the moment of the renewed bleeding, why does the *baraita* speak in terms of retroactivity at all?

### Rav Oshaya's Position

The *gemara* notes that *Rav Oshaya* also grapples with this question in what is cited as a *baraita*, though the attribution is textually problematic: *Rav Oshaya* is the known editor of *baraitot*, but he himself is never quoted within a *baraita*, and *Rabbi Yochanan*, an *amora*, appears in this same passage responding to him. The *rishonim* accordingly emend the text from *detanya* to *amar Rav Oshaya*. *Rav Oshaya* states that a *zav* who has a flow on his seventh day thereby causes that flow to *soter shelifanav* — to retroactively undermine the preceding period of *taharah*, treating it as continuous *tumah*.

*Rabbi Yochanan* responds to him: why should it undermine everything? Should it not cost only the day on which the flow occurred? The *gemara* immediately rejects the simple reading of *Rabbi Yochanan*'s response. By the rule of *mi-mah nafshach* — whichever way you turn it — the position is incoherent: if a flow on day seven creates retroactive *tumah*, then all the preceding days are undermined, since the seven days were never truly clean; and if the flow constitutes new *tumah* from this point forward only, then even day seven itself is not lost, since the new *tumah* simply begins now.

### Rabbi Yoshia's Response

The *gemara* therefore reinterprets *Rabbi Yochanan*: he must have said that the flow on day seven should not cause the loss of even one day, since it is a new *tumah* with no retroactive effect. *Rabbi Yoshia* then responds to *Rabbi Yochanan* that *Rabbi Yose* agrees with him — that a flow on the final day, after the day began in a state of *taharah*, constitutes a new *tumah* and does not retroactively undermine the preceding period.

The *gemara* now objects: but we have the *baraita* that says *Rabbi Yose* rules the person is *tamei mishkav u'moshav lemafrea*! If *Rabbi Yose* holds there is no retroactive *tumah*, how can the *baraita* use that language? The *gemara* resolves this: *shma mina metamei lemafrea miderabbannan* — the retroactive *tumah* stated in the *baraita* according to *Rabbi Yose* is only rabbinic. Biblically, the person was *tahor* during the interval between the *mikveh* immersion and the renewed flow. The retroactive *tumah* of *mishkav u'moshav* is a rabbinic stringency applied after the fact, but the biblical status during that period was *tahor*, and therefore the *korban pesach* was valid without any need for the *tzitz*.

### Miktzat HaYom Principle

Central to this entire discussion is the principle of *miktzat hayom k'kulo* — that part of a day counts as the whole day. This principle, familiar from the laws of *aveilut* where a mourner may rise from *shiva* at the start of the seventh day, applies here as well. When the woman immerses on Monday morning, the beginning of Monday counts as a full day of *taharah*, even if she subsequently bleeds later that day. This is the mechanism by which *Rabbi Yose* can say the day began in *taharah* — *miktzat hayom k'kulo* — and therefore the renewed bleeding is a new onset rather than a continuation.

However, this logic only applies when the day in fact began with *taharah*. The *gemara* then asks: according to *Rabbi Yose*, how can one ever arrive at a *zavah gedolah* who bleeds three consecutive days? If each day's renewed bleeding is simply a new onset, three consecutive days of *tumah* would never coalesce into the severe status of *zavah gedolah*. The *gemara* gives two answers. First, *bishofach* — she bled continuously for three days without interruption. Second, a more technically precise scenario: she bled during the *bein hashmashos* — the twilight period at the end of Sunday and again at the end of Monday, such that both days ended in *tumah* and Tuesday began in *tumah*. In this case, there was never any *miktzat hayom* of *taharah* at the start of any day to break the continuity, and therefore the three days coalesce into a single continuous *tumah* of a *zavah gedolah*.

This last scenario leads to an observation by *Rashi* and *Tosafot* about which twilight is the operative one for *miktzat hayom* — the beginning of the night or the beginning of the morning — a question that connects to broader discussions in other areas of *halacha*.

---

## Tzitz Timing & Aware (II)

### After Zerika Only

The *gemara* now returns to the question of timing: at what point in the *avodah* process must the *tumat hatehom* become known in order for the *tzitz* to be effective? *Mar bar Rav Ashi* states: the *tzitz* works for *tumat hatehom* only when the awareness came after the *zerikah* — after the blood was thrown. At the moment of *zerikah*, the person was ignorant and the *tumah* unknowable; the blood was thrown properly, and when the *tumah* was subsequently discovered, the *tzitz* renders the *korban* acceptable retroactively. But if awareness came before the *zerikah*, the *tzitz* does not apply and the *korban* is invalid.

The *gemara* challenges this from the *baraita* concerning *hamotzei meis mushkav l'rochbah shel derech* — a case where a dead body was found lying across the entire width of a path, making it impossible for the traveler to have avoided passing over it. The *baraita* states that for purposes of *trumah*, the person is *tamei*, but *l'nazir v'oseh pesach tahor* — for a *nazir* and one who brought the *korban pesach*, the person is *tahor*. The *baraita* uses the language of *tahor* — a language that implies one may act upon this status *lechatchila*, going forward. This seems to suggest that even before the *zerikah*, upon discovering the *meit* after walking over the path, the person could proceed to bring the *korban pesach* in the first instance.

The *gemara* therefore reformulates *Mar bar Rav Ashi*'s statement. Rather than a strict limit to post-*zerikah* awareness, the corrected ruling is: do not say that the *tzitz* works only when awareness came after the *zerikah* and not before; rather, even if awareness came before the *zerikah*, the *tzitz* works.

*Rashi* and *Tosafot*, however, draw back from the radical implications of this formulation. Based on other evidence including a *Tosefta*, they limit the ruling to the narrow window between *shechita* and *zerikah*. If awareness comes before the *shechita*, the *korban* cannot be brought. But once the *shechita* has been performed and the *avodah* has already commenced under conditions of *tumat hatehom*, the *kohen* may proceed to the *zerikah* and complete the offering. This is because the *avodah* began properly, in ignorance of an unknowable *tumah*, and may therefore be completed.

Even this limited position is striking: the *kohen* now knows the person is *tamei*, and yet *Rashi* and *Tosafot* say he may proceed with the *zerikah*. The language of *tahor* in the *baraita* is thus the language of *lechatchila* — it describes a permission to act, though the person is not truly *tahor* in fact. The *ritzuy* of the *tzitz* does not remove the *tumah*; it renders the *korban* acceptable. The owner may not eat the *korban pesach*, and must subsequently immerse and follow the normal process of *taharah*. The *ritzuy* means only that he has fulfilled his *korban pesach* obligation.

---

## Tumat HaTehom & Kohen

### Rav Yosef's Question

With this background established, the *gemara* returns to the unresolved question of whether *tumat hatehom* applies only to the *be'alim* — the owners — or also to the *kohen* performing the *avodah*. *Rav Yosef* poses a further question: if the *tzitz* does work for the *kohen* bringing the *korban pesach* or the *korban* of the *nazir*, does this principle extend to a *kohen* performing the *avodah* of other *korbanot* as well — for instance, the *tamid*, the daily offering?

### Rava's Kal VaChomer

*Rava* proposes a *kal v'chomer*: if *tumat hatehom* is permitted in a context where ordinary known *tumah* is not — namely, the *korban pesach* and *korban nazir*, where even an aware owner who is *tamei* cannot bring the offering — then certainly in a context where known *tumah* is permitted — such as the *tamid*, which may be brought even when all available *kohanim* are *tamei* — *tumat hatehom* should likewise be permitted. The logic seems compelling: the case where *tumah* is more stringently treated already accommodates *tumat hatehom*; the case where *tumah* is more leniently treated should do so *a fortiori*.

### Halacha Lemoshe Status

The *gemara* rejects this reasoning with a fundamental principle: *u'mi dayninan kal v'chomer me-halacha* — one cannot apply a *kal v'chomer* to a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. The very character of a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* is that it is an arbitrary received tradition, not derived through logic. Since *tumat hatehom* and the *ritzuy* of the *tzitz* are understood to be *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, one cannot use logical argumentation to extend their scope.

A proof for this principle is adduced from a debate between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Akiva*. The *halacha* that a *nazir* must shave and restart his *nezirut* upon contracting *tumah* from a bone the size of a barley grain is a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. *Rabbi Akiva* attempted to extend this by a *kal v'chomer* to a *revi'it* of blood from a corpse — which causes *tumah b'ohel* while the small bone does not — arguing that if the bone triggers the obligation to shave, the blood certainly should. *Rabbi Eliezer* responded: *etzem kese'orah halacha* — the rule concerning the bone is a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — *v'ein danin kal v'chomer mehalacha* — and one does not derive extensions of a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* through *kal v'chomer*.

Nonetheless, *Rava* then proposes an alternative: although *kal v'chomer* cannot be applied to an arbitrary *halacha*, a *gezeirah shavah* can be used to connect arbitrary *halachot* to one another. The word *b'moado* — "in its appointed time" — appears in the *pasuk* of the *pesach* and similarly in the *pasuk* of the *tamid*. A *gezeirah shavah* from *pesach* to *tamid* could in principle extend the *halacha* of *tumat hatehom* to the *tamid*. The logic here is that one arbitrary mechanism (*gezeirah shavah*) may legitimately be used to extend another arbitrary tradition, while a logical argument (*kal v'chomer*) may not.

---

## Tzitz Timing & Aware (II)

### Meis Across Road

The *baraita* describes the case of *hamotzei meis mushkav l'rochbah shel derech* in full. A dead body was found lying across the entire width of a road. Since it covered the whole width, it was physically impossible to traverse the road without having passed over or alongside the corpse. For purposes of *trumah*, such a person is considered *tamei* — the *tumah* is certain, not merely doubtful. But for the *nazir* and the one who brought the *korban pesach*, the person is *tahor*, because at the time of the encounter the *tumah* was unknowable — a true case of *tumat hatehom*.

This rule applies when the body covered the entire width with no room to pass. If there was a space at the edge through which a person could have walked, then even for *trumah* the person is *tahor* — the principle of *safek tumah b'reshut harabbim*, that a doubt of *tumah* in a public domain is resolved leniently, applies.

### Rashi/Tosafot Limit

Furthermore, this strict ruling — that when the entire width was covered one is *tamei* for *trumah* — applies only when the body was found intact. If it was *meshubar m'furak* — broken into pieces — the person is *tahor*, since it is possible to have walked between the gaps. This leniency does not apply, however, when the body is in a *kever*. *Rashi* understands *kever* here as a coffin, while *Tosafot* is troubled by this interpretation: if it is in a coffin, presumably someone knows about it, and it would not qualify as *tumat hatehom* at all. *Tosafot* therefore discusses whether *kever* means a purposefully constructed burial site and raises the question of what makes such a case unknowable. When the body is in a *kever*, even if it is in pieces, the person is *tamei*, because *kever m'tzarfo* — the grave or coffin unifies the pieces into a single source of *tumah*, and the *tumah* emanates from the entire structure.

The *baraita* further distinguishes by the manner of the traveler's passage. If one walked on foot, it remains possible that one navigated a gap between the pieces without directly passing over or creating an *ohel* above the body; therefore, one may be *tahor*. But if one was carrying a heavy load or riding an animal, it is impossible to have avoided contact or *ohel*, and the person is *tamei*. The mechanism for this stringency — presumably that a large load creates its own *ohel*, or that the width of one's passage while bearing a load makes avoidance of the body impossible — is acknowledged as requiring further analysis in the tractate of *Oholot*.

---

## Source of Tumat HaTehom

### Rabbi Eliezer's Source

Having established that *tumat hatehom* operates as a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, the *gemara* now inquires whether it has any basis in scripture. *Rabbi Eliezer* cites the *pasuk* regarding the *nazir*: *v'chi yamus meis alav* — if a dead body dies upon him, implying that the *tumah* must be directly and clearly upon him, *b'michuveres elav*, in something that was connected to and known by him. If the *tumah* was unknown to him, it is as if it was not "upon him" in the relevant sense, and he need not restart his *nezirut*. This establishes the principle by the *nazir*, but leaves open the source for the *korban pesach*.

### Rabbi Yochanan's Source

For the *korban pesach*, *Rabbi Yochanan* cites the word *lachem* — "to you" — that appears in the *pasuk* dealing with *pesach*: *o baderech rechokah lachem*. The *tumah* must be *michuveres lachem*, something connected and known to you. If it was not known, it falls outside the scope of the prohibition.

### Reish Lakish's Source

*Reish Lakish* derives the principle differently: *k'derech* — like a road or path, which is *galuy*, open and exposed to all. Just as a public road is known to everyone, so too *tumah* must be of the known, public variety. If it is not generally visible and knowable, it is not in the relevant category.

### Scriptural Source Challe…

The *gemara* objects to all three scriptural derivations. The *mishnah* and *baraita* define *tumat hatehom* with extreme precision: the *tumah* was unknown to even *one person* in the entire world. This is an extraordinarily narrow category. But the scriptural derivations would yield a much broader category. According to *Rabbi Eliezer*'s derivation, the category would be anything unknown to the person himself. According to *Rabbi Yochanan*'s derivation from *lachem* — the plural form, "to you" — it would require that the *tumah* be unknown to at least two people. According to *Reish Lakish*'s derivation from the analogy to a path, it would need to be unknown to the general public. None of these yields the precise *halacha* that even one person's knowledge anywhere in the world removes the classification of *tumat hatehom*.

### Halacha Lemoshe Conclusi…

The conclusion is therefore clear: *tumas hatehom hilchasa gemiri lah* — *tumat hatehom* is a received tradition, a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. *U'kra asmachta b'alma* — the scriptural verses are mere supports (*asmachta*), not the true source of the law. This conclusion retroactively explains the discussion earlier in the *sugya*: when *Rava* was asked to apply a *kal v'chomer* from *pesach* to *tamid*, the response that *tumat hatehom* is *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* was precisely the conclusion arrived at here. *Rashi* notes that the discussion we have just read was chronologically prior and that the *gemara* above presupposed its outcome.

---

## Tumat HaTehom Scenarios

### Body Across Road

The *mishna* describes in detail the specific scenarios that constitute *tumat hatehom*. The first case is *hamotzei meis mushkav l'rochbah shel derech* — finding a dead body lying across the entire width of a road. As analyzed above, this renders the person *tamei* for *trumah*, but *tahor* for the *nazir* and the one who brought the *korban pesach*, provided the *tumah* was unknowable at the time.

### Broken Body vs. Grave

The *mishna* introduces two further refinements. If the body was *meshubar m'furak* — broken into pieces — the person is *tahor*, since it is possible to have walked through the gaps without contact or *ohel*. However, if the body was in a *kever*, even if broken into pieces, the person is *tamei*, because *kever m'tzarpo* — the grave consolidates the pieces such that the entire burial structure transmits *tumah*, and one cannot argue that the gaps between the pieces provided a safe corridor.

### Manner of Travel

The *mishna* further distinguishes based on how the person was traveling. One who walked on foot and traversed a path over which a broken body lay may potentially have passed through the gaps and is therefore *tahor*. One who was carrying a load (*ta'un*) or riding an animal (*rachuv*) is *tamei*, because in those modes of travel it is impossible to have avoided contact or *ohel* over the body.

### Definition of Unknown

The *mishna* then provides the critical definitional statement: *eizo hi tumat hatehom* — what constitutes a *tumah* of the depths? *Kol shelo hekirah echad b'sof ha'olam* — any *tumah* that not one person in the entire world recognized or was aware of at the time. This is the operative definition: if even a single person, anywhere in the world, knew that the *tumah* was present at the time the person came into contact with it, the case does not qualify as *tumat hatehom*, and the *tzitz* does not apply.

### Exceptions to Definition

The *mishna* also addresses cases where a body was concealed not by being buried beneath the earth, but in other ways. If the body was *tamun b'teven, b'afar, u'v'tzrorot* — hidden in straw, loose soil, or stones — that still qualifies as *tumat hatehom*, assuming no one was aware of it. By contrast, if the body was in water, in darkness, or in a niche within a cave (*nikikei hasla'im*), that does not qualify as *tumat hatehom*. *Tosafot* explains that in those scenarios, someone presumably does know about it. Alternatively, even if no one specifically knows, those situations are *galuy* in character — with minimal effort the body could be seen or found — and therefore lack the quality of genuine inaccessibility that defines *tumat hatehom*.

### Tumat HaTehom Scope

Finally, the *mishna* states the limiting principle that opened this entire discussion: *v'lo amru ela tumat hatehom ela l'meit bilvad* — the sages said *tumat hatehom* only with respect to a corpse, and not with respect to other sources of *tumah* such as a *sheretz*. This returns us to the starting point of the *sugya*. The *gemara* had asked what case required this exclusion — if *tumat hatehom* works for the *be'alim*, then excluding *sheretz* makes sense because a person who is *tamei sheretz* on the fourteenth of *Nisan* could bring the *korban pesach* in any case (according to some opinions), or if not, the *tzitz* still would not help him even for corpse *tumah* in a way that needs demonstration. The *gemara*'s exploration of whether *tumat hatehom* applies to the *kohen* remained unresolved by direct proof, but the scope of *tumat hatehom* is in any case bounded: it is a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* applying to corpse *tumah* alone.

# Pesachim 82

## Intro: Pesach Tumah

### Pesach Tumah Overview

The overarching discussion on this *daf* concerns *tumah* of a *korban pesach*. The earlier portions of the chapter dealt with the case of the *tzibur*, then moved to the case of an individual, and examined how the *tzitz* operates: not to permit eating the meat, but to render the offering acceptable even when the meat or blood becomes *tamei*, and in certain cases even when the owners themselves become *tamei* under the category known as *tumat hatehom*. The *mishnah* now turns to the practical question of what is done with the meat once parts of the *korban pesach* have in fact become *tamei*.

### Post-Zrika Status

Before proceeding, it is important to recall a foundational principle: once the *korban pesach* has been brought and the *dam* has been *nizrak*, whatever occurs afterward does not affect whether one has discharged the obligation of bringing the *pesach*. If the meat subsequently became *tamei*, or if one failed to eat it, the bringing itself was valid so long as the offering was fit to be eaten at the time of the *zrikat hadam*. The question of the *mitzvah* of eating is a separate matter entirely. The *mishnah* now addresses how one handles the meat in cases where it did become *tamei* after the *korban* was brought.

## Mishnah: Burning Pes (II)

### Entire/Majority Tamei

The *mishnah* states: *nitmah kulo o rubo* — if the entirety or the majority of the *pesach* became *tamei* (whether before it was dismembered or through contact with something that affected the whole or most of it), *sorfin oto lifnei habirah me'atzei hama'arachah* — one burns it in the presence of the *Birah*, understood here to mean the *Beit HaMikdash*, using wood designated for the *ma'arachah*, the wood pile on the altar. The *gizbar*, the Temple treasurer, provides sanctified wood from the altar's stores, and one uses it to burn the *pesach* that became *tamei*.

### Kodshim Burning Rules

The general *halakhah* regarding *kodshim* that become *pasul* is, as the *Gemara* quoted in the second *perek* and will cite again briefly: *bakodesh ba'esh tisaref* — *kol shepasula bakodesh*. Any sacrifice that became invalid must be burned, and it must be burned on holy ground, in the environs of the *Beit HaMikdash*. This principle applies primarily to *kodshei kodashim* — sacrifices that, when valid, must be eaten within the immediate precincts of the *Beit HaMikdash* and may not leave the *Azarah*. The *pesach*, by contrast, may be eaten throughout all of *Yerushalayim*. As will emerge, this difference creates scenarios where burning outside the *Beit HaMikdash* area is permitted, since the meat itself — when *kosher* — was permitted to be eaten anywhere within *Yerushalayim*.

### Minority Tamei/Notar

The *mishnah* then addresses a less severe case: *nitma mi'uto* — only a minority of the meat became *tamei* — or the case of *notar*, where the meat was not *tamei* but simply remained uneaten as leftover. These are regarded as less severely negligent occurrences. In such cases, *sorfin oto bechatzeroteihen o al gagoteihen* — one burns it at home, in one's courtyard or on one's roof, presumably within *Yerushalayim* where the meat was being eaten. There is no requirement to bring it to the *Beit HaMikdash*. However, *me'atzei atzman* — one must use one's own firewood.

### Two Issues: Location & W…

There are two distinct issues operating simultaneously throughout this *mishnah*, and the *Gemara* will return to both. The first is where one burns it: burning it wherever one wishes is obviously easier, sparing one the need to bring it to the *Beit HaMikdash*. The second is what wood one uses. The *Gemara* will explain that when the entirety became *tamei*, the requirement to burn it before the *Beit HaMikdash* functions as a kind of fine — a consequence for allowing the entire *korban* to become *tamei* through negligence. The purpose, as will become clear, involves an element of public embarrassment designed to deter such negligence in the future.

## Tosafot: Balance

### Temple Wood Leniency

As for the leniency of using Temple wood, a conceptual difficulty immediately arises: the wood is *hekdesh*, sanctified property of the *Beit HaMikdash* — so how may it be used for burning *pasul* meat? *Rashi* and *Tosafot* both refer to another *Gemara* that employs the principle of *lev beit din matneh aleihem*. Since the wood is sanctified only in the sense of being property owned by the *Beit HaMikdash* — not sanctified in the manner of a *korban* itself — the *Beit HaMikdash* always retains, through a form of prior stipulation, the latitude to employ it in ways that do not constitute direct *hekdesh* usage. Burning *pasul korbanos*, for instance, falls within this conditional permission. The central authority overseeing the *Beit HaMikdash*, understood by *chazal* as a *beit din*, effectively retains control over how this property is deployed, and may stipulate that its *kedushah* does not apply under certain circumstances. This is a separate *sugya* in its own right, but it is the mechanism that makes the leniency of Temple wood workable.

### Reciprocal Balance

There is thus an interesting reciprocal structure in the *mishnah*: on one hand, when the entire *korban* became *tamei*, the offender is inconvenienced and compelled to bring it to the *Beit HaMikdash* area — a *chumra*; on the other hand, Temple wood is provided at no personal cost — a *kula*. *Tosafot* explicitly describes this balance, framing the provision of Temple wood as a counterweight to the harshness of having to perform the burning in a public location.

### Public Burning Purpose

*Tosafot* addresses the rationale directly. Since one is already being subjected to the considerable inconvenience and indignity of having to come to the *Beit HaMikdash* to perform this public burning — *kedei levaysho*, in order to shame him — the authorities did not further compel him to provide his own firewood. The public nature of the burning is embarrassing enough; requiring personal wood on top of that would be excessive. The two considerations are thus kept in careful balance: the location serves the purpose of deterrence through embarrassment, while the provision of materials offers modest relief.

## Mishnah: Burning Pes (II)

### Hatzikanim Category

The *mishnah* introduces one further category: *hatzeikanim*, the stingy people. These individuals would actually make the journey to the public burning area near the *Beit HaMikdash* — *bishvil lehenos me'atzei hama'arachah* — specifically in order to benefit from the Temple's firewood, even when they were not required to come. When only a minority of the *korban* became *tamei* or there was *notar*, they were entitled to burn it at home with their own wood. Yet to avoid the personal expense of providing firewood, they were willing to make the journey and suffer whatever public notice came with it. *Tosafot* addresses the obvious problem: if they are not among those obligated to come to the *Beit HaMikdash*, why should they be allowed to use the Temple wood there? *Tosafot* answers that if we refused to allow such people to use the Temple wood and insisted they provide their own, they would simply not burn the *korban* at all. Since they are evidently only willing to perform the burning under the condition of using public wood, we must accommodate them — otherwise the *tamei* meat or *notar* would go unburned entirely.

## Q&A: Negligence & Funds

### Negligence Assumption

One might ask whether *tumah* is always a reliable indicator of negligence — after all, a *sheretz* can simply find its way in, and there is nothing the owner could necessarily have done. And there is a second, related difficulty: if indeed the degree of negligence is uncertain, why should public funds be used to cover what may be private carelessness?

### Response: Presumption

The answer to the first question is that while one cannot determine negligence with certainty in every individual case, the general presumption is sound. If one is treating *hekdesh* with the vigilance it demands, one should be hyper-vigilant. The combination of negligence occurring *and* it affecting the entire *korban* — how did the whole thing become *tamei*? — makes significant carelessness a reasonable inference in the majority of cases, even if not in every one.

As for the public funds question, this is, admittedly, a somewhat ironic arrangement. *Tosafot*'s answer is that once the *Beit HaMikdash* has already imposed the substantial inconvenience and public shame of bringing the burning to a public location, it would be too much to additionally compel the person to supply the materials for, in a sense, his own public humiliation. That said, the person cannot simply choose to burn it in his backyard with his own wood — that option is not available.

### Gemara Answer: Purpose

The *Gemara* itself cuts directly to the rationale: *amar Rav Yosef amar Rav Chanina* — *kedei le-vayshan*, in order to embarrass them. The purpose is not to derive pleasure from shaming but rather to create a powerful disincentive, making bystanders sufficiently aware that they become more careful in their own practice.

A useful parallel is found in the *Gemara*'s discussion of why the *ba'al koreh* reads aloud for the congregant called to the Torah rather than the congregant reading himself. Among the reasons given is *shelo levayesh et mi she'ein lo* — so as not to embarrass those who cannot read. If some were to read and others not, those who cannot would be exposed. The same reasoning applies here: if some individuals were to bring their own wood to the public burning, thereby demonstrating their personal means or piety, those who come with public wood would be embarrassed by the contrast. Policy therefore requires uniformity.

One might further ask about the nature of the *lev beit din* — whose *beit din* is this? While the *Sanhedrin* formally operated in the *Lishkat HaGazit*, in the perspective of *chazal* all operations of the *Beit HaMikdash* fall under rabbinic oversight. The phrase *matneh aleihem* — the stipulation applies to the *etzim*, the wood — reflects the idea that a central rabbinic authority retained ultimate supervisory jurisdiction over *hekdesh* property and could calibrate its use accordingly.

## Braita: Leaving Jerusalem

### Departure from Jerusalem

The *Gemara* now presents a *braisa*: *v'chen mi sheyatzah mi'Yerushalayim venizkar sheyeish biyado basar kodesh* — and similarly, one who was departing from *Yerushalayim* and realized he had *shelamim* meat on his person. Since *shelamim* is *kodshim kalim*, there is greater latitude about where it may be burned than there would be for *kodshei kodashim*, where one would have no choice but to burn it within the *Beit HaMikdash* precincts.

### Tzofim Boundary

The relevant boundary marker is *Tzofim* — possibly *Har Tzofim*, or more precisely, the point from which one can still see *Yerushalayim*. *Rashi* understands it as the location beyond which *Yerushalayim* is no longer visible. Once one has passed that point, one is no longer considered to be within the environs of *Yerushalayim*.

### Beyond Tzofim

*Im avar Tzofim* — if one has already passed *Tzofim* — *sorefo bimkomo*: one burns it where one stands. We do not require a return journey, since the traveler is already beyond the effective orbit of the city.

### Within Tzofim Zone

*V'im lav* — if one has not yet passed *Tzofim* — *chozer vesorefo lifnei habirah me'eitzim hama'arachah*: one must return and burn it before the *Birah*, and one is permitted to use the firewood of the *Beit HaMikdash*. Two issues are again in play: the obligation to return and the availability of Temple wood.

## Gemara Q: Why Difference?

### Problem Statement
