The *Gemara* now poses a sharp question. In the *braisa*, the traveler who returns to *Yerushalayim* is permitted to use the wood of the *Beit HaMikdash*. But in the *mishnah*, the person in *Yerushalayim* who has a small portion of *tamei* meat or *notar* is told to burn it at home with his own wood. Why should the traveler returning to *Yerushalayim* be entitled to the Temple wood when the resident of *Yerushalayim* is not? This is the question on which the *Gemara* focuses — not whether someone should be required to return, but why one may use the Temple wood and the other may not.

### Guest vs. Homeowner

*Amar Rav Chama bar Ukva*: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. *Kan be'achsanya kan be'ba'al habayis* — the *mishnah* speaks of a homeowner; the *braisa* speaks of a guest. Why is the traveler leaving *Yerushalayim*? Because he does not live there. In the *braisa*, the person is an *achsanya*, a visitor who came to *Yerushalayim* for *Pesach* but is not a resident. We cannot reasonably expect such a person to have his own wood readily available. And by extension, even had he not yet begun his journey home but was still staying as a guest in *Yerushalayim*, he would similarly be entitled to use the Temple wood. The *mishnah*'s requirement of *me'atzei atzman* applies only to residents — *ba'alei batim* who live in *Yerushalayim* and are not given the option of going to the *Beit HaMikdash* to use public wood. They must remain at home and use their own.

### Two Guest Categories

*Rav Pappa amar*: one can further distinguish between two categories of visitors. *Kan shehecheshik baderech kan shelo hecheshik baderech* — whether one has already begun one's departure or not. A visitor who has not yet started leaving — who is still settled in *Yerushalayim* at his lodgings — is for the time being a temporary resident. Like any resident who wakes up each morning and must provide for himself, we can require him to obtain his own wood and burn the *korban* at home. But the *braisa* addresses one who has already set out on his journey. His mind and body are already outside of *Yerushalayim*, and to now demand that he locate a supplier of wood and manage the logistics of private burning would be unreasonable. In that case, he may proceed to the public burning with Temple wood.

### Rav Zvid: All Guests

*Rav Zvid amar l'olam k'da'amran me'ikara* — Rav Zvid clarifies that the original position was correct: the distinction is always and only between *achsanya* and *ba'al habayis*, regardless of whether one has already started one's journey. *Ve'af al gav de'hecheshik baderech* — even if one is mid-journey, the relevant factor remains one's status as a guest, not the journey itself. The reasoning is: *achsanya keivan delais lei* — a guest simply does not have his own property or resources in the city — *asu kemi she'ein lo* — and so they placed him in the same category as those without means to provide their own wood. Even absent the journey, this is the governing principle. If the sole question were the journey, the rule would be stated differently; the *braisa* mentions the journey not to establish it as the criterion, but — as *Rashi* notes — to teach that even one who has begun leaving must return, and not to limit the wood leniency to travelers only.

## Rashi Clarification

### Rashi: Return Demand

*Rashi* addresses the end of Rav Zvid's position by emphasizing what the *braisa* is primarily coming to teach: that even one who has already set out on his journey must turn around if he has not yet passed *Tzofim*. *Le'ashme'inan chazara nakat lah* — the mention of journey status is there to convey the *chazara*, the obligation to return, and not to define the condition for using the Temple wood. The entitlement to Temple wood, according to Rav Zvid, flows from *achsanya* status alone. *Velo mishum etzim de'hu hadin lelo hecheshik* — even a guest who has not yet started his journey is entitled to the wood.

### Unresolved: Why Return?

This raises a question that *Rashi* leaves somewhat open. One understands why a guest receives the leniency of Temple wood. But why is the guest in the *braisa* also required to return to the *Beit HaMikdash* area specifically? The *mishnah* tells residents they may burn at home. Why is the guest not given the same option — burn wherever you are, using your own or locally obtained wood?

### Two Possible Answers

Two possible answers suggest themselves. The first: the *braisa*'s instruction to return to the *Beit HaMikdash* area is not a standalone obligation but rather a conditional one. The obligation is to return to *Yerushalayim*; if one wishes to make use of the Temple wood, that requires going to the *Beit HaMikdash* precincts. But theoretically, if one wished to go to *Yerushalayim* and use one's own wood, that option might also exist. The *braisa* is not demanding a return to the *Beit HaMikdash* per se — it is offering a path that combines the return obligation with the convenience of Temple wood.

The second possibility: *achsanya* status may cut both ways. For a resident, we say "you are rooted here, stay home, burn it at home." For a guest who has already left his lodgings and set out on his journey, there is no longer a fixed location to which we can direct him. Once he must return in any case, we direct him to the appropriate communal location — the *Beit HaMikdash* area — rather than leaving him to improvise burning somewhere without proper resources. The *Gemara* itself does not resolve this fully.

## Braita: Forbidden Mix

### Private + Temple Wood

The *Gemara* now presents a *braisa* addressing forbidden combinations. If individuals come to burn *pasul* meat privately, in their own courtyards, using wood of the *ma'arachah* — *ein shomin lahem* — this is not permitted. Even in a case like that of the *tzikanim*, where we otherwise accommodate the use of Temple wood, we will not permit them to do so in a private setting.

### Public + Personal Wood

Conversely, if individuals come to burn in the public space before the *Birah* using their own personal wood — *ein shomin lahem* — this too is not permitted. The two considerations — location and wood — are not interchangeable. One cannot mix the leniency of one with the stringency of the other.

### Rav Yosef: Dignity

The *Gemara* readily explains the first prohibition: *dilma payish mineihu* — perhaps some Temple wood will remain after the burning, and since it would otherwise be *hekdesh*, any leftover would remain *hekdesh*. If that wood is in one's private yard and one keeps the remainder, *ve'atu bah lidei takala* — one will come to stumble by using the sanctified wood for ordinary purposes.

The second prohibition — why one may not use personal wood at the public burning site — is explained by *Rav Yosef*: *kedei shelo levayesh et mi she'ein lo* — so as not to embarrass those who lack personal resources. Once the practice at the public burning site involves private wood being brought by some, those who use the public wood are by implication marked as those without means. The policy of uniformity protects dignity. This principle recurs in several places in *halakhah*, including the practice among *Ashkenazim* where the congregant called to the Torah does not read aloud himself — so that *mi she'ein lo*, those who cannot read, are not exposed. Similarly, it has been suggested that the institution of the *mesader kiddushin* reciting the *birkat eirusin* arose because not all *chatanim* knew it, and to have some recite it and others not would embarrass those who could not. The uniform policy eliminates the distinction.

## Rav Papa: Suspicion

### Leftover Wood Concern

*Rav Pappa amar mipnei hachashad* — Rav Pappa offers an alternative reason for prohibiting personal wood at the public burning site: suspicion. If one brings one's own firewood, burns part of it, and then takes the remainder home, observers may suspect that the remaining wood is *hekdesh* wood being taken for private use.

### Non-Temple Materials

The practical difference between Rav Yosef and Rav Pappa becomes apparent in a case where one brings materials that are clearly not Temple wood — reeds or palm branches, for example, which burn quickly and would never be used for the *ma'arachah* on the altar. According to Rav Pappa, there is no *chashad* in such a case: no one would suspect these materials of being *hekdesh*. According to Rav Yosef, however, the prohibition would still apply — because bringing one's own materials, of any kind, to the public burning site introduces the invidious distinction between those who can and those who cannot provide their own.

### Tamid Parallel

A parallel debate appears in *Tamid*, for those familiar with that tractate. The *rosh hama'amad* — the officer overseeing the *kohanim* on duty that day — would station all *tamei kohanim* at *sha'ar hamizrach*, the eastern gate leading into the *Ezrat Nashim*, at the beginning of the day. *Amar Rav Yosef: kedei l'vayeshan* — in order to embarrass them, as a deterrent against allowing oneself to become *tamei*. *Rava amar: mipnei hachashad* — to prevent suspicion, since observers who do not see a *kohen* fulfilling his duties might assume he is neglecting his obligations or absconding to attend to private affairs. The visible presence at the gate makes clear that he is *tamei*, not absent without cause.

### Yosef vs. Papa

The difference between the two positions emerges again in a further case: *mefanki* — those who are idle or independently wealthy. If one has no employment to which one might plausibly slip away, no one would suspect dereliction of duty. According to Rav Pappa's *chashad* reasoning, such a person would not need to be stationed at the gate. According to Rav Yosef's embarrassment reasoning, the practice would still apply, since the purpose is deterrence through shame, not merely the management of perception.

## Intrinsic vs. Extrinsic

### Immediate Burning

The *mishnah* now introduces a distinction of fundamental importance. *Hapesach she'yatzah o shenitma yisaref miyad* — if the *pesach* went out of its permissible boundaries (i.e., left *Yerushalayim*) or became *tamei*, it is burned immediately.

### Delayed Burning

*Nitmu ha-ba'alim o she-meisu* — if the owners became *tamei* or died, such that there is no one entitled to eat the meat, the problem is not intrinsic to the meat itself but external to it. In such a case, *tu'ubar tzurato veyisaref beshishas'ar* — one waits until the meat's appearance degrades overnight, which renders it *notar* by the following morning. Since *pasul kodshim* cannot be burned on *Yom Tov*, and the 15th of *Nissan* is *Yom Tov*, burning is delayed until the 16th.

### R. Yochanan Dissent

*Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka omer* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka disagrees. Even when the owners died or became *tamei*, the meat should be burned immediately — *lefi she'ein lo ochlim*, because when there are no owners to eat it, this is tantamount to an intrinsic invalidity in the *pesach* itself.

### Principle Stated

The underlying principle is thus: *kol shepsulo b'gufo yisaref miyad* — whatever invalidity is intrinsic to the body of the *korban* itself is burned immediately. Invalidity that is external — whether a problem with the blood or a problem with the owners — requires waiting until the following morning. The debate between the *chachamim* and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka hinges on precisely which problems are classified as intrinsic and which as external.

## Gemara: Biblical Sources

### Tumah & Yatzah Sources

The *Gemara* now traces the *derasha* foundations of these laws. *Bishlama tamei ksiv* — the requirement to burn *tamei* meat is clear: *vehabasar asher yiga bechol tamei lo yei'achel ba'esh yisaref* — the Torah explicitly states that if the meat becomes *tamei* it may not be eaten and must be burned. But what is the source for the rule that *yatzah* — meat that left its designated zone — is also burned?

### Moshe-Aharon Dialogue

The *Gemara* derives *yatzah* from the exchange between Moshe and Aharon during the *miluim*. Aharon burned the *chatas* instead of eating it, and Moshe sought to understand why. The *pasuk* states: *hen lo huva et damo el hakodesh penimah* — the blood was not brought inside. For a *korban* whose blood is meant to be sprinkled on the outside, bringing the blood into the *heichal* would invalidate it and require burning. Moshe therefore asked: *madua lo achaltem et hachatas* — why did you not eat this *chatas*? Perhaps, he suggested, you brought the blood *lifnai velifnim*, into the innermost sanctum? Aharon replied: no. Moshe then asked: *shema chutz limchitzasah yatzah* — perhaps the meat left the boundary of the *Azarah* and that is why it was burned? Aharon again replied: no — *bakodesh hayasah*, it remained in the *kodesh*.

### Inference: Yatzah

The *Gemara* reads the exchange as implying: had the meat gone out — had it not remained *bakodesh*, *penimah* — it would have been appropriate to burn it. Alternatively, had the blood been brought too far *pnimah* into the *heichal*, it would similarly have required burning. *Miklal de'im nafkuh* — from the logic of Moshe's question we infer that *yatzah* is a ground for burning *pasul kodshim*. The *Gemara* thus treats these as the two primary scriptural anchors: *nitmah* from the explicit *pesuk* about *tamei* meat, and *yatzah* derived from the Moshe-Aharon dialogue.

## Expansion: Kodshim K (II)

### Question: Shelamim

The *Gemara* now asks: the source from the Moshe-Aharon exchange addressed *kodshei kodashim* — specifically the *chatas*, whose zone is the *Azarah*. *Kadashim kalim minalan* — where do we derive that *yatzah* applies equally to *kodshim kalim* such as *shelamim*?

### Different Zones

The difficulty is compounded by the difference in zones. For *kodshei kodashim*, the relevant boundary is the *Azarah*; crossing that line is a severe violation. For *kodshim kalim* like *shelamim*, the zone extends to all of *Yerushalayim*. It is therefore far from obvious that crossing the boundary of *Yerushalayim* carries the same severe consequence — invalidating the meat and requiring burning — as crossing the wall of the *Azarah* does for *kodshei kodashim*.

## Blood Invalidity Issues

### Blood Cases

The *Gemara* raises a further set of cases established throughout *Shas*: *lan dama* — if the blood was not thrown while it was still day and night fell; *nishpach dama* — if the blood was spilled; *yatzah dama chutz le-klaim* — if the blood was taken outside the *Azarah*. In all these situations, *de-kaima lan bi-sreifah* — it is well-established that the meat must be burned. These are problems not with the meat itself but with the blood. What is their scriptural source?

### Source Question

The question is whether these cases can be derived from existing *pesukim* or whether they rest on tradition. The *Gemara* identifies a *pasuk* through a *braisa* in the name of Rabbi Shimon.

### Rabbi Shimon Pesuk

*Rabbi Shimon omer*: the *pasuk* states — *ve-chol chatas asher yuva mi-damah el ohel moed le-chapeir ba-kodesh lo se-acheil ba-esh tisaref* — any *chatas* whose blood was brought into the *Ohel Moed* to effect atonement inside the *heichal* shall not be eaten but shall be burned with fire in a holy place. The phrase *ba-kodesh ba-esh tisaref* establishes two things: first, that a *chatas* invalidated through mishandling of the blood is burned; second, that it is burned *ba-kodesh* — on sanctified ground, within the *Azarah*. *Limed al chatas she-sreifasah ba-kodesh* — this teaches that a *chatas* rendered *pasul* by a blood problem is burned, and burned specifically in the holy area. From *kol she-pasula ba-kodesh*, the *pasuk* is expanded to apply to other *kodshei kodashim* with other invalidities, including the *imurei kodshim kalim* — the portions of *kodshim kalim* such as *shelamim* fats that must remain within the *Azarah*.

## Expansion: Kodshim K (II)

### No Pesuk: Tradition

When it comes to *kodshim kalim* as a whole — not merely their *imurei* but the meat itself — and for invalidities beyond *tumah*, the *Gemara* is forced to concede: *ela, kol psula ba-kodesh bi-sreifah* — the general rule that *pasul kodshim* must be burned, *lo shena kadashim kalim ve-lo shena kodshei kodashim*, whether *kodshim kalim* or *kodshei kodashim*, cannot be fully derived from *pesukim*. *G'mora g'miri lah* — it is a tradition. The sole *pesuk* we had for *kodshim kalim* addressed *tumah*; for other invalidities affecting *kodshim kalim*, we cannot find a satisfactory scriptural basis, and we must therefore rely on transmitted tradition, akin to the earlier discussion regarding *tumat hatehom*.

## Purpose of Pesuk

### Pesuk Indicates Place

Given that the obligation to burn *pasul kodshim* ultimately rests on tradition — *gemara gemiri lah* — what purpose do the *pesukim* serve? The *Gemara* resolves this by assigning each *pasuk* its own independent function. The *pasuk* of *bakodesh ba'esh tisaref* does not establish the fact of burning — that comes from tradition — but rather specifies the location: that things whose zone when valid was the *Azarah* must be burned in the *Azarah*. The *pesuk* is a locational instruction, not a burning instruction.

### 'Bakodesh' Zone

*Hahu miba'ei lei l'sreifa bakodesh* — that *pasuk* is needed to tell us that burning must occur *bakodesh*, in the holy area, specifically where its zone was *kodesh*. *Bakodesh ba'esh tisaref* thus informs us not that one burns *pasul kodshim* — that is known from tradition — but that one burns it within the boundaries of the zone that defined its permissible use.

## Purpose of Pesuk (II)

### Tumah Pesuk Purpose

This leaves a question about the *tumah pasuk* — *vehabasar asher yiga bechol tamei lo yei'achel ba'esh yisaref*. If burning is already known from tradition and location is taught by *bakodesh ba'esh tisaref*, why do we need this *pesuk*? The *Gemara* answers: *hahi l'gufeih itztareich* — this *pasuk* is needed for its own specific teaching, which could not have been inferred otherwise.

## Aharon's Chatas

### Why Aharon Story?

The *Gemara* asks a pointed question: if the *halakhah* that *pasul kodshim* must be burned is already known through tradition — *gemara gemiri lah* — going back as far as one cares to trace it, why did the *Torah* need to record the story of Aharon and the burning of his *chatas* at all? The entire premise of citing a narrative in the *Torah* is that we derive *halakhah* from it. If the *halakhah* is already established independently, what does the story add?

### Horaas Sha'ah

The response: *u'mishum maaseh shehaya kach haya* — the story of Aharon's *chatas* was not recorded in order to teach a general rule but simply as a historical account of what actually happened. It was a *horaas sha'ah* — a ruling specific to that moment and those circumstances — not a normative precedent for all generations.

### Rabbi Nechemia: Onen

Rabbi Nechemia offers a concrete halakhic grounding for this position: *bidmei aninut nisrefah* — the *chatas* was burned because Aharon was an *onen*, a mourner, on that day. A *kohen onen* may perform the *avodah* — *kohen onen makriv onen* — but an *onen* may not eat consecrated meat. Since every *kohen* available at that time was an *onen*, there was simply no one who could legitimately eat the *chatas*, and that is why it was burned. This was a one-time situation — *horaas sha'ah* — arising from entirely unique circumstances, and no general rule should be extracted from it.

## Tumah Question

### Tumah Common

The *Gemara* now addresses the remaining question about why the *tumah pasuk* is independently necessary. *Salka da'atach amina* — one might have thought to limit the burning obligation to those invalidities that are uniquely *korban*-related: *lan dama* (blood not thrown that day), *nishpach dama* (spilled blood), *yatzah dama* (blood taken outside), *nishchetah balaylah* (slaughtered at night) — all of these are forms of *pesul* that have no parallel in non-sacrificial contexts. *D'leisnhu b'chulin* — such invalidities simply do not occur with ordinary *chulin* food. One might therefore have confined the burning obligation to these distinctly sacrificial forms of *pesul*, reasoning that what makes a *korban pasul* in a *korban*-specific way retains its sacred character even in its invalidity and is therefore burned.

### Resolution: Still Burns

By contrast, *tumah* is commonplace. *D'v'chulin nami mipsal* — even ordinary non-consecrated food is rendered *pasul* by *tumah*; one cannot eat *chulin* that has become *tamei* either. One might therefore have argued that *tumah* is so mundane a form of *pesul* that it strips a *korban* of its elevated status, reducing it in effect to the level of an ordinary spoiled item. And if so — *v'tisgi lei bikvura* — perhaps one need not burn it at all but merely bury it, as one does with *tamei* food that is not *kodesh*. The *tumah pasuk*, *ka mashma lan*, therefore comes to teach that even *tumah*, notwithstanding its commonplace character, carries the full burning obligation when it affects *kodshim*.

## Rav Yosef Analysis

### Before Zrika

*Amar Rav Yosef*: the debate between the *chachamim* and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka must be carefully located in time. *Machlokes shenitm'u be'alim lifnei zrika* — the controversy over whether owner-related problems are intrinsic or extrinsic applies specifically to the case where the owners became *tamei before* the *zrikat hadam*. At the moment the *korban* was being brought, the problem was already present — the owners were already unable to eat the meat. Yet the problem is not in the *korban*'s body itself; it is in the owners. Here, Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka considers this intrinsic — *d'lo itchazi basar l'achilah*, the meat was never fit for eating at the defining moment — while the *chachamim* regard even this as external.

### After Zrika

However, *aval nitm'u be'alim l'achar zrika* — if the owners became *tamei* or died after the *zrikat hadam*, when the *korban* had already been properly brought and the meat was fully fit to be eaten at that moment — *divrei hakol psulah machamat davar acher* — everyone agrees this is an extrinsic *pesul*. Even Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka would concede that the subsequent loss of owners is categorically external to the *korban*.

### External Logic

The logic is straightforward: when the *korban* was brought, it was completely in order. The meat was *de-chazi l'achilah* — fit to be eaten. The problem that arose afterward is external, a circumstance that befell the owners, not a deficiency in the offering itself. *Psulo machamat davar acher* — its invalidity arises from something entirely outside the *korban's* body.

## Baraita Rule

### General Rule

The *Gemara* then cites a *braisa* presenting the general principle: *kol shepsulo b'gufo yisaref miyad* — whatever invalidity is intrinsic to the body of the *korban* is burned immediately.

### Specific Cases

*B'dam u'v'ba'alim te'uvar tzurato* — if the problem involves the blood or the owners, one waits for the night to pass and burns it the following morning, or after *Yom Tov* if applicable.

### Logical Link

The *braisa*'s pairing of blood problems and owner problems in the same category of delayed burning illuminates the interpretation. Problems of the blood — *lan dama*, *nishpach dama* and the like — necessarily occur before *zrikat hadam*, since once the blood has been properly thrown there are no further blood-related issues that could arise. Reading the *braisa*'s grouping accordingly: *ma dam lifnei zerikah af ba'alim lifnei zerikah* — just as blood problems occur before *zrikat hadam*, the owner problems referred to in the *braisa* are likewise those that occurred before *zerikah*. This supports Rav Yosef's reading that the debate between *chachamim* and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka concerns the pre-*zrikat hadam* scenario.

## R.Y. Ben Broka

### His Reasoning

According to the revised reading attributed to Rabbi Yochanan (the *amora*), the debate extends even to the post-*zrikat hadam* scenario. *Af l'achar zerikah nami machlokes* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and the *chachamim* debate not only the pre-*zerikah* case but also what happens after *zerikah*. Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's reasoning, even in the post-*zerikah* scenario, is that if there is no one to eat the meat, the meat itself is intrinsically compromised — *lefi she'ein lo ochlim*, the absence of owners renders it like a body without a purpose, which is itself an intrinsic defect.

### Rabbi Nechemia

Rabbi Yochanan the *amora* aligns Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka with Rabbi Nechemia: *Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka v'Rabbi Nechemia amru davar echad*. The parallel to Rabbi Nechemia is instructive. In the case of Aharon's *chatas*, the *kohanim* were *onenim* — mourners — and could not eat the meat despite the *korban* having been properly offered. This is a post-*zerikah* problem relating to the owners' capacity to eat, not a deficiency in the offering itself. Yet the meat was burned immediately. *Ve-ha aninut l'achar zerikah hi* — this *aninut* problem arose, or is to be treated as arising, in the context of the *zerikah* already having been performed. And despite the fact that the *kohen onen* did perform the *zrikat hadam* — since *kohen onen makriv onen*, an *onen* may perform the service — the inability to eat thereafter was deemed sufficient to require immediate burning.

### Application

The broader application is this: according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, when owners are unable to eat the meat — whether because they became *tamei* before the *zerikah* or, as Rabbi Nechemia's case illustrates, because they are *onenim* after the *zerikah* — the meat is treated as intrinsically invalid and is burned immediately. The *chachamim*, by contrast, maintain that even pre-*zerikah* owner problems are extrinsic, since the source of the *pesul* lies outside the *korban's* body, and delayed burning is therefore required. The dispute thus turns on whether *psulo b'gufo* — intrinsic invalidity — is defined by the moment of *zerikah* or by the source of the problem, a question that the *Gemara* on this *daf* brings into sharp focus.

---

---

# Pesachim 83

## Psul Begufо vs. Bedamo

### Psul Begufо Principle

The daf opens with a review of the foundational principle governing the burning of invalid *korbanot*. When a *korban* becomes *pasul* for an intrinsic reason — a *psul begufo* — it is burned immediately. When the invalidity is extrinsic, characterized in a *baraita* as *bedamo uviva'alim* (relating to the blood or the owners), the burning is deferred until the following day.

### R. Yochanan ben Beroka

This principle was applied in the previous *mishnah* to the *korban pesach* whose owners have died, leaving no one to eat it. Although this would seem to be an extrinsic defect, and therefore one might expect the burning to be deferred to the sixteenth, Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka maintains that even this constitutes a sufficiently intrinsic problem that the *pesach* is burned immediately. According to Rabbi Yochanan in the *Gemara*, this applies even when the owners died after the blood was sprinkled — as long as the meat has no one to eat it, that is treated as an intrinsic defect requiring immediate burning.

### Rava's Connection

The *Gemara* previously connected the position of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka to that of Rabbi Nechemiah, who articulated a similar principle. The daf now opens with Rava drawing a further connection — *Rava mosif af Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili* — identifying yet a third *tanna* who shares this approach.

---

## R. Yossi ha-Gelili

### Parim & Se'irim Nisrafim

Rava teaches that the position of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka — that even an extrinsic defect may necessitate immediate burning — reflects the view of Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili. As the *baraita* states: *Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili omer kol ha-inyan kulo eino medaber ella be-farim ha-nisrafim u-vi-se'irim ha-nisrafim lisrof psuleihem al beis ha-birah.*

The verse in Vayikra states: *ve-chol chatat asher yuva midamah le-chaper ba-kodesh lo te'achel ba-esh tisaref* — that a *chatat* whose blood is brought into the *kodesh*, into the *heichal*, may not be eaten but must be burned. The standard reading of this verse treats it as describing an invalidity: a *chatat* whose blood should have been applied on the outer *mizbe'ach* but was instead brought inside, thereby becoming *pasul*. Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili, however, reads the verse entirely differently. He maintains that the entire passage speaks of *chatat* offerings whose blood is *supposed* to be brought inside — namely the *parim ha-nisrafim* and *se'irim ha-nisrafim*, such as the *par* brought on Yom Kippur or the *par he'elem davar* brought when the *beis din* issues an erroneous ruling.

### Kohen Gadol's Par

This requires a brief review of the relevant *halacha*. When the *korban* is performed correctly — as with the *par* of the *kohen gadol* on Yom Kippur, whose blood is sprinkled inside the *heichal* — the carcass is taken and burned *el michutz la-machaneh*, outside the precincts of the *Beis ha-Mikdash*, as the verse states: *ve-et par ha-chatat ve-et se'ir ha-chatat asher huva et damam le-chaper ba-kodesh yotzi el michutz la-machaneh ve-sarfu va-esh et orotam ve-et besaram ve-et pirsham.*

Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili reads the verse in Vayikra as addressing precisely these *korbanot*, but teaching what is done when such a *korban* becomes *pasul*. Ironically, when performed correctly, the carcass is burned outside the *Beis ha-Mikdash*; but if something goes wrong and the *korban* is invalidated, it is burned *bakodesh* — within the grounds of the *Beis ha-Mikdash* itself. This is what Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili derives from the verse: *lisrof psuleihem al beis ha-birah*. The verse also establishes a *lo ta'aseh* against eating the meat of such offerings.

### Gemara's Challenge

The *Gemara* presses Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili: on your reading, the verse is concerned only with *parim ha-nisrafim* and *se'irim ha-nisrafim*. How then do we know that a normal *chatat* — one whose blood should have been applied on the outer *mizbe'ach* — becomes *pasul* if its blood is brought inside the *heichal*? This is the ruling that the broader tradition derives from this very verse. What is Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili's source for it?

### Aaron's Story

Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili responds by invoking the narrative of Aharon. The verse says: *hein lo huva et damah el ha-kodesh pnimah* — Moshe challenged Aharon, asking why he had burned the *chatat* rather than eating it, noting that its blood had not been brought inside. The *Gemara* infers: *michlal de'ee nafik hee... ee nami ayil dama, bisreifah* — from the very framing of Moshe's question, we derive that had the blood been brought inside, the *korban* would have been burned. Thus the invalidity of a normal *chatat* whose blood is brought inside, along with the requirement to burn it, is derived from this episode.

At this point, the *Gemara* returns to the original purpose of Rava's argument. The connection to Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili is: if even a defect relating to the blood — which might seem extrinsic — results in immediate burning (as inferred from the story of Aharon), then we see that Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili would treat even extrinsic problems as triggering immediate burning. That is the link to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds the same for a *pesach* without owners.

### Dam u'Vasar vs. Ba'alim

The *Gemara* then explains why Rabbi Yochanan himself declined to make this connection. Rabbi Yochanan holds that *dam u-vasar chada milsa hi, ba'alim milsa achrisei hi* — the blood and the flesh of a *korban* are one integrated matter, intrinsic to the physical reality of the *korban* itself, and a defect in either is therefore an intrinsic *psul*. A defect relating to the owners, by contrast, is genuinely extrinsic — it is a problem with the circumstances surrounding the *korban*, not with the *korban* itself. The story of Aharon and the burning of the *chatat* whose blood was brought inside is therefore no proof about a *korban* whose owners have died; those are categorically distinct situations. The debate between Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and the *chachamim* thus turns specifically on the case of the owners — the *ba'alim* — and whether that extrinsic defect suffices to require immediate burning or merely deferred burning.

---

## Atzmos, Gidin, Notar

### Mishnah Listing

The *mishnah* states: *ha-atzamos ve-ha-gidin ve-ha-notar yisrafu be-shishah asar* — the bones, the sinews, and the leftover meat of the *pesach* are burned on the sixteenth. Leftover meat (*notar*) is not meat that became *pasul* for some external reason, but rather the meat of a validly offered *korban* that was simply not consumed. The bones require burning because they contain marrow; since the *korban pesach* carries a prohibition against breaking its bones, the marrow cannot be extracted and burned separately. The sinews similarly require burning, as we will discuss. All of this is done on the sixteenth because burning cannot take place on the fifteenth, which is *Yom Tov*.

---

## Notar on Shabbat

### Sixteenth as Shabbat

The *mishnah* continues: *chal tet-zayin lihiyot be-Shabbos, yisrafu be-shiva-asar* — if the sixteenth falls on Shabbos, the burning is deferred to the seventeenth. In this scenario, the *pesach* was *notar* on the fifteenth, but one cannot burn on *Yom Tov*, so the burning is scheduled for the sixteenth; if the sixteenth is Shabbos, the burning must wait until the seventeenth.

### No Override Rule

The *mishnah* gives the reason: *lefi she'ein dochin lo et ha-Shabbos ve-lo et ha-Yom Tov* — burning *kodashim* does not override either Shabbos or *Yom Tov*. Even though burning *notar* is a *mitzvah*, it is insufficient to displace either of these days, as the *Gemara* will elaborate.

---

## Atzmos, Gidin, Notar (II)

### Rav Mari & Rav Yitzchak

The *Gemara* opens with a teaching: *Rav Mari bar Avuha amar Rav Yitzchak: atzmos kodshim she'shimshu notar metamin et ha-yadayim* — bones of *kodashim* that served *notar* convey *tumah* to the hands. The Rabbis instituted that *notar* meat imparts *tumah* of the hands as a measure to prompt *kohanim* to eat the meat before it expired: since *kohanim* were scrupulously careful about matters of *tumah*, attaching *tumah* to *notar* would motivate them not to allow meat to become *notar* in the first place. Rav Mari bar Avuha teaches that bones which "served" the *notar* — specifically by containing marrow within them — likewise convey *tumah*, since they are considered a *basis le-davar ha-assur*, a base or vessel for something forbidden.

### Marrow Status

The *mishnah* establishes that bones are to be burned on the sixteenth. A question immediately arises: *hani atzamos heichi dami?* — what exactly is the case? If the bones contain no marrow, there is no obligation to burn them; they should simply be discarded, for there is nothing of the *korban* remaining in them — a bone without marrow has no more sanctity than a piece of wood. The *Gemara* therefore concludes that the *mishnah* must be discussing bones that contain marrow. The marrow is *notar*, and it is that marrow which must be burned — which is why the bones are addressed in the *mishnah*. This discussion has implications for broader questions, such as whether bones of animals that never contained marrow have any *halachic* status whatsoever.

### Shimush Notar Debate

The *Gemara* then raises a structural question. Given that we are clearly burning the bones because of the marrow, why must we burn the bones together with the marrow? Why not simply break open the bones, extract the marrow, burn the marrow, and discard the bones? The *Gemara* assumes that the prohibition against breaking bones no longer applies once the *pesach* has become *notar* — so by the morning of the fifteenth or sixteenth, there should be no obstacle to breaking them. The *Gemara* therefore suggests that burning the bones whole (rather than extracting and burning only the marrow) implies something about the status of the bones themselves: *shema mina shimush notar milta hi* — we may infer that the act of "serving" *notar* confers upon the bones a status equivalent to *notar*, requiring that they too be burned.

The *Gemara* then challenges this inference by reversing the logic: *le'olam eima lach shimush notar lav milta hi* — perhaps the bones do not acquire any status from having served *notar*, and the bones themselves genuinely have no obligation to be burned. The reason they cannot simply be broken open is the *halakhic* force of the verse *ve-etzem lo tishberu bo* — do not break a bone of the *pesach*. The word *bo* is read not as a limiting term, but as applying even after the *pesach* has become *pasul*: *bo be-chasher ve-afilu be-fasul*. The prohibition against breaking bones continues to apply even the next morning when the *pesach* is *notar*.

The *Gemara* immediately objects: a *mishnah* taught that if one breaks a bone of a *tamei pesach*, one does not receive lashes, implying the prohibition does not apply to an invalid *pesach*. The *Gemara* resolves this tension by distinguishing between *sha'at ha-kosher* and its absence: *kan she-haitah lo sha'at ha-kosher, kan she-lo haitah lo sha'at ha-kosher*. A *pesach* that was validly offered and only later became *notar* — it had its *sha'at ha-kosher*, its moment of validity — retains the bone-breaking prohibition even after it has become *pasul*. But a *pesach* that was *tamei* from the outset and was therefore never valid never had a *sha'at ha-kosher*, and the prohibition therefore never applied to it and does not apply now.

### Sheviras Etzem

With this distinction in hand, the *Gemara* explains why we cannot simply break open the bones and extract the marrow: by the morning of the fifteenth, the *pesach* has become *notar*, but because it once had a *sha'at ha-kosher*, the prohibition against breaking its bones continues to apply. The bones must therefore be burned whole, together with the marrow inside them.

### Sha'at ha-Kosher

The *Gemara* then identifies the *tanna* behind this distinction. *U-man tanna de-shani leh?* — who is the *tanna* who draws this distinction? It is Rabbi Yaakov. As the *baraita* teaches: the verse *ve-etzem lo tishberu bo* prohibits breaking a bone of a valid *pesach* but not an invalid one. Rabbi Yaakov adds: *haitah lo sha'at ha-kosher ve-nifsal, yesh bo* — if it once had a moment of validity and subsequently became *pasul*, the prohibition applies. *Lo haitah lo sha'at ha-kosher, ein bo mishum sheviras etzem* — if it was never valid, there is no prohibition of bone-breaking.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *echad zeh ve-echad zeh, ein bo mishum sheviras etzem* — whether or not the *pesach* once had a *sha'at ha-kosher*, once it is now *pasul*, there is no prohibition of bone-breaking at all. On Rabbi Shimon's view, even the bones of a *pesach* that was validly offered may be broken freely the next morning when it is *notar*.

*Tosafot* makes a significant structural observation: Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon are not independently disputing one another, but are each offering their interpretation of the *tanna kamma*. The *tanna kamma* stated only that the prohibition applies to a *kasher pesach* and not a *pasul* one. The debate between Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon is over what constitutes *pasul*: Rabbi Yaakov holds that *pasul* means only those that were never valid, while Rabbi Shimon holds that any *pesach* currently *pasul* — regardless of its prior status — is excluded from the prohibition. This pattern, where later *tannaim* debate the meaning of an earlier ruling rather than independently asserting their own views, recurs throughout the *mishnah*, as seen for instance in the opening *mishnah* of *Pesachim* itself, where Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel debate the meaning of the earlier teaching about the two rows in a cellar.

### Bones Distinction

The *Gemara* now turns to a *baraita* that presents what seems to be a difficulty: *kol atzmos ha-kodshim ein te'unim sereifah* — all bones of other *kodashim* do not require burning — *chutz me-atzmos ha-pesach, mipnei ha-takalah* — except for the bones of the *pesach*, because of the potential for transgression. What does this mean?

The *Gemara* asks: what is the case regarding these bones of other *kodashim* that need not be burned? If they contain no marrow, there is no need to burn them in the first place — they would simply be discarded. So the *baraita* must be discussing bones that do contain, or once contained, marrow. Yet it says these bones of other *kodashim* need not be burned. If the principle of *shimush notar* — that serving *notar* confers *notar*-status upon the bones — were operative, why would these bones not also require burning?

This appears to challenge the conclusion that *shimush notar milta hi*. The *Gemara* resolves the challenge by explaining that the *baraita* is not discussing bones from which the marrow was removed after the *korban* became *notar*, but rather bones that were already stripped of their marrow when found. The question then becomes: when was that marrow removed?

### Stripped Bones

Two *amoraim* offer related explanations of this scenario.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: *kegon she-metzan chalutzin* — the case is one where the bones are found already stripped of their marrow. By bones of other *kodashim*, since there is no prohibition against breaking the bones, we may assume that the owners were careful to extract the marrow before the meat became *notar* — *kamei de-hava notar chalutzinhu* — and therefore the bones never served *notar*, and need not be burned: *velo havei shimush notar, velo ba'ei sereifah*. By the *pesach*, however, since breaking the bones is prohibited, the marrow could not have been removed before the *korban* expired; therefore, it is certain that the bones served *notar* before they were stripped, and they must be burned even now that they are hollow: *leva'tar de-hava notar hu de-chaltzinhu, ve-havu lehu shimush notar u-va'u sereifah*. This reading supports the principle that *shimush notar milta hi*.

Rav Zvid offers a somewhat different reading of the *baraita*. He explains: *kegon she-metzan tziburin tziburin* — the case is one where the bones are found in a large pile, and inspection of those on top reveals that they have been stripped of their marrow. By bones of other *kodashim*, since there is no prohibition against breaking the bones, one can assume not only that the stripped bones in hand had their marrow removed before *notar* set in, but one can further extrapolate that the same is true of the entire pile — *lekulu havei chalitz lehu ve-achul lehu* — and therefore none of the bones in the pile require burning. By the *pesach*, however, even if the bones on top were stripped, one cannot make a corresponding assumption about the rest of the pile — *dilma hani de-chaltzinhu u-le-hanach lo chaltzinhu* — since the prohibition against breaking bones would have made early extraction difficult or impossible, and the bones at the bottom of the pile may still contain *notar* marrow, requiring them to be burned.

On Rav Zvid's reading, the distinction between *pesach* and other *kodashim* does not rest on whether *shimush notar milta hi*, but on whether one can make a reliable assumption about the contents of stripped bones. The bones themselves need not be burned independently; only those that actually contain marrow need burning. The difference is simply evidentiary: for other *kodashim*, one may assume early extraction; for the *pesach*, one may not.

---

## Gidin & Gid Nasheh

### Gidin Classification

A general teaching is cited: *kol ha-gidin basar ninhu* — all sinews are classified as meat for *halachic* purposes, with one exception: *chutz mi-gidei tzavar*, the sinews of the neck, which are essentially inedible and are not counted as meat.

### Sinew Reference

The *mishnah* states that the *gidin* must also be burned on the sixteenth. The *Gemara* asks what kind of sinews the *mishnah* has in mind. If it refers to ordinary, edible sinews — *gidei basar* — then the *chiddush* is unclear: these are simply meat that was not eaten, and they are already subsumed under the general category of *notar*. There is no reason to list them separately. And if the *mishnah* refers to the sinews of the neck, which are inedible and not classified as meat, then on one hand one might argue that the *mishnah* is teaching that even these count as meat and must be burned; but on the other hand, if they are not really meat, why would they have any *notar* status at all?

The tension becomes sharp: for the *mishnah* to be making a *chiddush* by listing the sinews separately, it must be referring to sinews that are in some sense borderline — either nearly inedible but still technically meat, or technically permissible but practically uneaten. If it refers to ordinary sinews, the mention adds nothing. If it refers to the neck sinews, one must argue that even these are considered meat — which would be the *chiddush* — and that the obligation to burn them follows from their status as *notar*.

### Rav Chisda

Rav Chisda offers a different identification entirely: *lo nitzrecha ela le-gid ha-nashe* — the *mishnah* is speaking of the *gid ha-nashe*, the sciatic nerve, which is forbidden to eat. But if the *gid ha-nashe* is forbidden and cannot be eaten, why would there be an obligation to burn it as *notar*? The obligation to burn *notar* is linked to the *mitzvah* of eating the *korban*: one leaves over something that one was obligated to eat, and that leftover must be burned. The *gid ha-nashe* was never in the category of things to be eaten. Rav Chisda's answer is that the explanation follows Rabbi Yehuda's position.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda holds: *eino noheg ella be-achat* — the prohibition of the *gid ha-nashe* applies to only one of the two thighs. *Ve-ha-da'at machra'at shel yamin* — reason suggests it is the right thigh that is primary. Now, does Rabbi Yehuda mean that he has resolved the question and determined definitively that it is the right thigh? Or does he mean that while it is probably the right, he remains uncertain — in which case one would refrain from eating both the right and left *gidin* out of doubt? If Rabbi Yehuda retains a *safek* and therefore forbids both as a precaution, then one of the two *gidin* — the permissible one — could have been eaten but was not, and is therefore *notar* that must be burned. This would explain why the *mishnah* mentions the *gidin* as requiring burning.

### Mixed-Up Gidim

Rav Ika bar Chinena offers a related scenario: *kegon she-hukru le-vasof ve-nitarvu* — even if Rabbi Yehuda ultimately concludes with certainty that it is the right *gid* that is forbidden, the two *gidin* may have become mixed up. Once they are mixed up, one cannot identify which is which, and therefore both are left uneaten, with the permissible one becoming *notar* and requiring burning. This explains the *mishnah*'s listing of *gidin* as a case requiring burning even if one accepts that Rabbi Yehuda definitively identified the prohibited side.

### Shuman shel Gid

Rav Ashi offers yet another reading: *lo nitzrecha ella le-shumno shel gid ha-nashe* — the *mishnah* is not referring to the *gid* itself, but to the fat (*shuman*) surrounding the *gid ha-nashe*.

### Fat Status

As the *baraita* teaches: *shumno muttar* — the fat around the *gid ha-nashe* is technically permitted by Torah law. Nevertheless, *ve-Yisrael kedoshim hem ve-nohagim bo issur* — the Jewish people are holy and have adopted the practice of treating it as forbidden. This practice has the force of at least a rabbinic prohibition. The consequence is striking: since nobody eats this fat — though the Torah permits it — it necessarily remains as *notar* after the *pesach* meal, and the *mitzvah* to burn *notar* applies to it. The *mishnah* therefore lists *gidin* as requiring burning on the sixteenth because of the fat around the *gid ha-nashe* that was left over. There is a certain irony here: the *chumra* of treating permitted fat as forbidden results, in effect, in a *chumra de-ati lidei kulla* — everyone who eats a *korban pesach* inevitably transgresses the prohibition of *notar* with respect to this fat, since they cannot eat something they have undertaken not to eat.

### Outer vs. Inner Gid

Ravina proposes a final answer: *bechitzon* — the *mishnah* refers to the outer *gid*, and the explanation follows the ruling of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: *de-bei gidin hein* — there are actually two sinews. The inner one, *pnimi ha-samuch la-etzem*, running along the bone, is biblically forbidden and one is liable for its consumption. The outer one, *chitzon ha-samuch la-basar*, closer to the meat and not running the length of the bone, is only rabbinically forbidden — *ein chayavin alav*. Because of this rabbinic prohibition, the outer *gid* is left uneaten, even though it is biblically classified as meat. It therefore becomes *notar* and must be burned, and this is what the *mishnah* is teaching. The same logic applies as in Rav Ashi's explanation: a rabbinic prohibition results in something biblically permissible being left uneaten and consequently requiring burning as *notar*.

---

## Notar on Shabbat (II)

### Chizkiya's Proof

The *Gemara* now turns to the question raised by the *mishnah*: if the sixteenth falls on Shabbos, why can the burning of *notar* not override the prohibition of *Yom Tov*? After all, this is a positive commandment — should the *aseh* of burning *notar* not displace the *lo ta'aseh* of prohibited labor on *Yom Tov*? This question presents no difficulty with respect to Shabbos, which combines a *lo ta'aseh* with a *lo ta'aseh* and the additional severity of *chiyuv misah*, but *Yom Tov* seems more vulnerable to the override argument.

Chizkiya, and likewise the *tanna* of the school of Chizkiya, derives the answer from the verse: *ve-lo sosiru mimenu ad boker, ve-ha-notar mimenu ad boker ba-eish tisrofu*. The verse first prohibits leaving the meat until morning, and then commands that whatever remains be burned in the morning. Why does the verse need to say *boker* a second time? The first *boker* already establishes the prohibition. *Liten lo boker sheini le-sereifaso* — the second mention of *boker* teaches that the burning is assigned to a subsequent morning: do not burn the *notar* on *Yom Tov* itself; give it another morning. The Torah explicitly delays the burning to avoid conflict with *Yom Tov*.

### Abaye's Approach

Abaye derives the answer from a different verse: *olas Shabbos be-Shabbato* — the *olah* of Shabbos is offered on its own day. The verse implies: *ve-lo olas chol be-Shabbos* — the weekday sacrifice cannot be completed on Shabbos. This principle extends equally to *Yom Tov*: *ve-lo olas chol be-Yom Tov*. Even on the *mizbe'ach* itself, fat from a *korban* slaughtered on the fourteenth cannot be burned on *Yom Tov* night — it is a weekday sacrifice being completed on *Yom Tov*, which is prohibited. If one may not even complete the offering of a valid *korban* on *Yom Tov*, how much more so may one not burn *notar*, which is already an invalid remnant of the *korban*. The *kal va-chomer* establishes that burning *notar* is not permitted on *Yom Tov*.

### Rava's Logic

Rava derives the answer from yet another verse: *hu levado ye'aseh lachem* — on *Yom Tov*, only that which is directly related to eating is permitted; *hu ve-lo machshirav* — but not preparatory acts such as chopping wood for a fire; *levado, ve-lo milah shelo bi-zmanah* — and "alone" teaches that even *milah* not performed on its proper day may not override *Yom Tov*, despite the fact that *milah* performed on its prescribed eighth day overrides even Shabbos. Rava's point is that the Torah explicitly teaches, through the word *levado*, that *Yom Tov* cannot be displaced by commandments that do not pertain directly to food preparation on *Yom Tov* itself — even *mitzvot* as significant as *milah*. If that is true of *milah*, it is certainly true of burning *notar*.

### Rav Ashi Final

Rav Ashi offers what is perhaps the most direct and structurally elegant answer: *shabbaton de-Yom Tov aseh hu* — the *shabbaton* quality of *Yom Tov* is itself a positive commandment. *Yom Tov* is therefore not merely a *lo ta'aseh* but a combination of *lo ta'aseh* and *aseh*. *Ve-ein aseh docheh lo ta'aseh va-aseh* — a positive commandment can override a negative commandment standing alone, but it cannot override a negative commandment reinforced by a positive commandment. The *aseh* of burning *notar* therefore cannot displace *Yom Tov*, which carries both a prohibition against *melacha* and the positive requirement of *shabbaton* — rest. This is why *notar* may not be burned on *Yom Tov*, and *a fortiori* not on Shabbos.

---

---

# Pesachim 84

## Definition of Meat

### Meat Definition Intro

The daf opens with a continuation of the discussion surrounding the *korban pesach* — specifically, what constitutes *basar* (meat) for purposes both of fulfilling the *mitzvah* of eating the *korban* and of the *nosar* prohibition governing leftover meat. The preceding sugyot established that bones containing marrow follow the status of the marrow within them, and that various sinews — including the *gid hanasheh*, which one participant noted is more precisely a nerve (the sciatic nerve) than a sinew in the strict sense, though the term *gid* is used broadly for stringy tissue — had been under discussion. The present *mishnah* advances a formal and somewhat striking definition of what counts as *basar* in the context of a young animal offered as the *korban pesach*.

### Comparative Standard

The *mishnah* states: *kol hane'echal beshor gadol ye'achel begedi harach* — whatever would be edible in a large ox is likewise edible in a tender young kid. The inverse implication is equally significant: if a given tissue would *not* be edible in a fully grown ox, it does not qualify as *basar* even in the tender young animal, despite being edible in its current state. This is a formal, comparative standard — the edibility of the tissue is assessed not by reference to the animal being offered, but by reference to what its anatomical counterpart would yield in a large mature animal.

This is, on reflection, a quite surprising definition. One might have assumed that the relevant question is simply whether the tissue is edible now, at the time of eating the *korban*. Yet the *mishnah* imposes a standard that is partly external to the animal itself: a tissue that is perfectly edible in this young kid may nonetheless fail to qualify as *basar* if the corresponding part in a grown cow would be inedible. The consequence is apparently that one neither fulfills the *mitzvah* of eating the *korban pesach* through such tissue, nor would the tissue become *nosar* requiring burning if left over.

### Cartilage Analysis

The *mishnah* then includes *rashei knafayim* (the tops of the forelegs or shoulder joints — Rashi glosses this as *sheberosh gaf hakasef*) and *sachchusim* (cartilage, possibly of the ear or more generally) within the category of meat for these purposes. This inclusion is itself puzzling in light of the preceding standard: would the cartilage of an ear or the tip of a foreleg really be edible in a large ox? The apparent tension between the general rule and these specific inclusions drives the *gemara*'s discussion below.

### Cartilage Hardening

A note in the Artscroll edition illuminates an anatomical point that is crucial to understanding the *mishnah*'s logic: the skeleton of a young animal is composed largely of cartilage, much of which gradually hardens into bone as the animal matures. This means there is a broad class of tissues that are genuinely edible in a young lamb or kid offered as the *korban pesach* but which would, in the course of normal development, become hard bone — inedible and indeed breakable in the full sense. The formal definition of *basar* in the *mishnah* thus maps onto a real biological phenomenon: tissues that are presently soft and edible may have a future identity as bone. This transformation is what gives the comparative standard its practical bite, and it also clarifies why the prohibition of *sheviras etzem* (breaking bones) is not implicated by these tissues in their current state — they are not yet structurally bone.

---

## Mishnah Contradiction

### Rabba's Challenge

Rabba identifies a sharp internal contradiction in the *mishnah*. The opening clause establishes: *kol hane'echal beshor gadol ye'achel begedi harach* — if it can be eaten in a large ox, it counts as meat in the young kid; if not, it does not. Yet the closing clause includes *rashei knafayim* and *sachchusim* as meat. The problem: *vehani lo mistachli beshor gadol* — these very tissues cannot be eaten in a large ox. The general rule and the specific inclusion appear to be in direct conflict.

### Tannaim Debate

The *gemara*'s first resolution is striking: *ela tannai* — the two parts of the *mishnah* represent the opinions of two different *tannaim* that have been collated together without an explicit marker of disagreement. The *gemara* reconstructs the *mishnah* as follows: the first clause represents the majority view (*kol hane'echal beshor gadol ye'achel begedi harach, veshe'eino ne'echal lo*), while the second clause, beginning with *veyesh omrim* ("there are those who say"), represents a dissenting position holding that *rashei knafayim* and *sachchusim* count as meat even though they would not be edible in a large animal.

This solution — that Rebbi, in editing the *mishnah*, pasted together two opposing positions without clearly flagging the disagreement — is something the *gemara* generally resists. The editorial puzzle of why one would juxtapose contradictory rulings without a *veyesh omrim* or similar marker is worth noting, and indeed the *gemara* itself is somewhat uncomfortable with it. The more fundamental question underlying the debate is whether the criterion for *basar* is grounded in the tissue's present edibility or in some objective, forward-looking standard.

### Rava's Shalka

Rava offers a far more elegant resolution. He argues that there is no contradiction and no editorial patchwork: the *mishnah* is all one position, and a qualifying word has simply been omitted. The correct reading is *kol hane'echal beshor gadol beshalka* — whatever could be eaten in a large ox *if boiled* (*shalka*, or *beshaluk*, a form of thorough boiling that softens otherwise tough tissue) — that tissue *ye'echel begedi harach betzli*, may be counted as meat in the roasted young kid. And *mahein rashei knafayim vehasachchusim* — the specific examples are precisely the cartilaginous tissues that, though they could not be eaten raw or roasted in a large ox, *could* be eaten if thoroughly boiled.

This is a very satisfying resolution. The standard is not "edible in any state in a large ox" but "edible in the most favorable conceivable state — even boiled — in a large ox." The criterion for exclusion is therefore reserved for tissues that are so far beyond the pale of edibility that even boiling would not help. What exactly those would be in a large ox is left implicit, but the existence of such tissues is assumed. A *beraita* then confirms Rava's reading: *kol hane'echal beshor gadol beshalka ye'echel begedi harach betzali*, concluding with *u'mai hein — rashei knafayim vehasachchusim*. The *gemara* notes the philological curiosity that *shalka* is Aramaic whereas the *beraita* uses the Hebrew *beshaluk*, and also raises the broader question of whether this *beraita* is truly an independent tannaitic source or whether it so closely mirrors Rava's own language — the *beraita* appears nowhere else — that it may reflect the phenomenon whereby amoraic rulings, delivered in the *mishnaic* Hebrew register rather than Aramaic, were sometimes transmitted and received as independent *beraitot*.

The *mishnah* then adds that *gidim harachim* (soft sinews) also count as *basar*. The natural follow-up question is: what then is being excluded?

---

## Yochanan/Lakish Debate

### Hardening Sinews

An independent discussion is now introduced with the marker *itamar*, signaling a teaching from a separate context — the same dispute is in fact recorded in tractate Chullin, where the question of what constitutes food or meat has ramifications for susceptibility to *tumah*. The subject is *gidim shesofam lehakshot* — sinews that will eventually harden. These seem to be precisely the category of soft tissue that the *mishnah* was navigating: presently edible, but destined for inedibility as the animal matures.

### Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan holds: *nimnim aleihem bepesach* — one may count such sinews as one's portion in the *korban pesach*, meaning they qualify as *basar* and one can designate them as one's share of the offering. Since the *korban pesach* is communally purchased and eaten by a group, each participant has a designated portion; Rabbi Yochanan holds that soft sinews that will harden may constitute such a portion.

### Lakish Position

Reish Lakish disagrees: *ein nimnim aleihem bepesach* — one may not designate these sinews as one's portion. His reasoning is that the sinew's future state determines its present classification: since it will harden into inedibility, it is objectively not *basar*, even now. This position aligns with what appeared to be the plain sense of the *mishnah* — the determinant of *basar*-status is forward-looking.

On its face, Rabbi Yochanan's position seems intuitive: why should the future state of a tissue override its present edibility? Yet the *mishnah*'s comparative standard (*kol hane'echal beshor gadol*) seems to vindicate Reish Lakish.

### Yochanan's Reconciliation

Reish Lakish presses the challenge directly, citing the *mishnah*: *kol hane'echal beshor gadol ye'achel begedi harach* — the cartilage (*knafayim* and *sachchusim*) is included precisely because it *is* edible in a large animal; sinews that will harden apparently are not, and should therefore be excluded. How does Rabbi Yochanan respond?

### Liberal Edibility

Rabbi Yochanan's response is: *tanna hani vehu hadin lehanach* — the hardening sinews are analogous to the cartilage mentioned in the *mishnah*, because they too are theoretically edible in a large ox if boiled. *Mai ta'ama hani? — demitachli beshor gadol beshluka*. The cartilage qualifies because it can be eaten when boiled; *hacha nami mitachli beshor gadol beshluka* — so too these sinews, if boiled thoroughly, would be edible even in a large animal. Thus Rabbi Yochanan is not truly holding that one goes by present status alone; he is offering a more expansive understanding of what qualifies as potentially edible in the future. The debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish thus narrows: both agree in principle that the criterion is future edibility in the mature animal; they disagree about whether the thoroughly-boiled standard (*beshluka*) is sufficient to bring hardening sinews within the category of *basar*. Rabbi Yochanan's position, though intellectually coherent, is a generous application of the edibility standard, and the *gemara* notes that in the end it somewhat undercuts the sharpness of the original debate.

---

## Chulin Parallels

### Abbahu Challenge

Rav Yirmeyah sends a question to Rabbi Abbahu via Rav Avin: did Rabbi Yochanan truly hold that *gidim shesofam lehakshot* count as one's portion in the *korban pesach*, implying that one goes by present status (*batar hashta azlinan*)? For there is a parallel discussion in Chullin where Reish Lakish challenged Rabbi Yochanan's position with a *mishnah*, and the resolution of that exchange appears to yield a different conclusion.

### Skin Precedent

The Chullin precedent concerns the skin of the head of a tender young calf (*or harosh shel eigel harach*): can it become susceptible to *tumah* as *ochel* (food)? Rabbi Yochanan ruled: *ein mitamei* — it cannot, because it is not classified as food. Now, in its present state, the skin of a tender calf is in fact edible. If Rabbi Yochanan held that we go by present status, he should have ruled that it *is* food and *does* become *tamei*. His ruling that it does not become *tamei* implies that he actually holds *batar besof azlinan* — we follow the future status. The tension with his apparent position in the *pesach* context is, on its face, a genuine contradiction.

### Abbahu Response

Rabbi Abbahu's response to Rav Avin is sharp and dismissive: *derama lach ha lo chash lekimchei* — the one who posed this contradiction "was not careful with his wheat," meaning he was grinding carelessly, not attending to the quality of his material. Rashi explains the idiom: *lemah dehu tachin im chitin solet* — he was not discriminating between grinding wheat and grinding chaff. The question *seems* strong but betrays an inattention to what happened at the end of the relevant *sugya*.

### Yochanan Reversal

The point is that Rav Yirmeyah, in formulating the contradiction, knew the *beginning* of the Chullin discussion but not its resolution. In Chullin, Reish Lakish had challenged Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about the calf's skin with a *mishnah* that seemed to support going by present status — apparently cutting against Rabbi Yochanan's ruling there. Rabbi Yochanan responded that he did not accept that *mishnah* as authoritative, regarding it as a *da'as yachid* (a lone opinion). In rejecting that *mishnah*, Rabbi Yochanan was effectively abandoning any position that one goes by present status, and aligning himself with the view that future status governs — the very position of Reish Lakish in the *pesach* context. In other words, Rabbi Yochanan reversed himself: what appeared to be his position in the *pesach* debate (present status controls) was, upon further examination, a position he relinquished in Chullin. So the question Rav Yirmeyah posed to Rabbi Abbahu was indeed a good question — it revealed a real contradiction — but the answer was already embedded in the Chullin *sugya*: Rabbi Yochanan conceded the point and came around to Reish Lakish's view.

The upshot is that ultimately both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish agree that future status governs the classification of *basar*. The plain sense of the *mishnah* is vindicated: one must assess whether the tissue would be edible when the animal is mature. The *beshluka* standard (edibility if boiled) sets the outer boundary — something that could not be eaten even under those ideal conditions is not *basar*. But something presently edible that will become inedible as the animal grows is also not formally classified as *basar*, and cannot constitute one's portion in the *korban pesach*, and perhaps also is not subject to *nosar*.

---

## Rambam Analysis

### Rambam's Position

Before proceeding to the next *mishnah*, it is worth examining how the Rambam codifies the foregoing discussion. The relevant passage is in *Hilchos Chametz U'Matzah*, chapter 8, halachah 11 — though halachah 10 in that same chapter encapsulates the *mishnah* just studied. The Rambam writes regarding *gidim harachim shesofan lehakshot*: *af al pi she'einan re'uyim la'achilah atah, ne'echalin bePesach ve'ein nimnin aleihem* — even though they are not presently fit for eating, they may be eaten as part of the *pesach*, but one may not designate them as one's portion.

### Meat/Partnership

This ruling is illuminating and resolves a question that had lingered in the *mishnah* itself. The Rambam draws a distinction between two questions that the *gemara* somewhat conflates: first, whether the tissue counts as *basar* such that eating it discharges one's obligation; and second, whether it is substantial enough to constitute one's designated share (*nimnim aleihem*) in the *korban pesach*. According to the Rambam, such soft sinews that will harden do qualify as *basar* in the sense that one may eat them as part of fulfilling the *mitzvah* — since they are currently edible — but they do not rise to the level of a formal portion in the partnership of the *korban pesach*. This distinction addresses the earlier question of whether *nosar* implications would apply to other *korbanot*: the Rambam's reading suggests that the *basar* status (with its *nosar* implications) and the *nimnim aleihem* status are separate determinations with potentially different criteria.

### Roasting Procedure

Halachah 11 of the Rambam then describes the procedure for eating the *pesach*: one cuts meat and eats it, cuts bones at the joint (*min haparak*) rather than through them, and may separate joints without transgressing *sheviras etzem*. When one reaches the *gid hanasheh*, the Rambam instructs: *motzio* — remove it — and set it aside with the other inedible *gidim*, bones, and membranes (*kromos*) that emerge during the meal. Crucially, the Rambam emphasizes that one does *not* remove the *gid* before roasting, as one would normally do with other meat — instead, the *korban* is roasted whole and intact, with the *gid hanasheh* still inside. If the *korban* was cut into pieces rather than roasted whole, it is *kasher* after the fact (*bedi'eved*), as long as no limb is missing.

### Ra'avad Objection

The Ra'avad's objection to this ruling is fierce. In one of the more colorful passages of the *hassagot*, he writes: *bechai roshi ein issur gadol mizeh* — by his life, he has never seen a greater prohibition than roasting the *pesach* with the *gid hanasheh* inside, and moreover with its fat (*im shamno*), and with the fat beneath the sides (*tarba d'susei masnei*), and with the membranes of the head (*kromos shebarosh*), all of which are items that may not be eaten. The Ra'avad could not fathom how the Rambam would be unconcerned about *nosein ta'am* — the taste and flavor transferred from these forbidden or inedible components into the meat during roasting. His conclusion: *ve'im ezkeh ve'ochal mehaPesach veyaviu lefanai kizeh — hayisi chovto bakarka lefanav* — if he lived to see the *korban pesach* restored and someone brought him such a Pesach, he would throw it on the ground before him.

One may offer a partial defense of the Rambam: the fat of the *gid hanasheh* is a *derabanan* prohibition, not *d'oraisa*; the *gid* itself may not impart discernible taste; and the Rambam may have regarded these concerns as overridden by the *mitzvah* of roasting the *korban* whole and intact — even though, *bedi'eved*, one may be *yotzei* in other ways. The Ra'avad, of course, takes strong exception to that calculus.

---

## Nosar/Sheviras

### Lashes Distinction

The next *mishnah* addresses two prohibitions in tandem: *hashover et ha'etzem bePesach hatahor harei zeh lokeh arba'im* — one who breaks a bone of a valid (*kasher* or *tahor*) *pesach* incurs lashes. However, *aval hamoseir batahor eino lokeh arba'im* — one who leaves over the meat of a valid *pesach* (transgressing the prohibition of *nosar*) does not incur lashes. Similarly, *vehashover betamei eino lokeh arba'im* — one who breaks a bone of an invalid (*tamei*) *pesach* also does not incur lashes.

### Nosar Exemption

The *gemara* explains why *nosar* in a valid *pesach* does not incur lashes. A *beraita* cites the verse: *lo sosiru mimenu ad boker, vehanosar mimenu ad boker ba'esh tisrofu* — do not leave over from it until morning; that which remains until morning shall be burned in fire. Rabbi Yehuda derives from this that since the Torah follows the negative prohibition with a positive commandment (*asei*) — burn it — this constitutes a *lav hanitak l'asei*, a prohibition rectifiable through a subsequent positive act, and one does not receive lashes for such a prohibition. Rabbi Yaakov offers a different rationale: the transgression is *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — a purely passive violation, since leaving over meat requires no active deed, and passive violations do not incur lashes.

Rashi provides two complementary explanations of the *nitak l'asei* exemption. The first is substantive: the *asei* serves as a *tikkun*, a partial correction of the transgression — burning the *nosar* does not undo the leaving-over, but it is a remedial act that mitigates its severity. The second is formal-technical: the rules governing lashes require that the violation resemble the prohibition of *lo sachsom shor b'disho* (muzzling an ox while it threshes), and a *lav hanitak l'asei* structurally does not resemble that paradigm case. The interaction between these two explanations is itself instructive: formal categories in halachah typically track substantive rationales, even when, once a category is defined, its boundaries become formally determined.

### Tumah Pesach

The *gemara* then turns to the case of breaking a bone in an invalid (*tamei*) *pesach*. The verse states *v'etzem lo sishberu vo* — the word *bo* ("in it") is taken to limit the prohibition: *bo b'kasher, velo b'pasul* — only in a valid *pesach*, not in an invalid one. Rebbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) derives the same exemption differently, connecting the prohibition of breaking bones to the verses describing eating (*b'vayis echad ye'achel*): *kol hara'ui l'achilah yesh bo mishum sheviras etzem, veshe'ein ra'ui l'achilah ein bo mishum sheviras etzem* — only that which is fit to be eaten is subject to *sheviras etzem*; what is not fit to be eaten is not.

Rav Ami identifies the practical difference between the *Tanna Kamma* (who focuses on *kasher/pasul*) and Rebbi (who focuses on *ra'ui l'achilah*): a *pesach* offered in *tumah* by the community (*tzibur*). According to those who say the criterion is *kasher/pasul*: such a *pesach*, though technically *pasul* in nature, is permitted to be eaten — but it is still technically a *pasul korban*, so one would not transgress *sheviras etzem*. According to those who say the criterion is *ra'ui l'achilah* (fit to be eaten): since such a *pesach* is in fact permitted for consumption, one would transgress *sheviras etzem* if one broke a bone.

### Scope Resolution

Rav Yosef, however, disagrees with Rav Ami's framing. He argues that in the case of a *pesach* brought in communal *tumah*, *everyone* would agree there is no transgression for breaking a bone, since the *korban* is technically *tamei* even if consumption is permitted. Rav Yosef adds that Rebbi's position is oriented entirely toward leniency (*Rebbi l'akulei ka'asi*): Rebbi is not introducing an independent criterion that might sometimes *add* liability — he is only introducing an additional basis for *exemption*. Accordingly, Rebbi would concede that wherever the *Tanna Kamma* also exempts (i.e., in a *pasul* case), Rebbi certainly exempts as well. The debate between them, Rav Yosef says, arises specifically in the case of a *pesach* that *was* once *kasher* and then became *pasul* (*haysa lo sha'as kosher v'nifsal*): the *Tanna Kamma* would say it is subject to *sheviras etzem* (it was once *kasher*), while Rebbi would say it is not (since right now it is not fit to be eaten).

Abaye then weighs in: in *that* case as well (a *pesach* that was once *kasher* and became *pasul*), everyone would agree there is no transgression (*kulei alma ki hai gavna ein bo mishum sheviras etzem*), since it is currently *pasul*. The real debate, Abaye proposes, is the case of *sheviras etzem mibod yom* — breaking a bone on the fourteenth of Nissan before nightfall, when the *pesach* has been slaughtered but the time of eating has not yet arrived.

---

## Timing Issues

### 14th Breaking

Abaye's proposal brings the discussion to the case of breaking a bone before nightfall on the fourteenth. The animal is entirely *kasher*; the only issue is that the time for eating has not yet arrived. According to the *Tanna Kamma* (*kasher* is the criterion): it is *kasher*, and one transgresses. According to Rebbi (*ra'ui l'achilah* is the criterion): since right now it is not yet fit to be eaten (the time of eating has not arrived), one does not transgress.

### Marrow Cases

A challenge is raised from a teaching attributed to Rebbi himself: *nimnin al hamoach shebarosh ve'ein nimnin al hamoach shebekullis* — one may designate the brain marrow (accessible through the nasal cavity) as one's portion in the *pesach*, but one may not designate the marrow in the thigh bone (*kullis*) as one's portion. The reason one *can* designate the brain marrow is *hoil veyachol legorero ulehotzi'o* — it can be scraped out and extracted without breaking any bone. The marrow in the thigh bone, by contrast, cannot be extracted without breaking the bone.

The *gemara* challenges Abaye: if Rebbi holds that breaking bones before nightfall on the fourteenth does not constitute *sheviras etzem*, then one could simply extract the thigh-bone marrow before nightfall, and why could that not serve as one's portion? Abaye responds: *uletaimaich* — even by your own reasoning, one could also accomplish this after nightfall by applying a hot coal to the bone (*neisei gumreta, venichos aleih, venikla*), thereby burning rather than breaking the bone open. The *beraita* explicitly states: *aval hasoreif atzamos ein bo mishum sheviras etzem* — burning bones does not constitute *sheviras etzem*. So why can't the thigh-bone marrow serve as one's portion in any event?

### Burning Alternative

Two answers are given. Abaye himself says: *mishum pak paka* — we are concerned that in the process of burning the bone, the heat will cause other parts of the bone to crack and split, which would involve at least an indirect transgression (*grama*) of *sheviras etzem*. Rava offers a different concern: *mishum hefsed kodashim* — we are concerned about the destruction of sacred property (*kodashim*). If one applies fire to the bone, one may inadvertently burn some of the marrow itself. Although the marrow would eventually become *nosar* and require burning passively, it is preferable to allow that to occur on its own rather than to actively destroy a part of the *korban* that could theoretically have been consumed.

### Rabbinical Safeguard

Returning to Abaye's proposal that the *machlokes* concerns *sheviras etzem mibod yom*: the *gemara* resolves why, even according to Rebbi, one cannot designate the thigh-bone marrow as one's portion (and hence cannot extract it before nightfall) — *gezeirah mibod yom atu mishechasheicha*: the Rabbis decreed against breaking bones even before nightfall, lest people continue breaking bones after nightfall as well. Even if one does not transgress *d'oraisa* before nightfall according to Rebbi, the Rabbis forbade it as a protective measure. Since one is not permitted to break the bone even before nightfall, the marrow cannot serve as one's designated portion.

---

## Partial Disqualification

### Half-Limb Case

Rav Pappa proposes that the *machlokes* concerns *sheviras etzem* when the bone is *raw* (*bena*) — the animal has not yet been roasted. It is the fifteenth and the time of eating has arrived, but the animal is still uncooked. According to the *Tanna Kamma* (criterion: *kasher*), the animal is *kasher* and one transgresses. According to Rebbi (criterion: *ra'ui l'achilah*), since it is not yet in a state fit for eating, one does not transgress — because Rebbi's position is always intended to be a *kula*, an additional lenient ground.
