Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak counters: in that case, everyone agrees one transgresses — *de'chazi l'achilah, dematu lei ve'achil lei* — all it takes is roasting it, and it is fit to eat.

The *gemara* then determines that the dispute concerns *eiver sheyatza miktzato* — a limb half of which has gone outside the boundaries of Jerusalem and become *pasul yotzei*. The part that crossed the boundary is *pasul*; the part within Jerusalem remains *kasher*. According to the *Tanna Kamma*: since part of the limb is *kasher*, breaking the bone (which affects the entire limb) involves breaking a bone of a *kasher pesach*, and one transgresses. According to Rebbi: since half the limb is *pasul* and cannot be eaten, the limb as a whole is not *ra'ui l'achilah*, and one does not transgress. Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi argues that in this case, everyone would agree there is no transgression, since the limb (*eiver*) itself is *pasul* — even though part of it remains technically *kasher*.

A *beraita* confirms: *Rebbi Yishmael beno shel Rebbi Yochanan ben Beroka omer — eiver sheyatza miktzato veshavro, ein bo mishum sheviras etzem* — if a limb half extended outside Jerusalem's boundary and one broke it, there is no transgression, since at least the portion of the bone being broken is *pasul*. Tosafot notes a difficulty: from the perspective of the *kasher* portion, the bone *is* being broken; why should we focus only on the *pasul* portion? The precise formulation of this position is not without its difficulties.

### Fat Tail Case

The *gemara* then considers whether the *machlokes* applies to *shevirat ha'alyah* — breaking the bone of the fat tail. The fat tail (*alyah*) of the sheep is the part that is burned on the altar; it is not eaten by the participants. According to the *Tanna Kamma*: it is part of the *kasher korban*, and one might transgress. According to Rebbi: *hai eino ra'ui l'achilah, d'alyah l'gavoha salka* — the fat tail is not subject to eating; it ascends to the altar for the Divine Service, and therefore the criterion of *ra'ui l'achilah* is not met. One therefore does not transgress. Whether the fat tail in fact contains bone — and thus whether *sheviras etzem* is anatomically relevant here — is itself uncertain; participants noted that a sheep's fat tail is composed almost entirely of fat, though any structure supporting it would presumably have some bony element.

Rav Ashi objects to the framing entirely: regarding the fat tail, *vadai ein bah mishum sheviras etzem — d'vadai einah ra'uyah l'achilah klal* — it is certainly not subject to *sheviras etzem*, since it is certainly not fit to be eaten at all. Even the *Chachamim*, who do not use a *ra'ui l'achilah* criterion explicitly, must at minimum intend that *sheviras etzem* applies to portions of the *korban* that are in the realm of being eaten.

### Stripped Limb

Rav Ashi therefore locates the *machlokes* in the case of *eiver she'ein alav kezayis basar* — a limb stripped of meat, with less than a *kezayis* (olive-size) of meat remaining on it. According to the *Tanna Kamma* (criterion: *kasher*): the bone is part of a *kasher korban*, and one transgresses. According to Rebbi (criterion: *ra'ui l'achilah*): *be'inan shiur achilah ve'leika* — we require an edible amount on the specific limb being broken, and it is lacking. The *chiddush* here is significant: Rebbi's criterion is not about the *korban* as a whole, but about the specific piece in one's hand. If the bone one is about to break does not have a *kezayis* of meat on it, Rebbi exempts one from lashes.

### Meat Distribution

Ravina then addresses the extreme case: a limb with no meat at all. Surprisingly, Ravina holds that in *that* case, everyone agrees one does not transgress — *d'be'inan shiur achilah*. The assumption had been that even without meat, the bone might still count as part of the *korban*. Ravina insists there must be at minimum an edible amount associated with the bone.

### Internal Marrow

The next refinement: a limb that has a *kezayis* of meat not *at the point of breaking* but elsewhere on the limb (*bemakom acher*). This is the case that most directly tests whether Rebbi's criterion is tied to the immediate point of fracture or to the limb as a whole. And further: what if the limb has no external meat at the point of breaking, but contains a *kezayis* of marrow internally (*mibifnim*)? Rav Pappa rules that marrow on the inside (*moach mibifnim*) can satisfy the *kezayis* requirement — the marrow counts as the edible substance associated with the bone, even if it is not visible on the outside.

---

## Final Beraita

### Four Standards

A *beraita* is cited that encapsulates four distinct positions regarding when *sheviras etzem* applies, corresponding to the various approaches surveyed by the *amoraim*.

### Rebbi Standard

Rebbi's position in the *beraita* synthesizes his multi-pronged approach to leniency. He holds that one is liable only for a bone of a *kasher pesach* (not a *pasul* one); that if the *korban* had a *sha'as kosher* (a period of validity) and was subsequently disqualified, one is not liable (since right now it is *pasul* and not fit to be eaten); that if there is a *shiur achilah* (sufficient quantity for eating) on the limb, one is liable, and if not, one is not; that if the part is *ra'ui l'mizbeach* (fit for the altar, like the fat tail), one is not liable; that during the time of eating (*beshas achilah*) one is liable, but *shelo beshas achilah* (not during the time of eating, such as on the fourteenth before nightfall), one is not liable.

### Location Debate

The final dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerns the case of a limb with a *kezayis* of meat at one location but not at the point of breaking. Rabbi Yochanan holds *yesh bo mishum sheviras etzem* — one transgresses even if the *kezayis* is located elsewhere on the limb, not at the point of fracture. Reish Lakish holds *ein bo mishum sheviras etzem* — without a *kezayis* at the precise point of breaking, one does not transgress.

### Outside/Inside

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the *beraita*: *echad etzem sheyesh alav kezayis basar, ve'echad etzem she'ein alav kezayis basar* — the prohibition applies both when there is a *kezayis* of meat on the bone and when there is not. If "no *kezayis* of meat" means literally no meat at all, why would anyone be liable? There must be some edible substance present for the prohibition to apply. The *beraita* must therefore mean that even when there is no *kezayis* at the point of breaking but there is one elsewhere on the limb, one is still liable — supporting Rabbi Yochanan.

Reish Lakish deflects: the *beraita* does not mean "meat elsewhere on the limb" but rather refers to marrow inside the bone. *Echad etzem sheyesh alav kezayis basar mibachutz, ve'echad etzem she'ein alav kezayis basar mibachutz veyesh alav kezayis basar mibifnim bemakom shevirah* — one bone with external meat at the point of breaking, and another with no external meat but with internal marrow (*moach*) at the point of breaking. The *beraita* teaches that internal marrow satisfies the *kezayis* requirement. Reish Lakish thus concedes that marrow on the *inside* at the point of fracture counts — but insists that a *kezayis* located elsewhere on the exterior of the limb does not. Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, holds that a *kezayis* anywhere on the limb suffices for the prohibition to apply.

The discussion will continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Pesachim 85

## Breaking Bones

### Parameters & Exceptions

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion about the parameters of the prohibition against breaking a bone in the *korban pesach*. Two exceptions had already been established: one where the *pesach* is *pasul*, and another where it is not fit to be eaten. The Gemara had been probing what exactly is meant by "not fit to be eaten" — whether that represents an independent exemption built on the prohibition of *pasul*, or whether it is an extension of the same idea. That had been the position of *Rebbi*. Among the intriguing possibilities raised was that one would not transgress the prohibition on the fourteenth of Nisan itself, since the time for eating has not yet arrived — a striking formulation. The Gemara now focuses on the position that one does not transgress *sheviras etzem* when there is no meat on the bone at the moment of breaking, i.e., that the prohibition applies only when there is food on the bone at that time, such that it is currently fit to be eaten.

What becomes clear from the discussion that follows is that this exemption applies even when there was meat on the bone previously but it has since been stripped away. This is quite surprising. For most of us, the natural assumption would be that the whole point of the prohibition is to prevent one from chewing away at a bone after having eaten the meat off it — that once the meat is gone, one should not start chomping on the bone. Yet according to this view, if there is literally no meat on the bone at this moment, even if all the meat has been eaten off, one does not transgress the prohibition.

### Yochanan vs. Lakish

The Gemara immediately takes up a related debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish. The case is where there is meat somewhere on the bone, but not at the precise point where it is being broken. Does the prohibition apply? Rabbi Yochanan says yes, Resh Lakish says no — according to Resh Lakish, the prohibition requires that there be meat at the actual location of the break. A *braita* had been cited, which Rabbi Yochanan interpreted as supporting his view. Resh Lakish's response is that the *braita* is not making that point at all. Rather, the *braita* is emphasizing that even if the meat is not on the outside of the bone but on the inside — that is, it is *moach*, marrow — that still counts as "meat on the bone" for purposes of the prohibition. But the *braita* would not apply the prohibition when there is no meat at the specific location of the break.

### Marrow Prohibition

The Gemara now cites the *braita* formally, introduced with *ve-hatanya*. The *braita* states: *ve-etzem lo tishberu bo* — you shall not break a bone in the *korban pesach* — *echad etzem she-yesh bo moach ve-echad etzem she-ein bo moach* — whether the bone has marrow or does not have marrow. The prohibition applies in either case.

But the *braita* itself anticipates a counterargument: *u-mah ani mekayem ve-achalu et ha-basar ba-laila ha-zeh* — what do I do with the verse commanding the eating of meat? Perhaps one should actually be permitted — specifically and exclusively — to break bones that contain marrow. The logic would be: since marrow is the meat, and there is a *mitzvah* to eat the meat, perhaps that positive obligation should override the prohibition against breaking the bone.

The *braita* counters: *be-basar she-al gabbei ha-atzem* — the meat referred to in the verse commanding eating is the meat on the outside of the bone. One might think the verse extends even to the meat within the bone, i.e., the marrow. If so, what would we do with the prohibition? We would say it applies only to *etzem she-ein bo moach* — a bone without marrow — but that *be-etzem she-yesh bo moach*, a bone containing marrow, one should be permitted to break it and eat the marrow. And furthermore, *ve-al titmah* — do not be so astounded by this! After all, there is a general principle that a positive commandment can override a negative one. The *braita* then resolves the question: since the Torah repeats the prohibition against breaking the bone in the context of *Pesach Sheni*, and there was no need to repeat it — since the Torah already says *ke-chol chukkat ha-pesach ya'asu oto*, that *Pesach Sheni* follows all the rules of *Pesach Rishon* — the repetition must be teaching that the prohibition applies in every case: *echad etzem she-yesh bo moach ve-echad etzem she-ein bo moach*, whether or not there is marrow.

### Tosafot Objection

Tosafot raises a sharp objection to the *braita*'s *hava amina* — the very suggestion that the *aseh* of eating the meat should override the *lo taaseh* of breaking the bone. First, Tosafot notes, the rule that an *aseh* overrides a *lo taaseh* applies only when the two conflict simultaneously, not when the *aseh* requires a preparatory act that happens to violate the *lo taaseh* before the fulfillment of the positive commandment occurs. Breaking the bone in order to subsequently eat the marrow would be a preparatory act, not the *kiyum aseh* itself. Second — a point already raised by Rashi — there are other ways to access the marrow, such as burning the bone rather than breaking it. So the *hava amina* was not particularly compelling to begin with, and indeed the *braita* rejects it.

One might also ask: why not access the marrow from a different part of the bone? The answer is that while that may be technically possible, the question is whether the *mitzvah* of eating applies to every portion of meat on the bone, including the marrow — or whether the obligation to eat applies only to the external meat, leaving the marrow subject to the negative prohibition of *nosar* if not consumed, but not the subject of an affirmative *mitzvah* to eat. The *braita* ultimately makes clear: the prohibition against breaking the bone stands even in the presence of marrow.

### Limb Outside

The Gemara now asks a question from the *mishnah* that will be treated formally later: *ever she-yatza miktzato* — if a limb of the *korban pesach* partially extended outside of Yerushalayim. Since meat that goes outside Yerushalayim becomes *pasul*, one must cut away the outer portion. The *mishnah* prescribes: *choteich ad makom she-magia la-etzem* — cut the meat until reaching the bone — *ve-kolef ad she-magia la-perek* — peel the meat on the inner portion until reaching the joint — and then sever the limb at the joint. The meat that was peeled away on the inside, which is still *kasher*, is eaten; the bone is discarded.

The distinction between *choteich* and *koleif* is instructive. *Choteich* — cutting — is used for the outer meat, which is being discarded and can be handled roughly. *Koleif* — peeling — is used for the inner meat, which is being eaten, and which one handles more delicately; once the bone has been reached, one wants to peel the meat carefully away from the bone rather than hack at it.

The Gemara now asks a pointed question, presenting a position attributed to *Rava* from the previous day's discussion: if indeed the prohibition of *sheviras etzem* does not apply when there is no meat at the precise point of the break, then why must one go to the trouble of peeling all the meat off the inner portion of the limb until reaching the joint? Let the procedure be far simpler: peel away a small amount of meat right at the line, creating a strip of exposed bone with no meat at that spot, and then break the bone at that exposed location. The prohibition would not apply — because there is no meat at that precise point — and the process would be much easier. Why does the *mishnah* require stripping all the way to the joint?

### Abaye: Cracking

Abaye answers: *mishum paka* — because of cracking. If one breaks the bone at a spot that has been stripped of meat, the break will not be clean; it will create a crack that runs into the adjacent portion of the bone where meat is still present. Since the cracking effect extends to areas where there is still meat on the bone, one cannot simply strip a small section and break there — the breaking action itself will effectively constitute breaking a bone in a place where meat remains.

### Ravina: Marrow

Ravina offers a different answer. The case involves a *kulis* — a particular type of limb, understood to be a thigh bone that contains marrow. The answer that one could simply peel away a spot and break the bone overlooks the marrow on the inside of the bone, which also counts as meat at the location of the break. This is an important clarification, and in some ways it restores a more intuitive picture of the prohibition.

The debate throughout has been: does the prohibition apply when there is meat somewhere else on the bone but not at the point of breaking? But everyone agrees — once the bone is fully stripped of external meat and contains no marrow — that no prohibition applies. This is what struck us as counterintuitive at the outset. Ravina's answer reminds us that the scenario in which one might think no prohibition applies is actually far more limited than it sounds: even if all the external meat has been eaten off, as long as the bone contains marrow, that marrow is still "meat at the location" and the prohibition remains in force. The only case where no prohibition exists is when both the bone is stripped of external meat and the bone either has no marrow or contains less than a *kezayis* of marrow inside.

This fits with the Gemara's broader understanding of the relationship between *ve-achalu et ha-basar* and *ve-etzem lo tishberu bo* — the prohibition against breaking the bone is connected to the act of eating. Once the bone is entirely stripped and has no marrow, it is essentially refuse, no longer part of the eating process. Only then is the prohibition inapplicable.

---

## Pigul & Nosar

### Huna vs. Chisda

The Gemara now transitions to a related topic. *Ha-pigul ve-ha-nosar u-metame'im et ha-yadayim* — meat that is *pigul* or *nosar* causes *tumah* of the hands upon contact. This is a rabbinic enactment. The dispute is between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda: *chad amar mipnei chashdei kehunah*, one says it is because of *kohanim* who are suspected of acting improperly; *ve-chad amar mipnei atzlei kehunah*, the other says it is because of *kohanim* who are lazy.

The one who emphasizes *pigul* says *mishum chashdei kehunah*. How does *pigul* occur? A *kohen* who performs the *avodah* with the intent to eat the offering outside its designated time renders the offering *pigul*. This is an intentional, willful act — not a matter of negligence. What would motivate a *kohen* to do this? Rashi suggests *mipnei eivah* — out of hostility. A vindictive *kohen* might intend to invalidate someone's *korban*, or worse, to cause the owner — who would not know of the *pigul* — to eat the meat and thereby incur *karet*, even if unknowingly and therefore as an *ones*. In any case, the result is that the *korban* is invalidated.

The one who emphasizes *nosar* says *mishum atzlei kehunah* — lazy *kohanim* who fail to eat the meat within the required time, allowing it to become *nosar*.

### Deterrent Logic

A natural question arises: in both cases, there is already a negative prohibition. Making something *pigul* deliberately transgresses a *lav*, and eating *pigul* is punishable by *karet*. Allowing something to become *nosar* similarly violates a negative prohibition. Is that not sufficient deterrent? Why must the Rabbis additionally render such meat *tamei*?

Tosafot addresses this directly. He writes: *de-atzlu reshaim chamira lehu tumah* — for wicked people, *tumah* is a more serious deterrent than ordinary prohibitions. He cites the Gemara in Yoma, which teaches that *kohanim* treat the impurity of vessels more stringently than bloodshed. This reflects a broader truth about human nature and taboo: *kohanim* raised with an acute sensitivity to *tumah* — for whom contact with impurity is an ingrained and deeply felt prohibition — will be far more deterred by the prospect of *tumah* than by a technical violation of a *lav*. Chazal understood how to leverage disproportionate taboos as social deterrents. The same asymmetry shows up, regrettably, in many contexts: people who are fastidious about matters of *bein adam la-Makom* while relatively cavalier about *bein adam la-chaveiro*.

### Minimum Quantities

The Gemara then records another dispute: *mar masni kezayis u-mar masni kebetzah* — one teaches a *kezayis* and another teaches a *kebetzah* as the minimum quantity of meat that triggers this rabbinic *tumah*. The one who says *kezayis* holds that since the relevant prohibition — eating *pigul* or *nosar* — kicks in at a *kezayis*, the *tumah* should similarly apply from that quantity. The one who says *kebetzah* holds that since the standard minimum unit for *tumah* is normally the size of an egg, the same threshold should apply here.

---

## Yotzei & Tumah

### Extension Question

The Gemara poses a question: *yotzei* — meat that was taken outside its designated boundaries — is another way in which *korban* meat becomes *pasul*. The three standard categories of disqualified *korban* meat are *pigul*, *nosar*, and *tamei*. The current discussion is about when the Rabbis applied *tumah* to *pasul* meat, so *tamei* meat need not be discussed — it is already *tamei*. But what about *yotzei*? If meat of a *kodshei kodashim* offering is taken outside the *azarah*, or meat of *kodshim kalim* is taken outside Yerushalayim, does it also become *tamei*?

*Mi amrina nosar d'asi l'atzulei* — perhaps the Rabbis only made this enactment by *nosar*, because the problem there is laziness: one might simply fail to eat the meat in time. *Aval yotzei*, but when meat goes outside its boundary, *afukei b'yadayim lo mafik lei* — one does not simply carry it out by accident; it requires a deliberate act. Perhaps there was no reason to make the *gezeirah* of *tumah* for *yotzei*. Alternatively, *lo shna* — perhaps it makes no difference once the Rabbis decided to make *pasul* meat *tamei*, they applied it broadly without distinction, as a form of *lo plug*.

### Tumah Setarim

The Gemara attempts to resolve the question from the *mishnah* about a limb that partially went outside Yerushalayim: *choteich ad she-magia la-etzem, ve-kolef ad she-magia la-perek, ve-choteich*. The Gemara asks: if the Rabbis applied *tumah* to *yotzei*, then when you cut away the outer meat, how does cutting help? The outer meat that crossed the line is *tamei* — and it was touching the inner meat. Should not the inner meat also be *tamei*, making the whole enterprise pointless?

The Gemara answers: *tumas setarim hi* — it is *tumah* of a hidden, non-exposed surface. When two sections of meat are connected as part of one continuous piece on a bone, they are not touching in the halachic sense of *tumah* transfer. *Tumah* is transferred between exposed surfaces. If the outer and inner meat are joined and continuous, there is no exposed surface contact between them. Thus, the outer portion being *pasul* — and therefore *tamei* by the rabbinic enactment — does not render the inner portion *tamei*, because there is no *exposed* surface touching another exposed surface. The result is a remarkable halachic reality: half of a single continuous piece of meat can be *tamei* and the other half *tahor*.

This arises from the fact that we are mixing two legal models. We started with *issur* — certain meat is *pasul* — and from the *issur* we derived a rabbinic *tumah*. That *tumah* attaches precisely and only to the portion that is *pasul*. The remainder stays *tahor*, because *tumah* is not transferred through a hidden, internal connection.

This principle has a well-known application in a different context: the question of cutting fingernails before immersion in a *mikvah*. The actual concern is dirt beneath the nails creating a *chatzitzah*. Some authorities, however, have posited an additional layer — that if nails are long enough to require cutting, the portion that needs to be cut is already considered extraneous and creates a *chatzitzah* on the surface that would be exposed upon cutting. That reasoning reflects the same conceptual point: a continuous connection is different from two surfaces touching, and only separated surfaces that meet constitute genuine contact.

### Ravina: Food Units

Ravina complicates this resolution. He holds that *chiburei ochlin lav chibur hu* — when food is connected, it is not truly considered an indivisible unit. Because food by its nature is consumed in pieces, Ravina treats a connected piece of food as if it were already divided, *ke-man de-mifarshei dami*. According to him, the meat on the inside and the meat on the outside would be deemed as already separate, and the contact between them would count as exposed-surface contact — meaning the inside would also be *tamei*.

### Two Solutions

For Ravina, then, the *tumas setarim* answer does not work. But the Gemara provides an alternative: the case in the *mishnah* may simply involve a quantity below the threshold for *tumah*. According to the opinion that *tumah* applies from a *kezayis*, the case may involve less than a *kezayis* of meat having gone outside. According to the opinion that requires a *kebetzah*, the outside portion may be less than a *kebetzah*. Either way, there is an insufficient quantity to trigger *tumah* transfer, and therefore the inside remains *tahor*. The upshot is that one cannot prove from this *mishnah* whether the Rabbis applied *tumah* to *yotzei* or not, because there are explanations available that avoid *tumah* either through *tumas setarim* or through insufficient quantity.

### Group Transfer

The Gemara brings another attempt to resolve the question. *Ha-motzi besar pesach mi-chaburah le-chaburah* — one who transfers meat of the *korban pesach* from one group to another — *af al pi she-hu be-lo ta'aseh*, although doing so violates a negative prohibition — *tahor*, the meat remains *tahor*. The Gemara asks: does *tahor* here mean merely *tahor* but *assur be-achilah* — pure but forbidden to eat, because taking it out of the *chaburah* is like taking it out of its *mechitza* and invalidates it just as *yotzei* invalidates other *korbanot*? If so, we would see that *pasul* meat through *yotzei* is nonetheless *tahor* — proof that *tumah* was not applied to *yotzei*.

The Gemara responds: no, *tahor u-mutar* — the meat is not only *tahor* but remains fully permitted to eat. Taking meat from one *chaburah* to another, while a *lav*, does not invalidate the meat itself. The end of the *braita* then complicates matters: *ha-ochlo harei zeh be-lo ta'aseh* — one who eats this meat transgresses a negative prohibition. This makes clear the meat is *assur*, which implies it is indeed *pasul*. The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that *tumah* applies from a *kezayis*, if there is a *kezayis* — which is the threshold for the *lav* of eating — why is the meat *tahor*? This should be proof that *tumah* was not extended to the *pesach* case of *yotzei*.

### Pesach Carefulness

The Gemara accepts this proof — but only in part. *Yotzei be-pesach lo mibaya lan* — the case of *yotzei* by the *korban pesach* is not our question. *De-lo gazru Rabbanan tumah* — there, the Rabbis did not apply *tumah*. And the reason: *benei chaburah zrizin hein* — the members of the *chaburah* are vigilant. The setting of the *pesach* is one of intense communal focus, and the group is scrupulous; there is no need for the deterrent of *tumah* to prevent the meat from going outside its boundaries.

It is worth noting that this answer distinguishes *pesach* from other cases on the basis of its unique *psul*: the *psul yotzei* that applies specifically to leaving the *chaburah* is a *psul* that exists nowhere else in the world of *korbanot*. This particularity may itself be a reason not to extend the rabbinic *tumah* to it, in addition to the carefulness of the participants. By contrast, taking *pesach* meat outside Yerushalayim is the generic *psul yotzei* common to all *kodshim kalim* — and it is possible the Rabbis did apply *tumah* to that scenario, since the *lo plug* logic would be more relevant for a universal type of *psul*.

The same reasoning addresses why *tumah* of *nosar* was applied to *pesach* meat: unlike the *chaburah*-specific *psul*, *nosar* is a universal prohibition and the laziness concern is fully applicable.

### Regular Kodashim

The Gemara concludes: *ella ki ka mibaya lan, be-yotzei be-kodshim* — our real question is about *yotzei* in regular *kodshim*. And the Gemara declares *teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

One further point deserves attention. The Gemara's willingness to distinguish *pesach* from other cases suggests that the logic of *lo plug* — once we apply *tumah* to one form of *psul*, we apply it to all — is not being invoked here. The Gemara is treating each case on its own merits. This is significant because it implies that the extension of *tumah* to various forms of *psul* was a considered, case-by-case decision by the Rabbis, not a blanket rule.

---

## Hotzaah Mi-Chabura

### Source: Chutz

The Gemara now asks: *u-motzi besar pesach mi-chaburah le-chaburah minayin* — from where do we know there is a prohibition against taking *pesach* meat from one group to another? The source is the verse *ve-lo totzi min ha-bayit min ha-basar chutza* — do not remove the meat from the house outside. *Ein li ela mi-bayit le-bayit* — I might read this only as prohibiting carrying from one house to another. How do I know the prohibition extends even to two groups eating in the same house? The verse teaches *chutza* — meaning *chutz le-achilato*, outside the area designated for its eating. The word *chutza* expands the prohibition beyond the physical structure to anything outside the group's designated eating space.

### Bayit Abstraction

This points to a deeper conceptual move. The Torah speaks of *bayit* — the household — as the framework of the *pesach*: *seh le-veit avot, ish le-fi ochlo*, one sheep per household. Chazal abstracted the concept of *bayit* from its literal meaning. The designated group need not be one's literal family or physical house; any group of people who register together for the *pesach* constitutes the *bayit* that the Torah envisions. And correspondingly, the prohibition of taking the meat *chutz* — outside — is no longer tied to the physical walls of a house but to the boundaries of that designated group. The *chaburah* is the operative unit, and removing the meat from that unit is the transgression.

### Boundary Definition

This abstraction raises an important question: if a group is eating in a room and someone carries the meat outdoors — not into another group, simply outside into the open air — has a prohibition been violated? The analysis suggests that the prohibition is triggered specifically by bringing the meat *into another chaburah*, not merely by removing it from one's own. The reason is that once the concept of *bayit* is detached from a physical structure, the mere physical exterior is no longer the boundary. The *chaburah* can, in principle, move outdoors or into any space it chooses. What definitively marks the boundary is the existence of *another chaburah*: that is where "outside" becomes real and legally operative.

### Placement Required

Abaye rules: *ha-motzi besar pesach mi-chaburah le-chaburah eino chayav ad she-yaniah* — one who removes *pesach* meat from one group to another is not liable until he places it down. Taking it out is insufficient; there must also be a *hanacha*, an act of resting or depositing the meat in the other location.

### Hotza'ah Parallel

The reason: *hotza'ah ketiv bei, ke-Shabbos* — the verb *hotza'ah* is used here, as it is in the context of Shabbat. Just as the *melachah* of carrying on Shabbat requires both an *akirah* — a lifting — and a *hanacha* — a resting — so too here: *af hacha nami ad de-avid akirah ve-hanacha*. The complete act of *hotza'ah* requires both picking up and putting down. The parallel between *hotza'ah* on Shabbat and *hotza'ah mi-chaburah le-chaburah* for the *pesach* is being applied in full, including all its technical criteria.

### Dragging as Hanacha

The Gemara raises an objection from Rav Abba bar Mamal regarding the *parim ha-nisrafim* — the bulls burned outside Yerushalayim. These were carried out of the *azarah* on poles. The *mishnah* states that when the front carriers had already passed outside the wall of the *azarah* but the rear carriers had not yet left, the front carriers become *tamei* in their garments while the rear ones do not. The Gemara notes that the term *hotza'ah* is used here too — and yet the carriers had not yet stopped; they were mid-motion. How can *tumah* apply if the *hanacha* had not yet occurred?

The Gemara answers: *hu motzi la ve-hu mafrik la be-nigrarin* — they are dragging it along the ground, which counts as a *hanacha*. When an object is being dragged, it is in continuous contact with the ground, which is treated as the equivalent of being placed down, even though the motion continues. Tosafot extends this ruling, noting that even if the object is not literally touching the ground — as long as it is within three *tefachim* — it is treated as *nigrarin*.

The Gemara's importation of the technical laws of *hotza'ah* from Shabbat into the laws of the *korban pesach* is striking, and Tosafot begins to explore the full extent of that parallel.

---

## Limb Removal

### Cutting & Peeling

The *mishnah* is now treated formally. *Ever she-yatza miktzato* — if part of a limb went outside Yerushalayim. The prescribed procedure: *choteich ad she-magia la-etzem* — cut away the outer meat down to the bone — *ve-kolef ad she-magia la-perek* — then peel away the inner meat, which is still *kasher* and will be eaten, until reaching the joint — *ve-choteich* — and then sever the limb at the joint. The peeled meat from the inside is what one eats; the bone is discarded.

### Hatchet Method

The *mishnah* then contrasts this with regular *kodashim*: *u-vikdashim, choteich be-kupitz* — for ordinary *korbanot*, if part of a limb became *tamei* or went outside its boundary, one simply takes a hatchet and chops the invalid portion away. There is no concern about *sheviras etzem* in that case, and so one need not go through the delicate process of stripping the entire inner portion of meat from the bone.

### Gate Boundary

This leads to the *mishnah*'s discussion of precisely where the line falls at the gate of Yerushalayim.

---

## Gate Threshold

### Inner Doorjamb

*Min ha-agaf ve-lifnim ke-lifnim* — from the inner doorjamb inward is considered the inside of Yerushalayim. The *agaf* refers to the part of the doorway where the door closes and rests — the inner edge of the gate's frame. Everything from that point inward into the city is within the boundary.

### Outer Doorjamb

*Min ha-agaf ve-lachutz ke-lachutz* — from the outer doorjamb outward is considered the outside. The question of what happens in the space of the door itself — the thickness occupied by the door when closed — will be resolved shortly. As the analysis makes clear, determining the precise line is not a trivial matter. A gate has thickness: there is the inner face, the outer face, and the space in between. The *mishnah* draws the line at the two faces of the doorjamb, leaving the intermediate space to be determined by context.

### Windows & Walls

*Ha-chalonot ve-ovi ha-chomah ke-lifnim* — windows set into the wall and the thickness of the wall itself are considered as inside. If one is situated in a window recess or standing atop the wall within its thickness, that is halachically inside Yerushalayim. There is an internal logic here: as long as one has not passed beyond the wall entirely, one remains within the city. By contrast, when the gate is open and one is standing in the space normally occupied by the door itself, one may already be halachically outside — depending on which side of the inner *agaf* one stands. The same physical thickness of the wall yields different rulings depending on whether one is in a window or in the gate opening, because passing through the gate represents a different kind of spatial crossing than standing in a window.

---

## Prayer & Minyan

### Rav Yehuda

Rav Yehuda rules in the name of Rav: *ve-chein li-tefillah* — the same threshold applies for purposes of prayer. If someone is standing beyond the outer *agaf*, on the outside of the doorway, they are considered in a different space from those inside.

### Ben Levi

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees. He states: *afilu mechitzah shel barzel einah mafsekes bein Yisrael la-Avihem she-bashamayim* — even an iron wall does not divide between Israel and their Father in heaven. This is a deeply evocative teaching, particularly resonant at this time of year.

### Minyan Logic

The practical ruling that emerges from these two views is as follows. The principle of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — that no wall separates Israel from their Father in heaven — means that if a *minyan* is gathered in one location and someone is outside the building but able to hear the prayers, that person is still part of the *tefillah be-tzibbur*. Once a *tzibbur* is constituted in one space, individuals outside its walls can attach themselves to that *minyan*. The concern raised by Rav Yehuda — that the partition creates a spatial separation — is more acute when there is no *minyan* to begin with, and one needs to count people in different spaces toward the required quorum. Tosafot introduces a third category: whether someone outside the building is *yotzei* with *Kaddish* and *Kedushah* even when a *minyan* is already present. Whether this is truly distinct from the question of *tefillah be-tzibbur* or is essentially the same issue is itself a matter of discussion.

This discussion has practical implications for the status of the *ezrat nashim* and for questions about listening to prayer through windows or electronic media — though the latter involves considerations well beyond the present *sugya*.

---

## Gate Sanctification

### Leper Accommodation

The Gemara notes an apparent inconsistency between the two parts of the *mishnah*: the first part implies the *agaf* itself is on the outside; the second part implies it is on the inside. The resolution is: *kan be-sha'arei azarah, kan be-sha'arei Yerushalayim* — one ruling applies to the gates of the *azarah*, the other to the gates of Yerushalayim. The reason they differ is provided by Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak: *mipnei mah lo nitkadshu sha'arei Yerushalayim* — why were the gates of Yerushalayim not sanctified? *Mipnei she-metzoraim meginim tachteihem ba-chamah mipnei ha-chamah u-va-geshem mipnei ha-geshem* — because *metzoraim*, who must remain outside the walls of Yerushalayim, would shelter in the gate openings from the sun and the rain.

A *metzora* who is excluded from Yerushalayim has no home within the city walls. Like the four *metzoraim* in the story read as the *haftarah* during this period, they sit exposed outside the city gates. To provide them with at least the shelter of the gate doorway, the Rabbis — or more precisely, the *kedushah* was not extended to the gates during the original sanctification — left the gate space unsanctified, so that *metzoraim* could stand there without transgressing. To whatever extent it was possible to leave a strip of accessible space for them, it was done. Hence, in Yerushalayim, the *agaf* itself is treated as outside, not inside.

### Jerusalem vs. Azarah

This consideration does not apply to the gates of the *azarah*. A *metzora* has no standing at the *azarah* to begin with, and there is no reason to create an accessible strip at those gates. Accordingly, by the *azarah* gates, the *agaf* is treated as inside, part of the sanctified space.

### Nicanor Exception

However, there is one exception even within the *azarah*: *mipnei mah lo nitkadash sha'ar Nicanor* — why was the gate of Nicanor not sanctified in the same way as the other gates of the *azarah*? Nicanor's Gate is the primary gate of the *azarah*, the great eastern entrance. The reason it was also left with an unsanctified *agaf* space is: *mipnei she-metzoraim omdim sham u-machnisim behonot yadeihem* — because *metzoraim* stand there and insert their thumbs. On the eighth day of a *metzora*'s purification process, blood from a *korban* must be applied to the *behonot* — the thumb and big toe — of the *metzora*. But the *metzora*, who is not yet fully purified, cannot enter the *azarah*. The solution is for the *metzora* to stand in the gateway and extend their thumbs inward to receive the blood. To give the *metzora* a bit more room in which to stand, the space of the *agaf* at Nicanor's Gate was also left outside the boundary of sanctification.

The general principle thus emerges: for all the gates of Yerushalayim, the *agaf* is treated as outside because of *metzoraim*. For gates of the *azarah*, the *agaf* is inside — except at Nicanor's Gate, where it is outside, again because of the *metzora*'s purification procedure.

---

---

# Pesachim 86

## Windows & Wall Status

### Intro: Doorways

The *mishna* with which our *daf* opens addresses what happens when a limb from the *korban pesach* exits its designated zone — the zone being *Yerushalayim*, though we had already learned that the prohibition also encompasses leaving the *chabura*, the group of participants eating the offering. The *mishna* further specified that the disqualified portion must be removed, a practically complicated matter given that the meat is still on the bone.

The final clause of the *mishna*, which is our immediate focus, concerns the status of the doorway: is the space within a doorway considered inside the city or outside? And what of the space where the door itself closes? The *mishna* rules that windows and the thickness of the wall (*ovi ha-choma*) are treated as though they are on the inside of the city. This produces a striking asymmetry: once one crosses to the outer side of the door, one is definitively outside — yet that same wall thickness, when approached via a window or from above, is considered inside. The determining factor is not the physical location within the wall but precisely where one stands in relation to it.

### Rambam: House Focus

*Rashi* understands this *mishna* to be discussing the walls encircling *Yerushalayim* and the question of when one has exited the city — since taking any *korban*, any *kodshim kalim*, out of *Yerushalayim* renders it invalid. *Rambam*, however, reads the *mishna* in a notably different way. He understands it to be discussing specifically the *korban pesach* and the physical *bayit* in which it is consumed, drawing on the verse *lo totzi min ha-basar min ha-bayit chutza* — one may not take the meat outside the house. What constitutes "outside the house"? What if one is eating in a window embrasure? What if one is at the top of a wall without a roof? What if one is in the doorway itself?

The *Rambam*'s reading connects to an issue raised earlier in the *masechta*: whether the prohibition is exclusively about leaving the *chabura*, or whether the physical house also matters as an independent boundary. For *Rambam*, it is clear that the physical house matters — and thus the *mishna* is defining what counts as "the house" for purposes of the *korban pesach*. As we will see, however, the *gemara* reads the *mishna* in terms of *Yerushalayim* and *kedusha*, which is precisely where *Rashi*'s reading is grounded.

### Rooftops Unsanctified

The *gemara* opens with a statement of *Rav*: *gagin va'aliyot lo nitkadshu* — rooftops and upper stories were not sanctified with the *kedusha* of *Yerushalayim*. This immediately raises a conceptual difficulty: all of *Yerushalayim* is an area in which *kodshim kalim* may be eaten. Does that *kedusha* extend only to ground level? Can one eat such offerings on a rooftop?

### Kedusha Concepts

The question, though initially strange, admits of a principled resolution. The *kedusha* of *Yerushalayim* can be understood in two distinct ways. One way is to see it as an extension of the *beit ha-mikdash* itself — a more distant zone of sanctity continuous with the inner sanctity of the Temple. From this perspective, the relevant analogy is the *kedusha* of the *beit ha-mikdash* floor, where the *kohanim* walk barefoot and the sanctity is specifically bound to the ground surface. We encountered this principle earlier in discussing *kohanim* walking through blood — the very floor of the *mikdash* is sanctified, and contact with it is structurally significant. If *Yerushalayim* is understood as an extension of that sanctity, one might argue that only ground-level space participates in it, just as the *mikdash* itself is conceptually anchored to the floor.

The second way to understand the *kedusha* of *Yerushalayim* is not as an extended *beit ha-mikdash* but as proximity — a kind of sacred neighborhood or suburb of the *mikdash*, where one's relationship to the city itself, rather than to a specific floor, defines the sanctity. Under this second conception, vertical position might be irrelevant. These two frameworks produce different conclusions about whether rooftops and upper stories share the *kedusha* of the city.

A further illustration of the first framework emerges from the *mitzvah* of *lulav*. The verse *vesamachtem lifnei Hashem Elokeichem shivat yamim* — rejoicing before God for seven days — was understood by *chazal* to require taking the *lulav* in *Yerushalayim* for all seven days as a *mitzvah d'Oraisa*. Yet no one suggests this applies only to ground level. That is because in this context, *Yerushalayim* functions as a place of proximity, not as an extension of the *mikdash* floor. By contrast, when it comes to eating *korbanot*, where the analogy to the *beit ha-mikdash* is most operative, the question of ground-level sanctity becomes real.

A related point arises regarding the ramp (*kevesh*) leading up to the *mizbeach*: the *kohen* walking up that ramp is not at ground level, yet the ramp is clearly part of the sanctified structure. The reason is that the ramp is a permanent, integral element of the *mikdash*'s architecture — there is no space beneath it — and as such it is treated as part of the ground. This distinction between permanent structural features and the more ambiguous status of rooftops and upper stories is conceptually useful, even if not fully determinative.

### Hallel Rooftop Image

The *gemara* then challenges *Rav*'s ruling with a poetic statement transmitted by *Rav* in the name of *Rabbi Chiya*: *k'zayita Pischa v'Hallel paka igra* — when each person receives only a *k'zayit* of the *korban pesach* it means there is a great crowd, and their *Hallel* bursts through the rooftops. It is a vivid image: the house packed with people, each receiving just a *k'zayit*, and the power of their song overflowing. The phrase also rhymes in Aramaic, giving it an almost musical quality.

The challenge is: does this not imply that people were eating and saying *Hallel* on the rooftop itself — *d'achli b'igra v'amri b'igra*? The *gemara* rejects this reading: *d'achli b'ara v'amri b'igra* — they ate at ground level and then, after finishing, ascended to the rooftop to continue with *Hallel*. But then a further problem arises.

### Afikoman & Groups

We have a *mishna* that rules *ein maftirin achar ha-pesach afikoman*. The word *afikoman* is Greek. The Babylonian *Talmud* did not work from its Greek etymology — the *chachamim* therefore offered various interpretations of the word. *Rav* explains it to mean that after the *korban pesach* has been eaten, one must not uproot oneself from one *chabura* and join another *chabura*. We already learned that one cannot physically transfer the *pesach* from one group to another; *Rav* adds that even after eating is complete, one should not go and say *Hallel* together with a different group. The imagery evoked is that of a livelier gathering next door and the temptation to join their celebration. In fact, the word *afikoman* in Greek apparently refers to precisely this phenomenon — going from party to party after a meal — which *chazal* prohibited. Given this ruling, how could the people in the *gemara*'s scenario move up to the rooftop to say *Hallel*, leaving the location where they ate?

### Post-Meal Movement

The *gemara* resolves this with a distinction: *lo kashya — kan b'sha'at achila, kan shelo b'sha'at achila*. The prohibition against leaving one's group applies during the time of eating — even if one has personally finished, leaving at that moment creates the appearance of joining another group's eating. But once the time of eating has concluded for everyone, there is greater latitude of movement. It is then permitted to move — for instance, ascending to the rooftop — because one is not joining another group's meal but simply relocating after the meal is over.

One might have thought the distinction would turn on whether one joins another *chabura* or merely moves within one's own group. But the *gemara*'s principle is temporal rather than spatial: what matters is whether the time of eating has passed.

### Upper Chamber Kedusha

The *gemara* now brings a further challenge from a *baraita* attributed to *Abba Shaul*: *Aliyat Beit Kodesh Kadashim chamura mi-Beit Kodesh Kadashim* — the upper chamber above the *Kodesh Kadashim* is treated with even greater stringency than the *Kodesh Kadashim* itself. This is noteworthy given that today's *daf* would have ideally been studied on *Yom Kippur*, when the *Kodesh Kadashim* itself is so central.

The distinction is this: *Shebeit Kodesh Kadashim Kohen Gadol nichnas lo pa'am achas ba-shana* — the *Kohen Gadol* entered the *Kodesh Kadashim* once a year, on *Yom Kippur*. The upper chamber, however, was entered only once every seven years, or according to some opinions twice every seven years, and according to yet others only once every fifty years — *leda ma hi tzericha*, to inspect whether it required repairs. In one sense, this makes the upper chamber less significant: it was visited only for functional, structural purposes and had no ongoing ritual role. Yet its extreme infrequency of access was understood as reflecting a kind of heightened *chamur* quality.

The *Maharsha* connects this to a famous *midrash* regarding *sukkah*: the divine presence (*Shechina*) never descended below ten *tefachim*, and no human ever ascended within ten *tefachim* of the heavens — the impossibility of actual contact between the human and the divine, like the famous image of Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling where God and Adam's fingers do not quite touch. By this reading, since the *Shechina* resides in the *Kodesh Kadashim* but cannot descend fully below a certain threshold, the chamber *above* the *Kodesh Kadashim* is in some sense even closer to the divine presence than the room below it.

Whatever the theological rationale, the practical import of *Abba Shaul*'s ruling for our *gemara* is this: minimally, it implies that the chamber above the *Kodesh Kadashim* possessed the *kedusha* of the *mikdash* — otherwise, why speak of it in terms of greater *chamur* than the *Kodesh Kadashim*? And if an upper story has *kedusha*, it would seem to undercut *Rav*'s ruling that rooftops and upper stories were not sanctified.

### Access Defines Status

*Rav Yosef* pushes back: can one really derive a proof from the *Heichal*? By the *Heichal*, the verse states explicitly: *Vayiten David li-Shlomo b'no et tavnit ha-ulam* — David gave Shlomo the plans for the *ulam*, its chambers, its treasury rooms, *ve'aliyotav* — and its upper stories, *ve-Beit ha-Kapporet* — and even the *Kodesh Kadashim* where the *aron* stood. And the verse continues: *Hakol bi-chtav mi-yad Hashem alai hiskil* — everything came from God, God gave me the blueprints directly. Since the *Heichal* and all its upper stories were part of the divinely transmitted plan, it is unsurprising that those second-story chambers were sanctified. That tells us nothing about *Yerushalayim* generally or about the status of rooftops there.

The *gemara* then attempts a proof from elsewhere in the *mikdash* itself — not from the *Heichal* specifically: *ha-lishkot ha-bnuyot ba-kodesh u-ftuchot la-chol, tochan chol, ve-gaggoteihem kodesh*. Chambers that were physically built within the sacred zone but whose doors opened to the non-sacred area — their interior is *chol* and their rooftops are *kodesh*.

To understand this ruling, one must picture the layout. Imagine a chamber built into the outer wall of the *mikdash* complex, physically embedded within the sacred zone, but with its door opening outward toward *Har ha-Bayit* — not into the *Azara* itself. In such a case, the ground-floor interior of the chamber is functionally associated with the outside space to which it opens; those entering and using it come from the outside. Its floor is therefore treated as *chol*. But its roof, physically located within the sanctified zone, is *kodesh*.

The inverse ruling follows: *benuyot ba-chol u-ftuchot la-kodesh, tochan kodesh ve-gaggoteihem chol* — chambers built in the non-sacred zone but whose doors opened into the *kodesh* have their interiors treated as *kodesh* (because they are accessed and used by those in the sacred space), while their rooftops are *chol*. The governing principle is that access defines status: the interior of a space follows the direction from which it is entered and used. The rooftop, being equally accessible from neither side in the simple sense, follows the physical location of the wall in which the chamber is embedded.

*Rav Chisda* then redirects the analysis. The *gemara* had been using this *mishna* as evidence that rooftops can be *kodesh*, but *Rav Chisda* explains: *targuma Rav Chisda be-she-gaggoteihen shavin le-karka Azara* — we are actually speaking of a chamber that is underground, recessed into the terrain, such that its roof is flush with the floor of the *Azara*. In that case, the "rooftop" is not elevated above ground at all — it is level with the *Azara* floor. The "roof" of the chamber is in fact the floor of the *Azara*, and its *kedusha* follows from that ground-level status. There is no proof here for elevated rooftops having *kedusha*.

The *gemara* then presses on the *seifa* of that same *mishna*. If *Rav Chisda*'s interpretation holds — that we are always talking about underground chambers — then when the *mishna* rules *tochan kodesh ve-gaggoteihem chol* for chambers built in the *chol* but opening into the *kodesh*, those "rooftops" would have to be flush with the non-sacred ground outside. But wait: if we are describing underground chambers throughout, we are talking about *mechilot* — tunnels. And *Rabbi Yochanan* taught explicitly: *mechilot lo nitkadshu* — the tunnels were not sanctified. How, then, can the *gemara* say *tochan kodesh*?

The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between two classes of tunnels. *Rabbi Yochanan*'s ruling that tunnels are not sanctified applies to tunnels beneath *Har ha-Bayit* — those were deliberately left unsanctified to allow *tamei* individuals to exit the area without violating the *kedusha* of *Har ha-Bayit* above them. This is exactly the logic of the *mechilot ha-Kotel* tours available today. By contrast, tunnels or underground chambers whose openings are into the *Azara* — the sanctified precinct itself — do bear *kedusha*, because their access and use is from the sanctified zone. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s statement that tunnels beneath the *Heichal* are *chol* refers specifically to those whose opening is to the *chol* side. Tunnels beneath the *Azara* that open into the *kodesh* are themselves *kodesh*. The determining principle is consistently: where does the entrance face?

### Tunnels & Kedusha

To summarize what emerges from the foregoing: the *kedusha* of underground spaces follows from their point of access. Tunnels beneath *Har ha-Bayit* were kept unsanctified as a matter of deliberate policy — to allow *tamei* persons to depart without being in a sanctified zone. Tunnels that open into the *Azara* proper, however, carry *kedusha*. The same logic that defines the chamber interiors defines the tunnels: access determines status.

### Measuring Sticks

The *gemara* makes one more attempt to address the status of rooftops, this time from a *baraita* stating that the roof of the *Heichal* is *kodesh* — *gago shel Heichal kodesh*. But the *gemara* immediately counters with another teaching: *gagim halalu einu ochlim sham kodshei kodashim ve-ein shochtim sham kodashim kalim* — one cannot eat *kodshei kodashim* on those rooftops and one cannot perform *shechita* of *kodashim kalim* there. These are the defining acts of the *Azara*, the sanctified courtyard. Since neither can be done on the roof of the *Heichal*, that rooftop clearly does not have the *kedusha* of the *Azara*. If so, in what sense is it *kodesh*?

*Rav Chama bar Guria* answers: *l'otan shtei amot* — the reference to the roof being *kodesh* is connected to the two *amot*, i.e., the two measuring sticks (*amot* here meaning not the cubits themselves but the measuring rods). The *mishna* teaches: *Shtei amot hayu be-Shushan ha-Bira* — they kept two measuring sticks in the chamber called *Shushan ha-Bira* (a special room, named for the image of the city of Shushan carved above the eastern gate). One was kept at the northeast corner and one at the southeast corner. The northeastern stick was a half-finger larger than the official *amah* as transmitted from *Moshe Rabbeinu* — roughly 2% larger. The southeastern stick was a half-finger larger still — 4% larger than the *amah* of *Moshe*.

Why maintain measuring sticks of different sizes? *She-hayu umnim notlin bi-ketana u-machzirin be-gedola kedei she-lo yavo'u lidei me'ila* — craftsmen hired to work on the *mikdash* would receive their raw materials measured out by the smaller stick, and return the finished goods or unused materials measured by the larger stick. This ensured that they could not pocket any sacred materials: whatever they received was measured conservatively, and whatever they returned was measured generously, meaning they had to account for every last bit. Two different sizes were needed because *achat le-kesef ve-zahav ve-achat le-vinyana* — one for precious metals (where a 2% discrepancy is substantial) and one for building materials like stone and wood (where the margin could be larger). The point was not to make it impossible for the craftsmen to profit, but to incentivize extreme care with *hekdesh* property so as to guard against *me'ila*.

Returning to the main question: what does this have to do with the roof of the *Heichal* being called *kodesh*? *Tosafot* clarifies that the measuring sticks were not actually stored on the rooftop. *Shushan ha-Bira* was a depiction of the city of Shushan carved above the eastern gate of the *mikdash*, and that gate was one of the gates of the *Azara* itself. *Tosafot* therefore says: just as those eastern gates were sanctified enough to hold sacred vessels, so too was the roof of the *Heichal* sanctified in that same sense — *le-hatzni'a sham klei kodesh*, to store sacred implements there. But *Tosafot* immediately notes that *klei kodesh* do not actually require a sanctified location to be stored; you do not need *Azara*-level *kedusha* to house them. So the statement that the roof is *kodesh* means no more than that it was used for this purpose — it does not establish that the roof had the full *kedusha* of the *Azara*. The use of the word *kodesh* there is *lav davka*.

### Windows & Ground Level

The *gemara* now turns back to the *mishna* itself: *ha-chalonot ve-ovi ha-choma ki-fenim* — windows and wall thickness are like the inside. The *gemara* attempts to clarify how to account for these physically. For windows, it proposes that we understand them as *shaveh le-karka* — flush with the ground, as in a case where a building is constructed into the slope of *Yerushalayim*'s terrain, such that a window is at the same level as the city floor. Someone standing in that window embrasure is therefore at ground level.

*Rashi* notes that the *gemara*'s references to *Azara* in this context are not precisely meant — we are really discussing *Yerushalayim* as a whole. For the wall thickness (*ovi ha-choma*), though, the geometrical challenge is more acute: the whole purpose of a city wall is that it rises higher than the ground it surrounds, so how can the top of the wall be flush with the interior ground level?

### Secondary Walls

The *gemara* answers: *mishkachat lah be-var shura* — you find this in the case of a secondary wall. The verse in *Eichah* speaks of *cheil ve-choma* being mourned in the destruction of *Yerushalayim*, and *Rabbi Acha* (or *Rav Chanina*) explains these as *shura u-var shura* — the main wall and the secondary wall. *Rashi* describes an arrangement in which the outer wall of the city rises to full height, while inside, a lower inner or retaining wall runs parallel to it. The top of this secondary, lower wall can be flush with the interior floor of the city — just as the top of the *Kotel* today is roughly flush with the level of *Har ha-Bayit* and the *Kippat ha-Sela*. In that way, "the thickness of the wall" that is treated as being on the inside refers to the space associated with this inner retaining wall, the top of which is at ground level with the inner city.

The *gemara* does not reach a fully explicit resolution regarding the general status of rooftops in *Yerushalayim*. What emerges is a consistent effort to translate all the evidence into cases where surfaces are flush with the ground — the strong implication being that when a surface is genuinely elevated, it may not carry the *kedusha* of *Yerushalayim*, though this remains without a definitive ruling. The discussion throughout has also presented a challenge to the *Rambam*'s reading of the *mishna* as pertaining to the physical house of the *korban pesach*, since the *gemara* consistently frames the analysis in terms of *kedusha*, the sanctification of space, rather than merely the legal definition of a house for purposes of the offering.

---

## Dividing Groups

### Two Groups Separated

The *mishna* continues: *shtei chaburot she-hayu ochlot be-bayit echad* — two groups eating in one house. *Eilu hofchin et pneihem heilach ve-ochlim, ve-eilu hofchin et pneihem heilach ve-ochlim* — each group turns its face away from the other and eats in its own space.

*Rashi* reads this *mishna* as establishing that it is *permitted* to divide one *korban pesach* between two groups — a matter that will be debated in the *gemara*. The *mishna* thus tells us that two groups may eat one *pesach* in one house, each turning away from the other. *Rambam*, however, reads the *mishna* as stating a *requirement*: once you have committed to two groups eating in one house — whether from one or two *korbanot* — the boundary lines between them must be maintained visibly and clearly. The act of each group turning away from the other is not merely a permission but an obligation to ensure that the two groups do not become confused. The heating vessel (*micham*) may be placed between them without undermining this clarity, since it is a shared utilitarian object.

### Baraita: Division

The *gemara* establishes whose view the *mishna* reflects: *matnisin mani? Rebbi Yehuda hi* — the *mishna* follows *Rebbi Yehuda*. The source is a *baraita* on the verse *al ha-batim asher yochlu oto bahem* — the *pesach* shall be eaten in the houses in which you will eat it. The word *batim* is plural. One could read this as: every group eats in its own house, but a single *pesach* is eaten in multiple houses — i.e., divided between two groups. *Melamed she-ha-pesach ne'echal bi-shtei chaburot* — it teaches that a *pesach* may be eaten by two *chaburot*.

One might then have thought that just as the *pesach* itself can be divided, an individual can eat in two locations — starting with one group and then joining the other half of his *pesach* elsewhere. The *baraita* therefore continues: *talmud lomar be-bayit echad ye'achel* — "in one house it shall be eaten." The *gemara* reads this as *yochal* (the subject being the eater), meaning the *individual* must eat in one location, even if the *pesach* is distributed across two groups.

### Attendant Scenario

From this the *baraita* derives a practical ruling: *ha-shamash she-achal ke-zayit be-tzad ha-tanur* — if the attendant (*shamash*) was tending the oven while the *korban pesach* was roasting and he tasted a *ke-zayit* of it there, he has established his eating location as the small oven room. Since a *chabura* can consist of even one individual, and one must eat in only one place, he cannot now go to the main room to continue eating. *Im pikei'ach hu, memaleh karsav mimenu* — if he is wise, he eats his full share right there at the oven. And if the members of the main *chabura* wish to do him a kindness, *ba'in ve-yoshvin tzido* — they come and sit next to him. That is *Rebbi Yehuda*'s position.

### Rabbi Yehuda: One Place

*Rebbi Yehuda*'s ruling is thus that a person can eat in only one location. The logic of this is tight: wherever one first eats establishes one's *makom*, one's designated location. Even if that location is not where the rest of the *chabura* is eating, one is fixed there. The *chabura* is defined not only by group membership but by spatial commitment.

### Rabbi Shimon: Multiple

*Rebbi Shimon* reads the verse differently. *Al ha-batim asher yochlu oto bahem* — the plural *batim* teaches *melamed she-ochel ochel bi-shtei mekomot*: an individual *may* eat in two locations. He is not locked into his first eating spot. On the other hand, *Rebbi Shimon* reads *be-bayit echad ye'achel* more literally — the *pesach* must be eaten in one house, one group. One cannot divide a single *korban pesach* between two *chaburot*. *Rebbi Shimon* and *Rebbi Yehuda* thus arrive at opposing conclusions from the same verses, each one treating one clause as the restriction and deriving freedom from the other.

### Debate Resolution

The *gemara* explains: *Rebbi Yehuda savar yesh em la-masoret* — *Rebbi Yehuda* holds that we follow the *written* tradition, i.e., the *ketiv*. The word *ye'achel* as written can be read as *yochal* — the *person* must eat in one place. *Rebbi Shimon savar yesh em la-mikra* — *Rebbi Shimon* holds we follow the *pronunciation*, the *kri*. The word is read as *ye'achel* — the *pesach* shall be eaten in one house. Hence their disagreement over which clause restricts movement of the person and which restricts division of the offering.

*Rashi* clarifies *Rebbi Shimon*'s position: the requirement of *be-bayit echad* means that the primary eating of the *pesach* must take place with one *chabura* — it may not be divided from the outset. But as for an individual's movement: once the group has started eating together, a person may relocate within the house or even to other spaces, as long as he is not joining a different *chabura* eating a different *pesach*.

### Partition Setup

The *gemara* then presents a series of scenarios testing these principles. In the first: one group was eating one *korban pesach* together in one space, and then a *mechitza* was erected between two halves of the group. According to the view that a *pesach* may be eaten by two *chaburot* (*Rebbi Yehuda*'s position), they may continue eating — the *mechitza* does not create a problem. According to the view that a *pesach* may not be eaten by two *chaburot* (*Rebbi Shimon*'s position), the erection of the *mechitza* effectively divides what was one group into two, and they may no longer continue eating.

### Partition Removed

The second scenario involves two separate groups, each eating its own *korban pesach*, separated from the start by a *mechitza*. The *mechitza* is then removed. Does the new spatial configuration — now larger than the original space of either group — create a problem?

According to the view that a person may eat in two locations (*Rebbi Shimon*), it is fine: even if the expanded space constitutes a new location, that is permitted. According to the view that a person must eat in only one location (*Rebbi Yehuda*), there is a problem: although no one has moved, the space in which one now finds oneself is arguably a *new* and expanded space — and eating in a second location is prohibited. Note the asymmetry between the two cases: when a *mechitza* is erected to create a subset of the original space, the smaller space is contained within the original and does not constitute a truly new location. But when a *mechitza* is removed to create a *larger* space that was previously divided, that new, expanded space may be considered a different location altogether.

### Rav Ashi Challenge

*Rav Ashi* challenged *Rav Kahana*, who was presenting these cases as obvious settled rulings. *Rav Ashi* argued: *ibayei lach ibaya* — these should be posed as open questions, not taken for granted. The question of whether erecting or removing a *mechitza* constitutes a meaningful change — *siluk mechitza va-asiyat mechitza, ni havei k'vei mekomot u-k'vei chaburot dami o lav* — whether placing or removing a partition genuinely converts one space into two or two spaces into one for purposes of these *halachot* — remains genuinely unresolved, and *Rav Kahana* should have framed it as a *she'ela* rather than a *peshat*.

### Bride's Modesty

The final clause of the *mishna* states: *ve-ha-kallah hofechet panei-ha ve-ochelet* — the bride turns her face away and eats. *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* explains: *mishum she-hi bosha* — because she is embarrassed. As a newly married woman, she is self-conscious about eating in front of strangers — particularly in a room with men she does not know well. *Rashi* indicates that everyone's attention was naturally drawn to her as the new bride. The *chiddush* of the *mishna*, then, is not that she is required to turn away, but that she is *permitted* to do so without it appearing that she has separated herself into a different *chabura* or relocated to a different space. Her turning away is a matter of modesty, not a statement about group membership.

---

## Etiquette & Customs

### Rav Huna Visit

The *gemara* now introduces a series of narratives about proper conduct at a host's table, which connect back to the *mishna*'s mention of the bride turning her face. *Rav Huna brei d'Rav Nasan ikla l'vei Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* — *Rav Huna son of Rav Nasan* came to visit the house of *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak*. They asked him his name. He told them: *Rav Huna*. Everything that followed was, from the perspective of the household, a series of social missteps — each of which *Rav Huna* then proceeded to justify on the basis of principle.

### Couch Protocol

When they told him to sit on the *puraya* — the couch, the honored reclining place rather than an ordinary chair — he accepted immediately and sat. This was contrary to local etiquette, where a guest was expected to initially decline such an honor. *Rav Huna* justified himself: *kol ma she-yomar lecha ba'al ha-bayit asei* — whatever the *ba'al ha-bayit* tells you to do, you should do. There is a well-known principle of deferring to one's host. He added the qualifier *chutz mi-tzei* — except for "leave." Once the host tells you to leave, he is no longer functioning as your *ba'al ha-bayit*, and in any case you must go. The *Maharsha* adds a nuance: once told to leave, the relationship of *ba'al ha-bayit* and guest has dissolved, and there is no further obligation to follow his instructions.

### Wine Acceptance

Similarly, when they handed him a cup of wine, he accepted it at once without the customary show of reluctance. Again, local practice apparently called for an initial refusal. *Rav Huna* explained: *mesarvin mi-katan ve-ein mesarvin mi-gadol* — one pushes off and initially refuses when a person of lesser status makes an offer, but when someone of importance offers, one accepts immediately. By accepting their offer without hesitation, he was expressing that he regarded them as people of importance — his acceptance was itself a form of respect.

### Drinking Etiquette

When he then drank the cup in two sips (*terei zimnei*), they again noted this. The *baraita*: *ha-shoseh koso be-vas achas, harei zeh gargaran* — one who drinks a cup all in one gulp is considered a glutton. *Shnayim derech eretz* — two gulps is the proper, accepted manner. *Shlosha mi-gasei ha-ruach* — drinking in three small, slow sips conveys arrogance and excessive delicacy. *Rav Huna* had therefore drunk in two gulps precisely because that is *derech eretz*, the correct middle path.

### Face Turning

Finally, they observed that when he drank he did not turn his face away. *Rav Huna* replied: *Kallah hofeches panei-ha* — it is the bride who must turn her face; the *mishna* specifies only her. This is the reason the narrative about *Rav Huna*'s visit is introduced in the context of the *mishna*'s ruling about the bride: the *kallah hofeches panei-ha* is brought here to teach that turning one's face away while eating or drinking is not a general requirement of *derech eretz* but a specific dispensation — or rather accommodation — for the newly married woman who is too embarrassed to eat facing others. In ordinary circumstances, a man is not required to, and indeed may not need to, turn away.

### Yishmael Exception

The *gemara* then records a parallel episode. *Rabbi Yishmael be-Rabbi Yosi ikla le-vei Rabbi Shimon be-Rabbi Yosi ben Lakunya* — *Rabbi Yishmael* came to visit *Rabbi Shimon*'s house. They gave him a cup of wine; he accepted it immediately and drank it all in one gulp (*be-vas achas*). They challenged him: does the master not hold the principle that one who drinks a cup all at once is considered a glutton? He replied: *lo amru be-hai* — they did not say this ruling applies in this case, for three reasons. First, *koscha katan* — your cup is small. Second, *ve-yeincha matok* — your wine is sweet, making it easy and natural to drink quickly. Third, *ve-charsi rechava* — my stomach is large. When all three factors combine, drinking the whole cup at once is not gluttony but simply normal consumption. The principle is not absolute; the circumstances of the cup, the wine, and the person matter.

### Servant Protocol

The *gemara* closes with a brief teaching of *Rav Huna*: *bnei chabura nichnasim bi-shlosha ve-yotzin afilu be-echad* — a group that has hired a *shamash* (attendant) to serve them requires a minimum of three members before the attendant is obligated to serve them. He cannot be made to attend to just one or two people. When they leave, however, *ve-yotzin afilu be-echad* — he must continue attending to them even if only one remains, as they break up one by one.

*Rava* adds two conditions: *ve-hu de-ayeil be-idna de-ragil le-me'al* — this applies only if the group assembled at the normal time, within the attendant's normal hours of service. And *ve-hu de-ragash bei dayala* — it applies only if the *dayala* (the attendant) is alert to the possibility that the group may break up and prepared to serve them individually. *Ravina* adds: *ve-notel sechar damim* — if the attendant is in fact required to serve individuals after the main group has broken up, he is entitled to additional compensation. *Ve-tzarich achron le-hosif damim* — the last member of the group remaining, who causes the attendant the most extra service, must contribute additionally from his own pocket. *Ve-livsof yachloku ze im ze* — and ultimately the additional payment is divided among all the members of the group.

*Tosafot* notes that according to another reading, this passage is not about general *derech eretz* regarding hired attendants but speaks specifically in the context of a *chabura* assembled to eat the *korban pesach* — addressing the question of how many members must be present before one is obligated to wait for the others before beginning to eat.

*Hadran alach kefei tzon.*

---

---

# Pesachim 87

## Women & Korban Pesach

### Perek HaIsha Intro

We begin now the eighth *perek*, known as *HaIsha*, opening at the top of 87a. One topic that has not yet received focused treatment — though it has been alluded to in passing — is women's obligation in the *korban Pesach*. The present *mishna* opens precisely on this question, though it approaches it obliquely: since we have been discussing the *chavura*, the group that participates together in the *korban Pesach*, this *mishna* begins by asking which group a particular woman belongs to — a woman who is simultaneously a wife and a daughter. But the discussion will eventually extend to the broader question of women's obligation in the *korban Pesach* itself.

### Woman in Husband's House

The *mishna* opens: *haisha bizman shehi beveis ba'alah* — when a woman is in her husband's house, and both her husband (*shachat aleha ba'alah*) and her father (*shachat aleha aviha*) each slaughter the *korban Pesach* with her in mind, then *tochal mishel ba'alah* — we assume she wishes to be with her husband, and she eats from his *korban*.

This raises an immediate and important question beyond the matter of assumed preference: what exactly constitutes membership in a *chavura* for the *korban Pesach*? There is no indication in the *mishna* that she contributed money, or that any formal act of *kinyan* was performed. It sounds as though her inclusion is determined purely by intent — what was in her head, or what others assumed was in her head. One might ask whether this is an application of *zachin leadam shelo bifanav*, the principle that one may acquire a benefit on behalf of another without their explicit presence. That is certainly possible. But it is not obvious that a formal act of *kinyan* was performed at all. This remains something to explore: what precisely constitutes membership in the *chavura*?

### Woman Visits Father

A more complex case: *halcha regel rishon la'asos beveis aviha* — if on the first *Pesach* she went to her father's house, and both her father and her husband slaughtered the *korban Pesach* with her in mind, then *tochal bimakom shehi rotza* — she eats where she wishes.

Several ambiguities press upon this case. First, what is meant by *regel rishon* — is it the very *Pesach* during which she went to her father's house? Or does it refer to the following year, based on a pattern established when she spent the first *yom tov* after marriage at her father's home? Moreover, the *regel rishon* in question need not have been *Pesach* at all — perhaps she went to her father's house on *Sukkos*, thereby indicating a general preference for spending *yom tov* with her parents, and the question then arises for the following *Pesach*. The *mishna* is not clear on any of these points.

What is clear is that the *mishna* allows her preference to be determinative, and the *gemara* will raise the question of *breira* — retroactive determination — in connection with this ruling.

### Orphan & Trustees

A parallel case involves an orphan whose estate is managed by *apitropsin* — trustees or executors — and each of the two trustees slaughtered a *korban Pesach* intending to include the orphan in his group. Since the two *korbanot* are distinct, *yochal bimakom shehu rotze* — the orphan eats where he wishes. Again, the question immediately arises: does this not require a determination at the time of *shechita*? The *gemara* will address this.

### Slave Two Partners

The case of an *eved shel shenei shutfin* — a slave jointly owned by two partners — is categorically different. Here, *lo yochal mishel sheneihem*: the slave may not eat from either *korban*, and this is true even if one partner and the slave himself explicitly express their preference that the slave eat with one particular master.
