Since the slave belongs equally to the other partner, nothing may be done without both partners' agreement. If both partners agree, of course, the matter is straightforward — but explicit stated preference alone is insufficient without joint consent.

### Half-Slave Status

Finally, the case of *mi shechetzio eved vechetzio ben chorin* — someone who is half slave and half free, typically the result of one of two partners having emancipated his share. Such a person may not eat with his master, because we cannot take for granted that the master wishes to include him: this person is no longer fully his slave, and so the ordinary assumption that a master includes his slave in his *korban* no longer applies. Whether this person eats his own *korban* independently, or is dependent on his master's initiative, remains among the questions the *gemara* will resolve.

---

## Breira & Shechita

### Breira Inference

*Shema mina* — the *gemara* infers from this entire *mishna* that it operates on the principle of *yesh breira*: retroactive determination. If the woman's, or the orphan's, expressed preference after the fact can determine their group membership retroactively, then *breira* — the idea that a later choice reveals what the status was from the beginning — must be operative. Otherwise, once the *shechita* has passed, it would be too late; one cannot retroactively join a group.

### Tosafot Breira Timing

The *gemara* deflects this inference: *mai rotza beshat shechita* — what the *mishna* means by "where she wishes" is that she had already expressed her preference at the moment of *shechita*. *Tosafot* spells this out precisely: *davka beirura beshat shechita* — the expression of preference must be specifically at the time of *shechita*. If no preference was expressed and we hold *ein breira*, then *eino ochel lo mishel zeh velo mishel zeh* — she cannot eat from either, because she is not definitively a member of either group, yet she cannot eat from both, since one may only eat from a *korban Pesach* one is a member of.

### Text vs. Doctrine

This resolution, while logically coherent, is clearly a difficult reading of the *mishna*. The simple sense of *tochal bimakom shehi rotza* is that she decides after the *shechita*, and her subsequent choice retroactively determines her membership — which is precisely the principle of *breira*. The *gemara*'s reading, in which she had already chosen at the moment of *shechita*, is strained. This is not unusual: when there is a *machloket* over a principle, the *gemara* works to show how each side can accommodate the evidence against it, even at the cost of a forced reading. Though it should be noted that *breira* is itself a dispute among *tanna'im*, so it would not have been troubling to attribute this *mishna* to the *tanna* who holds *yesh breira*.

---

## First vs. Later Holidays

### Remini Question

The *gemara* raises a *remini* — a contradiction from a *braita*. Whereas our *mishna* treats the woman's presence in her husband's home as the default assumption and raises doubt only when she went to her father's house on the *regel rishon*, the *braita* says the opposite: *isha regel harishon ochelet mishel aviha* — on the first *regel*, one assumes that she wants to be at her father's house, with no need for any expressed preference.

### Father First Holiday

The *braita* thus establishes that the first *yom tov* after marriage is assumed to be spent at the father's house — a presumption so strong that even if she did not actively go there, we assume that is where she wants to be. This aligns with a well-known social practice, attested here as a long-standing reality: that the first *yom tov* of a newly married couple is spent at the wife's parents' home.

### Later Holidays Open

After the first *regel*, the *braita* says: *rotza ochelet mishel aviha, rotza ochelet mishel ba'alah* — she eats where she wishes, and it is an open question. This stands in contrast to our *mishna*, which seems to treat the husband's household as the ordinary default. The two sources appear to reflect different baseline assumptions about where a wife wishes to celebrate *yom tov*.

### Lo Kashya Women Types

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya* — it is not difficult. *Kan be-redufa leilech, kan be-she-eino redufa*: one teaching refers to a woman who tends to run back to her father's house (*redufa*), while the other refers to a woman who does not have that inclination. The presumptions differ depending on the type of woman. As the *pasuk* says, *az hayiti be-einav kemotzet shalom* — then I was in his eyes like one who finds peace. Rabbi Yochanan interprets this strikingly: *ke-kallah she-nimtza'at sheleimah be-veit chameha* — like a bride who is found wholesome and beloved in her father-in-law's house, and because she is so beloved there, *rotza leilech le-hashbi'ach be-veit aviha* — she wants to go back to her father's house to report how warmly she has been received. This is a notable twist: one would have expected that the woman returning to her parents is doing so because things are difficult with the in-laws. Rabbi Yochanan inverts this — it is precisely because she is so loved in her husband's home that she wants to share the news with her own family.

---

## Shir HaShirim Interp.

### Ishi vs. Bali

The *gemara* introduces a new *pasuk* — one that the mention of *kallah* and the dynamics of marriage seem to have called to mind. The verse from *Hoshea* reads: *ve-haya ba-yom ha-hu neum Hashem tikrei Ishi ve-lo tikrei li od Ba'ali* — on that day you will call me *Ishi* (my husband) and no longer call me *Ba'ali* (my master). The plain sense of the verse is that the name *Baal* will be expunged because of its association with idolatrous worship. But the verse also carries a resonance between intimacy and ownership: *ba'ali* carries connotations of possession, dominion, and a certain coarseness of relationship, whereas *ishi* evokes equivalence and closeness.

Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse: *ke-kallah be-veit chameha ve-lo ke-kallah be-veit aviha* — like a bride in her father-in-law's house, not like a bride in her father's house. The implication is that in her father-in-law's house she has arrived at the fullness of the relationship — the intimacy of *ishi* — whereas in her father's house she was still in the status of *arusah*, the betrothed, not yet having entered fully into the husband's domain. As a betrothed woman, *ba'ali* would not yet have applied; only in the father-in-law's house does the relationship achieve its complete form. The precise connection between the two parts of Rabbi Yochanan's statement remains somewhat elusive, and if a better interpretation is available, it should be offered.

### Sister Interpretation

The *gemara* continues with *Shir HaShirim*. The verse reads: *achot lanu ketanah ve-shadayim ein lah* — we have a little sister and she has no breasts. Rabbi Yochanan interprets: *zu Eilam* — this refers to the region of Eilam, near Bavel, where Daniel went into *galut*. Eilam *zachatah lilmod ve-lo zachatah l'lamed* — it merited to learn Torah but did not merit to produce teachers of Torah. The "breasts" (*shadayim*) represent Torah in its nurturing capacity: Eilam absorbed Torah but did not nourish others from it. It is worth noting that in its famous *Shir HaShirim* commentary, *Artscroll* translates the plain sense in ways that quietly incorporate the allegorical meaning — rendering *shadayim ein lah* as essentially "she has not yet reached spiritual maturity."

### Wall Imagery Torah

The verse continues: *ani chomah ve-shadai ke-migdalot* — I am a wall and my breasts are like towers. Rabbi Yochanan interprets: *ani chomah zu Torah* — the wall is the Torah. *Ve-shadai ke-migdalot elu talmidei chachamim* — the towers are the Torah sages. As Rashi explains, the image here is not nurturing but protective: *she-meginim al ha-dor* — they protect the generation, as towers protect a city. Rava offers a broader reading: *ani chomah zu Knesset Yisrael* — the wall is the Jewish people itself, and *shadai ke-migdalot elu batei knesiyot u-vatei midrashot* — the towers are the synagogues and houses of study. This reading is more inclusive, encompassing the entire people and its institutions rather than Torah study alone.

### Sons Daughters Verse

Rav Zutra bar Tuvia said in the name of Rav: what is meant by the verse *asher baneinu ke-neti'im megudalim bi-neureihem* — our sons are like young shoots growing in their youth — *binoteinu ke-zaviyot mechutavot tavnit heichal* — our daughters are like hewn cornerstones, fashioned in the image of the *heichal*?

*Asher baneinu ke-neti'im* — these are the young men of Israel *shelo ta'amu ta'am chet* — who have not yet had the taste of sin, referring in context to the domain of sexual transgression, including *zera le-vatalah* and *hirhurim*. They are still like young saplings, innocent of the sins that come with maturity. *Binoteinu ke-zaviyot* — the daughters, like cornerstones, *elu betulot Yisrael she-ogdot pitcheihen le-ba'aleihen* — these are the virgins of Israel who guard their openings for their husbands, protecting their virginity until marriage.

### Bloodline Symbol

How does the word *zaviyot* convey this? The *gemara* draws a comparison to the verse: *u-mal'u ke-mizrak ke-zaviyot mizbe'ach* — and they will be filled like the *mizrak*, like the corners of the altar. The *mizrak* is the bowl that catches the blood of the sacrifice at the corners of the altar. *Zaviyot* in both places involves the retention of blood — and so it evokes the retention of blood that signifies virginity. This is the plain sense of the interpretation. Rashi also suggests a second reading: that it refers to women who are meticulous about *hilchot niddah*, ensuring that marital intimacy does not occur during the forbidden period — *sochfot pitcheihen le-ba'aleihen* — meaning that it is the women who maintain this boundary even when the husband might urge otherwise.

A further verse is offered: *meizaveinu melei'im mefikkim mizan el zan* — our storehouses are full, giving forth produce upon produce. The word *mezavveinu* echoes *ke-zavit*, and *mizan el zan* may carry a play on *znut* — sexual desire. The picture is one of abundant desire that is nevertheless mastered.

### Desire Mastery

*Mechutavot tavnit heichal* — hewn in the image of the *heichal*, specifically of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *gemara* concludes: *eilu va-eilu mah ma'aleh aleihem ha-katuv ke-ilu nivnah heichal bi-yimeihem* — regarding both the men and the women who achieve mastery over their desires, Scripture regards it as though the *Beit HaMikdash* has been built in their days. This is the culminating point of the digression: the mastery of desire — whether in the form of young men untainted by sin or young women who guard their fidelity — is the spiritual equivalent of the construction of the *Mikdash*.

---

## Hoshea Narrative

### Four Prophets

Returning to the verse in *Hoshea* — *devar Hashem asher hayah el Hoshea ben Be'eri bimei Uziyahu Yotam Achaz Chizkiyahu malchei Yehudah* — the *gemara* notes that this opening formula parallels that of *Yeshayahu*: *chazon Yeshayahu ben Amotz asher chazah bimei Uziyahu Yotam Achaz Chizkiyahu*. The *gemara* observes: *be-ferek echad nitnab'u arba'ah nevi'im* — four prophets prophesied in the same period: *Hoshea, Yeshayah, Amos*, and *Michah*. *Tosafot* notes that *Michah* does not overlap perfectly with all four kings, but the approximation is close enough. Among these four, says the *gemara*, *ve-gadol she-be-chulam Hoshea* — the greatest was *Hoshea*, which is striking given that *Yeshayahu* fills over sixty chapters, while *Hoshea* is a relatively brief book. The proof text: *techilat devar Hashem be-Hoshea* — the beginning of God's word was with *Hoshea*. Rabbi Yochanan interprets this not as a chronological claim but as a hierarchical one: *techilah le-arba'ah nevi'im she-nitnab'u be-oto ferek* — *Hoshea* was the first, i.e., the greatest, among the four who prophesied in that era.

### God Complains

Now the *gemara* reconstructs the backstory to *Hoshea*'s command to take a wife of prostitution. This is all implied rather than stated in the text, and *Tosafot* makes the point explicitly: *mim-she-amar lo likahat eishet zenunim darish she-mistama kach amar lo ve-kach heishiv* — from the fact that God commanded him to take a prostitute wife, we infer that there must have been a prior exchange that the *gemara* now fills in.

God said to *Hoshea*: *banecha chata'u* — your children have sinned. The expected response: *ve-hayah lo lomar* — he should have said, *banecha hen* — they are Your children, *benei chanunecha hen* — the children of Your beloved, *bnei Avraham Yitzchak ve-Yaakov* — the children of the Patriarchs. Roll Your compassion upon them, God. Recognize that they are Yours.

### Hoshea Dismisses

Instead, *Hoshea* responded: *Ribbono shel olam, kol ha-olam shelcha hu* — Master of the Universe, the whole world is Yours. If the Jewish people have sinned, exchange them for another nation. This is presented as a radical failure of advocacy — the precise opposite of what a prophet was called to do.

### Prostitute Wife Lesson

God's response — *mah e'eseh le-zakein zeh* — what shall I do with this elder? The lesson had to be taught through experience. God instructed *Hoshea*: *lech ve-kach ishah zonah ve-holid lecha bnei zenunim* — go and take a prostitute wife and have children from her, children whose paternity is uncertain. *Ve-achar kach amar lo: shalcheha me-al panecha* — and afterward, divorce her. *Im hu yachol lishloa'ch* — let us see if he is able to. If you think it is so easy to cast off a people, let us see whether you can cast off your own wife and children.

### Gomer Name Meaning

*Va-yelech va-yikach et Gomer bat Divlayim* — he went and took a woman named *Gomer bat Divlayim*. The *gemara* now interprets these names. *Gomer*: Rav says *she-hakol gomrin bah* — all men finish with her, meaning all men have had relations with her. *Bat Divlayim*: *dibah ra'ah bat dibah ra'ah* — she has a wicked reputation, the daughter of a woman with a wicked reputation. *Shmuel* says: *she-metukah be-fi hakol ke-devilah* — she is as sweet to everyone as pressed dried figs — with an obvious sexual connotation. Rabbi Yochanan says: *she-hakol dushin bah ke-devilah* — all trample upon her like figs being trodden during their preparation — a coarse image, using *dash*, a word associated with threshing and also with sexual intercourse. These are among the more explicit passages in *aggadah*, and one does wonder about the all-male setting in which these interpretations developed and were transmitted.

A more elevated alternative is offered: Rabbi Yehudah says *Gomer* alludes to the time — *she-bikshu ligmor mamon Yisrael* — when the nations sought to finish off the wealth of Israel, as the *bayit rishon* period drew to its close and Israel was constantly besieged and looted. Rabbi Yochanan adds: *baze-zu ve-gamru* — not merely sought, but actually did so. As the verse says, *ki ibdam melech Aram va-yasimem ke-afar la-dush* — for the king of Aram had destroyed them and made them like dust for trampling.

### Children Names Prophecy

*Va-tahar va-teled lo ben* — she conceived and bore a son. God commanded *Hoshea*: *kera shemo Yizre'el* — call his name *Yizre'el*, recalling the blood of *Navot*'s vineyard and the sin of the house of *Achav*: *ki od me'at u-fakadti et d'mei Yizre'el al beit Yehu* — I will visit the blood of *Yizre'el* upon the house of *Yehu*. *Ve-hishbatti mamlechut beit Yisrael* — I will cause the sovereignty of the house of Israel to cease.

She conceived again and bore a daughter. *Kera shemah Lo Ruchama* — call her name *Lo Ruchama*, for *ki lo osif od arachem et beit Yisrael* — I will no longer have compassion on the house of Israel. The closing phrase of that verse, *ki naso esa lahem*, is difficult — literally it seems to speak of lifting or forgiving, and Rashi reads it rhetorically: do you think I will still forgive them?

Then a third child, a son: *kera shemo Lo Ami* — call his name *Lo Ami*, for *ki atem lo ami* — you are not my nation — *ve-anochi lo ehye lachem* — and I will no longer be for you.

### God Demands Divorce

After these two sons and a daughter were born, God said to *Hoshea*: *lo hayah lecha lilmod mi-Moshe rabecha* — should you not have learned from your teacher Moses? *She-keivan she-dibarti imo peirash min ha-ishah* — from the moment I spoke with him, he separated himself from his wife. *Af ata bdal atzmecha mimenah* — you too should now separate yourself from this woman. Divorce her.

### Israel Eternal Acquisiti…

*Hoshea* replied: *Ribbono shel olam, yesh li banim mimenah, ve-eini yachol lehotzi'ah ve-lo le-garshah* — I have children from her; I cannot expel her, nor can I divorce her. Note that expulsion and formal divorce are treated as two separate acts.

God responded: *u-mah ata she-ishtecha zonah u-vanecha bnei zenunim, ve-ei ata yode'a im shelcha heim im shel acherim heim* — you, whose wife is a prostitute and whose children may not even be yours — you cannot bring yourself to divorce her. Yet you told Me to simply exchange the Jewish people for another nation? *She-hein banai, bnei bechunai, bnei Avraham Yitzchak ve-Yaakov* — they are My children, the children of My chosen ones, the children of the Patriarchs. They are *echad me-arba'ah kinyanim she-kaniti be-olami* — one of four special acquisitions I have in this world. Torah — *Hashem kanani reishit darko*. Heaven and earth — *koneh shamayim va-aretz* (and it should be noted that *koneh* in biblical Hebrew can also mean "to create," as in *kaniti ish* at the birth of *Kayin*). The *Beit HaMikdash* — *har zeh kanah yeminecha*. And Israel — *am zu kanita*. *Ve-ata amarta ha'avireim be-umah acheret* — and you told Me to exchange them for another nation?

### Hoshea's Repentance

*Keivan she-yada she-chata* — once *Hoshea* understood that he had sinned, *amad le-vakesh rachamim al atzmo* — he stood to seek compassion for himself. This is noted pointedly: even now, his concern was for himself alone.

### Compassion for Israel

God said to him: *ad she-ata me-vakesh rachamim al atzmecha, bakesh rachamim al Yisrael* — before you worry about forgiveness for yourself, ask for compassion for Israel. That had been his obligation from the very beginning. *She-gazarti aleihem shalosh gezeirot ba'avurecha* — because of your sin, the three harsh edicts — the names *Yizre'el*, *Lo Ruchama*, *Lo Ami* — were issued. It is a striking theological move: all of the negative prophecies are attributed not to God's will but to *Hoshea*'s failure. There is a *yom kippur* resonance here — not merely seeking personal *mechilah*, but taking genuine responsibility for everything one has caused.

### Edicts Nullified

*Amad u-vikeish rachamim* — and so *Hoshea* stood and finally asked compassion for the Jewish people. *U-vatlah gezeirah* — the edict was nullified. The Jews were still destined for *galut*, but the harsh terms — *Lo Ami*, *Lo Ruchama* — were reversed. *Ve-hitchil le-varchem* — and God began to bless them through the mouth of *Hoshea*: *ve-hayah mispar bnei Yisrael ke-chol ha-yam* — they will be as the sand of the sea. *Ve-hayah bi-makom asher ye'amer lahem lo ammi atem, ye'amer lahem bnei El chai* — instead of being called "not My nation," they will be called "children of the living God." *Ve-nikbezu bnei Yehudah u-vnei Yisrael yachdav* — and Judah and Israel will be gathered together, reversing the rupture signaled by *Yizre'el*. *Ve-zartiha li va-aretz* — I will plant them in the land. *Ve-richamti et Lo Ruchama* — I will have compassion on *Lo Ruchama*. *Ve-amarti le-Lo Ami ammi atah* — and to those I called "not my nation," I will say: you are my nation.

What makes this *gemara* so theologically powerful is not merely that the negative prophecies are reversed — it is that they are revealed to have never been God's true intention. It is not simply that there was a period of *Lo Ami* that gives way to *Ami*; rather, God's whole point from the beginning was that He would never divorce Himself from the Jewish people, that they are always His children. The harsh decrees were entirely a lesson for *Hoshea*, and nothing that God ever willed for Israel. The poetic and literary flexibility of the *gemara*'s reading shifts the theology entirely. Furthermore, by making *Hoshea* the source of all the negative prophecies, the *gemara* extends a kind of theological vindication to the people: even the children born with a stigma of *bnei zenunim* — the metaphorical standing of Israel during this period — will be purified and reclaimed. Their identity as *bnei Yisrael* is not diminished by sin or punishment, because God's love and commitment never wavered.

---

## Commentary Authority

### Rabbinate Burden

Rabbi Yochanan says: *oi lo le-rabbanut she-mekaveret et ba'aleha* — woe to positions of authority, for they bury those who hold them. The proof: *she-ein lecha kol navi ve-navi shelo kippe'ach arba'ah melachim be-yamav* — every prophet in this group outlived four kings. As the verse says, *chazon Yeshayahu ben Amotz asher chazah al Yehudah vi-Yerushalayim bimei Uziyahu Yotam Achaz Chizkiyahu malchei Yehudah* — so all four of these prophets outlived four successive kings. Authority takes its toll.

### Yerovam Accepts Amos

Rabbi Yochanan then asks: *mipnei mah zachah Yerovam ben Yoash melech Yisrael le-himanot im malchei Yehudah* — why did *Yerovam ben Yoash*, a king of Israel, merit to be listed among the kings of Judah in the opening verse of *Hoshea*? *Mipnei shelo kibel lashon hara al Amos* — because he did not accept the *lashon hara* that was spoken against *Amos* the prophet. This is derived from the account in which *Amatzyah*, the idolatrous priest of *Beit El*, sent word to *Yerovam* that *Amos* had prophesied *bacherev yamut Yerovam* — that *Yerovam* would die by the sword. *Yerovam* responded (as supplied by the *gemara*): *chas ve-shalom* that the righteous *Amos* should have meant such a thing — and if he truly prophesied this, then *mah e'eseh lo, she-shechinah amrah lo* — what can I do? God told him so. We never find that *Yerovam* acted against *Amos*, and from his inclusion in the list we infer that he rejected the accusation entirely.

### Compassion in Anger

Rabbi Elazar says: *afilu bi-she'at ka'aso shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu, zocher et ha-rachamim* — even at the moment of God's anger, He remembers compassion. The proof: when God says *ki lo osif od arachem et beit Yisrael* — I will no longer have compassion on the house of Israel — the very phrasing invokes compassion even in its negation. When the verse says God will no longer have compassion, He could have said He would bring fierce anger; instead, He speaks in the language of compassion even while withdrawing it. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina draws the same point from the phrase *ki naso esa lahem* — even if read rhetorically as "will I forgive them?," the fact that forgiveness appears in the text at all, even as a rhetorical question within a moment of judgment, demonstrates that compassion is never entirely absent.

### Exile & Converts

Rabbi Elazar further says: *lo higla Hakadosh Baruch Hu et Yisrael le-vein ha-umot ela ke-dei she-yitvasfu aleihem gerim* — the only reason God exiled Israel among the nations was so that converts would join them, so that Israel scattered across the world would bring knowledge of God to the peoples and that people would come to convert. This is a striking repositioning of *galut*: it is no longer merely punishment for sin, but is revealed as part of a divine plan oriented toward the messianic future, toward the universal recognition of God. Moreover, it reflects a profoundly positive attitude toward *gerim* — indeed, it places the value of *gerus* at the very center of the purpose of Jewish history.

The verse cited is *ve-zartiha li va-aretz* — I will plant them to Me in the land. The *gemara* reads: *adam zoreia se'ah ella le-hachnis kama korin* — one plants a small measure of grain in order to harvest many barrels. So too, the Jewish people are planted in the lands of exile in order to bring in a harvest many times larger. It is worth noting the irony: in its plain sense, the verse speaks of planting Israel back in the land of Israel as part of the ultimate redemption. The *gemara* reads it as the planting of Jewish communities in the lands of exile as seeds for that very redemption.

### Nations Converted

Rabbi Yochanan extends this further, citing the verse *ve-richamti et Lo Ruchama ve-amarti le-Lo Ami ammi atah*: the final words — *le-Lo Ami ammi atah* — are read not only as the restoration of Israel's relationship with God, but as God's declaration to those who were never part of the nation in the first place: *you too shall be my people*. This is the vision of *gerus* as inseparable from the purpose of *galut*.

---

## Commentary Authority (II)

### Scattering Kindness

Rabbi Oshia adds from the verse *tzidkat pirzono be-Yisrael* — rendering *pirzono* as *pizron*, scattering: *tzedakah asa Hakadosh Baruch Hu be-Yisrael she-pizran bein ha-umot* — God performed an act of righteousness and kindness for Israel by scattering them among the nations. This goes beyond the point about converts: the scattering itself, regardless of the missionary dimension, was an act of divine grace.

---

## Heretic Debate

### Heretic Boasts

A *min* — likely a Jewish Christian in this context — said to Rabbi Chanina: *anan mallei mineichu* — we are better than you. His evidence: the verse says that *David* sat in *Edom* for six months (*ki sheishet chodashim yashav sham*) and wiped out many of the *Edomim*. You, when you had power, used it to destroy. Whereas we — *itnechu gaban* — you have been living among us for many years, *ve-lo avdinan lachu midi* — and we have not done anything to you.

### Chanina Response

Rabbi Chanina replied: if you want, I will have a student respond to this on my behalf — treating the question as too elementary to require his personal attention. Rabbi Oshia then took the case and said: do you know why you have not eliminated us? *Mishum de-lo yadeitu heichi ta'avdu* — because you do not know how to do it. If you were to destroy all of us — *tahlinu kulhu* — we are not all concentrated among you. We are scattered. And if you want to destroy *ma de-ika gabaichu*, those of us who are among you — *kari lachu malchuta ktiasta* — you would be called a murderous kingdom. You hold back not from virtue, but from reputation.

### Scattered Safe

This ties back directly to Rabbi Oshia's earlier point about scattering as divine kindness: the very fact that Israel is scattered prevents their total annihilation. What from one angle looks like the vulnerability of exile is, from another, the guarantee of survival. The concentration of Jewish communities in any single location is itself the danger; the dispersion is the protection. The passage has obvious resonances that do not need to be made explicit.

---

## Why Babylon Exile

### Roman Cruelty Escape

Rabbi Chanina explains: *yodea Hakadosh Baruch Hu et Yisrael she-einam yecholim lekabel gezerot achzariyot* — God knows that Israel could not endure the cruel decrees of *Edom*, meaning Rome. Had Israel remained in the land under Roman rule, the persecution would have been unendurable. *Le-fikach higlam le-Vavel* — therefore He exiled them to *Bavel*, where the conditions were far more tolerable.

### Babylon Deep Sheol

Rabbi Elazar adds: *lo higla Hakadosh Baruch Hu et Yisrael le-Vavel ela mipnei she-amukah ke-sheol* — God exiled Israel to *Bavel* because it is as deep as *sheol*, the underworld. The verse says *mi-yad sheol efdem, mi-mavet eg'alem* — from the hand of *sheol* I will redeem them, from death I will save them. Rashi understands this to mean that God would redeem them more swiftly precisely because they were in such a depth. There is something of a playfulness here: God decreed that they be in *sheol* and then declared He would redeem them from *sheol* — the decree creates the very occasion for the redemption.

### Aramaic Affinity

Rabbi Chanina says: *mipnei she-karov leshonam li-leshon toratan* — because the Aramaic language of *Bavel* is close to the language of their Torah. If exile was inevitable, at least *Bavel* provided linguistic and cultural kinship that made the preservation of Torah possible. This does not explain why *Bavel* over *Eretz Yisrael*, but if a destination outside the land was to be chosen, *Bavel*'s linguistic proximity made it the fitting choice.

### Mother's House Return

Rabbi Yochanan says: *mipnei she-shigram le-veit imam* — they were being sent back to their mother's house, as Abraham originated from *Aram Naharaim*, which is *Bavel*. The connection to the *mashal* offered at the beginning of the *daf* is clear: *mashal le-adam she-ka'as al ishto, le-heich meshagrah, le-veit imah* — when a man is angry with his wife, where does he send her? To her mother's house. And so God, as it were, in His anger with Israel, sent them back to the ancestral home.

### Three Returns

Rabbi Alexandri adds: *sheloshah chazru le-mata'atan* — three things returned to their origin. *Yisrael* — the Jewish people, who returned to *Bavel*, the land of Abraham. *Kesef Mitzrayim* — the money of Egypt that Israel took at the Exodus: *va-yehi ba-shanah ha-chamishit le-melech Rechavam alah Shishak melech Mitzrayim al Yerushalayim* — in the fifth year of King *Rechavam*, *Shishak* king of Egypt came up to Jerusalem and looted it, taking back the wealth that had left Egypt centuries before. And *ketav ha-luchot* — the script of the tablets: *va-ashabrem le-eineichem* — I broke them before your eyes. The *tanna* teaches: *ha-luchot nishberu ve-ha-otiyot porchot* — the tablets were broken, but the letters flew back to God, returning to their divine source. They were never destroyed; they returned to where they came from.

# Pesachim 88

## Galus to Bavel

### Ulla: Dates & Torah

The daf opens at the bottom of 87b, picking up a remarkable stretch of *aggadata* concerning the reasons Israel was exiled specifically to Bavel. Several explanations had already been offered: to gather *gerim*, to return to a place of ancestral origin, and because Bavel was experienced as something like *sheol* — a descent into the depths. There was also the consideration that Bavel was simply more hospitable to Jews than remaining in Roman-controlled Eretz Yisrael. The Gemara now adds a final teaching on the matter: *Ulla amar kedei she-yochlu temarim ve-ya'asku ba-Torah* — Ulla said that Israel went to Bavel so that they could eat dates and engage in Torah. The point is that dates were extraordinarily plentiful and cheap in Bavel, making it remarkably easy to earn a livelihood. Rather than framing the exile solely in terms of fleeing persecution, Ulla reframes it positively: the material ease of Bavel freed people to devote themselves to Torah study.

### Ulla's Dates Story

The Gemara immediately follows with an anecdote that enriches and complicates this teaching. Ulla, who was himself from Eretz Yisrael, once visited Pumbedita. The locals brought him a large basket of dates. He asked the price and was told: three baskets for a *zuza* — extraordinarily cheap. His reaction was sharp: *mala tana de-duvsha be-zuza u-Vavlayei lo aski be-Oraisa* — a basket of honey for a *zuza*, and the Babylonians still can't manage to learn Torah? That night, having overindulged, he suffered a severe stomachache from all the dates. His tone shifted completely: *mala tana samma de-mosa be-zuza be-Bavel, Vavlayei aski be-Oraisa* — a basket of poison for a *zuza* here in Bavel, and yet they still manage to learn Torah! The reversal is not merely comic. What began as a critique of Babylonian scholars for failing to capitalize on their material ease becomes an admiring acknowledgment that they pursue Torah even amid conditions that are, in their own way, challenging.

### Comfort & Growth

The lesson here is one worth taking seriously in any era of material comfort. The assumption — Ulla's initial assumption — is that easy living ought to translate straightforwardly into greater Torah study. The reality is more complicated. Ease can breed complacency just as readily as it enables devotion. This is the same irony captured in the famous Chassidic story, attributed to the Berditchever Rebbe, in which a *Litvak* and a *Chassid* encounter a wagon-driver (*ba'al agala*) repairing his wheel, hands filthy with mud, all the while *davening*. The *Litvak* sees a man too distracted and dirty to be praying properly. The *Chassid* looks up and says: *Ribono Shel Olam*, your people — even in the mud, even in their difficulties — are still turning to You. The Babylonians, stomachache and all, are a version of that wagon-driver. The circumstances aren't ideal, but the commitment is genuine and perhaps all the more impressive for it.

## Beis HaMikdash

### Yaakov's House

The Gemara continues with a teaching of Rabbi Elazar, who asks about the verse in which the nations of the world declare: *ve-halchu amim rabim ve-amru lechu ve-na'aleh el har Hashem el beis Elokei Ya'akov* — many peoples will come and say, let us go up to the mountain of God, to the house of the God of Yaakov. The question is pointed: why specifically the God of Yaakov, and not Avraham or Yitzchak? Rabbi Elazar explains that the distinction tracks how each of the Patriarchs referred to the site of the *Beis HaMikdash*. By Avraham, the verse says *asher ye'amer hayom be-har Hashem yeira'eh* — he called it a *har*, a mountain. By Yitzchak, the verse says *vayeitzei Yitzchak lasu'ach ba-sadeh* — his encounter with the Divine was in a *sadeh*, a field. But Yaakov called it a *bayis*, a house: *vayikra shem ha-makom ha-hu Beis El*. It is Yaakov's terminology — *bayis* — that the nations invoke when they speak of the destination of their future pilgrimage.

### Kibbutz Galuyos

The Gemara adds a related teaching from Rabbi Yochanan: *gadol kibbutz galuyos ke-yom she-nivreu vo shamayim va-aretz* — the day of the ingathering of the exiles will be as great as the day on which heaven and earth were created; it is nothing less than a new creation. The source is the verse in Hoshea: *ve-nikbetzu bnei Yehuda u-vnei Yisrael yachdav... ki gadol yom Yizre'el*, and this is connected to *ve-yehi erev va-yehi voker yom echad* — the emphasis on *yom*, day, evoking the language of creation itself. This teaching brings to a satisfying close the discussion that had begun earlier with Hoshea, anchoring it in the imagery of a renewed world.

### Bayis vs. Mountain

The distinction between *har*, *sadeh*, and *bayis* is worth dwelling on, because it goes to the heart of what the *Beis HaMikdash* represents as a theological idea. Rashi explains *bayis* simply as *makom meyushav* — a settled, inhabited place — though this leaves the deeper significance somewhat underarticulated.

The theological paradox at stake is one that Shlomo HaMelech himself named explicitly at the Temple's dedication: *hinei ha-shamayim u-shmei ha-shamayim lo yechalchelucha v'af ki ha-bayis ha-zeh asher baniti* — even the heavens and the highest heavens cannot contain You, and yet here is this house I have built. How does one speak of a particular location for an infinite God? If God is everywhere, what is the meaning of a specific place of presence? And yet if God is everywhere in an undifferentiated way, it can become experientially equivalent to God being nowhere — too abstract, too vast to relate to. The proliferation of altars *al he-harim ha-gevohim v'al ha-gevaot v'tachat kol etz ra'anan* — on the high mountains and the hills and under every leafy tree — reflects one answer to that problem: you encounter the divine in nature, at particular striking locations. Avraham at the *har* and Yitzchak in the *sadeh* represent encounters of that kind, real and meaningful, but diffuse.

The *chiddush* of the *bayis* is different. The verse says *ve-asu li mikdash ve-shachanti b'tocham* — make Me a sanctuary and I will dwell among them. The *bayis* is not a natural landmark but a human construction, a space that people actively build. And there is something remarkable about that. Har Sinai, where the Divine presence was arguably felt most intensely in all of history, has no lasting *kedusha*. The site of the *Mikdash* does. The things human beings build and consecrate, the spaces they deliberately create and dedicate, those carry a *kedusha* that endures in a way that natural encounters do not. This is *Hashem amar lishkon ba-arafel* — God chose to concentrate His presence in a space that is in some sense opaque, bounded, constructed. That concentration, that focus, is not a limitation of God but a gift to human beings: one place toward which all prayers and energies and intentions converge, one location that makes the unity of God tangible and relatable. The very specificity of the *bayis*, which might at first seem to work against a universal theology, turns out to be what enables it.

## Pesach Membership

### Orphan & Guardians

The Gemara now pivots to more strictly *halachic* terrain, returning to the *Mishnah*. The case is that of an orphan whose two guardians (*apitropsin*) each slaughtered a *korban Pesach* on his behalf. The orphan may eat from whichever of the two he chooses. The Gemara initially raises the question of *yesh breirah* — whether his retroactive choice can determine which *korban* was slaughtered on his behalf. Rabbi Zeira resolves this by invoking the principle of *seh l'vayit* — a lamb per household. The Torah frames the *Pesach* obligation in terms of the household unit, *seh l'veit avot seh l'vayit*, and that objective membership in a household is what determines inclusion, not individual consent or advance designation. The orphan is objectively part of both households and therefore was legitimately included in each *Pesach*. His choice between them is not an act of retroactive *breirah* but a selection from among memberships that were always genuinely his.

### Consent Requirements

A *baraita* spells out the framework in detail. A man may slaughter the *Pesach* on behalf of his minor sons and daughters, and on behalf of his male and female Canaanite slaves (*avdo ve-shifchato ha-kena'anim*), *bein mida'atam bein shelo mida'atam* — whether with their knowledge or without. He may not, however, slaughter on behalf of his adult children, his Jewish slaves (*avdo ve-shifchato ha-ivrim*), or his wife, without their explicit buy-in. A second *baraita* makes the same point from the reverse direction, establishing the two categories clearly: those who have no independent voice in the matter — minor children and Canaanite slaves — and those who must actively consent.

### Household vs. Consent

The Gemara in *Nedarim* makes explicit what is implicit here: the principle of *zachin* — doing something for a person's benefit without their knowledge — does not apply to *korban Pesach* membership. One cannot simply enroll someone in a *chaburah* as a favor. Membership in the *Pesach* group requires conscious, active participation, with the one exception being the case of minor children and slaves, whose inclusion is governed not by the principle of *zachin* but by the Torah's own category of *seh l'vayit*. They belong to the household as an objective fact, not as a matter of consent.

The interplay here between the model of *bayis* and the model of *chaburah* is fundamental. The Torah frames the *Pesach* in terms of the household; the Sages developed the concept of *chaburah* — a fellowship group whose membership need not track biological or domestic relationships. But how much does the original idea of *bayis* continue to operate even within the framework of *chaburah*? For minor children and slaves, it operates entirely, overriding even explicit objection. *Tosafot* notes, with reference to a discussion in Bava Metzia concerning *metzia*, that even an adult child who is financially dependent on his father (*samuch al shulchan aviv*) retains full independence for purposes of *Pesach*: *gedolim peshita d'yesh beyadam limchot afilu semuchin al shulchan avihen*. Once a child has reached *Bar Mitzvah*, no degree of financial dependence reduces that person to the status of a minor here. The criterion of *shelo mida'ato* — without their knowledge — must therefore refer to actual minors, whose inability to object effectively is taken for granted.

### Knowledge Defined

The apparent contradiction within the *baraita* is carefully resolved by the Gemara. The *baraita* says that for the independent categories — the wife, adult children, and Jewish slaves — the husband or father may only slaughter *mida'atan*, with their knowledge. But the *baraita* also suggests that in a case where no objection is raised, the wife is assumed to be included with her husband. These two statements seem to be in tension: if *mida'atan* is required, how can the silent wife be presumed included?

The Gemara resolves this by explaining that *mida'atan* does not mean active verbal consent. It means the absence of explicit protest. In a *stam* case — where nothing has been said either way — the wife is assumed to consent, just as the opening *Mishnah* assumed that a wife would ordinarily want to celebrate *Yom Tov* with her husband rather than her parents. The requirement of *da'at* is real, but the *da'at* can be presumed from silence. What the requirement excludes is the case where she has actively indicated otherwise.

Rava then addresses the case where the wife herself has slaughtered her own *korban Pesach*: *kivan she-shachtu ein lecha michuy gadol mizeh* — the act of *shechitah* itself constitutes the clearest possible statement of independent intention. She need not verbally protest; her action speaks for itself. This resolves the apparent contradiction at the end of the *baraita*, which says that while minor children and slaves who slaughter their own *korban* are nonetheless subsumed under the master's or father's *Pesach*, the wife is not — because her *shechitah* is itself an act of *michuy*, of opting out.

The underlying picture that emerges is one with two fully distinct categories and perhaps a third. Minor children and Canaanite slaves have no independent standing; the household defines them completely, and even active protest cannot alter that. Adults — wives, adult children, Jewish slaves — do have independent standing, and their buy-in is genuinely required; but that buy-in can be presumed from silence, and only an affirmative act of opting out removes them from the household's *Pesach*. Whether this presumption for the wife and adult children means they occupy a conceptually intermediate category — more firmly attached to the *bayis* than a complete stranger, requiring less explicit buy-in than a friend or neighbor — remains an open question that the Gemara does not fully resolve.

## Two Partners' Slave

### Rami's Question

The Gemara presents a challenge from Rav Eina Saba to Rav Nachman. The *Mishnah* states that a slave owned jointly by two partners (*eved shel shnei shutfin*) cannot eat from either partner's *Pesach*. Yet a *baraita* teaches the opposite: *ratzah mizeh ochel ratzah mizeh ochel* — he may eat from whichever of the two he wishes. The contradiction seems direct.

### Kapdan Partners

Rav Nachman's resolution — introduced with the playful exchange *mini u-minach tistayem shmai'ta* — is that the two sources are addressing different circumstances. The *Mishnah* speaks of partners who are hostile to one another (*bid'kapdi ahadadei*): each partner refuses to allow the slave to derive benefit from the other, and since each can invoke his ownership to exclude the slave from the other's domain, the slave is caught with no valid option. The *baraita*, by contrast, speaks of partners who are on good terms (*d'lo kapdi ahadadei*): neither objects to the slave participating in the other's *Pesach*, so his membership in both households functions as it does for the orphan with two guardians, and he may choose freely between them. The *chiddush* when they are hostile is that the power of each partner to deny benefits flowing from his ownership effectively removes the slave from the other's household for these purposes.

## Half-Slave Status

### Shammai-Hillel

The *Mishnah* presents the case of the *mi she-chetzyo eved ve-chetzyo ben chorin* — the person who is half slave and half free. Such a person cannot eat from his master's *Pesach*, since the master may reasonably object to including the free half of this individual in his *chaburah*; and he cannot bring his own *Pesach*, since his master has not authorized the slave half of him to participate in an independent group. Beit Hillel's original position — *mishna rishona* — was a practical accommodation: the person works one day for his master and one day for himself, dividing his labor accordingly. Beit Shammai objected.

### Forced Freedom

Beit Shammai's argument is striking in its moral directness. *Tikantem et rabo ve-et atzmo lo tikantem* — you have provided a solution for the master but not for the person himself. The difficulty is fundamental: *lisha shifcha eino yachol she-kevar chetzyo ben chorin* — he cannot marry a maidservant because he is already half free; *lisha bat chorin eino yachol she-kevar chetzyo eved* — he cannot marry a free woman because he is still half a slave. He is caught in a liminal status that makes it impossible for him to fulfill *pirya ve-rivya*. And the world, the Torah insists, was not created for desolation: *lo tohu vera'ah lashevet yetzarah*. Therefore, Beit Shammai rules, *kofin et rabo ve-oseh oto ben chorin* — we compel the master who still holds half of this person in bondage to emancipate him, and the former slave assumes a financial debt for half his assessed value. His legal status remains, in some technical sense, transitional, but the master's practical control over him has ended. He is for all operative purposes a free man.

### Agunah Parallel

*Ve-chazru Beit Hillel le-horot ke-Beit Shammai* — Beit Hillel ultimately reversed course and accepted Beit Shammai's ruling. The case of the half-slave carries a direct and powerful resonance for the situation of the *agunah* — the woman trapped in a marriage she cannot exit, unable to remarry, suspended in a comparable limbo. If the Torah and *Chazal* were willing to override the master's property rights and compel manumission to ensure that a slave could fulfill his capacity for life and family, the argument for doing everything halachically possible to free a Jewish woman from her marital limbo is at least as compelling.

The Gemara also notes an interesting debate among the *Rishonim* arising from the specific language invoked here. Beit Shammai grounds the ruling not in the narrow *mitzvah* of *peru u-revu* but in the broader value of *lo tohu bera'ah lashevet yetzarah*. This raises the question of whether a *eved* is obligated in *peru u-revu* at all — the Gemara elsewhere suggests he has the *mitzvot* of a woman, and women are generally not obligated in *peru u-revu*. Some *Rishonim* argue that the resort to *lo tohu bera'ah* proves the slave lacks the *mitzvah* as such but is still subject to this overarching value of settling the world. Others argue the *mitzvah* is present but that invoking this larger value makes the case for compulsion more forceful than the *mitzvah* alone would. *Tosafot*, who align slaves and women in this regard, develop the further question of whether *lo tohu bera'ah* generates some form of obligation for women as well — a discussion that opens into substantial terrain and that the shiur sets aside for another time.

## Master's Pesach

### Unspecified Animal

The *Mishnah* turns to a master who instructs his slave to slaughter the *Pesach* for him without specifying which animal. If the slave slaughters a goat (*gedi*), the master eats it — even if he is known to prefer lamb. If the slave slaughters a lamb (*taleh*), the master eats it — even if he is known to prefer goat. The *chiddush*, made explicit by the Gemara, is that since the master gave no specification, his personal preferences are simply irrelevant: *af al gav deragil betleh* and *af al gav deragil begdi* — regardless of habitual preference, the unspecified instruction gives the slave full discretion.

### Two Animals

If the slave, uncertain which animal the master wanted, slaughtered both, the master eats from the first one slaughtered (*yochal min ha-rishon*). The Gemara initially questions this: given the rule that one cannot be registered as a member of two *Pesachs* simultaneously (*ein nimnin al shnei pesachim k'echad*), how does it follow that one simply eats the first? *Tosafot* clarifies the issue: it is not merely that two *Pesachs* were slaughtered, but that there is a question about the relationship between the order of designation and the order of *shechita*. The resolution — as the Gemara indicates — is that the *Mishnah* refers to a king and queen, or people in a comparable position, and the ruling flows from their particular circumstances, as will become clear below.

### Stipulation Solution

If the slave forgot entirely what his master had specified, the Gemara teaches that he should slaughter both animals but make a careful stipulation: *im gedi amar li rabbi, gedi shelo ve-taleh sheli; ve-im taleh amar li rabbi, ha-taleh shelo ve-gedi sheli* — if my master told me a goat, then the goat is his and the lamb is mine; if he told me a lamb, then the lamb is his and the goat is mine. With this stipulation, both animals are valid *korbanot*; the only remaining uncertainty is which belongs to whom. The master is then consulted, and the question is resolved.

The Gemara raises an obvious difficulty: *mah she-kanah eved kanah rabbo* — whatever a slave acquires belongs to his master. How can the slave claim that one of the animals is *his* for these purposes? Abaye's resolution is ingenious: the slave should go to a shepherd who regularly does business with the master, one who has an interest in everything working out well (*ve-neicha lei be-takkanta de-rabbeh*). That shepherd gives the slave one of the animals *al menat she-ein le-rabbo reshut bo* — on the explicit stipulation that the master has no ownership claim over it. And this, the Gemara allows, is halachically effective: under ordinary circumstances, property given to a slave passes automatically to the master; but if the giver explicitly stipulates that the master shall have no claim, the property can remain with the slave. The independent ownership is thus created through the explicit *tenai* of the shepherd.

### Both Forgot

Finally, if both master and slave have forgotten what was specified, both *korbanot* are nonetheless valid, and both master and slave are exempt from *Pesach Sheni* — because when each animal was slaughtered and its blood thrown, it was fit to be eaten. The failure to actually eat the meat does not retroactively invalidate the *korban*. What matters is the fitness for eating at the time the *korban* was brought.

## King & Queen

### Royal Question

The Gemara now tells the story underlying the *Mishnah*'s ruling about two animals slaughtered without specification. A king and queen instructed their servants to slaughter the *Pesach* for them. The servants slaughtered two — one a lamb, one a goat — and came to ask which was which and how to proceed. The king deferred to the queen, whose knowledge of *halacha* was clearly superior. The queen in turn directed them to Rabban Gamliel.

### Don't Care Logic

Rabban Gamliel's ruling turned on a single observation about the king and queen: *kalla aleihem* — they simply do not care. People of their station have access to every type of delicacy; whether tonight's *Pesach* is lamb or goat is a matter of complete indifference to them. Since they have no preference, there is no unresolved question of designation to worry about. *Yokhlu min ha-rishon* — they eat from whichever was slaughtered first. For ordinary people, by contrast, who do have preferences and who would have had something specific in mind when they issued the instruction, neither animal can be definitively identified as the intended one, and so they would be unable to eat from either. The *Mishnah*'s ruling that one eats *min ha-rishon* thus applies specifically to cases — like the king and queen — where the owner is genuinely indifferent to which animal is used.

### Lizard Story

A second anecdote follows. On another occasion, a lizard (*lita'ah*) was found in the royal kitchen. The king and queen apparently ate their non-sacred food in a state of *tahara* (*chulin be-tahara*), and so there was concern that the discovery of a potentially dead reptile — a source of *tumah* — would render the entire meal impure. Again the king deferred to the queen, and the queen to Rabban Gamliel. Rabban Gamliel asked whether the kitchen was hot or cold. The servants said hot. He instructed them to throw a cup of cold water on the lizard. They did, and it began to thrash — it was not dead, merely prostrated by the heat. Rabban Gamliel declared the entire meal pure.

### Dependency Chain

The Gemara closes the episode with a wry observation: *nimtza melech talui be-malka, ve-nimtza malka teluyah be-Rabban Gamliel, nimtza kol ha-se'udah teluyah be-Rabban Gamliel* — the king turned out to depend on the queen, and the queen on Rabban Gamliel, so the whole meal depended on Rabban Gamliel. The surface meaning is literal — the *halakhic* validity of the meal was determined by Rabban Gamliel's ruling at each turn — but the deeper point is clear: the entire world, kings and queens included, depends ultimately on the *talmidei chakhamim* and their mastery of Torah.

The episode also touches, in passing, on the phrase *nashim da'atan kallah*. Here the term is clearly not pejorative. The king and queen are described as *kalla aleihem* in the sense that food preferences are simply not weighty matters to them — they have everything they could want. If the expression *nashim da'atan kallah* carries that same valence in other contexts, it would mean not that women reason poorly but that they do not treat certain things as weighty decisions requiring careful deliberation — a reading that is quite different from the more negative sense the phrase sometimes bears.

## Before Zerika

### Abaye's Rule

The Gemara now presents a teaching of Abaye that sharply qualifies the ruling about the slave who forgot what his master said. The *Mishnah* states that in a case where both master and slave have forgotten, they are both *yotzei* and exempt from *Pesach Sheni*. Abaye specifies: *lo shanu ela she-shachach achar zerika* — this applies only if the forgetting occurred after the *zrikas ha-dam*, the throwing of the blood on the altar. If neither master nor slave knows whose animal is whose at that point, the *korban* is nonetheless valid because at the decisive moment of *zerika* each animal was fit to be eaten.

### Fitness at Zerika

But *aval shachach lifnei zerika* — if the forgetting occurred before the blood-throwing — neither party knows at the critical moment of *zerika* whose animal is designated for whom. *De-chi izreik dam lo havi chazi la-achila* — when the blood was thrown, the animal was not genuinely fit to be eaten, because no one could identify it as their own. In that case, *chayavin la-asot Pesach Sheni* — they are obligated to bring a *Pesach Sheni*, since the first *Pesach* was never fully valid as a *korban* that was *rauy la-achila* at the time of *zerika*.

## Mixed Skins

### Blemish Found

The *baraita* presents a parallel case that draws on the same logic. Five people's Pesach skins (*oros*) became intermingled. Upon examination, a blemish (*mum*, specifically a *yabelet*, a wart) was found on one of the skins. Since a *Pesach* with a *mum* is invalid, one of the five *korbanot* was invalid — but no one can determine which one. All five skins are sent out to be burned, and the Gemara rules: *kulan yetzu le-veit ha-sereifa u-pturim mi-la'asot Pesach Sheni* — all are burned, and all five are exempt from *Pesach Sheni*.

### Impossible Identity

The claim that all five are exempt is immediately counterintuitive: four were surely valid, and four are therefore certainly exempt. But one person brought an invalid *korban Pesach* and should, in principle, be obligated in *Pesach Sheni*. Abaye's parallel teaching applies here: *lo shanu ela she-nisarvu achar zerika* — the exemption holds only if the skins became mixed up after *zerika*. At the moment of *zerika*, each animal's identity was known, and each of the four valid animals was *chazi la-achila*. The subsequent confusion does not retroactively undermine the validity of the *zerika*. But *aval nisarvu lifnei zerika* — if the mixing up occurred before the blood-throwing — then at the moment of *zerika* it was impossible to know which animal was the valid one, and therefore none of them was genuinely *chazi la-achila* in a meaningful sense. In that case, *chayav la-asot Pesach Sheni*.

### Stipulation Attempts

The Gemara then acknowledges the obvious problem: the ruling that all five are *patur* from *Pesach Sheni* is practically convenient but conceptually uncomfortable — one person among the five is in fact obligated. *Mishum de-lo efshar* — but there is simply no way to remedy the situation. The Gemara explores and rejects several potential solutions.

If all five were to bring a *Pesach Sheni*, four of them would be bringing *chulin la-azara* — non-sacred animals into the Temple courtyard — since four of the five are not actually obligated. If all five were to join together as a single *chaburah* for one *Pesach Sheni*, the *Pesach* would be eaten by four people who are not registered members of that sacrifice — *pesach ne'echal shelo li-menuav*.

A more creative solution is proposed: let each person bring his own animal on *Pesach Sheni* and make a stipulation — *i didi hava ba'al mum, hai de-aiti hashta lihavei pesach; i didi tam hava, hai de-aiti hashta lihavei shelamim* — if mine was the blemished one, let this animal I am now bringing serve as my *Pesach*; if mine was unblemished, let it be a *shelamim*. This elegant stipulation would allow each person to cover both possibilities without definitively committing to either. However, the Gemara rejects this as well: *mishum de-ika chaze ve-shok de-kohanim de-achli lei* — if the animal turns out to be a *shelamim*, the *kohen* must receive the *chaze* and *shok*, the breast and the thigh, which are not part of the *Pesach* protocol. And if all five eat it as a *Pesach Sheni*, then for four of them it is *Pesach shelo li-menuav*, being eaten outside one's registered group. The Gemara closes with the difficulty unresolved, noting that the discussion will continue.

# Pesachim 89

## Mixed-Up Pesachim

### Five Pesachim w/ Mum

The *gemara* opens with a *baraita* describing a case in which five different groups each brought a separate *korban Pesach*, and afterward the skins became mixed up. One of the animals was found to bear a *mum* (blemish), but it is unknown whose it was. The *gemara* modifies the scenario: the discovery occurred after the blood had already been thrown, meaning that at the time of *zerika* all five were presumptively valid. Since no one can identify which animal was blemished, all five carcasses must be burned — and, critically, none of the five groups knows whether they are the one obligated in a *Pesach Sheni*, so the *gemara* initially suggests that no one brings a *Pesach Sheni*. The *gemara* immediately objects: clearly one of the five *is* obligated. The problem is identifying who.

### Individual Pesach Sheni

The *gemara's* first proposed solution is to have each of the five bring his own *Pesach Sheni* with a *tenai* (stipulation): if my original offering was the blemished one, let this be my *Pesach Sheni*; if not, let it be a *shelamim*. The *gemara* objects: if it is a *shelamim*, the *kohen* must receive the *chazeh v'shok* (the breast and the side). So, one might suggest, simply give those portions to the *kohen* as a precaution — perhaps it is a *Pesach* and perhaps it is a *shelamim*, so cover both possibilities. But this fails: if the animal is in fact a *Pesach*, then the *kohen* who eats from it must be a registered member of that group — and eating the *chazeh v'shok* of a *Pesach* one is not enrolled in is forbidden. There is no clean way to handle the *chazeh v'shok*, and so this approach collapses.

### Priest Covers All

The *gemara* advances a second solution: *veneyti kol chad vechad kohen bahadeih* — let each of the five bring along a *kohen* to be a member of his group. Then the *kohen* would be entitled to the *chazeh v'shok* should it turn out to be a *shelamim*. But the *gemara* asks: what kind of *kohen* are we talking about? If he already brought his own *Pesach Rishon*, then he is not obligated in a *Pesach Sheni*, and if the animal being brought now is in fact a *Pesach Sheni*, then this *kohen* is eating from a *Pesach* to which he does not belong — *venimtza Pesach ne'echal shelo limnuyav*. If, on the other hand, this *kohen* did *not* bring a *Pesach Rishon* and is himself obligated in a *Pesach Sheni*, then the reverse problem arises: if the animal turns out to be a *shelamim* and not a *Pesach Sheni*, the *kohen* has failed to be *yotzei* his own *Pesach Sheni* obligation.

The *gemara* then proposes a refinement: *veneyti kol chamisha chad kohen* — let all five groups together bring in a single *kohen* who did not bring a *Pesach Rishon* and is thus obligated in a *Pesach Sheni*. This *kohen* conditionally registers with each of the five groups separately: if you are the one obligated in *Pesach Sheni*, I am part of your group; and likewise for each of the others. *Demia nafshach* — either way it works out. Exactly one of the five animals is a genuine *Pesach Sheni*, and from that one this *kohen* fulfills his own obligation. The remaining four are *shelamim*, and from those he receives the *chazeh v'shok* of a *shelamim*, to which he is fully entitled. He does not need to know which is which; the halakhic reality sorts itself out.

### Sanctify as Pesach

The *gemara* then raises a new difficulty: *ella mishum de'ka mema'et be'achilat shelamim* — even with the *kohen* solution in place, each owner is still bringing an animal designated either as a *Pesach Sheni* or, conditionally, as a *shelamim*. A *Pesach* must be eaten by daybreak of the fifteenth of Nissan, whereas a *shelamim* may be eaten through two days and one night. Since the owner must treat the animal as if it might be a *Pesach*, he is constrained to finish it by daybreak — thereby squandering the additional eating time that would have been available had it been a *shelamim*. *D'ilu Pesach l'yom valailah, v'ilu shelamim lishnei yamim valailah echad*: the time-frames are incompatible, and by treating it as a *Pesach* one potentially causes the meat of what is really a *shelamim* to become *notar*.

### Motar Pesach Money

The *gemara* proposes a solution: designate the animal not as an ordinary *shelamim* but as a *shelamim* arising from *motar Pesach* — leftover sanctified *Pesach* funds or animals. A *motar Pesach* brought as a *shelamim* is eaten only for a day and a night (not the full two days), matching the constraint already imposed by the *Pesach* possibility. Each person could declare: if my original offering was blemished, this is my *Pesach Sheni*; if not, let this be a *shelamim* that derives from *motar Pesach*.

According to Rashi, the *gemara* rejects this on the grounds that one cannot *initially* sanctify something as *motar* — leftovers, by definition, can only arise organically, not by stipulation. Tosafot, however, reads the *gemara* differently. No one would have thought to sanctify something explicitly as *motar*; rather, Tosafot understands the *gemara* to be proposing that one simply sanctify the animal as a *Pesach Sheni* outright, without any backup designation. If it then turns out that the person was already *yotzei* in Nissan and does not need a *Pesach Sheni*, the animal automatically acquires the status of *motar Pesach* — no stipulation required; that is simply the halakhic reality.

The *gemara*'s response to Tosafot's reading is that while this would technically work *bedi'avad*, it is problematic *lechatchila*: one should not sanctify an animal knowing it may end up as an unwanted *motar*. It would be preferable to stipulate the backup designation explicitly as a *shelamim*, even though that reintroduces the time-limitation problem.

### Semicha by Women

Leaving the time problem aside, the *gemara* identifies yet another obstacle: *ella mishum semikhah*. A *shelamim* requires *semicha* — the owner rests his hands on the offering — whereas a *Pesach* does not. If the animal is a *Pesach* and one performs *semicha*, he is pressing his weight on a *korban* without cause, which is a rabbinic concern. If the animal is a *shelamim* and one omits *semicha*, the obligation is unfulfilled.

The *gemara* notes that this problem is solvable — *hatanach anashim* — if the five individuals are women: women are not required to perform *semicha* on their *shelamim*. If the animal is a *Pesach*, no *semicha* is needed. If it is a *shelamim* of a woman, *semicha* is also not required. So for women's offerings this particular obstacle falls away.

### Dam Shfika Problem

Even with women's offerings, the *gemara* raises a further complication concerning the blood: *ella mishum matanot*. A *Pesach* requires only a single application of blood (*matanah achat*) on the *mizbeach*, whereas a *shelamim* requires two applications on diagonal corners, which together touch all four sides (*shtayim she'hein arba*). The *gemara* asks whether this matters: after all, the *Mishnah* teaches that *bedi'avad*, if any offering whose blood requires multiple applications had only one application made, it is still valid. So perform a single application and be covered in either case.

The *gemara* then raises a more fundamental distinction: *ella mishum de'ilu Pesach bishfika* — for a *Pesach* the blood is *poured* against the wall (*shefikh*), while for a *shelamim* it is *thrown* (*zerika*). Again the *gemara* notes that a *baraita* rules *bedi'avad* that anything meant to be thrown but instead poured is valid. But here the *gemara* draws the line: *aymur de'amrinan* — all of these *bedi'avad* leniencies apply only after the fact, *ee avad*, if one has already acted in such a manner. They cannot justify acting improperly *lechatchila*.

### Tosafot Objection

This brings us to the objection raised by Tosafot, which cuts to the heart of the entire discussion. Tosafot asks the obvious question: each of the concerns raised — limiting the time for *shelamim*, the *semicha* issue, the improper blood application — is relatively minor. Against these stands the possibility that one of the five individuals will fail to bring a *Pesach Sheni* that he is genuinely obligated in, risking *safek karet*. How can the *gemara* refuse all proposed solutions on *lechatchila* grounds when the alternative is *safek karet*?

Tosafot answers: *tov sheyidache safek karet beshev ve'al ta'aseh mimah she'ya'asu ruban shelo kehogen* — it is preferable to allow the possibility of *safek karet* through passive inaction than to require four out of five people to perform their *korbanot* improperly in order to protect the one. Invoking the principle of *omrim le'adam chet kedei she'yizkeh chaveirecha* — we do not tell one person to sin so that another may be acquitted — the *gemara* concludes that since the person in this predicament is in any case an *oneis*, we trust that he will be forgiven. At the very least, Tosafot is right to flag this as the obvious and pressing question underlying the entire passage.

---

## Father's Stipulation

### Who Gets There First

The *Mishnah* presents a case in which a father declares: *hareini shocheit et hapesach al mi she'ya'aleh mikem rishon l'Yerushalayim* — "I am slaughtering the *Pesach* for whichever of you arrives in Jerusalem first." He slaughters it, and the definition of "arriving first" is *rosho ve'rubo* — the majority of the body having crossed the threshold, analogous to the principle of *rosho ve'rubo basukka*. Whoever first achieved *rosho ve'rubo* inside Jerusalem retroactively satisfies the condition and is considered the one enrolled in the *korban*. Moreover, the *Mishnah* adds, *zachah be'chelko u'mezakeh et echav imo* — the first son who "wins" can then bring his brothers to join in with his portion.

### Incentive, Not Breira

The *gemara* immediately notes that this *Mishnah* appears to rely on *breira* — the principle of retroactive determination — which has been contested throughout these chapters. *Rabbi Yochanan* resolves this: *kedei lezarezan be'mitzvot kamar* — the father did not genuinely mean to create a legal stipulation. His declaration was purely motivational, intended to make his children eager and enthusiastic in the performance of *mitzvot*. In reality, the father had all his children in mind from the moment of *shechita*, so there is no actual *breira* involved.

The *gemara* finds support for this reading from within the *Mishnah* itself: *dika nami dektani u'mezakeh et echav imo*. If the father truly intended only the first-arriving son to be enrolled, there would be no mechanism by which that son could afterward bring his brothers into the group. As the very next *Mishnah* teaches, one can join or withdraw only until the moment of *shechita* — and once it is slaughtered, no new enrollments are possible. The fact that the brothers can join afterward proves that they were always implicitly included, and the father's statement was never a real condition.

The *Mishnah* is thus teaching us how to interpret this type of parental declaration as a matter of *halakha*: given the assumption that family members are considered included in the *Pesach* unless they actively object, the father's words are read as encouragement rather than exclusion.

### Daughters vs. Sons

A *baraita* is cited: *maase ve'kadmu banot le'vanim* — there was an incident in which daughters arrived in Jerusalem before the sons, so that *nimtzu banot zerizot u'vanim shefalim* — the daughters turned out to be the zealous ones and the sons the sluggards. Tellingly, the *baraita* does not say *nimtzu banot ochlot u'vanim einam ochlim* — it does not say the daughters ate and the sons did not. The only consequence noted is a matter of honor and zeal, which confirms that the father's stipulation was never meant as a binding legal condition determining who eats. It was entirely a device to spur eagerness in the performance of the *mitzvah*.

---

## Membership Changes

### Kezayit Minimum

The *Mishnah* teaches that one may continue adding members to a *chavura* for a *Pesach* as long as each member retains at least a *kezayit*-sized portion. There is no upper limit on the number of members, only this lower bound: *leolam nimnin alav ad sheyesh bo kezayit le'chol echad ve'echad*.

### Rav Shimon View

The *Mishnah* further states that members may join or withdraw until the moment of *shechita*. Rabbi Shimon goes further: *ad sheyizarek hadam* — withdrawal is permitted even after *shechita*, up until the blood is thrown on the *mizbeach*. This is a surprising position, as we will see qualified by the *gemara*.

### Replace Whole Group

The *gemara* asks what the *chiddush* of the *Mishnah* is. The answer: *de'af al gav de'mimnu alav chavura zu, chozer ve'nimnin alav chavura acheret* — even if one complete *chavura* had already registered for this *Pesach*, the entire group may be replaced by a new *chavura* before *shechita*. There is an opinion that at least one original member must remain, and it is this opinion that the *Mishnah* comes to exclude: complete replacement is permitted prior to *shechita*.

### Join/Withdraw Timeline

Abaye clarifies the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon: the disagreement concerns *withdrawal* only. The Rabbis derive from the verse *ve'im yim'at ha'bayit mehiyot miseh* that the *bayit* (i.e., *chavura*) may be reduced *michiyotei de'seh* — while the animal is still alive, i.e., before *shechita*. Rabbi Shimon reads *mehivaya de'seh* — until the animal has completed its process of being sacrificed, i.e., until the blood is thrown.

On joining, however, all agree: *nimnin ad shechita* — enrollment must occur before *shechita*. Rabbi Shimon does not extend his leniency to new enrollments after *shechita*, because the verse *bemichsas nefashot tachosu* — "according to the number of souls, slaughter" — is read as requiring that the count of members be established before the act of *shechita*. A member must be enrolled from the beginning of the sacrificial process; withdrawing, says Rabbi Shimon, remains possible until *zerika* since the *korban* is not yet complete until the blood has been thrown. This is confirmed by a *baraita* that states explicitly: *nimnin ad sheyishachat, u'moshchin ad sheyizarek hadam*.

---

## Uninvited Guest

### Solo Invitation

The *Mishnah* presents the case of *ha'memaneh imo acher be'chelko*: a member of a *chavura* goes ahead and invites someone to join the group without consulting his fellow members.

### Separate Portions

The *Mishnah* rules: *reshayim bnei chavura litein lo et shelo ve'hu ochel et shelo ve'hein ochlim et shelahem* — the other members of the *chavura* may give the inviting member his portion and have him eat it with his guest separately, while they eat their shares among themselves. As Rashi emphasizes, the language of *ve'hu ochel et shelo* implies a genuine physical separation into two distinct *chaburot*, not merely a portioning out while remaining at the same table. The one who issued the unauthorized invitation takes his share and the two of them form their own group, while the original members eat as their own group.

### Glutton Problem

The *gemara* then raises a question: *bnei chavura she'hayu yedeihem shel echad mehen yafot* — what if after joining together, one member turns out to eat disproportionately more than the others? The idiom is that his "hands are nice" — a polite way of saying he grabs and eats at an aggressive pace. May the group tell him *tol chelkecha u'tzei* — take your portion and leave?

Two positions are considered. One: the glutton may argue *ki kibbaltuhu* — you accepted me as a member of this group and the communal arrangement stands, you cannot now expel me. Two: the group may counter *ki kablinan le'tikkunei zevach* — we accepted you for the purpose of the *korban*, meaning to ensure that the meat would be consumed appropriately; we did not accept you on the assumption that you would eat disproportionately.

The *gemara* attempts to prove from the earlier case of the unauthorized invitation that the group can expel a disproportionate eater, reasoning that the case of the invited outsider is analogous to a person with a huge appetite. The *gemara* deflects this comparison: *deshani* — two people (the inviting member and his uninvited guest) are different from one overeater. Even if the two combined eat no more than a single normal portion, the group's right to expel them has nothing to do with quantity. *Matzi amri lei de'lo nicha lan inish de'garuch gaban* — they can simply say we do not want a stranger at our table; *kol de'chazina leh u'merachamana leh yativ ve'yeichol* — only someone we know and like is welcome to sit and eat with us. The case of the uninvited guest thus rests entirely on the social intimacy of the *chavura*, not on the financial concern of disproportionate eating. Whether the purely financial argument — the glutton eating more than his share — is itself grounds for expulsion remains the open question that the *gemara* proceeds to resolve.

---

## Shamash by Oven

### Shamash Eats First

The *gemara* introduces the case of the *shamash* (attendant) who was roasting the *Pesach* by the oven and inadvertently — or by taking a small taste — ate a *kezayit* of meat right there, *betzad tanur*. Having now eaten in that location, he cannot join the group in the other room to eat the *Pesach*, since the *Pesach* may not be eaten in two locations. *Im haya pikeach, memalei kreiso mimenu* — if he is smart, he should fill his stomach right there by the oven, since he cannot move to join the group in any case.

### Group Follows or Stays

Rabbi Yehuda teaches: *ve'im ratzu bnei chavurah la'asos tovah imo, bo'in ve'yoshvin betzido ve'ochlin* — if the members of the group wish to be kind to the *shamash*, they may come and sit beside him at the oven and eat there. *Lo ratzu, lo* — if they do not wish to do so, they are under no obligation; they are entitled to remain in the other room.

### Can't Force Shamash

The *gemara* asks: why can the *shamash* not demand that the group come to him? After all, the principle established earlier was that a member who accepted others into his group cannot then claim they are stuck with him — yet symmetrically, shouldn't the group be stuck with the *shamash* since they accepted him? The *gemara* answers: *shani hasam de'amri lei* — it is different here, because the group can say to the *shamash*: under what terms did we accept you? *Adaata de'nishdrach kaman* — we accepted you with the understanding that you would come to serve us, that you would attend upon us. *Limtrach lan u'ledidach lo kablinach* — we did not accept you on the understanding that we would have to be dragged after you. The *shamash*, by wandering off and eating by himself, broke the implicit terms of his membership; the group cannot be compelled to follow him.

---

## Communal Eating

### Baraita: Glutton Kicked…

A *baraita* now addresses both the *Pesach* case and an analogous case of communal eating. *Bnei chavurah she'yadav shel echad mehen yafot, reshayim lomar lo: tol chelkecha bekatzei* — the members of the group may tell a disproportionate eater to take his portion and leave.

Beyond the *Pesach* case, the *baraita* continues: *afilu chamisha she'asu sibolot* — even five people who organized a communal meal arrangement (like a rotating food cooperative, in which each member takes a turn providing the meal for all), and one of them turns out to eat far more than his share, *reshayim lomar lo: tol chelkecha u'tzei* — they may give him his portion and remove him from the arrangement. This seems to suggest that a disproportionate eater can be expelled from any communal eating arrangement, not only a *korban Pesach*.

### Real Question: Divide?

The *gemara* reframes the underlying question. According to one version of the discussion, it was never unclear whether a group could expel a disproportionate eater — that was always obvious. The real question is: *bnei chavurah reshayim lachalok o einam reshayim lachalok?* — may the members of a *chavura* simply *choose* to divide up their portions and eat separately, even absent any complaint of disproportionate eating? In other words, may they abandon the communal eating arrangement arbitrarily, without cause?

This question has a social and a financial dimension. The social dimension is whether the communal experience itself is obligatory.
