The financial dimension — as Rashi and later codes understand it — is whether members may reorganize into separate groups, since communal eating means sharing from a common source while separate eating means dividing the animal and potentially forming distinct *chaburot*. If one member eats more slowly than others, the communal arrangement disadvantages him; but if each gets a fixed portion, that risk is eliminated. The question is whether such a division is permitted.

### Proof: Only If Unequal

The *gemara* resolves this from the *baraita* itself: *yadav yafot — ein, ein yadav yafot — lo*. The *baraita* specifies that one may only remove a member — or, by extension, break up the communal arrangement — when there is disproportionate eating. Without such justification, the members may not unilaterally divide. *Shma mina* — this is the ruling. The default expectation is communal eating, and a member cannot demand separation without cause. This principle is codified in the *Rambam* and *Shulchan Aruch* for both *Pesach* and other communal eating contexts.

---

## Papa & Huna Story

### Papa Gobbles Four

The *gemara* brings a vivid illustrative story. Rav Papa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua *arivu rifta bahadi hadadei* — they pooled together for a meal, joining their food or contributions equally. While Rav Huna ate one portion, Rav Papa ate four.

### Huna Wants Out

Rav Huna demanded *palgi* — give me my separate portion; he no longer wished to eat communally. He proceeded to cite multiple proofs that a member is entitled to his portion and may eat separately when the arrangement becomes inequitable.

### Papa Refuses

Rav Papa responded *kavietun* — you accepted me as part of this group, invoking the same language used in the *Mishnah* and *baraita*. For each proof Rav Huna cited, Rav Papa gave a distinguishing answer: the case of the *shamash* is different because he withdrew from the group himself; the case of the *Pesach* is different because there the acceptance was *le'tikkunei zevach* — for the purposes of the offering — not a fundamentally social arrangement. When Rav Huna finally cited the *baraita* about *sibolot* — communal eating arrangements — which explicitly allows removal of a disproportionate eater from a social meal, Rav Papa conceded, and they divided their portions.

### Ravina Even Worse

Rav Huna then took his portion and *arav behadi Ravina* — joined together with Ravina for a meal. This time, while Rav Huna ate one portion, Ravina ate eight. Rav Huna exclaimed: *me'ah Papei ve'lo chada Ravina* — I would rather have a hundred Rav Papas than one Ravina.

---

## Pesach vs. Other Offerin…

### Pesach: Join Allowed

A *baraita* juxtaposes the rules governing new membership in a *Pesach* against those governing other *korbanot*. *Ha'memaneh acherim imo al Pesacho* — if one invites others to join in his *Pesach*, even after the animal has been sanctified, *ma'ot she'beyado chulin* — the money he receives from the new members becomes *chulin*. The new member gains a portion in the sanctified *korban*, and the money changes hands in a way that somehow transitions out of *kedushah*. The *gemara* will explain the mechanics of this further, but the practical result is that joining a *Pesach* even post-sanctification is possible and the financial arrangement is workable.

### Olah: No Transfer

By contrast, *ha'mocher olato ve'shalmav* — one who attempts to sell or transfer ownership in a sanctified *olah* or *shelamim* — *lo asah ve'lo klum*: the transaction is entirely void. Ownership of a *korban* that has already been sanctified cannot be transferred. Furthermore, the money given by the would-be purchaser — rather than becoming *chulin* as in the *Pesach* case — *yiplu le'nedavah*: it must go toward a communal donation for the *Beit HaMikdash*, since it was given in the context of *kedushah* and cannot simply revert to ordinary status. The *baraita* thus establishes a sharp contrast: the *Pesach* uniquely permits post-sanctification enrollment with the financial consideration becoming *chulin*, whereas *olah* and *shelamim* permit no transfer at all and any money involved must go toward a *nedavah*. The *gemara* will continue tomorrow to explain the conceptual underpinning of this distinction.

---

---

# Pesachim 95

## Pesach Rishon/Sheni

### Tammei/Rechoka Ptur

Before turning to the Gemara proper, it is worth addressing the Rambam's reading of the Mishnah that opened the previous discussion — a reading followed by virtually all the *meforshei hamishna* and which stands, remarkably, against the Gemara's own interpretation.

The Mishnah had asked: what is the difference between *tamei* and *derech rechoka* on one hand, and a case of *shogeg* or *mezid* on the other? Why did the Torah need to specify *tamei* and *derech rechoka* at all? The Mishnah concludes: *she-elu paturim mi-karet ve-elu chayavim be-hikaret* — these are exempt from *karet* and those are liable. The Gemara understood *elu chayavim* as referring to the *mezid*, but this is a strange reading since *mezid* was not the subject of the Mishnah's question.

The Rambam reads the Mishnah according to its plain sense — *peshat* — and his interpretation yields a fundamental conceptual distinction. A person who failed to bring *Pesach Rishon* because he was *tamei* or because he was on a *derech rechoka* falls into a category of *ptur* altogether. For such a person, the obligation of *Pesach Sheni* is an opportunity, not an atonement; even if he ultimately fails to bring *Pesach Sheni*, he is not *chayav karet* — his original exemption stands. By contrast, a person who missed *Pesach Rishon* for any other reason — *shogeg*, *mezid*, or *ones* of a different kind — requires *Pesach Sheni* to discharge his obligation. If he fails to bring *Pesach Sheni*, he is indeed *chayav karet*.

This is a major conceptual distinction in the nature of the *ptur*: for *tamei* and *derech rechoka*, the exemption is categorical; for all others, *Pesach Sheni* is essential for avoiding *karet*.

### Tikkun/Tashlumin

This reading connects, to some degree, to the Gemara's broader discussion of *tikkun* and *tashlumin*, though the Gemara's discussion of those concepts did not present a case in which someone was *mezid* on *Pesach Sheni* itself. Nonetheless, the conceptual relation is clear: where others understand *Pesach Sheni* as a *tashlumin* — a make-up — the Rambam's *chiddush* is that for the categories of *tamei* and *derech rechoka*, the person is in a state of total *ptur*, rendering *Pesach Sheni* fundamentally different in character. Strikingly, on this point all the major *meforshim* — the Bartenura and the others — follow the Rambam against the Gemara's own reading of the Mishnah.

---

## Cosmology & Mil

### Chazal Science

The Gemara on this *daf* contains a discussion of the *rakia*, the sun's path, and the nature of the cosmological dome — a topic of considerable importance for both historical and *halachic* reasons. The basic picture assumed by Chazal is that the *rakia* is an opaque dome, that the sun travels through its thickness from *alos hashachar* to *hanetz* and again from *shkia* to *tzeis*, which is why there is dim light escaping through the thickness of the dome during those transitional periods. According to Chazal's view, the sun then travels above the dome overnight, while *chachmei umot ha-olam* maintained that it travels below.

The Gemara records the striking statement: *amar Rebbe, nitzchu divreihem mi-divreinu* — Rabbi acknowledged that the position of the non-Jewish sages had prevailed over that of the Jewish sages. This is an important source for the Rambam's broader position that Chazal were not scientists and should not be treated as authorities in scientific matters, such that errors in their science or medicine are not theologically problematic.

There are those who find this threatening to the authority of Chazal and resist the conclusion. Rabbi Akiva Eiger, in his *Gilyon HaShas* on 94b, lower left-hand corner, writes — citing a position in the name of Rabbeinu Tam — that even though *chachmei umot ha-olam* were victorious, *haynu nitzachon beta'anot*: they had better proofs, but the truth still lies with the Jewish sages. As he puts it: *aval ha-emet kachachmei Yisrael* — in the end we are right, proof-shmoof. He supports this from the liturgical formulation *boke'ach chalonei rakia* — the very language of the sun passing through the windows of the *rakia* that we use in prayer shows that Chazal had it right all along. This illustrates the central debate: whether one can accept that Chazal could err in scientific matters.

### Duration Mil

Several important *halachic* conclusions emerge from this Gemara regarding the duration of a *mil*. The Gemara presents effectively three possible readings. One position yields thirty *mil* for twelve hours, or 720 minutes — making a *mil* 24 minutes. Another yields thirty-two *mil*, making a *mil* 22.5 minutes. A third reading understands the Gemara as giving forty *mil* for the twelve hours of the day, making a *mil* 18 minutes. We in practice rule that a *mil* is 18 minutes.

This ruling is highly practically relevant: the 18-minute limit for how long bread may be left before it becomes *chametz* — the time it takes to walk a *mil* — derives from this very Gemara. The matter is disputed: some hold 22.5 minutes and some 24, and indeed the physical distance of a *mil* (approximately one kilometer) and the type of terrain one traverses affect which figure is most accurate, but 18 minutes is the accepted ruling.

### Shkia/Tzeis

The same Gemara states that from *shkia* to *tzeis hakochavim* is four to five *mil*. Working through the arithmetic: if a *mil* is 18 minutes, then four *mil* is 72 minutes and five *mil* is 90 minutes. If a *mil* were 24 minutes, five *mil* would equal 120 minutes. This is the basis for *shitat Rabbeinu Tam*, who takes this Gemara seriously and holds that *Shabbat* is not concluded until 72 minutes after *shkia* — four *mil* at 18 minutes each. Those who are even more *machmir* in both dimensions wait 90 minutes, and some wait 120 minutes, combining Rabbeinu Tam's position with the most stringent reading of the *mil*.

### Cosmology Halacha

Why do we not rule like Rabbeinu Tam in practice? The Gemara in *Shabbat* that addresses the *halachic* question of when *Shabbat* begins contains a direct discussion of *tzeis hakochavim* and speaks of three stars becoming visible — and locates that moment at three-quarters of a *mil* after *shkia*, which at 18 minutes would be approximately 13.5 minutes. The Gra, the Geonim, and others hold that it is that Gemara — being the Gemara explicitly addressing the *halachic* boundary of when the next day begins — that governs. This Gemara, by contrast, is not about *tzeis hakochavim* as a *halachic* matter at all; it is a cosmological discussion about how long it takes the sun to traverse the full thickness of the *rakia*.

The reconciliation offered is elegant: as the sun begins its passage through the thickness of the dome, the stars near the top of the dome begin descending toward visibility. The first three visible stars — the *halachic* *tzeis hakochavim* — appear when only the initial portion of the sun's journey through the thickness has elapsed. By the time the sun has completed its full traversal, all stars, including those that began at the very top, will have descended into view; that full-traversal period corresponds to the four or five *mil* of this Gemara. Thus the 20-to-25-minute practice observed in Israel according to the Gra reflects the *halachic* Gemara in *Shabbat*, while the four-to-five-*mil* figure of our Gemara describes something else entirely.

### Geography Season

Geography and season introduce further complexity. Rabbeinu Tam and the *Baalei HaTosafot*, as well as the Ramban, lived in France and Germany, where twilight extends very late; a 72-minute *tzeis* is plausible — and sometimes even still light — in a northern European summer. The Vilna Gaon, reading the Gemara in *Shabbat* as the controlling source, arrived at a far shorter interval that accords naturally with conditions in Eretz Yisrael, where darkness falls much more quickly.

The question of whether duration from *shkia* to *tzeis* must vary by latitude and season is itself debated. One might also ask whether the cosmological model, which envisions the sun traversing a fixed thickness of the dome, should be thought of as describing a straight-line path or an arcing one, and how the shorter path inside the dome in winter versus the longer path in summer would affect the timing. These questions remain open within the discussion of the Gemara's cosmological framework, and no definitive resolution is offered.

---

## Mishnah Differences

### Chometz Chametz

The Mishnah now presents the differences between *Pesach Rishon* and *Pesach Sheni* in their actual performance.

*HaRishon assur be-val yeira'eh u-val yimatzei* — the first *Pesach* carries with it the full prohibition of owning *chametz*, connected as it is to *Chag HaMatzos*. There is a prohibition of *lo tishchat al chametz dam zivchi*, and the day before the *Pesach* the obligation of *tashbitu* already begins. *Ve-hasheini chametz u-matzah imo ba-bayit* — by *Pesach Sheni*, one may have *chametz* in the house alongside it. Indeed, it is intriguing whether one could theoretically eat bread alongside the *Pesach*, given that one is still required to eat it *al matzot u-merorim*. The *matzah* requirement is explicit; whether that itself precludes also having bread present is a question worth noting.

### Hallel Eating

*HaRishon taun Hallel be-achilaso* — the first *Pesach* requires recitation of *Hallel* at the time of eating it; *ve-hasheini ein taun Hallel be-achilaso* — the second does not. Both, however — *zeh ve-zeh te'unim Hallel be-asiyasan* — require *Hallel* at the time of the *korban*'s offering, when it is brought.

### Override Shabbat

*Ve-dochin et ha-Shabbat* — both *Pesach Rishon* and *Pesach Sheni* override *Shabbat*. Since each carries a fixed time obligation — *be-mo'ado* — and overriding *Shabbat* is rooted not specifically in its being a *korban tzibbur* but in the principle of *chiyuv she-kavuah lah zeman*, both are *docheh Shabbat*. The question of *docheh tumah*, however, applies only to *Pesach Rishon*, as will be seen. This is the position of the Mishnah, which the Gemara will note is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.

---

## Kekhol Chukat

### Gufo Classification

The Gemara now turns to the underlying derivation of which laws of *Pesach Rishon* apply to *Pesach Sheni*. The verse says: *ke-chol chukat ha-Pesach ya'asu oto* — the verse about *Pesach Sheni* states that one should observe it according to all the statutes of the *Pesach*. The Gemara reads this through a Baraita: *be-mitzvot she-be-gufo ha-katuv medaber* — the verse is speaking about obligations pertaining to the body of the *Pesach* itself, such as *tzli eish*, roasting over fire. 

What then of obligations that accompany the *Pesach* but are not literally the body of the *korban*? For these the verse says *al matzot u-merorim yochluhu* — they are included because they are *al gufo*, directly associated with the body of the *Pesach*. But might one go further and include things entirely extraneous to the body, like *bal yeira'eh u-val yimatzei*? For this the verse repeats by *Pesach Sheni*: *v'etzem lo yishberu vo*. The repetition of the bone-breaking prohibition, applied to *Pesach Sheni*, is not merely restatement; it serves to anchor the analogy. Just as *v'etzem lo yishberu vo* concerns the body of the *Pesach* itself, so all the applied laws must concern the body of the *Pesach* or what is directly *al gufo* — excluding things *chutz me-gufo*, however conceptually linked to the *Pesach* they may be. Even *lo tishchat al chametz dam zivchi*, though it concerns the *shechitat ha-Pesach*, is considered *chutz me-gufo* because it is not something done with the meat itself; one is simply *shochting* the animal while happening to own *chametz*.

The Gemara then draws an explicit tripartite classification. The three additional verses cited in connection with *Pesach Sheni* correspond neatly to three categories of obligation: *al matzot u-merorim* is a positive *mitzvat asei*; *lo yash'iru mimenu ad boker* — the prohibition of *notar* — is a *lo ta'asei she-nitak la-asei*, paired with the positive obligation of *ve-hanotar mimenu ba-esh tisrofu*; and *v'etzem lo yishberu vo* is a pure *lo ta'asei gamur*. The principle that emerges is: any obligation in any of these three categories applies to *Pesach Sheni* if it is *be-gufo*, and is excluded if it is *chutz me-gufo*.

The Gemara then asks: what is included by the *klal* of *al matzot u-merorim*? The answer is *tzli eish*, roasting — another *mitzvat asei* that is directly about the body of the *Pesach*. What *mitzvat asei* is excluded? *Tashbitu* — the positive obligation to destroy *se'or* — since it is not *al gufo*.

### Isi ben Yehuda

*Isi ben Yehuda* does not dispute the *halacha* but the derivation. He holds that *ya'asu oto* — the word *oto*, meaning "it" — already suffices to limit the laws to those directly concerning the body of the *Pesach*. The word *oto* is *davka*; it never needed to be expanded in the first place. He therefore has no need for the verse of *v'etzem lo yishberu bo* to perform a limiting function.

This raises the Gemara's counter-question: if Isi holds *oto* was already limiting, and the Rabbis required *v'etzem lo yishberu bo* to limit it back — what forced the Rabbis to think that *oto* was *lav davka* in the first place? The answer is that once the verse explicitly included *matzah* and *maror*, which are not the body of the *Pesach* but are *al gufo*, one might have inferred that *oto* was meant broadly — opening the possibility of including even *bal yeira'eh u-val yimatzei*. Once that inference is entertained, the entire structure becomes a *klal u-prat*, and the verse of *v'etzem lo yishberu bo* is needed to close it back down.

Conversely, having concluded that *v'etzem lo yishberu bo* limits the scope, what do the Rabbis do with *ya'asu oto*? They derive from it: *she-ein shochtin et ha-Pesach al ha-yachid* — ideally one should not bring *Pesach* alone, for an individual, but should seek a *chaburah*. The word *ya'asu* is plural while *oto* is singular — implying that multiple people should be joining together for a single *Pesach*. As the Gemara puts it: *de-kama de-efshar l'hiddurei mahadrinan* — as much as possible, one should seek to do it with a group.

This is admittedly not an absolute prohibition for *Pesach Sheni*. Unlike *Pesach Rishon*, where all of *Klal Yisrael* is bringing together, *Pesach Sheni* by its very nature is for the stragglers and the individuals who were unable to participate. Nevertheless the aspiration encoded in *ya'asu oto* is to recreate the communal character of *Pesach Rishon* as much as possible. The cry of *lamah nigara levilti hakriv et korban Hashem be-mo'ado be-toch bnei Yisrael* — the complaint of those who were left out — is precisely about belonging to the national act, and the ideal of *chaburah* at *Pesach Sheni* recovers something of that sense of communal participation.

Rashi goes so far as to say that *le-hiddurei* — the seeking after a *chaburah* — means that if one would otherwise be the only person bringing *Pesach Sheni*, we would actually render someone else *tamei* deliberately so that there would be a *chaburah* partner.

### Three Categories

Returning to the tripartite structure, the Gemara enumerates the categories and their examples in detail. What is excluded as a *mitzvat asei chutz me-gufo*? *Tashbitu* — the positive obligation to destroy leaven. What is included as a *lo ta'asei she-nitak la-asei*? *Lo totzi mimenu* — the prohibition against removing the meat from the *bayit* or from the *chaburah*. And what is excluded as a *lo ta'asei she-nitak la-asei* that is nevertheless *chutz legufa*? *Bal yeira'eh u-val yimatzei*, which is *nitak* to *tashbitu*.

A parenthetical gloss in the Gemara addresses the internal parallel: the reason *lo totzi* is treated as analogous to *notar* is that both create a *psul* — *notar* through remaining overnight, and *lo totzi* through removal from the *bayit*. The two are parallel types of invalidity affecting the *korban* itself.

It is significant that the prohibition of *lo totzi mimenu* applies to *Pesach Sheni*. This confirms that the laws of *chaburah* — remaining within the *bayit* associated with one's *korban* — apply to *Pesach Sheni* as well. What exactly *nitak la-asei* means in the case of *lo totzi* is not fully resolved: Rashi notes that unlike other cases discussed in the Talmud, this Gemara assumes one cannot remedy the violation by bringing the meat back inside, since the meat becomes *pasul* upon being removed.

### Lo Totzi/Chaburah

What is excluded as a simple *lo ta'asei gamur be-gufo*? *Al tochlu mimenu na* — the prohibition against eating the *Pesach* raw. That is a *lo ta'asei* directly about the body. And what simple *lo ta'asei* is excluded as *chutz legufa*? *Lo tishchat al chametz dam zivchi* — the prohibition against slaughtering the *Pesach* while owning *chametz*. This is the most striking exclusion. One might have thought that since the prohibition pertains to the very act of *shechitas ha-Pesach*, it should be treated as *be-gufo*. But the Gemara holds that it is nonetheless *chutz legufa* — it is not something one is doing *with the meat* but rather a condition of ownership that exists at the time of *shechita*. This distinction between acting upon the meat and circumstances accompanying the *shechita* marks the outer boundary of what counts as *mitzvah she-be-gufo*.

---

## Hallel Question

### Hallel Derivation

The Mishnah having established that *Pesach Rishon* requires *Hallel be-achilaso* while *Pesach Sheni* does not, the Gemara asks: where is this derived? Rav Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: the verse says *hashir yihyeh lachem ke-leil hiskadesh chag* — a song will be for you like the night consecrated with the festival. The night that is consecrated with a *chag* — the night of *Chag HaMatzos* — is *ta'un Hallel*. A night not consecrated with a *chag* — the night of *Pesach Sheni* — is not *ta'un Hallel be-achilaso*. As for *Hallel be-asiyasan*, both require it when bringing the *korban*, since the verse's exclusion is only of the *lailah* and not of the bringing during the day.

### Maggid Omission

One might ask: the Mishnah discusses *Hallel be-achilaso* and *Hallel be-asiyatan*, but it says nothing about *Maggid* — the recitation of *sippur yetziat Mitzrayim*. This is a striking omission. One might have thought that just as *matzah* and the *Pesach* itself require contextual explanation and *Maggid* gives meaning to *achilas ha-Pesach* — so much so that the Gemara elsewhere says that if *matzah bi-zman ha-zeh* is *de-rabbanan*, then *Maggid* is *de-rabbanan* — perhaps *Maggid* should apply to *Pesach Sheni* as well.

The assumption that *Maggid* is excluded from *Pesach Sheni* follows from the same logic as the exclusion of *Hallel be-achilato*: *Maggid*, like *Hallel*, is connected to *Chag HaMatzos* and not specifically to *achilas ha-Pesach*. The verse *ke-leil hiskadesh chag* ties both *Hallel* and implicitly *Maggid* to the sanctity of the *chag* itself. Just as a *sukka* requires no parallel obligation of *Maggid* despite the verse *le-ma'an yeid'u doroteichem*, so too *Maggid* retains independent status linked to *Chag HaMatzos* rather than to the eating of the *korban*.

That said, it is not entirely *pashut*. One could argue that *Maggid* is integral to how one eats the *Pesach* — that without articulating the symbolism of the *Pesach*, *matzah*, and *maror*, one has not fully performed *achilas ha-Pesach* itself. The statement *kol she-lo amar shlosha devarim eilu be-Pesach lo yatza yedei chovato* raises exactly this question: does failing to say the three things mean one has not fulfilled *Maggid*, or not fulfilled *Pesach*, or both? The Mishnah's silence here is thus significant — and it suggests that even in the Talmudic understanding, *Maggid* is more deeply tied to *Chag HaMatzos* than to *achilas ha-Pesach* as such.

### Philo Jubilees

Relevant here is pre-Mishnaic and extra-Mishnaic evidence. In the book of Jubilees — whose composition predates the Mishnah — the story of the first *Pesach* is told with an account of the night of *achilas ha-Pesach*: "All Israel was eating the flesh of the paschal lamb and drinking the wine and was lauding and blessing and giving thanks to the Lord the God of their fathers." Song and praise accompany the eating of the *Pesach*; there is no mention of *Maggid*.

Similarly, in Philo's account of the *Pesach* — also earlier than the Mishnah — he describes the *Pesach* gathering as unique among feasts: "Those who are to share in the feast come together not as they do to other entertainments to gratify their bellies with wine and meat, but to fulfill their hereditary custom with prayer and songs of praise." Again: *shira*, no *Maggid*.

This pattern of evidence is significant. The Mishnah's focus on *Hallel be-achilato* — rather than on *Maggid* — is not an accident. In an earlier stratum of practice, song and praise with the eating of the *korban Pesach* was the central performative act of the night. *Maggid* may represent a later, more explicitly expository development tied to the *chag* framework, while *Hallel* as sung praise is the more ancient accompaniment to the *Pesach* itself. The observation that the Mishnah is discussing *Hallel* but not *Maggid*, and that the external sources similarly know *shira* but not *Maggid*, is therefore meaningful in tracing the history of the *seder* night.

### Shechirah Hallel

The Gemara then turns to explain why *Hallel be-asiyatan* applies to both *Pesachim*. It offers two approaches. The first: *laila ka-mi-mai, yom lo ka-mi-mai* — the verse *ke-leil hiskadesh chag* excluded only the *Hallel* of the night; the *Hallel* of the day, accompanying the *shechita*, was never excluded.

The second approach is striking: *efshar Yisrael shochtin et pisecheihen ve-notlin lulaveihen ve-ein omrin Hallel?* Could it be that Israel is slaughtering their *pesachim* and taking their *lulavim* and not saying *Hallel*? This is virtually a rhetorical self-evidence argument — a form of reasoning from what is inconceivable. The Ramban derives from this that *Hallel* in the context of performing such *mitzvot* is *de-oraita*, at least in principle, though the precise texts of *Hallel* as we know them were composed by David, raising the same question that arises regarding *tefillah*.

A deeper question remains, however, and is acknowledged without a full resolution: why should *Hallel be-asiyah* — at the *shechita* — be more self-evident than *Hallel be-achilah*? Ordinarily, the *Hallel* of the *korban* in the Temple was associated with the *Levi'im*, whereas what is being described here is a *Hallel* connected to the *mitzvot* of *chag* and *simcha* by the *Yisraelim* themselves. If the argument is that one cannot possibly bring the *Pesach* without *Hallel*, why does that logic not apply equally at the moment of *achilas ha-Pesach*? The verse *ke-leil hiskadesh chag* provides the answer for the night, but the intuition that the *shechita* demands *Hallel* while the *achilah* does not — though derivable from the verse — is not intuitively obvious. This question deserves further investigation.

---

## Lina Requirement

### Tosefta Lina

The question of whether *Pesach Sheni* requires *lina* — an overnight stay in Jerusalem — is disputed among *Tannaim*. The Tosefta's discussion on this point includes a vivid depiction of what the absence of a *lina* requirement would look like in practice. According to Rabbi Yehuda, *Pesach Sheni* does not require *lina*, deriving this from the juxtaposition of the verse *u-fanita va-voker ve-halachta le-ohalecha* — you may turn in the morning and go to your tents — with *sheishet yamim tochel matzot*: the *lina* requirement applies only to what is eaten across the six days of *Chag HaMatzos*, and since *Pesach Sheni* carries no such *chag* extension, no *lina* is required.

The Tosefta renders this vividly: one who brings *Pesach Sheni* may enter Jerusalem, slaughter the *Pesach* in the *Azarah*, leave, and even get a haircut at Beis Pagi — the district just outside the walls — the same night. If someone has pressing obligations, such as a death in the family requiring him to become *tamei*, he need not remain. Bring the *Pesach*, and then attend to what must be attended to. The image of someone departing Jerusalem immediately after the *shechita* — eating the *korban* in Jerusalem and then leaving that same night — underscores how differently *Pesach Sheni* is structured from *Pesach Rishon*. Note that even absent the *lina* requirement, the *korban* itself must still be eaten within Jerusalem; one may not take it *chutz li-Yerushalayim*.

---

## Pesach Tumah

### Eating Tumah

A new discussion opens concerning the *Pesach she-ba be-tumah* — a *Pesach Rishon* brought in a state of communal *tumah*, when the majority of Israel is *tamei* and the *korban* is therefore offered in *tumah*. Even in such circumstances, certain categories of *tamei* individuals are excluded from eating it: *lo yochlu mimenu zavim ve-zavot niddot ve-yoldot*. Individuals whose *tumah* emanates from within their bodies — *zavim*, *zavot*, *niddot*, and *yoldot* — may not eat from the *Pesach*, even though it is being brought *be-tumah*. Their status is of a more personal and severe character of *tumah*, one that is not overridden by the communal dispensation that permits *tumah yotzei mi-chutz* — external *tumah* from a *meit* or *sheretz* — to trigger the *Pesach be-tumah* arrangement.

The practical consequence: they may not eat, but *hem pturim min ha-karet* — they are nonetheless exempt from *karet* for failing to eat.

### Eliezer Azarah

Rabbi Eliezer adds a further ruling: not only is there no *karet* for failing to eat, but even if *zavim* and *metzora'im* were to press into the *Azarah* during the time the *Pesach* was being brought *be-tumah*, Rabbi Eliezer holds they would be *patur* from *karet* for entering.

### Pesukim Tamei

The derivation from the verses: the Torah states *kol tahor yokhal basar* — all who are *tahor* may eat meat — and then, *ve-ha-nefesh asher tochhal basar mi-zevach ha-shelamim asher la-Hashem ve-tum'ato alav ve-nikhretah* — the person who eats *korban* meat while *tamei* is *chayav karet*. The Gemara reads these verses as connected: the prohibition generating *karet* applies to meat that is *ne'ekhal le-tahorim* — restricted to *tahor* people. When the *korban* is brought *be-tumah* and is not restricted to *tahor* people, it is *she-eino ne'ekhal le-tahorim*, and in that circumstance *ein tme'im chayavin alav mishum tamei* — the *tamei* person is not *chayav karet* for eating it. The *cheftza* of the *korban* has changed in status; the *karet* applies only to eating meat that belongs categorically to the *tahorim*.

For Rabbi Eliezer's ruling regarding *bi'at ha-mikdash*: the verse *ve-yishalchu min ha-machaneh kol tzarua ve-khol zav ve-khol tamei la-nefesh* — send out from the camp the *metzora*, the *zav*, and the *tamei meit* — is read as establishing the rule by parallel: when *tamei meit* are expelled from the camp, that is also when *zavim* and *metzora'im* are expelled. And conversely, when *tamei meit* are not expelled — when the *Pesach be-tumah* allows them in — *zavim* and *metzora'im* are also not expelled, and therefore cannot be held *chayav karet* for entering.

### Yosef Heikhal

Rabbi Yosef then raises the question: if *zavim* and *metzora'im* who press into the *Azarah* during a *Pesach be-tumah* are *patur* according to Rabbi Eliezer — what if such individuals pressed further, entering the *Heikhal*? Is the dispensation coextensive? *Mid'ishtaray tumat azarah, ishtaray nami tumat heikhal?* Once we have said the *Azarah* entry does not generate *karet* in this circumstance, does the same follow for the *Heikhal*? Or is the dispensation strictly limited to what was explicitly permitted — *ma d'ishtaray ishtaray, ma d'lo ishtaray lo ishtaray* — the *Azarah* was opened but the *Heikhal* was not?

### Rava Heikhal

Rava offers a resolution through two formulations from the same verse. One formulation: *ve-yishalchu min ha-machaneh* — *afilu miktzat machaneh*, even a partial part of the camp. The *Heikhal* is its own distinct *machaneh*; even a partial domain remains subject to its own rule. Since the dispensation was only for the *Azarah*, the *Heikhal* — being a distinct domain — retains its prohibition, and entry there would render one *chayav*.

A second formulation of Rava takes the opposite view, reading *ve-yishalchu min ha-machaneh* alongside *u-mi-chutz la-machaneh tishalchum*: the principle is that wherever the verse of expulsion applies, the *yishalchu min ha-machaneh* also applies. Since when a *Pesach be-tumah* is brought, even *tamei meit* need not leave the *Beit HaMikdash* at all, the full dispensation — including for the *Heikhal* — would apply, and one who presses into the *Heikhal* under these circumstances would likewise be *patur*.

---

---

# Pesachim 96

## Pesach B'Tumah

### Intro: Tumah Heter

Daf 96 picks up at the very bottom of 95b, in what feels like a wrap-up mode for the final *mishnayos* and the final *perek* dealing with *korban pesach*. The organization is admittedly somewhat unusual: the *mishnah* immediately preceding this passage concerned the differences between *pesach rishon* and *pesach sheini*, and the *mishnah* coming up will address the differences between *pesach l'doros* and the *pesach* brought in Egypt. Situated between these two discussions is a *sugya* about *pesach haba b'tumah* — the Passover offering brought when the majority of the community is ritually impure.

The relevant background is as follows. When the community is *tamei*, there is a general *heter* permitting the *pesach* to be brought and eaten in a state of *tumah*. However, this *heter* does not apply to one whose *tumah* emanates from his body itself — a *zav* or a *zavah* — so if such a person were to eat, he would not be *chayav kares*. The position of Rabbi Eliezer extends a parallel logic to *bi'as mikdash*: just as other *tamei* people are permitted to enter the Temple precinct, even a *zav* or *zavah* who enters would not be *chayav kares*. The *Gemara* then probes whether there might still be restrictions within Rabbi Eliezer's position — for example, whether entering the *heichal* proper would remain *chayav* even for an ordinary person.

### Rav Yosef: Emurim

Against this backdrop, Rav Yosef poses a question at the end of 95b. Returning now to the view of the Rabbanan — who permit only the *eating* of the *pesach* in a state of *tumah*, not *bi'as mikdash* — the question is whether the *heter* for eating extends further than the *basar* of the *pesach* itself. Specifically: *dachaku t'mei meisin v'achlu emurei pesach haba b'tumah* — if *tamei meis* individuals forced their way and ate from the *emurim* (the inner organs of the *pesach* that are burned on the *mizbeiach*) in a time when *tumah* is *muttar*, what is the *halacha*?

The question carries several layers of complexity. Eating *emurim* is already prohibited under the prohibition against a *zar* — indeed, every person, even a *kohen*, is a *zar* with respect to *emurim*. Setting that aside, the narrower question is whether there is an additional *chiyuv* for being *tamei* specifically when eating *emurim*. In an ordinary time, eating *emurim* while *tamei* would entail two distinct prohibitions: the *issur zar* and the *issur tumah*. In a time when *pesach haba b'tumah* is in effect, the *heter* clearly removes the *issur tumah* from eating the *basar*. But does it extend to the *emurim* as well?

The question is framed as follows: *mi d'ishari tumas basar ishari nami tumas emurim* — since the *tumah* prohibition with respect to the *basar* has been made permissible, does the same follow for the *emurim*? Or does one say *mai d'ishari ishari, mai d'lo ishari lo ishari* — what was permitted, was permitted; what was not, remains prohibited?

### Rava: Source

Rava answers by tracing the very source of the *tumah* prohibition as it applies to *emurim*. How do we know in the first place that there is any prohibition against eating *emurim* while *tamei*? The source is a *pasuk* dealing with *basar* — the verse (Vayikra 7:20) which says *mibasar zeivach hashelamim asher l'Hashem v'tumasov alav*. The phrase *asher l'Hashem* is otherwise redundant when describing *zeivach hashelamim*, and so it is interpreted as *l'rabos es ha'emurim* — to include the *emurim*, teaching that the *tumah* prohibition on eating applies to them as well.

### Parallel Rule

From this derivation, Rava articulates a governing principle: *kol heicha d'isa tumas basar isa tumas emurim; kol heicha d'lesa tumas basar lesa tumas emurim* — wherever the *tumah* prohibition on *basar* applies, the *tumah* prohibition on *emurim* applies; wherever it does not apply, neither does it apply to *emurim*. The conclusion: since in *pesach haba b'tumah* the *tumah* prohibition on the *basar* of the *pesach* is waived, the same waiver extends to its *emurim*. This is limited solely to the dimension of *tumah*. The *tamei* person who eats *emurim* remains *chayav* for eating them as a *zar* — that prohibition is entirely unaffected. He simply does not incur the additional *chiyuv* for *tumah*.

### Rabbi Zeira: Pesach Mitz…

Rabbi Zeira then asks a question that serves as a perfect bridge to the next *mishnah*: what was done with the *emurim* of *pesach Mitzrayim*? In Egypt, the lintel and doorposts served as a kind of *mizbeiach* for the *zerikah* of the blood. But where were the *emurim* burned? There was no actual *mizbeiach* in Egypt. This question naturally opens the discussion of what the *pesach* in Egypt looked like, and what distinguished it from the *pesach* of future generations.

---

## Pesach Mitzrayim vs L'Do…

### Abaye: Burning Emurim

Abaye offers two responses to Rabbi Zeira's question. First: *uman leima lan dela sheviski avdi* — who is to say they did not simply roast the *emurim*? Perhaps they made a small fire that functioned symbolically the way the *mizbeiach*'s fire would, just as the doorposts served as the place for the blood in lieu of the altar. Second, Rav Yosef had a *baraisa* teaching that there were three "altars" at the time of *pesach Mitzrayim* — the lintel and the two doorposts — each serving as a valid surface for *zerikah*. But beyond those, there was nothing else — *vesu midei achrinei lo havei* — and perhaps the *emurim* were simply not burned at all; they may have been roasted together with the rest of the animal and eaten.

### Mishnah: Differences

With this as a launching point, the *Gemara* transitions to the *mishnah*, which addresses: *mah bein pesach Mitzrayim lepesach dorot* — what were the differences between the *pesach* brought in Egypt and the *pesach* of future generations? The *mishnah* itself mentions only a few distinctions; the *Tosefta* is considerably more expansive, and we will return to it below.

### Pesach Mitzrayim Practic…

The *mishnah* enumerates three practices unique to *pesach Mitzrayim*. First: *mikcho mibe'asor* — the lamb or kid was to be taken on the tenth of the month, as commanded in the verse *be'asor lachodesh hazeh veyikchu lahem ish seh leveit avot*. Second: *ta'un hazayah ba'agudat ezov ve'al hamashkof ve'al shtei hamezuzot* — it required sprinkling with a bundle of hyssop (*agudat ezov*) on the lintel and the two doorposts. These two requirements — the tenth-day selection and the hyssop-on-doorpost application — applied only in Egypt and not to future generations.

### Eating Requirements

Third: *ne'echal bechipazon balaylah* — it was to be eaten hurriedly and at night. This, too, the *mishnah* presents as a distinctive feature, with the implication that the *pesach* of future generations is not bound by the urgency of *chipazon* in the same manner. It was eaten *balaylah echad* — in one night — a limitation the *Gemara* will interrogate further.

### Pesach L'Doros: Seven Da…

By contrast, *pesach dorot noheg kol shiv'ah* — the *pesach* of future generations extends over seven days. The *Gemara* will clarify that this cannot refer to the *korban* itself, since no one eats the *pesach* offering for seven days; rather it must refer to the prohibition of *chametz*, which applies for seven days in future generations. This introduces an interesting conflation within the *mishnah* between *pesach* as a *korban* (which has been the exclusive focus of the preceding five *perakim*) and *pesach* as a *yom tov* — the festival week with its *chametz* prohibition and *matzah* obligation. It is worth noting that shift.

---

## Textual Analysis

### Hazeh Principle

The *Gemara* now undertakes a systematic examination of how we know which practices were exclusive to *pesach Mitzrayim* and which were replicated for future generations. The organizing principle is the word *hazeh* — and related limiting terms such as *bo* and *mimenu* — which appear repeatedly throughout the *parshah* describing *pesach Mitzrayim*. The verse *be'asor lachodesh hazeh veyikchu* contains *hazeh*, which is read as a limitation: *hazeh mikcho be'asor ve'ein pesach dorot mikcho be'asor* — only *this* offering requires being taken on the tenth; future *pesachim* do not.

However, immediately a difficulty arises. The verse *ve'hayah lachem l'mishmeret ad arba'ah asar yom lachodesh hazeh* — which establishes a four-day inspection period (*bikur arba'ah yamim*) before *shechitah* — also contains *hazeh*. Applying the same logic would imply that this inspection requirement is also exclusive to *pesach Mitzrayim*, but that cannot be correct.

### Eating at Night

The *Gemara* similarly challenges: the verse *ve'achlu et habasar balaila hazeh* uses *hazeh* as well. Should we therefore say that *zeh ne'echal balaila ve'ein acher ne'echal balaila* — that *this* pesach is eaten at night and no other? In other words, is eating at night a restriction unique to *pesach Mitzrayim*?

### Va'avadta Extension

The answer, which will be given repeatedly throughout this section: *amar kra va'avadta et ha'avodah hazot bachodesh hazeh* — the Torah states at the end of the *parshah* that "you shall perform this service in this month," a verse that speaks in future terms, pointing toward *pesach dorot*. This verse functions as a *ribuy* — a general extension of everything done in *pesach Mitzrayim* to all future *pesachim*. Consequently, whenever the *Gemara* proposes that *hazeh* or *bo* limits a given practice to *pesach Mitzrayim*, the answer is that *va'avadta et ha'avodah hazot* comes and extends it to future generations. The limiting words therefore cannot serve to exclude the practice from *pesach dorot*; they must be doing something else entirely.

### Chatzot Debate

The word *hazeh* in *balaila hazeh* is then explained as serving a different purpose: it provides the textual basis for the dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah and Rabbi Akiva in *Berakhot* regarding the time limit on eating the *korban pesach*. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah derives from *va'avarti b'eretz Mitzrayim balaila hazeh* that the *pesach* may only be eaten until *chatzot*. Rabbi Akiva, however, holds that *hazeh* does not limit the eating to *chatzot*; rather, it excludes the following night — teaching that unlike *shelamim*, which may be eaten for two days and one intervening night, the *pesach* may not be eaten the night of the sixteenth. Each position thus finds a distinct function for *hazeh* without limiting the practice to *pesach Mitzrayim* alone.

### Four-Day Inspection

Returning to the *bikur arba'ah yamim*: the *Gemara* shows from a *baraisa* that the four-day inspection requirement is not limited to *pesach Mitzrayim* at all — it applies both to the *tamid* and to all future *pesachim*.

### Ben Bag Bag Source

Ben Bag Bag — known to most from *Pirkei Avos* but who appears here in a substantive *halachic* context — derives the obligation for the *tamid* to be inspected for four days before *shechitah* by a *gezeirah shavah*: the verse by *tamid* says *tishmeru l'hakriv li b'mo'ado*, and the verse by *pesach Mitzrayim* says *ve'hayah lachem l'mishmeret* — the word *tishmeru* and the word *mishmeret* share the same root. Just as *mishmeret* by the *pesach* means four days of inspection before *shechitah*, so too *tishmeru* by the *tamid* means four days of inspection before *shechitah*. And by *pesach dorot*, the verse *va'avadta et ha'avodah hazot bachodesh hazeh* likewise extends the four-day inspection requirement.

### Resolving Limits

The *Gemara* reconciles the apparent contradiction as follows. The word *hazeh* that appears in the verse establishing *bikur arba'ah yamim* does carry limiting force — but it excludes only *pesach sheini* from the requirement, not *pesach dorot* generally. The reasoning is that *pesach sheini* is structurally analogous to *pesach Mitzrayim* in that it pertains solely to the *korban* and carries no *yom tov* dimension, and therefore its exclusion from *bikur* is what the *hazeh* signals. Meanwhile, the *hazeh* that appears in the verse about taking the animal on the tenth day of the month carries a different limiting force: it restricts *that* specific requirement — *mikcho be'asor* — to *pesach Mitzrayim* alone.

The result is a principled but layered structure: essentially everything done in *pesach Mitzrayim* is replicated for *pesach dorot* by virtue of *va'avadta et ha'avodah hazot*, and the limiting terms scattered throughout the *parshah* are each assigned to exclude something specific — but nearly nothing is excluded wholesale from future *pesachim*. The only practice the *Gemara* definitively restricts to *pesach Mitzrayim* at this stage is *mikcho be'asor*.

---

## Phrase-by-Phrase Analysis

### Arel Prohibition

The *Gemara* continues its phrase-by-phrase survey. The verse states *v'chol arel lo yochal bo* — no uncircumcised person shall eat from it. Applying the same logic: *hacha nami bo eino ochel aval ochel b'pesach dorot* — perhaps the word *bo* limits this exclusion to *pesach Mitzrayim*, and an *arel* would be permitted to eat from future *pesachim*? The answer: *amar kra va'avadta et ha'avodah* — the extension verse replicates the practice. An *arel* is excluded from eating the *pesach* in all generations.

So what does the word *bo* accomplish here? *Bo eino ochel aval ochel hu b'matzah u'maror* — the *arel* is excluded from eating the *pesach* itself, but he may still eat *matzah* and *maror*. This is worth pausing over, because the need for a *pasuk* to teach this seems puzzling. If *matzah* and *maror* constitute independent *mitzvos*, why would anyone have thought an *arel* is excluded from them? One possibility is that the Torah might have been understood to prohibit even eating *maror* or *matzah* in the company of the *pesach* without actually eating the *pesach* itself, lest it appear as a pseudo-*pesach* observance. The *pasuk* therefore comes to clarify that eating *matzah* and *maror* is permitted even for an *arel*.

There is, however, a deeper conceptual point underlying this discussion. The Torah's primary *mitzvah* of *matzah* is not an independent *mitzvah* in the simple sense — it is tied to the manner of eating the *korban pesach*. *Chazal* derived a separate *mitzvah* of *achilas matzah* independent of the *korban*, but *maror* in our era is only *derabanan* precisely because there is no *korban pesach* — the *mitzvah* of *maror* is contingent on the *pesach*. If a person has no obligation or access to the *pesach* offering, it is not immediately obvious why he would have cause to eat *maror* at all. The *pasuk*'s teaching that the *arel* may eat *matzah* and *maror* is therefore not merely clarifying that he is *muttar* to do so in some formal sense; it is affirming that the *arel* retains a *chiyuv* in the independent *mitzvah* of *matzah*, and that eating *maror* — even without the *pesach* — is permitted to him and not prohibited as an apparent imitation of the *pesach* ritual.

### Ben Neichar

The verse continues: *kol ben nechar lo yochal bo* — no foreigner shall eat from it. The simple reading would indicate a non-Jew, but *Chazal* understood that a *pasuk* is unnecessary to exclude a non-Jew from a Jewish communal sacrifice. They therefore interpreted *ben nechar* to mean *shenitnachru ma'asav l'Aviv shebashamayim* — one who has become foreign to his Father in Heaven, i.e., an apostate who has renounced his faith.

As before, the *Gemara* asks: perhaps *bo* limits this exclusion to *pesach Mitzrayim*, and an apostate could eat from *pesach dorot*? *Va'avadta* extends it — the prohibition applies in all generations. What then is the *bo* teaching? *Bo hamarat dat poselet ve'ein hamarat dat poselet b'trumah* — for the *korban pesach*, apostasy (*hamarat dat*) disqualifies; but apostasy does not disqualify one from eating *terumah*. Even if the apostate in question is a *kohen* whose *terumah* would otherwise be permitted, renouncing his faith does not invalidate his *terumah* access. The *bo* thus localizes the disqualifying force of *hamarat dat* specifically to the *pesach*.

The *Gemara* then asks why the Torah needed both prohibitions — *arel* and *ben nechar* — when one might have seemed derivable from the other. *Ve'itztarich l'michtav arel ve'itztarich l'michtav ben nechar*. Had only the *arel* been written, one might have said the exclusion is due to something physically repugnant about the uncircumcised state — *mishum de'ma'is* — but that wouldn't apply to an apostate, who shows no external sign of his spiritual distance. Had only *ben nechar* been written, one might have said the exclusion is because he is not engaged in an act of worship — *de'ein libo lashamayim* — but an *arel* whose uncircumcision is involuntary (as in a family of hemophiliacs) may be entirely devout in his religious life and should not be excluded. Therefore both are necessary.

### Toshav and Sachir

The verse additionally states *toshav vesachir lo yochal bo* — a sojourner and a hired hand shall not eat from it. The *Gemara* asks the same structural question — perhaps *bo* limits this to *pesach Mitzrayim* — and gives the same answer: *va'avadta* extends it. As for what *bo* adds, the *Gemara* produces a formulation about *hamarat dat* that seems to duplicate what was just said about *ben nechar*. Rashi entirely crosses out these three lines, noting that they are incoherent. The reason is that in the rabbinic reading, *toshav vesachir* refers not to foreigners but to a Hebrew bondsman: a *toshav* is a *nirtza* — one who extended his servitude through *yovel* — and a *sachir* is a Hebrew slave serving a six-year term. According to *Chazal*, such individuals *do* eat the *korban pesach*, in tension with the *pasuk's* plain sense. The treatment of these verses in other contexts involves very particular readings of the relevant *pesukim*, and Rashi accordingly deletes these lines as not fitting with the rest of the *Gemara*.

### Circumcision Limit

The verse states *u'maltah oto az yochal bo* — circumcise your sons and slaves, and then you (and they) may eat from it. The *Gemara* asks: might *bo* limit this requirement of household circumcision to *pesach Mitzrayim*, such that future *pesachim* could be eaten even by one whose slaves and children are uncircumcised? *Va'avadta* extends the requirement. The *bo* then does its own narrower work: *bo b'kasher velo b'pasul* — this rule of not breaking bones applies to a valid *pesach* and not to an invalid one.

### Raw vs. Roasted

Similarly, the verse *al tochlu mimenu na* — do not eat of it raw — contains the limiting term *mimenu*. The *Gemara* asks: should *mimenu* restrict the prohibition on eating raw to *pesach Mitzrayim* only? *Va'avadta* again extends it. The *mimenu* is then assigned a different function, linked to an interpretation cited in the name of Rabba citing Rav Yosef, extending certain prohibitions — particularly the *issur* on an *arel* eating — to the domain of *ma'aser*, and clarifying that while an *arel* is prohibited from eating *terumah*, the parallel prohibitions concerning *ben nechar* and unmolled household members do not carry over to *terumah* in the same fashion. *Ve'ein milat zcharav ve'avadav me'akevet biterumah* — circumcision of one's sons and slaves is not a barrier to eating *terumah*, even though it is a barrier to eating the *pesach*.

### Breaking Bones

The verse *ve'etzem lo tishberu bo* — do not break a bone of it — likewise uses *bo*. The *Gemara* asks whether this prohibition might be limited to *pesach Mitzrayim* by virtue of *bo*. *Va'avadta* extends it; the prohibition on breaking bones applies to *pesach dorot* as well. Here, too, the residual function of *bo* is to specify *bo b'kasher velo b'pasul* — that the prohibition on breaking bones applies to a valid *pesach* and not to an invalid one.

---

## Summary & Transition

### Mitzrayim Unique

Having gone through the central limiting terms of the *parshah* systematically, the *Gemara* arrives at its conclusions. The practices replicated from *pesach Mitzrayim* for future generations include: eating at night, the exclusion of the *arel* and *ben nechar*, the requirement to circumcise one's household, the prohibition on eating raw, and the prohibition on breaking bones. The practice categorically restricted to *pesach Mitzrayim* — identified through *hazeh* with no countervailing *va'avadta* extension — is *mikcho be'asor*, taking the animal on the tenth of the month. The word *hazeh* by *bikur arba'ah yamim* excludes only *pesach sheini*, not *pesach dorot*, from the inspection requirement.

An interesting thread runs through the entire discussion: the *Gemara* acknowledges that *va'avadta et ha'avodah hazot bachodesh hazeh* functions as a general *ribuy* bringing the totality of *pesach Mitzrayim* experience into *pesach dorot*. The limiting terms are then assigned particular, targeted functions rather than wholesale exclusions. The logic is that when *Chazal* understood a practice to be inherently local to the Egyptian context, they found a limiting word to carry that message; everything else was presumed to carry forward.

### Tosefta Details

The *Tosefta* at the end of *perek* 8 fills out a richer picture. It identifies a number of similarities that one might not have expected: *pesach Mitzrayim* was also conducted in three shifts (*gimel kitot*), just as *pesach dorot* is; and just as in future generations the *pesach* must not have any portion left over until morning, the same *lo totiru* applied in Egypt.

Among the differences the *Tosefta* enumerates: in Egypt, certain subtle *psulim* such as *etnan* and *mechir* (the hire of a prostitute and the price of a dog, which later *halacha* disqualifies from being brought as a *korban*) did not yet apply — the Torah had not yet stated those prohibitions. Furthermore, *pesach Mitzrayim* required that the animal be taken *hu ushcheino* — one's own household together specifically with one's neighbor — whereas *pesach dorot* does not require neighbors; any *chabura* will do. In Egypt, each individual slaughtered in his own home (*kol echad ve'echad shocheit betoch beito*), whereas in future generations all of Israel slaughters in one communal place. And in Egypt, the requirement *lo tetze'u ish mipetach beito* — no one was to leave his home until morning — meant that one had to sleep (*telinas laylah*) precisely where one ate; by contrast, *pesach dorot* permits eating in one place and sleeping elsewhere.

---

## Summary & Transition (II)

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon dissents from the ruling that neighbors need not be included in *pesach dorot*. He argues that even for future generations, one should preferably conduct the *pesach* together with one's nearest neighbor rather than traveling to celebrate with a more distant friend. His reasoning is the cultivation of neighborly bonds — *kedei shelo yaniach adam shcheino hakarov el beito veyelech la'asot pesacho etzel chaveiro* — and he anchors this in the verse *tov shachen karov me'ach rachok*, "a near neighbor is better than a distant brother."

### Emurim Service

Returning to Rabbi Zeira's original question about the *emurim* of *pesach Mitzrayim*, the *Tosefta* provides the clearest answer: *pesach Mitzrayim lo hayah ta'un damim vechelev legabei mizbe'ach* — the *pesach* in Egypt did not involve bringing the blood and fat (*chelev*) to the *mizbeiach*, in contrast to *pesach dorot*. This directly resolves the *chelev* dimension of the question. The Israelites in Egypt performed *zerikah* on the doorposts rather than on the altar, and the *emurim* were never offered in the formal *hekter* sense. *Pesach dorot*, by contrast, does require the *damim* and *chelev* to go to the *mizbeiach* in the ordinary fashion.

---

## Temurah of Pesach

### Yehoshua's Tradition

The *Gemara* now turns to the next *mishnah*, which shifts from the *pesach Mitzrayim*–*pesach dorot* comparison to the laws of *temurah* as they apply to the *korban pesach*. Rabbi Yehoshua says: *shamati she'tmurat pesach kreivah utmurat pesach einah kreivah* — "I have heard that the *temurah* of a *pesach* is brought as a *korban*, and I have heard that the *temurah* of a *pesach* is not brought — but I cannot explain the difference between the two cases." The phrase *ve'ein li lefareish* is striking: Rabbi Yehoshua received the tradition but could not reconstruct its reasoning.

It is worth noting the characteristic posture of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer as transmitters of tradition — their strength lay in preserving and handing down received rulings with precision. Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, was of the newer school: deeply analytical, creative, and willing to reconstruct the *rationale* behind traditions rather than simply store them.

### Akiva: Nidcheh

Rabbi Akiva steps in: *ani afareish* — "I will explain." The key concept he introduces is *nidcheh* — an animal that has been "pushed away" or stigmatized. The *halacha* of *nidcheh* in the context of *korban pesach* operates as follows: if one sanctified an animal as a *pesach*, then lost it and sanctified a second one in its place, and the first animal subsequently reappeared — the first animal has been actively set aside. It was present, it could have been brought, and instead one designated another animal. That deliberate displacement is what constitutes *nidcheh*, and such an animal cannot itself be brought as a *shelamim*; it can only be redeemed once it develops a *mum*, with the proceeds used to purchase a *shelamim*.

Crucially, Rabbi Akiva argues that the *temurah* of a *pesach* simply mirrors the original *pesach*. The *chiddush* — and the reason Rabbi Yehoshua's tradition spoke specifically about *temurah* rather than the *pesach* itself — will emerge below.

### Before Shechitah

The first case: *hapesach shenimtza kodem shechitat hapesach*. If the lost animal was found before the new *pesach* was slaughtered, then at the moment of that *shechitah* there were two available animals. The owner actively chose the new one and thereby pushed away the old one. That old animal is *nidcheh* — stigmatized — and may not be brought directly as a *shelamim*. It must graze until it develops a *mum*, then be sold, and the proceeds used to buy a *shelamim*. And similarly, any *temurah* made from that *nidcheh* animal inherits its status: the *temurah* too cannot be brought directly and must wait for the same process.

### After Shechitah

The second case: *achar shechitat hapesach*. If the lost animal was found only after the new *pesach* was already slaughtered, then the old animal was never actively displaced — it was simply absent when the decision was made. The owner had no opportunity to bring it; its absence was not due to his deliberate choice. This animal is not *nidcheh*, and it can be brought directly as a *shelamim*. And likewise, any *temurah* made from it can be brought directly as a *shelamim*.

---

## Temurah Status

### Why Temurah?

The *Gemara* asks the obvious question: given that Rabbi Akiva's entire explanation focuses on the status of the original *pesach* — *nidcheh* or not — why did Rabbi Yehoshua's tradition concern itself with the *temurah* at all? Shouldn't the *mishnah* have discussed the original *pesach* directly? *Leima pesach kareiv upesach eino kareiv* — let it simply say: this *pesach* is brought and that *pesach* is not brought!

### Temurah Follows

The *Gemara* answers: *ha kamashma lan d'ika temurat pesach d'lo kareiv* — the tradition comes to teach us a *chiddush* about the *temurah* specifically. One might have thought that even if the original *pesach* is *nidcheh* and cannot be brought itself, the *temurah* — which was never personally pushed away — should always be eligible to be brought as a *shelamim*. The original animal was set aside; the *temurah* animal was never part of that drama. The *chiddush* is that this is not so: the *temurah* takes on the full status of the original *pesach*, and if the *pesach* was *nidcheh*, so too is its *temurah* — it cannot be brought directly and requires the same redemption process.

### Shechitah vs Chatzot

There is then a *machlokes* between Rabba and Rabbi Zeira regarding what precisely defines the threshold that renders a *pesach nidcheh*. Rabba holds: *kodem shechitah v'achar shechitah shaninu* — the *mishnah's* distinction is simply about whether the lost animal was found before or after the *shechitah* of the replacement *pesach*. If found before the *shechitah*, there were two animals available at the decisive moment, and the old one was actively passed over; if found only after, the *shechitah* had already occurred and there was no opportunity to choose the old one. Rabbi Zeira disagrees: *kodem chatzot v'achar chatzot shaninu* — the operative threshold is not *shechitah* itself but *chatzot*, midday. If the lost animal was found before *chatzot*, when the time for *shechitah* had begun but the owner still had time to act, its non-selection renders it *nidcheh*; if found after *chatzot*, it was effectively out of the picture at the critical moment.

### Rabbi Eliezer

The *Gemara* notes that this dispute maps onto a *machlokes tannaim*. The *baraisa* states: *hapesach shenimtza kodem shechitah yera'eh le'achar shechitah yikareiv* — if found before *shechitah*, it must graze until a *mum*; if found after, it is brought directly as a *shelamim*. Rabbi Eliezer in the *baraisa*, however, holds: *kodem chatzot yera'eh, le'achar chatzot yikareiv* — before *chatzot* it grazes, after *chatzot* it is brought directly. The rationale is that *chatzot* marks the moment when the *pesach* was effectively expected to have been brought; an animal that was missing at that moment was naturally removed from consideration, and its later reappearance does not retroactively make one's decision to bring the new animal an act of deliberate displacement.

### Rava: After Shechitah

Rava adds a further refinement regarding the *temurah* specifically. The *mishnah* implies that the *temurah's* status simply mirrors the original *pesach's* status — if the *pesach* was found after *shechitah* and is not *nidcheh*, neither is its *temurah*. But Rava clarifies: this is only true if both the finding of the original animal *and the act of temurah* occurred after *shechitah*. Specifically: *lo shanu ela she'nimtza achar shechitah ve'hemir bo achar shechitah* — the case of the *mishnah* where the *temurah* is brought directly applies only when the original was found after *shechitah* and the *temurah* was also made after *shechitah*. The reasoning is that if the act of *temurah* itself was performed before the *pesach* was slaughtered, then at the moment of *shechitah* there were two candidates — the original and the *temurah* — and bringing the designated *pesach* effectively pushed away both. But if the *temurah* was made only after *shechitah*, the *temurah* animal was never present as an option during the decisive moment and was never pushed away. The discussion of this final case is left open as the *daf* concludes, to be continued in the following shiur.

---

---

# Pesachim 97

## Pesach vs. Proceeds

### Nidcheh Status

The *mishnah* opens with a framework that has occupied the *sugyah* throughout: when a *pesach* that was not brought on *Pesach* may be offered itself as a *shelamim*, and when one may only wait for it to develop a *mum*, redeem its value, and use the proceeds. The organizing distinction turns on the concept of *nidcheh* — whether the animal was in some sense "pushed away," its availability rejected.

### Lost Before/After

The *mishnah*'s governing case involves an animal that was lost before *Pesach*. When the owner designates a replacement and subsequently slaughters it, the question is whether the original animal was available at the moment of *shechita*. If the original was found before *shechita*, then the act of *shechita* constitutes a rejection of that animal — one had it as an option and chose to slaughter the replacement anyway. In that case the original is considered *nidcheh*, stigmatized, and cannot be offered; only its monetary proceeds may be used. If, however, the original was found only after *shechita*, it was never available to be pushed away. The owner had no choice, and therefore the original retains its full *kedushah* and may be offered as a *shelamim*.

### Temurah Status

The *mishnah* extends this framework to *temurah* — the attempted transfer of *kedushah* from a sanctified animal to a non-sanctified one. Such a transfer does not dissolve the *kedushah* of the original; rather, both animals become *kadosh*. The *temurah*, the *mishnah* teaches, inherits the status of the original *pesach*. Whether the *temurah* itself may be offered or only its proceeds may be used tracks the status of the original — and this is the explanation of Rabbi Akiva.

---

## Rava on Temurah

### Found After Shechita

Rava refines the *mishnah*'s treatment of *temurah* with precision. He teaches: *lo shanu ella shenimtza achar shechita vehimur bo achar shechita* — the rule permitting the *temurah* to be brought applies only when the original *pesach* was found after *shechita*, meaning it was never *nidcheh*, and the act of *temurah* was also performed after *shechita*. In that scenario the *temurah* may be brought as a *shelamim*.

### Inherited Kedusha

The more complex case arises when the original was found before *shechita* — making it *nidcheh* — and the act of *temurah* was performed only afterward. One might reason that the *temurah* itself was never pushed away, since the *temurah* act postdates the *shechita*; the *temurah* animal, one might argue, came into its *kedushah* in an unencumbered state. Rava rejects this. *Temurah mikoch kedusha dechuya kaasai* — the *temurah* derives its sanctity from the original, and since the original's *kedushah* was *dechuya*, stigmatized, the *temurah* inherits that stigmatized status. It cannot be offered.

### Timeline Diagram

The distinction can be mapped visually. At ten in the morning the original sheep is lost. A new animal is then sanctified as *pesach*. At one in the afternoon *shechita* is performed on the replacement. Where was the original at the moment of *shechita*? If it was present — *nimtza kodem shechita* — then the act of *shechita* on the replacement simultaneously constitutes a rejection of the original; the owner had both animals available and slaughtered only the new one. That act of *shechita* is therefore a *dechiyah*, and the original becomes *nidcheh*. If an act of *temurah* is then performed on yet another animal, that new animal is a copy of a *nidcheh* original, and cannot escape the stigma. If, by contrast, the original surfaced only after *shechita*, it was never subject to rejection, and a *temurah* performed thereafter is likewise untainted.

---

## Abaye Challenges

### Im Kesev Question

Abaye challenges Rava from a *braitta* interpreting the phrase *im kesev* in the *parashah* of *shelamim*. The *braitta* asks: *ma talmud lomar im kesev*? What is this phrase adding? Rashi notes that either the word *im* or the word *kesev* appears to be superfluous, since subsequent verses already clarify the species. The *braitta* answers that the phrase comes *lerabos tmuras hapesach achar pesach shekreiva shelamim* — to include the *temurah* of a *pesach*, once the original *pesach* has been offered, in the category of what may be brought as a *shelamim*.

### Pasuk Teaching

The *braitta* thus establishes as a matter of derivation from the *pasuk* that a *tmuras pesach* — a *temurah* of a *pesach* — may be brought as a *shelamim* after the original *pesach* has been sacrificed.

### Non-Obvious Case

Abaye then presses the logical implication. He asks: *heichi dami* — what scenario is this *pasuk* actually addressing? If it is speaking of the case where the original was found after *shechita* and the *temurah* was also performed after *shechita* — *peshita*! Of course the *temurah* may be brought as a *shelamim*; the original was never *nidcheh*, and there is no stigma whatsoever. *Lama li kra* — why would a *pasuk* be needed for something so obvious? If the *pasuk* is teaching a *chiddush*, it must be addressing a scenario where there is reason to think the *temurah* cannot be brought — namely, Rava's scenario, where the original was found before *shechita* but the *temurah* was performed afterward. And if the *pasuk* says it can be brought, that would directly contradict Rava.

### Asmachta Resolution

The *Gemara* deflects this challenge. It says: *lo* — the *pasuk* can indeed be speaking of the simple case, where both the discovery and the *temurah* occurred after *shechita*. Even though that case is obvious, the *pasuk* is merely cited as an *asmachta*, a textual support, rather than as the actual source of the law. The *Gemara* thus insulates Rava's position from this line of attack.

---

## Pesach Pasuk Purpose

### Conversion to Shelamim

Since the *pasuk* is an *asmachta* in this context, the *Gemara* asks: *kra lama li ata* — if the phrase *im kesev* is not needed to teach the *temurah* rule, what is it actually teaching? The *Gemara* answers from a separate *braitta*. The word *kesev* comes *lerabos es hapesach l'alyah* — to include the *pesach* in the law of the fat tail. But first the *braitta* establishes the more fundamental teaching: a *pesach* that cannot be offered as a *pesach* is converted into a *shelamim*, and it follows all the laws of *shelamim*. The *Torah* never provides explicit detail about what is done with the fat of a *pesach*; we have only very general verses — one instructing that the blood of sacrifices be sprinkled on the *mizbeach* and the flesh eaten, and another commanding that the fat be burned — neither of which focuses specifically on the *pesach*. The *pasuk* in the *shelamim* section therefore teaches that the fat of a *pesach* is treated in all respects as the fat of a *shelamim*.

### Fat Tail Law

The word *kesev* specifically — "a lamb" — teaches that when a *pesach* that is a lamb is converted into a *shelamim*, the *alyah*, the fat tail, is included in what is offered on the *mizbeach*. This is a *chiddush*, since the fat tail is specific to sheep and is included in the *shelamim* service for lambs; the *pasuk* teaches that the same applies to a lamb *pesach* brought as a *shelamim*.

### Shelamim Laws

The word *im* teaches that all the full apparatus of *shelamim* obligations applies to a *pesach* that becomes a *shelamim*: *smicha* (the laying on of hands, which is not performed on a *pesach* itself), *nesachim* (the accompanying wine and flour offerings), and *tenufas chazeh ve-shok* (the waving of the breast and thigh). None of these apply to a regular *pesach*, but once the animal is converted into a *shelamim*, every *mitzvah* of *shelamim* applies to it.

### Goat Exclusion

The phrase *ve-im ez* — "and if a goat" — then interrupts the subject, and from this interruption the *braitta* derives that a goat does not require the fat tail. *L'me'at es ha-ez she-ein teuna alyah* — the goat is excluded from the fat tail requirement. This is relevant because a *pesach* may be either a lamb or a goat; if the *pesach* is a goat, the fat tail is not offered. One might note, as is evident to any observer of livestock, that goats do not in fact possess a substantial fat tail as sheep do. Rashi, aware of this, suggests that the *Gemara* seems to assume goats do have a fat tail, and uses this as evidence to that effect — though the resolution remains unclear.

---

## Rava Reversed

### Temurah Timing

The *Gemara* notes that some authorities teach Rava's statement not in connection with the end of the *mishnah* — which addresses when the *pesach* itself may be brought — but in connection with the beginning, which addresses when only proceeds may be used. In this reversed formulation, Rava's statement works as follows: *amar Rava lo shanu ella shenimtza kodem shechita vehimur bo kodem shechita* — the rule that the *temurah* may not be used itself applies when the original was found before *shechita* and the act of *temurah* was also performed before *shechita*.

### Shechita Effect

In this version, the reasoning is equally precise. If the *temurah* was performed before *shechita*, then at the moment of *shechita*, both the original and the *temurah* were present and available; the act of *shechita* on the replacement pushes away both of them. But if the original was found before *shechita* — making it *nidcheh* — while the act of *temurah* was performed only after *shechita*, the *temurah* can actually be brought. The reasoning: *ki kava shechita mi-de-chazi lei, mi-de-lo chazi lei lo kava* — *shechita* only establishes the status of *nidcheh* with respect to an animal that was actually available and fit at the time of *shechita*. An animal that did not yet exist as a *temurah* when *shechita* was performed was not something *shechita* could push away. Therefore, even though the *temurah* derives its *kedushah* from the original *nidcheh* animal, in this reversed version Rava holds that the *temurah* itself was never pushed off and may be brought.

---

## Pesach Hu Pasuk

### Pesach Hu Teaching

Abaye now challenges the reversed version of Rava's statement from a different *braitta*. This *braitta* focuses on the *pasuk* *pesach hu l'Adonai* — "it is a *pesach* to God" — and derives from the word *hu* that only the original *pesach* itself can be brought in certain circumstances, *ve-ein tmuras pesach kriva* — and in some cases the *temurah* of a *pesach* cannot be brought.

### Non-Obvious Teaching

Abaye applies the same logical methodology he used earlier. *Heichi dami* — what scenario does this exclusion address? If both the discovery of the original and the *temurah* act occurred before *shechita*, *peshita* — of course the *temurah* cannot be brought, since the *shechita* rejected both the original and the *temurah* simultaneously. *Lama li kra* — no *pasuk* is needed for that. If the *pasuk* teaches an exclusion, it must be addressing a case where one might have thought the *temurah* could be brought.

### Found Before, Temurah Af…

The non-obvious case is precisely Rava's reversed scenario: the original was found before *shechita* — making it *nidcheh* — and the act of *temurah* was performed after *shechita*. One might think the *temurah* is valid since it was never itself pushed away. The *pasuk* *pesach hu* comes to teach that even in this scenario, the *temurah* cannot be brought, because its *kedushah* originates from a *dechuya* source.

### Refutation Accepted

Unlike in the first version of the exchange, where the *Gemara* deflected Abaye's challenge by invoking *asmachta*, here the *Gemara* accepts the argument. *Tiyuvta de-Rava tiyuvta* — this is a knockdown refutation of Rava's reversed position. The *Gemara* does not reach for *asmachta* here because, as it observes, there was no other available interpretation of the *pasuk* — it had to be teaching this non-obvious case. And if it is teaching that case, Rava's reversed position is wrong: the *temurah* cannot be brought even when the *temurah* act postdates *shechita*, because it inherits the *nidcheh* status of the original. This outcome aligns with Rava's first version of the statement and the conclusion of the earlier analysis.

---

## Shmuel's Principle

### Chatas Parallel

The *Gemara* now introduces a sustained and initially cryptic teaching of Shmuel that will occupy the rest of the *daf*. Shmuel states: *kol she-b'chatas mesa, be-pesach kareiv shelamim* — any scenario that, if it occurred to a *chatas*, would require the animal to be left to die, if the same scenario occurred to a *pesach*, the *pesach* would be brought as a *shelamim*. And: *ro'eh, be-Pesach nami ro'eh* — any scenario that, if it occurred to a *chatas*, would require it to graze until it developed a *mum* and its value be transferred, the same would apply to a *pesach*.

It must be noted at the outset, as Rashi observes, that there is no logical necessity connecting the laws of *chatas* to the laws of *pesach*. The *pesach* framework centers on whether an animal is *nidcheh*, while a *chatas* presents entirely different halachic dynamics. Rashi therefore characterizes Shmuel's principle as *simana be-alma* — a mnemonic organizing device, not a logical derivation. Shmuel is not saying that the laws are structurally connected; he is saying that, as a matter of fact, the same scenarios that yield death in a *chatas* happen to yield *shelamim* status in a *pesach*, and similarly for grazing. If you want to know what to do with a *pesach* in a given situation, ask yourself what you would do with a *chatas* in the same situation.

Alongside Shmuel's opaque principle, Rabbi Yochanan states the matter with characteristic directness: *ein pesach kareiv shelamim ela she-nimtza achar shechita* — a *pesach* is brought as a *shelamim* only if it was found after *shechita*. Before *shechita* it was *nidcheh* and cannot be brought itself. This is precisely what the *mishnah* and all prior analysis have established. The question, then, is what Shmuel could possibly be adding.

### Chatas Meitot Cases

To unpack Shmuel's principle, one must first identify the cases in which a *chatas* is left to die. There is a well-known mnemonic: *Vitinnah* — recalling the verse that Timna was a concubine to Elifaz son of Amalek. The letters of *Vitinnah* encode five cases. Vav stands for *vlad chatas* — the offspring of a *chatas*, which carries the same *kedushah* but cannot be offered. Tav stands for *tmuras chatas* — the *temurah* of a *chatas*. Mem stands for *mesu be-aleha* — the owner died. Nun stands for *nichperu be-acher* — atonement was achieved through a different animal, the equivalent of the *avud* case we have been discussing throughout. And ayin stands for *avar shnaso* — the animal became more than a year old and is therefore no longer fit for a *chatas*.

### Pesach-Relevant Cases
