Not all five of these cases are applicable to a *pesach*. A *pesach* must be male, and a *chatas* is female; therefore *vlad pesach* is impossible, and similarly the *temurah* scenario in Shmuel's discussion is not about *temurah* of the *pesach* itself as a separate category. The cases that are relevant to *pesach* are: *avud* (the lost animal, which is precisely the case the *mishnah* discusses), *mesu be-aleha* (the owner died), and *avar shnaso* (the animal exceeded a year of age). With this inventory in hand, Shmuel seems to be saying that in all these scenarios — anywhere a *chatas* would die — the *pesach* is brought as a *shelamim*.

---

## Avar Shnaso Problem

### Reish Lakish View

Rav Yosef challenges Shmuel's principle. He asks: *kellala hu* — is this really a universal rule? He targets the *avar shnaso* case. The standard teaching is that *avar shnaso* belongs to the five cases where a *chatas* dies; this is the ayin of the *Vitinnah* mnemonic. However, the *Gemara* now introduces a dissenting opinion. Reish Lakish holds that *chatas she-avar shnaso ro'in osah ke-illu hi omedes be-veis ha-kevaros* — a *chatas* that has exceeded a year of age is treated as if it were standing in a graveyard that a *Kohen* cannot enter. There is nothing inherently wrong with the animal; it is simply inaccessible. Therefore, rather than being left to die, it grazes until it develops a *mum* and its value is transferred. Reish Lakish thus removes *avar shnaso* from the category of *chatas* that dies and places it in the category of *chatas* that grazes.

### Pesach Avar Shnaso

The problem for Shmuel's principle is that by *pesach*, the *avar shnaso* scenario yields the opposite result from what Reish Lakish says it yields by *chatas*. The *braitta* already studied — the one derived from *im kesev* — explicitly states that *pesach she-avra shnaso* is brought as a *shelamim*. The *braitta* lists it among the cases converted into a full *shelamim*, with *smicha*, *nesachim*, and *tenufas chazeh ve-shok*. So when the *pesach* exceeds a year, it is brought as a *shelamim*.

### Principle Fails

The collision is direct. According to Reish Lakish, a *chatas* that exceeds a year grazes. According to the *braitta*, a *pesach* that exceeds a year is brought as a *shelamim*. These are different dispositions in the same scenario. Shmuel's principle — that the *pesach* always follows the *chatas* — fails in this case. Rav Yosef's challenge stands.

---

## Avud Only

### Limited Scope

The *Gemara* answers: *ki kamar Shmuel be-avudim, bi-dchuyim lo amar* — Shmuel was speaking only about cases of *avud*, of a lost animal. He was not making a claim about every possible problem that could befall a *pesach* or *chatas*. The cases of *avar shnaso* and *mesu be-aleha* are outside the scope of his principle. His principle applies only to the scenario where the *pesach* was lost, a replacement was designated, and then the original was found — the scenario the *mishnah* is addressing throughout.

### Rabbi's View

Once the scope is narrowed to *avud* cases, the *Gemara* examines a *braitta* that sets out the law of a lost *chatas*. The *braitta* states: *hifrish chattaso ve-avda* — one designated his *chatas* and it was lost. He separated a second *chatas* in its place, and then the original was found; both are now standing before him. Rabbi holds: *achas meihen tikareiv ve-hashniyah tamus* — one is brought and the second is left to die. This is regardless of the timing; Rabbi makes no distinction about when the original was found.

### Chakhamim's View

The *chakhamim* disagree and introduce a temporal distinction. *Ein chatas mesa ella she-nimtzas le-achar she-nis-kapru ha-baalim* — a *chatas* is left to die only if it was found after the owners had already achieved atonement through the other animal. But — and this is somewhat counterintuitive — if the original was found before the second one was brought, a different rule applies. In that case, the owner had both animals available and chose one, thereby pushing the other aside. This very act of *dechiyah*, paradoxically, helps: because the animal was pushed away rather than simply abandoned, it does not carry the full unimpaired *kedushah* that would demand its death. Instead it grazes. So: found before atonement achieved — *ro'eh*; found after — *meisa*.

---

## Chatas-Pesach Mapping

### Chatas Scenarios

The *Gemara* maps the *chatas* framework onto the *pesach* question. By *chatas*, according to the *chakhamim*: if the original was found before the new one was brought and was pushed away, it grazes; if found after, it dies.

### Pesach Translation

Translating into *pesach* terms requires one conversion: *meisa* by a *chatas* corresponds to bringing the *pesach* as a *pesach* — meaning in the context of our discussion, the *pesach* may be brought as a *shelamim* without restriction. And *ro'eh* by a *chatas* — the animal grazes until it develops a *mum* — corresponds to the *pesach* being brought only through proceeds, the mode of using the money value rather than the animal itself.

### Perfect Match

The correspondence appears perfect. If the original *pesach* was found before *shechita* — analogous to the *chatas* being found before atonement — it was pushed away, it is *nidcheh*, and only the proceeds may be used. If found after *shechita* — analogous to the *chatas* found after atonement — it was never *nidcheh* and may be brought as a *shelamim*. Shmuel's principle, applied to *avud* cases with the *chakhamim*'s framework, perfectly recapitulates everything the *mishnah* and Rabbi Yochanan have been saying.

---

## Redundancy Problem

### Says Same Thing

This perfect correspondence is, in fact, the problem. If Shmuel's principle, applied carefully, yields exactly the same ruling as Rabbi Yochanan's straightforward before-and-after-*shechita* rule, then Shmuel is saying nothing new. He has simply restated the same position in a far more elaborate and obscure way. And yet the *Gemara* presents them as disagreeing. This cannot be right.

### Chatzot Alternative

The *Gemara* therefore concludes that Shmuel must be holding a different position — one that diverges from Rabbi Yochanan. The divergence, the *Gemara* proposes, lies in the determinative moment. Rabbi Yochanan holds that *shechita* is the key act: it is *shechita* that establishes whether the original was *nidcheh*. Shmuel, by contrast, holds that *chatzot* — noon — is the key moment. The question is not what happened relative to *shechita* but what happened relative to midday.

### Chatzot Disagreement

This produces a genuine disagreement. Under Rabbi Yochanan's view, a *pesach* lost and found before *shechita* — even if found after *chatzot* — is *nidcheh* and only its proceeds may be used. Under Shmuel's view, the relevant question is whether the animal was found before or after *chatzot*. If it was found after *chatzot* but before *shechita*, Shmuel would say it is brought as a *shelamim*; Rabbi Yochanan would say it is *nidcheh* and only the proceeds are used. This is a substantive disagreement, and it justifies the *Gemara*'s presentation of the two as opposing positions.

---

## Rabbi Position

### No Roeh

In order for Shmuel's *chatzot*-based position to work coherently within the *chatas* analogy, the *Gemara* concludes that Shmuel holds like Rabbi. Rabbi's view, stated in the *braitta*, is that whenever a *chatas* is lost and a replacement is designated, one is brought and one dies — period. Rabbi makes no distinction about when the original is found. There is no *ro'eh* case for Rabbi in a lost *chatas* scenario.

### Always Shelamim

Applied to *pesach*, this means: whenever a *pesach* qualifies as properly *avud* — lost at a relevant time — it is always brought as a *shelamim*. There is no scenario in the *avud* case where one uses only the proceeds.

### Time, Not Shechita

This means that what defines the *pesach* as *avud* is not whether *shechita* was performed while the animal was available, but whether the animal was lost at a time that is halachically relevant to the *pesach* service. The *shechita* act, for Shmuel, is not determinative. What matters is the temporal status of the *pesach* at the time of loss and recovery.

---

## Avud Definition

### Night Analogy

The *Gemara* now precisely defines what counts as *avud* for Shmuel's purposes. The analogous question for a *chatas* is whether a loss that occurred at night counts. The *Gemara* invokes a principle of Rava: *aveidas layla la shme aveda* — a loss at night is not called a loss. Why? Because *korbanos* cannot be slaughtered at night. The animal's absence during nighttime hours is completely irrelevant to its halachic function; nighttime is simply outside the operative window of the *korban*. A *chatas* lost at night and found by morning was never truly *avud* for halachic purposes.

### Rava's Principle

This principle — that a loss occurring entirely within an irrelevant time window does not constitute a halachic *avud* — is the structural key to understanding Shmuel's position.

### Pesach Analogy

The same logic applies to *pesach*. Before *chatzot*, the *pesach* cannot be slaughtered. The time before noon is simply outside the operative window of *pesach* service. Therefore, a *pesach* that was lost and found before *chatzot* was never truly *avud*; its absence was irrelevant to its function as a *korban pesach*.

### After Chatzot Rule

It follows that Shmuel's principle applies only to a *pesach* lost and found after *chatzot*. In that case, the loss occurred within the relevant window — the window when the *pesach* could and should have been slaughtered — and therefore the animal is genuinely *avud*. And in that scenario, following Rabbi's position that all *avudim* by a *chatas* lead to death, Shmuel holds that the *pesach* is always brought as a *shelamim*.

---

## Core Dispute

### Chatzot Determines

The *Gemara* now articulates the core of the disagreement. Shmuel's entire elaborate construction — the *chatas* analogy, the adoption of Rabbi's universal *meisa* position, the exclusion of pre-*chatzot* losses as non-*avud* — serves a single purpose: to establish that *chatzot* is the determinative moment. What defines a *pesach* as *nidcheh* or otherwise is whether it was properly *avud* at a relevant time, meaning after *chatzot*. Once that threshold is crossed, the *pesach* is always brought as a *shelamim*.

### Shechita Determines

Rabbi Yochanan's position is the direct contrary. For him, *shechita kava* — *shechita* is what establishes whether a *pesach* is *nidcheh*. The act of slaughtering the replacement, while the original is present and available, is the moment of rejection. Before that act, regardless of the time of day, the *pesach* is not yet definitively *nidcheh*. After that act, if the original was present, it is *nidcheh*.

### Avud Framework

Shmuel's invocation of the *chatas* framework implies that what matters is whether the *pesach* has the status of *avud* at a halachically relevant moment. For *chatas*, relevance is defined by the hours during which *korbanos* may be brought; loss at night is irrelevant. For *pesach*, relevance is defined by the hours during which *pesach* may be slaughtered, which begin at *chatzot*. Shmuel therefore holds that *chatzot*, not *shechita*, draws the critical line.

---

## Alternative Shechita

### Perfect Parallel

The *Gemara* considers an alternative reading: perhaps Shmuel holds like Rava — *shechita kava* — rather than adopting a *chatzot*-based position. Under this reading, Shmuel would hold Rabbi's position that all *avudim* by *chatas* lead to *meisa*, and would map this onto *pesach* by saying that *shechita* determines what counts as *avud* for *pesach*. The result would be a clean parallel: *chatas* found before *shechita* grazes (under this reading of *chakhamim*, who have a *ro'eh* case), *pesach* found before *shechita* uses proceeds; *chatas* found after *shechita* dies, *pesach* found after *shechita* is brought as *shelamim*.

### Before/After Shechita

This reading would make the *chatas*-*pesach* parallel structurally exact: in both cases, the dividing line is *shechita*, and in both cases the before-*shechita* scenario yields the "lighter" disposition (grazing / proceeds) while the after-*shechita* scenario yields the "heavier" one (death / *shelamim*).

### Redundancy Again

But this interpretation cannot stand, for the same reason the *Gemara* identified earlier. Rabbi Yochanan already says precisely this: *ein pesach kareiv shelamim ella she-nimtza achar shechita*. If Shmuel's principle, resolved through the *chatas* analogy with *shechita* as the determinant, yields the same ruling as Rabbi Yochanan, then Shmuel is saying nothing new. He and Rabbi Yochanan would be in complete agreement, stated in very different idioms, and the *Gemara* would have no basis for presenting them as debating.

### Rejected Interpretation

This interpretation is therefore rejected. Shmuel must be saying something that diverges from Rabbi Yochanan. And the only available divergence is the *chatzot* position.

---

## Final Resolution

### Rabbi Position Final

The *Gemara* arrives at its final resolution. Shmuel holds like Rabbi: *avuda le-misa azla* — any lost *chatas*, once it qualifies as genuinely *avud*, is always left to die. There is no *ro'eh* case in the *avud* scenario according to Rabbi (and by extension, according to Rabbi Shimon, who likewise holds that all five cases of *chatas* lead to death without exception). Shmuel adopts this maximalist position.

### Before Chatzot Excluded

The apparent counterexample — that by *pesach*, a loss before *chatzot* yields only the proceeds (a "lighter" outcome) — is not actually a counterexample. A *pesach* lost and found before *chatzot* is not considered *avud* at all. Just as Rava teaches that *aveidas layla la shme aveda* — loss at night is not called a loss for a *chatas* — because nighttime is outside the halachically operative window, the same logic governs *pesach*: before *chatzot*, the *pesach* cannot be offered, and a loss within that window is entirely irrelevant to its *korban* status. It does not enter Shmuel's analysis at all.

### Chatzot Determines Status

When a *pesach* is genuinely *avud* — meaning it was lost at a time when it could have been slaughtered, i.e., after *chatzot* — then, following Rabbi's principle applied to *pesach*, it is always brought as a *shelamim*. The act of *shechita* plays no role. Whether the replacement was slaughtered before or after the original was found is irrelevant under Shmuel's framework. All that matters is whether the loss occurred during the operative window of *pesach* service.

### Time-Based Status

The conclusion the *Gemara* extracts is explicit. *Lema'afukei mi-Rabbi Yochanan* — Shmuel's entire principle is designed to show that Rabbi Yochanan is wrong. Rabbi Yochanan holds *shechita kava* — the act of *shechita* is what establishes *nidcheh* status. Shmuel, through his *chatas* analogy, teaches *chatzot kava* — time is what matters. By grounding the analysis in the concept of *avud* and by invoking the parallel to the irrelevance of nighttime loss by a *chatas*, Shmuel argues that the question is always one of temporal status: was the *pesach* lost during a time when it was halachically relevant? If yes, it is *avud* in the full sense and is brought as a *shelamim*. If no — because the loss was before *chatzot*, outside the operative window — it does not even enter the *avud* framework. Time, not the act of *shechita*, is the determinative criterion.

---

---

# Pesachim 101

## Kiddush in Shul

### Intro: Shul Kiddush

The Gemara on 101b opens with a case involving those who recited *kiddush* in the synagogue — *otam bnei adam shekidshu bevet haknesses* — and asks what the halachic consequence of that *kiddush* is. The framing question is simple: has one fulfilled one's obligation, and if so, which obligation exactly?

### Rav's Position

Rav's answer is precise but initially surprising. He says *yedei yayin lo yatzu, yedei kiddush yatzu* — they did not fulfill the obligation regarding the wine, but they did fulfill the obligation of *kiddush*. The Rashbam explains that this is not a question about Shabbat *per se* but about *halachot berakhot*. Having recited *borei pri hagafen* in the *shul*, and then departing for home, the change of location — *shinuy makom* — means that if one wishes to continue drinking wine, a new *borei pri hagafen* is required. That is the principle of *shinuy makom*: a change of location, even if anticipated, requires a new *berakhah* on wine. The *kiddush* obligation itself, however, has been fulfilled even without a meal at that location. This *shinuy makom* question is flagged as a *berakhot* issue that the *Gemara* will return to at length; the immediate focus is the ruling that *yedei kiddush yatzu* — one is *yotzei kiddush* even though no meal was eaten in the *shul*.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel disagrees sharply. He holds *af yedei kiddush lo yatzu* — one has not fulfilled the *kiddush* obligation at all. His ruling rests on the fundamental principle that *ein kiddush ela bimkom seudah*: *kiddush* is valid only in the place where the meal will be eaten.

### Rav's Reasoning

Given Rav's position that one is *yotzei kiddush* in *shul*, the *Gemara* asks the obvious question: why then bother making *kiddush* again at home? The answer is *kedei lehotzi banav uvnei beito* — to discharge the obligation on behalf of one's children, spouse, guests, and household members who were not present in the *shul*. This invokes the general principle of *af al pi sheyotzei motzi* — even one who has already fulfilled an obligation may discharge it on behalf of others. Moreover, anyone who hears *kiddush* recited in *shul* and wishes to be *yotzei* with it may do so; those who already fulfilled their own obligation need not repeat it at home for their own sake.

### Shmuel's Reasoning

The *Gemara* presses Shmuel in the other direction: if one is *not* *yotzei* with *shul kiddush*, why recite it there at all? The answer is *le'afokei orchim yedei chovatan* — to discharge the obligation of the guests. Why are guests different? *De'achlu veshatu veganu bevei kenishta* — because they eat, drink, and sleep in the *shul*. As Tosafot notes, this does not mean literally in the sanctuary; rather, it refers to some side room that functions as the guests' quarters. For those guests, the *shul* itself is their *makom seudah*, and therefore the *kiddush* recited there is fully valid for them.

The *Gemara* then states explicitly: *de'azal Shmuel letameih* — Shmuel goes according to his own reasoning, namely *ein kiddush ela bimkom seudah*.

### Makom Seudah Principle

Several important practical consequences flow from this principle. The first is that *bimkom seudah* applies to each individual listener, not just to the person reciting *kiddush*. Even if the *ba'al habayit* making *kiddush* does so in a place where he himself will eat, a listener for whom that location is *not* a *makom seudah* is not *yotzei*. It makes no difference that it is a valid *makom seudah* for someone else. This point is practically significant because many people attend a *shul kiddush* without making sure they themselves have *mezonot*, reasoning that the rabbi had *mezonot* and therefore the *kiddush* was valid. That reasoning is incorrect. To be *yotzei* with any *kiddush* one hears — whether in *shul* or at someone's home — one must ensure it is a *makom seudah* for oneself, meaning that one has some food there. What exactly constitutes a sufficient *seudah* is a question to be addressed shortly.

A second point emerges from Tosafot's inference about the one reciting *kiddush* in *shul* for the guests. It sounds from the *Gemara* as though the person making *kiddush* is not one of the guests — perhaps the *shaliach tzibur* or some other congregant — and for him it is not a *makom seudah*. The *kiddush* therefore does not work for him, yet it is valid for the guests. One might ask whether this constitutes a *berakhah levatalah* for the *mekadesh*. The answer is that it is not entirely unlike the general case of *af al pi sheyotzei motzi*: even one who has already discharged his own obligation — or, in this case, for whom the *kiddush* does not apply — may still recite it to discharge others' obligations. It is not treated as a blessing made in vain because it is genuinely effective for the people who hear it.

### Tosafot on Bread

Before turning to modern practice, a word on what constitutes *makom seudah*. For now the discussion uses the term *mezonot*, but Tosafot addresses this directly. Looking at the first Tosafot on 101b, the phrase *teimu midi* — have a bit to eat — that appears in the relevant *Gemara* passages means specifically a bit of bread. Tosafot cites the usage in *perek kamma* of *Shevuot*, where people say "let's have a bit," and it means bread and wine — a small meal, but a meal. Tosafot further distinguishes: *mezonot* may suffice to qualify as *seudah shlishit* (the third Shabbat meal), as is also the rule in the *sukkah*, but not for the first two Shabbat meals — *Arvit* and *Shacharit* — which are the primary expressions of *kavod Shabbat* and require bread. The implication for *kiddush* is direct: since the first two Shabbat meals require bread, *kiddush bimkom seudah* for those meals must similarly mean bread.

### Modern Practice

What then of the widespread practice of making *kiddush* in *shul* when no one eats there — not even the guests, since that custom has long since disappeared? Tosafot himself acknowledges that in that case the *kiddush* should not be recited at all, as it would constitute a *berakhah levatalah*. Nonetheless the practice continues.

### Chazarat HaShatz Analogy

The explanation for this is that certain liturgical practices are instituted for a particular need, and once established they become part of the fixed *nusach* even after the original need no longer obtains. The paradigmatic example is *chazarat hashatz* — the repetition of the *Shemoneh Esreh*. The original *takkanah* was enacted for those who could not recite the prayer themselves. In an era without printed *siddurim*, when much of the liturgy was transmitted orally and people might not know long prayers by heart — particularly the extended *Shemoneh Esreh* of Rosh Hashanah, recited only twice a year — the *shaliach tzibur* repeated it on their behalf. The question therefore arises: now that virtually everyone knows the *Shemoneh Esreh*, should *chazarat hashatz* be abolished? Some did argue this, but practice has maintained it. It is now considered the established *nusach* of the community and is not regarded as a *berakhah levatalah*. Rav Soloveitchik went further, elevating the repetition to a distinct mode of prayer altogether — not the individual praying within the community, as in the silent *Shemoneh Esreh*, but the community praying as a corporate entity — a status that was not its origin but which it has since acquired. A parallel case is lighting *Chanukah* candles in the *shul*, where no one is *yotzei* and yet a *berakhah* is recited. Originally, by Tosafot's straightforward analysis, this should not be done. But once the practice was established, it became part of the liturgy. The same logic applies to *shul kiddush* in a place where no one eats.

### Preference Question

A related question concerns who should ideally recite *kiddush*. The principle of *shomea k'oneh* — that hearing a *berakhah* is like reciting it oneself — is fully valid for *kiddush*, so that being *yotzei* by listening is halachically equivalent to reciting it oneself. One might therefore ask: is there a preference for each person to recite *kiddush* individually, or is there value in hearing it from one person? Some argue the opposite — that hearing *kiddush* from one *mekadesh* is preferable because it fulfills the obligation *b'rov am*, as a communal act rather than as a series of individual recitations. As a general rule, it is better for someone who has not yet been *yotzei* to recite *kiddush* rather than someone who has, though these preferences are not absolute.

### Wine Not Required

Tosafot draws one further inference from this *Gemara*: it appears that drinking the wine is not required in order to be *yotzei kiddush*. Tosafot on 101b states: *af al pi shelo shatu, rak sheyitaom hamvarekh, o afilu echad meihem; ulchatchila tzarich sheyitaamu kulam* — even if the listeners did not drink, as long as the one reciting *kiddush* tasted, or at minimum one person did, there is *yetziat kiddush*. The ideal is for everyone to drink, but it is not strictly required for *yetziat kiddush*. The resulting picture is somewhat counterintuitive: one can hear *kiddush* and be *yotzei* without drinking the wine — even from a person who is himself not *yotzei kiddush* because he is not remaining for the *seudah* — yet the one thing one *must* do is eat a meal. There is a small irony here: the very act from which the *kiddush* obligation is formally discharged is not drinking wine but eating the *seudah*. That this is a function of *kiddush bimkom seudah* rather than of the wine *per se* is a point that will resurface in the fuller discussion below.

---

## Makom Seudah Evidenc (II)

### Ein Kiddush Principle

The *Gemara* now states the principle of *ein kiddush ela bimkom seudah* explicitly as a topic in its own right and examines it from multiple angles.

### Rashbam's Explanations

The Rashbam offers two reasons for the requirement. The first is that since *kiddush* is recited over wine, the wine must have some weight and significance — it is wine in the context of a meal, not a random glass. The second, drawn from the *pasuk* of *vekarata laShabbat oneg*, is that wherever one "calls" Shabbat — wherever *kiddush* is recited — that is where the *oneg Shabbat*, the enjoyment of Shabbat, should take place. The meal must be framed by the *kiddush*. This second reason raises a structural question: if the problem of *kiddush* not in the *makom seudah* is a flaw in the *kiddush* itself (the wine lacks weight), that is one thing. But if the problem is that the *seudah* lacks proper framing (the meal was not introduced by *kiddush*), that is another. This distinction bears on what exactly constitutes *makom seudah*, a question that is worked through in the cases that follow.

### Rav Huna's Case

A case involving Rav Huna illustrates *ein kiddush ela bimkom seudah* in practice. Rav Huna made *kiddush* and intended to eat, but then his candle blew out — *itfara lei shraga*. He then brought his vessels to the house of Rabbah his son, who had recently married and where there was light, and recited *kiddush* again and ate there. The *Gemara* concludes: *almah kasavar ein kiddush ela bimkom seudah* — this demonstrates that when one is no longer able to eat in the location where *kiddush* was recited, one must make *kiddush* again in the new location where the meal will take place.

---

## Shinuy Makom

### Rav Anan's Testimony

The *Gemara* had initially speculated that the restriction of *makom seudah* might apply only when moving from one building to another — *mibayit lebayit* — but not between different locations within a single building — *mimakom lemakom bechad beisa*. Rav Anan bar Tachlifa then testifies directly: *zimnin sagi'in havei kamina kamei d'Shmuel denachit me'igra le'ara vahadar mekadesh* — many times I was in the presence of Shmuel, and he would descend from the rooftop to the ground floor and only then make *kiddush*. Shmuel thus deliberately avoided making *kiddush* on the roof when the meal would be eaten downstairs, evidently because he considered the roof and the ground floor to be different *mekomot* even within the same structure. This testimony establishes that even a change of location within a single building can constitute a halachically meaningful *shinuy makom*.

---

## Makom Seudah Evidenc (II)

### Tosafot's Qualification

While the testimony of Rav Anan bar Tachlifa establishes that different floors within one building can be distinct locations for purposes of *kiddush bimkom seudah*, Tosafot introduces a qualification. Examining the phrase *mimakom lemakom bechad beisa*, Tosafot reads the case as involving a room-to-room change — *micheder levayit* — or a floor-to-floor change like *igra le'ara*. However, Tosafot rules that going from one corner of a room to another — *mipina lepina* — does not constitute a problematic *shinuy makom*. This is consistent with the later *Gemara* on *shinuy makom* and *berakhot*, which distinguishes *mipina lepina* from *mibayit lebayit*.

### House vs. Room Distincti…

Two clear extremes emerge from the discussion: moving from one building to another is unambiguously a new *makom* that invalidates *kiddush bimkom seudah*; moving from one corner of a room to another within a large space is not. The intermediate case — different rooms or different floors within the same building — is less clear from the *Gemara* itself.

On this intermediate case, Tosafot introduces a position drawing on the Yerushalmi. The relevant line in Tosafot reads: *nireh demodeh Shmuel im kiddesh beigra kedei leechol beara dechashiv kiddush bimkom seudah* — it appears that Shmuel would concede that if one made *kiddush* on the roof with the *intention* of eating downstairs, that would qualify as *kiddush bimkom seudah*. The presence of *intent* transforms the act. This is admittedly difficult to square with the plain sense of the *Gemara*, since if intent sufficed there would have been no reason for Shmuel himself to physically relocate before making *kiddush*. Tosafot's position is grounded in the Yerushalmi rather than in a direct reading of the Bavli. Nevertheless, this ruling of Tosafot is accepted as *halacha*: for two locations within the same building, if one had in mind to eat in the second location when making *kiddush* in the first, it qualifies as *bimkom seudah*.

The conceptual rationale relates to the framing function of *kiddush*. When one makes *kiddush* explicitly as a prelude to eating in the next room, the *kiddush* is understood as introducing the meal — the two are psychologically and functionally contiguous. It is only when the transition is an unplanned break, when one finds oneself eating elsewhere in a manner that was not anticipated, that the *kiddush* is seen as disconnected from the meal. The plain sense of the *Gemara*, it must be acknowledged, does not support this view — the implication of Shmuel's behavior is that even with intent it would not work, otherwise why relocate? But the Tosafot position based on the Yerushalmi is what has become normative practice.

### Shul Application

This ruling has direct application to the standard practice of many synagogues, where *kiddush* is recited upstairs in the sanctuary and the *seudah* is served downstairs in the social hall. On the plain reading of the *Gemara*, this ought not to work — moving from one floor to another is akin to *igra le'ara*, the very case Shmuel took pains to avoid. But on the basis of Tosafot's reading of the Yerushalmi, since the *kiddush* is made upstairs with explicit intent to eat downstairs in the same building, it qualifies as *bimkom seudah*. This is the accepted practice and is treated as *lechatchila*.

The distinction between two buildings and two locations within one building is thus the operative line: a *kiddush* made in *shul* can never discharge the obligation of someone who intends to eat at home — Shmuel is unambiguous on this — but a *kiddush* made in one part of a building can work for a meal eaten in another part, provided the intent was in place at the time of *kiddush*.

One important corollary bears repeating: the fact that *kiddush* qualifies as *bimkom seudah* for those present at a *shul kiddush* does not help those who are listening without themselves having food. One must have food — at minimum *mezonot* — at one's own location for the *kiddush* to count as *bimkom seudah* for oneself.

### Abaye's Account

The *Gemara* then cites a parallel case. Abaye relates: *ki havina bei mar* — when I was at the house of the Master (i.e., Rabbah, his teacher) — when Rabbah made *kiddush* on Friday night, he would say to the students: *teimu midi* — have a bit to eat right now before you go home. The reason: *dilma ad'azlitu le'ushpiza itfara lechu shraga* — perhaps by the time you travel to your lodgings, the candles there will have blown out. If that happens, *vela mekadesh lechu beveit achilah* — there will be no *kiddush* made in the place of eating, and *uvekidddusha dehacha lo nafkitu* — you will not have been *yotzei* with my *kiddush* here, *de'ein kiddush ela bimkom seudah* — because *kiddush* is valid only in the place of the meal. Therefore Rabbah insisted that students eat something before departing. This confirms both the principle of *ein kiddush ela bimkom seudah* and the personal nature of *bimkom seudah* — the students, even though they heard Rabbah's *kiddush*, must themselves eat in that place if they wish to be *yotzei* with it.

This *Gemara* establishes unambiguously that one who heard *kiddush* at a teacher's house must eat there in order to be *yotzei*, regardless of plans to eat elsewhere. It does not show, however, which dimension of *kiddush bimkom seudah* is operative: whether the problem is that the *kiddush* itself lacked weight, or that the subsequent meal will lack a proper *kiddush* introduction. Both problems are present simultaneously in all the cases discussed, so the theoretical question remains open.

### Bread vs. Mezonot

The phrase *teimu midi* — a bit to eat — appears in both the Rav Huna case and the Abaye case. What does that minimum consist of? As Tosafot argues, the word means bread: the parallel usage in *perek kamma* of *Shevuot* makes clear that "a bit to eat" means bread and wine — a small but genuine meal. For the first and second Shabbat meals, the *seudah* obligation requires bread, and therefore *kiddush bimkom seudah* for those meals must involve bread as well. This is Tosafot's position.

### Tosafot vs. Geonim

The *Geonim* disagree. They hold that one may be *yotzei kiddush bimkom seudah* with considerably less. There is even a position among the *Geonim* that drinking a *revi'it* of wine alone constitutes *bimkom seudah* — if one drinks a full *revi'it*, the *kiddush* wine itself provides the required context. This position would make the entire discussion of what one eats nearly irrelevant to the *kiddush* question, which seems to render much of the *Gemara*'s discussion beside the point. The accepted *psak* rejects this extreme and generally holds that *mezonot* — a *kezayit* of a grain-based food — satisfies *kiddush bimkom seudah*.

The dispute between Tosafot and the *Geonim* maps directly onto the two reasons the Rashbam offered. If the purpose of *bimkom seudah* is to give weight and significance to the *kiddush* (the first reason), then *mezonot* — or even a significant amount of wine — might suffice, since any meaningful eating context serves that function. If the purpose is that the *seudah* itself must be introduced by *kiddush* (the second reason, from *vekarata laShabbat oneg*), then for the first two Shabbat meals, which require bread, only bread can satisfy the requirement. The ruling that *mezonot* generally suffices indicates that the accepted position comes down on the side of the first reason: the function of *bimkom seudah* is to give context and significance to the *kiddush*, not to define the Shabbat meal.

### Home Kiddush Practice

This brings up a common practical scenario. Many people attend a *shul kiddush* on Shabbat morning, have wine, *kiddush*, and *mezonot* — satisfying the requirement of *kiddush bimkom seudah* by the accepted *psak* — and then return home. At home, do they make *kiddush* again before the Shabbat meal, or do they simply begin with *Hamotzi*? For many, reciting only *Hamotzi* without first making *kiddush* — or at least *borei pri hagafen* — feels wrong. It is not a *berakhah levatalah* to say *borei pri hagafen* if one wants to drink wine, but technically the *kiddush* obligation has already been discharged.

One approach is that both dimensions of *kiddush bimkom seudah* may in fact be operative simultaneously. The *mezonot* in *shul* gave sufficient weight to discharge the formal *kiddush* obligation and permitted eating for the rest of the morning. But the dimension of *vekarata laShabbat oneg* — that the *seudah* itself ought to be introduced by *kiddush* — remains unfulfilled, and the *kiddush* (or at least the *borei pri hagafen*) recited at home before the bread meal addresses that dimension. Both functions are thus satisfied. The straightforward *psak* in the *Shulchan Aruch* and *Poskim* holds that technically only *mezonot* is required and a second *kiddush* at home is not strictly necessary, but a strong argument can be made that both dimensions belong together.

### Rambam on Wine

Rambam's position is that wine should accompany all three Shabbat meals, not just the first two. For Rambam, the *borei pri hagafen* that introduces the second meal and — in his view — the third meal as well provides a consistent framework, and one can detect in his ruling both the dimension of giving weight to the *kiddush* and the dimension of *oneg Shabbat* being introduced by wine throughout Shabbat.

### Rabbah's Three Rulings

The *Gemara* now notes that while Rabbah generally ruled like Rav against Shmuel, Abaye records that in three specific cases Rabbah ruled like Shmuel. *Kol mili d'mar hava avid k'Rav, l'var mihani tlas d'avid k'Shmuel* — in everything else the Master followed Rav, but in these three he followed Shmuel.

### Three Cases

The three cases are: (1) *ma'avirin mibeged lebeged* — Shmuel's ruling that one may transfer *tzitzit* from one garment to another, removing the *mitzvah* from one garment in order to place it on another; (2) *madlikin miner lener* — Shmuel's ruling that on *Chanukah* one may use one lit candle to light another, without concern that this disrespects the first *ner Chanukah*; (3) *halachah k'Rabbi Shimon bigreirah* — that one may drag a bed, chair, or bench on Shabbat even though doing so might inadvertently create a furrow, in accordance with the principle of *davar she'eino mitkavein* as ruled by Rabbi Shimon. Rabbah followed Shmuel, who ruled like Rabbi Shimon against Rav's position. This last ruling is of enormous practical importance throughout *hilchot Shabbat*: without it, one could not walk on grass lest one inadvertently uproot it, and countless ordinary Shabbat activities would be prohibited.

The *Gemara* then explains how Rabbah could maintain this selective alignment. It was not that he arbitrarily adopted the *chumra* of each party — which would violate the principle that one cannot always take the stringent position from both sides of a dispute. Rather: *kechumrei deRav hava avid* — he followed Rav when Rav was *machmir*. But *kekulei deRav lo hava avid* — when Rav was the *meikel*, Rabbah did not follow him. In those three cases, Shmuel was the *machmir*, and Rabbah ruled accordingly. Tosafot notes the broader principle that one is permitted to take *chumrot* from different positions as long as they are not internally contradictory, and here Rabbah's approach was internally consistent. The application to *kiddush bimkom seudah* is that Rabbah, who generally ruled like Rav, here adopted Shmuel's *chumra* of *ein kiddush ela bimkom seudah*.

---

## Shinuy Makom (II)

### Yochanan's Position

The *Gemara* returns to the first half of the original dispute — not the *kiddush bimkom seudah* question, but the *berakhot* question: if one made *kiddush* in *shul*, reciting *borei pri hagafen* and drinking, and then moves to a new location, must one recite a new *borei pri hagafen*? Both Rav and Shmuel agreed that one must; the earlier discussion focused on the *kiddush* question. Now Rabbi Yochanan takes a different position entirely: *af yedei yayin nami yatza* — one has also fulfilled the *yayin* obligation, meaning no new *borei pri hagafen* is required even after a change of location.

Rabbi Yochanan goes according to a principle he is quoted as holding in the name of several transmitters — Rabbi Yochanan bar Abba citing Rav Chanin bar Abba citing Rav Assi citing Rabbi Yochanan: *echad shinui yayin ve'echad shinui makom ein tzarich levarech* — neither a change of wine (opening a new barrel) nor a change of location requires a new *berakhah*. It should be noted that while a change to a superior wine does not require a new *borei pri hagafen*, it does require *hatov vehametiv* if the new wine is better than what was on the table. The Rashbam and Tosafot both note this: changing wine barrels requires no new *borei pri hagafen*, but if the new wine is superior, *hatov vehametiv* must be recited. That question of *hatov vehametiv* is a separate discussion; the present point is whether *borei pri hagafen* must be repeated, and on that Rabbi Yochanan says no for both *shinuy yayin* and *shinuy makom*.

### Refutation of Yochanan

The *Gemara* immediately challenges Rabbi Yochanan with a *braita*: *shinuy makom tzarich levarech, shinuy yayin ein tzarich levarech* — a change of location requires a new *berakhah*, a change of wine does not. This *braita* is unambiguous: *shinuy makom* requires a new *berakhah*. The *Gemara* concludes: *tyuvta d'Rabbi Yochanan tyuvta* — Rabbi Yochanan's position is refuted. So *shinuy makom* does require a new *borei pri hagafen*. A question is noted: if one recited a *berakhah acharona* before leaving the first location, that would certainly break the continuity; but even absent a *berakhah acharona*, the objective change of location requires a new *berakhah rishona*.

### Rav Chisda's First Teach…

With the refutation of Rabbi Yochanan established, the *Gemara* turns to define what constitutes a *shinuy makom* requiring a new *berakhah*. The passage is: Rav Idi bar Abin was sitting before Rav Chisda, and Rav Chisda was seated and transmitting in the name of Rav Huna: *ha de'amrat shinui makom tzarich levarech, lo shanu ela mibayit lebayit* — what we said, that changing location requires a new *berakhah*, applies only when going from one *bayit* to another *bayit*. But *mimakom lemakom* — from one location to another — or more precisely *mipina lepina* — from one corner of a room to another — does not require a new *berakhah*. That is not considered a *shinuy makom*.

Rav Idi bar Abin then notes that this was actually already taught in a *braita* from the school of Rav Huna — or, according to some versions, from the school of bar Huna: *kevaseich* — just as you said. The *Gemara* then asks: was Rav Huna then just teaching his own opinion as if it were novel, when it already appears in a *braita*? The answer: *Rav Huna masnita lo shemia lei* — Rav Huna had never encountered this *braita* from the school of bar Huna. He formulated his ruling on his own authority, and it happened to align with what was already taught.

The operative parameters are thus: one building to another — definitely *shinuy makom* requiring a new *berakhah*; one corner of a room to another — definitely not *shinuy makom*. The intermediate case — different rooms or different floors within the same building — parallels the same ambiguity encountered in the *kiddush bimkom seudah* discussion. The term *bayit lebayit* in the *Gemara* can refer to different rooms within a building, so different rooms presumably create a *shinuy makom*, though this is not absolutely explicit. Moving from one visible space to another visible space within a room, on the other hand, does not. Whether having intent in mind helps in these intermediate cases — as Tosafot argued it does for *kiddush bimkom seudah* — is a question that the *Gemara* does not address directly here but is implicitly raised.

### Rav Chisda's Second Teac…

Rav Chisda then makes a further ruling, this time in his own name: *ha de'amrat shinui makom tzarich levarech, lo amran ella bidvarim she'ein te'unin berakhah le'achareihem bimkoman* — the rule that a *shinuy makom* requires a new *berakhah rishona* applies only to foods that do not require a *berakhah acharona* in the specific location where they were eaten. But for foods that *do* require a *berakhah acharona* in the specific place — *devarim hate'unin berakhah le'achareihem bimkoman* — one does not make a new *berakhah rishona* upon moving to a new location.

### Lekviat Kama Hadar

The reason: *lekvi'uta kama hadar* — one is, in effect, returning to the original established meal, the original *kevi'ut*. If food is of a kind that requires returning to its original location for the *berakhah acharona*, then any eating done elsewhere is seen as an extension of that original established eating, not as a new and independent event. The change of location does not sever the connection to the original *kevi'ut* because the person remains, by halachic logic, rooted in the original place.

A practical illustration: if one is drinking coffee and steps outside to continue, one must recite a new *berakhah* upon beginning to drink again outside. But when one finishes outside, does one need to return to the room where one started in order to recite *borei nefashot*? No — for foods in the category of *shehakol* or *ha'etz* and the like, the *berakhah acharona* may be said wherever one finishes. By contrast, for a *Hamotzi* meal, the *Gemara* speaks of *berakhah acharona bimkom seudah* — the principle that *Birkat Hamazon* ideally must be recited in the place where one ate. If one left that place, the *Poskim* discuss how far one may have gone before one is required to return. The point is that for a *Hamotzi* meal one is considered "rooted" in the original location in a way that one is not for casual eating.

### Bread/Mezonot Application

The Rashbam holds that this category of *devarim hate'unin berakhah le'achareihem bimkoman* — foods requiring a *berakhah acharona* in the place of eating — includes all *shivat haminim*, encompassing wine. This would mean that virtually every case of wine or grape products discussed throughout the *Gemara* falls into this category, which would make the entire discussion of *shinuy makom* and *borei pri hagafen* nearly irrelevant. For that reason, this view creates serious difficulties, and the *Gemara* itself is difficult on the Rashbam's reading.

### Tosafot's Debate

Tosafot therefore rejects the Rashbam's expansive reading. The relevant Tosafot rules: *lachen nireh deyayin vechol she'ar haminim lo havai bikhlal devarim hate'unin berakhah acharonah bimkomam, ella pas* — wine and the other *shivat haminim* are *not* in the category of *devarim hate'unin berakhah le'achareihem bimkoman*; only bread is. Or, more tentatively, bread and possibly *mezonot* — *vechol minei mezonot sheyesh bahem me'ein hamisha* — foods requiring *berakhah me'ein shalosh* — may also belong to this category, but that is uncertain.

The practical consequence is significant. For bread, and possibly for *mezonot*, changing locations while in the middle of eating does not require a new *berakhah rishona*, because the eating remains rooted in the original established *seudah* and the person will need to return to that location (or is halachically considered as rooted there) for *Birkat Hamazon*. For wine and other foods, a genuine *shinuy makom* does require a new *berakhah rishona*. This is the position that is accepted *lehalacha*.

The logic is somewhat counterintuitive: one might have expected that the more "established" a meal is, the more a change of location would sever it. The *Gemara*'s principle, by contrast, is the opposite: the more established the meal — the more it demands a return to the original location for the *berakhah acharona* — the less a change of location during the meal is treated as a rupture. The concept is *lekvi'uta kama hadar*: one is still deemed to be connected to the original *kevi'ut*, and eating done in another location is seen as an outshoot of that established meal, not a new experience.

This has a recognizable practical application. Consider a situation where a meal is served in one room and guests move to other rooms during the course of the meal, eating *mezonot* or drinking wine there. If the main *Hamotzi* meal is in one room, then the eating in other rooms during that meal is understood as an extension of the main meal and is covered by its *berakhot*. Casual eating, by contrast — *mezonot* eaten with no connection to a fixed *Hamotzi* meal, in one room and then in another — would require a new *berakhah* for the change of location, since there is no established *kevi'ut* to return to. The more fixed the meal, the more mobile the eating during it may be. This is the point of the well-known practice of having small pieces of bread by the washing station in some establishments — the concern being that the interval and change of location between *al netilat yadayim* and *Hamotzi* might constitute a *hefsek*, though the extent of what counts as a *shinuy makom* in that context depends on whether the two locations are visually connected and the general parameters discussed above.

### Rav Sheshet's Position

Rav Sheshet takes an entirely different and maximally stringent view: *echad zeh ve'echad zeh tzarich levarech* — whether one is in the middle of a *Hamotzi* meal or eating casually, a genuine *shinuy makom* always requires a new *berakhah rishona*. Rav Sheshet does not accept Rav Chisda's distinction between established and non-established eating. For him, the objective fact of being in a new location is always halachically significant and always requires a new *berakhah*.

It should be noted that this entire discussion has focused on the *berakhah rishona* upon returning to or continuing eating in a new location. Whether *shinuy makom* also requires a *berakhah acharona* before leaving the original location — as a sort of forced interruption — is a question Tosafot addresses with some ambiguity. According to Rav Sheshet, if a new *berakhah rishona* is always required upon moving, one might ask whether the act of moving itself constitutes a conclusion of eating at the first location requiring a *berakhah acharona* there. Tosafot's analysis of this point goes back and forth.

### Chavura Case

The *Gemara* now introduces a *braita* that bears on this: *bnei chavura shehayu mesubin lishtot, ve'akru ragleihem latzet likrat chatan o likrat kallah* — a group who were reclining and drinking, and they all got up to go welcome a wedding party. When they go out, *ein te'unin berakhah lemafrea* — they do not need to recite a *berakhah acharona* before leaving. When they return, *ein te'unin berakhah lechatchila* — they do not need to make a new *berakhah rishona*. All of this is treated as continuous. However, this applies only if they left someone behind — an elderly or ill person who could not join them. *Henihichu sham zaken o choleh* — the presence of that person creates continuity; the group is considered as though they remained. If they left no one behind, then when they go out they must recite a *berakhah acharona*, and when they return they must recite a new *berakhah rishona*. The *seudah* has been definitively interrupted.

Crucially, the *braita* uses the phrase *akru ragleihem* — "they uprooted their legs" — which implies that they were genuinely *kavu'a*, established and planted in their place. This is a *Hamotzi*-style meal, the type for which *Birkat Hamazon* must be recited in the *makom seudah*. Yet even for that type of established meal, a *shinuy makom* interrupts things, unless someone is left behind to maintain continuity. This seems to directly contradict Rav Chisda's ruling that established meals (*devarim hate'unin berakhah le'achareihem bimkoman*) are *not* subject to the *shinuy makom* requirement of a new *berakhah*. The *Gemara* therefore presents this as a *kashya* to Rav Chisda.

### Yehuda vs. Chachamim

The resolution lies in identifying the authorship of the *braita*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says: *man tana akira akirot? Rabbi Yehuda* — the author of this *braita*, with its emphasis on *akirah* (uprooting), is Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yehuda holds that even for an established *Hamotzi* meal, *shinuy makom* — without someone left behind to maintain continuity — interrupts the meal and requires both a *berakhah acharona* upon leaving and a new *berakhah rishona* upon returning. The *Chachamim*, however, disagree: even without someone left behind, the meal is considered continuous and no new *berakhot* are required. Rav Chisda's position, it emerges, aligns with the *Chachamim*: for an established meal, *shinuy makom* does not require a new *berakhah*. Rav Sheshet's maximally stringent position, on the other hand, aligns with Rabbi Yehuda. The debate between Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet thus maps onto the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* over whether *shinuy makom* during an established *kevi'at seudah* interrupts the meal. This will be developed in the following *daf*.

---
