In the second large Tosafot on this topic — beginning *chutz mi-bracha hasmucha lachaverta* — Tosafot takes up the blessings following the *haftara*. He notes that the blessing *d'tzur kol ha-olamim*, which culminates in *she-kol devarav hem emet v'tzedek*, presents a question not from the *nusach* of the *bracha* itself but from the way it is laid out in the *machzorim* (meaning, in the manuscripts of the period). In the printed Artscroll siddur, the passage flows continuously from *she-kol devarav hem emet v'tzedek* into *Ne'eman Atah Hu Hashem Elokeinu* and concludes with *Baruch Atah Hashem ha-Kel ha-Ne'eman b'chol devarav* — a single *bracha* with proper opening and closing. But Tosafot observed that in the *machzorim* as they were written, a paragraph break appeared between these two sections, giving the impression that the first portion lacked a closing *Baruch Atah* and the second lacked an opening one — *v'ein sham bracha lo b'chatimat harishona v'lo bifteichat hashniya*.

The obvious resolution is that there should be no such break — it is all one *bracha*. Tosafot explains: *v'nireh d'kula bracha achata hi, d'kula mishtayei b'ne'emanut u'va'amittut ha-makom* — the entire passage is one *bracha* because it revolves around a single theme, the faithfulness and truth of the Omnipresent. *Ne'eman Atah*, *ha-Kel ha-Ne'eman* — it is all the same idea. The paragraph break in the *machzorim* may have served as a pause during which the *shliach tzibur* would allow the congregation to respond. What is striking about this Tosafot is the nature of the question itself: the difficulty does not arise from the formal *nusach* of the *bracha* but from the typographical or scribal convention of paragraph breaks in the manuscripts. The white space apparently suggested to some readers that the text had been divided into two structurally separate *brachot*. This phenomenon connects in a fascinating way to the broader *Ashkenazi* practice of *piyutim* — the flexibility with which certain communities inserted liturgical poetry into the fixed *nusach hatfillah*, particularly on *Yamim Tovim*. The pause implied by the paragraph break may also reflect something like the *Sefardi* practice of a responsive moment between the *shliach tzibur* and the *tzibbur*.

### Sheva Brachot

The discussion of *Sheva Brachot* introduces one of the most structurally interesting applications of the *smucha lachaverta* principle. In the *Sheva Brachot* recited under the *chuppah*, the first three blessings — *shehakol bara lichvodo*, *yotzer haadam*, and *asher yatzar et haadam* — each open with *Baruch Atah*. Why should they? Regarding the first two, Rabbeinu Tam explains in the Tosafot that *shehakol bara lichvodo* and *yotzer haadam* open with *Baruch Atah* because they are short, one-line *brachot* that lack a *chatimah*: *lekach poteach b'varuch v'lo chatimah* — they are like blessings over fruit or *mitzvot*, where the opening *Baruch* is simultaneously the entire *bracha* and its conclusion, *ufitichat zazu hi chatimatan*.

The more subtle question is why *asher yatzar et haadam* opens with a new *Baruch Atah*. Since *yotzer haadam* immediately precedes it, one would expect *asher yatzar* to simply continue as *smucha lachaverta* without its own opening *Baruch Atah*. Tosafot's answer is elegant: *u-vaasher yatzar et haadam tzarich liftoach b'varuch she-im lo hayah poteach hayah nireh hakol bracha achat* — *asher yatzar* requires its own opening *Baruch Atah* precisely because without it, the two blessings would appear to be one continuous paragraph *bracha* together with *yotzer haadam*. The thematic proximity of the two passages — both dealing with the creation of the human being — combined with the fact that *yotzer haadam* is a one-liner rather than a paragraph *bracha*, means that without an explicit *Baruch Atah* at the start of *asher yatzar*, the whole sequence would be read as one long *bracha*. This requires *asher yatzar* to assert its independence explicitly through an opening *Baruch Atah*.

One might note that the machzor problem discussed above could theoretically have been solved with a similar device — inserting an explicit *Baruch Atah* to mark the division. But Tosafot's approach in both cases reflects the same underlying logic: structural independence requires formal markers, and in their absence the text will be read as continuous.

This analysis bears directly on a prominent practical question: may the *Sheva Brachot* be distributed among different people, as is universally done at weddings today? Several *poskim* have raised the objection that since the blessings following *asher yatzar* do not open with *Baruch Atah* — being *smucha lachaverta* — if each is given to a different person who has not personally just recited the preceding *Baruch Atah*, they are no longer truly *smucha* to anything. Rav Moshe Feinstein responded that this is not the correct understanding of *smucha lachaverta*: the exemption from opening with *Baruch Atah* is established at the level of the original institution of the *bracha*, not at the level of the individual's execution of it in any given instance. The *bracha* was established as *smucha lachaverta*, and it therefore does not require *poteach b'varuch*, regardless of who recites it or whether the preceding *bracha* was recited by the same person. An interesting corollary: if the *Sheva Brachot* were recited out of order such that no preceding *Baruch Atah* was said by anyone, Rav Moshe's reasoning would apparently still hold, since the institution itself carries the exemption.

The final blessing, *asher bara sasson v'simcha*, opens with its own *Baruch Atah* for a different reason: it is capable of standing entirely on its own. When *panim chadashot* are not present and only a single *bracha* is recited, it is this one, and a *bracha* that can stand independently must open with *Baruch Atah*.

---

## Kashya L'Ulla

### Ulla's Havdalah

With this context established, we turn to the opening of 105a: *kashya l'Ulla* — this is a difficulty for Ulla. To recall the background: Rav Yehuda sent Rav Yitzchak to observe what Ulla did for *havdalah*, and Rav Yitzchak in turn sent Abaye. The report that came back was that Ulla said only *Hamavdil bein kodesh l'chol*. The Rashbam understands this to mean that Ulla recited a simple one-liner — much like the *havdalah* of Rebbi.

### Tosafot Reading

Tosafot, however, takes a different approach. A one-liner would not generate the difficulty the *Gemara* now poses — if Ulla recited a one-liner, the answer would be obvious: a one-liner does not require a closing *Baruch Atah*. Tosafot therefore reads the episode differently: Ulla recited the full content of *havdalah* — *Hamavdil bein kodesh l'chol, bein or l'choshech, bein Yisrael l'amim* — but omitted the closing *chatimah* entirely. He said the opening *Baruch Atah* but did not end with one. The words *Baruch Hamavdil* that the *Gemara* records are thus read by Tosafot as the opening of a full *bracha* without a conclusion.

### Single Theme Bracha

This is what the *Gemara* finds difficult: how can Ulla recite an opening without a closing *chatimah* for a passage of that length? *Amar lach Ulla* — Ulla would respond: *hani nami k'birchat hamitzvot damyan* — this is analogous to a *birchat hamitzvah*. A *birchat hamitzvah* requires no closing *Baruch Atah*. Why not? *Mishum d'hoda'ah hi* — because it is a single *hoda'ah*, a single act of acknowledgment centered on one idea, with no diversification of themes. And so too here: *hacha nami hoda'ah hi*.

What does this mean in practice? Tosafot explains that the question of whether a *bracha* is "short" or "long" — whether it requires a closing — is not simply a matter of word-count or physical length. It is a question of thematic complexity. A *bracha* that introduces multiple distinct themes requires a closing *Baruch Atah* to signal its conclusion. A *bracha* that, however lengthy, circles around a single unifying theme does not. When Ulla recites *Hamavdil bein kodesh l'chol, bein or l'choshech, bein Yisrael l'amim, bein yom hashvi'i l'sheshet yemei hama'aseh*, every clause is a variation on the same concept — *hamavdil, hamavdil, hamavdil* — the one who distinguishes. The entire passage is therefore a single *hoda'ah* and does not require *chatimah*, even though it is extensive in length.

This connects directly to the point Tosafot made earlier about *HaTov vehaMetiv*, which also lacks a closing *Baruch Atah* not because of its brevity but because it does not introduce genuinely new themes. For those of us accustomed to thinking of length as the trigger for requiring a closing *bracha*, this is a striking reorientation: it is thematic multiplicity, not length, that determines structural requirements. One might note that by this logic, the blessing at the conclusion of the *Megilla* reading could similarly be analyzed — Tosafot raises this as well, though we do in fact require a *chatimah* there, suggesting either a divergence from Ulla's principle or a determination that the themes are sufficiently distinct to warrant one.

---

## Shabbat Establishes

### Friday Meal Case

The *Gemara* now introduces the case of Rav Chananya bar Shelamya and the students of Rav, who were seated at a meal on Friday afternoon. Rav Hamnuna Saba was attending to them. They said to him: *zil chazi im ikadesh yoma* — go and see if the day has become sanctified, if it has grown dark — *v'nifsik v'nikbeiyeh l'Shabata* — and then we will interrupt and establish Shabbat. The phrase "establish Shabbat" is not entirely transparent here, but the context of the later discussion suggests they intended to stop the meal, recite *Birkat Hamazon*, perform something like the *siluk hashulchan* that appears in Rav Yehuda's approach, and then begin a new meal designated as the *Shabbat* meal.

### Shabata Kava

Rav Hamnuna Saba — the very attendant they were about to dispatch on this errand — instead addressed them with a halachic ruling: *lo tzarichitu* — you need not interrupt your meal and formally reconstitute it as a Shabbat meal. *Shabata kava nafshah* — Shabbat establishes itself.

What does it mean that Shabbat establishes itself? Taken literally, this might suggest one need do nothing at all — the meal automatically becomes a *Seudat Shabbat* without any intervention, akin to the position of Rabbi Yossi. The *Gemara*'s subsequent discussion makes clear that the *Rishonim* do not read it that way. Rather, the meaning is that Shabbat's arrival is sufficient to transform the ongoing meal into a *Seudat Shabbat* — one need not stop, bench, and restart — but the obligation to make *Kiddush* remains. The meal becomes a *Seudat Shabbat* by virtue of Shabbat's arrival, and a *Seudat Shabbat* demands *Kiddush*. The practice of *poreis mapa u'mekadesh* is thus the appropriate response: you do not restart the meal, but you do make *Kiddush*.

### Ma'aser Parallel

*D'amar Rav* — the source for this principle is a ruling of Rav: *keshem she'Shabbat kova'at l'ma'aser kach Shabbat kova'at l'kiddush* — just as Shabbat establishes for *ma'aser*, so Shabbat establishes for *kiddush*.

The *ma'aser* rule requires some explanation. Grain that has been harvested but has not yet undergone *gmar melacha* — the completion of processing, meaning it has been threshed, winnowed, mounded, and brought into the house — may be eaten *achilas arai*, as casual snacking, even before *trumos u'ma'asros* have been separated. Once *gmar melacha* is complete, such casual consumption is forbidden. The *Gemara* teaches that the onset of Shabbat functions as a trigger: because eating on Shabbat carries the character of a sit-down, enjoyment-oriented meal — *seudah* — rather than snacking, any eating done on Shabbat is automatically classified as formal eating rather than *achilas arai*, even if it would otherwise qualify as snacking. Shabbat therefore *establishes* the eating as something more significant than it might otherwise be.

The parallel Rav draws to *kiddush* is direct: just as Shabbat arrives and transforms the nature of eating, redefining even casual snacking as *Seudat Shabbat*, so too Shabbat arrives and takes the ongoing Friday meal and gives it a new identity as *Seudat Shabbat*. You were eating a Friday afternoon meal; Shabbat arrived; that meal is now a *Seudat Shabbat*. Tosafot sharpens the parallel: the *halacha* of *ma'aser* holds that if one was snacking on grain in the field Friday afternoon and Shabbat began, that very grain one was snacking on can no longer be eaten casually — even mid-meal, the arrival of Shabbat redefines what is happening. Similarly, even mid-meal on Friday afternoon, the arrival of Shabbat redefines the nature of the eating being done.

*Kova'at l'kiddush* — Shabbat establishes itself *for* kiddush, not instead of kiddush. As the *Gemara*'s phrasing makes clear, the obligation to make *kiddush* is not dissolved; rather, Shabbat's transformative power means the meal itself now demands *kiddush*, and that *kiddush* can be satisfied through *poreis mapa u'mekadesh* without reconstructing the meal from scratch.

### Kiddush Not Havdalah

One might reason by analogy: just as the beginning of Shabbat transforms the nature of eating and establishes an obligation of *kiddush*, the end of Shabbat should similarly transform the nature of the meal — one who is eating *shalosh seudot* as Shabbat departs should find that meal automatically reclassified as weekday eating, which would then require *havdalah* before continuing. *Savar minah* — this inference seemed compelling. But Rav Amram reports: *hachi amar Rav, le'kiddush kova'as ve'lo le'havdalah kova'as* — Rav says explicitly that Shabbat establishes only for *kiddush* at the entry, not for *havdalah* at the exit. And this is the ruling we follow — if it were otherwise, one could never complete *shalosh seudot* past nightfall.

The asymmetry requires explanation, and the *Gemara* will address it later. At this point the practical consequence is clear: the ongoing *seudat Shabbat* is not disrupted by nightfall and does not require an interruption for *havdalah*. The meal retains its Shabbat character and may continue.

It is worth noting that this ruling simultaneously rejects two positions. It rejects Rabbi Yossi's view, which would have allowed the Friday meal to continue into Shabbat with no intervention whatsoever — since Rav's ruling establishes that *kiddush* is indeed required once Shabbat begins. And it rejects the stricter view that would have required one to stop the *shalosh seudot*, interrupt for *havdalah*, and only then continue eating.

### Kiddush Required

Lest the principle of *shabata kava nafshah* be misread as obviating *kiddush* entirely, the *Gemara* clarifies: *hani mili le'inyan mifsek de'lo mafsekinan* — this principle that Shabbat establishes itself operates only with respect to the requirement to interrupt. One need not stop the meal and reconstitute it. *Aval atchulei lo matchalinan* — but one may not begin eating on Saturday night without first making *havdalah*. The two obligations are parallel: the same way one may not begin eating on Shabbat night without *kiddush*, one may not begin eating on *Motzei Shabbat* without *havdalah*. Rav Soloveitchik has a full discussion of this parallel. The underlying logic appears to be that *kiddush* and *havdalah* serve to mark the boundaries of *Seudat Shabbat*, investing the eating with the identity of the day. *Kiddush* designates what follows as *Seudat Shabbat*; *havdalah* demarcates the eating from that point forward as weekday eating, distinguishing it from *Seudat Shabbat* at the boundary line.

---

## Eating Rules

### Before Havdalah

*Aval atchulei lo matchalinan* — one may not begin eating after dark without *havdalah*. This is an important practical ruling that is not always observed with sufficient care. *U-mifsak nami lo amrinan ella be'achilah* — the permission to continue eating without interruption applies only to eating; *aval be'shtiyah lo* — if one was merely drinking (not eating a meal), drinking does not carry the same status, and one would need to interrupt. *U-ve'shtiyah nami lo amrinan ella be'chamra ve'shichra* — and the rule about drinking applies specifically to wine and beer. *Aval maya leis lan bah* — but water is not a problem; water may be drunk even after nightfall before *havdalah*.

In summary: one may not begin eating once it is dark, because one must make *havdalah* before eating. One who was already in the middle of a Shabbat meal may continue eating but not drinking. Water alone may be drunk even without *havdalah*. Other beverages — milk and similar liquids — presumably are treated like wine and beer: they do not carry the continuity privilege of an ongoing meal, and one may not begin drinking them before *havdalah*. The legal category is apparently the formal starting of a meal with *Hamotzi*.

### Mincha Ma'ariv Eating

Tosafot raises an important question about the temporal framing of *shalosh seudot*. The *Gemara* here seems to assume that one can begin *shalosh seudot* after *Mincha*, even close to nightfall. Yet our *minhag* is not to begin eating between *Mincha* and *Ma'ariv*. Tosafot notes that Rabbeinu Tam took strong exception to Rabbeinu Meshullam, who apparently instituted the practice of eating between *Mincha* and *Ma'ariv*: *ka'as al Rabbeinu Meshullam she-hinhig le'echol bein Mincha l'Ma'ariv*. The *Midrash* states: *ha-shoteh mayim be'Shabbat bein hashmashos gozel et krovav ha-metim* — one who drinks water on Shabbat during *bein hashmashos* robs from the waters belonging to his deceased relatives. And Tosafot records that in the town of Lutier, those who ate between *Mincha* and *Ma'ariv* encountered *sakana* — danger — a report that Rabbeinu Tam apparently connected to this ruling.

### Dead & Waters

The reference to robbing the dead of their waters during *bein hashmashos* opens onto a dimension of this discussion that goes beyond formal *halacha*. There is a mystical understanding according to which the deceased are granted a reprieve from the fires of *Gehinnom* for the duration of Shabbat. That reprieve extends not merely until three stars appear but until the community has concluded its prayers and made *havdalah*. Under this understanding, there are two related concerns: first, that one should deliberately postpone *havdalah* in order to extend the deceased's day of relief; and second, that consuming water before *havdalah* constitutes a form of taking for oneself the waters in which the deceased are, so to speak, cooling themselves — *gozel et krovav ha-metim*.

This framework also bears on the question of *Kaddish*, which relates to the *nishamos* of the deceased, and on the *minhag* of *Tziduk Hadin* recited on *Motzei Shabbat*, connected to the tradition that Moshe Rabbeinu died at the departure of Shabbat during *bein hashmashos*. A *Gaon* cited by the Rosh notes further customs of that period: not to deliver a public lecture — *midrash* — between the *tefillos* of Shabbat afternoon and evening, *mishum de'chacham she-meis beis midrasho biteilim*, and more broadly the cessation of certain activities during this transitional time.

The practical *halachic* question embedded here is: from which moment does the prohibition against beginning to eat take effect — from *shkia* or from *tzeis hakochavim*? Tosafot does not resolve this cleanly, and the mystical considerations are woven through the discussion in a way that makes it difficult to separate the purely *halachic* from the *agadic*. Rabbeinu Tam's severity regarding the town of Lutier suggests these concerns were very real to the *Rishonim* and not merely rhetorical devices to encourage compliance.

The Rashbam adds a further distinction worth noting. In the passage *lo kapya mayya k'mi havdalah aval k'mi kiddusha kapya* — those who were lenient about water before *havdalah* on *Motzei Shabbat* would nonetheless be strict about it before *kiddush* on Friday night, *mishum kavod Shabbat*, and *ve'hachi hilchasa* — this is the operative ruling. Whatever leniency one might permit regarding water before *havdalah*, there is no comparable debate with respect to the entry of Shabbat and *kiddush*. Water before *kiddush* is not permitted, and the Rashbam states that this is the accepted *halacha*.

---

## Late Kiddush

### Ravina's Question

*Ba'ei minei Ravina me'Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* — Ravina asked Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: *mi she'lo kiddesh be'erev Shabbat mahu she'yekadesh al kol hayom kulo* — if one forgot to make *kiddush* on *erev Shabbat*, may one make *kiddush* throughout the entire following day? The question, as framed, concerns whether the Friday night *kiddush* — the full *kiddush* of *Mekadesh HaShabbat* — may be recited on Shabbat morning if one omitted it the previous night.

The phrasing *mi she'lo kiddesh be'erev Shabbat*, rather than *be'leilei Shabbat*, is worth pausing over. *Erev Shabbat* means the eve of Shabbat itself. The Rambam understands *kiddush* as a demarcation of the transition point, designating the beginning of Shabbat. *Kiddush* need not be made at the precise moment Shabbat begins; it functions to mark the opening of the day, and this demarcation can occur roughly around the beginning. By the Rambam's reasoning, *kiddush* does not inherently constitute *kabbalat Shabbat* — it is not the act by which Shabbat is accepted, but rather the act by which the beginning of Shabbat is formally designated. This means, for example, that one may make *kiddush* on Friday afternoon before Shabbat formally begins, and similarly that *havdalah* may be recited before *shkia* — without the *ner*, obviously — anytime from *Plag HaMincha* onward. This is in fact the operative *halacha*, though one should not do so unless there is pressing need, such as a *devar mitzvah*.

Ravina's question, then, could extend beyond the simple scenario of "can I make *kiddush* on Shabbat morning?" It could also be asking about a case where midnight has already passed — where it is no longer *erev Shabbat* even in the loose sense of "around the beginning" — whether *kiddush* may still be made at that point.

### Parallel to Havdalah

*Amar lei* — Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds by drawing a parallel. *Mi de'amar lei* — since it is established that the children of Rabbi Chiya say: *mi she'lo hivdil be'Motzei Shabbat mavdil v'holech kol hashavua kulo* — if one failed to make *havdalah* on *Motzei Shabbat*, one may make *havdalah* throughout the week, specifically through Tuesday night. The principle is that although ideally *havdalah* belongs to the boundary moment of *Motzei Shabbat*, if it was missed it can be discharged later — it has an extension period. *Hach nami* — so too, one who failed to make *kiddush on erev Shabbat* may make *kiddush* throughout the entire day of Shabbat.

The parallel produces a striking theoretical scenario: if one forgot *kiddush* entirely and then also extended *shalosh seudot* into very late Shabbat afternoon, one could conceivably make *kiddush* at that point and then, moments later, make *havdalah*. A good exam question: when can one make *kiddush* and two minutes later make *havdalah*? The answer: late Shabbat afternoon, having failed to make *kiddush* the previous night, and then *Plag HaMincha* arrives and *havdalah* becomes permissible.

### Tosefta Objection

*Esvei* — an objection is raised from a *Tosefta*: *leilei Shabbat v'leilei Yom Tov yesh bahen kiddush al ha-kos v'yesh bahen hazkara b'Birkat Hamazon* — the nights of Shabbat and *Yom Tov* have *kiddush* on the cup and have the mention of Shabbat or *Yom Tov* in *Birkat Hamazon*. *Shabbat v'Yom Tov* — during the day of Shabbat and *Yom Tov*, *ein bahen kiddush al ha-kos* — there is no *kiddush* on a cup; one makes *Borei Pri HaGafen* but not a formal *bracha* of *Mekadesh HaShabbat*. *V'yesh bahen hazkara b'Birkat Hamazon* — but the mention of Shabbat in *Birkat Hamazon* does still apply. If it were possible to make the Friday night *kiddush* on Shabbat day, then the *Tosefta*'s statement that there is no *kiddush* on the cup during the day would be false — one could always find oneself in such a case, having forgotten the night before.

### Normal Cases

The *Gemara* dismisses this objection straightforwardly: *amar lei, d'ei lo lo tana* — the *Tosefta* is not speaking of unusual cases. As a rule, one makes *kiddush* on the night of Shabbat and *Yom Tov*, not on the day; the *Tosefta* describes the normal situation. The unusual scenario where one has forgotten — and therefore may still make *kiddush* during the day — is not the subject of the *Tosefta*'s formulation. The *Gemara*'s ruling stands: *bedieved*, if one did not make *kiddush* on Friday night, one may still do so on Shabbat day.

---

## Kiddush Priority

### Kvod Yom & Lyla

A further question: *kvod yom v'kvod layla* — if one has limited resources and must choose between a superior Friday night meal and a superior Shabbat day meal, which takes precedence? The ruling is *kvod yom kodem* — the honor of the day takes precedence. One should invest more in the Shabbat day meal. This reflects the halachic recognition that the day of Shabbat carries its own distinctive significance, amplified by considerations from *Kabbalistic* tradition.

But what if one has only a single cup of wine? The *Gemara* rules: *omer alav kiddush hayom mipnei she'kiddush hayom kodem l'kvod yom* — one uses that cup on Friday night for *kiddush*, because the *kiddush* of Shabbat takes priority even over the honor-of-day principle that would otherwise favor the daytime meal. The word *kiddush hayom* here refers to the Friday night *kiddush* — the sanctification of Shabbat — not to the daytime *kiddush*. The question was whether to use the single cup of wine for *kiddush* on Friday night or to save it for the Shabbat day meal, making the meal more festive. The ruling is to use it for *kiddush*.

### Proper Time

*V'ei issa* — but if it were truly possible to make the Friday night *kiddush* during the day, one could save the single cup, use it for both the day meal and the *kiddush*, and achieve two outcomes with one cup. Why not adopt this strategy? The *Gemara* answers: *amar lei, chaviva mitzvah b'sha'atah* — a *mitzvah* is dear in its proper time. Even though *bedieved* one may make *kiddush* during the day, the ideal performance of the *mitzvah* is at its designated time. We do not deliberately defer a *mitzvah* from its proper moment to achieve an economy of means. *Kiddush* belongs to Friday night; the love and urgency with which Shabbat is greeted — the eagerness of its arrival — is expressed precisely by performing *kiddush* at that moment, not by manipulating it for convenience.

### Havdalah Economy

The *Gemara* then raises an apparent contradiction from the *Havdalah* case: *ve-hatanya* — a *Braisa* teaches that if one arrives home on *Motzei Shabbat* from *shul* — having already said *havdalah* in *Shmoneh Esrei*, which however does not discharge the *havdalah* that permits eating — and has only one cup of wine, one places it aside until after the meal: *menicho ad achar hamazon*, *u-meshalshelan kullan le-acharav* — one eats, benches, and only then says *havdalah* over the wine, chaining it onto *Birkat Hamazon*. The single cup serves both: after *Birkat Hamazon*, one recites *Borei Pri HaGafen* and flows directly into *havdalah*.

But here we *are* manipulating things to achieve two for the price of one, and we *are* permitting eating before *havdalah* in order to make this work. Why is *chaviva mitzvah b'sha'atah* not invoked here? Why don't we say: make *havdalah* immediately on the single cup of wine, don't worry about having wine for *Birkat Hamazon*, and do the *mitzvah* at its proper time? The *Gemara* is pointing out that we explicitly do not apply that principle in the *havdalah* case — we permit a delay, permit eating before *havdalah*, and arrange for the *havdalah* to follow *Birkat Hamazon*, all in order to use the single cup for both purposes. This apparently undermines the argument made for *kiddush*.

---

## Ayulei vs. Apukei

### Ayulei Yoma

*Shani lan bein ayulei yoma le-afukei yoma* — there is a fundamental distinction between ushering in the day and ushering it out. With respect to *ayulei yoma* — bringing in Shabbat — *kol kamma de-makdeminan leh adif u-mechabevinan leh*: the earlier we perform *kiddush*, the better, and we demonstrate our love for Shabbat by that eagerness. When Shabbat begins, one wants to show that one is embracing it, greeting it, declaring immediately that it has arrived. To postpone *kiddush* — to hold the cup of wine in reserve for the next day — would communicate the opposite: that one is not rushing to affirm Shabbat's arrival. *Chaviva mitzvah b'sha'atah* therefore has full force on the entry side. One does not defer *kiddush* even for a practical benefit.

### Apukei Yoma

With *apukei yoma* — sending Shabbat out — the calculus is reversed. *Machrinan leh ki heichi de'lo lehavei alan tituna* — we deliberately postpone *havdalah* so that Shabbat's departure should not feel like a burden being lifted, like we are rushing to be rid of it. There is an affirmative value in not hurrying Shabbat's conclusion. This connects to the general principle of extending Shabbat at its close — *tosefet Shabbat* at the outgoing end — and to the practice of lighting *Hanukkah* candles before making *havdalah* on *Motzei Shabbat*, which similarly signals that we are not eager to end Shabbat. The value of *chaviva mitzvah b'sha'atah* thus does not apply symmetrically: at entry, we press forward; at exit, we hold back.

### Havdalah Delay

This asymmetry justifies the strategic arrangement of the single-cup scenario on *Motzei Shabbat*: eat first, bench, and then make *havdalah* afterward — *menicho ad achar hamazon*. The delay is not mere convenience; it reflects the positive value of not rushing to conclude Shabbat. The *Borei Pri HaGafen* recited after *Birkat Hamazon* serves double duty, flowing directly into *havdalah*. One practical question: does the introductory paragraph of *havdalah* need to be said? Even without it, the arrangement works. And the meal one ate before *havdalah* is covered by the *bedieved* principle that if one has already eaten, *havdalah* can still be performed and is still valid — a point the *Gemara* will make explicit in the following section.

The same principle — that we are lenient about *havdalah* at the exit but strict about *kiddush* at the entry — is also why one who forgot *kiddush* on Friday night is told to make it on Shabbat day: *bedieved* it is valid, but every effort should have been made to perform it on Friday night, because *ayulei yoma* demands eagerness.

---

## Shemea Mina

### Havdalah on Cup

*Shema mina mehamasnisa tamni* — from this *Braisa* about coming home on *Motzei Shabbat* and having only one cup, eight things may be inferred. The first: *shema mina hamavdil be'tefila tzarich lehavdil al ha-kos* — one who has said *havdalah* in the *tefila* — in *Shmoneh Esrei* — must still say *havdalah* on a cup of wine. This is self-evidently implied by the *Braisa*: the person coming home from *shul* has already said *havdalah* in the *Shmoneh Esrei*, yet the *Braisa* describes him as needing to say *havdalah* at home. The *havdalah* in *davening* does not discharge the obligation; the *havdalah* that is *matir achila* must be said over the cup.

### Bracha Teuna Kos

The second inference: *shema mina bracha teuna kos* — *Birkat Hamazon* must be recited over a cup of wine. This is built into the very logic of the arrangement. The entire reason for deferring *havdalah* until after the meal — for eating first, benching, and then making *havdalah* — is that the cup of wine will be used for *Birkat Hamazon* as well. If *Birkat Hamazon* did not require a *kos*, there would be no reason to arrange things this way. The fact that the *Braisa* describes this strategic delay makes sense only if *Birkat Hamazon* requires a *kos shel bracha*.

### Minimum Shiur

The third inference: *kos shel bracha tzarich shiur* — the cup of blessing requires a minimum measure. If there were no minimum measure, one could solve the single-cup problem by pouring tiny amounts into two separate vessels and using each independently. The very fact that the *Braisa* treats this as a genuine problem — requiring a creative solution — implies that a *kos* must contain a minimum amount, which is a *revi'is*.

### Tasting Required

The fourth inference: *ha-mevarech tzarich she'yitom* — the one making the *bracha* must taste from the wine. This addresses a further potential solution: why not make *havdalah* over the cup, complete the *bracha*, and then set the wine aside untouched for *Birkat Hamazon*? If the person reciting the *bracha* were not required to drink from the wine, this would be a workable strategy. The fact that the *Braisa* does not contemplate it — and instead requires the elaborate arrangement of deferring *havdalah* — proves that tasting is obligatory. Tosafot notes that it need not be specifically the *mevarech* who drinks; someone present must taste. This reflects the tension between the *kos shel bracha*'s function as a *kos* designated for the *bracha* and the *birchat hanehen* dimension of the *Borei Pri HaGafen* recited over it.

### Tasting Disqualifies

The fifth inference: *ta'amo pagmo* — once one has tasted from the wine, the remaining wine in the cup is no longer usable for another *bracha*. This too follows from the logic of the *Braisa*. One might propose: have a *revi'is* and a half, drink a small amount for *havdalah*, and use the remainder for *Birkat Hamazon*. The *Braisa* does not suggest this solution, which implies it is unavailable. Once a sip has been taken, the remainder in the cup has been *pogem* — rendered unfit for use as a *kos shel bracha* in another context. Whether adding more wine to the cup would rehabilitate it is a further question; what is clear is that the wine remaining after tasting is treated as disqualified.

### Havdalah After Eating

The sixth inference: *ta'am mavdil* — *havdalah* is valid even after one has already eaten. The entire scenario of the *Braisa* involves a person who eats before making *havdalah* on the cup — because the single cup is being held in reserve for *Birkat Hamazon* and *havdalah* together. This *bedieved* scenario is presented without criticism of the eating itself (beyond the acknowledgment that one is not supposed to eat before *havdalah*), and *havdalah* is still performed and still valid at the end. The inference is clear: if one has eaten before *havdalah*, whether intentionally or not, one may still make *havdalah* afterward and discharge the obligation.

### Minyan Requirement

The seventh inference — that *Birkat Hamazon* requires a *kos* — invites Tosafot's important qualification. Tosafot observes: *ktzat mashma de'afilu be'yachid teuna kos* — the *Braisa* implies that even an individual benching alone requires a cup, since *ha-nichnas* — the person arriving home in the *Braisa* — appears to be alone. Tosafot then works through the question and concludes, tentatively, that perhaps the requirement applies specifically when there is a quorum of three. Yet Tosafot acknowledges that the straightforward reading of the *Gemara* — *shema mina bracha teuna kos* — suggests the requirement applies to any individual. In practice, of course, we do not regularly bench on a cup unless there is a *minyan* present. The gap between the *pshat* of the *Gemara* and common practice is notable. The reasoning offered by way of analogy — *ein omrim shira ela al ha-yayin*, that song requires wine — connects *Birkat Hamazon* to the category of formal, elevated religious expression that demands a cup. The full development of how this practice evolved, and why it is limited in practice to a *minyan*, remains a discussion for the *Rishonim*. To be continued.

---

---

# Pesachim 106

## One Cup Dilemma

### One Cup Setup

The daf opens in the midst of an extended discussion about *kiddush* and *havdalah*. The scenario under examination involves a person who arrives home on *motzaei Shabbat* with only a single *kos* of wine. He faces a dilemma: that cup is needed for *birkat hamazon*, yet he also needs it for *havdalah*. Tosafot permits him to eat his meal first — eating before *havdalah* — precisely so that he may have the cup available at the conclusion of *birkat hamazon*. He then proceeds to use that one cup for both *birkat hamazon* and *havdalah*.

### Eight Lessons

The Gemara derives a series of lessons from this *baraita*. Among the most significant: first, *birkat hamazon* requires a cup of wine, for if it did not, the scenario would present no difficulty in the first place. Tosafot notes that the plain reading implies this applies even when an individual recites *birkat hamazon* alone, without the presence of three or ten participants — though this is not standard contemporary practice.

Second, there must be a minimum required amount of wine — a *revi'it* — because if there were no minimum, one could simply divide the single cup into two cups and use each for a separate purpose.

Third, taking even a small sip of the wine from a cup renders the remainder *pagum* — unfit for ritual use — because otherwise one could simply sip a little for *birkat hamazon* and use the remainder for *havdalah*.

Fourth, the person making the blessing must actually drink from the cup, since if drinking were not required, the problem of *pagum* would never arise.

The Gemara further derives that two *kedushot* may be recited over a single cup — meaning *birkat hamazon* and *havdalah* may share one *kos* — and while the principle of *mitzvot chavilot chavilot* (bundling separate ritual acts onto a single vessel) is generally a concern, when no alternative exists, a single cup may serve both. Additionally, the Gemara identifies the *baraita*'s author as representing the position of Beit Shammai according to Rabbi Yehuda, on the basis of the order in which the *havdalah* blessings appear — fire (*aish*) before spices (*besamim*) — which is the reverse of our practice and corresponds to the Beit Shammai position in the earlier dispute about that order.

Finally, the *baraita* teaches that *ta'am mavdil* — the fact that he ate before *havdalah* — does not disqualify him from making *havdalah* afterward, at least in this permitted scenario.

### Rav Ashi's Logic

Rav Ashi raises a pointed observation. The Gemara had suggested that two separate lessons could be derived from the *baraita*: (1) that tasting wine renders the remainder *pagum* even if a sufficient quantity remains, and (2) that a minimum *shiur* of wine is required for a *kos shel beracha*. Rav Ashi argues that these are not two independent teachings but rather one unified concern — *chada milta hi*. The *baraita* may simply be describing a case where there is precisely a *revi'it* and nothing more. If so, when the person takes a sip, the remainder falls below the required *shiur*. There is no proof that the act of tasting creates any independent *pagum* status on wine that exceeds the minimum amount.

Tosafot clarifies that Rav Ashi does not necessarily dispute the underlying *halacha* of *pagum* — the Rashbam believes he does — but his point is that the *baraita* alone cannot establish it. The *baraita* does not indicate that the cup contained more than exactly a *revi'it*, so the only principle proven is the requirement for a minimum amount.

---

## Pagum Wine

### Stringent Authorities

The Gemara proceeds to discuss the practical scope of *pagum*. Rav Yaakov bar Idi was careful not to use a *chatzra* — a pitcher — that had been drunk from. Rav Idi bar Shisha was careful about a *kasa* — a cup — that had been drunk from. Mar bar Rav Ashi was careful even about a *chavita* — a barrel — that had been drunk from.

### What Pagum Means

The concept of *pagum* requires careful definition. At first glance one might think this concerns the principle of *mitzvot chavilot chavilot* — that once a vessel has been used for one *mitzvah* it cannot be used for another. But that is not the correct understanding. The issue is specifically that someone drank directly from the container. Once a person drinks directly from a pitcher, cup, or barrel, whatever remains in that container cannot be used for a ritual act, even if the quantity remains sufficient and even if the initial drinking had nothing whatsoever to do with any *mitzvah*. A person who tastes wine from a barrel to assess its quality — entirely outside any ritual context — has nonetheless rendered the remaining contents *pagum*.

The critical distinction is between drinking directly from a container and pouring from it. If one pours wine from a bottle into a cup and drinks from the cup, only the wine remaining in the cup becomes *pagum*; the wine in the bottle is entirely unaffected. Similarly — as other passages in the Gemara make clear — if before drinking one recites *borei pri hagafen* and pours into a smaller cup, the original container does not become *pagum*. The concern is therefore localized entirely to the container from which one drank directly.

The cases involving a pitcher and a barrel do present an imaginable scenario: one might come to a wine cellar, recite *kiddush* over a barrel, then open a tap and taste a bit. Even in that case, Mar bar Rav Ashi holds that what remains in the barrel has been rendered *pagum*.

The wine does not become prohibited for drinking by others — it may be consumed normally — but it may not be used by anyone, neither the original drinker nor anyone else, for *kiddush* or *havdalah*.

### Tosafot Bedieved

The Rashbam notes that the language used for these authorities is *kapid* — "was careful" — which sounds like a personal stringency rather than a firm ruling. Tosafot cites the Rashbam's view that this stringency applies only *lechatchila*, and that *bedieved* a *pagum* cup may be used. Tosafot then challenges this: if it is only a *lechatchila* concern, why did the Gemara need to permit eating the entire meal before *havdalah* to ensure the cup remained unused? Tosafot ultimately concludes that the concern is genuinely *bedieved* in nature, not merely a *lechatchila* preference — and that the Rashbam's reading is therefore difficult to maintain. Nevertheless, Tosafot adds a striking caveat: *mihu ra'uy Rashbam lismoch alav b'sha'at hadechak* — in a time of pressing need, it is appropriate to rely on the Rashbam's position. This is a remarkable statement about a near-contemporary authority: not a full agreement, yet a recognition that his view may serve as a legitimate basis in difficult circumstances.

### Yerushalmi Fix

A solution to the problem of a *pagum* cup appears not in the Bavli but in the Yerushalmi, quoted by the Rosh in *siman* 11. The Rosh writes: *uv'Yerushalmi mashma dekos pagum marbeh alav kol shehu umachshiro va'afilu b'mayim yachol letakno* — from the Yerushalmi it appears that a *pagum* cup may be restored by adding even a small amount to it, and even water suffices to fix it.

The logic is that by adding even a tiny amount, the cup is no longer one that was directly drunk from — it has received something new, and its status is thereby restored as fresh wine. Notably, one need not add back the precise quantity that was removed; any addition suffices to reconstitute the cup's identity.

This immediately raises a question: why did the Gemara not suggest this solution in the original scenario? Why not allow the person to drink a sip for *birkat hamazon*, add a drop of liquid, and then use the restored cup for *havdalah*? The Rosh addresses this: the wine in that case was already fully diluted to the maximum permissible ratio, and no additional water could be added without disqualifying it as wine. With no other wine available to add, the fix was unavailable.

### Practical Method

The Yerushalmi's principle is the basis for standard practice. After making *havdalah* and drinking a portion of the cup, one adds a drop of wine to the remaining contents and pours it back into the bottle. This restores the cup's status, so the returned wine is not considered *pagum*.

A subtle point must be observed, however. The logical direction of the restoration matters. One must add wine *into* the *kos* — bringing new wine to the container that was drunk from — and then pour the combined contents back into the bottle. One may not simply pour the *pagum* remnant from the *kos* back into the bottle, because that would be moving the *pagum* wine into the bottle rather than restoring the *kos* itself. Pouring *pagum* wine into a bottle creates a question of *rov* — if the bottle's wine constitutes the majority, the mixture may be acceptable *bedieved*, but *lechatchila* this approach is not followed. The proper practice is the reverse: pour fresh wine into the *kos*, thereby restoring it, and then return everything to the bottle.

The question of dilution that arose in antiquity — the Gemara's presumption that wine was routinely mixed with water in a three-to-one ratio — should not be confused with questions about alcohol percentage. The relevant measure is the proportion of original wine content relative to added water, not the strength of the drink.

---

## Sources & Foundations

### Zachor Source

A *baraita* now addresses the biblical basis for *kiddush* on wine. The verse *Zachor et yom haShabbat l'kadsho* — Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it — is interpreted as *zachrehu al hayayin b'knisato*: declare and commemorate it over wine at its entry. From this the *baraita* derives the obligation to recite *kiddush* over wine.

### Day vs. Night

The *baraita* initially reads the verse as establishing a daytime obligation — *yom haShabbat* — and asks how we know the obligation applies at night as well. The Gemara then reverses course: the primary logic actually points to *kiddush* at night, because it is at the entry of *Shabbat*, the moment of sanctification, that one declares its identity. The verse's reference to "the day" provides a secondary, additional source for the daytime *kiddush*.

Rav Yehuda states that the daytime *kiddush* consists solely of *borei pri hagafen* — nothing more. The elaborate text we know from Friday night does not apply during the day.

### Rav Ashi Unsure

The Gemara records a remarkable incident involving Rav Ashi. He arrived in Mechuza, and those present asked him to make for them *Kiddusha Rabba* — the daytime *Shabbat* *kiddush*. Rav Ashi did not know what was meant by this phrase, nor apparently did he know the practice. A cup of wine was placed before him. He reasoned: any ritual act involving wine begins with *borei pri hagafen*, so he would begin there. He extended the recitation of *borei pri hagafen*, waiting for some cue, until he observed an elderly man leaning forward to drink — signaling that the *kiddush* was complete. Rav Ashi then quoted to himself the verse from *Kohelet*, *hechacham einav b'rosho* — the wise man has his eyes in his head — congratulating himself for having had the foresight to start with *borei pri hagafen* regardless.

The episode is striking on multiple levels. Here is Rav Ashi — one of the latest and most authoritative *amoraim* — apparently unacquainted with the very existence of daytime *Shabbat* *kiddush* as a distinct practice, and navigating a public ritual by reading the crowd rather than by announcing his uncertainty. It underscores just how much of the *halacha* of this period was still in flux and how heavily practices were observed and transmitted through direct observation of teachers and community customs.

### Vayechulu Origins

Tosafot raises a significant question about the nature of *Vayechulu*. The plain reading of various Gemaras is that *Vayechulu* is never recited as part of *kiddush* at home — it belongs exclusively to *tefillat maariv* of *Shabbat*. The Gemara establishes the practice of saying *Vayechulu* in *tefilla*, but there is no corresponding institution of *Vayechulu* over the *kos*.

Why then do we say *Vayechulu* at home at all? Tosafot explains: it is recited at home not as part of *kiddush* but as a substitute for those family members who did not daven *maariv* and therefore did not say *Vayechulu* within *shmoneh esrei*. The *takana* is that they should fulfill this recitation.

Why is *Vayechulu* said aloud in *shul* after *shmoneh esrei*? Because when *yom tov* falls on *Shabbat*, the *maariv* service uses *Atah Vechartanu* and *Vayechulu* is omitted from *shmoneh esrei*. To ensure that *Vayechulu* is said by everyone even in that scenario, the rabbis instituted saying it publicly after *shmoneh esrei*. And so that no distinction should be drawn between one *Shabbat* and another — since most weeks *Vayechulu* is said within *shmoneh esrei* — the practice was extended to every *Shabbat*.

The upshot is striking: *Vayechulu* is fundamentally part of *tefillat maariv*, not of *kiddush*. Its recitation at home serves an independent function of ensuring family members fulfill their *maariv* obligation. *Kiddush* itself is constituted by the *brachos* that *Chazal* instituted — *borei pri hagafen* and *mekadesh haShabbat* — not by the recitation of *psukim*. Just as the *mitzvah* of *sippur yetziat Mitzrayim* is fulfilled through the rabbinic *seder* rather than by simply reading the *psukim* in *Shemot*, so too the *mitzvah* of *zachrehu al hayayin* is fulfilled through the rabbinic *brachos*, not through the reading of *Vayechulu*.

Whether the wine itself is required *mid'oraita* is a separate question. Tosafot suggests that the entire requirement to recite *kiddush* on wine may be only an *asmachta*, though he entertains the possibility that the wine is genuinely a biblical requirement while the obligation to drink may be only rabbinic.

### Rambam View

The Rambam, in *perek* 29 of *Hilchot Shabbat*, rules unambiguously that the *mitzvat aseh* of *kiddush* is biblical: *zachor et yom haShabbat l'kadsho* — meaning one must remember it with words of praise and sanctification, *zechirat shevach v'kiddush*. Crucially, the Rambam extends this equally to *havdalah*: the verse requires remembrance *b'knisato b'kiddush hayom uv'yetziato b'havdalah* — at its entry through *kiddush*, and at its exit through *havdalah*. Thus the Rambam presents *kiddush* and *havdalah* as perfectly coequal *d'oraita* obligations, both derived from *Zachor et yom haShabbat*.

The Rambam further states that *kiddush al hayayin* and *havdalah al hayayin* are *midivrei sofrim* — rabbinic in origin — clearly the consensus position, even as the Rambam emphasizes the biblical status of the verbal obligations themselves.

Regarding *Vayechulu*, the Rambam describes its recitation before *kiddush* as *minhag pashut b'chol Yisrael* — the universal Jewish custom. Unlike Tosafot, who treats *Vayechulu* as categorically independent of *kiddush*, the Rambam's formulation integrates it closely: the custom is to recite *Vayechulu*, then *borei pri hagafen*, then *mekadesh haShabbat*, then drink a *m'lo lugmav*. The Rambam does not treat *Vayechulu* as a mere appendage; rather, the universal practice incorporates it as part of the *kiddush* experience, through which one may also fulfill one's *d'oraita* obligation.

---

## Postponing Havdalah

### Havdalah Timeline

A *baraita* quoted by the sons of Rabbi Chiya establishes that one who failed to make *havdalah* on *motzaei Shabbat* may make it up later in the week. Rabbi Zeira states that this window extends through Tuesday — *ad revii b'Shabbat*, meaning through the end of Tuesday — since Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday are halachically associated with the preceding *Shabbat*, while Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday are associated with the coming *Shabbat*. This is not merely an abstract framework; it has practical grounding in the laws of conditional *gittin*, where stipulations framed as "after *Shabbat*" are understood to apply through Tuesday and "before *Shabbat*" applies from Wednesday onward.

The idea that one may formally demarcate the conclusion of *Shabbat* on a Tuesday, after presumably having performed *melacha* and eaten normally for two days, is admittedly striking. Yet the halachic principle holds that the formal act of *havdalah* still carries significance as an act of demarcation even then.

### Fire Exception

Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi limits the above: the make-up *havdalah* applies to all the standard components except the blessing over fire. The *beracha* over *aish* may not be recited later in the week. The reason is that the kindling of fire is associated with a specific historical moment — the original creation of fire at the close of the first *Shabbat*. The blessing is meant to commemorate *techilat yetzirah shel ha'ur* at the moment it occurred, and that moment is *motzaei Shabbat* itself. While the other elements of *havdalah* function as acts of demarcation that remain meaningful throughout those early days of the week, the fire blessing is tied to a singular historical commemoration and cannot be separated from its original context.

### Hand Washing

Rav Bruna cites a ruling in the name of Rav: *hanotel yadav lo yekadesh* — one who has already washed his hands for a meal should not then make *kiddush*. According to the Rashbam, the concern is *hefsek*: having washed for *hamotzi*, one must proceed directly to bread, and reciting *borei pri hagafen* for *kiddush* in the interval would constitute an interruption. The Rashbam therefore holds that in this situation one should ideally hear *kiddush* from someone else; if no one else is available, one may have no choice but to wash again afterward.

---

## Washing & Kiddush

### Rav Yitzchak Challenge

Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta challenges Rav Bruna's ruling sharply. He declares: Rav is barely gone and we have already forgotten his teachings! He then testifies from his own extensive direct observation of Rav's practice.

The challenge is also an occasion to note how unusually rich the discussions on this daf are in *ma'aseh rav* — actual observed practices — as opposed to theoretical argumentation. Because *kiddush* and *havdalah* occur every single *Shabbat*, Sages had constant opportunity to observe what their teachers actually did, and those observations saturate these sugyas in a way that is far less common in other areas of *halacha*.

### Rav's Flexibility

Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta reports: *zimnin dechaviva leih rifta mekadesh arifta, zimnin dechaviva leih chamra mekadesh achamra* — sometimes when Rav was inclined toward bread he made *kiddush* on bread, and sometimes when he was inclined toward wine he made *kiddush* on wine. This testimony has a double significance: it apparently introduces the idea that *kiddush* may be made on bread — a notion that seems to contradict everything previously discussed about *kiddush* on wine — and it bears on the *hefsek* question.

### Rashbam Hefsek

The Rashbam reads the passage literally: Rav would sometimes wash his hands in preparation for bread, then change his mind and make *kiddush* on wine. The point of the testimony is that Rav would change course midway — washing for bread, then interposing *kiddush* on wine before proceeding to *hamotzi* — and this demonstrates that doing so is not an impermissible *hefsek*, at minimum *bedieved*. The Rashbam's reading preserves the concern of *hefsek* in principle while showing that Rav's practice establishes that it is not fatal.

### Tosafot B'Makom

Tosafot rejects both the literal reading and the Rashbam's explanation. Rabbeinu Tam argues that *kiddush* on bread is simply not possible — one cannot fulfill the obligation of *kiddush* with *hamotzi*. What then does the passage mean?

Tosafot reframes the entire episode by invoking a teaching from the very beginning of the *perek*: Rav held that *kiddush* does not require *makom seudah* — one may make *kiddush* without eating a meal immediately afterward. The phrase "made *kiddush* on bread" does not mean he recited the *kiddush* text over a loaf; it means that when Rav intended to have a meal with bread he would structure his *kiddush* in connection with that meal, and when he preferred wine alone he would make *kiddush* without the meal context.

More importantly, Tosafot argues that the concern raised by Rav Bruna was never about *hefsek* at all. Since for Rav one could make *kiddush* divorced from the meal, there was a genuine concern that after washing, a person might make *kiddush*, then decide to skip the meal entirely — rendering his *netilat yadayim* a *beracha l'vatala* (a blessing recited in vain). The testimony of Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta responds to that concern: Rav himself would wash and make *kiddush* without worrying that he might abandon the meal afterward. The issue was never *hefsek*.

### Ashkenazi Practice

Once the concern of *hefsek* is removed entirely, the practical ramification becomes clear. Tosafot states explicitly: for those who hold *ein kiddush ela b'makom seudah* — that *kiddush* must be in the context of a meal — the connection between the washing, the *kiddush*, and the bread is so tight that there is no conceivable *hefsek* problem at all, and no risk that the meal will be abandoned. Indeed, Tosafot identifies the *minhag* of the *Ashkenazim* — meaning specifically the German-Jewish *Yekke* custom — as washing *davka* first, then making *kiddush*, then reciting *hamotzi*. For those raised in a different custom, this sequence may seem counterintuitive or even problematic, but Tosafot's reading demonstrates its impeccable logic: *kiddush bimkom seudah* means that the hand washing, *kiddush*, and *hamotzi* form a single unified act, all bound together around the meal.

---

## Alt. Beverages

### Chamar Medina

Tosafot raises the question of *chamar medina* — a regional beverage. The Gemara elsewhere states that *havdalah* may be made over *chamar medina*, a drink consumed socially rather than merely for thirst. Beer or a similar beverage serves as the paradigmatic example. The defining characteristic is that people drink it in a social setting even when not thirsty — it is a beverage of social significance in its locale. The question Tosafot poses is whether this latitude extends to *kiddush* as well, given the Gemara's apparent flexibility in allowing bread for *kiddush* on one hand and *chamar medina* for *havdalah* on the other.

### Bread Asymmetry

Tosafot's analysis produces an asymmetry. Bread may be used for *kiddush* — at least according to those who permit it — but not for *havdalah*. The reason is rooted in the concept of *kiddush bimkom seudah*: *kiddush* is defined by its connection to the meal, and bread is the meal itself. The loaf over which one recites *hamotzi* and the *kiddush* function belong to the same act. *Havdalah*, by contrast, does not require *makom seudah*; it stands independently. Because bread's eligibility derives entirely from its role in defining the meal, it has no analogous function in *havdalah* and cannot serve there.

The converse holds for *chamar medina*: it may serve for *havdalah* but its use for *kiddush* is uncertain. The connection of *kiddush* to the meal may demand something more substantial — wine or bread — rather than a mere social beverage.

### Practical Shiur

Whatever beverage is used for *kiddush* or *havdalah*, the required *shiur* remains a *revi'it* — approximately three and a half ounces. The argument that the *shiur* should be proportional to what is normative for that particular beverage is very late and finds no support in the Gemara or *rishonim*, where the assumption throughout is a standard *revi'it*. A practical solution for those wishing to use *chamar medina* — particularly in scenarios such as the nine days when wine is restricted — is to prepare a mixed drink, such as juice and spirits. Three and a half ounces of a mixed drink is far more manageable than drinking that quantity of undiluted liquor.

### Grape Juice Issue

The status of commercially available pasteurized grape juice is genuinely problematic. While the Gemara does acknowledge that unfermented wine — even wine pressed that same day — retains the status of *yayin*, such wine remains capable of fermentation. Pasteurized grape juice has had that capacity eliminated. It may therefore fall entirely outside the halachic category of *yayin*. The analogy to *mevushal* wine is suggestive. A responsum of the *Tzitz Eliezer* famously points out that one should first ask whether grape juice qualifies for *borei pri hagafen* before asking whether it qualifies for *kiddush* — let alone whether reconstituted grape juice (produced by removing water content, shipping, and reconstituting) would qualify.

The practical upshot: one should be considerably more *makpid* regarding the use of grape juice on Friday night, when *kiddush* carries its primary weight. On *Shabbat* day, where *chamar medina* is in any case widely relied upon and the halachic standards are less stringent, grape juice may be more readily accepted.

---

## Eating Before

### Ta'am Dispute

The final topic of the daf concerns eating or tasting food before *kiddush* or *havdalah*. Rav Huna, citing Rav, rules: *ta'am eino mekadesh* — if one has tasted food, one may no longer make *kiddush*. The question posed to Rav Huna is whether *havdalah* follows the same rule: *ta'am mahu sheyavdil* — does tasting food preclude *havdalah* as well?

Rav Huna himself answers that *ta'am mavdil* — tasting does not prevent one from making *havdalah*. Rav Assi disagrees and holds that tasting disqualifies one from *havdalah* just as from *kiddush*.

The underlying logic of the debate tracks the structural differences between the two obligations. *Kiddush* is intimately connected to the meal through *kiddush bimkom seudah*: it defines the opening of the meal, and once eating has already begun, the significance of that demarcating function is lost. *Havdalah*, which carries no *makom seudah* requirement, has a looser connection to eating, and it may therefore remain valid even if one has incidentally tasted something.

### Yirmiah Case

The dispute plays out in a vivid anecdote. Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba came to the home of Rav Assi as a guest. Rabbi Yirmiyah absentmindedly ate something after nightfall — *ishtali v'ta'im midei* — and then *havdalah* was brought before him, which he proceeded to recite. Rav Assi's wife observed this and pointed out to her husband: but you, Master, do not do this — you hold that one who has tasted may not make *havdalah*. Rav Assi replied: leave him alone — *shavkei* — he follows his own *rebbe*, who is Rav Huna, and Rav Huna holds that *ta'am mavdil*. He is acting in accordance with his own tradition and that is entirely acceptable.

The detail that Rav Assi's wife was familiar with her husband's ruling — and recognized the discrepancy immediately — reflects just how often this situation must have arisen in practice and how closely domestic life tracked halachic reasoning.

### Final Rulings

Rav Yosef cites Shmuel: *ta'am eino mekadesh, ta'am eino mavdil* — tasting disqualifies for both *kiddush* and *havdalah*. Rabba cites Rav Nachman citing Shmuel — a different tradition from the same authority — as ruling: *ta'am mekadesh v'ta'am mavdil* — tasting does not disqualify for either. Rava then rules definitively: *hilchesa ta'am mekadesh v'ta'am mavdil* — the *halacha* follows the lenient position in both cases. *Bedieved*, if one has tasted food, one may still make *kiddush* or *havdalah* after the fact.

The daf thus concludes by returning to the structural tension that has animated much of the discussion: *kiddush* and *havdalah* share the prohibition against prior eating, yet their different relationships to the meal — *kiddush* as meal-defining through *bimkom seudah*, *havdalah* as independent of the meal — generate distinct analytical frameworks. That same distinction explains why bread serves *kiddush* but not *havdalah*, and why the question of *ta'am* generates the disputing traditions that Rava ultimately harmonizes in a single lenient ruling.

---

---

# Pesachim 108

## Pre-Seder Eating

### Opening & Context

The daf opens at the very bottom of 107b, marking a transition in the tractate: we have moved from the laws of *kiddush* and *havdalah* into the practical concerns of *erev haseder* itself.

### Mincha Ketana Rule

The *mishnah* states that one may not eat before nightfall, beginning from *mincha* onward. The *gemara*, as it has already reiterated at the opening of the *perek*, specifies that this refers to *mincha ketana* — that is, from approximately 3:30 in the afternoon, meaning the prohibition effectively begins at 3:00 p.m. The concern is straightforward: one must not arrive at the *seder* already full, since the appetite for *matzah* must be intact.

### Permitted Snacks

Certain snacks remain permitted even during this restricted period. The *gemara* refers to *minei targima* — light foods such as fruits and vegetables. According to Tosafot, even small amounts of *mezonot* that are *kosher l'pesach* might be permitted. The *gemara* also describes people who would partake of *b'nei me'ayim* — bits of the intestines that were to be used for the meat eaten that night — as a kind of pre-meal appetizer. This is not merely tolerated but may even be preferable, since it whets the appetite. The *gemara* supports this notion through a *pasuk* cited as a *zecher ladavar*: *niru lachem nir v'al tizre'u el kotzim* — "plow for yourselves a plowed field and do not plant among the thorns." Just as one must prepare the field before planting, one should prepare the stomach before eating, and a small amount of food accomplishes precisely that.

### Rava's Wine

The *gemara* continues: Rava would make a point of drinking wine every *erev pesach* — *rava hava shati chamra kol ma'ale yoma d'pischa* — specifically in order to whet his appetite so that he would eat *matzah* with greater desire that evening. As Rava himself explains: *minan amina lei d'chamra migrar garir* — from where do I know that wine draws the appetite? From the *mishnah*, as we will see.

### Extra Cups Proof

Rava derives his principle from the *mishnah*'s ruling that between the prescribed cups — between the first and second and between the second and third — one is permitted to drink additional wine: *bein hakosot halalu im ratza lishtot yishte*. The question Rava presses is this: if wine were actually satiating, why would additional cups be permitted before the eating of *matzah*? Drinking between the first and second cup could fill one up before the *matzah* of *hamotzi*, and drinking between the second and third cup could impair one's appetite for the *matzah* of *afikoman*. The fact that the *mishnah* permits this extra drinking demonstrates that wine does not satiate but rather stimulates the appetite — *migrar garir*.

### 3rd–4th Cup Ban

This raises an obvious question: if wine whets the appetite, why is drinking between the third and fourth cups prohibited — *bein shlishi l'revi'i lo yishte*? Here the *gemara* shifts to a different concern entirely. The Rashbam explains that once *birkat hamazon* has been recited over the third cup, there is no further need to stimulate the appetite, since the primary *matzah* obligations have already been fulfilled. Accordingly, the *gemara* offers two reasons for the prohibition on drinking between the third and fourth cups. First, the Rashbam: *lo sharina lei dimichzei k'mosif al hakosot* — at that point, additional drinking merely looks like adding to the four cups with no justification, since the appetite-whetting purpose is no longer operative. Second, from the Yerushalmi: *kedei shelo yishtaker* — so that one should not become drunk and thereby be incapable of completing *hallel* at the end of the *seder*. The Yerushalmi itself then raises a counterpoint: has one not already become drunk from the wine consumed during the meal? The answer is that drinking during a meal, when the stomach is occupied with food, does not produce the same intoxicating effect as drinking after a meal on an empty stomach.

It is worth noting the character of this entire discussion. The arguments about whether wine whets or satiates the appetite are treated as logical and *halachic* in nature rather than empirical — a reminder that in the *gemara*'s framework, legal analysis and conceptual reasoning operate independently of observed physiological fact.

### Rav Sheshet Fast

The *gemara* records that Rav Sheshet would fast every *erev pesach*: *rav sheshet havai yativ b'tanisa kol ma'ale yoma d'pischa*. On first reading, one might assume this reflects an extreme stringency regarding the concern about appetite — that he did not believe that a small amount of eating was beneficial and simply refrained entirely.

### Korban Distraction

The *gemara* however entertains a different explanation. Perhaps Rav Sheshet held that the *mishnah*'s prohibition begins from *mincha gedola* — noon — and that the reason is not hunger but rather distraction from bringing the *korban pesach*: one must not be preoccupied with eating when the time for the offering has arrived. This would explain fasting from midday onward, though it leaves unexplained why he fasted the entire day. The *gemara* resolves this by citing the opinion of Ben Betira, who held that the *korban pesach* slaughtered in the morning of the fourteenth — *b'arba'asa lishmo* — is valid *bedieved*, because the entire day is in some sense fit for the *korban pesach*. Rav Sheshet would adopt the interpretive tradition that *bein ha'arbayim* refers not to the afternoon hours but to the period between the night of the thirteenth and the night of the fourteenth — meaning the entire day of the fourteenth — and therefore the concern about distraction from the *korban pesach* applies from the earliest hours of the day. This is a striking reading, and the *gemara* itself notes its strangeness on multiple levels: that the prohibition would apply even nowadays after the *churban*, that it would extend to the hours that are only *bedieved* valid for the *korban pesach*, and that even the smallest amount of eating would constitute distraction sufficient to trigger the prohibition.

Ultimately the *gemara* rejects this whole line of reasoning: *amri lo* — no, that was not Rav Sheshet's motivation at all. The answer is simply: *shani rav sheshet d'istnis havai* — Rav Sheshet was different because he was exceptionally finicky. For him, *de'ei ta'im b'zafra midi l'orsa lo havai mahani lei mikhla* — if he tasted even the smallest amount of food in the morning, he would have no interest in eating even come evening time. It was purely a matter of individual temperament, not a general ruling.

### Tosafot Nuance

Tosafot adds an important clarification regarding the nature of Rav Sheshet's practice. The phrase *havai yativ b'tanisa* — that he would sit in a fast — need not be taken literally to mean that he formally accepted a *ta'anis* upon himself. It may simply mean *shome'a atzmo mil'echol* — that he was careful not to eat. Alternatively, Tosafot suggests, he may have formally accepted a fast upon himself as a practical aid to memory, *kedei sheyisga v'yizaker mil'echol*, to help ensure he would not inadvertently eat. It is in this context that Tosafot introduces, almost as an aside, the famous custom of the firstborn fasting on *erev pesach*: *habechoros nahagu litanos erev pesach*. He cites this from *masechet Sofrim* — one of the minor tractates edited during the Geonic period, though likely containing earlier Tannaitic and Amoraic material — which records *she'ein misanin benissan ela bechoros be'erev pesach*. This custom is not the subject of the *gemara* here, but Tosafot takes the occasion to note its existence.

In summary, the prohibition against eating before the *seder* begins at *mincha ketana* — around 3:00 p.m. — and applies to substantial meals. It does not prohibit all food; small amounts of *minei targima* are permitted and may even be desirable for whetting the appetite. The prohibition extends to *matzah* the entire day, and according to Tosafot, arguably to *matzah ashirah* made with fruit juices, which might constitute a substantial enough eating to be prohibited from 3:00 p.m. onward.

---

## Haseiba

### Poor Person Rule

The *mishnah* establishes that *v'afilu ani shebe'yisrael lo yochal ad she'yeisav* — even the poorest person in Israel may not eat on *pesach* until he reclines. This statement will bear closer examination shortly; for now, the emphasis is on the universality of the requirement. No one, regardless of economic station, is exempt from *haseibah*.

### Matzah Maror

The *gemara* records: *matzah tzarich haseibah* — eating *matzah* requires reclining, since *matzah* is a symbol of freedom and *haseibah* is a symbol of freedom. *Maror ein tzarich haseibah* — *maror* does not require reclining. Indeed, it would be something of a mixed message to recline while eating *maror*, whose entire significance is bound up with the experience of enslavement.

### Wine Cups

When it comes to wine, the *gemara* records what appears to be a contradiction within the teachings attributed to Rav Nachman himself: *itmar mishmeih d'Rav Nachman tzarich haseibah*, and also *itmar mishmeih d'Rav Nachman ein tzarich haseibah*. One tradition requires reclining for wine; another does not. This is surprising, since one might have expected wine — the quintessential symbol of aristocratic freedom — to require *haseibah* unambiguously.

---

## Haseiba (II)

### All Cups Safe

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *v'lo pligi* — these two traditions do not actually dispute one another. One applies to the first two cups and the other to the last two. But the *gemara* then notes that this distinction is itself disputed — *amri lah l'hai gisa v'amri lah l'hai gisa* — with one view holding that the first two cups require *haseibah* because it is during the recitation of the *haggadah* that the movement from *shibud l'geulah* takes place, and another view holding that only the last two cups require *haseibah* because it is only after the *geulah* has been fully articulated that one stands in a genuine experience of freedom. Since neither resolution commands consensus, the *gemara* concludes: *idi v'idi ba'ei haseibah* — one should recline for all four cups. The Ran addresses the question of why we do not apply the general principle of *sfeika d'rabanan l'kula*. His answer is that *sfeika d'rabanan l'kula* operates when the scope of an established institution is uncertain in particular cases; it does not operate where applying it would entirely undermine the institution. If we were to apply leniency here, the result would be that *haseibah* is never required for wine — which would hollow out the institution entirely. Hence we require *haseibah* for all four.

It is worth noting in passing that cups two and three seem, on the merits, to be the strongest candidates for *haseibah*: by the end of the second cup, *asher ge'alanu* has been recited and the story of redemption has been told, and throughout the third cup the meal of *matzah* — the symbol of *cheirus* — has been eaten. The first cup stands prior to the telling, and the fourth cup follows the conclusion of the formal narrative. Yet despite this intuition, the *gemara* frames the choice as first-two versus last-two rather than cups two and three.

### Tosafot Meal Focus

Tosafot engages this question with nuance. He addresses why *matzah* continues to require *haseibah* even according to the view that limits wine's *haseibah* to the first two cups — since *matzah* comes after the second cup, after *birkat hage'ulah* has already been recited. He offers two answers, and they point in different directions conceptually.

The first answer is that *matzah* is the *ikar seudah* — the heart of the meal itself — and *haseibah* is fundamentally a feature of how one eats a meal, not merely of how one performs symbolic ritual eating. This is an important observation that reflects the original character of *haseibah* as described in the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states simply that a person may not eat until he reclines — *lo yochal ad she'yeisav* — without connecting *haseibah* to specific ritual acts at all. *Haseibah* was the posture of the wealthy Roman citizen at his meal; it was the meal itself that was symbolic. What the *gemara* does is reframe *haseibah* as an accompaniment to specific ritual eating acts — *matzah*, *yayin*, *maror* — and that is indeed how most people think about it today. But Tosafot here pulls back toward the original conception: the reason *matzah* requires *haseibah* regardless of where it falls in the narrative arc is that *matzah* is the meal, and *haseibah* belongs to the meal.

The second answer is that *matzah* is intrinsically inscribed as a symbol of *cheirus*, as the Torah itself records — *shelo hispik bitzekam lehachmitz ad shenigalu* — and therefore whenever *matzah* is eaten, it requires *haseibah*, whereas wine's symbolic significance is more dependent on its position within the structure of the *seder*. According to this second answer, *haseibah* for *matzah* is limited to the ritual *kezayit* at *hamotzi* and the *afikoman*, not to all *matzah* consumed during the meal.

Tosafot thus presents two distinct conceptual frameworks. According to the first, *haseibah* is fundamentally about the meal — and therefore applies to all *matzah* eaten during the meal. According to the second, *haseibah* is about symbolic ritual acts of *geulah* — and therefore applies only to the two primary *kezayit* obligations. The practical implications for eating *matzah* throughout the course of the meal differ accordingly, and many *rishonim* follow the more restrictive approach, limiting *haseibah* to the formal first and last *kezayit*. Tosafot, however, invites us to consider the broader conception embedded in the *mishnah*'s original formulation.

---

## Haseiba Positions

### Back Flat Issue

The *gemara* now turns to the physical mechanics of *haseibah*. Two positions are disqualified. First, *pirkadan lo shme haseibah* — lying flat on one's back does not count as *haseibah*. *Haseibah* requires reclining to the side; flat on the back is neither a normal eating position nor one that carries the requisite symbolic significance. Second, Rava rules: *haseibah yemin lo shme haseibah* — reclining on the right side does not constitute valid *haseibah*.

### Trachea Risk

The *gemara* adds a further concern regarding right-side reclining: *v'lo od ela shema yakdim kaneh l'veshet* — one risks having food enter the trachea before the esophagus, creating a danger of choking. This raises the question of why reclining on the right would produce this anatomical risk.

### Rashi Rashbam

Rashi and the Rashbam disagree on how to read the *gemara*'s medical concern. Rashi holds that the trachea and esophagus are oriented front to back rather than left to right. On his reading, the danger of food entering the trachea is not specifically associated with right-side reclining but with lying flat on one's back: in that position, the flap over the esophagus functions improperly, leaving the trachea exposed.
