Regarding passing between two palm trees: *lo amran ela d'la paskin'hu reshut harabim* — this is only dangerous when a public thoroughfare has not passed through the area. *Shedim* avoid the masses. *Aval paskin'hu reshut harabim* — if a public road passes between the trees, *leit lan bah* — there is no concern. The *shedim* prefer darker, more secluded areas, and where there is steady public traffic they will not linger.

### Borrowed Water Limits

Regarding borrowed water: *lo amran ela d'shailinhu katan* — the danger applies only if a minor did the borrowing, as a minor may not have been able to properly watch over the water, rendering it somehow more susceptible to demonic access. *Aval gadol leit lan bah* — if an adult borrowed the water, there is no concern.

Even if a minor borrowed the water, there is a further qualification: *ela basadeh* — the concern applies only in a field, where water is scarce. *D'la shechichi* — since water is not readily available, one risks actual competition with the *shed* for that water. *Aval ba'ir* — in a city, where wells are plentiful and water is accessible, *leit lan bah* — the *shed* will simply obtain water elsewhere.

And even in a field, *ela maya* — the concern applies only to water. *Aval chamra ve-shichra leit lan bah* — wine and beer are no concern, since the *shed* is evidently health-conscious and drinks only water. It should be noted that consuming multiple cups of wine creates its own danger through *zugot*, but that danger arises from the pairs themselves, not from competition with a *shed*.

### Spilled Water Rules

Regarding walking over spilled water: the Gemara specifies that the danger applies *ela d'la afsikinhu be'afra* — only when no dirt has been placed on the water to interrupt it — *ve-la taf behu ruka* — and no one has spit into it. The spilled water under discussion is primarily soiled water — what one might call household wastewater or sewage, since in antiquity one would pour out dirty water used for washing or other purposes. Something about the nature or perhaps the odor of such water attracts *shedim*. But if dirt is added, or if someone spits in it, the nature of the liquid is sufficiently altered that it is no longer an attractive gathering point.

*Aval hifsiknu o taf bo rok* — if either interruption occurs, *leit lan bah*, no problem. And further: *velo amran ela dela avar aleihu shimsha* — the concern applies only when the sun has not yet passed over the water, and *velo avar aleihu shittin nigrei* — when sixty footsteps have not yet crossed it. Once the sun has shone upon it, or sixty people have walked over it, the danger dissipates.

There is a final amelioration: *ela dela rachiv chamra velo sayim masanei* — the concern applies only if one is neither riding a donkey nor wearing shoes. If one has either protection — either riding or wearing shoes — *leit lan bah*, there is no danger.

### Witchcraft Exception

*Ve-hani milei* — all of these qualifications and leniencies apply *heicha deleika lemichash lechshafim* — in a place where there is no reason to worry about witchcraft being directed against a person. The protections address the *mazikin* acting in their ordinary, autonomous movements through the world. *Aval heicha de-ika lemichash le-chshafim* — but in a place where someone is actively directing witchcraft against a person, *af al gav de-ika kol hanei chaishinan* — even if one has taken all of the precautions described, one must still be concerned.

This is a striking assumption in the Gemara: that the same conditions which expose a person to *shedim* also render him susceptible to the effects of witchcraft. One might wonder whether the underlying conception is that witchcraft operates *through* the *shedim* — drawing on those same forces — such that vulnerability to one implies vulnerability to the other. Once witchcraft is actively being practiced against someone, however, the protections against the *shedim's* ordinary movements provide no defense.

The Gemara illustrates this with a story: a certain man was riding his donkey and wearing shoes — both protective conditions — yet his shoes shriveled and his leg withered. The only explanation the Gemara offers is that someone was directing witchcraft against him, and against that no physical precaution suffices.

One student raised a broader observation: the world of the Talmud is a deeply animated one, full of non-physical forces moving through physical space, such that even the simplest acts — walking between trees, stepping over a puddle — carry consequences because the world is populated by beings with whom one may come into conflict. This contrasts sharply with a modern materialist sensibility in which randomness stands at the center of unexplained events. The *Gemara's* world, by contrast, is profoundly personalized: misfortune has a cause, and that cause is often an encounter with a being that one provoked, however inadvertently.

---

## Dogs, Trees & Women

### Three Prohibited

A *brayta* is cited: *shlosha ain mimetzin velo mitmetzin* — there are three entities that one must not allow to become an intermediary between two people, and between two of which one must not place oneself. These are *hakelev veha-dekel veha-isha* — a dog, a palm tree, and a woman. Some add *af hachazir* — even a pig — and some add *af hanachash* — even a snake. The concern, as the subsequent discussion makes clear, relates to the demonic or witchcraft-related dangers associated with these entities.

### El/Lo Remedy

*Ve-im mimetzin* — if one of these did become an intermediary, what is the remedy? Rav Pappa teaches: *niftach b'El ve-nisayem b'El* — one should recite a *pasuk* that begins with the divine name *El* and ends with *El*. Alternatively: *niftach belo ve-nisayem belo* — one should begin with *lo* and end with *lo*.

Rashi identifies the *pasuk* for *El*: *El motziam mimitzrayim kito'afot re'eim lo, ki lo nachash beya'akov velo kessem beyisrael, ka'et ye'ameir leya'akov uleyisrael mah pa'al El* — a verse that opens with *El* and closes with *El*. This passage is particularly apt: it invokes *ki lo nachash beya'akov velo kessem beyisrael* — that witchcraft has no power over Israel — making it directly relevant to the danger at hand. Moreover, there is a structural resonance: just as one has been caught in the middle of something — sandwiched between entities — the remedy involves being sandwiched within a verse, with *El* on both sides.

For *lo*, Rashi cites: *lo ish El veyichazev uven adam veyitnecham, hahu amar velo ya'aseh vedibeir velo yekimena* — a verse that opens and closes with *lo*, though the final *lo* is not the very last word. Again, the content is apposite.

### Torah as Incantation

Tosafot raises a significant concern: the Rashbam's interpretation requires reciting *pesukim* as a protective incantation, yet it is generally prohibited to use Torah as a vehicle for healing or protection in this incantatory way — one ought to pray to God, not wield *pesukim* as magical instruments.

Tosafot offers two answers. First: *lehagen shari* — for protection, as opposed to healing an existing ailment, it is permitted, since the danger has not yet materialized and one is acting preventatively. The precise distinction between a preventative recitation and an incantatory one is not entirely transparent, but this is the answer given. Second, Tosafot cites another Gemara in Shabbos that permits reciting a *pasuk* when treating a dangerous fever, and reasons: *mishum sakana shari* — in a life-threatening situation, it is permitted; it is only for non-life-threatening illness that one may not use Torah as incantation.

This discussion touches on a deep tension in the world the Gemara describes. In a world saturated with demonic forces and witchcraft, the demand for protection is immediate and pressing. The mechanisms the Gemara offers — amulets, incantations, formulaic recitations — sit uneasily with a religious sensibility that insists the Torah is not a magic text, and that one's relationship with God is mediated through prayer, *mitzvos*, and *maasim tovim*, not through the deployment of sacred words as protective spells.

### Rabbeinu Chananel

To avoid this difficulty entirely, Rabbeinu Chananel offers a different interpretation: one does not recite *pesukim* at all, but rather composes a *tefillah* — a spontaneous prayer — that opens with *El* and concludes with *El*, or opens with *lo* and concludes with *lo*.

He provides examples. For *El*: *El Elohim Hashem hatzileni mikol ra mikol nezek asher beyadcha koach u-gevurah ki atah El* — God, the Lord, save me from all evil and all harm, for in Your hand is all power and might, for You are *El*. For *lo*: *lo titecheni Elohai ve-lo ta'azveni shamreni k'ishon bat ayin terem ekra ta'aneni ve'al tomar lo* — do not abandon me, my God, do not forsake me; guard me as the apple of the eye; before I call, answer me, and do not say no. In Rabbeinu Chananel's reading, then, the remedy is genuine *tefillah* — turning to God for protection — rather than an incantatory use of scriptural verses.

It should be noted that Tosafot's discussion preserves both the *Rashbam's* approach using *pesukim* and Rabbeinu Chananel's approach using *tefillah*, presenting them as alternative possibilities.

### Women as Niddah

The Gemara continues with a further specification: *hani bei tere de-matzu'ah lehu isha niddah* — if a *niddah* passes between two people. *Im techilas niddasah hi* — if she is at the beginning of her menstrual flow, *horegas achas mehen* — it will cause the death of one of them. *Ve-im sof niddasah hi* — if she is at the end of her period, *meriva osa beineihen* — it will cause a quarrel between them. The remedy is again to recite a verse or prayer beginning and ending with *El*.

### Niddah Discussion

This passage opens onto a broader historical concern. In many ancient societies there existed powerful taboos surrounding menstruating women — they were required to live apart from the rest of the community, forbidden to touch food lest they contaminate it, and treated as dangerous in ways that had nothing to do with the laws of *tumah*. In some communities these practices persist into the present day, with devastating consequences for women's welfare and safety.

Notably, the Torah itself does not reflect this attitude at all. *Niddah* in the Torah is treated as a category of *tumah* and a matter of *issur arayos*, nothing more. The Gemara in Masechet Niddah equally ignores these taboos in its *halakhic* analysis, ruling, for instance, that a husband and wife may sleep in the same bedroom during the *niddah* period — rejecting any notion of casting the woman out, and equally setting aside the concern about *yichud* that would normally apply when a man is secluded with a woman with whom relations are forbidden.

The passage before us, however, is not a *halakhic* discussion. It reflects a popular perception — present in the surrounding culture and apparently not entirely foreign to some strands of rabbinic thought — that a *niddah* carried with her some dangerous power or spiritual contamination beyond the domain of *halakhah*. Tosafot mitigates this somewhat by suggesting: *yesh mefareish im oseh lahen kishuf* — perhaps the concern is specifically about a *niddah* who is also actively practicing witchcraft, such that it is the combination of the two that creates the danger, not the *niddah* status by itself. That is somewhat ameliorating, though if women are in any case routinely assumed to be potential practitioners of witchcraft, the improvement is limited.

It is significant that this perception did find its way into practical life across the medieval period. Works such as the *Baraita de-Masechet Niddah* — a text quoted by *rishonim* including the Ramban, though its authorship is disputed and some regard it as Karaitic — are filled with taboos about menstruating women touching food, reciting *blessings*, or entering the *beit keneset*. In Ashkenaz in particular there developed a concern about whether a *niddah* could attend synagogue even on Yom Kippur, or engage in any form of sacred activity. The Rambam, for his part, was especially concerned about another adjacent phenomenon: the writing of angelic names on *mezuzot*, transforming a *mitzvah* into an amulet. The tendency to treat sacred objects and texts as sources of magical protection rather than as expressions of a rational *halakhic* relationship with God is a recurrent tension — one that the *Gemara's* own material here seems, despite itself, to fuel.

---

## Women Witchcraft

### Crossroads Women

The Gemara now addresses a related scenario: *hanei trei nashei yatvan b'parashat drachim ve-chada b'hai gisa dishvila ve-chada b'idach gisa umichavnan apaihu hadadi* — two women sitting at a crossroads, one on each side of the road, facing one another. *Vadai b'kshafim askinan* — this positioning is taken as certain evidence that they are engaged in witchcraft.

### Witchcraft Remedies

If one encounters this situation, *ieka darcha achrina leizil bah* — the first and best advice is to take an alternate route. If no other route is available and one has a companion, the two should grasp each other's hands and pass through together. If one is alone, *neima hachi* — one should recite the following: *Igeret azlat asya blusya mitkatla b'cheik tevel*. The first words — *Igeret, azlat, asya, blusya* — appear to be names of demonic entities; the concluding phrase means something like "may murderous arrows be driven into you." The Rashbam understands this as a curse directed at the *shedim* associated with the witchcraft, and indeed the verse concludes with an invocation of destruction against them: *k'tzar harugin heim b'chitzim* — they are already as if slain by arrows.

### Mikvah Encounter

A further scenario: *hai man d'paga b'it-teta b'idna d'salka mitvilas mitzvah* — a person who happens to encounter a woman at the very moment she is emerging from the *mikvah*, having immersed for the *mitzvah* of becoming permissible to her husband. If he then goes home and has relations before she does — *achda lei l'didei ruach znunim* — a spirit of licentiousness takes hold of him. If she has relations before he does — *achda lah l'didah ruach znunim* — it takes hold of her. The remedy in either case is to recite: *shfoch buz al nedivim vayashgem betohu lo darech* — "Pour contempt upon princes and make them wander in pathless wastelands," the apparent intent being that God should drive away the demonic spirit.

### Rav Yochanan Story

Tosafot, printed on the preceding page at 107a, raises an obvious difficulty from a well-known Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan would intentionally sit at the gates of the *mikvah*, so that women emerging from immersion would see him. The reasoning was that Rabbi Yochanan was renowned for his extraordinary beauty, and the Gemara operates on the assumption that what a man or woman contemplates at the moment of conception influences the appearance of the child. Rabbi Yochanan believed that if women looked at him as they left the *mikvah* and then held his image in mind when they later had relations with their husbands, their children would be beautiful and well-formed.

But this creates a tension: the Gemara before us suggests that encountering a woman as she emerges from the *mikvah* leads to a *ruach znunim* seizing one party or the other. Why was Rabbi Yochanan unconcerned?

Tosafot offers several resolutions. The first: *hacha depaga beshata desalka min hamayim* — our concern applies at the precise moment of emerging from the water, while Rabbi Yochanan was waiting at the *gates*, encountering women a few minutes later, already dressed and composed. The second: *hatam yasiv hacha paga* — Rabbi Yochanan was *sitting*, a settled, deliberate posture, while the danger described in the Gemara involves an inadvertent *bumping into* (*paga*), a sudden, unplanned encounter. The third resolution: *Rav Yochanan hava amar shfoch buz al nedivim* — Rabbi Yochanan himself would recite the protective verse, thereby neutralizing the danger. Of course, this third answer raises its own question — what of the woman, who might have relations before Rabbi Yochanan does? — but Tosafot does not address that directly.

---

## Dangerous Shades

### Shadow Dangers

Rav Yitzchak opens this section with an exegetical observation: what is the meaning of the verse *gam ki elech be-gei tzalmavet lo ira ra ki ata imadi* — "Even as I walk through the valley of the shadow of death I shall fear no evil, for You are with me"? What is this *gei tzalmavet*, this valley of the shadow of death, that represents such acute danger? The Gemara identifies it: *ze hayashen betzel dekel yechidi* — this is one who sleeps in the shade of a solitary palm tree. The linguistic connection is pointed: *betzel*, shade, resonates with *tzalmavet*, shadow of death. And note that the *shedim* are associated not merely with the trees themselves but specifically with their *shade* — making vulnerable any place where shade is cast.

Two specific shade-dangers are enumerated: the shade of a solitary palm tree, and *u-vetzel levana* — the shade of the moon, meaning the shadowed area created when moonlight is blocked by a wall or other obstacle.

Regarding the shade of a solitary palm tree: *lo amran ela dela nafal tula de-chavreih alaveih* — the danger applies only when the shade of another tree does not overlap with it. If the shade of a neighboring tree falls upon it as well, *leit lan bah* — there is no problem.

A *brayta* then specifies that the shade of a solitary palm tree in a *chatzer* — a courtyard — is dangerous, as is sleeping in moon shade. The Gemara works through this *brayta* analytically. If the concern is that no other shade overlaps, then even in an open field it would be dangerous — so why does the *brayta* specify a *chatzer*? The Gemara concludes: *shma mina be-chatzer af al gav de-nafal tula de-chavreih alaveih* — in a courtyard, the danger applies even when the shade of another tree overlaps, because the enclosed nature of the courtyard intensifies the danger. The *brayta* is thus teaching a stringency specific to the *chatzer*, not a limitation to it.

This raises a broader reflection: the Gemara's use of standard *halakhic* analytical language — *lo amran ela*, *shma mina*, the resolution of apparent contradictions between a *sugya* and a *brayta* — to analyze the laws of demonic shade is notable. One might wonder whether this reflects the Gemara's equal weighting of this material alongside *halakhic* discussions, or whether the analytical idiom is borrowed and applied somewhat mechanically. It is genuinely difficult to determine the tone of this material at this distance.

### Moon Shade Danger

Regarding moon shade: *u-v'tzila shel levana lo amran ela b'ma'arava* — the danger of moonlight shade applies only when the shade is cast to the west. The Rashbam explains that toward the end of the night the moon is in the east, and a wall facing east would therefore cast its shadow westward. Shade cast to the east — *aval b'madnacha leit lan bah* — presents no concern. This suggests that only a particular configuration of moonlight and shadow at a specific time of night activates the danger.

### Palm Tree Spirits

Continuing with the palm tree hazards: *hai man d'mafni agidda d'dikla* — one who relieves himself on the stump of a palm tree is seized by *ruach palga*, which may be the name of a specific demon or may refer to a disease — the Rashbam suggests a form of paralysis. One who leans his head against the trunk of a palm tree — *hai man d'matzli reisha agidda d'dikla* — is seized by the demon *tzrada*, which corresponds to a type of migraine headache, perhaps because the head is brought into direct contact with the tree.

### Stepping Over Trees

One who steps over a felled palm tree faces yet further danger: *im mikta katlo* — if the tree was cut down deliberately, he will be killed; *ee yakar u-mayas* — if it simply fell naturally, he will die. However, these dangers apply only if *dilo manach karei ilavei* — if he did not pause to rest his leg upon the trunk as he crossed. *Aval manach karei ilavei leit lan bah* — if he rests his leg on the tree while stepping over, there is no problem. The precise logic underlying this distinction is not explained, but it is presented as a matter of practical guidance.

### Five Shades Rule

The Gemara enumerates five dangerous shades: *tula d'dikla yechida* — the shade of a solitary palm tree; *tula d'kanda* — the shade of a *kanda* tree; *tula d'parcha* — the shade of a *parcha*, identified as a caper bush; *tula d'zarjeta* — the shade of a sorb tree; and, according to some, *af tula d'arva* — the shade of a boat, and *tula d'arveta* — the shade of a willow. (Some versions emend the opening number to four rather than five in light of the count.)

The Gemara then states a general principle: *kol dinapish anfei kashi tulei* — any tree with many branches has dangerous shade; *ve-kol d'kashi silvayei kashi tulei* — and any tree whose wood is very hard, or which has thorns, likewise has dangerous shade. The underlying intuition seems to be that the density of the canopy or the hardness of the wood creates conditions that *shedim* find congenial.

### Karumashe Exception

The *karumashe* tree — identified in some translations as a service tree — is explicitly excluded: *af al gav d'kashi silvayei lo kashi tulei* — even though its wood is hard, its shade is not dangerous.

The reason offered takes the form of a demonic folk narrative: *d'amrah lei sheida livrah* — a *sheida* said to her daughter, *pirchi nafshach mikrumashe* — fly away from the *karumashe* tree, avoid its shade — *d'ihu d'katol la'avuch* — for that tree is what killed your father. *Ve-katol l'didei* — and it went on to kill him too, apparently the son as well, despite his mother's warning. Whatever myth underlies this, the practical result is that *shedim* actively avoid the *karumashe* tree, and therefore its shade poses no danger.

Rav Ashi states: *chazivna l'Rav Kahana d'parish mikulu tulei* — I observed that Rav Kahana avoided all shades, as a matter of general precaution.

### Parcha Spirit Story

The Gemara now identifies the specific *shedim* associated with various locations. The spirit of the *parcha* tree is called *ruchi*. The spirit of the sorb tree is called *sheida*. The spirit that inhabits rooftops is called *rishpi* — an echo of *rishpei esh*, fiery bolts.

*Le-mai nafka mina* — why does it matter to know their names? *Likmiya* — for the writing of amulets. When composing a *kmiya* to protect someone from a specific demonic encounter, one must know the name of the *shed* to whom the amulet is directed.

Regarding the spirit of the *parcha* tree: *birya she-ein la einayim* — it is a creature without eyes. Again, *le-mai nafka mina* — of what practical consequence is this? *Ligzuzei lah* — so that one knows to simply run away from it, since without eyes it cannot follow.

This is illustrated by a story: a Torah student once went to relieve himself near a *parcha* tree and entered its shade. *Shama d'ka ati laveih* — he heard something coming toward him, the rustling of the approaching spirit. *Ve-gazilei* — and he ran, and was safe, since the eyeless *ruchi* could not pursue him. As he ran, he grabbed hold of a palm tree — itself associated with *shedim*, as we have seen — *tzavach dikla upaka hi* — and the palm tree cried out, and something burst. Whether it was the tree, the shade, or the demon is not entirely clear from the text.

### Sixty Demons Story

*Hazira d'tasamicha l'mata lo pachas mi-shishin sheedi* — a sorb tree located near a city harbors no fewer than sixty demons. *Le-mai nafka mina likmiya* — the practical implication is again for amulet-writing: one must know that the amulet must be written against sixty *shedim*, not just one.

The Gemara tells a story that brings this point to life. A certain officer — some leading figure in the city — would rest under a sorb tree near the city. *Alu bei shishin sheedi veistaken* — sixty *shedim* possessed him, and his life was in danger. He went to a certain rabbinic student for help, but this student did not know that a sorb tree near a city harbors sixty demons. *Kesav la kmiya l'chad sheeda* — he wrote a *kmiya* effective against only one *shed*. The student subsequently heard that the demons had hung a harp from the tree and were celebrating, singing mockingly: *sudreih d'mar ki tzurva m'rabanan badikna bei d'mar d'lo yada baruch ata* — that man's head-cloth makes him look like a Torah scholar, but we tested him and he doesn't even know a *bracha*. They were deriding him for not knowing that there were sixty of them — *d'lo yada baruch*, he doesn't know the first thing.

Then a second, properly informed rabbinic student arrived. *Kesav la kmiya d'shishin sheedi* — he wrote a *kmiya* directed against sixty *shedim*. *Panu m'naichu me-hacha* — and the demons were heard to say: clear out your belongings from here. They were expelled.

This story both reflects and reinforces the widespread practice of *kamea*-writing, which remained common through the medieval period and continues in some communities to the present day. The implicit lesson is that the practice requires genuine expertise: an amulet composed without full knowledge of what one is dealing with is not merely ineffective but almost farcical.

---

## Ketev Pestilences

### Ketev Types

The Gemara now turns to *Ketev Meriri*, a demonic pestilence referenced in the Torah and here associated by the Gemara with a specific class of dangerous spirit. *Trei katvei havei* — there are two forms of *Ketev*: *chad mikamei tihara* — one that operates before noon, and *ve-chad mibatar tihara* — one that operates after noon.

The one that operates before noon is called *Ketev Meriri*. *Umachzi b'kada d'kamcha* — it appears within a jug of *kamcha*, a type of sauce or compound, and looks like a stirring or mixing implement moving within it — perhaps describing a whirling, turbulent appearance.

The one that operates after noon is called *Ketev Yashud Tzahorayim* — echoing the *tzahorayim*, the afternoon or noon hour, mentioned in Tehillim. *Umachzi b'karna d'iza* — it appears among the horns of goats, *ve-hadar bei knafaya* — and wings or feathers surround it. Some translate this as a whirling sieve-like appearance; others emphasize the surrounding wings.

### Abaye Encounter

Abaye was once traveling with Rav Pappa on his right and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua on his left. *Chazya l'hahu Ketev Meriri d'ka ati l'apei* — he saw the *Ketev Meriri* coming toward him, specifically approaching from his left side. He responded by repositioning his companions: he moved Rav Pappa to the left and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua to the right.

Rav Pappa protested: *ana mai shna d'lo chashasht li* — why are you not concerned for my safety? Why am I being moved into the path of the *Ketev*? Abaye responded: *at sha'ata kayima lach* — it is a good time for you, meaning your *mazel* is currently strong. Since Rav Pappa was very wealthy and evidently blessed with considerable *mazel*, Abaye calculated that this protection would extend to the demonic encounter as well.

### Ketev Seasons

*Michad b'Tammuz ad shitser beh* — from the first of Tammuz through the sixteenth, just before the seventeenth of Tammuz, *vadai sh'chichi* — the *Ketev* powers are definitely prevalent. From that point onward — *safek sh'chichi safek lo sh'chichi* — there is uncertainty as to their prevalence. It is worth noting that this temporal proximity to the Three Weeks has generated discussion about whether some of the customs and stringencies surrounding that period were influenced by these beliefs about heightened demonic danger during this stretch of the summer calendar.

### Ketev Habitat

*U'mishtakchei b'tulei d'chatzva d'lo chatzvei garmida* — they are found in the shade of a *chatzva*, a type of low-growing grass that does not reach a *amah* in height. *U'btulei d'tzafra v'panya d'lo havei garmida* — and in the short morning and afternoon shadows that do not extend a *amah* in length. *Ve-hikar b'tulei d'veit hakisei* — but their primary dwelling place, where they are most to be found, is in the shade of the bathroom.

That, the Gemara suggests, is a fitting place to stop.

---

---

# Pesachim 112

## Health & Poverty Omens

### Causes of Blindness

The daf begins at the bottom of 111b with a teaching of Rav Yosef: *hani tlata milei yahiv arvona l'nehora* — these three things give a pledge toward blindness, meaning they make a person blind. The first is combing one's hair dry, without wetting it beforehand. The second is drinking in a drip-by-drip fashion — placing one's mouth directly to a dripping barrel. The third is putting on one's shoes while one's feet are still wet. These are presented as genuine practical concerns, even if their precise physiological rationale is not elaborated upon.

### Poverty Omens

The Gemara then turns to a series of behaviors said to lead to poverty. If one suspends objects in the house — food hanging from the ceiling in baskets, for instance — *kashi l'aniyuta*, this is difficult for poverty, meaning it causes poverty. As people say: *tala silta tala mazonei* — if you hang your basket, you have suspended your *mezonot*, your livelihood. This applies specifically to bread; if one hangs meat or fish to dry, *orcheih hu*, that is its normal manner of preservation, and there is no concern.

Similarly, having bran in the house is said to lead to poverty, perhaps because bran is symbolic of the food of the poor. And crumbs of bread left around the house also lead to poverty — reflecting a general rabbinic sensitivity toward the proper treatment of food, particularly bread. The Gemara elsewhere is quite exacting on questions of respect for food, and the disregard signaled by allowing crumbs to accumulate carries weight here as well.

### Demons & Spirits

The Gemara further notes that on Friday nights and on the nights leading into Wednesday, *mazikin* — demons or harmful spirits — hover over these crumbs and bran. Two spirits are named. The spirit presiding over food is called *Nakid*, a name the Rashbam connects to *naki*, cleanliness, linking it to the theme of treated food with care. The spirit presiding over poverty is called *Navel*, a word connoting degeneracy, which fits here as the spirit associated with the mistreatment and neglect of things.

### Uncleanliness & Poverty

The Gemara continues: *tza afuma d'chatzva*, if there is dirt on the mouth of a barrel or pitcher, *kashi l'aniyuta*, this leads to poverty. This connects to the *Navel* spirit and the theme of general uncleanliness. It is worth noting that while in other contexts the Gemara's concerns about dirt and hygiene may have an implicit connection to illness and what we would today understand as germ theory, here the Gemara is treating this specifically as a cause of poverty, not of sickness.

One might ask how we even know the meanings of the unusual vocabulary appearing in these passages — words that are uncommon even within the broader corpus of *Shas*. Sometimes meaning is recovered from context, sometimes from parallels elsewhere in the Talmud, and sometimes from traditions preserved by the *Geonim*, which are then cited by Rashi or the Rashbam. The *Aruch*, composed around the year 1000, represents a significant lexicographic effort, drawing on traditions that had been maintained within those roughly five centuries since the close of the Talmud. One cannot assume one hundred percent accuracy in every case, but these traditions deserve respect.

### Vision Hazards

The Gemara adds that one who drinks water from a dish rather than from a proper cup risks *bruktai* — a difficulty with eyesight, something like cataracts.

---

## Hand-Washing Practices

### Cress & Fear

Moving to the top of 112a, the Gemara states that one who eats *tachli* — watercress — and does not wash his hands afterwards will suffer *mafchid tlatin yomei*, an unexplained anxiety and fear lasting thirty days.

### Bloodletting Rules

One who undergoes *mesuchar* — bloodletting from the shoulders — and does not wash his hands afterwards will be fearful for seven days. This is clearly a reference to hand-washing after the procedure, and as we will see, it gives rise to a practice that is actually codified.

### Hair & Nail Care

One who gets a haircut — *shakil mazyei* — and does not wash his hands afterwards will be fearful for thirty days. One who has his fingernails removed and does not wash his hands afterwards will be fearful for one day — *v'lo yada mai kamafchid*, and will not even know why he is afraid.

These concerns are cited as the basis for actual practice. As Dr. Elman has demonstrated, anxiety about hair, nails, and demonic vulnerability was a prevalent motif in Zoroastrian and broader Persian culture, the environment in which the Babylonian *Chazal* lived, and this context helps explain why such concerns enter the Talmudic discussion.

### Shulchan Aruch Rules

The Shulchan Aruch, *Orach Chayim*, Siman 4, codifies the requirement of *netilat yadayim* in a broad range of circumstances:

> אֵלּוּ דְּבָרִים צְרִיכִים נְטִילָה בְּמַיִם: הַקָּם מֵהַמִּטָּה, וְהַיּוֹצֵא מִבֵּית הַכִּסֵּא, וּמִבֵּית הַמֶּרְחָץ, וְהַנּוֹטֵל צִפָּרְנָיו, וְהַחוֹלֵץ מִנְעָלָיו, וְהַנּוֹגֵע בְּרַגְלָיו, וְהַחוֹפֵף רֹאשׁוֹ... מִי שֶׁעָשָׂה אַחַת מִכָּל אֵלּוּ וְלֹא נָטַל, אִם תַּלְמִיד חָכָם הוּא תַּלְמוּדוֹ מִשְׁתַּכַּח, וְאִם אֵינוֹ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם יוֹצֵא מִדַּעְתּוֹ.

The Shulchan Aruch then continues:

> וְהַמַּקִּיז דָּם מֵהַכְּתֵפַיִם וְלֹא נָטַל יָדָיו מְפַחֵד שִׁבְעָה יָמִים. הַמְגַלֵּחַ וְלֹא נָטַל יָדָיו מְפַחֵד ג׳ יָמִים. הַנּוֹטֵל צִפָּרְנָיו וְלֹא נָטַל יָדָיו מְפַחֵד יוֹם אֶחָד וְאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ מִמָּה מְפַחֵד.

This is essentially a direct quotation of the Gemara's language, incorporated into the Shulchan Aruch. Notably, the Rambam does not include this material. This raises a broader and genuinely fascinating question about which elements of Talmudic sugyas dealing with *shedim* and *ruach ra'ah* enter the halachic literature and which do not.

The Shulchan Aruch did not phrase this as *chayav litol yadav* — one is obligated to wash — or as an *issur* not to wash. Nevertheless, he did record the consequence: *mafchid shlosha yamim*, fearful for three days; *mafchid shiva yamim*, fearful for seven days. The question of what makes it into halachic literature is thus in part a question of the author's sensibilities. Did Rav Yosef Karo feel this was important *hadracha* — practical guidance for living — even if not strict *halacha* in the narrow technical sense? And was the fact that he already had a *siman* on *netilat yadayim*, treating the halachic requirements of hand-washing, an occasion to include adjacent material relating to washing hands in other contexts? That too cannot be determined with certainty.

What is striking is how much of what now carries practical weight is a function of certain editorial decisions — by the Rambam and by Rav Yosef Karo — about what belongs within halachic discourse. One sees this even in practice today: people wash their hands after a haircut, but not necessarily after scratching their head, even though the Shulchan Aruch mentions both in the context of *tefillah*. The difference in uptake reflects exactly this process of selective reception.

### Rambam vs. Demons

A great deal of the material about *ruach ra'ah* and *shedim* does not appear in the Rambam. The various Gemaras that speak of the *ruach ra'ah* resting on the hands in the morning, or on food left uncovered, or on water placed near an open barrel — none of this is found in the Rambam. Rav Ovadia Yosef, *zichrono livracha*, addresses this explicitly in the context of whether food that was left under a bed while one slept constitutes a *safek sakana*. He cites the Rambam's implicit rejection of these concerns, invoking the principle of *nishtanu hateva* — nature has changed. Rather than saying the Gemara was mistaken, this approach holds that in the Rambam's era, the relevant natural or spiritual conditions no longer obtained in the same way. This reading was not original to Rav Ovadia; the *Lechem Mishnah* in *Hilchos Netilas Yadayim* makes a similar observation.

The question then becomes: how much does the Rambam's non-codification of this material function as an authoritative *shita* — a legitimate position that can weigh in halachic discussions, even when other authorities have codified the practice? This is a live question, particularly around *negel vasser* and the various *ruach ra'ah* concerns associated with morning hand-washing, food left under the bed, and so on. The Gemara we are studying concerns food left under the bed that becomes unfit for consumption because *ruach ra'ah shoreh aleihen* — an evil spirit rests upon it — even if it is covered with an iron vessel. The Gemara references *Tur* and *Shulchan Aruch*, *Yoreh Deah*, and points toward Rambam, *Perek* 12 of *Hilchos Rotzeach V'Shemiras Nefesh* — and, as one might expect, it is not there.

---

## Night Dangers

### No Water Nights

The Gemara teaches: *lo yishte adam mayim lo beleilei revi'iyot velo beleilei shabbatot* — a person should not drink water on Tuesday nights or Friday nights. This is an immediately striking statement; not drinking water at all on those nights would be a serious hardship in a world without alternative beverages readily available. The Rashbam immediately qualifies the prohibition, explaining it applies only when there is no light — drinking in the dark on those particular nights is forbidden. This qualification is the Rashbam's insertion to render the ruling intelligible, since the Gemara's text itself does not state this condition. *Damo berosho*, his blood is on his own hands, if he drinks. *Mipnei hasakana* — because of danger. *Mai sakana?* — *Ruach Ra'ah*, an evil spirit.

### Food Under Bed

A *baraita* teaches that food and drink placed under a bed — even if covered with an iron vessel — have *ruach ra'ah shoreh aleihen*, an evil spirit resting upon them, and may not be consumed.

### Protective Rituals

The Gemara asks: *v'ei tzechi mai takanteih* — if one is thirsty on one of these nights, what is the remedy? One option is to recite the seven *kolot* that David uttered regarding water — the passage from Psalms 29 beginning *kol Hashem al hamayim*, in which the phrase *kol Hashem* appears seven times — before drinking.

If one does not know that passage by heart, an alternative incantation is provided: *lu shafan anigron anirdafin* — terms the Rashbam does not even attempt to translate, apparently some form of incantation, perhaps the names of *shedim*. The speaker then declares: *bein kochvei yativna* — I sit among the stars — *bein balya lishmina azilna* — I go between the thin and the fat. The Rashbam explains this as a way of saying to the *shedim*: there are many people around you, thin ones and fat ones — leave me alone.

If neither option is available, one may wake a companion and say: *Planya bar Planta* — so-and-so son of so-and-so (notably using the mother's name as the second identifier) — *tzachina maya*, I am thirsty for water. Once one has declared this to another person, one may then drink. Alternatively, one may bang on the lid of the pitcher to frighten away whatever is lurking, or throw something into the water before drinking. The Gemara seems to present these in descending order of efficacy, though it does not say so explicitly.

### Rivers & Pools

A second *baraita* states: *lo yishte adam mayim lo min haneharot velo min ha'agamim balaila* — do not drink water from rivers or pools at night. *Mipnei hasakana* — because of danger. *Mai sakana?* — *Shavriri*, the spirit of blindness, which both causes blindness and refers to a particular spirit by that name.

If one is thirsty and in the field with no other water available, and there is a companion present, one says: *Planya bar Planta, amar li immi* — so-and-so son of so-and-so, my mother told me — *hizdaher mi-Shavriri* — beware of Shavriri. One then recites a diminishing incantation: *Shavriri, Briri, Riri, Yiri* — each iteration dropping a letter from the name, as if to make the spirit progressively disappear. One then declares *tzachina maya bekasi chivri* — I am thirsty for water in white vessels — and may then drink.

---

## Four Cups Obligation

### Tamchoi & Poor

The Gemara returns now to the *Mishnah*, specifically the ruling that even the poorest person — even one supported by the *tamchoi*, the communal soup kitchen that distributed food on a daily basis to those who could not afford two meals of their own — must nonetheless have *arba kosot* at the Seder. The *tamchoi* was primarily a food-based institution, not a monetary one, and its recipients were those most deeply without means. The Gemara's reading of the *Mishnah* is that even such a person must find a way to obtain four cups of wine regardless.

The Gemara asks: *pshita* — is this not obvious? After all, this is a rabbinic *mitzvah*, and even for biblical *mitzvot* there is a limit to how much a person is obligated to spend. For a positive biblical *mitzvah*, one need not spend more than a third or a fifth of one's assets. Why then is it obvious that even the destitute person must obtain the four cups?

The Gemara answers: *lo nitzrecha ela afilu le-Rabbi Akiva* — this ruling is needed specifically to address Rabbi Akiva's position.

### Akiva's Principle

Rabbi Akiva taught: *aseh Shabbatecha chol ve-al titztarech la-beriyot* — better that your Shabbos should be like a weekday than that you become dependent on others. The principle reflects a profound concern for financial independence and human dignity. The state of dependency, once entered, can be self-perpetuating; it can affect a person's self-image in ways that are lasting and damaging. Better to have no special food for Shabbos than to be forced into a position of taking loans and relying on others.

One might think that Rabbi Akiva would apply this same logic to *arba kosot*: if obtaining the four cups requires borrowing money or becoming dependent, one should forgo them. The *Mishnah*'s ruling comes to tell us that even according to Rabbi Akiva, the four cups must be obtained — even if it means taking loans. This is striking, and raises the question of what makes *arba kosot* different. The Rambam applies the principle of *pirsumei nisa* — publicizing the miracle — to explain this. The *arba kosot* are a fundamental vehicle for *pirsumei nisa*, and that mandate demands universal, unconditional participation. This is the same logic that underlies the inclusion of women in the obligation of the four cups — *af hen hayu be-oto ha-nes* — and as the Rav Soloveitchik points out, *pirsumei nisa* is the context in which such inclusive, near-absolute obligations are especially characteristic.

It is worth pausing to appreciate the tension here. On the one hand, we are told that *pirsumei nisa* breaks all normal limits and insists on complete universality. On the other hand, the Gemara earlier discussed who reclines at the Seder — and noted that a woman in the presence of her husband, or a student before his *rav*, may not recline. So the universality is not quite total. Nevertheless, the *arba kosot* represent a point at which the community's obligation to ensure participation is paramount — indeed, the Mishnah's first line establishes that the community must provide.

---

## Four Cups Obligation (II)

### D'vei Eliyahu

*Tana D'vei Eliyahu* teaches: even though Rabbi Akiva says one should make one's Shabbos like a weekday rather than become dependent, he would nonetheless agree that one must make *something* a little different — some small gesture to mark the day. The Gemara cannot fully come to peace with the idea of *aseh Shabbatecha chol* in its totality. *Mai nihu* — what would this small gesture be? Rav Pappa says: *kasa d'harsena* — a small dish of fish hash. Not a large expenditure; perhaps just a few extra pennies. The point is that one scrapes together what one can and does something, however small, to make Shabbos distinct.

The Shulchan Aruch, in the very first *siman* of *Hilchos Shabbos*, Siman 242, codifies this tension carefully: one who is already dependent on others for *tzedakah* or loans must still make every effort to honor Shabbos with what little he has of his own. The statement *aseh Shabbatecha chol* applies only to one who is in extremely straitened circumstances. Even then, the prescription is to be economical during the week in order to set something aside for Shabbos. The *Mishnah Berurah* attempts to harmonize the various statements in the Gemara and the competing values at stake; the Shulchan Aruch's bottom line seems to be that if the real choice is between doing nothing special and taking out loans, one should do nothing — but if one can scrape a few pennies together, one must do so.

---

## Akiva's 7 Teachings

### Commands 1-3

The Gemara now presents a *baraita*: *shivah devarim tzivah Rabbi Akiva et Rabbi Yehoshua beno* — Rabbi Akiva commanded seven things to his son Rabbi Yehoshua. Interestingly, we rarely hear of Rabbi Akiva's children. Rashi suggests that this Rabbi Yehoshua may be Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, a *Tanna* mentioned frequently elsewhere, on the basis of a Gemara that refers to Rabbi Akiva by the epithet *kereach*, bald — but Tosafos strongly disagrees. The phenomenon of the children of great men living in relative obscurity, always in the shadow of a towering parent, is poignant here.

The first teaching: *beni al teshev begovhah shel ir vesishaneh* — do not sit at the highest point of the city and try to learn there. The gathering place at the city heights will distract from study. The second: *ve-al tadur be-ir sherhosheha talmidei chachamim* — do not live in a city whose leaders are Torah scholars. The Rashbam explains: *detaridi begirsa velo taridi bemilei ditzibura* — they are too busy with their learning and not sufficiently occupied with communal needs. The third: *ve-al tikanes leveisecha pit'om, kol shekein leveit chaveirecha* — do not enter your own house suddenly, and certainly not your friend's house. Even with respect to one's own household, one must respect the privacy of other members; both Rashi and the Rashbam make this point explicitly. The teaching applies to all members of the household, not merely in situations where one suspects wrongdoing.

### Shoes & Breakfast

The fourth teaching: *ve-al timna min'alim meraglecha* — never go without shoes on your feet. The Gemara considers the wearing of shoes important, with implications for dignity and self-presentation that go beyond mere physical protection. The fifth: *hashkeim ve-echol bakayitz mipnei hachamah uvachoref mipnei hatzinah* — rise early and eat in the summer because of the sun and in the winter because of the cold. Whatever the precise logic of "because of the sun" or "because of the cold," the basic message is to have an early breakfast — the most important meal of the day.

---

## Akiva's 7 Teachings (II)

### Shabbos vs. Dependence

The sixth teaching brings us back to the principle already discussed: *va-aseh Shabbatecha chol ve-al titzatarech labriyos* — make your Shabbos like a weekday rather than become dependent on others. This is precisely why the Gemara cited this principle in the context of *arba kosot* — it is part of Rabbi Akiva's teachings to his son.

### Fortune & Blessing

The seventh teaching: *vehevei mishtadel im adam shehasha'ah mesacheket lo* — make efforts to associate with someone who is enjoying great fortune, so that perhaps some of it will rub off on you. This seems, on the surface, somewhat less pragmatic than the preceding advice — more in the realm of luck and mystical contagion than practical wisdom.

The Gemara, however, offers two readings. Rav Pappa says: this is not about buying from him or selling to him — that alone accomplishes little. Rather: *ela lemiavad shutafus bahadei* — try to go into business with him. This is very practical advice: if someone is having remarkable success, they may well know what they are doing, and becoming a partner in their venture is sound strategy.

But then Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak adds a deeper dimension by citing the verse from Iyov: *ma-aseh yadav berachta* — you have blessed the work of his hands. The principle derived is: *kol hanotel perutah mei-Iyov misbarech* — whoever received even a single *perutah* from Iyov was blessed. Anything that passed through his hands transferred blessing. On this reading, even buying from him or selling to him — any commercial contact that results in receiving something from the fortunate person — can transfer blessing. The advice thus has both a sober, pragmatic dimension and a more mystical, supernatural one. One may note the irony that Iyov ultimately lost everything — but the Gemara brackets that, since Iyov's reversal was caused by the *Satan*, not by any failure of his own fortune.

---

## Akiva to Shimon

### Great Tree Metaphor

The Gemara now shifts to five things Rabbi Akiva commanded to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai — *keshehuyu chavush beveit ha-asurim*, when Rabbi Akiva was imprisoned by the Romans for teaching Torah.

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai came to him and said: *Rebbi, lamdeni Torah* — Rebbi, teach me Torah. Rabbi Akiva refused, saying *eini melamdecha* — I will not teach you, I have already gotten myself into enough trouble. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai responded with a remarkable threat: if you do not teach me, I will tell my father Yochai — we almost never hear of Yochai himself, only of *bar Yochai* — and he will hand you over to the government. The audacity of this threat against a teacher already in Roman custody is startling. The Maharsha notes that Rabbi Akiva was already in prison, so the threat to make things worse for him carries its own irony. Further, what could Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai possibly report to the Romans? That Rabbi Akiva was teaching Torah — which is precisely why he was imprisoned. The very means of the threat thus defeats itself.

Rabbi Akiva responded: *yoter mi-mah sheha-egel rotzeh linok, haparah rotzah lehanik* — more than the calf wants to suckle, the cow wants to provide milk. He was not refusing out of lack of desire to teach; he was merely trying to be cautious. And Rabbi Shimon pressed the metaphor further: *u-mi al hasakana?* — and in your parable, who is in danger if it does not happen? *Vehalo egel hasakana* — it is the calf who is in danger, the one who will perish without the milk. The allusion is clear: Torah study for Rabbi Shimon was as vital as water for a fish — and this argument is precisely what Rabbi Akiva had used elsewhere to justify his own Torah teaching in the face of Roman prohibition. Rabbi Akiva conceded, and what follows is less formal Torah teaching than ethical instruction — perhaps a deliberate choice to avoid further legal jeopardy.

### Checked Books

The first teaching: *im bikashta leichanek, hitaleh be-ilan gadol* — if you want to go strangle yourself, hang from a big tree. The graphic image means: if you wish to take a bold or radical halachic position, find a great authority to support yourself from. This expression is found throughout Rabbinic literature; when an author is *mehadesh* something novel in a *teshuvah*, he will write *u-matzati ilan gadol litlot alav* — I found a great tree to support myself with — and cite the authority behind him.

The second teaching: *u-keshehatah melamed et bincha, lamdehu besefer muga* — when you teach your son, teach him from a corrected book. In an era when all texts were copied by hand, scribal error was a constant hazard. *Shabeshta kivan de-al al* — once a mistake enters a text, it stays. The Gemara asks: what does *muga* mean in this context? Rava (or, in another version, Rav Mesharshiya) says: *bechadta* — in a new book. The Rashbam adds that this may also mean the first time one is learning a new topic, when one is especially susceptible to absorbing errors uncritically.

Tosafos raises a striking objection: Rava himself holds that mistakes eventually correct themselves — *shabeshta mimmela nafka*, errors come out on their own. Is this not a contradiction? Tosafos resolves it: when a student is absorbing large quantities of material rapidly without yet being able to analyze it carefully, errors may self-correct once the student matures and begins to analyze more precisely. But when learning from a book, one tends to defer to the authority of the written text and never revisit one's initial understanding. The book becomes the authority, and the error is frozen in place. This is a genuinely insightful piece of educational psychology: the authority we assign to written texts makes their errors far more durable than errors absorbed in other ways.

The Maharsha adds his own note on the phrase *sefer she-eino muga* — he understands *chadta* as meaning a book that has simply never been proofread by anyone at all, making the primary concern the importance of at least one pass of editorial correction. This is a simpler reading than the "first time learning" interpretation. One might also ask: what kinds of books were being discussed in this period? Given that almost nothing was written down — other than *sifrei Torah* — the *sefer* in question may well be a *Sefer Torah*, which is interesting in its own right, since we tend to think of the *Sefer Torah* primarily in ritual terms — *kriat ha-Torah* — and not as a learning text. Yet in the Talmudic period, the *Sefer Torah* was evidently also the medium from which one began formal Torah study.

### Used Pot Metaphor

The third teaching: *lo tevashel be-kederah she-bishel bah chavercha* — do not cook in the pot your friend already used. *Mai nihu?* — what does this mean? *Grushah be-chayei ba-alah* — do not marry a divorced woman while her husband is still alive. The image of the "used pot" is, admittedly, an objectifying metaphor for women; it treats the divorced woman as a vessel that retains residue of its previous use.

The Gemara itself, however, significantly tempers this reading. *De-amar mar garush shenasa grushah arba de-ot ba-mitah* — if a divorced man marries a divorced woman, there are four minds in the bed: both parties are preoccupied with their former spouses. The concern is thus not asymmetrical — it applies equally to divorced men. The Gemara then asks whether the concern extends even to widows, who might be presumed less likely to actively think about their deceased husbands. The answer: *lefi she-ein kol etzba-ot shavot* — all fingers are not equal, a euphemism meaning that she will inevitably compare her new husband to the one she lost. This is at least a partial reversal of the objectification: here it is the man who is the object of comparison, not the woman. That said, one cannot ignore the practical consequence: divorced and widowed women are rendered even harder to remarry in a society that already diminishes their prospects, and one must acknowledge that reality honestly.

### Mitzvah & Profit

The fourth teaching: *mitzvah beguf gadol ochel peirot v'lo sachar* — a *mitzvah* with a large body: one eats the fruit and not for a fee. The Rashbam understands this as referring to lending money in a manner that is halachically permissible while still yielding profit — specifically, taking land as collateral and eating the fruit of that land while the loan remains outstanding, in a way that avoids the biblical prohibition of *neshech*. The virtue is in doing well while doing good: performing the *mitzvah* of lending to one who needs funds, and simultaneously making a legitimate profit.

### Pure Body Marriage

The fifth teaching: *mitzvah beguf tahor, nosei ishah v-lo banim* — a *mitzvah* with a pure body: marry a woman even if you already have children. This might seem paradoxical — what does marriage have to do with bodily purity in the ascetic sense? The Gemara's implicit reasoning appears to be the concern that a man who has already fulfilled *peru urvu* and remains unmarried will be chronically preoccupied with illicit sexual temptation. Marriage — even without the imperative of procreation — keeps one's *guf tahor*, one's bodily conduct in a sanctioned framework. The word *tahor* here thus refers not to ritual purity but to moral-behavioral propriety.

---

## HaKadosh's Commands

### Avoid Mockers

The Gemara now presents four things that Rabbeinu HaKadosh commanded his sons. The first: *al tadur b-shichnat tiv* — do not dwell in the place called *Shichnat Tiv*. Why? *Mishum d-leitzanei havu* — because they are mockers and skeptics, and *u-mashchu lach b-latzanusa* — they will draw you along into their culture of mockery and cynicism. This attitude is deeply corrosive to a life of Torah and to seriousness of purpose.

### Aramaic Bed

The second command: *v-al teshiv al mitah arammit* — do not sit on an Aramaic bed. Several readings are offered. One interpretation: *lo tigni b-lo kriyas shema* — do not go to sleep in the manner of a non-Jew, that is, without reciting *Shema*; one's sleep should begin with *tefillah* and *kriyas shema al ha-mitah*. The word *aramai* is used here in its generic sense of "non-Jew." Another reading: *lo tinsa giyurta* — do not marry a female convert, i.e., one whose bed was previously an Aramaic bed. A third reading takes the phrase literally: do not sit on a bed belonging to a non-Jewish woman — this stems from the story of Rav Pappa, who came to collect a debt from a non-Jewish woman; she allegedly killed her young child, placed the body in the bed, and when Rav Pappa rose from having sat there, accused him of the child's death in order to avoid repaying her debt. The concern, on this reading, is about practical danger and vulnerability to false accusation.

### Pay Taxes

The third command: *velo tavriach atzmecha min ha-machas* — do not try to escape your taxes. The *machas* was a specific form of tax — perhaps an import or transit duty — levied in the context of Roman governance. It is worth noting that certain *mishnayot* treat evading tax collectors without censure, and the *Yerushalmi* does not reverse this. But the *Bavli* introduces *dina d-malchuta dina* — the law of the kingdom is law — and with it, a fundamentally different attitude toward civic financial obligations. Rabbeinu HaKadosh, as the political head of the Jewish community and dependent on Roman goodwill, had strong reasons of his own for issuing this instruction. But the Gemara grounds it in entirely pragmatic terms: *dilma mishk-chu lach* — perhaps they will catch you — *veshakli minach kol de-it lach* — and take everything you have. As history has repeatedly demonstrated, tax evasion tends to be expensive when discovered.

---

## HaKadosh's Commands (II)

### Ox Danger

The fourth command: *ve-al ta-amod bifnei ha-shor she-oleh min ha-agam* — do not stand before an ox emerging from a swamp. *De-it beih satan mirakeid bein karnav* — the Satan dances between its horns. This is clearly a metaphor: the ox emerging from a swamp is agitated, unpredictable, and looking for trouble. Do not be the trouble it finds.

---

## Animal & Health Hazards

### Black Oxes Spring

Rabbi Shmuel qualifies the preceding warning: *beshor shachor* — this applies specifically to black oxen, which are particularly aggressive — *uveyomei Nissan* — and in the spring, when the natural world is in bloom and the animal's hormones are at their height.

Rav Oshaya taught: one keeps a distance of fifty *amot* — approximately seventy-five feet — from an ox that has never gored before, a *shor tam*. From an ox that has gored previously, a *shor mu-ad*, one should not even be within its line of sight. And in the name of Rabbi Meir: even if the head of the ox is buried in a basket eating its grain, *sak le-igra* — climb to the roof — *veshadi darga mitotach* — and kick the ladder away from beneath you. No ox is going to climb a ladder; the hyperbole is the point. Oxen are dangerous; maintain maximum distance.

### Animal Sounds

Rav teaches the proper vocalizations for managing various animals and situations. The call for oxen is *hein hein*. The call for a lion — though why one would need to call a lion is not obvious — is *ze ze*. The sound for moving camels is *da da*. And for pulling a boat, the Gemara offers *hayomei hi hi hileich vehileich chulya* — something like a rhythmic heave-ho, using the *h*-sound to coordinate effort. The Gemara's inclusion of these practical details is curious but evidently considered worth preserving.

### Leprosy Hazards

Abaye teaches that certain things lead to *davar acher* — leprosy. These are: *or* — untanned leather, specifically lying on hides that have not been properly processed; *dag* — specifically the fish called *shivuta* eaten in the spring; *kos chamim* — the remnants of a cup of *harshena* soup or porridge; *chamim* — scalding hot water thrown on oneself; *beitzim* — walking on eggshells; and *kinim levanim* — linen garments that have been washed and then left hanging for eight days without being laundered again, so that lice develop in them, and then worn. Each item in this list has its own Talmudic elaboration. The linen case is described as follows: *man demachvar livushei velo natir lei tamnaya yomei vehadar lavush leh, biryan hanach kinim, vekashin ledavar acher* — one who cleans linen garments and then leaves them for eight days without washing them, and then wears them, thereby produces lice — *vekashin ledavar acher*, and this leads to leprosy.

### Cats & Shoes

Rav Pappa teaches: *beita deit bei shunra, lo neil bei inshi belo masanei* — in a house that has a cat, one should not walk around barefoot. Why? *Mishum deshunra katel lechivya* — because cats kill snakes. *Ve-achal lei* — and eats the snake. *Ve-it bei dechivya garmei katekini* — but there are small bones within the snake, and *veyativ hei garma dechivya akarei* — if such a bone becomes lodged in one's foot, *lo nafik* — it cannot be extracted — *ve-istaken* — and one will be in mortal danger from the poison.

Conversely, in a house without a cat, one should not put on one's shoes in the dark. *Dilma mirach bei chivya* — a snake may have coiled inside the shoe — *velo yada ve-istaken* — and one will not know it is there until too late. In a place without cats to control the snake population, snakes in shoes were a genuine and life-threatening hazard. The story of a scorpion found nesting in a shoe on *erev Yom Kippur* at a yeshiva in Israel is a vivid reminder that for much of human history, and in much of the world today, such concerns are anything but theoretical.

---

---

# Pesachim 113

## R. Yishmael's Commands

### Mum B'Atzmecha

The larger thematic context of this daf flows from the Mishnah's ruling that even a pauper who subsists from the communal *tamchuy* must have *arba kosot* at the Seder. The Gemara traced this back to Rabbi Akiva's maxim that one should make one's *Shabbat* like a weekday rather than become dependent on others — a teaching he transmitted to his son as part of an ethical will. That, in turn, opened a sustained series of such charges: ethical instructions that sages transmitted to their students and children. One tradition records that Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, when confined together in prison, would discuss precisely these kinds of practical and ethical teachings rather than formal *halakha*.

Continuing in that vein, the Gemara cites three things Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi commanded Rabbi. The first is *al ta'as mum b'atzmecha* — do not make a wound in yourself. The Gemara immediately asks *mai hi*, what does this mean in practice? The answer: *lo tehavei lach dina bahadi tlata* — do not enter into litigation or business disputes with three people simultaneously. The concern is structural: one of the three becomes your opponent in court and the other two serve as his witnesses. You are three against one, and that is asking for trouble.

### Onaat Devarim

The second command is *v'al ta'amod al hamekach b'sha'at she'ein lecha damim* — do not examine merchandise when you have no money to purchase it. This is more than a counsel of self-interest; it touches on the biblical prohibition of *onaat devarim*, causing anguish through words or actions. The Gemara in Bava Metzia treats this at length. Here, the concern is raising the seller's expectations that you are a genuine buyer when you have no intention or means of purchasing. The Rashbam explains it as *mafsido* — causing a loss to the seller — because once you are seen handling an item and then setting it down, another potential buyer assumes something is wrong with it and moves on. Or, the seller loses time and other customers while attending to you. Either way, your presence and conduct generate a real harm to the owner, even without any explicit deceptive statement.

The third command — that if one's wife has gone to the *mikvah*, one should not be with her on the very first night when the immersion followed the biblical *niddah* count — generated some surprise. After all, the general understanding, reflected in the *poskim*, is that the first night after *mikvah* is considered a *mitzvah*. Rav explains the concern: *u'veniddah d'Oraita* — this refers to biblical *niddah* law, where a woman immerses seven days after the onset of bleeding without additional clean days. Since she may have been bleeding through those seven days, *hoil v'huchzak ma'ayan patuach* — her flow has been established as open — and there is concern that *dilma mashcha ziva*, perhaps some flow continues even after immersion, making relations potentially prohibited. The advice is therefore to wait a short additional period and verify that things have fully concluded. As the Gemara makes clear, this does not imply that women necessarily bleed for the entire seven days — most stop before then — it is simply a prudential buffer.

### R. Yossi's Commands

The Gemara then records three things that Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda commanded Rabbi. The first is *al tetzei yechidi balayla* — do not go out alone at night, a ruling we have already encountered in the Mishnah in connection with *shedim*. The second is *v'al ta'amod bifnei haner arom* — do not stand naked before a candle. The third is *v'al tikanes lemerchatz chadash* — do not enter a brand new bathhouse, on account of the fear that the floor might collapse. The practical concern is very concrete: in those bathhouses, bathers stood on a wooden floor directly above hot coals and steam. If the structure had not yet been tested, the floor might give way. How long must one wait before entering? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says twelve months.

### Candlelight & Epilepsy

The Gemara now circles back to explain the prohibition of standing naked before candlelight. A *braita* teaches: *ha'omed bifnei haner arom havei nichpeh* — one who stands naked before candlelight will develop epilepsy (*nichpeh*). Presumably, this is connected to some form of demonic influence, though the Gemara does not spell it out. The *braita* continues: *hamishamshe mitato le'or haner havayan lo banim nichpin* — one who has marital relations by candlelight will have children who are epileptic. The Gemara appears to understand this in terms of the mixing of categories: marital relations are presumed to belong to the dark, and epilepsy involves falling into unconsciousness when one should be awake — a confusion of the awake and asleep, the light and the dark. There is also the consistent Talmudic concern that the manner and circumstances of marital relations affect the character and wellbeing of the children conceived.

### Tinok Asleep

A further *braita* teaches: one who has marital relations on the same bed upon which an infant is sleeping — *oto tinok nichpeh* — that infant will become epileptic. Notably, the Gemara qualifies this in three ways, each narrowing the scope of the danger. First, *delo havei bar shata* — this applies only if the infant is less than a year old; once a year old, there is no concern. This seems counterintuitive from a moral standpoint — surely an older child's presence would be more problematic — but the Gemara's framework appears to be one of vulnerability: the younger the infant, the more susceptible to whatever spiritual forces are at play. Second, *deganei lahadei krayeh* — this applies only if the infant is sleeping at the foot of the bed; if the infant is sleeping at the head of the bed, there is no concern. Third, *dela manach yadeih alaveih* — this applies only when one does not place one's hand upon the child; if one places a hand on the child in a protective gesture while the child sleeps, there is no concern. The Gemara's logic seems to be that nakedness and the act of relations attract forces that are particularly dangerous to an infant's vulnerability, and that proximity, position, and physical protection all mediate that danger.

---

## Demons & Spirits

### Agrath Bath

The Gemara returns to explain the prohibition of going out alone at night. A *braita* teaches: *lo yetzei yechidi balayla* — do not go out alone at night — specifically not on Tuesday nights or Friday nights. The reason: *she'Igeret bat Machlat* — because Agrath bath Machlath, who is the queen of the *shedim*, *hi ushmoneh esreh ribo shel malachei chabalah yotzim* — she and 180,000 angels of destruction go out on these nights. Moreover, *kol echad ve'echad yesh lo reshut lechabel bifnei atzmo* — each of those 180,000 has individual permission to wreak havoc on its own.

### Chanina Encounter

Yet this does not match our experience of Tuesday and Friday nights. The Gemara explains that *me'ikara havu shechichi kulei yoma* — originally, these demonic forces were present every single day of the week. What changed? *Zimna chada paga beRabbi Chanina ben Dosa* — on one occasion, Agrath bath Machlath encountered Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa. She told him that were it not for the heavenly proclamation protecting him — *hizaheru beChanina u've'torato*, be cautious around Chanina and his Torah — she would have harmed him. Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa responded: if I am so significant in heaven, then I issue a decree — *she-lo ta'avri be-yishuv le-olam* — that you shall never be permitted to pass through inhabited areas. She pleaded with him, *bi-metuta minach*, please, *shevok li ravcha purta*, give me a little room. Whether she needed this space in order to have an opportunity to harm people or simply as living space is not entirely clear from the Gemara. What is notable is the phrase from earlier — that each of the 180,000 has *reshut lechabel*, permission to destroy — which suggests they are driven toward harm. In any case, Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa relented and permitted her the Tuesday nights and Friday nights, withdrawing his decree for those two nights only.

### Abaye & Agrath

*Ve-tu* — and furthermore — one might ask why Friday nights and Tuesday nights specifically became the designated danger nights. One suggestion raised is that every other night is either before or after a market day, so people are moving through the streets; Friday night, however, is when people are home, and perhaps that created a natural opening. In any event, some time later — *zimna achrita paga beih be-Abaye* — Agrath encountered Abaye. She said to him the same thing she had once said to Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa: were it not for the heavenly proclamation protecting *Nachmani* — Abaye's other name, which he bore because he was raised in the household of Rabbah bar Nachmani — and his Torah, she would have harmed him. Abaye, in response, issued the same decree she had once obtained a concession from: that she should never pass through inhabited areas. This time, it appears, he offered her no concession for Tuesday or Friday nights. This narrows the scope still further, and explains why the danger is not as prevalent as one might have expected from the initial framing.

### Narrow Alleys

The Gemara presses the point: *hacha chazinan de-avri* — but we do observe that *shedim* still seem to pass through inhabited places. The response: *hani gazyata ninhu* — these are instances of the narrow alleyways. The *shedim* travel on horses through the side alleys, and when those horses encounter people or other horses, *de-shamtei susaihu* — the horses bolt in fright, dragging the demons along with them into the more populated areas. They are not willfully entering *yishuv*; they are pulled in by their startled animals, and then must make their way back out. So the decree holds, but these edge-cases account for the occasional encounters that still occur.

---

## Urban Precautions

### Horses & Dogs

Rav gave practical urban advice to Rav Assi: *lo tadur be-mata delo tzanifei susya* — do not live in a city where horses do not neigh. The Rashbam explains that without horses, a city is vulnerable to enemies; horses provide the transportation and military capacity essential for both pursuit and escape. Similarly, *velo navach bah kalba* — do not live in a city where dogs do not bark, since dogs serve as a warning system against approaching danger. And do not live in a city *de-reish mata asya* — where the head of the city is a doctor. The reason given is that a doctor who leads the city will be too consumed by his medical practice to govern effectively. One variant of the text reads *de-reish mata Assi* — a subtle wordplay on Rav Assi's own name — implying: and I would not want you, Rav Assi, to be in charge of the city when you should be spending your time on Torah rather than politics.

### Multiple Wives

Rav also advised: *velo tnasiv tarti* — do not take two wives simultaneously. The concern is that two wives will conspire together against their husband. But then comes the surprising follow-up: *ve-i nasbat tarti nasiv telas* — if you have already taken two, take a third. The logic is that with three wives, any two who might conspire against the husband will have a third who can serve as an independent voice and protect him. One might wonder whether this simply escalates the problem indefinitely — four wives requiring five, and so on — but the apparent assumption is that it is more likely that coalitions fracture among three than they solidify, compared to the neat balance of two.

### Rav Kahana Labor

Rav said to Rav Kahana: *hafoch bi-nevielta* — it is better to involve yourself in trading animal carcasses as a livelihood *velo teifoch be-mili* — than to occupy yourself with words and idle talk. The point is that honest labor, even of an undignified kind, is preferable to living off speech or spending one's time in gossip and chatter. The practical instruction follows: *pshot nevielta be-shuka ve-shakil agra* — strip the carcass in the marketplace and accept your payment for it. And do not say, *velo teima Kahana ana ve-gavra raba ana ve-sanya bi milta* — do not say, "I am Kahana, I am a great man, such work is beneath my dignity." There is a genuine question whether Rav Kahana was actually a *Kohen*, or whether his name merely signaled a lineage associated with *kehuna*. Either way, Rav's message is clear: dignity of labor is not diminished by the nature of the work. The concern is entirely about the attitude one brings to earning a living.

The practical advice continues: *salkas le-igra sherusach be-hadach* — if you are climbing to a roof, take your provisions with you. Do not go on even a short excursion without food. And even if *me'ah karei be-mata be-zuza* — a hundred gourds are available in the market for a single *zuz*, *tuti knafecha lehavu* — make sure you have some of your own under your cloak. Even when food appears abundant and cheap, the prudent person maintains personal provisions.

Rav said to Chiyya his son: *lo tishti sama* — do not drink potions or medicinal preparations. The Rashbam's comment on this is remarkable: he says *al tisht samim* — do not take drugs — *mipnei shenikva lahem veset* — because your body will develop a pattern and dependence upon them; *v'libcha shocha* — your heart will always be craving them; *v'tachle maot* — and ultimately they will consume all your money. He adds explicitly that even for medical purposes one should avoid them if there is another option, because people become hooked even when they begin taking such substances for legitimate pain relief. The Rashbam's understanding maps with striking precision onto what we today recognize as addiction to narcotic pain medication.

Rav further told his son: do not take wide steps or jump over canals of water — which some understand as a warning against *pesi'ah gasah* — and *velo ta'aker kakka* — do not pull out teeth except as a last resort. Then: *velo tiknei b'chivya* — do not provoke a snake, and *velo tiknei b'arma'ah* — do not provoke an Aramean. The Gemara elaborates with a *braita*: there are three you do not provoke — *nochri katan*, a young non-Jew; *nachash katan*, a small snake; and *talmid katan*, a young student. Why? *D'malchuteihu achorei udneihu yativ* — their kingdom sits behind their ears, meaning their power is latent but coming. Do not be deceived by their present smallness into thinking you can harm them without consequence; they will grow into a position to retaliate.

---

## Business Advice

### Aivo Trading

Rav said to Aivo his son: *tarchi bach b'shma'ata tuva v'lo mistayei* — I have invested great effort in your learning and it is not proving successful. Come, *ta agmarcha milei d'alma* — let me teach you the ways of the world, some practical business wisdom.

The first piece of advice: *ad chala achraeicha zvincha zavin* — while the sand is still on your legs, sell your wares. Meaning: as soon as you return from a trading journey, sell immediately. Do not wait for the absolute best price; move your merchandise and repeat the cycle. *Kol milei zavin v'techaret* — you can sell almost anything and justifiably regret having gotten a lesser price than you might have. But *bar mechmra d'zvin v'lo techaret* — except for wine: sell wine as soon as possible and never regret it, because by the time you find a better buyer the wine may well have turned to vinegar.

Next: *sharei kisecha ptach, ptach sakeikha* — first open your money pouch, then open your sack of goods. Collect payment before delivering the merchandise; always position yourself holding the money rather than the goods when there is any ambiguity in the terms of a transaction.

Then: *kava me'ara velo kura me'igra* — a small measure from the ground is better than a large measure from the roof. The Rashbam explains this as preferring nearby trade with a smaller margin over distant trade with a potentially larger margin. The effort, risk, and uncertainty of distant commerce often outweigh the apparent advantage of a higher price.

### Beer Business

*Tamrei bechalozach levei sudna rahit* — if you have dates in your basket, run to the brewers. Do not let the dates sit to be eaten or to spoil; instead, convert them into beer immediately and make a substantial profit. The Gemara asks: *v'ad kama* — up to how large a quantity does this apply? Rava says: *ad tlata sa* — up to three *sa'im*. Beyond that quantity, presumably there is less danger of the dates being eaten up before you can brew with them, so the urgency is somewhat reduced.
