The profitability of the beer business is attested directly: *amar Rav Papa, ei lav deramina shikra lo i'atarei* — Rav Papa said, had I not gone into the beer business I would not have become wealthy. A parallel tradition attributes the same statement to Rav Chisda.

The Gemara asks: *mai sudna?* What does this Aramaic word for the brewers actually mean? Rav Chisda explains it as *sod na'eh* — a good secret. Perhaps the brewing process itself was a trade secret; or perhaps the real secret is that people do not appreciate how profitable it is to convert dates into beer rather than simply eating them. There is a further reading: *sod na'eh u'gemilut chasadim* — a good secret and acts of kindness — which appears to be a play on Rav Chisda's own name, *Chisda* evoking *chasadim*, suggesting that the profits of the beer trade enable one to engage in philanthropy.

### Credit Dangers

Rav Papa offered a pair of warnings about the dangers of credit and liens. *Kol agav gavi ba'ei* — anything involving a lien or a written obligation still has to be collected; do not treat it as money in hand. He may be referring specifically to the mechanism of *metaltalei agav mekarkei* — attaching a lien on movable goods through a lien on land — where the chattel is particularly difficult to trace and recover. More broadly: *kol ashrai safek ati safek lo ati* — anything extended on credit may or may not ever be paid; *ve-d'ati mus ravnei mineih* — and even if it comes, it may arrive in degraded form, paid out in small installments rather than all at once. The practical counsel is clear: avoid having extensive notes and outstanding loans; they are risky investments that rarely perform as expected.

---

## Jerusalem Wisdom

### War & Shabbat

Rabbi Yochanan transmitted three teachings in the name of the people of Jerusalem. First: *keshe'ata yotze lemilchama al tetze berishona ela tetze be'achrona* — when going out to war, do not go in the front lines but in the rear guard — *kedei shetikanes berishona* — so that you can be the first to return safely. The Maharsha notes that it might have been simpler to say that those in the front are killed first, but the Gemara instead phrases it positively.

Second — and strikingly, this appears here in the name of the people of Jerusalem rather than in the name of Rabbi Akiva alone — *va'aseh Shabat-cha Chol ve'al titztarech labriyot*: make your Shabbat like a weekday rather than becoming dependent on others. This may reflect that both Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan drew on a common Jerusalem tradition, or that the maxim circulated among different transmitters independently.

Third: *vehevay mishtadel im mi shehasha'ah mesacheket lo* — seek out and associate with those who are experiencing good fortune. This also appeared earlier in the context of Rabbi Akiva's teachings, suggesting again a shared or overlapping tradition.

### Rooftop & Marriage

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi transmitted three things in the name of the people of Jerusalem. The first: *al tarbe begnut mishum ma'aseh shehayah* — do not engage in behavior that is *gnut*, shameful or exposed, in light of the famous event that occurred. The Gemara understands this as a reference to the episode of David and Batsheva. The Rashbam, however, suggests that the correct reading is *al tirbe begagot* — do not do things on rooftops — since that is precisely the setting of the episode, and one should not assume that being on a rooftop means being out of sight.

The second teaching: *bitcha bagra, shachrer avdecha veten lah* — when your daughter reaches maturity, free your slave and marry her to him. The urgency here is about sexual awareness: once a daughter is of marriageable age and men — including slaves in the household — are of interest to her and she to them, one must act decisively. The structure of the advice reflects the patriarchal setting, where the father controls decisions about marriage; the parallel concern for young men appears in the Gemara's general exhortations to men to marry young, driven by the same awareness of the *yetzer hara*.

The third: *vehevay zahir be'ishtcha mechatanah rishon* — be careful with your wife in relation to her first son-in-law. The Gemara asks why. Two explanations are offered: *mishum ervah* — there is a concern about an illicit liaison, consistent with the sexual theme running through all three teachings — and *mishum mamon* — or perhaps the concern is financial, that she will shower him with excessive gifts out of her joy at her daughter's marriage. The Gemara concludes: *veha veha itnehu* — both concerns are real and valid.

---

## Righteous & Wicked

### Olam Ha-Ba

Rabbi Yochanan said: three people inherit the *olam ha-ba*. They are: *hadar be'eretz Yisrael* — one who lives in the Land of Israel; *hamigadel banav letalmud Torah* — one who raises his children for Torah study; and *hamavdil al hayayin b'motza'ei shabbatot* — one who makes *havdalah* on wine on *motzaei Shabbat*.

A student observed that Rabbi Yochanan himself lost all ten of his children while they were still young, which is poignant given his inclusion of *megadel banav letalmud Torah*. The Maharsha notes that the merit attaches to the act of raising children toward Torah, not to their ultimate success — so the reward belongs to the father regardless of outcome.

The question arises: what is the *chiddush* of making *havdalah* on wine? The Gemara answers: *d'mishayer mikiddusha l'avdalta* — that you reserve wine from *Kiddush* for *havdalah*. As Tosafot explains, if one has a limited supply of wine, one does not drink it entirely at *Kiddush* but holds some in reserve so that *havdalah* can be recited *al hakos*. This connects to the broader debate over whether *Kiddush* on bread is a true equivalent or only a *bedi'avad* option. The Maharsha's view, derived from this Gemara, appears to be that when wine is available, even a small quantity should be used for *Kiddush* — and if some can be preserved for *havdalah*, so much the better — rather than defaulting to *Kiddush* on bread in order to save the wine for *havdalah*.

The three categories — living in *Eretz Yisrael* rather than *chutz la'aretz*, raising one's children for Torah, and separating between *kodesh* and *chol* through *havdalah* — share a thematic coherence around the act of sanctification and separation: between holy and mundane land, between Torah-life and ordinary life, and between Shabbat and the rest of the week.

### Daily Proclamation

Rabbi Yochanan further said: three are proclaimed about each day by the Holy One Blessed be He. First: *al ravak hadar bikrach v'eino chotei* — a single man who lives in a large city, a *krach*, and does not sin. The *krach* is even larger than an ordinary *ir*, a metropolis with abundant opportunity for sin; remaining celibate in such an environment is an act of extraordinary self-mastery over the *yetzer hara*. Second: *v'al ani hamachzir aveida l'va'aleha* — a poor person who returns a lost object to its owner. Here too, the *yetzer hara* — the desire for money, sharpened by genuine need — is overcome. Third: *v'al ashir ham'aser peirotav b'tzina* — a wealthy person who tithes his produce in private. The wealthy man's *yetzer hara* is not toward keeping the *ma'aser* itself but toward the *ga'avah* of public display — announcing how much he is giving. Doing it quietly conquers that desire.

The Gemara provides a vivid illustration. When a *tanna* recited the teaching about the single man in a large city in the presence of Rava and Rav Safra — who was himself such a man, a bachelor living in a great *krach* — *tzahavu panav de-Rav Safra*: Rav Safra's face lit up. Rava immediately deflated him: *lav kigon mar* — we are not talking about you. Who do they proclaim about in heaven? *Kigon Rav Hanina ve-Rav Oshaya* — like Rav Hanina and Rav Oshaya. These two were shoemakers in the Land of Israel whose shop was located in the market adjacent to the brothel district. They made shoes for the prostitutes and delivered them directly into those premises. The women would look at them, but *lo madlu einaihu le-istakulei behu* — they kept their eyes averted and would not look back. The prostitutes were so struck by their conduct that when they took oaths, they swore *be-hayeihon de-rabbanan kaddishei de-be-ara de-Yisrael* — by the lives of the holy rabbis of the Land of Israel. That is the standard against which celestial proclamation is measured — not simply living a celibate life, but maintaining holiness under conditions of maximum exposure and temptation.

### God Loves

The Gemara continues with three whom God loves: *mi she-eino ko'es* — one who does not get angry; *u-mi she-eino mishtaker* — one who does not get drunk; and *ve-mi she-eino ma'amid al middosav* — one who does not stand on his dignity, who is willing to let go of grievances and not demand satisfaction when wronged. The Maharsha connects these three to the principle in Pirkei Avot that one who is beloved by people is beloved by Heaven. These three qualities define a person who interacts with others in a way that does not provoke, alienate, or burden those around him. They are, at their core, *bein adam la-chavero* virtues.

### God Hates

And three whom God hates: *ha-medabber echad ba-peh ve-echad ba-lev* — one who says one thing with his mouth while thinking another in his heart, the duplicitous person. *Ve-ha-yodei'a eidut be-havero ve-eino me'ido lo* — one who possesses testimony that would help his fellow and withholds it. And *ve-ha-ro'eh davar erva be-havero u-me'id bo yehidi* — one who witnesses his fellow committing a sexual sin and goes to testify against him alone, as a single witness. The grammatical distinction matters here: *bo* rather than *lo* — he testifies *against* him, not *for* him. And because testimony in matters of personal status and sexual prohibition requires a minimum of two witnesses to carry any legal weight — unlike monetary cases where a single witness at least triggers an oath — the sole witness accomplishes nothing legally. His testimony will not be believed or acted upon in court, and the only practical effect is to generate *shem ra*, an evil reputation that damages the subject without any legitimate process.

---

## Testimony & Hatred

### Tuvya & Zigud

The Gemara provides a concrete illustration: *ki ha deTuvya chata* — Tuvya sinned, presumably in some form of sexual transgression. *Va'ata Zigud lechudei* — Zigud came alone and gave testimony against Tuvya before Rav Pappa. Rav Pappa's response was to administer lashes — not to Tuvya, the one who had sinned, but to Zigud, the one who testified. *Tuvya chata veZigud minged?* Tuvya sins and Zigud gets lashes? The explanation: *de-chituv lo yakum ed echad be'ish* — one witness cannot rise against a person in these matters. *Ve'at lechudach asda'at bei* — you have testified by yourself. *Shem ra be'alma kamafket bei* — all you have accomplished is to spread an evil report about him. The Torah's demand for two witnesses in personal status matters is not merely procedural; it is protective. Without that threshold, the sole witness has not initiated a legal process but committed something that functions as *motzi shem ra* — libel.

This case raises questions that extend far beyond the Gemara's own context. The tension between protecting potential innocent victims of misconduct and protecting the accused from unverifiable accusations is real and urgent, particularly in the contemporary community. A lone witness reporting serious misconduct — sexual abuse, improper behavior — places the community in a difficult position. Dismissing the report entirely silences those who may be telling the truth; accepting it uncritically and acting punitively on that basis can destroy a person's life on the basis of an accusation that may be false. One important factor that emerges from the Gemara is whether there are other corroborating accounts — whether other people have reported similar patterns — as opposed to a single isolated claim with no supporting context.

### Permitted Hatred

The Gemara now turns to what the lone witness *may* do, given that he cannot testify. *Amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak amar Rav: mutar lesano'aso* — it is permitted to hate the person you have witnessed sinning, even though you may not testify against him. The verse cited: *ki tireh chamor sone'acha rovetz tachat masa'o* — if you see the donkey of someone you hate struggling under its burden. The Gemara asks: *mai sonay?* What kind of person are you legitimately hating here? If it is a non-Jew, that does not fit — the verse concerns a fellow Jew. And if it concerns just any Jew you happen to hate, the question arises: *umi shari lesanya?* Are you even permitted to hate a fellow Jew? Is this not a violation of *lo tisnah*?

The Gemara resolves: the verse must be speaking of a case where there are witnesses — *de'ika sahadi de'avid issura* — and the person has been publicly established as a habitual transgressor. But if there are witnesses, then *kuly alma nami misne sanei leh* — everyone should hate him; why does the verse say *your* enemy, as though it is specific to you? Therefore, the case must be the one described earlier: *d'hazye bei ihu dvar ervah* — you yourself saw him commit a sexual sin. That is why it is specifically *your* hatred: you know; others do not; and you may not tell them. Sexual sins are committed in private, and the *yetzer hara* operates most powerfully there, which is precisely why you who witnessed it are uniquely positioned to hate him while remaining unable to share what you know.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak goes further: *mitzvah lesanoso* — it is not merely permitted but a *mitzvah* to hate him, as the verse states *yirat Hashem sonei ra* — the fear of God is the hatred of evil.

### Report to Master

Rav Acha brei de-Rava asked Rav Ashi: *mahu lemeimrei leh lerabbeih lemisnaye* — what is the ruling regarding telling the person's master or employer, so that the master should also hate him? This is not a question of formal court testimony; it is a question of whether the lone witness has an obligation or permission to inform someone in authority over the transgressor — a *rebbe*, an employer — about the behavior he has witnessed, even though it cannot be formally proven.

Rav Ashi answers: *iy yada de'meheiman lerabbeih ke-bei terei* — if you know that you will be trusted by the master the way two witnesses are trusted — that is, if your report will be accepted and acted upon responsibly — then *leimrei leh*, you should tell him. *Ve-i lo lo leimrei leh* — and if you will not be trusted in that way, you should not tell him. The reason is that if you will not be believed, the only outcome is that you create *lashon hara* about the transgressor and do no good for anyone.

The underlying principle is about calibrating the communication of information to the likely consequence. When telling someone will actually help — will reach a person in a position to act wisely and protectively — then the information should be shared. When telling someone will merely generate suspicion, damage the accused, and accomplish nothing constructive, it should not be shared. This is a framework, not a formula; it requires real judgment about the specific situation, the relationship between the parties, and the reliability of the chain of communication.

### Hatred Breeds

Tosafot raises a pointed question on the discussion of subduing one's *yetzer hara* through action. The earlier teaching — familiar from elsewhere in the Talmud — holds that if you hate someone and his animal is struggling, you should attend to *his* animal before you attend to the animal of your friend whom you love, specifically in order to subdue the *yetzer hara* of hatred. But Tosafot asks: we just established that it is a *mitzvah* to hate this person. If so, what *yetzer hara* is there to subdue? Where is the improper desire here?

Tosafot's answer is searching and psychologically acute. *Kevan shehu soneh o, gam chavero soneh oto* — because once you hate him, even if justifiably, he will hate you back. *Kamayim hapanim lapanim ken lev haadam laadam* — as water reflects the face, so does the human heart reflect back to another human heart. Once he hates you back, you will hate him in return — and that secondary hatred has nothing whatsoever to do with the original sin you witnessed. It is pure mutual enmity, self-perpetuating and unjustified. *Uvah mitoch kach lidei sinah gemurah veshayach kfiyat hayetzer* — and from all of this one arrives at total hatred, and the suppression of the *yetzer hara* becomes relevant precisely there: you must work against the resentment, the counter-hatred, the escalation that your justified initial hatred has set in motion.

*Sinah goreret sinah* — hatred begets hatred. The Tosafot is making a sobering observation: even righteous hatred carries within it a mechanism of moral corrosion. You may be right about the first step; but the chain it sets off is not within your control, and it can consume you in hatred that bears no relationship to the original wrong. The *mitzvah* to subdue the *yetzer hara* in one's behavior toward a person one justifiably hates is, in the end, self-protective — a way of not allowing what begins as a principled moral response to degenerate into something far more destructive.

---

---

# Pesachim 115

## Daf Overview

### Opening

Today's daf is 115, and we pick up in the middle of 114b. A schematic of the *haggadah* has been distributed, which will serve as a useful reference throughout the discussion. The schematic traces the *seder* from start to finish, with the key instructional rubrics underlined so as to track how those instructions developed over time.

### Haggadah Flow

We have already discussed *Kadesh* and *Karpas*; *Urchatz* has not yet been addressed, and we will return to it in due course. The structure of the *haggadah* also involves the removal and restoration of the *shulchan*, which likewise awaits treatment. The instructions embedded in the rubrics are of particular interest, and the schematic will help situate each discussion as it arises.

---

## Maror Upfront

### Mishna Anomaly

The *gemara* on this daf engages with a striking feature of the *mishnah*: when the *mishnah* describes the vegetable dipped at the beginning of the *seder* — what we call *karpas* (though the *mishnah* itself does not use that term) — it identifies the vegetable as *maror*. This is puzzling, because we know that *maror* is meant to be eaten later, together with *matzah*, as the verse states: *al matzos u'merorim yochluhu* — "upon *matzos* and *maror* shall you eat it." The *gemara* therefore asks: by using *maror* at the beginning, have you not preempted performing the *mitzvah* of *maror* at the proper time?

### Intent Requirement

The *gemara* presents two ways of understanding why the *mishnah* permits this. Reish Lakish holds that *mitzvos* require intent — *mitzvos tzrichos kavana* — and therefore when one ate the *maror* at the outset for the purpose of *karpas*, one had no intent to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *maror*, and was thus not *yotzei*. The *chiddush* of the *mishnah*, on this reading, is that one may use *maror* upfront without fear of discharging the *mitzvah* prematurely, because intent is required.

### No Intent Req

The *gemara* then raises an alternative: perhaps the *chiddush* of the *mishnah* is precisely the opposite — that *mitzvos* do *not* require intent, and even so, we use *maror* upfront in order to have two dippings, with the *mitzvah* discharged early and the second dipping performed later. This seems bizarre on its face — one would have thought that if all you have is *maror*, you should simply skip *karpas* and wait until the proper time. But the *gemara* suggests that perhaps the *chiddush* is that we deliberately use it for both, precisely so that there will be two dippings. The *gemara* thus presents the question starkly: does the *mishnah*'s allowance of *maror* upfront prove that *mitzvos* require intent (and therefore it is safe to use *maror* early), or does it prove that even without intent, the two-dipping structure is worth performing *maror* out of sequence?

### Symbolism

It is worth pausing over a pedagogical dimension of this question. One of the responses children give at the *seder* — *halailah hazeh kulo maror*, "this night is entirely *maror*" — is recited before *maror* is formally introduced, which *Tosafot* works hard to resolve. But there is a broader symbolic logic worth considering: the *seder* begins with *Avadim Hayinu* and culminates in *geulah*. By the time one arrives at *matzah*, the blessing *Asher ge'alanu v'ga'al es avoseinu miMitzrayim* has been recited. Why, at that point, return to *maror*, the symbol of affliction?

It is not unreasonable to speculate that in the *mishnah*'s conception, *maror* at the beginning makes deliberate symbolic sense — just as *ha lachma anya* frames the *matzah* at the start as a symbol of poverty and slavery, while later, *matzah al shum mah* reframes it as a symbol of *geulah*, so too perhaps *maror* was meant to appear at the beginning as a symbol of *avdus*, before the *geulah* narrative has been completed. This would also explain why one says *halailah hazeh kulo maror* before the *maror* is brought, and why the two-dipping structure of the *mishnah* does not strike the *mishnah* itself as problematic at all. The *mishnah* never problematizes using *maror* upfront; only the *gemara* does.

That said, the *gemara* clearly does not understand the *mishnah* this way. The *gemara* assumes that the ideal is to eat *matzah* and *maror* together in the manner of the *Korban Pesach* — *al matzos u'merorim yochluhu* — and therefore treats the early *maror* as something requiring justification. Perhaps the conflation of *karpas* and *maror* in the *mishnah* reflects a transitional moment between the Temple-era model, where *matzah* and *maror* were eaten together with the *Korban Pesach*, and the later, more structured rabbinic *seder*, where each element is separately defined and sequenced.

### Braisa Evidence

The *gemara* then brings a *braisa* to challenge Reish Lakish's position. The *braisa* states: if one ate *maror* that was *demai* (produce whose *terumot* and *ma'asros* are uncertain), one has fulfilled the obligation. If one ate it without intent — *belo miskayvein* — one has fulfilled the obligation. And if one ate it in two separate portions, provided they are consumed within the time it takes to eat half a loaf of bread (*achilas pras*), one has also fulfilled the obligation. The absence of an intent requirement, stated explicitly in the *braisa*, seems to undermine Reish Lakish's position. The *gemara* responds: *tannai hi* — this is a dispute among *tannaim*.

### R. Yosei View

To substantiate this, the *gemara* cites a further *braisa*: Rabbi Yosei says that even if one dipped with the *maror* at the beginning (*af al pi shetiblu bachazeres*), it is still a *mitzvah* to bring back *chazeres* (the *maror*), *charoses*, and the two cooked dishes. The very fact that Rabbi Yosei calls bringing the *maror* back a *mitzvah* implies that the obligation was not yet discharged — which supports the view that *mitzvos tzrichos kavana*. The *gemara* pushes back: perhaps Rabbi Yosei holds *mitzvos einan tzrichos kavana*, and the *maror* was fully discharged upfront, but he requires bringing it back for the sake of the second dipping, so that there will be *trei tibulei* — two dippings — as a *hikara* for the children. The *gemara* deflects this by noting that if that were so, Rabbi Yosei would not have called the return of the *maror* a *mitzvah*, since it would be merely a procedural requirement rather than the fulfillment of a commandment. This, the *gemara* concludes, is how Reish Lakish's position survives as a view in a *tannaim* dispute.

---

## Blessings/2Dips

### Rav Huna

Before returning to the *gemara*'s discussion of intent, there is an important digression concerning the *blessings* recited when *maror* is used for both dippings. The *gemara* first addresses a preliminary matter — *mai shenei tavshilin*, what are the two cooked dishes on the *seder* plate? Rav Huna says beets and rice. Rava was careful always to have beets and rice, in deference to Rav Huna's statement. Rav Ashi notes from this that Rav Huna did not accept the view of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who held that rice is a type of grain, that one incurs *kares* for leavening it, and that one may fulfill the *mitzvah* of *matzah* with it on Passover — a position so marginal that the *gemara* treats it as effectively rejected. Chizkiya adds that even fish smeared with egg can count as two dishes. Rav Yosef clarifies that the two dishes must be two types of meat — one *zecher l'Pesach*, a remembrance of the Paschal offering, and one *zecher l'Chagiga*, a remembrance of the festival offering. Ravina adds that even a bone and the broth in which it was cooked can count as two.

*Tosafot* raises the question of whether, if *Shabbat* falls on *Erev Pesach* and the *chagiga* was not offered, one would have only a single cooked dish. He concludes that since the concern is about creating a visual distinction, this need not be applied in such cases, lest it confuse people. As for *Rashi*'s suggestion that one dish should be roasted (*tzli*), as a *zecher l'Pesach*, and the other cooked, as a *zecher l'Chagiga*, *Tosafot* demurs: since it is established that the *chagiga* too was eaten roasted, according to Beit Shammai, there would be no visual distinction, and so both may be cooked. Notably, nothing in the *gemara* suggests that these dishes are merely symbolic items to be gazed at rather than eaten.

The *gemara* then turns to the central question of this section. It states: *pashita* — it is obvious — that if one has *other* vegetables available for *karpas*, one makes *borei pri ha'adama* over the vegetable at the outset and later makes *al achilas maror* when one reaches the *maror* portion of the *seder*. There is no blessing conflict because the two acts of eating are entirely distinct.

The question arises only where all one has is *maror* — *chasa* — and one uses it for both the initial dipping and later for the *mitzvah* eating after *hamotzi*. In that case, what blessings does one recite, and in what order?

Rav Huna rules: at the outset, one recites *borei pri ha'adama* on the *maror* used for *karpas* and eats it. Later, when one reaches the *maror* eating after *hamotzi*, one recites *al achilas maror* and eats. The blessings are kept in their natural sequence — *borei pri ha'adama* comes first because it is the primary botanical blessing, and *al achilas maror* comes when one fulfills the *mitzvah*.

### R. Chisda Obj

Rav Chisda challenges Rav Huna's position sharply, at the top of 115a. His objection: after you have already stuffed your stomach with *maror* — *l'achar shemilei kreiso heimenu* — can you really turn around and recite *al achilas maror*, the blessing proclaiming that you are about to perform the *mitzvah* of eating *maror*? You ate *maror* an hour ago. The blessing *al achilas maror* is a *birchas hamitzvah* — a blessing on the act of the commandment — and reciting it after one has already been eating *maror* is simply not appropriate.

### R. Chisda Sol

Rav Chisda's solution is therefore: recite both blessings at the very beginning — *borei pri ha'adama* and *al achilas maror* — before the first dipping, and then eat the *maror* the second time, after *hamotzi*, without any additional blessing.

### Regional Practice

The *gemara* records that in Surya the practice followed Rav Huna, while the household of Rav Sheshes the son of Rav Yehoshua followed Rav Chisda. The fact that Surya maintained the practice of Rav Huna is puzzling — it implies that a community regularly had nothing but *maror* for both dippings, and deliberately chose that practice rather than simply obtaining another vegetable. This may itself reflect a view, perhaps unacknowledged by the *gemara*, that *davka* using *maror* upfront was considered appropriate or even preferable.

### Final Ruling

The *halakhah* is ruled like Rav Chisda: both blessings are recited at the outset.

### Tosafot Expl

What exactly is this dispute about? The simplest reading, as the *Rashbam* seems to suggest, is that it is simply an application of the earlier debate: if *mitzvos tzrichos kavana*, you were not *yotzei* *maror* upfront, so Rav Huna can defer *al achilas maror* until later; if *mitzvos einan tzrichos kavana*, you will be *yotzei* when you first eat the *maror*, and therefore both blessings must be made at the outset.

*Tosafot* disagrees. If the dispute were that simple, the objection would have been framed differently — Rav Chisda would have said *l'achar sheyatza hu chozer mevarech al achilas maror*, "after you have already been *yotzei*, can you still recite *al achilas maror*?" Instead, Rav Chisda says *l'achar shemilei kreiso heimenu* — after you have already been eating *maror*. This language, *Tosafot* argues, reflects a different concern: not that one has formally discharged the *mitzvah*, but that the propriety of reciting *al achilas maror* is compromised by the fact that one has been consuming *maror* throughout. Even granting, as *Tosafot* does, that *mitzvos tzrichos kavana* and therefore the *mitzvah* was not discharged at the first dipping, it is still unseemly to recite *al achilas maror* after extended prior consumption of *maror*.

The question that then arises is: how can one recite *al achilas maror* at the very beginning if one has not yet fulfilled the *mitzvah* with intent? *Tosafot* reasons that as long as one recites the blessing and begins the *mitzvah* — even in some preliminary way — the *berachah* remains valid even with an interruption before the *mitzvah* is completed. *Tosafot* compares this to *tekias shofar* on Rosh Hashanah: the primary *tekios* through which one is *yotzei* are those during *shemoneh esrei*, yet one recites the blessing before the earlier *tekios*, and the blessing remains connected to the *mitzvah* even after the full *amidah* and its repetition. The logic is that both acts — the earlier *maror* and the earlier *tekios* — are sufficiently connected to the *mitzvah* that the *berachah* can be considered to have begun on the *mitzvah*, and interruption does not sever that connection.

This discussion opens onto a broader question: to what extent is the *haggadah* itself a *hefsek*? Does it constitute an interruption that severs the connection between the blessings made early in the *seder* and the eating that follows? This is a major dispute among the *rishonim*. If the *haggadah* is a *hefsek*, then one would need a new *borei pri hagafen* on the second cup — and in fact one does — and one might also require a new *borei pri ha'adama* on the *maror*. *Tosafot* accepts that the *haggadah* is a *hefsek* and therefore a new *borei pri hagafen* is needed on the second cup. As for *borei pri ha'adama* on *maror*, *Tosafot* argues that it is not required because *maror* is covered by *hamotzi* — the bread blessing covers food eaten in the course of the meal.

But *Tosafot*'s position raises a further question, since *maror* is not a standard accompaniment to bread in the way that other foods are; it comes to the table because of a *mitzvah*, not as an ordinary part of the meal. *Tosafot* nonetheless holds that *hamotzi* covers it. What *Tosafot* does not require is that one recite *borei pri ha'adama* explicitly on *maror*, provided *hamotzi* has been said. And yet, *Tosafot* does maintain that the earlier *al achilas maror* — made upfront — remains in effect and need not be repeated, since the *berachah* was attached to the beginning of the *mitzvah* and retains its force even across the *hefsek* of the *haggadah*.

Standard *haggadah* texts reflect this by instructing that when one reaches *karpas*, one should have in mind — *umichavein liftor bivracha gam es hamaror* — that the *borei pri ha'adama* is intended to cover the *maror* as well. This works only on the assumption that the *haggadah* is *not* an interruption with respect to that blessing. As noted, nobody follows both stringencies simultaneously — requiring a new *borei pri ha'adama* for *maror* and also holding that *hamotzi* does not cover it. The practice simply never developed in that direction.

The *karpas* instructions also raise a separate point: the instruction to eat less than a *kezayis*. The *gemara* never specifies a quantity for *karpas*; the *Rambam* actually requires a *kezayis* and eats *davka* a *kezayis* of *karpas*. The practice of eating less than a *kezayis* developed from precisely the concern being discussed: if one eats a *kezayis*, one may incur an obligation to recite a *berachah achronah*, and given the uncertainty about whether the *haggadah* is a *hefsek* and whether one should be *yotzei* with *birkas hamazon*, the practice evolved to eat less than a *kezayis* and thereby sidestep the question altogether. Similarly, the instructions specify that *karpas* is dipped in salt water. *Tosafot* mentions that Rashi and other early Ashkenazic authorities had the practice of dipping in *charoses*, consistent with the view that *charoses* is itself a *mitzvah* as a *zecher l'tit* (a remembrance of the mortar). The *Rambam* also endorses dipping in *charoses*. This would cohere with a reading of the *seder* that places symbols of *avdus* prominently at the beginning — *charoses* and perhaps *maror* both upfront — before the *geulah* narrative takes over.

There are also debates about whether *karpas* should be eaten *b'haseiva*, reclining. If *karpas* is understood as part of the Roman-style appetizer course that evokes freedom, one would recline; if it is understood as a *zecher* to the bitterness of servitude, one would not. There is no clear resolution in the *gemara*, and the practice varies.

Finally, Rav Acha the son of Rava would make a point of obtaining other vegetables for *karpas* — *l'afukei nafshei mi'pelugta* — specifically to avoid this entire dispute. This itself reflects that there were communities for whom using *maror* upfront was simply standard, and perhaps even preferred, and that the halachic complications the *gemara* identifies were navigated differently in different places.

---

## Lvls Negation

### Principle

The *gemara* now introduces what is in many ways the most structurally significant principle governing how the *seder* is conducted: *mitzvos* — specifically two acts of *mitzvah* eating performed simultaneously — do not negate one another (*mitzvos ein mevatlos zu es zu*), as long as they are at the same level of obligation. However, the *gemara* states that when one obligation is *d'oraisa* and the other is *d'rabbanan*, the *d'rabbanan* does negate the *d'oraisa* (*asi d'rabbanan umevatel lei l'd'oraisa*).

The specific application is this: since *matzah* today is a biblical obligation (*d'oraisa*), independent of the *Korban Pesach*, while *maror* today is only rabbinic (*d'rabbanan*) — *maror* having been biblically mandated only in conjunction with the *Korban Pesach* — one may not eat them together. If one did so, the rabbinic obligation would negate the biblical one. What precisely does "negate" mean here? It is not simply that one cannot taste the *matzah* because of the *maror*; we will see shortly that one does not need to *taste* the *matzah* at all — swallowing *matzah* whole fulfills the obligation. Rather, there is a more fundamental claim: eating an item that carries a weaker obligation simultaneously with an item that carries a stronger obligation redefines the act itself. One can no longer call it an act of eating *matzah* in the full sense, because the act is simultaneously defined by a different, lesser obligation. The presence of the *d'rabbanan* is like an intrusion that prevents the act from being classified purely as an *achilas matzah d'oraisa*. This is a genuinely striking idea, and it appears to be specific to the domain of simultaneous *mitzvah* eating.

A comparison may be drawn to the principle of *kam lei b'drabba minei* — if one commits a capital offense simultaneously with a lesser offense, the lesser offense cannot be prosecuted separately because the act is entirely subsumed by the capital crime. Here, the logic runs in the opposite direction: one *wants* the more serious act to define the moment, but the presence of the weaker act prevents that from happening.

### Hillel View

Having established this principle, the *gemara* identifies the *tanna* who holds that *mitzvos ein mevatlos zu es zu*: it is Hillel. A *braisa* states that Hillel would wrap together *Pesach*, *matzah*, and *maror* and eat them at once, as derived from the verse *al matzos u'merorim yochluhu* — reading it as a requirement to consume them together. Since Hillel held that all three must be eaten together, he evidently held that when they are all at the same level of obligation (*d'oraisa*), they do not negate one another.

(It should be noted that there is also an *Amora* named Hillel mentioned earlier in this daf, quoted by Ravina in the name of Rav Mesharshiya the son of Rav Natan, stating that one should not wrap *matzah* and *maror* together. The *Ran* notes that this Hillel is an *Amora* and should not be confused with Hillel the *Tanna* quoted in this *braisa*. Given that the passage immediately preceding quotes Hillel the *Tanna*, the distinction is important.)

### Rabbis Disagree

Rabbi Yochanan reports that Hillel's colleagues disagree. The *braisa* in question interprets the verse differently: the Torah could have written simply *ye'achel*, "it shall be eaten." The use of *yokhluhu hu* — with the additional personal pronoun — signals that each item can be eaten individually. *Afillu ze bifnei atzmo v'ze bifnei atzmo* — even this one by itself and that one by itself. The Rabbis read the verse as permitting separate consumption, which might imply that eating them together is *prohibited*, perhaps because *mitzvos mevatlot zu es zu*.

### Rav Ashi Reinterp

Rav Ashi, however, challenges this reading of the Rabbis' position. Why, he asks, does the *braisa* say *afillu ze bifnei atzmo* — "even" each individually? The word *afillu* implies that separate consumption is permitted but less preferred, which suggests the Rabbis' concern is not that eating them together is forbidden, but rather that one might think it is *required*. Rav Ashi therefore reinterprets the *braisa*: the Rabbis are merely clarifying that one is *not obligated* to eat them together in the manner of Hillel — separate consumption suffices. But even the Rabbis would agree that eating them together would not be a problem. If so, even the Rabbis may hold *mitzvos ein mevatlos zu es zu*, at least when all obligations are at the same level.

### Current Law

The practical conclusion therefore follows from the *d'oraisa*/*d'rabbanan* distinction rather than from any dispute between Hillel and the Rabbis. All agree — or at least, the *gemara* does not determine otherwise — that when both *mitzvos* are at the same level, eating them together presents no problem. But since today *matzah* is *d'oraisa* and *maror* is *d'rabbanan*, eating them simultaneously allows the *d'rabbanan* to negate the *d'oraisa*, and they must be kept separate. Moreover, *Tosafot* considers whether even Hillel's requirement to eat them together (when biblically applicable) might have been an exception based on an explicit verse, while the general rule might still be *mitzvos mevatlot*. He concludes that since Hillel goes further and says one is *chayav* to eat them together, Hillel must hold as a general principle that *mitzvos ein mevatlos*; otherwise his ruling would require further justification.

### Procedure

The *gemara* therefore prescribes the following procedure: recite *al achilas matzah* and eat *matzah*; then recite *al achilas maror* and eat *maror*; then eat *matzah* and *maror* together, without any blessing, as a *zecher le-mikdash ke-Hillel* — in remembrance of the Temple, as Hillel did. This is precisely the formula we recite: *zecher le-mikdash ke-Hillel, kach haya Hillel oseh*.

*Tosafot* explains why the sandwich cannot come earlier. After eating *matzah*, one has discharged the *d'oraisa*, and *maror* remains as a *d'rabbanan*. If at that point one were to eat them together in a sandwich, the *matzah* in the sandwich would carry no *mitzvah* at all — it would be *reshus*, optional eating. This means the *matzah* in the sandwich would be at a lower level than the *d'rabbanan* *maror*, and the *maror* would be negated by the presence of something that carries *no* obligation. Conversely, eating *maror* first would have the same problem in reverse: when one subsequently ate *matzah*, the *maror* would be *reshus* relative to the *d'oraisa* *matzah* and would undermine it. The only moment when both can be combined without either negating the other is after both *mitzvos* have been separately discharged — at which point the combination is a *zecher* alone, carrying no independent obligatory weight, and therefore there is no concern of mutual negation.

---

## Dipping Rules

### Hand Wash Rule

Rabbi Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: anything that is dipped in liquid (*kol she'tibullo be'mashkeh*) requires *netilat yadayim* — washing of the hands. This is the *gemara*'s basis for the *urchatz* that precedes *karpas*: since one is dipping in liquid, hand-washing is required.

### Charoses Immerse

Rav Papa draws an inference from here: the *maror* must be immersed in *charoses* — *tzarich leshakkuei be'charoses* — because of *kappa*.

### Kappa Definition

What is *kappa*? There are two possibilities: either it refers to a type of insect or larva that could be present within the *maror* and that was thought to be dangerous, or it refers to the sap or juice within the bitter herbs themselves, which was considered harmful and which the *charoses* would counteract.

### Health Safety

*Tosafot* addresses the obvious question: if it is an insect, why would one be permitted to eat the *maror* at all? He answers with two points. First, it may be that the insect in question was one that never walked on the ground — hatched and grew entirely within the vegetable — in which case it might not be prohibited under the laws of *sheratzim*. Second, even if it would otherwise be a concern, the *halachic* threshold for assuming *bittul* or absence of insects may be met, allowing one to eat the *maror*. However, *chamira sakanta mei-issura* — danger to life is treated more stringently than ritual prohibition — and therefore, even if the halakhic basis for eating the *maror* is sound, protecting one's health requires the additional step of immersing in *charoses*. This is why the *gemara* insists on immersion. (One should note that checking lettuce and other *maror* vegetables for insects is a separate and serious matter, dealt with extensively in contemporary halachic literature.)

Rav Papa's inference about *charoses* immersion is based on the *netilat yadayim* requirement itself: if one did not need to immerse the *maror* in *charoses*, there would be no reason to wash hands before *karpas*, since one would not be touching liquid. The very fact that hand-washing is prescribed presupposes that one's hands will come into contact with liquid — i.e., the *charoses* into which the *maror* is dipped. The *gemara* raises the possibility that the aroma of the *charoses* alone might be sufficient to neutralize *kappa* without actual immersion, meaning the hands need never touch liquid. The *gemara* deflects this by suggesting that proximity to the liquid is enough to create a concern that one might inadvertently immerse, and therefore hand-washing remains required.

There is a broader question about the rationale for *netilat yadayim* before *tibulo be'mashkeh*. The *Rashbam* holds that the concern is that one's wet hands will make the food a *sheni le'tumah*, since any liquid that touched *tamei* hands becomes a *rishon*, which then renders the food it contacts *tamei* — parallel to the hand-washing before bread that is modeled on the practice of *kohanim* who ate *terumah*. *Tosafot* objects that on this logic, one should make a blessing on the washing, and one should also be required to do so throughout the year — neither of which is the case. *Tosafot* therefore argues that the concern is not about the food becoming *tamei* but about the person himself drinking the liquid and thereby making himself *tamei*. This explains why no blessing is required — it is not in the category of practices retained *zecher* to the *kohanim* and their *kedushah* — and why it is not practiced during the rest of the year. On *leil seder*, vestiges of practices associated with the *Korban Pesach* are maintained, and this is one of them.

The practical question of whether to make a blessing on *netilat yadayim* before *karpas* turns on this dispute: the *Rambam* requires a *berachah*, while *Tosafot*'s position implies that none is made. Similarly, whether one is *makpid* to wash hands before eating wet vegetables throughout the year reflects these underlying disagreements.

### Removal Rule

Rav Papa adds a further instruction: do not leave the *maror* immersed in the *charoses* — *lo nishke'inhu le'maror be'charoses*. Immerse it briefly to counteract *kappa*, then remove it. If left too long, the pungency of the spices in the *charoses* will not merely neutralize the dangerous element but will completely cancel out the bitter taste of the *maror* altogether. And as we will see immediately, tasting the bitterness is an essential requirement of the *mitzvah* of *maror* — *uv'einan ta'am mar ve'leika*, we need there to be a bitter taste and it must be present.

### Dual Washing

Rav Chisda instructed Rav Hamnuna to expound publicly the following teaching: one who washes hands before the first dipping (*tibul rishon*) must wash hands again before the second dipping (*tibul sheni*). At first glance this might seem redundant — after all, one washes hands before *hamotzi* in any case. The question is really whether the first washing before *karpas* can extend to cover the second eating.

### Hesach Concern

Rav Papa explains why the first washing cannot carry through to the second: since one recites the *haggadah* and the first half of *hallel* between the two dippings, there is a concern of *hesach ha-da'as* — a lapse of attention during which one may have touched an unclean part of the body. The rabbis raised the objection that in a *seder* context one knows in advance that a second dipping is coming, so why should there be *hesach ha-da'as* and why should two washings be needed? Rav Papa responds: on the contrary, the very fact that a second washing is discussed proves that this teaching was said specifically in the *seder* context — for it is precisely in the *seder* that there are two dippings. If it were a general teaching about non-*seder* contexts, why would two dippings arise? The reason a second washing is nonetheless required is the *haggadah* and *hallel* interposed between the two acts of dipping — a substantial interruption during which *hesach ha-da'as* is entirely possible.

This point about the *haggadah* as a potential *hesach ha-da'as* reinforces the broader discussion touched on earlier regarding whether the *haggadah* constitutes a *hefsek* for various *berachot*.

---

## Taste Maror

### Swallowing Rule

Rava states: one who swallows *matzah* whole — *bala matzah* — has fulfilled the obligation. One who swallows *maror* whole — *bala maror* — has not fulfilled the obligation.

### Taste vs Matzah

The reason is straightforward: the *mitzvah* of *maror* requires that one actually experience the bitter taste — *ta'am mar*. If one swallowed the *maror* whole without chewing, the bitter flavor never registered on the palate, and the experiential dimension of the *mitzvah* was not achieved. *Matzah*, by contrast, has no such requirement of taste; the obligation is one of *achilah* — eating — and eating is achieved even when one swallows without tasting.

### Together Whole

If one swallowed *matzah* and *maror* together in one gulp, one was *yotzei* *matzah* but not *yotzei* *maror*. This raises a question: should not the rule of *mitzvos mevatlos zu es zu* apply here as well? *Tosafot* addresses this and notes something of an irony: since the two items were swallowed together rather than *chewed* together, the eating of the *maror* does not impact the *definition* of the eating of the *matzah*. The *matzah* eating, being a simple swallow, is not shaped or defined by the simultaneous swallowing of the *maror*. The mutual negation principle appears to operate specifically where the two acts of eating are intertwined in the chewing and tasting, not where they are simply co-swallowed without that intermingling.

### Wrapped Rule

If one wrapped the *matzah* (or *maror*) in something inedible — *keracho b'siv* — and swallowed it, one was not *yotzei* even *matzah*. The reason is that the *matzah* never came into contact with the throat. This is a significant principle with practical implications for the question of medicines in capsules: if a substance is encased in something that prevents it from touching the throat, it does not constitute *achilah*, even if it is swallowed. (The gelatin of a capsule raises its own separate concerns, but the principle here concerns the act of eating itself, not the status of the casing.)

---

## Seder Plates

### Individual Plates

Rav Shimi bar Ashi rules that *matzah*, *maror*, and *charoses* must be placed before each and every individual participant in the *seder* — *matzah lifnei kol echad v'echad*, *maror lifnei kol echad v'echad*, *charoses lifnei kol echad v'echad*. Each person at the *seder* requires their own *seder* plate. The *gemara* takes this for granted as the norm.

### Table Removal

However, the ritual of removing and restoring the *shulchan* — the table or plate — is reserved for the *seder* leader alone. Rav Huna goes further and rules that *all* the *seder* items are placed before the one who recites the *haggadah* — and the *halakhah* follows Rav Huna in this regard.

### Kid Questions

The *gemara* explains the reason for removing the table: *kedei sheyakiru tinokos v'yishalu* — so that the children will notice the unusual behavior and ask questions. This is the pedagogical mechanism driving the *mah nishtana*.

### Abaye Question

The *gemara* then relates a famous incident. Abaye was once sitting before Rabbah when he saw the table removed early, before anyone had eaten. He exclaimed: we haven't eaten yet — why are they moving the table from before us?

### Rabbah Answer

Rabbah replied: you have exempted us from needing to recite *mah nishtana* formally — *patartanu milomar mah nishtana*. Your spontaneous question achieved precisely the goal that the removal of the table was designed to produce.

This is also reflected in the standard *haggadah* rubrics, which instruct: uncover the *matzos*, remove the *ke'arah* from the table, pour the second cup, and *then* — at that moment of puzzlement — the child asks *mah nishtana*. The *ke'arah* is then restored before *Avadim Hayinu* begins. The removal of the table is thus directly linked to the mechanics of the *mah nishtana* question.

### Tosafot Caveat

The *Rashbam* reads Rabbah's response literally: since Abaye's spontaneous question accomplished what *mah nishtana* was meant to accomplish, the formal recitation of *mah nishtana* is no longer required. The point of *mah nishtana* is to ask why this night is different; once that question has been asked naturally, the text is superfluous.

*Tosafot* resists this conclusion. *Tosafot* reads *kedei sheyakiru tinokos v'yishalu* not as: "the table is removed *so that* the child will ask *mah nishtana*," but rather as: "the table is removed so that the child will become curious and proceed to ask about various unusual practices." Abaye's question about the table removal was a trigger for broader curiosity — not a substitute for the formal text. *Tosafot* therefore holds that Abaye's question does not exempt one from reciting the formal *mah nishtana*, noting that the *gemara* does not describe the beginning of Abaye's full line of questioning but only his initial remark. The formal text of *mah nishtana* was still required. This reflects the broader question — to be developed further — of how fixed the text and ritual of the *seder* was in the *gemara*'s era, and how much was still evolving.
