# Pesachim 116

## Review: Kiddush–Karpas

### Kiddush, Urchatz, Karpas

Today's daf is 116, picking up at the bottom of 115b. To review what has been covered: the seder begins with *kiddush*, followed by *urchatz* — the washing of hands before dipping. The Gemara, though not the Mishnah explicitly, took for granted that one washes twice, explaining that this is on account of the dipping of *karpas* in liquid. The question of whether this is a general requirement — whether it is because one might render the food *tamei*, and whether a *bracha* is recited — was addressed, and the conclusion is that we do not make a *bracha*, though the Rambam does require one.

### Karpas Details

In the Mishnah, the vegetable used for *karpas* was *maror*. The Gemara gave the impression that *maror* was used only because no other vegetable was available, which is itself somewhat strange. As was suggested, there may in fact be a deliberate reason to use *maror* specifically at the outset: it fits with the fact that one of the four questions concerns *maror* before the *maror* has actually been eaten in its formal context, and the symbolism of *maror* begins, in a sense, from the very opening of the *seder*. Nevertheless, because of complications surrounding the recitation of *al achilat maror* — if *maror* is used both at the front and later — the practice developed to use other vegetables for *karpas*.

Regarding how much to eat: the Ashkenazic practice is to eat less than a *kezayit* in order to avoid the question of whether a *bracha achrona* is required, since the *haggadah* constitutes a *hefsek*. The Rambam, by contrast, holds that one specifically eats a *kezayit* because there is an obligation of *achilah*, which has the practical advantage of allowing one to have some food before the seder properly begins.

As for what to dip it in — the Gemara does not specify. The Rambam understands that one dips in *charoset*, which carries the symbolism of slavery and is fitting if *maror* was the primary vegetable used for *karpas*. Tosafot and other Ashkenazic authorities hold that one dips in something else, such as salt water or vinegar. The related question of whether one eats *karpas* with or without *haseiba* (reclining) turns on the same axis: if the dipping is understood as a symbol of slavery, one eats without reclining; if it is understood as the Roman custom of dipping before a meal — a gesture of freedom — then one reclines. This question is the subject of debate.

### Removing the Seder Plate

The last topic discussed previously was the removal of the *ke'arah*, the seder plate. Although the Mishnah speaks first of bringing what will be dipped and then bringing the *matzah*, *chazeret*, and *charoset*, the Gemara explains this second bringing in terms of removing the plate so that the *tinokot* will take notice. The Rashbam at the bottom of 115b writes:

> *Mitzvah hi la'akor et hashulchan kodem l'haggadah, ki heichi d'lehavay heker l'tinokot* — it is a *mitzvah* to remove the table before the *haggadah*, so that there should be something to stimulate the curiosity of the children.

He explains that in earlier times, each person had a small individual table that would be removed entirely during the *haggadah*. In our practice, we remove the *ke'arah* — containing *matzah*, *maror*, and the two cooked items — to the side of the table. The Rashbam notes that some have the custom of lifting the *ke'arah* onto the shoulder, or removing the bread from it, but he dismisses this as unnecessary and not an effective *heker* for the child. His view is that one should remove the *ke'arah* entirely, placing it at the corner, "as if they had already eaten," so that the child will notice and ask. This is analogous to the earlier practice of removing the small table.

In practice, right after *ha lachma anya* at the beginning of *maggid*, the plate is removed from the table. The second cup is poured, and at that moment the child asks *mah nishtanah*. After the questions, the *ke'arah* is brought back — precisely the sequence the Gemara describes. Indeed, Abbaye before Rabbah — when Rabbah removed the *ke'arah* — said, "Good, now we do not have to say *mah nishtanah*," which suggests that any genuine expression of curiosity can in principle substitute for the formal recitation of the *mah nishtanah*. Tosafot, however, is uncomfortable with omitting the formal text entirely, and understands that even after the question about the plate is asked, one still proceeds to recite the *mah nishtanah*.

## Yachatz: Lechem Oni

### Lechem Oni Definition

Moving now to *yachatz*. Four lines from the bottom of the page, Shmuel states: *lechem she-onim alav devarim harbeh* — "bread over which many things are said." The *haggadah* is recited in relation to the *matzah*, which is why the *matzah* remains uncovered and exposed throughout the telling. It is the symbol around which the story is woven. The term *onim* literally suggests proclaiming, though it may equally connote responding — *v'anita v'amarta lifnei Hashem Elokecha* — since the entire structure of the evening is one of question and response: the child asks *mah nishtanah* and the father responds. Either interpretation fits: the *haggadah* is both proclaimed over the *matzah* and given in answer to the questions.

### Lechem Oni Interpretati…

The Gemara then continues: *tanya nami hachi — v'it d'amri*: another version also teaches this, and some say *lechem she-onim alav devarim harbeh*. Then comes *davar acher*: *lechem oni* — the word *ani* is written without a *vav*, and just as a poor person typically possesses only a broken piece of bread rather than a whole loaf, so too here the *haggadah* should be recited over a broken piece of bread. This is the source of *yachatz*: because *maggid* is said over *lechem oni*, which represents bread of affliction, the *matzah* must be broken before *maggid* begins. A third interpretation adds that just as a poor person has no fuel to waste — the husband lights the fire while the wife kneads the dough and gets it into the oven immediately — so too in the making of *matzah* one must work efficiently so that the dough does not become *chametz*.

### Two vs. Three Matzot

The concept of *b'prusa* — using a broken loaf — raises an important halachic question: when one recites *hamotzi*, must the loaf be whole? May one of the two *lechem mishneh* loaves be broken? The debate among the *rishonim* is significant. Most *rishonim*, including the Rif, hold that two whole loaves are required even on *yom tov*. On *leil seder*, however, the Rif permits one of the loaves to be half, in keeping with *darko shel ani b'prusa*. The Rambam follows the Rif, using one and a half *matzot*.

One might question whether two loaves are even required on *yom tov* at all. The *torah* itself does not mandate it, and the usual rationale — the double portion of *man* that fell on *shabbos* — does not straightforwardly extend to *yom tov*, since one may both carry and prepare food on *yom tov*, so the need for a double portion is less obvious. Tosafot raises this question and notes a further complication from the liturgical phrase *v'attah kidashtanu*, suggesting that the *man* did fall in a double portion on *erev yom tov* as well.

### Tosafot on Three Matzot

Tosafot's own resolution is to use three *matzot*: two whole ones to fulfill *lechem mishneh*, and one broken one to represent *lechem oni*. This is our Ashkenazic practice. Tosafot writes:

> *Nira d'gam hamotzi tzarich l'varech al haprusa* — it appears that *hamotzi* must also be recited over the broken one.

He then describes the dispute among earlier authorities. The view of Rav Menachem of Yoni and Rav Yom Tov was that one recites *hamotzi* with *kavana* directed toward the broken *matzah*. The Ri, however — and this is the practice we follow — recites *hamotzi* over the whole top *matzah*, then lowers it, recites *al achilat matzah* with *kavana* directed toward the broken middle *matzah*, and cuts from both together. The practical *kavana* is: *hamotzi* on the top whole *matzah*, *al achilat matzah* on the broken *prusa*.

Technically, the *kezayit* requirement applies only to the *mitzvah* of *achilat matzah*, which could in principle be fulfilled from the broken middle alone. Nevertheless, the practice has developed to take a *kezayit* from both the top and the middle, and since there is never quite enough to go around, those present supplement from the pieces as needed. The bottom *matzah* serves as the third of the *lechem mishneh*; the half that was broken off during *yachatz* is set aside for the *afikomen*; and the remaining portion of the broken middle *matzah* is used for *korech*. This is how the various components of the *seder* cohere — though much of this elaborated detail is not found in the Gemara itself, and alternative arrangements were certainly possible.

## Charoset Debate

### Charoset Obligation

The Mishnah continues: *af al pi she-ein charoset mitzvah* — even though *charoset* is not a *mitzvah* according to the *tanna kamma*. If it is not a *mitzvah*, why do we bother with it at all? *Mishum kapa* — Rabbi Ami explains that it is to neutralize a dangerous sap or substance found in the *maror*. According to this view, *charoset* has no intrinsic symbolic purpose at the *seder*; it is purely a practical precaution.

Abbaye then analyzes this further. The *kapa* — the pungency or dangerous sap — of *chassa* (lettuce used as *maror*) is countered by radish; the *kapa* of radish is countered by cress; the *kapa* of cress is countered by hot water; and ultimately, *kapa* of all of them is countered by hot water. The text then produces an Aramaic incantation directed at the harmful substance and its seven daughters and eight daughters-in-law, which the Gemara includes without further elaboration.

Rabbi Eliezer — or Rabbi Tzadok — then declares that *charoset* is in fact a *mitzvah*. The question becomes: what is the nature of this *mitzvah*?

### Charoset Symbolism

Rabbi Levi says: *zecher le-tapuach* — to recall the *tapuach*. This refers to the well-known *midrash* found in tractate Sotah, that the women of Israel seduced their husbands under the *tapuach* trees (Shir HaShirim: *tachat hatapuach orarticha*), because the men had despaired of having children given Pharaoh's decrees. It was this act of faith and courage that produced the children of Israel and ultimately led to the *geulah*. As an aside, the translation of *tapuach* as "apple" is almost certainly incorrect — there were no apples in the ancient Near East — and the word likely refers to some other fruit, perhaps a citrus. Some suggest it could even be an *esrog*.

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different rationale: *zecher le-tit* — to recall the mortar. The *charoset* is thick and heavy, resembling the mortar the slaves worked with. Abbaye draws both concerns together: *tzarich le-kahavuye* — it must be made pungent, *zecher le-tapuach*; and *tzarich le-samchu-e* — it must be made thick, *zecher le-tit*.

A *baraita* consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's view adds: *tavlin zecher le-teven* — the spices recall the straw. There may be a wordplay here between *tavlin* and *teven*. The Rambam understands this literally, suggesting that one leaves whole pieces of spice — like cinnamon sticks — uncrushed, to more directly evoke straw. The *charoset* as a whole is described as *zecher le-tit*, recalling the mortar of Egyptian bondage.

### Charoset Preparation

Regarding the preparation: *tzarich le-kahavuye* and *tzarich le-samchu-e* — it must be pungent and thick. Tosafot adds *tzarich le-chapuyei* — it should also have a covering quality. The Yerushalmi notes: *ist avdi zecher le-dam* — there is also the symbolic recall of the blood, and this is why *charoset* is called a *mashkeh* — because wine is added, rendering it a liquid. At the time of eating, one dilutes the thick *charoset* somewhat with wine and vinegar, which is the reason it was already characterized as a *mashkeh* earlier in the discussion.

Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok reports that the merchants of *cherach* in Jerusalem would call out: "Come and take spices for the *mitzvah*" — meaning, the *mitzvah* of *charoset*. The general ruling follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, and we are therefore particular about the ingredients. The Rambam in his *Perush Hamishnayot* states that according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, one would even recite a *bracha — al achilat charoset* — though this is not standard practice.

The Geonim, in their responsa, prescribe preparing *charoset* from fruits to which the *Knesset Yisrael* is compared in *Shir HaShirim*: *tachat hatapuach orarticha*, *k'felach harimon*, *hate'enah chanta fageha*, *amarti eleh b'tamar*, *egoz el ginat egoz* — pomegranates, figs, dates, nuts — along with almonds, because *shekadim* evokes *shakad Hakadosh Baruch Hu al hakeitz*, God's vigilance over the moment of redemption. Hence the recipe includes nuts, wine, pomegranates, figs, dates, and so on.

A remarkable point was raised: Tosafot lived in medieval Europe at a time when Jews were accused of blood libels during Pesach, and yet the tradition includes a symbolic food that evokes blood. These historical echoes are not invented — someone heard something and misunderstood it. Such things have their tragic resonance.

## Mah Nishtanah Structure

### Four Questions

Moving now to the Mishnah on *maggid*: *mazgu lo kos sheni* — they pour the second cup of wine, after the *karpas* and *yachatz*, and now *v'kan haben sho'el* — the child asks. If the child does not know how to ask, the father prompts him. *Mah nishtanah halailah hazeh mikol haleilot?* — How is this night different from all other nights? The four distinctions enumerated in the Mishnah's version include: *chametz u'matzah* vs. *kulo matzah*; other vegetables vs. *maror*; roasted, boiled, and cooked meat vs. *kulo tzali*; and either *ein anu chayavin litbol* once or the question about dipping once vs. twice. We will see the Gemara's discussion of the dipping question shortly.

It is worth noting that not all versions of the Mishnah have four questions. The Rif has only three, omitting the *maror* question and retaining *matzah*, *tzali*, and dipping. The *tzali* question is also noteworthy: the Rashbam explains it as belonging to the time of the Beit HaMikdash. However, there is reason to think that even after the *churban*, the practice of eating specifically roasted meat on *leil seder* — *zecher la-pesach* — persisted in some communities, since an earlier Mishnah references *gufo shel pesach* being brought before the participants. That tradition was ultimately set aside under the influence of the Bavli's concern that displaying roasted meat might appear like eating *kodshim bachutz*.

### Response Structure

The Mishnah continues: *lefi da'ato shel ben aviv melamdo* — the father teaches according to the capacity of the child. *Matchil bignut u'mesayem beshevach* — he begins with denigration and ends with praise. This is the foundational structural principle of the *haggadah*: a narrative arc from darkness to light, from shame to glory.

### Dorsh Me'Arami Oved Avi

The Mishnah then states: *v'doresh me-arami oved avi ad she-yigmor kol haparsha kulo* — one expounds on *Arami oved avi* (Devarim 26:5) until he completes the entire passage. This is a remarkably open-ended, free-form structure. The basic components are: the *mah nishtanah* questions, a narrative from *avdut l'cheirut*, and the expounding of *Arami oved avi* as the textual framework.

Why use *Arami oved avi* rather than simply reading the account from *Shemot*? Because *Arami oved avi* is the one place in the *Torah* where the story of the Exodus appears in a ritual retelling context: the person bringing *bikkurim* recounts the story as his own. The distinction between *telling* and *retelling* is essential. A retelling allows the speaker to bring his own framing, to emphasize particular dimensions, to make the story genuinely personal. This is the nature of *doresh* — the intersection of the human with the divine, the *Torah she-be'al peh* enterprise applied not only to *halacha* but to the telling of the story itself. We use *Arami oved avi* as our framework in order to do a retelling of a retelling.

This also connects to the broader concept of *talmud Torah*. The *Tosefta* speaks of reciting *hilchot hapesach* as part of the *mitzvah*. The *chacham* is told *af atah emor lo ke-hilchot hapesach*. The phrase *baruch hamakom baruch hu, baruch shenatan torah le-amo Yisrael* functions as a miniature *birchat hatorah*. Thinking of *sippur yetziat mitzrayim* as a form of *talmud Torah* is a distinct theme embedded in the *seder*, and *doresh me-arami oved avi* is its classic expression — the rabbinic enterprise of *Torah she-be'al peh* applied to the telling of our story.

### Questioning Framework

The *mitzvah* of *haggadah* on *leil seder* is distinct from the daily obligation of *zecher li-yetziat mitzrayim* in several respects: it involves the symbols, it involves extended narration rather than mere mention, it involves expounding on verses. But perhaps the most significant distinction is the framework of questioning and responding. *Ki yishalcha bincha machar le-emor* — the *Torah* structures the transmission of the Exodus narrative as a response to a child's question. The entire apparatus of *kedei she-yish'alu ha-tinokot* — removing the plate, pouring the second cup — is constructed to elicit the question that the *Torah* itself expects. The type of engagement generated by genuine curiosity and responsive explanation is qualitatively different from any other mode of transmission.

### Child Asking Before Seei…

One might ask: how does the child ask questions about the *tzali* before he has seen it? He has not yet observed the roasted meat. Similarly, he has not yet experienced the second dipping — only one dipping has occurred. Tosafot's resolution is that when the plate is removed and the child asks what is happening, the father feeds him the cues: don't worry, there will be *maror*, there will be dipping, there will be more — and this prompts the child to formulate his questions in advance.

This difficulty leads to a striking interpretation found in the Rambam: *mah nishtanah halailah hazeh* is not the question — it is the beginning of the answer. The child asks whatever he asks, and the father then declares, *mah nishtanah halailah hazeh mikol haleilot* — "let me show you how different this night is" — presenting the child with the reality of the night's differences, which in turn prompts the child to ask *why*. The Rambam's formulation is analogous to *mah tovu*, which is similarly structured as a declaration rather than a genuine question. On this reading, *mah nishtanah* is what the father says — it is the beginning of the *haggadah* text rather than the child's question.

One further observation: by the time one reaches *rabban gamliel hayah omer kol shelo amar shlosha devarim eilu ba-pesach lo yatza yeday chovaso — pesach, matzah, u-maror*, three of the original four questions have already been answered through the course of the *haggadah*. The *mah nishtanah* is indeed answered — it is simply that the answer is embedded in a vast, rich narrative that intervenes before the explicit explanation of the symbols. In a sense, *rabban gamliel* is ultimately providing the direct answers that the *mah nishtanah* raised at the outset.

## Who Asks Questions

### Chacham Beno Shoalo

The Gemara: *tanu rabbanan — chacham beno shoalo*. If the son is capable of asking, the son asks. The emphasis is on *beno* — it is the son's wisdom that determines who initiates the question. *V'im eino chacham — ishto shoalto*: if the son cannot ask, the wife asks. *V'im lav — hu shoal et atzmo*: if there is no one else, he asks himself. Asking oneself is not a strange practice — it is a legitimate method of driving genuine inquiry.

### Talmidei Chachamim Asking

*V'afilu shnei talmidei chachamim she-yodi'in be-hilchot hapesach shoalin zeh la-zeh* — even two *talmidei chachamim* who are fully versed in the laws of Pesach ask one another, because the question-and-answer structure itself is essential to the *mitzvah*, independent of whether a child is present or capable. This is notable: the Gemara specifies *she-yodi'in be-hilchot hapesach* — they may know all the *halachot* and yet still be obligated to engage in questioning. Knowing the law does not exempt one from exploring the story.

### Dipping Once vs. Twice

The Gemara then takes up the dipping question from the *mah nishtanah*: *she-bechol haleilot anu matbilin paam achat halailah hazeh shtei pe'amim*. Rava challenges this formulation: is one really obligated to dip once every night? *Atu kol yoma lo sagi delo matbe'ei chada zimna?* Therefore, says Rava, the correct reading is: *shebechol haleilot ein anu chayavin litbol afilu paam achat* — on all other nights we are not obligated to dip even once, whereas tonight we dip twice.

Rav Safra then challenges even this: *chiyuva le-dardakei* — does one speak of an *obligation* to children? The framing of *chiyuv* seems out of place in something designed to arouse the children's curiosity. Rav Safra therefore proposes: *ein anu matbilin afilu paam achat* — on other nights we do not go out of our way to dip even once, whereas tonight we go out of our way to dip twice. This formulation carries the practical force of obligation without using the language of *chiyuv*. Just as the Mishnah's *anu ochlin she'ar yerakot* does not mean one is *obligated* to eat other vegetables on other nights — merely that one does not make a point of eating *maror* — so too here one does not ordinarily make a point of dipping, but tonight one does so twice.

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Rav's Approach

*Matchil bignut u'mesayem beshevach — mai bignut?* What is the "denigration" with which the narrative begins? Rav says: *matchila ovdei avodah zarah hayu avoteinu* — at the outset our forefathers were idolaters. On this view, the story of redemption is fundamentally a story of spiritual transformation: from worshipping foreign gods to being brought close to the service of God, culminating at *ma'amad Har Sinai*.

### Shmuel's Approach

Shmuel says: *avadim hayinu* — we were slaves. On this view, the story is about physical freedom and national liberation: from slavery to autonomy, from *avdut* to *cheirut*. Both approaches are present in the *haggadah* as we have it. Immediately after *mah nishtanah*, we recite *avadim hayinu le-Pharaoh be-Mitzrayim* — Shmuel's version, as the immediate and simple answer. Then, before the fuller elaboration, we say *mitchilah ovdei avodah zarah hayu avoteinu ve-achshav kervanu HaMakom la-avodato* — Rav's version, introducing the theological framing of the narrative. The *keneged arba'ah banim* section appears between these two, perhaps because before launching into an elaborate retelling, one must first calibrate the story to the different people around the table.

### Rav Nachman Anecdote

Rav Nachman said to Darru, his slave: *avda de-mappik leih mareih le-cheirut ve-yahiv leih kaspa ve-dahava — mai ba'ei le-meimar leih?* If a master were to free his slave and give him gold and silver, what should the slave say? It is a somewhat pointed question to pose to a slave, but Darru answered: *ba'ei le-oduyei u-le-shabbuchei* — he would thank him and praise him. Rav Nachman responded: *patartan mi-lomar mah nishtanah* — you have exempted us from reciting *mah nishtanah*. He then opened and said: *avadim hayinu*.

The anecdote is illuminating on several levels. It confirms that immediately after *mah nishtanah*, the opening words are *avadim hayinu* — consistent with Shmuel's structure. It also raises the question of what exactly exempted them from *mah nishtanah*: Darru gave an *answer*, not a question. This may support the Rambam's reading that *mah nishtanah* is itself the beginning of the answer rather than the question — for here too, an answer sufficed. But it remains somewhat puzzling, since Rav Nachman is about to give the answer, *avadim hayinu*, and how Darru's response parallels *mah nishtanah* is not entirely transparent. Earlier, when Abbaye asked Rabbah about the removed table, the question was clearly a genuine expression of curiosity and so substituted for the *mah nishtanah*. Here, the analogy is less straightforward.

A question was raised regarding whether the *avodah zarah* and the *avdut* are somehow connected — whether the bondage in Egypt was in some sense a *tikkun* for the idolatry of the ancestors. This is a much larger discussion, appropriate for *seder* night itself; the lecturer noted it as a possibility without affirming it as the primary reading.

Returning to the significance of *doresh me-arami oved avi* as a framework: the Mishnah does not appear to prescribe a fixed text for how one expounds on *arami oved avi* — it is meant to be a genuine, personal retelling. The fact that *patach ve-amar avadim hayinu* sounds like a fixed text may indicate that the principals agreed on a common text that already contained both Rav's and Shmuel's components, with each simply pointing to a different part of it. But the structure of *doresh* was originally meant to be one's own engagement with the *pesukim*.

## Rabban Gamliel's Three

### Three Things Obligation

*Kol shelo amar shlosha devarim eilu ba-pesach lo yatza yeday chovaso* — whoever did not say these three things on Pesach did not fulfill his obligation. The *rishonim* debate whether this is meant literally or as rhetorical emphasis. But even granting the literal reading, one must identify which *chiyuv* has not been fulfilled. The most natural answer is the *chiyuv* of *haggadah* — the obligation to tell the story. The telling of the story requires explaining the symbolism of what one is eating. Some *rishonim*, however, suggest that not fulfilling this obligation may also mean that one has not properly discharged the *chiyuv* of *achilat matzah*, *achilat maror*, or *achilat pesach* — that the *mitzvah* of eating these foods is not complete without integrating them into the narrative and explicating their significance.

### Pesach Explanation

*Pesach al shum she-pasach HaMakom al batei avoteinu be-Mitzrayim, she-ne'emar: v'amartem zevach pesach hu la-Adonai asher pasach*. The Pesach offering is explained as recalling God's passing over — or, according to some, saving — the houses of our ancestors. Tosafot points out that the *pasuk* itself instructs *v'amartem*, "and you shall say" — on the eating of the Pesach, one must articulate its meaning. The very *pasuk* that describes the Pesach commands its verbal explanation.

### Matzah & Maror

*Matzah al shum she-nig'alu avoteinu, she-ne'emar vayofu et habatzek asher hotziu* — the *matzah* represents the moment of liberation, the dough that had no time to rise. At this point in the narrative, *matzah* emphasizes freedom rather than affliction. *Maror al shum she-mar'ru ha-mitzriyim et chayei avoteinu be-Mitzrayim* — some have *marorin* following the language of the *pasuk* *she-ne'emar vay'mar'ru et chayayhem*. The *maror* recalls the bitterness of slavery.

### Integration of Symbols

The deeper point of *rabban gamliel* is that these symbols must be *pulled into the story* — not merely eaten, not merely displayed *b'fnei kol echad ve-echad*, but actively integrated into the telling and made part of the narrative itself. What he is requiring is not just the presence of the symbols but the articulation of their meaning in the context of the story of redemption.

Looking at the *haggadah*: after *tzei u'lemad* and the full *doresh me-arami oved avi*, after *dayenu* and the unfolding narrative, one arrives at *rabban gamliel omer kol shelo amar shlosha devarim eilu* — *pesach she-hayu*, *matzah zu*, *maror zeh* — and then, holding the *kos* and the *matzah*, one says *lefikhakh anachnu chayavim lehodot*. The story has been told, the symbols have been explained and integrated, and *therefore* — *lefikhakh* — one must break into praise, thanks, and *hallel*. This is the logical and experiential culmination of the *seder*'s first half.

## Bekhol Dor VaDor

### Personal Redemption

*Bekhol dor vador chayav adam lirot et atzmo k'ilu hu yatza mi-Mitzrayim* — in every generation, a person is obligated to see himself as if he personally left Egypt. The *pasuk* cited is *she-ne'emar ve-higadeta le-vincha bayom hahu leimor ba'avur zeh asah Hashem li be-tzeiti mi-Mitzrayim* — "you shall tell your son on that day, saying: it is because of this that Hashem did for *me* when I left Egypt."

### Hagada L'Bincha

This *pasuk* is the source of the *mitzvah* of *haggadah* itself, and the word *li* — "for me" — is what makes the *mitzvah* personal. It is the directive to make the story one's own, to experience it not as ancient history but as present reality. This connects to the Darru story: only if one genuinely feels that he has been redeemed — has been a slave who was freed and given gold and silver — is he in a position to naturally express the obligation of thanks and praise.

### Lefikhakh to Hallel

It is also worth noting that at this point in the Mishnah, we appear to have transitioned from the Mishnah *speaking about* the *haggadah* to the Mishnah *containing* the text of the *haggadah* itself. The formulation *lefikhakh anachnu chayavim lehodot lehalel le-shabe'ach le-fa'er le-romem le-hadar le-varech le-aleh u-lekales le-mi she-asa la-avoteinu ve-lanu et kol hanisim ha-eilu* — with its seven expressions of praise addressed to the One who performed these miracles for our ancestors and for us — is clearly not *halachic* formulation but *haggadah* text. Similarly, *u-mimavet le-chayim, me-avdut le-cheirut, mi-yagon le-simcha, me-avel le-yom tov, me-afeila le-or gadol, u-mishiabbud li-geulah — v'nomar lefanav halleluyah* is the transition into *hallel*.

The reason there is no *bracha* recited before *hallel* on *leil seder* — unlike *hallel* in its other contexts — is that a *bracha* is appropriate when one is performing a defined ritual act. But if one has truly achieved *lefikhakh anachnu chayavim* and *chayav lirot et atzmo*, then the *hallel* is not a formalized ritual obligation but a natural expression of religious feeling. One does not frame a genuine outpouring of the heart with a *bracha* — one simply sings.

A fascinating reading was offered by one of the participants: when *rabban gamliel* says *shlosha devarim*, the three things may refer not merely to *pesach, matzah, u-maror*, but to three structural obligations: (1) explaining the symbols, (2) *chayav adam lirot et atzmo*, and (3) *le-hodot ve-le-halel*. This is a striking and original interpretation, integrating the entire sweep of the *seder*'s *maggid* into a tripartite framework — though it does not appear to have been articulated by other authorities.

## Hallel: Timing & Amount

### Hallel Extent

*Ad heikan hu omer?* — How far does one recite *hallel* in the first half of the *seder*? The remainder will be completed after the meal.

### Beit Shammai vs. Hillel

*Beit Shammai omerim ad em habanim semeichah* — Beit Shammai holds that one stops before the second psalm of *hallel*. *U-Beit Hillel omerim ad chalamish le-mayno mayim* — Beit Hillel holds that one continues through the end of the second psalm, concluding with *chalamish le-mayno mayim*.

### Immediacy vs. Narrative

What accounts for this dispute? Beit Hillel's position is the more comprehensible: the second psalm opens with *betzeit Yisrael mi-Mitzrayim*, which speaks directly of the Exodus, and it concludes with *chalamish le-mayno mayim*, a powerful image of miraculous redemption. What Beit Shammai's reasoning might be is less obvious. The best interpretation is that for Beit Shammai, reciting *betzeit Yisrael mi-Mitzrayim* takes the speaker out of the immediacy of the experience. *Betzeit Yisrael* speaks of *them*, of a past event, of *Yisrael* when *they* went out — it is a narrative of others rather than an immediate personal experience. Beit Shammai may want to preserve the first-person vividness of the moment: *halleluyah*, the spontaneous praise, without slipping into third-person historical narration. Why the *hallel* is divided into two parts at all has to do with this same tension: the first half should feel immediate and personal; the second half, recited after the meal, completes the formal ritual of *hallel*.

## Geula Blessing Debate

### Tarfon's Version

*V'chosem bi-geulah* — the Mishnah requires concluding the first half of *hallel* with the *geulah* blessing. What is that *chatimah*? *Rabbi Tarfon omer: asher ge'alanu ve-ga'al et avoteinu mi-Mitzrayim* — and he did not conclude with a *chatimah*. On Rabbi Tarfon's view, this is a short *bracha* — *baruch atah Hashem elokeinu melech ha-olam asher ge'alanu ve-ga'al et avoteinu mi-Mitzrayim* — focused entirely on the past *geulah*, with no closing formula.

### Akiva's Version

Rabbi Akiva adds: *kein Hashem elokeinu ve-elokei avoteinu yagi'einu le-moadim u-le-regalim acherim ha-ba'im likrateinu le-shalom, semeichim be-vinyan irecha ve-sasim be-avodatecha, ve-nochal sham min ha-zevachim u-min ha-pesachim* — and he closes with *baruch atah Hashem ga'al Yisrael*. Rabbi Akiva does not merely lengthen the *bracha* — he adds an entirely new dimension: the orientation toward *future* redemption, toward the rebuilding of the *Beit HaMikdash*. This is deeply characteristic of Rabbi Akiva, who throughout the destruction period — and in the context of Bar Kochba — maintained a constant focus on future *geulah*. The *haggadah* on this view is not only a story culminating in *Har Sinai* but also a story pointing forward. How much the *seder* night's narrative incorporates the theme of future redemption is itself a significant question, and Rabbi Akiva answers it emphatically.

### Rishonim on Chatimah

Tosafot and the Rashbam both clarify that the earlier line of the Mishnah — *v'chosem bi-geulah* — is not a third opinion alongside Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva, but rather the earlier, unexplicated statement that the later *tannaim* are interpreting. The Mishnah presents the phenomenon, common in rabbinic literature, where an earlier formulation — *v'chosem bi-geulah* — is stated without elaboration, and subsequent *tannaim* debate what it means. Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva represent the two positions in that debate.

### Rambam's Girsa

The Rambam's reading of the earlier Mishnah — *chayav liros et atzmo* vs. *chayav l'haros et atzmo* — presents a telling textual variant. *Chayav lirot et atzmo* means one is obligated to actually *see* oneself as if having left Egypt — a demanding standard of genuine internalization. *Chayav l'haros et atzmo* means one is obligated to *present* or *demonstrate* oneself as if — a more accessible standard that is closer to the principle of "act as if, and understanding will follow." If one cannot fully feel the experience of redemption, at minimum one should conduct oneself as though one does, and through that embodied practice, the feeling may develop.

## Lifting Objects in Seder

### Lifting Matzah & Maror

Rava states: *matzah tzarich l'hagbi'ah* — when saying *matzah zu*, one lifts the *matzah*. *Maror tzarich l'hagbi'ah* — when saying *maror zeh*, one lifts the *maror*. This is a practical form of *show and tell*: the physical objects are raised to make vivid the connection between word and symbol.

### Not Lifting Meat

*Basar ein tzarich l'hagbi'ah* — the meat, however, should not be lifted. The reason: *lo od ela she-neireh k'ochlei kodshim bachutz* — it would appear as if one were eating *kodshim* outside the *Mikdash*. Here is the opposite principle from the earlier discussion of *tzali*: while there was historically a practice of eating specifically roasted meat on *leil seder* as a *zecher la-pesach*, and while some went so far as to roast a kid goat and refer to it as the *pesach*, the Bavli's concern is that publicly indicating the meat while discussing the *pesach korban* creates the appearance of consecrating offerings outside their proper context. Therefore, though some symbolism of the *pesach* is maintained, it is deliberately downplayed — the meat is not lifted, not pointed to in the way that *matzah* and *maror* are.

# Pesachim 117

## Suma Patur Haggadah

### Overview & Context

Daf 117b picks up near the conclusion of the *haggadah* section of the *seder*, in the passage preceding *motzi matzah*. The immediate context is the discussion flowing from Rabban Gamliel's famous ruling — *kol shelo amar sheloshah devarim eilu b'Pesach* — that whoever has not articulated the meaning of the three ritual objects has not fulfilled his obligation. The Gemara has established that the *seder* plate is placed before every participant, the foods integrating themselves into the very structure of the narrative. The child asks *ki yishalcha bincha machar l'amor mah zot*, questions rooted in the ritual foods, and the response culminates in *pesach, matzah, maror*, tying the foods and their symbolism into the act of telling. With this backdrop firmly in place, the Gemara opens a fascinating discussion about the precise contours of the *mitzvah* of *haggadah*.

### Suma Patur Derasha

Approximately three lines into the Gemara's new sugya — on 117b, beginning with the words *ella she'nireh koach kadshecha bachutz* — Rav Acha bar Yaakov makes a striking statement: *suma patur mi'lomar haggadah*, a blind person is exempt from reciting the *haggadah*.

### Ba'avur Zeh Tziyun

The textual basis for this ruling is the phrase *ba'avur zeh*, which appears in the verse *v'higadta l'vincha bayom hahu leimor ba'avur zeh asah Hashem li b'tzeisi miMitzrayim*. Chazal understand this phrase as the foundation of the entire *haggadah* obligation: *ba'avur zeh lo amarti ella b'shaas she'yesh matzah u'maror munachim lefanecha* — one recites the *haggadah* only when *matzah* and *maror* lie before him. The telling of the story is understood to be constitutively tied to the ritual foods themselves.

### Ben Sorer Comparison

The derivation proceeds by means of a *gezerah shavah*-like comparison to the laws of the *ben soreir u'moreh*. In that context, the verse says *bneinu zeh* — "this our son." Had the Torah wished simply to say "our son," it could have written *baneinu hu*. The extra word *zeh* teaches, as an accepted *drasha*, that both parents must be able to directly point to and see the child; blind parents are therefore excluded from bringing the case of the *ben soreir u'moreh*. The word *zeh* implies a direct, visual identification. Rav Acha bar Yaakov imports this logic: just as *zeh* in that context excludes the blind because they cannot directly perceive the referent, so too *ba'avur zeh* in the *haggadah* context requires a direct relationship to the ritual foods — and although a blind person relates to *matzah* and *maror* through touch and taste, the *zeh* of *ba'avur zeh* is understood to require visual engagement with the objects. Hence, *suma patur*.

It is worth noting, as the Gemara itself implicitly signals, that the motivation in the *ben soreir u'moreh* case was clearly to limit and ultimately eliminate the category. No such motivation operates here — the comparison is purely textual.

### Mareimar Challenge

The Gemara immediately challenges this ruling: *inei?* Is it really true? Mareimar reports that he asked the students in the academy of Rav Yosef — *man de'amar haggadah bei Rav Yosef* — who was it that actually recited the *haggadah* there? The answer: Rav Yosef himself. And Rav Yosef was blind. Similarly, in the academy of Rav Sheshet — also blind — it was Rav Sheshet himself who recited the *haggadah*. How, then, can the ruling of Rav Acha bar Yaakov stand?

### One Reciter Model

What this account incidentally reveals is that at these *sederim* there was a single reciter of the *haggadah*. This is notable and worth pausing on. While we have discussed previously how the *seder* is structured as a dialogue — a child asks and a father answers, a wife asks and a husband answers — the Gemara makes clear that one person was effectively the narrator. Everyone else plays their part by asking and by listening, while one figure carries the *sippur yetzias Mitzrayim*.

This raises a genuine question about the nature of the *mitzvah*. If I am the one asking and you are the one telling me the answer, am I participating in *sippur yetzias Mitzrayim*? The fuller model suggested by the Gemara is not simply that each person contributes their part to a collective telling, but rather that the principle of *shomea k'oneh* — that listening is halachically equivalent to speaking — operates here. The reciter recites; the listeners hear and are thereby considered as if they themselves have recited. That appears to be the structural understanding the Gemara is operating with.

The difficulty, then, is sharp: if a blind person is exempt from reciting the *haggadah*, how could Rav Yosef and Rav Sheshet — who were blind — have served as the *motzi* for an entire household of sighted people who were themselves obligated? One who is exempt cannot discharge the obligation of one who is obligated.

### Matzah Status Debate

The Gemara introduces a resolution by way of Rav Sheshet's own view: *kasavar rabanan matzah bizman hazeh d'rabanan*. Those sages held that the obligation to eat *matzah* in the present era is only rabbinic in force, since *matzah* and *maror* are in the Torah linked to the *Korban Pesach*, and in the absence of the *korban* some hold the obligation reduces to a rabbinic one. If *matzah* nowadays is rabbinic, then *haggadah* — which is pegged to *matzah* through *ba'avur zeh* — is likewise rabbinic. Following this reasoning, virtually everything done on *seder* night in our era would be rabbinic in origin; the only candidates for biblical standing might be *kiddush* and *birchas hamazon*.

### Rav Acha's Logic

The Gemara then turns to a sharp observation: the implication of Rav Sheshet's response is that Rav Acha bar Yaakov, who holds a blind person is *patur*, must hold that *matzah* nowadays is biblical — since his entire *derasha* only works if *haggadah* has biblical standing. But the Gemara notes a complication: *veha Rav Achai bar Yaakov hu d'amar matzah bizman hazeh d'rabanan* — Rav Acha bar Yaakov himself is on record holding that *matzah* nowadays is rabbinic! How then can he maintain that a blind person is exempt?

The resolution: *kasavar kol d'tikon rabanan k'ein d'oraisa tikun*. Even if the obligation is rabbinic, the rabbis patterned their rabbinic institutions after the structure of the biblical ones. Since biblically a blind person would be exempt, the rabbis extended that exemption to their rabbinic legislation as well. Rav Acha bar Yaakov's position is internally consistent: he holds *matzah* is rabbinic, yet the rabbinic framework replicates the biblical structure, and therefore a blind person remains exempt.

The Gemara then asks whether Rav Sheshet and Rav Yosef also accept this principle of *kol d'tikon rabanan k'ein d'oraisa tikun*. If they do, then even on a rabbinic level, a blind person should have been exempt — and they should not have served as the *motzi* for their households. The Gemara's answer is that they in fact reject the entire *derasha* of Rav Acha bar Yaakov.

### Ba'avur Zeh Rejected

The Gemara proceeds to dismantle the comparison to *ben soreir u'moreh*. *Bishlama hasam* — in the case of *ben soreir u'moreh* there is good reason to read the extra *zeh*: the verse could have written simply *baneinu hu*, yet it chose *baneinu zeh*. The superfluous *zeh* teaches that the parents must be able to point directly, which implies visual capacity. *Shema mina prat le'sumin* — the extra word comes specifically to exclude the blind.

But *aval hacha* — here, by *ba'avur zeh*, what else could the verse have written? The sentence wishes to express that the telling is occasioned by, and connected to, the ritual foods. The word *zeh* is not superfluous at all; it is required to identify the referent of *ba'avur*. One might not even know what *zeh* refers to without Chazal's interpretation — *v'higadta l'vincha bayom hahu leimor ba'avur zeh asah Hashem li b'tzeisi miMitzrayim* — what is the *zeh*? Chazal tell us: the *matzah* and the *maror*. But the word *zeh* was absolutely necessary to point to *something*; it was not added to exclude anyone. Therefore *ela ba'avur matzah u'maror d'asit* — the verse comes to link the *haggadah* to the *matzah* and *maror*, and the word *zeh* carries no exclusionary implication. The comparison to *ben soreir u'moreh* collapses, and with it the ruling that *suma patur*.

One might ask: why doesn't *ba'avur zeh* refer to the *Korban Pesach* rather than to *matzah* and *maror*? In the context of the surrounding *pesukim* — which speak of eating *matzah* for seven days and the prohibition of *chametz* — the *ba'avur zeh* is most naturally read in connection with *matzah*, and Chazal's reading reflects that contextual anchor.

### Haggadah Food Link

What emerges from this entire discussion is a set of important conclusions. First, there is near-universal agreement that if *matzah* were merely rabbinic, *haggadah* would be rabbinic as well. The obligation to recite *haggadah* on that particular night derives entirely from *ba'avur zeh*, which ties the telling to the ritual foods being present. Without a biblical obligation in *matzah*, there is no biblical *haggadah*. The entire reason *haggadah* is *d'oraisa* is because *matzah* is *d'oraisa*.

Second, Rabban Gamliel's statement — *kol shelo amar sheloshah devarim eilu b'Pesach, lo yatza yedei chovato* — reflects a tight, constitutive integration of *haggadah* with the ritual foods. Some *rishonim* take this literally: if one does not articulate the significance of the *pesach*, *matzah*, and *maror*, one has not fulfilled the obligation. Others say that while *b'di'eved* one may have fulfilled it, the fundamental conception of the *mitzvah* demands this integration. The *she'eilos* of the *seder* are questions about the foods; the answers are about the foods; the very timing of the obligation is derived from the presence of the foods. The Gemara considers and then rejects the possibility that a blind person — unable to see those foods — cannot fulfill the obligation, but the tight linkage between *haggadah* and *achilah* remains firmly established.

Third, the structure of the *seder* as one person reciting while others listen — with *shomea k'oneh* discharging the obligation of the listeners — is clearly reflected in the practice of Rav Yosef and Rav Sheshet.

---

## Hallelujah Etymology

### Hallel Overview

The Mishnah proceeds to the phrase *v'nomar lefanav shira chadasha Hallelujah*, and the word *hallelujah* itself becomes the occasion for a brief but analytically rich digression into etymology and textual structure.

### One Word Debate

Rav Yochanan's question concerns whether *hallelujah* and related compound expressions — *kes Yah* (from *ki yad al kes Yah milchama l'Hashem b'Amalek*), and *Yedidyah* (one of the names of Shlomo) — are each one word or two. The question has practical halakhic implications: if *Yah* stands alone as a separate word, it constitutes a divine name and is therefore *kodesh*, affecting how such texts may be handled and erased.

### Rav Rabba Split

Rav holds that *kes Yah* and *Merchavyah* are each a single word, leaving *hallelujah* and *Yedidyah* unaddressed. Rabba takes the more restrictive position that only *Merchavyah* is a single word; all the others are two words, each with *Yah* as an independent divine name. The Gemara then notes that Rav Chisda's position on *Merchavyah* is left unresolved — *teiku*. As for what Rav would say about *Yedidyah*, the Gemara brings a proof: Rav explicitly states that *Yedidyah* is divided into two — *yedid chol, Yah kodesh* — meaning the *Yah* component is a separate, sacred divine name. The implication for our *davening* is clear: *aneini b'merchav Yah* in *Hallel* — whether *Merchavyah* there is one word or two has direct consequences for how the word is treated.

### Intensifier Theory

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi takes a different analytical approach entirely. He asks *mai Hallelujah?* and answers: *hallulhu b'hillulim harbeh* — praise God with many praises. On this reading, the *Yah* suffix is not functioning as the divine name at all but rather as an intensifier, denoting abundance or superlative degree. Even if *hallelujah* is formally one word, its *Yah* component might simply amplify the praise rather than explicitly invoking God's name.

### God's Name Praise

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi then adds a further observation that argues on his own first position. He teaches that *Sefer Tehillim* employs ten distinct expressions of praise — among them *nitzuach*, *nigun*, *maskil*, *mizmor*, *shir*, *ashrei*, *tehillah*, *tefillah*, *hodaah*, and *hallelujah*. Of all these, *hallelujah* is the greatest: *shekolel shem v'shevach b'vas achas* — it contains both God's name and the act of praise within a single word. On this reading, *hallelujah* is one word, but the *Yah* within it does mean God — it is not merely an intensifier. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi thus appears to argue with himself: in one statement the *Yah* is an intensifier; in this statement it is the divine name embedded within praise.

---

## Hallel Origins

### Prophets Tikun

The Gemara now addresses the historical origins of *Hallel* as a liturgical institution. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that the prophets among the people established for Israel that they would recite *Hallel* on the occasions appropriate to it.

### Three Contexts

Three distinct contexts are identified: *al kol perek v'perek* — at every designated festival season, which the Rashbam interprets as *yom tov*; *al kol tzarah v'tzarah shelo tavo aleihem* — God willing it should never happen, but at every time of affliction and danger; and *u'kshe'nigalin, omrim oso al geulasan* — when they were redeemed, they would say it upon their redemption. The parenthetical *shelo tavo aleihem* is exactly that — parenthetical, expressing the hope that such affliction never occur; the operative point is that at the moment of redemption from affliction, this is what was recited. This framework would encompass events like *Chanukah*, and perhaps other moments of national deliverance.

### David Authorship

A *baraisa* records Rabbi Meir's view: *kol tushbachos ha'amuros b'sefer Tehillim, kulam David amram* — every single psalm in the Book of Psalms was composed by David. The basis is a *drasha* on the verse *kalu tefillos David ben Yishai*: read not *kalu* (ceased) but *kol elu* (all these), meaning everything in the book — even those psalms headed by other names such as *tefillah le'Moshe* or *livnei Korach mizmor* — was composed by David, though in the voices or names of those figures.

### Moshe at Sea

Given that attribution, the Gemara presses: *hallel zeh mi amaro?* Who actually composed and first recited *Hallel*? Rabbi Yose reports in the name of his son Elazar that it was *Moshe v'Yisrael* who said it *b'sha'ah she'alu min ha'yam* — when they came up from the Sea of Reeds. This stands somewhat in tension with Rabbi Meir's view, but establishes the crucial point that *Hallel* predates David. His colleagues challenge this, preferring the simpler assumption that David composed everything — but Rabbi Yose defends the antiquity of *Hallel* with two arguments.

### Necessity Proof

The first argument is a logical one: *efshar Yisrael shachtu et pischeihen v'natlu lulaveihen v'lo amru shirah?* Is it conceivable that Israel, throughout all the centuries before David, slaughtered their *Korban Pesach* and took their *lulav* and uttered no song of praise? Obviously, they must have been praising God at those moments, and if so, they must have been doing so with some established text — and this is evidently the text of *Hallel*. Hence *Hallel* must predate David.

A second, more striking, argument is cited: the idol of Michah was present and active — the *Rashbam* explains this as a euphemistic way of saying it stood in the period leading up to and overlapping with David's time — yet Israel was simultaneously reciting *Hallel*, which itself contains the verse *einayim lahem v'lo yiru, oznayim lahem v'lo yishme'u* — mocking those who have eyes but cannot see, ears but cannot hear. This implies *Hallel* was composed at a time when *avodah zarah* was a live reality, perhaps in the brief interval between *yetziat Mitzrayim* and the sin of the *eigel*. The text must have been ancient. These arguments are striking, though it is worth noting that they do not strictly *require* this specific text — they establish that *some* form of praise must have been ancient, and the *Hallel* text we possess is then assumed to be that ancient form.

### Ramban Defense

This discussion about the antiquity and nature of *Hallel* connects to a significant dispute among the *rishonim* regarding whether *Hallel* is *d'oraisa* or *d'rabanan*. The Rambam opens his *Sefer Hamitzvos* with fourteen principles for determining which commandments count as biblical. The first is that only biblical commandments are to be enumerated, not rabbinic ones. Among his critiques of the Ba'hag's list is the inclusion of *Hallel*: since the psalms that comprise it were written by David, how can *Hallel* be biblical?

The Ramban, in his *Hassagos* on *Sefer Hamitzvos*, mounts a sustained defense of the Ba'hag. He first challenges the Rambam's logic: the Rambam himself holds that *tefillah* — daily prayer — is a biblical obligation, yet the specific text of *tefillah* was not composed until the Men of the Great Assembly, long after the biblical period. Similarly, *benshen* is *d'oraisa* even though its particular text came much later. One can therefore have a biblical obligation without that obligation having been expressed in its current textual form from Sinai. The same argument applies to *Hallel*: the obligation could be biblical even if the specific psalms were composed by David.

The Ramban then adds that the Gemara in *Pesachim* itself attests to multiple traditions holding *Hallel* to be ancient — indeed, the Gemara's reasoning that Israel *must* have been praising God at *Pesach* and *lulav* supports the idea that this was never merely an institution invented late in the rabbinic period.

The Ramban proposes that the biblical basis for *Hallel* might be either a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* or — more suggestively — that it is subsumed within the biblical *mitzvah* of *simchas yom tov*. The verse *v'samachta l'fnei Hashem* implies that *simchah* before God is not merely physical — not just eating *basar u'shlamim* — but includes the spiritual dimension of praise and song in God's presence. On this reading, saying *Hallel* on *yom tov* is part of the fulfillment of *simchas yom tov* itself. This aligns with the earlier Gemara's framework connecting *Hallel* to *yom tov*, to redemption, and to the specific acts of taking *lulav* and slaughtering the *Korban Pesach* — all moments of heightened encounter with the divine presence.

---

## Inspiration Mood

### Simcha Shel Mitzvah

The Gemara derives from the contrast between *mizmor l'David* and *l'David mizmor* a fundamental principle about the conditions for divine inspiration. When a psalm is headed *l'David mizmor* — David's name precedes the song — this teaches that the *shechina* rested upon him first, and he then sang. When it is *mizmor l'David* — the song precedes — this teaches that he sang first, and the *shechina* rested upon him afterward.

Why would God wait? *She'eina shechina shora lo mitoch atzlut v'lo mitoch atzvut* — the *shechina* does not rest upon a person when they are lazy, nor when they are sad, nor when they are frivolous (*sechok*), nor when they are engaged in empty levity (*kalut rosh*), nor when they are occupied with trivial matters (*devarim betelim*). Rather, divine inspiration comes *ela mitoch devar simcha shel mitzvah* — specifically from a state of joyful engagement in *mitzvah*. The additional verse *ve'atah kchu li menagen, vehaya kenagen hamenagen vatehi alav yad Hashem* reinforces the point: it was the playing of the musician — an act of joyful engagement — that brought the divine inspiration upon Elisha.

### Mood for Halacha

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav extends this principle: the same requirement of a good and joyful state applies *vechen ledvar halacha* — to the rendering of halachic rulings as well. Rav Nachman adds a parallel application: the same is true for receiving a *chalom tov*, a good dream — one should enter sleep in a state of *simcha shel mitzvah*.

### Dreams Joy

These three applications — divine inspiration, *halacha*, and good dreams — are presented as structurally parallel, all requiring the same preparatory inner disposition of joy rooted in *mitzvah* engagement.

### Trembling Lips

A challenge is immediately raised. Rav Gidel in the name of Rav states: *kol talmid chacham hayoshev lifnei rabbo v'ein siftotav notfot mar tichzena* — any Torah scholar who sits before his teacher and whose lips are not dripping with bitterness, trembling in awe, his lips should be scorched. The proof text is from *Shir Hashirim*: *siftotav shoshanim notfot mor over* — his lips are like roses dripping myrrh. Read not *shoshanim* (roses) but *sheshonim* (those who learn); read not *mor over* (passing myrrh) but *mar avar* (bitterness that passes over). A student must come to his *rebbi* in a state of trembling awe — the opposite of the joyful ease suggested above. This is the same paradox invoked when explaining why one does not study Torah on *Tisha B'Av*: the joy of Torah study is itself an expression of the soul's delight, incompatible with mourning.

### Rebbe vs Student

The Gemara resolves the tension: *lo kashya — ha b'rabba, ha b'talmida*. The two descriptions apply to different parties. The *rebbi* may and should be in a state of *simcha* — the joy of *mitzvah* engagement that allows him to teach, to reach *halachic* conclusions, and to access deeper levels of understanding. The student, by contrast, must be in a state of trembling reverence before his teacher. The two postures are not contradictory; they characterize different positions in the relationship.

### Rabba's Method

Alternatively, the Gemara suggests that both descriptions apply to the *rebbi* himself, but at different moments. *Hachi hashta: ha mikmei depatach, ha levatar depatach* — one disposition belongs to before one begins to teach, the other to after. This is illustrated by the practice of Rabba: *mikmei d'patach l'rabbanan, amar milta d'bidichuta* — before he would open his lesson to the rabbinic students he would say something light, something humorous, *u'vadu rabbanan* — and the students would laugh, relaxing into a receptive frame of mind. *U'levasof yativ be'eimta u'patach b'shmata* — and then he would sit with a sense of solemnity and open the lesson itself. The humor served not as a distraction but as a vehicle to shift the students from their ordinary state into readiness for learning, whereupon the *rebbi* himself entered into the awe-filled space of Torah. One might ask whether these two states are truly contradictory: perhaps *gilu b're'adah* — joy and trembling combined — represents the ideal in which one engages Torah with both love and awe simultaneously. But the Gemara is here navigating a practical balance, and the model of Rabba suggests a temporal sequencing: levity to open, then gravity to sustain.

---

## Hallel Crises

### Moshe Israel

The Gemara returns to the question of *Hallel*'s origins with a *baraisa* that presents multiple competing Tannaitic positions, each locating the first recitation of *Hallel* at a different historical moment of crisis and redemption. The structure is uniform throughout: at each crisis, the protagonists recited *lo lanu Hashem lo lanu* — "not for us, God, not for us" — a form of petition acknowledging unworthiness while pleading for divine intervention, and the divine spirit responded *l'ma'ani l'ma'ani e'eseh* — "for My sake, for My sake I will act" (from Yeshayahu). This is striking: *Hallel* is here understood not merely as a post-redemption song of thanksgiving but as containing, at its culmination, a genuine *bakashah* — a petition for salvation — and a divine response promising redemption for God's own sake rather than Israel's.

Rabbi Eliezer holds that *Moshe v'Yisrael amru b'sha'ah she'amdu al ha'yam* — Moshe and Israel said *Hallel* while they were standing at the sea, before they crossed, during the moment of danger itself.

### Yehoshua Kings

Rabbi Yehuda holds that it was *Yehoshua v'Yisrael* who said it *b'sha'ah she'amdu aleihem malchei Kena'an* — when the kings of Canaan stood against them in battle.

### Deborah Barak

Rabbi Eliezer HaModai holds that it was *Devorah u'Barak* who said it *b'sha'ah she'amad aleihem Sisra* — when Sisra threatened them.

### Chizkiyahu

Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah holds that it was *Chizkiyahu v'siato* — Chizkiyahu and his circle — who said it *b'sha'ah she'amad aleihem Sancheriv* — when Sancheriv besieged Jerusalem.

### Three Friends

Rabbi Akiva holds that it was *Chananyah, Mishael v'Azaryah* who said it *b'sha'ah she'amad aleihem Nevuchadnetzar harasha* — when the wicked Nevuchadnetzar threatened to cast them into the fiery furnace.

### Mordechai Esther

Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds that it was *Mordechai v'Esther* who said it *b'sha'ah she'amad aleihem Haman harasha* — when Haman threatened the entire people. The list proceeds in historical order — from the Sea of Reeds through the Persian period — suggesting a cumulative argument: *Hallel* was not composed at one moment; it was always the prayer and song of Israel in its moments of greatest peril and greatest redemption.

The Rashbam notes that one reading of these positions holds they are not actually in dispute — each sage is pointing to a different historical instantiation of the same practice, collectively demonstrating that *Hallel* has always been recited at such moments. The structure is reminiscent of the ancient *selichot* and *ta'anit* liturgy — *mi she'anah l'Avraham Avinu... mi she'anah... mi she'anah* — where the catalog of divine responses to crisis becomes itself a form of prayer and praise.

What is particularly powerful about this *baraisa* is the location of *lo lanu Hashem lo lanu* — "not for us God, not for us" — as the pivot point of each account. This verse, which appears near the end of the *Hallel* we recite, carries a petitionary, even supplicatory quality. The *baraisa* is pointing out that *Hallel* contains within itself not only thanks for redemption already received but the cry of those still standing at the threshold of danger, pleading for divine intervention. The narrative arc of *lo lanu* followed by divine response *l'ma'ani e'eseh* captures the full movement from petition to promise.

### Chachamim View

The *Chachamim* offer a formulation that distinguishes itself from the individual Tannaitic positions. They reiterate the formula that *nevi'im shebeineihem tiknu l'Yisrael sheyihu omrim oso al kol perek u'perek v'al kol tzarah shelo tavo aleihem u'kshe'nigalin omrim oso al geulasan*. The key distinction in the *Chachamim*'s version appears to be the emphasis on recitation *al geulatan* — upon redemption — rather than specifically during the moment of threat. Where the individual Tannaim emphasize the crisis itself as the occasion for *Hallel*, the *Chachamim* stress the moment of deliverance. Both dimensions are present in the full *Hallel*, but the *Chachamim* place the center of gravity on thanksgiving for redemption rather than petition during danger.

---

## Hallelujah Perek

### Ends Perek

Rav Chisda rules that whenever *hallelujah* appears at a point of ambiguity in *Sefer Tehillim* — between the end of one *perek* and the beginning of another — it should be understood as *sof perek*, the concluding word of the preceding section.

### Begins Perek

Rava bar Rav Huna disagrees: *hallelujah reish pirka* — *hallelujah* is the opening word of the following section, not the conclusion of the preceding one.

### Between Sections

Rav Chisda reports having seen the *Sefer Tehillim* in the possession of Rav Chanin bar Rav, in which *hallelujah* was written precisely between two sections — *b'emtza pirka* — clearly because its owner was uncertain (*misafka lei*) whether it belonged to the end of one or the beginning of the other, and so placed it exactly in between as a way of expressing that uncertainty in the physical layout of the scroll.

### Consensus Begin

Rav Chanin bar Rava — distinct from Rav Chanin bar Rav cited just above — states that in fact *hakol modin*, everyone agrees, that the *hallelujah* following the verse *tehillas Hashem yedaber pi viyvarech kol basar shem kodsho l'olam va'ed* is *reish pirka*, the opening of the next section. This verse concludes one psalm; the *hallelujah* that follows it opens the next. Similarly, the *hallelujah* that follows *rasha yireh v'ka'as, shinav yichrok v'namas, ta'avas resha'im toveid* is likewise *reish pirka* — the opening of the next psalm, not the closing of that one.

### Ashrei Practice

The practical implication emerges in our *davening*. In *Sefer Tehillim* itself, psalm 145 (*ashrei*) concludes with *tehillas Hashem yedaber pi...* and does not end with *hallelujah*. Psalm 146 then opens *Hallelujah, halleli nafshi es Hashem*. When we recite *ashrei* in our prayers, however, we conclude with *hallelujah* — reflecting the liturgical practice rather than the strict *Tehillim* division. In a *Sefer Tehillim*, there is only one *hallelujah* at that juncture; in the printed *siddur*, it appears twice, because the liturgical tradition influenced the printed text. The Gemara's discussion clarifies that structurally that *hallelujah* is properly the beginning of the next *perek*, not the ending of *ashrei* — and indeed, several of the psalms that begin with *hallelujah* continue immediately with *halelu es Hashem* or similar language, which further supports reading *hallelujah* as an opening formula that flows into the body of the new section.

---

## Hallel Length

### Shammai Hillel

The Gemara now reconnects to the *Mishnah*'s dispute about how far one recites *Hallel* before the *berachah* that concludes the *haggadah* — that is, before *motzi matzah* and the main meal. Two *beraisos* record the dispute between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel, and the two versions seem to differ on how each position is formulated.

### Version One

In the first *baraisa*: Beis Shammai says one recites until *eim habanim simchah*, the final phrase of the first *perek* of *Hallel* (psalm 113). Beis Hillel says until *chalamish l'mayno mayim*, the final phrase of the second *perek* (psalm 114).

### Version Two

In the second *baraisa*: Beis Shammai says until *b'tzeis Yisrael miMitzrayim*, the opening phrase of the second *perek*. Beis Hillel says until *lo lanu Hashem lo lanu*, the opening phrase of the third *perek* (psalm 115).

At first glance these two versions seem simply to disagree about whether the stopping point is quoted as the last phrase of the *perek* one does say or the first phrase of the *perek* one does not say — an inclusive versus exclusive formulation. But the Gemara notices something significant: neither version mentions *hallelujah*, even though *hallelujah* appears between the two *perakim* at issue.

### Chisda Explains

Rav Chisda resolves the apparent discrepancy between the two versions of the dispute according to his own position that *hallelujah* is *sof perek*. On this reading, the full text of the first *perek* ends: *moshivi akkeres habayis, eim habanim simchah, Hallelujah*. And the second *perek* begins: *b'tzeis Yisrael miMitzrayim*. The one who says "until *eim habanim simchah*" holds *hallelujah* is *reish pirka* and therefore does not include it — stopping before the word *hallelujah*, which opens the next section. The one who says "until *b'tzeis Yisrael miMitzrayim*" holds *hallelujah* is *sof pirka*, meaning it was already included as part of the first *perek*, and one recites up until (but not including) *b'tzeis Yisrael miMitzrayim*.

### Rabba Explains

Rabba bar Rav Huna resolves the same discrepancy according to his position that *hallelujah* is *reish pirka*. On this reading, the second *perek* properly opens *Hallelujah b'tzeis Yisrael miMitzrayim*. The one who says "until *eim habanim simchah*" is citing the last phrase of the first *perek* inclusively — *ad v'ad bichlal*, up to and including — meaning one does say *eim habanim simchah*. The one who says "until *b'tzeis Yisrael miMitzrayim*" means up to but not including — *ad v'lo ad bichlal* — so the second *perek*, which begins with *hallelujah*, is not recited before the meal.

### Kashia Unresolved

Both resolutions, however, run into the same difficulty: if the word *hallelujah* is the crux of the debate — if the entire point of the dispute between the two versions is whether *hallelujah* belongs to the end of one *perek* or the beginning of another — then why doesn't either version of the dispute simply say "until *hallelujah*" or "until the *hallelujah* of *eim habanim simchah*"? The omission of *hallelujah* from both formulations is conspicuous. The Gemara raises this challenge — *v'neima Hallelujah shel eim habanim simchah*, why not simply say until *that* *hallelujah*? — and leaves it unresolved: *kashia*.

The halacha, the Gemara notes, is that *hallelujah* is *reish pirka* — the opening of the following section. The overall discussion leaves us with a richly detailed portrait of *Hallel*'s structure, its ancient origins, its function as both petition and thanksgiving, and the careful attention Chazal paid to its textual divisions and their practical implications for the *seder* night and for all *yamim tovim*.

---

---

# Pesachim 118

## Geula Blessing Tense

### Maggid Conclusion

The daf begins at the top third of 117b, approximately six lines before the lines widen, with the phrase *v'chosem b'geula* — the rule that one concludes the *maggid* section of the *seder* with the *beracha* of *geula*. As we have established from the *mishnah*, Rabbi Tarfon holds that this blessing consists of *asher g'alanu* alone, while Rabbi Akiva adds the prayer *ken Hashem elokeinu yagi'enu l'mo'adim acherim* — an expression of hope for the future — followed by a *chatima* at the end. The *gemara* now turns not to the debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon, but to a different question entirely: whether the concluding *chatima* should read *ga'al Yisrael* — in the past tense — or *go'el Yisrael* — in the present.

### Ga'al vs. Go'el

*Amar Rava*: the *beracha* concluding *Krias Shema* before *Shemoneh Esrei*, and the corresponding *beracha* at the conclusion of *Hallel* in the *Haggadah* — that is, the blessing at the end of the first two *prakim* of *Hallel* recited during *maggid* — both employ *ga'al Yisrael*, a reference to the past redemption from Egypt. By contrast, the *tzelusa* — the *Shemoneh Esrei* — uses *go'el Yisrael*. Indeed, all of the *berachos* of *Shemoneh Esrei* are framed in the present.

### Participial Form

It is worth noting that in biblical Hebrew the present-tense form is in fact a participial construction, and one could argue that Hebrew has no true present tense at all. When one says *ani shomer*, it can mean either "I am a guardian" — a noun — or "I am watching" — a verb in action. The participial form of *Shemoneh Esrei* thus functions as an ongoing descriptor: when we say *baruch atah Hashem rofei cholei amo Yisrael*, we are not merely recalling a past act of healing but affirming God as the one who continuously heals the sick of Israel — describing an active, ongoing relationship.

### Rachamei Concept

*Mai ta'ama d'rachamei ninhu* — the reason is that the *Shemoneh Esrei* is characterized as *rachamei*, a technical term the *gemara* employs in discussing *tefillah*, denoting the *bakasha* element, the quality of petition and request. Because *Shemoneh Esrei* is fundamentally an act of supplication directed toward the present and future, its formulations are cast accordingly in the present. *Amar Rabbi Zeira*: similarly, in *Kiddush* one says *asher kideshanu b'mitzvosav v'ratza vanu* — You have sanctified us in Your commandments in the past — whereas in *Shemoneh Esrei* one says *kadshenu b'mitzvossecha*, a petition: please sanctify us. The same principle applies: *mai ta'ama d'rachamei ninhu* — because of the *bakasha* dimension of *tefillah*.

---

## Kiddush Mention

### Exodus in Kiddush

*Amar Rav Acha bar Yaakov*: one is required to mention *Yetzias Mitzrayim* in *Kiddush*. This ruling requires justification, since one might have thought that *Kiddush* — at least on *Shabbos* — is thematically about *Ma'aseh Bereishis*, creation, and has no inherent connection to the exodus. The question is all the more pointed because there are two accounts of the *Aseres Hadibros* in the *Torah*, each giving a different rationale for *Shabbos*.

### Two Pesukim

The *gemara* supports this ruling by juxtaposing two verses. *Ketiv hacha*: *lema'an tizkor et yom tzetcha me'eretz mitzrayim kol yemei chayecha* — so that you shall remember the day of your departure from Egypt all the days of your life. *Uchetiv hatam*: *zachor et yom hashabbat lekadesho* — remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it. The *gemara* brings these two *pesukim* together to derive that the obligation of remembrance applies to both, and they are to be woven together in *Kiddush*. This is a striking derivation, because one might more naturally have derived the connection from the explicit verse in *Devarim* that ties *Shabbos* to the experience of servitude in Egypt — *vezacharta ki eved hayita b'Eretz Mitzrayim* — which connects the freedom of *Shabbos* directly to the memory of liberation.

### Gematria Atbash

*Tosafos* notes that the *Torah* establishes *zecher l'Yetziat Mitzrayim* in *Kiddush* on the basis of *lema'an tizkor*, and quotes a teaching — attributed to the *Maharam* of Rothenburg — that works through a more elaborate path. The word *befarech*, the crushing labor imposed upon Israel in Egypt, yields through *Atbash* letter substitution the letters that form the word *v'gal*, numerically equivalent to thirty-nine, corresponding to the thirty-nine *melachot* forbidden on *Shabbos*. The inference drawn is that when Israel was redeemed from Egypt, God removed from them the burden of those thirty-nine labors and granted them *Shabbos* — the right to rest from that very work. This is a more elaborate encoding of what the *Torah* itself already says: that you were a slave and you are now free, and *Shabbos* embodies that freedom. One could verify whether it is specifically the *Maharam* of Rothenburg being cited, as it is a somewhat late attribution for *Tosafos*.

### Beyond Shabbat

The *Rashbam* extends the principle: the obligation to mention *Yetzias Mitzrayim* applies not only to *Shabbos* but *bein b'kos bein b'tefillah* — both in *Kiddush* and in *Shemoneh Esrei*. He explains that *Shabbos* derives this obligation through the *gezeirah shavah* between *lema'an tizkor* (said by *Pesach*) and *zachor* (said by *Shabbos*), and that the remaining *Yamim Tovim* derive it from *Pesach* in turn. This accounts for why we say *zecher l'Yetziat Mitzrayim* in every *Kiddush* throughout the year. The case most in need of justification is *Shavuos*, whose connection to the exodus is least explicit in the *Torah* — and the *gemara*'s derivation there, through this chain of *pesukim*, is genuinely unusual. One might suggest that the *gemara* wishes to underscore not merely the thematic association but a formal textual obligation to remember the exodus as part of *Kiddush* itself, grounded in the verse *lema'an tizkor*.

---

## Sanctification Forms

### Kiddush Formulation

*Amar Rava bar Shila*: in *Shemoneh Esrei* one says *matzmiach keren yeshuah* — God causes the horn of salvation to sprout forth, expressed in the present — while in the concluding *beracha* of the *Haftarah* one says *Magen David*. Both locutions pertain to David, yet they differ.

### Redemption Language

The question naturally arises: why not say *Magen David* in *Shemoneh Esrei* as well, since *magen* appears in the present tense, just as we say *Magen Avraham*? The *Rashbam* explains, citing *Masechet Soferim* which records the *berachos* of the *Haftarah*: in *tefillah*, *matzmiach keren yeshuah* is more appropriate because the *Shemoneh Esrei* is *rachamei* — petition — and we are asking that God cause the horn of salvation to flourish for Israel. *Matzmiach keren yeshuah* looks forward to a future flowering of redemption, while *Magen David* — even grammatically present — is a more static concept, a descriptor of past protection rather than an aspiration toward future renewal. A second explanation attributed to *Rabbeinu Shlomo* — presumably Rashi — is that since we have already said *Magen Avraham*, having a second *beracha* ending with *magen* would be an undesirable redundancy; *trei chatimos k'hadadi lo shayach b'tzalla*. Both explanations can coexist.

### Haftarah Blessings

This raises the broader discussion of why we associate God's protection of David specifically with the phrase *Magen David* in the *Haftarah* blessing, which the *gemara* will address in the following section.

---

## Patriarchal Names

### Magen David

*Tani Rav Yosef*: the verse states *ve'asiti lecha shem gadol keshem hagedolim* — I will make for you a great name like the great ones. The *gemara* identifies this as the basis for saying *Magen David*, because God's promise to David parallels God's promise to Avraham. Who are *keshem hagedolim*? That refers to *Magen Avraham*. And indeed, God said to Avraham *ve'esecha l'goy gadol v'agadlah shemecha* — I will make you into a great nation and I will make your name great. David thus receives the same status, anchored in the same language of greatness.

### Three Patriarchs

*Amar Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish*: the verse *ve'esecha l'goy gadol* corresponds to what we say *Elohei Avraham*; *u'varechecha* corresponds to *Elohei Yitzchak*; *u'gadlah shemecha* corresponds to *Elohei Yaakov*.

### Fulfilled Promises

The *Maharsha* explains how these correspondences work. *U'varechecha* is realized through Yitzchak, because immediately after Avraham's death the *Torah* says *vayivarech Elohim et Yitzchak beno* — God blessed Yitzchak his son. Thus the fulfillment of God's promise that *u'varechecha* is seen played out in Yitzchak's life. We therefore say *Elohei Yitzchak* because the truth of God's promise became visible in Yitzchak. The connection to Yaakov is made in a somewhat different manner, but the overarching principle is consistent: we associate God's name with each patriarch because God's promises to them were fulfilled, and those fulfilled promises are what we invoke.

### Avraham Singular

*Yachol yachatmu bechulam* — one might have thought that the concluding *beracha* of *Shemoneh Esrei* should enumerate all three patriarchs: *baruch atah Hashem Magen Avraham Yitzchak v'Yaakov*.
