The *gemara* answers from the verse *v'heyeh berachah* — and you shall be a blessing — in the singular, not *v'hayu*. *Becha chotmin v'ein chotmin bechulan*: in you, Avraham, we conclude, and we do not conclude with all of them. The emphasis at the end is upon Avraham, because his is the beginning of the relationship. That is *Magen Avraham*, with the singular focus on Avraham.

---

## Shabbat vs. Yom Tov

### Pumbedita Elders

*Amar Rava ashchechihu l'savei d'Pumbedita d'yatvi v'ka'amri*: Rava recounts that he found the elders of Pumbedita sitting and saying: on *Shabbos*, whether in *Shemoneh Esrei* or in *Kiddush*, one says *Mekadesh HaShabbat*; on *Yom Tov*, whether in *Shemoneh Esrei* or in *Kiddush*, one says *Mekadesh Yisrael v'hazmanim*. That is, the distinction follows the day — *Shabbos* versus *Yom Tov* — and applies uniformly across both *tefillah* and *Kiddush*.

### Rava's Reasoning

Rava responded to the elders: *adarava* — on the contrary. The distinction ought to be based not on the day but on the context — *Shemoneh Esrei* versus *Kiddush*. In *Shemoneh Esrei*, whether *Shabbos* or *Yom Tov*, one should always say *Mekadesh Yisrael*. In *Kiddush*, on *Shabbos* one says *Mekadesh HaShabbat*, and on *Yom Tov* one says *Mekadesh Yisrael v'hazmanim*. So Rava maintains the distinction between *Mekadesh HaShabbat* and *Mekadesh Yisrael v'hazmanim* — but only in *Kiddush*, not in *Shemoneh Esrei*.

### Intrinsic Nature

The *gemara* then presents both rationales. *Ta'ama did'hu* — the reasoning of the Pumbedita elders: *Shabbat d'kevi'a v'kayama* — *Shabbos* is fixed and stands on its own; its *kedushah* is inherent and independent of any human role. Therefore, whether in *Shemoneh Esrei* or in *Kiddush*, one says *Mekadesh HaShabbat*, because God is the one who sanctifies the *Shabbos* without the involvement of Israel. On *Yom Tov*, by contrast, *d'Yisrael hu d'kavei leih* — it is Israel that establishes it. Israel determines whether a month is twenty-nine or thirty days, fixes the calendar, and intercalates the year. Through Israel's role the *kedushah* of the times flows. Hence: *Mekadesh Yisrael v'hazmanim* — God sanctifies Israel, and through Israel's partnership, the sacred times are established.

### Community Context

*Ta'ama didi* — Rava's own reasoning: *tzeluta d'bei rabim* — *Shemoneh Esrei* is, in its primary form, a communal prayer, said in the synagogue. When the community gathers in the *shul* on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, one wants to acknowledge that gathering by saying *Mekadesh Yisrael*, recognizing the *kedushah* of the people Israel assembled together. *Kiddusha d'bei chavi* — *Kiddush*, by contrast, takes place in the home, in a private setting. Therefore the distinction in *Kiddush* remains between *Mekadesh HaShabbat* for *Shabbos* and *Mekadesh Yisrael v'hazmanim* for *Yom Tov*.

One might deepen Rava's reasoning: it is not merely that the congregation is assembled, but that the assembly itself provides the occasion to affirm the covenant — *ki ot hi*, the *ot* and the *bris* between God and Israel — and therefore to emphasize *Mekadesh Yisrael*, the role of Israel in relation to *Shabbos* as well. Even though *Shabbat d'kevi'a v'kayama*, Israel is the party commanded to observe it, and that *bris* is what the communal *tefillah* seeks to give voice to.

### Individual Prayer

The *gemara* rejects Rava's distinction: *v'lo hi* — this argument does not hold. *Tzeluta b'yachid mi leita?* — does one not pray *Shemoneh Esrei* privately? *Kiddusha b'rabim mi leita?* — is *Kiddush* never recited communally? Since both *Shemoneh Esrei* and *Kiddush* can occur in either context, the distinction between public and private cannot be the operative difference. The *gemara* therefore reasserts that Rava's view is that one goes after the *ikar* — the primary context of each.

### Practical Evidence

*Ulla bar Rav nachit kamei d'Rava* — Ulla bar Rav went down to lead the *tefillah* before Rava as *shaliach tzibbur* (the term *nachit* reflects the ancient practice of praying from a lower position, calling out from the depths). He said the formula of the elders of Pumbedita — that is, in *Shemoneh Esrei* he said *Mekadesh HaShabbat* or *Mekadesh Yisrael v'hazmanim* depending on the day, rather than uniformly *Mekadesh Yisrael*. *V'lo amar lei v'lo midi* — Rava said nothing to him. *Alma hadar bei Rava* — this indicates that Rava himself reversed his position. Subsequently, Rav Natan the father of Rav Huna son of Rav Natan went down before Rav Papa and likewise said as the elders of Pumbedita. *V'shabchei Rav Papa* — Rav Papa praised him.

### Marimar Ruling

*Amar Ravina*: I came to Sura before Mareimar, and the *shaliach tzibbur* prayed according to the elders of Pumbedita. The assembled congregation tried to silence him — evidently expecting the uniform *Mekadesh Yisrael* of Rava's original position — but Mareimar said to them: *shavkuya* — leave him alone. *Hilchasa k'savei d'Pumbedita* — the *halakha* follows the elders of Pumbedita. At that, the congregation ceased its objections. An alternative *girsa* in the margin reads that it is the anonymous editorial voice of the *gemara* that declares *v'hilchasa k'savei d'Pumbedita*.

---

## Liturgical Variance

### Nuschaot Variance

What this entire discussion reveals — and it is important always to bear in mind when studying debates about liturgy — is how much these *beit midrash* disputes reflect actual divergent practices that existed in the communities. We see the same phenomenon elsewhere in our *gemara*, for example in the discussion around *Agosi* and how *Chazal* actually conducted themselves. Here, the people in the synagogue clearly thought the *shaliach tzibbur* was making an error — they tried to silence him — yet he was following a recognized tradition. The relationship between what was taught in the *beit midrash* and what communities actually practiced was clearly bidirectional, not simply top-down.

### Text Crystallization

This discussion also raises a more fundamental question: when exactly was the text of *Shemoneh Esrei* crystallized and finalized? The basic structure is attributed to *Anshei Knesses Hagedolah*, but the *gemara* itself — and related sources in the *Tosefta* — reflects an awareness of certain textual flux operating within defined parameters. The absolute solidification of the text, word for word, was a process that extended over time.

### Variants Parameters

There is, however, an important distinction to maintain: on one side, there are texts that represent acceptable variant *nuschaot* — formulations that circulated during a period before the text fully crystallized, each representing a legitimate tradition. On the other side, there is the question of unauthorized insertions — additions to the *tefillah* beyond its sanctioned structure. The *gemara* does speak to this: one may not make insertions into the first three *berachos*, while additions in the middle *berachos*, depending on their nature, may be permissible. These are two separate questions: the legitimacy of parallel textual traditions that predate full crystallization, and the prohibition against arbitrary personal additions.

### Oseh Hashalom

A striking case study is the practice of saying *Oseh Hashalom* at the conclusion of *Shemoneh Esrei* during the *Yamim Noraim* instead of the standard *Ha-mevarech et ammo Yisrael bashalom*. Rav Soloveitchik was strongly opposed to this practice, on the grounds that the *gemara* gives no indication that the *beracha* should be changed for the *Aseres Yemei Teshuvah*, and the *Geonim*, even when they inserted additions like *Zachreinu*, did not alter the text of the *berachah* itself. Yet fragments from the *Geniza* show that *Oseh Hashalom* was in fact a parallel text used during the year — not just during the *Yamim Noraim* — which suggests it was an authentic alternative *nusach* rather than an innovation. What apparently happened is that this alternative formulation came to be endorsed specifically for the *Yamim Noraim*. This illustrates precisely the distinction described above: a legitimate parallel text that predated full crystallization is categorically different from a new insertion. Even so, the practical reality is that even today there are differences in this matter between Artscroll and Koren siddurim, and between various communities that nominally follow the same *nusach*.

---

## Third Fourth Cups

### Cup Pouring

The *mishnah* turns now to the structure of the *arba kosot*. *Mozgu lo kos shlishi* — one pours the third cup and recites *Birkat Hamazon* over it. One then pours the fourth cup, *gomer alav et ha-Hallel* — completes the *Hallel* begun after *maggid* — and says *Birkat Hashir*, the blessing of song. It is striking that the *mishnah* completely leapfrogs over the major *mitzvos* of *achilah* — *matzah*, *maror*, and *koreich* — as well as *Shulchan Orech*, and proceeds directly from the blessings of *maggid* to the third cup. The *kosos* appear to be structuring the entire rhythm of the *mishnah*'s presentation. Notably, even *afikoman* — the second eating of *matzah* after the meal — receives no mention in the *mishnah*, despite not being obvious in the way that the meal itself might be. We will return to that topic when the *gemara* addresses *ein maftirin achar hapesach afikoman*.

One might speculate that some scholars have suggested that in the world of the *mishnah*, the eating of *matzah* and *maror* actually took place much earlier in the *seder* — before *maggid* — when the *mishnah* says *hevi'u lefanav* and *hevi'u lo matzah v'chazeret v'charoset ushnei tavshilin*, and that the telling was simultaneous with the eating. This would explain why the *mishnah* does not separately mark the moment of eating.

### Inter-Cup Drinking

*Bein hakosos hallalu* — between the earlier cups, that is between the first and second and between the second and third, *im rotze lishtot yishte* — one may drink additionally if one wishes. *Bein shlishi l'revi'i lo yishte* — between the third and fourth cups one may not drink. The *Rashbam* quotes the *Yerushalmi*: drinking after the meal, as opposed to during it, leads to intoxication. Additionally, some suggest the concern is about washing away the taste of the *matzah* — a consideration that becomes relevant once one has eaten the *matzah* and *afikoman* and the meal has concluded. We will develop this point further in the discussion of *ein maftirin achar hapesach afikoman*. *Tosafos* notes that the restriction between the third and fourth cups applies specifically to wine; water would be permissible even according to those who give the reason as protecting the taste of *matzah*, since water does not eliminate that taste.

### Hamazon Cup

*Amar lei Rav Chana le-Rava*: since the *mishnah* specifies that the third cup is poured for *Birkat Hamazon*, one might infer that *Birkat Hamazon* generally requires a *kos* — a cup of wine. *Amar lei*: this does not necessarily follow. *Arba kasei tiknu rabanan derech cheirut* — the rabbis instituted four cups as an expression of *cheirus*, freedom. *Kol chad v'chad na'avid bei mitzvah* — they wanted each cup to be associated with a *mitzvah*, so that one was not simply drinking without ritual purpose. They therefore designated the third cup for *Birkat Hamazon*. This does not demonstrate that *Birkat Hamazon* in general requires a cup; it demonstrates rather that on *leil ha-seder*, where cups were already mandated, they were each assigned to a *mitzvah*. This *gemara* also makes clear that the four cups are specifically four — *davka* — and no more, since the entire rationale is to assign each cup to a *mitzvah* within the *seder*.

---

## Hallel Completion

### Hallel End

*Revi'i omer alav gomer alav et ha-Hallel* — on the fourth cup one completes the *Hallel* begun during *maggid*, and *omer alav Birchat Hashir* — one recites the blessing of song at its conclusion.

### Blessing Debate

*Mai Birchat Hashir?* — what is this blessing? *Rabbi Yehuda omer Yehallelucha Hashem Elokeinu* — the standard concluding *beracha* of *Hallel*, which reads *Yehallelucha Hashem Elokeinu kol ma'asecha vachasidecha tzaddikim osei ritzonecha*, concluding with *baruch atah Hashem melech mehullal batishbachos*. According to Rabbi Yehuda, *Birchat Hashir* is simply the normal concluding blessing of *Hallel*. *Rabbi Yochanan omer*: it is *Nishmas Kol Chai*, the extended passage of praise familiar from *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov Pesukei D'Zimra*, which concludes with *Yishtabach* — *El melech gadol mehullal batishbachos, El hahoda'os, adon hanifla'os, habocher b'shirei zimrah, melech El chei ha'olamim* — also concluding with *batishbachos*.

### Internal Impetus

The *rishonim* raise a pointed question: why does the *mishnah* need to specify that one ends *Hallel* with a *beracha*? Surely, if one recites *Hallel*, one ends with the standard concluding blessing, just as one always does. The answer lies in the unique nature of how *Hallel* was introduced during *maggid*. The *Haggadah* frames the beginning of *Hallel* with the language of *lefichach anachnu chayyavim* — therefore we are obligated — and *chayyav liros et atzmo* — one is obligated to see oneself as if one personally left Egypt. The *Hallel* begins not from a formal external obligation marked by a blessing of *asher kiddeshanu*, but from this internal impetus — the person is living the experience of *geulah*, and the praise flows from within. For this reason, the *mishnah* never specifies that *Hallel* begins with a *beracha*, and indeed, this is our practice: the first half of *Hallel* in the *Haggadah* begins without a formal opening blessing.

---

## Hallel Completion (II)

### Ending Formula

The explicit statement that one says a blessing at the end of *Hallel* therefore serves a purpose: to tell us that despite the unconventional opening — without a *beracha* — there is nonetheless a proper concluding *beracha*. According to Rabbi Yehuda, that is the standard *Hallel* closing; according to Rabbi Yochanan, it is *Nishmas Kol Chai* leading into *Yishtabach*.

### Why Explicit

One proof that *Hallel* does not begin with a *beracha* on *leil ha-seder* derives precisely from the fact that the *mishnah* specifies the concluding blessing: if *Hallel* had begun with a *beracha* in the ordinary way, it would go without saying that it ends with one. The very need to state the ending formula demonstrates the unusual structure of the opening.

### Begin Without

This is consistent with our received practice: the first two *prakim* of *Hallel* during *maggid* — *Betzeit Yisrael mi-Mitzrayim* and *Lo Lanu* — are recited without a preceding blessing of *asher kiddeshanu*, because they emerge from the experiential moment of reliving the *geulah*.

### Ritual Transition

By the time we reach the conclusion of *Hallel* after the meal, however, the dynamic has shifted. We have eaten, the *afikoman* has been consumed, and we are no longer in that immediate experiential moment of *geulah*. We have recited *asher ga'al Yisrael* — the *geulah* was framed in the past — and we have moved into a more retrospective and ritual mode. In this mode, it becomes possible and appropriate to conclude with a formal blessing, *melech mehullal batishbachos*.

---

## Nishmat Extension

### Nishmat Alt

According to Rabbi Yochanan, the concluding blessing is *Nishmas Kol Chai*, not the standard *Hallel* ending. This view holds that in addition to or in place of the standard *Yehallelucha* closing, one recites the extended passage of *Nishmas* and concludes with *Yishtabach*.

### Dual Endings

The *Rashbam* understands Rabbi Yochanan not as excluding Rabbi Yehuda's view but as supplementing it: one ends *Hallel* with the standard *melech mehullal batishbachos* of *Yehallelucha*, then recites *Nishmas Kol Chai*, and concludes with *Yishtabach* ending in *melech chei ha'olamim*. On this reading, two *berachos* are recited at the conclusion — one at the end of *Hallel HaMitzri* and one at the end of *Nishmas*. Other *rishonim* disagree, holding that *Birchat Hashir* is a single blessing and the debate is between the two positions: we rule like Rabbi Yochanan, reciting *Nishmas* and ending with *Yishtabach*, and do not recite *Yehallelucha* as a separate concluding *beracha* for *Hallel*.

### Nuschaot Variance

The practical division between *Ashkenaz* and *Sefard* follows from these positions. *Ashkenazim* recite *Yehallelucha* before *Hallel HaGadol* — integrating the *Hallel* conclusion there — then recite *Nishmas* and conclude with *Yishtabach* as the single *Birchat Hashir*. *Sefardim* recite *Nishmas* first and follow it with the *Yehallelucha* passage, concluding with *melech mehullal batishbachos* as the *Birchat Hashir*.

### Minhag Variance

The result is genuine confusion in practice. At any *seder* table, people may find that their *Haggadot* direct them differently at this point. This reflects multiple layered *minhagim*, traceable directly to the terseness of the *gemara* and the divergent rulings of the *rishonim*. The presentation in the *Haggadah* under study helpfully distinguishes the two *nuschaot*: it notes that *Ashkenazim* say *Yehallelucha* at the first juncture (before *Hallel HaGadol*), while *Sefardim* say it at the later juncture after *Nishmas*.

---

## Hallel HaGadol

### Second Hallel

The *mishnah* and *gemara* introduce a second *Hallel* said on *leil ha-seder* after completing *Hallel HaMitzri* — *Hallel HaGadol*, the great *Hallel*, which is the passage *Hodu l'Hashem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo* that we say on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* within *Pesukei D'Zimra*.

### Alt Texts

*Divrei Rabbi Tarfon*: *Hallel HaGadol* begins from *Hodu l'Hashem ki tov*. *V'yesh omrim*: there is a view that it is *Hashem ro'i lo echsar*, the opening of *Mizmor L'David*. The *Rashbam* explains this alternative as an attempt to connect the theme of *Birkat Hamazon* — God's provision, *ta'aroch l'fanai shulchan* — to the *Hallel*, creating a bridge from the meal into praise.

### Extent Views

*Meheichan Hallel HaGadol?* — from where does *Hallel HaGadol* begin and how far does it extend? *Rav Yehuda omer*: from *Hodu* through to *Naharot Bavel* — the entirety of the *Hodu* chapter concluding with the following chapter. *Rabbi Yochanan omer*: from *Shir HaMa'alot*, two *prakim* earlier, through to *Naharot Bavel*. *Rav Acha bar Yaakov omer*: from the verse *ki Yaakov bachar lo Yah*, approximately half a *perek* before the *Hodu* chapter, through to *Naharot Bavel*. This debate directly maps onto the current liturgical practice: on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* in *Pesukei D'Zimra* we lead into *Hodu l'Hashem ki tov* with the preceding *perek* — which contains *ki Yaakov bachar lo Yah* — but do not begin from *Shir HaMa'alot*, which would be two *prakim* back. Interestingly, *Sefardim* do say *Shir HaMa'alot* at this point, reflecting Rabbi Yochanan's view.

### Greatness Name

*Lama nikra shemo Hallel HaGadol?* — why is it called the great *Hallel*? *Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: because *mipnei shehakadosh baruch hu yoshev berumo shel olam umachalek mezonot lechol beriyotav* — God dwells at the heights of the world and yet distributes sustenance to all creatures. This is expressed in the verse *noten lechem lechol basar ki le'olam chasdo* — He gives bread to all flesh, for His lovingkindness endures forever. While *Hallel HaMitzri* focuses on dramatic supernatural salvation, *Hallel HaGadol* encompasses God as creator, sustainer, and provider — the God of nature and of daily provision, *noten lechem lechol basar* alongside *vayotzi Yisrael mitocham*.

### 26 Times

*Amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: the *Hodu* passage contains twenty-six *haduos* — twenty-six repetitions of the refrain — corresponding to the twenty-six generations from creation until *matan Torah* at *Har Sinai*. During all those generations there was no *Torah* in the world, yet *vezanam bechasdo* — God sustained them through His *chesed*. *Noten lechem lechol basar ki le'olam chasdo* — He provided for all creatures even when they did not merit it through *Torah*. This is the extraordinary *chesed* that *Hallel HaGadol* celebrates: ongoing divine provision even before the covenant of *Torah* was established.

### Provision Theme

The fundamental distinction between the two *Hallels* is this: *Hallel HaMitzri* is about miraculous salvation — the supernatural, the dramatic, the sudden reversal of fate. *Hallel HaGadol* is about ongoing provision and the God of nature who quietly sustains all creation. On *Yamim Tovim*, when we recite formal *Hallel*, we focus on the miraculous and salvific dimension. In the *Pesukei D'Zimra* of every *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, we celebrate God as creator and sustainer. On *leil ha-seder*, in a way that is uniquely powerful, we bridge both dimensions: we begin with *Hallel HaMitzri*, the miraculous, and conclude with *Hallel HaGadol*, the providential — a transition from the drama of *yetziat Mitzrayim* into the ongoing *chesed* of daily life.

---

## Divine Goodness

### Debt Repayment

*Amar Rav Chisda*: what is meant by *Hodu l'Hashem ki tov*? The verse declares God good because of the manner in which God collects what is owed to Him. *Hodu lo shegoveh chovato shel adam betovato* — give thanks to God that He collects a person's debt using what God Himself has given. That is: when a person incurs a spiritual debt and God must collect it, He takes back only something He Himself previously bestowed.

### Mercy Examples

The *gemara* elaborates: if a wealthy person sins, God takes the ox — not the person himself. *De'ani besayo* — if a poor person, the sheep. *Yatom bebetzato* — an orphan, even more impoverished, loses the egg he was to eat for breakfast. *Almana betarnagoltah* — a widow loses her chicken. In every case, what God takes back is something God had given. He does not inflict suffering directly upon the person's body or life; He reclaims only from His own prior gifts.

### Chesed Reinterpret

What is remarkable about this teaching is the interpretive move it makes under conditions of hardship. *Chazal* lived through periods of persecution and deprivation, and the plain reading of *ki l'olam chasdo* — His *chesed* endures forever — could seem to mock reality. Yet this *gemara* does not acknowledge the problem. It does not say "and despite appearances, God is good." Instead, it simply reinterprets the situation: *baruch Hashem*, you know what? The fact that all that happened was God took away my wealth rather than harming me personally — that itself is the *chesed*. You find the *chesed* precisely where it is least visible, and the affirmation is all the more powerful for being arrived at through interpretation rather than through protest.

### Chazal Affirm

This is the approach of *Chazal* throughout: a constant, unwavering affirmation of God's *chesed* even within visible suffering, not by denying the suffering but by finding, through careful reading of the situation, the dimension in which God's goodness is operating. There is also the complementary framework, of course — that debts paid in *Olam Hazeh* need not be settled in *Olam Haba* — but that is not what this *gemara* is saying. What it is doing is something more striking: it reaffirms *chesed* through the act of interpretation itself.

---

## Parnassa Challenge

### Twice Difficulty

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *kashe mezonotav shel adam kiflayim kiyoledah* — the challenges of earning a livelihood are twice as difficult as childbirth. This is a man making the comparison, and the derivation is textual: by childbirth the *Torah* says *be'etzev teldi vanim* — with *etzev*, singular. Regarding sustenance it says *be'itzavon*, which carries the force of a more intensive or plural form, hence doubly difficult.

### Harder Geula

*Ve'amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *kashe mezonotav shel adam yoter min hageulah* — earning a livelihood is harder — that is, more miraculous, more requiring of divine involvement — than redemption itself. This is not a complaint. It is rather the recognition that the ongoing miracle of *parnassah* is greater than the miracle of *geulah*.

### Angel vs. God

The textual proof is elegant: regarding redemption, the *Torah* says *hamalach hagoel oti mikol ra* — the angel who redeems me from all evil. God sends an angel to accomplish redemption — *malach dealma*, just an angel. But regarding sustenance, the verse says *haElokim haro'eh oti* — God Himself shepherds me, God Himself is the one who ensures my provision. This is the *Mizmor l'David Hashem ro'i lo echsar* — God my shepherd, I shall not lack. The implications are striking: the sustained miracle of daily *parnassah* requires God's direct involvement in a way that even redemption from Egypt did not.

### Bodily Functions

*Amar Rav Elazar ben Azaryah*: *kashim nekavav shel adam keyom hamitah uvekri'at Yam Suf* — the functioning of a person's bodily orifices is as weighty a matter as the day of death and as the splitting of *Yam Suf*. The verse *miher tzo'eh lehipateach* — quickly will the bound one open — is immediately followed by *rogeh hayam vayehemu galav* — God stirs the sea and its waves roar. The juxtaposition evokes *Kri'at Yam Suf*. The Chasam Sofer drew the analogy explicitly: the bodily functions that sustain human life are as miraculous as the splitting of the sea — both are daily demonstrations of divine power that we habitually take for granted.

---

## Human Dignity

### Labor Curse

*Amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: when God said to Adam *kotz vedardar tatzmiach lach* — the ground will bring forth thorns and thistles — Adam's eyes filled with tears. *Amar lefanav*: Master of the Universe, shall I and my donkey eat from the same trough? Are we the same, both eating whatever grows from the ground? Once God added *beze'at apecha tochal lechem* — by the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread — *nitkarerah da'ato* — his mind settled. He understood: yes, I must labor, but the labor transforms the raw earth into *lechem* — into bread — something no animal can do. That transformation is the marker of human distinctiveness. The hard work is not a punishment so much as the price of a higher status.

### Dignity Work

*Amar Resh Lakish*: *ashreinu im amadnu barishonah* — it would have been better for us if we had remained in that first state, eating the grass of the field without labor. That would have been easier. The *gezeirat* of labor is hard. There is a real question here: is the dignity worth the effort?

### Animal vs. Human

*Ve'adayin lo paltinan minah* — and we have not fully escaped from the category of animals, says Resh Lakish. *Dekachlinan ishvei dedabra* — we still eat the grass of the field, meaning we still eat vegetables — which prompts the observation, familiar to anyone who has heard bread called "real food" and salad dismissed as "rabbit food," that the transformation from purely natural consumption to fully cultivated human food is never quite complete. The point is philosophical: human dignity requires effort and aspiration, not ease. The choice is between eating like an animal without effort and eating like a human being through toil — and even then, the boundary is never absolute.

### Seder Transition

This teaching functions as a powerful bridge at the close of *leil ha-seder*. The *seder* is *Leil HaSeder* — a fantasy of freedom, of *haseivah* and fine wine, of *afilu ani shebe-Yisrael lo yifchatu lo me'arba kosot* — even the poorest Jew must have four cups. But the *gemara* here acknowledges the reality: when we leave that fantasy and step back into ordinary life, it is simply hard to put food on the table. The miracle of daily *parnassah* — *kashe mikri'at Yam Suf* — is itself a continuation of the *geulah*. We carry *yetziat Mitzrayim* not only in the *seder* night but in the daily struggle, and seeing God's hand in that struggle is precisely what *Hallel HaGadol* calls us to do.

---

## Aggadic Excursus

### Holiday Honor

*Amar Rav Shishi mishmeih de-Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah*: anyone who demeans the *mo'adot* — and some understand this to refer specifically to *Chol HaMoed* — is as if he worships idols. The *gemara* derives this from the juxtaposition in the *Torah*: *elohei masechah lo ta'aseh lach* — do not make molten gods for yourself — is immediately followed by *et chag hamatzot tishmor* — you shall observe the festival of *matzos*. The adjacency implies equivalence in severity: denigrating the sanctity of the festival is akin to the gravest form of religious transgression.

### Lashon Hara

In the same context, *ve'amar Rav Sheshet mishum Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah*: anyone who speaks *lashon hara*, and anyone who accepts *lashon hara*, and anyone who testifies falsely against another, deserves to be thrown to the dogs — *ra'uy lehashlicho laklavim*. The verse by the *neveilah* says *lakelev tashlichun oto* — throw it to the dog — and is immediately followed by *lo tisa shema shav* — do not carry a false report. Reading *lo tashi* — do not cause one to arise — the *gemara* derives that one must not generate false reports, not merely receive them.

---

## Why HaMitzri

### Both Contain

The *gemara* poses the question: given that *Hallel HaGadol* contains references to both *Yetzias Mitzrayim* and *Kri'at Yam Suf*, why do we say *Hallel HaMitzri* — the standard *Hallel* — on *Yamim Tovim*? Why not simply say *Hallel HaGadol*?

### Five Three

*Tanu Rabbanan*: the two *Hallels* are distinguished by their thematic content. *Hallel HaMitzri* contains five subjects that *Hallel HaGadol* does not include in the same way, while *Hallel HaGadol* contains three subjects of its own. The five of *Hallel HaMitzri* are what make it specifically appropriate for *Yamim Tovim*.

### Five Topics

The five topics of *Hallel HaMitzri* are: *yetziat Mitzrayim*, the exodus; *kri'at Yam Suf*, the splitting of the sea; *matan Torah*, the giving of the *Torah*; *techiyat hameitim*, resurrection of the dead; and *chevlo shel Moshiach*, the birth pangs of the messianic era.

### Topic Sources

*Yetziat Mitzrayim dechtiv*: *betzet Yisrael mi-Mitzrayim* — as Israel went out from Egypt. *Kri'at Yam Suf*: *hayam ra'ah vayanos* — the sea saw and fled. *Matan Torah*: *he-harim rakedu che-eilim* — the mountains danced like rams, which the *midrash* understands as the trembling of *Har Sinai*. *Techiyat hameitim*: *ethalech lifnei Hashem be'artzot hachayim* — I will walk before God in the lands of the living, that is, in the world where there is only life, referring to resurrection. *Chevlo shel Moshiach dechtiv*: *lo lanu Hashem lo lanu* — not to us, O God, not to us — which refers to a period of suffering and subjugation. *Va'amar Rav Yochanan*: *lo lanu Hashem lo lanu* — this refers to the subjugation of the nations, from which Israel will ultimately be freed at the time of redemption. *Ika d'amri*: Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to the war of Gog and Magog, the final conflict preceding the coming of *Moshiach*.

### Context Diff

The underlying difference between the two *Hallels*, then, is not simply a list of topics but a fundamental difference in character. *Hallel HaMitzri* is the *Hallel* of the miraculous and salvific: dramatic, supernatural, spanning from Egypt through the end of days. *Hallel HaGadol* is the *Hallel* of nature and ongoing providence: God as the sustainer of all creatures, the provider of daily bread. On *Yamim Tovim* we want the *Hallel* that speaks to the miraculous dimension; in *Pesukei D'Zimra* of every *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* we want the *Hallel* that speaks to creation and provision. On *leil ha-seder*, we recite both — beginning with the miraculous and concluding with the providential.

---

## Lo Lanu Prayer

### Lo Lanu Intro

The *gemara* has identified *lo lanu Hashem lo lanu* as referring to *chevlo shel Moshiach* — the birth pangs of the messianic era. The verse, read in this context, expresses the suffering and subjugation of the period leading up to redemption: *lo lanu* — not by our merit, not for our sake — but for the sake of God's name and truth.

### Gog Magog

An alternative reading: *lo lanu Hashem lo lanu* refers specifically to *milchemes Gog u-Magog*, the eschatological war that precedes the final redemption. On this reading, *Hallel HaMitzri* contains within it a prayer and reference to the ultimate future deliverance, making it fitting not only for *Yamim Tovim* commemorating past salvation but also as an expression of hope for future redemption.

### Righteous Saved

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak mishum*: among the additional reasons *Hallel HaMitzri* is chosen is that it contains the *milut nafshan shel tzaddikim migehinnom* — the escape of the souls of the righteous from *Gehinnom*. The verse *ana Hashem malta nafshi* — please God, save my soul — is understood as a prayer for deliverance from the fires of *Gehinnom*. *Chizkiyah amar mishum*: it contains also the *yeridatan shel tzaddikim l'kivshan haeish v'aliyasan mimenu* — the descent of the righteous into the fiery furnace and their ascent from it, referring specifically to *Chananya Mishael v'Azarya*.

### Three Youths

The passage of *lo lanu Hashem lo lanu* is then read as a three-part prayer of the three young men before their ordeal: *lo lanu* — Chananya's declaration that it is not for our sake but for Yours; *ki l'shimcha ten kavod* — Mishael's appeal to God's honor; *al chasdecha v'al amittecha* — Azarya's invocation of God's *chesed* and truth. Together they are pleading: do not allow the nations to say You have abandoned us. Their prayer is one of *bakasha*. Upon their deliverance, the prayer transforms into praise: *hallu et Hashem kol goyim* — Chananya; *shabbechu'u kol ha'umim* — Mishael; *ki gavar aleinu chasdo* — Azarya; *ve'emes Hashem l'olam halleluyah* — all three together. The movement from *bakasha* to *shevach* mirrors the arc of *Yonah* in the belly of the fish: the cry from the depths, the salvation, and then the hymn of praise.

---

## Furnace Stories

### Nimrod Story

*Darsha Rav bar Shimon haShiloni*: when the wicked Nimrod cast Avraham our father into the fiery furnace, Gabriel said before God: *Ribbono shel olam*, let me go down and cool the fire and save this righteous one from the furnace.

### Singular Save

God replied to Gabriel: *ani yachid be'olami v'hu yachid be'olamo* — I am singular in My world, and he is the singular one in his world who believes in Me. We have a uniquely individual relationship, the one and only God with the one and only believer. *Na'eh l'yachid lehatzil et hayachid* — it is fitting for the Singular One to save the singular one. God Himself, not an angel, would save Avraham.

### Three Saved

Yet, *velifi shehakadosh baruch hu eino mekape'ach sechar kol biryah* — because God does not withhold the reward owed to any creature — Gabriel's offer was not dismissed without consequence. God said to him: *tizkeh v'atzil sheloshah mibnei banav* — you will merit to save three of his descendants. And those three were *Chananya Mishael v'Azarya*.

### Furnace Miracle

*Besha'ah shehipil Nevuchadnezzar harasha et Chananya Mishael v'Azarya l'soch kivshan haeish* — when Nevuchadnezzar cast them into the furnace — *amar Yurkamo sar habarad lifnei Hakadosh Baruch Hu*: Yurkamo, the angelic minister of frost and hail, came before God and said: Master of the Universe, let me descend and cool the furnace and save these righteous ones. Gabriel interjected: *ein gevuraso shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu bekach* — God's power is not demonstrated in that way. *Atah sar barad* — you are the minister of frost; that a frost angel can cool a fire is no great demonstration of divine might.

### Double Miracle

*Ela ani sar shel esh* — I am the minister of fire. *Eired v'akrir mibifnim v'akdiach mibachutz* — I will descend and cool from within, and heat from without, so that those inside the furnace will be saved while those surrounding it — the Babylonian soldiers who had stoked it — will be consumed. This is exactly what the story in Daniel records. *V'na'aseh nes betoch nes* — a miracle within a miracle: the same fire that burned hotter on the outside was cooling on the inside. The *gemara* adds, with a touch of humor: it is like asking of a thermos — it keeps cold things cold and hot things hot, but how does it know?

### Promise Fulfil

*B'otah sha'ah patach Gavriel v'amar*: at that moment Gabriel opened with the words *ve'emes Hashem l'olam* — the truth of God endures forever. God had promised Gabriel an opportunity to save the descendants of Avraham. Here was that moment. The proclamation *ve'emes Hashem l'olam* is Gabriel's affirmation that God fulfills His promises — that the *emet* of the divine word is not merely spoken but enacted across generations, from Nimrod's furnace to the furnace of Nevuchadnezzar, from Avraham to *Chananya Mishael v'Azarya*.

---

---

# Pesachim 119

## Hallel & Red Sea

### Hallel Intro

The daf under discussion is 119b. We pick up several lines into the page where the Gemara is expounding various *pesukim* from the *hallel*. The verse in question is *ve'emes Hashem le'olam haleluyah* — "God's truth endures forever, Halleluyah." We had already established in the preceding discussion that this verse was said by Gavriel when he was granted the right to save Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah. Now the Gemara introduces a new voice: *dagim shebayam amruha* — the fish of the sea said it — and connects the verse to the story of *yetziat Mitzrayim*.

### Fish & Exodus

The Gemara cites a teaching of Rav Huna: *Yisrael she-be'oto hador mikatney amanah hayu* — the Jewish people of that generation were of weak and small faith. This is elaborated by Rabba bar Mari, who expounds the verse in Tehillim, *vayamru al yam beyam Suf* — they rebelled against God at the *Yam Suf*. The teaching is that even at the very moment the sea was splitting, the *Bnei Yisrael* expressed doubt. They said to Moshe: just as we are coming up on one side, perhaps the Egyptians have found another path through the sea and are coming up on the other side.

### Angel & Kishon

In response to this crisis of faith, God said to the *sar shel yam* — the angel appointed over the sea — *pelot otam leyabashah*: spit out the Egyptians onto dry land, so that Israel could see that they had truly drowned. The angel of the sea replied: *Ribbono Shel Olam, klum yesh eved shenoten lerabo matanah vechozer venotel heimenah?* Is there ever a slave to whom a master gives a gift and then demands it back? You gave me all these Egyptians as food for the fish of the sea — you want me to return them?

God responded: *efra lecha echad umchetza shebahen* — I will pay you back one and a half times this in the future. The angel countered: *Ribbono Shel Olam, yesh eved shetoveh et rabo?* How could a slave ever make a claim against his master? I cannot request payment from You. God then offered a solution: *Nachal Kishon yihiyeh li arev* — the *Nachal Kishon* will serve as my guarantor. You will not need to demand it from Me; you can demand it from the *Nachal Kishon*, who will be held responsible.

Immediately, the angel of the sea complied and cast the Egyptians onto the dry land. *Uba'u Yisrael vera'u otam* — the *Bnei Yisrael* came and saw them, as it says: *vayar Yisrael et Mitzrayim met al sfat hayam* — Israel saw Egypt dead on the shore of the sea.

### Sisra Defeat

The Gemara then asks: *mai echad umchetza shebahen?* — what in fact was this promised payment of one and a half times? The answer involves a striking comparison. By Pharaoh it is written *shesh me'ot rechev bachur* — six hundred chosen chariots. By Sisra, it is written *tesha me'ot rechev barzel* — nine hundred iron chariots. Nine hundred is precisely one and a half times six hundred.

The fulfillment of the guarantee occurred as follows. When Sisra came to war against Israel, he attacked with his iron spears and weapons. God caused the stars to deviate from their orbits and come close to the earth to burn up Sisra's forces, as it says in *Shirat Devorah*: *min hashamayim nilchamu hakochavim* — from the heavens the stars fought against them. The heat made the iron weapons of Sisra's armies burning hot, so they ran to cool themselves in *Nachal Kishon*. At that moment, God said to *Nachal Kishon*: *lech vehashev ervonecha* — go and pay back your surety. *Miyad garafam Nachal Kishon vehishpicham layam* — immediately, *Nachal Kishon* swept them up and cast them into the sea, as it says: *Nachal Kishon garafam Nachal Kedumim* — the *Nachal Kishon* swept them away, the *nachal* of ancient times. *Mai Nachal Kedumim?* — *Nachal shenasa arev mi-kedem* — it had long ago been made the guarantor.

At that moment, *patchu dagim shel yam v'amru ve'emes Hashem le'olam* — the fish of the sea opened their mouths and declared: God's truth endures forever. God keeps His promises — not only to angels and to Israel, but even to the fish. The original promise was really made to the *sar shel yam*, but the fish received the fulfillment. The verse was thus said by the fish.

---

## Divine Response

### Akeres Habayis

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish turns to another verse from the *hallel*: *moshivi akeres habayis em habanim smeicha haleluyah* — He who causes the barren woman of the house to dwell as a joyful mother of children, Halleluyah. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains that *Kneses Yisrael* said to God: *Ribbono Shel Olam, smuni vanayich kachulda zu hadara be-ikrei habatim* — your children have made me like a weasel that dwells in the crevices of walls. On this reading, *akeres habayis* refers not to a barren woman but to the crevices of a house, and the *Rashbam* explains that *Kneses Yisrael* is saying: through their sins, they have caused me to become lowly, like a weasel hiding in the cracks. The second half of the verse — *em habanim smeicha* — reflects the reversal that comes with redemption. It may seem a curious choice of metaphor over the more obvious image of a barren woman; nonetheless, this is how the *Rashbam* reads the verse.

A further observation is worth making here. The *Rashbam* explains *smuni vanayich* — your children have made me thus — as referring to *hazekeinim vehachashuvim shebahem*, the elders and the distinguished ones among them, understanding *Kneses Yisrael* as the honorable leadership. In Kabbalistic thought, however, *Kneses Yisrael* refers to something metaphysical — almost an emanation of the divine that represents the Jewish people — rather than simply the physical nation. This accounts for the striking feature of the verse, where *Kneses Yisrael* appears as a distinct entity in conversation with God.

### Angels & Direct Action

A student raised a pointed question in connection with the previous aggadah about the *sar shel yam*: do we not say on *Shevi'i shel Pesach* — the seventh day of Pesach — *ani velo malach, ani velo acher*, that God acted alone at the *Keri'at Yam Suf* and not through any angel? The response here is nuanced. Even granting the principle of *ani velo malach*, it applies most directly to the *makkas bechoros* and the *yetziah* itself. The passage also says in that context *velo yiten hamashchis lavo el bateichem lingof* — and He will not allow the destroyer to enter your homes — which implies at least some engagement with the idea of an intermediary force, however God directed it. In the current story, the involvement of the *sar shel yam* concerns a secondary matter — having the Egyptians' bodies cast to the shore — not the splitting of the sea itself. Still, the question is well-taken, and the *Midrash* generally emphasizes *ani hu velo acher*, meaning there are indeed counter-voices within the *midrashim* and even within certain *pesukim*.

More broadly, the graphic and almost theatrical character of these *midrashim* — where angels bargain with God, where God makes promises and pays them back, where the *Nachal Kishon* becomes a legal guarantor — is difficult to assimilate into a comfortable theology. These stories have great power to seize the imagination, and in rabbinic literature this entire world of angelic personalities and divine negotiations is elaborated at length. In *Tanakh* itself, angels appear as part of a divine retinue that keeps its distance from the human drama — as in Yechezkel's visions or in the stories of the angels visiting Avraham. The only place in *Tanakh* where something like a personal discussion occurs in the divine presence is in Iyov, where the *Satan* comes before God to discuss Iyov's worthiness. In rabbinic literature, however, this dimension expands dramatically.

### Ahavti Ki Yishma

Rava offers an exposition of another *hallel* verse: *ahavti ki yishma Hashem et koli tachanunai* — I have loved that God has heard the voice of my supplication. Rava reads this as *Kneses Yisrael* speaking before God: *Ribbono Shel Olam, ematai ani ahuva lefanecha? Bishaa shetishma kol tachanunai* — when am I beloved to You? When You hear my supplication. Rather than reading *ahavti* simply as "I have loved," the *derasha* reads it in a passive or relational sense: I am beloved when You hear me. The moment of being heard is both the demonstration and the creation of the beloved relationship.

The following verse, *dalosi veli yehoshia* — I was poor and God saved me — is similarly read as *Kneses Yisrael* speaking to God: *Ribbono Shel Olam, af al pi shedala ani bemitzvot, lecha ani* — even though I may be poor in *mitzvot*, I belong to You. *Veli na'eh lehoshia* — it is fitting for You to save me. The appeal here is not based on merit but on relationship. The people say: not because of my *mitzvot*, not because I deserve it, but because of Your love and our unique bond — because I am true to You — save me.

---

## Rabbi Yishmael Teachings

### Nations Praise God

Rav Kahana relates that when Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi took ill, Rebbi sent to him a request: *emor lanu shenayim o shelosha devarim she'amarta lanu mishum avicha* — tell us two or three things that you have reported in your father's name, perhaps fearing these teachings would be lost. The *Rashbam* notes with interest that in multiple places in *Shas* we find this scenario of Rebbi asking Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi during illness to share his father's teachings, and that the answers given are not always the same. He suggests two possibilities: either Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi fell ill many times and each time Rebbi came to him received different teachings; or Rabbi Yishmael gave all of these teachings at one time, and the *Gemara* distributed them to different tractates, each in its appropriate thematic context.

Rabbi Yishmael relays his father Rabbi Yosi's interpretation of the verse *halelu et Hashem kol goyim shabechuhu kol ha'ummim* — praise God, all nations, laud Him, all peoples. The question is sharp: *umot ha'olam mai avidtaihu* — why would the nations be the ones praising God? Particularly in light of the verse's ending: *ki gavar aleinu chasdo* — for His kindness has been mighty *upon us*. The interpretation offered is: the nations should praise God for the wonders and mighty acts He has done *for them*, all the wonders of creation and the natural world. And if the nations who receive general providence should praise God, *kol sheken anu* — how much more so we, for whom God's special relationship and *chesed* has been particularly mighty.

### Future Gifts

Rabbi Yishmael then shares his father's teaching about the future: *atida Mitzrayim shetavi doron leMashiach* — in the future, at the end of days, Egypt will bring gifts to Mashiach. Mashiach will initially reason that he should not accept from them. But God will say: *kabel mehem* — accept it from them. *Achsanya asu levanai beMitzrayim* — they were a host to My children in Egypt. Even with all the enslavement, they did house them in the land. Immediately, *vaye'etayu chashmanim mini Mitzrayim* — the nobles of Egypt came forward.

Upon seeing Egypt's gifts accepted, Kush made a *kal vachomer* to itself: if Egypt, who enslaved Israel, will have their gifts accepted, how much more so I, who never enslaved them, will surely have my gifts accepted as well. God says: accept it. *Miyad Kush taritz yadav l'Elohim* — immediately Kush stretched its hands toward God.

Then Rome made its own *kal vachomer*: if these nations whose gifts are accepted, *anu she'anu acheihem* — we who are their brethren — the *Gemara* associating Rome with Eisav — how much more so should our gifts be accepted? Here, however, the response changes entirely.

### Rome Rejection

God says to Gavriel — the same Gavriel who appeared earlier in the daf — *ga'ar chayat kaneh* — rebuke, roar at the beast of the reed. Gavriel is to reject Rome's gift and *keneh lecha edah* — acquire for yourself the congregation of Israel. Rome is too evil to deserve acceptance.

An alternative reading of *ga'ar chayat kaneh* — *she-dara bein hakanim* — identifies this beast as the one that dwells among the reeds, evoking the verse *yechasmenah chazir miya'ar* — the wild boar of the forest will ravage her. This is the familiar association of Rome and Edom with the pig. The pig, of course, is the one non-kosher animal that possesses split hooves — it displays an outward sign of *kashrut* while being inwardly *treif*. Archaeologically, this association runs deep: in excavations of settlements from the First Temple period, one of the ways scholars identify Jewish versus non-Jewish villages is the complete absence of pig bones in certain sites, even where other signs of religious compromise are found.

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ga'ar be-chaya she-kol ma'aseha nichtavin be-kulmos echad* — rebuke the beast all of whose deeds are written with a single reed, meaning Rome always acts destructively against Israel and never otherwise. Every entry in its ledger is one of harm.

This is a striking contrast within the *aggadah*. Egypt, despite all the enslavement and the drowning of children in the Nile, is ultimately given credit for hosting Israel and its gifts are accepted in messianic times. Kush, which never persecuted Israel at all, is certainly included. But Rome is rejected absolutely. One might ask whether this reflects the sheer severity of Roman persecution — the Herodian persecutions, the destructions, the martyrdoms — or whether it reflects the lack of historical distance, since the *Amoraim* were still living under Roman authority. The Egyptians could be viewed with more equanimity precisely because their domination was centuries past. Whatever the reason, it is particularly striking in the context of this tractate, where we have seen throughout that aspects of the *seder* itself are consciously modeled on the banqueting customs of wealthy Romans — the reclining, the wine — even as this deep resentment and unwillingness to extend any forgiveness to Rome simultaneously runs through the discussion.

---

## Wealth & Exile

### Harugei Malchus

The Gemara continues its exposition of *pesukim* from the same *perek* of Tehillim. The verse *adat abbirim be-eglei amim* — the congregation of mighty ones among the calves of the nations — is read as a reference to the *harugei malchus*, the great martyrs killed by the ruling power. *She-shachtu abbirim ke-agalim she-ein lahem ba'alim* — they slaughtered the mighty ones like calves that had no owners, like ownerless animals, like they were nothing.

*Mitrapes be-ratzei chesev* — the *Rashbam* understands this as a reference to the practice of extending one's hand to receive money, suggesting that the oppressors would take bribes with promises of waiving their edicts, and then *ve'ein osim ratzon ba'alim* — they would not follow through and would proceed with their persecutions anyway.

### Pizar Amim

The verse *pizer amim keravot yechpatzu* — He scattered the peoples who desire battles — prompts the question: *mi garam lahem l'Yisrael she-yispazru l'vein umot ha'olam* — who caused Israel to be scattered throughout the nations of the world? *Keravot she-hayu chafetzim bahem* — their desire for *keravot*. One reading understands *keravot* as closeness: their desire to assimilate, to be close to the nations and to be like them, ultimately led to the loss of their distinct identity and to exile. A second reading, offered by the *Maharsha*, takes *karva* to mean war: Israel was too eager for military confrontation. In the time of the First Temple they refused to submit to Babylonian authority, and in the time of the Second Temple they refused to submit to Rome, and their insistence on going to war brought about their dispersion. The *Maharsha* acknowledges this is not the typical formulation of *Chazal*, which usually focuses on specific sins as causes of exile. But it is a notably provocative reading — and a historically grounded one — suggesting that had Israel been more willing to accept the authority of the ruling powers, they might have maintained their presence in the Land.

### Rome's Wealth

Continuing with his father Rabbi Yosi's teachings, Rabbi Yishmael reports: *tlas mei'ah v'shishim v'chamisha shvakim be-krach gadol shel Romi* — there were 365 marketplaces in the great metropolis of Rome. Each marketplace contained 365 castles, each castle had 365 stories, and each story contained enough grain to sustain the entire world. Rome was effectively hoarding all the world's sustenance.

Rabbi Shimon Berabi said to Rebbi — and some versions attribute it to Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi — *halalu l'man* — all this wealth, for whom is it ultimately stored? The answer: *lecha ul'chavercha ul'chavrosayich* — for you and your friends, meaning the people who occupy themselves with *Torah*. As it says: *sachrah ve-esnanah kodesh l'Hashem lo ye'atzer ve-lo yeichasen ki l'yoshvim lifnei Hashem yihyeh* — its hire and its wealth will be sanctified to God, it will not be stored up nor kept in treasure, for it will belong to those who dwell before God. All the grain and gold and silver that Rome accumulated will ultimately go to *Torah* scholars. Rav Yosef clarifies: *lo ye'atzer* refers to *beit otzar*, a storehouse of grain; *lo yeichasen* refers to *beit genizah*, a treasury of gold and silver. Both will be transferred.

---

## Yoshvim Lifnei

### Knowing Seats

The Gemara asks: *mai ki la-yoshvim lifnei Hashem* — what exactly does it mean that the wealth will go to those who sit before God? Rabbi Elazar answers: *zeh hamakir mekom chaveiro be-yeshiva* — this refers to one who is so regular a presence in the *beit midrash* that he knows where every other person sits. He knows this person's place and that person's place. Beyond the simple fact of regularity, the formulation *makir mekom chaveiro* carries a deeper resonance: you know everyone else's *makom*, you respect it, you do not take it, you do not displace anyone.

An alternate version: *zeh hamikabel pnei chaveiro be-yeshiva* — one who greets and welcomes every person who enters the *beit midrash*, because you are always there, always the fixture of the place. Both formulations — knowing where everyone sits and welcoming those who arrive — emphasize not only personal diligence in learning but a sensitivity to the community and to the other people present. It is a notable balance: being *yoshvim lifnei Hashem* is described not in purely solitary terms but in terms of awareness of and relationship to others who share the *beit midrash*.

### Sitrei vs Taamei

The verse continues: *ul-michaseh atik* — and for the one who covers the Ancient of Days. *Zeh hamichaseh devarim shekissah atik yomin* — this refers to one who covers up the things that God has covered up. *Umai nihu?* — and what are these things? *Sitrei Torah* — the hidden mysteries of the Torah, the esoteric secrets of *Ma'aseh Merkavah* and the like. One fulfills this by refraining from revealing what ought not to be revealed.

An alternate version: *zeh hamigaleh devarim shekissah atik yomin* — one who reveals things that have been concealed. *Umai nihu? Ta'amei Torah* — not *sitrei Torah* but *ta'amei Torah*, the reasons and meanings of the Torah. The distinction between the two is important. *Sitrei Torah* are the deep esoteric knowledge — the powerful mysteries that are not to be widely shared. *Ta'amei Torah* are the efforts to understand the meaning of *halachot*, of narratives, of *mitzvot* — to ask what they signify, what they teach, what lies beneath the surface. This is not hidden knowledge being inappropriately uncovered; it is precisely the kind of exploration and reflection that *mefarshim*, *midrashim*, and *parsha shiurim* are all engaged in.

### Maharsha Reasons

The *Maharsha* raises a pointed question: the Gemara says elsewhere that the Torah deliberately did not reveal *ta'amei ha-mitzvot* — the reasons for the commandments — precisely because once you know the reason, you might conclude it does not apply to you. The classic example is *lo yarbeh lo nashim pen yasur levavo* — the king shall not take many wives lest his heart turn away. Shlomo reasoned that he could take many wives without his heart turning, and he stumbled. So if the Torah withholds its reasons precisely to prevent such reasoning, how can the verse here praise one who *reveals* the reasons?

The *Maharsha* offers two responses. First, perhaps *ta'amei Torah* is distinct from *ta'amei mitzvot* specifically — they are not the same category. But the second answer is particularly compelling: it is only dangerous when the *Torah* reveals the reason, because then the person treats the reason as the entire substance of the *mitzvah* and discounts the commandment when they believe the reason does not apply. But when *you* work to discover the reason, it comes with the recognition that your conclusion is ultimately speculation — you have not supplanted the divine word, you have only approximated it. You understand that at the end of the day your reasoning remains tentative. This seems a very beautiful distinction: the pursuit of reasons is not only permitted but encouraged, so long as it is accompanied by the humility to recognize that the *Torah*'s authority does not depend on your having understood the reason correctly.

---

## Rav Kahana

### Lamnatzeach

Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi expounds the verse *lamnatzeach mizmor l'David zamru* — to the *menatzeach* a psalm of David, sing. Rather than reading *lamnatzeach* in its musical sense — some sort of musical instruction — the *derasha* reads it from the root *nitzachon*, victory: *l'mi shenotzchin oto ve-sameach* — to the One whom others are victorious over, and who is happy about it. *Bo u-re'eh shelo ke-middat haKadosh Baruch Hu middat basar v'dam* — come and see that God's way is not the way of flesh and blood. When a person of flesh and blood is bested by someone, he is distraught. But *haKadosh Baruch Hu notzchin oto ve-sameach* — when God is, so to speak, bested, He is glad. As it says: *vayomer le-hashmidam lulei Moshe bechiro amad baperetz lefanav* — God wanted to destroy them, were it not that Moshe His chosen one stood in the breach before Him. Moshe fought against God's decree and was victorious, and the Torah records it approvingly — *Moshe bechiro*, His chosen one.

This connects the present passage to the earlier *aggadah* in a meaningful way. We saw the angels bargaining with God, the *sar shel yam* arguing that God owes him payment. Gavriel negotiating. Now the Gemara teaches that this is not merely a feature of the angelic realm — it is built into our relationship with God as well. *Lamnatzeach* — God wants to be challenged, God wants to be argued with, God rejoices when we stand in the breach. It translates the somewhat unfamiliar image of angels arguing in the heavenly court into a human reality: this is the kind of relationship we are meant to have.

### God's Hand

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah expounds: *ve-yedei adam mitachat kanfeihem* — and the hands of a man are under their wings, from the opening vision of Yechezkel. The word *yedei* — hands, plural — is actually written as *yado*, with a *vav*, suggesting a singular reading. Whose hand? *Yado shel haKadosh Baruch Hu* — this is God's hand, *she-perusha tachat kanfei ha-chayot* — stretched out beneath the wings of the celestial beings that surround and, in a sense, shield the divine presence from direct access. And the purpose of this outstretched hand: *k'dei l'kabel ba'alei teshuvah* — to receive those who repent, *mipnei midat ha-din* — in spite of, or against, the attribute of strict justice.

This image is striking. The angelic wings serve as a barrier — they keep the human world at a distance from the divine. Yet God stretches His hand *beneath* those wings, reaching through the barrier specifically to draw in *ba'alei teshuvah*. The theme is consistent with what has come just before: the special intimacy that God maintains with Israel, the relationship that breaks through barriers. First we saw that God wants us to argue with Him. Now we see that even the structures of the heavenly court do not prevent God from reaching out to receive those who return to Him.

---

## Wealth History

### Yosef's Wealth

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *kol kessef ve-zahav sheba-olam Yosef likto ve-hevi'o le-Mitzrayim* — all the gold and silver in the world, Yosef gathered it and brought it to Egypt. As it says: *vayelaket Yosef et kol ha-kessef ha-nimtza be-eretz Mitzrayim u-ve-eretz Kena'an*. One might think this refers only to Egypt and Canaan, but the verse also says *ve-chol ha-aretz ba'u Mitzraymah* — all the lands came to Egypt — indicating that all the world's wealth was concentrated there. When Israel left Egypt, they took it all with them: *vayenatzlu et Mitzrayim* — they stripped Egypt. *Rav Assi* reads *vayenatzlu* as related to *metzudah* — a bird trap completely emptied of its grain; Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish reads it as *metzula she-ein bah dagim* — a pond emptied of all its fish. In either case, Israel departed with the entire world's accumulated wealth.

### Empire Succession

That wealth remained in Israel's possession until the reign of Rechavam, son of Shlomo, at which point Shishak king of Egypt came and took it from Rechavam — as recorded explicitly in *Tanakh*: *vayikach et otzrot beit Hashem ve-et otzrot beit ha-melech*. The Egyptians had reclaimed what Israel had taken from them.

Then came Zerach king of Kush and took it from Shishak — this is not in *pesukim* explicitly, Rashi notes it is tradition. Then Asa waged war against Zerach king of Kush and recovered it — this is recorded in *pesukim* — and sent it to Hadardimon ben Tavrimon, king of Aram, in exchange for protection against Baasha king of Israel. The Ammonites then took it from Hadardimon ben Tavrimon. Yehoshaphat came and took it from *Bnei Amon* — we have *pesukim* about Yehoshaphat going to war against *Bnei Amon*. It remained in the hands of the Judean kings until Achaz. Sancheriv came and took it from Achaz. Chizkiyahu then recovered it after the angel wiped out Sancheriv's armies — presumably Israel looted the devastated camp and recovered the wealth. It then remained with the Judean kings until Tzidkiyahu. The Kasdim came and took it from Tzidkiyahu. The Persians took it from the Kasdim. The Greeks — Alexander and the Hellenistic empires — took it from the Persians. Rome took it from the Greeks. *Ve-adayin munach be-Romi* — and it still sits in Rome.

This historical survey provides a satisfying closure to the teaching we encountered earlier: all of Rome's accumulated wealth will ultimately go to those who sit in *yeshiva*. Since the chain of this wealth traces back through empire after empire to the original taking from Egypt — itself a taking that was prophesied — there is a sense in which the wealth was always destined to return to Israel in the end.

### Three Treasures

Rav Chama beRabbi Chanina adds: *shalosh matmoniyot hitmin Yosef be-Mitzrayim* — three treasures Yosef buried in Egypt. One was revealed to Korach — that is the source of Korach's legendary wealth. One was revealed to Antoninus ben Asveirus — a figure identified tentatively with someone in the line of Roman emperors who bore the name Antoninus, possibly associated with Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus or Antoninus Pius. And one is still hidden and reserved *l'tzadikim l'asid lavo* — for the righteous in the time to come. It is notable that the distribution is not "everything goes to Israel" but rather one third each: one portion was revealed in antiquity, one in the Roman period, and one awaits the future.

---

## Korach Wealth

### Wealth Ruin

The Gemara cites the verse *osher shamur le-va'alav le-ra'ato* — wealth held in store for its owner, to his ruin. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says: *zeh oshro shel Korach* — this is the wealth of Korach. His wealth made him haughty, led him to believe he could challenge Moshe, and ultimately brought about his destruction. And the verse *ve-et kol ha-yakum asher be-ragleihem* — all the substance that was at their feet — prompts Rabbi Elazar to observe: *zeh mamono shel adam she-ma'amido al raglov* — this is a person's money that makes him stand on his feet, that gives him his sense of dignity and standing. It was that very dignity and pride, conferred by his enormous wealth, that drove Korach's rebellion and that was ultimately swallowed up along with him.

### 300 Mules

Rabbi Levi teaches: *masa shalosh me'ot pardot levanot hayu mafteichot beit genaziv shel Korach* — the load of three hundred white mules was the keys to Korach's treasure houses. And these were not the actual treasures — just the keys. Moreover, *vechulu aklidi ve-klifi de-galda ninhu* — they were all keys and locks made of leather, which are light. Even so, three hundred white mules were needed to carry them, which gives some sense of the staggering scale of the actual treasure. We had just seen that Rome possessed 365 marketplaces each with 365 castles each with 365 stories of provisions — and yet even Korach's wealth as described here strains the imagination.

---

## Hallel Enactment

### David Stone

The Gemara returns to *pesukim* in the *hallel*. The verse *odecha Hashem ki anisani* — I will thank You because You have answered me — was said by David, presumably in some moment of divine rescue from his many troubles. The following verse, *even ma'asu ha-bonim hayesa le-rosh pinah* — the stone rejected by the builders became the cornerstone — was said by Yishai, David's father. The context is the challenge to David's very legitimacy: he was the youngest and least considered of Yishai's sons, his lineage through Rus HaMoaviya was challenged by *talmidei chachamim*, and his right to kingship was questioned. Playing on the word *bonim* — reading it as *bonayim*, builders, i.e., *talmidei chachamim* — the verse says: those who build and who rejected him became the cornerstone. The *Maharsha* elaborates the full *midrash* about David's lineage being challenged and ultimately vindicated.

### Verse Attribution

The Gemara proceeds to assign various *hallel* verses to specific speakers at specific historical moments:

*Me'eis Hashem haysa zos* — this was from God, this thing — was said by Yishai, reflecting the astonishment that the rejected youngest son would become king. *Hi niflas be-eineinu* — it is wondrous in our eyes — is in the plural and so was said by *echav*, his brothers. *Zeh hayom asa Hashem* — this is the day God has made — was said by Shmuel, presumably at the moment of David's anointing. *Anna Hashem hoshia na* — was said by *echav*, David's brothers. *Anna Hashem hatzlicha na* — was said by David himself. *Baruch haba be-shem Hashem* — was said by Yishai. *Berachnuchem mi-beis Hashem* — was said by Shmuel. *Keil Hashem va-ya'er lanu* — was said by all of them together. *Isru chag ba-avotim* — was said by Shmuel. *Eli ata ve-odeka* — was said by David. *Elokai aromemeka* — was said by all of them together.

### Hallel Drama

The Gemara does not provide the full context for each of these attributions, but what it is clearly doing is bringing a generic sequence of praise verses to life by grounding each line in a specific voice and dramatic moment — the anointing of David, his brothers' reaction, Shmuel's proclamation, the communal response. This raises the intriguing possibility that the *hallel* was not merely recited but in some sense enacted when it was said, with different people taking different parts. We saw something similar earlier in the daf with the verse *lo lanu lo lanu*, where the same kind of dramatic assignment was implied. One can imagine that at certain points the saying of *hallel* had a quasi-theatrical character, with assigned roles bringing the text alive as something more than rote recitation.

---

## Doubling Verses (III)

### Custom Doubling

The Gemara now takes up a brief *halachic* discussion drawn from a *baraita* in Sukkah. *Makom shenahagu lichpol yichpol* — in a place where the custom is to double certain verses in the *hallel*, one doubles them. *Liphshot* — where the custom is to recite them straight without doubling, one does so. *Levarech acharav yevarech* — if the custom is to make a concluding *bracha* at the end of *hallel*, one makes it. *Hakol ke-minhag ha-medinah* — everything follows the local custom. The doubling referred to here is the repetition of verses such as *odecha Hashem ki anisani* and others near the end of *hallel* that are not repeated as written in the original *pesukim* but are recited twice as a matter of *minhag*.

---

## Bracha Status

### Bracha Before

Abaye clarifies: the debate and variation in custom described above applies only to the concluding *bracha* — whether one says a *bracha* at the end of *hallel* or not varies by locale. But *aval lefanav mitzvah levarech* — before *hallel*, one must make a *bracha*, as one makes a *bracha* before every *mitzvah*. This is based on Rav Yehuda's ruling in the name of Shmuel: *kol mitzvot mevarach aleihen over la'asiyasan* — for all *mitzvot*, one recites the *bracha* before performing them.

The Gemara asks: *mai mashma d'over lishna de-akdumi hu* — how do we know that *over* means "before" rather than something else? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites the verse *vayaratz Achima'atz derech ha-kikar vaya'avor et ha-Kushi* — Achima'atz ran through the valley and passed in front of the Ethiopian, meaning *avor* indicates passing in front, preceding. Abaye cites *ve-hu avar lifneihem* — he passed before them. A third version cites *vaya'avor malkam lifneihem ve-Hashem be-rosham* — their king passed before them with God at their head. The image of *over la'asiyasan* is thus of the *bracha* running ahead of the act, announcing and proclaiming and giving identity to the *mitzvah* — the *bracha* precedes and, in a sense, inaugurates what follows.

---

## Doubling Verses (III)

### Rabbi Doubling

A *baraita* records: *Rebbi kofel bidvarim* — Rebbi would double certain verses. *Rebbi Elazar ben Parta mosif bidvarim* — Rabbi Elazar ben Parta would add. Abaye explains that *mosif* means he would do more doubling than Rebbi: *mosif lichpol me-odecha le-mata* — he would extend the doubling beginning from the verse *odecha Hashem ki anisani*, which precedes *Anna Hashem hoshia na*. The *Rashbam* indicates that Rebbi's doubling began only from *baruch haba be-shem Hashem*, whereas Rabbi Elazar ben Parta doubled from an earlier point in the *hallel*.

---

## Future Seudah

### Yigdal Hayeled

Rav Avira expounded — sometimes attributed in the name of Rav, sometimes in the name of Rav Assi — on the verse *vayigdal ha-yeled vayigamel* — the child grew up and was weaned. This verse, which this week's *parasha* brought back to mind, is read not only literally in the context of Yitzchak's weaning but also as an allusion to the future. *Asid haKadosh Baruch Hu la'asos seuda la-tzadikim be-yom sheyigamel chasdo le-zaro shel Yitzchak* — God will in the future make a great banquet for the righteous on the day He fulfills His *chesed* to the descendants of Yitzchak, in the era of Mashiach. Just as Avraham made a great *mishteh* upon Yitzchak's weaning, *vaya'as Avraham mishteh gadol*, God will make the ultimate *mishteh gadol* in the future.

### Disqualifications

After the righteous eat and drink at this banquet, the question arises of who should lead the *birkat ha-mazon*. The *kos shel bracha* is offered to Avraham Avinu. He declines: *eini mevarach, sheyatza mimeni Yishmael* — I will not lead the blessing, for Yishmael came from me. I do not fully represent the *kedushah* of *Klal Yisrael*.

They offer it to Yitzchak. He declines: *eini mevarach, sheyatza mimeni Eisav* — for Eisav came from me. Not that Yitzchak sinned, but in this context of messianic completeness, he does not see himself as the right representative of the whole of Israel.

They offer it to Yaakov. He declines: *eini mevarach, she-nasasi shtei achayot be-chayeihen, she-asida Torah le-osran alai* — for I married two sisters while they were both alive, which the Torah would subsequently forbid. Again, he acted without wrongdoing — the Torah had not yet been given — but in the ultimate moment, he does not see himself as the complete representative.

They offer it to Moshe. He declines: *eini mevarach, shelo zachisi le-hikanes le-Eretz Yisrael, lo be-chayai ve-lo be-mosi* — for I did not merit to enter the Land of Israel, neither in life nor in death. The ideal of the Jewish people is living in *Eretz Yisrael*, and Moshe represents more of a transitional stage, the period of *galus* and wilderness.

They offer it to Yehoshua. He declines: *eini mevarach, shelo zachisi le-ven* — for I had no son. When genealogies are listed it says Yehoshua bin Nun and Nun and Yehoshua, and the line does not extend further. He cannot represent the full continuity of the Jewish people.

### David Worthy

They offer it to David. He accepts without hesitation: *ani avarech ve-li na'eh le-varech* — I will lead the blessing, and it is fitting for me to do so. *Shene'emar kos yeshuot esa u-ve-shem Hashem ekra* — as the verse from *hallel* says: I will raise the cup of salvations and call upon the name of God.

David, of course, was also a flawed individual in various ways, and he did not merit to build the Temple. Yet he alone accepts the role and declares himself fitting. The reason becomes clear: if the theme of *asid lavo* is the resurgence of *malchus beit David* and the coming of the Messiah — if what we are celebrating is precisely the continuity and survival and ultimate sovereignty of the Jewish people — then David is the figure in whom all of that is concentrated. He represents the *malchus* that looks forward to messianic times, the kingship that is never wholly extinguished. Moshe didn't enter the Land, Yehoshua had no descendants, but David is the figure around whom the messianic hope is organized. In this sense, *li na'eh le-varech* — it is genuinely fitting for him.

---

## Doubling Verses (III)…

### Repetition Concern

A question was raised about whether the practice of repeating words or verses in liturgical contexts — a concern that has grown increasingly prominent in certain communities with regard to chazzanim who repeat words in *tefillah* — connects to this discussion of doubling in *hallel*. This is indeed an undercurrent of the present passage. Whether the concern rises to a strictly *halachic* level is debated, and context matters significantly: repeating in the context of *Shemoneh Esrei*, where one is in the formal structure of a *bracha*, is a different matter from repetition in other settings. The fact that the Gemara here must give explicit license for the doubling of verses suggests that in general, such repetition requires justification. There is also a distinction between repeating an entire verse — which is what the *hallel* custom involves — and repeating individual words within a verse as a melodic device, though both have generated literature. The broader point stands: the Gemara's need to grant permission for doubling implies that doubling is not the default and should be approached with care.

---

## Bracha Status (II)

### Hallel Status

The discussion of the *bracha* before *hallel* actually conceals a non-trivial conceptual question. Abaye states as a matter of course that of course one makes a *bracha* before *hallel*, since one makes a *bracha* before every *mitzvah*. But this is not as obvious as it sounds.

Consider *keri'at Shema*: we say *Shema* every day in *davening*, and it is certainly a *mitzvah*, yet we do not say *asher kideshanu be-mitzvosav ve-tzivanu al keri'at Shema*. Instead we have *birkot keri'at Shema* — *Yotzer ha-Me'orot* and *Ahavat Olam* — which are not *birkat ha-mitzvah* in the classic sense but rather *brachos* that expand upon and draw out the themes of *Shema* as part of *tefillah*. They envelop *Shema* as part of the flow of prayer, rather than introducing it as a distinct commandment.

*Hallel* occupies an analogous position. It is said in the context of *tefillah* and has the character of prayer — it is praise addressed to God, not an action performed upon an object. The *chidush* — the genuine innovation — of saying *asher kideshanu be-mitzvosav ve-tzivanu al keri'at ha-hallel* is that it reconstitutes *hallel* as a *ma'aseh mitzvah*, a commandment-act, rather than treating it as an expansion of prayer. One might have thought, on the contrary, that since *hallel* is inherently *tefillah* in character, it would not receive a *birkat ha-mitzvah* at all, just as *Shema* does not receive one in the standard morning liturgy.

There is a further wrinkle: why do we not say a *birkat ha-mitzvah* before *birkat ha-mazon*? After all, benching is a *mitzvah* — yet we simply bench, without first saying *asher kideshanu be-mitzvosav ve-tzivanu le-varech al ha-mazon*. Because *birkat ha-mazon* is itself a *bracha*, a prayer, and once something is itself a prayer one does not generally introduce it with a separate *birkat ha-mitzvah*. This makes the practice with *hallel* all the more distinctive: here we do introduce a prayer with a *birkat ha-mitzvah*, making it simultaneously an act of praise and a formal commandment. The *Tosafos* understand the concluding *bracha* of *hallel* — recited according to our custom — as resolving this tension: the concluding *bracha* transforms the whole of *hallel* into an extended *bracha* structure, with the *bracha* of *asher kideshanu* at the opening and the concluding *bracha* at the close forming a unified framework. That is our custom, but it is worth appreciating that the conceptual question it answers is a genuine one.

---

## Afikoman Mishnah

### Mishnah Context

The Mishnah states: *ein maftirin achar ha-Pesach afikoman* — one does not conclude after the *Pesach* with an *afikoman*. This is identified as the answer to the *ben chacham* — the wise son — who asks about the statutes and practices of this night.

Before turning to the definition of *afikoman*, it is worth pausing on the framing of the Mishnah. The phrase *achar ha-Pesach* — after the *Pesach* — presupposes that one is eating a *korban Pesach*. This raises the broader question of whether this *perek* is speaking about *zman ha-mikdash* — the time of the Temple — or about post-Temple practice. The first Mishnah in the *perek* had said *u-va-mikdash hayu mevi'in lefanav gufo shel pesach*, which indicated that that particular Mishnah distinguished between Temple times and post-Temple practice.
