Several of the four questions referred to *halailah hazeh kulo tzali* — tonight everything is roasted — which could refer either to Temple times or to a post-Temple *minhag* to eat only roasted meat in commemoration. The present Mishnah, however, comes with no such distinction and appears to take for granted the context of *zman ha-mikdash*.

This impression is strengthened by looking at the final several Mishnayot of the tractate: *lo yochlu ha-Pesach achar chatzot*, *yishnamu lo yochlu ha-Pesach*, *birkhat ha-Pesach* — they all discuss eating the *Pesach*. And significantly, throughout the *perek*'s discussion of the *seder*, the eating of *matzah* and *marror* was not independently addressed. This is striking if the Mishnah were speaking about post-Temple practice — *matzah* and *marror* would be the central items. But if the context is *zman ha-mikdash*, where the *korban Pesach* is the primary obligation and the *matzah* and *marror* are its accompaniments, it makes sense that the Mishnah focuses on the *Pesach* and largely passes over the *matzah* and *marror*. The Gemara will bring them in as it develops the discussion, but the Mishnah's organization itself reflects a Temple-era framework.

### Afikoman Meaning

*Mai afikoman?* — what is this *afikoman*? Rav explains: *shelo ye'akor me-chabura le-chabura* — one may not leave one group eating the *Pesach* and go to eat with another group. There is a formal prohibition against eating the *korban Pesach* in two different *chaburot*, and the *Rashbam* adds that even eating other foods in a second *chabura* is prohibited, as it may lead to eating the *Pesach* itself in two places.

How does the word *afikoman* convey this meaning? The *Rashbam* attempts a reading of the word as a Hebrew compound, but more straightforwardly, *afikoman* is a Greek word — it refers to a kind of carousing that would follow a meal in Greek and Roman culture: *epikomion*, an after-party of visiting other people's homes, drinking wine, socializing from one gathering to the next in a licentious and festive manner. The Mishnah is saying: after eating the *Pesach*, don't go out for the *afikoman*, the Greek-style carousing. The Gemara reads this halakhically rather than morally — the concern is not the carousing per se but the violation of the rule about *chaburot*.

### Afikoman Dessert

Shmuel offers a different reading: the *afikoman* refers not to going elsewhere but to eating a dessert course here, in the same place. *Ke-gon urdilai li ve-gozlaya le-abba* — for example, fungi such as mushrooms for me, and pigeons for Abba, i.e., for Rav. These would be the kinds of delicacies one might eat as a dessert following the main meal. Similarly, Rav Chanina bar Shila and Rabbi Yochanan: *kegon temarim klayot ve-egozim* — dates, roasted grain, and nuts. *Tanya kevatch d'Rabbi Yochanan*: one may not eat dessert after the *Pesach*.

On this reading, the concern is entirely different: it is not about moving between groups but about obliterating the taste and flavor of the *korban Pesach* in one's mouth. The *Pesach* is meant to be the last thing one eats, so that its taste remains. The word *afikoman* would then have to be read in its Greek sense of a dessert course — an *epicomion* in the sense of an after-course — rather than the carousing sense. This latter explanation — preserving the taste of the *Pesach* — is how the contemporary practice of the *afikoman* piece of *matzah* is typically understood: the *matzah* is eaten last and nothing follows it, so that the taste of the *matzah* remains. The *Gemara*'s first explanation, however — rooted in the prohibition of *chaburot* — is in some ways closer to the literal Greek meaning of the word and to the cultural context in which the *seder* was formulated. The discussion will continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Pesachim 120

## Afikoman Concept

### Rav vs. Shmuel

The daf opens at the bottom of 119b, where the *mishnah* had stated: *ein maftirin achar hapesach afikoman* — one does not conclude after the *pesach* with an *afikoman*. It is striking that the final *mishnayot* of the tractate focus on the eating of the *korban pesach* rather than on *matzah* and *maror*, which go entirely unaddressed. This raises the broader question of how much this *perek* assumes *zman habayit* — the period when the Temple stood — versus *bizman hazeh*.

The term *afikoman* itself is a Greek word, and Rav's interpretation follows that etymology: the prohibition is against going to other *chavurot* — other groups' meals — in the manner of a Greco-Roman afterparty, with its carousing and inappropriate revelry. In the context of the *korban pesach*, the practical concern is that one might come to eat the *pesach* in two separate locations.

Shmuel's interpretation — the one with which we are all familiar — is that *afikoman* refers to eating *anything* after the *pesach*, on the presumption that doing so would displace the taste of the *korban pesach* from one's mouth. Notably, the *Gemara* has not yet stated this rationale explicitly; it is the operative concern behind Shmuel's position.

### Shmuel: No Food After Ma…

Following Shmuel's approach, the *Gemara* cites: *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* — not only after the *pesach* is there a prohibition, but even nowadays, after *matzah*, one may not eat anything. This ruling transforms the practical structure of the *Seder*: if nothing may follow the *matzah*, then the *matzah* must come at the very end of the meal. The familiar *afikoman* — the piece of *matzah* eaten at the conclusion of the *Seder* — exists precisely to ensure this: we eat it last so that nothing comes after it, thereby fulfilling the spirit of *ein maftirin achar hapesach afikoman* as applied to *matzah bizman hazeh*.

This is an important point: the eating of a final *kezayit* of *matzah* at the end of the meal is not a proactive institution celebrating some special importance of that last piece. It is, rather, the necessary consequence of the ruling that nothing may follow the *matzah*. Once you must have *matzah* last, the final piece becomes significant by default. The question of which *matzah* — first or last — bears the primary weight of the *mitzvah* will be addressed shortly.

### Matzah vs. Pesach Taste

The *Gemara* attempts to test Shmuel's position against the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* says *ein maftirin achar hapesach afikoman*, implying by its silence that after *matzah* there is no such problem. The *Gemara* deflects this with the principle of *lo mibaya ka'amar* — the *mishnah* is speaking in the form of "it goes without saying." The logic runs as follows: *lo mibaya achar matzah delo nafish tamayhu* — it goes without saying that after *matzah*, whose taste is weak and insubstantial, one should not eat anything afterwards; *aval achar pesach de-nafish ta'amei velo matzi avurei lei* — but after the *pesach*, which has a powerful taste that cannot easily be washed away, one might have thought there is no need to worry since the taste will linger on its own. The *mishnah* therefore teaches that even after the *pesach*, one may not eat.

This reading preserves Shmuel's position: the *mishnah* is not excluding *matzah* from the prohibition, but rather emphasizing that the prohibition extends even to the stronger-tasting *pesach*. The *mishnah* is thus operating in a *zman habayit* framework and innovating that even by *pesach* it is a concern — but of course the same concern applies *a fortiori* to *matzah bizman hazeh*.

Mar Zutra, however, reports a different version of the tradition — *Amar Rav Yosef amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* — in which Shmuel's ruling is precisely the opposite: *maftirin achar matzah afikoman*, meaning it is only a problem with the *korban pesach* and not with *matzah* nowadays. With this reversal, all the proofs and challenges trade places. The *mishnah* now seems to support this position — *achar hapesach hu de-lo*, after the *pesach* is the prohibition, *aval achar matzah maftirin* — and the *Gemara* counters again with *lo mibaya ka'amar*, though now in the reverse direction: it goes without saying you cannot eat after *matzah* since its taste is so weak, and the *mishnah* innovates regarding *pesach* that even its strong taste is a problem.

### Baraita: Matzah at End

The *Gemara* adduces a *baraita* to press the question further. A *baraita* states that one may eat one's fill of *sofganin*, *duvshunin*, and *iskartin* — various types of *mezonos* — on the night of *Pesach*, *uvilvad she-yochal kezayit matzah ba-achrona* — provided that the *kezayit* of *matzah* is eaten last. The *baraita* further specifies: *ba-achrona in, barishona lo* — at the end, yes; at the beginning, no.

This appears to support Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel's position that *matzah* must come at the end. However, the *Gemara* again deploys *lo mibaya ka'amar*: naturally it is permitted to eat *matzah* at the beginning when one has an appetite — *leteiavon* — it is even preferable that way. The *baraita* teaches us only that eating it at the end is also acceptable, despite the concern that by that point one may be overly satiated, rendering the eating *achila gassa*. The *baraita*, on this reading, establishes that eating *matzah* at the end is *permitted*, not that it is *required*.

The result is that neither version of Shmuel's teaching can be decisively confirmed or refuted from these *mishnayot* and *braitot*.

There is a deeper question lurking here: why should the concern about preserving the taste in one's mouth apply to *matzah* at all? The *Gemara* elsewhere was only concerned with the taste of *maror*, not *matzah* — indeed, swallowing *matzah* whole satisfies the *mitzvah*. One might therefore argue that the obligation to end with *matzah* is uniquely a *pesach*-related concern, grounded in the profound symbolism of the *korban pesach* in a way that does not transfer to *matzah*.

*Tosafot* raises this very question — *ve-im tomar achar pesach mai ta'ama ein maftirin* — why would it be specifically a concern after *pesach*, given that its taste is *stronger* than *matzah's*? *Tosafot* then cites the *Yerushalmi*, which offers a different rationale altogether: the *pesach* is eaten *al hasova* — in a state of satiation — as a safeguard against the prohibition of *sheviras atzem*. If one is ravenous, one might chew the bones and extract the marrow, violating the prohibition of *ve-etzem lo tishberu bo*. Eating the *pesach* at the end, when satiated, guards against this. *Tosafot* further notes that by *minchat* there is a related idea of eating *al hasova*, derived not from the concern about bone-breaking but from the notion that one should not leave the table of one's Master still hungry. Applied to *pesach*, there is also the consideration that finishing the *korban* while still craving more food would be inappropriate.

This gives us multiple convergent reasons for eating the *pesach* at the end of the meal: not eating it when ravenous, so as not to break bones; not finishing and feeling unsatisfied; and maintaining the taste. It is precisely because these reasons are so specifically tied to the *korban pesach* that their extension to *matzah* is not self-evident — and that is what the *Gemara's* debate reflects.

## Two Matzah Roles

### Rashbam: Last Kezayit

The *Rashbam* takes a unified view: the final *kezayit* of *matzah* is the essential *matzah mitzvah*. Since this last piece is eaten at the end — mirroring the *korban pesach*, which was also eaten at the end — it stands as a *zecher* for the *matzah* eaten together with the *pesach*, *ne'echelet im ha-pesach*. On this view, the final *kezayit* performs double duty: it is both the commemoration of *matzah al ha-pesach* and the fulfillment of the independent *mitzvat achilat matzah*.

This raises an immediate question: if the *mitzvah* is fulfilled with the final piece, why do we recite *al achilat matzah* at the beginning of the meal? The *Rashbam* addresses this by analogy to a discussion earlier in the tractate about *maror*, where a *bracha* is recited in advance of the actual *mitzvah* act. He contends that since one begins eating *matzah* at the start of the meal, the *bracha* is recited then — but the essential fulfillment occurs with the closing *kezayit*.

### Tosafot: Divided Roles

*Tosafot* proposes a cleaner and more elegant structure by assigning distinct roles to each *kezayit*. The first *kezayit* of *matzah* fulfills the independent *mitzvah* of *achilat matzah* — the *de'oraita* obligation that applies *bizman hazeh*. The final *kezayit* — what we call the *afikoman* — represents the *matzah* eaten together with the *pesach*: a *zecher l'pesach*, consumed at the end of the meal just as the *korban* was eaten at the end, with its taste lingering in the mouth.

On this reading, each piece has its own identity. The *al achilat matzah* is recited at the beginning because the *mitzvah* of *achilat matzah* is being fulfilled there and then. The final piece is separately meaningful as a symbolic re-enactment of the Temple *seder*. One might ask: if the final *kezayit* is *zecher l'pesach*, should *korech* not be eaten at the end, since that too commemorates eating *matzah* with the *pesach*? The practical structure of the *Seder* as we observe it renders this question somewhat academic, but it is worth noting.

### Seder Matzah Structure

In practice, the *Seder* begins with three *matzot*. The reason for three is that since one will be broken — and we want *lechem mishneh* — we need two whole ones; the third provides the one that will be broken. The middle *matzah* is broken because it represents *lechem oni*, the bread of affliction, over which the *Haggadah* is recited, since the *midrash* connects *oni* to *oneh* — responding, answering — and one answers over a broken piece.

The half that is set aside — classically, the larger half — becomes the *afikoman*. The *Gemara* itself never specifies what to do with this piece; all of this detail is developed by the *Rishonim*. At the point of eating, the *bracha* of *Hamotzi lechem min ha-aretz* is recited over the whole *matzah*, and the *al achilat matzah* is recited over the broken piece. A *kezayit* is taken from each. This arrangement — assigning *Hamotzi* to the whole and *al achilat matzah* to the broken — may seem unusual, since *birkat hanehenin* is not normally parceled out between pieces, but it functions as a way of giving each element a distinct role.

*Korech* uses the third *matzah*, the remaining whole one, giving it a role as well. The set-aside half then fulfills the final *kezayit* — the *afikoman* — eaten after the meal. In this way every piece of *matzah* finds its place in the *Seder* structure.

Regarding the practice of eating two *kezayitim* for the *afikoman*: the common reason given in *Seder* guides is that since the *afikoman* may fulfill the *de'oraita* obligation, some hold one should double the measure to satisfy the *shiur* of the *Chazon Ish*. It does not appear to reflect an independent *din* of *shnei kezayitim*.

## Matzah Independence

### Rava: Matzah De'Oraita

*Rava* states plainly: *matzah bizman hazeh de'oraita* — the obligation to eat *matzah* on the night of *Pesach* is biblical, even in the absence of the *korban pesach*. It is not merely a rabbinic enactment; it is a full-fledged Torah obligation that stands independently.

### Maror Rabbinic Status

By contrast, *maror* is *derabbanan* in our time. The *Gemara* explains: *d'chtiv al matzot u-merorim yochluhu* — the Torah states that the *pesach* is eaten with *matzah* and *maror*. The *maror* is therefore an accompaniment to the *pesach*: *bizman d'ika pesach yesh maror, bizman d'leika pesach leika maror* — when there is a *pesach* there is *maror*, when there is no *pesach* there is no *maror*. Since we no longer bring the *korban pesach*, the obligation of *maror* reverts to rabbinic standing.

One might think the same logic applies to *matzah*: it too is mentioned in the verse as an accompaniment to the *pesach*. The *Gemara* answers that the Torah *returns* to *matzah* — *matzah mahadeir hadei bei kra* — and establishes an independent obligation.

### Torah Source for Matzah

The *Gemara* points to the verse: *ba-erev tochlu matzot* — in the evening you shall eat *matzot*. If one asks any serious student of *Gemara* for the Torah source of the obligation to eat *matzah* on *Seder* night, this is the verse they will cite. The matter is, however, subtler than it first appears. The full verse reads: *barishon b'arba'ah asar yom la-chodesh ba-erev tochlu matzot ad yom ha-echad ve-esrim la-chodesh ba-erev* — from the fourteenth day of the first month in the evening you shall eat *matzot* until the twenty-first day of the month in the evening. This is a verse about all seven days.

What the *Gemara* effectively does is isolate the opening clause — *ba-erev tochlu matzot*, "in the evening you shall eat *matzot*" — treating the beginning of *Pesach* as establishing an independent, specific obligation for the first night, while severing it from the remainder of the verse. The Torah, in other words, was never legislating a distinct night-one obligation; it was describing the entire seven-day obligation. But the hermeneutical move of the *Gemara* reads into the opening words a *de'oraita* requirement unique to the first night, giving *matzah* its independent standing *bizman hazeh*.

### Rava bar Yitzchak: All R…

*Rava bar Yitzchak* takes a strikingly different position: *echad zeh ve-echad zeh derabbanan* — both *matzah* and *maror* are rabbinic in our time, and neither carries a biblical obligation. On this view, the verse *ba-erev tochlu matzot* is not establishing an independent obligation for *Seder* night at all. Rather, the *Gemara* responds to him, it speaks to the case of one who is *tamei* or on a distant road — *tamei ve-shehayah be-derech rechokah* — who is exempted from bringing the *korban pesach*. The verse teaches that even such a person must still eat *matzah* on that night, lest one think: since he is not eating the *pesach*, he need not eat *matzah* and *maror* either. The verse therefore addresses a *zman habayit* scenario and does not create an independent *bizman hazeh* obligation at all.

This is a striking position, because it implies that *matzah* exists as an obligation only when there is a *korban pesach* — yet independent of actually eating one. The person who cannot bring the *korban* because of *tumah* or distance is nonetheless obligated to eat *matzah* and *maror* at the time when the *korban* is brought. In our era, when there is no *korban* at all, neither *matzah* nor *maror* carries biblical force. According to *Rava bar Yitzchak*, there is no *de'oraita mitzvah* on *leil Seder*.

*Rava*, by contrast, responds that no additional verse is needed to teach the case of *tamei ve-derech rechokah*: *d'lo gra'ei me-areil u-ven neichar* — they are no worse than an *areil* (an uncircumcised person) or a *ben neichar* (an apostate), who likewise cannot eat the *korban pesach* yet are still obligated in *matzah* and *maror*, as the *baraita* teaches: *bo eino ochel aval ochel be-matzah u-maror*. The verse therefore must be doing something else entirely — establishing a biblical obligation independent of the *pesach*.

The *Gemara* adds that the verse covering *tamei* and *derech rechokah* is still necessary even if one knows each case individually, because arguments might be constructed to distinguish one from the other, and the Torah therefore covers both explicitly.

### Six Days Argument

The *Gemara* further develops the position of *Rava bar Yitzchak* by examining a second verse: *sheshes yamim tochal matzot u-va-yom ha-shevi'i atzeret la-Hashem Elokecha* — six days you shall eat *matzot* and on the seventh day is a solemn assembly. This verse mentions only six days of eating, not seven. The *Gemara* asks: *mah shevi'i reshut* — since the seventh day appears optional (it is a *Yom Tov* and eating *matzah* is clearly permitted but not commanded separately there), perhaps the entire six-day period is also optional? The hermeneutical principle is *davar she-hayah bi-khlal ve-yatza min ha-klal l'lamed* — something that was part of a general category and was singled out comes to teach about the entire category, not just itself. Since the verse singles out the seventh day and appears to render it *reshut*, the same status extends to all six days.

The logical conclusion is that throughout *Chol ha-Moed* and the final day, there is no obligation to eat *matzah*; if you choose to eat bread, eat *matzah*, but you are not compelled to. This would appear to extend to the first night as well — *yakhol af lailah ha-rishon reshut*? The *Gemara* answers: *talmud lomar al matzot u-merorim yochluhu* — the Torah verse about eating the *pesach* with *matzah* and *maror* establishes that on the first night there is an obligation. But this, as noted, is tied to the *korban pesach* in the time of the *Beit ha-Mikdash*.

For *bizman hazeh*, the obligation on the first night is derived from *ba-erev tochlu matzot*, and *Rava* holds this as a fully independent *de'oraita*. Since *matzah* is established as a biblical obligation, *maggid* — the recitation of the *Haggadah* — is also biblical, because the verse *ba-avur zeh* is conditioned on the presence of *matzah* and *maror* before you: *ba-avur zeh lo amru ela be-sha'ah she-yesh matzah u-maror munachim le-fanecha*. Without a *de'oraita matzah*, there is no *de'oraita maggid*.

According to *Rava bar Yitzchak*, by contrast, virtually every *mitzvah* of *leil Seder* is rabbinic. The only *de'oraita* obligations that night might be *birkat ha-mazon* and possibly *kiddush* for *Yom Tov* — though even the latter is complicated by the question of whether *kiddush* for *Yom Tov* carries biblical force in the same way as *kiddush* for *Shabbat*. We rule in accordance with *Rava*, and *matzah bizman hazeh* is thus *de'oraita*, *maror* is *derabbanan*, and *maggid* is *de'oraita*.

## Sleeping Rule

### Mishna Sleep Rule

The *mishnah* teaches: *yashnu miktzatan yochlu kulam, yashnu kulam lo yochlu* — if some members of the group fell asleep, the group may continue eating when they awaken; if all of them fell asleep, they may not continue. The context is the eating of the *korban pesach*: falling asleep creates an interruption analogous to departing from one *chavurah*, and resuming in such circumstances would be akin to eating the *pesach* in two separate settings.

One might also frame the concern as a variant of the *afikoman* prohibition: having fallen asleep and awoken, any further eating of *matzah* would constitute a new, post-meal eating — precisely the kind of *afikoman*-eating one is trying to avoid. The *Rashbam* frames the concern as resembling eating the *pesach* in two locations.

If some members remained awake, continuity is preserved and eating may resume. If all fell asleep, the communal meal has effectively ended, and resumption is forbidden.

### Rabbi Yose Distinction

*Rabbi Yose* introduces a distinction between types of sleep: *nishnamnemu yochlu, nirdemu lo yochlu* — if they merely dozed, they may continue eating; if they fell into deep sleep, they may not. Whether *Rabbi Yose* is being *meikel* or *machmir* relative to the anonymous *mishnah* is ambiguous: he may be restricting even the case where only some fell asleep (requiring that the sleep be light), or he may be permitting even the case where all fell asleep as long as the sleep was only a doze.

## Chatzot Deadline (II)

### Pesach Nosar After Chatz…

The *mishnah* states: *ha-pesach achar chatzot metamei et ha-yadayim* — the *pesach* after midnight renders the hands *tamei*. This is because the *pesach* becomes *nosar* — leftover meat that may not be eaten — once *chatzot* passes, since according to this *mishnah* the entire night is not available for eating the *korban pesach*; only until midnight. *Nosar*, when touched, imparts *tumah* to the hands, as will be discussed below. The final line of the *mishnah* generalizes: *ha-pigul ve-ha-nosar metamim et ha-yadayim* — both *pigul* and *nosar* render the hands *tamei*.

## Sleeping Rule (II)

### Rav Ashi Definition

The *Gemara* opens the discussion of *Rabbi Yose's* ruling by asking: *heichi dami nishnamnemu* — what exactly constitutes dozing? *Rav Ashi* defines it: *nim ve-lo nim, tir ve-lo tir* — sleeping but not quite sleeping, awake but not quite awake — the half-asleep state. The operational test: *dekari lei ve-ani* — you call the person and he responds, he reacts to his name; *ve-lo yada la-haduri sevara* — but if asked something that requires reasoning, he cannot generate a response on his own. However, *ve-chi midkeru lei midkar* — if you prompt him with the beginning of the thought, he can follow along and remember. He cannot produce independent reasoning, but he can track and respond to external prompts. This is a precise and recognizable phenomenological description of the hypnagogic state.

### Abaye-Rabbah Example

*Abaye hava yasiv kamei de-Rabbah* — *Abaye* was sitting before *Rabbah* during a *shiur*. *Chazah de-ka minanem* — he observed that *Rabbah* was dozing off. *Amar lei: nim ka naim mar?* — he asked, "Master, were you dozing?" *Amar lei: nimumei ka menamnemna* — "I was dozing, yes." And then *Rabbah* cited the *mishnah* — *nishnamnemu yochlu, nirdemu lo yochlu* — to demonstrate that his dozing, being only *nishnamnemu* and not *nirdemu*, did not constitute the kind of sleep that would have legal consequence. The *Rashbam* explains that the applicable context was not the *Seder* but rather a *taanit*: the *Yerushalmi* teaches that falling asleep can constitute the beginning of a fast, since one who sleeps has effectively ended his day. *Rabbah* was therefore using *Rabbi Yose's* distinction to establish that his doze was too light to count as the sleep that initiates a *taanit*.

## Chatzot Deadline (II)

### Rabbi Elazar Chatzot

*Rav Yosef* identifies the *tanna* behind the *mishnah's* ruling that the *pesach* becomes *nosar* at *chatzot*: it is *Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah*. A *baraita* records his derivation: the Torah says *ve-achaltem et ha-basar ba-lailah ha-zeh* — you shall eat the meat this night. *Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah* draws a *gezerah shavah* from the phrase *ba-lailah ha-zeh* to the verse *ve-avarti be-eretz Mitzrayim ba-lailah ha-zeh* — I will pass through the land of Egypt this night. Since the plague occurred at *chatzot*, the word *ha-zeh* implies a limit until midnight. Therefore the eating of the *pesach* also extends only until *chatzot*, after which it becomes *nosar*.

### Rabbi Akiva Challenge

*Rabbi Akiva* challenges this derivation. The Torah also says *ve-achaltem oto be-chipazon* — you shall eat it in haste. *Chipazon* refers to the moment when the Egyptians urgently expelled the Israelites — which occurred in the morning, not at midnight. Therefore the eating extends until the morning.

### Ad Boker Debate

The *Gemara* records the extended exchange between the two positions. The word *balaila* — "at night" — might seem superfluous if *chipazon* already establishes the deadline as morning. *Rabbi Akiva* explains: *balaila* is needed to teach that eating begins at night rather than during the day on which the *korban* was offered — since all other *korbanos* may be eaten beginning the day of their offering, one might have thought the *pesach* similarly begins in the afternoon. *Balaila* teaches that it is eaten only at night.

*Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah* counters that the nighttime-eating limitation could have been derived from *ad boker* — "until morning" — rendering *ha-zeh* available to teach the *chatzot* limit. *Rabbi Akiva* responds that without *ha-zeh*, the word *boker* might have been read as referring to the morning of the second night, implying that eating is permitted until the following morning. *Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah* rejoins: wherever the Torah writes *boker*, it means the first morning.

### Rava: Matzah Chatzot

*Rava* applies this dispute to *matzah*: *achal matzah bizman hazeh achar chatzot, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah lo yatza yedei chovato* — one who eats *matzah* in our time after *chatzot* has not fulfilled his obligation according to *Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah*. The *Gemara* initially objects that this is obvious — *peshita* — since *matzah* is linked to the *pesach*. But *Rava's* point is not trivial: one might have thought that since the Torah explicitly extracted *matzah* from its linkage to the *pesach* and established it as an independent *mitzvah*, the time constraints of the *pesach* no longer apply. *Mah u-ditema, ha apkei kra me-heiksha* — one might argue the verse detached *matzah* from the *pesach*. *Rava* teaches: *de-chi ahadrei kra, le-milsa ka-maisa ahadrei* — when the Torah restored *matzah* as an independent obligation, it retained the essential linkage in terms of time. *Matzah* is independent as a *mitzvah*, but its temporal framework remains bound to that of the *korban pesach*.

This is a significant *chiddush*: *matzah* is simultaneously a free-standing *de'oraita mitzvah* and temporally tethered to the *pesach*. One who eats *matzah* after *chatzot* has not fulfilled his obligation, according to *Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah* as applied by *Rava*. Consequently, *maggid* — which is linked to the *matzah* obligation — is also bounded by *chatzot*.

This is the basis for the widespread practice of trying to eat the *afikoman* before *chatzot*. It is worth noting the irony: *Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah* himself is one of the figures celebrated in the *Haggadah* for discussing the *Exodus* all night — *hayu mesaprim bi-ytziat Mitzrayim kol oto ha-lailah* — yet according to his own ruling, the *matzah* must be eaten by midnight. Some have noted that perhaps he believed elements of *maggid* not directly tied to the *matzah* could continue after *chatzot*; others suggest more creative solutions, such as the practice of one who ate an additional *kezayit* of *matzah* just before *chatzot* so that *mi-mah nafshach* he had fulfilled his obligation before the deadline, and could then continue the discussion through the night.

*Tosafot* acknowledges uncertainty about whether we rule like *Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah* or *Rabbi Akiva*, which is why not all authorities are equally stringent about the *chatzot* deadline.

A further question concerns the relationship between this *chatzot* and the *chatzot* mentioned in the first *mishnah* of *Berachot*, where *Rabbi Gamliel* implies that *keri'at shema* and certain *korbanos* extend until dawn (*amud ha-shachar*), while the *mishnah* sets *chatzot* as the deadline. *Tosafot* explains that in *Berachot*, the *chatzot* serves as a rabbinic fence — *be-di'avad*, if one missed it, one may still fulfill the obligation until dawn. But according to *Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah*, the *pesach's* limit at *chatzot* is grounded in the *gezerah shavah* to *ve-avarti be-eretz Mitzrayim ba-lailah ha-zeh*, making it a genuine biblical cutoff — *mamash* becoming *nosar* after midnight.

## Pigul & Nosar Tumah

### Two Reasons

The *Gemara* now returns to explain why *pigul* and *nosar* render the hands *tamei*. *Rav Huna* and *Rav Chisda* each offer a reason, with one addressing *pigul* and the other *nosar*. *Chad amar mishum chashdei kehuna* — one says the concern is *kohanim* who are suspected of deliberately intending to invalidate *korbanos*: a *kohen* who plans to eat the offering outside its proper time or place renders it *pigul*, and the rabbinic imposition of *tumah* serves as a deterrent. The rationale is that *kohanim* have an almost visceral aversion to contracting *tumah* while serving in the *Beit ha-Mikdash*, and the threat of *tumah* may deter misconduct that the biblical prohibitions alone do not. *Ve-chad amar mishum atzlei kehuna* — the other says the concern is *kohanim* who are lazy and negligent, failing to ensure the meat is consumed within its time and thereby allowing it to become *nosar*. The *tumah* designation for *nosar* is a rabbinic safeguard against this carelessness.

### Kezayit vs. Kibeitzah

A further dispute concerns the measure of *tumah*: *chad amar kezayit ve-chad amar ke-beitzah* — one holds that a *kezayit* of *pigul* or *nosar* causes the hands to become *tamei*, while the other holds it requires a *ke-beitzah* (egg-size).

### Measure Rationale

The *Gemara* explains both positions. *Man d'amar kezayit — ke-issuro*: the one who says *kezayit* reasons that since the prohibited *act of eating* these substances is defined by the measure of a *kezayit* — that being the minimum for the prohibition of eating *pigul* or *nosar* — the *tumah* that mirrors this prohibition should likewise be triggered by a *kezayit*. *Ve-man d'amar ke-beitzah — ke-tumato*: the one who says *ke-beitzah* reasons from the standard framework of food *tumah*, in which the operative measure is an egg-sized quantity. Even though *pigul* and *nosar* are prohibited foods, they remain within the world of *tumah* and should conform to its standard measure of *ke-beitzah*.

## Blessing Exemption

### Mishna Exemption

The final *mishnah* of the tractate teaches: *birkat ha-pesach poteret et shel zevach* — the blessing recited over the *pesach* exempts the *chagigah* and other *korbanos* eaten alongside it from requiring their own separate blessing. The reverse, however, does not hold: *beirach et ha-zevach, lo poter shel pesach* — if one recited the blessing over the other *korban*, that does not exempt the *pesach*. This is the position of *Rabbi Yishmael*. *Rabbi Akiva* disagrees entirely: *lo zu poteret zu ve-lo zu poteret zu* — neither exempts the other.

This is a striking *mishnah* on several levels. The very notion that one blessing can exempt another *korban* is curious: if the blessing is *le-echol ha-pesach*, how does it extend to the *chagigah*? And the question of the order — one presumably eats the *chagigah* before the *pesach*, to come to the *pesach al ha-sova* — makes it unclear how the blessing on the *pesach* could have preceded the eating of the *chagigah*.

### Yishmael Overlap

The *Gemara* explains *Rabbi Yishmael's* position through the lens of the laws of blood service. For standard *korbanos*, the blood is offered through *zerikah* — throwing the blood against the corners of the *mizbeach* from a distance, so that it splatters against two walls. For the *korban pesach*, the blood is offered through *shefichah* — pouring it at the base of the *mizbeach*. *Rabbi Yishmael* holds: *zerikah bi-khlal shefichah* — *zerikah* is subsumed within *shefichah*. That is, a *korban* that requires *zerikah* could, under *Rabbi Yishmael's* view, also have its obligation satisfied through *shefichah*.

### Akiva Opposition

*Rabbi Akiva* holds the opposite: *lo shefichah bi-khlal zerikah ve-lo zerikah bi-khlal shefichah* — neither method is subsumed within the other. They are categorically distinct blood rites, and neither can serve as a substitute for the other.

### Gemara Explanation

The *Gemara* derives the ruling of the *mishnah* from this dispute: because according to *Rabbi Yishmael*, *zerikah bi-khlal shefichah* — what was done with the blood of the *pesach* (*shefichah*) could in theory have been done for the other *korban* as well — the blessing on the *pesach* extends to exempt the other *korban*. The blood rites overlap, creating a sufficient nexus for the blessing to carry over. But *lo shefichah bi-khlal zerikah* — the *shefichah* of the *pesach* could not have served as *zerikah* for a *korban* that requires *zerikah*; therefore the blessing on the other *korban* does not extend to the *pesach*. According to *Rabbi Akiva*, since neither overlaps with the other, no blessing exempts the other in any direction.

It must be noted that this explanation is difficult to follow. The *bracha* is recited over the *eating* of the *korban*, not over the *hakravat ha-korban* or the blood service. It is unclear how the theoretical interchangeability of blood-sprinkling methods — *zerikah* and *shefichah* — should bear on whether the blessing recited over the eating of one *korban* extends to the eating of another. The *Rashbam* and *Tosafot* explain the connection, but the full resolution of how the *Gemara* ties blood rites to blessings over eating remains a question with which we will open the *siyum* tomorrow.

# Shekalim 3

## Shekalim in Daf Yomi

### Why Shekalim in Daf Yomi

We begin *Masechet Shekalim*, which we have in the *Yerushalmi*. A natural question presents itself: why is *Shekalim* included in *Daf Yomi* at all, given that it exists only as a *Yerushalmi* tractate? The answer is likely twofold. First, *Shekalim* is printed within the *Bavli*, and there is no other *Yerushalmi* tractate that receives this treatment. Second — and this may explain both why it appears in the *Bavli* and why it was included in *Daf Yomi* — *Shekalim* is the one tractate in *Seder Moed* that is otherwise unrepresented in the *Bavli*. Unlike *Seder Zeraim*, where only *Brachot* has *Bavli* coverage, *Shekalim* is the single omission in *Moed*, and being a short tractate, it may have been included for the sake of completion.

### Order of Masechtot

*Shekalim* appears after *Yoma* in the ordering of tractates within *Seder Moed*. The standard principle of organization is by the number of *perakim*, which generally — though not always — aligns with thematic and calendrical sequence. *Shabbat* and *Eruvin* come first naturally; *Pesachim* follows, since the verse *HaChodesh hazeh lachem* establishes *Nissan* as primary. *Yoma*, covering *Yom Kippur*, does not fit cleanly into that sequence, which is why the *Bavli* effectively reorders things so that *Rosh Hashanah*, *Yoma*, and *Sukkah* follow one another in the order of the *Tishrei* festivals. In truth, however, the structural order has *Yoma* coming before *Shekalim* simply because *Yoma* has more *perakim*. The reason *Shekalim* is nonetheless placed near *Pesach* in our study is probably because its subject matter — the collection of the half-shekel — begins on *Rosh Chodesh Adar* and is directed toward *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*, placing it squarely in the *Pesach* thematic orbit.

### Yerushalmi References

A practical note on referencing the *Yerushalmi*: citations are typically given either by *perek* and *halachah*, or by *amud* according to the original Venice printing. In that printing, each side of a page contained two columns, meaning that an *amud* designated a column — not a side. References to, say, 63c would designate column three of a given page, and columns could run up to *dalet* on each physical page. For our purposes, we will use the *Bavli* pagination format since that is how the tractate is organized before us.

It should also be noted that the *girsah* — the textual reading — of the *Yerushalmi* is considerably less stable than that of the *Bavli*. This is largely because the *Yerushalmi* was studied far less, and we effectively have only one complete manuscript: the Leiden manuscript. Other fragments exist, but the survival of this entire corpus rested on that single witness. This does not mean it is necessarily accurate — it is simply what we have. The instability of the text sometimes results from scribes who did not fully understand the *Yerushalmi*'s Aramaic and adjusted the text accordingly; at other times, it reflects genuine uncertainty about the correct reading.

### Roman Tax Parallels

Before turning to the *Gemara* itself, it is worth noting a historical parallel that illuminates why *Masechet Shekalim* was particularly relevant to *Eretz Yisrael*. Under Roman rule, there existed a form of annual taxation with some similarity to the half-shekel collection. Beyond the Roman Jewish tax, there was also a tax collected by the *Nasi* — the Patriarch — from Jewish communities not only within *Yisrael* but from the diaspora as well. This parallel between the ancient *shekalim* collection and the later institutional taxation of the Jewish community is worth bearing in mind as we work through this tractate.

---

## Adar Activities

### Road & Mikva Repair

After the opening discussion of collecting the *shekalim* beginning on *Rosh Chodesh Adar*, the *Mishnah* continues: *metaknin es hadrachim ve'es harechovot ve'es mikva'ot hamayim ve'osim kol tzorchei harabbim* — also in *Adar*, one fixes the roads and the alleys and the *mikva'ot*, and performs all the communal needs. The rationale is clear: the winter rainy season is drawing to a close, spring is approaching, and people will soon be traveling up *laregel* for the *yom tov*. The roads need to be cleared and repaired after the rains, and the *mikva'ot* — which were essentially holes in the ground collecting rainwater, not the refined structures we have today — need to be cleared of mud and debris that would render them unusable.

### Tzorchei Rabbim

The *Gemara* now quotes a *Mishnah* from *Moed Katan*: *eilu hein tzorchei harabbim* — these are the communal needs. This is a separate use of the category of *tzorchei harabbim*, and in *Moed Katan* the context is things that may be done on *Chol HaMoed*. The *Yerushalmi* quotes it here because of the thematic parallel, but this should not lead us to conclude that the following list consists of activities specific to *Adar*.

The *Mishnah* in *Moed Katan* lists: *danim dinei mamonot* — one may hold civil courts on *Chol HaMoed*; *udinei nefashot* — courts dealing with capital matters; *udinei makot* — or cases of lashes. The court system, in other words, continues to function. *Ufodin erchin vecharamin vehekdeshot* — one may also perform various transactions related to the *Beit HaMikdash*: redeeming property that has been consecrated. A brief note on terminology: *hekdesh* sanctifies the object itself; *cherem* is a form of dedication whose beneficiary — the *Kohanim* or the *Beit HaMikdash* — is a matter of some dispute; *erchin* involves a fixed value paid based on the age and gender of a person one designates. All these transactional activities relating to the *Beit HaMikdash* may be performed on *Chol HaMoed*.

*Umashkin es hasota* — one may also administer the *sotah* waters. This is somewhat striking, since it raises the question of how the *sotah* procedure fits into the category of *tzorchei harabbim*. The *Gemara* in *Sota* grapples with how much of the *sotah* procedure is to be understood as a legal process as opposed to a ritual performed in the *Beit HaMikdash*. *Usorfin es hapara* — one burns the *parah adumah* if ashes are needed. *Veorfin egla arufa* — one performs the *egla arufa* ceremony, which is clearly a communal concern. *Verotzin eved Ivri* — one pierces the ear of a Hebrew slave who wishes to become a permanent bondsman. This last item is somewhat puzzling, since it seems to be a private concern. It does involve the slave's household — *ishto ve'es banav* — so it affects multiple people, but why it qualifies as *tzorchei harabbim* is not entirely clear. *Umetarin es hametzora* — one performs the purification process for a *metzora*, which is a communal concern since one does not want a *metzora* remaining within the community.

### Why Quote Moed Katan

A question presents itself: the *Gemara* quotes this *Mishnah* from *Moed Katan* but does not develop it further or explain what it adds to our *Mishnah* in *Shekalim*. The reason the *Yerushalmi* introduces this *Mishnah* appears to be specifically because of its concluding items: *metzaynin es hakevarot* — designating graves — and *veyotzin al hakilayim* — going out to uproot *kilayim*. These are precisely the same two items with which our *Mishnah* in *Shekalim* concludes: *umetzaynin es hakevarot veyotzin af al hakilayim*. The citation is thus meant to illuminate those two specific *mitzvot* mentioned in our *Mishnah* and their parallel appearance in the context of *Chol HaMoed*.

### Graves & Kilayim

This parallel, however, immediately raises a difficulty. Our *Mishnah* instructs that one designates graves and uproots *kilayim* in *Adar*, and the *Mishnah* in *Moed Katan* says one does these same things on *Chol HaMoed*. But *Chol HaMoed Pesach* comes a full month after *Adar*. If it was already done in *Adar*, why must it be done again on *Chol HaMoed*? The *Gemara* will address this question in detail as we turn to the two topics in sequence.

---

## Marking Graves

### Rain Washes Away Marks

The *Gemara* asks directly: *lo kevar tzeinu me'Adar* — did we not already designate the graves back in *Adar*? Why would it be necessary to do so again on *Chol HaMoed*? The answer offered is: *tipatar she'yarad shetef shel geshamim ve'shafah* — one can explain the case as one where a heavy downpour of rain came and washed away the designations. The markers were made with lime painted on stones or on the ground, and a powerful rain could obliterate them entirely. If the rains were particularly heavy and prolonged, then even though the graves were marked in *Adar*, they might need to be marked again by *Chol HaMoed Nisan*.

A note on terminology: *tipatar* is the *Yerushalmi*'s way of contextualizing a teaching — explaining it as applying to a specific circumstance. It functions similarly to the *Bavli*'s *hacha bemai askinan*, though not identically. Both are means of establishing a particular contextual reading to resolve an apparent difficulty.

### Calendar & Rain Factors

A similar question is then asked about *kilayim*: *lo kevar yatzu me'Adar* — did they not already go out in *Adar* to uproot the errant sprouts? The answer here is: *tipatar she'haya hashana afeila ve'ein hatzmachim nikarim* — the year was *afeila*, and the sprouts were not yet visible. *Afeila* can mean dark, suggesting prolonged overcast or rainy conditions that obscured the sprouts. But it more likely refers to the calendar being out of alignment — the solar and agricultural seasons had not yet fully synchronized with the calendar. If the year had not been properly intercalated, *Adar* might fall earlier than its proper spring position, meaning that the sprouts had not yet emerged by the time the *Adar* inspection was conducted. Only by *Chol HaMoed Nisan*, when the season had genuinely warmed, did the sprouts become visible. This is also why the *Gemara* will shortly discuss the relationship between *ibbur hashanah* — adding a month to the year — and the agricultural calendar.

Our *Mishnah* uses the phrase *kol tzorchei harabbim*, which evokes the *Moed Katan* list of *tzorchei harabbim* for *Chol HaMoed*. The *Gemara* quotes that *Mishnah* but does not elaborate on it further in the context of *Adar*, since these are activities performed throughout the year, not uniquely in *Adar*.

### Ezekiel Source

Having established that grave designation is required both in *Adar* and potentially again on *Chol HaMoed*, the *Gemara* asks: *minayin l'tziyun* — what is the scriptural source for designating graves at all?

The tradition is transmitted through a chain of *Amoraim* — there is some textual uncertainty about the exact names involved, with different *girsaot* giving *Rav Yaakov bar Bas Yaakov* in the name of *Rav Chunya de'Bas Chavrin*, or *Rav Yaakov bar Acha* in the name of *Chunya de'Bas Chavrin*, or *Rav Uziel brei de'Rav Chunya de'Beis Chovrin*. The place name — *Beis Chovrin*, *Bas Chavrin*, and similar variants — appears to refer to a location in the *Negev*, possibly near *Nachal Chaverim* in the area of *Sde Boker*. It is striking that the *Tanna* may well have originated from that region.

One source brought for the designation of graves is the verse relating to the *metzora*: *ve'tamei tamei yikra* — "tamei, tamei, he shall call out." This is interpreted to mean that *tumah* itself announces its own presence — *kedei she'tehei hatumah koreiah befiha*, so that the impurity cries out to warn people away: *ve'omeret lach perosh*, "it says to you: separate yourself." By extension, all forms of *tumah* should make themselves known so that people can avoid them.

A second, more direct source is cited by *Rav Ila* in the name of *Rav Shmuel bar Nachman*, from *Yechezkel*: *ve'avru ha'ovrim ba'aretz ve'ra'ah etzem adam uvanah etzlo tziyun* — "and those who pass through the land will see a human bone and build a marker by it." According to its *peshat*, this verse describes marking a location in order to then move the bone, but from it the *Gemara* derives the practice of building a marker adjacent to a grave.

### Marker Requirements

The verse in *Yechezkel* mentions *etzem adam* — a human bone — and from this the *Gemara* derives that markers are placed specifically over bones: *mikan she'metzaynin al ha'atzamot*. This emphasis on bones is significant for two reasons. First, as we will see, a marker is not made over human flesh alone, because flesh decomposes and the marker would outlast its purpose. Second, the concern driving grave designation is that *Kohanim* not walk over the grave and contract *tumah be'ohel* — impurity transmitted by being under the same covering as human remains. Only bones generate *tumah be'ohel*, and only when present in sufficient quantity, with the exceptions of the skull and the spine, which convey *tumah* even as individual bones.

From *adam* — "of a man" — the *Gemara* derives: *mikan she'metzaynin al hashidrah ve'al hagulgoles*, that markers are placed even for the spine and the skull individually, as these generate *tumah be'ohel* even without the requisite quantity of other bones.

From *uvanah* — "and he shall build" — the *Gemara* derives that markers must be fixed structures: *mikan she'metzaynin al gabei even kevuah*, placed on a stone that is embedded in the ground rather than a loose movable stone. The reason is straightforward: *im omer at al gabei even telushah af hi holechet u-metamet be-makom acher* — if the marker is painted on a movable stone, that stone will be moved, and people will identify the wrong location as dangerous while remaining unaware of the real one.

From *etzlo* — "beside it" — the *Gemara* derives: *le-makom taharah tziyun* — the marker must be placed in *tahor* space, adjacent to but not directly over the grave. The purpose is to warn a person before they reach the danger zone, not after.

Each element of the verse thus yields a distinct *halachah* about how grave designation is to be performed.

### One vs Two Markers

The *Gemara* then addresses what to assume when one actually encounters a marker. If one stone is found marked, even though the proper practice is to place the marker away from the *met*, one cannot rely on this and assume safety: *af al pi she'ein mekayamin ken ha-ma'ahil aleha tamei*. Even though markers are not supposed to be placed directly over the *met*, the marker may have been placed incorrectly, or the *met* may have been positioned — *metzuyan*, perhaps folded over — such that it ended up directly beneath the marker. One who walks over a single marker must therefore treat oneself as *tamei*.

If, however, two marked stones are found, the analysis shifts: *ha-monach aleihem tahor u-vineihem tamei* — the stones themselves are in *tahor* space, and it is the area between them that is *tamei*. Two markers together clearly demarcate an area, and one may assume the stones stand at the edges with the grave between them. However, if the ground between the two stones was plowed — *haya charush be'ntayim* — one would not normally plow over a grave, so the two stones revert to the status of individual markers: *harey hen ki-yechidot*, with *tumah* assumed directly beneath each.

### Flesh vs Bones

A *Baraita* is now cited: *ein metzaynin al ha-basar* — one does not place a marker over human flesh that has no bones. The reason is *shema yitakel ha-basar* — lest the flesh decompose. Once the flesh is gone, the marker remains but the *tumah* does not, and the permanent marker will mislead people into thinking a location is *tamei* when it no longer is.

*Rabbi Yose bar Abun* posed a question before *Rabbi Mana*: *velo nimtza metamei teharot le-mafrea* — by declining to mark the location of flesh, will we not end up causing people to contract *tumah* unknowingly during the period before decomposition, treating themselves as *tahor* when they are in fact *tamei*? *Rabbi Mana* responded with a striking formulation: *mutav she-yitkalkelu vo la-sha'ah ve'al yitkalkelu vo le-olam* — it is preferable that there be a temporary period of error, during which people become *tamei* unknowingly, rather than establish a permanent error that causes people to treat themselves as *tamei* indefinitely when they are in fact *tahor*. This is a remarkable ruling: *Rabbi Mana* is willing to accept a *kula* — permitting people to be in a state of unwitting *tumah* for a limited time — in order to avoid an unnecessary permanent *chumra* that would wrongly restrict people forever.

---

## Kilayim Removal

### Original Uprooting

*Rav Yehuda* states — citing a *Baraita* — that the history of enforcing *kilayim* removal unfolded in three stages. The background is that when people failed to prevent errant seeds from growing in their fields — grape sprouts appearing among grain, for instance — the *beit din* would send inspectors to uproot the offending growth. In the first stage, *barishona hayu okrin umashlichin lifneihem* — they would uproot the *kilayim* and throw it down in front of the field owners. The owners, however, were delighted: *hayu smeichim she'yesh mocheh*. They were happy for two reasons. First, *achas she'hayu menachshin sadeoteihem* — the *beit din* was effectively weeding their fields for them, relieving them of the labor. Second, *ve'achas she'hayu nehenin min hakilayim* — they would then feed the uprooted growth to their animals and derive benefit from it, which, while perhaps technically permissible for *kilayim* that is not *kilei hakerem*, was nonetheless inappropriate behavior that the enforcement was inadvertently encouraging.

### Kilayim on Roads

Once *mishe-rabu ovrei aveira* — sinners multiplied and the perverse incentive became clear — the policy shifted: *hayu mashlichim al hadrahim* — they would throw the uprooted *kilayim* onto the public roads rather than in front of the owners, thereby preventing them from feeding it to their animals. Yet even this did not fully solve the problem: *hayu smeichim achas she'hayu menachshin sadeoteihem* — the owners were still happy, because the *beit din* was still doing their weeding for them.

### Field Becomes Hefker

The authorities therefore enacted a more severe measure: *hitkinu she'yehe mafkirin es kol hasadeh kullah* — they enacted that if a field was found to contain *kilayim*, the entire field would be declared *hefker*. Whether this meant the crops, the land itself, or both could be seized, the consequence was a genuine and serious financial penalty.

### Perverse Incentives

This sequence illustrates a broader phenomenon — one with a name in contemporary discourse — where a regulatory response to unwanted behavior produces the exact opposite of the intended effect. Each escalation in enforcement created a new perverse incentive: the *beit din*'s removal of *kilayim* was being exploited as a free agricultural service, and even throwing the growth into the road was insufficient. Only the threat of losing the entire field forced a change in behavior. It is the Talmudic enactment of *hefker* as a *knas* — a punitive fine — that finally produces the desired result.

---

## Hefker Beit Din

### Ezra's Proof

The *Mishnah*'s ruling that *beit din* can declare a field *hefker* as a penalty leads naturally into the classic principle of *hefker beis din hefker* — that property declared ownerless by *beit din* is indeed legally ownerless. The *Gemara* asks: *minayin she-hefker beis din hefker* — what is the source for this principle? The proof text comes from *Sefer Ezra*: *ve'chol asher lo yavo lishloshes yamim ba'atzas hasarim vehazkeinim yachoram kol rechusho vehu yibadel mikhal hagola* — whoever does not appear within three days, by the ruling of the leaders and elders, all his property shall be forfeited and he shall be expelled from the community. *Yachoram kol rechusho* — "all his property shall be banned" — is understood to mean that *beit din* can remove a person's ownership of property and render it available for anyone to take. This is explicitly a punitive context, a *knas*, and that is precisely the context of our *Mishnah* here.

It is worth noting that the *Bavli* applies *hefker beis din hefker* far more broadly, using it to validate ordinary *takkanot* of *beit din* in civil matters generally — not only punitive ones. But neither the *pasuk* from *Ezra* nor our *Mishnah* provides a basis for that broader application; both are squarely in the context of penalty.

### Ibbur Year Proof

The *Gemara* then asks: *minayin she-patur min hama'asrot* — how do we know that property declared *hefker* by *beit din* is exempt from *ma'asrot*? This might seem obvious — once something is *hefker* it is *hefker*, and all the normal consequences of *hefker* should follow. But the *Gemara* takes the question seriously.

*Rav Yonatan brei de'Rav Yitzchak bar Acha* attempts a proof from the following: *ein ma'avrin es hashana lo bisvi'is velo bemotzei shvi'is* — one does not add an intercalary month to a *shemittah* year or to the year following *shemittah*. The reason for not doing so in *shemittah* is that one does not want to extend the hardships of *shemittah* by an additional month. The reason in *motzei shvi'is* is that people desperately need the new grain, and adding a month delays the *Omer* offering and thereby postpones the permissibility of the new crop by an additional month. Nevertheless, *ve'im ibruha harei zu me'uberes* — if *beit din* did add such a month, the intercalation stands. And *vechodesh echad she'hu mosif lo patur min hama'asrot* — the added month, and anything that grows during it, is exempt from *ma'asrot*. Apparently, then, *beit din*'s act of adding a month is sufficient to create an exemption from *ma'asrot*.

### Refuting Ibbur Proof

*Rabbi Avun* rejects this proof decisively: *leit at shemia mineh klum* — you cannot derive anything from it. The reason *beit din* can add a month and thereby extend *shemittah* — resulting in an automatic exemption from *ma'asrot* — is not because of any general principle of *hefker beis din hefker*. It is because of the biblical mandate: *shamor es chodesh ha'aviv* — "observe the month of spring." *Beit din* has an explicit *mitzvah* to ensure that *Nissan* falls in its proper season. Their authority to intercalate derives directly from that *pasuk*, and the consequences of intercalation — including the extension of *shemittah* and the resulting *petur* from *ma'asrot* — flow from that biblical power, not from any act of *hefker*. The proof is therefore irrelevant to our question.

### Calendar Sync Condition

The *Gemara* had noted that *beit din* does not add an intercalary month in *shemittah* or *motzei shvi'is*. A clarification is offered by *Rav Mana*: *hada de'at amar barishona she'hayu hashanim ke'tiknan* — that rule applied in the early period, when the calendar years were properly synchronized. *Aval achshav she'einan hashanim ke'tiknan* — but now, when the calendar years are not in their proper alignment, *hi shemittah hi shel she'ar shenei shavua* — the same would apply to *shemittah* as to other years, meaning intercalation may proceed.

The meaning of "now the years are not properly aligned" has been understood in different ways. Some read it as referring to the period after the *Churban*, when *Yovel* was no longer observed and *shemittah* itself was perhaps only *derabanan* — though this reading is difficult since *shemittah* is observed even today. Others prefer a different *girsah*: not *hi she'shvi'is hi shel she'ar shenei shavua* but *hi shel motzei shvi'is hi shel she'ar shenei shavua* — meaning that *Rav Mana* is explaining specifically why *motzei shvi'is* can also have a month added: if an intercalation is being made, it is because the calendar genuinely requires it, the spring has not yet arrived, and therefore adding a month is warranted even in *motzei shvi'is*.

Additionally, *Rabbi Avun* had already noted a separate reason why intercalation in *shemittah* became permissible: *Rebbe* had relaxed the prohibition against importing vegetables from *chutz la'aretz*. Before that ruling, importing *chutz la'aretz* produce was forbidden — whether for reasons of *tumah* of *chutz la'aretz* soil or to support local agriculture. Once *Rebbe* permitted imports, the hardship of *shemittah* was substantially reduced, since one could continue eating imported vegetables even without domestically grown produce. The rationale for refusing to intercalate in *shemittah* — that it would extend the hardship — accordingly fell away.

### Leket Proof

Having rejected the *ibbur* proof, the *Gemara* asks: *ve'haida amar da* — where, then, is it actually demonstrated that *hefker beis din hefker* creates a *petur* from *ma'asrot*? The real proof comes from the following case: *gadi she'lo lukat tachtav kol ha-nogea ba'aretz harei hen shel aniyim* — a grain pile beneath which *leket* had not first been cleared. The *halachah* is that all the grain immediately touching the ground beneath the pile has the status of *leket*, which belongs to the poor. And since *leket* is *hefker*, it carries no obligation of *ma'asrot*. However, the *Gemara* recognizes that this is a rabbinic rule — biblically, not all the grain touching the ground is *leket*. This is therefore an enactment of the Rabbis, an act of *hefker beis din hefker*, and the fact that it generates a *petur* from *ma'asrot* demonstrates that *hefker beis din hefker* does indeed produce that consequence.

### Hefker Aniyim Dispute

*Rabbi Ami* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish* challenges this proof: *sedei Shammai hi zu* — that *halachah* follows only *Beit Shammai*. There is a famous dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* about *hefker la'aniyim* — whether one can declare property *hefker* selectively for the poor alone. *Beit Shammai* holds that *hefker* to a subset is valid *hefker*; *Beit Hillel* holds that true *hefker* must be available to everyone — one cannot remove ownership only toward the poor. According to *Beit Hillel*, therefore, grain that has been designated only for the *aniyim* never achieves the legal status of *hefker*, and the *aniyim* who take it would accordingly be required to separate *ma'aser* from it.

### Rabbinic Penalty Status

*Rabbi Yosei* resolves the difficulty: *shamanu she-patur min hama'aser divrei hakol mishum kensa* — everyone agrees, even *Beit Hillel*, that in this case the grain is exempt from *ma'aser*, and the reason is that it is a rabbinic *knas*. The debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* about *hefker la'aniyim* concerns a private individual's ability to make something *hefker* selectively. But what we have here is not a private individual's act — it is an enactment of *beit din*, an exercise of *hefker beis din hefker*, which is a fundamentally different category. Because it is a rabbinic penalty, it carries the full force of *hefker*, rendering the property completely ownerless — even if, practically, only the *aniyim* can collect it — and therefore even *Beit Hillel* would agree that no *ma'aser* is required. The *chiddush* being established here deserves emphasis: the principle of *hefker beis din hefker* does not merely mean that *beit din* has announced that anyone may take the property while the original owner retains ownership until someone does. Rather, the property is genuinely removed from the owner's possession before anyone takes it, achieving a true moment of ownerlessness — and it is that status which generates the *petur* from *ma'aser*.

---

## Shekel Collection

### 15th Adar: Changers

On the fifteenth of *Adar*, *shulchanot hayu yoshvin ba-medinah* — money changers were stationed throughout the towns and cities. This was done to make it convenient for people to exchange their currency for *machtzis ha-shekel*. The precise meaning of *medinah* here — whether it refers to *Yerushalayim* specifically or to the major population centers more broadly — involves some discussion, but the intent is accessibility.

### 25th Adar: Temple

On the twenty-fifth of *Adar*, *yoshvin ba-mikdash* — the money changers relocated to the *Beit HaMikdash*. This might seem counterintuitive: as the deadline approaches and urgency grows, why move the changers to fewer, more centralized locations rather than maintaining their broad distribution? One way to understand this is that by this point, the majority of the money had already been collected and was converging on *Yerushalayim* in any case. Those who had not yet paid would need to come to *Yerushalayim* to arrange their payment directly at the source. As one might say: if you register early, you can do it remotely; if you wait until the last moment, you have to come in person.

---

## Shekel Collection (II)

### Mashkon Seizure

From the time the money changers relocated to the *Mikdash*, enforcement intensified: *hitchilu le-mashken* — they began seizing property as collateral from those who had not yet paid. *Mashkon* refers to the taking of a pledge or lien — *beit din* would seize property and hold it until the *shekel* was paid. The goal was to ensure complete participation.

The *Mishnah* specifies who was subject to seizure: *leviyim ve-yisre'elim, gerim va-avadim meshuchrarim* — *Leviyim*, *Yisre'elim*, converts, and freed slaves. Any Jewish male adult, with defined exceptions, was subject to this enforcement.

### Kohanim Exempt

*Kohanim* were exempt from the seizure of their property, and the *Mishnah* offers one reason: *mipnei darchei shalom* — for the sake of peace. The *Kohanim* were the workers of the *Beit HaMikdash*, and seizing their property for contributions to the *Beit HaMikdash* would breed resentment and animosity. The sense of *darchei shalom* here is closely related to considerations of honor and dignity — a point the *Gemara* will restate as *darchei kavod*, ways of respect. One did not want the institution's own servants to be visibly subject to coercive enforcement. Women, slaves, and minors were also exempt — women and slaves because the *machtzis ha-shekel* obligation in the *Torah* is formulated for men, and minors because the obligation had not yet applied to them.

### Ben Bukhri Test

*Rabbi Yehuda* cites a testimony given by *Ben Bukhri* in *Yavneh* — the rabbinic center established after the *Churban* where sages with living memory of *Beit HaMikdash* practice convened to preserve that knowledge. *Ben Bukhri*'s formulation was: *kol kohen she-shokel eino chotei* — any *Kohen* who gave a *shekel* was not sinning. This implies that it was optional — one could give without transgressing, but one was not obligated. The framing presupposes that the *Kohanim* had made an argument that giving was actually problematic, and *Ben Bukhri* sought to counter at least part of that argument by establishing that giving was permissible.

### Kohanim Argument

The *Kohanim*'s argument was drawn from the verse *ve'chol minchat kohen kalil tihyeh lo te'achel* — any *minchah* of a *Kohen* must be completely burned and cannot be eaten. Their reasoning ran as follows: the communal sacrifices purchased with *shekalim* include the *Omer*, the *shtei ha-lechem*, and the *lechem ha-panim*. If the *Kohanim* contributed to the communal fund, they would hold ownership in those sacrifices. Since a *Kohen*'s *minchah* must be entirely burned, those communal *minchot* could no longer be eaten. In the interest of the *tzibbur*, they argued, the *Kohanim* must refrain from contributing their *shekel*. The argument has a certain psychological familiarity — much like a synagogue professional who reasons that his labor exempts him from financial contribution — but it served the *Kohanim*'s convenience remarkably well.

### RYBZ Response

*Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai*, the head of *Yavneh*, rejected *Ben Bukhri*'s formulation outright: *lo ki, ella kol kohen she'eino shokel chotei* — the correct position is the reverse: a *Kohen* who does *not* give a *shekel* is sinning. It is not that giving is optional; it is mandatory, and failure to give is a transgression. He acknowledged, however, the *Kohanim*'s interpretive move: *ella she-hakohanim dorshin mikra zeh le'atzman* — the *Kohanim* read this verse self-servingly, to their own benefit.

### Communal vs Private

The *Chachamim*'s rebuttal to the *Kohanim*'s argument turns on the fundamental distinction between private and communal sacrifices. The *Chachamim* argue: *chatat yachid meta, ein chatat tzibbur meta* — a private *chatat* whose owner dies must be left to die, but a communal *chatat* does not. This demonstrates that a communal sacrifice is not simply the aggregate of individual contributions — it is a categorically distinct entity, a corporate matter of the *tzibbur*. Similarly, *minchat yachid kareva kalil* — a private *Kohen*'s *minchah* is entirely burned — but this does not apply to a communal *minchah*. Once the *Kohanim*'s contributions are absorbed into the communal fund, they are no longer *Kohen* property in any relevant sense; ownership has transferred to the *tzibbur* as a distinct entity.

### Yehuda Objection

The *Gemara* raises a sharp objection: *meshivin le'adam davar she'eino modeh bo* — you cannot refute someone with a proof he does not accept. The proof from the *chatat* — the difference between a private *chatat* that must die and a communal *chatat* that does not — depends on a *halachah* that *Rabbi Yehuda* himself disputes. *Detnan: she'ein chatat tzibbur meta, Rabbi Yehuda omer tamus* — the *Mishnah* records that *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that a communal *chatat* also must be left to die. If *Rabbi Yehuda* does not concede the premise — that communal and private *chatat* differ in this respect — how can it serve as a proof against him?

The *Gemara* responds: even granting *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position, once an individual's contribution is handed over to the *tzibbur* — *keivan she-nimsar la-tzibbur ke'mi she-hu nidvas tzibbur* — it becomes communal property. It is no longer a proportional private stake in a shared asset; it has been subsumed into the collective. Therefore, even without conceding the *chatat* distinction, one can argue that the very act of contributing to the communal fund transforms the private contribution into a communal one, eliminating any basis for the *Kohanim*'s concern.

### Gematria Proof

An additional proof is offered by *Rabbi Berechiah*: the word *zeh* — "this is what they shall give" — has the *gematria* value of 12, representing the twelve tribes: *yud-bet shevatim yitnu* — all twelve tribes are obligated to give. This proof works against the *Kohanim*'s exemption, though it should be noted that the number twelve can be arrived at in more than one way given the complexities of tribal counting in the *Torah*.

### Pikudim Dispute

Finally, the *Gemara* presents a dispute between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Nechemia* on the meaning of *kol ha'over al ha-pikudim* — "all who pass through the counting." One opinion holds: *kol d'avar be'yama* — this refers to all who passed through the *Yam Suf*, meaning all *Bnei Yisrael* without exception are obligated to give. The other holds: *kol d'avar al pikudaya yitein* — only those included in *eileh ha-pekudim*, the standard census count, are obligated. Since the *Kohanim* — and the *Leviyim* — were counted separately in a distinct census, they would under this reading be excluded from the obligation entirely. This last view supports *Ben Bukhri*'s position, while the former supports *Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai*'s view that all of *Bnei Yisrael* — including the *Kohanim* — are obligated to give.

---

## Minor Exemptions

### Minor Definition

Returning to those exempt from the *mashkon* — the seizure of property — the *Mishnah* listed *katanim*, minors. The question of what constitutes a minor for purposes of the *machtzis ha-shekel* is answered by reference to the scriptural language of *me'esrim shanah va-ma'alah* — "from twenty years and above" — which appears in connection with the census and the *shekalim*. Under one *girsah*, a minor for this purpose is anyone under twenty, even if he has already reached halachic adulthood at thirteen.

### Paternal Obligation

Despite the minor's exemption, the *Mishnah* records: *ve'chol katan she-hitchil aviv lishkol al yado shuv eino posek* — any minor for whom the father has already begun to contribute, the father may not subsequently stop. Once the practice of giving on a son's behalf has been established, it has the force of a commitment that cannot simply be abandoned. This evokes the broader principle that once a practice has been undertaken three times it acquires a degree of binding force, though here the context is specifically the *machtzis ha-shekel*.

### Minor Seizure Rules

Although the minor's property is not subject to *mashkon* — forced seizure — the *Mishnah* indicates that contributions are still *requested* from a minor who has reached a certain threshold. Specifically, *hada deteimar bishetei se'arot* — this applies to one who has already grown two pubic hairs, signifying physical maturity and bar mitzvah status. Such a person is no longer a *katan* for other purposes and would therefore still be asked to contribute. But even so, his property is not seized.

The question of exactly when seizure becomes applicable is subject to a textual dispute. One *girsah* reads: *af al pi she-heivi shetei se'arot, ad she-yehei ben esrim* — even after developing two pubic hairs, property is not seized until he reaches twenty years of age. This is a striking *halachah*, suggesting that the *machtzis ha-shekel* obligation tracks a different threshold than ordinary halachic majority — following the *psukim* that speak explicitly of *me'esrim shanah va-ma'alah* rather than the standard bar mitzvah age of thirteen. Under an alternative *girsah* that lacks this condition, the two pubic hairs alone might be the operative threshold, though why they would be mentioned if the child has not yet reached thirteen remains difficult to explain.

---

---

# Shekalim 4

## Exemptions & Donations

### Kohanim Correction

We begin today with *daf* 4, picking up with the *mishna* at the bottom of 3b. Before proceeding, a brief correction to yesterday's reading of the final line preceding today's *mishna* is in order. The passage concerns the *Kohanim*'s claim that they were exempt from contributing the half-*shekel* on the grounds that doing so would render the communal *korban* a private one. The position of *Rav Ben Buchri* is that he challenged the *Chachamim* with the argument: *zu lo nidvas yachid* — is this not an individual donation? Would not the *Kohanim*'s contribution transform the *korban* into a private one? The *Chachamim*'s response is: *keivan she'nimtseru l'tzibur k'moshe hu nidvas tzibur* — once the funds are handed over for the communal *korban*, they become communal funds, regardless of their private origin. The *Kohanim*'s claim that they were exempt — a position associated with *Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai* — was therefore entirely without merit, even if self-servingly motivated. Once individual funds are designated for the communal offering, they assume the identity of communal property.

### Non-Seizure Rule

We now turn to the next *mishna*. *Af al pi she'amru ein memashkinin nashim va'avadim u'ketanim* — even though the rule is that one does not seize the property of women, slaves, and minors to compel payment of the half-*shekel*, since these individuals are not even obligated in the half-*shekel* to begin with. The property of free adult men, by contrast, could be seized as collateral once a certain period had passed without payment. But for the exempt categories — women, slaves, and minors — no *memashken* takes place.

### Voluntary Gifts

The *mishna* continues: *aval im shaklu mekablin mi'yadam* — but if they nonetheless wish to give voluntarily, their contribution is gladly accepted. Regarding *ketanim* specifically: as was noted in yesterday's discussion, once a minor reaches *bar mitzvah*, even though he is not obligated until the age of twenty — twenty being the age modeled after the *shekel* of the *Torah*, one of the rare areas in *halacha* where the age of twenty is halachically significant — one nonetheless encourages him to give. The present *mishna*, however, addresses those who are under *bar mitzvah*: we do not ask them to give, we will not be *memashken*, but if they wish to contribute, we accept their donation.

### Tosefta Mashal

The concept of *memashkenin* — seizing property — might initially seem incongruous in the context of contributing to the *korbanot*. The *Tosefta* in *Shekalim* (Perek 1, Tosefta 2) addresses this tension directly through a striking *mashal*. The *Tosefta* states: *mashkenu Yisrael al shikleihem k'dei she'yehu korbanot tzibur kreivin mei'hem* — the property of Israel was held as collateral so that the communal sacrifices would be brought from them. The *mashal* offered is that of a man who sustained an injury to his leg: *v'haya rofe kofeto u'mechattech b'visaro bishvil l'rafoso* — the doctor would bind him down and excise the infected flesh in order to heal him. So too, says God, we compel Israel to give their *shekel* — *k'dei she'yehu korbanot tzibur kreivin mei'hem mipnei she'korbanot tzibur mirtzin u'mechapprin bein Yisrael l'avihem she'bashamayim* — so that the communal sacrifices, which bring atonement and reconciliation between Israel and their Father in Heaven, will be brought from their own funds. The *mashal* captures something profound: what might appear coercive is in reality an intervention in Israel's deepest interest. The communal sacrifice is only truly communal — and thus truly atoning — when it is funded by all of Israel. The *memashken* ensures that each Jew has a genuine share in that offering, much as a physician's painful intervention serves the ultimate good of the patient.

---

## Non-Jewish Donors

### Shekel Rejection

The *mishna* now turns to an entirely different category: *ha'nochri v'ha'kuti she'shiklu ein mekablin mei'hen* — if a non-Jew or a Samaritan wishes to contribute their *shekel*, we do not accept it. This is not a general operating fund; the half-*shekel* goes directly toward the *korbanot tzibur*. The communal sacrifice by definition represents the Jewish community. Accepting contributions toward it from those outside the community would blur the very communal identity that the *korban tzibur* is meant to express. The *mishna* further specifies that we do not accept from them *kinei zavin v'kinei zavot* — bird offerings for a *zav* and a *zavah* — nor *kinei yoledet*, bird offerings for a woman who gave birth, nor *chatat* and *asham* offerings.

### Voluntary vs Obligatory

The operative principle is formulated clearly: *ze ha'klal — kol she'niddar v'nidav mekablin miyadan*, anything that is a *neder* or *nedavah*, a vow or free-will offering, we accept from them. *Kol she'eino niddar v'nidav, ein mekablin miyadan* — anything that is obligatory in nature, including the *shekel* itself, we do not accept.
