The distinction is between voluntary offerings, which a non-Jew may bring to acknowledge the God of Israel, and obligatory sacrifices, which are the expression of one's membership in the Jewish covenantal community. The former are welcomed; the latter are refused.

### Nidur Nidav Rule

The logic underlying this distinction bears emphasis. Obligatory sacrifices — *chatat*, *asham*, the birds of *zav* and *yoledet* — are intrinsically tied to a framework of Jewish religious obligation and identity. The *shekel* too, while a monetary contribution rather than an animal offering, partakes of this obligatory character. Accepting such contributions from non-Jews or Samaritans would imply that these individuals are members of the community whose obligations they are fulfilling — a claim the *mishna* categorically rejects.

### Ezra Precedent

The biblical grounding for this rejection is drawn from the book of *Ezra*: *lo lachem velanu livnot bayit l'Eloheinu* — "It is not for you and for us to build a house for our God." When the returnees from Babylonian exile began rebuilding the *Beit Hamikdash*, and the Samaritans offered to participate, they were refused. The Samaritans at that period presented themselves as willing partners, but the leadership of the Jewish community drew a sharp communal boundary. The concern was not merely abstract: accepting Samaritan funds for the *Beit Hamikdash* would have given them grounds to claim a stake in the Temple — that it was not solely a Jewish institution but a Samaritan one as well. The *mishna* invokes this precedent to anchor its own rejection of such contributions in explicit *pesukim*. While, as the *Gemara* will discuss, there are *Tannaic* opinions that Samaritans may hold a form of Jewish status, the communal dimension of the question — how a community defines its own boundaries — operates on a different register from the abstract question of individual personal status.

---

## Kolbon Fee

### Kolbon Obligation

The *mishna* now turns to an entirely distinct subject: the *kolbon*. The *kolbon* is a small surcharge — a money-changer's commission — paid when contributing the half-*shekel*. The practical context is that if one brings a full *sela* rather than an exact half-*shekel*, change must be made, and a fee is taken. More precisely — as will emerge from the analysis — it functions as a transaction fee rather than purely a change-making fee. The following are obligated in the *kolbon*: *Leviyim, Yisraeliyim, geirim*, and freed slaves — in short, all who are obligated in the half-*shekel*. Exempt are *Kohanim*, women, slaves, and minors.

### Kohanim Exempt

The exemptions for women, slaves, and minors are readily understood: they are exempt from the *shekel* obligation entirely, and if they choose to contribute voluntarily, we would not impose an additional surcharge. The exemption of *Kohanim*, however, requires a word of explanation. As discussed earlier, the *Kohanim* — according to *Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai* — are actually obligated in the half-*shekel*. Yet we do not seize their property to compel payment, out of *kavod*, a form of professional courtesy, so as not to publicly embarrass those who serve in the Temple. In the same spirit, we waive the *kolbon* fee for *Kohanim* even though they are technically obligated. The *Kohanim*, in any case, were already resistant to contributing; demanding a surcharge on top of their contribution would only further antagonize them.

Importantly, the money changers who collected the *kolbon* were not independent operators who could set their own commission. They were employees of the *Beit Hamikdash*, operating at the direction of the Temple administration. It was therefore within the institution's authority to waive the fee for certain categories of contributors.

*Ha'shokel al yedei Kohen al yedei isha al yedei eved al yedei katan patur* — if one gives a whole *shekel* on behalf of oneself and an exempt individual — say, oneself and a *Kohen*, or oneself and one's wife — one is exempt from the *kolbon*. The reasoning here is twofold: first, the other party would not have been subject to a *kolbon* had they contributed independently; second, one has given an exact *shekel* and no change need be made. One effectively piggybacks on the exemption of the party on whose behalf one is paying.

### Joint Payment

*V'im shakal al yado v'al yedei chavero chayav bekolbon echad* — but if one pays a full *shekel* for oneself and an obligated partner, one owes one *kolbon*, even though no change needs to be made and the payment is made in a single transaction. This is counterintuitive: if the logic of the *kolbon* were purely about the cost of making change, then a bundled payment should attract no fee at all. The better way to understand the *kolbon*, as emerges from this case, is as a transaction fee — not unlike a processing fee charged whenever a financial transaction takes place, regardless of whether change is made. Even when two people combine their payment into one efficient transaction, a single transaction fee remains due. What they save is the second fee; they do not escape the first. And when one bundles a contribution with an exempt party, one escapes the fee entirely by virtue of that party's exemption.

The case of *ha'noten sela v'notel shekel* — one who gives a full *sela* and receives back a half-*shekel* as change — incurs two *kolbonot*. On the transaction-fee understanding, this is intelligible: there is the standard transaction fee for the act of contributing, and there is an additional fee for the actual making of change.

---

## Kolbon Amount

### Fee Type

The *mishna* specifies the amount of the *kolbon*: *ma'ah kesef*, divrei *Rabbi Meir* — a *ma'ah*, which is a twenty-fourth of a *sela* and thus a twelfth of the half-*shekel*, according to *Rabbi Meir*. *Vachachamim omrim chatzi ma'ah* — the *Chachamim* say it is half a *ma'ah*, which amounts to approximately four percent of the half-*shekel*. Four percent is a meaningful surcharge; the typical money-changer's commission in other contexts was likely lower.

There is a further dispute regarding the destination of these collected *kolbon* funds. *Rabbi Meir* holds that the *kolbon* monies go to the same fund as the *shekel* itself — toward the *korbanot tzibur*. The *Chachamim*, by contrast, hold that it goes to the *shulchani* — to the money changer — or to other Temple funds. This dispute reflects a deeper disagreement about the nature of the *kolbon*: if it is truly an integral part of the *shekel* obligation (as *Rabbi Meir* maintains), it makes sense that it flows to the same purpose; if it is merely a service charge, it would naturally be directed elsewhere.

---

## Kolbon Fee (II)

### Rabbi Meir Dissent

*Rabbi Meir omer shenei kolbonot* — *Rabbi Meir* holds that even in the case of two individuals contributing jointly in a single transaction, two *kolbonot* must be paid rather than one. The *Gemara* will explain the basis of *Rabbi Meir*'s position at greater length in a later passage. In brief, *Rabbi Meir* holds that the *kolbon* is not merely a transaction fee but an inherent supplement to every half-*shekel* — a small margin added to ensure that the full, pure amount of the divine standard has been met. On this view, each half-*shekel* individually requires its own *kolbon*, and combining two contributions into a single payment does not merge the two separate obligations into one.

### Charity Waiver

*Ha'shokel al yedei ani v'al yedei shecheino v'al yedei ben iro patur* — one who pays on behalf of a poor person, a neighbor, or a fellow townsman — where the intent is genuine charitable giving rather than a lending arrangement — is exempt from the *kolbon*. The distinction from the earlier case of joint payment is meaningful: when two obligated individuals combine their contributions, both are truly giving, and the *kolbon* attaches to both. But when one person is simply being a *tzaddik* and paying on behalf of another without any expectation of repayment, that generosity exempts the payer from the surcharge. *V'im hilvan* — if, however, it turns out that one was merely lending the other the money, such that the recipient remains responsible for repayment, then the earlier rule applies and the *kolbon* is owed.

---

## Estate Partnership

### Undivided Estate

*Ha'achim hashutafin shechayavim bakolbon paturim mima'aser behema* — brothers who are partners — in the sense of an undivided inherited estate — and who are obligated in the *kolbon*, are exempt from *ma'aser behema*. The *mishna* here invokes one of the few contexts in *halacha* that recognizes something approximating the concept of a corporate entity. An estate that has not yet been divided among the heirs is not a conventional partnership between distinct individuals; it functions as a single unified entity. The animals belonging to such an undivided estate are subject to *ma'aser behema* as though they are owned by one entity. Conversely, such an estate, even if it must contribute multiple half-*shekalim* on behalf of each of the brothers, is treated as a single entity for purposes of the *kolbon* and is therefore exempt from paying multiple *kolbonot*. The analogy that some *meforshim* draw is to a father who pays on behalf of his children: just as a father's payment on his children's behalf does not multiply the *kolbon*, the estate's payment on behalf of the brothers does not multiply the fee.

### Corporate Entity

The inverse is also stated: *k'shechayavim b'ma'aser behema paturim min hakolbon* — when they are subject to *ma'aser behema* (that is, when the estate exists as a unified entity), they are correspondingly exempt from multiple *kolbonot*. The two obligations track one another: the status of the undivided estate as a single legal entity determines both its liability for *ma'aser behema* and its exemption from multiple *kolbon* payments.

### Partnership Corp

If, however, the brothers divided the estate and subsequently regrouped as a conventional partnership, the picture changes. A conventional partnership — as opposed to an undivided estate — is *patur* from *ma'aser behema* (since it is a *shutafut* of distinct individuals), but is *chayav* in the *kolbon*, because the partners are now multiple individuals who happen to be acting jointly, rather than a single corporate entity. It is worth noting that while most *meforshim* read *achim hashutafin* as a single case, the *Rambam* reads the phrase as referring to two distinct cases. The *Rambam* goes further and allows that an ordinary partnership — not only an undivided estate — can, under certain conditions, function as a corporate entity for these purposes. This is a striking position: the concept of a legal corporation, with all that it implies about the separate legal identity of the entity from its individual members, is exceedingly difficult to locate in *halachic* literature. That the *Rambam* finds room for it here is a matter of considerable interest.

---

## Kolbon Amount (II)

### Amount Dispute

As already quoted, the *mishna*'s definition of the *kolbon* amount is: *ma'ah kesef*, according to *Rabbi Meir*, and *chatzi ma'ah* according to the *Chachamim*. The *sela* is the full *shekel* of the *Torah*; the *shekel* in the language of the *Mishnah* refers to the half-*shekel* of the *Torah*. A *ma'ah* is a twenty-fourth of a *sela*, making it a twelfth of the half-*shekel*. A *chatzi ma'ah*, the *Chachamim*'s figure, is thus a twenty-fourth of the half-*shekel*, yielding approximately four percent. On the *Chachamim*'s view, the *kolbon* is a modest surcharge. On *Rabbi Meir*'s view, it is somewhat more substantial — and, as we shall see, carries a deeper theological significance.

---

## Samaritan Status

### Rabbi Ba Opinion

The *Gemara* now takes up the question of Samaritan status in greater depth. *Amar Rabbi Ba: tipater keman de'amar kuti kanochri* — the *mishna*'s ruling regarding Samaritans can be explained according to the opinion that a *kuti* has the status of a non-Jew. This is, however, a disputed position.

### Rebbi & Gamliel

The relevant *Tannaic* dispute is stated directly: *kuti kanochri divrei Rebbi* — Rebbi holds that Samaritans are like non-Jews in legal status, having not genuinely converted. *Rabban Gamliel omer kuti kiyisrael lechol davar* — Rabban Gamliel, by contrast, holds that Samaritans are to be treated as Jews in every respect.

### Rabbi Elazar View

*Amar Rabbi Elazar: matnitin banochri — habakutim lo* — Rabbi Elazar offers a more nuanced reading. The *mishna*, he argues, is speaking about non-Jews in its relevant provisions; with respect to Samaritans, the rules are different. On Rabbi Elazar's reading, Samaritans may well be Jewish in their individual status, but the context of *korbanot tzibur* and the communal *shekel* is governed by a different logic: even if Samaritans are technically Jews, the fact that they organized themselves as a distinct and often antagonistic community — as the episode in *Ezra* makes plain — justifies excluding them from communal boundaries even where their individual status might warrant inclusion. On the other hand, if a Samaritan presents himself as an individual wishing to bring an obligatory *korban*, Rabbi Elazar would accept it.

This position is reflected in the *Rambam*'s ruling as well. The *Rambam* holds that while Samaritans are excluded from the communal *shekel*, if a Samaritan brings a *korban chatat* — an obligatory sacrifice — it is accepted from him. The reasoning is that one should leave open the possibility that such an individual may wish to do *teshuva* and rejoin the broader Jewish community. This represents a fascinating interplay between the question of individual halachic status and the management of communal boundaries: the latter may be drawn more strictly than the former strictly requires, while still leaving certain doors open at the individual level.

The *Gemara* then cites the *drasha* on the word *adam* from the beginning of *Vayikra*: *adam ki yakriv mikem korban la-Hashem — adam lerabbos es hagerim*, the word *adam* comes to include *gerim*. That this needs to be derived through a *drasha* is itself somewhat notable, given that the Torah equates a *ger* with a native in numerous other contexts. An alternative version of the *drasha* reads *adam afilu nochrim* — even a non-Jew can bring a *korban*, consistent with our *mishna*'s ruling that free-will offerings are accepted from non-Jews. *Mikem*, "from among you," then serves to exclude apostates: *lehotzi es hamumrim* — an apostate cannot bring a *korban*. The *Korban HaEdah* suggests that *gerim* in this *drasha* would obviously include *Kutim*, though as the *Gemara* itself acknowledges, that somewhat begs the question of Samaritan status.

---

## Meir's Principle (III)

### Adam Derasha

The *drasha* on *adam ki yakriv mikem* thus establishes a range: *gerim* are included in the category of those who may bring offerings; apostates are excluded. The non-Jew occupies an intermediate position — welcome to bring a free-will *olah*, but unable to participate in obligatory communal offerings or the communal *shekel*. The *mikem* exclusion of apostates is particularly striking: the apostate, who was born Jewish, is denied a status that the voluntary *ger* and even the non-Jewish stranger enjoy. The internal logic of communal belonging, as these *derashot* articulate it, turns on commitment to the covenant — not merely biological origin.

---

## Meir's Principle (III)

### Gemara Parse

The *Gemara* now returns to parse the *mishna*'s ruling on non-Jews and Samaritans more precisely. The difficulty is that the *mishna* appears to address both non-Jews and Samaritans simultaneously throughout, while Rabbi Elazar's position requires the *mishna* to be read as addressing different groups in different clauses.

---

## Samaritan Status (II)

### Gemara Challenge

*Matnisin palig al Rabbi Eliezer* — the *Gemara* argues that the *mishna* itself contradicts Rabbi Elazar's position. Rabbi Elazar claims that the second portion of the *mishna* — the section listing obligatory sacrifices that are not accepted — addresses only non-Jews. The *Gemara* challenges this: *vechi yesh kinei zavim vezavot banochrim?* Do non-Jews even have the category of *zav* and *zavah*? These are categories of ritual impurity that simply do not apply to non-Jews. If the *mishna* says we do not accept the bird offerings associated with these conditions, it cannot be addressing non-Jews — for whom such offerings are entirely irrelevant. It must therefore be addressing Samaritans, for whom these categories do apply and from whom one might have thought such offerings would be accepted.

### Reisha Seifa

This leads to the *Gemara*'s resolution: *ella reisha banochrim vesifa beKutim* — the beginning of the *mishna* addresses non-Jews, and the end addresses Samaritans. The text invites the question of whether this division is satisfactory: *kein hu?* Is it truly the case that the beginning is about non-Jews and the end about Samaritans? And the *Gemara* affirms: *kein hu — reisha banochrim vesifa beKutim*.

This reading, however, creates its own difficulties. The beginning of the *mishna* explicitly lists both non-Jews and Samaritans together: *ha'nochri v'ha'kuti she'shiklu ein mekablin mei'hen*. To say the beginning is exclusively about non-Jews requires reading the explicit mention of *kuti* in the opening clause as part of the second section, which governs Samaritans. The best reading offered by the *meforshim* is that the *mishna* as a whole excludes both non-Jews and Samaritans from everything — the *shekel*, and the obligatory bird offerings alike. The beginning mentions both, and the end addresses Samaritans specifically with respect to the category of obligatory bird offerings, where one might have expected a more permissive ruling. Even so, fitting Rabbi Elazar's position into this framework remains a genuine challenge. It appears that the *mishna* explicitly refuses to distinguish between non-Jews and Samaritans in the way Rabbi Elazar would prefer. That said, the *Rambam* rules effectively in line with Rabbi Elazar — accepting an obligatory *korban chatat* from a Samaritan — suggesting that however he reads this *Gemara*, he does not consider the *mishna* to have definitively foreclosed that position.

---

## Stages & Specificity

### Yochanan Position

The *Gemara* now shifts to a related but distinct question: the basis on which contributions from non-Jews may be accepted or refused, depending on the stage of construction and the specificity of the donation. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan: batchila ein mekablin meihem lo davar mesuyam velo davar she'eino mesuyam* — at the outset, meaning when construction is beginning (as in the case of *Ezra* and the initial building of the *Beit Hamikdash*), we accept neither a *davar mesuyam* nor a *davar she'eino mesuyam* from non-Jews. A *davar mesuyam* is a designated, specific object — "I want to donate this *menorah* and have it placed at the entrance with my name on it." A *davar she'eino mesuyam* is general funds, fungible money with no specific designation. At the outset, Rabbi Yochanan holds, neither is accepted.

*Uvesof*, however — once the *Beit Hamikdash* is built and established, and its Jewish identity is beyond dispute — *mekablin meihem davar she'eino mesuyam*, we may accept general, undesignated funds from non-Jews. What we cannot accept even then is a *davar mesuyam*: a specific, named donation that would allow the donor to claim a proprietary connection to a particular feature of the Temple. The concern with a *davar mesuyam* is precisely that it creates a lasting association between the donor and the sacred object — a plaque, an inscription, a named installation — which implies a stake in the institution's identity.

### Reish Lakish

*Reish Lakish* takes a considerably more stringent position: *bein batchila bein besof ein mekablin meihem lo davar mesuyam velo davar she'eino mesuyam* — whether at the beginning or at the end, we accept from them neither specific nor non-specific contributions. Reish Lakish would refuse all monetary donations from non-Jews to the Temple, regardless of their form or timing. This is a remarkably exacting standard; it would have made the practical management of the Temple's finances quite demanding, given the degree of interaction between Jewish and non-Jewish communities that we know existed in this period. Archaeological evidence from synagogues in *Eretz Yisrael*, for instance, sometimes includes inscriptions suggesting non-Jewish donors — suggesting that on the ground, a position closer to Rabbi Yochanan's may have prevailed.

### Braita Bedek

A *braita* is then introduced: *ein mekablin meihem hekdesh unedava l'vedek habayit* — we do not accept from non-Jews sanctified objects or donations designated for *bedek habayit*, Temple maintenance and repair funds. The *braita* makes no distinction between *davar mesuyam* and *davar she'eino mesuyam*, and makes no distinction between the beginning and the end of the construction process. This appears to contradict Rabbi Yochanan's position, which permits non-specific contributions after the Temple is built. The *Gemara* therefore attempts to resolve the tension: *patar la* — explain it as speaking of *davar mesuyam*, of concrete, specific designated objects. The *braita*'s prohibition, on this reading, is limited to specific objects intended for *bedek habayit*, not to generic funds. This would preserve Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between specific and non-specific donations even in the context of maintenance funds.

### Generic Funds

The *Gemara* then turns to the question of what happens when non-specific funds end up being used for specific purposes. The case of *nesachim* is raised: if a non-Jew brings a free-will *olah* — which Rabbi Yochanan and even Reish Lakish would accept, as established earlier — accompanying *nesachim* (wine and flour) are required. *U'motar nesachim lo li-chlei shareit inun?* The principle is that surplus *nesachim* funds are redirected toward purchasing *klei shareit*, sacred Temple vessels. If we accept the non-Jew's *olah* along with its *nesachim*, we may wind up using the surplus to buy a specific object — a *davar mesuyam*. How can this be permitted even according to Rabbi Yochanan?

*Heitiv Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Bun*: a related challenge is raised from the laws of *arachin*. The opinion that allows non-Jews to make an *erech* — declaring the monetary value of a person as a donation — directs those funds to *bedek habayit*. Even according to Reish Lakish, how is it possible that a non-Jew's *erech* funds, which go to *bedek habayit*, are permissible?

The resolution is: *li-shemayim hu mitkavein u-mei-aleihem heim ba'im o l'vedek habayit o l'chlei shareit* — the donor's intent is directed toward heaven in a general sense; he is giving a *korban* or a donation without specifying where the funds should go. We then decide how to allocate the money — whether to operating funds, *bedek habayit*, or *klei shareit*. Because the donor cannot claim ownership over or association with any specific object purchased with the funds, the concern that motivates the prohibition does not apply. The same logic resolves the *nesachim* case: the non-Jew intends to bring his *olah*, and the allocation of surplus *nesachim* funds is our decision, not his. He cannot claim that his money went to purchase any specific vessel.

### Reish Lakish Standard

On Reish Lakish's view, it emerges that his objection is more precisely targeted than it first appears. The *pasuk* that underlies the prohibition — *lo lachem velanu livnot bayit l'Eloheinu* — is specifically about construction of the house. Reish Lakish's concern, even regarding *davar she'eino mesuyam*, is limited to funds that actually contribute to the building or structure itself. Generic operating funds — funds that, from the donor's perspective, are simply an offering directed to heaven with no connection to any specific structure or object — Reish Lakish is prepared to accept. The critical factor is whether the donor can claim a stake in the *bayit* itself. When the money is genuinely generic and could be used for anything at all, Reish Lakish's concern does not apply and he would accept it. When it goes, even indirectly, to the construction of the building, the prohibition of *lo lachem velanu livnot bayit* is triggered.

The practical upshot is that both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish agree that a specifically designated donation — a *davar mesuyam* — is never acceptable from a non-Jew. Rabbi Yochanan permits non-specific donations after construction is complete; Reish Lakish limits even that, refusing non-specific donations that are directed toward the structure, while permitting fully generic contributions. In both cases, the decisive factor is whether the donor can assert a proprietary claim over any identifiable element of the *Beit Hamikdash*.

---

## Meir's Principle (III)

### Divine Standard

The *Gemara* finally returns to the basis of *Rabbi Meir*'s position on the *kolbon*. *Kasavar Rabbi Meir benoten shiklo shalem shehu chayav bekalbon* — Rabbi Meir holds that even one who pays a standard half-*shekel*, without requiring any change, is nonetheless obligated in the *kolbon*. The reason: *kemin matbe'a shel esh hotzi hakadosh baruch hu mitachat kisei kevodo v'her'ahu l'Moshe v'amar lo: zeh yitnu* — the Holy One, Blessed be He, drew forth something resembling a coin of fire from beneath His Throne of Glory and showed it to Moshe, saying: "This shall they give." The implication of *zeh*, "this" — the divine, perfectly pure half-*shekel* of fire — is that nothing produced in this physical world can meet that standard of purity without some supplementation. Every material coin carries impurities that fall short of the divine ideal. Therefore, *Rabbi Meir* holds, every half-*shekel* must be accompanied by a small additional amount — the *kolbon* — to ensure that the full, true value of the divine standard has been honored. This is not a transaction fee in Rabbi Meir's understanding; it is a built-in margin of error required by the metaphysical gap between the earthly coin and its heavenly archetype.

This is why, in *Rabbi Meir*'s view, when one gives a full *sela* and receives a half-*shekel* in change, two *kolbonot* are owed: one is the ordinary transaction fee (as the *Chachamim* would also acknowledge), and one is the supplemental amount that accompanies every half-*shekel* by Rabbi Meir's own principle. And this is also why *Rabbi Meir* directs the *kolbon* funds to the same destination as the *shekel* itself — toward the *korbanot tzibur* — since the *kolbon*, on his view, is not a service charge but an integral extension of the *shekel* obligation, required by the very nature of what the *shekel* represents.

---

---

# Shekalim 5

## Double Kolbonot

### Meir: Two Fees

We pick up in the middle of 4b, dealing with a ruling in the *mishnah* concerning Rabbi Meir. Even when someone pays a full *shekel* on behalf of himself and another person, Rabbi Meir insists on two *kolbonot* — two separate fees. The *gemara* establishes that Rabbi Meir's position is that even someone who pays a straight half-*shekel* owes a fee. This is grounded in the idea that the *shekel* of fire that God showed Moshe — the half-*shekel* — must be perfectly pure. Since every real-world, non-Platonic half-*shekel* is somewhat less than perfect, a rounding fee is required. That is Rabbi Meir's rationale.

The *mishnah* then continues to a new case: *natan sela ve'notal shekel* — you gave a *sela* and received back a *shekel*. The terminology here is confusing: in the *mishnah*'s usage, a *sela* is a biblical *shekel*, and a *shekel* is a half-*shekel*. In practical terms, you gave a whole *shekel* and received back a half-*shekel* as change. The *mishnah* rules *chayav sheni kolbonot* — you are obligated in two *kolbonot*. This seems counterintuitive. One might assume this is simply a normal transaction — you give a whole and receive back a half — and that only one fee should apply.

### Rounding vs. Transaction

Why, then, does the *mishnah* require two fees? There are in fact two distinct rationales operating simultaneously. One *kolbon* is the standard rounding fee that Rabbi Meir requires any time a half-*shekel* is paid — the fee for the slight impurity of every real-world coin relative to the Platonic ideal. The second *kolbon* is a transaction fee, a service charge for the act of exchange itself. These are conceptually separate obligations: one concerns the nature of the coin, the other concerns the mechanics of the transaction.

### Attribution & Tosefta

Rabbi Elazar states: *amar Rabbi Elazar Rabbi Meir hee* — that line of the *mishnah* follows Rabbi Meir's opinion. It might seem surprising that a line appearing in the body of the *stam mishnah* should be attributed to a single named authority rather than representing the consensus position. However, the *Tosefta* explicitly identifies it as *divrei Rabbi Meir*, confirming Rabbi Elazar's attribution. Sometimes what we encounter in the Yerushalmi — as in the Bavli — is a citation of the beginning of a passage where the proof is actually located at the end. So here, the demonstration is not merely inferential — not simply that since Rabbi Meir always requires a fee for a straight half-*shekel*, he would require two in this exchange scenario — but that the *Tosefta* explicitly states, regarding the case of giving a whole and receiving back a half, that two *kolbonot* are required, *divrei Rabbi Meir*, which is precisely what Rabbi Elazar is asserting.

A *baraita* is then cited — *de'tanya* — which essentially quotes our *mishnah* and notes that if one pays on behalf of two people, the standard position is *kolbon echad*, one fee. Rabbi Meir, however, says *sheni kolbonot*, two fees. This confirms that Rabbi Meir's view is that every half-*shekel* payment carries its own standard fee, so that a full *shekel* given for two people incurs two *kolbonot*.

### Three Fees Total

The *gemara* then introduces a further position attributed to Rav, which is really presenting Rabbi Meir's view in a more developed form. Rav states: *al date'ih d'Rav gimel kolbonot inun* — according to Rav, meaning according to Rabbi Meir, the exchange scenario would actually produce not two *kolbonot* but three. This is also transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yirmiyah and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak: *echad she'ata noten v'echad she'ata notel v'echad l'dvar Torah* — one for the act of giving the whole coin, one for the act of receiving back the half, and one as the standard biblical-derived fee that always accompanies any half-*shekel* payment.

The *chachamim*, by contrast, would explain the *mishnah*'s ruling of two *kolbonot* as follows: a straight half-*shekel* by itself carries no fee according to the *chachamim*, but when you give a whole and receive change, you pay one *kolbon* for each side of the exchange transaction — one for giving, one for receiving. Why that bilateral transaction generates two fees while a unilateral payment generates none is, frankly, not fully transparent, and the *mefarshim* do not appear to resolve it in a manner that fully satisfies. The candid acknowledgment here is that the logic remains somewhat elusive.

---

## Chachamim Position

### Chachamim: Two Fees

The *chachamim*'s position, as just outlined, holds that the two *kolbonot* required when giving a whole *shekel* and receiving a half back are both transaction fees — one assessed for giving too much, and one for receiving the change. There is no additional biblically-derived rounding fee in this framework, since the *chachamim* do not accept Rabbi Meir's premise that every half-*shekel* payment independently incurs a fee. The structural tension in the *chachamim*'s position — why a two-sided exchange generates two fees while a straightforward payment generates none — remains genuinely difficult to resolve.

### Bavli Layer Issue

This is an appropriate moment to address a broader textual issue that bears on our learning throughout Shekalim. The doubling of language we have observed in this passage — where formulations appear to be repeated in slightly varied form, and certain transitions feel more abrupt than the *stam* of the Bavli typically produces — is not simply a stylistic feature of the Yerushalmi. There is a more fundamental explanation, rooted in a specific phenomenon affecting the text of Yerushalmi Shekalim in particular.

It has been noted that in an exchange with Professor Seth Schwartz, he mentioned that the Yerushalmi Shekalim has been heavily influenced by the Bavli. This points to a significant matter of *mesorah* and textual transmission.

### Sussman Manuscript

The great Yerushalmi scholar Sussman — who authored the introduction to the new edition transcribing the Ktav Yad Leiden — conducted a study some thirty years ago in which he demonstrated that the Yerushalmi as it appears in our printed text has two distinct layers. There is the original Yerushalmi layer, and a second layer that was heavily influenced by the Bavli and became integrated into the text. The specific circumstances of this integration appear connected to the decision to include Shekalim — the one tractate of *Moed* without its own Bavli — within the printed Bavli editions alongside the Yerushalmi text. In that process, some additional version, gloss, or parallel material became grafted onto the original, producing the composite Bavli-influenced layer visible in our current Yerushalmi Shekalim. The new transcription of the Ktav Yad Leiden makes this two-layer structure clearly visible. When the text appears to duplicate itself, or when transitions seem jarring, readers should be aware that this phenomenon of textual layering is a documented feature of this particular tractate.

---

## Brothers & Estates

### Partners Status

The *mishnah* turns to the case of *ha'achin ve'hashutafin* — the brothers and partners. Although the *Rambam* reads this as two distinct cases, the more natural reading treats it as a compound term, brothers who are also partners, that is, brother-partners. The *mishnah* states that those obligated in the *kolbon* are exempt from *ma'aser behemah*, and those obligated in *ma'aser behemah* are exempt from the *kolbon*.

The underlying logic is as follows. Obligation in the *kolbon* signals that you are treated as individuals rather than as a corporate entity. A standard partnership of multiple individuals is *chayav* in the *kolbon* — each individual who pays on behalf of others must pay a *kolbon* — but is exempt from *ma'aser behemah*, since *shutafut*, partnership, is exempt from *ma'aser behemah*. Conversely, exemption from the *kolbon* and obligation in *ma'aser behemah* reflects treatment as a corporate entity.

### Division & Return

The operative case is *beshe'hilku ve'chazru ve'nishtattfu* — they divided the estate and then chose to re-enter partnership. Having divided, each person's share is now private property. They then partner as individuals. That is a normal partnership: *chayav* in the *kolbon* as a collection of individuals, and exempt from *ma'aser behemah*. The reverse — *beshe'lo hilku*, they never divided — represents the one case in *halachah* that recognizes something analogous to a corporation rather than a partnership. An undivided estate exists as a unified entity, not merely as a sum of individual partners. In that case, the estate is treated as one body: exempt from the *kolbon* as a single entity, but *chayav* in *ma'aser behemah*.

### Breira Conditions

Rabbi Elazar introduces a significant qualification: the rule that dividing and then reconstituting yields a partnership rather than a reconstituted estate applies only when the division was *not* along symmetric lines — for example, one brother took the kid goats (*gedayim*) and the other took the adult male goats (*tyashim*), or the reverse. But if the division was symmetric — *gedayim k'neged gedayim, tyashim k'neged tyashim*, each party taking half of each category — then *hu chelko mish'at rishonah*, that is the portion that was always coming to that person from the moment of inheritance. This is the principle known in the Bavli as *yesh breira*: does a subsequent division retroactively clarify what was always each party's portion?

The point is subtle. When brothers inherit an estate, we might conceptualize each as holding an undivided fifty percent of every item. When they then divide the estate, if one takes the house and the other takes the car, there has clearly been a transaction — a swap of respective undivided interests — and the division has created something new. But if they split every category exactly in half, so that each takes the half of each type that was always naturally coming to him, then one might argue that no real transaction occurred, and that the division simply made explicit what was already implicit. That retroactive clarification — that this was always my portion — is the core of *breira*.

This generates important practical consequences. First, regarding the reconstitution of the estate: if the initial split was genuinely transactional, then when the brothers subsequently reunite their holdings, they have created a new partnership, not reconstituted the old corporate estate. But if the split was a natural taking of predetermined halves, then when they re-pool the assets, one might argue they have simply reverted to the original entity.

Second, and more concretely, there is the *halachah* of *lakuach*: animals that were purchased, as opposed to raised from birth in one's possession, are exempt from *ma'aser behemah*. If we view the division of the estate as a transaction — essentially a swap of undivided interests — then the animals each brother received are considered *lakuach* and exempt from *ma'aser behemah*. If, however, we view the equal split as merely a realization of each party's pre-existing share with no transaction taking place, then the animals carry no *lakuach* status and remain *chayav* in *ma'aser behemah*.

The term *breira* in this context might seem an imprecise application of the concept as it appears in other discussions, where it means explicitly that a later act reveals what was always the status of the earlier designation. Here the underlying logic is similar: we can only say that no barter occurred and that each party naturally received his inherent portion if we can retroactively say that this portion was always his. That is a form of *breira*, even if less dramatic than its other applications.

### Yochanan Rejects

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. Even in the case of a perfectly symmetric division — *gedayim k'neged gedayim, tyashim k'neged tyashim* — he holds *k'lakuach hen*: the animals are treated as purchased. Once you make any division, you have in effect exchanged your undivided interest in the full estate for a defined parcel of specific assets, and that exchange is a transaction. Therefore the animals you received are *lakuach* and exempt from *ma'aser behemah* regardless of whether the split was symmetric. As the *mishnah* in the relevant context teaches: *lakuach*, that which was purchased, or *she'nitan lo b'matanah*, that which was received as a gift, is exempt from *ma'aser behemah*.

The practical upshot, then, of the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan is whether a symmetric division of an estate constitutes a transaction that confers *lakuach* status, and correspondingly whether a symmetric re-pooling of assets reconstitutes the original corporate estate or creates a new partnership.

---

## Estate & Shekel

### Scenarios Depend

Rabbi Chiya in the name of Rabbi Yirmiyah raises a penetrating question: why can we not construct scenarios in which the brothers are *chayav* in both the *kolbon* and *ma'aser behemah* simultaneously, or exempt from both simultaneously? The *mishnah* treats these as always inverse — if you are *chayav* in one, you are exempt from the other — but Rabbi Yirmiyah challenges this by pointing to cases where the asset division is mixed.

If they divided the general property and monetary assets of the estate but did not divide the animals (*chalku hanekhasim velo chalku behemah*), then from the perspective of the *shekel* obligation, where we look at the general assets, each person holds private property and they are individuals — *chayav* in the *kolbon*. But from the perspective of *ma'aser behemah*, the animals remain undivided corporate property — also *chayav*. The reverse case (*chalku behemah velo chalku hanekhasim*) yields the opposite: the animals, now divided or recombined as a partnership, are either *lakuach* or a new *shutfus* — exempt from *ma'aser behemah*. And the general assets, still undivided as estate property, mean the estate pays the *shekel* as a single entity — exempt from the *kolbon*. So both exempt. This produces the counterintuitive result that one can be *chayav* in both simultaneously, or exempt from both simultaneously, depending on which assets have been divided.

### Majority Rule

Rabbi Mana clarifies: this is only so when the animals do not constitute the majority of the estate's assets. But if the animals are the majority of the assets (*im hayta behemah rov*), then they define the character of the estate overall — *hen hen iqar nechasim* — and the entire estate is assessed by reference to the animals regardless of what happened to the other assets.

### Status Puzzle

This analysis raises a striking and genuinely puzzling observation. The *shekel* is not an asset-based tax. It is a personal obligation — every individual Jew owes a half-*shekel*. Why, then, should one's status as a *shekel*-payer be defined by the estate one happens to have inherited jointly with siblings? Imagine someone who has lived independently for twenty years, has no relationship with his brothers, and then inherits a joint estate. Why should his identity vis-à-vis the *shekel* — a personal religious obligation — now be filtered through the lens of this inherited estate? The *mishnah*'s framework seems to assume that once brothers are co-heirs of an undivided estate, their *shekel* status is jointly determined by that estate. This is far from self-evident, and the strangeness is compounded by the fact that the determination shifts depending on which portion of the estate is divided and which is not.

### Money Source

One proposed resolution is that the relevant question is not the brothers' abstract personal status but rather from which account the *shekel* is actually being paid. If the *shekel* is drawn from the estate's communal funds, then the estate is the payer and the determination follows the estate's corporate status. If each brother pays from his own private funds, he is clearly an individual and pays accordingly. This approach has considerable explanatory power and was helpfully observed in the course of discussion. However, it creates a further difficulty with Rabbi Mana's ruling: why should the fact that the animals are the majority of the estate affect anything, if what matters is simply the account from which the *shekel* payment is drawn? One is presumably not paying the *shekel* in livestock. The persistent awkwardness of this suggests that something more than a simple "source of funds" rule is at work — perhaps that the character of the estate, as reflected in its primary asset class, somehow does define the personal status of its heirs in ways that remain difficult to fully systematize.

The *gemara* then asks a further question in the name of Rabbi Avin citing Rabbi Shimi: just because they are like one person for purposes of *ma'aser behemah*, how does that exempt them from the *kolbon*? The *kolbon* relates to the personal *shekel* obligation, not to animal ownership. The answer offered is that the exemption from the *kolbon* is not really about being conceptually one person at all. Rather, it follows from a separate *halachah*: when one person pays a full *shekel* covering multiple individuals' obligations simultaneously, even if as a gift or on their behalf, they pay only one *kolbon*, not one per person. The estate, drawing from its communal funds, is doing exactly that — paying one full *shekel* for multiple members — and therefore is exempt from multiple *kolbonot*. This seems to answer the question but immediately generates a new one: if that is the reason, it has nothing to do with the estate structure at all. Anyone who pays a full *shekel* on behalf of multiple people would be exempt. Why, then, does the *mishnah* differentiate between an undivided estate and one that has been divided and reconstituted? If the brothers divide and then reform as a partnership and still pay as a group, they would likewise be giving one coin for multiple people. The *gemara* points this out, noting the apparent contradiction with the *mishnah*'s ruling that divided-and-reconstituted brothers are indeed *chayav* in the *kolbon*. The *gemara*'s attempt at resolution — citing a tradition about two brothers-in-law who inherited from their respective fathers-in-law — is itself difficult to parse and, by the admission of the analysis here, does not fully resolve the underlying tension. The *mishnah*'s framework connecting estate status to *shekel* identity remains genuinely challenging.

---

## Kolbon Destination

### Meir: To Shekalim

The *mishnah* concludes this section by asking: *le'eichan hayu hakalbonot noplim* — to what use were the *kolbonot* put? The answer reveals much about how each authority understood the nature of the fee in the first place. Rabbi Meir says *l'shekalim* — the *kolbonot* were added directly to the *shekalim* funds. This is entirely consistent with Rabbi Meir's rationale that the *kolbon* serves to round out the *shekel* to its ideal measure. If its purpose is to complete the *shekel*, the natural destination is the general *shekalim* fund.

### Eliezer: To Nedavah

Rabbi Eliezer says *l'nedavah* — the funds go for *nedavah*, the communal free-will burnt offerings. These are the *olot* brought on the *mizbe'ach* during periods of inactivity to keep the altar continuously occupied. They are a type of communal *korban* but not among the standard obligatory communal sacrifices. The *kolbonot* thus support Temple activity in a related but distinct category.

### Shezuri & Azzai

Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's opinion — *riku'ei zahav tzipui l'beit kodshei hakodashim*, that the funds were used for gold plating in the Holy of Holies — is striking and its rationale is not entirely transparent. It calls to mind the fate of Korach's fire pans, which were beaten into coverings for the *mizbe'ach*, but why the *kolbonot* specifically should go to gold plating in the *kodesh hakodashim* is not immediately obvious.

Ben Azzai, by contrast, offers the most intuitive answer given the transactional understanding of the *kolbon*: *shulchanim hayu notlim otan bischaran* — the money changers took the *kolbonot* as their fee. If the *kolbon* is fundamentally a money-changing service charge, paying the changers with it is perfectly fitting. And some authorities say the funds went *l'hotza'at drachim* — to cover the travel and operational expenses of the entire collection process, sending agents out to collect the half-*shekels* and transport them.

The underlying conceptual divide is thus made explicit by the destinations: Rabbi Meir, who understands the *kolbon* as a rounding fee to perfect the *shekel*, sends it back into the *shekalim* fund. The others, who understand it as a transaction or operating fee, direct it toward the costs of conducting the collection — either to the money changers directly, or to the broader logistical expenses of the system.

---

## Collection & Transport

### Currency Exchange

The next *mishnah* opens with a practical *halachah* regarding the logistics of collection: *metzarfin shekalim ledarkonot* — one may exchange collected *shekels* into *darkonot*, which are gold coins (a term connected to the Greek or Persian monetary system). The rationale is *mipnei masa haderech* — to reduce the physical weight and burden of transporting the collected silver to the *Beit HaMikdash*. This is purely a logistical accommodation.

### Collection Horns

A further detail of the collection infrastructure is noted. Just as there were *shofarot* in the *Mikdash* itself — shaped like horns with a narrow slit at the top and a wide base, making it possible to deposit funds but impossible to extract them by hand — so too were such *shofarot* maintained in local communities throughout the country, *kach hayu shofarot b'medinah*. Whether *medinah* here refers specifically to Jerusalem or to the country at large is a matter of dispute among the commentators.

### Coin-Only Rule

The *gemara* raises a question: why exchange collected *shekels* specifically into gold coins? Why not convert them into diamonds or pearls for ease of transport? The answer is *shema tazil hamargaliyot venimtza hekdesh mafsid* — lest the value of precious stones decline, causing *hekdesh* to suffer a loss. Currency, backed by governmental fixed ratios, is relatively stable in value; commodities such as gems fluctuate.

This principle is confirmed by a cross-reference to *Mishna Bechoros*: *vechulan nifdin bechesef uveshaveh chesef, chutz mishkalim* — a range of obligations may be redeemed either with money or with money's equivalent in value, except for *shekalim*, which may only be redeemed with actual coins. The Yerushalmi cites Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's explanation: *shema yazilu hakeilim venimtza hekdesh mafsid* — lest vessels depreciate and *hekdesh* lose out. The same concern about value instability that prohibits redeeming *shekalim* with vessels or gemstones explains why, when transporting collected funds, only the conversion to gold coins — with their governmentally fixed exchange ratio to silver — is permitted.

---

## Theft Liability

### Truma Threshold

The *mishnah* then addresses the case of *bnei ha'ir sheshalchu et shikleihem* — a village that collected its *shekalim* and dispatched them to the *Beit HaMikdash* — and the funds were stolen or lost in transit. The question is: who bears the loss?

The answer turns on whether *nitrema hatruma* — whether the *trumah* has already been taken. Three times a year, the *Beit HaMikdash* would draw from the accumulated collected funds, removing the actual coins from the collection vessels and beginning to deploy them for the purchase of communal *korbanos*. This act of removal is called *terumah*. Crucially, when performing this *terumah*, the *Beit HaMikdash* drew not only on the funds physically present but on all funds yet to arrive — *min hagavuy umin ha'asid ligvos*, from what had been collected and from what would yet be collected. By drawing on anticipated funds, the *Beit HaMikdash* effectively treated the funds still in transit as already received. A village whose funds were on the road at the moment of *terumah* had, in a sense, already fulfilled its obligation, since the *Beit HaMikdash* had already counted on those funds.

### Before Truma

If the *terumah* has not yet been taken, the funds in transit remain the property of the village. They have not yet been received by the *Beit HaMikdash*, and the loss falls on the village. The carriers must therefore swear to the *bnei ha'ir* — *nishba'im livnei ha'ir* — that they were not negligent. And the *bnei ha'ir* themselves must contribute a second set of *shekalim* — *shoklim tachteichem* — to replace what was lost.

### After Truma

If the *terumah* has already been taken, the funds are considered constructively received by the *Beit HaMikdash*. The carriers are now effectively custodians of *hekdesh* property. They must swear to the *gizbarim*, the Temple treasurers — *nishba'im lagizbarim* — that they were not negligent, and the village is thereafter exempt from replacing the funds.

The *gemara* notes that this entire framework accords with the position that the *terumah* was indeed taken drawing on both collected and anticipated funds. According to an alternative view that the *terumah* was drawn only from funds physically present, even after the *terumah* act, funds still in transit would not yet be considered received, and the liability structure would differ accordingly.

### Old vs. New

A further point is established: *matnisa b'taklin chadashin, aval b'taklin atikin lo bada* — the *mishnah*'s collection system applies only to the current year's *shekalim*. Back-payments — funds owed from a prior year — could not be paid through the village collection and local *shofarot*. *Atikin bamikdash ve'ein atikin b'medinah*: old *shekalim* were accepted at the *Beit HaMikdash* directly but not through the local collection apparatus. The village infrastructure served only the current year's obligation.

---

## Oath Requirement

### Elazar Position

Rabbi Elazar states that this entire mechanism — taking an oath when the village funds are stolen or lost — follows exclusively the position of Rabbi Shimon. The problem is that one does not ordinarily take oaths regarding *hekdesh* property. If the money is *hekdesh*, what basis is there for a *shevuah*? Rabbi Elazar resolves this by anchoring the ruling in Rabbi Shimon's principle: *kodshim she'hu chayav be'achrayutan ke'nechasav hen* — sacred objects for which a person bears financial liability are treated as though they were ordinary personal property. Since the village bears liability for the lost funds before the *terumah*, those funds are treated as ordinary village property from a monetary perspective, enabling a standard oath to be taken.

---

## Oath Requirement (II)

### Yochanan Takana

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees with Rabbi Elazar's limitation and holds that the oath applies universally — *divrei hakol hi* — not only according to Rabbi Shimon. The basis, however, is different: *mishum shevuat takana* — the oath is a Rabbinic enactment. Even though biblically there is no oath on *hekdesh*, the Rabbis instituted one for reasons of policy: allowing the custodians of communal *shekalim* to simply say *oops* without consequence would reflect poorly on *hekdesh*, and people would not be sufficiently careful. The *takana* thus serves both to ensure diligence and to maintain respect for the sanctity of *hekdesh* funds.

According to Rabbi Yochanan, the full structure of the *mishnah* is explained as *takana*: swearing to the *gizbarim* when funds are considered received, and swearing to the *bnei ha'ir* when they are not, are both Rabbinic enactments for these policy reasons.

### Possible Bavli Import

This yields the *gemara*'s difficult question about Rabbi Elazar's position. In the scenario where the funds are considered already received — where *hekdesh* bears the loss and the carriers swear to the *gizbarim* — Rabbi Elazar faces a problem: the money is *hekdesh*, the owners are *hekdesh*, and there is no organic basis for a standard *shevuah*. Rabbi Elazar's framework, which relied on the villagers' liability to justify the oath, cannot easily account for this scenario.

The *gemara* offers an answer: *nishba'im livnei ha'ir bema'amad gizbarim* — they swear to the villagers in the presence of the *gizbarim*, not to the *gizbarim* themselves. The purpose is to prevent the carriers from being suspected of negligence or embezzlement by the villagers — not because the village has suffered a financial loss, but to protect the reputation of the carriers. The *gizbarim* are present but are not the recipients of the oath.

However, this answer is textually suspicious. The formulation *nishba'im livnei ha'ir bema'amad gizbarim* is a phrase that appears in the Bavli in a different discussion, addressing a different question. Several *mefarshim* point out that this line has been imported from the Bavli into this *sugya* of the Yerushalmi, where it does not naturally belong and answers a question the *sugya* is not actually asking. Tellingly, this line does not appear in the Ktav Yad Leiden. This is a concrete example of the Bavli layer that Sussman identified — a phrase grafted in from the Bavli that can be made to work, but only awkwardly, and which is absent from the manuscript tradition.

### Oath Binding

A final point is established: even if the *bnei ha'ir* volunteer to cover the lost funds themselves — thereby relieving *hekdesh* of any financial loss — the oath requirement is not waived. *Ein hekdesh yotzei belo shevuah* — *hekdesh* does not release a custodian without an oath. The *takana* is categorical: regardless of reimbursement, the carriers must swear. The purpose of the oath is not solely to ensure financial recovery but to maintain accountability and respect for *hekdesh* funds. Voluntary restitution by the village does not substitute for that.

---

## Individual Shekel

### Delivery Threshold

The *mishnah* moves to the case of an individual who has designated his *shekel* — *hifrish shkalo* — and then lost it. Rabbi Yochanan states that he is *chayav achrayuso*, he remains liable for the *shekel*, until *sheyimserena lagizbar* — until he actually hands it over to the *gizbar*. This is the intuitive position: personal liability attaches until physical delivery.

### Divine Ownership

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish offers a striking counterposition: *hekdesh birshut gavoha bechol makom shehi* — *hekdesh* is under the authority of the Most High wherever it may be. Once a person designates his *shekel* as *hekdesh*, the money belongs to God. God knows where it is. The bank of the *Beit HaMikdash* may not know its location, but the divine owner does. Accordingly, Reish Lakish holds that the individual is not liable once the *shekel* has been designated, since it is already, in an ultimate sense, in divine possession.

### No Replevin Needed

This position has significant implications for the broader *sugya*. If *hekdesh* belongs to God wherever it is, then the carriers who lost the village funds could theoretically argue: wherever it is, it belongs to *hekdesh*. Go retrieve it from the thieves. The *gemara* addresses this: *lo hi mishum takana* — the requirement for the village to pay a second time is itself a *takana*, not the strict letter of the law. Under Reish Lakish's view, *me'ikar hadin*, the *bnei ha'ir* would never owe a second payment. Once they designated the money as *hekdesh* — and once that money is wherever it is — *hekdesh*'s claim follows the money, and the village has fulfilled its obligation. The sole reason the village pays again, and the sole reason the oath is required, is the Rabbinic *takana*. It is a fascinating and somewhat striking conclusion: technically, no replevin would ever be required of the village at all.

---

## Fund Allocation

### Baraita Rule

The *mishnah* addresses a practical scenario: the village paid its *shekalim*, the funds were stolen or lost, the village levied a second collection and paid again, and then the original funds were found or returned by the thieves. Now there are two sets of funds in hand. What becomes of them?

The *mishnah* rules: *elu va'elu shekalim ve'ein olin lahem leshana haba'ah* — both sets of funds are *shekalim* for the current year, and neither can be credited toward the following year's obligation. One might think that since the second set was given under duress — the village had no choice but to pay again — it could be applied to next year's account and the village would receive credit. The answer is no: both sets have been designated as *hekdesh* and both are consecrated for the current year's *korbanos*.

A *baraita* then provides further detail: *harishonim noflim letaklin chadashin, hashniyim noflim letaklin atikin* — the first set of funds goes toward the new *shekalim* account for the current year's communal offerings, while the second set goes toward *taklin atikin*, the account for old *shekalim*, covering prior obligations and related expenses.

### Pinchas & Abba

The natural question is: in a case where two sets of funds exist, which is "first" and which is "second"? Rabbi Pinchas and Rabbi Abba debate this. One holds that *elu sheshalchu bnei ha'ir techila* — those that the village originally sent are "first," and those that the village was compelled to pay a second time are "second." This is the straightforward chronological reading: what was sent first is first, what was sent second is second.

The other holds a more counterintuitive position: *elu shehigi'u liydei hagizbarim techila* — whichever set actually arrived in the hands of the *gizbarim* first is considered "first." Since the original funds were stolen or delayed, it is quite possible that the replacement funds arrived at the *Beit HaMikdash* before the originals were recovered and returned. On this view, receipt rather than dispatch determines priority. The funds that reach the *gizbarim* first go toward the new account; those that arrive later go toward the old account.

---

---

# Shekalim 6

## Mishnah: Friend's vs Own…

### Opening Mishnah

We begin *daf* 6 with the *mishna* found on 5b. The *mishna* opens: *ha-nosei shekalo le-chavero ve-shaklo al yado* — one who carries his friend's *shekel* and gives it on his behalf. The phrase *al yado*, which we have encountered before, here means that you entrusted your *shekel* to a friend so that he could deliver it to wherever *shekalim* were being collected — at the local square or village — on your behalf.

### Me'ila from Friend's She…

The scenario continues: *ve-shaklo al yedei atzmo* — and he forgot, through an honest mistake, and deposited the *shekel* into the collection box for himself, intending it to discharge his own obligation rather than yours. This brings us immediately to the issue addressed on the previous *daf*: once a *shekel* is set aside, it has the status of *kodesh* — it is *hekdesh*. The *Gemara* there raised the question of how one could swear regarding *hekdesh*, since oaths do not apply to consecrated property. So when Reuven gave Shimon the *shekel*, Reuven had already sanctified it. When Shimon then deposited it toward his own obligation, he was taking a coin that was *hekdesh* belonging to Reuven and using it — not maliciously, not intentionally, but through honest error — to discharge his own financial duty. Here the *halacha* of *me'ila* (misuse of consecrated property) enters the picture.

The *mishna* rules: *im nitharma ha-trumah ma'al* — once the *terumah* is taken, *me'ila* applies. The *terumah* here refers to the moment when the *Beis HaMikdash* removes funds from the collection box and begins applying them. We learned previously that this act of *terumah* functions as the moment the *Beis HaMikdash* formally receives the money. For *me'ila*, the critical question is when was the money actually *used* — when was benefit accrued from it? The *mishna* teaches that this occurs at the point of *terumah*, when the funds are removed from the large collection box and put into active use. The *me'ila* does not take effect at the moment the misdirected *shekel* was placed in the box, but later, when the *Beis Din* draws the *terumah* from the collected *shekalim*.

### Own Hekdesh Funds

The *mishna* then turns to a second case: *ha-shokel shiklo min ha-hekdesh* — one who paid his *shekel* from *hekdesh* funds. Here the person did not use a friend's *shekel* but rather his own money that happened to be *hekdesh* — money he had consecrated to the *Beis HaMikdash*, or *ma'aser sheni* money, or *shmittah* money — and inadvertently used it to pay his *shekel* obligation.

### Me'ila Timing

Interestingly, for this second case the *mishna* does not focus on the *terumah* as the critical moment but instead on actual application of the funds: *ve-nitharma ha-trumah ve-karvah ha-behemah* — the *terumah* was taken and the animal was purchased and offered. Only at that point, *ma'al* — *me'ila* takes effect.

The *mishna* then raises the possibility that the funds in question were *mi-ma'aser sheni mi-dmei shvi'is* — from *ma'aser sheni* money or *shemittah* money. In that scenario, if one realizes soon enough, there is a remedy: *yokhal kenegdan* — one may eat corresponding food. As the *Gemara* will clarify, one can transfer the *kedushah*: wherever the *ma'aser sheni* money is, its sanctity is transferred to a different coin or food, and the corresponding food may then be eaten. The *shekel* obligation has effectively been discharged through ordinary funds once the *kedushah* is redirected.

One might ask why the same transfer mechanism is not available when one used *hekdesh* funds rather than *ma'aser sheni* funds. If one realizes before it is too late that one gave a *hekdesh* coin, why not simply declare that wherever the *hekdesh* money is, its *kedushah* should be transferred to another coin? The answer turns on the nature of the consecration: once the animal has been purchased and the funds have been concretely applied — reaching the level of *kedushas haguf*, intrinsic sanctity of an object designated as a *korban* — there is no redemption without a *mum* (blemish). But at the stage of money, which is one level removed from the actual *korban*, value-based *hekdesh* can be transferred. The *mishna*'s silence on this remedy for *hekdesh* funds therefore remains somewhat unclear, yet it is what we have.

### Terumah vs Korban Offeri…

A striking feature of the *mishna* as we have it is the apparent inconsistency between the two cases: the first hinges on *nitrama ha-trumah* as the critical moment, while the second hinges on *karvah ha-behemah*. This asymmetry will be the subject of the *Gemara*'s opening discussion.

---

## Gemara: Me'ila Timing De…

### Anan Teninan vs Beis Reb…

The *Gemara* opens by noting the apparent tension directly. *Anan teninan* — we teach in our *mishna* that the critical moment is *im karva ha-behemah*, when the animal is brought. But *detani devei Rebbi* — the school of Rebbi teaches differently: *im nitharma ha-trumah*, when the *terumah* is taken.

Here we encounter the broader question of what *mishna* the *Yerushalmi* itself had before it. It is worth noting — though it has not been stated until now — that the *Yerushalmi* is a complete misnomer. It is more accurately called *Talmuda de-vnei ma'arava* or *Talmuda shel Eretz Yisrael*; it was not written in Yerushalayim but somewhere in the Land of Israel. The *girsa* questions surrounding this passage are substantial. As we have our text, the first case of the *mishna* (your friend's *shekel*) identifies the *terumah* as the critical moment, while the second case (your own *hekdesh* funds) identifies the offering of the animal. The *Yerushalmi*'s *mishna*, it appears, was fully consistent — both cases were defined by when the animal was brought — and the tradition from Rebbi's school identifying the *terumah* moment was recognized as a separate variant. The *Yerushalmi* accordingly saw no internal contradiction in its *mishna*.

The *Gemara* then asks: *man tana* — who is the author of the position that the critical moment is when the *terumah* is taken? The answer: *Rebbi Shimon hi* — it is Rabbi Shimon. For Rabbi Shimon holds that the *kohanim* are meticulous (*zerizim hem*), and that the Temple pays the animal suppliers immediately upon delivery rather than waiting until the animal is actually offered. According to this position, money is considered "used" — and thus subject to *me'ila* — as soon as the *terumah* is drawn and the funds change hands to the supplier. The *chachamim*, by contrast, hold that payment is deferred until the animal is actually brought as a *korban*, out of concern that a problem might arise with the animal in the interim; the *Beis HaMikdash* therefore prefers to wait. Accordingly, in their view, the money is not "used" until that later moment.

One might press: why would the moment of *nitrama ha-trumah* specifically be when the supplier is paid? After all, the *terumah* is removed from the large collection box and the *Beis HaMikdash* only needs a handful of animals at any given time — not hundreds all at once. The *Gemara* nonetheless operates with the assumption that everyone agrees *me'ila* takes effect when the money is actually transferred to the supplier, and the dispute concerns only when that transfer occurs: immediately upon *terumah* according to Rabbi Shimon, or only upon the offering of the animal according to the *chachamim*. It is also worth noting the distinction between the financial liability question we examined yesterday — where the key moment for whether the donor has discharged his obligation was *nitrama ha-terumah*, agreed upon by all — and the *me'ila* question here, which requires not merely delivery but actual *use* of the funds.

### Ganav u'Lesof Chavero

The *Gemara* then raises a sharp difficulty: *ganav u'lesof chavero* — suppose I stole an *olah* belonging to someone else and brought it to the *Beis HaMikdash* and it was slaughtered without explicit designation. Whose *korban* would it be? Clearly the original owner's, since *stama leshem ba'alim ha-rishonim mishtakacha* — an undesignated offering is presumed to be for the original owners. The *Gemara* applies this principle to the *shekel* case: if Reuven put Shimon's money into the collection box without any explicit designation, the money was in effect Shimon's, and when the Temple eventually used it, it was Shimon's money being used. Where then is the *me'ila*? What exactly did Reuven misuse? If the funds automatically revert to their original owner's account, Reuven derived no benefit from them and committed no misuse.

### Mesuyam and Rabban Gamli…

The *Gemara* resolves this with a key concept: *amar Rav Yehuda tifshot bi-mesuyam* — we are dealing with a case where the coin is *mesuyam*, designated and identifiable. If the coin was somehow marked or distinguishable — scratched with a distinctive mark, for example — then when the Temple used it, the very act of using that identifiable coin constituted using it *on behalf of Reuven*, not Shimon. It is through this designation that the misuse becomes concrete: that identifiable coin was treated as Reuven's when in fact it belonged to Shimon.

The *Gemara* then cites a practice of *Beis Rabban Gamliel*: *mishel Beis Rabban Gamliel she-haya mitkaven ve-dochef le-toch ha-kuppa* — the house of Rabban Gamliel would not deposit their coins into the *shofar* and wait for the standard *terumah* collection. Instead, they would wait until the moment of collection and press their coins directly into the *kuppa* (basket) as the funds were being drawn. The *shofar* was a container shaped like an inverted funnel, with a narrow slot preventing anyone from reaching in once the money was deposited; coins dropped in anonymously could lie there for months until collected. The *kuppa*, by contrast, was the basket into which the collectors poured the funds during the *terumah* process — a process comparable to emptying a vending machine.

By placing the coin directly into the collectors' hands as they gathered the funds, the Rabban Gamliel household ensured their coin was identifiably theirs at the moment of use. This serves a dual purpose in the *Gemara*'s discussion: it explains what makes a coin *mesuyam* (immediate personal designation at the moment of collection), and it will also address the *shiyuraim* question that follows.

### Shiyuraim Concern

The *Gemara* presses further: *dechash lomar shema li-shiyuraim hanofku* — perhaps the concern is that even when the *terumah* is taken or the animal is brought, my particular coin might have been left behind as *shiyuraim* (leftovers not included in that collection cycle). The collectors did not necessarily empty the *shofar* completely; some coins might remain. If my coin was among those left behind, then even once an animal was purchased with other funds, my coin has not been "used" at all — so where is the *me'ila*?

The *Gemara* offers two responses. The first: *ella ke-Rabbi Meir* — it could be following Rabbi Meir, who holds *mo'alin be-shiyuraim*: *me'ila* applies even to the leftover coins, as if the very act of taking the *terumah* extends to encompass everything in the collection, including what was not removed. This is admittedly a difficult position to fully explain, and we will encounter Rabbi Meir's reasoning later. The second response: *o hi be-mesuyam* — or, as before, we are dealing with a designated coin, specifically following the practice of *Beis Rabban Gamliel* who deposited coins directly into the *kuppa*. Since the coin goes straight into what is actively being used, it cannot be among the *shiyuraim* by definition.

It is notable that the two answers — the *mesuyam* point and the Rabban Gamliel practice — appear in the *Gemara* in a somewhat inverted order relative to the two questions they address. What makes the coin mine rather than my friend's? The designation. What ensures it is not among the leftovers? Placing it directly into the *kuppa*. The *Gemara* here has presented both answers in service of both questions, even if the fit is somewhat reversed.

### Practical Benefit of Me'…

Having established that *me'ila* can in principle apply to this scenario, the *Gemara* turns to a further question: *ma neheneh?* — what practical benefit did Reuven actually receive? He never put the money in his pocket. He delivered it to the *Beis HaMikdash*; he simply called it his own. If there is no tangible gain, what is the *me'ila*?

Rabbi Avin answers in the name of the Rabbis: *mikivan she-Beis Din re'uya le-meshkino ve-lo mashkino ke-mo she-neheneh* — because if Reuven had not paid, *Beis Din* would have seized his property. The practical benefit of escaping that seizure constitutes the *hana'ah* that triggers *me'ila*. This raises a natural question: if this is the operative benefit, why was the *mesuyam* answer even necessary? Even if the coin were not designated — even if, as far as heaven is concerned, it was Shimon's *shekel* that was used — as far as *Beis Din* is concerned, it was Reuven's *shekel*, and Reuven walks away without anyone coming to collect from him. That practical benefit exists regardless of the *mesuyam* designation. This is a genuine difficulty with how the *Gemara*'s answers interlock, and the question of what exactly constitutes the act of *geneiva* in this case remains pointed.

---

## Transfer of Sanctity

### Ma'aser Sheni Transfer

Turning to the *mishna*'s ruling regarding *ma'aser sheni* money — that one may eat corresponding food — the *Gemara* explains the mechanism of transfer. The verse teaches *kol she-hu kodesh ein kedusha chala alav* — one cannot impose a second *kedushah* on something already sanctified. Therefore one cannot directly consecrate *ma'aser sheni* money for *machatzis ha-shekel*. But the solution the *mishna* provides is: bring a coin of *chulin* and declare — *ma'os ma'aser sheni be-chol makom she-hen harei hen mechulalin al sela zo* — wherever my *ma'aser sheni* money is, let its value be transferred onto this coin. That coin then takes on the *kedushah* of *ma'aser sheni*, and the original money is freed to serve as *shekalim*. The same applies to *shemittah* funds. One may similarly effect this transfer for both categories.

---

## Accumulating Shekali (II)

### Hamachnis Maos

The *mishna* on 6a opens with a new case: *ha-machnis ma'os ve-omer harei elu le-shekali* — one who saves coins over the course of the year, placing them into a box and declaring "these are for my *shekel*," accumulating penny by penny toward the *machatzis ha-shekel* obligation.

### Beis Shammai: Motar Neda…

When it comes time to pay, the person counts his coins and finds he has more than a half *shekel*. What is the status of the excess? Beis Shammai rules: *mosran nedava* — the leftover is *nedavah*, consecrated property used by the *Beis HaMikdash* for voluntary *olos* offered when the altar is not otherwise occupied. This reflects Beis Shammai's general position that *hekdesh b'ta'us* — consecration made in error — nonetheless takes effect. When one declared "these are for my *shekel*," the extra coins were unknowingly sanctified, and even though it was inadvertent, the *kedushah* holds.

---

## Transfer of Sanctity (II)

### Hekdesh Cannot Transfer

Why does the *mishna* offer a transfer remedy for *ma'aser sheni* but not for *hekdesh* funds? The verse states *ach bechor asher yivakar ba-behema lo yakdish ish oso* — do not sanctify a *bechor* that is already sanctified. The principle derived is *kol she-hu kodesh ein kedusha chala alav*: a second *kedushah* cannot take effect on something already consecrated. Therefore one cannot consecrate *ma'aser sheni* money toward the *machatzis ha-shekel* by imposing a new *kedushah* directly upon it. The transfer remedy works for *ma'aser sheni* not by adding a new *kedushah* but by redirecting the existing one. *Hekdesh* funds, as general consecrated property, presumably pose similar structural issues — though exactly why the *mishna* omits the parallel remedy for *hekdesh* is not fully clarified here.

---

## Accumulating Shekali (II)

### Beis Hillel: Motar Chulin

Beis Hillel rules: *mosran chulin* — what is left over is ordinary, non-consecrated property. Since one only intended to sanctify the half *shekel*'s worth, anything beyond that was consecrated in error, and *hekdesh b'ta'us* does not take effect. It should be noted that the distinction between the exact coins one sanctified and those one did not is not obvious when they are commingled — this involves a kind of *breira*, a retroactive identification of which coins were sanctified, which introduces its own complexities. But the fundamental principle Beis Hillel applies is that whatever exceeds the half *shekel* was never intended to be consecrated.

### Shea'avi Mehen

If, however, one said not "these are my *shekel*" but rather *she-avi me-hen shekali* — "I will draw from these funds for my *shekel*" — then both Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel agree: *she-ha-motar chulin*, whatever remains is *chulin*. In this formulation one never declared all the coins sanctified; one merely indicated that from within this pool of money a *shekel*'s worth would be used. The excess never entered any category of *hekdesh* at all, and the question of *hekdesh b'ta'us* does not arise.

### Chatat Comparison

A parallel: if one declared "these coins are for my *chatat*" (*korban* of sin-offering), both Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel agree that the leftover is *nedavah* — not *chulin*. Why does the *chatat* case not produce the same debate as the *shekel* case? Because the *chatat* has no fixed price. When one sets aside one hundred dollars for a *chatat* and finds an animal for ninety, it was never clear at the outset how much would be needed; therefore the entire sum was sanctified. The ten-dollar remainder was fully consecrated and must go toward *nedavah*. (If one said *she-avi me-hen chatasi* — "I will draw from these for my *chatat*" — then again everyone agrees the leftover is *chulin*.)

---

## Rabbi Shimon's Expla (II)

### Shekalim vs Chatat

Rabbi Shimon explicates the distinction directly: *ma bein shekalim le-chatat? Ella she-shekalim yesh lahem kitzva, le-chatat ein la kitzva.* — What is the difference between *shekalim* and a *chatat*?
