The *shekel* has a fixed amount set by the Torah; anything beyond that amount can be recognized as a mistake, allowing Beis Hillel to rule the excess *chulin*. The *chatat* has no fixed amount; there is therefore no conceptual basis for calling any portion of the set-aside funds an error.

### Rabbi Yehudah Objects

Rabbi Yehuda challenges this reasoning: *af shekalim ein lahem kitzva* — even the *shekel* has no absolutely fixed amount. The evidence: *she-ke'she-alu Yisrael min ha-gola hayu shoklim darkonot* — when Israel returned from exile at the beginning of the *Beis Sheni* period, they gave *darkonot*, coins worth a *shekel* and a half (three half-*shekalim*), presumably because rebuilding the *Beis HaMikdash* required greatly increased funding.

---

## Shekel Amount History

### Darkonim Collection

When the Jewish people returned from exile, the amount collected was not a half-*shekel* but rather a *darkon* — a coin that functions as a *shekel* and a half. The *Yerushalmi* derives this from the verse in Nechemya: *ve-ha'amadnu aleinu mitzvat la-teit shlishit ha-shekel ba-shanah la-avodat beis eloheinu* — we undertook the commandment to give a third of a *shekel* per year for the service of the *Beis HaMikdash*. The *Yerushalmi* in the name of Rav Acha further derives from this verse that one is required to give one's *shekalim* three times per year, and it is through that triple donation that the initial giving totals a *shekel* and a half. How precisely a "third" of a *shekel* generates a *shekel* and a half is not entirely transparent in the *Gemara*'s exposition — the verse may be read as "three" rather than "a third," or it may be that the *shekel* denomination current at the time of the return from exile was itself considerably larger, making a third of it equivalent to a half *shekel* of the biblical standard, and the triple annual collection then yields one and a half.

### Amount Changes

The progression continued: *chazru lishkol sela'im* — they subsequently reverted to giving a full *sela* (a full *shekel*), and later still *chazru lishkol teva'im* — they returned to giving a *tiv'a*, which is a half-*shekel*, the standard biblical obligation.

### Dinarim Rejected

Finally, *bikshu lishkol dinarim* — they wished to lower the amount further, to give a *dinar*, which is a quarter of a *shekel*. This was not accepted: *ve-lo kibelu aleihem* (or *meihem* in the *Bavli* version of the *mishna*, where the wording implies the authorities refused to accept it rather than the people refusing to adopt it). One may not go below the half-*shekel* obligation, though one may go above it. It is worth noting that the Roman tax on Jews following the revolt — the *Fiscus Judaicus* — was fixed at two *dinarim*, equivalent to a half-*shekel*, a striking historical echo.

---

## Rabbi Shimon's Expla (II)

### Rabbi Shimon Replies

Rabbi Shimon responds to Rabbi Yehuda's objection: *af al pi chen yad kullan shava* — even so, everyone's contribution is equal. Yes, the absolute amount has varied across different historical periods; but at any given moment, a fixed amount applies uniformly to every Jew. This is fundamentally different from the *chatat*, where at any single point in time *ze mevi be-sela ve-ze mevi be-shtayim ve-ze mevi be-shalosh* — one person may bring a *chatat* worth a *sela*, another worth two, another worth three, depending on their means and circumstance. The *shekel* therefore possesses, at every specific moment in history, the character of a fixed amount, and that fixity is precisely what allows the excess to be recognized as a *ta'ut*.

---

## Fistful vs Pennies Debate

### Mechnis Prutot Case

The *Gemara* now asks: what exactly is the case about which Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel disagree? Rabbi Yosei in the name of Rabbi Elazar: the debate concerns *machnis prutot* — one who accumulates coins penny by penny, placing them in a box over time and declaring them for one's *shekel*.

### Fistful Consensus

But, the *Gemara* continues, if instead one grabbed a fistful of coins and said "all of these are for my *shekel*" (*eilu shekali*) — and it happens that the fistful contains more than a half *shekel*'s worth — then *kuli alma modei she-ha-motar nedava*: everyone would agree the leftover is *nedavah* (consecrated), not *chulin*. In this case, one grabbed everything deliberately and declared it all consecrated; had one bothered to count, one would have known there was extra. There is no real error, and therefore even Beis Hillel would agree the excess is *hekdesh*.

### Rabbi Chiya's Reversal

Rabbi Chiya (citing Rabbi Ba in the name of Rabbi Elazar) reverses this position entirely. According to this view, the debate of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel is again about the case of penny-by-penny collection. But when one grabs a fistful and says *eilu shekali*, the conclusion is the opposite: *kuli alma modei she-ha-motar chulin* — everyone agrees the leftover is *chulin*. The reasoning runs in the other direction: precisely because one grabbed a fistful and said "this is for my *shekel*," it is clear one intended only a *shekel*'s worth from what is in hand, and the excess was never meant to be consecrated. It is not entirely obvious why Beis Shammai would concede here, given Beis Shammai's general view that *hekdesh b'ta'us* takes full effect; one of the commentators suggests it is because the grab-and-declare scenario is not genuinely a *ta'ut* at all — one could easily have counted before speaking — and thus even Beis Shammai recognizes the intent was limited.

### Proof from Mishnah

Rabbi Chiya offers proof from our *mishna* in support of Rav Bibi's position (that when one says *eilu* with a fistful, the leftover is *chulin*). The proof runs through Rabbi Shimon's statement: *ma bein shekalim le-chatat? Ella she-shekalim yesh lahem kitzva ul'chatat ein lahem kitzva* — in what case is Rabbi Shimon distinguishing *shekalim* from *chatat*? It cannot be the case where one said *she-avi me-hen*, "I will draw from these," because in that case everyone already agrees the leftover is *chulin* for both *shekalim* and *chatat*. Similarly, there would be nothing to distinguish if the case were the same formulation for both. The *Gemara* reasons: *man anan kayamin* — what case are we actually discussing? It must be the case where one said *eilu shekali* — the fistful scenario. And Rabbi Shimon says that in that case, since the *shekel* has a fixed amount, *motar chulin* — the leftover is *chulin*; whereas by *chatat*, which has no fixed amount, *motar nedava*. This proves that when one grabs a fistful and says *eilu*, the leftover is *chulin* — even Beis Shammai agrees — which is Rav Bibi's position.

The *Gemara* then notes that a later *mishna* states *mosar shekalim chulin* — leftover *shekel* money is *chulin* — and asks whether this too proves Rav Bibi's position. The answer is that this does not constitute a strong proof: one can read that *mishna* as dealing with the standard penny-collection case and as going according to Beis Hillel. It is not a *chiddush* that the *mishna* rules like Beis Hillel; the question of whether Beis Shammai would agree in the fistful-of-coins case remains separate.

---

## Hekdesh B'Ta'ut Cases

### Set Aside Shekel Wrongly

The *Gemara* now turns to cases of *hekdesh b'ta'ut* — consecration made in error. The first case: *ha-maphrish shekalo ve-savar she-hu chayav ve-nimtza she-eino chayav* — one sets aside a coin as one's *shekel*, believing oneself obligated, and it turns out one was not. Perhaps one's wife had already given on one's behalf, or one had forgotten that one had already given. The ruling: *lo kadash* — it was not sanctified. This is the position of Beis Hillel: *hekdesh b'ta'us* does not take effect.

### Two Shekalim, One Owed

The second case: *ha-maphrish shenayim ve-savar she-hu chayav shenayim ve-nimtza she-eino chayav ela echad* — one set aside two *shekalim*, believing one owed for two years (last year's and this year's), and it turns out one had in fact paid last year's obligation. One is only *chayav* one. One declared "these two are for my *shekalim*." The first coin is clearly valid. What of the second? The *Gemara* asks: *ha-shaini mah avid lei?*

### Chatat Parallels

The *Gemara* seeks to derive an answer from the parallel *chatat* case: *hifrish chataso ve-savar she-hu chayav ve-nimtza she-eino chayav* — one set aside a *chatat* animal and was not in fact obligated; *lo kidsha* — it was not sanctified, consistent with Beis Hillel. But: *hifrish shenayim ve-savar she-hu chayav shenayim ve-nimtza she-eino chayav ela echad* — one set aside two *chatat* animals and was only obligated for one. The second animal: *ela ro'eh* — it must graze (i.e., it retains a degree of sanctity and grazes until it develops a *mum*, at which point it can be redeemed). The *Gemara* applies the same reasoning to the *shekel* case: *hacha nami* — so here too the second *shekel* would have some sanctified status. The *Yerushalmi*'s language here is striking: rather than bringing a textual proof, it advances a *svara* (logical reasoning) by drawing on the *chatat* scenario. Some commentators emend the *girsa* to present an explicit text rather than a logical inference.

### Partial Effect Logic

What is the underlying logic that distinguishes setting aside one item in error from setting aside two where only one is valid? The *mefarshim* explain: if one sanctifies a single coin and the *hekdesh* is entirely mistaken, Beis Hillel says it does not take effect at all. But if one sanctifies two simultaneously and the *kedushah* validly applies to one of them, then even where one's intention regarding the second was mistaken, perhaps the partial effectiveness of the consecration causes it to take hold across the entire declared set. Since the *kedushah* is working for one, it works for both — even the erroneous portion.

The *Gemara* then connects this directly to the earlier fistful-of-coins debate. When one grabs a fistful and says *eilu shekali*, and the *kedushah* takes effect for the half-*shekel*'s worth contained within, does it also take effect for the excess on the grounds that a partial *hekdesh* has been activated? This is exactly the question the earlier dispute addresses. If the answer from the two-*shekalim* case proves that partial *hekdesh* extends to the whole, then even in the *eilu* scenario the leftover would be *nedavah*, not *chulin* — which cuts against Rav Bibi's position. The *Yerushalmi* thus weaves the two debates together: *heicha at omarta elu* — how could you have said before that when one declares *eilu* the leftover is *chulin*, given that partial consecration apparently extends to the whole?

---

## Collection Practices and…

### Three Yearly Collections

From the verse in Nechemya — *shlishit ha-shekel ba-shanah* — Rav Acha derives that one is required to give one's *shekalim* three times per year. The initial large donation at the time of the return from exile — a *darkon* — can be understood as three half-*shekalim* spread across three collection seasons, totaling a *shekel* and a half. The verse's phrasing encodes a triple rhythm of giving. This connects to the broader *Beis HaMikdash* practice: three times annually the *terumah* was drawn from the *shofrot*, three baskets (*kuppot*) each holding three *se'in* were used, and three collection removals were made — a pervasive theme of three running through the entire *shekel* system.

### Appeal Limit

From the same source the *Gemara* derives: *she-ein matrichin al ha-tzibur yoser mi-shalosh pe'amim ba-shanah* — one should not burden the community with more than three appeals per year. This principle speaks directly to communal fundraising practice. It is an open question how many contemporary synagogues observe this guidance.

### Theme of Three

Rabbi Avin notes that the number three is embedded throughout the *shekel* institution, all traceable back to this verse: three *se'in* per basket, three baskets, three times of *hafrashos* (removals) from the *shofrot*. The verse's reference to "a third" — or "three" — becomes the symbolic and structural backbone of the entire collection system, from the baskets used to the frequency of draws to the number of times the community is approached.

---

## Symbolic Meaning of Half…

### Noon Atonement

The *Gemara* closes with a series of *derashot* on the symbolic significance of the *machatzis ha-shekel*. Why a half? One *tanna* answers: *lefi she-chatu bi-machatzit ha-yom yitnu bi-machatzit ha-shekel* — because Israel sinned at midday, they give a half-*shekel* in atonement. The sin of the golden calf (*cheit ha'egel*) occurred at the sixth hour, midday, as derived from the verse *ki boshesh Moshe* — read as *ba shesh*, "the sixth hour came." The half-*shekel* mirrors the half-day at which the sin occurred. It should be noted that in the order of the Torah, *Ki Tisa* and the *machatzis ha-shekel* command appear before the account of *cheit ha'egel*; Rashi and others understand the passage as being out of chronological sequence, and all these *derashot* presuppose that the *machatzis ha-shekel* was instituted as a *tikkun* for the *cheit ha'egel*, even if textually it precedes it.

### Six Geraim

A second *derasha*: *lefi she-chatu be-shesh sha'os ba-yom yitnu machatzit ha-shekel de-avei sheisha garmisin* — because they sinned in the sixth hour, they give a *machatzis ha-shekel*, which equals six *garmisin*. This formulation emphasizes not the "half" aspect but the number six, corresponding to the six hours of daylight at which the sin occurred. One practical difference noted between these two approaches: since we know one may give *more* than a *machatzis ha-shekel* when circumstances require a larger denomination, the symbolic emphasis differs. According to the first *derasha*, the symbolic goal is always a "half" of whatever coin is current. According to the second, the goal is that whatever is given should equal six of some smaller unit.

### Ten Dibrot

Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rabbi Nechemia, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai: *lefi she-avru al Aseret HaDibrot yitein kol echad va-echad asara geira* — because Israel transgressed all ten of the *Aseret HaDibrot*, each person gives ten *geira*. A *shekel* equals twenty *geira*, and a half-*shekel* therefore equals ten — corresponding to the ten commandments violated at the time of the golden calf.

### Sale of Yosef Connection

Rabbi Berachia and Rabbi Levi in the name of Rabbi Shimon Lakish offer a striking *derasha*: *lefi she-machru bechora shel Rachel be-esrim kesef* — because the brothers sold the firstborn son of Rachel (Yosef) for twenty *kesef*, everyone gives and redeems his firstborn with twenty *kesef*. The *pidyon ha-bechor* is five *shekalim*, and this *derasha* identifies the twenty *kesef* of Yosef's sale with twenty *dinarim* (since a *dinar* is a *kesef*), which at four *dinarim* to a *shekel* equals five *shekalim*. The brothers sold Yosef — Yaakov's (through Rachel's) firstborn — for five *shekalim*, and we pay five *shekalim* to redeem our firstborn sons.

### Ten Brothers' Share

Finally, Rav Pinchas in the name of Rav Levi: *lefi she-machru bechora shel Rachel be-esrim kesef venafal kol echad va-echad meihem teiva* — each of the brothers (ten in total; Binyamin was not present) received two *kesef* from the sale of Yosef. Two *kesef*, i.e., two *dinarim*, equals a half-*shekel* — the *tiv'a*. Therefore we each give a half-*shekel* to atone for each individual brother's share in the sale. One might object that the tribe of Yosef himself would be exempt — and the *Gemara* leaves this aside. But the arithmetic is clean: twenty *kesef* divided among ten brothers yields two *kesef* each, which is exactly a half-*shekel*, the precise amount of the *machatzis ha-shekel* obligation.

---

---

# Shekalim 7

## Leftover Funds Rules

### Shekel Leftovers

The daf we pick up on is 6b, which opens with a *mishnah* that extends the discussion from the previous session concerning what happens when someone sets aside extra money for their *shekel*. The prior discussion focused on whether such a designation constitutes *hekdesh* in error — *hekdesh ta'us* — or a legitimate sanctification. The present *mishnah* broadens the inquiry to the general question of leftover funds sanctified for various *korbanos*: when such funds cannot be applied to their original purpose, what becomes of them?

The *mishnah* opens: *mosar shekalim chullin* — leftover money for a *shekel* is *chullin*. This reflects the position of *Beis Hillel* that since the *shekel* obligation has a fixed amount, any excess was contributed inadvertently — a *ta'us* — and therefore never achieved *kedushas hekdesh* in the first place.

### Asirit HaEifah

The *mishnah* continues: *mosar asirit ha'eifah* — leftover funds designated for the *asirit ha'eifah* offering. This refers specifically to the *minchat choteh* brought within the framework of the *korban oleh v'yored*, the sliding-scale *chatas* applicable to a defined set of transgressions enumerated at the end of *Parshas Vayikra*. For someone too poor to bring an animal, the minimum permissible offering is a tenth of an *eifah* of flour, which functions as a *chatas* substitute. Leftover funds for this, together with leftover funds for *kinei zavim*, *kinei zavos*, and *kinei yolodos* — the bird-pairs brought by a *zav*, *zavah*, and a woman who has given birth — as well as for *chataos* and *ashamos* generally, all carry the same ruling: *mosran nedavah*, the surplus goes to the *nedavah* fund.

It is worth pausing here. In the cases of *kinei zavim* and *kinei yolodos*, not both birds constitute a *chatas*. As the *pasuk* in *Tazria* specifies: one bird is an *olah* and one is a *chatas*. Yet the *mishnah* treats the entire fund as falling under the *chatas* rule. The simpler reading is that since a *chatas* is present within the package, and since the entire offering serves a *taharah* purpose — for *zav*, *zavah*, and *yolodes* alike — the whole fund is treated with the stringency of *chatas* funds. The *mishnah* emphasizes the *chatas* dimension because that is what drives the *halacha*.

The *nedavah* referred to here is not a personal voluntary offering but rather a communal fund — *kaitz hamizbeach* — drawn upon by the *Beis HaMikdash* to bring *olahs* when the *mizbeach* would otherwise stand idle.

### Chatat & Asham Rule

The *mishnah* states the general principle: *zeh haklal — kol sheba leshem chatat umishum ashmah, mosran nedavah* — anything designated as a *chatas* or an *asham*, its surplus goes to *nedavah*. This is understood to be *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*.

### Voluntary Offerings

The *mishnah* then addresses the voluntary offerings. *Mosar olah le'olah* — leftover money set aside for a personal *olah* goes toward another *olah*. The distinction between this and *nedavah* is significant: *nedavah* is a communal contribution to the *Beis HaMikdash*'s standing fund, whereas here the individual retains the surplus and applies it to his next personal *olah*. An *olah* is a free-will sacrifice, not an obligatory or sin-related one, and therefore the funds are not locked into a specific obligation but may be carried forward.

Similarly, *mosar minchah laminchah* — surplus *minchah* funds are saved for the individual's next *minchah*. And *mosar shelamim shelamim* — leftover *shelamim* funds go toward a future personal *shelamim*.

### Pesach to Shelamim

*Mosar hapesach lishlamim* — leftover money for a *korban pesach* goes toward a *shelamim*. One might ask: why not simply hold those funds for the following year's *pesach*? The answer lies in what was learned in *Masechet Pesachim*: after *Pesach*, both the animal itself and any funds designated for it undergo a conversion of status to *shelamim*. The leftover money therefore cannot remain designated as *pesach* funds.

### Nazirite Leftovers

The *mishnah* closes with the *nazir*. *Mosar nezirim l'nezirim* — if funds were collected communally for multiple *nezirim*, any surplus is held for the next *nazir* who requires assistance, since the funds are not specific to any one individual. However, *mosar nazir lindavah* — if an individual *nazir* set aside money for his own *korbanos*, any surplus goes to *nedavah*. The *nazir*'s obligation is highly particular to his specific period of *nezirus*, much like a *chatas*, and therefore the leftover money cannot simply be carried forward.

---

## Shekel Death Question

### Rav Yehuda's Query

The *gemara* opens with a vivid report. *Amar Rabbi Yosi: ad d'anan taman* — while I was still there, in *Bavel* — *shami'a kal Rav Yehuda sha'il l'Shmuel*: I heard the voice of Rav Yehuda asking Shmuel. The phrasing is striking: not merely "I heard that Rav Yehuda asked," but rather "I heard the voice of Rav Yehuda asking" — an almost graphic recollection that perhaps suggests he was nearby but unseen, or that the exchange made a vivid impression.

The question Rav Yehuda posed to Shmuel: *hefrish shiklo u'mes* — someone sanctified his *shekel* and then died. What becomes of the money? Shmuel's answer: *yiplu l'nedavah* — it falls to the *nedavah* fund.

### Ta'us Doctrine

This ruling requires unpacking. Our *mishnah* opened by stating *mosar shekalim chullin* — surplus *shekel* money is *chullin*. But that ruling applies to the case of *hekdesh ta'us*: the person was dropping coins into a container and inadvertently exceeded the half-*shekel* threshold without realizing it. That excess was never intentionally sanctified; it was a mistake.

Here the case is entirely different. The person properly and deliberately sanctified his *shekel* — the sanctification was legitimate — and then he died. This is not *ta'us*. The funds are genuine *hekdesh*. Since *Beis Shammai* does not accept the *ta'us* doctrine and holds that even accidentally over-sanctified *shekel* funds are genuine *hekdesh* going to *nedavah*, and since our case presents deliberate sanctification followed by death, the ruling is that such funds go to *nedavah*. The *ta'us* element that would render the funds *chullin* is entirely absent.

---

## Asirit HaEifah Dispute

### Yam HaMelach

The *gemara* now raises a dispute concerning the ruling by the *asirit ha'eifah*. The pronoun *shelo* in the *mishnah*'s phrase *mosar asirit ha'eifah shelo* — the surplus of *his* *asirit ha'eifah* — points toward a specific individual. The *gemara* identifies this as the *Kohen Gadol*, who is obligated to bring an *asirit ha'eifah* every day, half in the morning and half in the afternoon, as a daily *minchah*. This is a *chovah* — an obligatory offering — but it is categorically different from the *minchat choteh* of the *oleh v'yored* discussed in the *mishnah*.

Rabbi Yochanan rules: *yolichem l'Yam HaMelach* — you cast them into the Dead Sea. There is nothing that can be done with them.

### Mishnah Contradiction

The *gemara* immediately presses: *masnisa peligah al Rabbi Yochanan* — our *mishnah* contradicts Rabbi Yochanan directly. The *mishnah* lists *mosar asirit ha'eifah* among those whose surplus goes to *nedavah*. How can Rabbi Yochanan rule that it must be disposed of?

### Minchat Choteh

Rabbi Yochanan resolves this: *patar lah* — he explains the *mishnah* as referring specifically to the *asirit ha'eifah sheminchat choteh shel kol Yisrael* — the *asirit ha'eifah* that functions as the *minchat choteh* for the general population, the offering brought within the sliding-scale *chatas* system. That is what the *mishnah* addresses. But the *Kohen Gadol*'s daily *asirit ha'eifah* is an obligatory *minchah* of an entirely different character — it is not a *chatas* substitute at all.

This distinction, though, invites scrutiny. The general principle observed throughout the *mishnah* is that obligatory funds with no remaining designated use go to *nedavah*. This applies to *shekalim*, to *nazir* korbanos, to the birds of a *zavah* even though one is an *olah*. Why would the *Kohen Gadol*'s *minchah* be different? The rule of *nedavah* does not appear to be limited to *chatas*-category offerings. If surplus obligatory funds generally go to *nedavah*, Rabbi Yochanan's position is difficult to understand.

One possible resolution: the *Kohen Gadol*'s *asirit ha'eifah* occupies an unusual intermediate position. On one hand, the *Kohen Gadol* is an individual bringing what functions as a private obligation; on the other, his daily service is also bound up with the general operations of the *Beis HaMikdash* in a way that sets it apart from a typical private *chovah*. Perhaps Rabbi Yochanan views this unique status as removing the *minchah* from the ordinary *nedavah* framework. Still, this remains difficult, and Rabbi Eliezer's position — *yiplu l'nedavah* — seems to follow naturally from the broader principle.

---

## Pesach Conversion

### Bavli Derasha

The *gemara* reports another teaching transmitted by Rabbi Yosi: *ad d'anan taman* — while I was still in *Bavel* — he heard a *derasha* that they make there. *Abba bar Ba* raised the following question about a Babylonian exegesis: *minayin shehapesach mishtaneh l'shem shelamim?* — from where do we know that a *pesach* converts to a *shelamim*? The verse cited is *v'im min hatzon korbano l'zevach shelamim* (the opening of the *shelamim* section in *Vayikra*). The Babylonian *derasha* reads: *kol shehu min hatzon ba shelamim* — anything that comes from the flock, if not used for its original purpose, becomes a *shelamim*.

### Olah Challenge

Abba bar Ba then challenges this *derasha*: *harei olah* — but consider an *olah*! An *olah* also comes from the flock. Why, then, would surplus *olah* funds not also become a *shelamim*? And of course we know they do not — surplus *olah* funds go toward another *olah*.

The response: *davar she'eino ba ela min hatzon* — something that comes *only* from flocks. *Yatzat olah shehi ba'ah af min habakar* — an *olah* is excluded because it may be brought from cattle as well, not exclusively from the flock. The phrase *v'im min hatzon* therefore encompasses only offerings that are exclusively flock-animals. A *pesach* qualifies; an *olah* does not.

### Min Hatzon Parse

But this does not end the analysis. *Hayatzivun? Harei asham?* — is this really correct? What of an *asham*? An *asham* comes only from sheep — specifically from male sheep, rams — and not from cattle. If the principle is that *min hatzon* indicates an exclusively flock-based offering, the *asham* should also be included, and surplus *asham* funds should become *shelamim*. We know they do not.

Rav Bun bar Kahana answers: *davar shehu ba mikol hatzon* — the verse points to something that comes from *all types* of flocks. *Tzon* encompasses both sheep and goats. A *shelamim* may come from either sheep or goats; a *pesach* similarly may come from either. But an *asham* comes only from rams — not from goats. Therefore, *yatza asham she'eino ba ela min ha'eilim bilvad* — the *asham* is excluded because it does not come from the full range of *tzon*.

At this point, however, a counter-pressure emerges within the *gemara*. In all other contexts, the prefix *min* is understood as *l'ma'et* — to exclude, to indicate a subset. Yet here we are reading *min hatzon* as inclusive of both sheep and goats. How can *min* be expansive?

Rav Mana answers: *hachi nami min l'ma'et* — yes, *min* here is also excluding, but what it excludes is not goats but rather certain characteristics of sheep themselves. Specifically, it excludes females — a *pesach* may only be male — and it excludes animals older than one year. The *min* narrows *within* the category of sheep-and-goat flocks by excluding females and two-year-old animals, thereby pointing us specifically toward the *pesach*. Meanwhile, *tzon* itself still encompasses both sheep and goats, which excludes the *asham*.

The *gemara* then presses: *v'gabei asham nami min l'ma'et hu she'eino ba ela min ha'eilim* — could we not equally read *min* with regard to the *asham* as excluding goats? The *gemara* resists this reading; the *pshat* of *tzon* as covering the full range of flocks is what excludes the *asham*, and the *min* is reserved to narrow within that range toward the specific parameters of a *pesach*.

### Logical Reasons

The *gemara* then returns to why surplus *pesach* funds should become *shelamim* rather than *olah*, even though a textual argument could in principle be constructed from the *olah* verse as well. Rabbi Avun offers: *meshanim davar shehu l'achila l'davar shehu l'achila, v'ein meshanim davar shehu l'achila l'davar she'eino l'achila* — we convert something that is eaten into something that is also eaten; we do not convert something that is eaten into something that cannot be eaten. A *pesach* is eaten; a *shelamim* is eaten; an *olah* is entirely consumed on the *mizbeach*. We therefore read the *pesach* into the *shelamim* passage, not the *olah* passage.

Rabbi Yose bar Abun adds a parallel consideration: *meshanim kodashim kalim l'shem kodashim kalim, v'ein meshanim kodashim kalim l'shem kodashei kodashim* — we convert *kodashim kalim* into *kodashim kalim*, not *kodashim kalim* into *kodashei kodashim*. A *pesach* is *kodashim kalim*; a *shelamim* is likewise *kodashim kalim*; but an *olah* is *kodashei kodashim*. We therefore prefer the *shelamim* reading.

What is striking here is the interplay between *derasha* and *sevara*. One might assume that a *drasha* from a *pasuk* is determinative on its own, operating mechanically. But here the *gemara* reveals that there was a genuine choice between two possible *pesukim* — either the *olah* passage or the *shelamim* passage could have served as the basis for the conversion of *pesach* funds. The *sevaros* of Rabbi Avun and Rabbi Yose bar Abun are what tilt the reading toward *shelamim*. Similarly, the earlier argument about whether the *asham* or the *pesach* is the subject of the *drasha* reflects a choice in how to parse the verse, guided by substantive legal logic. This illustrates how *derasha* and *sevara* function together rather than in isolation.

---

## Shechita Intent

### Shelamim Intent

The *gemara* now addresses the conditions required for an actual *pesach* animal — not merely surplus funds — to convert to a *shelamim* after the holiday has passed. Rabbi Yosi reports that in *Bavel* they held: *ein hapesach mishtaneh l'shem shelamim ela im ken shechato l'shem shelamim* — the *pesach* does not convert to a *shelamim* unless it was specifically slaughtered with the intent of a *shelamim*. This is more restrictive than what was taught in *Pesachim*, where any *she'lo lishmo* intent — slaughtering it for something other than *pesach* — sufficed for the conversion.

### Any Non-Pesach

Rabbi Chanina disagrees: *afilu shechato l'shem olah* — even if you slaughtered it with the intent of an *olah*, any intent other than *pesach* suffices to convert it to a *shelamim*.

### Any Korban Intent

Rav Illa explains the basis for Rabbi Yochanan's position that even slaughter for an *olah* converts the animal to a *shelamim*: the *drasha* of *v'im min hatzon korbano l'zevach shelamim* — once it is slaughtered *l'zevach*, for any other *korban*, it becomes a *shelamim*. The word *zevach* is read broadly: any act of slaughter directed toward *some* sacrificial purpose — not necessarily *shelamim* specifically — triggers the conversion.

The *gemara* then raises the question: *u'mishtaneh l'machshevet pasul* — does the animal also change with respect to *machsheves pasul*, invalid intent? The specific case is where someone slaughtered the *pesach* with the intent of an *olah* and simultaneously entertained the thought of throwing the blood the following day — a *pigul* thought. Does the *olah* intent interact with the *pigul* thought in any legally significant way?

The *gemara* notes, *miko makom pasul hu* — regardless, it would be invalid. But the *gemara* refines this: if you say *mishtaneh l'machshevet pasul* — if the *olah* intent gives the animal a kind of dual identity such that the slaughter is not purely *shelamim* but is somehow colored by the *olah* designation — then adding a *pigul* thought produces *pasul* but not *pigul*. The compounding of the *olah* designation alongside the improper intent keeps it from achieving full *pigul* status. However, if you say *ein mishtaneh l'machshevet pasul* — the *olah* intent carries no independent weight and the slaughter is treated as straightforward *shelamim* slaughter — then the *pigul* thought takes full effect and produces *pigul*.

The *nafka mina* is significant. *Pigul* entails a separate Torah violation committed at the moment of the improper slaughter, and one who eats *pigul* is *chayav kareis*. *Pasul* merely invalidates the offering without the additional consequences.

---

## Pesach Post-Holiday

### She'lo Lishmo Rule

The *gemara* now addresses the case of *lishmo u'she'lo lishmo* — where the slaughterer declares a dual intent simultaneously, both for *pesach* and for *shelamim*, during the rest of the year (*bish'ar yemos hashana*). For the conversion of *pesach* to *shelamim* to take effect, the animal must be slaughtered *she'lo lishmo* — not for *pesach*. What happens when the intent is split?

### Neutralization

Rabbi Avin bar Bun bar Chiya in the name of Shmuel bar Abba reasons: *mikeivan she'ein lo shem* — since the *pesach* during the rest of the year has no designated status, the dual declaration of *lishmo u'she'lo lishmo* effectively cancels itself out, as if the slaughter were performed *bishitika* — in silence, without any verbal designation. And if performed in silence, the animal is *kasher*, since once the *Pesach* holiday has passed, the animal's original *pesach* identity is understood to have lapsed without requiring active uprooting.

### Dual Intent

This raises the question: if *lishmo u'she'lo lishmo* neutralize one another and produce the same result as silence, what would be the *halacha* if someone slaughtered it *lishmo* but then intended to sprinkle its blood *she'lo lishmo*? Could one argue that the separated *lishmo* and *she'lo lishmo* — one at *shechita* and one at *zrika* — also neutralize? The *gemara* resists this extension. One might argue that when the acts are separated temporally, the first act (*shechita lishmo*) already defines the animal and takes precedence, precluding any subsequent neutralization.

### Challenge to Neutralizat…

A challenge follows: if we say that *lishmo u'she'lo lishmo* in combination neutralize and produce the result of silence, then the same logic could presumably extend to cases where the two intents were somehow articulated sequentially rather than simultaneously. Why does neutralization apply only to the combined declaration?

### Silence Question

Rabbi Abba Mari raises a more fundamental challenge: *ma nomar bishitika kasher o nomar bishitika pasul?* — where do we derive the premise that silence produces a *kasher* result in the first place? Can we not equally say that slaughtering the *pesach* in silence during the rest of the year is *pasul* — that it retains its *pesach* identity and requires active redefinition?

This maps precisely onto the question in the *Bavli* of whether *pesach bish'ar yemos hashana ba'ei akira o lo ba'ei akira* — whether the *pesach* requires active uprooting of its old name during the rest of the year. The *Yerushalmi* frames this as: does silence produce *kasher* or *pasul*? The *gemara* leaves this unresolved.

---

## Nazirite Leftovers

### Order Rule

The *mishnah* ruled that surplus funds of an individual *nazir* go to *nedavah*. The *gemara* now probes a foundational ambiguity: a *nazir* brings three *korbanos* — an *olah*, a *shelamim*, and a *chatas*. If a *nazir* set aside a combined sum for all three and there was money left over, how do we characterize the surplus? Is it surplus *chatas* money? Surplus *olah* money? Surplus *shelamim* money? The answer matters because the rules differ.

Rav Chisda rules: *v'hu shekarva chatato besof* — it depends on which *korban* was offered last. Since the funds are understood to flow toward the last offering brought, the surplus takes on the identity of that *korban*. If the *chatas* was the last offered, the surplus is *chatas* surplus, going to *nedavah*. If the *shelamim* was brought last, *mosar shelamim shelamim* — the surplus goes toward a future *shelamim*.

### Chatat Identity

Rav Zeira disagrees: *afilu karvu shelamim l'besof, halacha achas hi benazir* — even if the *shelamim* was brought last, there is one unified *halacha* for the *nazir*: since a *chatas* is part of the *nazir*'s package of obligations, any surplus is treated as *chatas* surplus and goes to *nedavah*. The same logic underlies the *mishnah*'s ruling about *kinei zavim* and *kinei zavos*: the presence of a *chatas* within the bundle stamps the identity of the entire fund.

### Maos Setumim

A *baraisa* is cited in support of Rav Zeira: *elu hein maos setumim — kol shedmei chatas mesos meuravas bahen* — these are the undesignated funds: any fund into which *chatas* money was ever mixed. The *chiddush* of the *baraisa* follows: *va'afilu hifrish dmei chatas mitokhan maos setumim hein* — even if someone later separated out the *chatas* money from the pool and set it aside distinctly, the remaining funds are still treated as *maos setumim*, undesignated funds with *chatas* identity. Since *chatas* money was once part of this pool, that status persists regardless of subsequent separation. Applied to the *nazir*: since *chatas* funds were always part of the *nazir*'s designated pool, any surplus is treated as *chatas* surplus, regardless of which *korban* was offered last.

### Meila Principle

A *baraisa* is then cited in support of Rav Chisda. If someone designated funds specifically for a *chatas* and separately designated the remainder for his other *nazir* korbanos, and then died: *moalin b'kulan v'ein moalin b'miktzasan* — one who uses *all* of these funds has committed *me'ilah*, but one who uses only *some* of the funds has not. The reason: the remaining fund is a mixture of *olah* and *shelamim* designations. *Me'ilah* applies to *kodshei kodashim* such as an *olah*, but not to *kodashim kalim* such as a *shelamim*. If you use only part of the fund, perhaps those coins were going toward the *shelamim* portion, and *me'ilah* does not apply. Only if you take the entire amount can you be certain you have used funds designated for an *olah* and thereby committed *me'ilah*. Significantly, the *baraisa* does not say that if the man died the funds go to *nedavah* because the *chatas* money was once mixed in — which supports Rav Chisda's position that the *chatas* does not automatically dominate the identity of the entire fund when clearly separated.

---

## Bread & Wine

### Bread Rots

The *gemara* now turns to the non-animal components of the *nazir*'s obligation. Rav Chisda rules: *mosar lachmo shel Nazir yirkav* — surplus funds designated for a *nazir*'s bread offering must be left to rot. This parallels the earlier ruling about the *Kohen Gadol*'s *asirit ha'eifah* according to Rabbi Yochanan — certain surplus funds that cannot be used for their original purpose and do not fit the *nedavah* framework must simply be disposed of.

### Unique Offering

The *gemara* explains why the bread cannot be redirected. One might suggest using it for a similar offering — the way surplus *olah* funds go to another *olah* — or saving it for another period of *nezirus*. Neither works. As for the first option: *she'ein l'cha lechem kareiv l'atzmo* — there is no such thing as a bread offering brought independently. The *nazir*'s bread has no parallel that could receive the funds. And as for applying it to a future *nezirus*: *she'ein l'cha nezirus belo lechem* — every period of *nezirus* requires its own independent sanctification for the bread. Funds designated for one *nezirus* cannot serve another. Therefore: *mosar lachmo shel Nazir yirkav* — the surplus must rot.

### Wine Rots Too

Rav Yosef initially reasoned by analogy: just as the bread must rot, so too the surplus wine funds — *mosar niscav* — should also be left to rot, for the same reasons: the wine cannot be brought independently and cannot be transferred to another *nezirus*.

### Wine to Nedavah

Rav Yossi bar Rabbi Bun disagrees: *mosar niscav kodshei kodashim inun v'yiplu l'nedavah* — the surplus wine funds have the status of *kodshei kodashim* and therefore fall to *nedavah*. The *nesachim* — wine libations — are entirely consumed on the *mizbeach* without being eaten, which gives them *kodshei kodashim* status. Unlike the bread, which is *kodashim kalim*, the wine shares the *kodshei kodashim* character that makes *nedavah* the appropriate disposition for surplus funds.

---

## Kodashei Kodashim

### Three Positions

The *gemara* draws together three *amora'im* who have each articulated, in their own domain, the principle that surplus *kodshei kodashim* funds go to *nedavah*:

First, Shmuel, as reported by Rabbi Yosi who heard it in *Bavel* — *hefrish shkalov u'meis yiplu l'nedavah*: surplus *shekel* funds of a man who died go to *nedavah*. The *shekel* is not a *chatas*, yet its surplus goes to *nedavah*.

Second, Rabbi Eliezer — *mosar asirit ha'eifah shelo yiplu l'nedavah*: surplus funds of the *Kohen Gadol*'s *asirit ha'eifah* go to *nedavah*. This is the *asirit ha'eifah* of the *Kohen Gadol* — a *minchah* obligation, not a *chatas* — yet Rabbi Eliezer holds it goes to *nedavah*. (Rabbi Yochanan, recall, disagreed and ruled *Yam HaMelach*.)

Third, Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Bun — through his interpretation of Rav Chisda's position — holds that surplus *nazir* wine funds, as *kodshei kodashim*, go to *nedavah*.

The *gemara* aligns these three: *shloshtan amru davar echad* — all three expressed one principle. What ties them together is precisely the *kodshei kodashim* character of their respective surpluses. The rule of *nedavah* for leftover sanctified funds is thus not confined to the *chatas* category alone. Rather, the broader principle emerges: when obligatory funds of *kodshei kodashim* status have no remaining designated application, they go to *nedavah*. The distinction between what *yirkav* (rots) and what becomes *nedavah* tracks the distinction between *kodashim kalim* — such as the *nazir*'s bread — which cannot easily be redirected, and *kodshei kodashim*, which finds its natural home in the *nedavah* framework.

---

## Charitable Funds

### Ransom Rules

The *mishnah* now shifts from *hekdesh* to *tzedakah* funds designated for specific *mitzvah* purposes — the analogy to sanctified funds being structurally significant. *Mosar shvuyim l'shvuyim* — surplus funds collected generally for *pidyon shvuyim* are retained for future captives. *Mosar shavuy l'oto shavuy* — if funds were collected for a particular captive and there was a surplus after his ransom, that surplus belongs to him.

### Poor Funds

Similarly, *mosar aniyim l'aniyim* — general surplus funds for the poor are saved for future cases. *Mosar ani l'oto ani* — surplus funds raised for a specific poor person go to that individual. The parallel to *hekdesh* is evident: funds designated for a specific purpose or a specific person follow that designation.

### Burial Funds

*Mosar hametim lametim* — general surplus burial funds are saved for future burial needs. *Mosar hamet* — surplus raised for a specific deceased person is disputed. The *tanna kamma* holds it goes *l'yorshav* — to his heirs, since the funds were designated for him and what he would have owned passes to his heirs. Rabbi Meir holds the surplus must remain in escrow — *yehei munach ad she-yavo Eliyahu* — since it is unclear whether it should be used for additional honor to the deceased or passed to his heirs. Rabbi Natan holds the surplus is used for additional honor of the deceased — building a tombstone and providing for the dignity of his burial.

The underlying question is unique to the *met*: unlike the *ani* or the *shavuy*, the deceased cannot express a preference. The question is whether we assume the deceased would have wanted the funds to benefit his heirs, or to be applied to additional honor for his grave.

---

## Burial Excess

### Mistaken Collection

The *gemara* presents a specific case: *gavu lo be-chezkas she-ein lo v'nimtza she-yesh lo* — funds were collected for burial on the assumption that the deceased was penniless, and it then emerged that he had his own resources and did not need the collected funds. What becomes of the money?

### Heirs vs Mistake

Rav Yirmiyah initially inclined to say: *motar hamet l'yorshav* — apply the standard rule and give the surplus to the heirs, since the money was designated for the deceased regardless of the circumstances. Rav Idi of *Chutra* challenged him: *de-lo kiven ela leh* — the collectors only gave because they believed the deceased needed it. This is a fundamentally different case from the standard *mosar hamet*. There, the funds were genuinely needed and something was left over; here, the entire collection was predicated on a mistaken assumption. The whole enterprise was a *ta'us*, and the funds should be returned to the donors. Rav Yirmiyah pushed back: *ana lo amari — at mena lach?* — "I didn't assert that position — where do you get yours?" The *gemara* here turns on a question of *sevara*: who bears the burden of proof in characterizing the collection as either a legitimate designation-with-surplus or an error ab initio?

### Tombstone Use

A *baraisa* in the name of Rabbi Natan expands on his ruling from the *mishnah*: *motar hamet yibaneh lo nefesh al kivro* — the surplus is used to build a tombstone at the grave site. Additionally, *v'ya'aseh lo ziluf al gabei mitato* — some of the funds may be used to sprinkle wine over the coffin during transport, which served as a practical measure to address the odor of decomposition in an era without refrigeration. The *baraisa* also rules: *ein podin shavuy be-shavuy* — you do not redeem one captive with funds designated for another captive, and *ein govin tallit be-tallit* — one does not collect a cloak for a cloak, meaning funds collected for one specific item may not simply be redirected to a comparable item. The exception: *v'ein memachin be-yad parnasin le-kach* — one does not object to the charity officers making such redirections, because when funds are given to communal charity administrators, there is an implicit understanding that they have discretion over allocation.

### Righteous Memorial

A *baraisa* adds the famous teaching of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *ein osin nefashot la-tzaddikim* — one does not build tombstones for the righteous. *Divreihem hen hen zichronam* — their teachings, their words, their legacy: that is their memorial. The righteous do not require physical monuments; what they leave behind in Torah and deed constitutes their lasting remembrance. This teaching also implicitly cautions against the veneration of graves as physical sites, redirecting the instinct toward honoring the substance of what the *tzaddik* transmitted.

---

## Yochanan & Eliezer

### Hiding Encounter

The *gemara* closes with a narrative. Rabbi Yochanan *hava masmach ve-azal* — was being supported as he walked, leaning on Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, apparently due to his considerable weight. Rabbi Eliezer — a Babylonian who had come to *Eretz Yisrael* — saw Rabbi Yochanan approaching. *U-mitmar leh mi-kamei* — he went and hid.

### Yochanan's Complaint

Rabbi Yochanan, observing this through Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, remarked: *hani tarti milayu hadein Bavla avad bi* — this Babylonian has done two things to me. *Chada d'lo sha'al bishlomei* — first, he did not ask after my wellbeing, he offered no greeting. *V'chada d'mitmar* — and second, he fled into hiding, as if he could not bear to be in my presence.

### Babylonian Custom

Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, who happened to be present, explained: *kach minhagin gav'hon* — that is simply their practice over there in *Bavel*. *D'zeira lo sha'al bishlomeih d'rabba* — a person of lesser stature does not ask after the wellbeing of someone of greater stature. In Babylonian practice, greeting a *rav* as one greets a friend — *shalom alecha* — would itself be inappropriate, a kind of presumptuous familiarity. The absence of a greeting, far from being discourteous, is the proper expression of deference.

### Scripture Basis

Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi supports this practice from the verse: *re'uni ne'arim venichba'u, veyshishim kamu amadu* — "Young ones saw me and hid; elders rose and stood." The verse distinguishes two forms of honor: the elders rise and stand, an active demonstration of respect; the young ones — those of lesser standing — see the great figure and *hide*. Their concealment is itself the expression of awe. They cannot simply walk by; they cannot presume to offer a greeting; and so they withdraw entirely, an act that paradoxically manifests reverence through absence.

### Idol Analogy

To illuminate Rabbi Eliezer's behavior, Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi posed a pointed question to Rabbi Yochanan: *mahu me'avar kamei d'hadein tzalmaya?* — is it permitted to walk in front of this idol? Rabbi Yochanan replied: *ma palig lei y'kar?* — what honor are you showing it by avoiding it? *Avor kumei v'samei eynech* — walk right past it and close your eyes. By refusing to walk in front of an idol, one inadvertently confers upon it a kind of gravity and significance. The correct response is to walk past it with eyes averted — demonstrating indifference rather than awe. Treating the idol like something so weighty that you cannot pass before it is itself a form of reverence.

### Respect Shown

The analogy is then applied directly: *ah, ya'os Rabbi Eliezer avad* — you see, Rabbi Eliezer did right. Since Babylonian practice holds that a lesser person does not greet a greater one — because greeting is what you do with a peer, not with one before whom you stand in awe — to walk before Rabbi Yochanan and remain silent would have been the most conspicuous disrespect. Rabbi Eliezer was simply not prepared to do that. And so he hid. *D'lo avar kamach* — he did not walk past you. His concealment was not avoidance; it was reverence expressed in the only form Babylonian protocol permitted him.

The *gemara* will continue this encounter in the following *daf*, where Rabbi Yochanan's further concerns will be addressed.

---

---

# Shekalim 9

## Log & Kos Measures

### Log De'Oraita

The daf opens at the bottom of 79b, in the midst of a digression prompted by the mention of the baskets used for *terumat halishka* — the three annual removals of coins from the chamber where the *shkalim* were deposited. That discussion gave rise to a broader inquiry into the sizes of various measures not made explicit in certain *mishnayot*, including the size of the *kos* used for *kiddush* and the *arba kosot*. We now pick up with a further discussion of measures.

*Amar Rabbi Chanin*: the biblical *log* — the *log de'oraita* — is equivalent to the *tmunta atikta*, the old measure used for measuring fish brine in Tzipori. So now we know. This establishes the biblical *log* in terms of a contemporaneously recognizable standard.

### Log & Honey

*Amar Rabbi Yona*: *vachachamnala* — and I recognized it — that in the house of Rabbi Yannai they would use this same measure to measure honey. The word *mechilin*, to measure, is the same root used in the *Mechilta*, the Tannaitic work on Shemot — a term conveying the sense of gathering or collecting. The discussion here concerns volume, not weight, even though honey is considerably heavier than wine.

### Shminis Measure

A *baraita* teaches that *chatzi shminis tabernis hayeshana* — half of the ancient Tiberian *shminis* — is another measure relevant to this discussion. The *Korban HaEdah* understands this as equivalent to a *revi'it*, since half of a *shminis* (an eighth) yields a sixteenth, though the *shminis* itself, being an eighth, would need to be doubled to reach a *revi'it*. In any case, this represents another ancient measure that has a recognizable modern equivalent.

### Why 'Ancient'?

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: this ancient Tiberian *shminis* — *didan hu* — is really one of ours; we know what a *shminis* is and we have that measure today. So why is it called *atika*, the ancient one? *Min begin de'hava beyomei* — because it exists in our days. And some say that the ancient one actually used to be smaller, and then it was made larger, so the one we currently call the Tiberian *shminis* is larger than the ancient standard, which is why we must specify the ancient one. And there is yet another view: *de'azla* — that it was then re-shrunk, but *velo azla kema de'hava* — it was not shrunk back to its original size. In either case, the current Tiberian *shminis* does not precisely match the ancient measure, and therefore the ancient one must be specified by name.

### Kos Dimensions

What is the *shiur* of a *kos*? Rabbi Yose Berabbi Bun in the name of Rabbi Yose ben Pazai, and Rabbi Yose bar Bibi in the name of Rabbi Shmuel, states: *etzba'im al etzba'im rom etzba u'mechtza veshlish etzba* — two *etzba'ot* by two *etzba'ot* by one and a third plus one half, that is, 1.833 *etzba'ot*. This is a striking discrepancy: the *Bavli* in Pesachim gives the dimensions as two by two by 2.7, not two by two by 1.833. None of the commentators printed alongside the *Yerushalmi* even address this line, so it may be that they did not have it in their text, or that there is some other explanation — but it is clearly a different size than what the *Bavli* records.

---

## Wine & Tumah

### Dried Wine

If wine dries up — *yavesh* — a *revi'it* of wine, when congealed, will be the size of a *kazayit*. This appears in a number of places in the *Bavli* as well, where it is assumed that a congealed *revi'it* equals a *kazayit*. The relevance to *Shabbat* is presumably this: if one carries dried wine, the *shiur* for carrying is a *kazayit*, since the dried wine is not being mixed with water and therefore one goes by the full size of the *kos*, by the *revi'it*, and a dried-up *revi'it* of wine becomes a *kazayit*. These are the words of Rabbi Natan.

### Rabbi Natan

The sages of Keisarah — Rabbi Yose bar Bibi in the name of Shmuel — note that Rabbi Natan's position here follows that of Rabbi Shimon. Just as Rabbi Shimon holds that one is only *chayav* for carrying wine on *Shabbat* if one carries a *revi'it* — not a quarter of a *revi'it* of concentrate — so too Rabbi Natan holds that the *revi'it*, when it dries up and congeals, becomes a *kazayit*.

The question is not in dispute: a *kazayit* is understood to be the quantity that a *revi'it* becomes when it congeals. The debate concerns only the *Shabbat* carrying context. Why do we go by a *revi'it* rather than by what is normally used when dealing with concentrate — a quarter of a *revi'it*? Some *nosei kelim* explain that one only uses the quarter-*revi'it* size when dealing with the concentrate in liquid form, because in that form it is significant: water can easily be added to reconstitute it into a full *revi'it*. When it is in congealed form, that small a quantity loses its significance. However, the *Gemara* here is suggesting that Rabbi Natan may actually hold that even in liquid concentrate form one needs a full *revi'it*, and therefore in congealed form one needs a *kazayit* — and this is consistent with Rabbi Shimon's position that even liquid wine goes by a *revi'it*, not a quarter of a *revi'it*. A note from one of the students identifies the *Tosafot* in Pesachim as making a related point about a different standard finger-width used in Tzipori, which would affect the dimensional calculations — a detail worth following up.

---

## Neveilah Blood

### Mule Story

The *Gemara* transitions from the question of a *revi'it* that congeals to a related topic involving blood. Rabbi Simon in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reports: *maaseh be-pirdat Rabbi she-metah* — there is a story involving the mule of Rabbi (Rebbi), which died. *Ve-tiharu et damah mishum neveilah* — and they declared its blood not problematic on account of *neveilah*, because *neveilah* applies to the meat, not to the blood. This, however, raises a significant question. In various areas of *halakha*, blood is treated similarly to meat: would the blood of a *neveilah*, if there were enough of it to constitute the equivalent of a *kazayit* of meat, itself be *tamei*? The story says the blood was *tahor* — but was it *tahor* categorically, or only because there was not enough of it?

### Blood Amount

*Ve-sha'al Rabbi Eliezer et Rabbi Simon*: Rabbi Eliezer asked Rabbi Simon, *ad kama* — how much blood would have been considered acceptable? Is the blood categorically *tahor*, or is there a threshold amount? *Velo ashkhach beh* — and Rabbi Simon did not respond to him. He went instead to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi himself, who said: *ad revi'it tahor yoter mirevi'it tamei* — up to a *revi'it* it is *tahor*, more than that is *tamei*. The reasoning is that a *revi'it* of blood, when it congeals, becomes a *kazayit*, and just as a *kazayit* of meat is *tamei*, so too a *revi'it* of blood would be *tamei* — and the reason the blood in the story was *tahor* was that it was less than a *revi'it*. It is slightly puzzling that the text says *yoter mirevi'it tamei* rather than *revi'it veyoter tamei*, but the *Gemara* does not pause on that formulation. The *mefarshim* clarify that biblically only the meat is *metamei*; rabbinically, blood becomes *tamei* once it reaches a *revi'it* in quantity.

### Bibi's Version

Rabbi Bibi was sitting and retelling this same story, when Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna — or bar Kahana — posed the same question: when they said the blood was *tahor*, did they mean up to a *revi'it* it is *tahor* and beyond that *tamei*, or was it categorically *tahor*? *Uva'at beh* — and he kicked him. The *Korban HaEdah* understands this as the questioner going to Rabbi Simon himself, who this time, rather than simply ignoring the question, responded with a kick.

### Paltar Bread

Rav Zerika challenged whoever did the kicking: *begin dasha'al lakh at ba'at beh* — he asked you a legitimate question, why did you kick him? The reply: *begin dila hava da'ati bi* — because my mind was not settled, I was not in a good frame of mind, so I kicked him. And what caused this unsettled state? *Da'amar Rabbi Chanin*: the verse in Devarim, *vehayu chayekha teluyim lekha mineged* — your life will hang before you — refers to one who must purchase grain for an entire year without owning land, relying entirely on others for his food supply. *Ufachadeta laila veyomam* — and you will be afraid night and day — refers to one who purchases from the *sadki*, the retailer, buying week to week with no reserves. *Lo ta'amin bechayecha* — you will not trust your life — refers to one who buys *pas paltar*, already-baked bread from the baker, having no grain stores of his own whatsoever. *Ve-ana samichna a-paltar* — and I rely on the baker's bread — he was saying that this is his situation, one of perpetual anxiety about where his sustenance will come from.

This is a remarkable explanation. It does not fully account for why the pattern of refusing or kicking recurred, but it frames it as a reflection of an ongoing psychological state of insecurity. There is a broader historical context worth noting: in *Eretz Yisrael* under Roman rule there was a period of significant inflation, after which the Roman government subsidized bread, which gave rise to various leniencies regarding *pas paltar*. Whether that context illuminates this passage is unclear, but the connection between reliance on the baker's bread and a state of existential anxiety would have resonated sharply in that environment.

### Halakha Decision

Stepping back from the story, the *Gemara* asks: *u-ma kado* — so what is the actual *halakha*? Is the blood of a *neveilah* categorically *tahor*, or is it *tamei* above a certain threshold?

### BenPesora

A *baraita* — indeed a *mishnah* in Eduyot — states: *Heid Rabbi Yehoshua ben Pesora al dam neveilah she-hu tahor* — Rabbi Yehoshua ben Pesora testified that the blood of a *neveilah* is categorically *tahor*. This seems to establish clearly that it is not a question of quantity but of categorical status.

### Sheretz Blood

An attempt is made to reinterpret the word *tahor* in that *mishnah*: perhaps *tahor* means only that the blood does not render food susceptible to *tumah* — it is not *machshir* — but that it is itself a source of *tumah*. This would be a remarkable re-reading of a simple declaration of *tahor*. The *Gemara* challenges this immediately. The *mishnah* in Machshirin states: *dam sheretz ki-bsaro* — the blood of a *sheretz* is like its flesh: *metamei ve-eino machshir* — it causes *tumah* exactly as the flesh of a *sheretz* does but does not render food susceptible. And then the *mishnah* continues: *ve-ein lanu ke-yotzei bo* — nothing else is like this. No other blood has the quality of being *metamei* but not *machshir*. Therefore, that quality cannot be ascribed to the blood of a *neveilah*, because the *mishnah* explicitly says only the blood of a *sheretz* occupies that singular category. Furthermore, the *shiur* for the blood of a *sheretz* to convey *tumah* is the same as for its flesh — the size of a lentil.

### Amoraim Split

*Ve-amar Rav Yosef plig ba terei amora'ei* — Rav Yosef states that this question, whether blood of a *neveilah* is *metamei*, is actually a dispute between two *amora'im*: one says *tamei* and one says *tahor*. The one who says *tamei* follows Rabbi Yehuda, who cites a *mishnah* that records the debate between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel, where according to Beis Hillel the blood of a *neveilah* is *metamei*. The one who says *tahor* follows the *mishnah* of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Pesora, cited above. Thus the question of whether blood of a *neveilah* is fundamentally *tahor* or *tamei* is both a *machlokes tanna'im* and a *machlokes amora'im* mapping onto those respective Tannaitic positions.

### Advuma's Proof

*Amar lei Rav Advuma de-min Nachusa*: this works out well — *ve-yeus de-Rebbi Yehudah moreina de-bei nesi'ah havei* — because Rabbi Yehuda was effectively the *posek* for the house of the *nasi*, and we recall that the house of the *nasi* at that time was Rebbi's household — the household whose mule had died in the opening story. So when they declared the blood *tahor* because it was less than a certain amount, that was consistent with the ruling of Rabbi Yehuda: he holds that blood of a *neveilah* is indeed *tamei* rabbinically once it reaches a *revi'it* (at which point it congeals into a *kazayit*), and the blood in the story was *tahor* only because it fell below that threshold. This neatly resolves the narrative: the story was proceeding according to Rabbi Yehuda's *psak*, not according to the categorical *tahor* view of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Pesora.

It is worth noting that the *Yerushalmi* here reflects quite naturally on the fact that Rebbi — who was not only the political leader but the pre-eminent *talmid chacham* of his generation — nonetheless had a dedicated in-house *posek*. The *Bavli* regularly discusses the rabbis who served in this capacity for the *Reish Galusa*, whose household raised its own set of halakhic challenges. Here, however, it is more surprising: one imagines how much time Rebbi actually had for the *beis medrash* while running the entire political and communal apparatus. The assumption that he needed a *posek* for the day-to-day *she'eilot* of his own home raises genuine questions about the realities of his schedule.

---

## Beyond Suspicion

### Appearance Issue

The *Gemara* returns to the *mishnah*, which expresses concern not that the one collecting *terumat halishka* might steal, but that if something later changes in his financial circumstances — whether he becomes richer or poorer — people will attribute it to theft from the *lishka*. Therefore, the system is designed so that he is beyond any possible suspicion. As one participant notes, this concern extends beyond the individual: it would cast aspersions on the entire *Beis HaMikdash* system and the integrity of the institution. The *mishnah*'s invocation of *ve-yissem neki'im*, however, is read at the individual level as well.

### Body Search

A *baraita* taught by Rabbi Yishmael: a *kvat* — possibly a person with long, flowing hair or locks — should not perform the removal, because of *mipnei hachashad*, the appearance of impropriety (coins could be concealed in such hair). Another *baraita* states that the *gizbarim* would conduct a thorough pat-down — *mepaspasin be-kilkelin*, inspecting his hair or garments — before and after entry. Furthermore, they would speak with him continuously — *medabberin hayu immo she-hu nichnas ad she-hu yotzei* — from the time he entered to the time he exited, to prevent him from swallowing any coins.

One might ask: why not simply fill his mouth with water before he enters, so that he could not swallow anything? This was indeed raised.

### Bracha Issue

*Amar Rav Tanchuma*: *mipnei habracha* — because of the *bracha*. In passing, the *Gemara* reveals that when the designated official would lift the money out with the basket, he would recite a *bracha*, just as one recites a *bracha* on taking *terumah* of grain. This is a striking detail: the entire act of removing funds from the collective chamber has been ritualized as *terumat halishka*, with its own accompanying *bracha*. The mouth therefore could not be filled with water, as that would prevent the *bracha* from being recited.

The degree to which this act was ritualized is worth pausing on. What is functionally a transfer of funds from one room to another — coins collected in a chamber being moved to a operational account — was transformed into a solemn ritual complete with formal pronouncements, prescribed questions and answers, tarping procedures, and a *bracha*. This ritualization will become even more apparent as the *mishnah* continues.

### Clean Twice

Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: in Torah, *Nevi'im*, and *Ketuvim* we find that a person must not only be innocent before God but must also be seen as beyond reproach by other people — *latzet yedei habriyot* — just as one must be clean before *HaMakom*.

### Three Sources

*BaTorah minayin*: from the verse *ve-yissem neki'im meHashem u-miYisrael* — you shall be clean both before God and before Israel. *BaNevi'im minayin*: the verse *El Elohim Hashem veYisrael hu yeda* — God knows and Israel will know — from the episode in *Ever HaYarden* where the tribes were suspected of building a *bamah* for rebellion, and they declared their innocence before both God and the people. *UvaKetuvim minayin*: *u-matzah chen vesechel tov be'einei Elohim ve'adam* — you will find favor in the eyes of both God and people.

### Cleanest Pasuk

Gamliel Zuga asked Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Bun: *eizo hi hamchuvarta she-bekulan* — which of these three *psukim* most clearly and cleanly captures this standard? The answer: *ve-yissem neki'im meHashem u-miYisrael*, because the term *naki* — clean — most directly conveys the idea of being completely free from any suspicion or blemish, and it explicitly demands this cleanliness both before God and before the people of Israel.

---

## Terumat Ritual

### Gamliel Timing

The *mishnah* describes an interesting practice of Beis Rabban Gamliel. *Shel Beis Rabban Gamliel hayah nichnas ve-shiklo beyado bein etzbe'otav* — Rabban Gamliel would time his entry so that his *shekel* was held between his fingers, *vezarko lifnei hatoram* — and he would throw it directly in front of the one performing the removal at precisely the moment of the *terumah* act — *ve-hatoram mitkaven vetochavo letoch hakuppah* — and the one performing the removal would have *kavanah* and insert it into the basket. The motivation was to ensure that his money would be among the funds actually used for the *korban*, and not left behind among the remainder.

One wonders how this was permitted, given that it might cause others to feel their money was left behind. But Rabban Gamliel was the *nasi*, and the prerogative of position apparently extended this far.

### Take Terumah?

The one performing the removal does not simply proceed: *ein hatoram torem ad she-hu omer lahem etrom* — he first asks those supervising, "Shall I take the *terumah*?" *Ve-hen omrim lo terom* — and they say, "Take it." This exchange is performed three times — *shalosh pe'amim* — before he proceeds.

### Tarping System

*Tarma harishona*: after the first removal — presumably at Pesach time — the money left behind was covered with a tarp, *chippah be-katavliot*. This ensured that when new funds accumulated and the second removal was made at Shavuot, the *terumah* would be taken only from the new money piled atop the tarp, not from the previously-addressed funds. The second removal was similarly covered. *Shlishit lo haya mechape* — the third removal required no covering, since no new funds would be arriving afterward.

The reason for the tarp is rooted in the *terumah* model: just as one cannot take *terumah* from a new heap by drawing from a pile on which *terumah* has already been taken — *ein tormin min hachadash al hachadash* only from untouched grain — so too here, the removal must come from fresh funds, not from funds already addressed by a prior removal.

*Lama haya mechape*: why cover it at all? *Shema yishkach veyitrom min hadavar hatarum* — lest he forget and take from what has already been taken, which would be invalid.

### Three Regions

*Tarama et harishona leshem Eretz Yisrael*: the first removal was designated for those who lived in Israel, whose funds arrived earliest. *Ve-hashniya leshem krachim hamukaffin la* — the second for the cities and lands surrounding Israel. The phrase is notable: *krachim hamukaffin* normally refers to cities surrounded by a wall (as in the laws of *Megilla*), but here *mukaffin la* means surrounding Israel — a creative reuse of familiar terminology. *Ve-hashlishit leshem Bavel ve-leshem Madai ve-leshem medinot hayam* — the third for Babylonia, Media, and all the distant lands, whose funds arrived latest.

### Grain Analogy

The *Gemara* addresses the practice of Rabban Gamliel through an analogy from *terumah* of grain. *Ilu hayu shney krayim ve-toram mi-echad mehen al chavero* — if one had two mounds of grain and took *terumah* from one on behalf of both, the *terumah* applies to both and the second mound is certainly covered. So why did Rabban Gamliel insist his specific coin be in the basket? If the removal is taken from the communal funds and covers all the funds including the remainder, his money is represented whether or not it was physically scooped. The *Gemara* answers: *nachas ruach hi lahem* — it gave them personal satisfaction — *shelo yehe korban mitkarev ela mishelahem techila* — they wanted their money to be the first used toward the purchase of a *korban*. Not that one would not be *yotze* otherwise — obviously everyone would be — but the emotional and symbolic significance of having one's own money go first mattered to them.

### Barayta Pronouncements

A *baraita* elaborates the formal proclamations made during each removal. For the first: *harei zo me'Eretz Yisrael al kol Yisrael* — this is from the funds of Israel, for the sake of all of Israel. The *Tosefta* is even more explicit, recording the full text of each pronouncement and noting that after the first removal the tarp was put down, *mipnei she'anshei Surya ba'im ve-shoklim aleha* — because the people of Syria would come and add their contributions on top of it, necessitating separation. For the second: *harei zo me'Ammon u-miMoav u-mikrachim hamukafin le-Eretz Yisrael* — from Ammon, Moab, and the surrounding lands — for all Israel. For the third: *harei zo miBavel u-miMadai u-mimedinos harchokos al kol Yisrael* — from Babylon, Media, and the distant lands — for all of Israel. The funds were acknowledged by origin, but the act was performed for all of *Klal Yisrael*.

---

## Shirayim Status

### Tarp Slip

*Shamat et hakattabaliyot* — if the tarp slipped accidentally, *nasu kullan shirayim* — everything becomes mixed together and takes on the status of *shirayim*, remainder funds. This is the *Tosefta*'s understanding: the mixing was accidental. The consequence is that one cannot now take the second removal from the mixed pile, since it cannot be distinguished which funds are new and which were already addressed. Following the *terumah* model strictly — one cannot take *terumah* from a pile already subject to a prior removal — the entire mixed pile is treated as *shirayim* and unavailable for the next formal removal.

---

## Third Collection

### Gold Coins

*Shelishit hi hayta ha-ashira she-bekullan* — the third collection was the richest of all. *She-haya bo istariyot shel zahav* — it contained these gold *istariyot* (possibly a type of gold coin or, according to some, fine garments), *darkonot shel zahav* — and gold *darkonot*. As discussed earlier in the masechta, when contributions were being transported from great distances, it was practical to convert them into more valuable denominations, which is why the third collection — from Babylon and the distant lands — arrived in gold. Strictly speaking, converting to gold does not necessarily mean the total monetary value was greater; one is simply expressing the same wealth in higher-denomination coins. Nevertheless, there are independent reasons to think the third collection genuinely represented greater wealth. First, it had the longest window of collection, from Sukkot until Pesach — approximately half the year. Second, it is well attested that the financial situation of the Jewish community in Bavel was substantially stronger than in *Eretz Yisrael*. Third, the sheer geographic spread and likely population of the diaspora communities in Babylon and beyond may have exceeded that of *Eretz Yisrael* itself. Those who chose not to return from exile were in many cases economically integrated and prosperous. The third collection, therefore, was almost certainly wealthier not merely in coin type but in aggregate value — which would explain why it also had to last the longest, sustaining the *Beis HaMikdash* operations for the six months between Sukkot and Pesach, while the first collection only had to last the two months from Pesach to Shavuot.

---

## Shirayim Status (II)

### Basket Cycle

A *baraita* details the cycling procedure among the three baskets used at each removal. *Natal min harishona af al pi sheyesh barishona natal min hashniya* — they took from basket one even though there was still some left in basket one, and moved to basket two; *natal min hashniya af al pi sheyesh bashniya natal min hashlishis* — and from basket two even though there was still some left, to basket three. This refers to the three baskets from the Pesach removal that needed to fund the *korbanos* until Shavuot. They would cycle through them: use basket one, then two, then three — *shalma shlishis chozer lishniya* — when basket three was exhausted, return to basket two — *shalma shniya chozer lishona* — when two was done, return to basket one.

### Exhausted Baskets

*Shalmu shloshtan* — if all three baskets were exhausted before the next *terumah* was due, what then? *Chozer veshokel* — one returns and collects anew. The precise mechanics of this are not fully clarified: since contributions would be arriving continuously from outlying regions, there would likely be funds available, but the exact procedure of *chozer veshokel* — whether it means soliciting new contributions specifically or simply drawing on funds already received but not yet formally included — remains unclear.

### Meir: Use Shirayim

Rabbi Meir has a simpler solution: *chozer lishirayim* — return to the remainder funds, the *shirayim*. If the three baskets are exhausted, simply draw on the money left behind from the prior removal.

### Sanctified?

Rabbi Meir continues: *mo'ilin b'shirayim* — *me'ilah* applies to the *shirayim*, because *shema yitztarchu lahem b'sof* — you may need to draw on those funds again. This hints at a fundamental disagreement about the status of the remainder funds. According to the *chakhamim* who dispute Rabbi Meir, the *shirayim* lose their *kedushah* after the *terumah* is taken — analogous to the *terumah* of grain model: after *terumah* is removed from *tevel*, the remaining grain becomes *chullin*. So too the remaining funds, according to the *chakhamim*, revert to a non-*kodesh* status, available for the *Beis HaMikdash*'s discretionary operating expenses but no longer subject to *me'ilah* as consecrated *korban* funds. Rabbi Meir rejects this: the remainder funds remain *kodesh*, *me'ilah* applies to them, and one may therefore draw on them if needed.

What is remarkable — as the lecturer notes in closing — is what the *chakhamim*'s position implies: they constructed this elaborate ritual called *terumat halishka*, modeled on the *terumah* of grain, with the consequence that after the *terumah* act the remaining funds are formally desanctified. They truly converted what was essentially a logistical transfer of communal money into a ritual with real halakhic consequences for the sanctity of the funds left behind.

---

## Third Collection (II)

### Pinchas Chain

The *Gemara* connects the foregoing discussion of Rabbi Meir to a famous statement attributed to him in the name of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair — a statement whose structure forms the organizing principle of the *Sefer Mesillas Yesharim*. *V'chein hayah Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair omer* — this is what Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair used to say:

*Zerizus mevia l'idei neki'os* — alacrity brings to cleanliness. *Neki'os mevia l'idei taharah* — cleanliness brings to purity. *Taharah mevia l'idei kedushah* — purity brings to holiness. *Kedushah mevia l'idei anavah* — holiness brings to humility. *Anavah mevia l'idei yiras cheit* — humility brings to fear of sin. *Yiras cheit mevia l'idei chasidus* — fear of sin brings to *chasidus*, which denotes some combination of scrupulousness, generosity, and high piety. *Chasidus mevia l'idei Ruach HaKodesh* — that brings to divine inspiration. *Ruach HaKodesh mevia l'idei techiyas hameitim* — divine inspiration brings to resurrection of the dead. *Techiyas hameitim mevia l'idei Eliyahu zachor latov* — and resurrection brings about Elijah, who is bound up with the entire process of *mashiach* and final redemption.

The connection to Rabbi Meir's statement is admittedly tenuous. The suggestion is that Rabbi Meir, in insisting that the remainder funds remain *kodesh* so that they may be drawn upon if needed, exhibits a kind of careful *zerizus* — covering all bases, leaving nothing unguarded — and it is this quality of care and vigilance that serves as the opening link in Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's chain.

### Pinchas Proofs
