The *Gemara* supplies a scriptural proof for each link in the chain. *Zerizus mevia l'idei neki'os dechsiv ve-chilah mikapeir* — perhaps reading *ve-chilah* as *be-chulah*, doing something completely and fully, which leads to a cleansing. *Neki'os mevia l'idei taharah dechsiv ve-chiper aleha ha-kohen ve-taherah* — he atoned and she became pure. *Taharah mevia l'idei kedushah dechsiv ve-tiharo ve-kidsho* — this connection is transparent: *taharah* is a precondition for entering the *Beis HaMikdash* and encountering the holy. *Kedushah mevia l'idei anavah dechsiv ki cho amar ram ve-nisa shochein ad ve-kadosh shemo marom ve-kadosh eshkon ve-es daka ushfal ruach* — God, who is most exalted and holy, directs his presence toward the lowly and humble in spirit. So holiness — understood through God's own attribute of holiness — translates into a turn toward humility. *Anavah mevia l'idei yiras cheit dechsiv eikev anavah yiras Hashem* — as a result of humility comes fear of God. *Yiras cheit mevia l'idei chasidus dechsiv ve-chesed Hashem me'olam ve'ad olam al yere'av* — God's eternal kindness rests upon those who fear him; *yirat cheit* thus flows into *chasidus*, though here *chasidus* is expressed through God's *chesed* rather than the human quality directly. *Chasidus mevia l'idei Ruach HaKodesh dechsiv az dibarta ve-chazon la-chasidecha* — you have spoken in a vision to your pious ones, so the *chasid* merits *Ruach HaKodesh*. *Ruach HaKodesh mevia l'idei techiyas hameitim dechsiv ve-natati ruchi bachem ve-chiyitem* — I will put my spirit within you and you will live again, the vision of Yechezkel, so *Ruach HaKodesh* leads to resurrection. *Techiyas hameitim mevia l'idei Eliyahu dechsiv hinei anochi sholeach lachem et Eliyah ha-navi lifnei bo yom Hashem ha-gadol ve-ha-nora* — behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome day of God.

---

## Closing Mishnah

### Fixed in Israel

The *perek* closes with another statement in the name of Rabbi Meir: *kol mi she-kavu'a be-Eretz Yisrael* — whoever is permanently settled in Israel, not merely visiting but truly fixed there, *u-medaber bi-lashon ha-kodesh* — and speaks in the holy tongue, *ve-ochel perotav be-tahara* — and eats his food in *tahara* — threading together the themes of *kedushah* and *tahara* — *ve-koreh Kriyat Shema ba-boker u-va-erev*, and recites *Kriyat Shema* morning and evening — *kemevaser she-ben olam ha-ba hu* — he is assured of being a son of the World to Come.

The connection to the preceding discussion is not immediately transparent, but the statement draws together the themes of the *perek*: the sanctity of the land, the purity with which one conducts oneself, the holy language, and the acknowledgment of God morning and night. With this the *perek* concludes: *hadran lach perek bi-shlosha prakim*.

What we have seen across this entire daf is the thoroughgoing ritualization of *terumat halishka* — what began as a practical accounting procedure for communal Temple funds was transformed into a solemn act with prescribed language, formal questioning, tarping protocols, a *bracha*, geographic designations, and real halakhic consequences for the status of funds left behind. The *chakhamim*'s insistence that the *shirayim* lose their *kedushah* after the act — modeled explicitly on *terumah* of grain — and Rabbi Meir's counter-position that they remain *kodesh* and subject to *me'ilah*, are not merely administrative disagreements. They reflect a fundamental question about the nature of this act: is it a ritual transformation, with the accompanying consequences that once the act is complete the remainder reverts to ordinary status, or is it an ongoing consecration that leaves the entire pool of funds in a perpetually holy state?

---

---

# Shekalim 10

## Communal Funds Overview

### Opening & Transition

We begin *daf* 10 with a new *perek*, picking up from the bottom of *daf* 9b. The preceding material described how the money was physically removed from the chamber — a procedure called *trumat halishka*, the taking of the *truma* from the *lishka*. That process, as we saw, was deliberately fashioned to resemble the taking of *truma*, with the remainder designated as *shirayim*. Questions surrounding what remained and whether it retained sanctity will be revisited briefly. This new *perek* turns our attention to a different question: what was actually done with the funds? We have been saying all along that the money went toward *korbanos tzibur*, communal sacrifices. Now the *mishna* gives us the specifics.

### Terumah Usage

The *mishna* opens with the question: *hatruma mah hayu osin bah* — what would they do with the *truma*? Note that the term *truma* is employed deliberately; it is not simply asking what was done with the *shekalim*. This framing continues to emphasize the *truma*-like character of the withdrawal. The answer: *lokchim ba temidin umusafin veniskeyhen* — they would purchase the *korbanos tzibur* with it: the *temidin*, the two daily sacrifices; the *musaf* offerings, which consist largely of *olos* together with a *chatas*; and the *nesachim*, meaning the wine, grain, and flour that accompanied them — all of the *korbanos tzibur* with their attendant offerings brought upon the *mizbe'ach*.

### Non-Animal Offerings

The *mishna* continues: *ha'omer ushtei halechem v'lechem hapanim* — the *omer*, the *shtei halechem* brought on *Pesach* and *Shavuos*, and the *lechem hapanim*, which also constitutes a *korban tzibur*. These are non-animal *minchos* that qualify as *korbanos tzibur* and are therefore purchased from the communal fund. The *mishna* concludes: *v'chol korbanos hatzibur* — and all *korbanos tzibur*. Were this the *Bavli*, one would expect the *gemara* to ask *kol l'rabos mai* — what does the inclusive word "all" come to add? The *Yerushalmi* does not raise that question, and, as we shall see, neither does the *gemara* that follows.

---

## Omer & Shemita

### Watchers Payment

The *mishna* then introduces an interesting case: *shomrey sefichin beshvi'is notnim sachar mitrumas halishka* — the people who watch the wild growth during *shemita* are paid from the *trumat halishka*. What is the background? During the *shemita* year, one does not plant the grain that will be harvested for the *omer*. Instead, one takes grain that has grown spontaneously from dropped seeds — the *sefichin*, the wild growth. But to ensure there is something available to cut, one must hire people to watch over designated fields, preventing others from taking the grain, while not acting in a proprietary manner that would itself violate *shemita*. The watching is done on behalf of the *beis din*, the *mikdash*, and *klal Yisrael*. Once the grain is ready, it is harvested and taken into the possession of the *beis hamikdash*. The key point is that you can pay these workers from the *trumat halishka* even though you are not paying for the *korban* object itself.

### R. Yosi View

*Rabbi Yosi* goes further: *af harotze mitnadve shomer chinam* — if someone wishes to volunteer as a watcher without compensation, watches the grain for the sake of the *beis hamikdash* without being hired, and then himself harvests and donates the grain to the *beis hamikdash*, that is also acceptable. Rabbi Yosi may have been more tentative about deploying the communal funds to cover secondary needs of the *korban*; his solution is to allow someone to donate their time freely and simply give over the grain as a gift.

### Tzorchei Korban

The underlying principle at work is *tzorchei korban k'korban* — the needs that enable a *korban* to be brought may be funded from the same source as the *korban* itself. This principle opens a broad range of possibilities, several of which we will explore as we proceed.

### Sages' Objection

The *chachamim* respond: *amru lo, af ata omer she'ein ba'in ela mishel tzibur* — do you not yourself admit that the *korbanos* may only be brought from communal funds? This sets up the central debate of the *gemara*: may an individual make a private donation to the *beis hamikdash* for the purpose of a communal sacrifice? If I bring my own sheep and declare that I give it wholeheartedly to the *beis hamikdash* for use as a *tamid* on behalf of *klal Yisrael*, is that permissible?

The *chachamim*'s objection to Rabbi Yosi's model is that when a private individual watches the grain and then cuts and donates it, the wheat has been his personal property — and his personal property becoming a donation is not acceptable to the *chachamim* for a *korban tzibur*. We want communal sacrifices purchased with communal funds. Private donation, even for a communal purpose, is rejected. One might ask whether the concern is purely one of appearances — that no one should be able to say "that was my *korban*" when the whole point is that it is being brought on behalf of *klal Yisrael* — or whether there is an objective halachic deficiency: that the act of purchasing communally is constitutive of *korban tzibur* status, and a private donation, however sincerely given, cannot replicate it. As we shall see, the *gemara*'s own discussion suggests the concern is specifically about the *korban* itself, not about communal purpose in general.

---

## Private Donations

### Gemara Framing

The *gemara* does something structurally interesting: it skips over the opening of the *mishna* and goes directly to this debate, planning to double back to the beginning later. It opens with the question *mah ra'u* — why was this practice established? This connects to a *mishna* in *Taanis*, which records that there were eight occasions, *zman atzei hakohanim ve'ha'am*, on which eight families each had a designated date for contributing wood to the *beis hamikdash*. The question immediately arises: since wood for the *mizbe'ach* must be communally owned, does the fact that these families contributed their own private wood not raise precisely the problem of private donations for communal purposes?

### Eight Families

Each of the eight families had its own date — a fact that, as we shall see, had historical roots. Although the *beis hamikdash* would normally purchase communal needs from the *shekel* funds, wood presents an interesting case: it is communally owned, yet it is not a *korban* proper. Where does it come from? That question will be addressed in later *mishnayos*. For now, the issue is whether the entire institution of family wood donations — individual property given over for communal use — is subject to the debate between *Rabbi Yosi* and the *chachamim*.

### Wood Donations History

The *baraisa* explains: *besha'ah she'alu Yisrael min hagolah* — when the Jewish people returned from exile in the days of *Ezra*, *velo matzu etzim balishkah* — there was no wood in the *lishka*. The temple was being rebuilt and the wood stores were empty. *Ve'amdu elu ve'nisnadvu etzim mishel atzmam* — these eight families rose and donated wood from their own resources, *u'mesarum latzibur* — and freely gave it over for communal use. *Ve'hikrivu mehem korbanos tzibur* — and *korbanos tzibur* were brought upon those fires. *Ve'hisnu imahem nevi'im shebeineihem* — the prophets among them — presumably *Chaggai*, *Zecharyah*, and *Malachi*, the last of the prophets — stipulated with them: *she'afillu lishkah meleiah etzim* — even in the future, when the storehouses are full of wood, *ve'amdu elu ve'nisnadvu etzim mishel atzmam* — if these families wish to continue donating their wood, we will not refuse on grounds that we have enough. Moreover, *shelo yehei korban miskarev ella mishelahem techilah* — we will use their donated wood first, as the first wood upon which offerings are brought that week.

This institution is striking. Not only do the *chachamim* accept private wood donations, but they ensure that the donated wood takes precedence, and the dates themselves become family holidays. If anything, this seems *more* problematic than the case of *Rabbi Yosi*, since the families' identity is permanently bound up with the practice.

### R. Yacha's Analysis

*Amar Rabbi Yacha d'Rabbi Yose* — Rabbi Yacha the son of Rabbi Yosi says: that entire institution follows the approach of *Rabbi Yosi*, as Rabbi Yosi holds that one may contribute one's own time and resources for the sake of the *beis hamikdash* for communal purposes. The wood donation institution thus reflects only *Rabbi Yosi*'s view, not the view of the *chachamim*.

### Core Distinction

*Rabbi Yose b'shem Ila* — or, as others have it, *Rav Assi b'shem Rabbi Ila* — responds: *divrei hakol hi* — the *mishna* actually represents a unanimous position. *Mah peligan* — where does the disagreement between *Rabbi Yosi* and the *chachamim* lie? *Beguf d'korban* — concerning the *korban* itself. Can the actual object to be offered come from a private donation? That is contested. *Aval bemachshirei korban* — but for things that enable the *korban* to be brought, such as the wood, *kol ama modei* — everyone agrees that *shehi mishtaneh korban yachid lekorban tzibbur* — one can take something that was privately owned and dedicate it for communal purposes. Thus private donations are universally accepted for attendant matters; only for the *korban* itself do the *chachamim* resist.

What precisely is the concern with the *korban* itself? It does not appear to be a worry that the object never truly becomes communal property, since the *chachamim* readily accept private donations for other communal needs. The concern seems to be something more specific to the *ikar* of what is placed upon the *mizbe'ach* — the thing that most essentially represents the community before God. For that, no individual should be able to say "that is mine." Everything else is, as it were, a sideshow; but the *korban tzibur* itself must be purchased communally. Whether this is a policy sensitivity or an objective halachic requirement that communal purchasing constitutes *korban tzibur* status is not spelled out by the *Yerushalmi*.

---

## Kohen Gadol Garments

### Tunic Case

A *baraisa* is now cited: *isha she'asta kutonet livnah* — if a woman made a white tunic, *keshera* — it may be used for the *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur*, *uvilvad she'timserena letzibbur* — provided she freely gives it over to the community. The case involves the white linen garments worn by the *kohen gadol* during the *Yom Kippur* service.

### Consensus Position

*Rabbi Yacha d'Rabbi Yose* initially says this follows *Rabbi Yosi*'s position — that one may donate privately for communal purposes. But *Rabbi Yose b'shem Ila* responds again: *divrei hakol hi* — everyone agrees to this. *Mah peligan* — the debate is only *beguf d'korban*, concerning the *korban* itself. *Aval bemachshirei korban, kol ama modei* — for anything that enables the *avoda* to be performed, everyone agrees you may accept private donations and convert them to communal use. The white garments of the *kohen gadol* are *machshirei korban* — they enable the *avoda* — but they are not themselves the *korban*. This is admittedly somewhat counterintuitive, given the particular weight attached to the *kohen gadol*'s *bigdim* on *Yom Kippur*, but the formal classification is clear: the garments facilitate the *avoda*; they are not what is offered. The *Yerushalmi* does not explain precisely why the line is drawn exactly at the *korban* itself.

### Wood & Holiday

The *gemara* now offers additional proof that even the *chachamim* accept private donations for communal purposes other than the *korban* itself. A *baraisa* teaches: *otam yamim nohagim beshaat korban ushelo beshaat korban* — those eight days are observed as family *yom tovs* whether it is the era of *korbanos*, i.e., the time of the *beis hamikdash*, or not. *Rabbi Yosi*, however, says: *einam nohagim ella b'shaat korban bilvad* — they are observed only during the era of *korbanos*.

It is worth noting the *Yerushalmi*'s different formulation: instead of the *Bavli*'s *bizman beis hamikdash* and *shelo bizman beis hamikdash*, the *Yerushalmi* uses *beshaat korban* and *shelo beshaat korban*. The point, of course, is the same.

Now, when the text says this *pliga d'Rabbi Yose* — that this *baraisa* argues with *Rabbi Yosi* — it does not refer to the *Rabbi Yosi* of the original *mishna*, but rather to the *amora* *Rabbi Yosi* (*Rav Assi b'shem Rabbi Ila*) who had argued that even the *chachamim* accept private wood donations. The proof runs as follows: if the *chachamim* debate *Rabbi Yosi* regarding whether the family holidays apply outside the *beis hamikdash* era, both sides presuppose that the institution of family wood donations exists and is legitimate. The *chachamim* themselves thus accept the institution. This contradicts *Rabbi Acha*'s position that the institution reflects only *Rabbi Yosi*'s view, and supports *Rabbi Yosi* the *amora*'s contention that the *chachamim* universally accept private donations for non-*korban* matters. The *gemara* accordingly adjusts either the *girsa* or the attribution.

### Holiday Status

The proof is reinforced by a second *baraisa*: *amar Rabbi Eliezer bei Rabbi Tzadok anu hayinu mi'bnei San'ah ben Binyamin* — we are descendants of the house of *San'ah ben Binyamin*, one of the eight families, whose designated date was the tenth of *Av*. Once, *Tisha b'Av* fell on *Shabbos* and was therefore postponed to *motza'ei Shabbos* — which coincided with this family's holiday. *V'hayinu mit'anim v'lo meshlimin* — we began the fast but did not complete it, because the family holiday was powerful enough to override even the completion of the *Tisha b'Av* fast. This demonstrates that the family holidays were observed *after* the destruction of the *beis hamikdash* — for one would not observe *Tisha b'Av* during the era of the *beis hamikdash*. Since *Rabbi Yosi* does not accept the holidays in that era, and yet the *chachamim* clearly do, the *chachamim* must accept the entire institution of private wood donations. The conclusion stands: the *chachamim* agree with private donations for all attendant matters, and their disagreement with *Rabbi Yosi* is confined to the *korban* itself.

---

## Omer Sources

### Geographic Limit

Having addressed the debate over private donations, the *gemara* doubles back to the opening of the *mishna* and its list of communal offerings, including the *omer*, the *shtei halechem*, and the *lechem hapanim*. The *gemara* now notes: *masnisin d'Rabbi Yishmael* — our *mishna* follows the position of *Rabbi Yishmael*, who holds that *ein omer ba min haSurya* — the *omer* cannot be brought from *Surya*. *Surya* refers to lands bordering *Eretz Yisrael* that were conquered by *Dovid HaMelech* — roughly corresponding to territories in present-day Syria and Jordan — whose status with respect to the sanctity of *Eretz Yisrael* was disputed. If the *omer* could come from *Surya*, there would be no need to hire watchers of wild growth in *Eretz Yisrael* during *shemita*; one could simply bring grain from *Surya*, where *shemita* either does not apply or at least does not apply biblically. The very fact that our *mishna* describes hiring watchers within *Eretz Yisrael* demonstrates that our *mishna* holds one must bring the *omer* from *Eretz Yisrael* proper — and that is the view of *Rabbi Yishmael*.

### Ten Holiness Levels

The *gemara* invokes the famous *mishna* in *Kelim*: *eser kedushos hein* — there are ten levels of holiness ordered by geography, each more sacred than the last. *Eretz Yisrael mekudeshes mikol ha'aratzos* — the land of Israel is holier than all other lands. *U'mah hi kedushasah* — what is the expression of its holiness? *Shemevi'im mimenah ha'omer v'habikurim u'shtei halechem* — only from produce grown in the land of Israel may one bring the *omer*, the *bikurim*, and the *shtei halechem*. The *gemara* here cites the relevant *pesukim*: by *shtei halechem* the verse says *mimoshvoseichem*; by the *omer* the verse says *v'ktzartem es ktzirah* — the cutting of its harvest, indicating specifically the land's own harvest. It is striking that the primary expression of *Eretz Yisrael*'s sanctity is framed not in covenantal or historical terms, but in terms of the land itself — what grows from its soil. *Rabbi Chiya b'shem Rabbi Yirmiya* states that this *mishna* in *Kelim* proceeds according to *Rabbi Yishmael*, who holds the *omer* cannot come from *Surya*, as the *mishna*'s identification of *Eretz Yisrael*'s holiness with the *omer* implies that other opinions might permit the *omer* from *Surya*.

### Syria Excluded

*Rabbi Yishmael*'s position is derived from a *drashot* in *Shvi'it*. The *pasuk* states *be-charish u-va-katzir tishbot* — you shall rest from plowing and from harvesting. *Rabbi Yishmael* reads this as follows: plowing is always a *reshus*, a discretionary act — there is no mitzvah to plow. Therefore, when the verse says to cease harvesting, it means harvesting that is likewise a *reshus*. But harvesting that is a *mitzvah* — specifically the cutting of the *omer*, of which the verse says *v'ktzartem es ktzirah* — is excluded. The consequence is twofold: one need not refrain from cutting the *omer* on account of *shemita*, and one may even cut it on *Shabbos*. This is the principle *yatza katzir ha-Omer she-hu mitzvah* — the cutting of the *omer* is exempted because it is a *mitzvah*.

### Mitzvah Connection

The *gemara* then notes: *Rabbi Yishmael ke-da'ateih* — *Rabbi Yishmael* here is consistent with his own reasoning, *de-amar Rabbi Yishmael ein Omer ba min ha-Surya* — that the *omer* cannot come from *Surya*. The connection is as follows: if the *omer* must come from *Eretz Yisrael* specifically, that specificity lends the act of cutting a genuine *mitzvah* character. But if one could bring it from *Surya*, the cutting would lack that essential character — there would be less ground to call it a *mitzvah* and therefore less basis for overriding *shemita* or *Shabbos*. The *Yerushalmi* at face value almost seems to argue that the geographic requirement itself creates the *mitzvah* quality. The *mefarshim*, however, explain it differently: if one could bring the *omer* from *Surya* where *shemita* does not apply, there would be no pressing need to permit cutting in *Eretz Yisrael* on *shemita*. The fact that *Rabbi Yishmael* permits it implies that *Eretz Yisrael* is the only option — *ke-da'ateih*, consistent with his position.

### Planting Issue

A further question is raised: *ha-hen omer mahu she-yizarei bi-tchila* — since we are discussing wild growth (*sefichin*), might one be permitted to actually plant the seeds during *shemita* for the purpose of the *omer*, given that harvesting the *omer* is itself a *mitzvah* that overrides *shemita*? *Rabbi Chiya bar Ada* posed this question before *Rabbi Mana*. The response: *lo nimtza ke-kometz al ha-kilayim she-einam ne'echalim* — this would render the grain forbidden, since what grows from seeds planted in violation of *shemita* would itself be *assur*. When one takes the *korban mincha*, the *kometz* is placed on the *mizbe'ach* and the remaining *shirayim* must be fit for eating. If the grain grew from prohibited planting, the *shirayim* would be *einam ne'echalim* — not fit for consumption. This parallels what the *Bavli* derives from a *pasuk* in *Yechezkel* — *mimashkeh Yisrael min hamuttar l'Yisrael* — that one may not bring a *korban* from *ma'achalos assuros*.

The response to this objection invokes a principle from what was recently learned in *Pesachim*: there are five *korbanos tzibur* that may be brought in a state of *tumah* but may not be eaten in a state of *tumah* — only the *Pesach* may be eaten *b'tumah*, since the point of the *Pesach* is specifically to be eaten. Nevertheless, those *korbanos tzibur* are brought despite being unfit for eating. If a *korban* may be brought even when the *shirayim* cannot be eaten — as in the case of *tumah* — perhaps the same logic could apply here. The difference, of course, is that *tumah hutra b'tzibur* is a special dispensation for communal sacrifice brought in *tumah*; whether the same principle could be extended to *shemita*-tainted grain is left unresolved. The *mishna*'s discussion of wild growth implicitly answers the question in the negative: wild growth, not planted grain, is the prescribed path.

---

## Sanctity Transfer

### Banker Mechanism

Returning to the *mishna*'s provision that those who watch the wild growth during *shemita* are paid from the *trumat halishka*, the *gemara* now addresses a fundamental technical problem: how does one actually pay workers with sanctified money? Normally, when sanctified funds are used to purchase an object, the *kedusha* transfers from the money to the object — you buy an animal, the *kedusha* moves to the animal, and you now have a sanctified *korban*. But when paying for labor, there is no object to which the *kedusha* can transfer. So how is this done without a violation of *me'ila*?

The *gemara* describes the mechanism: *notel ma'ot min hashulchani* — you go to the banker — a money changer who also functions as a lender with available funds — and the banker pays the workers and the harvesters from his own unsanctified funds. This happens *ad she-lo yikarev ha-Omer* — before the *omer* is brought. Then, *mevi ma'ot mi-trumat halishka* — you take the sanctified *trumat halishka* funds, and *mechallelan alav* — you transfer their *kedusha* onto the harvested grain. The grain that the worker brings is now sanctified. The worker has already been paid by the bank, so he turns over the grain. The sanctified money, now desanctified, is used to repay the banker. In short: the bank pays the worker; the worker freely gives the grain; the *kedusha* transfers from the communal funds to the grain; the bank is repaid with what is now unsanctified money.

### Retroactive Value

The *gemara* raises a question: *v'tavo ken* — is this truly appropriate? The problem is that the grain itself may not be worth the amount paid to the workers. You paid a hundred *shekel* in labor costs to watch grain that, as a raw commodity, is worth far less. How can you transfer a hundred *shekel* of *kedusha* onto grain worth twenty? *Rabbi Yitzchak b'shem Rabbi Ba* answers: *kol mah she-yiten hein hein damav misha'ar rishona* — whatever you pay retroactively constitutes the value of the object. If *shemita* conditions drive up the cost of labor disproportionately, those labor costs become the assessed value of the grain. Just as the final cost of a product often reflects the labor embedded in it, so here the grain's value is retroactively set at the amount paid on its behalf.

### Stone Carvers

A *baraisa* then applies the same mechanism to a different case: *af l'pitchei avanim ken* — you do the same for those who carve stones for the *beis hamikdash*. *Notel ma'ot mi-shulchani ve-noten le-chotzvin ve-lasatatin* — you have the banker pay the hewers and the stone-carvers, *ad she-lo tinaten al gabei ha-dimos* — before the stone is placed on the *dimos*, the layer of stones already in place. *U-mi-she-nitanah al ha-dimos* — once the stone is set in the structure, *mevi ma'ot mi-trumat halishkah u-mechallel aleha* — you bring the sanctified funds and transfer the *kedusha* to the finished stone, then repay the banker with the now-desanctified money. The *gemara* asks the same question here — *v'tavo ken*? — noting that the cost of stone carving may not equal the simple commodity value of the stone. *Rabbi Yose be-reibi Bun b'shem Shmuel* gives the identical answer: *kol mah she-yiten hein hein damav misha'ar rishona* — retroactively, whatever was paid is the assessed value of the stone. The *mefarshim* explain the practical situation: the carvers may have been paid for ongoing labor including wasted stones and failed attempts, costs that would normally not factor into the market price of a single finished stone. Nevertheless, retroactively, that total outlay becomes the stone's assessed value.

One cannot help but note that this is a remarkably precise description of the *beis hamikdash* construction process — the *dimos*, the hewing, the cutting — very likely reflecting Herodian-era stonework.

---

## Korban Types

### Red Heifer & Scapegoat

The next *mishna* lists further items purchased with the *shekel*, some of which might not be immediately obvious as falling into the category of *korban tzibur*. *Parah* — the *parah adumah*, the red heifer, is not a standard *korban*; it is slaughtered outside the *beis hamikdash*, though it is called a *chatas* and is treated in many respects like a *korban* — its blood is sprinkled toward the *beis hamikdash*. It may be purchased with the communal funds. *Ve-sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* — the goat sent to *Azazel* is not a *korban* at all. Why then may it be purchased from the *shekel*? Because one does not know in advance which of the two *Yom Kippur* goats will be designated for *Azazel* and which for the *mizbe'ach*. Since both must be purchased together, both are acquired with the communal funds.

### Ritual Items

*Lashon shel zehorit* — the crimson strand. This is not the strand tied to the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* at the cliff; rather, this is the strand thrown into the fire of the *parah adumah*, as the *Torah* prescribes adding hyssop and the crimson thread to the burning. This is therefore considered part of the *korban* itself, analogous to the way *nesachim* are considered part of the *korban tzibur*.

### Ramps

*Kevash para ve-kevash sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* — the ramps. When the *parah adumah* was led out to where it would be slaughtered, a special double-ramp structure was constructed — a ramp atop a ramp — to protect it from *tumah*. Similarly, a designated exit ramp was built for the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach*, because crowds would surround and attack the man leading the goat — pulling its hair, shouting at it to carry away their sins and leave. A protected passage was therefore required. *U-leshon shebein karnav* — and the crimson strand between its horns, another element of the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* ritual. All of these come from the *trumat halishka*.

### City Infrastructure

*Ve-amat hamayim ve-chomat ha'ir u-migdaloteha ve-chol tzorchei ha'ir* — the water channel, the walls of Yerushalayim, its towers, and all the city's needs. These obviously are not *korbanos*; accordingly, they do not come from the *trumat halishka* but rather from the *sheyarei halishka*. Recall that the previous material established that when the *truma* is taken from the *shekel* funds, what remains in the chamber is desanctified — except according to *Rabbi Meir*. That desanctified remainder, the *sheyarei halishka*, may be used for non-*korban* and even non-sacred purposes, such as reinforcing the walls of Yerushalayim and attending to the city's municipal needs.

---

## Leftover Funds

### Abba Shaul

*Abba Shaul* adds a dissenting note: *kevash para kohanim gedolim osim mishel atzmam* — the ramp for the *parah adumah* was actually built from the private resources of the *kohanim gedolim*, without recourse to communal funds at all.

### Investment Strategy

The *mishna* then asks: *motar sheyarei lishkah mah hayu osim bahen* — what was done with the remainder of the *sheyarei halishka*? You had funds that were desanctified and used for the city's needs; now the year ends and even those funds have not been fully spent. What do you do with them? *Lokchim bahen yeinot shemanim ve-saltot ve-haschar lehekdesh* — you would purchase wine, oil, and flour, sell them to the people coming to the *beis hamikdash*, and the profit would go to the *hekdesh*. In essence, the *beis hamikdash* would invest its leftover funds by running a small commercial operation.

### R. Yishmael

This is the view of *Rabbi Yishmael*: use the money to generate returns. Whoever administered these funds — the *gizbar* and his staff — would put the money to work, potentially through subcontractors or a side business selling provisions to pilgrims.

### R. Akiva

*Rabbi Akiva* disagrees: *ein mistakrin beshel hekdesh* — one does not conduct business with *hekdesh* funds. It is not appropriate for the *hekdesh* to operate commercially. The concern is twofold: first, it undermines the sanctity of the institution — one does not want the *beis hamikdash* to appear focused on profit. Second, there is the risk: markets decline. One does not take risks with funds held in sacred or communal trust.

### Poor Funds

*Af lo mishel aniyim* — *Rabbi Akiva* applies the same principle to funds collected for the poor. If the *tzedaka* collectors have a surplus, they should not invest it commercially. Again, the concern may be appearance — those administering communal charity funds should not appear to be profiting from them — or it may be the principle of *ve-heyitem nekiyim*, ensuring transparency and cleanliness in the handling of others' money. Either way, *Rabbi Akiva* holds that neither *hekdesh* nor charitable funds should be put to work in commercial ventures.

---

## Terumah Remainder

### Gold Plating

The *mishna* turns from the *sheyarei halishka* to the leftover *truma* itself. *Mosar hatruma ma hayu osim bah* — what was done with the *truma* funds that remained at year's end? The *mishna* answers: *rikuei zahav tzipui leveit kodesh hakodashim* — gold plating for the walls of the *kodesh hakodashim*. Why gold plating for the *kodesh hakodashim* of all things? It is difficult to explain why this in particular is the appropriate use for leftover *shekalim*, given that the *truma* was designated for *korbanos tzibur*.

### Kayitz Option

*Rabbi Yishmael* says: *mosar ha-peros kayitz hamizbe'ach* — the leftover from *peros* goes toward the *kayitz hamizbe'ach*. What is *peros*? The *gemara* will address this. The *kayitz hamizbe'ach* is the practice of bringing voluntary *olos* when the *mizbe'ach* would otherwise stand idle — ensuring that the *mizbe'ach* always appears active and not, as it were, neglected. *Rabbi Yishmael* says that any leftover would go to fund these voluntary burnt offerings. This at least makes intuitive sense: you are using the *shekel* for some form of *korban*, even if not an obligatory one.

*Mosar truma liklei shares* — what is done with the leftover *truma* proper? According to this view, it goes toward purchasing the *klei shares*, the vessels of the *beis hamikdash*. Why the *klei shares* and not something more directly related to *korbanos* is again not immediately obvious.

### R. Akiva Alt

*Rabbi Akiva* says: *motar truma le-kayitz hamizbe'ach* — the leftover *truma* goes to the *kayitz hamizbe'ach*. This is more readily understood: the *truma* was collected for *korbanos*; the *kayitz hamizbe'ach* provides *korbanos*; the usage is consistent with the original purpose of collection.

### Nesachim Option

*Mosar nesachim liklei shares* — the leftover from the *nesachim* fund goes to the *klei shares*. *Rabbi Chananya Segan HaKohanim* — the assistant *kohen*, who presumably had firsthand expertise — says: *mosar nesachim kayitz hamizbe'ach* — no, the leftover *nesachim* funds go to the *kayitz hamizbe'ach*, because the *nesachim* are offerings fully consumed upon the *mizbe'ach*, and the *kayitz ha-mizbe'ach* consists of *olos* similarly consumed in their entirety. The functional similarity suggests that usage. *Mosre hatruma likli shares* — and the leftover *truma* funds, those go for the *klei shares*. *Ve-ze ve-ze lo hayu modim be-peirot* — and both of them would not agree regarding *peiros*. What *peiros* means in this context remains to be addressed in the next *daf*.

The underlying principle seems to be that each type of leftover fund should be directed toward uses that are analogous or parallel to its original function, though the *mishna* and *gemara* do not spell out the reasoning with full clarity. It is also worth noting that the question of what *mosre nesachim* means is itself somewhat obscure: if the *nesachim* were purchased with *trumat halishka* funds, then leftover *nesachim* funds would simply be leftover *truma*. The more natural reading may be that *mosre nesachim* refers to private *nesachim* funds — an individual who set aside money for the *nesachim* of his personal *korban*, had a surplus, and donated that surplus to the *beis hamikdash*. In that case *mosre nesachim* would be a distinct category of private leftover, separate from the communal *truma*.

---

## String Weights

### Three Strings

*Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman b'shem Rabbi Yonasan* teaches: *gimel leshonos hen* — there are three strings. *Shel sa'ir ba-sela* — the one used in the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* ritual costs or weighs one *sela*. *Shel metzora be-shekel* — the one used in the purification ritual of the *metzora* costs half a *sela*, which is one *shekel*. *Shel para bishtei sela'im* — the one used for the *parah adumah* weighs two *sela'im*. *Rabbi Chunya bras chavrin* in the name of *Rabbi Ba bar Zavda b'shem Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafsa* says the string for the *parah adumah* was two and a half *sela'im*. Some formulate this as ten *zuz* — since there are four *zuz* to a *sela*, two and a half *sela'im* equals ten *zuz*; this is a trivial variant in expression rather than a substantive dispute.

### Weight Rationales

Why the different weights? The string for the *parah adumah* must be heavy because it is thrown into the fire, and it must be substantial enough to actually reach and burn in the flames. The string for the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* is twice as heavy as that of the *metzora* because it was divided in half: one portion was left at the rock, and the other portion was tied between the horns of the goat. Thus it needed to begin at twice the size of a string used in its entirety.

---

## Staff Payments

### Sage Teachers

*Rabbi Yehuda b'shem Rabbi Shmuel* teaches: *talmidei chachamim ha-melamdin es ha-kohanim hilchos shechita hilchos kabala hilchos zerika* — the *talmidei chachamim* who would teach the *kohanim* the laws of *shechita*, *kabala*, and *zerika* — the slaughter, reception of the blood, and sprinkling — *notlin secharan mi-trumas ha-lishka* — were paid from the *trumat halishka*. This reflects the assumption embedded in the *gemara* that rabbinic scholars held the relevant expertise and served as instructors to the *kohanim* in the performance of the *avoda*.

This ruling is surprising. The *trumat halishka* was designated for *korbanos tzibur*, and the whole thrust of the preceding discussion has been that even attendant matters connected to *korbanos* are not paid from the *truma* proper. How then can salaries for *talmidei chachamim* — teaching staff — come from this fund? There is no object to which the *kedusha* of the money could transfer. This question will recur with the cases that follow.

### Blemish Inspectors

*Rabbi Yifta bar Redifa b'shem Rabbi Ami* adds: *mevakrei mumei kodshim* — the inspectors who would examine sacrificial animals for disqualifying blemishes — *notlin sechar mi-trumas ha-lishka* — were also paid from the *trumat halishka*. Again, this is not the *korban* itself but rather an enabling function — ensuring the animals offered are *kasher*.

### Scribal Correction

*Rabbi Acha, Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiya b'shem Rabbi Simlai* teaches: *magihei Sefer HaAzara notlin secharam mi-trumat halishka* — the correctors of the *Sefer HaAzara* were also paid from this fund. What is the *Sefer HaAzara*? Some *mefarshim* identify it with the authoritative *Sefer Torah* kept in the *beis hamikdash*, which was produced by a process of comparing three separate manuscript versions of the *Torah* and following the majority where they differed — a procedure described in rabbinic literature. This *Sefer Torah* served as the master text against which all others were corrected. Some *mefarshim* read *Sefer HaAzara* as referring to the *Sefer Torah* from which the *kohen gadol* would read in the *azara* on *Yom Kippur* — which had to be proofread and corrected regularly. Others note a variant *girsa* of *Sefer Ezra*, identifying it with the text that *Ezra HaSofer* brought back from Babylonia, regarded as the most accurate version.

### In-House Judges

*Gidul bar Binyamin b'shem Rav Assi* (some read *gezerot* instead of *gezelot*) adds: *shenei dayanei gezelot* — two judges who handled theft cases within the *beis hamikdash* and could take on no other occupation — *notlin secharam mi-trumat halishka*. These were the standing in-house *dayanim* of the *mikdash*, and they too were paid from the *truma* fund.

The cumulative problem is evident: all of these — teaching *kohanim*, inspecting animals, proofreading *sifrei Torah*, adjudicating disputes — are paid from the *trumat halishka*, which is supposed to be reserved for *korbanos tzibur*. There is no obvious *korban*-related object to which the *kedusha* of the payment could transfer.

---

## Parochet Weavers

### Payment Source

*Shmuel amar nashim haorgot baparochet* — women who weave the *parochet*, the great curtain of the *beis hamikdash* — whenever the *gemara* discusses weaving or sewing, it characteristically mentions women — *notlin secharam mi-trumat halishka* — they too are paid from the *trumat halishka*. *Rabbi Chuna* disagrees: *lo, mi-trumat Bedek HaBayit* — they are paid not from the *trumat halishka* but from the funds of *bedek habayit*, the fund designated for maintaining and repairing the physical structure of the *beis hamikdash*.

### Conceptual Debate

*Mah palig* — what is the underlying conceptual disagreement? *Shmuel avid lei kikorban* — *Shmuel* treats the *parochet* as analogous to a *korban*: it is essential to the *avoda* and its funding belongs with the *korban* funds. *Rav Huna avid lei kibinyan* — *Rav Huna* treats the *parochet* as part of the building's structure. Is a curtain part of the architectural structure, or is it a hanging appended to it? *Rav Huna* holds it is like the structure, and therefore its funding belongs with *bedek habayit*.

### Resolution

The broader and more fundamental question is how *any* of the payments in this entire section can come from the *trumat halishka*. The *trumat halishka* is sanctified money designated for *korbanos tzibur*, and throughout this *daf* we have insisted that even attendant matters — *machshirei korban* — do not come from it. How then does it pay for teachers, inspectors, scribes, judges, and weavers?

The answer that the *mefarshim* provide is admittedly somewhat deflating in its formalism: the *beis din* stipulates at the outset that if and when the *trumat halishka* funds are used for any of the following purposes, those funds retroactively never acquired sanctity for that use — they are treated as *chulin* for that purpose and may therefore be applied freely. The practical result is a movement from a tightly defined regime — sanctified funds usable only for *korbanos tzibur* — to a far more flexible arrangement in which the *beis din*, through a retroactive condition, can desanctify the funds for a wide range of communal and *mikdash*-related needs that extend well beyond the *korban* itself.

---

---

# Shekalim 11

## Terumat HaLishka Uses

### Omer & Shabbat

Before turning to the daf proper, it is worth clarifying a point from the previous day's discussion about the cutting of the *omer* and its relationship to *Shabbat*. The question arose whether the *omer* could be cut before the appointed day — and if so, whether it would be *bedi'eved kasher* to do so in advance. According to the Bavli, both propositions cannot coexist: if cutting the *omer* early is valid *bedi'eved*, then it would never be necessary to override *Shabbat*, since one could simply cut it beforehand. There is some question regarding the *psak* of the Rambam on this point, but the basic tension between the two positions is clear.

### Terumat HaLishka Overview

We also ended the previous daf with a long list of permitted uses for *terumat ha-lishka* — the funds removed from the Temple treasury chamber. This requires some framing. An earlier *mishnah* had stated that *terumat ha-lishka* is designated exclusively for *korban tzibur*, the communal sacrifices. It did include the ancillary cost of stationing guards over the grain for the *omer*, but the emphasis was squarely on the *korban tzibur* itself. By contrast, the *mishnah* under current discussion (Mishnah 2) demonstrates just how narrowly defined that principle really is: one may spend *terumat ha-lishka* on the *parah adumah* itself, but not on the ramp constructed for its ritual — only what pertains directly to the *korban tzibur* qualifies.

Yet the list at the bottom of 10b appears to contradict this by enumerating a host of non-sacrificial expenditures funded by *terumat ha-lishka*: rabbinic students who taught the *kohanim* the laws of *korbanot*, the *shnei dayanei gzeirot* (or according to some, *gzeilot*) — judges in Yerushalayim who maintained fixed salaries to adjudicate ongoing cases — and even the women who wove the *parochet*. What any of this has to do with *korban tzibur* is not immediately apparent.

The *Mishnat Eliyahu*, one of the commentaries on the Vilna printing based on the *Gra*, addresses this. It cites a *Rashi* in Kesubos who explains that *beit din* was empowered to stipulate from the outset that certain funds would be directed toward these purposes, and that such funds would therefore never have been considered sanctified for the standard purpose of *korban tzibur*. This is the principle of *lev beit din matneh* — the rabbis can condition a sanctification at its very inception, such that designated sums are retroactively deemed never to have held the ordinary *kedushah*. The *Mishnat Eliyahu* adds further: the verse prohibiting the maintenance of an unchecked *sefer Torah* — *al tishkan be-oholecha avla* — obligated individuals to have their scrolls examined, and when *beit din* observed that the public was neglecting this duty, they directed *terumat ha-lishka* toward paying professional proofreaders to do the checking.

It is worth pausing to appreciate the broader structure of these funds. The *terumat ha-lishka* was the primary fiscal mechanism for collecting revenue from the entire Jewish population — not only those in the Land of Israel — for the needs of the *beit ha-mikdash*. From the outset, the authorities knew that far more money would be collected than was needed for the *korbanot tzibur* alone. The *shiyarei ha-lishka* — the funds remaining after the three baskets were drawn — was in a very real sense a planned operating surplus, not an accidental one. This explains why the *mishnah* could allocate the *shiyarei ha-lishka* even toward projects as expansive as repairing the city walls of Yerushalayim (*chomat ha-ir u-migdaloteha mi-shiyarei ha-lishka*). What rested under the tarp — the funds already processed through the *terumah* procedure — constituted the *shiyarei ha-lishka* and could be applied to a wide range of purposes. The two subsequent rounds of *terumah* drawn from newly arriving provincial contributions were then placed on top of the tarp. The whole system appears to have been structured with this intentional surplus in mind.

### Magihei Sifrei

One of the items in that list merits special attention: the *magihei sifrei ha-azarah* — those who would proofread and correct the *sifrei Torah* kept in the Temple courtyard, or perhaps the communal scrolls used there. The precise scope of their work is itself a matter of discussion. One interpretation holds that they circulated in Yerushalayim checking individuals' *sifrei Torah* against the authoritative temple copy; another holds that the reference is to the *sefer Torah* read by the *kohen gadol* in the *azarah* itself.

### Three Torah Scrolls

This brings us to a famous and striking source in *Avot de-Rabbi Natan* (paralleled also in the *Sifrei* on the *pasuk* in *Vezot ha-Berachah*, *me'onah Elohei kedem*), which illuminates what the proofreading work of the *magihei sifrei ha-azarah* may have been responding to.

*Gimel sefarim nimtze'u ba-azarah* — three *sifrei Torah* were found in the Temple courtyard. The *baraita* does not specify exactly when, but the episode appears to describe a one-time authoritative adjudication of textual variants. The three scrolls diverged from one another in several places, and the procedure adopted was to follow the reading attested by two of the three scrolls against the one.

### Textual Variants

The three variant pairs the *baraita* records are as follows. The first scroll was called *sefer me'onah*, because it read *me'on Elohei kedem*, while the other two read *me'onah* — the form we have today. The majority prevailed and *me'onah* was retained. The second scroll was called *sefer za'atuti*, because it read *za'atutei bnei Yisrael* in a passage where the other two read *vayishlach et na'arei bnei Yisrael* — an entirely unfamiliar word in place of *na'arei*. Again the two-scroll majority was followed. The third scroll was called *sefer hi*, because it recorded eleven instances where *hi* was spelled *heh-yud-aleph* rather than *heh-vav-aleph*; the other two agreed on a different count, and again the majority ruled.

This is a remarkable source for questions surrounding the text of the *Torah* and the existence of early textual variants. The connection to the *magihei sifrei ha-azarah* becomes clear: once the authoritative text was established, the temple scrolls served as the standard against which all other *sifrei Torah* were checked. The proofreaders' function was thus to preserve and propagate the canonically settled text. This episode also stands as an early precursor to the later work of the Masoretes — who developed a comprehensive system of counting every letter to ensure the text would never again be subject to such uncertainty — though that enterprise came many centuries later.

---

## Braita: Fund Sources

### Ketoret & Korbanot

We now pick up at the opening of 11a. The *amora* Rabbi Chizkiyah cites a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Yehudah, which enumerates in organized fashion what each fund is used for. The *baraita* begins precisely where one would expect: *ha-ketoret ve-chol korbanot ha-tzibur ba'in mi-terumat ha-lishka* — the *ketoret* and all communal sacrifices are purchased from *terumat ha-lishka*. This is entirely consistent with the purpose for which the half-shekel was collected.

### Altars & Vessels

The *baraita* then turns to the gold altar and all the sacred vessels: *mizbe'ach ha-zahav ve-chol klei shareit ba'in mi-motar nesachim* — these come from the surplus funds of the *nesachim*, the wine and flour libations accompanying the *korbanot*. We will return later to the precise mechanism by which a surplus arose from the *nesachim*. For now, the logic is that since the *nesachim* are burned entirely on the altar with no human benefit, any surplus from them is appropriately directed toward other Temple objects that are similarly wholly devoted to the *beit ha-mikdash* — either the *mizbe'ach* or the *klei shareit*. How large a surplus the *motar nesachim* actually generated, given the expense of maintaining the golden altar and all the sacred vessels, will become clearer when we examine the *nesachim* system in detail.

The *mizbe'ach ha-olah* — the outer altar for burnt offerings — along with the *heichal* and the *azarot*, any repairs needed for these spaces, would come from *shiyarei ha-lishka*. As already noted, the *shiyarei ha-lishka* could be applied to an extraordinarily broad range of purposes.

### Interior vs. Exterior

The *baraita* then distinguishes between the interior Temple spaces and those beyond the *azarah*: repairs needed *chutz la-azarot* — outside the *azarah* proper, in external areas — would come from *lishkat bedek ha-bayit*, a dedicated fund supported by voluntary donations specifically for Temple repair. This creates an apparent anomaly: one would naturally assume that funds donated to *bedek ha-bayit* would be used for the interior and most sacred parts of the structure, yet the *baraita* allocates those funds to the exterior while directing *shiyarei ha-lishka* — the less sacred surplus — toward the inner spaces.

The *Gra* resolves this by pointing out that the Bavli's version of this *tosefta* reverses the order: in the Bavli's *girsa*, the *mizbe'ach ha-olah*, the *heichal*, and the *azarot* are funded from *bedek ha-bayit*, while repairs to areas outside the *azarah* come from *shiyarei ha-lishka*. This is far more intuitive: the sanctified donations of *bedek ha-bayit* fund the sanctified interior, while the desanctified *shiyarei ha-lishka* — which could even go toward city walls — covers the outer perimeter. The *Gra* accordingly emends the *baraita* in our text accordingly.

### Me'ilah Question

The *gemara* then raises a pointed difficulty. A separate *baraita* teaches that *avnei ha-mizbe'ach ha-heichal ve-ha-azarah mo'alin bahem* — one can transgress *me'ilah* with respect to the stones of the *mizbe'ach*, the *heichal*, and the *azarah*. According to the Yerushalmi's *girsa*, these structures were funded from *shiyarei ha-lishka*. But *shiyarei ha-lishka*, as we learned, was desanctified once the *terumah* was drawn. The *gemara* therefore asks: *v'chi yesh me'ilah bi-shiyarayim?* — can there be *me'ilah* with respect to desanctified funds and the objects purchased with them?

### Rabbi Meir Kedusha

The *gemara* answers: the *baraita* follows the position of Rabbi Meir, who held that *mo'alin bi-shiyarayim* — the *shiyarayim* do retain *kedushah* even after the *terumah* is drawn. Rabbi Meir's reasoning was that those funds might still be needed during the year for *korbanot tzibur* should the primary funds run short, and therefore their *kedushah* remains operative.

Rabbi Chiya sharpens this: Rabbi Meir's position that the *shiyarayim* retain *kedushah* applies only *betoch shnato* — within the year of that *shekel* — because that is the year in which one might still draw on those funds for *korbanot*. At year's end, once those funds can no longer be used for that year's *korbanot*, their *kedushah* lapses. This creates a further difficulty: according to Rabbi Meir, you cannot draw on the *shiyarei ha-lishka* during the year for construction purposes — those funds must remain available for *korbanot tzibur*. But once the year ends and you can finally use them for construction, they have already become desanctified. The *me'ilah* question thus reasserts itself.

This is precisely why the Bavli's reversed *girsa* is superior: if the interior structures are funded from *bedek ha-bayit* — sanctified voluntary donations — then *me'ilah* applies straightforwardly. The external areas, funded from *shiyarei ha-lishka*, would not carry *me'ilah*, and no contradiction arises. The Yerushalmi's *girsa*, which reverses this, is left in genuine difficulty.

It is worth noting that the Rambam rules in accordance with the Yerushalmi here, a decision that the *Kesef Mishneh* finds puzzling given the Rambam's general stated principle of following the Bavli. One resolution sometimes offered is that in tractate Shekalim — where the Yerushalmi constitutes the primary and natural locus of discussion — the Rambam felt justified in preferring the Yerushalmi over the Bavli. More broadly, careful scholarship has shown that the Rambam did not uniformly subordinate the Yerushalmi; in cases where he deemed it appropriate, he would rule according to Tannaitic sources, the Yerushalmi, or the *Tosefta* even against the Bavli.

---

## Korban Requirements

### Four Items Required

Still within Rabbi Chizkiyah's citation of Rabbi Yehudah's *baraita*, the discussion shifts from questions of funding to the minimum ritual prerequisites for offering *korbanot*. The first position states: *ha-shulchan ve-ha-menorah ve-ha-mizbechot ve-ha-parochet me'akvin et ha-korbanot* — the table (*shulchan*), the candelabrum (*menorah*), the altars (*mizbechot*), and the curtain (*parochet*) are all prerequisites that impede the bringing of *korbanot* if absent. This is a striking claim: these are all features of the *heichal*, the inner sanctum, yet *korbanot* are offered in the outer courtyard. One of the *mefarshim* suggests reading this functionally — each of these is required for its particular associated service: the *parochet* for the *Yom Kippur* service, the *menorah* for the lighting, the *shulchan* for the *lechem ha-panim*. In their absence, the corresponding service cannot be performed.

### Chakhamim Opinion

The *chakhamim* disagree sharply: *ein lecha me'akev et ha-korban ella ha-kiyor ve-chano bilvad* — the sole prerequisite for bringing *korbanot* is the laver and its base, the *kiyor* and the *kan*. None of the interior furnishings are indispensable. The *Gra* is dissatisfied with this *girsa* and emends it to read *ha-karkov ve-ha-keren* — features of the outer *mizbe'ach* — arguing that what is logically indispensable is a properly constituted altar, not the laver. His emendation is based on a parallel Bavli discussion elsewhere. Regardless, neither the first opinion nor the *chakhamim* here cite their *pesukim*, which is unusual.

The broader context of this debate is the well-known principle in the Bavli, cited in Megilla and elsewhere, that *makrivin af al pi she-ein bayit* — one may offer *korbanot* even without a standing *beit ha-mikdash*. This becomes practically significant in contemporary discussions about ascending to the Temple Mount and offering a *korban pesach*, and the question naturally arises: what is the minimum institutional infrastructure required? This *baraita* addresses exactly that question.

### Interior vs. Exterior

Rabbi Chanina provides the resolution: *kan ba-avodas she-bifnim, kan ba-avodas she-ba-chutz* — the two positions are not actually in conflict; they address different domains. For the outer service — the standard *korbanot* on the outer altar — the only prerequisite is the *kiyor* and the *kan*; that is the only required element in the outer space. For the inner service — the burning of *ketoret*, the *Yom Kippur avodah*, and related rituals — one requires the *shulchan*, the *menorah*, and the other interior furnishings.

The *gemara* had also noted positions by Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yose bar Chanina, both of whom derive these requirements from the word *nochach* in the *Torah* — wherever a Temple object is described as positioned *nochach* (opposite/facing) something else, that object is indispensable; where the text uses *tzela* (side) or *simah* (placement), various other views disagree about whether *me'akeiv* status applies. The difficulty that all of these positions raise is that in *beit sheni* there was no *aron* — yet the inner *avodot* were performed. How this was managed according to any opinion that treats the *aron* as *me'akeiv* remains unresolved.

---

## Parah Adumah

### High Priests Arrogance

Rabbi Chanina opens a new topic: *shachatzit gedolah hayetah bi-vnei kohanim gedolim* — there was a great haughtiness among the *kohanim gedolim*. The *mishnah* had taught that the *kohen gadol* would spend his own personal funds to build the ramp over which the *parah adumah* was led to the place of burning. Rabbi Chanina characterizes this practice as an expression of arrogance: they would spend in excess of sixty talents of gold on such a ramp, and *shehayah kivsho shel parah omed* — even though a ramp from the previous *parah* ceremony already existed, *velo hayah echad mehen motzi parato be-kivsho shel chavero* — no *kohen gadol* would use the ramp built by his predecessor. Each would demolish the existing ramp and construct a new one at his own expense.

### Shimon HaTzadik

Rebi Ulla challenges this characterization before Rebi Mana from a *baraita*: Shimon HaTzadik, during his long tenure as *kohen gadol*, presided over two *parah adumah* ceremonies, and the *baraita* explicitly states *lo be-kivesh she-hotzi et zo hotzi et zo* — the ramp used for the first ceremony was not the one used for the second. The objection is pointed: *is lach le-meimar Shimon HaTzadik shachatz hayah?* — would you say that Shimon HaTzadik was motivated by arrogance? Clearly there is a substantive requirement to use a freshly dedicated ramp for each ceremony, independent of any personal vanity. The individual *kohanim gedolim* may have been guilty of excessive expenditure, but the practice of constructing a new ramp was not itself rooted in mere arrogance.

### Parah Ornamentation

The resolution offered is that the special treatment accorded to the *parah* ceremony reflects *silsul* — a kind of elevation and ornamentation deliberately cultivated around this ritual. Numerous special stringencies surrounded the *parah adumah*, some of them also linked to the ongoing debates with the *Tzeddukim*, who interpreted its laws differently. In certain areas the rabbis were more lenient specifically to undercut the *Tzeddukim*'s position; in others they were exceptionally stringent, and the distinctive treatment of the ramp belongs to this larger pattern.

A *baraita* adds: *zizin u-ktalim hayu yotzin mikan u-mikan* — protrusions and walls jutted out from both sides of the ramp, *kedei she-lo yeitzu ve-yatzitzu ha-kohanim ve-yitame'u* — so that the *kohanim* would not lean over the sides, lose their footing, or otherwise risk becoming *tamei* through inadvertent contact with something below. The ramp was therefore ornamented and reinforced not merely for aesthetic reasons but to maintain the ritual purity of everyone involved in the ceremony.

---

## Year-End Surplus

### Yishmael Business

The discussion now turns to what is done with leftover *shiyarei ha-lishka* — the desanctified surplus — at the end of the year. Rabbi Yishmael holds that one may purchase oil, wine, and flour with those funds and sell them to pilgrims and visitors in Yerushalayim, pocketing the difference as profit for *hekdesh*.

### Akiva Prohibition

Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *ein mishtakrin be-shel hekdesh* — one does not engage in business ventures with *hekdesh* funds. He applies the same prohibition to funds held in trust for the poor. The question underlying the dispute is whether the objection is one of propriety — it looks unseemly for *hekdesh* to be operating commercial enterprises — or whether it is a concern about the risk inherent in any business venture. One does not expose funds that belong to others, whether to *hekdesh* or to the poor, to the possibility of loss.

### Risk & Investment

The *gemara* resolves this tension by means of a conditional arrangement: *im bayit di-yiheh hefseida didach ve-agra de-tarveichon* — if the investor is willing to absorb any loss personally while splitting any profit with *hekdesh*, then *shari*, it is permitted. Under such terms the *hekdesh* funds face no risk; the investor functions as a guarantor of the principal, and whatever commercial gain results is shared. Even Rabbi Akiva would agree to this structure, since the concern about exposing trust funds to risk is entirely neutralized.

### Entrusted Funds

Two parallel cases illustrate this principle. Rabbi Chiya bar Adda was entrusted with the estate funds (*midal de-yatmi*) of orphans and wished to invest them. He approached Rabbi Imi, who ruled: if you are willing to bear any losses yourself and to share the profits equally, it is permitted. Similarly, Rabbi Chiya bar Adda himself acted on the same terms when similarly entrusted. The *gemara* acknowledges that this arrangement has some of the structural characteristics of a loan with interest (*ribbit*): the investor guarantees return of principal (making the relationship resemble a loan) while also receiving a share of profits. Ordinarily such an arrangement would be rabbinically problematic, but the authorities permitted it here for the benefit of orphans.

The conceptual boldness of permitting even *hekdesh* to benefit from this arrangement deserves emphasis. The plain meaning of *ein mishtakrin* suggests something intrinsically problematic about *hekdesh* engaging in commerce — not merely a concern about risk, but a dignity concern: one does not want *hekdesh*, which is sustained by sacred collections, to be seen operating as a merchant. Yet the *gemara* frames the entire prohibition as purely a risk-management question and permits the arrangement as soon as the risk is removed.

---

## Motar Peirot

### Yishmael Profits

The *mishnah* contains an ambiguous reference to *motar peirot* — the leftover of the fruits — and states that Rabbi Yishmael directed these funds toward *kayitz ha-mizbe'ach*, the voluntary *olot* brought when the outer altar would otherwise stand idle.

### Rejection Motar

Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Chanina Sgan ha-Kohanim are recorded as not having accepted the category of *motar peirot* at all. The *gemara* now works to determine what *motar peirot* actually means, and why Rabbi Akiva rejected it.

### Fourth Se'ah

Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef explains the *mishnah* as follows: *motar peirot* refers to *sechar la-hekdesh* — the profit the Temple made by going into business with the *shiyarei ha-lishka* funds, in the manner Rabbi Yishmael described. *Motar nesachim*, by contrast, is identified as *zu se'ah revi'it* — "the fourth *se'ah*." To understand this, one must appreciate the Temple's commercial arrangements with its suppliers of *nesachim*. A supplier would contract at the beginning of the year to provide, say, four *se'ah* of wine per *shekel*. If prices rose during the year so that the market rate fell to three *se'ah* per *shekel*, the supplier was still contractually obligated to deliver four. The Temple always captured the benefit of price fluctuations in its favor while bearing none of the downside. The surplus that accumulated through this systematic advantage is the *motar nesachim* — what the *gemara* here calls *se'ah revi'it*, the "fourth *se'ah*" that the market no longer required the supplier to provide but the contract still did.

On this reading, Rabbi Akiva's rejection of *motar peirot* is entirely consistent: since *motar peirot* means the profit from commercial activity, and Rabbi Akiva prohibits *hekdesh* from engaging in commerce, he naturally refused to acknowledge this category.

### Heaping Measure

Rabbi Yochanan interprets the *mishnah* differently. According to him, *motar peirot* is the *se'ah revi'it* — the price-fluctuation surplus — and *motar nispacham* is *le-beirutzin*, the profit from heaping measures. When the Temple purchased liquid commodities, the supplier was required to fill the measuring vessel without smoothing off the top; any amount that heaped above the rim belonged to the Temple. When the Temple subsequently sold that commodity, it would measure out precise, level quantities. The cumulative difference between heaped purchases and level sales generated a consistent and not insignificant profit stream, particularly given the extraordinary volume of *nesachim* consumed daily.

### Certification System

Rabbi Yochanan's identification of *motar nispacham* with heaping raises a question: does this not constitute the Temple engaging in commerce — precisely what Rabbi Akiva prohibited? The answer lies in understanding the actual mechanism by which *nesachim* were supplied. Worshippers did not purchase their *nesachim* directly from Temple officials. Instead, upon arriving, a worshipper would pay a fixed price to a Temple administrator and receive receipts (*pitkin*) specifying the type and quantity of *nesachim* required. The worshipper then proceeded to an independent contractor who would exchange the receipts for the actual *nesachim*. At the end of the day, the contractor returned to the Temple with the receipts and was reimbursed. Officially, the Temple was never selling anything directly; it was merely reimbursing a contractor. Yet since the Temple was the ultimate buyer of all the commodities, it was positioned to capture the benefit of heaping measures at the point of purchase, while the contractor measured out level quantities to the worshippers. The net surplus accumulated to the Temple through this intermediated structure.

Even Rabbi Akiva concedes the legitimacy of this arrangement, since the Temple never directly engaged in buying and selling with the public. The certified-contractor system insulated *hekdesh* from direct commerce. Given the volume of *korbanot* brought daily, even a fractional percentage of surplus per transaction compounded into substantial *motar nispacham*.

### Business Paradox

The *gemara* then asks: given that Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef identifies *motar peirot* as the profit from business ventures, it is clear why Rabbi Akiva rejected it — he prohibits *hekdesh* from engaging in business. But according to Rabbi Yochanan, who identifies *motar peirot* with the price-fluctuation surplus (*se'ah revi'it*), why did Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Chanina Sgan ha-Kohanim decline to endorse *motar peirot*? The price-fluctuation mechanism is a contractual advantage, not a commercial venture — everyone agrees to it. The *gemara* answers: they did not reject the *phenomenon* of *motar peirot*; they rejected only what Rabbi Yishmael said you do with it. Rabbi Yishmael directed these funds to *kayitz ha-mizbe'ach*; Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Chanina held that such funds should go instead toward *klei shareit*, because *motar nesachim* funds are designated for *klei shareit*, and *motar peirot* is essentially a form of *motar nesachim*.

The *gemara* then raises the question of *beirutzei yachid* — profits from heaping in the context of individual, private *korbanot*. Most of the *nesachim* purchased through the contractor system were funded by private individuals, not communal funds. If the heaping surplus derives from individual expenditure, how can it be channeled toward communal purposes like *kayitz ha-mizbe'ach* or *klei shareit*? The *gemara* invokes a principle: as long as an individual fully transfers what he has given over to the public domain — as the woman who wove a priestly garment and donated it to the *tzibur* renders it fully communal — individually sourced funds that are entirely surrendered can be used for communal purposes. The private source of origin does not permanently characterize them. One further question is raised concerning *beirutzei yavesh* — heaping of dry measures, as distinct from liquid. The distinction may rest on whether the heaping material ever occupied the interior of the sanctified vessel: liquid that fills a vessel touches its walls and airspace and is thereby sanctified; dry goods that heap above the rim were never within the vessel's contained airspace. Whether the Temple could claim that surplus as well, and on what grounds, is left without a fully satisfying resolution.

---

## Motar HaKetoret

### Ketoret Purchase

The *mishnah* now turns to *motar ha-ketoret* — the handling of year-end surplus *ketoret*. The practice was to purchase, at the start of each year, 365 portions (*manot*) of *ketoret* — one for each day of the solar year — plus three additional portions for the *Yom Kippur* service, totaling 368. The difficulty is structural: the *shekalim* cycle and the *ketoret* purchase were calibrated on a lunar year basis, which is shorter than the solar year. Consequently, there was a regular annual surplus. Over several years this surplus could theoretically be absorbed in a leap year, but this created a serious problem: *korban tzibur* must be purchased with that year's consecrated funds. The leftover *ketoret* from the previous year retained its old year's *kedushah* and could not simply be carried over and used as though it were newly sanctified. How, then, was the surplus *ketoret* reintegrated into the next year's service?

### Desanctification

The *mishnah* describes the solution: *mafrishin mimenu sechar ha-umnin* — one designates a portion of the surplus *ketoret* as the wage owed to the craftsmen (*umnin*) who produced it. One then performs *challalah* — a transfer of *kedushah* — from the *ketoret* onto the coins that represent the workers' payment: *u-mechalelalin oto al me'ot ha-umnin*. The surplus *ketoret* is thereby desanctified. The *ketoret* is then repurchased with newly consecrated *shekalim* of the new year, and through the purchase it is re-sanctified under this year's *kedushah*. If the new funds are already available, the repurchase is made from them; if not, it is made from the old funds.

### Multi-Step Transfer

The *gemara* immediately asks: this transfer of *kedushah* onto the workers' wages — what exactly does it accomplish? The *umnin* cannot use sanctified funds; *kedushah* cannot simply land on an abstraction. *Velo nimtza hekdesh mitchalel al ha-melachah* — one cannot transfer *kedushah* onto labor, which is not a tangible object.

Rabbi Simon ben Bisna describes the precise multi-step procedure that resolves this. The administrator brings a sum of desanctified money — the amount owed to the *umnin*. He then transfers the *kedushah* of that money onto some physical object in the Temple, say the masonry of the building (*ha-binyan*), thereby stripping the money of its *kedushah* and leaving it as ordinary currency. He then takes the *ketoret* that the *umnin* have delivered — which the *umnin* own, having supplied their own raw materials and labor — and transfers the *kedushah* of the *ketoret* onto that money. The *ketoret* is thereby desanctified.

### Umnin Payment

Now the *umnin* are paid: *ve-notnin otah le-umnin be-scharan* — the desanctified *ketoret* is given to them as their wages. The craftsmen, who had delivered the finished *ketoret* and are owed payment, receive the *ketoret* itself back as compensation in lieu of cash. The analogy is apt: they come and deliver a finished product worth a certain amount, and instead of cash, they are paid with the equivalent value of the very product they delivered.

### Repurchasing

But now the Temple needs that *ketoret* for the coming year. So it immediately repurchases the *ketoret* from the *umnin* using newly consecrated *shekel* funds. Through this purchase, the *kedushah* of the new year's *shekalim* transfers onto the *ketoret*, and the money passes to the *umnin* as fully desanctified currency they can use freely. The entire sequence achieves what was needed: the old *kedushah* is removed from the *ketoret*, and new *kedushah* of the current year is applied to it through purchase with this year's consecrated funds.

### Remnant Funds

This leaves a further question: after the *kedushah* of the *ketoret* was transferred onto the intermediate sum of money in the first step of the process, what becomes of that money? It now carries the *kedushah* of last year's *ketoret*.

*Rebbi* suggests it be given to the house of Garmo and the house of Avtinas — the families who held hereditary expertise in the preparation of the *ketoret* and the *lechem ha-panim* respectively — as payment for services rendered. Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak qualifies: this is appropriate only if the Temple in fact owed those families money from the prior year, since this money carries last year's *kedushah*. The *mefarshim* explain that using last year's *terumat ha-lishka*-derived funds for payment of services is consistent with what we established at the outset — that *lev beit din matneh* permits directing such funds toward certain non-*korban* Temple services.

Rabbi Ba, citing Rabbi Chiya in the name of Rabbi Yosi, offers an alternative: use those funds for *kayitz ha-mizbe'ach* — the voluntary *olot* that fill idle time at the outer altar. This serves as the general fallback use for surplus sanctified funds.

### Ketoret Vessel

Rabbi Ba bar Kahana then raises what appears to be a contradiction in Rabbi Chiya bar Ba's statements, noting that in one place he seems uncertain about the proper use of these funds while in another he states it clearly. The *gemara* resolves this: when Rabbi Chiya bar Ba expressed uncertainty, he already knew the answer regarding *kayitz ha-mizbe'ach* — that is obvious. What he was uncertain about was whether the funds could also be directed toward *klei shareit*. That remained the open question.

The daf closes with a debate on a related matter concerning the *ketoret* itself. Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina rules: *pitma be-chulin — pesulah* — if the *ketoret* was ground in a non-sanctified vessel, the *ketoret* is invalid. His reasoning is the verse *kodesh hi* — it is holy — which he interprets as requiring that the very production of the *ketoret* occur within a sanctified vessel: *she-teheh havayatah ba-kodesh*. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees and rules it valid: *kodesh hi* means only that the *ketoret* must be purchased from sanctified funds (*mi-terumat ha-lishka*); it does not require that the grinding itself take place in a *keli shareit*. Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Bun notes that these two positions parallel the broader dispute between Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan on related questions of *kedushah* and production, and the discussion of their respective supports is left for the following daf.

---

---

# Shekalim 12

## Ketoret & Kli Share (III)

### Ketoret: Kli Shares Deba…

The discussion opens mid-tractate with the question of what is done with the *ketoret* — how it is desanctified and resanctified for use in the coming year. The *Gemara* records a debate over whether the *ketoret* must be prepared in a *kli shares* (a consecrated service vessel). Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Chanina holds that it must be made in a *kli shares*, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that this requirement does not apply.

### Shmuel & R. Yochanan

Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Bun then aligns these positions with two Babylonian *amoraim*: the view of Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Chanina, who requires a *kli shares*, corresponds to the position of Shmuel, while the view of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who does not require one, corresponds to Rabbi Yochanan.

To demonstrate this alignment, the *Gemara* invokes the *mishnah* that will appear shortly: *hamakdish nechasav v'hayu bahen devarim reuyim lekorbanot tzibur* — someone who sanctifies all of his property, among which are items fit only for *korbanot tzibur* (public offerings). When one says generically "I sanctify all my property," that dedication goes by default to *bedek habayit*, the temple maintenance fund. Yet if the property contains animals or items fit for *korbanot*, a further question arises as to how their sanctity is treated — a matter the upcoming *mishnah* will address in detail. For now, the *Gemara* focuses on a specific line within that discussion.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that the only item in one's private property that is fit exclusively for a *korban tzibur* — and not for any *korban yachid* — is the *ketoret*. Animals, flour, and all other such items can always be brought as private offerings; *ketoret* alone is categorically restricted to communal use.

This raises an immediate difficulty. If the *ketoret* must be prepared in a *kli shares*, how could *ketoret* found in a private home be considered fit for Temple use? Rabbi Hoshaia resolves this by explaining that the *mishnah* can be read as referring to a craftsman from the family of Beit Avtinas — the hereditary guild entrusted with producing the *ketoret* — who received *ketoret* as his wages. It was established practice to compensate these workers with *ketoret*, meaning the worker would possess at home *ketoret* that had, in fact, been prepared inside the Temple in a *kli shares*. When he subsequently sanctifies all his property, this *ketoret* in his possession is genuinely fit for Temple use.
