One might wonder: wasn't it established previously that the workers were not actually paid with the *ketoret* itself, but rather that the *ketoret* was used as part of an exchange in which they ultimately received money? The answer is that we will encounter precisely this question in the upcoming *mishnah*, where the possibility of paying workers directly with the *ketoret* — at least according to Rabbi Akiva's view — will be considered. For now, this explanation suffices to account for how a private individual could possess *ketoret* prepared in a *kli shares*.

The *Gemara* then raises a further question from Rabbi Chuni before Rabbi Yossi: if the *ketoret* was indeed made in a *kli shares*, the principle is that something sanctified through a *kli shares* cannot be redeemed. A standard item sanctified for *bedek habayit* can be redeemed by transferring its monetary value — that is *kedushat damim*, sanctity of monetary worth — but once an item has been sanctified through a *kli shares*, its intrinsic use has been consecrated and it may not be redeemed. How then can the entire mechanism of desanctifying and resanctifying the *ketoret* function, if the *ketoret* was produced in a *kli shares*?

The answer given is: *velo deShmuel hi?* — is this not itself Shmuel's position? The question of how to redeem *ketoret* made in a *kli shares* is answered by Shmuel's general principle of *kal hu b'mosar* — that a leniency applies to leftover public offerings. Beit Din stipulates that when funds were used to purchase *korbanot tzibur* and those offerings turn out to be leftover at year's end, greater flexibility is permitted in handling the resulting *hekdesh*. The mechanics of this leniency are not made fully explicit, but the principle is clear: ordinary restrictions that apply to individual offerings are relaxed in the context of communal leftover offerings.

## Leftover Offerings

### Shmuel: Redeem Unblemish…

The *Gemara* now demonstrates Shmuel's leniency directly. The case: *hossiru temimim* — at the end of the year, unblemished animals remain that had been sanctified with public funds from the prior year. By Rosh Chodesh Nisan, the new year commences and these animals, purchased with the old year's *terumah* funds, can no longer be used. What is to be done? Shmuel rules: *nifdin temimim* — they are redeemed even though they are unblemished, which completely contravenes the standard rule that a *korban* may only be redeemed once it has acquired a *mum* (a blemish). Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *lo nifdin kefsulei hamukdashim* — they are not redeemed as if they were disqualified offerings; rather, one waits until the animal acquires a *mum* and then redeems it in the normal manner.

This debate, it emerges, directly parallels the earlier question. Shmuel's position that *ketoret* made in a *kli shares* can nonetheless be redeemed finds its logical foundation in this same leniency: Shmuel allows latitude in redeeming public leftover offerings that would not be permitted by normal rules. Rabbi Yochanan, who requires waiting for a *mum*, correspondingly holds that the *ketoret* was not made in a *kli shares* — because if it were, the standard prohibition against redemption would apply and no mechanism would be available.

### Leftover Sin Offering

The *Gemara* extends the analysis: *hossiru se'irim* — what if what remains at year's end is not animals designated for an *olah* but male goats (*se'irim*) designated for a *chatat* (sin offering), as used in *musaf* services? According to Shmuel, would even these be redeemable while unblemished?

A *kal vachomer* (argument from the lenient to the stringent) is proposed: *im olah nifdeist lo kol sheken chatat?* — if an *olah* can be redeemed while unblemished, how much more so should a *chatat* be redeemable?

The *Korban HaEdah* explains the logic of this *kal vachomer* as follows. In the case of the *olah*: if we had not redeemed it while unblemished and had instead waited for it to acquire a *mum*, the animal would still ultimately have been repurchased and re-sanctified as an *olah*, remaining within the same category. The money from its redemption would return to fund another *olah*. In the case of the *chatat*, however, had we not redeemed it while unblemished and had waited for a *mum*, the animal could never have served as a *chatat* again — a *chatat* of an individual cannot be redeemed, but a *chatat tzibur* that becomes blemished is indeed redeemable, and that money would go to *kayitz hamizbeach* (supplementary burnt offerings), not back to a *chatat*. By permitting redemption while the animal is still *tamim* (unblemished), we allow the original animal to be reused as a *chatat* and kept within its proper category. This is why the *chatat* presents a *kal vachomer* over the *olah*: the benefit of early redemption is even greater for the *chatat* than for the *olah*.

### R. Yochanan: Normal Rules

According to Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, no such latitude exists. Rav Zeira rules *yireu* — they are left to graze until they acquire a blemish, at which point normal rules of redemption apply.

### Repurposing as Offering

Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak then introduces a far more radical position: *m'kayitzin bahen es hamizbeach* — the leftover sin offering animals, rather than being redeemed and the money used for *kayitz hamizbeach*, are repurposed directly as *olot* (burnt offerings). He is not merely saying they are redeemed and the money goes toward an *olah*; he is saying the *chatat* animal itself is brought as an *olah*.

### Sin → Burnt Offering

The *Gemara* challenges this sharply: *yeish chatat shek'reiva olah?* — has one ever heard of a *chatat* being brought as an *olah*? The only precedent for transferring sanctity between categories is the ruling that a *pesach* can become a *shelamim* under certain circumstances. But a *chatat* becoming an *olah* is unheard of.

Two explanations are offered in response. Rabbi Yossi states: *shani she'ein korbanot tzibur nikva'in ela b'shechitah* — public offerings are different, in that their identity is not definitively fixed until the moment of slaughter. Even after an animal has been sanctified as a *chatat tzibur*, its precise identity remains open until *shechitah*. This is presented as a natural feature of *korbanot tzibur* — an inherent rule that was perhaps not previously known — which allows for a change of purpose right up to the moment of the offering.

Rabbi Chiyya offers a second explanation: *tnai beis din hi al hamotar sheyikrevu olot* — it is a stipulation of Beit Din that all leftover public offerings shall be brought as *olot*. This approach does not rely on a natural legal rule but on a proactive rabbinic stipulation that gives the institution the flexibility to redirect these funds and animals as circumstances require. This same principle — that Beit Din's stipulation underwrites the broader financial mechanics of the *terumah* funds — was already implicit in what was discussed regarding the use of *terumah halishkah* for purposes beyond the direct purchase of *korbanot*, such as support of *talmidei chachamim* who teach the laws of the offerings.

## Mishnah: Ketoret

### Sanctifying Property

The *Gemara* now arrives at today's *daf*, 12a, and the *mishnah* itself. *Hamakdish nechasav v'hayu bahen devarim reuyim lekorbanot tzibur* — one who sanctifies all of his property and among those possessions are items fit for *korbanot tzibur*. As established, the only item in private hands that could be fit exclusively for a *korban tzibur* and not for a *korban yachid* is the *ketoret*. The *mishnah* therefore addresses what is to be done with such *ketoret*: *yinatnu l'umnin b'scharan* — it should be given to the craftsmen (the *umnin*, the workers who produce the *ketoret*) as their wages. This is the ruling attributed to Rabbi Akiva.

The rationale for this prescription reflects an important constraint. Even though the sanctification was the act of a private individual, and even though that individual's *ketoret* cannot actually be used for the Temple offering — since the *korban tzibur* must be purchased with public funds — the item cannot simply revert to *bedek habayit* either. As will emerge more clearly in the continuation of the *mishnah*, items that are fit for *korbanot* cannot simply be absorbed into the general *bedek habayit* pool without being channeled toward their proper purpose.

## Ketoret & Kli Share (III)

### R. Akiva's Position

Rabbi Akiva's position raises a difficulty in light of the earlier debate. If the *ketoret* was made in a *kli shares*, how can it be redeemed at all? The *Gemara* applies the earlier answer: Rabbi Akiva's position is consistent with Shmuel's leniency, which permits redemption of leftover public offerings under circumstances where standard rules would normally prohibit it.

## Mishnah: Ketoret (II)

### Paying Workers

Rabbi Akiva therefore rules that the *ketoret* itself is handed directly to the workers as payment: *shehayu notnim b'scharan ketoret* — they gave them *ketoret* as their wages. This is possible because Rabbi Akiva evidently holds that *ketoret* may be made outside of a *kli shares*, or that the *ketoret* in question was already produced in a *kli shares* and came into the worker's possession through prior payment, as explained earlier.

Ben Azzai objects to this approach and provides an alternative: *mafrishim mehen sechar ha'umnin* — one first sets aside the monetary amount to be paid to the workers; *umechallelin osam al hama'ot* — one then transfers the *kedushah* of the *ketoret* onto that money; *v'al ma'ot ha'umnin venotnim osam la'umnin bischaran* — one gives the *ketoret* to the workers as their wages now that it has been desanctified; *vechozrin velokechin osam mitrumah chadasha* — and then one repurchases the *ketoret* using new *terumah* funds. In this way, the workers are compensated, the *ketoret* is formally desanctified and resanctified with proper public funds, and it is now available for use in the Temple service.

## Ketoret & Kli Share (III)s…

### Ben Azzai's Objection

The *Gemara* then explains why Ben Azzai rejects Rabbi Akiva's simpler approach of direct payment: *she'ein hekdesh mitchalel al hamelacha ela al hama'ot* — sacred property cannot be desanctified by transferring its *kedushah* onto abstract labor; it can only be transferred onto tangible money. If the *ketoret* is handed to a worker as wages, where does the *kedushah* go? It cannot transfer onto the act of work performed, since work is not an object. The *kedushah* has no recipient and the desanctification is therefore invalid.

What Rabbi Akiva's position would require is that *kedushah* can in fact transfer onto abstract *melachah* (labor), which is a genuinely striking idea. Alternatively, one might understand his position as relying on some form of stipulation — though it is noted that here we are dealing with a private *hekdesh*, not a public one, so the standard formulation of *kol mah she'daas Rabonan adaata* (all that one does is conditional upon rabbinic approval) may not straightforwardly apply.

## Mixed Property Animals

### R. Eliezer: All Bedek

The *mishnah* then addresses a different scenario: *hamakdish nechasav v'hayu bahen behemah re'uyah legabei hamizbeach* — one who sanctifies all of his property and among those possessions are animals fit for the altar. Unlike *ketoret*, animals could in principle be brought as either a *korban tzibur* or a *korban yachid*, so the issue is not which category of offering they serve but rather what type of *kedushah* attaches to them in the context of a generic, undifferentiated sanctification.

The *mishnah* specifies: *zecharim unekevot* — there were both male and female animals. Rabbi Eliezer rules: *zecharim yimachru l'tzorchei olot unekevot yimachru l'tzorchei zivchei shelamim* — the males are sold to people who need to bring an *olah*, and the females are sold to people who need to bring a *shelamim*. The money from these sales — *vedmeihem yiplu im she'ar nechasim l'bedek habayit* — is pooled with the rest of his property for *bedek habayit*.

Rabbi Eliezer's position rests on the principle that a generic sanctification is always for *bedek habayit*. Even these animals, though they are fit for the altar, are owned by the temple treasury in the capacity of *bedek habayit*. However, since they have been caught in the net of *hekdesh* and are capable of serving as *korbanot*, they cannot simply be absorbed into the general fund without being channeled toward the altar. The solution is to sell them to individuals who need those specific offerings: an unblemished male is sold to someone who needs to bring an *olah*. When that person purchases the animal, the *kedushah* of *bedek habayit* transfers to the money paid — which now goes to the *bedek habayit* fund — and the purchaser re-sanctifies the animal as his own *korban*. Both goals are thereby achieved: the animal reaches the altar, and the temple maintenance fund receives its value.

One might ask whether the animal could simply have been sold to the *shekalim* fund for a *korban tzibur*. The answer is that the *shekalim* funds are themselves already *kadosh*, and *kedushah* cannot be transferred onto something that is already consecrated. A transfer of *kedushah* requires unsanctified money as its recipient.

### R. Yehoshua: Olah Status

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees. In his view, the *kedushah* is not uniformly *kedushat bedek habayit* for all items; rather, a generic *kedushah* takes on the character appropriate to the object it attaches to. For the house, the car, and the furniture, the sanctity becomes *bedek habayit*. For the animals, however — since they are fit for the altar — the generic sanctification crystallizes into a *kedushat korban*. Rabbi Yehoshua therefore rules: *zecharim atzman yikrevu olot* — the males themselves are brought as *olot*. That is how the *kedushah* expresses itself when it encounters an unblemished male animal.

For the females, however, there is a further limitation. Since the generic sanctification was fundamentally directed toward *bedek habayit*, which means total dedication to the Temple with no benefit accruing to the owner, the only *korban* identity that can properly express this character is that of an *olah* — which is entirely consumed on the altar. A *shelamim*, most of which is eaten by the owner, is too different in character from a *bedek habayit* sanctification for the *kedushah* to crystallize in that form. Therefore, Rabbi Yehoshua rules that even the females receive a *kedushat olah* in terms of their sanctity — yet since females cannot be brought as an *olah*, the practical ruling is: *yimachru l'tzorchei zivchei shelamim* — they are sold to people who need to bring a *shelamim* (since the animal itself can still serve that function when re-sanctified by a buyer), *veyavi bidmeihem olot* — and the proceeds are used to purchase an *olah*. *U'shear nechasim yiplu l'bedek habayit* — everything else in the estate goes to *bedek habayit*.

### Akiva & Pappias

Rabbi Akiva weighs in: *ro'eh ani es divrei Rebbe Eliezer midivrei Rebbe Yehoshua* — he prefers Rabbi Eliezer's position over Rabbi Yehoshua's, for the reason that *Rebbe Eliezer hishveh midosav* — Rabbi Eliezer is internally consistent, treating the entire sanctification uniformly as *bedek habayit*, whereas *Rebbe Yehoshua hillek* — Rabbi Yehoshua introduces a distinction, allowing the *kedushah* to bifurcate depending on the object. It is worth noting the verbal echo: at the opening of the *mishnah* Ben Azzai criticized Rabbi Akiva's approach as *eino min hamiddah*, and here Rabbi Akiva turns the same language back in a different direction, praising Rabbi Eliezer for *hishveh midosav* — measuring with a single consistent standard.

Rabbi Pappias then reports: *shamati k'divrei sheneihem* — I heard that in practice both approaches were applied, meaning the ruling depended on the circumstances.

### Explicit vs. Generic

The resolution is as follows. *Hamakdish b'feirush* — if the person was explicit in his sanctification, specifying his animals alongside the rest of his property, we follow Rabbi Eliezer. By making animals an explicit category in his declaration while not specifying that they should be for *korbanot*, he signals that he intends them all to be treated the same. *Hamakdish stam* — if the sanctification was entirely generic, without explicit mention of animals, we follow Rabbi Yehoshua, and the *kedushah* differentiates itself according to the nature of each object.

## Wine, Oil, Birds

### Non-Animal Items

The *mishnah* continues with a third scenario: *hamakdish nechasav v'hayu bahen devarim hara'uyim legabei hamizbeach* — one who sanctifies property that contains items fit for the altar, but not as animal *korbanot*. The examples given are *yeinot u'shmanim* — wine, which could serve as *nesachim* (libations), and oil, which could serve as *menachot* (meal offerings), and *ofot* — birds, which, though they are an animal offering, are placed in a distinct category here.

Rabbi Eliezer rules: *yimakru l'tzorchei oto hamin* — these items are sold for use in their respective categories. The wine is sold to someone who needs *nesachim*, the oil to someone who needs *menachot*, and the birds to someone who needs to bring a bird offering. In this way, the items are directed toward their proper Temple use.

### Attribution Problem

What becomes problematic is the end of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling here: *sheyavi bidmeihen olot* — the proceeds from these sales go toward an *olah*. This is striking, because a ruling that uses the proceeds for an *olah* sounds like Rabbi Yehoshua's approach, not Rabbi Eliezer's. Under Rabbi Eliezer's logic, the proceeds should go to *bedek habayit*.

Several commentators resolve this by emending the text's attribution, reading *Rabbi Elazar* rather than *Rabbi Eliezer* — treating this as an independent, third opinion. Alternatively, one might argue that Rabbi Eliezer himself distinguishes between large livestock and inanimate items or birds, conceding in this more limited context to an approach resembling Rabbi Yehoshua's. The logic for such a distinction, however, remains unclear. In any case, the structure of the ruling — sell the items for their proper use, and direct the proceeds toward an *olah* — is essentially a Rabbi Yehoshua-type position, whether or not it is Rabbi Eliezer himself saying it. *V'shear nechasim yiplu l'veit habayit* — and everything else in the estate goes to *bedek habayit*.

## Bedek Habayit Traits

### Generic → Bedek

The *Gemara* quotes a *baraita* from Temurah that enumerates the characteristics unique to *kodshei bedek habayit* as against *kodshei mizbeach*. The first principle: *stam hekdeshos l'bedek habayit* — a generic sanctification defaults to *bedek habayit*. This is the rule operative in our *mishnah*. It is worth pausing to note that this default is not as obvious as it might appear. The *Beit Hamikdash* maintained multiple funds, including the large and important fund of *shirei halishkah*, which financed walls and infrastructure. The question arises: when one writes a check to the Temple, as it were, why does it go specifically to *bedek habayit* and not to one of these other funds? The answer, it seems, is that those other funds were structurally tied to the *shekel* contributions and the surpluses of *terumah halishkah*, and were not open to voluntary individual contributions. The only fund available for an individual to donate to generically was *bedek habayit*.

### Universal Application

The second characteristic: *hekdesh bedek habayit chal al hakol* — the sanctity of *bedek habayit* can take effect on any object whatsoever. Unlike *korbanot*, which are restricted to unblemished animals meeting specific requirements, there is no categorical restriction on what can be sanctified for *bedek habayit*. Any item of value may be dedicated.

### Me'ilah on Growth

The third characteristic: *u'moalin b'giduleihen* — there is *me'ilah* (the prohibition against misappropriating sacred property) on things that grow from items sanctified as *bedek habayit*. This reflects a fundamental conceptual difference between *kedushat bedek habayit* and *kedushat korban*. The *kedushah* of *bedek habayit* is essentially *kedushat damim* — sanctity of monetary value and ownership. The Temple owns the item. Therefore, when that item produces fruit, offspring, or milk, those products also belong to the Temple and are subject to the laws of *me'ilah*.

The *kedushah* of a *korban*, by contrast, is about identity and purpose — not ownership in the ordinary sense. If I sanctify an animal as a *shelamim*, its identity is that of a sacrificial offering. But its offspring and its milk are extraneous to that identity; they are not caught up in the same *kedushah* and do not belong to the Temple by virtue of the animal's *korban* status. That is why *me'ilah* applies to the growth of *bedek habayit* items in a way it does not apply to the growth of *kodshei mizbeach*.

### No Kohen Benefit

The fourth characteristic: *v'ein bahem hana'ah l'kohanim* — the *kohanim* receive no benefit from *kodshei bedek habayit*, in contrast to *kodshei mizbeach*. Even from an *olah*, which is burned entirely on the altar, the *kohanim* benefit by receiving the hide. From *bedek habayit* items, however, everything goes entirely toward the repair and maintenance of the Temple, and no priestly benefit is derived.

The *Gemara* then observes that the *baraita* aligns with Rabbi Eliezer's position from our *mishnah*, as his ruling consistently treats generic sanctification as *bedek habayit* in all cases.

Rabbi Yochanan identifies the scriptural source for Rabbi Eliezer's approach in the verse *ish ki yakdish et beito kodesh l'Hashem* — "a man who sanctifies his house as sacred to God." The *Gemara* reasons that *beito* here cannot mean literally his residential dwelling, since that is addressed in a separate verse. Rather, *beito* means his household — all of his property. And since the verse discusses sanctification going to the Temple without specifying any particular type of offering, the default conclusion is that it all goes to *bedek habayit*.

## Property vs. Flock

### Rav Zeira's Reading

Rav Zeira, citing Rav Huna in the name of Rav, proposes a limiting principle regarding the scope of the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. According to Rav Zeira, the dispute applies only when one sanctifies mixed property — a household containing both animals and other items — in which case the question arises of whether the animals receive a differentiated *kedushah*. However, if one explicitly sanctifies only a flock of animals — *aval hamakdish edro* — then all agree that the sanctification goes *l'mizbeach*, since there are no non-animal items requiring a different treatment and no reason to split the *kedushah*.

### R. Ba's Alternative

Rabbi Ba bar Huna, also citing Rav, reads the *mishnah* in the opposite direction. In his view, the debate in the *mishnah* occurs precisely in the case of *hamakdish edro* — one who sanctifies only his flock. That is the scenario where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree about whether the animals receive *kedushat bedek habayit* or *kedushat mizbeach*. But if one truly sanctified mixed property of all kinds, even Rabbi Yehoshua would agree that everything goes to *bedek habayit*.

This is a challenging reading of the *mishnah*, because the *mishnah* explicitly states that *she'ar nechasim* — the other property — goes to *bedek habayit*, implying that there is indeed other property present. Under Rabbi Ba's reading, one would need to say that the other property consists of animals that are not fit for *korbanot* — those that are too old, already blemished, or otherwise disqualified — and it is only those that go to *bedek habayit*. This is acknowledged to be a difficult reading. The *Gilyon HaShas* essentially supports this interpretation as the only way to make Rabbi Ba's position work, but the strain on the text is clear.

### R. Yochanan: Same Debate

Rabbi Yochanan takes a third approach, one that cuts through the entire distinction: *lo shanu* — it makes no difference. Whether one sanctified mixed property or only a flock of animals, the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua applies in exactly the same way. Rabbi Eliezer would always hold that everything is *l'bedek habayit*, and Rabbi Yehoshua would always hold that for animals the *kedushah* takes on a *korban* character.

## Redeeming Bedek

### Redemption Status

With this the *Gemara* turns to a new question, one that cuts to the heart of the conceptual distinction between *kedushat bedek habayit* and *kedushat mizbeach*. Rav Huna in the name of Rav Avu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states: *kodshei bedek habayit shepadaan temimim yatzu l'chulin* — if items consecrated as *bedek habayit* were redeemed while they were still unblemished, they exit their consecrated status completely and become fully *chulin* (profane).

This question has genuine depth. Everyone agrees that one can explicitly sanctify an unblemished animal as *bedek habayit* — that is, one can deliberately dedicate an unblemished sheep to the temple maintenance fund rather than as a *korban*. (The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua concerns only the generic case.) When such an animal is subsequently redeemed, does it become entirely *chulin*, or does some residual status remain?

The conceptual tension is as follows. The *kedushah* of *bedek habayit* is primarily a *kedushah* of ownership and monetary value — the Temple owns the item and derives value from it. When that monetary value is transferred to a substitute through redemption, in principle the *kedushah* should depart entirely from the original object, since the object's only relevance was its value. This contrasts with *kedushat korban*, where the *kedushah* is bound up with the animal's identity and purpose, such that even after redemption some residual identity remains. The *halacha* is well established that even after a *korban* with a *mum* has been redeemed, certain restrictions continue to apply — one may not shear it or milk it — because the identity of the animal as a former *korban* does not entirely dissolve.

The ruling of Rav Huna is that for *kodshei bedek habayit*, the redemption is complete: the item exits fully to *chulin*. The *Gemara* then asks whether the *mishnah* confirms this. The *mishnah* in Temurah, which listed the characteristics unique to each type of sanctification, states concerning *kodshei mizbeach*: *veladan vechalavan asur l'achar pidyonan* — the offspring and the milk of a redeemed *korban* remain forbidden even after redemption. Implicitly, then, by *kodshei bedek habayit*, the offspring and milk would be *mutar* — permitted. This seems to support the ruling that *bedek habayit* sanctity does not leave behind a residual restriction.

### Rav Chisda's Ruling

Rav Chizkiyah in the name of Rav Chisda clarifies the precise scope of the ruling. The statement that *kodshei bedek habayit shepadaan temimim yatzu l'chulin* applies when the animals were redeemed and subsequently acquired a *mum*. In that case, once the *mum* appears after redemption, the animal may be used without restriction. If, however, the animal remains unblemished after redemption, there is at least a rabbinic-level restriction against using it immediately — it would look inappropriate to take an unblemished animal that was sanctified and immediately put it to mundane use. So the blanket statement of Rav Huna requires qualification: full permissibility comes when the animal acquires a *mum* after having been redeemed.

### Milk & Children

The *Gemara* reconciles this with the *mishnah*'s more limited language. Rabbi Yose in the name of Rav Chisda notes that the *mishnah*'s implication — that by *kodshei bedek habayit* the offspring and milk are permitted after redemption — refers to the case before the animal acquired a *mum* after redemption. In that stage, when the animal itself cannot yet be freely used, the milk and offspring are nonetheless permitted. Only once the animal acquires a *mum* does the fuller permissibility apply, extending to the animal itself. This distinguishes the *mishnah*'s more limited *heter* (permissibility of milk and offspring) from Rabbi Yochanan's broader ruling (full permissibility), by placing them at different stages of the animal's post-redemption history.

---

---

# Shekalim 13

## Bedek HaBayit Redemption

### Intro & Approach

Today's daf is 13, and we pick up at the very bottom of 12a. This passage proved difficult at the end of the previous shiur — and rightly so, as it is much debated among the commentators. The explanation presented here follows that of the *Tosafot HaRosh*, which is, on balance, the simplest available.

### Unblemished Redemption

The *gemara* opens with a statement transmitted by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, citing Rabbi Abahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kodshei bedek ha-bayit she-pe'd'an temimim yatze'u le-chullin* — animals sanctified for *bedek ha-bayit* that were redeemed while still unblemished exit entirely into the domain of the ordinary.

To understand this, one must recall the fundamental distinction between the two types of *kedushah*. *Kedushah* of *bedek ha-bayit* is essentially a sanctity of ownership — the Temple treasury acquires a proprietary interest in the animal. As such, even if one sanctifies an unblemished animal for *bedek ha-bayit* (which one is technically not supposed to do, yet if done — whether explicitly or through the generic *kiddush* discussed in our *mishnah* — the *kedushah* takes effect), and subsequently redeems it without a *mum*, one is entitled to do so. Since this *kedushah* is about ownership rather than purpose, the animal upon redemption has no residual *kedushah* whatsoever — it is *yatza le-chullin* in the fullest sense.

This stands in contrast to a *korban*, which, even after developing a *mum* and being redeemed, retains a residual sanctity: one may not shear it, work it, or benefit from its milk.

### Mizbe'ach Contrast

The *gemara* then invokes a *mishnah* — *matnitin amar ken* — noting that a *mishnah* in Chullin supports this. That *mishnah* addresses a case of *kodshei mizbe'ach* where a *mum* preceded the act of sanctification. The *mishnah* there distinguishes between two scenarios. If an animal is sanctified for a *korban* and subsequently develops a *mum*, the original *kedushah* was a full *kedushat korban*, and even after redemption some residual *kedushah* remains. However, if the animal already had a *mum* when sanctified, it was never truly fit for the *mizbe'ach*, and the *kedushah* it received is not a genuine *kedushat mizbe'ach* in the full sense.

### Chullin Mishnah

There is something analogous between sanctifying an already-blemished animal for the *mizbe'ach* and sanctifying something directly for *bedek ha-bayit* — in both cases the animal was never truly fit for the altar at the moment of sanctification. The *mishnah* in Chullin teaches that when a *mum* preceded the *kedushah* for the *mizbe'ach*, the ruling is *vladan va-chalavan mutar le-achar pidyonan* — the offspring and the milk are permitted after redemption. The *gemara* takes this to mean the animal is entirely *yatza le-chullin*. By analogy, the same ought to be true when the animal was sanctified directly for *bedek ha-bayit*, and perhaps even without any *mum* at all.

Similarly, a *mishnah* in Temurah articulates the contrast from the other direction: *kodshei mizbe'ach* that are sanctified and then develop a *mum* result in a ruling of *vladan va-chalavan asur* — the offspring and milk remain forbidden after redemption. The *mishnah* implies by contrast that *kodshei bedek ha-bayit* would yield *vladan va-chalavan mutar*. Again, however, the cases being contrasted all involve a *mum* at some stage, whether before or after sanctification.

### Chizkiyah's Challenge

At this point Rav Chizkiyah in the name of Rav Chisda raises a challenge — *hipatir* — essentially rejecting the proposed analogy. Following the reading of the *Gra*, the response is that one cannot draw a proof from the case of a *mum* to the case of an unblemished *bedek ha-bayit* animal. In the cases under discussion, the animal at least had a *mum*; it is not necessarily true that an unblemished *bedek ha-bayit* animal would be equally and completely desanctified upon redemption.

One might ask: is the comparison not compelling? If the *kedushah* never had the character of *kedushat mizbe'ach* — either because the animal was blemished at sanctification or because it was sanctified directly for *bedek ha-bayit* — the *kedushah* in both cases ought to be fully removable. Yet the *gemara* maintains the distinction. One possible rationale is practical: if one sees an animal being used freely after redemption but the animal is unblemished and known to have been sanctified, that creates a far more significant public impression than seeing the same with a visibly blemished animal. So even if the *kedushah* types are genuinely comparable, the presence of a *mum* is what in practice allows for complete *yetzi'ah le-chulin*, and one cannot extrapolate to the unblemished case.

Rabbi Yosei in the name of Rav Chisda then reasserts — *matnitin amrah ken* — still insisting the *mishnah* supports complete desanctification. The full arc of his argument draws on both the implicit contrast (from the Temurah *mishnah*) and the parallel (from the Chullin *mishnah*), but in every case the textual basis involves a *mum*. The *gemara*'s conclusion is therefore that while the analogies are suggestive, one cannot derive a definitive ruling about unblemished *bedek ha-bayit* redemption from these sources alone — since in all the supporting cases, a *mum* is present.

The argument from our own *mishnah* is ultimately the strongest. Rabbi Chizkiyah in the name of Rabbi Yosei insists: *kodshei bedek ha-bayit she-pe'd'an temimim yatze'u le-chullin*. The proof is that if they did not fully exit into *chullin*, one could never impose a *kedushat mizbe'ach* upon them afterward. Yet our *mishnah*, according to Rabbi Yehoshua, says that the unblemished animals from a generic *kiddush* — once belonging to *bedek ha-bayit* — are sold, the proceeds go to *bedek ha-bayit*, and the buyer goes on to bring an *olah*. How could that buyer bring the animal as a *korban* if it still retained any residual *kedushah*? One can only sanctify something for a *korban* if it is completely *chullin*. This is a powerful proof from our *mishnah* that unblemished *bedek ha-bayit* animals, once redeemed, are fully desanctified.

---

## Female Sanctity Stat (II)

### R. Shimon Gender

The *gemara* now turns to a new set of questions arising from a *mishnah*, asking what *kedushah* — if any — attaches to animals sanctified for the wrong purpose by reason of gender. The case: *hifrish nekevah le-olato u-le-fischo u-le-ashamo* — one set aside a female animal and sanctified it as an *olah*, or as a *pesach*, or as an *asham*, all of which require a male. The first position is that such an animal is *oseh temurah* — it possesses enough *kedushat korban* that were one to attempt an exchange (*temurah*), the *kedushah* would take effect on the substitute animal. The very act of *temurah* is a biblical prohibition, but the *halacha* is that although one transgresses, the second animal nonetheless becomes *kadosh* while the first retains its *kedushah*.

Rabbi Shimon, however, distinguishes: *le-olato oseh temurah* — for an *olah*, yes, the female achieves enough *kedushat korban* to make *temurah*; *le-fischo u-le-ashamo ein oseh temurah* — but for a *pesach* or an *asham*, no. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda then transmits in the name of Rabbi Shimon an even broader position: *le-olato le-fischo u-le-ashamo ein oseh temurah* — for none of them does it make *temurah*.

These two positions attributed to (or in the name of) Rabbi Shimon thus represent a tripartite range: the first *tanna* holds that all three achieve *kedushah* sufficient for *temurah*; Rabbi Shimon distinguishes *olah* from the others; and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in Rabbi Shimon's name says none of them achieve such *kedushah*.

### Bird Precedent

Rabbi Yochanan explains the reasoning of the first Rabbi Shimon — the one who distinguishes *olah* from *pesach* and *asham*: *sheken matzinu nekevah be-of kesherah lavo olah* — since a female bird is entirely valid to be brought as an *olah*, the concept of "female" is not foreign to the *parshah* of *olah*. Consequently, when one sanctifies a female animal as an *olah*, that animal is sufficiently within the *parshah* to acquire genuine *kedushat korban*, and it therefore makes *temurah*. By contrast, a female is entirely foreign to the *parshah* of *pesach* and *asham*, and therefore acquires no such *kedushah*.

### R. Yochanan Compare

Rabbi Yochanan then explains the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, who says that even for an *olah* the female makes no *temurah*: *im min be-mino hu chaluk alav, kol sheken min she-eino* — if something of the same fundamental type but differing in a single characteristic (like age) is already so different as to not receive *kedushah*, how much more so something of the wrong gender entirely.

The illustrative case is from a *baraita*: an *asham* requiring a one-year-old for which one brought a two-year-old, or requiring a two-year-old for which one brought a three-year-old — *lo yatza*. One is not *yotzei* with the *korban*. And most *mefarshim* read the following line, *Rabbi Shimon omer kol atzman einam kedoshim*, to mean that the animals do not even become *kadosh* at all. Since the tradition of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda is attributed to Rabbi Shimon, the reasoning follows: if even a difference of one year in an animal that is otherwise entirely appropriate — right species, right gender, right in every other respect — suffices to prevent *kedushah* according to Rabbi Shimon, then certainly the wrong gender falls entirely outside the *parshah*.

---

## Sanctity Distinction (II)

### Sanctity Categories

At this point in the analysis it becomes necessary to introduce a more precise conceptual framework than the simple *mizbe'ach*/*bedek ha-bayit* dichotomy. The more exact categories are *kedushat haguf* and *kedushat damim*.

*Kedushat haguf* is intrinsic sanctity: the object itself is to be used — the animal itself is to be brought as a *korban*, the beam itself is to be incorporated into the *Beit HaMikdash*. *Kedushat damim* is a sanctity of value: the object itself will not be used, but will be sold and the proceeds used in its stead. These categories cross-cut the *mizbe'ach*/*bedek ha-bayit* distinction. A stone sanctified to be built into the *Beit HaMikdash* has *kedushat haguf* that is *le-bedek ha-bayit*. And there exists a category of *kedushat damim le-mizbe'ach* — a sanctity of proceeds designated for the *mizbe'ach* — which is the key to understanding several of the cases that follow.

---

## Female Sanctity Stat (II)

### R. Abba Pesach/Asham

Rabbi Abba clarifies why Rabbi Yochanan's original question — why not extend the reasoning to *asham* as well, since leftover *asham* funds go toward an *olah*, and an *olah* as a bird can be female — does not succeed. The difference is this: by a *pesach*, *gufo karev shelamim* — the animal body itself is brought as *shelamim* after *Pesach*. A female is therefore genuinely within the *parshah* of *pesach* because the animal itself can serve in that capacity. By contrast, by an *asham* and an *olah*, *ein gufo karev olah* — the *asham* animal itself is never brought as an *olah*; only its redeemed value is transferred. The animal body itself thus never serves as an *olah*, and the connection is too attenuated.

---

## Sanctity Distinction (II)

### R. Yehoshua Female

This distinction leads directly to an important analysis of Rabbi Yehoshua's position in the *mishnah*. Rabbi Yochanan states: *Rabbi Shimon ve-Rabbi Yehoshua shneihem amru davar echad* — Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua effectively say the same thing. How so? Rabbi Yehoshua says in the *mishnah* that when one sanctifies all one's property generically, the unblemished female animals acquire *kedushat olah* — yet in practice one sells them and uses the proceeds for an *olah*, while the animals themselves go as *zivchei shelamim*. The implication is that the female animal acquires *kedushat olah* in a meaningful sense, yet one is permitted to sell it *without* a *mum*. How can an animal with *kedushat olah* be redeemed without a *mum*?

### Redemption Mechanism

The answer is that the female's unsuitability for an *olah* is itself a significant enough deficiency that it pushes the *kedushah* out of the domain of *kedushat haguf* and into the domain of *kedushat damim*. It was never truly sanctified in its body for use as an *olah*; its *kedushah* from the outset was only as proceeds — *kedushat damim*. This explains the apparent paradox: since the *kedushah* is *kedushat damim*, the animal can be sold without a *mum*. But since the *kedushah* is *le-mizbe'ach*, the proceeds must be used for an *olah*.

### Proceeds Purpose

This subtle category — *kedushat damim le-mizbe'ach* — is what enables this hybrid result: the animal may be redeemed without a *mum* because it was always about its proceeds rather than the thing itself; yet the proceeds are designated *le-mizbe'ach*, so they must go toward an *olah*. This explains both Rabbi Yehoshua in the *mishnah* and, by parallel, Rabbi Shimon's position that a female for an *olah* does not make *temurah* — since one who has only *kedushat damim* cannot make *temurah*.

---

## Generic Sanctification

### Generic Olah Creation

Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rabbi Shimon Lakish now turns to the textual basis for Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling. The verse cited is *daber el Aharon ve-el banav ve-el kol bnei Yisrael ve-amarta aleihem ish ish mi-beit Yisrael asher yakriv la-Hashem le-olah* — the general rule for *korbanot* is that a generic *kedushah* applied to animals creates *kedushat olah*. The verse's scope, *hakol kareiv le-olah*, makes the *olah* the default category.

The verse then specifies *tamim zachar* — unblemished male — for one's desire. The question arises: if only males are mentioned, from where does Rabbi Yehoshua include females in the *kedushat olah*? The answer is *talmud lomar ba-bakar* — the word "cattle" is generic and encompasses females as well, extending the *kedushah* to unblemished females.

### R. Elazar Extension

Rabbi Elazar (the text switches from Rabbi Eliezer, since Rabbi Eliezer's position in the *mishnah* is that everything goes to *bedek ha-bayit*, making the attribution there problematic; the *mefarshim* accordingly emend to Rabbi Elazar) goes further than Rabbi Yehoshua. He holds that the generic *kedushah* creates *kedushat olah* not only on unblemished cattle and sheep but on everything fit for the *mizbe'ach* — birds, flour, wine, oil. His proof text is the same verse: *asher yakriv la-Hashem le-olah — hakol kareiv olah*, everything that is *ra'uy le-mizbe'ach* receives *kedushat olah*.

Rabbi Abahu in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains: *ta'ama de-Rabbi Elazar* — the same verse that Rabbi Yehoshua used. Where Rabbi Yehoshua stops at cattle and sheep, Rabbi Elazar reads the entire opening phrase as universal in scope and understands *ba-bakar* not as a limitation on what receives *kedushah* but as a limitation on what may be brought *itself* as opposed to through its proceeds.

### Scripture Bakar

The question is then asked: if you use *ba-bakar* to include females (overriding the explicit *zachar*), why not also use it to include blemished animals (overriding the explicit *tamim*)? The *gemara* answers with a striking idiom — *shivta de-kadka beineihem*, the rod of the loom is between them, meaning there is a world of difference between the two extensions. Unblemished females are fundamentally fit to be brought as *korbanot* — just not as an *olah* specifically. Blemished animals, by contrast, are fundamentally unfit to be brought as *korbanot* at all. The *bakar* extension only reaches as far as animals that are, in principle, within the *parshah* of *korbanos*.

### Bird Redemption Trap

This leads to an important question about birds in Rabbi Elazar's system. According to Rabbi Elazar, when one gives a generic *kedushah*, a bird receives *kedushat olah*. Yet the bird cannot be brought itself — *de-chtiv ba-bakar ve-lo ofot*, the verse specifies cattle and not birds as what may be brought directly. But a bird also cannot be redeemed, because *ein la-of pidyon* — there is no mechanism for redeeming a bird. So the bird has *kedushah* but can neither be used nor redeemed. 

Rabbi Yosei clarifies by citing a principle of Rabbi Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Zeira: *kol she-eino yachol likrov lo hu ve-lo dameha lo kidshah ela hekdesh tamid* — anything that can be neither brought nor redeemed through its proceeds receives only a standing *kedushah* and does not get *kedushat olah* through the generic *kedushah*. In Rabbi Elazar's system, therefore, the bird receives *kedushat damim* but cannot have it realized — it is a *kedushah* that, given the generic context, is trapped without *pidyon* or *korban*. The upshot is *lo kidshah ela kedushat damim* in this attenuated, unrealizable sense.

The question is raised: how does this square with the earlier statement of Rabbi Yochanan that a female bird's eligibility for an *olah* is precisely what makes the female animal's *kedushah* meaningful enough to make *temurah*? The answer appears to be that these are two different contexts. When one *explicitly* sanctifies a female animal as an *olah*, the bird precedent gives that act enough halachic traction that the animal acquires *kedushat haguf* and makes *temurah*. But when the *kedushah* arises from the generic *kiddush* of Rabbi Elazar's *mishnah*, the limiting verse (*ba-bakar ve-lo ofot*) intervenes and pushes the bird into a different category — one where the *kedushah* cannot be actualized either through the animal itself or through its proceeds.

---

## Temurah & Tameia

### Female Pesach Fit

Returning to the dispute about whether a female sanctified for a *pesach* makes *temurah*, the *gemara* records that Rabbi objects to applying Rabbi Shimon's ruling to the *pesach* case: *Ein ani ro'eh divrei Rabbi Shimon be-Pesach she-mosar Pesach ba shelamim*. A female is genuinely within the *parshah* of *pesach* because if one fails to bring it as a *pesach*, it may subsequently be brought as *shelamim*. Since the animal itself can be brought in that capacity, the female is not so foreign to the *pesach* that it should be denied *kedushat korban*.

### Tameia Definition

The *gemara* continues to probe the basis for denying *kedushat korban* to inappropriate animals. The verse invoked is *ve-im kol behemah teme'ah asher lo yakrivu mimenah korban la-Hashem* — the verse concerning a *teme'ah* animal (such as a camel) that one attempts to sanctify as a *korban*. The question is what falls into the category of *teme'ah* for this purpose. One approach, associated with the position of Rabbi Shimon, reads *teme'ah* broadly: *afilu teme'ah be-oto ha-shem* — even something inappropriate by reason of any disqualifying characteristic is in the category of *teme'ah*. This reading would consign a female sanctified for an *olah* to the *teme'ah* category and deny it *kedushah* sufficient for *temurah*.

Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rabbi Elazar, however, reads it more narrowly: *kol she-eino ra'uy likarev lo kan ve-lo be-makom acher* — only something that cannot be brought here or anywhere as a *korban* falls into the *teme'ah* category. A female, by contrast, while not fit for this specific *korban*, is fit *le-karev be-makom acher* — it can be brought as some other *korban*. Therefore *yatzat nekevah le-olah* — the case of a female for an *olah* is excluded from the *teme'ah* category, and it does make *temurah*.

### Bestiality Exception

Rabbi Avun and Rabbi Bun raise a challenge: what about an animal that has been used in an act of bestiality (*haroveiah ve-hanirva*)? Such an animal is *she-einam reuyim likarev lo kan ve-lo be-makom acher* — completely unfit for any *korban*, anywhere, under any circumstances. Yet the *halacha* is that if one sanctifies such an animal, it does achieve enough *kedushat mizbe'ach* to make *temurah*. If the criterion for exclusion is that an animal cannot be brought anywhere, how does an animal involved in bestiality avoid that exclusion?

### Tameia Strict

Rabbi Zeira responds: *af ani lo amarti ela teme'ah mamash* — I only ever meant *teme'ah* in the strictest sense: a genuinely *tame* species, like a camel. The word *teme'ah* in the verse means precisely that — a non-kosher animal. It does not extend to animals that are disqualified for other reasons, even if they are entirely unfit for the altar. Consequently, animals involved in bestiality, though completely unfit, are not in the category of *teme'ah mamash* and therefore do make *temurah*. And similarly, a female sanctified for an *olah* — which is certainly not a *tame* species — is not in the *teme'ah* category, and would make *temurah*.

The practical consequence of this conclusion is that one cannot use the *teme'ah* verse to exclude wrong-gender animals from *temurah*. The category of *teme'ah* is reserved strictly for non-kosher species, and anything outside that narrow category retains sufficient *kedushat mizbe'ach* to make *temurah* — leaving the broader dispute about the *nature* of the *kedushah* acquired by a female animal (whether *kedushat haguf* or *kedushat damim*) unresolved by this textual route.

---

## Supplier Contracts

### Monthly Prices

The *gemara* now arrives at the final *mishnah* of the *perek*, which is considerably more straightforward. *Achat li-shloshim yom meshari'in et ha-lishkah* — once every thirty days, the Temple administrators would fix prices for the commodities they were purchasing: flour, wine, oil, and similar supplies needed for the *korbanot*. The prices set at the beginning of the month governed all transactions for that month, until the next price-setting at *Rosh Chodesh*.

### Price Lock

The mechanism works as follows. Suppose the Temple agreed with a supplier to provide flour at four *se'ah* per *shekel*. If during the month market prices rise so that the going rate is now only three *se'ah* per *shekel* — *yaspik me-arba*, the supplier must nonetheless deliver four *se'ah* per *shekel* as agreed. The original contract price holds.

### Temple Benefit

Conversely, if the original agreement was three *se'ah* per *shekel* and the price drops so that four *se'ah* can be had for a *shekel* — *yaspik me-arba*, the supplier must deliver at the more favorable rate of four. *She-yad hekdesh al ha-elyonah* — the hand of *hekdesh* is always on top. In either direction of market movement, the Temple always benefits.

### Quality Returns

Beyond the price terms, there are quality guarantees. *Im hitli'ah* — if the flour became wormy, even after delivery and payment, the supplier bears responsibility: *solet hitli'ah lo*, it is the supplier's loss. Similarly, *im hichmitz yayin hichmitz lo* — if the wine turned sour, that too falls to the supplier.

The supplier's exposure continues until the moment of use: *eino mekabel ma'osav ad she-yehei mizbe'ach mirtze* — the supplier does not have an unqualified right to retain payment until the *mizbe'ach* has accepted the offering. Up until that point, the right of return remains in force.

### Payment Terms

The final ruling, transmitted in the name of Rabbi Shimon, introduces a modification out of fairness to the supplier: *miyad hayu mekablin et ma'oseihen* — payment would be given immediately upon delivery. Why is the Temple not concerned that it is surrendering its leverage before the offering is made? *Ha-kohanim zerizim heim* — the *kohanim* are diligent and will use the materials promptly. Since in practice the gap between delivery and offering is negligible, there is no reason to impose an unfair payment delay on the supplier.

With that, the *perek* concludes.

---

---

# Shekalim 14

## Temple Officials

### Opening remarks

Today's daf is 14, though we begin in the middle of 13a with the opening of a new *perek*. The shift in tone is immediately apparent: after the dense and often challenging discussions that preceded, the *gemara* now moves into a markedly different register. The *mishnah* and the *gemara* that follows offer something of a respite — a sustained look at the people and personalities who populated the *Beis HaMikdash*, and the remarkable things they did there.

### First Mishnah

The *mishnah* opens: *Elu hen hamemunim shehayu bamikdash* — these are the appointed ones, those who held some administrative position in the *Beis HaMikdash*. The context is entirely natural given where we have been: having discussed the collection of the *shekel*, what to do with the *shekel* funds, and how prices were set for the suppliers, we are now firmly in the world of *Beis HaMikdash* administration. The *mishnah* accordingly catalogs the various officials and what each one oversaw.

### Officials overview

*Yochanan ben Phinehas al hachotamos* — Yochanan ben Phinehas oversaw the *chotamos*, the receipt system. As we have already seen, this was the mechanism by which worshippers would pay money, receive a stamp or token, and then bring that token to a supplier who would provide them with wine and other *nesachim*. *Achiyah al hanesachim* — Achiyah then oversaw the *nesachim* themselves: one official handled the receipt, the other fulfilled it. *Matya ben Shmuel al hapisos* — Matya ben Shmuel oversaw the *pisos*, the lots drawn to determine which *kohein* would receive the more sought-after assignments. *Petachia al hakinim* — Petachia oversaw the bird sacrifices, an administratively challenging role that we will examine more closely when the *gemara* returns to him. People would bring money to a communal container, and the *Beis HaMikdash* would acquire the birds and offer the sacrifices within the same day — a demanding logistical undertaking.

### Petachiah = Mordechai

At this point the *mishnah* takes a striking turn: *Petachia zehu Mordechai* — this Petachia was in fact Mordechai. The reason he was called Petachia, the *mishnah* explains, is *shehaya poseach devarim vedorsham veyodeia beshiv'im lashon* — because he would open up closed matters, explicate difficult things, and knew seventy languages. There is something notable about the *gemara* performing this kind of *drash* on the name of a character mentioned within the *mishnah* itself, a technique more familiar from the Torah's own treatment of figures like Yisro with his multiple names. But a second, more pressing question arises: if Petachia is Mordechai, then we are dealing with a figure from the very first generation of the *Beis HaMikdash Hasheini*. Does that mean all the officials listed here served in that same early generation?

### Generation question

This question is real. The *mishnah* also mentions Elazar — presumably the biblical Elazar — who oversaw the *Parochet*, and Pinchas, who dressed the *Kohanim*, presumably the *Kohen Gadol*. These are figures one would associate with a period far earlier than Mordechai, and the identification compounds the difficulty of treating this list as a roster of contemporaries. One plausible resolution is that the line *Petachia hu Mordechai* is a later gloss, a secondary layer added to the *mishnah*, and that if it is removed, the remainder of the list can be understood as describing one particular generation — perhaps toward the end of the *Mikdash* period, overlapping with the early *tanna'im*. That would make considerably more sense. It is also worth noting that Elazar and Pinchas are the only two names in the *mishnah* that appear without a patronymic, without a *ben*, which itself sets them apart and may support the view that they represent a separate tradition. Additionally, Mordechai was not a *kohein*, introducing a tribal inconsistency if he is placed among the *Beis HaMikdash* officials in a straightforward reading. The goal of the *mishnah* in naming individuals at all seems primarily to convey the texture and variety of the different roles — and to give *kavod* to those who performed them.

### More officials

*Ben Achiya al cholei me'ayim* — Ben Achiya oversaw digestive ailments among the *kohanim*, an office that turns out to have real medical substance, as the *gemara* will explain. *Nachunya chofer shichin* — Nachunya dug wells. *Gevini kruz* — Gevini was the announcer. *Ben Gever al ne'ilas she'arim* — Ben Gever oversaw the locking of the gates at night; while the *levi'im* performed the actual guarding, he served as the head administrator. *Ben Babi memuneh al hapakiya* — Ben Babi oversaw the *pakiya*, the twisting of the wicks, as we will see. *Ben Arza al hatziltzal* — Ben Arza oversaw the chimes, the signal for the *levi'im* to begin their singing. *Hugras ben Levi al hashir* — Hugras ben Levi oversaw the choir itself.

### Beit Garmo & Avtinas

The *mishnah* then turns to two institutions of a different character: *Beis Garmo al ma'aseh lechem hapanim* and *Beis Avtinas al ha-ketores*. We have already encountered both of these families in earlier discussions, where the *ketores* was mentioned in connection with payments to *Beis Garmo* and *Beis Avtinas*. What distinguishes them from the administrative officials listed above is that these were *kohanim* households who held hereditary secrets — *Beis Garmo* knew how to prepare the *Lechem HaPanim*, and *Beis Avtinas* knew how to prepare the *ketores*. These were not administrative posts in the same sense; the knowledge lived within the family and was transmitted only within it. Finally, the *mishnah* lists *Elazar al haParochet* and *Pinchas al haMalbush*, who dressed the *kohanim* — and as noted, these two stand without patronymics, raising again the question of which generation is being described and whether all of these figures truly belong to the same historical moment.

---

## Merit debate

### Rav Chizkiyah debate

The *gemara* opens with a dispute between Rav Chizkiyah and *Rabbanan*. *Chad amar kasherei dor vador ba limnot* — one position holds that the *mishnah* is not describing a single generation at all. Rather, it singles out, from all the generations in which the *Beis HaMikdash* stood, those individuals who were most deserving of recognition — the *kasherei*, the upstanding ones of each era. On this reading, the figures in the *mishnah* can come from any number of different historical periods, united only by the fact that they merit special mention. *Vecharna amar mi shehaya be'oto dor mana* — the other position is more prosaic: the *mishnah* simply lists whoever happened to be serving in the generation of the author of the *mishnah*. This is not a selection of the best from across history; it is merely an account of who held each post at one particular time.

### Yoma reference

The practical consequence of this debate emerges through a connection to a *mishnah* in *Yoma*. That *mishnah* discusses various individuals and families who contributed to the *Beis HaMikdash*, and it concludes with a distinction: *al harishonim hu omer zecher tzadik livracha* — about the former ones it says "the memory of the righteous is a blessing," while *aval acharonim hu omer shem reshaim yirkav* — about the latter ones it says "the name of the wicked shall rot." The *mishnah* in *Yoma* mentions *Beis Garmo* and *Beis Avtinas* among those who did not share their knowledge with others, placing them ambiguously between the clearly praiseworthy and the clearly blameworthy.

According to the position that our *mishnah* in *Shekalim* deliberately selects the *kasherei* of each generation, all those mentioned — including *Beis Garmo* and *Beis Avtinas* — fall under *zecher tzadik livracha*. According to the position that the *mishnah* simply records whoever was there, no particular merit is implied, and the *shem reshaim yirkav* of the *Yoma mishnah* would apply to them.

### Garmo/Avtinas status

The question of whether *Beis Garmo* and *Beis Avtinas* are to be counted among the righteous or the wicked is thus genuinely unresolved at this stage, and the *gemara* will return to it. The ambivalence is understandable: on the one hand, they performed their sacred tasks with skill and faithfulness; on the other, they refused to transmit that knowledge to anyone outside their families. Whether that refusal constitutes a failing serious enough to place them in the *shem reshaim yirkav* category, or whether it is mitigated by their genuine service, depends on which reading of our *mishnah*'s purpose one adopts.

---

## Organizing traditions

### Rabbi Akiva

The *gemara* continues with Rav Yona citing the verse from Isaiah: *lachen achalek lo barabim v'et atzumim yachalek shalal* — "therefore I will divide for him among the great, and with the mighty he will divide the spoil." *Zeh Rabbi Akiva* — this refers to Rabbi Akiva, *she'hitkin midrash halachot v'agadot*, who established — or organized — the *halachot* and the *aggadot*. The *gemara* does not define this precisely, but the weight of the description falls on the word *yachalek*, to divide and distribute: Rabbi Akiva took what preceded him in a disorganized state and sorted it into conceptual categories. *Tosafos* glosses *agadot* here as *midrash halacha*, which is noteworthy, since we do not ordinarily associate Rabbi Akiva's legacy with *aggadah* in the looser sense. The standard formulation of Rabbi Akiva's domain is rather the world of *nega'im* and *ohalot*. The precise meaning of what he "established" here remains worth examining.

### Knesset HaGedolah

A second opinion divides the verse differently. *V'yesh omrim elu anshei knesset hagedola* — some say the verse refers to the members of the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*. The question then becomes: *ela ma tiken* — what exactly did they establish? The answer given is *zeh klalot u'pratot* — they established the framework of *kelal* and *prat*, the general and the particular, the foundational hermeneutical categories of rabbinic legal reasoning. The *gemara* appears to read the two halves of the verse as referring to two different figures or groups: *achalek lo barabim* to Rabbi Akiva, and *v'et atzumim yachalek shalal* to the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*. What is striking throughout is the consistent emphasis on *organization* as the great intellectual achievement. Whether it is Rabbi Akiva sorting *halachot* and *aggadot* into categories, or the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* structuring legal reasoning around *kelal* and *prat*, the creative act being celebrated is not simply the generation of new law but the arrangement and structuring of what was already there into a coherent, transmissible form.

### Sofrim & numbering

Rabbi Abbahu then cites the verse *mishpachat Sofrim yoshvei Yabetz* — the family of the *Sofrim* who dwell in Yabetz — and asks: *mah Talmud lomar Sofrim*? Why were the early generations of rabbis called *Sofrim*? The answer is famous: *ela she-asu et haTorah sfurot sfurot* — they made the Torah into numbers. They organized the material numerically, creating mnemonics that would allow the traditions to be preserved, remembered, and transmitted accurately.

### Numerical mnemonics

The *gemara* immediately offers a cascade of examples: *chamisha lo yitremu trumah* — five people may not separate *terumah*; *chamesh esreh nashim potrot tzaroteihen* — fifteen women exempt their co-wives from *yibbum*; *shloshim v'shesha kretot baTorah* — thirty-six *kretot* in the Torah; *shlosha asar davar ne'emru b'neveilat ha-of hatehorah* — thirteen things are said regarding the carcass of a *tahor* bird; *arba avot nezikin* — four main categories of damage; *avot melachot arba'im chaseir achat* — the *melachot* of *Shabbat* are forty minus one. These are all openings of *mishnayot*. The organizing principle is numerical: a number anchors each tradition, makes it memorable, and serves as a check on the integrity of transmission.

### Torah she-be-al-peh

What is genuinely illuminating about this *gemara* is its recognition that the process of *Torah she-be-al-peh* involves not merely the development or evolution of *halacha* but, in a crucial sense, the *organization* of the material. When the *gemara* says that the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* established *halachot*, it may mean that they took existing practices — things people were already doing — and articulated them as formal law. They looked at what was being observed and gave it shape and expression. And then the early rabbis took that articulated material and structured it further: thematically, numerically, mnemonically. The entire enterprise of *Torah she-be-al-peh* as we have received it is, on this account, inseparable from the labor of organization.

### Ezra the Scribe

The *gemara* then draws a parallel to Ezra: *le-Ezra ha-Kohen ha-Sofer* — Ezra the *Kohen* the *Sofer*. *Mah Talmud lomar Sofer*? *Ela keshem she-hayah Sofer be-divrei Torah kach hayah Sofer be-divrei Chachamim* — just as he was a *Sofer* in matters of Torah, so was he a *Sofer* in matters of the Sages. The *gemara* is saying that the same way the early rabbis numbered and structured their oral traditions, Ezra numbered the written Torah. This is the work we associate with the early Masoretes: counting how many *psukim* the Torah contains, how many times *hi* is written versus *hu*, how many times a word is spelled *maleh* versus *chaser*, what is the midpoint of the Torah in words and in letters. All of this serves to guarantee the accuracy and integrity of the text, exactly as the numerical mnemonics of the *mishnah* serve to preserve the oral tradition.

There is a deeper point embedded here about the very word *sefer* and the word *sofer*. The simplest sense of *sofer* derives from *lesaper* — to tell, to narrate — and a *sefer* is a book that tells a story. But *sofer* also means to count, *lispor*. The two meanings are not incidental to one another: embedded in the concept of a book is the idea of structure, numbering, organization. A *sefer* is not a random collection; it has *psukim*, it has sections, it has a counted and verifiable form.

---

## Bread parable

### Labor metaphor

Rabbi Chagai in the name of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman offers one of the most beautifully constructed images in this section of the *gemara*: *harishonim charshu v'zar'u nichshu kisschu idru katzru amru dashu zaru berru tachnu hirkidu lashu kitfu v'afu* — the early ones plowed, planted, weeded, hoed, harvested, gathered into piles, threshed, winnowed, sorted out the chaff, ground, sifted, kneaded, patted down the dough, and baked it. They did every single step required to transform raw grain into bread. They did everything necessary to make Torah accessible to us.

### Our struggle

*V'anu ein lanu mah le'echol* — and we have nothing to eat. After all that labor, after every stage of preparation was completed on our behalf, we still struggle to access the Torah. The image is not merely rhetorical. What came before the *mishnah*? What had to be done to the inchoate mass of oral traditions, practices, and teachings that preceded it in order to produce the organized, articulated, transmissible document we now simply open and read? We arrive at *daf yomi* each morning, open the *gemara*, and read a *mishnah* — and we rarely pause to ask how much labor was invested in getting that *mishnah* to the form it is now in. Just as one can purchase a loaf of bread without pausing to consider the full chain of agricultural and manufacturing labor behind it, one can study *mishnah* without reckoning with the generations of organizing, articulating, and structuring work that made it possible. The *gemara* insists that we pause and reckon.

---

## Angels & donkey

### Angel comparison

This leads directly to the famous formulation: *in havon kadma'in malachin, anan benei enash* — if the earlier ones were like angels, then we are merely people. *V'in havon benei enash, anan chamorin* — and if they were people, then we are donkeys. Rabbi Mana adds: at that moment I said, *afilu k'chamorei d'Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair lo daminan* — we are not even comparable to the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair. This self-deprecating observation sets up the story that follows.

### Donkey joke

The quip is precise: it is not merely that we are donkeys. We are not even *good* donkeys. The donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair sets an extraordinarily high bar — as the story will make clear.

### Donkey refuses food

*Chamortei d'Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, ganvuha listim b'leilya* — the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair was stolen by bandits in the middle of the night. *Avdat temira gavon tlata yomin* — they kept him hidden with them for three days. *V'lo ta'ama klum* — and the donkey refused to eat anything. After three days, *amru l'machzara* — they decided to return him. They did not want to have a dead donkey on their hands and then be found out. *Afikuha, azlat v'kamat lah al tar'a d'mareh* — they let him go, and he went and stood at the door of his master's home, braying. Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair said to those around him: *pitchun l'hada aluvta* — open up the door for this forsaken one. *D'it lah tlata yomin d'lo ta'ama klum* — it has gone three days without eating anything. He knew that his donkey would not eat away from home.

### Proper feeding

They opened the door and brought the donkey in. Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair said: *yehavun lah klum te'echal* — give him something to eat. They gave him barley, *v'lo ba'at l'meichal* — and he refused to eat it. They reported this to Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair. He asked: *metaknin inun* — have you properly prepared it, removing the stones and chaff? They said yes. He asked further: *v'harimtun demai* — have you separated the *demai*? The barley had been purchased from an *am ha'aretz*, and while one is normally permitted to feed an animal *demai* without separating *terumot u'ma'asrot* — since the obligation is only rabbinic and feeding animals is more lenient — they had indeed assumed they could do so. But Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair had taught them a *halacha*: *halokeiach zera lebeheimah* — if one purchases *demai* for planting, or for feeding animals, or flour for tanning leather, or oil for a lamp, *patur min hademai* — one is exempt from separating *terumas ma'aser*. So they had assumed, correctly by the letter of the law, that they could feed the donkey without separating.

### Donkey machmir

Yet the donkey refused. Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's response is remarkable: *mai na'avid lah leha aluvta, de'ee machmera agarmah al atzmah* — what can we do for this poor creature? It is *machmir* on itself. The donkey, of its own accord, was applying a standard beyond what was halachically required of it. The wordplay is delightful: a *chamor* that is *machmir*. And the word *atzmah* — itself, literally "its bone" — echoes the Aramaic *garma*, also meaning bone and also meaning oneself, a linguistic coincidence that the *gemara* savors. They went, separated the *demai*, and then the donkey ate. Which also explains, of course, why it had refused to eat during its three days with the bandits — they were surely feeding it *tevel* and *gezel*. The donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair was more scrupulous in its observance than we are. That is the point.

---

## Petachiah mysteries

### Petachiah greatness

The *gemara* returns now to Petachia from the *mishnah*: *bo u'rei mah gadol hu kocho shel oso ish, poteiach devarim vedorsham* — come and see how great was the power of that man; he could open up hidden things and explicate them. And he knew *shiv'im lashon*, seventy languages.

### Sanhedrin languages

A *baraita* is cited about the language requirements for a *sanhedrin*: *sanhedrin she-yesh bo shnayim she-yecholim ledaber v'khulam reuyim lishmoa* — if among the seventy members of a *sanhedrin* two can speak all languages and the rest can at least understand them, *harei zu reuyah le-Sanhedrin*, that is the minimum for a valid *sanhedrin*. If three can speak all seventy languages, that is an average *sanhedrin*. Four speakers of all languages constitutes a *wise* *sanhedrin*.

### Yavneh scholars

*U'veYavneh hayu vo daled* — and at Yavneh there were four: Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Ben Chakhinai, and Rabbi Elazar ben Masya. These four could speak all seventy languages, making the *sanhedrin* of Yavneh a *chakhmah*, a wise one.

### Drought & omer

Rav Chisda then relates: *pa'am achas yavsha Eretz Yisrael* — once there was a drought in the Land of Israel, and they did not know from where to bring the *omer*. There was a mute person who put one hand on a rooftop and one on the top of a lean-to structure. They brought him before Petachia. Petachia asked: is there a place called *Gagot Tzrifim* or *Tzrifim Gagot*? They went there and found grain suitable for the *omer*. Petachia had interpreted the mute person's mime as indicating a place name.

### Blight story

Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Bun tells a similar story: *pa'am achat nishtadef kol ha-olam kulo* — once there was a blight on the entire world, not only in Israel, and they again did not know where to find grain for the *omer*. A mute person placed one hand over his eyes and the other over the opening of a well. They brought him before Petachia, who asked: is there a place called *Ein Sokher* or *Sokher Ein*? They went there and found what they needed.

### Three women

Then: *Gimel nashim heviu kineihan* — three women brought their *kinim* to Petachia, who oversaw the bird offerings. This story illuminates, from a different angle, why someone of Petachia's unique abilities was needed for that post. The challenge was not only the logistical complexity of birds getting mixed up — the subject of an entire tractate *Kinnim* — but also the problem of discerning the *intent* behind the offerings brought.

### Eye danger

The first woman said *le-einati* — for my *einati*. *Savrin lemeimar shofat ke-ma'ayan* — the natural reading was that she had experienced a flow like a wellspring, meaning she had bled outside her regular menstrual period and was a *zavah*, who must bring a *korban*. Petachia said: *be-aynah sakanta* — no, she means she was in danger in her eye, her life was at risk, and she is bringing this as a *nedavah*, a voluntary offering. The difference is halachically significant: a *zavah* brings a *chatat* and an *olah*; a *nedavah* is simply an *olah*.

### Sea danger

The second woman said *le-yamati* — for my *yamati*. Again the obvious reading was *shofat ke-yam*, that she had a flow like an ocean, making her a *zavah*. Petachia said: *be-yama sakanta* — no, she was endangered at sea, and this too is a *nedavah*.

### Wolf danger

The third woman said *le-zivati* — for my flow. This one seemed unambiguous: *zavah mamash*, she is plainly a *zavah*. Yet Petachia said: *ze'ev ba litol et benah* — a wolf came to take her child, she was saved, and this too is a *nedavah*. In each case Petachia was reading something — body language, context, demeanor — that allowed him to reinterpret what appeared on the surface to be a declaration of *zavah* status as something else entirely. This is the gift that made him indispensable: the ability to open what was closed, to see what others could not perceive.

---

## Ben Achiah health

### Stomach ailments

*Ben Achiya* oversaw *cholei me'ayim* — digestive ailments among the *kohanim*. The *gemara* now explains why this was such a persistent problem.

### Diet problems

*Al yedei she-hayu ha-kohanim holchim yecheifim al ha-ritzpah* — because the *kohanim* went barefoot on the stone floors, and they had to consume enormous quantities of meat from the *korbanot* — all the *chatat* and *asham* offerings that were brought. Apparently in the *Beis HaMikdash* they drank only water, no other beverage being available to them. This combination — cold stone floors underfoot, vast meat consumption, and water as the sole drink — led chronically to *cholei me'ayim*, stomach ailments.

### Wine remedies

*Va-havei yeda* — and Ben Achiya knew which wine would be good for the stomach, whether for settling it or for acting as a laxative, and which wine would have the opposite effect. He had, in other words, a practical pharmacological expertise in applying the right wine to the specific condition the *kohein* was suffering from. The role was as medically substantive as any other on the list.

---

## Nechunya wells

### Well digging

*Nechunya chofer shichin* — Nechunya dug wells. *She-hayah chofer shichin u-me'arot* — he would dig wells and caves and other excavations to ensure access to water for the *Beis HaMikdash* and for people traveling the roads.

### Cold water

*Va-havei yeda hai dein keif mekorar* — he knew which type of rock, if you dug into it, would yield cold water, the kind of cold underground water that was needed.

### Hot water

And he knew *sharvruri* — where there were streams of hot water running through the earth, and how far down those streams ran.

### Son's death

*Amar Rabbi Eliezer: umet bno btzama* — Rabbi Eliezer observes: and yet Nechunya's son died of thirst. This is the theological shock at the heart of the passage. Here was a man whose entire life's work was ensuring that others had water, and his own son died without it.

### Divine justice

The *gemara* responds with the famous declaration of Rabbi Chanina: *man de'amar Rachmana vatran, yivaterun bnei me'ohi* — whoever says that God is a *vatran*, that He simply lets things slide and does not ultimately exact what is owed, his own stomach should be let go in kind. The point is not to be taken literally but to underscore with force: God is not a *vatran*. There is *middas hadin*. *Ela ma'arich ruchyei, vegabe di'dei* — God may be *erech apayim*, He may extend the time before collecting, but ultimately He collects what is owed. The answer to the theological problem, on this account, is that we must believe in *cheshbon shamayim* even when we cannot follow it. There is a just accounting; we simply do not always see how it works.

### God's account

What this means practically is that when someone appears to be flourishing despite their sins, one should not conclude that God has simply forgiven and forgotten. The patience of *erech apayim* is not the same as acquittal. God will ultimately collect. And correspondingly, when someone appears to be suffering despite their righteousness, one should not conclude that the suffering is unjust. There is an accounting we cannot always access.

### Hairbreadth measure

Rabbi Acha then offers a different angle through a *drasha*: the verse says *u-sevivav nis-ara me'od*, which literally means that around God there is a great whirlwind. But Rabbi Acha reads *nis-ara* from the root *se'ara*, hair: *medakdek imahem ke-chut ha-se'ara* — God is as precise with those who surround Him as a hairbreadth. The closer one is to God, the higher the standard to which one is held. A great *tzaddik* is measured with extraordinary precision — precisely because he is capable of being held to that standard, and precisely because his conduct reflects on how God is perceived by the world.

### Awe of closeness
