Rabbi Yosi offers a distinct but related formulation. The verse *v'nora hu al kol sevivav* — "He is awesome upon all those who surround Him" — yields the interpretation: *mora-o al ha-krovim yoser min ha-rechokim* — His awe rests more heavily upon those who are close than upon those who are far. This is not simply a restatement of Rabbi Acha's point. Where Rabbi Acha emphasizes God's exacting precision as something imposed from without, Rabbi Yosi may be pointing to something that emerges from within the person of great closeness: the awe that one carries by virtue of proximity to the divine creates its own inner demand for a higher standard. The exact conceptual distinction between these two positions is subtle, but the difference may be between an externally imposed accountability and an internally generated one — the *tzaddik*'s own heightened consciousness of the divine, which demands more of him than the ordinary person's relationship to God demands of them.

One of the commentators notes a further dimension to the Nechunya story: because Nechunya was so deeply invested in the area of water — it was his defining virtue — the standard applied to him *within that domain* was extraordinarily high. Even a minor failing in precisely that area would be held against him with the precision of *ke-chut ha-se'ara*. This would explain not just that he was punished, but why the punishment came in the very domain of his greatness — a dimension that connects naturally to *midah k'neged midah*.

---

## Chasid daughter

### Chasid tragedy

Rabbi Chagai in the name of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman relates a *ma'aseh*: there was a *chasid* who throughout his life would dig wells, pits, and caves to provide water for travelers. On his daughter's wedding day, she was washed away by a river. The tragic irony is structurally identical to the Nechunya story: a man of extraordinary virtue in the domain of water is struck precisely through water, and on the happiest day of his family's life.

### Refuses comfort

The entire community came to console him. He refused to accept consolation, like Yaakov Avinu before him — and as with Yaakov, the parallel invites attention, since Yaakov's inconsolable grief turned out to rest on a misapprehension. Here too the *chasid*'s refusal to be comforted carries within it an implicit *ta'ana* against God's justice. He was not merely grief-stricken; he was, at some level, refusing to accept that what had happened was right.

### Pinchas questions

Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair came to console him and was also refused. He turned to those present and asked: *dein hu chasid'chum*? This is your *chasid*? He who refuses consolation, who refuses to accept God's justice, who maintains a *ta'ana* against the divine — this is the man you call righteous? They explained to him the full story: what the man had done throughout his life with water, and how his daughter had died.

### Pinchas refuses

Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's response is remarkable: *efshar she-hayah mekhabed es boro b'mayim v'hu mekape'ach b'mayim* — is it possible that this man honored his Creator with water, and now God is going to cut him off through water? Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair refused to accept this as true. His refusal was not the same as the father's refusal. The father refused consolation because he believed the tragedy had occurred and could not accept it as just. Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair refused to believe the tragedy had occurred at all in the way it appeared.

### Daughter alive

*Miyad naflah havarah ba'ir* — immediately a commotion arose in the city. The daughter appeared, alive.

### Two readings

*Ait d'amri b'suchsa istabchis* — some say she had grabbed a branch as she was swept along by the river and survived. *V'ait d'amri malach yarad kidmus Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair v'hitzilah* — and some say an angel descended in the likeness of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and saved her. The two versions carry different implications. If she survived naturally — grabbed a branch, was carried to safety — then Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's theological confidence is vindicated: God truly would not do this. His intervention was declaratory, not causal. If an angel descended in his likeness, then his intervention was itself the cause of her survival; she would have died without it, and it was his refusal to accept the injustice that changed the outcome.

### Responses differ

This story is in deliberate dialogue with the Nechunya story that preceded it. In both cases, a great man dedicated to providing water is struck through water. In the Nechunya story, the answer given is that God is not a *vatran* — the accounting always works out, even if we cannot follow it, and we must accept the result with faith. The *chasid*'s first response — inconsolable grief, refusal to accept, implicit *ta'ana* — represents one human posture before inexplicable suffering. Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair represents a different one: not acceptance of injustice as a fact, but refusal to accept that this could be God's will, and insistence on finding another explanation. The difference between the father and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair is not that one was angrier or less faithful. It is that the father accepted the tragedy as real and then could not reconcile it with divine justice, while Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair would not accept it as real in the first place. He refused to believe that God would do such a thing to such a person.

---

## Gevini announcer

### Announcements

*Gvini kruz* — Gevini was the *kruz*, the announcer of the *Beis HaMikdash*. *She-aya machriz b'Beis HaMikdash* — he would make announcements to call everyone to their positions. His call was: *Imdu HaKohanim l'avoda* — *kohanim*, to the *avodah*; *Leviim l'duchanam* — *levi'im*, to your stations for the *shira*; *Yisrael l'maamadam* — and Israel, to the *maamad*, the communal representation that stood witness to the *korban tamid*.

### Loud voice

*Agrippas HaMelech shama kolo ad cheis parsa'os* — King Agrippas heard his voice eight *parsa'os* away. One may reasonably assume some element of exaggeration in the account, but the point is clear: his voice was extraordinary in its power and reach. *V'nasnu lo matanos harbeh* — and the king gave him many gifts, presumably as an expression of admiration and encouragement.

---

## Ben Gever gates

### Gate locking

*Ben Gever al ne'ilas she'arim* — Ben Gever oversaw the locking of the Temple gates, the *levi'im* being the ones who actually performed the task of guarding.

### Krias hagever

The *gemara* records that Rav Kumi of the school of Rav Shila translated *krias hagever* — the phrase used elsewhere to denote the time for the *trumas hadeshen* — as *kra gavra*, "the man called out," meaning the announcer's proclamation. This connects *krias hagever* to the *kruz*, the announcer, rather than to the crowing of a rooster. When challenged — why not translate it as *kra tarnagola*, "the rooster crowed," which is how *gever* is usually understood to function in that phrase? — the reply is: but our *mishnah* speaks of a *Ben Gever*, a man named Ben Gever. Would you then call him *bar tarnagola*, the son of a rooster? The joke lands, and the point is made: the translator preferred to render *gever* as a human being, in keeping with the *mishnah*'s use of the name, rather than as a rooster.

---

## Ben Babi charity

### Wick twisting

*Ben Babi al hapaki'a* — Ben Babi oversaw the *pakiya*, which was the twisting of the wicks, the *ptilos* used in the *menorah*.

### Parnasin refused

The *gemara* then relates that Rabbi Yosi came to the town of *kuphra* and sought to appoint *parnasin* — administrators for *tzedaka* distribution, people who would oversee how charity funds were managed and dispersed to the poor. They refused to accept the appointment.

### Parnasin honor

Rabbi Yosi addressed them: *zachah limanos im gedolei hador* — Ben Babi merited to be counted among the great ones of his generation in the *mishnah*, and he oversaw the twisting of wicks — not a task of monumental significance compared to the others listed. *Atem she-atem nimnaim al chayei nefashos* — you, by contrast, would be appointed to matters of life and death. The poor depend on those who administer charity. *Vechol sheken* — how much more, then, should you merit to be counted among the great. The argument is that the responsibility of *parnasin* is not a burden to be avoided but an honor that dwarfs many of the celebrated Temple roles; those who administer the welfare of the destitute are engaged in something of ultimate human importance.

---

## Ben Arza chimes

### Signal chimes

*Ben Arza al hatziltzal* — Ben Arza oversaw the chimes, or the like of a triangle or gong, that served as the signal for the *levi'im* to begin their music. The *gemara* cites the relevant procedure: when the *tamid* offering was being brought, the *sagan* — the deputy High Priest — would wave with cloths at a distance to signal readiness. *V'heikish ben Arza al hatziltzal* — Ben Arza would then strike the chimes. And with that signal, the *levi'im* would commence their singing and instrumental music at the precise moment the offering was brought.

---

## Hugras song

### Choir overseer

*Hugras ben Levi al hashir* — Hugras ben Levi, who was himself of Levitical lineage, oversaw the *shir*, the actual choral singing of the *levi'im*.

### Beautiful melody

*Amar ava neima yeseira haya yodeia* — it was said that he possessed an exceptionally beautiful melody. *V'amru alav al Hugras ben Levi she-haya mane'ima es kolo bezemer* — he was able to make his voice extraordinarily melodious in song, and to accompany himself with music.

### Kohanim amazed

*U-khshehaya no'es gudalo besoch piv, haya motzi kama minei zemer* — when he would place his thumb inside his mouth, he could produce many different types of remarkable sounds — something akin to a complex form of whistling or vocalization that allowed him to generate multiple voices or tones simultaneously. *V'hayu kol ha-kohanim nizrakim lo bevat rosh* — and all the *kohanim* would be startled, taken aback, by the sheer power and beauty of his music. The word *nizrakim* conveys something close to being physically moved or jolted by the experience. It is a fitting note on which to pause, capturing as it does the living reality of what the *Beis HaMikdash* was at its best: a place where the most gifted people dedicated their most extraordinary talents to the service of God.

---

---

# Shekalim 16

## Shofars & Aron

### Intro & Mishna

Today's *daf* is 96b. We pick up in the *Gemara* right after the *Mishna* on 96b. The *Mishna* mentions two sets of things that numbered thirteen: thirteen *shofrot*, which will be discussed in later *Mishnayot*, and a fascinating story connected to the thirteen bowings performed in the *Beit HaMikdash*. The house of Rabban Gamliel and the house of Rabbi Chananya Sgan HaKohanim had a tradition to add a fourteenth bowing opposite *Deir HaEtzim*, the room where the wood was stored, based on their tradition that the *Aron* was hidden beneath that very room.

### Shofar Design

The *Gemara* opens with a *tani*: *hashofrot ha'elu akumot hayu, tzarot milmala v'rechavot milmata, mipnei haramaim* — these *shofrot* were bent, narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, as a safeguard against cheats. The pyramidal shape with its narrow slot at the top made it impossible to insert one's hand and remove the money, and the curved interior made it equally impossible to fish anything out with an implement.

### Fourteen Bowings

The *Mishna*'s reference to the fourteenth bowing opposite *Deir HaEtzim* opens the gateway to the *Gemara*'s extended discussion of the *Aron*. The *Aron* was not present in the *Bayit Sheni* — and the question now to be addressed is: what became of it?

---

## Aron Location

### Eliezer: Exile

The *Gemara* presents a *tani beshem Rabbi Eliezer*: *ha'aron gala imahem l'Bavel* — the *Aron* was not hidden beneath the *Beit HaMikdash* at all; it was taken into exile in Bavel along with all the other vessels of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *Gemara* asks *mai taama* — what is the basis for this view? The proof-text is the verse *lo yivater davar amar Hashem* — nothing shall be left behind, said the Lord. The word *davar* is interpreted as *dibrot*, the *Aseret HaDibrot*, meaning that even the vessel containing the Ten Commandments would not be spared from exile. A supporting verse is then adduced: *bitshuvat hashana shelach hamelech Nevuchadnetzar v'yevi'ehu Bavel im klei chemdat Beit Hashem* — at the turn of the year, Nevuchadnetzar sent and brought the king of Israel to Bavel along with the most precious vessels of the House of God. The *Gemara* asks *eizu klei chemdat Beit Hashem* — which vessel is the most precious? *Zeh ha'aron* — it is the *Aron*. According to this view, then, the *Aron* was carried off to Bavel together with the rest of the Temple's treasures. This of course creates a *tiyuvta* against the *Mishna* — but it should be noted that the source for Rabbi Eliezer's position is a *Baraita*, not the *Mishna* itself.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish takes a different position: *bimkomo haya ha'aron nignaz* — the *Aron* was hidden in its own place, namely beneath the *Kodesh HaKodashim*. His proof-text is the verse *vayarichu habadim vayira'u rashei habadim min hakodesh al pnei hadevir v'lo yira'u hachutza* — the poles of the *Aron* extended so that their tips could be seen from the *Kodesh HaKodashim* toward the *devir*, yet they could not be seen outside. The *Korban HaEdah* notes that the end of this verse reads *vayiheyu sham ad hayom hazeh* — and they remained there until this very day. While the plain sense is that this phrase refers to the time of composition in *Melachim*, during the period of the *Bayit Rishon*, Reish Lakish reads *ad hayom hazeh* expansively: wherever you are reading this verse, that is where the *Aron* remains — hidden beneath the *Kodesh HaKodashim*.

Having cited this verse, the *Gemara* notes an internal tension: the verse begins *vayira'u* — they were seen — yet concludes *v'lo yira'u hachutza* — they were not seen outside. The resolution offered is *nirim v'lo nirim* — they were seen and yet not seen. The poles protruded into the *parochet*, the curtain, so that *boltim v'yotzim kishnei dadei ha'isha* — they pressed outward like a woman's breasts. One could perceive their form through the curtain, but the poles themselves remained invisible. This imagery belongs to a broader set of erotic or nurturing motifs associated with the *Aron* and the *keruvim*, which elsewhere are described as intertwined like lovers. The operative point, however, is the end of the verse — *ad hayom hazeh* — which establishes that the *Aron* remains in that place to this day.

### Rabbanan

The *Mishna*'s own position is that of *Rabbanan*: *belishkat ha'etzim haya ha'Aron ganuz* — the *Aron* was hidden beneath the wood-storage room. No verse is adduced in support; it is presented simply as a received tradition.

### Kohen's Discovery

The *Gemara* then relates the *ma'aseh*: a *kohen* who had a physical *mum* and was therefore barred from performing the *avodah* was assigned to peel wood in *lishkat ha'etzim*. As he worked, *vera'ah et haritzpah shehi meshunah machavroteiha* — he noticed that one section of the floor looked different from the rest. He went to tell a colleague — *bo re'eh et haritzpah hazot shehi meshunah machavroteiha* — but *velo hispik ligmor et hadavar ad sheyatzata nishmato* — before he could finish speaking or show his colleague precisely where the unusual section lay, he died. From this they knew with certainty — *veyadu beyichud shesham Aron ganuz* — that he had discovered the hiding place of the *Aron*, and this is the very tradition referred to in the *Mishna*. The incident raises an obvious question: why could others not simply inspect the floor of *lishkat ha'etzim* themselves? Presumably the anomaly required extremely close attention to detect, and the knowledge died with the *kohen*.

### Digging & Fire

A *Baraita* of Rabbi Oshaya then describes what happened when someone tried to act on this knowledge: *hikishu aleiha bekurnas* — they struck the floor with a heavy sledgehammer-like implement, *veyatza esh vesarfato* — and fire emerged and burned him. It is possible, as one reading of the *Baraita* suggests, that this refers to the same *kohen* — that this is a parallel account of how he died. But the more natural reading is that others, having learned the approximate location, attempted to dig and were struck down by the fire. The episode is, as the lecturer notes, evocative of the deadly booby-traps of ancient lore: the hidden *Aron* is guarded by divine fire, and any attempt to unearth it is met with destruction.

---

## One or Two Arons

### Two Arons Theory

A *Baraita* in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish asserts: *shnei aronot hayu mehalchin im Yisrael bamidbar* — two *aronot* traveled with Israel through the wilderness. One contained the *Torah* — meaning the *luchot* — and one contained the *shivrei luchot*, the broken tablets. The proposal is motivated by tensions in the biblical text: if one follows the *pesukim* carefully, there is apparent confusion about whether the *Aron* traveled with the camp, whether it preceded them, and when exactly various events occurred. Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish resolves this by positing two distinct arks.

### Pessukim Evidence

The first *Aron*, the one containing the *luchot*, *haya munach be'ohel mo'ed* — remained within the *Ohel Mo'ed*. This is derived from the verse *va'aron berit Hashem uMoshe lo mashu mi-kerev ha-machaneh* — the *Aron* of the covenant of God and Moshe did not move from the camp. The significance of this formulation becomes clear by contrast with the second *Aron*, the one containing the *shivrei luchot*: *haya nichnas v'yotzei imahem* — that one would go out with them when they traveled and when they went to war. The verse *va'aron berit Hashem nose'a lifneihem latur lahem menucha* — the *Aron* of the covenant of God traveled before them to seek out a resting place — refers to this second *Aron*. Similarly, the verse *kuma Hashem v'yafutzu* belongs to this second *Aron* that went out with them to battle. What initially appeared to be a contradiction — sometimes the *Aron* stays in the camp, sometimes it goes before them — is resolved by the existence of two separate arks.

### One Aron Only

*Rabbanan*, however, maintain that there was only ever one *Aron*: *aron echad haya*. The single occasion on which it went out to war was at the time of Eli, when it was captured by the *Plishtim* — and that was an exceptional and unauthorized act, not standard practice. In support of the rabbinic view, the *Gemara* cites the verse *oy lanu mi yatzilenu miyad ha-elohim ha-adirim ha-eleh* — woe to us, who will save us from the hands of this great God? — which was the *Plishtim*'s cry upon seeing the *Aron* being brought out. The *Gemara* reads this as indicating that the *Plishtim* had never before witnessed such a thing in all their days — *mila d'lo chamun mi-yomeihon* — which implies that taking the *Aron* to battle was a genuine novelty, not a regular practice. This supports the rabbinic position that it went out only that once.

### More Evidence

Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish, however, adduces counter-evidence from *Nach*. The first is the episode of Sha'ul and Achiya: *vayomer Sha'ul le-Achiya hagisha aron ha-elohim* — Sha'ul said to Achiya, bring forth the *Aron* of God. Yet, the *Gemara* notes, *v'halo aron beKiryat Ye'arim haya* — the *Aron* was in Kiryat Ye'arim at the time! If Sha'ul was calling for the *Aron*, there must have been a separate *Aron* that could be brought to the battlefield. The *Rabbanan* respond that what Sha'ul was calling for was not the *Aron* at all but rather the *tzitz*, which is referred to here as *aron ha-elohim* perhaps because it too carried divine communication in some sense. The *Gemara* acknowledges that this is a difficult reading.

The second proof-text adduced by Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish is from the story of Uriya and David: *ha'aron v'Yisrael v'Yehuda yoshvim basukkot* — the *Aron* and Israel and Judah are dwelling in booths, out on the battlefield. Yet *v'halo aron beTzion haya* — the *Aron* was in Tzion at the time. Must there not be a second *Aron* that had gone out with the troops? The *Rabbanan* explain that *sukkot* here does not mean literal field-tents; it refers to an impermanent dwelling, *she-adayin lo nivna beit ha-bechira* — because the permanent Temple had not yet been built. Uriya's point was that the *Aron* in Yerushalayim was still housed only in a temporary structure, not in a fully established home — which was reason enough not to enjoy his own home. The plain sense of the verse does support Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish's reading, but the *Rabbanan* find a way to read *basukkot* as a reference to impermanence rather than to a battlefield location.

---

## Hidden Items

### Manna & Oil

From the time the *Aron* was hidden — *mishenignaz ha'aron* — various other sacred objects were hidden alongside it. The first is the *tzintzenet ha-man*, the container of *manna*, about which the verse says *kach tzintzenet achat v'hanach otah lifnei ha-edut lemishmeret* — take a container and place it before the testimony as a safekeeping. Since it was placed *lifnei ha-edut*, alongside the *Aron*, the assumption is that whatever befell the *Aron* also befell the *manna*. The second is the *tzlochit shemen ha-mishchah*, the flask of *shemen hamishcha*, about which the verse says *shemen mishchat kodesh yihyeh zeh li ledoroteichem* — this shall be sacred anointing oil for Me throughout your generations. A *hekesh* is drawn between the two: just as the *tzintzenet ha-man* was *lemishmeret ledoroteichem*, so too the *shemen hamishcha* was preserved for all generations, and both were therefore hidden with the *Aron*.

### Aaron's Staff

Also hidden alongside the *Aron* was *maklo shel Aharon u-frachav u-shkedav* — Aaron's staff together with its blossoms and its almonds. Here too the verse instructs that the staff be placed *lifnei ha-edut lemishmeret le'ot livnei meri* — before the testimony as a safekeeping for a sign for the rebellious. The repeated formula of *lemishmeret* — preserved for all generations — establishes that the staff, like the other items, was to endure forever, and was accordingly hidden when the *Aron* was hidden.

### Philistine Gift

Finally, *v'argaz she-shigru Plishtim asham l'Elohei Yisrael* — the box of gifts that the *Plishtim* sent as a guilt-offering to the God of Israel when they returned the *Aron* — was also hidden with it. When the *Plishtim* returned the *Aron*, they sent a golden box alongside it, and the verse instructs *tasimu ba-argaz mitzido* — place it in the box next to the *Aron*. Since the verse places this gift-box *next to* the *Aron*, the tradition understands that it permanently remained beside it. As the *Gemara*'s *Kodesh HaKodashim* grew crowded with all these objects, whatever ultimately happened to the *Aron* happened to all of them together.

---

## Yoshiyahu Hides

### Yoshiyahu

*Mi genazo* — who actually hid the *Aron*? *Yoshiyahu genazo* — it was Yoshiyahu. Not the last of the kings of Judah, but one who was already perceptive enough to see what was coming. *Keivan sher'ah shekatuv* — when he saw what was written in the verse *yolech Hashem otcha v'et malkecha asher takim alecha el goy asher lo yadata atah va'avotecha* — God will take you and the king you set over yourself to a nation that neither you nor your ancestors have known — he understood the exile was coming, and acted accordingly: *amad u-genazo* — he arose and hid it.

### Pessukim Proof

The proof-text for Yoshiyahu's action is the verse *vayomer laleviyim hamevinim lechol Yisrael hakedoshim l'Hashem tnu et aron hakodesh babayit asher banah Shlomo ben David melech Yisrael ein lachem masa bakatef* — he said to the Levites, place the sacred *Aron* in the house that Solomon son of David built; you shall no longer carry it on your shoulders. The straightforward reading of this verse is that it refers to the biblical era when the *Aron* was carried on the shoulders. But the *Gemara* reads it as Yoshiyahu's instructions to hide the *Aron* beneath the *Beit HaMikdash*. His reasoning: *im goleh hu imachem l'Vavel, ein atem machzirim oto od limkomo* — if it goes into exile with you to Bavel, you will never have the opportunity to bring it back. Therefore *ein lachem masa bakatef* — this object will no longer be transported at all; it must be secured before the exile comes. The verse concludes: *ela atah ivdu et Hashem Eloheichem ve'et amo Yisrael* — now serve God your God and His people Israel. This is read as a *midrashic* interpretation embedded in the *pesukim*, one that assumes the *Aron* was indeed hidden rather than exiled.

---

## Shemen HaMishcha

### Oil Recipe

Since the *shemen hamishcha* was mentioned among the items hidden with the *Aron*, the *Gemara* takes the opportunity for an extended digression on this remarkable substance. The *Torah* specifies its recipe: *v'atah kach lecha besamim rosh — mor dror chamesh me'ot, u-kinman besem machtzito chamishim u-matayim, u-kneh bosem chamishim u-matayim, u-kidah chamesh me'ot beshekel hakodesh, v'shemen zayit hin*. Adding up the aromatic components — *she-hen elef u-chamesh me'ot manin* — yields 1,500 *maneh* of fragrances to be combined with a single *hin*, twelve *log*, of olive oil. The question immediately arises: how does such a small quantity of oil absorb such a vast quantity of fragrance?

The answer is as follows. The oil served as the medium into which the fragrances were steeped. *She-hayu sholkim bo et ha-ikarim* — one would use the oil to boil the roots and herbs of the spices — according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda offers a different procedure: first *sholkan haya bemayim* — one would boil the fragrant materials in water, fully saturating them, so that they could absorb no more liquid. Then *venosein shemen al gabeihen* — one would place the oil on top of them. Since the materials were already fully saturated with water and could absorb no more, *mishaa shekalat et hare'ach, haya maaviro* — once the oil drew out the fragrance from the saturated herbs, it was removed, now bearing the full aromatic quality. This is the technique *kederech shehapitamim osim* — the way professional perfumers work.

### Meir vs Yehuda

The practical difference between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda lies in the sequence and medium. For Rabbi Meir, the oil itself is the cooking medium from the outset — the spices are boiled directly in the oil. For Rabbi Yehuda, the spices are first saturated with water so that the oil, when added, cannot be absorbed into the spices but instead draws only the fragrance out. Rabbi Yehuda's method, drawn from the practice of professional perfumers, ensures maximal transfer of fragrance into the oil with minimal absorption of the oil itself into the spice material.

### Oil Miracle

A *Baraita* in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Ilai states: *shemen hamishcha she-asa Moshe bamidbar, ma'aseh nissim na'asu vo mitchila v'ad sof* — the *shemen hamishcha* that Moshe prepared in the wilderness was miraculous from beginning to end. It began as only twelve *log* — *shene'emar shemen zayit hin*, a *hin* being twelve *log*. Yet even the simple act of smearing the oil onto the fragrant materials to absorb their scent would, by ordinary reckoning, have used up all twelve *log* before any oil remained — *al achas kama v'chama* when one considers that fire evaporates oil, the wooden structure of the *mishkan* absorbs it, and the cooking vessel absorbs more. And yet from these twelve *log*, the following was accomplished: *umimenu nimshachu hamishkan v'chol kelav, hashulchan v'chol kelav, hamenorah v'chol keleiha* — the entire *Mishkan* and all its vessels were anointed; *umimenu nimshachu Aharon Kohen Gadol u-vanav kol shivat yemei hamilu'im* — Aaron and his sons were anointed every day for all seven days of the inauguration; and *umimenu nimshachu kohanim gedolim u-melachim* — from it, every subsequent *Kohen Gadol* and king was anointed.

The miracle is further illuminated by a *derasha* on the verse *shemen mishchat kodesh yihyeh zeh li ledoroteichem*. The word *zeh* in *gematria* equals twelve, and the *midrash* reads: the twelve *log* with which it began — *ledoroteichem* — that same amount was always there, generation after generation. Like the *nes Chanukah*, the oil was never diminished. One began with twelve *log*, performed all of this with it, and twelve *log* always remained.

---

## Uses of Oil

### King Anointing

The *Gemara* now turns to the uses of the *shemen hamishcha* in the investiture of kings and *kohanim gedolim*. The principle is: *melech betchila ta'un meshicha* — when someone becomes king for the first time, establishing a new royal line, anointing is required. This applies to the founding kings, such as Shaul and David. *Melech ben melech ein ta'un meshicha* — but a king who is the son of a king does not require anointing, since kingship is fundamentally hereditary. The *pasuk* cited is *kum mishcha'ehu ki zeh hu* — arise and anoint him, for this is the one. The word *zeh* implies that *this one* requires anointing, but not his son.

### Kohen Gadol

The rule is precisely the opposite for the *Kohen Gadol*: *aval Kohen Gadol ben Kohen Gadol, afilu ad asara doros, ta'un meshicha* — a *Kohen Gadol* who is the son of a *Kohen Gadol*, even if the position has passed through ten generations, still requires fresh anointing. The underlying logic is structural: kingship is intrinsically hereditary, so no new act of investiture is necessary — to perform one would actually undermine the sense of natural succession. The office of *Kohen Gadol*, by contrast, is not intrinsically hereditary. The *Gemara* in *Horayot* acknowledges that a son has some priority, all else being equal, but priority is not the same as automatic inheritance. Since the *Kohen Gadol*'s status is not self-transmitting, each holder of the office — including the son of a previous *Kohen Gadol* — requires a fresh act of anointing to be invested in that status.

The same principle governs the miraculous preservation of the oil: *v'chulo kayam la'atid lavo* — all of it will be intact into the future as well, as the verse *shemen mishchat kodesh yihyeh zeh li ledoroteichem* promises. The *derasha* on *zeh* — numerically twelve — reinforces that the original twelve *log* will always remain whole.

### Which Kings

The *Gemara* now specifies when, exceptionally, a king who is the son of a king does require anointing: *ein moshchin melech ben melech ela mipnei hamachlokes* — only when there is a dispute over succession. Several historical examples are enumerated. Shlomo was anointed because of the competing claim of Adoniyahu. Yoash was anointed because of Atalyahu's usurpation. Yehoachaz was anointed because his brother Yehoyakim, who was two years older, had a competing claim. Yehu was anointed because of Yoram. The *Gemara* then raises a question against the inclusion of Yehu: a broader principle is now asserted that anointing with *shemen hamishcha* applies only to *malchei Beit David*, the kings of the Davidic dynasty, not to *Malchei Yisrael*, the kings of the Northern Kingdom. If so, the inclusion of Yehu and Yoram — kings of the North — in this list is problematic. The *Gemara* answers: trim those words from the *Baraita*. The list should end with Yehoachaz, and the mention of Yehu was not a reference to *shemen hamishcha* at all.

---

## Historical Kings

### Aromatic Oil

The *Gemara* then raises a further question: *v'halo Yoshiyahu genazo* — did Yoshiyahu not hide the *shemen hamishcha* together with the *Aron*? If so, how could Yehoyakim and Yehoachaz have been anointed with it? The answer is attributed to Ada: *bafarsimon nimshach* — they were anointed with plain aromatic oil, not with the true *shemen hamishcha*. The *shemen hamishcha* had been hidden by Yoshiyahu, and so the anointings of Yoshiyahu's sons were performed with an aromatic substitute.

Some of the *meforshim* draw from this an additional insight: since the anointing of Yehu too was presumably done without *shemen hamishcha* — as it occurred before Yoshiyahu but among *Malchei Yisrael* in any case — the reference to anointing with a substitute oil could extend to *Malchei Yisrael* as well under certain conditions. This would mean one need not strike the words about Yehu from the *Baraita* at all, since those anointings used only aromatic oil. And even with aromatic oil, the practice was reserved for situations of genuine uncertainty about succession — to perform it unnecessarily would subtly undermine the sense of hereditary legitimacy.

---

## Uses of Oil (II)

### Horn vs Pitcher

The *Gemara* adds a further distinction regarding the vessel from which kings are anointed: *ein moshchin hamelachim ela min hakeren* — kings are anointed from a horn, not from a simple container. The horn, like a cornucopia, evokes abundance, permanence, and the proclamation of a new reign. The proof comes from the contrast between Shaul and Yehu on one hand, and David and Shlomo on the other. *Shaul v'Yehu nimshakhu min hapakh* — Shaul and Yehu were anointed from a simple pitcher — *hayta malkhutam malkhut overet* — and their dynasties were temporary and did not endure. *David u-Shlomo nimshakhu min ha-keren* — David and Shlomo were anointed from a horn — *hayta malkhutam malkhut kayyemet* — and their dynasty was permanent. The verse *matzmiach keren yeshua* — the One who causes the horn of salvation to flourish — carries precisely this symbolism of royal permanence and saving power associated with the *keren*.

### No Kohen Kings

*Ein moshchin kohanim melachim* — one does not anoint *kohanim* as kings. The *Gemara* here touches on the danger of combining religious and political authority in a single figure, a concern that resonates especially in light of the *Chashmonaim*. At one level the prohibition is about *meshicha* specifically — anointing for kingship is restricted to *malchut Beit David* — so the problem with anointing a *kohen* as king subsumes the general problem of anointing anyone outside the Davidic line. But there is also a distinct and pointed objection to *kohanim* taking kingship, rooted in the principle *lo yasur shevet miYehuda* — the scepter shall not depart from Judah. Rabbi Yehuda Antundaraya derives from this verse that kingship cannot belong to any other tribe.

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba adds a second verse: the Torah describes the king's obligation to write a *Sefer Torah* so that *lema'an ya'arich yamim al mamlachto hu u-vanav bekerev Yisrael* — his kingship should extend, he and his children. *Mah ketiv batreih* — what does the very next verse say? *Lo yihyeh lakohanim haleviyim* — juxtaposed immediately to the king and his children is the statement that this role does not belong to the *kohanim*. Reading the two verses as a single thought, kingship shall extend to his children — and this is not for the *kohanim*.

The *Ramban*, as is well known, comments in his *perush* on the verse *lo yasur shevet miYehuda* in connection with the *Chashmonaim*, noting that they transgressed by taking upon themselves the kingship. He also observes that *Chanukah* receives virtually no treatment in the *Mishna* — mentioned only once incidentally in *Bava Kamma* — and suggests that this reflects the *Tanna'im*'s disapproval of how the *Chashmonaim* claimed royal authority, a silence that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who understood himself as a descendant of David HaMelech, may have deliberately maintained.

---

## Historical Kings (II)

### Sons ID

The *Gemara* now works to identify the sons of Yoshiyahu mentioned across different biblical texts. Rabbi Yochanan says: *hu Yochanan hu Yehoachaz* — the same person is referred to in one text as Yochanan and in another as Yehoachaz. An apparent difficulty is raised: *v'ha ketiv habechor Yochanan* — in *Divrei Hayamim* the firstborn is listed as Yochanan — yet Yehoachaz was not the *bechor*. The resolution is *bechor lemalchuto* — he was first in *malchus*, meaning the first of Yoshiyahu's sons to reign. This is precisely the context we discussed earlier: Yehoachaz was anointed because Yehoyakim, who was two years older, had a competing claim. Yehoachaz/Yochanan received the kingship first despite not being the oldest.

Rabbi Yochanan further states: *hu Shalom hu Tzidkiyahu* — similarly, the same person appears in one text as Shalom and in another as Tzidkiyahu. But a textual problem immediately arises: *veha ketiv hashlishi Tzidkiyahu vehareviei Shalom* — one *pasuk* lists the third son as Tzidkiyahu and the fourth son as Shalom, making them appear to be two distinct individuals. The resolution: *gimel letoldot* — he was the third in birth order — *dalet lemalchus* — but the fourth of Yoshiyahu's sons to reign. Tzidkiyahu and Shalom were the same person, but two different aspects of his identity are being enumerated in different places.

The *Gemara* then addresses the significance of each name. The name *Tzidkiyahu* — *shetzidak alav midat hadin* — reflects the fact that he justified upon himself the divine judgment. The straightforward reading is that Tzidkiyahu accepted the justice of God's verdict when he was taken into exile by Nevuchadnetzar, acknowledging that divine justice had been done — a poignant acceptance given that this was the king whose eyes were put out. Some *meforshim* read the phrase differently, citing a passage in the *Bavli* suggesting that Nevuchadnetzar himself gave Tzidkiyahu this name as a kind of oath — *ka-yifra'acha* — that God would exact punishment from him if he rebelled, and of course he did rebel. This reading is forced, and the plain sense of the *Gemara* here is that Tzidkiyahu himself justified and accepted God's judgment.

As for the name *Shalom*, the *Gemara* reads it with dark irony: *shebeyamav shalma malchut beit David* — in his days the kingship of the house of David came to completion, to its end. *Shalom* as *shlemut* — finality, completion. Reish Lakish then adds a tradition on a different level: *lo Shalom hava shemo v'lo Tzidkiyahu hava shemo — ela Mattanya* — neither Shalom nor Tzidkiyahu was his original name. He was born Mattanya. This is not *midrash* but *peshat*, since the verse states explicitly: *vayimloch melech Bavel et Mattanya dodo tachtav vayasev et shemo Tzidkiyahu* — the king of Bavel placed Mattanya, his uncle, on the throne and changed his name to Tzidkiyahu. The text is clear: Nevuchadnetzar renamed him.

---

## Aron Contents

### Six-Tefach Amah

Rabbi Yochanan states: *be'ama shel shisha tefachim haya ha'aron asui* — the *Aron* was constructed using an *amah* of six *tefachim*. This is consistent with Rabbi Meir's position, recorded elsewhere in a *Mishna*: *Rabbi Meir omer kol ha'amot hayu beinoniyot* — Rabbi Meir holds that all the *amot* used in the *Beit HaMikdash* were standard six-*tefach* ones. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, distinguishes: *amot habinyan shisha* — structural *amot* were six *tefachim* — *v'shel kelim chamisha* — but the *amot* used for vessels were five *tefachim*. The *Aron*, being a *keli*, would according to Rabbi Yehuda have been built with a five-*tefach amah*.

Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the *Aron* used a six-*tefach amah* thus reflects Rabbi Meir's position.

### Length Calc

According to Rabbi Meir's view — *al daiteh d'Rabbi Meir*, the six-*tefach amah* — the *Gemara* works out the dimensions in detail. The *Torah* specifies the *Aron*'s length as *amatayim vachetzi* — two and a half *amot*. At six *tefachim* per *amah*, this yields: one *amah* equals six, a second *amah* equals six, a half-*amah* equals three — a total of fifteen *tefachim* in length.

Within the *Aron* were four *luchot*: two whole and two broken. The verse *asher shibarta v'samtam ba'aron* — that which you broke, place them in the *Aron* — is read to indicate that both the intact *luchot* and the *shivrei luchot* were stored in the same *Aron*. This is consistent with the *Gemara*'s ruling elsewhere: *luchot v'shivrei luchot munachin ba'aron*. The *luchot* were square — six *tefachim* by six *tefachim* — as the *midrashic* tradition understands them, contrary to the familiar rectangular or arched popular image.

Placing the *luchot* in the length of the *Aron*: if the two intact *luchot* account for six *tefachim* each (twelve total), and the two broken ones are assumed to occupy the same space (stacked), then twelve *tefachim* of the fifteen-*tefach* length are accounted for. Three *tefachim* remain. Subtract half a *tefach* for each of the two walls — leaving two *tefachim* — and these two *tefachim* accommodate the *Sefer Torah*, which was six *tefachim* long but only two *tefachim* wide.

### Width Calc

The *Aron*'s width was *ama vachetzi rochbo* — one and a half *amot*. At six *tefachim* per *amah*, this yields: one *amah* equals six, half an *amah* equals three — nine *tefachim* total. The *luchot* being six *tefachim* wide, six *tefachim* of the nine are occupied. Three *tefachim* remain. Half a *tefach* for each wall accounts for one *tefach*, leaving two *tefachim*. These two *tefachim* provide *shirush makom* — breathing room, access space — alongside the *Sefer Torah*, allowing it to be removed when needed. Practically, this could mean one *tefach* of clearance on each side, providing access on both sides of the *Sefer Torah*.

Whether the four *luchot* were stacked two and two, or arranged side by side in a more rectangular configuration, depends on textual variants: one *girsa* reads that each *luach* was six *tefachim* by six *tefachim* (square), the other *girsa* reads three by six (rectangular). With the reading of three, the *luchot* would be arranged side by side in the width rather than stacked, which would yield a more intuitively familiar shape — though the *midrashic* tradition favors the square.

### Five-Tefach

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish holds that the *Aron* was constructed using a five-*tefach amah* — *be'ama bat chamisha tefachim haya ha'aron* — which corresponds to Rabbi Yehuda's view that vessels were measured by a five-*tefach amah*. *V'ha'aron keli hu* — the *Aron* is a vessel — and therefore falls under Rabbi Yehuda's rule.

At five *tefachim* per *amah*, two and a half *amot* yields: five plus five plus two and a half — twelve and a half *tefachim* in length. Six and six for the four *luchot* (twelve *tefachim*) leaves only half a *tefach*. With walls of one *etzba* (a quarter-*tefach*) on each side — accounting for the half *tefach* — there is no room whatsoever for the *Sefer Torah* inside the *Aron*. This is not an oversight; it is the basis for Rabbi Yehuda's position, derived from the verse *v'samtem oto mitzad aron berit Hashem* — place it beside the *Aron* — which he reads as *outside* the *Aron*.

In the width dimension — one and a half *amot* at five *tefachim* per *amah* — five plus two and a half yields seven and a half *tefachim*. Six *tefachim* for the *luchot*, leaving one and a half *tefachim*. After walls of one *etzba* each (a half-*tefach* total), one *tefach* remains. This is divided into half a *tefach* on each side — *chatzi tefach mikan v'chatzi tefach mikan lishilut* — a minimal clearance. Here there is no room for the *Sefer Torah* in the width either. According to this view, the *Sefer Torah* was stored externally in a special box attached to the side of the *Aron*.

---

## Aron Construction

### Three Boxes

The *Gemara* now addresses how Betzalel actually constructed the *Aron*. Rabbi Chananya holds: *shalosh teivot asao* — he made three separate boxes, *shtayim shel zahav v'achat shel etz* — two of gold and one of wood. These were made independently and then assembled: the wooden box was inserted into one golden box, and then the second golden box was placed inside the wooden one, so that the *Aron* had gold on the inside, wood in the middle, and gold on the outside. The verse *v'tzapita oto zahav tahor mi-bayit u-mi-chutz* — plate it with pure gold inside and outside — is fulfilled by the two golden boxes. The additional verbal form *v'tzipanu* — and he plated it — indicates the covering of the top edge where the boxes meet, so that the separate rims were joined and covered with gold plating.

### One Box

Reish Lakish disagrees: *teivah achat asah* — he made one box. The procedure was simple: start with the wooden box, then plate it with gold. The verse *v'tzapita oto zahav tahor mi-bayit u-mi-chutz* describes this standard plating. The additional *v'tzipanu*, according to Rav Pinchas, indicates *le-havi bein neser le-neser* — that the gold plating was applied even between the individual planks of the wooden construction, covering every crevice so that no wood was left exposed anywhere. The *Aron* was thus entirely encased in gold, including the joints between its constituent wooden elements.

---

## Luchot Writing

### Five Each

The *Gemara* now turns to how the *luchot* were written. Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel holds: *chamishah al luach zeh v'chamishah al luach zeh* — five *dibrot* on one *luach* and five on the other. This is the familiar division, implying the first five — broadly characterized as *bein adam la-Makom* — on one tablet, and the second five — *bein adam la-chavero* — on the other. The *Torah* itself never specifies this arrangement explicitly, but it is the natural assumption given that there are ten and two tablets.

### Ten Each

The *Rabbanan* hold: *asarah al luach zeh v'asarah al luach zeh* — all ten on each tablet, so that each *luach* contained the full *Aseret HaDibrot*. The proof-text is *va-yaged lachem et brito asher tzivah etchem la-asot aseret ha-devarim va-yichtivem al shenei luchot avanim* — He told you His covenant, commanding you to observe the ten words, and He wrote them on two tablets of stone. The *Rabbanan* read *aseret ha-devarim va-yichtivem al shenei luchot* to mean that all ten were written on each of the two tablets.

### Front & Back

Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai goes further: *esrim al luach zeh v'esrim al luach zeh* — twenty on each tablet. His reasoning is that the same ten were written on each tablet both front and back, so that each tablet bore twenty inscriptions — ten on each face.

### All Sides

Rabbi Simai extends the count further: *arbaim al luach zeh v'arbaim al luach zeh* — forty on each tablet, meaning all four sides of each *luach* were inscribed. The proof-text is *mi-zeh u-mi-zeh hem ketuvim* — from this side and from that side they are written — which Rabbi Simai understands as referring to all four faces of the tablet, like a *tetroga*, the Greek word for a four-sided figure — a cube or rectangular solid. One might expect the count to continue to eighty or more, but the *Gemara* does not pursue it further.

### Ocean Metaphor

Chananya ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua offers a different conception entirely. He does not count the *dibrot* and multiply them across surfaces. Instead, he says: *bein kol dibur v'dibur, dikdukeiha v'otioteiha shel Torah* — between each *dibur* and the next, all of the minute explications and letters of the *Torah* were written in the white space. The entire *Torah she-be'al peh*, in all its detail, was embedded in the space between the great *dibrot*.

His proof-text is a verse from *Shir HaShirim* describing something *memula'im ba-tarshish* — filled with *Tarshish*, which he understands as the name of the great sea, the ocean. Reish Lakish, whenever he would encounter this *pasuk*, would say: *yafe limadani Chananya ben achi Rabbi Yehoshua* — he taught me well. The metaphor is this: *mah ha-yam hazeh bein gal gadol le-gal gadol galim ktanim* — just as between every great wave in the ocean there are countless small ripples and eddies — *kach bein kol dibur v'dibur, dikdukeiha v'otioteiha shel Torah* — so between every great *dibur* and the next, there were all the fine details and letters of the *Torah*. The great *dibrot* are the towering waves, and between them, implicit and infinite, is the *Torah she-be'al peh* in all its detail. One might observe that this image anticipates the metaphor of the *yam shel Talmud*, though the explicit connection is not drawn.

### Sefer Torah

Finally, the *Gemara* addresses the question of where the *Sefer Torah* was placed: inside the *Aron* or outside it, at its side.

According to Rabbi Yehuda, whose position flows from the five-*tefach amah* calculation that left no interior room, the *Sefer Torah* was placed *mitzad* — on the outside of the *Aron*, in a specially fashioned box, *k'min gluskamya asuyah lo mi-bachutz*, affixed to the exterior. The proof-text is *v'samtem oto mitzad aron berit Hashem* — place it beside the *Aron of the covenant*.

According to Rabbi Meir, whose six-*tefach amah* calculation does leave room inside, the *Sefer Torah* was placed inside. His proof-text is the verse *v'natata et ha-kaporet al ha-aron milma'ala… v'el ha-aron titein et ha-edut asher etein eilecha* — place the *kaporet* on the *Aron* from above, and into the *Aron* place the *edut* which I will give you. The *edut* here is understood to include the *Sefer Torah*, and the verse directs that it be placed inside the *Aron* before the *kaporet* is set in place. The apparent difficulty — that the *kaporet* seems to have already been placed before the instruction to insert the *edut* — is resolved by the principle *ein mukdam u-me'uchar ba-Torah*: the *Torah*'s narrative sequence does not always follow chronological order. The practical sequence was: place the *Sefer Torah* inside first, then cover the *Aron* with the *kaporet*.

---

## Divine Tablets

### Fire Writing

The *Gemara* closes with a statement of Rabbi Pinchas in the name of Reish Lakish: *ha-Torah she-natan lo ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu le-Moshe, netanah lo esh levana charuta be-esh shechora* — the *Torah* that the Holy One gave to Moshe was given to him as white fire engraved upon black fire. Whether the letters were of white fire written on a black background, or black fire inscribed upon a white one — as black ink upon a white surface — the text describes fire interwoven with fire: *hi esh mevulla'a be-esh, esh chatzuvah me-esh, u-netunah me-esh*. Fire intertwined with fire, fire hewn from fire, given out of fire. The proof-text is *mi-ymino esh dat lamo* — from His right hand, a fiery law for them. All of the preceding discussion — the physical dimensions of the *Aron*, the geometry of the *luchot*, the layout of the *dibrot*, the techniques of the perfumers, the weight of the gold and the wood — ultimately gives way to this conclusion: whatever the *luchot* were physically, their essence was divine fire, irreducible to any material container.

# Shekalim 17

## 13 Prostrations & Gates

### Intro: 13 Lists

The *mishna* on which we now focus appears in the context of a broader enumeration: thirteen *shofarot* — the containers used to collect donated funds — thirteen *shulchanot*, and thirteen *hishtachavayot*, prostrations. The *mishna* proceeds in a kind of inverted order, addressing these three topics in reverse sequence. Having just concluded the discussion of a fourteenth *hishtachavaya* and the spot where the *aron* was hidden, the *mishna* now returns to explain the thirteen prostrations, then the tables, and will eventually arrive at the *shofarot*. We thus follow a structure of ABC followed by CBA.

### Prostration Locations

The *mishna* opens: *heichan hayu hishtachavayot ellu?* — where were these prostrations? The answer: four in the north, four in the south, three in the east, and two in the west — all within the *azarah*. The *mishna* adds: *k'negedan shlosh esrei she'arim* — corresponding to the thirteen gates of the *azarah*.

A question arises naturally here: who precisely was performing these prostrations, and where were they standing when they did so? The *mishna* earlier mentions Chananya *segan ha-kohanim* as performing fourteen prostrations, and Rabban Gamliel is mentioned in that context as well. The ordinary *yisrael* would not have free access throughout the *azarah*, and access deeper into the compound was restricted to *kohanim*. The precise choreography of where one stood while performing the *hishtachavaya* remains, on the face of the *mishna*, unclear.

### South Gates

Moving through the gates themselves, the *mishna* lists the southern gates from west to east — that is, beginning at the southwest corner: *Sha'ar ha-elyon*, the upper gate; *Sha'ar hadelek*, the gate of fuel or fire; *Sha'ar habechorot*, the gate of the firstborns; and *Sha'ar hamayim*, the gate of water.

According to the *Korban ha-edah*, *Sha'ar hadelek* was located opposite the *lishkat ha-etzim* — the chamber where the wood for the altar was stored — and the wood would be brought through there. *Sha'ar habechorot* was used because the *bechorot* were slaughtered in the south of the *azarah*. But a genuine difficulty presents itself: we normally understand that a *yisrael* bringing a *korban* would enter through *Sha'ar Nikanor* in the east, wait in the *ezrat Yisrael*, and the *kohen* would receive the animal and bring it slightly north of the *mizbeach* for *kodshei kodashim* or to the south for *bechorot*. The notion that an ordinary Israelite would enter through a side gate and hand off the animal directly to a *kohen* at that location is not the standard picture we carry. Perhaps one could suggest that the *yisrael* never fully entered the *azarah* but stood in the gateway itself; perhaps there was a narrow passage allowing movement around the courtyard's perimeter. The choreography remains genuinely puzzling.

Similarly, the *Sha'ar hadelek* is distinct from the *lishkat hadelek* — the chamber for firewood — which was located in the *ezrat nashim*. Why then a separate gate for firewood on the south wall of the *azarah* itself? These questions do not find easy resolution.

### Sha'ar Hamayim

The *mishna* asks: *velamah nikra shemo Sha'ar hamayim?* — why was it called the gate of water? The answer: *shebo machnisim tzluchit shel mayim be-chag* — it is through this gate that they would bring in the flask of water for *nisuch hamayim* on *Sukkot*. The *mishna* in Tractate *Sukkah* describes the elaborate ceremony of *Simchat Beit ha-Shoevah* involving a procession through the *ezrat nashim*, yet here we have the water entering through a side gate in the south wall of the *azarah*. Once again, the exact topography of the ceremony does not resolve neatly.

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds: *bo ha-mayim mifachim* — from there the waters will pour, like from a *pach*, a jug. *Ve-atidin lihyot yotzin mitachat miftan ha-bayit* — and they are destined to emerge from beneath the threshold of the *bayit*. This is an allusion to a *pasuk* in *Yechezkel* that the *gemara* will spend most of the rest of the *daf* elaborating, concerning a miraculous river that will flow forth from the *Beit Hamikdash le-atid lavo*.

### North Gates

From the south we turn to the northern gates, listed from northwest to southeast: *Sha'ar Yechanyah*, *Sha'ar hakorban*, *Sha'ar hanashim*, and *Sha'ar hashir*.

*Sha'ar Yechanyah* was named for king *Yechanyah*, who exited through it when he was taken into exile. Though the *bayit* was destroyed and rebuilt, the name was preserved — and the *gemara* will offer its own version of the events surrounding his departure.

*Sha'ar hakorban* is explained by the *Korban ha-edah* as the gate through which the *kodshei kodashim* were brought in, those offerings that required *shechitah* in the north. Again, the same topographical puzzle applies: does this mean that the owner of the *korban* would approach this side gate and present the animal there, while we normally assume entry through *Sha'ar Nikanor* and the animal being walked northward past the *mizbeach*? The *mishna* seems to indicate functional use for these lateral gates, but precisely how they were incorporated into the normal flow of *avodah* remains an open question.

*Sha'ar hanashim* is explained in the *Korban ha-edah* as the gate through which women would enter to perform *smicha* on their *korbanot*, or at least to accompany them — there being a well-known dispute about whether women perform *smicha* at all. Yet we generally understand that women entered through *Sha'ar Nikanor*, since the *ezrat nashim* was the outermost roofed courtyard accessible to them. A separate women's gate on the north wall of the *azarah* itself is an unusual datum.

*Sha'ar hashir* was presumably the gate adjacent to the chamber where the Levitical instruments were kept. The *gemara* also associates that area with the *Beit Hamoked*, where the *kohanim* would warm themselves by the fire kept burning there, and where a *lishka* of sorts was maintained.

### East Gates

In the east there was *Sha'ar Nikanor* — the great gate — and two smaller side gates, *pashpashim*, one on each side of it. These three together account for the three prostrations on the eastern side of the *azarah*. Significantly, the *mishna* here refers unmistakably to the main entrance to the *azarah* proper — the *sha'ar* through which *yisrael* would enter the *ezrat Yisrael* — which strongly suggests that the entire enumeration is indeed tracing a circuit of the *azarah* and not some outer precinct.

### West Gates

Finally, behind the *Kodesh Kodashim*, on the western wall, were two gates — *u-shenayim ba-ma'arav lo hayah lahem shem* — and these two had no name at all. In the land of Israel, where virtually every stream and hilltop carries multiple names accumulated through layers of history, it is striking that the two westernmost gates of the holiest courtyard in the world went unnamed.

---

## Gemara: 13 vs 7

### Abba Yose Position

The *gemara* opens by identifying whose view the *mishna* represents: *Abba Yose ben Yochanan hi de-amar k'neged yud-gimmel she'arin* — this is the position of Abba Yose ben Yochanan, who holds that the thirteen prostrations corresponded to thirteen gates. Whether *k'negedan* means literally "directly in front of" those gates or more loosely "corresponding to them in number" remains somewhat ambiguous — though the word *keneged* elsewhere in this very tractate implies physical positioning opposite a specific location.

### Rabbis Disagree

The Rabbis, however, dissent: *shiva she'arim hayu ba-azarah* — there were only seven gates in the *azarah*. The *gemara* specifies *ba-azarah*, which confirms that the entire discussion concerns the *azarah* proper. How one reduces thirteen to seven is not fully worked out, but possibilities include: not counting the two unnamed western gates, not counting the two side gates of *Sha'ar Nikanor*, and disputing the existence of certain others. The Rabbis thereby face the obvious question: if there were only seven gates, what accounts for thirteen prostrations?

### Breaches & Chashmonaim

The answer is historically charged: *yud-gimmel peratzot hayu bah she-peratzum malchei Yavan* — there were thirteen breaches made in the wall of the *azarah* by the Greek kings. *Ve-chazru u-gedarum benei Chashmonai* — the *Chashmonaim* came and repaired them. *U-vegazru k'negdan yud-gimmel hishtachavuyot* — and they established, opposite those thirteen sites, thirteen prostrations.

The word *k'negdan* here may well mean physically in front of those repaired breaches. The symbolism is striking: prostrations specifically at the sites of the violation. Rather than simply forgetting the breaches, the *Chashmonaim* enshrined the memory of persecution and perseverance in the choreography of the *avodah* itself. The places that had been broken became the very spots at which one bowed in gratitude and awe.

---

## Living Waters

### Waters Intro

Because the *mishna* mentioned *Sha'ar hamayim* and introduced the phrase *bo ha-mayim mifachim* — the waters pour forth — the *gemara* now embarks on an extended treatment of the prophecy of water flowing from the *Beit Hamikdash*. The *pasuk* in *Zechariyah* states: *ve-hayah ba-yom ha-hu yetze'u mayim chayim mi-Yerushalayim* — on that day, living waters will flow out from Jerusalem. This sets the stage for the *gemara*'s interpretation of the extended vision in *Yechezkel*, which will occupy most of the remainder of the *daf*.

### Water Growth Pattern

A *baraita* is cited describing the progressive growth of the stream in extraordinary detail. The water originates in the *Kodesh Kodashim* itself and begins in the most minute quantities, growing larger and more powerful as it flows outward through successive zones of the *Beit Hamikdash*.

From the *Kodesh Kodashim* to the *parochet*, the stream is *ke-karnei silei ve-chilei* — like the antennae of small insects, specifically snails, the tiniest possible trickle. From the *parochet* to the golden altar — which stood in the *kodesh*, directly opposite the *menorah* and the *shulchan* — the stream grows to *ke-karnei chagavim*, like the antennae of grasshoppers, somewhat thicker. From the golden altar to the *azarah* (understood here to encompass the *ezrat nashim* as well, as the water is about to exit the structure), the stream is *ke-chut shel sheti*, like a thread of warp — the thinner of the two components of the weave. From the *azarah* to the *miftan ha-bayit*, the threshold, it becomes *ke-chut shel erev*, the woof, slightly thicker still. And from that point outward, *ke-fi ha-pach* — pouring like a jug. This is the very word, *mefachim*, used in the *mishna*.

The symbolism here runs counter to what one might expect. We normally think of *kedushah* as most concentrated at its source — the *Kodesh Kodashim* — and attenuating outward. But the stream of living water begins infinitesimally small at its origin and becomes a roaring river as it moves outward into the world. This is reminiscent of *kol demamah dakkah* — the still small voice — where the most profound divine presence arrives in the quietest form. Rivers in nature follow the same pattern: beginning from a small source and growing mightier as tributaries join.

### Yechezkel Vision

The *gemara* now turns to the text of *Yechezkel*'s vision directly, providing the underlying *pesukim*. *Ve-hinei mayim mifachim min ha-katef ha-yemanis* — behold, water pouring from the right side, that is the south, since one orients oneself facing east, making the right hand the south. *Va-yavod elef ba-ammah* — he measured a thousand *amot* eastward. *Mei afsayim* — *ad karsula*, water up to the ankles.

Another thousand: *mei birkayim* — *ad arkuba*, up to the knees. Another thousand: *mei masnayim* — *ad masnya*, up to the loins. And after yet another thousand *amot*, the stream becomes a *nachal asher lo uchal la-avor* — a river I could not cross. The *gemara* interprets: *afilu le-virani gedolah einah yecholah la-avor bo* — even the largest ship cannot navigate it.

The *gemara* cites a *pasuk* from *Yeshayahu* — *ve-tzi adir lo ya'avrenu* — no great vessel shall cross it — and then asks *mipnei mah*, why? *Ki ga'u ha-mayim mei sachu* — because the waters have risen, *waters to swim in*. What does *sachu* mean? Rabbi Chuna notes that in his locale swimmers were called *sachuna*, confirming that *sachu* means to swim.

A second *derasha* on the same word is then offered: Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Bun reads *sachu* not from *lischot* (to swim) but from *siach* (to speak). The waters are *mayim de-mistalin be-alma* — waters that will be spoken about throughout the world — because of their miraculous character.

### Zechariyah Wellspring

The *gemara* now cites a *pasuk* in *Zechariyah*: *ba-yom ha-hu yihiyeh makor niftach le-veit David u-le-yoshvei Yerushalayim le-chata't u-le-niddah* — on that day a wellspring will be opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for *chatat* and for *niddah*.

The *gemara* understands *chatat* here not as a sin-offering in the ordinary sense but as a reference to the *parah adumah*, which is called a *chatat* and whose preparation requires *mayim chayim* — naturally flowing spring water. A *niddah* may also immerse in *mayim chayim*. Thus the *pasuk* is read as speaking directly about the ritual uses of this miraculous stream.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonasan elaborates: from the house of David and throughout the inhabitants of Jerusalem — that is, as the waters flow from the *Beit Hamikdash* through the royal quarter and into the broader city — *kesherim le-niddah ve-la-chatat*. The waters remain pure *mayim chayim* throughout that range and may be used for both purposes.

### Mixed Waters Status

From that point onward, however, *mei ta'arovot heim* — they are mixed waters. Rainwater and other sources have joined the stream, and it can no longer be considered pure *mayim chayim*. The practical consequence: *kesherim le-niddah, pesulim le-mei chatat*. A *niddah* may still use these waters for *mikveh* purposes, since the admixture of rainwater does not disqualify a *mikveh* as such, but the water is no longer valid for preparing *mei chatat* for *parah adumah*, which requires *mayim chayim* specifically.

### Katafres Waters

Rabbi Elazar offers a different position. He agrees that from the house of David and throughout Jerusalem the waters are *kesherim le-niddah ve-la-chatat*. But from that point on, he describes the waters not as *mei ta'arovot* but as *mei katafresot* — waters flowing down an incline, a *katafres* being a sloped surface. His ruling: *pesulim le-niddah ve-la-chatat* — invalid for both.

Why should an incline invalidate the water even for *niddah*? The *mefarshim* assume that Rabbi Elazar also presupposes that rainwater has mixed in. If so, the water is predominantly rainwater — and running rainwater, where the majority is not *mayim chayim*, is invalid for *mikveh* since a *mikveh* of predominantly rainwater must be still rather than flowing. Moreover, the question of *katafres* and *chibur* — whether water running down a slope is still considered connected to the body of water above — is a distinct issue in the *gemara* elsewhere. If the sloped section is not considered *mechubar* to the main stream, it would be treated as an independent body of rainwater runoff, invalid entirely.

### Flow to Seas

Returning to *Yechezkel*: *ha-mayim ha-eileh yotzim el ha-Gelilah ha-Kadmonah* — these waters flow toward the eastern country. The *gemara* identifies the *Gelilah ha-kadmonah* as *yam shel Samcho* — the lake of Samcho, which Rashi identifies as the Hula Lake in the northern *Galil*. *Ve-yaredu el ha-aravah* — they descend to the *aravah* — this is *yam shel Tiveria*, the Sea of *Kinneret*. *U-va bo ha-yamah* — and they enter the ocean — this is *yam ha-melach*, the Dead Sea. *El ha-yamah ha-mutzaim* — toward the sea that issues forth — this is *ha-yam ha-gadol*, the Mediterranean.

Why is the Mediterranean called *mutzaim*, meaning the one that issued forth or overflowed? Because it overflowed its boundaries twice in history. Once in the generation of *Enosh*, when *avodah zarah* prevailed and the Mediterranean overflowed and submerged a third of the inhabited world. And once in the generation of *haflagah*, the Tower of Bavel. Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina says: the first time it went as far as *Kalbareia* — apparently a region the *Korban ha-edah* identifies with southern Italy, while others suggest it refers to Calabria specifically. The second time it reached the shores of *Barbaria*, the Barbary Coast of North Africa. Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Chanina reverses the geography: the first time to *Barbaria*, the second time only as far as *Akko* and *Yafo* on the coast of Israel itself. The *gemara* then cites *Iyov*: *tavo ve-lo tosif* — until here you shall come and no further — reading *poh* as an allusion to *Yafo* and *ad poh* as *Akko*.

The *gemara* then asks: it makes sense for the miraculous river to flow into the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea — *bishvil le-mitkan*, in order to sweeten their waters, as the *pasuk* itself says the salty waters will be healed. But why does the river flow into the *Kinneret* and the lake of *Samcho*, which are already fresh water? The answer: *le-rabot dagatam* — to increase their fish. *Le-minei minei tihyeh dagatam* — there will be multitudes of species of fish in those waters. This is followed by a striking supporting report: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel testifies that when he went to *Tzeidan*, they brought before him more than three hundred species of fish in a single dish.

### River Trees

Back to the *pasuk* in *Yechezkel*: *ve-nirpe'u ha-mayim* — the waters will be healed. *Be-tzeitav u-gevav ve-lo yirpe'u le-melach nittanu* — the swamps and marshes will not be healed, for they are given over to salt. The *gemara* notes an apparent internal contradiction: the verse opens by saying the waters will be healed and closes by saying they will not be healed. The resolution: *makom hu u-shemo velo yirpe'u* — *velo yirpe'u* is not a statement of outcome but a place name. The location by the edge of the river is called "Velo Yirpe'u."

On both banks of the river grow all manner of food-bearing trees: *lo yibol alehu* — their leaves will not wither; *ve-lo yitom piryo* — their fruit will never cease; *le-chadashav yivaker* — they will blossom and bear forth each month; *pe'riyo le-ma'achal ve-alehu li-trufa* — the fruit is for food, and the leaves are for medicine.

### Future Fruit Cycles

A *baraita* is cited with a debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi concerning the production cycles of the future:

Rabbi Yehuda reasons from the present: in this world, grain takes six months to ripen and trees take twelve months. In the future, applying a consistent ratio of one-to-two, *tvua osa le-chodesh echad* — grain will ripen in one month, and *ilan osa li-shnei chodashim* — trees in two months. His reading of *le-chadashav yivaker* is that the tree produces every two months.

Rabbi Yosi goes further. In this world the same cycle applies, but in the future, *ha-tvua osa le-tet-vav yom* — grain will ripen in fifteen days, and *ilan osa le-chodesh echad* — trees in one month. He reads *le-chadashav* as one month per fruit cycle, not two. His proof: in the days of *Yoel* there was a miracle in which grain grew in fifteen days, and the *omer* was brought from it — as the *pasuk* states: *ki nasan lachem et ha-moreh li-tzedakah ve-yored lachem geshem moreh u-malkosh ba-rishon* — the early and late rain came in the first month, which is *Nissan*, meaning that from the rain in *Nissan* the grain ripened in time for the *omer*, a span of fifteen days.

The *gemara* then asks: if Rabbi Yosi holds that trees produce every month, what does he make of the plural *le-chadashav*, "its months"? He reads it as *be-chol chodesh ve-chodesh yihiyeh meivaker* — every single month the tree will be producing; the plural simply indicates monthly recurrence.

### Healing Properties

The *gemara* then addresses the verse's statement that the leaves will be *li-trufa*, for healing. Rabbi Yochanan interprets: *tarfei matzitz aleh ve-taraf mezona* — reading the word with a *tes*, as *taraf*, meaning food — so that the leaves can even serve as food. Why reinterpret the verse when fruit for food and leaves for medicine already seems a sufficiently generous arrangement? The *gemara* does not explain.

Rav and Shmuel offer two readings of *trufa le-hatir peh*: one says it means *le-hatir peh she-le-mala* — to open the mouth above, that is, to cure the mute and restore their speech; the other says *le-hatir peh she-le-mata* — to open the mouth below, meaning to cure the barren or to relieve constipation. Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi make the same distinction more explicitly: one says *le-hatir peh akarot*, to make barren women fertile; the other says *le-hatir peh ilmim*, to restore speech to the mute.

---

## Yehoyachin Story

### Nebuchadnezzar Siege

Having mentioned *Sha'ar Yechanyah* and the reason for its name, the *gemara* now narrates the events leading to *Yechanyah*'s exile. *At motza be-sha'ah she-ala Nevuchadnetzar le-chan* — when Nebuchadnezzar came up to this place, *ba ve-yashav lo be-dafni shel Antochia* — he came and encamped at the walls of Antioch. This is strikingly far from Jerusalem, and yet the *Sanhedrin* went out to meet him there — a preemptive act reminiscent of *Yochanan ben Zakkai*'s famous capitulation to Vespasian in the period of the *Bayit Sheni*. The *Sanhedrin* said to him: *he-izman ha-bayit ha-zeh le-hacharev?* — Has the time come for the *Beit Hamikdash* to be destroyed? Take care of it and proceed.

Nebuchadnezzar replied: *oso she-himlachti aleichem* — the king I appointed over you — *teneihu li ve-ani holech* — give him to me and I will leave. Which is, in fact, precisely what transpired historically: he deposed *Yechanyah* and took him into exile. The *Sanhedrin* went and informed *Yehoyachin melech Yehuda*: Nebuchadnezzar wants you.

### Keys Returned

Upon hearing this, *Yehoyachin* took the keys of the *Beit Hamikdash*, ascended to the roof of the *heichal*, and addressed God: *le-she-avar hayinu ne'emanim lach* — in the past we were trusted by You; *va-hayu maftechotecha mesurim lanu* — Your keys were entrusted to us. *Achshav she-einanu ne'emanim* — now that we are no longer found trustworthy — *harei maftechotecha mesurim lach* — here are Your keys returned to You. It is a remarkable act — part resignation, part theological statement, a formal acknowledgment that the stewardship has ended.

### Keys Fate

A dispute among *amora'im* follows: one says *zarkan ve-od lo yardu* — he threw the keys upward and they have not come down yet. The other says *ba ke-min yad ve-natalta mi-yado* — a hand emerged from heaven and took them. The two versions carry different theological valences: in the first, the keys hang suspended — unreturned, unclaimed, awaiting *redemption*; in the second, heaven actively receives them back, a gesture of acknowledgment from above.

### Nobles' Response

*Kivan she-ra'u kol chorei Yehuda ken* — when all the nobles of Judah witnessed this, *alu le-rosh gagotseihem ve-naflu ve-meitu* — they ascended to their rooftops and threw themselves off, dying. The *gemara* identifies this in the *pasuk* of *Yeshayahu*: *massa gei chizayon mah lach eifo ki alita kulech le-gagosei* — what has happened to you that you have all gone up to the rooftops? The city is in tumult.

This account is not without halakhic resonance. These *midrashim* describing mass suicide in moments of religious catastrophe were cited by the *Chachmei Ashkenaz* in the medieval period — particularly in the context of the Crusades — as precedent for martyrdom, demonstrating that this mode of response to persecution had classical roots in *aggadic* tradition.

---

## 13 Tables

### Tables Overview

The *mishna* now proceeds to the thirteen *shulchanot* — the second item in the inverted ABC-CBA structure. *Yud-gimmel shulchanos hayu ba-Mikdash* — thirteen tables were in the *Mikdash*.

### 8 Marble Tables

*She-monah shel shayish be-veit ha-mitbachayim* — eight made of marble in the *Beit Hamitbachayim*, the slaughterhouse. *She-aleihem medichim et ha-kirvayim* — on these they would wash out the innards and organs of the slaughtered animals, removing refuse. Marble was chosen because it keeps the meat cold, preventing spoilage.

### West Ramp Tables

*U-shtayim be-ma'arav ha-kevesh* — two on the west of the ramp of the *mizbeach*: one of marble and one of silver. The marble one was for placing the *eivarim* — the limbs of the offerings — again to keep them cool before they were carried up to the *mizbeach*. The silver one was for the *klei shares*, the service vessels, which could be kept on silver without the same concern about temperature.

### Ulam Tables

*U-shtayim ba-ulam mi-bifnim al petach ha-bayit* — two in the *ulam*, just inside the entrance to the *heichal*. One was of marble, the other of gold. *Al shel shayish notnin lechem ha-panim bi-chnisaso* — on the marble table they would rest the *lechem ha-panim* upon its arrival, as it was brought in for placement. *Ve-al shel zahav be-yetziaso* — on the gold table it rested upon removal. *She-maalin ba-kodesh ve-lo moridin* — because one ascends in *kedushah* and does not descend. The bread would thus move from a lesser to a greater material on its way out, culminating on gold.

### Gold Showbread Table

And of course there was the famous thirteenth: *echad shel zahav mi-bifnim she-alav lechem ha-panim tamid* — the one golden table inside, on which the *lechem ha-panim* rested continuously. This is the *shulchan* known from the *Torah* itself — one of the original vessels of the *Mikdash* — and its presence among the thirteen is what completes the count.

---

## Tables Gemara

### Silver vs Marble

A *baraita* variant surfaces: rather than *shel shayish* — marble — for the table on which the *lechem ha-panim* rested upon entry, it says *shel kesef* — silver. Rabbi Yosi in the name of Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak, and Rabbi Chanina citing Rabbi Yochanan, rule: *leit kan shel kesef* — silver was not used. *Mipnei she-hu martiach* — because silver would heat the bread, causing it to spoil. Some have a variant *girsa* in which the concern was the opposite — that marble would cool the bread too much — but in our text the concern is that silver retains heat in a way that would be damaging.

### Showbread Miracle

At this point the *gemara* raises an obvious objection: surely there were sufficient miracles operative in the *Beit Hamikdash* that such practical concerns are irrelevant? Is it not taught in a *baraita*: *zeh echad min ha-nissim she-na'asu be-Beit HaMikdash* — this is one of the miracles that occurred in the *Beit Hamikdash* — *keshem she-hayu manichim oto cham, kach hayu motzi'im oto cham* — just as they placed the *lechem ha-panim* on the table while it was hot, so too they removed it a full week later and it was still hot, still completely fresh. The verse is cited: *lasum lechem cham be-yom hilakcho* — bread as hot as the day it was taken. If a miracle of this magnitude was in place, why concern ourselves with whether the table was marble or silver?

### No Relying on Miracles

The response: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states, *ein mazkirin ma'aseh nissim* — one does not invoke miracles. The parallel formulation in the *Bavli* is: *ein somchin al ha-nes* — we do not rely on the miracle. The practical arrangements of the *Mikdash* were to be made responsibly, as though no miraculous intervention could be counted upon. If God then chooses to perform a miracle, all the better; but the design of the *avodah* must not be predicated on the assumption that a miracle will occur.

### Old Bread Query

A question is posed before Rabbi Ami: *lo hayah sham lechem, mahu le-hanicho le-Shabbat ha-ba'ah?* — if in some unusual circumstance there was no new *lechem ha-panim* ready on *Shabbat*, could the old loaves remain on the *shulchan* for an additional week — two weeks in total? The verse requires *lechem ha-panim lefanai tamid* — the showbread must always be before Me — and perhaps that *tamid* allows for continuous presence even beyond the normal weekly cycle.

### Continuous Bread

Rabbi Ami responds: *ve-nasata al ha-shulchan lechem panim lefanai tamid* — the verse says "place bread before Me always." *Lechem panim afilu pasul* — even if the bread is technically invalid.
