The precise meaning of *pasul* here is somewhat unclear — does the bread become invalid by remaining more than a week? — but the operative ruling is that it must remain *lefanai tamid*, before God continuously. The bread therefore may remain in place beyond the standard week if no new bread is ready. Additionally, Rabbi Ami's comment implies: *ve-ein lo notar* — there is no prohibition of *notar* applicable here, consistent with the principle that an offering on top of the *mizbeach* is not subject to *notar*, and a similar logic apparently applies to the *shulchan*.

---

## Solomon's 10 Tables

### Solomon's Tables

The *mishna* now raises an additional dimension: *asarah shulchanos asah Shlomo* — Solomon made ten additional *shulchanot* beyond the original one, replicating the golden *shulchan* of *Moshe*. The biblical source: *va-ya'as shulchanos asarah va-yanach ba-heichal chamisha mi-yamin ve-chamisha mi-smol* — he made ten tables and placed five on the right and five on the left within the *heichal*.

### Placement Reconciliation

The ordinary reading of "right" and "left" when facing east would yield south and north. But this creates an immediate problem: *ein ha-shulchan kasher ela be-tzafon* — the *shulchan* is only valid when placed on the northern side, as the verse commands *ve-et ha-shulchan titen al tzela tzafon* — place the table on the northern side. If Solomon's additional tables were arranged north and south of the original, some of them would be more northerly than the original, violating the requirement that it occupy the northern position.

The resolution: *chamisha mi-yamin shulchano shel Moshe ve-chamisha mi-smolo* — the "right" and "left" do not mean north and south of the room, but east and west relative to *Moshe*'s original *shulchan*. The ten tables flanked the original on either side, meaning they were arrayed east and west of it, not north and south. The original *shulchan* thus remained in the northernmost position as required.

### Moses' Table Only

The standard ruling: *af al pi chein lo hayah mesader ela be-shel Moshe bilvad* — even so, the *lechem ha-panim* was arranged only on *Moshe*'s original table, not on any of Solomon's ten additions. The verse is cited: *et ha-shulchan asher alav lechem ha-panim* — "the table upon which the *lechem ha-panim* rests" — the definite article indicating one specific table.

### All Tables Theory

Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehudah takes the striking minority position: *al kulan hayah mesader* — the showbread was arranged on all eleven tables. He derives this from the verse *et ha-shulchanos va-aleihem lechem ha-panim* — using the plural *ha-shulchanos* and *aleihem*. This is, as the *gemara* does not hesitate to note, quite shocking. Not only did Solomon add vessels to the inner *heichal* — itself already a bold act, given the Torah's particularity about the sacred vessels — but according to Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehudah, an entirely separate *avodah* was established, with additional loaves baked and arranged on all ten new tables as well. The *gemara* simply records this view without further analysis, leaving it to stand in its remarkable solitude.

---

---

# Shekalim 18

## Tables & Menorahs

### Tables Orientation

The daf opens by continuing the discussion of thirteens in the *beis hamikdash*, which serves as the framework leading into the thirteen *shofaros* — the collection boxes — that are the central subject of our *masechta*. Having already treated thirteen prostrations and thirteen *shulchanot*, the Gemara now addresses the exact placement and orientation of those tables. The backdrop is that in the time of *Shlomo*, ten additional *shulchanot* were added — five to the right and five to the left of *Moshe*'s original *shulchan* — and a parallel set of ten *menorot* was likewise added. A *baraisa* is cited recording a dispute on the matter: *mizrach u'ma'arav hayu netunim* — *Rebbi* holds that the *shulchanot* were oriented east-west; *Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon* holds they were placed north-south, *tzafon ve-darom*.

### Beis Hamikdash Diagram

To appreciate what is at stake, consider the layout of the *heichal*. The interior space runs forty *amot* from the entrance to the *kodesh kodashim*, with an additional twenty *amot* for the *kodesh kodashim* itself. The *shulchan* stood to the north and the *menorah* to the south, each positioned within the inner half of the forty-*amah* space.

The Gemara notes the difficulty with the north-south position: *nimtza shulchan ba'darom* — if the ten additional *shulchanot* are lined up north to south, *Moshe*'s *shulchan* would no longer be the northernmost. Since halachic significance attaches to the northernmost position, this creates a problem. The same issue applies to the *menorah*, which the *pasuk* places specifically to the south (*temana*): were the additional *menorot* arranged north-south, *Moshe*'s *menorah* would no longer be the southernmost. By contrast, if the *shulchanot* and *menorot* are aligned east-west — that is, with each additional vessel running parallel to *Moshe*'s, neither protruding further north nor further south — all the vessels are equally accessible and the primacy of *Moshe*'s originals is uncompromised.

### Shulchan Placement

A *baraisa* provides direct textual evidence in favor of the east-west orientation. *Ha-shulchan hayah natun me-chatzi ha-bayit u'vifnim* — the *shulchan* was positioned on the inner half of the house, meaning from the halfway point of the forty-*amah* space inward. It was drawn *mashuch min ha-kotel shtei amot u'mechetza k'lapei tzafon* — two and a half *amot* from the northern wall. The reason a gap of two and a half *amot* was needed between the *shulchan* and the wall is functional: the *lechem hapanim* had to be approached from both sides, with the old bread being removed and the new bread inserted simultaneously, requiring access from each flank.

The *menorah*, the *baraisa* continues, was situated opposite the *shulchan* on the southern side of the *heichal*. Given that there are only two and a half *amot* between the *shulchan* and the northern wall, there is simply no room for any additional *shulchanot* between it and the wall. This *baraisa* thus clearly presupposes an east-west arrangement and constitutes strong evidence against the north-south view.

The *Korban HaEdah* and the *Tachlin Chadatin* both note the significance of how the *Yerushalmi* handles this evidence. Rather than engaging in elaborate *ukimtot* to salvage the north-south position — as the *Bavli* might do — the *Yerushalmi* simply presents the *baraisa* and moves on. The *Tachlin Chadatin* makes this observation explicit: *v'gam stam matnitin de'Menachot kevata de'Rebbi v'lav orcha d'Yerushalmi le'ha'arich be'pilpula shelo aliba de'hilchata* — the plain *mishna* of Menachot accords with *Rebbi*'s position, and it is not the way of the *Yerushalmi* to extend its dialectic in support of a view that does not reflect the *halacha*. This reflects a genuine and pronounced methodological difference between the two Talmuds.

### Golden Altar

The *baraisa* continues with the *mizbeach ha-zahav*: *haya natun be-emtza ha-bayit* — it was positioned exactly in the middle of the *heichal*, dividing the house at its midpoint, *cholek et ha-bayit mechatziya u'lifnim*. Interestingly, the *Yerushalmi* notes that it was *meshuch kima k'lapei chutz* — drawn slightly outward — so that it was not positioned directly between the *menorah* and the *shulchan* but slightly toward the entrance, leaving an open space between the two vessels. The sole function performed at the *mizbeach ha-zahav* was the burning of the *ketoret*: twice daily, in the morning and afternoon, a *kohen* would offer the incense there. Since the entire *heichal* is roofed, animal sacrifices would not be appropriate in that space. On *Yom Kippur*, blood from the inner sacrifices was also applied to the corners of the *mizbeach*, but the regular daily rite was exclusively the burning of *ketoret*.

The *baraisa* notes that all these vessels — *shulchan*, *menorah*, and *mizbeach ha-zahav* — were *me-shlish ha-bayit u'lifnim*, positioned from a third of the house inward. This apparent contradiction with the earlier statement of "half" is resolved by the *Bavli*: "half" counts from the entrance to the *kodesh kodashim* — twenty *amot* of forty; "a third" counts the entire structure including the *kodesh kodashim* — twenty *amot* of sixty.

### Solomon's Menorahs

The Gemara now turns to the ten *menorot* that *Shlomo* added: *eser menorot asah Shlomo*, as the *pasuk* in *Divrei Hayamim* states — *vayasas menorat ha-zahav eser ke-mishpatam vayitein ba-heichal chamesh mi-yamin u'chamesh mi-smol*, five on the right and five on the left. The question of what "right" and "left" mean here parallels the problem of "north" and "south" discussed above. If one faces east — the standard orientation, reflected in the word *kedem* meaning both "east" and "in front," and in *temana* (south) deriving from *yamin* (right) — then right is south and left is north. That would once again leave *Moshe*'s *menorah*, which is required to be the southernmost, surrounded by others to its south. The Gemara resolves this: *chamisha mi-yamin menorato shel Moshe v'chamisha mi-smolo* — five on each side of *Moshe*'s *menorah*, but oriented east-west, not north-south.

### Menorah Lighting

Even after establishing their placement, a second debate emerges: were all ten additional *menorot* actually lit in practice, or only *Moshe*'s original? One view holds that only *Moshe*'s *menorah* was kindled: *lo haya mavir ela b'shel Moshe bilvad*. The basis is a *pasuk* in *Divrei Hayamim* that refers to the *menorah* in the singular — *menorat ha-zahav ve-neiroteha le'va'er ba-erev ba-erev* — the golden *menorah* and its lamps to kindle every evening. *Rabbi Yosei be-Rabbi Yehuda* takes the opposing view: *al kullan haya mavir* — all of them were lit. His proof is from another *pasuk* in *Divrei Hayamim* that uses plural language — *ve-et ha-menorot ve-neiroteihen le'va'aram ke-mishpat lifnei ha-dvir zahav sagur* — the *menorot* and their lamps to kindle them as required before the *dvir* (the *kodesh kodashim*).

This is a striking dispute. The instinct to say that *Shlomo*'s additional vessels were not actually used for their intended ritual purposes is understandable. The *Torah*'s entire account of the *mishkan* seems to invest the specific *keilim* and their arrangement with profound significance — indeed, the *Torah* begins its description with the *aron* and works outward to the structure itself. To multiply the primary vessels and operate them all in parallel would represent something qualitatively different from constructing the *Beis Hamikdash* at a grander scale. One can therefore appreciate the inclination to read the singular *pasuk* as indicating that, in practice, only *Moshe*'s original *menorah* was ever kindled.

### Gold Purification

The *pasuk*'s description of *Shlomo*'s *menorot* as being made of *michlot zahav* — the purest of gold — introduces a *baraisa* that illuminates the extraordinary refining process involved. *Tani Rabbi Yehuda be-shem Asi*: *haya Shlomo notel elef kikarei zahav u'machnisam la-kur u'motzian ad she'hu ma'amidam al echad* — *Shlomo* would take a thousand talents of ore, place it in a furnace, and reduce it until only one talent of pure gold remained. This is not as paradoxical as it sounds; the process of smelting gold ore to remove impurities is, in fact, how gold is refined even today, and raw ore can contain a very high proportion of dross. The phrase *michlot zahav* is thus read as *kilei zehavo shel Moshe* — they exhausted, through this intense purification, the gold of *Moshe*'s original *menorah* and then some, so great was the quantity processed. The purpose: *likayem mah she-ne'emar kikar zahav tahor asah otah* — to fulfill the Torah's requirement that the *menorah* be of pure gold, which demanded that all impurities be burned away.

### Moshe's Menorah

A *baraisa* adds a remarkable detail about *Moshe*'s own *menorah*. *Maaseh bi-menorat zahav she-asah Moshe ba-midbar* — when *Moshe* fashioned the golden *menorah* in the wilderness, *ve-hayata yeteira dinar zahav* — it came out one *dinar* heavier than the prescribed *kikar*. It was run through the furnace eighty times — *ve-hikhnisuha la-kur shmonim pa'am* — and yet *lo chasra klum*: nothing could be reduced from it. The Gemara explains: *ad de-lo yakum al burarei havi chasar sagi* — before gold reaches its absolutely pure state, repeated smelting continues to drive off impurities and reduce the mass; *min de-kayaum al burarei lo chasar klum* — once it has reached its ultimate purity, there is nothing left to burn away. The furnace does not consume gold itself, only its impurities. *Moshe*'s *menorah*, having been fashioned at the level of ultimate purity, could not be reduced further no matter how many times it was fired. The extra *dinar* was an irreducible part of the purest gold itself. This is, as noted, a rather striking passage — the suggestion that *Moshe*'s *menorah* came out slightly heavier than expected is puzzling, but the Gemara's resolution transforms it into a testament to the extraordinary purity of that vessel.

---

## Thirteen Shofaros

### Shofaros Categories

The Gemara now arrives at the immediate subject of our *perek*: the thirteen *shofaros* that stood in the *beis hamikdash*. These were collection boxes of a distinctive pyramidal shape — narrow at the top, widening downward — designed so that money could be dropped in but could not be retrieved by hand. Each *shofar* bore an inscription indicating the designated purpose of funds deposited in it.

The thirteen designations were as follows. Two boxes were for *shekalim*: one inscribed *taklin chadatin* (new shekels) for the current year's half-shekel obligation, and one inscribed *taklin atikin* (old shekels) for those paying in arrears from the prior year. Two boxes were for *kinim* — bird sacrifices: one labeled *kinim* generically, and one labeled *gozlei olah* for chick *olos*. One box was for *etzim* (wood for the altar). One was for *levonah* (frankincense). One was for *zahav la-kaporet* (gold for the *kaporet*, the cover of the *aron*, although the *mefarshim* understand this broadly as gold for the *klei shares* generally). The remaining six were designated for *nedavah* — free-will offerings — which would be used for *kayitz ha-mizbeach*, the fund that kept the altar continuously active when private *korbanot* were not being brought.

The existence of boxes for *levonah* and *etzim* reflects a significant halachic development. While the *Torah* specifies *olah*, *shelamim*, and the various types of *mincha* as forms of voluntary sacrifice, the *Chachamim* recognized two additional categories not explicitly mentioned in the *Torah*: the *minchat nesachim* offered independently of any animal sacrifice, and *ketoret* as a private donation. Moreover, the *etzim* are treated by *Chazal* with something approaching the status of a *korban* — *mipnei she-hu ke-korban* — as the *pasuk* uses the term *korban ha-etzim*. The *Bavli* even raises the question of whether privately donated wood should have salt applied to it, as required of all sacrificial offerings — *al kol korbanecha takriv melach*. This expanded range of voluntary offerings is thus not derived from the explicit text of the *Torah* but articulated by rabbinic tradition.

### Old & New Shekels

The inscriptions *taklin chadatin* and *taklin atikin* served a clear administrative function. New shekels (*taklin chadatin*) were for the current year's contribution, which would be collected, stored in the *lishkah*, and drawn upon three times yearly in the *terumat ha-lishkah* to fund the communal *korbanot*. Old shekels (*taklin atikin*) — *mi she-lo heivi eshtakad shokel li-shanah ha-ba'ah* — were for those who had not contributed in the prior year and were now making up the arrears.

### Bird Sacrifices

The two bird *shofaros* introduce a dispute between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *Chachamim*. *Rabbi Yehuda* held that both the *kinim* box and the *gozlei olah* box were designated for *olot* exclusively — one for mature pigeons (*torim*) and one for young doves (*benei yonah*), simply two forms of voluntary bird *olot*. The *Chachamim*, however, drew a sharp distinction: the box labeled *gozlei olah* was indeed for voluntary *olot*, but the box labeled *kinim* was split — *echad chatas ve-echad olah* — half for *chatas* and half for *olah*. This reflects the common purification scenario in which a woman — a *zivah* or a *yoledes* — is obligated to bring two birds, one as a *chatas* and one as an *olah*. Rather than personally acquiring, transporting, and presenting live birds to the *beis hamikdash*, she could simply deposit the monetary equivalent into the *kinim* shofar, leave, and be assured that by the end of the day the priests would have offered the appropriate number of sacrifices on behalf of all who had contributed. This system presupposes a fixed market price for birds, so that the total amount deposited could be evenly divided between *chatas* and *olah* obligations.

### Wood & Incense

The minimum for a wood donation is addressed in the *mishna*: *harei alai etzim, lo yifchos mi-shnei gezirin* — one who accepts upon himself to donate wood may not bring less than two logs. The minimum for frankincense is: *lo yifchos mi-kometz* — no less than one handful. These minima govern not only physical donations but also the monetary value that must be deposited in the respective *shofaros*.

### Gold & Kaporet

For gold, the minimum is: *lo yifchos mi-dinar zahav* — no less than one gold *dinar*. The *shofar* for *zahav la-kaporet* — gold for the *kaporet* — raises a conceptual question, since the *kaporet* (the cover of the *aron*) was already constructed and in place. The *mefarshim* therefore understand *kaporet* here generically, as referring to the *klei shares* more broadly, notwithstanding the somewhat unusual terminology.

### Free-Will Offerings

The six remaining *shofaros* were for *nedavah*. The Gemara explains: *lokchim bah olos* — the funds collected in these boxes were used to purchase animal *olot*. The meat went entirely to God (*ha-basar la-Shem*), as is the nature of an *olah*, while the hides went to the *kohanim* (*ha-orot la-kohanim*). These *olot* served as *kayitz ha-mizbeach* — keeping the altar fires occupied at all times, even when no private *korbanot* were being brought.

The legal basis for diverting surplus *chatas* and *asham* funds into this *olah* account is derived from a *midrash* of *Yehoyada ha-kohen gadol*: *asham hu asham asham la-Hashem* — the *pasuk* in *Melachim* states that the silver of *asham* and *chatas* funds shall not be brought into the *beis Hashem* but shall belong to the *kohanim* (*kesef asham ve-kesef chatot lo yuva beis Hashem la-kohanim yihyu*), while another passage indicates that such funds go *la-Shem*. The resolution: one brings an *olah* from such funds, such that the meat goes entirely to God while the hides go to the *kohanim* — *nimtze'u shnei kesuvim kayamim*, both verses are fulfilled simultaneously. This is the source for the rule that *mosar chatas* — money set aside for a *chatas* that exceeded the actual cost — is redirected to *kayitz ha-mizbeach*. A parallel instance of *kohanim* independently interpreting *pesukim* for halachic purposes appears earlier in the *masechta* (3b), where the *kohanim* derived from *ve-chol minchat kohen kalil tihyeh* an exemption from the half-shekel obligation.

---

## Chatas Money Debate

### R. Yehuda's View

A *baraisa* records *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position: *lo haya shofar shekalim bi-Yerushalayim mipnei ha-ta'aroves* — there was no *shofar* designated for *chatas* bird money in Jerusalem, because of the problem of mixture. This is a striking claim, since it amounts to a rejection of what the *mishna* describes as established practice. *Rabbi Yehuda*, living roughly a century after the *churban*, is arguing that the system described by the *Chachamim* could not have operated as stated, because it is fundamentally incompatible with the laws of *chatas*.

The concern is specific: *shema tamus achas meihen* — suppose one of the donors dies after depositing money into the *kinim* shofar but before it is spent. The money she deposited for a *chatas* is now *dmei chatas meisa* — money designated for a *chatas* whose owner has died — and such money must be allowed to be lost (*yamus*). Once it is mixed with the other funds in the shofar, the entire sum is compromised. *Ve-nimtzu dmei chatayot meisos me'uravot bahen* — money of a *chatas meisa* is now indistinguishably mixed throughout the collection, rendering the whole fund unusable.

*Rabbi Yehuda* does not invoke principles of *bitul* or *rov* as solutions, presumably because he holds *min be-min lo batil* — like-kind is not nullified by like-kind. Even the *Chachamim* who disagree regarding *bitul* accept that *oilin lo mevatlin zeh et zeh* — sacrificial coins do not nullify one another. There is also the conceptual possibility of simply disregarding the eventuality (*lo chayish*), since persons have a *chazakah* of being alive, but *Rabbi Yehuda* does not accept this as sufficient grounds to permit the entire arrangement in principle.

### Baraisa Evidence

Against *Rabbi Yehuda*, the Gemara cites a *baraisa*: a woman who has an obligation to bring bird sacrifices — either as a *yoledes* or as a *zavah* — may bring the monetary value, *dmei kan*, deposit it in the *shofar*, and thereafter eat *kodashim* that same evening. *Ve-einah chosheshet shema nis'atzlu bahen* — she need not be concerned that the *kohanim* were negligent and failed to offer the sacrifices that day. And, crucially, *ve-ein kohen choshesh shema dmei chatas meisa me'ureves bahen* — the *kohen* officiating need not be concerned that the money of a *chatas meisa* is mixed into the fund. This *baraisa* directly contradicts *Rabbi Yehuda* on two counts: it presupposes that *chatas* money was in fact deposited in a *shofar*, and it explicitly dismisses the concern about a deceased donor's funds being mixed in.

### Bittul Solutions

The Gemara proposes a possible solution: *nivrar arba zuzei ve-nishdi be-nahara* — designate four *zuzim* (representing the compromised *chatas* funds) and cast them into a river, thereby segregating and removing the tainted money. This would be analogous to the method sometimes employed in cases of *avodah zarah* that has become mixed with other items, where one symbolically separates and discards the forbidden element once *bitul* has already taken effect.

### No Breirah

The Gemara rejects this approach on behalf of *Rabbi Yehuda*: *Rabbi Yehuda leisa lei breirah* — *Rabbi Yehuda* does not accept *breirah*. It should be noted that the term *breirah* here is applied somewhat loosely: classic *breirah* involves making an act whose content is retroactively defined by future events (as in designating *terumot u'maasrot* to be the portion that will remain at a future date). What is described here is closer to a declaratory fiction — asserting that the four *zuzim* being cast away are specifically the ones that were compromised. Whether or not this constitutes *breirah* in the formal sense, *Rabbi Yehuda*'s non-acceptance of it as a legal mechanism leaves him without a remedy. The conclusion is therefore that according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, *chatas* money could not be placed in a communal *shofar*; individuals obligated in a bird *chatas* must bring the sacrifice directly and personally.

---

## Wood Donation Minima

### One Log vs. Two

Having established that the minimum wood donation is two logs, the Gemara raises a related question: if someone said *harei alai eitz* — "I hereby obligate myself to bring a single log" — can one log constitute a valid minimum, or is the floor always two? The question turns on whether a single log (*gezer echad*) has independent halachic standing as a *korban* unit.

### Yoma Evidence

*Rav Elazar* resolves the question from the *mishna* itself: *masnisa amrah kein — shezeh korban bifnei atzmo ve-zeh korban bifnei atzmo* — each log has independent status as a *korban*. The proof is from a *mishna* in Yoma: *shnayim be-yadam shnei gizrei etzim* — when wood was brought onto the *mizbeiach* each morning as part of the *tamid* service, two *kohanim* participated, each carrying one log independently. The fact that the *Torah*-ordained morning service assigns each *kohen* an individual log demonstrates that a single log is a functionally complete sacrificial unit. Accordingly, one who stipulates *harei alai eitz* is obligated in one log and no more.

### Mizbeach Dimensions

A digression addresses the physical dimensions of the wood on the *mizbeiach*. *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* teaches: the logs were an *amah* in thickness — *uvyan amah be-amah be-amah sochaktes*, measured in the generous *amah sochaktes* (a loosely measured *amah*, somewhat larger than exact) — but less than an *amah* in length, *amah gedumah*, a truncated *amah*. This produces an unusual proportionality in which the logs were essentially cubic or even wider than they were long. *Rav Chuni be-shem Rav Ami* adds a comparison to the arm of a balance scale (*turtani*), suggesting a specific shape. The *amoraim* then explain the unusual dimensions.

### Log Length Requirement

*Rabbi Shmuel be-Rabbi Yitzchak* provides the rationale: *mipnei she-lo hayah makom ha-ma'arachah ela amah* — the designated space for the woodpile on the *mizbeiach* was only one *amah* by one *amah*. Therefore the logs could not protrude beyond that square, requiring that they be shorter than one *amah* in length. This is illustrated by a *baraisa* enumerating the successive *amah*-wide sections of the *mizbeiach*'s upper surface: *amah ha-yesod*, *amah ha-soveiv*, *amah ha-karkov*, *amah ha-keranot*, and *amah ha-ma'arachah*. Working inward, with one *amah* given to the *keranot* on each side and one *amah* for the *karkov*, one arrives at a one-by-one *amah* central space for the *ma'arachah* — the woodpile. Because the logs must fit entirely within this space, they are cut to less than a full *amah* in length.

---

## Incense Minima

### Incense Handful

For *levonah* donated to the *beis hamikdash*, the minimum is one *kometz* — one handful. The Gemara derives this through a *gezeirah shavah* linking the *azkarah* of *lechem hapanim* to the *azkarah* of the *mincha*.

### Azkarah Connection

The connection works as follows. By *lechem hapanim*, the *pasuk* states: *ve-nasata al ha-ma'arachah levonah zakah ve-hayetah la-lechem le-azkarah* — the *levonah* placed in spoons upon the *shulchan* alongside the showbread serves as its *azkarah*, its memorial portion. By the *mincha*, the *pasuk* states: *ve-kamatz misham melo kumtzo mi-soltah u'mi-shamnah al kol levonatah ve-hiktir ha-kohen et azkaratah* — the *kohen* takes a *kometz*, a full handful, of the *mincha* and burns it as the *azkarah*. Since both contexts use the term *azkarah*, a *gezeirah shavah* connects them: *mah azkarah ha-amurah le-halan milo kometz, af azkarah ha-amurah kan milo kometz* — just as the *azkarah* of the *mincha* is a full handful, so too the *azkarah* of the *lechem hapanim* consists of a full *kometz* of *levonah* per arrangement, burned weekly when the old bread is removed and the new is set in place.

### Two Spoons Question

This raises an immediate difficulty. By *lechem hapanim* there were two arrangements (*ma'arachot*), each accompanied by its own spoon of *levonah*, yielding a total of two *komatzim* of *levonah* burned each week. If the minimum unit is derived from the *azkarah* of *lechem hapanim*, should not the minimum be two *komatzim* rather than one — *af azkarah ha-amurah kan shnei komatzim*?

### Each Kometz Independent

*Rabbi Ila* resolves this by demonstrating that each *kometz* of *levonah* by the *lechem hapanim* is halachically independent. The argument proceeds through an internal analysis of the *lechem hapanim* itself: the *halacha* is that a *kometz* of the *mincha* that is *chaser* — lacking even a minimal amount — is invalid. If one of the two spoons of *levonah* by the *lechem hapanim* were slightly deficient while the other were slightly in excess, they could not be combined to make up the shortage, because if we treated them as a single unit we would never be able to say that one alone is invalid. The very fact that a deficient *kometz* is invalid on its own proves that each spoon is evaluated independently, as a self-contained unit. Consequently, one *kometz* is a complete and valid minimum — just as each *kohen* who carried a single log of wood in the morning performed a complete act, so too each *kometz* of *levonah* stands on its own.

### Kohen's Handbreadth

A final question concerns the measuring standard for the *kometz*: since a *kometz* is literally a handful measured by the *kohen*'s fingers, whose hand determines the measure? *Rabbi Yosei* in the name of *Rabbi Ila* says: *ha-mitnadev levonah meivi k'kumtzo shel kohen* — the donor must bring an amount corresponding to the handbreadth of the *kohen* who will offer it. According to some, this means the *kohen gadol*; according to others, it means the largest *kohen* available, ensuring that however large the officiating *kohen*'s hand, the amount donated will suffice. *Rabbi Chizkiyah be-shem Rabbi Yirmiyah* offers a lenient view: *afilu be-kometz ba'alim* — the donor may measure by his or her own handful, without regard for the *kohen*'s hand size.

---

## Gold Donation Minima

### Gold Coin Amount

For gold donations, the *mishna* establishes: *lo yifchos mi-dinar zahav* — one may not give less than one gold *dinar*. *Rabbi Elazar* clarifies: this minimum applies *ve-hu she-hizkir tzurah* — when the donor explicitly specifies coins, i.e., refers to a particular minted form of gold. In that case, the minimum denomination is one gold *dinar*, which in the Roman period represented a substantial sum.

### Generic Gold

However, if the donor did not specify a form — *im lo hizkir tzurah* — but simply said "I will give gold" generically, then *meivi afilu tzinora* — even a tiny amount, such as a gold needle, is acceptable. The determination of the minimum thus turns on whether the donor's language invoked a specific monetary unit or referred to gold as a material substance without further specification.

---

---

# Shekalim 19

## Six Nedavah Boxes

### Priestly Families

The daf opens at the bottom of 18b, continuing the discussion of the *shofarot* — the various donation boxes in the *Beit HaMikdash* — which collected money for different types of offerings and Temple needs. We have already worked through the first seven boxes, each designated for a specific purpose, such as logs of wood, frankincense, and gold. The Gemara now turns to six additional *shofarot*, all designated for *nedavah* — voluntary offerings — also known elsewhere as *keitz hamizbeach*, referring to *olot* brought on the *mizbeach* during periods when no other sacrificial activity occupied it. This fund also received proceeds from leftover money originally designated for a *chatat* or an *asham*, as indeed the *mishnah* had discussed, citing the interpretation of *Yehoyada Kohen Gadol*.

The *gemara* opens with the question: why were there six *shofarot* for *nedavah* when every other designation had only one? The first answer comes from Rav or Chizkiya: *kineged shisha batei avot* — corresponding to the six family houses of the priests. By way of background, the *kohanim* were divided into twenty-four *mishmarot*, each serving approximately twice a year. Each *mishmar* was further subdivided into *batei avot*, with one family house operating each day of the week and all families serving together on *Shabbat*, yielding six family houses per *mishmar*.

The word *kineged* here is worth examining carefully. Sometimes *kineged* means only that a number is symbolically parallel to another — a pleasing correspondence. But here *kineged* seems to mean something more literal: each *shofar* was actually assigned to a specific day of the week. If you deposited money into the Sunday *shofar*, that money was designated for the *korbanot* brought on Sunday; the Monday *shofar* for Monday *korbanot*, and so on. Why would such a system be necessary rather than simply maintaining a single communal fund drawn upon as needed? The *Korban HaEdah* explains: if one family's day of service was particularly busy and drew heavily on the communal *nedavah* fund, while another family's day was quieter, the busier family would benefit more — in the form of hides or portions of *korbanot* belonging to the family on duty that day. To prevent disputes over the unequal distribution of these benefits, *chazal* instituted separate boxes for each day so that each family would draw only from its own day's fund and could not complain about how resources were allocated across the week.

### Six Animal Types

Bar Pedaiah offers a different explanation: *kineged shisha behemot* — corresponding to six types of animals. The enumeration runs as follows: a cow (*par*), a calf (*egel*), a goat (*sa'ir*), a ram (*ayil*), a young goat (*gedi*), and a lamb (*taleh*). Just as with the explanation based on *batei avot*, one can ask whether *kineged* here is purely symbolic or whether it means the funds in each box were literally designated to purchase a specific type of animal. Here too, it would appear that each *shofar* was marked — or assumed — to fund *olot* of a particular species.

### Six Korban Origins

Shmuel offers yet another reading: *kineged shisha korbanot* — corresponding to six types of *korbanot*, meaning six distinct origins of the funds deposited. These are: *kinei zavim*, *kinei zavot*, *kinei yoldot*, *chatatot*, *ashamot*, *menachot*, and *asirit ha-eifah*. The count requires some explanation, since several of these are obligatory rather than voluntary offerings, and the total enumeration seems to exceed six, suggesting some question about the *girsa*. The commentators understand that what the *shofar* received was not the *korban* itself but leftover money originally sanctified for these purposes. Funds remaining after a *chatat*, an *asham*, a *minchah*, or an *asirit ha-eifah* — including the *Kohen Gadol*'s daily personal *minchah* — would be deposited here. This explanation is the hardest to follow intuitively: while it is clear why you might want separate boxes based on the day of service or the species of animal, why the *origin* of the funds would necessitate distinct *shofarot* is considerably less obvious.

### Large Volume Rationale

Rabbi Yochanan provides a simpler, more pragmatic answer: *al yedei she-hanedava meruba ribbu lo shofarot harbe* — because the *nedavah* donations were so numerous and the fund so large, they simply maintained multiple *shofarot*. On this reading, there is nothing architecturally meaningful about the number six; it is merely that the volume of money flowing into this fund — from leftover *chatat* and *asham* funds, from personal donations, and from other sources — was so great that a single box could not accommodate it.

### Preventing Family Disputes

The *Korban HaEdah*'s explanation, which has already been introduced, provides the most detailed rationale for the system based on *batei avot*. The passage reads that since each family working on a given day would be entitled to whatever benefit derived from the *korbanot* brought on that day — whether hides, meat portions, or other entitlements depending on the type of *korban* — a single communal *nedavah* fund would have generated constant disputes. A family whose day was busy but which drew little from the *nedavah* fund would resent a family whose day drew heavily on those same communal resources. To forestall such conflicts entirely, each family was given its own dedicated *shofar*, and each family's entitlements were tied exclusively to what was raised and used on its own day. The logic holds even if it leaves some questions open — for instance, what happened to unclaimed funds from one family's box when the next *mishmar* rotated in — but the structural intention is clear: separate funds prevent quarrels.

It is worth noting that there is a certain tension in how we picture the *kehuna* here. On one hand, the *kohanim* are renowned for their precision and diligence in the *avodah*. On the other hand, the Talmud records their intense competitiveness and passion. These qualities are not contradictory — they are expressions of the same fervor applied in different directions.

To summarize the different explanations: some link the six *shofarot* to the six days of the priestly family rotation; others link them to the six species of sacrificial animals; still others to the six origins from which *nedavah* funds derived; and Rabbi Yochanan simply notes the large volume of donations as the practical impetus.

---

## Yehoyada & King's Boxes

### Two Locations

The *gemara* now cites the *pesukim* bearing on the collection boxes from the time of *Yehoyada HaKohen*. Two biblical passages describe the donation arrangements: *Melachim* records that *Yehoyada* took a box and placed it *etsel hamizbeach miyamin* — beside the *mizbeach* on the right — while *Divrei HaYamim* (chapter 24) records that the king ordered the box to be placed *beshaar beit Hashem hachutza* — at the outer gate of the Temple. The statement of Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rav Yonatan is that there were in fact two separate *nedavot*, two distinct collections — which accounts for the two divergent descriptions. The *pasuk* of *Divrei HaYamim* also seems to indicate that the money from one collection was used to purchase *klei shareit*, while *Melachim* says explicitly that the money was *not* to be used for *klei shareit* — further evidence that two different boxes with two different purposes are being described.

### King's Reform

The *baraita* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael reconciles the two locations somewhat differently. Rav Huna explains: *mipnei ha-teme'im* — because of those in a state of *tumah*. The *Korban HaEdah* elaborates: there was originally only one *nedavah* box, and *Yehoyada* placed it inside, *etsel hamizbeach*, within the *azarah*. The king subsequently ordered it relocated to the outer gate — outside the *azarah* — so that those who were *temei met* or *tamei sheretz*, who were permitted to enter the *Har HaBayit* but not the *azarah*, could also contribute.

### Reconciliation

The *Korban HaEdah* ultimately concludes that the evidence compels the view that there were indeed two separate *nedavot* — one for interior use and one for exterior access — since the contradictions between the two biblical accounts extend not only to the location of the box but also to its designated purpose. One was used for *klei shareit*; the other was not. These simply cannot be describing the same box at two moments in time.

---

## Found Coins Principle

### Shekalim-Nedavah Case

With the close of the preceding *perek*, the *gemara* transitions into a new topic: what is the halachic status of coins found in ambiguous locations — that is, between two *shofarot* designated for different purposes? The *mishnah* opens: *ma'ot she-nimtzu bein ha-shekalim la-nedavah* — coins found between the *shofar* for *shekalim* and the one for *nedavah*. The rule: if they are closer to the *shekalim* box, they go to *shekalim*; if closer to the *nedavah* box, they go to *nedavah*; and if equidistant — *mechtza l'mechtza* — they go to *nedavah*.

This invokes the halachic principle of *karov* — proximity. This principle holds that when the origin of an object is uncertain, we assume it came from the nearest source. The *Bavli* derives this principle from the passage about the *eglah arufah* — the city closest to an unidentified corpse bears the responsibility. (Famously, Rabbi Yirmiyah asked what happens if the corpse's foot is in one jurisdiction and the rest is in another — and was reportedly expelled from the *beit midrash* for that question.)

### Circular Arrangement

A difficulty immediately presents itself: how can a coin be found *between* the *shekalim* box and the *nedavah* boxes? On a linear arrangement, these two would be at opposite ends of the row, not adjacent. The answer, provided by Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Pinchas, is that the *shofarot* were arranged in a circle — *k'min brukhliya hayu osin* — like some sort of circular vessel. In a circular arrangement, the *nedavah* boxes at one end of the arc could be adjacent to the *shekalim* box at the other, making the scenario of a coin found between them perfectly plausible.

This resolves the scenario posed by the *mishnah* but does not fully explain why the *mishnah* omits so many other possible scenarios — coins between *shekalim* and *kinnim*, between *gozlei olah* and *etzim*, between *levonah* and *zahav*, and so on. The *gemara* does not address all of these omissions, and a number of possible combinations go undiscussed.

### Other Box Pairs

The *mishnah* then extends the same proximity principle to additional pairs of *shofarot*: between *etzim* and *levonah*, closer to either goes to that box; *mechtza l'mechtza* goes to *levonah*. Between *kinnim* and *gozlei olah* — the *kinnim* being, according to Rabbi Meir's view, pairs designated for *chatat-olah* combinations, and *gozlei olah* being birds designated exclusively as *olot* — closer to either goes to that box; *mechtza l'mechtza* goes to *gozlei olah*.

### Home Coins

The final case moves outside the *Beit HaMikdash* entirely: coins found at home between a person's regular funds (*chullin*) and their *maaser sheni* money — funds that must be brought to *Yerushalayim* and used to purchase food and offerings. The same proximity rule applies: closer to the *chullin* wallet goes to *chullin*; closer to the *maaser sheni* pouch goes to *maaser sheni*; and equidistant goes to *maaser sheni*. The *mishnah* articulates the underlying principle: *zeh haklal, holchin achar hakarov l'hakel; mechtza l'mechtza l'hachmir* — we follow proximity to rule leniently; when equidistant, we rule stringently.

This last case is the most intuitive: when in doubt, treat the money as consecrated in order to play it safe. The earlier cases are more complex, and the *gemara* will work to explain why the *nedavah* default — and the *gozlei olah* and *levonah* defaults — represent the *machmir* position in each of those contexts.

One might also ask why these ambiguities cannot be resolved simply through conditional *pidyon* — a stipulated redemption. One might say: if this coin is *nedavah*, transfer its sanctity to a second coin; if it is *shekalim*, transfer its sanctity to a third coin, so that each category ends up properly designated. The *mishnah* does not pursue this approach, and the *gemara* will not fully explain why.

### Why Nedavah Default

The *gemara* asks directly: why, when coins are equidistant between *shekalim* and *nedavah*, do they go to *nedavah* and not to *shekalim*? Two answers are offered.

The first: *shema yiplu l'shirei halishka* — lest they fall to *shirei halishka*, the surplus Temple funds. If the coin is placed in the *shekalim* box and turns out to be *nedavah* money, it may end up treated as leftover *terumah* funds — which, by an established stipulation, could be used for the walls of *Yerushalayim* and other broadly civic purposes. But money genuinely consecrated as a *nedavah* for an *olah* cannot be redirected to such non-sacrificial purposes. Therefore we cannot risk placing *nedavah* money into the *shekalim* channel, since that risks its eventual misappropriation for uses incompatible with its sanctity.

The second answer invokes a halachic parallel: *mechtza l'mechtza k'mi she-met* — being equidistant is like the case of one who died. Specifically, this refers to someone who set aside a *shekel* and then died before delivering it to the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *gemara* records that Rabbi Yosi reports having been present in *Bavel* and heard Rav Yehuda ask Shmuel: if someone separated his *shekel* and died — *hifrish shiklo u-met* — what is done with those funds? The answer: *yiplu l'nedavah* — they go to the *nedavah* fund. This principle is consistent with the treatment of other stranded sacred funds: just as leftover money from a *chatat* or an *asham* goes to the *nedavah* fund when the original purpose cannot be fulfilled, so too a *shekel* whose owner has died cannot be applied to the *shekel* obligation — that obligation was personal — and so it flows into the *nedavah* fund as a general consecrated resource. The *nedavah* thus serves as a halachic catchall for sanctified money that can no longer be applied to its designated purpose.

The analogy to equidistant coins follows: a coin that might be a *shekel* but cannot be established as such is analogous to a *shekel* that cannot be used — and therefore, like that *shekel*, it defaults to *nedavah*.

The first answer — concern over *shirei halishka* — reflects an asymmetry of risk: placing genuine *nedavah* money into the *shekalim* channel may ultimately lead to its use for non-sacrificial purposes, which is worse than the reverse. The second answer is more structural: *halakha* converts unusable *shekel* funds into *nedavah* funds, and the equidistant coin is treated as a case of an unusable *shekel* and converted accordingly.

A related case is then mentioned: if the *Kohen Gadol* separated money for his *asirit ha-eifah* — the personal *minchah* he brings daily — and then died, what is done with it? Rabbi Yochanan says it must be disposed of — cast into the *Yam HaMelach* — and cannot be converted into *nedavah* funds. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees and says it goes to *nedavah*. Without resolving all the details that distinguish the *Kohen Gadol*'s *minchah* from other stranded funds, what is evident is the same underlying theme: *nedavah* serves as the natural repository for sanctified funds that have lost their original purpose — which is precisely why, under conditions of doubt, coins default to that category.

The *Rambam* offers an interesting synthesis of the default rules throughout the *mishnah*. Rather than relying solely on the two reasons given by the *gemara* for the *nedavah* default, the *Rambam* suggests that *l'hachmir* — stringency — is itself the organizing principle. Going to *nedavah* rather than *shekalim* is more stringent because the *nedavah* fund is used exclusively for *olot*, all of which is entirely consumed on the *mizbeach*, whereas the *shekalim* fund supports communal *korbanot* that include *chatatot*, from which *kohanim* eat. Similarly, *gozlei olah* is more stringent than *kinnim* because *kinnim* include a *chatat*, while *gozlei olah* are pure *olot*. By parallel reasoning, *levonah* is more stringent than *etzim* because *levonah* is itself a *korban* that is fully burned, making it a more complete form of *hekdesh* than wood, which is only fuel. This explains the three default rules — *shekalim* to *nedavah*, *kinnim* to *gozlei olah*, *etzim* to *levonah* — as all expressions of the single principle of *machmir*, even though the *gemara* does not spell out this reasoning explicitly for each case.

---

## Kinnim-Olah Resolution

### Initial Challenges

The *gemara* now addresses a more serious set of difficulties raised by the *mishnah*'s ruling that equidistant coins between *kinnim* and *gozlei olah* go to *gozlei olah*. The problem is twofold.

First: *v'yesh chatat kreviha olah* — if the coin was money designated for a *chatat* bird, how can it simply be applied toward an *olah*? Even granting the general principle that leftover *chatat* funds become *olah* funds, this is typically in the context of non-bird offerings. Bird *korbanot* operate under distinct rules, and using *chatat* money directly for an *olah* — especially in bird form — is not straightforward.

Second, and more urgently: what about the woman who deposited money for her *kinnim* — typically a pair of birds, one as a *chatat* and one as an *olah*, brought by a woman after childbirth or by a *zav* or *zavah* as part of a purification process? This is not a discretionary offering. Without the *chatat*, her purification is incomplete. If her money is now diverted to the *gozlei olah* fund, her *korban* will not be brought, and she will not achieve *taharah*. This is a serious problem — not the misallocation of a freewill donation, but the failure to complete an obligatory purification process.

### Conversion Stipulation

The first problem — using *chatat* money for an *olah* — is answered by Chizkiyah in the name of Reish Lakish: *tnai beit din hu al hamosarot she-yikrevu olot* — it is a standing stipulation of the rabbinic court that leftover or unresolved funds originally designated for a *chatat* should be brought as *olot*. This is an application of the broader principle *kol hamakdish ada'ata d'rabbanan makdish* — whoever consecrates does so subject to the conditions established by the Sages. Since *beit din* has issued a blanket stipulation, any money set aside for a *chatat* that cannot be used for its original purpose automatically assumes the status of *olah* funds by virtue of that standing condition.

### Supplier Obligation

The second problem — securing the woman's purification when her money has been reallocated — is addressed by Rav Yitzchak: *tnai beit din hu; hamefasek et ha-kinnim, hu mefasek et ha-psulot ve-et ha-avudot* — it is a standing stipulation of the rabbinic court that the supplier of the birds is obligated to make good any birds that are lost or found invalid, beyond the initial supply he delivers. The arrangement works as follows: the *beit din* holds a certain sum in its *kinnim* box and contracts with a bird supplier — in exchange for the advantages of regular, high-volume Temple business, the supplier accepts unfavorable contractual conditions, including the obligation to replace any birds that turn out to be *pasul* or that go missing. Under this standing stipulation, the box's uncertainty is included within that obligation. If there is a doubt whether a particular coin belonged to the *kinnim* fund, the supplier must provide the corresponding bird anyway. The money goes to the *gozlei olah* fund, but the woman's *korban* is secured through the supplier's contractual liability. The only party who bears the cost is the supplier — but that is the arrangement he accepted as a condition of doing business with the *Beit HaMikdash*.

This has no bearing on questions of ordering or timing of the two birds within the *kin* — those are matters for Masechet Kinnim — but it does fully resolve the concern about the woman's purification.

The *gemara* then notes that the *mishnah*'s closing rule — *zeh haklal, holchin achar hakarov; mechtza l'mechtza l'hachmir* — is sufficient to cover all the unlisted scenarios, such as coins between *ktores* and *etzim*, or between *levonah* and *zahav l'kapara*. The principle of *machmir* governs them all, even though the *gemara* does not specify which side is *machmir* in each of these cases.

---

## Found Money Jerusale (II)

### Sellers' Context

The *gemara* now moves to a new and well-known *mishnah* — one cited frequently in the *Bavli* — dealing with money found in various parts of *Yerushalayim*. *Ma'ot she-nimtze'u lifnei sochrei beheima* — coins found in front of the animal sellers in *Yerushalayim* — are assumed, *le'olam*, at all times of the year, to be *maaser sheni* money.

### Maaser Assumption

The reason for this assumption is the sheer prevalence of *maaser sheni* funds in *Yerushalayim*. A farmer with a substantial yield might have the equivalent of thousands of dollars in *maaser sheni* money — a tenth of his produce — which he would bring to *Yerushalayim* whenever he made the pilgrimage. That sum could be far more than he could spend on food during his stay. The money would circulate: shared with friends, relatives, or given to others. But the primary and classic use of *maaser sheni* money was to purchase food consumed *lifnei Hashem*, and the paradigmatic expression of *achilah lifnei Hashem* is *shelamim*. The *mishnah* therefore assumes that the dominant use of *maaser sheni* funds in *Yerushalayim* was to purchase animals for *shelamim* — so much so that virtually all the money flowing through the animal market was *maaser sheni* funds.

### Seasonal Variation

Outside the immediate context of the animal market, the presumption differs. *Uv'har habayit* — on the *Har HaBayit* — found coins are presumed *chullin*. In the rest of *Yerushalayim*, the ruling depends on the time of year: *bish'ar kol yemot hashana*, during regular periods of the year, coins are presumed *chullin*; but *uv'sh'at haregel*, during the pilgrimage festival period, all coins found in *Yerushalayim* are presumed *maaser sheni*, because the entire city is flooded with pilgrims carrying their *maaser* funds.

### Sweeping Rationale

The question then arises: if during the *regel* all coins in *Yerushalayim* are presumed *maaser sheni*, why does the same not apply to the *Har HaBayit*? The answer lies in a practice unique to *Yerushalayim*: the streets were swept daily. Because of this daily sweeping, any money found in the street could be assumed to have been dropped recently, and its identity could therefore be determined based on the current time of year. During the *regel*, recent money is *maaser* money. Outside the *regel*, recent money is *chullin*.

The *Har HaBayit*, by contrast, was not swept regularly. Two factors exempted it from this need: first, people were forbidden from entering the *Har HaBayit* with dust on their feet, so it accumulated little debris; second, the elevated and wind-exposed terrain contributed to natural cleaning. Because the *Har HaBayit* was not swept daily, money found there could not be assumed to be recently dropped — it might have been lying there for weeks or months. Therefore one cannot rely on the time of year to determine its status, and it defaults to *chullin* year-round.

---

## Found Meat Rules

### Temple Courtyard Meat

The *mishnah* turns from money to meat. *Basar ha-nimtza ba-azarah* — meat found in the Temple courtyard. The only meat present in the *azarah* was from offerings: *olot*, which are dismembered and burned on the *mizbeach*, and *chatat* and *asham*, the portions of which are eaten by the *kohanim* in the *azarah*. The rule is: if the meat is in the form of *eivarim* — whole limbs — it is assumed to be *olah*, since that is how an *olah* appears after slaughter (dismembered). If it is *chatichos* — cut into slices or portions — it is assumed to be *chatat*, since that is how the *kohanim*'s portion appears. *Shelamim* would not remain in the *azarah*, as that is a *kodshim kalim* and the *be'alim* take it out immediately.

### Jerusalem Meat

Meat found in *Yerushalayim* itself — outside the *azarah* — is presumed to be *shelamim*. This follows naturally from the previous discussion: if the dominant use of *maaser sheni* money is to purchase animals as *shelamim*, then the meat found in the city is most likely *shelamim* as well.

In either case, whether the meat is assumed to be *olah*, *chatat*, or *shelamim*, the *mishnah* rules: *ta'avor tzurato v'yeitzei l'beit hasreifah* — one must allow its form to pass, meaning allow a day to pass until it becomes *nosar* (*noticeably stale and no longer fit*), and then burn it at the *beit hasreifah*.

---

## Outside Jerusalem Me (II)

### Limb-Piece Distinction

Meat found outside *Yerushalayim* — in the surrounding territory — follows a different set of presumptions. If found in the form of whole *eivarim*, it is presumed to be *neveilah* — an animal that was not slaughtered through *shechitah*. The reasoning is straightforward: one does not bother to dismember a *neveilah* into neat cuts; it would be discarded whole, thrown to dogs, or sold in bulk to non-Jewish butchers. If, however, the meat is found as *chatichos* — properly cut portions — it is presumed *mutarot*, kosher and permitted. The assumption in this latter case is that one is operating within a generally Jewish context, and in the absence of any reason to suspect improper *shechitah* or *treifah*, the meat may be consumed.

---

## Found Money Jerusale (II)

### Har HaBayit Exception

Returning to the question raised earlier about money found on the *Har HaBayit*: if the *Har HaBayit* is the location of all the *shofarot* and is awash with *shekalim*, *kinnim*, and other consecrated funds, why is money found there presumed *chullin*?

The *gemara* answers with a principle cited by Rabbi Ba and Rabbi Chiyya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *chazakah she-ein ha-kohen motzi min ha-lishka ma'ot ad she-hu mechalalan al beheimah* — there is a presumption that a *kohen* does not remove funds from the treasury chambers (*lishka*) without immediately transferring their sanctity onto the animal or object for which they are intended. In practice, consecrated money does not circulate on the *Har HaBayit* in its sanctified state; the moment it is removed from the *shofarot*, it is immediately applied toward its designated purpose and effectively desanctified as money. Any loose coins found on the *Har HaBayit* are therefore most likely *chullin* — either because they were never sanctified in the first place, or because they represent already-transferred funds now in the hands of the supplier or worker.

This remains somewhat puzzling, since even if money is converted quickly upon removal from the *shofarot*, donors must presumably bring funds onto the *Har HaBayit* before depositing them. However, the logic of the *chazakah* — reinforced by the absence of regular sweeping — supports a default of *chullin* for any coin found there.

---

## Found Meat Rules (II)

### Nosar Concern

The *mishnah*'s requirement to wait before burning meat found in the Temple courtyard or in *Yerushalayim* — *ta'avor tzurato* — prompts a closer discussion of what underlying concern drives that ruling.

### Invalidation Debate

Rabbi Eliezer in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya explains: *hisi'a da'at ta'un ibbur tzurah* — the act of taking one's eyes off sacred meat, *hesi'ach hadaat*, itself renders it invalid. According to the *Bavli*, *hesi'ach hadaat* from *basar kodesh* creates a *psul*. Therefore, even if the meat found was slaughtered today and would otherwise be perfectly fresh and valid, the fact that it was left unattended — that no one maintained proper attention over it — has already disqualified it. One cannot consume it or offer it as is; one must wait until it is definitively *pasul* due to age (*linah*) and then burn it.

Rabbi Yosi demurs: *veya'ot* — is that reading truly compelling? He argues that *hesi'ach hadaat* is not the operative concern. Rather, *l'ochlo ein ata yachol, shema nitkalkela tzuraso* — the reason one cannot eat it is simpler: perhaps the meat's form has already passed, meaning it may already be a day old and therefore *nosar*. Since we do not know when the meat was left there, we cannot be certain it is still within the time permitted for consumption or offering. Therefore we wait another day until it is definitively *pasul* through *linah* and can be burned. On Rabbi Yosi's view, *hesi'ach hadaat* has nothing to do with it; it is purely a question of age and the possibility that the meat is already *nosar*.

---

## Outside Jerusalem Me (II)

### Strung Meat Exception

The *gemara* notes an exception to the rule that whole limbs found outside *Yerushalayim* are presumed *neveilah*. If the limbs were *machruzot* — strung together on a cord — this clearly indicates they came from a butcher's market, since *neveilah* would not be packaged and displayed in that manner. Strung limbs are therefore presumed kosher and *mutarot*.

### Nine Shops Case

The *gemara* now brings the well-known case of the nine shops: nine butcher shops sell non-kosher meat and one sells kosher meat. If a person does not remember which shop he purchased from — *nischalef lo* — he must be concerned (*choshesh*) that it came from a non-kosher shop, even though nine out of ten are non-kosher. The principle at work here is *kavuah*: when the object of doubt was associated with a fixed location — a shop that stands in its place — the halachic status is treated as an even fifty-fifty doubt regardless of the actual numerical ratio. The fixed presence of the shops prevents the ordinary application of *rov*. If, however, the meat is simply found in the street — *nimtza* — the question is abstract and one goes by *rov*: the majority of butchers is followed, and the meat is treated as if it certainly came from one of the nine non-kosher shops and is forbidden.

In the reverse configuration — nine kosher shops and one non-kosher shop — the same structural distinction applies. If the person does not remember which shop he visited, it is *kavuah* and treated as a fifty-fifty doubt, so he must be concerned even though only one of nine is non-kosher. But if the meat is found in the street, one goes by *rov* and may eat it.

### Non-Jew's Meat Status

Rabbi Yochanan rules that meat found in the possession of a non-Jew — *ha-nimtza b'yad nochri* — is treated like meat found in the town square, *k'nimtza b'platya*. In other words, the question of which shop the non-Jew visited is not treated as *kavuah* from the halachic questioner's perspective. Since the Jew asking the question was not the one who stood in the shops, the *kavuah* principle does not apply to him; for him, it is equivalent to finding meat on the ground and one follows *rov* accordingly.

However, a further nuance is raised: if a non-Jew simply has meat, how can one invoke the majority of butchers at all? Perhaps he did not acquire the meat from a butcher but slaughtered his own animal — a horse, for instance — in his barn. Rabbi Yosi clarifies: the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan applies specifically when one saw the non-Jew emerge from the Jewish butchers' market (*makolin shel Yisrael*). In that case, it is known that he obtained the meat from a butcher; the only question is which one. And then one follows *rov*. If one has no knowledge of where the meat came from, no such inference is available.

### Trust Stories

The *gemara* closes with an illustrative incident from *Tzippori*. A certain person wanted to purchase meat from a *shochet* who refused to sell to him. The customer then sent a non-Jewish acquaintance to buy the meat on his behalf — and succeeded. He went back to the *shochet* and boasted that he had outsmarted him. The *shochet* replied: I knew what you were doing, and so I gave your agent *neveilah* meat. The question that arises is whether this admission undermines the trustworthiness of the *shochet* going forward — not only for this customer, but for all the butchers of *Tzippori*.

The case was brought before Rebbe. Rabbi Yirmiyah in the name of Rabbi Chanina reports Rebbe's ruling: *lo kulam minei me-asar makolin de-Tzippori* — one cannot, on the basis of this *shochet*'s statement, forbid the butchers of *Tzippori*. The admission of one butcher selling *neveilah* to a non-Jew in a specific act of spite does not cast suspicion on the general reliability of the market. Other butchers' establishments are not implicated. As for the *shochet* himself who made this statement, his personal trustworthiness is a separate question — but that too is left for continued discussion.

---

---

# Shekalim 20

## Meat Identity & Rav

### Intro: Money & Meat

The daf opens by picking up from the bottom of 19b, where the *mishna* deals with moneys that are found and the question of determining their identity. The *gemara* transitions from this into a parallel concern: finding pieces of meat and trying to determine which *korban* they came from — or whether the meat might be *nevela* rather than legitimately slaughtered. This latter issue, the identity and permissibility of found meat, becomes the primary focus as the *gemara* opens on 20a.

### Rav in Bavel

The *gemara* introduces the subject with a brief but significant biographical note: *Rav nachas l'saman* — Rav descended there, to Bavel. The phrase *ki asa Rav leBavel* appears in the *gemara* in Gittin as well, referring to Rav's famous transition from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel, where he was foundational in establishing the great *yeshivot*. Upon arriving, *chamzu meikilin* — he found that the Babylonian community was being lenient regarding meat, presumably meat found in the hands of non-Jews or meat that had not been continuously observed. And so, *v'chamir aleihon* — he was *machmir* upon them.

This is identified with the larger Talmudic category of *basar she-nisalem min ha-ayin* — meat that has passed out of one's sight. The *gemara*'s concern in that discussion is, on its face, quite far-fetched: the worry that if you look away from your meat for a moment, someone might come and substitute a different piece in its place. But the context here is important. Rav saw a community that was being broadly lenient — perhaps too quick to assume that found meat, or meat from an unobserved source, was permissible without proper scrutiny into whether it might have come from a *treif* animal. In response to that ambient leniency, he adopted an exaggerated stringency. It is worth noting, then, that some of what follows may represent *chumra* in the sense not merely of choosing the stricter of two standard *din* positions, but of an additional stringency exceeding normal halachic expectation.

### River Meat Story

The *gemara* then records a story. A certain man, *chad bar nash*, went to wash his meat by the river. The precise meaning of the Aramaic phrase is unclear, but the context is straightforward: he was washing his meat along the riverbank, it slipped from his hands — *ve'inshetsa* — and was carried downstream. He ran after it and retrieved it, *chazar bimisvaneih*, apparently with it in his sight the entire time, or at least nearly so. He sought to resume eating it.

Rav, who we have just been told was in a *machmir* mode, said to him: *assur lach* — it is forbidden to you. The reasoning: *hahi shatif nahara ve'aisi chauri denevela tachosai* — one might say that this river washed away another piece of meat, perhaps *nevela*, and deposited it in place of yours twenty feet downstream, and this is what you retrieved rather than your own.

The absurdity of this concern is self-evident, and the *gemara* itself frames it as precisely that — an extreme stringency. If you drop your meat in a river and retrieve it a few moments later, the realistic probability that an identical-looking piece of *nevela* happened to float into the exact same spot is negligible. And yet the story is presented here, one must understand, in direct response to a community that was being cavalier about the origins of their meat.

### Bird Snatching

A second story follows in the same vein. A man, *chad bar nash*, was walking in the marketplace carrying some meat, when a bird swooped down — *chatafah minei* — and snatched it from him. He ran after it, watched it drop a piece of meat, and retrieved what he assumed to be his own. Rav again declared it forbidden: *assur lach*. The reasoning: *dilma basar d'neveila hava teina* — perhaps the bird was already carrying a piece of *nevela* when it grabbed his meat, dropped the *nevela*, and flew off with his kosher piece. What he retrieved, then, would not be his own meat at all.

Again, this is plainly fantastical as a realistic concern. The only way to make sense of it is as a deliberately overstated stringency, a response to the atmosphere of excessive leniency Rav encountered upon arriving in Bavel. Unless one watched the bird uninterruptedly every single second, one cannot be certain of the exchange — and under the rubric of *basar she-nisalem min ha-ayin*, even a brief lapse in observation opens the door, however theoretically, to this kind of substitution.

---

## Found Objects

### Wine Flasks

The *gemara* now turns from meat to wine. The river known as Ginai flooded and washed away some flasks of wine — *shatif zikin*. The case came before Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Elazar, and they ruled: *yachkmon shapaya kitreihon* — let the wine pourers or wine sellers identify their knots. That is, if the owners had made distinctive knots on their flasks, and they can recognize those identifying marks, they may reclaim their property.

This case represents a meaningful contrast to Rav. Whereas Rav was *machmir* even when the meat had seemingly been in sight the entire time, here at least some recovery is permitted — provided there is a *siman*, an identifying mark. The implication is that without a *siman*, a similar concern would presumably apply to wine as well; but with one, the owner may reclaim it.

### Cheese Wheels

A parallel case: certain jugs — *nuknika* — were found in the *beit knesset* of *Buli*. The word *Buli* refers, as noted, to an administrative governing body, a Greek term — the *boule* — related, in fact, to the word that forms part of *pruzbul*. This particular *beit knesset* was presumably associated with a wealthy or civic community. The case came before Rabbi Yirmiyah, who ruled: *yachkmon sakuraya avidatehon* — let the craftsmen, those who made the identifying marks, recognize their handiwork. If they can identify their own marks on the vessels, they may assume the jugs are theirs and reclaim them.

The pattern is consistent: identification via *siman* is the key that unlocks the right to reclaim an otherwise found object.

### Roasted Goat

A markedly different case now: a roasted goat — *gdi tzli* — was found in the main street of Gufta, a *stratya*, which is a major thoroughfare (a Greek term familiar from the Bavli, from which words like "street" and "estrada" derive). *Ve'hitirua* — they declared it permissible. This stands in striking contrast to Rav's extreme stringencies.

The permissibility rested on two distinct grounds — not two reasons for a single leniency, but two separate concerns that were each resolved. First, *mishum metziah*: the question of whether one is even permitted to keep a found object, or whether one must seek out its owner. Second, *mishum rov mahallchei drachim*: the question of whether the meat itself was permissible, resolved by the fact that the majority of those who pass through that thoroughfare are Jewish.

On the first point, a *baraita* is cited: one who saves an object from a lion, from marauding troops, from an ocean wave, from a river current, or who finds something on a major street or plaza — *harei elu shelo*, it belongs to the finder. The reason: *mipnei shehabe'alim mityashin mehen* — the owners have surely despaired of recovering it. If you drop your wallet in Times Square, you do not expect to see it again. In all such cases, *ye'ush* is immediate and automatic, and the finder acquires the object.

On the second point, *rov mahallchei drachim* — the majority of passersby — resolves the concern of *shechitat nochri*. One may assume the meat was slaughtered by a Jew and is therefore kosher.

This is quite striking. One might have imagined additional concerns: perhaps the reason someone dropped a roasted goat in the street is itself a signal that something was wrong with it; perhaps even if the *shechita* was done by a Jewish *shochet*, the animal might have been a *treifah*. But the *gemara*, drawing on the logic of the *mishna* and the earlier discussions, is willing to follow normal probabilities and declare the meat permissible — a position entirely at odds with the stringencies of Rav just discussed.

### Ye'ush Principle

The *gemara* elaborates on the *mishum metziah* principle. *Ye'ush* — the owner's loss of hope — operates as an automatic mechanism in certain defined circumstances. In contexts where recovery is objectively impossible or virtually so (an object about to be devoured by a lion, washed away by a river, or lost in the middle of a major public thoroughfare), the law does not require the owner to consciously articulate despair. The hopelessness is presumed, and the finder accordingly acquires the object.

It is worth noting the terminology here. *Rov mahallchei drachim* is not itself the category being resolved; rather, it is the *reason* to be lenient about the underlying category, which is the concern about *nevela* and non-Jewish meat. *Mishum metziah*, meanwhile, is itself the category being addressed. The phrasing is slightly unusual but precise.

### Goat Validation

The story of the roasted goat concludes with a remarkable postscript: *ve'ishtachach min d'vei Rabbi* — it was subsequently discovered that the meat had in fact originated from the household of Rabbi. The factual outcome thus confirmed the halachic reasoning. Not only did the *gemara* bracket Rav's stringencies and arrive at a more lenient position, but the empirical reality bore out that the lenient ruling was correct.

Similarly, a wheel of cheese — *igoola d'goofna*, literally a pressed circular wheel — was found in the inn of Levi, an establishment apparently doing brisk business with high foot traffic. Here too, permissibility was declared on two grounds: *mishum metziah*, since the inn's throughput made *ye'ush* immediate, and *mishum rov mahallchei drachim*, resolving the concern of *gvinat ovdei kochavim*, since the majority of patrons were Jewish. The same *baraita* about saving objects from lions and rivers and major thoroughfares is cited again in support. And again, the story concludes with a validating postscript: *ve'ishtachach mid'Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yosei* — the cheese turned out to have come from the household of Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yosei.

---

## Theory vs Practice

### Mani's Challenge

Rabbi Mani addressed Rabbi Yose with a challenging observation: *ve'anan chamian rabanan machrizin* — all of this is fine in theory, but in practice, we actually see that *rabanan* are more stringent, not about the *kashrut* question, but about *returning* the object. That is, even in cases where *ye'ush* has technically occurred and the finder is halachically entitled to keep the object, people nonetheless announce their find and attempt to return it to the owner.

This is a fascinating inversion of the expected trajectory. If you had predicted that the *gemara* would end with a *chumra*, you would have guessed it was reverting to Rav's position on *kashrut*. Instead, the *chumra* appears in the domain of *metziah* and *hashavas aveidah* — returning lost objects. Note too that if the objects had *simanim*, as implied by the cheese and goat stories, *ye'ush* alone does not fully settle the owner's claim — the *siman* remained a live avenue for identification and return, and apparently people acted on it.

### Yona's Wallet

Rabbi Yose responded to Rabbi Mani with a personal anecdote. He said: you, Rabbi Mani, I know you personally would not keep such a wallet even if you found it in Times Square. But *Rabbi Yona abuch* — your father Rabbi Yona — did not say that. What did he say? *Halevai kad nishkach min piyusa ulegav* — he said: I only wish that if I find a wallet, I find it in the middle of a major thoroughfare — meaning, I hope I find it in a place that allows me to keep it. In other words, Rabbi Yona expressed the quite natural sentiment of hoping to be in circumstances where the *halacha* permits him to keep what he finds, rather than being obligated to seek out the owner.

### Practice Reality

Yet the *gemara* concludes: *ve'afilu kein, ashkach velo nasiv* — even so, when he actually found something, he did not keep it for himself. In practice, Rabbi Yona's behavior was more stringent than his stated theory.

There is something genuinely arresting about this passage. In the Bavli, the characteristic direction of such anecdotes is the opposite: "my father was greater than I — he would wait twenty-four hours between meat and milk; I, *nebach*, wait only until the next meal." The son is less rigorous than the father. Here, we have the son being more *frum* than the father — at least in terms of the stated theoretical position. And the *gemara* adds that even the father, in practice, returned what he found.

More strikingly still, consider the asymmetry in where stringency is applied. Most people's instinct, if they were going to be more *machmir* in one domain, would be the *kashrut* dimension rather than the *hashavas aveidah* dimension. And if one were going to identify a gap between theory and practice, the common expectation would be that the *yetzer hara* pushes a person toward leniency in practice relative to their theoretical *psak*. Here it is the exact reverse: the *psak* is lenient, but real people with real objects and real owners in front of them act with greater stringency in practice. The criterion for being more *frum* turns out to be returning the lost object, not holding the meat to a higher standard.

This discussion also effectively brackets Rav's stringencies. The Yerushalmi makes no attempt to rehabilitate Rav's position on *basar she-nisalem min ha-ayin*. Even the note that Rav was *machmir* because he found an unusually lenient community in Bavel — meaning the Eretz Yisrael tradition was different — does not salvage his rulings here. In the Bavli as well, of course, Rav's move to Bavel is what gave his stringencies their foothold; but the present daf makes clear that at least in the Palestinian tradition, his concerns were not the governing standard.

---

## Animals Jerusalem

### Mishna Animals

The *gemara* now turns to the next *mishna*, which returns to the broader theme of identifying found objects and their halachic status. *Beheimah shenimtzeit miyerushalayim ve'ad migdal eder* — an animal found anywhere between Jerusalem and Migdal Eder. Migdal Eder is a nearby village, and *uchmidasah lechol ruach* — that radius applies in all directions around Jerusalem. Found animals in this zone are assumed to have originated in Jerusalem.

The extension of the radius is necessary because, unlike pieces of meat, live animals move on their own. An animal might have started in Jerusalem, been designated as a *korban*, and wandered out. We therefore apply the same presumption about Jerusalemite animals even at some distance from the city walls.

Given this presumption, the *mishna* rules: *zecharim olos* — male animals found in this zone are to be treated as *olos*, since males are eligible for *olas*. *Unekeivot zivchei shelamim* — females, which cannot be brought as *olos*, are presumed to be *shelamim*.

The logic of the *shelamim* presumption connects to the earlier discussion: the prevailing use of *ma'aser sheni* funds in Jerusalem generated a constant stream of *shelamim* offerings, making *shelamim* the statistically dominant *korban* in the city. The assumption that found females are *shelamim* follows naturally from this demographic reality.

Rabbi Yehuda adds a qualification: *hara'uy lapesachim kodem haregel shloshim yom* — if the animal is fit for a *pesach* offering (a male sheep or goat under one year old), and we are within thirty days before Pesach — from after Purim onward — then we presume it is a *pesach* offering. At that season, the most likely purpose for such an animal is the *korban pesach*.

### Status Problem
