This raises the obvious question: if the prior *mishna* established that the dominant *korban* in Jerusalem is *shelamim* — so much so that even found meat is presumed to be *shelamim* — why do we not assume that male animals are also *shelamim*? After all, a *shelamim* may be male or female alike.

The *gemara* will engage with this difficulty in the discussions that follow. It is worth noting that the question has no fully satisfying answer at this stage. Perhaps the ruling is simply a *chumra* — treating the animal as an *olah* because that is the stricter of the two possibilities for a found male animal. But then one wonders whether it is consistent with the earlier tendency to follow likelihoods, which there led to *leniency* rather than to *stringency*. The *gemara* does not resolve this tension cleanly.

---

## Takanot Found Animal (II)

### Nesachim Rule

*Barishonah* — originally, the rule was *hayu memashkenin et motzah ad shehu mevi nesacheha* — they would take collateral from the person who found and turned in the wandering animal until he brought the *nesachim* — the libation offerings that accompany an *olah*. The finder, it seems, was expected to bear the cost of the *nesachim*, even though the animal was not his *korban* to begin with.

The result was predictable: *chazru lihyot manichin osah uvorchin* — people began abandoning the animals and fleeing in the opposite direction whenever they saw a stray sanctified animal. No one wanted the financial and logistical burden of supplying *nesachim* for someone else's *korban*. In response, *hitkinu beit din shenesacheha ba'in mishal tzibbur* — the *beit din* enacted that the *nesachim* for such found animals would be supplied from communal funds. This enactment is one of the items that belongs to a broader list of seven.

### Seven Takanot

Rabbi Shimon introduces these seven enactments of *beit din* — *shivah devarim hitkinu beit din*. The case of the found animal is one of them. Among the others:

A non-Jew who sent a *korban* from overseas — *nochri she-sholach olato mimedinat ha-yam* — and included funds for *nesachim* will have the *nesachim* brought from his own money; if he did not send funds, the *nesachim* are brought from communal funds. We know the tragic story of what happened when this principle was violated at the end of the Second Temple period, but the operative rule is that a non-Jew's *korban* is not turned away for lack of *nesachim* funds when the donor is simply inaccessible.

Similarly, *ve-chen ger she-met* — a convert who died without heirs. Because a convert who dies without children is considered to have no legal heirs, his estate is technically *hefker*. If he left behind animals that had been sanctified as *korbanos*, and his estate includes funds for *nesachim*, those funds are drawn upon; if not, communal funds are used. The case raises some interesting questions about how a lien on a seized estate would operate in practice, but the operative *takana* is clear: if there are no funds available, *nesachim* come from *mishal tzibbur*.

In both cases — the non-Jew overseas and the deceased convert — the common denominator is that the owner of the *korban* is not accessible to be asked for payment.

---

## Takanot Found Animal (II)

### Tenai Beit Din

The *mishna* then introduces a distinct conceptual category: *u-tenai beit din hu* — and this is a *tenai beit din*. The phrase now takes on a more specific meaning than the earlier *takanos*, which were primarily about funding. *Tenai beit din* in this context means a stipulation through which *beit din* defines how *kedusha* itself operates — adjusting the rules by which sanctified property is governed.

The first application: *al kohen gadol she-met she-tehe minchato kereva mishal tzibbur* — when the *kohen gadol* dies, his daily *mincha* offering (brought half in the morning and half in the afternoon) continues to be brought, funded from communal property. Rabbi Yehuda adds that it comes *mishal yorshim* — from the heirs of the deceased *kohen gadol*. The implicit assumption in Rabbi Yehuda's view is that the dead *kohen gadol* retains some continuing obligation even after his death, such that his heirs bear the cost.

*U-shelemah hayetah kereva* — Rabbi Yehuda adds further that when it is brought under these circumstances, it is brought as a whole unit, not divided into two halves as the *kohen gadol* himself would have divided it.

The subsequent *takanot* more clearly exemplify the *tenai beit din* mechanism in its technical sense. *Al ha-melach ve-al ha-etzim she-ha-kohanim ne'otim ba-hem* — a stipulation that the salt and wood in the *beit hamikdash*, which were designated for use in the *korbanos* and for salting meat per the verse *al kol korbancha takriv melach*, the *kohanim* may use for roasting and salting the *korban* meat that they themselves eat. This would ordinarily constitute *me'ilah* — misappropriation of consecrated property — since the salt and wood are *hekdesh*. The *tenai beit din* operates here not merely to redirect funds but to define the scope of the *kedusha* itself: by stipulating from the outset that these items may be used for this purpose, the *beit din* prevents the *me'ilah* category from applying.

*Ve'al haparah shelo ye'u mo'alin be'afarah* — and a stipulation that there be no *me'ilah* with the ashes of the *parah adumah* after it has been burned. The question of why *me'ilah* would apply at all is itself worth examining — the fact that the ashes are used for a *mitzvah* does not by itself negate *me'ilah*, since *mitzvos lav lehanos nitnu*.

*Ve'al hakinim hapesulot* — regarding invalid bird offerings. If birds purchased from the *shofer* fund turned out to be *pasul*, the first answer is that replacement birds are supplied from communal funds. Rabbi Yosi, however, holds that the supplier himself must replace *pasul* birds — *hamaspek et hakinim hu maspek et hapesulot* — as a condition of his supply contract. This is, once more, an application of *tenai beit din* in the sense of stipulating conditions that govern how the relationship between the consecrated objects and the parties involved will operate.

---

## Gemara Challenge

### Hoshaya Value

The *gemara* now confronts the *mishna* about found animals directly. Rabbi Oshaya Rabba — *Rebbi Oshaya the great* — proposes: *lavo bidmeihem shanu* — the *mishna* is not speaking of bringing the animals themselves; it is speaking of bringing their monetary value. The procedure he envisions is one of transfer: the finder takes the found animal, transfers its *kedusha* to money, and with that money purchases the appropriate *korbanos*.

The reason for this maneuver is to cover multiple bases. We are not certain whether this animal is an *olah* or a *shelamim*. If we bring the animal itself as an *olah*, we may be wrong. But if we transfer the *kedusha* conditionally to money — if it is an *olah*, this money is sanctified as an *olah*; if it is a *shelamim*, this other money is sanctified as a *shelamim* — we can then bring both an *olah* and a *shelamim* with their respective funds, one representing the original animal and one as a new *korban*, and the bases are covered. The problem is that the *mishna* does not describe this procedure; it speaks of the animal itself.

### Yochanan Objection

Rabbi Yochanan objected: *omrin lo l'adam tze u-meal b'kodshim?* — do we tell a person to go and commit *me'ilah* with consecrated property? The *meforshim* note that Rabbi Yochanan does not literally mean the *me'ilah* prohibition in the technical sense here, but he is invoking the principle that one may not redeem a *korban* that has no *mum* — no blemish — transferring its *kedusha* to money. That is the operative prohibition: *podeh tmimim*, redeeming an unblemished animal, is not permitted under normal circumstances. How can Rabbi Oshaya Rabba suggest doing exactly this?

### Majority Solution

Rabbi Yochanan therefore proposes the simpler answer: *manach acharei harov* — you follow the majority. There is no need to cover bases or transfer *kedusha* to money. The animal itself is brought; you apply the rule of *rov* and treat it accordingly. Males are brought as *olos* because we follow the majority.

But this raises the persistent difficulty: why are males *olos* rather than *shelamim*? Rabbi Yochanan appears to address this by suggesting that if you found a flock of animals, you assess the makeup: *im rov zecharim olah, im rov nekeivot zivchei shelamim* — if the majority are male, the animals are *olos*; if the majority are female, they are *shelamim*. The problem with this reading, as the *gemara* immediately notes, is that *shelamim* can come from both males and females — *ein shelamim ba'in min hazecharim u-min hanekeivot* — so even a majority of males does not resolve whether they are *olos* or *shelamim*. And what happens if you find only one animal? The answer remains unclear, and the *meforshim* genuinely struggle here.

The *gemara* then suggests: *motzi'an l'chullin v'chozer v'oseh osan olos* — take them out to *chullin* and then make them *olos*. This would involve a conditional transfer: if the animal is an *olah*, transfer its *kedusha* to money; if it is a *shelamim*, transfer it to other money; then use that money to acquire an *olah* and a *shelamim*, and then retransfer the *kedusha* from the *olah* money back to the animal, restoring it as an *olah*. But as the *meforshim* note, this procedure is deeply problematic — we have never heard of redeeming an unblemished animal with the intent of re-sanctifying it, and the *mishna* nowhere describes anything like this. Some *meforshim* suggest this is not an answer at all, but rather a rhetorical continuation of the question: *do you want him* to perform this elaborate and questionable procedure? The discussion is genuinely unresolved.

### Zeira Parallel

Rabbi Zeira offers a more coherent answer. *K'ma d'at amar taman* — the same logic applied in the previously discussed case applies here. We have been learning for the past two days that leftover money from a *chatat* or *asham* goes to the *nedava* fund — the *olah* fund. Whether someone dies after separating his *shekel*, or whether various ambiguities arise about sanctified funds, the operative rule is: *yiplu l'nedava*, it goes into the *olah* fund. This has been established as *tenai beit din* for those cases.

Rabbi Zeira argues: *tenai beit din hu al avudot sheyikrevu olos* — *beit din* stipulates the same for lost animals. When you find a lost animal and do not know whether it is an *olah* or a *shelamim*, *beit din*'s standing stipulation determines that it becomes an *olah*. Just as the doubt about leftover money is resolved by the *nedava* rule, the doubt about a found animal's status is resolved by the same framework. Anyone who sanctifies an animal implicitly accepts all the conditions that *beit din* has stipulated, whether or not he is explicitly aware of them — a greatly expanded application of the principle of *kol hamikadesh ada'ata derabanan mikadesh*.

### Meizid Question

Rabbi Yosi raised a pointed question to Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha: *ein zeh meizid?* — is this not *meizid*, willful misapplication? In all the other cases of *tenai beit din* involving leftover funds, the money was *passively* redirected. Here, one is *actively* and *knowingly* taking an animal that might be a *shelamim* and treating it as an *olah*. Does that not cross the line into intentional misapplication of *kedusha*?

The response: *mideka tnai beit din ein zeh meizid* — since it is all part of the conditions of *beit din*, there is nothing improper about it. The stipulation is not a circumvention; it is the foundational framework within which all acts of *hekdesh* operate. The person who sanctified the animal did so within a system that has these rules built in from the start. Acting in accordance with those rules, even if one knows the animal might have been a *shelamim*, is not *meizid* — it is simply following the system as *beit din* defined it.

---

## Leftover Funds

### Shekel Death

The *gemara* records that Rabbi Yosi heard, when he was still in Bavel, the sound of Rabbi Yehuda asking Shmuel: *hifrish shekalo u-meis* — someone separated his *shekel* but died before giving it; what is the *halacha*? Shmuel replied: *yiplu l'nedava* — it falls into the *nedava* fund. This is consistent with everything we have seen: when funds have been set aside for a communal purpose and circumstances prevent their use, they go to the *olah* fund.

### Yochanan Eliezer

A distinct question: *umosar asiris haeifa shelo* — what if the *kohen gadol* sanctified money to be used for his daily *asiris ha-eifa* and there are leftover funds? Here the rulings diverge in an interesting way. Rabbi Yochanan says: *yolichem l'Yam HaMelach* — those funds are cast into the Dead Sea, not placed into the *nedava* fund. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees and says: *yiplu l'nedava* — they follow the same rule as everything else, and go into the *nedava* fund.

It is not immediately clear why Rabbi Yochanan treats this case differently. The *nedava* fund has absorbed leftovers from *chatat*, *asham*, the *shekel* of one who died, and found animals — but not, apparently, the surplus funds of the *kohen gadol*'s personal daily *mincha*. One possible distinction is that the *nedava* fund is traditionally associated with communal or quasi-communal *korbanos*, or with *korbanos* of the *chatat* and *asham* type, whereas the *kohen gadol*'s *asiris ha-eifa* is neither of those. But the *gemara* does not spell out the reason, and the ruling stands: Rabbi Yochanan says *Yam HaMelach*, Rabbi Eliezer says *nedava*.

---

## Daily Minha

### Sanctify Timing

The *gemara* now turns to a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about the mechanics of the *kohen gadol*'s daily *asiris ha-eifa*. The Torah states that it is brought *machatzisah baboker u-machatzisah ba'erev* — half in the morning, half in the afternoon.

Rabbi Yochanan holds: *chotzah osah ve'achar kach mekadeshah* — first the whole *isaron* of flour is prepared in a non-*kli shares*, then it is divided into two halves, and only then is each half placed in a *kli shares* and thereby sanctified. Sanctification follows the division.

Reish Lakish holds the reverse: *mekadeshah ve'achar kach chotzah osah* — the entire *isaron* is first placed in a *kli shares* and sanctified as a whole, and only then is it divided into two halves. Sanctification precedes the division.

### Half Lost

The *gemara* challenges Rabbi Yochanan from a *baraita*: *makriv mechtzo u-mechtzo avad* — one half was brought in the morning and the other half was then lost or became *tamei*. In such a case, an entirely new whole *isaron* is made, divided in half, and the fresh half is brought in the afternoon; the remaining half of the new preparation goes to waste.

The question for Rabbi Yochanan is: if the half that was left over was not yet in a *kli shares* — since according to his view the second half would not have been sanctified yet — why should it go to waste? Simply do not sanctify it and there is no problem. The fact that it must be wasted implies it was already sanctified, which supports Reish Lakish.

Rabbi Yochanan's answer: *she-ken afilu ma'os yelchu l'Yam HaMelach* — even the money that was set aside for the *kohen gadol*'s *asiris ha-eifa* goes to the *Yam HaMelach* if it cannot be used, as Rabbi Yochanan himself ruled just now. This implies that even without being placed in a *kli shares*, the funds already bear a *kedusha* — what one might call *kedushas peh*, the *kedusha* of verbal designation. Once something is earmarked for the *asiris ha-eifa*, even without the formal sanctification of a *kli shares*, it acquires a status that requires disposal. The leftover half of the *isaron* is similarly governed by its designation, and must be wasted even according to Rabbi Yochanan's view. The contradiction from the *baraita* is thus resolved.

The question of why the *kohen gadol*'s leftover money cannot simply be used for the following day — which would seem the obvious solution — is addressed: if the *kohen gadol* died, there is no tomorrow; and if the *mincha* itself has been in a *kli shares* overnight, it is *pasul* because of *lina*.

### Two Priests

A further *baraita*: *nimtze'u shnei chatza'in krevim u-shnei chatza'in avudin* — there is a scenario in which two halves are brought and two halves must be discarded. This occurs when one *kohen gadol* dies after bringing his morning half, and a new *kohen gadol* is appointed for the afternoon. The new appointee brings a whole, divides it, and brings his afternoon half. The morning half leftover from the first *kohen gadol* and the second half from the new *kohen gadol*'s preparation — both must be disposed of.

*V'sani ala* — a *baraita* teaches: *mechtza rishon u-mechtza sheni te'uber tzurasan v'yeitzu l'veis ha-sreifa* — both halves, the first priest's and the second's, must have their form allowed to pass — that is, one waits until they are *pasul b'lina* from being left overnight — and then they are burned. This is a stronger form of disposal than simply casting into the *Yam HaMelach*; it implies full *kedusha* requiring burning. And in particular, the second half of the new *kohen gadol*'s preparation — why would that necessarily have been placed in a *kli shares*? According to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that sanctification comes after division, there would have been no need to sanctify the second half at all.

### Isaron Sanctified

The *gemara* resolves this by citing Rabbi Yishmael: *isaron mekadesh keshe-ha-kohen mitkarev techila* — the *isaron* is sanctified when the *kohen* first approaches to perform the service. The *Korban Ha-Eda* explains: when the *kohen* measures out the *isaron* of flour, he does so in a *kli shares*. Therefore, even according to Rabbi Yochanan, the flour is actually placed in a *kli shares* and thereby sanctified before it is divided. Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about dividing before sanctifying described only the sequence of the formal act of dividing relative to the formal act of *mekadesh*; but in practice, *l'chatchila*, the *isaron* is always measured in a *kli shares* from the very beginning of the preparation.

This effectively undermines the practical difference between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. Since *l'chatchila* one always starts with a *kli shares*, the result is the same in practice. Rabbi Yochanan was speaking *b'diavad* — describing what happens if someone waited to place it in a *kli shares* until after dividing it; but normative practice would always sanctify the *isaron* first. The *baraita* about burning the leftover halves therefore poses no real challenge to Rabbi Yochanan, since it describes the standard procedure in which the *kli shares* is used from the beginning.

---

## Priest Initiation

### First Service

The *gemara* now introduces a rule about priestly initiation. *Keshe-kohen mitkarev techila la'avoda meivi asiris ha-eifa shelo* — when a *kohen* first enters the *avodah*, he brings his own *asiris ha-eifa* and himself performs the offering. This applies to any *kohen* beginning his service for the first time — not only the *kohen gadol* who brings it daily, but any *kohen* on his inaugural day.

*B'diavad*, the question of what happens if a *kohen* performed the *avodah* without having first brought his *asiris ha-eifa*: *echad kohen gadol ve'echad kohen hedyot she'avdu ad shelo heviu asiris ha-eifa shelahen* — whether a *kohen gadol* or an ordinary *kohen*, if they performed the *avodah* before bringing their initiatory *asiris ha-eifa* — *avodatan keshera b'diavad*, the service is valid after the fact, though the *Gra* has the reading *pesulah*, that it is invalid. The practical difference between these two readings is significant.

### Two Portions

Rabbi Mani then poses a case: *meimar bo bayom shenitkarev techila la'avoda bo bayom nimna lihyot kohen gadol* — suppose a man's very first day of *avodah* coincides with the day he is appointed *kohen gadol*. He has two obligations: the *asiris ha-eifa* as an initiating *kohen* beginning his service, and the regular daily *asiris ha-eifa* as *kohen gadol*. Does he bring two separate *asiris ha-eifas* — *meivi shtayim, achat l'chinucho ve'achat l'chovat hayom* — one for his initiation and one for his daily obligation? Or can a single offering serve both purposes?

The case is framed as *ba'i* — a genuine inquiry — though it is formally stated as a ruling. The question of whether the initiatory *asiris ha-eifa* and the daily obligatory one are two conceptually distinct offerings, requiring two physical performances, or whether one can discharge both, is left somewhat open by the text.

### Baking Timing

Finally, the *gemara* addresses the word *tufini* in the verse *tufini minchat pitim takriv* — the *mincha* must be baked. *Besha'at hava'a tufini* — at the time of bringing it, it must be freshly baked; *ve'ein beshachris tufini* — it may not be baked the night before, and there is no *tufini* in the morning sense that it is prepared before morning. Reading the verse carefully, since it says *takriv* alongside *tufini*, the baking must coincide with the time of offering; it cannot have been done beforehand.

This creates an apparent tension with a *baraita* cited from tractate *Middot* that describes an official announcement made before daybreak: *he'emidu osei chavitin la'asot chavitin* — those who make the *chavitin* (the technical term for the *kohen gadol*'s *asiris ha-eifa*) rise and begin their work. This sounds like the baking begins well before dawn, in darkness, contradicting the rule that the baking must be contemporaneous with the *hakrava*.

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba resolves this: *la'asot chamim lerivucha lirachva* — the pre-dawn announcement was not about beginning the actual baking. It was about heating the water and preparing the fire in advance, not the baking itself. The baking itself waited until the morning. The *gemara* continues with this discussion in the next session.

---

---

# Shekalim 21

## High Priest's Mincha

### Mincha Sources

The penultimate *daf* of *Shekalim*, 21b, opens by continuing a discussion that arose from the *mishnah*'s concern with who brings the *korban* of the *kohen gadol* once he has died — specifically his daily *minchah*, the *asirit ha'eifah*, brought half in the morning and half in the afternoon. The *gemara* now turns to how this *minchah* is prepared under ordinary circumstances before addressing the exceptional cases.

The relevant *pesukim* in Vayikra are worth laying out in full. The Torah introduces the obligation with the words *zeh korban Aharon u-vanav asher yakrivu l'Hashem beyom himashach oto* — this is the offering of Aharon and his sons that they shall bring to Hashem on the day he is anointed. The offering itself is *asirit ha-eifah solet tamid, machatzitah va-voker u-machatzitah ba-arev* — a tenth of an *eifah* of fine flour as a *tamid*, half in the morning and half in the afternoon. The method of preparation is given as *al machavat ba-shemen te'aseh, murbachet tivienah* — on a frying pan with oil, brought *murbachet*, a term understood to mean repeatedly baked. The offering is then described as *tufinei minchat pitim*. The concluding *pasuk* states: *ve-ha-kohen ha-mashiach tachtav mi-banav ya'aseh otah chok olam l'Hashem kalil tuktar* — the anointed *kohen* who succeeds him from his sons shall perform it, an eternal edict to Hashem, it shall be burned entirely. This final *pasuk* is the source for the requirement that the *kohen gadol* brings it every day, and it will also serve as the basis for several subsequent *derashot*.

### Frying vs. Baking

The *gemara* records a dispute about the order of preparation. *Rabbi Yosi b'shem Rabbi Chanina* holds: *metagnah v'achar kach ofah otah* — first you fry it and then you bake it. *Rabbi Acha b'shem Rabbi Chanina* reverses this: *ofah v'achar kach metagnah* — first you bake it and then you fry it.

### Tufinei Wordplay

The word *tufinei* then becomes the basis for a series of wordplays, each yielding a slightly different reading. One interpretation reads *tufinei* as *te'afena na* — bake it while it is still *na*, meaning partially raw or not fully baked. A second reading, attributed to *Rabbi*, is *te'afena na'eh* — bake it so that it looks nice. A third reading, attributed to *Rabbi Dosa*, is *te'afena riba* — bake it many times. There are variant textual readings noted in the margins throughout, but these three are the primary positions recorded.

### Linking Debates

The *gemara* then draws an explicit connection between these wordplays and the earlier dispute about the order of preparation: *atyan ilayn pelugta kehani pelugvata* — this debate flows from the same root issue as that debate. The one who says *te'afena na'eh*, bake it so it looks nice, corresponds to the position that you bake it first and fry it afterward (*ofah v'achar kach metagnah*), because baking first preserves the attractive appearance of the finished product. The one who reads *te'afena na*, bake it while quasi-raw, corresponds to the position that you fry it first and then bake it (*metagnah v'achar kach ofah*), since by the time you reach the baking stage it has already been partially cooked through frying and is thus no longer fully raw.

---

## Mincha Cont.

### Tamei & Mum

The *gemara* now returns to the exceptional cases raised by the *mishnah*: *lo sof davar shemet, ela afilu nitma ve'afilu nidcha mimum* — it is not only when the *kohen gadol* dies that this issue arises; even if he has become *tamei* or has been disqualified due to a physical *mum*, the *minchah* must still be brought. This observation carries its own implications. Normally, a person who is *tamei* can still have a *korban* brought on their behalf. But the *pasuk* says *ve-ha-kohen ha-mashiach tachtav ya'aseh otah* — he performs it. The assumption here is that the *kohen gadol* must himself be fit to bring the offering. When he is *tamei* or disqualified, the question of who brings it — and from whose funds — becomes relevant.

One might ask whether a *tamei kohen gadol* would simply be replaced. The answer is nuanced: on *Yom Kippur*, when the *kohen gadol* becomes *tamei* and is needed, we do indeed appoint another in his place — *memanim acher tachtav*. But if on an ordinary day he happens to become *tamei* and his presence in the *Beis HaMikdash* is not otherwise required, we do not routinely substitute him. As for who funds the *minchah* in such a case, it is not entirely clear from the text. If he is alive but *tamei*, having his heirs pay would be strange; presumably he would fund it himself, with another *kohen* performing the service — but the *gemara* does not spell this out.

### Sons Bring It

The *gemara* then poses the fundamental question: *minayin shemet velo minu acher tachtav she-tehe minchato keriva mishel yorshin?* — from where do we derive that when the *kohen gadol* dies and no replacement has been appointed, his *minchah* continues to be brought, and that it comes from the estate? The answer is a *derasha* on the concluding *pasuk*: *mibanav ya'aseh otah*. Reading the *pasuk* in isolation — not as a reference to the newly anointed *kohen gadol* who comes from the sons of the previous one, but simply as *mibanav ya'aseh otah*, his sons shall perform it — we derive that the sons bring the *minchah* after the *kohen gadol*'s death. Since the question of when sons would bring it only makes sense after their father's death, this constitutes both the source for the obligation and, by implication, the source for the estate's financial responsibility.

### Whole or Halves

A further question follows: *yachol yevienah lachatza'in?* — perhaps when the sons bring it after the *kohen gadol*'s death, they should bring it in the same manner he did — half in the morning and half in the afternoon? The *gemara* answers from the same *pasuk*: *talmud lomar otah* — *ya'aseh otah*, it shall be performed as a whole. Since the final *pasuk*, which is being read to address the posthumous situation, does not specify the splitting into halves, we derive that when the sons bring it, they bring it as a single whole unit. *Kulah amarti* — as one complete offering. This is the position of *Rabbi Yehuda*.

---

## Funding Source

### Yehuda: Heirs

The *mishnah* records the dispute about the source of funds. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds: *mishlo yorshin* — it comes from the estate of the deceased *kohen gadol*. Furthermore, *shleima hayta kerevah* — it is brought as a complete unit, not in two halves.

### Shimon: Tzibur

*Rabbi Shimon* holds: *eina ba'ah ela mishel tzibur* — it comes only from communal funds. His proof is from the word *chok olam* at the end of the *pasuk*. The *derasha*, as cited by the *Korban HaEdah*, runs as follows: *mi she-berit kerutah lo* — from the one for whom the world is covenanted, that is, God. *Chok olam* is read as referring to the *Owner* of the *olam*, God, and hence the funding comes from what belongs to God — the communal treasury of the *Beis HaMikdash*. The word *kalil tuktar* — it is burned entirely — further confirms that it is brought as one whole unit. There is thus no dispute between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* on the question of *kulah* versus *chatzi*; both agree it is brought whole. The dispute is exclusively about the source of funds.

### Scriptural or Rabbinic?

A difficulty now surfaces. In our *mishnah*, *Rabbi Shimon* presented the rule that the *minchah* comes from communal funds as one of the *takanot* enacted by *Beis Din*. Yet here the *gemara* has shown *Rabbi Shimon* deriving this very rule from a *pasuk*. Is it *de'oraita* or *takana*? *Rabbi Abba bar Mamal* raises this tension explicitly: *machlafa shitatei de-Rabbi Shimon* — *Rabbi Shimon* is contradicting himself. There it seemed that in principle it would come from the *yorshin*, with the *takana* shifting it to communal funds; here he derives from scripture that it comes from communal funds.

*Rabbi Chiya bar Ba* responds — though in the characteristic style of the Yerushalmi it is difficult to know if his remark is affirmation or further question — *v'lo ya'ut hu makshe?* Is this not a well-posed difficulty?

### Resolution

*Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha* in the name of *Rabbi Abbahu* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* provides the resolution. *Dvar Torah hu she-tehe ba min ha-tzibur* — it is indeed biblical that it comes from the *tzibur*. However, one might have thought this means a special appeal had to be made each time — *hayiti omer yigbu lah*, I would have thought they collect for it specifically. The *takana* enacted by *Beis Din* was *she-hitkinu she-tehe ba mi-trumat ha-lishka* — that it should be funded not through a special collection but from the *Trumas HaLishkah*, the standing treasury of the *Beis HaMikdash* used for communal sacrifices.

This is a subtle but important distinction. The *Trumas HaLishkah* is designated for *korbanos tzibur* — communal offerings. The *minchah* of the *kohen gadol* is formally his personal *korban*, not a communal one. The *takana* permits drawing on those funds even for this *korban*. The underlying biblical principle, then, is that the community bears financial responsibility; the *takana* specifies from which communal fund the money is drawn. The two positions are thus complementary rather than contradictory. This dual resolution has a certain conceptual elegance: the *minchah* of the *kohen gadol* occupies a liminal space, simultaneously personal and institutional. During his lifetime, the personal dimension is foregrounded — it is his *korban*, from his funds. After his death, when it continues to be brought, the institutional, *Beis HaMikdash* dimension comes to the fore, and the communal treasury absorbs the cost.

---

## Whole Unit Implications

### Tamid Concept

With the ruling established that the *minchah* is brought as a whole unit, the *gemara* explores the practical implications. *Rabbi Yosei amar Rabbi Yochanan* raises a question: *sheleimah be-shacharis u-sheleimah bein ha-arbayim* — is it still brought in two distinct presentations, a whole in the morning and a whole in the afternoon? Or *sheleimah be-shacharis u-beteilah bein ha-arbayim* — is it brought whole in the morning and nothing in the afternoon?

The *gemara* appears to resolve this by invoking the word *tamid* — *minchat tamid* — which appears in the *pasuk*. The category of *tamid* by definition requires a morning and an afternoon component: the *korban tamid* is once in the morning and once in the afternoon, the *ketores* is twice daily, the *menorah* is *tamid* through the night. A single morning offering cannot constitute a *tamid*. Therefore, on the assumption that *tamid* demands two daily presentations, the conclusion is that a complete unit is brought in the morning and a complete unit in the afternoon.

### Oil & Frankincense

With this resolved — at least as an *im timtzi lomar* — the *gemara* moves to the next question. Ordinarily, the *kohen gadol* brings half an *issaron* of flour with one and a half *log* of oil in the morning and half an *issaron* with one and a half *log* in the afternoon. Now that a full *issaron* is being brought in the morning and a full *issaron* in the afternoon, what happens with the *shemen*? *Shlosha lugin shacharis u-shlosha lugin bein ha-arbayim* — is the oil also doubled to three *log* each time? Or does it remain *log u-mechetza shacharis v-log u-mechetza bein ha-arbayim* — one and a half in the morning and one and a half in the afternoon, unchanged?

The *gemara* further extends the question to the *levonah*. By a normal *minchah* two *kematzim* of *levonah* are brought. In the standard configuration, one *kometz* accompanied each half — one in the morning and one in the afternoon. Now that each presentation is a full *issaron*, does each presentation get two *kematzim*, so that *shnei kematzim shacharis u-shnei kematzim bein ha-arbayim*? Or does each presentation retain one *kometz*?

To illustrate the structure of the problem: the full recipe is one *issaron* of flour, three *log* of oil, and two *kematzim* of *levonah*. In the standard split, each half-presentation receives half an *issaron*, one and a half *log*, and one *kometz*. The question is whether, now that the half-presentation has been expanded to a full *issaron*, the oil and *levonah* scale up proportionally or remain at their split-level amounts.

### Oil Proportion

*Rabbi Chizkiyah* addresses the question of the oil: *kula lamdu shlosha lugin mi-tamid she-bein ha-arbayim* — we derive the three *log* per *issaron* from the standard *tamid* offering of a sheep, which requires one *issaron* of *soles* with a *revi'it ha-hin* of oil, equal to three *log*. *Mah lehallan shlosha lugin, af kan shlosha lugin* — just as there it is three *log* per *issaron*, so too here it is three *log* per *issaron*. Once the flour of each presentation constitutes a full *issaron*, the standard ratio demands three *log* of oil to accompany it.

*Rabbi Yose* addresses the *levonah* question analogously: *kula lamdu l-kometz mi-minchas chotei* — the principle of the *kometz* of *levonah* in this *minchah* is derived from the *minchas chotei*, and *mah lehallan shnei kematzim, af kan shnei kematzim* — just as there, two *kematzim*, so here, two *kematzim*. The exact logic of why *shnei kematzim* per full unit follows from the *minchas chotei* is less explicit in the text, and the commentators offer various explanations.

---

## Sacred Items Rules

### Wood & Salt Use

The *gemara* now turns to a series of rabbinic ordinances governing *kedushas hamikdash* and the laws of *me'ilah*. The first concerns the *kohanim*'s use of wood and salt. The wood and salt designated for the *korbanos* — the wood for the altar fire and the salt for salting the sacrificial meat — were permitted by *Beis Din* for use by the *kohanim* to roast and salt the portions of the *korban* they themselves receive. *Rabbi Shimon Nachmani beshem Rabbi Yonasan* explains the legal background: *badin hayah she-yiheyu mo'alin bahen* — by rights there should have been *me'ilah* in using these sacred materials for personal consumption. *Ve-hen gazru shelo yim'alu bahen* — and they legislated that there would be no *me'ilah*. This is the *tnai Beis Din*, the condition under which the *kohanim* operate in their use of Temple property.

### Red Heifer Ashes

The *gemara* then transitions to the ashes of the *parah adumah*. The *mishnah* had indicated that these ashes are exempt from *me'ilah*. The *gemara* cites a *baraita* that confirms: *chatasi* — the word *chatasi* in the relevant *pasuk* teaches that *me'ilah* applies to the animal itself once sanctified, *bah mo'alin v-ein mo'alin be-afrah* — you have *me'ilah* in it but not in its ashes. Since the animal is called *chatas*, *me'ilah* applies to the animal; once burned into ashes, the *me'ilah* falls away.

This raises a question: if the Torah itself exempts the ashes from *me'ilah*, why did the *mishnah* need to present this as a rabbinic enactment? *Rabbi Abbahu* explains a three-stage historical development. Originally, the ashes were biblically exempt from *me'ilah*, and in that period people were using them freely — applying them medicinally to wounds, for example. Because the absence of *me'ilah* led to misuse, *Beis Din* imposed rabbinic *me'ilah* on the ashes as a protective measure. However, once people became aware of this *gezeirah*, they became excessively reluctant to engage with the ashes at all — to the point that they would not even be sprinkled with them for purification. The rabbis therefore reversed the *gezeirah* and returned to the biblical baseline: no *me'ilah* in the ashes. The pattern here — biblical exemption, interim rabbinic stringency, and then reversal — parallels the structure we saw in the discussion of communal versus personal funding of the posthumous *minchah*: a biblical principle, a *takana* that modified practice, and a subsequent return (or refinement) that brings us back to the underlying rule.

### Bird Replacement

The final *takana* in this section concerns the *kinnim* — bird offerings brought by a woman after *niddah*. The scenario is that a woman purchased birds from a supplier for her *korban*, but those birds died or were found to be *pesulos*. Without replacement, the woman would assume her *korban* had been brought and consider herself *tehorah*, while in fact it had not. *Rabbi Yitzchak* states: *tenai Beis Din hu — ha-maspek es ha-kinim hu maspek es ha-pesulos ve-es ha-avudos* — it is a condition imposed by *Beis Din* that the supplier who provides the birds bears responsibility to replace any that are lost or invalid. This was the arrangement under which suppliers conducted business with the *Beis HaMikdash*.

---

## Spittle Purity

### Meir's Position

With the conclusion of this *perek*, the *gemara* enters the final chapter of *Shekalim*. The *mishnah* addresses the *halachic* status of *rokim* — spit found in Yerushalayim. The concern is real: the spit of a *zav*, *zavah*, or *metzora* carries the status of an *av ha-tumah*, and if one cannot determine the source of spit found in a public space, one must assess its presumptive status. *Rabbi Meir* rules: *kol ha-rokim ha-nimtza'im bi-Yerushalayim tehorin* — all spit found in Yerushalayim is presumed *tahor*, *chutz mi-shuk ha-elyon* — with the exception of spit found in the upper marketplace, which is presumed *tamei*.

### Yose: Location

*Rabbi Yose* disagrees with this simple geographic division and instead distinguishes between the central and marginal paths throughout the city. *Bish'ar kol yemot ha-shanah* — during the rest of the year, outside the festival season, *she-ba-emtza temei'im* — spit found in the middle of the road is *tamei*, because the central path is where the general population travels without concern for *tumah* and *taharah*, and *zavim* and *zavos* will inevitably be found there. *She-ba-tziddin tehorin* — spit on the margins of the road is *tahor*, because those who walk on the sides of the road are presumed to be consciously avoiding the masses, which is attributed to a concern for *taharah* rather than mere preference.

### Festival Reversal

At the time of the *regel*, however, the presumptions reverse entirely. *She-ba-emtza tehorin, she-ba-tziddin temei'im* — the center is *tahor* and the margins are *tamei*. During the *regel*, the entire population is concerned with maintaining *taharah* for entry to the *Beis HaMikdash*, and thus the masses walking in the center are overwhelmingly *tahor*. Those on the margins, precisely because they are avoiding the crowds, are more likely to be among the minority who are *tamei* and who keep to the sides so as not to *metamei* others. As the *gemara* states: *mipnei she-hamu'atin mistalkin la-tziddin* — it is the minority that retreats to the margins.

---

## Vessel Purity

### Descent to Mikvah

The *mishnah* turns from spit to *kelim* — vessels found in Yerushalayim. The question is whether such vessels may be presumed *tahor* for use with *kodashim* or *terumah*. The *mishnah* establishes a geographic framework based on proximity to the *mikvah*. A vessel found on the road that descends to the *mikvah* is presumed *tamei*: the evident reason it is there is that its owner was bringing it to be immersed.

### Ascent from Mikvah

A vessel found on the road ascending from the *mikvah* is presumed *tahor*, on the assumption that it has already been immersed. The *mishnah* attributes this ruling to *Rabbi Meir*, who states *she-lo ke-yeridatan aliyatan* — the descent and the ascent are not symmetric in what they imply. The physical layout of the *mikvah* apparently involved separate paths for those going down and those coming up — a feature consistent with excavated *mikvaos* at the *Beis HaMikdash* which contain a central divider on the stairway.

### All Vessels Pure

*Rabbi Yose* takes a more sweeping position: *kulam tehorim* — all vessels found in Yerushalayim may be presumed *tahor*. This is a striking counterpoint to his position on spit, where he was more stringent than *Rabbi Meir* about *tumah* in public spaces. *Rabbi Meir* was more lenient about spit — presuming it *tahor* everywhere except the upper marketplace — while being more restrictive about which *kelim* may be presumed *tahor*. *Rabbi Yose* was more stringent about spit in the center of the road but more permissive about vessels. The positions do not align neatly by general tendency, which is worth noting.

### Grave Implements

*Rabbi Yose*'s blanket leniency for vessels has one exception: *chutz min ha-sal ve-ha-magrefah ve-ha-maritza ha-meyuchadin le-kevaros* — a basket, a shovel, and a *maritza* that are identifiably associated with graves are always presumed *tamei*. These implements are so specifically associated with *tumah* that no presumption of *taharah* can attach to them, whatever the general rule about vessels in the city.

---

## Slaughter Knife

### 14th Nisan Knife

A *sakin* — a slaughtering knife — found on the fourteenth of Nisan presents a distinctive case. On the fourteenth, people are actively engaged in *shechitah* of the *Korban Pesach*, and any knife found that day may be used *miyad*, immediately, without first taking it to the *mikvah*. The reasoning is straightforward: anyone who wished to use a knife on the fourteenth would have had to immerse it on the thirteenth, because immersion requires *ha'arev shemesh* — waiting for nightfall — before the vessel is fully *tahor*. A knife immersed on the fourteenth could not be used until nightfall. Therefore, any knife one finds on the fourteenth of Nisan must have already been immersed on the thirteenth and is thus presumptively *tahor*.

### 13th Nisan Knife

If the knife is found on the thirteenth, the situation differs. *Shoneh u-matbil* — one must take it to the *mikvah*, because it is possible the owner had not yet immersed it and planned to do so later that day. Since immersion on the thirteenth would leave the knife *tahor* by nightfall and thus usable on the fourteenth, we cannot presume it has already been immersed. This requirement is somewhat puzzling given *Rabbi Yose*'s ruling that all *kelim* in Yerushalayim are presumed *tahor* — perhaps the *mishnah* here reflects *Rabbi Meir*'s position, or perhaps the heightened standards of *kodashim* impose special requirements regardless.

### Cleaver Cases

A *kofitz* — a cleaver — is treated differently because of its different function. A cleaver is not used for *shechitah*; it is used for dismembering the *korban*. Moreover, by the *Korban Pesach* it cannot be used at all for dismembering, since *kol etzem lo yishberu bo* — no bone of the Pesach offering may be broken. The cleaver is therefore needed not on the fourteenth but on the fifteenth, for the other *korbanos* of the *regel*. This means the cleaver could legitimately be taken to the *mikvah* on the fourteenth — immersion on the fourteenth means it is *tahor* by nightfall and usable on the fifteenth. Accordingly, if one finds a cleaver on the fourteenth, its status is ambiguous: it may have been immersed already or may not yet have been immersed. *Baze u-vaze* — whether found on the thirteenth or the fourteenth, *shoneh u-matbil* — one must immerse it again.

If the fourteenth falls on *Shabbat*, the calculation shifts: since one cannot immerse on *Shabbat*, anyone who needed the cleaver for *Yom Tov* would have had to immerse it on the thirteenth. In that case, a cleaver found on that *Shabbat-Erev Pesach* may be used *miyad*. Similarly, a cleaver found on the fifteenth of Nisan may be used immediately, because the latest the owner could have immersed it was the fourteenth, and nightfall of the fourteenth renders it *tahor* for the fifteenth.

### Tied Together

If a cleaver is found tied together with a *shechitah* knife — *nimtzeit keshurah im sakin* — then *harei hu ke-sakin*, it is treated like the knife. Since the two implements are bound together, we presume they were brought to the *mikvah* at the same time. Therefore, the cleaver is presumed to share the *taharah* status of the knife: if found on the fourteenth, both may be used immediately.

---

## Spittle Purity (II)

### Non-Jewish Presence

Returning to explain *Rabbi Meir*'s exception for the *shuk ha-elyon*, the *gemara* now supplies the reason. *Rabbi Akiva beshem Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* explains: *katzin shel nochrim hayu sham* — there was a garrison of non-Jews stationed in the upper marketplace. The relevance is that *chazal* treated non-Jews *le-chumra* as having the status of a *zav*, a source of *tumah* in their spittle. Because of this significant non-Jewish presence — apparently a Roman garrison, which would also explain the dramatic detail about wild donkeys being killed there, presumably to feed the garrison's animals or as part of its activity — the upper marketplace was distinguished from the rest of the city as a place where one could not presume the spit to be *tahor*. *Rabbi Meir* accordingly exempted all other parts of Yerushalayim while singling out this one location.

---

## Carcass Blood

### Dead Donkey

The brief mention of the garrison and the animals killed there leads the *gemara* into an extended digression triggered by the subject of blood and *tumah*. The digression begins with a story from the household of *Rabbi* (*Rebbi*): *maaseh be-pirdah shel beis Rebbi she-meisah* — there was an incident with a donkey in *Rebbi*'s household that died. The ruling given was *u-tihara damah mishum neveilah* — its blood was declared *tahor* on the grounds that the *tumah* of *neveilah* applies to flesh, not to blood.

### Elazar's Frustration

*Rabbi Elazar* asked *Rabbi Siman*: *ad kama?* — until how much blood does this *taharah* apply? Is the blood categorically *tahor* in all quantities, or is there a threshold beyond which the blood becomes significant enough to be treated as equivalent to a *kezayis* of flesh and thus *tamei*? *V-lo agivei* — *Rabbi Siman* gave him no answer. This non-response left *Rabbi Elazar* deeply frustrated, as the *gemara* records.

### Yehoshua Ruling

*Rabbi Elazar* then brought the question to *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*, who answered: *ad revi'is tahor, yosei mikan tamei* — up to a *revi'is* the blood is *tahor*; beyond a *revi'is* it is *tamei*. A parallel account describes *Rabbi Bibi* telling over this incident, and *Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna* raising the same question — *ad kama?* — with the same answer given. In the parallel account, however, the respondent kicks the questioner, and *Rabbi Zerika* remonstrates: you kick someone who asks you a question? The respondent explains: *bigin d'lo havay da'ati bi* — because my mind was not settled. He then cites a teaching of *Rabbi Chanin* on the verse *ve-hayu chayecha telu'im lach mineged* — your life will be suspended before you — applied to three levels of precarious livelihood: one who buys a year's worth of grain but has no field of his own, one who buys from a grain supplier, and one who buys from a baker (*paltera*), each stage representing a more tenuous existence. *V-ana samichna a-paltera* — and I rely on the baker, meaning his own mental state was such that he could not compose himself to answer.

The *gemara* then addresses what appears to be a contradiction. The *mishnah* in *Taharos* — cited as *tman tninan* — states that *dam ha-sheret mitamei ke-vesaro* — the blood of a *sheretz* causes *tumah* like its flesh — and then adds *u-mitamei v-eino machshir*, it causes *tumah* but does not render food susceptible to *tumah*. And the *mishnah* concludes: *v-ein lanu ke-yotzei bo* — there is nothing else like this combination of being *metamei* without being *machshir*. This would seem to contradict the ruling that blood of *neveilah* beyond a *revi'is* is *tamei* — for that too would be *metamei* without being *machshir*, and yet the *mishnah* says there is nothing like *sheretz* blood in this regard. One might try to resolve the earlier *mishnah* about *neveilah* blood being *tahor* by reading *tahor* narrowly — meaning not *machshir* but still *tamei* — but the *sheretz* *mishnah*'s statement that nothing else shares this combination would undercut that reading. The *gemara*'s response is that *v-ein lanu ke-yotzei bo ke-shiyur tumato* — there is nothing else with this combination at the *same minimum measure*: the *sheretz* causes *tumah* at the tiny measure of *ka-adasha*, like a lentil, while *neveilah* blood — if it is indeed *tamei* — operates at a larger threshold. These are thus not the same phenomenon.

### Amoraim Dispute

Ultimately *Rabbi Yose* frames the matter as an explicit dispute between two *amoraim*: *peligi bah trei amora'in* — two *amoraim* disagree about this. *Chad amar tamei* — one holds that blood of *neveilah* is categorically *tamei*; *ve-chad amar tahor* — the other holds it is categorically *tahor*. *Man d'amar tamei ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — the one who holds it is *tamei* follows the position of *Rabbi Yehuda*, who — drawing on a dispute between *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* — understands that both schools agree blood of *neveilah* is *tamei*, differing only about the measure. *U-man d'amar tahor ke-Rabbi Yehoshua ben Betira* — the one who holds it is *tahor* follows the position of the *mishnah* attributed to *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Betira* that the blood of *neveilah* is *tahor*.

The resolution for the story of *Rebbi*'s donkey follows: *Rav Dimi d'min Nechusha* notes that *Rabbi Yehuda* — the one who says *neveilah* blood is *tamei* beyond a *revi'is* — was *moreinah de-vei nesiah*, the *posek* for *Rebbi*'s own household. The ruling they gave, that the blood was *tahor*, therefore fits within *Rabbi Yehuda*'s own framework, since presumably the amount in question was under a *revi'is*.

---

## Road Behavior

### Normal Year

Having mentioned *Rabbi Yose*'s distinction between central and marginal roads, the *gemara* now elaborates the practical behavior expected in each period. During the ordinary year — outside the festival season — *ha-teme'im mehalchin shibbolet* — the *tamei* individuals walk *shibbolet*, meaning straight down the center path (*shibbolet* understood as *lashon shevil*, a path or throughway). *Ve-ha-tehorim mehalchin min ha-tzad* — the *tehorim* walk on the margins. *Ve-ha-tehorim mehalchin stam* — the *tehorim* walk without announcing themselves, *ve-ha-teme'im omrim lahem: peroshu* — and it is the *tamei* individuals in the center who call out to those at the margins: keep your distance.

### Festival Period

During the *regel*, the dynamic inverts entirely. *Ha-tehorim mehalchin shibbolet* — the *tehorim* walk in the center. *Ve-ha-teme'im mehalchin min ha-tzad* — the *tamei* individuals walk on the margins. *Ha-teme'im mehalchin stam* — the *tamei* individuals walk without announcing themselves, *ve-ha-tehorim omrim lahem: peroshu* — and the *tehorim* in the center call out to those on the margins to keep their distance. The dominant group in each period — those who walk openly in the center — are the ones who announce their status to the minority at the margins.

---

## Grave Implements ID

### Abba Shaul Term

The *mishnah* had identified three grave-related implements as always presumed *tamei*: the *sal* (basket), the *magrefah* (shovel), and the *maritza*. The *gemara* records that *Abba Shaul hayah korei otan tziporin* — *Abba Shaul* would call the *maritza* by the name *tziporin*, meaning fingernails or claws, because the implement was shaped like a fingernail. *Man d'amar maritza* — the one who uses the term *maritza* in the *mishnah* understands it as *she-maritza et ha-even le-veit ha-kevarot* — that it causes the stone to run or slide toward the gravesite, that is, it was used to push or move stones in a cemetery.

### Three Implements

The three implements — basket, shovel, and *maritza* — are thus defined by their function: they are tools specifically associated with burial work. Their identification with graves is so clear that no general presumption of *taharah* for vessels found in Yerushalayim can override the inference drawn from their form and function.

### Tied Implements

A *baraita* then addresses the case of tied implements in the grave-implement context: *ha-sakin keshurah lah harei zeh kemotah* — a knife tied to one of these grave implements is treated like the grave implement itself. This stands in apparent tension with the ruling in the *mishnah*, which held that a *kofitz* tied to a *sakin* takes on the *sakin*'s status. Here the *baraita* reverses the direction: when a knife is tied to a grave implement, the knife takes on the grave implement's status. Some commentators suggest these are not contradictory but address different configurations — perhaps the *baraita* speaks of two knives found together, where the status of one informs the presumption about the other. The tension between the *mishnah* and this *baraita* is left unresolved.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 3

## Nissan vs Tishrei

### Intro & Shlomo Review

Today's *daf* is 3, and we pick up at the bottom of 2b, in the middle of the discussion of *Nissan* being *Rosh Hashanah* for kings. To clarify a point from the previous session: the evidence used was in the context of Shlomo's Temple construction, because the counting of years for the building of the *Beis Hamikdash* was reckoned as the 480th year from *Yetzias Mitzrayim* and the fourth year of Shlomo's reign — and from this we learn that the counting from *Yetzias Mitzrayim* begins from *Nissan*. Similarly, the count for *Jewish* kings begins from *Nissan*. As we will see today, the count for non-Jewish kings runs from *Tishrei*.

This actually makes a great deal of sense. The command *hachodesh hazeh lachem rosh chodashim* — "this month shall be for you the first of the months" — was the *chiddush* of the *Torah*. Naturally, in the agricultural cycle upon which the ancient calendar was based, *Tishrei* was the beginning: it marks the onset of the planting season and thus, organically, the start of the year. The *Torah* came along and declared that the Jewish people would instead count from the month of *geulah*, from the month of redemption. *Nissan* became *rosh chodashim*. And now the *Gemara* is establishing that not only the months but also the years — at least for Jewish kings — are counted from *Nissan*.

### Torah's Nissan Mandate

The *Gemara* takes it for granted that *Nissan* is month number one in terms of the *Torah*'s numbering of the months. The *Torah* itself never uses the familiar names — *Nissan*, *Tishrei*, *Cheshvan*, *Kislev*, *Iyar* — those names are in fact non-Jewish, Persian in origin, and only begin appearing in *Tanach* after the first *churban bayis*, which is why we find them in *Ezra*, *Nechemia*, and *Megillas Esther*. The *Torah* instead refers to the months as *hachodesh harishon*, *hachodesh hasheini*, and so on. Yet it is clear from the *Torah* itself that this numbering begins from *Nissan* — as for example when it instructs the *korban pesach* in the second year, it specifies *bachodesh harishon*, and it is obvious that *Nissan* is the first month.

The *Gemara*'s question, which was introduced at the end of the previous *daf*, is distinct from the question of month-numbering. Granted that the months are numbered from *Nissan* — are the *years* also counted from *Nissan*? That is, when the *Torah* counts the years from *Yetzias Mitzrayim*, does the year increment when *Nissan* arrives? In principle one might expect the year-count to follow a different rhythm from the month-count — and indeed, we ourselves today do precisely that: we increment the year at *Tishrei* for *Rosh Hashanah* purposes, while still numbering the months from *Nissan*. So the question is a genuine one.

### Aharon & Moshe Evidence

The *Gemara* attempts to prove that years are counted from *Nissan* by means of the following argument. The *Torah* records that Aharon died at *Hor Hahar* in the fifth month — counting from *Nissan*, that is *Av* — *bachodesh hachamishi*. Then, the book of *Devarim* opens with Moshe delivering his great address, which begins in the eleventh month — that is, *Shevat*. Both events are stated to belong to year forty. We know the death of Aharon came before Moshe's speech — and we will demonstrate this explicitly in the next segment — so the two events, in month five and month eleven of the same year, bracket the period during which no year-increment occurred.

Now *Tishrei* is the seventh month. It falls precisely between month five and month eleven. If *Tishrei* were the *Rosh Hashanah* for counting years — meaning the year would increment when *Tishrei* arrived — then Moshe's speech in month eleven would have to be year forty-one, not year forty. Since the *Torah* places both events in year forty, nothing between month five and month eleven can be *Rosh Hashanah* for the year-count. Months six through eleven are all eliminated. The logical conclusion is that year forty-one begins only after month eleven — pointing to *Nissan*, month one, as the point of year-increment.

### Shevat Alternative

The *Gemara* immediately raises a seemingly absurd counter-suggestion: who says the death of Aharon in month five came *before* Moshe's speech in month eleven? Perhaps it was the other way around — Moshe spoke in *Shevat* first, and Aharon died six months later. In that case, one could place the year-increment anywhere from month six through month eleven, since the gap between the two events would have run in the opposite direction. Needless to say, such a reading of *Sefer Devarim* is virtually inconceivable — the entire structure of the book presupposes that Moshe is giving his farewell address on the eve of entering the land, and it contains retrospective references to events including Aharon's death. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* entertains the logical possibility and proceeds to refute it by means of an independent proof establishing the correct chronological sequence — which it will address in the following section.

## Aharon Death Sequence

### Canaanite King = Sichon

The *Gemara* establishes that Aharon's death preceded the battle with Sichon, and that Moshe was still alive when Sichon was defeated. The opening of *Sefer Devarim* explicitly states that Moshe delivered his address *acharei hakoso es Sichon Melech ha'Emori* — "after he struck Sichon king of the Amorites." So Sichon's defeat was a precondition for Moshe's speech.

Now the question becomes: was Sichon still alive when Aharon died? The *Gemara* answers by pointing to a verse in *Bamidbar* that reads: *Vayishma haKena'ani Melech Arad yoshev haNegev* — "and the Canaanite king of Arad who dwelt in the south heard." This verse appears immediately following the account of Aharon's death. The natural reading of the juxtaposition is that this king "heard" about Aharon's death and attacked on account of it — meaning he was alive and active at that point. And if this king can be identified with Sichon, then we know Sichon was still alive after Aharon died, which in turn means Moshe's speech — delivered after Sichon's defeat — necessarily came *after* Aharon's death. The normal sequence of the *Torah* is thus confirmed.

### Rashi: Clouds Departed

Rashi explains that the verse *mah shmua shama* — "what report did he hear?" — is answered as follows: he heard that Aharon had died, *v'nistalku ananei hakavod*, and that the clouds of divine glory had consequently departed. With the protective *ananei hakavod* gone, the nation was exposed and vulnerable, and the king therefore concluded that *nitna reshu lalechem b'Yisrael* — there was now an opening to wage war against Israel. This reading is not merely an inference from juxtaposition; it reads the very motivation of the attack as caused by Aharon's death, making clear that Aharon was already dead at the time.

This interpretation is then supported from the verse itself: *Vayir'u kol ha'eda ki gava Aharon* — "and the whole congregation saw that Aharon had died," which appears immediately before the king's attack. The connection between seeing and the departure of the clouds is unpacked in the following passage.

### Ki's Four Functions

Rabbi Abbahu teaches: *al tikri vayir'u ela vayeira'u* — do not read "they saw" (*vayir'u*) but rather "they were made visible" or "exposed" (*vayeira'u*). Rashi explains with the single word *nitgalu ha'eda* — the congregation became exposed. The shift in reading hinges on a *derashah* that the departure of Aharon, whose merit sustained the *ananei hakavod*, left the people unprotected and literally uncovered before their enemies.

This *derashah* is introduced by reference to a principle stated by Resh Lakish: the word *ki* functions in four different ways — *ei* (if), *dilma* (lest), *ela* (rather/but), and *de'ha* (because). The point here is that the *ki* in *vayir'u kol ha'eda ki gava Aharon* is being read not as a simple "that" — not as "they saw *that* Aharon died" — but in its causative sense: they were exposed *because* Aharon died.

It is worth pausing on these four functions. *Ei* means "if," as in *ki tifga shor oyevcha* — "if you encounter your enemy's ox." *Dilma* means "lest" — and this differs from "if" in a crucial way. Rashi's example is *ki tomar bilvavcha rabbim ha-goyim ha-eleh mimenni* — "lest you say in your heart, these nations are more numerous than I." The word "lest" is not conditional: "if" implies that there would be a contrary consequence in the opposite case, whereas "lest" implies no such conditionality — you simply should not entertain this thought, full stop. *Ela* means "rather" or "but," and Rashi illustrates this with a single *pasuk* containing two different uses: *Vatomer lo tzachakti ki yare'ah — Vayomer lo ki tzachakt* — "she said I did not laugh because she was afraid — he said, no, *rather* you did laugh." *De'ha* means "because" or "for the reason that."

There is actually a fifth common function of *ki* — namely "when," which operates similarly to *ka'asher*, as in *ki tissa et rosh benei Yisrael*. Rashi tends to subsume this under *ei*, since *im* in Hebrew can also function as "when" — as in *im kesef talveh et ammi* — and the distinction between "if" and "when" can be treated as a nuance within the same usage.

Interestingly, the straightforward *peshat* of *ki* in the *pasuk* under discussion — the simple meaning of "that," as in "they saw *that* Aharon had died" — does not fit neatly into any of the canonical four functions of *ki* enumerated by Resh Lakish. Tosafot notes that this sense of "that" can be understood under the function of "when," which Rashi places under *ei* since *im* sometimes means "when." But the observation stands that the plain reading is not one of the four listed functions, which makes the enumeration somewhat incomplete as a comprehensive account of the word's range.

### Sichon ID Baraita

Having established the reading of the Canaanite king's attack from a *derashah* perspective, the *Gemara* now addresses the identification itself. The *Gemara* objects: *mi dami* — how can we compare? The verse speaks of *Kena'an*, whereas we are trying to prove something about Sichon. A *baraita* resolves this by establishing that this figure bore multiple names: *Sichon* because he resembled a wild colt (*ayyar*) in the desert; *Kena'an* was the name of his kingdom (*al shem malchuto*); and his personal name was *Arad*. A second version of the *baraita* gives *Arad* the etymology of resembling a wild ass (*arohd*) in the desert, while maintaining that *Kena'an* was his kingship and his personal name was Sichon. Tosafot cites an interesting *midrash* suggesting that Sichon actually *disguised* himself as a Canaanite king, perhaps so that the Israelites would pray for salvation from the Canaanites — which would be ineffective, since he was actually an Amorite.

With considerable effort, then, what might seem like an obvious reading of the *Torah* has been established through textual proofs and a *baraita*: Aharon died before Sichon's defeat, and Moshe's speech in *Shevat* came after Aharon's death in *Av*, both within year forty. The year-increment between months five and eleven is thus ruled out, which eliminates *Tishrei* as *Rosh Hashanah* for this counting.

## Month Elimination

### Mishkan/Cloud Proof

Having eliminated *Tishrei* and all months between *Av* and *Shevat*, the *Gemara* still needs to eliminate the months that remain — those earlier in the year. Perhaps *Rosh Hashanah* falls in *Iyar* (month two), *Sivan* (month three), *Tammuz* (month four), or *Av* (month five) itself? And what about *Adar* (month twelve)?

The *Gemara* first dismisses *Iyar*: *lo salka da'atach* — this is inconceivable. The verse states that the *Mishkan* was erected on the first of the first month — *Nissan* — in the second year: *vayehi bachodesh harishon bashanah hashenis b'echad lachodesh hukam hamishkan*. And the very next passage states that in the second year in the second month — *Iyar* — the cloud departed from above the *Mishkan*: *vayehi bashanah hashenis bachodesh hasheni na'alah he'anan me'al mishkan ha'edus*. Both events are designated as occurring in the second year. If *Iyar* were *Rosh Hashanah*, the departure of the cloud would have been in year three. Since it is called the second year — *midekai b'Nissan v'karei shanah shenis, v'kai b'Iyar v'karei shanah shenia* — clearly the year did not increment at *Iyar*. *Iyar* is therefore not *Rosh Hashanah*.

### Matan Torah Proof

*Sivan* is likewise eliminated. The verse introducing *Matan Torah* reads: *bachodesh hashlishi l'tzeis Bnei Yisrael me'Eretz Mitzrayim* — "in the third month of the going out of the Children of Israel from Egypt." It does not say "in the third month, in the *second* year of the going out." If *Sivan* were *Rosh Hashanah*, the year would have incremented by the time they stood at *Har Sinai*, and the verse would have needed to say "in the second year." Since it says no such thing, *Sivan* is eliminated as well.

### Shlomo Temple Proof

After *Sivan* is ruled out, the *Gemara* still faces three remaining candidates: *Tammuz*, *Av*, and *Adar*. Rather than eliminating each individually, Rabbi Eliezer resolves all of them at once by returning to the verse about Shlomo. The verse states: *Vayachel livnot bachodesh hasheni b'sheni b'shnas arba l'malchuto* — "and he began to build in the second month, on the second, in the fourth year of his reign." The word *sheini* — second — appears twice in close succession. The first *sheini* clearly refers to the second month, counted in the standard manner from *Nissan*: that is, *Iyar*. The second *sheini* must also refer to the second month — but now, the second month of that year of Shlomo's kingship. This means the year of Shlomo's kingship is itself counted from *Nissan*. The verse thus provides direct textual proof that years — and not just months — are numbered from *Nissan*. This eliminates *Tammuz*, *Av*, and *Adar* simultaneously.

### Ravina Day Challenge

Ravina challenges this reading: perhaps *b'sheni* means the second *day* of the month, not the second month? The *Gemara* rejects this on two grounds. First, whenever the *Torah* wants to specify a day of the month, it always uses the construction *bachodesh* — "of the month" — such as *b'asor bachodesh* or *b'chamisha lachodesh*. A bare *basheini* without *bachodesh* would be anomalous as a day-reference. Second, one might suggest that *basheini* means Monday — the second day of the week — but this too is rejected: we never find the days of the week mentioned in *Tanach* except in the context of Creation, and apart from references to *Shabbos* and *erev Shabbos*, the day of the week is never specified. Finally, a *gezeirah shavah* is applied: the second *sheini* in the verse is linked to the first *sheini*, and just as the first *sheini* unambiguously refers to a month, so too the second *sheini* refers to a month — specifically, the second month from the point at which the king's year is incremented. The year of Shlomo's kingship is thus conclusively shown to be counted from *Nissan*.

## Jewish vs Non-Jewish

### Complete Baraita

The *Gemara* now cites a *baraita* that collects and formalizes all the proofs assembled above: *minayin she'ein monim lahem l'mlachim ela miNissan?* — from where do we know that we count for kings only from *Nissan*? The *baraita* marshals each proof in turn. It cites the verse connecting Shlomo's construction of the Temple to the 480th year from *Yetzias Mitzrayim*, establishing the parallel between the two counting systems. It then cites the verse about Aharon's death, *vaya'al Aharon hakohen el Hor Hahar al pi Hashem*, and the verse that places Moshe's address in year forty, month eleven — *vayehi b'arbaim shanah b'ashti asar chodesh* — demonstrating that *Tishrei* is not *Rosh Hashanah*. It then invokes the passage *acharei hakoso es Sichon* and the story of the Canaanite king's attack — *vayishma hakena'ani... vayiru kol ha'eda ki gava Aharon* — to establish the correct chronological sequence. Finally it proceeds through the elimination proofs: the Mishkan-cloud evidence ruling out *Iyar*, the *Matan Torah* verse ruling out *Sivan*, and the Shlomo verse providing the positive proof for *Nissan*.

### Rav Chisda Ruling

Rav Chisda qualifies the entire preceding discussion: *lo shanu ela l'malchei Yisrael* — all of the above applies only to Jewish kings. When counting the regnal years of non-Jewish kings, the year increments not at *Nissan* but at *Tishrei*: *aval l'malchei umos ha'olam miTishrei mininan*.

This distinction raises an interesting question about the nature of this counting system. Is the system for Jewish kings something the *Sages* created and imposed, or are they simply observing and codifying the system that was actually in practice? In the case of non-Jewish kings, it seems clear that the *Gemara* is simply adopting their own counting convention. The case of Jewish kings is somewhat more ambiguous — and in practical terms, how long this system remained operative is itself uncertain, given the disrupted succession of kings through the *Chashmonaim* period and beyond.

## Nehemiah Year Twenty

### Kislev to Nissan

The proof that non-Jewish kings are counted from *Tishrei* derives from the book of *Nechemia*. The *Gemara* cites two verses: the opening of the book, *vayehi bachodesh Kislev shnas esrim* — "and it was in the month of *Kislev* in year twenty"; and a verse from the second chapter, *vayehi bachodesh Nissan shnas esrim l'Artachshashta hamelech* — "and it was in the month of *Nissan* in year twenty of King Artaxerxes." *Kislev* is the ninth month and *Nissan* is the first month of the following spring. Yet between these two events — one in *Kislev* and the other in *Nissan* — the year number remains unchanged at twenty. If *Nissan* were *Rosh Hashanah* for non-Jewish kings, the *Nissan* event should have been called year twenty-one. Since it is still year twenty, *Nissan* is evidently not the *Rosh Hashanah* for non-Jewish kings. The conclusion, by elimination, is that the year increments at *Tishrei*.

At this stage of the discussion, the *Gemara* notes that the month names used in *Nechemia* are Babylonian-Persian names, reflecting the post-exilic reality in which the Jewish community had absorbed the nomenclature of the surrounding culture. This was the cultural context in which names like *Kislev*, *Tammuz*, and *Adar* entered Jewish usage — names that in some cases carry pagan associations (such as *Tammuz*, a Babylonian deity), yet which became embedded in the Jewish calendar.

### Event Sequence Logic

Before accepting the proof, the *Gemara* raises a preliminary objection: how do we know that the event in chapter one of *Nechemia* (*Kislev*) preceded the event in chapter two (*Nissan*)? Perhaps the *Nissan* event happened first, and the fact that the year had not yet incremented is simply because *Nissan* had just passed or the *Kislev* event came later in the same year after *Nissan*.

A further objection: the verse in *Kislev* merely says "year twenty" without specifying *whose* year twenty. Perhaps this "year twenty" refers to a different counting system entirely — perhaps some general era-based count — whereas only the *Nissan* verse explicitly ties the count to Artaxerxes. How do we know both verses are counting the same king's regnal years?

Rav Papa resolves the second question via a *gezeirah shavah*: both passages use the identical phrase *shenas esrim* — "year twenty." The repetition of the exact phrase in both places establishes that both are counting the same system, and specifically the same king's year. *Mah hatam l'Artachshashta af hacha l'Artachshashta* — just as the *Nissan* verse explicitly counts Artaxerxes's years, so too the *Kislev* verse counts Artaxerxes's years.

### Nehemiah Narrative

The *Gemara* then addresses the sequence question directly via a *baraita*: the things that Chanani said to Nechemia were said in *Kislev*, and those were the things that Nechemia subsequently reported to the king in *Nissan*. The *baraita* is supported by an extended close reading of the relevant *pesukim*.

Chapter one of *Nechemia* opens: *Divrei Nechemia ben Chachalyah — vayehi bachodesh Kislev shnas esrim va'ani hayiti b'Shushan habirah* — Nechemia was in the capital city of Shushan. *Vayavo Chanani echad me'achai hu v'anashim miYehudah* — and Chanani, one of his brothers, came along with other men from *Yehudah*. Nechemia asked them about the condition of the Jewish remnant in the land and about *Yerushalayim*. They reported: the survivors left from the exile are there in the land in great misery and shame, *v'chomat Yerushalayim meporetzet ushe'areha nitzetu va'esh* — the walls of *Yerushalayim* are broken down and its gates have been consumed by fire.

This account is the event of *Kislev*. Then in chapter two, *Nechemia* reports this to the king in *Nissan*: he is serving wine before the king, *vayehi bachodesh Nissan shnas esrim l'Artachshashta hamelech yayin lefanav*, and the king notices his distress — *madua panecha ra'im v'ata eincha choleh* — "why do you look so troubled, since you are not sick?" — and diagnoses it: *ein ze ki im roa lev* — "this must be bitterness of heart." Nechemia, after first offering the obligatory salutation *hamelech l'olam yichyeh*, explains that the city of his forefathers' burial lies desolate and its gates have been consumed by fire. The king asks what he seeks; Nechemia offers a silent prayer to God and then petitions: *im al hamelech tov* — if it pleases the king — to be sent to *Yehudah* to rebuild the city of his forefathers. The king, with the *shagal* seated beside him, agrees and asks how long the journey will take. Nechemia provides a timeframe, the king is pleased, and Nechemia is sent forth.

### Tishrei Confirmed

The sequence is thus plain from the *peshat* of the text itself: Nechemia received the report from Chanani in *Kislev*, was distressed by it, and months later — in *Nissan* of the same year — the king noticed his distress and the matter came to a head. One event is clearly the cause and precondition of the other. Both are called year twenty of Artaxerxes. Since *Nissan* — the first month of spring — arrived between *Kislev* and the later event without triggering a year increment, the year for non-Jewish kings does not increment at *Nissan*. The conclusion stands: for non-Jewish kings, the year increments at *Tishrei*.

## Darius Contradiction

### Chaggai Adar-Av

An apparent contradiction now emerges from the book of *Chaggai*. The *Gemara* cites a verse: *u'veyom esrim v'arba'ah lachodesh bashishi bishnas shtayim l'Daryavesh* — on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month in the second year of Darius — and then a later verse referring to the seventh month without specifying a new year number. Rashi notes that from the context of the preceding *pasuk* it is clear that the seventh month is still year two of Darius. Since the seventh month is *Tishrei*, and we have said that *Tishrei* is *Rosh Hashanah* for non-Jewish kings, the year should have incremented. Yet both events — month six and month seven — are counted as year two. This suggests that for Darius, the year *did not* increment at *Tishrei*, implying instead that *Nissan* was his *Rosh Hashanah*.

Furthermore, the *Gemara* draws on a *baraita* that records: the completion of the Temple building took place on the third of *Adar* in year six of Darius — *v'shitzia beita dena ad yom talata leyarch Adar dehi shenas sheis lemalkus Daryavesh malka*. And a separate tradition records that at that same time, the following year, Ezra began to bring back a major wave of *aliyah*. The verse in *Ezra* then states: *vayavo Yerushalayim bachodesh hachamishi hi shenas hashvi'is lamelech* — he arrived in *Yerushalayim* in the fifth month, which is year seven of the king. The fifth month of year seven is *Av*. Between the *Adar* of year six and the *Av* of year seven, *Nissan* intervened. If *Nissan* were the increment point for Darius, *Av* of that year would have been year *eight*, not year seven. Since it is called year seven, *Nissan* evidently did not function as *Rosh Hashanah* for Darius in this period — which coheres with the principle that non-Jewish kings count from *Tishrei*.

### Rav Yosef Challenge
