Rav Yosef raises the core difficulty. The evidence from *Chaggai* — where month seven is still called year two — seems to require that *Nissan*, not *Tishrei*, was the *Rosh Hashanah* for Darius. This directly contradicts the rule established for non-Jewish kings, and stands in tension with the *Ezra* evidence just cited, which fits *Tishrei* as the increment point.

### Kasher King Theory

Rabbi Abbahu proposes a resolution: *Coresh Melech Kasher haya* — Coresh was a righteous king. And therefore, *lepichach manu lo kemalchei Yisrael* — they accordingly counted his years as one counts for Jewish kings, that is, from *Nissan*. This would explain why in *Chaggai* the year did not increment at *Tishrei* — because for a king of this moral stature, *Nissan* was the operative *Rosh Hashanah*.

This resolution is striking, but it raises an immediate practical difficulty. The entire discussion of non-Jewish kings has operated on the assumption that "non-Jewish kings count from *Tishrei*" is a stable rule. To introduce an exception based on the personal righteousness of a king — so that Jewish scribes and prophets would be using a fundamentally different calendar counting for this particular king — is hard to picture as a practical reality. Would the community really have maintained a parallel and divergent year-count for this king while everyone around them was counting differently?

### King Name Identity

There is also the textual problem that the suggestion invokes *Coresh*, while the *Chaggai* passages are about Darius. The *Gemara* therefore cites a *baraita*: *hu Coresh hu Daryavesh hu Artachshashta* — this king bore all three names. *Coresh* because he was a *kasher* king — and Rashi notes the wordplay between *Coresh* and *kasher*. *Artachshashta* was his royal title, *al shem malchuto*. And *Daryavesh* was his actual personal name. Rashi qualifies this identification, noting that this is not the original *Coresh* — the famous Cyrus who issued the initial decree permitting the rebuilding of the Temple — but a later king who happened to share the name *Coresh*, given that royal names were reused in antiquity. The identification of the original *Coresh* as a righteous figure is not outlandish — certain traditions even invoke a phrase like *Coresh avdi*, "Coresh my servant," in prophetic contexts — but the claim that his successors operated under a distinct year-counting regime remains difficult.

## Unresolved Difficulty

### Calendar Change Problem

Rav Yosef presses the objection. Even granting that Darius-Coresh was a *melech kasher* and was therefore counted like Jewish kings from *Nissan*, this creates a self-contradiction within the *pesukim* themselves. The *Chaggai* evidence implies that during the earlier period of Darius's reign — when the year did not increment at *Tishrei* — he was being counted from *Nissan*, consistent with the *kasher* designation. But the later *Ezra* evidence — where *Av* of year seven follows *Adar* of year six without the intervening *Nissan* triggering a new year — implies that by that later point the year was *not* incrementing at *Nissan*, which means the counting had reverted to *Tishrei*. One cannot have it both ways. If he was a *melech kasher* who counted from *Nissan*, then the *Ezra* passage should read year eight; if he counted from *Tishrei*, the *Chaggai* passage should show an increment at *Tishrei*. The two sets of *pesukim*, drawn from the same king's reign, appear to operate under mutually inconsistent calendar assumptions.

Furthermore, Rav Yosef objects: *mi dami? hasam Coresh hacha Daryavesh* — how can you simply conflate them? One king is called *Coresh* and the other *Daryavesh*. The *baraita*'s identification that they are one and the same person addresses this, but the underlying contradiction in the calendar assumptions remains.

### Soured King Theory

The *Gemara* proposes an answer: *lo kashya — kan kodem she-hichmitz, kan achar she-hichmitz* — there is no difficulty. The earlier *Chaggai* evidence dates from the period *before* Darius soured — when he was a righteous king and was counted from *Nissan*. The later *Ezra* evidence dates from after he had *hichmitz* — a term drawn from the imagery of wine turning to vinegar, or dough souring — when he had deteriorated morally. At that later stage, the counting reverted to *Tishrei* as for all non-Jewish kings.

The connection between *chametz* and moral deterioration is noted — the *chametz* imagery of *yetzer hara* is embedded in the very term *hichmitz* here.

### Kahana Objection

Rav Kahana challenges this: who says Darius soured? The *pasuk* from *Ezra* records that when Ezra was returning to the land, the king — identified as Artaxerxes/Darius — issued a remarkably generous directive to the treasury officials: *u'mah chashchan* — whatever is needed — whether rams, bulls, lambs, grain, salt, wine, or oil — *kelamar kahanya di b'Yerushalem* — whatever the priests in *Yerushalayim* request for the sacrifices — *leheve mityahiv lahem yom b'yom* — let it be provided to them on a daily basis from the royal treasury, *u'd'la shalu* — without them even needing to ask. A king who voluntarily funds the *Beis Hamikdash* from his own treasury, unsolicited, hardly seems like a king who has "soured."

### Self-Interest Motive

Rav Yitzchak responds to Rav Kahana directly: *matuncha* — your very proof contains the answer. What does the end of the verse say? *Di lehevon mehakarvin nichochin l'Eloah shemaya u'matzlin l'chayei malka u'vnohei* — "that they may offer pleasing aromas to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and for his sons." The king's generosity was not altruistic; it was entirely self-interested. He was purchasing prayers for his own life and the lives of his children. The *Gemara* notes with gentle irony that perhaps one should not be too critical of a patron whose self-interested contributions result in prayers and sacrifices — and the discussion of whether self-interested generosity constitutes genuine virtue will be taken up on the following *daf*.

# Rosh Hashanah 5

## Nissan/Bal Tacher Intro

### Nissan Rosh Hashanah

Today's daf is 5, and the Gemara continues its discussion of the principle that Nissan is *Rosh Hashanah l'regalim* — it marks the beginning of the cycle for the *moadim* and for the prohibition of *bal tacher*, the obligation not to delay bringing one's sacrifices, vows, and other religious obligations. The Gemara had already surveyed, on the previous daf, a Baraita presenting a range of opinions about when exactly one transgresses *bal tacher*: whether it requires three *regalim* proceeding in order beginning from Pesach (the assumption of the Mishnah, which makes Nissan the *Rosh Hashanah*), or whether any two or any single *regel* suffices. Now the Gemara turns to working through the various *pesukim* that serve as the basis for these positions.

### Overnight in Jerusalem

One of the matters addressed in this context is the obligation to remain overnight in Jerusalem after bringing one's *olat re'iyah* and *shalmei chagigah*. As Rashi explains on this daf, the verse *ufanita vaboker ve-halachta le-ohalecha* — "you shall turn in the morning and go to your tents" — is not speaking of the morning of *Yom Tov* itself, for that is precisely the day one is obligated to appear in the *Azarah*. Rather, it speaks of the morning following *Yom Tov*, after one has brought the *olat re'iyah*. The pilgrim remains overnight and departs the next morning — which is the first day of *Chol Ha-moed*.

### Pesach/Sukkot Connection

The Gemara draws a connection between Pesach and Sukkot to establish this overnight requirement: just as Pesach carries an obligation of *linah* — remaining overnight — so too does Sukkot: *mah Chag Hamatzot ta'un linah af Chag Hasukkot ta'un linah*. The derivation of the Sukkot obligation from the Pesach verse is achieved by linking the two festivals through their respective *pesukim*.

It is worth noting that the explicit verse about going home in the morning appears only in connection with Pesach and not with Sukkot. This is not coincidental. By Sukkot, the Torah already assumes one spends the entire week in Jerusalem — *ve-samachta lifnei Hashem Elokecha shivat yamim*, "you shall rejoice before the Lord your God for seven days." Sukkot falls at the end of the harvest season; one has gathered everything in, and taking a week in Jerusalem is entirely natural. Pesach, by contrast, falls in the middle of the agricultural year, with the wheat harvest still underway. The pilgrim must return quickly to his fields. Hence the explicit verse directing him to wait until morning before setting out — *ufanita vaboker ve-halachta le-ohalecha*. Tosafot raises the question whether there might not be a general obligation to remain overnight after bringing *korbanot* regardless of this specific verse, but the Gemara proceeds with the derivation as stated.

## Tashlumin/Shavuot

### Three Regalim Position

The Gemara then turns to a question about the positions of Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon. Both of these opinions hold that *bal tacher* is transgressed only after three *regalim* — either any three in proper order or the three in sequence. The difficulty arises concerning *tashlumin* on Shavuot: the principle that if one failed to bring the required *korbanot* on the first day of a *regel*, one has the remaining days of that *regel* to make them up. For Shavuot, the accepted rule is that the full seven days following the first day serve as *tashlumin*. According to the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon, the Torah's repetition of all three *chagim* is used to establish the requirement of three *regalim* for *bal tacher* — not to link the festivals to one another. So if the repetition is being used for that purpose, how do Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon derive the seven-day *tashlumin* period for Shavuot?

### Rabba bar Shmuel

The Gemara answers: *nafka lehu midetani Rabba bar Shmuel* — they derive it from what Rabba bar Shmuel teaches. The Baraita states: *Rabba bar Shmuel amar Torah — manei yamim ve-kadesh chodesh*, count days and sanctify the new month. The underlying idea is that *Rosh Chodesh* is a single day, because the unit you count to arrive at it is the day — twenty-nine or thirty of them. By analogy: *manei yamim ve-kadesh Atzeret*, count days and sanctify Shavuot. Just as *Rosh Chodesh*, being counted in units of days, is itself one day, so too Shavuot should, by that logic, be one day.

### Shavuot Dual Nature

But the Gemara immediately challenges this: surely when counting toward Shavuot, one counts not only days but weeks. The Torah emphasizes *sheva shabbatot temimot tihyena* — seven complete weeks — and indeed there is a *mitzvah* to count the weeks during *Sefirat Ha-omer* as well as the days. The verse *ve-od Chag Shavuot katuv* — "Chag Shavuot" is written — further suggests a concept of the *chag* extending across a week. The result is a fascinating dual identity for Shavuot: it is counted in units of both days and weeks. As a one-day *Yom Tov*, the festival lasts a single day; but as a *regel* for the purposes of bringing *korbanot*, it carries the weight of a full week. The week-long dimension does not express itself as *Yom Tov* throughout, but manifests in the context of *korbanot* brought as *tashlumin*. This is a striking way to think about Shavuot — that its very identity is simultaneously singular and weekly, and that the week is not merely a rabbinic extension but reflects something intrinsic to what Shavuot is.

## Bal Tacher List

### Baraita's List

The Gemara now turns to unpacking the full Baraita that enumerates the categories subject to *bal tacher*. The list includes: *chayvei damim, erchin, charamim, hekdeshot, chataot, ashamot, olot, shelamim, tzedakot, ma'asrot, bechor, ma'aser*, and *Pesach*. The Gemara jumps first to *Pesach* at the end of the list, though there is much to say about the items that precede it.

### Pesach Exception

The Gemara asks: *u-Pesach bar mikra b'regalim hu?* Can the *korban Pesach* be brought on the other *regalim*, such that one could be *over* on *bal tacher* by not having brought it on Shavuot and then Sukkot? The answer is no: *Pesach zimna kvi'a lei* — Pesach has a fixed, immovable time. If you brought it on the fourteenth of Nissan, you brought it; if you did not, it is simply gone — *idchaya lei*. There is no opportunity on the other *regalim* to remedy the omission. Accordingly, Rav Chisda says: *Pesach k'dei nasba* — the mention of Pesach in the list was for nothing. It appears because it is a long enumeration of obligations, and Pesach was swept along with the rest — what the Gemara elsewhere calls *shigra d'lishna*, the momentum of speech. In substance, it does not belong in the list.

### Rav Sheshes Pesach

Rav Sheshes offers an alternative reading. *Mai Pesach?* he asks — what does "Pesach" in the Baraita mean? He answers: *shalmei Pesach* — a *shelamim* that originated from a *Pesach* sacrifice. The scenario is as follows: one sanctified an animal as a *korban Pesach*, the animal was lost, another was brought in its place, and then the original was found. The found animal, which had been a *korban Pesach*, now carries the status of *shelamim*. That animal is subject to the obligation of being brought within three *regalim* and is therefore subject to *bal tacher*.

### Shelamim Pesach Vs Regul…

But the Gemara challenges Rav Sheshes: if it is simply a *shelamim*, why was it necessary to specify? The Baraita has already listed *shelamim*. The answer is that there are two distinct cases: a *shelamim* that originates from a *Pesach* (*shelamim habaim machmat ha-Pesach*) and an ordinary *shelamim* (*shelamim habaim machmat atzman*). One might have thought — *salka daitach amina* — that since the animal originated as a *Pesach*, perhaps it retains a quasi-*Pesach* character: *ho'il u-machmat Pesach ka-atu, ke-Pesach dami*. Rashi explains this to mean that perhaps one would be *over* already at the first opportunity — at the very first *regel* — just as one transgresses by missing the fourteenth of Nissan. The Baraita therefore teaches that this is not so: once the animal has assumed the status of a *shelamim*, it follows the normal rules of *shelamim* and may be brought within three *regalim*.

### List Conceptual Issues

Having established what Pesach means in the Baraita, one must step back and confront some of the conceptual difficulties that run through the entire list of obligations subject to *bal tacher*. The foundational verse — *ki tidor neder la-Shem Elokecha lo te'acher leshalmo* — speaks of one who makes a *neder*, a vow, and delays fulfilling it. Yet several items on the list sit uneasily with that framework.

The first difficulty concerns *damim* and *erchin*: monetary obligations one accepts to pay to the Temple treasury. These at least fit the category of a vow — one undertakes to pay a sum, and delays. Slightly more surprising are *hekdeshot* — cases where one sanctifies an object, such as a piece of property, directly to the Temple. When one says *hikdashti et ha-mechonit* — "I sanctify my car to the Temple" — the ownership transfers immediately at the moment of speech. *Mi amirato legavoah kemesirato lehedyot* — one's verbal declaration to the Most High is equivalent to a physical transfer to an ordinary person. So one might ask: in what sense is the owner "delaying"? The Temple already owns the object. The delay is merely in delivery. Yet the Baraita includes *hekdeshot* under *bal tacher*. This is already a notable extension.

More striking still is the inclusion of *chataot* and *ashamot*. A *chatat* or *asham* arises from an obligation — one sinned *be-shogeg*, or incurred a specific liability — without any vow whatsoever. The verse speaks of *lo te'acher leshalmo*, of not delaying to fulfill one's *neder*. Yet no *neder* was made. The clock begins running and after three *regalim* one has transgressed *bal tacher* simply by not having brought a *korban* one was obligated in through circumstance, not through speech. Similarly with *olot u-shelamim* in their obligatory forms — *olat re'iyah* and *shalmei chagigah* — one did not undertake a vow to bring them, yet they fall under the same prohibition. This is a significant expansion of what *bal tacher* covers.

And then the list reaches *tzedakot, ma'asrot, bechor*, and — most surprisingly — *leket, shikcha, and pe'ah*, which have not yet appeared in the Baraita's formal derivations but which will be addressed. These obligations are not directed toward the Temple at all, and some of them arise not from any verbal act but simply from how one conducts one's harvest. The strangeness of this list should not be understated.

## Parashat Nedenim

### Neder/Nedavah

The Gemara now presents the Baraita's systematic derivation of each category from the verse in *parashat nedarim*. The verse reads *ki tidor neder la-Shem Elokecha lo te'acher leshalmo* — when you make a vow to the Lord your God, do not delay fulfilling it. The Baraita begins: *ein li ela neder* — I know only a *neder*, meaning a case where one says "I accept upon myself to bring a *korban*." But what about a *nedavah* — where one sanctifies the animal directly? The Baraita derives the inclusion of *nedavah* by a *gezerah shavah*: the word *neder* appears here, and the word *neder* also appears in another context alongside *nedavah* — *o neder o nedavah zevach korbano*. Just as there the *neder* encompasses the *nedavah*, so here too: *af kan nedavah imo*.

### Harei Zo Olah

This first extension — from *neder* to *nedavah* — is a genuine *chidush*, though perhaps not the most dramatic one. When one says *harei zo olah* and directly sanctifies an animal, one might argue that the vow is immediately and fully fulfilled the moment the words are spoken: the animal is sanctified. What remains to be done? Yet the Baraita teaches that the ultimate fulfillment of such a sanctification is the actual bringing of the *korban*, and until that occurs, the full purpose of the vow remains unrealized. The *chidush* is real but comprehensible: the *nedavah* is in essence a vow whose climax has not yet been reached.

### Money/Property Vows

The Baraita continues: *ki tidor neder la-Shem Elokecha* — the words *la-Shem Elokecha*, "to the Lord your God," teach us about things given entirely and directly to God. *Elu ha-damim, ha-erchin, ha-charamim, ve-ha-hekdeshot* — these are monetary evaluations, *erchin* (fixed Torah valuations), *charamim*, and *hekdeshot*. Rashi explains the derivation from *la-Shem Elokecha* specifically: unlike *korbanot* in which the *kohanim* receive a portion — even an *olah* yields the hide to the *kohen* — these categories go entirely to God, and are therefore learned from the phrase that emphasizes the divine destination.

As noted, the inclusion of *hekdeshot* carries a real conceptual *chidush*. Once one sanctifies an object and transfers its ownership to the Temple, the delay one is subject to under *bal tacher* concerns something one no longer owns — the Temple already holds title. Nevertheless, the Baraita teaches that the obligation to bring it, to actually deliver and realize the sanctification, remains and is subject to *lo te'acher leshalmo*.

### Obligations Not Vows

The next phrase — *ki darosh yidrashenu Hashem Elokecha me'imach*, "for God will seek it out from you" — extends *bal tacher* to obligations not grounded in a vow at all. *Elu chata'ot va-ashamot olot u-shelamim* — these are *chataot, ashamot, olot*, and *shelamim*. The word *yidrashenu*, "He will seek it," denotes a divine demand rather than a vow the person undertook. For *chataot* and *ashamot*, the obligation arose from circumstance or sin. For *olot u-shelamim*, Rashi explains that the reference here is to *olat re'iyah* and *shalmei chagigah*, which are obligatory festival offerings.

This raises a genuine difficulty. Tosafot notes that *olat re'iyah* and *shalmei chagigah* have a fixed time — *ze man kvi'a lehu* — and the general rule is that if one did not bring them on the *regel*, one is no longer liable: *avar ha-regel ve-lo chag eino chayav be-achrayuto*. If that is so, one would expect no *bal tacher* to apply, since the obligation has simply lapsed. Tosafot answers that if one actually sanctified an animal for this purpose and then did not bring it, the situation is different. Even if the personal obligation to bring an *olat re'iyah* has expired, the animal itself carries a *kedushah* as an *olah* and must be brought. It is not the personal *chiyuv* of the *regel* that generates the *bal tacher*, but the sanctity of the animal that was designated and not offered. This distinction — between the lapse of the personal obligation and the ongoing status of the consecrated animal — is Tosafot's resolution, and it is instructive.

### Divine Ownership Vows

The final clause — *Hashem Elokecha* — generates the inclusion of *tzedakot, ma'asrot*, and *bechor*. Rashi notes the connection: by *tzedakah* the verse says *ve-lecha tihyeh tzedakah lifnei Hashem Elokecha*, and by *ma'aser* the verse says *ve-achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha ma'asar degancha tiroshcha ve-yitzharecha*. The phrase *Hashem Elokecha* links these categories to the same overarching principle.

## Bal Tacher List (II)

### Tzedakah/Maasrot/Leket

The inclusion of *tzedakah* is comprehensible, at least: charity can be given through a vow, and when one designates money as *tzedakah* money, it assumes a kind of *kedushah* or legal status, learned out from the world of *terumot, ma'asrot*, and *nedarim*. There is a verbal element — one obligates oneself, and the money's status changes through that speech act.

*Ma'aser* carries a similar structure. The *ma'aser* is verbally separated and thereby sanctified — *kol ma'asar ha-aretz mi-zera ha-aretz la-Shem hu*. What does it mean that it belongs to God? One gives it to the *Leviyim*, or to the *aniyim*, or fulfills it in other ways — but the foundational religious act is the separation of the tithe to God. When Yaakov says *ve-chol asher titein li aser asrenu lach* — all that You give me I will tithe to You — what does it mean to give the tithe to God? The forms of fulfillment vary, but the conceptual anchor is that this is God's portion, separated through one's word. At least *ma'aser* and *tzedakah* are tethered, however loosely, to the sphere of *hafla'ah* — the speech act that changes the legal status of a thing.

*Leket, shikcha*, and *pe'ah*, however, are another matter entirely. These are agricultural gifts to the poor — gleanings dropped during harvest, forgotten sheaves, and the corners of the field left unharvested. They are not sanctified through speech. They do not go to the Temple. They arise from the structure of how one harvests — from what one drops, from what one forgets, from what one leaves. How does one transgress *bal tacher* in connection with them? The verse uses the word *me'imach* — from you, or from among you — and the Baraita's derivation from *et he-ani imach*, "the poor person who is with you," will be examined next. But conceptually, this is the strangest inclusion in the entire list. One is not delaying a vow, not delaying the delivery of something whose ownership has transferred, not even failing to bring a fixed obligatory offering. One is simply not distributing leavings of one's field to the poor. And yet this falls under *lo te'acher leshalmo*.

## Parashat Nedenim (II)

### Community Obligations

The Baraita derives the inclusion of *leket, shikcha*, and *pe'ah* from the word *me'imach* in the verse — "from among you." The Torah's phrase *et he-ani imach*, "the poor who is with you," is read as identifying a category of obligations that arise not from one's relationship to God or the Temple but from one's relationship to *amecha* — those within one's community, one's society. This is a radically different conceptual foundation. Everything that came before was about one's obligations to the Most High, whether through vows, sanctifications, or imposed obligations. *Leket, shikcha*, and *pe'ah* begin with the horizontal dimension — one's responsibility to those around one.

Tosafot raises the practical puzzle: how does one actually transgress *bal tacher* with *leket, shikcha*, and *pe'ah*? The prohibition runs for three *regalim* — but what precisely is being delayed? The normal case is that one leaves the *leket* and *shikcha* behind in the field and the *pe'ah* at the corner. One does not "give" them; one leaves them. Tosafot offers two scenarios. In the first — involving a *be-aveirah* — one violated the obligation by going back and collecting what should have been left, and now must redistribute it to the poor. The *bal tacher* would apply to the failure to effect that redistribution. In the second scenario — which does not begin with a violation — there are no poor people nearby to collect the leavings. The owner gathers them indoors to preserve them, holding them on behalf of the poor. In this case, having taken possession of these goods for distribution, one must distribute them within three *regalim*, and failure to do so constitutes *bal tacher*.

This is also the moment to reflect on the logic of the *regel* as the unit of measurement for *bal tacher* across all these categories. The obvious reason the *regel* serves as this unit in the world of *korbanot* and *hekdesh* is that the pilgrimage is when one has the opportunity to go to Jerusalem and actually bring or deliver what one owes. Missing the first *regel* meant missing one's first opportunity; Rabbi Meir holds one is therefore *over* after just one *regel*. But does this logic extend to *leket, shikcha, pe'ah, ma'asrot*, and *tzedakot*? These have nothing to do with Jerusalem. Yet perhaps, as one might suggest, there is a secondary logic: the *regel* is when all of *Klal Yisrael* gathers, and if there is ever a natural moment to settle one's obligations to the poor and to society, it is when the community assembles together. The *regel* thus carries significance not only for one's relationship to God and the Temple but for one's relationship to the community — and the inclusion of these agricultural and charitable obligations in *bal tacher* forces us to recognize that dimension of the *regel* as well.

## Lo Tacher Leshalmo

### Offering Not Substitute

The Baraita concludes its derivation with two additional principles. The first: *lo te'acher leshalmo — hu ve-lo chilufo* — "to fulfill it": the obligation applies to the offering itself, not to its substitute. One does not transgress *bal tacher* with respect to a substitute. The second: *ve-hayah becha cheit ve-lo be-korbancha cheit* — "the sin will be in you and not in your *korban*." If one transgressed *bal tacher*, the *korban* itself remains valid. We will examine both principles in turn.

### Chilufim Definition

What is a *chilufo* — a substitute? The Gemara clarifies: it is an animal sanctified as a replacement for a lost or defective offering. One sanctifies animal A as an *olah*, it is lost, one sanctifies animal B in its place, and then animal A is found. Animal B was the substitute — the *chilufo* — of animal A.

### Olah/Shelamim Substitutes

If the original offering was an *olah* or *shelamim*, a substitute can be brought — the substitute animal is a valid *korban* that may be offered. One might ask: if the substitute can be brought, should one not be *over* on *bal tacher* for failing to bring it within three *regalim*? The Baraita seems to say one is not.

### Chatat Substitutes

If the original offering was a *chatat*, the situation is different: a *chatat* whose owner was atoned for through another offering must be left to die — *le-mitah azla*. If the substitute cannot be brought at all, there is obviously no *bal tacher* to transgress. The *bal tacher* presupposes a *korban* that ought to be brought and has not been.

### Gemara's Challenge

The Gemara presses: *ella mai chilufav* — so what exactly is the case where the verse needs to tell us there is no *bal tacher* on the substitute? If the substitute can be brought, one ought to be *over*; if it cannot be brought, of course one is not *over* — that is self-evident, just as with a *chatat* that dies. What is the scenario where a verse is required to exclude the substitute from *bal tacher*?

### Todah/Substitute Case

Rav Sheshes answers: *chilufei todah* — a substitute of a *todah* thanksgiving offering. The relevant teaching is from Rav Chiyya: if a *todah* became mixed with its *tmurah* (or its substitute, the animal sanctified in its place after the original was lost), and one of the two animals then died, the surviving animal has no remedy — *chavertah ein lah takkanah*. Why? A *todah* is brought together with forty loaves of bread; the substitute animal does not come with bread. If you do not know which animal is the *todah* and which is the substitute, you are in an impossible position: bring it with bread, and perhaps it is the substitute — *chametz* would be brought in the *Azarah* without authorization; bring it without bread, and perhaps it is the *todah* — which requires the bread as part of its offering. With both animals present, one could bring both along with the forty loaves and declare: whichever is the *todah*, these loaves are connected to it. But when one animal has died and only the other remains, this solution is no longer available. The surviving animal cannot be brought.

So here is the case: the surviving animal is theoretically a valid *korban* — it is either a *todah* or a *tmurah/chilufo* — but in practice it cannot be offered. This is not the same as a *chatat she-metah* where the animal dies and there is nothing left. Here there *is* an animal, and one might think that because the animal exists and could theoretically be a *todah* requiring bringing, one might be *over* on *bal tacher* for not bringing it. The verse therefore teaches: *lo te'acher leshalmo — hu ve-lo chilufo* — the substitute is excluded. Since the animal standing before you might be the *chilufo*, and the *chilufo* is excluded, you are not *over* on *bal tacher*.

## Chilufim/Defects

### Mum Transfer Case

The Gemara now examines a different scenario involving substitutes and defective offerings. Suppose an animal sanctified as an *olah* or *shelamim* develops a *mum* — a disqualifying blemish — during the period between the *regalim*. A blemished animal cannot be offered as a *korban*, but one is permitted to transfer the sanctity: one redeems the blemished animal through money and uses that money to purchase and sanctify a new animal. The question is how this transfer of sanctity affects the *bal tacher* clock.

### Rava on Mum Mid-Holiday

According to the majority view, the scenario is readily analyzed: the original animal had passed through two *regalim*, developed a *mum*, and the sanctity was transferred to a new animal before the third *regel*. The new animal then passes through one *regel* without being brought. Has one transgressed *bal tacher*? The question is whether the new animal should be treated as a continuation of the same *kedushah* — in which case the three *regalim* have effectively passed — or whether the clock resets with the new animal.

Rava explains the case as it applies according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that *bal tacher* is transgressed after even a single *regel*. According to Rabbi Meir, there would seem to be no scenario where the transfer of sanctity matters: if the *regel* has already passed, one is already *over* on *bal tacher* on the original animal; if the *regel* has not yet passed, then transferring the sanctity mid-interval simply means the new animal will face whatever *regel* comes next, just like any other newly sanctified *korban*. What difference does the exchange make?

Rava's answer: the case involves a *mum* that developed in the middle of a *regel* — say, on the third day of Pesach — with the sanctity transferred to a new animal before Pesach ends. The first animal did not pass through the complete *regel*; the transfer occurred mid-*regel*. The new animal likewise did not receive its sanctity at the start of the *regel* but only mid-way through. The question is: if the new animal fails to be brought on that same Pesach, is it as though a complete *regel* passed over it — since taken together with the first animal the full *regel* was spanned — or does the clock reset to zero with the new animal's sanctification?

### Clock Resets

The Gemara teaches: *ka mashma lan* — the verse comes to tell us that the clock resets. The new animal is treated as freshly sanctified from the moment the *kedushah* was transferred to it. Even though the *kedushah* derives from the original animal (*mikach kama ka-ati*), one does not say the new animal is treated as though the entire *regel* passed over it. *Bal tacher* requires a complete *regel* to pass over *this* animal, and this animal only received its sanctity partway through.

### Neder Vs Nedavah

This scenario also illustrates a conceptual distinction between *neder* and *nedavah*. If one said *harei alai olah* — "I accept upon myself to bring an *olah*" — then the *bal tacher* question centers on the person: has the vow-maker fulfilled his obligation? The focus is on the individual's unrealized undertaking. But if one said *harei zo olah* — "this animal is an *olah*" — the focus shifts entirely to the animal: has this specific animal been offered within three *regalim*? When the *kedushah* is transferred to a new animal, that new animal has not yet had three *regalim* pass over it, and therefore there is no *bal tacher*. This contrast between *neder* and *nedavah* — between the obligation resting on the person versus the sanctity resting on the object — is essential to understanding how *bal tacher* operates across different categories.

## Ve-hayah Becha Cheit

### Sin in Owner

The Baraita's second concluding principle: *ve-hayah becha cheit ve-lo be-korbancha cheit* — the sin of *bal tacher* inheres in the owner, but the *korban* itself is not rendered invalid. Even if one transgressed by delaying too long, the offering may still be brought and is still accepted.

### Bechor/Maaser Parallel

The Gemara notes that this principle is also derived from a Baraita attributed to Rabbi Meir — referenced as *Acherim*, others, a name used for Rabbi Meir in certain contexts. The Baraita asks: perhaps a *bechor* that was not brought within its first year should be treated like disqualified *hekdesh* and become invalid? The verse answers: *ve-achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha ma'asar degancha tiroshcha ve-yitzharecha u-vechorot bekarcha ve-tzonacha* — you shall eat before the Lord your God your *ma'aser* of grain, wine, and oil, and the *bechorot* of your cattle and flocks. The verse links *bechor* to *ma'aser* — *makish bechor le-ma'aser*. Just as *ma'aser* can be given in a later year (the Torah explicitly contemplates a three-year clearing cycle, demonstrating that *ma'aser* from one year can be distributed more than a year late), so too *bechor* is not invalidated by late bringing. This implies that the *korban*, more generally, is not rendered *pasul* by the transgression of *bal tacher*.

### Deriving from Bechor

The Gemara raises the question: given this derivation from *bechor* and *ma'aser*, is the verse *ve-hayah becha cheit ve-lo be-korbancha cheit* needed at all? Could we not derive the validity of a late-brought *korban* from the *bechor/ma'aser* analogy alone?

### Bechor Not Ratzon

The Gemara answers: *itzterich* — both derivations are necessary. One might have argued that the *bechor/ma'aser* analogy proves the point only for *bechor* itself. Why? Because *bechor* is fundamentally a gift — *lav bar hartza'ah hu*, it is not oriented toward *hartza'ah*, the seeking of divine favor. Rashi explains that *bechor* is something one gives as a donation; its bringing is not primarily about achieving *ratzon*, divine acceptance and favor.

### Sanctification Vs Connec…

Other *kodashim* — *olah*, *shelamim*, *chatat* — are fundamentally different in character. These *korbanot* are oriented toward connection with God; there is an inherent element of *le-ratzon*, of being desired and accepted. The Torah frequently describes these offerings in terms of *hartza'ah* — the *korban* "comes before God" in a way that involves divine reception and favor. *Bechor* and *ma'aser*, by contrast, are fundamentally sanctifications: one separates what belongs to God and gives it over. What does one do with the *ma'aser*? Give it to the *Leviyim*, give it to the *aniyim*. The primary religious act is the separation, the acknowledgment that this portion belongs to God. It is not the vehicle through which one achieves *ratzon* or connection. Therefore, even if one grants that *bechor* is not disqualified by late bringing, one might argue that *olah* and *shelamim* — *korbanot* oriented toward *ratzon* and divine acceptance — perhaps should be: perhaps a *korban* brought after *bal tacher* is transgressed cannot achieve *ratzon*, and therefore cannot be *oleh le-shem chovah* for the owner.

There is an additional consideration that pushes toward this concern. The concept of *mitzvah haba'ah be-aveirah* — a *mitzvah* fulfilled through a transgression — might suggest that the delayed *korban* itself is tainted. If the very act of bringing it now involves, in some sense, the *aveirah* of having waited, perhaps the *ratzon* dimension of the *korban* is compromised. This is precisely the worry the verse *ve-hayah becha cheit ve-lo be-korbancha cheit* comes to address.

### Ben Azzai Pigul

The Gemara adds a teaching of Ben Azzai that makes this necessity even clearer. The Gemara notes that one might think the verse *lo te'acher leshalmo* is also needed to establish that a *bal tacher* offering is not *ratzon*. Ben Azzai teaches: the verse by *pigul* — an offering invalidated through improper intent during the *avodah* — states *ha-makriv oto lo yeichashev lo, pigul yiheyeh*: it will not be desired. One might reason: just as *pigul* involves a thought that pervades the act of offering and renders it *lo yeiratzeh*, not desired, perhaps *bal tacher* similarly renders the eventual *korban lo yeiratzeh*? The verse therefore states *ve-hayah becha cheit ve-lo be-korbancha cheit*: the *cheit* — the wrongdoing — remains in the person, but the *korban* itself is entirely unblemished. Not only is it *kasher* in the technical sense; it retains the full dimension of *ratzon*. *Oto lo yeratzeh* — only *that* (*pigul*) is not desired; *ve-ein me'acher nidro b'lo yeiratzeh* — one who delays his vow does not thereby make his *korban* undesired.

The question of what *ve-hayah becha cheit ve-lo be-korbancha cheit* comes to add, given that these principles might seem derivable from the *bechor/ma'aser* analogy and from Ben Azzai's teaching, will carry us into the next daf.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 6

## Delayed Korban Valid

### Becha Chet Baraita

The *gemara* on 6a continues its sustained treatment of *bal te'acher* — the prohibition against delaying the fulfillment of one's vow to bring a *korban*. To orient ourselves: the preceding discussion had introduced a *baraita* that interprets the phrase *becha chet* ("the sin shall be upon you") as teaching that *becha chet v'lo b'korban'cha chet* — the sin is yours, but it does not invalidate the *korban* itself. The *gemara* did not dispute this ruling; rather, it observed that the point seemed obvious, since we already know from the case of a *bechor* that a *korban* brought after the proper time remains *kasher*. The *gemara* then raised a possible distinction: perhaps the *korban* is technically *kasher* but lacks *hartza'ah* — it is not found acceptable, not *b'nei hartza'ah*. Both Rashi and Tosafot note the centrality of *kappara* here, but the concept extends more broadly to the notion that a *korban* must find favor before God, that there is an aspect of *yehi ratzon* — of the offering being desired — which is central to the very act of *avodah*. The *bechor*, by contrast, is primarily about the act of separation and sanctification; the actual offering is secondary. But for other *korbanot*, the question of *hartza'ah* is fundamental.

So the *gemara* sought to resolve the matter by pointing out that the *baraita*'s teaching — that the *korban* is not invalidated — is needed to address precisely this concern. Yet the *gemara* then presses further: even granting that, we might have derived the same ruling from another source.

### Ben Azzai & Pigul

The *gemara* notes that the ruling could have been derived from Ben Azzai. A *baraita* teaches: Ben Azzai says, the verse by *pigul* states *lo yeratzeh hamakriv oto* — the one who brings a *pigul* offering, it shall not be considered favorably for him. The word *oto*, "it," singles this out as the problem. One might have thought, the *baraita* reasons, that since the Torah says *lo te'acher leshalmo* — do not delay fulfilling your vow — someone who delays his *neder* would likewise be in the category of *belo yeratzeh*, his *korban* rendered unacceptable like *pigul*. Therefore the verse says *oto*: it is *pigul* that is *belo yeratzeh*, but the one who merely postpones his vow is not in this category. His delay is a sin upon him, but it does not compromise the acceptability of the *korban*.

Thus, the *gemara* observes, we already know from Ben Azzai's *drasha* that postponing a vow does not invalidate the offering. One might ask why the *gemara* insists that different Tannaitic sources cannot simply derive the same *halacha* from different *drashot* — and indeed, the *gemara*'s move here is to press that every source must be teaching something new. So if the point about the *korban*'s validity is already known, what does the phrase *becha chet* come to teach us?

### Sin on Person

The *gemara* reinterprets the *drasha* entirely. Rather than *becha chet v'lo b'korban'cha chet* — the sin is on you, not on your *korban* — the verse is now read as *becha chet v'lo b'ish'techa chet*: the sin falls upon you, not upon your wife.

### Wife's Death Context

This interpretation requires context. The *gemara* invokes a teaching of Rabbi Yochanan — or, some say, Rabbi Elazar — that *ein ishto shel adam meitah ela im ken mevakshin mimenu mamon v'ein lo*: a man's wife does not die unless heaven demands from him a monetary obligation that he is not fulfilling. What does this mean in context? Rashi understands it as referring to stolen money left unrepaid. Tosafot, more attuned to the passage at hand, explains it as referring to an unfulfilled vow — *mevakshin mimenu mamon*, heaven is calling in the pledge he made and has not satisfied. The consequence of non-fulfillment is rendered in vivid terms: the one who sleeps beside you is taken from you. One might then have assumed — *havah amina* — that the same punishment applies even to *bal te'acher*, the mere postponement of a vow. Therefore the verse teaches: *becha chet*, the sin focuses on you alone, it is not collective punishment. Non-fulfillment is one matter; postponement is another — and postponement does not trigger collective consequences.

### Collective Punishment Context

This, of course, is a striking and theologically charged teaching. The original *baraita* had said the sin falls on you and not on your *korban*; the *gemara* now reads it as saying the sin falls on you and not on your wife. That the two readings coexisted and the *gemara* chose to pursue the second is itself noteworthy.

It is worth acknowledging the discomfort this teaching provokes. The *Torah* itself seems to deny collective punishment in the starkest terms: *lo yumtu avot al banim u-vanim lo yumtu al avot* — fathers shall not be put to death for sons, nor sons for fathers; *ish b'chet'o yumatu* — each person is put to death for his own sin.

### Collective Punishment

And yet the tradition is not entirely uniform on this point. There are contexts — particularly around *avodah zarah* — where something resembling collective punishment appears. The verse in Devarim states, in the context of one who gives his children to *Molech*, *v'natati et panai ba-ish ha-hu u-ve-mishpachto* — I shall set My face against that man and against his family. What did his family do? Interestingly, Onkelos there translates *mishpachto* not as "his family" but as "his supporters," evidently seeking to preserve the principle of individual culpability by reading the collective as a community of willing participants. But the plain sense of the verse does point toward something collective. By *ir hanidachat*, the *gemara* resolves the difficulty by saying that the innocent are separated out and only the guilty are killed — but the Rambam famously rules that the guilty men are executed together with their wives and children, which is a position the other *rishonim* find deeply troubling, and which even pertains to a court-imposed punishment, not merely divine retribution.

One student offered a more structural reading: in the case of *avodah zarah*, what is at stake is not personal guilt spreading to family members, but rather the need to eradicate every trace of the corrupt influence. The family, on this reading, is not guilty — but the entire ecosystem connected to the *avodah zarah* must be cleansed, just as *shabbor teshabber matzevoteihem* demands the destruction of all vestiges. This is why *ir hanidachat* exists as a category — not because everyone in the city is equally culpable, but because the contamination must be fully excised. The same logic may explain why the concern extends to the family by *Korach* as well: one does not leave behind a four-year-old who will grow up to seek vengeance and carry on the rebellion. Rashi on the verse *v'ish hu b'mishpachto* takes a different approach, suggesting that the family is implicated because a corrupt figure — Rashi's example is a tax collector — typically has the complicity of the entire household. Rashi thus attempts to reframe the collective punishment as collective guilt.

In any event, the *gemara* here is working within a tradition that acknowledges, particularly in connection with *avodah zarah* and unfulfilled vows, some notion of collective consequences radiating outward from the individual. The *mishna* in Ketubot lists *noderet v'eina mekayyemet* — a wife who makes vows and does not fulfill them — as grounds for divorce without the *ketubah*. One might ask what her unfulfilled vows have to do with the husband. The *gemara* there explains it through this very same idea: unfulfilled vows can bring punishment upon the family. The same theme runs through our passage.

What the *gemara* here accomplishes is to narrow it: whatever applies in the case of outright non-fulfillment of a vow, it does not apply to mere postponement. *Becha chet* — the sin is on you, and not visited collectively. Though even the tradition acknowledges that *ba'avon nedarim*, for the sin of violating vows, a person's children may die — a statement embedded in the *halacha* of Ketubot — the *gemara* limits the collective dimension. Postponement is a sin, but it is an individual one.

---

## Motza Sefatecha Dras (II)

### Why Need Motza

The *gemara* now turns to a *baraita* on the closing verse of the *bal te'acher* passage: *motza sefatecha tishmor v'asita ka'asher nadarta l'Hashem Elokecha nedavah ka'asher dibarta beficha* — what comes forth from your lips you shall observe and do, as you vowed to Hashem your God, a *nedavah*, as you spoke with your mouth.

The *baraita* proceeds to identify multiple obligations within this verse. *Motza sefatecha* — this is a *mitzvat asei*, a positive commandment. *Tishmor* — this is a *mitzvat lo ta'asei*, a negative prohibition. And *v'asita* — this constitutes an *azharah l'veit din she'yasucha*, a charge to the court to compel the person to act.

But the *gemara* immediately challenges each element. Why do we need a *mitzvat asei* from *motza sefatecha*? We already have *u'vata shama v'havatem shama* — the verse commanding one to come to the place God chooses and bring all one's sacrifices there; that is already an explicit positive obligation. Why do we need *tishmor* as a negative prohibition? We already have the explicit *lo te'acher leshalmo* — do not delay fulfilling it — at the beginning of the passage; that is *bal te'acher* in its plainest form. And why do we need *v'asita* to teach that the court must compel someone to bring his *korban*? This too we already know: *yakriv oto*, as expounded in a *baraita* from Vayikra, teaches *she'kofin oto ad she'yomar rotzeh ani* — you compel him until he says "I am willing." *Yakriv oto* is read not as "he brings it" but as "you cause him to bring it" — the court presses the person into compliance. The resolution of the apparent contradiction between compulsion and *l'rtzono* — that it must be according to his will — is the famous principle that deep down a person wishes to fulfill his obligations; the *yeitzer hara* stands in the way, and the court beats the *yeitzer hara* out of him until his true desire is revealed. The Rambam discusses this principle at length in the context of the coerced *get*.

Tosafot notes that there are other *gemarot* indicating that the court generally compels performance of positive *mitzvot* — one thinks of the case of someone refusing to don *tefillin* or sit in a *sukkah* — and so the question of why we need a special verse for *korbanot* is pointed. The answer is that by *korbanot* one might have thought the Torah's explicit insistence on *l'rtzono* would preclude compulsion; the verse therefore tells us that compulsion applies even here.

The *gemara* then notes that since we apparently derive all three elements from other sources, the passage *motza sefatecha* must be doing something different — namely, extending these obligations beyond the domain of *korbanot*, to include *kodshei bedek habayit* and *tzedakah* as well.

---

## Tzedakah & Bedek (III)

### Categories Drasha

The *baraita* reads the entire clause of *motza sefatecha... ka'asher nadarta... nedavah... ka'asher dibarta beficha* as a series of categories to which the obligations of *bal te'acher* apply. *Ka'asher nadarta l'Hashem Elokecha* — this is a *neder*, the formula *harei alai*, a personal obligation. *L'Hashem Elokecha* — these are *chatat, asham, olah*, and *shlamim*, the various *korbanot* brought to God, whether obligatory or voluntary. *Nedavah kemashmao* — a *nedavah* in the straightforward sense, as distinguished from a *neder*: whereas a *neder* is *harei alai* — I obligate myself — a *nedavah* is *harei zu* — I sanctify this object. *Ka'asher dibarta* — what you spoke: these are *kodshei bedek habayit*, donations to the *beit hamikdash* in a non-*korban* form, where one sanctifies the monetary value of an object and transfers its ownership to the Temple treasury. And finally, *beficha* — with your mouth: *zu tzedakah*, this refers to *tzedakah*.

On the connection of *beficha* to *tzedakah*, Tosafot cites the verse *yatza mipi tzedakah* — "righteousness went forth from My mouth" — which explicitly links the word for *mouth* with *tzedakah*. This conjunction, *beficha zu tzedakah*, carries enormous resonance in later halachic literature and becomes a standard formula in discussions of whether *bal te'acher* applies to charitable pledges.

It should be noted that this list, as the *gemara* presents it here, is somewhat shorter than the list as it appeared in the preceding sugya. Conspicuously absent is *leket, shikcha, u'peah* — a category that Tosafot had already flagged as difficult from multiple angles: there is no act of speech that creates the obligation (making *beficha zu tzedakah* inapplicable), and the very concept of *bal te'acher* sits uneasily in that context, since either you left the *leket* in the field or you did not. The fact that this category does not appear in the *gemara*'s current formulation is notable.

The court's role in enforcement applies across this entire list, not only to *korbanot*. The Rambam rules that one who fails to give the appropriate amount of *tzedakah* is subject to compulsion by the court — a ruling that flows directly from this sugya's extension of *kofin oto* to the full scope of *bal te'acher*. Much of the *halacha* of *tzedakah* is also elaborated at the beginning of Bava Batra.

One question left open by the *gemara* is how to categorize a pledge made to a synagogue or communal institution that does not fit neatly as *tzedakah* to the poor. Does such a pledge fall under *bedek habayit* as an extension of that category, or does it fall under *tzedakah*, or perhaps simply under the general rubric of *neder*? The *gemara* does not address this directly.

---

## Motza Sefatecha Dras (II)

### Two Stages

The *gemara* now introduces a crucial distinction. After exhausting the question of why each element of *motza sefatecha* is needed when we already have other sources, the *gemara* offers its definitive answer: *chad amar v'lo afrish v'chad afrish v'lo akriv* — one verse speaks to the case where the person has taken a vow but has not yet separated an animal, and the other speaks to the case where the person has already sanctified the animal but has not yet brought it as a *korban*. Both stages involve *bal te'acher*, and each requires its own source.

And *u'tzricha* — you need both. If we only knew that *bal te'acher* applies when the person has taken a vow without yet separating an animal — *mishum delo kaim l'diburei*, because he has not yet acted on his words, his vow remains unsatisfied — one might have thought that once the animal is sanctified, the obligation is effectively in the Temple's possession already, and there is no further *bal te'acher* for the delay in physically delivering it. *Kol heicha de'isa b'igaza de'rachmana isa* — wherever the animal is, it is as if it sits in the divine storehouse. So we need the verse to tell us there is *bal te'acher* even in the second stage.

Conversely, if we only knew that *bal te'acher* applies when the animal has been sanctified and is being held without delivery — *dekamoshi gabei*, because there is something concrete that belongs to *hekdesh* and is being withheld — one might have thought that mere words, a vow without any physical action, are not sufficient to trigger *bal te'acher*. *Dibura lo kelum hu* — words alone amount to nothing in this context; *bal te'acher* requires that there be an actual object being held back from the *beit hamikdash*, somewhat analogous to *lo ta'ashok sechar sachir* — withholding a laborer's wages. Therefore both verses are necessary.

This raises an interesting question that the *gemara* itself does not address: if someone says *harei alai olah* — taking a vow — and then two *regalim* pass, and then he sanctifies an animal, and then two more *regalim* pass, and then he brings it — has he violated *bal te'acher*? Are these two distinct forms of *bal te'acher* such that sanctifying the animal resets the clock on the second stage, or does the original vow define the entire period from start to finish? The *gemara* does not say the clock resets, and presumably it does not, but the existence of two distinct dimensions of *bal te'acher* — the unfulfilled vow and the unsacrificed animal — is worth marking.

### Neder & Nedavah

The *gemara* raises a sharp difficulty with this two-stage framework. It notes that the word *nedavah* appears in both of the relevant verses — and by definition, a *nedavah* involves saying *harei zu*, thereby immediately sanctifying the animal. So if a *nedavah* always comes with a sanctified animal, how can one of the verses be addressing the case where the person has only spoken and not yet sanctified anything? *U'nedavah ksiv* — *nedavah* is written in both verses.

The *mishnah* makes the distinction explicit: *eizehu neder? ha'omer harei alai olah* — a *neder* is when one says "I take upon myself an *olah*." *V'eizehu nedavah? ha'omer harei zu olah* — a *nedavah* is when one says "this animal shall be an *olah*," immediately sanctifying the object. The difference has practical consequences: if it is a *neder* and the animal dies or is stolen, the person remains obligated and must bring another, since his personal commitment (*harei alai*) is still outstanding. If it is a *nedavah* and the animal dies or is stolen, he is exempt, since he never took on a personal obligation — he only sanctified the animal, and once it is gone, so is the obligation.

So the *gemara* asks: how can one verse be addressing the pre-sanctification stage when *nedavah* — written in both verses — means the animal has already been sanctified?

Rava resolves this. *Mashkachat lah kegon d'amar: harei alai olah al m'nat she'eini chayav b'achrayushah* — the case is where a person says: I accept upon myself the obligation of an *olah* on the condition that I will not be responsible for it if something happens to it after I sanctify it. This is technically a *neder* — it involves a personal obligation, *harei alai* — but it carries the halachic consequence of a *nedavah* with respect to *achrayut*: if the animal dies, he is not obligated to replace it. Rava is thus saying that the word *nedavah* in the verse that addresses the pre-sanctification stage refers not to a classic *nedavah* — *harei zu* — but to a *neder* that has assumed *nedavah*-like consequences through this stipulation.

In summary: the first verse addresses a *neder* in the classic sense (*harei alai*) or a *neder* qualified to resemble a *nedavah* in its consequences — in both cases, no animal has yet been physically sanctified. The second verse addresses the case where the animal has already been sanctified, whether through a classic *nedavah* (*harei zu*) or through a *neder* that has been actualized by designating a specific animal. Both stages trigger *bal te'acher*, and both require their own scriptural source.

---

## Tzedakah & Bedek (III)

### Rava Tzedakah

Having established the framework of *bal te'acher*, the *gemara* now turns to Rava's striking position on *tzedakah*. Rava declares: *utzedakah mechayev alah le'alter* — regarding *tzedakah*, one immediately becomes obligated. The violation of *bal te'acher* for *tzedakah* does not wait for three *regalim*; it is instantaneous. *Mai ta'ama? Dekaimi aniyim* — the reason is that the poor are present. The *regel* functions as the defining window of opportunity for *korbanot* — when one is *oleh l'regel* is when one has the opportunity to bring the offering. By *tzedakah*, every day that the poor are around constitutes such an opportunity. Failure to act is therefore an immediate transgression.

The *gemara* responds *pshita* — this is obvious — and one might expect that to end the discussion. But the *gemara* clarifies that it was not obvious: one might have thought that since *tzedakah* appears in the same *drasha* as *korbanot*, it should follow the same schedule — *ad de'avrei alei gimmel regalim ke'korbanot*. Therefore Rava tells us: *hatam hu de'leitnehu de'talinehu Rachmana b'regalim* — there, by *korbanot*, the Torah pegged the obligation to the *regalim*, which is when the opportunity arises. *Aval hacha*, here by *tzedakah*, it is not about *regalim* — *de'shchichi aniyim* — the poor are always present.

---

## Rava Severity (III)

### Rava I: Immediate

This is the first of three escalating statements from Rava about the severity and scope of *bal te'acher*. The immediate obligation for *tzedakah* — *mechayev alah le'alter* — is Rava's most extreme formulation, and it raises practical questions about what "immediately" means. Does one have even a short period to get one's affairs in order before writing the check, as it were? And does the obligation exist continuously, since the poor are always around?

---

## Tzedakah & Bedek (III)

### Tosafot Limitation

Tosafot, commenting on 4a, pulls back from the full force of Rava's position. Tosafot writes: *hani mili dekaimi aniyim, aval lo mechayev lehadori basreihu kol zman she'lo avru aleha shalosh regalim* — this applies when the poor are right in front of you. But if poor people are not directly present, one is not required to go searching for them; the obligation would still be governed by the three-*regalim* framework. Tosafot thus preserves Rava's principle while containing it: the immediacy of the obligation is activated by direct encounter with the poor, not by the abstract existence of poverty in the world.

---

## Rava Severity (III)

### Rava II: One Regel

The second of Rava's statements: *keivan she'avar alav regel echad, over b'asei* — once a single *regel* has passed without the person fulfilling his vow, he transgresses a positive commandment. The *mitzvat asei* of *u'vata shama v'havatem shama* — the obligation to bring one's sacrifices to the place God chooses — is violated as soon as the first opportunity is missed. Three *regalim* must pass to trigger *bal te'acher* proper, the *lo ta'asei*, but even one *regel* triggers a violation of the *asei*.

The *gemara* challenges this from a *baraita*: the case of the *vlad shlamim*, the offspring of a *shlamim* sacrifice. A witness testified: *hayesa lanu parah shel zivchei shlamim*, we once had a cow that was a *shlamim*, *v'achalnuhu b'Pesach*, we ate it at Pesach, *v'achalnu valdah shlamim b'chag*, and we ate its offspring as a *shlamim* on *Sukkot*. The *gemara* asks: why was the offspring not brought by *Shavuot*? According to Rava, one *regel* was already enough to trigger a violation of the *asei*. Did they not transgress by letting *Shavuot* pass?

Mar Zutra, in the name of Rava, answers: *kegon she'hayesa cholah b'Atzeret* — perhaps the animal was ill at *Shavuot*, and an ill animal may not be brought as a *korban*; therefore the delay was justified. Rav Ashi offers a different resolution: *mai v'achalnu valdah shlamim b'chag* — what does "on the *chag*" mean? He reads *chag* as referring to the next holiday, which would be *Shavuot* itself, not *Sukkot*. The *gemara* objects that this reading is linguistically strained: *kol heicha de'tani Pesach tani Atzeret* — wherever the *tanna* mentions Pesach and then wishes to refer to *Shavuot*, he calls it *Atzeret*. If he simply says *chag*, he means *Sukkot*. So Rav Ashi's reading is rejected, and Mar Zutra's answer — illness at *Shavuot* — stands.

### Rava III: Daily

The third of Rava's statements: *v'amar Rava, keivan she'avru alav gimmel regalim, b'chol yom va-yom over b'bal te'acher* — once three *regalim* have passed, one transgresses *bal te'acher* anew every single day. The rationale is practical as well as moral: if the transgression were a one-time event, once the person is already *over*, there is no further urgency to bring the *korban*. By declaring a fresh violation each day, the Torah maintains constant pressure on the person to remedy the situation.

---

## Rava Severity (III)

### Baraita Challenge

The *gemara* challenges Rava's third statement from the same *baraita* cited earlier: *echad bechor v'echad kol ha-kodashim, keivan she'avru aleihem shana belo regalim, regalim belo shana, over b'val te'acher* — whether it is a *bechor* or any consecrated animal, once a year without *regalim* or *regalim* without a year have passed, one transgresses *bal te'acher*. The *gemara* reads this as implying that the transgression happens once, at the threshold, not repeatedly each day. So is there a contradiction with Rava?

Rav Kahana responds: *man dekamosi shapir kamosi* — whoever raises this question raises it well. *Mikhdei, tana alavai kamahadar* — the *tanna* of that *baraita* is trying to find every possible scenario in which one transgresses. If you were trying to exhaust all the cases, you should have added: and after three *regalim*, every single day. Since he did not say that, presumably the *tanna* does not hold like Rava.

The *gemara* pushes back: *v'idakh, tana le-mikvei b'lav kamahadar* — the other side responds that the *tanna* is only interested in defining the parameters of the *lav*, when it first takes effect. *B'lav yeteira lo kamahadar* — counting the accumulation of subsequent violations is not his concern. He defines the threshold; Rava defines the ongoing consequence. The two positions are not contradictory — they address different questions. Rava's three statements therefore stand unchallenged: *tzedakah* is immediate, an *asei* is violated after one *regel*, and after three *regalim* a new violation accrues every day.

---

## Calendar Problem

### Lesser Measure

The *gemara* now turns to analyze the *baraita* itself in more detail. *Gufa*: the *baraita* teaches that *bal te'acher* is triggered by the lesser of three *regalim* or one year. *Bishlama regalim belo shana meshakchat lah* — the case of three *regalim* without a full year is easily constructed: if one makes a vow just before Pesach, then *Shavuot* and *Sukkot* follow within the same calendar year, giving three *regalim* in less than twelve months.

### Year Without Regalim

But *ela shana belo regalim heichi meshakchat lah* — how do you construct the inverse case, a full year without three *regalim*? A normal year always contains three *regalim*. The *gemara* notes that this is easy *l'man de'it lei kesidran* — for the opinion that requires the *regalim* to pass in their proper sequence (*Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot*). Under that view, a vow taken between *Pesach* and *Sukkot* could result in a year passing before completing the sequence *kesidran*. But for the opinion that any three *regalim* suffice, regardless of order — *l'man deleit lei kesidran* — any three *regalim* in any sequence count. How would you then construct a full year without three *regalim*?

### Rabbi Solar Year

The *gemara* answers: *bishlama le-Rebbi, de'meshakchat lah b'shana me'uberet* — for Rebbi, there is a ready answer, derived from a *baraita* about the redemption of a sold house in a walled city, which must be redeemed within a "full year." Rebbi holds: *gimel me'ot v'shishim v'chamisha yamim keminian yemos hachama* — 365 days, according to the count of the solar year. The Sages hold: *monei yud-bet chodesh miyom l'yom* — twelve months from day to day, and if the year was a leap year, the seller gains the extra month.

Under Rebbi's view, a year is 365 solar days, irrespective of the Hebrew calendar. In a leap year, the Hebrew calendar adds an extra month, making the lunar year 383 or 384 days. If one sanctifies an animal right after *Pesach* in a leap year — say, on the first of *Iyar* — and defines the year as 365 days, that span of 365 days will end before the next *Pesach* arrives. Since the leap year pushed the next *Pesach* further away (because it takes approximately 384 days to reach the same date again), 365 days will expire while one is still in *Adar Beit*, before the next *Pesach*. Three *regalim* have not yet recurred — the new *Pesach* has not come — yet 365 days have passed. So according to Rebbi, one can have a full year without three *regalim*.

### Shavuot Fluctuation

But for the Sages, who define a year by the same calendar date twelve (or thirteen) months later, the problem remains: under a normal calendar, the same date always brings you back after three *regalim*. The *gemara* resolves this by citing a teaching of Rabbi Shemaya: *Atzeret pe'amim heh, pe'amim vav, pe'amim zayin* — *Shavuot* can fall on the 5th, 6th, or 7th of Sivan, depending on whether *Nisan* and *Iyar* are both full months (30 days each, giving the 5th), both deficient (29 days each, giving the 7th), or one full and one deficient (giving the 6th).

This fluctuation creates the possibility of a full year without *Shavuot* occurring again on or before its previous date. If one took a vow on the 6th of *Sivan* in a year when *Shavuot* fell on the 5th, and the following year *Shavuot* falls on the 7th, then when the anniversary arrives — the 6th of *Sivan* of the following year — *Shavuot* has not yet occurred that year. The 6th of *Sivan* has come again (completing a full lunar year from the same date), but the festival of *Shavuot* is still one day away. A full year has elapsed without three *regalim* having passed through that date.

### Acherim Fixed

The *gemara* then asks: who argues with Rabbi Shemaya's position that the date of *Shavuot* can fluctuate? The answer is *Acherim* — identified as Rabbi Meir — who hold that the holidays shift by a fixed number of days each year. A *baraita* teaches: *Acherim omrim, ein bein Atzeret l'Atzeret, ein bein Rosh Hashanah l'Rosh Hashanah ela arba yamim bilvad* — from one year's *Shavuot* to the next, the calendar shifts by exactly four days. This is because a Hebrew year contains 354 days, and dividing by seven leaves a remainder of four. So each subsequent year's holidays fall four weekdays later than the previous year's. *V'im haysa shanah me'uberet, chamisha* — in a leap year, the shift is five days rather than four, because the added month is always a fixed 29-day month, and 29 divided by seven leaves a remainder of one, adding one more day to the shift.

The elegance of the *Acherim* system lies in its perfect regularity — no month-length variation, no fluctuation in the date of *Shavuot*. One might ask why such a clean calendar was not adopted in practice. The answer, as noted, is that other constraints — such as the prohibition against *Rosh Hashanah* falling on certain days of the week — require the flexibility of variable month lengths, and that system is what prevents adoption of the fully fixed calendar that *Acherim* envision.

# Rosh Hashanah 7

## Bal Te'acher & Heir

### Heir & Bal Te'acher

The *daf* opens by continuing a discussion of *bal t'acher* — the prohibition against delaying the fulfillment of sacrificial vows or obligations. The Gemara has already established that *bal t'acher* is not limited strictly to vows: one who is obligated to bring a *chatas* or an *asham* is equally bound by this prohibition even without having taken a formal vow. With that background in place, Rabbi Zeira poses a pointed question: *yoresh mahu b'bal t'acher* — does an heir who inherits a consecrated animal transgress *bal t'acher* if he delays bringing it?

The case requires careful analysis. The heir did not take the original vow, and the obligation does not arise from any personal act on his part. It stems entirely from the fact that he has inherited a sanctified animal. This distinguishes him both from the classic case of a person who makes a vow and from the case of one obligated in a *chatas* or *asham*, where the obligation originates directly with the individual. On the other hand, there is a general verse — *u'vashta shama v'heveisa shama* — enjoining one to bring one's *korbanot* to the *Beis Hamikdash*, and perhaps that general obligation is sufficient to link the heir to *bal t'acher* as well.

### Textual Derivation

The Gemara resolves the question by citing a *braisa* taught by Rabbi Chiya. The Torah uses the phrase *me'imach* — "from you" — and the Gemara derives from this: *prat l'yoresh*, you are held liable, not your heir. The *yoresh* is therefore exempt from *bal t'acher*.

The Gemara immediately asks: is not this same word *me'imach* already needed to derive the inclusion of *leket*, *shichcha*, and *peah* within the category of *bal t'acher* — a derivation noted earlier as among the more surprising extensions of this prohibition? The Gemara resolves this elegantly: *kari be me'imach v'kari be imach* — the word *me'imach* yields two teachings simultaneously. The base word *imach* — "with you" — establishes the obligation regarding the poor person's gifts, while the prepositional *mem* of *me'imach* adds the limiting teaching: "you," not your heir.

The upshot is significant: although *bal t'acher* does not require the person to have made the vow himself — as proven by its application to *chatas* and *asham* — it does require that the obligation originate with the person. An heir who inherits a sanctified animal may still be obligated by the positive commandment of *u'vashta shama v'heveisa shama* to bring it, but he does not transgress *bal t'acher*.

## Women & Bal Te'acher

### Women's Status

Rabbi Zeira's second question follows directly: *isha mah hi b'bal t'acher* — is a woman subject to *bal t'acher*? At first glance this seems puzzling, since a woman who takes a vow is certainly obligated to fulfill it. The difficulty, however, lies in the relationship between *bal t'acher* and the *regalim*. The entire Gemara has been developing the connection between *bal t'acher* and the pilgrimage festivals, treating the failure to bring a *korban* during a *regel* as the operative moment of delay. Since women are not obligated in *aliyah l'regel* — they may remain home while their husbands make the pilgrimage — a woman never squanders a concrete opportunity to bring her *korban* in the manner that triggers *bal t'acher*. She was never in Yerushalayim, never passed through the *Beis Hamikdash*, and therefore, one might argue, never incurred the specific *ikhur* — the delay — that *bal t'acher* targets.

The counter-possibility raised in the Gemara is that women are included in the *mitzvah* of *simcha* — the rejoicing of the festival — based on the verse *vesamachta ata u'veisecha*, "you and your household shall rejoice." If so, a woman has an obligation to be in Yerushalayim for the *regalim*, and the logic of squandered opportunity would apply to her just as it does to men.

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye responds to Rabbi Zeira by affirming the force of the *simcha* argument: since a woman is obligated in *simcha*, she has reason to be in Yerushalayim, and therefore *bal t'acher* applies to her. The Gemara, however, immediately complicates Abaye's position by citing another statement in his name: *isha ba'alah mesamchah* — "a woman is made joyful by her husband." This statement seems to undercut the claim that a woman's independent presence in Yerushalayim is required, and the Gemara asks whether Abaye is being consistent.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

The tension between these two statements of Abaye gives rise to an important dispute between Rashi and Tosafot regarding the precise meaning of *isha ba'alah mesamchah*.

Rashi understands this phrase to mean that a woman fulfills the obligation of *simcha* through her husband's provision — specifically, through receiving nice clothing and similar gifts — and she has no independent requirement to partake of the *shalmei simcha* at all. On this reading, a woman need not be in Yerushalayim at all; the husband's departure for the *regel* while providing for his wife at home is sufficient. Accordingly, a woman would never have the concrete opportunity to bring her *korban* to the *Beis Hamikdash* that is the basis of *bal t'acher*.

Tosafot, in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, reads the statement differently. The obligation of *simcha* does fall upon the husband rather than the wife, but this means that the husband must bring the *shalmei simcha* — it is his obligation to do so. The wife, however, would still be present in Yerushalayim to eat from those *korbanot*, even if the act of bringing them is not hers. The distinction is between the obligation to bring and the opportunity to partake. On Tosafot's reading, the question of *bal t'acher* for women becomes more nuanced: even if she eats in Yerushalayim, it is not her own obligation to appear before the *Beis Hamikdash* in the manner that creates a squandered opportunity.

The Gemara then notes — in response to an implicit question — that according to Rabbi Zeira himself, who raised the question, the relevant framing must be his own view that women are included in *simcha* through the *korbanot*; otherwise, on the view that women have no connection to these sacrifices at all, there would be no basis for the question in the first place. The question of whether *bal t'acher* applies to women thus ultimately hinges on deeper disagreements about what defines a "squandered opportunity": whether it requires an obligation to be present in the *Beis Hamikdash*, an obligation to be in Yerushalayim, or whether *bal t'acher* operates independently of the *regalim* altogether as a function of calendar time.

## Bechor & Year

### When Year Begins

The Gemara turns from *bal t'acher* to a related question about time: *bechor me'eimatai monim lo shana* — from when does one begin counting the year for a *bechor*? The Torah requires that a firstborn animal be eaten *shana b'shana*, year by year. The question is what event starts the clock.

Abaye holds that the year begins *me-sha'ah she-nolad* — from the moment of birth. Rav Acha bar Yaakov holds it begins *me-sha'ah she-ra'uy l'hartza'ah* — from the moment the animal becomes fit to be brought as a *korban*, which is eight days after birth.

### Tam vs. Ba'al Mum

The Gemara resolves the apparent dispute by distinguishing between two cases: *ha b'tam, ha b'ba'al mum* — the two opinions are not actually in conflict but address different scenarios. For an unblemished animal (*tam*), which is fit to be brought as a *korban*, the year does not begin until it is eligible to be offered, namely eight days after birth. For a blemished animal (*ba'al mum*), which will never be brought as a *korban* but will instead be slaughtered and eaten by the *kohen* outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, the year begins immediately upon birth, since there is no reason to wait.

A question arises: can a *ba'al mum* really be eaten on the very day it is born? Rashi notes that a newborn animal might be a *nefel* — a non-viable animal — and therefore unfit for consumption. The Gemara answers that there are cases where it is evident at birth that the animal completed a full gestation (*de-kim lei b'de-ika de-kalu lo chodashav*), and in such cases one may indeed begin eating it immediately and the year commences from that day.

## Four New Years Braitta

### Nissan & Months

Having concluded the immediate *bal t'acher* discussion and the question of the *bechor*'s year, the Gemara introduces a *braisa* — *tanu rabbanan* — that enumerates additional *roshei shanah* not included in the *Mishnah*. The *braisa* states: *b'echad b'Nissan, Rosh Hashanah l'chodashim* — the first of Nisan is the new year for months. Nisan is month one, Iyar is month two, and so on throughout the year.

The *braisa* also lists: *l'iburim* — for leap years; *l'trumat shekalim* — for the collection of new *shekel* funds for the communal sacrifices; and, according to some, even for house rental contracts. Each of these will be discussed in turn.

The Gemara first asks: *l'chodashim mina lan* — how do we know Nisan is the first month? The answer comes from the verse *hachodesh hazeh lachem rosh chodashim* — "this month shall be for you the first of months," from the passage in which the Torah designates the month of the Pesach offering as month one.

But this is somewhat circular: how do we know which month the Pesach offering was brought? The verse tells us it was brought in month one — but which month is that? The answer is provided by a second verse: *shamor et chodesh ha'aviv v'asita pesach* — observe the month of the *aviv*, the spring ripening of the grain, and bring the Pesach. We know from agricultural reality that this ripening occurs in Nisan.

### Aviv Proof

The Gemara sharpens the derivation. *Eizehu chodesh she-yesh bo aviv? Hevei omer zeh Nisan* — which month has the ripening of the grain? That is Nisan. And this month is called *rishon*, first.
