The Gemara anticipates objections: perhaps Iyar should be considered the month of *aviv*, since some grain ripening extends into it? The answer: *be'inan aviv v'leika* — the full sense of *aviv* is not present in Iyar. Perhaps Adar, since some early ripening occurs there? The answer: *be'inan rov aviv v'leika* — Adar lacks the *majority* of the ripening. The Gemara then asks: but does the verse actually say "the majority" of the ripening? This challenge stands.

### Tishrei & Harvest

Rav Chisda therefore offers a different prooftext: *ach b'chamishah asar yom la-chodesh ha-shevi'i b'aspe'chem et tvuat ha'aretz* — "but on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you gather in the produce of the land," referring to Sukkot. *Eizehu chodesh she-yesh bo asifah? Hevei omer zeh Tishrei v'kari lei shevi'i* — which month is characterized by the ingathering? Tishrei. And it is called the seventh month. Since Tishrei is the seventh, Nisan is the first.

But again the Gemara objects: perhaps the seventh month refers to the seventh counting from Iyar, making the ingathering month Marcheshvan? The answer: *be'inan asif v'leika* — Marcheshvan lacks the full ingathering. And Elul? Perhaps the ingathering begins there, counting from Adar? Again: *be'inan rov asif v'leika* — the majority of the ingathering is not in Elul. And again the Gemara presses: does the verse actually say "majority"?

### Kabbalah & Prophecy

Ravina then concedes the point: *devar zeh mi-torat Moshe Rabbeinu lo lamadnu* — we cannot prove the identity of Nisan with certainty from the Torah alone. The agricultural anchors are suggestive but not definitive; there is always the possibility of a one-month shift. Rather, *mi-divrei kabbalah lamadnu* — we learn it from the books of *kabbalah*, meaning the prophetic writings: the *Nevi'im* and *Ketuvim*.

The critical evidence comes from post-exilic texts, in which numbered months are explicitly identified with named Babylonian months. Because this identification occurred after the return from Babylonian exile, these texts uniquely correlate the traditional numbering with specific named months, thus providing a fixed point of reference.

The Gemara adduces several such verses: from Zechariah, *beyom esrim v'arba'ah la-ashtei asar chodesh hu chodesh Shevat* — the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is Shevat. Since Shevat is eleven, Nisan is one. From Esther: *ba-chodesh ha-asiri hu chodesh Tevet* — the tenth month is Tevet, confirming Nisan as one. From Nehemiah: *b'arba'ah asar la-chodesh ha-tshi'i b'Chislev* — the ninth month is Kislev. From Esther again: *ba-chodesh ha-shelishi hu chodesh Sivan* — the third month is Sivan. And: *shneim asar hu chodesh Adar* — Adar is the twelfth, so Nisan is the first. Finally, the most explicit verse: *ba-chodesh ha-rishon hu chodesh Nisan* — "in the first month, which is Nisan."

The Gemara asks why all the other *amora'im* did not simply quote that last verse. The answer is that *dilma rishon rishon l'milta* — "first" there might mean the first month in which this particular story began, not necessarily that Nisan is first in the monthly order. Hence the other verses, each linking a numbered month to a named month, are necessary.

### Month Nomenclature

Tosafot raises a meta-level question: even granting all of these verses, how do we know which month is "Nisan"? The derivation from the prophets assumes we already know the order and identity of the months. The answer is that we do have an independent tradition (*kabbalah*) establishing the sequence of the months — the prooftexts serve to correlate the numbered months of the Torah with the named months already known by tradition.

The Yerushalmi states the historical situation explicitly: *shemot ha-chodashim alu b'yadam mi-Bavel* — the names of the months came up with the Jewish people from Babylonia. Before the exile, the Torah uses numbered months, and the earlier books of *Tanakh* employ descriptive agricultural names — *yerach ha-eitanim* for Tishrei (the month of the strong ones, when the forefathers were born), *yerach Bul* (the month of falling leaves and the feeding of stored produce to animals), and *yerach Ziv* (the month of the blossoming of trees). Tosafot's point is that there was a three-stage transition: first, numbered months only; then, descriptive agricultural designations beginning to serve as names; finally, the adoption of the Babylonian month names upon the return from exile — the names now familiar as Nisan, Iyar, Sivan, and so on. Some of these Babylonian names have associations with Babylonian deities, a fact that raises its own questions.

## Nissan & Leap Years

### Intercalation Rules

The *braisa* also lists Nisan as *Rosh Hashanah l'iburim* — the new year for leap years. The Gemara challenges this: does one really determine leap years starting from Nisan? That would mean deciding a full twelve months in advance. But a *braisa* teaches: *ein me'avrin ha-shanah lifnei Rosh Hashanah* — one does not intercalate the year before Rosh Hashanah, meaning before Tishrei. And if one did so prematurely, it does not take effect. Under exceptional pressure — for instance, if there is fear of a governmental decree preventing intercalation later, or if the *nasi* may not be available — one may intercalate immediately after Rosh Hashanah. But in any case, *ein me'avrin ela Adar* — the only month that may be added is a second Adar, since the purpose of intercalation is to ensure that Pesach falls in the spring, and the adjustment is therefore made immediately before Pesach.

### Confusion Risk

One reason cited in the Gemara for not intercalating too late in the year concerns the thirty-day pre-Pesach learning period: *sho'alin b'hilchot ha-Pesach kodem l'Pesach sheloshim yom* — we begin publicly teaching the laws of Pesach thirty days before the festival. One opinion held that intercalation must occur before Purim, because once the public teaching of the laws of Pesach begins, people internalize the message that Pesach is thirty days away. If the rabbis then declare an intercalated year, adding another thirty days, the community will have been sent a contradictory message. Rashi explains the danger: people will have already begun preparing for Pesach in earnest, and when told it is now a leap year, they may not believe the announcement and may inadvertently observe Pesach in Adar Sheni, failing to recognize the true Pesach when Nisan arrives. The concern is analogous to the boy who cried wolf — repeated false signals desensitize people to the real one.

The opinion permitting intercalation through the end of Adar responds that the community understands intercalation to be a matter of calculation (*chushbana*), and they will accept that the rabbis finalized their determination only now. People know that such decisions can come late, and will adjust accordingly.

### Endpoint Function

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies what the *braisa* means when it calls Nisan the *Rosh Hashanah* for *iburim*: *hafsakat iburim* — it is the *termination* of the opportunity for intercalation, not its initiation. Since intercalation can only occur in Adar, the last moment to declare a leap year is the last day of Adar. Once the first of Nisan arrives, the previous year can no longer be made a leap year. This is confirmed by the *Mishnah* in tractate *Eduyot*, which teaches that one may intercalate the year throughout all of Adar — up to its very last day.

Thus, the *braisa*'s inclusion of Nisan as *Rosh Hashanah l'iburim* reflects not the beginning of a leap year's declaration, but the closing of the prior year's window. Our *Mishnah*, by contrast, is interested in how years begin — not how prior years end — and therefore does not include *iburim* in its list.

## Nissan & Shekalim

### Fresh Funds Rule

The *braisa* further designates Nisan as *Rosh Hashanah* for the *trumat shekalim* — the collection of new funds for the communal sacrifices. Rabbi Yoshiah derives this from the verse *zot olat chodesh b'chodsho l'chodshei ha-shanah* — "this is the burnt offering of each month in its month, for the months of the year." The phrase *l'chodshei ha-shanah* implies renewal: the communal sacrifices must come from fresh, newly collected funds each year. The starting point for this renewal is Nisan, linked by the same phrase *l'chodshei ha-shanah* to the verse that identifies Nisan as the first month.

This connection is reinforced by a *gezeirah shavah* — the verse governing new *korbanot* uses *chodshei ha-shanah* (months and year together), and the verse establishing Nisan uses the same language. This shared phrasing links them: the renewal of communal sacrificial funds begins in Nisan. The Gemara notes that one cannot apply a verse where "year" appears with "months" to a different verse where "year" appears alone (as in *me-reishit ha-shanah*, associated with Tishrei), precisely because the presence of "months" is the operative link.

### Old vs. New Funds

The practical law is stated by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *korbanot tzibbur ha-ba'im b'echad b'Nissan, mitzvah l'havi min ha-chadash* — for the communal sacrifices beginning on the first of Nisan, there is a *mitzvah* to bring them from the newly collected funds. *V'im hevi min ha-yashan, yatza* — if one brought them from old funds, the obligation is still discharged; the sacrifice is valid. *Ella she-chisar mitzvah* — but the specific *mitzvah* of renewal has been missed. A parallel *braisa* confirms this ruling.

### Private Donations

A further law follows: *yachid she-nitnadav mishelo* — if a private individual donates an animal from his own property to be used as a communal sacrifice, it is valid (*ksherim*), provided he truly transfers it to the community — *u'vilvad she-yimserem l'tzibbur*. The Gemara asks: is this not obvious? If he genuinely transfers it, why would there be any concern? The answer is that one might have worried that even an ostensibly sincere transfer retains some element of personal attachment — perhaps the donor will continue to think of the animal as his own. The Gemara therefore rules that we take him at his word: if the transfer appears complete and he declares it complete, we accept it. The *korban* is now fully the community's.

As for why our *Mishnah* does not include Nisan as *Rosh Hashanah* for *shekalim*: since the law permits bringing from old funds *b'diavad*, it is not absolute. The ruling lacks the definitive quality that would warrant inclusion in the *Mishnah*'s list of the four primary new years.

## Nissan & House Rentals

### Default Meaning

The *braisa* concludes with the position of *yesh omrim*: Nisan also serves as *Rosh Hashanah* for rental contracts. The *tanna'im* of the *braisa* teach: *ha-maskir bayit l'chaveiro l'shanah* — one who rents a house to another for "a year" counts twelve calendar months from the rental date, returning to the same day of the calendar year regardless of whether that spans twelve or thirteen months. But *v'im amar l'shanah zu* — if one says "for this year," the contract runs until the end of the current year, defined as the last day of Adar. Once the first of Nisan arrives, the year has turned. Thus, even if the rental began on the first of Adar, the arrival of Nisan — just thirty days later — constitutes the end of that year.

The Gemara adds that even authorities who hold that "one day in a year counts as a full year" for certain purposes (such as counting the years of a king's reign) do not apply that principle here. The reason: *d'lo tarach inish l'migar beisa l'vatzir mi-tlasin yomin* — no one bothers to draw up a rental contract for less than thirty days. Therefore, the minimum period implied by "this year" in a rental context is a full month, and a rental of less than a month would be read as extending through to the end of the *following* year.

### Rainy Season Logic

The Gemara asks why the "end of the year" in rental contracts should be tied to Nisan rather than Tishrei. The answer is practical and intuitive: *stam ki agar inish beisa, l'chulu yemot geshamim agar* — when someone rents a house, they typically want it for the rainy season. The rainy season in Eretz Yisrael begins after Tishrei. No one wants to be evicted or to begin apartment-hunting at the onset of the rainy season. Therefore, defining the "end of the year" as Tishrei would create exactly this hardship, and it is inconceivable that rental convention would operate this way.

### Minority View

The first opinion in the *braisa*, as well as the author of our *Mishnah*, does not include Nisan as *Rosh Hashanah* for rental contracts. Their reasoning: *b'Nisan nami shchichi mitri* — rain occurs in Nisan as well. April showers are a reality, and no renter is more comfortable being evicted in Nisan than in Tishrei. If both months can bring rain, there is no principled reason to fix the "end of the year" at either one; local custom and context must determine what parties meant by "this year."

### Tosafot on Payment

One might think that the amount paid would resolve ambiguity — if the rent paid is clearly six months' worth at the going rate, and the contract runs from Rosh Chodesh Adar to Rosh Chodesh Nisan, surely the parties intended one month, not one year. Tosafot cautions against this inference: even if the sum seems inconsistent with the stated duration, we do not necessarily conclude the contract meant something other than what it says. The excess payment could be construed either as a *matanah* — a gift, essentially a signing bonus — or as a *pikadon*, a deposit the tenant expects to recover. Which of these applies has significant halakhic consequences, but neither reading allows us to simply read the sum as decisive evidence of the parties' intent regarding the duration. Tosafot's caution reflects a broader principle in *dinei mamonot*: payment alone cannot override the literal terms of a contract when those terms are susceptible to multiple readings.

## Elul vs. Tishrei

### Rabbi Meir Position

Having exhausted the discussion of Nisan, the Gemara returns to the *Mishnah*'s next entry: *b'echad b'Elul, Rosh Hashanah l'ma'aser behema* — the first of Elul is the new year for the animal tithe. The Gemara asks: *manni* — who is the anonymous author of this ruling? The answer is Rabbi Meir, as explicitly stated in a *Mishnah* elsewhere: *Rabbi Meir omer b'echad b'Elul, Rosh Hashanah l'ma'aser behema*.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

The *Mishnah* then immediately states the minority view: *Rabbi Eliezer v'Rabbi Shimon omrim b'echad b'Tishrei* — the first of Tishrei is the new year for *ma'aser behema*. This creates a structural puzzle. The opening of the *Mishnah* established Nisan as *Rosh Hashanah l'melachim u'l'regalim*. The Gemara has already determined, based on an earlier *braisa*, that the rule of *regalim* for purposes of *bal t'acher* — namely that the *regalim* must be observed in order beginning with Pesach — is the position of Rabbi Shimon. Then the *Mishnah* adopts the view of Rabbi Meir for *ma'aser behema* (Elul rather than Tishrei), and immediately cites Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer as dissenting on that question.

### Rabbi's Selectivity

Rav Yosef explains that Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi — *Rebbi* — is the *Mishnah*'s redactor, and he exercises deliberate selectivity: *v'nasiv lei aliba d'tana'i* — he chooses among the positions of the *Tanna'im* as he sees fit. *B'regalim savar lah k'Rabbi Shimon* — on the question of the *regalim* and *bal t'acher*, he follows Rabbi Shimon. *U'v'ma'aser behema savar lah k'Rabbi Meir* — on the question of *ma'aser behema*, he follows Rabbi Meir. The *Mishnah* is thus a composite, drawn from two different authorities, each authoritative in his own domain according to Rebbi's judgment.

## Beyond Four Years

### Additional Candidates

The resolution of the *Mishnah* through Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon creates a new problem. If Rebbi adopts Rabbi Shimon's position on the *regalim*, then the first of Nisan (for kings) and the fifteenth of Nisan (for *regalim*) are two separate entries — yet both fall in Nisan. Adding Elul (for *ma'aser behema*), Tishrei (for years, *shemitah*, and *yovel*), and the fifteenth of Shevat (for trees), we already have five entries, not four. But now a *braisa* raises the number further: *shisha asar b'Nisan, Rosh Hashanah l'omer* — the sixteenth of Nisan is the new year for the *Omer*, marking the beginning of permitted consumption of the new grain; and *shisha b'Sivan, Rosh Hashanah l'shtei halechem* — the sixth of Sivan (Shavuot) marks the new year for the *shtei halechem*, after which new grain may be brought as a *Mincha* offering.

These additions would bring the total to six or seven, depending on how one counts. Rava would go from four to six; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, who counts by months rather than individual dates, should still reach five, since Sivan would constitute a new month.

### Rav Papa's Answer

Rav Papa offers the first resolution: *ki chashiv, midei d'chaya m'ortsa — midei d'lo chaya m'ortsa lo kachashiv* — the *Mishnah* counts only those new years that begin the night before, i.e., at nightfall at the onset of the new day. The *Omer* and the *shtei halechem* are brought in the middle of the day; they do not commence at nightfall and therefore are excluded from the count.

The Gemara objects: the *regalim* are also effective only during the day — one can only bring *korbanot* in the daytime — yet the *regalim* are counted. Rav Papa responds that the *regalim* are different: the underlying obligation to bring the *korbanot* arose long before the *regel* itself. The *regel* is not the beginning of the obligation but the moment at which delay becomes a violation. Since the obligation *mechayav v'kai* — was already in place — the *regel* functions as a terminus rather than an initiation.

The Gemara further presses: *Yovel* also takes effect only in the daytime — *ta'aviru shofar b'chol artzechem*, the blowing of the shofar that activates *Yovel*, is understood to occur during the day of Yom Kippur. Yet *Yovel* is included in the *Mishnah*. The Gemara responds that the *Mishnah* here follows the position of Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that *Yovel* already takes effect from Rosh Hashanah — the night before Yom Kippur — not from Yom Kippur itself.

### Rav Sheshet's Logic

Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi offers a simpler principle: *ki kachashiv midei d'lo tali b'ma'aseh* — the *Mishnah* counts only those new years that are not dependent on an action. Dates that carry inherent significance by virtue of the calendar alone are included; dates whose significance derives from a specific act performed on them are not. The sixteenth of Nisan is not really a date — it is the day on which the *Omer* is brought, and it is that act of bringing which matters. Similarly, the sixth of Sivan is the date of the *shtei halechem* offering, and the significance is action-dependent.

The Gemara raises the same objection: the *regalim* are also action-dependent — they are about bringing *korbanot*. Rav Sheshet responds: *bal t'acher mimela chaya* — the *regalim* function differently. They make one liable not for having done something on that day, but for *not* having done something. It is the failure to act that the date activates, not the action itself. The date has independent significance as the point at which liability crystallizes.

And again the Gemara presses: *Yovel* also requires blowing the shofar, an action — yet it is listed. Again the answer: the *Mishnah* follows Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, for whom *Yovel* takes effect from Rosh Hashanah.

### Rav Ashi's Method

Rav Ashi provides a final, clean resolution: *arba'ah Roshei Hashanim hen she-hen b'arba'ah Roshei Chadashim* — there are four new years, and they fall on four first-of-the-month dates. The *Mishnah* counts only those *roshei shanah* that fall on the first of a month. The sixteenth of Nisan and the sixth of Sivan are immediately excluded on this basis. The *regalim* in the context of *bal t'acher* refer primarily to the fifteenth of Nisan — already counted as part of the Nisan block — and do not add a separate new year on a different first of a month.

The Gemara raises one remaining difficulty: the fifteenth of Shevat (*Tu B'Shevat*), as held by Beit Hillel, is not the first of the month. Rav Ashi's principle would require that the new year for trees fall on the *first* of Shevat, which is Beit Shammai's position. The Gemara therefore concludes: *sheloshah l'divrei hakol* — three of the four new years are agreed upon by everyone and fall on the first of their respective months. The fourth — the new year for trees — is a matter of dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Rav Ashi's principle of counting only first-of-the-month *roshei shanah* applies as an absolute rule to three, and by Beit Shammai's reckoning also to the fourth.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 8

## Ma'aser Behema Debate

### Two Verses Read

The daf opens five lines from the top with the position of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon: *be'echad beTishrei* — the *rosh hashanah* for *ma'aser behemah* falls on the first of Tishrei. Having spent considerable time unpacking *echad beNisan* — including an extensive treatment of *bal te'acher* and a *baraisa* enumerating the various ways Nisan functions as a *rosh hashanah* — the Gemara now moves on to the remaining *roshei shanah*, beginning with the dispute over *ma'aser behemah*.

Rabbi Yochanan observes that both the *tanna kamma* (who holds Elul) and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon derive their respective positions from the same verse in Tehillim: *levushu charim hatzon ve'amakim ya'atfu var yitro'u af yashiru* — "The sheep are clothed with coverings, and the valleys are cloaked in grain; they burst forth in trumpeting, even give song." The verse is read as a description of the sheep's mating season, with the "covering" (*levushu*) understood as one sheep mounting another, and the "cloaking of the valleys in grain" and "bursting forth in song" as simultaneous agricultural markers that help identify the precise time of year.

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rabbi Meir holds that the sheep mate *bizman she'amakim ya'atfu var* — at the time when the valleys are first cloaked in grain, which is in Adar, before the barley is ripe and ready for harvest. If mating occurs in Adar, then, given a gestation period of five months — Nisan, Iyar, Sivan, Tammuz, Av — the sheep give birth in Av. Since the primary birthing season concludes in Av, the *rosh hashanah* for *ma'aser behemah* falls in the month immediately following, which is Elul.

### Rabbi Elazar/Shimon

Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon read the verse differently. They focus not on the phrase *ve'amakim ya'atfu var* but on *yitro'u af yashiru* — when the stalks of grain rustle in the wind and "give song," a phenomenon that occurs only in Nisan once the grain has grown tall enough. According to their reading, the primary mating season occurs in Nisan. The sheep therefore conceive in Nisan, give birth five months later in Elul, and accordingly the *rosh hashanah* for *ma'aser behemah* is Tishrei, the month after Elul.

### Gemara Resolution

The Gemara objects to both readings. Against Rabbi Meir: does the verse not also mention *yitro'u af yashiru*, implying that mating happens in Nisan as well? The Gemara answers: *hahu be'aflei* — that refers to the late-mating sheep, those who mate after the primary season. Against Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon: does the verse not also say *ve'amakim ya'atfu var*, implying mating in Adar? The Gemara answers: *hahu becharifta* — those are the early ones who begin mating already in Adar.

Rava then reformulates the dispute entirely. In truth, *kulei alma* — everyone agrees that the primary mating period occurs in Adar (as the *pasuk* first states) and that the primary birthing period is therefore in Av. The dispute is not really about sheep biology at all. Rather, it concerns how to read the verse *aser te'aser*, the doubled language of tithing, which the Gemara takes as linking *ma'aser behemah* to *ma'aser dagan* and asks: in what sense are they linked?

It is worth noting a difficulty here: if both sides agree that birthing occurs throughout both Av and Elul — with Av being primary and Elul being secondary — then it is hard to understand why anyone would place the *rosh hashanah* after the primary birth period but before the late births are complete. Logic would seem to demand that the new year begin only after the entire birthing process has concluded, which would mean Tishrei in any case. This is a genuine *he'arah* on the structure of the dispute as initially framed, though Rava's reformulation ultimately moves the argument away from this point.

---

## Logic vs Form

### Rabbi Meir Logic

Rava explains that Rabbi Meir reads the linkage between *ma'aser behemah* and *ma'aser dagan* as a conceptual parallel: *makish ma'aser behemah le-ma'aser dagan* — just as the *rosh hashanah* for grain is determined by the logic of the agricultural cycle, so too the *rosh hashanah* for animals. The principle he identifies is *samuch le-gemaro isuro* — the tithing year begins at the point juxtaposed to the completion of the process. By grain, the new year is Tishrei, because Tishrei is when *Chag Ha-asif* — the Feast of Ingathering — marks the end of the harvest cycle. So too by animals, the new year begins right after the primary birthing period concludes, which is in Elul, immediately following the Av births.

### Elazar/Shimon Form

Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon also invoke the linkage between the two *ma'asrot*, but they apply it as a simple formal equation rather than an analogical argument: *mah ma'aser dagan Rosh Hashanah shelo Tishrei, af ma'aser behemah Rosh Hashanah shelo Tishrei* — just as grain has its *rosh hashanah* in Tishrei, so too animals have their *rosh hashanah* in Tishrei. It is a *Tishrei-Tishrei* comparison with no further derivation needed.

The dispute thus comes down to whether the *hekesh* operates by shared logic or by shared form. Rabbi Meir says the Torah links the two tithes to teach that the same underlying rationale — beginning the year *samuch le-gemaro* — governs both. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say the Torah simply places both tithes under the same calendar date.

### Sukkot Asif

The identification of Tishrei as the *rosh hashanah* for grain is itself rooted in the agricultural cycle. *Sukkot* is *Chag Ha-asif*, the festival of ingathering, when the harvest is being gathered in. It is the moment when one agricultural year concludes and the next begins, which is why the *rosh hashanah* for *ma'aser dagan* is anchored to Tishrei. Rabbi Meir draws on this logic and extends it by analogy to animals, placing the *rosh hashanah* for *ma'aser behemah* in the month immediately following the primary birth season.

One might note that even by grain, the new year is proclaimed while the ingathering process is still technically underway — *Sukkot* is when you are still gathering, not when the last stalk has been processed. This raises the same structural question as before: does the new year mark the end of the primary phase of a process, even if secondary elements are still ongoing? It seems that this is indeed the principle, and it applies consistently to both grain and animals.

---

## Tishrei Applications

### Documents Dating

The Gemara now turns to the *mishnah*'s statement that Tishrei is *rosh hashanah le-shanim* — the new year for years. The Gemara asks *le-mai hilchata*, what is the practical application? Rav Pappa answers: *le-shtarot*, for the dating of documents. As the *mishnah* teaches elsewhere, a predated document is invalid while a postdated document is valid, which means one must always know when the year increments in order to write the correct year on a deed or contract. The new year for that purpose begins on the first of Tishrei.

### Kings Distinction

This immediately raises a difficulty: the *mishnah* stated at the outset that the first of Nisan is *rosh hashanah le-melachim*, the new year for kings — and Rav Chisda had explained that this too is *le-shtarot*, for dating documents. Which month is it, then, Nisan or Tishrei?

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. The distinction is between *malchei Yisrael* and *malchei umot ha'olam*. Documents dated by reference to Jewish kings increment the regnal year in Nisan, consistent with the special significance of Nisan as the beginning of the months for the Jewish people. Documents dated by reference to non-Jewish kings increment in Tishrei. Depending on which king's reign is being used as the dating reference — and the Gemara notes that certain documents were customarily dated by non-Jewish kings for reasons of *shalom malchut* — the year would increment at different times.

### Two Time Cycles

This distinction points toward something deeper. Tishrei is the natural beginning of the agricultural year; the agricultural cycle begins with planting in the fall, and *Sukkot* — which falls in Tishrei — is *b'tzeit hashanah* or *b'tekufat hashanah*, the going out of the year and the turning of the year's cycle. Just as the school year begins in September because children historically returned from helping on the farm when the planting season commenced, so too the natural agricultural year begins in Tishrei.

The Torah then introduces a second system: *hachodesh hazeh lachem rosh chodashim* — this month shall be for you the first of the months. With the Exodus and the revelation at Sinai, a new dimension of time is introduced: not just the natural agricultural cycle but a historical and redemptive mode of reckoning time, counted from God's intervention in human history. This explains why the months are numbered from Nisan while the years are numbered from Tishrei — they reflect two genuinely different cycles operating simultaneously. The numbering of years from creation, used when we write 5774 or similar, also increments from Tishrei, as *beTishrei nivra ha'olam* is a foundational assumption. Interestingly, the Gemara does not mention *briyat ha'olam* as a practical application for the dating of *shtarot*, listing only *melachim* — a point worth reflection.

It bears noting as well that Babylon, from which many of the month names in our calendar derive, also began its year in Nisan. Spring, when things come alive after winter, is a naturally compelling starting point for a year — both as a redemptive moment and as a natural one. So Nisan, too, has claims on being a natural beginning of the year, which further explains why two valid systems of reckoning exist.

### Astronomical Year

The Gemara then introduces a second opinion on the meaning of *le-shanim*. According to Rabbi Zeira, Tishrei is the new year *litkufa* — for the astronomical cycle. The idea is that in order to reckon where the sun and stars were positioned at the time of creation, one must know that the creation occurred in Tishrei, in accordance with the view of Rabbi Eliezer that *beTishrei nivra ha'olam*. The astronomical cycle, meaning the calculation of *tekufot* and the position of the celestial bodies relative to where they were *beshat briyat ha'olam*, is therefore anchored to the first of Tishrei.

One might ask: what practical difference does this make? We can calculate where everything is now, and work backwards to any point in history regardless of which month we designate as the starting point. The *Tosafot* engages at length with this question and addresses the computations of *tekufot*, though this is a complex area. The most accessible *nafka mina* is *Birkat HaChama*, the blessing recited when the sun returns to the position it occupied at the time of creation, which is a calculation anchored to the *tekufa* from creation. It is worth noting, however — and this is a striking point raised in the discussion — that our practice for *Birkat HaChama* places the event in Nisan, not Tishrei, despite our general assumption that *beTishrei nivra ha'olam*. The *Tosafot* notes that according to Rabbi Eliezer, the world was actually created on the 25th of Elul, meaning that Adam was created on the first of Tishrei — *Rosh Hashanah* — and according to Rabbi Yehoshua, the equivalent starting point falls in Adar, with Adam's creation on *Rosh Chodesh Nisan*. These competing assumptions underlie the different astronomical reckonings.

---

## Yom HaDin

### Day Judgment

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a third application of *rosh hashanah le-shanim*: *ledin*, for judgment. Tishrei marks the beginning of the year in the sense that on *Rosh Hashanah* one is judged for the coming year. The proof text is *mereishit hashanah ve'ad acharit shanah* — God surveys the land, and by extension His people, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year, meaning that at the outset of the year He renders judgment for what will unfold by its end: *mereishit hashanah nidon mah yehei be-sofah*.

The Gemara asks: how do we know this refers to Tishrei? From the verse *tiku bachodesh shofar bakese l'yom chageinu ki chok l'Yisrael hu mishpat lelohei Yaakov* — sound the *shofar* on the new moon, on the *kese*, on our festival day, for it is a statute of Israel, a judgment of the God of Jacob. The Gemara identifies the holiday in question through the phrase *bakese* — the day when the moon is "covered" and barely visible. *Eizu chag shehachodesh mitkaseh bo* — which holiday falls on the day when the month is hidden? Only *Rosh Hashanah*, which occurs on the first of the month when the moon is still a sliver. All other *chagim* fall on the fifteenth, when the moon is full.

The *Tosafot* records a debate among the *baalei Tosafot* connected to this. One opinion held that *chodesh mitkaseh bo* was a reference to the fact that on Tishrei the *korban musaf* of *Rosh Chodesh* was subsumed — not brought separately, since only the *musaf* of *Rosh Hashanah* was offered. A *Tosefta* refutes this by establishing clearly that a separate *korban musaf* of *Rosh Chodesh* is indeed brought on *Rosh Hashanah*. The opinion then retreats to a narrower claim: the *pesukkim* obscure the *Rosh Chodesh* identity of the day, and our *tefilot* similarly do not highlight that aspect — in our *mussaf she-moneh esrei* we do not draw attention to it being *Rosh Chodesh*. To this, Rabbeinu Tam responds that we actually do: the line *olat hachodesh u'minchatah* is explicitly included in the *musaf* of *Rosh Hashanah*. This insertion is attributed to Rabbeinu Tam, and it is in accordance with his view that our practice follows — we recite that line making explicit reference to the *korban* of *Rosh Chodesh* as well.

### Partnership Beit Din

The Gemara introduces a *baraisa* deriving from *ki chok l'Yisrael hu mishpat lelohei Yaakov* a striking principle: *ein Beit Din shel ma'alah nichnasim ladin ela im ken kidshu Beit Din shel matah et hachodesh* — the heavenly court does not convene for judgment unless and until the earthly *beit din* has sanctified the month.

This is a profound expression of the partnership between God and Israel that runs throughout Jewish law. Just as *Torah she-bichtav* gives the written framework and *Torah she-ba'al peh* fills it with interpretive life, so too the calendar operates through a collaboration: God creates the natural rhythm of the moon, but Israel must observe it, testify to it, and declare it holy. The *moadim* are designated not merely by nature but by human declaration — *asher tikre'u otam*.

What is particularly striking here is the application of this principle to the context of *din*. *Yom HaDin*, the day of judgment, carries an aura of pure submission — of the subject standing before an absolute authority. Yet even *Yom HaDin* only exists because Israel creates it through *kiddush hachodesh*. The day of our judgment is, in a profound sense, a day we bring into being.

This theme has a natural extension to the second day of *Rosh Hashanah*. The second day exists only because of *sfeika d'yoma*, a doubt — it is a *minhag* rooted in uncertainty, not in any direct divine declaration that it is a *yom hadin*. One might therefore have thought that the second day carries no weight as a day of judgment. Yet the same logic operates: by treating it as *Rosh Hashanah*, by declaring it and living it as such, we actually constitute it as a *yom hadin*. And if what makes it a *yom hadin* is the communal act of creating it, then its *din* is naturally a collective one — not the individual judgment of the first day but a judgment for the community as a whole. This connects as well to the idea, found in certain *midrashic* sources, that the first day's *din* is strict while the second day's is sweetened, and to the concept at the heart of *Hoshana Rabbah* where the final seal of the *din* is itself subject to further softening.

### Nations Judgment

A second *baraisa* on the same verse asks: *ein li ela le-Yisrael* — perhaps *Rosh Hashanah* is a day of judgment only for the Jewish people? *Umos ha'olam minayin?* — how do I know that the nations are also judged? The answer is drawn from the second half of the verse: *mishpat lelohei Yaakov* — it is the judgment of the God of Jacob, and since He is the universal God, judgment extends to all. The function of *ki chok l'Yisrael* is then to teach something different: *Yisrael nichnasim techilah ladin* — Israel enters judgment first.

The Gemara supports this with a parallel principle stated by Rav Chisda: when a king and his community both stand before the court, *melech nichnas techilah ladin* — the king is judged first. The proof text is *mishpat avdo u-mishpat amo* — first the judgment of His servant (understood here as the leader or king), and afterward the judgment of the nation.

Two explanations are offered for why the king — and by analogy Israel — is judged first. The first is *lav orach ar'a lemeikam malka avraei* — it is a matter of honor; it is undignified to leave the king waiting outside in the corridor while others are being processed. The second: *mikamei de-lifush charon af* — it is better to be judged before God's anger increases. As God proceeds through the judgments of those being tried and witnesses more and more sin, the divine anger intensifies, and one is better positioned at the beginning of the queue.

This second explanation invites reflection. Framing it as an advantage for those judged first seems to run counter to an equally natural reading: the king, or Israel, bears the greatest responsibility. If there is widespread sin or failure, the one who was in the best position to prevent it — the leader, the nation charged with being *or lagoyim* — should perhaps bear the heaviest judgment. From that perspective, being judged first is not a privilege but an expression of heightened accountability. The *pasuk* in Amos — *rak etchem yadati mikol mishpechot ha'adamah al kein efkod aleichem et kol avonotechem* — precisely frames Israel's unique relationship with God as the basis for a more demanding judgment, not a lighter one. The Gemara's framing of this as an advantage is thus somewhat surprising, and the underlying logic remains worth examining.

---

## Shemitah Year

### Shemitah Proof

The *mishnah* also lists *shemitah* among the things for which Tishrei is the *rosh hashanah*. The Gemara asks: *menalan*, how do we know the seven-year *shemitah* cycle increments in Tishrei rather than Nisan?

The derivation proceeds by *gezerah shavah*. The verse *u-vashanah ha-shvi'it shabbat shabbaton la-hashem tihyeh la-aretz* uses the word *shanah* — year. The verse *mereishit hashanah ve'ad acharit shanah*, which we established refers to Tishrei, also uses the word *shanah*. We therefore learn *shanah shanah* from Tishrei. Could we not equally learn it from Nisan, using the verse *rishon hu lachem le-chodshei hashanah*, where *shanah* is also mentioned? The Gemara rules this out.

### Shanah Types

The Gemara's reasoning is that one derives *shanah* (unqualified year) from *shanah* (unqualified year), but one does not derive *shanah* from a verse where *shanah* appears in the context of *chodashim* — months. The verse *rishon hu lachem le-chodshei hashanah* mentions *shanah* in conjunction with *chodesh*, making it a reference to the year in terms of its months. The verses governing *shemitah* and the verse *mereishit hashanah* do not mention *chodashim* — they speak of *shanah* simply. One therefore draws the *gezerah shavah* between the simple *shanah* references, all of which point to Tishrei.

More conceptually: the significance of Nisan as *rosh hashanah* is tied to its identity as the beginning of the *chodashim*, the months. That is its domain. For the larger agricultural and cyclical year — *shemitah*, *yovel*, and related laws — we operate within the natural agricultural calendar that predates the Sinaitic revelation about month-counting, and that calendar begins in Tishrei.

---

## Yovel Release

### Rosh Hashanah vs Yom Kip…

The Gemara asks: the *mishnah* includes *yovelot* among the things for which Tishrei is the *rosh hashanah* — but is *yovel* really from the first of Tishrei? The Torah explicitly says *be-yom ha-kippurim ta'aviru shofar be-chol artzechem* — the *shofar* of *yovel* is sounded on *Yom Kippur*, the tenth of Tishrei! The Gemara answers: the *mishnah* reflects the position of Rabbi Ishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who gives the first of Tishrei a distinct role even in *yovel*.

### Middle Zone Limbo

The *baraisa* records Rabbi Ishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's view as follows. The verse *ve-kidashtem et shnat ha-chamishim shanah* — "you shall sanctify the fiftieth year" — would seem superfluous, since the Torah already specified *be-yom ha-kippurim ta'aviru shofar*. The word *tishrei* is already established from the *shemitah* analysis as the month when years begin; therefore the verse *sanctify the year* teaches that the year's sanctity as *yovel* begins from the start of the year — from *Rosh Hashanah* — even though the shofar and formal declaration come on *Yom Kippur*. From here: *mitkadeshet ve-holechet* — the sanctity grows progressively from *Rosh Hashanah* onward.

### Ten Days Limbo

What then is the practical consequence of this view? *Me-Rosh Hashanah ad Yom Kippur*, during the ten days between the two, the slaves would not go home (*lo hayu avadim niftarin le-vateihem*) and would not be enslaved to their masters (*ve-lo mishtabdin le-adoneihem*). They were in a *limbo* — neither free nor bound. They would eat, drink, and rejoice (*ochlin ve-shotin ve-smechin*), and could even wear crowns on their heads (*ve-atroteihem be-rasheihem*), living as though already elevated. When *Yom Kippur* arrived, *beit din* would sound the *shofar* — corresponding to the verse *u-kratem dror ba-aretz le-chol yoshveha*, "you shall proclaim liberty throughout the land" — and only then would the slaves actually return home and the fields revert to their original owners.

This progression has a beautiful resonance: the ultimate redemption does not arrive instantaneously. There is a preparatory middle period in which the old order is already loosened and the new one anticipated, but the final liberation requires its own distinct moment. The image parallels ideas of *itchalta de-geula*, the beginning of redemption that precedes its full realization.

### Rabbis Yom Kippur

The Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Ishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka. According to them, everything in *yovel* — both the beginning and end of its sanctified status — is anchored exclusively to *Yom Kippur*. The verse *ve-kidashtem et shnat ha-chamishim shanah* teaches them something different: *shanim atah mekadesh, ve-ein atah mekadesh chadashim* — you sanctify years, not months. This is taken as a ruling that the obligation of *beit din* to perform an act of *kiddush* is limited to the sanctification of the *yovel* year; there is no parallel obligation of *beit din* to formally sanctify the months in the manner associated with *yovel*. This is a striking position, running somewhat against the standard assumption that *beit din*'s act of *mekudash mekudash* is an indispensable requirement for *kiddush hachodesh* in the ordinary sense.

### Cycle Duration

A further *baraisa* addresses the question of what happens at the *end* of the *yovel* year. The verse *yovel hi shnat ha-chamishim shanah* — "it is the *yovel*, the fiftieth year" — is read as defining the year's boundaries precisely. One might have thought that just as the *yovel* year accretes its sanctity from *Rosh Hashanah* onward (per Rabbi Ishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka), so too at the end there might be a tapering-off period extending into the *Yom Kippur* of year fifty-one — *mitkadeshet ve-holechet be-sofah* — a symmetrical de-acclimatization. The verse comes to exclude this: only the fiftieth year is sanctified; the fifty-first is not.

The Rabbis, who have no acclimating period to begin with, derive a different lesson from the same verse: *shnat hamishim atah moneh, ve-ein atah moneh shnat hamishim achat* — you count this year as fifty, not as year one of the next cycle. This is directed against the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *shnat hamishim oleh le-kan u-le-kan* — the fiftieth year counts both as the last year of the previous cycle and as year one of the next, making the *yovel* cycle effectively forty-nine years rather than fifty. The majority view, established by this verse, is that year fifty has a single identity — it is the fiftieth and nothing more — and year one of the new cycle begins the following year, making the full cycle fifty years.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 10

## Orlah & Planting

### Rosh Hashanah Intro

The daf opens with a *baraita* addressing the question of *Rosh Hashanah* for planting — *netia* — which is distinct from the role of the first of *Tishrei* in other agricultural contexts. As we have seen, the first of *Tishrei* serves as the *Rosh Hashanah* for *shmita* and *yovel* in the sense that those cycles are calibrated to the calendar year: what year of the *shmita* cycle is it? What year of the *yovel* cycle? Those are universal determinations that apply to everyone equally.

The question of *netia* is different. It concerns the age of a particular tree that a particular person planted: how many years old is this tree? The Torah in *Vayikra* establishes that the fruit of a tree is forbidden as *orlah* for its first three years, that the fourth year's fruit carries the status of *neta revai* — which must be redeemed and consumed in *Yerushalayim*, or the fruit itself brought and eaten there — and that only from the fifth year onward may the fruit be eaten without restriction. One might have assumed that "three years" means three years from the tree's planting date, counted day to day. The *Mishna*, however, teaches that *Tishrei* — *Rosh Hashanah* — is the point at which a tree's age increments. A tree planted even a month before *Rosh Hashanah* already enters its second year when *Rosh Hashanah* arrives. In theory, a tree planted on *Rosh Chodesh Elul* would complete its three years of *orlah* in a little over two calendar years. The fruit of *orlah* is not merely forbidden for consumption; it is forbidden even in benefit — one may do nothing with it whatsoever.

### Three Planting Methods

The *baraita* begins: *echad hanotea* — whether one plants directly; *ve'echad hamavrich* — or performs *mavrich*, the technique of bending a branch underground so that it emerges from the earth at a new location and effectively becomes a new tree, while still drawing nutrients from the original; *ve'echad hamarkiv* — or performs *markiv*, grafting, which joins a branch to a different root system. All three methods are treated as constituting a new planting for the purposes of *orlah*.

*Tosafot* notes a complexity regarding *markiv*: other sources suggest that bending a branch without severing it from the original tree does not constitute a new planting and that *orlah* does not apply. *Tosafot* resolves this by distinguishing between a case where the connection to the original tree is never cut — in which case the "new" growth is really just a branch extending in an unusual direction and *orlah* does not apply — and a case where the connection is eventually severed. When we say that *markiv* constitutes a new planting, we refer to the latter case, where the branch is ultimately cut off from its source.

### 30-Day Rule

The *baraita* continues: if one performs any of these three acts of planting *erev shevi'it* — the eve of the *shmita* year — at least thirty days before *Rosh Hashanah*, then *altah lo shana* — it counts as a year, meaning that when *Rosh Hashanah* arrives, the tree is already considered to have entered its second year for *orlah* purposes. Such a tree may also remain in the ground during *shvi'it*. But if the planting occurred fewer than thirty days before *Rosh Hashanah* — that is, from *Rosh Chodesh Elul* or later, since *Elul* has twenty-nine days — then it does not count as a year, the tree remains in its first year when *Rosh Hashanah* arrives, and it must be uprooted during *shmita*.

At this stage of the *Gemara's* analysis, the thirty-day requirement is provisionally understood as serving two purposes simultaneously: for *shmita*, it reflects the concept of *tosefet shvi'it* — one must add time to the *shmita* year and refrain from prohibited agricultural activity before *shmita* actually begins, and this *tosefet* period is thirty days. For *orlah*, it reflects the requirement that enough time elapse before *Rosh Hashanah* for *Rosh Hashanah* to meaningfully increment the tree's year. As we will see, the *Gemara* will ultimately revise this understanding.

### Fruit Restrictions

The *Gemara* then introduces a striking and counterintuitive *halakha* on the top of 11a. Although *Rosh Hashanah* increments the tree's year at the front end, there is a corresponding extension at the back end: *u'feiros netia zo asurim ad Tu B'Shvat* — the fruits of this planting remain forbidden until *Tu B'Shvat*, the fifteenth of *Shevat*, following the view of *Beis Hillel*. Specifically, if the tree is in its third year and the *orlah* prohibition is still operative, that prohibition extends beyond the *Rosh Hashanah* that nominally marks the entry into the fourth year and continues until *Tu B'Shvat*. Likewise, the *neta revai* status of the fourth year extends into what would otherwise be the fifth year, remaining in effect until the next *Tu B'Shvat*.

The logic is as follows. For its first three years, a tree has the status of *netia* — a sapling — and its years are counted by *Rosh Hashanah* in *Tishrei*. But once it has completed three years, it becomes an *ilan* — a full-grown tree — and for an *ilan*, the *Rosh Hashanah* is *Tu B'Shvat*. Thus there is a peculiar transitional moment: the tree is no longer a *netia* but not yet at its *Rosh Hashanah* as an *ilan*. The third year's *orlah* therefore continues until *Tu B'Shvat*, and the *revai* of the fourth year likewise continues to the following *Tu B'Shvat*.

---

## Orlah/Reva'i Calendar

### Tu B'Shvat Transition

To illustrate concretely: suppose a tree is planted roughly one month before *Rosh Hashanah*. When *Rosh Hashanah* arrives, the tree enters year two. The following *Rosh Hashanah* brings it to year three. The third *Rosh Hashanah* would, on a simple reading, bring it into year four and free it from *orlah*. But since the tree is now an *ilan* and its new year runs from *Tu B'Shvat*, the *orlah* of the third year continues until *Tu B'Shvat* of what is calendrically year four. Only at that *Tu B'Shvat* does the *revai* status take effect, and only at the following *Tu B'Shvat* does the tree become fully *mutar* — permitted without restriction.

### Misalignment Issue

One might observe that this arrangement seems less favorable than simply using *Tu B'Shvat* as the *Rosh Hashanah* for the tree throughout its entire life. If *Tu B'Shvat* governed from the beginning, the years would count cleanly from *Tu B'Shvat* to *Tu B'Shvat*, and the tree's fruit would become permitted at the same point it currently does. Moreover, the mixed system that begins with *Rosh Hashanah* and then extends to *Tu B'Shvat* is actually disadvantageous compared to a pure *Tu B'Shvat* system. Consider a tree planted between *Rosh Hashanah* and *Tu B'Shvat*: under the current system, *Rosh Hashanah* has already passed and cannot increment the tree's year until the following *Rosh Hashanah*, so the tree begins year two relatively late. Under a pure *Tu B'Shvat* system, however, the first *Tu B'Shvat* after planting would already bring the tree into year two, giving it more credit. Thus the current arrangement — counting from *Rosh Hashanah* at the front but extending to *Tu B'Shvat* at the back — is actually the least advantageous of the possible configurations. One suggested rationale is that *Tu B'Shvat* ensures that a full rainy season has been experienced; planting before *Tu B'Shvat* but well into the rainy season might not provide that assurance, and hence some extension makes sense.

### Biblical Sources

The *Gemara* asks: *minalan hani mili* — what is the source for all of this? Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, with some uncertainty as to whether this tradition comes via the name of Rabbi Yanai, that the source is in *Vayikra*. The verse says: *shalosh shanim yihyeh lachem arelim lo ye'achel* — for three years it shall be *orlah*, it shall not be eaten — *u'vashanah ha'revi'it* — and in the fourth year. The *Gemara* reads the conjunction *u'* connecting the fourth year to the prior verse as indicating that the forbidden status does not simply end when the third year ends at *Rosh Hashanah*, but extends *into* the fourth year — specifically until *Tu B'Shvat*. Similarly, the verse continues: *u'vashanah ha'chamishit tochal et piryo* — and in the fifth year you shall eat its fruit — with the *revai* status similarly extending into the fifth year until its *Tu B'Shvat*. The *Gemara* summarizes: there are times when one is already calendrically within the fourth year — after the third *Rosh Hashanah* but before *Tu B'Shvat* — yet the fruit is still forbidden as *orlah*. And there are times when one is already calendrically within the fifth year yet the fruit still carries the status of *revai*.

---

## 30-Day Debate

### Rabbi Meir: One Day

The *Gemara* now turns to the thirty-day requirement and asks: *leima de-lo ke-Rabbi Meir* — shall we say this ruling does not accord with Rabbi Meir? For Rabbi Meir holds that *yom echad ba-shanah chashuv shanah* — one day within a year counts as a full year. We have already encountered this principle in the context of kings' regnal years. The *Gemara* adduces a parallel from a *baraita* concerning the ages of sacrificial animals.

The Torah uses several terms for cattle: *egel* — a calf — alone; *egel ben bakar* or simply *ben bakar*; and *par* or *par ben bakar*. Rabbi Meir holds that wherever the Torah says *egel* alone, the animal must be in its first year; where it says *ben bakar*, it must be in its second year; and where it says *par*, it must be in its third year. Accordingly, *par ha-amur ba-Torah stam* — a *par* mentioned in the Torah without further qualification — must be *ben esrim ve-arba'ah chodesh ve-yom echad*, twenty-four months and one day old. That is, according to Rabbi Meir, once the animal has entered its third year by even one day, it is halachically a three-year-old. Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, requires *ben esrim ve-arba'ah chodesh u-shloshim yom* — twenty-four months and thirty days — before it may be called a three-year-old *par*. One day is insufficient.

It is worth noting a conceptual question that arises here: are we saying that the animal *is* three years old, which one day serves to establish, or are we saying that the defining criterion is simply being *into* one's third year? Rabbi Meir's position as understood by the *Gemara* is that the animal is defined as a *ben shalosh* — a three-year-old — and that one day into the third year is sufficient to confer that definition.

By analogy, if one day at the back end suffices to make an animal a three-year-old according to Rabbi Meir, then presumably, by the same logic, one day of planting before *Rosh Hashanah* should suffice to increment the tree's year. Yet the *Mishna* requires thirty days — apparently contradicting Rabbi Meir.

### Rava's Kal Vachomer

The *Gemara* responds: *afillu teima Rabbi Meir* — one may still attribute this ruling to Rabbi Meir. When did Rabbi Meir say one day counts? *Be-sof shanah* — at the end of a year. But *bit-chilat shanah lo amar* — he did not say so at the beginning of a year. It may be that a partial day at the end of a counting period, which marks the completion of that period, carries different weight than a partial period at the very start of a new count.

Rava challenges this distinction with a *kal vachomer*: *velav kal vachomer hu?* If anything, a partial period at the *beginning* should be easier to count than at the end, not harder. His proof is from the laws of *niddah*.

### Niddah Example

Rava's argument proceeds as follows. In the Torah's framework of *niddah*, a woman who begins menstruating counts seven days from the onset of bleeding, after which she immerses in a *mikvah* on the night following the seventh day. Consider a woman who begins bleeding at 1:00 PM on Sunday. That Sunday counts as day one of her seven days — even though only a portion of Sunday remained when the bleeding began. Yet when she reaches the beginning of the seventh day, *Shabbos*, the mere onset of *Shabbos* does not count as the completion of day seven; she must wait until *Shabbos* ends to immerse. The beginning of day seven does not discharge the final day.

Thus: *she'ein t'chilat ha-yom oleh lah be-sofah* — the start of a day does not count for her at the end — yet *sof ha-yom oleh lah bit-chilatah* — the end of a day *does* count for her at the beginning. A few hours of Sunday at the start of the count are sufficient to constitute day one, but the arrival of *Shabbos* is not sufficient to constitute day seven. This demonstrates that it is *easier* to count a partial unit at the beginning of a process than at the end. Therefore — *eino din* — if by cattle we allow one day at the end to count as a full year, how much more so by trees should we allow one day at the beginning to count as a year. Rabbi Meir should therefore not require thirty days.

*Rashi* cautions against a common misapplication of this passage. Some have erroneously inferred from the principle that *sof ha-yom oleh lah bit-chilatah* that the final hours of the day on which bleeding ceases can count as the first of the seven clean days. This is entirely incorrect; the *Gemara* here is discussing the biblical counting of seven days from the onset of bleeding, not the rabbinic system of seven clean days following the cessation of bleeding — two entirely distinct frameworks.

### Trees vs. Cows

One might ask: if the *kal vachomer* from *niddah* shows that beginnings are easier than ends, why do we not count a partial period at both the beginning *and* the end for cattle? The answer is that cattle and trees operate on fundamentally different calendrical systems. For cattle, the count runs from the animal's birthday: how many years have elapsed since the date of birth? The only opportunity for a partial-count credit is at the back end, when the animal has completed two full years and enters its third. There is no "beginning" in the same sense, because the count simply starts at birth. For trees, by contrast, the count is governed by a specific calendar date — *Rosh Hashanah* — which increments the tree's year. Here, the only opportunity for partial-count credit is at the front end: did the tree get planted before that date, and if so, does even a small amount of time before the date suffice to allow *Rosh Hashanah* to increment it into year two? The analogy from *niddah* is being used to establish the principle that partial periods are easier to credit at the start of a process than at its end, and this principle is then applied: if cattle get credit for one day at the end, trees should certainly get credit for one day at the beginning.

### Rabbi Eliezer: Rooting T…

The *Gemara* then turns to Rabbi Eliezer's position. If the ruling requiring thirty days before *Rosh Hashanah* accords with Rabbi Eliezer — who requires thirty days for the cattle to be considered a *par* — then, the *Gemara* objects, one would need *shloshim u-shloshim*, sixty days in total. Why? Because there is a separate consideration for trees that does not apply to cattle: a newly planted tree must first *take root* — *klita* — before it can be considered planted in any meaningful sense. Only after it has rooted does the clock begin running on its time in the ground.

This principle emerges from a *baraita* dealing with *shmita*: *ein note'in ve'ein mavrichin ve'ein markivin erev shvi'it pachos mi-lamed yom lifnei Rosh Hashanah* — one may not plant, bend, or graft within thirty days before *Rosh Hashanah* of *shmita*, and if one did, *ya'akor* — it must be uprooted. Rabbi Yehuda says: for *markiv*, only three days are required to take root; if it has rooted more than three days before *shmita*, it need not be uprooted. Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Shimon say: two weeks suffice for rooting.

These opinions concern how long it takes for a planted tree to become genuinely rooted in the earth. *Tosafot* reads the *Gemara*'s conclusion as abandoning the earlier assumption that the thirty-day pre-*shmita* period reflects *tosefet shvi'it*. Rather, the concern is purely practical: one may not plant a tree in such a way that it will take root *on shmita* itself. The only question is therefore how long rooting takes. The first opinion holds thirty days; Rabbi Yehuda holds three days; Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Shimon hold two weeks.

The same principle applies to *orlah*. Rav Nachman says in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: *le-divrei ha-omer lamed* — according to the opinion that rooting takes thirty days — *tzarich lamed u-shloshim* — for *orlah* purposes one needs thirty days for rooting plus another thirty days to count as a year, a total of sixty days before *Rosh Hashanah*. According to the opinion that rooting takes two weeks, one needs two weeks plus thirty days before *Rosh Hashanah*. Even according to Rabbi Yehuda who requires only three days for rooting, one would need thirty-three days, not thirty. How then does the *Mishna* say that thirty days suffices?

---

## Reconciling 30 Days

### The 30-Day Problem

The problem is sharp: whatever opinion we adopt regarding rooting time, it would seem that thirty days alone cannot satisfy both the rooting requirement and the additional time needed for *Rosh Hashanah* to meaningfully increment the tree's year. Even the most lenient opinion — Rabbi Yehuda's three days for rooting — would require thirty-three days total before *Rosh Hashanah*. The *Mishna*'s thirty-day rule appears insufficient on any account.

### Double-Duty Solution

The *Gemara* resolves this by reversing the initial assumption. Rather than saying that the thirty-day requirement reflects *tosefet* or the time needed to count as a year, the *Gemara* concludes: *ela le-olam Rabbi Meir* — in fact, this *baraita* accords with Rabbi Meir. *Ve-chi ka'amar lamed li-klita* — when the *baraita* says thirty days before *Rosh Hashanah*, it refers entirely to the time needed for rooting. The first-opinion *baraita* holds that rooting takes thirty days; this is also the position assumed in the *shmita* context. And Rabbi Meir, who requires only one day to count as a year, provides the solution.

But if one needs thirty days for rooting *and* then at least one additional day to count as a year, one would need thirty-one days, not thirty. The *Gemara* answers: *kasavar yom sheloshim oleh le-kan u-le-kan* — the thirtieth day does double duty. Consider a tree planted on the last day of *Av*. Day thirty is the twenty-ninth of *Elul*. During the first portion of that thirtieth day, the rooting process completes — the tree is now genuinely planted. During the remaining hours of that same day, it has already begun its count as a rooted tree, and those hours constitute the "one day" before *Rosh Hashanah* that Rabbi Meir requires. When *Rosh Hashanah* arrives, the tree has both rooted and had at least one day of counted time, and *Rosh Hashanah* can therefore increment it into year two. The last day of the thirty-day period performs dual service: it is simultaneously the final day of the rooting process and the first day of the year-count.

### Shmita Conclusion

This resolution also clarifies the *shmita* ruling. The reason one must uproot a tree planted within thirty days of *shmita* is not *tosefet* — it is not that one has transgressed the prohibition of agricultural labor during the *tosefet* period. The reason is that the tree will take root *on shmita* itself. If a tree planted within thirty days has not yet rooted by *Rosh Hashanah*, it will root during *shvi'it*, which is prohibited. Accordingly, *tosefet* is a separate concern and does not drive the uprooting requirement; the uprooting requirement is driven solely by whether the tree roots before or during *shmita*. As *Tosafot* reads the *Gemara*, these two considerations — the *tosefet* prohibition and the rooting prohibition — are independent, and violating *tosefet* does not automatically trigger uprooting if the tree nevertheless roots before *shmita* begins.

---

## Prooftext Debate

### Rabbi Meir: Genesis

The *Gemara* now introduces a more fundamental textual basis for the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Yochanan observes: *bi-shteihem mikra echad darshu* — both derived their positions from the same verse. The verse in question is from the flood narrative in *Bereishit*: *vayehi b'achat u-shesh me'ot shanah ba-rishon b'echad la-chodesh charevu ha-mayim me'al ha-aretz* — it came to pass in the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first of the month, that the waters dried from upon the earth.

Rabbi Meir derives his position from the phrase *b'achat* — on the first, the first day. The verse describes this as occurring in the six hundred and first year. From the fact that one day of the year — the very first day — is described as constituting or characterizing that year, Rabbi Meir infers *shema mina yom echad ba-shanah chashuv shanah* — one day within a year counts as a full year.

The logical force of this derivation is admittedly puzzling. The verse is simply saying that this occurred during the six hundred and first year — it is not claiming that 601 full years have elapsed. Nevertheless, Rabbi Meir reads it as though the single day mentioned is treated as though it represents the entire year, yielding the principle that one day in a year is counted as a year.

### Rabbi Eliezer: Genesis

Rabbi Eliezer derives from the same verse a very different lesson. He focuses on the phrase *ba-rishon b'echad la-chodesh* — in the first month, on the first of the month. His reading: *yom echad hu de-aya ba-chodesh ve-ka kara lei chodesh* — it is only one day into the month, yet the verse calls it a month. From this he infers *yom echad ba-chodesh chashuv chodesh* — one day within a month counts as a full month.

Here too the reading is strained: the verse is stating the date — the first of the month — not claiming that the month is complete. Yet Rabbi Eliezer reads it as conferring upon that one day the status of a full month.

### Day-Month-Year Analogy

Having established from the verse that one day counts as a month, Rabbi Eliezer proceeds by analogy. The relationship of a day to a month parallels the relationship of a month to a year. Just as a month is composed of days, and one unit (a day) suffices to count as the whole, so too a year is composed of months, and one unit (a month) suffices to count as the whole. Therefore *shloshim yom ba-shanah chashuvim shanah* — thirty days within a year count as a full year. The number thirty is used because a month always has at least thirty days — a month is by definition at least thirty days — and therefore a month, as the operative unit of a year, is represented by thirty days.

One might ask why we say thirty specifically rather than, say, twenty-nine, since a lunar month can be twenty-nine days. The implicit answer is that thirty days represents a complete, round month, the minimum period that is unambiguously a full month.

---

## Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

### Rabbi Eliezer Timeline

The *Gemara* has been working with verses from the flood narrative — the six hundred and first year, the first month, the first of the month — in establishing the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer. This naturally raises the question of what month that "first month" refers to. The flood narrative pre-dates the establishment of *Nissan* as the first month in the context of the Egyptian exodus, so the question of whether the Torah's original month-count runs from *Tishrei* or from *Nissan* becomes directly relevant to how we read those very verses. The *Gemara* accordingly turns to a *baraita* in which this dispute is addressed directly.

Rabbi Eliezer says: *bi-Tishrei nivra ha-olam* — the world was created in *Tishrei*. *Bi-Tishrei noldu avos* — the forefathers were born in *Tishrei*. *Bi-Tishrei mesu avos* — the forefathers died in *Tishrei*, the assumption being that they lived out complete years and therefore died in the same month they were born. *Bi-Pesach nolad Yitzchak* — Yitzchak was born on *Pesach*, which constitutes an exception to the *Tishrei* pattern. *Bi-Tishrei asidin lehiga'el* — the future redemption will occur in *Tishrei*.

### Shared Remembrances

Rabbi Eliezer holds that *be-Rosh Hashanah nifkeda Sarah Rachel ve-Channah* — on *Rosh Hashanah*, Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah were *nifkadu* — remembered by God, meaning they became pregnant. This is why we read those passages on *Rosh Hashanah*: it is a day of divine remembrance and response. Sarah was remembered on *Rosh Hashanah*, conceived, and gave birth six months later on *Pesach* — hence Yitzchak's birth on *Pesach* rather than *Tishrei*. *Be-Rosh Hashanah yatza Yosef mi-beis ha-asurim* — on *Rosh Hashanah* Yosef was released from prison, as Pharaoh remembered him on that day. *Be-Rosh Hashanah batla avoda me-avoseinu be-Mitzrayim* — on *Rosh Hashanah* the labor imposed upon our ancestors in Egypt ceased, even before the actual redemption.

*Bi-Nissan nigalu* — they were redeemed in *Nissan*. *Bi-Tishrei asidin lehiga'el* — the future redemption will occur in *Tishrei*.

According to Rabbi Eliezer, then, *Tishrei* is the primary month for virtually everything: creation, the births and deaths of the forefathers, the future redemption, and the foundational acts of divine memory and liberation. The only exceptions that must be assigned to *Nissan* are the actual exodus itself and Yitzchak's birth — the latter being forced by the prior commitment to *Rosh Hashanah* as the time of Sarah's *pikida*.

### Rabbi Yehoshua Timeline

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees, assigning primacy to *Nissan*. *Bi-Nissan nivra ha-olam* — the world was created in *Nissan*. *Bi-Nissan noldu avos* — the forefathers were born in *Nissan*. *Bi-Nissan mesu avos* — they died in *Nissan*. *Bi-Pesach nolad Yitzchak* — Yitzchak was born on *Pesach*. Both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree on this point. And because Yitzchak was born on *Pesach*, Rabbi Yehoshua likewise agrees that: *be-Rosh Hashanah nifkeda Sarah Rachel ve-Channah* — Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah were remembered on *Rosh Hashanah*. Both Tannaim share this conclusion, since it follows necessarily from Yitzchak's birth on *Pesach*. Rabbi Yehoshua also agrees that *be-Rosh Hashanah yatza Yosef mi-beis ha-asurim* — Yosef was freed on *Rosh Hashanah* — and that *be-Rosh Hashanah batla avoda me-avoseinu be-Mitzrayim* — the forced labor in Egypt ceased on *Rosh Hashanah*. These are grounded in the idea of *Rosh Hashanah* as a day of *zikaron* — divine remembrance — which both Tannaim accept.

The key difference is at the cosmic and eschatological level: *bi-Nissan nigalu u-vi-Nissan asidin lehiga'el* — they were redeemed in *Nissan* and the future redemption will also occur in *Nissan*. Rabbi Yehoshua thus presents a more complex picture: the primary rhythms of creation, the lives of the forefathers, and the ultimate redemption all center on *Nissan*, yet certain specific events — the *pikida* of Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah; the release of Yosef; the cessation of Egyptian servitude — are nonetheless assigned to *Rosh Hashanah* in *Tishrei*, reflecting that month's enduring character as a time of divine attention and response. The full elaboration of how these positions are grounded in the verses of the flood narrative will be the subject of the next daf.

# Rosh Hashanah 11

## World Creation Debate

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

The *gemara* opens with a *baraita* that frames one of the great calendrical disputes of rabbinic literature: when precisely was the world created? The *baraita* is found at the very bottom of 10b, and serves as the foundation for the extended discussion on 11b.

*Rabbi Eliezer omer*: *be-Tishrei nivra ha-olam* — the world was created in *Tishrei*. Following from this premise, *be-Tishrei noldu avot* and *be-Tishrei metu avot* — the forefathers were born and died in *Tishrei*. There are, however, notable exceptions to the *Tishrei* pattern within Rabbi Eliezer's own position: *be-Pesach nolad Yitzchak* — Yitzchak was born on Pesach — and *be-Rosh Hashanah nifkeda Sarah Rachel ve-Chanah* — Sarah, Rachel, and Chanah were remembered (that is, became pregnant) on Rosh Hashanah. As will become clear from the *gemara*, these two items are related: if Sarah was remembered on Rosh Hashanah, the calculation requires that Yitzchak be born approximately six to seven months later, which points toward Pesach. Rabbi Eliezer further holds that *be-Rosh Hashanah yatza Yosef mi-beit ha-asurim* — Yosef was freed from prison on Rosh Hashanah — and *be-Rosh Hashanah batlah avodah me-avoteinu be-Mitzrayim* — the forced labor in Egypt ceased on Rosh Hashanah, even though the actual redemption, *be-Nissan nigalu*, took place in Nissan. And crucially: *be-Tishrei atidin lehigael* — the future redemption will occur in *Tishrei*.

### Rabbi Yehoshua Position

Rabbi Yehoshua's position is a systematic inversion. *Be-Nissan nivra ha-olam* — the world was created in Nissan. *Be-Nissan noldu avot*, *be-Nissan metu avot* — the forefathers were born and died in Nissan. He concedes the same exceptions: *be-Pesach nolad Yitzchak*, and *be-Rosh Hashanah nifkeda Sarah Rachel ve-Chanah*. He likewise agrees that Yosef was freed and the labor ceased on Rosh Hashanah. Where he sharply diverges from Rabbi Eliezer is on the future redemption: *u-be-Nissan nigalu u-be-Nissan atidin lehigael* — just as they were redeemed in Nissan, so too will the future redemption come in Nissan.

### Textual Analysis

The *gemara* now proceeds to unpack the textual proofs on both sides, focusing on the verses from the creation narrative itself. Each position turns on close readings of the vegetation imagery in the first chapter of *Bereishit*, and it is to those proofs that the *gemara* immediately turns.

---

## Eliezer Vegetation Proof

### Vegetation Verse

The *gemara* cites the *baraita* presenting Rabbi Eliezer's proof from vegetation: *mina'in she-be-Tishrei nivra ha-olam?* — from where do we know the world was created in *Tishrei*? *She-ne'emar*: *vayomer Elohim tadshe ha-aretz deshe esev mazria zera etz peri oseh peri* — God said, let the earth be covered with grass, seed-bearing herbage, and fruit trees making fruit. *Eizu chodesh she-ha-aretz motzia deshaim ve-ilan maleh perot?* — what month is it when the earth brings forth grass and the tree is filled with fruit? *Hevei omer zeh Tishrei* — it must be *Tishrei*.

### Tishrei Fruit Season

The intuition behind Rabbi Eliezer's proof is straightforward: apple-picking season falls in September, in the beginning of autumn. That is when trees in the Northern Hemisphere — and, as the *gemara* assumes, in the Mediterranean climate of *Eretz Yisrael* — are filled with ripe fruit. The key word in the verse is *maleh perot*: the tree is already full with fruit. This points to *Tishrei*, not to spring.

### Grass Growth Climate

There is, however, a complication regarding the grass portion of the verse. *Rashi* draws attention to the difference between two possible *girsaot*. Our standard text reads *motzia deshaim* — the earth brings forth, or sprouts, its grass — which would seem to suggest a spring context, since in the Mediterranean climate grass sprouts in the spring, not the fall. But *Rashi* appears to have had the *girsa* of *mele'ah deshaim* — that the earth is already coated and covered with grass — consistent with his comment that *tadshe ha-aretz titkaseh ve-titlabesh bi-deshaim*, the earth should be clothed and covered in grass. This is also the reading the *Bach* explicitly adopts in his textual emendation.

The distinction matters because it bears on the contrast the *gemara* will draw with Rabbi Yehoshua's proof. The verb *tadshe* in Rabbi Eliezer's verse, under this reading, implies a full coating of grass already in place, whereas Rabbi Yehoshua's verse uses *vatotzei* — the earth *brought forth* — which connotes initial sprouting. Under the *Bach*'s *girsa*, then, Rabbi Eliezer's verse describes a world already blanketed with grass and laden with fruit — both signs of *Tishrei* fullness — while Rabbi Yehoshua's verse describes a world just beginning to produce, which fits Nissan.

The *gemara* does not, it should be noted, dwell at length on the grass question; its primary focus is on the contrast between *etz peri* and *etz oseh peri* — whether the tree is already a full fruit-bearing tree or merely beginning to produce. That contrast carries the weight of the dispute.

### Tishrei Rains

Rabbi Eliezer's proof is further reinforced by an observation about the rainy season. *Ve-oto ha-perek zman revia hayta* — that period is the time of *revia*, the beginning of the rains. The rains begin to fall in *Cheshvan*, shortly after *Tishrei*. *Ve-yardu geshamim ve-tzamchu* — the rains descend and the vegetation sprouts. The *gemara* cites the verse from *Bereishit* 2: *ve-ed ya'aleh min ha-aretz ve-hishka et kol pnei ha-adamah* — a mist rose from the earth and watered the entire surface of the ground — as an allusion to this cycle.

It is worth pausing on the term *revia* itself. The word does not mean "a fourth" or "a quarter" in this context; it is connected rather to imagery of fertility and penetration — the rain that waters and fertilizes the earth, a motif running through the agricultural imagination of *Chazal*. It is because of this seasonal reality that we begin reciting *mashiv ha-ruach u-morid ha-gashem* and *ve-ten tal u-matar* in the *Tishrei*-*Cheshvan* period. The world's fertility cycle, on Rabbi Eliezer's view, begins in *Tishrei*.

---

## Yehoshua Vegetation Proof

### Sprouting Verse
