Rabbi Yehoshua's proof runs in the opposite direction. *Mina'in she-be-Nissan nivra ha-olam?* — from where do we know the world was created in Nissan? *She-ne'emar*: *vatotzei ha-aretz deshe esev mazria zera ve-etz oseh peri* — and the earth brought forth grass, seed-bearing herbage, and a tree *making* fruit. Following the *Bach*'s *girsa*, *motzia deshaim* in this verse connotes the earth just beginning to push out grass — initial sprouting, not a full covering. And the critical distinction: it is not *etz peri*, a full fruit tree, but *etz oseh peri* — a tree in the process of producing fruit, not yet laden with it. *Hevei omer ze Nissan* — this is Nissan.

### Nissan Fertility

Rabbi Yehoshua adds a second dimension beyond the botanical. *Ve-oto ha-perek zman behema ve-chaya ve-of she-mizdavjin ze im ze* — that is the season when domesticated animals, wild animals, and birds mate with one another. The spring is the season of animal fertility. The *gemara* cites the verse *livshu charim ha-tzon* — the meadows are clothed with flocks — which the *gemara* used earlier in a different context to establish that the *rosh hashanah* for sheep and for *ma'aser behema* falls in *Elul* or *Tishrei*, precisely because their mating season is in Nissan. The connection between the imagery of creation and the fecundity of the natural world is most powerfully evoked by spring.

### Full Stature Creation

One might ask: how does Rabbi Eliezer respond to the verse *etz oseh peri*, which sounds like the tree is not yet full of fruit — fitting Nissan, not *Tishrei*? The *gemara* answers: *hahu li-vracha le-dorot hu de-chtiv* — that phrase was written not to describe the state of the trees at the moment of creation, but to convey the blessing for all future generations, namely that trees possess the capacity and nature to produce fruit. The word *oseh* indicates what the tree *does* — its essential character — not its momentary state. At the moment of creation itself, under Rabbi Eliezer's view, the trees were already filled with fruit. It was *Tishrei*.

---

## Full Stature Doctrine

### Maturity Concept

The *gemara* now turns to Rabbi Yehoshua's response to the counter-challenge. Rabbi Yehoshua must explain the verse *etz peri* — a full fruit tree — which sounds like the tree is already mature and laden, consistent with *Tishrei*. The answer invokes a famous principle attributed to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *kol ma'aseh bereishit be-komasan nivre'u* — all creations of the six days were created already in their full stature. Adam and Chava were not created as one-day-old infants; the trees were not created as saplings. All things came into being fully formed. Therefore, *etz peri* does not indicate that the fruit was already present, but only that it was a mature, full-grown fruit tree — which it would be even in Nissan, when the fruit was just beginning to develop. The *etz peri* describes the tree's full physical stature; the *etz oseh peri* describes the fruit's early emergence.

### Consent Doctrine

The *gemara* continues: *leda'atan nivre'u* — they were created with their acquiescence, or will. This is a striking and philosophically provocative idea. God, as it were, asked the things of creation whether they wished to be created. There is an obvious circularity here — how can a tree consent to its own creation before it exists? — and the *gemara* does not resolve this directly. The image may point to some pre-existent potential or form, perhaps analogous to the Platonic notion of forms entering the physical world, or to the Kabbalistic idea of the will to create as itself a kind of primordial reality that precedes the act of creation. What is powerful about the idea is the sense that the natural world is not merely passive and inert, but participates in some sense in its own coming-into-being. The *gemara* elsewhere contains related images — the sun and moon arguing with God, the trees resisting God's original intention that the bark taste like the fruit — all suggesting a conception of nature as possessing something like will and interiority.

### Distinctive Form

*Letzevyonam nivre'u* — they were created according to their distinctive form and appearance. *Rashi* understands *tzevyonam* as referring to the particular shape and character that defines each created thing. The *gemara* derives this from the verse *vayechulu ha-shamayim ve-ha-aretz ve-chol tzeva'am* — the heavens and earth and all their hosts were completed — reading *tzeva'am* not as "their hosts" but as *tzevyonam*, their distinctive forms. *Al tikrei tzeva'am ela letzevyonam*.

How does this answer the question about *etz peri*? It establishes that *etz peri* means the tree was created at the full size and form of a fruit tree — that is, fully mature, with all its defining characteristics — without necessarily meaning it was at that moment laden with ripe fruit. Under Rabbi Yehoshua's reading, it was Nissan, the fruit was beginning to emerge (*etz oseh peri*), and the *etz peri* language signals only that the tree stood at full stature.

---

## Patriarchs Birth Tishrei

### Etanim Month

The *gemara* now addresses the second major item in the dispute: the birth of the *avot*. Rabbi Eliezer says the forefathers were born in *Tishrei*. *Mina'in she-be-Tishrei noldu avot?* — from where? *She-ne'emar*: *vayikahalu el ha-Melech Shlomo kol ish Yisrael be-yerach ha-Etanim ba-chag* — all of Israel gathered to King Solomon in the *yerach ha-Etanim*, in the month of *Etanim*, on the festival. This verse, from the books of *Nevi'im*, refers to the dedication of the *Beit HaMikdash* and the month of *Sukkot* — hence *ba-chag*. The month is not called by its Babylonian name (*Tishrei*, which enters Hebrew usage only in the books of the exile and the post-exilic period, such as *Esther*, *Ezra*, and *Nehemiah*) but by an older Hebrew name: *Etanim*.

*Yerach she-noldu bo etanei olam* — the month in which the strong ones of the world were born, meaning the *avot*.

### Etanim Strength

*Mai mashma de-hai etan lishna de-takifei hu?* — from where do we derive that the word *etan* connotes strength? The *gemara* cites two verses. First: *etan moshavakha ve-sim ba-sela kinecha* — your dwelling place is strong and secure. Second: *shimu harim et riv Hashem ve-ha-etanim mosedei aretz* — hear, O mountains, the contention of God, and the *etanim*, the foundations of the earth. In this verse, *etanim* appears in parallel with *harim* — mountains — and is associated with the idea of foundations. The *etanim* are thus both strong and foundational.

### Mountains Fathers

The identification of *etanim* with *harim* (mountains) opens the door to a further *midrashic* connection. The *gemara* cites the verse from *Shir Ha-Shirim*: *kol dodi hinei zeh ba medaleg al he-harim mekapetz al ha-geva'ot* — the voice of my beloved, behold he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills. In the *midrashic* reading, this describes the coming of redemption: *medaleg al he-harim bi-zchut avot* — leaping over the mountains by the merit of the *avot*, who are identified with mountains; *mekapetz al ha-geva'ot bi-zchut imahot* — bounding over the hills by the merit of the *imahot*, who are associated with valleys. One *midrash* is being established by another: since we know from the second verse that *etanim* parallels *harim*, and since from *Shir Ha-Shirim* we learn that *harim* refers to the *avot*, the month of *Etanim* is identified as the month in which the forefathers were born.

There is something worth dwelling on in the imagery itself. The association of mountains with fathers and valleys or hills with mothers is not arbitrary. Beyond the physical symbolism of protrusion and indentation, there is the deeper image of fertility: valleys are where things are planted and where growth happens. The gendered imagery of land — Mother Earth, the earth as feminine vessel — runs through the agricultural imagination of *Chazal*. The mountains stand firm, the valleys receive and nurture.

This also opens onto a larger question about the two models of creation. The autumn model, associated with *Tishrei*, evokes a world already fully formed, mature, and ready. It is also the beginning of the agricultural cycle, the time when human beings must begin their work — planting, initiating, participating in the earth's productivity. The spring model evokes a world in the process of becoming, bursting forth naturally. One might argue that *Tishrei*, with its fully formed world and the beginning of the planting season, suggests a model in which human creativity and partnership with the divine are central: the world is given, and you must now till it and bring forth its fruits. *Nissan*, by contrast, suggests nature's own spontaneous outpouring, with the human being more the beneficiary than the initiator.

---

## Patriarchs Birth Nissan

### Ziv Blossoming

Rabbi Yehoshua's parallel proof for the birth of the *avot* in Nissan draws on a verse from the building of the *Beit HaMikdash*: *vayehi bi-shmonim shanah ve-arba me'ot shanah le-tzet bnei Yisrael me-eretz Mitzrayim ba-shanah ha-revi'it be-chodesh Ziv* — and it was in the four hundred and eightieth year after the departure of Israel from Egypt, in the fourth year, in the month of *Ziv*. The next words in the verse — *hu ha-chodesh ha-sheni* — make explicit that *chodesh Ziv* is the second month, i.e., *Iyar*.

The argument is: *be-yerach she-noldu bo zivtanei olam* — in the month in which the luminaries of the world were born, meaning the *avot*. *Rashi* acknowledges a difficulty here: the verse explicitly identifies this as the second month, which is *Iyar*, not *Nissan*. *Rashi* offers two approaches. The first is that by the time we reach the second month, the *avot* had already been born (in *Nissan*), making this a somewhat strained reading. The second is more elegant: the term *chodesh Ziv* refers not strictly to *Iyar* but to the season of *Tkufat Nissan* — the spring season — which extends into *Iyar*. The name *Ziv* captures the radiance of spring, not a specific month. One must acknowledge, however, that the verse is explicit in identifying this as the second month, which creates some tension for Rabbi Yehoshua's proof.

### Blossoming Bracha

The *gemara* now addresses what the other side does with the opposing verse. Rabbi Yehoshua's camp must explain *yerach ha-Etanim*, which Rabbi Eliezer read as pointing to the birth of the *avot* in *Tishrei*. The answer: *ha-tam de-takifei be-mitzvot* — it is called *Etanim* because that period is strong in *mitzvot*. *Rashi* lists them concisely: *shofar, Yom Kippurim, sukkah, lulav, aravah, nisuch ha-mayim*. The month of *Tishrei* is dense with *mitzvot*, and so it is called *Etanim* — the strong month — but this is no indication that the *avot* were born then.

Symmetrically, Rabbi Eliezer must explain *chodesh Ziv* if he holds the *avot* were born in *Tishrei*. The answer: *hahu de-it beih ziva le-ilanei* — it is the month that has a radiance and beauty about the trees, when the trees are blossoming. That is what *Ziv* means — the glow of spring blossoms — not a reference to the birth of luminaries.

This leads to *Rav Yehuda*'s famous teaching: *ha-i man de-nafik be-yomei Nissan ve-chazei ilanei de-melavlevei* — one who goes out during *Nissan* and sees trees beginning to blossom recites: *Baruch she-lo chisar me-olamo klum u-vara vo briyot tovot ve-ilanot tovot le-hanot ba-hen bnei adam* — Blessed is the One who has not left His world lacking anything, and has created good creatures and good trees for human beings to derive pleasure from them — even from their visual beauty, not only from their fruit. This *bracha* is recited once a year upon seeing blossoming trees in spring, and *Rav Yehuda* cites it precisely to illuminate what *Ziv* — radiance — means in the context of *Iyar*.

### Death Parallels

The *gemara* now draws the logical corollary: *man d'amar be-Nissan noldu be-Nissan meitu* — whoever holds they were born in Nissan holds they died in Nissan; *man d'amar be-Tishrei noldu be-Tishrei meitu* — whoever holds they were born in *Tishrei* holds they died in *Tishrei*.

The proof comes from Moshe's declaration: *ben me'ah ve-esrim shanah anochi ha-yom* — I am 120 years old *today*. The word *ha-yom* is exegetically significant: *she-ein talmud lomar ha-yom* — there was no need to say "today." *Ma talmud lomar ha-yom? Ha-yom malu yamai ve-shenotai* — today my days and years are precisely complete. This teaches that *ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu yoshev u-memale shenoteihem shel tzaddikim mi-yom le-yom mi-chodesh le-chodesh* — God fills out the years of the righteous to the precise day. The proof verse: *et mispar yamecha amale* — I will fill the number of your days. Therefore, if the *avot* were born in *Tishrei*, they died in *Tishrei*; if in Nissan, they died in Nissan.

---

## Yitzchak Pesach Birth

### Sarah Promise

On the birth of Yitzchak on Pesach, both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree: *be-Pesach nolad Yitzchak*. The source is the verse *la-mo'ed ashuv eleicha* — I will return to you at the appointed time — spoken by the *malachim* to Sarah. The *gemara* reads *mo'ed* as *Yom Tov*: the next *Yom Tov* you will have a child.

But when exactly was this promise made? *Eimat kai?* — at what point? *Ileima be-Pesach* — if it was Pesach, *ve-ka'amar lah be-Atzeret* — and they told her she'd give birth by *Shavuot* — *be-chamishim yomin mi ka yalda?* — how can one give birth in fifty days? *Ela de-ka'ei be-Atzeret ve-ka'amar lah be-Tishrei* — perhaps it was *Shavuot* and they said she'd give birth by *Sukkot* — *be-chamisha yarchei mi ka yalda?* — one cannot give birth in five months. *Ela de-ka'ei be-Chag ve-ka'amar lah be-Nissan* — it must have been *Sukkot*, and they promised her by Nissan. That is at least six months — the minimum for a viable birth. This establishes that Yitzchak was born in Nissan, specifically on Pesach.

### Leap Year Need

The *gemara* immediately presses: *ve-akati be-shita yarchei mi ka yalda?* — but can one give birth in only six months? Six months alone is still insufficient. The *gemara* answers: *tanya, ota shanah me'uberet hayta* — it was a leap year. With the intercalation of an extra *Adar*, the period from *Sukkot* to Pesach extends to seven months, which makes the birth viable.

### Impurity Calculation

Even with a leap year, a further complication arises: *ki madli mar yomei tum'ah batzrei lehu* — if you subtract the days during which Sarah was *tameh* and unable to conceive, the window shrinks to less than seven full months. *Rashi* on the *Torah* notes that the very day the *malachim* arrived, *oto yom pirsa Sarah niddah* — Sarah became a *niddah* on that day, which is alluded to in the verse *acharei beloti hayta li edna*. It also explains why Avraham did not serve the *malachim* the dough that Sarah prepared — because she had become a *niddah* while preparing it, rendering the food *tamei*. If she became a *niddah* upon the angels' arrival, she could not conceive immediately, and the effective window is shortened by at least a week or two.

### Seventh Month Birth

The resolution comes from *Mar Zutra*: *afilu man d'amar yoledet le-tish'ah eina yoledet le-ktu'im* — even the opinion that holds that a full-term pregnancy lasts nine months maintains that those nine months must be complete months; but *yoledet le-shiv'ah yoledet le-mikuta'im* — when a woman gives birth in the seventh month, the birth can occur even partway into the seventh month. The *gemara* supports this from the verse *vayehi li-tkufat ha-yamim* regarding Chanah — *mi'ut tkufot shtayim u-mi'ut yamim shnayim* — the minimum of *tkufot* is two (i.e., two seasons, or six months) and the minimum of days is two, so Chanah gave birth just two days into the seventh season. Thus a birth just at the beginning of the seventh month is *halakhically* recognized.

Applying this to Yitzchak: with a leap year, the period from *Sukkot* to Pesach is seven months. Even subtracting a week or two for Sarah's *niddah* period, the birth falls just at the opening of the seventh month — and such a birth is valid. This is how the *gemara* establishes that Yitzchak was born on Pesach.

It bears noting that all of this is consistent with the prior *gemara*, which assumes the *malachim* visited in *Tishrei*. This would align naturally with the next line: *be-Rosh Hashanah nifkeda Sarah* — Sarah was remembered on Rosh Hashanah, also in *Tishrei*.

---

## Three Women Remembered

### Rosh Hashanah Zichron

The *gemara* turns to the principle that Sarah, Rachel, and Chanah were all remembered on Rosh Hashanah. The underlying theme is that Rosh Hashanah is the day of *zikaron* — remembrance — and *pekida* — visitation, or divine intervention. These are not merely abstract categories; they are the central theological characterization of the day. *Shabbaton zichron teru'ah* — a day of rest, a memorial of the shofar blast — is the verse that anchors Rosh Hashanah as the day of divine remembrance.

### Rachel Chana

The *gemara* establishes the Rosh Hashanah connection through a *gezeira shava* — a textual analogy — using two parallel chains of derivation. The word *zechira* (remembrance) appears in connection with Rachel — *vayizkor Elokim et Rachel vayiftach et rachmah*, God remembered Rachel and opened her womb — and in connection with Chanah — *vayizkerah Hashem*, God remembered her. Since Rosh Hashanah is described as a day of *zichron*, *atya zchira zchira* — the same term connects these divine acts of remembrance to Rosh Hashanah.

### Sarah Pekida

The connection to Sarah employs a parallel *gezeira shava* using the word *pekida*. The verse by Chanah says *ki pakad Hashem et Chanah* — God *visited* Chanah. The verse by Sarah says *va-Hashem pakad et Sarah* — God visited Sarah. Since Chanah's *pekida* has been linked to Rosh Hashanah through *zchira*, Sarah's *pekida* is linked to Rosh Hashanah through *pekida*.

### Timeline Tension

This creates an apparent tension with what the *gemara* established moments earlier. The *gemara* there placed the visit of the *malachim* to Avraham and Sarah during *Sukkot*, with Yitzchak born on Pesach the following year. But now the *gemara* says Sarah was remembered on *Rosh Hashanah* — two weeks before *Sukkot*. How do the two fit together?

One resolution — which accords better with the verse *la-mo'ed ashuv eleicha* — would read the timeline as follows: the *malachim* visited on Pesach (as *Rashi* hints, noting that Lot baked *matzah* for them when they departed to Sedom, suggesting it was Pesach night). They announced a child would come *la-mo'ed* — at the next *mo'ed*, i.e., the next *Yom Tov*. Six months later, on Rosh Hashanah, God remembered Sarah (*be-Rosh Hashanah nifkeda*), and seven to seven-and-a-half months later — in a leap year — Yitzchak was born on Pesach. This reading integrates the two *gemarot* more smoothly, and it is the approach *Tosafot* labors to work through. However, the present *gemara* seems to assume the visitation occurred in *Tishrei*, which complicates the picture. The two traditions sit in tension, and *Tosafot* devotes considerable effort to resolving the difficulty.

---

## Joseph Liberation

### Joseph Forgot

*Be-Rosh Hashanah yatza Yosef mi-beit ha-asurim* — Yosef was freed from prison on Rosh Hashanah. The thematic connection to Rosh Hashanah is profound: the story of Yosef's imprisonment is essentially a story of *forgetting* — the *sar ha-mashkim* (chief cupbearer) forgot Yosef after he promised to remember him: *ki im zechartani itach*, and *velo zachar sar ha-mashkim et Yosef*. The redemption from this forgetting comes through divine *zichron* — the same divine memory that is the central theme of Rosh Hashanah.

### Tekua Shofar

The textual source is the *pasuk* from *Tehillim*: *tiku va-chodesh shofar ba-keseh le-yom chageinu ki chok le-Yisrael hu mishpat le-Elohei Yaakov* — blow the shofar on the month, on the concealed day of our festival, for it is a statute for Israel, a judgment of the God of Yaakov. This verse, as established earlier in the *masechta*, refers to Rosh Hashanah. The *pasuk* continues: *edut bi-Yehosef samo be-tzeito al eretz Mitzrayim* — a testimony was set upon Yosef when he went out over the land of Egypt. The juxtaposition of the Rosh Hashanah *pasuk* with Yosef's elevation over Egypt demonstrates that Yosef was freed and elevated on Rosh Hashanah.

One additional note: the *daf* at this point in the text has an unusual appearance — a *hagah* (marginal gloss) that pushes down the entire layout of the page, sitting atop the *Tosafot* rather than below it. This gloss represents a later commentator's attempt to resolve the question of when exactly the *malachim* visited — whether at Rosh Hashanah, Sukkot, or Pesach — a question that *Tosafot* also engages. It is perhaps unique in *Shas* for a *hagah* to reshape the page layout so dramatically.

---

## Labor Cessation

### Work Stopped

The *gemara* continues with another point on which all agree: *be-Rosh Hashanah batlah avodah me-avoteinu be-Mitzrayim* — the forced labor ceased on Rosh Hashanah. The actual redemption came later, in Nissan, but the *bitul avodah* — the cessation of the oppressive work — began on Rosh Hashanah. This parallels, as noted earlier, the structure of the *yovel*, where the *shofar* of *Yom Kippur* announces freedom but the transition unfolds over time.

The textual proof employs a *gezeira shava* on the word *sevel* (burden): *ve-hotzeisi eschem mi-tachat sivlot Mitzrayim* — I will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt — is linked to *ha-sirotiv mi-sevel shichmo* — I removed the burden from his shoulder — from the *pasuk* of *tiku va-chodesh shofar*, which is a Rosh Hashanah verse. The same root *s-v-l* appears in both, connecting the removal of Egypt's burden to Rosh Hashanah.

### Leil Shimurim

Now the *gemara* returns to the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on the future redemption, and this is where the two positions crystallize most sharply. *Be-Nissan nigalu* — they were redeemed in Nissan — and *be-Tishrei atidin lehigael* — in *Tishrei* will the future redemption come — according to Rabbi Eliezer. The proof: *atya shofar shofar* — a *gezeira shava* on the word *shofar*. *Tiku va-chodesh shofar* refers to Rosh Hashanah; *ba-yom ha-hu yitaka be-shofar gadol* refers to the great shofar of Messianic redemption. Just as the *yovel* shofar, blown on *Yom Kippur* of *Tishrei*, represents the announcement of freedom, so too will the great shofar of the future redemption sound in *Tishrei*.

Rabbi Yehoshua responds: *be-Nissan nigalu u-be-Nissan atidin lehigael* — in Nissan they were redeemed, and in Nissan will they be redeemed in the future. The proof: *amar kra leil shimurim* — the verse says *leil shimurim* (Shemot 12:42). How does Rabbi Yehoshua read this? *Leil ha-meshumar u-va mi-sheshet yemei bereishit* — a night that has been guarded and awaited since the six days of creation. This Pesach night was designated from the very beginning of the world as the night of redemption — both the first redemption and the future one.

The one who says *Tishrei* reads *leil shimurim* differently: *laila ha-meshumar min ha-mazikin* — a night guarded from harmful forces, alluding to the protection of the firstborn during *Makas Bechoros*, when *lo yiten ha-mashchit lavo el bateichem lingof* — the destroyer was not permitted to enter the Israelite homes.

### Nissan Tishrei Theology

It is worth pausing over this debate, because the question of whether the future redemption will come in Nissan or in *Tishrei* is not merely calendrical — it carries genuine theological weight. The argument for Nissan is intuitive and almost irresistible: if the first redemption came in Nissan, and Nissan is marked as *rishon hu lachem le-chodshei ha-shanah* — first among the months — and the entire month carries the character of *geulah*, then the future redemption should be a continuation and culmination of that original *geulah*. The imagery of Nissan is powerful: the movement from the dead of winter to the blossoming of spring, from darkness to light, from slavery to freedom. It is natural, organic, and cyclically satisfying.

The position that the future redemption will come in *Tishrei* is harder to grasp. *Tishrei* is the time of divine judgment, of God's memory and intervention in the world — *Rosh Hashanah* and *Yom Kippur*. One might argue that in *Tishrei*, the world does not simply blossom of its own accord; rather, it is human beings who must initiate, plant, and partner with the divine. The beginning of the agricultural cycle is the beginning of human creative responsibility. The future redemption, on this view, will not simply be a repeat of the original *geulah* — where *Bnei Yisrael* were, as it were, carried out passively — but will be one in which greater human partnership and initiative are required. This is an intellectually provocative thought, even if the *gemara* does not spell it out explicitly. The *shofar shofar* connection at least anchors it liturgically in the existing structure of Rosh Hashanah.

---

## Mabul Flood Dating

### Yehoshua Mabul Date

The *gemara* now applies the same *Tishrei*-versus-Nissan dispute to the dating of the *mabul*. The verse says the flood began in the second month, on the seventeenth day. *Ve-azdu le-ta'amaihu* — they each follow their own reasoning. Rabbi Yehoshua says: *oso yom Yud-Zayin be-Iyar haya* — that day was the 17th of *Iyar*, because he counts from Nissan, making *Iyar* the second month.

### Kima Stars

What is significant about this date? *Yom she-mazal Kima shokeia ba-yom* — it is the day when the constellation *Kima* is setting during the day. *Rashi* identifies *Kima* with the Pleiades. *Rashi* here also provides a full list of the twelve zodiacal constellations in their Hebrew names: *Taleh* (Aries), *Shor* (Taurus), *Teomim* (Gemini), *Sartan* (Cancer), *Aryeh* (Leo), *Betula* (Virgo), *Moznayim* (Libra), *Akrav* (Scorpio), *Keshet* (Sagittarius), *Gedi* (Capricorn), *Deli* (Aquarius), *Dagim* (Pisces). The mnemonic is: *Hatshaf Av Maakt-Gadad*.

The *Kima* is in the setting phase during the day in *Iyar*, because by then the cycle of constellations has moved on from where it was at the start of Nissan. *U-mayanos mitma'atim* — the underground wellsprings are diminishing in spring, as the winter rains and snowmelt taper off. This is the natural state of affairs in *Iyar*. Therefore, *u-mitoch she-shinu ma'aseihem* — because the generation of the *mabul* perverted their ways — *shina ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu aleihem ma'aseh bereishit* — God altered the natural order against them. *Ve-he'ela mazal Kima ba-yom* — God made *Kima* rise during the day, in the opposite of its normal pattern — *ve-natal shenei kochavim mi-Kima ve-heivi Mabul la-olam* — and God took two stars from *Kima* and brought the flood upon the world. The stars of *Kima* functioned as plugs in the great heavenly storehouse of water; removing them opened the floodgates.

### Zodiac Signs

The constellations rotate through the sky in a twelve-part cycle. In Nissan, Aries (*Taleh*) is in the ascendancy as the day begins, and each subsequent constellation takes over in roughly two-hour intervals. Six months later, in *Tishrei*, the cycle is inverted — what was at the top in Nissan is now at the bottom, and vice versa. This rotating structure is the framework for understanding both the astronomical claims about *Kima* and the calculation of the *tekufot* (seasonal reckonings) — to which the *gemara* will turn shortly.

### Eliezer Mabul Date

Rabbi Eliezer holds that *oso yom Yud-Zayin be-Marcheshvan haya* — that day was the 17th of *Marcheshvan*, the second month counting from *Tishrei*. On his calendar, *Kima* is rising — *ola* — during the day in *Marcheshvan*, which is actually consistent with the natural pattern of that month. In *Marcheshvan*, the underground wellsprings are increasing — *mayanot mitgabrim* — as the winter rains begin. So the question the *gemara* will raise is: if this is already the natural state of affairs in *Marcheshvan*, what exactly did God *change* (*shina*) to bring the flood?

---

## Mabul Flood Dating (II)

### Boiling Water Sin

The answer to that question comes from Rav Chisda: *be-rotchin kilkelu be-rotchin nidonu* — they sinned with boiling liquid and were punished with boiling liquid. The sin refers to sexual immorality — the *aveira* associated in *Chazal*'s reading with the generation of the *mabul*, involving unnatural unions. The punishment was that the floodwaters were not merely cold water but boiling hot. This is the *shina* — the alteration of the natural order — according to Rabbi Eliezer: not that water came in the wrong season, but that the water itself was supernaturally hot.

The proof for the hot water: *ktiv hacha va-yashoku ha-mayim* — the waters *abated*, using the root *sh-k-k*; *ve-chtiv hatam ve-chamat ha-melech shachachah* — and the king's fury (*chamat*) abated, the same root. Since *chemah* connotes fiery rage and heat, the shared root implies that the floodwaters, like a king's fury, required *cooling down* — demonstrating that they had been boiling hot.

---

## Calendar Resolution

### Jewish Counting

The *gemara* presents a surprising resolution in the form of a *baraita*: *chachmei Yisrael monin la-mabul ke-Rabbi Eliezer u-le-tekufa ke-Rabbi Yehoshua* — the Jewish sages count the *mabul* dates following Rabbi Eliezer (i.e., from *Tishrei*, making the second month *Marcheshvan*), but they reckon the *tekufot* (seasonal divisions of the year) following Rabbi Yehoshua (i.e., from Nissan). This is not consistent.

### Non-Jewish Counting

*Chachmei Umot Ha-olam monim af hem ke-Rabbi Yehoshua* — the sages of the nations are consistent: they count both the *mabul* dates and the *tekufot* from Nissan, following Rabbi Yehoshua throughout.

### Tekufa Reference

Both *Rashi* and *Tosafot* explain the significance of how one counts the *tekufot*: the seasonal reckoning takes the moment of creation as its point of reference. The *tekufa* calculation works backward from a fixed starting point, which must be the beginning of the world. Therefore, whichever month one uses as the reference point for the *tekufot* implicitly reveals which month one believes the world was created in. If the *chachmei Yisrael* reckon the *tekufot* from Nissan, they are, in effect, ruling that the world was created in Nissan — *be-Nissan nivra ha-olam* — even while they apply the *Tishrei* calendar to the *mabul* narrative in the *Torah*.

### Conclusion Ambiguity

What then is the final ruling? The *gemara* leaves the question unresolved in a striking way. The entire tradition of *tekufa* calculation — the backbone of the Jewish calendar's seasonal reckoning — implicitly assumes the world was created in Nissan. Yet so much of the liturgy of Rosh Hashanah assumes *be-Tishrei nivra ha-olam*: *zeh ha-yom haras olam*, *zeh ha-yom techilat ma'asecha* — this day is the birthday of the world, this day is the beginning of Your works.

The result is that both traditions — Nissan as the month of natural creation and *Tishrei* as the month of providential creation, judgment, and human partnership — remain alive simultaneously in Jewish consciousness and practice. The tension is not resolved; it is inhabited. The agricultural calendar begins in *Tishrei*; the redemptive calendar begins in Nissan. The world was created in *Tishrei* for purposes of divine judgment and human accountability; it was created in Nissan for purposes of natural birth and cosmic renewal. Both things are true, and the *gemara* on 11b ends, characteristically, by leaving us to hold both.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 12

## Creation to Year Categor…

### Constellations & Creation

The discussion of creation-era chronology — when the constellations were set in place, when the waters rose — reaches its natural conclusion here. The debate over the *girsa* turns on a question of seasonal plausibility: the rising of waters and the melting of snows fit the spring far better than the fall, as does the ascending of Aries. Rashi's formulation is that the *tekufot* represent the moment we imagine the constellations and the sun to have been placed — which occurred on the fourth day of creation, when the luminaries were created — and the computation of that moment proceeds from Nisan. Both the *chachmei umot ha'olam* and the *chachmei Yisrael* appear to converge on Nisan as the basis for this calculation.

### Nisan vs. Tishrei Tension

This consensus will prove startling when the *Gemara* later encounters a discussion in which our very liturgy reflects the position that the world was created in Tishrei. The tension between the computational tradition anchoring creation in Nisan and the liturgical tradition anchoring it in Tishrei remains unresolved. One might be tempted to resolve it by positing two planes — *alah b'machshava*, the world arose in thought in one month, and came into being in another — but the *Gemara* itself leaves this open.

### Vegetables & Ma'aser Year

The *Gemara* now returns from its extended excursus on the *pesukim* of Noach and the *mabul*, and resumes the list in the *mishnah* of domains for which the first of Tishrei constitutes the *rosh hashanah*. The next item on that list is *u'leyerakot* — for vegetables. The operative concern is *ma'aser yerek*: one may not tithe from one year onto the next. If, for example, a farmer has twenty bushels from this year and ten from the following year and attempts to designate a tithe covering all thirty, the portion taken on behalf of the ten units of the second year's produce is legally ineffective — and this is true even *bedi'avad*. Beyond the question of cross-year tithing, the year-designation for *ma'asrot* also determines which *ma'aser* applies within the seven-year cycle: *ma'aser ani* in years three and six, and *ma'aser sheni* in years one, two, four, and five.

---

## Vegetables Cross-Year Mi…

### Year Boundary Rules

Two conceptually distinct questions arise whenever the year-boundary for *terumot u'ma'asrot* is at stake. The first is the calendar date: when does the new year begin? For vegetables, the answer is the first of Tishrei. The second is the operative event: what must have occurred by that date to assign the produce to one year or the other? By *ma'aser behemah*, the relevant event is the birth of the animal — whether it was born before or after *rosh chodesh Elul*, or before or after the first of Tishrei, depending on how one rules in that debate. For vegetables, as the *Gemara* will demonstrate, the operative event is the moment of picking.

### Calendar Date vs. Event

These two questions — the fixed calendar date and the determining event — operate in tandem. The date answers *when* the year turns; the event answers *what* must have happened to place the produce on one side of that boundary or the other. Neither question is trivial, and the *Gemara* treats them as analytically independent.

---

## Braita Analysis

### Three Categories Listed

The *Gemara* cites a *braita*: *u'leyerakot u'lema'asrot u'lenedarim* — not just vegetables, but also *ma'asrot* generally, encompassing fruit and grain, and also vows. The *Gemara* immediately asks: why does the *braita* mention both *yerakot* and *ma'asrot*? If *yerakot* means the *ma'aser* obligation as it pertains to vegetables, is that not simply a subset of *ma'asrot*?

### Rabbinic vs. Biblical Ma…

The answer is that the two categories are legally distinct: *tana d'rabbanan v'tana d'oraita*. The obligation of *ma'aser* on vegetables is rabbinic — *ma'aser yerek* is *derabbanan* — while *ma'asrot* in the second clause refers to the biblical obligations on grain, olives, and grapes. This raises a significant question: what precisely falls within the biblical obligation? Reading the *Gemara* plainly, it sounds as though anything other than vegetables would be biblical, which would include all fruit. Whether *ma'aser* on fruit is indeed *d'oraita* is a major dispute among the *rishonim*. Rashi, throughout *Shas*, maintains that the Torah's obligation of *terumot u'ma'asrot* applies only to *degancha tiroshcha ve'yitzharecha* — the five grains, oil from olives, and wine from grapes — and that everything else, including fruit, is rabbinic.

### Fruit Tithes Debate

Tosafot here raises a lengthy counter-argument rooted in the *Yerushalmi*, which seems to indicate that all fruit carries a biblical *ma'aser* obligation, with vegetables alone being the rabbinic exception. Tosafot marshals this tradition at length, arriving at the formulation *mishma d'she'ar kol peyros d'oraita* — that all other fruit is biblical. Yet Tosafot ultimately reverses course. Several lines later, Tosafot concludes with the words *aval i efshar lomar kein* — "but it is impossible to say this" — because in numerous places throughout the *Gemara*, the rabbis treat fruit *ma'aser* as rabbinic. Tosafot thus ultimately aligns with Rashi's position: the biblical obligation applies only to grain, olives, and grapes.

### Ordering Rationale

A further question presses: why does the *braita* list the rabbinic category (*yerakot*) before the biblical one (*ma'asrot*)? The *Gemara* answers with a principle invoked in multiple places: *aydi d'chaviva lei akdamah* — the *tanna* is partial to rabbinic enactments and places them first in order to give them weight, so that people will not treat them lightly.

### Mishna Word Choice

The *Gemara* then turns to the *tanna didan* — the author of our *mishnah* — who mentions only *yerakot*, without using the broader term *ma'asrot*. The explanation offered is *tana d'rabbanan v'chol shekein d'oraita*: by specifying the rabbinic category, one conveys the obligation for the biblical category *a fortiori*. Rashi understands the *kal va'chomer* as follows: if there is a fixed date for the rabbinic *ma'aser* that governs year-boundaries, then certainly there is a fixed date for the biblical obligation. Alternatively, the *kal va'chomer* runs in the other direction: if the rabbinic category — which was modeled on the biblical one — operates by the first of Tishrei, then certainly the biblical category, which served as the model, operates the same way.

The *Gemara* then asks why the *mishnah* did not simply say *ma'aser*, which would have generically included both rabbinic and biblical obligations. Tosafot explains that had the *mishnah* used the generic term *ma'aser*, it might have been construed as encompassing *ma'aser behemah* as well — and whether the first of Tishrei governs *ma'aser behemah* is itself a matter of dispute. By saying *yerakot* instead, the *tanna* avoids any implication about *ma'aser behemah*. Tosafot further notes that the term *ma'asrot* in the *braita* does not carry the same connotation of *ma'aser behemah*, since across Tannaitic literature *ma'asrot* refers to the multiple tithes separated from produce — *ma'aser rishon*, *ma'aser sheni*, *ma'aser ani* — and not to the animal tithe.

### Two Vegetable Types

The *Gemara* asks one final question about the *mishnah*'s language: why *yerakot* in the plural rather than *yerek* in the singular? The answer is that the plural alludes to two distinct categories of vegetables, each with a different standard of *gmar melacha* — the completion of processing — after which one may no longer eat even *arai*, casual snacking, without first separating *terumot u'ma'asrot*.

### Bundled vs. Unbundled

For vegetables that are sold in bundles — asparagus, broccoli, and similar produce that is typically bound together for market — the *gmar melacha* occurs when they are bundled, at which point they are fully processed and ready for sale. For vegetables that are not bundled — such as loose tomatoes or lettuce — the *gmar melacha* occurs when the vessel is filled: *mi'she'yimalei et ha'keli*. If the vessel is never filled, then the *gmar melacha* is determined by the end of the harvest. It is critical to note that this distinction governs the point at which casual eating becomes prohibited — it does not govern year-assignment for *ma'asrot*, which is always determined by the moment of picking. The plural *yerakot* thus signals that while all vegetables share the same rule for year-assignment, they differ with respect to this separate question of *gmar melacha*.

---

## Picking & Day Boundary

### Picking Erev & After

A *braita* presents the following case: a person was picking vegetables in his garden on *erev Rosh Hashanah* before sunset and continued picking after sunset. Given that picking after sunset would constitute *melachah* on *Yom Tov*, the *Yerushalmi* resolves this by positing a non-Jewish worker who, on his own initiative — *adaata d'nafshei* — continued the harvest after dark.

### Yom Tov & Obligation

Even granting that the post-sunset picking may have involved a *Yom Tov* violation, the *braita* rules that both batches remain *chayav b'terumot u'ma'asrot*. The *Yom Tov* concern does not vitiate the *ma'aser* obligation.

### Picking Moment Decisive

More importantly for the conceptual framework, the *braita* rules that *ein tormin u'ma'asrin mi'zeh al zeh* — one may not take *terumah* or *ma'aser* from the pre-sunset batch on the post-sunset batch, nor vice versa. This establishes not merely the date — the first of Tishrei — but the operative event: the moment the produce is picked determines which year it belongs to. Produce picked five minutes before sunset and produce picked five minutes after sunset cannot be tithed against one another, because they belong to different years. The rule is stated explicitly: *lo min ha'chadash al ha'yashan velo min ha'yashan al ha'chadash*.

### Year Cycle Application

The *braita* then spells out the consequence for the seven-year cycle. If it is the second year of the cycle transitioning into the third: produce picked before sunset — belonging to year two — requires *ma'aser rishon* and *ma'aser sheni*, the latter being eaten in Jerusalem. Produce picked after sunset — belonging to year three — requires *ma'aser rishon* and *ma'aser ani*, the tithe designated for the poor. Four *nafka minot* thus emerge in sequence: (A) the calendar date is the first of Tishrei; (B) the operative event is the moment of picking; (C) produce from one year may not be tithed against produce from another year; and (D) the applicable *ma'aser* within the cycle is determined by the year of picking.

---

## Ma'aser Ani Years 3 & 6

### Ma'aser Ani Source

The *Gemara* now digresses briefly to establish the biblical source for *ma'aser ani* in years three and six. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives it from the verse: *ki techaleh la'aser et kol ma'aser tevuatcha ba'shanah ha'shlishit shenat ha'ma'aser* — "when you finish tithing all the tithe of your produce in the third year, the year of the tithe" — followed by *ve'natata la'Levi la'ger la'yatom ve'la'almana*. Ordinarily, *ma'aser rishon* goes to the Levi and *ma'aser sheni* is eaten in Jerusalem by its owner. The inclusion of *ger*, *yatom*, and *almana* as recipients marks this as the year of *ma'aser ani*.

### Only One Other Tithe

The phrase *shenat ha'ma'aser* — the year of *the* tithe — is interpreted to mean that in this year there is only one other *ma'aser* besides *ma'aser ani*. The inference is that *ma'aser sheni* is suspended: only *ma'aser rishon* and *ma'aser ani* apply.

### Ma'aser Rishon Continuity

The *Gemara* raises an objection: perhaps *shenat ha'ma'aser* means that even *ma'aser rishon* is suspended, leaving only *ma'aser ani* altogether? This is resolved by the verse: *v'el ha'Levi'im tedaber v'amarta aleihem ki tikchu mei'et b'nei Yisrael et ha'ma'aser asher natati lachem mei'itam b'nachalatchem* — "and to the Levites you shall speak... the tithe that I have given you from them as your inheritance." The verse links *ma'aser rishon* to an inheritance: just as an inheritance has no interruption — *ma nachala ein lah hefsek* — so too *ma'aser rishon* has no interruption. It follows that *shenat ha'ma'aser* signifies the suspension of *ma'aser sheni* only, not of *ma'aser rishon*.

### Second Braita Confirmati…

A second *braita* confirms this reading independently. The same verse — *ki techaleh la'aser... shenat ha'ma'aser* — is quoted, and the same conclusion is reached: only *ma'aser rishon* and *ma'aser ani*, while *ma'aser sheni* is suspended. The *braita* then asks whether *ma'aser rishon* might also be suspended, and resolves this from a different verse: *u'va ha'Levi* — "and the Levi shall come" — which appears in the context of the third year. The verse *u'va ha'Levi ki ein lo chelek v'nachala imach v'ha'ger v'ha'yatom v'ha'almana* singles out the Levi distinctly, alongside the *ger*, *yatom*, and *almana*, demonstrating that even in the year of *ma'aser ani*, the Levi continues to receive his tithe. The ruling is thus: *u'va ha'Levi kol zman sheba ten lo* — whenever the Levi comes, give to him — even during the third year.

### R. Eliezer ben Yaakov

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov maintains that the verse *u'va ha'Levi* is unnecessary for this derivation. The earlier verse — *v'el ha'Levi'im tedaber... asher natati lachem b'nachalatchem* — linking *ma'aser rishon* to an inheritance already suffices: *ma nachala ein lah hefsek, af ma'aser rishon ein lo hefsek*. Just as an inheritance admits no interruption, *ma'aser rishon* admits no interruption, and the continuity of the Levi's entitlement is established without need of the additional verse.

---

## Vows & Year Term

### Vow Duration & Expiry

The *braita* on vows rules as follows: one who vows not to derive benefit from another person "for a year" counts twelve months from day to day — that is, returning to the same date on the calendar, accounting for leap years. However, if the vow was formulated as "for this year" — *lishana zo* — the vow expires when the first of Tishrei arrives, since that marks the end of the current year.

### One-Day Vow Suffices

Even if the vow was taken on the twenty-ninth of Elul — *b'esrim v'tisha b'Elul* — once the first of Tishrei arrives, *altah lo shanah*: the year is complete and the vow expires, even though the vow was in force for only a single day.

### Self-Affliction Exception

The *Gemara* notes that this outcome holds even according to those who hold that one day in a year is ordinarily insufficient to be counted as a full year — as debated extensively regarding trees and rental agreements, where one camp required the new year to arrive only after at least a month's residence. In the case of vows, everyone agrees that a single day suffices. The reason is *letzaarei nafshia kavilah alei* — in making a vow, a person takes upon himself an act of self-affliction, and that self-affliction is achieved immediately, from the very first moment. Unlike a rental arrangement in which the practical benefit of the lease accumulates over time, the purpose of a vow of self-denial is accomplished from the instant the restriction takes effect. One need not endure the vow for a prolonged period for it to have been meaningful; even a single day of deprivation constitutes a genuine act of *inui*, and thus the most minimal reading of "this year" — even a single day — is legally sufficient.

---

## Stage-Based Designation

### Mishnah Stage Rules

The *Gemara* now cites a *mishnah* from tractate *Ma'asrot*: *ha'taltan mishetitzmach* — fenugreek is governed from the time it sprouts; *ha'tvuah v'ha'zeitim misheyavi'u shlish* — grain and olives are governed from the time they have reached a third of their ripeness. This *mishnah* introduces a layer of complexity: while the calendar date (the first of Tishrei) is uniform across all categories, the operative event — the stage of development that assigns a given crop to a given year — differs by type of produce. Grain and olives are assigned by *shelish* (a third ripening); fenugreek by sprouting. Fruit, not mentioned here, will be assigned by blossoming. The *Gemara* has not yet explained why these different stages apply to different plants, but the question is noted.

### Shelish from Shmita

The *Gemara* focuses first on the rule of *shelish* for grain. Rav Assi cites Rabbi Yochanan — with some transmitters attributing it to Rabbi Yose HaGlili — who derives this from the verse concerning *hakhel*: *miketz sheva shanim b'mo'ed shnat ha'shmitah b'chag ha'sukkot* — "at the end of seven years, at the appointed time of the year of *shmita*, during *Sukkot*." The verse presents an apparent difficulty: if it is *at the end* of seven years, then *Sukkot* must already be in the eighth year. Why does the Torah call it *shnat ha'shmitah*? The answer is: *kol tvuah shehevia shelish bi'shvi'it lifnei Rosh Hashana, atah noheg bah minhag shevi'it bi'shminit* — any grain that reached a third of its ripeness during the seventh year before *Rosh Hashanah* retains the sanctity of the *shmita* year even when harvested in the eighth year. The verse calls it *shnat ha'shmitah* because there is still grain being harvested in that eighth year that carries *kedushat shevi'it*, having crossed the *Rosh Hashanah* threshold while already a third ripe.

### Challenge to Shelish Mea…

Rav Zeira raises two challenges to this derivation. The first: perhaps the verse does not speak of the sanctity of fruit at all, but rather of a continuation of *shmita* practices — an extension of *shmita* law until *Sukkot*, analogous to the principle of *mosifin me'chol al ha'kodesh*, adding from the ordinary into the sacred. The *Gemara* dismisses this by reading the word *asif* — used in the verse *v'chag ha'asif b'tzet ha'shanah* — as referring to active harvesting, not to the general practices of *shmita*. If *Sukkot* is called the time of *asif*, it means people are harvesting then; one does not harvest during *shmita*, so the verse must be addressing grain that is being harvested, grain that grew during *shmita* and is now being cut in year eight.

The second challenge, pressed by Rav Zeira (or Rabbi Yirmiyah), is more pointed: granted that some grain harvested at *Sukkot* has *kedushat shevi'it*, how do you derive that the operative stage is precisely *shelish*? Even if we accept that grain harvested on *Sukkot* grew during *shmita*, how do we know it was *specifically* a third ripe before *Rosh Hashanah*, as opposed to some lesser stage? The *Gemara* answers: the rabbis knew — *v'kayam lehu l'rabbanan* — that any grain ready to be harvested on *Sukkot* was, by definition, a third ripe before *Rosh Hashanah*. The temporal relationship between the stage of *shelish* and the point of harvestability is established knowledge.

### Precision of Law Required

At this point a deeper objection surfaces: even granting that *shelish* is the operative standard, how can a legal line be drawn at such a biologically imprecise threshold? What difference does a hair's breadth make — a grain that is just barely at *shelish* versus one that is barely less? The response is definitive: *kol midat chachamim ken hi* — this is the very nature of rabbinic legal measurement. The law draws lines and those lines hold without exception. The *mikvah* requires *arba'im se'ah* of water; *arba'im se'ah* minus a *kurtav* — a thumbnail's volume — and one cannot immerse: *b'arba'im se'ah chaser kurtav eino yachol litbol bahen*. A piece of food the size of an egg (*k'beitza*) imparts *tumah* of foodstuffs; a *k'beitza* minus a single sesame seed (*shum-shum*) does not. A piece of cloth three by three handbreadths (*sheloshah al sheloshah*) is susceptible to *midras* tumah from a *zav*; remove a single thread and it is not. Law requires defined thresholds; the question of whether one can always detect the precise threshold with certainty is beside the point. All measurements — including *beitza* and *mikvah* — are calibrated according to the aggregate norm and applied as consistently as humanly possible. The imprecision inherent in biological development no more undermines the *shelish* standard than the variability of individual throats undermines the egg-size standard for *tumah* of foodstuffs.

### Shelish Applications

Tosafot draws a unifying conclusion from this discussion: the various stage-markers that appear throughout *Ma'asrot* — sprouting (*mishetitzmach*) for fenugreek, blossoming for fruit, third-ripening for grain and olives — are all, in fact, applications of the *shelish* principle. Each marker identifies the moment at which the produce in question reaches what is functionally equivalent to a third of its full development. The reason the *mishnah* does not simply say *misheyavi'u shlish* for all categories is that by most produce there are identifiable, visible signs that correspond to this stage and can be described concretely, whereas for grain and olives no such convenient external sign exists, so the quantitative measure of *shelish* must be stated explicitly.

### Taltan & Seed Planting

The *Yerushalmi* offers a further confirmation of this framework specifically regarding fenugreek. The word *mishetitzmach* — from the time it sprouts — is interpreted by Rabbi Zeira in the *Yerushalmi* through a *derashah* on the verse *aser te'aser et kol tevuat zarecha*: a thing that is planted and sprouts. What is excluded? That which has not yet reached *shelish*, because less than *shelish* ripe, the seeds are not yet fit for replanting. Once the seeds of the fenugreek are fit to be planted, *mishetitzmach* applies — and this is precisely the *shelish* threshold expressed in a form appropriate to fenugreek. The convergence of the *Bavli* and *Yerushalmi* on this point, as Tosafot notes, confirms that the diverse stage-markers throughout *Ma'asrot* are all expressions of a single underlying principle: the moment a crop's seeds are viable for replanting marks its legal transition into the category of produce subject to *ma'aser* year-assignment.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 13

## Critical Moment Overview

### Development Stage Questi…

The daf opens in the midst of a fundamental question: at what stage of development does one examine a crop in order to determine which year it belongs to? The year itself is established by *rosh hashanah* — the first of *tishrei* — which determines one's position in the *shemita* cycle, whether produce from one year may be taken on another, and related matters. But the operative question is which developmental milestone triggers the assignment to a given year.

By way of review, a *braita* cited at the close of the previous daf (12b, approximately ten lines from the bottom) establishes:

> תנן התם: התלתן משתצמח, והתבואה והזיתים משיביאו שליש.

That is, fenugreek goes by the time it sprouts, while grain (*tvuah*) and olives go by *havi'u shalish* — once they have developed a third. What exactly does "a third" mean? The agricultural scholar Yehoshua Felix, in his work on agriculture in the land of Israel during the period of the *mishna*, explains that *hevi'u shalish* means that the grain's weight has reached one third of its ultimate weight — a definition that renders the criterion more quantifiable, even if still difficult to assess by the naked eye.

The *gemara* further clarifies that by fenugreek, *titzmach* means *titzmach lizraim* — it has sprouted to the point where the seeds are fit for replanting. *Tosafot* draws a conceptual link here: *havi'u shalish* in grain similarly means that the seeds within have reached a stage at which they are viable for replanting.

### Vegetable Picking

The case of vegetables was addressed through a *braita* in the earlier discussion, which taught that the critical moment for vegetables is *lekita* — the act of picking. Vegetables picked before *rosh hashanah* belong to the preceding year; those picked after belong to the new year.

### Obligation vs. Dating

Before proceeding to the main discussion, an important distinction must be drawn — one that generates much of the confusion in this sugya. There are two entirely separate questions that both invoke the concept of *hava'at shalish*, and it is critical not to conflate them.

The first question is: when does produce become obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot*? This is a question about the status of the produce itself — is it sufficiently developed to be considered food or fruit such that the obligation of tithing attaches? *Tosafot* notes that the opening *mishnayot* of tractate *Ma'asrot* enumerate the various signs of development for different types of fruit and produce, and explains that all of these are simply applications of the single principle of *hava'at shalish* — the moment at which tithing obligations begin. Before this point, even if one were to designate *terumah*, it would have no legal effect. After *hava'at shalish* and until *gmar melacha* — the completion of processing — one may snack from the produce but is not obligated to tithe until processing is complete. After *gmar melacha* (such as heaping grain into a pile and bringing it into the house, or bundling vegetables), even snacking is prohibited without tithing. For this entire framework, *hava'at shalish* serves as the universal threshold across all produce types.

### Chaviv Framework

This first framework — the question of when the *chiyuv* in *terumot u'ma'asrot* begins — applies uniformly. Everything, whether fruit, vegetables, or grain, goes by *hava'at shalish* as the entry point into the tithing system. The gradient runs from before *hava'at shalish* (no obligation, tithes ineffective) through the window between *hava'at shalish* and *gmar melacha* (snacking permitted, tithing effective if done) to after *gmar melacha* (snacking prohibited, full obligation).

### Year Determination

The second question — the one actually under discussion — is categorically different: which *year* does the produce belong to? This matters for *shemita* status, for *maaser sheni* versus *maaser ani*, for the prohibition of taking from one year's produce on another year's, and so on. The year is determined by *rosh hashanah*, but the question is: which developmental milestone locks in the year?

Here, unlike in the obligation framework, the answer varies by produce type. The milestone differs depending on whether one is dealing with grain, fruit, or vegetables.

### Produce-Type Moments

The different milestones for different produce categories are as follows. For *yerek* (vegetables), the determinative moment is *lekita* — picking. For *tvuah* (grain) and olives, it is *hava'at shalish* — a third developed. For *peiros* (fruit trees), it is *chanata* — blossoming. And for *kitniyot* (legumes and seeds such as rice, millet, poppy, and sesame), the answer will prove to be *hashrashah* — taking root — for reasons the *gemara* will explain.

To illustrate with grain: if wheat is planted in one year and growing, but does not reach *shalish* until the following year, it belongs to the year in which it reached *shalish*. The *chiyuv* question and the year-dating question are answered by the same criterion for grain, but for vegetables and fruit they diverge entirely. The confusion arises because the terminology of *shalish* appears in both frameworks, but for distinct purposes.

---

## Sukkot Proof & Chall (II)

### Source of Third

With the framework clarified, the *gemara* returns to the primary inquiry: what is the source for the rule that a third of development determines the year to which grain belongs?

> מנא הני מילי?

### Sukkot Verse Logic

Abaye transmits in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, who transmits it in the name of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, a derivation from the following verse:

> מקץ שבע שנים במועד שנת השמיטה בחג הסוכות.

The verse speaks of "the end of seven years, at the appointed time of the *shemita* year, on *Chag HaSukkot*." The *gemara* presses: if we are at the end of seven years, it is already the eighth year — the *sukkot* referred to falls in year eight, not in the *shemita* year. Why then does the verse call it "*shnat hashmita*" — the *shemita* year?

The answer: the verse is teaching that any grain (*tvuah*) which had developed a third before *rosh hashanah* of the *shemita* year — even if it continues growing into the eighth year — retains the sanctity of *shemita* produce. The verse calls it the *shemita* year because some produce, by virtue of having reached *shalish* before *rosh hashanah*, still carries *shemita* status even as it is harvested in the eighth year.

But this teaches only that the timing of *hava'at shalish* relative to *rosh hashanah* is consequential for *shemita* status. It does not yet establish why the specific threshold of a *third* is the operative criterion. A further step is needed.

### Precision Challenge

Rabbi Zeira raises a prior challenge entirely. Perhaps, he suggests, the verse is not speaking about the sanctity of produce at all. Perhaps it simply means that the laws of *shemita* extend into the eighth year as a matter of calendar — one continues abstaining from labor even past *rosh hashanah*, similar to the principle of *mosifin mechol al hakodesh*, adding from the weekday onto the holy. In that reading, no inference about produce development can be drawn.

The *gemara* rejects this: *lo salka daitach*. The verse elsewhere says:

> וחג האסיף בצאת השנה באספך את מעשיך מן השדה.

The festival of *asif* at the end of the year, when you gather in your produce from the field. The word *asif* appears twice — once as the name of the festival (*Chag HaAsif*) and once in the phrase *be'aspecha* (when you gather). Since the gathering is already stated explicitly in *be'aspecha*, the *asif* in the festival's name must be conveying something additional.

The *gemara* reads *asif* here not as gathering (*asifah*) but as harvesting (*katzir*). This is somewhat striking, since one does not typically harvest grain at *sukkot* time — Felix notes it is legumes that are harvested then, not grain. Nevertheless, the *gemara* interprets the verse to be saying: if you are harvesting grain at *sukkot* time, that grain is still called "at the end of the year" (*betzeit hashanah*) — meaning it remains connected to the preceding year. And the logic is: if grain is harvested at *sukkot*, it must have reached *shalish* before *rosh hashanah* of the previous year. Thus whatever reached *shalish* before *rosh hashanah* is considered part of the previous year. The criterion of a third is derived by retroactive inference: since grain harvested at *sukkot* is connected to the prior year, and since the *gemara* establishes that this requires having been a third developed before *rosh hashanah*, it follows that reaching a third is the operative moment.

Rabbi Yirmiyah then poses a challenge to Rabbi Zeira: can the rabbis really distinguish between grain that is a third developed and grain that is less than a third? Is such precision achievable — and is it really possible to retroactively conclude from the fact of a *sukkot* harvest that the grain must have been precisely a third developed by *rosh hashanah*?

### Measurement Standards

Rabbi Zeira responds sharply:

> לאו אמינא לך? לא תיפק נפשך לבר מהלכתא. כל מדת חכמים כן הוא.

"Have I not told you — do not take yourself outside the halakhic system. This is how all rabbinic measurements work."

He illustrates with a series of parallel cases: a *mikveh* requires forty *sa'ah* of water — forty *sa'ah* minus a thumbnail (or, as *Tosafot* says, even minus a single drop) is invalid. Food contracts impurity if it is the size of an egg; an egg minus a sesame seed does not. A piece of cloth is susceptible to *midras* impurity if it measures three by three *tefachim*; remove a single thread and it is not. In each case, the threshold is a formalized estimate grounded in a real-world correlation — the forty *sa'ah* corresponds to the volume of water needed to cover a person's body; the egg corresponds to the amount of food that fills the gullet — but the rabbis do not claim scientific precision. They establish an average, formalize it, and it becomes the *halacha*, even if perfect precision in every individual case is unattainable.

The same applies to *shalish*. Based on what can be harvested at *sukkot*, the rabbis established the working criterion that grain harvested then must have been a third developed before *rosh hashanah*. That estimate is then formalized as the rule, and one does the best one can to assess it.

---

## Omer Story & Ownership

### Omer Source Question

Following the discussion of whether the criterion of *shalish* can be practically identified, Rabbi Yirmiyah withdraws his challenge — not because Rabbi Zeira's defense satisfied him, but because separate evidence demonstrates that the rabbis can indeed distinguish between more and less than a third.

That evidence emerges from a question posed by Rav Kahana's colleagues:

> עומר שהקריבו ישראל בכניסתן לארץ מהיכן הקריבו?

When *Bnei Yisrael* entered the land of Israel under Yehoshua, they brought the *omer* offering. Where did the grain for this *omer* come from? They entered the land on the tenth of *Nissan* and brought the *omer* six days later, on the sixteenth. The grain they found growing had been cultivated and was developing before they arrived.

### Non-Jewish Grain Problem

The problem: the Torah specifies regarding the *omer*:

> קצירכם — ולא קציר נכרי.

"Your harvest" — not the harvest of a non-Jew. Grain that was grown under the auspices of non-Jews would not be valid for the *omer*. Yet this is precisely the grain they found upon entry. How could they have used it?

### Omer Verification

Before answering, the *gemara* questions the premise: did they actually bring the *omer* that first year?

> ממאי דאקריבו? דילמא לא אקריבו?

### Eating New Grain

The *gemara* responds: *lo salka daitach*. The verse in Yehoshua states:

> ויאכלו מעבור הארץ ממחרת הפסח מצות וקלוי.

They ate from the produce of the land on the day after *pesach*. The implication of *mimocharat haPesach* — on the morrow of *pesach* — is that prior to that point they had not eaten from the land's grain. What changed on the day after *pesach*? They had brought the *omer*, which is offered on *mimocharat haPesach*, and it was the *omer* that permitted the new grain. The verse thus implies that they did indeed bring the *omer*, and only after doing so did they eat from the new grain.

### Pesach Terminology

This verse raises an interesting side observation. *Tosafot* cites a challenge from Rav Avraham Ibn Ezra — notably one of the very few instances where *Tosafot* quotes this Sephardic authority. The challenge concerns the meaning of *pesach* in the phrase *mimocharat haPesach*. In the Torah, the term *pesach* generally refers to the day on which the *korban pesach* is slaughtered — the fourteenth of *Nissan* — while the holiday itself is called *Chag HaMatzot*. If so, *mimocharat haPesach* would mean the fifteenth of *Nissan* — which is the first day of *yom tov*, not the first day of *chol hamoed*. This would actually support the rabbinic position that the *omer* is brought on the sixteenth — the day after the first day of *yom tov* — rather than the Sadducean interpretation that it is brought on the day after the first *Shabbat* following the holiday. Ibn Ezra notes, however, that the word *pesach* can also refer to the festival itself, and various resolutions are offered.

The *gemara* clearly reads *pesach* as referring to the fifteenth of *Nissan*, making *mimocharat haPesach* the sixteenth, which is the day the *omer* was brought and which then permitted the new grain. Some *rishonim*, including the Rambam, hold that this verse in Yehoshua itself constitutes the strongest proof that the *omer* is brought on the sixteenth — the day after the first day of *yom tov* — since the verse says *mimocharat haPesach*, not *mimocharat hashabbat*. Yet the persuasiveness of this proof depends entirely on how one reads the word *pesach*, which is itself precisely what is in dispute.

### Ownership Criterion

Returning to the main question, the *gemara* asks how, given the prohibition of *ktzirchem velo ktzir nochri*, *Bnei Yisrael* could have used the grain growing in the land for the *omer*. Rav Kahana answers:

> כל שלא הביא שליש ביד נכרי.

The determinative criterion for whether grain is considered Jewish or non-Jewish is *hava'at shalish*. If the grain reached its critical threshold of a third of development while in the possession of a non-Jew, it is identified as non-Jewish grain. If it reached a third under Jewish possession, it is Jewish grain. When *Bnei Yisrael* entered the land, some of the grain had not yet reached a third; they took possession; it reached *shalish* under their auspices; and thus it was valid as Jewish grain, usable for the *omer*.

This demonstrates that *hava'at shalish* functions as the criterion not only for dating produce to a particular year, but also for determining the "ownership identity" of grain — whether it is considered to have grown under Jewish or non-Jewish jurisdiction.

### Discernment Challenge

This answer is cited by Rabbi Yirmiyah as evidence that the rabbis can indeed distinguish between grain that has and has not reached a third. But Rabbi Yirmiyah himself then raises a challenge: how do we know that when *Bnei Yisrael* entered the land they actually had to assess whether the grain had reached *shalish* or not? Perhaps the grain had not sprouted at all by the time of entry, such that it developed entirely from zero to full under Jewish possession, with no assessment of partial development required. In that scenario, the story would not prove that partial development can be gauged.

> ודילמא אתו ולא קים להו — אבל היכא דאתו ריבעא בין שליש לפחות משליש לא קים להו.

Perhaps where grain was a quarter developed — somewhere between a third and nothing — one still could not determine which side of the threshold it had crossed.

### Grain Development Timeli…

The *gemara* immediately rules out the scenario in which no development had occurred at all upon entry:

> דכתיב: ויעלו מן הירדן בעשור לחודש.

They ascended from the Jordan on the tenth of the month. The *omer* was brought on the sixteenth. If the grain had not sprouted at all on the tenth, it could not have grown from zero to fully harvestable in five days.

But the *gemara* presses: suppose it had developed a quarter by entry. The same problem remains — how could it have grown from a quarter to fully harvestable in five days?

The *gemara* offers a resolution:

> ארץ צבי כתיב בה.

The land of Israel is described as *eretz tzvi* — the land of the deer. As Rashi explains:

> מה צבי קל ברגליו מכל החיות אף ארץ ישראל קלה לבשל פירותיה מכל הארצות.

Just as the deer is the swiftest of all creatures, so too the land of Israel ripens its fruit faster than all other lands. This miraculous quality explains how grain could develop from a partial stage to full harvest-readiness in five days.

But the *gemara* notes that this same reasoning cuts against the proof. If one invokes *eretz tzvi* to explain growth from a quarter to full in five days, the very same logic could explain growth from zero to full in five days — in which case the grain may not have been partially developed at entry, and no assessment of *shalish* would have been necessary. The question of whether *Bnei Yisrael* could actually discern the threshold is thus left unresolved.

---

## Sukkot Proof & Chall (II)

### Asif Language Challenge

The *gemara* returns to the core derivation for the criterion of *shalish* — the reading of *Chag HaAsif betzeit hashanah* as referring to the harvest of grain at *sukkot* time. Rabbi Chanina challenges this interpretation:

> מי מצית אמרת דהאי אסיף קציר הוא?

How can you claim that *asif* in this verse means harvesting (*katzir*) rather than gathering? The verse elsewhere states:

> באספך מגרנך ומיקבך.

When you gather in from your granaries and your wine vats. Clearly *asifah* means bringing stored produce inside, not harvesting from the field. Moreover, the master teaches that this very language — *psolet goren v'yekev* — is what the Torah uses to indicate the materials from which *sechach* may be made. One makes the *sukkah*'s covering from the remnants of the granary and wine vat, meaning plant matter that grows from the ground and is not susceptible to *tumah*.

Rashi explains the force of the challenge: if the word *asif* is already being used in the *drasha* of *Sukkot* to teach what *sechach* is made of — the remnants of the *goren* and *yekev* — then the phrase *Chag HaAsif* is simply another name for *Chag HaSukkot*, and it is entirely the festival's designation. There is no surplus in the word *asif* that would allow for the additional derivation that grain harvested at *sukkot* must have been a third developed before *rosh hashanah*. The entire *drasha* that yielded the criterion of *shalish* collapses.

### Proof Destroyed

Rabbi Zeira responds with a measure of dismay:

> האי מילתא הוה בידן, ואתא רבי חנינא שדא בה נרגא.

We had this *drasha* in our hands, and Rabbi Chanina came and threw a hammer into it.

It is worth noting that this exact expression — "we had a good thing and someone came and threw a hammer in it" — occurs very rarely in *Shas*, and with a striking parallel. In tractate *Sukkot*, the *gemara* derives from the same verse of *Chag HaAsif* the rule that *sechach* must be made from the remnants of the granary and wine vat — material that grows from the ground and is not susceptible to *tumah*. There too, Rabbi Chanina raises an objection (perhaps frozen wine could serve as *sechach*), and there too the *gemara* uses this same image of a hammer being thrown. The convergence suggests a deliberate verbal and conceptual connection between the two sugyot, both of which depend on the same verse and encounter the same challenger.

With the *Sukkot* proof demolished, the question reverts: where does the rule of *shalish* for grain actually come from?

---

## Deuteronomy Source

### Three/Third Wordplay

A new source is now proposed from a *braita* in the name of Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef:

> ועשת את התבואה לשלוש השנים.

This is the verse from *Vayikra* in which God promises that the produce of the sixth year will suffice for three years — the sixth year itself, the *shemita* year, and the year following *shemita* while waiting for the new harvest. Rabbi Yonatan derives the rule of *shalish* through a *drasha*:

> אל תקרי לשלוש אלא לשליש.

Do not read *lishlosh* — "for three years" — but rather *lishlish* — "for a third." The verse then teaches: the *tvuah* is considered *asui* — complete, established — once it has reached a third of its development. This is a classic al-tikrei *drasha*, trading on the similar sounds of *lishlosh* and *lishlish*, and it provides the foundation for the rule that grain goes by *hava'at shalish*.

### Redundancy Question

The *gemara* objects: we need this verse for its straightforward meaning — *p'shat* — which is that God promises an abundance of produce to sustain the Jewish people through the *shemita* and *yovel* years. If the verse is consumed by this *drasha*, how does its literal promise get conveyed?

### Completion Concept

The *gemara* answers: *ksiv kra achrina* — the literal content is already taught by a different verse:

> וזרעתם את השנה השמינית ואכלתם מן התבואה ישן עד השנה התשיעית.

You will plant in the eighth year and eat from the old produce until the ninth year. The blessing of abundance — that the sixth year's produce sustains through the *shemita* and into the year of the new harvest — is thus already taught by this verse. The verse *ve'asas et hatevuah lishlosh hashanim* is therefore available for the *drasha* of *lishlish*, teaching that once grain has reached a third of its development it is considered complete and is determined by the year in which that threshold was crossed.

---

## Kitniyot Takeover

### Legume Categories

The *mishna* teaches:

> האורז והדוחן והפרגין והשומשמין שהשרישו לפני ראש השנה — מותרין בשביעית, ומתעשרין לשנה שעברה; ואם לאו — אסורין בשביעית, ומתעשרין לשנה הבאה.

Rice (*orez*), millet (*dochan*), poppy (*pargin*), and sesame (*shumshamin*) — if they took root (*hishrishu*) before *rosh hashanah*, they are permitted in the *shemita* year and are tithed according to the previous year. If not, they are subject to the restrictions of *shemita* produce and tithed according to the following year.

The operative criterion for these *kitniyot* is thus *hashrashah* — taking root — rather than *lekita* (picking), *hava'at shalish* (a third developed), or *chanata* (blossoming). This is immediately puzzling. All other criteria correspond to meaningful stages of maturation. *Hashrashah* is the very beginning of growth — the plant has barely begun to exist. Why should this earliest of stages be determinative?

### Moment Summary

Rava provides a useful summary of the landscape:

> אמרו רבנן: אילן — בתר חנטה; תבואה וזיתים — בתר שליש; ירק — בתר לקיטה.

Trees go by *chanata* (blossoming); grain and olives go by *shalish* (a third developed); vegetables go by *lekita* (picking). Into which of these categories do *kitniyot* fall?

### Vegetable Logic

Rava answers his own question. Logically, legumes most resemble vegetables — certainly rice and sesame do not seem like fruit trees, and while their kernel-like seeds might suggest grain, the intuitive categorization, as Rashi frames it, is with *yerek*. If *kitniyot* are like vegetables, the determinative moment should be *lekita* — picking.

### Convenience Logic

But there is a problem with applying *lekita* to *kitniyot*. As Rava explains:

> מתוך שעשויין פרחין פרחין — עשו רבנן בתר השרשה.

*Kitniyot* are picked on an ongoing, continuous basis — the pods are harvested repeatedly over an extended season. Rashi explains that *prachin prachin* refers to cracking open the pods continuously over time. Because of this pattern of ongoing, spread-out picking, any given batch of legumes will contain a mixture of produce picked before and after *rosh hashanah*. If the criterion were *lekita*, determining which year's produce one is dealing with at any given moment would be perpetually confused.

The solution the rabbis adopted was *hashrashah* — taking root. Even though the legumes are harvested over a long period, the planting — and therefore the rooting — happens all at once, at the beginning of the season. By pegging the determining moment to *hashrashah*, one has a single unambiguous point in time that applies to all the legumes in a given planting, regardless of when they are individually harvested.

There is a further question that Rashi's analysis raises: why should convenience drive the legal rule? Shouldn't the halacha follow an intrinsic stage of development rather than what is administratively tidy? The answer is that *kitniyot* in this context is entirely rabbinic in nature. Since the underlying obligation is rabbinic, the rabbis have latitude to structure the rule in whatever way is most workable — and they chose *hashrashah* precisely because it provides a clean, unified moment.

Regarding vegetables (*yerek*), the logic of *lekita* is that vegetables grow continuously, always getting larger and ripening further. At any given moment, the vegetable is connected to the current period of growth. It is not, so to speak, "from" an earlier year in the way that a tree's fruit, once it has blossomed, is locked into its year. The vegetable's identity at any moment reflects its most recent period of growth, and thus the moment of picking determines its year.

### Mixing Solution
