Abaye challenges Rava's rationale. The concern about a mixture of pre- and post-*rosh hashanah* produce is real, but why is *hashrashah* the only solution? Why not simply follow the mixing procedure described elsewhere?

> ויצבור גורנו לתוכו.

Pile the threshing floor together — take all the harvested legumes, pile them together, and separate *terumot u'ma'asrot* from the entire mass. If the old and new produce are thoroughly mixed in the pile, any ten units one designates as *maaser* will contain a proportional representation of old and new. If 40% of the pile is old and 60% new, then the designated *maaser* will consist of four parts old and six parts new, which then serves as *maaser* for the respective portions — old for old, new for new — without any confusion.

This solution does not address every complication — if the two years carry different *halachot* (one being *maaser sheni* and another *maaser ani*, or one being *shemita*), the mixing trick does not resolve the substantive discrepancy. But as a method of avoiding confusion over old-and-new mixing, it seems functional.

### Equal Distribution

A *braita* in the name of Rabbi Yosi ben Kipar citing Rabbi Shimon Shezuri provides a case in point: Egyptian fava beans (*pol hamitzri*) planted for their seeds (in which case they go by *hashrashah*) — some of which took root before *rosh hashanah* and some after. The *braita* states that one may not take *terumot u'ma'asrot* from one batch on behalf of the other, since one may not tithe from new produce on behalf of old or vice versa. Yet the solution offered is precisely what Abaye proposed:

> צוברו גורנו לתוכו — ונמצא תורם ומעשר מן החדש שבו על החדש שבו ומן הישן שבו על הישן שבו.

Pile the threshing floor together and the *maaser* one takes will automatically represent an equal distribution — the old-produce portion of the *maaser* covers the old produce and the new portion covers the new.

### Distribution Dispute

Rava responds to Abaye's challenge:

> רבי שמעון שזורי גמרת? רבי שמעון שזורי סבר יש בילה; רבנן סברי אין בילה.

The *braita* follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, who holds *yesh bilah* — that solid matter genuinely mixes such that any sample drawn from the pile will reflect an equal distribution. The rabbis, however, hold *ein bilah* — that solids do not truly mix in this way, and there is no guarantee of equal distribution. Since the general rabbinic position is *ein bilah*, the mixing trick cannot be relied upon, and *lekita* as the criterion for *kitniyot* would produce an intractable mixture problem. It is for this reason that the rabbis established *hashrashah* as the determinative moment.

### Halachic Ruling

Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports in the name of Shmuel:

> הלכה כרבי יוסי בן כיפר שאמר משום רבי שמעון שזורי.

The *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri. The mixing procedure is valid, and one may rely on equal distribution.

### Shmuel Contradiction

This ruling immediately creates a difficulty. If Shmuel holds that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's position of *yesh bilah*, then we have an apparent contradiction with a different statement of Shmuel's:

> לכל אין בילה חוץ מיין ושמן.

For all substances, there is no *bilah* — no equal mixing — with the exception of wine with wine and oil with oil. Only liquids mix equally; solids do not. This directly contradicts the attribution of *yesh bilah* to Shmuel.

### Finish Time Standard

The resolution, which the *gemara* introduces here and will elaborate in the following amud, is that Shmuel does indeed hold *ein bilah* for solids. The statement that he rules like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri must be understood differently. There is a third principle of Shmuel's that mediates:

> הכל הולך אחר גמר פרי.

Everything goes by when the fruit finishes developing — *gmar pri*.

Shmuel does not actually hold that *kitniyot* go by *hashrashah*. Rather, he holds that they go by *gmar pri* — when growth is complete. Under this view, if one has beans that rooted before *rosh hashanah* and beans that rooted after *rosh hashanah*, the mixing trick works not because of *yesh bilah* but because there is no mixture in the first place. All the beans — regardless of when they took root — finish developing in the following year. They therefore all belong to the same year, and there is nothing to mix. Shmuel's endorsement of the *braita*'s solution is not an endorsement of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's *yesh bilah* position; it is an endorsement of the outcome, arrived at by an entirely different route.

This makes for a subtle and somewhat counterintuitive result: Shmuel is cited as ruling like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, but he does not actually agree with Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's reasoning. He agrees with the practical conclusion in the *braita*'s case while rejecting the theoretical foundation. The *gemara* will return to clarify this further on the following amud.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 14

## Shliach & Kavanah

### Get Delivery Requirements

We learned in *Masechet Gittin* that if a man sends a *get* through a *shliach*, the *shliach* must declare *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam* — that the *get* was written and signed in his presence. This declaration ensures the *get* is valid. The *gemara* explains the reasons behind this requirement: whether the concern is to confirm the authenticity of the signatures, or to ensure that the writing of the *get* was performed *lishmah*, for the sake of the specific woman. This illustrates a vital *yesod* in *halacha* regarding the trust we place in a *shliach*.

### Intent in Mitzvot

This discussion leads to a broader principle: whenever we perform a *mitzvah*, we must ensure it is done with the proper *kavanah*. Even though we are in *galus*, our *avodah* is to refine ourselves and the world around us until we merit the *geulah* with the coming of *Mashiach*, *bimeherah beyameinu*, *amen*.

---

## Ice & Snow on Shabbat

### Melting Ice

If one simply leaves ice in a cup and allows it to melt on its own, there is no problem of *molid*, because no active *ma'aseh* is being performed — it happens *mimeila*, on its own. Accordingly, one may place ice in a drink, but one may not crush it. The *Mishnah Berurah* clarifies in *seif katan* 35 that the liquid resulting from the ice is *misbatel* into the water already present in the cup.

### Snow on Garments

The *Shulchan Aruch* discusses in *siman* 320, *seif* 10 what is to be done when snow lands on one's clothes. The *Mechaber* rules: *hayah sheleg al begadav menaran* — if there is snow on his garments, he may shake them off. The reasoning is that snow is not *nivla*, not absorbed into the fabric, and therefore there is no *issur* of *melaben*. However, the *Rema* notes that one should be *machmir* if there is no great *tzorech*.

### Walking on Snow

Walking on snow is *muttar*. The *gemara* explains that since the crushing of snow underfoot is incidental to the normal act of walking, it does not constitute the *melacha* of *risuk*. It is simply the ordinary *derech* of movement, and is therefore permitted on *Shabbos*.

---

## Terumah & Mishkan

### Terumah Definition

In this week's *parsha*, *Parshat Terumah*, we find the first instruction for building the *Mishkan*. The *Torah* says: *vayikchu li terumah me'eis kol ish asher yidvenu libo tikchu es terumasi* — take for Me an offering from every man whose heart motivates him; you shall take My offering. The word *terumah*, usually translated as contribution or offering, derives from the root *rom*, meaning to lift up. When a person gives with a full heart, he is not merely giving an object — he is elevating himself and the object along with him. The *Ramban* explains that the central purpose of the *Mishkan* was to be a place where the *Shechinah*, the Divine Presence, could rest among *Bnei Yisrael*. And how is that achieved? Through *asher yidvenu libo* — through the willingness of the heart.

### Keruvim & Shechinah

Later in the *parsha*, when describing the *keruvim* atop the *aron*, the *Torah* states that their faces were *ish el achiv*, one toward the other. *Rashi* notes that this was the case when *Bnei Yisrael* were doing the will of *Hashem*. When they were not, the *keruvim* turned away. Everything depends on the heart. When there is true *nedivus lev* — a genuine generosity of spirit — the physical structure becomes a home for the *Shechinah*. May we all merit to give from the heart and thereby create a place for *Hashem* in our lives.

---

## Traits & Yetzarim

### Teshuva Process

This is the path of perfect *teshuva*: to take every part of one's personality and bring it back to its source, back to *HaKadosh Baruch Hu*.

### Holy Boldness

Similarly with the trait of *azut*, boldness — a person should not be impudent toward other people, but he should possess *azut d'kedushah*, holy boldness, to stand up for truth and not be embarrassed before those who mock him in his service of *Hashem*.

### Divine Roots of Traits

Every trait, even those that appear negative on the surface, has a root in the divine. The work of a person is to elevate these traits and employ them according to the will of the *Borei*, the Creator. This is what it means to serve *Hashem* with both of one's *yetzarim* — both the *yetzer hatov* and the *yetzer hara*. When we take the energy of the *yetzer hara* and channel it into our passion for *Torah* and *mitzvos*, we are performing the highest level of *avodah*.

### Strong Drives & Mussar

This is why the holy *sefarim* teach that a person who has a very strong *yetzer* — a powerful internal drive — has the potential to reach far higher levels than someone who is naturally quiet and passive. The more fire a person carries within, the more he can ignite his soul to burn with a love for *Elokus*, for Godliness. But if he fails to work on his *middos*, that same fire will consume him in negative desires and anger. Therefore, the study of *mussar* and the refinement of character is the foundation of everything. Without it, even our holy actions can be tainted by ego. May we all merit to find the path of balance and to use every part of ourselves to bring *giluy Shechinah* — the revelation of the Divine Presence — into this world.

---

## Trumas Halishkah

### Preventing Suspicion

We can extend this concept to other areas of life as well. The *Mishnah* in *Masechet Shekalim*, chapter 3, *Mishnah* 2, discusses the process of *trumas halishkah* — the taking of money from the chamber of the *Beis HaMikdash* in order to purchase the *korbanos tzibbur*, the communal sacrifices. The *Mishnah* states that the person who entered to withdraw the coins was forbidden to wear a garment with sleeves that could conceal money, and was not permitted to wear shoes, sandals, *tefillin*, or a *kameia*, an amulet — because if he were to become wealthy afterward, people might suspect that he had secreted money from the *lishkah* in his clothing or footwear. The *Mishnah* concludes with the principle: *lefi she'adam tzarich latzeis yedei habriyos k'derech shetzarich latzeis yedei HaMakom* — because a person must satisfy the requirements of his fellow human beings just as he must satisfy the requirements of the Omnipresent.

### V'Heyitem Nekiyim

This is based on the *pasuk*: *v'heyitem nekiyim me'Hashem u'mi'Yisrael* — you shall be clean before *Hashem* and before Israel. A fundamental principle emerges from here: it is not sufficient for a person to know in his own heart that he is acting honestly. It is not enough to say, "I know I am honest, *Hashem* knows I am honest, and I do not care what people think." Of course, when it comes to performing *mitzvos*, one should not be swayed by those who mock him — as the *Rema* rules in the very first *siman* of the *Shulchan Aruch*: *v'lo yisbayesh mipnei bnei adam hamal'igim alav*, a person should not be embarrassed before those who mock him for his service of *Hashem*. However, when it comes to matters of integrity — to money and honesty — we bear a responsibility to be above suspicion, and to conduct ourselves in such a way that even someone seeking to find fault will be unable to do so.

---

## Trumas Halishkah (II)

### Kiddush/Chillul Hashem

This standard applies to anyone who holds a public position, to anyone who handles money belonging to others — whether a *gabbai tzedakah*, a treasurer of a *shul* or communal organization, or a person in business. Everything must be transparent, with no room for misunderstanding. This is part of the concept of *kiddush Hashem*: when people observe a *shomer Torah u'mitzvos* acting with the highest levels of integrity and scrupulously avoiding even the appearance of impropriety, great *kavod* is brought to *Hashem* and to the *Torah*. Conversely, if a person acts carelessly and invites suspicion — even if he is in fact innocent — this can lead to *chillul Hashem*, a desecration of the Name of Heaven. We must therefore keep this principle ever before our eyes: *v'heyitem nekiyim me'Hashem u'mi'Yisrael* — always striving to be clean and pure both in our relationship with *Hashem* and in our relationship with our fellow human beings.

---

## Shema Timing

### Kohanim & Shema Time

The *Mishnah* at the opening of *Masechet Berachot* asks: *me'eimatai korin et shema be'arvit* — from what time do we recite the *shema* in the evening? The answer given is: *mishe'ah shehakohanim nichnasim le'echol bitrumatan* — from the time that the *kohanim* enter to eat their *terumah*.

### Tana's Foundation

The *gemara* there raises a question: *tana heicha ka'i dekatani me'eimatai* — where did the *tana* stand before this that he is now asking "from when"? The *gemara* answers that he is proceeding from the *pasuk* of *beshachbecha uv'kumecha* — the *Torah* instructs us to recite *shema* when we lie down and when we rise. The *Mishnah* therefore asks, "from when" is the time of lying down? This is the fundamental starting point of *Shas*, of the entire *Talmud Bavli* — beginning with the precise timing of a *mitzvah*.

---

## Nishmat Prayer

### Nishmat Segulah

*Nishmat kol chai* carries this same light and the same power. The text of *Nishmat* is composed of language that can be found within *Birchat HaMazon*, and it is for this reason that many *Chasidishe sefarim* teach that the recitation of *Nishmat* is a *segulah* for *parnassah*. Just as *Birchat HaMazon* is a blessing for physical sustenance, *Nishmat* is a blessing for the soul — and in saying it, we tap into that same flow of abundance.

### Birchat HaShir

The *Nishmat* prayer is called the *Birchat HaShir*, the blessing of song, and it is the ultimate expression of gratitude. It reminds us that every breath is a gift from the Almighty — *kol haneshama tehallel Yah*, every soul shall praise God. When we say *Nishmat kol chai*, we acknowledge that our very life force comes from Him. The connection between *Nishmat* and *Birchat HaMazon* reveals that our physical needs and our spiritual essence are one — they must not be separated, for everything flows from the same source. May we always merit to say these words with a full heart and to recognize the miracles that surround us each and every day.

---

## Slave Sales

### Slave Freedom

We are in *Masechet Gittin*, 44a. The *Mishnah* teaches: *hamocher avdo la'akum yatza lecheirut* — if a person sells his slave to a non-Jew, the slave goes free. This is a *knas*, a penalty, that the *Chachamim* imposed upon the owner because he has caused the slave to lose his ability to perform *mitzvos*.

### Akiva's Position

The *gemara* raises the question of what the *din* is if the slave is sold only for a limited period — for example, for thirty days. The *gemara* cites a *machloket* between *Rebbi Akiva* and the *Chachamim*. *Rebbi Akiva* holds that even if the slave is sold for a single day, *yatza lecheirut* — he goes free — because the owner has already caused him to forfeit *mitzvos*. Furthermore, the *gemara* makes clear that the owner cannot simply reclaim the slave; the *beis din* compels the owner to repurchase him from the non-Jew, even at a high price, after which the slave goes free. This mechanism ensures that owners are dissuaded from ever placing a slave in the hands of someone who will cause him to cease observing *Torah u'mitzvos*.

### Manumission Document

*Amar Abaye* — and this ruling is corroborated by a *baraita* in accordance with *Abaye*'s position: *hamocher avdo l'oved kochavim yatza lecheirut v'tzarich lichtov lo get shichrur umacharav* — if a person sells his slave to a non-Jew, he goes free, and the master is required to write him a bill of manumission. *Amar Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*: *bameh devarim amurim?* When does this apply? *Shelo katav alav ono* — when he did not write a formal bill of sale for the slave. *Aval katav alav ono, zeh hu shichruro* — but if he did write a bill of sale, that document itself constitutes the slave's manumission.

### Terumah Disqualification

The *Mishnah* further states: *hamocher avdo l'oved kochavim poslo meloechol b'terumah* — one who sells his slave to a non-Jew thereby disqualifies the slave from eating *terumah*. Even if the slave technically retains his status as a slave and would otherwise be eligible to eat *terumah* as a member of a *kohen*'s household, once he has been sold to a non-Jew he is disqualified. *Ve'im hayah rabbo kohen, ma'achilo b'terumah* — if his master was a *kohen* and previously fed him *terumah*, he may no longer do so.

### Rebbi Yosei's Case

*Amar Rebbi Yosei*: in this case — *lo amru yatza lecheirut* — they did not say he goes free, *ela sheyichtov lo rabbo shichrur veyomar lo harei atah ben chorin* — unless his master writes him a formal manumission and declares to him: you are hereby a free person.

---

## Damages & Tikkun

### Land Quality Hierarchy

With *hadran alach hamocher avdo*, we complete the fourth *perek* of *Masechet Gittin* and begin *Perek* 5, *Perek Hanizakin*. The *Mishnah* opens: *shamin lahem b'idit* — when assessing payment for damages, collection is made from the best quality land; *uva'al chov b'veinonit* — a creditor collects from medium quality land; *uchtuvas ishah b'ziburis* — and a woman's *ketubah* is collected from the poorest quality land.

### Rebbi Meir Ketubah

*Rebbi Meir* disagrees with this last ruling and holds: *af chtuvas ishah b'veinonit* — even a woman's *ketubah* is collected from medium quality land.

### Free Property Priority

The *Mishnah* then enumerates several laws instituted *mipnei tikkun ha'olam*, for the betterment of the world. Among them: *ein nifrahin minechasim meshubadim bimkom sheyesh nechasim b'nei chorin* — we do not collect from sold, encumbered property when free property exists, *ve'afillu hen ziburis* — even if the free properties are of the poorest quality. Thus, if a debtor sold his best land but retained poor-quality land, the creditor must collect from the free poor-quality land rather than pursue the *lokeach*, the purchaser of the encumbered property.

The *gemara* asks for the reasoning behind this rule. The answer is *mipnei tikkun ha'olam*: if buyers knew their purchased property could be seized even when the seller retained other assets, no one would be willing to purchase land. Commercial stability requires that purchasers enjoy security in their acquisitions. Therefore, as long as *b'nei chorin* — free property — remains available, the creditor must proceed there first.

### Orphan Protection

The *Mishnah* further states: *ein nifrahin minechasei yetomim ela min haziburis* — we do not collect from orphans' property except from the poorest quality land.

### Tikkun Rationale

The *gemara* seeks the reason for this special treatment of orphans. *Amar Rebbi Yochanan*: *mishum china* — for the sake of grace, meaning that we wish to encourage people to lend money to orphans and to engage in transactions with them, while simultaneously protecting the orphans' interests so that they do not lose their finest assets. An additional reason given is that orphans are not privy to the business dealings their father may have entered into, and they are therefore extended the benefit of the doubt, with collection limited to the poorest quality land. All of this falls under the overarching principle of *tikkun ha'olam*.

---

## Mah Nishtanah

### Four Questions

Why is this night different from all other nights? *Shebechol haleilos anu ochlin chometz umatzah halaila hazeh kulo matzah* — on all other nights we eat *chometz* and *matzah*; on this night only *matzah*. *Shebechol haleilos anu ochlin shear yerakos halaila hazeh maror* — on all other nights we eat other vegetables; on this night *maror*. *Shebechol haleilos anu ochlin basar tzali shaluk umvushal halaila hazeh kulo tzali* — on all other nights we eat meat roasted, boiled, or cooked; on this night only roasted. *Shebechol haleilos anu matbilin paam achas halaila hazeh shtei peamim* — on all other nights we dip once; on this night twice.

### Reclining

*Shebechol haleilos anu ochlin bein yoshvin uvein msubin halaila hazeh kulanu msubin* — on all other nights we eat either sitting or reclining; on this night we all recline. Reclining is the symbol of freedom and royalty.

### Rambam Version

The *Rambam* notes that the version of *mah nishtanah* differs slightly depending on whether it is recited *bizman habayis* or *bazman hazeh*. The question regarding roasted meat, for instance, was asked only *bizman habayis*, when the *korban Pesach* was offered. These distinctions reflect the different realities of the *seder* across the two eras.

---

## Haggadah Narrative

### Story Elaboration

After the questions are posed, the father responds: "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt," and he proceeds to narrate the entire *Haggadah*. Anyone who elaborates further on the story of what happened to *Bnei Yisrael* in Egypt is considered praiseworthy. Moreover, in every generation a person is obligated to see himself as though he himself had just gone out from the slavery of Egypt.

### Symbolic Foods

One then recites the sections explaining the significance of the *Pesach*, the *matzah*, and the *maror*. The *Pesach* represents the Almighty's passing over the houses of our ancestors in Egypt. The *maror* recalls that the Egyptians embittered the lives of our ancestors. The *matzah* commemorates the redemption. We are therefore obligated to thank, to praise, to glorify, and to extol the One who performed all these miracles for our ancestors and for us.

### Hallel & Second Cup

One then begins *Hallel*, reciting through the end of the second chapter, concluding with the words *chalamish l'maino mayim*. He then recites the *beracha* of *asher ge'alanu* — "Who has redeemed us and redeemed our ancestors from Egypt" — and concludes "Blessed are You *Hashem*, *ga'al Yisrael*, Who has redeemed Israel." He then drinks the second cup while reclining on his left side.

---

## Seder Meal Order

### Hamotzi & Brachot

*Halacha* 2: After the second cup, one recites the *beracha* of *hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz* over the whole *matzah*, and then recites *al achilas matzah* over the broken piece.

### Matzah & Maror

One then takes a *kezayit* from the whole *matzah* and a *kezayit* from the broken piece and eats them together. He subsequently recites *al achilas maror*, dips the *maror* in *charoses*, and eats it — being careful not to leave the *maror* in the *charoses* for too long, lest the taste of the *maror* be nullified. He then wraps *matzah* and *maror* together, dips them in *charoses*, and eats them without an additional *beracha*.

### Afikoman

*Halacha* 3: He then eats his meal, eating and drinking as he wishes. At the conclusion of the meal he eats of the meat of the *Pesach* — at least a *kezayit* — and eats nothing after it. *Bazman hazeh*, in our times, he eats a *kezayit* of *matzah* at the meal's end and eats nothing afterward, so that the taste of the *matzah* — or, in Temple times, the taste of the *Pesach* — lingers in his mouth.

### Brachot & Cups

*Halacha* 4: He then recites *Birchat HaMazon* on the third cup and drinks it. They pour the fourth cup, he completes *Hallel* and recites *Birchat HaShir*, which is the *beracha* of *yehalelucha Hashem Elokeinu*. He then recites the *beracha* on the fourth cup and drinks nothing afterward.

---

## Limud & Kinyan

### Learning Modes

Returning to the *beis hamedrash* — to finding one's *limud*, one's *seder*, and one's proper place within the world of Torah study — whether one is learning an *amud* of *gemara* per day, a *daf*, or studying *b'iyun*, the essential goal remains the same: to make a *kinyan*.

### Kinyan Concept

When we think about what a *kinyan* means — *shtar*, *kessef*, and all the formal modes of acquisition — the most important dimension is that one truly owns the material, that one genuinely understands it. This means having a *biyur* on every single word one says, truly internalizing and possessing what one has learned.

---

## Chatzot Timing

### Moshe's Caution

*David HaMelech* would say: *ani me'orer hashachar ve'ein hashachar me'orer osi* — I awaken the dawn, and the dawn does not awaken me. The *gemara* asks: what was the difference between *Moshe Rabbeinu* and *David HaMelech*? Why did *Moshe Rabbeinu* say *kechatzos* — "approximately midnight" — whereas *David HaMelech* knew the precise moment of *chatzos*? The *gemara* answers that *Moshe Rabbeinu* in fact knew exactly when *chatzos* was. He said *kechatzos* because he was concerned that the *itztagninei Paroh*, the astrologers of *Paroh*, might miscalculate the moment and then declare that *Moshe* was a *badai* — a liar.

### David's Kinnor

*David HaMelech*, by contrast, possessed the *kinnor*. The *kinnor* informed him of the exact moment of *chatzos*.

### Torah Learning

With that precise knowledge, *David HaMelech* was able to rise at exactly *chatzos* and engage in *Torah* learning until the break of morning.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 15

## Overview & Framework

### First Mishna Scope

With today's daf, we complete the first *mishna* of Masechet Rosh Hashanah. It is worth pausing to appreciate the structural peculiarity: the entire *masechet* spans approximately 34 *daf*, and the very first *mishna* occupies roughly half of it. The remaining *mishnayot*, which will feel somewhat more immediately relevant, begin only now.

The subject matter of this first *mishna* has been the rules governing the new year for *terumot uma'asrot* and *shvi'it*, and the distinctions that apply to different categories of produce.

### Produce Categories

The *mishna* establishes the following framework. Grains and olives are determined by *shalish* — reaching one-third of their growth. Fruit trees are determined by *chanatah* — blossoming. Vegetables are determined by *lakitah* — picking. Legumes are determined by *hashrashah* — the moment of taking root.

A clarification is worth noting here regarding the vegetable rule. *Tosfot* points out that the significance of picking by vegetables is effectively equivalent to *g'mar peri* — the moment the fruit finishes developing — since picking follows almost immediately upon that completion. There is similarly one opinion for legumes that also locates the determining moment at *g'mar peri*. *Tosfot* appears to mean this seriously: if one could construct a scenario in which *g'mar peri* occurred in one year and picking in the following year, *Tosfot* would have us go by *g'mar peri* for vegetables, not by *lakitah* — even though all the available evidence speaks only in terms of "picked before Rosh Hashanah" or "picked after Rosh Hashanah." *Tosfot* is attempting to resolve other difficulties by recasting the rule in terms of *g'mar peri*.

### Etrog Hybridity

The particular focus of the *gemara* at this stage has been the *etrog*, which presents a uniquely hybrid character. Because the *etrog* continues to grow throughout the year and continuously benefits from rainfall at all times, it is treated in certain respects like a vegetable. Specifically, when it comes to *terumot uma'asrot*, the year is determined by when the *etrog* is picked — following the vegetable rule. However, for *orlah* and *shemitah*, it follows the tree rule and goes by *chanatah* — blossoming.

What makes this particularly striking is the following: even though for *ma'aser* purposes the *etrog* is treated like a vegetable and goes by when it is picked, the calendar marker that is used is *tu b'shvat* — not the first of *tishrei*. The story of *Rabbi Akiva* who picked an *etrog* after *echad b'shvat* and before *tu b'shvat* and followed the practice of *Beit Hillel* while *Beit Shammai* played it safe illustrates precisely this hybrid structure. We treat the *etrog* like a vegetable for purposes of determining *ma'aser* by picking, yet the date we consult is the *shvat* date appropriate to trees. The *etrog* is, in every sense, a legal hybrid.

---

## Etrog Dual Status

### Rabba's Statement

The *gemara* at the bottom of 14b begins with a statement by Rabba bar Rav Huna. His initial formulation reads: *amar Rabba bar Rav Huna hashta d'amar Rabban Gamliel etrog achar lakitah* — now that *Rabban Gamliel* says the *etrog* follows picking, *issuro k'yerek* — its prohibition is like a vegetable, and therefore *Rosh Hashanah shelo tishrei* — its Rosh Hashanah should be *tishrei*, like a genuine vegetable.

This was a debate between *Rabban Gamliel* and *Rabbi Eliezer*. *Rabbi Eliezer* held that the *etrog* follows tree rules in all respects, while *Rabban Gamliel* ruled that for *ma'asrot* it follows the vegetable rule and goes by picking. Rabba bar Rav Huna's initial statement attempted to be consistent with *Rabban Gamliel*: if we go by picking, we should also go by *tishrei* as the Rosh Hashanah. The *gemara* challenges this from a *braita*.

### Braitta Evidence

The *gemara* challenges with a *braita*: *Rabbi Shimon Elazar* rules that if one picked an *etrog* on the eve of *tu b'shvat* before the sun had set, and then went back and picked again after the sun had set, one may not take *terumah* and *ma'asrot* from one batch on behalf of the other. The implication is clear: picking is the operative factor, and *tu b'shvat* is the determining date — both simultaneously. The *braita* thus establishes explicitly that the *etrog* is a hybrid: it goes by picking in the manner of a vegetable, yet uses *shvat* as the calendar marker in the manner of a tree.

The *gemara* therefore revises Rabba bar Rav Huna's statement: *af al gav d'amar Rabban Gamliel etrog achar lekita k'yerek, Rosh Hashanah shelo Shevat* — even though *Rabban Gamliel* says the *etrog* follows picking like a vegetable, its Rosh Hashanah is nevertheless *shvat*. The revised formulation acknowledges the hybrid, rather than attempting to iron it out.

### Tu B'Shevat Impact

The practical stakes of this hybrid status become clear when the *shemitah* cycle causes a change in the *type* of *ma'aser* being taken — not merely whether produce belongs to the old or new year. Consider the third year of the *shemitah* cycle entering the fourth: in the third year, one takes *ma'aser ani*, while in the fourth year, one takes *ma'aser sheni*. For an *etrog* picked before *tu b'shvat*, even if picked four months after *rosh hashanah* of *tishrei*, the operative calendar marker is *tu b'shvat*. The type of *ma'aser* taken will accordingly reflect the prior year's status.

By contrast, for other fruit trees, the *chanatah* is what counts. A peach, for instance, that blossoms before *tu b'shvat* and is picked late in year four — when the *shemitah* cycle calls for *ma'aser sheni* — will nonetheless require *ma'aser ani*, because the blossoming occurred before *tu b'shvat* in a *ma'aser ani* year. Picking has no effect by ordinary fruit. The *etrog* at least has the advantage that its status is determined closer in time to when one is actually ready to eat it, but even so, the *tu b'shvat* date can still assign it to a different year than the one in which it is actually being consumed.

### Etrog Diagram

To make this concrete, consider the *shemitah* cycle as follows: *shemitah* precedes year one, followed by year two, three, and four. In year two and year four, *ma'aser sheni* is taken; in year three, *ma'aser ani* is taken. The *tu b'shvat* that falls partway through year three — approximately one-third into it — is the dividing line for the *etrog*. An *etrog* picked before that *tu b'shvat*, even though it has been four months since *rosh hashanah* of *tishrei* and the world around it is operating under year-three *ma'asrot* rules, is still assigned to year two and thus requires *ma'aser sheni*. Only after *tu b'shvat* does the *etrog* cross over into year three and become subject to *ma'aser ani*.

The *gemara* also explains why the example of the *etrog* is drawn from the third year entering the fourth — rather than the more standard example of the second year entering the third that is used for other produce. The incidental teaching embedded in this choice is that the *etrog* tree is particularly delicate — *kashi lei yada* — and is easily damaged by handling. During *shemitah*, when the orchard is *hefker* and everyone is freely picking, the tree sustains damage and will take until well into the third year after *shemitah* to begin producing fruit again. Consequently, for the *etrog*, there simply is no fruit to be picking in a scenario of the second year entering the third; the first realistic opportunity for a harvest following *shemitah* is the third year entering the fourth. Hence the *gemara* uses that case as its example. This is not necessarily to say that every *etrog* tree in *Eretz Yisrael* suffers this fate every *shemitah* cycle — it may be that many trees recover sooner — but it reflects a common enough pattern, particularly given how the *etrog*'s soft fruit is especially vulnerable to the rough handling of open public access.

The *etrog* is singled out for vegetable-like status precisely because its fruit remains on the tree continuously from year to year, always benefiting from ongoing rainfall, unlike ordinary fruit that blossoms, grows, and must be picked within a fixed season.

---

## Months vs. Seasons

### Calendar Date Question

The *gemara* records that *Rav Yochanan* posed a question to *Rabbi Yannai*: *esrog rosh hashanah shelo eimasai* — when is the Rosh Hashanah of the *etrog*? Given the hybrid status of the *etrog* and the argument that it might consistently follow the vegetable rule with *tishrei* as its Rosh Hashanah, this was a genuine question. *Rabbi Yannai* answered simply: *shvat*.

*Rav Yochanan* then pressed further: *shvat dechodashim o shvat detkufah* — do we mean the calendar month of *shvat*, or *shvat* as a seasonal marker? The seasons of the year are each associated with a *tkufah*: *tkufas tishrei* is autumn, *tkufas teves* is winter, *tkufas nissan* is spring, and *tkufas tammuz* is summer. *Tkufas shvat*, as *Rashi* explains, means one month into winter — reckoned by the solar calendar. Since the lunar and solar years periodically diverge, the question arises whether we should track the calendar month called *shvat* or whether we should track the seasonal moment that the month of *shvat* was originally meant to represent.

One might ask why this question was not raised more broadly about every instance in which the *mishna* specifies a date — *rosh chodesh tishrei* for grain, *tu b'shvat* for trees, and so on. The suggestion is that the question was specifically directed at the *etrog* because the *etrog*'s status is already so tailored and anomalous that one might expect its date to be calibrated differently as well — perhaps seasonally rather than calendrically.

### Calendar Month Resolution

*Rabbi Yannai* responded: *dechodashim* — we go by the calendar month. *Tosfot* notes that this question could equally have been raised with respect to the first of *shvat* in the *mishna*, even independently of the *etrog*, since the same tension between calendar month and astronomical season applies throughout. The conclusion, however, is unambiguous: the calendar date governs.

### Leap Year Question

The *gemara* records a further query: *Rava* asked *Rav Nachman* — and some attribute the question to *Rav Yochanan* asking *Rabbi Yannai* — *haysa shanah m'uberess mahu*: if the year is a leap year, what is the law? In a leap year an extra month is intercalated, which shifts the relationship between the calendar and the seasons. One might think that *tu b'shvat*, being in some sense sensitive to seasonal conditions, should shift accordingly — that in a leap year the marker for the *etrog*'s *ma'aser* year should move. The response is *halach achar rov shanim* — we follow the majority of ordinary years and do not adjust for the leap year. The calendar date remains constant. This is, in a sense, internally consistent: if one wants to be sensitive to seasonal considerations, the very purpose of intercalating a leap year is to bring the lunar calendar back into alignment with the seasons — so the calendar date already reflects the seasonal adjustment. And if one simply wants to follow the calendar, then the date does not shift. Either way, *tu b'shvat* remains *tu b'shvat*.

---

## Rava's Scenarios

### Sixth→Seventh

*Rava* presents two cases involving the *etrog* and the *shemitah* cycle. The first: *esrog bat shishis shenichnesah l'shevi'is* — an *etrog* that blossomed in the sixth year and was picked in the seventh year. *Rava* rules: *peturah min hama'aser upeturah min habiur* — it is exempt from *ma'aser* and exempt from *biur*. *Biur* — the obligation to remove and make ownerless one's *shemitah* produce once that species of produce is no longer available in the field — is a marker of *kedushas shvi'is*, the sanctity of *shemitah*. Because the *etrog* blossomed in the sixth year, it carries no *kedushas shvi'is*, and therefore there is no *biur*. And it is exempt from *ma'aser* as well, for reasons that the *gemara* will clarify.

### Seventh→Eighth

The second case: *bat shevi'is shenichnesah l'shminit* — an *etrog* that blossomed in the seventh year and was picked in the eighth. *Rava* rules: *peturah bema'aser vechayeves beviur* — exempt from *ma'aser* and obligated in *biur*. This is where the scenario becomes genuinely striking. The *etrog* blossomed in *shemitah* and therefore carries *kedushas shvi'is*, which is why it is obligated in *biur*. Yet it is exempt from *ma'aser* — even though it was picked in the eighth year, a year in which *ma'aser* would ordinarily apply. The apparent tension between these two determinations is precisely what drives the subsequent discussion.

### Scenarios Diagram

To map this out clearly: in the first scenario, the tree blossoms before *tu b'shvat* of the seventh year — that is, in the sixth year — and the *etrog* is picked after *tu b'shvat*, now in the seventh year. For *shemitah* purposes, the *chanatah* in the sixth year means no *kedushas shvi'is* and no *biur*. For *ma'aser* purposes, the *lakitah* in the seventh year means no *ma'aser* — since one does not take *ma'asrot* from seventh-year produce. The result is that both obligations are absent, and they are absent for different reasons grounded in different operative moments.

In the second scenario, the tree blossoms in the seventh year — carrying *kedushas shvi'is* — but is picked in the eighth year. Here the obligations seem to pull in opposite directions: *kedushas shvi'is* (from blossoming in the seventh) argues for *biur*; picking in the eighth (a year of *ma'aser*) would seem to argue for *ma'aser*. Yet *Rava* rules that there is *biur* but no *ma'aser*. The resolution of this apparent paradox is what *Abbaye* now challenges.

---

## Abbaye's Challenge

### Abbaye's Logic

*Abbaye* responds to *Rava*'s ruling with a penetrating challenge. He opens by saying: *bishlama seifa* — I understand the second part of your statement. You say the *etrog* blossomed in the seventh year and was picked in the eighth: it is obligated in *biur* because it has *kedushas shvi'is*, and once you have established that it is a *shemitah* fruit, the exemption from *ma'aser* follows naturally, since *shemitah* fruit does not require *ma'asrot*. That is a consistent, strict ruling — *l'chumra* — which treats the *etrog* as a *shemitah* fruit throughout.

But *ella reisha peturah min habiur amai* — what about the first part of your ruling? There you say it is blossomed in the sixth year and you say no *biur* because you go by *chanatah*. Very well. But if you go by *chanatah* to determine that it lacks *kedushas shvi'is*, then it should follow that for *ma'aser* purposes as well, it should be treated as a sixth-year fruit — which means it should be obligated in *ma'aser*. Why does *Rava* say it is also exempt from *ma'aser*?

*Abbaye*'s underlying assumption, in other words, is that *ma'aser* follows *shemitah* status. If the *shemitah* status is determined by *chanatah* and the *chanatah* was in the sixth year, then the *ma'aser* status should likewise be that of a sixth-year fruit — and a sixth-year fruit is obligated in *ma'aser*. Yet *Rava* says it is exempt. Why?

### Rava's Response

*Rava*'s response is arresting in its practicality. He says: *yada kol memashmeshin ba v'at amrat titchayev bema'aser* — everyone's hands are grabbing at it, and you are saying it should be obligated in *ma'aser*? His argument is not a formal legal principle but an observation about reality. During *shemitah*, even if a tree technically lacks *kedushas shvi'is* — because it blossomed in the sixth year — the reality on the ground is that nobody is protecting it. The fruit of this tree grows during the *shemitah* year, when all agricultural produce is *hefker* by convention, and people are freely helping themselves. A fruit that in practice is accessible to all and is not protected — *eino min hamishomar* — cannot generate an obligation of *ma'aser*.

There is a principle in the laws of *ma'aser* that produce must be *mishumar* — guarded, protected — for the *ma'aser* obligation to apply with full force. Since the *etrog* growing during *shemitah* is in practice accessible to the public even if it is not legally *hefker*, one cannot realistically impose an obligation of *ma'aser* upon it.

This argument would potentially be bounded: if one had an enclosed *etrog* orchard and could actually prevent public access during *shemitah*, the situation might be different. The answer is that even then the fruit would not be fully *mishumar* in the relevant sense, since the social reality of *shemitah* would still pertain. But the theoretical question of whether a perfectly enclosed orchard would generate *ma'aser* liability is a genuine *nafka mina* from *Rava*'s reasoning.

### Rashi's Reading

*Rashi* offers a reinterpretation of the entire exchange that deserves careful attention, because it changes the framework considerably. According to *Rashi*, *Rava* in fact agrees with *Abbaye*'s premise: *ma'aser* follows *shemitah* status. The two rulings therefore become internally consistent on their own terms.

In the second scenario — blossomed in the seventh, picked in the eighth — the *etrog* has *kedushas shvi'is*, and since *ma'aser* follows *shemitah* status, it is exempt from *ma'aser*. *Abbaye* had no difficulty with this part.

In the first scenario — blossomed in the sixth, picked in the seventh — the *etrog* lacks *kedushas shvi'is*, and therefore, if *ma'aser* follows *shemitah* status, it should be obligated in *ma'aser* as a sixth-year fruit. *Abbaye*'s question was precisely: why then does *Rava* say it is exempt?

And *Rava*'s answer, on *Rashi*'s reading, is: you are technically correct that it lacks *kedushas shvi'is* and therefore should be obligated in *ma'aser* as a sixth-year fruit. But the practical reality is that this *etrog* is growing during *shemitah*, and people are treating it as *hefker* and picking it freely. Even though halachically it is not *hefker*, it is also not *mishumar*. Since it is not protected, the obligation of *ma'aser* cannot practically take hold. This is *Rava*'s justification for the exemption — not a rejection of *Abbaye*'s logical framework, but an acknowledgment that practical reality overrides the theoretical obligation in this specific case.

---

## Hamnuna vs. Braitta

### Hamnuna Position

*Rav Hamnuna* offers a sweeping formulation. He says: *bat shishit shenichnesa l'shvi'it le-olam shishit* — a sixth-year *etrog* entering the seventh year is, in all respects, always sixth-year produce. And *bat shvi'it shenichnesa l'shminit le-olam shvi'it* — a seventh-year *etrog* entering the eighth year is, in all respects, always seventh-year produce. The *shemitah* status established at *chanatah* is permanent and comprehensive, governing both *biur* and *ma'aser* consistently and without qualification.

### Braitta Challenge

The *gemara* challenges *Rav Hamnuna* from a *braita* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda* citing *Rabbi Shimon*: an *etrog* that blossomed in the sixth year and was picked in the seventh is exempt from *ma'aser* and exempt from *biur*. The exemption from *biur* is intelligible — it is a sixth-year fruit without *kedushas shvi'is*. But the *braita* gives the reason for the exemption from *ma'aser* as follows: *she-ein lecha davar she-chayav bema'aser ella im ken gadal b'chiyuv v'nilkat b'chiyuv* — nothing is obligated in *ma'aser* unless it both grew in a year of *ma'aser* obligation and was picked in a year of *ma'aser* obligation. Since it was picked in the seventh year, when there is no *ma'aser*, it is exempt — not because of its *shemitah* status from *chanatah*, but because picking in *shemitah* independently exempts it.

For the second scenario — blossomed in the seventh, picked in the eighth — the *braita* says it is exempt from *ma'aser* and exempt from *biur*. The exemption from *ma'aser* is understandable, since it is *shemitah* produce. But the exemption from *biur* is justified by the parallel logic: *she-ein lecha davar she-chayav bebiur ella im ken gadal b'shvi'it v'nilkat b'shvi'it* — nothing is obligated in *biur* unless it both grew and was picked in the seventh year. Since it was picked in the eighth year, it has no *biur*.

This *braita* introduces a fundamentally different framework: the determining moment for each obligation is a combination of when the fruit grew and when it was picked, and only when both conditions point to *chiyuv* does the obligation apply. This directly contradicts *Rav Hamnuna*, who says the *shemitah* status at *chanatah* is permanent and exclusive.

### Gemara Resolution

The *gemara* maps out the contradictions precisely: *reisha kashya le-Rav Hamnuna, seifa kashya bein le-Rabba bein le-Rav Hamnuna* — the first part of the *braita* poses a difficulty for *Rav Hamnuna*, and the second part poses a difficulty for both *Rabba* and *Rav Hamnuna*.

The first part: in the sixth-into-seventh scenario, the *braita* says no *ma'aser* because it was picked in the seventh — consistent with *Rabba*'s outcome (though perhaps not his exact reasoning) but contradicting *Rav Hamnuna*, who would say the sixth-year status means *yes* to *ma'aser*.

The second part: in the seventh-into-eighth scenario, the *braita* says no *biur* because it was picked in the eighth. *Rabba* says yes *biur* (because it blossomed in *shemitah*), and *Rav Hamnuna* likewise says yes *biur* (since it is always seventh-year produce). Both are contradicted by the *braita*'s ruling that picking in the eighth exempts from *biur*.

The *gemara* resolves the impasse by declaring *tannai hi* — this is a dispute among *tannaim*. It then presents and expands a *braita* that reads: *esrog achar lekitaso lema'aser ve-achar chanataso l'shvi'is* — the *etrog* follows picking for *ma'aser* and blossoming for *shemitah*. That is the majority position that has governed our discussion throughout. Against this, *ve-raboseinu nimnu be-Usha ve-amru achar lekitaso bein lema'aser bein l'shvi'is* — the rabbis took a vote in *Usha* and said that the *etrog* follows picking for both *ma'aser* and *shemitah*.

### Usha Vote

The *gemara* asks: *shvi'is man dchar shmeih* — *shemitah* was never mentioned in the first opinion; what is the dispute about? The *gemara* supplies the missing context: the first opinion holds that for *shemitah* the *etrog* goes by *chanatah*, and the rabbis who voted in *Usha* held that even for *shemitah* the *etrog* follows *lakitah*.

The *braita* of *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda* — the one that said no *biur* because the *etrog* was picked in the eighth year — represents precisely the *Usha* minority position: that *lakitah* matters even for *shemitah* laws. The accepted ruling, as established by the *Usha* vote, rejects this position. For *shemitah* purposes, it is only *chanatah* that counts. Only for *ma'aser* does *lakitah* operate, and that is what *Rabba* and *Rav Hamnuna* are debating — with the rejected minority *braita* accounting for the position that introduced *lakitah* even into *shemitah* law.

---

## Yochanan & Lakish

### Always Sixth Status

*Rav Yochanan* and *Resh Lakish* are both reported to hold: *etrog bashishit shenichnesa lishvi'it le-olam shishit* — a sixth-year *etrog* that blossoms in the sixth year retains its sixth-year status in all respects, even as it continues to grow enormously during the seventh year. The fact that the bulk of its physical growth and enlargement occurred during *shemitah* is irrelevant; the status is locked in at the moment of *chanatah*.

### Tiny Fruit Rule

When *Ravin* came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported in the name of *Rav Yochanan*: if an *etrog* blossomed in the sixth year and at that time was only the size of an olive — *afilu kezayit* — and by the time it was the seventh year it had grown to the size of a loaf of bread — *venasa kikar* — it is nevertheless obligated in *ma'aser* as sixth-year produce, and is considered *tevel* until properly separated. No matter how dramatically it grew during *shemitah*, its *ma'aser* status remains anchored to the moment of *chanatah* in the sixth year. One might intuitively feel that a fruit that grew so dramatically during *shemitah* should take on the character of *shemitah* produce — but the halacha is unequivocal: *chanatah* determines status, and that determination is final.

---

## Tree Ripening Patterns

### Nechemia Position

The *gemara* introduces a new *braita*: the rule that fruit trees go by *chanatah* and by *tu b'shvat* applies when a tree has two *breichot* — two periods of ripening — per year. The *gemara* notes that the borrowed term *breicha* (literally a brood or clutch, used of pigeons) means here something like two cycles of fruit ripening, and clarifies *k'ein shtei breichot* — like two broodings, meaning the tree produces and ripens fruit at multiple times throughout the year.

*Rabbi Nechemia* qualifies the rule: *aval ilan ha'oseh breichah achat* — but a tree that produces fruit in only one cycle per year — such as palm trees, olives, and carobs — follows a different rule. *Af al pi shechanto peiroteihem kodem tu b'shvat, mitasrin l'shanah haba'ah* — even if their fruits blossomed before *tu b'shvat*, they are tithed as belonging to the coming year, not the previous year. In other words, for single-cycle trees, we go by *g'mar peri* — when the fruit finishes ripening — rather than by *chanatah*.

This is a radical qualification of everything that has been said. The entire framework of the first chapter — trees go by *chanatah*, and *tu b'shvat* is the dividing date — was built on the assumption of trees with multiple ripening cycles. For single-cycle trees, *Rabbi Nechemia* says, we actually go by the ripening itself.

### Reasoning

The underlying logic parallels the discussion about legumes. By legumes, the *gemara* noted that while the real operative moment might ideally be *g'mar peri*, legumes are picked at various times throughout the year and we cannot use a single uniform marker; so we use *hashrashah* instead as a fixed, early, uniform date. Similarly, *Rabbi Nechemia* is reasoning about trees as follows: the reason we use *chanatah* and *tu b'shvat* as the fixed marker for most trees is that trees with multiple ripening cycles produce fruit at many different times, making *g'mar peri* an unworkable standard — it will fall at different dates for different clusters of fruit. So we look backward to the blossoming, which tends to occur in a concentrated window around *tu b'shvat*, and use that as a single, fixed point.

But if a tree only produces fruit once per year — one *breichah* — then *g'mar peri* is not scattered across the calendar. It happens at a single, identifiable time. In that case, there is no practical need to retreat to the earlier and more uniform marker of *chanatah*. We can simply use *g'mar peri* itself. The choice between *chanatah* and *g'mar peri*, in other words, is driven by practical convenience in establishing a fixed and workable standard — not by an independent principle about what categorically determines the year for trees.

The difficulty is that *Rabbi Nechemia* does not explicitly frame the shift as being between *tu b'shvat* and *rosh hashanah*, but between blossoming and finishing. Nonetheless, the structural logic appears to be: when trees blossom matters because it is a convenient single marker; when there is only one ripening, the ripening itself serves as that single marker equally well.

### Carob Practice

*Rav Yochanan* reports: *nahagu am becharuvin k'Rabbi Nechemia* — the people practiced with carobs in accordance with *Rabbi Nechemia*. Since carobs ripen only once per year, the common practice was to go by the ripening rather than the blossoming. This is notable, and as will become clear, it implies that the laws of *ma'aser* for trees are rabbinic in character — otherwise such latitude in practice would be difficult to justify.

---

## White Figs Challenge

### White Figs Timing

*Resh Lakish* challenges *Rav Yochanan* from the case of *bnot shuach* — white figs. The ruling is: *shevi'it shelahen shniyah mipnei she'osot l'shalosh shanim* — their *shemitah* year is the second year of the cycle, because it takes three years for them to ripen fully. The implication is that a white fig that blossomed in the *shemitah* year will only be picked two years later, in the second year after *shemitah*, and it will carry *kedushas shvi'is* at that point because of its *shemitah* blossoming.

### Problem

This presents a direct challenge to *Rav Yochanan*'s endorsement of the *Rabbi Nechemia* position. White figs ripen only once — they are quintessentially a single-*breichah* tree. According to *Rabbi Nechemia*'s logic, single-cycle trees should go by *g'mar peri*, not by blossoming. Yet the white fig's *shemitah* status is determined by its *chanatah* in the *shemitah* year, not by when it is picked two years later. *Resh Lakish* pressed this contradiction, and *Rav Yochanan* fell silent — *ishtik* — offering no response.

### Rabbinic vs. Biblical

*Rabbi Abba Ha-Kohen son of Rabbi Yose Ha-Kohen* asks why *Rav Yochanan* was silent. Surely he could have said: *amina lach ana Rabbi Nechemia* — I was citing *Rabbi Nechemia*, and you are citing the rabbinic majority against him. That is not a challenge directed at me; I was simply reporting *Rabbi Nechemia*'s view.

The *gemara* anticipates that *Resh Lakish* could have responded: *shavket Rabbanan ve-avdet k'Rabbi Nechemia* — are you entitled to set aside the majority rabbinic position in favor of *Rabbi Nechemia*? And *Rav Yochanan* could have answered: *ki amina lach ana nahagu* — I was not stating the normative *halacha*; I merely reported that the people practiced in accordance with *Rabbi Nechemia*. You are telling me something about *issura* — about the binding halacha — and that is a separate question.

But then *Resh Lakish* could have pressed further: *bemakom issura ki nahagu shavkinan lehu* — if the normative halacha is violated, how can you simply report the practice as if it were acceptable? This is precisely why *Rav Yochanan* should not have remained silent.

*Rabbi Abba Ha-Kohen* explains the resolution. *Rav Yochanan* could have distinguished between the two domains entirely. When I endorsed the practice of going by *g'mar peri* for carobs, I was speaking about *ma'aser* — *ma'aser charuvin derabbanan*, *ma'aser* for trees is rabbinic law. In the realm of rabbinic law, there is flexibility to go sometimes by *g'mar peri* and sometimes by *chanatah*, depending on practicality. That is why the people's practice can be accommodated.

But the challenge from white figs involves *shemitah* — *ve-at amret li shvi'is de-oraisa*. *Shemitah* law for trees is biblical. In the domain of biblical law, one cannot apply the same flexibility. Of course we go by *chanatah* for *shemitah* — the leniency *Rabbi Nechemia* introduced, and which the people followed regarding carobs, was never meant to apply to biblical-level obligations. *Rav Yochanan* was silent not because the question was unanswerable, but because — as *Rabbi Abba Ha-Kohen* suggests — the answer is sufficiently obvious that the silence may indicate *Rav Yochanan* did not consider the challenge to have genuinely engaged his position in the first place.

---

## Summary & Conclusion

### Trees Recap

To summarize the terrain covered: the general rule for trees is that *ma'aser* is determined by *chanatah* and the marker date is *tu b'shvat*. This rule has been qualified in two directions. First, the *etrog* — because of its continuous growth throughout the year — goes by *lakitah* for *ma'aser*, while still using *tu b'shvat* as the calendar marker and going by *chanatah* for *shemitah* purposes. Second, trees that ripen in a single cycle per year — such as carobs and, by implication, palms and olives — may go by *g'mar peri* rather than *chanatah*, at least for *ma'aser*. The practice of the people followed *Rabbi Nechemia* on this point for carobs, suggesting that in the realm of *ma'aser* for trees, there is sufficient latitude to make such an adjustment.

### Rabbinic Flexibility

The overarching theme that emerges from the final sugya is that the flexibility of the dating rules corresponds directly to the level of the law being applied. Where the obligation is rabbinic — as *ma'aser* for trees is *derabbanan* — there is room to choose whichever standard of measurement is practically workable and most accurately captures the intention of the law, whether blossoming, ripening, or picking. Where the obligation is biblical — as *shemitah* is *de-oraisa* — the rules are fixed and the flexibility disappears. The case of white figs, which require three years to ripen and yet take their *shemitah* status from the year of blossoming, illustrates precisely that for biblical-level *shemitah* obligations, the calendar of *chanatah* governs without exception, regardless of how long the fruit takes to mature. The entire discussion thus concludes, appropriately, on the theme of the distinction between *de-rabbanan* and *de-oraisa* as the organizing principle behind the apparent complexity of produce-year determinations.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 17

## Arba'ah Devarim

### Intro to Four Things

The daf begins with a series of statements by Rabbi Yitzchak relating to *din*, and we pick up approximately ten lines before the text widens on 16b. The Gemara introduces: *arba'ah devarim mekari'in gezar dino shel adam* — four things that tear up a person's final judgment. This evokes the broader theme running through the sugya: even after a *din* has been rendered, it is not necessarily immutable. There remains the possibility of reversal, and these four things are precisely that mechanism.

### Tzedakah

The first is *tzedakah*, derived from the verse *v'tzedakah tatzil mimavet* — charity will save from death.

### Tze'akah

The second is *tze'akah* — crying out to God — derived from the verse *vayitz'aku el Hashem batzar lahem mimtzukoteihem yotzi'em*: they cried out to God in their travail, and from their anguish He took them out.

### Shinui Hashem

The third is *shinui hashem* — changing one's name — derived from the verse in which God tells Avraham: *Sarai ishtecha lo tikra et shemah Sarai ki Sarah shemah* — you shall not call her Sarai, for Sarah is her name — followed immediately by the blessing that she would bear a son.

### Shinui Ma'aseh

The fourth is *shinui ma'aseh* — changing one's deeds — derived from *vayar Elokim et ma'aseihem*, God saw the deeds of the people of Nineveh, and *vayinachem ha'Elokim al hara'ah asher diber la'asot lahem v'lo asah* — God relented from the evil He had spoken of doing to them.

### Teshuvah Connection

Three of these four map directly onto the famous liturgical formula: *teshuvah, tzedakah, tefillah ma'avirin et ro'a hagezeirah* — repentance, charity, and prayer avert the evil decree. Notably, *shinui hashem* is absent from that formulation. One explanation is that *shinui hashem* may itself be a means of achieving *teshuvah*: the Rambam discusses how changing one's name is an expression of the desire to become a new person, to identify as a different kind of individual. Alternatively, the Maharsha argues that *shinui hashem* is categorically different from the other three, in that it is not about reversing an evil decree so much as changing a status quo for the better — Sarai did not have children, and now she can. In that sense it is not quite of the same weight as the others, which are truly mechanisms of *mekari'in gezar dino*.

### Shinui Makom

The Gemara adds: *v'yesh omrim af shinui makom* — and some say that changing one's place also belongs on this list — derived from *vayomer Hashem el Avram lech lecha me'artzecha*, and only afterward *v'e'escha l'goy gadol*, you will become a great nation. Here again, as with *shinui hashem*, the verse speaks more about achieving a greater fortune than about being saved from an evil decree.

### Teshuvah Integration

The Rambam also addresses *shinui makom* in the context of *teshuvah*: moving to a new place can represent a fresh start with a clean slate, and beyond that, the Rambam consistently emphasizes how one's surroundings and environment shape one's conduct and standards of behavior. In this way, both *shinui hashem* and *shinui makom* can be understood as dimensions of *teshuvah* more broadly conceived.

---

## Hakbilat P'nei Rav

### Greeting Master

The Gemara transitions to another statement of Rabbi Yitzchak, though the theme now shifts away from *din*: *chayav adam lehakbil p'nei rabo baregel* — a person is obligated to greet his master on the festivals. The scriptural source is the question posed to the Shunamite woman when she set out to visit Elisha after her son died: *madua at holechet elav hayom lo chodesh v'lo shabbat* — why are you going to him today? It is not *Rosh Chodesh* and it is not *Shabbat*. The Gemara reads this as a *michlal*: by implication, on *Rosh Chodesh* and *Shabbat* one is indeed obligated to go. Of course, the *tanna* spoke of *regalim*, not *Rosh Chodesh* and *Shabbat*. The connection is admittedly not entirely clear, and the difficulty of demanding a visit on every *Rosh Chodesh* and every *Shabbat* would make the requirement unduly burdensome. There is another Gemara that addresses this at greater length, and we will not pursue it further here.

### Taharah Baregel

Rabbi Yitzchak continues: *chayav adam l'taher atzmo baregel* — a person is obligated to purify himself on the festivals. The scriptural source is *uv'nivlatam lo tiga'u* — do not touch the carcasses of unclean animals. A *braisa* elaborates: one might have thought this verse prohibits ordinary Israelites from touching a *nevelah*. The *talmud lomar* is the verse *emor el hakohanim bnei Aharon* — it is the *kohanim* who bear the prohibition against *tum'ah*, not ordinary Israelites. In fact, a straightforward *kal v'chomer* confirms this: if even the more severe *tum'ah* of a human corpse applies only to *kohanim* and not to ordinary Jews, how much more certainly does the lighter *tum'ah* of an animal carcass not apply to them. If so, what is the meaning of *uv'nivlatam lo tiga'u*? It must be speaking in the context of the *regel*. The *rishonim* debate whether this constitutes a genuine prohibition or rather practical advice — that in order to perform *aliyah laregel* and bring a *korban* at the *Beis Hamikdash*, one would need to be in a state of *taharah*, and the verse is thus providing guidance rather than issuing a formal prohibition. Moreover, if it is a formal prohibition, one might reasonably assume it applies only when *aliyah laregel* is actually practiced — what logical basis would it have in the absence of a *Beis Hamikdash*?

### Post-Churban Aliyah

When these two obligations — greeting one's master and immersing in a *mikveh* — are considered together, it becomes apparent that Rabbi Yitzchak, who lived after the *Churban Habayis*, seems to be attempting to recreate something of the *aliyah laregel* experience in a world without a Temple. Where once one would ascend to the *Beis Hamikdash*, stand in the presence of the *Shechina*, and fulfill *lo yera'u fanai reikam* — appearing before God's presence not empty-handed — now the practice involves purifying oneself in a *mikveh* and proceeding to greet one's *rav*. The effect is unmistakably to substitute the *talmid chacham* for the *Beis Hamikdash* as the locus of the *regel* experience — a striking post-*Churban* reimagining of the festival pilgrimage.

---

## Three Books

### Books Intro

The Gemara now turns to a statement of Rav Kruspedai — whose Aramaic name, incidentally, is the word for *tzitzis* — citing Rabbi Yochanan: *shlosha sefarim niftachim b'Rosh Hashanah* — three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah. It is worth pausing to appreciate that none of this is self-evident. The idea of a *yom hadin*, of *ketivah* and *chatimah*, of books being opened — these are particular metaphors and conceptual frameworks that Chazal are introducing and developing. The basic notion that Rosh Hashanah is a time when we beseech God for a good year, and that there are moments when particular things — rain, fruit, and so forth — are determined, does not by itself imply the full-blown theology of a *yom hadin*. These are being built step by step throughout the sugya.

### Tzaddikim and Resha'im

The three books are as follows. *Tzadikim gemurim* — the completely righteous — are immediately written and sealed for life: *nechtavim v'nechtamim l'altar l'chayim*. *Resha'im gemurim* — the completely wicked — are immediately written and sealed for death: *nechtavim v'nechtamim l'altar l'mitah*.

### Beinonim Suspended

*Beinonim* — the intermediate category — are suspended: *tluyim v'omdim me'Rosh Hashanah v'ad Yom Hakippurim*. If they merit, they are written for life; if they do not merit, they are written for death. One notices here that the familiar two-stage process of *ketivah* and *chatimah* does not quite work out as straightforwardly as one might assume. The *tzadikim* and *resha'im* receive both stages immediately; the *beinonim* do not actually receive the *ketivah* until Yom Kippur. So the picture is not that everyone is written on Rosh Hashanah and sealed by Yom Kippur. Rather, the *beinonim* have a period of suspended judgment in which they are not yet written at all.

### Sefer Chayim

Rabbi Abin derives these categories from the verse *yimachu misefer chayim v'im tzaddikim al yikatevu* — let them be erased from the book of life and not be written with the righteous. The Gemara reads: *yimachu misefer* — to be erased from the book — this is the book of the *resha'im gemurim*, who are removed from the book of life; *chayim* — the book of life — this is the book of the *tzadikim*; and *v'im tzaddikim al yikatevu* — they will not yet be written with the righteous — this refers to the *beinonim*, whose writing is deferred. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives similarly from Moshe's plea: *ve'im ayin mechani na misefercha asher katavta* — if not, erase me from the book that You have written. *Mechani na* — the erasure — refers to the book of the *resha'im*; *misefercha* — Your book — is the book of the *tzadikim*; and *asher katavta* — that You have written — refers to the *beinonim*, whose writing is still pending.

It is also worth noting that the Gemara's language for the *resha'im* is not that they are written in a book of death, but rather that they are erased from the book of life. This connects to a broader question in Chazal's conception of *gehinnom*: is it a place of active punishment, or is it simply the absence of eternal life? The Rambam, among others, understands *gehinnom* as the soul's extinction rather than as an underworld of torment — and the language of *mechiyah*, erasure, rather than inscription in a book of death, is consistent with that reading.

### Rishonic Approaches

The obvious difficulty with this Gemara is that its apparent premise — that the righteous live and the wicked die — does not correspond to observable reality. The *rishonim* offer three main responses.

The Ramban effectively turns the Gemara into a tautology: the words *tzaddik* and *rasha* here do not denote moral categories but legal ones — *tzaddik bedino* and *rasha bedino*, one found innocent and one found guilty. The righteous in this Gemara are those whom God has judged worthy of life; the wicked are those judged worthy of death. This makes the Gemara's only real *chiddush* the timing — that the decision is made on Rosh Hashanah — but it says nothing about the moral criteria God employs. This reading is not very compelling as *peshat* and not particularly illuminating as theology.

The Rambam attempts to read the Gemara more literally, maintaining that it really does concern whether one's *mitzvot* outweigh one's *avonot* or vice versa, while acknowledging that God's calculus is opaque to human perception. Sins we consider minor may weigh heavily; acts we consider great may not. In the end the accounting is precise, even if we cannot follow it — which is not always satisfying when one observes an apparent *tzaddik* dying young or a *rasha* flourishing.

Tosafot offers what has become the standard response of Chazal to the problem of *schar va'onesh* in general: defer the reckoning to the world to come. According to Tosafot, the Gemara is not speaking about whether a person will live or die in the coming year but about whether they will merit *chayei olam haba*. A *tzaddik* is determined to merit the world to come; a *rasha* is determined not to. This dissolves the empirical problem but raises its own difficulty: why would a yearly judgment be needed for a determination that logically belongs at the moment of death? And it is entirely at odds with the liturgical context of Rosh Hashanah, which is concerned with the year ahead rather than with final eschatological destiny.

---

## Final Day Judgment

### Beis Shammai

The Gemara now introduces a *braisa* from Beis Shammai on an altogether different plane of judgment — not the annual determination on Rosh Hashanah but the *yom hadin* at the end of days, the final judgment of the messianic era and the time of *techiyat hameitim*. *Gimel kitos hein l'yom hadin* — three groups stand for the final day of judgment: one of *tzadikim gemurim*, one of *resha'im gemurim*, and one of *beinonim*.

### Tzaddikim and Resha'im F…

*Tzadikim gemurim* are immediately written and sealed for *chayei olam* — eternal life. Notice the shift in language from the earlier Gemara: where before it said *l'chayim*, here it says *l'chayei olam*, eternal life — appropriate to this eschatological setting in which physical, bodily existence in the world to come is presumably what is at stake. *Resha'im gemurim* are sealed immediately for *gehinnom*. Again, the language changes: in the earlier Gemara it said *l'mitah*, death; here it says *l'gehinnom*. The verse cited is from Daniel: *rabim miyeshenei admat afar yakitzu* — many who sleep in the dust will awaken — *eileh l'chayei olam*, these to eternal life, *v'eileh lachaparot l'dira'on olam*, those to shame and eternal damnation.

### Beinonim Purification

The *beinonim*, according to Beis Shammai, *yordim l'gehinnom umitzaftzefin v'olim* — go down to *gehinnom*, cry out, and rise up. The verse from Zechariah reads: *veheiveisi et hashlishit ba'esh* — I will bring the third group into the fire — *vetzaraftim ketzruf es hakesef uvechantim kivechon es hazahav* — I will smelt them as one smelts silver and test them as gold is tested — *hu yikra bishmi va'ani e'eneh oto* — he will call out in my name and I will answer him. The fire of *gehinnom*, for the *beinonim*, is thus a process of purification rather than final destruction — an idea that has obvious structural parallels to the Catholic doctrine of Purgatory. Through this process, the *beinonim* earn their place in eternal life. *Va'alehem amrah Chanah: Hashem meimis umechayeh, morid she'ol vaya'al* — God brings death and life, brings down to the underworld and brings up — this refers to those who go through *gehinnom* and emerge.

Beis Shammai's framework is thus essentially one of strict *din*: the *tzadikim* earn eternal life, the *resha'im* are condemned, and the *beinonim* must undergo a purgative process before they can merit *chayei olam*. Even Beis Shammai acknowledges some mechanism for the *beinonim* to ultimately attain reward, but it comes only after punishment.

### Beis Hillel Compassion

Beis Hillel takes a more compassionate position: *v'rav chesed mateh klapei chesed* — the One who is great in *chesed* will tip the scales toward *chesed*. For Beis Hillel, at least some of the ordinary *beinonim* are spared the need for purification altogether — God leans in their favor from the outset. Regarding them David says *ahavti ki yishma Hashem et koli* — I rejoice that God has heard my supplication. Tosafot notes that the fuller context of that psalm includes *afafuni chevlei mavet*, the bonds of death surrounded me, and *daloti v'li yehoshia*, I was poor and God saved me — meaning even one who was undeserving, even one who was deserving of death, God ultimately had compassion and saved. Another reading of *daloti*: the root *dal* means to draw up, as in drawing water — God lifted this person up even from the depths of their deserved fate. That is the *rav chesed mateh klapei chesed*.

### Minim and Apikorsim

Having established the three basic groups, the Gemara turns to those who deserve special — and especially severe — treatment: *haminim v'hamasorot v'ha'apikorsim* — the heretics, the informers, and the *apikorsim* — along with *she'kafru baTorah* (those who denied the Torah), *she'kafru bit'chiyat hameitim* (those who denied resurrection), *she'pirshu midarchei tzibur* (those who separated themselves from the ways of the community), *she'natnu chititam b'eretz chayim* (those who put their fear upon the living — meaning those who exercised oppressive authority over others), and *she'chat'u v'hichti'u et harabim* — those who sinned and caused the masses to sin — with Yerovam ben Nevat and his colleagues cited as the paradigmatic examples.

Rashi illuminates these categories: *minim* are those who perverted the words of the living God to produce sectarian movements — the *Tzadukim* and *Baitosim* — while *apikoros*, as the Gemara in Sanhedrin defines it, means one who denigrates *talmidei chachamim*, thereby undermining rabbinic authority. The *masorot* — informers — correspond to those who separate from the ways of the community. What is striking in Rashi's readings is that the emphasis falls not on private heterodoxy but on the public dimension: *chat'u v'hichti'u et harabim*, leading the masses astray. It is not merely that a person holds incorrect views privately, but that they corrode the community's relationship with Torah and its leadership.

### Eternal Gehennom

These figures *yardu l'gehinnom v'nidonim bah l'dorot dorot* — go down to *gehinnom* and are judged there for generations upon generations. After twelve months, ordinary severe sinners have their bodies destroyed and their souls burned; but for this category there is no terminus. *Gehinnom kala v'hein einam kalin* — even *gehinnom* itself will come to an end, but their punishment will not. The verse: *v'tzuram l'valot she'ol* — their form will wear out the underworld, meaning they will outlast *gehinnom* itself, which is categorically not a good thing. The verse continues: *mizvul lo*, which refers to the Temple — *v'ein z'vul ela Beis Hamikdash*, as in *bano baniti beit z'vul lach*. Their punishment is thus tied to having, through their sins, stretched their hand against the *Beis Hamikdash* — which Rashi interprets as meaning that their conduct caused the destruction of the Temple, with Yerovam ben Nevat serving as the archetypal figure. *Va'alehem amrah Chanah: Hashem yeichatu m'rivav* — those who war against God shall tremble.

Rava adds a sharp and pointed observation: *v'inhu mishafirei shafirei b'nei Mechuza* — and these people are none other than the finest of the fine of Mechuza, the most cosmopolitan and wealthy of his own city. Rava had a well-documented critical relationship with the affluent populace of Mechuza, and here he is unambiguous: *v'kari lehu b'nei gehinnom*.

---

## Poshei Yisrael

### Poshei Definition

The Gemara returns to clarify the structure of Beis Hillel's position. *U'Beis Hillel omrim v'rav chesed mateh klapei chesed* — but what about the verse that says the third group is brought into fire? *Hatam b'poshei Yisrael begufan* — that verse refers specifically to *poshei Yisrael begufan*, Jewish sinners with their very bodies, not to ordinary *beinonim*. The normal *beinonim* God tips in favor of compassion; those who carry *poshei Yisrael begufan* sins must be purified. The distinction is thus one of quality, not quantity. A *beinoni* who is fifty-fifty but whose sins include sins of this severe category must undergo the purgative process; a *beinoni* whose sins are merely ordinary receives God's compassion directly.

### Tefillin Identity

*Poshei Yisrael begufan mai ninhu* — what exactly is this category? *Amar Rav: karkafta d'lo manach tefillin* — a head that never wore *tefillin*. This is a striking and perhaps surprising definition. One might have expected something far more grave. The significance, however, lies not merely in the neglect of a *mitzvah* but in what *tefillin* represents. Chazal teach *ki shem Hashem nikra alecha* — God's name is called upon you — *elu tefillin sheberosh*, this refers to the *tefillin* on one's head. Wearing *tefillin* is not simply an action performed with one's body; it is the very marking of one's body and personhood with a Jewish identity, with identification with Torah and with God. Unlike other *aveirot* — desecrating *Shabbat*, eating *treifos* — which are performed *b'gufa* but are nonetheless specific acts, not wearing *tefillin* is a statement about the identity of the person's very self. It is less like an action and more like rejecting the identity that should define one's being. In this sense it parallels, to some degree, the category of one who reversed his *bris milah* or never received one.

### Tosafot Qualifications

Tosafot, aware that in the period of the *Ba'alei HaTosafot* there were Jews who did not consistently wear *tefillin* or *mezuzah*, works carefully to limit the scope of this ruling.
