First, he cites the *Mechilta*: *haosek baTorah patur min hatefillin* — one who is engaged in Torah study is considered as if wearing *tefillin*, since *tefillin* embody the principle *l'ma'an tihye Torat Hashem b'ficha*. Learning Torah substitutes for the *mitzvah*. Second, Rabbeinu Tam specifies that the category of *poshei Yisrael begufan* applies only when the *mitzvah* is *bezuyah alav* — despised in one's eyes — as in *d'megunah alav retzuah shel tefillin sheberosh*, one who finds the very strap of *tefillin* repugnant. By contrast, one who refrains because he fears he cannot maintain the standard of *guf naki* required — as discussed in connection with Elisha Ba'al Knafayim in *Bameh Tomnin* — is not in this category. Finally, and most broadly, Tosafot notes: *v'chol hanei d'shmatin b'shelo asah teshuvah* — all of this applies only where the person did not do *teshuvah*. *Teshuvah* fixes it entirely.

### Nations' Sinners

*Poshei umot ha'olam begufan* — the parallel category among the nations — *amar Rav b'aveirah*, Rav defines this as sexual sin. Here too the logic is that this category of sin involves the body in its totality, the entire person rather than a particular act or limb.

### Abusive Leaders

A further category is introduced: *she'natnu chititam b'eretz chayim* — those who instilled fear in the land of the living. Rav Chisda identifies this as *parnas hamatil eimah yeteirah al hatzibur shelo l'shem shamayim* — a communal leader who imposes excessive fear upon the community not for the sake of Heaven. Exerting authority and inspiring appropriate reverence may at times be legitimate, but doing so for personal aggrandizement rather than for Heaven's sake places one in the company of the gravest sinners. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav extends this: any such leader will not see a child who is a *talmid chacham* — derived from *lo yireh kol chachmei lev*. This consequence, while far less severe than the fiery punishments described earlier, is significant in its own right.

---

## Chesed and Measure

### Kovsho v'Nosei

Returning to Beis Hillel's position, the Gemara asks: *heichi avid* — how exactly does God tip the scales toward *chesed*? Two approaches are given. Rabbi Eliezer says *kovsho* — God submerges or suppresses the sins — from *yashuv yerachamenu yikhbosh avonoteinu*, God will suppress our sins. Rabbi Yose bar Hanina says *nosei* — God lifts them off — from *nosei avon v'over al pesha*, bearing sin and forgoing transgression. The precise distinction between these two modes of divine compassion is subtle. One reading is that *kovsho* acknowledges the sin but brackets it — the sin is not erased but the person is spared punishment. *Nosei* is more thoroughgoing — the sin is actually lifted off, carried away, as though relieved from the person's burden. Rashi frames it through the image of scales: *kovsho* is to press down on the side of the *mitzvot* so that they outweigh the sins; *nosei* is to lift the sins themselves so they do not weigh down the scale. Rashi's metaphor is apt but, as the Gemara notes, it is his own elaboration rather than the language of the text itself.

### Ma'avir Rishon

A *Tanna devei Rabbi Yishmael* introduces the concept of *ma'avir rishon rishon* — God passes over the first sin, overlooking it, and this is the *middah*. The word *middah* here carries a double resonance: on the one hand it means the measure or attribute by which God acts; on the other, *middah* implies precision, exact calculation — and there is something quietly ironic in declaring that the precise measure is to forego precision. One reading connects *v'chen hi hamiddah* to the *Yud Gimmel Middot* of *rachamim*, making *ma'avir rishon rishon* itself one of the attributes of divine mercy. Rava adds an important qualification: *veavon atzmo eino nimchak* — even when God passes over the first sin, it is not erased. If in the end the person accumulates a majority of sins, that forgiven sin gets added back to the ledger and counted against them.

### Forgiveness Reciprocal

Rava also derives a principle of *middah keneged middah* in the realm of compassion: *kol hama'avir al middotav* — whoever is willing to forgo their own precise accounting, who does not demand exact judgment against those who wrong them, and instead says *mochel*, I forgive — God will respond in kind. *Nosei avon v'over al pesha: lemi nosei avon? L'mi she'over al pesha* — for whom does God bear sin? For the one who himself passes over sins done against him. The reciprocity is direct and explicit: our willingness to forgive other human beings becomes the very basis for God's willingness to forgive us.

### Rav Huna Story

This principle finds dramatic confirmation in the story of Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua, who became gravely ill. Rav Pappa came to visit and, seeing that Rav Huna's condition was dire, instructed those present to prepare *zavda* — an accompanying care package, meaning *tachrichim*, burial shrouds — for the journey ahead. In the end, Rav Huna recovered. Rav Pappa, understandably embarrassed, eventually encountered Rav Huna and asked: *mai chazit* — what did you see, what transpired at the threshold of death? Rav Huna answered: yes, the decree against me was as you saw. But God said to the heavenly court: *hoil v'lo mokim bemileih* — since he does not stand upon his own accounting, since he is willing to forgo things done against him — *lo takumu bahadei* — we too should not be exacting against him. The heavenly judgment was reversed on the grounds that Rav Huna did not demand that others be held to precise account for wrongs done to him. This is not mere *drasha* but a report of what was actually witnessed in the heavenly tribunal.

### She'erit Nachalato

The verse cited — *nosei avon v'over al pesha lish'erit nachalato* — to the remnant of His heritage — contains a qualification. Rabbi Acha bar Chanina notes: *alyah vekotz bah* — this is like a fatty tail, delicious but with a thorn. The promise that God forgives is real, but it is not universal. *Lish'erit nachalato v'lo lechol nachalato* — God forgives the remnant of His inheritance, not the entirety. Who is *she'erit nachalato*? *Lemi shemesim atzmo keshirayim* — those who make themselves like leftovers, like the residue, meaning those who are humble and do not assert themselves with haughtiness. Only such people will receive this divine forgiveness.

---

## Justice vs. Compassion

### Tzaddik and Chasid

Rav Huna identifies a scriptural tension: *tzaddik Hashem bechol derachav* — God is a *tzaddik* — and *chasid bechol ma'asav* — God is a *chasid*. Is He exacting or compassionate? The resolution: *betchilah tzaddik* — initially, God seeks to judge with precise justice — *ulevasof chasid* — but when justice alone would condemn too many, He turns to compassion.

### Chesed and Din

Rabbi Eliezer identifies a parallel tension: *velecha Hashem chesed* — You are compassionate — versus *ki atah tishalem le'ish kema'aseihu* — You compensate each person precisely according to their deeds. Again, the resolution runs in the same direction: *betchilah ki atah tishalem kema'aseihu*, God first applies the precise measure of justice; *ulevasof velecha Hashem chesed*, when justice threatens to overwhelm, compassion takes over.

### Rav Chesed v'Emet

Ilfi — or some say Ilfa — raises a further contradiction: *v'rav chesed* — God is great in compassion — and *v'emet* — God is truth. Compassion or truth? *Betchilah b'emet*, God begins with truth; *ulevasof rav chesed*, He ends with great compassion. One might object that in the verse itself, *chesed* precedes *emet*. Perhaps that ordering is itself the message: God recognizes from the outset that truth alone will be insufficient, that the eventual recourse to *chesed* is already anticipated at the moment of judgment. The commitment to truth is genuine but is framed from the beginning within the larger horizon of compassion.

---

## Yud Gimmel Middot

### Moshe's Lesson

The Gemara now arrives at the *Yud Gimmel Middot* themselves. The verse: *vayavor Hashem al panav vayikra: Hashem, Hashem, El rachum v'chanun erech apayim*. Rabbi Yochanan teaches — and prefaces with *ilmalei mikra katuv iy efshar l'omro*, were it not written in the verse one could not say such a thing — that God wrapped Himself like a *shliach tzibbur* and showed Moshe the *seder tefillah*, the order of prayer. The language of *vayavor* evokes the rabbinic phrase *over lifnei hatevah* — passing before the ark to lead the congregation — and the Gemara reads God's act of passing before Moshe as precisely this: demonstrating how to lead in prayer, how to invoke divine compassion. God said to Moshe: whenever the Jewish people sin, let them perform this rite before Me — the recitation of *Hashem, Hashem* — and I will forgive them. This is the foundation for the centrality of the *Yud Gimmel Middot* throughout *selichot* and the *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah*.

### Compassion Beforehand

The Gemara elaborates on the opening words: *Hashem, Hashem* — *ani hu kodem sheyecheta adam v'ani hu l'achar sheyecheta adam v'ya'aseh teshuvah* — I am God before a person sins, and I am God after a person sins and does *teshuvah*. The repetition of the divine name thus encodes two temporal dimensions of God's compassion: a compassion that precedes and sustains even before sin occurs, and a compassion that awaits and receives the sinner after the fact, sustaining them until they do *teshuvah*.

### Brit Middot

Rav Yehuda teaches: *berit kerutah l'Yud Gimmel Middot she'einam chozrot reikam* — there is a covenant forged with the thirteen *middot* such that whoever recites them will not return empty-handed. The verse: *hineh anochi koreit berit* — behold I am making a covenant — which follows the revelation of the *Yud Gimmel Middot*, confirms that the covenant is bound to those very attributes. Their recitation is therefore not merely liturgical expression but the activation of a *berit*, a covenantal commitment by God Himself to receive Israel's prayer with compassion. Tosafot undertakes an extended discussion of exactly how to count thirteen from the words of the verse, a question also debated among the *Ge'onim* and *rishonim* — how each word or phrase maps onto one of the thirteen attributes — but the Gemara itself here does not enumerate them individually, passing directly to the teaching of the *berit* that guarantees their efficacy.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 18

## Teshuvah & Gezar Din

### Yochanan's Teshuvah

The daf opens with a statement of Rabbi Yochanan: *gedola teshuva she-mekara'at gzar dino shel adam* — great is *teshuva*, which tears up the *gzar din*, the divine decree against a person. The proof text is from Yeshayahu: *hishmen lev ha-am ha-zeh ve-oznav hachbed ve-einav hasha pen yireh ve-einav u-ve-oznav yishma u-levavo yavin va-shav ve-rafa lo* — the heart of this people has become fat and their ears heavy and their eyes blind, lest they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and their heart understand; and they will do *teshuva*, and they will be healed. The verse appears to demonstrate that *teshuva* works even after a *gzar din* has already been issued.

### Papa's Challenge

Rav Papa immediately challenges this reading: *ve-dilma lifnei gzar din* — who says this verse is talking about after *gzar din*? Perhaps this is speaking about *teshuva* performed before any decree has been issued at all, in which case the verse proves nothing about overturning an existing judgment.

### Healing Proof

The response is pointed: *ve-rafa lo ktiv* — it says "and he will be healed." The Gemara asks: what kind of thing requires healing? *Hevei omer zeh gzar din* — it must be that there was already a decree, something harmful already set in motion, that now requires a cure. The language of healing thus signals the prior existence of a *gzar din*, confirming that *teshuva* can indeed tear it up.

---

## Meitivei Baraita

### RH to YK Window

A *meitivei* objection is raised. A *baraita* states: *hashav bein Rosh Hashanah l'Yom ha-Kippurim mochalin lo* — one who returns in *teshuva* between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is forgiven. But if one does not do *teshuva* during that window — *afilu heivi kol eilei nevayot she-ba'olam ein mochalin lo* — even if he brings all the fat rams of the world as sacrifices, he will not be forgiven. The implication is that after the *gzar din* is finalized at Yom Kippur, no reversal is possible, which directly contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's position.

### Yachid/Tzibur Split

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya, ha b'yachid ha b'tzibur* — it is not difficult; one source speaks of a *yachid*, an individual, and the other of a *tzibur*, a community. The principle emerging from this resolution is a significant one: *teshuva* can tear up a *gzar din* only for a *tzibur*, not for a *yachid*. After Yom Kippur, the *gzar din* of the individual stands. This is, admittedly, a radical qualification of Rabbi Yochanan's opening statement.

---

## Rain Decree Case

### Wicked→Teshuvah

A second *meitivei* objection now complicates the picture further. The *baraita* describes a scenario where God's inspection of the Land of Israel for good or ill operates throughout the year. The case for good: *harei she-hayu Yisrael resha'im gmurim b'Rosh Hashanah* — suppose Israel were completely wicked on Rosh Hashanah, and it was therefore decreed — *v'pasku lahem gshamim mu'atim* — that they would receive only a small amount of rain. Then, later in the year, *u-lesof chazru bahen* — they reversed themselves, they returned to God. Note the unusual language: the *baraita* uses *chazru*, "they reversed," rather than *asu teshuva*, "they did *teshuva*." The problem is now stark: *l'hosif aleihem i efshar, she-kvar nigzera gzeira* — you cannot add to the decree because the *gezeira* was already issued.

### Timing Solution

Yet the *gzar din* is not simply left to operate harshly. The resolution: *ela Hakadosh Baruch Hu moridam bizmanan* — God brings the rain at precisely the right time, *al ha-aretz ha-tzricha lahen* — and upon exactly the lands that need it. Even a small quantity of rain, delivered with perfect timing and precision of location, can suffice. The *gezeira* stands, but through its optimal execution, the *teshuva* has its effect. The decree itself is not nullified, but it is, in a sense, fulfilled in the most beneficial way possible.

### Righteous→Backslide

The reverse scenario: *harei she-hayu Yisrael tzaddikim gmurim b'Rosh Hashanah* — suppose Israel were completely righteous on Rosh Hashanah, and it was decreed — *v'pasku lahem gshamim merubim* — that they would receive an abundant rainfall. Then they *chazru bahen* — they slid back into sin. Again the problem: *l'fachot meihem i efshar, she-kvar nigzera gzeira* — you cannot reduce what was decreed, because the *gezeira* was already issued.

### Bad Timing

Yet here too the system finds a way to register the change in conduct: *ela Hakadosh Baruch Hu moridam she-lo bizmanan* — God sends the rain at the wrong time, when rain does damage rather than benefit, *al aretz she-eina tzricha lahen* — on the land that does not need it. The great quantity of rain is delivered, faithfully fulfilling the decree, but its effects are largely nullified. Once again, the *gzar din* is honored in letter while the people's subsequent behavior has its consequence.

---

## Tear Up vs Within

### Challenge Logic

The Gemara steps back and poses a sharp question. If, as Rabbi Yochanan teaches, *teshuva* genuinely has the power to *kera'* — to tear up — the *gzar din*, why in the case of the wicked who repented did God not simply tear up the decree of meager rain altogether? Why work within the constraint of the original judgment at all, adjusting only its timing and placement, rather than fully reversing it?

### System Preference

The Gemara answers: *shani hatam de'efshar behachi* — there it is different, because it was possible to achieve the desired result while working within the existing framework. The Gemara affirms, however, that *if* working within the system were not possible — *ai hachi nami* — God would indeed tear up the *gzar din* entirely. The operating principle is thus one of minimal intervention: as long as the decree can be fulfilled in a way that honors the changed circumstances, that approach is preferred. But the capacity to fully void a *gzar din* remains.

---

## Jonah & Psalms

### Jonah Reversal

The Gemara notes that the reading of Sefer Yonah on Yom Kippur provides a clear instance of this very principle in action — God reverses His decree entirely in response to the repentance of a *tzibur*. The imagery of the Book of Yonah is precisely about a divine decree being issued and then revoked, and this is of course a *tzibur*, not a *yachid*, which is consistent with what has been established.

### Sea Voyage Psalm

The Gemara then brings *ta shema* from the *pesukim* in Tehillim describing those who go down to the sea in ships — *yoredei hayam be'oniyot, osei melacha bemayim rabim* — those who do their work on the great waters. They see the wondrous works of God: *vayomar vaya'amod ruach se'ara vateromeim galav, yachogu veyanu'u kashikor* — a great storm wind arises, the waves mount high, the sailors stagger and reel like drunkards. Then: *vayitz'aku el Hashem batzar lahem* — they cry out to God in their distress. And God saves them. *Yodu l'Hashem chasdo* — they give thanks to God for His kindness.

### Inverted Nuns

Here the Gemara makes a striking observation. In the text of these *pesukim* in Tanakh, there appear special typographical markings — inverted *nun* letters — at the beginning of the relevant verses, precisely where the passage appears. The Gemara notes: *aseh lahen simaniyot k'achin ve'rachin she'baTorah* — God made these little signs, similar to the *achin* and *rachin* of the Torah, those words or markers which introduce a qualification or limitation. Rashi relates this to the inverted *nun* found in the passage of *vayehi binsoa* — it is exactly that form of textual indicator. These inverted *nun* letters function, as the Gemara puts it, like an asterisk attached to a grand promise: the verses describe God's magnificent salvation of those who cry out at sea, but the asterisk signals that this promise is not unconditional.

### Asterisk Meaning

What does the asterisk — the qualification — mean? The Gemara explains: *tza'aku kodem gezar din na'anin* — if they cried out to God before *gzar din*, they will be answered. *Tza'aku le'achar gezar din einan na'anin* — if they cried out after *gzar din*, they will not be answered. This would seem to cut against the earlier principle that a *tzibur* can always reverse its *gzar din*. The Gemara responds: *hani nami keyichidim dami* — these sailors, even if many of them are aboard, are regarded as *yechidim*, as individuals, not as a *tzibur* in the relevant sense. They do not constitute a communal body whose collective repentance carries the force needed to overturn a communal decree.

---

## Akiva's Timing

### Bluriah Challenge

The Gemara now brings a further dispute. *Sha'ala Bluriya hagiyoret* — Bluriah the convert posed a challenge to Rabban Gamliel. She noted an apparent contradiction in the Torah: on the one hand, *asher lo yisa panim* — God does not show favor or partiality; on the other hand, *yisa Hashem panav eilecha* — God will lift His countenance toward you. Is God partial or is He not? It is worth noting that in the *She'iltot* the word *be'Torat'chem* — "in your Torah" — does not appear in this version of the story, since that formulation is typically used when a non-Jew challenges the rabbis, whereas Bluriah was herself a convert; perhaps the question was posed before her conversion.

### Debtor Parable

Rabbi Yosei HaKohen was designated to respond. He offered a *mashal*: *emshol lakh mashal l'mah hadavar domeh* — to what may this be compared? To a person who lent his friend a hundred *maneh*, and they went before the king, and the borrower swore by the life of the king that he would repay by a certain date. The time arrived and he did not pay. He then came before the king to seek forgiveness. The king said to him: *elboni machul lach* — my personal offense I forgive you; *lech u-fayes et chaveircha* — go and appease your friend who is owed the money, for that debt remains outstanding.

### God vs Man

The application: *kan bein adam la-makom kan bein adam la-chavero* — the two verses refer to two different categories of sin. When it comes to sins *bein adam la-makom*, between a person and God, *yisa Hashem panav eilecha* — God lifts His countenance and forgives. But *asher lo yisa panim* — God will not show favor when the sin is *bein adam la-chavero*, between one person and another, and the human victim has not yet been appeased.

### Akiva Resolve

Rabbi Akiva, however, offered a different resolution. He read the two verses as referring not to two categories of sin, but to two temporal stages: *kan kodem gzar din kan le'achar gzar din* — one verse speaks of before *gzar din*, the other of after *gzar din*. Before *gzar din*, God will forgive; after *gzar din*, He will not. The Gemara responds that this still does not contradict the earlier framework: *hacha nami be-yachid* — here too we are speaking of a *yachid*. Rabbi Akiva's rule thus applies to the individual, consistent with what has been established throughout.

---

## Yachid Reversible

### Twin Cases

Having repeatedly reached the conclusion that after *gzar din* a *yachid* cannot reverse the decree, the Gemara now signals that this is itself a matter of Talmudic dispute. *Ve-gzar din de-yachid tannai hi* — the question of whether the *gzar din* of a *yachid* can be overturned is a *machloket tannaim*, a dispute among the Tannaim. The *baraita* presents two parallel cases: *shnayim she-alu le-mita ve-cholyan shaveh* — two people who fell ill with the same illness, and *shnayim she-alu le-gardom* — two people brought before the court to be judged for a capital crime (*gardom*, from the Latin, refers to the place of execution, something like a gallows). In both cases the two individuals were in identical situations — same illness, same verdict — yet their outcomes diverged: one recovered and one died; one was acquitted and one was executed.

### Meir's Prayer

Rabbi Meir's explanation for this divergence: the difference was not in what happened externally but in the quality of prayer. *Zeh hitpalel tefilla shleima ne'eneh ve-zeh lo hitpalel tefilla shleima lo ne'eneh* — one prayed a complete, full prayer and was answered; the other did not pray a complete prayer and was not answered. This raises the deeper question of why one prayer was answered and another not — Rabbi Meir's answer is the qualitative difference in the *tefilla* itself. It is an attempt to account for the variance in outcome, attributing it to the depth and wholeness of the individual's supplication.

### Elazar Timing

Rabbi Elazar offers an entirely different explanation: *kan kodem gzar din kan le'achar gzar din* — perhaps one of the individuals had already been assigned a *gzar din* by Rosh Hashanah, while the other had not. Their situations looked identical on earth, but in heaven one had an unalterable decree against him and one did not. On this reading, the *gzar din* of the *yachid* cannot be reversed — the variation in outcome simply reflects a difference in what was decreed on Rosh Hashanah, not any differential response to prayer.

### Yitzchak Both Times

Rabbi Yitzchak, however, takes the position we have been looking for: *yafa tze'aka la-adam bein kodem gzar din bein le'achar gzar din* — crying out is beneficial for a person both before *gzar din* and after *gzar din*. Notice that Rabbi Yitzchak uses the language of *tze'aka*, crying out, echoing the earlier context of the sailors at sea and the language of urgent supplication, rather than specifically *teshuva*. His position is that even for a *yachid*, even after a *gzar din* has been issued, there remains the possibility of reversal. He does not resolve the question of why one person survived and another did not — but he establishes the principle that the gate is never fully closed for the individual either.

---

## Tzibur Gezar Din

### Jeremiah Contradiction

Having now affirmed that for the *yachid* the matter is debated, the Gemara pivots to the *tzibur* — which we have been treating as the straightforward case for reversibility — and asks: *ve-gzar din d'tzibur mi mikra?* — who says the *gzar din* of a *tzibur* can be torn up at all? The proof comes from a pair of verses in Yirmiyahu that appear to contradict one another. One verse says: *kabb'si me'ra'ah libbech* — cleanse your heart from evil, implying that atonement is possible. The other says: *im t'khabb'si baneter v'tarbi lach borit nikhtam avonech l'fanai* — even if you scrub yourself with lye and use abundant soap, your sin remains stained before Me. The second verse seems to say that no amount of purification can remove the sin — suggesting that even for the *tzibur* there is a point of no return.

### Shevu'ah Factor

The Gemara resolves: *lo kashya, kan b'gezar din she'yesh immo shevu'ah, kan b'gezar din she'ein immo shevu'ah* — it is not difficult; the two verses refer to different categories of *gzar din*. One speaks of a *gzar din* without a *shevu'ah*, and there the *tzibur* can have its decree torn up. The other speaks of a *gzar din* that is accompanied by a divine oath, a *shevu'ah*, and there even the collective cannot reverse the decree. The Gemara has thus introduced yet another layer in the hierarchy of divine judgment: the question is not only whether a decree has been issued, not only whether it has been sealed, not only whether it applies to an individual or community — but also whether God has bound the decree with an oath.

---

## Shevu'ah Oath

### Eli Oath Source

The Gemara now asks: from where do we know that there is such a category as a *gzar din* accompanied by a *shevu'ah* that cannot be torn up? The proof text: *ul'khen nishba'ti l'veit Eli im yitkapper avon beit Eli b'zevach u'v'minchah* — I have sworn concerning the house of Eli that the sin of the house of Eli will not be atoned for by sacrifice or meal-offering. God here explicitly takes an oath that the decree against the house of Eli is irrevocable, at least through the means of sacrifice. This is the source for the category of *gzar din she'yesh immo shevu'ah*.

### Torah Loophole

But the Gemara will not let this stand unchallenged either. Rava says: *b'zevach u'v'minchah eino mitkapper, aval mitkapper b'Torah* — the sin cannot be atoned through sacrifice or meal-offering, as the oath specifies, but it *can* be atoned through Torah study. The oath closes one door but leaves another open — the *shevu'ah* was specific to the mode of *kaparah*, not to the possibility of atonement altogether.

### Chesed Factor

Abaye goes further: *b'zevach u'v'minchah eino mitkapper, aval mitkapper b'Torah u'v'gemilut chasadim* — it can be atoned through Torah and through *gemilut chasadim*, acts of lovingkindness. Abaye adds to Rava's formulation the dimension of ethical engagement with the world beyond the *beit midrash*.

### Eli Descendants

The reason this is not merely theoretical becomes apparent immediately: *Rabbah v'Abaye mi'devei Eli ka'atu* — Rabbah and Abaye were both descendants of the house of Eli. The question of whether the curse of Eli's line could be mitigated was, for them, an entirely personal one. It should be noted that there is a question in the *rishonim* whether the first statement should be attributed to Rava or Rabbah — most prefer Rabbah, since Eli was a *kohen* and Rava was not, though Rashi notes that perhaps through his mother's line Rava too descended from Beit Eli, which would raise the interesting question of whether the curse followed the maternal line as well.

### Lifespan Evidence

The Gemara provides a striking demonstration of the differential effect of Torah alone versus Torah together with *gemilut chasadim*. *Rabbah d'asak b'Torah chaya arba'in shanin* — Rabbah, who engaged primarily in Torah learning, lived forty years. *Abaye d'asak b'Torah u'v'gemilut chasadim chaya shitin shanin* — Abaye, who engaged in Torah *and* in *gemilut chasadim*, lived sixty years. The context matters: without any *kaparah* at all, members of Eli's line apparently died far younger than even forty, as the subsequent *baraita* will show. Even forty years represented a partial atonement through Torah; sixty represented a fuller one through Torah combined with active kindness.

Tosafot notes a potential tension here: in *Perek Chelek*, Abaye himself says to Rabbah that the master possesses Torah *and* *gemilut chasadim* — implying that Rabbah too had significant *gemilut chasadim*. Tosafot resolves this by saying that *mikol makom Abaye asik tifei minei* — nevertheless, Abaye was more *oseik* in it than Rabbah was. There is a meaningful distinction between performing acts of kindness and making *gemilut chasadim* a defining commitment and orientation of one's religious life. Abaye had made it such a commitment, and the lifespan differential reflects it.

This is, it should be noted, a remarkably powerful statement emanating from within the rabbinic world itself: the difference between a life lived entirely within the *beit midrash* and a life in which Torah study propels one outward into acts of care for others carries, according to this *gemara*, real and measurable consequence.

---

## Eli Family Torah

### Death at 18

The Gemara now presents a *baraita* that provides concrete context for the severity of the curse upon Eli's house. *Mishpacha achas haysa bi-Yerushalayim she-hayu meseha mesim bnei yud ches shanah* — there was a family in Jerusalem in which all the young men died at eighteen years of age. The family came and reported this pattern to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.

### Zakkai Diagnosis

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked them: *shema mi-mishpachat Eli atem?* — perhaps you are from the family of Eli? He cited the verse: *ve-chol marbis beischa yamusun anashim* — all the multitude of your house shall die as men in their prime. His response to their plight was direct: *lechu ve-isku ba-Torah va-chyu* — go and engage in Torah study, and you will live.

### Torah Success

*Halchu ve-isku ba-Torah va-chyu* — they went, they learned Torah, and they lived. *Ve-hayu korin osam mishpachat Yochanan al shemo* — they were thereafter called the family of Yochanan, in his honor. It is worth noting that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai prescribed Torah alone, without explicitly adding *gemilut chasadim* — though this need not be read as a contradiction to Abaye's formulation. One might also observe the broader symbolic resonance: the *korbanos* that once atoned, and whose channel was closed by the oath, have been replaced in the post-*churban* world by Torah study — itself understood as the successor to the sacrificial service. The sin of Beit Eli was rooted in the abuse of priestly power; its remedy is found in the democratizing, non-hierarchical pursuit of *talmud Torah*.

---

## Tzibur Sealed

### Never Sealed

Rav Shmuel bar Inya, citing Rav, introduces a further principle: *minayin le-gezar din shel tzibur she-eino nechtam?* — from where do we know that the *gzar din* of a *tzibur* is never finally sealed? The implication is remarkable: not only can the communal decree be torn up even after issuance, but it is never truly sealed in the first place — the door always remains open.

---

## Tzibur Sealed (II)

### Sealed Verse

The Gemara immediately challenges this claim. The very verse cited earlier — *nechtam avonech lefanai* — your sin is sealed before Me, with *nechtam* serving as a play on *nechtam* — seems to imply that there is such a thing as a sealed communal decree. This was, after all, Yirmiyahu's address to the entire people.

### Can Tear Up

The Gemara resolves: *ela af al gav she-nechtam nikra* — even if it is sealed, for a *tzibur* the *gzar din* can still be torn up. The sealing does not carry the same finality for a community as it might for an individual. The *tzibur* retains the capacity to reverse even what has been sealed against it.

### Isaiah Proof

The proof text: *ka-Hashem Elokeinu be-chol koreinu eilav* — like Hashem our God, whenever we call out to Him. The *be-chol* — whenever, at all times — establishes the permanent and unconditional availability of divine responsiveness to communal prayer, even in the face of a sealed decree.

---

## Yachid Seek Days

### When Found

The Gemara then takes up the verse from Yeshayahu: *dirshu Hashem be-himmatz'o* — seek God when He can be found. The word *be-himmatz'o*, "when He can be found," introduces a temporal qualification: God is not equally available at all moments. For the *tzibur*, as just established, He is available *be-chol koreinu eilav* — at all times. But the verse *dirshu Hashem be-himmatz'o* applies to the *yachid*, for whom divine receptivity is circumscribed by timing.

### Ten Days RH-YK

*Amar Rabbah bar Avuha: elu asarah yamim shebein Rosh Hashanah le-Yom ha-Kippurim* — these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. It should be noted that there are not literally ten full days between the two holidays — there are seven or eight, depending on whether Rosh Hashanah is observed for one or two days. The count of ten is arrived at inclusively, counting Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur themselves. These *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah* constitute the window during which even the *yachid* finds God particularly receptive, and during which the *gzar din* of the individual can potentially be reversed.

### Naval Reprieve

A proof for this ten-day framework is adduced from the story of Naval: *vayehi ke'aseret hayamim vayigof Hashem et Naval* — it was after ten days that God smote Naval. The Gemara asks: *yud yemei mai avidtaihu?* — what was the significance of those ten days? Rav Yehuda citing Rav answers: they corresponded to the ten meals Naval had given to David's servants — Rashi understands this not as ten separate occasions but as ten people served at one meal, yet constituting ten discrete acts of hospitality, which earned Naval a ten-day reprieve. Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha, however, offers the answer that ties directly to our discussion: *elu asarah yamim shebein Rosh Hashanah le-Yom ha-Kippurim* — God granted Naval the ten days of the *Aseret Yemei Teshuvah* as an opportunity to do *teshuva*, and only after those days had elapsed and he had failed to repent did God bring His judgment upon him.

---

## RH Procession

### Bnei Maron

The Gemara now returns to the *mishna*, which states: *be-Rosh Hashanah kol ba'ei olam overin lefanav kivnei maron* — on Rosh Hashanah all those who enter the world pass before God like *bnei maron*. The phrase *kivnei maron* requires explanation.

### Sheep Counting

In Bavel, the phrase was translated as *kivnei amrana*, and Rashi explains: *kekvasim shemonin otam le'asran, veyotzin zeh achar zeh befetach katan she'ein yecholim latzet k'echad* — like sheep that are counted for the tithe of *ma'aser behema*, passing single file through a narrow opening, one after another, since they cannot exit together. This is the image of God as shepherd passing the flock through individually, counting and assessing each one.

### Mountain Pass

Reish Lakish explains *kivnei maron* differently: *kema'alot Beit Maron* — like those ascending the ascents of Beit Maron, a narrow mountain road where, with a deep valley on either side, travelers must proceed one at a time, with a sheer drop on both sides. ArtScroll and Steinsaltz suggest this may refer specifically to Har Meron in northern Israel, which has just such a steep and dangerous path. This is arguably the most viscerally frightening of the three images: one walks a narrow precipice, a small misstep sending one plunging into the valley below. It captures the sense of life hanging by a thread, the precariousness of one's judgment.

### Soldiers Ready

Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, offers the third interpretation: *k'chayalot shel Beit David* — like the soldiers of the house of David. Rashi connects *maron* to *lashon marut v'adnut*, a language of mastery and lordship. But Steinsaltz notes that manuscripts read *kivnumeron* rather than *kivnei maron*, and that the word derives from the Latin *numerus*, borrowed also into Greek as *numeron*, meaning a military unit — *anshei tzava*. Moreover, there exists in Greek the expression of people standing *like a numeron*, as soldiers stand for inspection. This etymology almost certainly underlies Rav Yehuda's reading. The imagery here is one of pride and readiness: soldiers who have prepared themselves, polished their equipment, and stand at attention for inspection. It evokes a very different emotional posture from the other two — not the helplessness of the sheep nor the terror of the precipice, but the dignity of one who has done the work and stands ready to be reviewed.

Each of these three images captures something distinct about the experience of standing in divine judgment on Rosh Hashanah: the trusting helplessness of the sheep before the shepherd; the terrifying fragility of the mountain pass; the prepared, upright bearing of the soldier before his king.

### One Glance

Having described how all of humanity passes in procession before God — individually, one by one — the Gemara immediately adds the counterpoint. *Amar Rabbah bar bar Chana amar Rabbi Yochanan: v'chulan niskarin b'skira achat* — and yet all of them are surveyed in a single glance. God beholds every human being individually, yet encompasses them all simultaneously. The judgment is personal and particular, and it is also total and instantaneous.

### Mishnah Support

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that this principle is already implicit in the *mishna* itself, which closes with the verse *hayotzer yachad libam hamevin el kol ma'aseihem* — He who fashions their hearts as one, who understands all their deeds. The Gemara clarifies: the verse does not mean that God unifies all human hearts into a single unity — we observe that the world is manifestly not unified in that way. Rather, *hayotzer yachad libam* means that God sees all hearts as one, *ro'eh yachad libam*, perceiving every individual heart simultaneously, *u-mevin el kol ma'aseihem* — and understands every deed of every person at once. The many are seen individually; the many are also seen together. Both are true.

---

## Six Rosh Chodesh

### Six Month List

The *mishna* continues: *al shisha devarim ha-shuluchim yotzim* — on account of six matters, messengers go out to announce the *rosh chodesh* to distant communities. The six months are: Nisan, on account of Pesach; Av, on account of the fast; Elul, on account of Rosh Hashanah — since one cannot send messengers on Rosh Hashanah itself to announce when Rosh Hashanah is, messengers are sent after *rosh chodesh Elul*, and since Elul is almost always twenty-nine days, communities can calculate Rosh Hashanah accordingly; Tishrei, on account of the regulation of the holidays — after Rosh Hashanah, messengers are sent out to confirm or correct the date of *rosh chodesh Tishrei* so that the subsequent *mo'adim* can be properly observed; Kislev, on account of Chanukah; and Adar, on account of Purim. Shavuot does not require its own messengers because it is calculated from Pesach.

### Temple Pesach 2

The *mishna* adds: *ve-cheshe-haya beit ha-mikdash kayam, yotzim af al Iyar mipnei pesach katan* — when the Temple stood, messengers also went out for Iyar, on account of *Pesach Sheni*, so that people who had been unable to bring the *korban pesach* in Nisan would know the correct date on which to bring it in Iyar. This detail confirms that the *mishna*'s framing is from a post-*churban* perspective — the *pesach* mentioned in the context of Nisan refers to *chag ha-matzot*, not to the *korban pesach*, since the special provision for the Temple period is noted separately.

---

## Six Rosh Chodesh (II)

### Minor Fasts

The Gemara asks: *ve-lifok nami ateivet ve-tamuz?* — why not also send out messengers for Tevet and Tammuz, so that communities know when to observe the fasts of *asarah b'Tevet* and *shiva asar b'Tammuz*? This leads into a broader discussion of the halakhic status of the minor fast days.

---

## Zechariah Fasts

### Four Fasts

The Gemara cites Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida, who asks: what is the meaning of the verse in Zechariah — *ko amar Hashem Tzevaos: tzom ha-revi'i ve-tzom ha-chamishi ve-tzom ha-shvi'i ve-tzom ha-asiri yihiyeh le-veit Yehudah le-sason u-le-simcha* — so says the Lord of Hosts: the fast of the fourth, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become for the house of Judah days of joy and gladness. The prophecy was delivered in the context of the return from exile and the rebuilding of the Temple, when the people asked whether the fasts they had observed through the period of destruction should continue. The answer was that those fast days would be transformed into days of rejoicing.

But the verse creates an internal tension: *kari lei tzom ve-kari lei sason ve-simcha* — it calls the same days both a fast and a time of joy and gladness. The Gemara treats this as a difficulty requiring resolution.

### Peace Determines

Rav Pappa resolves it: *biz'man she-yesh shalom, yihyu le-sason u-le-simcha* — when there is true peace, when times are good and the Temple stands, those days are transformed into days of joy. *Yesh gzeiras ha-malchus* — when there is governmental persecution, when the people are actively oppressed, *tzom* — they are observed as fast days. This is the extreme of suffering: the fast days are mandatory expressions of mourning under conditions of oppression.

### Three States

*Ein gzeiras ha-malchus, ein shalom* — when there is neither active oppression nor true peace — in other words, the condition of exile without persecution, roughly describing much of Jewish history in the diaspora — then *ratzu mis'anim ratzu ein mis'anim*: if the community wishes to fast, it may; if not, it is not obligated. The minor fast days in such a middle-ground period are optional. This has genuine halakhic implications: in principle, under conditions that are neither shalom nor governmental persecution, an individual or even a community could elect not to observe the minor fasts.

### Tisha B'Av Special

*Ei hachi Tisha B'Av nami?* — if that is so, the same logic should apply to Tisha B'Av, which also appears in the Zechariah verse. The Gemara firmly rejects this: *shani Tisha B'Av ho'il ve-huchplu bo tzaros* — Tisha B'Av is different, because multiple catastrophes accumulated upon it. *De-amar Mar: be-Tisha B'Av charav ha-bayis be-rishona u-ve-shniya, ve-nilkeda Beitar, ve-nechrasha ha-ir* — the Temple was destroyed both the first and second time, Beitar was destroyed, and the city was plowed over. Tosafot notes that while multiple tragedies also befell *shiva asar b'Tammuz*, the weight of Tisha B'Av is qualitatively different — not only does it carry the burden of the same tragedy having occurred twice, but the *churban* itself, the destruction of the Temple, is so fundamental a catastrophe that it places Tisha B'Av in a category of its own. Tisha B'Av is also distinguished in that it begins from the night before, whereas the other fasts do not — though the full elaboration of these distinctions awaits the study of *Maseches Taanis*.

---

## Fast Days Order

### Month Numbers

A *baraita* is now cited that unpacks the Zechariah verse by identifying each of the four fasts. Rabbi Shimon prefaces the discussion by noting that there were four matters on which Rabbi Akiva offered interpretations with which he himself disagrees.

### Breach Tammuz

*Tzom ha-revi'i* — the fast of the fourth month — is *shiva asar b'Tammuz*, the 17th of Tammuz, the month counted as the fourth from Nisan. *Shebo hufke'ah ha-ir* — that is when the city of Jerusalem was breached. The proof text: *b'tisha lachodesh vayechazak ha-ra'av ba-ir ve-lo hayah lechem l'am ha'aretz, va-tibaka ha-ir* — on the ninth of the month the famine was severe and the city was breached. The verse says the ninth, yet we observe the fast on the 17th. Tosafot explains: in the first Temple the city was indeed breached on the ninth of Tammuz, but in the second Temple it was breached on the 17th, and since it is the second Temple's chronology that governs our practice, the fast is observed on the 17th. However, Tosafot also cites a remarkable passage from the Yerushalmi: the *baraita* there reads the date as the 17th even for the first Temple, and explains that while the verse says the ninth, the correct date was actually the 17th — but such was the turmoil and distress of that moment that the people got the date wrong. *Mitoch tirdasam ta'u b'cheshbonam* — in the midst of their anguish they erred in their reckoning. And the Torah records the date as they believed it to be, even though the actual date was the 17th. This is a striking claim: that the *pasuk* records a mistaken date out of a kind of deference to the perception of those who experienced the catastrophe.

### Burn Av

*Tzom ha-chamishi* — the fast of the fifth month — is Tisha B'Av: *shebo nisraf beis elokeinu* — the day on which the House of our God was burned.

### Gedaliah 3 Tishrei

*Tzom ha-shvi'i* — the fast of the seventh month — is the third of Tishrei: *shebo neherag Gedalyah ben Achikam* — the day on which Gedalyah ben Achikam was murdered by Yishmael ben Nesanyah. The *baraita* draws a pointed lesson: *l'lamedcha she-shkulah misasan shel tzaddikim k'sreifat beis elokeinu* — to teach you that the death of the righteous is as weighty in God's eyes as the burning of the Temple. The assassination of Gedalyah appears in the same list as the destruction of the Temple, and is given equivalent halakhic status. One might note the painful irony: Gedalyah accepted lashon hara about the plot against his life, and was murdered as a result — yet it is he who is called righteous and his death that receives this weight.

### Siege Teves

*Tzom ha-asiri* — the fast of the tenth month — according to Rabbi Akiva is *asarah b'Tevet*, the tenth of Tevet, the month of Tevet being the tenth counting from Nisan. *Shebo samach melech Bavel al Yerushalayim* — that is when the king of Babylon laid siege to Jerusalem, as the verse states: *ben adam ksov lecha et shem hayom hazeh, et esem hayom hazeh, samach melech Bavel al Yerushalayim* — son of man, inscribe for yourself the very name of this day, this very day, on which the king of Babylon drew close to Jerusalem. The question is then asked: why is *asarah b'Tevet* listed last in the verse, as the fourth in the sequence, when chronologically the siege occurred first — before the breaching, before the destruction, before the assassination of Gedalyah? Rabbi Akiva's answer: *k'dei l'hasdir chadashim k'tiknan* — the verse lists the fasts in calendar order of their months, not in chronological order of the events. The sequence goes fourth month, fifth month, seventh month, tenth month — reflecting the month numbers, not the sequence of historical events.

### Report 5 Teves

Rabbi Shimon disagrees with Rabbi Akiva's reading of *tzom ha-asiri*. *Ella tzom ha-asiri zeh chamishah b'Tevet* — the fast of the tenth is not *asarah b'Tevet* at all, but rather the fifth of Tevet. What happened on the fifth of Tevet? *Shebo ba'ah shemuah la-golah she-hukta ha-ir* — that is the day on which the report reached the exile that the city had been destroyed. The proof: *vayehi b'shteim esre shanah b'asiri b'chamishah lachodesh legalutenu, ba elai ha-palit mi-Yerushalayim leimor, hukta ha-ir* — in the twelfth year of our exile, in the tenth month on the fifth of the month, the refugee from Jerusalem came to say that the city had been struck down. The fifth of Tevet was when the exiles — those who had been sent away to Bavel a decade or more before the *churban* — first heard the news of the Temple's destruction. *Va-asu yom shemuah k'yom sereifah* — and the day of hearing the report was treated as equivalent to the day of the burning itself, just as in matters of *aveilut* the moment of receiving tidings of a death carries its own weight.

### Shimon Order

Rabbi Shimon's logic is elegant: *she-ani omer rishon rishon ve-achron achron* — I maintain that the events are listed in perfect chronological order. The siege came first (*asarah b'Tevet* by Rabbi Akiva's reading), then the breaching of the city (*shiva asar b'Tammuz*), then the destruction of the Temple (*Tisha B'Av*), then the assassination of Gedalyah (*third of Tishrei*), and finally — the report reaching the exile (*fifth of Tevet*). By identifying *tzom ha-asiri* as the fifth of Tevet rather than the tenth, Rabbi Shimon achieves both goals simultaneously: the months remain in ascending numerical order, *and* the historical events are listed in the precise sequence in which they unfolded. *Ve-hu omer al rishon achron ve-al achron rishon* — whereas Rabbi Akiva, in placing the siege last in the list, has the first event appearing at the end and uses the ordering of months alone as his rationale. *Va-ani moneh l'seder pur'anut* — Rabbi Shimon concludes: I list them in the order of the catastrophes themselves. The daf concludes here, and we will resume tomorrow with a full understanding of the fast days that underlie this discussion.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 19

## Megillat Ta'anit Status

### Rav vs. Rabbi Yochanan

The daf opens with an *itmar* — a recorded dispute among Amoraim — presenting two diametrically opposed positions regarding *Megillat Ta'anit*. Rav and Rabbi Chanina (some versions read Rav Huna and Rabbi Chanina) hold *batla Megillat Ta'anit* — the scroll of fasts has been annulled. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagree, maintaining *lo batla Megillat Ta'anit* — its halakhic status remains intact.

### What is Megillat Ta'anit

*Megillat Ta'anit* is an ancient document dating from the Second Temple period, listing all the dates on which fasting and *hesped* (eulogizing) are prohibited — minor festivals that were decreed for the Jewish people, many connected to events of the Temple era or to the Hasmonean period. Chanukah, as we will see, is among the days listed. The document is notable for its brevity: each entry consists of the date and a terse half-sentence explanation of the historical event it commemorates, making it a source of genuine historical significance for the Second Temple period. It is written in Aramaic — the vernacular of the time — and was actually committed to writing even during the era of oral tradition, which is why it is called a *megillah* in the first place.

We do possess manuscript copies of *Megillat Ta'anit*, though not from the original period, and there is an excellent modern critical edition by the Israeli scholar Vered Noam. In addition to the core text, there exists a *scholion* — later elaborations written in the Talmudic or post-Talmudic period — which at times reflects the Gemara's own discussions of the entries. This is relevant to the *sugyot* surrounding Chanukah as well: the *scholion* traditions about the miracle of the oil show evidence of having been shaped and hybridized by the Gemara's own treatment of the topic.

The central halakhic question, then, is whether the status of these minor festival days endures. Most of the events they commemorate were tied to the Second Temple and have little resonance for later generations. Did those days retain their character as minor *yamim tovim*, continuing to prohibit fasting and eulogizing? Or, with the absence of the Temple and the changed circumstances of exile, did they lose that status?

### Five Fast Days Reversed

The Gemara begins its analysis by connecting the question to the earlier discussion of the five fast days mentioned in Zechariah. The verse may be read as follows: when there is peace — *bizman sheyesh shalom* — those days that had been fast days will turn into days of rejoicing; when there is no peace — *ein shalom, tzom* — they revert to being fast days. Rav and Rabbi Chanina apply this paradigm to *Megillat Ta'anit*: just as the five fast days lose their character as days of rejoicing when the *Beit Hamikdash* is absent and revert to their original nature as days of mourning, so too the minor holidays of *Megillat Ta'anit* lose their festive status in the post-*churban* reality.

The analogy is admittedly strange. The five fast days began as days of tragedy — their natural state is mourning. During the era of the Second Temple they were transformed, paradoxically, into days of rejoicing, a kind of "last laugh" of history. With no *Beit Hamikdash*, they revert to that natural state. By contrast, the days in *Megillat Ta'anit* began as days of celebration — their natural state is festivity. One might argue they should retain that status even without the Temple. The very comparison thus seems to cut against Rav and Rabbi Chanina's position. Nevertheless, that is the analogy they offer.

### Fundamental vs. Continge…

Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi respond to this argument directly. It is specifically the five fast days whose festive status is *explicitly* tied by the verse to the existence of the *Beit Hamikdash* — *talia Rachmana bevinyan Beit Hamikdash*. Those days' transformation into days of joy was always conditional on the Temple's presence. But the days listed in *Megillat Ta'anit* carry no such condition. Their status as holidays is not contingent on the *Beit Hamikdash*, and therefore — *kidekai kai* — they stand on their own terms. Stated more simply: the five fast days are fundamentally fast days that were temporarily elevated; without the Temple they revert. The *Megillat Ta'anit* days are fundamentally holidays; without the Temple, they remain holidays.

---

## Lod Fast on Chanukah

### Lod Fast Declared

Rav Kahana raises a challenge from a recorded incident: *ma'aseh vegezeru ta'anit beChangukah beLod* — there was a case in Lod where a fast was declared on Chanukah. Whether the motivation was a need for rain or some other pressing circumstance, those who declared the fast were treating Chanukah as a day on which the prohibitions of *Megillat Ta'anit* no longer applied — that is, they were acting in accordance with the position of *batla Megillat Ta'anit*.

### Public Demonstration

The response of the Sages was swift and public. Rabbi Eliezer went and bathed, and Rabbi Yehoshua went and got a haircut — acts that explicitly violated the norms of a fast day, performed openly to demonstrate that they did not recognize the fast's validity. They then declared to those who had fasted: *tze'u vehit'anu al mah shehit'anitem* — go now and make a fast as *teshuvah* for having fasted. Their willingness to do so publicly shows that *lo batla Megillat Ta'anit* — the prohibition on fasting on Chanukah remained in force.

### Tosafot: Holiday vs. Fas…

Before one concludes from this incident that it constitutes proof against *batla Megillat Ta'anit*, Tosafot makes an important observation. One might have thought that the Mishnah's continued treatment of Chanukah as a holiday — with candle-lighting and *Al Hanissim* — itself proves *lo batla Megillat Ta'anit*. Tosafot rejects this inference. It is entirely possible to hold *batla Megillat Ta'anit* and still light Chanukah candles. The candle-lighting and commemoration of the miracle stand independently of the question of *Megillat Ta'anit*'s annulment. *Batla Megillat Ta'anit* addresses only whether a day has the status of a minor *yom tov* such that fasting and *hesped* are forbidden on it — not whether other *mitzvot* associated with that day continue to be observed.

### Status Independence

This distinction is critical. What the people of Lod were doing was precisely this: they acknowledged Chanukah as a day of candle-lighting while treating the fasting prohibition as annulled — holding that *batla Megillat Ta'anit* removes only the *ta'anit* prohibition, not the observances connected to the miracle itself. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua rejected that position, insisting that *lo batla Megillat Ta'anit* — Chanukah retains its full status including the prohibition on fasting. The halakhic status of Chanukah as a day of *hadlakat nerot* and its status as a day on which fasting is forbidden are conceptually separable, even if in practice both apply.

---

## Chanukah's Special Status

### Chanukah Has Mitzvah

Rav Yosef draws a conclusion from the Lod incident: the incident demonstrates *lo batla Megillat Ta'anit*, at least with respect to Chanukah. But this leads to an immediate qualification: *shani Chanukah d'ika mitzvah* — Chanukah is different because it has a specific *mitzvah*, namely candle-lighting. One cannot simply extrapolate from Chanukah's retained status to the retained status of all other days in *Megillat Ta'anit*.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye presses back: if we are in a position of *batla Megillat Ta'anit* for the other days, why not go further and eliminate Chanukah entirely — including its candle-lighting? Why should the existence of a *mitzvah* associated with a day preserve its status if we are annulling the framework within which that day's significance was established? In other words, if *batla Megillat Ta'anit* sweeps away the minor holidays, why does the associated *mitzvah* of Chanukah save it?

### Pirsumei Nisa Argument

Rav Yosef refines his answer: *shani Chanukah demefarsam nisa* — Chanukah is different because the miracle was very public. The principle of *pirsumei nisa* — publicizing the miracle — carries particular weight. Whether this means the miracle itself was objectively greater in its visibility, or that the value placed on publicizing it gives Chanukah an enduring significance that other *Megillat Ta'anit* days lack, the implication is that Chanukah occupies a distinct halakhic category that survives the general annulment.

### Rashi: Social Entrenchme…

Rashi reads the situation somewhat differently. He writes: *kevar hu galuy lechol Yisrael al yedei shenahagu bo mitzvah vehiziku bo keshel Torah velo nachon levattla* — it is already manifest throughout all Israel, through the practice of its *mitzvah*, and they have treated it with the force of Torah law, and it would not be proper to annul it. For Rashi, Chanukah's retention is not primarily a function of objective factors like the nature of the miracle, but of social and communal entrenchment. It has become so deeply embedded in Jewish practice that reversing it is simply not a viable option — and that social reality is itself halakhically significant.

---

## 3rd Tishrei Holiday

### God's Name Removed

The Gemara now turns to another entry in *Megillat Ta'anit*, introduced as a further challenge: *be-telasa be-Tishrei beteilit adkarata min shtaraya* — on the third of Tishrei, the mention of God's name was removed from legal documents. This terse Aramaic formulation — characteristic of the original text — sounds at first like a negative development, but the explanation that follows reveals otherwise.

### Greek Decree & Reversal

The explanatory gloss reads: *she-gazra malchut Yavan gezerah shelo lehazkir Shem Shamayim al pihem* — the Greek kingdom decreed that the Jewish people could not mention God's name. When the Hasmoneans were victorious — *gavra malchut Chashmonai ve-nitzchum* — they instituted that God's name should be mentioned, even in legal documents. The formula they established for such documents was: in the year such-and-such of Yochanan the *Kohen Gadol*, *le-El Elyon* — to the Most High God. The presence of these Hasmonean entries in *Megillat Ta'anit* reflects the centrality of that period to the document as a whole.

### Desecration Concern

When the Sages heard of this practice of writing God's name in legal documents, they raised an objection: *limachara zeh poreh et hovo* — tomorrow a person will repay his debt, the IOU will be returned to him, and *ve-nimtza shtar mutal be-ashpah* — the document will wind up discarded in the trash, with God's name on it. The concern for the desecration of God's name in mundane discarded documents led the Sages to reverse the Hasmonean innovation and prohibit writing God's name in secular legal instruments.

### Made into Holiday

The success of this reversal — changing an entrenched practice in the business world — was itself considered a significant achievement, and the day was therefore made into a *yom tov*. It is worth noting that while coins and documents from this period do survive, including references to Yochanan the *Kohen Gadol*, no archaeological evidence of the formula *le-El Elyon* in documents has been found. Whether that means the practice never became widespread or that the Sages' intervention succeeded quickly is an open question.

---

## Tzom Gedaliah Problem

### Why Another Holiday?

Rav Acha bar Huna's question now generates one of the more striking dialectical moments in the *sugyia*. The Gemara assumes that the third of Tishrei entry was added to *Megillat Ta'anit* during the post-*churban* period — which would demonstrate *lo batla Megillat Ta'anit*, since they were still actively adding to it after the Temple's destruction. The Gemara initially tries to deflect this by saying the event occurred during the *Beit Hamikdash* era. But then a further question arises: if this happened during the time of the *Beit Hamikdash*, why was there any need to add the third of Tishrei as a minor holiday? During the Temple period, as we have established, the five classical fast days were transformed into days of rejoicing. Tzom Gedaliah — the fast of Gedaliah — was among them. The third of Tishrei is precisely the date of Tzom Gedaliah. So during the *Beit Hamikdash* period, it was already a holiday. Who needed to create a new one?

The irony is almost comic: Tzom Gedaliah, a fast commemorating a profound tragedy at the close of the First Temple period, had become a day of celebration — *lesason u'lesimcha* — during the Second Temple era. There was, so to speak, no fast to override. Why add it to *Megillat Ta'anit*?

### Strengthening via Days B…

The Gemara's answer, offered in the name of Rav, is precise: *lo nitzercha ela lesur shelefanav* — the purpose of designating the third of Tishrei as a *Megillat Ta'anit* day was not to make the day itself a holiday (it already was one), but to extend the prohibition on fasting to the day *before* it — the second of Tishrei. A *Megillat Ta'anit* day, being rabbinic, carries the effect of prohibiting fasting on the days both before and after it, and that is what the designation was intended to achieve.

The Gemara then raises a further objection: the day before the third of Tishrei is the second of Tishrei, which is the day after Rosh Hashanah — and since one does not fast on the day after a *yom tov*, why would any additional designation be necessary? The Gemara answers that Rosh Hashanah's status as a *yom tov* is biblical, and *d'Oraita lo baei chizuk* — biblical holidays do not require the halakhic "strengthening" that extends their prohibition to surrounding days. Only rabbinic designations carry that strengthening effect on adjacent days.

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic

A *Beraita* explicitly articulates this principle: the days written in *Megillat Ta'anit* — being *divrei sofrim*, rabbinic enactments — prohibit fasting on the days both before and after them; *Shabbat* and *yom tov* — being *divrei Torah*, biblical law — prohibit fasting only on the day itself, not on the surrounding days. *Divrei Torah lo tzrichim chizuk* — what rests on biblical authority does not need strengthening. *Divrei sofrim tzrichim chizuk* — rabbinic enactments do require that additional reinforcement.

The same logic applies to Tzom Gedaliah: though it had become a day of rejoicing during the Second Temple period, its halakhic basis rests on verses in Zechariah — *divrei kabbalah*, which the Gemara treats similarly to *divrei Torah*. Therefore, even as a holiday, Tzom Gedaliah would not extend its prohibition to the day before it. The Hasmonean-era addition of the third of Tishrei as a distinct *Megillat Ta'anit* day — a rabbinic designation — was thus purposeful: it extended the *ta'anit* prohibition to the second of Tishrei, something Tzom Gedaliah alone, as a quasi-biblical holiday, could not accomplish.

---

## 28 Adar: Roman Edict

### Roman Persecutions

Rav Tuvi bar Masna raises yet another entry from *Megillat Ta'anit*, this time from the Adar section: *be-esrim u-tumnia beih asas besorta tava le-Yehuda'ei, de-la i-idun m-Oraisa* — on the twenty-eighth of Adar, a good report reached the Jews, that they would not have to remove themselves from the Torah. Six words of explanation for six words of date. The Hebrew gloss then elaborates: the ruling government had decreed *shelo ya'asku ba-Torah* — that they could not engage in Torah study — *shelo yimolu es beneihem* — that they could not perform *brit milah* — and *she-yechalelu Shabbasos* — that they must violate *Shabbat*. This set of three decrees is recognizable as the pattern of Hadrianic persecution following the Bar Kokhba revolt, placing this event in the mid-second century.

### Seeking Influence

The Gemara then asks: *ma asa Yehuda ben Shamua ve-chaverav* — what did Yehuda ben Shamua and his colleagues do? Yehuda ben Shamua was a student of Rabbi Meir, himself a student of Rabbi Akiva, which firmly locates him in the post-*churban* period, in the middle to later second century. *Halchu ve-natlu eitza mi-matronisa achas* — they went and sought advice from a certain *matronisa*, a woman of high social standing in Rome, *she-kol gedolei Romi metzuyin etzlah* — with whom all the great Roman officials were to be found. Her influence over these officials gave her the access that Yehuda ben Shamua and his group needed.

### Night Protest & Appeal

Following her advice, they organized a nighttime protest — perhaps because it was safer, perhaps because the sounds of a crowd carry differently at night, or because the psychological weight of numbers feels greater in darkness. Their public declaration took the form of an appeal to shared ancestry: *lo acheichem anachnu* — are we not your brothers? *Velo benei av echad anachnu* — do we not share the same father, Yaakov? *Velo benei em achas anachnu* — do we not share the same mother, Rivka? *Mah nishtaninu mikol umma velashon* — why have we been treated differently than all other nations? The argument invoked the historical kinship between Esau and Jacob, the ancestors of Rome and Israel respectively, as a basis for appealing to Roman tolerance. The Romans generally extended a degree of religious tolerance to peoples who acknowledged their pantheon; those who did not — and Israel was uniquely in this category — strained that tolerance to its breaking point.

### Decree Reversed

Nevertheless, the appeal succeeded. *Ve-oto hayom asu yom tov* — and that day was made into a *yom tov*. Comparing this to the third of Tishrei, one is struck by the enormous disparity in significance: on one hand, a procedural religious achievement regarding God's name in commercial documents; on the other, the reversal of a decree that would have effectively suppressed Torah study, *brit milah*, and *Shabbat* observance. Both were made into *yamim tovim* — the same halakhic designation for very different magnitudes of historical event.

---

## Post-Churban Usage

### Addition Post-Churban

The Gemara now draws out the implication of the twenty-eighth of Adar entry. If *Megillat Ta'anit* had been annulled at the *churban* — *batla Megillat Ta'anit* — how could new days have been added to it afterward? The Gemara assumes from the verses in Zechariah that if the annulment occurred, it occurred at the moment of the *churban*. Yehuda ben Shamua is unambiguously post-*churban*. Adding a *yom tov* to *Megillat Ta'anit* in his time suggests the framework was still operative — *lo batla Megillat Ta'anit*.

### Pre-Churban Dating

The Gemara attempts to deflect this by suggesting that the events underlying both entries — the third of Tishrei and the twenty-eighth of Adar — took place during the *Beit Hamikdash* era. The Gemara then establishes, from the *Mishnah* in tractate *Kelim*, that Yehuda ben Shamua transmitted halakhot in the name of Rabbi Meir — and Rabbi Meir was definitively post-*churban*. This makes the claim that Yehuda ben Shamua's activities occurred during the *Beit Hamikdash* period impossible. The Gemara therefore concedes that the issue is unresolved and declares: *tannai* — this is itself a dispute among *Tannaim*.

### Tannaitic Dispute

A *Beraita* is cited: Rabbi Meir holds that the days listed in *Megillat Ta'anit* — *bein bizman sheBeit Hamikdash kayom uvein bizman she'ein Beit Hamikdash kayom asurin* — whether or not the Temple stands, retain their prohibitive status. This fits perfectly: Yehuda ben Shamua, Rabbi Meir's student, was operating under the assumption that *Megillat Ta'anit* remained active even post-*churban*, consistent with his teacher's view. Rabbi Yose takes the opposite position: *bizman sheBeit Hamikdash kayom asurin mipnei shesimcha hi lahem* — when the Temple stands they are days of joy and are forbidden; *ein Beit Hamikdash kayom mutarin mipnei she'avel hu lahem* — when there is no Temple they become permitted, because they are now days of mourning. Rabbi Yose goes even further than simply annulling the days: he regards them not merely as neutral but as actually transformed into days of loss and grief, symmetrically inverting the transformation they underwent when the Temple stood.

### Halacha: Chanukah & Purim

The Gemara then presents what appears to be a tension between two halakhic rulings — one stating *batlu* and one stating *lo batlu* — and resolves it: *kan baChanukah u'Purim, kan b'sha'ar yomei* — the ruling of *lo batlu* refers to Chanukah and Purim, which retained lasting significance; the ruling of *batlu* refers to all other days in *Megillat Ta'anit*, which lost their status after the *churban*. The reasons for Chanukah's retention have already been explored above — the entrenchment of its *mitzvot*, the weight of *pirsumei nisa*, and in Rashi's reading, the social impossibility of reversing it. Purim, one might add, rests on a biblical book entire unto itself; whatever basis *Megillat Ta'anit* might have provided for it, its retention hardly required that framework. All other minor holidays of the Second Temple period — including the twenty-seventh of Iyar commemorating the cessation of tribute to the Greeks, and all the other Hasmonean-era commemorations — were annulled, and we no longer observe any halakhic restrictions on them.

---

## Sending Shlichim

### Elul Shlichim

The Gemara now returns to the *Mishnah*. *Al Elul mipnei Rosh Hashanah* — *shlichim* were dispatched in Elul so that distant communities could determine when Rosh Hashanah would fall, on the assumption that Elul would be only twenty-nine days. Since witnesses could not be dispatched on Rosh Hashanah itself — it would already be too late — they had to go in advance.

### Tishrei Shlichim

*Ve'al Tishrei mipnei takanat hamo'adot* — they would go out again in Tishrei to confirm when Tishrei had been established, reinforcing for those communities the precise date of the *mo'adot*. This second dispatch would serve as a backup, ensuring that even if the first message had not arrived clearly, communities would know with certainty when the month began.

### Always 29 Days?

The Gemara questions the need for a second dispatch. If *shlichim* had already gone out in Elul, they would have communicated the assumption that Elul was twenty-nine days and Rosh Hashanah fell accordingly. Why go out again for Tishrei? The Gemara considers whether the answer might be that Elul could theoretically be thirty days — but then cites the statement of Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana in the name of Rav: from the time of Ezra onward, *lo matzinu Elul me'ubar* — we have never found Elul to have been thirty days. This tradition is connected to a close reading of the *pesukim* in Ezra, which Tosafot suggests implies Elul was thirty days at some earlier moment.

### Theoretical Possibility

The Gemara's response is crucial: *lo matzinu d'lo itztarich* — the fact that it has never happened is not because it is structurally impossible, but simply because the circumstances never required it. *Ha itztarich, m'abrinan leh* — if circumstances demanded, we would make Elul thirty days. What circumstances might warrant this? Rashi suggests it relates to the desire not to have Yom Kippur fall immediately adjacent to Shabbat. Tosafot disputes this, arguing that such a consideration does not qualify as *tikkun mo'adot* in the full sense the Mishnah intends, and that the relevant scenario is simply if witnesses came late and could not testify on the thirtieth day of Elul. In that case, Elul would be extended to thirty days, and *shlichim* for Tishrei would be essential.

---

## Tikkun HaMo'adot

### Better Wrong RH

The Gemara confronts a significant tension: if Elul could conceivably be thirty days, one could argue that the *Beit Din* should simply refuse to accept such testimony — protecting people from celebrating Rosh Hashanah on what they had assumed to be the right day, only to have it shifted. The Gemara rejects this. *Mutav titkalkal Rosh Hashanah v'lo yitkalkelu kulhu moadot* — it is better that Rosh Hashanah be "ruined" — meaning that some communities observed it on the wrong day due to the assumption of a twenty-nine day Elul — than that all the *mo'adot* be compromised.

### Moon Sighting Priority

The principle at stake is *tikkun hamo'adot*: the proper fixing of the festivals. The *mo'adot* must be established based on the actual appearance of the moon — testimony from witnesses who saw the new moon — and the *Beit Din* cannot manipulate that process to avoid inconvenience. Even if accepting testimony that Elul was thirty days causes communities who had assumed twenty-nine days to have observed Rosh Hashanah incorrectly, that is a lesser harm than undermining the integrity of the entire *mo'ed* system by refusing valid testimony. The *shlichim* for Tishrei must therefore always go out, because there always remains the theoretical possibility — however rarely realized — that Elul was a full thirty-day month.

### Lunar Basis

The Gemara infers from the language of the Mishnah itself — *tikkun hamo'adot* — that the *mo'adot* are indeed grounded in the actual appearance of the moon, not in a fixed arithmetic cycle. The months are lunar-based and tied to real astronomical events, and the entire system of witnesses and *Beit Din* declaration exists precisely because the calendar is responsive to that appearance, not predetermined independently of it.

---

## Chanukah & Purim

### Listed in Mishnah

The Mishnah lists Kislev and Adar as months for which *shlichim* are dispatched — Kislev for Chanukah and Adar for Purim. This is entirely consistent with the Gemara's earlier conclusion that Chanukah and Purim are the two rabbinic holidays that survived the annulment of *Megillat Ta'anit* and retain lasting significance requiring communal coordination.

### Adar Sheni Omission

A closer look at the Mishnah reveals a notable omission: when a leap year is declared, the Mishnah does not mention sending *shlichim* for Adar Sheni, even though Purim is celebrated in Adar Sheni. The Gemara notes this gap: *ve'ilu nitabra hashanah yotzim af al Adar Sheni mipnei Purim lo katani* — the Mishnah does not include this as a required dispatch. This silence is significant and requires explanation.

### Majority: Rishon Suffices

The Gemara's explanation: *matnitin d'lo k'Rabbi* — the Mishnah does not follow the view of Rabbi. The majority position holds that all *mitzvot* applicable in Adar Sheni may be performed in Adar Rishon — that is, if one observed Purim in Adar Rishon, one has discharged the obligation. Since the *shlichim* dispatched in Adar Rishon already enabled communities to observe Purim at that point, there is no need for a second set of *shlichim* for Adar Sheni.

### Rabbi: Need Sheni

Rabbi disagrees: *mitzvot ha-noahgot be-sheni einan nohagot be-rishon* — the *mitzvot* specific to Adar Sheni cannot be performed in Adar Rishon. Observing Purim in Adar Rishon does not count. Purim must be observed in Adar Sheni. Therefore, *shlichim* must go out for Adar Sheni as well, so that communities know precisely when Purim falls. The Mishnah's silence on this point aligns it with the majority position and against Rabbi's view.

---

## Adar Rishon Length

### Fixed vs. Variable

The Gemara proceeds to analyze the underlying debate more carefully, asking whether the omission of *shlichim* for Adar Sheni in the Mishnah necessarily tracks the dispute between Rabbi and the majority about whether Adar Rishon discharges the Purim obligation — or whether it might reflect a separate question entirely.

### Need Depends on Length

The Gemara raises an alternative framing: even if everyone agrees that Purim must be observed in Adar Sheni, the question of whether *shlichim* are needed for Adar Sheni depends on whether communities can independently calculate when Adar Sheni begins. If Adar Rishon is always a fixed number of days, communities know when it ends and therefore when Adar Sheni begins — making *shlichim* unnecessary. But if the length of Adar Rishon is variable, communities cannot make that calculation on their own, and *shlichim* become necessary to communicate the start of Adar Sheni.

### All Combinations Possible

A remarkable tradition is cited: Rabbi Simai testified in the name of Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi — the last three prophets, present at the dawn of the Second Temple era — that when there are two Adars, *sheratzu la'asot sheneihem mele'im osim* — one may make both full (thirty days); *sheneihem chaseirim osim* — or both lacking (twenty-nine days); *echad malei ve'echad chaser osim* — or one full and one lacking. All combinations are permissible. The practice in the exile (*baGola*) before the return had followed this flexible approach, accommodating a range of arrangements.

### Rav: Always 30-29

Against this, a ruling attributed to Rav (*Rabbeinu*) establishes a default: *le'olam echad malei ve'echad chaser* — always one full and one lacking, with Adar Rishon being the full thirty-day month and Adar Sheni being the twenty-nine-day month — *ad sheyivadei lach shekave'u Rosh Chodesh bizmano* — unless one has explicit testimony that Adar Sheni was sanctified in its proper time, meaning that the preceding month was twenty-nine days and the new moon appeared on day thirty. Without such testimony, the default assumption is thirty-day Adar Rishon and twenty-nine-day Adar Sheni.

---

## Adar Before Nissan

### 29 Day Rule

A ruling was sent to Mar Ukva: *Adar hasamuch leNissan* — the Adar immediately preceding Nissan, whether in a regular year or as Adar Sheni in a leap year, is always twenty-nine days. This is consistent with Rav's position that Adar Sheni is the *chaser* month — and it provides a practical anchor: whatever uncertainty may exist about Adar Rishon, the month that connects directly to Nissan is always twenty-nine days.

---

## Shabbat Violation

### Two Months Only
