The Mishnah teaches that witnesses were permitted — indeed required — to violate *Shabbat* in order to testify about the new moon of two months: Nissan and Tishrei. These are the months whose proper establishment has cascading consequences for the *yamim tovim* — Pesach on the one hand, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and Sukkot on the other.

### Nachman's Challenge

Rav Nachman challenges the rule regarding Nissan in light of the ruling just transmitted to Mar Ukva. If the Adar preceding Nissan is always twenty-nine days, then everyone already knows when Nissan will begin — on day thirty of Adar, without any need for witness testimony. Why then should witnesses violate *Shabbat* to testify? Their testimony changes nothing about when Nissan falls. The entire apparatus of *chilul Shabbat* for lunar testimony is premised on the calendar being dependent on that testimony — but if the answer is already known, what purpose does the *Shabbat* violation serve?

### Mitzvah of Testimony

The Gemara responds with a fundamental principle: *mishum de-mitzvah lekadesh al ha-re'iyah* — there is an independent *mitzvah* to sanctify the month based on actual testimony about the moon's appearance. This *mitzvah* exists regardless of whether the calendar's outcome depends on the testimony. The obligation to witness and formally declare the new moon is not merely instrumental — it is not only a means to an end of establishing the correct date — but is itself a religious obligation. And since that *mitzvah* exists, the *Shabbat* violation is warranted to fulfill it, even when the calendar result could theoretically have been determined without the witnesses.

### Alternative: Adar Varies

The Gemara offers an alternative reading of the entire exchange. According to some (*ika de-amrei*), Rav Nachman's statement is inverted: if Adar is *always* twenty-nine days, then one understands *why* witnesses violate *Shabbat* for Nissan — because of the *mitzvah* of sanctification through testimony. But if Adar's length varies, then the witnesses' testimony is materially necessary to determine when Nissan begins, and in that case a different solution would be available: simply assume Adar is thirty days and sanctify Nissan on day thirty-one, without requiring *Shabbat* violation. The Gemara leaves this tension — between these two ways of reading the *Shabbat* violation for Nissan — for further analysis, picking up with the question on the following daf of whether the evidence cuts in favor of a fixed or variable Adar.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 20

## Adar's Length

### Adar Fixed Length

The discussion on daf 20 continues the broader inquiry into the lengths of certain months and whether the *shluchim* — the messengers sent to announce *Rosh Chodesh* — needed to travel for months whose length was in principle already fixed. The background assumption, which will be challenged, is that certain months preceding critical holidays were always twenty-nine days: *Elul* before *Tishrei*, and the *Adar* preceding *Nissan* — whether a standard *Adar* or *Adar Sheini* in a leap year — were always *chaser*, twenty-nine days. This would give communities a reliable basis for knowing when *Rosh Chodesh Tishrei* and *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* would fall, even without receiving the messengers' report.

To set the stage, the *Gemara* on 19b brings a *drasha* transmitted by Rabbi Simai in the name of Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi: regarding the two *Adarim* of a leap year, if the court wished, it could make both of them full (*malei*, thirty days), both of them deficient (*chaser*, twenty-nine days), or one full and one deficient — and such was the practice in the *golah*. In the name of Rav, however, it was said that the proper approach is for the first *Adar* to be full and the second deficient, unless one has definite knowledge that the first *Adar* had been fixed at twenty-nine days in its proper time. On this view, the default assumption is thirty and twenty-nine.

Against this background, a tradition was sent to Mar Ukva: *Adar hasamuch leNissan le'olam chaser* — the *Adar* immediately preceding *Nissan* is always twenty-nine days, regardless of whether it is a regular *Adar* or an *Adar Sheini*.

### Witnesses & Shabbat

Rav Nachman challenges this position from our *Mishnah*: on two months, witnesses violate *Shabbat* to come and testify — for *Nissan* and for *Tishrei*, because the holidays of those months depend on getting the dates right. Since *Nissan* follows *Adar*, the difficulty is immediate: if *Adar* is always twenty-nine days, then *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* is automatically day thirty — fixed and known in advance. Why, then, would witnesses need to violate *Shabbat* to testify about it? Their testimony would be superfluous; the date is predetermined regardless of what they say.

### Mitzvah Lekadesh

The *Gemara* initially deflects: *mishum d'mitzvah lekadesh al har'iyah* — there is a *mitzvah* to sanctify the new month on the basis of witness testimony, and for the sake of fulfilling that *mitzvah* properly, the witnesses violate *Shabbat* even when the date could technically be determined without them. On this reading, even if we know when *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* will be, we nevertheless want to anchor the sanctification in actual testimony.

This prompts an alternative formulation in the name of Rav Nachman — *ika de'amri*, some say — that actually the *Mishnah* can be read in the opposite direction, as support for the view that *Adar* is always twenty-nine. The logic runs as follows: if *Adar* is always twenty-nine days, and therefore we already know which day will be *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*, and that day happens to fall on *Shabbat*, we would still have the witnesses travel on *Shabbat* — because *mitzvah lekadesh al pi hare'iyah*, we want to perform the sanctification through testimony. This accounts neatly for why witnesses violate *Shabbat* for *Nissan* even if the date is fixed.

By contrast, if *Adar* is variable — sometimes twenty-nine, sometimes thirty — the *Gemara* asks why witnesses would ever need to violate *Shabbat* at all. If day thirty of *Adar* falls on *Shabbat* and the court has not yet fixed the month, could they not simply delay, leave the witnesses to come on Sunday, and declare Sunday — day thirty-one — as *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*? The court would avoid any violation of *Shabbat* and still conduct the sanctification based on testimony. The *Gemara* responds: this works only if day thirty falls on *Shabbat*. But the *Mishnah*'s case is that day thirty-one falls on *Shabbat* — that is, Friday is already day thirty, and if witnesses are to testify for that day, they must travel on *Shabbat*. At that point the court has no flexibility to delay; they cannot push *Rosh Chodesh* to day thirty-two. The witnesses must travel, and the case of violating *Shabbat* is necessary regardless.

### Rav Kahana's Test

Rav Kahana now presses the matter further. The *Mishnah* concludes: *keshehamikdash kayam mechallelin af akulahu mipnei takanat hakorban* — when the *Beit HaMikdash* stood, witnesses would violate *Shabbat* for every *Rosh Chodesh*, not only *Nissan* and *Tishrei*, because the *korbanot* of *Rosh Chodesh* needed to be brought on the correct day. This is Rav Kahana's proof: the fact that witnesses violate *Shabbat* is not, in principle, an expression of the abstract *mitzvah* to sanctify on the basis of testimony. If it were, they would violate *Shabbat* for every month, not only *Nissan* and *Tishrei*. The restriction to *Nissan* and *Tishrei* — in the period without the *Mikdash* — shows that witnesses violate *Shabbat* only when something practical hangs in the balance: the actual date must be uncertain and its determination must have concrete consequences.

The *Gemara* draws the inference directly: *midekulahu lav mishum d'mitzvah lekadesh al pi hare'iyah* — from the fact that witnesses violate *Shabbat* for every month when the *Mikdash* stood, and only for *Nissan* and *Tishrei* when it did not, it follows that the reason for violating *Shabbat* is not the general desire to sanctify through testimony. It follows that the reason it applies to *Nissan* and *Tishrei* specifically is that the date is genuinely uncertain — and that means *Adar* cannot be fixed in advance. The *Gemara* concludes: *tiyuvta* — a decisive refutation. The position that *Adar* is always twenty-nine days is rejected. *Adar* can be either twenty-nine or thirty days, depending on testimony.

### Adar Variable

This is the *Gemara*'s conclusion for this section: *Adar* preceding *Nissan* is not invariably twenty-nine days. Its length was determined by when witnesses testified to having seen the new moon. The assumption of a fixed, predetermined *Adar* cannot be sustained.

---

## Elul 30 Days

### Ulla's News

With the parallel assumption about *Elul* still in place — *miyemot Ezra va'eilach lo matzinu Elul me'ubar*, that from the days of Ezra onward *Elul* was never made thirty days — the *Gemara* now introduces a striking report. *Ki ata Ulla* — when *Ulla* came from Eretz Yisrael, he announced: *ibruhu l'Elul* — they made *Elul* thirty days. The confidence we might have had that *Elul* was always twenty-nine, providing certainty about when *Rosh Chodesh Tishrei* would fall, has now been undermined as well. Just as *Adar* turns out not to be invariably twenty-nine, so too *Elul* was on at least one occasion extended to thirty days.

*Ulla* himself adds: *yadai chavrain b'Bavel mai tivuta avdinan b'hadaihu* — our colleagues in Babylon should know what a favor we did for them by making *Elul* thirty days. *Tosafot* sharpens the implicit objection: what exactly is the favor? From the Babylonian perspective, one might have preferred that *Elul* simply remain twenty-nine days without exception — that way *Rosh Hashanah* would be fully predictable, and there would be no need for a second day of *Yom Tov* observed in the diaspora due to uncertainty. If the calendar were perfectly fixed, the "favor" of adjusting *Elul* carries a hidden cost.

### Metaya & Yarka

The *Gemara* presses: *mai tivuta* — what was the benefit? Two answers are given. *Ulla amar mishum yarka* — *Ulla* himself says: because of vegetables. *Rav Acha bar Chanina amar mishum metaya* — Rav Acha bar Chanina says: because of dead bodies.

The concern of *metaya* — dead bodies — arises when *Shabbat* and *Yom Kippur* would fall on consecutive days. In such a case, there would be two full days on which burial is impossible: one cannot bury on *Shabbat* (even through non-Jews) and one cannot bury on *Yom Kippur*. In climates without refrigeration, two consecutive days of inability to bury a corpse poses a serious practical problem. The calendar is therefore adjusted — *Elul* is made thirty days — to prevent *Yom Kippur* from falling immediately adjacent to *Shabbat*.

The concern of *yarka* — vegetables — arises when *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* fall consecutively. Without refrigeration, if one picks fresh vegetables on Friday for *Shabbat*, and *Yom Tov* immediately follows, the vegetables will have wilted by the time *Yom Tov* arrives. Making *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* non-consecutive ensures that fresh vegetables can be gathered the day before each.

### Reason Differences

The *Gemara* asks: *mai beinayhu* — what practical difference does it make which reason one invokes? The case that distinguishes them is *Yom Kippur* falling immediately after *Shabbat* rather than before it. According to the one who says the concern is *metaya*, we would adjust the calendar to prevent that configuration. According to the one who says the concern is *yarka*, there is no vegetable issue on *Yom Kippur* itself, since one fasts on *Yom Kippur*; and after *Yom Kippur*, one can simply go pick fresh vegetables — *l'orta tarach u'maity* — so there is no need to adjust the calendar for that case.

The *Gemara* then observes that the *metaya* concern is so serious that even according to the one who says the primary reason is *yarka*, one would certainly also adjust for *metaya*. The real dispute, then, is over *yarka* alone. When *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* are consecutive — which, of course, occurs regularly in our experience — would one adjust the calendar? According to the *yarka* view, yes: *maavrin*, one adds a day to the previous month. According to the *metaya* view alone, no: *efshar b'amamei* — non-Jews can bury the dead on the first day of *Yom Tov*, so consecutive *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* does not create the two-day burial crisis. And as for vegetables on *Yom Tov*, *efshar b'chamimei* — one can keep them warm or heated to preserve them adequately. The vegetable concern is not severe enough to override the calendar.

As is well known, our calendar reflects the *metaya* position: *Yom Kippur* never falls on a Friday or a Sunday, but *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* do fall consecutively.

### Babylon's Climate

One might ask why *Ulla* singles out the Babylonians as the recipients of this favor. The *Gemara* answers: *l'didan chavila lanu alma* — for us in Babylon, the world is intensely hot. The concerns that motivate the calendar adjustment — decomposing bodies and wilting vegetables — are far more acute in the humid heat of Babylon than in the more temperate, Mediterranean climate of Eretz Yisrael, where *lo chavilu alma* — the conditions are simply not as severe. The Babylonians, therefore, have particular reason to be grateful that the court in Eretz Yisrael adjusted *Elul* to prevent these problems. *Tosafot*'s irony remains unresolved by the *Gemara*: one might still prefer a fully predictable calendar to the benefits gained by the adjustment.

---

## Calendar Manipulation

### Adding Days Query

The previous discussion raises a deeper question: when the court makes *Elul* thirty days to prevent *Yom Kippur* from falling adjacent to *Shabbat*, are they doing so in response to the testimony of witnesses, or are they simply manipulating the calendar for their own reasons, independent of the moon? And if the latter, how can this be justified?

### Verse Limit

The *Gemara* brings a *braita* taught by Rabba bar Shmuel: one might think that just as we intercalate the year — adding an extra month — for a need (*l'tzorech*), so too we might add a day to a month for a need, regardless of the moon. But the verse teaches: *hachodesh hazeh lachem rosh chodashim* — *kazeh re'eh v'kadesh*, see and sanctify. One must first see — that is, receive testimony — and only then sanctify. The calendar cannot be manipulated at will based purely on external concerns.

### Rava's Distinction

Rava resolves the apparent tension: *lo kashya — kan l'avro kan lekadsho*. There are two distinct ways of overriding the astronomical testimony. *Le'avro* means delaying: witnesses appeared on day thirty and testified, but the court suppresses their testimony and makes the month thirty days, pushing *Rosh Chodesh* to day thirty-one. *Lekadsho* means advancing: the witnesses did not appear on day thirty, and the court sanctifies it as *Rosh Chodesh* without any testimony, making the previous month only twenty-nine days.

Rava's point is that the verse's requirement — *re'eh v'kadesh*, see then sanctify — limits only early sanctification. Doing it *le'avro*, a day late, still respects the basic procedure: witnesses testified, and the court sanctified, even if slightly delayed. But advancing — *lekadsho* — without prior testimony directly violates *kazeh re'eh v'kadesh*. Therefore, what the case of *Elul* demonstrates is permissible delay (*le'avro*), not impermissible early sanctification.

### Manipulation Limits

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi articulates the limits that follow from this distinction: *me'aymin al ha-edim al ha-chodesh she-nir'ah bi-zmano le-avro* — the court may even intimidate witnesses who saw the moon at the expected time in order to silence them, thereby allowing the month to be extended. The court can actively suppress testimony in order to delay *Rosh Chodesh*. But: *v'ein me'aymin al ha-edim al ha-chodesh she-lo nir'ah bi-zmano le-kadsho* — the court may not intimidate witnesses to testify that they saw the moon a day before they actually did, in order to advance *Rosh Chodesh* to an earlier day. Suborning false testimony to enable early sanctification is categorically prohibited. The hierarchy, at this point in the *Gemara*, is: delay is permissible (and the court may even silence witnesses to achieve it); early sanctification is not, and procuring false testimony to enable it is certainly not.

### Rabbi Yochanan Opposite

This position is now challenged. *Rav Yehuda Nesi'ah* — understood by *Tosafot* to be a later figure who was a contemporary of *Rabbi Ami*, not the immediate grandson of Rav Yehuda HaNasi — sent word to *Rabbi Ami*: be aware that throughout the lifetime of *Rabbi Yochanan*, he would consistently teach the exact opposite. *Me'aymin al ha-edim al ha-chodesh she-lo nir'ah bi-zmano le-kadsho* — the court would in fact intimidate witnesses to testify that they saw the moon a day early, even though they had not actually seen it, in order to advance *Rosh Chodesh*. *Af al pi she-lo ra'u, yomru ra'inu* — even though they did not see it, they would be made to say: we saw it. This is a striking position: not merely adjusting the calendar without witnesses, but actively procuring false testimony to do so.

### Abaye's Solution

Abaye resolves the contradiction between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan by distinguishing between months: *ha be-Nisan u-ve-Tishrei, ha bi-shear yarchei* — one ruling applies to *Nissan* and *Tishrei*, the other to the remaining months. For *Nissan* and *Tishrei*, whose dates govern the holidays and carry the greatest practical weight, the court has maximum latitude: it will adjust the calendar in either direction, and if necessary will even procure false testimony to do so. For other months, the court will only delay — silencing witnesses and doing it late — but will not advance *Rosh Chodesh*, and certainly will not procure false testimony.

### Rava's Answer

Rava offers a different resolution. The *braita* of Rabba bar Shmuel — which asserted that we may not adjust months at will and must be guided by testimony — does not represent the normative ruling. It is *Acherim hi* — it is the position of *Acherim*, identified as *Rabbi Meir*. The *braita* records: *Acherim omrim*, others say, *ein bein Atzeret l'Atzeret v'ein bein Rosh Hashanah l'Rosh Hashanah ela arba'ah yamim bilvad* — from one *Shavuot* to the next, or from one *Rosh Hashanah* to the next, the shift is only four days. In a leap year, five. This is because a standard Hebrew year of 354 days is fifty weeks with four days remaining; any given date shifts exactly four days from one year to the next (five in a leap year).

If one could confidently assert this four-day shift as invariable, it implies a perfectly predictable calendar — which is only possible if the calendar is not being adjusted at will. Rava reads this statement, however, as describing what would happen if the court always followed pure astronomical reality without any intervention. The *Gemara* reads it as the position of *Rabbi Meir* alone, who held that we do not manipulate the calendar at all. But the majority position is that we do adjust it as needed, and the statement of Rabba bar Shmuel that generated our difficulty is itself only the minority view of *Rabbi Meir*. According to the consensus, the calendar can be manipulated — extended, advanced, and in certain contexts even supported by suborned testimony — without restriction.

### Rav Dimi Logic

Rav Dimi of Nehardea teaches the opposite order of preference from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *m'aimin al ha'edim al hachodesh shelo nira bizmano l'kadsho* — the court is more willing to procure false testimony to advance *Rosh Chodesh* than to silence witnesses and delay it. His reasoning turns on appearances: *ha mechzi k'shikra, ha lo mechzi k'shikra* — one scenario looks like a lie and the other does not.

The logic is as follows. If nobody actually saw the moon, but the court arranges for witnesses to testify that they saw it — and therefore declares today *Rosh Chodesh* — this will not be publicly apparent. A bystander who did not see the moon will simply assume it was visible and he missed it, or that conditions were different elsewhere. The court's manipulation is invisible. But if witnesses genuinely saw the moon and the court suppresses their testimony and announces that tomorrow — day thirty-one — will be *Rosh Chodesh*, bystanders who saw the moon clearly the night before will find this declaration absurd and transparently false. *Mechzi k'shikra* — it looks manifestly like a lie.

The irony, which the *Gemara* leaves standing, is striking: the court would prefer to procure actual false testimony if it does not look dishonest, over suppressing genuine testimony in a way that is visibly implausible. The concern with appearances of manipulation outweighs the concern with the underlying dishonesty of the manipulation itself.

The section closes with the conclusion that the court has broad latitude to adjust the calendar as needed. Whether one follows Abaye's distinction between *Nissan* and *Tishrei* versus other months, or Rava's position that the entire restriction belongs to the minority view of *Rabbi Meir*, the normative ruling allows calendar adjustment — including, under some views, the procurement of false testimony — when the need arises.

---

## Astronomy & Moon

### Shmuel's Claim

Having established that the calendar can be manipulated, the *Gemara* pivots to the astronomical expertise that underlies calendar determination. *Amar Shmuel*: *yachilna l'situnei l'chulei gola* — I could set up the calendar for the entire exile. *Shmuel*, renowned as a master of astronomy, is asserting that his command of the astronomical calculations was sufficient to establish the calendar independently, without relying on witness testimony from Eretz Yisrael — foreshadowing what ultimately occurred in the era of Hillel the Second.

### Before/After Chatzot

*Abba*, the father of Rabbi Simlai, put *Shmuel* to the test. He asked: do you know what is meant by the line taught in the *sod ha'ibbur* — the secret of intercalation, a cryptic compendium of the principles governing the calendar — *nolad kodem chatzot o nolad achar chatzot*? Does it matter whether the *molad* — the astronomical moment at which the moon moves out of conjunction — occurs before or after midday (*chatzot*)? And if so, why?

*Shmuel* admitted he did not know. *Abba* responded: if you do not know the meaning of this line, there must be many other things you do not know. The claim to be able to set up the calendar for the entire exile was premature.

### Night & Day

When *Rav Zeira* ascended to Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted back the following teaching: *tzarich she-yehai layla v'yom min hachodesh* — it is required that both night and day belong to the month.

This is a cryptic formulation and attracts extensive commentary — the *Ba'al HaMa'or* (Rav Zerachyah HaLevi, twelfth century) devotes a substantial treatment to these few lines alone, which gives some measure of how dense and contested this passage is.

### Old Moon Visible

*Rashi* reads the principle *tzarich she-yehai layla v'yom min hachodesh* as follows. The moon is invisible for twenty-four hours around the time of conjunction: the old moon, moving in a counterclockwise direction relative to the sun, is visible only at the very end of the night — the last hours before sunrise — as it precedes the sun. It then sets before the sun and is invisible through the day. As it approaches the sun it becomes invisible entirely. After conjunction, the new moon moves out from behind the sun and becomes visible at the very start of night, immediately after sunset, then sets while it is still night.

Given this, *Rashi* connects the principle to the earlier discussion of calendar manipulation. Suppose witnesses saw the old moon during the night of day thirty, the day that has the potential of being sanctified as *Rosh Chodesh*. Even if the court wished to manipulate the calendar and declare that same day — that same daytime — as *Rosh Chodesh* based on alleged sighting of the new moon, this is impossible. People saw the old moon during the night just hours before. They know the new moon cannot have appeared in the intervening hours. The astronomical reality is publicly known, and the manipulation would be transparent — *mechzi k'shikra* in the most literal sense. The requirement that both night and day belong to the month thus sets an outer limit on calendar manipulation: the court cannot sanctify a day as *Rosh Chodesh* when the old moon was visibly present just hours earlier that same night.

### Visibility Prediction

Returning to the question *Abba* posed to *Shmuel*: the significance of whether the *molad* falls before or after *chatzot* is now explained. The *Gemara* operates on the premise — stated explicitly though difficult to reconcile with precise astronomical observation — that once the moon has moved six hours out of conjunction, it will be visible near the time of sunset (*samuch l'shkiat hachamah*). On this assumption: if the *molad* occurs before midday, then six hours later it will be visible at or near sunset, meaning witnesses could conceivably see the new moon that same evening. If the *molad* occurs after midday, then six hours later the sun will have already set and the moon will be below the horizon; it cannot be visible that night.

The formula, therefore, is: *molad kodem chatzot — beyadua shenireh samuch l'shkiat hachamah*; *lo nolad kodem chatzot — beyadua shelo nireh samuch l'shkiat hachamah*. If the *molad* is before midday, it is known that the moon will be visible near sunset. If it is not before midday, it is known that it will not be visible near sunset.

### Contradict Witnesses

*Rav Ashi* supplies the practical purpose of this astronomical knowledge: *l'achchushei sahadi* — to contradict witnesses. If witnesses claim to have seen the new moon at sunset on a given day, but the *molad* is known to have occurred after midday, their claim is astronomically impossible. The court can reject their testimony on that basis. Conversely, if the *molad* is known to have been before midday, the sighting is plausible. Astronomical calculation thus serves as a check on the integrity of witness testimony, not as a replacement for it.

### 24-Hour Cycle

*Rav Zeira* further transmits in the name of *Rav Nachman*: *kaf daled sha'ei machasei sihara* — the moon is concealed for twenty-four hours. This twenty-four-hour period is divided differently depending on location. *Ledidan* — for us in Eretz Yisrael — six hours of the old moon's invisibility and eighteen hours of the new moon's invisibility. *Ledidehu* — for them in Bavel — six hours of the new moon's invisibility and eighteen hours of the old moon's invisibility.

The practical application is again, as *Rav Ashi* states: *l'achchushei sahadi*, to contradict witnesses. If a witness in Eretz Yisrael claims to have seen the old moon within the last six hours before the new month, that is plausible; but if more than six hours have elapsed since the old moon was last visible, the claim is impossible. The figures differ for Bavel.

This passage is admittedly very difficult. Astronomically, the period during which the moon is invisible around conjunction is approximately thirty-six hours — nine degrees of arc in each direction at half a degree per hour — not twenty-four. Furthermore, the distinction between Eretz Yisrael and Bavel, which are approximately one time zone apart, would not seem to produce such a dramatic reversal in the invisibility periods for old versus new moon; they observe the same astronomical events with roughly an hour's difference.

### Geography Effect

One attempt at explanation runs as follows, on the *Gemara*'s own premise that six hours of separation from conjunction suffices for visibility. Consider the case where the *molad* occurs just after midday (*chatzot*). In this scenario, the new moon will become visible only six hours later, which by that point is after sunset — the moon is already below the horizon. The new moon is therefore invisible from the moment of conjunction until after the next sunrise: eighteen hours. The old moon, for its part, had been invisible for the final six hours before conjunction (as it was too close to the sun). So in this scenario: six hours of old moon invisibility, eighteen hours of new moon invisibility.

Now consider the opposite case: the *molad* occurs just before midday. The new moon becomes visible six hours later, right at sunset. The new moon is therefore invisible for only six hours. The old moon, last visible eighteen hours before conjunction, was invisible for eighteen hours. So in this scenario: eighteen hours of old moon invisibility, six hours of new moon invisibility.

The geographic explanation then proposes that the one-hour time difference between Bavel and Eretz Yisrael — Bavel being further east — shifts a *molad* that falls just before midday in Eretz Yisrael to just after midday in Bavel (or vice versa). This shift moves the scenario from one case to the other, reversing the distribution of six and eighteen hours between old and new moon. The two statements in the *Gemara* — *ledidan* six of the old and eighteen of the new, *ledidehu* six of the new and eighteen of the old — thus describe the same *molad* event as experienced from two different longitudes, where the one-hour offset is exactly sufficient to place the *molad* on opposite sides of midday.

The explanation is elegant, though it depends on the *Gemara*'s assumption that six hours from conjunction suffices for visibility — a figure that does not correspond to the actual astronomical requirement of approximately nine degrees of arc, representing closer to eighteen hours. Nonetheless, on the *Gemara*'s own terms, this geographic account coherently explains why the division of the twenty-four-hour concealment period is inverted between Eretz Yisrael and Bavel.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 21

## Layla v'Yom Min HaChodesh

### Requirement Statement

The *gemara* returns to a principle stated earlier: *tzarich sheyehei layla veyom min hachodesh* — both the night and the day of *Rosh Chodesh* must belong to the new month. Before unpacking the precise halachic implications, the *gemara* asks *minalan* — what is the source for this requirement?

### Yochanan & Reish Lakish

Two *amoraim* offer independent verse-based derivations. Rabbi Yochanan cites the phrase *me'erev ad erev* — "from evening to evening" — which establishes that a halachic day runs from one evening to the next, encompassing both night and the following day as a single unit. Reish Lakish draws from the verse governing the eating of *matzos* for seven days, which specifies *ad yom ha'echad ve'esrim lachodesh ba'erev* — until the twenty-first at night — again demonstrating that a day extends from the preceding evening up to, but not including, the following night. In both cases the underlying point is simply that a halachic day consists of night followed by day.

### Abaye & Rava Debate

*Mai beinaihu* — what practical difference exists between these two sources, given that both arrive at the same conclusion? Abaye answers that the difference is purely a matter of *mashmach dorshin* — which verse one derives the principle from — with no halachic consequence. Rava disagrees: *chatzos laila ika beinaihu* — the practical difference concerns *chatzos*, midnight. The verse from the *matzah* context presupposes that the obligation to eat *matzah* on the first night extends until midnight, meaning the first night of *Pesach* is in effect divided at *chatzos*. This division will bear on the question of whether the entire preceding night of *Rosh Chodesh* must belong to the new month, or whether only the portion from *chatzos* onward need do so.

### Rashi's Explanation

What does the requirement that both night and day belong to the new month actually mean in practice? Rashi understands this as a rabbinic concern, and accordingly treats the cited verses as mere *asmachtos*. The underlying issue, according to Rashi, is one of appearances: if the old moon was visible on a given night, *Beis Din* may not turn around and declare the following day *Rosh Chodesh*. As the *gemara* established earlier, at least twenty-four hours — and in practice closer to thirty-six — must elapse between the last sliver of the old moon and the appearance of the new one. If witnesses saw the old moon the night before and *Beis Din* were to declare the very next day *Rosh Chodesh*, it would be patently obvious to the entire community that the calendar was being manipulated. People who had seen the old moon with their own eyes would recognize the declaration as a fraud.

According to Rashi, then, the question of *chatzos* amounts to the following: if the old moon was seen in the first half of the night — before *chatzos* — is it sufficiently removed in time that *Beis Din* could declare the following day *Rosh Chodesh* without it being conspicuously obvious? Or must the old moon have been unseen even after *chatzos* before such a declaration becomes acceptable? This is the halachic dispute between the two sources as Rashi reads it.

### Rabbeinu Chananel

Rabbeinu Chananel offers a substantially different reading, one that accounts more naturally for why the *gemara* invokes biblical verses at all. In his view, the requirement is not primarily about appearances but about an objective astronomical condition: the entire day declared as *Rosh Chodesh* must fall after the *molad*, the moment of lunar conjunction. The *molad* is the instant the moon moves, even infinitesimally, off the precise alignment with the sun and earth — the astronomical new moon, invisible to the eye but real as an astronomical event.

### Molad & Visibility Gap

The *gemara* has been operating throughout this passage with the assumption that the new moon becomes visible approximately six hours after the *molad*. In practice, as is noted, the gap is closer to sixteen to eighteen hours — but the *gemara*'s working figure is six. This gap matters enormously for Rabbeinu Chananel's reading.

Consider the normal case: witnesses testify that they saw the new moon on Monday night at, say, 7:00 PM. They come before *Beis Din* the following morning, still within the halachic day of Monday. *Beis Din* declares Monday *Rosh Chodesh*. If the moon became visible at 7:00 PM Monday evening, then the *molad* — occurring at least six hours earlier — took place at approximately 1:00 PM on Sunday. This means that all of Monday, beginning at nightfall Sunday, falls well after the *molad*. The entire day of *Rosh Chodesh* is thus *min hachodesh* — from the new month.

But now consider a different scenario. Suppose the moon, by the end of a long month, has traveled far enough behind the sun that it becomes visible in the early morning — say, 7:00 AM on Monday. Witnesses see it at dawn, testify that day, and *Beis Din* declares Monday *Rosh Chodesh*. If the moon was visible at 7:00 AM, the *molad* occurred approximately six hours earlier, around 1:00 AM Monday. But that means Monday night — from nightfall Sunday until 1:00 AM — was still part of the old moon's phase, pre-*molad*. Part of Monday belonged to the old month. According to Rabbeinu Chananel, this is precisely what the requirement *layla veyom min hachodesh* precludes: you cannot declare Monday *Rosh Chodesh* unless the entire day, including the night with which it began, falls after the *molad*.

There is of course a perfectly valid version of even the early-morning scenario. If the *molad* occurred at, say, 5:00 PM on Sunday — too soon after conjunction for visibility — and the moon only became sufficiently separated by 7:00 AM Monday, then all of Monday (which began at Sunday nightfall, after 5:00 PM Sunday) is post-*molad*, and the declaration is valid.

*Tosafot* disagrees with Rabbeinu Chananel's framework as a matter of practical *halacha*, holding that what matters is when the moon was visible, not when the *molad* occurred. But Rabbeinu Chananel's reading does have the advantage of explaining why the *gemara* reaches for biblical verses — it is making a substantive legal point, not merely a rabbinic ruling about appearances.

### Chatzos & Matzah

Under Rabbeinu Chananel's reading, the debate about *chatzos* takes on a different character as well. The question becomes: must the entirety of Monday night — from nightfall through dawn — be post-*molad*, or is it sufficient that the portion of Monday night from *chatzos* onward falls after the *molad*? The connection to *matzah* is structural: since the obligation to eat *matzah* on the first night of *Pesach* runs until *chatzos*, the night is in a sense legally divided at that point. The verse therefore might imply that if the post-*chatzos* portion of the night is from the new month — i.e., the *molad* occurred before *chatzos* — that suffices, even though the earlier part of the night was technically pre-*molad*. This is Rabbeinu Chananel's understanding of how *chatzos* enters the analysis.

It should be noted that in practice, *Rosh Chodesh* was always declared during the day in question, often only after witnesses arrived and testified. If they saw the moon the night before, they would travel and arrive the following morning; if they saw it at dawn, they would testify later that same day. In either case, the declaration was always retrospective, applying to a day that was already underway. This is one reason why, to this day, one does not repeat *Shemoneh Esrei* if *Yaaleh V'yavo* was forgotten on the first night of *Rosh Chodesh* — because the formal *kiddush hachodesh* was never accepted at night, and the status of that first night was always uncertain until testimony was received.

### Fixed Calendar Practice

One might ask: given that we now have a fixed calendar, what relevance does this discussion of the *molad* retain? The answer is that the fixed calendar itself was constructed with precisely this gap in mind. When the *molad* is announced in synagogue — one is stating that the astronomical conjunction occurs at a particular hour — *Rosh Chodesh* is then the following day. Now one understands why: even according to the *gemara*'s more conservative estimate, it takes at least six hours after the *molad* for the moon to become visible. In practice it is closer to eighteen hours, and so the calendar is structured such that *Rosh Chodesh* falls the day after the *molad* is announced. It is also worth noting that the *molad* is announced in Jerusalem time — a reflection of the fact that *kiddush hachodesh* was always anchored in *Eretz Yisrael*, and we preserve that orientation even in the fixed calendar.

---

## Sefeika DeYoma in Bavel

### Rav Nachman Principle

The *gemara* now shifts from astronomy to the practical challenge facing communities in *Bavel* — distant lands that received no timely word from *Eretz Yisrael* about when *Rosh Chodesh* had been declared. Rabbi Zeira cites Rav Nachman: *kol sefeika lekamei shadinan* — any doubt about when *Rosh Chodesh* falls is resolved by pushing forward, not backward. That is, the concern is always that the previous month may have been thirty days rather than twenty-nine, which would shift *Rosh Chodesh* — and therefore the fifteenth, the day of the *Yom Tov* — one day later than assumed. The practical result is that communities observe both the fifteenth and the sixteenth as *Yom Tov*, out of uncertainty. The months that matter most in this context are *Nissan* and *Tishrei*, and the months immediately preceding them — *Adar* and *Elul* — are treated as standard twenty-nine-day months.

### Discovery Principle

One might ask: why is the concern exclusively about the month being longer than expected — making *Rosh Chodesh* a day later — and not also about the possibility that the month was shorter, making *Rosh Chodesh* a day earlier? In that case, should we not also keep the fourteenth as *Yom Tov*? The *gemara* addresses this directly: *trei yarchei chasiri kala it lehu* — if two consecutive short months occurred, the word would get out. Rashi clarifies that this does not refer to *Elul* and *Av* as the consecutive pair — by *Rosh Hashanah* there would not necessarily have been enough time to learn that *Elul* was a short month. Rather, the relevant pair is *Av* and *Tammuz*. In a normal calendar pattern, *Tammuz* is twenty-nine days and *Av* is thirty. If *Av* were also only twenty-nine, that would mean two consecutive short months, and that would have become known by the time *Elul* arrived. Since no such news came, one can safely assume *Av* was thirty days, and there is therefore no reason to fear that *Rosh Chodesh* fell a day earlier than assumed.

### Two-Day Observance

The practical upshot is that communities in *Bavel* observe both the fifteenth and sixteenth as *Yom Tov* — *chamiser veshitser avdinan* — due to the uncertainty of which day is truly the fifteenth. They do not, however, observe the fourteenth, because that would require assuming two consecutive short months, and such a scenario would have become known.

### Levi's Silence

The *gemara* now presents a remarkable story. Levi, who had come from *Eretz Yisrael*, found himself in *Bavel* on the eleventh of *Tishrei* — the day after *Yom Kippur* as reckoned in *Bavel*. Observing the Babylonian Jews cheerfully cooking and eating, he quipped: *bassim tavshila de-Bavla'ei beyoma rabba de-Ma'arava* — the pots of the Babylonians are smelling very good today, on the great day of *Eretz Yisrael*, i.e., *Yom Kippur*. *Elul* had been declared thirty days in *Eretz Yisrael*, which pushed *Rosh Hashanah* — and consequently *Yom Kippur* — one day later than the Babylonians had assumed.

Those present immediately asked Levi to testify formally — if he knew it was *Yom Kippur* in *Eretz Yisrael*, why not declare it and bring them to stop eating? Levi refused: *lo shamati mipi beis din mekudash* — I did not personally hear *Beis Din* declare *mekudash*. Rashi explains: the *halacha* requires that messengers depart only after explicitly hearing *Beis Din*'s formal declaration. Even in a case where the previous month passed its thirtieth day without witnesses, making it logically certain that the following day is *Rosh Chodesh*, the messengers do not depart until *Beis Din* formally accepts testimony the next day and pronounces *mekudash*. Levi had not witnessed that declaration and therefore declined to offer formal testimony.

### Tosafot's Decentralizati…

*Tosafot* finds this extraordinarily difficult. Regardless of technicalities about hearing *mekudash*, Levi knew — or knew with overwhelming probability — that today was *Yom Kippur* in *Eretz Yisrael* and that the Babylonians were eating in violation of one of the most severe prohibitions in the Torah. How could he remain silent on a technicality?

*Tosafot* first attempts to create a small measure of genuine uncertainty. Levi had departed from the vicinity of *Beis Din* approximately twenty minutes before nightfall on the thirtieth of *Elul*. While it was practically inconceivable that witnesses could have arrived, been examined, and had their testimony accepted in those final minutes, it was not logically impossible. Perhaps, in theory, the process was concluded in moments — *chick-chak* — and the thirtieth became *Rosh Chodesh* after all. *Tosafot* acknowledges this is barely a possibility, but uses it to argue that Levi's certainty was not absolute.

Yet even this concession leaves the problem largely intact. If one is ninety-nine-point-nine percent certain that the Babylonians are eating on *Yom Kippur*, how does a technical procedural scruple justify silence? Here *Tosafot* makes a genuinely startling move. He invokes the principle that *Beis Din*'s calendar determinations are binding even when in error — even when the witnesses were mistaken, even when the declaration was made intentionally contrary to reality. The declaration is what creates the sacred day, not the underlying astronomical event. *Tosafot* then extends this logic: the Babylonian community had collectively identified a particular day as *Rosh Hashanah* and consequently another as *Yom Kippur*. That communal identification, even without a formal *Beis Din* declaration, was binding for them. The result is that there could be a valid *Yom Kippur* in *Eretz Yisrael* on one day and a valid *Yom Kippur* in *Bavel* on a different day, with both being halachically legitimate.

This is a striking position. It projects, at least theoretically, a paradigm of decentralized calendar authority — two communities, each with a binding calendar, neither invalidating the other. *Tosafot* is careful to note that the historical Jewish community never actually tolerated two permanently divergent calendars; the battles of the *geonic* period over calendar authority — ultimately resolved in favor of *Bavel* — make clear how intolerable that situation was recognized to be. But *Tosafot* uses this framework to explain why Levi's silence was not, in fact, halachically indefensible: the Babylonians' day was their binding *Yom Kippur*, and Levi's testimony could not retroactively undo that.

---

## Messenger Routes & Zones

### Rav Yochanan Ruling

The *gemara* records that Rav Yochanan issued a public proclamation: *kol heicha d'matu shluchei Nissan v'lo matu shluchei Tishrei l'avdu trei yomei* — wherever the messengers of *Nissan* reached but the messengers of *Tishrei* did not, the communities there must keep two days, as a *gzeira* lest *Nissan* lead to leniency regarding *Tishrei*.

### Geographic Zones

To understand this ruling, one must appreciate the geographic reality. *Yerushalayim* is the center. Messengers depart after *Rosh Chodesh* to inform surrounding communities of when the month was declared. For *Nissan*, they leave on the first of the month and can travel for approximately twelve days before *Pesach* on the fourteenth — two *Shabbatot* during which they cannot travel are subtracted from the fourteen available days. For *Tishrei*, they can only begin on the second of the month (not on *Rosh Hashanah* itself), lose two *Shabbatot* and *Yom Kippur* to travel restrictions, and thus reach only a ten-day journey's radius before *Succos* on the fifteenth.

The result is a set of concentric zones. Communities close to *Eretz Yisrael* — within the ten-day radius — receive messengers for both *Nissan* and *Tishrei*, know the exact date of both *Pesach* and *Succos*, and keep one day. Communities beyond the twelve-day radius receive messengers for neither and must keep two days for both. But there is an intermediate zone: communities between ten and twelve days' journey receive the *Nissan* messengers but not those of *Tishrei*. They know the correct date of *Rosh Hashanah* and therefore *Pesach*, but do not receive timely word for *Succos*.

### Uniformity Requirement

For these intermediate communities, Rav Yochanan ruled that they must nonetheless keep two days of *Pesach* as well — *gzeira Nissan atu Tishrei*. The concern is one of internal consistency: if they keep only one day of *Pesach* (since they know the date), they will likewise keep only one day of *Succos*, even though for *Succos* they genuinely do not know. A community cannot have a split practice — one day for *Pesach* and two for *Succos* — without the distinction becoming blurred over time. Uniformity requires that the same rule apply to both festivals.

### Aibo & Chiyya Story

The *gemara* brings a narrative that illustrates both the ruling and the difficulty of implementing it. Rabbi Aibo bar Nagri and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, both students of Rav Yochanan, happened to visit a community that fell precisely in the intermediate zone — reached by *Nissan* messengers but not those of *Tishrei*. They observed the community keeping only one day of *Pesach*, and they said nothing. Word reached Rav Yochanan. He was displeased: *lav amina l'chu* — did I not tell you? In this zone, two days of *Pesach* are required, on account of *gzeira Nissan atu Tishrei*. The story echoes the earlier tale of Levi's silence — a pattern of rabbinic figures declining to intervene in calendar practice — but here the concern is entirely rabbinic in character, about maintaining uniform observance across the two major festival seasons.

---

## Two-Day Yom Kippur

### Rava's Practice

The *gemara* records that Rava *hava ragil d'hava yateiv b'taanita trei yomei* — Rava was accustomed to fasting two days of *Yom Kippur*. As Levi's story illustrated, one could never be absolutely certain in *Bavel* that *Elul* had indeed been twenty-nine days. If *Elul* was thirty days, the day one took to be the tenth of *Tishrei* was actually the ninth, and the real *Yom Kippur* fell the following day. Since Rava could not be certain on which of the two days *Yom Kippur* actually fell, he fasted both.

### Rava Vindicated

*Zimna chada ishtakach k'vateih* — on one occasion Rava turned out to be correct. *Elul* that year was indeed thirty days, and the community had misidentified *Yom Kippur*. Rava cited this vindication as confirmation of his practice.

### Rabbeinu Chananel

Rabbeinu Chananel, however, enters an important qualification. Even granting that the practice was understandable, it was not an *obligation* and should not be mistaken for one. The principle stated elsewhere in the *gemara* — *d'miyemot Ezra v'eilach lo matzinu Elul meubar*, that since the days of Ezra *Elul* has never been thirty days — reflects the standard expectation. Rava's fasting was *milta yeteira* — an extra stringency, something beyond the letter of the law. *Rabbeinu Chananel* writes explicitly: *lo chovah hu alav* — it was not incumbent upon him. And if someone undertook such a stringency, Rabbeinu Chananel notes, it was not something deserving of particular praise — one should not congratulate oneself for going beyond what is required when the underlying concern is not a genuine one under normal circumstances.

### Rav Nachman Story

The *gemara* then presents a story that vividly captures why the prospect of two consecutive days of *Yom Kippur* was so daunting. Rav Nachman fasted throughout *Yom Kippur*. At *Ne'ilah* — at the very close of the day — a man arrived and informed him: *lemachar yoma rabba b'maarava* — tomorrow is *Yom Kippur* in *Eretz Yisrael*. *Elul* had been thirty days; rav nachman had fasted on the ninth of *Tishrei*, and the true *Yom Kippur* was the following day.

### Nachman's Curse

Rav Nachman asked the man where he was coming from. The man answered: from *Damharia*. Rav Nachman, playing on the name, replied: *dam tehei acharitao* — blood should be the end of you. Rashi explains that this reflects the tremendous anguish of being told, at the very conclusion of an exhausting fast, that one must fast again tomorrow. The *gemara* also has Rav Nachman quote: *kalim hayu rodfenu* — swift were our pursuers. The bitter irony being: you came so quickly with this news. Had you arrived a few days later, it would have been too late to matter. As it stands, Rav Nachman faced the physical and spiritual challenge of two consecutive days of fasting.

---

## Tekufas Teves & Leap Year

### Solstice Rule

Rav Huna bar Avin sent a ruling to Rava: *kad chazit de-mashka tekufas Teves ad shis-asar be-Nissan* — if you observe that *tekufas Teves*, the winter solstice season, extends into the sixteenth of *Nissan*, then *abrah le-hahi shata* — declare a leap year for that year. The concern is straightforward: *Pesach* must fall in the spring. If the winter season has not yet given way to spring by the fifteenth of *Nissan*, then *Pesach* — which falls on the fifteenth — is occurring in winter, not spring. A leap month must be added so that the following year's *Nissan* falls properly in the spring season. Rav Huna adds: *v'lo tachosh lahem* — do not be concerned that such a declaration is somehow improper, for there are adequate grounds to do so.

### Verse Basis

The biblical anchor for this requirement is the verse *shamor et chodesh ha-aviv* — guard the month of spring. The word *chodesh* refers to the lunar month, the moon's renewal; the word *aviv* refers to the solar spring season. The verse thus enjoins that the lunar month of *Nissan* must coincide with the solar season of spring — *she-tehe be-chodesh Nissan*, that the spring should fall within the month of *Nissan*.

### Rashi's Explanation

One might ask: if the spring needs only to fall within *Nissan*, perhaps it suffices for spring to begin by the fifteenth, i.e., by *Pesach* itself. And if spring only begins on the sixteenth — one day late — why not simply add a day to one of the preceding months rather than an entire leap month? Rashi addresses both questions. On the first: the word *chodesh* in the verse implies *chadesh* — newness, waxing. The moon is still growing, still renewing itself, only through the fourteenth of the month. From the fifteenth onward it begins to wane. Therefore, for the month to be a *chodesh* in the full sense — a waxing, renewing month — the spring must begin by the fourteenth, not the fifteenth. On the second: since the spring must begin by the fourteenth rather than the fifteenth, a single-day adjustment to a preceding month would be insufficient. The gap requires a full thirty-day leap month — *ibur hashana* — to bring *Nissan* back into proper alignment with the solar spring.

### Adjustment Limits

This leads to a further question: if one could see in advance that *Pesach* would fall a day or two late, why not preemptively extend one or two of the preceding months by a day? The answer involves limits on how much imbalance is permissible in the calendar. A normal year has six thirty-day months and six twenty-nine-day months. One can extend this to seven thirty-day months and five twenty-nine-day months. Whether one may go as far as eight and four is a matter of dispute — some permit it, others do not, and according to some readings even eight and four is forbidden. If one has already used up the permissible single-day adjustments and cannot make a double adjustment, there is no alternative to declaring a full leap year.

---

## Moon Phases at Sea

### Seafarer's Marker

Rav Nachman addressed a practical challenge facing those who traveled at sea: *atun delo yadisu bikviya diyarcha* — you will be on the ocean and will have no way of knowing when *Beis Din* declared *Rosh Chodesh*. Without knowing the exact date, how will you know when the fourteenth of *Nissan* arrives and it is time to destroy *chametz*? Rav Nachman provided a lunar marker: *ki chazisu seira demashlim leyoma* — when you see that the moon "completes the day," i.e., sets precisely as the sun rises, then *biar* u *chamira* — destroy your *chametz*. That moment signals that you are at the midpoint of the month, around the fifteenth of *Nissan*.

### Astronomical Marker

The *gemara* then clarifies the astronomy behind this marker. At the middle of the month, the sun and moon are diametrically opposite one another, with the earth between them. This means that at sunset, the full moon rises on the opposite horizon; it then remains visible throughout the entire night; and at sunrise, it sets. The moon literally "completes" the day — its light fills the night from end to end, setting just as the sun comes up. This is the phenomenon that marks the fifteenth of the month.

### Land vs. Sea

The *gemara* then raises a difficulty. If this phenomenon marks the fifteenth, yet *chametz* must be destroyed on the fourteenth, why did Rav Nachman give this marker to seafarers? The *gemara* resolves this: *ledidu demaglu lehu alma* — for those on land, where the horizon is clear and visibility is enhanced, this phenomenon is actually observable on the fourteenth. The geometry of visibility from land versus sea creates a slight difference in how the positions of sun and moon appear relative to the horizon. For those at sea, the marker occurs on the fifteenth; for those on land with a clear, open horizon, effectively on the fourteenth. The *gemara* does not fully resolve the precise optical explanation, and the details of how enhanced horizon visibility shifts the apparent timing remain somewhat unclear.

---

## Shabbat Override

### Nissan & Tishrei

The *mishna* states: *al shenei chadashim mechalelin et haShabbos* — for two months, witnesses may violate *Shabbos* in order to testify about the new moon. Those two months are *Nissan* and *Tishrei*. For all other months, while witnesses might in principle come forward, the urgency that would justify overriding *Shabbos* applies only to these two.

### Festival Dependency

The reason is that *Nissan* and *Tishrei* are the hinge upon which all the *Yamim Tovim* turn. The *mishna* notes: *shebahen shluchim yotzim leSurya uvehen metaknin et hamoadot* — for these months the messengers go out to the surrounding lands, and the entire festival calendar is organized around them. *Pesach* depends on the correct dating of *Nissan*; *Rosh Hashanah*, *Yom Kippur*, and *Succos* all depend on *Tishrei*. For these months, the stakes of accurate testimony are high enough to override *Shabbos*.

### Formal Declaration

The *gemara* notes an apparent contradiction. The *mishna* says messengers go out for *Nissan* and *Tishrei*, implying not for other months. Yet an earlier *mishna* states that messengers go out for all six months. Abaye resolves this: for all months, *shluchim yotzim me'urta* — messengers can depart already at nightfall. If the preceding month was thirty days and no *Rosh Chodesh* was declared on the thirtieth, by nightfall one knows that the following day is *Rosh Chodesh*, and messengers may depart. But for *Nissan* and *Tishrei* — *ad sheyishme'u mipi Beis Din mekudash* — even when it is certain that today is *Rosh Chodesh*, messengers do not depart until they have explicitly heard the formal declaration of *mekudash* from *Beis Din*. This level of procedural rigor reflects the singular importance of these months.

### Verse Derivation

The *gemara* then asks: what is the scriptural basis for overriding *Shabbos* to testify about the new moon? The verse states: *eleh moadei Hashem asher tikre'u otam bemo'adam* — these are the appointed times of God, which you shall proclaim in their proper time. The imperative to proclaim the festivals at their correct time overrides *Shabbos* — *al keri'atam atah mechalel* — it is the act of declaring *Rosh Chodesh* itself that may override *Shabbos*. However, *v'ei atah mechalel al kiyuman* — one does not override *Shabbos* merely to ensure that the message reaches distant communities, i.e., the sending of messengers does not itself override *Shabbos*.

### Ben Zakkai's Takana

The *mishna* then records that when the *Beis Hamikdash* stood, witnesses would violate *Shabbos* to testify for all twelve months — *mechalelin af al kulam mipnei takanat hakorban* — because each month's *korban mussaf* depended on knowing the correct date. After the *Beis Hamikdash* was destroyed, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai ruled that *Shabbos* may be violated for testimony only regarding *Nissan* and *Tishrei*: *vechi yesh korban?* — is there still a *korban*? Without the *Beis Hamikdash*, the weight that had attached to every month's testimony no longer exists, and only the two months with direct festival significance continue to justify the override.

### Post-Mikdash Reality

This *takana* of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai is often classified among his *takannot zekher lamikdash* — enactments made in memory of the Temple. But it is worth understanding his legislative program more precisely. Many of his rulings, including this one, are not so much attempts to preserve pre-Destruction practice as they are honest acknowledgments that the world has fundamentally changed. The earlier *mishna* on this daf noted that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai also ruled that witnesses may be accepted even after *mincha* time — a leniency made possible precisely because there is no longer a *korban* whose preparation depends on immediate action. Similarly here: by restricting the *Shabbos* override to *Nissan* and *Tishrei*, he is not memorializing the *Mikdash* but responding to the new post-*Mikdash* reality in which only the festival calendar remains as a pressing halachic concern. The *takannot* of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai are thus better understood as legislation for a new era than as nostalgia for the one that was lost.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 22

## Shabbat Violation

### Clear or Unclear

The daf begins by picking up from the *mishna* on 21b, which opens with the principle: *bein she-nira be'alil bein she-lo nira be'alil, mechallelin alav et ha-Shabbat* — whether the new moon was seen clearly or not clearly, witnesses may violate *Shabbat* to come and testify. One might have thought: if the moon appeared on a perfectly clear night and everyone could see it, surely there are witnesses who live closer to Jerusalem who did not have to violate *Shabbat* to get there — why should I, who live far away, be entitled to violate *Shabbat* to travel and testify when others will certainly arrive without any violation? The *mishna* rejects this reasoning: every witness who has seen the moon should come, because one never knows what will happen. Perhaps all the others will turn out to be invalid for some reason, and this witness's testimony will be the one on which *kiddush ha-chodesh* ultimately rests. The term *mechallelin* here implies not merely permission but obligation — if you have seen the moon, you must go.

### Rabbi Yosi Disagrees

*Rabbi Yosi omer*: if the moon was seen *be'alil* — clearly — then you do not violate *Shabbat*, because there will certainly be other witnesses available who did not need to travel far. The *mishna* then records an illustrative incident: more than forty pairs of witnesses were on their way to testify, and *Rabbi Akiva* detained them in Lod, reasoning that since so many people had seen the moon, there was no need for all of them to violate *Shabbat* — others closer to the destination would testify.

### Rabban Gamliel Policy

*Rabban Gamliel* sent word to *Rabbi Akiva*: *im me'akeiv attah et ha-rabbim, nimtza makhshilam le-atid lavo* — if you prevent the masses from coming now, you will cause them to stumble in the future. The concern is that next year, a witness will remember that the last time he made the long journey on *Shabbat*, he was turned away, and so he will not bother to go. This will undermine the entire institution of *kiddush ha-chodesh* going forward.

What is striking here is the nature of *Rabban Gamliel*'s argument. He is not claiming that this particular witness is necessary for the present *kiddush ha-chodesh* — it is entirely possible that forty other pairs will suffice without this one. Rather, the justification for *chilul Shabbat* is a macro-level policy consideration: in order to preserve the long-term functioning of the institution, it is necessary to maintain a norm of universal participation. This raises a conceptually interesting point: the *chilul Shabbat* is warranted not because of the micro-necessity of this individual witness, but because of the broader systemic requirement. This is somewhat analogous to the principle of *hativu sofam mishum techilatan* — permitting the return journey of those who traveled to save a life, even though the return itself involves no *pikuach nefesh*. The discussion there in *Beitzah* concerned rabbinic prohibitions, but the analogy is instructive: sometimes broader institutional considerations shape what is permitted.

---

## Be'alil Definition

### Psalms Source

The *gemara* asks: *mai mashma de-hai alio* — what is the linguistic basis for understanding *be'alil* as meaning "clearly"? *Rabbi Abba* cites the verse from Psalms 12:7: *imrot Hashem imrot tehorot, kesef tzaruf be'alil la-aretz, mezukak shivatayim* — the utterances of God are pure utterances, like silver refined *be'alil la-aretz*, purified sevenfold. It should be noted that standard English translations render *be'alil la-aretz* as referring to an earthenware crucible — the vessel in which silver is smelted. The *gemara*, however, reads the word *be'alil* as conveying purity and clarity, deriving from it the sense of something refined and clearly visible. Exactly what is done with *la-aretz* on that reading is left somewhat unclear. In any case, the root conveys refinement, purity, and clarity — and indeed, in modern Hebrew *nirah be'alil* means "clearly visible."

### Fifty Gates Debate

The verse's phrase *mezukak shivatayim* — refined sevenfold, meaning forty-nine — connects to a famous *midrash* that serves as the basis for a debate between Rav and Shmuel. One of them says: *nun sha'arei bina nivra'u ba-olam* — fifty gates of wisdom were created in the world, *ve-kulan nitnu le-Moshe chasar achat* — and all of them were given to Moshe except one, so Moshe possessed forty-nine. The source for this is the verse *va-techasrehu me'at me-Elokim* — you have diminished him only slightly from the divine. Forty-nine levels, then, represents the pinnacle of human wisdom, corresponding to the *shivatayim* — the seven sevens — of the verse.

### Kohelet's Ambition

Based on this, *bikesh Kohelet li-heyot ke-Moshe* — Kohelet aspired to attain the same level of wisdom as Moshe. A heavenly voice responded with the end of the verse: *ve-katuv yosher divrei emet* — and what is written straight in the words of truth? *Ve-lo kam navi od be-Yisrael ke-Moshe* — there arose no prophet again in Israel like Moshe. So Kohelet was told: you cannot be like Moshe.

The other opinion in the Rav-Shmuel debate responds: the prohibition *lo kam navi* refers specifically to a *navi* — a prophet. In the realm of kingship, Kohelet could indeed achieve that same level. So the aspiration itself was not the problem. The problem, according to this view, is the second clause of the verse: *bikesh Kohelet li-don dinim she-ba-lev, she-lo be-eidim ve-she-lo be-hatra'ah* — Kohelet sought to adjudicate cases based on his perception of people's innermost thoughts and motivations, without external witnesses and without formal warning. Because he was so wise, he believed he could see through to the truth without formal legal procedure. The heavenly voice responded with the words of truth inscribed in the Torah: *al pi shnayim eidim yakum davar* — on the testimony of two witnesses shall a matter be established.

The lesson is striking: however brilliant the judge, the legal system cannot be run on the basis of private insight. The world must be governed by objectively ascertainable facts, by formal procedure, not by the genius of any individual. This resonates with the famous observation about *Rabbi Meir* — that the *halacha* was not ruled like him because he was so penetrating that no one else could follow his reasoning. Raw intellectual brilliance, however extraordinary, does not override the institutional requirements of communal law.

---

## Shazpar Story

### Forty Pairs

The *mishna* records the incident of forty pairs of witnesses on their way to testify about the new moon, who were detained in Lod — apparently on their way to Yavneh, which was the seat of the *beit din* in the post-*Churban* period, and which is indeed closer to Lod than Jerusalem, making the journey more plausible in terms of covering the distance before the day's end.

### Shazpar's Role

A *braita* corrects the apparent attribution to *Rabbi Akiva*: *amar Rabbi Yehudah, chas ve-shalom she-Rabbi Akiva ikvan* — it never occurred to *Rabbi Akiva* to detain them, for he well understood the principle that witnesses must come even at the cost of *Shabbat*. Rather, it was *Shazpar rosh shel Gader* — a figure named Shazpar, the head of Gader (perhaps modern Gedera, near the coast, in the vicinity of Ashkelon) — who detained them. And *Rabban Gamliel* sent word and had him deposed from his position as a consequence of this action. This is quite a different story than one involving *Rabbi Akiva*.

### Day 30 Question

A related question arises, though it is not made fully explicit in the text: is the license to violate *Shabbat* specifically tied to cases where the *beit din* will be declaring the month on day 30, making it a twenty-nine-day month? If the moon was not seen on the night of day 30 and day 31 will automatically be *Rosh Chodesh* regardless, why would anyone violate *Shabbat* to come testify? There is still the question, raised earlier in the *gemara*, of whether there is a *mitzvah* to perform *kiddush ha-chodesh al pi ha-re'iyah* — based on actual testimony — even on day 31 when the calendar outcome is not in doubt. Whether that *mitzvah* alone would suffice to justify *chilul Shabbat*, and whether it would do so even if it were certain that many others had clearly seen the moon, remains not fully resolved.

---

## Valid Witnesses

### Father and Son

The next *mishna* addresses who may come to testify. *Av u-veno she-ra'u et ha-chodesh yelechu* — a father and son who have both seen the new moon should both go to testify. The *mishna* immediately clarifies: *lo she-mitztarfin zeh im zeh* — not that they combine together as a single valid pair of witnesses, since relatives cannot testify together. Rather, *she-im yippasel echad mehem, mitztaref ha-sheni im acher* — if one of them is disqualified for some reason, perhaps because he does not describe the moon's details correctly, the other remains available to pair with a different witness. Since we accept many more witnesses than the bare minimum of two, having a father and son travel together is no different from having ten unrelated people travel together — not all of them will be needed, but it is prudent to have backup.

### Rabbi Shimon Relatives

*Rabbi Shimon* goes further: *av u-veno ve-kol ha-kerovim kesherim le-edut ha-chodesh* — a father and son and all relatives are in fact *kasher* as witnesses for testimony about the new moon, even when combining together. This is a significant ruling that goes beyond the first clause of the *mishna*, and the *gemara* will search for its rationale.

### Tuvyah Story

*Rabbi Yosi* introduces a relevant incident: *ma'aseh be-Tuvyah ha-rofe* — the story of Tuvyah the doctor, who saw the new moon in Jerusalem together with his son and his freed slave. This was during the period of the *Beit ha-Mikdash*. The *kohanim* accepted Tuvyah and his son but invalidated the freed slave.

### Beit Din Reversal

When the group came before the *beit din* — the rabbinic court, which had ultimate authority — the court accepted Tuvyah and the freed slave and invalidated the son, on the grounds that Tuvyah and his son were relatives who could not testify together, whereas the status of the freed slave presented no such problem.

### Priestly vs. Rabbinic

The subtext of this episode is not subtle. The *kohanim* were exercised about the freed slave — a man of slave lineage, a former *Kena'ani* — even though he was now a full Jew. The *kohanim*, whose entire institutional identity rests on the principle of *ab u-veno*, of patrilineal descent and hierarchical lineage, were naturally sensitive to questions of status and lineage. They were unbothered by the father-and-son combination because that very structure is the foundation of *kehunah* itself. The rabbis, by contrast, were not impressed by lineage — for them, the freed slave's Jewish status was unimpeachable and irrelevant to his reliability as a witness, while the issue of relatives testifying together was the operative concern. This episode encapsulates in miniature the difference between the priestly and rabbinic approaches to communal hierarchy.

---

## Moshe Aharon Source

### Verse Interpretation

*Rav Levi* provides the textual basis for *Rabbi Shimon*'s ruling: *de-chtiv va-yomer Hashem el Moshe ve-el Aharon be-eretz Mitzrayim lemor, ha-chodesh ha-zeh lachem* — God commanded both Moshe and Aharon together regarding the sanctification of the new month. Since Moshe and Aharon were brothers, this implies that *edut zu tehi kesherah bachem* — this testimony is valid even when given by brothers or other relatives.

### Rabbanan Response

The *rabbanan* counter: the verse does not imply that brothers are qualified as joint witnesses. Rather, *edut zu tehi mesurah lachem* — this matter is entrusted to your leadership and responsibility. The verse addresses the leaders of the generation and indicates that *kiddush ha-chodesh* is their charge, not that it may be performed by relatives acting as co-witnesses.

### Type of Testimony

This debate opens a broader question: is testimony about the new moon a classic form of *edut* — formal legal testimony directed against a person — or is it something categorically different, more akin to reporting a state of affairs? In *halacha*, most formal testimony concerns events: a person did this act, committed this violation. Here, witnesses are simply stating a fact they observed — we saw the moon. The reason such factual statements usually still require two witnesses is likely not conceptual but practical: formal *halacha* generally demands direct evidence rather than circumstantial inference. But the *edut ha-chodesh* case raises the question of whether it truly belongs in the category of classic testimony at all.

### Lichtenstein View

A related framing was offered by Rav Aharon Lichtenstein: the operative verse governing classic testimony is *ki yakum ed hamas ba-ish* — when a witness rises up against a person. Formal *edut* is, at its core, testimony directed against someone. Testimony about the new moon is not directed against any person at all. It may therefore fall outside the classical category of testimony, which would explain why the normal rules of eligibility — including the disqualification of relatives — might not apply. This is related to the broader principle of *ed echad ne'eman be-issurin* — one witness is trusted regarding prohibitions — where again the testimony is not against a person but reports a state of affairs, and where accordingly the rules are significantly loosened.

---

## Rav Huna Challenge

### Conflicting Rulings

*Rav Chana bar Abba* ruled: *hilcheta ke-Rabbi Shimon* — the *halacha* follows *Rabbi Shimon* that relatives are *kasher* for *edut ha-chodesh*. *Rav Huna* challenged him: but *Rabbi Yosi* recorded the story of Tuvyah and his son being rejected by the *beit din* — and you are ruling like *Rabbi Shimon*?

### Rav Silence

*Rav Chana bar Abba* responded: I stated this ruling — *hilcheta ke-Rabbi Shimon* — in the presence of Rav many times, and Rav never objected. This silence, he argued, constituted implicit approval.

### Reversed Positions

*Rav Huna* then revealed the problem: how exactly did you present the positions to Rav? *Rav Chana* admitted that he had stated the positions in reverse — he attributed the ruling permitting relatives to *Rabbi Shimon* and the invalidating position to the other opinion. Since Rav heard the ruling as "*Rabbi Shimon* says relatives are invalid" and agreed, he was actually endorsing the stricter position. His silence was not an endorsement of the lenient ruling at all.

### Shmuel's Ruling

*Tavi brei de-Mari Tavi* reported in the name of *Mar Ukva* in the name of *Shmuel*: *hilcheta ke-Rabbi Shimon*. The question, of course, is which version of *Rabbi Shimon*'s position is being endorsed. Some manuscripts add the word *ein* — *ein hilcheta ke-Rabbi Shimon* — though this is clearly a later gloss, since the Aramaic formulation would be *leit* rather than *ein*. The general assumption, consistent with the plain reading of the *gemara* and with the story of Tuvyah's son being rejected, is that the *halacha* does not validate relatives for *edut ha-chodesh* — but the final conclusion remains genuinely murky.

---

## Invalid Witnesses

### Disqualified List

The *mishna* enumerates the categories of witnesses who are invalid: those who play dice (*ha-mesachek ba-kuvya*), those who lend money at interest (*malveh be-ribbit*), those who race pigeons (*mafrichei yonim*), those who engage in commerce with *shevi'it* produce (*socharei shevi'it*), and slaves (*avadim*). This is the well-known *mishna* from *Sanhedrin*.

### General Rule

The *mishna* then articulates the governing principle: *kol edut she-ein ha-ishah kesherah lah, af hen einan kesherim lah* — any testimony for which a woman is invalid, these categories of persons are likewise invalid. Tosafot notes an important distinction: this principle applies to those who are individually unfit. The earlier discussion about relatives was different — each relative is individually a *kasher* witness; the only question was whether they could combine. But the persons listed here are unfit as individuals, and everyone agrees they cannot testify for *kiddush ha-chodesh*.

### Woman's Testimony

The one domain in which a woman's testimony is accepted is to testify that another woman's husband has died, thereby permitting the widow to remarry. The rabbis granted very broad latitude for this category of testimony — *edut ishah* — including accepting hearsay (*ed mipi ed*). And by the rule of the *mishna*, these otherwise disqualified categories are likewise accepted for this testimony.

### Gazlan Categories

*Rav Ashi* draws out the implication: *zot omeret, gazlan de-divreihem, kesherim le-edut ishah* — this teaches that a rabbinic-level *gazlan* is valid for testimony about a woman's husband's death, but a biblical *gazlan* is not. The listed individuals are classified as *gazlan de-divreihem* — only rabbinically considered to be acting with the mentality of a thief — and it is only on that basis that they retain validity for *edut ishah*.

### Severity Question

This raises an obvious difficulty: several items on the list appear to involve biblical violations. Lending at interest and trading in *peirot shevi'it* are not obviously mere rabbinic offenses. Why are these individuals classified as only rabbinic *gazlanim*?

### Tosafot & Rashi

Tosafot offers two explanations. First, the *mishna* may be referring specifically to subcategories of these transgressions that are only rabbinic violations — there are indeed rabbinic forms of interest and rabbinic forms of prohibited *shevi'it* commerce. Second, and more conceptually interesting: a person who engages in these activities is typically able to rationalize his behavior and does not fully appreciate that he is committing a clear biblical violation. If a person genuinely does not perceive what he is doing as a serious transgression, then his willingness to engage in it does not demonstrate the same preparedness to put his testimony up for sale as would an out-and-out theft. It is this psychological dimension — the capacity for self-rationalization — that keeps him in the rabbinic rather than biblical *gazlan* category.

*Rashi* takes a somewhat different approach. Even if the violation is in fact biblical, these activities do not involve overtly taking something from another person — they are not straightforward theft. Because the nature of the interaction does not constitute the direct appropriation of someone else's property, it does not rise to the level that would make a person's testimony fundamentally untrustworthy. Only genuine, direct theft — the act of taking what manifestly belongs to someone else — raises the concern that the person's testimony can be bought.
