Absent that, even biblical violations of a financial character do not cross the threshold that invalidates one for *edut ishah*.

---

## Practical Provisions

### Transport Help

The *mishna* turns to the practical arrangements made for witnesses traveling to testify. If a witness saw the new moon but is unable to walk, he is transported on a donkey on *Shabbat* — and if necessary, even carried on his bed. The *Shabbat* violation is warranted by the same logic that permits the witness himself to travel.

### Defense & Supply

If people are lying in wait to waylay them along the route, the witnesses may carry weapons — sticks or arms — on *Shabbat*. If the journey is long, they may take provisions of food. All of this may be done despite it being *Shabbat*, because the testimony cannot be effective unless the witnesses actually arrive.

### Time Constraint

The limiting condition is that the journey must be completable within a night and a day — that is, the witness must be able to arrive before the following nightfall, since testimony delivered after the day of *Rosh Chodesh* has ended serves no purpose.

### Verse Justification

The *mishna* derives its authorization for *Shabbat* violation from the verse: *eleh mo'adei Hashem asher tikre'u otam be-mo'adam* — these are the appointed times of God that you shall proclaim in their proper time. The phrase *be-mo'adam* — in their time — implies that the proclamation must be made at the right moment even if that requires overriding *Shabbat*.

---

## Character Witnesses

### Vouching System

The *mishna* on 22b opens the new *perek* — though the discussion continues seamlessly from the previous chapter — with the following rule: *im einan makirin oto* — if the *beit din* does not recognize the witnesses who have come to testify, *meshalchin imo acher le-ha'ido* — they send another person along with the witness who can vouch for his trustworthiness and identity. This practice arose in response to the problem of sectarians attempting to manipulate the calendar by submitting false testimony. Originally, the *beit din* accepted testimony from any person who walked in. Once the *Baitusim* began corrupting the process, the rabbis instituted a requirement that only recognized witnesses, or those vouched for by recognized parties, would be accepted.

### One vs. Pair

The *gemara* immediately asks: *mai acher, chad* — does the *mishna* mean they send one additional person? The *gemara* questions whether one character witness would be sufficient, since the normal rules of *edut* require two witnesses.

### One Sufficient

At the level of the *mishna*'s plain meaning, one character witness does seem to be what is intended. The *mishna* uses singular language, and it would be reasonable to think that the *beit din*'s institutional discretion in setting up this character-witness system would allow them to accept a single vouching individual.

### Pappa's Solution

*Rav Pappa* resolves the apparent contradiction between the *mishna* and a *braita* (which implies two character witnesses are needed) by reinterpreting the *mishna*: *mai acher, zug acher* — when the *mishna* says "another," it means another *pair*, not a single individual. The basis for requiring a pair is the principle *mishpat kesiv bei* — the verse associates *mishpat*, the ordinary rules of a law court, with the process of *kiddush ha-chodesh*, which means the normal requirement of two witnesses applies to the character witnesses as well. As is acknowledged, this is a somewhat strained reading of the *mishna*, which clearly seems to speak of one person being sent. But the *gemara* commits to it in order to harmonize the two sources.

### Rabbi Nehorai

The *gemara* then cites a *braita*: *ma'aseh be-Rabbi Nehorai she-halach eitzel ha-eid le-ha'id alav be-Shabbat le-Usha* — Rabbi Nehorai traveled on *Shabbat* to Usha to serve as a character witness for another witness. This demonstrates not only that the witness himself may violate *Shabbat*, but that the character witness may do so as well — for without the character witness, the primary witness will not be accepted, making the entire exercise pointless. The logic is the same: whatever is necessary to make the testimony effective is permitted.

### Two Witnesses Needed

The *gemara* addresses the apparent implication that a single character witness suffices, since only *Rabbi Nehorai* is mentioned. Two explanations are offered. The first: there was in fact another character witness traveling with *Rabbi Nehorai*, but the *braita* only mentions *Rabbi Nehorai* because the *chiddush* — the novel point — is that even a figure of his stature would violate *Shabbat* merely to serve as a character witness. *Rav Ashi* offers a variant: the second character witness was already present in Usha; only *Rabbi Nehorai* needed to violate *Shabbat*, because the other witness was already there. In either case, there were indeed two character witnesses. The *chiddush* of the story, according to *Rav Ashi*, is that one should not hesitate to violate *Shabbat* on the assumption that the second witness might not be there — even in a case of uncertainty about whether one's own presence will be sufficient to complete the pair, one should go. The simple reading of both the *mishna* and the *braita* would allow a single character witness, but the *gemara* maintains that two are required.

---

## Reports vs. Witnesses

### Ulla's Report

When Ulla arrived from *Eretz Yisrael* and reported that the new month had been sanctified there, *Rav Kahana* noted that the question of credibility should not be limited to Ulla specifically.

### Revelation Principle

*Rav Kahana* articulates the principle: *lo mibaya Ulla, de-gavra raba hu* — it goes without saying that Ulla, a great scholar, can be trusted. *Ela afilu inish de-alma nami meheman* — even an ordinary person would be trusted to report what happened. Why? *Kol milta de-avida le-igluyi, lo meshakri bei inshei* — anything that is destined to become publicly known, people do not lie about. If the month was indeed sanctified, word will spread and the truth will emerge regardless. Anyone who falsely reported that *Rosh Chodesh* had been declared would quickly be exposed. The self-correcting nature of the information therefore removes the incentive to lie and makes any messenger credible.

### End-of-World Report

A *braita* confirms this: *ba echad be-sof ha-olam ve-amar kiddshu beit din et ha-chodesh, ne'eman* — someone who comes from the ends of the earth and reports that the *beit din* sanctified the month is believed.

### Identity vs. Revelation

This creates a striking asymmetry: witnesses who appear before the *beit din* to testify directly about the moon must be recognized or vouched for, while a messenger who simply reports the fact of *kiddush ha-chodesh* can be trusted even if completely unknown. The reason is structural. A witness who appears in person might be a sectarian impersonating a legitimate witness, or simply an unknown figure whose reliability cannot be assessed. But a reporter of a communal event is protected by the revelation principle — the facts will become known regardless, and a false report will be quickly exposed. The requirements therefore track the nature of the risk, not a uniform standard of trustworthiness.

---

## Baitusim Plot

### Original Openness

*Barishonah hayu mekabelin edut ha-chodesh mikol adam* — originally, the *beit din* accepted testimony about the new moon from any person without restriction. No prior recognition was required.

### False Testimony

*Mishe-kilkelu ha-Baitusim* — once the *Baitusim* corrupted the process. A *braita* elaborates: *pa'am achat bikshu Baitusim le-hat'ot et ha-chakhamim* — on one occasion the *Baitusim* sought to deceive the Sages about when *Rosh Chodesh* fell. They hired two people for four hundred *zuz* to give false testimony about when the new moon had appeared. Their motivation, as noted earlier, was to manipulate the calendar so that *Pesach* would fall on *Shabbat* — which would cause the day after *Pesach* to coincide with the day after *Shabbat*, thereby aligning the rabbinic calendar with the *Baitusim*' practice of counting fifty days from the Sunday after *Pesach* for *Shavuot*.

### Undercover Agent

*Echad mishelanu ve-echad mishelahem* — one of the two hired men was, as it turned out, sympathetic to the rabbinic cause. The *Baitusim* did not know this. He was not planted as a formal undercover agent; his sympathies simply lay with the rabbis, and when hired to deliver false testimony, he saw an opportunity to expose the scheme.

### Ridiculous Details

Their man testified first and departed. Then the second man — the one with rabbinic sympathies — was brought before the *beit din* and asked: tell us how you saw the moon. He proceeded to deliver the following account: *olei hayiti be-ma'aleh Adumim* — I was going up the ascent of Ma'aleh Adumim. I saw the moon crouching between two rocks. Its head resembled a calf, its ears resembled a goat, its horns resembled a deer, and its tail was between its thighs. I peered closely at it and fell backwards in astonishment. The absurdity of this description — the moon crouching like a beast with animal features — was clearly designed to expose the fraud. And to remove all doubt, he added: *harei masayim zuz tzerurim li be-sidini* — and here, tied in my garment, are the 200 *zuz* I was paid to say this.

### Confession

He then explained his motivation: *shamati she-Baitusim mevakshim le-hat'ot et ha-chakhamim* — I heard that the *Baitusim* were plotting to deceive you. I went along with it and took the money, he said, because I was afraid that someone less principled would come and actually succeed in misleading you. So he played along in order to expose the plot.

### Response & Reform

The *beit din*'s response: *masayim zuz netunim lecha be-matanah* — keep the 200 *zuz* as a gift. The person who hired him — the *Baitusim* agent — was brought to the post and flogged. And from that moment on, *hitkinu she-lo yehu mekabelin ela min ha-makirim* — they instituted the policy of accepting testimony only from recognized individuals. The entire recognition-and-vouching system of the *mishna* flows directly from this episode.

---

## Bonfire System

### Beacon Method

*Barishonah hayu masi'in masu'ot* — originally, the communication of *Rosh Chodesh* across *Eretz Yisrael* and into the *golah* was accomplished by a system of mountaintop bonfires. The principle is elegant: if people are stationed on successive mountain peaks and each lights a fire upon seeing the previous peak's fire, a message can travel hundreds of miles in minutes — a communication daisy chain of extraordinary efficiency.

### Sabotage

*Mishe-kilkelu ha-Kusim* — when the *Kusim* (with some manuscripts reading *Baitusim*) interfered by lighting false fires at unauthorized times. The difference between the sabotage of the testimony system and the sabotage of the bonfire system is worth noting. A person who delivers false testimony in person puts his reputation on the line; as the *gemara* noted earlier, people do not lie about things that will eventually be revealed. But lighting a bonfire on a mountaintop at night is entirely anonymous. Nobody knows who lit it, and the revelation principle does not apply. The communication channel was therefore vulnerable in a way that personal testimony is not — it could be hacked. The *Kusim* (or *Baitusim*) exploited precisely this vulnerability.

### Technical Details

The *mishna* describes the physical apparatus: *mevi'in kelonsa'ot shel erez aruchim* — they would take long cedar poles, together with reeds, olive wood, and flax fiber, wrapping the materials together with rope into a bundle at the top of the pole. The beacon-lighter would then go to the mountain peak, ignite the materials, and wave the fire *u-molik u-mevi u-ma'aleh u-morid* — forwards and back, upward and downward. Tosafot explains that the waving motion was necessary to ensure the signal could not be mistaken for a natural phenomenon such as a shooting star.

### Mountain Chain

The chain of beacons ran: from *Har ha-Mishchah* — the Mount of Olives — to Sartaba, from Sartaba to Grofina, from Grofina to Havran, from Havran to Beit Baltin.

### Full Coverage

*U-mi-Beit Baltin lo zazu misham* — from Beit Baltin, the final station in the chain, they did not move until *she-ro'eh kol ha-golah lefanav ke-madurat esh* — until the entire exile was illuminated before them like a great bonfire. The entire *golah*, covering hundreds of miles, received the signal effectively instantaneously.

### Messenger Switch

Once the *Kusim* began lighting false fires and the system was compromised, *hitkinu she-yehu sheluchim yotzim* — the rabbis switched to dispatching human messengers to communicate *Rosh Chodesh*. Messengers, unlike bonfires, are accountable individuals who put their reputations on the line. The communication system that was so elegant and instantaneous had to be abandoned for something far slower because the channel had been hacked — the price of sabotage was paid in time and efficiency for generations afterward.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 24

## Moon Directionality

### Before/After Sun

The *gemara* opens by examining the astronomical framework used to test moon witnesses, picking up at the very bottom of 23b. The *mishnah* had already established that witnesses who claim to have seen the new moon before the sun — *lifnei hachammah* — have said nothing valid, *lo amar klum*. The *gemara* now unpacks why, and extends the analysis to a second axis of questioning: north versus south.

The underlying astronomy is as follows. The moon moves counterclockwise relative to the sun. When the moon is in exact conjunction with the sun — perfectly aligned — it is completely dark, since only its far side is illuminated. This is the *molad*. The moon becomes visible only some hours later, once it has moved sufficiently away from the sun that it is no longer blinded by solar glare. At that point, the new moon trails just behind the sun. The old moon, by contrast, sits just ahead of the sun — it is visible in the final moments before sunrise and then sets before the sun does. The new moon is the mirror image: invisible during the day because the sun is too bright, it becomes visible after sunset because the sun has already set and the moon is trailing just behind. This is why the new moon must be seen *after* the sun, *leachar hachammah*, and any witness who says otherwise is simply describing something that cannot be true.

### North/South Position

The second axis of questioning — *litzfonah* or *lidromah*, to the north or to the south — requires a more careful treatment of the sun's path. In the northern hemisphere, the sun does not travel directly east to west but arcs toward the south: rising in the east, curving southward, and setting in the west. Given this trajectory, something that is *lifnei hachammah*, in front of the sun as it moves, lies more to the north; something that is *leachar hachammah*, behind the sun, lies more to the south. The *gemara* therefore equates *lifnei hachammah* with *litzfonah* (north) and *leachar hachammah* with *lidromah* (south).

## Moon Indentation

### Pegima Definition

Abaye, however, reframes the question entirely. The question of *lifnei* versus *leachar*, he argues, is not simply asking whether the moon leads or trails the sun — that question is already settled, and the answer must be that it trails. Rather, Abaye understands the question as: *pegimata lifnei hachammah o leachar hachammah* — is the indentation, the lacking side of the moon, facing toward the sun or away from it?

This is physically straightforward once stated. The moon is illuminated by the sun; whichever portion faces the sun is lit, and whichever portion faces away is dark. The *pegimah*, the lacking or indented side, is therefore always the side facing away from the sun. A witness who claims that the indented side was facing toward the sun has described an optical impossibility. *Im amar pegimata lifnei hachammah, lo amar klum* — if he says the indentation faced the sun, he has said nothing.

### Moon Embarrassment

This physical law is anchored in a *midrashic* teaching. Rabbi Yochanan derives it from the verse in Job: *hamshal ufachad imo oseh shalom bimromav* — dominion and fear are with Him, He makes peace in His celestial heights. The peace referred to is this: *me'olam lo ra'ata chammah pegimata shel levanah* — the sun has never seen the indentation of the moon. The reason given is *dechalsha da'atah* — so that the moon would not become despondent. This evokes the well-known *midrash* in which the moon complained that two luminaries of equal size cannot share the sky, and God diminished it. Given that humiliation, it would be an additional cruelty to allow the sun to see the moon's lacking side — its nakedness, as it were — and so the *pegimah* always faces away.

### Rainbow Symbolism

The same verse teaches that the sun has also never seen the indentation of the rainbow, *pegimata shel keshet*, for a different reason: *delo limru ovdei chammah girei ka mashdaya* — lest the sun-worshippers say that God is shooting arrows. A rainbow, viewed as an archer's bow, has its concave side facing the direction from which arrows are shot. The Ramban notes that the rainbow's significance as a covenantal sign lies precisely in this reversal: God holds the bow with its concave side facing upward and away, the posture of one who surrenders his weapon, as if to say He will not shoot down upon the earth. The raindrops of the *mabul* may be understood as the arrows — a connection the *gemara* surfaces here, though the precise astronomical relationship between the sun's position and the arc of the rainbow remains a matter for further investigation.

## Moon Directionality (II)

### Summer/Winter

Returning to the north-south question, the *gemara* presents an apparent contradiction. One *baraita* states that a witness who says the moon was to the north, *litzfonah*, has given valid testimony, while one who says it was to the south, *lidromah*, has said nothing. A second *baraita* says precisely the opposite: *lidromah devarav kayamin*, south is valid, while *litzfonah lo amar klum*, north is invalid. This second formulation, at least, coheres with the analysis above, in which the new moon trailing the sun would be to the south.

The *gemara* resolves: *lo kashya*, there is no difficulty. *Kan bimot hachammah, kan bimot hageshamim* — one *baraita* refers to summer and the other to winter. The explanation that best captures the astronomical reality, as the *Meiri* articulates it, is as follows. In winter, the sun's arc is shorter: it rises in the southeast and sets in the southwest. In summer, the arc is longer: it rises in the northeast and sets in the northwest. The question being posed to the witnesses is where on the horizon the moon set. In winter, the correct answer is that it set in the south; in summer, in the north. The apparent contradiction dissolves once one distinguishes between the two seasons. Rashi offers a different explanation that is considerably more difficult to unpack astronomically, and the *Meiri*'s reading is to be preferred.

A further contextual note: the earlier *mishnah* mentions that these examinations took place in a great courtyard in Jerusalem — *chatzer gedolah hayta biYerushalayim* — in the time of Rabban Gamliel the Elder, when the *Beit HaMikdash* still stood. But the proceedings we are now reading about involve Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, post-destruction, and the seat of the court had moved to Yavneh. Rabbi Akiva, as discussed in an earlier *sugya*, detained witnesses in Lod on their way to Yavneh. The astronomical calculations thus properly apply to wherever the testimony is being accepted — which, after the *churban*, was Yavneh.

## Witness Height Testimony

### Two vs Three Marda'ot

The *gemara* turns to a different dimension of witness testimony: the height of the moon above the horizon. The *baraita* states that if one witness says the moon was two *marda'ot* — some unit of measurement, roughly understood as saddle-lengths — above the horizon, and another says three, their testimony is considered consistent: *edutan kayamet*. A modest imprecision in observation is accepted; we do not expect witnesses to be perfectly precise instruments.

### Three vs Five Marda'ot

However, if one says three and the other says five, that is too great a discrepancy: *edutan beteila*, their combined testimony is nullified, since one cannot say they witnessed the same thing. Nevertheless, *aval mitztarfin le'edut acheret* — they may combine with other testimony. The reason is that we do not assume either witness is lying; each retains his *chazakah* of being *kasher*. Rashi explains that the witness who said three can pair with another who says three, and the one who said five with another who says five. The parallel in tractate *Sanhedrin* regarding discrepancies in testimony about timing is instructive, though the precise mechanics interact with other discussions there.

## Indirect Sightings

### Water/Glass/Clouds

The *gemara* now addresses several forms of compromised or indirect sightings. If witnesses say *re'inuhu bamayim* — we saw its reflection in the water — or *ba'ashashit* — through a glass or lantern — or *be'avim* — in the clouds — *ein me'idim alav*, such testimony is insufficient. The concern is that what was seen may have been a glowing patch mistaken for the moon.

### Partial Visibility

The *mishnah* also addresses the case of *chetzyo bamayim chetzyo barakia* — half in reflection and half directly visible in the sky — or half obscured by clouds and half directly seen. The *gemara* notes a logical puzzle: if a witness who claims to have seen the entire moon through a reflection or cloud has said nothing, why does the *mishnah* need to tell us that seeing only half under such conditions is also invalid? Of course it is. The *gemara* resolves that the *mishnah* is not speaking of a witness who saw only half; rather, he saw half of the moon directly in the sky and the other half only as reflected in water, or only through cloud cover. Even that partial directness is insufficient. The entirety must be seen without any obstructing or distorting medium.

### Episodic Sighting

Another *baraita* addresses the case of witnesses who say *re'inuhu v'shuv lo re'inuhu* — we saw it and then could no longer see it. Such testimony is also invalid. One might object: the new moon is visible for only a few minutes after sunset before it sets; is it not inevitable that witnesses saw it and then it was gone? Must they have watched it continuously?

Abaye clarifies. The *baraita* is not describing a case where the moon simply set in the ordinary course of events. Rather, *re'inuhu me'aleinu* — they saw it incidentally, in passing — *v'shavnu lir'oto mida'ateinu* — and then returned deliberately, intending to examine it carefully enough to testify — *velo re'inuhu*, and at that point could no longer see it. *Mai ta'ama* — what is the legal concern? *Kuvisha de'eiva b'alma hu d'chaza* — perhaps what they originally glimpsed was merely a rounded cloud. The fact that they could not relocate it when they looked intentionally suggests that the initial sighting was not reliable. Notably, the *gemara* does not require that a witness intend to testify at the moment of sighting — that is a separate discussion arising in *Makkot* and elsewhere. What it does require is that when a witness harbors enough doubt to go back and verify, and verification fails, the original sighting cannot serve as testimony.

## Sanctification Ritua (II)

### Mekudash Declaration

The *gemara* now arrives at the ritual of formal sanctification. *Rosh Beis Din omer mekudash, vechol ha'am onim acharav mekudash mekudash* — the head of the court declares *mekudash*, sanctified, and all those present respond: *mekudash, mekudash*. The significance of this public assent is considerable. The entire thrust of the tractate has been that *Beis Din* holds the power to fix the calendar, rooted in the principle of *asher tikre'u osam* — it is you, the people, who call and designate the festivals. The verbal affirmation of the assembled community is not mere ceremony; it is the enactment of that authority.

## Sanctification Debat (II)

### Tanna Kamma

The *tanna kamma* of the *mishnah* holds that the sanctification declaration is performed regardless of whether the moon was seen in its time — that is, whether the previous month was a short twenty-nine-day month or a long thirty-day month. Even when the thirtieth day arrives and it is self-evidently *Rosh Chodesh* without any sighting of the moon, the act of communal declaration is still performed. The analogy offered is the *mitzvah* of *veKidashtem et shenat hachamishim shanah* — the *yovel* year must be formally sanctified even though its identity is perfectly clear after forty-nine years of counting. The act of sanctification is not merely informational; it is constitutive.

## Sanctification Ritua (II)

### Moshe Declaration

The *gemara* seeks biblical grounding for the declaration formula. Chizkiyah bar Gamda in the name of Rabbi Yossi ben Shaul in the name of Rabbi derives from the verse *Vayidaber Moshe et mo'adei Hashem el Bnei Yisrael* — and Moshe declared the festivals of God to the children of Israel. Moshe, as the representative of the people and head of the court, is the archetype for the *rosh beis din* who pronounces *mekudash*. The word *vayidaber*, with its connotation of authoritative declaration rather than mere communication, is the source.

### People's Authority

The response of the people — *mekudash, mekudash* — is derived by Rav Pappa from the verse *asher tikre'u osam* — which you shall proclaim. The verb *tikre'u* is in the plural, addressing the entire community. The *gemara* additionally reads it as *asher tikre'u atem* — you, the people, shall call. Notably, as a student points out, the letter *vav* is in fact absent from the text of *atem* in the verse, making this not merely a homiletical play but a genuine textual variant reading. The power of establishing the calendar is thus explicitly vested in the community, not only in its representative. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives from *eileh heim mo'adai* — these are My festivals — that the people themselves must pronounce *mo'adai*, "My appointed times."

### Double Affirmation

Why is *mekudash* said twice? The *gemara* derives this from the plural form *mikra'ei kodesh* — holy convocations, in the plural — implying that the affirmation must itself be plural. The double *mekudash* also functions similarly to the double *amen* known elsewhere: a heightened, emphatic assent that internalizes and reinforces the reality being declared. An analogy is drawn to the *birkat hachodesh* recited in the synagogue before *Rosh Chodesh*, in which *chaverim kol Yisrael* and *venomar amen* may represent these two layers of communal affirmation, though the parallel is inexact since that announcement precedes the new month by several days.

## Sanctification Debat (II)

### R. Elazar Tzadok

Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok holds that the declaration is performed only when the moon was not seen in its time — that is, only on a twenty-nine-day month. If it was already a thirty-day month, with *Rosh Chodesh* having arrived automatically, the declaration is not performed.

### Plimo Position

Plimo takes the opposite view, and it is a striking one: *bizmano ein mekadeshin oso* — precisely when the month is a twenty-nine-day month, you do *not* make the declaration; *shelo bizmano mekadeshin oso* — only when it is a thirty-day month do you declare it. Rashi offers a strained explanation — *she'aino tzarich chizuk*, it does not need reinforcement — which is difficult to understand. The position seems nearly inexplicable, and the lecturer acknowledges it as such.

### R. Elazar Shimon

Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds that neither situation requires the declaration: *bein kach uvein kach ein mekadeshin oso* — in either case, no formal *mekudash* is pronounced. His textual basis is the verse *veKidashtem et shenat hachamishim shanah* — from which he derives that *shanim ata mekadesh*, one sanctifies years, but *ve'i ata mekadesh chodashim*, one does not formally sanctify months. The acceptance of the witnesses' testimony is sufficient; no ritual act of declaration accompanies it.

This position is surprising given the entire thrust of the tractate. The masechet consistently emphasizes that *Beis Din* actively and authoritatively creates *Rosh Chodesh*, not merely identifies it. The absence of a formal *mekudash, mekudash* could suggest, on the contrary, that *Beis Din* is simply adjudicating the astronomical facts rather than exercising a constitutive power — that *Rosh Chodesh* is made by the astronomical reality and *Beis Din* merely clarifies what that reality is. But that reading stands in tension with, for instance, the power of *Beis Din* to fix the calendar even against witness testimony, or to establish a different day if it chooses. We are left with four distinct positions: the *tanna kamma* (always), Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok (only on a short month), Plimo (only on a long month), and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon (never).

### Ruling

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok* — the law follows Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, and the declaration is made only on a twenty-nine-day month. Abaye notes that this ruling is supported by a later *mishnah*, which he introduces to buttress the *halakhic* conclusion.

## Missed Window

### Me'ubar Outcome

The *mishnah* Abaye cites states: if the *Beis Din* saw the moon — indeed, all of Israel saw it — the witnesses were examined, and yet they did not manage to pronounce *mekudash* before nightfall, *harei ze me'ubar* — the month is thereby automatically a thirty-day month. The opportunity has passed; the month is *me'ubar*.

From this language Abaye infers: *me'ubar in, mekudash lo* — the *mishnah* says it is *me'ubar*, implying it is not *mekudash*, meaning one does not go back the next day and make the declaration retroactively. Had the *mishnah* wanted to indicate that the *Beis Din* could simply try again the next day, it would have said *harei ze yekadshuhu lemachar* — let them sanctify it tomorrow. The fact that it instead says *me'ubar* closes off that possibility.

### Me'ubar Language

The *gemara* pushes back: perhaps the *mishnah* had no choice but to use the language *harei ze me'ubar*. Why? Because one might have thought that since the moon was seen by *Beis Din* and by all of Israel — *isparsema*, it was publicly known — perhaps the *Beis Din* would be compelled not to allow it to become *me'ubar*, and even having missed the moment of declaration, would be required to maintain it as a twenty-nine-day month. *Kamashmalan* — the *mishnah* informs us that no, the opportunity is lost and the month is *me'ubar*. The *mishnah*'s choice of words was thus dictated by the need to exclude that possibility, not necessarily to exclude retroactive sanctification on a later day.

### Retroactive Option

Rashi, however, derives from this textual choice a further conclusion: the reason the *mishnah* cannot say *yekadshuhu lemachar* is that such a formulation might have implied declaring the previous day as *Rosh Chodesh* retroactively, and the *mishnah* intends to rule that out. *Kamashmalan* — you cannot go back and retroactively sanctify an earlier day. Yet the Rambam, as will emerge from a later *mishnah*, actually rules that retroactive sanctification is possible — that on day thirty-one, *Beis Din* could retroactively sanctify day thirty. This represents an important dispute in how the *mishnah*'s language is understood, and the question is not definitively resolved in this *sugya*.

## Moon Images

### Gamliel's Aids

The *gemara* now returns to the examination of witnesses, introducing a famous detail about Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh. *Demut tzurot levana hayu lo l'Rabban Gamliel b'tavla u'vekotel aliyato* — Rabban Gamliel had images of the moon's various phases on a tablet and on the wall of his upper chamber. *Shebahen mareh et hedyotot* — with these he would show the laypeople: *hakezeh ra'ita o kazeh*, did it look like this or like this? Much as an eye examination presents options to the patient, Rabban Gamliel used visual aids to clarify and verify the witnesses' testimony, since a picture communicates what words cannot easily convey.

### Lo Ta'asun Iti

The *gemara* immediately raises an objection: *u'mi shari*? Is this even permitted? The verse says *lo ta'asun iti* — you shall not make with Me — which the *gemara* interprets as *lo ta'asun kidmut shamshai*, do not make likenesses of those things that attend to God. Celestial bodies, as attendants of the divine, would appear to fall within this prohibition. How then could Rabban Gamliel maintain images of the moon?

### Abaye Limit

Abaye responds: *lo asra Torah ela shamashim she'efshar la'asot kemotan* — the Torah only prohibited making likenesses of those celestial attendants that are genuinely replicable by human hands. One can make a model of the moon, but one cannot actually produce the moon itself — the celestial luminaries are not truly replicable and thus do not fall under this prohibition. What, then, is prohibited? The *gemara* introduces a *baraita* that specifies.

## Prohibited Images

### Temple Items

The *baraita* enumerates several categories of prohibited replicas. *Lo ya'aseh adam bayit tavnit heichal* — a person may not construct his house in the likeness of the *heichal*. He may not make his *achsadra*, his portico, in the form of the *ulam*, the entrance hall. He may not make his courtyard corresponding to the dimensions of the *azarah*. He may not make a table corresponding to the *shulchan* of the *Beit HaMikdash*, and he may not make a *menorah* corresponding to the *menorah* therein.

### Menorah Specifics

However, there is an important qualifier regarding the *menorah*. *Aval oseh shel chamisha v'shel shisha v'shel shemonah* — one may make a *menorah* of five, six, or eight branches. *Shel shiva lo ya'aseh* — a seven-branched *menorah* one may not make, even of other metals, since the seven-armed form itself is the prohibited shape, not merely a golden one. The question of what it means to "replicate" the *menorah* becomes more nuanced when one considers the position of *Tosafot*, who notes that the obligation for the *menorah*'s full ornamentation — the *gevi'im*, *kaftorim*, and *perachim* described in the Torah — applies only to a gold *menorah*. For any other material, such ornamentation is not required. This means the threshold for creating a prohibited "replica" is actually lower than one might think, since even a simple seven-armed structure without elaborate ornamentation could qualify.

Rabbi Yossi the son of Rabbi Yehuda extends the prohibition further: *af shel eitz lo ya'aseh* — even a wooden *menorah* may not be made, *k'derech she'asu Beis Chashmonai* — in the manner of the Hasmoneans, who made a *menorah* from wooden spears when they recaptured the Temple and had no metal *menorah* available. This proves that a wooden *menorah* can qualify as a valid *menorah*. The sages respond to Rabbi Yossi: *misham ra'aya*? You cite that as a proof? *Shfudin shel barzel hayu* — those were actually iron spears, *vehifum b'va'atz* — covered with a dull metal alloy resembling lead. They were not truly wooden, and in any case were the best available substitute under emergency conditions. The *gemara* adds that as the Hasmoneans grew wealthier they replaced the wooden *menorah* with silver and eventually with gold.

The practical implications of this *baraita* are significant and contested. The question of whether Orthodox synagogues may have seven-armed *menorot* arises naturally. Some *acharonim* note that the prohibition is specifically against a replica functional for use as the *menorah* itself; others focus on the shape alone. The Temple Institute's claim that their *menorah* is not a replica because they intend to use it is a bold position. These questions are not resolved by the *gemara* but follow directly from it.

### Human Faces

The *gemara* returns to Abaye's initial limitation: the Torah only prohibits making things genuinely replicable and connected to God. The *baraita* being read identifies the prohibited categories as those of the Temple. But then a further challenge arises. The *gemara* cites another *baraita*: *kol hapartzufot mutarin chutz mipartzuf adam* — all forms are permissible except the human face. If Abaye's principle is that only what is truly replicable is prohibited, why should the human face be prohibited at all?

Rav Huna the son of Rav Idi reports: I heard from Abaye's teaching that a separate *derashah* covers this case. The same verse *lo ta'asun iti* is read as *lo ta'asun oti* — do not make Me. Why would making a human face constitute making God? Because of *tzelem Elokim* — the human being is created in God's image, and the human face is therefore a representation of God. This is a striking statement: the prohibition on making a human face is grounded not in the fear of idolatry toward another god, but in the recognition that the human visage itself embodies the divine image, and replicating it is therefore too close to attempting to represent God Himself.

One might then ask: if making a human face alone is already prohibited, why does the *gemara* need a separate prohibition against the four-faced angel, one of whose faces is a human face? *Tosafot* addresses this: even if someone else had already made the human face, one would still be prohibited from completing the other three faces around it. The prohibition on the four-faced figure is thus not entirely superfluous.

### Angels List

The *baraita* extends further: *lo ta'asun kidmut shamashai hameshamshim lefanai b'marom* — do not make images of those that serve before Me in the celestial heights. The *gemara* enumerates: *ofanim, serafim, chayot hakodesh, malachei hasharet* — the celestial *ofanim*, the *serafim*, the *chayot hakodesh*, and the ministering angels. All images of this class of heavenly beings are prohibited.

Abaye responds: *lo asra Torah ela shamshai shebimador ha'elyon* — the Torah only prohibited the attendants of the highest celestial sphere. Those in the lower spheres, such as the planetary bodies, the sun, and the moon, are not included. The *gemara* then challenges even this: since when are the celestial bodies of the lower sphere permitted? A *baraita* cites the verse *asher bashamayim mimaal* — that which is in the heavens above — *lerabot chamah ulevanah kochavim umazalot*, to include the sun, moon, stars, and constellations; and *mimaal lerabot malachei hasharet*, the heavenly angels. The *gemara* responds: *ki tanya hahee l'ovdam* — that *baraita* speaks of making them for the purpose of worshipping them. If the purpose is worship, then obviously even a small worm is forbidden — as the verse continues to include everything: mountains, valleys, rivers, oceans, and even the tiniest creature.

So there are two distinct concerns operating in parallel throughout this discussion. The first, rooted in the *aseret hadibrot*, is the prohibition against making any image for the purpose of worshipping it — whether it be another god or a representation of God Himself. This is the *avodah zarah* concern in its most direct form, and it applies to literally everything. The second, rooted in *lo ta'asun iti*, is a prohibition against making things that are too closely connected to God even without any intent to worship — because such representations are an inappropriate embodiment of the divine. This second prohibition applies to: replicas of the Temple and its vessels; the human face, on account of *tzelem Elokim*; and all categories of celestial angels. The question that remains is whether the sun, moon, and stars fall under this second prohibition as well.

## Celestial Reps

### Challenge

The *gemara* presses the question directly: *ve'asiya gredata misharay* — is making celestial bodies simply permitted, without any purpose of worship? A *baraita* states explicitly: *lo ta'asun kidmut shamashai hameshamshim lefanai, k'gon chamah ulevanah kochavim umazalot* — do not make likenesses of those that attend to Me, such as the sun, moon, stars, and constellations. How then could Rabban Gamliel have maintained such images?

### Gamliel Loophole

The *gemara* answers: *shani Rabban Gamliel, de'acherim asu lo* — Rabban Gamliel is different because others made them for him. Rashi understands "others" as non-Jews. The prohibition is on making; owning an object made by someone else is a separate matter.

### Signet Ring

The *gemara* then raises a parallel case. Rav Yehuda had a signet ring that featured a human face, and it too had been made by others. Yet Shmuel said to him: *Rav Yehuda, shinina* — sharp one — *samei einei didei*, rub out its eyes. Even though someone else had made it, Rav Yehuda could not retain it in its complete form as a human image.

This seems to present a problem: if the prohibition is on making, and Rav Yehuda did not make it, why did he have to deface it? The answer introduces the rabbinic concern of *chashad* — suspicion. Even if one has not made a prohibited image, owning a three-dimensional human figure raises the concern that observers will suspect one of worshipping it.

### Signet Details

The *gemara* elaborates through a *baraita* distinguishing between protruding and indented seals. *Tabaat chotamo bolet* — if the signet ring's seal is protruding, three-dimensional — *assur lehanichah*, it is forbidden to wear, because the image stands out and people will suspect idolatrous intent; however, *mutar lachtom bah*, it may be used to make an impression, since the resulting impression will be indented. Conversely, *chotamo shokeia* — if the seal is indented — *mutar lehanichah*, one may wear it, since no three-dimensional image is displayed; but *assur lachtom bah*, one may not use it to make an impression, since doing so produces a protruding, three-dimensional image. The concern of *chashad* thus attaches specifically to the three-dimensional nature of a display, not to the mere ownership of the object.

## Context & Intent

### Public Prayer

The *gemara* now asks: is the concern for *chashad* really so robust? In Nehardea there was a famous synagogue — *bei kenishta de-Shaf veYasiv* — which contained a statue, *andarta*. Some understand the name to mean that the congregation had cleared rubble and rebuilt, or even that stones from the *Beit HaMikdash* had been transported there and used in its construction. Despite the presence of this statue, Rav, Shmuel, Shmuel's father, and Levi all prayed there, *velo chaishi le-chashada* — with no concern about the appearance of suspicion. How can we say *chashad* is a serious concern if these great *amoraim* paid it no heed?

The *gemara* answers: *rabbim shani* — a public place is different. Where masses of people gather, no one suspects idolatrous intent, because a person who genuinely wished to worship an idol would not do so publicly. The *chashad* concern is reserved for private contexts.

### Gamliel as Nasi

This resolution creates a new problem for Rabban Gamliel. His use of moon images was apparently in a private setting — he met with witnesses in his upper chamber. Why was he not subject to the concern of *chashad*? The *gemara* answers: *keivan de-nasi hu, shechichi rabbim gabei* — since he was the *Nasi*, his home functioned as a public forum. People streamed to him constantly, making his household effectively a public space even when the meeting was nominally private.

### Disassembled

Alternatively, the *gemara* offers: *de-prakim hava* — perhaps Rabban Gamliel's images were composed of separate components that were assembled and disassembled as needed. An object that exists only in assembled form for functional use, and is otherwise kept in pieces, does not carry the appearance of a cultic object and therefore raises no concern of *chashad*.

### Educational Purpose

A third resolution: *le-hitlamad avid* — he did it for educational purposes, *dikhtiv lo tilmad la'asot* — as the verse teaches, do not learn how to do as the nations do, *aval ata lamed lehavin ulehorot* — but you may learn in order to understand and to teach. This principle, *lemaaseh*, that learning for educational understanding is distinct from learning to practice, may resolve either the biblical concern — that educational purpose removes the prohibition of making outright — or only the rabbinic concern of *chashad*, depending on how the *gemara*'s resolution is read. The text does not definitively adjudicate between these two possibilities.

## Modern Issues

### Modern Ownership

The concern of *chashad* and its application to ownership raises questions that extend well beyond antiquity. Rav Ovadia Yosef, addressing the question of why Jews may own busts and human figurines, notes that in Iraq and throughout the Sephardic world, wealthy Jewish families routinely commissioned portrait busts of themselves without any rabbinic objection. He argues more broadly that the *chashad* concern is contextual: if nobody would reasonably suspect that you are worshipping a G.I. Joe or a decorative bust, the rabbinic prohibition grounded in *chashad* may not apply in contemporary circumstances.

### Art Definition

What remains unresolved is the more fundamental question of what constitutes a prohibited image in the first place — particularly the distinction between two-dimensional and three-dimensional representations. *Tosafot* raises the possibility that because the sun and moon are perceived as two-dimensional, even a two-dimensional depiction of them might be prohibited. For the human face, by contrast, some argue that because the human form is three-dimensional in reality, a two-dimensional painting does not constitute a true representation and might therefore be permitted. The practical history is somewhat the reverse: the traditional community has been considerably more reluctant to depict human faces, even in two dimensions, than it has been to draw a picture of the sun. Yet as the *gemara* makes clear, a child's crayon drawing of the sun raises the same underlying question of *lo ta'asun iti*. The precise contours of what constitutes a prohibited representation — in terms of dimensionality, completeness, medium, and intent — remain genuinely open questions that the *sugya* surfaces but does not resolve.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 25

## False Witnesses & Author…

### Morning & Evening

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 27b opens a fascinating series of stories that bring the *perek* to a close. The case involves two witnesses who came and testified: *reinuhu shacharit bamizrach* — we saw it in the morning in the east, meaning the old moon still visible before sunrise, *vearavit bamaarav* — and in the evening in the west, meaning the new moon appearing just after sunset. On its face, this sounds precisely like what one would expect: the old moon visible in the eastern sky before dawn, and the new moon glimpsed in the western sky at dusk.

The problem, however, is astronomical. As the *daf* has established in the preceding pages, the moon passes through a period of invisibility as it transitions from old to new. It comes so close to the sun — within roughly eight degrees — that it cannot be seen, and only becomes visible again once it has moved far enough away. The *Gemara* regards this invisible interval as at least twenty-four hours; the *Rambam* considers it closer to thirty-six. The critical point is that a window of only twelve hours — from morning to evening of the same day — is simply insufficient. The moon could not have been seen in the morning as the old moon and then again in the evening as the new moon within that span. It would not have moved enough.

### Impossibility Objection

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*: *ede sheker hem* — these witnesses are giving false testimony. Whether they were intentionally lying or had simply misidentified what they saw, it is astronomically impossible for both observations to be true. Notably, the *mishnah* indicates that some prior inspection of the witnesses occurred — seemingly by Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri — before they were forwarded to Yavne.

### Gamliel Accepts

Despite this, *vekiblam Rabban Gamliel* — Rabban Gamliel accepted their testimony. This is a striking datum: even in the face of apparent astronomical impossibility, Rabban Gamliel was willing to validate what the witnesses reported.

### Seen Then Unseen

A second case follows. Two witnesses reported: *reinuhu bizmano* — we saw it in its time, meaning on the night of the thirtieth day, which would make that day *Rosh Chodesh* — *uveleil iburo lo nira* — and on the following night, the night of the thirty-first, it was not seen. This case does not even require an astronomical diagram. If the new moon was genuinely sighted on the night of the thirtieth, it should certainly be visible the following night as well. And once again, *vekiblan Rabban Gamliel* — Rabban Gamliel accepted this testimony.

A closer reading of the language, however, raises the question of whether the second clause — *lo nira*, it was not seen — belongs inside or outside the witnesses' direct testimony. The grammatical shift from first person (*reinuhu*, we saw it) to the passive third person (*lo nira*, it was not seen) suggests that the narrator, not the witnesses, is speaking when reporting the second night's invisibility. Under this reading, what the witnesses said was simply: "We saw it on the thirtieth night" — end of testimony. Then, separately, on the following night, nobody saw the moon. The narrator observes this fact. This reading makes considerably better sense of the story's dynamics: *Kiddush HaChodesh* had already been declared on the basis of the testimony, and now the absence of the moon on the subsequent night raises questions retroactively.

### Pregnant Woman

*Amar Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas*: *ede sheker hem* — they must be lying. His objection is delivered with graphic force: *Hech meidin al isha sheyalda ulemachar kreisa bein shineiha* — how can you testify that a woman gave birth, and the next day her pregnant belly is jutting out between her teeth? If the moon truly gave birth to a new month on the first night, how is it possible that the very next night there is no moon to be seen?

### Retroactive Annulment

The story at this point raises two intertwined questions. The first is practical: perhaps the moon simply was not visible on the second night due to clouds or some other interference; the absence of a sighting need not prove the earlier testimony false. The second is legal: by the time anyone is questioning this, *Kiddush HaChodesh* had already been declared. Can one retroactively annul what has already been sanctified? The scenario suggests that the witnesses may have been reporting late — that is, after the actual night in question — and the possibility existed to validate their testimony retroactively. Or alternatively, now that the following night has passed without a sighting, the question becomes whether one can undo an already-accepted *kiddush hachodesh*.

### Political Confrontation

*Amar lo Rabbi Yehoshua*: *ro'eh ani et devarekha* — Rabbi Yehoshua says to Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas that his argument is compelling. Notice that even this mild concession is expressed in the most non-confrontational of terms. Rabbi Yehoshua does not say outright that the witnesses are false or that *Rosh Chodesh* must be annulled; he simply remarks, in effect, that the argument is well-taken.

Even this measured statement was intolerable to Rabban Gamliel. He sent to Rabbi Yehoshua: *Gozrani alekha she-tavo etzli be-maklekha u-ve-me'otekha be-Yom HaKippurim she-chal lihyot be-cheshbonekha* — I decree that you must come to me with your walking staff and your money on the Yom Kippur that falls out according to your reckoning. Since Rabbi Yehoshua had declined to accept the thirtieth of *Elul* as *Rosh Chodesh Tishrei*, by his calculation *Elul* was thirty days long, pushing *Yom Kippur* a day later than Rabban Gamliel's reckoning. The decree was that Rabbi Yehoshua must appear before Rabban Gamliel at Yavne on what was the eleventh of *Tishrei* according to Rabban Gamliel — but what was *Yom Kippur* according to Rabbi Yehoshua's own counting, apparently violating the sanctity of the day.

---

## Authority Separation

### House of Hillel

The *Gemara* in *Berakhot* develops the broader pattern of conflict between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua at greater length, though our *daf* does not. What is relevant here is the structural reality: Rabban Gamliel was from the house of Hillel, the line that would eventually produce Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi himself. He was not merely the political head but also a major Torah authority — the two roles fused into one. Nobody ever claimed he was necessarily the greatest scholar in absolute terms, but he was a significant *talmid chacham*, and he held both offices simultaneously.

### Babylon Separation

In *Bavel*, this combination was never attempted. The *Resh Galuta* held political authority, and nobody expected him to be a *talmid chacham* — indeed the *Gemara* records his occasional halakhic missteps with candor. The heads of the *yeshivot* of Neharde'a and Pumbedita held the Torah authority. The two spheres were kept entirely separate.

### Gamliel's Sensitivity

In *Eretz Yisrael*, however, where the two roles converged in one person, a heightened sensitivity naturally followed. When Rabbi Yehoshua was widely regarded as the greater scholar, any casual remark from him — even as understated as *ro'eh ani et devarekha* — could be perceived as a challenge to the authority of the *Nasi*. The pattern of Rabban Gamliel's reactions throughout this period, including the famous episode concerning *Tefillat Arvit* whether it is *reshut* or *chovah*, reveals a recurring dynamic: Rabban Gamliel overreacted to Rabbi Yehoshua specifically, seemingly to assert who ultimately set the parameters of authority. Significantly, it is Rabbi Yehoshua — not Rabbi Dosa, who actually voiced the sharper and more confrontational objection — who bears the brunt of Rabban Gamliel's response. The reason is not hard to find: Rabbi Dosa was not perceived as a rival to his authority in the same way that Rabbi Yehoshua was.

### Geographic Divide

The geographic dimension adds further texture to the drama. Rabbi Yehoshua resided in Peki'in in the northern Galilee, while Rabban Gamliel was in Yavne, a considerable distance to the south. Traveling on the day Rabbi Yehoshua regarded as *Yom Kippur* — carrying a staff and money — would have been no small matter in any sense.

---

## Akiva's Consolation

### Akiva Seeks Permission

*Halach Rabbi Akiva umatza'o meitztar* — Rabbi Akiva went and found Rabbi Yehoshua in a state of distress. Rabbi Yehoshua was Rabbi Akiva's *rebbe*, and so Rabbi Akiva approached with studied deference: *yesh li lilmod shekol ma she'asah Rabban Gamliel asuy* — I can demonstrate from a verse that whatever Rabban Gamliel did is done; it may not have been astronomically accurate, but it is legally effective. He then asks permission to share what he claims Rabbi Yehoshua himself had taught him — *tarshini lomar lefanecha davar echad shelimadtani* — a framing of extraordinary psychological intelligence. By asking permission and attributing the teaching back to his *rebbe*, Rabbi Akiva has already secured Rabbi Yehoshua's engagement before a single word of the argument has been offered.

### Moadei Declaration

The verse he cites is *eleh moadei Hashem mikraei kodesh asher tikre'u otam* — these are the appointed times of God, the holy convocations, that *you* shall declare. The word *otam* — them — is read homiletically through the lens of *atem* — you — yielding a threefold emphasis: *atem afilu shogegin, atem afilu mezidin, atem afilu mut'im* — the declaration is binding whether made in error, intentionally, or as a result of having been deceived. What matters is the act of declaration by the authorized body; the astronomical reality does not override it. The critical question — how far this principle extends beyond *kiddush hachodesh* to all of *Torah she-be'al peh* — will be addressed further below.

---

## Dosa's Submission

### Yehoshua Consults

Rabbi Yehoshua remained troubled and went to Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas himself — the one who had most forcefully articulated the objection — to ask what he should do. Here was someone who had publicly said *ede sheker hem*, who had deployed the striking analogy of the pregnant woman. What did he think Rabbi Yehoshua ought to do?

---

## Torah She-be'al Peh

### Scope of Authority

This is precisely the moment to pause and consider the deeper question the narrative raises. Everyone agrees that in the domain of *kiddush hachodesh* the verse *asher tikre'u otam* hands authority entirely to the human court: *bein shogegin bein mezidin bein mut'in* — in error, deliberately, or as victims of deception. But what about *Torah she-be'al peh* more broadly? If a *beit din* interprets a *pasuk* in a manner that does not accord with the original divine intent — not through bad faith but through genuine *pesak* — is that interpretation binding? Has God given over the power of interpretation to human authorities in such a way that *their* meaning becomes the operative halachic meaning, regardless of original intent? Or does a wrong answer remain wrong, and does it need to be corrected even at the cost of disrupting established practice? This is a fundamental question in the *rishonim*, with profound implications for how one understands the nature of *Torah she-be'al peh* as a whole.

---

## Dosa's Submission (II)

### Audit Argument

Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas responded to Rabbi Yehoshua with the same essential message Rabbi Akiva had offered, though grounded in a different argument. *Im ba'im anu ladun achar beis dino shel Rabban Gamliel* — if we are going to call into question decisions made by Rabban Gamliel's *beit din* after the fact, then *tzerichim anu ladun achar kol beis uveisin she'amad miymos Moshe ve'ad achshav* — we would have to conduct a full audit of every *beit din* decision going back to the time of Moshe. Once decisions are made, they are binding. The alternative — treating each ruling as permanently subject to re-examination by those who disagree — is the collapse of legal authority altogether.

### Seventy Elders

The proof text is drawn from the scene of the seventy elders ascending with Moshe, Aharon, Nadav, Avihu, and the elders of Israel: *shene'emar Vaya'al Moshe ve'Aharon Nadav va'Avihu veshivim miziknei Yisrael*. The *midrash* asks: *velamah lo nitparshu shemosan shel zekenim* — why does the Torah not specify their names? The answer: so that future generations would not be subjected to invidious comparisons. Had the names been recorded, one could always ask whether a later *beit din* member was truly the equal of those named luminaries. Since their names are withheld, the seventy represent anonymous authority — standing in for any legitimate *beit din* in any generation.

### Equivalent Courts

*She-kol sheloshah vesheloshah she'amdu beis din al Yisrael harei hu keveis dino shel Moshe* — any three members of a *beit din* standing over Israel are considered the equivalent of Moshe's own court. The institution, not the individuals, carries the authority.

---

## Torah She-be'al Peh (II)

### Ramban's Approach

The *rishonim* debate precisely this question of original intent versus binding interpretation, and it is worth tracing the contours of that debate carefully. The *Ramban*'s position is that since the text of *Torah she-bikhtav* is inherently capable of bearing multiple meanings, God grants the Torah *al da'at shelahem* — in accordance with the understanding of the authorized interpreters. The text is meant to mean what they say it means. On this view, questions of original intent are simply not operative once the *beit din* has issued its ruling in good faith.

### Lo Bashamayim Hi

A student in the shiur raised a point that deserves extended attention: it is precisely Rabbi Yehoshua who, in the famous story of the *Tanuro shel Achnai* in *Bava Metzia*, stands up and declares *Lo bashamayim hi* — the Torah is not in heaven. A heavenly voice (*bat kol*) itself endorsed Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on the *tanur*, and Rabbi Yehoshua responded that it makes no difference, because the Torah has already been given to human authorities. The contrast with his behavior on our *daf* is striking: here he is the one being compelled to accept a ruling he believes to be wrong, while in the *Tanuro shel Achnai* he is the one asserting that human interpretation overrides heavenly input. One might ask whether Rabbi Yehoshua learned his lesson from this episode, subsequently embracing for *Torah she-be'al peh* the principle he had been forced to accept here specifically regarding *kiddush hachodesh*. Perhaps he drew a distinction: in the realm of the natural sciences — where the moon either was or was not in a particular position — there are objective facts and one can simply be wrong. But *Torah she-be'al peh* is inherently open-ended; the text genuinely admits of multiple meanings, and therefore is properly given over to human determination. Many authorities would prefer to draw the line the opposite way — limiting the binding-regardless-of-accuracy principle to *kiddush hachodesh* alone, and not extending it to *Torah she-be'al peh* at large. But the *Tanuro shel Achnai* tradition, attributed to Rabbi Yehoshua, sits in considerable tension with that more limited reading.

### Masechet Horayot

One might raise the further question: if *beit din* authority is truly binding regardless of error, how does one account for the laws in *Masechet Horayot* requiring the *Sanhedrin* to bring a special *korban* when it rules in error and the community acts on that ruling? The existence of that *korban* implies that the ruling was in fact wrong, not merely that it was authoritative. The full reconciliation of *Masechet Horayot* with the principle of *atem afilu shogegin* is a substantial topic in its own right and cannot be resolved here, but it stands as an important check on any overly absolute formulation of rabbinic authority.

---

## Reconciliation

### YK Travel

*Natal maklo u-meotav beyado* — Rabbi Yehoshua took his staff and his money in his hand *vehalach l'Yavne etzel Rabban Gamliel b'yom shechal Yom Hakippurim lihyot b'cheshbono* — and went to Yavne to Rabban Gamliel on the day that fell out as *Yom Kippur* according to his own reckoning. He made the journey, with staff and money, on what he personally believed to be *Yom Kippur*.

### Kiss & Dual Role

When Rabban Gamliel saw him approach, *amad mi-kiso*, he rose from his seat, *u-neshako al rosho* — and kissed him on the head. *Amar lo: bo b'shalom rabbi v'talmidi* — come in peace, my master and my student. *Rabbi b'chochma* — my master in wisdom, acknowledging without reservation that Rabbi Yehoshua was the greater scholar. *V'talmidi shekibalta devari* — and my student in that you accepted my ruling and submitted to my authority.

The *baraita* that follows elaborates this with additional nuance. *Amad mi-kiso u-neshako al rosho. Amar lo: shalom alecha rabbi u-talmidi. Rabbi she-limaditani Torah ba-rabbim* — my master, in that you taught me Torah publicly, *u-talmidi she-ani gozer alecha gezeira ve-ata mekayemah ke-talmid* — and my student in that when I issue a decree you fulfill it as a student would. The *ke-talmid* here is telling: Rabban Gamliel is mapping the political relationship onto the rabbinic one, suggesting that because his political authority has halachic implications, Rabbi Yehoshua's submission carries the character of a student's deference to a teacher, even though the actual relationship of greater scholarship runs in the other direction.

*Ashrei ha-dor she-ha-gedolim nishma'im la-ktanim* — praised is the generation in which the great ones are willing to listen to lesser ones. *Kal va-chomer ktanim li-gedolim* — how much more so should lesser ones listen to their leaders. The *Gemara* questions the logic of calling this a *kal va-chomer*: surely the lesser ones listening to the greater is simply a *chiyuv*, an obligation — what is the *kal va-chomer*? The answer: *ela mitokh she-ha-gedolim nishma'im la-ktanim, nosh'in ktanim kal va-chomer be-atzman* — when those of great stature are willing to submit, the example they set inspires those of lesser stature to internalize the principle of deference all the more deeply. The act of public submission by the great becomes a formative precedent for how the community as a whole relates to authority.

---

## Moon Cycle Science

### Rabbi Chiya Story

A parallel story is introduced through a *baraita* concerning Rabbi Chiya. *Rabbi Chiya chazyei l'sihara d'hava kai b'tzafra d'esrin v'tisha* — Rabbi Chiya saw the moon on the morning of the twenty-ninth. The situation required some unpacking. The moon visible in the morning of the twenty-ninth was the old, waning moon. The problem was with the new moon. Once the old moon disappears — becoming invisible as it passes close to the sun — it will not reappear until approximately thirty-six hours later. In this case, by the time the new moon would become visible (after sunset), it would already be technically the night of the thirty-first, making it too late to declare *Rosh Chodesh* on day thirty. Rabbi Chiya had wanted to make the upcoming day, the thirtieth, into *Rosh Chodesh* — meaning he needed the new moon to appear that evening. But the moon would not cooperate.

*Shakal kala patak beh* — he picked up a clod of earth and threw it at the moon. *Le'orta be'ina lekadoshei bach ve'at kaimet hacha?* — Tonight I need to sanctify you, and you're still hanging around? *Zil ikasi* — go hide yourself! He was telling the old moon to become invisible so the new moon could emerge in time. When Rebbe heard about this, he said to Rabbi Chiya: *Zil le-Ein Tav* — go to Ein Tav, the designated location for *kiddush hachodesh*, *vekadshei leyircha* — and sanctify the month there, *veshalach li simana* — and send me a coded message: *David Melech Yisrael Chai VeKayam* — David King of Israel lives and endures.

The choice of coded message is suggestive on two levels. *Rashi* notes that David is traditionally compared to the moon. But there is another dimension: Rebbe's household claimed descent from David HaMelech, and *David Melech Yisrael Chai VeKayam* simultaneously signaled that as *Nasi* — in the lineage of David — he had the authority to perform *kiddush hachodesh* even when the astronomical facts were less than fully cooperative. The contrast with the earlier period of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua is instructive: whereas that era was marked by open conflict, here, just two generations later, Rabbi Chiya is enlisted as a cooperating agent. Rabban Gamliel's position had, in effect, prevailed.

### Cloud Illusion

A further *baraita* recounts another case. *Pa'am achat nitkashru shamayim be'avim* — once the sky filled with clouds, *venidmet dmut levana be'esrim vetisha lachodesh* — and there appeared in the sky what looked like the new moon on the twenty-ninth of the month. *Vechasvurim ha'am lomar Rosh Chodesh* — the people thought it was *Rosh Chodesh*, which would have made the preceding month only twenty-eight days long — an impossibility if the calendar is functioning correctly. *Uvikesh Beit Din lekadsho* — and the *beit din* moved to sanctify it.

### Lunar Minimum

Here Rabban Gamliel intervened — but this time not on the basis of pure authority. *Kach mekublani mibeis avi aba* — this is the tradition I have from my grandfather's house: *ein chiddusha shel levana pechusa* — the new moon cannot come in less than a full lunar cycle.

### Precise Calculation

The lunar cycle is: twenty-nine days, *vamechetza* — and half a day, meaning twelve hours — *ushnei shlishei sha'ah* — and two-thirds of an hour, which is forty minutes — *ve'ayin gimel chalakim* — and seventy-three *chalakim*. This figure — 29 days, 12 hours, 44 minutes, and 3 seconds — is precisely the average synodic month as it would be expressed in the Hebrew calendar's unit system, accurate to within 0.2 seconds of the modern measured value.

### Chalakim Division

The *chelek* is one 1080th of an hour. Why 1080? The *Rambam* notes that it is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 9, making it highly flexible for astronomical calculation. At 1080 *chalakim* per hour, the rate is 18 *chalakim* per minute. Thus 73 *chalakim* equals four minutes and one *chelek* — or, more precisely, four minutes and three seconds — bringing the total to 29 days, 12 hours, 44 minutes, and 3 seconds. This is as precise as the *chalakim* system permits; making the unit finer would introduce the need for a smaller subdivision.

One should note, however, that Rabban Gamliel's formulation specifies *ein pechusa* — not less than this. The modern astronomical measurement of the actual lunar month varies by as much as nine hours above and below the average depending on the time of year and orbital mechanics. So while the average is captured with extraordinary precision, individual months can deviate substantially. Rabban Gamliel's tradition captures the average, not the minimum possible length of a specific month.

### Funeral Statement

*Ve'oto hayom meta imo shel Ben Zaza* — on that same day, the mother of Ben Zaza died. *Vehispidah Rabban Gamliel hesped gadol* — and Rabban Gamliel delivered a major eulogy and organized a large public funeral. *Lo mipnei sherauya lekach* — not because she was particularly distinguished, but *ela kedei sheyedu ha'am shelo kidshu Beit Din et hachodesh* — in order to make clear to the people that the *beit din* had not sanctified the month. In contrast to the earlier story, where Rabban Gamliel asserted authority against the astronomical facts, here he was on the side of the astronomy, using the public funeral as a declaration that the twenty-ninth was not and could not be *Rosh Chodesh*.

It is also worth noting, as a structural matter, that the authority to perform *kiddush hachodesh* is vested specifically in the *Nasi* — not, for instance, in the *Av Beit Din*. This is documented in *Sanhedrin* as well. The reason is not incidental: the unified calendar is the single most powerful instrument of communal coherence for *Klal Yisrael*. It is fitting, therefore, that responsibility for it rests with the one person who speaks for the entire people — the political and spiritual head.

---

## Akiva's Consolation (II)

### Atem Emphasis

Returning now to the *baraita* about Rabbi Akiva's consolation of Rabbi Yehoshua, the *Gemara* presents a more expanded version of the exchange. When Rabbi Akiva found Rabbi Yehoshua in distress, Rabbi Yehoshua gave voice to his anguish without speaking in the first person — a studied indirection. *Ra'uy lo sheyipol lemitah yod-bet chodesh ve'al yigzor alav gezeirah zo* — it would be fitting for him to lie sick in bed for twelve months rather than be forced to undergo what Rabban Gamliel had decreed. Rabbi Akiva then asked leave to share a teaching — *tarshini lomar lefanecha davar echad shelimadtani*, framing it as something Rabbi Yehoshua himself had taught him, a framing that enlisted his *rebbe*'s own commitment before a word of argument was made.

The verse is *asher tikre'u otam be'moadam*, with the word *otam* playing on *atem* — you. The word appears three times in the relevant passages, yielding the three-fold principle: *afilu shogegin, afilu mezidin, afilu mut'im* — even in error, even intentionally, even when deceived. In each case, it is the human declaration — *atem*, you — that is binding. Whether the declaration was made in a *beit din* that got the astronomy wrong, whether it was accepted based on testimony that turned out to be impossible, whether witnesses had deceived the court — in all these cases, what the *beit din* declared is what *moadei Hashem* consists of. The question of how broadly to extend this principle beyond *kiddush hachodesh* to *Torah she-be'al peh* generally remains live, as discussed above.

### Yehoshua Consoled

*Amar lo: Akiva nichamtani nichamtani* — Rabbi Yehoshua said: Akiva, you have consoled me. This echo — *nichamtani nichamtani*, the word said twice — is a recognizable trope of Rabbi Akiva's encounters elsewhere, though there it is typically with his students. Here it is with his *rebbe*.

In this version of the story, the consolation provided by Rabbi Akiva was sufficient; Rabbi Yehoshua did not require the additional confirmation he sought from Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas.

---

## Judge Your Generation

### Verse Citation

*Vayomer Shmuel el ha-am Hashem asher asa et Moshe ve'et Aharon ve'omer vayishlach Hashem et Yeruba'al ve'et Bedan ve'et Yiftach ve'et Shmuel* — Shmuel addresses the people in a verse that places all these figures in a single category as those whom God had sent.

### Judge Identities

*Yeruba'al zeh Gid'on* — Yeruba'al is Gideon, who fought against *Ba'al* worship. *Velamah nikra shemo Yeruba'al? She-asa meriva im ha-Ba'al* — hence the name, meaning "let Ba'al contend." *Bedan zeh Shimshon* — Bedan is Shimshon, *de-ati mi-Dan*, who came from the tribe of Dan. *Yiftach k'mashma'o* — Yiftach is Yiftach, well known, the judge whose tragic vow involving his daughter is recorded in the Book of Judges.

### Lightweight Pairing

The problem is that these figures do not obviously belong in the same category. A different verse groups Moshe, Aharon, and Shmuel together as the great authorities of their respective periods. Placing Gideon, Shimshon, and Yiftach in the same verse as Shmuel therefore creates an apparent incongruity. *Shakal ha-katuv shelosha kallei olam ke-shelosha chamurei olam* — the verse weighs three *kallei olam*, three of the world's lightweights, against three *chamurei olam*, three heavyweights, and treats them as equivalent. The term *kallei olam* is notably pointed — it is not merely that Gideon, Shimshon, and Yiftach are lesser figures; *kallei olam* implies they are the biggest lightweights imaginable.

### Generation Equality

*Lomar lecha: Yeruba'al be-doro ke-Moshe be-doro, Bedan be-doro ke-Aharon be-doro, Yiftach be-doro ke-Shmuel be-doro* — to tell you: Gideon in his generation stands as Moshe in his; Shimshon in his generation stands as Aharon in his; Yiftach in his generation stands as Shmuel in his. This is not a claim about absolute spiritual or intellectual parity. Rather, it is a statement about authority: whatever authority Moshe held for his generation, the appointed leader of a later generation holds for that generation. The standard is not comparative greatness across time but authorized function within a generation.

### Lightweight Power

*She-afilu kal she-be-kallim ve-nitmana parnas al ha-tzibbur, harei hu ke-abbir she-be-abbirim* — even the most lightweight of the lightweights, once appointed as a *parnas*, a community leader, is considered as the mightiest of the mighty. One might ask whether this principle is specifically about lay leadership — *parnas* suggesting political authority — or whether it extends to Torah interpretation. The answer is that in the figure of Rabban Gamliel, and in the *shofet* of the Torah, both roles are embodied simultaneously.

---

## Judge Your Day

### Time Absurdity

*U-vata el ha-kohanim ha-Levi'im ve'el ha-shofet asher yihyeh ba-yamim ha-hem* — you shall come to the *kohanim* and the *shofet* who will be in those days. The *Gemara* asks the obvious: *v'chi ta'aleh al da'at'cha she-adam holech etzel dayan she-lo hayah be-yamav?* — would it enter your mind that a person could go to a judge who was not alive in his time? The verse's formulation — *the judge who will be in those days* — would be absurd if it meant anything other than the judge of your own generation. The verse is therefore teaching precisely through its apparent redundancy.

### Your Generation

*Ein lecha leilech ela etzel shofet she-be-yamav* — you have no recourse but to go to the judge of your own generation. There is no other option, no mechanism for bypassing your contemporary authority in favor of an idealized earlier one.

### Anti-Nostalgia

The *Gemara* then invokes the verse from *Kohelet*: *Al tomar mah hayah she-ha-yamim ha-rishonim hayu tovim me-eleh* — do not say, "How is it that the earlier days were better than these?" Do not bemoan the loss of superior earlier leadership.

### Rashi: Self-Blame

*Rashi* explains: *lefi she-ha-dorot hayu tovim be-tzaddikim min ha-aharonim* — if the earlier generations had better leaders, it is because the people of those generations were themselves at a higher *madrega*. If you are unhappy with your leaders, it is ultimately your own fault, a function of the collective spiritual standing of the generation. The conclusion would be: do not blame your leaders; they reflect who you are. This reading, however, sits awkwardly with the broader argument of the *sugya*, which is not about explaining why leadership declines, but about asserting that current leadership has full binding authority regardless of comparative stature.

### Tosafot: Office

*Tosafot* reads the verse differently. The warning against nostalgia is not because everyone has declined together and you simply get the leaders you deserve. Rather, *she-ein lecha ela shofet she-be-yamecha* — you have only the judge of your time, and authority has nothing to do with relative greatness. It is conferred by office and role. The person who holds the *shofet*'s office in your generation holds it with full legal authority, irrespective of whether earlier holders were greater scholars or more pious individuals. Tosafot's reading is more coherent as a statement of the *sugya*'s main point: authority is institutional, not graduated according to comparative merit.

---

## Rambam Powers

### Reversal Principle

The well-known principle is that a later *beit din* cannot reverse an earlier *beit din* unless it is greater in wisdom and number — *ad she-yehiyeh gadol mimenu be-hochmah u-ve-minyan*. What "greater in number" means precisely is not entirely clear, since all *battei din* of the same category are nominally the same size. But the wisdom criterion clearly establishes that a court of diminished scholarly standing cannot overturn its predecessors. Since the trajectory of generations is understood as generally downward, this in practice means that very few rulings can ever be reversed.

### Legislative vs. Interpre…

The *Rambam*, however, draws a distinction that emerges from this very *sugya* and the *midrashim* surrounding it. This limitation on reversal — the requirement to be greater in wisdom and number — applies to the *legislative* capacity of the *beit din*: its power to enact takkanot, issue gezerot, and establish communal practices that were not derived from interpretation of *Torah she-bikhtav*. But the *interpretive* capacity — the authority to determine what the *pesukim* themselves mean in terms of *Torah she-be'al peh* — operates on a different plane. Here, the principle of *ke-Yiftach be-doro ke-Shmuel be-doro* applies in full.
