The judge of your generation is your authoritative interpreter of *Torah she-bikhtav*, and his interpretation is binding.

### Central Authority

This does not mean that any *beit din* anywhere can unilaterally reinterpret *Torah she-bikhtav*. The *Rambam* insists that this reinterpretive authority belongs only to the *Beit Din ha-Gadol*, the central *Sanhedrin*. Only the body that stands as the authoritative representative of all Israel can exercise this function.

### Reinterpretation

But the theoretical implication is significant: a later *Beit Din ha-Gadol*, even if it were at a lower absolute *madrega* than its predecessors, could in principle arrive at a different interpretation of *Torah she-bikhtav* — and that interpretation would become the binding *halacha*. The parallel to *kiddush hachodesh* is direct: just as the *beit din* can declare *Rosh Chodesh* in a manner that is not astronomically optimal and have that declaration stand as the halachic reality, so too can the *beit din* interpret a *pasuk* in a manner that may not represent the original intent and have that interpretation stand as the binding law. *Lo bashamayim hi* — in both cases, it is not what the heavens say but what the authorized human court says.

---

## Reconciliation (II)

### Public Submission

The *baraita*'s concluding observation — *Ashrei ha-dor she-ha-gedolim nishma'im la-ktanim* — deserves one final reflection. What Rabban Gamliel acknowledged by kissing Rabbi Yehoshua and calling him *rabbi u-talmidi* was not merely a personal gesture of reconciliation. It was a public act: *Rabbi she-limaditani Torah ba-rabbim*, you taught me Torah publicly, in front of others. Rabbi Yehoshua's submission — appearing with staff and money on what he regarded as *Yom Kippur* — was itself a public act visible to all who saw him arrive in Yavne. The great ones who are willing to submit, even when they believe themselves to be right, set the defining example for what communal deference to authority looks like. It is *mitokh she-ha-gedolim nishma'im la-ktanim* — from seeing the great ones submit — that the lesser ones learn to carry the argument themselves. Authority, in this *sugya*, is not merely asserted from above; it is modeled and internalized through precisely these acts of visible, costly submission.

---

## Beit Din Seeing

### Three Scenarios

With the conclusion of the third *perek*, the new *perek* opens. It is notable that the division here between *perakim* is somewhat puzzling — we remain squarely in the midst of the theme of *kiddush hachodesh*, which had been the subject of the preceding material. The opening *mishnah* presents three distinct scenarios involving who sees the new moon and under what circumstances a formal declaration can be made.

### All Israel Case

The first case: *Ra'u Beit Din v'chol Yisrael, nekharu ha'edim v'lo hispiku lomar mekudash ad shechashicha* — the *beit din* and all of Israel saw the new moon, the witnesses were examined, but they did not manage to say *mekudash* before nightfall. *Harei zeh m'ubar* — the month is pregnant, meaning thirty days, and *Rosh Chodesh* is the following day. The remarkable point here is that it makes no difference that everyone knew the moon had appeared. The formal declaration must be made, and it must be made before nightfall. Failure to complete the process in time means the month is automatically extended.

### Beit Din Alone

The second scenario: *Ra'u Beit Din bilvad* — only the *beit din* saw the moon, without the broader populace. Since they have a full day available and are not racing the clock, the procedural question becomes: do they need external witnesses? They themselves are the witnesses. The *mishnah*'s answer is: *Ya'amdu shnayim v'ya'idu bifneihem* — two members of the *beit din* stand apart and serve as witnesses before the remaining members, who then hear the testimony and declare *mekudash mekudash*. Even when the court itself has seen the moon, the formal structure of witness-and-declaration must be replicated within the court's own procedures.

### Three Members

The third scenario: exactly three members constitute the *beit din* and they saw the moon. If two break off to serve as witnesses, only one remains — insufficient to form a court. The solution: *yoshivu mekhavereihem etzel hayakhid* — they recruit two additional qualified individuals to join the remaining one, reconstituting a new *beit din* of three, before whom the two can then testify.

### Individual Powerless

The *mishnah* concludes with the principle: *she-ein hayakhid ne'eman al yedei atzmo* — an individual cannot, on his own authority, sanctify the month. The word *ne'eman* here carries a particular nuance — it is not merely that an individual lacks authority, but that there is no mechanism by which a single person can make such a declaration operative. Read against the background of the Rabban Gamliel narratives, this functions as a structural check: however forceful the *Nasi*'s assertion of authority, the act of *kiddush hachodesh* remains inherently institutional, requiring the formal structure of a *beit din*.

---

## Gemara Challenge

### Seeing > Hearing

The *Gemara* enters into tension with the *mishnah* through a well-established principle: *lo tehei shmi'ah gedolah me-re'iyah* — hearing should not be greater than seeing. The logic is straightforward: if seeing something with one's own eyes is held to be the most direct form of knowledge, then formal testimony — which is a verbal report of what someone else saw — should not be more powerful than direct personal observation. If the *beit din* has already seen the moon, they know what they know. Why should they need to go through the formal procedure of witness acceptance at all?

### Redundant Case?

Applying this principle to the *mishnah*, the *Gemara* asks: *Lama li lemitni ra'u Beit Din v'chol Yisrael?* — why does the *mishnah* need to teach the case where both the *beit din* and all Israel saw the moon? *Salka da'atakh amina*: one might have thought that since everyone saw it and the matter is entirely public, the month should simply not be made pregnant even without a formal declaration. The *mishnah* therefore needs to tell us: no, *mekudash* was not said, and *harei zeh meubar*.

### Declaration Required

The answer is thus: even when the fact is universally known, the formal declaration is indispensable. The procedural act of saying *mekudash mekudash* is not merely evidentiary — confirming what is already known — but constitutive: it is the declaration that creates the halachic reality of *Rosh Chodesh*. Without it, the knowledge is legally inert.

The *Gemara* then pushes further: since the *mishnah* teaches the case of universal observation, why does it also need to mention the case of *chakirat edim*, formal examination of witnesses? The *Gemara* suggests these are two separate sub-cases of the opening clause. *Salka da'atakh amina*: in the case where witnesses were formally examined and a legal process was begun during the day, perhaps — analogous to *dinei mamonot* — the conclusion of the process could extend into the night. The formal initiation of the proceeding would anchor it to the day, and *mekudash mekudash* could then be said after nightfall.

### Dinei Mamonot

In ordinary monetary litigation, the *mishnah* in *Sanhedrin* establishes that *dinei mamonot danim bayom vegomrim balayla* — financial cases are heard during the day but may be concluded at night. One might think the same flexibility should apply to *kiddush hachodesh*: if the examination of witnesses was conducted during the day, the declaration could be made after dark.

### Ki Chok Verse

The *Gemara* rejects this on the basis of a *pasuk*: *Ki chok leYisrael hu mishpat lelohei Yaakov* — for it is a statute for Israel, a judgment unto the God of Jacob. *Eimat havei chok?* — when is it established as a statute? *Begmar din* — at the conclusion of the judgment. *Veka kari lei rachmana mishpat* — and the Torah calls it *mishpat*, meaning the judicial act, which must take place by day. *Mah mishpat bayom af hacha nami bayom* — just as *mishpat* is by day, so too the conclusion of this process must be by day. Unlike *dinei mamonot*, *kiddush hachodesh* cannot span the day-night boundary; the declaration must be completed while it is still daytime.

The *mishnah*'s underlying assumption — that even firsthand knowledge does not substitute for the formal process of witness testimony and declaration — thus stands in ongoing tension with the *Gemara*'s principle that *shmi'ah* should not exceed *re'iyah*. The resolution of this tension, and its implications for each of the *mishnah*'s three scenarios, will be the work of the next *daf*.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 26

## Lo Tehei Shemiah

### Lo Tehei Shemiah

The daf begins by wrapping up the issues of *kiddush hachodesh* and picking up at the bottom of 25b, approximately ten lines from the bottom. The *mishna* there assumes that even if the *beit din* saw the new moon themselves, they must still go through the formal process of testimony. The *gemara* challenges this assumption by invoking the principle of *lo tehei shemiah gedolah mereiyah* — hearing testimony should not be greater than seeing directly. If seeing the new moon is sufficient knowledge, why must members of the *beit din* break off and formally testify to the others?

### Nighttime Seeing

Rav Zeira resolves the difficulty: the case in the *mishna* is one where they saw the moon at night. Since the entire process of accepting witnesses — and indeed the pronouncement of *mekudash* — must take place during the day, their act of seeing at night does not carry the legal weight of a formal act of testimony. One might immediately object: even if their nighttime seeing cannot function as formal testimony, they still *know* what they saw. Why must they hear witnesses the following morning?

The *gemara*'s answer is precise and important. The principle of *lo tehei shemiah gedolah mereiyah* does not go so far as to say that mere *knowledge* eliminates the need for formal process. Rather, the principle holds that an act of *seeing* is equivalent in legal status to an act of *hearing testimony* — but just as hearing testimony must occur during the day, so too the act of seeing that would substitute for it must occur during the day. Since they saw it at night, that seeing cannot function as the formal equivalent of testimony, and a fresh formal process is required the next morning. The new moon's visibility at night makes this situation entirely natural: they see it after sunset, but cannot validate the month until the morning.

### Three Witnesses Case

The *mishna* then presents a second case: if only three judges saw the moon, and two cannot break off to testify because an insufficient number would remain on the *beit din*, two must step aside and be replaced by additional judges so that testimony can be formally accepted. The *gemara* asks the same question — why not invoke *lo tehei shemiah gedolah mereiyah* here as well? The *gemara* considers giving the same answer as before (they saw it at night), but then objects: *haynu hach* — that is identical to the first case and adds nothing new.

The *gemara* therefore explains that the second case is needed for a novel point stated at its end: *ein hayachid ne'eman al yedei atzmo* — a single individual cannot constitute a *beit din*. One might have thought that since monetary cases may be adjudicated by a single *mumcheh*, a recognized expert, perhaps the new moon could similarly be sanctified by one such individual. The *mishna* therefore teaches that this is not so. God told Moshe — despite being the greatest *mumcheh* the Jewish people has ever had — that Aharon must be with him, as derived from the verse *vayomer Hashem el Moshe ve'el Aharon be'eretz Mitzrayim lemor hachodesh hazeh lachem*. The deeper reason is that the *beit din* here functions not merely to render a legal decision but to represent the Jewish people as a whole, which requires a collective body rather than a single individual.

### Eid Naasah Dayan

The *gemara* now raises the principle of *eid na'aseh dayan*. The *mishna* envisions a scenario where a member of the *beit din* might himself have been in a position to serve as a witness to the moon. The concern is not the case of *eid hameid na'aseh dayan* — where one testifies and then immediately turns to serve as the judge of one's own testimony — but rather the case of *eid sherah*: a *dayan* who personally saw the moon and is now listening to others testify. Does the fact that he could have been a witness disqualify him from serving as a judge?

The *gemara* raises the possibility that the *mishna* follows the view of the Rabbis and not that of Rabbi Akiva. As taught in a *baraita*: if a *sanhedrin* witnessed a murder, Rabbi Tarfon holds that some of them may serve as witnesses while others serve as judges. Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *kulam na'asu eidim ve-ein eid na'aseh dayan* — all of them are considered witnesses, and a witness cannot become a judge.

---

## Eid Naasah Dayan

### Rabbi Tarfon

Rabbi Tarfon's view, as stated in the *baraita*, is that when a *sanhedrin* has witnessed a capital crime, the group may divide its roles: some will testify while others, together with additional judges, will adjudicate. Seeing the event does not disqualify one from serving as a judge, provided one does not personally testify. The witnessing itself leaves room for a formal distinction between the role of *eid* and the role of *dayan*.

### Rabbi Akiva

Rabbi Akiva takes the more stringent position: *kulam na'asu eidim* — everyone who saw it is rendered a witness — and *ein eid na'aseh dayan*, a witness cannot subsequently serve as the judge in that very case. The act of witnessing the crime itself, not merely the act of testifying, is what triggers the disqualification.

### Capital Crimes Only

The *gemara* resolves that even according to Rabbi Akiva, the *mishna* regarding the new moon is unproblematic. Rabbi Akiva's rule applies exclusively to *dinei nefashot*, capital cases, where the Torah states *ve-shaftu ha-eda ve-hitzilu ha-eda* — the congregation shall judge and the congregation shall seek to save the accused. In capital cases, one who has seen the crime committed is so emotionally and cognitively invested that he cannot maintain the dispassionate distance needed to seek out arguments in the defendant's favor. The graphic reality of witnessing a killing registers in a way that forecloses the kind of impartial advocacy the Torah demands of judges in capital matters. For *kiddush hachodesh*, however, even Rabbi Akiva agrees that having seen the moon does not disqualify one from participating in the adjudicative process.

---

## Tosafot Classification

### Three Categories

Tosafot, in the *dibbur hamatchil* beginning with the word *uve-eid*, provides a crisp summary of three distinct legal contexts in which *eid na'aseh dayan* operates differently. In the case of testimony about the new moon, which is *de-oraita*, one who merely saw the moon — *eid haroeh* — may nonetheless serve as a judge; the seeing does not disqualify. In the case of *kiyum shetarot*, the validation of signatures on documents, which is Rabbinic in origin, even *eid hameid na'aseh dayan* — one who actually testified may turn around and serve as the adjudicating judge. And in *dinei nefashot*, capital cases, even *eid haroeh eino na'aseh dayan* — even one who merely saw the act, without ever testifying, is disqualified from serving as judge.

The result is a spectrum: at one extreme, *kiyum shetarot* is the most permissive (even the testifying witness may judge); in the middle, *kiddush hachodesh* permits the one who saw to judge; and at the other extreme, *dinei nefashot* disqualifies even the one who only saw but never testified. This leaves open, as a *she'elah*, where ordinary *dinei mamonot* and cases involving lashes — which are neither capital nor merely monetary — would fall along this spectrum.

---

## Transition to Shofar

### All Except Cow

With the issues of *kiddush hachodesh* concluded, the *masechet* now transitions to its *shofar* section. The *mishna* states: *kol hashofarot ksheirim* — all horns are valid for use as a *shofar* — *chutz mishel parah*, except for a cow's horn — *mipnei shehu keren*, because it is a *keren*. This formulation immediately invites scrutiny: what precisely is the significance of calling it a *keren*, and why would that disqualify it?

### Keren Definition

Rabbi Yosi challenges the reasoning directly. He argues that one cannot exclude a cow's horn on the grounds that it is called a *keren*, because all *shofarot* are referred to as *keren* as well. His proof is from the verse in Yehoshua concerning the fall of the walls of Yericho: *bimshoch bkeren hayovel heimah ya'alu bahar* — when the *keren hayovel* is drawn out, they shall go up the mountain — and the verse continues, *b'shom'achem et kol hashofar*. Since a *yovel* — which as the *gemara* will establish means a ram — has its horn called both *keren* and *shofar*, the terminology of *keren* alone cannot be the basis for distinguishing a cow's horn.

---

## Cow Horn Debate

### Rabbi Yosi Proof

Rabbi Yosi's challenge stands. Even a ram's horn — which is unambiguously valid — is referred to in Scripture as a *keren*. If the *mishna*'s reason for invalidating a cow's horn were simply that it is called a *keren*, that reason would equally invalidate every *shofar*, since rams' horns are likewise called *keren*. The objection therefore demands a stronger account of the distinction.

### Rabbis Response

The Rabbis respond by refining the claim. All other horns, they argue, are called both *shofar* and *keren* — *kol hashofarot ikru keren ve-ikru shofar*. The term *shofar* applies to rams' horns, as derived from the *pasuk* at Har Sinai: *bimshoch hayovel heimah ya'alu bahar*, followed by *vayehi kol hashofar holech vechazek me'od* — there the *yovel* (ram's horn) is explicitly called a *shofar*. A cow's horn, by contrast, is only ever called a *keren*, never a *shofar*. The proof is the verse: *bechor shoro hadar lo ve-karnei re'eim karnav* — horn language is associated with the bovine, while the word *shofar* never appears in that context.

### Shor Par

Rabbi Yosi counters that a cow's horn *is* called a *shofar*, based on the verse *ve-titev la'Hashem mishor par* — my offering will be more pleasing to God than a *shor par*. The *gemara* asks: if it is a *shor*, why say *par*, and if it is a *par*, why say *shor*? The answer: *shor par* is a contraction for *mi-shofar* — from the *shofar*. The double language signals that the animal's horn is itself called a *shofar*.

The Rabbis respond to this by invoking Rav Masna's interpretation: the verse refers to an animal that was a *shor* — that is, a one-day-old — yet was as large as a *par* (a fully grown animal), since at the time of creation animals were formed in their fully developed state. The word *par* thus describes the size, not the species, and the verse does not establish a general term *shofar* for a cow's horn.

The debate at this point is granular — trading *pesukim* to establish whether *shofar* ever applies to a bovine horn — and the *gemara* itself seems to recognize the unsatisfying character of this exchange. Both Ulla and Abaye will offer alternative explanations that move away from the philological argument entirely.

### Golden Calf Link

Ulla proposes what he presents as the real reason underlying the Rabbinic position: *hainu ta'ama de-Rabbanan ke-Rav Chisda*. Rav Chisda had asked why the *kohen gadol* does not enter the inner sanctum on Yom Kippur wearing his golden vestments when performing the *avodat pnim*. The answer: *ein kategor na'aseh sanegore* — the prosecutor cannot become the defense attorney. Gold evokes the *chet ha-eigel*, the sin of the Golden Calf, and therefore cannot be the instrument through which the *kohen gadol* approaches God in the innermost sanctum on the day of atonement. Similarly, a cow's horn evokes the *eigel* and cannot serve as the instrument through which Israel approaches God on Rosh Hashanah.

The *gemara* then subjects this parallel to sustained scrutiny. Does not the blood of the ox (*dam par*) enter the *kodesh kodashim* on Yom Kippur? The *gemara* answers: blood no longer appears as a cow — *ishtani ishtani*, it has been transformed. What about the *aron*, the *kapores*, and the *keruvim*, all of which are gold and reside permanently inside the inner sanctum? The *gemara* distinguishes: the principle of *ein kategor na'aseh sanegore* applies to what the *kohen gadol* himself brings in and uses — *chotei bal yakriv* — the sinner may not approach using objects that evoke the sin. The permanent furnishings of the sanctuary are not being actively wielded by the approaching worshipper. What about the *kaf* and *machtah*, the fire pan and incense ladle, which are gold and which the *kohen gadol* does carry in? The *gemara* answers with the principle of *chotei bal yisna'eh* — the sinner may not adorn or beautify himself with things that evoke his sin. Clothing, which integrates with one's identity and presents one's person, is categorically different from the vessels one happens to carry.

The *gemara* then presses: the *kohen gadol* does wear gold vestments outside the inner sanctum for the other services on Yom Kippur — why is that permitted? The answer: *mi-pnim* — only within the innermost sanctum is the prohibition operative.

This leads to the sharpest objection: the *shofar* is blown outside, not within the *kodesh kodashim* — *shofar mi-bachutz hu*. So why should the *kategor-sanegore* logic apply? The *gemara* responds with a striking statement: *keivan de-le-zikaron hu ke-pnim dami* — since the *shofar* functions to raise Israel's memory before God, it is as if it penetrates directly into the innermost sanctum. The *shofar* pierces through to God's presence, so its use is treated as though it were an act performed *lifnai ve-lifnim*.

Yet the *gemara* simultaneously notes that the *mishna* stated the reason for excluding the cow's horn as *mipnei shehu keren* — which sounds like a terminology-based argument, not the *kategor-sanegore* reasoning. The *gemara* resolves this: *chada ve-od ka'amar* — the *mishna* is making two points, not one. The primary reason is *ein kategor na'aseh sanegore*; the secondary, additional point is *mipnei shehu keren*. Rabbi Yosi, for his part, maintains that neither argument succeeds: the *kategor-sanegore* reasoning applies only within the *kodesh kodashim*, and the *keren* terminology applies equally to all *shofarot*.

### Multiple Segments

Abaye offers a third independent rationale: *shofar echad amar Rachmana ve-lo shnayim u-shloshah shofarot* — the Torah specifies a single *shofar*, not two or three. And later in the *masechet* we will see that one may not insert one *shofar* inside another and blow. The problem with a cow's horn is that *keivan de-kaei gildei gildei* — it is visibly layered, growing in segments year by year — *michzei ke-shnayim u-shloshah shofarot*, it appears as though it were two or three *shofarot* joined together, in violation of the requirement for a single *shofar*.

The *gemara* once again invokes *chada ve-od ka'amar* — both this reason and the *keren* terminology are cited by the *mishna*, the former being the primary one. Rabbi Yosi responds: *keivan de-michubar ahadadi*, since the segments of a cow's horn are all organically connected, it constitutes a single unit — *chad hu*. And the *keren* terminology, as before, applies to all horns equally. The *gemara* thus records an impasse between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosi, with the *gemara* itself appearing somewhat frustrated by the back-and-forth over the *keren* terminology and generating successive new arguments precisely because the original *mishna*ic formulation seems inadequate on its own terms.

---

## Ramban Pshat

### Bone vs Marrow

The Ramban composed a famous *drasha le-Rosh Hashanah* that functions effectively as a running commentary on the *halakhot* of *shofar* and *tefillah* addressed in this *masechet*. One of the first topics he addresses is this very question about the cow's horn. He argues that the entire debate about whether a cow's horn is called a *shofar* or a *keren* misses the plain meaning of the *mishna*. The *mishna* does not say the cow's horn is excluded *mipnei she-nikra keren* — because it is *called* a *keren*. It says *mipnei she-hu keren* — because it *is* a *keren*, because of what it actually *is*.

The Ramban's explanation is structural. A cow's horn contains no marrow; it is solid bone throughout. To convert it into a functioning musical instrument, one must carve out and hollow the bone, which makes the resulting instrument an essentially manufactured object. By contrast, a ram's horn contains marrow that can be scooped out, leaving a naturally hollow vessel that is ready to function as a *shofar* with minimal intervention. The cow's horn must be *fashioned* into an instrument; the ram's horn *is* one naturally. The invalidation thus rests on the distinction between a natural *shofar* and a manufactured horn instrument — which is what *keren* properly denotes in this context.

This reading elegantly sidesteps the philological debate in the *gemara* and grounds the exclusion in the physical character of the instrument rather than in its nomenclature.

### Tosafot Hollow

Tosafot makes a related observation in addressing why the *mishna* does not also exclude the horn of the *re'eim* (wild ox), since the *re'eim*'s horn is likewise called *keren* in Scripture. Tosafot answers: *ve-shema einam chalulim* — perhaps the *re'eim*'s horns are not naturally hollow — *ve-einam re'uyim le-shofar*, and therefore they are not fit to serve as a *shofar* in any case, rendering it unnecessary for the *mishna* to exclude them explicitly. Tosafot does not state that this is the *reason* for the cow's horn's disqualification; he is explaining only why no explicit exclusion was needed for the *re'eim*. The Ramban, however, points out that Tosafot's observation reflects the very same physical insight — the relevance of whether a horn is naturally hollow — and that the Ramban's reading of the *mishna* essentially makes this the operative principle that the *mishna* itself is invoking.

---

## Yovel as Ram

### Rabbi Akiva Travels

The *gemara* asks: *mai mashma de-hai yovla lishna de-dichra hu* — what is the source for understanding the word *yovel* to mean a ram? The word appears throughout the *sugyot* of *kiddush hachodesh* and *shofar*, and the assumption that it refers specifically to a ram's horn has been taken for granted. A *baraita* is cited: Rabbi Akiva testified that when he traveled to Arabia, *hayu korin le-dichra yovla* — the local population referred to a ram as a *yovel*. This vernacular usage provides the philological anchor for the term as it appears in the Torah.

### Vernacular Evidence

This exchange introduces a broader methodological point. The *gemara* uses Rabbi Akiva's observation as an instance of a legitimate form of lexicographic inquiry: difficult or rare words in the Torah or in *mishnaic* literature can sometimes be illuminated by how those words, or cognates of them, are used in the living vernacular — whether by local populations, traveling merchants, or the everyday speech of those close to the rabbis. Just as modern scholars of ancient Semitic languages compare biblical vocabulary with contemporary Arabic or Aramaic usage to reconstruct original meanings, the *tanna'im* and *amora'im* employed an analogous method.

---

## Vernacular Examples

### Akiva Examples

The *gemara* presents several further instances of Rabbi Akiva learning the meaning of scriptural or *mishnaic* terms from vernacular usage encountered in his travels. When Rabbi Akiva went to *Galya* (perhaps Gaul), he found that the local population called a *niddah* a *galmuda* — Tosafot notes this illuminates a *pasuk*. When he went to Africa, he found the local population called a *ma'ah* (a small coin) a *kesitah*, which clarifies the meaning of *me'ah kesitah* in the Torah — it means one hundred *danki*, a known monetary unit. Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) similarly reported that when he traveled to the coastal islands, the people there called selling *kirah*, which explains the verse *asher karisi li* — meaning "which I acquired for myself." And Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish reports that in a place called *Kan Nishraya*, a bride was called *ginfi* (possibly from the Greek for bride) and a rooster was called *sikhvi* — the latter illuminating the verse *mi shat batuchot chochmah o mi natan la-sikhvi binah* (Job 38:36), where *sikhvi* refers to the rooster who knows when to crow at dawn.

### Levi Stories

The *gemara* then narrates the story of Levi, who encountered a man who said to him *kavan ploni* — "I was *kove'a* so-and-so." Levi did not understand the term and had to consult the study hall, where his colleagues explained that the man meant he had stolen from that person, as in the verse *ha-yikba adam Elohim ki atem kove'im oti* — "will a man rob God, for you have robbed Me?" — said in the context of withholding *ma'aser* and *terumah*. Notably, the root appears in a *pasuk* and is not purely vernacular, which makes it surprising that Levi did not recognize it.

### Rava Approach

Rava from Barnish told Rav Ashi that had he been in Levi's position, he would not have needed to consult the study hall. Instead, he would have engaged the man directly with a series of questions: *heichi kav'ach*, *be-mai kav'ach*, *ve-amai kav'ach* — how did you *kove'a* him, with what, and why? From the man's answers, Rava would have reconstructed the meaning by context. This is offered as a clever method of lexicographic inquiry through targeted questioning — essentially the same method one uses when one has forgotten someone's name and keeps the conversation going in hopes of reconstructing the context.

The *gemara* adds that Levi did not take this approach because *midei de-issura ka'amar leih* — he sensed the man was describing something of a transgressive nature and did not want to probe further into the details.

### Maidservant Words

The *gemara* then presents a series of cases in which the Rabbis — meaning the rabbinic students in the academy — did not know the meaning of certain words appearing in *mishnaic* or biblical texts, and learned them through the vernacular usage of the maidservant in Rabbi's household.

They did not know what *serugin* meant (a word that appears in a *mishna*), until they heard the maidservant chastise the students who were entering the study hall in clusters with pauses between them: *ad matay atem nichnasim serugin serugin* — "how long will you keep entering in *serugin serugin*?" From this they understood that *serugin* means intermittently, in broken intervals.

They did not know what *chaluglogot* were — a type of vegetable relevant to certain *halachot* of a *zav*. One day they saw the maidservant rebuke a man who was scattering his *parpachinei* (purslane) about, saying *ad matay atah mefazer chaluglogecha* — and they identified *chaluglogot* as purslane.

They did not know what *salselah* meant in the verse *salselah u-teromemeka* (Proverbs 4:8), meaning to cherish or adorn. They heard the maidservant say to a man who was constantly fussing with his hair, *ad matay atah mesalsel be-sa'arecha* — "how long will you keep *mesalsel* your hair?" — and understood the word to mean playing with or adorning.

They did not know what *ve-titateiha be-matate ha-shmad* (Isaiah 14:23) meant. They heard the maidservant say to her companion *shikuli tatita ve-tati beita* — "take your broom and sweep the house" — and understood *matate* to mean a broom.

Finally, they did not know what *yehavcha* meant in the verse *hashlech al Hashem yehavcha ve-hu yechalkelecha* (Psalms 55:23) — "cast upon God your burden and He will sustain you." Rabbah bar bar Chanah reported that one day he was traveling with a nomadic Arab who, seeing him carrying a load, said *shekol yehavcha u-shdi agmalai* — "take your *yehavach* and throw it on my camel." From this he understood that *yehav* means one's burden or load.

---

## Rosh Hashanah Shofar

### Description

The *mishna* now describes the *shofar* used in the *Beit HaMikdash* on Rosh Hashanah: *shofar shel Rosh Hashanah shel ya'el pashut* — it was made from the horn of a *ya'el* (ibex), and it was straight. *U-fiv metzupeh zahav* — and its mouthpiece was plated in gold. This description pertains specifically to the practice in the *Beit HaMikdash*.

### Trumpets Role

*U-shtei chatzotzrot min ha-tzedadim* — two silver trumpets were positioned on the sides. All three instruments would sound together, but the respective durations were calibrated to signal the primary instrument of the day: *shofar maarich ve-chatzotzrot mekatzrot* — the *shofar* would sustain its sound while the *chatzotzrot* would cut off early. The reason: *she-mitzvat hayom ba-shofar* — the central *mitzvah* of the day is the *shofar*, and the *chatzotzrot* serve only as accompaniment. The primacy of the *shofar* is audibly demonstrated by the extended *shofar* tone sounding alone after the *chatzotzrot* fall silent.

### Fast Day Shofar

On fast days, the arrangement was the inverse. *U-ve-ta'aniyot be-shel zecharim kfufim* — the *shofarot* used were the twisted horns of rams — *u-fihen metzupeh kasef* — and their mouthpieces were plated in silver. *U-shtei chatzotzrot ba-emtza* — the two *chatzotzrot* were placed in the center, not the sides — *shofar mekatzrot ve-chatzotzrot maarichot* — the *shofar* cut off while the *chatzotzrot* sustained their sound. *She-mitzvat hayom ba-chatzotzrot* — on a fast day, the primary *mitzvah* is the *chatzotzrot*.

The context for these blowings on fast days is the additional six *berachot* recited in the *shemoneh esrei* on communal fast days for rain. Two of those six additions are *zichronot* and *shofrot*. After each of these *berachot* in the repetition, the *kohanim* (at least in the *Beit HaMikdash*) would sound the *shofar* and *chatzotzrot*. Outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, blowings were done as well, though without the full ceremonial apparatus of center-and-sides placement and precious metal plating.

The *chatzotzrot* as instruments of calling out to God have their own independent biblical basis — *ki tavo'u milchama be-artzechem al ha-tzar ha-tzorer etchem ve-hareiotem ba-chatzotzrot* — and the integration of *chatzotzrot* into the *tefillot* of *ta'anit* reflects this distinct scriptural mandate. The parallels between fast-day practice and the *shofar* of Rosh Hashanah are worth noting even if they are not identical in their sources.

### Rosh Hashanah vs Yovel

The *mishna* then states that *yovel* is equivalent to Rosh Hashanah with respect to the *tekiot* and the *berachot* — meaning the number of blasts and the structure of *malchuyot*, *zichronot*, and *shofrot*. This equation sets up the next section's debate about whether the horn types used on Rosh Hashanah and *yovel* must in fact be identical.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda View

### Yehuda Distinction

Rabbi Yehuda disputes the first part of the *mishna* on two fronts. He holds that Rosh Hashanah and *yovel* are not equivalent in the type of horn used, and that the horn for Rosh Hashanah itself differs from what the *tanna kamma* describes. *Be-Rosh Hashanah tokiyim be-shel zecharim* — on Rosh Hashanah one blows with rams' horns — *u-ve-yovel be-shel yeilim* — and on *yovel* with ibex horns. So Rabbi Yehuda actually reverses the *tanna kamma*'s assignment: ibex (*ya'el*, straight) for *yovel*, ram (*zachar*, bent) for Rosh Hashanah. He explicitly maintains a distinction between the two occasions rather than treating them symmetrically.

### Levi Classification

Rabbi Levi adds a further dimension: *mitzvah shel Rosh Hashanah ve-shel Yom Kippurim bi-kfufim* — the ideal for both Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is bent horns — *ve-shel kol ha-shanah bi-fshutim* — while for all other occasions (meaning the fast-day *shofarot*) straight horns are used. Rabbi Levi thus agrees with Rabbi Yehuda that Rosh Hashanah calls for a bent horn, but disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda's distinction between Rosh Hashanah and *yovel*: for Rabbi Levi, both Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur (*yovel*) are alike in requiring a bent horn.

The *gemara* reconciles Rabbi Levi's view with the *mishna* by noting that the *mishna* already records Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that *zecharim* (rams) are used on Rosh Hashanah, and a *baraita* makes explicit what the *mishna* only implies: *Rabbi Yehuda omer be-Rosh Hashanah yotzim be-shel zecharim kfufim* — rams are bent. Rabbi Levi is therefore understood as following this *tanna*. The *gemara* explains why Rabbi Levi did not simply rule *halakha ke-Rabbi Yehuda*: had he done so, one might have thought he also accepts Rabbi Yehuda's distinction between Rosh Hashanah and *yovel*, with *yovel* using a straight horn. By specifying that both Rosh Hashanah and *yovel* take bent horns, Rabbi Levi makes clear he agrees with Rabbi Yehuda only on the Rosh Hashanah side, not on the differentiation.

The resulting picture is that all three positions — *tanna kamma*, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Levi — take distinct stances along two axes: (1) whether Rosh Hashanah and *yovel* are the same or different, and (2) whether the horn for Rosh Hashanah is straight (*pashut*) or bent (*kafuf*). *Tanna kamma* holds them the same and straight; Rabbi Yehuda holds them different (Rosh Hashanah bent, *yovel* straight); Rabbi Levi holds them the same and both bent.

---

## Bent vs Straight

### Core Debate

The *gemara* now asks *be-mai kamifligi* — what exactly is the underlying disagreement between the *tanna kamma* and the others regarding the Rosh Hashanah *shofar*? Both sides agree that the *shofar* must work; the dispute is about the preferred shape. The *gemara* frames the answer in terms of the symbolic meaning each shape carries for the day of Rosh Hashanah.

### Straight Symbolism

One view holds that *be-Rosh Hashanah kama de-pashit inish dateih tfei ma'alei* — on Rosh Hashanah, the more one's *da'at* is directed straight, the better. The idea is that Rosh Hashanah is fundamentally about approaching God directly — not about self-abnegation or prostration, but about bringing one's prayers and one's very self straight to God. A straight horn symbolizes and embodies that direct, forward-directed orientation.

### Bent Symbolism

The opposing view holds *kama de-khayif inish dateih tfei ma'alei* — the more one is bent over, the better. This conception of Rosh Hashanah emphasizes supplication, self-negation, a sense of being weighed down by one's inadequacy, the posture of one who comes before the King not in confidence but in humility and contrition. A bent horn embodies that downward, inward orientation of *teshuvah* and shame.

By contrast, those who hold that Rosh Hashanah calls for a straight horn would agree that *be-ta'aniyot kama de-khayif inish dateih tfei ma'alei* — on fast days, the bent posture is appropriate, since fast days are precisely about confronting sin and communal guilt. On Yom Kippur, meanwhile, the *yovel* aspect — the proclamation of freedom — calls for a straight, outward, announcing posture: *ve-Yom Kippurim kama de-pashit inish dateih tfei ma'alei*.

### Tanna Kamma

The *tanna kamma* thus holds that Rosh Hashanah is best approached with a *pashut*, straight, direct orientation toward God. This is not the day of self-flagellation and guilt — that belongs to the fast days. Rosh Hashanah is the day of coronation, of drawing close, of presenting oneself to the King in a posture of dignity and directness. The *tanna kamma*'s preference for a straight horn on Rosh Hashanah reflects this theological orientation.

---

## Shofar Direction

### Animal Symbolism

The discussion of straight versus bent horns intersects with the question of which animal the horn comes from — and each animal carries its own symbolic weight. A ram's horn evokes the *akeidah*, the binding of Yitzchak, and all that entails: self-sacrifice, surrender, the willingness to give everything up. It evokes a posture of submission and the negation of self before God. An ibex (mountain goat) horn, with its proud, outward-reaching form, projects a very different imagery — directness, confidence, even pride. The *gemara* focuses on the *pashut-kafuf* axis, but the animal dimension reinforces the same symbolic contrast.

### Direction Question

There is a deeper question underlying this entire discussion: to whom or toward what is the *shofar* directed? Is the *shofar* directed *to you* — meaning it is a call addressed to the listener, meant to awaken the hearer to repentance and fear — or is it directed *to God* — meaning it is part of Israel's prayer, functioning as an instrument through which we send our supplications upward? If the *shofar* is directed to you, then the bent posture makes perfect sense for Rosh Hashanah: the *shofar* breaks through your self-satisfaction, bends you, induces fear and reflection. But if the *shofar* is directed to God — if it is the mechanism of *zikaron* before God — then the straight, direct, upward-directed shape is more fitting. Rashi's commentary implies this second understanding.

### Tosafot Symbolic

Tosafot engages at length with the question of how we *poskin* — how we rule in practice on the question of bent versus straight. Tosafot concludes that this is presumably a matter of *lechatchila* only — a symbolic preference about the ideal form of the *shofar* — and not a question of strict *halakha* that would render one's obligation unfulfilled if not observed. Tosafot does note, however, that one could read the discussion as *halakha le-ma'aseh*, such that using the wrong shape would mean one has not properly fulfilled the *mitzvah* — which is hard to accept in light of the opening *mishna* of this section, which declares that all *shofarot* are *kasher*. The normative conclusion is therefore that the preference for one shape or another is a matter of *lechatchila* and symbolic significance, not a *me'akeiv* disqualification. Nevertheless, the underlying question of what the *shofar* is fundamentally about — a summons to *teshuvah* directed inward at the listener, or an instrument of prayer directed outward toward God — is far from merely symbolic. It goes to the heart of how one understands the *mitzvah* of *shofar* on Rosh Hashanah.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 29

## Mitzvot, Kavanah, Bal To…

### La'atzeis vs. La'avor

The *daf* before us is 29, with which we finish the third *perek* and enter into the fourth and final *perek* of *Rosh Hashanah*. We pick up three lines from the bottom of 28b, in the midst of a discussion of several central issues that *Rava* has introduced across the preceding pages. One was *mitzvot lav lehanot nitnu* — whether deriving benefit from fulfilling a *mitzvah* constitutes a technical violation of the prohibition against *hana'ah* from certain objects. A related but distinct example helps clarify the stakes: dissecting a corpse for medical knowledge is permitted even though such knowledge has enormous value, because it does not constitute *hana'ah* in the relevant technical sense.

A second issue was whether *kavanah* is required to fulfill a *mitzvah* — *mitzvot tzerichot kavanah*. All of the evidence from the *Mishnayot* seemed to require *kavanah*, understood as an awareness and intent that what one is performing is a *mitzvah* act. *Rava* disagrees, arguing that the *Mishnayot* speak only of intent to perform the act itself, not of labeling it as a *mitzvah*. Finally, the discussion transitioned into the issue of *bal tosif* and *bal tigra* — the prohibition against adding to or subtracting from a *mitzvah*. If *mitzvot* require no *kavanah*, it should be alarmingly easy to transgress *bal tosif*, since anything done during the time of a *mitzvah* might automatically become incorporated into it — as in the case of sleeping in a *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret*.

Now *Rava* attempts to reconcile these tensions. He states: *la'atzeis lo ba'ei kavanah* — to fulfill one's obligation, one does not need *kavanah*. But *la'avor ba'ei kavanah* — to transgress *bal tosif*, one does need intent. The reasoning is elegant. Taking a *lulav* and *etrog* on *Sukkot* is self-defining as a *mitzvah* act; no special intent is required for it to count. But if one holds a pencil in the same hand, nothing about holding a pencil is objectively a *mitzvah* act. To incorporate it into the *mitzvah* and thereby transgress *bal tosif*, one would need *kavanah* — the explicit intent to expand the *mitzvah* act to include it. Similarly, sleeping in a *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret* is not, by itself, an act that is self-evidently a *mitzvah*; one might simply be sleeping outdoors. To transgress *bal tosif* by extending the seven-day *mitzvah* into an eighth day, one would have to consciously frame that act as a *mitzvah* act.

### Lulav & Intentionality

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this formulation. It invokes the earlier case of *matan damim* — the application of blood — in which *Rabbi Yehoshua* held there is a problem of *bal tosif* even without apparent *kavanah* to expand the *mitzvah*. If *Rava's* principle is correct, *Rabbi Eliezer* could simply have responded that there is no *kavanah* present and therefore no violation. This is in fact one possible reading of *Rabbi Eliezer's* statement: *lo ne'emar bal tosif ela k'shehu l'atzmo* — *bal tosif* is only operative when one performs the expansion on its own terms; here the additional applications are the product of the bloods having become mixed, leaving the *kohen* no choice. That resolution may be precisely what *Rabbi Eliezer* intended.

Nevertheless, the *Gemara* treats this as a significant challenge to *Rava's* formulation and presses further.

### Bizmano vs. Shelo Bizmano

*Rava* now refines his position: *la'atzeis lo ba'ei kavanah* — to fulfill one's obligation, no intent is needed. But to transgress *bal tosif*, the critical variable is *bizmano* — whether the act is performed during the time of the *mitzvah*. If it is *bizmano*, then *lo ba'ei kavanah* — even without intent, something can naturally become incorporated into the *mitzvah* act, and one may transgress *bal tosif*. Thus in the case of *matan damim*, the additional applications occur *bizmano*, within the performance of the *mitzvah* itself, and therefore become incorporated without any conscious intent to expand it. *Aval shelo bizmano* — not during the time of the *mitzvah*, as in sleeping in the *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret* — nothing defines that act as part of the *mitzvah*, and therefore *ba'ei kavanah*: explicit intent is required to incorporate it and thereby transgress *bal tosif*.

This resolves several of the earlier cases. The extra blessing of *birkat kohanim* involves *kavanah*, while the blood application does not, but is *bizmano*. The *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret* is neither accompanied by *kavanah* nor is it *bizmano*, and therefore presents no *bal tosif* concern.

### Types of Kavanah

This resolution, however, opens a further question: does *lo ba'ei kavanah bizmano* mean that literally everything one does while performing the *mitzvah* is automatically incorporated? That cannot be right — if one happens to be wearing a ring or holding one's glasses while taking the *lulav*, one surely has not transgressed *bal tosif*. The answer lies in clarifying what kind of *kavanah* is under discussion at each stage. When *Rava* says *mitzvot lo ba'ei kavanah* — that *mitzvot* do not require *kavanah* — he means one need not specifically intend to perform a *mitzvah*; intent to do the act itself suffices to render one *yotzei*. Similarly, *la'avor bizmano lo ba'ei kavanah* means one need not intend to expand the *mitzvah* consciously, but one does still have to intend to do the act in a way that makes it incorporated into what is being performed. The person applying blood four times is aware that he is making those applications, even if he did not intend to expand the *mitzvah*. The person who is wearing a ring is not intending to incorporate the ring into the *lulav* act at all. The distinction, then, between *kavanah* to frame something as an expanded *mitzvah* act — which one does not need *bizmano* — and *kavanah* to do the act in a way that connects it to the *mitzvah* performance — which one still needs — is where the precise and admittedly narrow line must be drawn.

---

## Kavanah LeHotzi

### Rav Zeira's Shofar

The *Gemara* now introduces a new dimension of *kavanah* through the instruction of *Rav Zeira* to his attendant: *ikaven u'tka li* — have *kavanah* when you blow the *shofar* and blow for me. This instruction adds something beyond the question of *mitzvot tzerichot kavanah*. Even granting *Rava's* view that *mitzvot* do not require *kavanah* to render oneself *yotzei*, blowing the *shofar* for another person introduces a distinct requirement: *kavanah lehotzi* — the intent not merely to blow, but specifically to help discharge the other person's obligation. It is not enough that the blower intends this as a *mitzvah* act of *tkias shofar* in general. For the act to become the other person's act — to connect to them — the blower must consciously intend to link that blowing to this specific listener. This is the principle of *ad sheyichavein shomeia umashmia* — both the hearer and the one causing the sound to be heard must have *kavanah*, but the *kavanah* required of the *mashmia* is specifically *kavanah lehotzi*.

### Shomea & Mashmia

A *baraita* is then cited in challenge: *niskavein shomeia velo niskavein mashmia, niskavein mashmia velo niskavein shomeia, lo yatza — ad sheyichavein shomeia umashmia*. Both must have intent; if either is lacking, the obligation is not discharged. The *Gemara* observes that this *baraita* describes the intent of the *mashmia* in parallel with the intent of the *shomea*: just as the hearer need only intend to fulfill his own obligation, so apparently the blower need only intend to fulfill his own obligation. No additional, distinct *kavanah lehotzi* seems to be required of the blower — the *baraita* speaks of them in identical terms. This is a compelling challenge to *Rav Zeira's* requirement.

### Overhearing Behind Shul

The *Gemara* raises a related case. Someone was walking behind a *beis haknesses* or living in an adjacent house and happened to hear the *shofar* or *megillah*: *im kivein libo yatza, v'im lav lo yatza* — if he had intent, he fulfilled his obligation; if not, he did not. The *Gemara* immediately notes the problem: even if this incidental listener had intent, what does it matter? *Lo kamichavein adaata dideih* — the blower had no awareness of this person at all and certainly had no intent to discharge his obligation.

The *Gemara* resolves this by invoking the case of the *shliach tzibbur*: we are speaking here of the one who blows or reads in an official congregational capacity. When one serves in that role, the nature of the position itself carries a blanket intent — *dedaateih achulei alma*, his intent extends to whoever hears, anyone in the world who needs to be *yotzei* with this performance. He does not enumerate individuals; he understands he is performing the *mitzvah* for the community, and that extends to whomever is within hearing range.

### Shliach Tzibur

This distinction between the *shliach tzibbur* and a private individual is made explicit by *Rabbi Yosi*. In the same *baraita* tradition, *mashmia lefi darko* — the blower performs it in his usual manner without special intent — is clarified as follows: *bameh devarim amurim — bishliach tzibbur*. This standard applies to the *shliach tzibbur*, for whom ordinary, unstated intent suffices precisely because his role presupposes he is blowing for others. *Aval beyachid — lo yatza ad sheyitkaven shomea umashmia*: but a private individual blowing for someone else requires explicit *kavanah lehotzi* — he must specifically intend to discharge that person's obligation. While the earlier *baraita* appeared to describe the intent of *mashmia* and *shomea* in identical terms, *Rabbi Yosi's* distinction makes clear that a private individual who wishes to serve as the means through which another person fulfills the *mitzvah* must have an active, directed intent to that effect.

In practical terms, this applies at the *Shabbat* table as well. A person making *Kiddush* for others who has not specifically thought of those present should at minimum express a blanket intent to discharge the obligation of anyone who hears and wishes to be *yotzei*.

### Two Levels of Intent

This raises a pointed question: can one simultaneously hold both *Rava's* position that *mitzvot einan tzerichot kavanah* and the requirement of *kavanah lehotzi*? The answer is that these are two categorically different questions. When one performs the *mitzvah* act oneself — taking the *lulav*, blowing the *shofar* — the question is whether the absence of conscious *mitzvah*-intent prevents the act from counting. *Rava* says it does not; the act itself is sufficient. But when one wishes to fulfill one's obligation through someone else's act, an entirely different problem arises: what makes that other person's act one's own? The blower is performing the act; the listener is not. For the blowing to be constituted as the listener's act, some connecting link must exist — and that link is the *kavanah lehotzi* of the blower, the conscious intent to extend that act toward the listener. Without it, the sounds produced are simply sounds; they do not become the listener's *mitzvah* act. These are thus two distinct layers of the *kavanah* question, and it is entirely coherent to hold both simultaneously.

As for the practical *halacha*: the *rishonim* and *poskim* debate the rule for *mitzvot tzerichot kavanah*. The general tendency is to require *kavanah* for *de'oraita* obligations, while for *derabanan* obligations there is more room to rule *bedi'avad* that they do not require it — though the matter remains subject to significant dispute. The requirement of *kavanah lehotzi*, by contrast, is applied across the board wherever one person seeks to discharge another's obligation.

The discussion of *kavanah lehotzi* also raises the question of which *mitzvot* are even susceptible to the mechanism of discharging another's obligation through one's own performance. The answer is that this is fundamentally limited to auditory *mitzvot* — *brachot*, *mikra megillah*, *tkias shofar* — governed by the principle of *shomea ke'oneh*, that hearing is as if one has spoken. Yet even within this category, nuance remains. It is relatively straightforward to understand why hearing words of *tefillah* or *brachot* and responding *amen* is as if one said them — one heard the words, assented to them, and is thus connected to them. It is somewhat more difficult to understand how hearing the sounds of the *shofar* is equivalent to having placed the ram's horn to one's lips. Similarly, the *mitzvah* of *krias megillah* involves not merely hearing words but reading them from a physical scroll — whether hearing them read constitutes reading them oneself is a question that generates debate among the *rishonim*. The common thread that unifies *shofar*, *megillah*, and *brachot* under *shomea ke'oneh* is their auditory character, even if the precise mechanism differs across the categories.

---

## Moshe's Hands & Serpent

### Hands of Moshe

The *perek* concludes with an *aggadeta* that grows directly from the preceding discussion of *kavanah*. The *Mishnah* cites the verse: *Vehaya ka'asher yarim Moshe yado vegavar Yisrael, vechaasher yaniach yado vegavar Amalek* — when *Moshe* raised his hand, *Yisrael* prevailed; when he lowered it, *Amalek* prevailed. The *Mishnah* immediately poses its rhetorical question: *vechi yadav shel Moshe osos milchamah o shores milchamah?* Did *Moshe's* hands make the war, or break the war? What kind of power is being ascribed here?

The answer: *ella lomar lecha* — to tell you that whenever *Yisrael* would look upward at the raised hands and would direct their hearts to their Father in Heaven — *meshabdin es libam la'avihem shebashamayim* — they would prevail; and when they would not, they would fall.

### Serpent on Pole

The same interpretive move is applied to a second story: *aseh lecha saraf vesim oto al nes*, make a fiery serpent and place it upon a pole, and anyone who was bitten would look at it and live. Again the rhetorical question is posed: *vechi nachash meimis o nachash michayeh?* Can a serpent bring death, or can a serpent bring life? And again the same answer: when *Yisrael* would look upward and subjugate their hearts to their Father in Heaven, they would be healed; when they would not, they would waste away.

### Removing Magic

This *aggadeta* operates on two levels simultaneously. On one level, it is making a point about the religious significance of *kavanah* that goes well beyond its halachic parameters. The preceding discussion treated *kavanah* as a technical question of what is required for an act to count, and whether intent is needed to transgress *bal tosif*. Here, the *Mishnah* enlarges the picture: *kavanah* — understood as directing one's heart toward God — is what gives a physical act its religious meaning and its capacity to connect one to the divine. The act without that orientation is empty; the act with it becomes a conduit for relationship with *avihem shebashamayim*.

On a second level, the *Mishnah* is actively demystifying narratives that could be read very differently. Both stories — the hands of *Moshe* and the serpent on the pole — could easily be read as accounts of direct magical efficacy. One might conclude that certain physical acts or objects carry inherent power, and the Torah is cataloguing them. This reading would be deeply at odds with the Torah's fundamental opposition to magic, incantation, and necromancy. The *Mishnah* therefore reframes these stories entirely: the object or gesture was never the operative force. It was always the *kavanah* — the interior act of turning toward God — that was doing the work. Whether this reframing constitutes the *pshat* of the *pesukim* is a larger question, but the interpretive intent of the *Mishnah* is unmistakable.

---

## Bar Da'at Requirement

### Obligation Principle

The *Mishnah* now establishes a principle that was already implicit in the preceding discussion of *kavanah lehotzi*: *cheresh, shote, v'katan ein motzi'in es harabim yedei chovasan* — a deaf-mute, a *shote* (a person not anchored in rational reality, with a fuller definition reserved for discussion elsewhere), and a minor cannot discharge the public from its obligations. The governing principle is stated explicitly: *ze haklal — kol she'eino mechuyav badavar eino motzi es harabim yedei chovasan* — whoever is not themselves obligated in a matter cannot be the one through whom the community discharges its obligation.

### Cheresh, Shote, Katan

All three of these categories — *cheresh*, *shote*, and *katan* — share the halachic status of not being *bar da'as*, not being persons of legal understanding and capacity. It is worth noting that the category of *cheresh* carries a complex modern history: the advent of sign language and the demonstrated cognitive capacities of deaf individuals led to a significant reconsideration of this category in later halachic literature. But within the framework of the *Gemara*, these three are treated as formally outside the circle of halachic obligation, and one cannot discharge the obligation of the *tzibbur* through the act of someone who does not themselves bear that obligation.

---

## Who's Obligated Baraita

### General Categories

A *baraita* now enumerates those who are obligated in *tkias shofar*: *hakol chayavin bitkias shofar — Kohanim, Levi'im, v'Yisraelim, geirim, va'avadim meshuchrarim* — all are obligated: *Kohanim*, *Levi'im*, *Yisraelim*, converts, and freed slaves. To this list are added *tumtum*, *androgynous*, and *mi shechetzyo eved v'chetzyo ben chorin* — the *tumtum*, the *androgynous*, and the half-slave, half-free person — because in each of these cases there is some aspect of the individual that may carry the relevant obligation.

### Tumtum Status

The *baraita* states: *tumtum eino motzi lo es mino v'lo es she'eino mino* — a *tumtum* cannot discharge another *tumtum* and cannot discharge someone who is clearly male. A *tumtum* is a person whose genitalia are concealed, and the question of whether the individual is male or female is therefore empirically unknown. Given that women are not obligated in *tkias shofar*, and given that one *tumtum* blowing for another *tumtum* creates the possibility that a female is attempting to discharge a male, the discharge fails: the part of the *tkiah* generated by what may be a female cannot satisfy the obligation of what may be a male.

### Androgynous Status

An *androgynous* — a person possessing both male and female primary anatomy — can discharge another *androgynous* but cannot discharge a clearly male person. The distinction here is conceptually important. A *tumtum's* status is an empirical unknown: every *tumtum* may be male or female, depending on what lies beneath, and this may differ from case to case. An *androgynous*, by contrast, presents a question of legal classification that applies uniformly to the entire category: all *androgynous* individuals share the same halachic status, whatever that status turns out to be. The three possibilities are that they are classified as male, as female, or as a distinct third category. Whichever classification is correct applies equally to all members of the category — and therefore one *androgynous* can discharge another, since they share the same classification. However, none of these three possibilities is equivalent to a fully male individual, and therefore an *androgynous* cannot discharge a clear male. It is worth noting that even here, the female exemption from *shofar* is functioning as a background premise throughout these discussions without being explicitly stated — a striking feature of how the *Mishnah* and *baraita* are structured.

### Half-Slave Status

*Mi shechetzyo eved v'chetzyo ben chorin eino motzi lo es mino v'lo es she'eino mino* — the half-slave, half-free person cannot discharge another half-slave and cannot discharge a fully free male. The reasoning for the inability to discharge another half-slave is that the *tkiah* produced by a half-slave is itself of a compromised halachic character: the portion of the blow generated by the *eved* component of the individual cannot serve as a *tkias mitzvah* for the *ben chorin* component of the listener. Since the *tkiah* is not a complete and uncompromised *tkias mitzvah*, it cannot satisfy the full obligation of even another half-slave.

### Self-Discharge Issue

*Rav Huna* initially rules that the half-slave, half-free person can at least discharge his own obligation — *le'atzmo motzi*. *Rav Nachman* challenges this: what distinguishes the inability to discharge another from the inability to discharge oneself? The same structural problem applies internally. *Lo ati tzad avdus didey u'mafki tzad cheirus didey* — the slave-component of his own *tkiah* cannot discharge the free-person component of himself. The *tkiah* is indivisible; one cannot say that only the part of the blow that comes from the free aspect of himself is the operative *tkiah*. The entire act is compromised. *Rav Nachman* therefore concludes: *af le'atzmo eino motzi* — even his own obligation he cannot discharge through his own blowing. A *baraita* is cited in confirmation: *mi shechetzyo eved v'chetzyo ben chorin af le'atzmo eino motzi*.

---

## Blessings Discharge

### All Brachos Rule

A *baraita* is taught by Abba, son of *Rav Zeira*: *kol habrachos kulan, af al pi sheyatza motzi* — all *brachot*, even if one has already fulfilled the obligation oneself, one may repeat the *bracha* to discharge another's obligation. The principle that one who has already been *yotzei* can nonetheless be *motzi* others applies broadly to *brachot* as a category.

### Bnei Hanaa Exception

There is, however, an exception: *chutz mibirchas halechem u'birchas hayayin* — except for *birkat halechem* (*Hamotzi*) and *birkat hayayin* (*Borei Pri HaGafen*). These are *birchat hanehenin* — blessings of benefit, rooted in the fact that the one reciting them is about to derive physical benefit from food or drink. *V'im lo yatza motzi* — if one has not yet made the *bracha* for oneself, one can make it and thereby discharge another as well. But *v'im yatza, eino motzi* — if one has already said *Hamotzi* or *Borei Pri HaGafen* for oneself, one cannot say it again for someone else. A *birchat hanehenin* is not framed as a *mitzvah* one is performing on behalf of another; it is anchored in the speaker's own benefit. If that benefit is not a present reality for the speaker, the *bracha* has no valid footing.

### Integrated Blessings

*Rava* raises a question about the intersection of these two categories: what of *birchat hanehenin* that has become incorporated into a *birchat hamitzvah* — specifically, *birchat halechem shel matzah* and *birchat hayayin shel kiddush hayom*? When one says *Hamotzi* on *matzah* at the *Pesach Seder*, or *Borei Pri HaGafen* as part of *Kiddush*, is this still a *birchat hanehenin* to which the restriction applies? Or since the obligation of *Kiddush* and the *mitzvah* of *matzah* are operative, has the *birchat hanehenin* been absorbed into the *birchat hamitzvah* frame, rendering it one capable of being repeated to discharge another even after one has already fulfilled it oneself?

The question can be sharpened further. *Kiddush* can theoretically be made without *Borei Pri HaGafen* — if one had already recited *Borei Pri HaGafen* on wine before *Shabbat* began, as sometimes occurs when *Purim* falls on *Erev Shabbat*, the *halacha* in *Pesachim* is *pores mapah umekadesh*, and *Kiddush* would begin from the second *bracha*, since the *birchat hanehenin* has already been covered. Similarly, in a theoretical case where one had already said *Hamotzi* on *matzah* that does not qualify for the *mitzvah*, the subsequent eating of *mitzvah*-*matzah* would require only *al achilas matzah*, not *Hamotzi* again, since the *hana'ah* dimension was already covered. This means that even within *Kiddush* and the *Seder*, the *Hamotzi* and *Borei Pri HaGafen* are not intrinsically part of the *mitzvah* obligation — they are present because one is about to benefit, and if that dimension is already covered, they drop out.

### Rav Ashi Example

*Rav Ashi* reports: *ki havainan bei Rav Pappa, hava mekadesh lan* — when we were in the house of *Rav Pappa*, he would make *Kiddush* for them. *Vechi hava ati ariseih midabra, hava mekadesh lei* — and when his sharecropper came in from the field, he would make *Kiddush* for him as well, including *Borei Pri HaGafen*, without distinguishing between the two instances. Since *Rav Pappa* did not skip the *Borei Pri HaGafen* even when reciting *Kiddush* for the sharecropper after having already made *Kiddush* for himself — and since the sharecropper was presumably also drinking the wine and needed *Borei Pri HaGafen* — this serves as a practical ruling that the *Borei Pri HaGafen* embedded in *Kiddush* can be recited to discharge another's obligation even after one has already fulfilled one's own. The *birchat hanehenin* in that context is treated as having been absorbed into the *birchat hamitzvah*.

This ruling has interesting practical ramifications. The question of what happens when one is serving as *mesader kiddushin* before *birchat eirusin* — where the custom is to say *Borei Pri HaGafen* on wine, though the *Gemara* never makes this a formal requirement and the *halacha* is that it can be done without wine — is one that careful *mesadrei kiddushin* are alert to. Since in that context the *Borei Pri HaGafen* was never packaged into a formal *birchat hamitzvah*, those making the *bracha* without personally drinking face a *birchat hanehenin* without personal *hana'ah*. One solution practiced by those aware of this concern is to place a small amount of wine on one's fingers and taste it after handing the cup to the groom.

Separately, it should be noted that *Borei Pri HaGafen* on *Shabbat* morning operates differently from *Borei Pri HaGafen* on *Friday night*. On *Shabbat* morning, the *Kiddush* is essentially the practice of beginning one's meal with wine, without the full *mitzvah* character of *Friday night Kiddush*. Therefore, the *Borei Pri HaGafen* said on *Shabbat* morning is truly a straight *birchat hanehenin*, and one who has already said it cannot repeat it for someone else. If one made *Kiddush* at *shul* and subsequently returns home, one makes a new *Borei Pri HaGafen* not because one is repeating *Kiddush* in some enriched sense but simply because one is now drinking wine anew in a different setting, and a new *birchat hanehenin* is required.

### Chinuch Rule

The *baraita* continues: *lo yifros adam prusah le'orchin ela im kein ochel imahem* — one should not break bread for guests unless one is eating with them. This states the basic rule for *Hamotzi* as a *birchat hanehenin*: without personal benefit, one may not say it for others. *Aval pores hu levanav ulevnei beiso kedei lechancham bemitzvot* — but one may break bread for one's children and household members in order to train them in *mitzvot*. For the sake of *chinuch*, one may say a full *bracha* — even a *birchat hanehenin* — even without personally fulfilling the obligation or without the personal *hana'ah* that would normally be required. This principle has important practical application: when training children to recite *brachot* or perform *mitzvot*, one may recite the complete *bracha* together with or for them, rather than substituting an imperfect formulation.

### Hallel & Megillah

Finally: *u've'hallelu u've'megilla af al pi sheyatza motzi* — for *Hallel* and *megillah*, even if one has already fulfilled one's own obligation, one may repeat the performance and the associated *brachot* to discharge another person's obligation. In practice, when helping someone fulfill the *mitzvah* of *megillah*, we would ideally have the person recite the *brachot* themselves and have the reader read the *megillah* on their behalf. But if they are unable, the reader may make the *brachot* again even after having already fulfilled his own *mitzvah*.

---

## Rosh Hashanah & Shabbat

### Mishnah Context

The fourth and final *perek* of *Rosh Hashanah* opens: *Yom Tov shel Rosh Hashanah she'chal lihyot b'Shabbos* — the *Yom Tov* of *Rosh Hashanah* that falls on *Shabbat*. One might ask why the *Mishnah* adds *Yom Tov shel* — why not simply say *Rosh Hashanah she'chal lihyot b'Shabbos*? For *Sukkot* and *Pesach*, the qualifier *Yom Tov* distinguishes the *Yom Tov* day from *Chol HaMoed*; but *Rosh Hashanah* has no *Chol HaMoed*, so the phrase seems redundant. It may simply be a stylistic parallel to the formula used for the other *yamim tovim*. But it is also possible that it alludes back to the opening *Mishnah* of the *masechet* — *arba'ah rashei shanim hem*, there are four *rosh hashanahs* — and signals that we are now speaking specifically of the *Yom Tov shel Rosh Hashanah*, not of the other three.

This is an appropriate moment to note how strikingly the *masechet* has, in its structure, downplayed the centrality of *Rosh Hashanah* as *Yom Tov*. The opening *Mishnah* treats *Rosh Hashanah* as one of four calendrical markers. The second *Mishnah* mentions it as one of four times the world is judged — *arba'ah perakim bashana ha'olam nidon* — without evoking its *Yom Tov* character. *Kiddush HaChodesh* then dominates the first *perek*, extends through the second, and bleeds into the third. Even the third *perek*, when it finally addresses *Rosh Hashanah* practices, does so without naming *Rosh Hashanah* explicitly — it simply says *kol hashofarot kesherim*. The Torah itself never calls this day *Rosh Hashanah*; and one might have expected *Chazal* in this *masechet* specifically to heighten its identity as *Yom HaDin*. Instead, this *Mishnah* is effectively the first place in the entire *masechet* where *Rosh Hashanah* is addressed squarely as a *Yom Tov*.

### Temple vs. Outside

The *Mishnah* states: *ba'Mikdash hayu tokin, aval lo ba'medina* — in the *Mikdash* they would blow the *shofar* on *Shabbat*, but not outside. What "outside" means requires some interpretation: it could mean outside the *Mikdash* compound within *Yerushalayim*, or it could mean outside *Yerushalayim* entirely. Given that the *Mishnah* later indicates that *Yerushalayim* had a wider radius for permissible blowing than *Yavneh*, the more likely reading is that *ba'medina* refers to places outside of *Yerushalayim*.

### Rabban Yochanan's Edict

After the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*: *hiskin Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai yihyu tokin b'chol makom sheyesh bo Beis Din* — *Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai* enacted that they would blow wherever there was a *Beis Din*. It is worth noting that the *Mishnah* does not frame this as *zecher laMikdash*, a commemoration of *Mikdash* practice. The *Mishnah* simply states that the practice was continued in the presence of a *Beis Din*, without characterizing it as memorial. Whether that framing is implied will be revisited in the *Gemara*.

### Rabbi Elazar Dispute

*Rabbi Elazar* disputes the breadth of *Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai's* enactment: *lo hiskin Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai ela be'Yavne bilvad* — the enactment applied only to *Yavneh*, the central *Beis Din* and the seat of Jewish leadership after the *Churban*, not to every *Beis Din* everywhere. The *Chachamim* respond: *echad Yavne v'echad kol makom sheyesh bo Beis Din* — whether *Yavneh* or any place with a *Beis Din*, the enactment applies equally.

### Jerusalem Advantage

Beyond the dispute between *Rabbi Elazar* and the *Chachamim*, the *Mishnah* adds: *v'od zos hayisa Yerushalayim yesira al Yavne* — *Yerushalayim* had an additional advantage over *Yavneh*. Any city in the environs of *Yerushalayim* — one that could see *Yerushalayim*, could hear its *shofar*, and was close enough that its inhabitants could come — they too would blow on *Shabbat*. In *Yavneh*, by contrast, blowing was restricted to those immediately present at the *Beis Din* itself. *Yerushalayim's* gravitational pull thus extended the permissibility of *Shabbat* blowing outward to its surrounding towns in a way that *Yavneh's* authority did not.

---

## Shofar on Shabbat Problem

### Verses Reconciliation

The *Gemara* now asks the foundational question: *minan hanei milei* — what is the source for the idea that blowing *shofar* on *Shabbat* is problematic at all? *Levi bar Lachma* citing *Rabbi Chama bar Chanina* offers the following: one verse says *shabbason zichron teruah* — a day of rest, a *remembrance* of blasting — implying that on this day there is only a memorial of the blasts, not actual blasting. Another verse says *yom teruah yihyeh lakhem* — it shall be for you a day of actual blasts. *Lo kashya* — there is no contradiction: the verse referring to remembrance applies when *Rosh Hashanah* falls on *Shabbat*, while the verse of actual blasting applies when *Rosh Hashanah* falls on a weekday. The two verses thus encode a biblical distinction between *Rosh Hashanah* on *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashanah* during the week.

### Rava's Logic

*Rava* challenges this directly: *im mid'Oraisa* — if the prohibition is biblical, *hi b'Mikdash heichi takinan* — how could they blow in the *Mikdash* at all? If the Torah itself prohibits blowing on *Shabbat*, no rabbinic or practical consideration can override it in any venue, not even the *Mikdash*. Furthermore, *halav melakha hi?* — and in any case, is blowing *shofar* even a *melakha*? *D'tana d'vei Shmuel*: the school of *Shmuel* teaches from the verse *kol melekhes avoda lo ta'asu* that blowing the *shofar* (*tkias shofar*) and removing baked bread from the walls of an oven (*ridyat hapas*) are excluded from the category of prohibited *melakha* — they are highly skilled acts (*chokhma*) but not *melakha* in the halachic sense. If blowing *shofar* is not *melakha*, there would be no biblical basis for its prohibition on *Shabbat* to begin with — and therefore no need for a verse to exclude it.

### Carrying Concern

*Rava* therefore offers a different resolution: *mid'Oraisa mishra sharei* — biblically, blowing *shofar* on *Rosh Hashanah Shabbat* is entirely permitted. The prohibition is *derabbanan*. *Rabba* explains the rabbinic reasoning: *hakol chayavin bitkias shofar v'ein hakol beki'im bitkias shofar* — everyone is obligated in *tkias shofar*, but not everyone knows how to blow it. *V'im yitlenu b'yado v'yeilekh etzel baki lilmod, v'ya'avirenu arba amos b'reshus harabim* — one would take the *shofar* in hand and carry it to an expert to learn how to blow it, and in doing so would carry it four *amot* in a *reshus harabim*, violating *Shabbat*. To prevent this from happening, the Rabbis decreed that *shofar* is not blown on *Shabbat* — a protective *gezeirah* against the likely transgression of carrying.

### Lulav & Megillah

*Rabba* extends this same rationale to account for two other *mitzvot* that are similarly not performed on *Shabbat*: *v'hainu ta'ama d'lulav v'hainu ta'ama d'megilla* — the same concern underlies the rabbinic prohibition against taking the *lulav* and reading the *megillah* on *Shabbat*. In each case, the worry is that people will carry the object — *lulav*, *megillah*, *shofar* — to an expert, and the fear of that *Shabbat* violation leads the Rabbis to prohibit the *mitzvah* performance entirely on *Shabbat*.

### Mikdash Exemption

The rabbinic protective decree does not apply in the *Beis HaMikdash*. This is a broader principle: the Rabbis did not extend their protective *gezerot* into the *Mikdash* context. Therefore, the *Mikdash* continued to blow even on *Shabbat*, not because of a biblical privilege but because the rabbinic *gezeirah* was inapplicable there.

### Yerushalmi View

The *Yerushalmi* takes a different approach. It does not reject the biblical reading offered at the outset of the *Gemara's* discussion. Rather, the *Yerushalmi* appears to maintain that there genuinely is a biblical distinction between *Rosh Hashanah* on *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashanah* on a weekday — that the two verses do in fact encode a real biblical differentiation — and it engages directly with that distinction rather than resolving it away in favor of a purely rabbinic explanation.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 31

## Tamid Service Structure

### Morning Tamid

The *daf* before us is 31b, picking up approximately fourteen lines from the bottom of the page with the word *mizeh*. The *mishnah* had established that once — when witnesses had not arrived on *Rosh Hashanah* — the *Levi'im* said the wrong *shira* at the afternoon *tamid*. As a result, the Rabbis instituted a *takana* not to accept witnesses after *mincha* time, so that if they had not arrived by then, everyone would know that the day would not be sanctified.
