Even so, people refrained from *melacha* for the remainder of the day, so that the day would not be treated lightly in subsequent years — the concept of *kedusha achat* — though that is not our present focus.

Before proceeding, it is worth noting that with this *mishnah*, we have established that the topic of *Kiddush HaChodesh* appears in every single *perek* of *Rosh Hashanah*: it concluded the first *perek*, ran through the entirety of the second, opened the third (*ra'u beit din v'chol Yisrael*), and now in the fourth *perek* it resurfaces again. This is almost certainly not coincidental. Calendar control was one of the central points of contention between the *Perushim* and the *Tzedukim*, and whoever controlled the calendar controlled the entire liturgical life of the community. The repeated prominence of *Kiddush HaChodesh* throughout the tractate reflects how high the stakes were.

The *Gemara* opens this passage with a challenge from Rav Acha bar Huna. The *baraita* he cites describes precisely what would be done with the *shir shel yom* — the daily psalm — on *Rosh Hashanah*. At the morning *tamid*, when witnesses had almost never yet arrived to testify to the new moon, the practice was to recite the ordinary *shir shel yom* for that day of the week, exactly as recorded in our *siddur* for each weekday. The *yom tov* identity of *Rosh Hashanah* was not yet reflected in the morning *tamid*.

### Musaf Service

Once witnesses arrived and it became clear that the day was indeed *Rosh Hashanah*, a *musaf* offering would be brought, and the *shir* sung at *musaf* was *Harninu l'Elohim uzenu* — the opening of Psalm 81. The association is evident: the *mizmor* contains the verse *tik'u vachodesh shofar bakese l'yom chagenu ki chok l'Yisrael hu mishpat l'Elohei Yaakov* — "Blow the *shofar* at the new moon, at the appointed time for our festival, for it is a statute for Israel, a judgment of the God of Jacob." This psalm was the fixed *shir* for *musaf* on *Rosh Hashanah*.

### Afternoon Tamid

At the afternoon *tamid*, the *shir* recited was *Kol Hashem yachil midbar* — Psalm 29. The running theme of that psalm is the voice of God reverberating through all of creation: *kol Hashem bakoach, kol Hashem behadar, kol Hashem shover arazim* — the voice of God in power, in splendor, shattering cedars. *Rashi* adds that it evokes *zechut kol shofar shel matan Torah* — the merit of the *shofar*'s voice at Sinai, the mountain trembling as all of nature trembles before the divine voice. The thematic connection to *Rosh Hashanah* is thus twofold: the motif of *kol* and *teruah*, and perhaps even an echo of *ma'aseh bereshit* imagery, the sound of God causing all creation to shudder.

### Thursday Rosh Hashanah

A more complex situation arises when *Rosh Hashanah* falls on Thursday — which does occur in our calendar, and is precisely why one can encounter a three-day *yom tov* sequence in *Tishrei*. The difficulty is that the regular *shir shel yom* for Thursday is *Harninu l'Elohim uzenu* — the very same psalm designated as the fixed *shir* for *musaf* on *Rosh Hashanah*. If that psalm is recited at *shacharit* as the ordinary weekday *shir*, what is there left to say at *musaf*?

The *baraita* resolves this by dividing Psalm 81 into two halves. The *musaf* retains the first half — the section containing *tik'u vachodesh shofar* — which is the essential *Rosh Hashanah* *shir* and therefore must remain fixed at *musaf*. The *shacharit* then uses the second half of the psalm, beginning *hasiroti misevel shichmo* — "I removed the burden from his shoulder" — which speaks of *Yosef* going out over the land of Egypt, a resonance with *Rosh Hashanah* in a different register: the tradition that *Yosef* was released from prison on *Rosh Hashanah*, as discussed in the first *perek*. So in the morning one recites the second half, concerning *Yosef's* liberation; at *musaf* one recites the first half, concerning the *shofar* blast of the new moon.

This, of course, presupposes that one knows by *shacharit* that it is *Rosh Hashanah*. A student raises the pointed question: how could one know by the time of the morning *tamid*, given that the court would not have been examining witnesses before sunrise? The answer is that in practice one almost never would know at that point — and that is precisely the point. The default practice was always to say the ordinary *shir shel yom* at *shacharit* even on *Rosh Hashanah*, since the witnesses would virtually never arrive that early. The division of the psalm into two halves applies when one happens to know in advance, or when witnesses are processed with exceptional speed. The *baraita* addresses the case where witnesses arrive after *shacharit* has already concluded: *ve-im ba'u eidim achar tamid shel shachar* — if witnesses came after the morning *tamid*, then at *musaf* one says *Harninu* again, even though it was already said at *shacharit*. The *baraita* explicitly permits this repetition: *af al pi shechozer v'chofla b'musaf*.

### Pre-Takana Practice

The *Gemara* now uses this case to address a question left open from the *mishnah*: in the period before the *takana*, when witnesses had not yet arrived at *mincha* time and there was genuine uncertainty about whether the day was *Rosh Hashanah*, did the *Levi'im* recite nothing, or did they say the ordinary weekday *shir shel yom*?

The *Gemara* proposes that an inference can be drawn from the Thursday scenario. If when one does not yet know at *shacharit*, one says the ordinary weekday *shir shel yom*, this explains how the situation of *af al pi shechozeil v'chofla b'musaf* can arise at all: one recited the ordinary Thursday *shir* at *shacharit* not knowing it was *Rosh Hashanah*, then witnesses arrived, and so one repeated *Harninu* at *musaf*. This implies that when one does not know, one says the weekday *shir* — which would resolve our question about *mincha*.

The *Gemara* deflects this inference: *shani hatam de-shir de-yoma hu* — that case is different, because saying the ordinary weekday *shir* at *shacharit* was entirely standard practice even on days when one *did* know it was *Rosh Hashanah*. The weekday *shir shel yom* was always the norm at the morning *tamid* on *Rosh Hashanah*, regardless of one's knowledge. So there is no difficulty in saying it when one does not yet know; it is what one would say anyway. At *mincha*, however, the situation is the reverse: on any *Rosh Hashanah* where one knew it was the holiday, one would never say the weekday *shir shel yom* at *mincha*. Accordingly, when there was uncertainty at *mincha* time, one might indeed say nothing rather than something categorically inappropriate. The inference thus fails: the two contexts are not parallel.

---

## Weekly Shir Shel Yom

### Sunday–Friday Shir

The *Gemara* now pivots from the specific *Rosh Hashanah* practice to the broader question of what was said as the *shir shel yom* throughout the week in the *Beit HaMikdash*. A *baraita* is cited: *Rabbi Yehuda omer mishum Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Akiva — and it provides the foundation for the *shir shel yom* as preserved in our *siddur* to this day, parallel to a *mishnah* in *Tamid*.

On the first day, Sunday, they would say *Lashem ha'aretz umlo'ah* — Psalm 24 — because God *kanah v'hikna v'shalit b'olamo*: he acquired the world, transferred dominion to mankind, and ruled over it all.

On the second day, Monday, they said *Gadol Hashem u'mehulal me'od* — Psalm 48 — because God *chilek ma'asav umalach aleihem*: he divided his creations — splitting the waters above from the waters below on the second day — and ruled over them. *Rashi* explains the connection via the end of that psalm, *be'elokeinu har kodsho*, the holy mountain of God — the separation of the firmament from the waters creates a domain, as it were, from which God rules.

On the third day, Tuesday, they said *Elokim nitzav b'adat El* — Psalm 82 — because God revealed the land and established it for habitation: *shegila eretz b'chochmato v'hichin tevel la'adato*. The language is somewhat poetic, and one senses a liturgical resonance in these explanations themselves.

On the fourth day, Wednesday, they said *El nekamot Hashem* — Psalm 94 — because that was the day the luminaries were created, and God will ultimately exact punishment from those who worship them. It is striking that what was created to provide light and warmth is filtered here through the lens of *avodah zarah* — idolatry — and that the *shir* for the day of creation of the sun and moon speaks of divine vengeance against those who worship them. This is reinforced by the verse in *Devarim*: *asher chalak Hashem Elokecha otam l'chol ha'amim asher tachat kol hashamayim* — which the tradition reads as God apportioning the celestial bodies to the nations, as an implicit warning.

On the fifth day, Thursday, they said *Harninu l'Elohim uzenu* — Psalm 81 — because God created birds and fish to praise his name: *shebara ofot v'dagim leshabeach lishmo*. The connection is somewhat loose — many psalms speak more explicitly of praising God through the beauty and diversity of nature — and the lengthy reference in the psalm itself to *edut biYosef samo b'tzeto al eretz Mitzrayim* seems remote from the theme of creation's fifth day. The *Gemara* does not resolve this, and one is left noting that the selection is not always a perfect thematic match.

On the sixth day, Friday, they said *Hashem malach ge'ut lavesh* — Psalm 93 — because God completed his work and ruled over it: *shegamar melachto umalach aleihem*. With the creation of human beings, there is now a kingdom over which to reign.

### Shabbat Shir

On the seventh day, *Shabbat*, they said *Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbat* — Psalm 92 — which is self-evidently appropriate. However, the explanation given reframes it rather strikingly: *l'yom shekulo Shabbat*, for a day that will be entirely *Shabbat*, namely the seventh millennium of history, when the world will cease to exist entirely — a day of complete cessation, modeled on the seventh day of creation.

At this point Rav Nechemia raises an objection: *mah ra'u chachamim l'chalek bein ha'perakim halalu*? Why does the explanation for *Shabbat* shift from creation-past to eschatology-future, when all the preceding days were anchored in what God did at creation? Why not simply say: on *Shabbat*, God rested — *al shem sheshavat*? The answer is that what is being debated here reflects a disagreement with the position of Rav Kattina.

### World Duration Debate

Rav Kattina teaches: *shita alfei shenei havei alma, v'chad charuv* — the world will exist for 6,000 years, and one millennium it will be destroyed. The proof-text is *v'nisgav Hashem levado bayom hahu* — God alone will be exalted on that day — and a divine "day" equals a thousand years. On this view, *mizmor shir l'yom haShabbat* refers forward to that single millennium of destruction, which parallels the seventh day of rest.

Abaye disagrees: *trei charuv* — the world will be destroyed for two millennia. His source is *yechayenu miyomayim* — after two days he will revive us — understanding the *techiyat hameitim* as occurring after a two-thousand-year hiatus. On Abaye's view, the millennium of Psalm 92 cannot refer to the future destruction (which lasts two millennia, not one), and the *shir* must be understood as referring to the *Shabbat* of creation in the past. Thus the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rav Nechemia maps onto the dispute between Abaye and Rav Kattina: those who read the future into the *shir* follow Rav Kattina's schema of a single millennium of destruction; those who read the past follow Abaye.

One might ask why it would be appropriate to sing about a period when the world no longer exists, when there are no human beings and no history — a "day" of cosmic emptiness. The answer is not entirely clear. *Shabbat* as *me'ein olam haba* typically refers to something spiritually elevated and living, not to the silence of a destroyed cosmos. Nor does the connection between the first six days and creation obviously demand that the seventh day gesture toward destruction rather than divine rest. The *Ramban* in *Bereishit* develops the idea that each millennium of history models a day of creation, tracing the parallels across all six thousand years — and that broader framework is the backdrop for this entire discussion.

---

## Shabbat Services

### Musaf Ha'azinu

Having established the *shir shel yom* for each weekday and the morning *tamid* of *Shabbat*, the *Gemara* turns to the *musaf* of *Shabbat*. Rav Chanan bar Rava says in the name of Rav: the *shir* at *musaf* on *Shabbat* followed the mnemonic *HaZi"V La"Kh* — standing for the opening words of six sections of *Ha'azinu* (Deuteronomy 32). The six divisions are: *Ha'azinu hashamayim* (the opening), *Zechar yemot olam*, *Yarkivehu al bamotei aretz*, *Vayar Hashem vayina'atz*, *Lulei ka'as oyev agur*, and *Ki yadin Hashem amo*. The first four sections comprise six verses each; the final two are eight verses each.

Rav Chanan bar Rava adds that this same division governs the *aliyot* when *Ha'azinu* is read as the weekly Torah portion in the synagogue — *kederach shechalukim kan kach chalukim b'veit haknesset*.

It is admittedly somewhat puzzling that *Ha'azinu* — a poem of rebuke, warning, national sin, and the specter of divine retribution — would be the *shir* of *musaf* on *Shabbat*. The poem is not, by any measure, uplifting in the conventional sense. Yet it is one of the great *shirot* of the *Torah*, and as we will see, the overall plan was to incorporate all the *shirot* of the *Torah* into the Shabbat services.

### Mincha Songs

Rabbi Yochanan teaches that at *mincha* on *Shabbat* — the afternoon *tamid* — they would say *az yashir Moshe* (the *Shirat Hayam*, Exodus 15), followed by *mi kamocha* (the second half of that same *shira*), and then *az yashir* from the *shira* of the well, *ali be'er enu lah* (Numbers 21). Combined with *Ha'azinu* at *musaf*, the result is that between *musaf* and *mincha* on *Shabbat*, all of the *shirot* of the *Torah* are recited: *Ha'azinu*, *Az Yashir*, and *Ali Be'er*. The systematic completeness of this arrangement helps explain why *Ha'azinu* was selected for *musaf* despite its sobering tone — it is part of a comprehensive program to encompass all the *Torah's* songs on the day of *Shabbat*.

### Cycle or Complete

A question is raised: *hani kulhu b'chad shabta amrinhu* — are all six sections of *Ha'azinu* recited on a single *Shabbat* (with distinct musical breaks between them), or does each *Shabbat* receive one section, cycling through the six over the course of six weeks? Similarly for the *mincha shirim*.

The *Gemara* resolves the question from a *baraita* in which Rabbi Yosi states that by the time the *musaf* has gone through one cycle, the afternoon *tamid* has gone through two. This clearly implies a rotating schedule: one section per *Shabbat*. After six weeks one completes one cycle of *Ha'azinu* at *musaf*, and after three weeks one completes one cycle of the *mincha shirim* — hence two cycles of the *mincha shirim* for every one cycle of *Ha'azinu*.

This is rather startling in its implications. On any given *Shabbat*, the section of *Ha'azinu* assigned to *musaf* might be something as stark as *vayar Hashem vayana'atz mikinas banav uvnotav vayomer astira panai mehem* — God saw and was provoked by his sons and daughters, and said, I will hide my face from them. To recite just a fragment of *Ha'azinu*, stripped of even the limited consolation that comes at the poem's conclusion, seems deeply unusual as a *musaf shir* on *Shabbat*. Yet the *halakha* appears to accept precisely this.

---

## Shechina's Exile

### Ten Journeys

The *Gemara* now shifts its frame entirely. Having discussed the *shir shel yom* in the context of the *Beit HaMikdash*, and with *Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's* role in the post-*churban* order on the horizon, the *Gemara* offers a remarkable teaching. Rav Yehuda bar Idi says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *eser masaot nasa Shechina* — the *Shechina* moved through ten stages of departure from the *Beit HaMikdash* at the time of the *churban*, and this is established from verses. In parallel — *uchnegdam galta Sanhedrin* — the *Sanhedrin* went into exile from its seat in the *Beit HaMikdash*, and this is known from tradition.

The ten journeys of the *Shechina* are as follows. First, from the *kaporet* — the cover of the *aron* — to the *keruvim*: from the place between the wings where the divine voice would speak (as in *v'noadeti l'cha sham v'dibarti itcha me'al hakaporet*) to atop one of the large freestanding *keruv* statues that stood in the *Heikhal* of Solomon's Temple. Second, from one *keruv* to the other. Third, from the *keruvim* to the threshold of the *Heikhal* — the transition point between the inner sanctuary and the entrance hall, the *ulam*. Fourth, from the threshold into the *chatzer*, the open courtyard. Fifth, from the *chatzer* to the *mizbeach*.

At this point the sequence moves upward and outward. Sixth, from the *mizbeach* to the roof. Seventh, from the roof to the surrounding wall. There is some uncertainty in the text here — *Rashi's* reading has the *Shechina* going to the roof of the *Heikhal*, which does create a slight impression of doubling back; the *Gra* has a somewhat different version. In any case, the trajectory is consistently outward. Eighth, from the wall into the city of Jerusalem. Ninth, from Jerusalem to *Har Hazeitim*, the Mount of Olives, the mountain to the east of the city. Tenth, from the mountain into *Midbar Yehudah*, the wilderness, and from there *altah v'yashvah bimkomah* — it ascended and returned to its place, as Scripture says: *eilech ashuva el mekomi* — I will go and return to my place (Hosea 5:15).

### Verse Sources

The *Gemara* now systematically provides the scriptural basis for each stage of this departure.

The first three stages — *kaporet* to *keruv*, *keruv* to *keruv*, *keruv* to threshold — are supported by two verses. The initial location on the *kaporet* is established from *v'noadeti l'cha sham v'dibarti itcha me'al hakaporet* (Exodus 25:22). The movement to the *keruvim* is implicit in *vayirkav al keruv vayauf* — God rode upon a *keruv* and flew (Psalm 18:11) — though some editions of the text excise this verse because it is not explicitly set in the context of the exile of the *Shechina*. The transition from *keruv* to threshold is from *uchvod Elokei Yisrael naalah me'al hakruv asher hayah alav el miftan habayit* — the glory of the God of Israel lifted from the *keruv* upon which it had rested, to the threshold of the house (Ezekiel 9:3).

It bears noting that these verses are drawn from across a wide span of the biblical corpus. The *Gemara* is not reading a continuous narrative; it is weaving together texts from different contexts to construct this progression. The rabbis understood the various prophetic visions — particularly in *Yechezkel* — as windows into a coherent process of divine withdrawal.

For the stage from threshold to *chatzer*: *vayamalei habayit et he'anan v'hachatzer malah et nogah kvod Hashem* — the house was filled with the cloud and the court was filled with the radiance of God's glory (Ezekiel 10:4). The word *nogah*, radiance or shining, is significant. The *Torah* and prophets frequently describe the *kavod Hashem* as something that shines — a visible luminosity, perceived through the cloud because it is too intense to behold directly. When the texts speak of the *Shechina* departing, they are likely describing the departure of this physical-phenomenological shining as well, not merely an abstract theological absence.

From *chatzer* to *mizbeach*: *va'ere et Hashem nitzav al hamizbeach* — I saw God standing upon the altar (Amos 9:1).

From *mizbeach* to roof: *tov lashevet al pinat gag* — it is better to sit on a corner of the roof (Proverbs 25:24). The verse is read as though God declares: better to ascend to the roof, to remove from this place.

From roof to wall: *hinei Hashem nitzav al chomat anach* — behold, God standing on a wall of *anach* (Amos 7:7).

From wall to city: *kol Hashem la'ir yikra* — the voice of God calls out to the city (Micah 6:9).

From city to *Har Hazeitim*: *vaya'al kevod Hashem me'al toch ha'ir vaya'amod al hahar asher mikedem la'ir* — the glory of God lifted from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain to the east of the city (Ezekiel 11:23).

From the mountain to the wilderness: *tov shevet b'eretz midbar* — better to dwell in a wilderness land (Proverbs 21:19).

And finally the departure from earth to the heavenly realm: *eilech ashuva el mekomi* — I will go and return to my place (Hosea 5:15).

### Six Months Wait

The *Gemara* adds a teaching of Rabbi Yochanan that deepens the pathos of this entire account: *sheshah chodashim nitkavah Shechina l'Yisrael bamidbar* — the *Shechina* waited in the wilderness for six months, *shema yachzeru b'teshuvah* — hoping that Israel would repent, so that it would not have to leave. When *teshuvah* did not come, God declared, as it were: *tipach atzmam* — let their very bones be blasted — as the verse concludes: *v'einei resha'im tichlena umanos avad mihem v'sikvasam mapach nafesh* — the eyes of the wicked will be consumed, escape will be lost to them, and their hope will be the gasping of a soul (Job 11:20).

The image is profoundly moving. The *Torah* itself speaks of God's commitment to dwell *b'toch tumotam* — in the midst of Israel's impurity — the divine decision to remain present even amid human sinfulness. Here that commitment reaches its limit, but even so, the departure is slow, stage by stage, each transition carrying the possibility that things might turn around. Six months of waiting. Ten stages of withdrawal. The *Shechina* is not swept away; it reluctantly retreats, holding on as long as possible before the final departure.

The *Maharsha* notes that the six months corresponds to the period from *Asarah B'Tevet* — when the siege of Jerusalem began — to the *Tisha B'Av* of the following year when the Temple was burned: in fact that is eighteen months, not six, but the six-month interval marks the distance from *Asarah B'Tevet* to the breach of the walls on the ninth of *Tammuz* of the same year.

---

## Sanhedrin's Exile

### Jerusalem Moves

The *Gemara* now describes the parallel exile of the *Sanhedrin*, which is known not from biblical verses but from tradition: *galta Sanhedrin migemara*. The *Sanhedrin* moved from *Lishkat HaGazit* — the Chamber of Hewn Stone within the *azarah* of the *Beit HaMikdash* — to *chanut*, the shops. These were the commercial stalls lining the base of *Har Habayit*, evocative of the *Cardo* corridor in Jerusalem that archaeologists have excavated. From *chanut* they moved further into central Jerusalem proper.

### Post-Churban Moves

After the *churban*, the *Sanhedrin* left Jerusalem for *Yavne* — this is the famous transition effected by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. From *Yavne* they moved to *Usha*, then back to *Yavne*, then back to *Usha* — *Rashi* explains that the *Sanhedrin* followed the *Nasi*, and the *Nasi* — whether Rabban Gamliel or his successors — moved back and forth between the two cities. Thereafter: from *Usha* to *Shefaram*, from *Shefaram* to *Beit Shearim* (where the extensive necropolis excavations have uncovered sarcophagi associated with the house of the *Nasi*), from *Beit Shearim* to *Tzippori*, and finally from *Tzippori* to *Tverya*. The verse cited for the final stage is *v'shachotam me'eretz tedaberi* — brought low from the earth, you will speak — and indeed *Tverya* lies below sea level, the lowest of all these locations.

One should note that calling these movements an "exile" in the same sense as the departure of the *Shechina* is somewhat forced. After leaving Jerusalem, the relocations are not exile in any straightforward sense — the *Sanhedrin* is moving around within the land, following the *Nasi*. The imagery of exile serves primarily to create the structural parallel: as the *Shechina* moved through ten stages and finally departed, so the *Sanhedrin* moved through ten stages and eventually ceased to function as a central body.

There is, however, a deeper parallel that is worth dwelling on. The *churban* of the *Beit Rishon* was associated most prominently with religious sin — *avodah zarah*, *gilluy arayot*, *shefichat damim* — and accordingly what departed was the *Shechina*, the manifest divine presence. The *churban* of the *Beit Sheni* was attributed to *sinat chinam*, and what that phrase seems to capture in the tradition is a catastrophic failure of communal leadership and unity — the *Kamtza and Bar Kamtza* stories in *Gittin*, the inability of the Rabbis to exercise the leadership the moment required. Accordingly, what went into exile in the *Beit Sheni* period was not the *Shechina* but the *Sanhedrin*, the institutional seat of Jewish communal and halachic authority. The parallel is not accidental: each destruction exiled what was most central to the spiritual life of that era.

### Six Exiles

Rabbi Eliezer offers a different count: not ten but six exiles of the *Sanhedrin*. His proof-text is *ki heishach yoshvei marom kiryah nisgavah yashpilena yashpila ad aretz yagi'ena ad afar* — counting the verbs and clauses yields six, not ten. Rabbi Yochanan adds: *umisham atidin l'iga'el* — and from that place they are destined to be redeemed, as Scripture says *hitna'ari mei'afar kumi shvi* — arise, shake off the dust, return to your seat (Isaiah 52:2). Just as the *Shechina*, after its departure, would ultimately return to dwell among Israel in the time of redemption, so too the *Sanhedrin*, after its wandering, would ultimately be restored.

---

## Fixed Court Location

### Takana Established

Returning now to the *Rosh Hashanah* context of *Kiddush HaChodesh*, the *mishnah* records: *amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha*, and yet this additional *takana* was enacted by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. Even if the *rosh beit din* was located elsewhere on any given day, the witnesses for the new moon would not be required to seek him out — they would go only to the fixed location of the *vaad*, the court's regular seat. The practical motivation is clear: if witnesses find the court is in one place one month and somewhere else the next, they will eventually stop making the effort to come at all. The entire system of testimony for *kiddush hachodesh* depends on making the process as predictable and welcoming as possible.

Beyond the practical logic, this *takana* connects to a broader shift we have been observing throughout this *perek*: the move from *Mikdash* to *Torah*, from hierarchy to a somewhat more decentralized form of religious authority. The willingness to say that the *beit din* can function without its head being physically present, that witnesses need only arrive at a fixed location, reflects the same spirit that produced the other *takanot* of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai — building a functioning, sustainable Jewish community in a post-*Mikdash* reality.

### Woman's Case

The *Gemara* now adduces a case study. A certain woman received a summons to appear before *Amemar* in *Nehardea*. On the day appointed, *Amemar* happened to be in *Mechuza*. The woman refused to travel to *Mechuza*, and the court in *Nehardea* wrote a *pticha* — a document placing her in contempt — against her. Rav Ashi challenged *Amemar*: how could you do this? Does our *mishnah* not teach that even if the *rosh beit din* is elsewhere, the witnesses — and by logical extension, litigants — need only go to the fixed location?

### Amemar's Response

*Amemar* replied: *hani mili* — that principle applies in *eidut hachodesh*, testimony for the new moon. In that context, the concern is institutional: if witnesses are sent on a chase after the *rosh beit din*, they will stop coming altogether, undermining the entire system. But here — *abda lova l'ish malva* — the borrower is a slave to the creditor. In a monetary dispute, the debtor is obligated to present herself before the creditor's chosen forum. The lender did the borrower a favor by extending credit; the debtor cannot claim the convenience protections designed to encourage voluntary witnesses to come forward. The policy underlying the *takana* simply does not apply in the same way to ordinary litigation, where the parties are in an adversarial relationship and the creditor has legitimate interests of his own.

---

## Nine Takanot

### Introduction

A *baraita* is cited: the *Kohanim* may not ascend the *duchan* wearing their sandals — this is the practice in the *beit knesset*, corresponding to the practice of going barefoot in the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *Gemara* there explains that if a *kohen* bends down to tie a loose sandal, onlookers might think he is disqualified from *Birkat Kohanim* for some reason. The *baraita* identifies this as one of the nine *takanot* of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.

The nine *takanot* deserve enumeration. Together they represent Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's comprehensive reorganization of Jewish life in the aftermath of the *churban*, and one of their most striking features is how consistently they embrace the new reality rather than attempting to preserve the old one. They are not primarily about memorializing the *Mikdash*; they are about building a functioning *Torah*-centered community for the long exile.

### Six in This Chapter

Six of the nine *takanot* appear in this *perek*. They include the five enacted by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai that are recorded in the *mishnayot* of this chapter: blowing *shofar* in *Yavne* even when *Rosh Hashanah* falls on *Shabbat*; taking the *lulav* for all seven days; not eating *chadash* (new grain) on the entire sixteenth of *Nisan* rather than only until *musaf*; accepting witnesses for the new moon after *mincha* time (the original practice that preceded the *takana* we have been discussing); and the rule that witnesses always go to the fixed location of the court regardless of where the *rosh beit din* is. Plus the sixth: the *duchan* without sandals, which the *Gemara* notes is mentioned here even though it is formally at home elsewhere (*sota*).

One might wonder how the sandal *takana* fits within the overarching theme of the others. A suggestion raised in the course of the *shiur* is illuminating: this *takana* places Rabbinic authority squarely over *Kohanim* in their performance of *Birkat Kohanim* outside the *Mikdash*. It is the Rabbis dictating the protocol of *Kohanic* ritual in a decentralized, non-*Mikdash* context — thus reinforcing Rabbinic authority over priestly practice, which is itself a hallmark of the post-*churban* realignment.

### Nisan/Tishrei

The seventh *takana* — the first in the order of the *perakim*, found in the opening chapter — is that after the *churban*, witnesses desecrating *Shabbat* to travel and testify to the new moon would be permitted to do so only for *Nisan* and *Tishrei*: the months that govern *Pesach* and *Rosh Hashanah*/*Yom Kippur*, the pillar festivals whose dates most profoundly affect all of Israel. In the time of the *Mikdash*, precision in the calendar for every month mattered greatly because of the *korbanot* and the Temple calendar. Post-*churban*, the urgency is limited to the months that matter for the community's observance of the great festivals. This *takana* is, again, a perfect expression of the same spirit: recognizing the changed reality and calibrating practice accordingly.

### Convert's Sacrifice

The eighth *takana* concerns the convert's bird-sacrifice obligation. The *baraita* teaches: a convert who undergoes conversion nowadays is required to set aside a *rova* — a quarter-*dinar* — for his *kinim* (bird-offerings), so that when the *Beit HaMikdash* is rebuilt he can complete his conversion process by bringing the obligatory sacrifice. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, however, reports that Rabbi Yochanan already convened a vote and nullified this requirement *mipnei hatakala* — because of the danger of misuse. Money set aside for *hekdesh* in one's home is sanctified; one might inadvertently misappropriate it, incurring *me'ila*.

Beyond the technical concern, the thrust of this ruling is striking. To require the convert to set aside this money is to tell him: your conversion is incomplete; you remain in a kind of suspended state, awaiting the rebuilding of the Temple to finish what you started. The psychological and theological burden of that message — you are a *ger* but not quite fully one — is enormous. Rabbi Yochanan's ruling removes that burden. Do not set aside the money; do not hold onto the idea that your conversion is pending. You are fully a *ger*. Here too, the look is forward, not backward.

### Ninth Takana Debate

The ninth and final *takana* is itself a matter of dispute, debated by Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak — and with that, the *daf* reaches its limit. The resolution of that debate, and the identification of the ninth *takana*, will be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 32

## Ninth Takkanah Debate

### Ninth Takkanah Intro

The daf opens at the bottom of 31b, continuing the discussion of the nine *takkanot* of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. Eight have already been enumerated: six in the current *perek*, one in the previous *perek*, and one concerning a *ger* who converts nowadays and should not set aside money for a *korban* — all of them, in various ways, reflecting the transition away from the *Mikdash*. The identity of the ninth *takkanah* is the subject of a dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak.

### Rav Pappa: Kerem Reva'i

Rav Pappa holds that the ninth *takkanah* concerns *kerem reva'i* — the produce of a vineyard in its fourth year. As taught in the *Mishnah*, *kerem reva'i haya oleh l'Yerushalayim mahalach yom l'chol tzad*: fourth-year fruit was to be brought to Jerusalem and consumed there. Although one could technically redeem the fruit on money even just outside Jerusalem's limits, the Rabbis instituted that within a day's travel of Jerusalem, one must bring the fruit itself, so as to adorn the marketplaces of Jerusalem with produce. The cities marking this boundary were: *Eilat* in the north, *Akravat* in the south, Lud in the west, and the Jordan in the east. Ulla — and some say, Rabba bar bar Ulla, citing Rabbi Yochanan — explains the rationale: *k'dei l'ateir shukei Yerushalayim b'peirot*, so that the markets of Jerusalem would be adorned with fruit.

### Rabbi Eliezer's Concerns

A *braita* illustrates the practical impact of this *takkanah*. Rabbi Eliezer had *kerem reva'i* to the east of Lud, near the village of Kfar Tavi — that is, in the direction of Jerusalem, within the prescribed boundary. Not wishing to bring the fruit himself, he was on the verge of declaring it *hefker* for the poor, hoping they would take it. His students stopped him: *kvar nimnu chaveirecha alav v'hitiruhu* — your colleagues already voted and permitted it, meaning they annulled the original *takkanah*. The reference to "colleagues" (*chaveirim*) is, according to Rav Pappa, a reference to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai himself, who — post-*Churban* — recognized that the purpose of the original enactment no longer applied, Jerusalem being destroyed and under Roman rule, and accordingly annulled it. This fits squarely within the recognized genre of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's *takkanot*: an acceptance of post-*Churban* reality and an adjustment of the law accordingly.

### Rav Nachman: Red String

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak disagrees. He identifies the ninth *takkanah* with the *lashon shel zehorit* — the red string used in the Yom Kippur *avodah* in connection with the *seir l'azazel*. This is, notably, not a post-*Churban* enactment at all, but rather a *takkanah* rooted in the period of the *Beit HaMikdash* and its *korbanot*.

### Red String Stages

A *braita* describes the three stages of this practice. Originally, the red string was tied at the entrance of the *Ulam*, the hallway to the *Heichal*, on the outside. If it turned white after the *korban* was brought, the people would rejoice; if it did not turn white and remained red, they would be anguished, sensing that their sins had not been atoned. This public visibility of the result created distress, so the Rabbis enacted that the string be tied instead on the inside of the doorway — but people would still peer through and look. Finally, the authorities enacted that half the string be tied to the rock at the site where the goat was thrown over and the other half between the horns of the goat itself, entirely removing it from public view. According to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, it was this final stage — concealing the string from public sight — that was the *takkanah* of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.

### Chronological Proof

The *gemara* proceeds to examine why each sage rejects the other's position. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains why he does not follow Rav Pappa: if the one who annulled the *kerem reva'i takkanah* were Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the students would not have said to Rabbi Eliezer "your *chaveirim* annulled it," since Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was not Rabbi Eliezer's colleague but his *rebbe* — a generation above him. The *gemara* responds on behalf of Rav Pappa: since it was the students speaking to Rabbi Eliezer, it would have been disrespectful for them to say "your *rebbe* annulled it," as if invoking a higher authority to override him. As a matter of *derech eretz* they said "colleagues" when they meant the *rebbe*. That is a reasonable resolution.

The more formidable challenge, however, runs in the opposite direction — against Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak. The *gemara* asks: in the days of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, was the red string actually turning white? A *braita* teaches that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai lived 120 years — forty years devoted to business, forty to learning, and forty to teaching. Any act of communal leadership, then, belongs to his final forty years. But a second *braita* teaches that *arba'im shanah kodem shenechrav habayit* — for the forty years preceding the *Churban*, the red string did not turn white; it remained red. And we know from the *Mishnah* that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai made his *takkanot mishcharav habayit* — after the *Churban*. Working backwards: if the *Churban* is year zero, then Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was teaching for the forty years prior, going back no more than thirty-nine years before the *Churban*. But the string had already ceased to turn white forty years before the *Churban*. The entire *takkanah* of the red string — which presupposes that the string *sometimes* turned white and *sometimes* did not — must therefore have been instituted before Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's tenure of leadership. His active role post-dates the period in which the *takkanah* could have been made.

### Resolution: Young Yochan…

The *gemara* offers a resolution: during those forty years that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was a *talmid yoshev lifnei rabo* — a student sitting before his *rebbe* — he was not merely learning independently. He was present in the context of active *halachic* life and occasionally offered a suggestion: *amar milta*, he said something. *V'istaber tameih* — they found it reasonable, *v'karu rabo mishmeih* — and his *rebbe* attributed the ruling to him by name. The analogy is almost reversed from academic convention: rather than the *rebbe* taking credit for the student's insight, the *rebbe* attributed it to the student. So the *takkanah* could technically be ascribed to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai even from his years as a student.

That said, this resolution is clearly a stretch. The *takkanah* of the red string fits none of the recognizable characteristics of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactments: it is not post-*Churban*, it is not a response to the transition away from the *Mikdash*, and it requires a convoluted chronological reconstruction. The primary case for the ninth *takkanah* remains, with greater naturalness, Rav Pappa's position of *kerem reva'i*.

One participant noted the striking correspondence between the 120-year life of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and that of Moshe Rabbeinu — similarly divided into thirds, with the final forty years constituting the period of public leadership. The parallel may be deliberately drawn by *Chazal* to suggest that just as Moshe led the Jewish people through the transformative rupture of leaving *Mitzrayim*, so too Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai guided Israel through the no less radical rupture of the *Churban* — a transition from one mode of national and religious existence to another.

---

## Malchuyos Structure

### Overview of Debate

We turn now to the top of 32a and the *Mishnah* that introduces the liturgical structure of *musaf* on Rosh Hashanah — specifically the placement of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* within the *Shemoneh Esrei*. The *Ba'al HaMaor* holds that *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* are recited in every *tefillah* of *Shemoneh Esrei* on Rosh Hashanah, but the standard ruling, and the assumption of the *gemara*, is that we are speaking exclusively about *musaf*.

The normal structure of *musaf* consists of seven *brachot*: *Avos*, *Gevuros*, *Kedushat Hashem* (culminating in *Ha-El HaKadosh* or *HaMelech HaKadosh*), *Kedushat HaYom* (ending with *Mekadesh HaShabbat v'Yisrael v'HaZmanim*), *Avodah* (*Retzei*), *Modim*, and *Birkat Kohanim* (*Sim Shalom*). To incorporate the three additional *brachot* of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* while maintaining a total of nine rather than ten, two elements must be combined. The dispute is over which ones to combine and where.

### Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri

The *Mishnah* presents the position of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri: *omer Avos u'Gevuros u'Kedushat Hashem v'kolel malchuyos imahem v'eino sokeia* — one recites *Avos*, *Gevuros*, and *Kedushat Hashem*, incorporating *malchuyos* together with them, without sounding the *shofar* at that point. Then, in the center of the *Shemoneh Esrei*, one says *Kedushat HaYom* together with *zichronos* and sounds the *shofar*; then *shofros* with the *shofar*; and finally *Avodah*, *Modim*, and *Birkat Kohanim*. According to this position, *malchuyos* is placed early — subsumed within *Kedushat Hashem* — and the *tekiyot* are sounded only in connection with *zichronos* and *shofros*, both of which fall in the center of the prayer.

### Rabbi Akiva's Objection

Rabbi Akiva objects: *im eino tokeia l'malchuyos lama hu mazkir?* If one is not going to sound the *shofar* with *malchuyos*, why mention *malchuyos* at all? This reflects a clear understanding of the intimate relationship between *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* on the one hand, and the *tekiyot* on the other. One can understand this relationship in either direction: either the *tekiyot* are the vehicle through which the prayers ascend — as the post-*tekiyah* formula *tikabel b'rachamim u'v'ratzon seder shofroteinu* suggests — or conversely, the verbal themes give meaning and content to the *tekiyot*, characterizing what the blasts are about. In either case, Rabbi Akiva insists, the *tekiyot* and the three liturgical themes are inextricably bound together, and to detach the *shofar* from *malchuyos* is to undermine the coherence of the entire structure.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva's own position, then, is: *omer Avos u'Gevuros u'Kedushat Hashem v'kolel malchuyos im Kedushat HaYom v'tokea* — one includes *malchuyos* together with *Kedushat HaYom* and sounds the *shofar* at that point. Then *zichronos* with the *shofar*, then *shofros* with the *shofar*, and then the final three *brachot*. All three themes — *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* — come in the center of the *Shemoneh Esrei*, each accompanied by *tekiyot*, and *malchuyos* is merged with *Kedushat HaYom* rather than with *Kedushat Hashem*.

This is, of course, the position we follow. Its traces are visible throughout the *musaf* liturgy. The *chatimah* of *Kedushat HaYom* in *musaf* reads *Baruch Atah Hashem mekadesh Yisrael v'Yom HaZikaron*, but with the addition of *Melech al kol ha'aretz* — a four-word *malchuyos* phrase that becomes the *chatimah* of *malchuyos* merged with *Kedushat HaYom*. Significantly, this combined *chatimah* is preserved in all the *Shemoneh Esrei* prayers of Rosh Hashanah, not only *musaf*, even in those *tefillos* where the full *piyutim* of *malchuyos* are not recited.

### Gemara's Response

Yet the *gemara* does not simply affirm Rabbi Akiva's stated logic. The *gemara* deflects his rhetorical challenge — *lama hu mazkir?* — by responding that *malchuyos* is said because *the Torah requires it*: *Rachmana amar*. The obligation to recite *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* exists independently of any connection to the *tekiyot*; they are a required liturgical element in their own right. The *gemara* thus strips Rabbi Akiva's argument of its full force. Rather than reading him as making a fundamental claim about the inseparability of these themes from the *shofar*, the *gemara* reduces his point to something more modest: if you are not sounding the *shofar* with *malchuyos*, at least say nine *pesukim* rather than ten — *shinui*, do something to mark the difference. The argument becomes considerably weaker when interpreted this way. The *gemara* clearly understands that *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* can in principle function as an independent liturgical form, decoupled from the *tekiyot*.

### Conceptual Analysis

This debate points toward a deeper question about the meaning of Rosh Hashanah itself. The position of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, in pushing *malchuyos* to an earlier, less central position and withholding the *tekiyah* from it, implicitly decentralizes *malchuyos* as a theme and places *zichronos* and *shofros* at the center. This may reflect a conception of Rosh Hashanah primarily as a *yom hadin* — a day of judgment. *Zichronos* (God's remembrance of His creatures) and *shofros* (the *shofar* as a cry before the King) are the operative themes; *malchuyos* provides necessary background context — God as King explains why there is judgment — but it is not the focus.

Rabbi Akiva's position, by contrast, places all three themes in the center with equal weight, each receiving its own *tekiyah*. This allows *malchuyos* to function as a genuinely central theme, not merely a backdrop. One can read Rosh Hashanah as a *yom shel malchus* — a day of proclaiming God's kingship over creation — with *zichronos* and *shofros* as expressions of that sovereignty rather than as the primary substance of the day.

Interestingly, our received liturgy reflects traces of both positions. The *ub'chen* paragraphs — *ub'chen ten pachdecha*, *ub'chen ten kavod*, *ub'chen tzadikim*, culminating in *v'timloch Atah Hashem levadecha* — which appear after *Gevuros* and before *Kedushat Hashem*, suggest a *malchuyos*-themed liturgy associated with *Kedushat Hashem* that may preserve a strand of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's approach. The *chatimah* of *HaMelech HaKadosh* serves as a *malchuyos* conclusion to this section. And the *chatimah* of *Melech al kol ha'aretz* is preserved in all the *tefillos* of Rosh Hashanah even outside of *musaf*, as a remnant of the *malchuyos* theme integrated into *Kedushat HaYom*. In practice, as often observed in *halachic* liturgical disputes, both positions leave their mark on the final *nusach*.

---

## Biblical Sources

### Rabbi Eliezer Sources

The *gemara* now asks: from where do we derive that one recites *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* at all? A *braita* presents the view of Rabbi Eliezer, who derives all three from a single verse in Leviticus 23: *shabbaton zichron teruah mikra kodesh*. He reads *shabbaton* as a reference to *Kedushat HaYom* — the sanctity of the day as expressed in the liturgy. *Zichron* yields *zichronos*. *Teruah* yields *shofros*. And the concluding phrase *mikra kodesh* is understood as an instruction to sanctify the day through the prohibition of *melacha*.

The notable absence from Rabbi Eliezer's derivation is *malchuyos*. This is consistent with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's framework — where *malchuyos* occupies an earlier, less central position — rather than Rabbi Akiva's. The verse as Rabbi Eliezer reads it maps onto precisely the liturgical order Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri prescribes: *Kedushat HaYom*, *zichronos*, *shofros*, with *malchuyos* elsewhere.

### Rabbi Akiva Reading

Rabbi Akiva offers a minor textual objection to Rabbi Eliezer's reading: why did he place the *mikra kodesh* prohibition of *melacha* at the end, when the word *shabbaton* — which he uses for *Kedushat HaYom* — appears first in the verse? One should begin by noting that *shabbaton* refers to the prohibition of *melacha*, and then proceed to the liturgical themes of *zichron* and *teruah*. Rabbi Akiva therefore reads the verse as: *shabbaton* — sanctify the day by refraining from *melacha*; *zichron* — *zichronos*; *teruah* — *shofros*; *mikra kodesh* — *Kedushat HaYom*. The substantive outcome is largely the same, with *zichronos* and *shofros* still derived from *zichron teruah*, but Rabbi Akiva places *Kedushat HaYom* at the end — a curious inversion, given that in his own liturgical arrangement, *Kedushat HaYom* comes before *zichronos* and *shofros*.

### Rabbi Yosi's Derivation

On the question of *malchuyos*, the *gemara* presents a *braita* in which Rabbi Yosi bar Yehudah offers an alternative derivation. He argues that *malchuyos* need not be derived from the phrase *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* adjacent to the Rosh Hashanah passage in Leviticus (as *Rebbi* suggests elsewhere). Rather, a derivation is available from the passage in Numbers 10 concerning the *chatzotzros* — the silver trumpets. The verse reads: *u'tekatem b'chatzotzros al olosaychem v'al zivchei shalmaychem vehayu lachem le'zicharon lifnei Elokeichem Ani Hashem Elokeichem*. From this passage, *u'tekatem b'chatzotzros* yields *shofros* (by loose association of blasts); *vehayu lachem le'zicharon* yields *zichronos*; and *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* yields *malchuyos*.

### Binyan Av Logic

What makes Rabbi Yosi's derivation structurally significant — and this is where the *gemara* identifies a *binyan av* — is not simply that it provides a source for *malchuyos*, but that it wraps all three themes together in a single passage, and crucially, together with *tekiyah*. The verse in Numbers 10 links *teki'at chatzotzros*, *zichronos*, and *malchuyos* in one breath. By contrast, the derivation from Leviticus 23 (*Ani Hashem Elokeichem u'vachodesh hashvi'i*) places *malchuyos* prior to the verse describing *shabbaton zichron teruah*, thereby separating it from *zichronos* and *shofros* and from the *tekiyah*.

The Numbers passage, in other words, supports precisely the Rabbi Akiva position: all three themes come together, all three are associated with *tekiyah*, and *malchuyos* is not pushed earlier and removed from center stage. As Rashi in his commentary on the Torah emphasizes, it is the *chatzotzros* passage that provides the textual basis for the entire structure of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* as a unified liturgical category. The *binyan av* principle then extends: wherever *zichronos* appear in the liturgy, *malchuyos* accompanies them — they are not separable themes.

This also clarifies the underlying logic of the earlier dispute. The derivation that places *malchuyos* adjacent to *Kedushat Hashem* (from *Ani Hashem Elokeichem u'vachodesh hashvi'i*) has *malchuyos* introduced before the characterization of the day in *shabbaton zichron teruah*, leaving *tekiyah* disconnected from *malchuyos*. The derivation from the *chatzotzros* passage has all three bound together with *teki'ah* from the outset. The textual choices, in other words, are not merely academic; they directly generate the competing liturgical arrangements.

---

## Yavneh to Usha

### Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka

The *gemara* reports an episode that confirms which position became normative. When the *Beit Din* sanctified Rosh Hashanah in Usha, Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka descended before the *amud* and led the prayer in the manner of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri — incorporating *malchuyos* with *Kedushat Hashem*, away from the center and without *tekiyah*.

### Yavneh Practice

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel responded immediately: *lo hayu nohagin ken b'Yavneh* — this is not how things were done in Yavneh. Whatever the theoretical debate between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva, the practice that had been established in Yavneh did not follow Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's arrangement.

### Rabbi Akiva Adopted

The following year — or, as Rav Chisda clarifies, *l'yom sheni l'shanah haba'ah*, on a different occasion — Rabbi Chanina, son of Rabbi Yose HaGlili, descended and led the prayer in the manner of Rabbi Akiva, placing *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* in the center, each accompanied by *tekiyot*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel affirmed: *kach hayu nohagin b'Yavneh* — that is precisely how it was done in Yavneh. This confirmed that the practice follows Rabbi Akiva.

The *gemara* notes incidentally that these are not merely hypothetical positions argued in the study hall. Different communities maintained different liturgical traditions, and the Rabbis were working to determine which tradition to make authoritative. The survival of variant traditions — visible even in the Cairo *Genizah* — reflects the genuine diversity of early liturgical practice.

### Shimon's Position

A subtlety requires clarification. The *gemara* raises the question: does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel hold entirely like Rabbi Akiva? On one point he does not. Rabbi Akiva holds that *Kedushat HaYom* comes as the fourth *bracha* — immediately after *Kedushat Hashem* — because *mah matzinu b'chol makom bi-revias*, wherever the sanctity of the day is mentioned it comes in the fourth *bracha*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, by contrast, holds like the position stated elsewhere — *mah matzinu b'chol makom ba'emtza*, the sanctity of the day always falls in the center of the *Shemoneh Esrei*. He therefore places *Kedushat HaYom* with *zichronos* (the middle of the three *malchuyos-zichronos-shofros* grouping) rather than with *malchuyos*. As Rabbi Zeira clarifies, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel agrees with Rabbi Akiva that *malchuyos* belongs in the center of the *Shemoneh Esrei* and that *tekiyot* accompany all three themes; his disagreement concerns only where *Kedushat HaYom* is attached within that center group.

This question of placement is not merely technical. If *Kedushat HaYom* is attached to *malchuyos*, the *chatimah* — *Mekadesh Yisrael v'Yom HaZikaron* — frames the day primarily as a *yom shel malchus*. If it is attached to *zichronos*, the same *chatimah* frames it primarily as a *yom hadin* focused on divine remembrance. Notably, the final *nusach* — *Baruch Atah Hashem Melech al kol ha'aretz mekadesh Yisrael v'Yom HaZikaron* — manages to fold both emphases into a single *chatimah*: the kingship language of *malchuyos* together with the *Yom HaZikaron* of *zichronos*.

---

## Number of Verses

### Ten Verses Required

The *Mishnah* states: *ein pochtin me'asarah malchuyos me'asarah zichronos me'asarah shofros* — one must not recite fewer than ten *malchuyos*, ten *zichronos*, and ten *shofros*. The *gemara* asks what the ten *malchuyos* correspond to. Rabbi Levi answers: *k'neged asarah hillulim she'amar David b'sefer Tehillim* — the ten praises of God found in Psalm 150, *halleluhu b'teka shofar*. There the word *hallelu* appears in connection with various musical instruments, and counting yields ten instances — hence ten *malchuyos*, consonant with the theme of praising the divine king. Rabbi Yochanan offers a different correspondence: the ten *malchuyos* correspond to the *asarah ma'amarot* — the ten utterances by which the world was created — connecting the theme of God's kingship on Rosh Hashanah directly to the creation of the world.

### Rabbi Yochanan: Three Ve…

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's lenient position is then stated: *im amar shalosh shalosh mi-kullan yatza* — if one recites three from each category, one has fulfilled the obligation.

### Debate Clarified

The *gemara* examines what "three from each category" means. One possibility is that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri means three *pesukim* from *Torah*, three from *Nevi'im*, and three from *Ketuvim* — for each of the three liturgical themes — yielding nine *pesukim* per theme. If so, the debate is between the *Tanna Kamma*'s requirement of ten and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position of nine, a modest dispute of one *pasuk*. Alternatively, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri may mean one *pasuk* from *Torah*, one from *Nevi'im*, and one from *Ketuvim* — three *pesukim* total per theme, one from each of the three sections of *Tanach*. On this reading the debate between ten and three is substantial.

### Seven Verses Option

A *braita* introduces a further position: *ein pochtin me'asarah malchuyos me'asarah zichronos me'asarah shofros; v'im amar sheva mi-kullan yatza, kenegid shiva reki'im* — ten is the ideal, but *be-diavad* seven suffices, corresponding to the seven firmaments. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's own formulation in this *braita* is: *ha-poches lo yifchos mi-sheva* — one should not recite fewer than seven; *v'im amar shalosh mi-kullan yatza, kenegid Torah Nevi'im v'Kesuvim*. The final phrase clarifies decisively that when he speaks of "three," he means one *pasuk* from each of the three sections of *Tanach* — not three *pesukim* from each section. The debate, then, is indeed between ten and three, with seven as a middle position.

### Rav Huna's Ruling

Rav Huna rules in the name of Shmuel: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's lenient position, meaning that even *be-diavad*, three *pesukim* per theme — one from *Torah*, one from *Nevi'im*, one from *Ketuvim* — constitutes a valid fulfillment.

---

## Verse Selection Rules

### Excluding Puranus

Once it is established how many *pesukim* are required, the *gemara* turns to which *pesukim* may and may not be selected. The first rule: *ein mazkirin* — one does not recite *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, or *shofros* that relate to *puranus* — suffering and punishment. The liturgy of Rosh Hashanah is oriented toward hope and redemption, and evoking divine wrath directed at Israel is inappropriate on this day.

### Torah-Ketuvim-Nevi'im

The prescribed order for the *pesukim* is: one begins with *Torah*, proceeds through *Ketuvim*, and concludes with *Nevi'im*. This is counterintuitive, since the standard order of *Tanach* is *Torah*, *Nevi'im*, *Ketuvim*, and one might expect the *nusach* to follow suit. Several explanations have been offered by the *Rishonim*, but the most illuminating frames the order in liturgical-temporal terms: the *pesukim* from *Torah* look backward — to foundational moments of creation, covenant, and election. The *pesukim* from *Ketuvim* (predominantly from *Tehillim*) speak to the present — how we praise and encounter God now, how the themes of *malchus*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* express themselves in our ongoing life. The *pesukim* from *Nevi'im* look forward — toward the Messianic redemption and the ultimate realization of these themes. The order thus reflects a temporal arc from past through present to future.

### Examples of Bad Verses

The *gemara* provides examples of *pesukim* that are prohibited because of their association with *puranus*. For *malchuyos*: *Chai ani neum Hashem Elokim im lo b'yad chazaka u'vizroa netuya u'vichema shfucha emloch aleichem* — "As I live, says God, with an outstretched hand and poured-forth wrath I will rule over you." Although Rav Nachman is quoted as saying that even this severe expression of divine anger would be acceptable — for if God vents His anger on us and ultimately redeems us, so be it — nevertheless, since the verse is stated *b'ritcha*, in heat and anger, we do not invoke it at the beginning of the year: *b'ritcha b'reisha d'shata lo madchrinan*.

For *zichronos*: *vayizkor ki basar hema ruach holech v'lo yashuv* (Psalm 78:39) — "He remembered that they were flesh, a wind that passes and does not return" — which, in context, is preceded by verses describing Israel's rebellions in the wilderness.

For *shofros*: *tiku shofar ba'Giva chatzotzra ba'Rama* (Hoshea 5:8) — a passage associated, in its context, with the punishment of Benjamin.

### Allowed: Non-Jews

An important qualification follows: *aval im bau lomar malchuyos, zichronos, u'shofros shel puranus shel ovdei kochavim, omer* — if the *pesukim* of punishment describe calamity befalling the nations rather than Israel, they may be recited. Examples are given. For *malchuyos*: *Hashem malach yirgezu amim* — "God reigns; let the nations tremble"; and *Hashem melech olam va'ed avdu goyim m'artzo* — "God reigns forever; nations will be driven from His land." For *zichronos*: *Zechor Hashem livnei Edom es yom Yerushalayim ha'omrim aru aru* — "Remember, God, against the children of Edom the day of Jerusalem, who said, 'Raze it, raze it.'" For *shofros*: *v'Hashem Elokim b'shofar yitka v'halach b'sa'aros Teiman* — God will blow the *shofar* and go in the storms of the south — followed by the continuation, *Hashem Tzva'os yagen aleihem*, God of hosts will protect them (the Jewish people). These are permitted. The universalist dimension of Rosh Hashanah as a day of divine sovereignty over all nations does not preclude — and in some sense accommodates — the hope for divine protection of Israel and judgment of her enemies.

### No Individual Memory

The *gemara* further rules: *ein mazkirin zichron shel yachid* — one does not recite *zichronos* referring to God's remembrance of an individual, even a positive remembrance. The themes of the *Shemoneh Esrei* are communal and national, and the *zichronos* of Rosh Hashanah must reflect that character. Examples of prohibited individual-remembrance verses: *zachreini Hashem birtzon amecha* — "Remember me, God, in the goodwill of Your people" (Psalm 106:4); and *zachrah li Elokai l'tovah* — "Remember me, my God, for good" (Nehemiah 13:31).

### Zichronos vs. Pikdonos

The *gemara* then introduces a related question: does *pikdon* — God's fixed-time remembrance of someone — count as *zichron*? Rabbi Yosi holds that *pikdonos harei hem k'zichronos* — instances of the root *pakad* are equivalent to *zichronos*. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: only the root *zachar* qualifies. The distinction is conceptual. *Zachar* implies constant, ongoing awareness — keeping something continually in mind. *Pakad*, by contrast, implies a fixed-time remembrance or a scheduled visitation — remembering something at an appointed moment. *V'Hashem pakad et Sarah*, for instance, describes God's visit to Sarah at a specific, pre-designated time. The *gemara* in the name of the *Maharsha* connects this to the broader distinction: *zichronos* connotes continuous divine attention, whereas *pikdonos* connotes episodic, time-bound intervention.

### Sarah Exception

Even granting Rabbi Yosi's position that *pikdonos* count as *zichronos*, the verse *v'Hashem pakad et Sarah* would seem to be the remembrance of an individual — and thus prohibited on the grounds stated above. The *gemara* addresses this: *keivan d'atu rabbim mimena* — since the many came from her, since all of *Klal Yisrael* descended from Sarah, the remembrance of Sarah is effectively the remembrance of the entire people. *K'rabbim damya* — it is treated as if it were the remembrance of the collective.

# Rosh Hashanah 33

## Malchuyot/Zichronot/ (II)

### Melech Mentions

The *daf* begins in the middle of *masechet* Rosh Hashanah 32b, continuing the discussion of the *psukim* of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*. The *Gemara* had been examining which verses qualify for each of the three liturgical sections of the *musaf* prayer — a matter that turns, in part, on a dispute between Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Yehuda.

### Psalm 24 Analysis

The *Gemara* turns to Psalm 24, which contains the phrase *Melech Hakavod* in multiple iterations. Reading through the *perek*: *se'u she'arim rasheichem vehinas'u pitchei olam veyavo Melech Hakavod* — one mention of *Melech*. *Mi zeh Melech Hakavod Hashem izuz vegibor* — a second mention. *Hashem gibor milchama se'u she'arim rasheichem use'u pitchei olam veyavo Melech Hakavod* — a third. *Mi hu zeh Melech Hakavod* — a fourth. *Hashem tzeva'ot hu Melech Hakavod selah* — a fifth. Since only three verses from *Ktuvim* are required, Psalm 24 alone could furnish more than enough.

The *Gemara* records: *rishona shtayim shniya shalosh divrei Rabbi Yose* — Rabbi Yose holds that the first *pasuk* of the *perek* yields two counts of *Melech*, and the second *pasuk* yields three. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *rishona achas shniya shtayim* — the first *pasuk* counts for only one mention, and the second for only two. The reason, explains *Rashi*, is that the rhetorical question *mi zeh Melech Hakavod* does not yet identify God as *Melech* — it is a question, not an affirmation, and Rabbi Yehuda declines to count it. Rabbi Yose treats the question as rhetorical and counts it nonetheless.

What is striking about this dispute is the underlying principle it reveals: the count of *malchuyos* is not simply a count of *psukim* but of affirmative mentions of *Melech* within *psukim*. A single *pasuk* containing multiple qualifying mentions can count more than once.

### Universal Kingship

A related case makes this even sharper. The *Gemara* cites *zimru Elohim zamru zamru le'malkeinu zamru ki melech kol ha'aretz elohim* — this verse contains both *malkeinu* and *melech kol ha'aretz*. Rabbi Yose counts this as two, since two mentions of kingship appear. Rabbi Yehuda counts it as only one. *Rashi* explains that *malkeinu* — "our King" — refers to God only as King of Israel, and Rabbi Yehuda requires that a *malchuyot* verse express universal kingship, *melech al kol ha'aretz*. The verse *meloch elohim al goyim elohim yashav al kisei kodsho* counts as only one for both opinions: it speaks of God reigning over the nations, satisfying the universality requirement, but "sitting on the throne" is not the explicit language of *Melech* and therefore contributes only a single count.

### Double-Purpose Verses

The *Gemara* then addresses the possibility of using a single *pasuk* to serve double duty. A verse containing both *zichron* and *teruah* — such as *shabbaton zichron teruah mikra kodesh* — may, according to Rabbi Yose, be recited once as part of *zichronos* and again as part of *shofros*: *omrin im hazichronos v'omrin im hashofros divrei Rabbi Yose*. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *eino omer ela im hazichronos bilvad* — you may say it only in the *zichronos* section. The same dispute applies to a verse containing both *malchut* and *teruah*, such as *Hashem Elokav imo uteruas melech bo*: Rabbi Yose permits it for both *malchuyos* and *shofros*; Rabbi Yehuda limits it to *malchuyos* alone.

### Teruah vs Shofar

The reason for Rabbi Yehuda's position becomes explicit in the third case. The verse *yom teruah yiheyeh lachem* — the very *pasuk* from which the observance of Rosh Hashanah as a day of *teruah* is derived — cannot count for the *shofros* section, says Rabbi Yehuda: *eino omer kol ikar*. The word *teruah* does not specify *shofar*, and Rabbi Yehuda requires explicit mention of *shofar* for a verse to qualify for the *shofros* section. *Rashi* supports this reasoning by noting that *teruah* also appears in connection with *chatzotzros* — trumpets — and is therefore not intrinsically tied to *shofar*.

This raises a genuine question. The *Torah* itself characterizes Rosh Hashanah as a *yom teruah* and *zichron teruah*, and yet *Chazal* designated the third *bracha* of *musaf* as *shofros*, not *teruos*. One might suggest that *Chazal* chose to emphasize *shofar davka* in order to underscore that the central instrument is the *shofar*, and not the *teruah* in its broader sense. This also opens the *shofros* section to a wider range of *psukim* — including those from *Har Sinai* — that could not otherwise have been included. There is a further dimension here noted by the *Ramban* from a Kabbalistic perspective: *tekiah* is associated with *midas harachamim* while *teruah* is associated with *midas hadin* — the staccato, fragmented quality of *teruah* evoking something more like crying out or being struck. The *Torah* itself seems to confirm this distinction: *v'chi tavo'u milchamah b'artzechem vaharei'otem bachatzotzros* — in wartime, you sound *teruah* — while *uvyom simchaschem utkatem bachatzotzros* — on days of rejoicing, you sound *tekiah*. Perhaps, then, the third *bracha* was deliberately framed as *shofros* rather than *teruos* precisely to avoid overemphasizing that more severe, *din*-laden resonance, while also allowing the Sinaitic imagery of *shofar* to enrich the section.

---

## Torah Brackets

### End with Navi

The *Gemara* now addresses the requirement governing the structure of each of the three sections: *im hishlim matchil b'Torah umashlim b'Navi*. The *Gemara* immediately asks whether *im hishlim* implies that ending with *Torah* is only *bdi'avad* — after the fact — but *lechatchila* one would end with a verse from *Navi*.

### Torah Framing

The *Gemara* resolves the text through revision. The initial formulation is: you begin with *Torah* and end with *Navi*. Rabbi Yose says: you should end with *Torah*, and if you ended with *Navi*, you have fulfilled your obligation *bdi'avad*. In practice, the structure is: three *psukim* from *Torah*, three from *Nevi'im*, three from *Ktuvim*, and then a final *pasuk* from *Torah* to close the section. This is how we end each of the three sections — completing the ten *psukim* with a verse of *Torah*.

### Vatikin Practice

A *baraita* confirms this: Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Yose transmitted that the *vatikin* — the pious ancients, those most exacting in observance — would always conclude with a *pasuk* from *Torah*.

### Malchuyot Shortage

This framework immediately creates a problem. For *zichronos* and *shofros*, there is no shortage of *psukim* from *Torah* — *ika tuvah*, there are plenty. But for *malchuyos*, only three *psukim* from *Torah* are readily available: *Hashem Elokav imo uteruas melech bo*, *vayehi biYeshurun melech*, and *Hashem yimloch l'olam va'ed*. If the structure demands three opening *Torah* verses plus a closing *Torah* verse, four *Torah* verses of *malchuyot* are required. And we need ten verses total — the *Gemara* asks: *v'anan be'inan asar v'leka*? Where is the fourth *Torah malchuyot* verse?

---

## Malchuyot/Zichronot/ (II)

### Fourth Malchuyot

The *Gemara* answers with a *baraita* cited by Rav Huna: *ta shema* — Shema Yisrael.

### Shema as Malchuyot

The *baraita* proposes that *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* qualifies as a *malchut* verse. The reasoning is that the declaration of God's absolute singularity — one God over all — evokes the concept of kingship, and presumably universal kingship at that. *Divrei Rabbi Yose*. Rabbi Yehuda, characteristically more restrictive, does not accept this: *einah malchut*. The *Gemara* then offers two further candidates: *v'yadata hayom vahashevota el l'vavecha ki Hashem hu ha'Elokim ein od*, and *ata hareita ladaat ki Hashem hu ha'Elokim ein od milvado*. Again, Rabbi Yose accepts these; Rabbi Yehuda does not.

This raises a deeper conceptual question about *malchuyot* itself. Is the purpose of *malchuyot* to invoke God's absolute and exclusive dominion — such that verses affirming there is no other God would qualify? Or is *malchuyot* specifically about the imagery of kingship in its juridical, relational sense — a king who rules over his subjects and exercises power over them? If the latter, then verses like *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* may not fully evoke that dimension, even if they affirm monotheism in its most fundamental form. The question remains open, embedded in the disagreement between Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Yehuda.

### Musaf Prayer Verses

Turning to the actual text of the *musaf* prayer as it is recited today, we can trace how these *psukim* were incorporated. The *malchuyos* section opens with *Atah zachartanu* and proceeds through the *kedushas hayom*, incorporating as well the *korban musaf* verses beginning *uminchasam veniskeihem uvachodesh hashvii*. The *malchuyos psukim* themselves include *Aleinu leshabei'ach*, which introduces the theme of universal kingship, and concludes the *psukim* sequence with *kakatuv beTorasecha Hashem yimloch le'olam va'ed* — the verse on which all opinions agree — followed by *lo hibit aven beYaakov... Hashem Elokav imo utru'as melech bo*, then *vayehi biYeshurun melech behis'asef roshei am yachad shivtei Yisrael*. These are the three universally accepted *Torah* verses. The fourth, debated, verse — *ki Hashem hu ha'Elokim* — is also present in the *musaf* text, as part of the passage *veyadata hayom vehasheivosa*. Finally, *uvTorasecha kasuv leimor Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad* appears as the closing *Torah* verse of the section.

The *shofros* section, similarly, opens by evoking *Har Sinai* — *Atah nigleisa ba'anan kevodecha* — and draws on Sinaitic verses: *vayehi kol shofar chazak me'od*, *vayehi kol hashofar holeich vechazeik me'od*, *vechol ha'am ro'im es hakolos ve'es halapidim ve'es kol hashofar*. What is striking is that the section concludes with the verse *uveyom simchaschem uvemoadeichem uveroshei chodsheichem uskatem bachatzotzros al olosaychem* — a verse that speaks explicitly of *chatzotzros*, not *shofar*. This is the same phenomenon, in mirror image, that we observed with the *malchuyos* section: in both cases, the final *pasuk* is not perfectly on-point, yet it was selected for inclusion. The *Gemara* does not highlight this, but it is clearly visible from the text of the prayer itself.

---

## No Hallel/Musaf Timing

### Shofar in Musaf

The *Gemara* cites the *Mishnah*: the *shliach tzibur* for the morning service leads *Shacharis*, but it is the second — the *ba'al musaf* — who sounds the *shofar*. The reason given is *mishum de'berov am hadrat melech* — in order to maximize the community's presence when the *shofar* is blown. The more people present, the greater the honor to God as King. The same logic would seem to require reciting *Hallel* during *musaf* as well, to ensure maximum attendance — but we do not do that. Conversely, the principle of *zrizim makdimim lemitzvot* — the zealous perform *mitzvos* at the earliest opportunity — would seem to argue for blowing *shofar* in *Shacharis*. The *Gemara* notes this tension directly: each principle seems to lead to a different conclusion for each practice.

### Historical Edict

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the matter: *be'shat gzerat hamalchut shanu* — this ruling was established at the time of a royal edict. *Rashi* explains that there was a decree forbidding *shofar* blowing, and so the community waited until the government's agents had departed — which happened to be during *musaf* — and then blew. Even after the decree was lifted, the practice was not reverted: *lo avidnan ke'meikara*, because of concern that dangerous conditions might return.

### Intrinsic Connection

*Tosafot* cites the *Yerushalmi*, which offers a more nuanced account of the historical edict and also a more intrinsic reason for the *musaf* timing. On the historical side, the *Yerushalmi* explains that the enemies of Israel misinterpreted the *shofar* as a call to war — *tru'at milchama* — and attacked the community. The solution was to wait until after the community had visibly gone through the full *tefillah* — *Kriyat Shema*, *davening*, *keriat haTorah* — at which point the authorities understood it was religious observance: *binimusei hinhu askin*, they are engaged in their own practices. The intrinsic reason the *Yerushalmi* offers is that the *teruah* verses on Rosh Hashanah appear in the context of the *mussafim* in the *Torah* — *yom teruah* and *zichron teruah* arise in the context of the communal *korbanot* of the day. If *musaf* represents the identity of the day — what makes Rosh Hashanah what it is — then the *tekios*, which are equally constitutive of that identity, properly belong there as well.

### Angels' Question

The *Mishnah* also teaches that the first *shliach tzibur* recites *Hallel* — not on Rosh Hashanah, but on days when *Hallel* is said, since the *ba'al Shacharis* leads directly into *Hallel* from *chazarat haShatz*. The structure of the *Mishnah* makes clear that *Hallel* is not said on Rosh Hashanah. The *Gemara* asks *mai ta'ama* — why not? — and records a remarkable passage: Rabbi Abbahu teaches that the angels said before God, *Ribono Shel Olam*, why do the people of Israel not sing *shirah* before You on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur?

### Divine Judgment

God answers: *efshar melech yoshev al kise din v'sifrei chayim v'sifrei meitim ptuchim lefanav v'Yisrael omrim shirah?* — Is it possible that the King sits on the throne of judgment with the books of life and death open before Him, and Israel sings praises? The day is one of awe, not of *simcha*, and *Hallel* — as an expression of joyous praise — is therefore inappropriate.

### Fasting on RH

This passage raises broader questions about the character of Rosh Hashanah. How much does the *yom hadin* theme override the *yom tov* dimension? There is in fact a direct halachic consequence: whether one may fast on Rosh Hashanah. Some *poskim* permit it, reasoning that as a *yom hadin* the gravity of the day overrides the ordinary prohibition against fasting on *Yom Tov* — and the passage just cited, that *Hallel* is inappropriate because judgment hangs in the balance, would seem to support that view. Others prohibit it, citing a *midrash* that portrays Israel approaching Rosh Hashanah not in black garments and covered in ash, as one would expect of someone standing trial, but dressed in fine white clothing, confident that God will judge them favorably. The image of *kidnei maron* — the flock passing before the shepherd — and the simultaneous sense of awe and trust make the proper emotional posture of the day genuinely complex and contested.

---

## Shofar Restrictions

### Tchum Boundary

The *Mishnah* now lists a series of restrictions governing the *shofar* on *Yom Tov* of Rosh Hashanah. The first: *ein ma'avirin alav et hat-chum* — one may not carry the *shofar* beyond the *tchum*, even for the purpose of enabling someone else to fulfill the *mitzvah*. This holds despite the fact that the *mitzvah* is *d'Oraisa*.

### Melacha Restrictions

Further: *v'ein mefaktin alav et hagal* — one may not move a pile of stones to uncover a buried *shofar*; *v'lo olim b'ilan* — one may not climb a tree; *v'lo rochvin al gabei behema* — one may not ride an animal; *v'lo shatin al penei hamayim* — one may not float across water. These prohibitions are recognizable from an earlier *Mishnah* in *Beitzah* that catalogues the classic list of *shevutim* — rabbinic prohibitions on *Yom Tov*. The *Gemara* explains that the *mitzvah* of *shofar* is a positive commandment (*asei*), while *Yom Tov* is governed by both a positive and a negative commandment.
