A positive commandment cannot override a combination of positive and negative, and therefore the biblical restrictions stand. As for the rabbinic *shevutim*: *hashta d'rabbanan amrat lo, d'Oraisa miba'aya* — once we have established that the rabbinic prohibitions are not overridden, the biblical certainly are not. The *Gemara* frames this as *zu v'ein tzarich lomar zu* — this ruling, and it goes without saying that one. Once the *mitzvah* of *shofar* cannot override *Yom Tov* at the biblical level, the rabbinic *shevutim* are equally protected.

### Cutting Shofar

The *Mishnah* states: *v'ein chotchin oto bein bidavar shehu mishum shevut uvein bidavar shehu mishum lo ta'aseh* — one may not trim or shorten the *shofar*, whether the means of doing so is only a rabbinic violation or a biblical one. The *Gemara* identifies the rabbinic case as using a *magal* — a sickle, an unusual implement for this purpose, which constitutes a *shinui*, a deviation from the normal manner of performing a prohibited act, rendering it only rabbinically forbidden. The biblical case is using a regular *sakin* — a knife — which constitutes a normal act of *tikkun kli*, fixing a vessel, and is therefore a biblical prohibition. The same *zu v'ein tzarich lomar zu* logic applies.

### Cleaning Shofar

The *Mishnah* permits placing water or wine into the *shofar* to clean it: *aval im ratza litten letocho mayim o yayin, yitten*. Water and wine are permitted; urine is not. The *Gemara* attributes this *halacha* to Abba Shaul: *mayim o yayin mutar k'dei l'tzachzacho* — to clean and polish it — while *mei raglayim assur mipnei hakavod* — urine is forbidden because it is disrespectful to an object used for a *mitzvah*, the same principle that governs respectful handling of *ketores* and other sacred items.

---

## Women/Children

### Women Blowing

The *Mishnah* states that children are not prevented from blowing the *shofar*. The *Gemara* infers that women, by contrast, are prevented — *hanashim m'akvin*. *Rashi* explains this on the basis that women are entirely exempt from positive time-bound commandments (*mitzvat asei shehazman grama hi*), and that for them to blow would raise the concern of *bal tosef* — adding to the commandment. Nearly all *rishonim* take issue with *Rashi* on this point. *Bal tosef* ordinarily refers to someone who is obligated and expands the scope of a *mitzvah* beyond its proper bounds — it is not obviously applicable to someone who is entirely exempt. Most *rishonim* prefer a different rationale: if the *mitzvah* is not incumbent upon a person, then the *shofar* might otherwise be considered *muktzeh* on *Yom Tov* and blowing it a form of prohibited music-making. On that analysis, blowing *shofar* without a *mitzvah* context generates incidental problems that would ordinarily make it inappropriate.

### Children Learning

As for children: not only does one not prevent them from blowing, but one actively engages with them — *aval mitaskin imahem ad sheyilmedu*. The *Gemara* will elaborate on what this active involvement entails and how it navigates the competing concerns of *chinuch*.

---

## Kavanah Issues

### Blower's Intent

The *Mishnah* states: *vehamitasek lo yatza* — one who blows in an incidental, non-purposive manner has not fulfilled his obligation. This is the issue of *kavanah*: blowing the *shofar* requires intent to perform the *mitzvah*. Mere incidental production of the sounds — *misasek* — does not count.

### Listener's Intent

Similarly: *vehashomea min hamitasek lo yatza* — one who hears the *shofar* from someone who was blowing without intent to perform the *mitzvah* has also not fulfilled the obligation. The chain of *kavanah* must be intact on both ends. Both rulings set the stage for the *Gemara*'s later analysis of precisely how much intent is required and what form it must take.

---

## Shofar Restrictions (II)

### Positive Mitzvah

The *Gemara* consolidates the underlying principle: *shofar asei hu ve-Yom Tov asei v'lo ta'aseh ve-ein asei docheh lo ta'aseh ve-asei* — the *mitzvah* of *shofar* is a positive commandment, while *Yom Tov* is governed by both a positive commandment and a negative commandment. The rule that a positive commandment overrides a negative does not apply when the negative is accompanied by a positive as well. Therefore, *shofar* cannot displace *Yom Tov* restrictions at the biblical level, and by extension the rabbinic *shevutim* are equally shielded.

It is worth noting that the *Gemara* does not pause to analyze whether individual *shevutim* might be overridden on other grounds — for instance, the position of the *Aruch* that a single rabbinic prohibition may be overridden for the sake of a *mitzvah* on *Shabbat* in certain circumstances. Once the *Gemara* has established that *shofar* does not override *Yom Tov* at the biblical level, it treats the *shevutim* as equally protected, without requiring independent justification for each.

---

## Women/Children (II)

### Bal Tosif

Returning to the question of women, the *Gemara* cites a *baraita* that contradicts the *Mishnah*'s apparent prohibition: *ein m'akvin lo es hanashim v'lo es hatinokos miltkoah b'Yom Tov* — one does not prevent women *or* children from blowing on *Yom Tov*. Abaye resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — ha Rabbi Yehuda ha Rabbi Yosi v'Rabbi Shimon*. The *Mishnah*'s restrictive position reflects Rabbi Yehuda's view; the *baraita* reflects the view of Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon.

The underlying dispute concerns *smicha* — the laying of hands on a *korban*. Rabbi Yehuda holds that only *Bnei Yisrael*, males, perform *smicha*; women do not. Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon hold that women may perform *smicha* on a voluntary basis — *nashim somchot reshut*. They are not obligated, but they are permitted. This maps onto the broader question of women's relationship to positive time-bound commandments. Even granting the exemption, does that exemption also constitute exclusion? Or may women choose to perform such *mitzvos* on an optional basis?

One approach — appearing in the context of *chagigah* — is that even if there are incidental rabbinic concerns, we permit women to perform these *mitzvos* *kedei la'asot nachat ruach lenashim*, to give women a sense of inclusion. This is a meaningful statement about the value of inclusion, but it does not fully resolve the underlying *halachic* question about women's relationship to the *mitzvah* itself. A stronger approach holds that exemption is not the same as exclusion: a woman who performs a *mitzvas asei shehazman grama* is not engaged in a meaningless act — she is performing the *mitzvah*, albeit on an optional basis, and as *eino metzuveh ve'oseh* she still receives *schar*. On this view the incidental concerns about *muktzeh* or improper use of *kodshim* fall away, because the woman is actually performing a genuine act of *mitzvah*.

### Halacha Psak

*Tosafot* rules, in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yose: *af al gav desatama desifra ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — even though there is a *stam* ruling in the *Sifra* following Rabbi Yehuda — *halacha ke-Rabbi Yose*, because *denimuko imo* — Rabbi Yose's reasoning accompanies his ruling — and because of *ma'aseh rav*: Michal the daughter of Shaul wore *tefillin*, and the wife of Yonah made the *aliyah la'regel*. A further precedent involves women performing *smicha* in the *ezras nashim*. Women are therefore permitted to blow *shofar* if they choose to do so. This also overrides the secondary concerns about *muktzeh* and music-making.

### Women's Bracha

The remaining question, which occupies the bulk of *Tosafot*'s discussion, is whether women who perform a *mitzvas asei shehazman grama* make a *bracha*. This is the question that divides *Ashkenazi* and *Sefardi* practice. *Ashkenazim* rule that women do make a *bracha*, even on *mitzvos* from which they are exempt. *Sefardim*, following the *Rambam*, rule that women do not — since they were not commanded, they cannot say *vetzivanu*.

The *Ashkenazi* position rests on two possible foundations. One is that *vetzivanu* means *Klal Yisrael* — the Jewish people as a whole were commanded, and even though women individually were not, they may recite the *bracha* as members of that collective. The stronger approach is that the exemption is not equivalent to exclusion from the commandment altogether. On this reading, women were fundamentally addressed by the commandment but granted an exemption; if they choose to waive the exemption and perform the *mitzvah*, they re-enter the category of the commanded, and the *bracha* is appropriate. They cannot, however, be *motzi* men, since men retain a higher level of obligation that women cannot match.

The practical significance of the *bracha* question is considerable. When women do not make a *bracha*, the implicit message is that the act is not truly a *mitzvah* for them. When they do, the *bracha* powerfully affirms that they are performing a genuine act of religious obligation. This difference is observable in practice: in *Sefardi* communities, where the *Rambam*'s ruling prevails, women often feel considerably less connection to *mitzvos asei shehazman grama*, whereas the *Ashkenazi* practice of making a *bracha* communicates, in the most direct terms available, that the *mitzvah* is genuinely theirs. When it comes to *shofar* on Rosh Hashanah in particular, virtually all women feel deeply connected to the obligation, and many would be surprised to learn that they are technically exempt — which itself testifies to the power of the *bracha* in shaping that sense of *chiyuv*.

It is worth noting that certain *mitzvos* that are formally time-bound carry their own independent basis for women's obligation — *kiddush* is linked to *zachor* and *shamor*, and *matzah* is connected to the prohibition of *chametz* — and these are therefore distinct from the general category of *mitzvas asei shehazman grama*.

### Chinuch Age

The *Gemara* now turns to a contradiction within the *Mishnah* regarding children. The first clause says *mitaskin imahem ad sheyilmedu* — you actively engage with children to teach them. A *baraita* extends this even to *Shabbat*: *afilu b'Shabbat*. But the second clause says *ein me'akvin* — you merely do not interfere. The *Gemara* notes that *mitaskin* implies an active *lechatchila* encouragement, while *ein me'akvin* suggests only passive non-interference — not encouragement. *Lo kashya*: the two clauses address different cases.

### Shabbat Blowing

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a child who has reached the age of *chinuch* and one who has not. There are two ways to read the distinction, leading to opposing conclusions.

On one reading: for a child below the age of *chinuch*, there are no *chinuch* concerns about *Shabbat* violation, so one may actively engage — even on *Shabbat*, even though no one else is performing a *mitzvah* today. For a child at the age of *chinuch*, one does not actively encourage because there is a *chinuch* obligation regarding *Shabbat* that must be respected, but one also does not interfere — particularly on Rosh Hashanah, when the *shofar* connection is itself valuable.

On the other reading: for a child below the age of *chinuch*, one does not interfere but does not actively involve; for a child at the age of *chinuch*, the *chinuch* obligation of Rosh Hashanah counterbalances the *chinuch* of *Shabbat*, and one may actively encourage blowing the *shofar*.

The *Shulchan Aruch* and the *Rama* do not adopt the *girsa* that includes *afilu b'Shabbat*; the standard *girsa* in practice reads *afilu b'Yom Tov*. The *Rama* rules clearly that for a child who has reached *chinuch*, and when it is *Yom Tov* rather than *Shabbat*, one actively involves the child — teaches, encourages, and blows the *shofar* alongside him. This is especially meaningful given that on Rosh Hashanah the child may not have reached the *beis haknesses* to hear the *tekios* himself. One may also make a *bracha* for the sake of *chinuch*, as was established in an earlier discussion.

This section also clarifies an important practical boundary for adults. The *Rama* rules that after one has fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *shofar*, blowing for mere enjoyment — without any connection to *mitzvah* or *chinuch* — is forbidden, because it constitutes making music on *Yom Tov*. The *Taz* disagrees, arguing that on Rosh Hashanah the *shofar* cannot be considered problematic in any context. The *Rama*'s ruling prevails: *lechatchila*, blowing the *shofar* for purely recreational purposes after the *mitzvah* has been fulfilled is not permitted. Blowing in the context of *chinuch* — even if the adult must demonstrate the sounds himself — remains entirely legitimate.

---

## Kavanah Issues (II)

### Musical Intent

The *Gemara* engages with a fine point of *kavanah* arising from the *Mishnah*'s reference to *misasek*. The case of *hatokea lashir* — blowing the *shofar* for musical purposes — appears to suggest that the only disqualifying lack of intent is complete incidentality, *misasek* in its strictest sense. If a person deliberately produces the sounds of a *shofar* but for musical rather than *mitzvah* purposes, the implication might be that he *is* *yotzei*. The *Gemara* then cites Rava, who rules explicitly: *hatokea lashir yatza* — one who blows for music has fulfilled the obligation.

### Motzi Intent

The *Gemara* declines to confirm Rava's ruling from this passage, because *dilma tokea lashir nami misasek kari lei* — perhaps "blowing for music" is itself classified as *misasek*, and the *Mishnah* is simply saying that any blowing outside a *mitzvah* intent is disqualifying. The boundary of *misasek* is thus left uncertain.

A separate but related issue of *kavanah* emerges: does the blower need intent not only to perform the *mitzvah* himself, but specifically to *motzi* the listener? The *Mishnah* says that hearing from a *misasek* does not fulfill the obligation — implying that if the blower *did* intend to perform the *mitzvah* for himself, the listener would be *yotzei* even without the blower having intended to exempt him. This would contradict Rabbi Zeira, who instructed his attendant: *ikavein u-tkah li* — have intent specifically to blow *for me*, meaning intent to *motzi* the listener is required, not merely intent to perform the *mitzvah*.

The *Gemara* deflects: *dilma ayidi d'tani resha mitasek, tana seifa nami mitasek* — the *Mishnah* is structured around the theme of *misasek* throughout, and the *seifa* about the listener merely parallels the *reisha* about the blower. The *Mishnah* does not affirmatively rule that intent to *motzi* is unnecessary; it simply does not address that question. It remains possible that intent to exempt the listener is indeed required, as Rabbi Zeira holds.

---

## Sound Sequence

### Nine Sounds

The *Mishnah* introduces the *seder tekios*: *shalosh shel shalosh shalosh* — three sets of three sounds each, yielding nine *kolot* in total. The biblical source for three *teruos* is that the word *teruah* appears three times in connection with the obligation: *yom teruah yiheyeh lachem*, *zichron teruah* (twice on Rosh Hashanah), and *v'ha'avarta shofar teruah* for *Yovel*. From other *psukim* it is derived that a *tekiah* precedes and follows each *teruah*, producing the structure of *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* three times — nine sounds altogether.

### Tekiah Timing

*Shiur tekiah k'shalosh teruos* — the duration of a *tekiah* equals the duration of three *teruos*. This establishes a proportional relationship: the *tekiah* is the full, sustained sound, and the *teruah* is a fragmented version of it. One standard reading is that a *teruah* — the set of broken sounds — equals one third the length of a *tekiah*, and three *teruos* together equal one *tekiah* in length. Understood this way, a *teruah* is essentially a *tekiah* that has been broken into fragments: in quantity and quality, the *teruah* is a shattered *tekiah*. The *Ramban* raises the possibility that the two sounds differ in quality as well as duration — that the *tekiah* and *teruah* are intrinsically different types of sound, one straight and one undulating — but the standard position is that the only distinction is one of length.

### Teruah Beats

*Shiur teruah k'shalosh yevavot* — the minimum duration of a *teruah* is the length of three beats, where a *yevavah* is the basic unit of sound. Thus each individual sound within the *teruah* set must last at least three beats.

---

## Sound Sequence (II)

### Distinct Sounds

The *Gemara* addresses the case of *takah b'rishonah u-mashach b'shniyah k'shtayim* — if a person blew the first *tekiah* and then extended the second *tekiah* to double length, intending for it to count as both the concluding *tekiah* of one set and the opening *tekiah* of the next. The ruling is *ein b'yado ela achat* — it counts as only one. Each sound must be a distinct, discrete unit; one cannot stretch a single *tekiah* to serve as two.

### Teruah Type

The *Gemara* presents a dispute about the nature of the *teruah* sound itself. The word *yom teruah* is rendered in the Aramaic *targum* as *yom yevava* — a day of wailing, derived from *vateyabev em Sisra* — the mother of Sisera wailing at the window. The question is what form that wailing takes: *mar savar genuchi ganach* — one view holds it is a moan, a sustained but broken sound, corresponding to what we call *shevarim*; *umar savar yeluli yalil* — the other view holds it is a high-pitched wail, a staccato cry, corresponding to what we call *teruah* in its technical sense. This is the source of the fundamental *machloket* that underlies our practice of sounding *shevarim*, *teruah*, and the combination *shevarim-teruah*: because it was uncertain which form of *teruah* the *Torah* intended, we perform multiple variants to satisfy both opinions.

---

## Missed Shofar

### Late Shofar

The *Mishnah* addresses the case of *mi she'berach v'achar kach nizdamen lo shofar* — a person who recited the *brachot* of *mussaf*, including the sections of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*, without having a *shofar* available, and who subsequently obtained one. In the context of the *Mishnah*, the relevant *brachot* are those of *Shmoneh Esrei* itself — not the later-developed *birkat hamitzvah* of *lishmoa kol shofar*, which arose once the *shofar* blowing was separated from the *Shmoneh Esrei* and the standalone *brachot* were required. In the original framework, *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* within *musaf* constituted the *halachic* envelope of the *shofar* obligation.

### Separate Fulfillment

The *Mishnah* rules: *tokeia u-meiri u-tokeia shalosh pe'amim* — one blows *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* three times, even without the surrounding *brachot* of *Shmoneh Esrei*. This is a significant *chiddush* in both directions: *bdi'avad*, one may recite *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* without *shofar*, and one may blow *shofar* without the enveloping *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*. Although these elements are conceptually intertwined — the *shofar* blowing occurs within and because of those *brachot* — they are not mutually indispensable.

### Individual Obligation

*K'shem she'shliach tzibur chayav kach kol yachid v'yachid chayav* — just as the *shliach tzibur* is obligated, so is every individual. This statement addresses a potential misunderstanding: since the *shliach tzibur* is the one who blows the *shofar* in the communal setting, one might think that the obligation is communal rather than personal. The *Mishnah* clarifies that the *mitzvah* belongs to each individual. In the context of *musaf*, this also raised a practical challenge: the *psukim* of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* were not widely memorized, and without *siddurim*, ordinary people had no way to recite them independently.

### Shliach Motzi

Rabban Gamliel addresses this directly: *shliach tzibur motzi et harabim yedei chovatan* — the *shliach tzibur* can exempt the community. Here Rabban Gamliel is speaking about the *Shmoneh Esrei* of *musaf* with its *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* — not about the *shofar* blowing itself. The practical issue is clear: how can people fulfill the obligation of reciting these *psukim* in *Shmoneh Esrei* if they do not know them? Rabban Gamliel's ruling — that the *shliach tzibur* can be *motzi* the community — resolves this, and the fuller implications of that ruling will be developed in the discussion that follows.

---

---

# Rosh Hashanah 35

## Blessings & Shofar

### Daf Introduction

This daf — daf 35, the final daf of Masechet Rosh Hashanah — opens by picking up in the middle of 34b. The *mishna* there records the case of *mi sheberach*: one who recited the *brachot* first and was subsequently provided with a *shofar*, proceeds to blow — *tokeia, marea, vetokeia* — after the fact. The *mishna* thus makes explicit what has been the taken-for-granted assumption throughout: the *brachot* in question are the *brachot* of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*, and they are sufficiently independent of the *shofar* that each can stand alone when circumstances require. If no *shofar* is available, one davens *shemoneh esrei* with *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* but without *tekios*; if a *shofar* becomes available afterward, one blows without renewed mention of any *bracha*. The separate *bracha* over *shofar* blowing — which becomes a fixed feature once the practice of blowing *tekios* outside of *shemoneh esrei* is established — develops later, in the time of the *Geonim*.

### Malchuyos Framework

Although the *mishna*'s treatment of the *seder habrachot* makes the integration of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* with the *tekios* explicit — *malchuyos vetokeia*, *zichronos vetokeia*, *shofros vetokeia* — it is worth noting that this is a point on which Rabbi Akiva himself is emphatic: *im eino tokeia lama hu mazkir* — if one is not blowing, what purpose does mentioning them serve? For Rabbi Akiva, the two are inherently intertwined.

### Shofar Primary

The *gemara* states tersely: *tama* — the reason the *mishna* permits the separation is *delo havei lei shofar meikara*, that the *shofar* was unavailable from the outset. The inference follows: *ha havei lei shofar meikara*, once a *shofar* is available, *ki shama lehu aseder brachot shama lehu* — one hears the *tekios* in the course of the *brachot* themselves. The normal state of affairs presupposes their integration.

### Private Davening Case

The *gemara* then records the case of Rav Pappa bar Shmuel, who rose to daven privately and instructed his attendant: *ki nahirna lach, tka li* — when I signal you, blow for me. Since he was davening silently and not serving as *shliach tzibur*, there was no communal structure through which anyone could know when he had completed each *bracha*. He therefore arranged a personal signal so that the *tekios* could be coordinated with his private *shemoneh esrei*.

### Minyan Requirement

Rava, however, rejects this arrangement: *lo amru ela bechaver ir* — they only permitted the *tekios* to be blown during *shemoneh esrei* in the context of a *minyan*, a *chaver ir*, which Rashi explains as a communal gathering. A *braita* confirms: *keshehu shoman shoman al haseder ve'al seder habrachot* — when one hears the *tekios*, one hears them in order and in the order of the *brachot*. The *braita* then specifies: *bemei devarim amurim*, this applies *bechaver ir*; *aval shelo bechaver ir*, when there is no *minyan*, one still hears the *tekios* in their proper order — *tokeia, marea, vetokeia* — but not in coordination with *shemoneh esrei*.

## Braita: Obligation

### Hearing in Order

The *braita* continues with a striking series of distinctions. *Veyachid shelo taka chavero tokeia lo* — if an individual has not blown *shofar*, another may blow on his behalf. *Veyachid shelo berach ein chavero mevarech alav* — but if an individual has not davened *shemoneh esrei*, another cannot daven for him. The *braita* then adds: *umitzvah betokein yoteir min hamevarchin* — the greater *mitzvah* belongs to the blowers rather than the blessers. The practical application: if two villages face one another, one with a *baal tokeia* and one capable of conducting *shemoneh esrei*, and one must choose — *holchin limakom shetokein ve'ein holchin limakom shemevarchin* — one goes to the village that blows, not the one that prays.

### Individual via Others

The *gemara* initially challenges this as obvious — *pshita*: *hai d'oraisa hai d'rabbanan*, the *tekios* are biblical while *tefillah* and *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* are rabbinic. The *gemara* responds that the real novelty is this: even if one village offers a certain *baal tefillah* while the other offers only a doubtful *baal tokeia*, one would still choose the *safek* of a *d'oraisa* over the *vadai* of a *d'rabbanan*.

### D'oraisa vs. D'rabbanan

This distinction — *tekios* as *d'oraisa* and *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* as *d'rabbanan* — is important and deserves attention, because it runs against a position that Rashi appears to hold in several places, and which the *Ramban* and other *rishonim* cite this *gemara* to challenge. The *Torah* does say *yom terua yihyeh lachem* and *zichron terua yihyeh lachem*, but what precisely those phrases mandate — how many *tekios*, how many *teruos* — is not spelled out explicitly. The liturgical construction of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*, by contrast, is far more derived and inferential, and the general assumption in halachic literature is that liturgy — outside perhaps *shema*, *birkat hamazon*, and *birkat hatorah* — is rabbinic in character. This *gemara* reinforces that assumption in the clearest of terms.

### Rashi's Integration

The difficulty is that Rashi, in a number of places, seems to hold that *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* carry *d'oraisa* force. The answer Rashi would give — though he does not state it explicitly here — is tied to his interpretation of a *gemara* discussed the previous day, where the phrase *tekios m'akvot zo et zo, brachot m'akvot zo et zo* appears. Most *rishonim* read that phrase as saying that the *tekios* are each indispensable to one another and the *brachot* are each indispensable to one another — that is, one cannot take partial credit for a partial set. Rashi, however, reads it differently: one is not *yotzei* the *tekios* without the *brachot*, and one is not *yotzei* the *brachot* without the *tekios*. They must come together. Of course, the *mishna* itself makes clear that they can come apart in extenuating circumstances. What Rashi must therefore mean is that there are two levels of fulfillment: when combined, the *tekios* together with *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* constitute the full *d'oraisa* *kiyum* of the *mitzvah*; when separated, each becomes diminished. At that stage of separation, only the *shofar* blowing retains its *d'oraisa* character. *Malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* without the *tekios* are rabbinic. Hence, in the case the *braita* discusses — two villages, one offering only *tekios* and one offering only *tefillah* — the two are already separated, and at that point the *tekios* alone are *d'oraisa*. This *gemara* is therefore not a disproof of Rashi, because Rashi would argue that the very scenario under discussion is one of separation, and therefore the ranking the *braita* assigns is correct even on his view. Rashi's deeper position is that at a *d'oraisa* level, *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* belong together with the *tekios* — they are an integral part of the *d'oraisa* shofar obligation when performed in combination.

### Communal Prayer

The *braita*'s requirement that *tekios* during *shemoneh esrei* occur only with a *minyan* is itself significant. It supports those who hold that one only blows *tekios* during *chazarat hashatz* — for if the integration were permitted during silent *shemoneh esrei*, there would be no obvious reason to limit it to a *minyan*. What this seems to be saying is that the power of combining *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* with the *tekios* inheres specifically in the *tefillat hatzibur* — the community praying as a unified body.

Rav Soloveitchik articulates a useful conceptual distinction here: one's silent *shemoneh esrei* in a *minyan* is *tefillah b'tzibur* — prayer that takes place in the presence of a community — whereas *chazarat hashatz* is *tefillat hatzibur* — the entire community praying as a single unit through the mouthpiece of the *chazzan*. What this *gemara* would then be saying is that the integration of *shofar* and *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* as a unified act of prayer belongs to the *tefillat hatzibur* specifically — not to each individual's private prayer, even when that prayer occurs in the presence of others.

One way to sharpen this further: if *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* are derived from the *chatzotzros* — from the verse *al hatzar hatzorer eschem v'hareyosem bachatzotzros* — then the *chatzotzros* represent a fundamentally communal calling-out, the communal mode of *simcha* and petition, and that is precisely where the integration of *tekios* with *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* finds its home.

Those who permit the *tekios* during silent *shemoneh esrei* in a *minyan* would need to argue that even in individual silent prayer, there is a communal dimension present — we are all davening our private prayers as part of a community — and that communal dimension suffices. But the *braita*'s restriction to *bechaver ir* seems to work against that view, since that communal dimension exists in any *minyan* setting, not only in *chazarat hashatz*.

The *braita*'s final distinction — that one can be *yotzei* *tekios* through another's blowing but cannot be *yotzei* *shemoneh esrei* through another's davening — flows naturally from this framework. The *tekios* belong to the communal sphere and can therefore be conveyed through a *shomea k'oneh*-type mechanism. *Tefillah*, however, is something that must originate from within the individual. A number of *rishonim* cite a *Yerushalmi* explaining that *shomea k'oneh* does not operate for *tefillah*, *krias shema*, and similarly personal obligations, because these require initiation from the person themselves. One cannot piggyback on another's prayer with God. The *zimun* and the institution of the *shliach tzibur* provide the only recognized structures through which one person's prayer can serve another — and that is what sets the stage for the debate that follows.

## Shliach Tzibur Debate

### Gamliel Position

The *gemara* presents a *braita* that frames the central dispute of this section. The opening position states: *kesheim sheshliach tzibur chayav kach kol yachid veyachid chayav* — just as the *shliach tzibur* is obligated, so too every individual is obligated to daven his own *shemoneh esrei*. Rabban Gamliel disagrees and holds that the *shliach tzibur* is *motzi* everyone — the entire congregation fulfills its obligation through the *chazarat hashatz*.

A *braita* then records the exchange between Rabban Gamliel and the *chachamim*. The *chachamim* challenge him: *lidvarecha lamah tzibbur mispallelin?* — according to you, why does anyone bother with a private *shemoneh esrei*?

### Preparation Purpose

Rabban Gamliel's answer is striking: *kedei lehasdir shliach tzibur tefillaso* — in order to give the *shliach tzibur* an opportunity to prepare, to say it through once so that he has it straight before repeating it. Beyond that purpose, there is, according to Rabban Gamliel, no real function to private *shemoneh esrei* when one is in the presence of a *tzibur*.

This takes Rabban Gamliel considerably further than simply saying that the *shliach tzibur* can serve as a vehicle for those who do not know the *tefillah*. What he appears to be saying is that when one is present in a *tzibur*, the relevant mode of prayer is *tefillat hatzibur*, not *tefillat yachid*. One is praying to God as part of a community, in a different mode entirely. The only reason the individual's private *shemoneh esrei* exists in that context is as a preparation for the *shliach tzibur's* repetition.

This raises the question of whether Rabban Gamliel intends this as a general principle applying throughout the year, or specifically for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. The most natural reading of his position, applied broadly, would be that whenever one is present in *shul*, in a *tzibur*, the private *shemoneh esrei* serves no independent purpose. One is fully included in the communal prayer.

### Eino Baki Only

The *chachamim* respond with a counter-question: *lamah shliach tzibur yored lifnei hateivah?* — if the *shliach tzibur* is not *motzi* anyone, why do we have *chazarat hashatz* at all? The *chachamim* answer: *kedei lehotzi es she'eino baki* — in order to be *motzi* the person who does not know the *tefillah* by heart. On this reading, *chazarat hashatz* has a single technical function: providing a vehicle for the *eino baki*. It does not constitute a communal prayer that discharges the congregation's individual obligations. Those who know the *tefillah* remain responsible for their own.

This represents a genuinely radical divergence of underlying conceptions. Rabban Gamliel holds that in the context of a *tzibur*, private prayer effectively disappears — there is *tefillat hatzibur* and nothing else. The *chachamim*, understood on their most extreme reading, hold that there is no real *tefillat hatzibur* at all — only a technical mechanism to assist the *eino baki* — and individuals remain entirely responsible for their own obligations.

### Gamliel's Response

Rabban Gamliel pushes back: *keshem shemotzi et she'eino baki kach motzi et habaki* — the same mechanism that works for the *eino baki* works for the *baki* as well. The reason it works is not a technical workaround for those who cannot daven, but rather the inherent nature of communal prayer: the *shliach tzibur* speaks for the entire community, and that representation functions equally regardless of each individual's personal proficiency.

### Concession Claim

Rabba bar Bar Chana then reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *modim chachamim le-Rabban Gamliel* — the *chachamim* conceded to Rabban Gamliel. Rav, by contrast, maintains: *adayin hi machloket* — it remains an unresolved dispute.

The *gemara* then records that when Rabba bar Bar Chana transmitted Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the *chachamim* conceded, Resh Lakish pushed back — *iflag alei Resh Lakish* — and himself said *adayin hi machloket*. So we have Rabbi Yochanan maintaining that the *chachamim* conceded, while Rav and Resh Lakish both maintain the debate stands unresolved.

## Dispute Resolution

### Nachman's Reading

The *gemara* then asks: did Rabbi Yochanan really say the *chachamim* conceded? This question arises because another tradition in his name states: *hilchata ke-Rabban Gamliel* — we rule like Rabban Gamliel. If one rules on a matter, that implies the underlying dispute is still live. *Miklal d'peligi* — the very act of ruling presupposes an ongoing disagreement. So Rabbi Yochanan cannot simultaneously hold that the *chachamim* conceded and that we rule like Rabban Gamliel.

### Limited Scope

The resolution comes from Rabbi Chanah Tzippora'ah, who clarifies what Rabbi Yochanan's tradition actually stated in full: *halacha ke-Rabban Gamliel be-vrachot de-Rosh Hashanah ve-shel Yom Kippurim* — we rule like Rabban Gamliel specifically in the *brachot* of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. This implies that in those cases the *chachamim* still dispute Rabban Gamliel, and we are ruling against them. For ordinary *tefillah* throughout the year, the same debate may persist, and we rule like Rabban Gamliel there as well. The mention of Yom Kippur alongside Rosh Hashanah in this context is somewhat surprising, since the earlier discussion focused on Rosh Hashanah. The *Ran* resolves this by pointing out that throughout this chapter, *Yom Kippur* consistently refers to the Yom Kippur of *yovel*, which carries the same *brachot* as Rosh Hashanah. That is what the *gemara* means here when it pairs the two.

### Rabbi Meir Position

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's statements through Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's reading. When earlier traditions said *modim chachamim le-Rabban Gamliel*, they did not mean the *chachamim* of our *mishna* reversed themselves. They meant that another Tanna — Rabbi Meir — agrees with Rabban Gamliel. A *braita* is then cited: *brachot shel Rosh Hashanah ve-shel Yom HaKippurim shliach tzibur motzi et harabim yedei chovasan, divrei Rabbi Meir* — the *shliach tzibur* fulfills the congregation's obligation in the *brachot* of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur; this is the position of Rabbi Meir. The *chachamim* in that *braita* respond with the same language as our *mishna*: *keshem sheshliach tzibur chayav kach kol yachid veyachid chayav*. The *chachamim* of our *mishna* thus never conceded; what Rabbi Yochanan reported was simply that Rabbi Meir stands alongside Rabban Gamliel.

### Ruling & Debate

On this reading, the position of the *chachamim* in our *mishna* — that each individual remains obligated — stands unretracted. We rule like Rabban Gamliel, and there is a supporting *tanna* in the form of Rabbi Meir, but the dispute itself remains active. Whether the debate extends to ordinary *tefillah* throughout the year or is confined to Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and whether we rule like Rabban Gamliel in all cases or only those, are questions this passage leaves partially open. What is clear is that the *halacha* follows Rabban Gamliel for the *brachot* of Rosh Hashanah.

## Length Problem

### Distinction Question

Having established that we rule like Rabban Gamliel specifically for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the *gemara* asks: *mai shna hani* — what is different about those days? Why does Rabban Gamliel's principle apply with particular force there?

### Many Verses

The initial proposal is *mishum d'nafishei krai* — because there are many verses in *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*, making the *tefillah* far longer and more complex than what most people could manage independently.

### Verse Shortcut

The *gemara* immediately refutes this: Rav Chananel says in the name of Rav that once one has said *u'vetoratcha katuv leimor* — "and so it is written in Your Torah" — one need not actually quote the *pasuk*. If the verse problem can be circumvented so easily, why would the multiplicity of verses be the reason for Rabban Gamliel's special ruling?

### Many Blessings

The *gemara* therefore corrects itself: *ela mishum d'avshei brachot* — no, the true problem is the sheer number of *brachot*. Even granting that one can substitute the formula *u'vetoratcha katuv leimor* for the individual verses, there remain three complete *brachot* — *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* — that constitute a substantial and unusual addition to the standard *shemoneh esrei*. That length and complexity is what most people cannot manage alone, and that is why Rabban Gamliel's position carries particular force on Rosh Hashanah.

### Verses Required?

The simple reading of the *gemara* — and not the reading Rashi adopts — is that the formula *u'vetoratcha katuv leimor* provides a way of dispensing with the verses in *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* altogether. This creates an apparent difficulty: earlier in the tractate the *gemara* debated how many *pesukim* are required — ten according to some, three according to others — but nobody suggested fewer than three. How can this *gemara* imply that a summary formula suffices?

### Two Tracks

Tosafot resolves this by proposing two distinct tracks. If one chooses to cite *pesukim* in *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*, a minimum number applies — whether three or ten according to the relevant opinion. But one is not compelled to quote *pesukim* at all. One may instead say *malchuyos* and append *kemo shekatuv b'toratcha*, *kemo shekatuv al yedei nevi'echa*, *kemo shekatuv b'divrei kodshecha* — invoking each section of Tanach by reference without quoting — and that suffices. The minimum-verse rules govern only those who elect to quote; if one does not quote at all, the summary formula is a complete alternative.

### Three-Verse Link

The *Ran*, in explaining the *Rif*'s position, offers a different reading. He argues that the *Rif* understands the formula *u'vetoratcha katuv leimor* not as an alternative track but as an interpretation of the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who requires only three *pesukim* — one from Torah, one from *Ketuvim*, and one from *Nevi'im*. On this reading, the phrase *u'vetoratcha katuv leimor* itself counts as the *pasuk* from Torah, a parallel phrase for *Nevi'im* serves as the second, and the phrase for *Ketuvim* as the third. We rule like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri that three suffice, one from each section, and these formulaic phrases are themselves the fulfillment of that requirement. This is thus not a third alternative separate from the ten-or-three debate; it is a way of satisfying the three-*pasuk* requirement with the most minimal possible formulation.

### Rashi's Reading

Rashi refuses the premise that *u'vetoratcha katuv leimor* provides a shortcut for *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* at all. Rashi holds that where the *gemara* speaks of *nafishei krai* — too many verses — it is referring to the *pesukim* of *musaf*, the verses associated with the *korban* offering, not to the verses of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*. The formula *u'vetoratcha katuv leimor* applies to the *musaf korban* verses, allowing one to reference them without quoting them in full. When the *gemara* then shifts and says the real problem is *avshei brachot*, Rashi understands that to mean the *pesukim* of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* — because those *brachot* are long and their verses cannot be replaced by the formula. On Rashi's reading, the formula is unavailable for *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*, and those *pesukim* must be recited in full.

### Musaf Verses

Tosafot takes sharp issue with Rashi's reading. For Tosafot, it is the *musaf* verses — not the *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* verses — that cannot be replaced by a formula. The reason is theologically significant: *tefillah* serves as a replacement for the *korbanot*, and if one wants the *musaf* prayer to function as a substitute for the *musaf* offering, one must verbalize the actual *pesukim* describing that offering. *Mikraot shel musaf tzarich l'hazkir l'olam sheheim b'makom hakorbanot* — the verses of *musaf* must always be stated explicitly because they stand in place of the *korbanot*. The formula works for the verses of *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros*, not for the *musaf korban* verses. Rashi and Tosafot thus arrive at precisely opposite conclusions about which set of verses is reducible.

### Rosh Chodesh Musaf

Tosafot raises a further question about the *musaf* of Rosh Chodesh, which coincides with Rosh Hashanah. Rashi holds that both the Rosh Hashanah *musaf* and the Rosh Chodesh *musaf* must be mentioned. Tosafot disagrees on whether the *pesukim* must be recited and also on whether Rosh Chodesh itself should be explicitly mentioned. Tosafot rules that one need not mention Rosh Chodesh explicitly; it is already subsumed in the phrase *milvad olat hachodesh u'minchatah* — the standard formulation — and for the *chatat* one says *b'shnei se'irim l'chaper u'shnei tmidim k'hilchatam*, which is the very language of our established *nusach*. The *Ran* offers a striking rationale for why Rosh Chodesh should not be highlighted: if one emphasizes that the day has the status of Rosh Chodesh, people will begin thinking of it primarily as Rosh Chodesh and recall that on a two-day Rosh Chodesh the second day is the true Rosh Chodesh, thereby undermining the sanctity of the first day of Rosh Hashanah. By not drawing attention to the Rosh Chodesh dimension, we protect the integrity of the day itself.

These are the debates concerning which *tefillah* we are discussing, a point worth making explicit: the entire discussion about the *shliach tzibur* being *motzi* everyone, and about the length of the *brachot*, concerns the *musaf* prayer. According to most *rishonim* and the accepted *halacha*, *malchuyos*, *zichronos*, and *shofros* are said only in *musaf*, not in every *tefillah* of Rosh Hashanah.

## Preparation Issues

### Mental Ordering

Rav Elazar states a general principle: *l'olam yasdir adam tfilato v'achar kach yitpallel* — a person should always first order his prayer mentally and only then daven. This is especially relevant in an oral culture without *siddurim*, where one must carry the entire *tefillah* in one's head before beginning.

### Special Occasions

Rav Abba qualifies this: *mistabra milta d'Rabbi Eliezer b'vrachot shel Rosh Hashanah v'shel Yom HaKippurim v'shel prakim* — the principle applies specifically to the *brachot* of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and *prakim* — the infrequent prayers, such as the *shemoneh esrei* of Yom Tov. These are *tefillot* one does not normally say, and one must prepare as one would prepare *leining* before *leyning* — do not get up without having practiced. For the daily *tefillah*, however, which one knows by heart, no such preparation is required.

### Yehuda Exception

The *gemara* challenges this from the practice of Rav Yehuda, who would order his *tefillah* even before his regular daily prayer. If Rav Abba says the daily *tefillah* requires no preparation, how do we account for Rav Yehuda's practice?

### Monthly Davening

The *gemara* resolves this: *shani Rav Yehuda*, Rav Yehuda is exceptional — *keivan d'matzli mitlatin yomin l'tlatin yomin*, because he davened only once a month. There is a *gemara* elsewhere indicating that those immersed in constant Torah study may be exempt from prayer during their learning. Rav Yehuda would complete his review of his entire learning — Rashi suggests he would *chazar* through *Shas* once a month — and upon completing that cycle, he would pause and daven. For Rav Yehuda, therefore, *k'prakim dami* — each instance of davening is like a Yom Tov prayer, an infrequent event requiring advance preparation.

## Communal Exemption

### Field Workers

A *baraita* transmitted by Rabbi Abba bar Avira in the name of Rav Shimon Chasida states: *poter haya Rabban Gamliel afilu am she'basadot* — Rabban Gamliel would exempt even the people in the fields. This is not merely saying that those present in *shul* are *yotzei* through the *shliach tzibur*; it implies that Rabban Gamliel's principle, taken to its logical conclusion, extends even to those who cannot come to *shul* at all. The *tefillat hatzibur* speaks for the entire community, and the entire community — including those prevented from attending — is represented by it.

### City Objection

The *gemara* raises an immediate objection. If those in the fields are exempt, does it not follow — *kol sh'ken* — that those who remain in the city should certainly be exempt? But that conclusion seems wrong. Those in the fields have no choice; they are working and cannot attend. Those who are in the city, however, could come and choose not to — and by not coming, they are *poresh min hatzibur*, separating themselves from the community. This is comparable to the principle of those who stand behind the *kohanim* during *birkat kohanim* and are therefore not included in the blessing: by positioning themselves outside the gathered community, they exclude themselves.

### Necessity Criterion

The resolution, brought by Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida, limits Rabban Gamliel's exemption precisely: *lo patar Rabban Gamliel ella am she'basadot* — he exempts only those in the fields, meaning those prevented from attending by necessity, *mishum d'anisei bim'lacha* — because they are compelled by their labor. Those in the city who could attend but do not are not exempted; *aval ba'ir lo*. They have separated themselves from the community and therefore cannot claim the benefit of its communal prayer.

### Full Attendance

An additional condition is implied by the Ran and grounded in the *Rif*: even for those who do attend, the exemption applies only to those who are present from the beginning to the end of *chazarat hashatz* — *shamu me'reshitah v'ad sofah*. Partial attendance does not suffice. One is either fully part of the communal *tefillah* or one is not.

### Communal Nature

The theological thrust of Rabban Gamliel's position comes into clearest focus here. His exemption is not predicated on a mechanism of *shomea k'oneh* — the principle by which hearing another's recitation serves as one's own. Rabban Gamliel himself made this clear earlier: in the context of a *tzibur*, he sees no need for private *shemoneh esrei* at all, not merely because one can be *yotzei* through the *shliach tzibur*, but because the mode of prayer in a communal setting is fundamentally different. It is *tefillat hatzibur* — the prayer of the entire community as a unified entity — and that prayer is offered by one *shliach tzibur* on behalf of the whole. This is not one person discharging another's individual obligation; it is an entirely different category of prayer in which all members of the community participate by virtue of being part of that community. For those unable to be physically present due to genuine necessity, they remain part of that community and therefore part of its prayer. Those who absent themselves by choice have severed that connection and cannot be included.

---

*Hadran alach Yom Tov u'slika lah masechet Rosh Hashanah.*

---

---

# Yoma 2

## Masechet Organizatio (II)

### Welcome & Overview

Welcome to the beginning of *Masechet Yoma* and to our return to the Bavli. The placement of *Masechet Yoma* within *Shas* raises an immediate question about organization. In the *Mishnayot*, the *masechtot* of *Moed* are arranged in a particular sequence, but in the standard printed Bavli edition the order differs. The reason is that the Bavli organizes *masechtot* by size — defined by number of *perakim* — so *Shabbos* comes first as the largest, followed by *Eruvin* and then *Pesachim*.

### Order in Bavli vs Mishna

Once you have the three *masechtot* of *Yoma*, *Sukkah*, and *Rosh Hashanah*, it is easy to reorganize them to follow the calendar sequence of the *yamim tovim*. The year's *regalim* begin with *Nisan*, as the *Torah* treats *Pesach* as the opening of the festival cycle, and so the Bavli places *Pesachim* first, followed by *Rosh Hashanah*, *Yoma*, and *Sukkah* — a perfect chronological arc. In the *Mishnayot*, however, *Yoma* precedes *Rosh Hashanah*, and *Shekalim* follows *Yoma*. The *Daf Yomi* cycle we are now following adheres to the *Mishnayot* order, placing *Yoma* before *Rosh Hashanah*. Interestingly, the *Daf Yomi* continues to follow the *Mishnayot* sequence even after *Yoma*, proceeding to *Sukkah*, then *Beitzah*, then *Rosh Hashanah* — the actual order of the *Mishnayot* — rather than the reorganized Bavli sequence.

### Timeline & Length

*Masechet Yoma* runs to approximately eighty-eight *daf*, making it a roughly three-month commitment. After *Yoma*, nearly every remaining *masechet* in *Moed* is approximately one month in length — with *Sukkah* being a partial exception — leaving us about eleven months until the completion of *Seder Moed*.

---

## Kohen Gadol Separati (II)

### Seven-Day Separation

The *masechet* opens: *shivat yamim kodem Yom HaKippurim mafrishin kohen gadol mibeito lelishkat parhedrin* — seven days before *Yom Kippur*, they would separate the *kohen gadol* from his home and bring him to the *Lishkat Parhedrin*. Seven days before *Yom Kippur* is *Tzom Gedaliah*, meaning the separation took place right at the start of the *Aseret Yemei Teshuva*, immediately after the two days of *Rosh Hashanah*. The *Lishkat Parhedrin* was a chamber situated at the boundary between the *Ezrat Nashim* and the *Ezrat Yisrael*, essentially at the entrance to the *azara*, and this is where the *kohen gadol* would remain for the entire week leading up to *Yom Kippur*.

---

## Masechet Organizatio (II)

### Eight Perakim Structure

It is worth pausing to note the literary architecture of *Masechet Yoma* itself. The *masechet* contains eight *perakim*, of which the first seven deal entirely with *Avodat Yom HaKippurim* — the Temple service — while only the eighth addresses *Yom Kippur* as we observe it today: the *inuyim*, *teshuva*, and the experience of the day itself. This parallels the very structure described in the opening *Mishna*: seven days of preparation culminating in the eighth day, which is *Yom Kippur* itself. Seven *perakim* of preparation leading to the eighth, which is the day — there is an elegant structural parallel that is difficult to regard as coincidental.

A comparable structure appears in *Masechet Shabbat*, where six *perakim* deal with preparatory matters and issues of carrying before the seventh *perek*, *Klal Gadol*, finally lists the *lamed-tet melachot* — as if the six preceding *perakim* represent the six days of labor leading to the seventh, which is *Shabbat* itself. The *Rambam* mirrors this in his *Mishneh Torah*, where six introductory *perakim* precede the seventh *perek* that begins the laws of the *lamed-tet melachot*. The same numerological structure — seven leading to eight — appears to be operative here in *Yoma*.

---

## Kohen Gadol Separati (II)

### Substitute Kohen

Continuing the *Mishna*: *u'matkinin lo kohen acher tachtav shema ye'arei bo psul* — they would also prepare another *kohen* as a stand-in in case the *kohen gadol* were to become disqualified. Since he was carefully sequestered and protected during this period, the most plausible concern for *tuma* was that he would experience a seminal emission. The stand-in was not the regular *segan*, the designated deputy *kohen gadol*, but rather a specifically designated understudy appointed for this contingency.

### Backup Wife & Ein Ladava…

*Rabbi Yehuda omer af isha acheret matkinin lo* — Rabbi Yehuda adds that they would also prepare for him a second wife, in case his wife should die during this period. The basis is the *pasuk*: *v'chiper ba'ado u-va'ad beito* — "he shall atone for himself and for his household" — and *beito zo ishto*, "his household" means his wife. A *kohen gadol* who is unmarried is invalid to perform the *Yom Kippur* service. There is a broader principle running through *halacha* — touching on the *shliach tzibbur* and members of the *Sanhedrin* as well — that being married draws a person out of a purely self-oriented existence and renders him more capable of representing and empathizing with others. Here the requirement is grounded in a *pasuk*, but the thematic resonance with those other contexts is notable.

The *Mishna* records the objection raised against Rabbi Yehuda: *im ken ein ladavar sof* — if so, there is no end to the matter. If we worry that his wife might die, we should also worry that the backup wife might die, and then we should need a third, and a fourth, and so on. The response implicit in the objection is instructive about the nature of *halachic* risk assessment. The concern about the *kohen gadol* becoming *tamei* through seminal emission is a reasonable likelihood and therefore warrants a contingency plan. But the concern that his wife will suddenly die is far-fetched; and if we entertain far-fetched possibilities, we cannot stop — *ein ladavar sof*, reductio ad absurdum. A reasonable approach prepares for seminal emission but does not spiral into unlimited contingency planning for a wife dying and a backup wife dying after her.

---

## Parah Adumah Parallel

### Kohen Hasoref Separation

The *Gemara* now cites a parallel *Mishna* from *Masechet Parah*: *shivat yamim kodem srifat hapara hayu mafrishin kohen hasoref et hapara mibeito lelishka she'al p'nei habira, tzfonah mizrachah* — similarly, seven days before the burning of the *para aduma*, the *kohen* who would burn it was separated from his home to a chamber that was "on the face of the *bira*," in the northeast.

### Lishkat Beis Even

This chamber was called the *Lishkat Beis Even* — the Chamber of Stone. Why the name? *Shekol ma'aseha bichlei glalim bichlei avanim uvichlei adama* — because all vessels used there were made of *glalim* (dried animal dung), stone, and unworked earth. Critically, none of these materials are susceptible to *tuma*: stone vessels, vessels of dried dung, and unfired mud — not fired *cheres* (earthenware) but simply hardened sun-dried earth — cannot become *tamei*. The chamber was named for the stone vessels that so characterized its contents.

### Stringencies & Sadducees

The *Gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason they insisted on exclusively *tuma*-proof vessels? The answer: *keivan detvul yom kasher bapara* — because, as we are taught, a *tvul yom* is valid for the *para aduma*. And not merely valid — they would go out of their way to ensure that the *kohen* performing the burning was in fact a *tvul yom*.

The *Mishna* in *Masechet Para* records: *metama'im hayu hakohen hasoref et hapara u'mativlin oto* — they would render the *kohen* who burned the *para* *tamei* and then immerse him in the *mikveh*, after which he would begin the *avoda* as a *tvul yom*, while still in the diminished state before nightfall completed his purification. The reason: *lehotzi miliban shel tzedukim* — to uproot the position of the Sadducees, *shehayu omrim bime'orvei shemesh hayta ne'eset* — who held that the *para aduma* could only be performed by someone who had achieved complete *tahara* after nightfall.

This is a striking deliberate choice. Normally the Rabbis, even when something is technically permitted, would prefer to perform a *mitzva* in the most *lechatchila* manner possible. Here they went in the opposite direction — actively engineering a state of *tuma* — to publicly demonstrate the rabbinic position against the Sadducees. It is worth remembering how significant the Sadducean presence was in the Temple. As Josephus and other sources make clear, many *kohanim* were Sadducees. The Sadducees did not, strictly speaking, reject *Torah Sheba'al Peh* as a matter of principle the way the later *Karaim* did, but they had fundamental interpretive differences with the Rabbis on certain critical questions. The Sadducee question was live and consequential in the Temple's operation, and this is precisely why — as we will see later in the *masechet* — the *kohen gadol* is made to swear on *Erev Yom Kippur* that he will follow the rabbinic approach and not the Sadducean one.

### Tosafot on Tvul Yom

Now, once they allowed themselves this leniency in order to make a point, they counterbalanced it with extreme stringency in all other aspects. *Tiknu rabanan klei galal uchelei avanim uchelei adamah* — they instituted that all vessels used would be ones incapable of receiving *tuma*, *kedei dela lezalzlu bah* — so that this single leniency would not allow the whole procedure to be treated lightly.

*Tosafot* takes the analysis a step further and significantly tempers the apparent radicalism of the *Mishna*. *Tosafot* says: *lav betumah d'Oraisa timuhu* — they never actually rendered him *tamei* with biblical-level *tuma*. They would never have allowed the *kohen* to be genuinely, biblically *tamei*. Indeed, from the *perek Ein Dorshin* we know that even the garments of those who ate *kodshim* — *kohanim* who ate *korbanos* — were considered *tamei* for the purposes of the *para aduma kohen*, so stringent was the standard. How could one imagine they would permit genuine biblical *tuma*?

Rather, *Tosafot* explains, citing the *Mishna* in *Parah* 3: *samchu yadeihem alav veshavu veomrim lo ishi Kohen Gadol red tevol achas* — they would lay their hands on him and tell him, "My lord, *kohen gadol*, go and immerse once." The act that rendered him "*tamei*" was merely the touch of another person. Because the *kohen* performing the *para* was being held to such an extraordinary standard of *tahara* — whereby even contact with *kohanim* who ate *korbanos* constituted *tumah* for him — this rabbinic-level *tuma* from that touch was what he immersed from. He was then a *tvul yom* not from biblical *tuma* but from a *tumah derabanan*.

*Tosafot*'s reading is that the so-called leniency was barely a leniency at all; if anything, the entire procedure began from a platform of extraordinary *chumra*, since the *kohen* was already being treated as if any human contact made him *tamei*. The single point of "leniency" — immersion and then proceeding as a *tvul yom* — was itself an expression of rabbinic-level *tuma* from an almost trivial contact, not genuine biblical impurity.

---

## Chamber Location & Signi…

### Why Stone & Northeast

The *Gemara* asks two further questions about the *Lishkat Beis Even*: why was it called *beis even* (we have explained this above), and *mai shna tzfonah mizrachah* — why specifically was this chamber located in the northeast?

*Keivan de-chatat hi ve-chatat teuna tzfonah* — because the *para aduma* is called a *chatat*, and a *chatat* is performed in the north side of the *mizbe'ach*. Additionally, *al nochach pnei ohel moed* — the *para aduma* is performed facing the *Ohel Moed*, meaning the *kohen* stood on *Har HaMishcha* — the Mount of Olives (*Har HaZeitim*), which lies to the east of *Har HaBayit* — and faced westward toward the *Beis HaMikdash*, sprinkling the blood in that direction. Since the *para aduma* is called a *chatat*, which ordinarily indicates the north, and since it is physically performed to the east with the *kohen* facing the *Beis HaMikdash*, *tekinu lah rabanan lishkat tzfonah mizrachah* — the Rabbis established her preparatory chamber in the northeast, *ke-heichi de-lehvei leh hekera*, so that it symbolizes both dimensions at once — the north of *chatat* and the east of the actual performance on *Har HaMishcha*.

### Definition of Bira

The *Gemara* then asks *mai bira* — what does the phrase *al p'nei habira* mean? Two *Amoraim* disagree. *Rabbah bar Bar Chana* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* says: it was a specific location on *Har HaBayit* that was called *bira* by name. *Resh Lakish* disagrees and says: the entire *Mikdash* is referred to as *bira* — as in the phrase *habira asher hachinoti*, the "capital" or "fortress" that *David HaMelech* said he had prepared. On this reading, *al p'nei habira* tells us only that the chamber faced or was adjacent to the *Beis HaMikdash*, without specifying its exact location.

### Inside vs Outside Ezrah

*Tosafot* draws an important distinction between the two chambers — the one for the *para aduma* and the one for the *kohen gadol*. The *Lishkat Parhedrin*, in which the *kohen gadol* was sequestered before *Yom Kippur*, was located within the *azara* proper: *lishkas parhedrin she-bnuyah bekodesh* — because all of his *avoda* on *Yom Kippur* would take place within the *azara*, the *heichal*, and the *Kodesh Kodashim*, it was fitting that his preparatory chamber also be within the sanctified space.

By contrast, the *kohen* of the *para aduma* performed his *avoda* outside the *Beis HaMikdash* entirely — on *Har HaMishcha* — and therefore *perishaso le-lishkah she-al p'nei habirah u-she-chutz la-azrah*: his chamber was one that was outside the *azara* proper, perhaps in the *Ezrat Nashim* or elsewhere on *Har HaBayit*. The principle is elegantly consistent: the location of the preparatory chamber mirrors the location of the *avoda* for which the *kohen* is being prepared.

---

## Seven-Day Source

### Tzivah-Tzivah Source

Having established the practice, the *Gemara* asks *mena hanei milei* — from where do we derive the requirement for a seven-day separation? *Rabbi Minyomi bar Chilkiyah* in the name of *Rav Machasiyah bar Idi* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* cites the *pasuk* from *Parshat Tzav* concerning the *milu'im*: *ka'asher asah bayom hazeh tziva Hashem la'asot lechaper aleichem* — "as he has done this day, so God has commanded to do, to atone for you." During the *milu'im*, *Aharon* and his sons were separated for seven days in the courtyard of the *Mishkan* in preparation for the inauguration of the *avoda* on the eighth day. The *pasuk* at the close of that episode appears somewhat redundant — God commanded to do this, and God commanded to atone for you — but the *Gemara* reads the two verbs as carrying distinct referents.

*La'asot* — "to do" in the future — means *elu ma'aseh parah*: when you similarly perform this type of act in the future, do it as you did today, with a seven-day separation before the eighth. *Lechaper* — "to atone" — means *elu ma'asei Yom HaKippurim*: this refers to the *avoda* of *Yom Kippur*. Neither the *para aduma* nor *Yom Kippur* had yet been commanded at the point of the *milu'im*, but the *pasuk* indicates that both are anticipated.

The *Gemara* immediately asks: *bishlama kulei kra befarah lo misukam* — the entire *pasuk* cannot be referring only to the *para aduma*, because it says *lechaper* and *ufarah lav bas kaparah hi* — the *para aduma* is not an act of *kapara*. While it is true that *chatat* can mean purification rather than sin-atonement, and indeed by *Yom Kippur* itself the *pasuk* speaks of *v'chipper es mikdash ha-kodesh u-mi-tumos Bnei Yisrael* — cleansing from *tumah* — the *Gemara* treats *kapara* as not applicable to the *para aduma*. So the *pasuk* must be addressing two things.

But then perhaps the entire *pasuk* refers only to *Yom Kippur*? The *Gemara* answers by invoking a *gezeira shava* of *tziva-tziva*: *ela yalif tziva tziva*. The *pasuk* at the *milu'im* says *tziva Hashem la'asot*. The *pasuk* opening the commandment of *para aduma* says *zos chukas hatorah asher tziva Hashem*. Both use the word *tziva*. This *gezeira shava* links the *milu'im* passage to the *para aduma* passage, and since the *milu'im* involved seven days of separation preceding the eighth day of inauguration, we learn that the *para aduma* similarly requires a seven-day separation. And *lechaper* remains available to indicate *Yom Kippur*.

But why not construct a *tziva-tziva gezeira shava* with *Yom Kippur* instead? After all, the *pasuk* at the conclusion of the *Yom Kippur* section says *vaya'as ka'asher tziva Hashem es Moshe* — "and he did as God had commanded Moses." The *Gemara* answers: *danin tziva d'lifnei asiya mitziva d'lifnei asiya, v'ein danin tziva d'le'achar asiya mitziva d'lifnei asiya*. We link a *tziva* that precedes the act to another *tziva* that precedes the act. The *pasuk* by the *milu'im* says *tziva... la'asot* — "commanded to do" — commanding before the performance. The *para aduma* likewise opens with *asher tziva Hashem* — commanding before the act. But the *Yom Kippur* *pasuk*, *vaya'as ka'asher tziva*, appears at the end, after the entire *avoda* has been described — it is a *tziva d'le'achar asiya*, a command-reference after the fact. We therefore do not link it to the command-reference that precedes the act.

### Timing of Command

What of the possibility that *la'asot* refers to all *korbanos*, since the *Torah* also says *beyom tzovoso es bnei Yisrael lehakriv es korbanaihem* — "on the day He commanded the children of Israel to bring their offerings" — which is also a *tziva* preceding an act of bringing? The *Gemara* answers: *danin tziva mitziva, v'ein danin tzovoso mitziva*. The *milu'im* *pasuk* says *tziva* and the *para aduma* *pasuk* says *tziva* — an exact verbal match. The *korbanot* *pasuk* uses *tzovoso*, a different conjugation.

The *Gemara* anticipates an objection: does the precise form of the word really matter? *Detana devei Rebbi Yishmael* — from the school of *Rebbi Yishmael*, who is known for his somewhat broader hermeneutical approach relative to *Rebbi Akiva*, we find that he makes a *gezeira shava* between *veshav hakohen* and *uva hakohen* in the laws of *tzara'as* — *shav* and *ba* are entirely different words, yet *zu hi shiva zu hi bia*, since "returning" and "coming" mean the same thing in that context, he links them. If *Rebbi Yishmael* is willing to link two completely different words on the basis of shared meaning, why should an inexact match between *tziva* and *tzovoso* prevent a *gezeira shava*?

The *Gemara* answers: *hanei mili heicha d'leika d'dami lei* — that principle applies only when there is no better option, when the closest match available is a semantic one. But *aval heicha d'ika d'dami lei* — where there is an exact verbal match available, *mid'dami lei yalfinan*, we derive the law from the closer match rather than the more distant one. Since *tziva* and *tziva* are an exact match, we prefer that linkage over *tziva* to *tzovoso*.

This discussion opens into a broader reflection on the nature of *gezeira shava* and the *mesorah* underlying it. The *Ramban*, in his *Hassagot* on the *Rambam*'s *Sefer Hamitzvot*, raises the following question: if a *gezeira shava* requires a *mesorah* going back to *Sinai*, why does the *Gemara* suggest alternatives — why not use this *gezeira shava*, why not use that one? If the *mesorah* fixed the precise *gezeira shava*, there would be nothing to discuss. The *Ramban* answers that the *mesorah* was not the exact formulation of the *gezeira shava* but rather the underlying *halacha* itself — the tradition that a seven-day separation was required for the *para aduma* and *Yom Kippur*, derivable via *gezeira shava* from the *milu'im*. Within that framework, it remained to determine which precise linguistic link best instantiated the derivation. The *mesorah* established the *what*; the *drasha* works out the *how*.

This bears on a broader question that has occupied both *Rishonim* and contemporary scholars: when *Chazal* derived *halacha* from *pesukim*, were they genuinely discovering laws through exegesis, or were they retroactively anchoring already-established traditions in scriptural language? The *Ramban*'s approach suggests the latter was at least sometimes operative — the tradition preceded the *drasha*, and the *drasha* expressed it in a canonical form. That does not make it an *asmachta*; the *Ramban* holds that the practice itself traced to *Har Sinai*. But the specific *gezeira shava* formulating that practice in terms of *tziva-tziva* may have been a post-facto articulation of what was always known.

---

## Alternatives Rejected

### All Korbanos Rejected

The *Gemara* works through a series of alternative applications for the seven-day separation derived from *milu'im*, rejecting each in turn. First: *ve'eima tziva d'korbanos* — perhaps the principle applies to all *korbanos*, requiring every *kohen* to observe a seven-day separation before performing any Temple service. This is not unreasonable on its face: *kohanim* serve only briefly, and a week of preparation prior to service would be fitting.

The *Gemara* raises the counter-suggestion: *niba'ei prisha l'chulei mishmeres beis av* — one could require each *beis av* (the daily subdivision of the weekly *mishmar*) to prepare for its day of service. Each *kohen* knows in advance which day of the week his *beis av* is scheduled to work; he could simply begin his seven-day preparation the week before. The objection is answered on principled grounds: *donin davar shekavu'a lo zman midavar shekavu'a lo zman* — we derive from *milu'im*, which was a singular fixed occasion, only to things that similarly have a single fixed time. *Korbanos* are brought every day of the year; they are not a single special occasion of sufficient gravity to demand the kind of preparation that *milu'im* models.

### Regalim Rejected

Perhaps the requirement should apply to the *regalim*, the pilgrimage festivals — a far more significant category than quotidian *korbanos*? The *Gemara* rejects this as well: *donin davar shenoheg pa'am achas b'shana midavar shenoheg pa'am achas b'shana* — we learn from something that occurs once a year to something that occurs once a year. The *regalim*, though individually significant, occur three times a year as a group, and are not analogous to a single unique annual occasion. The *milu'im* was once in a lifetime; the relevant structural parallel is to something that occurs exactly once annually, not three times.

### Specific Regalim Rejected

Could the principle apply to one specific *regel*? Two candidates present themselves. *Ei Chag HaMatzos* — *Pesach* might be chosen because *hakesuv* opens the calendar cycle with it, as the *Torah*'s festival legislation begins with *Pesach*. Or *ei Chag HaSuccos* — *Sukkot* might be chosen because *ho'il u'merubah mitzvosav*, it carries the greatest concentration of *mitzvos* among the *regalim*, receives the most detailed treatment in the *pesukim*, and carries the eschatological weight of *Zechariah*'s prophecy that all nations will gather *lachog es Chag HaSuccos*.

The *Gemara* rejects both with a single principle: *donin prishas shiva l'yom echad miprishas shiva l'yom echad, v'ein donin prishas shiva l'shiva miprishas shiva l'yom echad* — we learn seven days of preparation for a single day from the model of seven days of preparation for a single day. *Chag HaMatzos* and *Chag HaSuccos* each last seven days; preparing for them would be a seven-day preparation for seven days, not for a single climactic day. The *milu'im* model is specifically seven unsanctified days leading to one special eighth day, not seven days leading into a seven-day *yom tov*.

---

## Shemini Atzeret Status

### Rav Ashi's Argument

The *Gemara* raises one further candidate: *ve'eima shemini* — perhaps the principle should apply to *Shemini Atzeret*, since *Sukkot* would then serve as seven days of preparation for the single day of *Shemini Atzeret* — precisely the structure of *d'prishas shiva l'yom echad*. The *Gemara* rejects this on formal grounds: *donin davar she'ein kedusha lefanav midavar she'ein kedusha lefanav* — we derive from a scenario in which the preparatory period carries no inherent sanctity to another such scenario. Before the *milu'im*, the seven days were ordinary. Before *Yom Kippur*, the *Aseret Yemei Teshuva* are *chol*. But the seven days of *Sukkot* are *yom tov*, days of *kedusha*, and one cannot derive from seven unsanctified preparatory days to seven sanctified *yom tov* days.

One might attempt a *kal vachomer*: if something with no sanctity before it still demands such extensive preparation, then surely something with seven days of *kedusha* before it should demand even more. *Rav Ashi* offers a more fundamental objection: *mi ika midi de'ikar regel lo ba prisha tafel didei ba prisha* — is there any case in which the primary *regel* does not require preparation, yet its appendage does? *Sukkot* is the main *regel*; *Shemini Atzeret* is, in some sense, its culmination. If we do not require a seven-day preparation for *Sukkot* itself, it is absurd to require one for *Shemini Atzeret*.

### Pazarkeshav Framework

The *Gemara* preempts an objection: *va'afillu leman de'amar shemini regel bifnei atzmo hu* — even granting the view that *Shemini Atzeret* is an independent *regel*, that independence is limited to the matters summarized by the acronym *pazarkeshav*.

*Pei* — *payis bifnei atzmo*: a new lottery (*payis*) is conducted on *Shemini Atzeret* for the distribution of *korbanos* among the *mishmarot*, rather than continuing from wherever *Sukkot* left off. Even if some *mishmarot* had brought fewer bulls over the seven days of *Sukkot*, *Shemini Atzeret* starts fresh with a new lottery, treating itself as entirely independent. *Zayin* — *zman bifnei atzmo*: a *Shehecheyanu* is recited on *Shemini Atzeret*, as opposed to the last day of *Pesach*, which does not receive its own *Shehecheyanu*. *Reish* — *regel bifnei atzmo*: it has its own name (*Shemini Atzeret*) and its *mitzvot* differ from those of *Sukkot* — there is no *lulav* and no *sukka* obligation. *Kuf* — *korban bifnei atzmo*: its *musaf* offering does not follow the descending pattern of the seventy bulls over *Sukkot* but has its own distinct form; notably, the *Torah* introduces it with an independent formulation, *u'vayom hashmini*, rather than the continuation pattern used for the intermediate days. *Shin* — *shir bifnei atzmo*: the *shir shel yom* on *Shemini Atzeret* differs from those of *Sukkot*. The *shir shel yom* throughout *Sukkot* reflected the theme of gathering produce and the obligations of *matnot aniyim* — *va'ger, ve'aniyecha, ve'ha'almanah ve'hayatom, lo ta'azvenu* — appropriate to harvest time. The *Shemini Atzeret shir* is distinct, though *Rashi* notes *v'lo pirshu lanu eizeh shirah* — it was not transmitted to us which *shir* it was; *Tosafot* cites the tradition that it was *Lamnatzeach al hashminit*. *Vet* — *bracha bifnei atzmo*: it has its own *bracha*. *Rashi* cites a *Tosefta* regarding a special blessing given to the king; *Tosafot* offers the more practically relevant explanation that in *Birkat HaMazon* and *Shemoneh Esrei* the *chag* is identified not as *Chag HaSukkot* but as *Shemini Chag HaAtzeret*, reflecting an independent identity.

### Tashlumim Status

Despite all these dimensions of independence, *Shemini Atzeret* nevertheless retains a subordinate relationship to *Sukkot* in one critical respect: *le'inyan tashlumin tashlumin derishon hu* — with regard to making up missed *korbanos*, it functions as *tashlumim* of the first day. If one failed to bring the *korban chagiga* on the first day of *Sukkot*, one may bring it on any of the subsequent days of *Sukkot* — and this makeup window extends through *Shemini Atzeret* as well. A missed *chagiga* of *Sukkot* can be remedied on *Shemini Atzeret*. This means that however independent *Shemini Atzeret* may be across the six dimensions of *pazarkeshav*, it remains, in this one dimension, the tail end of *Sukkot*. And that is precisely *Rav Ashi*'s point: if *Sukkot* itself does not require a seven-day preparation, then *Shemini Atzeret* — which remains *Sukkot*'s *tashlumim* — cannot require one either. The question of how to balance *Shemini Atzeret*'s independence against its continuing relationship to *Sukkot* will receive further treatment as we continue.

---

---

# Yoma 3

## Miluim & Seven Days

### Setup: Preparation Paral…

The *Gemara* on today's *daf* opens by addressing the question raised by the *Mishnah*: what is the biblical basis for the seven-day preparation of the *Kohen Gadol* prior to the *Avodah* on *Yom Kippur*, during which he was separated from his household? A parallel *Mishnah* in *Parah* records an identical seven-day preparation for the *kohen* who would perform the *Parah Adumah* ritual. The *Gemara* has been seeking the source for both of these practices. The answer it has been exploring derives from the verse describing the *Miluim* — the seven-day consecration period before the *kohanim* inaugurated the *Avodah* in the *Beit Hamikdash*. The verse there reads: *kaasher asah bayom hazeh tsivah Hashem la'asot lekaper alechem* — "as was done on this day, so God commanded to do, to atone for you" — which the *Gemara* interprets as a divine directive to replicate this paradigm in future contexts.
