Two such contexts are identified: *Parah Adumah*, derived through a *gezerah shavah* on the word *tsivah*, and *Yom Kippur*, linked through the word *lekaper*.

### Gezerah Shavah: Tzivah

The connection to *Yom Kippur* via *lekaper* is admittedly broad, since *lekaper* could refer generically to any *korban*. The *Gemara* therefore adds a restriction: the referent must resemble *Yom Kippur* — it must be a special, singular event, not a routine offering. Furthermore, it must be a one-day event, which immediately rules out the *regalim*.

### Excluding Regalim

Having eliminated the three pilgrimage festivals, the *Gemara* considers whether *Shemini Atzeret* might serve as the intended one-day event. At the top of 3a, the *Gemara* raises this possibility seriously, noting that *Shemini Atzeret* does indeed stand as an independent day in six distinct respects, encapsulated in the mnemonic *Pezer Keshev*.

### Shemini Atzeret Independ…

These six dimensions of independence are as follows. *Payis*: a new lottery is conducted for the *korbanot*, initiating a fresh cycle of priestly divisions. *Zman*: a new *Shehecheyanu* is recited, distinct from the final day of *Chag Hamatzot*. *Regel bifnei atzmo*: it functions as an independent *regel*, with none of the distinctive practices of *Sukkot* — no *sukkah*, no *lulav*. *Korban bifnei atzmo*: it has its own independent *korban* rather than continuing the pattern of the *Sukkot Musaf* cycle. *Shir*: the *shir shel yom* sung during the *korbanot* on *Shemini Atzeret* is distinct — *Rashi* notes that the *shir* for *Sukkot* would be based on *matanot aniyim*, whereas *Shemini Atzeret* has its own. *Bracha bifnei atzmo*: it receives a distinct blessing — *Rashi* suggests this may refer to a special blessing offered to the king, or alternatively that in *Shmoneh Esrei* and in *Birkat Hamazon* it is given its own unique appellation: *Yom Hashmini Chag Ha'atzeret hazeh*.

### Tashlumin Link

Yet despite all of these markers of independence, *Shemini Atzeret* remains unmistakably bound to *Sukkot* in one critical legal respect: it is a *tashlumin* day. The *Mishnah* teaches that one who failed to bring the *korban chagigah* on the first day of the *regel* may make it up on any subsequent day of the festival — *chogeg veholech kol haregel kulo* — and may even bring it *beyom tov acharon shel chag*, on the final day, which is *Shemini Atzeret*. The *Rambam* extends this to the *olat re'iah* as well. Accordingly, *Shemini Atzeret* functions as a makeup day for obligations incurred during *Sukkot* itself.

### Shemini Atzeret Ruled Out

It would therefore be incoherent to require a seven-day separation before *Shemini Atzeret* while not requiring one before *Sukkot*, since *Shemini Atzeret* is clearly the culmination of *Sukkot*. This rules out *Shemini Atzeret* as a candidate, and the *Gemara* concludes that the seven-day preparation must point to *Yom Kippur*.

### Shavuot Candidate

The *Gemara* now turns to the next obvious candidate. Having eliminated *Pesach*, *Sukkot*, and *Shemini Atzeret*, the remaining one-day *Yom Tov* is *Atzeret* — the *Chazal*ic term for *Shavuot*. This appears structurally ideal: the *Miluim* involved seven days of preparation followed by one culminating day, and *Shavuot* is precisely a one-day event. The *Gemara* frames the question: *deparisha shiva leyoma chad* — why not say the seven-day separation for a one-day event applies to *Shavuot*?

### Rava's Distinction

Rava answers: *danin par echad ve'ayil echad mipar echad ve'ayil echad, le'apukei Atzeret dishnei eilim ninhu* — we derive from one *par* and one *ayil* to a case of one *par* and one *ayil*, thereby excluding *Shavuot*, which involves two *eilim*.

### Par & Ayil Comparison

The logic becomes clear upon examining the relevant verses. At the culmination of the *Miluim*, on the eighth day as recorded at the beginning of *Parshas Shmini* (Vayikra 9), *Aharon* is commanded: *kach lecha egel ben bakar lechatat ve'ayil le'olah* — one calf for a *chatat* and one ram for an *olah*. Turning to *Yom Kippur* in *Acharei Mos*, the verse reads: *bezot yavo Aharon el hakodesh bepar ben bakar lechatat ve'ayil le'olah* — again, one animal from the cattle family for a *chatat* and one ram for an *olah*, both for *Aharon*. The parallel is exact.

By contrast, the special *Avodah* of *Shavuot* — not the *Musaf*, but the offering brought *al halachem* in conjunction with the *shtei halechem* as recorded in *Emor* (Vayikra 23:18) — reads: *shivat kvasim tmimim bnei shana, ufar ben bakar echad ve'eilim shnayim yihyu olah l'Hashem*. Here, first, there are seven sheep. Second, the *par* is brought as an *olah*, not a *chatat* — already a significant difference. And third, there are two *eilim*, not one. The *Gemara* therefore concludes that *Yom Kippur*, which is identical to the *Miluim* in the structure of *Aharon*'s offering, is the correct parallel, while *Shavuot* is excluded.

---

## Korban Details

### Miluim Offerings

To lay this out precisely: on the eighth day of the *Miluim*, *Aharon* brought an *egel ben bakar lechatat* and an *ayil le'olah*. The *Bnei Yisrael* in turn brought a *se'ir izim lechatat*, an *egel*, and a *keves bnei shana le'olah*. The structure for *Aharon* — one bovine for a *chatat* and one ram for an *olah* — is what anchors the comparison.

### Yom Kippur Offerings

On *Yom Kippur*, the parallel is precise. *Aharon* brings *par ben bakar lechatat ve'ayil le'olah* — exactly matching the *Miluim*. For *Bnei Yisrael*, the verse specifies *shnei se'irei izim lechatat ve'ayil echad le'olah*. While the communal offering is not identical to the *Miluim*'s structure for *Bnei Yisrael*, it shares a recognizable pattern. But it is *Aharon*'s offering that is the focus, since the separation being discussed pertains to the *Kohen Gadol*, and here the correspondence is complete.

It is worth noting that the *Gemara* is deliberately setting aside the *Musaf* in these comparisons. The *Musaf* of *Yom Kippur* appears in *Parshas Pinchas*, where the verse reads: *par ben bakar echad ayil echad kevasim bnei shana shiva tmimim* — a *par*, an *ayil*, and seven *kevasim*, all as *olot*. This *Musaf* is unambiguously a separate matter from the special *Avodas Yom Hakippurim* of *Acharei Mos*. Indeed, by the *Miluim* as well, the eighth day happened to be *Rosh Chodesh*, so there was a *Musaf* on that day too — but that is similarly bracketed. What is being compared is the unique *Avodah* of the day, not the standing *Musaf*.

### Shavuot Differences

Returning to *Shavuot*: the offering brought *al halachem* — the special *Avodah* tied to the *shtei halechem* — presents multiple divergences from the *Miluim*. Most obviously, there are two rams rather than one. Additionally, the *par* is an *olah* rather than a *chatat*, which is itself already a structural difference. And there are seven *kevasim* alongside. Any one of these would distinguish *Shavuot* from the *Miluim*; all three together make the comparison untenable.

### One or Two Rams

The *Gemara* now raises an internal complication. The argument above — that *Yom Kippur* parallels the *Miluim* because both feature one *par* and one *ayil* — holds smoothly according to the view that there is only one *ayil* on *Yom Kippur*. But there is an opinion that on *Yom Kippur* there are in fact two *eilim* — in which case the parallel breaks down. The *Gemara* asks: *mai ika lemeimar?* — what can be said according to that opinion?

### Rabbi's View: Same Ram

A *baraita* is cited. *Rabbi* holds: *ayil echad hu ha'amur kan hu ha'amur beChumash Pikudim* — the single *ayil* mentioned in *Acharei Mos* and the *ayil* mentioned in *Chumash Pekudim* (i.e., *Pinchas*) are one and the same ram. According to *Rabbi*, therefore, the *Musaf* of *Yom Kippur* in *Pinchas* does not introduce an additional *ayil*; rather, the single *ayil* listed there is identical to the one in *Acharei Mos*, and there is in total only one ram.

### Yom Kippur Musaf

The *Musaf* passage in *Pinchas* reads: *uve'asor lachodesh hashvi'i hazeh mikra kodesh yihyeh lachem ve'inisem es nafshoseichem... vehikravtem olah la-Shem... par ben bakar echad ayil echad kevasim bnei shana shiva tmimim* — along with accompanying *menachos* and *nesachim*, followed by the qualification *milvad chatas hakippurim ve'olat hatamid uminchatah veniskeihem*. The passage is clearly structured as a *Musaf* and is fully independent of *Acharei Mos*. Moreover, the *par* here is an *olah*, whereas in *Acharei Mos* the *par* is a *lechatat* — this alone demonstrates they are different animals. And the seven *kevasim* in *Pinchas* have no parallel in *Acharei Mos*. The only potential overlap is the *ayil le'olah* that appears in both — and it is precisely about this *ayil* that *Rabbi* and *Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Shimon* disagree.

The peculiarity of *Rabbi*'s position is notable. Logic would suggest these are entirely separate offerings. One might even argue that if *Rabbi* wished to identify the *Pinchas ayil* with something in *Acharei Mos*, it would be more natural to link it with the *ayil* of *Bnei Yisrael* rather than the *ayil* of *Aharon*, since a *Musaf* is a communal offering and the *ayil le'olah* of *Bnei Yisrael* in *Acharei Mos* likewise has a communal character. Yet *Rabbi*'s stated position is that the *ayil* of the *Musaf* is the same as *Aharon*'s *ayil* — a puzzling equation that the *Gemara* leaves largely unexplained.

The larger context of the *Avodah* in *Acharei Mos* is worth recalling briefly. *Aharon* brings his *par*, performs the *viduy*, and sprinkles the blood — the famous *achas ve'sheva* — in the *Kodesh Kodashim*. The two *se'irim* of *Bnei Yisrael* play their central roles: one goes *la'Azazel*, the other undergoes the blood-sprinkling ritual *ve'chiper ba'ad kol adas Bnei Yisrael*. The *ayil le'olah* for *Aharon* and the *ayil le'olah* for *Bnei Yisrael*, by contrast, are dispatched with relative brevity — *vayatza ve'asah es olaso ve'es olas ha'am*. These *olot* are not the focal point of the day's *Avodah*.

### Rabbi Eliezer: Two Rams

*Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Shimon* disagrees: *shnei eilim hem ha'amur kan veha'amur beChumash Pikudim* — the two references to an *ayil* are two distinct rams. According to him, *Yom Kippur* involves not one but two rams, which would undermine the claimed parallel to the *Miluim*.

### Reconciliation

The *Gemara* resolves this: *afilu teima Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Shimon* — even according to *Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Shimon*, the comparison holds. *Hasam chad dechovas hayom vechad demussafim* — there, one ram belongs to the special *Avodah* of the day (*chovas hayom*) and the other belongs to the *Musaf*. As *Tosafot* observes, there was also a *Musaf* on the eighth day of the *Miluim* — because it happened to coincide with *Rosh Chodesh* — and yet that *Musaf* is not what anchors the comparison. It is the *chovas hayom* that matters, and as regards the *chovas hayom*, even *Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Shimon* agrees: one *par lechatat* and one *ayil le'olah* for *Aharon* — precisely mirroring the *Miluim*. The parallel therefore stands regardless of which opinion one follows on the question of one ram or two.

---

## Rosh Hashanah Excluded

### Rosh Hashanah Question

Having addressed *Shemini Atzeret* and *Shavuot*, the *Gemara* now raises *Rosh Hashanah* as another candidate for the one-day event to which the *Miluim* seven-day preparation might apply. *Rosh Hashanah* is a one-day *Yom Tov*, and its *Musaf* includes a *par* and an *ayil* — *par ben bakar echad ayil echad* — alongside seven *kevasim*, as recorded in *Pinchas*: *uve'echad lachodesh hashvi'i... par ben bakar echad ayil echad kevasim bnei shana shiva tmimim*. All are *olot*. If one were looking merely for a one-day occasion with a *par* and an *ayil*, *Rosh Hashanah* presents itself as a plausible candidate.

### Rav Abbahu: Tzibur

Rav Abbahu answers: *danin par ve'ayil shelo mipar ve'ayil shelo, le'apukei Atzeret ve-Rosh Hashanah detzibur ninhu* — we compare one person's *par* and *ayil* to another person's *par* and *ayil*, thereby excluding both *Shavuot* and *Rosh Hashanah*, whose *korbanot* are *korban tzibur*. The *Miluim* offering was *Aharon*'s own; the *Yom Kippur* offering likewise belongs to *Aharon* personally. The *Musaf* of *Rosh Hashanah*, by contrast, is a communal *korban* that any *kohen* can bring on behalf of the entire community.

### Private vs. Communal

This distinction is highly significant for the question of the separation itself. The entire seven-day preparation is a separation of the *Kohen Gadol*. The reason for that separation is directly tied to the uniquely personal character of his role — it is his *korban*, his *Avodah*, his day. The *Musaf* of *Rosh Hashanah* carries no such personal dimension; any *kohen* can bring it, funded by communal *shekalim*, on behalf of the entire *tzibbur*. The *Miluim* and *Yom Kippur* share a personal dimension that *Rosh Hashanah* does not.

### Kach Lecha Debate

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this reasoning. *Hani nicha leman de'amar kach lecha mishelcha* — this works well if one holds that the phrase *kach lecha* means "take from your own funds." Both the *Miluim* passage (*vayomer el Aharon kach lecha egel ben bakar*) and the *Yom Kippur* passage (*kach lecha egel ben bakar lechatat*) use this phrase, indicating a private expenditure. But what of the view that even *kach lecha* refers to communal funds? A *baraita* records this debate:

*Kach lecha mishelcha ve'aseh lecha mishelcha* — wherever the *Torah* says *kach lecha* or *aseh lecha*, it means private funds. The contrast is with *vyikchu eleicha* — "they shall take to you" — as in *vyikchu eleicha shemen zayit zach*, where the plural subject and the preposition *eleicha* (rather than the reflexive *lecha*) indicate communal sourcing. This is the position of *Rabbi Yoshiyah*.

*Rabbi Yonatan* disagrees: *bein kach lecha bein vyikchu eleicha mishel tzibur* — regardless of the formulation, the funding is always communal. According to *Rabbi Yonatan*, even the offering brought on the eighth day of the *Miluim* came from communal funds, and there would be no basis for the distinction Rav Abbahu drew.

### Rabbi Yonatan View

The debate between *Rabbi Yoshiyah* and *Rabbi Yonatan* bears on various other instances of *kach lecha* and *aseh lecha* throughout the *Torah*. When the *Torah* instructs regarding the *shemen hamishcha* — *ve'atah kach lecha besamim rosh mor dror* — or regarding the *chatzotzrot* — *aseh lecha shtei chatzotzrot kesef* — was Moshe required to fund these from his own resources, or were these communal expenses? *Rabbi Yoshiyah* would say private; *Rabbi Yonatan* would say communal.

### Midrashic Explanation

If the funding is always communal, the *Gemara* asks, *umah talmud lomar kach lecha?* — why does the *Torah* use this personal formulation at all? The answer given is: *kevayachol, mishelcha ani rotzeh yoter mishelahem* — as it were, God expresses a preference: I would rather it come from you than from them. *Rashi* offers two readings of this *kevayachol*. The first: if it were halakhically permissible for the offering to be privately funded, God would prefer that — but since it must be communal, it remains communal, with the personal language expressing a kind of divine wish. The second: the *kevayachol* itself signals that one should not speak too plainly of God preferring the offering of an individual over that of all of *Klal Yisrael* — hence the qualification "as it were." The notion of God preferring *Moshe* or *Aharon*'s private contribution to a gift from all of Israel is theologically striking, and the *Gemara* hedges it accordingly. Yet the *Torah*'s phrasing does seem to gesture toward the singular importance of these individuals in God's design.

### Ark Metaphor

A parallel textual contrast reinforces the point. *Abba Chanan* in the name of *Rabbi Eliezer* observes: one verse says *ve'asita lekha aron etz* (Devarim 10) — "make for yourself an ark of wood," addressed to Moshe in the singular — while another says *ve'asu aron atzei shitim* (Shemot) — "they shall make an ark of acacia wood," in the plural, inclusive of all of Israel. *Ha-keitzad?* — how can both be true? *Rabbi Eliezer* answers: *bizeiman she-Yisrael osim retzono shel Makom*, when Israel fulfills God's will, the *aron* is described as belonging to the entire community; *bizeiman she-ein Yisrael osim retzono shel Makom*, when they fall short, the *aron* is described as belonging to Moshe alone — *ke'ilu shel Moshe hu*. The midrashic point maps onto the theme of communal versus individual: God's relationship with the *tzibbur* is conditional on their conduct, but the *tzaddikim* among them maintain their singular standing regardless.

### Consensus: Aharon's Offe…

The *Gemara* ultimately concludes that in the specific cases of the *Miluim* and *Yom Kippur*, there is no debate — even *Rabbi Yonatan* would agree that these are *Aharon*'s private *korbanot*. The reason is that the *Torah* in both places explicitly contrasts *Aharon*'s offering with that of *Bnei Yisrael*. At the *Miluim*, the text first instructs *Aharon* — *vayomer el Aharon kach lecha egel ben bakar* — and then pivots to the community — *ul'vnei Yisrael tedaber leimor*. This explicit juxtaposition leaves no ambiguity: *kach lecha* here unmistakably means *Aharon*'s own. The phrase *Shma mina kach lecha mishelcha hu* — hear from this that *kach lecha* means from his own — is not merely a general inference but a conclusion mandated by context.

Similarly on *Yom Kippur*, after *Aharon* is instructed to bring *par ben bakar lechatat ve'ayil le'olah*, the next verse distinguishes *ume'et adat Bnei Yisrael yikach shnei se'irei izim lechatat ve'ayil echad le'olah*, and then the text adds: *ve'hikriv Aharon es par hachatas asher lo* — "and *Aharon* shall sacrifice the *par* of the *chatat* that is his." Why does the *Torah* restate "that is his" (*asher lo*) once *Aharon*'s offering has already been contrasted with that of the community? *Shma mina, hai lo mishelo hu* — this teaches definitively that it is funded from *Aharon*'s personal resources.

*Tosafot* raises a pointed question here: why does any of this matter? The relevant legal distinction for purposes of the comparison to the *Miluim* is not who funded the offering but for whom it comes — whose *kapparah* it achieves. Both the *Miluim* and *Yom Kippur* offer a *korban* on behalf of *Aharon* himself; the *Musaf* of *Rosh Hashanah*, by contrast, comes on behalf of the entire *tzibbur*. That distinction is self-evident and requires no derivation about funding sources. *Tosafot* leaves this as an open question. Nevertheless, the *Gemara*'s essential point stands: the *Miluim* and *Yom Kippur* share an intimate personal character — they are *Aharon*'s *korban*, for *Aharon*, from *Aharon* — that the communal *Musaf* of *Rosh Hashanah* simply does not replicate.

---

## Alternative Models

### Rav Ashi: Par & Ayil

Rav Ashi now offers a cleaner and more direct answer, one that cuts through the entire question of funding: *danin par lechatat ve'ayil le'olah mipar lechatat ve'ayil le'olah, le'apukei Rosh Hashanah ve'Shemini Atzeret detarvaihu olas ninhu* — we derive from a case of *par lechatat ve'ayil le'olah* only another case sharing that identical structure, thereby excluding *Rosh Hashanah* and *Shemini Atzeret*, where the comparable offerings are both *olot* rather than a *par lechatat* paired with an *ayil le'olah*. There is no need to invoke the question of private versus communal funding. The structural dissimilarity in the *korban* itself is sufficient.

### Ravina: Kohen Gadol

Ravina offers yet another approach: *danin avoda be'kohen gadol me'avoda be'kohen gadol, le'apukei kulu kushyasen d'lav avoda be'kohen gadol ninhu* — we compare an *Avodah* performed by a *Kohen Gadol* to another *Avodah* performed by a *Kohen Gadol*, thereby elegantly excluding all the problematic candidates at once. *Shemini Atzeret*, *Shavuot*, and *Rosh Hashanah* all have *Musaf* offerings that any *kohen* can perform — there is nothing unique about the *Kohen Gadol*'s role. The *Miluim*, by contrast, was *Aharon*'s singular moment of initiation as *Kohen Gadol*, and *Yom Kippur* is the one day each year on which the *Avodah* uniquely requires the *Kohen Gadol*. The separation is thus grounded not merely in a formal parallel of offerings, but in the nature of the *Avodah* itself as belonging specifically to the *Kohen Gadol*.

### Ravina Alt: Place

An alternate version of Ravina's position is also recorded: *danin avoda techila bemakom me'avoda techila bemakom* — we compare an initial *Avodah* in a particular place to another initial *Avodah* in a particular place. Here the emphasis shifts from the identity of the performer to the nature of the space being inaugurated.

### Avodah Techila Explained

The *Gemara* asks: *mai techila?* — what does "initial" mean in this context? If it means "first time a *Kohen Gadol* functioned" — well, the *Miluim* was the very first time *Aharon* served as *Kohen Gadol*, and by extension, the first time anyone played that role. What corresponds on *Yom Kippur*? *Rashi* explains: the first occasion on which the *Kohen Gadol* had the opportunity to perform a *korban tzibbur* requiring uniquely the *Kohen Gadol* would have been *Yom Kippur*. But the *Gemara* notes that this formulation collapses back into the previous point about the *Kohen Gadol* — *hainu kamaisa*. The genuinely distinct reading, therefore, is: *avoda techila bemakom* — the first initiation of a place. On the *Miluim*, it was the first time the *Avodah* was performed officially with *kohanim* on the *mizbeach hachitzon*. (The seven preparatory days prior involved *Moshe*, not the *kohanim*, and were not official *Avodah* in the full sense.) On *Yom Kippur*, it was the first time an *Avodah* was performed in the *heichal* and the *kodesh kodashim*.

### Preparation Philosophy

This range of approaches is worth pausing to appreciate, because they reflect genuinely different understandings of what the seven-day preparation is for. One approach — the *Kohen Gadol* model — suggests that the preparation is about the person: this is a day that uniquely requires the *Kohen Gadol*, and he must ready himself for a role that is his alone. The preparation is an inward process of getting oneself to the appropriate level, sanctifying oneself in one's person for the singular responsibility one must bear. Another approach — the *avoda techila bemakom* model — shifts the focus from the person to the place. The preparation is about the relationship between the person and the sacred space he is about to enter. It is not simply that he needs to be prepared; he needs to be prepared *in order to enter that space properly*, because the space makes an absolute demand on whoever crosses its threshold. *Bezot yavo Aharon el hakodesh* — by this shall *Aharon* enter the sanctuary — underscores that the entry itself is conditioned on a prior process. These are related but genuinely different orientations, and the shiur's final discussion will return to this distinction.

---

## Parah Adumah Status

### Parah Differences

Now that the *Gemara* has so thoroughly established the parallels between the *Miluim* and *Yom Kippur* — identical *korbanot* of *par lechatat ve'ayil le'olah*, both belonging personally to *Aharon*, both uniquely requiring the *Kohen Gadol*, both constituting inaugural *Avodot* in their respective sacred spaces — one element that the present discussion has quietly pushed aside becomes conspicuous by contrast: *Parah Adumah*. The *Parah Adumah* requires no *Kohen Gadol*, is not performed in the *Beit Hamikdash*, involves no *par lechatat ve'ayil le'olah*, and shares none of the features that have been marshaled to connect *Yom Kippur* to the *Miluim*. The *Gemara* now addresses this directly.

### R. Yochanan: YK Only

When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *matni chada* — Rabbi Yochanan taught only one application. *La'asos lekaper eilu ma'asei Yom Hakippurim* — from the *Miluim* verse he derives only the *Avodas Yom Hakippurim*, not the *Parah Adumah*. After everything we have seen about how precisely *Yom Kippur* mirrors the *Miluim*, this position makes eminent sense. Every element of comparison has pointed to *Yom Kippur*; *Parah Adumah* shares none of them.

### R. Yehoshua: Both

Yet *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* taught two applications — or, according to some, it was *Reish Lakish* who taught both: *la'asos eilu ma'asei parah, lekaper eilu ma'asei Yom Hakippurim* — the word *la'asot* is taken to refer to the *Avodas Parah* and *lekaper* to the *Avodas Yom Hakippurim*. This is, of course, the reading we encountered on the previous *daf*, deriving both practices from the single verse in the *Miluim*.

### Maala B'alma

If *Rabbi Yochanan* holds that only *Yom Kippur* is derived from the *Miluim*, then the *Mishnah*'s mention of a seven-day preparation for *Parah Adumah* requires a different explanation. The *Gemara* responds: *ma'ala b'alma* — it was simply an added stringency, not a biblical derivation. The seven-day preparation for the *kohen* performing *Parah Adumah* was a rabbinic enhancement, not a requirement rooted in the *Miluim*.

### Tzaddukim Context

This fits seamlessly into the broader context of the *Parah Adumah* procedure. As *Tosafot* observes, the Rabbis had introduced a notable leniency into the *Parah Adumah* — the burning could be performed by a *tevul yom*, a *kohen* who had immersed in the *mikveh* that very day but had not yet waited until nightfall for the sunset that would complete his purification. This leniency was deliberate: *le'hotzi mi-liban shel Tzaddukim* — to confute the *Tzaddukim*, who insisted that only one who had fully completed his purification cycle (i.e., who had waited until nightfall after immersion) could perform the *Parah*. The Rabbis, by using a *tevul yom*, publicly demonstrated their rejection of the *Tzaddukim*'s position. Having accepted that unusual leniency, they compensated by heaping on a series of additional stringencies — and the seven-day separation was one of them. It was not derived from the *Miluim*; it was a *ma'ala b'alma*, a rabbinic enhancement in the context of this particular controversy.

### Yochanan Contradiction

A difficulty arises, however, from another *Amoraic* tradition. A chain of transmission — *Rabbi Minyumi bar Chelkiya* quoting *Rabbi Machasya bar Idia* quoting *Rabbi Yochanan* — records that *Rabbi Yochanan* himself interpreted the *Miluim* verse as deriving both *Parah* and *Yom Kippur*: *la'asos eilu ma'asei parah, lekaper eilu ma'asei Yom Hakippurim*. How can both traditions bear the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*?

The resolution: *hahi deRabbay* — the teaching that derives both is not *Rabbi Yochanan* speaking in his own name, but *Rabbi Yochanan* transmitting the position of his *rebbe*, namely *Rabbi*. When *Ravin* came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he clarified: *Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Yishmael* — that the full *baraita*-like derivation of *la'asos eilu ma'asei parah, lekaper eilu ma'asei Yom Hakippurim* was a tradition *Rabbi Yochanan* conveyed in the name of *Rabbi Yishmael*, not his own independent ruling. *Rabbi Yochanan* in his own name derived only *Yom Kippur*.

*Tosafot* notes that the *Gemara* could simply have resolved the contradiction by saying it is a dispute among *Amoraim* about what *Rabbi Yochanan* actually held — a formula the *Gemara* uses elsewhere. The present resolution, however, is more precise: one tradition is in his own name, the other in the name of a prior authority.

Stepping back: we now have two fundamental positions. Either both *Parah Adumah* and *Yom Kippur* are derived from the *Miluim* — in which case we are looking for something more generic that ties all three together — or only *Yom Kippur* is derived from the *Miluim*, and the seven-day preparation for *Parah Adumah* is a *ma'ala b'alma* rooted in the *Tzaddukim* controversy. The latter view is in many respects more intellectually satisfying: having now demonstrated so exhaustively the precise correspondences between the *Miluim* and *Yom Kippur*, the derivation of *Yom Kippur* alone makes the analogy far more compelling and coherent. The *Parah Adumah*, for all its importance, simply does not share the profile.

---

## Reish Lakish Challenge

### Me'akev Question

*Reish Lakish* now challenges *Rabbi Yochanan* directly: *mehacha kayalphat?* — is this really where you derive the *Yom Kippur* preparation? If the *Miluim* is your source, there is a significant problem. By the *Miluim*, anything written in the passage is *me'akev* — legally essential. The *Gemara* will establish this principle explicitly in a later discussion: every detail of the *Miluim* was indispensable to the validity of the process, and failure to observe any of them would have invalidated the entire consecration. If we learn the seven-day preparation from the *Miluim*, should it not likewise be *me'akev*? Should a *Kohen Gadol* who did not undergo the full seven-day separation be disqualified from performing the *Yom Kippur Avodah*?

### Backup Kohen

*Reish Lakish* adduces evidence from the *Mishnah* itself. The *Mishnah* states: *u-matkinin lo kohen acher* — a backup *kohen* is designated in case the *Kohen Gadol* becomes unfit. Now, does this substitute require a seven-day separation of his own? The *Mishnah* uses the word *matkinin* for the backup — a different verb entirely from *mafrishin*, "they separate," which is used for the *Kohen Gadol* himself. If the backup also required seven days, the *Mishnah* would have used consistent language, or at least mentioned the requirement explicitly. The absence of any mention of a seven-day preparation for the substitute — *ve-lo tani mafrishin* — is telling. The *Mishnah* presumably envisions that the backup, if called upon, performs the *Avodah* without having undergone the full seven-day preparation.

### Not Biblical

If a *Kohen Gadol* can perform the *Yom Kippur Avodah* validly without seven days of prior separation, then that seven-day preparation is clearly not *me'akev*. But if it is not *me'akev*, it cannot have been derived from the *Miluim*, where everything written is *me'akev*. *Reish Lakish* therefore concludes: the seven-day preparation cannot be learned from *Miluim* — and *Rabbi Yochanan* must look elsewhere.

---

## Sinai Source

### Yochanan Response

*Rabbi Yochanan* accepts the challenge and pivots to an entirely different source: *amar mi-Sinai* — I derive it from *Har Sinai*. The seven-day preparation is not learned from the *Miluim* at all; it is learned from what happened when *Moshe* ascended to receive the *Torah*.

### Sinai Verse

The scriptural basis: *vayishkon kvod Hashem al Har Sinai vayichasehu he'anan sheshet yamim, vayikra el Moshe bayom hashvi'i* — the glory of God rested on *Har Sinai* and the cloud covered it — or covered *Moshe*, as *Rashi* understands — for six days, and on the seventh day God called to *Moshe*. Moshe was present in the divine ambient for six days, enveloped in the cloud at the foot or on the slopes of the mountain, before being summoned to ascend to the summit for the definitive encounter with God.

### Machane Shechina

The *Gemara* derives a general principle: *shekol hanichnas bemachaneh shechina teun perishat shisha* — anyone who is to enter into the *machaneh shechina* requires a six-day preparation. The *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur* is entering into the most intimate divine presence — *bezot yavo Aharon el hakodesh* — and therefore requires the six-day preparation that Moshe underwent before ascending *Har Sinai*.

### Machane Technical

A terminological clarification is needed here. The formal halakhic designation *machaneh shechina* refers to the sanctity of the *azarah*, the Temple courtyard. Yet ordinary *kohanim* entered the *azarah* regularly, and *Israelites* could enter it without any prior preparatory period; all that was required was *tahara*. Clearly, it is not entry into the *azarah* that mandates a six-day preparation. In this context, *machaneh shechina* carries a more restricted meaning: it refers to entry into the *kodesh* and the *kodesh kodashim* — perhaps even more precisely, only the *kodesh kodashim* itself, since ordinary *kohanim* entered the *heichal* to light the *menorah* and arrange the *shulchan* without any extended preparation.

### Seventh Day Rabbinic

If the biblical basis is six days, why does the *Mishnah* specify seven? *Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira*'s concern provides the answer: the seventh day is a rabbinic addition driven by anxiety over *tumat beito* — the potential impurity of his household, specifically his wife. The concern is that if the *Kohen Gadol* has marital relations with his wife on the sixth night — the night leading into what would be the sixth full day of preparation — his wife might become a *niddah* during or immediately after the act. In such a case, even if he had no knowledge of it at the time, he would be rendered *tamei* for seven days, since the *Torah* teaches that a man who has relations with a *niddah* is *tamei* for seven days. To guard against any possibility of this *tumah* still being present on *Yom Kippur*, the Rabbis added a seventh day of separation from his household. The six-day preparation is biblical; the seventh is rabbinic.

### Philosophy Shift

It is worth pausing on the profound conceptual difference between this source and the *Miluim* model. The *Miluim* model points to a structured process of sanctification — preparing the *kohen* for a special *Avodah*, analogous to the inauguration of the *Mishkan* itself. It carries a somewhat formal, institutional character: you are being readied for a particular role, in a particular place, through a prescribed process of consecration. There is a sense in which the preparation is about achieving the right status or condition for the *Avodah* one is about to perform.

The *Sinai* model is categorically different. *Moshe* was not being sanctified to perform a particular *Avodah*. He was preparing himself to encounter God. The six days were not about status or role — they were about the quality of presence one brings to a meeting with the divine. *Machane shechina* here is not a technical halakhic category but a description of the most intimate proximity to God's presence. The *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur* is not merely performing the *Avodah*; he is entering into an encounter — *bezot yavo Aharon el hakodesh*. The entry into the *kodesh kodashim* is not a procedural step but an ascent.

This distinction may illuminate how *Yom Kippur* is experienced more broadly. The days of *Elul* begin a process of drawing near; the *Aseret Yemei Teshuva* deepen it; and on *Yom Kippur* itself, one finally arrives at the summit — just as *Moshe* spent six days in the cloud before being called into the full divine presence on the seventh. The *Kohen Gadol*'s seven-day preparation, understood through the *Sinai* paradigm, becomes a map for the entire season of *teshuva* and encounter with God: a gradual approach, day by day, through the cloud, toward the moment of the *Kohen Gadol*'s entry into the *kodesh kodashim* — which is, for all of *Klal Yisrael*, the moment of standing before God.

---

---

# Yoma 4

## Two Sources Debate

### Yochanan's Miluim

The fourth *daf* of *Yoma* opens with a question that is both halachic and deeply conceptual: what is the source for the seven-day separation of the *kohen gadol* prior to *Yom Kippur*, and by extension, the analogous separation of the *kohen* who performs the *parah adumah*? Until this point in the *sugya*, the dominant position has been that of Rabbi Yochanan, who derives the practice from the *miluim* — the inauguration of the Tabernacle — on the basis of the verse *ka'asher asah bayom hazeh tzivah Hashem la'asot lechaper aleichem*. The comparison to the *miluim* is in many respects natural and compelling: both involve a preparation for a specific *avodah* in the *Beit Hamikdash*, and the Gemara had already characterized the relationship as *techilah bamakom* — a sense of initiating or consecrating the space and its service. The *korban* of the *kohen gadol* is central, and the entire structure focuses on the person who must perform the *avodah* and what is required to make him capable of performing it.

As for the *parah adumah*, there is a second tradition in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that excludes it from this model entirely: the *parah adumah* is, on this view, only a rabbinic matter related to *tumah and taharah*, and does not belong to the fundamental framework derived from the *miluim*. The alternative tradition that includes the *parah adumah* within the model strains to identify a common denominator, but that tension is acknowledged.

### Lakish's Sinai Model

Reish Lakish disputes the *miluim* derivation on a pointed logical ground: if the seven-day separation were truly modeled on the *miluim*, it would be indispensable, and yet we know that a substitute *kohen* — the understudy — would not require the same preparation even *bedi'avad*. This demonstrates, in Reish Lakish's view, that the practice cannot be grounded in the *miluim* framework at all. Instead, he grounds the requirement in Moshe's experience at Har Sinai, reading the relevant verse to mean that Moshe was enveloped in the cloud for six days before ascending to receive the Torah — a period of preparation before his encounter with God. The *kohen gadol* similarly requires such preparation, though not for seven days: the seventh day is added as a precaution against *tumah* and is not part of the fundamental model. Likewise, the *parah adumah* would not be grounded in this model; its seven-day separation would be a *tumah* concern rather than a reflection of the core principle.

This distinction is conceptually significant. Reish Lakish's model shifts the entire frame of reference: the preparation is not about enabling an *avodah*, not about the ritual mechanics of what the *kohen gadol* must do on *Yom Kippur*, but about the encounter with God itself. Just as Moshe needed six days of preparation before standing in the divine presence, the *kohen gadol* needs preparation before entering the *Kodesh Hakodashim* — before stepping into *Machaneh Shechinah* in its most precise and exalted sense, not merely the *Beit Hamikdash* in general but the innermost chamber where the divine presence is concentrated. And thinking about how this framework applies to us, it places the emphasis on the inner preparation for encountering God rather than on the proper execution of the Temple service.

### Water vs. Blood

The Gemara at the top of *daf dalet amud aleph* records Rabbi Yochanan's response to Reish Lakish. Rabbi Yochanan says: *bishlama lidi* — it works well according to me, since I derive the seven-day separation from the *miluim*, for that fits precisely with a *baraita* we will encounter shortly: *zeh v'zeh mazzin alav kol shiva mikol chatatot shehayu sham* — both the *kohen* preparing for the *parah adumah* and the *kohen gadol* preparing for *Yom Kippur* would have the ashes of the *parah adumah* sprinkled upon them every single day throughout the seven-day period, drawing from all the various red heifers whose ashes were stored. Rashi explains that they would preserve the ashes of earlier *parot adumot* rather than wait until one supply was entirely exhausted, and indeed cites a tradition that the ashes of Moshe's original *parah* never ran out entirely. The sprinkling was not merely a functional act of achieving *taharah*; if that were all, one would sprinkle only on the third and seventh days. Sprinkling every single day points to a deeper ritual dimension. And what is the parallel? The *miluim* itself involved some act of sprinkling — with blood — every one of the seven days. The daily sprinkling in the preparation for *Yom Kippur* is thus analogous to the daily sprinkling throughout the *miluim*.

Rabbi Yochanan presses his point: *ela ledidach* — but according to you, Reish Lakish, *haza b'Sinai mi havi* — where does any preparatory sprinkling exist at Har Sinai? This speaks strongly in favor of the *miluim* model. Reish Lakish responds: *ultamich mi nicha* — but wait, why is it good even according to you? In the *miluim* the sprinkling used blood; here we use water — the waters of the *parah adumah*. These are not the same thing. The Gemara immediately deflects this: *ha lo kashya*, for Rav Chiyya teaches in a *baraita* that *nichnesu mayim tachat dam* — water entered in place of blood. We acknowledge the substitution and do not claim identity. The reason is clear: there are no fixed *korbanot* in the days leading up to *Yom Kippur* from which blood could be taken, and using the blood of a *korban* for sprinkling without explicit Torah mandate would be a misuse of the offering. Therefore, the only meaningful sprinkling available is that of the *parah adumah*, and we apply the model as best the circumstances allow. But the point stands against Reish Lakish: *ela ledidach, haza b'Sinai mi havi* — according to your model, there is no basis for the sprinkling at all.

### Initiation vs. Encounter

Reish Lakish's response to the challenge is *maala b'alma* — a qualitative enhancement, something added once the core practice is already in place. His position is that the fundamental requirement — analogous to Moshe's preparation at Har Sinai — calls only for six days, with a seventh added for *tumah* concerns. The sprinkling is similarly an elaboration: once the practice of separation exists, the ritual is enriched with additional acts that deepen the sense of preparation and heighten the solemnity of what is being built toward. Rashi suggests that the sprinkling functions as a form of preparation for entering *Machaneh Shechinah* — not merely to achieve *taharah*, but to create and sustain a daily ritual of readiness. Each day of sprinkling intensifies the cumulative experience of buildup, of the *kohen gadol*'s consciousness that he is approaching something extraordinary, that he is preparing to enter into the most direct form of divine encounter available to any human being. Reish Lakish is entirely willing to concede that certain features of the seven-day separation — the *tumah* considerations, the sprinkling — do not flow organically from his model. But at the core, he insists: conceptually, this is about standing before God, about the preparation for that encounter, not about a *Beit Hamikdash* ritual that enables the *avodah* in the manner Rabbi Yochanan envisions.

The two models thus represent genuinely different conceptual frameworks. For Rabbi Yochanan, the axis of the preparation is the *avodah* — the *kohen gadol* must be prepared to perform the service, and the seven-day separation, like the *miluim*, is a process of enabling and initiating that service. For Reish Lakish, the axis is the *encounter* — the *kohen gadol* must be prepared to enter into the divine presence, and everything in the seven days is oriented toward that.

---

## Textual Derivations

### Baraita on Miluim

The Gemara now brings a *baraita* in support of each position. For Rabbi Yochanan: *tanya k'vateih d'Rabbi Yochanan* — the derivation begins from the verse *u-vezot yavo Aharon el hakodesh*, "with this Aaron shall enter into the sanctuary." The word *bezot* — in the feminine — does not straightforwardly match *par ben bakar*, a bull, and *ayil*, a ram, both masculine. Rashi explains that the feminine *bezot* points to some additional process — a *perishah*, a separation — that must accompany Aaron's entry into the *Kodesh Hakodashim*. And what process? *Be-inyan miluim* — what we find in the *miluim*. What does the *miluim* tell us? *Aharon piresh shivah ve-shimesh yom echad* — Aaron separated for seven days and then served on the eighth. Furthermore, *u-Moshe masar lo kol shivah* — Moshe served as the effective *kohen* throughout the seven days of the *miluim*, *kedei le-chanecho ba-avodah* — in order to prepare Aaron for the *avodah*. The preparation was not a passive retreat but an active training process.

*Ve-af le-dorot* — and so too for all generations: the *kohen gadol* separates for seven days and serves on the day of *Yom Kippur*. And *shene talmidei chachamim mi-talmidav shel Moshe* — two *talmidei chachamim* drawn from the disciples of Moshe serve as his companions throughout the seven days, *mosrin lo kol shivah, kedei le-chanecho ba-avodah* — transmitting to him the entire sequence of the *avodah*, preparing him as Moshe prepared Aaron. The *baraita* concludes with a reference to the passage in the *Mishnah* that the *kohen gadol* is separated from his house seven days before *Yom Kippur* to the *Lishkat Parhedrin*.

### Tzedukim & Sages

The *baraita*'s specification that the two sages represent *talmidei Moshe* carries a pointed implication: *le-afokei Tzedukim* — to exclude the *Sadducees*. The two sages must be representatives of the authentic *mesorah*, the true tradition, as opposed to what the *baraita* regards as a perverted or false tradition. They stand in for Moshe — the transmitter of the unbroken chain — and in doing so they validate the *kohen gadol*'s service as continuous with that original chain of transmission. Each day they would walk the animals before the *kohen gadol*, instruct him, and rehearse the *avodah* with him, precisely paralleling what Moshe did for Aaron throughout the *miluim*. The entire structure is reconstructed: a substitute Moshe in the form of two *talmidei chachamim*, a successor-Aaron in the form of the *kohen gadol*, and a seven-day preparation that mirrors the *miluim* almost exactly.

The *baraita* then adds, *u-cheshem she-mafrishim kohen gadol kach mafrishim kohen ha-soref et ha-parah* — just as one separates the *kohen gadol*, so does one separate the *kohen* who burns the *parah adumah*. Rashi notes that this addition sits uneasily within the elegant model because it doesn't fit the *miluim* parallel. The *miluim* analogy was constructed specifically for the *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur*; the *parah adumah* is a different matter entirely, which is why, as noted earlier, one tradition attributed to Rabbi Yochanan excluded it. According to Rashi, this inclusion is therefore best understood as an appended rabbinic extension — not the *ikkar* of what the verse teaches — and the *parah adumah*'s seven-day separation is in a different category from the *kohen gadol*'s.

### Bezot Derivation

A potential objection now arises: the verse *bezot yavo Aharon el hakodesh* contains the word *bezot* — but *bezot* is needed simply for its straightforward meaning, to specify the *korban* through which Aaron enters! How can you use it to imply an entire seven-day preparatory process? The Gemara answers that if the Torah had intended only to specify the *korban*, it would have written *bezeh* or *be-eileh* — forms that match the masculine *par* and *ayil*. The use of the feminine *bezot* signals that something additional is implied: *mashma mi-na tarti* — the language teaches two things at once. The *korban* is specified, and simultaneously a further preparatory process is required. The grammatical anomaly is the opening through which the *drasha* enters.

### Future Generations

Even with *bezot* doing double duty, there remains a further hermeneutic need, and this is where *ka'asher asah bayom hazeh* becomes essential. One might have read *bezot yavo Aharon* as applying only to the first time Aaron entered the *Kodesh Hakodashim* — a one-time initiatory act, analogous to the *miluim* which, after all, was performed only once to inaugurate the *kohanim* and the *Mishkan*. Indeed, the entire *parasha* of *Acharei Mot* is addressed to Aaron rather than to future generations, which the Vilna Gaon pointedly observes: the parasha does not even mention *Yom Kippur* explicitly until its very end. The primary framing is *bezot yavo Aharon* — here is what Aaron must do if he wishes to enter. The annual *Yom Kippur* observance is appended at the conclusion. One might therefore have concluded that the seven-day separation was required only for Aaron himself, as a personal initiation, or only for the first *Yom Kippur* — the first entry into the *Kodesh Hakodashim* — as an inauguration of that space.

The verse *ka'asher asah bayom hazeh tzivah Hashem la'asot lechaper aleichem* closes this interpretive opening: *la'asot* — to do this in future generations. This is what the Gemara means by *tashma* — "come and hear": the two possible limitations (first *kohen gadol* only, or first *Yom Kippur* only) are foreclosed by this verse, which commands that the practice continue *le-dorot*. And it is worth noting that these two limitations correspond precisely to the two ideas the Gemara had already raised in the closing lines of the previous *daf*: the uniqueness of Aaron as a person and the inauguration of the *Kodesh Hakodashim* as a space. Both were potential grounds for restricting the requirement to a single historical moment, and both are overridden by *ka'asher asah bayom hazeh*.

This also illuminates something important for Reish Lakish's position: the entire framing of *bezot yavo Aharon* — not a general rule but a focused account of Aaron's access to God — resonates deeply with the idea that the preparation is fundamentally about the encounter, not merely about the mechanics of service. Even within Rabbi Yochanan's framework, the *parasha*'s structural emphasis on Aaron as an individual approaching God supports what Reish Lakish highlights.

### Asmachta Framework

Before moving on, it is important to pause at a significant qualification introduced by Tosafot. The discussion has proceeded as though the seven-day separation and its associated practices — especially the daily sprinkling — are grounded in a genuine *d'Oraita* requirement. Tosafot challenges this directly: *delav le-gamrei drasha gemura hi* — this is not truly a complete Torah-level derivation. The substitution of water for blood is only possible, Tosafot argues, because the entire derivation from the *miluim* is an *asmachta b'alma* — a rabbinic practice that finds textual support in the Torah without being strictly commanded by it.

Moreover, Tosafot notes — citing Rashi's commentary on the *Chumash* — that the verse *ka'asher asah bayom hazeh* in the *miluim* passage most naturally refers not to the eighth day but to the first day: Moshe told the people on day one of the *miluim*, "continue this practice for the next seven days." On this reading, the verse is not establishing a future Yom Kippur obligation at all; its *peshat* is internal to the *miluim* narrative itself. *V'keivan d'asmachta b'alma hu* — since it is only *asmachta*, we need not be troubled by the substitution of water for blood, for the entire structure is a rabbinic framework that models itself on the *miluim* without claiming to replicate it with full halakhic precision.

The more interesting question, however, is not whether to classify this as *d'Oraita* or *d'Rabbanan*, but what the underlying conceptual model is. And for Rabbi Yochanan, that model is unambiguously the *miluim*: the initiation and ongoing annual preparation of the *kohen gadol* for his unique service, with all the attending ritual elaboration that concept entails.

---

## Chronology Dispute

### Moshe in Cloud

The Gemara now brings a *baraita* supporting Reish Lakish: *Moshe ala be-anan ve-niskasa be-anan ve-niskadesh be-anan kedai le-kabel Torah le-Yisrael bi-kedusha* — Moshe ascended into the cloud, was covered by the cloud, and was sanctified by the cloud, in order to receive the Torah for Israel in a state of holiness. The verse cited is *vayishkon kevod Hashem al Har Sinai* — the cloud of God rested on Har Sinai. The *baraita* adds: *zeh hayah ma'aseh achar Aseret HaDibrot she-hayu techilah le-arba'im yom* — this event occurred after the Ten Commandments had been given, and it initiated the forty days that Moshe would spend atop Har Sinai. This is the view of Rabbi Yose HaGelili.

To appreciate why this reading is at all contested, it is necessary to understand the structure of the *pesukim* at the end of *Parashat Mishpatim*. What is not always appreciated is that *parashat Mishpatim* is a direct continuation of the *Aseret HaDibrot* — the civil laws are an elaboration of what was communicated at Sinai. Throughout the entire *parasha*, Moshe is still on the mountain in the same encounter. At the very end of *Mishpatim*, the narrative shifts: God tells Moshe to come back up with Aaron, Nadav, Avihu, and seventy elders. Moshe descends, reports everything to the people — *vayavo Moshe vayisaper la-am et kol divrei Hashem ve-et kol ha-mishpatim* — the people respond with *na'aseh*, a covenant is enacted, the *dam habrit* is sprinkled on the people. Then the elders ascend with Moshe for that brief, extraordinary vision of God. Then comes the command: *aleh eilai ha-harah ve-heyeh sham* — come up and be there, and I will give you the *luchos*. Moshe and Yehoshua rise; to the elders he says, stay here. And then: *vayishkon kevod Hashem al Har Sinai vayichaseihu he-anan sheshet yamim vayikra el Moshe bayom ha-shevi'i* — the cloud covered the mountain for six days and God called to Moshe on the seventh — *vayavo Moshe be-toch he-anan vaya'al el ha-har vayehi Moshe ba-har arba'im yom ve-arba'im lailah*.

The *peshat* of these *pesukim* is strikingly clear: after *matan Torah*, after the *dam habrit*, after the vision of the elders, God calls Moshe up for a forty-day stay, and there is a six-day period of the cloud covering the mountain before God calls to Moshe on the seventh day. This is exactly Reish Lakish's position, and Rabbi Yose HaGelili reads it accordingly: those six days were preparation, those forty days were Moshe's time with God, and it is this model that underlies the *kohen gadol*'s seven-day separation.

### Yose: After Torah

Rabbi Yose HaGelili's reading is thus precisely aligned with what one would call the *peshat* of the *pesukim*. The cloud covered Har Sinai, Moshe was enveloped in it for six days, and on the seventh God called him — *le-kabalei she'ar Torah* — to receive the remainder of the Torah. The forty days of Moshe on the mountain began on that seventh day, after the *Aseret HaDibrot* had already been given. This is Rabbi Yose HaGelili's position: *shene'emar vayishkon kevod Hashem al Har Sinai* — that *parasha* at the end of *Mishpatim* is an event chronologically subsequent to the *Aseret HaDibrot*, not a recap of events preceding them.

### Akiva: Before Torah

Rabbi Akiva disagrees in a striking way. He reads *vayishkon kevod Hashem* not as the cloud covering Moshe but as the cloud covering the mountain — *vayichaseihu he-anan le-har*, the cloud covered the mountain, not Moshe. And this entire passage, in his reading, is not a narrative of events following the *Aseret HaDibrot* but a summary-recap of everything from *Rosh Chodesh* — the first of Sivan, when Israel arrived at Har Sinai. The six days of the cloud were the six days leading up to the *Aseret HaDibrot*, and the call to Moshe on the seventh day was the call immediately preceding the giving of the Torah.

Why does Rabbi Akiva take this unusual reading? One reason emerges from the text of *Parashat Yitro* itself: there, God calls to Moshe just before the *Aseret HaDibrot* — *vayikra Hashem el Moshe rosh ha-har vaya'al Moshe* — and the content of that call is to warn the people to stand back. At the end of *Mishpatim*, God again calls Moshe — *vayikra el Moshe bayom ha-shevi'i mitoch he-anan* — but without explicit content. Rabbi Akiva understands this second *vayikra* as a summation of the same event narrated in *Yitro*, with the entire closing paragraph of *Mishpatim* functioning as a retrospective account, not a new one. The cloud covered the mountain from *Rosh Chodesh*, the *Aseret HaDibrot* were given on the seventh day, and then Moshe entered the cloud and ascended for forty days — all of this is retrospectively summarized.

But this creates a problem for Reish Lakish's model. If the six days of cloud-covering preceded the *Aseret HaDibrot* rather than following them, and if the cloud covered the mountain rather than Moshe personally, then there is no six-day personal preparation of Moshe — and Reish Lakish's derivation loses its textual basis. Moreover, as was already noted, Moshe was going back and forth throughout the *Sinai* narrative; a continuous six-day preparation simply cannot be fitted into that picture if the events took place before *matan Torah*.

### Vayikra Question

What then does Rabbi Akiva do with the *vayikra el Moshe bayom ha-shevi'i*? If Moshe and all of Israel were standing there together at that moment, the calling is not to summon Moshe into a cloud or to draw him up the mountain for a forty-day stay — those events came later. So what was the *vayikra* for? This question needs resolution.

### Honor Explanation

The Gemara records the answer: *velo ba ha-kasuv ela le-chalek kavod le-Moshe* — the verse came only to give honor to Moshe. It was a public singling out of Moshe before all of Israel at the moment of *matan Torah* — a calling of his name before the assembled nation, to distinguish him and accord him recognition as the one through whom the Torah was being transmitted. This is, of course, the same explanation given by Rabbi Elazar: *Moshe ve-chulan omdin velo ba ha-kasuv ela le-chalek lo kavod le-Moshe*. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva's position supports Rabbi Elazar's formulation, and the two are now aligned.

A question immediately arises: if the divine voice that called Moshe was heard only by Moshe and not by the assembled people — *moshe shama ve-chulan lo shamu* — how does calling his name give him public honor? The Gemara later provides two resolutions. The first: *ha b'Sinai ha b'Ohel Moed* — at Sinai, it was a one-time event in which everyone heard; from the *Ohel Moed* onward, God spoke to Moshe privately. The second: *ha b'kriya ha b'dibur* — even at *Ohel Moed*, one might distinguish between the initial calling of Moshe's name, which was heard by all, and the content of the subsequent divine speech, which only Moshe heard. Each day, in this reading, the nation could hear God call Moshe's name — a public declaration of his unique status — even if the message that followed was exclusively between God and Moshe.

---

## Six Days Meaning

### Natan: Purification

The Gemara records several explanations of the six-day preparation, offered by different *tanna'im*. Rabbi Natan says: *velo ba ha-kasuv ela le-morek achilah ve-shtiyah she-bi-m'av la-asomo ke-malakhei ha-sharet* — the text came only to purge Moshe's physical digestive substance, to make him like the ministering angels. Rashi reads this as directly connected to the period in the cloud: the six days served to cleanse Moshe of his corporeality, to strip away as much physical substance as possible so that he could sustain forty days without eating or drinking — *lechem lo achal u-mayim lo shatiti*. The preparation for the divine encounter required diminishing the body's claim on the person, approximating the angelic state that continuous divine proximity demands. Notably, Rashi observes that this explanation is specific to Moshe and cannot straightforwardly be generalized to the *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur*, for we do not require the *kohen gadol* to abstain from food throughout his seven-day preparation.

### Matya: Fear & Awe

Rabbi Matya ben Cheresh offers a different explanation: *velo ba ha-kasuv ela le-ayem alav* — the text came only to strike fear upon him. *Kedei she-tehei Torah nitenet be-eimah be-ret u-ve-ze'ah* — so that the Torah should be given in awe, trembling, and perspiration. The Maharsha notes that this explanation and Rabbi Natan's, placed as they are immediately after Rabbi Akiva's position in the *baraita*, are best read as explanations not of the six days themselves but of the *vayikra el Moshe* — what was the function of that act of calling? One answer was to give honor. Another, Rabbi Natan's, is that even a single divine call was sufficient to purge Moshe's physicality. Rabbi Matya ben Cheresh's answer is that it was to instill fear in Moshe's heart before he received the Torah.

### Rejoicing + Fear

The *baraita* supports this with the verse *ivdu et Hashem be-yirah ve-gilu bi-ra'adah* — serve God with fear and rejoice in trembling. The Gemara asks: *mai ve-gilu bi-ra'adah*? What does it mean to rejoice in trembling? Rav Adda bar Matna said in the name of Rav: *bi-mekom gilah sham tehei ra'adah* — at the very place of rejoicing, there too must be trembling. The reception of Torah is a supreme elevation — and it is precisely that elevation that must be accompanied by the profoundest awe. The two do not cancel each other; they coexist, each intensifying the other.

This balance resonates powerfully with the *Yom Kippur* context. The death of the *shenei benei Aharon* at the threshold of *Kodesh Hakodashim* stands as the paradigm of what happens when one approaches the divine presence without the proper disposition of fear. *Bezot yavo Aharon* — with this, and only this rigorous preparation, may Aaron enter. The *vayikra*, the trembling that accompanied it, and the entire preparatory process serve to hold together the exaltation of encounter with the sobriety of standing before the living God.

Rashi reads these explanations as connected to the position of Rabbi Yose HaGelili, where there is a genuine six-day preparatory period in the cloud. The Maharsha, however, suggests they may equally fit Rabbi Akiva's reading, in which case they explain the significance of the single act of *vayikra el Moshe* rather than of an extended period of preparation. On either reading, the conceptual message is the same: the encounter with the divine demands a total reorientation of the person — physical, emotional, and spiritual.

---

## Soloveitchik Analysis

### Lakish Recap

At this point it is worth pausing to draw together the two conceptual models as they have emerged across the *sugya*, with the help of Rav Soloveitchik's analysis in Rav Aharon Lichtenstein's work on *Maseches Yoma* — a *daf*-by-daf presentation of Rav Soloveitchik's *chiddushim* on the *masechta*, of which the first extended treatment addresses precisely this debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. Reish Lakish's model, Rav Soloveitchik suggests, is in a certain sense the more straightforwardly intuitive one. It is not about the *avodat Yom HaKippurim* as such; it is about the God encounter itself — the act of entering the *Kodesh Hakodashim* and standing in the immediate divine presence — and it is about creating the state of *kedusha* that makes such an encounter possible. The *kohen gadol* must prepare himself as Moshe prepared himself before ascending into the cloud.

### Yochanan Deepened

Rabbi Yochanan's model requires more unpacking. On the surface, one might say it is simply about enabling the *avodah* — a preparatory ritual that allows the service to proceed. But Rav Soloveitchik argues for something richer: the seven-day separation, modeled on the *miluim*, does not merely prepare the *kohen gadol* to perform the service. It elevates his status, reaffirming and in a sense reconstituting him as the *kohen gadol* fit for this unique service. Just as the *miluim* established the *kohanim* in their priestly identity — transforming Aaron from a private individual into the *kohen gadol* — the annual seven-day preparation repeats this process on a yearly basis. It is not a rehearsal; it is a renewal of his very standing as the *kohen gadol* appropriate for *Yom Kippur*. This is why, on Rabbi Yochanan's model, the *baraita*'s derivation from *bezot yavo Aharon* is so apt: the verse is not primarily about logistics but about identity and access — *bezot*, through this process, Aaron may enter.

### Aaron Representation

Rav Soloveitchik extends this further. The Vilna Gaon had already noted that *Parashat Acharei Mot* is addressed to Aaron, not generically to future *kohanim* or to the nation — and the annual observance is added only at the *parasha*'s conclusion. This framing suggests that to enter the *Kodesh Hakodashim*, even in future generations, the *kohen gadol* must in some sense enter as Aaron — must be constituted as Aaron's representative and successor in that role. The seven-day preparation, modeled on the *miluim* through which Aaron was first established, re-enacts that establishment each year. And this is where the *shenei talmidei chachamim* — the two sages who attend the *kohen gadol* throughout the seven days — take on their full significance: they are substitute Moshe figures, standing in for the one who first prepared Aaron. The result is a recreation of the *miluim* relationship: a substitute Moshe prepares a substitute Aaron to enter the *Kodesh Hakodashim* as Aaron's authorized successor. *Bezot yavo Aharon* — and by extension, *bezot* will every *kohen gadol* who is truly constituted as Aaron's representative enter.

### Rituals Essential

This framework also illuminates why the preparation cannot be performed for the substitute *kohen* — the understudy who stands ready in case the primary *kohen gadol* becomes disqualified. One might think: if the preparation is so important, why not prepare the understudy as well? Rav Soloveitchik's answer is that the process of elevation can only build upon an existing foundation. The seven-day preparation does not create a *kohen gadol* from scratch; it elevates a *kohen gadol* into his *Yom Kippur* identity. The substitute has no such foundation — he does not carry the baseline status of *kohen gadol* — and therefore the process of elevation cannot be applied to him. *Bedi'avad*, he may perform the service if necessary, but there is no mechanism for giving him the preparation that properly belongs to his role, because that preparation presupposes the role already exists.

Finally, and more broadly, all of the surrounding practices — the daily sprinkling, the two attending sages, the provisions made for the understudy — are not secondary concerns or administrative details. They are part of the comprehensive structure of *miluim*-modeled preparation. If the entire purpose is to make the *kohen gadol ra'uy la-avodah* — genuinely fit to perform the service — then everything that ensures he will be able to do so is, at its root, derived from that same conceptual source. The *shnei talmidei chachamim* teaching him the *avodah* each day, the sprinkling with the ashes of the *parah adumah*, the provisions for *taharah* — all of these are components of the single *miluim*-derived process that culminates in the *kohen gadol*'s service on *Yom Kippur*.

---

## Calendar Dispute

### Sixth vs Seventh

The Gemara turns to identify the underlying disagreement between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva, locating it in a broader dispute among *tanna'im*: *b'shishah b'chodesh nitnah Torah le-Yisrael* — the Torah was given on the sixth of Sivan; *Rabbi Yosi omer b'shivah bo* — Rabbi Yosi says on the seventh. This calendrical dispute is the engine that drives the different readings of the *pesukim* in *Mishpatim*.

### Yose's Logic

If the Torah was given on the sixth of Sivan, then the seventh day at the end of *Parashat Mishpatim* — *vayikra el Moshe bayom ha-shevi'i* — cannot refer to the seventh day of Israel's encampment at Sinai, for the Torah had already been given on the sixth. One cannot, on this reading, place the call to Moshe on the seventh day before *matan Torah* — the sixth was *matan Torah*, the seventh has to be afterward. Therefore, Rabbi Yose HaGelili must read the closing *parasha* of *Mishpatim* as an event subsequent to the *Aseret HaDibrot*, in which Moshe was enveloped in the cloud for six days and called on the seventh to begin his forty-day ascent.

### Akiva's Logic

Rabbi Akiva, holding that Torah was given on the seventh of Sivan, has no difficulty reading the closing *parasha* of *Mishpatim* as a recap from the beginning. The cloud settled on the mountain from *Rosh Chodesh*; there were six days until the seventh, when God called to Moshe at the moment of *matan Torah*; and then afterward Moshe entered the cloud and went up for forty days. *Vayikra el Moshe bayom ha-shevi'i* refers to the seventh of Sivan, the very day the Torah was given — not to a post-*Sinai* preparatory period. On this reading, *mishkan kevod Hashem* covered the mountain, not Moshe himself.

### Forty Days Math

The Gemara then works through the chronological arithmetic. According to Rabbi Akiva, who holds Torah was given on the seventh, Moshe began his forty-day ascent on the seventh of Sivan. Counting from the seventh: twenty-four days remain in Sivan, plus sixteen days of Tamuz — that is forty days. Moshe came down on the seventeenth of Tamuz and broke the *luchos*. The *cheshbon* works precisely, and *Shivah Asar b'Tamuz* as the day the *luchos* were broken is confirmed.

### Yose's Inclusion

According to Rabbi Yose HaGelili, however, who holds Torah was given on the sixth, the forty days began on the seventh — the day after *matan Torah* — and six additional days of preparation preceded even that. Adding six days of preparation plus forty days in the cloud to the sixth of Sivan pushes the descent past the seventeenth of Tamuz, arriving instead at the twenty-third. The Gemara presses: how does Rabbi Yose HaGelili maintain that the *luchos* were broken on the seventeenth?

Rabbi Yose HaGelili's answer is remarkable: *arba'im de-tura be-hadi shisha de-prisha* — the forty days on the mountain included the six days of preparation. The six days of cloud-covering were not a separate period that preceded the forty days; they were the first six of the forty days themselves. Only from the seventh day onward was Moshe actively in God's presence receiving Torah; the first six days were embedded within the forty, serving as the preparation that opened the encounter. This means Moshe spent only thirty-four days in direct divine communication — but the forty days is counted from the beginning of his ascent into the cloud, preparation included. There is something quietly profound in this: the journey to stand before God is itself part of the standing before God.

---

## Cloud Entry Problem

### Honor, Not Call

The final section of the *daf* takes up what Rabbi Elazar had already stated and what Rabbi Akiva's position implied: *vayikra el Moshe bayom ha-shevi'i* was not to summon Moshe upward but *le-chalek kavod le-Moshe* — to give him honor before the assembled people. The Gemara confirms that this ruling supports Rabbi Elazar's formulation.

### Cloud Contradiction

But now a sharp textual contradiction emerges. At the end of *Sefer Shemot*, the Torah states: *ve-lo yachol Moshe lavo el Ohel Moed* — Moshe could not enter the *Ohel Moed* because of the *anan*. The divine presence in the cloud was so concentrated that Moshe could not penetrate it. Yet the closing verse of *Parashat Mishpatim* states: *vayavo Moshe be-toch he-anan* — Moshe came into the midst of the cloud at Har Sinai. What is it? Can Moshe enter the cloud or not?

### Hearing Problem

Before resolving that contradiction, the Gemara addresses the challenge to Rabbi Elazar's claim that the *vayikra* was *le-chalek kavod le-Moshe*. If God's voice, when addressed to Moshe, was heard only by Moshe — *Moshe shama ve-chulan lo shamu* — how does calling his name confer public honor? This principle is derived from the *pasuk* in *Sefer Bamidbar*: *u-ve-vo Moshe el Ohel Moed lishmo'a et ha-kol midaber eilav* — *midaber eilav*, directed toward him alone, meaning only Moshe heard. If the divine calling was private, it cannot publicly distinguish Moshe.

### Sinai vs Ohel

The Gemara's first resolution: *lo kashya, ha b'Sinai ha b'Ohel Moed* — the two cases are different. At Har Sinai, the calling was a single extraordinary event that all of Israel heard; subsequently, at the *Ohel Moed*, the divine speech was exclusively private. Sinai was a unique communal revelation in which the calling of Moshe's name was a public act — *lechalek kavod le-Moshe* before the whole nation. The ongoing private communications from the *Ohel Moed* are a different mode entirely.

An alternative resolution is also offered: *ha b'kriya ha b'dibur* — even at the *Ohel Moed*, one can distinguish between the calling — *kriya*, the address by name — and the content of the speech — *dibur*. The calling of the name might always have been audible to those present; only the substance of what God said was restricted to Moshe. On this reading, it was always publicly known that God was calling Moshe, even if the content of divine speech was not shared. This is a striking possibility: the nation perpetually witnesses God naming Moshe, confirming his unique relationship with God, even as the specific words of Torah pass between them privately.

### Divine Force

Returning to the core contradiction — Moshe cannot enter the *anan* at the *Ohel Moed*, yet he entered the *anan* at Har Sinai — the Gemara resolves it through a remarkable teaching: *melamed she-tefaso Hakadosh Baruch Hu le-Moshe ve-hivi'o ba-anan* — God took hold of Moshe and brought him into the cloud. Moshe did not himself penetrate the divine presence; God drew him in. This is not Moshe crossing a threshold under his own power, but God extending himself to bring Moshe inside. The encounter, in other words, is entirely on God's initiative — God makes it possible, God enables the entry, God guarantees the path.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael reinforces this with a *gezeirah shavah*: it says *be-toch* here at Sinai, and it says *be-toch* elsewhere — *vayavo'u benei Yisrael be-toch ha-yam* — the people went into the *midst* of the sea, where the waters formed walls: *ha-mayim lahem chomah*. As there a path was made through what would otherwise be impassable, so here: God opened a path for Moshe through the cloud. Moshe was not in the full substance of the divine cloud; there was a channel, a *shvil*, through which he could pass without being consumed.

The *daf* closes, then, on precisely this tension — the impossibility and the possibility of the divine-human encounter held together. Moshe cannot enter the *anan*; God brings him in. The path exists, but only because God creates it. The *kohen gadol* prepares for seven days, goes through every stage of the process, and yet the entry into the *Kodesh Hakodashim* is only possible because God permits it and sustains it. That is the final image *daf dalet* leaves us with: the encounter with God is utterly beyond human capacity to engineer, and yet it is made real through the combination of human preparation — rigorous, sustained, ritually elaborate — and divine accommodation. *Bi-mekom gilah sham tehei ra'adah* — the rejoicing and the trembling belong together, at Sinai and on *Yom Kippur* alike.

---

---

# Yoma 5

## Separation Models

### Intro: Two Models

We pick up in the middle of daf 4b, approximately twelve lines from the bottom, in the midst of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding the two models for the *kohen gadol*'s days of separation. Rabbi Yochanan holds that we learn the requirement from the *miluim* — the process of consecrating Aharon, his sons, and the *kohen gadol* for the *avodah* — and accordingly the separation is oriented around preparation for *avodah*. Reish Lakish, by contrast, holds that the source is the six days Moshe spent in the *anan* at the outset of his forty days following Har Sinai, before he entered the *anan* to be with God; accordingly, the focus is on the *kohen gadol*'s entry into the *kodesh kodashim* and is less *avodah*-centered. We also noted previously the position associated with Rav, that even Rabbi Yochanan's model — preparation for *avodah* — can be understood as elevating the *kohen gadol* to a higher status, perhaps even as a representative of Aharon himself, which would explain why the process applies only to the *kohen gadol* and not to the designated stand-in.

### Vayikra Purpose

Within that broader discussion of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, the *gemara* engages with the *pesukim* describing God calling to Moshe *mitoch ha'anan*. The question is: what was the purpose of *vayikra el Moshe* at Har Sinai, before the *aseret hadibrot*? The *gemara* answers: *lachlok lo kavod* — to bestow honor upon Moshe. The *gemara* then pivots to the *vayikra el Moshe* at the opening of *Vayikra*, where it is similarly followed by *vayedaber Hashem elav*. The question: why does *kriya* precede *dibur* — why does God first call to Moshe before speaking? The answer is *lilmedcha derech eretz shelo yomar adam davar lachavero ela im ken kora'o*: it teaches proper conduct — one does not simply begin speaking to someone without first addressing them by name and inviting them into the conversation. God called to Moshe, in effect saying, "Moshe, I wish to speak with you," and only then began. This teaching is identified as supporting the principle of Rabbi Chanina, who stated the same rule as a general norm of human conduct.

### Moshe Distance

As we noted at the close of the previous session, the opening *pasuk* of *Vayikra* must be read in juxtaposition with the final *pasuk* of *Shemot*: Moshe could not enter the *ohel moed* because the *anan* rested upon it — *ki shachan alav ha'anan* — and so God had to call out to Moshe, drawing him into at least some form of encounter. A striking *midrash* addresses the apparent asymmetry: at Har Sinai, Moshe entered into the *anan*, yet at the *ohel moed* he did not. Two answers are offered — that at Har Sinai God compelled Moshe into the *anan*, and that God carved a path for him through it. Both responses grapple with the profound question that the *gemara* returns to repeatedly in the context of Har Sinai: the nature and very possibility of a genuine human-divine encounter. These questions are alive precisely because entering the *anan* is not something a human being simply does of his own accord.

## Calling Before Speaking

### Derech Eretz Principle

The *gemara* identifies the principle underlying *vayikra el Moshe* as *derech eretz*: one does not speak to another person without first calling to them. The formulation is *shelo yomar adam davar lachavero ela im ken kora'o* — a person should not address something to his fellow unless he has first called to him. This is basic social conduct: before launching into substance, one acknowledges the other person, says their name, invites them into the exchange. The *gemara* cites this as supporting the teaching of Rabbi Chanina, who articulated the same principle independently.

### Privacy Assumption

The *gemara* proceeds to the word *lemor* at the close of the opening *pasuk* of *Vayikra*: *vayedaber Hashem elav me'ohel moed lemor*. The question becomes: what does *lemor* add? Rav Menashya Rabba derives from here a fundamental principle of confidentiality — *minayin la'omer davar lachavero shehu be'bal tomar ad she'yomar lo lech emor*: from where do we know that if someone tells you something, you are prohibited from repeating it until they explicitly tell you to go and say it? The source, as the *gemara* reads it, is this very *pasuk*.
