Rashi understands it as a play on *lemor* — *lav emor*, do not say — meaning one may not repeat what was told to him unless explicitly authorized. The Maharsha understands it more directly from the *pshat*: since the *pasuk* continues with *daber el Bnei Yisrael*, God had to explicitly instruct Moshe to transmit the communication outward. Had that instruction not been given, Moshe would have had no license to repeat what he heard, even to others, even if the content itself was not negative. This is a critically important principle, and one that deserves more emphasis in contemporary teaching. The prohibition of *rekhilut* is understood as the prohibition against being a gossip — carrying information from person to person — and this applies even when the content is not negative. The deeper point is that one must assume all verbal communication is private unless explicitly released.

### Speech as Relational

The deeper insight is that every verbal communication is relational — it belongs to the relationship between the two parties involved, not to the world at large. It is not simply information that happens to have been transmitted; it is an exchange between two people, and treating it as freely shareable public information violates that relational dimension. This is not only about the other person's privacy but about the fundamental nature of speech as a bond between speaker and listener.

One small curiosity in passing: by the *vayikra* to Avraham, the text reads *vayikra el Avraham Avraham* — his name is said twice. Here, it reads only *vayikra el Moshe*, without the doubling. This is a good question and is left open.

## Miluim Essentials

### Both Hold Essentials

The *gemara* now returns to the core issue. It observes: *mikhlal de-tarvaihu sevira lehu miluim kol ha-katuv ba-hen me-akkeiv ba-hen* — it is implicit from the structure of the debate that both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish agree that in the *miluim* itself, every written component was indispensable. The logic is as follows: Reish Lakish challenged Rabbi Yochanan by saying that if the *miluim* is the model, one should conclude that just as in the *miluim* every requirement is essential, so too the seven-day separation of the *kohen gadol* should be essential *bedi'avad*. Rabbi Yochanan did not dismiss the premise — he did not say "who told you everything in the *miluim* is *me'akev*?" His silence on that point confirms that both disputants share that assumption.

### Miluim vs. Future

The *gemara* then introduces a related dispute, explicitly attributed: *de-itmar miluim* — there is a recorded debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina. One holds *kol ha-katuv ba-hen me-akkeiv ba-hen* — every single element written in the *miluim*, if not performed, invalidates. The other holds *davar ha-me-akkeiv le-dorot me-akkeiv ba-hen she-eino me-akkeiv le-dorot ein me-akkeiv ba-hen* — only those elements of the *miluim* that are generally essential in future generations are essential in the *miluim* itself; elements that are not *me'akev* in other contexts are likewise not *me'akev* in the *miluim*.

The *gemara* then resolves the attribution: *tistayeim* — we can conclude that Rabbi Yochanan is the one who holds everything is *me'akev*, since Reish Lakish challenged him on precisely that basis and he did not reject the premise. Rabbi Chanina, then, is the one holding the more limited position.

The question becomes: *mai beinaihu* — what are the concrete cases in dispute? That is, which components of the *miluim* are not generally *me'akev* in other contexts, and would therefore be at the center of this debate?

### Semicha Analysis

Rav Yosef identifies *semikhah* as the first point of disagreement. The *miluim* involved *semikhah* on the *korbanot* — Aharon and his sons leaned their hands upon the offerings. And yet in general, while *semikhah* is required on *korbanot*, failure to perform it does not invalidate the offering *bedi'avad*. According to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that everything in the *miluim* is *me'akev*, even the *semikhah* on the *korbanot* of the *miluim* would have been indispensable. According to Rabbi Chanina, since *semikhah* is not *me'akev* in other contexts, it would not have been *me'akev* in the *miluim* either.

### Blood and Kapara

The *gemara* then asks: *ul'dorot minalan delo me'akkeva* — from where do we know that *semikhah* is not *me'akev* in future generations? The answer is a well-known *braisa*: *v'chi semikhah mechaperes* — does *semikhah* actually achieve *kapara*? *V'halo ein kapara ela b'dam* — ultimately, *kapara* is achieved only through the blood, as the *pasuk* states: *ki hadam hu banefesh yechaper*. The *gemara* understands this *pasuk* to mean that the blood, and the blood alone, determines whether a *korban* is valid *bedi'avad*. This encompasses the *shechita* and the *zerikat hadam*; everything else, while required, does not ultimately prevent *kapara* if omitted. The word *ela* is decisive here — it is not merely that blood is *part* of *kapara*, but that it is the *only* determinant of *kapara*. The *gemara* then presses: *u'mah talmud lomar v'samach v'nirtza* — if blood alone achieves *kapara*, why does the Torah juxtapose *semikhah* with *v'nirtza*, implying that the offering is accepted on account of the *semikhah*?

### Semicha Paradox

The *braisa* resolves this with a striking formulation: *she'im asa l'semikhah shiyurei mitzvah ma'aleh alav hakatuv k'ilu lo chiper v'chiper* — if one treated *semikhah* as a marginal detail, as something optional, and accordingly omitted it, the Torah regards it as though he did not achieve *kapara* — and yet he did achieve *kapara*. This is a genuine paradox. Technically, *bedi'avad*, as long as the *dam* was handled correctly, the person has fulfilled his obligation. But *semikhah* is not merely a procedural nicety — it is part of the *kapara* process itself. Its absence does not prevent *kapara* from taking effect, but it means the *kapara* is incomplete in some meaningful sense. The Torah therefore treats the person as though he failed to achieve *kapara*, even while acknowledging that he did. This formulation is applied specifically to *semikhah* here, and as we will see, it is applied in an analogous way to *tenuphah* as well.

The key distinction is: *semikhah* is not *me'akev* in the technical sense that prevents one from being *yotzei*, but it is part of the *kapara* process. Its omission does not invalidate; it impoverishes.

## Non-Essential Components

### Waving

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak identifies *tenuphah* — the waving of portions of the *korbanot* and the bread — as the next point of disagreement. *Tenuphah* is a standard feature of certain *korbanot*, such as *shelamim*, where the *shok hayamin* and *chazeh hatenuphah* are waved. The question is whether failure to perform *tenuphah* in the *miluim* would have been *me'akev*. According to Rabbi Yochanan, yes; according to Rabbi Chanina, since *tenuphah* is not *me'akev* in future generations, it would not have been *me'akev* in the *miluim* either.

The *gemara* then asks: *ul'dorot minalan delo me'akkeva* — from where do we know *tenuphah* is not *me'akev* in future generations? A *braisa* is cited that mirrors the *semikhah* discussion almost exactly: *v'chi tenuphah mechaperes* — does waving actually achieve *kapara*? *V'halo ein kapara ela b'dam*, as the *pasuk* says. So why does the Torah say *letnuphah lechaper*? *Im asa'o letnuphah shiyurei mitzvah ma'aleh alav hakatuv k'ilu lo kiper v'chiper* — the same formulation: it is as if he did not achieve *kapara*, and yet he did. The conclusion is parallel: *tenuphah* is not *me'akev* in the technical sense, but it is part of the *kapara* process, and its omission is not trivial.

The *gemara* is now building a list of components performed in the *miluim* that are not generally *me'akev* in other contexts. Each item on this list represents a point of contention between Rabbi Yochanan, who holds all of them were *me'akev* in the *miluim*, and Rabbi Chanina, who holds that none of them were. The first two items are *semikhah* and *tenuphah*.

### Seven-Day Separation

Rav Papa identifies *prisha shiva* — the seven-day separation — as the next item. This is, of course, the very issue that Reish Lakish used to challenge Rabbi Yochanan: if the *miluim* is the model, why should the seven-day separation of the *kohen gadol* not be *me'akev bedi'avad*? Rabbi Yochanan had no answer, confirming that he holds it was *me'akev* in the *miluim*. Rabbi Chanina, by contrast, would hold that since we do not find the separation to be *me'akev* in future generations, it would not have been *me'akev* in the *miluim* either.

One must be careful about what *me'akev* means in this context. By *semikhah* and *tenuphah*, the question is whether a particular act during the *avodah* of the *korban* was indispensable. Here, *me'akev* means something broader: would the failure to maintain the seven-day separation in the *mishkan* have prevented the consecration — of the *mishkan* itself and of the *kohanim* — from taking effect? The goal of the *miluim* was not just the offering of *korbanot* but the inauguration of the *mishkan* and the installation of the *kohanim* into their *avodah*. So *me'akev* here refers to *me'akev* the *miluim* as a whole, not merely a specific *korban*.

The *gemara* asks: *ul'dorot minalan delo me'akkeva*? How do we know the separation is not *me'akev* in future generations? The answer is derived from our own *mishnah*: the *mishnah* speaks of preparing a stand-in *kohen gadol* for Yom Kippur, yet it does not say that the stand-in must undergo a seven-day separation. This indicates that while separation may be required, its absence does not invalidate. One can say either that the concept of separation never applies in future generations at all, or — more instructively — that even where it does apply, it is not *me'akev*. The *mishnah*'s silence regarding the stand-in's separation supports the latter reading.

### Dressing & Anointing

Ravina identifies *ribui shiva u'meshicha shiva* — the seven days of dressing and the seven days of anointing — as the next and most far-reaching item on the list. During the *miluim*, Moshe dressed Aharon and his sons in the *bigdei kehunah* day after day, and anointed Aharon and the garments. This was the very act of consecration. But in future generations, we do not find that the failure to repeat this process for all seven days is *me'akev*.

This is a striking escalation. If one could still accept that failing to do *semikhah* or *tenuphah* does not invalidate, since those are relatively peripheral acts during the *avodah*, the idea that the entire dressing and anointing process could be dispensed with seems radical. After all, the dressing and anointing were not incidental features of the *miluim* — they were its very substance, the mechanism of consecration. And yet, says Rabbi Chanina, since this level of detail is not *me'akev le-dorot*, it would not have been *me'akev* in the *miluim* either.

### Tetzaveh vs. Acharei Mot

To understand what is and is not *me'akev le-dorot* regarding dressing and anointing, the *gemara* turns to the relevant *pesukim*. In *parshat Tetzaveh*, where the command of the *miluim* is given, it says: *uvigdei hakodesh asher le'aharon yihyu levanav acharav lemoshcha vahem ulemalei vam et yadam* — the sacred garments of Aharon will belong to his sons after him, to anoint them through the garments and to install them into office. Then the next *pasuk* says *shivat yamim yilbasham hakohen tachtav mibanav asher yavo el ohel moed lisharet bakodesh* — for seven days the *kohen* who succeeds him shall wear them. On the face of it, this seems to require seven days of wearing the garments for any future *kohen* who will enter the *ohel moed* — which Rashi identifies as referring to the *kohen gadol* on Yom Kippur.

Yet the *parsha* at the end of *Acharei Mot*, when describing the future *kohen gadol* who will perform the Yom Kippur *avodah*, says only: *asher yimshach oto va'asher yemale et yado* — the one who was anointed and whose hands were filled, that is, who was dressed in the garments. No mention of seven days.

### Minimum Requirements

A *braisa* is cited that resolves this apparent contradiction: *ein li ela nitraba shiva venimshach shiva* — I know only that if one was dressed for seven days and anointed for seven days, the new *kohen gadol* has achieved his status. But what about *nitraba shiva venimshach yom echad* — dressed seven days but anointed only one day — or the reverse? *Minayin*? From where do I know that *bedi'avad* even that suffices? The answer is *talmud lomar asher yimshach oto va'asher yemale et yado mikol makom* — because *Acharei Mot* uses the simple formulation without specifying seven days, *bedi'avad* even a single instance of each suffices.

This is the basis for the halachic ruling codified by the Rambam in *Kelei Hamikdash*. The Rambam states that in *Bayit Sheni*, where there was no *shemen hamishcha*, a *kohen gadol* was consecrated through *ribuy begadim* alone — wearing the eight garments repeatedly for seven days. He describes the process: the *kohen* would dress in the eight garments, remove them, and replace them each day for seven days, as the *pasuk* says *shivat yamim yilbasham hakohen tachtav mibanav*. Similarly, just as dressing is seven days, so too anointing is seven days — *ukesheim sheribuy begadim shiva kach meshicha shiva*. Yet *bedi'avad*, if he performed the *avodah* before completing all seven days of dressing or all seven days of anointing, the *avodah* is valid, *ho'il venistarbeh o nimshach pa'am achat* — since he was dressed or anointed even once.

The Ra'avad adds a fascinating qualification: this requirement of seven days applied specifically to prepare the *kohen gadol* for *avodat Yom HaKippurim* — for entering the *kodesh kodashim* — not for the ordinary status of *kohen gadol*. The *pasuk* in *Tetzaveh* itself, with its phrase *asher yavo el ohel moed*, supports this: Rashi reads it as referring to Yom Kippur entry. This nicely accords with the Soloveitchik reading that the seven-day process creates a distinct *kohen gadol* status specifically oriented toward *avodat Yom HaKippurim*, over and above ordinary *kehuna gedolah*.

The upshot for our debate: Rabbi Chanina holds that the minimum for future generations — even a single day of dressing and a single day of anointing — establishes the baseline, and therefore had the *miluim* been conducted with only that minimum, it would have been valid. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the first time around, every detail of the seven-day process was absolutely essential.

## Kakah and Textual Proof

### Kakah Exactness

The *gemara* now turns to the textual justification for Rabbi Yochanan's position — the position that every component of the *miluim* was *me'akev*. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna cites the *pasuk* from *Ve'ata Tetzaveh*, at the close of the *miluim* command: *ve'asita le'aharon ulevanav kakha kechol asher tziviti otacha* — you shall do for Aharon and his sons *kakha*, exactly like this, as all that I have commanded you. *Kakha ikuva hu* — the word *kakha* signals that the requirement is exact. Every detail specified must be performed precisely as stated; nothing may be omitted. This is the textual anchor for the position that all is *me'akev*.

### Pesach Gezeirah

The *gemara* then raises a difficulty: *teinach* — that works well for everything written in *Tetzaveh*. But what about things performed in *Tzav* — where the *miluim* was actually enacted — that do not appear in *Tetzaveh*? Rashi identifies the *urim ve'tumim* as one such element: it is mentioned in *Tzav* but not in *Tetzaveh*. If *kakha* in *Tetzaveh* is the source for *me'akev*, how do we extend that to elements appearing only in *Tzav*?

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers: *yalif pesach pesach* — a *gezeirah shavah* is made on the word *pesach* (*petach ohel moed*), which appears repeatedly and somewhat superfluously in both *Tetzaveh* and *Tzav*. Through this *gezeirah shavah*, whatever is *me'akev* in *Tetzaveh* is equally *me'akev* in *Tzav*.

### Three Proofs

Two additional proofs are offered. Rav Mesharshiya cites *veshamrtem et mishmeret Hashem* from *Tzav* — the injunction to guard the charge of God — which in itself underscores that everything recorded there must be scrupulously observed, and carries the force of *ikuva*. Rav Ashi cites the phrase *ki chein tziveisi* — "because thus I was commanded" — which Moshe invokes in the context of the *miluim*; this too signals that every element is *me'akev*, since it frames the entire undertaking as an exacting divine command.

## Eighth Day Emphasis

### Nadav Avihu Death

Since we concluded with the phrase *ki chein tziveisi*, the *gemara* pursues a digression: the *baraisa* records that this phrase — along with its variants *ka'asher tziveisi* and *ka'asher tziva Hashem* — appears three times on Yom HaShmini, the eighth day. Why this threefold repetition? The context is important: after seven days of the *miluim* ritual, the eighth day arrives as the culmination. Aharon brings his first *korban* as *kohen gadol*, the glory of God appears, and then Nadav and Avihu, sons of Aharon, bring an unauthorized offering and die. In the aftermath of this tragedy, Moshe continues to instruct Aharon and his surviving sons to carry on with the *avodah*.

### Mincha Eating

The first instance of *ki chein tziveisi* appears when Moshe instructs Aharon and his sons to eat the remaining *mincha*: *kechu et hamincha hanoseres me'ishei Hashem ve'ochuha matzot etzel hamizbe'ach ki chein tziveisi*. Despite the fact that Aharon and his sons are *onanim* — in the state of acute mourning for their sons and brothers who have just died — Moshe tells them they must eat the *mincha* anyway, and grounds this in the fact that he was commanded to say so.

### Chattas Question

The second instance — *ka'asher tziveisi* — comes when Moshe observes that the *se'ir hachattas* has been burned rather than eaten. He challenges Aharon: *achol tochlu osa bakodesh ka'asher tziveisi* — you should have eaten it in the sacred precinct, as I commanded. Here again the phrase appears in the context of insisting that the *avodah* must continue despite the mourning, with Moshe pointing to his own *tzivui* as the mandate.

### Shlomim Permission

The third instance — *ka'asher tziva Hashem* — precedes the episode of the *chattas* in the sequence of *pesukim*. Here Moshe instructs them to eat the meat of the *shelamim* — the *shok haterumah* and the *chazeh hatenuphah* — even while they are *onanim*: *velach ulevane'icha ito lechok olam ka'asher tziva Hashem*. This too grounds the instruction in divine command rather than Moshe's own authority.

### Rashi's Reading

Rashi explains the significance of the third instance — *ka'asher tziva Hashem*, "as God commanded" — by noting that here Moshe is explicitly distinguishing his words from his own authority: *velo me'elai ani omer* — "I am not saying this on my own." After the tragedy of Nadav and Avihu, and after the difficult instruction to eat the *mincha* and *shelamim* in a state of acute mourning, Moshe underscores that all of this comes directly from God. He is not improvising. Rashi notes that this statement is made in the context of reassuring them after they had already burned the *chattas*: even now, continue to follow the divine directive, because I am only transmitting what God has commanded. Whether the precise sequence of *pesukim* fully supports Rashi's reading is a matter for consideration, but the essential point is clear: Moshe's three invocations of divine command on the eighth day serve to underscore the non-negotiable, God-given character of everything he has instructed.

## Missing Components

### Michnasayim

Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina raises a difficulty: the *michnasayim* — the priestly breeches — are never mentioned in the *parsha* of the *miluim* command when it speaks of dressing Aharon and his sons. Yet they are clearly part of the *bigdei kehunah*. One view holds that the phrase *vezeh hadavar asher ta'aseh lahem lekadeish osam lekahen li* — "this is the thing you shall do for them to sanctify them to serve Me" — includes the *michnasayim*, since *zeh* points back to everything previously described in *Tetzaveh*, where the *michnasayim* do appear among the priestly garments. The *gemara* accepts this: since the *parsha* commanding the *miluim* is at the close of *Tetzaveh*, and *Tetzaveh* opens with a full account of all the priestly garments including the *michnasayim*, the word *vezeh* contextually draws all of those garments into the *miluim* requirement.

### Esheris Ha'eiphah

The same phrase *vezeh hadavar* is also used to derive the inclusion of the *asiris ha'eiphah* — the daily meal-offering — which a new *kohen* brings upon first entering the *avodah*, and which the *kohen gadol* brings in halves each day. This offering is not mentioned explicitly in the *miluim* parsha either. The *gemara* derives its inclusion through a *gezeirah shavah* of *zeh zeh*: the *parsha* elsewhere that introduces the *asiris ha'eiphah* also begins with the word *zeh*, and the word *vezeh* in the *miluim* context therefore draws it in.

The *gemara* notes a distinction between the two derivations: the *michnasayim* fits naturally under *vezeh* because it appears in the same contextual unit — the *inyana de-bigadim* at the opening of *Tetzaveh* — and is therefore easily read as included by implication. The *asiris ha'eiphah*, by contrast, belongs to a different *parsha* entirely, and cannot be included by contextual reading alone. It requires the independent *gezeirah shavah* of *zeh zeh* to bring it in.

A further observation: toward the close of this discussion, the *gemara* cites Rav Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai — *minayin she'af mikra parsha me'akev* — from where do we know that even the formal announcement of the *parsha* is *me'akev*? At the beginning of *Tzav*, before the *miluim* begins, Moshe assembles the entire congregation and says: *ze hadavar asher tziva Hashem* — this is the thing God has commanded. If Moshe had not made this announcement, says Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, they would not have been *yotzei*. The derivation: *afilu dibur me'akev* — even the verbal announcement is *me'akev*, since *ze hadavar asher tziva Hashem* — the very *word* (*davar*) is included in what God commanded (*asher tziva Hashem*), and therefore even that carries the force of *ikuva*.

## History to Halacha

### Contradiction Resolution

With these discussions complete, the *gemara* raises a new question: *keitzad hilbishan* — how did Moshe dress Aharon and his sons? Before engaging, the *gemara* itself objects: *mai de-heva heva* — what was, was. Why do we care how Moshe dressed them? That is mere history, and the *gemara* does not traffic in idle historical speculation. So the question is reformulated: *ela keitzad malbishin le'atid lavo* — how will we dress the *kohanim* in the future, when the *beit hamikdash* is rebuilt and a new *miluim* process takes place? By reframing the question as a halachic one — what are the requirements going forward — the inquiry becomes relevant.

But even this reframing invites a question: why not simply say what was required at the time of the original *miluim* and derive the future requirement from that? The *gemara*'s deeper answer is that the question is not idle historical speculation at all, even in its original form. The real motivation is *lemisbar karai* — to resolve contradictions between *pesukim*. The *pesukim* in *Tetzaveh*, where the *miluim* is commanded, and the *pesukim* in *Tzav*, where it is enacted, appear to describe the dressing process differently. Resolving the contradiction requires understanding precisely how Moshe dressed Aharon and his sons. That is not history for its own sake; it is textual analysis driven by a genuine *kashya* in the *pesukim*.

### Future World Query

The *gemara* adds a further observation: *le'atid lavo nami lechsheyavo Aharon uvanav uMoshe imahem* — in the future world, when the resurrection occurs, we will be able to ask Moshe and Aharon directly what they did, and they will provide the historical testimony. This is not *lo bashamayim hi* — it is not turning to heaven for halachic rulings. Resurrected figures who were present and can report what actually occurred are providing factual information, not halachic *pesak*. Their testimony will then resolve the question definitively.

### Order Contradictions

The specific contradiction in the *pesukim* is this: in *Tetzaveh*, the dressing of Aharon and his sons is described in one way, and in *Tzav*, it is described differently. The question of the order — whether Aharon was fully dressed first and then his sons, or whether they were all dressed together, garment by garment — is not resolvable without carefully working through what each set of *pesukim* implies. The *gemara* now proceeds to analyze precisely this.

## Dressing Order Dispute

### Two Dressing Orders

The dispute is between the sons of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yochanan. One holds *Aharon ve'achar kach banav* — Aharon was fully dressed first in all his garments, and only then were his sons dressed. The other holds *Aharon u-vanav be-vat achat* — Aharon and his sons were dressed together, meaning garment by garment, each person receiving one garment before the next garment was applied to anyone.

### Cloak/Hat Agreement

Abaye notes that on one point there is no dispute: regarding the *kutonet* (the cloak) and the *mitznefet* (the turban/hat), everyone agrees that *Aharon kodem* — Aharon was dressed in these garments before the sons. This is because both in *Tetzaveh* (the command) and in *Tzav* (the execution), the *pesukim* begin with Aharon receiving the *kutonet* and the *mitznefet* before the sons are mentioned at all. So *bein betzava'ah bein be'asiyah*, whether in the command or in the fulfillment, Aharon receives the *kutonet* and the *mitznefet* first, and this is uncontested.

### Belt Dispute

The dispute centers on the *avnet* — the belt. The *avnet* was applied last, after the *kutonet* and the *mitznefet*. At this point the *pesukim* diverge. In *Tzav*, it says *vayachgor oto ba'avnet* — he belted *him* (Aharon) — and then *vayachgor otam* — he belted *them* (the sons), suggesting a sequential process: Aharon was fully completed, belt and all, before Moshe turned to dress the sons at all. In *Tetzaveh*, by contrast, it says *ve'chagarta otam avnet* — and you shall gird *them* with the belt — combining Aharon and the sons in a single act, which suggests that all were dressed together up to the belt stage and then belted as a unit.

The one who holds *Aharon ve'achar kach banav* — first Aharon, then the sons — relies on *Tzav*: *oto* and then *otam*, a sequential completion. The one who holds *Aharon u-vanav be-vat achat* — all together — relies on *Tetzaveh*: *ve'chagarta otam*, a unified act.

Each position must then account for the other's proof-text. The one who holds they were dressed together explains the separation in *Tzav* (*oto* and then *otam*) as conveying not a difference in process but a difference in garment: *avneto shel kohen gadol lo zehu avneto shel kohen hedyot* — the *avnet* of the *kohen gadol* is not the same as the *avnet* of the ordinary *kohen*. The *avnet* of the *kohen gadol* is composed of four strands — three wool and one linen — making it *shaatnez*. The Torah does not specify the material of the ordinary *kohen*'s *avnet*, and there is a dispute about whether it matches the *kohen gadol*'s or is a simpler linen belt. According to this view, the reason *Tzav* separates *oto* from *otam* is precisely to indicate that the two belts are different — not that the process was sequential.

### Sequential Uninterrupted

Conversely, the one who holds *Aharon ve'achar kach banav* — the sequential reading — must explain the unifying language of *Tetzaveh*'s *ve'chagarta otam*. He explains that *otam* is brought together to convey that the *avnet* of the *kohen gadol* and the *avnet* of the ordinary *kohanim* are the same.

The *gemara* then raises the obvious question on the *be-vat achat* position: *u-ve-vat achat mi meshakhachat lah* — how is it even physically possible to belt four people simultaneously? The answer is *lo tzrikha de-akdim* — it does not mean literally simultaneous. Rather, the belting of all of them was done as a single uninterrupted process. One after another the belts were applied, but without any interruption between them — not completing Aharon's belt and then proceeding to dress the sons in their other garments before returning to belt them. The belts were applied in immediate succession, and in that sense it was *be-vat achat* — at one time, as a unified act.

We will continue tomorrow at 7:15, beginning on daf 5a, four lines from the top, with *amar Rav Ashi*.

# Yoma 6

## Wife Separation

### Miluim/Har Sinai Recap

The daf opens, approximately eight lines from the top of *vav amud aleph*, with the *gemara* revisiting the discussion that occupied the preceding four days. The *mishna* states *mafrishin kohen gadol mibeto* — the *kohen gadol* is separated from his house for seven days prior to the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur*, during which time he would reside in the *Lishkat Parhedrin* within the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *gemara* asks: *lama mafrishin?* — why do we separate him? Its own reply is almost impatient: *kideka'amarnan* — as we have already said. Either according to Rabbi Yochanan, who derived the seven-day separation from the model of the *miluim*, or according to Reish Lakish, who derived it from *Har Sinai* — the reasoning has already been established over the preceding discussion.

### Beto = Wife

Having dispatched the general question, the *gemara* turns to the specific word *mibeto*. The word *bayit* throughout *Shas* commonly refers not merely to a physical dwelling but to a man's wife — the Aramaic word for wife, *devataiyu*, itself reflects this usage — and the *gemara* takes for granted that the *mishna*'s phrasing means he was separated from his wife. This is consistent with the *pasuk* of *Yom Kippur*, *vechiper ba'ado uve'ad beto*, which the *gemara* elsewhere reads as *beto zu ishto*, his wife, and which is why the *kohen gadol* is required to be married on *Yom Kippur*. The *gemara* now asks: *mibeto lama pirash?* — specifically why was he separated from his wife? Why couldn't his wife join him in the *Lishkat Parhedrin*?

### Lishkat Parhedrin

The *gemara* frames this as a genuine question and proceeds to seek the reason. Before it offers an answer, the question itself implicitly presupposes that the *Lishkat Parhedrin* was not possessed of the full *kedushah* of the *azarah* — otherwise the question would be self-answering, since one may not even sit in the *azarah*, let alone sleep there or engage in marital relations. The nature of the *lishkah*'s sanctity is itself a matter that the *gemara* will address in greater detail.

## Wife Separation (II)

### Tumah Concern

The *gemara* presents a *baraita*: *Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira omer, shema timatze ishto safek nida veyavo aleha* — lest his wife turn out to be a *safek niddah* and he come upon her. The reason for separation is not, as one might have supposed, rooted in the *miluim* model or the *Har Sinai* model — it is a *tumah* concern. The *kohen gadol* must be *tahor* on *Yom Kippur*, and if his wife is present and they are living as husband and wife, there is a risk that he will have relations with her while she is in a state of *niddah*, thereby contracting a seven-day *tumah*.

## Safek Niddah

### R. Yehuda ben Beteira

A man who has relations with a woman who is a *niddah* acquires, in addition to the grave prohibition entailing *karet*, the *tumah* of the *niddah* herself — a seven-day *tumah*. The *baraita* of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira thus grounds the entire institution of separation in a concern for *tumah* rather than in any conceptual framework of spiritual preparation. This is itself a striking feature of the *gemara*'s approach, to which we will return.

### Atu Bershei

The *gemara* immediately raises an objection: *atu bersha'ei askinan?* — are we dealing with wicked people? He would never knowingly have relations with his wife when she is definitely a *niddah*, or even when she is a *safek niddah*. The prohibition itself would restrain him, quite apart from any *tumah* concern.

### Timing Safek

The *gemara* therefore refines the scenario: *ela shema yavo al ishto vetimsa safek nida* — rather, the concern is that he will have relations with his wife permissibly, and only afterward will she discover blood, creating a retroactive *safek* as to whether she was a *niddah* at the time of relations. The act is done entirely in good faith; the *safek* arises after the fact. While the *gemara* could have stated the concern in terms of her definitely becoming a *niddah* mid-act, it frames it as a *safek* in order to describe a scenario that is both more realistic and more common — they have relations with no indication of any problem, and then some time later a bloodstain is discovered. The question is then whether that retroactive *safek* is sufficient to render the husband *tamei*.

## Rav Chisda Position

### R. Akiva/Rabbanan

The rabbis brought this concern before Rav Chisda. His response — *keman?* — cuts to the issue: this would only be a legitimate concern according to Rabbi Akiva, *d'amar niddah metama bo'alah*, who holds that the *niddah* renders her husband *tamei* retroactively. The *rabbanan*, by contrast, hold *ein niddah metama bo'alah* — the *niddah* does not render her husband *tamei* in this way.

### 24-Hour Retroactive

This requires explanation. The *rabbanan* do not deny that a man who has relations with a definite *niddah* is *tamei*. The question concerns the mechanism of *tumah* when the woman's status as *niddah* is established only retroactively. The first *mishna* in *Niddah* establishes that when a woman finds blood — whether through an internal examination or on her garments — she is *temeiah* retroactively for the preceding twenty-four hours (absent a more recent internal check that would shorten the window). This retroactivity governs objects she handled: anything she touched in the prior twenty-four hours is retroactively *tamei*. The debate is whether this retroactive *tumah* extends to her husband as well. The *rabbanan* hold that it does not — *psychologically*, as it were, the concern that one's wife might retroactively turn out to have been a *niddah* during any prior act of relations would make marital life untenable, and the sages did not extend the retroactivity that far. Rabbi Akiva disagrees and holds that even the husband is rendered *tamei* retroactively. Rav Chisda's point is therefore that if this is the governing concern behind the separation, it would only be operative according to Rabbi Akiva.

## Rav Chisda Position (II)

### Three Scenarios

Rav Chisda, however, does not leave it there. He responds to the rabbis: *afilu teima rabanan* — even granting the position of the *rabbanan*, the concern remains. The *rabbanan* only dispute Rabbi Akiva regarding *achar achar* — the "after of the after," a time period beyond approximately thirty seconds following relations. The *gemara* identifies three distinct temporal scenarios.

The first is immediate discovery: she checks the moment they separate and finds she is bleeding. In that case, there is a presumption that she was already a *niddah* during relations, with implications even for the obligation to bring a *korban*. The second scenario is discovery within approximately thirty seconds — enough time to rise from the bed and perform a rinse. In that window, the *safek* is genuine and real at a biblical level, and everyone agrees that the husband would be *tamei*, since it is a true *safek* whether she was a *niddah* during the act itself. The third scenario is discovery after that thirty-second window. It is here that the debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *rabbanan* applies: only Rabbi Akiva would extend retroactive *tumah* to the husband in that case; the *rabbanan* would not. Rav Chisda's point is that even according to the *rabbanan*, there is a real window — the first thirty seconds — during which everyone agrees the husband would be *tamei* at a biblical level. The concern is not merely theoretical.

## Safek Niddah (II)

### Time Periods

So the *gemara*'s description of the concern is precise: the scenario is not that she was bleeding while they were having relations, but that a period of time elapsed afterward — corresponding to the middle window — during which discovery would create a genuine, biblically-grounded *safek* as to the husband's *tumah* status. It is precisely that realistic scenario which motivates the separation.

## Conceptual Questions

### Spiritual Model Q

At this point, a deeper question presents itself. Why does the *gemara* ground the separation entirely in this *tumah* concern — a secondary, practical matter — rather than in a more primary conceptual framework? One might have supposed that the very models the *gemara* invoked earlier — *miluim* and *Har Sinai* — themselves supply a compelling reason for the *kohen gadol* to be separated from his wife. Why is *tumah* offered as the explanation rather than the concept of spiritual preparation or elevated consecration implicit in those models?

### Miluim Immersion

On reflection, the *miluim* model may not carry the weight one expects here. The verse *mipetach ohel moed lo teitzu shivat yamim pen tamutu* — "you shall not depart from the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days lest you die" — describes an immersion into the life of the *kehunah* and the *avodah* of the *Mishkan*. The *miluim* was about initiating the *kohanim* into their role, inaugurating the space, and conferring upon them the status of *kehunah*. As has been discussed elsewhere, the Rav understood the *Yom Kippur* process in terms of imparting the *kohen gadol* with a special status. But the *miluim* model is not essentially about shedding the material self or transcending the physical world — it is about full immersion into a new institutional role. One could therefore argue that even within the *miluim* model, having one's wife present while fully inhabiting the priestly role is not obviously contradicted.

### Har Sinai Emphasis

The *Har Sinai* model, however, is considerably more difficult to dismiss. The forty days Moshe spent on the mountain were characterized by complete abstinence: *lachem lo achalti umayim lo shatiti* — he ate no bread and drank no water. The *gemara* notes that perhaps the first days were to purge him of food. And the three days prior to *matan Torah*, the verse states *al tigshu el isha* — the separation from women was explicit. Moshe's own permanent separation from his wife, *Tzipporah*, alluded to in *chazal*'s reading of various passages, underscores that in the *Har Sinai* model the separation from one's wife is intrinsic and self-evident. It is therefore genuinely puzzling why, according to Reish Lakish who derives the seven-day separation from *Har Sinai*, the *gemara* should need any additional explanation grounded in *tumah* concern. According to that model, the reason for the separation from the wife seems entirely self-evident from the paradigm itself. This question does not receive a clear answer in the *gemara*.

## Lishkat Status

### Rashi

A second question concerns what Rashi calls the *havaminah* of the question itself. When the *gemara* asks why the *kohen gadol* could not have his wife present in the *Lishkat Parhedrin*, it implicitly assumes she could be there and they could live as husband and wife. But how is that conceivable? Is the *Lishkat Parhedrin* not within the *Beit HaMikdash*? Rashi addresses this directly. He writes: *tavo ishto imo sham* — let his wife come with him there, *sheharei al korchacha Lishkat Parhedrin lo haysa kedushah* — because by necessity the *Lishkat Parhedrin* could not have had the *kedushah* of the *azarah*. Rashi's reasoning: *she-ein yeshiva ba-azarah ela le-malchei beis David kol she-kein shechivah* — one may not even sit in the *azarah* other than kings of the Davidic line, and certainly not lie down. The *kohen gadol* must sleep during his seven days, and therefore the *lishkah* in which he slept cannot have possessed the sanctity of the *azarah* proper. Since it lacks *azarah* sanctity, the question then arises why his wife could not be there with him.

### Tosafot Q

Tosafot, however, presses further. Granting that the *Lishkat Parhedrin* lacked the *kedushah* of the *azarah*, it still would have had at minimum the *kedushah* of *Har Habayit*. As a *baraita* in *perek Bachatzot* states, *kol Har Habayit machaneh Leviyah hu* — the entire Temple Mount has the status of *machaneh Leviyah*, and a *ba'al keri* — one who has had a seminal emission — may not enter *machaneh Leviyah*. If the *kohen gadol* were to have marital relations in the *Lishkat Parhedrin*, he would thereby become a *ba'al keri*, who is forbidden even on *Har Habayit*. So even before the *tumah* of *boel niddah* becomes relevant, the very act of relations would render him a *ba'al keri* and disqualify him from remaining in that space. Why then is *ba'al keri* not itself the stated concern?

### Underground Tunnel

Tosafot resolves this by reframing the *havaminah* entirely. The question is not why his wife cannot join him in the *Lishkat Parhedrin* as it actually existed, but rather: why was the separation not conducted in a *mechilah* — an underground tunnel beneath *Har Habayit*? The *gemara* in *perek Ketzad Tzolin* establishes that underground chambers were not sanctified with the *kedushah* of the temple precincts above them, *de-mechilot lo nitkadshu*. Had the *kohen gadol* resided in such a tunnel, neither *azarah* sanctity nor *Har Habayit* sanctity would apply, and presumably marital relations could have taken place there. It is against that *havaminah* — residence in an underground space devoid of *kedushah* — that the *tumah* concern of *boel niddah* serves as the answer.

This has an interesting implication. If the *havaminah* is that the *kohen gadol* might have been situated in an underground tunnel, then the concern about fulfilling the models of *miluim* or *Har Sinai* — particularly Reish Lakish's model in which the *kohen gadol* must be in some sense *nichtav be'anan*, enveloped in the divine cloud — would seem to require his presence in or near the *Mishkan* or *Beit HaMikdash* itself, not merely in some subterranean space beneath it. This is, of course, only the *havaminah*. In the event, since his wife does not accompany him, the *kohen gadol* is in the *Lishkat Parhedrin* itself, located on *Har Habayit* grounds — whether with the sanctity of *Har Habayit* or even of the *azarah*, depending on the question of which space its entrance opens onto, a matter the *gemara* will address separately.

## Ba'al Niddah Mikvah

### Mikvah Timing Q

The *gemara* now presents an inference by Rav Zeira: *shema mina ba ve-nidal eina ke-nida ve-tovel be-yom* — from this discussion one can infer that the *tumah* of a *ba'al niddah* — a man who has had relations with a *niddah* — is not identical to the *tumah* of the *niddah* herself, and specifically that he may immerse in the *mikvah* during the daytime of the seventh day, not waiting for the following night.

The reasoning requires unpacking. A *niddah* counts seven days from the beginning of her menstrual flow and goes to the *mikvah* at nightfall — the conclusion of the seventh day, not during the day. This is because the Torah states *shivat yamim tihyeh ve-nidatah*, and the full seven days must elapse. Many *meforshim* explain that since a menstrual period can last up to seven days, there is a Torah-level concern that bleeding might continue through the seventh day itself, and therefore immersion must wait until nightfall. The verse *ve-tehi tumatah alav* — "her *tumah* shall be upon him" — indicates that the husband acquires her *tumah*, but the question is whether he acquires it in precisely the same form she has it, including the requirement to wait until nightfall on the seventh day.

### Timeline Scenario

Rav Zeira argues that the *tumah* concern driving the separation reveals the answer. Consider the scenario: the *kohen gadol* comes to the *Beit HaMikdash* to begin his seven-day separation. The concern is that he might have had relations with his wife immediately before arriving — perhaps at eleven in the morning, before coming at noon. If that act rendered him a *ba'al niddah*, when does his seventh day occur? If he arrived at noon on the first day, the seventh day would be *Yom Kippur* itself. If he were like a *niddah* and could only immerse at nightfall of the seventh day, he would go to the *mikvah* the night of *Yom Kippur* — and then, since *tvilah* requires *haarev shemesh* (the setting of the sun following immersion) for full *taharah*, he would not be completely *tahor* until *motzaei Yom Kippur*, after the service is long over.

### Day Seven Mikvah

The point, as Michael correctly observed in the course of the discussion, is that he did not come at noon on day one — we must worry about the worst-case scenario, namely that he had relations a moment before his arrival. So day seven lands precisely on *Yom Kippur*. If he could go to the *mikvah* during the day of the seventh — as is the standard rule for ordinary seven-day *tumot* — then by nightfall of *Yom Kippur*, which is simultaneously the *haarev shemesh* following his daytime immersion, he would be completely *tahor* and eligible to perform the *avodah*. The fact that the *gemara* frames the separation as a solution to the *tumah* concern therefore proves that the *ba'al niddah* goes to the *mikvah* during the daytime of the seventh day. *Ella lav shema mina boel niddah eino ke-niddah* — this demonstrates that he is not like the *niddah* in this respect.

The conceptual logic is elegant. The reason a *niddah* waits until nightfall is connected to the possibility that menstruation may continue throughout the seventh day. The *ba'al niddah* has the *tumah* without the menstruation — and as a *tumah* of seven days, it follows the normal pattern of seven-day *tumot*, which permit daytime immersion on the seventh day. A woman who is a *zavah* (with non-menstrual flow) goes to the *mikvah* on the day of the seventh; one who becomes *tamei* through contact with a *meit* completes the sprinkling of ashes on the seventh day. The *ba'al niddah*, as a seven-day *tumah* without the specific menstrual dimension, belongs to that category and goes to the *mikvah* during the day.

## Textual Support

### Niddah Exception

The *gemara* now tests Rav Zeira's position against textual sources. *Meitvei* — an objection is raised. A *mishna* states: *kol chayavei tvilos tvilosan ba-yom* — all those obligated in *tvilah* immerse during the daytime. The only exceptions are a *niddah* and a *yoledet* (a woman who has given birth), whose *tvilah* is at night: *tvilosan ba-laylah*. The *mishna* lists only *niddah* and *yoledet* as exceptions. Since *ba'al niddah* is not listed among the exceptions, it would appear he follows the standard rule and goes during the day — consistent with Rav Zeira, and a challenge to anyone who would dispute him.

### Category Inclusion

The *gemara* deflects: *niddah ve-chol de-asi mi-ribui* — "*niddah*" in the *mishna* refers to a *niddah* and everyone who falls within the chapter of *niddah tumah*. Since the *ba'al niddah*'s *tumah* derives from the *niddah*, he is subsumed within the term *niddah* as used there. Therefore no inference can be drawn from his absence in the list of exceptions — he may well be included among those who wait for nightfall.

### Dead Body Comparison

A second challenge is mounted. A *mishna* in *Zavim* states: *ba'al keri ke-maga sheretz* — one who has had a seminal emission is like one who touched a *sheretz* (a dead creeping creature). The *mishna* thereby groups these *tumot* together, and separately groups the *ba'al niddah* with *tamei meit* — one who became *tamei* through contact with a corpse — as both being seven-day *tumot* of the status of *av ha-tumah*. Contact with a *meit* is in fact the most severe form of *tumah* — an *avi avot ha-tumah* — yielding the status of *av* to the one who touches it. A *ba'al niddah* similarly acquires an *av ha-tumah* status, for seven days. The *mishna* appears to equate them, and since *tamei meit* goes to the *mikvah* during the day of the seventh (via the sprinkling of ashes), the same should apply to *ba'al niddah* — supporting Rav Zeira.

### Duration Not Timing

The *gemara* responds: *lo letumatan* — the *mishna* is not making this comparison for the purpose of *tvilah* timing. It is comparing them only with respect to the duration of *tumah* — both are seven-day *tumot* rather than one-day *tumot*. Since the Torah states explicitly that both are seven-day *tumot*, the *mishna* does not need to teach that; it therefore must be teaching something else.

### Mishkav/Moshav

That something else is found in the *seifa* of the *mishna*: *ella shechamur mimennu boel niddah* — in one respect, the *ba'al niddah* is more stringent than the person who contacted a corpse. That stringency is *shemetamei mishkav umoshav betumah kallah letamei ochlin umashkin* — he renders the seat or bed upon which he rests *tamei*, with a *tumah kallah* that goes on to make food and liquids *tamei*.

This requires some elaboration. Among the special categories of *tumah* enumerated in *Tazria-Metzora*, a *zav*, *zavah*, *niddah*, and related persons generate a particular type of *tumah* for anything they sit or lie upon — even without direct contact, merely by having their weight supported. A seat or bed that bears the weight of a *zav* or *zavah* acquires the status of *mishkav* or *moshav* and becomes an *av ha-tumah* in its own right, not merely a *rishon*. This is the distinctive *tumah* of objects that bear the weight of those whose *tumah* derives from a bodily condition. A person who contacts a corpse, despite the severity of that *tumah* in other respects, does not generate this *mishkav/moshav* effect.

The *ba'al niddah* occupies a middle position. He acquires enough of the *niddah*'s *tumah* to generate *mishkav* and *moshav* — he too renders what he sits upon *tamei* even without contact. But his *mishkav* and *moshav* are not an *av ha-tumah*; they are only a *rishon le-tumah*. The *rishon* level means he can render food and liquids *tamei* but cannot render persons or vessels *tamei* — that requires the level of *av*. The *mishna* is teaching this unique intermediate status of the *ba'al niddah*, and it is for this purpose — not for *tvilah* timing — that it groups him with *tamei meit*. No inference about daytime immersion can therefore be drawn from the *mishna*.

## R. Chiyya Baraita

### Seven-Day List

The *gemara* now brings a decisive source. *Tanya devei Chiyya* — a *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Chiyya is taught. It lists the various seven-day *tumot*: *ha-zav ve-ha-zavah ve-ha-metzora ve-ha-metzora'at* — a man or woman with these flows, or a man or woman with *tzara'at*.

### Ba'al Niddah Listed

The *baraita* continues: *u-voel niddah u-tmei meit* — and a *ba'al niddah*, and one who became *tamei* through contact with a corpse. All of these are seven-day *tumot*, and *tevilatan ba-yom* — they all immerse during the daytime. The *baraita* then states the lone exception: *niddah ve-yoledet tevilatan ba-laylah*. The *ba'al niddah* is listed explicitly and unambiguously among those who immerse during the day.

### Rav Zeira Victory

*Dayka* — this is a direct and explicit contradiction to the challengers, and it vindicates Rav Zeira completely. His position is definitively established: *boel niddah eino ke-niddah* in this respect — the *ba'al niddah* goes to the *mikvah* during the day of the seventh, not at nightfall. Consequently, the entire structure of the separation works: the *kohen gadol* arrives on day one, even if the very worst-case scenario obtained (relations immediately before arrival), day seven is *Yom Kippur*, he immerses during the day, nightfall brings *haarev shemesh*, and he is completely *tahor* for the *avodah*.

## Death Tumah Q

### Logical Parallel

The *gemara* now turns to what initially seems like a logical parallel concern. If the reason for separating the *kohen gadol* from his wife is to prevent the *tumah* of *boel niddah*, one might equally ask: why is there no comparable concern about *tumat meit*? Any human being in his proximity might die, and death-contact *tumah* is also a seven-day *tumah*. Once the *gemara* has established that *tumah* concern is the driving rationale, the question follows naturally: *tefrisho mitumat meit* — you should also separate him from any contact with other human beings, lest someone die near him during the seven days and render him *tamei meit*.

### Hutrah Baitzibur

Rav Tachlifa, the father of Rav Huna, in the name of Rava, responds: *zot omeret* — this teaches us something. The fact that no one suggests such a separation indicates that *tumat meit hutrah hi be-tzibbur* — *tumah* from contact with a corpse is not merely overridden for the sake of a *korban tzibbur*, it is fully *hutrah*, completely permissible, as if there were no prohibition at all. The principle learned in *Pesachim* is that if the *kohanim* are *teme'im* and there is a *korban tzibbur* — especially one with a fixed time that must be brought today — the *korban* is brought even in a state of *tumah*. The question, however, is whether this represents *hutrah* — no violation whatsoever — or *dchuya* — a prohibition that is overridden under duress but remains a violation. Rav Tachlifa argues that since no effort is made to isolate the *kohen gadol* from potential *tumat meit*, it must be that *tumat meit* is *hutrah* entirely, and therefore there is nothing to avoid.

### Status vs Contact

Why then must he be separated from his wife? Because the category of *tumah* that is *hutrah be-tzibbur* is specifically contact-based *tumah* — *tumat meit*, touching a *sheretz*, and similar externally contracted *tumot*. A *tumah* that derives from a personal bodily status, such as *niddah*, *zav*, *zavah*, or *boel niddah*, is not *hutrah be-tzibbur*. The *kohen gadol*'s becoming a *boel niddah* is not the kind of *tumah* that is overridden for a *korban tzibbur*, and therefore it remains a genuine obstacle to his service on *Yom Kippur* — which is precisely why the separation from his wife is necessary.

## Ravina Refinement

### Dchuya Status

Ravina offers an alternative framework. Even granting that *tumat meit* is only *dchuya be-tzibbur* — overridden rather than fully permissible — one still would not require the *kohen gadol* to be isolated from all other human beings. Ravina's position is that even under *dchuya*, one would work to avoid *tumah* where possible, but the concern is tempered by a different consideration.

### Frequency Argument

*Tumat meit lo shechicha* — contact with a corpse simply does not happen with sufficient frequency to warrant preemptive isolation. Someone dying in the presence of the *kohen gadol* during a seven-day period is a statistically remote possibility. By contrast, the possibility that his wife will find herself in a state of *niddah* — even unexpectedly, even outside her anticipated *veset* — is considerably more common. The *gemara* does not dismiss *tumah* concerns entirely; it calibrates the level of preventive action to the realistic probability of the *tumah* occurring. Contact *tumah* from a corpse is rare enough that no special measures are required, even under *dchuya*. *Niddah* status is common enough that it does warrant the precaution of separation.

It is worth noting in passing that the *gemara* will need to revisit this framework when it addresses the practice of sprinkling the ashes of the *parah adumah* on the *kohen gadol* throughout the seven days — a practice that is itself entirely concerned with *tumat meit*. That discussion will require further examination of the interplay between *hutrah* and *dchuya*.

## Hutrah vs Dchuya

### All Tamei Scenario

The *gemara* now examines the practical difference between *hutrah* and *dchuya* in a concrete scenario. Setting aside the specific context of *Yom Kippur*, consider a Monday when the *beit av* — the subgroup of *kohanim* assigned to serve that day — are all *teme'im*. A *korban tzibbur*, specifically the *tamid*, must be brought. The *kohanim* of the *mishmar* who are not assigned to Monday are elsewhere in Jerusalem, having come for the week's service. It would take minimal effort to summon a few *tehorim* from among those available to perform the *avodah* instead.

### Nafka Mina

The *nafka mina* between *hutrah* and *dchuya* is precisely this: under *dchuya*, since *tumah* is still a problem that we merely override when we have no alternative, we would make the effort to find *tahor kohanim* if they are accessible. Under *hutrah*, since there is no prohibition at all in bringing a *korban tzibbur* with *temei'im*, there is no reason to make even the minimal effort to find alternatives.

### Rav Nachman

Rav Nachman holds *hutrah hi be-tzibbur* — it is completely permissible. Accordingly, *lo mahadrinan* — we do not go to the effort of summoning *tehorim* from another *beit av*. The *teme'im* may serve; there is nothing to remedy.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet holds *dchuya hi be-tzibbur* — it is overridden rather than permitted. Accordingly, *u-mahadrinan* — we would make the effort to find *tahor kohanim* who could perform the *avodah*, since the *tumah* remains problematic even if ultimately permitted under duress.

## Extreme Hutrah

### Tame'im With Tahorim

An alternative and more extreme version of the debate is reported. Some say the dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet applies even in a case where the *beit av* of that day contains both *teme'im* and *tehorim* — that is, where there are *tahor kohanim* readily available within the very same group assigned to serve. Even in that case, Rav Nachman would say the *teme'im* may serve alongside or instead of the *tehorim*.

### Contact Tumah Hutrah

The basis for this extreme position: *de-chol tumat meit be-tzibbur rachmana sharya* — any *tumat meit* in the context of a *korban tzibbur* is simply permitted by the Torah, without qualification. The prohibitions in the Torah against a *tamei kohen* performing the *avodah* were never stated with respect to a *korban tzibbur*. There is no violation — and therefore no preference for the *tahor kohen* over the *tamei* one when it comes to bringing the *korban tzibbur*. This is an admittedly radical position, but it flows directly from an uncompromising application of *hutrah*.

## Korban Categories

### Pesach Status

Tosafot introduces an important distinction that clarifies the scope of the entire debate. The *korban pesach* presents a borderline case. On one hand, it overrides *Shabbat* and *tumah* and has a fixed time, features associated with *korban tzibbur*. On the other hand, it is not truly a *korban tzibbur* in the full sense: it is not brought by *Klal Yisrael* as a corporate entity through a single offering, but rather each household brings its own. It comes *be-khnufya* — en masse, as a large group — but it is not brought in *shutfus*, in partnership, as one collective *korban*. Tosafot notes: *chashiv ke-korban tzibbur* in some respects, but *keivan de-lav kulhu meisi chad pesach be-shutfus*, since they do not all bring a single shared *korban*, it is not a fully constituted *korban tzibbur*.

### True Tzibbur Only

Tosafot's framework is consequently as follows. The extreme position of *hutrah* — the position that even with *tehorim* available, *teme'im* may serve without any preference for the *tahor* — applies only to a genuine *korban tzibbur*, a single offering brought on behalf of all of *Klal Yisrael* as a collective. That is the context in which the Torah's prohibition against *tamei* service was never stated in the first place.

### Yachid Consensus

For a *korban yachid* — an individual offering — even one with a fixed time, everyone agrees that we operate under *dchuya* at most. Accordingly, everyone agrees that we would seek *tehorim* to bring it if they are available. The *korban pesach*, being a *korban yachid* brought *be-khnufya*, falls into this category: even according to the view that holds *hutrah* for a true *korban tzibbur*, everyone would agree to seek *tahorim* for the *korban pesach*.

### Kohen Gadol Korban

The same logic applies to the *kohen gadol*'s personal *korban* on *Yom Kippur*. Even though it has a fixed time and cannot be postponed — and even though in some respects it functions similarly to a *korban tzibbur* — it is at the end of the day a *korban yachid*: *keivan de-korban yachid hu, mahadrinan atahorin le-chulei alma* — since it is a personal offering, everyone agrees we would try to ensure the *kohen gadol* is *tahor*. That is the overarching reason the seven-day separation is taken seriously: the *kohen gadol*'s personal offerings on *Yom Kippur* demand *taharah*, because even those who hold *hutrah* for a true *korban tzibbur* would insist on *tehorim* for a *korban yachid*. With that, Tosafot's framework neatly ties together the entire discussion of *hutrah* and *dchuya* and its application to the *kohen gadol*'s service.

---

---

# Yoma 7

## Tumah Hutra/Dechuya

### Hutra vs. Dechuya

The discussion on this *daf* opens with one of the classic questions in the laws of *korbanot*: what is the nature of *tumah* in the context of a *korban tzibur*? The two positions are *tumah hutrah b'tzibur* and *tumah dechuya b'tzibur*. Is *tumah* simply permitted for a *korban tzibur* — meaning the Torah's prohibition against bringing a *korban b'tumah* was never stated for *korbanot tzibur* in the first place, so that bringing such a *korban* while *tamei* constitutes no violation whatsoever? That is the position of *hutra*: there is no prohibition, no impropriety, and nothing to apologize for. Or is the position *tumah dechuya*? According to this view, there is in fact a prohibition, and one is technically violating it, but the mandate to bring the *korban tzibur* overrides the prohibition. The violation is acknowledged even as it is permitted — and that acknowledgment carries practical consequences, because in an ideal world one would prefer to avoid the violation entirely, and that preference would shape certain decisions about minimizing the degree of *tumah* involved.

### Pikuach Nefesh Analogy

A structurally parallel question applies to *pikuach nefesh* on *Shabbos*. When one breaks *Shabbos* to save a life, is this *chilul Shabbos* that one is permitted to commit, or is it not considered *chilul Shabbos* at all — meaning it is precisely what one is supposed to do on *Shabbos* when a life is at stake, regardless of what activities are required? The question is not merely theoretical. If one believes that saving a life overrides *Shabbos* but still constitutes a technical violation, one might be tempted to minimize the violation even at the cost of increasing risk to the patient. The literature on *pikuach nefesh* is unequivocal: do not hesitate, do not make calculations, go ahead and do whatever is necessary. The dominant message is to act without delay. An important qualification does apply — if it is possible to accomplish the same goal in a manner that does not involve *chilul Shabbos* and this involves no additional difficulty or risk, one should certainly do so. But that caveat does not undercut the primary principle; it refines it at the margins.

### Tumah Meis vs. Yotzei

This question connects directly to the *Kohen Gadol*'s service on *Yom Kippur*. If he were to become *tamei*, he would proceed with the *avodah* regardless — the question is how much effort must be invested in preventing that outcome, and that depends precisely on whether we say *hutra* or *dechuya*. One further clarification is important at the outset: this entire debate concerns *tumas meis* or a similar externally contracted *tumah*, that is, *tumah* resulting from contact with something outside the person's body. A *tumah yotzei migufo* — such as *ba'al keri* for a man, or contact with a *niddah* — involves the transfer of a personal status rather than external contact, and such *tumah* is not overridden under any circumstances. Those cases must simply be avoided. The debate is limited to *tumas meis*.

### Melachot on Shabbat

A related question concerns the performance of *melachot* on *Shabbos* within the *Mikdash* for the sake of a *korban tzibur*. Is *Shabbos* overridden — *nidcheh* — for the *korban tzibur*, or does it simply not apply at all? While the same derivations in the *Gemara* that address *tumah* are applied to the *Shabbos* question as well, and the *pesukim* that permit bringing a *korban Pesach* or a *korban tzibur* on *Shabbos* are the same as those relevant to *tumah*, the *Gemara* does not appear to contain a direct discussion of whether the performance of *melachot* for a *korban tzibur* on *Shabbos* constitutes *hutra* or *dechuya*. There seems to be an implicit assumption that it is *hutra*.

---

## Rav Nachman vs. Sheshet

### Rav Nachman Extreme

The debate is between *Rav Nachman*, who holds *hutra*, and *Rav Sheshet*, who holds *dechuya*. To appreciate the full force of their disagreement, one must consider the more extreme formulation of their positions, which appears toward the end of 6b. *Ika de'amrei* — some say — that when *Rav Nachman* says *hutra*, he means it even in the most extreme case. The scenario: the *kohanim* who constitute today's shift, the *beis av*, include both *temeim* and *tehorim*, and they need to bring the *tamid*, which is a *korban tzibur* with a fixed time. *Rav Nachman*'s extreme position is that even so, one may have the *temeim* bring the *tamid*. Why bother asking the *tahor kohen* to do it? It is a *korban tamid*, a *korban tzibur* — there is simply no problem at all. This is a genuinely radical formulation: even when a *tahor* alternative is trivially available, *hutra* means there is no reason to prefer it.

### Minchat Ha-omer

*Rav Sheshet* asks: where do I derive my position of *dechuya*? He cites a *braita*: a *kohen* was standing and bringing the *minchat ha-omer* — a flour offering — and as he was holding it, it became *tamei*, perhaps because a *sheretz* fell into it. The *braita* states that he announces the problem and a substitute is brought. The text has an interesting marginal variant (*girsa*): rather than the *kohen* himself calling out, the people around him check whether a substitute is available; if so, they inform him, and if not, they tell him to proceed quietly. Either way, the operative point is the same — one prefers to obtain a *tahor* substitute. This demonstrates that even for a *korban tzibur* with a fixed time, there is a preference for *taharah*, which is precisely what *dechuya* would predict.

### Pikeach Ve-Shtok

The curious instruction — *hevei pikeach ve-shtok*, "be wise and keep quiet" — demands explanation. If bringing the *tamei* offering is fully permitted, why the instruction to remain silent? And if it is not permitted, how can silence make it acceptable? The *Gemara* notes the tension embedded in this phrase with the word *miha* — *ketani miha* — which signals that something here is not entirely straightforward. The phrase itself will be revisited repeatedly as the *sugya* develops.

### Sheyirayim Exception

*Rav Nachman* concedes one point. He says *modina* — he would admit — *heicha de'ika sheyirayim le'achilah*: where the *korban* has remnants (*sheyirayim*) that are intended to be eaten, he acknowledges the preference for *taharah*. The principle of *tumah hutrah b'tzibur* permits bringing the *korban b'tumah*, but it does not extend to *eating* it *b'tumah* — with one exception. One might ask: which *korban* may even be eaten *b'tumah*? The *korban Pesach*, as established in *Pesachim*, because the essential purpose of the *korban Pesach* is the *achilah*, not the *hakravah*. Every other *korban* — even when the *hakravah* is permitted *b'tumah* — may not be eaten *b'tumah*. Therefore, if the *korban* in question has *sheyirayim* that are eaten, there is good reason to prefer a *tahor* substitute: not because the *hakravah* itself demands it, but because one wants the *sheyirayim* to be available for eating rather than discarded. Importantly, *Rav Nachman* notes that in this context the discussion involves the *korban* becoming *tamei*, not the *kohen* — though for present purposes the practical difference is not yet significant.

### Minchat Nesachim

A second *braita* is cited in parallel. A *kohen* was bringing the *minchat nesachim* — the flour, oil, and wine that accompany certain *olot* and *shelamim* — for bulls, rams, and sheep, and it became *tamei* in his hand. The *braita* states that a substitute is to be sought, and if none is available, he is told *hevei pikeach ve-shtok* — keep quiet and proceed. This case is actually sharper than the *minchat ha-omer*: the *minchat nesachim* is entirely burned on the *mizbeach* and no *kometz* is taken; there is no *sheyirayim* for eating. The preference for *taharah* here cannot be explained by the *sheyirayim* rationale. The *Gemara* raises the question of which *korban* is under discussion. Is this perhaps the *musaf* of *Sukkot*, with its full complement of bulls, rams, and sheep — a paradigmatic *korban tzibur*? That would be a formidable challenge to *Rav Nachman*: if it is a *korban tzibur* with a fixed time, and we still prefer *taharah*, that supports *dechuya*.

---

## Fixed Time Key

### Par Avodah Zarah

*Rav Nachman* responds: no, we are not discussing a *korban musaf*. He recategorizes the three animals. The *parim* — the bulls — refer to the *par avodah zarah*, the bull brought as an *olah* when the entire *Klal Yisrael* sins with *avodah zarah*. This is indeed a *korban tzibur*, since it is brought on behalf of the community. Yet *af al gav de-tzibur hu* — even though it is a communal *korban* — *keivan delo kevi'a lei zman*, since it has no fixed time, *mahadrinan* — we pursue a *tahor* alternative. This is the critical point, stated explicitly: what determines whether *tumah* is overridden is not that a *korban* is a *korban tzibur*, but that it has a fixed time. A *korban tzibur* without a fixed time does not override *tumah*. This can be demonstrated from the opposite direction as well: a *korban Pesach* is brought by individuals, yet because it has a fixed time — and indeed because the entire Jewish people bring it simultaneously — it carries the character of a *korban tzibur*. Even more strikingly, the *korban* of *Aharon ha-Kohen* on *Yom Kippur* — which is personal, possibly funded from his own resources — overrides *tumah* entirely, because it must be brought that very day.

### Aaron's Ram

The *eilim* — rams — in the *braita* refer to *eilo shel Aharon*, Aaron's ram on *Yom Kippur*. This is a *korban yachid* with a fixed time. *De-af al gav de-kevi'a lei zman* — though it has a fixed time, *keivan de-yachid hu*, since it is a *korban yachid* and not a *korban tzibur*, *mahadrinan* — we prefer to bring it *b'taharah*. The *korban* does override *tumah* because of its fixed time, but because it lacks the additional dimension of being a *korban tzibur*, it does not receive the full force of *hutra*, and we would prefer *taharah* when possible.

### Sheep with Omer

The *kevasim* — sheep — are identified as the sheep brought together with the *omer* on the second day of *Pesach*. The discussion thus circles back to the *minchat ha-omer* discussed earlier. Here the rationale for preferring *taharah* is *de'ika sheyirayim le'achilah* — as *Rav Nachman* already conceded, when there are *sheyirayim* to be eaten, the preference for *taharah* exists even within his position of *hutra*.

### Fixed Time Principle

The structure of *Rav Nachman*'s response can now be stated as a general principle: the override of *tumah* — whether framed as *hutra* or *dechuya* — is predicated on a fixed time, not on the *tzibur* character of the *korban*. A non-fixed-time *korban* does not override *tumah* or *Shabbos*, even if it is a *korban tzibur*. A fixed-time *korban* does override *tumah* and *Shabbos* — whether or not it is a *korban tzibur*, though a *korban yachid* with a fixed time earns somewhat less deference than a *korban tzibur* with a fixed time. The explanations for the *braita*'s preference for *taharah* are therefore subsidiary: in one case the *korban* has *sheyirayim*; in another it is a *yachid* *korban* even if fixed-time; and in the third it is a *korban tzibur* without a fixed time. None of these cases presents the clean scenario of a *korban tzibur* with a fixed time for which *Rav Nachman* maintains *hutra* without qualification.

This still leaves a pressing question, however. The *par avodah zarah* is not a fixed-time *korban*. If the override of *tumah* depends entirely on fixed time, and not on *tzibur* status alone, why does the *braita* instruct *hevei pikeach ve-shtok* and permit it to be brought *b'tumah* at all? By *Rav Nachman*'s own logic, a non-fixed-time *korban* should simply be invalid when brought *b'tumah*. This is the question that opens the next discussion.

---

## Ritzuy Tzitz

### Person Tamei Rule

*Tosafot* provides the resolution. There is a fundamental distinction between two types of *tumah* situations: cases in which the *person* — the *kohen* performing the *avodah* — is *tamei*, and cases in which the *object* — the *korban* itself — is *tamei*. When the *kohen* is *tamei*, the only mechanism that permits the *avodah* is the override rooted in fixed time. If the *korban* does not have a fixed time, there is no override, no *hutra*, no *dechuya* — the *kohen* simply cannot perform the *avodah*.

### Object Tamei Exception

When the *korban* itself is *tamei* — the blood, the meat, the flour offering — a distinct principle applies: *ritzuy tzitz*. The *tzitz* that the *Kohen Gadol* wears on his forehead, inscribed *Kodesh l'Hashem*, functions to validate *korbanot* that were brought while *tamei*. This principle applies regardless of whether the *korban* is a *korban tzibur* or a *korban yachid*, and regardless of whether the *korban* has a fixed time. The *tzitz* operates specifically when the *objects* are *tamei* — the blood, the meat, the fat — not when the *people* are *tamei*. For the *par avodah zarah*, then, when its *minchat nesachim* became *tamei*, the *ritzuy tzitz* is what permits the *avodah* to proceed and validates the *korban bedieved*.

### Keep It Quiet

This also explains the instruction *hevei pikeach ve-shtok*. The *korban* is not supposed to be brought *b'tumah*; for a non-fixed-time *korban*, there is no override when the objects are *tamei*. But *bedieved*, once the *korban* is in the process of being brought, the *ritzuy tzitz* will validate it after the fact. The instruction "keep quiet" reflects precisely this *bedieved* character: the impropriety is acknowledged — one does not announce that a *tamei korban* is being brought — but the validity of the *korban* is secured through the *tzitz*. The principle of *sha'at ha-dechak k'bedieved dami* — a situation of constraint functions like *bedieved* — may further explain why the *kohen* is permitted to proceed rather than halt entirely. An important distinction must be maintained here: the *ritzuy tzitz* does not atone for a sin the way a *korban* atones; rather, it validates the *korban*, declaring it acceptable. The concern of the *Beis HaMikdash* is whether *bedieved* the *avodah* stands, and the *tzitz* answers that question in the affirmative.

---

## Fixed Time Key (II)

### Korban Categories

The framework that emerges from this discussion can be organized into four categories. First, a *korban tzibur* with a fixed time — such as the *tamid*, the *musaf*, or the *Yom Kippur* communal offerings — fully overrides both *tumah* and *Shabbos*. According to *Rav Nachman*, this is *hutra* in the fullest sense: even *lechatchila* there is no need to prefer a *tahor kohen* over a *tamei* one. Second, a fixed-time *korban yachid* — such as the *eilo shel Aharon* on *Yom Kippur* or the *asiris ha-eifah* of the *Kohen Gadol* — also overrides *tumah* and *Shabbos* by virtue of its fixed time, but because it lacks the *tzibur* dimension, there is a preference for *taharah* even according to *Rav Nachman*. Third, a *korban tzibur* without a fixed time — such as the *par avodah zarah* — does not override *tumah* or *Shabbos*. If the *kohen* is *tamei*, the *avodah* is simply invalid. If the *korban* object is *tamei*, the *ritzuy tzitz* will validate it *bedieved*, and the instruction *hevei pikeach ve-shtok* applies. Fourth, a non-fixed-time *korban yachid* — the vast majority of individual *korbanot* — similarly cannot override *tumah* or *Shabbos*, and if the person is *tamei*, the *korban* is invalid. If the object is *tamei* and the *ritzuy tzitz* is functioning, there may be *bedieved* validity, though in practice the communal dimension present even in the *par avodah zarah* case does not exist here.

One might ask how *temei* *kohanim* can be present in the *azarah* at all in the scenario where *Rav Nachman* says the *tamei kohanim* may bring the *tamid*. One plausible construction: the *kohanim* begin as *tehorim*, and one becomes *tamei* in the midst of performing the *tamid* — perhaps through an accidental *neveila* when the *shechita* goes wrong — and the question is whether the others must stop or whether he may continue alongside them. The *heter* to be in the *azarah* while *tamei* would be coextensive with the *heter* to bring the *korban*, and only applies for the purpose of that specific *avodah*.

---

## Braita: Dam Tamei

### Dam Shitma

The *Gemara* now introduces a *braita* dealing with a case of *dam she-nitma*: the blood of an *olah* became *tamei* and was thrown on the *mizbeach b'shogeg*, unintentionally — either because the *tumah* was unintentional or because the throwing itself was inadvertent, a question debated in the *Gemara*. If *b'shogeg*, the *braita* rules *hurtzah* — it is valid. If *b'meizid*, intentionally, *lo hurtzah* — it is not valid. The surface meaning of *lo hurtzah* is that the *korban* is entirely invalid. However, as the *Gemara* will clarify, the *ritzuy tzitz* ensures *bedieved* validity even in a case of *b'meizid*, and *lo hurtzah* is interpreted elsewhere to mean that the owners or the *kohanim* are penalized — they do not derive benefit from the *korban* — even though the *korban* itself stands. The straightforward question is: if we are dealing with a *korban tzibur*, why should the distinction between *shogeg* and *meizid* matter at all? If *tumah hutrah b'tzibur*, nothing problematic happened. The *Gemara* resolves this immediately: *ki tanya hahee d'yachid* — this *braita* is about a *korban yachid*. The validity *bedieved* in the *shogeg* case is because of the *tzitz*.

### Tzitz Works Objects
