The *Gemara* introduces the principle of *ritzuy tzitz* directly: the *tzitz* functions only when the objects — the blood, the meat, the fat — are *tamei*, not when the people are *tamei*. The *korban* objects that have become *tamei* are validated by the *tzitz bedieved*. When the *kohen* himself is *tamei*, the *tzitz* cannot help; only the override from fixed time applies in that scenario.

### Tzitz Braita

The *Gemara* cites a *braita* that elaborates the *ritzuy tzitz* principle: it applies to the blood, the meat, the fat — all the constituent parts of *korbanot* that may become *tamei* — whether the *korban* is *yachid* or *tzibur*, whether the *tumah* was *b'shogeg* or *b'meizid*, *b'ones* or *b'ratzon*. In all these cases, the *tzitz* renders the *korban* valid. Note that this *braita* states the *tzitz* works *bein b'yachid bein b'tzibur* — for both individual and communal *korbanot*.

### Non-Fixed Tzibur

This raises an immediate question: why does the *braita* find it necessary to state that the *tzitz* works for a *korban tzibur*? If *tumah hutrah b'tzibur*, then there is no problem in the first place — the *korban tzibur* brought *b'tumah* is perfectly valid without any assistance from the *tzitz*. Who needs the *tzitz* for a *korban tzibur*? *Rav Nachman* responds: *amar lach Rav Nachman — ki tanya ha-tzitz mirtzeh ad'yachid*. The mention of *korban tzibur* in the *braita* was incidental; the primary purpose of the *tzitz* rule is for the *korban yachid* case. Once the *braita* was stating that the *tzitz* validates *tamei* *korbanot*, it included *korban tzibur* for completeness — but the *tzibur* does not actually need the *tzitz*. Alternatively — *ve-iba'is eima* — even if you want to say the mention of *korban tzibur* is meaningful, it refers specifically to *korban tzibur* without a fixed time, such as the *par avodah zarah*. That category does not have *tumah hutrah* or *tumah dechuya* — it has no override at all based on its own character — and therefore when the *korban* objects become *tamei*, the *tzitz* is what validates them *bedieved*.

---

## Pigul/Notar

### Pigul Disqualified

Having established that the *tzitz* validates *korbanot* that were brought *b'tumah*, the *Gemara* asks: how do we know the *tzitz* applies specifically to *tumah* and not to other forms of invalidity? The *pasuk* that describes the *tzitz* — *v'nasa Aharon et avon ha-kodashim* — uses the language of sin and atonement without specifying what type of invalidity it addresses. One might suppose the *tzitz* renders acceptable all invalidly brought *korbanot*. The *Gemara* systematically eliminates alternatives. *Pigul*: a *korban* brought with the intent to eat it at the wrong time — the *pasuk* states explicitly *lo yeratzeh*, it shall not be accepted. There is no *ritzuy* possible for *pigul*; the *pasuk* forecloses it. The *tzitz* cannot override an explicit *lo yeratzeh*.

### Notar Issue

*Notar*: the sin of leaving meat from a *korban* past the permitted time of eating. The *pasuk* states *lo yechashev* — it shall not be reckoned. This is from the same *parasha* as *pigul*. Moreover, *notar* arises only after the *korban* was already valid and accepted — it is a post-hoc problem, occurring after the *avodah* was completed. There is no need for the *tzitz* to validate the *korban* for a problem that arises after the *korban* is already good. Both *pigul* and *notar* here likely encompass, between them, the two related forms of invalid intent: an intention of the wrong time (*pigul* proper, or *chutz lizmano*) and an intention of the wrong place (*chutz limkomo*), which are addressed by the same *pesukim* of *lo yeratzeh* and *lo yechashev*, as discussed extensively in *Rashi* and *Tosafot*.

### Tumah Only

By process of elimination, *tumah* is the only remaining category of invalidity to which *ritzuy tzitz* can apply. *Pigul* is explicitly excluded by *lo yeratzeh*. *Notar* either arises too late or is similarly excluded. *Tumah* alone is left as the form of invalidity that the *tzitz* can address.

### Hutrah Logic

The *braita* does not merely stop with this logical conclusion but adds a substantive reason why *tumah* in particular is the appropriate domain for *ritzuy tzitz*. The *braita* states: *she-hutrah mi-klalah b'tzibur* — because we know that *tumah* has instances where it is set aside entirely, namely the *korban tzibur* context. There is an established precedent, a category within the law, where *tumah* does not stand as an absolute barrier. Given that *tzitz* is going to function for some category of invalidity, and given that *pigul* and *notar* are explicitly excluded, it makes sense — indeed it is fitting — that *tumah* should be the category where *tzitz* provides its assistance, precisely because *tumah* is the type of invalidity that the Torah itself has shown some flexibility about in the context of *korban tzibur*.

One significant observation: this *braita* uses the term *hutrah* — *she-hutrah mi-klalah b'tzibur* — and the *Gemara* recognizes that this precise vocabulary, in a context where the *Rav Nachman / Rav Sheshet* debate uses those same technical terms, constitutes apparent support for *Rav Nachman*. The *Gemara*'s response is *tannai hi* — it is itself a debate among *tannaim*. *Rav Sheshet* holds that he has *tannaim* who use the language of *dechuya*, as evidenced by the *braitot* on the earlier *amud*. The *braita* here that says *hutrah* represents the other side of that *tannaitic* debate. It is only the specific use of the word *hutrah* in the *braita* that constitutes a challenge to *Rav Sheshet* — not the halakhic mechanics of how the *tzitz* functions, which are unaffected by whether one holds *hutra* or *dechuya*.

---

## Abaye's Framework

### Implication Analysis

*Abaye* now enters to frame the debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* — which concerns whether the *tzitz* must be worn to function — in terms of the *hutra/dechuya* debate. If one holds *hutra*, the *korban* brought *b'tumah* for a *korban tzibur* is valid without any assistance; the *tzitz* is not needed in that scenario and its wearing or non-wearing is irrelevant to the outcome. If one holds *dechuya*, the *korban* is valid but remains in a liminal state — there was something problematic about it — and the *tzitz* can play a meaningful supporting role. *Rabbi Yehuda*, who holds the *tzitz* must be worn on the forehead to function, implies a certain understanding: since the *tzitz* must actively be worn to have an effect, its contribution is a real and necessary one. This is more consistent with a *dechuya* framework in which the *tzitz* is doing actual work. *Rabbi Shimon*, who holds the *tzitz* always functions even when not being worn, suggests a different picture: the very existence of the *tzitz* in proper condition suffices, pointing perhaps to a *dechuya* understanding in which, even though the validity is acknowledged to be in a somewhat lower register, the *tzitz* functions as a constant structural feature of *korban* validity rather than a moment-by-moment active intervention.

### Broken Tzitz

*Abaye* states that one point of agreement between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* is clear: *venishbar ha-tzitz — de-chulei alma lo peligi de-lo mirtzeh*. If the *tzitz* is broken — if it no longer exists as a functional object — all agree that it does not make *korbanot* acceptable. A broken *tzitz* has no *ritzuy* function.

### On Peg Debate

The debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* is located precisely in the case where *detalui be-kuchta* — the *tzitz* is hanging on its peg, sitting in the *Kohen Gadol*'s storage, intact but not being worn. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that only when it is on the forehead does it function. *Rabbi Shimon* holds that even when it is hanging on its peg, so long as it is fit to be worn, it functions.

---

## Wearing Tzitz

### Yehuda: Must Wear

*Rabbi Yehuda* derives his position from the juxtaposition of two phrases in the *pasuk*: *al mitzcho* — on his forehead — and *venasa Aharon et avon ha-kodashim* — he will lift off the sin of the sanctified things. Reading these two phrases together, *Rabbi Yehuda* understands that the *tzitz* lifts off the *avon* of the *korbanot* specifically when it is on the forehead. Only the act of wearing the *tzitz* on the forehead activates its function.

### Shimon: Always Works

*Rabbi Shimon* derives his position from a different part of the same *pasuk*: *tamid leratzon lahem lifnei Hashem* — it shall always be for acceptance before God. He reads *tamid leratzon* as a standalone statement: the *tzitz* always makes *korbanot* acceptable, regardless of whether it is being worn at any given moment. On his reading, *al mitzcho* tells us the placement of the *tzitz* — on the forehead — while *tamid leratzon* independently declares its constant efficacy.

### Constant Consciousness

*Rabbi Yehuda* must account for the word *tamid*, which on its face seems to imply something constant even when not being worn. He explains: *hahu tamid she-lo yassiach da'ato mimeno* — *tamid* means that when the *tzitz* is worn, the *Kohen Gadol* must be constantly conscious of it, never allowing his attention to lapse. It does not mean the *tzitz* must be worn continuously, but that wearing it must be accompanied by uninterrupted awareness.

### Tefillin Analogy

The *Gemara* draws an explicit parallel to *tefillin*. *Rabba bar Rav Huna* teaches: *chayav adam lemashesh be-tefillin be-chol sha'ah ve-sha'ah* — a person wearing *tefillin* is obligated to touch them constantly, continuously invoking his awareness of them. This is learned *kal va-chomer* from the *tzitz*: if the *tzitz*, which contains only one divine name — *Kodesh l'Hashem* — demands *al mitzcho tamid*, understood as constant consciousness when wearing, then *tefillin*, which contain many divine names, certainly demand constant awareness when worn. *Tosafot* notes that this is not a formally rigorous *kal va-chomer* — the divine names of *tefillin* are concealed within boxes while the name on the *tzitz* is exposed, and the *bigdei kehunah* may carry distinct demands from personal *mitzvot* — but the conceptual comparison between *tzitz* and *tefillin* is genuine and significant. There is a broader parallel worth noting: just as *tefillin shel rosh* corresponds in certain respects to the *tzitz*, the *tzitzit* parallels the *bigdei kehunah* more broadly. These analogies suggest that even in the absence of the *Beis HaMikdash*, the personal *mitzvot* of *tefillin* and *tzitzit* carry forward something of the *kedushah* of the *Mikdash*'s service.

### Shimon: Fitness

*Rabbi Shimon* responds to *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position by clarifying what *al mitzcho venasa* means in his own reading. He does not dispute that the *tzitz* has a connection to the forehead; he argues that the *pasuk* establishes fitness, not active wearing, as the operative criterion. *Ra'ui le-metzach mirtze — she-ein ra'ui le-metzach eino mirtze*: when the *tzitz* is fit to be placed on the forehead — meaning it is whole and intact — it functions. When it is not fit — meaning it is broken — it does not function. The phrase *al mitzcho venasa* thus tells us the condition of fitness rather than the requirement of actual wearing. This is precisely the line that *Abaye* identified: all agree that a broken *tzitz* does not function (*la-apukei nishbar ha-tzitz de-lo mirtze*), while the debate is about a *tzitz* that is intact but not being worn.

*Rabbi Shimon* reinforces his position with the case of the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur*. There are times during the *Yom Kippur avodah* when the *Kohen Gadol* is not wearing the *tzitz* — specifically during the *avodah* performed in the inner sanctuary, the *Heichal*, where he wears only the white garments and not the golden ones. If a *korban* were to become *tamei* during those moments, *Rabbi Shimon* argues, the *korban* would still be valid, because the *tzitz* is fit to be worn even though it is not being worn at that moment. *Rabbi Yehuda* responds that the *Yom Kippur* case is not evidence for the *tzitz*'s function at all: *hanach le-Kohen Gadol be-Yom Kippurim she-tumah hutrah lo b'tzibbur* — the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur* operates under the principle of *hutra b'tzibbur* for a fixed-time *korban*. The validity of those *korbanot* when *tamei* does not depend on the *tzitz* in any way; it follows from the *tumah hutrah b'tzibur* principle itself. Therefore *Rabbi Yehuda* cannot be refuted by that case — it provides no information about whether the *tzitz* functions when not worn.

The *Gemara* draws out the implication: *micklal de-Rabbi Yehuda — Rabbi Shimon savar tumah dechuya hi b'tzibbur*. If *Rabbi Shimon* thought the *Yom Kippur* case was a valid proof for the *tzitz* functioning when not worn, that means *Rabbi Shimon* holds *dechuya*. If it were *hutra*, the *Yom Kippur* case is trivially valid and the *tzitz* is irrelevant; there would be nothing to prove. The fact that *Rabbi Shimon* thinks the *tzitz* has a role to play even there — even for the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur* — reflects his view that *dechuya* applies: there is something slightly in need of correction, and the *tzitz* provides that correction. *Rabbi Yehuda*, on the other hand, says the *tzitz* has no role on *Yom Kippur* for that *avodah*, because *hutra* makes the whole question moot.

This settles the alignment *Abaye* identified: *Rabbi Yehuda* holds *hutra*, and therefore the *tzitz* must be actively worn when it does function, since the *tzitz* is not needed in the main *korban tzibur* scenario at all. *Rabbi Shimon* holds *dechuya*, and therefore the *tzitz* has a perpetual structural role — it is always doing something, even when not actively worn, because the validity of *korbanot* brought *b'tumah* always remains in a *dechuya* register that the *tzitz* continuously addresses. The requirement of fitness — being fit to be placed on the forehead — is what *Rabbi Shimon* derives from *al mitzcho venasa*, and this fitness, not active wearing, is what activates the *ritzuy*.

---

---

# Yoma 10

## Yeridat HaDorot

### Intro: Yeridat HaDorot

Today's *daf* is 10, and we pick up on 9b, where the *gemara* has been engaged in a rich and far-reaching dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerning *yeridat hadorot* — the question of whether earlier generations were spiritually greater than later ones. This discussion is deeply connected to the question of the *binyan beit hamikdash*: why was the First Temple rebuilt after seventy years, whereas the Second Temple, once destroyed, has never been rebuilt? It is important to keep that backdrop in mind as we turn to the following narrative.

### Reish Lakish in Jordan

*Reish Lakish hava sachi b'Yardena* — Reish Lakish was bathing in the Jordan River. Rabbah bar Bar Chana, a Babylonian *amora* who was spending time learning in Eretz Yisrael, approached and stretched out his hand to help Reish Lakish out of the water. Reish Lakish's response was, to say the least, unexpected: *Eloha sanei lechu* — your God hates you. As a proof-text, he cited the verse from Shir HaShirim: *Im chomah hi nivneh aleha tirat kasef v'im delet hi natzur aleha luach arez* — "If she is a wall, let us build upon her a tower of silver; and if she is a door, let us board her up with a plank of cedar."

### Wall vs. Door Metaphor

The interpretation Reish Lakish draws from this verse is as follows: *Im asitem atzmechem k'chomah v'alitem kulchem b'yimei Ezra* — had you made yourselves like a wall and ascended together in the time of Ezra, for the majority of Jews living in Babylonia chose to remain there rather than return for the building of the Second Temple. A wall is a single unified structure; had all of Israel come up together, *nimshaltem k'kasef she'ein rakav sholeit bo* — you would have been likened to silver, into which no rot can penetrate.

But as it was, *achshav she'alitem k'dalatot* — now that you came up like doors. Rashi explains the metaphor: a door is only a small piece of the wall, the part that opens and closes; it is something partial and incomplete. Now that you came up like a door, *nimshaltem k'arez she'harakav sholeit bo* — you are likened to cedar, into which rot can set.

The *gemara*'s implication, as Rashi frames it, is that this parable addresses the very question animating the prior discussion: why has there been no *binyan beit hamikdash*? Why was the Second Temple destroyed and not rebuilt? Reish Lakish answers: it is the fault of the *bnei bavel* who did not come up in the time of Ezra. It is not that later generations are of lesser spiritual stature — indeed, Torah learning under oppression may be at a higher level than in earlier times. The reasons for our diminished national status lie elsewhere, in historical and communal failures rather than individual decline. The *Maharsha* develops this reading beautifully by connecting the wall-and-door imagery to the actual historical circumstances of Sefer Ezra: had so many of Israel ascended, they would have constituted a wall in the literal sense, making the fortifications unnecessary against the hostile Samaritans and others who sought to obstruct the rebuilding. As it was, only enough came up to guard the doors — a partial and vulnerable presence.

### Arez & Sasmagor

*Mai arez?* — what exactly is the *arez* being referred to? Ulla answers: *sasmagor*. This term may simply be a Babylonian name for a variety of cedar, but Rashi also understands it to denote a particular worm that eats through the cedar from the inside, leaving the outer shell intact while the interior rots away. *Mai sasmagor?* — what is the metaphor of *sasmagor*? Rabbi Abba answers: *bat kol* — the Second Temple had the outer shell of sanctity but lacked the inner fullness. During the period of the Second Temple, there was no true *nevuah*, no complete divine presence — only the distant echo of a *bat kol*.

This is grounded in a *baraita*: *mishemetu nevi'im acharonim Chaggai Zechariah u'Malachi nistalka Ruach HaKodesh m'Yisrael v'adayin hayu mishtamshim b'bat kol* — once the later prophets, Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi — who bridged the transition from the First to the Second Temple — passed away, the *Ruach HaKodesh* departed from Israel; yet they still made use of a *bat kol*. The *bat kol* is not the actual *Ruach HaKodesh*; it is, as the name suggests, the daughter of a voice — a distant echo, some residual form of divine inspiration. Saul Lieberman noted that in the Bavli, the *bat kol* carries genuinely metaphysical connotations, whereas in the Yerushalmi the term often bears no supernatural weight, referring simply to a rumor or emerging consensus.

So the point is not that the Second Temple was built by spiritually inferior people, but that the circumstances of its construction — the incomplete *aliyah*, the subjugation to foreign powers — meant that the *shechina* could not rest there as it had in the First Temple. The cedar is still cedar; but the *sasmagor* has done its work from within.

---

## Mezuzah in Mikdash

### Reish Lakish's Silence

The *gemara* now raises a pointed internal question about the story just told: *Reish Lakish mi mishata b'haday Rabba bar bar Chana?* — would Reish Lakish really have spoken with Rabbah bar Bar Chana at all? The issue is this: *u'ma Rebbi Elazar d'marei d'artza d'Yisrael hava v'lo hava mishata Reish Lakish badei* — Rabbi Elazar, who was regarded as the master of the sages of Eretz Yisrael, a figure of towering stature, and yet Reish Lakish would not speak with him in public. The reason: *d'man d'mishata Reish Lakish badei beshuka yavlu lei iska b'lo sa'adi* — whoever Reish Lakish would speak with publicly, people would consider that person so completely trustworthy that they would conduct business with him without witnesses. Therefore, Reish Lakish was extraordinarily careful about whom he would be seen speaking with in public, because his public acknowledgment of a person served as a powerful character endorsement. If he would not extend this to Rabbi Elazar, he certainly would not have extended it to Rabbah bar Bar Chana.

### Rav Pappa's Solution

Rav Pappa resolves the problem: *shadi gavra beinaihu* — one of the figures in the story must be exchanged. Either it was Reish Lakish swimming in the river and it was Zeiri who helped him out, or it was Rabbah bar Bar Chana who stretched out his hand and it was Rabbi Elazar who was swimming. The story as originally told must have involved a pairing that is historically plausible — one of the two names as transmitted to us must be a substitution for the original.

The *gemara* notes that when they came before Rabbi Yochanan — which, Rashi observes, suggests it was Reish Lakish involved, given the famous relationship between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan — Rabbi Yochanan responded to the substance of the teaching.

---

## Yeridat HaDorot (II)

### Rabbi Yochanan's Response

*Amar lei lav hai hu ta'ama* — Rabbi Yochanan says: that is not the reason. *Ee nami seliku kulhu b'yemei Ezra, lo havi sharya Shchina b'mikdash sheni* — even if all of Israel had ascended in the time of Ezra, the *shechina* would not have rested in the Second Temple. This is not a question of demography or communal solidarity. The reason lies in a deeper theological principle, derived from the verse: *Yaft Elokim l'Yefet v'yishkon b'ahalei Shem* — God will beautify Yefet, but He will dwell in the tents of Shem. Even though God grants expansion and even beauty to the descendants of Yefet, the divine presence rests only in the tents of Shem. Since the Second Temple was built under Persian auspices — and the *gemara* will now examine whether Persia descends from Yefet — its construction was not purely within the domain of Shem, and therefore the *shechina* could not rest there fully, regardless of how many Jews ascended. The classic *midrash* reads *yaft Elokim l'Yefet* as a synthesis — the beauty of Yefet finding its home in the tents of Shem — but Rabbi Yochanan reads it as a dichotomy, a structural limitation on where the *shechina* can dwell.

---

## Yaft Elokim Leyafet

### Persia & Yafet

The *gemara* raises the foundational question behind Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: *u'Parsayei minalan d'miYefet ka'asu* — from where do we know that the Persians descend from Yefet? The verse that enabled the second *beit hamikdash* to be built was given by Koresh, a Persian king. For Rabbi Yochanan's argument to stand, Persia must be identified as a nation of Yefet's lineage. To establish this, the *gemara* turns to the *pasuk* listing the sons of Yefet: *Bnei Yefet Gomer u'Magog u'Madai v'Yavan v'Tuval u'Meshech v'Tiras.*

### Sons of Yafet

The *gemara* proceeds to identify each of these nations. *Gomer* is *Garmamya* — a term our *girsa* records as *Garmamya*; the *Gra* has the reading *Germanya*. Steinsaltz identifies it with a region north of Assyria, likely Phrygia or a neighboring area; on geographic grounds, an identification with a Near Eastern or Caucasian region is far more plausible than a Western European one, since all of these nations belong to the ancient Near Eastern world.

*Magog* is *Kandya*. The Steinsaltz identifies this with Scythia; there is also a *girsa* of *Gothya*, referring to the Goths, a people of Asia Minor or further north. *Madai* is *Makdonya* — Macedonia, the region north of Greece proper; notably, Alexander the Great was Macedonian, representing a distinct ethnic and political identity from the Greek city-states to the south.

*Yavan k'mashmao* — Yavan is Greece, as is well known. *Tuval* is *Beis Onaiki*, identified as Bithynia in northwest Asia Minor. *Meshech* is *Mosya*, associated with the region along the Sea of Marmara and the Dardanelles.

*Tiras* is the subject of a dispute. *Pleigei bar Simai ve-Rabbanan* — one opinion holds it is *Beis Taryaiki*, identified as Thrace, which fits within the Greek geographic sphere. The other opinion, cited by Rav Yosef in a *baraita* — *Tiras zu Pras* — holds that *Tiras* is Persia. This identification, of course, is the linchpin of the entire argument. If Persia descends from Tiras, and Tiras is the youngest of the sons of Yefet, then the verse *yaft Elokim l'Yefet* applies to the Persian kingdom, and Rabbi Yochanan's point stands.

One might ask: how do we know to identify *tzeirei hatzon* — "the young of the flock" — in the verse from Yirmiyahu as Persia and not as some other nation? A *talmid* visiting Eretz Yisrael raised this question before one of the *rabbinan*, citing the verse in Daniel where the ram (*ayil*) represents the kings of Media and Persia, and the he-goat (*tzfir hasayir*) represents Greece. If *tzon* can include both rams and goats, perhaps the "young of the flock" refers to Greece rather than Persia? The *talmid* was told he was asking a question born of ignorance of the *peshat*. The identification of *tzeirei hatzon* as Persia does not rest on the *pasuk* in Daniel at all. Rather, *tzeirei hatzon* means simply "the youngest of the sons" — and the youngest of the sons of Yefet is Tiras, which is Persia. No metaphor of rams or goats is involved.

### Sakastan Geography

Moving through the same passage of *Parshat Noach*, the *gemara* notes, by way of Rav Yosef's teaching, that *Sabta* and *Sabtecha* — which appear in the verse listing the sons of Kush — are identified with *Skistan Gavyata*, the outer Sakastan, and *Skistan Brayta*, the inner Sakastan. This region has been identified by scholars with Sakastan or Drangiana, a territory spanning west Afghanistan and eastern Iran. The outer and inner designations envision concentric rings; the distance between them — the gap between the outer and inner circles — is a hundred *parsi*, approximately a mile, while the circumference of the outer circle is a thousand *parsi*. It should be noted that these are the sons of Kush, descendants of Cham, not sons of Yefet — a distinction the *gemara* implicitly acknowledges as it moves through the *pesukim*.

### Nimrod's Cities

The *gemara* continues working through the genealogical narrative of *Parshat Noach*. After the listing of Yavan's descendants, the *gemara* arrives at Kush, who fathered Nimrod. The *pasuk* states: *va-tehi reishit mamlachto Bavel v'Erech v'Akad v'Calneh* — the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, and Erech, and Akad, and Calneh. *Bavel kemashmao* — Babylonia is Babylonia, no further identification needed. *Erech* is *Orichot*, identified by archaeologists as Uruk, a major ancient city in what is now Iraq. *Akad* is *Bashkar* in the *gemara*'s terminology, corresponding to the ancient Akkadian civilization. *Calneh* is *Nofar Ninphi*, whose precise identification remains uncertain.

### Ashur's Cities

From that land, *Ashur* went out. Rav Yosef teaches that *Ashur* is *Silak* — Seleucia, one of the successor kingdoms established after Alexander divided his empire among his generals, encompassing Syria, Mesopotamia, Iran, and India, though the eastern portions quickly broke away.

*Vayiven et Ninveh* — and he built Ninveh. *V'et Rechovot Ir v'et Kalach*. Ninveh requires no identification; it is the famous city known from Sefer Yonah. *Rechovot Ir* is identified as *Perat de'Meshan* — a region along the Euphrates. *Kalach* is *Perat de'Borsi*, another location along the Euphrates.

Regarding the final clause — *v'et Resen bein Ninveh uvein Kalach hi ha'ir hagedolah* — which is the great city, Ninveh or Resen? The *Maharsha* notes that had *Kalach* been the great city, the verse would have said *v'et Kalach ha'ir hagedolah* explicitly. The word *hi* — "it is" — refers back to one of the previously named cities, making the referent either Ninveh or Resen. The *gemara* resolves this: since Yonah later says *v'Ninveh hayetah ir gedolah l'Elohim mahalach sheloshet yamim*, we derive that Ninveh is *ha'ir hagedolah*. Resen is identified as *Aktispon* — Ctesiphon, the Persian capital, a striking identification. Of course, the relative size of cities could have shifted between *Bereishit* and Yonah, but the *gemara*'s point is that the textual witness of Yonah settles the question.

### The Giants

Still within the broader survey of nations and notable figures, the *gemara* turns to a passage from Bamidbar: *v'sham Achiman Sheshai v'Talmai yelidei ha'anak* — and there were Achiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the sons of the giant, whom the scouts encountered upon entering Canaan.

A *tanna* derives their attributes from their names. *Achiman* — from the root *yamin*, the right hand — was *meyuman shebe'achin*, the strongest among the brothers. *Sheshai* — *she'mesim et ha'aretz keshchitut* — he lays the earth waste, so massive that his every step destroys what lies beneath him. *Talmai* — *she'mesim et ha'aretz telamim telamim* — he makes the earth into furrows wherever he walks, such is his enormous weight. 

A *davar acher* adds that each of these giants built a city: Achiman built the city of Anat, Sheshai built Alush, and Talmai built Talbosh. And as for *yelidei ha'anak* in general — *she'ma'anikim hachamah bekumatan* — they were so tall that the sun appeared to hang around their necks like a necklace, the *anak* suggesting a necklace or collar in Hebrew.

---

## Rome & Persia

### Rome Falls to Persia

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said in the name of Rabbi: *atidah Romi shetipol beyad Pras* — Rome is destined to fall into the hands of Persia. To understand the significance of this statement, one must appreciate that from the perspective of *Chazal*, Rome was a colossus of apparently limitless power. The dream of Yaakov with the ladder, as interpreted in the famous *midrash*, envisions the successive kingdoms that would dominate Israel, with Rome ascending and seemingly never descending. The question — when would Roman dominion ever end? — was urgent and without an obvious answer.

At the same time, Persia during the *talmudic* period was a genuine rival power. The Sassanian Persian Empire was not a theoretical threat but a real military force on Rome's eastern frontier. Indeed, in the early seventh century, the Persians conquered the entire Middle East from Rome before eventually losing it. So the prospect of Persian dominance over Rome was not entirely fanciful. It is also worth noting the historical irony that the Babylonian *amoraim* who had this discussion were themselves living under Persian rule, giving the question of which empire would prevail an immediate and personal dimension.

The proof text is the verse from Yirmiyahu: *lachen shim'u atzat Hashem asher ya'atz el Edom... im lo yis'chavum tze'irei hatzon* — the young of the flock (*tzeirei hatzon*) will drag them away, referring to Edom, which *Chazal* identify with Rome. The identification of *Edom* with Rome, and later with Christianity through the continuity of the Holy Roman Empire, represents a layered transference in rabbinic thought: *Esav* in the Torah represents *Edom*, *Edom* in the biblical period was Rome as the subjugator of Israel, and Rome eventually became Christianity.

Rava bar Ulla challenges the identification: *mai mashma dehai tze'irei hatzon Pras?* — what indicates that the young of the flock means Persia? Perhaps it means Greece? After all, in Daniel's vision, the ram (*ayil*) with horns represents the kings of Media and Persia (*ha'ayil asher ra'ita ba'al hakarnayim malchei Madai uPharas*), and the he-goat (*tzfir hasayir*) represents Greece (*u'tzfir hasayir melech Yavan*). Since *tzon* encompasses both sheep and goats, why couldn't *tze'irei hatzon* refer to Greece?

The answer, as we have already seen, is that the identification of *tzeirei hatzon* with Persia does not rest on a metaphor drawn from Daniel at all. *Tze'irei hatzon* means the youngest of the sons — the youngest of the sons of Yefet, which is Tiras, which is Persia. The entire argument about Daniel's ram and he-goat is therefore a misreading of the original derivation.

### Kal VaComer

Rabbah bar Bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yehuda be-Rabbi Ilai: *atida Romi she-tipol be-yad Pras* — Rome will fall in the hands of Persia. A *kal vachomer* is offered in support. The first *beit hamikdash* was built by the descendants of Shem — built by Shlomo — and destroyed by the Kasdim; yet the Kasdim subsequently fell before the Persians. The second *beit hamikdash* was built under Persian auspices — under Koresh — and destroyed by Rome. How much more so, then, should Rome fall to the Persians.

Even on its own terms the *kal vachomer* is not entirely compelling. One might object that the very historical sequence it cites — Persians defeating Kasdim, then Romans defeating Persians — argues against the conclusion rather than for it. The *kal vachomer* seems to be working with the logic that if the Persians, who were merely the *enablers* of the *beit hamikdash*, were capable of toppling those who destroyed the *first* Temple, how much more so will they be able to topple those who destroyed something they themselves built. But the argument's force is at best suggestive rather than probative.

### Rav's Correction

Rav disagrees entirely: *atida Pras she-tipol be-yad Romi* — it is Persia that will fall into the hands of Rome, not the reverse. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged him: *banuyei be-yad saturei?* — will the builders fall in the hands of the destroyers? The Persians are the ones who allowed the *beit hamikdash* to be rebuilt; Rome destroyed it. How can it be that the builders would be overcome by the destroyers?

### Builders vs. Destroyers

Rav's response is terse: *in, gezerat ha-melech hi* — yes, it is God's decree. That is simply how history will unfold, regardless of the moral asymmetry between builders and destroyers. Some voices add that Persia is not entirely innocent in any case — *inhu nami ka satrei bei knishta* — they too destroy synagogues, and should not be idealized as the permanent good guys. A *baraita* supports Rav's position: *atida Pras she-tipol be-yad Romi*, and two reasons are given — their destruction of synagogues, and the divine decree that builders should sometimes fall before destroyers. The destroyers, after all, are proficient at destruction.

### Mashiach & Rome

Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: *ein Ben David ba ad she-tifshot malchut Romi ha-resha'ah be-chol ha-olam kulo tish'ah chodashim* — the son of David, the *mashiach*, will not come until the wicked kingdom of Rome has spread its dominion over the entire world for nine months. This is a sobering statement. Rather than imagining an immediate counterbalance to Roman supremacy, Rav Yehudah envisions the most desperate possible scenario: Rome reaching its maximum extent across the entire world, and only then, at the nadir, the redemption arriving.

The duration of nine months is derived from the verse in Michah: *lachen yitnem ad eit yoledah yaladah v'yeter achiv yeshuvun al bnei Yisrael* — therefore He will deliver them until the time that the woman giving birth gives birth, and the remnant of his brothers will return. The birth process takes nine months, and so Rome's universal dominion will last nine months before the *mashiach* comes.

With that, the *aggadic* passage concludes and the *gemara* returns to the *mishnah*.

---

## Mezuzah in Mikdash (II)

### Mishnah: Chambers

*Tanu Rabbanan: kol ha-lishkot she-hayu ba-mikdash lo hayah lahen mezuzah* — all the chambers in the Temple did not have a *mezuzah*, *chutz milishkat parhedrin* — except for the *Lishkat Parhedrin*, which was designated as the residence of the *Kohen Gadol* in the seven days before Yom Kippur and therefore had a *mezuzah*.

### Rabbi Yehudah's Objection

Rabbi Yehudah objects: were there not many chambers in the *beit hamikdash* in which people lived — *kohanim* sleeping there during their watches — and none of those had a *mezuzah*? His argument is that the mere fact of living in a chamber within the *beit hamikdash* does not by itself create a *mezuzah* obligation. The case of the *Lishkat Parhedrin* was therefore exceptional, not because it was genuinely lived in but for a different reason. According to Rabbi Yehudah, the *mezuzah* in the *Lishkat Parhedrin* was not a biblical obligation at all: *ela Lishkat Parhedrin gzeira hayta* — it was a rabbinic decree, and we will see shortly what that decree was meant to accomplish. The other chambers, although inhabited, did not receive a *mezuzah*, and Rabbi Yehudah's position implies that there is a fundamental reason why chambers in the *beit hamikdash*, even inhabited ones, are exempt. Notably, in the *Tosefta* Rabbi Yehudah's position appears in the exact opposite formulation — there he holds that the inhabited chambers of the *beit hamikdash* do require a *mezuzah* — making this a significant textual tension.

---

## Mezuzah Analysis

### Definition of Bayit

*Amar Rabbah kasavar Rabbi Yehudah*: Rabbah explains Rabbi Yehudah's reasoning. Rabbi Yehudah holds that *kol bayit she'eino asui limot hachama ulimot hageshamim eino bayit* — any structure that is not made to be lived in throughout the year, both summer and winter, does not have the legal status of a *bayit* and therefore does not require a *mezuzah*. No room in the *beit hamikdash* is inhabited year-round; people sleep there for a few days at most. Accordingly, no room qualifies as a *bayit* for purposes of *mezuzah*.

### Winter/Summer House

Abaye challenges Rabbah's formulation. The *pasuk* in Amos states: *vehikeiti beit hachoref al beit hakayitz* — I will strike the winter house along with the summer house. These structures are called *batim* — houses — even though each is used for only part of the year. Rabbah responds: *beit choref ubeit kayitz ikri, bayit stam lo ikri* — it is called a winter house or a summer house with a modifier, but it is not called simply a *bayit* without qualification. A house that requires a seasonal descriptor to identify its function has not attained the full *halachic* status of *bayit*. The modifier itself signals its limitation. Just as a place might be called a winter house or summer house, it is still not simply a house — much as a dish might be labeled "Chicago-style pizza" rather than simply "pizza."

### Sukkah & Mezuzah

Abaye then raises a more pointed challenge to Rabbah's construction of Rabbi Yehudah's position. If Rabbi Yehudah holds that only a structure suited for year-round habitation requires a *mezuzah*, why does Rabbi Yehudah rule that a *sukkah* during *Sukkot* requires a *mezuzah*? *Rabbi Yehudah mechayiv, veChachamim potrin* — Rabbi Yehudah obligates, and the *chachamim* exempt. Here the positions are exactly reversed from what we might expect: Rabbi Yehudah is the more demanding opinion regarding the *sukkah*, yet apparently more lenient regarding the chambers of the *beit hamikdash*. Furthermore, a *baraita* teaches that Rabbi Yehudah would require the *sukkah* to participate in an *eruv*, to have a *mezuzah*, and to have *ma'aser* separated from produce brought into it — treating the *sukkah* in all respects as a genuine dwelling.

### Ma'aser Discussion

The *gemara* pauses to clarify the *ma'aser* requirement, which is the most legally telling of the three obligations Rabbi Yehudah imposes on the *sukkah*. One might suggest that the *eruv* and *mezuzah* requirements are merely rabbinic. But if the *ma'aser* obligation applies, it must be biblical in nature — and this proves that Rabbi Yehudah treats the *sukkah* as a genuine *bayit* with full biblical force.

Why can't the *ma'aser* obligation in such a case be merely rabbinic? Because we would never institute a rabbinic *ma'aser* obligation in a category that closely resembles a biblical *ma'aser* obligation — doing so risks the person separating *trumot u'ma'asrot* from this grain to cover other grain, where one is rabbinic and the other biblical, and that cross-application would be invalid. The concern is precisely that nothing obvious distinguishes the grain brought into a *sukkah* from grain brought into a permanent house; an observer would easily assume both carry the same status, leading to the serious error of applying a *hafrashat ma'aser* that does not work across different categories of obligation.

Tosafot raise an important objection here: there are in fact documented cases of rabbinic *ma'aser* obligations, so why is the *gemara* so confident that we would not institute one here? Tosafot's answer is that when there is something that clearly marks the category as different — such as a distinct species of food — the risk of cross-application is minimal. But when grain enters a *sukkah* rather than a permanent home, there is nothing immediately apparent to an observer that signals a different legal category. Therefore in such a case we could never make the obligation merely rabbinic, and it must be biblical.

This confirms that Rabbi Yehudah treats the *sukkah* as a biblical *bayit* during *Sukkot*. Yet the *gemara* has just explained Rabbi Yehudah's leniency toward the chambers of the *beit hamikdash* on the grounds that they are not year-round dwellings. How can both positions be attributed to Rabbi Yehudah?

### Rava's Clarification

Abaye proposes that the debate about the *sukkah* and the debate about the *Lishkat Parhedrin* are not about the same time period: during the seven days of actual use — whether the seven days of *Sukkot* or the seven days in which the *Kohen Gadol* resides in the *Lishkat Parhedrin* — everyone agrees that the obligation applies *de-oraisa*. The debate would then be only about the rest of the year.

Rava rejects this: *ve-Sukkat heChag be-chag katani* — the *mishnah* or *baraita* explicitly frames the debate about the *sukkah* as occurring during *Sukkot* itself. The disagreement between Rabbi Yehudah and the *chachamim* is not about an empty *sukkah* in the off-season; it is about the *sukkah* during the *chag*, when someone is actively living there. Therefore one cannot resolve the tension by localizing each debate to a different time period.

### Distinct Reasons

*Amar Rava*: the resolution is that each case has its own entirely distinct reasoning. *Sukkah taima le-chud ve-lishka taima le-chud* — the *sukkah* debate and the *lishka* debate are each driven by their own independent *halachic* logic, and the reversal of positions between Rabbi Yehudah and the *chachamim* in each case is not a contradiction.

Regarding the *sukkah*: *Rabbi Yehudah le-taimei de-amar sukkah diras keva ba'inan* — Rabbi Yehudah follows his own well-known position, debated at the beginning of *Masechet Sukkah*, that a *sukkah* must be a permanent structure (*diras keva*). He holds that a *sukkah* can be one hundred *amot* tall because he understands the *mitzvah* as requiring genuine permanent-style dwelling. If the *sukkah* is treated as a permanent dwelling during the *chag*, it has the full status of a *bayit* and is obligated in a *mezuzah*. The *chachamim*, by contrast, hold *diras arai ba'inan* — the *mitzvah* is specifically fulfilled through a temporary dwelling; a *sukkah* by definition is constructed for seven days and then dismantled. Precisely because it is inherently temporary, it never achieves *bayit* status and is exempt from *mezuzah*. This debate is purely about the *halachic* character of a *sukkah* as such.

### Forced Dwelling

The *lishka* in the *beit hamikdash* presents an entirely separate issue. The question here is not about the permanent or temporary nature of the structure, but about the nature of the inhabitation itself. *Rabbanan savri dira be'al korcha shemeih dira* — the *chachamim* hold that even a forced dwelling — a dwelling one is compelled to occupy against one's will — constitutes a *dira* in the full legal sense. The *kohanim* who sleep in the chambers of the *beit hamikdash* are required to be there; the *Kohen Gadol* is sequestered in the *Lishkat Parhedrin* for seven days under compulsion. Yet the *chachamim* maintain that compulsion does not negate the status of *dira*, and therefore the *mezuzah* obligation applies biblically.

*Rabbi Yehudah savar dira be'al korcha lo shemeih dira* — Rabbi Yehudah disagrees. A forced dwelling is not a genuine *dira*. Part of what constitutes a *bayit dira* is that the occupant has real authority and autonomy over the space. One who is effectively imprisoned there — even if the "imprisonment" is the sacred duty of the *Kohen Gadol* — does not truly inhabit that space in the legal sense. Therefore, no chamber in the *beit hamikdash*, however lived-in it may appear, carries a biblical *mezuzah* obligation.

### Decree on Lishkat

If Rabbi Yehudah exempts all *beit hamikdash* chambers from *mezuzah* on biblical grounds, why is there a *mezuzah* in the *Lishkat Parhedrin* at all? *U'miderabbanan hu detiknu lah shelo yomru Kohen Gadol chavush be'veis ha'asurim* — it is a rabbinic enactment, instituted so that people should not say that the *Kohen Gadol* is being held like a prisoner in a jail. Here the reasoning is internally coherent in a striking way: Rabbi Yehudah exempts the chambers precisely *because* he views forced habitation as analogous to imprisonment. And it is *because* he views the *Kohen Gadol's* sequestration as resembling imprisonment that he mandates the *mezuzah* — to visibly dispel that impression, to signal that this is a genuine dwelling place of the leader of Israel and not a detention cell.

The *chachamim* and Rabbi Yehudah thus agree on the *practical* outcome for the *Lishkat Parhedrin* — it has a *mezuzah* — but disagree on the legal basis. The *chachamim* hold it is a biblical obligation, because forced habitation is still *dira*. Rabbi Yehudah holds it is a rabbinic enactment, because forced habitation negates *dira* status, but the enactment is necessary to ensure the dignity and perceived freedom of the *Kohen Gadol*. We will continue with this analysis on the next *daf*.

---

---

# Yoma 11

## Lishkat Parhedrin Mezuzah

### Lishkat Parhedrin Review

To situate the discussion on *daf yud-alef*, it is worth briefly recalling where we left off. The *tanna rabbanan* taught that all the *lishkot* in the *Mikdash* did not have a *mezuzah* — with one notable exception: the *Lishkat Parhedrin*. The rationale offered was that the *Kohen Gadol* resided there for at least the week preceding Yom Kippur, giving it the character of a *beit dirah*. Rabbi Yehuda pushed back: there were other *lishkot* with *batei dirah* that nonetheless lacked a *mezuzah*, so mere habitation cannot be the distinguishing factor. He did not dispute that the *Lishkat Parhedrin* had a *mezuzah* — that was universally agreed upon — but he questioned the given rationale. Rava resolved this by designating the *mezuzah* there as a *gezeirah*: *shelo yomru Kohen Gadol chavush b'veit ha-asurim* — so that people should not say the *Kohen Gadol* is imprisoned. Without a *mezuzah*, the enforced seclusion might carry the appearance of incarceration rather than sacred preparation.

### Gates & Mezuzot

With the *Lishkat Parhedrin* as backdrop, the *Gemara* now pivots to the broader laws of *mezuzah*, a discussion that will occupy the remainder of this *daf* and extend into the next. The *Torah* commands *mezuzot* on *mezuzot beitecha uvisharecha* — on the doorposts of your house and on your gates. The expansive term *uvisharecha* raises an immediate question: which gates are included? A *tanna rabbanan* teaches: *echad sha'arei batim, v'echad sha'arei chatzerot, v'echad sha'arei medinot, v'echad sha'arei ayarot* — the gates of houses, of courtyards, of countries, and of cities are all included. The Gemara formulates this obligation in strikingly deliberate language: *yesh bahen chovat mitzvah lamakom* — there is upon them the obligation of the *mitzvah* for the Place. This is an unusual formulation, and it carries significance worth noting.

### Chovat Mitzvah

The phrase *chovat mitzvah lamakom* stands out precisely because it does not simply say that these places are *chayav b'mezuzah*. The *Siach Yitzchak* observes that this phrasing underscores the divine-command dimension of the obligation, as distinct from any protective benefit the *mezuzah* might confer.

### Protection vs Mitzvah

This distinction between protection and divine command surfaces in the famous narrative in *Gemara Avodah Zarah* concerning Onkelos. After his conversion, Roman officials repeatedly came to bring him in for questioning, and each exchange ended with the official himself converting. When Onkelos explained the *mezuzah* on his doorpost — noting that while a human king sits within and his servants stand guard outside, the *Kadosh Baruch Hu* has his servants within and he himself, as it were, stands guard over them — the officials were overwhelmed. The *mezuzah*, in other words, carries a genuine dimension of divine protection. The *Gemara* elsewhere connects the *mezuzah* to long life, which is one reason offered for why even a rented dwelling requires a *mezuzah*.

### Divine Command

Yet one might have thought: if protection is the *mezuzah*'s function, why extend the obligation to city gates and national borders? One's household *mezuzot* would presumably suffice to protect the family. The answer that emerges is that the obligation in those more expansive venues is not primarily about personal protection at all — it is because *Hashem*'s *mitzvah* says *uvisharecha* without qualification, and that broad wording includes them. Hence the deliberate phrasing: *chovat mitzvah lamakom*. Even where the protective rationale does not obviously apply, the commandment extends there nonetheless.

---

## Mezuzot Obligation

### Three Gate Categories

The *baraita* thus establishes three (or four) categories of gates: those of houses, courtyards, country borders, and cities — all carrying the obligation. The Torah's use of the plural *uvisharecha*, unqualified, is the textual basis for this expansion.

### Chovat Mitzvah

As noted above, the formulation *yesh bahen chovat mitzvah lamakom* is unexpectedly elaborate. Rather than a straightforward *chayav*, the *baraita* uses language that foregrounds the obligation as one owed to God rather than derived from personal benefit. This framing will become important as the *Gemara* probes cases where the protective rationale cannot easily apply.

### Protection vs Mitzvah

The tension between the *mezuzah* as talisman and the *mezuzah* as pure divine command is not merely academic. If it were purely about protection, one could argue that private homes suffice and public gates need not be included. The *Onkelos* story illustrates that protection is indeed a real dimension — but the *Gemara*'s point is that even absent a protective function at the national level, the obligation persists because of the divine command.

### Divine Command

The upshot is that the *mezuzah* obligation is expansive not because protection scales proportionally to the size of the gate, but because the *mitzvah* itself is directed at *Hashem* — *chovat mitzvah lamakom* — and the Torah's language of *uvisharecha* captures all of these categories.

---

## Avulei D'Mechuza

### Mechuza Gates

The *Gemara* now confronts a specific case: Abaye asked Rav Safra about *hani avulei deMechuza* — the city gates of Mechuza — and why the *rabanan* did not affix *mezuzot* to them. Rav Safra answered that the gates of Mechuza were constructed in the manner of a fortification — *chizuk d'akra* — with a structure more resembling military fortification than a habitable throughway. The architectural character of these gates, then, seemed to place them outside the normative category of gates that require a *mezuzah*.

### Inhabited Chambers

This answer is immediately challenged. Even if the gate itself resembles a fort, at the end of the day — *sof sof* — there is typically some habitable chamber within such a gate structure, where the city watch (*shomer*) resides. And there is a *baraita* that makes precisely this point: a *beit haknesset* that contains a *beit dirah* for the *chazzan* of the congregation — meaning its caretaker — is *chayevet b'mezuzah*. If habitation within a gate-like structure generates the obligation in a *beit haknesset*, the same logic should apply to the gates of Mechuza.

### Sakana & Danger

Abaye therefore offers a different resolution: *mishum sakana* — on account of danger. The explanation lies in a distinction the *Gemara* will now articulate regarding the frequency of *mezuzah* inspection. A *mezuzat yachid* — a private *mezuzah* — must be inspected *pa'amayim b'shavua*, twice within a *shemitah* cycle of seven years. But a *mezuzat rabbim* — a *mezuzah* in a public location — need only be inspected *pa'amayim b'yovel*, twice in a fifty-year *yovel* cycle. The reason, as Abaye implies, is *sakana*: inspecting public *mezuzot* exposes the inspector to danger.

### Artavin Fine

This danger is illustrated by a story cited in the name of Rabbi Yehuda: there was a certain *Artavin* — whether this is a professional title or a personal name is uncertain — who was inspecting *mezuzot* in the upper marketplace of Tzipori. A government official found him and fined him a thousand *zuz*. The reason for the fine, as the *Gemara* makes clear, is that publicly checking what is affixed to a gate could be perceived by the non-Jewish authorities as some form of incantation or witchcraft — casting a hex on the city's gate. This perception made public *mezuzah* inspection genuinely dangerous, especially in a city under foreign dominion. It is worth noting that the obligation to check still exists — the *sakana* merely reduces its frequency, it does not eliminate it.

---

## Checking Frequency

### Inspection Intervals

The *baraita* establishes two distinct intervals for *mezuzah* inspection: private *mezuzot* require checking twice in a seven-year *shemitah* cycle, while public *mezuzot* — those affixed to communal or civic gates — require checking only twice in a fifty-year *yovel* cycle.

### Rot & Theft

Rashi explains the underlying rationale for checking at all: *shema nirkava o nignava* — perhaps the *klaf* has rotted due to exposure to the elements, or perhaps it has been stolen. These are the two practical concerns that necessitate periodic inspection.

### Tefillin Contrast

This stands in interesting contrast to *tefillin*, which, if worn regularly, do not require checking from a strict *halachic* standpoint. The reason is straightforward: if you wear your *tefillin* every day, you know they have not been stolen, and regular handling gives you adequate awareness of their condition. A *mezuzah* affixed within the wall of a doorpost, by contrast, may deteriorate unnoticed or disappear without the homeowner realizing it. It is only *tefillin* that have been sitting unused for a long time — inherited *tefillin*, backup pairs, or *tefillin* found in an old storage room — that would require checking before use.

### Public Danger

The *Tosafot Yeshanim* identifies an additional rationale for the less frequent inspection of public *mezuzot*: even setting aside formal governmental decrees against fulfilling *mitzvot*, a person inspecting a *mezuzah* on a public gate risks being suspected of practicing some form of improper ritual. The *Artavin* story above illustrates precisely this. One might also suggest — though others dispute it — that the many people passing through public gates provide a kind of constant informal surveillance that makes theft or deterioration less likely; but this reasoning is not without difficulty, and that is precisely why multiple answers are offered.

### Rav Chaim Ruling

A practical question arises from the formulation "twice in seven years": could one discharge the obligation by checking on one day, and then checking again the very next day, and then not again for seven years? Rav Chaim Kanievsky rules that this does not work. The intent of the ruling is that the *mezuzah* be checked once roughly every three and a half years — the two required checks are to be spread across the *shemitah* cycle, not discharged consecutively. One cannot satisfy "twice in seven" by checking twice in two days and considering the obligation fulfilled for the next seven years.

---

## Exemptions Overview

### Six Exempt Structures

With the general obligation established, the *Gemara* now turns to structures that are exempt from the *mezuzah* requirement. Rav Kahana taught before Rav Yehuda: *beit hateven* (a storehouse for straw or grain), *beit habakar* (a barn), *beit ha'etzim* (a woodshed), and *beit ha'otzarot* (a general storehouse) — these are all *peturim min hamezuzah*, exempt from the *mezuzah* obligation.

### Women Bathe

The stated reason for the exemption is: *mipnei shehanashim ne'otot bahen* — because women are *ne'otot* in them. The *Gemara* immediately asks: what does *ne'otot* mean? And the first answer offered is *rochtzot* — they wash there. This is puzzling: one would not ordinarily expect women to be bathing in a barn or a woodshed, and it is not immediately clear why bathing in a location would exempt it from *mezuzah* in any case. Rashi explains that *ne'otot* in the sense of *rochtzot* implies that these are places where people are unclothed — *arumot* — and it would therefore be disrespectful to *Shamayim* to have a *mezuzah* in such a location. The rationale, then, is *kavod shamayim*: the *mezuzah* contains the divine name and should not be placed where there is an element of immodesty.

### Rav Yehuda Dispute

Rav Yehuda challenges this framing. The implication of the teaching that these structures are exempt *because* women wash there would be that *stam* — by default, without that qualifier — they *would* be obligated. Rav Yehuda disputes that inference.

### Rav Papa Teaching

Independently, Rav Papa taught that a barn (*refet bakar*) is exempt from *mezuzah* — without providing any reason. This teaching will become relevant to the resolution that follows.

### Ne'otot Reinterpreted

The resolution offered is a reinterpretation of *ne'otot*. Rather than meaning that women *bathe* (*rochtzot*) there — which would make dignity or modesty the reason for the exemption — *ne'otot* is reread as *mitkashtot*: women *adorn themselves* there. And the *Gemara* now reformulates the teaching accordingly: *af al pi shehanashim mitkashtot bahen, peturin* — even though women go there to adorn themselves with perfumes and cosmetics, the structures are still exempt. The reason is not immodesty but the fact that adorning oneself in a space does not constitute sufficient *beit dirah* to trigger the obligation. One might have thought that because women regularly occupy these spaces for cosmetic purposes, they might qualify as habitable — *salka datach amina dirah hi* — but the teaching establishes that this threshold is not met.

---

## Beitcha Definition

### Beitcha Dwelling

A *baraita* now provides a textual grounding for these exemptions. The Torah's term *beitcha* — "your house" — is read to mean *hamiyuchad lach*, a place designated for *you* and your habitation: *beit dirah*, a genuine dwelling place for people.

### Exemption List

On this reading, the following are excluded: *beit hateven*, *beit habakar*, *beit ha'etzim*, and *beit ha'otzarot* — all are *peturin min hamezuzah* not because of any issue of modesty or immodesty, but simply because they are storehouses and working structures, not human dwelling places. This is one coherent position.

### Women Adorning

Yet immediately another view is introduced: *v'yesh mechayvin* — there are those who obligate these structures. According to this view, even storehouses may require a *mezuzah* in certain circumstances. The point of contention is precisely what *ne'otot* means and whether a place where women adorn themselves rises to the level of *dirah*.

### Bathhouses Debate

This disagreement then extends to a further list of places: *beit hakisei* (a toilet), *beit habursaki* (a tannery), *beit hamerchatz* (a bathhouse), and *beit hatevilah* (a *mikvah*). These structures, it is said, are exempt because *shenashim ne'otot bahen* — women are *ne'otot* there. But here the disagreement about the meaning of *ne'otot* becomes critical once more, as it determines whether the exemption rests on immodesty or on absence of *dirah*.

---

## Filth & Immodesty

### Four Filthy Places

The *Gemara* enumerates four additional categories of exempt structures: *beit hakisei*, *beit habursaki*, *beit hamerchatz*, and *beit hatevilah*. These are spaces associated with physical impurity, filth, and undress.

### Bathing Character

The stated shared characteristic of all four is again *shenashim ne'otot bahen* — that women are *ne'otot* there.

### Bathhouse Repetition

A glaring difficulty now surfaces: the *bathhouse* appears twice in the discussion — once as part of the category where *nashim ne'otot*, and now again as an independently listed exempt structure. If *ne'otot* means *rochtzot* (bathing), then the place-where-women-bathe and the bathhouse are identical categories, and we have needlessly repeated ourselves.

### Public vs Private

The resolution offered is that the two mentions of *beit hamerchatz* refer to different types of bathhouses: one is *merchatz d'rabbim* — a public bathhouse frequented by many people — and the other is *merchatz d'yachid* — a private bathhouse belonging to an individual or household. One might have thought that only the public bathhouse, with its greater *zohamah* (filth and disorder), would be exempt, while a private bathhouse, which is kept cleaner and more orderly, might be considered sufficiently *mechubad* to require a *mezuzah*. The teaching therefore clarifies that even a private bathhouse is exempt.

### Filth & Nudity

The underlying explanation for the exemption of all these places — tannery, toilet, bathhouse, mikvah — converges on two related concerns: *nifsha zuhamah* (the pervasiveness of filth) and the presence of unclothed people. Either or both of these conditions renders the location unsuitable for the *mezuzah* and its divine name.

---

## Two Opinions

### Structure Type

The *Gemara* now summarizes the debate between Rav Kahana and Rav Yehuda as a *machloket tannaim*. Rav Kahana holds that the determinative criterion is the *type of structure*: *beitcha hamiyuchad lach* — structures that are not designated as human dwelling places are simply not covered by the Torah's *beitcha*, regardless of any question of cleanliness or modesty.

### Dignity Standard

Rav Yehuda holds that the criterion is *kavod* — dignity and cleanliness. On his view, what exempts the filthy places (*beit hakisei*, *beit habursaki*, *beit hamerchatz*, *beit hatevilah*) is not their structural classification but the fact that they involve *zohamah* and undress, rendering them incompatible with the dignity required of a location housing the divine name.

### Core Agreement

Both positions agree on the fundamental exemptions: *beit hateven*, *beit habakar*, *beit ha'etzim*, and *beit ha'otzarot* are exempt on any account. The dispute concerns the filthy and immodest places. According to Rav Kahana's reading, the tanna who obligates these structures does so because they may qualify as *dirah*; according to Rav Yehuda's reading, the tanna who exempts them does so because of their inherent lack of dignity. Both positions can be correlated with specific tannaitic sources, and the *Gemara* concludes that the conflicting teachings reflect a genuine *machloket tannaim* — not a contradiction within a single view.

The practical upshot, which the *Gemara* underscores, is that while everyone agrees that a *beit hakisei* is exempt, the real dispute concerns structures like *beit hateven*: is it exempt because it is not a *beit dirah* (Rav Kahana's tanna), or could it be obligated under some readings (the competing tanna)? Similarly, the question of *beit sha'ar* — the small passageway or vestibule leading to a gate — emerges as potentially *machloket*: the *Gemara* in *Menachot* teaches that a *beit sha'ar*, an *achsadra*, and a *mirpeset* (balcony) are *chayav b'mezuzah*, whereas our *baraita* here exempts them. The *Tosafot* address this tension and offer two resolutions: either the obligation in *Menachot* is *mid'rabbanan* while our *baraita* speaks *mid'oraita*, or the distinction is functional — a *beit sha'ar* that opens into a *beit dirah* requires a *mezuzah*, while one that does not is exempt.

---

## Holy Precincts

### Temple Mount

The *baraita* continues: *yachol she-ani merabeh af Har HaBayit v'ha-lishkot v'ha-azarot* — one might have thought to extend the *mezuzah* obligation even to the Temple Mount, the *lishkot* of the *Mikdash*, and the *azarot*.

### Holy Exemption

The *baraita* responds by invoking the word *beit*: just as *bayit* refers to a place that is *chol* — ordinary, non-sacred — so too the obligation applies only to *chol* structures. Holy places — *kodesh* — are exempt. This is the source for the ruling that a *beit haknesset* does not necessarily require a *mezuzah* from Torah law.

### Contradiction

This creates a dramatic problem. The *Gemara* has just established that *kodesh* places are exempt from *mezuzah*, and yet the very case that opened our discussion — the *Lishkat Parhedrin* and *Sha'ar Nikanor* — assumed that they *had* a *mezuzah*. How can holy precincts be exempt if these locations within the *Beit HaMikdash* had *mezuzot*?

### Torah vs Rabbinic

The first resolution follows directly from the distinction already employed earlier in the *sugya*: the *baraita* establishing the exemption of *kodesh* places speaks *mid'oraita*. The *mezuzah* of the *Lishkat Parhedrin*, by contrast, was either a rabbinic enactment or — more precisely — a *gezeirah* of a very specific character: *shelo yomru Kohen Gadol chavush b'veit ha-asurim*. This is not even a standard *mid'rabbanan* obligation; it is a one-case exception driven by considerations of *marat ayin* (appearance). So: *mid'oraita*, all *kodesh* places are exempt. On the rabbinic level, there is a *machloket* — the *rabanan* inclined toward requiring *mezuzah* on some of these places, while Rabbi Yehuda disagreed. And the *Lishkat Parhedrin* sits in a yet different category — a specific *gezeirah* that does not reflect a general rabbinic obligation.

### HaMeiri Purpose

The *HaMeiri* offers a strikingly different resolution. He asks: what do we mean by *kodesh* as the exempting criterion — is *kodesh* a matter of *location* or of *use*? On the *HaMeiri*'s reading, a place used for a holy *purpose* is exempt from *mezuzah*. A place that is merely *located* within the Temple precinct but is used for a mundane function might still be obligated. On this reading, the *Lishkat Parhedrin* — used as the *Kohen Gadol*'s personal dwelling — is not used for a *kodesh* purpose, and therefore falls under the obligation.

### HaMeiri Sanctified

The *HaMeiri* then goes further, however, and articulates a harder version of his position: if an area is *mekudash* — formally sanctified — it does not require a *mezuzah*, regardless of what it is used for. This is a more categorical statement.

### Lishkat Status

This brings us back to the question of whether the *Lishkat Parhedrin* was sanctified at all. Rashi indicates that the *Lishkat Parhedrin* was *not* sanctified — *lo nitkadesh*. This is consistent with other discussions about the *Lishkat Parhedrin*: the *Kohen Gadol* was permitted to sit there (he cannot sit in the *Beit HaMikdash* proper), and there were questions about whether his wife could be present. If the *Lishkat Parhedrin* was not formally sanctified, then on the *HaMeiri*'s own principle — that only *mekudash* locations are exempt — it would be straightforwardly obligated in *mezuzah*. And that is precisely what we find. Far from being a contradiction, the *mezuzah* of the *Lishkat Parhedrin* fits perfectly: it is an unsanctified place used for habitation, and therefore requires a *mezuzah* on its own merits. The *gezeirah* reasoning of Rava may then be supplementary, or may address the *Sha'ar Nikanor* aspect of the question rather than the *Lishkat Parhedrin* itself.

---

## Sha'ar HaMadi

### Six Exempt

Bar Shmuel bar Yehuda taught before Rabbah: six types of gates are exempt from *mezuzah*: *beit hateven*, *beit habakar*, *beit ha'etzim*, *beit ha'otzarot*, *sha'ar haMadi*, and *sha'ar she'eino mekureh* (an unroofed gate).

### Counting Error

Rabbah immediately challenges him: *patachta b'shisha v'siyamta b'shiva* — you began with six and ended with seven. The list as recited includes *sha'ar she'eino gavoah yud* — a gate that does not reach the requisite height of ten *tefachim* — bringing the total to seven.

### HaMadi Dispute

Bar Shmuel explains: in truth, there are six undisputed exemptions, and one — *sha'ar haMadi* — is the subject of a *tannaitic* dispute. Hence the count of six refers only to the uncontested cases.

### Meir vs Sages

The *baraita* on *sha'ar haMadi* reads: *kippa* — a domed or arched gateway — Rabbi Meir obligates (*mechayev*) in *mezuzah*, while the Sages exempt (*potrim*). Both agree that if the legs of the arch reach ten *tefachim* in height, it is *chayevet b'mezuzah*.

### Architecture Details

The architectural details are as follows. A standard gate obligated in *mezuzah* must be ten *tefachim* high and four *tefachim* wide. The *sha'ar haMadi* presents a complication: the gate is formed by an arch, so that while the overall structure reaches ten *tefachim* in height, the arch curves inward such that at the top, the opening is less than four *tefachim* wide. However, if one considers the bricks embedded in the wall on either side of the arch, and were one to "complete" those bricks across the top as if they formed a straight lintel, the total width would reach four *tefachim*.

### Abaye Clarifies

Abaye clarifies the undisputed cases and the precise locus of the dispute. If the arch's legs are not straight for three *tefachim* at the base — even if the overall height is ten — everyone agrees there is no *mezuzah* obligation: *lav klum hi*. Similarly, if the legs are straight for three *tefachim* but the structure does not reach ten *tefachim* overall, again everyone agrees it is exempt.

### Hidden Bricks

The dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages concerns exactly one case: the arch reaches ten *tefachim* in height, its legs are straight for three *tefachim* at the base, but the opening at the arch is less than four *tefachim* wide — *v'ein b'rochbah daled*. However, the bricks embedded in the surrounding wall, if extended notionally across the arch — *yesh b'chakuk l'hashlimah l'arba'ah* — would complete the four-*tefachim* width. Rabbi Meir holds *chokekim l'hashlim*: we extend the bricks notionally, completing the width, and the gate is therefore obligated. The Sages hold *ein chokekim l'hashlim*: we do not complete fictitiously, and since the actual opening is less than four *tefachim* wide, the gate is exempt. This principle — whether notional extension of a partial structure can complete a halachic measurement — is analogous to the more familiar principle of *gud asik* applied to vertical extensions, and the *machloket* here is essentially its horizontal equivalent. We will continue from here in the next *shiur*.

---

---

# Yoma 13

## Backup Kohen Gadol

### Baraita Setup

The daf opens on 12b with a *baraita* — cited also in Masechet Horayot — addressing what happens when a *kohen gadol* is rendered unfit for service and a replacement is appointed in his stead, only for the original to regain his fitness. The *baraita* itself is a *Tosefta*, and its original context in Horayot is not specifically about Yom Kippur; Horayot deals broadly with positions of communal authority — king, *kohen gadol*, *Sanhedrin* — and therefore the question it raises is a general one. The *baraita*'s language, *u'minu acher tachtav*, "they appointed another in his place," suggests a scenario where no backup was already waiting in the wings, unlike the Yom Kippur preparation discussed in the *mishnah*. Nevertheless, the scenario is clearly relevant: the *kohen gadol* is incapacitated, someone serves in his place, and then the original recovers. The *baraita* is unequivocal on one point: *rishon chozer la'avodato* — the first *kohen gadol*, once fit again, returns to his position. The question is what becomes of the second.

### Rabbi Meir

*Rabbi Meir* holds that the second *kohen*, having served in the capacity of *kohen gadol*, retains that status for the remainder of his life. In practice this means he is bound by all the *mitzvot* of *kehuna gedola*: he may not marry a widow, he may not allow his hair to grow wild or rend his garments upon the death of a close relative, he does not leave the *Beit HaMikdash* during a bereavement, and he wears all eight priestly garments when performing the *avoda*. What *Rashi* does not explicitly address — and what remains an open and somewhat striking question — is whether he would also be obligated in the daily *mincha* offering that a *kohen gadol* brings each morning and afternoon. Two *kohanim gedolim* each bringing that offering simultaneously would be a peculiar state of affairs.

### Rabbi Yose

*Rabbi Yose* disagrees. He agrees that the first *kohen gadol* returns to his role, but he holds that *sheni eino ra'ui lo l'Kohen Gadol v'lo l'Kohen Hedyot* — the second is fit neither to serve as *kohen gadol* nor as an ordinary *kohen*. He cites a historical precedent: the case of Yosef ben Illem of Tzippori, who served as a stand-in for the *kohen gadol* and was thereafter ruled by the sages to be disqualified from both roles. This is not presented as a new ruling but as applied precedent.

### Eivah & Maalin

The *Gemara* explains the reasoning behind each half of *Rabbi Yose*'s position. Why can he not serve as *kohen gadol*? *Mishum eivah* — because of the enmity it would generate. The entire institution of the *kohen gadol* is premised on there being a singular figure at the apex of the *kehuna*. Having two individuals simultaneously bearing the title of *kohen gadol* creates an intolerable rivalry. Why, then, can he not revert to serving as a *kohen hedyot*? Because of the principle of *maalin bakodesh velo moridin* — once elevated in sanctity, one cannot be demoted. His appointment to the role of *kohen gadol*, even if temporary, constitutes a real elevation that cannot simply be undone.

The practical implication is this: his true *halachic* status remains that of a *kohen gadol*, but he is prevented from actively exercising that status in the *Beit HaMikdash* due to the conflict it would create. This is not a denial of his status; it is a suspension of its expression.

### If He Performs

*Rabbah bar bar Chana* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* rules: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yossi*. And *Rabbi Yose* himself concedes — *u'modeh Rabbi Yossi she'im avar ve'avad avodato kesherah* — that if the second *kohen* went ahead and performed the *avoda* in defiance of this ruling, the *avoda* would be valid *bedi'avad*. This is a significant concession, because if a *kohen hedyot* were to perform the *avoda* in the eight golden garments of the *kohen gadol*, the *avoda* would be invalid. The fact that it is valid here confirms that his underlying status truly is that of a *kohen gadol*. The ruling is only that we do not permit him to exercise it — not that the status is fictional.

*Rav Yehudah* in the name of *Rav* similarly rules *halacha ke-Rabbi Yossi*, and the implication follows that all the *halachot* that apply to a *kohen gadol* — particularly in the context of bereavement, such as the prohibition against *keriah* and allowing one's hair to grow wild — would also apply to him. The debate, it emerges, reduces to a single practical question: may he actively perform the *avoda*? On that point alone, *Rabbi Yose* says no, on account of the conflict it would generate.

### Met Rishon

*Rav Yehudah* in the name of *Rav* adds a second ruling: *u'modeh Rabbi Yossi she'im met rishon she'chozer la'avodato* — if the first *kohen gadol* dies, the second steps into his place as the new *kohen gadol*. The *Gemara* asks: is this not obvious? If we have established that his status is genuinely that of a *kohen gadol*, of course he would succeed to the role upon the first one's death. The *Gemara* answers that one might have thought otherwise — *tzar mechayim*. As long as the first *kohen gadol* is alive and knows that this person is waiting to assume his position the moment he dies, that itself constitutes a kind of rivalry, an ominous presence that shadows him during his lifetime. One might therefore have thought that to prevent even this form of conflict, the second would not be permitted to succeed even upon the first's death. The ruling tells us we are not concerned about that. The succession is legitimate.

This point is directly relevant to the *mishnah*'s discussion of the Yom Kippur backup *kohen gadol*: should the original become permanently incapacitated or die, the stand-in assumes the role in full. Both *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yose* agree that the substitute acquires the personal status of a *kohen gadol*; their dispute concerns only whether he may actively serve in that capacity during the original's lifetime.

---

## Backup Wife Debate

### Rabbi Yehuda

The *Gemara* now returns to the *mishnah* itself, which raises the question of whether a backup wife should also be prepared for the *kohen gadol* before Yom Kippur. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that indeed *af isha acheret matkinin lo* — they should prepare another woman for him as well. The verse states *ve'chiper ba'ado uva'ad beito*, "and he shall atone for himself and for his household," and the *halacha* understands *beito* to require that he be married. Should his wife die on Yom Kippur, he would no longer fulfill that requirement. Therefore *Rabbi Yehuda* argues for a designated backup wife.

### Infinite Regression

The *Chachamim* object: *im ken ein ladavar sof* — if you are going to worry that his wife might die and therefore prepare a backup, you must worry that the backup will die as well, and there is no end to this logic. The *Gemara* takes this objection seriously and asks why the *Rabbanan* themselves are not equally troubled. They are, after all, concerned that the *kohen gadol* might become *tamei* — which is why a backup *kohen gadol* is appointed in the first place. Why not worry about his wife dying as well?

### Tumah Shchicha

The *Rabbanan* respond: *tumah shchicha* — *tumah* is common. Becoming *tamei* through seminal emission, contact with another *tamei* person, and similar causes is a relatively frequent occurrence. *Mitah lo shchicha* — death, by contrast, is not so common. The possibility that this particular person will die on this particular day is remote enough that we are not required to prepare for it.

### Two Deaths

*Rabbi Yehuda* accepts this logic but applies it asymmetrically. He is willing to be concerned about the unlikely event that one person — the *kohen gadol*'s wife — might die. *Lemitah de'chad chayshinan* — that level of concern is reasonable. *Lemitah detartei lo chayshinan* — that both the wife and the backup wife would die is too remote a scenario to warrant concern. The *Rabbanan* disagree.

### Zariz Argument

The *Rabbanan* respond sharply: once you allow yourself to worry about unreasonable possibilities, there is no principled stopping point.
