If the chance of one woman dying is already low enough to be dismissed as *lo shchicha*, what is the difference between worrying about that and worrying about two deaths? The *Rabbanan* further challenge *Rabbi Yehuda*'s framework by noting that he has no defensible threshold — if he is concerned about unlikely scenarios, he should be concerned about all unlikely scenarios with equal consistency.

### Two Tamei

The *Gemara* then turns the challenge back on the *Rabbanan* themselves: if they are concerned about the *kohen gadol* becoming *tamei*, they should equally be concerned that both the *kohen gadol* and his backup might become *tamei* on Yom Kippur. The *Rabbanan* respond: *Kohen Gadol zariz hu* — the *kohen gadol* is careful and meticulous, so the concern is much diminished. The *Gemara* probes: if he is so careful, why appoint a backup at all? The answer: *keivan de'avdinan lei tzarah* — precisely because there is a competitor waiting in the wings, he will be all the more vigilant. The backup functions not merely as a contingency but as an incentive. This is quite different from death, which no amount of vigilance can prevent. *Tumah* is avoidable; death is not. That is the fundamental asymmetry between the concerns raised by *Rabbi Yehuda* and those of the *Rabbanan*.

---

## Backup Wife Problem

### Nisu'in Required

Having established that *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position has some merit, the *Gemara* now asks how the backup wife arrangement would actually work in practice. The first obstacle: *beito amar Rachmana* — the *Torah* requires *beito*, his household, meaning an actual wife. Simply having another woman designated in the wings is meaningless if he is not married to her. Fine, the *Gemara* says — he does *kiddushin* with her before Yom Kippur, thus making her his wife.

But the *Gemara* presses further: *v'hachama de'lo kanis lah lav beiso hu* — as long as he has not brought her into his home as his wife, she is not yet his *beito*. The *Torah*'s language of *beito* implies not merely *kiddushin* — betrothal — but *nisu'in*, actual cohabitation, the second stage of marriage in which the couple begins to live together as husband and wife. The Torah's own usage elsewhere reflects this distinction: *ki yikach ish isha uva eileiha* — the "taking" of a wife is associated with physical union; *asher eiras isha velo lekacha* — betrothal is distinct from the consummation of the marriage. The *Gemara* understands *bayit* throughout to refer to *nisu'in*, not merely *kiddushin*.

### One Wife Only

Once the *Gemara* establishes that *nisu'in* is required, a second problem emerges immediately. If he has already done *nisu'in* with the backup wife, he now has two wives simultaneously. But the verse says *beito* — his household, singular — *velo bishnei batim*, not two households. This is a striking point: in a society that formally permitted polygamy, the *Gemara* reads the Yom Kippur requirement as implicitly restricting the *kohen gadol* to one wife, at least for purposes of the *avoda*. The idea of a singular *kohen gadol* who represents the apex of the *kehuna* resonates here with the idea of a singular wife who defines his *bayit*. Just as there cannot be two *kohanim gedolim* serving simultaneously — a point the *Gemara* made earlier in connection with *eivah* — there cannot be two *batim* on Yom Kippur.

The *Gemara* suggests that he could simply divorce the backup wife — but if he divorces her, he is back to square one, with only one wife and no contingency if she dies. The *Gemara* therefore proposes a *get* issued *al tenai* — a conditional divorce — as the mechanism for maintaining exactly one wife at all times.

### Rashi Caveat

Before following the *Gemara* through its discussion of conditional *gittin*, it is important to note what *Rashi* says explicitly about this passage. He writes: *v'chol sugya zo ein teirutzim she'ba yecholim la'amod ki yesh lahem teshuvot rabot* — every single suggestion the *Gemara* is about to offer is subject to numerous objections. *Ve'eino ella kemelamdin otanu v'im tomar ken yesh lehashiv ken v'eino meshiv kol teshuvot she'yesh lehashiv* — it is as if the *Gemara* is teaching us by process of elimination, answering one problem at a time to lead us toward the final correct formulation, without stopping to enumerate every possible objection to each intermediate proposal. *Ki be'achat hu mesalko leteretz inyan acher ad she'he'emidah al mechona* — each step is rejected for a single reason, redirecting the inquiry, until the discussion is finally settled.

This caveat is important because, as will become apparent, many of the proposals the *Gemara* entertains are obviously flawed. *Rashi* preempts the reader's impatience: yes, the suggestions are inadequate in more ways than the *Gemara* acknowledges at each step. The point is not to present watertight proposals but to think through the problem systematically.

The difficulty is fundamentally created by the requirement of *nisu'in*. If *kiddushin* alone sufficed, the solution would be straightforward: betroth the backup wife on the condition that *kiddushin* take effect at the moment his first wife dies. The *kiddushin* would be calibrated to activate precisely when needed and remain inert otherwise. There would be no overlap, no period of two simultaneous wives. But since *nisu'in* — the lived reality of establishing a household together — cannot be effected by a condition triggering at a future moment, the couple must actually begin living together before Yom Kippur. And once they have done so, the *Gemara* must grapple with how to ensure that at any given moment during Yom Kippur, he is married to exactly one woman.

### Conditional Get

The mechanism the *Gemara* pursues is a *get al tenai* — a conditional bill of divorce. The goal is to craft conditions such that whichever wife needs to be "available" at any moment is in fact his wife, and whichever does not need to be available is not. The *Gemara* will work through a series of formulations — most of them flawed in obvious ways — before arriving at what it considers a workable arrangement.

---

## Get Solutions

### Get If Dies

The first proposal: he says to the backup wife, *harei zeh giteich al menat shetamuti* — "here is your *get* on the condition that you die." This is plainly useless: if she dies, she has no need of a *get*, and he would in any case be left with only wife number one. The *Gemara* immediately rejects this.

Second attempt: *harei zeh giteich al menat shelo tamuti* — "here is your *get* if you do not die." The logic here is more coherent: if the backup wife survives Yom Kippur, the *get* takes effect and she is out of the picture, leaving him married to wife number one alone. If she dies, the *get* does not take effect — but she is dead, so that problem resolves itself, and he remains married to wife number one. The *Gemara* notes that this arrangement handles the basic cases: *ilu lo meita nitgarsha lah* — if she lives, she is divorced; *v'im meita, kaima hacha* — if she dies, wife number one remains.

But the *Gemara* then identifies the fatal flaw: *dilma lo meita v'hava lah gita dehai gita u'meita chaverta* — perhaps she does not die and the *get* therefore takes effect divorcing her, but then wife number one dies. In that case, he has no wife at all. The entire point of the backup wife arrangement was to ensure he always has a wife. This formulation fails to cover the scenario it was designed for.

### Get If Doesn't Die

The *Gemara* considers several further permutations. What if the condition is *al menat shetamus achas michem* — "if one of you dies"? This also fails: if neither dies, the condition is not met and he remains married to both; if one dies, the *get* takes effect for the surviving wife — and he has no wife.

The *Gemara* also raises an independent objection grounded in *Rava*'s ruling: *harei zeh giteich al menat shelo tishtei yayin kol yemei chayai* — a *get* conditioned on a restriction that applies for the entire duration of the husband's life is not valid as a *get*, because *kerisut* — the concept of severance — requires that the divorce effect a clean separation during the lives of both parties. A condition that binds them together indefinitely is inconsistent with the nature of a *get*. This rules out any formulation that ties the condition to the death of either party across the full span of a life.

### Midday Overlap

The *Gemara* makes its most significant advance with the formulation: *harei zeh giteich al menat shelo tamus chaverta* — "this is your *get* if wife number one does not die." Now the logic is considerably closer to the goal. If wife number one survives Yom Kippur, the backup's *get* takes effect and he is left married to wife number one alone. If wife number one dies, the condition is not met, the *get* does not take effect, and he remains married to wife number two. The *Gemara* acknowledges this: *ilu meita chaverta megarsha, v'im meita ha, kaima ha* — whichever wife survives, there is exactly one wife at the end of the day.

But a new and subtle problem emerges: *dilma meita chaverta b'palga d'avoda* — what if wife number one dies in the middle of the day? If she dies at noon, then her death means the *get* does not take effect — he remains married to wife number two. But for the first half of the day, both wives were simultaneously his. The *avoda* of the morning was performed with *shnei batim*, two households, in violation of the requirement of *beito*. The retroactive invalidation of the *get* confirms that the first half of the day was problematic. The question of when exactly wife number one dies creates an unavoidable window of overlap.

### Both Conditional

The *Gemara* arrives at the solution of issuing conditional *gittin* to both wives simultaneously. To wife number two, the *kohen gadol* says: *harei zeh giteich al menat shelo tamus chaverta* — "this is your *get* if wife number one does not die." To wife number one, he says: *harei zeh giteich al menat she'ekanes ani l'veit haknesset* — "this is your *get* if I go into a *beit knesset*."

The two conditions work in tandem. If wife number one survives the day, her *get* does not take effect — she remains his wife — and wife number two's *get* does take effect, leaving him with one wife. If wife number one dies during the day, wife number two remains his wife. The residual problem of the midday overlap — if wife number one dies at noon, what about the morning? — is resolved by the trigger mechanism of the *kohen gadol*'s own action. If he sees that wife number one is about to die, he goes into the *beit knesset* (or performs whatever act serves as the designated trigger), thereby activating her *get* retroactively, so that she is considered divorced from the start of that day. The retroactive *get* eliminates the overlap.

The choice of "entering a *beit knesset*" as the trigger is, as the *Gemara* implicitly acknowledges, a somewhat arbitrary substitute for what one would really want to say, which is "if you die" — a condition that cannot be attached to a *get* because of the *kerisut* principle. Some other observable act must be designated instead, one the *kohen gadol* can choose to perform or withhold as circumstances require.

This entire discussion is, as *Rashi* cautioned, more a framework for thinking through the problem than a fully worked-out practical solution. Each step clears one obstacle while leaving others unaddressed, and the *Gemara* is transparent that many objections could be raised that it does not stop to answer.

### Rav Ashi

*Rav Ashi* — and some say *Rav Avira* — now raises a fundamental challenge to the premise that drove the entire discussion. The *Gemara* assumed throughout that the word *bayit* in the verse *ve'chiper ba'ado uva'ad beito* must refer to a single wife, making it impossible for the *kohen gadol* to have two wives simultaneously on Yom Kippur. But does *bayit* really carry this restriction elsewhere in *halacha*?

*Rav Ashi* points to *yibbum*: *shtei yevamot ha'ba'ot mi'bayit echad* — the scenario of two wives from one household is the first *mishnah* of Masechet Yevamot and forms the basis of the entire tractate. The verse governing *yibbum* states *asher lo yivneh et beit achiv* — "that he not build his brother's *bayit*" — yet we never restrict *yibbum* to a man who had only one wife. If *bayit* means "one wife," all of *Yevamot* would be undermined. The *Gemara* responds that *yevimto yevimto* — the word "*yevimto*," his sister-in-law, is written in a form that is understood to include even multiple wives in the obligation of *yibbum*.

*Ravina* — and some say *Rav Shravya* — presses further: if *bayit* implies *nisu'in* rather than *kiddushin*, then *yibbum* should not apply to an *arusah*, a betrothed woman with whom *nisu'in* has not yet taken place. Yet *halacha* clearly holds that an *arusah* is subject to *yibbum*. The *Gemara* answers from the word *ha'chutzah* in the *yibbum* passage, which implies a woman still "outside" her husband's house — i.e., one with whom *nisu'in* has not yet occurred — is nonetheless included in the *parasha* of *yibbum*.

*Rav Ashi*'s challenge is a serious one: the entire edifice of the *Gemara*'s discussion of conditional *gittin* was built on the premise that *beito* means one wife and that *nisu'in* is required. Both premises require special *derashot* to be sustained when tested against other areas of *halacha*. This does not invalidate the readings, but it shows that the *Gemara* is aware of the tension and addresses it directly.

---

## Onen Status

### Normal Kohen

The *Gemara* introduces a new *baraita*: *Kohen Gadol makriv onen v'eino ochel* — a *kohen gadol* brings offerings even when he is an *onen*, an immediate mourner in the period between a relative's death and burial, but he does not eat from the *korbanot* during that period. This ruling contrasts with the rule for an ordinary *kohen*, who may not perform the *avoda* at all while an *onen*. For a *kohen hedyot*, doing the *avoda* as an *onen* would invalidate the service entirely.

### Kohen Gadol Exception

The basis for the *kohen gadol*'s exception is the verse *u'min ha'Mikdash lo yeitzei* — "and from the *Mikdash* he shall not go out" — which applies in the context of bereavement. The *kohen gadol* is commanded to remain at his post even when a close relative has died. He therefore continues the *avoda* in a state of *aninut*. However, his exemption extends only to the performance of the service itself; he remains prohibited from eating *korbanot* while an *onen*, since the permission flows from the specific requirement that he not abandon his post, not from any broader suspension of *aninut* status.

*Rava* comments on the phrase *kol ha'yom* — "the whole day" — used by *Rabbi Yehuda* in this connection, understanding it initially to mean that we would even compel the *kohen gadol* to leave his home during a bereavement in order to perform the *avoda*. *Abaye* challenges this: *Rabbi Yehuda* himself rules, in the case of an ordinary *kohen* who was in the middle of the *avoda* when he learned that a relative had died, that he must stop immediately — *maniach avodato v'yotzei*. If *Rabbi Yehuda* holds so stringently about the *aninut* invalidating an ordinary *kohen*'s *avoda*, how could he simultaneously hold that for the *kohen gadol* we drag him out of his house and make him perform the *avoda* as an *onen*?

### Gezeira Shema

*Rava* therefore revises his interpretation of *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position. When *Rabbi Yehuda* says *kol ha'yom*, he does not mean we compel the *kohen gadol* to perform the *avoda*; rather, he means the opposite. He holds that *rabbinically*, the *kohen gadol* should not perform the *avoda* during the entire day of the death, even though biblically he is permitted and even required to do so. The concern is *gezeira shema yokhal* — a rabbinic precautionary measure lest he come to eat from the *korbanot*. Since performing the *avoda* and eating from the *korbanot* are normally coupled activities, there is a concern that if he performs the *avoda* as an *onen* he might come to eat as well, which would be prohibited. At night, however, *Rabbi Yehuda* agrees he may perform the *avoda*, because biblical *aninut* applies only during the day of death; at night, even if rabbinical *aninut* applies, eating from *korbanot* consumed at night would not constitute a biblical violation. Therefore the rabbinic concern is limited to the daytime.

### Tomorrow's Topic

The connection of this *baraita* to the larger discussion of Yom Kippur will be taken up in the next session. The scenario the *Gemara* is building toward is this: if the *kohen gadol*'s wife dies during the Yom Kippur *avoda* — the very contingency that generated the entire discussion of conditional *gittin* and backup wives — he becomes an *onen* at that moment. Can he continue the *avoda*? Biblically, as established, a *kohen gadol* continues his service even as an *onen*, grounded in *u'min ha'Mikdash lo yeitzei*. But does *Rabbi Yehuda*'s rabbinic concern apply here as well, given the context of Yom Kippur? That question, and its implications for the entire structure of the Yom Kippur service, will be the focus of the next daf.

---

---

# Yoma 14

## Backup Wife & Onen

### Backup Wife Review

The daf opens by returning to the conclusions reached in the previous session regarding how the *kohen gadol* could maintain his marital status in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda — always married to exactly one wife at precisely the right moment. The *gemara* had understood that the word *beito* requires not merely *kiddushin* but full *nissuim*, an actual lived reality of having established a household together. Had *kiddushin* alone sufficed, the solution would have been straightforward: one could simply stipulate that the *kiddushin* with the second wife takes effect the moment the first wife dies. But *nissuim* cannot be activated by a retroactive stipulation in that manner, since it reflects an existing domestic reality rather than a formal legal status. The *gemara* was therefore forced to construct a more complicated framework — not one in which the marriage takes effect upon some future event, but one in which a *get* takes effect retroactively.

This second complication was compounded by the *gemara*'s further assumption that the *kohen gadol* must be married to precisely one wife, no more and no fewer. That assumption was challenged from the case of *yibum*, where the word *bayis* is used and the obligation applies even with two wives and even after mere *erusin* before *nissuim*. Both of the *gemara*'s working assumptions were thus called into question by the *yibum* parallel, yet the *gemara* ultimately held its position and concluded that the *kohen gadol* would need to be married to two wives simultaneously, each of whom has received a *get* formulated under different conditional terms, arranged so that regardless of which wife dies, he will retroactively have been married only to the surviving one at any given moment. In this way, the *gemara* constructed what amounts to a mechanism for a non-married *agun* — a striking conceptual creation.

### Onen Question

With that background established, the *gemara* now raises a further question: if the *kohen gadol*'s wife dies, would he not become an *onen*? The relevant *halacha* is that a *kohen gadol*, unlike a *kohen hedyot*, is permitted to continue performing the *avodah* even as an *onen*, as the verse states *u-min ha-mikdash lo yeitzei v'lo yechalel et mikdash elohav* — he does not leave the *beit ha-mikdash* even when an immediate relative dies. He therefore continues performing the *avodah*. It should be noted that as an *onen* he cannot eat from the *korbanot*, but since it is Yom Kippur and no one eats in any case, this would seem to present no difficulty.

A parenthetical point is worth raising here. The simple reading of the *pesukim* actually does not list a *kohen gadol*'s wife among the relatives to whom he would become *tamei*. The Torah lists his father, mother, siblings — *le-aviv u-le-imo, le-achiv u-le-achoto* — but the plain sense of the text does not mention a wife. Indeed, regarding a *kohen hedyot*, the verse *lo yitama ba'al be-amav le-hachalo* was understood by some as indicating that a husband-*kohen* cannot become *tamei* for his wife at all. Nevertheless, *chazal* derive from the phrase *ki im le-she'ero ha-karov elav* — "his flesh that is close to him" — that *she'ero zo ishto*, his wife is included in this category. The *Rambam* understands the *kohen hedyot*'s obligation regarding his wife to be Rabbinic in origin, and even so the Rabbis deemed it serious enough to override the *tumah* restrictions of *kehuna*. The assumption throughout, then, is that a *kohen* — whether *gadol* or *hedyot* — is an *onen* upon the death of his wife.

### Gezeirah Challenge

The potential problem arises not from the *avodah* itself but from a ruling of Rabbi Yehuda. The *gemara* at the top of 14a states: *she-eino oved kol hayom* — according to Rabbi Yehuda, a *kohen gadol* who is an *onen* may not perform the *avodah* for the entirety of that day. The reason is *gezeirah shema yochal* — a Rabbinic precautionary decree lest, if permitted to serve, he come to inadvertently eat from the *korbanot*, which an *onen* is forbidden to do. This is, it must be acknowledged, a striking piece of reasoning, since it overrides the explicit biblical verse *min ha-mikdash lo yeitzei* by means of a Rabbinic concern about a secondary violation.

Rav Adda bar Ahava posed a challenge to Rava: does Rabbi Yehuda truly prohibit the *kohen gadol* from performing the *avodah* out of concern he might eat from the *korbanot*? After all, the *mishna* itself, in articulating Rabbi Yehuda's position, states *af isha acheret matkinim lo shema tamut ishto* — we set aside a backup wife for him lest his primary wife die. The implication is that if his wife does die, his backup wife takes her place and he continues performing the *avodah* — and we do not appear concerned that he will come to eat from the *korbanot* as an *onen*.

### Yom Kippur Exception

The response is direct: *hachi hashta*? The cases are not comparable. In the situation described in our *mishna*, the *kohen gadol* is serving on Yom Kippur — *keivan de-Yom Kippurim hu, de-kulei alma lo achli* — since it is Yom Kippur, no one eats at all. Under such circumstances, *hu nami lo ati le-meichal* — he too will not come to eat; the concern simply does not apply. On a normal day, however, *de-kulei alma achli* — everyone is eating — and the *kohen gadol* as an *onen* might inadvertently come to eat from the *korbanot* as well. The *gezeirah* was never extended to Yom Kippur, where the entire environment of fasting renders it inapplicable.

### Onen Resolved

The *gemara* then raises a question that might have occurred to anyone following the previous day's discussion. It asks: *midi de-aninut lav chala alei* — but in what sense is he even an *onen* to begin with? The entire elaborate construction of conditional *gittin* was designed precisely so that if his wife dies, she would be considered retroactively divorced from him at that moment. *Ve-ha migarsha* — she is already divorced from him! He therefore would have no *onen* status at all, since the woman who died was not, retroactively, his wife.

The *gemara* responds: *tirda de-libeih mi la mitrad* — true, technically he is not an *onen*, but he will surely be emotionally distracted by his wife's death. This answer is, however, somewhat difficult to follow. Even granting that Rabbi Yehuda's original *gezeirah* was motivated by a concern lest he eat, it is not obvious why mere emotional distraction should generate the same concern. The apparent incompleteness of this resolution suggests that the question about *aninut* may have been raised from a position that did not accept the entire framework of conditional *gittin* and retroactive divorce developed in the previous *sugya*, and may have been operating with a different understanding of how the backup wife arrangement would function. In any case, the *gemara* brackets the retroactive-divorce solution in order to pursue the *aninut* question, and with this, the discussion of the first *mishna* — concerning the seven-day separation, the backup *kohen*, and the backup wife — is concluded.

---

## Seven-Day Preparation

### Seven Days Start

The *gemara* now moves to a new *mishna*, which addresses the substance of the *kohen gadol*'s seven-day stay in the *beit ha-mikdash* and what he would actually do during that time. The opening line of the *mishna* is: *kol shivat hayamim* — all seven days, referring to the period during which he is sequestered in the *beit ha-mikdash* before Yom Kippur.

### Daily Services

The *mishna* specifies the *avodot* the *kohen gadol* performs during these seven days. *Hu zorek et hadam* — he performs the *zerikat hadam* for the *tamid*, the daily offering. *U-maktir et haktoret* — he offers the *ketoret*, which was brought in two installments, half in the morning and half in the afternoon. *U-meitiv et haneirot* — he also tends to the *menorah*, cleaning out the wicks and lamps in the morning, since the cleaning takes place in the morning and the lighting in the evening.

### Service Scope

It is worth pausing to observe what the *mishna* is describing. The *zerikat hadam* and *ketoret* are directly relevant to the Yom Kippur *avodah*, though on Yom Kippur the *ketoret* will be offered in the *kodesh ha-kodashim* rather than on the outer *mizbeiach ha-chitzon*. The *meitiv et haneirot*, however, is not something specifically associated with the Yom Kippur *avodah* at all. This suggests that the seven-day period is not simply a rehearsal of Yom Kippur-specific rituals but rather a full immersion in the *avodah* of the *beit ha-mikdash* generally — a comprehensive bootcamp to get the *kohen gadol* acclimated to everything that takes place in the *mikdash*. This makes particular sense given that in the later period the position of *kohen gadol* was often purchased, meaning the officiant might have little prior experience performing the *avodah*. The parallel to the *miluim* — the seven-day inauguration period during which the *kohanim* were first initiated into their service in the *mishkan* — is apt. The seven-day structure serves as both practical preparation and a reenactment of that inaugural model.

The *mishna* further specifies *u-makriv et ha-rosh ve-ha-regel* — he would offer the head and the first leg of the *tamid* lamb onto the ramp of the *mizbeiach*, as part of the process by which the dismembered limbs were brought up in stages. Notably, he does not perform the *shechita* — which can be performed even by a non-*kohen* — but does perform the key *avodot* that constitute the heart of the *tamid* service.

There is something worth noting in the overall character of these seven days. The *gemara* elsewhere takes care to underscore that even tasks that might seem mundane, such as the *terumat ha-deshen* — the removal of ashes from the altar — carry genuine *avodah* significance and ought not be regarded as beneath the dignity of the service. There is no sense in the *gemara* that any of these daily *avodot* are peripheral. On the contrary, they represent the full range of what it means to serve in the *beit ha-mikdash*.

### Year-Round Rights

As for the rest of the year, the *mishna* states: *im ratzah le-hakriv makriv* — if the *kohen gadol* wishes to offer a *korban* on any given day, he may do so. He holds no fixed assignment outside the seven preparatory days and Yom Kippur itself, but should he appear on any ordinary day he retains the prerogative to perform whatever *avodah* he chooses. *She-kohen gadol makriv chelek be-rosh ve-notel chelek be-rosh* — the *kohen gadol* may offer first and receives the first portion. He may, in effect, step to the front of any line. Whether with respect to the performance of the *avodah* or the apportionment of the *korban*'s meat, the *kohen gadol* exercises a standing right of precedence on any day of the year he chooses to exercise it.

---

## Parah Adumah & Tumah

### Mishnah Authorship

The *gemara* now raises a question about the authorship of our *mishna*. *Amar Rav Chisda: d'lo ke-Rabbi Akiva* — Rav Chisda states that the *mishna* cannot be following the position of Rabbi Akiva. This requires explanation, since a *baraisa* taught earlier (not in our *mishna* but in a *baraisa* associated with the preceding discussion) established that during the seven days, the ashes of the *parah adumah* would be sprinkled upon the *kohen gadol* each day. The question is how this practice interacts with Rabbi Akiva's distinctive and radical position concerning the effect of the *parah adumah*.

### Rabbi Akiva Paradox

Rabbi Akiva's position is stated clearly: *tahor she-nafal alav haza'ah, tamei* — if the waters of the *parah adumah* are sprinkled upon a person who is already *tahor*, he becomes *tamei*. This is the full extension of the paradoxical logic inherent in the *parah adumah*: it makes *tamei* people *tahor*, and makes *tahor* people *tamei*. One might have assumed that this paradox — while true of those who handle or carry the ashes — does not extend to the person upon whom the sprinkling is performed. The plain sense of the Torah's description of the *parah adumah* says nothing about the sprinkled-upon *tahor* person becoming *tamei*; presumably, if you are already *tahor*, being sprinkled upon changes nothing for you. But Rabbi Akiva holds that the reversal is absolute and applies in both directions.

If Rabbi Akiva is correct, a severe practical problem emerges for the seven-day preparation period. Each day, ashes are sprinkled upon the *kohen gadol* to ensure his *tahara*. But if on any given day he happens to already be *tahor*, the sprinkling would render him *tamei* — not with a seven-day *tumah* requiring a new count, since this form of *tumah* only lasts until immersion and nightfall, but *tamei* nonetheless for the remainder of that day. The consequence would be that he cannot perform the *avodah* on any of the seven days, since each day's sprinkling might have rendered him *tamei*. The *mishna*, which envisions him performing the daily *avodot* throughout the seven-day period, therefore cannot accord with Rabbi Akiva's view.

The *baraisa* on which this discussion turns states: *veyizah ha-tahor al ha-tamei* — the *tahor* person sprinkles upon the *tamei*. *Al ha-tamei tahor* — if sprinkled upon the *tamei* person, the result is that the *tamei* person becomes *tahor*. *Ve-al ha-tahor* — and if upon a *tahor* person — *tamei* — he becomes *tamei*. This is the position of Rabbi Akiva.

The Sages, however, dispute this. Their position is: *ein ha-devarim ha-lalu amurim ela be-davar ha-mekabel tumah* — the operative rule of *al ha-tamei* is not about the *status* of the person (whether currently *tamei* or *tahor*), but rather about whether the thing being sprinkled upon is *capable* of receiving *tumah* at all. A valid sprinkling requires that the object sprinkled be of a type susceptible to *tumah*. The teaching addresses the case of one who intended to sprinkle upon an animal — which cannot become *tamei* — but whose sprinkling landed on a person, or vice versa. According to Rashi, what defines the act is not the intent but what actually occurred. If the sprinkling in fact landed on a person (who can become *tamei*), it constitutes a valid act of sprinkling and any water remaining on the hyssop may still be used. If it landed on an animal (which cannot become *tamei*), the act of sprinkling was invalid and the remaining water on the hyssop is disqualified.

### Rabbis Limit Paradox

The Rabbis, then, are not endorsing Rabbi Akiva's radical extension of the paradox; they are limiting it. They insist that the *parah adumah*'s paradoxical reversal is to be constrained, not amplified. To this, Rabbi Akiva essentially replies: you are correct that it is logically strange, but that is precisely the point. *Amarti echkama ve-hi rechoka mimeni* — Shlomo HaMelech declared that he sought wisdom and found it distant from him; the *parah adumah* represents that category of divine statute that resists rational comprehension. The reversal is real, it is absolute, and it applies even to the *tahor* person who is sprinkled upon.

The *gemara* then asks: does the Rabbinic position truly hold that the one who performs the sprinkling — the *mazeh* — is *tahor*? The verse states explicitly: *u-mazeh mei ha-niddah yechabes bgadav ve-ha-nogea be-mei ha-niddah yitma ad ha-arev* — the one who sprinkles must launder his garments and becomes *tamei*, and the one who touches the water also becomes *tamei*. Not only does the Torah make the *mazeh tamei*, it imposes upon him the additional requirement of laundering his garments — a stringency beyond what applies to the *nogea*, who merely touches the water. Two distinct categories are thus explicitly delineated, both *tamei*, with the *mazeh* being treated more stringently than the *nogea*. How then can the Rabbis claim the *mazeh* is *tahor*?

### Sprinkling Terms

The *gemara* explores this through a careful analysis of the operative terms in the Torah's description. The initial attempt to reinterpret *mazeh* as referring to the *nogea* is immediately rejected: the *pasuk* mentions *both* the *mazeh* and the *nogea* in the same verse as distinct individuals with different *halachot*, so they plainly cannot be identical. The *mazeh* requires laundering of garments; the *nogea* does not. These are clearly two separate categories.

The *gemara* therefore offers an alternative reinterpretation: perhaps *mazeh* in the verse does not refer to the person actually performing the sprinkling but to the person who *carries* the water — the *nosei*. Let the Torah have simply written *nosei* if that is what it meant; why write *mazeh*? The answer: the word *mazeh* teaches that one becomes *tamei* only if one carries a quantity sufficient for performing the *haza'ah*, i.e., the minimum required for a valid sprinkling.

This raises a further question: this resolution is workable according to the opinion that a *haza'ah* requires a minimum *shiur* of water. But according to the opinion that *haza'ah ein tzericha shiur* — that there is no minimum quantity and even the tiniest drop of water is sufficient to render a *tamei* person *tahor* — what does the word *mazeh* add?

### Mazeh & Mazin Tahor

The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between the quantity required at the point of contact and the quantity required in the vessel. Even according to the position that no minimum amount of water need actually land upon the person receiving the sprinkling — *hani mili agava de-gavra*, there is no minimum that need hit the recipient — there is nonetheless a minimum quantity required in the vessel itself at the outset of the act. *Aval be-mane tzericha shiur* — in the vessel, a minimum is needed. The *mishna* specifies this practically: the water must be sufficient that one can dip the heads of the hyssop stalks and produce a sprinkling. If there is so little water that immersing the hyssop absorbs it entirely and no sprinkling can take place, the act cannot be performed. This minimum, while practically motivated, functions as a formal requirement.

The Rabbinic position thus emerges as follows: the *mazeh* in the verse refers not to the sprinkler himself but to the *nosei*, the one who carries the water without being engaged in the act of sprinkling. The word *mazeh* establishes that one is *tamei* from carrying only if carrying the requisite minimum. The critical principle the Rabbis assert is: *ha-mazeh ve-ha-mazin alav tahor* — both the one who performs the sprinkling and the one upon whom the sprinkling is performed remain *tahor*, regardless of whether they begin as *tahor* or *tamei*. The *nogea*, who merely touches the water without being part of the sprinkling act, becomes *tamei*. The Rabbis thus draw the sharpest possible contrast with Rabbi Akiva: where Rabbi Akiva amplifies the paradox of the *parah adumah* to its maximum reach, the Rabbis constrain it, insisting that those directly engaged in the legitimate process of *haza'ah* are entirely shielded from its paradoxical reversal.

### Sunset Sprinkling

Returning to the original question about the *kohen gadol*'s seven-day preparation, Rav Chisda had said the *mishna* cannot accord with Rabbi Akiva. Abaye responds: *afilu teima Rabbi Akiva* — one can maintain the *mishna* even according to Rabbi Akiva, and it is simply a matter of scheduling. The *kohen gadol* performs the *avodah* throughout the entire day, *u-fanya* — and toward evening, just before sunset, one sprinkles upon him. He then immerses in the *mikvah*, and *ve-avid ha-erev shemesh* — nightfall arrives and he is fully *tahor*. Even if the sprinkling rendered him *tamei* in those final minutes before sunset, the immersion and the arrival of nightfall resolve his status before he needs to perform any further *avodah* the next morning. The entire problem, according to Abaye, is merely a logistical one of timing.

It is notable that the *gemara* does not entertain the possibility of simply omitting the daily sprinkling, which would sidestep the problem entirely. The practice of daily *haza'ah* appears to be a settled consensus — though as was noted in an earlier passage, there is an opinion that it was performed only on the third and seventh days rather than every day, which would at least have reduced the tension.

---

## Service Order Debate

### Mishnah Order

With the *parah adumah* discussion concluded, the *gemara* turns to the specific *avodot* enumerated in the *mishna* and examines their order. The *mishna* lists *u-maktir et ha-ketoret u-meitiv et ha-neirot* — the *kohen gadol* first offers the *ketoret* and then tends to the *neirot*. The *gemara* notes: *alma, ketoret be-reisha ve-hadar neirot* — it is apparent from our *mishna* that in the order of the morning *avodot* in the *beit ha-mikdash*, the *ketoret* comes first and the *neirot* afterward.

### Tamid Order

The *gemara* immediately juxtaposes this with a passage from *masechet Tamid*, which presents the order of the daily service through a sequence of three separate *mishnayot*, each describing the duties of a different *kohen*: first, the one who was assigned the cleaning of the inner *mizbeiach*; then the one who was assigned the *menorah*; and only thereafter the one who was assigned the *ketoret*. The sequence is thus: inner *mizbeiach*, *menorah*, *ketoret* — with the *menorah* clearly preceding the *ketoret*, the inverse of our *mishna*'s order.

### Different Authors

To resolve this apparent contradiction, Rav Huna suggests that *masechet Tamid* was authored by Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah. This is a surprising name to identify as the author of an entire tractate, but the reasoning follows. The *gemara* then challenges this attribution: *ve-ha ipcha shemia lan* — in fact, the opposite is the case, for Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah is demonstrably a *contrary* voice within *masechet Tamid*, not its author. The evidence appears in a *baraisa* that presents the standard ruling regarding the *zerikat ha-dam* of the *tamid*: at the northeast corner, one throw of blood covers the north and east sides; at the southwest corner, one throw covers the south and west sides — two throws that address all four corners. The *baraisa* then records that *Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah meshane ba-Tamid* — Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah treats the *tamid* differently. He agrees about the northeast corner, but holds that at the southwest corner one performs two separate applications rather than a single throw: first the west, then the south. He thus explicitly diverges from the *stam* of *masechet Tamid*. One cannot therefore identify him as its author; he is its dissenting voice.

Rabbi Yochanan therefore reformulates the resolution: *man tana seder Yoma Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah hu* — it is the *seder* of *Yoma* that was authored by Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah, not *Tamid*. The two tractates simply reflect different *tannaitic* opinions: the author of *Tamid* holds that the *menorah* precedes the *ketoret*; Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah, author of *Yoma*, holds that the *ketoret* precedes the *menorah*. Different authors, different rulings, no contradiction.

The *gemara*, however, is not satisfied. *U-remi seder Yoma a-seder Yoma* — there is a contradiction *within* the *mishna* of *Yoma* itself. A later *mishna* in our tractate discusses the four daily lotteries (*paysaot*) that determined which *kohanim* performed which *avodot*. The second lottery assigned specific tasks in sequence: *shechitah*, *zrikah*, cleaning of the inner *mizbeiach*, cleaning of the *menorah*, bringing the limbs of the *tamid* to the ramp. The third lottery then announced: *chadashim la-ketoret bo'u ve-hapisu* — anyone who has never yet had the privilege of offering the *ketoret* should come and participate in this lottery, since the *ketoret* was considered a *segulah* for wealth, and to prevent the same *kohen* from monopolizing this privilege, only first-time participants were eligible. The clear implication of this sequence is that the *menorah* comes before the *ketoret*, aligning with *masechet Tamid* — yet directly contradicting the earlier *mishna* of *Yoma* that placed the *ketoret* first.

### Abaye's Split

Abaye resolves the internal contradiction in *Yoma* with a solution that reframes the entire discussion: *kan be-tivat shtei neirot, kan be-tivat chamesh neirot* — the different *mishnayot* are not in fact describing different orderings of the same act, because the tending of the *menorah* was not performed as a single continuous act. It was divided into two stages: five lamps first, then two lamps afterward. When one *mishna* says the *menorah* comes before the *ketoret*, it refers to the first five lamps. When another says the *ketoret* comes before the *menorah*, it refers to the final two lamps. The *ketoret* was offered in between the two parts of the *menorah* service.

This elegant solution means that both statements are simultaneously correct: the *menorah* (in its first installment of five) *does* precede the *ketoret*, and the *ketoret* *does* precede the *menorah* (in its final installment of two). The apparent contradiction dissolves once the *menorah* service is understood as a split act rather than a unified one.

### Blood vs Incense

The *gemara* then notes a complication. Abaye himself, in a separate context, was known to teach the order of the morning *avodah* from a received tradition — *mesader maaracha mishmeih de-gemara* — and in that tradition it was the *dam ha-tamid*, the blood of the daily offering, that divided the two parts of the *menorah* service, not the *ketoret*. If Abaye's own tradition placed the *dam* as the divider, how can his resolution of the contradiction rest on the *ketoret* being the divider?

### What Divides Lamps

The response is that this, too, is a *tannaitic* dispute: *ha de-Abba Shaul, ha de-Rabbanan* — one position reflects the view of Abba Shaul, the other the view of the Rabbis. The *baraisa* makes this explicit: *lo yeitiv et ha-neiros ve-achar kach yaktir, ella yaktir ve-achar kach yeitiv* — one should not complete the *tivat ha-neirot* in full and *then* offer the *ketoret*; rather, one should offer the *ketoret* and then complete the *menorah*. This is the Rabbinic position, preserving Abaye's resolution: the *ketoret* interrupts the two parts of the *menorah*, with five lamps first, then *ketoret*, then two lamps. Abaye's own tradition about the *dam* as the divider follows Abba Shaul.

### Verse Interpretation

Abba Shaul's position is: *meitiv ve-achar kach maktir* — one completes the *menorah* fully and only then offers the *ketoret*. His reasoning derives from the verse: *ba-boker ba-boker be-heitivo et ha-neirot yaktirena* — in the morning, when he tends the lamps, he shall burn the *ketoret*. Abba Shaul reads this sequentially: first complete the *neirot* in their entirety, and *then* burn the *ketoret*. If the *menorah* must be divided at all, the interruption for Abba Shaul is the *dam ha-tamid*, not the *ketoret*, with the *ketoret* coming only after the *menorah* is finished.

The Rabbis read the same verse differently: *be-idan ha-tava tehei haktarat ketoret* — the phrase *be-heitivo et ha-neirot yaktirena* does not mean "after completing the lamps, then burn the *ketoret*," but rather "during the period of tending the lamps, burn the *ketoret*." The *ketoret* is thus offered in the *midst* of the *menorah* service, not after it. This is the reading that supports Abaye's resolution of the contradiction, and the debate between Abba Shaul and the Rabbis — over which act interrupts the two halves of the *menorah*, and over how to read the verse — will continue into the next session.

# Yoma 16

## Ketoret & Nerot Order

### Ketoret/Nerot Sequence

The *sugya* we enter today picks up in the middle of daf 16, and it is worth pausing to recall where we have been. The animating question of the previous discussion was a seeming contradiction in the order of two daily *avodot*: the burning of the *ketoret* and the kindling of the *nerot*. Our *mishnah* described the *kohen gadol* performing the *ketoret* and then the *nerot*, but this appears to reverse the standard order found elsewhere, where the *nerot* precede the *ketoret*. The *gemara*'s principal resolution was that the *nerot* were not performed as a single unit. Rather, five lamps were cleaned in the early morning, followed by the *ketoret*, and then the remaining two lamps were kindled. *Mishnayot* that list *ketoret* before *nerot* refer to the five-cleaning phase followed by the *ketoret*, while those listing *ketoret* and then *nerot* refer to the *ketoret* followed by the final two. That was the core answer.

### Tamid vs. Yoma Authors

Along the way, however, the *gemara* had entertained another approach: the apparent contradiction might simply reflect a dispute between *tannaim*, since the *mishnayot* in *Masechet Tamid* were composed by a different author than those in *Masechet Yoma*. This is not unusual; the *gemara* frequently resolves contradictions between tractates by attributing them to different authorities. What was striking about this particular answer was its ambition — it did not merely assign one discrete ruling to a different *tanna*, but rather attributed the entirety of *Masechet Tamid* to a single individual.

### Rabbi Shimon ben Meshulma

That individual was the relatively obscure *tanna* Rabbi Shimon ben Meshulma, whose name surfaced in a *braita* in connection with matters of *avodah*. The structure of the argument — a contradiction touching on Temple service, resolved by ascribing an entire *masechet* to one *tanna* — now serves as the template for the *sugya* we are entering.

## Shechita Location Contra…

### Two Chamber Locations

The new *sugya* is only formally connected to *Yoma*; it is not about *Yom Kippur* or the daily *avodah* in a direct sense. The connection is structural: just as we resolved the *ketoret*/*nerot* tension by assigning *Masechet Tamid* to a single author, the *gemara* now applies the same analytical move to a contradiction between *Masechet Tamid* and *Masechet Middot*. The contradiction concerns the location of the *shechita* chamber within the *beit hamoked* — that large hall where fires were kept burning so that priests who had immersed could warm themselves. *Masechet Tamid* mentions the chamber used for slaughtering *korbanot* in one location within the *beit hamoked*, while another *mishnah* in *Tamid* places it in a different chamber entirely.

### Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov…

The *gemara*'s resolution is to ascribe all of the *mishnayot* of both *Masechet Tamid* and *Masechet Middot* to a single *tanna*: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

### Eliezer's Forgetfulness

The proof for this attribution is a *mishnah* in *Middot* where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is enumerating the various chambers and their uses, and at a certain point he says simply: I have forgotten what this chamber was used for. One might ask why such an admission is significant. The answer is that it is only remarkable if Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov was himself the *stam* — the anonymous voice — of those *mishnayot*. If he were merely a *tanna* being cited, there would be no reason for him to inventory the rooms and confess ignorance about one of them. His acknowledgment of forgetting functions as an implicit signature: he is speaking in the role of author, cataloguing what he knows and flagging where his knowledge fails. That is the first proof that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is the author of *Masechet Middot*.

## Eastern Wall & Sightline

### High Walls Exception

The *gemara* now adduces a second, more elaborate proof from another *mishnah* in *Middot*. That *mishnah* states: *kol hakotalim she'hayu sham hayu gevohim* — all the walls in the *beit hamikdash* were very high, *chutz mikotel mizrachi* — except for the eastern wall. The reason given is that the *kohen* who burns the *parah* stands on *Har HaMishcha* and must be able to align his vision with the opening of the *heichal* at the moment of sprinkling the blood.

### Priest's Position

This requires some unpacking. The *Torah* commands *vehiza el nochach pnei Ohel Moed* — he must sprinkle toward, and in the direction of, the opening of the *Ohel Moed*. The *halachic* understanding is not merely that he faces the general direction of the *mikdash*, but that he must actually have a direct line of sight to the doorway of the *heichal* itself — the *pnei Ohel Moed* of the *Torah* being identified with that opening. The *kohen* stands on *Har HaMishcha* — the Mount of Olives — to the east, and must look westward, straight through the succession of gates, all the way to the *heichal* door.

### Temple Layout Diagram

To appreciate the geometric challenge this poses, one must picture the layout. To the east is *Har HaMishcha*. Further west is *Har HaBayit* with the *beit hamikdash* compound. Looking from east to west from *Har HaMishcha*, one would first encounter the outer retaining wall with its eastern gate, then the space of the *soreg* and *cheil* before the *ezrat nashim*, then the *ezrat nashim* itself with its gate, then the gate of *Shaar Nikanor* leading into the *ezrat yisrael*, then the open courtyard with the *mizbeach*, and finally the *ulam* — the antechamber — and the *heichal* beyond it. All of these gates happen to be perfectly aligned along the east-west axis, so that if everything were on a single level and the *kohen* were looking straight ahead, he could in principle see from *Har HaMishcha* all the way through to the *heichal* door.

The complication is that the terrain is not level. The *har habayit* rises as one moves westward, and rather than one continuous incline, the layout consists of a series of flat terraces separated by steps. One stands on a flat surface, climbs a set of steps, stands on the next flat surface, climbs again, and so on. The effect, viewed from the side, is a staircase of platforms: *ezrat nashim*, a rise, *ezrat yisrael*, a rise, the area of the *mizbeach*, a rise, and then the *ulam* and *heichal*. The challenge for the *kohen* standing on *Har HaMishcha* is this: if he is looking in a perfectly horizontal line — and the assumption throughout this discussion is that he is neither looking upward nor downward, but straight ahead — can his line of sight actually reach the *heichal* doorway? Or is it blocked by the accumulated rises of the terrain?

### Height Calculation

The *gemara* will now work through the arithmetic of those rises carefully. The height differential between the outer wall and the floor of the *heichal* is the key datum. If the total rise from the *kohen*'s line of sight at the outer wall to the floor of the *heichal* is less than twenty *amot*, then, since all doorways were twenty *amot* tall, some portion of the *heichal* doorway would remain visible even looking perfectly straight. If the rise equals or exceeds twenty *amot*, nothing of the doorway would be visible, and one would need either to stand higher or to have a lower outer wall.

## Steps & Rises Detail

### Soreg to Ezrat Nashim

The *gemara* assembles the relevant measurements from *mishnayot* in *Middot*. From the *soreg* — the latticework fence that marked the boundary before the *ezrat nashim* — to the *ezrat nashim* itself, there were twelve steps. Each step was half an *amah* in height and half an *amah* in depth. Twelve steps at half an *amah* each yields a rise of six *amot*. So from the level of the *soreg* — and the outer eastern wall is in this vicinity, before the *ezrat nashim* — one has already climbed six *amot* by the time one reaches the *ezrat nashim*.

### Nashim to Yisrael Steps

From the *ezrat nashim* to the *ezrat yisrael*, there were fifteen steps, each again half an *amah* tall. Fifteen times a half is seven and a half *amot*. These are the famous fifteen *ma'alot* associated with the fifteen *Shir HaMa'alot* psalms, which the Levites would chant upon them. So adding this rise to the previous: six *amot* from the outer wall to the *ezrat nashim*, plus seven and a half *amot* from the *ezrat nashim* to the *ezrat yisrael*, gives a cumulative rise of thirteen and a half *amot*.

### Mizbeach to Ulam

Finally, from the area beyond the *mizbeach* — moving through the *ezrat kohanim* — to the *ulam*, there were another twelve steps, each again half an *amah* tall, for a further rise of six *amot*. Adding six to thirteen and a half gives a total rise of nineteen and a half *amot* from the level of the outer eastern wall to the floor of the *ulam* and *heichal*. Since the doorways were all twenty *amot* tall, a *kohen* looking in a perfectly straight horizontal line from outside the eastern wall would, in theory, just barely be able to see the bottom half-*amah* of the *heichal* doorway — the threshold itself would be just at or barely above his line of sight.

## Low Wall Necessity

### Barely Sufficient Height

This calculation creates an apparent difficulty for the passage we are analyzing. The *mishnah* in *Middot* states that the eastern wall was specifically kept low so that the *kohen* on *Har HaMishcha* could see the *heichal* opening. But if the total accumulated rise is only nineteen and a half *amot* and the doorways are twenty *amot* tall, then even with a wall of normal height, he ought to be able to see at least the bottom half-*amah* of the opening. Why, then, was a specially low wall necessary?

## Middot Attribution P (II)

### Challenge to Rabbanan

This is precisely the *gemara*'s logical challenge. If *Masechet Middot* follows the view of the *rabbanan* — the majority opinion that does not introduce any additional rise before the *ulam* — then the nineteen-and-a-half-*amah* calculation is complete, and the bottom half-*amah* of the *heichal* doorway remains visible. In that case, the *kohen* on *Har HaMishcha* could manage a direct sightline without any special accommodation. Why, then, would the *mishnah* in *Middot* bother specifying that the eastern wall had to be low? The explicit statement that the wall was kept low implies that without this concession, visibility would have been impossible — but according to the *rabbanan*'s dimensions, visibility is achievable, barely. The special low wall is therefore unexplained if *Middot* follows the *rabbanan*.

## Low Wall Necessity (II)

### Eliezer's Extra Rise

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, however, introduces an additional element that changes the calculation. He states: *ma'alah haysa sham* — there was a rise in the area before the *ulam*, one *amah* tall — *ve-duchan nesuna lah*, and upon it was set a platform — *u'vo shalosh ma'alot shel chatzi chatzi amah* — with three steps, each half an *amah*. This was the *duchan* where the Levites would stand to sing. The critical point is the one-*amah* rise that precedes it. Before one even reaches the steps leading up to the *ulam*, there is an additional one-*amah* elevation. This means the total rise from the outer eastern wall to the floor of the *ulam* is not nineteen and a half *amot*, but at minimum twenty and a half *amot*.

### Extra Rise Blocks View

Once this additional *amah* is factored in, the arithmetic shifts decisively. The doorways are twenty *amot* tall. The total rise from the outer wall to the *heichal* floor is now at least twenty and a half *amot*. A *kohen* standing outside the eastern wall and looking in a perfectly straight, level line would find that even the very top of the *heichal* doorway is half an *amah* below his line of sight — the bottom of the opening is, in effect, underground from his perspective. No part of the *heichal* doorway is visible from a straight horizontal sightline at the level of the outer eastern wall.

Now the necessity of a low outer wall becomes clear. If the outer eastern wall were as high as the other walls, the *kohen* could only look through the gate at the top of that wall — which means his line of sight would be horizontal at the height of the gate. With a total rise of twenty and a half *amot* before the *heichal* floor, the *heichal* doorway would be entirely out of view. But if the eastern wall is low, the *kohen* can stand a bit higher relative to the wall — or rather, the low wall does not constrain his line of sight from above, and he can find an angle from *Har HaMishcha* that clears the wall and still reaches the *heichal* opening. The low wall is therefore directly necessitated by Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's additional *amah* of rise before the *ulam*.

## Middot Attribution P (II)

### Low Wall Proves Eliezer

The *gemara* states this explicitly: *ee amrat bishlama Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov hi* — if the *stam* author of *Middot* is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, then we understand perfectly why the eastern wall had to be low. The *heichal* opening is rendered invisible by the additional rise he describes, and only a low wall allows the *kohen* on *Har HaMishcha* to find a sightline. *Ela ee amrat rabbanan* — but if the author is the *rabbanan*, the total rise is only nineteen and a half *amot*, and the bottom half-*amah* of the door remains visible. There is then no compelling reason for the *mishnah* to mandate a low eastern wall. The very existence of that ruling in *Middot* is therefore proof — *shema mina* — that *Masechet Middot* is authored according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

## Rav Adda's Alternative

### Rabbi Yehuda Attribution

At this point, Rav Adda bar Ahava offers an alternative: *ha mani Rabbi Yehuda hi* — perhaps the *stam* of *Masechet Middot* follows the view of Rabbi Yehuda, not Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. Under this reading, Rabbi Yehuda would be the one who provides the reason why the eastern wall had to be low, and it would have nothing to do with an additional rise before the *ulam*.

### Mizbeach Centered Positi…

Rabbi Yehuda's relevant opinion is found in a *braita*: *hamizbe'ach memutza ve-omed be-emtza azara* — the *mizbeach* was positioned exactly at the midpoint of the *azarah*. This stands in contrast to the arrangement we may assume from other sources, where the *mizbeach* was somewhat off-center. Rabbi Yehuda insists it was precisely centered.

### Mizbeach Dimensions

The *braita* elaborates: the *mizbeach* was thirty-two *amot* wide. Ten *amot* of it were directly opposite the opening of the *heichal* — *esser amot keneged pitcho shel heichal* — with eleven *amot* extending to the north and eleven *amot* extending to the south. This, Rabbi Yehuda says, is how we know it was aligned precisely with the *heichal* and its walls. The *heichal* itself was twenty *amot* wide; its doorway was ten *amot* wide, with five *amot* of wall on each side, and the walls themselves were six *amot* thick. Eleven *amot* on each side of the central ten equals twenty-two *amot* total to the edge of the *mizbeach*, which corresponds to the doorway width plus the wall thickness on each side. The *mizbeach* was thus exactly in line — *mechuvon keneged heichal ve-kotlav* — with the *heichal* and its walls.

Now, if the *mizbeach* was exactly centered in the *azarah* north-to-south — and the *azarah*'s width was 135 *amot* — the midpoint would be at 67.5 *amot* from either wall. The *mizbeach*, being thirty-two *amot* wide, would therefore span from 51.5 *amot* to 83.5 *amot* from the southern wall — positioned symmetrically around the center.

Why does this matter for the *kohen* on *Har HaMishcha*? Because the *mizbeach* was nine *amot* tall. If the *kohen* is looking straight through the succession of eastern gates toward the *heichal*, and the *mizbeach* stands directly in his line of sight — centered precisely opposite the *heichal* doorway — then it constitutes a nine-*amah*-tall obstruction directly in his path. Even though the rise from the outer eastern wall to the floor of the *azarah* near the *mizbeach* is only about six *amot*, the *mizbeach* itself rises an additional nine *amot* above that floor, placing its top fifteen *amot* above the baseline. The *kohen*'s horizontal line of sight — aimed at the *heichal* doorway, which begins nineteen and a half *amot* above the baseline — would have to clear the *mizbeach*'s nine-*amah* summit. In fact, with the *mizbeach* centered directly in front of the *heichal*, the obstruction is unavoidable from a straight horizontal sightline at wall level. Hence, the eastern wall needed to be low: if it is low, the *kohen* can stand at a higher elevation on *Har HaMishcha*, adjust his line of sight upward enough to clear the *mizbeach*, and still see the *heichal* opening beyond it.

### Mizbeach Height Blocks V…

To be precise: a low wall does not resolve an obstruction by removing the obstruction itself. Rather, lowering the wall allows the *kohen* to stand higher in relation to the top of the wall, so that instead of being constrained to look through the gate opening at a fixed height, he can look from a slightly elevated vantage on *Har HaMishcha* and sight over both the outer wall and the *mizbeach* to the *heichal* beyond. If the outer wall were very high, the *kohen* would be forced to look at a very steep downward angle from whatever height on *Har HaMishcha* would allow him to see over it, and at that angle the *heichal* opening would not be directly in view. With a low wall, he can choose a gentler angle that clears the *mizbeach* and reaches the *heichal* door.

So according to Rav Adda bar Ahava's reading, the necessity of the low eastern wall is accounted for by Rabbi Yehuda's position that the *mizbeach* was centered — making it a direct visual obstruction — rather than by Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's additional *amah* of rise before the *ulam*.

## Refute Yehuda Attribution

### Mizbeach Not Centered

The *gemara* now challenges Rav Adda's proposal sharply. If *Masechet Middot* follows Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yehuda's defining claim is that the *mizbeach* was exactly centered in the *azarah*, then *Middot* itself should reflect this. But, the *gemara* says, the dimensional data recorded in *Masechet Middot* — when worked through carefully — shows that the *mizbeach* was *not* at the midpoint of the *azarah*. It was mostly in the south. And if *Middot* contradicts Rabbi Yehuda's very premise, *Middot* cannot be attributed to Rabbi Yehuda.

### Azarah Dimensions

The *gemara* cites the *mishnah* in *Middot*: *kol ha-azara hayta orech me'ah u-shemonim v-sheva al rochav me'ah u-sheloshim v-chamesh* — the entire *azarah* was 187 *amot* from east to west and 135 *amot* from north to south. For the east-to-west dimension of 187, the *mishnah* accounts for each component: 11 *amot* for the space where *Yisrael* could stand, 11 *amot* for the *kohanim*, 32 *amot* for the *mizbeach*, 22 *amot* for the space between the *ulam* and the *mizbeach*, 100 *amot* for the *heichal* with the *ulam*, and 11 *amot* behind the *beit hakapporet*. Adding these: 11 + 11 + 32 + 22 + 100 + 11 = 187. The east-to-west dimension is confirmed.

### North-South Measurements

Now the north-to-south dimension of 135 *amot* is broken down, and this is what concerns us. The *mishnah* enumerates: *hakevesh v'hamizbe'ach shishim u-shtayim* — the *kevesh* (the ramp leading up to the *mizbeach*) and the *mizbeach* together occupied sixty-two *amot*. The *mizbeach* itself was 32 by 32, and the *kevesh* was 32 *amot* long and 30 *amot* wide at the base, so together they span 62 *amot* in the north-to-south direction. Then: *min hamizbe'ach v'lataba'ot chet amot* — from the *mizbeach* to the *taba'ot* (the rings in which the animals' necks were placed for slaughter in the north) was eight *amot*. *Makom hataba'ot esrim v'arba* — the space of the rings themselves was twenty-four *amot*. *Min hataba'ot lashulchanot arba* — from the rings to the tables used for rinsing the innards was four *amot*. *Min hashulchanot lananasim arba* — from the tables to the *nanasim* (the pillar-posts with hooks for flaying the animals) was four *amot*. And *min hananasim lakotel* — from the *nanasim* to the wall — was eight *amot*.

### Mizbeach South Position

Tallying these figures: the *kevesh* and *mizbeach* account for 62 *amot*; to the rings, another 8, making 70; the rings themselves are 24, making 94; to the tables, another 4, making 98; to the *nanasim*, another 4, making 102; and to the wall, another 8, making 110. The *mishnah* does not explicitly state the span of the *nanasim* themselves or of the tables, though one of the large *Rashis* on this passage works through those figures. Accounting for the remaining space to reach 135 *amot*, and dividing it between the gap from the *kevesh* to the southern wall and the space of the *nanasim* — *Rashi* assumes an equal division, placing approximately ten and a half *amot* on each side — one arrives at the position of the *mizbeach* in the north-to-south axis.

If there are ten and a half *amot* between the southern wall and the start of the *kevesh* and *mizbeach*, and the *kevesh* and *mizbeach* span 62 *amot*, then the *mizbeach* extends from ten and a half *amot* from the southern wall to seventy-two and a half *amot* from the southern wall. The midpoint of 135 *amot* is 67.5 *amot*. The *mizbeach*'s center would therefore be at approximately 41.5 *amot* from the southern wall — which is not the midpoint of the *azarah* at all. The overwhelming majority of the *mizbeach* lies in the southern portion. *Ha rubo demizbe'ach bedarom kai* — most of the *mizbeach* is in the south.

### Final Eliezer Proof

The conclusion follows directly: *v'ei salka da'atach middot Rabbi Yehuda hi, mizbe'ach be'emtza azara mi meshkachat lah?* — if you think *Middot* follows Rabbi Yehuda, you cannot find the *mizbeach* at the center of the *azarah*. The data in *Middot* places it off-center, in the south. Rabbi Yehuda's central premise — *hamizbe'ach memutza ve-omed be-emtza azara* — is flatly incompatible with the dimensions recorded in *Middot* itself. Therefore, *Middot* cannot be authored according to Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Adda bar Ahava's alternative attribution fails.

The *gemara* therefore returns to its earlier conclusion: *ela lav shema mina Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov hi, shema mina* — you must conclude that *Masechet Middot* is authored according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. The need for a low eastern wall is explained by his additional *amah* of rise before the *ulam*, which pushed the total elevation above the twenty-*amah* height of the doorways and made a direct sightline impossible without the accommodation of a lower outer wall. This conclusion also coheres with the earlier proof from Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's confession of forgetfulness, which only makes sense if he was the *stam* voice of the *masechet*. With both proofs converging, and the alternative attribution to Rabbi Yehuda refuted by the *masechet*'s own dimensional data, the *gemara* is satisfied: the *stam* of *Masechet Middot* is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — and with that, the original contradiction between *Tamid* and *Middot* regarding the *shechita* chamber finds its resolution.

---

---

# Yoma 17

## Beit HaMoked Rooms

### Intro: Sheep Room

Today's daf is 17, and the *gemara* is in the middle of resolving a contradiction between *Middot* and *Tamid* concerning the locations of the various rooms within the *Beit HaMoked* and how they were used. The reason this discussion appears here at all follows the structure established earlier in the tractate: the *gemara* had already shown a contradiction between *Yoma* and *Tamid* regarding the order of the lighting of the *nerot* and the burning of the *ketoret*, and resolved that the *stam mishnayot* of *Tamid* have a different author than the *stam mishnayot* of *Yoma*. The same methodology is now applied to *Middot* and *Tamid*.

The specific contradiction is this: the *mishna* in *Tamid* states that *lishkat telayim hayta b'miktzoa tzafonit ma'aravit* — the chamber used for the sheep of the *korban tamid* was in the northwest — while the *mishna* in *Middot* places it in the southwest. The primary resolution already established by the previous daf is that the author of *Middot* is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds a different view than the author of *Tamid* as to the room's location and function.

### Rabbi Eliezer b. Yaakov

To appreciate the discussion, it helps to orient ourselves physically. The *Beit HaMikdash* runs along a north–south axis, with the *Ezrat Nashim* to the east leading through *Shaar Nicanor* into the *Ezrat Yisrael*. The *mizbeach* stands in the courtyard, with the *ulam* and the *heichal* beyond it. Along the northern side of the complex lay the *Beit HaMoked*, a large chamber kept warm with a fire — *Tosafot* notes that one purpose of this fire was to supply wood for the *mizbeach* — and this chamber contained four corner rooms, each with a distinct function. The *mishna* in *Tamid* places the sheep-room in the northwest; the *mishna* in *Middot* places it in the southwest. That is the contradiction, and the initial answer is simply that the two tractates reflect different authors, with *Middot* authored by Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

The conclusion at the end of the previous daf's discussion is: *ella shema mina Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov hi, shema mina* — we may conclude that the author of *Middot* is indeed Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, whose views differ from those of the author of *Tamid* on the layout and use of those rooms.

One might ask: does it even matter? This discussion is not *halakha* in any practical sense, let alone *hilkhata limshicha*. The tractate *Middot* is largely historical in character. The *gemara* engages with it here only because the contradiction presents a structural problem that demands resolution, and the methodology parallels the resolution applied earlier in *Yoma*.

### Perspective Solution

A second answer is now introduced: *Rava brei deRav Yitzchak amar hai lishka akzuyei makziya* — Rava son of Rav Yitzchak says that this chamber was positioned at the edge, straddling the boundary. As *Rashi* explains, *aktzuyei* suggests something both designated and extended. The *gemara* elaborates: *de'ati mitzafon mitchazi lei bedarom, v'de'ati midarom mitchazi lei betzafon* — when one approached from the north, the room appeared to be in the south, and when one approached from the south, it appeared to be in the north.

*Tosafot*'s reading of this is that the chamber was not clearly in either the northwest or the southwest but occupied something like a middle position between them. From different vantage points, one would naturally describe it differently — as northwest from the south, and as southwest from the north. This is not a deeply satisfying answer, since one might reasonably expect the *mishna* simply to place it in the west, or more precisely at the midpoint of the western side. Nevertheless, the point stands: the two descriptions are not contradictory accounts of two distinct locations, but rather two perspective-dependent descriptions of a single room that occupied the space between the two corners.

### Lechem HaPanim

At this point a second contradiction is introduced, and it is this second contradiction that will ultimately determine which of the two answers — different authors or perspective-dependence — is more persuasive. The *gemara* notes: *u-mistabra d'vi-ma'arav d'romi havah* — it makes more sense to say the room was really in the southwest. Why? *De-raminan lechem hapanim a-lechem hapanim* — because there is an additional contradiction between *Tamid* and *Middot* concerning which room was used for the *lechem hapanim*, and it is the resolution of that second contradiction that will point us to the southwest.

The contradiction runs as follows. The *mishna* in *Middot* explicitly labels each of the four rooms: the southwest was for the sheep (*tlayim*), the southeast was for the *lechem hapanim*, the northeast held the stones of the *mizbeach* that had been defiled by the Greeks and preserved by the Chashmonaim, and the fourth room was the passage down to *Beit HaTevilah*. These designations are explicit and unambiguous in *Middot*.

The *mishna* in *Tamid*, by contrast, starts with the sheep-room and then lists the remaining three rooms without giving their compass coordinates. Assuming one proceeds counterclockwise — the standard direction of movement in the *mikdash* — the order would place the second room as the room for the seals (*chotamot*), then the *Beit HaMoked* proper, and then the *lechem hapanim*. In this reading, the *lechem hapanim* room ends up in the southeast. But this does not coincide with the location assigned by *Middot*.

It should be noted that not every divergence between the two listings constitutes a genuine contradiction. The fact that one source mentions the Chashmonaic stones and another does not, or that one mentions the descent to *Beit HaTevilah* in a different position, may reflect different emphases or overlapping functions. The two firm contradictions are: where was the sheep-room, and where was the *lechem hapanim* room?

### Southwest & Clockwise

The resolution now offered is elegant. The *mishna* in *Tamid* does not tell us in which direction its author is listing the rooms — it merely starts with the sheep-room and proceeds. If we make two assumptions simultaneously, both contradictions dissolve. First, we assume that the author of *Tamid*, even though he called the sheep-room "northwest," actually agrees it was really in the southwest — the room was between the two corners, and he simply described it from his vantage point as northwest. Second, we assume that the author of *Tamid* listed the rooms not in the customary counterclockwise direction but clockwise.

If the sheep-room is really in the southwest, and the author proceeds clockwise, the subsequent rooms will fall in the northwest, then the northeast, then the southeast. This places the *lechem hapanim* in the southeast — precisely where *Middot* places it. The contradiction evaporates. *Amar Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua: mar kachashiv derech yamin, u-mar kachashiv derech smol* — one source counts moving to the right (counterclockwise), and the other counts moving to the left (clockwise).

Moreover, this solution provides the proof that the room truly was in the southwest: *i amrit bishlama b'ma'arav d'romi havah, hainu d'metartzat lechem hapanim a-lechem hapanim* — if you say the room was in the southwest, then the resolution of the *lechem hapanim* contradiction works out. *Ella i amrit tzfoni ma'aravi havah, sof sof mai tirutza de-lechem hapanim?* — but if you insist the room was really in the northwest, merely described as southwest from a certain angle, then there is no way to reconcile the *lechem hapanim* contradiction regardless of which direction you list. *Ella lav shema mina b'ma'arav d'romi havah, shema mina* — you must conclude that the room was fundamentally in the southwest.

### Kol Pinot Objection

The *gemara* immediately raises an objection. *Ve-ha amar: kol pinot she'ata poneh lo yehu ela derech yamin* — does not a principle exist that all turns in the *mikdash* must be to the right? When one ascends the ramp of the *mizbeach* or moves through the Temple, one always turns toward the right, which, when facing the center of the space, means one moves counterclockwise. How then can we posit that the author of *Tamid* listed the rooms in a clockwise direction?

The *gemara* answers: *hani mili be'avoda* — that principle governs the actual performance of the *avoda*. When a *kohen* is engaged in *avodah*, his physical movements must be to the right and therefore counterclockwise. *Aval hacha, hushbana b'alma hu* — but here the author of *Tamid* is merely listing rooms for the purpose of enumeration. An author listing chambers in a text is not performing *avodah*; the principle of *kol pinot derech yamin* simply does not apply.

To summarize: the two contradictions between *Tamid* and *Middot* — the location of the sheep-room and the location of the *lechem hapanim* room — can both be resolved without positing different authors. Both tractates agree the sheep-room was roughly between the northwest and southwest corners, in reality closer to the southwest. The apparent discrepancy in the *lechem hapanim* room's location reflects nothing more than the fact that one author listed the rooms clockwise and the other counterclockwise. Alongside this resolution stands the earlier answer that the *stam* voice of *Middot* is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and differs from the *stam* voice of *Tamid*. That identification rested on two independent grounds: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's own statement in another *mishna* that he forgot what a particular room was used for — a remark that makes sense only if he is the *stam* author of *Middot* — and the fact that his view elsewhere about the structure of the *mikdash* aligns with the distinctive features of *Middot*'s description.

---

## Kohen Gadol Rights

### General Principle

With the discussion of the *Beit HaMoked* rooms resolved, the *gemara* returns to its primary topic: the *kohen gadol* in the context of *Yom Kippur* preparation. The *mishna* had established that the *kohen gadol* performs the entire *avoda* himself during the seven days preceding *Yom Kippur*. The *gemara* now broadens the discussion to a general principle that applies throughout the year: the *kohen gadol* has the prerogative, on any day, to perform any *korban* he wishes before others, and to take the first portion from any division of *korbanot*.

*She-kohen gadol makriv chelek berosh* — the *kohen gadol* offers up first. *Ve-noteil chelek berosh* — the *kohen gadol* takes first from the division of meat or bread.

### Mishnah Examples

The *braita* elaborates on both dimensions of this privilege. *Keitzad makriv chelek berosh?* — How does he exercise the right to bring first? He may appear on any day of the year and say: *olah zu ani makriv* — I wish to bring this *olah*. *Mincha zu ani makriv* — I wish to bring this *mincha*. He is given precedence and his offering goes first.

*Keitzad noteil chelek berosh?* — How does he take first from the division?
