He may say: *chatat zu ani ocheil* — I wish to eat from this *chatat*. *Asham zeh ani ocheil* — I wish to eat from this *asham*. He is given the first portion. Similarly: *ve-noteil challah mi-shtei challot* — he takes one of the two loaves brought on *Shavuot*.

This last example begins to define the outer boundary of the privilege. He takes one of two — not both. He is one individual, and presumably there is a limit on how large a "first portion" he may claim.

### Four/Five/Half

The question of how large the *chelek berosh* can be becomes acute when the *braita* turns to the *lechem hapanim*. There are twelve loaves. Half of twelve is six. But the *braita* says the *kohen gadol* takes four or five — not six. Then *Rebbi* (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) states: *le'olam chamesh* — it is always five, because the verse says *ve-hayetah le'Aharon u-le-vanav*, indicating that Aaron and his sons each receive half, meaning the *kohen gadol* is entitled to a full half of whatever is being divided. Somehow, then, five must constitute half — though precisely how that works remains to be explained.

### Braita Contradiction

The *gemara* immediately flags the internal incoherence of the *braita*. *Ha gufa kashya* — the text is itself contradictory. The opening clause says the *kohen gadol* receives one of the two loaves on *Shavuot* — that is half, which sounds like *Rebbi*'s position. The middle clause says four or five of the twelve loaves of *lechem hapanim* — that is clearly less than half, which sounds like the Rabbis' position. The final clause is *Rebbi*'s explicit statement that he always gets five and always gets half. So the *braita* appears to begin with *Rebbi*, shift to the Rabbis, and then end with *Rebbi* again. *Reisha ve-seifa Rebbi, metzi'ata Rabbanan?* — Can the *braita* really be bouncing back and forth between two positions in this way?

### Abaye's Reading

*Amar Abaye*: *reisha u-metzi'ata Rabbanan* — both the opening and middle clauses reflect the position of the Rabbis. The Rabbis hold that the *kohen gadol* may receive his first portion, but it must be less than half. The reason the first clause says he receives one of the two loaves on *Shavuot* is not because one out of two equals half, but because you do not give the *kohen gadol* a fractional loaf. *Modu Rabbanan be-frusah de-lav orach ar'a le-meitiv le-kohen gadol* — the Rabbis concede that it would be beneath the dignity of the *kohen gadol* to give him a broken piece. So even though the Rabbis say he gets less than half, when there are only two loaves, he receives one whole loaf — he rounds up to the nearest whole unit. Both the first and middle clauses thus reflect the Rabbis. Only the final line is *Rebbi*, who says he always gets exactly half.

### Why 4 or 5

The four or five of the middle clause requires further explanation. Under normal circumstances, the twelve loaves of *lechem hapanim* are divided on *Shabbat* between the outgoing *mishmar* (the weekly rotation of *kohanim* departing) and the incoming *mishmar* (those arriving to serve the coming week). There is a dispute among the Rabbis in tractate *Sukkah* about how this division works.

According to the Rabbis cited there, *nichnas noteil shesh ve-yotzei noteil shesh* — the incoming group takes six and the outgoing group takes six, with no special payment allocated for closing the Temple gates. Thus the full twelve loaves are divided, and half of twelve is six. The *kohen gadol*, who must take less than half, takes five — one less than six. That is the reading that gives five.

According to Rabbi Yehuda, however, the incoming group receives seven — two of which constitute payment for closing the gates that the outgoing group had opened — and the outgoing group receives five. The two loaves set aside as gate-closing payment are not part of the general pool; they are designated from the outset. So the real pool for division is ten. Half of ten is five, and one less than half is four. That is the reading that gives four.

Thus when the *braita* says four or five, both figures represent the same Rabbinic position — that the *kohen gadol* takes one less than half — applied to two different understandings of the baseline pool: twelve (giving five) or ten (giving four).

### Rava's Reading

*Rava amar: kula Rabbi hi* — Rava offers an alternative reading in which the entire *braita* represents *Rebbi*'s position that the *kohen gadol* always takes exactly half. On this reading, the first clause — one of the two loaves on *Shavuot* — is straightforwardly half. The middle clause — four or five of the *lechem hapanim* — also works as half, because *Rebbi* holds like Rabbi Yehuda that two loaves are always set aside, leaving ten, of which half is five. How does four also qualify as half? The *gemara* explains: *lo kashya — ha de-ika mishmar ha-mit'akev, ha de-leika mishmar ha-mit'akev* — it depends on whether there is a *mishmar ha-mitakev*, a group of *kohanim* holding over.

### Mishmar HaMitakev

The *mishmar ha-mitakev* is a group of *kohanim* present in the *Beit HaMikdash* on a given *Shabbat* not because it is their assigned week, but because they have stayed over from or in anticipation of an adjacent *Yom Tov*. On *Yom Tov* itself, all twenty-four *mishmarot* would come up to *Yerushalayim* as *oleh l'regel* and serve together, dividing the offerings equally. The scenario that creates the *mishmar ha-mitakev* is when *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* are juxtaposed — either *Yom Tov* falls immediately before or after *Shabbat*, or there is a single intervening day that makes travel impractical.

Concretely: if *Yom Tov* falls on a Friday, all *kohanim* are already in *Yerushalayim* for the *regel* and naturally remain through *Shabbat* as well. If *Yom Tov* falls on a Sunday, *kohanim* who want to be present for *Yom Tov* will arrive on *erev Shabbat* and remain through *Shabbat* before the *regel* begins. And if there is a single weekday between *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* — say, *Yom Tov* falls on a Thursday or a Monday — *kohanim* may well choose to remain in *Yerushalayim* rather than make the journey home and back within a day or two. These *kohanim* who are present on *Shabbat* due to *Yom Tov* proximity but who are not the assigned *mishmar* for that *Shabbat* are the *mishmar ha-mitakev* — they hold over, whether arriving early or staying late.

Such *kohanim* are permitted to serve and are entitled to a portion, but not an equal share, precisely because their presence is voluntary. The *halakha* established for them is that all the visiting *kohanim* collectively receive two of the twelve loaves, and the remaining ten are divided between the two *mishmarot* actually assigned to that *Shabbat*.

Now, applying this to *Rava*'s reading: even assuming *Rebbi*, who holds like Rabbi Yehuda that two loaves are always designated as gate-closing payment, in the scenario where there is no *mishmar ha-mitakev*, the pool is ten and half is five — *kohen gadol* gets five. In the scenario where there *is* a *mishmar ha-mitakev*, those *kohanim* receive two additional loaves, leaving eight for division — and half of eight is four. Thus four and five both represent exactly half under *Rebbi*'s position, applied to different scenarios.

*Ei ika mishmar ha-mitakev mi-shmoneh ba'i le-miflag, ve-shakil arba* — if there is a holding-over *mishmar*, the division is from eight and he takes four. *Ei leika mishmar ha-mitakev me-eser ba'i le-miflag, ve-chamesh ba'i le-miflag ve-shakil chamesh* — if there is none, the division is from ten and he takes five.

The *gemara* then notes one remaining difficulty with *Rava*'s reading: if the middle clause already accounts for both four and five as half under various scenarios, why does *Rebbi* need to add the statement *le'olam chamesh* — it is always five? On *Rava*'s reading, that final clause seems to contradict the middle clause by restricting the amount to always five and excluding four. The *gemara* treats this as a difficulty (*kashya*), conceding that the simpler reading is *Abaye*'s.

### Rebbi vs. Rabbanan

To summarize the dispute: *Abaye* reads the *braita* such that the middle clauses reflect the Rabbis, who hold that *chelek berosh* must be less than half — with the qualification that one rounds up to a whole unit when only fractional amounts would otherwise result. The final clause is *Rebbi*, who holds that the *kohen gadol* is entitled to exactly half, *mechtzah le'Aharon u-mechtzah le-vanav* as the verse implies. *Rava* reads the entire *braita* as *Rebbi*'s position, with four and five both representing half under varying scenarios of *mishmar ha-mitakev* and the application of Rabbi Yehuda's gate-closing allocation.

The underlying dispute between *Rebbi* and the *rabbanan* is thus whether the *chelek berosh* of the *kohen gadol* must always be strictly less than half, or whether he is entitled to precisely half. The *gemara*'s discussion on this point continues on the following daf.

---

---

# Yoma 18

## Kohen Gadol Preparation

### Beis Din's Role

The *mishnah* of daf 18 brings us to the transition from the *kohen gadol*'s weeklong preparation into the specific protocols of *Erev Yom Kippur* itself. Having concluded the discussions of the regular *avodot* — the *nerot* and *ketores* and the structural details drawn from Middot and Tamid — we now arrive at a more action-oriented section of the tractate, focused on the *kohen gadol* as *Yom Kippur* approaches.

The *mishnah* opens: *masru lo zekeinim mizekinei Beis Din* — elders from the elders of *Beis Din* were assigned to him. The subject of *masru* is left anonymous; the *zekeinim* are the grammatical object, not the subject. What this establishes is that at this stage in the process, the *kohen gadol* came under the formal auspices of *Beis Din*. This is consistent with a broader assumption found throughout the *Gemara* — one that emerged repeatedly in the discussions in Shekalim — that everything that transpired in the *Beis HaMikdash*, even the conduct of the *kohanim* and the leadership of the *kohen gadol* himself, ultimately operated under the authority of *Beis Din*.

### Beis Din Representation

What is worth pausing over is the precise nature of *Beis Din*'s role here. Soloveitchik observes that *Beis Din* does not function solely as an adjudicating body or even merely as the authoritative interpreter of *Torah* law. In many contexts, *Beis Din* acts as the representative of *Klal Yisrael*. The parallel to the *eglah arufah* is instructive: when *veyatzu zekanecha ve'shoftecha* — the elders and judges go forth — they are acting not as a court rendering legal decisions but as the representatives of the people. Similarly here, *Beis Din*'s presence with the *kohen gadol* embodies the fact that the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* is performed on behalf of and for the sake of the entire Jewish people.

At the same time, *Beis Din* in this context may simultaneously represent *Torah* authority — and those are genuinely distinct roles. When the elders oversee the *kohen gadol* before *Yom Kippur*, there is both a representational dimension (they stand for *Klal Yisrael*) and a supervisory one (they stand for *Torah* law and its proper execution). It is worth holding both of these in mind as we proceed.

### Reading the Service

The *mishnah* continues: *vekorin lefanav b'seder hayom* — they would read before him the order of the day's service. The word *korin* here is significant. This appears not to be a how-to manual or step-by-step instructional guide, but a reading from the *Torah* itself — the *pesukim* of *parshas Acharei Mos*. This is a striking detail, because not everything about the *avodas Yom HaKippurim* is made fully explicit in the plain meaning of those *pesukim*; there are procedural elements that require tradition beyond the text.

The *mishnah* then records that they would say to him: *Ishi Kohen Gadol, kra attah be'ficha* — Mr. *kohen gadol*, read the passages yourself, *shemma shachachta*, in case you have forgotten, *o shemma lo lamad'ta*, or perhaps you never learned it at all. That second possibility — that a *kohen gadol* might never have learned the *avodah* — obviously calls for explanation, and the *Gemara* will address it shortly.

---

## Animal Parade & Desp (II)

### Animal Parade

On *Erev Yom HaKippurim Shacharis*, the *mishnah* describes the following procedure: *ma'amidim oto be-Sha'ar HaMizrach* — they would station him at the eastern gate, at *Sha'ar Nicanor*, the entrance to the *Azarah* — *uma'avirin lefanav parim ve-eilim u-kevasim*, and they would parade before him oxen, rams, and sheep. The purpose is stated explicitly: *kedei sheyehei makhir ve-ragil ba'avodah*, so that he should recognize the animals and be fluent in the *avodah*.

### Roleplay Explanation

This raises an obvious question: what is the point of parading these animals before him? Even an ignorant person knows what a cow looks like. The Maharsha explains — and this accords with an intuition one might independently arrive at — that this was not a zoological identification exercise. What they were actually doing was a full roleplay. They would say: here is the ox — now walk toward it, now perform the *shechitah*, now take this and move it here. The point was not intellectual knowledge but physical, embodied familiarity, so that on *Yom Kippur* itself the sequence would flow as second nature rather than requiring conscious recollection at each step. Acting it out with the actual animals makes the choreography intuitive in a way that reading the *pesukim* cannot.

One might wonder why this roleplay was not performed every day of the preparatory week leading up to *Yom Kippur*, which would seem to offer an even better opportunity to ingrain the sequence. That question remains. What the *mishnah* does record is that this particular parade took place on the morning of *Erev Yom Kippur*.

Some modern interpreters have drawn a connection between this scene and *Ma'aseh Bereishit* — Adam in the garden with the animals brought before him — noting that the *avodah* liturgy recited on *Yom Kippur* itself begins precisely with the creation narrative. The textual basis for this parallel is admittedly thin, since there is no mention of naming the animals here, but the structural resonance is worth noting.

---

## Seminal Emission Con (II)

### Food Restrictions

The *mishnah* records that throughout the seven days of preparation, *lo hayu mon'in mimenu ma'achal u-mishteh* — they did not withhold food and drink from him; he could eat what he wished. But *Erev Yom Kippur im chasheichah* — as nightfall of *Erev Yom Kippur* approached — *lo hayu manichin oto leechol harbeh mipnei shehama'achal meivi et hasheinah*: they would not allow him to eat a large meal, because eating heavily leads to sleep. This is somewhat paradoxical: at the very moment when everyone else is eating their *se'udah hamafseket* in preparation for the fast, the *kohen gadol* was actually limiting his intake. The reason is that he needed to remain awake the entire night preceding *Yom Kippur*, out of concern that if he fell asleep, he would have a seminal emission, become *tamei*, and be unfit for the *avodah* — necessitating recourse to the backup *kohen gadol*.

---

## Ignorant Kohen Gadol

### Gemara's Question

The *Gemara* now confronts the difficulty embedded in the *mishnah*'s language. The phrase *shemma shachachta* — perhaps you forgot — is at least comprehensible, if a little surprising. But the phrase *o shemma lo lamad'ta* — or perhaps you never learned it — is genuinely puzzling. *Mi mokminan ki hai gavna?* — would we ever actually appoint a *kohen gadol* who had never learned the *avodah*? He has never read *parshas Acharei Mos*?

One might add: even *shachachta* deserves scrutiny. If a *kohen gadol* is truly *gadol bechochma*, how does one forget what is written in *Acharei Mos*? And if this is not his first year serving as *kohen gadol*, then presumably he performed the entire *avodah* just twelve months prior — how is forgetting even a possibility?

### Kohen Gadol Requirements

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* in response. The Torah's phrase *vehakohen hagadol me'echav* — the *kohen* who is greater than his brethren — is read to require that the *kohen gadol* be genuinely superior to the other *kohanim* in concrete respects. The *baraita* lists these: *bekoach*, physical strength; *benoy*, impressive appearance; *bechochma*, wisdom and intelligence; *ube'osher*, wealth. These criteria are not arbitrary. Physical impressiveness — height, strength, distinguished appearance — projects the authority and gravitas that leadership requires. Empirically, of course, there is no correlation between these qualities and actual capability, yet they generate the impression of authority in the eyes of the people, and that impression itself has social and institutional value.

*Acherim omrim* — others add a further ruling: if the ideal candidate lacks wealth, the other *kohanim* are obligated to contribute from their own resources to endow him, based on the reading *gadlehu mishel achav* — make him great from what belongs to his brethren. The point for our discussion is clear: given that a *kohen gadol* must be *gadol bechochma*, how could it ever occur that he failed to learn — or forgot — the *avodas Yom HaKippurim*?

### Bayis Rishon/Sheni

Rav Yosef resolves the difficulty with a single distinction: *lo kashya kan be'Mikdash Rishon kan be'Mikdash Sheni* — there is no difficulty; the two cases refer to different historical contexts. In the *Beis HaMikdash Rishon*, *kohanim gedolim* were appointed in accordance with the proper criteria — *gadol bechochma, be'osher, bekoach* — and the concern that a *kohen gadol* had never learned the *avodah* was simply inapplicable. In the *Beis HaMikdash Sheni*, however, the position became susceptible to purchase and political manipulation, and under those conditions an ignorant *kohen gadol* was a genuine possibility.

The *Gemara* illustrates this with the case cited by Rav Assi: *tarkava de'dinari* — a basketful of gold dinars — *aylah lah Martha bas Baithos le'Yannai malka*, Martha the daughter of Baithos brought to King Yannai, *al de'ukmei le'Yehoshua ben Gamla be'khanei ravrevi* — to have Yehoshua ben Gamla appointed to the high priesthood. Baithos was a name associated with great wealth elsewhere in the *Gemara* (one recalls the famous case of Baithos ben Zonin and the question of *matzos* made with molds), and his daughter apparently inherited substantially from that estate.

A striking question arises from Rashi's comment on this passage. Rashi notes that Martha was an *almanah* — a widow — which raises an immediate difficulty: a *kohen gadol* is prohibited from marrying a widow. How could Yehoshua ben Gamla, once appointed *kohen gadol*, remain married to her? The *Rambam*'s ruling in *hilchos issurei biah* is relevant here: he holds that the prohibition for a *kohen gadol* regarding an *almanah* applies specifically to the act of *bi'ah* in that relationship, and uniquely — unlike the parallel prohibitions applicable to ordinary *kohanim* regarding *zonah*, *chalulah*, and *grushah* — he receives *malkos* for relations with an *almanah* even without prior formal *kiddushin*: *lo yichalel, keivan sheba'ala chillela*. This makes the scenario in which a *kohen gadol* was already married to a widow at the time of his appointment genuinely complex from a halachic standpoint — and indeed raises the further question of whether *vichaper ba'ado uvead beito* could be fulfilled when *beito* is *beito ha'asura lo*.

Tosafot adds a separate observation: the *Yannai HaMelech* referenced in this story cannot be the well-known Yannai HaMelech, since other *Gemaros* indicate that he himself served as *kohen gadol* and would not have sold the position to another. Tosafot therefore maintains that this refers to a different king named Yannai.

There is also a tradition in the *Yerushalmi* relevant to the question of seminal emission and the *kohen gadol*: one of the *nissim* of the *Beis HaMikdash* was that the *kohen gadol* never experienced a seminal emission. This yields two possible responses to the concern raised by the *mishnah*. The first is the principle of *ein somchin al hanes* — one does not rely on miracles, and practical precautions must be taken regardless. The second aligns with Rav Yosef's distinction: that particular *nes* belonged to the era of the *Bayis Rishon*, and in the diminished circumstances of the *Bayis Sheni*, one could not assume its continuation. The very need for the precautions described in our *mishnah* reflects that *yeridah*.

---

## Animal Parade & Desp (II)

### Goats Excluded

A *baraita* notes that the goats were also paraded before him during the week — *af hase'irim*. Yet our *mishnah* makes no mention of goats. The *Gemara* asks: *tana didan mai ta'ama lo tani se'irim?* — why does our *mishnah* omit them? The answer: *keivan d'al cheit ka'asi* — since the goats come for the sin of *Klal Yisrael* (one is the goat sent over the cliff, the other is brought as a *korban*), the sight of them would cause *chalsha da'atei* — a sinking of the spirit, a despair — as the *kohen gadol* contemplates the weight of the nation's sins that he is being called to atone for.

The *Gemara* then asks: *ee hachi, par nami* — if so, what about his own *par*, his ox? That too comes for sin. The *Gemara* answers: *keivan d'alav v'al echav hakoanim hu d'asi* — the ox comes for him and for his fellow *kohanim*. Regarding the *kohanim*, *meida yada lei* — he is personally acquainted with them; he knows who among them may be transgressing. *U'mahader lei b'teshuva* — he can bring a fellow *kohen* into his confidence, address him directly, and guide him toward *teshuva* before *Yom Kippur*. He has some degree of agency and influence.

### Influence Distinction

With *Klal Yisrael* at large, there is no such agency. *U'vechulu Yisrael lo yada* — he does not know who the sinners are among the broader people, and he cannot influence them. That helplessness is what generates the deeper despair when confronting the goat. *Amar Ravina*: this is the meaning of the folk saying, *ee bar achasach daila, havi chazi b'shuka kamei lo sachloof* — if your nephew is a tax collector, don't walk in front of him in the marketplace. The implication is that with one's own family and close circle, one is exposed, known, and subject to accountability. The *kohen gadol* feels that accountability with the *kohanim* — if one of them is sinning, he would know about it, and he could act. With the rest of Israel, he has no such knowledge or leverage, and the despair is correspondingly greater.

The result is that the roleplay with animals during the week is conducted with the oxen, rams, and sheep — but conspicuously without the goats. This is no small omission: a substantial portion of the entire *Yom Kippur avodah* centers on the goats — the *shechitas hase'ir*, the *lot* drawing, and the dispatch of the goat over the cliff. To conduct the roleplay without any of that is notable.

The *Gemara*'s conclusion here also opens a related question that will receive fuller treatment in the eighth *perek*: to what extent is *teshuva* a necessary component of *kaparah* when *korbanos* are present? Without *korbanos*, the entire focus of *kaparah* falls on *teshuva*, but whether *teshuva* was strictly required in order to achieve atonement when the *korbanos* themselves were being brought is a significant *machlokes* that will be addressed later.

---

## Seminal Emission Con (II)

### Foods Causing Emission

The *mishnah* stated that on *Erev Yom Kippur* as darkness fell, they would not allow him to eat heavily in order to prevent sleep and the resulting risk of seminal emission. A *baraita* elaborates on what Rabbi Yehuda ben Nakusa proposed: *maachilin oto solet uveitzim kedei lehamssu* — they would feed him fine flour products and eggs, as a kind of purgative to clear his digestive system, ensuring he would not be interrupted during the *avodah*. But this proposal was rejected: *kol sheken sheata mevio lidei chimum* — on the contrary, these are precisely the foods that generate bodily heat, meaning they stimulate sexual arousal and are liable to produce the seminal emission one is trying to avoid.

A further *baraita* cites Sumchus in the name of Rabbi Meir: *ein maachilin oto lo avi* on *Erev Yom Kippur* — that is, no *alef*, no *vav*, no *yud*: no *etrog*, no *yayin yashan* (old wine), no *beitzim* (eggs). An alternative version expands the acronym to *avavi*: *etrog*, *beitzim*, *basar shamen* (fatty meat), and old wine. Some add white wine as well — *mipnei shehayayin lavan meivi et ha'adam lidei tumah* — because white wine brings a person to *tumah*, meaning seminal emission. Notably, the concern about the night of *Erev Yom Kippur* is particularly acute: any *tumah* incurred on a previous day would allow time to immerse in a *mikveh* and recover before *Yom Kippur*, but a seminal emission on *Erev Yom Kippur* night would leave the *kohen gadol* unfit for the *avodah* with no opportunity to rectify it.

### Zav vs. Baal Keri

The *Gemara* now broadens the discussion into the underlying *halachic* framework concerning these foods. A *baal keri* — a man who has had a seminal emission — becomes *tamei* regardless of what caused it: whether sexual thoughts, a nocturnal emission with no identifiable cause, or certain foods. The cause is irrelevant to the *tumah*.

A *zav* is categorically different. *Zivah* is a non-seminal penile flow (associated by some with gonorrhea), and the *Gemara* understands that *zivah* cannot be attributed to an external cause — *machmat ones*. If a man had this type of emission following sexual arousal, or after consuming foods that can precipitate such a physiological response, it is considered externally caused and he does not acquire the status of *zav*. What is striking is that although the *Gemara* is entirely clear that *zivah* is not semen, it nonetheless assumes that the same types of triggers — sexual thoughts and certain foods — can produce this flow as well. The physiological parallel is drawn even where the substances differ entirely.

The *Gemara* states: *zav tolin lo bema'achal uvechol minei ma'achal* — for a *zav*, one may attribute the emission to food, even to overeating generally, regardless of specific food categories.

### Foods for Zav

Elazar ben Pinchas then cites Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira with a more specific ruling: *ein maachilin oto lo chagavi velo gabam* — you should not feed a *zav* the following foods when he is counting his seven clean days. The acronym *chagavi* yields: *chalav* (milk), *gevina* (cheese), *beitzah* (egg), *yayin* (wine). The acronym *gabam* yields: *mei gerisin shel pol* (a pounded-bean soup), *basar shamena* (fatty meat), and *muryaas* (a type of fish preparation). The overlap with the foods mentioned earlier in the context of the *kohen gadol* — particularly eggs, wine, and fatty meat — is evident, though the list for the *zav* is more expansive and includes dairy products not mentioned in the earlier context.

### Five Things Tumah

The *baraita* concludes with the phrase *velo kol devarim hamevi'in lidei tumah* — and not any foods that bring to *tumah*. The *Gemara* asks: *le'atuyei mai* — what does that phrase add? The answer is that it comes to include what the rabbis taught elsewhere: *chamisha devarim mevi'im et ha'adam lidei tumah* — five things that lead to seminal emission. They are: *hashum* (garlic), *hashachalim* (which Rashi identifies as cress), *hachalglogot* (purslane), *habeitzim* (eggs), and *hagargir* (which the Mesorah identifies as garden rocket, or arugula).

### Arugula Digression

The mention of *gargir* prompts a short *aggadic* digression. A *tanna* in the name of Rabbi Meir identifies the *orot* gathered in the field (mentioned in a Biblical passage) as *gargir*. Rabbi Yochanan asks: *lama nikra sheman orot?* — why are they called *orot* (literally, lights)? The answer: *sheme'irot et ha'einayim* — because arugula illuminates the eyes, meaning it is beneficial for eyesight.

Rav Huna adds a practical instruction: *hamotzeh gargir* — if one comes across wild arugula growing in a field, *im yachol le'achlo ochlo* — if you can tolerate eating it (arugula being notoriously bitter), then eat it for the health benefit. *Ve'im lo, ma'aviro al gabei einav* — and if you cannot stomach it, simply pass it across your eyes, and even that will benefit the eyesight.

Rav Papa qualifies this: this is specifically true of *gargira dematzra* — arugula that grows at the edge of the field, where it receives no nutrients from neighboring plants, leaving it in a purer, more concentrated form. This is Rashi's explanation of the distinction.

### Guest Etiquette

Rav Gidal cites Rav with a practical ruling that connects the concern about seminal emission to the context of a guest staying in someone else's home: *achsanai lo yochel beitzim* — a guest should not eat eggs while at someone's house. The reason, given what the *Gemara* has established about eggs and seminal emission, is that a nocturnal emission on someone else's sheets and in someone else's bed would be a source of embarrassment. Relatedly: *velo yishan betalito shel ba'al habayit* — a guest should not sleep using the host's cloak as a blanket. If he were to have a seminal emission under the host's garment, it would be obvious and shameful. Rashi suggests an alternative reading of this second concern: the embarrassment might run in the other direction — the guest, by sleeping with the host's cloak, might discover evidence of the host's own emission. Either way, the practical counsel is clear.

---

## Traveling Marriages

### Rav's Announcement

The *Gemara* now introduces a closely related discussion, arising naturally from the concern about men away from home and their management of sexual desire. Rav, when he would visit Darshish, *makhriz* — he would make a public announcement: *man havya leyoma?* — who would be with me for today? Rav Nachman would do likewise when he traveled to Shachnatziv.

### Bigamy Question

The *Gemara* immediately raises a difficulty from a *baraita*: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that a man may not marry a woman in one country and then go and marry another woman in a different country, because their children may eventually encounter one another without knowing they share a father, and a brother and sister may end up marrying — thereby filling the land with *mamzerut*. The verse applied to this concern: *u-malah ha'aretz zimah* — the land will be filled with licentiousness. How, then, could Rav and Rav Nachman take wives in different places they visited?

### Reputation Solution

The *Gemara* answers: *Rabbanan kali it lehu* — the rabbis had a recognized reputation. Their names were known throughout the Jewish world. Unlike an ordinary person named Shmuel whose children in two different cities might not identify each other as half-siblings, the children of Rav or Rav Nachman would identify their father by name and standing. When two people were considering marriage and discovered they both had the same famous father, they would know immediately. The concern about inadvertent incest therefore does not apply.

Rashi also notes that Rav would divorce these women afterwards — *veteitze le'achar mikan* — both for the woman's sake (she should not remain bound to him between infrequent visits) and to explain why he would need to make the announcement anew each time he arrived.

### Dam Chimud Issue

But the *Gemara* presses further. Rava ruled: *tav'uha lehinasay* — if a groom pressed his betrothed to advance the wedding date, and she agreed (*venitpaisah*), she requires *shiva neki'im* — seven clean days — because the suddenness of the demand likely caused excitement that may have led to spotting. This phenomenon is called *dam chimud* — the blood of desire or excitement. If so, how could Rav or Rav Nachman marry a woman and proceed to relations the same day, given that the very announcement of the intent to marry would itself trigger the concern of *dam chimud*?

This principle of *dam chimud* connects to a number of further *halachic* applications worth noting. It underlies the practice that a *kallah* does not go to the *mikveh* more than four days before the wedding; the approach of the wedding creates ongoing concern about excitement-related spotting. There is a division among the *Rishonim* on the scope of this concern: some hold that a woman must check herself daily after the *mikveh* as the wedding draws closer, since proximity to the wedding continuously intensifies the concern. The majority position, however, holds that the concern is specifically tied to *suddenness* — the shock of an unexpected demand — rather than to the general anticipation of a wedding one has been planning and preparing for.

### Yichud Solution

The *Gemara* offers two answers. The first: *Rabbanan adoyi havei mode'i lehu, mikdam havei makdimi umashadrei shlucha* — the rabbis would announce their arrival ahead of time by sending a messenger. Rather than making the announcement upon arrival, they would send someone in advance to find a suitable woman and to allow her time to go to the *mikveh* and count the seven clean days before he arrived. This fundamentally changes the picture: it is no longer a sudden announcement but a structured, advance arrangement.

The second answer: *yichudi havei miyachadi lehu* — they would have *yichud* with these women, and the principle of *pas besalo* applies: *lefi she-eino domeh mi she-yesh lo pas besalo le-mi she-ein lo pas besalo* — it is not the same for one who has bread in his basket as for one who does not. Rashi understands this to mean that they would not actually have relations; the knowledge that the woman was available to him was sufficient to reduce the urgency of the desire, and so no actual intercourse occurred.

### Tosafot Objection

Tosafot objects to this conclusion on two grounds. First, *pas besalo* — if you have bread in your basket, the natural thing is to eat it. Second, even on its own terms, the woman would not be accessible for relations during the week the *Gemara* presupposes them to be together, precisely because of the *dam chimud* concern — so in what sense is it *pas besalo* at all?

The *Ri* proposes an alternative reading: the announcement was never about marriage or sex explicitly. Rav and Rav Nachman announced only that they were seeking *yichud* — someone to share a room with them. Because sex was never mentioned in the announcement, the *dam chimud* concern does not arise; it was the suddenness of a sexual proposal that triggers that concern, not the mere prospect of *yichud*. If sexual relations ultimately occurred during the stay, it would not be precipitated by a shocking announcement.

---

## Oath & Instructions

### Transfer Authority

The *mishnah* now describes the final transfer of the *kohen gadol* as *Yom Kippur* eve concludes: *masru ziknei Beis Din le-ziknei kehunah* — the elders of *Beis Din* handed him over to the elders of the *kehunah*. The symbolic structure here is clear: he passes from the oversight of those who represent *Torah* authority and *Klal Yisrael* into the hands of his own priestly colleagues. They bring him to *Beis Avtinas*, where the *ketores* was prepared, since what follows centers on the *avodas haketores* — the most technical and contested element of the *Yom Kippur* service.

### Ketores Oath

The *mishnah* records that *v'hishbi'uhu* — they administered an oath to him. The substance of the oath is declared: *Ishi Kohen Gadol* — the assembled elders address him — *anu shluchei Beis Din, v'ata shlucheinu u-shliach Beis Din* — we are emissaries of *Beis Din*, and you are our emissary and the emissary of *Beis Din*. The Maharsha notes an allusion in the oath formula — *mi she-shachan shemo babayis hazeh* (the One whose name dwells in this house) — to the *pasuk* in the *parsha* of *Yom Kippur* describing God as *hashochen itam betoch tumasam*.

The content of the oath: *shelo teshaneh davar mikol mah she-amarnu lach* — that he will not deviate from anything they have taught him. The specific concern is the dispute between the *Perushim* and the *Tzadukim* regarding the *ketores*: the *Tzadukim* held that the incense was placed on the coals before entering the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, while the *Perushim* held that he entered first and only then placed the incense on the fire. Given that a large proportion of the *kohanim* in the *Bayis Sheni* period were *Tzadukim*, and the *kohen gadol* himself may well have been one, this oath was not ceremonial — it was the rabbinic establishment's means of ensuring that the *avodah* was performed according to the *halacha* as they understood it.

### Emotional Response

*Hu poresh v'bocheh v'hem porshim v'bochin* — he would go apart and weep, and they would go apart and weep. He wept at being suspected; they wept at being compelled to suspect him. The emotional valence of this moment is striking, and the *mishnah* preserves it without further comment.

### Staying Awake Methods

The *mishnah* then describes how the *kohen gadol* was kept awake throughout the night. If he was a scholar, *doreish* — he would deliver a *shiur* himself. *Ve'im lav* — if he lacked the capacity to deliver but could comprehend, *talmidei chachamim darshin lefanav* — Torah sages would lecture before him. *Ve'im ragil likrot* — if he was literate and could at least read fluently, he would read from *Tanakh* on his own. *Ve'im lav, korin lefanav* — and if even that was beyond his capacity, others would read to him.

### Books Read

The *mishnah* specifies which books were read to him in that final case: *be'Iyov uve'Ezra uve'Divrei HaYamim* — Iyov, Ezra, and Divrei HaYamim. Ezra, written largely in Aramaic (the spoken vernacular), would be accessible and engaging, with narrative directly relevant to the *Beis HaMikdash* and its restoration. Iyov offers rich philosophical substance. Divrei HaYamim contains sections of dense genealogy alongside narrative — potentially less immediately gripping, though some portions are highly relevant. Zecharya ben Kevutal adds his testimony: *pa'amim harbeh karisi lefanav be'Daniel* — I read to him from Sefer Daniel on many occasions, with its compelling narrative sections well-suited to holding a listener's attention through the night.

### Oath Authority Debate

The *mishnah*'s account of the oath contains an ambiguity that divides the *Rishonim*. After recording that the *ziknei Beis Din* handed the *kohen gadol* over to the *ziknei kehunah*, the text says *ve'halchu lahem ve'amru lo* — they departed and said to him. The question is whether the *amru lo* refers to the *ziknei Beis Din* — meaning they administered the oath before departing — or whether it refers to the *ziknei kehunah* — meaning the *Beis Din* elders left, and it was the priestly elders who then administered the oath.

The Ramban maintains that it was the *ziknei Beis Din* who administered the *shevuah*, not the *ziknei kehunah*. This reading carries a coherent institutional logic: the rabbinic establishment, representing *Torah* authority and standing guard against *Tzaduki* practice, retains direct supervisory involvement in this critical moment. The alternative reading — that *Beis Din* departed and the responsibility passed entirely to the *ziknei kehunah* — frames the scene quite differently, leaving the priests themselves as the guarantors of correct practice. The ambiguity in the *mishnah*'s language, and the debate it generates, reflects the broader question of exactly how the relationship between rabbinic and priestly authority was structured at this climactic moment before the *avodas Yom HaKippurim*.

---

---

# Yoma 24

## Terumat HaDeshen Debate

### Intro: Tanna Kamma vs R.…

The daf begins with the Gemara's declaration of *nima ketana'ei* — let us see whether this matter is connected to a *tannaitic* dispute. The issue at hand concerns a debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer regarding the *terumat hadeshen*, the priestly service of removing ashes from the altar.

By way of background: every morning, the *kohen* performed a ritual removal of a small amount of ashes from the top of the *mizbe'ach*, placing them beside the altar's ramp. This is the *terumat hadeshen* proper. Separately, the Torah states: *vefashat et begadav velavash begadim acherim vehotzi et hadeshen el michutz lamachaneh el makom tahor* — "he shall remove his garments and put on other garments, and carry the ashes outside the camp to a pure place." According to the simple reading of the *pesukim*, this is one continuous act. According to *Chazal*, however, these are two distinct acts. The daily morning ritual involves removing only a small amount. The second act — changing clothes and transporting the ashes outside the *mikdash* — was performed only when needed, when the accumulated ashes had to be cleared away, a kind of periodic removal.

### Two Acts of Ash Removal

This second act, the *hotza'at hadeshen*, is essentially a garbage removal: cleaning out the excess ashes from the *mizbe'ach*. The Torah's phrase *vefashat et begadav* — "he shall remove his garments" — introduces a change of clothing before carrying the ashes out.

What does he change into? The *tanna kamma* says he changes into other *bigdei kehunah* — priestly garments — simply of lesser quality. One would not wish to soil one's regular priestly garments with ash-removal work, so dedicated, less fine garments were set aside for this purpose. They are still *bigdei kehunah*, however, merely not the finest. This is a significant detail: if the clothing requirement is still *bigdei kehunah*, it strongly implies that this act is still an *avodah* of the *mikdash*. The question therefore poses itself in stark terms: is taking out the ashes an *avodah*?

### Garment Requirements

This question of garments becomes the pivot of the debate. The *tanna kamma* holds that the *kohen* who performs the *hotza'at hadeshen* wears four *bigdei kehunah*, and that a *kohen* with a blemish — a *ba'al mum* — may not perform it. Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, holds that even a *ba'al mum* may perform the ash removal. While Rabbi Eliezer does not directly address the garment question, his ruling about the *ba'al mum* carries an unmistakable implication: since a *ba'al mum* is disqualified only from performing a genuine *avodah*, allowing him to perform this act signals that Rabbi Eliezer does not regard it as an *avodah* in the full halachic sense.

### Is Ash Removal Avodah?

The central question thus crystallizes: is the *hotza'at hadeshen* — the occasional clearing of accumulated ashes — classified as an *avodah*? The *tanna kamma* appears to say yes: it requires four *bigdei kehunah* and an unblemished *kohen*. Rabbi Eliezer appears to say no: even a *ba'al mum* may perform it.

This *baraita* debate is then taken up by two *Amoraim*, Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, who raise a further question: does the same dispute apply not only to the *hotza'at hadeshen* but also to the daily morning ritual of the *terumat hadeshen* itself?

### Yochanan vs Reish Lakish

One would naturally assume that the daily morning *terumat hadeshen* is universally regarded as an *avodah*. After all, a lottery — a *payis* — was held among the *kohanim* each morning specifically to determine who would perform it, suggesting considerable dignity and formal status. Rabbi Yochanan therefore reads the *tannaitic* dispute narrowly: the debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer concerns only the *hotza'at hadeshen*, the occasional clearing-out. The morning *terumat hadeshen* is not in dispute; everyone agrees it is an *avodah*, requires four *bigdei kehunah*, and may not be performed by a *ba'al mum*.

Reish Lakish disagrees, and his position is considerably more radical.

### Reish Lakish Radical View

Reish Lakish argues that Rabbi Eliezer's leniency extends even to the daily morning *terumat hadeshen*. According to Reish Lakish's reading of Rabbi Eliezer, even that daily ritual — the one celebrated with a morning lottery — is not an *avodah*, and could therefore be performed by a *ba'al mum*. This is a striking claim. The entire elaborate *payis* procedure, with all its solemnity, would be surrounding an act that Rabbi Eliezer, in Reish Lakish's understanding, does not classify as a formal *avodah* at all.

### Two Garments = Not Avodah

Reish Lakish's proof derives from the *pesukim* themselves. The Torah describes the *terumat hadeshen* as follows: *velavash hakohen mido bad umichnesei bad yilbash al besaro* — "the *kohen* shall wear his linen tunic, and linen breeches shall he wear upon his flesh." The verse mentions only two garments: the linen cloak and the linen breeches. The belt and the turban are conspicuously absent. Reish Lakish reads this as significant: the Torah does not require the full four-garment set for the *terumat hadeshen*. Since a genuine *avodah* requires all four *bigdei kehunah*, the fact that only two are mentioned indicates this is not a full *avodah*.

The Gemara then cites a *baraita* (*nima ketana'ei*) that illuminates the debate. The *baraita* asks: why does the verse say *yilbash* ("he shall wear") in addition to *al besaro* ("upon his flesh")? Could it not simply have said *al besaro*? The word *yilbash* is redundant and must therefore teach something additional.

Rabbi Yehudah answers: *lehavi mitznefet ve-avneit leharama* — to include the turban and the belt in the *terumat hadeshen*. On his reading, the Torah mentions only two garments but the extra word *yilbash* teaches us that all four are required. This clearly implies that the *terumat hadeshen* is a genuine *avodah*.

Rabbi Dosa, however, offers a different interpretation of the same word *yilbash*. He reads it as permitting a *kohen hedyot* to wear the garments that had been worn by the *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur*. The *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur* wears the same four-white-garment ensemble: linen tunic, linen breeches, linen belt, and linen turban — identical to those of the ordinary *kohen*. Rabbi Dosa argues that the word *yilbash* implies reuse: these garments can be worn by another *kohen* for the *terumat hadeshen*.

*Rebbe* (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) rejects this on two grounds. First, *de-avneito shel kohen gadol lo zeh avneito shel kohen hedyot* — the belt worn by the *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur* is pure linen, whereas the ordinary *kohen*'s belt is *kilayim* (a wool-and-linen blend, permitted in the Temple context). They are different garments and cannot simply be substituted. Second, *bigadim shenishtamesh bahen kedusha chamura teshamesh bahen kedusha kala* — garments used for a weightier level of sanctity (the *Yom Kippur* service of the *kohen gadol*) cannot then be used for a lighter level of sanctity (an ordinary daily service). *Rebbe* therefore rules that the *yilbash* teaches something else entirely: *lerabbot hashachakim* — even worn or faded garments remain valid for priestly service. The Torah does not insist on fresh, brand-new garments each time.

The Gemara then addresses the *pasuk* regarding after *Yom Kippur*, where it says *vehinicham sham* — "and he shall leave them there." *Rebbe* understands this as *melamed sheteunim genizah* — the garments of the *kohen gadol* used on *Yom Kippur* must be stored away (buried) and never reused, not for another *Yom Kippur* and not for any other service. Rabbi Dosa, who permits reuse, understands *vehinicham sham* as teaching only that these garments may not be used for a *subsequent* *Yom Kippur*. Each *Yom Kippur* demands its own set of new garments — the significance is in the uniqueness of each *Yom Kippur*, not in the sanctity of the garments as such. The garments themselves, on this reading, carry no inherent prohibition against reuse in ordinary priestly service throughout the year.

Having surveyed these opinions, the Gemara asks: does this *baraita* debate reflect a disagreement about whether *terumat hadeshen* requires all four garments? Perhaps Rabbi Dosa and *Rebbe* — who deploy the word *yilbash* for purposes other than teaching the four-garment requirement — hold that only two garments are needed, consistent with Reish Lakish's position that it is not a full *avodah*.

The Gemara rejects this inference decisively: *dekulei alma avodah hi* — everyone agrees it is an *avodah*. The debate between Rabbi Yehudah on the one hand and Rabbi Dosa and *Rebbe* on the other is not about whether four garments are required — they all agree four garments are required — but only about whether the word *yilbash* is needed to teach this. According to Rabbi Yehudah, without *yilbash* one might have thought two garments suffice, and *yilbash* is therefore needed to teach us four. According to Rabbi Dosa and *Rebbe*, no verse is needed for this; it is obvious that a full *avodah* requires all four garments, and therefore *yilbash* must be teaching something else — either the reusability of the *kohen gadol*'s garments (Rabbi Dosa) or the validity of worn garments (*Rebbe*).

### Tosafot on Reish Lakish

*Tosafot* presses the implications of Reish Lakish's position further. According to Reish Lakish, it is not merely that *Rabbi Eliezer* regards *terumat hadeshen* as a non-*avodah*; rather, Reish Lakish holds that even according to the *tanna kamma*, the *terumat hadeshen* does not require all four *bigdei kehunah*. Since only two are required, it cannot be a full *avodah* by anyone's reckoning. The entire debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer, on this reading, is only about whether it is appropriate to allow a *ba'al mum* to perform the act — not about whether the act is technically classified as an *avodah*. Even the *tanna kamma* would agree that technically, a non-*kohen* could perform it; the *tanna kamma*'s concern is only that allowing a *ba'al mum* to do so simply *pasht nisht* — it is unseemly, even if not formally prohibited.

*Tosafot* notes that this raises a related question: if it is not an *avodah*, why does the *kohen* wear *bigdei kehunah* at all? This leads into a separate *sugya* about whether *bigdei kehunah nitnu lehanos bahem o lo nitnu lehanos bahem* — whether priestly garments may be used for purposes other than formal *avodah*. That discussion, while connected, need not be pursued here.

### Positions Compared

To summarize the landscape of opinions: Rabbi Yochanan reads the *tannaitic* dispute as narrowly as possible. The daily morning *terumat hadeshen* is uncontroversially an *avodah* — everyone agrees on this, it requires an unblemished *kohen* and all four *bigdei kehunah*. The only debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer concerns the *hotza'at hadeshen*, the occasional clearing-out, where the *tanna kamma* calls it an *avodah* and Rabbi Eliezer does not.

Reish Lakish offers the most radical view. In his reading, Rabbi Eliezer's position extends even to the daily morning *terumat hadeshen*, which he too regards as a non-*avodah*. More than that, *Tosafot* explains that according to Reish Lakish, even the *tanna kamma* does not regard *terumat hadeshen* as a full *avodah* in the sense requiring four garments — the entire dispute is only about the appropriateness of allowing a *ba'al mum* to perform an act that, technically speaking, is not a formal Temple service at all.

The Gemara, through its analysis of the *baraita*, restores the natural order: *dekulei alma avodah hi*. Everyone agrees the *terumat hadeshen* is an *avodah*; the word *yilbash* is deployed differently by different *tannaim* precisely because they all take for granted that all four garments are required.

---

## Amount of Ashes

### Rabbi Avin's Query

The Gemara now pivots from the question of the *avodah*'s status to a different question about the *terumat hadeshen*: *terumat hadeshen bekamah* — how much ash is actually removed in the daily morning ritual? This question applies specifically to the daily ritual, not the periodic clearing-out; when the altar had to be cleaned of accumulated ashes, the *kohen* simply removed as much as was necessary. But the morning *terumat hadeshen* involved a precise, defined quantity. Rabbi Avin poses the question.

### Proposed Sources

Three potential sources are proposed, each yielding a different quantity. The first is *terumat ma'aser* — the *terumah* that the *levi'im* separate from their *ma'aser*, which constitutes one-tenth of one-tenth, a tithe of the tithe. Perhaps the morning *terumat hadeshen* similarly involves one-tenth of the ashes on the altar. The second proposed source is *terumat Midyan*, the allocation set aside from the spoils of the war against Midyan, which was apportioned at one-fiftieth for one group and one-five-hundredth for another. Perhaps the ash removal follows one of these fractions. *Tosafot* notes that ordinary *terumah* (the standard separation from grain) and *challah* are not considered, since those carry no fixed proportion — one may give more or less — whereas the above two sources involve specific, fixed quantities, making them more plausible analogues.

### Kometz Measure

The resolution is provided by a *baraita* of Rabbi Chiya. The Torah uses the word *veheirim* — "he shall lift" — in the context of the *terumat hadeshen*, and the same word *veheirim* appears in connection with the *kometz* of the *mincha* offering, where the *kohen* takes a handful from the flour. By means of a *gezerah shavah*, the measure for the ash removal is derived from the *kometz* of the *mincha*: just as the *kohen* takes a handful (*kometz*) of the *mincha*, so too he removes a handful's worth of ash in the morning *terumat hadeshen*. As Rashi notes, since one cannot plunge a hand into the still-hot coals and embers of the altar fire, the *kohen* estimates the equivalent of a *kometz* — according to Rashi, at least a *kometz* — and removes that amount, placing it beside the ramp.

---

## Four Avodat Categories

### Rav's Four Avodot

Having established that the *terumat hadeshen* is a genuine *avodah*, the Gemara now moves to a broader and consequential question: not merely whether ash removal is an *avodah*, but what category of *avodah* it belongs to. Rav introduces a classification: *arba avodos zar chayav aleihem mita* — there are four Temple services for which a non-*kohen* (*zar*) who performs them incurs *heavenly* death (*mita bidei shamayim*). The Torah states: *vehazar hakarev yumat* — "the foreigner who draws close shall die." While it is clear that a *zar* may not perform any Temple service at all, there is a distinction between lesser violations (which are forbidden but do not carry the death penalty) and the most weighty category of violations that the verse specifically assigns a capital sanction.

### The Four Listed

Rav's four are: *zerikat hadam* (throwing the blood of a sacrifice against the altar), *haktarah* (burning — whether limbs of an *olah*, the innards of any *korban*, or the burning of incense), *nisuch hamayim* (the water libation performed on *Sukkot*), and *nisuch hayayin* (the wine libation that accompanied any *korban* requiring a *mincha*). These four, and only these four, carry the sanction of death for a *zar* who performs them.

### Levi Adds HaDeshen

Levi disagrees with Rav's list and adds a fifth: *af terumat hadeshen* — even the daily morning ash removal. This is a striking position. Earlier in the *sugya*, Reish Lakish had argued that a non-*kohen* could technically perform the *terumat hadeshen*. Now Levi goes to the opposite extreme: not only is *terumat hadeshen* an *avodah* (consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's view, which the Gemara endorsed), but it belongs to the most severe category, such that a *zar* who performs it is deserving of death. As the Gemara notes, Levi also taught this in a *baraita*: *af terumat hadeshen* is included among the *avodot* for which a *zar* incurs *mita*.

---

## Rav's Two Criteria

### Avodah Tammah Defined

The Gemara now probes the reasoning behind these positions. *Mai ta'ama d'Rav* — what is Rav's reason for limiting the capital category to four and excluding *terumat hadeshen*?

The answer is built on two separate *derashot* from the same *pasuk*: *ve-atah u-vanecha itcha tishmeru et kehunaschem lechol devar hamizbe'ach umibeis laparochet va'avadetem avodat matanah etein et kehunaschem vehazar hakarev yumat* — "And you and your sons with you shall guard your priesthood for every matter of the altar and for what is within the curtain, and you shall serve — a service of gift I give your priesthood — and the stranger who draws near shall die."

The word *va'avadetem* — "and you shall serve" — yields the first criterion through a *derashah*: *avodah tammah* — a completing service, one that is the final stage of a process. This excludes interim services. One might ask: surely *kabalat hadam* (receiving the blood) and *holachat hadam* (carrying the blood to the altar) are also services that require a *kohen* — why are they not on the list? The answer is that those are intermediate stages. Only the final act — the act after which nothing further remains to be done with that element — qualifies as *avodah tammah* and carries the capital sanction for a *zar*. Throwing the blood on the altar is the final stage of the blood service; burning the sacrificial portions is the final stage of the fire service; the libations are final acts unto themselves.

### Placing Not Removing

The second criterion is derived from the words *avodat matanah* — "a service of giving/placing." The play is on the root *natan* — to give, to place. The *derashah*: *matanah litein* — an *avodah* that involves placing something. *Velo avodat siluk* — and not an *avodah* that involves removing something. The *terumat hadeshen*, though it may satisfy the first criterion (it is a final act with nothing further required of those ashes), fails the second: it is an act of removal, not of placement.

### HaDeshen Is Siluk

Rav therefore holds that *terumat hadeshen* does not belong to the capital category, not because it lacks finality but because it is *avodat siluk* — a service of removal — rather than *avodat matanah* — a service of placing. Both criteria must be met: the service must be a concluding act (*avodah tammah*) and it must involve placing something, not removing it (*avodat matanah velo avodat siluk*). *Terumat hadeshen* satisfies only one of the two; it therefore stands outside the capital category.

---

## Levi's Position

### All Altar Matters

Levi, who includes *terumat hadeshen* in the capital category, reads the *pasuk* differently. He focuses on the phrase *lechol devar hamizbe'ach* — "for every matter of the altar." For Levi, this phrase is expansive: it encompasses all final-stage Temple services relating to the altar, whether they involve placing or removing. *Terumat hadeshen* is unquestionably connected to the altar and is unquestionably a concluding act — and that, according to Levi, is sufficient.

### Scope Debate

The Gemara presses the dispute. If Levi reads *lechol devar hamizbe'ach* as including all altar-related *avodot* whether of placement or removal, what, in Levi's view, does *avodat matanah* teach? For Rav, *avodat matanah* restricts the category to placement-*avodot*; if Levi does not use it for this restriction, what does he do with it?

Levi's answer: *avodat matanah* is not deployed to distinguish placing from removing; instead, its teaching is redirected to the phrase *umibeis laparochet* — "and within the curtain." Rav uses the phrase *lechol devar hamizbe'ach* to include things that are not done on the altar itself but are still final-stage placement-*avodot* — specifically, *sheva hazayot shebifnim veshebimetzora*, the seven sprinklings performed inside the *kodesh hakodashim* on *Yom Kippur* and the sprinklings of oil associated with the *metzora*'s purification. These involve placing (sprinkling) but not on the altar proper. According to Rav, the phrase *lechol devar hamizbe'ach* extends the capital category to include them even though they are not performed on the altar.

Levi, however, derives this extension from *devar vechol devar* — from the fact that the verse uses *kol* ("every") in the phrase *lechol devar hamizbe'ach*. The word *kol* includes the sprinklings not on the altar. This frees *avodat matanah* in Levi's reading to serve a different function: establishing that within the enclosed interior spaces (*mibeis laparochet*), only placement-*avodot*, not removal-*avodot*, carry the capital sanction. Outside, *terumat hadeshen*-style removal is included in the capital category; inside, only placement qualifies.

Rav, for his part, does not accept a *derashah* from *devar vechol devar* — the doubling of the noun to teach two inclusions. He does not expound the *kol* as a separate teaching; for him, *avodat matanah* does the entire work of excluding removal, and the verse's scope does not change depending on interior versus exterior location.

### Reconciliation

The Gemara raises a formal objection to Levi's reading. If *lechol devar hamizbe'ach* (general) is followed by *avodat matanah* (specific), one should apply the hermeneutical principle of *klal ufrat*: the general statement is limited by the specific one that follows it. A general statement followed by a specification means only what the specification includes — namely, placement, not removal. How, then, can Levi insist that *lechol devar hamizbe'ach* includes removal-*avodot* like *terumat hadeshen*?

The Gemara's answer turns on the syntax of the *pasuk*. The phrase *umibeis laparochet va'avadetem avodat matanah* connects *avodat matanah* specifically to *mibeis laparochet* — the interior space within the curtain. It is only there — within the *heichal* and *kodesh hakodashim* — that the specification of *avodat matanah* (placement, not removal) applies. Outside, the general phrase *lechol devar hamizbe'ach* stands unqualified, and removal-*avodot* are included.

But the Gemara immediately presses: if Levi restricts *avodat matanah* to *mibeis laparochet*, should he not equally restrict *avodah tammah* to *mibeis laparochet*? If *va'avadetem* teaches *avodah tammah*, and Levi reads *va'avadetem* as connected specifically to *umibeis laparochet*, then the requirement of *avodah tammah* would only apply inside — meaning outside, even an intermediate-stage service could generate capital liability for a *zar*. That cannot be right.

The Gemara resolves this with a structural observation: *va'avadetem hadar arbei kra* — the *va'avadetem* doubles back and reconnects to the broader context. The *vav* (the conjunctive "and") at the beginning of *va'avadetem* ties it to the wider framework of the *pasuk*, maintaining *avodah tammah* as a universal criterion. The restriction of *avodat matanah* to *mibeis laparochet* is a bracketing specific to that phrase alone; *avodah tammah*, by virtue of the *vav*, remains a general requirement throughout.

The upshot is as follows. Rav has two criteria that apply universally: the service must be a concluding act (*avodah tammah*), and it must involve placement (*avodat matanah*), not removal (*avodat siluk*). Levi has one universal criterion — *avodah tammah* — and one criterion that applies only inside the roofed interior spaces: within the *heichal* and *kodesh hakodashim*, the service must also be placement, not removal. Outside, *avodah tammah* alone suffices, and *terumat hadeshen*, which is the final act of ash-removal from the altar, qualifies.

---

## Menorah & Avodah Tes (II)

### Menorah Steps

The Gemara now tests the *avodah tammah* criterion by working through the preparation of the *menorah* step by step, asking at each stage whether that stage constitutes the concluding act.

Rava poses the question: *avodat siluk beheichal mahu* — what is the rule for a removal-*avodah* performed within the *heichal* (as distinct from the *kodesh hakodashim*)? Is the *heichal* treated like the interior (*mibeis laparochet*), requiring both *avodah tammah* and the placement criterion? Or is it treated like the exterior (*bachutz*), where *avodah tammah* alone suffices and even removal can generate liability? The Gemara concludes from the verse's language — *umibeis laparochet*, which can be read as the combined *umibeit* — that the interior criterion applies to both the *kodesh hakodashim* and the *heichal*. Anywhere under roof within the *mikdash* building, a removal-*avodah* would not qualify for the capital category.

This has a direct application to the *menorah*, whose service takes place in the *heichal*.

### Cleaning to Lighting

The Gemara now proceeds through the stages of *menorah* preparation. After cleaning the *menorah*, the *kohen* places new wicks — should a *zar* be liable for this? No: there is still the placing of the oil to follow. Should he be liable for placing the oil? No: there is still the *hadlakah*, the actual lighting, to follow. At each stage the same logic applies — *it is not yet done*. The process continues until one arrives at the lighting itself.

### Lighting Not Avodah

When the Gemara finally arrives at *hidlik le-hayyav* — should a *zar* be liable for lighting the *menorah*? — the answer is both surprising and striking: *hadlakah lav avodah hi* — the lighting of the *menorah* is not an *avodah*. This is counterintuitive in the extreme. The lighting of the *menorah* is the moment of the *menorah*'s purpose; a whole *parasha* begins *beha'alotecha et haneirot el mul penei hamenorah*. Yet precisely there, the Torah does not specify *benei Aharon hakohanim*; nowhere in the context of the *menorah* lighting does the Torah restrict the act to *kohanim*. And because it is not formally classified as an *avodah*, a *zar*'s performing it does not carry the capital sanction — and more than that, as the Rambam will explain, a *zar* may perform it outright.

### Hatzat Proof

A *baraita* confirms the distinction. The verse states: *venatnu benei Aharon hakohen esh al hamizbe'ach ve-archu etzim al ha-esh* — "and the sons of Aaron the *kohen* shall place fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire." There, the Torah says *benei Aharon hakohanim*. The *baraita* derives: *limed al hatzatat alita she-lo te-he ela bekohen kasher uvicheli sharet* — this teaches that the kindling of the initial twig-fire (*hatzatat alita*) must be performed by an unblemished *kohen* using sanctified vessels. The kindling of the altar-fire twigs is an *avodah*. The lighting of the *menorah* is not.

---

## Rambam Synthesis

### Wood as Haktarah

The Rambam draws out the full implications of the Gemara's analysis. He rules that *hakatarah* — the burning of sacrificial material — encompasses not only the offering itself but also the wood arranged for the fire. *Ketzad haktarah? Vehamesidar shenei gezirei etzim al hama'arachah harei hu kemaktir evarim vehayav mita she-ha-etzim korban hen* — one who arranges the two logs of wood on the pyre is like one who burns the sacrificial limbs, and if a *zar* does so he is deserving of death, because the wood itself has the status of a *korban*. Elsewhere the Gemara even raises the question of salting the wood just as one salts sacrificial offerings, so closely is the wood identified with the sacrificial act.

---

## Menorah & Avodah Tes (II)

### Light vs. Burning

The Gemara's resolution of the *menorah* paradox turns on a fundamental distinction. The lighting of altar-wood twigs (*hatzatat alita*) is part of the burning process; it participates in the *haktarah* of the offerings that will be consumed by that fire. Its purpose is to burn. By contrast, the lighting of the *menorah* — *hadlakah* — is not aimed at burning anything. The wicks and oil are consumed, yes, but consumption is merely the necessary means; the purpose is *light*. The *menorah*'s function is illumination, not combustion, and because the act of lighting aims at creating light rather than performing a burning-service, it is not an *avodah* in the halachic sense that would restrict it to an unblemished *kohen* performing it under the capital sanction.

---

## Rambam Synthesis (II)

### Non-Kohen May Light

The Rambam takes this Gemara to its logical conclusion, going further than the Gemara's bare statement. He rules: *vechen hadlakat haneirot kesherah bezarim* — the lighting of the *menorah* is valid even if performed by a non-*kohen*. This is not merely an observation that a *zar* is not liable for capital punishment if he lights it; the Rambam holds that *lechatchilah*, a *zar* may legitimately perform this act. The *kohen* must perform the cleaning (*hatavah*) of the *menorah*, which is an *avodah*, but the actual kindling may be done by anyone.

### Removed & Lit Outside

The Rambam extends this ruling even further. *Vehotziam lachutz mutar lezar lehadlikan* — the *menorah* may be taken out of the *heichal* and a non-*kohen* may light it there. One would never have imagined that the *menorah* could be lit outside its proper place in the *heichal*, yet the Rambam rules that this too is permitted, precisely because *hadlakah* is not an *avodah* — the locational requirements for *avodot* simply do not apply to it. The Rambam derives this directly from the Gemara's determination that lighting the *menorah* is not classified as a Temple service at all.

---

## Wood-Stacking Test

### Wood Logs Question

Having established that the *hatzatat alita* (kindling the altar-twigs) is an *avodah* while *hadlakah* (lighting the *menorah*) is not, the Gemara turns to the arrangement of the two logs (*shnei gezirei etzim*) placed on the *ma'arachah* each morning. The question is: does this act constitute an *avodah tammah* — a concluding, final-stage service — or is it an interim step?

---

## Wood-Stacking Test (II)

### Two Interpretations

The Gemara records a dispute on this point. One position holds that the arrangement of the two logs is an *avodah tammah* — it is the culmination of the fire-preparation process. From the perspective of the fire itself, once the wood is arranged the fire-service is complete; the *korbanot* that will subsequently be offered are a separate process. On this view, a *zar* who performs this act is *chayav* (as the position of Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan). The second position holds that the wood arrangement is only an interim step — it is preparatory to the burning of the *korbanot*, which is the true purpose and conclusion. The wood is never an end in itself; it exists only to receive and consume the offerings. This position reads the entire sequence — wood arrangement, carrying of limbs, burning of limbs — as a single continuous process, and the wood arrangement falls in the middle of it.

---

## Baraita Support

### Rav's Baraita

The Gemara closes by noting that each position — Rav's and Levi's — finds support in a *baraita*. A *baraita* aligning with Rav lists the *avodot* for which a *zar* incurs *mita* without including *terumat hadeshen*: *zerikat hadam*, whether performed inside the *heichal*, within the *kodesh hakodashim*, or at various other points; the squirting of blood in the bird-*chatat* (*hamaza bechatas ha'of*); the pressing-out of the remaining blood (*hamimatzei*); the burning of the bird-*olah* (*hamaktir b'olas ha'of*) — these being variants of the blood and burning categories; and the libation (*hamenasech*) of three *log* of water or three *log* of wine. This list corresponds precisely to Rav's four categories (blood-throwing, burning, water libation, wine libation) without adding *terumat hadeshen*.

### Levi's Baraita

A second *baraita* aligns with Levi. This *baraita* places *terumat hadeshen* at the head of the list — *hamayrim et hadeshen* — and proceeds to include *sheva hazayot shebifnim veshebimetzora* (the seven sprinklings of blood performed inside the *kodesh hakodashim* on *Yom Kippur*, and the oil sprinklings of the *metzora*), and *hamaleh al gabei mizbe'ach bein davar kasher bein davar pasul* — one who burns something on the altar, whether the item is valid or invalid, provided it is something that, once placed on the altar, is permitted to remain there.

The *sugya* thus concludes with the two positions each anchored in *tannaitic* tradition. The underlying debate is about the scope of *avodah tammah* — how broadly or narrowly to define what constitutes a "completing service" — and whether *avodat siluk* (removal) can ever meet that definition outside the interior of the *mikdash* building. And the great *chiddush* with which the *daf* ends: the lighting of the *menorah*, which one would have supposed to be the quintessential *avodah*, turns out not to be an *avodah* at all.

---

---

# Yoma 25

## Context & Setup

### Daf Overview

Daf 25 begins approximately ten lines from the bottom of the preceding page — just before the passage where the lines widen and the words *lama mafisim* appear. In some editions of the Gemara this passage is set off by two dots, indicating a new discussion, while in others it is not. The reason for this ambiguity is that the Gemara is not returning to quote a new Mishnah; rather, it is resuming an earlier thread. The bulk of the material on daf 24b had been devoted to the question of what constitutes an *avoda*, whether a *kohen gadol* or a non-*kohen* performed it, and the attendant question of *chiyuv mita*. That detour addressed the *trumat hadeshen* from multiple angles — its timing, the requirement to change garments, whether the *hotzat hadeshen* and the *trumat hadeshen* are themselves *avodot*, how much ash is removed, and whether a *zar* who performs the *trumat hadeshen* incurs the death penalty. Now, having concluded that discussion, the Gemara returns to the original subject: the lottery held in connection with the *trumat hadeshen* during the ordinary days of the year — not on Yom Kippur.

It is worth noting in passing that the *rishonim* debate whether on Yom Kippur itself the *kohen gadol* performs the *trumat hadeshen* or whether another *kohen* does so, since the *trumat hadeshen* is performed at night and the question is whether the requirement that all the day's *avodot* be done by the *kohen gadol* extends to this nighttime service. That debate, however, pertains to Yom Kippur; the present discussion concerns the rest of the year.

### Lottery Context

The prior material established that a *payis* — a lottery — was held to determine who would perform the *trumat hadeshen*. That lottery touched off a long chain of associated *halachot*. Now the Gemara returns: *lama mafisim* — why would they conduct the lottery at all? The Gemara swiftly pivots: the real question is not why a lottery exists but why it is done four separate times rather than once at the beginning of the day.

---

## Purpose of Lotteries

### Four Lotteries

The deeper question the Gemara raises is: given that several fixed services are assigned by lottery each day — one lottery for the *trumat hadeshen*, another for the *tamid*, a third for the *ketores*, and so forth — why not conduct a single lottery at the outset of the day and assign all the regular daily duties in one stroke? Why are there four separate lottery events?

### Commotion & Excitement

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *kedai lehargish kol ha'azara* — in order to create a commotion throughout the entire Temple courtyard. The purpose of repeating the lottery process multiple times is to generate excitement, movement, and a sense of heightened significance. Each new lottery would send a wave of activity through the *Beis HaMikdash*: priests running, officers assembling, the entire *azara* stirred into motion. Rabbi Yochanan derives this from the verse in Psalms (55:15): *asher yachdav namtik sod, b'veis Elohim nehalech b'ragesh* — "together we would share sweet counsel; in the house of God we would walk with commotion." The *ragesh*, the commotion, is understood to reflect the animated, purposeful energy that was meant to pervade the Temple.

### Verse Analysis

It is worth observing the *pshat* of the verse alongside the *drash*. The word *sod* in the verse — which can mean "secret" or "counsel" — is parallel to *yachdav*, "together," suggesting that *sod* here refers to a gathering of wise and understanding people, a *sod chachamim v'nevonim*. That is the *pshat*: a group convening together in the house of God, moving with commotion. The *drash* that the Gemara invokes focuses on the *ragesh*, using it to explain the halakhic requirement for multiple lotteries.

There is also something worth observing in the juxtaposition of *sod* and *ragesh* even in the *drash*: the combination of something mysterious or esoteric alongside all this movement and commotion creates a powerful sense of importance and gravity. While the Gemara itself does not draw that comparison, the contrast is striking — unlike the secret rituals of the surrounding nations, which derived their mystique from deliberate concealment, the *Beis HaMikdash* achieved a related effect through transparency paired with animated ceremony. Indeed, the lottery ceremony was conducted inside a chamber rather than in the open *azara*, so it was not entirely visible to all — a point that reinforces the element of *sod* even while the *ragesh* was public.

---

## Clothing Dispute

### Weekday vs. Priestly

The Gemara next addresses the question *bameh mafisim* — in what garments did the *kohanim* stand when they participated in the lottery? Rav Nachman holds they wore *bigdei chol*, their ordinary weekday clothes. Rav Sheshet holds they wore *bigdei kodesh*, their priestly vestments. The dispute is not framed around a principled question of whether *bigdei kehuna* are required or permitted for non-*avoda* activity; the arguments on both sides are grounded entirely in human psychology.

### Rav Nachman Rationale

Rav Nachman reasons: if all the *kohanim* were already standing in their *bigdei kehuna*, then a bully — *ba'alei zero'ot* — who did not win the lottery could simply push forward and perform the service before anyone could stop him. Being already dressed and ready, he could race to the *mizbeach* and perform the *trumat hadeshen* before the proper winner could assert himself. Having everyone in weekday garments creates a necessary delay: the winner must first go change, and during that interval the officers can ensure the correct person proceeds. The weekday clothing, in other words, serves as a practical safeguard against unauthorized seizure of the *avoda*.

### Rav Sheshet Rationale

Rav Sheshet reasons the opposite way. If the *kohanim* are in their weekday garments, then the winner of the lottery — because the *avoda* is so precious and dear to him, *agav chavivuteih* — will be too excited to wait to change and will run up to perform the service without putting on his *bigdei kehuna*. To prevent this, everyone should already be dressed in *bigdei kehuna* from the outset. The two positions thus represent two different analyses of human nature: Rav Nachman worries about the aggressive usurper; Rav Sheshet worries about the overeager winner.

### Tamid Source

Rav Nachman cites a source from the Mishnah in Tamid. As Tosafot notes, that Mishnah appears immediately after the passage describing the lottery for the *trumat hadeshen*, making it contextually relevant.
