The verse in Vayikra reads: *u-fashat et bigdei habad asher lavash be-vo'o el hakodesh ve-hini'cham sham verachatz et besaro bamayim umekadesh uvein ha'azarah v'lavash et begadav* — he shall remove the linen garments he wore when he entered the holy place, leave them there, bathe his body in water in a holy place, and put on his garments. The *Gemara* thus has: *u-fashat, rachatz, v'lavash* — take off, immerse, put on.

Rabbi Meir's principle is *makish pshitah le-levishah*: he draws an analogy between taking off and putting on. The same way that, when putting on the garments, the *Kohen* first dresses and then washes his hands — that is, the washing follows the putting on — so too when taking off the garments, he first removes them and then washes his hands. The washing after taking off comes *after* the act of undressing.

The *Rabbanan* articulate the analogy differently: *mah levishah keshehu lavush mekadesh* — the same way that when he performs the washing associated with *levishah* he is still dressed (he has just put the garments on), *af pshitah keshehu lavush mekadesh* — even when he performs the washing associated with *pshitah* he is still dressed. In other words, the washing for taking off the garments occurs *before* he removes them, while he is still wearing them.

Both opinions thus agree that neither washing relates to the *bigdei chol*: the first washing is about the old *kodesh* garments being removed, not about the new garments being put on. Accordingly, there is no hand-washing at the very first transition, when the *Kohen Gadol* moves from his weekday clothing to the *bigdei zahav* — because at that point there are no *bigdei kodesh* being taken off. The sole debate is the timing: does the washing for taking off precede or follow the act of removal?

This resolves the students' challenge. They had assumed Rabbi Meir's position was that two washings bracket the donning of new garments — one before and one after. Rav Pappa demonstrates that this is a misreading. According to Rabbi Meir, the two washings associated with any given *mikvah* immersion are: one for taking off the previous *bigdei kodesh* (done *after* removing them) and one for putting on the new *bigdei kodesh* (done *after* dressing). Both washings still occur — one flanking the *mikvah* on either side — but their logic is entirely about the garments being changed, not about preparation for the new ones. At the very first transition, since the *Kohen Gadol* is removing *bigdei chol*, not *bigdei kodesh*, even Rabbi Meir would agree there is no hand-washing before the *mikvah*.

### Baraisa Support

The students push back against Rav Pappa's resolution. *Umi matzis amart hachi* — how can you say that? They cite a *Baraisa*: *pirsu sadin shel butz beino uvein ha'am, pashat veyarad v'taval, ala v'nistapeig, hevi'u lo bigdei zahav, v'lavash v'kidesh yadav v'raglav* — this is the view of the *Rabbanan*. Then: *Rabbi Meir omer, pashat v'kidesh yadav v'raglav, veyarad v'taval, ala v'nistapeig, hevi'u lo bigdei zahav, v'lavash v'kidesh yadav v'raglav* — Rabbi Meir says he took off his clothes and *then* washed his hands, descended and immersed, arose and dried himself, was brought the gold garments, dressed, and washed his hands.

The students understand this *Baraisa* to be describing the first change of garments — from *bigdei chol* to *bigdei zahav*. If so, Rabbi Meir explicitly requires a hand-washing before going to the *mikvah* even at this first transition, which contradicts Rav Pappa's claim that no washing would occur at the *chol* → *zahav* transition. This *Baraisa*, they argue, proves that Rabbi Meir's washing *does* relate to the new garments, not merely to the old *kodesh* garments being removed.

### Final Reconciliation

Rav Pappa's response — or rather the *Gemara*'s acceptance of the challenge — is captured in the terse rejoinder: *ei tanya, tanya* — if it is taught in a *Baraisa*, it is taught. The *Baraisa* is authoritative, and if it explicitly places a hand-washing at the first transition according to Rabbi Meir, that must be accepted.

The final picture, then, is as follows. According to Rav Pappa's analysis, both the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Meir agree that the hand-washings relate to the *bigdei kodesh* being removed and donned, not to the *bigdei chol*. The sole dispute is one of timing: the *Rabbanan* hold that the washing for taking off *bigdei kodesh* occurs while one is still dressed, whereas Rabbi Meir holds it occurs after the garments have been removed. The *Baraisa*, however, introduces a further complication by recording that even at the first transition, from weekday clothing to *bigdei zahav*, Rabbi Meir requires a hand-washing before descending to the *mikvah*. Whether this means Rabbi Meir's position is in fact about preparing for the new *bigdei kodesh*, or whether it reflects some other dimension of his reasoning, the *Baraisa* stands as it has been taught.

---

---

# Yoma 39

## Context & Daily Order

### Daf 39 Setup

Daf 39 opens a new *perek*, and it is worth pausing to situate ourselves within the broader structure of the tractate. The *mishnayot* of Yoma have been doing a great deal of pulling in and out — offering framework about what happens during the rest of the year alongside the specific *avodot* of Yom Kippur. We discussed the lots drawn to distribute the various daily *avodot*, the *Kohen Gadol* going to the *mikvah*, the broader rule that anyone entering the *Beit HaMikdash* immersed, and then returned to the drawing of the lots and how they were specially fashioned. The *mishnah* states that the lots were originally made of *eshkora* wood, and then notes that *Ben Gamla asah shel zahav* — Ben Gamla had them made from gold — which led to a wider discussion about individuals who contributed special things to the *Beit HaMikdash* and those who withheld their talents from contributing in a more expansive way. That entire discussion was a digression. Now we are genuinely entering the stride of the *avodah* itself, and the pull-backs to the wider world of the year will diminish significantly as we move forward. The new *perek* opens with the words *tarof b'kalfi*.

### Tamid Service Review

Before arriving at the lot-drawing, it is helpful to recall the sequence of what has already taken place in the morning. The *Kohen Gadol* first performs *shechitah* on the *tamid* and catches its blood. He then enters and performs *zerikah* of the blood on the *mizbe'ach*. After that, he goes in to tend to the *menorah*, burn the *ketoret*, and complete the work of the *menorah*, and then, upon exiting, he places the *evarim* of the *tamid* on the *mizbe'ach*. This entire opening sequence — the *tamid*, the *ketoret*, the *menorah*, and the placing of the *evarim* on the *kevesh* — is performed while wearing the *bigdei zahav*. That constitutes the first stage of what will be five changes of clothing — three in *bigdei zahav* and two in *bigdei lavan*.

### Clothing Changes

Having completed stage one in *bigdei zahav*, the *Kohen Gadol* transitions into *bigdei lavan* for stage two. In this second stage, wearing the white garments, he stands before his *par* — whose head is oriented toward the west while it faces south — and performs the *viduy*. This *viduy* is among the first acts performed in *bigdei lavan*.

### Location Setup

Having completed the *viduy* over his *par*, the *Kohen Gadol* now moves to the location for the lot-drawing. The *mishnah* states: *ba lo l'mizrach azara l'tzfon ha'mizbe'ach* — he proceeds to the eastern section of the *azara*, to the north of the *mizbe'ach*. It is here, still in *bigdei lavan*, that he will draw lots over the two *se'irim* and proceed with the lottery.

---

## Lot Drawing Process

### Tarof B'Kalfi

The *perek* opens with the procedure itself. *Tarof b'kalfi* — he mixes around within the box that holds the lots. *V'he'ela shenei goralot* — he draws out two lots. One is inscribed *lashem*, for God, and one *la'azazel*, for Azazel. The act of mixing and drawing is not merely procedural — as we will see, the *Gemara* will probe why mixing is required at all and what the properties of the box must be.

### Sgan & Rosh Beit Av

Two figures stand alongside the *Kohen Gadol* during this ceremony: *hasgan mimino* — the *sgan*, the assistant *Kohen Gadol*, on his right — and *v'rosh beit av mismolo* — the head of the *beit av*, the priestly family whose day Yom Kippur falls on, on his left. The *sgan* functions essentially as the vice *Kohen Gadol*. His primary role is readiness — should the *Kohen Gadol* become disqualified, the *sgan* steps in to serve in his place. Beyond that, the *sgan*'s regular function carries little independent weight, which will become significant later. The *rosh beit av*, by contrast, has significance only on this one day, corresponding to his family's weekly *mishmar* divided by days.

### Hand Signaling

After the lots are drawn, the side on which the lot inscribed *lashem* appears determines the subsequent ceremony. *Im ala shem al biyamino* — if the lot bearing God's name came into the *Kohen Gadol*'s right hand, which was the auspicious *siman*, the *sgan* standing on his right would say: *ishi Kohen Gadol, hagbe yemincha* — Mr. *Kohen Gadol*, raise up your right hand. *V'im ala shem al bismolo* — if it came into his left hand, the *rosh beit av* on his left would say: *ishi Kohen Gadol, hagbe smolcha* — Mr. *Kohen Gadol*, raise up your left hand. In this way, the lot bearing God's name is elevated publicly, making clear which goat it designates.

### Placement on Goats

Following the signal, the *Kohen Gadol* places the lots onto the two goats. This is grounded in the *pasuk*: *v'natan al shenei hase'irim goralot* — literally placing the lots upon them. The goats are already positioned before him in alignment with the hands in which the lots rest, so that each lot naturally rests opposite the goat it designates.

### L'Hashem Chatat

After placing the lots, the *Kohen Gadol* pronounces: *lashem chatat* — for God, a sin-offering. He does not explicitly designate the other as *la'azazel*; that is inferred. *Rabbi Yishmael* holds that he need not say *chatat* at all, but only *lashem*, because the language of the *pasuk* itself is *goral echad lashem v'goral echad la'azazel*, and further *asher ala alav hagoral lashem v'asahu chatat* — but the primary designation is *lashem*, which stands in contrast to *la'azazel*, indicating the direction of the offering rather than merely its category. Upon hearing God's explicit name, the people respond: *baruch shem kevod malchuto l'olam va'ed*.

---

## Theology of YK

### Two Goats Theme

It is worth pausing over the theological landscape that this ceremony inhabits, because it differs substantially from the way we tend to think about Yom Kippur today. If one reads the *pesukim* in the Torah carefully, the dominant theme surrounding the *Kohen Gadol*'s *par* and the *seir l'Hashem* is not personal atonement — it is the cleansing of the *mikdash* itself. The Torah articulates this directly: *v'chiper al hakodesh mitumot benei Yisrael umipisheihem l'chol chatatam* — he atones for the sanctum from the impurities of the Children of Israel and from their transgressions, all their sins. The concept of *chatat* in this context is better understood not as "sin-offering" in the narrow sense, but as a cleansing agent, much as the same term describes the offering brought by a *yoledet* or a *zav* at the end of their purification process.

The underlying metaphysical picture is this: sin, in the Torah's conception, does not merely injure the sinner. It dirties up the *mikdash* in a metaphysical sense — it creates, so to speak, stains upon the *mikdash*. Yom Kippur is therefore the once-a-year cleaning crew. The *Kohen Gadol* enters and removes all the accumulated metaphysical grime that has sullied the sacred space over the preceding year. The significance of this is profound: *v'shachanti betocham*, God dwells among the people, *hashochen itam betoch tumatam* — God is willing to tolerate the *tumah* to a degree and continue to dwell in our midst. But that *tumah* must be cleansed annually for God's presence to remain. The focus, then, is national — the continued indwelling of the divine presence within the nation — rather than the individual's personal atonement.

The *seir la'azazel*, by contrast, is the vehicle for addressing individual sin: *v'nasa alav et kol avonotam el eretz gezeira* — it bears upon itself all their iniquities to a desolate land. The personal dimension of Yom Kippur, the one most prominent in our religious consciousness, is concentrated in the scapegoat.

### Blood Detergent

One scholar's formulation captures this beautifully: the blood is the metaphysical agent, the detergent. The blood, as the seat of life, is the medium through which *tumah* is removed. This understanding reinforces the point that the sacrificial blood rites of the *Kohen Gadol* on Yom Kippur are fundamentally about cleansing the sacred space, not about individual absolution in the first instance.

### L'Hashem Focus

This is why the emphasis throughout the *mishnah* and the broader ritual falls so heavily on the *seir l'Hashem* — the one designated *lashem chatat*. The right hand is preferred for it, the announcement of *lashem chatat* belongs to it, the *la'azazel* goat is not even explicitly named in the proclamation. It may be honest to acknowledge, at least personally, that in popular consciousness the attention often gravitates toward the *seir la'azazel* — the dramatic image of the goat being sent off the cliff, the red string turning white as confirmation of atonement. But the Torah's own emphasis and the *mishnah*'s structure both place the weight on the *seir l'Hashem* and the *par hachatat*, the instruments of the *mikdash*'s purification.

### Lots Problem

This raises a genuinely puzzling philosophical question. If Yom Kippur is about owning responsibility, about not blaming forces beyond one's control, about the exercise of freedom and choice — what is the significance of drawing lots, an act that appears to introduce randomness into the most consequential ceremony of the year? This question connects to an earlier theme in the tractate: lots are used daily to distribute the *avodot* among the *kohanim*. The centrality of the *goral* in both contexts deserves reflection. One might argue, as has been suggested, that what appears to be chance is in fact *siyata dishmaya* — divine guidance — just as in the Book of Jonah the falling of the lot is understood not as arbitrary luck but as the revelation of divine providence. But exactly how that meaning translates into the theological substance of the Yom Kippur *avodah* remains an open question, one worth pursuing further.

---

## Lot Debate

### Why Shake Box

The *Gemara* asks: *lama itraf b'kalfi?* Why is it necessary to mix up the lots in the box? Why not simply reach in and draw one? The answer is: *ki heichi d'lo nechavein v'lishkol* — so that the *Kohen Gadol* should not intentionally try to draw the lot inscribed *lashem* into his right hand by feeling for it.

### Box Properties

*Amar Rava*: the *kalfi* was made of wood and was not sanctified — *shel etz hayeta v'shel chol hayeta*. Note the contrast: the lots themselves, as the earlier *mishnah* established, were made of gold by Ben Gamla. The box, however, was neither gold nor silver nor sanctified. Furthermore, *v'eina machazeket ela shtei yadayim* — it was only large enough to fit two hands. Ravina probes these properties. He understands the two-hand constraint: *ki heichi d'lo nechavein v'lishkol* — a tight space prevents the *Kohen Gadol* from maneuvering to feel the inscription on a lot before grasping it. (It also anticipates the other opinion, discussed below, in which both the *sgan* and the *Kohen Gadol* insert their right hands simultaneously — which would require room for exactly two hands.)

### Unsanctified Box

But why was the box not sanctified? *Nikadshe* — let it be sanctified! The *Gemara* answers: *im ken havei lei kli sharet* — if it were sanctified, it would become a *kli sharet*. And *kli sharet d'etz lo avidnan* — we do not make *klei sharet* from wood. Fine, then make it from gold or silver and sanctify it. The *Gemara* responds: *HaTorah chasa al mamonam shel Yisrael* — the Torah has concern for the money of Israel; it does not wish us to expend unnecessary funds. This principle is derived from the case of the *metzora*: the Torah requires the *metzora* to clear out his house before the *kohen* inspects it for the plague, even though, were the vessels found impure, most could simply be taken to the *mikvah*. The rabbis explain that this is done to protect the *metzora*'s pottery vessels, which cannot be purified once declared *tamei*. The inference is that the Torah goes to extraordinary lengths to protect even small amounts of money, even for someone who may well have deserved his condition.

This answer is admittedly puzzling. The *Beit HaMikdash* was furnished throughout with gold and silver. The *Kohen Gadol*'s white garments alone cost twelve or eighteen *maneh*. To invoke financial concern as the reason for one small wooden box — when the lots themselves are gold — seems incongruous. One possible resolution, noted during the discussion, is the distinction between private donations and public funds: the lots of Ben Gamla were made from his personal wealth, whereas the box was maintained from the public treasury, and the Torah is particularly attentive to communal funds. Whether that distinction fully resolves the tension may be debated.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

The *Gemara* now introduces a *tannaitic* dispute. *Matnitin d'lo k'hai tanna* — our *mishnah* does not accord with the following *tanna*. In a *braisa*, *Rabbi Yehuda* says in the name of *Rabbi Eliezer*: *hasgan v'Kohen Gadol machnisin yadeihen b'kalfi* — both the *sgan* and the *Kohen Gadol* insert their hands into the box. According to this view, it is not the *Kohen Gadol* alone drawing one lot in his right and one in his left; rather, each man inserts his right hand and draws one lot apiece. The lot that emerges in the *Kohen Gadol*'s right hand is still the more significant, but the *sgan* actively participates in the drawing itself.

The procedure under this view unfolds as follows: if the lot inscribed *lashem* comes up in the right hand of the *Kohen Gadol*, the *sgan* says *ishi Kohen Gadol, hagbei yemincha* — raise your right hand. If, however, it comes up in the right hand of the *sgan*, then the *rosh beit av* speaks — not to the *sgan*, but to the *Kohen Gadol*: *dvar milcha* — say your words. The *Kohen Gadol* then pronounces *lashem chatat* over the animal positioned opposite the *sgan*'s hand, and he retains the role of designation even when the drawing itself was the *sgan*'s.

### Non-Avodah Role

This arrangement raises a significant question that requires attention before the *Gemara*'s own resolution. According to the first version in our *mishnah*, the *Kohen Gadol* holds one lot in his right and one in his left. But *avodah* performed with the left hand is *pasul*. Additionally, on Yom Kippur all *avodot* must be performed by the *Kohen Gadol* himself — yet Rabbi Eliezer's version has the *sgan* performing part of the act. How can either version work?

Rashi addresses this, noting in what may be a later gloss that the drawing of the lots must be understood as not constituting an *avodah* at all — it is what might be termed a *hechsher avodah*, a preparatory act that enables the *avodah* proper but does not itself carry the formal status of *avodah*. This explains why it can be performed with the *Kohen Gadol*'s left hand or with partial participation from the *sgan* without formal disqualification. Yet this framing creates its own conceptual tension: if the act lacks *avodah* status, can it still be *meakev* — can its omission invalidate the service? And conversely, does labeling something a *hechsher avodah* necessarily remove it from the category of the indispensable? The discussion of *shechitah*, for instance, which is *ksheirah b'zar* — valid even when performed by a non-*kohen* — raises the same question: is it an *avodah* or not? What we label an *avodah* is itself a genuine and unresolved question that threads through the subsequent *halakhic* analysis.

Similarly, the *kalfi* itself presents an interesting structural puzzle: it was used exclusively in the context of the *Beit HaMikdash*, yet because it was not formally sanctified it did not attain the status of *kli sharet*. Function and formal identity do not necessarily coincide.

### Hand Debate

The *Gemara* identifies the underlying point of contention between the *mishnah* and Rabbi Eliezer's view: *b'mai kamiphligi?* What is the disagreement about? *Mar savar yemina d'sgan adif mismala d'Kohen Gadol* — one position holds that the right hand of the *sgan* is preferable to the left hand of the *Kohen Gadol*, presumably from the perspective of how the act should be performed, even if it is not technically an *avodah*. *U'mar savar ki hadadi ninhu* — the other position holds that the two options are roughly equivalent, and once they are equivalent there is no reason to involve the *sgan* at all; the *Kohen Gadol* alone should perform the act.

### Rabbi Hanania

The *Gemara* then asks: *u'man hai tanna d'palig alei d'Rabbi Yehuda?* — who is the *tanna* behind our *mishnah*, the one who says the *Kohen Gadol* uses both hands? The answer is striking: *Rabbi Hanania Sgan HaKohanim hu* — it is Rabbi Hanania himself, who served as the *sgan*. And as the *braisa* records, Rabbi Hanania explains the *sgan*'s position on the right in purely functional terms: *she'im i'eir bo psul b'Kohen Gadol nichnas sgan u'meshammesh tachtav* — in case a disqualifying event befalls the *Kohen Gadol*, the *sgan* is ready to step in and serve in his place. The *Gemara* infers from this formulation that according to Rabbi Hanania, this readiness is the *sgan*'s sole function during the lot-drawing; had the *sgan* been actively drawing a lot, Rabbi Hanania would not have described his role exclusively in those terms. It is, as observed, quite remarkable that it is the *sgan* himself who most restricts the *sgan*'s role.

---

## Shimon HaTzaddik

### YK Signs

The *Gemara* now turns to a celebrated *aggadic* passage. *Tanu Rabbanan*: during the forty years that Shimon HaTzaddik served as *Kohen Gadol*, the lot inscribed *lashem* would always come up in his right hand — *arba'im shana she-shimmesh Shimon HaTzaddik haya goral oleh b'yamin*. The red string, *lashon shel zehorit*, would always turn white. The western light of the *menorah*, *ner ma'aravi*, remained perpetually burning. The fire on the *mizbe'ach* burned powerfully without constant feeding. And there was a *bracha* in the bread — the *omer*, the *shtei halechem*, and the *lechem hapanim* — such that a *kohen* who received even a *kezayit* would be fully satisfied, or would even have food to spare.

### Decline Begins

After the time of Shimon HaTzaddik, all of these signs began to waver. The lot was no longer always in the right hand — *p'amim oleh b'yamin p'amim oleh b'smol* — sometimes right, sometimes left. The red string no longer always turned white — *p'amim malbin p'amim eino malbin* — sometimes it would whiten and sometimes it would not.

### Further Signs

Simultaneously, the other signs of divine favor also became unreliable. The *ner ma'aravi* — *p'amim dolek p'amim kaveh* — sometimes continued burning beyond the other lights, sometimes was extinguished before them. The fire on the *mizbe'ach* — *p'amim mitgaber p'amim ein mitgaber* — sometimes burned powerfully on its own, sometimes the *kohanim* had to feed it continuously throughout the entire day. And instead of blessing in the bread, a curse was sent: *nishtalecha me'eira ba'omer uvishtei halechem uvlechem hapanim*. Each *kohen* now received not even a *kezayit* but the equivalent of a lentil — *kefol* — which the Maharsha notes is significant, because a *kezayit* is the minimum amount upon which *birkat hamazon* is recited and is the threshold for *sevi'ah*. Below that threshold, neither the capacity for satisfaction nor the fitness for *bracha* is present. This is not merely the withdrawal of miraculous blessing but the positive infusion of a curse — a qualitatively different and more alarming deterioration.

The reaction among the *kohanim* was telling: *hatznu'in moshchin et yedeihen* — the more modest ones withdrew their hands, unwilling to take even their portion, while *hagarganim notlin v'ochlin* — the voracious ones grabbed and ate. One individual became notorious for seizing not only his own portion but his colleague's as well, and was called *ben hamtzan* — son of the oppressor or thief.

A brief *Tosafot* on 39a addresses this: *Tosafot* notes that all the *garganim* were grabbing aggressively, so why was this particular individual singled out for the epithet? The answer: he did not merely grab from the communal distribution — he took directly off another person's plate. This crossed a qualitatively different line.

One further observation: one might think the most appropriate response would be simply to take one's allotted portion and eat it as a *mitzvah*, not to withdraw. While taking from the *lechem hapanim* may not constitute an individual *mitzvah* for a *kohen* in the precise sense, the *Gemara* seems to view the behavior of the modest ones as the admirable response to an impossible situation — though this is a nuanced point.

*Rabbah bar bar Shila* and *Rava* both offer *pesukim* grounding the negative sense of *chamtzan*: *Elokei faltzeiniy miyad rasha, mikaf me'avel v'chometz* — and *limdu heitev dirshu mishpat, ashru chamotz* — where *chamotz* clearly designates someone who has done violence or wrong to another.

### Shimon Death

The *Gemara* then records an *aggadic* narrative of striking power. *Tanu Rabbanan*: in the year that Shimon HaTzaddik died, he told those around him: *b'shana zo hu meit* — this year, he will die, referring to himself in the third person. When asked how he knew, he replied: *b'chol Yom HaKippurim haya mizdamen li zaken echad lavush levanim v'atuf levanim, nichnas imi v'yatza imi* — every Yom Kippur an elder figure would appear to him in the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, clothed in white and wrapped in white, entering with him and leaving with him. *V'hayom nizdamen li zaken echad lavush shechorim v'atuf shechorim, nichnas imi v'lo yatza imi* — but this time, the elder appeared clothed in black and wrapped in black, entered with him and did not leave with him. He understood this as an unmistakable sign of his impending death. After *Sukkot*, he fell ill for seven days and died. The *Yerushalmi* addresses the obvious difficulty — the Torah states *v'chol adam lo yihyeh b'ohel mo'ed b'vo'o el hakodesh* — and answers that this figure was not an *adam* but a *malach*.

### Divine Name

After Shimon HaTzaddik's death, *v'nimneu echav hakohanim levarech bashem* — his fellow *kohanim* refrained from blessing with the explicit divine name. Rashi explains that during the *Beit HaMikdash* era, blessings — including *birkat kohanim* — were ordinarily recited with the *shem hameforash*. After Shimon HaTzaddik, the *kohanim* considered themselves unworthy of this practice and discontinued it.

An important nuance emerges here: the subject is *echav hakohanim* — his fellow priests in the plural — not merely subsequent *Kohanim Gedolim*. This implies that his presence had elevated the entire generation to a level of worthiness, such that even ordinary *kohanim* were fit to pronounce the *shem hameforash* in blessing. With his death, that elevation was lost for all. *Tosafot* in *Sotah*, as cited, links this to the *Sifrei*'s principle that God's name may be proclaimed only where the divine presence is revealed — *bechol makom asher ani nigla sham tazkir shemi*. The *Ri* explains: the *kohanim* refrained *lefi she-lo zachu shuv l'giluy Shechina* — because they no longer merited the full revelation of the *Shechina* that the pronouncing of the divine name required. This reading harmonizes the cessation of the name with the broader pattern of the *Shechina*'s gradual withdrawal.

### Final Forty Years

A further and starker deterioration is recorded. *Tanu Rabbanan: arba'im shana kodem churban ha-Bayit* — for the forty years preceding the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*, not a single positive sign remained. The *goral* no longer ever came up in the right hand; it was always the left. The red string never turned white. The *ner ma'aravi* never outlasted the other lights. And — a new and ominous sign — *v'hayu daltos Heichal niftachos me'aleihen* — the doors of the *Heichal* would open by themselves, as though welcoming the enemy in.

It was Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai who rebuked the doors directly: *Heichal Heichal, mipnei mah attah mave'is et atzmecha?* — why do you trouble yourself with these signals? *Yode'a ani b'cha she-sofcha atid l'ichorev* — I know you are destined to be destroyed. *U'chevar nitnaba alecha Zecharia ben Iddo* — and Zecharia ben Iddo has already prophesied this: *p'tach Levanon dlatecha v'tochal esh b'arozecha* — open your doors, O Lebanon, and let the fire consume your cedars.

### Lebanon Midrash

The *Gemara* appends a brief but beautiful *midrashic* coda. *Amar Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tablai*: why is the *Beit HaMikdash* called *Levanon*? *Shemalbin avonoteihem shel Yisrael* — because it whitens the sins of Israel, parallel to the red string that turned white. *Amar Rav Zutra bar Tuvia*: why is it called a forest — as in *Beit Yaar HaLevanon*? *Mah yaar melavlev, af Beit HaMikdash melavlev* — just as a forest blossoms, so too the *Beit HaMikdash* blossomed. For when Solomon built the *Beit HaMikdash*, he planted within it trees of gold of every kind, and they would produce fruit in their seasons. When the wind blew through them, the fruit would fall, providing sustenance for the *kohanim*. When the enemies finally entered the *Heichal*, the golden trees withered and dried — *u'ferach Levanon umilal* — the blossom of the Lebanon became bereaved. But the passage closes with consolation: *v'atid HaKadosh Baruch Hu l'hachzira lanu* — the Holy One will yet restore it to us, as the verse promises: *paroch tifrach v'tagel af gilat v'ranen kevod haLevanon nutan lah* — it shall blossom and rejoice, for the glory of the Lebanon shall be given to it.

---

## Sensory Reach

### Ten Utterances

Returning to the *halakhic* material, the *Gemara* records: *eser pe'amim mazkir Kohen Gadol et HaShem bo bayom* — ten times the *Kohen Gadol* pronounces God's explicit name on Yom Kippur. Three in the first *viduy* over his *par*: the *pasuk* language includes *Ana HaShem chatati*, *Ana HaShem kaper na*, and *lifnei HaShem titharu* — each containing the explicit name. Three again in the second *viduy* recited on behalf of the *kohanim*. Three in the *viduy* recited over the *seir hamishtalei'ach*, the goat sent off. And one at the lot-drawing, when he declares *lashem* or *lashem chatat*. That totals ten.

### Voice Range

When the *Kohen Gadol* pronounced the explicit divine name, *v'nishma kolo b'Yiricho* — his voice could be heard all the way in Jericho. *Amar Rabba bar bar Chana*: the distance from Jerusalem to Jericho is ten *parsaot* — a *parsa* being four *mil*, each *mil* eight thousand *amot*, making the distance roughly twenty miles.

### Ketoret Smell

The auditory marvels were matched by olfactory ones. *V'tzir daltos haHeichal nishma b'shmona techumei Shabbat* — the creaking of the hinges of the *Heichal* doors when opened could be heard within eight *techumei Shabbat*, that is, sixteen thousand *amot*. *Izim sheb'Yiricho hayu mitatshot mereiach haktoret* — the goats in Jericho would sneeze from the scent of the *ketoret* reaching all that distance. *Nashim sheb'Yiricho einan tzerichin l'hitbasem mereiach ketoret* — the women of Jericho had no need for perfume, as the fragrance of the *ketoret* was sufficient. As for the women of Jerusalem, only the *kalot* — the brides — needed additional perfume beyond what the *ketoret* provided, because a *kala* requires substantially more fragrance than an ordinary woman. This observation is attributed to the Maharsha as well. *Tosafot* raises the question of whether benefiting passively from the *ketoret*'s scent might be prohibited, and answers that the prohibition applies only to an active seeking-out of the smell — *shelo yikrevu atzmam lizeh kedei lehariach yoter* — not to passive benefit.

### Ketoret Stories

Two *aggadic* accounts round out this section. *Rabbi Yosi ben Dugla* reports that his father kept goats in the mountains of Michmar, and those goats would sneeze from the scent of the *ketoret*. *Rabbi Chiya bar Avin* said in the name of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha*: an elder once told him that he had visited Shiloh — the site of the ancient *Mishkan* — and could still smell the *ketoret* emanating from between the cracks in the walls, a fragrance lingering long after the *Mishkan* had ceased to stand.

---

## Hagralah Meakev?

### Rabbi Yannai

The *Gemara* now turns to the central *halakhic* question of the lot-drawing's indispensability. *Amar Rabbi Yannai: aliyat goral mitoch kalfi meakevet* — drawing the lot from the box is *meakev*; if it is not performed, the subsequent designation of the animals as *lashem* and *la'azazel* is invalid and one cannot proceed. *Hanacha eina meakevet* — but the physical placement of the lots on top of the animals, which the *pasuk* prescribes, does not prevent *yetziat* the obligation if omitted.

### Rabbi Yochanan

*V'Rabbi Yochanan amar: af aliya eina meakevet* — Rabbi Yochanan goes further: even the drawing of the lot from the box is not *meakev*. If the *Kohen Gadol* simply assigned the roles arbitrarily — declaring this one *lashem* and that one *la'azazel* without performing the lot-drawing — the service would be valid *b'di'avad*.

### Order Debate

The *Gemara* situates this debate within the broader *tannaitic* dispute between *Rabbi Yehudah* and *Rabbi Nechemia* regarding the order of the Yom Kippur *avodot* performed outside the *Kodesh HaKodashim*. Note that in this context *bachutz* — "outside" — refers specifically to anything outside the *Kodesh HaKodashim* itself, encompassing the *Heichal* and the larger *azarah*. Rabbi Yehudah holds that if the prescribed order of acts performed in *bigdei lavan* outside the *Kodesh HaKodashim* is altered, *b'di'avad* the service remains valid. Rabbi Nechemia holds that even outside the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, order is *meakev* and a deviation invalidates. The *Gemara* assumes that this debate about the consequence of disordering acts may translate directly into whether performing the act at all is *meakev*.

### Hagralah Status

Two possible readings of this correlation emerge. The first reading: according to Rabbi Yehudah, who is more lenient about acts outside the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, everyone would agree that the *hagralah* is not *meakev* — it is performed in *bigdei lavan* outside the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, so Rabbi Yehudah would certainly not require it strictly. The debate between Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yochanan thus operates only within the framework of Rabbi Nechemia's stricter view. According to Rabbi Nechemia, the one who says the *hagralah* is *meakev* accords with his position, while the one who says it is not *meakev* even according to Rabbi Nechemia reasons that *hagralah lav avodah hi* — the lot-drawing is not a formal *avodah*; it is a *hechsher avodah*, and Rabbi Nechemia's strictures apply only to acts that constitute genuine *avodah*.

The second reading inverts the analysis: according to Rabbi Nechemia, who is strict even outside the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, everyone would agree that the *hagralah* is *meakev* — even this non-*avodah* act, when prescribed by the Torah, must be performed. The debate between Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yochanan then takes place within the framework of Rabbi Yehudah's more lenient view. According to Rabbi Yehudah, who normally gives latitude regarding acts outside the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, the one who says the *hagralah* is not *meakev* accords straightforwardly with his position. But the one who says it is *meakev* even according to Rabbi Yehudah argues: *shani hacha d'tana bei k'ra* — here it is different, because the Torah emphasizes this act repeatedly. The *pasuk* uses the phrase *asher ala alav hagoral* — and indeed repeats the language of *aliya* — implying that this act of the lot coming up must occur and cannot simply be bypassed.

The result is a genuinely unresolved tension: on one hand, the *hagralah* is not a formal *avodah* — it can be performed with the left hand, it can involve the *sgan*, suggesting a more lenient *halakhic* status. On the other hand, the Torah's explicit and repeated formulation points to the lot-drawing as something the Torah itself insists upon. Whether that tension resolves toward leniency or stringency depends on which *tanna*'s framework one adopts and which reading of their debate one follows.

---

---

# Yoma 40

## Hagralah Me'akev?

### Yannai vs. Yochanan

We pick up at the bottom of 39b with a question that has been developing: is the *hagralah* — the actual act of drawing lots — *me'akev*, that is, indispensable to the validity of the *avodah*, or is it merely the ideal procedure that can be bypassed *bedi'avad*?

This was the subject of a dispute between Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yochanan. Rabbi Yannai holds that *aliyat hagoral mitoch hakalpi me'akevet* — the drawing of the lot from the box is indispensable. Rabbi Yochanan holds that it is not *me'akev*; the designation of the animals can be valid even without the formal lottery.

### Order Outside Kodesh

The *gemara* asks whether this dispute tracks a more fundamental debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemia regarding whether the sequential order of services performed *outside* the *Kodesh Kodashim* is *me'akev*. Rabbi Yehuda holds, broadly, that the order outside the *Kodesh Kodashim* is not *me'akev* — and the *gemara* understands this to imply that certain things done outside may not be *me'akev* in substance either. Rabbi Nechemia insists that even outside the *Kodesh Kodashim* the order is *me'akev*.

The *gemara* considers whether there might be a lineup between these positions: perhaps Rabbi Yochanan, who says the *hagralah* is not *me'akev*, follows Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yannai, who says it is, follows Rabbi Nechemia. The *gemara* then notes, however, that the alignment is not clean in either direction. One could argue that even according to Rabbi Yehuda the *hagralah* is *me'akev* because the Torah repeats the phrase *asher ala*, *asher ala* — a doubling that would indicate indispensability. Conversely, one could argue that even according to Rabbi Nechemia the *hagralah* is not *me'akev*, because it is not technically an *avodah* at all — as evidenced by the fact that a non-*Kohen Gadol* can perform it and it may be done with the left hand.

### Mitzvah Lehagril

The *gemara* now brings the first *braitah* in support of Rabbi Yochanan. The text reads: *mitzvah l'hagril, v'im lo higril kasher* — it is a *mitzvah* to draw the lots, and if one did not draw them, it is nevertheless valid. This appears to be straightforward evidence that *bedi'avad* the *hagralah* is not *me'akev*.

### Mitzvah in Mikdash

Before proceeding, it is worth pausing on the word *mitzvah* in this context. When the *gemara* uses *mitzvah* in the context of *avodah* in the *Mikdash*, it does not carry the same meaning as an individual's personal obligation in the conventional sense — the question of whose *mitzvah* it is becomes blurred when we are discussing communal ritual and Temple service. The *Geonim* actually distinguished a third category alongside *asei* and *lo ta'asei*, called *mitzvot tzibburiot* — communal laws. In this context, *mitzvah* simply means this is the proper, prescribed way to perform the service, but *bedi'avad* if it is not done, the procedure is still valid.

The *gemara* says that this *braitah* works well according to one reading of the dispute — specifically the reading in which both Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yannai agree that according to Rabbi Yehuda the *hagralah* is not *me'akev*, and the debate is only about whether Rabbi Nechemia would also agree. On that reading, the *braitah* can simply be attributed to Rabbi Yehuda, and there is no difficulty.

The problem arises according to the other version of the dispute, in which Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yochanan are debating not within Rabbi Nechemia's position but within Rabbi Yehuda's, such that Rabbi Yannai holds that even Rabbi Yehuda would say the *hagralah* is *me'akev*. On this reading, the *braitah* stating it is not *me'akev* has no one to attribute it to. Everybody would say it is *me'akev*, and yet the *braitah* says otherwise.

### Hagril vs. Haniach

The *gemara* resolves this difficulty by amending — or reframing — the text of the *braitah*. Instead of reading *mitzvah lehagril*, "it is a *mitzvah* to draw the lot," the *gemara* proposes reading *mitzvah lehaniach*, "it is a *mitzvah* to place the lot on the head of the animal." On this reading, the *braitah* is saying that *bedi'avad* if you drew the lot but did not actually place it upon the animal's head, the procedure is still valid. This does not say anything about whether drawing itself is *me'akev*.

### Tosafot Interpretation

Tosafot, in the second comment on 40a, notes that this emendation is not meant literally — the *gemara* is not physically rewriting the *braitah*. Rather, as Tosafot explains: *eino magiah braitah, ela perushei kamefaresh* — it is an interpretive gloss. When the *braitah* says *lo higril*, it means "did not complete the lot-process," which can include the act of placement. So the *braitah* is being reread to refer to *hanachah* — the placing of the lot — not to the drawing itself.

### Higril and Hitvadah

The *gemara* then brings a second *braitah* to challenge this further. This *braitah* reads: it is a *mitzvah* to draw the lot (*lehagril*) and to recite the *viduy* — the confession; if one did not draw the lot and did not recite the *viduy* (*lo higril v'lo hitvadah*), it is nevertheless valid (*kasher*). This introduces a new element: not only does the *braitah* say the *hagralah* is not *me'akev bedi'avad*, it says the same of the *viduy* — the confession — which is separately striking.

The *gemara* anticipates that we might again apply the same solution used for the first *braitah* — that *lo higril* here also means "did not place the lot" — and rejects this on the basis of what comes next.

### Shimon's Position

The *braitah* continues: Rabbi Shimon says, *lo higril kasher, lo hitvadah pasul* — if you did not draw the lot, it is valid; but if you did not recite the *viduy*, it is invalid. Rabbi Shimon thus takes a position that diverges from the *Tanna Kamma* specifically on the question of *viduy*: everyone agrees on the lot, but Rabbi Shimon insists the *viduy* is *me'akev* while the *Tanna Kamma* holds it is not.

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* now challenges the reinterpretation. If we read *lo higril* as "did not place the lot" throughout this *braitah*, then the implication of Rabbi Shimon's concession — that *bedi'avad* not placing is acceptable — would be that *not drawing altogether is me'akev*. That is, Rabbi Shimon would be implicitly agreeing that drawing the lot is indispensable, with only the placement being dispensable *bedi'avad*.

But this cannot be Rabbi Shimon's position. The *gemara* demonstrates this from another teaching: *met echad meihen meivi chaveiro shelo behagra'ah* — if one of the two goats died, Rabbi Shimon holds that you bring a replacement without performing any new lottery. This is a strikingly radical ruling: not only does Rabbi Shimon hold that the drawing of the lot is not *me'akev*, he holds that the entire procedure of pairing the animals and designating them jointly is not *me'akev*. If the *se'ir lecha'tat* drops dead after *shechitah*, you can simply take a new goat and send it as the *se'ir la'Azazel* without repeating the *hagrala* process at all.

### Me'akev Framework

It is worth stepping back at this point. We have this major debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yannai, with considerable back-and-forth over whether the *hagralah* is *me'akev*. And now we discover that there is a *Tanna* — Rabbi Shimon — who very clearly holds it is not. However, Rabbi Shimon's position is being treated as exceptional and bracketed. The discussion proceeds within the assumption of those who regard the overall process as *me'akev*, asking only whether the drawing specifically is *me'akev* within that framework.

### Shimon Agrees

The *gemara* resolves the challenge regarding this second *braitah* by explaining that Rabbi Shimon was actually uncertain what the *rabbanan* meant when they said *bedi'avad* you do not have to do the lot. So Rabbi Shimon responds in two hypothetical registers: *i hagra'ah hagra'ah mamash kamarisu* — if you mean literally that you do not have to draw the lot, then I fully agree, and I will only argue with you about the *viduy*, where I think it is *me'akev*. *I hagra'ah d'kamrisu haynu hanachah* — but if what you meant by "not doing the lot" is only that you do not have to place the lot on the animal's head while you still hold that drawing is required, then I argue on both points. In other words, Rabbi Shimon is clarifying his position: if the *rabbanan* agree with him that drawing is not *me'akev*, he has only one disagreement with them — the *viduy*. If they only mean that placement is not *me'akev* while drawing remains required, he disagrees on both counts.

The *gemara's* conclusion is that the plain sense of the *braitah* is that both the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Shimon hold that drawing the lot is not *me'akev*. The *gemara*'s attempt to reframe their words as referring to *hanachah* runs into Rabbi Shimon's radical position, which demonstrates that the language really does refer to drawing. The *gemara* therefore attributes the framework position to Rabbi Shimon explicitly and acknowledges that the reinterpretation proposed earlier does not fully resolve all the textual evidence.

### Me'akev Assumption

One might ask: is it not strange that something so central to the *avodah* — or something so fundamental to a *korban* generally — should simply not be *me'akev*? The answer lies in a general principle that *Chazal* apply throughout the laws of *korbanot*. Outside the *Mikdash*, the assumption is that if the Torah says to do something, not doing it means you are not *yotzei* — there is no question. But in the laws of *korbanot*, where there is a vast number of details and particulars, *Chazal* begin with the opposite baseline: the assumption is that most details are *not me'akev* unless the Torah somehow underscores or repeats the requirement, or unless the Torah uses the language of *chok* — which does appear in the context of *Yom Kippur* and would indicate indispensability. Without such an indicator, many procedural details of *korbanot* are presumed to be *lech'tchila* requirements only. This principle applies broadly — even outside *Yom Kippur*, in the laws of *chatat* for instance, if only one of the four corners of the *mizbeach* received its placement of blood rather than all four, *bedi'avad* one may still be *yotzei*.

---

## Par vs. Seira Order

### Par vs. Seira

The *gemara* now turns to a different *braitah* bearing on the same question. The *braitah* states: *arba'ah me'akvin b'de'oraisa* — four things are *me'akev* by Torah law. Among them: *par me'akev et ha'seira* — the *par* prevents the *seira* from being valid (if the *seira* goes out of sequence before the *par*), but *ein ha'seira me'akevet et hapar* — the *seira* does not prevent the *par* from being valid if the *par* goes out of sequence.

To understand this, the *par* here refers to the *Kohen Gadol's* bull, and the *seira* is the goat brought as *l'Hashem chatat* — not the *se'ir hamishta'leach*, but the communal goat whose blood is brought inside as part of the purification of the *Mikdash*. Both animals play roles in the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur*, but their services are interleaved in a specific sequence.

### Service Sequence

Rashi provides a remarkably clear summary of the entire order of services involving the *par* and *seira*, evidently having surveyed the broader *sugya* and compiled the sequence from across the relevant discussions. The order is as follows:

First, the *Kohen Gadol* recites *viduy* on the *par* — the first *viduy par*, covering himself and his household. Then he performs the *hagrala* — the drawing of the lots on the two goats. Then he recites a second *viduy* on the *par*, this time encompassing the *kohanim* as well. He then performs *shechitah* of the *par* and enters the *Kodesh Kodashim* carrying the *kaf* and *machtah* to offer the *ketoret*. He then gives the blood of the *par* on the *kaporet*. He then returns and performs *shechitah* of the *seira*, takes its blood, and gives it on the *kaporet* as well. Then he gives the blood of the *par* on the *parochet*, followed by the blood of the *seira* on the *parochet*. Finally, he mingles the two bloods and applies them to the inner *mizbeach*.

### Inside/Outside Kodesh

Looking at this sequence, we can identify which services are performed inside the *Kodesh Kodashim* and which are not. The services inside the *Kodesh Kodashim* are: the blood of the *par* on the *kaporet*, the blood of the *seira* on the *kaporet*, and the *ketoret*. The *parochet* sprinklings and the inner *mizbeach* are already outside the *Kodesh Kodashim*, in the *Heichal*. The *gemara* clarifies that the rule about *par* preventing *seira* applies only to *matanot shebifnim* — the services performed inside the *Kodesh Kodashim*. This matters because, as we noted earlier, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemia debate whether order is *me'akev* outside the *Kodesh Kodashim*, and the rule here operates specifically within the domain where order is unambiguously *me'akev*.

### Which Avoda?

The *gemara* then reframes the entire question. Rather than asking which animal — *par* or *seira* — disrupts the other when it goes out of sequence, the *gemara* suggests that the real issue is which *avodah* was performed out of order, and whether the particular *avodah* that was displaced belongs to the *par* or the *seira*. Framing it as *par* versus *seira* is somewhat misleading; the *gemara* wants to understand the precise scenario in terms of which specific act was jumped.

### Par Before Hagrala

The *gemara* proceeds to analyze the scenario in which the *par* "goes first." The only meaningful way in which the *par bifnim* — the inside service of the *par* — could jump the line is if the *Kohen Gadol* performed the blood sprinklings of the *par* inside the *Kodesh Kodashim* before having performed the *hagrala* at all. That is: the *hagrala* should have been done prior to the *shechitah* of the *par*, but the *Kohen Gadol* went ahead and completed all the services of the *par* — including the *matanot bifnim* — without yet having drawn the lots. The *braitah* says that in this scenario, the *seira* does not prevent the *par* from being valid — meaning *bedi'avad* the *par* is still good. 

The *gemara* draws an inference: if doing all the inside services of the *par* while skipping the *hagrala* entirely still renders the *par* valid, this constitutes evidence that the *hagralah* is not *me'akev*. Because the only reason this out-of-sequence *par* service should be permissible is that the *hagralah* it bypassed was not indispensable to begin with.

The logic depends on understanding what was "out of order." If the *par* service skipped over the *hagrala*, and we say *bedi'avad* this is acceptable, we are implicitly saying that the fact that the *hagrala* had not yet been performed did not invalidate the *par* service. And if the *hagrala* is what was skipped, then its non-*me'akev* status must be the operative reason.

### Order vs. Act

The *gemara* immediately raises a counter. Perhaps this proves only that the *order* of the *hagrala* is not *me'akev* — that is, it can be performed later — but not that the *hagrala* itself is dispensable. There is a meaningful distinction between saying "the order doesn't matter as long as you do the thing" and "the thing itself can be omitted." The *gemara* thus preserves the possibility of holding: *bedi'avad* the *seder* is not *me'akev*, but the *hagrala* itself remains *me'akev*.

The *gemara* then considers another scenario: perhaps the *par* "going first" refers not to the *matanot bifnim* jumping ahead of the *hagrala*, but to the sprinklings of the *par* on the *parochet* — which are *beheichal*, outside the *Kodesh Kodashim* — jumping ahead of the *seira's* sprinklings *bifnim*. This would explain why it is not *me'akev*: these sprinklings are outside the *Kodesh Kodashim*, and according to Rabbi Yehuda, the order outside is not *me'akev*. The *gemara* cites this: *Rabbi Yehudah hi de'omar devarim hana'asim bevigdei lavan mibachutz lo me'akvei*.

But the *gemara* pushes back: the *braitah* explicitly states *matanot shebifnim* — it is specifically talking about services inside the *Kodesh Kodashim*. This eliminates the option of attributing the leniency to the location being outside. The *gemara* therefore returns to the conclusion that the scenario involves the *par bifnim* having been done before the *hagrala*, and attributes the ruling to either Rabbi Shimon — who broadly holds the entire lot-process is not *me'akev* — or to Rabbi Yehuda, with the qualification that even Rabbi Yehuda can distinguish between order not being *me'akev* and the act itself being *me'akev*: *d'nehi d'sidra lo me'akev, hagralah miha me'akva*.

---

## Shimon's Philosophy

### Scapegoat Alive

The *gemara* now examines a *braitah* that illuminates the theological foundations of Rabbi Shimon's radical position. The *braitah* is grounded in the *pasuk* concerning the *se'ir hamishta'leach*: *ya'amad chai lifnei Hashem lechaper alav l'shalach oto la'Azazel ha'midbarah* — the goat designated for *Azazel* shall stand alive before God to atone upon it, to send it off to *Azazel* in the wilderness. The *braitah* asks: until when must this goat remain alive? What is the last moment at which, if the goat dies, one would not be *yotzei*?

### Lekapaer Debate

The *braitah* presents a dispute. Rabbi Yehuda says: *ad she'as matan damo shel chaveiro* — the *se'ir la'Azazel* must remain alive until the moment the blood of its counterpart, the *se'ir la'Hashem*, is offered. Once the blood of the *se'ir la'Hashem* has been presented inside, if the *se'ir la'Azazel* then dies, one is still *yotzei*. Rabbi Shimon says: *ad she'as viduy devarim* — the *se'ir la'Azazel* must remain alive only until the moment the *viduy* — the confession spoken over it — has been recited. Once that *viduy* is complete, even if the goat dies before being sent over the cliff, one is *yotzei*.

### When Purpose Done?

Strikingly, both positions agree that the *se'ir la'Azazel* does not have to survive until the moment it is actually pushed off the cliff. Its function can be complete before that physical act. The disagreement is only about when that function is fulfilled. This is a remarkable shared premise: the dramatic act of sending the goat into the wilderness is not the operative moment of *kaparah*.

The order of events around the *se'ir la'Azazel* should be borne in mind. After the lottery, the *se'ir la'Hashem* is slaughtered and its blood is brought inside the *Kodesh Kodashim*. Then the *Kohen Gadol* recites the *viduy* over the *se'ir la'Azazel* — this *viduy* includes a confession on behalf of all of Israel. Only after that is the goat sent off to *Azazel*. The gap between the *viduy* and the sending is potentially several minutes. If the goat dies in that interval, the question becomes: is this after or before the critical threshold?

### Blood vs. Words

The *gemara* explores the textual basis for each position. The word *lechaper alav* in the *pasuk* — "to atone upon it" — is the crux. Rabbi Yehuda reads *lechaper alav* through the lens of *kaparat damim*: in the vocabulary of *Yom Kippur*, *kipper* refers to the blood rite in the sanctuary. The parallel phrase *v'chila mechaper et hakodesh* — "when he has finished atoning for the sanctuary" — uses *kipper* to mean exactly that. *Ma lehalan bechaparat damim, af kan bechaparat damim* — just as in that context *kipper* means the blood rite, so here it means the same: the *se'ir la'Azazel* must remain alive until the *se'ir la'Hashem's* blood has effected its *kaparah* inside.

Rabbi Shimon reads *lechaper alav* differently: *bechaparat devarim hakatuv medaber* — the text is speaking of *kaparah* through words. Rashi explains that the force of Rabbi Shimon's reading lies in the pronoun *alav* — "upon it." The immediately preceding antecedent of that pronoun is the *se'ir la'Azazel* itself. So *lechaper alav* means "to effect *kaparah* upon *it* — upon the *se'ir la'Azazel*." And the *kaparah* that pertains to the *se'ir la'Azazel* is not a blood rite — it has none — but rather the *viduy* spoken over it. Hence, once that *viduy* is complete, the purpose of the animal has been fulfilled.

### Tosafot Linkage

Tosafot offers a deeper reading of this dispute that goes beyond the question of which act constitutes *kaparah*. According to Tosafot, the fundamental question underlying this *braitah* is the degree to which the *se'ir la'Azazel* is linked to — dependent upon — the *se'ir la'Hashem*.

### Linked/Unlinked

According to Rabbi Yehuda, who says the *se'ir la'Azazel* must remain alive until the *damim* of the *se'ir la'Hashem* are completed, the two animals are intrinsically bound together. The validity and completion of the *se'ir la'Azazel* is dependent on what happens to the *se'ir la'Hashem*. This is why the *hagrala* — the lottery that establishes their paired identity and their respective destinies — is *me'akev*: you cannot separate the two animals' fates, and the lot-drawing is the act that joins them.

According to Rabbi Shimon, who says the *se'ir la'Azazel* only requires the *viduy* and is then complete, the two animals are fundamentally independent. The *se'ir la'Azazel* achieves its *kaparah* through what is done directly *to it* — not through what is done to its partner. Once that *viduy* is complete, the fate of the *se'ir la'Azazel* is no longer tied to its counterpart. This is precisely why Rabbi Shimon can hold that if one animal dies, you simply bring a replacement without repeating the *hagrala* — the two were never indivisibly linked to begin with.

### Theology

The theological implications, as Tosafot's reading makes clear, are profound. If the two animals are linked — if personal *kaparah* depends on the blood rite in the sanctuary — then the confession of Israel's sins and the purification of God's sanctuary are bound together as a single cosmic event. Individual atonement cannot occur independently of the cleansing of the *Mikdash*. If, on the other hand, the two are unlinked, then what the *Kohen Gadol* does to purify the *Mikdash* and what he does to achieve personal atonement for the people are two distinct processes, each standing on its own terms. The *Azazel* goat's *kaparah* through the *viduy* is a self-contained act; it does not wait upon the blood rite any more than the blood rite waits upon it.

---

## Reversing Lots

### Switch Hands?

A student of Rabbi Akiva poses a question: if the lot for *la'Hashem* was drawn in the left hand rather than the right — *ala b'smol* — is it permissible to transfer it to the right hand? Can the *Kohen Gadol* effectively reverse the mechanical result of the drawing after the fact?

### Tzadokim Concern

Rabbi Akiva's answer is not a categorical legal prohibition but rather a concern of a different kind: *al titnu makom l'tzadukim lirdos* — do not give the *Tzadokim* grounds to rebel. That is, the appearance of manipulating the results of the lottery would undermine confidence in Pharisaic authority over Temple procedure, providing the *Tzadokim* an opening to challenge the legitimacy of the *avodah*. The implication of this answer is striking: were it not for this concern, one presumably *could* make the switch.

### Hagralah vs. Reverse

The *gemara* seizes on this implication and asks: but if the *hagralah* is *me'akev*, how could one reverse the lot at all? If the identity of the goat is determined by the lottery result and that result is indispensable, then ignoring it and switching the lot to the other hand should be prohibited on substantive grounds — not merely on grounds of appearance.

### Switch Both

Rava resolves this: what the student was asking, and what Rabbi Akiva addressed, was not simply flipping the lot from left to right. Rather, the question was *mah she'yachaziru lo u'l'se'iro l'yamin* — whether one could reverse *both* the lot *and* the goat simultaneously. That is, if the lot for *la'Hashem* ended up in the left hand, one would switch which lot is held in which hand *and simultaneously* exchange the positions of the two goats, so that the goat now on the right is still the one over which the *la'Hashem* lot was drawn. The actual pairing of lot to animal is preserved; only the physical positioning changes. This would not constitute reversing or ignoring the lottery result — the lot's designation follows its goat. Rava thus shows that the question was about external presentation, not about overriding the *hagrala*.

### Integrity

Rabbi Akiva's concern nevertheless stands: even this technically valid maneuver should not be done, because it *looks* like manipulation of the lottery. The integrity of the lottery system — and by extension, the trust that the public places in the Pharisaic management of the *avodah* — demands that no appearance of rigging be tolerated, regardless of whether the action would technically be permissible.

---

## Placing Lots

### Asher Alav

The *gemara* now brings a *braitah* that introduces a distinction between two formulations: had the Torah written *et hasa'ir asher alav hagoral* — "the goat upon which the lot rests" — one might have thought that the lot must remain physically placed upon the animal throughout. But the Torah actually wrote *asher ala alav hagoral* — "upon which the lot ascended" or "which the lot fell upon" — using the past tense.

### Not Me'akev

The *braitah* derives from this: *keivan she'ala, shuv eino tzarich* — once the lot has been drawn and designated the animal, you do not have to keep it placed on the animal. The plain sense is that *hanachah* — the placement of the lot upon the goat's head — is not *me'akev*. Once drawn, you are *yotzei* even without physically placing the lot on the animal.

### Lechatchila?

The *gemara* asks a sharper question: does this mean you do not even have to place the lot *lechatchila* — from the outset, as an initial matter? Could the *braitah* be saying that the placing of the lot is not even *mitzvah* — not even the preferred procedure? The *gemara* considers this unthinkable. Surely there must at minimum be a *mitzvah* to place the lot upon the animal's head.

### Hagralah Yes/Hanachah No

The *gemara* concludes that the *braitah* must mean: *bedi'avad*, after the fact, if you did not place the lot on the animal, you are still *yotzei*. This is a *bedi'avad* ruling, not a negation of the *lechatchila* requirement. The inference follows: *shema mina hagralah me'akevet, hanachah lo me'akevet* — the drawing of the lot is *me'akev*, but the placing of the lot is not. The word *asher ala* — "that was drawn" — is what matters; the subsequent act of pressing the lot onto the animal's head is not essential.

### Rava Moment

Rava, however, offers a different reading that avoids drawing any inference about the *hagralah*. He says: had the Torah said *asher alav*, I would have thought the lot must remain placed on the animal all the way until *shechitah*. The Torah's use of *asher ala* teaches instead that you need not keep the lot on the animal throughout — it need only be placed momentarily. The *braitah* is not saying placement is entirely dispensable; it is saying that *lechatchila* the placement need only be for a moment. The requirement of placement exists, but it is of brief duration.

### Avoids Hagralah

Rava's reinterpretation is strategically significant. By reading the *braitah* as addressing the duration of placement rather than its presence or absence, he avoids any implication that the drawing itself is or is not *me'akev*. The *braitah* becomes entirely about the mechanics of *hanachah* — how long must the lot rest upon the animal — and says nothing about whether the lot must have been drawn in the first place.

---

## Synthesis

### Reinterpretations

Throughout this *sugya*, multiple *braitot* appeared to indicate that the *hagralah* — the drawing of the lots — is not *me'akev*. In each case, the *gemara* reinterpreted them as referring not to the drawing but to the *hanachah* — the placing of the lot upon the animal's head — which is indeed not *me'akev bedi'avad*. The drawing itself remains, under this reinterpretation, an indispensable act.

### Shimon Radical

The one clear exception is Rabbi Shimon, whose position is explicit and cannot be reframed: he holds not only that the drawing of the lots is not *me'akev*, but that the entire paired process — the starting of the two animals together, the drawing, the designation — is dispensable *bedi'avad*. If one goat dies after the lot has been drawn, a replacement can be brought and sent as the *se'ir la'Azazel* without any renewed *hagrala*. This is a radical position that the *gemara* brackets when analyzing the mainstream view.

### Viduy Status

Similarly, there is a position that the *viduy* — the confession — is not *me'akev*, which is equally striking from the perspective of those for whom personal confession is the emotional and spiritual center of *Yom Kippur*. This position challenges us to recognize that the Torah's framework for *Yom Kippur* centers on the blood rites and the purification of the *Mikdash*, not on the confessional and penitential process that later tradition has come to emphasize.

### Cosmic Link

Tosafot's insight, as we explored, is that the debate is not merely about which acts are technically essential. It reaches to a deeper theological question: are the personal atonement for Israel — symbolized by the *se'ir la'Azazel* and its *viduy* — and the cosmic purification of the *Mikdash* by blood inextricably linked, or are they independent processes? Rabbi Yehuda links them, and in doing so makes the *hagrala* — the act that binds the two animals into a unified ritual — essential. Rabbi Shimon unlinks them, and in doing so frees the personal atonement from dependence on the sanctuary rite. Whether that link exists is not merely a technical *halacha* question; it is a question about the relationship between individual human confession and the metaphysical renewal of God's dwelling place.

---

---

# Yoma 41

## Hagralah Me'akev

### Hagralah Overview

The *daf* begins with a question that carries over from the preceding discussion: is the *hagralah* — the actual drawing of lots on Yom Kippur to designate the two goats — *me'akev*, meaning essential to the validity of the ceremony? If the *kohen gadol* simply designated the goats verbally, without performing the lottery, would the service be acceptable *bedi'avad*?

To orient the question: Rabbi Shimon holds a uniquely expansive position. Based on his reading of the verse *yaamad chai lifnei Hashem lechaper alav*, as Tosafot understands it, Rabbi Shimon maintains that the *sheir hamishtaleach* is not linked to the fate of the other *sheir* at all — the two animals function independently. Consequently, for Rabbi Shimon, not only is the *hagralah* not *me'akev*, even the entire pairing is not *me'akev*; *bedi'avad*, each goat stands on its own. But Rabbi Shimon is the outlier. The question under discussion concerns everyone else: granted that the pairing is required, must the designation specifically emerge from the lottery, or could a verbal declaration suffice? This debate is attributed to Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yannai, and connects as well to the broader tannaitic dispute — involving Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Nechemiah, and others — over which procedural steps are *me'akev* in general.

### Goral Oseo Chatat

The *gemara* brings a *braita* as evidence. The verse reads: *asher alah alav hagoral l'Hashem ve'asahu chatat* — "upon which the lot fell for God, and he shall make it a *chatat*." The *braita* reads *ve'asahu chatat* not as a future act of Aaron designating it verbally, but as an already completed act of the *goral*: the *goral* is what had already made it a *chatat*. From this the *braita* derives: *hagoral oseo chatat ve'ein hashem oseo chatat* — the lot makes it a *chatat*, and not the name. The "name" here refers both to the invocation of God's name *l'Hashem* and, more pointedly, to verbal designation. No verbal declaration by itself can consecrate the goat as the *chatat*; only the act of the lot falling upon it achieves that designation.

This is a striking conclusion. If the *hagralah* were not *me'akev*, then verbal designation would be the only conceivable alternative for specifying which goat is the *chatat* and which is the *sheir la'azazel*. The *braita* forecloses that alternative entirely.

### Kal Vachomer

The *braita* itself, however, anticipates a counterargument. One might reason through a *kal vachomer*: consider the case of birds (*kinnim*), where a pair of birds — one to be a *chatat* and one to be an *olah* — can be designated through verbal declaration, while drawing lots plays no role whatsoever. If verbal designation works in a context where lots are entirely ineffective, how much more so should verbal designation work in the context of the Yom Kippur goats, where the lot *does* function? The *talmud lomar* answers: *ve'asahu chatat* — the *goral* makes it a *chatat*, and the verbal name does not.

The *gemara* then raises a technical difficulty with this *kal vachomer*. The *kal vachomer* draws a comparison between the moment of the *hagralah* (by the goats) and the moments when verbal designation works (by the birds). But as we will see shortly, verbal designation of birds is effective only at two specific times: at the moment of purchase (*lekichah*) or at the moment the *kohen* performs the *melikah* (*asiyah*). The drawing of lots for the goats occurs at neither of those moments — it is not the time of *lekichah* and it is not the time of *asiyah*. So how can the *braita* compare them?

Rava resolves this by re-reading the *kal vachomer* more carefully. The argument should be understood as follows: in the case of birds, lots *never* work — not at *lekichah*, not at *asiyah*, not at any point. And yet verbal designation does work at those two specific moments. Now contrast this with the goats: there the lot *does* work — not at the time of *lekichah* or *asiyah*, but at some point. Surely, then, verbal designation should work at *lekichah* or *asiyah*, the moments where it demonstrably functions by birds. The *braita* responds: no — because we have the verse explicitly telling us that only the *goral* makes it a *chatat*, not the verbal designation, at any moment. The verse is the *talmud lomar* that overrides the *kal vachomer*.

### Sifra Proof

Having established the *braita*'s position, the *gemara* bolsters it further. *Stam Sifra mani* — the anonymous voice of the *Sifra* (Torat Kohanim, the tannaitic halakhic commentary on Vayikra) is, by tradition, Rabbi Yehuda. He is the unnamed author of the *Sifra*. And the *Sifra* teaches: *hagoral oseo chatat ve'ein hashem oseo chatat* — the lot makes it a *chatat* and not the verbal designation. *Alma hagrala me'akva* — this demonstrates that the *hagralah* is *me'akev*. Because if verbal designation cannot work, there is no other mechanism available; the *goral* is the only path, which means it is indispensable.

### Conclusion

The *gemara* concludes: *tyuvta deman d'amar hagrala lo me'akva tyuvta* — this is a decisive refutation of the view that the *hagralah* is not *me'akev*. The position that it is *me'akev* prevails for all opinions. Earlier in the discussion there was uncertainty about whether this was a debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemiah; now the *gemara* concludes that even Rabbi Yehuda — the most permissive voice on *me'akev* questions — would hold that the *hagralah* is *me'akev*.

One detail remains worth noting. The *hagralah* is *me'akev* even though it is not categorized as an *avodah* in the technical sense: it need not be performed by a *kohen*, and the *kohen gadol*'s left hand or the *segan* can perform it. This is a striking combination — something that is *me'akev* yet is not an *avodah*. The question of what precisely gets labeled an *avodah* — and what the halakhic consequences of that designation are (who may perform it, whether it must be done *be'yamin*, and the like) — is a broader discussion. The *hagralah* illustrates how *me'akev* and *avodah* are not coextensive categories. And Rabbi Shimon, of course, remains the outlier: for him, not only is the *hagralah* not *me'akev*, but the entire pairing is not *me'akev* either, and *bedi'avad* the two goats are independent of one another.

---

## Birds Designation

### Rav Chisda

Having drawn in the case of birds as part of the *kal vachomer* discussion, the *gemara* now completes that topic. Rav Chisda states: *ein hakinnim mitparshot* — a pair of birds (*kinnim*) does not become designated, meaning one as a *chatat* and one as an *olah*, except at one of two moments: *o bi-lekichat ba'alim* — at the time of the owner's purchase, or *o be-asiyat ha-kohen* — at the time of the *kohen*'s act, that is, the *melikah*.

This is a remarkable *halakha*. A person — typically a *yoledet*, a *zav*, a *metzora*, or another individual completing a purification process — must bring two birds, one a *chatat* and one an *olah*. Ordinarily one would assume that consecration must accompany acquisition, or at least that designation must be made early. Here, the pair can be acquired as a unit, entirely undesignated, and the specification of which bird is which can be deferred. But if it is deferred past the moment of purchase, it can only then be established at the moment of *melikah* itself. There is no intermediate window.

The *chiddush* of Rav Chisda's ruling, as one might note, is not the *lekichah* moment — one can designate any *korban* at the time of purchase. The *chiddush* is rather the other side: if you did *not* designate at the time of purchase, you do not lose the ability to designate forever; you retain it until *asiyah*. Nothing in between counts.

### Two Moments

Rav Shimi bar Ashi asks: what is the source for Rav Chisda's ruling? He answers from two verses. By the *yoledet*, the verse says *ve-lakacha shtei torim o shnei bnei yonah* — "and she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons" — and specifies *echad le-olah ve-echad le-chatat*, one for an *olah* and one for a *chatat*. The verb of taking (*lekichah*) thus anchors designation to the moment of purchase. By contrast, the verse concerning the *zav* says *ve-asah ha-kohen echad chatat ve-echad olah* — "the *kohen* shall make one a *chatat* and one an *olah*" — which implies that until the *kohen*'s act, it has not yet been determined which is which. Similarly by the *metzora*. These two verses establish the two and only two valid moments of designation.

### Purification Birds

The birds in question are those brought as part of the purification process for the *yoledet*, the *zav*, and the *metzora* at the completion of their *tahara*. These *korbanot* consist of pairs of birds — either turtledoves or young pigeons — one designated as a *chatat* and one as an *olah*. The prevalence of bird *korbanot* in this context reflects a practical reality: pigeons and doves required minimal upkeep, were inexpensive, and were a readily available source for sacrifice. The *korban* of birds served as the *korban ani* option in the sliding-scale obligations of these individuals, making it accessible across economic circumstances.

The *gemara* then raises a challenge. The *braita* we encountered earlier — *ve'asahu chatat*, *hagoral oseo chatat ve'ein hashem oseo chatat* — is now being examined again. The *kal vachomer* embedded in that *braita* compares the case of the goats to the case of birds. But the *gemara* objects: *deha hacha, delav shat lekichah velav shat asiyah hi* — by the Yom Kippur goats, the drawing of lots occurs at a moment that is neither *shat lekichah* nor *shat asiyah*. The comparison is therefore flawed unless we re-read what the *kal vachomer* is actually arguing, which Rava proceeds to do, as discussed above.

### Money Designation

A further challenge is introduced. The *gemara* brings a case from the laws of *tum'at mikdash v'kodashav* — the sin of someone who, while ritually impure, entered the *Mikdash* or consumed consecrated food unknowingly. This transgression falls under the *korban oleh ve-yored*, the sliding-scale offering whose form depends on the offender's economic status. A poor person brings birds; a middle-tier person brings birds as well; a wealthy person brings a sheep.

The case: a poor person (*ani*) commits this transgression and sets aside money (*hefrish ma'ot l'kino*) for the pair of birds he is obligated to bring. He then becomes wealthy (*ve-he'ashir*), which means his obligation has shifted to bringing a sheep. He then verbally divides his pile of money, saying: this half is for my *chatat* and this half is for my *olah*. What is the *halakha*?

The *braita* rules: the half he designated as *chatat* money can be supplemented with additional funds to purchase the sheep *chatat* he now owes — *mosif u-meivi chovato midmei chatato*. However, the half designated as *olah* money cannot be used toward his *chatat* obligation — *ve-ein mosif u-meivi chovato midmei olato* — since he declared it for an *olah*, and a sheep *chatat* requires no accompanying *olah*. That leftover *olah* money would be used to purchase a bird *olah* as a freewill offering (*nedavah*).

### Rich vs Poor

Rav Sheshet raises a pointed difficulty with this *braita*, setting aside entirely the question of *when* designation can occur. He cites a tradition in the name of Rabbi Eliezer citing Rabbi Yehoshua: if a wealthy person who was obligated to bring a sheep instead brought the bird offering of a poor person, *lo yatza* — according to Rabbi Yoshiya, he has not fulfilled his obligation. If that is so, asks Rav Sheshet, once this man became wealthy, the pile of money he set aside for birds is no longer relevant to his *korban* at all — he cannot be *yotzei* with what it would purchase. How, then, can any designation of that money into *chatat* and *olah* portions have any halakhic significance? He is no longer in the category of one who brings these birds. *Kevan delo yatza, heichi kava* — since he would not fulfill his obligation, how can the designation be operative?

---

## Yatzei Obligation

### Yoshiya: Lo Yatzei
