The *gemara* now presents the two positions directly. Rabbi Yoshiya holds: *lo yatza* — a wealthy person who brings the lesser offering of a poor person does not fulfill his obligation. Going down the scale is simply invalid. This is the position attributed earlier to Rabbi Eliezer in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yoshiya endorses it.

### Chaga: Yatzei

Rabbi Chaga, however, transmits a tradition also in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya — creating two conflicting traditions attributed to the same authority — that *yatza*: a wealthy person who brought the lesser offering does fulfill his obligation *bedi'avad*. According to Rabbi Chaga's version, once a person has actually brought the lesser *korban*, it is accepted after the fact.

If Rabbi Chaga's position is correct, then the wealthy person who set aside money for birds while poor is not necessarily removed from the category. *Bedi'avad*, had he brought those birds, he would have been *yotzei*. Therefore, when he divides the pile and designates half for *chatat* and half for *olah*, the designation is meaningful — and we are not forced to read the *braita* as imprecise or as describing a pre-enrichment event.

---

## Birds Designation (II)

### Resolution

With the two positions on the table, the *gemara* resolves the question about the *braita*'s scenario. If one follows Rabbi Yoshiya's stricter view that *lo yatza* — that a wealthy person cannot be *yotzei* with a poor person's offering — then the person who became rich is entirely out of the category, and his designation of the money into *chatat* and *olah* portions is meaningless. The *gemara* therefore says we must read the *braita* as imprecise (*shekvar amar me'inyuto*): the *braita* actually means that he made the designation while still poor, and then became rich. The *braita* presents the two events in the wrong order or runs them together loosely.

Furthermore, once we are already reading the *braita* as imprecise about the order of events, we can also say: not only did the designation precede the enrichment, but the designation itself occurred at the moment of *hafrasha* — at the time he set aside the money, the same act of separation constituted the designation. It was one stage, not two.

Under Rabbi Chaga's view that *yatza*, the *braita* need not be read as imprecise at all, and the scenario can be taken literally: he designated the money after becoming rich, and this was effective at some intermediate moment — which would pose the original difficulty about *lekichah* and *asiyah*.

The *gemara*, even under Rabbi Chaga's view, ultimately re-reads the *braita* to say: *ela eima ve-achar kach lakach ve-amar* — the "afterwards" in the *braita* refers not to a verbal splitting of money, but to actually going and purchasing a bird and *at that moment* declaring the other half of the money for the other *korban*. The act of purchasing one bird (*preda achas*) serves as the *shat lekichah* for the designation of the remaining money.

Rav Pappa fills in the practical details. Rather than taking the entire pile of money and buying two birds simultaneously, the person takes half the money and buys a single bird — say, designating it as an *olah*. The very act of purchasing that one bird at *shat lekichah* automatically designates the remaining pile of money as *chatat* money. Now, since there is still money remaining (not a bird), it can be supplemented and used to buy the sheep *chatat*. This is the meaning of *mosif u-meivi chovato midmei chatato*. The bird purchased as an *olah* would simply be brought as a *korban nedavah*.

Conversely, if the bird he purchased was the *chatat*, the remaining money is *olah* money — and that cannot be redirected toward his *chatat* obligation. That is the second part of the *braita*, *ve-ein mosif u-meivi chovato midmei olato*. And the *chatat* bird itself? *Azla le-misa* — it must be left to die, since it was designated as a *chatat* that can no longer be brought and birds have no mechanism of *pidyon* (redemption): unlike livestock, a blemished bird cannot have its *kedusha* transferred to money.

The term *preda* used by the *gemara* for a single bird from the pair is a technical rabbinic term: just as *kan* refers to the pair (a "nest"), *preda* refers to one of the two, derived from the notion of separation.

---

## Yatzei Obligation (II)

### Metzora Proof

Returning to the dispute between the two traditions attributed to Rabbi Hoshaya — one via Rabbi Elazar saying *lo yatza* (a rich person bringing a poor person's offering does not fulfill the obligation), the other via Rabbi Chaga saying *yatza* — the *gemara* introduces a *braita* from the laws of *metzora* to clarify.

The *metzora* also has a sliding-scale offering. The *braita* rules: if a poor *metzora* brought the richer *korban*, *yatza* — he has fulfilled his obligation. If a rich *metzora* brought the lesser offering of a poor person, *lo yatza* — he has not. This is presented as a clear ruling. Presumably the same logic would apply to the *korban oleh ve-yored* in general, which would support the *lo yatza* position.

### Oleh V'Yored

However, the *gemara* then distinguishes: *metzora* is a special case. The Torah uses the word *zot* — "this shall be the law of the *metzora* on the day of his purification" — which is an exclusionary term indicating precise adherence to the specified form. Therefore, going down on the scale is invalid. Yet the same verse contains the word *torat* — "the *torat* of the *metzora*" — which is inclusive, extending the law to cover someone who goes *up* the scale. Hence by *metzora*: going up works, going down does not.

The *gemara* confirms this from a *braita*: the word *torat* comes to include a poor *metzora* who brought the richer *korban* — *yatza*. One might think that even going down should work. The *talmud lomar zot* — the word *zot* excludes that possibility.

Why not apply this principle to *korban oleh ve-yored* generally? Because the additional word by *metzora* — *ve-im dal hu*, "and if he is impoverished" — is taken as a limiting term, indicating that these precise rules (both the inclusion of going up and the exclusion of going down) apply specifically to *metzora* and are not meant to be generalized. For *korban oleh ve-yored*, lacking these words, Rabbi Chaga's tradition would hold that *bedi'avad* even going down on the scale fulfills the obligation.

---

## Red String

### String on Scapegoat

The *gemara* returns to the *mishnah*'s description of the Yom Kippur service. After the lots are drawn and the goats are designated, the *mishnah* records: *kashar lashon shel zehorit be-rosh sheir hamishtaleach* — he tied the *lashon shel zehorit* (the red string) on the head of the *sheir hamishtaleach*, the goat to be sent over the cliff. Notably, the *mishnah* says "head," not "horns." *Ve-he'emido keneged beit shilucho* — he then stood the goat facing the gate from which it would be sent away. *Ve-la-nishchat keneged beit shechitato* — and for the one that would be slaughtered, he placed it opposite the place of slaughter.

The *mishnah* thus describes two actions: the tying of a red string (mentioned explicitly for the *sheir hamishtaleach*) and the placement of each goat at its respective station.

### Second String Question

A question arises from the *mishnah*'s language. When it says *ve-la-nishchat keneged beit shechitato*, does this phrase go back to the first verb — meaning that a red string was also tied on the goat designated for slaughter, placed at the point around its neck from which it would be slaughtered — or does it go back only to the second verb, meaning that only the placement of the animal opposite its slaughter site is described, with no red string on this goat at all?

The more grammatically proximate reading would attach this clause to the verb of standing/placing. But the *gemara* explores both possibilities.

### No Mixing

A *braita* taught by Rav Yosef provides the evidentiary basis. It repeats the *mishnah*'s language but adds: *shelo yitarev zeh be-zeh* — so that the two goats should not become confused with one another, *ve-lo yitarev be-acherim* — and should not become confused with other goats.

### Neck String

The *gemara* now reasons from this addition. If *ve-la-nishchat* refers to a red string tied around the neck of the goat designated for slaughter — *ei amart akshira kai* — then both goats bear red strings, and the two strings distinguish them from each other and from other animals. This works perfectly: the *sheir hamishtaleach* has its string on its head (between the horns), and the *sheir la-Hashem* has its string around its neck. Different placements; same color — but placement suffices to distinguish them.

But if *ve-la-nishchat* refers only to placement — *ela ei amart ahamada kai* — then only one goat (the *sheir hamishtaleach*) has a string. *Nehi de-va-chavreih lo mi'arev* — granted, the one designated for slaughter won't be confused with the one being sent away, since that one has a string and this one does not. *Be-hai katar beih u-ve-hai lo katar beih*. But *u-ve-achrinei mi'arev* — it could still be confused with other goats, since nothing on it marks it as distinct. The requirement *shelo yitarev be-acherim* would then remain unsatisfied for the goat designated for slaughter.

Therefore: *ela lav, shma mina akshira kai* — the clause about the slaughtered goat must refer to tying a string. The *gemara* concludes: *shma mina* — there is indeed a red string tied around the neck of the *sheir la-Hashem*, the goat designated to be slaughtered as the *chatat*.

This is a striking conclusion — one that does not appear to be reflected in the standard liturgical descriptions of the *avodah* found in the *machzor*. Yet the *gemara* concludes it definitively. The practical logic is asymmetrical: the *sheir hamishtaleach* needs its string both to be identifiable and because that string will later be split when the goat reaches the cliff — requiring sufficient length for that purpose. The goat that remains in the *azarah* and is slaughtered would not encounter any other goats, so practically speaking it is less in need of the marking, but the *gemara*'s reading of the *braita* requires the string nonetheless.

---

## Red String (II)

### Two Strings

Rabbi Yitzchak's statement that follows addresses two types of *lashon shel zehorit* — and this connects back to the strings just discussed. One of those two strings is the one of the *sheir hamishtaleach*; the other is the red string (*sheni tola'at*) thrown into the pyre of the *parah adumah* — the Red Heifer. Both are called *lashon shel zehorit* in rabbinic tradition, and Rabbi Yitzchak notes that he received a tradition about these two strings: one requires a *shiur* (minimum size) and the other does not — but he does not know which is which.

---

## String Minimums

### Two String Types

Rabbi Yitzchak states: *shtei leshonot shamati* — I have received teachings about two strings. *Achat shel parah ve-achat shel sheir hamishtaleach* — one pertaining to the *parah adumah* and one pertaining to the *sheir hamishtaleach*. *Achat tzericha shiur ve-achat einah tzericha shiur* — one requires a minimum measure and the other does not. *Ve-lo yadana he minayhu* — and I do not know which is which.

### Scapegoat Minimum

Rav Yosef proposes a resolution. *Shel sheir hamishtaleach deva'i chaluka, ba'i shiur* — the string of the *sheir hamishtaleach* requires a minimum measure, because that string must be split in two. As we will see later in the tractate, the string is divided: one half remains tied between the horns of the goat as it is sent off, and the other half is kept at the cliff, enabling those present to observe when it turns white — the traditional sign that the Yom Kippur atonement has been accepted. Since the string must be divided and still function in both capacities, it requires a minimum length sufficient for this purpose.

### Parah No Minimum

By contrast, *shel parah delo va'i chaluka, lo ba'i shiur* — the string of the *parah adumah* does not need to be split and thus has no minimum measure. Any quantity, however small, satisfies the requirement of throwing *sheni tola'at* into the fire.

### Weight Question

Rami bar Chama challenges this conclusion. Even if the *parah adumah*'s string has no minimum *length*, it may still require minimum *weight*. The verse by the *parah adumah* uses the language *ve-hishlich* — "and he shall cast it" — which implies a throwing with force and trajectory. If the string is so light and wispy that it flutters rather than falls into the fire, can that be called *ve-hishlich*? There may therefore be a minimum *weight* requirement, even if not a minimum length.

### Tanna Debate

Rava responds: *koved tanna'i hi* — the question of whether the string must have weight sufficient to fall into the fire is itself a dispute among *tanna'im*. According to the *tanna* who holds that the string need not fall in a directed fashion, even a string that flutters into the fire is valid, and no minimum weight is required. According to that view, the *parah adumah* string truly has no minimum — neither of length nor of weight. The full range of opinions on this question, and how they map onto the various types of red strings involved in the Yom Kippur and *parah adumah* rituals, will be addressed in the discussion that follows.

---

---

# Yoma 42

## Service Overview & Red S…

### Service Steps & Red Stri…

Before turning to the substance of today's *daf*, it is worth pausing to situate ourselves within the *avodat Yom Kippur* as we have been tracking it. The first step of the day is the *kohen gadol*'s *vidui* over his *par*, performed in the northern portion of the *azarah*. The second step is the *goralot*, the drawing of lots over the two goats. The third step — and the one that has been occupying the *Gemara*'s attention — is the tying of the red string. The fourth step is a second *vidui* over the *par*, this time on behalf of all the *kohanim*.

The question arises: who ties the red string in this third step? The relevant term is *kashar* — he ties — but there is no clear discussion requiring the *kohen gadol* specifically to perform it. More fundamentally, the red string tied onto the goat designated *la'azazel* is not mentioned anywhere in the Torah. The Torah does mention red strings in other contexts, and the *Gemara* has been drawing comparisons between them. According to the *Mishnah*, the red string is placed on the goat *la'azazel*, which is then stationed near the gate from which it will depart. The *Gemara* also records that a red string is placed around the neck of the goat designated *l'Hashem* — a detail that, as far as can be determined, is not echoed in the liturgical retellings of the *avodah*.

### Red String Placement

The comparison that has been driving this discussion is between the red string of the *sa'ir* and the red string of the *parah adumah*. The red string used in the *parah adumah* ritual — together with the *eitz erez* and the *ezov* — is cast into the burning of the *parah*. This is where the issue of minimum weight arises: the verse uses the word *v'hishlich*, "and he cast it," and there is a question whether this implies that the object must fall immediately and directly when thrown, rather than floating down slowly. Does the red string need a minimum weight to ensure it descends with the directness that "casting" implies? That debate about *koved* is what the *Gemara* now resumes.

### Three Red Strings

There are in fact three red strings discussed in connection with these rituals: the string of the *parah adumah*, the string of the *sa'ir hamishtalach*, and the string of the *metzora* — the latter used in the purification process described in the Torah. All three will figure in the discussion of minimum weight requirements, each carrying a different amount for reasons that will become clear.

---

## Weight Minimums Debate

### Rava: Weight Debate

The *Gemara* on the bottom of 41b states: *amar lei Rava, koved tana'i hi* — Rava declares that the question of whether the red string of the *parah adumah* requires a minimum weight is in fact a dispute among *tanna'im*. The *Gemara* notes that, unlike the red string of the *sa'ir*, the string of the *parah adumah* does not need to be divided in two; the only question there is one of weight.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye raises a challenge to this: *eitiveih Abaye, keitzad hu oseh*? A *Mishnah* concerning *parah adumah* states *korchan beshiyarei lashon* — one wraps the *erez* and *ezov* with the remnant of the red string. The word *shiyarei* seems to imply that the string was indeed cut, suggesting a minimum length — and therefore a minimum weight — is required for the *parah adumah* string as well. The *Gemara* responds: *eima biznav lashon* — this does not mean a literal remnant from having been cut, but rather a frayed end, like the fringe at the bottom of a comb. The *shiyarei* here refers to the appearance of fraying, not to an actual division of the string.

### Flame vs. Fire Debate

*Amar Rabbi Chanin amar Rav*: if the *eitz erez*, *ezov*, and red string were caught by the flame and burned before actually falling into the fire — that is, they were held over the conflagration and the flame consumed them — is the ritual valid? Rabbi Chanin rules *kesheirah*: being consumed by the flame, even without physically falling in, is sufficient. The *Gemara* challenges this from a *braita*: *nishavhev halashon* — if the string gets charred, one must bring another string and sanctify it by casting it in. Mere charring is not enough; it must fall into the fire. Abaye resolves the contradiction: *kan dekolchas, kan demichsefes* — it depends on the type of fire.

### El Toch Requirement

If the fire has very high leaping flames, and the string is consumed while held aloft above it, one has not fulfilled the requirement, because the Torah says *el toch srefat haparah* — into the very midst of the burning of the *parah*. But if the flames are low, then being consumed at that low level is tantamount to being within the fire itself, because one is so close to the physical source of the combustion. The critical point is not that the string must physically strike the ground or the pile on the bottom, but that it must be close enough to the base of the flame to count as being *el toch* — within the midst. Being consumed by a high flame, far removed from the source, does not satisfy this criterion.

### Three Weight Standards

Returning to the question of minimum weight: *ki ata Rav Dimi amar Rabbi Yochanan — shalosh leshonot shamati*. When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that he had heard a teaching about the three red strings — that of the *parah adumah*, that of the *sa'ir hamishtalach*, and that of the *metzora*. Each has a different weight requirement: one must weigh ten *zuz*, one two *sela'im*, and one one *shekel*. The proportions are easy to remember: ten, two, and one. However, Rabbi Yochanan could not explain which weight belongs to which context.

### Ravin Explains Weights

When Ravin subsequently came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he provided the explanation in the name of Rav Yonatan, at the top of 42a. The *parah adumah* string must weigh the most — ten *zuz* — because it must be cast into the fire and fall in directly. The *sa'ir hamishtalach* string requires two *sela'im*, the intermediate amount, because it must be long enough to be divided into two portions. It is admittedly somewhat indirect to use weight as a proxy for length — weight only serves as a reliable indicator of length if one assumes a standard thickness of string — but that is the logic employed. The *metzora* string requires only one *shekel*, since neither of the previous considerations applies: it does not need to be cast into fire and it does not need to be divided.

One might ask why the *metzora* string needs any minimum at all. The *Gemara* does not offer a clear explanation for this baseline requirement. Rav Yochanan adds: *pligi vah Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta v'rabanan* — there is a dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta and the Sages specifically about the *parah* string. One says it must weigh ten *zuz*, the other says merely one *shekel*. The memorable quality of this dispute is its symmetry: one goes to the highest extreme, the other to the lowest, and nobody assigns the *parah* the middle value of two *sela'im*. The mnemonic offered is the famous phrase *echad hamarbeh v'echad hamamit, uvilvad sheyachaven libo laShamayim* — whether one does more or less, what matters is that one's heart be directed toward Heaven.

### Debate Focus Corrected

At this point, Rav Yirmiyah of Dipti corrects what he sees as a misidentification of the debate's subject: *lo b'parah pligi, ela bisi'arei hamishtalach pligi* — the dispute between the extreme of ten and the extreme of one is not about the *parah adumah* string at all, but about the *sa'ir hamishtalach*. Why one would insist on such a heavy string for the scapegoat, while another would permit the lightest possible string, is not fully explained — though one might speculate that preventing the string from blowing off or breaking during the goat's journey could motivate a heavier requirement.

### Death & Scapegoat Link

The *Gemara* then notes: *ve-hahu yoma nach nafshei de-Rav Ya bar Kisi* — on that very day when this dispute was being debated, Rav Ya bar Kisi passed away. *Ve-anchu vah siman* — they placed this as a mnemonic to remember that the debate concerned the *sa'ir hamishtalach* rather than the *parah adumah*: *Rav Ya bar Kisi mechaper ke-sa'ir hamishtalach* — Rav Ya bar Kisi atones like the scapegoat atones. On the surface this is presented as a simple memory device, but it opens onto one of the more theologically striking passages in this section of the *Gemara*.

The principle at work here is *mitat tzadikim mechaperet* — the death of righteous individuals brings atonement. This idea merits reflection precisely because it tends to be underemphasized in traditional discourse, perhaps because it was appropriated so centrally by Christian theology in connection with the death of Jesus. But here it appears straightforwardly in the *Gemara* as an accepted theological datum, analogized to the *sa'ir hamishtalach*. The parallel is evocative: the goat carries the sins of the community; the *tzadik*, one might say, carries its merit. Both are in some sense removed from the community — one cast away to the wilderness, the other taken by death — and yet both, by their departure, effect some form of metaphysical atonement.

This also invites reflection on why the *sa'ir la'azazel* itself brings atonement, which is theologically difficult in its own right. Unlike a *korban* offered on the altar — where one can understand the symbolism of a life given to God, perhaps even representing the offerer's own life as in the logic of the *akeidah* — the scapegoat is not offered to God at all. It is sent away, driven off a cliff, dispatched to *Azazel*, whatever that means. The mechanics of its atonement remain genuinely opaque. The *Gemara* connects these two opaque forms of atonement — the scapegoat and the death of the righteous — and allows that parallel to stand without resolving either.

Regarding terminology: the word *lashon* — literally "tongue" — is the term used in rabbinic Hebrew for the red string, as opposed to *chut*, which is the biblical term found in *chut ha-shani*. A *lashon* in this context refers specifically to a string or cord, and more precisely to the distinctive red string used in these rituals.

---

## Slaughterings Debate

### Which Needs Kohen?

The *Gemara* now introduces a new parallel to the three-string discussion: *amar Rabbi Yitzchak, shtei shechitot shamati* — Rabbi Yitzchak says he heard a teaching about two *shechitot*: one of the *parah adumah* and one of the *par* of the *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur*. Just as the three strings had different weight requirements that were debated and disputed, these two *shechitot* differ in their requirements regarding whether a *zar* — a non-*kohen* — may perform them: *achat kesheirah be-zar*, one is valid if performed by a non-*kohen*, *ve-achat psulah be-zar*, the other is not. And *ve-lo yadana hei mineihu* — he does not know which is which.

One might suppose the answer is obvious. But the question is genuinely complex. By *Yom Kippur*, there is a general principle that everything must be performed by the *kohen gadol*. Yet the *Gemara* has already established that certain actions on *Yom Kippur* are not considered *avodah* and therefore may not require the *kohen gadol* — the drawing of the lots being one example. *Shechitah* is normally *kesheirah be-zar* in all contexts. Does that remain true even on *Yom Kippur*? And conversely, why should the *parah adumah* — performed outside the *Mikdash* entirely — require a *kohen* for its *shechitah*?

### Rav vs. Shmuel

*Itmar* — there is a recorded dispute: *Rav u-Shmuel*. One says the *shechitah* of the *parah* is *psulah be-zar* and the *shechitah* of the *kohen gadol*'s *par* on *Yom Kippur* is *kesheirah be-zar*; the other says the opposite. The *Gemara* then attempts to assign the positions: *tistayem de-Rav hu de-amar parah psulah* — it can be concluded that it is Rav who holds the *parah* is invalid when performed by a non-*kohen*.

The evidence for this attribution comes from Rabbi Zeira, who says *shechitat parah be-zar psulah*, and then from Rava's comment on that ruling: *Elazar ve-chukah shaninu bah* — the reason is that the *parah adumah* pericope in *Parashat Chukat* repeatedly invokes *Elazar ha-kohen*, and the *parsha* opens with the phrase *zot chukat ha-Torah*. The word *chok* signals that something is absolutely binding and indispensable. The combination of the *chok* language and the repeated emphasis on *Elazar* yields the ruling that a *kohen* is required. Since Rav appears to be affirming and explaining this ruling, he is identified as its author.

The symmetrical argument applies to *Yom Kippur*: the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* is framed by *Bezot yavo Aharon* and concludes with *ve-hayeta zot lachem l'chukat olam*, again combining the personality of *Aharon* with the language of *chok*. By the same logic, everything on *Yom Kippur* should require a *kohen gadol*. But the *Gemara* responds: *shechitah lav avodah hi* — *shechitah* is not an *avodah*. Just as the drawing of the lots was not considered an *avodah* and could theoretically be performed by someone other than the *kohen gadol*, *shechitah* is similarly excluded from the *avodah* category, and therefore from the *kohen gadol* requirement on *Yom Kippur*. According to Rav, then, the *Yom Kippur par* can be *shechted* by a non-*kohen gadol* — indeed by a *zar* — while the *parah adumah* requires a *kohen*.

### Shechitah Not Avodah

Why is *shechitah* not an *avodah*? Rashi's explanation points to the evidence from the opening *parsha* of *Vayikra*: the Torah describes the owner bringing the *korban* and performing *shechitah*, and only then introduces *bnei Aharon* to receive the blood. The *kohanim* enter the picture after the *shechitah*, which is evidence that *shechitah* does not require a *kohen* as a general rule. Since the criterion for being an *avodah* is that it requires a *kohen*, the general permissibility of *shechitah* by a non-*kohen* is evidence that it is not an *avodah*. Once it is not an *avodah*, even on *Yom Kippur* it is excluded from the *kohen gadol* requirement.

Tosafot offers a different explanation: *shechitah* is not an *avodah* because it is a procedure required even outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. *Melikah* — the nipping of a bird's neck in the *Mikdash* — is a uniquely Temple ritual and therefore an *avodah* requiring a *kohen*. But *shechitah* is performed universally: for ordinary meat, for *korbanot*, for the *eglah arufah* outside the *Mikdash*. This universality defines it as something that, even when it takes place in the *Mikdash*, retains a non-*avodah* character. The actions that are genuinely *avodah* — receiving the blood, moving the blood, throwing the blood on the altar — are all uniquely Temple acts.

### Rav Sheshet's Point

The *Gemara* presses: if *shechitah* is not an *avodah* on *Yom Kippur*, why is it *psulah be-zar* by the *parah adumah*? Is the *parah adumah* not even a *korban* — it is sanctified with the sanctity of *kadshei bedek ha-bayit*, like a beam of wood consecrated for Temple use, not with intrinsic sacrificial sanctity — so should it not be *a fortiori* permissible with a *zar*? The *Gemara* responds: *amar Rav Sheshet b'rei d'Rav Idi, midi d'hava amara'os negaim* — consider the inspection of *nega'im*. Examining the spot of *tzara'at* is not an *avodah*; it is performed wherever the afflicted person is found, outside the *Mikdash* entirely. Yet it requires a *kohen*. This disproves the inference that whatever is not an *avodah* may be performed by a non-*kohen*.

The logical point here is important. Just because every *avodah* requires a *kohen* does not mean that every requirement of a *kohen* indicates an *avodah*. There are non-*avodah* functions that nonetheless require *kehunah*. The *parah adumah* process is entirely outside the *Mikdash* and is not about *avodah* at all — but if the Torah requires a *kohen* for some part of it, it requires a *kohen* for all of it, including *shechitah*. Inside the *Mikdash*, where the framework is *avodah*, one excludes *shechitah* from the *kohen gadol* requirement because it is not an *avodah*. Outside the *Mikdash*, that framework does not apply, and if the *kohen* requirement is there at all, it governs the entire process.

### Distraction Question

The *Gemara* continues: *she-lo yasi'ach da'ato mimena* — Rav's understanding of the phrase *v'shachat osah le'fanav*, "and he shall slaughter it before him," is not that someone else performs the *shechitah* in *Elazar*'s presence, but that *Elazar* himself performs the *shechitah* while being fully psychologically present, not distracted. This is one of the remarkable features of the *parah adumah* ritual — the requirement of mental presence and attentiveness.

Shmuel, who holds the *parah adumah* does not require a *kohen* for *shechitah*, reads *v'shachat osah le'fanav* straightforwardly as indicating that someone else performs the *shechitah* while *Elazar* supervises. Where does Shmuel then derive the non-distraction requirement? From the verse *v'saraf et ha-para le'einav* — he shall burn it before his eyes. That verse establishes the requirement of attentive presence at the burning. Rav, by contrast, uses both verses: one to establish the non-distraction requirement at the *shechitah*, the other to establish it at the *sreifah*. The *Gemara* explains why both are needed: had the Torah only specified non-distraction at the *shechitah*, one might have thought that once the process is underway, the *kohen* may become inattentive during the burning. Had it only specified at the *sreifah*, one might have thought that only the culminating act — when the *parah* actually becomes *eifer* — requires full attention, but the *shechitah*, as merely a preparatory step, does not. *Tzricha* — both verses are necessary.

### Distraction Exclusions

The *Gemara* then asks: *lemutei mai* — by specifying that non-distraction is required at *shechitah* and *sreifah*, what is being excluded? The *Gemara* considers and rejects the possibility that gathering the ashes and filling the water are excluded, since the verse *le-mishmeret le-mei nidah* — "for a safeguarding for the waters of sprinkling" — establishes that those processes too require watchful attention. The actual exclusion is: *ela lemutei hashlachat eitz erez ve-ezov u-sheni tola'at* — the throwing of the cedar, hyssop, and red string into the fire. Since these items are not the *parah adumah* itself — *delav gufah de-para ninhu* — all the other actions concern the *parah* directly, but these are auxiliary additions. If one performed the throwing of these items while distracted, it remains *kasher*.

### Alternative Opinions

The *Gemara* records additional versions of the debate: *Rav Ami amar kasher, Rav Yitzchak Napcha amar psulah* — Rav Ami rules the *shechitah* of the *parah* by a *zar* is valid, Rav Yitzchak Napcha rules it invalid. And *Ula amar kesheirah*, though some report Ula as having said *psulah*. These are further attestations of an ongoing dispute that runs throughout this *sugya*.

---

## Proof from Daytime

### Braita's Logic

*Masiv Rav Yehoshua bar Abba l'siyu'ei le-Rav* — Rav Yehoshua bar Abba brings a challenge in support of Rav's position, which holds that the *shechitah* of the *parah adumah* is *psulah be-zar*. The source is a *braita* that addresses which parts of the *parah adumah* process must be performed during the day. The structure of the argument is as follows.

The *braita* begins: *ein li ella hazat meimeha she-ein kesheirah be-isha ke-ve-ish ve-ein kesheirah ella bayom* — we know that the sprinkling of the purification water cannot be done by a woman as it can by a man, and it can only be done during the day. From this foundation, the *braita* asks: how do we derive that the other parts of the process — *shechitah*, receiving the blood, sprinkling the blood, burning the *parah*, and throwing the cedar, hyssop, and red string into the fire — also must be done during the day? The answer: *Talmud lomar, zot chukat ha-Torah* — the word *Torah* here is inclusive, drawing everything under the same category. Since the sprinkling must be daytime, and everything is grouped together, all other parts of the process must also be daytime.

But perhaps the daytime requirement extends further still — to gathering the ashes, filling the water, and the *kiddush* of putting the ashes in the water? *Talmud lomar, zot* — the word *zot* is limiting; not everything falls within the category.

### Torah Language Logic

The obvious question is: what criterion determines what falls inside the category and what falls outside? The *braita* states: *achar she-riba ha-katuv u-mi'et, amarta, harei anu le-meidin kulam me-hazat meimeha* — after the Torah both included and excluded, one reasons that everything is learned from the sprinkling. The logic is: just as the sprinkling cannot be done by a woman (only by a man) and can only be done during the day, we will apply both of those criteria to the other parts of the process.

### Category Logic

The category determination then proceeds: *hо'il ve-ein kesheirah be-isha ke-ve-ish ein kesheirah ella bayom* — since the other parts of the process share the criterion of requiring a man rather than a woman, we will also apply the criterion of daytime to them. *Af ani arbeh shechitata ve-kabbalat dama ve-hazat dama ve-sreifata ve-hashlachat eitz erez ve-ezov u-sheni tola'at* — I will include the *shechitah*, the receiving of the blood, the sprinkling of the blood, the burning, and the throwing of the wood and red string. All of these share the criterion of not being performable by a woman; therefore, by analogy to the sprinkling, they all require daytime.

*U-motziani asifat afara u-milui mayim ve-kiddush* — I will exclude the gathering of the ashes, the filling of the water, and the *kiddush*. Why? *Ho'il ve-ksheirim be-isha ke-ve-ish* — since those can be done by either a man or a woman, they do not share that restricting criterion, and therefore *ksheirim nami be-yom u-va-lailah* — they may be performed at night as well. The logic is essentially: those things that already share one of the two restrictive features of the sprinkling will be assumed to share the other; those that share neither restrictive feature share neither.

### Rashi on Judgment

A remarkable *Rashi* must be noted here. Rashi comments on the *braita*'s logic of inclusion and exclusion, observing that *ve-lo peiresh mah ribah u-mah mi'at* — the Torah does not specify what falls into which category. *U-mei'atah lo masran ela le-hitbonen bah et ha-emet ve-et ha-yashar* — and therefore the Torah handed it over to the Sages only to reason into it, to find out what is true and what is right. The word *yashar* — straight, upright — here suggests that the Torah deliberately left this categorization to rational and moral judgment. It is a striking formulation: not *da'at Torah* in the sense of an authoritative ruling, but an explicit invitation to the exercise of reasoned human judgment within the halakhic framework.

### Woman Exclusion Logic

This leads to the central argument of the *braita* as a proof that *shechitah be-zar psulah*. The *Gemara* asks: *ve-ha mai tiyuvta* — in what way is this actually a challenge to the position that *shechitah* can be done by a non-*kohen*? The apparent argument is: *eilema mid-paslinan be-isha paslinan nami be-zar* — from the fact that we disqualify a woman, we disqualify a non-*kohen*; the exclusion of women is really about their not being *kohanim*, and therefore it demonstrates that *shechitah* requires a *kohen*.

### Sprinkling Exception

But the *Gemara* objects: *haza'ah tochi'ach* — the sprinkling itself disproves this inference. The sprinkling cannot be done by a woman but can be done by a non-*kohen*. So the exclusion of women is not necessarily about requiring a *kohen*. If the sprinkling — which was the paradigm case from which the whole argument was derived — requires a man but not a *kohen*, then perhaps *shechitah* also merely requires a man without requiring a *kohen*.

Abaye responds: *hainu tiyuvteih* — this is precisely why it remains a challenge. *Isha mai ta'ama* — what is the basis for excluding a woman from *shechitah* and from burning and from receiving the blood? For the sprinkling, we know from explicit *pesukim* (*ish tahor*, *ish tahor*) that it must be a man, and separately that a non-*kohen* is valid. But for the *shechitah* and burning — where does the exclusion of a woman come from? The only basis in the text for excluding a woman from those parts of the process is *Elazar ve-lo isha* — the verse specifying *Elazar*, which excludes a woman. But if that is the basis, then *zar nami* — a non-*kohen* is likewise excluded, since the specification of *Elazar* implies *Elazar ve-lo zar*, not *Elazar* and not a non-*kohen*. The exclusion of woman in this part of the process is inseparable from the exclusion of the non-*kohen*; both flow from the same verse. Therefore, one cannot argue that *shechitah* requires a man but not a *kohen* — for those two conclusions are driven by separate textual grounds only in the case of the sprinkling, not for *shechitah* and the other parts of the process.

---

## Pesukim Reading

### Ulla's Framework

*Amar Ulla kol ha-parsha kullah mashma motzi miyad mashma u-mashma mimela* — Ulla offers a general observation about the entire *parsha* of *parah adumah*: throughout the section, the verses oscillate between *mashma* — the simple, natural reading of the text — and *motzi miyad mashma* — exceptions that deviate from what the text plainly implies. Sometimes the rabbinic ruling follows naturally from the plain sense of the verse; sometimes the ruling deliberately departs from it.

### Mashma Definition

A note on terminology is in order here. The word *mashma* — "it sounds like," "it implies" — is closely related to the word *pshat*, but they are not identical. We commonly assume *pshat* means the plain, simple sense of a verse: what the text would have meant to its original audience. But in rabbinic usage, *pshat* more precisely refers to the standardized, canonically accepted rabbinic reading. This is evidenced by the *Gemara*'s locution *pshuto ke-mashmao* — the *pshat* of this verse is as it sounds. If *pshat* simply meant the plain sense, this phrase would be tautological. Rather, *mashma* is the genuinely plain sense of the text — what the words naturally imply — while *pshat* is the accepted rabbinic interpretation, which sometimes coincides with *mashma* and sometimes does not. What Ulla is saying, then, is that throughout the *parah adumah parsha*, the rabbis sometimes follow the natural sense and sometimes depart from it.

### Elazar Requirement

The *Gemara* now reads specific verses. *Ve-nasattem otah el Elazar ha-kohen* — and you shall give it to *Elazar ha-kohen*. The rabbinic reading is: *otah Elazar ve-lo le-dorot Elazar* — for this generation, it must specifically go to *Elazar*; for future generations, the requirement of *Elazar* specifically does not apply. The question is: what does apply *le-dorot*? Here the *Gemara* records two opinions. *Ika de-amri: le-dorot be-kohen gadol* — some say that for future generations, the *parah adumah* requires a *kohen gadol*. *Ve-ika de-amri: le-dorot be-kohen hedyot* — others say it requires only an ordinary *kohen*.

The *mashma* of the text, if one were asked to extrapolate from the Torah's repeated emphasis on *Elazar*, might suggest someone elevated — perhaps a *segan*, a second-in-command, someone close to the level of *Elazar* without being the *kohen gadol* himself. But neither opinion follows that middle path. The question is whether the departure from *Elazar* goes up (to *kohen gadol*) or down (to ordinary *kohen*).

### Gezera Shava

*Bishlama le-man de-amar le-dorot be-kohen hedyot* — if you hold that an ordinary *kohen* suffices for future generations, this is straightforward: the Torah's specific mention of *Elazar* applied only to that moment, and afterward any *kohen* suffices. But if you hold that future generations require a *kohen gadol* — *mena leh*? Where does that come from? *Gamar chukah chukah mi-Yom ha-Kippurim* — a *gezera shava*: the Torah uses the word *chok* in the context of *parah adumah* and uses the same word *chok* in the context of *Yom Kippur*. Just as *Yom Kippur* requires a *kohen gadol*, so too *parah adumah* requires a *kohen gadol*.

This conclusion is striking in its implications. Throughout this *sugya*, the working assumption has been that the *Yom Kippur* service requires a *kohen gadol* and the *parah adumah* requires an ordinary *kohen*. Those two rituals — which the Torah presents as the defining communal *avodot* of their respective domains, each with a specific personality attached (*Aharon* for *Yom Kippur*, *Elazar* for *parah adumah*) — translate into the same institutional requirement *le-dorot* according to this opinion: in both cases, only a *kohen gadol*. The prevailing assumption runs the other way — *Yom Kippur* becomes *kohen gadol*, *parah adumah* becomes ordinary *kohen* — but the *gezera shava* collapses that distinction entirely, binding these two great rituals together through the shared word *chok*, so that the personality of *Aharon* and the personality of *Elazar* become, for all future generations, the same office.

---

---

# Yoma 44

## Shechita & Blood

### Shechita

The *mishna* that opens the daf picks up in the middle of 43b, returning to the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur*. The *Kohen Gadol* has completed his second *viduy* — the first having been for himself and his household alone, the second extending to all the *kohanim* — in fulfillment of the principle *yavo zakai veyechaper al hachayav*: he who is pure should come to bring atonement for others. As was noted, this already places extraordinary weight on the *viduy* itself, identifying him as *zakai* even before any *korban* has been brought.

With the *viduy* concluded, the *mishna* proceeds: *shachato* — he performed the *shechita* of the cow. *Kibeyl bamazrak et damo* — he himself received the blood in the *mizrak*. Every act of the *avodah* is performed by the *Kohen Gadol* personally.

### Blood Stirring

There is, however, one task he is not required to perform: continuously stirring the blood to prevent it from congealing. This is not itself an *avodah*, but it is a practical necessity — under normal circumstances, blood would be dashed immediately upon the altar, but here the *Kohen Gadol* must first bring the *ketores* into the *Kodesh Hakodashim* before attending to the blood. The *mishna* therefore states that he hands the blood to another, *lemishehu memareis vo*, who stirs it *al harovat harevi'i shebeheichal* — on the fourth step of the *Heichal* — so that it should not congeal. The precise location of this step will require discussion.

### Fire Pan Prep

Next, *nato machta* — he took a fire pan — *ve'ala lerosh hamizbeach*, ascended to the top of the outer altar, and pushed the coals to either side, digging out from the fully consumed inner embers. This coal will be used for a separate fire pan dedicated to the *ketores* of *Yom Kippur*. Indeed, as will emerge, a distinct wood pile was created specifically for this purpose — a special fire on top of the great outer altar, separate from the fires already burning there, whose sole function was to generate coals for the incense that would be brought into the *Kodesh Hakodashim*.

---

## Fire & Vessels

### Special Fire

The *mishna* now elaborates at length on the contrasts between the normal daily service and what is done on *Yom Kippur*, in a sustained back-and-forth that constantly pulls the reader between the ordinary and the extraordinary. The first such contrast concerns the fire pile itself. He placed the gathered coals *al harovat harevi'i sheba'azarah* — on the fourth step in the *Azarah* — which is presumably the same set of steps viewed from the other direction: one being the fourth step descending from the *Heichal*, and the other the fourth step ascending from the *Azarah*.

### Silver/Gold Pans

*Bechol yom hayah choteh beshel kesef umeareiv betoch shel zahav* — every ordinary day, a *kohen* would shovel out the coals using a silver fire pan and then transfer them into a gold one, bringing the gold pan into the *Heichal* to place upon the golden altar. The silver pan is used for the initial digging because shoveling burning coals with gold is damaging to the metal; silver is more durable. Both, of course, are *klei shareit*.

*Uvayom hazeh choteh beshel zahav uvah hayah machnis* — but today, he would not perform two transfers at all. He would dig out the coals directly with a gold fire pan and carry that same pan straight into the *Kodesh Hakodashim*. The *Gemara* will explain that the elimination of the double transfer is a matter of *chulsha d'Kohen Gadol* — sparing the *Kohen Gadol* unnecessary exertion — since the subsequent *avodah* of placing the incense from vessel to hands while holding the fire pan is already extraordinarily demanding.

The *Rashash*, however, suggests a different reading: that this is simply the *pshat* of the *psukim*. The Torah states *v'lakach mlo hamachta gachalei esh me'al hamizbeach... u'mlo chofnav ktoret samim daka v'hevi mibeit laparochet* — the very fire pan from which the coals are taken is the one brought inside. The *Rashash* further argues that *hayom* — "today" — when contrasted with "every day" throughout this *mishna*, refers not merely to the special *Yom Kippur ketores* of the *Kodesh Hakodashim*, but to all the *ketorot* performed that day, including those of the morning and afternoon. *Rashi*, however, maintains that the contrast applies only to the special inner *ketores* of *Yom Kippur*, and the subsequent discussion follows *Rashi*'s assumption.

### Coal Measures

*Bechol yom choteh b'shel arba'ah kavin umeareiv betoch shlosha kabin* — every ordinary day he would start with a pan that held four *kavin* and pour into one that held three. The reason is practical: when transferring between vessels, some spillage is inevitable, so you begin with more than the target amount. *Vehayom choteh bishlosha kabin uvahen hayah machnis* — but today, since he uses only one pan throughout, he digs out three *kavin* and that same pan is carried inside.

*Rabbi Yose* differs on the normal-day quantities: *bechol yom choteh b'shel se'ah* — ordinarily he would begin with a full *se'ah*, which is six *kavin*, and pour into three. Today, by contrast, three *kavin* are both dug and carried, the same bottom line as the first opinion.

### Pan Weight

*Bechol yom hayta kveda* — every ordinary day the fire pan was heavy. *Vehayom kala* — today it was lighter, made of thinner gold. This is not merely a gesture toward the *Kohen Gadol*'s comfort in general; it is a necessity given the extreme physical demands of the *avodah* that follows. He must carry both the fire pan and a vessel of incense, and then transfer the incense from the vessel into both of his hands while still holding the fire pan — manipulating the pan with his arms and elbows. Every reduction in weight and every increase in maneuverability matters enormously.

### Pan Color

Accompanying the difference in weight is a difference in the handle: *bechol yom hayta yadah ketzarah* — ordinarily the handle was short; *vehayom aruchah* — today it was long. A longer handle allows for better leverage, makes the pan easier to carry at the elbow, and facilitates the difficult manipulation of transferring the incense from vessel to hands.

*Bechol yom haya zehava yarok* — on ordinary days the gold of the pan was *yarok*. It should be noted that *yarok* in *mishnaic* usage encompasses both green and yellow, as *Tosafot* observes elsewhere from the *mishna* concerning an *etrog* that requires the specification *yarok ke-karti* — green like a leek — which would be unnecessary if *yarok* unambiguously meant green. Here, *yarok* likely indicates a yellowish-green tone. *Vehayom adom* — today it was red gold, a richer and more distinguished hue. This is attributed to *Rabbi Menachem*.

### Incense Quality

*Bechol yom makriv pras b'shacharit u'fras bein ha'arbayim* — every day a half-*maneh* of incense was burned on the golden altar in the morning and a half-*maneh* in the afternoon. *Vehayom mosif melo chofnav* — and today an additional *melo chofnav*, a double handful, was burned in the *Kodesh Hakodashim*. *Bechol yom hayta daka* — ordinarily the incense was ground very finely. *Vehayom daka min ha-daka* — today it was the finest of fine. On this point, virtually everyone agrees that the contrast refers specifically to the special *Yom Kippur* incense.

### Kohen Movement

*Bechol yom kohanim olim b'mizracho shel kevesh v'yordim b'maaravo* — ordinarily, *kohanim* would ascend on the eastern side of the ramp and descend on the western side. This is because of the general principle of always turning to one's right: walking forward, your right is to your east, and continuously facing the center while circling the altar produces a counter-clockwise movement. This is the basis for many analogous practices in Jewish life.

*Vehayom Kohen Gadol oleh b'emtza v'yored b'emtza* — but today the *Kohen Gadol* would go up and down through the middle. Since the entire *Beit HaMikdash* is cleared of other *kohanim* during his *avodah*, there is no practical need to stay to one side; and beyond the practical, this expresses the *kavod* of the *Kohen Gadol* — as *Rashi* puts it, he is like a *ben bayit*, at home, free to walk wherever he wishes.

It is worth noting a variant reading found in the *Yerushalmi* and the *Rambam*: *vehayom olim b'emtza v'yordim b'emtza*, in the plural. This is understood to mean that a retinue of *kohanim* would precede the *Kohen Gadol* up the altar — not performing any *avodah*, but serving as his honor guard. This presents an entirely different picture: rather than an empty *Beit HaMikdash* with a solitary figure ascending, one imagines ranks of *kohanim* marching before him, which would itself be a powerful expression of *kevod Kohen Gadol*.

*Rashi* also mentions, though its source is not immediately evident in the *Gemara*, that the *Kohen Gadol* could ascend the altar even *shelo le-tzorech* — even when not strictly required to do so.

*Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees with the premise: *l'olam Kohen Gadol oleh b'emtza v'yored b'emtza* — at all times, not only on *Yom Kippur*, the *Kohen Gadol* may ascend in the middle. For him, *Yom Kippur* does not create this privilege; the *Kohen Gadol* always enjoys it.

### Washing

*Bechol yom Kohen Gadol mekadesh yadav v'raglav min hakiyor* — every day he would sanctify his hands and feet at the *kiyor*, the communal laver. *Vehayom min hakiton shel zahav* — but today, since he undergoes multiple immersions and would wash his hands and feet adjacent to each *tevillah*, a special golden vessel filled with water was brought to him at the site of the *mikveh*. He would not need to descend to the communal *kiyor*.

*Rabbi Yehuda* again applies this distinction universally: the *Kohen Gadol* always washes from his own golden vessel, not the shared *kiyor* — an executive privilege, as it were, befitting his station.

### Fire Piles

*Bechol yom hayu sham arba ma'arachot* — ordinarily there were four wood piles with fire on the top of the outer altar. *Vehayom chamesh* — and today five. The fifth is the special pile created exclusively to produce the coals for the *ketores* of *Yom Kippur*. This is the view of *Rabbi Meir*. *Rabbi Yose* holds that ordinarily there were three, and today four. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that ordinarily there were two, and today three. All opinions agree, however, that one additional pile was added specifically for today's coal-gathering, making the total one more than usual.

---

## No One Present

### Stirrer Problem

Having completed the *mishna*'s survey of contrasts between ordinary days and *Yom Kippur*, the *Gemara* turns to a difficulty embedded in the description of the blood-stirrer. He is positioned on the fourth step of the *Heichal* — yet the verse states *ve-chol adam lo yihyeh b'Ohel Mo'ed* — no one may be present in the *Ohel Mo'ed* when the *Kohen Gadol* enters *lechaper bakodesh*, to perform the *kapparah* in the sanctuary.

*Amar Rabbi Yehuda tani shel heichal* — the answer is that these are not steps within the *Heichal* itself, but steps *leading to* the *Heichal*. The matter is clarified when one considers that no actual steps inside the *Heichal* are known to have existed. The *Heichal* and the *Ulam* are treated as a single unit; the steps in question are those ascending from the *Azarah* toward the *Ulam*-*Heichal* complex. The blood-stirrer stands outside this unit entirely, on the fourth step going down — which corresponds to the *rovat revi'i sheba'azarah* mentioned in the *mishna* as the step of the *Azarah*, the same steps viewed from below.

### No One in Ohel

A *baraita* then explores the scope of the prohibition systematically. The verse *ve-chol adam lo yihyeh b'Ohel Mo'ed* — one might have thought this applied even to the *Azarah* at large. The verse therefore says *be-Ohel Mo'ed*, limiting the prohibition to the *Ohel Mo'ed* proper. One might then have thought it applies only to the *Ohel Mo'ed* of the desert generation; the verse adds *bakodesh* — *b'vo'o lechaper bakodesh* — extending it to the sanctified space of future generations, including *Shilo* and the *Beit Olam*.

*Tosafot* notes a broader question: why do some laws require an explicit verse to include future *batei mikdash* while others are assumed automatically to apply? Among *Tosafot*'s answers is that *tumah*-related laws may differ: since the *Ohel Mo'ed* was portable, its actual tent structure could become *tamei*, while the *Mikdash*'s sanctity inheres in the *makom* itself — even after the structure is gone. These distinctions may be why *tumah*-related derivations sometimes require explicit inclusion.

### Blood Offerings

The *baraita* continues: from the phrase *be-sha'at haktoret* one might have learned only that the prohibition applies during the burning of the incense. How do we know it applies equally during *matan damim* — during the sprinkling of the blood of the *par* and the *sa'ir* on the golden altar and in the *Kodesh Hakodashim*? *Talmud lomar b'vo'o lechaper* — the verse says *b'vo'o lechaper*: all acts of *kapparah* performed in the sanctified space are included.

One might then have thought the prohibition ends once the *Kohen Gadol* enters. The verse adds *ad tzeito* — until he leaves. The *baraita* then delineates the order of precedence: his own *kapparah* precedes his household's, his household's precedes that of his *kohen* brethren, and the *kohanim*'s precedes that of the entire community — corresponding respectively to the two *viduyim* on the *par* and the *viduy* on the *sa'ir*. The *Gra* notes that this formulation is slightly problematic, since the *Kohen Gadol* never actually separates his personal *kapparah* from that of his household — his first *viduy* already reads *ani u'veiti*. The *Gra* accordingly emends the text to read simply him-and-his-household before the *kohanim*.

The *Gemara* then asks: why would one have initially assumed the verse refers only to the burning of the *ketores*? The phrase *lechaper bakodesh* seems more naturally associated with blood than with incense. *Rava*, and similarly *Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi* and *Rav Elazar*, answer from the continuation of the verse: *ve-chipper ba'ado u've'ad beito u've'ad kol kehal Yisrael*. What single act of *kapparah* on *Yom Kippur* covers all of these simultaneously — him, his household, the *kohanim*, and all of Israel? Only the burning of the *ketores* in the *Kodesh Hakodashim*, which is performed once and for all. The blood offerings are staggered — the *par* for himself and the *kohanim*, the *sa'ir* for all Israel — but the *ketores* is brought once, encompassing everyone equally.

---

## Ketores Atonement

### Ketores Mekapper

This leads to a pointed question: *ve-ketoret mechaperet?* — since when is the *ketores* understood to be a vehicle of *kapparah*? We know blood effects atonement; blood is explicitly connected to *kapparah* throughout the Torah. But the *ketores*? Other rituals performed in the *Mikdash* — the lighting of the *Menorah*, the *Lechem Hapanim* — are not associated with *kapparah*. The act of burning the *ketores*, conceptually, seems to belong to an altogether different register: it is about the *encounter* with God, about the conditions that allow the *Kohen Gadol* to enter the *Kodesh Hakodashim* in safety. The entire opening of the *parasha* — *bizot yavo Aharon el hakodesh*, *ki be'anan era'eh al ha-kaporet* — frames the *ketores* not as atonement but as the modality of divine encounter. This is why the question is genuinely sharp.

The *Gemara* answers: *in, detani Rabbi Chananya* — yes, we learn that *ketores* atones. The proof is from the episode following the rebellion of *Korach*, where *Aharon* runs into the midst of a plague and *vayiten et ha-ketores vaykhaper al ha-am* — he placed the *ketores* and it atoned for the people. The *ketores* demonstrably has the power to effect *kapparah*. While this observation is correct, it should not be taken to reduce the entire role of the *Yom Kippur ketores* to this one function; the *pshat* of the *psukim* clearly invests it with a much richer significance. The *kapparah* function is real but not exhaustive.

### Lashon Hara

*Tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* specifies what the *ketores* atones for: *lashon hara*. The connection to the *Korach* episode is evident — the sin there was the misuse of speech, the inciting of people through rhetoric, the pernicious power of language deployed destructively. *Lashon hara* in *Chazal*'s usage is broader than mere gossip; it encompasses any wicked and harmful deployment of speech.

Furthermore, *yavo davar she-bachashai* — something that is conducted in private, in concealment. The *ketores* is burned in the covered space of the *Heichal*, within the innermost sanctum, away from public view. *Ve-yechaper al ma'aseh chashai* — let it atone for things done in private, for slander whispered away from the public eye. One might observe that while this connection between *lashon hara* and the *ketores* is deeply instructive as *mussar*, the *pshat* of *Yom Kippur* invests the *ketores* with something far more profound.

---

## Ulam/Mizbeach

### Separation Rule

The *Gemara* now cites a *mishna* from tractate *Keilim* that discusses different levels of *kedusha*: *porshin mibein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach* — at the time of the burning of the *ketores*, people would separate not only from the *Heichal* and *Ulam* (which are already covered by the prohibition of *ve-chol adam lo yihyeh*) but from the entire space between the *Ulam* and the *mizbe'ach* as well. This space *bein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach* has its own elevated level of *kedusha* within the *Azarah*, and that status expresses itself through this requirement of separation. The *Gemara* will ultimately conclude that this requirement is rabbinic in character — though, as will be seen, the matter is somewhat nuanced.

*Tosafot* raises the obvious question: if no one can be in this space during the *ketores*, what of the man stirring the blood, who is standing on one of those very steps? The answer is that the rabbinic prohibition applies to those present without purpose; someone actively engaged in a necessary task is not in violation.

### Rav Elazar

*Amar Rav Elazar*: the statement of the *mishna* — that people must vacate the space *bein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach* at the time of the *ketores* — does not refer to the *ketores* of *Yom Kippur* burned in the *Kodesh Hakodashim*. *Lo shanu ela besha'at haktarat heichal* — it refers specifically to the daily *ketores* burned on the golden altar inside the *Heichal*. *Aval besha'at haktarah di-lifnai vela-lifnim* — but when the *ketores* is burned in the innermost sanctum on *Yom Kippur*, *meheichal parshi* — people must vacate the *Heichal* and *Ulam* — *mibein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach lo parshi* — but they need not vacate the outer space between the *Ulam* and the *mizbe'ach*.

This is a striking and counterintuitive ruling. One would naturally expect that the most significant *avodah* of the year — the *ketores* burned in the *Kodesh Hakodashim* on *Yom Kippur* — would require the greatest degree of separation, extending outward as far as possible. Yet *Rav Elazar* argues the reverse: the closer the burning is to the *bein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach*, the more it triggers the requirement to vacate that space. When the burning occurs right there in the *Heichal*, the proximity creates an obligation to clear even the adjacent outer area. When the burning occurs deep within the *Kodesh Hakodashim* — a distinct and more remote zone — it does not project outward to compel evacuation of the space near the *mizbe'ach*. The logic is one of proximity: the outer zone must be cleared when the sacred act is nearby; when the act is in a different, more inward domain, that zone is not affected.

The implication is also that on a daily basis — not only *Yom Kippur* — whenever the morning or afternoon *ketores* is burned on the golden altar, everyone must vacate the space *bein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach*. Twice every day, this separation is required.

### Rabbi Yose

A *baraita* is then cited from *Rabbi Yose*: *keshem she-porshin mibein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach besha'at haktarah, kach porshin besha'at matan dam par kohen mashiach u-par helem davar shel tzibbur u-se'irei avodah zarah*. Just as one separates from this space during the burning of the *ketores*, so too does one separate when the blood of the *par kohen mashiach* — the special *korban* brought when the *Kohen Gadol* himself sins — or the *par helem davar shel tzibbur* — the communal sin-offering when the entire community acts in error — or the *se'irei avodah zarah* — the goats brought when a *beit din* rules erroneously on matters of *avodah zarah* — is brought into the inner sanctum.

The conceptual principle underlying this extension is *lechaper bakodesh*: any act of *kapparah* performed within the *kodesh*, whether on *Yom Kippur* or at another time of year, triggers the same requirement of separation. The daily *ketores*, according to *Rav Elazar*, also qualifies because it too is an act of *kapparah* — specifically, as the *tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* taught, for *lashon hara*. Any *kapparah* performed in the *Heichal* obligates evacuation not only of the *Heichal* itself but of the outer space as well.

---

## Kedusha Levels

### Heichal Status

Having established this picture, the *baraita* continues with a question of its own: *u-mah ma'ala yesh bein ha-heichal le-vein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach?* — if one must vacate *both* the *Heichal* and the outer space during these acts of *kapparah*, in what respect is the *Heichal* on a higher level of *kedusha* than the space *bein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach*? If both must be vacated at the same moments, what distinguishes them?

### Two Contexts

The *baraita* answers: *ela shebeheichal porshin bein besha'at haktarah bein shelo besha'at haktarah* — because from the *Heichal* one must separate whether it is the time of the *ketores* or not. *U-mibein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach ein porshin ela besha'at haktarah* — but the outer space must be vacated only during the *ketores*. The *Heichal* must be cleared even at times that are not the burning of the *ketores* — that is, when blood offerings are being brought inside during these other occasions of *kapparah* (the sprinklings of the *par* and *sa'ir* on *Yom Kippur*, and the blood of the special *korbanot* enumerated above). The outer space, by contrast, need only be cleared during the actual burning of incense.

This is the practical expression of the *Heichal*'s higher status: it must be vacated more broadly, including at moments when the outer zone is not affected.

### Gemara Challenge

The *Gemara* then challenges *Rav Elazar*'s position. If *Rav Elazar* is correct that the *mishna*'s reference to *ketores* means specifically the daily *ketores* of the *Heichal* — and not the *Yom Kippur ketores* of the *Kodesh Hakodashim* — then the *baraita*'s statement of the *Heichal*'s superior status is incomplete. According to *Rav Elazar*, there is an additional distinction: you must vacate the *Heichal* when the *ketores* is burned in the *Kodesh Hakodashim* (on *Yom Kippur*), but you do *not* need to vacate the outer space at that time. Why doesn't the *baraita* cite *this* as the most telling difference between the two zones?

*Besha'at haktoret miha parshi* — even *Rav Elazar* agrees that the outer space must be vacated during the *ketores*. *Mai lav besha'at haktoret di-lifnai vela-lifnim?* — could it not be that this refers to the *Yom Kippur ketores* of the *Kodesh Hakodashim*? If so, the *baraita* should have said: the superiority of the *Heichal* lies in the fact that you must vacate the *Heichal* even when the *ketores* is being burned in the innermost sanctum, while the outer space need not be vacated at that time.

### Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves this: *lo, besha'at haktarah deheichal* — *Rav Elazar* insists that when the *baraita* says *besha'at haktarah*, it means the *ketores* of the *Heichal*. That is indeed the reference point throughout. The *Gemara* then asks: *ei hachi, ha-ma'ala bekulo?* — if so, why doesn't the *baraita* articulate the *full* superiority of the *Heichal*? Specifically, the *Gemara* formulates the missing distinction: *de'ilu meheichal parshi bein besha'at haktarah dideih bein besha'at haktarah di-lifnai vela-lifnim* — you vacate the *Heichal* whether you are burning the *ketores* there or burning it in the *Kodesh Hakodashim*. But *mibein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach lo parshi ela besha'at haktarah deheichal* — from the outer zone you must vacate only when the *ketores* is burning in the *Heichal* proper.

The *Gemara* answers: *hachi katani* — this is precisely what the *baraita* is saying. When it states that you vacate the *Heichal* both *besha'at haktarah* and *shelo besha'at haktarah*, the word *haktarah* is being used consistently to refer to the daily burning on the golden altar. On this reading, *besha'at haktarah* means: during the burning of the *ketores* on the golden *mizbe'ach*; *shelo besha'at haktarah* means: at some other time — namely, when the *ketores* is burned inside the *Kodesh Hakodashim* on *Yom Kippur*, or when blood is being sprinkled. The *Heichal* must be vacated during both. But the outer zone need only be cleared during the first — the *ketores* of the *Heichal*. So the *baraita* does capture exactly the distinction *Rav Elazar* requires; it simply does so implicitly, by using *haktarah* in the narrow sense throughout.

The *Gemara* adds a further nuance: *ve-ika hai ma'ala* — there is yet another dimension of the *Heichal*'s superior status that could be articulated, namely a conceptual one: *de'ilu meheichal parshi bein bi-kdushah dideih bein bi-kdushah di-lifnai vela-lifnim* — you vacate the *Heichal* whether the sanctifying act is its own *avodah* or the *avodah* of the *Kodesh Hakodashim*. *Ve'ilu mibein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach lo parshi ela bi-kdushah deheichal* — the outer zone must be cleared only when the sanctifying act belongs to the *Heichal*'s own domain.

### Rava's Argument

*Amar Rava*: there is a proof from all this that the *kedushah* of the *Ulam* and the *Heichal* are *chada milta* — a single level. *De'isalkadachta shetei kedushot ninhu* — if one were to say they are two distinct grades of holiness, then the requirement to vacate the *Ulam* on *Yom Kippur* (which the *Gemara* earlier treated as falling under the *de'oraita* prohibition of *ve-chol adam lo yihyeh*) would be rabbinic. And if vacating the *Ulam* is rabbinic, then the requirement to vacate the space *bein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach* would be a rabbinic decree resting upon another rabbinic decree — *gezeirah li-gezeirah* — which is impermissible. Therefore, the *Ulam* and the *Heichal* must share one unitary level of *kedushah*, both governed by the *de'oraita* prohibition.

### One Space

The *Gemara* responds with a different structural resolution: *lo, Ulam u-vein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach chada kedushah hi; Heichal ve-Ulam shetei kedushot* — the conceptual unity is not between the *Ulam* and the *Heichal*, but between the *Ulam* and the outer space beyond it. The *Heichal* and the *Ulam* are, in fact, two distinct levels of *kedushah*. The outer space and the *Ulam* share one level — and therefore the requirement to vacate both is based on a single *halacha*, not a compound of two separate rabbinic enactments.

The structural picture, then, is as follows: the *Heichal* proper and the *Ulam* are physically one complex — one roofed, enclosed space leading into the next. The outer zone, partly open, shares the *Ulam*'s grade of *kedushah* by virtue of its proximity and the absence of any intervening barrier. *Kivan d'lo mafsik midi* — there is nothing separating the outer space from the *Ulam*; the transition is invisible, making it easy to inadvertently step in. The *mizbe'ach ha-chitzon*, by contrast, serves as a natural physical and conceptual divider between that zone and the rest of the *Azarah*, making the boundary obvious. This is why the rabbinic requirement stops at *bein ha-ulam vela-mizbe'ach* and does not extend to the entire *Azarah*: the *mizbe'ach* itself is *mafsik*, and the danger of accidental entry into the *Ulam* does not threaten one standing at a safe distance behind it.

---

---

# Yoma 45

## Shoveling Coals

### Silver to Gold Transfer

The daf opens in the middle of 44b with the *mishnah*'s discussion of the shoveling of hot coals from the top of the altar — a necessary preliminary to the *ketoret* service of *Yom Kippur*. The *mishnah* states: *bechol yom haya choteh beshel kesef u-me'arah letoch shel zahav* — on every ordinary day the *kohen* would shovel the coals using a silver vessel and then pour them into a gold one. The *Gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason for this two-vessel system? The answer is *HaTorah chasa al mamonam shel Yisrael* — the Torah is concerned with the waste of Jewish money. Gold is a soft metal, and using it to shovel directly into the coals would cause rapid deterioration. Therefore, the silver vessel absorbs that wear, while the gold vessel — brought in for the actual service — is preserved.

### Yom Kippur Gold Vessel

On *Yom Kippur*, however, the procedure changes: *vehayom choteh beshel zahav uva haya machnis* — today he shovels directly with the gold vessel and carries it in with that same vessel. The *Gemara* explains: *mishum chulshat Kohen Gadol* — because of the physical weakness of the *Kohen Gadol*, who has been fasting, one does not wish to burden him with unnecessary manipulation of vessels.

### Pesuk-Based Approach

The *Rashash* notes that there is arguably a more straightforward reason rooted in the *pesukim* themselves: the plain sense of the verse implies that the same vessel used to shovel the coals is the one brought into the *Kodesh Kodashim*. This raises a further question about the scope of the *mishnah*'s discussion. *Rashi* understands the *mishnah* as referring specifically to what is distinctive about the *ketoret* of the *Kodesh Kodashim*. But one might read the *mishnah* more broadly — that certain special practices observed on *Yom Kippur* applied even to the regular morning and afternoon *ketoret*, not only to the inner service. The question of whether the single-vessel procedure on *Yom Kippur* reflects a *pesuk*-based requirement or merely an accommodation to the *Kohen Gadol*'s condition bears on which reading of the *mishnah* is correct.

### Quantity Debate

The *mishnah* also records that on a normal day the *kohen* would shovel with a vessel holding four *kabin* and pour into one holding three, whereas on *Yom Kippur* he shoveled directly with the three-*kav* vessel. A *baraita* is then cited teaching that one *kav* of coals would scatter when the transfer was made — consistent with going from four to three — while another *baraita* states that two *kabin* would scatter. The *Gemara* observes: *bishlama hach detani kav* — the position of one extra *kav* scattering corresponds to the *Rabbanan*, who say four is poured into three. But who holds that two would scatter? *Lo Rabbanan ve-lo Rabbi Yosi* — not the *Rabbanan* (four to three) and not *Rabbi Yosi* (six to three, which would yield three extra).

The answer is given in the name of *Rav Shizbi* citing *Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka*: he shoveled with four, as the *Rabbanan*, but poured into a vessel holding only two *kabin*, yielding two extra. So we now have three positions: the vessel brought in held two, three, or (according to *Rabbi Yosi*) that you shoveled with six. *Rav Ashi* then resolves the difficulty with *Rabbi Yosi*'s position: *afilu tema Rabbi Yosi* — one can even maintain *Rabbi Yosi*'s view, since the six-*kav* measure was a *se'ah midbarit* — a wilderness measure — whereas the vessel that received the coals held three *kabin Yerushalmi'ot*, the larger Jerusalem measure. Since a *se'ah midbarit* equals five *kabin Yerushalmi'ot*, only two *kabin* would be extra, which accounts for the *baraita* that teaches two scatter.

---

## Fire Pan Modifications

### Thin Gold & Long Handle

The *mishnah* continues to enumerate the differences between the ordinary daily procedure and that of *Yom Kippur*. A *baraita* elaborates: *bechol yom hayetah guldah avah ve-hayom rakah* — on a normal day the wall of the fire pan was thick, while on *Yom Kippur* it was thin. *U-ve-chol yom hayetah ketzarah ve-hayom arucha* — the handle was short on ordinary days, but long on *Yom Kippur*. The reason: *kedei she-tehei zero'o shel Kohen Gadol mesaya'ato* — so that the *Kohen Gadol*'s arm could assist him in manipulating the vessel. This is in anticipation of the subsequent service in which the *Kohen Gadol*, holding the fire pan in one hand and the incense in the other, must pour the incense using his arms and elbows in a confined space.

### Niashti Ring/Sheath

Another *baraita* records the teaching of *Ben Ha-Segan* — the son of the deputy *Kohen Gadol* — that *bechol yom lo hayah lah niashti ve-hayom hayah lah niashti*: on ordinary days the fire pan did not have a *niashti*, while on *Yom Kippur* it did. The word *niashti* is unusual and lacks a clear parallel in other contexts, so its meaning must be inferred from the commentators.

### Rashi Sound Theory

*Rashi* explains that the *niashti* was a ring (*taba'at*) attached to the vessel that would clatter against the metal as the *Kohen Gadol* walked — *she-mekashkesh u-mashmi'a kol* — producing a sound upon his entry. The conceptual basis is the principle of *ve-nishma kolo be-vo'o*: when the *Kohen Gadol* enters the *heichal*, there should be some audible signal of his approach. On ordinary days this is accomplished by the bells of the *me'il*. On *Yom Kippur*, however, he wears only the *bigdei lavan* — the white garments — which have no bells. *Rashi*'s position is therefore that the ring on the fire pan served as a substitute, at least when the *Kohen Gadol* was carrying it, for the sound that the *me'il* would ordinarily produce.

### Tosafot Leather Sheath

*Tosafot* quotes *Rashi* and then notes that the *Yerushalmi* reads *nartik* rather than *niashti* — and *nartik* denotes a sheath. The *Riva* interprets this as a leather covering wrapped around the handle: *k'ein nartik shel or haya asui saviv yada* — like a pot holder placed around the handle to prevent burning. The question this raises is: why was such protection not needed on ordinary days? The answer offered is that the concern was not the initial carrying of the fire pan into the *Kodesh Kodashim*, which is a matter of minutes, but rather the later retrieval. After the *Kohen Gadol* placed the *ketoret* on the coals, he would go and perform the other *avodos*, and only afterward return to retrieve the fire pan — which by that point had been sitting with burning coals inside for an extended time, rendering the handle dangerously hot. Furthermore, on *Yom Kippur* the gold was thinner and the fire pan had a longer handle, both of which may have affected heat distribution. *Tosafot*'s explanation — that the issue is prolonged exposure during the interval before retrieval — accounts for why this protection was needed specifically on *Yom Kippur* and not on ordinary days.

---

## Gold Types

### Seven Gold Types

The *mishnah* states that on ordinary days the fire pan was made of *zahav yarok* — yellow-green gold — while on *Yom Kippur* a red gold was used. *Rav Chisda* teaches: *shiva zehavim hem* — there are seven types of gold. He enumerates them as follows. First, plain *zahav* and *zahav tov* — standard gold and good gold — derived from the verse in *Bereishit*: *ve-zahav ha'aretz hahi tov*, which implies that there is ordinary gold and then a superior grade. Third, *zahav Ofir* — gold from the land of *Ofir* — which is presumably distinguished by its origin and attendant quality. Fourth, *zahav mufaz* — gold that resembles *paz*. *Rashi* explains that *paz* shines like a precious stone, *matzhiv k'margalit*. Fifth, *zahav shachut* — literally "drawn" gold — which *Rashi* describes as gold so soft and pliable it can be drawn out like a thread. Sixth, *zahav sagur* — "closed" gold — described as being of such exceptional quality that *besha'ah sheniftach kol hachanuyot nisgaru*: when this gold comes to market, all the other gold shops close, unable to compete. Seventh, *zahav parvayim*.

### Red Gold Symbol

*Zahav parvayim* is explained: *she-domeh l'dam ha-parim* — it resembles the blood of oxen. This is the red gold used for the fire pan on *Yom Kippur*.

### Gold & Kaparah Link
