The *pasuk* contains both the verb *v'lakach* — taking — and the verb *v'hevi* — bringing. The *gemara* had previously established that *v'hevi* applies to both the coals and the *ketoret*, teaching that both must be brought in a single act of conveyance. Now the question is whether *v'lakach* also extends to cover *melo chofnov*.

The distinction is significant. If *v'lakach* applies to *melo chofnov*, then the material between the fingers was never the subject of a formal act of *lekichah* — taking. It simply ended up there inadvertently, without having been actively taken. If, on the other hand, *v'lakach* does not extend to the *chafinah* and the operative requirement is only *melo chofnov v'hevi* — the correct measure brought in — then whatever finds its way into the space between the fingers is subsumed within the *melo chofnov* and is legitimately included.

### Rav Papa Clarifies

The *gemara* thus frames the precise question as follows. *Hachi kamibaia lei: melo chofnov v'hevi beinun v'ika* — perhaps only the *v'hevi* is operative here, such that all that is required is that the *melo chofnov* be brought, and what happens to be present in the hands is included accordingly. *O dilma v'lakach v'hevi beinun* — or perhaps one requires both the act of taking and the act of bringing, and the material between the fingers, never having been formally taken, is excluded: *v'ha lika*. The *gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teiku*.

One might note that the *gemara* is assuming throughout that the material between the fingers falls within the category of *melo chofnov* at all. One could have argued that it is by definition external to *melo chofnov*. But the *gemara* appears to presuppose that conceptually it counts as part of the handful — the only question being whether the absence of a formal *lekichah* disqualifies it.

## Variations in Acts

### Kemitzah Normal Way

Rav Papa now shifts to questions about variations in the formal execution of *kemitzah* and *chafinah* themselves. He begins: *pishita li* — it is obvious to me that *melo kumtzo* means the *kemitzah* should be performed in the normal manner in which people scoop. *Rashi* understands the standard method to be a downward-scooping motion into the palm. But what about variations?

### Kemitzah Variations

*Ba'ei Rav Papa*: If one performed *kemitzah b'rashei etzbaotav* — using only the tips of the fingers, such that the palm faces downward and the flour is scooped upward into the palm — what is the ruling? What if done *milmata l'mala* — from below upward, meaning with the back of the hand facing down and scooping from below, in the manner of a shovel? *Rashi* identifies this as in fact the most natural scooping motion for many people. And what if performed *min hatzedadim* — from the sides? *Rashi* explains this to mean placing the hand flat and drawing the flour over the edge of the palm rather than scooping downward into it. In all of these cases: *mahu* — what is the ruling?

### Teiku on Kemitzah

The *gemara* answers *teiku* across all variations. The underlying question may be understood in two ways. One is that the *gemara* presupposes that a formally defined act is required and is asking what falls within the acceptable range of that act. The other framing, more relevant in the parallel discussion of *chafinah*, concerns how much the act must be ritualized and precisely defined: perhaps once an act of *kemitzah* is required, it carries with it formal parameters, and any departure from those parameters is problematic.

## Stuff Between Finger (II)

### Teiku

As already noted in the previous segment, the *gemara* concludes with *teiku* on the question of the material between the fingers in *chafinah*. The question of whether *v'lakach v'hevi* are both operative, or only *melo chofnov v'hevi*, remains unresolved.

### Two Interpretations

There are two ways to understand what the underlying concern is. One reading focuses on the naturalness of the act: the act of *lekichah* captures only what is intentionally taken, and incidental inclusion between the fingers falls outside of that. A second reading emphasizes inadvertent inclusion: the act of scooping with both hands may produce material that is not genuinely part of *melo chofnov* at all, having entered not through the scooping motion but passively. These two framings lead to overlapping but somewhat distinct analyses of what would be required to resolve the question.

## Variations in Acts (II)

### Chafinah Normal Way

Rav Papa now turns to the same type of questions regarding *chafinah*. *Pishita li* — it is obvious to him that *melo chofnov* refers to the normal manner in which people scoop with both hands. *Rashi* describes this as bringing both hands together at an angle, scooping the *ketoret* up simultaneously into both palms. But the variations raise questions.

### Chafinah Variations

*Ba'ei Rav Papa*: What if one scooped with the tips of the fingers — *b'rashei etzbaotav* — with the palms facing downward and the flour gathered upward? What if performed *milmata l'mala*, with the backs of the hands downward, scooping from below at a downward angle? What if performed *min hatzad*, drawing the material over the edges of both hands rather than scooping actively? And since *chafinah* involves two hands, an additional question arises that has no parallel in *kemitzah*: what if one performed *chafinah b'zo u'v'zo v'kervan zu etzel zu* — scooping first with one hand, then with the other, each gathering one hand's worth independently, and only then bringing the two together? Rather than performing the double-handed scooping in a single integrated motion, the two hands acted sequentially and were joined afterward.

### Teiku on Chafinah

The *gemara* answers *teiku* on all of these variations. It is worth noting that these questions take for granted that a formal act of *chafinah* is required — a point that was itself left unresolved earlier, where the *gemara* entertained the possibility that *melo chofnov* is only a measure and not a required act. Here Rav Papa assumes the act is necessary and asks how precisely it must conform to the normal method. The questions about *chafinah* are thus parallel to those about *kemitzah*, even if the underlying nature of *chafinah* as a ritual act remains, as we shall see, of a somewhat different character.

## Kometz into Vessel

### Kometz on Wall

Rav Papa asks a further question, now concerning the *kometz* from the *mincha* and its placement into the *kli sharet*. As part of the *mincha* service, after performing the *kemitzah*, the *kohen* must take the *kometz* and place it into a service vessel. This act parallels *kabalas dam* — the catching of blood in a vessel after *shechitah*. Just as the blood must be received into a vessel to be sanctified for the *avodah*, so too the *kometz* must be placed into a *kli sharet*. The question is what constitutes valid placement.

*Ba'ei Rav Papa: dveka l'kometz b'dofnei demana* — what if the *kohen* pressed the *kometz* against the inner wall of the vessel rather than letting it fall to the floor? The *kometz* is technically inside the vessel, but it is adhering to the wall rather than resting at the base. *Mai* — what is the ruling?

### Two Answers

Two possibilities are articulated. *Tocho beinun v'ika* — perhaps all that is required is that the *kometz* enter the interior space of the vessel, in which case sticking it to the wall is perfectly valid, since it is plainly within the interior. *O dilma hanacha betocho ke'tikno beinun v'hacha leika* — or perhaps one requires placement in the normal manner, meaning that the *kometz* must rest on the floor of the vessel as is standard, and here, with the *kometz* adhering to the wall, that requirement is not met.

This question reflects a broader uncertainty about the nature of the requirement. Is the operative concern the act of placing — and any departure from the standard placement is deficient? Or is it the function of the *kli sharet* — the capacity of the vessel to sanctify what is contained within it? If the latter, one must ask what mechanism the *kli sharet* employs: does it sanctify things that rest within it, or things that are within its airspace? These are questions discussed in other *gemoros*. *Rashi* on the previous *amud* had employed the language of *nitkaven* — intentionality — in the context of the *chafinah* question, but there the concern was about the word *v'lakach*. In the present context, the *gemara* frames the question more in terms of whether the act was performed in the standard manner.

Practically, one might wonder what would be done if a *kohen* had placed the *kometz* against the wall and the validity was uncertain: could he simply remove it and replace it at the base? The *gemara* does not resolve this.

### Tosafot: Kli Sharet

*Tosafot* cite a relevant *gemara* from *Zevachim* 88: *amar Shmuel, kli sharet ein mekadeshin ela mibifnim* — a *kli sharet* sanctifies only from within. This raises the precise question of what constitutes *bifnim*. If sanctification requires the item to be within the interior of the vessel in a meaningful sense, one must determine whether adhesion to the inner wall satisfies that criterion or whether it requires the item to rest within the hollow space in the standard manner. This possibility — that the question is about the nature of the *kli sharet*'s function rather than only about the form of the act — is a lens through which the question can be read.

### Inverted Vessel

*Ba'ei Mar Bar Rav Ashi*. Carrying forward Rav Papa's approach of posing these speculative questions, Mar Bar Rav Ashi asks: *afcheih lemana* — what if one inverted the vessel, turning it upside down, *v'davkia l'kometz b'ar'isa* — and stuck the *kometz* to what had been the floor of the vessel? The *kometz* is stuck to what was originally the base, but the vessel is now inverted so that it no longer functions as a container in any standard sense. *Mahu* — what is the ruling?

### Two Readings

Two interpretations of this case are possible. One reading, which the lecturer adopts as primary, takes *ar'isa* to mean that the *kometz* is literally stuck to the floor of the vessel, but the floor is now facing downward. The *kometz* is affixed to the underside of the inverted vessel. On this reading, the item is clearly not within *toch* — the interior — of the vessel in any meaningful sense, since the vessel is inverted and not functioning as a container. The question of whether *hanacha betocho beinun v'ika* — whether placement within the interior satisfies the requirement — becomes pressing, since on this reading the interior requirement is simply not met.

*Tosafot*, however, read the case differently. They understand the base of the vessel to be curved, such that when the vessel is inverted, its concave base creates a hollow on the underside. On this reading, the *kometz* placed within that curved hollow might be considered to be within a space analogous to the interior of the vessel, and the question is whether such a space counts as *toch*. This reading of *Tosafot* is based on another *gemara* and preserves the possibility that the item could still be considered inside some form of *toch*. The *gemara* does not resolve the question.

## Chafinah Volume

### Smooth or Heaping

*Ba'ei Rav Papa*: *melo chofnov she'amru — mechukakot o gedushos* — when the *halacha* speaks of *melo chofnov*, is that measure to be understood as smoothed out or heaping? Regarding the *kometz* of a *mincha*, the *kemitzah* is *machuk* — smoothed with the thumb and the small finger to an even, level measure. What is the status of *melo chofnov* for the *ketoret*? Does one smooth out the top of the double-handfuls? That would seem physically difficult, since both hands are occupied. Does one heap it? Or is the measure something else?

### T'fufot Answer

*Amar lei Rav Ashi l'Rav Papa: ta shema*. Rav Ashi directs Rav Papa to a *braita*: *melo chofnov she'amru — lo mechukakot v'lo gedushos ella t'fufot*. The prescribed measure is neither smoothed out nor heaping, but *t'fufot* — with a slight, gentle curvature at the top. It is not a leveled-off measure, which may in any case be physically impossible without a free hand to smooth it, and it is not a heaping measure, which would exceed *melo chofnov*. Rather, it has a gentle rounded curve at the top. The *braita* thus resolves Rav Papa's question.

## Blood Reception Rules

### Blood Spill Rule

The *gemara* now introduces the *mishna* from which the rules about spillage before and after reception are derived, which will serve as the paradigm for the *chafinah* discussion that follows. The *mishna* states: *nishpach hadam al haritzpa v'asfo pasul* — if after *shechitah* the blood fell directly to the ground and was then scooped up and placed in the vessel, it is invalid. The blood must be caught from the animal directly into the vessel. However, *min hakli al haritzpa v'asfo kasher* — if the blood was properly received in the vessel and subsequently spilled onto the ground, and was then gathered and placed back in the vessel, it is *kasher*. Once the blood has been properly received in the vessel and sanctified therein, a subsequent spill and recovery does not disqualify it.

### Dam Me'hapar

The *gemara* asks: *mina hani milei* — what is the source for these rules? *Detanu rabanan*: the verse states *v'lakach midam hapar* — the *kohen* shall take from the blood of the ox. *Midam hapar* means *midam hanefesh* — from the lifeblood, the forceful flow that gushes from the severed arteries following *shechitah*. Not *midam ha'or* — not the blood seeping from the skin, from subcutaneous capillaries, from a superficial cut. And not *midam hatamtzit* — not the residual blood that drains out slowly after the main flow has ceased. The blood used for the *avodah* must be the lifeblood proper.

### Hermeneutic Analysis

The *gemara* then moves the *mem* from *midam hapar* to derive a second rule. Reading it as *dam me'hapar yekabelenu* — the blood must be caught directly from the ox — teaches that the blood cannot first hit the floor and be subsequently scooped up. It must travel straight from the animal into the vessel.

One might have argued that the *mem* in *midam hapar* should be read in its natural sense as *from*, meaning only *some* of the blood — not all of it — need be caught. But this reading is rejected.

### All Blood Required

*V'amar Rav Yehuda*: the *kohen* receiving the blood must catch all of the blood — *kol damo shel par* — as derived from the verse *v'chol dam hapar yishpoch el yesod hamizbe'ach*, which speaks of pouring all the blood. This requirement is *lechatchila*; *bedieved*, if not all the blood was caught, it may still be valid. But since the *lechatchila* obligation to catch all the blood is established from elsewhere, the *mem* of *midam* is not needed to limit the obligation to only *some* of the blood. Therefore, the *mem* is available to be repositioned.

### Hermeneutic Rules

The *gemara* spells out the mechanics of this derivation: *gurin u'mosifin v'dorshin* — one may subtract a letter from one location, add it to another location, and then perform the *derasha*. Here, the *mem* is removed from *midam* and appended to *hapar*, yielding *dam me'hapar*, from which it is derived that the blood must come directly from the animal.

## Blood Rules to Ketoret

### Chafinah Scatter Q

*Ba'ei Rav Papa*: Having established the paradigm of the blood spill, Rav Papa now applies it to *chafinah*. *Nitpazer ha-ktoret mi-melo chofnov mahu* — if, in the course of transferring the *ketoret* from the *chafinah* into the *kaf* (the ladle), some of the *ketoret* scattered and fell to the ground, what is the ruling? Can it be gathered from the ground and added back? The situation is precisely parallel to the blood falling to the ground before proper reception: the *chafinah* corresponds to *shechitah*, and the placing of the *ketoret* into the *kaf* corresponds to *kabalas dam* in the vessel. So does the same rule apply — that what hit the ground before being received in the vessel is disqualified?

### Hand as Throat

*Yado k'tzavar behema dami u'psula* — one possible answer is that the *kohen*'s hand, which holds the *ketoret*, is like the throat of the animal. Just as the blood, once it leaves the throat, must flow directly into the vessel and cannot first hit the ground, so too the *ketoret*, once it leaves the hands, must go directly into the *kaf*. What scattered to the ground was never properly received and is therefore *pasul*.

### Hand as Kli Sharet

*O dilma k'kli sharet dami v'lo psula* — or perhaps the *kohen*'s hand is to be regarded as a *kli sharet*. The *kohen*'s body is sanctified, and in many contexts we objectify the *kohen*'s body as functioning like a vessel of *kedusha*. If so, the *ketoret* was already received into the *kli sharet* — the hands — at the moment of the *chafinah*. The transfer from the hands into the *kaf* is not analogous to catching the blood from the animal. The relevant reception already occurred, and the subsequent scatter would be equivalent to blood that was properly received in a vessel and then spilled — which, as the *mishna* established, is *kasher*.

### Teiku

The *gemara* concludes with *teiku*. The *Rambam*, in his ruling on this matter, takes the stringent position and treats it as a *safek*, ruling that the *ketoret* should not be offered but that if it was, it is valid *bedi'eved*. Nevertheless, there are strong conceptual reasons, as the *gemara*'s analysis itself reflects, to distinguish this case from the blood paradigm.

### Why Chafinah Not Kemitzah

The *Tosafot Yeshanim* note a striking feature of Rav Papa's question: he raises the scatter question only with respect to *chafinah* and not with respect to *kemitzah*. Why? If we are concerned about whether the *ketoret* must go directly from the hands into the *kaf*, one would expect the same question to arise regarding the *kometz* from a *mincha* going into its vessel.

### Analogy Difference

The *Tosafot Yeshanim* explain: *peshita de-gabei kometz havei k'tzavar behema* — it is self-evident that the *kometz* must go straight into the vessel, just as the blood must go straight from the animal's throat. The analogy is direct and admits no question.

### Four Avodot Model

Why is the analogy so direct? *Lefi she-yesh arba avodot ba-mincha ke-neged arba avodot shel dam*. As demonstrated in *Menachot*, the four stages of the *mincha* service parallel the four stages of an animal *korban*: *kemitzah* corresponds to *shechitah*, the placing of the *kometz* into the vessel corresponds to *kabalas dam*, the conveying of the vessel to the *mizbe'ach* corresponds to *holacha*, and the burning of the *kometz* corresponds to *zerikah*. Because *kemitzah* is formally parallel to *shechitah*, and placing the *kometz* in the vessel is formally parallel to *kabalas dam*, the blood rules apply directly. There is no question.

By contrast, *aval b'ketoret mibaiya lei* — the question does arise regarding the *ketoret*. *Lefi she-ein kli l'chafinah ela mishum d'lo efshar* — the *ketoret* is placed into the *kaf* not because there is a formal ritual requirement of *kabbalah bi-kli*, but only because physically one cannot simultaneously hold the *ketoret* in both hands, carry the fire pan, and bring everything into the *Kodesh Kodashim*. The placement in the *kaf* is a practical necessity, not a formal *avodah* step. *Delo dami l'kemitzah* — the *chafinah* is not parallel to *shechitah* in the same structural way, and the placing of the *ketoret* into the *kaf* is not parallel to *kabalas dam*.

### Leftover Status

*Tosafot* add a further distinction. When *kemitzah* is performed, the leftover — the *shirayim* — is of an entirely different character from the *kometz*: the *kometz* goes to the *mizbe'ach* and the *shirayim* are eaten. This mirrors *shechitah*, where the blood goes to the *mizbe'ach* and the meat is eaten. The two portions are categorically distinct. With *ketoret*, by contrast, the portion that is offered and the portion that is left behind are not categorically distinct in the same way. The leftover *ketoret* from one day is simply offered on another day. There is no structural separation between *kometz* and *shirayim* as there is in both the blood and the *mincha* contexts. This further confirms that *chafinah* does not occupy the same structural role as *kemitzah* and *shechitah*, and therefore the blood rules do not apply with the same self-evidence.

This analysis illuminates why the entire trajectory of Rav Papa's questions is so significant. At one end, the *gemara* entertained the possibility that no act of *chafinah* is required at all — perhaps only the measure matters. Working through the questions, we assumed an act is required but found it to be of a fundamentally different quality than *shechitah* or *kemitzah*. And now, at the far end of the trajectory, the *Rambam* rules that *chafinah* is a full *avodah* and *machshava* invalidates. The conceptual journey from "perhaps no act is needed" to "it is a complete *avodah* subject to *pigul*" is considerable. The connections running throughout — *yad kohen k'tzavar behema*, the parallel to *kaparas korbanot* — reinforce the theme the *gemara* has been developing of the *ketoret* as something that *mechaper* in the manner of a *korban*.

## Thought in Chafinah

### Rambam Rules

Before turning to Rav Papa's question, it is worth noting how the *Rambam* rules on the matter. The *Rambam* states: *chafinat ha-ketoret avoda* — the act of *chafinah* is an *avodah*, and *ha-machshava poselet bo* — a *machshava* invalidates it. This ruling takes a clear position on what the *gemara* is about to leave unresolved. As will become apparent, the *gemara*'s attempted proof that *machshava* is operative in *chafinah* is ultimately incomplete, which makes the *Rambam*'s confident ruling all the more striking.

### Pigul in Chafinah

*Ba'ei Rav Papa: chishev b'chafinat ketoret* — if a *kohen* had an improper thought (*machshava*) while performing the *chafinah* of the *ketoret* — for instance, intending to offer it at a wrong time, on the eleventh of *Tishrei* — *mahu*? Is it invalidated? The thought of intending to perform a *korban* at the wrong time is the classic *machshevet pigul*, which is operative only during the performance of an *avodah*. The question, then, is whether *chafinah* is an *avodah* such that *machshava* is effective during it.

### Learn or Not

*Mi amrinan yalif melo melo mi-mincha*: do we apply the *gezeirah shavah* of *melo melo* and derive *chafinah* from *mincha*, where we know the *kemitzah* is like *shechitah* and *machshava* is operative? *Ma hatam mahanya bah machshava hacha nami mahanya bah machshava* — just as there a *machshava* is effective, so too here? *O lo* — or perhaps not, since the arguments developed above suggest that *chafinah* does not occupy the same structural role as *kemitzah*, and may not therefore be a full *avodah* subject to invalidation by *machshava*.

### Tevul Yom Braita

*Amar lei Rav Ashi bar Ashi l'Rav Papa: ta shema*. Rav Ashi bar Ashi offers a proof. *Hosif Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva added to the list of items that, if a *tevul yom* touches part of them, all of them are invalidated: *ha-solet*, the flour of a *mincha*; *ha-ketoret*, the incense — both the daily *ketoret* and that of Yom Kippur; *ha-levona*, the frankincense associated with the *lechem hapanim*; and *ha-gechalim*, the coals. The rule is *shenaga tevul yom b'miktzatan pasal et kullan* — if a *tevul yom* touches part of any of these, the entire quantity in the vessel is invalidated. A *tevul yom* has the status of *sheni l'tumah*; ordinarily, one might have supposed that only the individual piece touched would be affected, while the remainder, as physically separate objects, would remain *tahor*.

### Kli Sharet Unity

The reason all of them are invalidated is that a *kli sharet* unifies everything contained within it. When a *kli sharet* sanctifies the contents through *kedushat ha-guf* — intrinsic sanctification — everything within the vessel is treated as a single unified entity. A *tevul yom* touching any part therefore affects the whole.

### Time Matters Logic

*Kasalka datach*: the *gemara* builds on this as follows. *Mi-depasal tevul yom pasla nami lina* — since a *tevul yom* invalidates these items, so too *lina* — overnight — invalidates them. The connection is that both *tevul yom* and *lina* are consequences of the same underlying reality: the *kli sharet* elevated the items to *kedushat ha-guf*, and things with *kedushat ha-guf* that remain overnight become invalid. If the *kli sharet* operates this way — creating a unified *kedusha* — then *lina* is also effective. And since *lina* means time is operative, *machshava* — intention relating to time — is also operative.

It should be noted that the word *kasalka datach* here is unusual. Ordinarily this phrase introduces an assumption that will subsequently be challenged. Here, the *gemara* does not challenge it, but simply proceeds with the assumption. Similarly, *veha'tanya*, which typically introduces a challenge, sometimes functions as a support.

### Proof Gap

However, a fundamental problem with the proof must be acknowledged. The entire argument establishes that *lina* and *machshava* are operative on the *ketoret* once it is in the *kli sharet*. But the original question was whether *chafinah* is an *avodah* at all — whether a *machshava* entertained during the *chafinah* is effective. The proof addresses whether *machshava* relating to time can invalidate these items; it does not prove that the act of *chafinah* is itself an *avodah* during which such a *machshava* would operate. The *gemara* takes for granted, as *kasalka datach*, that *chafinah* is an *avodah* — but that is precisely the point that needs to be proven. This is why the *Rambam*, in ruling that *machshava* is operative, begins by asserting as a premise *chafinat ha-ketoret avoda hi* — the act of *chafinah* is an *avodah*. He recognizes that this must be stated as a premise, because the *gemara*'s proof does not establish it.

## Thought in Coals

### Pigul in Coals

*Ba'ei Rav Papa: chishev b'chatiyat gechalim mahu* — if a *kohen* entertained an improper thought while scooping the coals, what is the ruling? *Rashi* presents two versions of what the improper thought might be: either one intends to perform the *ketoret* at the wrong time, or one intends to use the coals themselves at the wrong time. The question is whether the scooping of the coals is an *avodah* in its own right or at least an *avodah* as part of the *ketoret* service.

### Preparatory Like Main

*Machshirei mitzvah k'mitzvah dami* — perhaps preparatory acts to a *mitzvah* are treated as the *mitzvah* itself. The scooping of the coals is preparatory to the burning of the *ketoret*. If the *chafinah* of the *ketoret* is an *avodah*, perhaps this preparatory act is similarly elevated to the status of an *avodah*, and a *machshava* during it is therefore effective.

This principle — *machshirei mitzvah k'mitzvah dami* — has broad applications beyond the present context. It bears on questions such as when a *berachah* is recited for the preparation of an object used in a *mitzvah*, whether *hiddur mitzvah* applies to preparatory acts, and similar questions. But the answers are not uniform across contexts, and one cannot simply assume the same ruling applies everywhere.

### Teiku

*Teiku* — the question remains unresolved. The *gemara* does not know whether the scooping of the coals, as a *machshir* to the *ketoret* service, is elevated to the status of an *avodah* such that *machshava* during it is operative.

This unresolved question reflects the remarkable conceptual arc traversed across this daf. We began with the possibility that the *chafinah* might not require any formal act at all — only the correct measure. We proceeded through questions about the precise form the act must take, how rigidly it is defined, whether the analogy to blood reception governs, and ultimately whether it constitutes a full *avodah* subject to *pigul* machshava. And now we extend the question one step further, to whether even the preparatory act of coal-scooping shares in that status.

## Left Hand Holacha

### Left Hand Question

The *gemara* now takes up a question that was raised earlier in the *mishna* but whose analysis was deferred: *holacha b'smol mah* — what is the ruling regarding the conveyance of items into the *Kodesh Kodashim* when done with the left hand? The issue of *holacha* is of particular theoretical interest. On the one hand, *holacha* is one of the four *avodot* of a *korban*, and certain disqualifications — such as being performed by a *pasul kohen* or being accompanied by a *pigul* thought — apply to it. On the other hand, the *gemara* elsewhere refers to *holacha* as an *avodah she-efshar l'vatla* — an *avodah* that can theoretically be dispensed with, since if the *shechitah* was performed adjacent to the *mizbe'ach* no *holacha* is necessary. *Holacha* is, at its core, simply conveyance from point A to point B. How much does it carry the full formal weight of a ritual *avodah*?

### Kaf in Left Hand

*Amar lei Rav Sheshet: tanituha* — we have already taught this in our *mishna*: *natol et hamachtah b'ymino v'et ha-kaf b'smolo* — the *kohen* takes the fire pan in his right hand and the *kaf* containing the *ketoret* in his left hand. The *kaf* is carried into the *Kodesh Kodashim* in the left hand. Since we have been drawing the analogy throughout this sugya between *chafinah* and *shechitah*, placing the *ketoret* in the *kaf* and *kabalas dam*, and bringing the *ketoret* into the *Kodesh Kodashim* and *holacha* of the blood to the *mizbe'ach* — this answer assumes that the *holacha* of the *ketoret* is parallel to *holacha* of *korbanot*. If the *ketoret*'s conveyance can be performed with the left hand, presumably ordinary *holacha* can as well.

### Olah Limb Precedent

The *gemara* asks: why not derive the permissibility of left-hand *holacha* from a different source? *Ha-regel she-ha-yamin b'smolo l'veit ha-ora l'chutz* — when the *kohen* carries the limbs of the *olah* to the *mizbe'ach*, the right hind leg is carried in his left hand. This would appear to demonstrate that *holacha* can be performed with the left hand.

### Essential vs. Non-Essent…

The *gemara* rejects this as a proof. *Im mei-hatam hava amina hani mili holacha d'la me'akva kapara* — from that source alone, one would conclude only that a *holacha* which is not essential to the atonement can be performed with the left hand. The burning of the limbs of an *olah* on the *mizbe'ach* is not *me'akva* — not necessary for *kapara*. The *kapara* of the *korban* is achieved without the burning of individual limbs.

### Me'akva Restriction

*Aval holacha d'me'akva kapara* — but a *holacha* that is essential to the atonement — such as the carrying of the blood to the *mizbe'ach*, the carrying of the *kometz* to the altar, or the bringing of the *ketoret* into the *Kodesh Kodashim* — one might have thought that such a *holacha* cannot be performed with the left hand, precisely because of its essential role. *Ka'mashma lan* — the *mishna* therefore teaches us that even *holacha d'me'akva kapara* can be performed with the left hand.

This point is striking in light of everything discussed across the daf. We began by questioning whether *chafinah* even required a formal act. We ended by using the *chafinah*'s conveyance into the *Kodesh Kodashim* — which is performed with the left hand — as the proof that even essential *holacha* may be done with the left hand. The *gemara* is not merely saying that the *ketoret*'s *holacha* is like *korbanot*; it is arguing in reverse — that because the *ketoret*'s *holacha* permits the left hand, the more essential forms of *holacha* in *korbanot* also permit it. The argument flows in both directions, and the full analogy between the *ketoret* service and the animal *korban* service is assumed to be operative throughout. The discussion of this point continues on the following daf.

# Yoma 49

## Chafina & Blood Service

### Chafina Overview

Daf 49 opens precisely at its first word, and the subject at hand is the significance of the various acts comprising the *chafina* and the subsequent placement of the *ketoret*. The process unfolds in three stages: taking the *ketoret* from its original container into the hands, transferring it into the ladle, and then conveying it — in this case, into the *kodesh kodashim*. These three stages correspond, to a meaningful degree, to three stages in the service of a standard *korban*: the *shechita*, the separation of the portions designated for the altar from the remainder, the placing of the blood into the vessels, and then the conveyance of the blood to the altar.

The *gemara* had raised various questions about whether the *chafina* itself must be performed with one's hands or whether a vessel could be used instead. Throughout the preceding *daf*, the *chafina* was treated as a significant ritual act — a necessary and substantive component of the service — and considerable discussion surrounded its precise parameters. More significantly, the *gemara* explored the question of what happens if *ketoret* spills between the moment of *chafina* and the moment it is deposited into the ladle: is that a problem analogous to blood spilling on the ground? Is the hand containing the *ketoret* comparable to the throat of the animal? This comparison is not merely rhetorical; it underscores the degree to which these *avodot* parallel the *avoda* of the blood, *hadam*.

The *Tosafot Yeshanim* and *Tosafot* noted two respects in which the parallel is imperfect. First, the placement of the *ketoret* into the vessel functions more as a means of conveyance than as an *avoda* in its own right. Second, the taking of the *ketoret* from its container does not replicate the act of separating what goes on the altar from what does not — a distinction that is structurally integral to *shechita* — and therefore the equivalence between the two processes is not self-evident. These considerations left open the question of the degree to which the rules governing the blood service could be imported into the *chafina* service, or vice versa.

### Avodah Status Debate

Nevertheless, the *gemara* ultimately does not reach a definitive resolution on this question, and it goes on to note that a thought of *pigul* can occur even during the act of *chafina* — a point that strongly implies the *chafina* is itself a full-fledged *avoda*. The *Rambam* draws precisely this conclusion: the *chafina* is an act of *avoda*. This conclusion having been tentatively reached, the *gemara* proceeds to explore whether requirements known to apply to the blood service should be imposed on the *chafina* as well, and conversely, whether a leniency found in the *chafina* might apply back to the blood.

### Holacha & Left Hand

The discussion then shifts from the *chafina* and the placement into the ladle to the conveyance — the *holacha* — into the *kodesh kodashim*. The *gemara* raises the question: can the *holacha* of the blood be performed with the left hand? The reasoning offered is that since the conveyance of the *ketoret* is done with the left hand, perhaps the *holacha* of blood may likewise be done with the left hand, assuming a genuine equivalence between the two. This was, in fact, the tentative conclusion with which the previous *daf* closed: perhaps the conveyance of blood could be performed with the left hand, just as the conveyance of *ketoret* is performed with the left hand.

---

## Baraita Challenge

### Invalid Persons

It is at this point that the *gemara* introduces a *meitivei* challenge — an objection drawn from a *baraita*. The *baraita* states: *zar ve-onen, shikkor u-va'al mum* — a non-*kohen*, an *onen* (a *kohen* who has suffered the loss of an immediate relative on that very day), a *shikkor* (a *kohen* who is intoxicated — a matter of some dispute between *Rashi* and *Tosafot* as to whether this applies only to wine or extends to other intoxicants as well), and a *ba'al mum* (a *kohen* with a physical blemish) — all of these individuals are forbidden from performing the *avoda*, and if they do perform it, the *avoda* is invalidated. These prohibitions derive from explicit *pesukim* and are extended by the *gemara* through interpretation. The *baraita* specifies that these individuals invalidate the service in three of the four classic *avodot*: *kabbala* (catching the blood), *holacha* (conveying the blood), and *zerika* (throwing the blood). Notably absent from this list is *shechita*, because *shechita* is *kasher be-zar* — valid even when performed by a non-*kohen*. Whether *shechita* is equally valid when performed by an *onen*, a *shikkor*, or a *ba'al mum* is a separate question left for another context.

One may observe that the *baraita*'s structure falls into two natural groups. The first — *zar*, *onen*, *shikkor*, *ba'al mum* — concerns the personal status of the individual, his standing *be-gavra*, so to speak. The second group — sitting and use of the left hand — concerns the manner in which the *avoda* is performed, not the status of the performer. This distinction has logical coherence and also reflects the mnemonic rhythms of oral tradition, where organizing material as a group of four followed by a group of three creates a certain cadence that facilitates memory.

### Left Hand Forbidden

The *baraita* then continues: *ve-chen yoshev* — and similarly if the *kohen* is seated — and *ve-chen smol* — and similarly if he uses the left hand — all of these invalidate the service. Crucially, this prohibition against the left hand applies not only to *kabbala* and *zerika*, but explicitly also to *holacha*, the very act of conveyance. The *gemara* therefore declares: *pasul* — all of this is invalid. And then: *tiyuvta* — this is an outright contradiction of what was argued yesterday, namely that *holacha* could be performed with the left hand.

### Rav Sheshet Problem

The *gemara* now raises an acute difficulty. If Rav Sheshet was the one who had argued that *holacha* could be performed with the left hand based on the analogy to the *ketoret*, how could he not have known of this *baraita*? In fact, the *gemara* reveals that Rav Sheshet did know this *baraita* — for it was Rav Sheshet himself who in a different context used this same *baraita* to challenge a different position. This makes his earlier argument all the more puzzling.

---

## Non-Kohen Holacha

### Amoraim & Tannaim

The *gemara* explains how we know that Rav Sheshet was acquainted with this *baraita*: Rav Sheshet said to the *amora* of Rav Chisda — that is, to the one who served as Rav Chisda's personal announcer — the following question. Before continuing with the substance of the exchange, it is worth pausing to clarify a terminological ambiguity. The term *amora*, used in this context, does not refer to the great *amoraim* of the *gemara* — figures such as Rava, Abaye, Rav Sheshet, and Ravina — but rather to the individual who served as a kind of human loudspeaker for a leading sage. In the era before any form of amplification, a scholar would whisper his teaching to this *amora*, who would then announce it loudly to the assembled audience. Similarly, the term *tanna* in this context does not refer to the *tannaim* of the *mishnaic* era — figures such as Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon — but rather to those whose function was memorization and recitation of fixed oral texts.

The *Mishna*, it should be recalled, was not committed to writing in the time of Rebbi. What Rebbi accomplished was the fixing of a textual tradition — an oral textual tradition — by harmonizing and standardizing competing oral versions. Once the text was fixed, Rebbi would call in a group of *tannaim*, repeaters and memorizers — the word *tanna* derives from the root meaning "to repeat" — and transmit the text to them verbally. They would memorize it precisely and then travel to different cities and towns to disseminate it word for word. As Saul Lieberman observed, what was wanted in such a *tanna* was a strong memory and very little creativity, since any individual stylistic contribution would corrupt the tradition. The earliest writings of the *mishnaic* text likely date to the beginning of the Geonic period, though certain tannaitic texts such as the *Sifra* and *Megillat Ta'anit* may have been committed to writing earlier.

The *amora* as announcer — from the root meaning "to say" or "to declare" — served a parallel function in the lecture hall: not to memorize but to project. These were the lowercase *amora* and lowercase *tanna*, distinguished from the capital-letter *Amoraim* and *Tannaim* who are the subjects of the Talmudic tradition.

### Rav Sheshet's Query

Returning to the *gemara*: Rav Sheshet instructed Rav Chisda's *amora* to pose the following question to Rav Chisda: *holacha be-zar mahu* — what is the law regarding whether a non-*kohen* may perform the *holacha*? Just as a non-*kohen* may perform *shechita*, which is *kasher be-zar*, might he similarly perform *holacha*? This question is particularly apposite because *holacha* is characterized as a *melacha she-efshar levatla* — a type of act that can theoretically be dispensed with, since if the *shechita* is performed adjacent to the *mizbeach*, no conveyance is necessary at all.

### Non-Kohen Permitted

The *amora* — whether after consulting Rav Chisda or perhaps responding immediately — answered: *keshera* — it is valid. And he added: *u-mikra mesayeini* — I have a verse that supports this position.

### Pesach Evidence

The supporting verse comes from *Divrei Hayamim*: *vayishchatu hapesach*, they — the owners — slaughtered the *pesach*; *vayizreku hakohanim miyadam*, the *kohanim* threw the blood from their hands — meaning from the hands of the owners — *vehaleviyim mafshitim*, and the *levi'im* flayed the animals. The inference is that the owners were holding the vessels containing the blood and handing them over for the *zerika*, which means the owners themselves performed the *holacha*. The sequence, as reconstructed, would be: the owner performs the *shechita*, the *kohen* performs the *kabbala* — since that is uncontested as requiring a *kohen* — and then gives the vessel back to the owner, who carries it to the *kohen* near the *mizbeach*, who performs the *zerika*. This intermediate carrying by the owner would constitute *holacha* performed by a *zar*.

### Zar Forbidden

Rav Sheshet then challenged this reading by citing the very *baraita* under discussion: *zar ve-onen, shikkor u-va'al mum, be-kabbala u-ve-holacha u-ve-zerika pasul* — the *zar* cannot perform *holacha*. How, then, can the verse from *Divrei Hayamim* be taken as evidence that a *zar* may do so?

---

## Baraita Challenge (II)

### Rav Sheshet Learned

The *gemara* now resolves the apparent contradiction in Rav Sheshet's own position — how he could have argued on the previous *daf* that *holacha* may be done with the left hand, while in a later exchange invoking a *baraita* that explicitly prohibits it. The answer is chronological: *batar de-shama, hadar bei* — after he himself was challenged with this *baraita* and came to learn it, he subsequently retracted his earlier position. The order of events, then, was as follows. First, Rav Sheshet reasoned that *holacha* could be performed with the left hand, drawing on the analogy to the *ketoret*. He was then challenged with the *baraita* that explicitly prohibits *holacha* with the left hand. Once he learned that *baraita* and accepted its ruling, he was able to turn around and deploy the same *baraita* in a later context to challenge Rav Chisda's *amora* on the question of *holacha* by a *zar*.

The conclusion that emerges is that both positions argued for yesterday are rejected: *holacha* cannot be performed with the left hand, and *holacha* cannot be performed by a non-*kohen*. Although *holacha* is in principle less weighty than some other *avodot* — it is the sort of act that can sometimes be bypassed entirely — when it is in fact performed, its invalidity under these conditions stands.

The *Tosafot Yeshanim* address the residual difficulty directly: *ve-chen smol kashya, u-matnitin ein reaya* — the prohibition of the left hand is a difficulty, but the fact that it is used by the *ketoret* is not a proof to the contrary, because by the *ketoret* there is simply no alternative — *mishum de-lo efshar*. One hand must hold the fire-pan and the other must hold the ladle; the two-handed requirement inherent in *melo chofnav* means the left hand must be involved, and accordingly the left hand was given a special dispensation specifically for *Yom Kippur*. As the *gemara* in another context states, the left hand was specially validated for use on *Yom Kippur* in this regard.

One might further argue — and this returns to the broader theme running through the entire discussion — that the acts performed in connection with the *chafina* do not precisely parallel the *avodot* connected with the blood in the first place. The *chafina* is not the *shechita*, the placement into the vessel is not the casting of the blood, and perhaps the *holacha* of the *ketoret* is likewise not the *holacha* of the blood. The question of whether *pigul* can apply during *chafina* cuts in one direction; the question of whether spillage is a disqualifying problem cuts in another. The analogy is real but contested, and the *gemara* has not closed the issue entirely. Two possible grounds of distinction exist: first, the ongoing and unresolved question of whether these *chafina*-related acts carry identical legal weight to blood-related acts; and second, even granting that they are generally equivalent, the left-hand usage by the *ketoret* is forced by necessity and cannot serve as a precedent for elective left-hand use in the blood service.

---

## Maise Itzba

### Passive Role

The *gemara* returns to Rav Chisda's position, noting that it was based on an actual *pasuk* from *Divrei Hayamim*. The verse seemed to indicate that the owners — *zarim* — were performing the *holacha* of the blood. The *gemara* responds: *d'avid maise itztaba* — the *zar* was merely acting as a passive pedestal. The *zar* held the vessel, the *kohen* took it from him and performed the *zerika*, but this does not mean the *zar* conveyed the blood. Rather: the *kohen* performed the *kabbala*, then conveyed the vessel, handed it to the *zar* — who simply extended his hand and held it stationary, functioning as little more than a stand — and then the *kohen* performed the *zerika*. The *zar* did not perform any act; he was entirely passive, inanimate in his role. Because he performed no action, there is no *avoda* to invalidate.

### Shabbat Parallel

This concept of *maaseh istaba* — passive pedestal — appears in several *rishonim* in connection with the first *mishna* of *Shabbat*, where the *gemara* describes scenarios involving a poor person standing outside and an owner inside a house, exchanging an object. One scenario has the poor person take the bread from the owner's hand, thereby performing the full *melacha* of carrying from inside to outside. In that case, the poor person is liable. But the *rishonim* ask: what of the owner? If he simply held out his hand and the poor person took the object, the owner apparently bears no liability. Why not? Is he not at least a *mesayeia* — a passive facilitator — and subject to some level of concern on the grounds of *lifnei iver*? The answer given by the *rishonim* is precisely *maaseh istaba*: the owner was utterly passive, performing no act whatsoever, and an individual who is completely inert — acting as an inanimate object — cannot have any act attributed to him.

One student in the course of this discussion raised the challenge that a human being cannot truly be completely passive — even the act of holding something still requires some muscular engagement, some micro-movement. This is a sharp observation that goes to the heart of what it means to perform an *avoda* or a *melacha* through another's body, and it is a difficulty that the invocation of *maaseh istaba* does not fully dissolve.

---

## Chafina Parameters

### Another's Chafina

Rav Pappa poses a series of questions about the parameters of the *chafina*, turning now to the question of who must perform it. The verse states *ve-lakach melo ha-machta* or *u-melo chofnav*, specifying that the *ketoret* must fill his hands — but does it say that he personally must perform the act of scooping? Perhaps it suffices that his hands be full. This raises the question: *chafan chaveiro ve-nasan le-toch chofnav mahu* — what if one person performs the *chafina* and then pours the *ketoret* into the hands of the *Kohen Gadol*? On one hand, one might say: *melo chofnav ba'inan ve-ika* — we require that his hands be full, and they are full, and the act of *chafina* with hands was performed, even if not by his hands. On the other hand: *o dilma ve-lakach ve-heivi ba'inan* — perhaps the requirement of *ve-lakach*, "he shall take," applies to the *melo chofnav* as well, and the same person must perform both the taking and the bringing. Or at minimum, the taking must be done by the *Kohen Gadol* himself. The *gemara* leaves this question unresolved: *teiku*.

### Kohen Dies

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked a closely related question: *chafan u-met* — what if the *Kohen Gadol* performs the *chafina*, transfers the *ketoret* into the ladle, and then dies? *Mah she-yikanes acher be-chafinato* — can another *Kohen Gadol* enter and use the *chafina* performed by the first one? This is structurally analogous to the previous question — a different person continues the service — except that here both the first and second individuals are *Kohen Gadol*, and the question is specifically whether the same person must complete what he started.

### Chronology Dispute

At this juncture, before the *gemara* addresses the substance of the question, it pauses for a digression. Rabbi Chanina responded to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's question by saying: *bo u-re'ei she'elas ha-rishonim* — look at the question that the earlier ones asked. This phrasing implies that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was the younger of the two, asking about a question that the previous generation had already raised. But a contrary inference seems available: elsewhere, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said that it was Rabbi Chanina who permitted him to do a certain thing — the very fact that he sought permission from Rabbi Chanina implies that Rabbi Chanina was the senior authority. The *gemara* takes up this chronological puzzle before returning to the *halakhic* substance.

### Cress Juice Digress

The specific permission Rabbi Chanina granted was: *hitir li lishtot shachlayim be-Shabbat* — Rabbi Chanina permitted me to drink cress juice on *Shabbat*. The *gemara* immediately objects: *pshita* — surely that is obvious. A *mishna* teaches that one may eat any food even for medicinal purposes, and one may drink any beverage for medicinal purposes, as long as it is in fact a food or a beverage rather than a medicine per se. If cress juice is a normal beverage, of course one may drink it. The *gemara* therefore clarifies: the question was not whether one may drink cress juice, but whether one may *grind* it — *lishchok* — and then drink it on *Shabbat*. The act of grinding raises a separate concern. The *gemara* then asks: under what circumstances? If there is genuine danger to life, of course it is permitted — *mishra shari*. If there is no danger, it is of course forbidden regardless. The *gemara* resolves: there was indeed danger. The question Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi posed to Rabbi Chanina was: does cress juice actually provide healing — *mi masya* — such that one could be *mechallel Shabbat* to prepare it? Or does it have no medical efficacy at all, in which case one cannot be *mechallel Shabbat* for its sake? And Rabbi Chanina permitted it.

The *gemara* then asks: why consult Rabbi Chanina specifically on this matter? The answer: *mishum de-baki be-refu'ot* — because Rabbi Chanina was knowledgeable in medicine. The evidence: Rabbi Chanina himself said that in all his years, no one ever came to ask him about a wound from a white mule who had survived — implying that he received many medical inquiries, and that wounds from white mules were universally fatal or permanently unhealing. The *gemara* challenges: but we do see people surviving such wounds. The response: *eima ve-chayat* — perhaps the intent is that the wound never fully healed, not that the person necessarily died. A further challenge: but we do see such wounds heal. The final response: *be-sumkan inu ve-chivan reish kara'aihu kami* — the particularly virulent cases refer to a mule that is reddish in body but has white legs.

Having established that Rabbi Chanina was a physician, the *gemara* notes that the evidence for who was the elder sage is actually the opposite of what was initially assumed. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi went to Rabbi Chanina not because Rabbi Chanina was his superior in wisdom but because he needed accurate medical information. He called him *Rabbi* Chanina — using the honorific — but that establishes Rabbi Chanina's authority rather than his age relative to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. *Shma mina d'Rabbi Chanina kashish* — we see that Rabbi Chanina was the elder of the two. The meaning of *she'elas ha-rishonim*, then, must be reinterpreted: not that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was of the earlier generation, but rather that when Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked his question, Rabbi Chanina said to him: "The question you are asking is the kind of question that the earlier generation already asked." It is a compliment to the depth of the question, not a chronological statement about the questioner.

### Back to Chafina

Returning now to the substance of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's question — and the *gemara* anticipates an immediate difficulty. How could Rabbi Chanina have treated the question of whether another *Kohen Gadol* may use the *chafina* of the first as a legitimate *halakhic* question, when Rabbi Chanina himself held that *be-par ve-lo be-damo shel par* — the *Kohen Gadol* must begin his service with the live *par*, not with the blood of the *par*? If that is so, then as soon as the first *Kohen Gadol* dies, the next *Kohen Gadol* must go all the way back to the beginning — to the slaughter of the *par* itself. And since Rabbi Chanina also holds that *ketoret* done before the *shechita* of the *par* is invalid, the entire sequence would need to be repeated. The question of whether the second *Kohen Gadol* can use the first one's *chafina* would be moot: of course he must do everything over.

The *gemara* therefore clarifies that Rabbi Chanina was not saying the question was legitimate from his own perspective. Rather, he was addressing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on his own terms. The fact that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked whether another *Kohen Gadol* can continue from the *chafina* reveals that he assumes *be-par va-afilu be-damo shel par* — that the next *Kohen Gadol* does not need to restart from the live animal, but can continue from the blood. Given that assumption, the question about the *chafina* is a genuine one: since you hold that the blood of the *par* suffices, you need not restart from the slaughter; but does the *chafina* of the deceased *Kohen Gadol* suffice for the one who succeeds him, or must he perform his own? *She'ilato ki-she'elat ha-rishonim* — your question, said Rabbi Chanina to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, is of the same type as those asked by the earlier generation.

The essential distinction between the two questions is this: the first question (Rav Pappa's) concerns whether any *chafina* performed by someone other than the *Kohen Gadol* can be used by him; the second (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's) concedes that the *chafina* must be that of a *Kohen Gadol*, but asks whether it must be done by the *same* individual who completes the service. These are related but distinct questions.

---

## Chofen V'Chozer

### Rav Pappa's View

Rav Pappa now addresses the question of whether the answer to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's question depends on whether *chofen ve-chozer ve-chofen* applies. The term *chofen ve-chozer ve-chofen* refers to whether the *Kohen Gadol*, upon entering the *kodesh kodashim*, must perform the *chafina* a second time — pouring the *ketoret* from the ladle back into his hands before releasing it onto the coals — or whether he may pour it directly from the ladle. Rav Pappa reasons as follows: if *chofen ve-chozer ve-chofen* applies — if one must indeed perform an additional *chafina* inside the *kodesh kodashim* — then another person can enter using the *chafina* of the first dead *Kohen Gadol*, because the critical *chafina* will in any case be performed again, this time by the one who actually completes the service. The act of *chafina* will be fulfilled, and it will be his own. But if there is no *chofen ve-chozer ve-chofen* — if the *ketoret* is poured straight from the ladle — then the question of whether another person may complete the service using the original *chafina* is a live and unresolved one.

### Rav Huna Reply

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua responded to Rav Pappa with the opposite reasoning. If *chofen ve-chozer ve-chofen* applies — if there is a second *chafina* inside the *kodesh kodashim* — then in fact another *Kohen Gadol* cannot use the original *chafina*, because: *ee efshar she-lo yechsar ve-she-lo yotir* — it is impossible that the second *chafina* will be exactly the same size as the first. The measure of *melo chofnav* taken on the outside and the measure of *melo chofnav* performed inside the *kodesh kodashim* will inevitably differ, because different hands have different sizes, and because the physical act of re-scooping is not identical to the original act. If both *chafina* acts are part of the *avoda* and both must match, continuity between two different people cannot be maintained. But if there is no *chofen ve-chozer ve-chofen* — if the *ketoret* is poured straight from the ladle — then the question is genuinely open: the second *Kohen Gadol* is using the first's *melo chofnav* without performing his own, and the question is whether that is permissible.

### Interior Chafina

The *gemara* moves to resolve the question of *chofen ve-chozer ve-chofen* by citing a *baraita* that describes in vivid detail what the *Kohen Gadol* does when inside the *kodesh kodashim*. The *baraita* states: *ocheiz et ha-bazikh* — he takes the ladle (referred to here as *bazikh* rather than *kaf*, though the vessels are similar) — *be-rosh etzbe'otav* — at the tips of his fingers — *ve-yeish omrim be-shinav* — some say using his teeth — *u-ma'aleh be-godlo* — and he lifts it with his thumbs — *ad she-magia le-vein atzilei yadav* — until it reaches between his elbows. What this describes is a complex physical maneuver by which the long-handled ladle is repositioned so that the bowl of the ladle, held beneath the arm and pressed against the body, can be tilted or maneuvered such that the *ketoret* is transferred back into both hands. The use of one's teeth is mentioned as one method — which is somewhat remarkable given that the *gemara* elsewhere indicates that using one's teeth is inappropriate, though *Tosafot* acknowledge that in situations where there is no alternative, it may be unavoidable.

### Incense Placement

Two opinions are recorded about how the *ketoret* is then placed upon the coals. The first opinion: *ve-tzavra* — he heaps it, placing the entire quantity in a mound — *ke-dei she-ashana shoha la-vo* — so that the smoke will rise slowly, giving the *Kohen Gadol* time to complete the act and exit before the cloud of smoke envelops him. The second opinion: *mifazra* — he scatters it across the coals — *ke-dei she-ashana memaheret la-vo* — so that the smoke rises quickly.

This debate is not merely technical. The *Kohen Gadol* is in the innermost sanctum, at the most intimate moment of the entire *Yom Kippur* service — an encounter of extraordinary weight and singularity. Does one set the incense in a mound, creating a delay before the smoke ascends, so as to withdraw before the encounter fully occurs — in effect, arranging the encounter but not remaining present for it? Or does one scatter it, causing the smoke to rise immediately, so as to be fully present at the moment when the cloud rises and the encounter is most immediate? This is a question of profound symbolic resonance, evoking the broader debate about whether one approaches the divine encounter or withdraws from it at the decisive moment.

### Avodah Hardship

After describing this intricate procedure, the *baraita* declares: *ve-zu hi avoda kasha she-be-Mikdash* — this is the most difficult *avoda* in the Temple. The *gemara* immediately responds: *zu hi ve-tu lo?* — is this really the hardest, and nothing else compares? Is there not also *melika* — the slicing of a bird's neck from behind with the fingernail — and *kemitza* — the particularly difficult smoothing of the *mincha* dough in the hand? The *gemara* therefore amends: *ela zu hi avoda kasha mi-me'ah avodot she-be-Mikdash* — rather, this is one of the hardest among the many *avodot* in the Temple.

What the *baraita* makes unmistakably clear, in any event, is that the procedure involves transferring the *ketoret* from the ladle back into the hands — the *chofen ve-chozer ve-chofen* is not optional but required. The *Kohen Gadol* does not simply pour from the ladle directly onto the coals; he performs a second *chafina* inside the *kodesh kodashim* and releases the *ketoret* from his hands. The *gemara* concludes: *shma mina chofen ve-chozer ve-chofen* — we learn from this that indeed a second *chafina* is required inside the *kodesh kodashim*, and the incense must be released from the hands. *Shma mina* — this is established.

The remaining unresolved question is whether another person may use the *chafina* of one who has died — that is, whether the second *Kohen Gadol* who enters may rely on the *chafina* performed by the first. Given that he will in any case perform his own *chafina* inside the *kodesh kodashim*, as the *baraita* establishes, the question of whether he is the one who did the initial *chafina* on the outside may be secondary. But as Rav Huna's argument makes clear, if the two *chafina* acts must correspond in measure — and it is physically impossible that they will — then even this route is problematic.

---

## Shechita Succession

### Live Animal Start

The *gemara* turns to the parallel question regarding the blood service: *shachat u-meis* — what if the *Kohen Gadol* slaughtered the *par* and then died? Can another *Kohen Gadol* take over from the point of the blood, or must he return to the beginning and slaughter again?

### Two Positions

The fundamental question is formulated as: *mi amrinan be-par va-afilu be-damo shel par* — do we say the verse's reference to "the cow" (*be-par*) encompasses even the blood of the cow, meaning the blood serves as a valid stand-in for the animal itself? Or: *be-par ve-lo be-damo shel par* — "with the cow" means specifically the cow, and entry into the service must begin with the living animal, not merely its blood?

### Four-Way Dispute

Four *amoraim* weigh in. Rabbi Chanina holds *be-par ve-lo be-damo shel par* — one must begin with the live cow. Reish Lakish holds *be-par va-afilu be-damo shel par* — even the blood suffices as a starting point. Rabbi Ami holds *be-par ve-lo be-damo shel par*, in agreement with Rabbi Chanina. Rabbi Yitzchak holds *be-par va-afilu be-damo shel par*, in agreement with Reish Lakish.

### Blood Represents Life

Rabbi Ami then challenges Rabbi Yitzchak. If the blood of the *par* truly represents the animal itself — such that beginning with the blood is equivalent to beginning with the live cow — then by that same logic, one should be able to join a *Korban Pesach* group even after the *shechita*, as long as the blood has not yet been thrown. The *halakha* is that participants may join or withdraw from a *pesach* group only until the *shechita*; once the animal is slaughtered, the group is fixed. But if the blood represents the living animal, why should the *shechita* be the cutoff? The blood is still present and still represents the *korban*. The challenge is direct: *ve-i isa, ad she-yizarek mibei lei* — if what you say is correct, the rule should be that one may join until the blood is thrown, not until the *shechita*.

### Pesach Joining Rule

The *gemara* responds: *shani hasam, de-ksiv min ha-seh* — there it is different, because the verse writes *min ha-seh*, "from the sheep." The verse that speaks of reducing or enlarging the group of participants uses the term *seh* — from the being of the *seh*. This generates the *drasha*: *mi-chayusa de-seh* — from the life of the *seh*, the sheep being alive. The ability to add or remove participants is linked specifically to the period when the animal is alive, not to the period when the blood is present. The *pesach* rule, then, is an exception derived from its own verse, and does not refute the broader principle that blood represents the animal in other contexts.

---

## Blood Represents Ani (II)

### Seh-Seh Linkage

The resolution, then, is that the *pesach* rule is established through a *gezera shava* — a linkage between *seh* in the context of the *pesach* and *seh* in the context of reducing the group. Since the word *seh* recurs in both contexts, the *halakha* of joining the group is tied to the life of the *seh* specifically. This makes the *pesach* the exception rather than the disproof: the restriction to adding participants only while the animal is alive is a unique feature of *pesach* derived from its own verse, and it does not undermine the general principle that blood represents the living animal in other *avodot*.

---

## Shechita Succession (II)

### Peter Chamor Parallel

Mar Zutra extends the discussion in a striking direction. The *mishna* states that a *peter chamor* — the firstborn of a donkey — cannot be redeemed with a calf, nor with a non-domesticated animal, nor with a slaughtered sheep, nor with a *treifa*, nor with a crossbreed, nor with a *koy*, but only with a *seh*. The question Mar Zutra poses is: why can it not be redeemed with a slaughtered sheep? If the blood of the sheep still represents the animal — if the blood of a slaughtered animal is halakhically equivalent to the living animal — then why should the dead sheep not serve for *pidyon peter chamor*?

The comparison might seem strained: in the case of the *par* on *Yom Kippur*, the blood is being brought in service of a *korban*, representing the life offered on the altar, and there is a compelling reason to say the blood stands in for the animal. But in the case of *pidyon peter chamor*, there is no *korban* being offered, and one might think the blood simply has no representational function at all. Nevertheless, the *gemara* does not immediately dismiss the comparison on those grounds.

---

## Blood Represents Ani (II)

### When Blood Represents

The *gemara* responds to Mar Zutra's challenge by invoking the same resolution used previously: *shani hasam, de-yalif seh seh mi-Pesach* — there it is different, because the requirement of *seh* for *pidyon peter chamor* is derived by *gezera shava* from *pesach*, and just as by *pesach* the *seh* must be alive, so too by *pidyon peter chamor* the *seh* must be alive. The *seh-seh* linkage thus has double duty: it both establishes the restriction for the *pesach* joining rule and extends that requirement to *pidyon peter chamor*.

What is particularly striking about this final discussion is its scope. The debate over whether the blood of the *par* represents the living animal — which one might expect to be a narrow question about the Yom Kippur *avoda* — is being applied as a *global* principle across the entire spectrum of *halakha*. The *gemara* entertains the possibility that if the blood represents the living animal for purposes of the *par* service, it might represent the living animal for the *pesach* joining rule, and even for the *pidyon* of a *peter chamor*. The *gezera shava* from *seh* to *seh* is what limits this expansion, but the very fact that the *gemara* considers the expansion at all reveals how fundamental and far-reaching the underlying conceptual question is. The discussion of whether a second *Kohen Gadol* can continue the service where the first left off is not merely a practical question about Yom Kippur procedure; it touches on the deepest question of what blood represents in the sacrificial system. This question will continue into the following *daf*.

---

---

# Yoma 53

## Kohen Gadol Entry

### Holy of Holies Entry

Daf 53 opens at precisely the moment we have been building toward throughout the tractate: the *Kohen Gadol* stands inside the *Kodesh Kodashim*. He has passed through the curtains, he stands near the rock — or, in the *Bayit Rishon*, beside the *Kodesh Kodashim* itself. He sets down the fire pan, and through a process debated earlier — whether he needed to perform *chofin v'chozer v'chofin*, scooping and re-scooping — he managed to transfer the incense from the ladle back into his hands and place it onto the fire pan. The chamber fills with smoke, and he prepares to leave.

### Mishnah Drama

Before entering the *sugyot* proper, it is worth pausing on something that might seem self-evident but is genuinely worth naming: the *Mishnayot* of this tractate have employed a persistent rhetorical technique of pulling out and pulling in. Each time the reader expects to finally arrive at the *avodah*, the Mishnah steps back — "and the rest of the year they would do it this way" — before drawing the narrative back in toward the center. The effect is dramatic. Had the Mishnah simply recited the procedure in sequence, the moment would not feel as momentous. By constantly supplying the larger context and then narrowing back toward the singular, we are made to feel the full weight of what the *Kohen Gadol* is doing: an act so utterly unique that it can only be appreciated against the backdrop of everything it is not.

---

## Tzedokim Dispute

### Incense Verse

A *Tanu Rabbanan* at the top of 53a introduces a *beraita* anchored in the verse *v'natan et haketoret al ha'esh lifnei Hashem* — "and you shall place the *ketoret* on the fire before God." The *beraita* understands *lifnei Hashem* as a directive: when you are in the presence of God, when you are inside the *Kodesh Kodashim*, do not place the *ketoret* on the fire pan outside and then carry it in already burning. This is the *lehotzi mi'liban shel Tzedukim* — the verse is meant to uproot the position of the *Tzedukim*.

It is worth recalling the context: during the seven days of preparation before *Yom Kippur*, the *Kohen Gadol* was instructed in the proper procedure and made to take an oath that he would not follow the *Tzedukim* practice. Much of the anxiety surrounding the *Kohen Gadol*'s potential death inside the *Kodesh Kodashim* was historically connected to concern that he might conduct the *avodah* according to *Tzedukim* custom.

### Tzedokim Position

The *Gemara* now asks: *mai darosh* — what did the *Tzedukim* actually derive? Their position is rooted in the verse *ki b'anan eraeh al hakaporet*, which appears in the opening of *Acharei Mos*: *v'al yavo b'chol et el hakodesh mibeit laparochet el pnei hakaporet asher al ha'aron v'lo yamut ki b'anan eraeh al hakaporet*. The *Tzedukim* read this as follows: since God appears upon the *kaporet* in a cloud, if you wish to enter, you must enter enveloped in a cloud. *Ki b'anan* is not a description of God's presence but a condition on the *Kohen Gadol*'s entry — he must come in already surrounded by the cloud of burning *ketoret*. Hence their ruling: *yitaken mibachutz v'yachnis*, prepare it outside with the incense already burning, and then carry it in.

### Chazal Refutation

The *Chachamim* respond: has it not already been stated explicitly — *v'natan et haketoret al ha'esh lifnei Hashem*? The *ketoret* is placed on the fire in the presence of God, which clearly means inside the *Kodesh Kodashim*. If so, what do we do with *ki b'anan eraeh al hakaporet*?

### Maaleh Ashan

Rather than reading *anan* as a reference to the cloud of God's normal theophanic appearance, *Chazal* concede — and this is notable — that the *anan* here indeed refers to the cloud produced by the *ketoret*. But *melamed she-noten bah ma'aleh ashan*: the verse is teaching that the *ketoret* must contain the herb called *ma'aleh ashan*, that ingredient which causes the smoke to rise in a straight column rather than dispersing. The *ki b'anan eraeh* means: when you come to encounter Me, ensure that the *ketoret* creates a proper *anan* — but it must be created inside, not brought in from outside.

One might ask: would the *ketoret* not produce smoke regardless, even without *ma'aleh ashan*? A reasonable reading of the *Gemara* is that *ma'aleh ashan* is a specific plant — indeed a proper name, not a generic descriptor — and that without it there would still be smoke, just not the ideal upward-streaming column. Alternatively, the verse may be understood more broadly as requiring any substance that ensures a robust cloud: *v'chisa mikkol makom*, the cloud must cover the *kaporet* by whatever means works. Both readings remain in play, and the *Gemara* will revisit this question.

---

## Ki BeAnan Erah

### First Source

Having established that *ki b'anan eraeh* teaches the requirement for *ma'aleh ashan*, the *beraita* then adds: *u'minayin she-noten bah ma'aleh ashan?* — and from where do we know this requirement? *Talmud lomar v'chisa anan haketoret et hakaporet*: the second verse makes it explicit that the cloud of the *ketoret* must cover the *kaporet*. The *Gemara* immediately questions this structure.

### Second Source

*Kra bi kra?* — do you need one verse to prove another? You already cited *ki b'anan eraeh* as the source for *ma'aleh ashan*, and now you cite a second verse to confirm it?

*Amar Rav Yosef hachi ka'amar*: the two verses are not redundant. *Ein li ela aleh ma'aleh ashan* — I might have thought only the leaf of the *ma'aleh ashan* plant suffices. *Ikar ma'aleh ashan minayin* — from where do I know the root of the plant may also be used? *Talmud lomar v'chisa*: the additional verse extends the obligation to include even the root, which is perhaps less potent than the leaf.

*Abaye* challenges this: but the *beraita* itself teaches the opposite — the root is *better* than the leaf! As it says: *natan b'ikar ma'aleh ashan haya mitamer v'oleh kemakel* — when one placed the root in the *ketoret*, the smoke would rise straight as a pole *ad shemagia lishmei kora*, until it reached the ceiling beams, and then *memashmesh v'yored bakotalim* — it would feel its way downward along the walls, *ad shenitmaleh habayit ashan*, until the chamber was filled with smoke, as it says in *Yeshayahu*, *v'habayit yimalei ashan*. So the root produces the superior result.

*Ela amar Abaye hachi ka'amar*: reverse it. The first verse establishes that the root suffices — that is already known to be the ideal. The second verse, *v'chisa*, comes to extend the requirement to the leaf as well, even though it is the lesser option, teaching that even with the leaf, provided the cloud ultimately covers the *kaporet*, the *avodah* is valid.

---

## Death Penalty

### Empty Entry

The *beraita* notes that if one failed to include *ma'aleh ashan*, or omitted even one of the ingredients of the *ketoret* — *shechisar achat mikol samaneha* — the offender is *chayav mita*. Many will recognize this formulation from the *Pitum HaKetoret* recited on *Shabbos*. But the *Gemara* presses: *v'teipuk lei de-kamayeh biah reikanit* — why is the death penalty derived from the improper burning? Let the offender be liable for *biah reikanit*, purposeless entry, since without a valid *ketoret* he has no legitimate reason to be inside the *Kodesh Kodashim* at all.

The background is the verse *v'al yavo b'chol et el hakodesh... v'lo yamut*, from which *Chazal* understand two separate liabilities: the first, *al yavo b'chol et v'lo yamut*, prohibits any unauthorized, purposeless entry — this is *biah reikanit*; the second, *v'lo yamut ki b'anan eraeh*, teaches that if the *ketoret* is not done properly, the offender is liable as well. The *Gemara*'s question is: these two liabilities will typically coincide — anyone who burns the *ketoret* improperly also lacks a valid *avodah* purpose and thus has committed a *biah reikanit*. Why do we need a separate liability for the burning?

*Amar Rav Sheshet*: the two liabilities exist independently to cover cases of partial knowledge. If someone was *shogeg* — unaware — of the prohibition of *biah reikanit* but fully intentional (*mezid*) regarding the improper burning, he cannot be held liable under the first rubric but can be held liable under the second. The point is not to find a scenario where one occurs without the other in practice, but to ensure liability attaches to whichever violation he was *mezid* about.

### Two Incense

*Rav Ashi* pushes further: *afilu teima hizid bazu uvazu* — even if he was *mezid* about both, it is still possible to burn the *ketoret* improperly without any *biah reikanit*. How? *Kegon de'ayeil shtei haktarot* — a case where he brought in two *ketorot*, *achat shleima v'achat chasera*: one complete and one lacking. *Abi'ah lo mechayev* — he is not liable for *biah reikanit*, because his entry was justified by the valid *ketoret* he carried in. His presence inside the *Kodesh Kodashim* was legitimate. But once he has burned the valid one, he then proceeds to burn the deficient one. *Ahaktara mechayev* — for that burning he is liable, because he burned a lacking *ketoret*, *de-kamaktir ketoret chasera*. His entry was legitimate; his subsequent action was not.

---

## Ki BeAnan Erah (II)

### Two Verses

Having established the two-verse framework, the *Gemara* now returns to examine the four *amoraic* explanations of why both *ki b'anan eraeh al hakaporet* and *v'chisa anan haketoret et hakaporet* are necessary. *Amar Rav Yosef*: as discussed above, one verse teaches the leaf and the other extends to the root — or, in *Abaye*'s reversal, one establishes the root and the other extends to the leaf.

### Mishkan Mikdash

*Rav Sheshet amar*: the two verses serve an entirely different purpose. *Ein li ela Ohel Moed* — I know only that this *avodah* applies in the *Ohel Moed* of the desert, since the *psukim* throughout this section center on *v'chein ya'aseh l'Ohel Moed hashochein itam b'toch tumatam*. How do I know the same requirement applies in the permanent *Mikdash* — in *Shilo* or in the *Beis Olamim* on *Har HaBayis*? *Talmud lomar v'chisa*: the additional verse extends the cloud-covering requirement to every place where God's presence dwells.

The *Gemara* objects: we already derive the equivalence between *Ohel Moed* and *Mikdash* from the words *hashochein itam b'toch tumatam* — wherever God causes His presence to dwell, the obligation applies.
