So the extra verse is not needed for that. *Ela hacha kamar*: try again. *Ein ela b'Yom HaKippurim* — I know only that this requirement applies on *Yom Kippur*. *B'sha'ar yemei hashanah minayin* — from where do I know it applies throughout the rest of the year? *Talmud lomar v'chisa*: the additional verse extends the obligation to the daily *ketoret* burned in the *Heichal*.

This is a striking expansion. The natural assumption has always been that the emphasis on *ma'aleh ashan* and the cloud of the *ketoret* is specifically a *Yom Kippur* concern, connected to the *Kohen Gadol*'s entry into the *Kodesh Kodashim*. But *Chazal* now establish that the requirement — including the attendant *chiyuv mita* for failing to fulfill it — applies equally to the *ketoret* burned twice daily on the golden altar in the *Heichal*. Indeed, when the *Gemara* discussed the family that guarded the secret knowledge of producing the *ketoret*, that discussion concerned the *daily* offering. We say every *Shabbos* in *Pittum HaKtoret*: *chisar achat mikol samaneha chayav mita* — and now we understand why this applies even outside the context of *Yom Kippur*.

There is something deeply meaningful here. The encounter with God that the *ketoret* is meant to facilitate — what the verse *ki b'anan eraeh al hakaporet* points toward — is not confined to the singular moment of *Yom Kippur*. Even in the daily offering, some shadow of that encounter, some echo of the intense divine presence, is being sought and required. The daily *ketoret* is in some sense modeled after, and reaches toward, the *Yom Kippur* experience. The same conditions, the same standards, and the same consequences attach — not with the same intensity, but with the same underlying orientation.

### Obligation Contingency

*Rav Ashi amar*: *chad lemitzvah v'chad le'akeiv* — one verse establishes the obligation *lechatchila*, and the second tells you that the requirement is *me'akeiv* even *bedi'eved*. Without the second verse, one might have thought that failure to achieve the proper cloud is a deficiency but does not invalidate the *avodah*. *Tosafos* adds: since everything in *Yom Kippur* is generally *me'akeiv* by virtue of the word *chukkah*, this reading may be more naturally applied to the extension of the requirement to the rest of the year — both verses together teach that the daily *ketoret* too must have the cloud in order to be valid.

### Punishment Warning

*Rava amar*: *chad le'onash v'chad le'azhara* — one verse provides the punishment, the other the prohibition. *V'lo yamut* is the *onash*, the consequence; *ki b'anan eraeh* serves as the *azhara*, the warning: do not enter this way unless you have the proper cloud. *V'al yavo ki b'anan eraeh*: the prohibition is not to enter without the *anan*; *v'lo yamut* is the consequence if one does.

---

## Death Penalty (II)

### When Applies

A *tanya* elaborates: *Rebbi Eliezer omer* — *v'lo yamut* is the *onash*, *ki b'anan eraeh* is the *azhara*. The verse structure supports this: *v'al yavo bechol et el hakodesh... v'lo yamut ki b'anan eraeh al hakaporet* — do not enter without the *anan*, and if you do, you will die.

### Acharei Mos

The *beraita* then poses a series of questions about the *parsha*'s temporal position. *Yachol yiheyu shneihem amurim kodem misat bnei Aharon* — perhaps both the prohibition and the consequence were communicated to *Moshe* and *Aharon* before the sons of *Aharon* died? After all, one might reason, it would only be just that they were warned beforehand if they were to be punished. *Talmud lomar acharei mos shnei bnei Aharon* — the heading of the *parsha* tells us it was said afterward.

But then perhaps *yachol yiheyu shneihem amurim achar misat shnei bnei Aharon* — maybe both the prohibition and the consequence were given only after they died, meaning they had received no warning beforehand at all? *Talmud lomar ki b'anan eraeh al hakaporet* — the *lashon asid*, the future tense "I will appear," indicates that this was given before God's presence had yet appeared on the *kaporet*.

*Amar Rava amar kra ki b'anan eraeh — v'adayin lo nireh*: I will appear, and I have not yet appeared. Since by the time of *Acharei Mos* God had already appeared in the *Mishkan* on *yom hashmini*, this must have been stated before *yom hashmini* — before the *Mishkan* was erected. *Ha keitzad*? How to reconcile? *Azharah kodem misah*: the warning — *ki b'anan eraeh* — was given before they died, before the *Mishkan* was erected. The prohibition was communicated beforehand. But *v'lo yamut*, the articulation of the *onash*, was stated only *achar misah*, after they died.

This is a striking *Gemara*, and it is worth pausing on several dimensions. First, it has effectively read *ki b'anan eraeh* not as referring to the *anan haketoret* — as *Chazal* argued against the *Tzedukim* earlier — but as referring to God's ordinary theophanic cloud. If the verse meant "I will appear [in the cloud of *ketoret*]," the future tense would not prove that it was said before *yom hashmini*; it would simply mean that on a future *Yom Kippur*, when you perform the *avodah*, I will appear. The proof only works if *anan* refers to God's standard *anan* of divine presence, and the claim is that God had not yet appeared on the *kaporet* specifically. But even then, the end of *Sefer Shemos* describes God's *anan* filling the entire *Mishkan* — and the *Gemara* accepts that this refers to the whole structure, not specifically *al hakaporet*. So the verse's emphasis on the *kaporet* is what allows it to be read as pointing to something yet to occur.

The additional dimension is halachic: the *Gemara* presupposes that punishment would be unjust without prior warning of both the prohibition and the consequence. The visceral biblical account — the fire going forth from before God and consuming *Nadav* and *Avihu* — is being fully halachized. The deaths cannot be understood merely as a collision with overwhelming divine power; they must be framed within the architecture of prohibition, forewarning, and willful violation.

### Paskening

*V'ela mai ta'ama i'anush* — but if the punishment required prior warning of the consequence, and that was only given after their death, why were they punished at all?

*Keditanya, Rebbi Eliezer omer*: they died *al she'horu halacha bifnei Moshe Rabban* — because they issued a *halachic* ruling in the presence of their teacher. *Mah darash*? The verse states that the sons of *Aharon* placed fire on the altar. From this they derived: *af al pi she'esh yoredes min hashamayim, mitzvah lehavoi min ha'hedyot* — even though fire descends from Heaven, one is still obligated to add fire from a mundane source. This is in fact the correct *halacha*. But they ruled on it independently, *bifnei rabban*, without deferring to *Moshe*. And the connection to the earlier theme is unmistakable: on *yom hashmini*, immediately before their act, fire had come down from Heaven — *vatetzei esh milifnei Hashem*. They then brought their own *esh* in addition, ruling by their own authority that this was required even in the face of the divine fire. It is also worth noting that the verse says *esh zarah asher lo tziva osam* — a foreign fire which He had not commanded them — which suggests the problem lay not merely in the *ketoret* itself but in the nature of their action.

### Multiple Explanations

*Tosafos* notes that in *Toras Kohanim* there is a wide *machloket* among the *tannaim* as to why they died. *Ika man d'amar misinai natlu* — they finally received their punishment for the improper behavior when they saw God at *Har Sinai*, where it says *vayochlu vayishtu*, eating and drinking while beholding the divine presence. *V'is de'amri*: they used to say, "when will these two old men die, and we two will lead the generation" — an impatient ambition regarding *Moshe* and *Aharon*. Others say *parua rosh hayu* — they entered with disheveled hair. Others say *shtuyei yayin hayu* — they were intoxicated, which the juxtaposition with *yayin veshichar al tesht* immediately following their death suggests. And others say *mechusarei begadim hayu* — they lacked some of the required priestly vestments. *Uviferek Arba Misos nami maisi lah* — these explanations are also cited in the chapter of the four capital punishments.

---

## Walking Backwards

### Shlomo's Journey

Having concluded that the *Kohen Gadol* exits *derech kenisato*, walking backwards the way he came in, the *Gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — from where is this derived?

*Amar Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yonatan*: the source is the verse concerning *Shlomo*, *vayavo Shlomo labamah asher beGivon Yerushalayim* — Shlomo came to the altar which is in *Givon*, Jerusalem. The verse oddly appends "Jerusalem" to a journey that went *to* Gibeon — it should have said he went *from* Jerusalem. *Vekhi mah inyan Givon etzel Yerushalayim*? The *Gemara* explains: *makish yetziato miGivon liYerushalayim levi'ato miYerushalayim liGivon* — by linking Gibeon and Jerusalem without the word "from," the verse connects his departure from Gibeon back to Jerusalem with his original approach from Jerusalem to Gibeon. Just as he went *panav klapei bamah* — facing the altar as he traveled toward it — so too when he departed from Gibeon back to Jerusalem, he continued to face the altar, walking backwards.

### Daily Application

This practice is not confined to the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur*. Just as we saw the *ketoret* requirement extended from the singular *Yom Kippur* moment into a daily obligation, the same pattern operates here with the backwards departure. *V'khein kohanim ba'avodatam* — the *kohanim* when performing their *avodah*, *uleviyim beduchnam* — the *levi'im* at the *duchan* as they sing, *v'Yisrael bema'amadam* — and the *Yisrael* representatives who stood in the *azarah* daily to represent the people for whose sake the *korbanot* were brought — when they leave, *lo hayu machzirim peneihem veholechim*, they would not turn their backs and walk away. Rather *metzadedim peneihem veholechim* — they would angle themselves sideways. Perhaps a full backwards walk is more appropriate when one is alone, as when leaving the *Kodesh Kodashim*; in the more crowded *azarah* one angles the face to the side rather than walking directly backward, but the back is never turned to the altar.

### Students Leaving

*V'khein talmid haniftar merabbo*: a student taking leave of his *rebbe* similarly does not turn his back, but faces to the side as he departs. The movement from *Mikdash* to *Torah* is an unmistakable and pointed one. In the absence of the *Mikdash*, *Torah* — embodied in the *rebbe* — is our center. The same reverence that governed departure from the *Kodesh Kodashim* and from the *azarah* now governs departure from the presence of one's teacher.

### Rabbi Stories

*Ki ha d'Rabbi Elazar*: when *Rabbi Elazar* would take leave of *Rabbi Yochanan*, the procedure varied depending on who was departing first. If *Rabbi Yochanan* wished to walk away, *Rabbi Elazar* would prostrate himself and remain in place until *Rabbi Yochanan* was no longer visible. If *Rabbi Elazar* himself was taking leave, *havei ka'azil l'achoreih* — he would walk backwards, *ad d'michsi minei d'Rabbi Yochanan* — until he had passed out of *Rabbi Yochanan*'s sight. The logic is clear: once the *rebbe* can no longer see him, turning his back would not be disrespectful.

### Rava Backwards

*Rava*, similarly, *kad havei miptar mineih d'Rav Yosef* — when taking leave of *Rav Yosef* — *havei azil l'achoreih*, he would walk backwards. The consequence: *ad d'minadp'in karaei* — his legs would strike against objects, *u'mitpayan askofta d'vei Rav Yosef dama* — and the doorposts of *Rav Yosef*'s house would be smeared with blood. He was willing to absorb that cost. This detail carries an unmistakable resonance — blood on the doorpost — though perhaps unintended.

*Amru leih l'Rav Yosef hachi avid Rava*: people reported this to *Rav Yosef*, who was blind and could not see it himself. Notably, even though *Rav Yosef* could not see *Rava* departing, *Rava* continued to walk backwards — because others could see, and because respectful conduct in the presence of one's *rebbe* is not simply a matter of being observed by him. *Amar Rav Yosef: yehei ra'ava d'tairem reishach a'kula karcha* — may it be God's will that your head be raised over the entire city, which *Rashi* understands as a blessing to become *Rosh Yeshiva*. *Maharsha* reads it as a blessing to lead both competing *yeshivot* — both his own and *Abaye*'s.

### Prayer Steps

*Amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: the same principle extends to *tefillah*. One who prays must take three steps backward at the conclusion of *Shemoneh Esrei* — *v'achar kach yiten shalom* — and only afterward recite the *oseh shalom* farewell. Note the order: first the steps, then *oseh shalom*. One might have expected the farewell to precede the departure, but there is a logic here: by saying goodbye one implicitly casts oneself as already outside the encounter. Instead, one first demonstrates the distancing — the physical stepping back — and then, once that breach has been created, sums up the experience with *oseh shalom bimromav hu ya'aseh shalom*. This too models after our central *avodah*: just as the *Kohen Gadol* exits the *Kodesh Kodashim* before completing his benediction to the assembled people, here the physical withdrawal precedes the formulaic conclusion.

### Dog Vomit

*Amar leih Rav Mordechai*: once one has taken those three steps back, one must stand there — *hatam miba'ei leih l'meikam* — and not immediately return to where one was standing. *Mashal l'talmid haniftar merabo* — the comparison returns to the *rebbe*-student relationship: *im chozer l'altar, domeh l'kelev sheshav al ke'o* — if he steps back and immediately returns, it is like a dog returning to its vomit. The image is jarring, and its exact significance is not entirely transparent. One reading: the act of stepping back is itself a kind of self-abasement, an *anochi afar va'efer* — an acknowledgment of one's smallness before the divine or before the *rebbe*. To immediately return negates that act of abasement, reversing the debasement just performed. Whatever the precise valence of the image, the practical instruction is clear: after the three steps back, one stands for a moment. One does not simply stride back to one's seat or to where one was standing before. The leave-taking must mean something.

---

---

# Yoma 54

## Walking Backwards

### Kohen Gadol Exiting

Today's daf is 54. We begin on 53b, where the previous discussion centered on the manner in which the *kohen gadol* would walk backwards out of the *kodesh kodashim*, and how that practice was then transposed: first to walking backwards when departing from one's *rebbi* — a transference of the sense of the sacred center from the *Mikdash* to Torah and its representative — and then further still to a direct encounter with God, namely the three steps backward taken upon completing *shmoneh esrei*.

### Three Steps Backward

The *Gemara* on 53b introduces a *tanya*: *hamispalel tzarich sheyafsiya shalosh pesiot leachora* — one who prays must step three steps backward upon concluding. Afterward, he recites *oseh shalom*. The *tanna* adds a strikingly harsh consequence: *veim lo asa ken, ra'uy shelo hitpalel* — if he did not do this, it would have been better for him not to have prayed at all. Rashi, citing the phrase *ra'uy hayo lo im lo hitpalel kemit'to*, does not substantially alter the plain meaning: the manner in which one ends the prayer affects the entire character of the prayer, rendering the whole worthless if the conclusion is improper.

### Direction of Greeting

In the name of Shmaya, the *tanna* teaches that one should give *shalom* first to the right and then to the left — *shenoten shalom liyamin veachar kach lismol*. The proof text is *mimino esh das lamo*, indicating that God's right hand is associated with the giving of Torah. A second verse is added: *yipol mitzidcha elef urevava miminecha* — a thousand shall fall at your side, but a myriad at your right. The *Gemara* anticipates an objection: perhaps the preference for the right in the first verse merely reflects the ordinary human practice of using the right hand? The second verse answers this, since it concerns not an act of giving but a general framework of divine favor toward the right.

### Rava Corrects Abaye

Rava observed Abaye turning first to his own right when reciting *oseh shalom bimromav*. He corrected him: *mi savart liyamin didach?* — do you think it means your right? No. *Lismol didach dehu yemino shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — one should first turn to one's own left, which is God's right. Since one is departing from God's presence, giving *shalom* to the right means orienting toward God's right — which, from the worshipper's perspective, is to one's own left. This is indeed the practice observed today.

### Three Steps & Bowing

Chiya brei deRav Huna reported that he observed Abaye and Rava take the three backward steps with a single prostration — *dipsilu shalosh pesiot bechriyah achas* — remaining bowed throughout the steps rather than stepping and bowing separately. This connects to the earlier discussion of Rabbi Eliezer, who would prostrate himself upon the ground until Rabbi Yochanan had departed.

This concludes the *Gemara*'s treatment of walking backwards — a fascinating intersection of *Mikdash* practice and *tefilla*. The discussion transitions naturally to a related intersection: the *kohen gadol*'s brief prayer in the *heichal* upon exiting the *kodesh kodashim*.

---

## Kohen Gadol's Prayer

### Short Prayer & Weather

Returning to the *Mishna*, the text states: *umitpalel tefilla ketzara bevayis hachitzon* — he would recite a short prayer in the outer chamber. The *Gemara* asks: *mai mitzlei* — what would he actually say? Rava bar Rav Adda and Ravin bar Rav Adda both report in the name of Rav: *Yehi ratzon milifanecha Hashem Elokeinu shetehei shana zo geshuma ushchuna* — may it be Your will that this year be rainy and hot.

### Shchuna Interpretation

The *Gemara* immediately questions the inclusion of *shchuna*: is an overly hot year a desirable thing? *Ella eima* — rather, the prayer should be read conditionally: *im shchuna tehei geshuma* — if it is going to be too hot, may it at least also be rainy, to offset the heat. This was fundamentally a concern about the crops and the agricultural livelihood of the people, not personal comfort. It is worth noting that the liturgical prayer of Yom Kippur, recited after the *avodah*, expands this into a considerably longer paragraph — but the *Gemara* here identifies this as the essential core.

The fact that, of all possible petitions, this concern about weather is singled out speaks to the reality of an agricultural society: the single most pressing matter for national welfare was whether the year would bring adequate rain.

### National Concerns Prayer

Rav Acha brei deRava adds, in the name of Rav Yehuda, a concluding section to the prayer that extends beyond meteorological concerns. Notably, the language shifts at this point from Hebrew into Aramaic.

### Dominion of Yehuda

The extended prayer includes: *lo ya'adi avidi shultana mibei Yehuda* — may dominion not be removed from the house of Yehuda. This reflects the belief that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was a direct descendant of David HaMelech, and that even during the period of the *Bayis Sheni*, when the Jewish people lived under foreign rule, they retained a degree of political autonomy through the Davidic line of the *nasi*. The *kohen gadol*, representing the nation at a national level, would pray that this measure of self-governance not be taken away. The petition is a powerful one: it frames the preservation of Jewish political identity as a matter of collective religious concern.

### Economic Sufficiency

The prayer continues: *velo yihiyu amcha Yisrael tzrichim leparnas ze mize* — may Your people Israel not need to support one another for *parnassa*. This broadens the prayer from weather to economic well-being. The *Maharsha* connects this to a famous *Gemara* in Berachos in which David's advisors suggest that, in a time of universal poverty, the people should simply do commerce with one another — to which the response is that if everyone is poor, there is no new money entering the system. The prayer is therefore for a genuinely productive year, not merely an internal redistribution of existing resources — what one might call a positive balance of payments.

### National vs. Individual

The prayer concludes: *velo tikanes lefanecha tefilas ovrei drachim* — and may the prayers of those traveling on the roads not enter before You. Travelers, for obvious reasons, pray that it not rain. But their self-interested, individual petitions are of far lesser weight than the national need for proper rainfall. The *kohen gadol* explicitly asks that God not heed those private concerns when they conflict with collective welfare.

---

## Chanina ben Dosa

### Rain on the Road

The *Gemara* now introduces a story about *ovrei drachim* and prayer. Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa was traveling on the road — *Rebbi Chanina Ben Dosa hava ka azil be-orcha* — when rain began to pour down upon him. He prayed: *Ribbono Shel Olam, kol olam kulo be-nachas ve-Chanina be-tza'ar?* — Master of the Universe, all the world is at ease, and Chanina alone is in distress? *Pasak mitra* — and the rain stopped.

### Rain Reversal

When he arrived home, he prayed again: *Ribbono Shel Olam, kol olam kulo be-tza'ar ve-Chanina be-nachas?* — all the world is now suffering because on my account You stopped the rain, and I alone am comfortable? *Ata mitra* — and the rain resumed. The story is striking: certain figures — among the *tanna'im* and *amora'im* — possessed an immediacy of divine responsiveness such that God would follow their word in both directions. The logic of Chanina ben Dosa's conduct is coherent: if God will equally hear him when he arrives home and asks for the rain to resume, he can permissibly pray to have it stopped while still on the road.

### Rav Yosef's Question

Rav Yosef raises the pointed rhetorical question: *mai ahani lei tzelutei de-kohen gadol legabei Rebbi Chanina Ben Dosa?* — what value does the *kohen gadol*'s prayer have in a world where Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa exists? The implication is that Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's direct line to Heaven renders the formal institutional prayer almost superfluous.

---

## Long Prayer Concern

### Fear of Death

The *Gemara* now presents a *baraita* about a *kohen gadol* who extended his prayer at length — *she-herich bitfilato*. The *kohanim* outside began to discuss whether to send someone in after him; they feared he might have died inside the *kodesh kodashim*. Just as they were about to enter, he emerged.

### Defense of Prayer

They asked him: *mipnei mah herachta bitfilatcha* — why did you pray for so long? He replied: *kashe be-eineichem she-hitpalalti aleichem ve-al Beis Hamikdash she-lo ye-charev?* — Is it problematic in your eyes that I prayed on your behalf and for the *Beis Hamikdash* that it should not be destroyed?

This is an interesting moment. One wonders at what point during the *Bayis Sheni* they genuinely feared its destruction, or whether the *Gemara* is projecting backwards, imagining that even in the time of the *Bayis Sheni* there was awareness of the precariousness of the *Mikdash*'s continued existence.

### Warning Against Length

The *kohanim* replied: *al targil la'asot ken* — do not make a habit of this. They cited an existing teaching: *lo hayah ma'arich bitfilato kedei she-lo le-hav'it et Yisrael* — he was not supposed to extend his prayer, so as not to frighten the people of Israel. The citation formula *she-harei shaninu* suggests they were quoting the literary corpus of the *Mishna*, which is slightly anachronistic, though the underlying principle clearly predates its formulation. The lesson is clear: even the most sincere and self-sacrificing prayer — offered for the sake of the people and the *Mikdash* itself — is inappropriate when its prolonged duration causes the congregation genuine distress. Being a *tzaddik* for others does not override the obligation not to alarm them.

---

## Aron's Fate Dispute

### Shtiyah Stone

The *Mishna* says: *mishenitlo ha-Aron* — from the time the *aron* was removed. Notably, it does not say *mishe-nignaz*, from the time it was hidden, but *mishe-nital*, from the time it was taken — language that implies it was carried away, not concealed in place. This leads to the position that the *aron* was exiled to Babylonia.

Before engaging the dispute directly, the *Mishna* introduces a related detail: *even hayetah sham mi-yemot nevi'im rishonim* — there was a stone there from the days of the early prophets, *ve-shtiyah hayetah nikreit* — and it was called the *Shtiyah* stone, the foundation stone. It stood *gavoha min ha-aretz shalosh etzba'ot* — three fingerbreadths above the ground.

Several questions arise regarding this stone. Was the *aron* placed upon it? Was it always visible, or was it beneath the ground during the period of the *aron* and only exposed after? The *Gemara* does not resolve these physical questions, and the dimensions invite further discussion: three fingerbreadths is barely an inch — quite modest — and the rock associated with the Dome of the Rock is considerably more imposing. Various sources do identify the *Even Shetiyah* with that rock, and archaeological analysis of the *Har Habayit* dimensions provides *halachic* authorities a basis for determining the approximate location of the *azarah* — hence the existence of sanctioned tours that can navigate around the *azarah* boundaries. But the precise correlation remains uncertain. The *Gemara* itself records only that upon this stone the *kohen gadol* would place the incense, and that it served as a substitute for the *aron* in the ritual of the *Bayis Sheni*.

The subsequent *Mishnayos* detail the *kohen gadol*'s actions after leaving the *kodesh kodashim*: he retrieves the blood of the ox from the one who had been stirring it, re-enters to sprinkle — *achat lemalah vesheva lematah* — one above and seven below, without intending to strike high or low specifically but rather *kematzlif*, with a flicking or whipping motion. He counts: *achat, achat ve'achat, achat veshtayim, achat veshalosh* — and so on through seven. He exits, places the blood on one of the two gold pedestals in the *heichal* — a dispute exists between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda as to whether there were one or two such pedestals — then performs the identical procedure with the blood of the goat, and subsequently mixes the two bloods together, pouring from vessel to vessel to combine them thoroughly.

### Four Positions

Returning to the language *mishe-nital*, the *Gemara* says: *tana ke-man de-amar aron galah le-vavel* — the *tanna* of the *Mishna* holds like the opinion that the *aron* was exiled to Babylonia. A *baraita* is then cited presenting four positions on the fate of the *aron*.

### Eliezer: Exiled

Rabbi Eliezer says: *aron galah le-vavel* — the *aron* was exiled to Babylonia. The proof text is *va-yeviehu vavel im klei chemdat beis Hashem* — Nevuchadnezzar brought him to Babylonia together with the most desirous vessels of the House of God. What is the most desirous vessel? The *aron*. A second verse is added: *va-yeitzei mi-bat Tzion kol hadarah* — from the daughter of Zion all her glory departed. The *Gemara* reads *hadarah* as *chadarah* — the innermost chamber. What is found in the innermost chamber? The *aron* with the *luchot*. Thus two verses together establish that the *aron* was taken into exile.

### Shimon: Buried

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says: *aron bimkomo nignaz* — the *aron* was buried in its place, beneath the floor of the *kodesh kodashim*. His proof is from the verse: *va-ya'arichu ha-badim min ha-kodesh al pnei ha-dvir* — the tops of the poles extended from the *kodesh* to the face of the *dvir* — and *va-yihyu sham ad ha-yom hazeh* — and they were there until this day. If the poles were still in place until the time of the verse's writing, the *aron* never moved; it must have been concealed in place.

### Ulla's Report

This position conflicts, however, with a report from Ulla. Ulla states that Rabbi Matya ben Charash once asked Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai — when they were together in Rome — whether, given that Rabbi Eliezer teaches us from two verses that the *aron* was taken to Babylonia, what Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai himself maintained. Rabbi Shimon replied that he holds *aron bimkomo nignaz*, as demonstrated by the verse about the poles remaining *sham ad ha-yom hazeh*. Thus the *Braitah* and Ulla's report disagree about Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's position: the *braitah* attributes to him the view that the *aron* was exiled, while Ulla's account presents him as holding that it was buried in place. Both versions stand without resolution.

### Rabba's Challenge

Rabba challenged Ulla's reasoning: *mah mashma* — what exactly does *va-yihyu sham ad ha-yom hazeh* prove? Does every occurrence of *ad ha-yom hazeh* in the *Tanach* imply permanence and continuity for all time?

### Counter-Example

Rabba marshals a counter-example. The verse states: *ve-es ha-yevusi yoshev Yerushalayim lo horishu benei Binyamin va-yeshev ha-yevusi es benei Binyamin be-Yerushalayim ad ha-yom ha-zeh* — the Jebusites dwelling in Jerusalem were not driven out by the children of Binyamin, and the Jebusites dwelt with the children of Binyamin in Jerusalem until this day. Does this mean that *benei Binyamin* remained continuously in Jerusalem? A *baraita* shows otherwise. Rabbi Yehuda teaches that for fifty-two years no man passed through Yehuda — the land was entirely desolate. This figure is derived from the *gematria* of *behema* (בהמה), which equals fifty-two, tied to the verse describing the utter desolation of the land. Additionally, Rabbi Yosei derives from a *gezeirah shava* on the word *bris* that for seven years the land suffered *gofris va-melach* — sulfur and salt — rendering it entirely untillable. Yet the verse had said *benei Binyamin* remained *ad ha-yom ha-zeh*. Clearly, then, *ad ha-yom ha-zeh* does not guarantee uninterrupted continuity.

### Sham Significance

The *Gemara* offers a response: *hacha chtiv sham* — in the verse about the *aron*'s poles, it says *va-yihyu **sham** ad ha-yom hazeh*, with the word *sham* — "there." The counter-example regarding the Jebusites and *benei Binyamin* lacks this word. The word *sham*, it is argued, implies continuity of presence — they remained precisely there, without displacement. However, this distinction is itself then challenged. The verse about the five hundred men of Binyamin who went to Har Seir and struck the remnant of Amalek similarly concludes *va-yeshvu **sham** ad ha-yom hazeh* — yet after Sancheiriv came and displaced all the nations (*va-asir gevulot amim*), they certainly were no longer there. Thus *sham* does not in fact guarantee permanence. *Tyuvta* — the challenge stands, and the support from this verse is withdrawn.

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's position that the *aron* is buried in place may still be correct, but it can no longer be derived from this verse.

### Chamber of Wood

Rav Nachman introduces a fourth position: the *chachamim* say that the *aron* was hidden in the *lishkat dir ha'etzim* — the chamber of wood, where timber was stored for the *mizbe'ach*. It was concealed beneath the floor of that chamber, not beneath the *kodesh kodashim* and not carried into exile.

### Priest's Discovery

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that the *Mishna* of *Shekalim* — studied before *Yoma* — actually corroborates this. A certain *kohen* was going about his business in that chamber and noticed that a section of the floor looked different from the others — Rashi explains that one tile was slightly raised, suggesting the ground had been disturbed. He went to tell his companion what he had found, but *velo hispik ligmor et hadavar* — he was not able to finish saying what it was before *ad sheyatza nishmato* — his soul departed. They thereby knew definitively that the *aron* was concealed in the *lishkat ha'etzim*.

### Wormy Wood Account

A *tanna devei Rabbi Yishmael* gives an alternative, more elaborate account. Two *kohanim* with physical blemishes — who were therefore unfit for the *avodah* — were assigned the task of removing wormy wood from the chamber's stores, going through the timber piece by piece. The axe of one of them slipped and fell — and a fire emerged from beneath the floor and consumed it. From this, too, it was known that the *aron* was hidden there — an event not unlike, as one might observe, the Indiana Jones motif of lethal sacred discovery.

---

## Poles & Parochet

### Seen/Not Seen

Rav Yehuda points out a textual contradiction. One verse states *va-yir'u rashei ha-badim* — the tops of the poles were seen. Another states *ve-lo yera'u ha-chutzah* — they were not seen outside. How can both be true? The resolution: *nirin ve'ein nirin* — they were seen, yet not fully seen.

### Lengthening Poles

A *baraita* elaborates. One might have thought that *va-yir'u rashei ha-badim* means merely that the poles were visible in their normal position alongside the *aron*. But the *kodesh kodashim* was 20 by 20 *amot*, and the *aron* itself was only two and a half *amot* long. Even with the staves inserted, in their ordinary centered position they would not have reached the front wall or the curtain. Therefore *talmud lomar va-ya'arichu ha-badim* — they were lengthened, meaning they were shifted forward. The *Maharsha* understands this not as a miraculous elongation but as a physical repositioning: the staves were slid through their rings toward the front of the *aron* so that their tips extended toward the entrance curtain. One might then think the staves broke through — but *ve-lo yera'u ha-chutzah* — they were not visible outside. *Ha keitzad?* How then? *Dochkin uvoltin veyotzin ba-parochet* — they pressed against and protruded through the fabric of the *parochet*, creating visible protrusions without actually penetrating to the exterior.

### Poles as Breasts

The *Gemara* describes what this looked like: *ve-nir'in ki-shnei dadei isha* — they appeared like the two breasts of a woman. The supporting verse is from *Shir Hashirim*: *tzror ha-mor dodi li bein shadai yalin* — a bundle of myrrh my beloved is to me; he rests between my breasts.

This imagery is, of course, extraordinary, and it opens the door to what follows. *Shir Hashirim* deploys not merely romantic but deeply erotic language to describe the relationship between *Bnei Yisrael* and God — calling upon the most powerful of human drives, the desire for union and intimacy, and translating it into the encounter between Israel and the Divine. This is not unique in the history of religious literature — mystical and erotic poetry intersect in various Eastern traditions and in Sufi Islam — but within the Jewish corpus it is *Shir Hashirim* that carries this freight most explicitly, and it is the imagery of that work that now begins to animate the *Gemara*'s description of the *aron* and the *kodesh kodashim*.

The connections are striking. The word *mor* — myrrh — is an ingredient of the *ketoret*, the incense. The *ketoret* was placed between the *badim* — the poles of the *aron*. *Bein shadai yalin* — he rests between my breasts — maps almost precisely onto this act. The *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur* enters the innermost chamber bearing the *ketoret* and places it *bein ha-badim*. The language *heviani ha-melech chadarav* — the king has brought me into his chambers — resonates with the *kohen gadol*'s entry, and notably, the chamber-word *cheder* was already invoked earlier when the *Gemara* read *hadarah* as *chadarah* to identify what the Babylonians took from the innermost room. Even the technical legal term for unauthorized entry into the *kodesh kodashim* — *bi'ah reikanit*, an empty entry — uses the word *bi'ah*, which is also the biblical term for conjugal union. The erotic register is not incidental; it is structurally embedded in the *Gemara*'s entire treatment of the *kodesh kodashim*.

What is also notable is the gender inversion in these passages. In most of *Shir Hashirim* and in most rabbinic metaphor, God is the man and *Bnei Yisrael* is the woman. Here, God becomes the beloved — the one entered, the one approached — the *aron* protruding like breasts through the curtain. The *kohen gadol* approaches. The imagery is of the most intimate penetration of the innermost, and the *Gemara* presents this not as scandal but as the ultimate expression of sacred relationship.

---

## Keruvim & Erotica

### Exposing Keruvim

Rav Ketina teaches: *be-sha'ah she-Yisrael olim la-regel, megalin lahem et ha-parochet* — when Israel would go up for the pilgrimage festivals, they would draw back the *parochet*. Even though the people were not permitted inside the *heichal*, the gates of the *heichal* and the *azarah* were aligned, so that with the curtains of each successive doorway drawn aside, one could see straight into the *kodesh kodashim* from the *azarah*.

### Keruvim Intertwined

What they were shown was this: *umar'im lahem et ha-kruvim she-hayu me'urim zeh ba-zeh* — they were shown the *keruvim* intertwined with one another. The *keruvim* — the two angelic or human forms atop the *aron* — were not standing apart. Miraculously, they were found intertwined, like lovers. The pilgrims were told: *re'u chibatchem lifnei ha-Makom ke-chibat zachar u-nekevah* — see how beloved you are before God, like the love between male and female. The phrase *zachar u-nekevah* — male and female — is notably more physical and corporeal than the softer *ish ve-ishah*, and the imagery is unmistakably erotic.

### Maturation & Exposure

A question immediately arises: is not this exposure itself a violation of the essential privacy of what takes place in the *kodesh kodashim*? Is not the entire point that the most intimate occurs in the most concealed space? How can the very intimacy be put on display?

### Bride Metaphor

Rav Chisda raises a related challenge. The *Torah* states *ve-lo yavo'u lir'os ke-vala et ha-kodesh* — they shall not come to see as the holy is being swallowed up, referring to the prohibition against the *Levi'im* witnessing the sacred vessels being wrapped before transit. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains this as applying when the vessels were being placed into their protective coverings. If such extreme privacy applied in the *Mishkan*, how can the *Gemara* describe public exposure of the *keruvim*?

Rav Nachman answers with a *mashal*: it is like a bride. *Kol zeman she-hi be-veit aviha, tzenu'ah mi-ba'alah* — as long as she is in her father's house, even after *kiddushin*, she maintains modesty with her husband. *Keivan she-ba'ah le-veit chamiah, einah tzenu'ah mi-ba'alah* — once she enters the domain of her father-in-law's household, at the stage of *nisu'in*, she no longer maintains that same modesty with her husband.

The application: in the time of the *Mishkan*, *Bnei Yisrael* and God had just been married. The relationship was new, and God — here cast explicitly as the woman — required privacy, as a new bride would. Hence the prohibition on viewing the vessels. By the time of the *Beis Hamikdash*, they had been living together for centuries. The relationship had matured, and it was now appropriate, on occasion, to draw back the curtain and allow the people to witness the intimacy of God's love for them.

There is an additional dimension worth noting in the *mashal*. The phrase *veit chamiah* — the father-in-law's house — carries the implication that *God* is now entering *our* domain, *our* land, *our* *Har Habayit*. In an ancient patriarchal framework, the wife moves to the husband's family home. If God is the wife and *Bnei Yisrael* is the husband, then God's *Shekhinah* dwelling on *Har Habayit* is God moving into our land, our home — making the *Mikdash* less the exclusive domain of the Divine and more a shared space in which *Bnei Yisrael* are *ba'al ha-bayis*. This sociological dimension is genuinely empowering, even as it operates within a patriarchal symbolic framework.

### Divorce & Remarriage

A student raises the question: what about the episode of the *kohen* who died upon discovering the *aron*'s location in the *lishkat ha'etzim*? If the mature relationship permits exposure, why was he struck down?

Rav Nachman's answer: *nisgarsha kamart?* — you are speaking of after the divorce. *Nisgarsha chazru le-chibasan ha-rishonah* — after a divorce and remarriage, the relationship reverts to its initial stage. After the *Churban Bayis Rishon*, the relationship was sundered. The *Bayis Sheni* represents a remarriage — a new beginning — and therefore the early-stage modesty returns. The *kohen* in the *Bayis Sheni* who came upon the hidden *aron* was approaching the most intimate space at a time when privacy had been re-established. The fire was not merely a protection of a physical secret; it was the restoration of appropriate sacred boundaries.

---

## Wall Carvings

### Keruvim Images

The *Gemara* now asks a structural question. The discussion of the poles protruding through the *parochet* and the *keruvim* intertwined — to which *Beis Hamikdash* does each refer? If it is the *Bayis Rishon*, there was no *parochet* in the same sense — there was a wall, though the doorway did have a hanging curtain. If it is the *Bayis Sheni*, there were no *keruvim* — the actual statues of the *keruvim* rested atop the *aron*, and the *aron* was absent from the *Bayis Sheni*.

The *Gemara* resolves this through a series of distinctions. Rav Zeira in the name of Rav reports that there were thirteen *parochos* in the *Mikdash*: seven corresponding to the seven gates of the *azarah*, one at the entrance to the *heichal*, one at the entrance to the *ulam*, two at the *dvir* — the inner wall of the *kodesh kodashim* — arranged with openings facing in opposite directions, and two more on the upper story of the *kodesh kodashim*, used for entry when maintenance work was needed above. The point is that even in the *Bayis Rishon*, where the *kodesh kodashim* was sealed by a wall, the doorway in that wall was hung with a curtain — which is where the poles would have protruded.

### Carved Decorations

Rav Acha bar Yaakov then argues that the discussion of the *keruvim* being shown to the pilgrims refers to the *Bayis Sheni*, where actual *keruvim* statues were absent — but where images of *keruvim* were present. He cites the verse: *ve-es kol kiros ha-bayis misav pituhe miklayos kruvim ve-simaros u-feturei tzitzim ve-tzipa zahav miyashar al ha-michuka* — all the walls of the house were covered with engraved braided carvings of *keruvim*, palm trees, and open flowers, and gold was inlaid into the carvings. So even in the *Bayis Sheni*, these carved images lined the inner walls.

### Man Intertwined

The verse continues, and Rabba bar Shila interprets the phrase *ke-ma'ar ish ve-livya* as *ke-ish ha-me'urav be-livyah shelo* — like a man intertwined with his consort. Even the carved *keruvim* on the walls depicted them in an embrace. Thus even in the *Bayis Sheni*, pilgrims could be shown these images and told: see how beloved you are before God.

### Desecration

Reish Lakish provides the tragic counterpoint. When the non-Jews entered the *heichal* — in the context of the *Bayis Sheni*'s destruction — they saw the *keruvim* intertwined, *me'uravim zeh ba-zeh*. They took them out into the marketplace — *hotziu'um la-shuk*. They transported what was most interior, most private, most sacred into the most public and commercial of spaces.

### Loss of Reverence

And they said: *Yisrael hallalu she-birchasam bracha ve-kilalasam klala — ya'asku bi-dvarim hallalu?* — this Jewish people, whose blessings are genuine blessings and whose curses are genuine curses — they should be engaging in *these* things, with sexuality in the *kodesh kodashim*? *Miyad hizilum* — immediately they denigrated them.

### Intimacy vs. Defilement

The proof text is from *Eikhah*: *kol mechabdeha hizziluha ki ra'u ervatah* — all who honored her have made her contemptible, because they saw her nakedness. The citation from *Eikhah* may point toward the destruction of the *Bayis Rishon*, in which context the actual *keruvim* statues atop the *aron* would have been the objects removed — a possibility more viscerally disturbing, and perhaps even more powerful as an image of desecration.

The final irony is profound. Sexual intimacy between husband and wife can be the most powerful, the most holy, and the most sacred of human experiences — but removed from its context, exposed in the marketplace, stripped of relationship and meaning, it becomes pornographic. The *keruvim*' embrace in the *kodesh kodashim*, within the living relationship between *Bnei Yisrael* and God, was the most exalted expression of that love. Taken out by those who had no part in that relationship, no framework for understanding it, and carried into the *shuk*, it was immediately reduced to scandal and used as a pretext for contempt.

The *Gemara* thus ends with a powerful contrast: all of the elaborate procedures that govern entry into the innermost chambers — the *kohen gadol*, the *Yom Kippur* service, the curtains and the incense and the walking backwards — all of it exists to protect and sanctify that innermost moment of union. The *churban* did not merely destroy the *Mikdash*; it violated the most intimate of sacred spaces and dragged its contents into the marketplace. *Kol mechabdeha hizziluha ki ra'u ervatah.*

We will pick up from here tomorrow.

---

---

# Yoma 55

## Keruvim & Jewish Art

### Keruvim Imagery

The daf we take up today picks up in the middle of 54b. The preceding *gemara* dealt with the remarkable imagery of the *keruvim* in the Holy of Holies — their intimate, even erotic dimension — and the significance of the *Kohen Gadol*'s entry into the innermost chamber. The *gemara* quoted from *Shir HaShirim*: *tzror ha-mor dodi li bein shadai yalin* — powerful imagery of God and Israel in the closest of embraces. The *gemara* also drew on the phrase *hevi'ani ha-melech chadarav* and reflected on the very word *bi'ah* — entry — as applied to the placing of the incense between the *badim*. All of this points to the charged, intimate quality of the *avodah* in the *kodesh kodashim*.

What makes this imagery so striking is precisely its hiddenness. The *kohen gadol* alone, once a year on *Yom Kippur*, was privileged to enter — and yet, as the *gemara* noted, on the *regalim* there was a certain revealing of the *keruvim* to *Bnei Yisrael*. The *gemara* also explored how this imagery can be misunderstood when taken out of context, when the sacred is brought into the *shuk* and degraded.

### Machzor Illustrations

Before moving on, there is an important *Tosafot* on 54a — the *Tosafot* beginning *keruvim detzurta* — that uses the *gemara*'s discussion of the *keruvim* engravings in the *Beit Sheni* as a launching point for a broader discussion of Jewish art. The *Tosafot* records a *shaylah* he received: *nishalti al otam she-metzayrim ba-machzorim tziyurat chayot ve-ofot* — I was asked about those who draw images of animals and birds in *machzorim*. Anyone who has visited a Jewish museum or browsed illuminated medieval *machzorim* knows exactly what this refers to: pastoral scenes, fantastical creatures, often deliberately altered in some way to address these very concerns.

The *Ba'al Tosafot* responds: *ilu vadai lo yafeh osim* — they are certainly not acting properly. But his reason is not a technical prohibition; it is *she-mitoch she-mistaklin ba-tziyurim ha-lalu ein mekavnim libam la-Avinu she-ba-shamayim* — because people spend time looking at the pictures and fail to direct their hearts to their Father in Heaven. They are distracted from *davening*.

### Lo Ta'aseh Pesel

He then clarifies: *ein kan issur de-lo ta'aseh lekha fesel* — this does not constitute a violation of the biblical prohibition of making a graven image. He explains that most of the images we see were made by non-Jews, and furthermore, *ve-afilu chashda leika* — there is not even a concern of being suspected of idol worship. Why not? *Lekka ba-tziyurim she-hani mi-nitzva'im be-alma, ve-ein ba-hem mamashut klal* — these are mere colors, mere pigment on a page; they have no physical substance. The concern of *chashda*, of appearing to worship an image, applies only to *chotam bolet* — something that is engraved or protrudes in three dimensions, not to flat illustration.

*Tosafot* proceeds through a full analysis of what types of images might be problematic under *lo ta'aseh lekha fesel*, including the *gemara*'s expansion of that category to figures representing human forms or celestial bodies, and separately, when even the mere possession of an object raises suspicion of worship. This *Tosafot* is essential reading for any *halachic* discussion of Jewish art. The short version: the gravest concerns are confined to three-dimensional figures, not to two-dimensional illustration — and certainly not to photography, which by nearly all opinions falls outside the scope of these prohibitions entirely.

---

## Foundation Creation

### Shitiyah Stone

The *gemara* now identifies the stone at the base of the *kodesh kodashim* as the *Even ha-Shitiyah* — the Foundation Stone. A *tanna* teaches: *shemimmenah hushtat ha-olam* — from it the world was founded. The *gemara* notes that the *mishnah* aligns with the opinion that says *mi-Tzion nivra ha-olam* — the world was created from Zion — since this stone stands in Zion, on *Har ha-Bayit*. It was the first thing created, and everything was built outward from it.

### Sides & Ocean

A *baraita* then records a three-way dispute. Rabbi Eliezer says: *olam me-emtzaito nivra* — the world was created from its middle. The verse cited — *be-tzeket afar la-mutzak u-regavim yedubaku* — suggests something like a core foundation around which the clods of earth coalesced. The world grew outward from a center point.

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees: *olam min ha-tzedadim nivra* — the world was created from the sides, with the snow and rain and the forces of nature converging from multiple directions simultaneously to form the earth. Rashi explains the verse *ki la-sheleg yomar hevei aretz* as God commanding the snow to become land; the various elements came together from the periphery inward.

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha offers a third position: *even yara ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu ba-yam, mimmenah nishtat ha-olam* — God cast a stone into the ocean and from that stone the world was founded. The verse *al mah adaneha hotbe'u, o mi yara even pinatah* — on what were its sockets sunk, who cast the corner stone — supports the image of creation rising from primordial waters. This resonates with *Bereishit* itself, which begins with an undifferentiated ocean that is then separated to allow dry land to emerge, and with ancient cosmological myths of cities and civilizations rising from the sea.

### Zion Creation

Against these naturalistic accounts, the Sages say simply: *mi-Tzion nivra ha-olam* — the world was created from Zion. The proof-text is from *Mizmor le-Asaf*: *mi-Tzion michlal yofi Elohim hofia* — from Zion, the epitome of beauty, God appeared — which the *gemara* reads as *mimenu michlal yofyo shel olam*, from it the beauty of the world was established.

The difference between these positions runs deeper than cosmology. The Sages' view places a spiritual-religious reality — Zion, the connection between heaven and earth, the site of the *Beit HaMikdash* — at the origin of all existence. Everything emanates from a spiritual essence. The other opinions, by contrast, allow nature a measure of independence: earth from earth, heaven from heaven, ocean giving rise to land. The Zion opinion sees creation as suffused with divine purpose from its first moment.

### Generations Dispute

A further *baraita* records the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer ha-Gadol: *eleh toldot ha-shamayim ve-ha-aretz be-hibaram, be-yom asot Hashem Elohim eretz ve-shamayim* — these are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created. He reads this as teaching that *toldot shamayim mi-shamayim nivre'u, toldot ha-aretz me-aretz nivre'u* — the offspring of the heavens, meaning the sun, moon, and stars, emerged from the heavens themselves, while the offspring of the earth — plants, trees, and presumably animals and humans — sprouted from the earth. Rashi develops this in his commentary on *Bereishit*.

Against this, the Sages maintain *elu va-elu mi-Tzion nivre'u* — both heaven-things and earth-things were created from Zion. The same verse from *Mizmor le-Asaf* supports the claim: *diber va-yikra aretz mi-mizrach shemesh ad mevo'o, ve-omer mi-Tzion michlal yofi Elohim hofia* — God called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting, and from Zion, the fullness of beauty, God appeared. Everything originates from that single spiritual center.

---

## Blood Sprinkling

### Sprinkle Procedure

The *gemara* now returns to the *avodah* itself. The *kohen gadol* took the blood from the one who had been stirring it and re-entered the *kodesh kodashim*. The *mishnah* describes the procedure: *ve-hizah mimenu achat le-ma'alah ve-sheva le-matah* — he sprinkled from it once upward and seven times downward. Crucially, *ve-lo hayah mitkavein lehazot lo le-ma'alah ve-lo le-matah* — he did not intend to sprinkle either up or down specifically.

### Kematzlif Motion

What, then, did he do? *Ela kematzlif* — he moved like one lashing. The *gemara* asks *mai kematzlif?* and records that Rav Yehudah demonstrated it physically: *ke-minagda* — like someone administering lashes.

Several dimensions of this comparison deserve unpacking. First, the motion involved: giving lashes is primarily an arm movement rather than a wrist movement. A flick of the wrist alone would not be an effective lash; the force comes from the shoulder and arm. This suggests that the *kohen gadol*'s motion was large and deliberate, not a mere finger-snap. Second, the question of when the release occurs: when administering lashes, the blow lands at the end of the downward arc. If the sprinkling follows the same logic, the blood is released at the lowest point of the motion.

Rashi elaborates: *ke-matah ba-retzu'ah she-machil min ha-ksafayim u-makkeh ve-holekh le-matah* — like striking with a strap, beginning from the shoulders and moving sequentially downward, hitting in a line. This suggests a deliberate, sequential, linear motion. *Tosafot* in *Zevachim*, by contrast, seems to indicate a less targeted motion — more consistent with the *mishnah*'s statement that he was not aiming up or down specifically. The precise mechanics remain somewhat unclear.

### Not Hitting Kapporet

A *tanna* then provides an important clarification: *kshehu mazeh eino mazeh al ha-kapporet ela keneged ovyah shel ha-kapporet* — when he sprinkles, he does not sprinkle onto the *kapporet* itself, but rather opposite its thickness. None of the blood actually strikes the *kapporet*. *Keneged ovyah* — opposite its thickness — means in front of the side face of the lid, not on its upper surface.

To understand this spatially: if the *aron* is oriented west-to-east, with the *kohen gadol* entering from the east and facing west, then *al pnei ha-kapporet kedmah* — on the face of the *kapporet* eastward — refers to the eastern-facing thickness of the lid. *Li-fnei ha-kapporet* — in front of the *kapporet* — means the seven downward sprinklings are done in front of it, not touching it. The *tanna* goes further: even the one upward sprinkling does not strike the surface; it goes past it.

### Rashi vs Chananel

The *tanna* adds a further detail: *kshehu mazeh le-ma'alah, mitzadeid yado le-matah* — when he sprinkles upward, he angles his hand downward; *kshehu mazeh le-matah, mitzadeid yado le-ma'alah* — when he sprinkles downward, he angles his hand upward.

Rashi and Rabbeinu Chananel dispute what this means. Rashi understands *mitzadeid yado le-matah* as the back of the hand facing downward — so for the upward sprinkling, the hand is oriented with the back facing down, in an underhand or somewhat awkward position. For the downward sprinkling, the back of the hand faces up. Rabbeinu Chananel reads it precisely the opposite way: *mitzadeid yado le-matah* means the palm faces downward. For the upward sprinkling, the palm is down, the fingers point upward, and the blood is flicked upward — a natural and easy motion. For the downward sprinkling, the palm faces upward and the fingers point down, which is indeed physically more awkward.

Rabbeinu Chananel also clarifies the spatial orientation: the upward sprinkling travels higher than the *kapporet* and then falls to the ground; the downward sprinklings are directed at the level of the *kapporet*'s thickness — what the *Yerushalmi* calls its *mitzcha*, its forehead — and then fall to the ground as well. One reason suggested by the *mefarshim* for the palm-upward position for downward sprinklings is that with the palm facing down, the blood would run back into the sleeve.

---

## Torah Redundancy

### Repetition Question

The *gemara* now undertakes a hermeneutic analysis of the relevant *pesukim*. By the *par*, the *Torah* says: *ve-lakach midam ha-par ve-hizah be-etzba'o al pnei ha-kapporet kedmah* — he shall take from the blood of the ox and sprinkle with his finger upon the face of the *kapporet* eastward — and then: *ve-lifnei ha-kapporet yazeh sheva pe'amim min ha-dam be-etzba'o* — and before the *kapporet* he shall sprinkle seven times. So the *par*: one *al*, seven *lifnei*.

By the *se'ir*, the *Torah* says: *ve-asah et damo ka'asher asah le-dam ha-par* — he shall do with its blood as he did with the blood of the ox — and then repeats: *ve-hizah oto al ha-kapporet ve-lifnei ha-kapporet*. Since the *Torah* already established the equation *ka'asher asah le-dam ha-par*, why does it need to say it again explicitly? That repetition demands interpretation.

### Before Not On

Rav Chisda's approach, as cited by Rav Acha bar Yaakov: the repetition is *le-akushei al ve-lifnei* — to link the word *al* (on) with the word *lifnei* (in front of). The logic: *mah lifnei de-lav al, af al de-lav al* — just as *lifnei* does not literally mean "on" (since you sprinkle in front of, not onto, the *kapporet*), so too *al* does not literally mean "on." Everything is done in front of, not on. The phrase *al ha-kapporet* in this context means in the presence of, or opposite, the *kapporet* — not directly upon it.

This is a striking interpretive move. The *Torah* uses the word *al*, which naturally means "on," but the repetition of the verse by the *se'ir* — after the equation has already been established — teaches us that *al* here carries the meaning of *lifnei*.

### Which Redundancy

The *gemara* challenges this: one could argue the opposite. Perhaps the *al* by the *par* is the extra element, since once the *se'ir* is linked to the *par*, you could have learned the upward sprinkling from the *se'ir* retrospectively. If *al* is the extra phrase, then *al* teaches the literal meaning — everything is done *al*, actually on the *kapporet*, including the seven *lifnei* sprinklings. On this reading, even *lifnei* means *al*.

The *gemara* resolves this with *hai mai* — what kind of a question is that? If the seven *lifnei* by the *se'ir* is what is extra — used to teach the principle that nothing is literally *al* — then the *al* by the *par*, which is also extra once the equation is established, has a use: it serves as the basis for the *binyan av* taught in the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, that *al pnei ha-kapporet kedmah* establishes a general principle: wherever *panim* appears, it means eastward. That *pasuk* has independent work to do.

But if instead we say the *al* by the *par* is the extra element, teaching that everything literally means *al*, then the *lifnei* by the *se'ir* would be entirely superfluous — there would be nothing to do with it. Since this reading leaves a *pasuk* without any function, it cannot be correct. Therefore the first reading stands: the *lifnei* by the *se'ir* is the extra element, and it teaches that *al* does not mean literally "on." The *al* by the *par* carries a separate lesson about *panim* meaning east. The upshot: one sprinkling upward and seven downward, none of them actually touching the *kapporet*.

---

## Quantity Derivation

### Below Seven

The *gemara* now works through a careful logical derivation of the quantities for both *par* and *se'ir*. A *baraita* spells out the reasoning step by step.

By the *se'ir*, the *Torah* says *ve-hizah oto al ha-kapporet ve-lifnei ha-kapporet* — from *oto* (literally "it," in the singular) we derive that the *al* above is one. How many below by the *se'ir*? That is not stated. The *gemara* proposes a derivation: *ne'emru damim le-matah ba-par ve-ne'emru damim le-matah ba-se'ir* — it says blood below by the *par* and blood below by the *se'ir*; *mah le-matah ba-par sheva, af le-matah ba-se'ir sheva* — just as below by the ox is seven, so too below by the goat is seven.

But one might argue the opposite: *ne'emru damim le-ma'alah ba-se'ir ve-ne'emru damim le-matah ba-se'ir* — the *se'ir* itself says above and below; *mah le-ma'alah ba-se'ir achat, af le-matah ba-se'ir achat* — just as the *se'ir* says one above, maybe it is one below as well. Learn the *se'ir* from itself rather than from the *par*.

The *gemara* says: *nireh le-mi domeh* — let us see which is more comparable. *Danin matah mi-matah ve-ein danin matah mi-ma'alah* — learn below from below, not below from above. So learn the seven from the *par* rather than the one from the *se'ir*'s own upper count.

The counter-argument: *danin gufa mi-gufa ve-ein danin gufa me-alma* — learn a thing from itself, not from elsewhere. Since the *se'ir* itself says one above, learn one below from its own internal evidence, not from the *par*.

This impasse is resolved by the equation *ka'asher asah le-dam ha-par*: *she-ein talmud lomar ka'asher asah, u-mah talmud lomar ka'asher asah? she-yihyu kol asiyotav shavot* — the equation is there to make all the acts equal. *Keshem she-le-matah ba-par sheva kakh le-matah ba-se'ir sheva* — just as below by the ox is seven, so below by the goat is seven.

### Category Principle

Now the corresponding question about above: how many times above by the *par*? The *par* itself does not specify. By parallel reasoning the *gemara* asks: learn it from above by the *se'ir*, which is one — *mah le-ma'alah ba-se'ir achat, af le-ma'alah ba-par achat*. Or learn from within the *par* itself: *mah le-matah ba-par sheva, af le-ma'alah ba-par sheva* — just as the *par* is seven below, perhaps it is seven above as well. Once again both directions of reasoning are valid in isolation.

The counter-argument applies again: *danin gufa mi-gufa* — learn the *par* from itself. And once again the equation resolves it: *keshem she-le-ma'alah ba-se'ir achat, kakh le-ma'alah ba-par achat* — just as above by the goat is one, so above by the ox is one.

### Equivalency Role

The equation *ka'asher asah le-dam ha-par* thus does double work. On the one hand, it establishes that below by the *se'ir* is seven, learned across from below by the *par*. On the other, it establishes that above by the *par* is one, learned across from above by the *se'ir*. The key principle operating throughout is *danin ma'alah mi-ma'alah ve-ein danin ma'alah mi-matah* — above is learned from above, not from below — and *danin matah mi-matah ve-ein danin matah mi-ma'alah* — below from below, not below from above.

Once the equation performs this work, it renders certain other phrases redundant: the explicit mention of *al ha-kapporet* by the *se'ir* (since the one above can be derived from the equation) and the explicit mention of *ve-lifnei ha-kapporet* likewise (since the seven below can be derived from the equation). These newly redundant elements then carry the interpretive lesson: *lifnei* does not mean literally *al*, and therefore *al* itself does not mean literally *al*. The full picture — one above, seven below, nothing touching the *kapporet* — is now established through the interplay of the equation and the redundancies it creates.

---

## Counting Order

### Meir vs Yehudah

With the quantities established, the *gemara* turns to how the *kohen gadol* counted aloud. A *baraita* cites two positions. Rabbi Meir says the count is: *achat, achat ve-achat, achat u-shtayim, achat ve-shalosh, achat ve-arba, achat ve-chamesh, achat ve-shesh, achat ve-sheva* — one; one and one; one and two; one and three... up to one and seven. Rabbi Yehudah says: *achat, achat ve-achat, shtayim ve-achat, shalosh ve-achat, arba ve-achat, chamesh ve-achat, shesh ve-achat, sheva ve-achat* — one; one and one; two and one; three and one... seven and one.

### No Disagreement

The *gemara* resolves: *ve-lo plugi* — they do not actually disagree. *Mar ke-asrei u-mar ke-asrei* — each follows his own regional counting convention. The difference is simply whether one says "twenty-one" or "one and twenty" — whether the larger number comes first or the current count comes first. Both are valid conventions for keeping track.

### Continuing Count

All opinions agree, however, on one crucial point: *ha-haza'ah ha-rishonah tzrikhah minyan im kol achat ve-achat* — the first sprinkling must be counted continuously together with each of the seven. That is, even after completing the one upward *haza'ah*, the *kohen gadol* does not simply begin a separate count of one through seven; he incorporates the first into each subsequent count.

Rabbi Elazar gives one reason: *she-lo yiteh ba-haza'ot* — so that he should not err among the sprinklings. Rashi understands this differently: *she-yehei lo shehut bein-tayim latet libo le-minyan she-lo yiteh* — by reciting the longer count each time, he is slowed down and must give deliberate attention to the number. This prevents careless rushing. One might have thought the purpose was to ensure the first *haza'ah* is not accidentally counted as one of the seven — but Rashi does not seem to be saying that; rather, it is purely a matter of deliberateness and care.

### Verb Repetition

Rabbi Yochanan derives this requirement from the *pasuk* itself: *ve-lifnei ha-kapporet yazeh sheva pe'amim* — the verb *yazeh* (he shall sprinkle) is stated. *She-ein talmud lomar yazeh* — the verb was not necessary; the text could simply have said "seven times." *U-mah talmud lomar yazeh? Le-lamed al ha-haza'ah ha-rishonah she-tzrikhah minyan im kol achat ve-achat* — the repetition of the verb teaches that the original *haza'ah* must continue to be enumerated alongside each of the seven. On Rabbi Yochanan's reading, this is not merely a pragmatic safeguard but a requirement derived directly from the *pasuk*.

### Counting Difference

What is the practical difference between Rabbi Elazar's explanation and Rabbi Yochanan's? *Ika beinaihu de-lo manah ve-lo ta'ah* — the case where he did not count and yet did not make a mistake. According to Rabbi Elazar, the counting is a secondary concern — a precaution against error — so if in fact no error occurred, the *avodah* is valid even without the explicit count. According to Rabbi Yochanan, counting together with the first is a positive requirement derived from the *pasuk* itself, so failure to count is a deficiency regardless of whether a mistake was made.

---

## Single Pedestal

### Yehudah Confusion

After the sprinkling in the *kodesh kodashim*, the *kohen gadol* exits and places the blood on the pedestal (*kan*) in the *heikhal*. The *gemara* now raises a *mishnah* from elsewhere: Rabbi Yehudah says *lo hayah sham ella kan achat bilvad* — there was only one pedestal, used for both the blood of the *par* and the blood of the *se'ir*. Why not two? Because *mishum de-mekhalfei* — they would get confused and might pick up the wrong bowl, not knowing which is the ox's and which is the goat's.

### Challenge Writing

The *gemara* challenges: why not simply have two pedestals and write on each one — this is the *par*, this is the *se'ir*? The answer: *Rabbi Yehudah leit lei kesivah* — Rabbi Yehudah does not believe that writing alone can be trusted to prevent confusion in practice. People will not reliably pay attention to written labels, especially under the pressure and intensity of the *avodah*.

But this raises an immediate difficulty. If Rabbi Yehudah does not trust writing, how does he account for the *thirteen shofarot* in the *Beit HaMikdash* — each designated for a different purpose by means of writing? Surely they were distinguished by their inscriptions. And yet we find that Rabbi Yehudah himself describes those inscriptions as the means of differentiation.

### Thirteen Shofarot

A *baraita* lists the thirteen *shofarot* and their designations. *Taklin chadatin* — new shekels (the current year's contribution); *taklin atikin* — old shekels, for one who had not paid the previous year; *kinim* — bird sacrifices of the *tor* (pigeon variety); *gozlei olah* — *bnei yonah* (turtledove variety); *etzim* — donations for wood for the altar; *levonah* — donations of incense (notably, one can make a private *nedavah* of incense, which is burned on the outer *mizbeach* — a remarkable *chiddush*, since there is no explicit *Torah* source for private incense donations, and it results in incense being offered in three distinct locations: the daily service on the gold altar in the *heikhal*, the *Yom Kippur* service in the *kodesh kodashim*, and this private donation on the outer altar); *zahav la-kapporet* — gold donations for the Temple vessels (Rashi: *klei shareit*); and six *shofarot* for general *nedavah*, into which surplus funds were eventually channeled. That accounts for all thirteen. Rabbi Yehudah describes the inscriptions on each.

This creates the difficulty: Rabbi Yehudah himself says the thirteen *shofarot* were distinguished by writing. He clearly accepts written designations as effective in that context. Why, then, does he not accept writing as sufficient to distinguish between the *par* blood and the *se'ir* blood, or between the obligatory and voluntary bird funds? The resolution to this tension will be taken up in the next session.

---

## Bird Sacrifices

### Dead Owner Decree

When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported: *amri be-ma'arava, gezeirah mishum chatas she-meitu ba'aleha* — they said in *Eretz Yisrael* that the absence of a separate *shofar* for obligatory bird funds is a rabbinic decree, on account of the *chatat* whose owner has died. The concern is as follows: if money from an obligatory bird fund — which is composed of half *chatat* and half *olah* contributions — becomes mixed with the general voluntary bird fund, and in the interim the owner of one of those *chatat* contributions dies, then birds will be purchased and brought with funds belonging to a *chatat* whose owner is no longer alive. This is prohibited. Rather than risk such an outcome, the Rabbis decreed that no separate *shofar* should be maintained for obligatory bird contributions at all. The precise implications of this decree will be explored further in the following session.

---

---

# Yoma 56

## Mixed Money Concern

### Dead Owner Problem

Today's *daf* is 56, and we pick up in the middle of 55b. The *Gemara* was trying to figure out why Rabbi Yehuda required only one pedestal rather than two. The first suggestion was that he did not trust labeling — that people fail to pay attention to writing — and that this concern was reflected in his position regarding the separate *shofrot* in the *Beis Hamikdash* for obligatory bird offerings, which are divided between *chatas* and *olah*, and those that are pure *nidavah*, which are entirely *olah*. The concern was about mixtures.

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he offered a different explanation: *gezeira mishum chatas shemesu ba'aleha* — the concern is not about confusing the free-will money with the obligatory money, but specifically about a *chatas* whose owner has died. The underlying problem is that someone may contribute money for an obligatory *chatas* and then die before the sacrifice is brought. Even if this happens on the same day, if by the time the money is used the owner has died, the *korban* would be invalid. The "mixture" is not a mixture of two different designations, but rather a mixture within the pool of *chatas* money — some of it potentially belonging to a person who has since died.

### Overseas Sacrifice

This prompts an immediate objection: *umi chaishinan*? Are we really concerned about this? The *Mishnah* teaches that *hasholeach chatato mimedinat hayam* — one who sends his *chatas* from overseas — *makrivin oto be-chezkat she-hu kayam*: the sacrifice is brought on the presumption that the owner is still alive. That is precisely the same scenario. The person is not present, the sacrifice is brought in his absence, and we rely on the *chazaka* that someone alive when the money was given is presumed to still be alive. Why should placing money in a box and walking away be any different? Rabbi Yehuda presumably does not dispute the ruling about the overseas *chatas*.

### Definite Contamination

The *Gemara* resolves this: *ela mishum chatas shemesu ba'aleha vadai* — the concern is not merely that the owner *might* have died, but that he *definitely* has died. Under ordinary circumstances, the principle of *chazaka* applies: if someone was alive when the money was deposited, we assume he remains alive, and the money may be used. But consider the following scenario: money is deposited throughout the day, and then word reaches the *Beis Hamikdash* that one of the contributors died that very day. Now the priests know with certainty that somewhere in that box is money that cannot be used. The problem is that they cannot identify which specific coins came from the deceased. The money is irretrievably mixed together, and this is the *ta'aroves* — the mixture — that creates the problem. Because such a scenario will occasionally arise, the practice of collecting money and using it without the contributor present was avoided entirely.

This is plainly distinct from the case of the overseas *chatas*, where there is no mixing — a single person sent a specific animal or specific funds, and nothing is intermingled with anyone else's contribution.

### Remove Money Solution

The *Gemara* then proposes a seemingly elegant solution: *v'nivror arba'a zuzei v'nishdi b'maya v'hanach mishtarin* — take four *zuz* (Rashi calculates this as roughly the average cost of a bird offering), remove that amount from the box, throw it into the ocean, and let the remainder be permissible. The idea is to simply remove from the pool an amount equivalent to the invalid contribution and declare the rest usable.

This is a striking suggestion. It would be analogous to saying: if some *treif* product is mixed into a pot, simply take a spoonful out and assume that was the *treif* portion. This is not how *kashrus* works. The underlying logic the *Gemara* may be reaching toward is that the money should in principle be *batel b'rov* — nullified within the majority — and perhaps we are only dealing with a rabbinic stringency that blocks that nullification. In situations where *bitul* ought to apply in principle but is blocked by stringency, the *Gemara* elsewhere sometimes permits the reasoning known as *she-ani omer* — "I can claim" — to achieve a similar result. For instance, if two boxes (one of *terumah* and one of *chulin*) fall into two larger containers (also one *terumah* and one *chulin*), and one cannot tell which box fell into which, the *Gemara* permits assuming the *chulin* fell into the *chulin* and the *terumah* into the *terumah* — reasoning that since *bitul* would have applied anyway given the rabbinic nature of the prohibition, we can allow ourselves to make favorable assumptions. The *Gemara* here may be suggesting something similar: in principle the money should be *batel*, and taking out a fixed sum and assuming it was the invalid portion functions as a kind of *she-ani omer*.

### Bittul Question

The reason this solution fails for Rabbi Yehuda is then given: *leis lei breira* — Rabbi Yehuda does not hold of *breira*. The *Gemara* will explain exactly what *breira* is and why its absence blocks this approach. But it is worth noting at this stage that the solution being proposed — taking four *zuz* and assuming they are the ones that must be removed — is actually not quite *breira* in the classical sense, a distinction the *Gemara* will return to.

---

## Breira Concept

### R. Yehuda & Breira

The *Gemara* now asks: *minalan*? How do we know that Rabbi Yehuda does not hold of *breira*? Before examining the proofs, it is worth establishing clearly what *breira* means. *Breira* is not the same as the quasi-magical *she-ani omer* maneuver just discussed. *Breira* is rather the concept that something undefined in the present can have its identity retroactively determined by what happens later. There is a certain deterministic or retrospective quality to it: something that is indeterminate now becomes determinate through a future event, and that future event is then treated as if it had already determined the matter from the beginning.

### Wine Separation Case

The proof is sought from a *Mishnah*: *haloke'ach yayin mibein hakutim* — one who purchases wine from Samaritans. Samaritans are assumed to have taken *terumah* and *maaser* for their own consumption, but they cannot be trusted to have done so on behalf of others. If someone purchases wine from them at *bein hashmashos* on *erev Shabbos* — just as it is becoming dark — what is to be done? One cannot separate *terumah* and *maaser* on *Shabbos*, but the wine cannot be drunk without those separations having been made.

### Wine Process Detail

The *Mishnah* records that Rabbi Meir permits the following procedure: one stands and declares, *shnei lugin she-ani asid le-hafrish harei hein trumah* — "the two *log* that I will separate [after *Shabbos*] shall be *trumah* from this moment." Similarly, one designates ten *log* as *maaser rishon* and nine as *maaser sheini*, all defined by reference to whatever amounts one will actually set aside after *Shabbos*. To make the arithmetic clear: if one has 102 *log* of wine, two *log* become *trumah*, leaving 100. Ten of those become *maaser rishon*, leaving 90. Nine of those — ten percent of the remaining 90 — become *maaser sheini*.

This declaration is made before *Shabbos* sets in, and then one may drink from the wine on *Shabbos* without concern, because whatever one drinks will not be the portion one will later designate. The portions one will later set aside are already deemed to have been the *trumah* and *maaser* from the moment of the original declaration. One then *u-meichal ve-shoseh mi-yad* — immediately goes ahead and drinks. Rashi interprets *meichal* as *mechaleil* — redeeming the *maaser sheini* onto a coin — while Tosafos reads it as *matchil*, meaning one simply begins drinking right away, since the act of redemption is beside the point at this stage.
