---

# Yoma 58

## Mixing Bloods

### Topic Overview

Today's daf is 58, and we pick up at the very bottom of 57b. The passage begins with the phrase *im dama hapar letoch dam hase'ir* — "if the blood of the ox fell into the blood of the goat" — and our *mishnah* is read as going *keman de'amar me'arvin lekrannot*, like the opinion that holds the bloods are mixed even for the horns.

To appreciate the question at hand, it is worth reviewing the full sequence of the *Yom Kippur* blood service. The *kohen gadol* performs one-and-seven sprinklings inside the *kodesh kodashim* on the *kaporet*, then one-and-seven directed toward the *parochet* — not on the *parochet* itself, though there was a dissenting opinion, but toward it. He then proceeds to the *mizbeach hazahav*, the golden altar, where he applies blood on the four horns and sprinkles seven times on top.

By way of contrast: when the *par he'elam davar shel tzibur* — the ox brought on behalf of the entire community that sinned based on a ruling of the *beis din* — is brought, one does seven sprinklings on the *parochet*, as opposed to the one-and-seven of *Yom Kippur*. This distinction was noted by the *Tosafos Yeshanim*. On *Yom Kippur*, we learn the one-and-seven structure from *vechein ya'aseh le'ohel moed*. And while on the golden altar a standard inner offering would require only the four horns, on *Yom Kippur* one also adds seven sprinklings on top.

### Par He'elam Davar

The scriptural basis for the *Yom Kippur* procedure is the *pasuk* (Vayikra 16): *veshachat es hase'ir vehevi es damo mi'beis laparochet ve'asah es damo ka'asher asah ledam hapar* — "he shall slaughter the goat and bring its blood within the curtain and do with its blood as he did with the blood of the ox." This makes clear that the *par* and the *se'ir* are kept separate: the *se'ir* is even slaughtered after the *par*. The verse *vechein ya'aseh le'ohel moed* then extends the same structure to the *parochet* sprinklings — they too are performed separately, one after the other, just as they were separate inside the *kodesh kodashim*. Although the *gemara* dealt elsewhere with the *be'di'avad* case of their becoming mixed, the *lechatchila* procedure is distinct applications.

The question now turns to the *mizbeach hazahav*. The *pasuk* states: *veyatzah el hamizbeach asher lifnei Hashem vechiper alav velakach midam hapar umidam hase'ir venasan al karnot hamizbeach saviv* — "and he shall go out to the altar that is before God and atone for it, and he shall take from the blood of the ox and from the blood of the goat and place it on the horns of the altar all around." When the *pasuk* subsequently says *vehizah alav min hadam be'etzba'o sheva pe'amim* — "and he shall sprinkle upon it from the blood with his finger seven times" — the language *min hadam*, "from the blood" in the singular, indicates that at the point of the seven sprinklings there is no question: the bloods are combined. But what of the application on the horns? The *pasuk* there says *midam hapar umidam hase'ir* — is that a combined mixture or two separate applications?

### Rav Yoshiya Principle

This is the subject of the debate before us. Our *mishnah* clearly holds they are mixed, but the *gemara* introduces the underlying dispute. It was stated: *Rav Yoshiya veRav Yonasan* — one says *me'arvin*, you mix them, and one says *ein me'arvin*, you do not.

The *gemara* concludes that it is Rav Yoshiya who holds they are mixed, based on a general principle known elsewhere. In questions of scriptural interpretation, Rav Yoshiya maintains: *af al gav delo ksiv yachdav keman dechsiv yachdav dami* — even when the *Torah* does not explicitly write the word *yachdav*, "together," it is treated as if it had. That is, a *vav* conjoining two items establishes a default presumption of combination.

This principle plays out in the famous case of *umakeh aviv ve'imo mos yumos* — "one who strikes his father and his mother shall be put to death." Does this mean one must have struck both, or does striking either one suffice? The *vav* is ambiguous: it can mean "and" (together) or "or" (each separately). Rav Yoshiya holds that the default reading of a *vav* is combination, and when the *Torah* means something separate, it requires additional contextual clues or another *pasuk* to override that default. Thus, when the *pasuk* says *midam hapar umidam hase'ir*, Rav Yoshiya reads that as a combined mixture by default.

### Yoshiya vs. Yonasan

A *baraita* makes the debate explicit. Rav Yoshiya: *v'lakach midam hapar umidam hase'ir — me'uravin*, "they should be mixed." This is simply his standard interpretive position applied here. Then, at the top of 58a, Rav Yonasan says: *lo — mizeh bifnei atzmo umizeh bifnei atzmo* — "no; from this one separately and from that one separately." Exactly as expected: where Rav Yoshiya reads a *vav* as implying combination, Rav Yonasan reads it as indicating two distinct, independent entities.

### Once Argument

The *gemara* then raises the possibility that even Rav Yonasan might agree to mixing in this particular case: *shani hacha d'chsiv achas* — here it is different, because the word *achas*, "once," appears. Where? Rashi explains that this refers to Shemos 30 — the passage in *Tetzaveh* describing the construction of the *mizbeach haktoret*. There it says: *v'chiper aharon al karnosav achas bashana midam chatas hakippurim achas bashana yichaper alav l'doroseichem* — "Aaron shall atone for its horns once in the year, from the blood of the *Yom Kippur* sin-offering, once in the year shall he atone for it throughout your generations." The double use of *achas* — "once" — in proximity to the *mizbeach hazahav* indicates that the atonement is performed as one unified act, which implies that the bloods are combined. This is far more contextually relevant than a verse appearing twenty *pesukim* later in Vayikra, and it makes considerably better sense as the textual basis for the argument.

### Midam Separate

Rav Yoshiya then presses the point in the *baraita*: *halo kvar ne'emar achas* — "has it not already been stated 'once'?" — meaning even according to you, Rav Yonasan, the word *achas* compels combination. Rav Yonasan responds: *halo kvar ne'emar midam hapar umidam hase'ir* — "has it not already been stated 'from the blood of the ox and from the blood of the goat'"? Had the *Torah* intended one mixture, it would have written *midam hapar v'hase'ir* — the *se'ir* appended to the ox. Since it repeats *midam* — "from the blood of" — separately for each, it signals distinct applications. As for *achas*, Rav Yonasan reads it to mean: do not perform each blood's application twice. *Achas v'lo shtayim midam hapar, achas v'lo shtayim midam hase'ir* — "once and not twice from the blood of the ox, once and not twice from the blood of the goat." The "once" limits repetition, not separation.

A second *baraita* then resolves: *v'lakach midam hapar umidam hase'ir — shem'uravin zeh b'zeh*, they are mixed together. Should one ask whether they might be separate, *talmud lomar achas* — the *Torah*'s use of *achas* settles it in favor of combination. The *gemara* notes this *baraita* follows Rav Yoshiya's position, and *Tosafos* observes that the need to derive mixing from *achas* does not necessarily mean the *baraita* rejects Rav Yoshiya's principle about the *vav* — it may simply be adding an additional proof. The upshot is that there are two independent grounds for the combined position: the default reading of a conjunctive *vav*, and the verse's use of *achas* to indicate a single unified act of atonement. Rav Yonasan's dissenting view — that the horns are done with each blood separately, and only the seven sprinklings on top require mixture — nonetheless stands as a legitimate position in the *baraita*.

---

## Mixture Procedure

### Pouring Procedure

Having established the debate over whether the bloods are mixed for the horns, the *mishnah* describes the practical procedure: *nassan es hamalei b'reikan* — "he poured the full one into the empty one." The sequence in the *mishnah* is: *eirev dam hapar l'soch dam hase'ir* — he poured the blood of the ox into the bowl holding the blood of the goat. One might expect the reverse — pouring the smaller quantity into the larger — but the last service performed had been the *se'ir* at the *parochet*, so that is the bowl the *kohen* is already holding. He then retrieves the *par* blood from wherever it was resting and pours it in. The reversal that follows — pouring the combined full bowl back into the now-empty bowl — is simply good mixing technique, like combining two glasses: you pour back and forth to achieve a thorough blend. The bowls must have been of similar capacity to accommodate both volumes simultaneously.

### Vessel in Vessel

Against this background, Rami bar Chama posed a question to Rav Chisda. In an ordinary case — not *Yom Kippur* — if one placed one *mizrak* (receiving bowl) inside another and performed *kabbalas hadam* (collection of the slaughtered blood) with the inner bowl while holding the outer one, what is the *halacha*? Is this a *chatzitzah* — an interposition between the *kohen*'s hand and the bowl he is meant to be holding — or not? Rami bar Chama initially thought the answer might be found in the *mishnah*'s phrase *nassan es hamalei b'reikan*, reading it to mean that one literally placed the full bowl inside the empty bowl and proceeded to carry both to the altar. Rav Chisda corrected him: the *mishnah* simply means that the contents of the full bowl were poured into the empty bowl, not that one bowl was physically nested inside another. Nevertheless, the question itself is worth pursuing.

### Min B'Mino

The precise issue is: *min b'mino chotzetz* — does an object of the same type as what it is obstructing constitute a *chatzitzah*? A bowl inside a bowl is the same category of object. Does that matter? One might argue that when the interposing material is of the same type as the primary object — *min b'mino* — it should not be considered a foreign interruption at all, and thus not a *chatzitzah*.

### Vessel Proof

The *gemara* attempts a proof: *ta shma* — come and hear. If a *kohen* was standing on a vessel during the *avodah* rather than directly on the floor of the *azarah*, the *avodah* is invalid. The *kohen* must stand barefoot on the floor of the *Mikdash*, and similarly his body must be in direct physical contact with the *klei sharet* he is using. The same sanctifying logic that applies to the floor connects through the *kohen*'s body to the vessels. A *kohen* standing on a vessel, or on his companion's foot, has his *avodah* rendered invalid because he is not in direct contact with the floor.

This might seem to prove that *min b'mino chotzetz* — two feet, both body parts, still constitute a *chatzitzah* — but the *gemara* deflects.

### Foot Exception

*Shani regel d'lo matzi mevatel lei* — a foot is different because it cannot be annulled. What does this mean? The concept of *bitul* in the context of *chatzitzah* functions as follows: if one can treat the interposing object as effectively merged with, or part of, the primary object, then it loses its identity as a foreign body and ceases to constitute a *chatzitzah*. Two vessels of the *Mikdash* can in principle be treated as one unified entity — together they are all the same sacred service-ware, and one can conceptually subsume the inner within the outer. But one cannot do this with another person's foot. That foot belongs to someone else, will always be reclaimed, and therefore retains its permanent identity as a separate, foreign object. It can never be *mevatel* — subsumed — into the primary entity, and thus always remains a *chatzitzah* regardless of the *min b'mino* consideration.

### Chatzitzah Concept

This discussion prompts a broader examination of the concept of *chatzitzah*. The *halacha* holds that if one is not *makpid* — not particular — about something resting on one's body, it does not constitute a *chatzitzah*. The clearest application is by *tevilah* in a *mikveh*: a bandage that one wishes to have on one's body is not a *chatzitzah*, even though it physically prevents water from reaching the skin beneath it. Why should the absence of subjective objection remove the legal barrier?

Two conceptual frameworks address this. The first holds that *chatzitzah* requires the object to be identifiable as a foreign body — a thing actively out of place. An object that the person affirmatively wants there lacks that identity; it is not foreign matter, and therefore it is not legally defined as a *chatzitzah* at all, regardless of whether water physically reaches the skin beneath it. The second framework goes in the opposite direction: the object is acknowledged to prevent contact, but when the person does not mind its presence, it becomes *tafel* — secondary, effectively treated as an extension of the body itself. The water therefore reaches "the body," including what has been subsumed into it.

The gap between these two frameworks is considerable. The first approach requires only that the object not be actively defined as foreign; the second requires that it be positively defined as part of the body. Contemporary *halachic* debates about *chatzitzah* often hinge precisely on this divide — for instance, whether a protective ear-plug worn by a woman with an ear infection constitutes a *chatzitzah* during *tevilah*. Rav Ovadia Yosef's basic approach is that since the woman currently needs the plug for medical reasons, it is considered part of her body at this moment. Rav Moshe addresses the question differently, noting that if the plug is coated with a permeable material such that water could theoretically seep through over time, the object cannot be considered a complete barrier, and there are additional grounds for leniency. The underlying principle — that something theoretically permeable is not a *chatzitzah* — will re-emerge momentarily in the *gemara*'s discussion of the *siv*.

Returning to the question of *mevatel lei*: Rashi explains the phrase in the context of the foot as follows: *d'lo mivatlei chaveiro es raglo ad sheyigmor avodaso* — the companion will not surrender his foot for the duration of the service; he will want it back immediately. A foot therefore always retains its character as something separate, which prevents it from ever being subsumed.

### Derech Sheirud

A second version of the question is then presented: some say the issue here is not *chatzitzah* at all — one can assume *min b'mino* is not a *chatzitzah* — but rather *derech sheirus bekach o ein derech sheirus bekach*: is it considered an appropriate manner of service to perform the *avodah* with one vessel nested inside another? This would be a distinct concern, unique to the sanctity of Temple service, separate from the physical question of contact and interposition.

### Two Vessels One Service

The *gemara* resolves both dimensions with a *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *es kol klei hashareis asher yesharsu bam bakodesh* — "all the holy vessels with which they shall serve in the sanctuary." The plural form *bam* — "with them" — is read as authorizing *shnei kelim v'sheirus echad*: two vessels serving as one unit of service. This teaches simultaneously that (a) a vessel within a vessel is not a *chatzitzah*, and (b) it constitutes proper *derech sheirus*. Both concerns are resolved in a single stroke by the scriptural phrase. The *gemara* thus concludes leniently on all fronts.

### Sieve Question

Rami bar Chama then poses a related question to Rav Chisda: *hiniach siv b'soch hamizrak v'kibeil bo es hadam mahu* — if one placed a palm-bast (a coarse porous plant fiber) inside a *mizrak* and collected the blood through it, what is the *halacha*? Unlike the previous case of *min b'mino*, here the *siv* is an entirely different substance — *min beshe'eino mino* — so the question of *chatzitzah* is more acute. On the other hand, the *siv* is porous: if left long enough, the blood will eventually seep through. Is that porousness sufficient to remove its status as a *chatzitzah*, given that right now the blood has not yet penetrated to the vessel itself?

### Porous Materials

Rav Chisda replied that the answer may be found in a *mishnah* concerning *parah adumah*: if a sponge was dropped into the purification water, one cannot use the water absorbed within the sponge, but one can use the water remaining in the vessel around it. Why can one use that surrounding water if some of it sits atop the sponge without touching the vessel floor? The *gemara* answers: *shani maya deklishi* — water is different, being extremely non-viscous; water seeps through porous materials with great ease. The principle of *machalchel* — porousness rendering something not a *chatzitzah* — holds in principle, but the question is one of degree. Blood, being more viscous, may require so long to seep through the *siv* that we would not say it has effectively passed.

A second version of the tradition reports that Rav Chisda did in fact reach a conclusion: for liquids (*bedam kasher*) the *siv* is not a *chatzitzah*, since the liquid will eventually permeate. For solids (*bekometz pasul*) — if one lined the vessel with this fibrous material and placed a handful of a *minchah* upon it — the *siv* would be a valid *chatzitzah*, since a solid will not seep through at all. The ruling thus establishes an important general principle in the laws of *chatzitzah*: a substance that is permeable to liquids, even if the liquid has not yet passed through it at the moment of use, is not considered a *chatzitzah* for liquids. This parallels the reasoning invoked in contemporary discussions of ear plugs and similar cases.

### Tosafos Distinction

*Tosafos* raises a question from a *gemara* in Sukkah that addresses taking a *lulav* through a handkerchief used as a handle. The *gemara* there considers whether this constitutes *lekichah al yedei davar acher* — taking via an intermediary — and whether that might itself be valid as an act of *lekichah*, especially when the handle is fashioned from *lulav* material and thus *min b'mino*. If *lekichah* through an intermediary can be valid, why does the *gemara* here treat vessel-within-vessel as a *chatzitzah* question at all?

*Tosafos* answers by drawing a fundamental distinction. When one uses an outer vessel as a handle and holds the inner one through it, that might indeed be classified as *lekichah al yedei davar acher* — and if the outer vessel functions as a handle, it may be acceptable. But when one grips a vessel such that an intermediary comes between the hand and the intended vessel — not a handle, but an obstruction — the question is one of *chatzitzah*, not merely of defining the act of taking.

More fundamentally, *Tosafos* points to a conceptual divide between *lulav* and *klei sharet*. The obligation by *lulav* derives from *ulekachtem lachem* — "you shall take for yourselves" — which defines a required act. The question is whether taking through a handle still constitutes *lekichah* as an act. But the requirement by *klei sharet*, as the *Ritzba* explains: *gabei klei sharet bechol inyan min beshe'eino mino chotzetz d'nihi dechi avid k'ein beis yad mikrei lekichah* — even if in the *lulav* context taking via a handle might be valid, *gabei klei sharet deksiv v'lakach hakohen*, where the *Torah* requires the *kohen* to take directly, the demand is *be'atzmo shel kohen* — the *kohen*'s own body must be in contact. That is a requirement of direct physical connection, not merely of performing an act of acquisition. The *chatzitzah* concern is therefore far more acute in the realm of Temple service than in the realm of *lulav*, because there the demand is bodily contact itself, not simply the performative definition of taking.

---

## Outer Altar Horns

### Northeast Start

We turn now to the *mishnah*'s account of the application of blood on the golden altar and then the outer altar. The *pasuk* states: *veyatzah el hamizbeach asher lifnei Hashem vechiper alav velakach midam hapar umidam hase'ir venasan al karnot hamizbeach saviv* — "and he shall go out to the altar that is before God, and he shall atone for it, and he shall take from the blood of the ox and from the blood of the goat and place it on the horns of the altar all around." The *mizbeach asher lifnei Hashem* is the *mizbeach hazahav*, the golden altar, as it stands closest to the *kodesh kodashim*.

The *mishnah* describes the procedure: *hitchil mechatei v'yored* — he would begin applying the blood, and his finger would move in a downward motion. The corners are addressed in the sequence: northeast, northwest, southwest, southeast. The *mishnah* then notes: *makom shehu matchil b'chatas al mizbeach hachitzon* — the place where one begins a *chatas* on the outer altar — *misham haya gomer al mizbeach hapnimi* — is where one finishes on the inner altar. On the outer altar one ascends the ramp, turns right (counter-clockwise), and descends; this ends at the southeast corner. Correspondingly, on the inner altar one begins at the northeast and travels counter-clockwise, ending at the southeast. The southeast of the outer altar is thus both the starting point for that service and the finishing point of the inner service.

The reason one does not simply begin at the first corner encountered upon exiting is derived, as the *gemara* will explain, from the word *veyatzah* — one must be fully outside before commencing.

### Rabbi Eliezer Stationary

Rabbi Eliezer holds: *bimkomo haya omed umachatei* — he would stand in place and apply the blood without walking around the altar at all. This is because the golden altar measured only *amah al amah* — one cubit by one cubit — no larger than a single horn of the outer altar. Given its small dimensions, Rabbi Eliezer holds that one can reach all four horns from a single position.

### Direction Variation

Rabbi Eliezer also teaches: *ve'al kulam haya nosein milmatah lemalah chutz mizo shehayta lefanav shehaya nosein mima'alah lematah* — on all the corners he would apply from bottom to top, except for the one directly in front of him, on which he would apply from top to bottom. This directional variation is consistent with the *tana kamma*'s position as well, since the first opinion implicitly requires different handling of the nearest corner.

### Rashi Explanation

Rashi explains the practical reasoning. The golden altar is two *amot* high — approximately three feet — which places the horns above the natural height of one's arm. To reach them, the *kohen* must extend his arm upward at an angle. When reaching corners that are farther away, one can manage the bottom-to-top motion without difficulty. But for the corner directly in front of one's body, if one attempts the same upward motion, the blood will run back down along the finger and into the palm. Therefore, for the nearest corner the *kohen* must reverse direction — applying from the top downward — so that the blood does not run into his hand. Rashi phrases it: *she'im moshcha milmatah lemalah hadam zav letoch beis yado* — "if he drew it from bottom to top, the blood would flow into his palm." This is why the first opinion, which has the *kohen* walking around the altar and standing directly in front of each corner in succession, consistently applies *mechatei veyoreid* — always top-to-bottom — since every corner is the "nearest" one in turn.

### Seven Sprinklings

After completing the application on the four horns, the *kohen* sprinkles seven times on *taharo shel mizbeach* — the "purity" of the altar. This language is borrowed from the *pasuk* in Vayikra: *vetaharo vekidesho mitum'ot benei yisrael* — "and he shall purify it and sanctify it from the impurities of the Children of Israel." The precise location of these seven sprinklings will be discussed on subsequent dapim.

### Base Pouring

The remainder of the blood — *shirei hadam* — is poured at the base of the outer altar. Specifically, it is poured at *yesod hamaaravi shel mizbeach hachitzon* — the western base of the outer altar. This is because after completing the inner service, the *kohen* exits and arrives first at the western side, so the western base is the natural first point of contact. For the blood of the outer altar's own *chatas* service, the remainder is poured at *yesod hadromi* — the southern base — because the *kohen* descending the ramp of the outer altar arrives first at the southern base.

### Blood Disposal

*Elu va'elu mit'arvin ba'amah* — all the bloods, regardless of which base they were poured upon, would eventually merge and flow together through the trough and channel in the floor of the *azarah*, emerging into *nachal Kidron*. There, *venimkarim legananim* — they were sold to gardeners, as the blood was rich in nutrients and served as fertilizer. However, *umo'alin bahem* — until the gardeners actually paid for it, the blood retained its sanctified status and was subject to the prohibition of *me'ilah*. This will be discussed in a future *sugya*.

---

## Vayatzah Exegesis

### Moving Outside

The *gemara* now examines the word *vayatzah* in the *pasuk* *veyatzah el hamizbeach asher lifnei Hashem*. A *baraita* is cited in the name of Rabbi Nechemiah: since we find by the *par ha'elam davar* — the communal ox brought for an inadvertent national sin — that *shehakohen omed chutz lamizbeach umazeh al haparochet besha'ah shehu mazeh* — "the *kohen* stands outside the altar and sprinkles toward the *parochet* while he is sprinkling" — one might think the same applies on *Yom Kippur*: that the *kohen gadol* must likewise stand outside the golden altar when he sprinkles toward the *parochet*. The *baraita* therefore teaches from *veyatzah el hamizbeach*: the *yetziah* — the going out — occurs only after the *parochet* sprinkling, not during it.

### Par Ha'Elam Davar

The *baraita* explains: until the moment of *veyatzah*, the *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur* is *lifnim min hamizbeach* — on the inner side of the altar, standing between the altar and the *parochet*. From that position he performs the one-and-seven sprinklings directed toward the *parochet*. Only afterward does *veyatzah* apply — he exits to the outer zone to perform the service on the golden altar's horns. This stands in contrast to the *par he'elam davar*, where the *kohen* stands outside and sprinkles from there.

It is worth noting the spatial dimension here. The *heichal* is forty *amot* deep; the golden altar stands twenty *amot* in, and the *parochet* is at the far wall. Sprinklings directed toward the *parochet* across that distance — particularly according to Rabbi Eliezer's position that they must actually strike the *parochet* — present obvious practical challenges.

### Lifnei Hashem

A second *baraita* addresses the phrase *asher lifnei Hashem* — "which is before God." Rabbi Nechemiah now takes this as a proof for the *par he'elam davar* context: since on *Yom Kippur* we know the *kohen* stands *lifnim min hamizbeach* — inside, between the altar and the *parochet* — and sprinkles while there, one might think the same applies by *par he'elam davar*. The second *baraita* derives from the phrase *mizbeach ketoret hasamim lifnei Hashem* — "the altar of spices that is before God" — that it is the *mizbeach* that is *lifnei Hashem*, not the *kohen*. The *kohen* by *par he'elam davar* therefore stands *chutz lamizbeach* — outside — and sprinkles from there.

### Yom Kippur Sequence

The distinction between the two services thus becomes fully articulated. On *Yom Kippur*, the *kohen gadol* performs the one-and-seven sprinklings toward the *parochet* while standing *inside* — between the altar and the *parochet* — and only after completing that stage does *veyatzah* occur, moving him to the outer position for the horn applications. By *par he'elam davar*, the *kohen* stands *outside* the altar for the seven sprinklings toward the *parochet*, reflecting the greater intimacy of the *Yom Kippur* service.

### Clarification

The *gemara* thus reads the sequence as follows: the *kohen gadol* performs the seven and one on the inner altar while standing *between* the altar and the *parochet*. Then, after those are complete, *veyatzah el hamizbeach* — he exits to the outer zone. This ordering is reinforced by the plain reading of the *pasuk*, which places *veyatzah* as a distinct subsequent act rather than a description of his position during the *parochet* service. The heightened intimacy of the *Yom Kippur* rite — the *kohen* positioned closer to the *kodesh kodashim* during the sprinkling — is a notable feature of the overall service.

---

## Starting Corner

### Rabbi Akiva

The *gemara* now records a *baraita* debating which corner of the golden altar to begin with. Rabbi Akiva holds: *mikeren mizrachit dromit, dromit maaravit, maaravit tzonit, tzonit mizrachit* — southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast. This is a clockwise direction, beginning from the southeast.

### Rabbi Yose HaGalili

Rabbi Yose HaGalili holds: *mikeren mizrachit tzonit, tzonit maaravit, maaravit dromit, dromit mizrachit* — northeast, northwest, southwest, southeast. This is the counter-clockwise direction we encountered in the *mishnah*, beginning from the northeast.

The *baraita* then draws an elegant symmetry: *makom she-Rabbi Yose HaGalili matchil, sham Rabbi Akiva posek* — where Rabbi Yose HaGalili begins, Rabbi Akiva ends; *makom she-Rabbi Akiva matchil, sham Rabbi Yose HaGalili posek* — where Rabbi Akiva begins, Rabbi Yose HaGalili ends.

### Consensus

Before analyzing the disagreement, the *gemara* establishes a point of consensus: *dekulei alma miha be-hu kerren depaga beresha lo avid* — everyone agrees one does not begin with the first corner encountered upon exiting the altar. That first corner would be on the western side, since one exits from the inner zone toward the west. Both Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yose HaGalili begin on the eastern side.

### Exit Requirement

Why does no one begin with the first corner encountered? Shmuel explains: *veyatzah el hamizbeach* — *ad denafik mikulei mizbeach* — you must be completely outside the altar before commencing. The *vayatzah* is not merely directional guidance but a prerequisite: the *kohen* must fully exit the altar zone before he is permitted to begin the horn applications. The corners encountered on the western side, which one naturally passes in exiting, therefore cannot be the starting point.

### Counterclockwise

The *gemara* then raises the question of why Rabbi Akiva goes clockwise at all. The general rule — derived by Rami bar Yechezkel from the *yam* (the great basin) constructed by Solomon — is that all turnings in the Temple are counter-clockwise. The *pasuk* in *Divrei Hayamim* (I Melachim) describes the twelve molten cattle supporting the *yam*: *shlosh panim tzonah, shlosh panim yamah, shlosh panim negbah, shlosh panim mizrachah* — three facing north, three west, three south, three east. Moving from north to west is counter-clockwise movement, establishing the principle: *shekol pinot sheata poneh lo yehu ela derech yamin lemizrach* — all turnings shall be only rightward, toward the east — that is, counter-clockwise as seen from the inside.

The *gemara* considers whether Rabbi Akiva might simply reject this principle, but concludes otherwise: *dekulei alma it lehu de-Rami bar Yechezkel* — everyone accepts Rami bar Yechezkel's rule. The debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yose HaGalili is instead about whether the counter-clockwise rule derived from the *yam* — which stands outside in the *azarah* — applies equally *inside* the *heichal*. *Mar savar yalfinan panim mi-chutz* — one holds we apply the same rule to the inside; *umar savar lo yalfinan panim mi-chutz* — the other holds we do not learn the inner from the outer.

### Return Obligation

The *gemara* adds a further dimension via the principle of Reish Lakish: *ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot* — one does not pass by an opportunity to perform a *mitzvah*. If a *mitzvah* opportunity presents itself, one may not bypass it in favor of performing a different *mitzvah* first. Applied to the altar service: by rights, the *kohen* should begin with the very first corner he encounters upon exiting. The fact that he does not — because *veyatzah* requires him to be fully outside before starting — means he has involuntarily bypassed the western corner.

### Directional Logic

This creates the obligation articulated by the *gemara*: *ve-keivan de-yahiv be-hahu keren, hadar asi le-hahu keren de-chayiv lemisav be-reisha* — once he has applied blood at whatever corner he begins with, he must then return to the corner he was forced to bypass first. Since that bypassed corner is the first one he actually encountered — and *ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot* obligates him to return to it — the corner he missed becomes the next obligation.

For Rabbi Yose HaGalili, who begins at the northeast, this is seamless: he was forced to bypass the western corners on his way out, begins at the northeast as the first available eastern corner, and can then proceed counter-clockwise (northwest, southwest, southeast) in the standard direction, naturally returning to what he missed.

For Rabbi Akiva, however, the forced bypass works differently. Rabbi Akiva begins at the southeast — and to return to the first corner missed after being forced fully outside requires moving in the clockwise direction. The counter-clockwise principle therefore does not override the obligation imposed by *ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot* once a bypass has already occurred. The apparent paradox of Rabbi Akiva's clockwise movement is thus resolved: it is not that he rejects the counter-clockwise rule, but rather that the obligation to return to the bypassed corner takes him in the opposite direction. What remains to be resolved — and will be addressed tomorrow — is the underlying dispute between the two opinions over why one begins in the north and the other in the south.

---

---

# Yoma 59

## Blood Mixing Debate

### Avodah Overview

The daf opens at the very first word of 59a, picking up in the midst of discussing the *kohen gadol*'s *avodah* on Yom Kippur. To orient ourselves: after completing the sprinkling inside the *kodesh kodashim*, the *kohen gadol* slaughters the *se'ir*, performs the *se'ir*'s blood service — one and seven — and then performs the *par*'s blood service — likewise one and seven. This differs from other *korbanot* brought on the inside, such as the *par* for the collective sin of *Bnei Yisrael*, where the *kohen gadol* would stand further inward and sprinkle seven times toward the *parochet* — not one and seven — without specifically aiming at the *parochet*, though contact would be acceptable if it occurred. The *seder ha'avodah* reflects a movement from greater to lesser intensity even as it proceeds from outer to inner space. Now, the *gemara* turns to the service on the *mizbe'ach hazahav*, the golden altar.

### Mixed Blood Question

A preliminary question concerns the horns of the *mizbe'ach hazahav*: does the *kohen gadol* mix the blood of the *par* and the *se'ir* together before applying it to the horns, or does he keep them separate? The verse reads *midam hapar umidam hase'ir* — "from the blood of the bull and from the blood of the goat" — and the question is whether this phrase prescribes a mixture or merely lists the two bloods as distinct applications. Our *mishna* assumes that the bloods are mixed; later, when the *gemara* reaches the seven sprinklings on the top of the altar, it will note that the verse's phrasing of *min hadam* again clearly refers to the mixed blood.

### Corner Order Debate

Two issues govern the application of blood to the horns of the *mizbe'ach hazahav*. The first is whether the *kohen gadol* stands in one place and applies the blood to all four corners from where he stands — covering a space of an *amah al amah* — or whether he walks around the altar. The second, which the *gemara* is presently addressing, is the order in which he visits the four corners. Our *mishna* records that he begins at the northeast corner and proceeds counterclockwise, which is the standard movement in the *azarah*. A *braita* records that Rabbi Akiva holds he begins at the southeast corner and proceeds clockwise. The *gemara* explains that normally one would encounter the western corners first, but the verse *veyatza el hamizbe'ach* — "and he shall go out to the altar" — requires the *kohen gadol* to leave a space and begin from an outer, eastern corner. Since he originally passed by the western corner, he naturally wants to return to it first. Starting from the north means going counterclockwise — back to the northwest — and starting from the south means going clockwise — back to the southwest. The rule of *avid denafik* ("go back to the one you bypassed") thus produces a difference in clockwise versus counterclockwise direction depending on which eastern corner one begins at.

## Clockwise Explanations

### Missed Corner Logic

The first explanation for Rabbi Akiva's clockwise circuit is precisely the practical logic just described: since one must start at an eastern corner due to *veyatza el hamizbe'ach*, the natural instinct is to then proceed first to the western corner that was bypassed. Starting from the southeast leads one to the southwest next — a clockwise movement. Starting from the northeast, as Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds, leads one to the northwest — a counterclockwise movement. The underlying debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yose HaGlili, then, is whether to begin in the south or the north, which is a question the *gemara* addresses separately.

### Walking vs. Standing

The *gemara* offers a second explanation. *Ve'iba'it eima* — if you prefer, one may explain the clockwise movement differently. Were we to hold that *hakafa beregel* — the circuit is performed by walking around the altar — then everyone, including Rabbi Akiva, would agree that one turns counterclockwise, exactly as one does throughout the *azarah*. *Dekulei alma lo paligi depenino yemina* — there is no dispute that one turns to the right, i.e., counterclockwise. In that case, the argument between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yose HaGlili is not about clockwise versus counterclockwise at all. Rather, the dispute is *ha beha kamiflegi*: one *tanna* holds *hakafa beyad* — the circuit is performed by standing in place and moving the hand — while the other holds *hakafa beregel* — one actually walks around. If *hakafa beregel*, all agree: counterclockwise. If *hakafa beyad*, and one is simply standing and placing blood at the four corners with one's hand, there is room to deviate from the standard counterclockwise convention.

A third version follows: *ve'iba'it eima*, everyone in fact agrees it is *hakafa beyad* — no one walks around this altar, which is only an *amah al amah*. The debate is whether when performing *hakafa beyad*, one follows the same convention of moving counterclockwise that governs walking (*yalfinan miyad miregel*), or whether one does not draw that analogy (*lo yalfinan*). Rabbi Akiva may hold that standing in place and placing blood with the hand need not mirror the directionality of walking, and therefore clockwise is permitted. This does not yet explain *why* one would go clockwise — only that it is not prohibited.

### Hakafa Resolution

The *gemara* now challenges the third explanation. Can it really be said that Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds *hakafa beyad*? The end of our *mishna* states: *Rabbi Eliezer omer bimkomo haya omed umechatei* — Rabbi Eliezer says he would stand in his place and apply the blood. The *gemara* notes: *michlal* — it follows implicitly — that the *tanna kamma* of the *mishna* disagrees with Rabbi Eliezer and holds that one does walk around. And that *tanna kamma*, as the *braita* reveals, is Rabbi Yose HaGlili. Therefore, Rabbi Yose HaGlili clearly holds *hakafa beregel*, and the third explanation collapses. The *gemara* concludes: *ela mechvarta kedi'shamin'ei me'ikara* — the better answer is what we said originally. Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds *hakafa beregel* and goes counterclockwise; Rabbi Akiva — on at least one account — holds *hakafa beyad* and therefore may go clockwise.

To summarize the three explanations for Rabbi Akiva's clockwise circuit: first, the law of returning to the bypassed corner, which produces a different circuit depending on where one starts; second, that Rabbi Akiva holds *hakafa beyad* and therefore is not bound by the directionality of walking; and third — though ultimately rejected — that everyone holds *hakafa beyad* and the debate is whether hand movement follows the same convention as foot movement.

## Altar Comparison

### Inner vs. Outer

The *gemara* now explains the underlying disagreement about whether one walks around the *mizbe'ach pnimi* or stands in place. *Mar savar savar de'mizbe'ach pnimi kishavrei de'mizbe'ach chitzon* — one position holds that just as the verse mandating blood application to the horns of the outer altar implies walking around, so too the parallel language regarding the inner altar implies walking around. The two are treated symmetrically.

The opposing position — that of Rabbi Eliezer in the *mishna*, or Rabbi Akiva in this discussion — holds: *kulei mizbe'ach pnimi bimkom chad karna de'mizbe'ach chitzon kai* — the entire inner *mizbe'ach* occupies the same footprint as a single horn of the outer altar, both measuring an *amah* by an *amah* (the inner altar is an *amah* by an *amah* by two *amot* in height, compared to the outer altar's horn which is an *amah* by an *amah* by an *amah*). Just as a priest applying blood to a single horn of the outer altar stands at that horn and places the blood without walking, so too the priest at the inner altar stands in place and applies the blood to all four corners from where he stands.

### Theological Implications

This structural debate opens onto a deeper conceptual question. Is the *mizbe'ach pnimi* an independent entity, to be treated in parallel with the outer altar in its own right? Or is it, when functioning in its blood-atonement capacity, more properly understood as a kind of extension or subsidiary of the outer altar — analogous to one of its horns?

The observation is apt that characterizing the entire inner altar as equivalent to a single horn of the outer altar somewhat diminishes its independent status. Yet one might refine the point: when the inner altar functions as the site of *ketoret*, it stands entirely in its own right. It is specifically in its blood-*kappara* role — where it parallels the atonement function of the outer altar — that it may be understood as an extension of that altar, like one of its horns. The deeper you penetrate into the *Mikdash*, the more you might expect independence. Yet in the specific context of blood service, the inner altar's role may be seen as a prolongation of what happens outside — a glimpsing, through the inner chamber, of what the outer altar is ultimately about. The inner altar offers, as it were, an occasional window into the blood-*kappara* function whose primary theater is the outer altar.

## Two Priests Testimony

### Two Priests Found

*Tanya* — a *braita* records: *amar Rabbi Yishmael, shenei kohanim gedolim nishtayru be-Mikdash Rishon* — Rabbi Yishmael said: two *kohanim gedolim* survived to the time of the destruction of the First Temple. This itself is remarkable, since the First Temple period is associated with a stable, non-rotating *kehuna gedola*, unlike the Second Temple era with its frequent succession of high priests. That two *kohanim gedolim* remained at the *churban* is historically striking, and what follows is even more so.

### Hand vs. Foot

*Zeh omer beyadi hikafti* — one of them said: when I performed the *avodah* of Yom Kippur, I performed the circuit with my hand; I stood in place. *Ve-zeh omer beraglai hikafti* — the other said: I walked around by foot. Here we have firsthand testimony, from practitioners who actually performed the service, disagreeing on how they did it.

### Scriptural Reasoning

What is remarkable is that neither priest appeals simply to tradition. *Zeh noten ta'am lidevrav ve-zeh noten ta'am lidevrav* — each one provides a scriptural rationale. The one who walked around cited: *saviv de-Mizbe'ach Pnimi ke-saviv de-Mizbe'ach Chitzon* — the language of encircling the inner altar is parallel to the language of encircling the outer altar; just as you walk around the outer, you walk around the inner. The one who stood in place cited: *kulei Mizbe'ach Pnimi bimkom chad karna de-Mizbe'ach Chitzon kai* — the entire inner altar is like a single horn of the outer altar, and at a single horn you stand in place.

What is striking is that these practitioners — presumably with access to living memory of the service across generations — are reasoning directly from *psukim*, not from received tradition handed down by predecessors. The *kohanim gedolim* appear to have had substantial latitude in working out the details of the *avodah* from scripture, rather than from an unbroken chain of practice.

### Pluralistic Resolution

The *Rashash* is troubled by this, because another *gemara* asserts that there was no genuine *machloket* in Israel from the time of Moshe until the death of Yosef ben Yo'ezer — the earliest recorded dispute being the question of *semicha* on *korbanot* brought on *Yom Tov*, which arose only toward the end of the Second Temple period. How then can there be a dispute between two *kohanim gedolim* at the end of the First Temple?

The *Rashash* — found in the *Tosafot Yeshanim* on 59b — offers two answers. The first: had they actually convened and taken a formal vote, they might have reached a conclusion. The fact that each reasoned independently to a different practice does not constitute a true *machloket*. The second answer, which he finds supported in the *Yerushalmi*, is the more penetrating one: *i avid hachi avid, i avid hachi avid* — either way is valid. Each priest reasoned from scripture to a legitimate practice, and neither was asserting that the other's approach was wrong. There is no true dispute here — just two plausible approaches to an unresolved question. As the *Rashash* frames it, citing the *Yerushalmi*: according to Rabbi Yishmael's understanding, they do not disagree at all.

This reframing is genuinely illuminating. Rather than reading the *braita* as a record of an ancient *machloket*, one can read it as a record of two legitimate traditions, each grounded in scripture, each reflecting a coherent understanding of the inner altar's relationship to the outer. The fact that each priest quotes *psukim* rather than tradition supports this reading: they are not asserting exclusive validity — they are each explaining the basis for their own practice.

## Finger Movement Direction

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

The *mishna* records: *Rabbi Eliezer omer bimkomo haya omed umechatei* — Rabbi Eliezer says the *kohen gadol* would stand in his place and apply the blood. This position, as established, reflects the view that *hakafa beyad* governs the inner altar. Standing in one place, with different corners at different distances from the priest, raises a further question: in which direction does the finger move when applying the blood — *mimala lemata* (from above to below, i.e., up-down) or *mimata lemala* (from below to above, i.e., down-up)?

The underlying concern is practical: when the corner being anointed is directly in front of the priest, a down-up movement risks causing the blood to run down onto the priest's sleeve, soiling his garments. An up-down movement is therefore the required default when facing the corner directly. When the corner is distant, however, the concern about soiling the sleeve recedes, and a down-up movement may be easier, especially when stretching across a distance.

### Rabbi Meir Version

A *braita* records a debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda as to what exactly Rabbi Eliezer said. According to Rabbi Meir's version: *Rabbi Eliezer omer bimkomo haya omed umechatei* — he stood in place — *ve'al kulan haya nosein mimala lemata* — and for all the corners he performed the movement from above to below, up-down — *chutz me'oso sheb'alachson* — except for the one at the diagonal, the farthest corner. That one, which requires the greatest reach, he performed *mimata lemala*, from below to above, down-up. The logic: when you must stretch to the most distant corner, pulling the finger upward as it moves across the altar surface keeps the blood from falling off the tip; a downward motion at such a distance is harder to control. Consequently, Rabbi Meir's version of Rabbi Eliezer defaults to up-down everywhere, with a single exception for the most distant corner.

### Rabbi Yehuda Version

Rabbi Yehuda offers a different version of Rabbi Eliezer's position. He too agrees that Rabbi Eliezer stood in place. But: *ve'al kulan hu nosein mimata lemala* — for all corners the default movement is down-up — *chutz mizu shehayesa lefanav mamash* — except the one directly in front of him — *shenosein mimalla lemata* — that one he performs up-down — *ki heichi d'lo litsran manei* — so that his garments should not become soiled.

According to Rabbi Yehuda's version of Rabbi Eliezer, down-up is the inherently easier movement and the natural default. The sole exception is the corner directly in front, where the risk of blood running down the sleeve requires the up-down motion. According to Rabbi Meir's version, up-down is the default, with down-up permitted only where the stretch makes it necessary.

Crucially, both versions agree on two points: the corner directly in front is always up-down, and the corner farthest away is always down-up. The debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerns the two intermediate corners — are they governed by the default of up-down (Rabbi Meir) or the default of down-up (Rabbi Yehuda)?

By extension, when the *kohen gadol* is walking around the outer altar (*mizbe'ach hachitzon*), every horn is directly in front of him at the moment he applies the blood, and everyone agrees the motion there is up-down.

## Seven Sprinklings Site

### Tahoro Definition

After completing the circuit of the four horns, the *kohen gadol* performs seven sprinklings on the top of the *mizbe'ach hazahav*. The verse governing this reads: *vehizah alav min hadam sheva pe'amim* — and he shall sprinkle upon it from the blood seven times. The verse uses the phrase *al tohoro shel mizbe'ach*, which our *mishna* echoes. But what precisely is *tohoro*? Where on the altar are these seven sprinklings to be performed?

Rabbah bar Rav Shila proposes: *palgei demizbe'acha* — the half of the altar. He invokes the linguistic parallel to *tzahornayim* — midday — where *tohar* or *tzohar* has come to mean the midpoint of the day. Thus *tohoro shel mizbe'ach* means the middle of the altar — not the top, but the midpoint on the wall. Rashi interprets this as referring to the midpoint of the wall, analogous to how blood is applied to the midpoint of the outer altar's sides.

### Clearing Ashes

A *Tosefta* is then cited as a challenge: *keshehu mazeh, eino mazeh lo agab ha'efer velo agab hagechalim* — when he sprinkles, he does not sprinkle on top of the ashes or on top of the coals. Rather, *choteh gechalim ilach ve'ilach* — he sweeps the coals to either side — and then performs the sprinkling. This *braita* makes clear that the sprinkling is done on the *top* of the altar. If the ashes and coals must be pushed aside to create an exposed surface for the sprinkling, then the seven are performed on the roof, not on the side wall.

In light of this, Rabbah bar Rav Shila revises his answer: *al giluyeih demizbe'acha* — on the exposed part of the altar. The coals are pushed aside, the golden surface is exposed, and the blood is sprinkled there. This is the *tahoro* — the uncovered, pure surface of the altar top. The *gemara* cites the verse *uke'etzem hashamayim latahar* — "like the very sky in its purity" — as an evocative parallel, though one cannot help but notice the resonance: the exposure of the altar's pure surface recalls that extraordinary moment at Sinai, where the elders beheld the divine presence, and the text describes the sky in its clarity. The uncovering of the altar's surface for this most intimate blood service of the year calls forth an image of radical visibility, of stripping away what ordinarily conceals. The verse at Sinai adds that they sat and ate — an act of consummate intimacy that would, of course, be entirely out of place on Yom Kippur. The blood, seven times applied to this exposed surface, occupies that liminal space between concealment and encounter.

## North-South Placement

### North vs. South

A *braita* records: *Chananya omer betzad tzfoni hu noten* — Chananya says the sprinkling is done on the northern side of the *mizbe'ach*. *Rabbi Yossi omer betzad dromi hu noten* — Rabbi Yossi says it is done on the southern side. This debate is directly connected to the earlier dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva about where one begins the circuit of the horns.

### Curtain Theory

The *gemara* asks: *bemai kamifligi* — what is the underlying dispute? *Mar savar pitcha bedarom kai* — one holds the opening is in the south; *umar savar pitcha betzafon kai* — the other holds the opening is in the north. The question is how many curtains separated the *heichal* from the *kodesh kodashim*. If there were two curtains, the *kohen gadol* would exit through the space between them from a point in the south; if there was only one curtain, he exits to the north. The direction of exit determines where he stands when he begins the circuit of the horns, which in turn determines where the circuit concludes, and it is at the conclusion of the circuit that the seven sprinklings are performed.

### Circuit End Rule

This is the principle: *dekulei alma meiha heicha degamrinan matnot dekarnot hatam yahiv agago* — everyone agrees that the seven sprinklings on the top of the altar are performed at the same location where the circuit of the horns concluded. If one started from the northeast (Rabbi Yose HaGlili, one curtain, exit to the north), the circuit ends in the south, and the seven are done on the southern part of the roof. If one started from the southeast (Rabbi Akiva, two curtains, exit to the south), the circuit ends in the north, and the seven are done on the northern part.

The scriptural basis is: *Vetiaro vekidesho* — you shall purify it and sanctify it. *Mekom shekidesho, sham tiaro* — where you sanctified it, where you completed the circuit (*kivuvim* being *kiddush*), there you shall purify it (the roof sprinkling being *tihur*). Notably, the word *tiaro* evokes *tohoro shel mizbe'ach*, the language of the *mishna* — suggesting that *tihur* specifically is associated with the top of the altar and the seven sprinklings there.

## Remnant Blood

### Proximate Base Rule

After completing the seven sprinklings, the *kohen gadol* exits and spills the remnant blood (*sheraye hadam*) at the base (*yesod*) of the outer altar. The *mishna* states: *sheraye hadam haya shofech liyesod maaravi shel mizbe'ach hachitzon* — the remnant is spilled at the western base of the outer altar. For blood of ordinary *korbanot* performed outside, the remnant is spilled at the southern base. The underlying principle, as the *gemara* develops it, is proximity: one spills at the base one encounters first. Coming out of the *heichal*, one encounters the western base; coming down from the ramp after service at the outer altar, one encounters the southern base.

The *Tosafot* note that the verse invoked — *el yesod mizbe'ach ha'olah asher petach ohel moed* — appears in Vayikra 4, in the context of the *par he'elam davar*, one of the few *korbanot* also brought inside. *Petach ohel moed* is in the west, and the verse is applied by extension to the Yom Kippur service as well. The *braita* elaborates: perhaps *yesod hamizbeiach* in that verse refers to the southern base — *atah omer yesod dromit o eino ela yesod maaravit?* The answer is derived by analogy: from the case of exiting the *heichal*, where the verse explicitly names the western base, we derive the principle of proximity — *besamuch lo*, the nearest one. Once that principle is established, it applies equally to ordinary sacrificial service at the outer altar, where the nearest base after descending the ramp is the southern one.

### Yishmael vs. Shimon

A second *braita* records divergent positions. Rabbi Yishmael says: *zeh vezeh yesod maaravi* — both the Yom Kippur blood and the ordinary sacrificial blood are spilled at the western base. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says: *zeh vezeh yesod dromit* — both are spilled at the southern base. Rabbi Yishmael's position is comprehensible: rather than deriving the principle of proximity from the case of leaving the *heichal* and extending it to the outer altar, he derives the fixed principle of *west* from the explicit verse and applies it universally. The inner sanctuary, as it were, is *koveia* — it sets the rule. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's position, however, is initially puzzling: the verse says *petach ohel moed*, which is in the west — why would he say the southern base?

### Altar Position Theory

Rav Ashi resolves this: *kasavar pitcha badarom kai* — Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai holds that the entrance of the *ohel moed* was in the south of the altar's position. That is, the *mizbe'ach* was positioned such that when the *kohen gadol* exited the *heichal*, the base he actually encountered first was the southern base. According to his understanding of the altar's placement in the *azarah*, the southern base was the proximate one — and therefore *both* cases yield the southern base. The debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai thus reduces to a factual disagreement about where the *mizbe'ach hachitzon* was positioned relative to the exit of the *heichal*.

An addendum: the school of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, when transmitting Rabbi Yishmael's teaching, reported it as saying *zeh vezeh yesod dromit* — the same as their own position. Rashi softens this: the school tradition was that Rabbi Yishmael had in fact retracted his position. The *gemara* preserves the observation: *mashchuha gavra legabeih* — the school drew the person's view toward their own. Both the western and southern bloods ultimately drained into a common channel, flowed out through the *azarah*, and emptied into the *Nachal Kidron*, where they were sold; the proceeds raised the question of *meilah*.

## Meila and Blood

### Meila Debate

A *braita* teaches: *mo'alin b'damim*, said as *divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir holds that there is *meilah* by blood. *Rabbi Shimon vachachamim omrim: ein moalin bahen* — Rabbi Shimon and the Sages say there is no *meilah* by blood. The statement of the Sages is categorical — it is not restricted to blood after the *mitzvah* has been performed, but appears to apply even before the blood has been sprinkled. This is striking: of all the parts of a *korban*, the blood is the one that actually effects *kappara*, and yet it is precisely the blood that is exempt from *meilah*.

### Biblical Agreement

The *gemara* asserts: *lo pligi ela miderabbanan* — even Rabbi Meir, who says there is *meilah*, is speaking only of Rabbinic *meilah*. *Ala mid'oraisa ein moalin bahem* — at the Biblical level, everyone agrees there is no *meilah* by blood. How the *gemara* derives this conclusion precisely is a matter elaborated in the *Tosafot*, which we do not develop here. The point is that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages is narrowed to the Rabbinic level, while the Biblical exemption is treated as universal.

### Blood for You

*Minani mili* — what is the scriptural source? *Amar Ulla amar kra: lachem* — Ulla says, the verse states: *va'ani natati lachem al hamizbeach lechaper* — "I have given it for you upon the altar to atone." The blood is *lachem* — for you. *Meilah* applies only to *kodshei Hashem* — that which belongs entirely to God, as the verse states: *ki timol maal mikodshei Hashem*. The part of a *korban* that is *lachem* — that the owner eats, or that effects atonement for the owner — does not fall under *meilah*. Thus, by way of example, the meat of a *shelamim* carries no *meilah* even before slaughter, since it will ultimately be eaten. Only the *cheilev* and *emurim* after the blood has been sprinkled become fully *kodshei Hashem* and subject to *meilah*. Blood, the verse tells us, is given for your sake — *lachem*, for you — and therefore, however central it is to the *avodah*, it is not characterized as something offered to God in the way that the flesh and fat are. The Torah describes the burning of fats and limbs as *reiach nichoach* and *lechem ishai* — God's sustenance, as it were. The blood achieves *kappara* but is nowhere described as a gift to God.

This is genuinely startling. The blood, which is the operative agent of atonement, the element placed on the *mizbe'ach lechaper* — is *lachem*, yours, not God's. Therefore no *meilah*.

The school of Rabbi Shimon offers a parallel derivation: *lekappara nesati* — I have given it to you that it should achieve atonement for you — *velo lemeilah* — not so that it should cause you transgression. The point is essentially the same: blood is there for the benefit of the worshiper, not as an object belonging exclusively to God.

### Before and After

Rabbi Yochanan cites yet another verse: *ki hadam hu banefesh yechaper* — for the blood is that through which, by virtue of the soul, atonement is achieved. From the word *hu* — it — Rabbi Yochanan derives: *hu hu lifnei kappara ke'achar kappara* — the status of blood before atonement is the same as after atonement. Since there is no *meilah* after the blood has been sprinkled and the *mitzvah* performed — *na'asis mitzvaso*, the *mitzvah* is done — the same is true before as well.

The *gemara* raises the obvious challenge: *ve'eima le'achar kappara kilifnei kappara* — why not derive the opposite? Just as before atonement one might assume there is *meilah* by blood, perhaps after atonement there is likewise *meilah*. The *gemara* responds: there is no category of *davar she-na'asit mitzvaso* — something whose *mitzvah* has been completed — that retains *meilah*. Once a *mitzvah* is performed, the object no longer has the character of *kodshei Hashem* in that operative sense. Since after the blood is sprinkled there is certainly no *meilah*, the verse's *hu* — equating the two — imports that exemption to before the sprinkling as well.

### Two Cases Exception

But the *gemara* objects: is it really true that nothing retains a prohibition after its *mitzvah* is done? *V'harei trumas hadeshen* — what of the removal of the ashes? The ashes placed at the base of the altar (*vesamo etzel hamizbeiach*) remain forbidden for benefit even after the ritual has been completed. This appears to be a counterexample: the *mitzvah* is done, yet *issur hana'ah* — prohibition of benefit — and perhaps even *meilah* — remains. Rashi infers that since benefit is prohibited, the *kedusha* has not departed, and *meilah* applies as well. The *Tosafot* qualifies this: *issur hana'ah* does not necessarily entail *meilah*, but even granting only *issur hana'ah*, the principle that "nothing retains prohibition after its *mitzvah* is done" seems to be falsified.

The *gemara* responds: *mishum de-havei trumas hadeshen u-vigdei kehuna shnei kesuvim habayim ke-echad, ve-chol shnei kesuvim habayim ke-echad ein melamdin* — because *trumas hadeshen* and *bigdei kehuna* are two verses that come as one, and whenever two verses come together to teach the same rule, they do not establish a general principle; instead, they mark off exceptions. The *bigdei kehuna* at issue are the *kohen gadol*'s Yom Kippur garments: the verse *vehinnicham sham* — "and he shall leave them there" — means they cannot be reused, remaining *assur behana'ah* even after the *avodah* is concluded. Together, *trumas hadeshen* and the Yom Kippur priestly garments form two explicit scriptural cases of post-*mitzvah* prohibition. The rule of *shnei kesuvim habayim ke'echad ein melamdin* holds that where the Torah must specify the same rule twice, it is doing so because that rule is *not* general — those two cases are the exceptions that prove the opposite rule. Everything else, once the *mitzvah* is done, becomes permitted. Blood, therefore, follows the general rule: no *meilah* after the *mitzvah* is done, and no *meilah* before it either.

# Yoma 60

## Dam: Me'ilah & Restricti…

### Blood Disposal Overview

The daf opens at the very top of the page, picking up from where the *Mishnah* had described the disposal of sacrificial blood on *Yom Kippur*. After the blood of the inner service is poured at the base of the outer *mizbeach* — both the special *Yom Kippur* blood deposited on the western side and the ordinary *korbanot* blood deposited on the southern side — all of it flows together through an underground channel into *Nachal Kidron*, the Kidron wadi, where it is sold as fertilizer. Before the sale, the money paid redeems the *kedusha* onto itself; but even before that point, a question arises concerning *me'ilah*.

One might expect that only a rabbinic *me'ilah* would apply at this stage, since the *mitzvah* has already been performed. Yet the *Gemara* makes a bolder claim altogether.

### No Me'ilah Before Mitzvah

The *Gemara* states that there is no *me'ilah* on the blood of *korbanot* even before the *mitzvah* is performed — even while the blood is still sanctified and being brought to the *mizbeach*. This is a striking ruling, and the *Gemara* establishes it on the basis of three distinct *pesukim*.

### Three Pesukim Analysis

The three textual sources are *natati lachem* ("I have given it to you"), *lechaper* ("for atonement"), and the word *hu* in the phrase *ki hadam hu*. The logic of *lechaper* is particularly significant: blood is not being offered to God in the way that limbs and flesh are. Rather, it is placed on the *mizbeach* in order to effectuate *kapara* — but it is not itself an offering. The word *natati lachem* similarly implies that the blood is given over for human purposes, i.e., for the *kapara*, not for the domain of *me'ilah*.

The word *hu* carries its own distinct implication: just as there is no *me'ilah* on blood after the *mitzvah* is done — since at that stage the *mitzvah* is complete — so too there is no *me'ilah* before the *mitzvah* is done. The underlying logic, derived from *hu*, is that the pre-*mitzvah* and post-*mitzvah* statuses mirror each other. The *Gemara* then asks: why not conclude instead that *me'ilah* applies both before and after? The answer is that we know, as a general principle, that *me'ilah* does not apply after a *mitzvah* has been fulfilled — except for a handful of recognized exceptions — and those exceptions serve to prove the general rule.

### Exceptions Prove Rule

The *Gemara* identifies two categories as exceptions: *trumat hadeshen* and *bigdei kehunah*. The ritual placement of ashes (*trumat hadeshen*), performed each morning on the side of the *mizbeach*, remains forbidden in benefit even after the ashes are deposited, and the *bigdei kehunah* worn by the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur* cannot be used again after the service. These two cases, the *Gemara* argues, constitute what is known as *shenei kesuvim habayim ke'echad* — two scriptural exceptions that, rather than establishing a rule, actually demonstrate that the rule runs in the opposite direction. Two exceptions prove that in all other cases, the restriction lapses once the *mitzvah* is done.

It is worth noting a significant *Tosfos* on this point, which was discussed previously. Regarding *trumat hadeshen*, *Rashi* reasons that since benefit from the ashes remains forbidden after the *mitzvah*, we may infer that the *kedusha* persists and that *me'ilah* technically applies. *Tosfos*, however, disagrees: it is not necessary to say that *me'ilah* applies to *trumat hadeshen*, only that it remains *assur behana'ah* — forbidden in benefit. That prohibition after the *mitzvah* is itself sufficient to qualify as an exception and thereby establish the general rule that everywhere else the restriction falls away.

### Rabbi Dosa Position

The *Gemara* then raises a complication: according to *Rabbi Dosa*, the *bigdei kehunah* of *Yom Kippur* may in fact be used afterward — not for a subsequent *Yom Kippur*, but by a regular *kohen* for ordinary service, since the white garments of the *Kohen Gadol* are identical in form to those worn by a regular *kohen*. As *Rashi* notes, this position may seem somewhat ironic — one might have thought that using the *Kohen Gadol*'s garments for a lesser service represents a descent in *kedusha* — but for *Rabbi Dosa* the operative concern is the uniqueness of each *Yom Kippur*. Each year's service requires fresh garments; reuse for *another* Yom Kippur is prohibited, but use by a *kohen hedyot* is entirely permissible. Under *Rabbi Dosa*'s view, the *bigdei kehunah* are no longer prohibited after the *mitzvah* is completed, and therefore cannot serve as the exception that proves the rule.

### Eglah Arufah Exception

With *bigdei kehunah* disqualified as an exception under *Rabbi Dosa*, the *Gemara* substitutes a different case: *eglah arufah*. The heifer whose neck is broken remains forbidden in benefit even after the *mitzvah* of the neck-breaking is performed. Together with *trumat hadeshen*, this gives us two exceptions — and with two exceptions, the rule goes the other way: in all other cases, the restriction lapses after the *mitzvah*. Therefore blood, like everything else, should be permissible after the *mitzvah* is done, and since that is so after the fact, it is likewise free of *me'ilah* even beforehand.

The *Gemara* then asks what happens according to the opinion that maintains that even two exceptions are not conclusive — that two cases could themselves establish the rule rather than prove its opposite. In that case, additional textual support is needed. The *Gemara* responds that each exception contains an extra limiting word: *vesamo* (regarding *trumat hadeshen*, "and he shall place it there") and *veha'arufah* (regarding *eglah arufah*, "the one with the broken neck") — both implying that the restriction applies uniquely to these cases. Even for the opinion that two exceptions are insufficient, the combination of two exceptions plus two *mi'utim* — four limiting indicators in total — is more than adequate to establish that these are the exceptions and that the general rule is leniency after the *mitzvah*.

### Blood Exclusions

Having established that there is no biblical *me'ilah* on blood even before the *mitzvah* is done, the *Gemara* now asks: why were three separate *pesukim* needed to make this point? If every *amora* simply selected one of the three words — *natati lachem*, *lechaper*, or *hu* — as sufficient to exclude blood from *me'ilah*, what work are the other two words doing?

The *Gemara* answers that the three exclusions are not all about *me'ilah*. Each word excludes blood from a different restriction that normally applies to *korbanot*:

One word excludes blood from *nosar*. If blood was left over and not applied to the *mizbeach*, and someone ate it, he would incur the biblical prohibition of eating blood — but not the separate *karet* penalty for eating *nosar*. *Rashi* notes that this is not merely a case of avoiding double punishment: even if one was *shogeg* with respect to the blood prohibition but *mezid* with respect to *nosar*, no penalty for *nosar* attaches. The blood simply does not fall within the category of *nosar* at all.

A second word excludes blood from the prohibitions associated with *tumah*. Eating blood while in a state of *tumah* does not incur the separate prohibition of eating *kodshim* in a state of ritual impurity — the *tumah* restriction that applies to sacrificial flesh does not apply to blood.

A third word, as already discussed, excludes blood from *me'ilah* itself.

This is a remarkable cluster of exclusions. It is one thing to say that *me'ilah* does not apply to blood, since *me'ilah* is a somewhat narrow category — it requires that something be *meyuchad* for God, dedicated to the divine domain, and one could argue that blood, for all its centrality to the *mizbeach*, is being granted to the people (*natati lachem*) and is therefore outside that domain. But *nosar* and *tuma* restrictions flow from the inherent *kedusha* of the offering itself. The idea that blood escapes all of these restrictions — that it is, as it were, freed from the normal stringencies of *korbanot* — is a profound and somewhat startling *chiddush*.

### Pigul & Matir Hu

The *Gemara* notes that there is a fourth prohibition associated with *korbanot* — *pigul* — and asks whether blood likewise escapes liability for *pigul*. The answer is yes, and moreover, no special *pasuk* is needed to derive this exclusion. The *Gemara* cites a principle: *kol sheyesh lo matirin bein l'adam bein l'mizbeach chayavin alav mishum pigul* — anything that becomes permissible (either for human consumption or for the *mizbeach*) by virtue of another act performed upon something else is subject to *pigul*. Thus, the meat of a sacrifice becomes permissible to eat because of the *zrikat hadam*; the *imurim* become permissible on the *mizbeach* because of the *zrikat hadam*; the remnant of a *mincha* becomes permissible because of the *kometz*. In each case, the thing that becomes permissible is the *mutar*, the B, while the thing that permits it — the A — is the *matir*. *Pigul* applies to the *mutar*, not to the *matir*.

Blood, however, is itself the *matir*. *V'hadam atzmo matir hu* — the blood is not the thing that becomes permissible as a result of some other act; it is the thing that does the permitting. Therefore, *pigul* cannot apply to it by definition, without any special verse being needed.

*Rashi* provides the *pesukim* from which this principle is derived. The broader implication is that blood is not simply one component of the *korban* among others — it occupies the structural position of the act that enables all the other components. Everything else in the *korban* derives its permitted status from what the blood does. All the restrictions of *korbanot* — *pigul*, *nosar*, *tumah*, *me'ilah* — attach to the thing that receives its status through the sacrificial process. The blood, which stands at the other side of that equation as the *matir* itself, remains categorically outside all of them. This connects directly to the theme of *lechaper* and *natati lachem*: the blood represents the very essence of the sacrificial act, and it is perhaps for that reason — counterintuitive as it seems — that none of the derivative restrictions of the *korban* framework can reach it.

---

## Inner Service Completion

### Service Order Review

With the discussion of *dam* concluded, the *Gemara* now steps back to survey the whole arc of the inner *avodah*. The *Kohen Gadol* wears the white garments twice on *Yom Kippur*; the first and more extensive wearing encompasses the entire inner service. What has he done during this period? He has performed the *ketoret*, the blood of the *par*, and then the blood of the *se'ir*. The one major component of the *Yom Kippur* service not yet addressed at this point is the *se'ir la'azazel*, the scapegoat — but that takes place in the *azarah*, not inside the *heichal*. He performs a *viduy* over it and sends it off; the dramatic account of its dispatch over the cliff lies ahead. For now, the focus is on what the *Kohen Gadol* has accomplished through the inner service.

### Pesukim Emphasis

The *Torah*'s own language underscores the significance of this completion. The *pasuk* reads: *vechila mekapper et hakodesh* — when he finishes atoning for the sanctuary — and then proceeds to describe the stages. The sequence in the *pesukim* is notably structured around three distinct locations, each marked with its own *kapara*:

After the *kodesh kodashim* and the *parochet*, the *pesukim* already signal a major stage of completion: *vechila mekapper et hakodesh*, which corresponds to *kodesh kodashim*. Then: *veyatza el hamizbeach asher lifnei Hashem vechiper alav* — even before reaching the *mizbeach*, the text emphasizes that the *kodesh kodashim* and the *parochet* together have achieved a substantial measure of *kappara*. The *Kohen Gadol* then proceeds to the *mizbeach*, where he performs the sprinkling with the mixed blood of the *par* and the *se'ir* upon the *karnot*, followed by the seven sprinklings. And then comes the full closure: *vechila mekapper et hakodesh ve'et Ohel Moed ve'et hamizbeach* — "and he completed atoning for the sanctuary, and the Tent of Meeting, and the *mizbeach*." These three phrases correspond precisely to the three components: *kodesh kodashim*, *parochet* (*Ohel Moed*), and *mizbeach*. The *pasuk* ends: *ve'hikriv et hase'ir hehai* — and he brought forward the living goat. He is done with the inner service; what remains is the *se'ir la'azazel*.

### Nine Steps Enumerated

Reconstructing the order of the service clarifies the structure of what follows. The sequence runs as follows: first, the *shechitat hapar* — performed in the northern section of the *azarah* (this is step one); second, the *chafinat haketoret*, the scooping of the incense (this will become significant shortly, and may be listed as step 2a); third, the *hakravat ketoret*, the burning of the incense inside; then, retrieving the blood of the *par* (step 3a); after which come the sprinklings of *dam hapar* inside the *kodesh kodashim* — first *achat*, then *achat ve'achat*, *achat ve'shtayim*, and so on; then the *shechitat hase'ir*; then the sprinklings of *dam hase'ir* inside the *kodesh kodashim*; then the sprinklings of both bloods on the *parochet*; then the mixing and application of the combined blood on the *karnot* of the *mizbeach*, followed by the seven sprinklings there. Finally, the *shirayin* — the pouring of the remaining blood at the base of the outer *mizbeach*. Looking at those *pesukim* again against this ordered sequence, the *Torah*'s emphasis on completion and *kapara* at each stage comes into sharp relief.

---

## Order & Sequence Rules

### Out of Order Principle

The *Mishnah* now states: *kol ma'aseh Yom HaKippurim ha'amur al haseder — im hikdim ma'aseh lachaveiro lo asa klum*. The entire *Yom Kippur* service, which has been given an ordered sequence, must be performed in that order; if one act was performed before another, that act accomplished nothing.

An important conceptual point must be underscored here. One might think that performing an act out of order contaminates everything that follows, rendering subsequent steps also disordered and therefore invalid. But that is not how the *Mishnah* reads the rule. Only the act that jumped the line is invalid; it counts as nothing and is treated as though it never happened. Everything that was properly performed before it remains valid, and everything that would have followed it in order simply continues from where it should have been. The errant act is set aside; it did not actually constitute an *avodah* at all, so it cannot render anything else disordered.

### Interruption Protocol
